medicine.title: Ascending Aorta Dilation in the Fontan
medicine.abstract: Ascending aorta dilation is a known finding in the congenital heart disease population and specifically in patients who have undergone single ventricle palliation.We present 3 patients with single ventricle physiology who underwent single ventricle palliations and had severe ascending aorta dilation.Guidelines for the management of these patients are lacking, and decisions are made on a case-by-case basis.There are case reports of aortic dissection, but true risk remains unknown. Weighing the risks of surgery versus conservative management in patients with single ventricle physiology is challenging.Surgical intervention on dilated aortas in patients with single ventricle physiology is perilous but possible in the correct circumstances.
medicine.text:
Dilation of the ascending aorta is a known complication in patients with single ventricle physiology who undergo aortic arch reconstruction., ,  Aortic dissection is rare in this population but is not nonexistent., ,  Currently, guidelines exist for ascending aorta dilation in patients with bicuspid aortic valve or connective tissue diseases but not for patients with congenital heart disease or specifically, patients who have undergone single ventricle palliation. We present 3 patients with single ventricle physiology who underwent single ventricle palliation with initial arch reconstruction and had severe ascending aorta dilation in adulthood. Two of the patients underwent surgical revision, whereas 1 patient has been monitored clinically.

Case 1 is a 35-year-old man with a right ventricular–dominant atrioventricular canal with atresia of the left atrioventricular valve, subaortic stenosis, and coarctation. He was initially palliated with a Damus-Kaye-Stansel (DKS) anastomosis, central shunt, and tube graft from the ascending to descending aorta. He then underwent a hemi-Fontan procedure with takedown of the central shunt and 10-mm tube graft reconstruction. His third-stage palliation consisted of a nonfenestrated lateral tunnel Fontan. At 19 years of age, he had persistent transverse arch obstruction, so he underwent a complete aortic arch reconstruction. He was then lost to follow-up; upon re-presentation, he was found to have moderate neo-aortic insufficiency, normal single ventricular function, and severe ascending aorta dilation (neo-aorta measured 43 mm, ascending aorta just above the DKS anastomosis measured 62 × 71 mm) () along with significant fatigue. Because of his symptoms and neo–aortic valve insufficiency, he met the criteria for surgical intervention on his neo–aortic valve, and intervention would also be performed on his severely dilated ascending aorta. He underwent neo–aortic valve replacement with a 29-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion), ascending aorta and hemiaortic arch replacement with a 38-mm hemashield graft, and tube graft takedown. He tolerated the procedure well and is now at 6 months postsurgery with improvement in symptoms.

Case 2 is an 18-year-old man with hypoplastic left heart syndrome who was initially palliated with a Norwood/DKS procedure followed by right-sided superior cavopulmonary anastomosis and finally a fenestrated extracardiac Fontan was found to have progressive ascending aorta dilation. After the Fontan procedure, the patient had left pulmonary artery stenosis that required stenting, and he had fenestration closure. Initially he was evaluated by serial echocardiography throughout his life, but during puberty he had interval growth of his ascending aorta over 1 year, so a computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, which showed the following dimensions: 40 × 40 mm at the neo–aortic root, 49 × 49 mm in the middle ascending aorta, and 65 × 72 mm in the distal ascending aorta (). After presentation in our combined cardiovascular surgical conference and in shared decision-making with the patient, the decision was made to proceed with surgery. He underwent ascending aorta replacement with a 32-mm hemashield graft. He had an uneventful postoperative course and is now 2 years out from surgery. His postprocedural exercise tolerance has improved although he was asymptomatic before surgery.

Case 3 is a 36-year-old man with hypoplastic left heart syndrome who was initially palliated with a Norwood/DKS procedure followed by right-sided superior cavopulmonary anastomosis and finally a fenestrated lateral tunnel Fontan was found to have progressive ascending aorta dilation. His history also included multiple episodes of hemoptysis that required multiple cardiac catheterizations and eventual left lower lobectomy. On his most recent CT scan, he was found to have severe ascending aorta dilation (neo–aortic root measured 42 × 43 mm, middle ascending aorta measured 62 × 72 mm) (). CT scan from 2 years prior had equivocal measurements to his most recent scan, although his CT scan from 7 years ago showed the middle ascending aorta measuring 55 × 66 mm. His most recent echocardiogram depicted a hypertrophied right ventricle with moderate systolic dysfunction and mild neo–aortic valve insufficiency. Discussions have been held with the patient about risk of dissection and currently, the patient wishes not to undergo surgery and to be monitored clinically. He is currently normotensive with beta-blockers and is asymptomatic.

Current management guidelines for ascending aorta dilation exclude significant congenital heart disease lesions with and without surgical intervention on the aortic arch. There is presently no consensus on the risk of ascending aorta dissection in this population and at what diameter this risk increases.

Management of the dilated ascending aorta in patients with a bicuspid aortic valve and/or connective tissue diseases has been thoroughly studied, and strong evidence is available as to the risk of dissection in these groups. Significantly less evidence is available for patients with significant congenital heart disease such as conotruncal anomalies and for patients with single ventricle physiology. We present 3 patients with single ventricle physiology who had significant ascending aorta dilation after Norwood operation. Two of these patients underwent surgical intervention, and 1 patient continues to be monitored clinically.

One of the patients who underwent surgical intervention also had moderate neo–aortic valve insufficiency, which made the decision to proceed with intervention more evidenced based. Having ascending aorta dilation alone, however, is not a current guideline. Dissection in both bicuspid aortic valves and in Marfan patients is most common with aortic root dilation and presents the biggest risk of morbidity and mortality., The risk has been quantified in these groups of patients, and distinct measuring tools such as absolute or indexed aortic root size and/or ascending aorta–to-height ratio can be used. Progressive stiffness of the ascending aorta has been seen the further patients get from their Fontan palliation and has been associated with diastolic and systolic dysfunction, which are known risk factors for aortic dissection and poor 30-day outcomes, as well as volume indices. There currently is a paucity of data to determine which congenital heart disease patients and specifically single ventricle physiology patients with previous interventions on their aorta would benefit from intervention and who are at the highest risk. Future multicenter observational studies could help in the clinical decision-making of these patients.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Irisin alleviates oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis in glucocorticoid-induced rat osteonecrosis of the femoral head via the integrin αVβ5/Bach1/Nrf2 signaling pathway
medicine.abstract: Glucocorticoid (GC)-induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) is associated with oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis. Irisin, the cleaved form of fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5, attenuates oxidative stress and apoptosis in numerous types of cells, including osteoblasts, osteocytes and cardiomyocytes. The present study aimed to investigate the role of irisin and the mechanism behind GC-induced ONFH in vivo, as well as oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis in vitro. In the present study, GC-induced ONFH was established in rats by intramuscular injection of methylprednisolone, with irisin administered by intraperitoneal injection; the FHs were then assessed by micro-CT, histology, immunohistochemistry and TUNEL staining. In vitro, murine osteoblastic MC3T3-E1 cells were treated with dexamethasone (DEX), and oxidative stress, apoptosis and Nrf2 signaling were evaluated by dihydroethidium/JC-1 staining, flow cytometry, reverse transcription-quantitative PCR and western blotting. Irisin prevented the development of GC-induced ONFH in rats, and alleviated oxidative stress and apoptosis in DEX-treated osteoblasts. To determine the underlying mechanisms by which irisin exerted beneficial effects on DEX-treated osteoblasts, the present study investigated Nrf2 signaling cascades. Irisin induced Nrf2 signaling cascade activation in MC3T3-E1 cells and Nrf2 silencing by targeted short hairpin RNA reversed the beneficial effects of irisin on DEX-treated osteoblasts. Further mechanistic analysis revealed that irisin physically interacted with integrin (ITG) αVβ5 on osteoblasts, activating Erk1 signaling. This activation promoted nuclear export of Bach1, a competitive suppressor of Nrf2, thereby relieving Bach1-mediated suppression of antioxidant response elements. Consequently, irisin enhanced Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and upregulated its target genes [heme oxygenase, NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1, glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit], reducing reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial membrane potential loss. Pharmacological inhibition of ITG αVβ5 or Erk1/2 abolished irisin-induced Bach1 export, Nrf2 activation and cytoprotective effects. Collectively, the present study indicated that irisin may mitigate GC-induced ONFH and osteoblast apoptosis via the ITG αVβ5/Bach1/Nrf2 signaling pathway, highlighting its therapeutic potential.
medicine.text:
Glucocorticoids (GCs) are used as part of the therapeutic regimen for certain types of autoimmune and allergic diseases due to their immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory effects. However, their prolonged and excessive use can lead to serious adverse effects, such as GC-induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH). This condition affects 9-40% of patients receiving long-term GC therapy and is the most common cause of non-traumatic ON (,). ONFH is characterized by progressive joint pain and dysfunction, which may require hip replacement surgery (). Despite the association between GCs and ONFH, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms remain elusive.

GC-induced excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and accumulation, as well as subsequent oxidative stress and apoptosis in osteoblasts, serve pivotal roles in the development of ONFH (-). GCs not only stimulate ROS generation by activating the NOX isozyme family proteins, but also impair ROS scavenging by inhibiting antioxidant enzymes (). Excessive ROS can oxidize biological macromolecules, impede protein function and cause cell death (). Moreover, ROS can induce apoptosis via both the death receptor- and mitochondria-mediated pathways (). Conversely, blocking ROS and oxidative stress partially prevents GC-induced ONFH and apoptosis (,).

Nrf2 is a key component participating in the endogenous antioxidant mechanism; under physiological conditions, it exists in the cytoplasm, binding to Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), with rapid degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system maintaining relatively low Nrf2 levels (,). Under excessive oxidative stress, Nrf2 plays an antioxidant role by dissociating from Keap1, translocating from the cytoplasm to the nucleus and binding to antioxidant response elements (AREs) to initiate the transcription and expression of antioxidative gene [including heme oxygenase (HO)-1 and NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase (NQO)1] (,,). Notably, Nrf2 activation may attenuate GC-induced oxidative stress injury and subsequent osteoblast apoptosis ().

Bach1 is a heme-sensitive transcription factor belonging to the CNC basic leucine zipper family, which serves as a critical regulator of oxidative stress responses by competitively binding to AREs in target gene promoters (). Under physiological conditions, Bach1 dimerizes with small Maf proteins to suppress the expression of antioxidative genes, thereby amplifying cell susceptibility to oxidative damage (,). The functional interplay between Bach1 and Nrf2 is a key axis in redox homeostasis. While Nrf2 activates ARE-driven transcription to enhance antioxidant defenses, Bach1 antagonizes this process by displacing Nrf2 from ARE sites, thereby suppressing the expression of genes (,). This competitive inhibition establishes a dynamic equilibrium wherein cell redox status dictates the Bach1/Nrf2 ratio, ultimately determining oxidative injury outcomes (). Thus, modulating Bach1 activity offers a promising therapeutic strategy for mitigating oxidative stress.

Irisin is a peptide hormone derived from the cleavage of fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) in skeletal muscle and myocardium during exercise. Since its discovery in 2012, irisin has attracted attention for its role in inducing the browning of white adipose tissue, and its beneficial effects on metabolic disorders such as obesity and insulin resistance, and on cardiovascular disorders such as atherosclerosis and heart failure (,). Irisin is also involved in bone metabolism, and modulates the proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis of osteocytes, osteoblasts and osteoclasts (-). Moreover, exogenous irisin has been shown to inhibit the apoptosis of osteoblasts and osteocytes (,,). Irisin decreases ROS production and attenuates oxidative stress and apoptosis in different cell types, including osteoblasts, cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells (,,). Furthermore, irisin treatment can increase the nuclear levels of Nrf2 in various cells (,,).

It was hypothesized that irisin may prevent GC-induced ONFH, and protect osteoblasts from oxidative stress and apoptosis through a Nrf2-dependent mechanism. The present study aimed to investigate the function and mechanism of irisin in GC-induced ONFH and to evaluate its therapeutic potential for this condition. The findings of the present study may provide novel information regarding the pathogenesis and treatment of GC-induced ONFH.

Animal experimental and care procedures were approved by the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, China; approval no. XJTUAE2025-1953) and were performed following the Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments guidelines () and National Research Council's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals guidelines (). In total, 60 male Sprague-Dawley rats (age, 10 weeks; weight, 280-360 g) were obtained from the Experimental Animal Center of Xi'an Jiaotong University. Rats were housed under controlled conditions (22±2°C, 50±10% relative humidity, 12-h light/dark cycle) with ad libitum access to standard chow and water. All animals were acclimated for 7 days prior to the experiments. Rats were randomly assigned into three groups (n=20/group) using a random number table, as follows: i) Control, rats received an equal volume of saline by intramuscular injection; ii) Model, rats received methylprednisolone (MPS; 20 mg/kg/day; Pfizer, Inc.) by intramuscular injection for the first 3 days of each week for 3 weeks; iii) Irisin, rats received the same MPS regimen and, immediately after each MPS injection, irisin (100 μg/kg; cat. no. 067-29A; Phoenix Pharmaceuticals, Inc.) by intraperitoneal injection. Rats in the Control and Model groups received an equal volume of saline. All animals were monitored daily throughout the experimental period for general condition, body weight, and food and water intake. Pre-defined humane endpoints were as follows: Loss of ≥20% of initial body weight; sustained loss of appetite or inability to access food or water for >24 h; severe lethargy, hunched posture or ruffled fur; inability to right itself or to ambulate; labored or rapid respiration; persistent hypothermia (rectal temperature <35°C); or any other sign of severe, unrelieved pain or distress. Any animal meeting one or more of these criteria would have been euthanized immediately by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (200 mg/kg body weight), followed by cervical dislocation to confirm death. No animal reached any of the humane endpoints during the present study. During the experimental period, two rats in the Control group died unexpectedly. Although these animals received only saline injection without MPS, their deaths may be attributable to complications associated with the injection procedure (cervical spine injury during handling or individual sensitivity to the stress of repeated intraperitoneal injection). In the Model group, five rats died before the endpoint, likely due to MPS injection-associated complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, severe infection or multi-organ failure, which are known adverse effects of high-dose GC administration (). In the Irisin group, four rats died, potentially due to similar MPS-related toxicities, as irisin was administered concurrently and may not have fully rescued the acute systemic toxicity of MPS. These 11 rats were all found dead during routine daily inspections and none of them had exhibited any of the pre-defined humane endpoints prior to death. Ultimately, 18 rats in the Control, 15 in the Model and 16 in the Irisin group were included in the analysis.

Sample size was calculated for pairwise comparisons using the formula for two-sample proportions as follows:

where n is the required sample size per group; Zα/2 is the critical value of the standard normal distribution corresponding to the Bonferroni-adjusted two-tailed significance level; Zβ is the standard normal value corresponding to 80% power; and p1 and p2 are the expected proportions of ONFH incidence in the two groups being compared.

To account for multiple comparisons, the significance level was adjusted using Bonferroni's correction (α'=0.05/3≈0.0167), giving a two-tailed critical value of Zα/2=2.39. Power was set at 0.80 (Zβ=0.84). Based on pilot experiments, the expected ONFH incidence was ~0% in the Control group, 80% in the Model group and 20% in the Irisin group. The largest required sample size was obtained for the comparison between the Model and Irisin groups (p1=0.80, p2=0.20). According to the aforementioned formula, a minimum of 10 rats/group was required. Considering potential attrition, 20 rats were initially assigned to each group.

All histological and micro-computed tomography (CT) analyses were performed by investigators blinded to group allocation. The GC-induced ONFH model was established according to a previous study (). For the ONFH model induction, rats received daily intramuscular injection with MPS (20 mg/kg/day; Pfizer, Inc.) for the first 3 days of each week for 3 weeks, while the rats in the Control group received equivalent saline. After each MPS injection, the Irisin group was administered with irisin (0.1 ml; 100 μg/kg) and the remaining groups received an equal volume of saline. The dose of irisin used in the present study has been used in previous studies (,).

All rats were euthanized by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital at a dose of 200 mg/kg body weight 3 weeks after the last MPS injection, at the end of week 6. Animals were placed in a quiet area and monitored until complete cessation of vital signs. Death was confirmed by the absence of chest wall movement, lack of palpable heartbeat, absence of corneal and toe pinch reflexes and fixed/dilated pupils, sustained for ≥5 min. Subsequently, a secondary physical method (cervical dislocation) was performed to ensure death before tissue harvesting. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the approved animal care protocol and AVMA Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals (2020 Edition) (). Micro-CT, immunohistochemical (IHC) and histomorphological analyses were performed on the collected FH of sacrificed rats at the end of week 6.

Rat FHs were collected, preserved in 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 48 h, and scanned with high-resolution micro-CT (Y. Cheetah) at 9 μm/pixel resolution. DataViewer software (version 1.5.6.2, Bruker Corporation) was used to reconstruct the three-dimensional image of representative samples. Within the subchondral region of interest, the trabecular (Tb) bone parameters were calculated, including bone volume/total volume fraction (BV/TV), Tb separation (Tb.Sp) and thickness (Tb.Th) ().

The rat FHs were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 48 h. After decalcification in 10% EDTA (pH 7.4) at room temperature for 4 weeks (the solution being refreshed every 3 days), the specimens were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series and embedded in paraffin. The specimens were sectioned to a thickness of 5 μm, stained with hematoxylin for 5 min and eosin for 2 min at room temperature, and examined under a light microscope (Olympus Corporation). All histological and immunohistochemical procedures, including H&E, IHC and TUNEL staining, were performed on separate serial sections (5 μm) cut from the same paraffin-embedded FH blocks. Dihydroethidium (DHE) staining was performed on separate fresh-frozen sections (5 μm) prepared from the same FHs.

Fresh-frozen FH sections (5 μm) were prepared at −20°C and incubated with DHE (10 μM; cat. no. D7008; Sigma-Aldrich; Merck KGaA) for 30 min at 37°C in the dark. The sections were then rinsed three times with PBS and the nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (1:1,000) for 5 min at room temperature. Images were captured under a fluorescence microscope (BX53; Olympus Corporation) using the red channel (excitation, ~535 nm; emission, ~610 nm), and the fluorescence intensity in the subchondral bone was quantified using ImageJ (version 1.53t; National Institutes of Health) by two researchers blinded to the treatment groups.

To detect apoptosis and oxidative stress-associated protein expression in rat FH tissue, IHC staining was performed. The FH tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 48 h, decalcified in 10% EDTA (pH 7.4) at room temperature for 4 weeks, dehydrated in a descending alcohol series, cleared in xylene and embedded in paraffin. Sections (5 μm) were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated through a descending ethanol series, and subjected to antigen retrieval in 10 mM citrate buffer (pH 6.0) at 95-100°C for 15 min. After which, endogenous peroxidase was quenched with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 10 min and the sections were blocked with 10% normal goat serum (cat. no. SL038; Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd.) for 30 min at 37°C. Sections were then incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against total caspase-3, cleaved caspase-3, HO-1 and NQO1, followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were treated with DAB for 10 min; brown staining was considered positive expression, and the sections were counterstained with hematoxylin for 5 min at room temperature. Images were captured using a light microscope (BX53; Olympus Corporation). The numbers of HO-1-, NQO1-, total caspase-3- and cleaved caspase-3-positive cells were counted in five randomly selected fields of view per section by two researchers blinded to the experimental groups, and were expressed as the number of positive cells per field.

Apoptosis in rat FH sections and in MC3T3-E1 cells was detected by TUNEL staining using the In Situ Cell Death Detection kit (Fluorescein; cat. no. 11684795910; Roche Diagnostics GmbH) for tissue sections and the In Situ Cell Death Detection kit (TMR red; cat. no. 12156792910; Roche Diagnostics GmbH) for cultured cells, in accordance with the manufacturer's protocols. Adjacent serial sections (5 μm) obtained from the same paraffin-embedded FH blocks used for H&E and IHC staining were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated, permeabilized with proteinase K (20 μg/ml) for 15 min at room temperature, rinsed three times with PBS and incubated with 50 μl TUNEL reaction mixture for 60 min at 37°C in the dark. MC3T3-E1 cells grown on coverslips were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 10 min and incubated with 50 μl TUNEL reaction mixture under the same conditions. In both cases, nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (1:1,000) for 5 min at room temperature, rinsed three times with PBS and mounted with an anti-fade mounting medium; TUNEL-positive nuclei appeared green in tissue sections and red in cultured cells, whereas all nuclei were stained blue with DAPI. Sections and coverslips were examined under a fluorescence microscope (BX53; Olympus Corporation). For tissue sections, five randomly selected fields of view per section were analyzed, and the apoptotic rate was calculated as the percentage of TUNEL-positive cells among DAPI-stained cells by two researchers who were blinded to the experimental groups. For MC3T3-E1 cells, five randomly selected fields of view per sample were analyzed and the percentage of TUNEL-positive cells among DAPI-stained cells was calculated by two researchers blinded to the treatment groups (saline control, DEX 10 μM and DEX 10 μM plus irisin 100 ng/ml).

Western blotting of rat FH tissue and MC3T3-E1 cells was performed using a unified protocol. FH tissue was harvested, washed with ice-cold PBS, and homogenized in RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche Diagnostics GmbH) using a tissue grinder. MC3T3-E1 cells treated with DEX (10 μM) with or without irisin (100 ng/ml) for 48 h were lysed in the same RIPA buffer. Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C and the supernatants were collected. Protein concentrations were quantified using a BCA Protein Assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Equal amounts of protein (30 μg/lane) were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (MilliporeSigma). The membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat dried milk in TBS-0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) for 1 h at room temperature, and then incubated overnight at 4°C with the following primary antibodies against HO-1, NQO1, SOD1, BCL-2, BAX, cleaved caspase-3, total caspase-3 and GAPDH. After three washes with TBST, the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit or anti-mouse IgG secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) reagent (Tiangen Biotech Co., Ltd.) and the blots were semi-quantified using ImageJ. GAPDH served as the loading control. Comprehensive antibody information (dilution, cat. no. and supplier) is provided in .

Murine osteoblastic MC3T3-E1 cells obtained from the China Center for Type Culture Collection were cultured at 37°C in 5% humidified CO2 in α-MEM (Sigma-Aldrich; Merck KGaA) supplemented with 10% FBS (cat. no. F2442; Sigma-Aldrich; Merck KGaA) and 100 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin for 3 days. To identify the roles of irisin on dexamethasone (DEX)-treated MC3T3-E1 cells, cells were treated with DEX (10 μM; cat. no. D4902; Sigma-Aldrich; Merck KGaA) alone or in combination with irisin at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2. Irisin was used at a low dose (10 ng/ml) or a high dose (100 ng/ml), unless otherwise indicated; the dose-response was first established across a range of 1, 10 and 100 ng/ml in the Cell Counting Kit (CCK)-8 assay. The duration of treatment was assay-dependent: 24 h for DHE and JC-1 staining, 48 h for flow cytometric analysis and western blotting, and 72 h for the CCK-8 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) assays.

MC3T3-E1 cell proliferation was assessed using a CCK-8 kit (Dojindo Laboratories, Inc.). The cells were seeded at a density of 5,000 cells/well into a 96-well plate, and then administered saline (vehicle control), DEX (10 μM) or DEX (10 μM) plus irisin (1, 10 or 100 ng/ml), as previously described (,). The cells were cultured for 72 h at 37°C and 5% CO2 in an incubator. After adding 10 μl CCK-8 reagent to each well and incubating for 2 h, absorbance was recorded at 450 nm.

The cytotoxicity of DEX and irisin was tested using an LDH Cytotoxicity Detection kit (cat. no. MK401; Takara Bio, Inc.) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, cells were seeded at a density of 5×104 cells/well in 12-well plates. Following 72 h administration of DEX (10 μM) and irisin (1, 10 or 100 ng/ml) at 37°C, the LDH activity released into the culture supernatant was detected and normalized to total LDH activity (supernatant + cell lysate). The absorbance was read at 490 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). All experiments were performed with five replicates.

MC3T3-E1 cell apoptosis was assessed by flow cytometry using an Annexin V FITC apoptosis detection kit (cat. no. 556547; BD Biosciences) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, following 48 h DEX (10 μM) treatment in the presence or absence of irisin (100 ng/ml) at 37°C, cells were resuspended in 500 μl binding buffer, incubated with 5 μl each Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI) for 15 min in the dark at room temperature, then analyzed using a BD FACSAria III flow cytometer (BD Biosciences). Data were analyzed using FlowJo version 10 (BD Biosciences). Total cell death was defined as the sum of PI- and Annexin V-positivity.

MC3T3-E1 cells were treated with DEX (10 μM) with or without irisin (100 ng/ml) at 37°C for 48 h, washed with ice-cold PBS, and lysed in ice-cold RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche Diagnostics GmbH) for 30 min on ice. Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C, the supernatants were collected and protein concentrations were quantified using a BCA Protein Assay kit. An aliquot of the lysate was reserved as the input control. Equal amounts of protein (500 μg/reaction) were pre-cleared with 20 μl Protein A/G-agarose bead slurry per reaction (cat. no. sc-2003; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Inc.) for 1 h at 4°C with gentle rotation; the pre-cleared lysates were then divided equally and incubated overnight at 4°C with anti-ITGB5 (2 μg) or normal mouse IgG (2 μg) as a negative control. The immune complexes were captured with a further 20 μl of the same bead slurry for 4 h at 4°C with gentle rotation, washed five times with ice-cold PBS and eluted by boiling in SDS-PAGE sample buffer for 10 min. The eluates and the input samples were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE, transferred onto PVDF membranes (MilliporeSigma) and subjected to western blotting for ITGB5 and irisin as aforementioned.

Total RNA was extracted from MC3T3-E1 cells using TRIzol® reagent (Invitrogen; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.), and first-strand cDNA was synthesized using a RevertAid First Strand cDNA Synthesis kit (cat. no. K1622; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) according to the manufacturer's instructions (65°C for 5 min, 42°C for 60 min and 70°C for 5 min). qPCR was performed using TransStart® Tip Green qPCR SuperMix (TransGen Biotech Co., Ltd.) with the following thermocycling conditions: Initial denaturation at 94°C for 30 sec, followed by 40 cycles of 94°C for 5 sec and 60°C for 30 sec, followed by melt-curve analysis. Primer sequences are listed in . Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2−ΔΔCq method () and normalized to Gapdh expression.

MC3T3-E1 intracellular ROS levels were measured using dihydroethidium (DHE) staining, as previously described (). Briefly, following 24 h treatment with DEX (10 μM) in the presence or absence of irisin (100 ng/ml) at 37°C, the cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature and stained with DHE (10 μM) for 30 min at 37°C in the dark. Images of the cells were then captured under a fluorescence microscope (BX53; Olympus Corporation). Fluorescence intensity was calculated with ImageJ by two researchers blinded to the treatment groups.

Malondialdehyde (MDA; cat. no. S0131S), glutathione (GSH; cat. no. S0052) and total superoxide dismutase (SOD; cat. no. S0101S) levels in MC3T3-E1 cells were measured using commercial kits (Beyotime Biotechnology) according to the manufacturer's protocols. NADPH oxidase activity was measured using a commercial kit (cat. no. A127-1-1; Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute) according to the manufacturer's instructions, as previously described ().

Cell apoptosis was quantified by a Cell Death Detection ELISAPLUS kit (cat. no. 11774425001; Roche Diagnostics GmbH) according to the manufacturer's instructions. This photometric sandwich immunoassay detects cytoplasmic histone-associated DNA fragments (mono- and oligonucleosomes). Briefly, cells were lysed and the cytoplasmic fraction was incubated with anti-histone-biotin and anti-DNA-peroxidase in streptavidin-coated wells for 2 h at room temperature; after washing, ABTS substrate was added and the absorbance was measured at 405 nm (reference, 490 nm) using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). Values were normalized to the untreated control.

To knock down the expression of Nrf2, Bach1 and integrin (Itg)b5, short hairpin (sh)RNAs targeting Nrf2, Bach1 and Itgb5, together with a scrambled control shRNA (referred to hereafter as sh-C), were cloned into the lentiviral vector LV3 (H1/GFP&Puro) (Shanghai GenePharma Co., Ltd.). Lentiviral particles were generated by co-transfecting 293T cells (cat. no. CRL-3216; American Type Culture Collection) with the transfer (10 μg), packaging (psPAX2; 7.5 μg) and envelope (pMD2.G; 5 μg) plasmids at a ratio of 4:3:2 using Lipofectamine® 3000 (Invitrogen; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) at 37°C for 6 h. Subsequently, the supernatants were harvested at 48 and 72 h, centrifuged and filtered (0.45 μm). MC3T3-E1 cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 1×105 cells/well and, at ~50% confluence, were transduced with the viral supernatant at a multiplicity of infection of 50 in the presence of polybrene (5 μg/ml) for 24 h at 37°C. Stable clones were then selected with puromycin (2 μg/ml) for 10 days and maintained in 1 μg/ml puromycin. The targeting sequences of the shRNA constructs were as follows: sh-C, 5'-CAACAAGATGAAGAGCACCAA-3'; Nrf2 sh1, 5'-CCAAAGCTAGTATAGCAATAA-3'; Nrf2 sh2, 5'-GCCTTACTCTCCCAGTGAATA-3'; Bach1 shRNA, 5'-GCGTACACAATATCGAGGAAT-3'; and Itgb5 shRNA, 5'-CGCCTTCAACAAGTTCAACAA-3'. Knockdown efficiency was confirmed by RT-qPCR for all targets and by western blotting for Nrf2, demonstrating ~95% reduction in Nrf2 expression, 70% reduction in Bach1 and 95% reduction in Itgb5 in the stable cell lines. Stable cell lines were used for all subsequent experiments.

MMP was measured using JC-1 MMP Assay Kit (cat. no. C2006; Beyotime Biotechnology) according to the manufacturer's protocols. Briefly, MC3T3-E1 cells were seeded in 12-well tissue culture plates at 5×104 cells/well. Following 24 h treatment with DEX (10 μM) in the presence or absence of irisin (100 ng/ml) at 37°C, the cells were stained with JC-1 working solution (2 μM) for 20 min at 37°C in the dark, washed twice with JC-1 staining buffer, and images were captured under a fluorescence microscope (BX53; Olympus Corporation). The JC-1 aggregate/monomer (red/green) fluorescence ratio was quantified using ImageJ.

To inhibit chromosome region maintenance 1 (CRM1)-dependent nuclear export, cells were pretreated with LMB (cat. no. L2913; Sigma-Aldrich; Merck KGaA) at 20 nM in serum-containing medium for 1 h at 37°C, after which the cells were incubated with DEX (10 μM) with or without irisin (100 ng/ml) for the indicated times (24 h for immunofluorescence, DHE and JC-1 staining; 48 h for western blotting) in the continued presence of LMB. Control cells received an equal volume of vehicle (methanol:water, 7:3).

To inhibit ITG αVβ5, cells were pretreated with 10 μM cilengitide (cat. no. HY-16141; MedChemExpress) in serum-containing medium for 1 h at 37°C, after which the cells were incubated with DEX (10 μM) with or without irisin (100 ng/ml) for 24 h (immunofluorescence) or 48 h (western blotting) in the continued presence of cilengitide. Control cells received an equal volume of vehicle (DMSO; final concentration ≤0.1%).

Immunofluorescence staining was performed as previously described (). Briefly, MC3T3-E1 cells grown on coverslips were treated with DEX (10 μM) with or without irisin (100 ng/ml) for 24 h at 37°C, in the presence or absence of cilengitide or LMB as indicated. The cells were then fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 10 min and blocked with 10% normal goat serum for 30 min at 37°C. For the co-localization of irisin and ITG αVβ5, the cells were incubated overnight at 4°C with rabbit anti-irisin and mouse anti-ITG αV/β5 antibodies, followed by incubation with Alexa Fluor® 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. For the detection of Bach1 and F-actin, the cells were incubated overnight at 4°C with rabbit anti-Bach1 antibody, followed by incubation with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG for 1 h at room temperature in the dark; F-actin was stained with Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated phalloidin for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. In both cases, nuclei were counterstained with DAPI and the cells were mounted with an anti-fade mounting medium. Images were acquired using a confocal microscope (TCS SP8 STED 3X; Leica Microsystems GmbH) with LAS X software (Leica Microsystems GmbH); co-localization and nuclear Bach1 fluorescence intensity were analyzed using ImageJ.

Nuclear and cytoplasmic protein fractions were prepared using the NE-PER™ Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction Reagents (cat. no. 78833; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, MC3T3-E1 cells were washed twice with ice-cold PBS and lysed in ice-cold CER I buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Following the addition of CER II buffer and centrifugation at 16,000 × g for 5 min at 4°C, the supernatant was collected as the cytoplasmic fraction. The pellet was resuspended in ice-cold NER buffer, vortexed for 15 sec every 10 min over 40 min at 4°C, and centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C; the resulting supernatant was collected as the nuclear fraction. Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay kit, and equal amounts of nuclear protein were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and subjected to western blotting as aforementioned. Nrf2 and Bach1 levels in the nuclear fractions were normalized to PCNA, which served as the nuclear loading control.

To inhibit MEK/Erk signaling, cells were pretreated with 10 μM U0126 (cat. no. 9903; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) in serum-containing medium for 1 h at 37°C, after which the cells were incubated with DEX (10 μM) with or without irisin (100 ng/ml) for 48 h in the continued presence of U0126. Control cells received an equal volume of vehicle (DMSO; final concentration ≤0.1%).

All tests were conducted ≥3 times, and the results are presented as the mean ± SD. Multiple groups were compared using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for pairwise comparisons. Comparisons between two groups were performed using independent-sample t-tests. P<0.05 was considered to indicate a statistically significant difference. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20.0 (IBM Corp.).

To evaluate the effect of irisin on GC-induced ONFH, a rat model was established by intramuscular injection of MPS (). The incidence rates of ONFH were 0.0 (0/18) in the Control group, 80.0 (12/15) in the Model and 12.5% (2/16) in the Irisin group. Histomorphometric analysis of H&E-stained FH sections () revealed marked ON in the Model group, characterized by sparse and disorganized Tb bone, as well as abundant empty osteocyte lacunae within the subchondral region. By contrast, irisin-treated animals exhibited well-preserved Tb architecture and a notable decrease in the number of empty lacunae. To evaluate the subchondral Tb architecture of FHs, micro-CT was used. The Model group exhibited notable structural changes in subchondral trabeculae, including bone mass loss and cystic degeneration, compared with the Control (). In the Irisin group subchondral trabeculae were relatively intact and well distributed. Quantitative analysis of microstructural parameters () confirmed that MPS significantly decreased BV, BV/TV and Tb.Th, while increasing Tb.Sp. Conversely, irisin significantly reversed these deleterious changes, restoring BV, BV/TV and Tb.Th, and decreasing Tb.Sp relative to the Model group. Collectively, these results indicated that irisin effectively attenuated MPS-induced ON and Tb bone loss in the FH.

The present study examined the protective mechanisms of irisin by assessing oxidative stress and apoptosis in the FH. Compared with the Control group, the Model group exhibited significantly elevated levels of ROS, as detected by DHE fluorescence staining, however, irisin treatment significantly decreased ROS accumulation (). Consistently, IHC analyses revealed that irisin upregulated the expression of the antioxidant enzymes HO-1 and NQO1 in FH sections (). TUNEL staining demonstrated that irisin significantly attenuated MPS-induced apoptosis in osteocytes and osteoblasts in the FH (). Concurrently, IHC analysis of total and cleaved caspase-3 in FH sections showed that MPS increased the immunoreactivity of both forms, whereas irisin markedly reduced cleaved caspase-3 without substantially altering total caspase-3 expression (). Western blot analysis of FH tissue confirmed these observations at the molecular level, showing that irisin upregulated the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 and downregulated the pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and cleaved caspase-3, thereby restoring the BAX/BCL-2 ratio toward control levels and inhibiting the caspase-3 activation pathway (). Collectively, these results suggested that irisin may protect against MPS-induced ONFH by simultaneously suppressing oxidative stress and apoptosis in the FH.

It has been shown in previous studies that DEX induces intracellular ROS production, leading to oxidative stress injury and cell death in osteoblasts (,). To determine the role of Nrf2, shRNA-mediated knockdown was performed, Nrf2 mRNA levels were markedly reduced in sh-Nrf2 cells compared with in sh-C cells (). To investigate the cellular mechanisms underlying irisin-mediated protection against oxidative stress, MC3T3-E1 osteoblasts were exposed to DEX with or without irisin. DEX significantly increased intracellular ROS levels, as evidenced by intensified DHE fluorescence, which was effectively attenuated by irisin co-treatment (). Notably, Nrf2 silencing largely abolished the antioxidant effect of irisin, with ROS levels comparable to those in the DEX group (). Furthermore, DEX induced notable MMP dissipation, indicated by the loss of JC-1 aggregates (red fluorescence) and increased green monomer fluorescence, whereas irisin preserved MMP; this protection was abrogated by Nrf2 knockdown (). Biochemically, DEX resulted in elevated MDA levels and NADPH oxidase activity, alongside depletion of GSH and SOD; irisin co-administration reversed these alterations (). At the molecular level, western blot analysis revealed that DEX significantly increased the expression of p67phox, and decreased the expression levels of SOD1 and SOD2; irisin co-treatment reversed these DEX-induced alterations, restoring SOD1 and SOD2 expression, and reducing p67phox expression. These effects were blocked by Nrf2 silencing (). Collectively, these findings indicated that irisin may mitigate DEX-induced oxidative stress in a Nrf2-dependent manner, thereby preserving mitochondrial integrity and enhancing cellular antioxidant defenses.

To evaluate the cytoprotective effect of irisin on GC-injured osteoblasts, cell viability and membrane integrity were assessed. Irisin dose-dependently restored the cell viability compromised by DEX, as determined by CCK-8 assay () and significantly decreased DEX-induced LDH release (). These results indicated that irisin can improve cell survival under GC stress.

The present study also examined apoptosis. ELISA quantification of cytoplasmic histone-associated DNA fragments (mono- and oligonucleosomes) showed that irisin co-treatment markedly attenuated DEX-induced apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner (). Furthermore, TUNEL staining confirmed that irisin reduced the proportion of apoptotic cells, with greater protection observed at the high compared with the low dose ().

To substantiate the anti-apoptotic effect of irisin, flow cytometry with Annexin V/PI double staining and western blot analysis were performed. DEX significantly increased the population of apoptotic cells, which was significantly suppressed by irisin co-treatment. Notably, this protective effect was largely reversed following Nrf2 silencing by shRNA (). Consistently, western blot analysis revealed that DEX markedly increased BAX expression and decreased BCL-2 expression, thereby elevating the BAX/BCL-2 ratio, and increased the cleaved caspase-3/total caspase-3 ratio; irisin co-treatment reversed these alterations, restoring BCL-2 expression, and reducing BAX and cleaved caspase-3 toward control levels. These regulatory effects were also inhibited by Nrf2 knockdown (). Collectively, these findings demonstrated that irisin protects osteoblasts from DEX-induced apoptosis in a Nrf2-dependent manner.

As Nrf2 is a master regulator of the cellular antioxidant response and its activation has been implicated in cytoprotection (,,), the present study aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying the protective effect of irisin. It was hypothesized that irisin mitigates oxidative stress by modulating the Nrf2 pathway. DEX significantly decreased the protein expression of Nrf2 in MC3T3-E1 cells (), whereas co-treatment with irisin reversed this DEX-induced downregulation, restoring Nrf2 protein levels. As Nrf2 functions primarily as a transcription factor (,), the present study examined its downstream targets. Consistent with the DEX-induced decrease and the irisin-induced restoration of Nrf2 protein, DEX significantly reduced the protein levels of HO-1, NQO1 and GCLC, whereas co-treatment with irisin significantly upregulated all three relative to the DEX group, restoring them toward control levels (). To determine whether this upregulation occurred at the transcriptional level, the present study quantified the mRNA expression levels of these genes. Irisin markedly elevated the mRNA levels of Hmox1, Nqo1 and Gclc in the presence of DEX (). Notably, irisin co-treatment did not significantly restore the DEX-induced reduction in Nrf2 mRNA levels (), which remained significantly lower than in the control group, whereas Nrf2 protein expression was fully restored by irisin (). This dissociation between Nrf2 mRNA and protein levels suggests that irisin acts post-translationally, most likely by stabilizing the Nrf2 protein. To confirm the role of Nrf2 in mediating irisin-induced antioxidant effects, shRNA-mediated knockdown was performed (). Knockdown of Nrf2 markedly decreased Nrf2 protein and mRNA levels and, consequently, reduced the expression of both NQO1 and HO-1 at the protein and mRNA levels (), confirming that the expression of these antioxidant enzymes requires Nrf2. Collectively, these findings demonstrated that irisin may alleviate DEX-induced oxidative injury by activating the Nrf2 signaling pathway, primarily via a post-translational mechanism that stabilizes the Nrf2 protein and enhances the transcription of antioxidant genes.

To elucidate how irisin activates Nrf2, the present study examined the expression of Keap1, the canonical cytoplasmic suppressor of Nrf2. Western blot analysis showed that irisin did not significantly alter Keap1 protein levels compared with DEX treatment alone (). Subcellular distribution of Nrf2 and its competitive suppressor Bach1 was subsequently assessed. Subcellular fractionation revealed that irisin significantly increased Nrf2 nuclear accumulation while decreasing nuclear Bach1 levels (). Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that irisin decreased Bach1 nuclear retention (). Therefore, it was hypothesized that the promoting effect of irisin on Nrf2 may be associated with its facilitation of Bach1 nuclear export.

To verify whether Bach1 nuclear export is required for irisin-induced protective effects, cells were treated with LMB, a CRM1-dependent nuclear export inhibitor. LMB significantly blocked the irisin-induced decrease in nuclear Bach1 (). Functionally, LMB abolished the ability of irisin to attenuate intracellular ROS generation (), restore MMP (), upregulate HO-1 and SOD1 () and modulate apoptotic proteins (BCL-2 upregulation; BAX and cleaved caspase-3 downregulation; ). These data indicated that irisin-induced cytoprotective effects depend on Bach1 nuclear export.

To establish the causal role of Bach1, shRNA-mediated knockdown of Bach1 was performed; Bach1 mRNA levels were markedly reduced in sh-Bach1 compared with sh-C cells (). Functionally, LMB abolished the ability of irisin to attenuate intracellular ROS generation and to restore MMP (). In Bach1-knockdown cells, LMB failed to block the protective effects of irisin, as shown by the restored expression of SOD1, HO-1 and BCL-2, and the reduced expression of BAX and cleaved caspase-3 relative to cells treated with DEX + irisin + LMB (). These results demonstrated that the inhibitory effect of LMB on irisin may be dependent on the presence of Bach1. Collectively, these findings indicated that irisin can promote CRM1-dependent nuclear export of Bach1, thereby relieving Bach1-mediated suppression of Nrf2 and enabling Nrf2 nuclear accumulation to drive antioxidant and anti-apoptotic gene expression.

Having established that irisin promotes CRM1-dependent nuclear export of Bach1, the present study investigated the upstream signaling events governing this process. As Erk1/2 phosphorylation is implicated in Bach1 nuclear translocation (), the present study examined the effect of irisin on Erk1 activation. Western blot analysis revealed that irisin significantly increased the phosphorylation of Erk1 in DEX-treated MC3T3-E1 cells, without altering total Erk1 levels (). To determine whether Erk1 activation is required for irisin-induced Bach1 nuclear export, cells were pretreated with U0126, a specific MEK/Erk inhibitor. U0126 prevented the irisin-mediated reduction of nuclear Bach1 () and blocked the irisin-induced upregulation of Nrf2 target genes, Hmox1, Nqo1 and Gclc (). These results are consistent with a requirement for MEK/Erk signaling in irisin-mediated Bach1 nuclear export and subsequent Nrf2 activation.

Previous studies have identified ITG αVβ5 as a functional receptor for irisin in various cell types, including intestinal epithelial cells, osteocytes and adipocytes (,,). To verify this interaction in the present experimental system, immunofluorescence double staining was performed. Confocal microscopy revealed prominent colocalization of irisin with ITG αVβ5 on the surface of DEX + irisin-treated osteoblasts (). To provide biochemical evidence for a physical interaction, the present study performed co-IP assay. Immunoprecipitation with an anti-ITGB5 antibody followed by immunoblotting for irisin detected a specific band at 24 kDa, whereas only a faint non-specific signal was observed in the IgG control (). These data demonstrated that irisin may physically associate with ITG αVβ5 in osteoblasts. To assess the functional relevance of this interaction, the present study employed both pharmacological and genetic approaches. Treatment with cilengitide, an ITG αV inhibitor, significantly attenuated irisin-induced Erk1 phosphorylation () and prevented the irisin-mediated reduction of nuclear Bach1 (). To achieve greater specificity, ITGB5 was silenced using shRNA (sh-Itgb5) (). Knockdown of Itgb5 phenocopied the effects of cilengitide: Irisin failed to induce Erk1 phosphorylation () and decrease nuclear Bach1 levels (). Collectively, these results established that irisin may engage ITG αVβ5 to activate Erk1 signaling, which in turn drives CRM1-dependent Bach1 nuclear export, enabling Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and antioxidant gene expression.

GC-induced ONFH is a debilitating orthopedic condition characterized by progressive bone cell death and articular collapse (,). Although the pathogenesis of ONFH is multifactorial, mounting evidence indicates that excessive oxidative stress and osteoblast apoptosis serve pivotal roles in its development (-,). In the present study, irisin, a myokine derived from FNDC5, effectively protected against GC-induced ONFH both in vivo and in vitro, with the underlying molecular mechanism involving the ITG αVβ5/Erk1/Bach1/Nrf2 signaling pathway.

The present in vivo results showed that irisin administration significantly decreased the incidence of MPS-induced ONFH in rats, preserved Tb bone microarchitecture and attenuated oxidative stress and apoptosis in FH tissue, as evidenced by DHE staining, TUNEL assay and IHC analysis of HO-1 and NQO1. These findings are consistent with previous reports on the role of irisin in bone metabolism (,,,). Colaianni et al () reported that low-dose irisin administration increased cortical bone mass and modulated osteoblast gene expression in vivo without inducing adipose tissue browning. Zhang et al () demonstrated that exercise-induced irisin promoted bone formation and systemic irisin administration revealed new regulatory mechanisms in bone metabolism. Zhu et al () generated osteoblast-lineage-specific FNDC5/irisin knockout mice and demonstrated that irisin deficiency led to lower bone density, delayed bone development and impaired exercise-induced bone strengthening. In vitro, irisin protected MC3T3-E1 osteoblasts from DEX-induced oxidative stress and apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanistically, irisin activated the Nrf2 signaling pathway, as evidenced by increased nuclear accumulation of Nrf2 and upregulation of its downstream target genes, including Hmox1, Nqo1 and Gclc. This is in line with the study by Zhang et al (), which demonstrated that FNDC5/irisin alleviated oxidative stress and cardiomyocyte apoptosis via Nrf2 activation in a doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity model. Notably, shRNA-mediated knockdown of Nrf2 abolished irisin-induced protective effects against ROS accumulation, MMP loss and apoptosis, confirming that Nrf2 is essential for irisin-mediated cytoprotection.

The present study identified Bach1 as a key mediator linking irisin to Nrf2 activation. Under physiological conditions, Bach1 competes with Nrf2 for binding AREs, thereby suppressing the transcription of antioxidant genes (). Wang et al () recently demonstrated that the Bach1/HO-1 pathway may serve a crucial role in regulating oxidative stress and ferroptosis, highlighting the importance of this regulatory axis in cell redox homeostasis (). Studies have established that Bach1 inhibition protects osteoblasts against oxidative damage by enhancing Nrf2/ARE signaling activation, and that pharmacological Bach1 inhibition promotes nuclear export of Bach1 and induces Nrf2 nuclear accumulation (,). The present data demonstrated that irisin promoted nuclear export of Bach1, leading to decreased nuclear Bach1 levels and consequent relief of Nrf2 suppression. This conclusion is supported by two complementary lines of evidence: LMB, a CRM1 inhibitor, blocked irisin-induced Bach1 nuclear export and abrogated irisin-mediated protective effects; secondly, shRNA-mediated knockdown of Bach1 rendered LMB ineffective, demonstrating that the inhibitory effect of LMB was dependent on the presence of Bach1. These results established a causal role for Bach1 nuclear export in irisin-mediated Nrf2 activation.

The present study investigated the upstream signaling events governing irisin-induced Bach1 nuclear export. Irisin induced Erk1 phosphorylation in DEX-treated osteoblasts, whereas pharmacological inhibition of Erk1/2 with U0126 blocked both Bach1 nuclear export and irisin-induced cytoprotective effects, thereby establishing Erk1 as a requisite intermediate in this cascade. Accordingly, the present study aimed to identify the upstream receptor responsible for irisin-induced Erk1 activation. Accumulating evidence has identified ITG αVβ5 as a functional receptor for irisin in various cell contexts, including osteocytes, hippocampal neurons and vascular endothelial cells (,-). Specifically, irisin has been shown to bind ITG αVβ5 and activate the Erk1/2 signaling pathway (,). Consistent with this, a recent study demonstrated that irisin signals via ITG αVβ5 to induce Erk1/2 phosphorylation and that pharmacological inhibition of αVβ5 with cilengitide effectively suppresses this activation (). In the present study, co-IP and immunofluorescence co-localization confirmed the physical interaction between irisin and ITG αVβ5 in osteoblasts. Functional inhibition of ITG αVβ5 with cilengitide abrogated irisin-induced Erk1 phosphorylation and Bach1 nuclear export, and genetic knockdown of Itgb5 using shRNA produced similar effects, indicating that ITG αVβ5 may serve as the upstream receptor for irisin in osteoblasts. Collectively, these findings demonstrated a complete signaling cascade: Irisin bound ITG αVβ5, activated Erk1 phosphorylation, promoted nuclear export of Bach1, relieved Bach1-mediated suppression of Nrf2 and ultimately enhanced antioxidant gene expression to counteract oxidative stress and apoptosis.

The Nrf2 signaling pathway is a central hub in the protection against GC-induced ON and multiple therapeutic strategies converge on this axis (,,). For example, Han et al () demonstrated that chlorogenic acid activated the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway via p21 upregulation to protect MC3T3-E1 cells from DEX-induced mitochondrial apoptosis. Similarly, Chen et al () reported that microRNA-3175 activated Nrf2 signaling by targeting DCAF1, thereby inhibiting DEX-induced oxidative injury in osteoblasts. The present findings extend these observations by identifying a novel upstream regulatory mechanism: Irisin promoted nuclear export of Bach1, a competitive suppressor of Nrf2, thereby relieving Nrf2 from transcriptional inhibition and enhancing antioxidant gene expression. This Bach1-centric mechanism distinguishes the present study from those that directly modulate Nrf2 stability or degradation and underscores the therapeutic potential of targeting the Bach1/Nrf2 axis as a complementary strategy for ONFH treatment.

Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. First, there was a species mismatch between the in vivo (Sprague-Dawley rats) and in vitro (murine MC3T3-E1 cells) experiments. Although this combination is common in preliminary investigations (,), it introduces potential inconsistencies in cross-species protein expression and antibody reactivity. Therefore, future studies employing rat-derived osteoblast cell lines are warranted to confirm the key findings. Additionally, the pharmacological tools used in the present study have inherent limitations. LMB is a general inhibitor of CRM1-mediated nuclear export rather than a Bach1-specific inhibitor and cilengitide inhibits multiple αV ITGs including αVβ3, αVβ5 and αVβ8 (). Although the present study performed sh-Bach1 and sh-Itgb5 knockdown to genetically compensate for these limitations, future studies using specific inhibitors or blocking antibodies may validate the specificity of these interactions. Additionally, the present study did not directly verify whether U0126 alone affects baseline oxidative stress or apoptosis in control cells; therefore, future studies should include appropriate control experiments to exclude potential off-target effects of pharmacological inhibitors such as U0126. Moreover, the present study did not directly examine key signaling components of the proposed αVβ5/Erk1/Bach1/Nrf2 pathway, such as p-Erk1, nuclear Bach1 and nuclear Nrf2, in FH tissue. Future studies employing more advanced techniques, such as single-cell RNA sequencing or spatial transcriptomics, are warranted to delineate the cell type-specific activation of this pathway in vivo. Finally, the evidence for direct binding between irisin and ITG αVβ5, while strengthened by co-IP and sh-Itgb5 data, relied on functional and biochemical association rather than direct biophysical measurement. Future studies using surface plasmon resonance or biotin-labeled binding assays may clarify the direct binding kinetics.

Despite the aforementioned limitations, the present study provided evidence that irisin protected against GC-induced ONFH through the ITG αVβ5/Erk1/Bach1/Nrf2 signaling pathway. The present findings provide new insights into the molecular regulation of bone metabolism and redox homeostasis, and highlight the therapeutic potential of irisin for the prevention and treatment of ONFH. Future studies should focus on optimizing irisin delivery methods, evaluating its long-term safety and efficacy in preclinical models and translating these findings into clinical application.

medicine.title: Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection of an Anomalous LAD in an Adult With Fontan Palliation
medicine.abstract: Evaluating chest pain in patients with Fontan palliation can be a daunting task given the spectrum of pathology, surgical history, and multisystem involvement.A 32-year-old man with double inlet left ventricle status post-Fontan palliation was transferred to our facility with 3 days of chest pain, dyspnea, and a sense of impending doom. An electrocardiogram and troponin trend were consistent with an acute coronary syndrome. Coronary angiography revealed 100% occlusion of the mid–left anterior descending with a linear lucency and intramural hematoma consistent with spontaneous coronary artery dissection type IV. He underwent cutting balloon angioplasty and was discharged on antiplatelet therapy and follow-up imaging to assess for fibromuscular dysplasia.Chest pain is common among patients with congenital heart disease (CHD). Knowledge regarding spontaneous coronary artery dissection in the CHD spectrum is limited. Chest pain differentials for patients with CHD should include evaluation for acquired conditions, particularly as this population ages.
medicine.text:
A 32-year-old man presented to an emergency department with 3 days of chest pain, dyspnea, and a sense of “impending doom.” Initial electrocardiogram showed dynamic changes in the anteroseptal leads, whereas high-sensitivity troponin I level was 650 ng/L and peaked at 26,113 ng/L. He was transferred to our facility for cardiac catheterization in the setting of complex congenital heart disease (CHD).

The patient had a history of double inlet left ventricle (DILV) with L-malposition of the great arteries and had undergone lateral tunnel Fontan palliation. His history also includes paroxysmal atrial flutter; home medications included reduced-dose apixaban because of epistaxis. He was last seen in an adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) clinic 5 years prior and was lost to follow-up.

Given the patient’s classic presentation for acute coronary syndrome (ACS), there was concern for a nonatherosclerotic etiology of myocardial ischemia such as a thromboembolism or spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD).

The patient was taken to the cardiac catheterization laboratory for coronary angiography. An anomalous left anterior descending (LAD) artery arose from a common trunk with the right coronary artery without atherosclerosis. The mid LAD was 100% occluded with a linear lucency near the occluded segment, suggesting the presence of thrombotic material and a dissection (, ). The LAD lesion was wired with difficulty because of the long length of the occlusion, and the wire entered multiple side branches. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) was performed before angioplasty to confirm wire positioning in the true lumen, because flow was not restored by wiring alone. IVUS showed a compressed vessel lumen throughout the vessel's course, from distal to proximal; where the vessel caliber was large, the lumen remained severely compressed, likely because of retrograde expansion of the intramural hematoma (,  and ). Because of the delayed presentation, the authors considered it possible that thrombus had time to develop in the lumen of the vessel, accounting for the thrombotic appearance distally. The wire was confirmed to be in the true lumen, and balloon angioplasty was performed with a 2.0 × 30 mm semicompliant balloon to re-establish flow to the distal vessel. IVUS was repeated following plain old balloon angioplasty (POBA) and again after cutting balloon angioplasty. The distal LAD, once flow was restored, had a normal lumen without dissection (, ). Type IV SCAD was most consistent as the vessel was 100% occluded.

Because the patient complained of ongoing chest pain, cutting balloon angioplasty was performed with a 2.5 × 15 mm Wolverine cutting balloon (Boston Scientific) to fenestrate the intima and decompress the intramural hematoma, and this strategy restored TIMI flow grade 3 to the distal LAD. Stenting was deferred given association with worse outcomes in SCAD. An individualized treatment strategy was determined through extrapolation of POBA and cutting balloon practice as well as the need for chronic anticoagulation. We recommended triple antithrombotic therapy with aspirin, clopidogrel, and apixaban for one week followed by clopidogrel and apixaban for 30 days, with a plan to de-escalate to single therapy apixaban indefinitely (with his history of atrial flutter). The patient was previously on a dose-reduced apixaban because of epistaxis; he was agreeable to therapeutic apixaban at discharge. β-Blocker dosing was increased to reduce myocardial oxygen demand.

The patient experienced significant improvement in his chest pain following percutaneous coronary intervention. His echocardiogram showed low-normal ventricular systolic function with a regional wall motion abnormality of the systemic single left ventricle extending from the base to distal wall segments sparing the apex (, , ). Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the head and neck vessels was without evidence of fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). He was discharged 2 days after percutaneous coronary intervention with plans to complete CTA of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis as an outpatient. Cardiac rehab was recommended to be initiated after a month without recurrence of symptoms. Follow-up occurred with his local cardiologist 2 weeks after discharge, and he noted significant symptomatic improvement. He returned for follow-up evaluation in our ACHD clinic 5 months after his hospitalization with resolution of his wall motion abnormalities (, , ). Antiplatelet therapy was discontinued, and therapeutic dose apixaban for known history of atrial arrhythmias was continued. He was encouraged to participate in light- to moderate-intensity activities with gradual increases but to avoid high-intensity activities such as heavy weightlifting or sprint- or burst-type activities.

Chest pain is a common presenting symptom in patients with CHD to the emergency room and can have a range of etiologies including cardiac, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, and psychologic pain. Differentiating among these etiologies can pose unique challenges becausee these patients have complex anatomies, extensive surgical histories, and lack traditional risk factors for coronary atherosclerosis. In this case, a young man with Fontan palliation presented to emergency care with an acute worsening of his chronic chest pain and a new sense of “impending doom.” His assessment was consistent with ACS, and he was referred to a higher level of care with ACHD providers for specialized evaluation.

DILV is diagnosed when more than 50% of both atria are connected to 1 dominant ventricle through either 2 atrioventricular valves or 1 common atrioventricular valve, effectively creating single-ventricle pathology. This pathology is commonly associated with transposition of the great arteries (TGA), and patients with TGA can have variable coronary anatomy.

SCAD is a dissection in an epicardial coronary artery not associated with atherosclerotic disease and not iatrogenic. The LAD is the most affected vessel. There are 4 angiographic classes of SCAD. Our patient was diagnosed with type IV SCAD, which is defined as a totally occluded vessel and requires evaluation with intracoronary imaging following re-establishment of coronary flow. The true incidence of SCAD is believed to be unknown because of misidentification in the setting of young age and absence of traditional risk factors. SCAD is commonly associated with women, FMD, and stressful events. SCAD has commonly been associated as a pathology exclusive to women, although studies have shown these events can occur in men. Because of this misconception, SCAD may have been underdiagnosed in the male population. Management of SCAD varies and is dynamic as more cases are identified in the general population. The goal for this patient’s management was to reestablish flow to his distal coronary artery conservatively to reduce the risk of dissection propagation. Medical management was driven by his coronary intervention and comorbidities with dual antiplatelet therapy following recommendations for POBA management and apixaban for atrial arrhythmia thromboembolism prophylaxis.

This patient had a wall motion abnormality on echocardiography. Unlike in anatomically typical hearts, wall motion segmental anatomy was cautiously interpreted in this patient. This is a stark contrast to traditional ischemic evaluation in adult cardiology. Based on the complexity of the anatomy of DILV, TGA, anomalous coronary artery, and lack of cross-sectional imaging in our patient, we are unable to clearly ascribe whether SCAD of the LAD correlated to the location of the wall motion abnormality. Because of the improvement in the wall motion abnormality following revascularization, we cautiously attribute the wall motion abnormality to the SCAD event. There is no standard for grading wall motion in patients with DILV. As patients with complex CHD continue to live longer, it is foreseeable that we will see more episodes of ACS in this population, with etiologies including SCAD, thromboembolism, and atherosclerotic plaque rupture.

To our knowledge, this is the first reported case in the academic literature of SCAD in a patient with Fontan palliation. The pathology of this patient’s ACS is particularly important in that SCAD is an acquired nonatherosclerotic etiology of ACS distinct from more commonly considered etiologies of Fontan-related coronary ischemia such as thromboembolism or coronary malperfusion. This case highlights the importance of evaluating for acquired etiologies of ACS in patients with complex CHD even in the absence of traditional atherosclerotic risk factors. SCAD should be considered as an etiology of ACS in men as well as women. As the population of patients with CHD continues to age, it becomes even more imperative for primary care providers, cardiologists, subspecialists, and emergency room providers to recognize and impart appropriate chest pain evaluations in the setting of combined congenital and acquired heart disease risks.

There are several diagnostic limitations in this case. A complete evaluation for an embolic source was not performed by cross-sectional imaging or transesophageal echocardiography; however, no intracardiac thrombus was identified on transthoracic echocardiography. Overall, the clinical picture and angiography were felt to be explained by a type 4 SCAD event. A CTA of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was ordered to complete screening for extra-coronary FMD but remains incomplete at the time of submission.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Search Interest in Alleged COVID-19 Treatments During the Pandemic and the Impact of Mass News Media Coverage Based on Google Trends and Media Cloud Data: Retrospective Analysis
medicine.abstract: During a public health emergency, interest in unsafe or illegitimate medications can delay appropriate treatment and foster medical mistrust.The aim of this study is to assess the relationship between search interest and media coverage of 3 purported COVID-19 treatments: hydroxychloroquine, ivermectin, and remdesivir.The authors obtained daily US-based Google Trends and Media Cloud data from 2019 through 2022, conducted national-level anomaly detection, and assessed the state-level association of treatment-specific search interest and media coverage by regressing search interest against daily media coverage, and vice versa, for each treatment using a 2-stage process. This allowed us to explicitly model the questions: (1) does a state have any of the outcomes (search interest or media coverage), and (2) given a nonzero outcome, how much is it impacted by the exposure?Search interest and media coverage of all 3 treatments were significantly elevated during the study period. Anomaly detection identified several periods of higher-than-expected activity; anomalies in search interest and media coverage showed similar temporal patterns within treatments. There were distinct patterns of media source bias across treatments: while the plurality of top sources for all treatments were rated “Left” or “Left Leaning,” ivermectin was covered by the highest number of “Right”-biased sources, and remdesivir had the highest coverage by “Center” or unbiased sources. Significant associations between media coverage and search interest were observed for all 3 treatments. Media coverage had the strongest impact on same-day search interest for hydroxychloroquine (21.3% increase, 95% CI 20.1%-22.5%) and ivermectin (18.3% increase, 95% CI 16.8%-19.7%), and a more modest impact for remdesivir (12.8% increase, 95% CI 11.8%-13.8%). For hydroxychloroquine and remdesivir, this same-day effect was more transient, while interest in ivermectin remained elevated at a comparable level 1 and 2 days after media coverage. When evaluating the separate impact of search interest on media coverage, the associations were much weaker for all 3 treatments and all lagged conditions.During a public health emergency, the information accessed by populations can directly influence health-seeking behaviors, potentially resulting in life-threatening consequences. Given the observed associations between treatment-related news media coverage and public interest in those treatments, our results suggest that news media serve as a powerful mechanism for experts to inform the landscape of public opinion and to reach audiences during future public health emergencies.
medicine.text:
Throughout the early COVID-19 pandemic, several repurposed drugs were evaluated as potential COVID-19 treatments in the United States, including hydroxychloroquine, ivermectin, and remdesivir. Hydroxychloroquine, an antimalarial and antirheumatic drug, received an emergency use authorization from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 in March 2020, but this was soon revoked after clinical trials showed harmful cardiovascular side effects at the doses being dispensed []. Ivermectin, an antihelminthic, was proposed as an antiviral agent for COVID-19 in early 2020, leading to the initiation of several randomized controlled trials between mid-2020 and 2021 []; however, results were generally inconsistent and inconclusive, leading the FDA, the US National Institutes of Health, and the World Health Organization to recommend against its use in 2021 []. Remdesivir, an antiviral originally developed to treat hepatitis C, was approved by the FDA for persons hospitalized with COVID-19 in October 2020 after multiple clinical trials showed moderately improved outcomes among hospitalized cases []. Public interest in these treatments varied over time, driven partially by governmental, political, and media responses to current events []. For hydroxychloroquine and then ivermectin, public demand for the drugs caused international pharmacy shortages, and in the case of ivermectin—a drug commonly used for livestock deworming—shortages of veterinary ivermectin as well [,]. Beyond causing shortages, public interest in unsafe or untested or off-label medications during a public health emergency can delay access to appropriate treatments and foster mistrust in the medical system, a detriment at both individual and population levels. Therefore, both for situational awareness and interventional purposes, it is critical for health and policy communities to understand how the public obtains medical information during an emerging crisis.

One method of evaluating public interest in medical information is the use of internet search data. These data can serve as a large-scale, near real-time proxy for public interest by providing insight into what information people seek online, including the subject, timing, and frequency of specific topics. A recent study in Switzerland found that 55% of Google searches were informational (as opposed to transactional or navigational) [], and in 2019, roughly 7% of Google searches (about 1 billion searches daily) were related to health []. This makes internet search data—publicly available through Google Trends (GT)—an attractive tool for health information research []; indeed, GT was used extensively throughout the pandemic to measure population engagement with public health messaging on topics like masking, vaccines, and misinformation, as well as interest in COVID-19 more broadly [,].

Another way to gauge public interest in a topic is by assessing relevant news media coverage—a data source that is particularly useful for topics such as uncommon medications, which would rarely enter the public zeitgeist otherwise. The impact of news media on public interest and changing health behaviors has been well studied [,], including during the COVID-19 era [,,]. Previous research by our team and others has assessed a variety of health-related topics and their relationship with news media coverage using services like Media Cloud (MC) [], an open-source content analysis tool that collects time series of national and subnational news media coverage, comprising data from more than 50,000 news sources since its inception. The bulk of MC’s corpora comprises news stories from web-based media sites, which is particularly relevant, as 86% of US adults reported getting news from an online source in 2023 [].
