Interestingly, the relationship between public interest and media coverage is not unidirectional; studies in communication theory demonstrate that the media can also serve as a reflection of public opinion rather than functioning solely as its driver—a phenomenon known as the “reflection hypothesis.” [] As interest in a topic increases, people begin searching for things they see in the news, while in response, the news covers things it knows people are interested in [].

Our study investigated the possibility of bidirectional relationships between online search interest and media coverage to evaluate exposure to and access to health-related information during the COVID-19 pandemic. Specifically, we examined (1) the extent to which US news sources covered supposed COVID-19 treatments, (2) the extent of public interest in these treatments, as reflected by online search interest, and (3) the relationship between these data sources within the United States.

We used 2 primary data sources to assess the relationship between treatment-related news media coverage and treatment-related search interest in the United States: MC and GT. All data were obtained for the period from January 2019 through December 2022 using the queries “hydroxychloroquine,” “ivermectin,” and “remdesivir” for both MC and GT (more details on how data were obtained can be found in the Supplemental Methods in ). Data from 2019 were included in the analysis to provide a prepandemic baseline for each of these search terms; data collection ceased in 2022 after a sustained period of low search interest and media coverage of all 3 terms.

Daily treatment-related news media coverage data were downloaded from MC’s national- and state-level news corpora. This was done by visiting the Media Cloud website [], creating a free account, logging in, and entering a keyword, such as “ivermectin.” We used the Boolean “ANY” to match any phrase including a treatment name in the headline. A custom time frame from January 1, 2019, through December 31, 2022, was applied. We restricted the analysis to single-word treatment keywords. In MC, one-word queries return any media containing that word anywhere in the content. News corpora include media articles published in either national (eg, Reuters) or state-specific news sources (eg, Arkansas Times) and report the daily normalized content percentage (ie, the number of corpus-specific articles reporting on a topic of interest on a given day divided by the total number of corpus-specific articles on the same day).

Daily treatment-specific Google search interest data were downloaded using the GT dashboard at both the national level and, separately, the state level. This was done by visiting the GT website [], entering a keyword, such as “ivermectin,” and clicking “Explore.” A custom time frame from January 1, 2019, through December 31, 2022, was applied. We restricted the analysis to single-word treatment keywords. When a search term is entered into GT, the platform returns data for all searches that include that word, not only exact matches. Thus, querying “ivermectin” captures search interest from all queries containing that string, including contextual phrases such as “ivermectin covid,” “ivermectin dose,” and “ivermectin treatment,” without requiring these to be specified individually. As a result, our single-term queries do not restrict the data to exact-match searches and are unlikely to underestimate aggregate search interest. Although misspellings and variant spellings are not directly captured by our methodology, the use of a search topic rather than a search term enables retrieval of all related terms, including misspellings. When comparing interest over time across the 3 treatment terms and topics, the patterns were incredibly similar, and thus we retained only results from our original term query.

GT returns a normalized index of relative search interest scaled from 0 to 100, where 100 represents the peak search volume within the queried window. Because daily observations are only available for query windows of approximately 9 months or less, and because each query is independently normalized to its own within-window maximum, a 2-pass extraction procedure was used to obtain a consistent daily series across the full study period. In the first pass, the 4-year window was divided into 9 contiguous approximately 6-month subwindows, and daily data were retrieved for each term-geography-subwindow combination (1377 queries). Each resulting series was internally consistent but expressed on its own local 0 to 100 scale, with 100 anchored to the highest-search day within that subwindow. In the second pass, a single 4-year query was issued for each term-geography cell (153 queries), returning weekly observations on a common 0 to 100 scale anchored to that cell’s 4-year peak. Daily subwindow series were then rescaled using min-max rescaling, mapping each subwindow’s local minimum and maximum onto the corresponding values from the 4-year reference series, preserving day-to-day variation while reexpressing each subwindow on a common scale. Rescaled subwindows were concatenated to produce 153 daily series of 1461 observations each.

To identify peaks in treatment-related search interest and media coverage, we performed anomaly detection for each treatment in the respective time series at the national level using the anomalize package in R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing) [], with α set at .001, using the traditional seasonal decomposition by LOESS (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing) method for time series decomposition and the generalized extreme studentized deviate test for anomaly detection. For each detected anomaly, we conducted additional internet searches for potentially relevant current events that could have resulted in atypical media attention or public awareness.

In addition to strict media mentions, MC provides a list of top words in the headlines of a random sample of content matching the query. These top words were used to create word clouds using the wordcloud2 R package after excluding the words “covid,” “covid-19,” and “coronavirus.” [] Finally, we acquired bias ratings for the top 10 media sources for each treatment query primarily from the AllSides website [,]; bias ratings were obtained from the Media Bias/Fact Check website [] when AllSides [,] did not rate a particular media source. Ratings were pulled from mid-pandemic (2021) assessments when possible, or from the closest assessment to that time when not.

To visualize geographic heterogeneity in search interest and media coverage, we created heatmaps at the state level for each treatment using ggplot2 (Figure S1 in ) []. Using treatment-specific regression models, we assessed the state-level relationship between treatment-specific media coverage and search interest. We considered 3 confounders in the models: political leaning, rurality, and social vulnerability.

As COVID-19 treatments were highly politicized during the initial stages of the pandemic [], we hypothesized that statewide political leaning may have differentially influenced interest in and coverage of specific treatments. We measured statewide political leaning as the percentage of a given state that voted for the Republican Party candidate in the 2020 presidential election, on a 0 to 100 scale [].

Social vulnerability may also have played a role in treatment interest, given its association with reduced access to health care services []. Reduced interaction with health care providers and services has previously been associated with riskier health choices and poor health outcomes, providing evidence that social vulnerability may influence treatment-seeking behavior [,]. We measured social vulnerability using the COVID-19 Community Vulnerability Index, which provides a state-level measure of access to health care, taking economic, structural, and demographic barriers into account []. State-level scores are scaled continuously from 0 to 100, where 100 represents the highest level of vulnerability.

Lastly, we included rurality in the models, first as a proxy for known barriers to health care that could potentially influence off-label medication use [], and second because of ivermectin’s widespread use on farms as a livestock deworming agent, which we hypothesized could influence search interest, especially among farming communities. Rurality was measured using the 2021 US Census Bureau Urban and Rural dataset [], which provides the percentage of a given state’s population that lives in rural settings, measured on a 0 to 100 scale, with 100 being the most rural.

Additional covariates were considered for inclusion in this analysis and were ultimately rejected. Specifically, we did not feel that broadband access is a confounding factor in the relationship between GT and MC, as broadband access is unlikely to influence whether the media covers COVID-19 treatments (Figure S2 in ). However, for due diligence, we acquired a broadband access dataset (US FCC Broadband Data Collection, FCC National Broadband Map) [,] for May 2024 (the earliest version of the dataset we could locate) and discovered that the median percentage of the United States served by broadband (≥100/20 Mbps) is 94% (IQR 80%-99%), the median percentage for underserved (≥25/3 Mbps but <100/20 Mbps) is 5% (IQR 0.4%-17%), and the median unserved (<25/3 Mbps) is 0% (IQR 0%-0%). These numbers were similar when stratifying by urban/rural status. We therefore chose not to include broadband access in our analysis.

Because both search interest and media coverage are bounded indices (0‐100) rather than true continuous or count data, we regressed search interest against daily media coverage, and vice versa, for each treatment using a 2-stage process. This allowed us to explicitly model the questions: (1) does a state have any of the outcome (search interest or media coverage), and (2) given a nonzero outcome, how much is it impacted by the exposure? To do this, we used the glmmTMB package in R [] to fit 2 generalized linear mixed models. First, we fit a logistic model to assess the impact of exposure on presence/absence of the outcome. Second, we fit a conditional log-normal model for all nonzero outcomes. This approach was chosen to account for overdispersion in the data because, across most days and states in the dataset outside of the anomalies, there was little search interest or media coverage of the selected COVID-19 treatments.

Media coverage was scaled by dividing values by the root mean square, and the other covariates were mean-centered and scaled by dividing values by the SD to ensure comparability and equal contribution in the regression analysis and to aid interpretation. We included “state” as a random intercept to control for interstate variability in the impact of covariates on exposure. Media coverage and search interest were assessed at 3 relative time points—nonlagged (same day), lagged 1 day, and lagged 2 days—using the timetk R package []. Multicollinearity was assessed by checking the variance inflation factors for the models. Model results are presented as adjusted odds ratios (ORs, logistic model) and adjusted risk ratios and percent differences (conditional model), with 95% Wald CIs. Multiple comparisons were accounted for using the Bonferroni method, with P<.001 considered significant. All analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.x) [].

To assess whether residual spatial autocorrelation existed beyond what was accounted for by the state-level random effect, we applied the Moran I measure to the state-level mean residuals from all 36 models (18 model pairs across binary and conditional parts), using a queen contiguity spatial weights matrix (Table S1 in ). E-values, which quantify the minimum strength of association that unmeasured confounders would need to have with both the treatment and the outcome to fully explain away a specific treatment-outcome association, conditional on the measured covariates, were calculated using the EValue R package [].

This study used publicly available aggregated state-level data that do not contain individual-level or identifiable information. Because the data are deidentified and publicly accessible, this study does not constitute human participants research and is therefore exempt from institutional review board approval.

Nationally, the median search interest (out of 100) during the pandemic period (January 2020 through December 2022) was 2.2 (IQR 1.6‐3.0) for hydroxychloroquine, 6.0 (IQR 1.9‐9.9) for ivermectin, and 2.2 (IQR 1.5‐3.3) for remdesivir, compared to 0.5 (IQR 0.3‐0.6), 1.0 (IQR 1‐1), and 0 (IQR 0‐0) for the respective treatments in 2019. Nationally, the median media coverage during the pandemic was 0.05% (IQR 0.02%‐0.13%) for hydroxychloroquine, 0.01% (IQR 0%‐0.04%) for ivermectin, and 0.03% (IQR 0.01%‐0.1%) for remdesivir, compared to median coverage of 0% for each treatment in 2019.

Anomaly detection identified periods of atypical search interest (A) and media coverage (B). Search interest in hydroxychloroquine peaked in July 2020 with media coverage increasing sharply in March 2020 and remaining high until mid-November 2020. While search interest in ivermectin had several small anomalies prior to 2021, interest peaked in late August/early September 2021, with a second large peak occurring in January 2022. Media coverage of ivermectin peaked and stayed elevated during this same period. Finally, search interest in remdesivir peaked in late April 2020 and decreased quickly; media coverage was high throughout 2020, and coverage remained sporadically elevated through the end of the study period.

shows the top 10 national-level media sources with the highest number of stories matching each treatment query and their bias as determined by 1 of 2 media bias reporting websites during the COVID-19 pandemic. Unsurprisingly, all top sources were web-based. While some sources covered all treatments at a high level (eg, nytimes.com and washingtonpost.com were in the top 10 for all 3 treatments), there were distinct patterns of bias (). The plurality of sources for all treatments were considered “Left” or “Left Leaning”; ivermectin was covered by the highest number of “Right”-biased sources, and remdesivir had the highest coverage by “Center” or “unbiased” sources.

For each treatment query, sources are ranked by the number of stories mentioning the treatment over the study period. Each source’s political bias rating and the year of that assessment were obtained from AllSides or, when unavailable, Media Bias/Fact Check [-].

C: Center.

LL: Left Leaning.

L: Left.

Rating from Media Bias/Fact Check.

R: Right.

RL: Right Leaning.

When assessing the co-occurrence of words and phrases in media sources covering each of the treatments (Figures S3A-C in ), the most striking qualitative difference was in the categories of words appearing alongside the drugs. Specifically, ivermectin appeared to be reported more frequently in association with specific individuals (Figure S3B in ) than media mentioning hydroxychloroquine (Figure S3A in ) or remdesivir (Figure S3C in ), although the top co-occurring word for hydroxychloroquine was “Trump” by a wide margin. In Google searches, people seemed most interested in understanding what hydroxychloroquine is and the uses of ivermectin (eg, “for humans” and “for dogs”). Curiously, for remdesivir, several co-occurring terms included the manufacturer and searches for remdesivir stock rather than its uses ().

Per Google, “Top searches” are terms most frequently searched together with the queried term in the same session within the chosen category and region; “Rising searches” are terms with the greatest growth in volume over the period, shown as a percentage increase relative to the prior period, with “Breakout” indicating growth exceeding 5000%.

When controlling for average state political leaning, rurality, and social vulnerability, we found significant, positive associations between media coverage and search interest across all 3 treatments for the questions: (1) does a state have any of the outcome (A and B), and (2) given a nonzero outcome, how much is it impacted by the exposure (C and D)?

For public search interest, the odds of having any interest peaked at a 1-day lag for both hydroxychloroquine (OR 3.48, 95% CI 3.32-3.64) and remdesivir (OR 3.06, 95% CI 2.91-3.23), relative to their immediate, no-lag baselines (ORH 2.37, 95% CI 2.29-2.46 and ORR 1.96, 95% CI 1.89-2.05; A). Conversely, ivermectin maintained remarkably stable threshold OR across all time frames, ranging tightly from an OR of 2.36 (95% CI 2.31-2.42) at no lag to 2.39 (95% CI 2.33-2.45) at a 1-day lag. In contrast to this delayed or sustained public search behavior, the relationship with media coverage showed immediate temporal decay across all treatments. The highest odds of a treatment having any media coverage occurred with no lag for hydroxychloroquine (OR 2.29, 95% CI 2.22-2.36), ivermectin (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.85-2.00), and remdesivir (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.92-2.05); all associations steadily weakened as the lag extended to 2 days.

Conditional log-normal models evaluating the volume of search interest or media coverage among nonzero observations revealed similar patterns to the logistic models (C and D). For example, hydroxychloroquine again demonstrated the most pronounced effects of the 3 treatments; media coverage increased same-day search interest by 21.3% (95% CI 20.1%-22.5%), and search interest increased same-day media coverage by 30.4% (95% CI 26.3%-31.6%). Unlike the logistic models, the timing of the exposure relative to the outcome had a much more limited effect. While hydroxychloroquine search intensity steadily waned over the lag periods, falling to 17.7% (95% CI 16.6%-18.8%) at a 2-day lag, remdesivir search interest peaked at a 1-day lag (15.7%, 95% CI 14.8%-16.6%) before declining by day 2 (14.7%, 95% CI 13.8%-15.6%). Ivermectin displayed notable consistency throughout, with conditional search interest remaining stable between 17.2% and 18.2% (95% CI range: 15.7%-19.7%), and conditional media coverage steady around 16% across all timeframes (C and D). Notably, despite remdesivir demonstrating a strong association with the initial onset of public search interest, its relationship with subsequent media coverage was the weakest observed, yielding an 8.4% (95% CI 7.6%-9.3%) increase at no lag that decreased to only 4.6% (95% CI 3.6%-5.6%) when lagged 2 days (D). All regression values and fitness statistics can be found in Tables S2 and S3 in .

To evaluate the vulnerability of these findings to unmeasured confounding, we calculated E-values for both the logistic and conditional models. For the logistic models, the associations proved highly robust; an unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with both treatment exposure and the outcome by a risk ratio ranging from 1.82 to 3.05 (based on the lower confidence limits) to fully explain away the observed probabilities of generating any search interest or media coverage. For the conditional models, the E-values were transformed into percentage changes to align with the effect size scale. These results indicate moderate to high robustness depending on the treatment. To shift the observed percentage changes in volume to the null, an unmeasured confounder would need to independently produce an effect ranging from a 22.9% change (for remdesivir media coverage at a 2-day lag) up to a 90.8% change (for hydroxychloroquine media coverage at no lag). While the findings for hydroxychloroquine remain highly robust against unmeasured confounding, the more modest E-values for remdesivir’s delayed media coverage suggest those estimates are more sensitive to moderate unmeasured confounding (Table S2 in ).

In this study, we identified significant public interest in 3 purported COVID-19 treatments—hydroxychloroquine, ivermectin, and remdesivir—as represented by anomalies detected in heightened search interest in these medications during the pandemic period. Additionally, we found significant associations between news media coverage and all 3 treatments. Our bidirectional design allows us to evaluate the reflection hypothesis—the proposition that media coverage functions as a mirror of existing public interest rather than its driver—directly against the data. If public interest were the primary driver of media coverage, we would expect search interest to predict subsequent media coverage at least as strongly as coverage predicted search interest. Instead, we observed a consistent asymmetry: across all 3 treatments and all lag structures, the association between media coverage and subsequent search interest was substantially stronger than the reverse, with the association between search interest and media coverage for remdesivir decreasing to a 4.6% (95% CI 3.6%-5.6%) increase at a 2-day lag. This pattern suggests that, for these purported COVID-19 treatments during this period, the influencing role of news media outweighed its reflective role. The reflection hypothesis is unlikely to be entirely inoperative; coverage and interest are mutually reinforcing, and our aggregate, state-level design cannot adjudicate causal direction at the individual level or rule out unmeasured events driving both series simultaneously. Rather, we have found that, in a fast-moving emergency dominated by many scientific and clinical unknowns, public interest appears to have followed media attention more than preceded it. This distinction matters for public health practice, as it implies that proactive, accurate news coverage can shape the information landscape rather than merely echo public sentiment that has already formed.

At the beginning of the pandemic, substantial uncertainty surrounded the epidemiology of COVID-19 and the effectiveness, safety, and availability of potential treatments. As scientific evidence accumulated, public health guidance evolved accordingly to reflect updated knowledge []. Although changing recommendations are expected during the early stages of a novel pathogen outbreak, inconsistent or insufficiently transparent messaging may have contributed to public confusion. In this environment, many individuals increasingly relied on nonexpert sources such as politicians, public figures, and celebrities for health-related information rather than traditional public health authorities []. Scholars have long noted that media reporting practices can further shape public risk perception; anecdotal framing and selective emphasis may lead audiences to draw inaccurate conclusions about the magnitude or nature of risk []. Additionally, because many journalists lack formal training in statistics or probability, complex or preliminary scientific findings may not always be critically evaluated before dissemination to mass audiences, potentially amplifying misunderstanding or misinterpretation [].

These dynamics may have been compounded by declining access to medical guidance: recent studies report that the percentage of Americans who regularly see a primary care physician has steadily decreased from 2014 to 2022, meaning regular communication with licensed medical providers is becoming more limited for many communities across the United States []. Together, these factors may have contributed to the general public’s increasing reliance on news media for guidance during the COVID-19 pandemic. Indeed, over the last several years, perceived US media influence on government decisions has grown among the public and will likely continue to have an outsized influence on the public interest []. In communication research, this aligns with media system dependency theory, which assumes that the impact of information provided by news media on audience perceptions is a function of how dependent an audience member is on mass media as a source for acquiring information important to them []; that is, the more likely someone is to turn to news media for personally relevant information, the more dependent on it they become. Importantly, research has found that this dependency is what drives changes in behavior, not media usage alone. While our study did not directly assess media usage or dependency at the individual level, the patterns observed, particularly the strong, temporally immediate association between media coverage and search interest, are consistent with media system dependency theory and highlight the importance of integrating communication theory into future epidemiologic analyses of health information seeking.

We found that the effect of media coverage on same-day search interest was largest for hydroxychloroquine, an initially FDA-authorized treatment with early potential that ultimately proved ineffective and dangerous [], followed by ivermectin, an incredibly popular but inappropriate treatment for COVID-19, and remdesivir, the only treatment that remains FDA-approved for use [,]. Although ivermectin produced an intermediate same-day effect, it was the only drug for which search interest stayed significantly elevated at a comparable level 1 to 2 days after coverage by media outlets, whereas the effects for hydroxychloroquine and remdesivir were more transient. One possible explanation for this sustained response is that people may receive information about ivermectin more frequently through non-news media sources, such as personal networks, social media, or podcasts, which may see continued high levels of engagement days to weeks after posting, depending on the platform []. Another hypothesis for why search interest in ivermectin remained elevated rather than tracking closely with day-to-day media coverage relates to trust in traditional media. Research by Ladd [] suggests that individuals who distrust traditional news media sources are more likely to rely on preexisting political beliefs to form opinions rather than incorporating new information supplied by news media. At least one study [] has found that higher belief in COVID-19 vaccine misinformation and conspiracy thinking was associated with increased use of ivermectin and/or hydroxychloroquine, although the results were not stratified by specific treatment. In a more recent article, Ladd and Podkul [] argue that when media credibility is lost, so is its capacity to influence the public. In this context, diminished trust in traditional media and reliance on alternative information channels may attenuate or delay the observable impact of news coverage on public search behavior.

We note several limitations in this analysis. First, the state-level analysis includes only state-level media outlets, as MC cannot track state-level readership of national news sources. Given that many individuals rely heavily on national media outlets for news, the media exposure used in this analysis may be skewed if individuals within a state engage differently with national-level vs state-level news outlets. Additionally, larger states had relatively larger news media corpora than smaller states; however, no corpus included fewer than 30 sources, indicating that sample sizes were sufficient to assess news media coverage at this geographic scale. While the associations reported here were broadly robust to unmeasured confounding, the E-values for remdesivir’s delayed media coverage were comparatively modest, indicating that those particular estimates are more sensitive to moderate unmeasured confounding and should be interpreted with corresponding caution. Notably, MC does not capture sentiment (ie, the emotions and attitudes contextualizing a news report about a particular issue), meaning that we were unable to comment on whether the treatment-related news media sources were reporting positively or negatively on purported treatments. Future studies should assess the content and sentiment of health-related news articles to understand the kind of language that is most likely to prompt heightened search interest, so those techniques can be leveraged to improve health communication strategies. Relatedly, our analysis captured only 2 information channels, news media (via MC) and search behavior (via GT), and did not measure exposure to other sources that may have influenced health information seeking during the study period, including social media platforms, podcasts, messaging applications, and personal networks. This is particularly relevant for ivermectin, for which we hypothesized that non-news channels may have contributed to the sustained search interest we observed; without data from these sources, we cannot directly test that hypothesis or quantify the relative contribution of alternative information channels to public interest in any of the 3 treatments.

Limitations in the use of GT data also exist. GT normalizes search interest independently for each geographic region (ie, state). Consequently, a search value of 100 in one state does not represent the same search volume as a search value of 100 in another state. For example, if Maryland has 500 total searches and 50 are for “ivermectin,” the scaled search interest value would be 100. If California has 5,000,000 total searches and 100 are for “ivermectin,” which might also yield a value of 100, even though the underlying population-level search behavior is completely different. Thus, these results are not intended to be compared between states; our analysis is intended to assess temporal patterns in our outcomes of interest, while accounting for state-level variation in search behavior and media coverage. Lastly, search interest was only captured for the population using Google as their primary search engine; people using alternative engines such as Microsoft Bing or DuckDuckGo were not captured in our study, and these users might differ in characteristics such as political leaning that could make their search behavior fundamentally different from that of Google users. However, in the United States, the Google search engine accounts for nearly 90% of market share []; we are, therefore, confident that our results capture most relevant search interest.

Several features of the media environment have continued to evolve since the end of our study period in 2022, with implications for how these findings should be applied to future public health emergencies. The audience for traditional and web-based news outlets (the corpus captured by MC) has continued to fragment, with a growing share of the public encountering health information through algorithmically curated social feeds, messaging applications, video platforms, and individual content creators rather than through identifiable news organizations [,]. The continued contraction of local news coverage may further widen the gap between national and subnational information environments that our state-level analysis was only partially able to capture [].

More recently, the integration of generative AI into search and the growth of conversational information-seeking may alter both what “search interest” reflects and how the public is exposed to health claims [,], potentially decoupling search behavior from discrete news events in ways our lag-based framework was not designed to detect. For example, in 2024, only 1% of COVID-19-related search queries were answered by AI; this increased to more than 66% by 2025 []. However, these shifts do not undermine our central finding that news media coverage was strongly and contemporaneously associated with public search interest during the COVID-19 pandemic; rather, they suggest that the relative influence of traditional news media may be diminishing, and that the sustained, media-independent interest we observed for ivermectin may become a more common pattern as alternative information channels assume a larger role. Consequently, while news media remains an important lever for public health communication, future efforts will likely need to engage a broader and more decentralized set of information channels to reach at-risk populations effectively.

Regardless of the quality of public health messaging available to the general public, social media, news outlets, and political and public figures will continue to be major influences on how individuals seek health-related guidance. During a public health emergency, the information that populations access can directly influence health-seeking behaviors, with potentially life-threatening consequences. More broadly, positive media coverage of unsafe or unapproved medications can deter individuals from trusting and accessing safe alternatives that are more likely to be efficacious in preventing disease progression. Given the observed associations between treatment-related news media coverage and public interest in said treatments, our results suggest that news media serve as a powerful mechanism for experts to inform the landscape of public opinion and to reach audiences during future public health emergencies.

medicine.title: Bdnf mRNA‐LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models
medicine.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA‐lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID‐19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non‐invasive delivery of mRNA‐encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood‐brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA‐LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age‐related and neurodegenerative disorders.
medicine.text:
Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have been propelled into the global spotlight by the rapid development and deployment of mRNA‐based vaccines during the COVID‐19 pandemic. These vaccines not only demonstrated the feasibility of large‐scale mRNA production but also validated lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) as a clinically viable platform for nucleic acid delivery. Beyond infectious diseases, the modularity, safety and rapid manufacturability of mRNA‐LNP systems have catalysed interest in their application across a spectrum of conditions, including cancer, metabolic disorders and neurological diseases, with over 70 mRNA‐based therapies currently in clinical trials (Reviewed in [, , , ].)

Age‐related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), represent some of the most pressing challenges in medicine. Notably, mild cognitive impairment in midlife (age 50–60) predicts severe decline in later life []. As such, interventions that delay or mitigate cognitive deterioration have the potential to significantly reduce the societal and economic burdens of an ageing population. However, current therapeutic strategies to manage age‐related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disorders largely focus on symptomatic treatment or are only modestly disease modifying.

One major obstacle in developing effective therapeutics for neurological diseases is the blood‐brain‐barrier (BBB). To circumvent this barrier, several direct delivery methods have been developed, including intravenous‐guided intracerebral injection, intrathecal administration and convection‐enhanced delivery []. While these approaches enable precise targeting to specific brain regions, they are inherently invasive, often requiring surgical procedures and pose risks such as infection, tissue damage and limited patient compliance. In contrast, systemic delivery methods, such as intravenous or subcutaneous injection, are less invasive and more amenable to repeated administration. These alternative approaches, however, suffer from poor brain bioavailability and their systemic distribution increases the likelihood of off‐target effects in peripheral organs []. Intranasal delivery can provide a nose‐to‐brain route that bypasses the BBB by exploiting the olfactory and trigeminal neural pathways. This route enables direct access to the brain from the nasal cavity, facilitating rapid transport of molecules to the central nervous system without entering systemic circulation. Recent studies have demonstrated its utility in delivering peptides [], nanoparticles [] and nucleic acids [, , , , ] to the brain.

Neurotrophic factors, such as brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF) and glial cell line‐derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) are essential regulators of neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity and cognitive function. Among all neurotrophic factors, BDNF is a particularly potent modulator of learning and memory, shown to enhance synaptic density and neurogenesis [, , , , ]. Reduced BDNF expression is observed in both serum and brain tissue as humans age and is also reduced in patients with AD and other neurodegenerative conditions [, , , ]. Consistently, elevating BDNF levels has been found to improve cognition in AD animal models [, ] and higher baseline serum BDNF levels are associated with a reduced risk of developing dementia []. Furthermore, in an AD clinical trial, cerebrolysin plus donepezil was shown to increase serum BDNF, with larger BDNF increases correlated with greater cognitive improvements [].

Here, we report the development of a therapeutic to deliver mRNA encoding neurotrophic factors intranasally to the brain. Our therapeutic is designed to bypass systemic circulation by targeting the nasal epithelium as a local site of therapeutic protein production. As a proof of concept, we used this platform to intranasally deliver mRNA encoding Bdnf , resulting in BDNF production and secretion by the nasal epithelium. Treatment improved cognitive performance in both aged mice and 5xFAD mice, a model of Alzheimer's disease. Our findings provide preclinical evidence supporting the feasibility and efficacy of this strategy in mitigating cognitive decline and stimulating neurogenesis, offering a promising avenue for the treatment of age‐related cognitive and neurodegenerative disorders.

Olfactory neurons project axons through the cribriform plate to form a direct interface between olfactory stimuli in the environment and the CNS. To exploit this feature, we used intranasal delivery of the clinically validated BioNTech COVID‐19 mRNA backbone to deliver mRNA to the nasal passage. In vitro transcribed mRNA was encapsulated into LNPs and administered intranasally to mice under light anaesthesia (Figure ). To assess the distribution of LNPs and the sites of mRNA‐driven protein expression, mice were administered with mRNA encoding a luciferase reporter and the near infrared dye, DiR, was incorporated into the LNP formulation. IVIS imaging of the skull, brain and peripheral organs of treated mice showed that after intranasal administration, DiR‐labelled LNPs were restricted to the respiratory and olfactory epithelia (Figure  and []), while luciferase protein expression was restricted to the respiratory epithelium (arrow) (Figure  and []). Importantly, neither DiR nor luciferase signals were detected in the lung or other peripheral organs. Overall, LNP‐mRNA did not migrate beyond the nasal cavity or enter the lower respiratory tract, highlighting the specific and contained nature of intranasal mRNA‐LNP delivery.

To assess which cells in the respiratory epithelium take up and express mRNA‐LNP, we delivered mRNA encoding the Cre recombinase to reporter mice harbouring a floxed STOP cassette upstream of the tdTomato gene []. From this we observed robust tdTomato expression within epithelial cells (marked by α tubulin) within the olfactory and respiratory epithelia (Figure ).

BDNF is a neurotrophic factor with potent neurorestorative and synaptic plasticity‐enhancing effects []. Despite strong evidence in the literature for the benefits of elevated BDNF levels across neurodegenerative disorders, its efficacy in clinical settings has been limited by its inability to cross the BBB. Given its promise as a therapeutic, we selected Bdnf mRNA for proof‐of‐concept assessment of our LNP‐mRNA neurotrophin delivery strategy.

Endogenous BDNF is synthesised as a precursor (pre‐pro‐BDNF) that undergoes sequential cleavage to generate either pro‐BDNF or mature BDNF (mBDNF). Importantly, the ratio of mBDNF to pro‐BDNF influences cognitive function, with excess pro‐BDNF associated with synaptic dysfunction and impaired learning and memory [, ]. To avoid these deleterious effects and increase only mature BDNF, we engineered an mRNA construct encoding the mature BDNF domain fused to its native signal peptide (Figure ).

To confirm that this modified mRNA was secreted and produced detectable protein, we transfected HEK293T cells with mBdnf mRNA or Gfp control mRNA, collected supernatants, then quantified BDNF by ELISA. Substantial amounts of BDNF were detected in the media of cells transfected with mBdnf mRNA at a range of doses while BDNF secretion was undetectable from Gfp control cells (p < 0.001; Figure ). In a time course of transfection, we collected and replaced media at regular timepoints after transfection and showed sustained BDNF production, with secretion detectable from 2 h post‐transfection, peaking at 24 h post‐transfection and still being secreted into cell culture media for up to 4 days post‐transfection (p < 0.001; Figure ).

Given that mBDNF is an established regulator of neural stem cell (NSC) proliferation [, ] and neuronal differentiation [], we assessed the biological activity of our synthetic BDNF by examining its effects on adult hippocampal neural stem and progenitor cells (NSPCs) and SH‐SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. When NSPCs were grown in HEK293T conditioned media (from mBdnf or Gfp mRNA treated cells), we found media from mBdnf treated cells showed enhanced proliferation over consecutive passages (p = 0.007; Figure ) and gave rise to more secondary neurospheres across plating dilutions (p = 0.04; Figure ), indicating enhanced self‐renewal.

To assess the ability of mRNA‐encoded synthetic BDNF to enhance neuronal differentiation, SH‐SY5Y cells were induced to differentiate in the presence of either recombinant BDNF or conditioned media from mBdnf or Gfp‐transfected HEK293T cells. Compared to cells that did not receive BDNF (Gfp controls), recombinant BDNF (50 ng/ml) and mBdnf conditioned media‐treated cells showed a greater average total neurite length per neuron (p = 0.04‐0.049) and increased average number of branches per neuron (p = 0.01‐0.03; Figure , quantified in G). Overall, these data indicate that synthetic mBdnf mRNA can drive the production of bioactive BDNF with neuronal differentiation activity similar to that of the recombinant protein.

We next evaluated mBdnf mRNA activity in vivo. mBdnf and Gfp control mRNA were encapsulated into LNPs (92 and 76 nm in diameter respectively, PDI = 0.13‐0.17 and zeta potential = ‐8.69 to ‐4.95 mV, based on a zetasizer; encapsulation efficiency = 96.9‐98.4% based on a RiboGreen assay) (Figure ). 24 h after a single intranasal dose of LNP‐mRNA, RTqPCR was used to assess mBdnf mRNA levels in treated mice. Primers were designed that spanned the novel fusion site between the BDNF signal peptide and mature domain to distinguish synthetic from endogenous Bdnf mRNA. Remarkably, mBdnf transcript levels were 1000–50 000‐fold elevated in the respiratory epithelium, olfactory epithelium and olfactory bulb of mBdnf‐treated vs Gfp control mice (p <0.0001‐0.04; Figure ), demonstrating significant increases in mBdnf expression and verifying delivery to the CNS. Similarly, after 2x doses, BDNF protein levels were augmented in mBdnf‐treated brains compared to controls, by both western immunoblotting (Figure , p = 0.045) and immunohistochemistry in the olfactory bulb and hippocampus (Figure ).

Notably, the elevated BDNF levels we observed in the brains of mice receiving intranasal mBdnf mRNA‐LNP may reflect an increase in endogenous levels, rather than evidence of successful intranasal delivery of encoded synthetic protein. To distinguish endogenous from synthetic BDNF, we delivered a single intranasal dose of mRNA‐LNP encoding mBdnf fused to a C‐terminal HA tag. Staining for the HA tag showed robust BDNF‐HA protein expression in the olfactory bulb (Figure ). Low levels were also observed in the hippocampus (Figure ). Overall, these data confirm that intranasal mBdnf mRNA‐LNP leads to augmented BDNF protein expression in the CNS and that synthetic BDNF can be delivered to the brain via the nose.

We next assessed the functional effect of mBdnf mRNA‐LNP treatment on behavior. As in humans, mice display a decline in cognitive performance as they age [], and this correlates with an age‐related decline in brain BDNF levels []. Aged (18 mn) mice were intranasally treated with Gfp or mBdnf LNP‐mRNA and underwent behavioral assessments of cognition; the open field test, novel object recognition test, Y maze for working memory and Y maze for spatial memory (Figure ). Young (3mn) animals were also behaviorally tested.

In the open field test, there was no effect across age or treatment on the proportion of time spent at the periphery of the arena, which measures anxiety‐like avoidance behavior (p = 0.2‐0.7; Figure ). Both Gfp and mBdnf‐treated aged mice travelled a shorter total distance and had a lower average speed than young mice (p = 0.0006‐0.09; Figure ). In the novel object test, used to evaluate recognition memory, mBdnf mRNA‐LNP‐treated mice showed enhanced memory performance compared with Gfp‐treated age‐matched controls (p = 0.03). Memory scores in mBdnf mRNA‐LNP‐treated mice were also not significantly different from young controls (p = 0.8) suggesting therapeutic delivery of mBdnf mRNA‐LNP rejuvenated memory function in aged mice (Figure ). Similarly in the Y maze test for working memory, mBdnf mRNA‐LNP‐treated aged mice showed significantly enhanced memory compared to Gfp‐treated age‐matched controls (p = 0.0007), and memory performance in aged mBdnf mRNA‐LNP‐treated mice was again indistinguishable from young control animals (p = 0.7; Figure ). Finally, in the Y maze for spatial memory, aged mBdnf mRNA‐LNP‐treated mice again showed enhanced memory performance compared to aged Gfp mRNA‐LNP‐treated controls (p = 0.009), and memory capacity of mBdnf treated mice was equivalent to control young animals in this test (p = 0.7; Figure ). These results demonstrate that once‐a‐week mBdnf mRNA‐LNP intranasal delivery can enhance memory performance in older animals, significantly improving age‐related cognitive decline.

Doublecortin (DCX) is a marker for neurogenesis [], expressed in newly generated neurons and reflective of plasticity and learning. Further reflective of improved memory performance, after 4x LNP doses, mBdnf mRNA‐LNP‐treated aged mice showed a 2.4‐fold increase in the number of DCX positive cells in the hippocampus compared to Gfp‐treated controls (p = 0.004; Figure ). The DCX+ cells of mBdnf‐treated aged animals were also more arborised than in Gfp treated controls (p = 0.005; Figure ). Notably the number and arborisation of DCX+ cells in both aged treatment groups were less than in young mice. This indicates that following mBdnf mRNA‐LNP therapy, neurogenesis is not completely restored to that of a young animal, however the effects of intranasal mBdnf mRNA‐LNP are nonetheless sufficient to return cognitive performance to a youthful state. Importantly, we did not observe any significant effect of treatment on weight gain (p = 0.6 (males) and 0.9 (females) (Figure ) and overall treated mice appeared healthy and showed no obvious side effects.

Our LNP therapy contains PEG, and anti‐PEG antibodies have been observed in patients treated with other PEGylated drugs [, ]. Since mBdnf mRNA‐LNP therapy can involve repeated intranasal dosing, development of anti‐PEG antibodies may impair therapeutic efficacy over time [, ]. To address this concern, we assessed the presence of anti‐PEG antibodies in the serum of LNP‐treated and untreated animals that had received 4x LNP doses, by ELISA; however no anti‐PEG antibodies were detected in control or Bdnf mRNA‐LNP treated animals (Figure ). In addition, cationic lipids, including the ALC‐0315 lipid used here, can promote inflammatory responses when injected []. While this property can be advantageous in vaccine settings, it may be less desirable for therapeutic applications. Accordingly, we assessed inflammation in animals that received 4x doses of intranasal LNP. Compared to untreated controls, we did not find elevated levels of IL‐6, IL‐33 or IFNγ in the sera of treated animals (p = 0.3‐0.99, Figure ) or of IL‐6 or IFNγ in the nasal mucus following lavage (Figure ). IL‐33 fell below detectable levels across all nasal mucus samples (not shown). We also did not observe elevated immune cell infiltration in the nasal passage by H&E staining (p = 0.7‐0.9, Figure ). To assess inflammation within the brain we assessed microglia (Iba1+) and astrocyte (GFAP+) cells in the olfactory bulb, hippocampus and parietal cortex of mBdnf and Gfp mRNA‐LNP treated animals and untreated controls. Across these regions we did not observe a difference in the number of Iba1+ or GFAP+ cells per unit area (p = 0.2‐0.99; Figure ). Overall, these data show that intranasal mRNA‐LNP dosing does not lead to elevated inflammation in the nasal and olfactory epithelium or within the CNS.

BDNF mRNA and protein levels are reduced in postmortem brains from individuals with AD, including in the hippocampus and cortical regions. In AD animal models, increasing BDNF signalling improves neuronal and synaptic integrity and cognitive performance, while higher circulating BDNF levels in AD patients are associated with better cognitive function [, , ]. To test mBdnf LNP‐mRNA as a potential therapeutic for AD, we used the 5xFAD mouse model []. 5xFAD mice serve as a rapid onset “humanised” model of AD, with AD‐associated brain pathologies detectable from 2 months of age and cognitive decline apparent from 4 months [, ].

To evaluate early intervention, 5xFAD animals were treated with Gfp or mBdnf mRNA‐LNP twice weekly from 2 mn of age (total 16x doses). From 4 mn of age animals underwent behavioral assessments, continuing LNP‐mRNA twice weekly doses during testing (8x doses during testing, 24 total doses) (Figure ). Treated mice were also compared to untreated, age‐matched wild type controls. No significant difference was observed between groups in the proportion of time spent at the periphery of the open field test (p = 0.1‐0.9; Figure ), however, across the novel object recognition test, Y maze for working memory and Y maze for spatial memory, mBdnf mRNA‐LNP treated animals performed significantly better than Gfp treated counterparts (p = 0.001‐0.04; Figure ) and were not significantly different from age‐matched wild type (WT) controls (p = 0.6‐0.95). No difference was observed between treatment groups in the average speed or total distance travelled in any test, although wild type animals travelled slightly faster and a greater distance in the Y maze for working memory (Figure ). As in aged mice, no difference in weight gain was observed between Gfp and mBdnf‐treated animals (p = 0.4‐0.7, Figure ) and no anti‐PEG antibodies were found in the serum of either treated group (Figure ). There was also no difference in levels of IL‐6, IL‐33 or IFNγ between either LNP‐treated group and untreated controls in the serum (Figure ). Together these data show that intranasal delivery of mBdnf mRNA‐LNP twice a week can prevent cognitive decline in an aggressive mouse model of familial Alzheimer's disease.

Following behavioral testing and 24 total LNP doses, 5xFAD animals also underwent a histological assessment of the hippocampus. The role of amyloid plaques in AD is controversial [], however therapeutic antibodies targeting plaques do show some clinical efficacy and are approved for clinical use (Reviewed in []). We observed no difference in the amyloid plaque load (p = 0.3) or number of GFAP+ cells (p = 0.6; Figure ) between treatment groups, indicating that mBdnf mRNA‐LNP treatment did not impact this aspect of AD disease progression. DCX staining, however, showed that mBdnf‐treated 5xFAD mice had more DCX+ cells within the hippocampus (p = 0.004) with a greater average total neurite length (p = 0.04; Figure ). Similarly, mBdnf‐treated animals had more neurons (NeuN+ cells) in the CA3 and dentate gyrus regions of the hippocampus compared to Gfp‐treated controls (p = 0.004 and 0.008; Figure ), indicating that mBdnf mRNA‐LNP therapy can prevent AD‐dependent neurodegeneration. Taken together, these data highlight the therapeutic potential of mBdnf mRNA‐LNP to promote neurogenesis, suppress neurodegeneration and enhance cognitive function in multiple forms of cognitive decline.

Neurotrophic factors are long‐standing candidates for cognitive decline, and BDNF rescues memory in rodent and primate models of Alzheimer's disease [], but delivery has required intraparenchymal surgery [, , ] or bolus protein that degrades in the nasal mucosa within hours []. Here we show that intranasal Bdnf mRNA‐LNP increases BDNF protein levels in the brain and improves memory in both aged mice and the 5xFAD model of Alzheimer's disease. Treated aged animals outperformed controls across a variety of memory tests, with augmented neurogenesis correlating with behavioral rescue. Because mRNA encoding synthetic BDNF is the therapeutic and persists at the site of dosing, this system turns the nasal and olfactory epithelium into a local “drug factory”, elevating neurotrophic levels in the CNS 24 h after dosing. Overall, our data establish re‐dosable in situ synthesis as a route to sustained neurotrophic exposure in the ageing or neurodegenerative brain.

Our work aligns with extensive evidence in the literature highlighting the therapeutic potential of BDNF in the CNS [, , ], and our study is corroborated by a recent independent study showing that intranasal delivery of BDNF and IL‐10 encoding mRNA‐LNP was also therapeutic in a preclinical model of traumatic brain injury []. Moreover, several recent studies have shown that intranasally delivered BDNF protein can improve neuronal function across multiple disease models; intranasally BDNF was shown to reduce trigeminal hyperalgesia in a migraine model [], although only at very high protein doses (40‐80 µg/kg); BDNF‐loaded exosomes promoted remyelination in a model of multiple sclerosis []; BDNF‐loaded extracellular vesicles improved post‐ischaemic recovery and synaptic plasticity [] and intranasally delivered BDNF protein reversed depression‐like behaviors, enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced oxidative stress in mice [].

Despite these promising outcomes, delivery of BDNF protein, either as naked or delivered in the vectors discussed above, has several key limitations. Nasally applied proteins are subject to rapid degradation in the mucosa, diffuse inefficiently through olfactory and trigeminal pathways and exhibit short half‐lives due to receptor‐mediated internalisation and degradation [, , ]. In addition, vesicle‐based delivery systems impose fixed cargo limits and require cell culture‐dependent manufacturing, introducing batch variability and limiting scalability (Reviewed in []).

In contrast, delivery of Bdnf mRNA enables local, in situ synthesis of peptides following cellular uptake by nasal epithelial cells. Moreover, we have shown here that in vitro mRNA‐driven BDNF protein expression is detectable for up to 4 days, demonstrating prolonged therapeutic exposure from a single dose. Importantly, mRNA translation amplifies the delivered mRNA cargo, generating greater and sustained amounts of peptide compared to what can be feasibly delivered by a bolus of purified protein. Lastly, mRNA‐LNPs are cost‐efficient, GMP‐standardised, chemically defined and highly scalable, making them well suited for clinical translation. While promising, we have not yet performed a formal pharmacokinetic analysis of BDNF in vivo after intranasal mRNA‐LNP dosing and therefore cannot precisely define the concentration‐time profile in the brain; our current conclusions about exposure are based on in vitro secretion kinetics and behavioral and histological readouts rather than direct PK measurements. Regardless, these data support the basic therapeutic potential of BDNF‐encoded mRNA‐LNP nose drops to enhance BDNF levels in the CNS.

It is also of note that this study delivered mRNA encoding a modified Bdnf mRNA sequence. Endogenous BDNF is synthesised as pre‐pro‐BDNF and subsequently cleaved into pro‐BDNF or mature BDNF (mBDNF). These isoforms exert opposing biological effects: while mBDNF activates TrkB signalling to promote synaptic plasticity and neuronal survival, pro‐BDNF engages p75NTR, triggering apoptotic pathways, synaptic pruning and long‐term depression. Consistently, elevated pro‐BDNF levels are associated with learning and memory impairments [, ], and individuals carrying a Val66Met polymorphism, which prevents activity‐dependent BDNF secretion, show similar cognitive deficits []. The modified BDNF design used here avoids these detrimental effects. This design has also previously been shown to yield functional BDNF capable of supporting neuronal differentiation and survival [, ] and here we similarly observed enhanced NSPC proliferation and neuronal differentiation in cells cultured in conditions media from mBdnf mRNA‐transfected HEK293T cells. Notably, other studies have delivered the full‐length BDNF sequence, including the pro‐domain, using MSC‐derived vesicles [], clathrin nanoparticles [] or AAV vectors [] and reported functional recovery and cognitive improvements in models of stroke, HIV/neuroAIDS, neurodevelopmental pathology and depression. As such, intranasal delivery of full‐length Bdnf mRNA may also have positive effects on neuronal viability, neurogenesis and memory‐based behaviors.

This work focused on BDNF, its clinical translational potential is supported by an ongoing first in human Phase I trial of MRI guided entorhinal‐cortex delivery of AAV2‐BDNF in those with early AD and cognitive impairment []. Notably, delivery of mRNA encoding other neurotrophic factors such as NGF or GDNF would also be of interest in future work. In rodent and non‐human primate models of Parkinson's, direct brain infusion of GDNF has been shown to protect dopaminergic neurons, increase dopamine levels and improve motor outcomes [, , ]. Similarly, targeted delivery of NGF to basal forebrain cholinergic neurons has been found to enhance neuronal function and prevent degeneration in animal models of AD [, ]. In parallel, a substantial body of work has shown that intranasal NGF can bypass the blood‐brain barrier and reach multiple brain regions via the olfactory pathway [, ], supporting its potential use for Alzheimer's disease and related indications, however a clinical trial investigating intracerebral injection of AAV2‐NGF was shown safe but did not affect AD clinical outcomes []. In addition, intranasal insulin has been investigated in preclinical models and clinical studies as a strategy to enhance central insulin signalling. Pilot trials in individuals with mild cognitive impairment or AD reported improvements in memory and cerebral glucose metabolism, reductions in white‐matter hyperintensity progression and alterations in CSF inflammatory markers. Larger trials and meta‐analyses, however, have reported heterogeneous cognitive outcomes and its clinical efficacy remains to be established [, , ]. Together, these findings reinforce the broader concept that increasing neurotrophic factors via intranasal delivery can provide non‐invasive, functionally meaningful access to the brain for peptide and protein therapeutics, avoiding recombinant protein production and providing a more sustained release of encoded neurotrophics.

In the aged‐mouse experiments, mice received 4 doses once a week for 4 weeks, with significant effects on memory detectable after just two doses. It is possible that additional repeated or earlier dosing would yield greater behavioral improvements. Younger animals, without baseline cognitive impairment may also benefit from mBdnf mRNA‐LNP therapy, although, as these animals show robust behavior in learning and memory‐based tasks, the ability to detect an effect in this age group would require more challenging tasks. We also observed that mBdnf mRNA‐LNP dosing resulted in increased neurogenesis as indicated by DCX staining. This increase is unlikely to reflect an immediate transcriptional or maturation response within 24 h, but rather the cumulative effect of repeated BDNF exposure on synaptic strength, progenitor survival and neuronal differentiation, or the maintenance of an immature neuronal population over the total 4 weeks of treatment. Future studies using longitudinal dosing paradigms, lineage tracing and complementary synaptic or proliferation markers would more precisely define the temporal and mechanistic basis of this effect.

In 5xFAD mice we found that mBdnf mRNA‐LNP, delivered from 8 weeks of age (16 doses before behavioral testing and 8 doses during behavioral testing, 24 total doses), improved memory and increased hippocampal neuronal numbers and neurogenesis, however, it did not alter amyloid plaque burden. This aligns with previous studies showing that BDNF does not directly modify amyloid pathology []. The observed benefits are likely explained by enhanced neuronal resilience, synaptic reinforcement and circuit function in the presence of ongoing pathology. In this context, mBdnf mRNA‐LNP should be considered a neurorestorative or symptom‐modifying approach rather than one that targets the underlying amyloid cascade. Importantly, combination treatments using mBdnf mRNA‐LNP and AD therapies such as anti‐amyloid antibodies may act synergistically by reducing plaque development while preserving or restoring neuronal health.

Importantly, although we observed robust effects within the hippocampus, intranasal LNP delivery is not inherently region‐specific, and BDNF signalling can exert broader effects across multiple brain regions (Reviewed in []). Given that BDNF effects are context‐dependent and may vary with cell type, circuit state and regional TrkB expression, sustained or repeated upregulation could, in principle, alter synaptic balance, excitability or plasticity in unintended ways. Although no overt adverse phenotypes were observed in this study a more comprehensive assessment of biodistribution, dose dependence and long‐term CNS safety will be required in future work to define the therapeutic window of this approach. This is particularly relevant for translation, as dementia therapy would require repeated administration, raising questions about nasal mucosal tolerance, local irritation and potential inflammatory or immune‐mediated responses to both the LNP formulation and expressed cargo. Here we provide initial safety data, including body weight monitoring, serum IL‐33, IL‐6 and IFN‐γ levels, and nasal and brain histology (Iba1 and GFAP), which did not reveal major inflammatory activation under the dosing conditions used; however, these measurements represent an early safety screen rather than an exhaustive evaluation, and more detailed longitudinal studies will be needed to characterise chronic dosing risks before this strategy can be trialled in AD patients.

In addition, the translational relevance of our intranasal dosing regimen must be interpreted in the context of substantial anatomical and physiological differences between mice and humans. In this study, mice received 1 µg mRNA in 10 µL intranasally, equivalent to approximately 0.05 mg/kg for a 20 g animal. Body‐surface‐area scaling to humans (Km
 mouse = 3; human = 37) [] indicates an equivalent dose of 0.004 mg/kg or 0.24 mg for a 60 kg adult. Notably, the shorter nasal passages and proportionally greater olfactory epithelium in rodents also favour more direct access to the olfactory bulbs, whereas the human olfactory region is located in the superior nasal cavity, 4 – 7 cm from the nostrils. The longer and more compartmentalised human nasal cavity, differences in airflow dynamics and mucociliary clearance, and greater inter‐individual variability in nasal anatomy are therefore likely to influence deposition patterns, residence time and overall CNS exposure to LNP‐mRNA formulations. These species differences, together with variation in nasal microbiota, epithelial‐barrier properties and immune tone, mean that dose, frequency and device design optimised in rodents cannot be directly extrapolated to humans. Moreover, the larger human brain and greater anatomical separation between nasal entry sites and deep targets mean that rodent studies may overestimate the efficiency of delivery to distal regions in patients. It is worth noting, however, that multiple groups have shown efficacy in brain delivery with intranasal administration in primates and humans [, , , ].

While our findings provide proof‐of‐concept that intranasal LNP‐mRNA can increase BDNF levels across multiple brain regions in mice, they do not permit reliable prediction of human regional BDNF concentration gradients or deep‐brain exposure. Regions closest to olfactory and trigeminal entry pathways, including the olfactory bulb and ventral frontal/olfactory cortical areas, may be the most plausible initial targets, whereas delivery of mRNA‐encoded protein cargo to the entorhinal cortex or deep hippocampal and associative cortical regions remains uncertain and will require dedicated biodistribution and PK/PD studies in larger‐brained species.

Lastly, optimisation of both the mRNA and LNP components could enhance therapeutic outcomes. mRNA modifications such as codon optimisation and reduction of secondary structure can increase mRNA yield and prolong expression []. 5’ and 3’ UTR engineering can also influence mRNA stability and translation [, ] and promote expression in specific cell types []. LNP modifications such as ApoE‐binding ligands and alternative lipid compositions could further refine cellular uptake and distribution or allow the LNP itself to enter the brain []. Nonetheless, the mRNA‐LNP formulation used in this study permits efficient delivery to the olfactory and respiratory epithelium and produces substantial cognitive improvements in both aged animals and an AD mouse model. While future refinements may further enhance this system, the current formulation already exhibits surprisingly robust effects.

Taken together, these findings establish intranasal LNP‐mRNA delivery as a versatile and non‐invasive platform with broad therapeutic potential. Beyond BDNF, this approach may be applicable to diverse CNS diseases, offering a promising pathway toward future neuro‐regenerative therapies.

Templates encoding the coding sequences of mRNA therapeutics were purchased as gBlocks (IDT, Integrated DNA Technologies). Sequences were restriction enzyme cloned into a T7‐driven mRNA expression plasmid, based on the Pfizer‐BioNTech vaccine backbone and assembled plasmid sequences confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Verified plasmids were linearised by BspQ1 restriction enzyme (NEB, #R0712L) digestion and mRNA synthesised by in vitro transcription using the HiScribe T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit (NEB, E2080L), including a 5’ cap CleanCap Reagent AG. mRNA for in vitro use was generated using standard UTP. mRNA for in vivo use was generated using N1‐Methylpseudouridine‐5’‐Triphosphate (TriLink BioTechnologies, N‐1081). Any residual DNA template was removed using DNase I (37°C, 15 min). mRNA was precipitated using LiCl (NEB, E2040S) and mRNA quantity and quality assessed using a Nanodrop.

In vitro transcribed mRNA was encapsulated into LNPs for delivery to mice. LNP‐mRNA was made up to the following composition: 47.5% ALC‐0315, 10% DSPC Helper lipid, 40.5% Cholesterol, 1.8% ALC‐0159 (PEG) and 0.2% DiR dye in a microfluidic mixer (NanoAssemblrTM IgniteTM nanoparticle formulation system, Cytiva) and at a target molar ratio of 6:1 (cationic lipid:mRNA). The LNP‐mRNA solution was exchanged for 10x volume 0.01M Tris buffer using Amicon Ultra‐15 Centrifugal filters (Millipore, UFC903008) and centrifuged (2000 g) to remove ethanol. Processed LNP‐mRNA complexes were stored in 0.01M Tris and 10% (w/vol) sucrose. Encapsulation efficiencies were assessed using the Quant‐iTTM RiboGreen RNA assay (Invitrogen, R11490). The size, uniformity and zeta potential of LNPs was determined using a Zetasizer (Malvern Panalytical).

HEK293T or SH‐SY5Y cells were transfected with mRNA using LipofectamineTM MessengerMaxTM Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen, LMRNA001), according to the manufacturer's instructions.

BDNF protein levels in cell culture media supernatants were quantified using the Total BDNF Quantikine ELISA kit (In Vitro Technologies, DBNT00), according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Anti‐PEG antibody levels were assessed in the sera of treated animals using the Mouse anti‐PEG IgG ELISA kit (Creative Diagnostics, DEIA6159), according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Inflammatory cytokines were assessed in the sera of treated animals using IL‐33 (Abcam, Ab213475), IFNγ (Abcam, Ab282874) and IL‐6 (Abcam, Ab222503) ELISA kits, according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Mice were lightly anaesthetised using 2.5% isoflurane and 1% O2. Mice were gently scruffed and 5 µl mRNA‐LNP, containing 0.5 µg mRNA was administered dropwise to each nostril (1.0 µg mRNA in 10 µl total volume) using a P20 pipette.

Total RNA was extracted from the olfactory bulb, respiratory epithelium and olfactory epithelium of LNP‐mRNA treated mice using the Isolate II RNA Mini Kit (Bioline, BIO‐52073), following the manufacturer's instructions. RNA (100 ng) was used as a template for cDNA synthesis using the iScript cDNA synthesis kit (Biorad, #1708891) according to the manufacturer's instructions. RTqPCR was performed in a 384‐well plate using a QuantStudioTM 6 Real‐Time PCR machine (ThermoFisher) using the following primers:

Bdnf F 5’ CATGAAGGCGCACTCCGAC 3’

Bdnf R 5’ GCCTTTGGATACCGGGACTTT 3’

Gapdh F 5’ TTCACCACCATGGAGAAGGC 3’

Gapdh R 5’ CCCTTTTGGCTCCACCCT 3’

Samples were run using the following cycling conditions: Initial hold (50°C, 2 min), 40x cycles (95°C, 15 sec; 60°C, 1 min; 72°C, 1 min) and melt curve analysis (72°C, 2 min; 95°C 1 min; 60°C 1 min). Data was analysed using the 2−ΔΔCT method [].

Freshly dissected brain tissue from mBdnf or Gfp LNP‐mRNA‐treated animals was dissociated into a single cell suspension using a tissue homogeniser in RIPA buffer (1% (vol/vol) Triton‐X 100, 0.1% (w/vol) SDS, 1% (w/vol) sodium deoxycholate, 10 mM Tris‐HCl pH 7.5, made up in H2O) containing 1x cOmpleteTM EDTA‐free protease inhibitors (Merck, 1187358001). Samples were incubated at 4°C for 10 min on a roller and centrifuged (10,000 g, 10 min) to remove cellular debris. The supernatant was transferred to fresh tubes. Total protein concentrations were determined using a PierceTM BCA Protein Assay kit (ThermoFisher, #23225) according to the manufacturer's instructions. A total of 20 µg protein per sample was loaded onto a 4–20% Tris‐Glycine SDS‐PAGE gel (Bio‐Rad, #4561094), electrophoresed and transferred onto a nitrocellulose membrane (LI‐COR, 926–31092). Membranes were blocked in TBS‐based Intercept Blocking Buffer (LICOR, NC1660550) and incubated O/N at 4°C with primary antibodies against BDNF (Invitrogen, PA5‐85730; 1:500) and alpha tubulin (Abcam, Ab7291; 1:1000). Following TBST washes, membranes were incubated for 1 h at RT IRDye 800CW Goat anti‐rabbit IgG and IRDye 680RD Goat anti‐mouse IgG at 1:10,000. Membranes were washed, imaged using the Odyssey Infrared Imaging System (LI‐COR) and analysed using Image Studio software (LI‐COR)

Hippocampi from 12‐month‐old C57Bl/6 mice were isolated under a dissecting microscope. Tissue was incubated with AccutaseTM (Stemcell, #07922) for 30 min on ice, followed by 10 min at 37°C and mechanically dissociated using a pipette. Dissociated tissue was passed through a 70 µm cell strainer (Corning, 431751) into cell culture plates containing NeuroCultTM proliferation media (Stemcell, #05702), supplemented with 800 ng/ml Heparin (Stemcell, #07980), 20 ng/ml EGF (Stemcell, #78006.1) and 20 ng/ml FGF (Stemcell, #78003.1). Cells were grown as free‐floating neurospheres in 37°C and 5% CO2. Cells were passaged every 5–7 days using AccutaseTM and replated at 10,000 cells/cm2.

SH‐SY5Y cells were grown at 37°C in 5% CO2 in DMEM/F12 (Gibco, 11320033) supplemented with 1x GlutaMAXTM (35050061), 1% (vol/vol) penicillin‐streptomycin (Gibco, 15140122) and 10% (vol/vol) FBS. Cells were passaged using TrypLE and replated at 10,000 cells/cm2.

SH‐SY5Y cells were differentiated as described [], with minor modifications. Briefly, cells were seeded at 50% confluency onto poly‐D‐lysine (Gibco, A3890401) and laminin (Sigma, L2020) coated chamber slides (Merck, Z734756) in DMEM/F12 (Gibco, 11320033) supplemented with 1x GlutaMAXTM (35050061), 1% (vol/vol) penicillin‐streptomycin (Gibco, 15140122) and 10% (vol/vol) FBS. The following morning media was replaced with conditioned media from HEK293T cells transfected with mBdnf or Gfp mRNA in Stage I media (DMEM/F12, 1x GlutaMAXTM, 1% (vol/vol) penicillin‐streptomycin, 2.5% (vol/vol) FBS and 10 µM retinoic acid. Cells were cultured for 5 days before media was replaced with Stage II conditioned media (Neurobasal‐A (Gibco, 10888022), 20 mM KCl, 1x B27TM (Gibco,17504044), 1x GlutaMAXTM, and 1% (vol/vol) penicillin‐streptomycin with or without 50 ng/ml recombinant BDNF (Gibco, 450‐02)). Cells were cultured for an additional 5 days before downstream staining and analysis.

For histological analysis, mice were perfusion fixed with PBS followed by 4% (w/v) PFA (Sigma, P6148). Brains were dissected and post‐fixed for 24 h in 4% PFA (w/v) at 4°C on a roller. Brain tissue was mounted in 2% (w/v) low gelling temperature agarose (Merck, A9414) and stored at 4°C until sectioning using a Vibratome (Leica). 30 µm coronal sections were blocked and permeabilised in 0.03% (vol/vol) Triton‐X 100 and 10% (vol/vol) FCS or 10% NGS (Invitrogen, 500622) for 1 h at RT and incubated O/N at 4°C in 10% FCS containing primary antibodies. The following morning sections were washed in PBS (3×5 min washes) and incubated with species‐specific secondary antibodies for 1 h at RT. Sections were washed, incubated with DAPI for 10 min at RT, washed and mounted onto SuperfrostTM slides (Bio‐Strategy Pty Limited, EPBRSF41296SP) in ProLongTM Diamond antifade mounting medium (Invitrogen, P36962).
