For assessment of nasal inflammation, mice were perfusion fixed as described above and skulls fixed in 4% (w/v) PFA (Sigma, P6148) overnight at 4°C on a roller. Skulls were decalcified in 0.5 M EDTA (Promega, V4231) for 14 days, followed by graded ethanol dehydration (30%, 50% and 70% overnight). Skulls were paraffin embedded and 10 µm sections cut on a microtome. Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on deparaffinized slides with Harris haematoxylin for 30s. Slides were rinsed in water, differentiated in acid alcohol with 10 rapid dips to remove excess staining and washed in water. Sections were blued in Scott's bluing solution for ∼8 sec, washed in water for 3 min and briefly rinsed in 70% (vol/vol) ethanol for 30 s before counterstaining twice in eosin. Following staining slides were dehydrated through graded ethanol, cleared in two changes of xylene for 2 min each and mounted. Sections were imaged using a 3DHistech Slide Scanner (3DHistech).

Confocal images were acquired using a Marianas 3i spinning disk or Leica TCS SP8 STED confocal microscope. 20–40 µm Z‐stacks were acquired at 0.34 µm (40x magnification) or 0.78 µm (20x magnification) steps. Maximum Intensity Projections were generated and analysed in Image J (Version 2.16.0/1.54j). Cell numbers were quantified on auto‐thresholded images using the ‘Analyze Particles’ function. DCX+ neuron neurite analysis was performed using the NeuronJ plugin.

SH‐SY5Y neurite analysis was performed using AutoNeuriteJ.

GFAP and Iba1‐positive cell counts were quantified in Fiji/ImageJ. Fluorescence channels were thresholded to generate binary masks and combined with the corresponding DAPI channel using the Image Calculator AND operation. Cells were quantified from the resulting binary images using the Analyse Particles function with matched thresholding and particle‐size parameters applied across all samples.

This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines set out in the Australian Code for the Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes. All experiments were conducted with approval of The University of Sydney Animal Ethics Committee (2024/AE002511 and 2025/AE000223). Mice were housed 2–5 to a cage with standard cage enrichments and provided with food and water ad libitum. Mice were housed in ventilated cages on a 12‐hr light/dark cycle.

For behavioral testing, light levels were standardised at 100 lux using a lux meter (Lutron LM‐81LX, S041136) and the temperature maintained at 22°C. Behavioral tests were performed in the light phase of the light‐dark cycle and only one test was performed per day. Prior to testing all mice were habituated to the operator and habituated to the room for at least 30 min prior to testing. All mice were returned to their home cage following testing. Animals were recorded from above using a webcam (WebCam C615 (Logitech; Lausanne, Switzerland) and data analysed using Any‐maze software (ANY‐maze, Version 7.20).

The open field was performed as described []. Each mouse was placed into a 40 × 40 cm square arena with 30cm high black walls. Mice were allowed to freely explore for 10 min and ambulation assessed and the proportion of time spent at the periphery of the arena was used as a measurement of anxiety.

The novel object recognition test was performed as described [, ]. Briefly, each mouse was placed into a 40cm2 square arena with 30cm high black walls. In session 1 animals were given two identical objects and allowed to freely explore for 10 min. Animals were returned to their home cage for 2 h. Upon returning to the arena, one of the objects from session 1 was replaced with a novel object in session 2. Animals were allowed to freely explore for 10 min. The ratio of time spent with the novel versus familiar object in session 2 was used to assess recognition memory.

Two tests were performed in the Y maze, as described []. In both tests each mouse was placed into a Y shaped maze with three arms at 120° to each other. Each arm was 30 cm long, 5 cm wide and 20 cm high. Visual cures were placed at the end of each arm to assist with spatial orientation. Animals began both tests in the ‘home arm’. The other two arms were defined as arm A and B. In the Y maze for working memory animals were allowed to freely explore the maze for 5 min. The sequence of entries into each arm was assessed, with one ‘spontaneous alternation’ defined as a mouse having entered each of the three arms within three consecutive arms entries. The proportion of spontaneous alternations was defined as the number of alternations/(total number of arm entries – 2) and used as a measurement of working memory.

In the Y maze for spatial memory, in session 1, each mouse was placed into the Y maze with either arm A or B blocked from entry (novel arm). Animals were allowed to freely explore the remaining two arms for 10 min. Animals were returned to their home cage for 2 h. Upon return to the Y maze all arms were open, and animals were allowed to freely explore for 5 min. The time spent in the previously closed ‘novel arm’ compared to the familiar arm, was used as a readout of spatial memory.

All statistical analysis was performed in Prism Graphpad (version 10.4.0). Statistical tests used and the number of replicates per experiment are described in the figure legends.

medicine.title: Contrasting Patterns of Seascape Genetics in Acropora cf. tenuis and Their Symbiotic Algae
medicine.abstract: Theory suggests that pairs of mutualist species will often co‐disperse and share the same dispersal patterns, though the extent to which this happens remains unclear. Photosynthetic corals constitute an example of this dynamic, as they rely on algal symbionts to meet their energetic needs, yet many acquire their symbionts environmentally after their larval dispersal phase. Consequently, corals and their symbionts may exhibit similar or contrasting patterns of genetic variation across the seascape, with implications for their evolutionary and ecological processes. Here, we densely sample corals of the key reef‐building taxon Acropora cf. tenuis and their algal symbionts across a reefscape in the central Philippines to examine genetic variation across space. Four distinct coral taxa show genetic evidence of long‐distance dispersal, including weak or absent isolation by distance signals and parent‐offspring pairs at widely spaced sites. These coral taxa all host a single group of algal symbionts from the genus Cladocopium, which shows landscape genetic structure independent from its coral hosts. In fact, Cladocopium genetics vary with both latitude and depth, potentially indicating genome‐wide local adaptation at a finer spatial scale than that seen in their hosts. Genetic variation at markedly different spatial scales between host and symbiont may be beneficial for hosts if these differences enable them to acquire symbionts adapted to their settlement environments.
medicine.text:
The spatial scale of genetic variation differs widely between species, from globally panmictic dragonflies to tuataras that exhibit genetic structuring on the sub‐kilometre scale (Moore et al. ; Troast et al. ). These contrasting patterns stem partially from differences in dispersal. Longer dispersal distances can lead to higher connectivity and more homogeneity between sites, blunting the effects of drift and inbreeding for smaller populations. Shorter dispersal may enable spatial heterogeneity and local adaptation as populations evolve to tolerate their immediate environment (Slatkin ). However, patterns of genetic variation may also be driven by co‐dispersal among closely associated species, such as mutualistic pairs or host‐microbe holobionts. How dispersal shapes landscape genetic structure in such associations remains poorly understood (Hand et al. ).

Some theorists have suggested that the evolution of mutualisms should rely heavily on parent to child transmission of symbiotic partners, and therefore codispersal of the mutualist pair (Ewald ). This is certainly true in some cases. A wide variety of terrestrial plants, for example, transmit their mycorrhizal partners directly from parent to offspring (Johnston‐Monje et al. ; Laurent‐Webb et al. ). However, the real world provides contradictory examples, including the many species of corals that acquire their algal obligate symbionts environmentally, a situation that some authors have described as a “paradox” (Hartmann et al. ). Environmental acquisition of mutualist symbionts occurs across taxa, and is especially common in the marine realm, including in many species of corals (Russell ). Photosynthetic corals play critical roles in maintaining global biodiversity and human wellbeing, and depend on algal symbionts for their nutrition and survival (Fisher et al. ; Mellin et al. ). While corals and symbionts form obligate mutualist associations, they can disperse separately, making them an ideal study system to understand the extent to which mutualists show similar patterns of dispersal.

Most reef‐building corals depend on photosynthetic algae living within their tissues to produce up to 95% of the carbohydrates they need to survive (Muscatine and Cernichiari ). These algal symbionts belong to multiple genera, and individual corals can acquire symbionts in one of two ways. “Brooding” species of corals often transmit their symbionts vertically from parent to offspring, producing larger larvae that carry their own symbionts. By contrast, most “broadcast” spawning corals release gametes directly into the water column, where they form smaller larvae that acquire symbionts from the environment post‐settlement (Harii et al. ). The second life history strategy, employed by corals of the genus Acropora, leads to the potential for corals and their algal symbionts to exhibit different patterns of genetic variation across space (Boutet and Schierwater ). However, the extent to which corals and their symbionts show similar or disparate patterns of dispersal remains unclear.

Fortunately, population genetic methods allow direct observation of patterns of spatial genetic variation, as well as indirect inference about dispersal through isolation by distance methods (Pinsky et al. ). For example, analyses of 
Stylophora pistillata
 and 
Pocillopora verrucosa
 on the Great Barrier Reef found far higher cross‐reef connectivity and genetic homogeneity in the latter species, with estimated mean dispersal distances of 2100 to 5200 m in 
P. verrucosa
 but just 23 to 102 m in 
S. pistillata
 (Meziere et al. ). Algal symbionts of corals may or may not show the same level of connectivity as their hosts. Some evidence shows algal symbionts exhibiting genetic differentiation at finer spatial scales than their coral hosts (Davies et al. ). This could imply consistent differences in both connectivity and local adaptation between corals and their symbionts. Estimating dispersal kernel spreads from isolation by distance (IBD) relationships requires an effective population size, which cannot be estimated from linkage disequilibrium methods for haploid organisms such as algal symbionts (Rousset ; Santos and Coffroth ; Waples et al. ). However, comparing the significance of IBD relationships between taxa can still reveal important differences in the extent to which geography structures genetic variation (Jenkins et al. ). Our limited understanding of how landscape genetic patterns differ between corals and their algal symbionts is especially critical for corals of the genus Acropora. This keystone genus of branching corals associates with a variety of algal symbiont strains acquired environmentally after their larval dispersal phase (Cumbo et al. ). All species of Acropora are broadcast spawners, and their asymbiotic larvae drift in the water column for days to weeks before settling (Nishikawa et al. ). Acropora in the Indo‐Pacific, including the Philippines, mostly associate with symbionts from genus Cladocopium, though they can also associate with symbionts of other genera (Davies et al. ; Matias et al. ; Matsuda et al. ; Torres et al. ). Acropora are sensitive to heat waves and face a growing threat from anthropogenic climate change (Pratchett et al. ). In addition, some Acropora populations exhibit local genetic adaptation to higher temperatures at both the regional and intra‐reef scales, as do their algal symbionts (Howells et al. ; McClanahan et al. ; Thomas et al. ). Consequently, understanding Acropora landscape genetics matters for applied conservation questions concerning connectivity, reserve design, and adaptation to anthropogenic change (Arafeh‐Dalmau et al. ).

Here, we examine landscape genomic patterns of Acropora cf. tenuis and its algal symbionts in the central Philippines to test whether host and symbiont exhibit congruent or disparate dispersal patterns. The samples for this study are from the Philippines, which is situated within the Coral Triangle, known as the global epicentre of marine biodiversity (Veron et al. ). While our samples were morphologically identified as Acropora tenuis, recent research on the Great Barrier Reef has revealed at least three sympatrically occurring but non‐interbreeding cryptic species within corals previously identified as 
A. tenuis
 (Matias et al. ). Research at broader spatial scales has found additional divergence, with some authors suggesting that true 
A. tenuis
 does not exist in the Philippines (Bridge et al. ).

Our spatially dense sampling took place along two different 200 km stretches of reefscape on Cebu and Leyte islands, which facilitated assessment of isolation by distance patterns. Prior study of multiple species of reef‐dwelling anemonefish across this same seascape found clear isolation by distance patterns and estimated dispersal kernel spreads on the order of 10 km (Catalano et al. ; Fitz et al. ; Pinsky et al. ). Here, we test for similar patterns in Acropora cf. tenuis and its algal symbionts. Specifically, we examined whether (1) specific algal symbiont genotypes associated with specific A. cf. tenuis host genotypes and (2) host and symbionts showed similar or contrasting degrees of genetic isolation by distance. Ultimately, we aimed to unpack the interacting relationships between genetic variation in corals, genetic variation in their algal symbionts, and physical location in space.

Field sampling was conducted from January to April 2016 across 47 sites in the Visayas region of the central Philippines, including areas surrounding the Camotes Sea and Cebu Strait. Sites were distributed across Cebu Province, including Cebu Island (n = 27 sites) and the Camotes Islands (n = 5), as well as Leyte Province (n = 15). Sites were selected to be approximately 10 km apart to capture ecologically relevant dispersal distances and enable testing for isolation by distance patterns in the study region (Figure ).

At each site, we characterized benthic cover using line point intercept transects. Three 15 m transects were deployed haphazardly parallel to shore, and the bottom type was recorded at 20 cm intervals along each transect. Following benthic surveys, we conducted a separate belt transect survey at each site by swimming parallel to shore within a 2 m wide belt for approximately 1 h or until 20 samples were collected. During these surveys, we measured the maximum length, width, and depth of every A. cf. tenuis colony encountered and recorded the time of collection. We collected small tissue samples (approximately 2 cm × 2 cm) from 20 colonies per site, ensuring that sampled colonies were spaced at least 10 m apart to avoid resampling the same genet. A towed GPS unit was used to record the coordinates of each sampled colony. If fewer than 20 samples were obtained during the initial survey, an additional dive was conducted to complete the target sample size (depth information was not collected during these additional dives).

Acropora cf. tenuis specimens were identified in the field based on morphological characteristics described in Veron's “Corals of the World” (Veron ). Key characteristics used for identification included: (1) colony growth form characterized by corymbose clumps, (2) long and tubular axial corallites, and (3) neatly arranged and slightly flaring radial corallites. Field identification focused on the combination of branching pattern, corallite structure, and overall colony architecture rather than relying on any single morphological trait. Detailed close‐up photographs were taken of each collected specimen and are available at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.sf7m0cgnr.

In total, we collected 258 samples during initial surveys and 394 samples on additional dives. Tissue samples were preserved in 95% ethanol for genetic analysis. All samples were collected under Gratuitous Permit 0129‐17 and transported to the United States under CITES export permit 4733. The Texas A&M Corpus Christi Genomics Core Laboratory performed all DNA extraction using an Omega E‐Z 96 tissue DNA kit, as well as double digest restriction‐site associated DNA sequencing (ddRadSeq) library preparation (Peterson et al. ), and sequencing. After attempted library preparation using SbfI and MluCI failed to produce sequenceable libraries, we then used the enzymes SphI and EcoRI and targeted fragment sizes of 500–600 basepairs. All sample libraries from the second round of preparations were pooled and then sequenced across two Illumina HiSeq4000 2 × 150 bp lanes to mitigate the possibility of variation introduced by lane effects.

We did initial quality control and 3′ read trimming with FastP version 0.23.4 (Chen et al. ), visualized the results with MultiQC (Ewels et al. ), de‐duplicated and compressed the read files with the Clumpify function from BBtools version 39.06, re‐ran FastP for 5′ read trimming, and re‐paired unpaired reads with BBtools (Bushnell ). We parallelized analysis with GNU Parallel version 20,200,122 (Tange ). Full scripts with parameters are available on Github at https://github.com/pinskylab/Atenuis_Philippines (to be replaced with a Zenodo DOI upon manuscript acceptance). The pre‐processing scripts were developed from Bird (). We then mapped the trimmed reads to genomes from 
Acropora tenuis
 (Shinzato et al. ), Cladocopium goreaui (Martin‐Cuadrado et al. ), Durusdinium trenchii (Dougan et al. ), and Symbiodinium kawagutii (Martin‐Cuadrado et al. ), all downloaded from NCBI, using BWA version 0.7.17 (Li and Durbin ). The ‘
Acropora tenuis
’ genome assembly available on NCBI comes from Japan and is therefore unlikely to represent true 
A. tenuis
 (Bridge et al. ). Given the broad taxonomic uncertainty and extensive presence of cryptic species within Acropora cf. tenuis, this genome likely represents a congener to our samples, rather than a conspecific. Consequently, we also mapped reads to genomes from 
A. gemmifera
 (Shinzato et al. ), 
A. muricata
 (State Key Lab for Bioelectroincs ), and 
A. selago
 (Shinzato et al. ) for comparison. Across individuals, a median of 41,236.5 reads, or 74% of total reads, mapped to the 
Acropora tenuis
 genome from NCBI. Lower percentages of reads (68% ‐ 69%) mapped to the other Acropora genomes. A median of 14,424.5 reads, or 15% of the total, successfully mapped to the Cladocopium goreaui genome, 2771 reads (2.4% of total) mapped to the Symbiodinium kawagutii genome, and 1447 reads (1.5% of total) mapped to the Durusdinium trenchii genome.

After sorting and indexing the resulting bamfiles with Samtools version 1.20 (Li et al. ), we called SNPs using FreeBayes version 1.3.10 (Garrison and Marth ), resulting in 2,491,826 Acropora SNPs across 652 individuals and 596,153 Cladocopium SNPs across 644 individuals. Nearly all individuals showed substantial missing data, with 184 (28%) of individuals showing more than 99.9% missing data after selecting only loci with a minimum quality score of > 30 and a minimum depth of > 3. More than half of individuals (359, 55%) were missing more than 90% of possible SNPs. We iteratively filtered SNPs and individuals using functions from vcftools and vcflib (Danecek et al. ; Garrison et al. ), in order to preserve the maximum number of each, as described in O'Leary et al. (). Ultimately, we retained all SNPs present in at least 85% of individuals and all individuals with at least 50% non‐missing data. After quality filtering, we were left with 2269 SNPs and 301 individuals in the Acropora assemblies, and 2059 SNPs and 310 individuals in the Cladopium assemblies. We pruned SNPs for physical linkage using Plink2 by examining SNPs across a 50 bp window size and pruning those with r
2 > 0.5 (Chang et al. ). This process left us with 1838 SNPs in Acropora and 873 SNPs in Cladocopium. To further verify our results, we created a second, higher quality dataset with all SNPs present in at least 85% of individuals and all individuals with at least 90% non‐missing data. This dataset included 238 individuals and 1846 SNPs after linkage pruning.

We also verified our key results using a separate pipeline based on ANGSD (Korneliussen et al. ). After excluding only samples with > 99% missing data, we used ANGSD to calculate Identity by State (IBS) matrices for the remaining (N = 390) samples using the—doIBS function. IBS is assumption‐free, robust to variation in coverage and sequencing depth between samples, and only requires SNPs to be repeatable between at least two individuals (Matz and Black ). For the ANGSD pipeline, we retained all SNPs with a minimum quality score of 20 and a minimum map quality of 25.

We calculated distance to shore for each sample using the global shorelines dataset from OpenStreetMap, downloaded on March 28, 2025 (OpenStreetMap contributors ).

A. tenuis
 was traditionally believed to be a common coral species across shallow reefs in the western Pacific ocean and Red Sea. However, recent research has suggested it comprises at least 11 morphologically similar but evolutionary distinct species (Bridge et al. ; Veron ). Multiple species of 
A. tenuis
 lookalikes have been identified co‐occurring on the same reefs in Australia, Okinawa, and the South Pacific (Bridge et al. ; Matias et al. ; Zayasu et al. ). While some of these A. cf. tenuis populations have been provisionally reassigned to new nominal species, those in Southeast Asia (including the Philippines) have so far only been defined as Acropora sp(p). The authors of a recent taxonomic revision note that this should be considered “an unresolved clade requiring further sampling and analysis” (Bridge et al. ). Here we refer to our samples as Acropora cf. tenuis to reflect both the species' traditional classification and current taxonomic uncertainty.

We determined the number of genetic clusters within the fully filtered Acropora SNP data using a Discriminant Analysis of Principal Components (DAPC) including the top 500 principal components, to capture the maximum amount of variation, as recommended by the package authors (Jombart and Collins ). We determined the optimal solution by comparing Bayesian Information Criteria (BIC) for all solutions between 1 and 16 clusters. We calculated principal components eigenvectors and eigenvalues using Plink2 version 2.00a5.10 in order to visualize these clusters in PCA space and quantify the percent of genetic variation accounted for by each principal component. We also examined the top three principal components for linear correlation with latitude, longitude, distance to shore, and depth. We repeated all cluster assignments using the low missingness (< 10% missingness) dataset to confirm that cluster assignments were not driven by missing data, and re‐ran ADMIXTURE with this dataset to confirm that the analysis converged on the same number of ancestry groups. We further verified these results using a hierarchical clustering dendrogram of the Identity by State distances, generated using the ‘hclust’ function from the R package Vegan version 2.7‐6 (Oksanen et al. ).

We quantified genetic distance between clusters by calculating FSTs between groups using the Hierfstat R package version 1.1.10 (Goudet ). We then reshuffled all individuals between each pair of taxa and recalculated the FST 1000 times in order to simulate a null distribution of genetic distances. To assign statistical significance to the pairwise genetic distance between clusters, we compared each observed between‐group FST to its simulated null distribution and calculated the percentile of the null distribution greater than the observed FST.

We also evaluated ancestry for each individual sample using ADMIXTURE version 1.3.0 and all possible numbers of ancestry groups between 1 and 16 using a cross validation procedure (Alexander et al. ). This approach found ancestry groups that corresponded closely to the genetic groups found by the DAPC. Given these consistent differences and the substantial genetic differentiation between these groups despite their broadly overlapping ranges (see Results), we referred to these groupings as “taxa,” which we numbered arbitrarily one through four with the most individuals assigned to cluster one and the fewest assigned to cluster four. We used the DAPC to assign each Acropora individual to a genetic cluster, and re‐filtered SNP data separately within each cluster (Section ). We used slightly different iterations of SNP and individual removal, but with the same final cutoffs as described above. After pruning, we ended with 116 individuals and 2308 SNPs in Taxon 1, 69 individuals and 1689 SNPs in Taxon 2, 57 individuals and 1221 SNPs in Taxon 3, and 53 individuals with 1213 SNPs in Taxon 4. We identified potential clones using the KING coefficient calculated in Plink2 using a cutoff of 0.354 (McMaster et al. ).

We used non‐parametric Kruskal‐Wallis tests in R to test for differences in mean latitude, depth, and distance to shore between genetic clusters. We calculated isolation by distance (IBD) patterns for each genetic group individually in accordance with Sheets et al. (). We assessed isolation by distance in both one dimension (along the coast of Cebu) and two dimensions (all sites together). We did not analyse one‐dimensional patterns along the coast of Leyte because of insufficient coral samples along that coastline. We calculated pairwise linearized FST and the pairwise geographic distance between each pair of sampling sites, a methodology that has been previously validated for estimating dispersal (Pinsky et al. ). Only sites with at least two individuals were considered for FST calculations. For the two‐dimensional IBD assessment, we took the natural logarithm of these distances, following the equation for isolation by distance in two dimensions (Rousset ). Mantel tests were conducted comparing the genetic and geographic distance matrices using the Vegan package. In order to compare the strength of IBD relationships between taxa, we calculated confidence intervals around regression slopes by using the standard error of the regression slope as the standard deviation for 1000 normally distributed slopes centered on the estimated regression coefficient. We then quantified the percentage of these resampled regression slopes that were greater than zero, indicating a positive relationship between geographic and genetic distance. We also evaluated calculated per‐taxon IBD slopes and standard errors using distances calculated from the individual‐level identity by state matrices, and quantified the percentage of those slopes that were greater than zero.

Finally, we identified putative parent/offspring pairs from Acropora SNP data using the GetMaybeRel() function of the Sequoia package version 3.0.3 in R with no age priors, assuming all individuals as hermaphrodites (Huisman ). We verified the identities of clones and first degree relatives using a dendrogram of the clustered IBS data as described in (Barfield et al. ).

To identify the taxonomic composition of the symbionts in our samples, we compared the percent of reads mapped to genomes from three common genera of algal symbionts (Cladocopium goreaui, Durusdinium trenchii, and Symbiodinium kawagutii). To identify environmental correlates of symbiont composition, we used Kruskal‐Wallis tests to compare the relative percentages of reads mapped from each individual to each genus to depth, distance to shore, latitude, island, and host coral genetic grouping. In nearly all individuals, by far the most reads mapped to the Cladocopium goreaui genome, leading us to proceed with further analysis for only these assemblies (see Supplemental Figure  for percent of reads mapping to each symbiont genome, Supplemental Table  for information on individual samples dominated by Durusdinium, and Supplemental Table  for individual samples dominated by Symbiodinium).

Similarly to Acropora, we used a DAPC and paired PCA to evaluate the number of genetic clusters and to visualize genetic groupings in PCA space. We found only one genetic cluster, and consequently did not subdivide our Cladocopium population for subsequent analyses.

We also ran an ADMIXTURE analysis for the Cladocopium genotypes using the—haploid flag, again evaluating all possible numbers of ancestry groups between 1 and 16 using cross‐validation. We assigned Cladocopium genomes to groups based on the taxon (1–4) of their Acropora host, calculated FSTs between those taxa, and calculated associated p‐values using the same resampling procedure for simulated null distributions described in Section . After SNP filtering, more individual samples were found with > 50% data present for the Cladocopium assemblies than for the Acropora assemblies, meaning that some (n = 10) Cladocopium samples could not be assigned to a specific taxon of host.

We used linear regression to compare the top three principal components of the Cladocopium genomes to latitude, longitude, distance to shore, and depth. We assessed isolation by distance in both one and two dimensions using a Mantel test from the Vegan package in R following the same methodology as described in Section . Confidence intervals around slopes were calculated similarly to the Acropora samples. To account for differences in sample size and geographic distribution of samples between the Acropora clusters and the full set of Cladocopium samples, we also evaluated isolation by distance patterns for Cladocopium within each genetic grouping of Acropora and reported distributions for those slopes as well. As above, we repeated this analysis using individual level Identity by State matrices.

Finally, we used two partial Mantel tests to evaluate the influence of geographic distance on genetic distance between Cladocopium populations while controlling for genetic distance between Acropora populations, as well as the influence of genetic distance between Acropora populations on the genetic distance between Cladocopium populations while controlling for geographic distance. We did not test for kin pairs within the Cladocopium samples, as they are haploid (Santos and Coffroth ). All analyses using R packages were performed using R version 4.4.1 and all Python analyses were performed in Python 3.9.25.

Our analysis revealed four distinct genetic clusters within the Acropora cf. tenuis genetic data. The four cluster solution resulted in the lowest BIC for the DAPC, closely followed by the five cluster solution (Supplemental Table ). Lowering the number of PCs below 200 resulted in the five cluster solution returning a slightly lower BIC than the four cluster solution, but we ultimately chose to retain four clusters for consistency with the ADMIXTURE results. With k = 4 clusters, all numbers of PCs > 3 resulted in identical cluster assignments. All of the cluster assignments in the low‐missingness subset were identical to the assignment using the full dataset, using both DAPC and ADMIXTURE. These clusters appear distinct in PCA space, with more than 50% of the genetic variation loading on the first two principal components. However, some intermediate individuals may represent hybrids (Figure ). Likewise, the ADMIXTURE analysis with four ancestry groups resulted in the lowest cross validation error, with the five ancestry groups in second place (Supplemental Table ). Most individuals showed a clearly dominant ancestry group, with 99% of individuals having more than half of their ancestry coming from a single group and 90% of individuals having at least 7/8th of their ancestry from a single group (Figure ). Representative photos for individuals of each genetic group can be seen in Supplemental Figure .

The ancestry groups found with the ADMIXTURE analysis corresponded well but imperfectly to the genetic clusters resolved by DAPC. The vast majority (298/301, 99%) of individuals assigned to a cluster by DAPC had greater than 1/2 ancestry fraction coming from that same cluster, and 90% (271/301) had at least 7/8 of their ancestry from that cluster. Cluster assignments using HClust also agreed for more than 98% of individuals (Supplemental Table  and Supplemental Figure ).

Pairwise FST comparisons between these genetic clusters ranged from 0.10 to 0.16 (Table ). For each pairwise comparison, the actual FST was higher than 100% of the simulated resamples with shuffled individuals.

These four genetic clusters were not separated in space. Each cluster occurred in at least 60% (26/43) of sampling sites and on both islands (Figure ). Taxa did appear somewhat structured by latitude (Kruskal‐Wallis test, p‐value = 0.00026, n = 301), with Taxon 2 having the highest median latitude (10.59°N) and Taxon 3 having the lowest (10.00°N). There was a marginally significant association between genetic grouping and average depth (Kruskal‐Wallis test, p‐value = 0.07, n = 97), with Taxon 1 having the greatest depth (4 m) and Taxon 4 having the lowest median depth (3 m). There was no association with distance to shore (Kruskal‐Wallis test, p‐value = 0.22, n = 301). We found no association between the number of genetic reads mapped per sample and taxon (Kruskall‐Wallis test p = 0.22, n = 301). Within taxa, principal components did not show strong associations with latitude or depth (Supplemental Figure ).

For two out of four taxa, there was on average a positive correlation between two‐dimensional geographic distance between populations in log meters and genetic distance in pairwise linearized FST. However, the correlations for Taxa 1 and 2 were negative, and all confidence intervals from resampling slopes overlapped with zero (Figure ). Moreover, none of the relationships between genetic distance and geographic distance were statistically significant (p < 0.05) when using a Mantel test (Supplemental Tables  and ). The strongest relationship, found in Taxon 4, was largely driven by three closely related individuals collected from sites at the north and south ends of Cebu, and excluding these individuals substantially reduced the percentage of positive IDB slopes in 1D for this taxon (Table ). These individuals collectively account for the high FST values seen in some pairwise comparisons (Figure ). Overall, a lack of strong IBD patterning suggests a high degree of genetic mixing within each cryptic Acropora taxon.

Pedigree analysis within the cryptic Acropora taxa found five putative parent/offspring pairs, or seven if both putatively clonal individuals at site CEB_01 were included (Supplemental Table ). All parent/offspring pairs were genotyped at a minimum of 1000 of the same SNPs and showed a minimum log likelihood ratio of 4, indicating that the paired individuals were 104 times more likely to represent parent/offspring pairs than they were to represent unrelated individuals. All of the pairs except for one also occurred in the low‐missingness dataset, and all of the pairs were also identified by HClust (Supplemental Figure ). Three of these pairs were defined as clones in the original clone scan with KING, and are marked in Figure  with a letter C. Nearly all of the pairs occurred at widely spaced sites (Figure ). These results suggest that long (> 50 km) dispersal distances are possible across a single generation.

We identified the vast majority of algal symbionts as the genus Cladocopium across all four Acropora taxa and 43 sites. More than 98% (644/652) of individual samples had a higher number of reads successfully map to the 
C. goreaui
 genome than either the D. trenchii or S. kawagutii genomes. Three individuals, two of which belonged to Taxon 1 and one of which belonged to Taxon 4, had the highest number of reads map to D. trenchii. One Acropora individual, which belonged to Taxon 1, had the highest number of reads map to S. kawagutii (Supplemental Tables  and ). There was no significant relationship between percent of reads mapped to a given genus of symbiont and host Acropora taxon (n = 298, all p > 0.5). Likewise, there was no significant association between relative number of reads mapping to different symbiont genera and either depth (Kruskal‐Wallis test, p = 0.71, n = 97) or distance to shore (Kruskal‐Wallis test, p = 0.13, n = 295). Finally, linear regression models for each symbiont genus found no association between percentage of symbiont reads mapping to that genus and sample depth (n = 97, all p > 0.3). Since Cladocopium was by far the dominant symbiont genus for this dataset, we proceeded analysing only symbiont DNA mapped to the 
C. goreaui
 genome. While our sampled Cladocopium are unlikely to belong to 
C. goreaui
 specifically, 
C. goreaui
 constitutes the only currently available genome assembly for the genus Cladocopium. Therefore, we refer to reads mapped to the 
C. goreaui
 genome by the more general term Cladocopium.

Cladocopium did not show the same genetic groupings as their Acropora hosts. Principal components and discriminant analysis of principal components did not reveal distinct genetic clusters within the Cladocopium SNP profiles (Figure ). The BIC for the DAPC was minimized by finding a single cluster, and BIC increased monotonically with the number of clusters up to at least 16 clusters (Supplemental Table ). ADMIXTURE resolved three ancestry groups within the Cladocopium, but these ancestry groups did not obviously correspond to those found in their Acropora hosts (Figure ). However, there was a noticeable structuring of ancestry with latitude (Figure ).

Based on this PCA, Cladocopium populations do show evidence for genetic structuring in space across both regional and microhabitat scales. The second principal component of the Cladocopium genomes had a significant linear relationship to latitude (linear regression, p = 0.00027, n = 310). Similarly, there is a significant relationship between the first principal component of the Cladocopium genomes and host coral depth (p = 0.000013, n = 107) (Supplemental Figure ).

Cladocopium populations associated with different Acropora cryptic taxa showed weak differentiation with extremely low FSTs. However, reshuffling individuals between taxa and recalculating FSTs of the associated Cladocopium populations reveals that while weak, some of these FSTs were significantly stronger than would be expected from random association (Table ).

Cladocopium showed more consistent patterns of genetic isolation by distance than did their coral hosts. Mantel tests found significant positive associations between pairwise linearized FST and geographic distance in one dimension along the coast of Cebu (p = 0.002, n = 23 sites) and between pairwise linearized FST and log geographic distance in two dimensions across the entire study area (p = 0.001, n = 36 sites). A higher percentage of the resampled slopes (99.7%) were positive than they were for any of the Acropora taxa, and the 95% confidence interval did not overlap with zero (Figure ). When we analysed IBD slopes for Cladocopium within each cryptic taxon separately to control for differences in sample size and geographic distribution of samples between Cladocopium and Acropora taxa, a higher percentage of IBD slopes were positive for the Cladocopium samples than for the Acropora samples in four out of four taxa for the one‐dimensional analysis, and in two out of four taxa for the two‐dimensional analysis (Table ). In the two‐dimensional analysis, a higher percentage of IBD slopes were positive for three out of four Cladocopium samples than for the Acropora samples after excluding one potential clone. For Taxon 3, both Cladocopium and Acropora resampled IBD slopes were positive for a large fraction of the draws, with a slightly higher percentage in Cladocopium for one‐dimensional analyses, and slightly higher for Acropora for two‐dimensional analyses (Table ). Results from the low‐missingness dataset showed similar patterns, with majority positive slopes for all Cladocopium groups, and more consistent IBD patterns in Cladocopium than Acropora for the two taxa with remaining sample sizes of n ≥ 10. Acropora showed stronger IBD patterns for Taxon 3 and Taxon 4 in this dataset, though the low number of remaining sites (< 7) means this result should be interpreted with caution (Supplemental Table ). IBD slopes using identity by state matrices were more consistently positive for all taxa than were IBD slopes using pairwise linearized FST. Since analysis using identity by state matrices relies on individual pairwise differences rather than the population‐level differences commonly used for dispersal analysis, the positive slope ratios calculated from these matrices are not directly comparable with results using pairwise linearized FST. Still, IBD slopes using identity by state distances were more likely to be positive for Cladocopium than Acropora in 6/8 analyses, and equally likely to be positive in the remaining two analyses (Supplemental Table ).

Geographic distance had a stronger influence on Cladocopium genetic similarity than did host Acropora genotype. A partial Mantel test assessing the relationship of FSTs between Cladocopium populations and FSTs between Acropora populations conditioned on geographic distance was not significant (p = 0.347, n = 36 sites). Conversely, a partial Mantel test of between‐population Cladocopium FSTs and geographic distance conditioned on Acropora between‐population FSTs was significant (p = 0.004, n = 36 sites).

This study used dense genetic sampling across a seascape to infer patterns of dispersal and, more broadly, spatial genetic variation in Acropora cf. tenuis corals and their algal symbionts. Unexpectedly, we found four genetically distinct but sympatrically distributed groups of Acropora within our sample. All of the taxa exhibited genetic patterns across the study area consistent with long‐distance dispersal, and we found putative parent/offspring pairs at widely spaced sites. However, all genetic clusters of Acropora hosted primarily a single type of algal symbiont belonging to the genus Cladocopium. Cladocopium genotypes were structured more strongly by geographic location rather than host genotype. When comparing dispersal across hosts and symbionts, the algal symbionts showed greater genetic structure in space than did their Acropora hosts.

Prior study of Acropora cf. tenuis suggests this species actually constitutes multiple morphologically similar species. In particular, the Acropora cf. tenuis group in Southeast Asia is poorly defined in terms of both genetics and morphology and may constitute multiple lineages (Bridge et al. ). Our results strongly support the existence of at least four sympatric genetic groups within Acropora cf. tenuis in the Philippines, along with some hybridization between those groups. Multiple analysis methods converged on four groups in our samples and assigned individual corals to groups with a high level of consistency, despite their lack of differentiation in space. Combining these lines of evidence, we consider these groups to be cryptic taxa, possibly constituting distinct members of a species complex. In particular, our ADMIXTURE results suggest limited interbreeding between the four ancestry groups, though the existence of mixed ancestry in some individuals implies that intermittent hybridization between these genetic clusters can occur.

Species definitions in Acropora are frequently ambiguous, with extensive hybridization between species (Ladner and Palumbi ; Wu et al. ). Closely related Acropora species may be best defined as “syngameons,” or groups of two or more related species that are genetically distinct, yet regularly interbreed (Ladner and Palumbi ). Given the apparently incomplete genetic separation of genetic groups within A. cf. tenuis individuals in our dataset, these populations may fit that definition. While prior studies of Acropora species complexes have found microhabitat differences associated with different cryptic taxa (Ladner and Palumbi ; Matias et al. ), we found only weak evidence of microhabitat differentiation between the cryptic taxa found here, defined in terms of depth and distance to shore. However, we had incomplete data on individual coral depths, which may have hindered our ability to observe such differentiation. Our results underscore the need for further study of Acropora taxonomy in the Philippines, which would allow us to uncover potentially differing distributions, ecological roles, and conservation needs of these previously conflated taxa.

Broadcast spawning corals, including Acropora, often show long distance connectivity through dispersal of their pelagic larvae. For example, a study of connectivity among 
Acropora austera
 populations in Mozambique found genetic near‐panmixia across a 384 km stretch of coastline (Duvane et al. ). A genetic study of 
A. hyacinthus
 and 
A. digitifera
 in Micronesia found isolation by distance patterns in both, but only on the spatial scale of thousands of kilometres (Davies et al. ). Research on 
Pocillopora verrucosa
, a coral belonging to a different genus but with a similar reproductive mode to Acropora, on the Great Barrier Reef estimated dispersal distances anywhere between 21 and 52 km using isolation by distance relationships to estimate dispersal kernel spread (Meziere et al. ).

Patterns of spatial genetic variation in each cryptic Acropora taxon studied here are consistent with long larval dispersal distances. We found no significant isolation by distance slopes in one or two dimensions despite dense sampling across 200 km. Confidence intervals for all slopes overlapped with zero, and resampling slopes resulted in substantial percentages with non‐positive slopes. For one taxon (Taxon 2), the best‐fit slope was less than zero. Taxon 4 also showed an average negative isolation by distance slope in the one‐dimensional analysis after excluding clones. All of this suggests minimal or no isolation by distance within the Acropora samples at 200 km scales. While still not significant, Taxon 3 had marginally stronger isolation by distance patterns than the other taxa, which may indicate shorter average dispersal in that taxon. However, this could also be due to lower effective population size.

Unlike the results presented here, multiple studies of reef fishes in this same area of the Philippines have found clear isolation by distance patterns, which were then used to estimate dispersal kernel spreads. A 2010 study of anemonefish 
Amphiprion clarkii
 across Cebu and Leyte found a dispersal kernel spread of 11 km, with a confidence interval of 4–27 km (Pinsky et al. ), with additional research showing that dispersal varied both seasonally and interannually (Catalano et al. ). A study in the sister taxon Amphiprion biaculeatus found a similar dispersal kernel spread of 8.9 km, with a confidence interval of 2.3–18.4 km (Fitz et al. ).

The lack of any consistent isolation by distance pattern in Acropora across exactly the same geography as that used in the Amphiprion studies suggests longer, and perhaps much longer, dispersal distances for Acropora corals than their co‐occurring reef fishes. Rousset () recommends a square sampling area for isolation by distance patterns of at least 10 times the dispersal distance of the study organism. In the case of this approximately 200 km by 100 km area, this guideline would suggest that clear isolation by distance patterns would have been apparent for dispersal distances of less than 10 to 20 km. The lack of such patterns suggests that Acropora dispersal may regularly exceed this threshold. Conversely, significant isolation by distance patterns in Cladocopium at the 200 km by 100 km scale suggest average dispersal distances below 20 km in this taxon.

Kinship analysis using multiple methods added further evidence to this hypothesis, finding six pairs of closely related individuals of Acropora separated by at least 45 km, and only one pair co‐occurring at the same site. While these distances are mostly long, they are not implausible given the oceanography of the area and the life history of broadcast spawning corals. Some of the distances between close kin pairs found here fall within the calculated range of dispersal kernel spread for Acropora taxa on the Great Barrier Reefs calculated by Meziere et al. (). Larvae of many Acropora species experience precompetency periods of three to 7 days before they are able to settle (Randall et al. ), and they may survive for 50 or even 100 days in the lab (Connolly and Baird ; Miller et al. ; Nishikawa and Sakai ). Dispersal models fit to genetic data suggest that dispersal times of more than 60 days are common in some Acropora species (Davies et al. ). Given that our study site exhibits mostly open coastlines, with surface current speeds that may exceed 0.5 m per second during the seasonal monsoons, we can expect these competency times to result in long‐distance larval transport (Catalano et al. ).

While three of these pairs were identified as possible clones by KING, this seems less plausible than close kin given known Acropora life history. Acropora do not produce asexual larvae and self‐fertilize only rarely (Boutet and Schierwater ; Willis et al. ). Clonal genotypes in other Acropora are most often found within a few meters of each other, as they are derived from physically fragmented adult corals (Howlett et al. ). However, some species of Acropora may be more prone to reproduction by fragmentation than others, and coral fragments have occasionally been documented to settle and grow after transportation by strong typhoons, such as those common in the Philippines (Anticamara and Tan ; Pipithkul et al. ). It is possible though unlikely that these putative clone pairs result from fragmentation during strong storms and subsequent cross‐island transportation.

Alternatively, coral polyps under acute stress occasionally detach themselves completely from the coral skeleton and form a “pseudo‐planula” in a process known as “polyp bailout”. These detached polyps can later settle in a new location and grow into a new colony. Polyp bailout was originally documented in the 1940s (incidentally, in a species of Acropora cf. tenuis), but remains an understudied process in coral ecology (Schweinsberg et al. ). Whether the related individuals in our dataset represent true clones or first degree relatives, our finding of closely related individuals at widely spaced sites provides strong evidence of long‐distance gene flow across a single generation.

Cladocopium taxonomy remains poorly resolved, with only a handful of formally recognized species out of potentially hundreds in nature (Butler et al. ; Davies et al. ). Some species of Cladocopium associate with specific coral hosts, especially but not exclusively hosts that transmit their symbionts vertically (Thornhill et al. ; Turnham et al. ). However, other named species of Cladocopium are generalists, found across thousands of kilometres and multiple hosts, including multiple species of Acropora (Butler et al. ). Extremely low FSTs between Cladocopium populations found in different coral taxa further imply that the taxonomic variation in our Acropora samples is not reflected in their algal symbionts. A study of co‐occurring Acropora cf. tenuis cryptic taxa on the Great Barrier Reef also found a common pool of Cladocopium symbionts between cryptic taxa (Matias et al. ). Similarly in our study, we find a single genetic grouping of Cladocopium shared between all Acropora taxa. While ADMIXTURE resolved three ancestry groups, all groups were present in all Acropora taxa, showing structure with geography (latitude) rather than host. Our finding of weakly significant genetic differentiation between Cladocopium in different Acropora taxa could imply some symbiont selectivity by coral hosts, or it could result from common environmental factors structuring both host taxon occurrence and Cladocopium genotype. For example, we found that the Acropora taxa exhibited slight latitudinal differences in their distributions, and we found that latitude structured genetic variation in Cladocopium as well. This finding could result from neutral variation across the seascape, or it could represent adaptive genetic differences relating to differences in temperature along the latitudinal gradient.

Studies of Acropora taxa on other reefs have also found genetic variation in symbionts that is structured by environmental factors separately from coral host genomes. Genetic variation of Cladocopium found in Acropora cf. humilis in the Coral Sea depends largely on environmental variables such as thermal stress, light attenuation, and latitude, and only very slightly on host genotype (Marzonie et al. ). 
Acropora hyacinthus
 in Palau host mostly Cladocopium, and the genomes of those Cladocopium vary both between reefs and with depth (Armstrong et al. ). However, studies in other Acropora taxa, including 
A. hyacinthus
 and 
A. digitifera
 in Micronesia, have found host specialization between different Cladocopium lineages (Davies et al. ). It is worth noting that all of the Acropora taxa in our study are likely closely related, as evidenced by the relatively low FSTs between the groups. Other co‐occurring Acropora species in the central Philippines may selectively host different lineages of Cladocopium, or even other symbiont genera. However, within this A. cf. tenuis species complex, genetic variation in algal symbionts appears to be more driven by geography and environment than host genetic variation. This result is consistent with the study of Acropora cryptic taxa on the Great Barrier Reefs, where a common pool of Cladocopium found across hosts nonetheless exhibited significant genetic variation with distance to shore (Matias et al. ).

In our study, Cladocopium exhibited significant isolation by distance patterning in both one and two dimensions. Resampled IBD slopes were more consistently positive than those found in Acropora, even when controlling for sample size, for all of the taxa in one dimension and for three of four taxa in two dimensions. Our Cladocopium samples also exhibited spatial genetic variation at fine scales, as evidenced by the strong correlation between the second principal component of the algal genomes and depth. Partial Mantel tests also revealed that genetic distance between Cladocopium populations depended on geographic distance, when controlling for genetic distance between Acropora populations more strongly than the inverse. All of these lines of evidence indicate that within these Acropora populations, geography and environment structure symbiont genetic variation more strongly than does the genome of the host.

Despite these differences in genetic structure, the relative dispersal distances in the two taxa are difficult to measure directly. The slope of the relationship between geographic and genetic distance is inversely related to dispersal kernel spread, with steeper slopes implying shorter dispersal distances (Rousset ). However, the slope is also inversely related to effective population size, with larger effective population sizes resulting in shallower slopes (Rousset ). Without effective population size estimates for these taxa, dispersal cannot be estimated. In addition, differences in effective population size could explain some of the differences that we observed. For example, the weakly steeper slopes of some Acropora IBD relationships compared to the Cladocopium relationship could result from much higher effective population sizes in the latter. Microscopic Cladocopium can inhabit a variety of hosts and may also live freely in the water column or benthos (Bell and Quigley ; Lim et al. ). The inverse relationship, however, is highly unlikely, namely that Acropora corals have substantially higher effective population sizes than Cladocopium in our study region. Therefore, the generally stronger isolation by distance patterns in Cladocopium, along with the observed patterns of landscape genetic variation, most likely indicates that Acropora disperse much further than their algal symbionts.

Our methodology for symbiont population genetics is non‐traditional, but not unprecedented. While studies of symbiont diversity historically relied on specific markers such as ITS‐2, SNP based methods can increase taxonomic precision and interpretability (Cooke et al. ; Eriksson et al. ). Host targeted ddRAD, such as used here, can lead to low numbers of symbiont reads per sample, and may have been a factor in our high number of symbiont samples with inadequate data for downstream analysis (Primov et al. ). Still, other studies have shown “remarkably consistent results” between RAD‐seq methods and ITS‐2 typing for assessing symbiont genera within samples, and good agreement between the methods at finer taxonomic resolutions (Frade et al. ; Rios et al. ). One key caveat to our methodology is that we have no way of identifying samples hosting multiple co‐dominant Cladocopium species, an issue that also occurs with ITS‐2 based methods (Davies et al. ). However, even if our samples hosted extensive unexpected co‐dominant lineages, our fundamental conclusions about symbiont genetic turnover across space would remain unchanged.

Corals are not the only marine animals that acquire photosymbionts from their settlement environment. Other examples include giant clams and jellyfish (Astorga et al. ; Butler et al. ; Fitt and Trench ). In a very different marine environment, deep sea snails inhabiting hydrothermal vents also acquire their chemosynthetic bacterial partners horizontally (Breusing et al. ). Similarly to our finding that Cladocopium genotypes depend on geography and depth more strongly than host taxon, the genetics of snail microsymbionts depend more strongly on site‐specific environmental variables than on the genetics of their hosts. Environmental acquisition of shorter‐dispersing symbionts can enable a far‐dispersing host to acquire symbiont strains adapted to their specific local conditions (Breusing et al. ). Our results suggest the possibility of similar dynamics at play in Acropora in the Philippines. We found low genetic structuring in populations of four different Acropora taxa across a two hundred kilometre span on multiple islands, suggesting limited potential for genome‐wide local adaptation. Conversely, we found genetic variation in Cladocopium associated with latitude and depth, both of which determine the environmental conditions to which corals are exposed.

Our results revealed differing patterns of spatial genetic variation in Cladocopium and their Acropora hosts, despite their close symbiotic relationship. The contrast between extensive within‐species connectivity in Acropora, contrasted with the spatial geographic structuring in Cladocopium, creates evolutionary advantages for the holobiont. Long dispersal distances enable genetic connectivity between far‐flung populations, but can limit local adaptation when parents and offspring settle in very different conditions (Kawecki and Ebert ). This may be a particular problem in the marine realm, where species tend to exhibit longer dispersal distances than do terrestrial taxa (Kinlan and Gaines ). Here we see Acropora cf. tenuis larvae traversing potentially hundreds of kilometres of latitudinal span, as well as tens of meters of depth gradient, and ultimately settling in markedly different environments than their parents. Acquiring symbionts from the settlement environment may allow far‐dispersing marine taxa to take advantage of locally adapted symbiont genotypes.

Given these differences, simulations of gene flow and evolution in corals should consider modelling coral hosts and their algal symbionts as distinct yet interacting components within a single framework. The close ecological relationship between Acropora and their Cladocopium symbionts does not require parallel patterns of landscape genetics, as the taxa exhibit contrasting patterns of speciation, gene flow, and possibly adaptation. Continued study of close symbiont pairs, including corals, will be important for understanding how species interactions shape the co‐evolution of dispersal.

All authors contributed to the interpretation of results and reviewed and revised the manuscript.

medicine.title: Erosive tooth wear in young adults and progression from adolescence in the Fit Futures longitudinal cohort study
medicine.abstract: This study aimed to determine the prevalence and severity of erosive tooth wear (ETW) among Norwegian young adults aged 26–27, and to assess its progression from adolescence (age 16–17), using data from the Fit Futures Study (FF).The study included 560 participants in a cross-sectional analysis at age 26–27, of whom 225 were also assessed at age 16–17 for longitudinal analysis. ETW was evaluated using intraoral photographs and graded according to the Visual Erosion Dental Examination (VEDE) system.At age 26–27, ETW was observed in 81% of the participants, with lesions extending into dentin present in almost half of the individuals (49%). Males exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of ETW (86%), compared to females (76%, p = 0.006). Significantly more erosive lesions were found on first molars (47%), compared to both central (26%) and lateral (14%) incisors (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis revealed that 78% of the participants experienced progression of ETW from age 16–17 to 26–27, while the incidence of ETW among those unaffected at baseline was 73%. No sex differences were observed in the proportion of participants showing progression. Progression was more frequent on first molars than on maxillary incisors (36% vs. 21%, p < 0.001).The findings demonstrate that ETW is a highly prevalent condition that progresses from adolescence through early adulthood. The results underscore the need for early diagnosis, preventive strategies, and public health interventions to address modifiable risk factors.
medicine.text:
Erosive tooth wear (ETW), characterized by loss of dental hard tissue caused by non-bacterial acids, is a growing concern in dentistry. Loss of dental hard tissue associated with ETW may lead to hypersensitivity, aesthetic impairment, reduced occlusal height, and pulpal damage []. As ETW is irreversible, it poses significant challenges for both patients and dental professionals if further deterioration is not adequately controlled.

While dental caries levels among Norwegian 18-year-olds have declined [], ETW appears to be emerging as a more prominent oral health challenge. A considerable amount of research has addressed the epidemiology of ETW, primarily focusing on pediatric and adolescent populations and relying largely on cross-sectional designs []. The global prevalence of ETW is estimated to lie between 20 and 40% in these age groups []. In Norway, studies among adolescents report higher prevalences, ranging from 38–59%, with dentin involvement observed in 15–20% [, ]. However, no updated prevalence estimates have been published over the past decade.

Research on ETW in adult populations remains limited. Prior Norwegian studies reported prevalences of 20% among adults with a mean age of 39 [] and 38% among 18-year-olds []. A large study of European adults (mean age 44 years) reported moderate or severe ETW in 72% of the participants []. In general, studies of adult cohorts show a substantial variation in ETW prevalences, ranging between 2 and 100% [], making it challenging to establish a reliable estimate of the overall burden of ETW in adult populations.

Longitudinal data are scarce, difficult to compare, and only a few are based on recent samples. In the Nordic countries, the reported incidence varies between 13 and 76%, with an average follow-up time of 5 years [–]. These marked differences in incidence are also seen in studies from other regions, ranging from 7–39% [–]. The existing studies differ substantially in data collection, age of the sample, follow-up time, diagnostic criteria, scoring systems, and methods of assessment. There is a need for contemporary longitudinal studies with sufficient follow-up time and consistent methodology to better characterize ETW progression.

Although available data suggest that ETW is a common condition [], its long-term implications for patients’ oral health, healthcare resources, and service capacity are uncertain. Systematic monitoring of ETW prevalence and progression is therefore essential to improve our understanding of its broader public health consequences. To address this gap, the present study aimed at determining prevalence and severity of ETW in a cohort of young Norwegian adults (age 26–27) and evaluating how ETW had progressed from adolescence (age 16–17).

This study is based on data from Fit Futures (FF), a longitudinal population-based health study, conducted over three study waves. The first (FF1) and last (FF3) waves included dental examinations.  shows the selection process for the current study. Minor discrepancies in sample sizes compared to earlier publications from this cohort [] reflect subsequent dataset updates.

FF1 was carried out in 2010/2011 and invited all first-year upper secondary school students (n = 1,117) in Tromsø and Balsfjord, two neighboring municipalities in Northern Norway. The second study wave (FF2) was conducted during 2012/2013 and invited all participants from FF1 and other students attending the third year of upper secondary school in the same municipalities (n = 1,127). All participants from FF1 and FF2 were invited to FF3, conducted during 2021/2022. In total, n = 715 (65% of invitees) participated in FF3 [].

To ensure an age-homogenous study population, eligibility for the ETW analyses was restricted to participants aged 16–17 years at FF1, corresponding to 26–27 years at FF3. In FF1, ETW grading was performed on a randomly selected subsample (n = 383), and the baseline prevalence of ETW for this sample has been reported previously []. In FF3, ETW was recorded for 560 participants aged 26–27, constituting the cross-sectional sample of the present study. Of these participants, 225 had available ETW data at age 16–17 and therefore comprised the longitudinal sample for analyses of ETW progression. To assess potential selection bias, participants with and without ETW data were compared by sex and educational program at each stage of the selection process, including the initial random selection for ETW grading at FF1, attrition between FF1 and FF3, and data availability within FF3.

The participants in FF completed extensive questionnaires, and in FF1 and FF3 clinical dental examinations were done, including intraoral photographs obtained by trained clinical personnel using a standardized camera setup (Canon EOS 60D; Canon 105 mm macro lens; Sigma EM-140 DG ring flash). Photographs were taken using cheek/lip retractors and dental mirrors to enhance visibility, lighting, and angulation of the photographs. For assessment of ETW, the following images were used: facial surfaces of the upper anterior teeth, occlusal surfaces of the upper and lower teeth, and palatal surfaces of the upper anterior teeth. ETW grading in this study was based solely on two-dimensional intraoral photographs with no direct clinical examination for ETW.

ETW was assessed and graded by three experienced and calibrated clinicians in FF1 []. In FF3, the assessments were performed by a different group of examiners, except one of the examiners who participated in both the FF1 and FF3 assessment teams. Grading of ETW in FF1 photographs was performed as part of the original FF1 assessment [], and incorporated into the present dataset without re-grading. Grading of ETW in FF3 photographs was performed specifically for the present study. The grading procedure of ETW was the same in FF1 and FF3, and the examiners were blinded to participant identity during grading. Each examiner scored surfaces independently on individual forms, and the final grade for each surface was determined by majority agreement across the three examiners. A total of 12 surfaces were registered as index teeth for ETW: facial and palatal surfaces of all maxillary incisors and occlusal surfaces of all first permanent molars.

Grading of ETW was performed according to the Visual Erosion Dental Examination (VEDE) system: grade 0 = no ETW; grade 1 = initial loss of enamel, no dentin exposed; grade 2 = pronounced loss of enamel, no dentin exposed; grade 3 = dentin exposed, < 1/3 of the surface involved; grade 4 = dentin exposed, 1/3–2/3 of the surface involved; grade 5 = dentin exposed, > 2/3 of the surface involved []. For analytical purposes, VEDE grades were further combined into three categories at the surface level: 0 (no ETW) = VEDE grade 0; 1 (mild ETW, only in enamel) = VEDE grades 1–2; 2 (severe ETW, into dentin) = VEDE grades 3–5. Participants were subsequently categorized using the same three-category scale, based on the highest ETW score recorded on any surface: 0 (no ETW on any surfaces); 1 (mild ETW on at least one surface, but no severe ETW); 2 (severe ETW on at least one surface). Progression between FF1 and FF3 was calculated for each surface as the difference between the FF3 and FF1 ETW score. Surfaces were categorized as showing no progression, progression by one severity grade (+1; e.g. from grade 0 to 1, or from grade 1 to 2), or progression by two severity grades (+2; from grade 0 to 2). An individual progression score (sum score) was computed as the sum of positive changes across the 12 eligible tooth surfaces, each surface allowing a maximum progression of two grades (range 0–24). Surface-pairs with missing data at either timepoint were assigned a value of zero for this score, as described in Missing data management.

For the 560 participants included from FF3, 6,720 tooth surfaces were eligible for ETW scoring. Of these, 438 (7%) were illegible: 391 (89%) due to ‘other reasons’ (e.g. orthodontic appliances or low-quality images), 39 (9%) due to restorative treatment such as fillings or crowns, and 8 (2%) due to developmental disturbances. Most of these excluded surfaces were palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors (85%), followed by occlusal surfaces of first molars (14%) and facial surfaces of maxillary incisors (1%). In the sub-sample with longitudinal data from FF1 and FF3 (n = 225), 261 of 2,700 eligible surfaces (10%) were illegible: 248 (95%) for ‘other reasons’, and 13 (5%) for restorative treatment. Most exclusions were of palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors (59%), followed by facial surfaces of maxillary incisors (30%) and occlusal surfaces of first molars (12%). Missing values were disregarded in the analysis, as they represented ≤ 10% of the dataset. Given the low proportion and the nature of the missing data (illegible tooth surfaces), no imputation was performed. For the individual progression score (see Grading procedure), missing surface-pairs were treated differently. Rather than being excluded, they were assigned a value of zero, since grading was not possible. A sensitivity analysis testing the robustness of the progression score to missing data is described under Statistical analyses.

Calibration was based on the same intraoral photographs and procedure at both FF1 and FF3. Examiner scores were compared against a reference standard established through consensus among examiners on a set of intraoral photographs developed at the University of Oslo for calibration of the VEDE system, as previously described []. Calibration was performed in two rounds, allowing calculation of inter- and intra-observer agreement (weighted kappa) at both time points. Inter-observer agreement was ‘almost perfect’ (κ = 0.81–1.00) and intra-observer agreement was ‘substantial’ or higher (κ ≥ 0.61) at both FF1 and FF3 [].

This study was approved by the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics (REK) (2022/481763). Informed and written consent was collected from all the participants, and the participants had the opportunity to withdraw from the study at any time. The processing of personal data in the project was assessed by the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research (Sikt).

The statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.4.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) within RStudio version 2024.09.1 (RStudio, PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Descriptive statistics were reported as frequencies and summary measures. Chi-square tests were used for comparisons between categorical variables at the individual level. To assess the robustness of the progression score to missing data, a sensitivity analysis compared the score distribution between participants with complete data on all 12 surfaces and the full sample, testing the association between the number of missing surfaces and the score using Spearman’s rank correlation. Surface-level analyses used mixed-effects logistic regression, with participant as a random intercept to account for clustering of surfaces within individuals. The outcome was a binary indicator of progression (any increase in ETW category from FF1 to FF3). Two separate models were fitted, with tooth region (incisors vs. molars) or jaw (maxillary vs. mandibular) as the fixed effect. A binary rather than ordinal outcome was used, as the number of two-grade progressions was limited in some comparisons. The significance level was set at 0.05.

Participants assessed for ETW at FF1 (n = 383) did not differ significantly from those not assessed (n = 563) by sex (p = 0.87) or educational program (p = 0.92). Participants lost to follow-up between FF1 and FF3 (n =158) did not differ significantly from those retained (n = 225) by sex (p = 0.051) or educational program (p = 0.18). Similarly, among FF3 participants aged 26–27, those without ETW data (n = 74) did not differ significantly from those included in the ETW analysis (n = 560) by sex (p = 0.055), though a marginal difference was observed by educational program (Fisher’s exact p = 0.050), with participants without ETW data somewhat more often enrolled in vocational rather than general study programs.

Of the 560 participants included from the FF3 study, 53% (n = 297) were females. ETW was present in 81% of the participants (n = 452); 31% (n = 176) had only mild ETW, while 49% (n = 276) had at least one surface with severe ETW. The overall prevalence of ETW and the prevalence of severe lesions were both significantly higher in males than in females (). No sex differences were observed in the prevalence of only mild ETW.

Variation in both the number of affected surfaces and the severity of ETW was observed across the sample (). Significantly more erosive lesions were found on first molars (47%) compared with central (26%) and lateral (14%) incisors (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analyses were performed in the subgroup of participants (n = 225) who were examined and graded for ETW at both ages 16–17 and 26–27. Baseline data from FF1 have been published previously []. There were slightly more females in the sub-sample, 54% (n = 121). The prevalence of ETW increased from 38 to 83%. The sex distribution and severity of ETW is shown in . Males exhibited significantly more ETW than females at both examination ages.

RR: Relative risk; CI: confidence interval; ETW: Erosive tooth wear; Mild ETW: lesions in enamel; Severe ETW: lesions into dentin; FF1: Fit Futures 1; FF3: Fit Futures 3.

Sex differences in severity of ETW have been calculated using chi-square test with a statistically significant p < 0.05.

ETW was assessed on 2,439 surfaces, 869 occlusal surfaces on first molars, 823 facial surfaces, and 747 palatal surfaces on maxillary incisors. A quarter of the surfaces (n = 644) deteriorated with either one or two severity grades (). The proportion of surfaces affected with mild lesions increased from 6% (n = 137) to 23% (n = 555), and the proportion of surfaces with severe lesions increased from 3% (n = 68) to 10% (n = 241). Decreased severity was registered for 2% (n = 43) of all surfaces. These were classified as stable in the statistical analyses.

Progression was significantly more frequent on first molars (36%, n = 317) compared to maxillary incisors (21%, n = 327, p < 0.001). On maxillary incisors, progression was more common on palatal surfaces (42%, n = 314) than on facial surfaces (2%, n = 13). Progression occurred more frequently on mandibular first molars (42%, n = 184) compared to maxillary first molars (30%, n = 133, p < 0.001). Mandibular first molars also exhibited the highest proportion of surfaces with progression of two severity grades (). No facial surfaces of maxillary incisors deteriorated with two severity grades.

Of the participants, 78% (n = 176) demonstrated a worsening of ETW. Among these, 108 participants showed progression limited to one-grade increases (no surface progressed by two grades), whereas 68 participants showed at least one instance of a two-grade increase. There were no significant sex differences in the proportion of participants showing any progression. In FF1, 140 individuals had no ETW (VEDE-score = 0 on all surfaces). Of these, 102 were scored with mild or severe ETW in FF3, giving an incidence of 73%. The distribution of the progression score is shown in . The score had a mean of 3.4 (standard deviation [SD] = 3.1) and a median of 3 (Q1–Q3: 1–5), with an observed range of 0–14. The distribution was right-skewed, with most participants clustering at the lower end of the scale. A sensitivity analysis comparing participants with complete data on all 12 surfaces (n = 159) to the full sample showed a higher progression score among complete-case participants (median 4, Q1–Q3: 1–6) than in the full sample. The number of missing surfaces was negatively correlated with the progression score (Spearman’s rho = −0.29, p < 0.001).

In this cohort study, the prevalence of ETW was 81% among young adults aged 26–27 years, with almost half having lesions involving the dentin. Between ages 16–17 and 26–27, the incidence of ETW was 73%, and 78% of the participants included in the longitudinal analyses showed progression of ETW over this period. For most participants, this progression was limited to a small number of surfaces. Direct comparison with previous studies is challenging due to methodological differences between studies. However, a recent large German cohort study, following participants over a comparable 9-year period, reported considerably lower prevalence, incidence, and progression than observed in the present study []. This applied both to adolescents followed into early adulthood (12–20 years: 19% prevalence, 11% incidence, 10% progression) and among an older adult population (43–52 years: 54% prevalence, 39% incidence, 30% progression). These comparisons suggest that ETW is both more prevalent and more likely to progress in the present study population.
