In the context of the ongoing debate regarding whether and at what point ETW should be classified as an oral disease [], our findings suggest that ETW may contribute considerably to hard tissue loss in adolescents and young adults. The present study demonstrated a 29% increase in severe ETW over a 10-year period, and although tooth wear generally increases with age [], the observed progression in this study appears to exceed what would be expected from normal age-related changes []. In a Norwegian study based on data from 1989–1991, individuals were followed from age 15 to 21, and only 3% of participants with ETW progressed to severe ETW []. These results support the view that ETW in this age group appears more pronounced now than earlier and should be regarded as an oral disease rather than a physiological consequence of aging.

The observed increase in ETW progression may, considering previous literature, be influenced by a combination of behavioral factors and broader contextual influences, including contemporary dietary habits, lifestyle-related exposures, and socioeconomic conditions. Dietary acids are identified as a key determinant of ETW [], and a recent experimental study showed a rapid progression of ETW when exposed to cola beverage []. At the same time, consumption of acidic beverages continues to rise globally and in Norway [, , ]. Furthermore, a considerable proportion of young adults have limited health literacy, potentially reducing the effectiveness of preventive efforts []. In this context, how ETW is conceptualized influences prevention, clinical management, and even health policies. Viewing progressive ETW as a physiological phenomenon may delay diagnosis and intervention, whereas recognizing it as an oral disease could facilitate earlier and more effective strategies. Further research is needed to clarify which behaviors and exposures most strongly influence ETW progression.

The current study demonstrated a significantly higher prevalence of erosive lesions in men compared with women. Although findings in the literature are not entirely consistent, a recent systematic review concluded that male sex is generally associated with a higher risk of ETW []. Several explanations have been proposed, including differences in enamel thickness, greater masticatory muscle strength, and higher consumption of carbonated beverages among men [, ]. Genetic susceptibility has also been suggested as a contributing factor []. Associations between enamel-formation gene variants and reduced ETW risk have been reported in females, and genome-wide findings indicate that both individual and sex-related differences in ETW susceptibility may partly reflect genetic variation [, ].

Although men in the present study had a significantly higher prevalence of ETW, the proportion of participants showing progression did not differ significantly between the sexes. These findings suggest that the observed sex difference may already have been established by early adulthood. The NORDMO 2025 report, which describes the intake of discretionary drinks (energy drinks, sugary beverages, and light or sugar-free beverages) in the Nordic region [], shows that among children, males consumed significantly more than females. In adults, however, no sex differences in intake were observed. This may indicate that some behavioral patterns relevant to ETW risk become less differentiated by sex with increasing age.

One of the major challenges in interpreting and comparing epidemiological studies on ETW is the lack of a universally standardized scoring system. Over the years, a variety of indices have been developed, each with distinct definitions, cut-off values, and levels of detail []. This heterogeneity limits the comparability of findings across studies.

The use of the VEDE system in the present study was retained to ensure comparability with the FF1 material from 2016 []. For analytical purposes, the six VEDE grades were collapsed into three categories reflecting clinically meaningful thresholds. VEDE provides a clear diagnostic distinction between mild and severe ETW by differentiating between exposed and non-exposed dentin and is suitable for demonstrating the progression of ETW over time []. However, limitations related to the clinical identification of exposed dentin have been reported, and dentin exposure has not been shown to correlate with the amount of tissue loss []. Other grading systems for tooth wear have been introduced over time, including the Basic Erosive Wear Examination (BEWE), which does not rely on dentin exposure for grading []. Nevertheless, a comparative evaluation found both VEDE and BEWE to be reliable for their intended purposes []. In this context, the use of VEDE was considered appropriate for the aims of the present study.

In the present study, calibrated examiners assessed ETW using intraoral photographs rather than direct clinical evaluation. Although assessment of depth and texture is more challenging and depends on image quality, intraoral photographs provide higher diagnostic quality than study models and allow repeated scoring when required []. Intra-oral scanning (IOS) is a more objective and sensitive method for assessing ETW; however, limitations remain regarding its ability to detect small changes in tissue loss across the full dentition, partly due to scan alignment and the lack of intraoral reference points [, ]. More recently, paired IOS supported by artificial intelligence has been suggested as a promising approach, primarily by reducing analysis time, although concerns related to clinical interpretation and overtreatment persist [].

This study has several strengths and limitations. A key strength is the longitudinal design with a 10-year follow-up period, which allows for evaluation of changes in ETW over time. All ETW assessments were performed according to protocol by experienced and calibrated examiners. FF provides a population-based sample, which enhances the generalizability of the findings. However, attrition between FF1 and FF3 has previously been shown to result in a study population at FF3 with a higher level of educational attainment compared with the general Norwegian young adult population []. This may limit the representativeness of the FF3 sample. A further limitation concerns the progression score used to characterize individual-level progression, which should be interpreted as a conservative estimate. Missing surface-pairs were assigned a value of zero, and participants with more missing data showed lower progression scores than those with complete data. Missing surfaces were also not evenly distributed. On palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors in particular, this most plausibly reflects the presence of bonded orthodontic retainers, which can obstruct visual assessment of these surfaces. Retainer status was not recorded, and this remains an assumption.

There was approximately a 10-year interval between the evaluation of erosive lesions at FF1 and FF3, with only partial overlap between examiner teams. This could introduce a systematic difference in grading between the two time points; however, it is unlikely to represent a major limitation, as only 2% of surfaces were scored with lower severity at FF3 than at FF1.

The findings in this study indicate that ETW is a common condition in early adulthood, which may have implications at several levels. For individual patients, ETW may lead to hypersensitivity, pain, reduced masticatory efficiency, and aesthetic concerns, which can affect daily function and quality of life []. For oral health professionals, these findings emphasize the importance of systematic monitoring and identifying individuals at risk, as well as the underlying risk factors, to enable targeted early interventions aimed at limiting further progression. Management of advanced ETW is resource-intensive and may impose substantial direct costs on patients and society []. Taken together, these findings suggest that ETW may extend beyond an individual clinical problem to represent a broader public health concern.

This study shows that ETW is prevalent among young adults, with progression from adolescence observed in the majority of participants over a 10-year follow-up period. The high prevalence of ETW extending into dentin suggests tooth wear beyond normal physiological changes at this age, and may support considering ETW in this age group as an oral disease rather than a physiological condition. These findings highlight the need for early identification of individuals at risk, effective preventive strategies, and systematic monitoring in young individuals.

medicine.title: Beyond the double-helix: non-canonical nucleic acid structures as drug targets and therapeutics
medicine.abstract: Nucleic acids adopt a rich repertoire of non-canonical structures beyond the iconic double helix — G-quadruplexes, i-motifs, triplexes, R-loops, Z-DNA/Z-RNA, and junctions — with roles in genome stability, transcription, replication, and translation. Yet the biological evidence for these conformations varies widely, from direct in vivo validation to largely indirect biochemical inference. We organize this review around a distinctive therapeutic duality: non-canonical structures may serve as molecular targets for small molecules, peptides, and nucleic acid-based modulators, while some are also engineered as therapeutic agents in their own right. For each structural class, we critically assess structural principles, biological evidence, and detection methods, explicitly distinguishing direct in vivo validation from cell-based and biochemical observations and noting the limitations of current detection strategies. Comparing translational maturity across classes through the lens of target versus agent, we identify key challenges — structural selectivity, mechanistic attribution, target engagement, and delivery — that must be resolved to fully realize the therapeutic potential of non-canonical nucleic acid structures.
medicine.text:
Nucleic acids are fundamental biomolecules that encode and regulate genetic information. Beyond the canonical B-form double helix, DNA and RNA adopt a diverse array of non-canonical structures, including G-quadruplexes (G4s), i-motifs (iMs), triplexes, R-loops, Z-DNA/Z-RNA, and DNA junctions. These conformations have been implicated in transcription, replication, translation, and genome stability, although the supporting evidence varies substantially across structural classes and experimental systems [, ]. Establishing their in vivo relevance remains difficult: current methods for monitoring non-canonical structure formation and its downstream consequences offer limited spatial and temporal resolution, while the complexity of the intracellular environment further obscures structure-specific effects. These constraints have slowed the transition from correlative observations to mechanistic understanding of non-canonical nucleic acid structures in vivo.

Most of these structures were initially seen as biophysical curiosities, relevant in vitro but of marginal cellular relevance. Over the past decades, advances in chemical biology, sequencing-based structure mapping, and live-cell imaging have overturned that view, revealing non-canonical structures as potential regulatory elements concentrated at functionally privileged loci such as promoters, enhancers, telomeres, untranslated regions, and viral genomes. Their implication in cancer, viral infection, neurodegeneration, and inflammatory diseases has intensified interest in their biological mechanisms [–]. This functional relevance also opens a therapeutic dimension uncommon among biomolecules: non-canonical nucleic acid structures can serve as drug targets— modulated by small molecules, peptides, or aptamers — or be engineered as therapeutic agents that adopt non-canonical folds to bind cellular targets with high affinity. Most molecules in drug development are either targets or therapeutics, but rarely both; non-canonical nucleic acid structures can be either, bringing the point of intervention to the level of gene regulation and genome architecture. This duality — target versus agent — frames the present review.

Importantly, targeting non-canonical nucleic acid structures embedded within genomic and transcriptomic contexts represents a fundamentally different therapeutic paradigm compared to classical protein-directed strategies. Rather than modulating downstream effectors, such interventions act directly on the structural layer that encodes and organizes genetic information, with the potential to influence several biological processes, like transcriptional and replication programs, RNA processing and chromatin architecture. In other words, non-canonical motifs provide structural “handles” on the genome and transcriptome, through which gene regulation and genome organization can be perturbed with spatial and possibly locus-specific precision. Thus, in the context of next-generation therapeutics, this shift from a protein-centric to nucleic acid-centric intervention paradigm can drive and boost future therapeutic strategies to operate at the level of nucleic acid topology and conformation.

This review addresses a central question: can non-canonical structures serve as drug targets, as therapeutics, or both? We first survey the major structural classes and their biological contexts, then evaluate the evidence for their therapeutic exploitation as targets or therapeutics, discussing these structures not merely as passive markers but as active architectural elements that can be selectively targeted or engineered. We argue that this structure-centric view potentially underpins a new generation of therapeutics, and assess the challenges that must be overcome to translate this structure-centric approach into clinical reality.

Non-canonical nucleic acid structures are alternative folds diverging from the well-known Watson-Crick B-form double-helix. The iconic duplex structure is composed of two antiparallel DNA strands wound around a common axis to form a right-handed double helix, in which guanine pairs with cytosine and adenine pairs with thymine [, ]. According to the proposed model, due to the hydrophobicity of nucleotide bases, the hydrophilic sugar-phosphate backbone lies on the exterior of the double helix, facing the surrounding water, also influenced by the hydrophobic base stacking and Van der Waals interactions, which minimize the bases’ exposure to the solvent [, , ]. Once considered biochemical curiosities, non-canonical structures are now detected at regulatory hotspots across the genome and transcriptome, where they form in specific sequence and cellular contexts. Their formation is likely governed by local sequence, supercoiling, pH, ionic composition, cell cycle, external ligands, and competition or cooperation with other folds.

In this section, we will outline the structural principles and stability determinants of each structure, highlighting methods used to detect and map them in vitro and in cell, and summarize their principal biological functions. Also, for each structural class, the proposed biological relevance is presented as the context that historically motivated the development of structure-specific detection methods. However, these biological interpretations should be considered in light of the methodological limitations discussed subsequently, particularly when evidence relies on indirect, probe-dependent, or antibody-based detection.

G-quadruplex (G4) structures, discovered by Gellert and collaborators in 1962 [], are formed in G-rich sequences and arise by the stacking of two or more G-tetrads (also known as G-quartets), consisting of a quasi-planar arrangement of four guanines stabilized by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds (Fig. ). Hoogsteen pairing between guanines involves the N1 and N2 donors of one base hydrogen-bonding to the O6 and N7 acceptors of the adjacent guanine, yielding eight hydrogen bonds per planar G-tetrad and a 90° angle between neighboring G bases [, ]. Tetrad–tetrad interactions strongly contribute to G4 stability, thanks to stacking between hydrophobic tetrads, which offer a large π-surface that favors stable π–π interactions, and facilitate cation coordination [, ].

Cations, especially alkali metal ions, are crucial for G4 stabilization and structural maintenance. In their absence, the arrangement of the polyanionic nucleic acid strands is electrostatically unfavorable due to the presence of four negatively charged sugar-phosphate backbones and the negatively charged cavities between tetrads, underscoring the essential role of cation binding in G4 stability [, ]. These ions centrally coordinate the O6 atoms of each G within the G4 axial channel, involving electrostatic and donor–acceptor interactions with the free electrons of the oxygen. The cations also contribute to electrostatic compensation by lowering the repulsion between the phosphate oxygens [–]. The intrinsic cation properties, such as size, charge, and cost of dehydration, together with ion concentration, govern G4 folding and stability. A hierarchical order was proposed for several mono- and divalent cations (Sr2+ > Ba2+ > K+ > Na+ ≈ NH4+ ≈ Rb+ >> Li+) [, ]. The most physiologically relevant cations, potassium (K+) and sodium (Na+), have been shown to strongly influence G4 structure, with K+ preferentially occupying sites between successive G-quartet layers, while smaller ions such as Na+ may also coordinate within the plane of an individual tetrad [].

G4s are highly polymorphic, and this variability arises from changes in (i) the number of G-quartets, (ii) the presence of loops (propeller, diagonal, and lateral) and bulges (discontinuities between tetrads in the same strand), (iii) strand stoichiometry (uni-, bi-, or tetramolecular), (iv) strand polarity, leading to parallel, antiparallel, and hybrid topologies [, , ], and (v) non-canonical quartets and additional base pairing schemes (Fig. ). The relative strand orientation imposes constraints on the glycosidic bond angles of guanines within a given quartet (leading to syn or anti-orientations). Unlike G4 DNA, which exhibits strong topological diversity, RNA G4 adopts mostly parallel topologies and tends to be more thermodynamically stable than the corresponding DNA ones. These properties result from the ribose 2′-hydroxyl group (2′-OH), which favors the anti-glycosidic conformation, excluding the syn/anti arrangements required for antiparallel or hybrid folds [, ]. In addition, in vitro analyses revealed that the ionic environment (cation type and concentration; molecular crowding) and the length, position, and geometry (propeller, lateral, diagonal) of the loops, as well as the presence of bulges and flanking sequences, also play important roles in G4 folding. Furthermore, under cellular and in vivo conditions, the G4 folding and stability are also governed by the interaction with proteins or small molecules, cellular localization, cell cycle, and cellular processes (replication and transcriptional activity), as well as epigenetic modifications [, –]. Very recently, it was also demonstrated that ultraviolet (UV) radiation induces, in cellulo, widespread and persistent G4 formation, distinguishing it from other genotoxins [].

Biologically, G4s have been reported to be involved in several processes. DNA G4 formation in promoter regions is proposed to influence transcription, and this has been explored in depth for oncogenic promoters, such as C-MYC, KRAS, or B-MYB, as well as in prokaryotic systems (both bacteria and archaea) such as H. volcanii, T. barophilus, P. aeruginosa, and S. aureus [–]. The biological roles summarized below should therefore be interpreted as being supported to different extents by in vitro, cellular, and in vivo evidence, rather than as uniformly established mechanisms. The RNA G4 (rG4s) in untranslated regions (5′-UTRs) or coding regions regulate translation, ribosome processivity, and splicing decisions [, , –]. Recently, cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) revealed how G4s can act as barriers to the chromosomal DNA replication machinery, leading to DNA replication arrest []. At telomeres, G4s modulate access of telomerase and shelterin components, shaping replication and end-protection, whereas in viruses, G4s can influence genome replication and translation [–].

These processes involve multiple interactions with several G4-binding proteins [–], including nucleolin, a multifunctional and predominantly nucleolar protein with DNA- and RNA-binding activity; the RNA helicase DHX36 (also known as RHAU); the transcription factor SP1; and the RNA-binding protein FMRP. Beyond proteins, small molecules (G4 ligands; later discussed in the “G-Quadruplex” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section) may also modulate G4 roles by stabilizing or destabilizing the structure [–]. G4 ligands have gained increasing interest in recent years, with some molecules reaching clinical trials [–]. G4 ligands may find several applications in anticancer or antiviral therapies [, , , ]. G4 formation is believed to be transient in cells; yet data on G4 lifetime are scarce; G4 formation tends to be cell cycle-regulated, with a maximal accumulation during S phase, corresponding to DNA replication, and lowest levels during G2/M, when transcription and replication are curtailed and histone modifications promote chromatin condensation [–]. Interestingly, using single-molecule fluorescence imaging and time-dependent chemical trapping of unfolded G4s in living cells reveals that G4s can fluctuate between folded and unfolded states or G4/dsDNA (double-stranded DNA) equilibrium, suggesting that G4s naturally undergo structural fluctuations in cells [, ]. These observations do not exclude the presence of challenging, “long-lived” G4s, for which transitions can be difficult to follow, as in human telomeric repeat or TRF2 messenger RNA (mRNA) [, ]. More recently, the visualization of RNA G4 was also reported using fluorescence lifetime microscopy (FLIM) and TOR-G4 as a dye [].

The discovery, validation and mapping of G4 have been performed at different levels. G4 evaluation generally starts by using computational methods such as G4Hunter or other reported algorithms to estimate potential G4-forming sequences across the genome and transcriptome []. Early computational approaches such as Quadparser and QGRS Mapper relied largely on sequence-pattern rules [–]. More flexible prediction methods were subsequently developed, including G4Hunter, which evaluates G-richness and G-skewness to generate a G4-propensity score [] and PQSfinder, which allows imperfect or atypical putative G4-forming motifs to be identified []. On the RNA side, a specific method called G4mer was proposed to predict rG4 formation, classify rG4 subtypes and evaluate the effects of genetic variants across the transcriptome [].

After G4-forming sequence prediction, in vitro characterization is generally performed to validate the identified candidate sequences. Several biophysical and biochemical methodologies have been described in the last decades to understand the ability of G4-prone sequences to assemble into G4, considering the intrinsic properties of G4 or their responses when interacting with specific probes, for which guidelines have been reported []. This is exemplified for the sequences found in the B-MYB promoter, for which we used no less than ten different methods to validate G4 formation []. Each of these methods, however, carries intrinsic limitations that no single technique can fully resolve. Most of these assays are performed under ionic strength, cation identity, and molecular crowding conditions that only approximate the nuclear environment, meaning that robust in vitro folding does not by itself guarantee that the same sequence adopts a G4 conformation within the chromatin environment.

Despite overwhelming evidence that G4-prone sequences actually fold in vitro, their actual formation in cells has long been a matter of debate. Fortunately, several techniques are now available to support G4 formation in a biologically relevant environment. Recently, in-cell nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy emerged as a complementary source for atomically resolved information on the structure, dynamics, and interactions of G4 within the intracellular space of living cells [–]. This approach, however, typically requires microinjection or electroporation of oligonucleotides at concentrations well above endogenous levels, and remains largely restricted to short, exogenously introduced sequences rather than single-copy endogenous loci within their native chromatin context.

Additionally, DNA and RNA G4 formation in cells can be validated using several high-throughput sequencing techniques, such as G4-seq, G4-CUT&Tag, G4Access, rG4-seq, G4RP-seq, Keth-seq, and SHALIPE-seq, by which Song et al. extensively discussed and summarized these and other methods reported in the literature []. It is important to note that the reported in-cell G4 frequencies should therefore be interpreted as method-dependent estimates rather than absolute counts because these sequencing-based methods do not all interrogate G4 formation within intact, living cells to the same degree. For example, the original G4-seq protocol is applied to purified and naked genomic DNA under conditions that favor (K+) or disfavor (Li+) G4 folding; it therefore reports the G4-forming potential of a sequence outside its native chromatin context, whereas methods such as G4-CUT&Tag and G4Access are performed on native or minimally processed chromatin and more directly reflect in-cell structural status.

Moreover, molecular probes provide an additional approach to study and visualize G4 structures in cells and in vitro, namely using antibodies or fluorescent ligands. The most commonly used antibody is BG4, a single-chain variable fragment that specifically recognizes G4s and allows applications from fixed-cell immunofluorescence, where punctate G4 staining of genomic DNA is observed, to genome-wide mapping, as previously mentioned []. This is also a powerful technique to assess how ligands mediate and induce in-cell G4 formation. Yet, attention should be paid to the origin of this antibody, as one commercial version also named “BG4” actually corresponds to a different protein (an IgG) of questionable selectivity! It is equally important to note that the immunofluorescence experimental protocol requires chemical fixation (such as formaldehyde or methanol), which can itself alter chromatin architecture and potentially induce or eliminate G4 structures that would not be present in the unfixed cell in its native state. Thus, the punctate BG4 signal therefore represents a fixed “snapshot” rather than a direct observation of a dynamic structure in a living cell. Moreover, although BG4 was raised against a synthetic parallel-stranded G4, its relative affinity across the full diversity of endogenous G4 topologies, including antiparallel and hybrid folds, remains incompletely characterized, so BG4-based maps may under- or overrepresent specific structural subclasses.

In addition to classical antibodies, and to surpass their limitations, nanobodies were also developed against the C-MYC G4 and the TBA aptamer. Each nanobody is raised against a single G4-forming sequence or topology, and may function as topology- or sequence-specific reporters rather than general-purpose detection tools, limiting their applicability to a smaller number of loci for which a validated binder currently exists [, ]. More recently, a genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor termed G4-Flame was reported for the spatiotemporal evaluation and high-resolution visualization of G4-DNA dynamics in real-time in living systems (nucleus and mitochondria) []; however, different challenges are encountered, such as fluorescent proteins photobleaching for long-term G4 dynamics monitoring or applicability to in vivo studies due to limited tissue penetration of visible light. In addition, having been described only recently, it has not yet been independently validated across multiple laboratories or cell types, and its performance at low-abundance loci remains to be established.

On the small-molecule side, fluorescent ligands such as SiR-PyPDS, TASQ derivatives, QUMA, DAOTA-M2, or TOR-G4 (both read out by fluorescence lifetime imaging, FLIM) have been demonstrated to enable live-cell visualization with improved photostability and cellular permeability [, , , –]. A common limitation to all ligand-based visualization approaches is that these probes are themselves G4-interacting, and often G4-stabilizing, molecules, which can shift the folding equilibrium toward the G4 conformation, so that the reported signal reflects a ligand-stabilized population rather than necessarily the unperturbed, steady-state abundance of G4 in the cell. Not long ago, the PCL conjugate, composed of the conjugation of PhenDC3 with a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable imidazopyrazinium chemilumophore, was described as the first chemiluminescent probe for selective G4 visualization in vitro and in cells []. Once again, as with the fluorescent ligands above, the chemiluminescent readout of PCL depends on PhenDC3 engaging and stabilizing its target G4; so, its signal should likewise be interpreted as reporting a stabilized rather than a fully native population.

Furthermore, G4-ligand-conjugated oligonucleotides have also been demonstrated to constitute an alternative method for selective binding and detection of individual G4 structures in cells [, –].

Taken together, and despite the advances and information that we can obtain, no currently available methods (biophysical, sequencing-based, antibody-based, or ligand-based) can unambiguously establish the abundance, dynamics, and functional relevance of a G4 structure at a specific genomic locus in an unperturbed living cell. In addition, most molecular probes risk reporting a shifted equilibrium. Sequencing-based maps depend heavily on the specific protocol and can differ from one another, and the most direct biophysical readouts, such as in-cell NMR, remain restricted to a small set of model sequences. Therefore, a convergent and multi-method approach, as illustrated above for the B-MYB promoter [], should be seen as a recommended approach for initial G4 characterization, whereas developing methods capable of reliably capturing G4 formation within its native chromatin environment remains the major challenge for this class of non-canonical nucleic acid structures.

The i-Motifs (iMs), also known as i-DNA, are pH-sensitive four-stranded structures formed by cytosine-rich sequences through intercalation of hemiprotonated C:C+ base pairs. iMs were discovered in the 1990s at École Polytechnique by Maurice Guéron et al. [, ]. The fundamental building unit consists of C:C+ base pairs with one proton actually shared between the two cytosines at the N3 position. The relatively low pK of this group explains why this structure is stable primarily under slightly acidic conditions. iMs are also stabilized by the C4–N4 and C2–O2 dipole bonds, which also contribute to the stability of the iM (Fig. ) [–]. Unlike G4s, in which π–π interactions stabilize the structure [], base stacking between consecutive C:C+ pairs is extremely limited.

In contrast to DNA G4 structures, strand orientation is fixed for iM: two strands in one direction (forming a parallel-stranded duplex), and two strands in the opposite direction (forming another parallel-stranded duplex). This limits iM structural polymorphism, yet there are other sources of variation: iM can be formed from the arrangement of a single strand, thus being called intramolecular iM, or from the arrangement of two or four strands, thus being called bimolecular or tetramolecular, respectively, and this also affects the presence of loops and overhangs in the structure [, ]. Intramolecular iMs contain three loops, while bimolecular iMs contain two and tetramolecular iMs do not contain loop regions, thus presenting negatively charged regions at their ends. iMs can be classified into two topologies based on the position of the outermost hemiprotonated cytosine pair, that is, 3′E and 5′E, where the pair lies at the 3′- or 5′-end, respectively []. The 3′E form is typically more stable, owing to more favorable sugar-phosphate interactions, due to the balance of repulsive forces between phosphate groups and attractive forces between sugars. Finally, just like G4s, iMs can accommodate bulges, with non-C nucleotides interrupting C-tracks and causing base- and position-dependent destabilization. RNA can also assemble in an iM structure, but this structure is less stable due to the 2′ OH groups of the ribose sugars [].

iM structures exhibit pronounced pH sensitivity; yet, their formation and stability are influenced by other factors, such as sequence composition, epigenetic modifications (like cytosine methylation by DNA methyltransferases), and environmental conditions (temperature, cation presence, and molecular crowding agents), which affect the midpoint conformational transitions (pHT value) [, , ]. iM formation under in vivo conditions is not controlled by one variable alone and is not independently adjustable but physiologically regulated. It is better viewed as the result of primary sequence propensity plus cellular context, especially crowding, negative supercoiling, and protein interactions [].

The electrostatics of the iM are fundamentally different from a G4. The linear density of negative charges is actually low, because the backbone is stretched and has one positive charge per base pair. Under in vitro conditions, divalent and transition metal ions such as Ag+ and Cu2+, as well as molecular crowding or dehydration agents, can modulate iM stability [–]. Also, it is reported that the ability of C-rich sequences to fold into the iM structure follows the order Cs+ > Na+ > K+ > Li+ for monovalent cations, and they do not directly affect the topology []. Thus, different factors contribute to iM stability under near-physiological conditions, encouraging to explore the structure’s role in biological processes, despite its pH dependency should not be directly extrapolated to the intracellular environment. Because C-rich sequences are the direct counterpart of G4-forming sequences, iM-prone sequences are also found in gene promoter regions close to transcription start sites, telomere, and centromere, allowing authors to hypothesize their role in biological processes like DNA transcription, replication, repair, or recombination, offering new therapeutic approaches for cancer and disease treatment. However, the biological implications attributed to iMs should be interpreted cautiously because their cellular detection remains strongly dependent on experimental conditions and on probes whose specificity is still under debate. The transcriptional regulation also involves mechanisms based on protein–iM interactions, namely the interaction of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L-like (hnRNPLL) in the case of the iM structure located on the BCL-2 oncogene [, ]. Small molecules have been reported to bind to iM, leading to transcriptional repression by preventing protein binding and proposed to be used as tools for iM detection [, ], although the selectivity and specificity of these effects have been questioned [, ]. iM formation has been proposed to be interdependent on G4 in human cells and is over-represented at G1 phase, during high levels of transcription [].

The pipeline for iM characterization is similar to G4, keeping in mind that the arsenal of iM techniques and probes is more limited. The discovery and prediction of iM-prone sequences starts using bioinformatic algorithms, followed by an extensive biophysical and biochemical analysis. Recently, Tao et al. reported all the existing methodologies for iMs identification and characterization, ranging from spectroscopic to genomic approaches, as well as summarizing the impacts of internal and external factors on iM formation and stability []. Unlike G4 characterization, where assay conditions primarily affect topology and stability, iM biophysical characterization is fundamentally conditioned by the assay pH itself, since folding requires hemi-protonated C:C+ pairs. Most spectroscopic and biochemical protocols are performed at mildly acidic pH (typically, 5.5–6.6) to guarantee a measurable signal, which by design does not test whether the same sequence would fold under the slightly alkaline pH of human cells (pH 7.0–7.4) []. Besides thermodynamic stability, kinetic factors strongly influence iM folding, especially at near-neutral pH. At this pH, under in vitro conditions, complete iM formation can become extremely slow (days or weeks). In addition, “imperfect” iMs can become kinetic traps, preventing the assembly of thermodynamically favored, fully C:C+ paired iMs []. This kinetic dependence has an important practical consequence because different laboratories using different folding protocols can report distinct results for the same sequence, complicating direct comparison across studies. On the other hand, the use of molecular crowding agents such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) has been used to raise the stability of iM to near-neutral pH values in vitro []. Whether such synthetic crowding conditions faithfully reproduce the specific macromolecular environment of the nucleus remains unverified.

An antibody for iM was also developed, termed iMab, and used to confirm the presence of iM structures in human cell nuclei, showing their dependence on both pH and the cell cycle []. Additionally, the same antibody was demonstrated to selectively bind to intramolecular and intermolecular iM structures []; however, contrary evidence reported that the iMab antibody binds single-stranded cytosine-rich sequences and unfolds iM []. This observation means that a positive iMab signal in iM-CUT&Tag [] and iM-IP-seq [, ] genomic methods may reflect the presence of a C-rich single-stranded region rather than a folded iM and may explain the surprising observation that iMab picks sequences in the genome that are completely unable to form a stable iM at physiological pH (e.g. the human telomeric motif). Once again, unlike the G4 field, which benefits from several independent mapping strategies (vide supra, “G-Quadruplex” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section), all genome-wide iM maps published to date rely on this same contested antibody, leaving the field without an independent method capable of cross-validating its own genomic landscape. Moreover, these studies have employed distinct protocols, differing particularly in whether acidic buffers are used to maintain iM folding, which can affect iM formation and may not accurately reflect the intracellular environment.

Some doubts on iM formation in cells remain, therefore unanswered, and additional tools are needed. Complementary methods, like in-cell NMR, were applied to evaluate the structure formation within the intracellular space of living cells and concluded that iM DNA levels are strongly depleted in living human cells [, , ], suggesting that only the most stable iM-forming sequences in vitro remain folded in cells. It is worth noting that this conclusion represents a significant revision of earlier in-cell NMR work reporting that iM structures formed from naturally occurring genomic sequences were stable and persisted in the nuclei of living human cells []. The more recent, cell cycle-resolved study substantially revised this view, illustrating how methodological refinement, rather than a single definitive experiment, has progressively reshaped the field’s confidence in the extent of iM formation in cells.

A question remains open regarding the number of iM formed within cells: are these structures as frequently formed as G4s, or much rarer and limited to the most favorable sequences? Answering this question is further complicated by the fact that the only genome-wide sequencing-based iM maps available to date depend entirely on the iMab antibody, as discussed above. Thus, any future estimate of genome-wide iM abundance will remain provisional until an antibody-independent, chromatin-based mapping method, analogous to G4Access for G4, becomes available for this structural class.

Triplex nucleic acid structures are three-stranded assemblies in which a third strand binds to the major groove of a purine-rich duplex through Hoogsteen or reverse Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds, keeping the original Watson-Crick structure intact []. The third strand (or TFO, for triplex-forming oligonucleotide) lies parallel or antiparallel to the purine-rich strand of the duplex, depending on the motif involved [, ]. Binding via Hoogsteen or reverse Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds depends on orientation and sequence composition [, ]. The TFO can be DNA or RNA, but non-natural modifications such as peptide nucleic acid (PNA) also allow triplex formation. RNA third strands often bind with higher affinity, owing to the 2′-OH constrained backbone [, ]. The third strand binding can be performed in two distinct ways and depends directly on the nucleotide composition. In the first scheme, a pyrimidine-rich third strand binds parallel to the purine strand (Y-type), forming the canonical base triplets T:A-T (thymine recognizing an A-T base-pair) and C+:G-C (protonated cytosine recognizing G-C, as protonation at the N3 position of the cytosine in the third strand is required, as for iM formation) []. The formation of C+:G-C base triplets requires cytosine protonation, making this motif pH-dependent and favored by slightly acidic conditions [, ]. The second binding mode involves purine-containing third strands binding in an antiparallel manner (R-type), generating A:AT (adenine recognizing A-T) and G:GC (guanine recognizing G-C) triplets, which are stable at neutral pH and less pH-dependent, but more sensitive to ionic conditions, especially di-cation concentration. These TFOs, which can be G-rich, may be prone to competing G4 formation (Fig. ) [, ].

Beyond pH, the stability and formation of triplex structures depend on multiple environmental factors. Sequence composition plays a crucial role, with optimal formation occurring at polypurine/polypyrimidine tracts typically containing uninterrupted runs of purines and pyrimidines, and cation composition, in particular divalent cations like Mg2+ and Ca2+, can enhance triplex stability by screening electrostatic repulsions and promoting appropriate structural alignment [, , ]. By contrast, under cellular and in vivo conditions, these parameters are physiologically constrained, and factors such as DNA supercoiling and negative torsion open the major groove and induce energetically favorable triplex formation [, ]. Moreover, chemically modified nucleic acids and synthetic nucleic acid analogues, originally developed primarily for antisense and therapeutic applications, have also been shown to enhance triplex formation, as modifications to the backbone of the third strand. For example, locked nucleic acid (LNA), 2′-O-methyl (2′-O-Me) or PNA modifications may stabilize the triplex. Modified bases such as pseudoisocytosine or 5-methylcytosine have also been shown to increase stability [, ]. These specific modifications contribute to enhanced triplex stability, which can be rationalized by the permanent protonation at the N3 position in pseudoisocytosine and possibly by altering the pKa and hydrophobicity of 5-methylcytosine [, , ]. These features favor the formation and maintenance of the protonated base states required for efficient Hoogsteen hydrogen bonding, thereby stabilizing the triplex structure under physiological or near-physiological conditions.

Triplexes may be involved in multiple biological processes. The natural intramolecular triplex DNA (H-DNA) can form at mirror-repeat sequences during transcription and replication by stalling polymerases, potentially influencing local chromatin structure and gene expression, and causing genome instability [, , ].

TFOs were proposed, as early as the late 1980s by the Dervan and Hélène labs, as potential tools for sequence-specific gene targeting and regulation [, ]. Several reviews address recent progress in blocking transcription, recruiting effectors, or steering repair at specific sites via triplex formation [, ].

A related but slightly different strategy has recently emerged. It involves polypurine reverse Hoogsteen hairpins (PPRHs). These DNA hairpins, formed by intramolecular reverse Hoogsteen bonds, bind to polypyrimidine stretches in dsDNA via Watson-Crick base pairing, thereby forming a triplex and displacing the complementary strand of the duplex, potentially allowing G4 formation [].

Triplex characterization is performed using a plethora of methods, including bioinformatics (Triplexator and 3plex), biophysical, biochemical, and genomic approaches [, , , ]. Some ligands have also been reported to recognize triplex structures. One of the earliest examples was the benzo[e]pyridoindole derivative (BePI), which showed preferential binding and intercalation to triplex over duplex DNA []. However, although several ligands can bind triplex DNA, not all display true structural selectivity, as some also interact with duplex DNA or bind through nonspecific intercalation. In contrast, other compounds have been reported to exhibit improved selectivity, including neomycin, an effective groove-binding stabilizer of DNA triple helices, and benzopyridoquinoxaline derivatives, which have shown preferential recognition of triplex DNA [, ]. More recently, flavone-derived compounds have also been reported to bind triplex DNA more strongly than duplex DNA, further expanding the range of potential triplex-selective ligands []. Antibodies targeting triplex structures (Jel 318 and Jel 466) were used for immunofluorescence studies of DNA triplexes. However, these antibodies are not universally selective under all conditions [, ]. Beyond selectivity concerns, immunofluorescence detection with Jel 318 and Jel 466 requires fixation, raising the same fixation-artefact concerns discussed for BG4 in the “G-Quadruplex” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section. More critically, both antibodies were shown to inhibit replication and transcription in isolated nuclei by approximately 20% upon binding, indicating that they are not simply passive reporters but also perturbators of the very processes under study. This feature, probably true for most compounds targeting nucleic acids, complicates the interpretation of any downstream functional readout obtained in their presence []. Moreover, these probes exhibit distinct nuclear and chromosomal staining patterns, suggesting differences in their recognition properties and modes of triplex binding.

More recently, a chemoproteomic approach using a photo-crosslinking triplex-selective probe (photoBQQ) [] was proposed for monitoring triplex DNA dynamics and enrichment of triplex structures for sequencing, as well as enabling the direct profiling of the endogenous protein interactome of triplex DNA in living cells, using Jel 466 as an orthogonal positive control. Thus, the methods represent a methodological step beyond antibody-based imaging toward unbiased cell-based validation.

Regarding sequencing methods, and differently from G4 and iM, which use mainly antibody-based methods, an alternative approach was reported for triplex and termed Triplex-seq []. This methodology is a deep-sequencing method that systematically maps the interaction space between an oligo library of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) triplex-forming oligos  and a particular dsDNA triplex target site (TTS).

R-loops consist of three distinct nucleic acid strands formed by a DNA:RNA hybrid duplex and an associated displaced single-stranded DNA, as first demonstrated by the Davis group in 1976 [–].

Structurally, the DNA:RNA hybrid duplex does not adopt the canonical B-form geometry of dsDNA, instead occupying an intermediate duplex conformation between the A and B forms, actually closer to the A form. This shift is driven by the stronger rigidity of the RNA strand and by the 2′ hydroxyl group, imposing a C3′-endo sugar pucker, which narrows the major groove and widens the minor groove relative to B DNA (minor groove width 8.5 to 10.5 Å versus 7.4 Å for canonical B-DNA) [–]. Additionally, it is also reported that glycosidic torsion angles in the DNA strand are around −120°, whereas those in the RNA strand are in the range −140° to −160° []. Compared to DNA and RNA duplexes, the distinct flexibility of the RNA:DNA hybrid duplex in stretching and in twist-stretch coupling arises mainly from its different base pair inclination within the helical structure, consistent with its α-form and mixed sequence composition []. This distinctive geometric signature, rather than sequence alone, allows structure-specific factors such as RNase H to recognize the hybrid independently of its functional context [].

The structure forms co-transcriptionally, favored by RNA polymerase that unwinds the DNA double-helix. This allows the nascent RNA to hybridize to its complementary DNA template strand, creating a stable or transient DNA:RNA hybrid, while displacing the non-template DNA strand into a single-stranded loop configuration (Fig. ) [, , ]. These DNA:RNA hybrids are not randomly distributed, and genome-wide maps reveal enrichment at promoters and terminators, CpG islands, replication origins, ribosomal DNA, and telomeres, as well as at mitochondrial replication regions and repetitive tracts such as CGG or GAA repeats [, –]. The physical size of R-loops varies widely with the genomic context. Promoter-proximal R-loops are typically short, confined to a few tens of base pairs, whereas elongation-associated R-loops show a median length of approximately 300 bp and can extend to several kilobases [, ]. Importantly, larger R-loop peaks observed in some genome-wide maps may result from clustering of multiple shorter and individual R-loops, rather than from a single continuous hybrid.

R-loop formation exhibits strong sequence specificity, with G-rich transcripts and C-rich template strands representing the most favorable configurations, liberating a G-rich DNA strand. The enhanced thermodynamic stability of G-C base pairing in DNA:RNA hybrids compared to equivalent DNA:DNA interactions provides the driving force for R-loop nucleation and extension [, ]. The displaced single-stranded DNA can adopt secondary structures that further stabilize the R-loop, and G4 is one of the structures frequently formed on G-rich displaced strands [, ]. These G4/R-loop hybrid structures exhibit enhanced stability and represent important regulatory complexes that influence transcription, replication, and chromatin organization (Fig. ) [, ].

R-loop abundance is dynamic over the cell cycle, typically peaking in S phase when transcription and replication collide and being resolved before mitosis by dedicated enzymes (RNase H1 and RNase H2) and helicases (SETX and DHX9) that reset the template [, , ]. Because of their similar A-form-like structure, which is poorly compatible with nucleosome wrapping, R-loop formation is intrinsically coupled to local chromatin state [, ]. In vitro, RNA:DNA hybrids have been shown to prevent nucleosome deposition, and genome-wide R-loop-enriched regions correspondingly show increased DNase I hypersensitivity and reduced nucleosome occupancy [, ]. Notably, this relationship is bidirectional, with R-loop formation promoting local chromatin decondensation, while their resolution facilitates chromatin re-compaction []. Thus, R-loops should therefore be viewed as both consequences and drivers of local chromatin accessibility, rather than purely functional byproducts of transcription.

Furthermore, R-loops serve as critical regulators of gene expression at multiple levels of transcriptional control. At promoter regions, R-loops can either facilitate or inhibit transcription initiation depending on the specific genomic context and associated protein factors [, ]. Activating R-loops promote chromatin decondensation and recruits the transcriptional machinery, while repressive R-loops can block access of transcription factors to their binding sites [, , , ].

Abnormally expressed and over-abundant R-loops become detrimental to the cell under certain circumstances, namely when RNA processing/export is impaired, topoisomerases or RNase H pathways are compromised, under replication stress or oncogenic hyper-transcription, or as a result of stabilizing features of other structures like G4, which trap hybrids [, –]. These long-lived structures impede replication forks and elongating RNA polymerase, provoking transcription-replication conflicts and aberrant gene regulation, or triggering genome instability contributing to cancer and neurodegenerative disease contexts [–].

Some algorithms, such as QmRLFS-finder or R-loopAtlas, have been developed to predict R-loop formation sites and propensity [, ]. Biophysical and biochemical methods such as gel-based assays, single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) or magnetic tweezers can be employed for R-loop characterization in vitro []. Yet, these biophysical assays are typically performed on short synthetic RNA:DNA hybrid substrates or plasmid-based model systems rather than on endogenous genomic loci, limiting their ability to capture the influence of native chromatin context on R-loop structure. Interestingly, a genetically encoded sensor, termed RHINO, was recently proposed as an alternative method for studying the abundance and dynamics of cellular R-loops through live-cell imaging []. As this method relies on overexpression of an exogenous engineered protein, it raises the same concerns discussed for G4-Flame in the “G-Quadruplex” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section regarding potential perturbation of the native RNA:DNA hybrid equilibrium. Notably, the authors reported that RHINO foci have been observed in the nucleus and nucleoli but with poor colocalization with S9.6 antibody signal, an unresolved discrepancy that raises the question of whether these two detection tools report on the same underlying population of RNA:DNA hybrid structures.

R-loop detection in cells relies primarily on the S9.6 antibody, which exhibits high specificity and affinity for DNA–RNA hybrids, and on the use of antibody-based approaches such as DRIP-seq and its variants [, , , ]. However, their performance was recently questioned since it was also described the ability of S9.6 to interact with double-stranded RNA(dsRNA) with weaker affinity than with RNA–DNA hybrids, which can generate many false-positive signals [–]. Therefore, S9.6-based signals alone cannot be considered definitive evidence of R-loop formation and should be supported by RNase H digestion controls and, whenever possible, with other orthogonal detection methods. To overcome this limitation, the R-ChIP method, based on exogenous catalytically inactive RNase-H1 enzyme, which presents higher affinity compared with the S9.6 antibody, was proposed for the detection of R-loop structures without their resolution [, ]. More recently, a similar approach, now based on the use of RNase H3 (enDR3), allowed genome-wide R-loop profiling in vivo and ex vivo []. A major limitation of these methods, and shared with the RHINO sensor previously discussed, is the requirement to express a mutant, exogenous RNase H1 in cells, which may not be feasible in all experimental systems and can itself generate artifacts if the overexpressed protein outcompetes or interferes with endogenous RNase H1 activity []. Nevertheless, RNase H-derived probes recognize the RNA hybrid moiety rather than the complete three-stranded R-loop and may detect populations distinct from those identified using S9.6. Consequently, no single method currently provides a definitive genome-wide map of R-loops, and cross-validation using independent approaches remains necessary. Beyond that, the experimental protocols are once again based on chemical fixation, highlighting the concerns already discussed in the previous sections.

Z-DNA and Z-RNA represent distinctive left-handed double-helical conformations of nucleic acids, in contrast to the conventional right-handed B- and A-form structures []. This structure, proposed by Wang et al. in 1979 [], is narrower and more elongated than right-handed duplexes, with a zig-zag pattern giving its name, which results from alternating sugar-phosphate backbone conformations where one base in each pair adopts the syn-conformation while its complement remains in the anti-conformation (Fig. ) [, ].

The closer proximity of phosphate groups in Z-form also creates increased electrostatic repulsion, making Z-nucleic acids thermodynamically less stable compared to B-forms at moderate ionic strength []. The optimal sequence requirement for Z-DNA formation involves purines adopting a syn-conformation and pyrimidines keeping an anti-conformation, creating the alternating pattern necessary for a stable Z-form structure []. Nevertheless, studies reveal that alternation is not an absolute requirement for Z-form adoption: specific conditions, involving chemical modifications or ionic environments (Mg2+, Ca2+, Li+, Na+; high concentrations needed for the last two cations), can also induce the formation of Z-structures []. Chemical modifications like methylation at the N7 position of guanine, which creates positive charges that neutralize phosphate repulsion, or bromination at the C8 position of G and the C5 position of C, promote the syn conformation and play crucial roles in stabilization []. Physiologically, during transcriptional processes, RNA polymerase movement generates negative supercoiling waves behind the elongation complex, creating torsional stress that favors Z-form adoption in susceptible sequences. This transcription-induced supercoiling can drive Z-form conversion even under physiological salt conditions where Z-nucleic acids would otherwise be unstable [, ]. Thus, these conformations are alternatively termed “flipons” because they present dynamic transitions between left- and right-handed forms; however, despite their structural features being well known and recognized, an effective understanding of their role in biological processes remains unanswered. This interconversion favors duplex opening, allowing the formation of other structures like G4, for example.

It is important to note that Z-DNA is thermodynamically less stable than B-DNA under standard physiological ionic conditions, and its in vivo formation depends on negative supercoiling, most commonly generated transcriptionally, or on binding by Z-DNA-stabilizing proteins that offset the energetic cost of the transition [, ]. This dependence means that Z-DNA formation is expected to be transient and locus-specific rather than a constitutive genomic feature, consistent with the dynamic, transcription-coupled signal (observed by chemical footprinting approaches discussed below). Accordingly, the proposed in vivo functions of Z-DNA and Z-RNA should be interpreted in the context of the available detection approaches, for which cross-validation between antibody-based and antibody-independent methods remains limited.

In the genome, flipons cluster at promoters and enhancers and provide dynamic regulatory switches responding to transcriptional activity and chromatin remodeling. Recent advances in understanding Z-nucleic acid biology have revealed their critical roles in viral defense, autoimmune diseases, and cancer pathogenesis, being associated with Zα domain proteins (ADAR1 and ZBP1), which recognize Z-structures [–], but also to DNA and RNA G4 through the Zβ domain, as recently demonstrated []. Interestingly, ADAR1 demonstrated the ability to promote A-to-Z transitions in dsRNA under near-physiological conditions [, ]. Additionally, in vivo evidence displayed the importance of Z-DNA conformational change, demonstrating that Z-DNA is formed during fear learning in the prefrontal cortex of mice and reduced during extinction learning [].

The characterization of flipons is also grounded in the use of several methods, first for prediction through the use of specialized algorithms such as ZSeeker, Z-DNABERT, and Z-Hunt [, –]. These approaches identify sequences with the potential to adopt a Z-conformation but do not demonstrate that the structure forms in cells or in vivo. Experimental investigation involves classical spectroscopic methods, including circular dichroism (CD), NMR, and smFRET; biochemical approaches based on labeled nucleobases; and genomic methods such as ZIP-seq and Z22-based CUT&Tag [, , –], as critically summarized by Zhang et al. []. Anti-Z-DNA antibodies, including Z-D11 and Z22, have also been used to detect Z-DNA in vitro and in cellular samples [, , ]; however, antibody-based evidence should be interpreted cautiously because probe binding can stabilize or, in the case of Z22, induce the B-to-Z transition []. Consequently, the detected signal may not represent the unperturbed endogenous Z-DNA population. Recently, these antibodies were combined with cryo-EM to enable structural characterization of the Z-DNA conformation and to clarify how these antibodies recognize it [].

Beyond antibody-based approaches, chemical methods have also been developed to map Z-DNA genome-wide. Permanganate/S1 nuclease (KEx) footprinting and kethoxal-assisted single-stranded DNA sequencing (KAS-seq) exploit the exposed or chemically accessible single-stranded character of the B-Z junction to detect Z-DNA formation transcriptome-wide on a timescale of seconds to minutes, providing indirect evidence for transient, transcription-coupled Z-DNA formation independently of antibodies [, ]. Complementary chromatin-domain approaches, such as Zα-domain-based ChIP-seq, have similarly been used to map putative Z-DNA-forming sites without relying on Z-D11 or Z22 []. Cross-validation among chemical, Zα-domain-based, and antibody-based approaches remains limited and represents an important direction to establish a consensus genome-wide Z-DNA landscape.

DNA junctions are branched nucleic acid structures that arise wherever three or more helical arms converge at a single point (branch point) []. They are typically formed in direct repeats (DR; multiple consecutive tandem repeats) or inverted repeats (IR; the first and second half of the sequence are reverse complementary), which influence the formation of three-way DNA junctions (3WJ or TWJ) or four-way DNA junctions (4WJ or FWJ), respectively (Fig. ) [, ]. Bioinformatic analysis demonstrated that IRs account for over 6 million occurrences in the human genome (approximately 206 per 100 kb) and 1.6% of autosomal DNA, while DRs are present in 13.1% (1–9 bp-long) and 18.6% (10–100 bp-long) [, ].

The best-studied member of this family is the 4WJ, also known as cruciform DNA or Holliday junctions (HJ), being theoretically described for the first time by J. R. Platt in 1955 [] and then postulated in 1964 by R. Holliday as a structural intermediate to explain gene conversion during homologous recombination []. Their formation occurs by reciprocal exchange of single strands between two homologous duplexes. Contrary to other structures, their formation is based on the release of accumulated torsional stress via a “transfer-twist” mechanism during DNA supercoiling [–]. In solution, the junction can adopt two principal conformations, namely the stacked-X form (comprising isoform I and isoform II), in which the four helical arms pair into two coaxially stacked antiparallel duplexes, or the open-planar X form, in which all four arms extend toward the corners of a square with approximate fourfold symmetry (Fig. ) [–]. Thus, mechanistically, the formation of a 4WJ (Holliday junction) is initiated by the alignment of two homologous duplex DNA molecules, followed by single-strand nicks at equivalent positions on strands of the same polarity [, ]. Then, the nicked strands dissociate, and each invades the opposing duplex, establishing a heteroduplex region that is sealed by DNA ligase to yield the covalently closed four-stranded X-shaped intermediate [, , ].

The transition between the open-X and stacked-X forms is dynamic and reversible, being critically dependent on the nature and concentration of cations in solution, the pH and the presence of recognition elements like proteins or small molecules [, , –]. Under near-physiological ionic conditions, the stacked-X conformation predominates, and it was the first to be crystallographically confirmed by Ortiz-Lombardía et al. [], while the open-X form is the biologically active conformation recognized by branch migration enzymes and resolvases [, ]. In the absence or low cation concentration, electrostatic repulsion between the four negatively charged phosphate backbones forces the structure to adopt the open-planar X form, in which four arms extend into a square-planar arrangement, creating an accessible and C4-symmetric central cavity [, ]. Upon addition of divalent cations, such as Mg2+, charge neutralization at the phosphate backbone allows the four arms to pair up into two quasi-continuous antiparallel B-DNA duplexes joined by a crossover, running antiparallel and crossing in a right-handed manner with an inter-duplex angle between 40° and 60°, driving the transition to the compact stacked-X conformation (Fig. ) [, , , ]. Additionally, the structural integrity at the branch point is maintained by van der Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds between the phosphate groups of one duplex and the major groove of the other [].

Alternatively, the 3WJ, also known as slipped-strand DNA, hypothesized by Arthur Kornberg in 1964 and later coined by the Ned Seeman group in 1982 [], configures the simplest branched DNA structure, consisting of three double-stranded arms converging at a branch point and can be classified as a Y-junction or T-junction depending on arm geometry (Fig. ) [, ]. Unlike the 4WJ, the 3WJ connects three duplex domains through a central node where strand continuity is maintained with no helix-helix coaxial stacking, resulting in a distinctly different conformational behavior also influenced by cations [, , –]. They are characterized by a C3-symmetric hydrophobic central cavity (10–15 Å diameter) whose dimensions and geometry are modulated by the sequences flanking the branch point, providing a tractable target for selective small-molecule recognition (later discussed in the “DNA junctions” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section) [, , ]. This type of junction can be perfectly or imperfectly complementary at the branch point due to base mismatches or improper alignment []. In the absence of unpaired bases at the branch point, fully complementary 3WJs (termed as 3H) adopt an extended, symmetric trigonal geometry with roughly equal angles between the arms; however, this arrangement is geometrically strained, as the three B-form helices cannot simultaneously satisfy their preferred helical parameters at the crossing point [, , , ]. To accommodate this steric incompatibility, the junction undergoes local backbone distortions and forced unstacking of the strictly complementary bases at the node, creating a central cavity [, ]. To overcome that, the introduction of one or more unpaired nucleotides at the branch point relieves this mechanical strain by acting as a flexible hinge. This eliminates the need for node distortion, disrupts the trigonal symmetry, and causes one arm to fold toward the others, yielding a more stable, asymmetric Y-shaped conformation often stabilized by the coaxial stacking of two adjacent helices [, , ]. Thus, a naming convention has been established for imperfect junctions, namely terming 3HS2 the 3WJ containing two unpaired nucleotides at the branch point and 2HS2HS1 for two unpaired nucleotides on one arm adjacent to the branch point and a single unpaired nucleotide on another arm [].

Biologically, DNA junctions (3WJ and 4WJ) appear transiently during DNA replication, recombination, and repair, and their proper processing is essential for both genome stability and controlled genetic maintenance [, , ]. The 3WJ arises at replication forks, during recombination events that do not involve active replication, and in several repair pathways, where they need to be remodeled to allow synthesis or ligation to proceed [, , , ]. DNA junctions have also been described to occur in viral genomes, notably in the inverted terminal repeats of adeno-associated virus (AAV), where they act as structured replication origins and integration signals [, ]. Already, the 4WJ plays a pivotal role in homologous recombination and double-strand break (DSB) repair, yielding either crossover or non-crossover products and influencing genetic diversity and genome stability, as well as in replication fork regression and on the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway [, –]. Furthermore, these junctions also engage a wide range of proteins, including branch migration and resolvase enzymes (RuvA/RuvB/RuvC, GEN1, and MUS81-EME1), site-specific recombinases (λ integrase), and junction-recognizing small molecules that modulate their stability and conformational dynamics [, , , , , ].

The identification and characterization of DNA junctions, similarly to the other structures, are based on the combination of bioinformatic, biophysical, and genomic evidence. In contrast to other non-canonical structures, there are currently no widely adopted genome-wide prediction tools or algorithms dedicated to 3WJ and 4WJ prediction, and most efforts instead combine sequence-based identification of DR, IR and palindromic repeats with biochemical knowledge of recombination and repair hotspots [, , ].

Then, the hypothesized DNA junctions are assembled in vitro and subsequently characterized using an array of structural and biophysical methods to evaluate formation and geometry ranging from the classical native gel electrophoresis, smFRET, X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy [, , –] to the recently reported steady or time-resolved cryo-EM studies for DNA junctions [–]. Beyond that, biochemical assays are used to track nuclease cleavage, ligation, and remodeling by recombinases, helicases, and resolvases [–]. Unlike other non-canonical structures, for which dedicated high-throughput sequencing-based approaches have been developed, genome-wide detection of DNA junctions relies primarily on methods that map recombination intermediates, DNA repair events, and protein-associated DNA structures, such as CC-seq [], X-seq [], single-stranded DNA sequencing (ChIP-SSDS) [], or END-seq [, ]. More recently, a dedicated method for 4WJ, termed HJSeq, uses a Holliday-junction-binding peptide to directly capture the structure and represents, to date, the only genome-wide method providing direct structural evidence of junction location rather than an indirect proxy based on its processing or repair [].

Notably, sequence-independent monoclonal antibodies capable of directly recognizing 4WJ structures, termed 2D3 and 4B4, were developed for affinity purification and for immunofluorescence-based detection in cells [–], but have never been coupled to high-throughput sequencing, representing a promising complement and avenue to previously reported direct and indirect genomic methods. Additionally, 4WJ structures were also reported to form in cell as demonstrated by electron microscopy in prokaryotes and by bidimensional electrophoresis in eukaryotes [, ].

As previously evidenced, non-canonical structures play potential biological roles and, in certain cases, may contribute to several pathologies like cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, or infectious diseases. Thus, mechanistic insights now provide a blueprint for potential intervention in structures such as G4, iM, triplexes, R-loops, Z-DNA, and DNA junctions, which can be stabilized or destabilized to tune gene expression, stall replication, or sensitize tumors to therapy. As introduced above, therapeutic strategies that treat non-canonical nucleic acid structures as drug targets differ fundamentally from classical protein-directed approaches, because they directly act at the DNA and RNA levels. In this section, we will focus on how distinct therapeutic approaches (Fig. ) can recognize, stabilize, or destabilize specific structures in order to control biological processes.

The most well-known approach to target G4s is based on the use of small molecules, also termed G4 ligands, which interact with G4s. Such ligands affect cell growth by interfering with telomere maintenance, stabilizing G4s in oncogene promoters and modulating gene expression, regulating helicase unwinding and replication, or regulating post-translational G4s in 5′-UTR mRNA regions []. Because G4s offer unique structural features (planar tetrad faces, specific grooves, and loop pockets) and their cation-stabilized cores do not exist in canonical duplex DNA/RNA, they present druggable epitopes with the potential for selectivity by topology, locus, and cell state.

Many G4 ligands share hallmark features, namely a planar and extended aromatic scaffold that allows end-stacking on exposed tetrads via π–π interactions, flexible side chains that engage the grooves/loops interface and also carry one or more positive charges to enhance electrostatic contacts with the polyanionic backbone []. These common features are both a blessing and a curse: while the rational design of G4-specific compounds may be proposed (as these features are lacking in other nucleic acid structures), selective binding to a specific G4 remains challenging, as most quadruplexes share these features. Depending on scaffold and substituents, these ligands can stabilize or destabilize specific G4, and in some cases exhibit preference for one topology (parallel, antiparallel or hybrid), loop composition/length, and groove dimensions.

To date, thousands of small molecules targeting these structures have been developed and are deposited in the G4 Ligand Database (G4LDB) [–]. These molecules can be grouped according to chemical families and can include porphyrins, naphthalene diimides, quinolones, phenanthrolines, acridines, bisquinoliniums, and macrocycles and natural products [, , , , –]. Despite progress in G4 ligand design and synthesis, a complementary and efficient evaluation regarding their binding mode and nature of the interactions with G4s is necessary. Thus, several experimental approaches (biophysical and biochemical) are employed to characterize G4/ligand interactions and can be divided into structure-based methods, affinity and apparent affinity-based methods, high-throughput methods, affinity chromatography, and microarrays []. Very recently, a machine learning-based tool, termed AGAPE (Computational G-quadruplex Stabilization Prediction), was designed to predict the stabilizing potential of small molecules targeting G4s and aiming to accelerate the discovery of selective G4-targeting compounds [].

Depending on the biological mechanism and the therapeutic purpose, G4 ligands can be applied as stabilizers or destabilizers, with the latter representing an emerging approach regarding G4 ligands (Fig. ). In the first case, a number of compounds have been described, and several are commercially available, such as PDS, BRACO-19, and PhenDC3. Interestingly, some of these molecules exhibit the ability to modulate G4 structures in vitro in terms of topological conformation upon ligand binding, like PhenDC3 and PyDH2 [, ].

In sharp contrast to this long list of G4 ligands, very few of them entered clinical trials (Table ). CX-3543 (Quarfloxin; NCT00955786) was the first G4 ligand to enter clinical trials in 2005. Other molecules have achieved the same milestone since then, such as CX-5461 (Pidnarulex; NCT02719977), APTO-253 (NCT02267863), and more recently QN-302 (NCT06086522) [–]. Beyond these advances, a rising trend is being developed by exploring the synergistic combination of G4 ligands and chemotherapeutic drugs to sensitize cancer cells [].

G4 ligands enrolled in Clinical Trials studies

Beyond their application in cancer and other diseases, bacterial G4s are increasingly being explored as potential targets for innovative antimicrobial strategies. Putative G4-forming sequences have been identified in several pathogenic bacteria, including P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, E. coli, N. gonorrhoeae, M. tuberculosis, and H. pylori, stimulating the development of small molecules capable of targeting bacterial G4 structures. To date, several ligands (NDI-10, PDS, L20, and Ni-salphen) targeting bacterial G4s have been reported [, , –], supporting bacterial G4s as emerging antimicrobial targets. However, important challenges remain and are identified compared to human G4s, particularly efficient intracellular accumulation. The bacterial envelope represents a major barrier to small-molecule uptake, including the thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria, which strongly restricts small-molecule entry by passive permeation, and the outer membrane and efflux systems characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria.

A second emerging class comprises destabilizers, sometimes referred to as molecular helicases, that aim to disfavor G4 formation or promote helicase access where pathological G4s impede replication or translation []. So far, only a handful of small molecules have been shown to effectively destabilize G4 structures (PhpC, 2′-FC3, ANC, TANC, and DANC) [–], but mainly PhpC stands out for destabilizing and for its ability to modulate G4s at a transcriptome-wide scale [, , , ].

Despite these advances, major challenges remain regarding G4 targeting in relation to selectivity: even if most molecules have a marked preference for G4s over ssDNA and dsDNA, multiple off-targets may be present as multiple G4s coexist within a cell. This lack of topology- and locus-selectivity is a plausible contributor to why, to date, no G4 ligand has completed the full clinical trial process, since stabilizing off-target G4s in essential regulatory regions may translate into dose-limiting toxicity and side effects.

Additional factors need to be addressed, such as intrinsic chemical properties that influence therapeutic application (poor solubility and toxicity), delivery, and stability (barrier-crossing ability, nuclease resistance, and endosomal escape). Cell context dependency also poses a challenge because chromatin state, local cation composition, strand polarity, and competition with G4-binding proteins and helicases complicate effective ligand binding [].

To address these challenges, precise targeting and delivery of G4 ligands using ligand conjugates constitute a future avenue. For example, associated with the detection properties previously mentioned, oligonucleotide-ligand conjugates can also be used for precise therapeutics, forming a dual tool for both G4 detection and therapeutics [, –]. Another study reported the conjugation of G4 ligands (pyridodicarboxamide and pyridostatin) and nucleolin protein with a CRISPR system to selectively facilitate single or multiple targeted G4 folding within specific genomic loci [].
