This methodology allows intra-G4 selectivity, which is one of the main limits to clinical application of G4-binding ligands, compared with traditional G4 ligands, resulting in cell proliferation arrest, differentiation inhibition, and cell senescence []. Other CRISPR-based ligand conjugates were reported in the so-called ATENA strategy (Approach to Target Exact Nucleic Acid alternative structures) []. ATENA demonstrated that selective targeting of the C-MYC G4 leads to the suppression of transcripts regulated exclusively by one of its promoters (Fig. ). In addition, the development of G4-PROTACs (Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras) and RIBOTACs (Ribonuclease Targeting Chimeras), which couple G4 binders to recruiting modules for E3 ubiquitin ligases and RNase L, respectively, has gained prominence, and several examples have already been reported in the literature [–].

Alternatives for G4 targeting based only on oligonucleotides were also explored. Brooks et al. reported a short oligonucleotide connected by an abasic linker capable of binding to 5′ and 3′ regions flanking the C-MYC G4 and modulating promoter activity with a significant and dose-dependent effect on transcription []. Moreover, antisense strategies have also been explored for G4 modulation. Aiming to increase the G4-dependent translation inhibition of MAOB mRNAs, Turcotte and Perrault synthesized G-ASOs (unmodified DNA or 2′OMe) capable of recognizing and inducing a new rG4 folding, leading to enhanced G4-dependent translational repression in vitro and in cells []. In a distinct paradigm, inspired by the destabilizing rational effects of small molecules, Pirota et al. developed a PNA conjugate to selectively disrupt G4 within the SNCA gene promoter, observing a decrease in both SNCA mRNA and α-synuclein protein content [].

More recently, another emerging approach, started in 2020, is based on the targeting of functional G4 structures using L-RNA aptamers (also known as spiegelmers), which are entirely composed of L-ribonucleotides and exhibit superior biostability and nuclease degradation resistance compared to natural D-aptamers (further explained in “Non-canonical nucleic acids as therapeutics” section). This technology was developed and applied to the G4 field by the Kwok group, which demonstrated that L-RNA aptamers can effectively regulate G4-mediated cellular processes by inhibiting G4–protein interactions and/or modulating transcription and translation, influencing gene expression both in vitro and in vivo [–]. Moreover, several conjugation and modification strategies have been developed to improve the cellular delivery and functionality of L-RNA aptamers, including conjugation with cell-penetrating peptides, antisense oligonucleotides, and fluorogenic compounds, as well as aptamer cyclization [–]. The SELEX methodology underlying aptamer selection is discussed in detail in “Non-canonical nucleic acids as therapeutics” section.

On the peptide side, which for some authors is considered the next generation of G4-interacting ligands, several strategies have been developed (Fig. ). The use of biologically active peptides for therapeutic intervention instead of the whole protein aims to surpass the limitations of using whole proteins because of their high manufacturing cost, laborious structure prediction, dynamic nature, and inefficient penetration due to their size and unavailability for oral administration []. Sharma et al. summarized all the advances in targeting G4 using peptides and discussed their relevance through a comprehensive and detailed review (Table ) []. G4-binding peptides can be classified according to their binding attributes, such as binding modes (tetrads, loops, and bulges), shape of the molecule and the chemical composition []. QW10 (QQWQQQQWQQ) is a 10-mer peptide demonstrating sequence-specific behavior, both stabilizing and destabilizing G4s found in the C-MYC oncogene and at telomeres, respectively [–]. Bicyclic peptides identified by phage display were also described by the Balasubramanian group as an alternative class of G4 ligands, with high affinity for C-KIT2 G4 structures and high selectivity over duplex DNA []. Another short peptide derived from the DHX36 helicase, termed DM039, exhibits selectivity toward G4 with preferential binding to C-MYC G4 []. Concerning RNA G4, the Kwok group reported Pep11 as a peptide binder that binds specifically to RNA G4s []. More recently, the same group proposed the rational design of chimeric peptides, combining Pep11 with a native peptide (Rhau18) derived from the endogenous DHX36 protein, reporting a 10-fold enhancement over the individual modules, selectivity for rG4s and functional activity on translation and telomerase activity [].

Moving to PNA, this class of nucleic acid analogues stands out for its exceptionally high affinity and specificity toward nucleic acids, resistance to nuclease and protease degradation, and ability to invade dsDNA []. The Calmyc PNA was shown to invade C-MYC G4 to form two 3-tetrad PNA–DNA hybrid G4s [].

Similarly to G4, the iM follows the same therapeutic rationale. Most of the studies reported in the literature evaluated the iM targeting using small molecules, which are characterized by heteroaromatic scaffolds π-extended with strategic cationic or hydrogen-bonding substituents. Unlike G4, which often succeeds by flat end-stacking, effective iM binders tend to rely on loop/groove recognition and end-capping of the intercalated stack rather than indiscriminate stacking on a terminal plane. This may happen because iMs expose four very different grooves, two extremely narrow ones that should not allow insertion of any compound unless the structure is deformed, and two very shallow and wide grooves, poorly compatible with small ligand binding [–]. Examples of iM ligands are deposited in the G4LDB database, and the most relevant were recently reviewed [, ]. The first study addressing the interaction between an iM structure and a small molecule was conducted with TMPyP4 []. Yet, this molecule is known to interact with many different nucleic acid structures, and this compound cannot be considered as iM-specific. Since then, other compounds such as phenanthroline derivatives, acridone derivatives or natural products were reported to bind to iM [–]. Interestingly, one peptidomimetic ligand, called PBP1, beyond selectively targeting iM, showed a remarkable ability to induce the structure from the unstructured ssDNA conformations and led to an upregulation of gene expression [].

One of the most promising ligands reported to date was the benzothiophene-2-carboxamide (NSC309874), which binds selectively to PDGFR-β iM with the ability to downregulate PDGFR-β promoter activity and transcription in vitro []. Despite the promising results, supported by luciferase reporter assays, Taq polymerase stop assays and the selective knockdown of PDGFR-β, it may be premature to conclude that the observed effects are exclusively mediated through transcriptional regulation. The reported outcomes should always be viewed as supportive but not definitive evidence of the proposed mechanism. This highlights the need for more comprehensive and extensive studies, including, for example, analyses of nascent RNA in iM-mutant and wild-type cell lines, as well as integrated transcriptomic and proteomic approaches. Thus, a comprehensive experimental workflow will be essential for elucidating and confirming that the intended mechanism underlies the observed effects and to discriminate or discover potential alternative or parallel mechanisms that may contribute to the observed effects. Therefore, a complete confirmation is needed for the effective validation of new molecules as specific, selective and effective iM binders, and the same rationale is true for compounds targeting other non-canonical structures.

In the case of the BCL2 promoter oncogene, two molecules were identified to carry distinct behaviors: IMC-48 stabilizes the iM structure, upregulating expression and modulating lymphoma biology, while IMC-76 disrupts iM formation and promotes hairpin structures, leading to transcriptional repression of the BCL2 oncogene []. In another study addressing other iM DNA sequences were shown to be very weak ligands or to have no quantifiable interaction []. Yet, the selectivity of these ellipticine derivatives remains to be firmly established.

Another molecule, reported by King et al., was demonstrated to stabilize iM accompanied by the formation induction in cells after 71795-ligand treatment []. Aiming to screen and to explore the potential duality of molecules, studies with commercial ligands or molecules usually applied to target G4, such as PDS, berberine, or PhenDC3, were also done; however, no binding was found [, ]. The Randazzo group also explored the use of G4 ligands as iM-binding molecules []. They demonstrated that some compounds could interact with both G4 and iM DNA in vitro, acting as multi-target-directed agents, and highlighted the importance of testing G4-targeting compounds against the iM counterpart. Very recently, the Li group identified a new carbazole derivative termed G51 as a unique dual-targeting ligand that simultaneously destabilizes the iM and stabilizes the G4, consequently suppressing C-MYB expression efficiently []. A second study reported an iM-templated target-guided synthesis strategy that yields a 1,4-triazolyl carbazole ligand with high affinity and selectivity for telomeric iM DNA over G4 and duplex forms, resulting in potent telomerase inhibition [].

Contrary to G4, there are no iM ligands in clinical trials, and research remains largely at the pre-clinical/in vitro and cellular stages. Due to this, strategies envisioning drug repositioning can be adapted and approved drugs can be screened for emergent targets. Thus, one of the studies aimed to explore mitoxantrone, widely applied in clinics as a chemotherapeutic, as a potential iM binder []. Results demonstrated that mitoxantrone can bind, induce folding of and stabilize iM formation, even at physiological pH; however, behavior in a full cellular context remains to be fully established.

Research on iM ligands remains sparse, a major bottleneck for the field, highlighting the need to discover new ligands, map their interactions with iM-prone sequences, define their specificity, and determine whether they recognize the folded iM or actively promote its unfolding. The compounds listed so far not only bind to iM but sometimes also recognize other structures, including duplex DNA or G4s. Also, the doubts on the limited stability at physiological pH and in vivo persistence have direct implications for druggability. Hence, if only the most stable iM-forming sequences remain folded at physiological pH inside cells, stabilizing ligands may only be pharmacologically relevant at a narrow subset of loci, constituting an additional challenge — or opportunity — for the rational targeting of iM structures at specific genomic locations and for subsequent clinical translation. Unlike G4, current iM-targeting strategies remain largely confined to the in vitro biochemical characterization and cellular-level binding, with no compound having advanced to a stage where clinical potential can be meaningfully assessed.

Finding a truly specific iM ligand is more challenging than finding a specific G4 ligand because the latter offers several interesting recognition epitopes such as terminal G-quartets, although a terminal-quartet interaction is also the principal driver of the limited cross-topology selectivity, since most G4-forming sequences expose structurally similar terminal tetrads regardless of overall fold. The situation is further complexified by possible artefacts, as discussed by Granzhan or Dejeu: several of the iM-ligands described so far exhibit poor selectivity or affinity [, ].

The ATENA methodology, applicable to G4 as mentioned before, and based on a CRISPR conjugation with a ligand, was employed for iM targeting []. In this iM approach, the system was conjugated with the RVS peptide led to a significant increase in P1-driven (~2-fold increase) C-MYC transcription in contrast to the transcriptional repression observed upon MYC-G4 targeting. The methodology’s success was only possible due to previous research conducted by the Waller group that identified a new class of short peptides capable of recognizing with high affinity and specificity iMs over G4s [].

Triplex structures can potentially form endogenously in both DNA and RNA contexts. In genomic DNA, intramolecular triplexes such as H-DNA can form at appropriate sequence motifs [, ], whereas triple-helical structures have also been described within long noncoding RNAs, including MALAT1, PAN, and MENβ []. Thus, therapeutic targeting of these structures is of utmost relevance, and the approaches can range from the use of small molecules in the case of H-DNA that does not need an external sequence to form a triplex, to oligonucleotide-based drugs designed to exploit triple helix formation with dsDNA, also known as TFOs.

Small molecules may once again be used to stabilize or disrupt triplexes, depending on the pathological molecular role’s context (Fig. ). The triplex stabilizers typically bind by three distinct mechanisms, namely by intercalating between stacked base triads, capping the triplex end or recognizing the groove/loop that strengthens Hoogsteen contacts without duplex binding.

To date, several molecules have been reported to interact specifically with triplex structures since 1992 [] (for a comprehensive review see []). However, the field remains largely underexplored, and most of the studies among small molecules and triplexes were conducted more than 25 years ago, with no reported molecules in clinical trials and most studies conducted in vitro. More recently, the small molecule approach was re-launched and explored as a strategy for modulation of a triple helix in the MALAT1 lncRNA, which is involved in a variety of cancers and its knockdown was shown to decrease oncogenic mechanisms. The first study identified two compounds (compounds 5 and 16) using a small molecule microarray (SMM) approach and observed reduced Malat1 RNA levels and branching morphogenesis in the organoid tumor model, while the second designed and synthesized nine novel analogues of a diphenylfuran-based small molecule DPFp8 [, ]. Later, the quercetin plant flavonoid molecule was evaluated as a MALAT1 triplex-binding molecule and shown to downregulate MALAT1 expression []. However, quercetin has also been reported to interact with G4 structures [, ], highlighting its limited structural selectivity across different non-canonical nucleic acid conformations. More recently, screening assays based on the TR-FRET technique allowed the identification of strong MALAT1 binders []. To our best knowledge, this comprises the only available studies addressing the therapeutic use of small molecules against triplex structures. The previously mentioned lack of selectivity was also found in other well-known G4 binders, namely Thiazole Orange, which was used to detect triplex DNA in heterochromatin of Drosophila and Rhynchosciara []. Interestingly, other flavonoids, in this case the fisetin (FIS) molecule, were shown to be able to stabilize the triplex structure and to result in a remarkable increase in fluorescence signal upon triplex recognition via an excited-state intramolecular proton transfer mechanism [].

The most well-known and established triplex strategy among the scientific community is based on the use of TFO (12–28 long) to bind to polypurine sequences in DNA, via Hoogsteen or reverse-Hoogsteen base pairing, creating a third strand that invades the major groove of dsDNA and forms unique base triplets. The first reports were published in 1987 [, ]. This mode of recognition provides high specificity for gene targeting, minimal off-target effects, and the potential to silence or modify genes directly at the DNA level, allowing its applicability, for example, in cancer therapy [, ]. One advantage of the TFO approach is that only a small amount of oligonucleotide is needed to achieve significant inhibition of the target gene, and the gene-silencing effects induced by TFOs tend to last longer when compared with other nucleic acid-based strategies such as small interfering RNA (siRNA) []. However, TFO technology faces fundamental limitations to its successful application, such as the need for homopurine target sequences, acidic conditions for pyrimidine-motif triplexes (when C+:G-C triplets are involved), and challenges in efficient DNA delivery. Beyond these sequence and delivery constraints, chromatin context represents an additional and often underappreciated barrier to TFO efficacy in vivo. This dependence on local chromatin state (nucleosome formation and DNA accessibility) means that biochemical triplex-forming capacity measured on DNA in vitro does not reliably predict genomic target accessibility in cells, widening the gap between the biochemical feasibility and cellular validation tiers of evidence for this approach.

TFOs have demonstrated significant potential in cancer therapy through targeted inhibition of oncogene expression, and C-MYC was the first oncogene to be targeted this way. The designed TFOs targeted the nuclease-sensitive region upstream of the P1 promoter, P2 promoter, or both at the same time, resulting in the inhibition of gene transcription or enhanced anti-cancer efficacy of gemcitabine [–]. However, the observation of reduced gene expression or enhanced therapeutic activity following TFO treatment does not, by itself, establish that formation of the intended triplex at the targeted genomic locus is the causal mechanism. As previously discussed for iM-targeting ligands, orthogonal mechanistic validation, including comparison with structure-disrupting target mutations and complementary analyses of transcriptional and downstream molecular responses, is required to distinguish the intended mechanism from alternative or parallel effects. More recently, TFO effects were assessed in the HER2 oncogene, with the induction of apoptosis in tumors, whereas cells without amplifications process lower levels of DNA damage []. Moreover, TFOs induced copy number-dependent DNA double-strand breaks and activated p53-independent apoptosis in HER2-positive cancer cells and human tumor xenografts. Inspired by these results, Yang et al. explored the encapsulation of TFOs in nanoparticle delivery systems to enhance their therapeutic efficacy []. They found an 80-fold improvement in TFO efficacy compared to naked TFOs using the TFO@ZW-128 nanoparticle system. Alternatively, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), such as the TAT peptide (derived from HIV-1 TAT protein), and Penetratin (from the Antennapedia homeodomain), have also emerged as alternatives for nucleic acid transfection [, ]. CPPs have been widely investigated to facilitate the cellular uptake and intracellular delivery of nucleic acids; in this context, their role refers to general transfection rather than selective delivery to specific cells or tissues.

Beyond drug delivery systems, other TFO modifications can be made to enhance their potency, namely at the primary level (bases, backbone, and sugar modifications) as well as by conjugation with intercalants []. Among several molecules reported in the literature, such as platinum-conjugated or TFO metallonuclease-conjugated, psoralen stands out for its capacity to efficiently intercalate between bases and can provide a covalent linkage by forming an adduct on photoreaction with the stacked pyrimidine [, , ]. This intercalator was first described and conjugated by the Hélène group, introducing psoralen into the 5′-end of a TFO []. Since this time, other advances have been made, and more recently, Mikame et al. developed a 1′(one)-psoralen-conjugated triplex-forming oligonucleotide (OPTO) to increase the thermodynamic stability of the corresponding triplex by the intercalation of psoralen and the combination with LNA and 5-methylcytosine modifications improved the applicability of this strategy [, ].

Regarding chemical backbone modifications, to improve stability, binding or resistance to nucleases, and focusing on RNA, which gained relevance in the last decades, PNA is emerging as a promising ligand for triple-helical recognition of RNAs. Structurally, they are characterized by a charge-neutral pseudopeptide backbone, which confers high binding affinity and specificity toward complementary sequences. They have been shown to modulate biological function and control dynamic conformational equilibria of complex folded RNAs, evidencing their potential as a research tool and therapeutic compound for RNA targeting []. Additionally, morpholino oligonucleotides represent another important class, particularly in developmental biology and in vivo studies using, for example, zebrafish models. Morpholinos consist of nucleobases attached to morpholine rings linked through non-ionic phosphorodiamidate bonds, contributing to abolishing nuclease degradation and electrostatic repulsion. In the context of triplex formation, morpholinos have been shown to promote stable triple-helix assembly and to reduce the dependence on magnesium ions, with early studies demonstrating that pyrimidine morpholino oligonucleotides can form stable triplex structures under physiologically relevant conditions [, ]. Despite these advances, the morpholino-specific triplex literature remains relatively limited compared with the broader RNA-triplex field.

Furthermore, the design of artificial nucleosides can be seen as a future avenue to improve the performance of oligonucleotides. Wang et al. reported that the introduction of 2-amino-4-methoxypyridinyl pseudo-dC (4OMeAP-dC) and 2-amino-3-methylpyridinyl pseudo-dC (3MeAP-dC) nucleosides can selectively recognize the CG base pair, including multiple CG inversion sites, and form a stable triplex structure against the hTERT promoter, leading to its inhibition [].

The rationale behind therapeutic strategies against R-loops depends on the specific functions of R-loop structures in pathologies, i.e. whether it is necessary to destabilize or induce their formation.

The therapeutic strategies to resolve R-loops aim to enhance their clearance, protecting against genomic instability observed in cancer or neurodegeneration. RNase H1 augmentation using gene therapy or small-molecule activators of RNase H1 can increase R-loop resolution, reducing transcription-associated DNA damage and inflammation in tumor and neuronal contexts [, ]. This enzyme was identified as a functional antagonist of R-loops and has been extensively used as a tool for R-loop elimination in laboratory studies. Additionally, enhancing accessory pathways, such as the AND-1 DNA-binding protein, induces RNase H1 recruitment, leading to stimulation of its endonuclease activity []. These results thus provide preclinical evidence for a therapeutic strategy targeting accessory pathways. Moreover, the modulation of helicases may enhance the unwinding of DNA:RNA hybrids and/or inhibit m6A modifications, preserving genome integrity in diseases marked by R-loop accumulation [, ].

An opposite strategy relies on R-loops induction, aiming to trigger DNA damage responses and apoptosis in cancer cells. Once again, RNase H1 plays a central role, and its inhibition is intended to increase R-loop accumulation, leading to replication stress and selective cytotoxicity in rapidly dividing tumor cells []. Topoisomerase 1 (TOP1) inhibitors (camptothecin, irinotecan, or topotecan) may achieve the same results, avoiding the removal of the torsional stress generated by R-loop formation and guiding R-loop removal by helicases or RNaseH1/H2 [].

Interestingly, no R-loop-specific molecules have been reported; however, some evidence showed that G4 ligands (CX-5461 and Pyridostatin) can increase R-loop levels and genome instability in human cancer cells while simultaneously stabilizing G4s [, , , ]. Thus, this crosstalk illustrates a broader and complex structural behavior among R-loops and G4. Therefore, future strategies designed to selectively modulate R-loop levels should consider the possibility that they may simultaneously perturb G4 populations at the same loci, and vice versa, complicating attribution of downstream phenotypes to either structure individually and limiting the locus-specific interpretability of both cellular and clinical data.

Additionally, other molecules ranging from PARP, ATR, or TOP inhibitors to alkylating agents have been shown to target factors that prevent or resolve R-loops, leading to genomic instability incompatible with cancer cellular viability. For an extended and comprehensive review about the pharmacological induction of R-loops in cancer cells, please consider this authoritative review [].

Based on these, future directions can be outlined. Considering the dynamic profile of R-loop structure formation, their selective targeting using small molecules can be challenging, largely because of the difficulty in distinguishing R-loop structures from canonical double-stranded nucleic acids and from DNA:RNA hybrid regions. Therefore, future efforts should be concentrated on exploring cancer-relevant pathways associated with R-loop metabolism and on identifying proteins that directly regulate R-loop dynamics. Such strategies may provide more tractable therapeutic targets and facilitate the development of effective R-loop-based anticancer therapies; however, it is important to recognize that targeting R-loop regulatory proteins is likely to produce systemic effects, rather than enabling locus-specific therapeutic interventions. Furthermore, the tissue- and context-dependent functions of R-loops represent an additional challenge, complicating the selection of therapeutic strategies aimed at either resolving or inducing R-loop accumulation. Consequently, a deeper understanding of the molecular and cellular contexts in which R-loops contribute to tumorigenesis will be essential for the successful translation of R-loop-targeted therapies into clinical practice.

The Zα domain of ADAR1 and ZBP1 proteins can recognize Z-structures and contribute to Z-nucleic acid biology processes, being hypothesized that influencing these proteins will result in subsequent interference with Z-DNA/Z-RNA. However, recent work shows that it is also capable of recognizing and binding to A-DNA and to G4 (DNA and RNA) [, ]. Thus, this broader binding repertoire complicates the assumption that pharmacologically engaging Zα-domain proteins can constitute a specific perturbation of Z-DNA/Z-RNA biology.

The curaxin CBL0137 molecule, which completed phase I/II clinical trials (NCT01905228), was found to activate ZBP1 and trigger Z-DNA formation in cells, which induced ZBP1-dependent necroptosis in liver cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts as well as reversed immune checkpoint blockade unresponsiveness in mouse models of melanoma [–]. Similar effects were found in NK/T-cell lymphoma (NKTCL) in vitro and in in vivo models, aside from synergistic antitumor effects found when combined with PD-1 antibody and cisplatin []. Moreover, the conducted RNA-seq analysis revealed that CBL0137 molecules exert their antitumor effect primarily by interfering with DNA damage repair. Collectively, these studies indicate that, although CBL0137 can bind to and stabilize Z-DNA, its activity is not restricted to this structure, highlighting its lack of genuine Z-DNA specificity and illustrating how a compound can reach clinical phase while the mechanistic level and cellular validation of a structure-specific effect remain unresolved. Very recently, an outstanding work conducted by Yan Xu’s lab elucidated the first high-resolution structure of the complex between a Z-DNA/curaxin alongside the first observation in living human cells of the complex using in-cell  19F NMR [].

Additionally, other reports identified potential inhibitors (lithospermic acid and Regaloside B) that bind to the ADAR1 Zα domain and could help to accelerate the pace of ADAR1 research, modulating RNA editing processes, offering potential therapeutic avenues for diseases associated with aberrant ADAR1 activity []. At this stage, these compounds are best regarded as proof-of-concept starting points for Zα-directed ligand discovery rather than as validated pharmacological tools.

Besides, expanding the chemical and reagent toolkit beyond the above-described molecules will be important for isolating the Z-DNA/ZBP1 mechanism experimentally. More recently, the development of the NanoZ method, a nanoparticle-based screening platform, identified, from the screening of 2000 compounds, Alexidine as a novel small-molecule Z-DNA inducer capable of modulating transcription in cells []. It was found that Alexidine efficiently promoted the B-to-Z transition, increased Z-DNA formation in cells, and modulated transcription.

Looking ahead, we believe that progress will depend on unravelling Z-DNA/Z-RNA-specific pharmacology from the broader activities of curaxin and Zα/Zβ-domain proteins, given recent evidence that these domains also bind G4 with high affinity.

DNA junctions represent underexplored targets now gaining recognition for their roles in genome maintenance and as targets for innovative cancer therapy. The ability to design small molecules that exploit unique structural cavity features formed at the junction branch point, such as symmetry, hydrophobicity, shape, and charge complementarity, offers a path to structure-specific DNA targeting, addressing one of the central limitations of classical genotoxic agents, namely the lack of true sequence or structure specificity. Thus, junction binders have direct interest as potential replication inhibitors, since stalling the replication fork in rapidly dividing cells can trigger DNA damage signaling and selectively kill cancer cells with compromised checkpoint responses.

The concept of exploiting DNA junctions as druggable targets rests on structural tools developed decades before any therapeutic application was conceived. Kallenbach’s pioneering work on the design and immobilization of 4WJ, their biophysical characterization and interaction with fluorescent dyes [, ], paved the way for the initiation of ligand-binding studies, providing the scientific and experimental basis that has enabled the modern design of drugs targeting these junctions.

The first molecules shown to bind junctions with high affinity were not small molecules but short peptides. The hexapeptides WKHYNY and WRWYCR, originally isolated by Segall et al. from a combinatorial peptide library screened for inhibitors of bacteriophage λ integrase, bind directly to the center of 4WJ in their square-planar conformation and competitively block junction-processing enzymes [–]. This structure-selective, sequence-independent mode of inhibition established the principle that a single ligand class could interfere with junction resolution. Later, the same group reported the WRWYRGGRYWRW peptide as an improved version of previous binders [], and other researchers reported, for the first time, cyclic peptides with increased specificity for 4WJs [, ].

Once this principle had been demonstrated, initial studies were performed with dyes such as stains-all, propidium iodide and TMPyP4, which are limited in terms of selectivity for B-DNA or other non-canonical structures. Chemists then turned their attention to the rational design of synthetic non-peptidic ligands, taking into account the DNA junctions’ properties. The evolution of DNA junction ligands is covered by recent authoritative reviews authored by Ivens et al. [] and the Monchaud group [, ]. Distinct families were designed and synthesized against 3WJ and 4WJ, ranging from bis-acridine ligands, azacryptands, and triptycene derivatives to supramolecular helicates, organometallic pillarplexes [, –]. Recently, the Song group reported for the first time the synthesis of photoswitchable metallohelices with antimicrobial properties []. Alongside these approaches, the combination of peptide and supramolecular chemistry is being extensively explored by the Vázquez-López group, who have reported in recent years the development of (metallo)peptide helicates [–]. Interestingly, in parallel studies, Yin et al. screened and identified a VE-822 molecule (also known as berzosertib), a first-in-class ATR kinase inhibitor already in Phase I/II clinical trials, which can also promote assembly and stabilization of DNA Holliday junctions in vitro and in cells, induce telomeric DNA damage, and sensitize cells to doxorubicin [, ]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first molecule capable of inducing DNA junction formation that has been reported to have entered clinical trials; however, it is not truly junction-specific, as it can also recognize ATR kinase.

Although numerous ligands have been reported to target specifically DNA junctions, all other compounds currently remain at the preclinical stage, and no specific DNA junction-targeting compound has yet entered clinical trials, thus providing an opportunity and an attractive avenue for the development of novel and therapeutically viable molecules.

Despite this structurally diverse ligand toolbox, the gap between in vitro proof-of-concept and clinical candidate remains wide, and this reflects intrinsic challenges of the target rather than a lack of medicinal chemistry effort. A first obstacle is intrinsic to the target itself: unlike other structures, such as the G4, which fold from thousands of relatively stable and sequence-defined genomic motifs, DNA junctions are short-lived reaction intermediates of low steady-state abundance, so a ligand should shift a transient structural equilibrium toward the junction rather than simply occupy a pre-existing or persistent site. Compounding this, the junction cavity is not a rigid pocket but dynamic and responsive to the cations and sequence, which can also affect the ligand’s selectivity. A second obstacle, from a pharmacological and medicinal chemistry perspective, is that the most potent junction ligands identified to date are large, rigid, and cationic, properties historically associated with poor cell permeability and oral bioavailability. Finally, because no method yet allows a junction to be visualized being bound and stabilized by a small molecule inside a living cell in real time, “on-target” activity is inferred almost entirely from indirect readouts (γH2AX foci, micronuclei, or synergy with DNA-repair inhibitors), none of which fully unravel junction-specific effects from more general genotoxic responses [, ]. Together, these obstacles help explain why, after two decades of rational design as well as structural and biophysical validation, DNA-junction ligands remain confined to the preclinical stage.

Alongside the development of new molecules, new techniques have also been developed to characterize the selectivity toward different non-canonical DNA structures and junction/ligand interactions. A broad range of techniques has been applied, ranging from classical methodologies [CD, fluorescence, NMR (in vitro and in cell lysates), and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS)] to DNA junctions’ specific methods such as TWJ-screen assay, multiplex polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE), and fluorescence intercalator displacement (FID) [, , –, , , ].

Beyond small molecules and peptides, DNA junctions can be targeted using engineered junction-binding proteins and catalytically inactive resolvases [, , ]. Looking ahead, future avenues can be drawn by designing junction-decoy oligonucleotides that trap junction-binding proteins, PROTAC systems or genomic engineering strategies (CRISPR) that modulate the sequence contexts in which junctions arise, opening complementary paths for therapeutic and mechanistic intervention.

The uneven therapeutic attention received by different non-canonical DNA structures likely reflects a combination of factors rather than any single cause, such as the later mechanistic validation of some motifs, technical barriers intrinsic to the structures themselves (e.g. the pH-dependence of iM formation, or the transient, dynamic nature of DNA junctions), and, in some cases, still-unresolved questions about whether an established biological role translates into a genuinely druggable, locus-specific vulnerability. At the same time, the historical record only partially supports the broader idea that the later discovery, the greater technical difficulty of detection, or an intrinsically lower translational potential alone can account for the disparity, suggesting that additional scientific and translational biases have shaped the current therapeutic landscape. Later discovery, in particular, is not by itself a sufficient explanation because some structures, like triplex DNA, were in fact hypothesized years before the G4 and the iM, the two most studied non-canonical folds, yet neither has attracted a comparable share of therapeutic development. This historical perspective is well supported by a recent detailed historical chronology of the field [].

What tracks more consistently with translational uptake is the early availability of validated, structure-specific detection tools together with a clearly articulated disease association capable of organizing a research community. The G4 field, for instance, benefited relatively early from both a rational ligand-targeting strategy, through indirect telomerase inhibition, and the development of a widely adopted structure-recognition antibody, BG4, whereas comparable structure-specific tools have emerged later or remain less well established for several other non-canonical nucleic acid structures.

Having examined in the previous section the non-canonical structures as targets for exogenous modulators, we now turn to the reverse side and revise these structures as active therapeutics, harnessing them as a potential functional scaffold and evidencing their intrinsic target versus drug duality.

Thus, in this section we will examine some of these structures, such as G4 and iM aptamers or engineered oligonucleotides (PPRH; Fig. ), highlighting that nucleic acid structure can be treated not only as targets to be perturbed, but also as a programmable platform for disease intervention, contributing to the basis for next-generation nucleic acid-centric therapeutics.

Aptamers (Table ) represent a class of oligonucleotide therapeutics that achieve exquisite molecular recognition of cellular targets, such as proteins, small molecules, ions, or even whole cells, through their ability to fold into complex three-dimensional structures. These single-stranded DNA or RNA molecules are also termed “chemical antibodies” because they bind to their targets with antibody-like specificity and affinity while offering distinct advantages in terms of thermodynamic and chemical stability, lack of immunogenicity, serum nuclease resistance, enhanced cellular uptake and easy synthesis, and modification potential [].
