The SELEX (Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment) process is the technology for aptamer discovery, enabling identification of high-affinity binding sequences from oligonucleotide libraries. The process begins with randomized oligonucleotide libraries typically containing 20–80 random nucleotides flanked by defined primer binding regions for amplification. Target binding occurs under controlled conditions, followed by partitioning to separate bound from unbound sequences []. Then, the binding sequences are amplified through PCR or RT-PCR for DNA or RNA aptamers, respectively. Selection pressure increases progressively through reduced target concentrations, decreased incubation times, increased washing stringency, and introduction of negative selection steps using related but non-target molecules. Typically, 8 to 15 selection rounds are required to achieve efficient binding populations. Ideally, SELEX protocols should include a counter-selection step, in which the selected aptamers are incubated with a negative control target [].

Notably, several reported aptamers are guanine-rich and can adopt a stable G4 structure. This may reflect the higher negative charge density of G4 nucleic acids relative to duplex DNA, which promotes interactions with positively charged protein pockets, and structural features (loops and bulges) that allow specific sites for protein recognition []. The most notable example of a G4-forming DNA sequence is AS1411, which binds nucleolin and was the first evaluated in phase I/II clinical trials (NCT01034410 and NCT00740441) for acute myeloid leukemia and renal cell carcinoma. Although AS1411 did not advance to approval, it demonstrated the feasibility of G4-based aptamers as therapeutic agents. Several other biologically relevant aptamers are also known to adopt G4 structures, including the thrombin-binding aptamer, NU172 (Phase II clinical trials; Clinical Trials number NCT00808964), the anti-HIV-1 integrase aptamer, STAT3-, HMGB1-, and ATP-binding aptamers [–]. Despite these encouraging examples, G4 formation by aptamers remained underexplored. Recently, Cucchiarini et al. demonstrated that, among >1400 aptamer sequences, many of them (1/4 and 1/6 for DNA and RNA aptamers, respectively) are capable of forming G4 structures. Interestingly, G4 formation by some of these sequences was not envisioned in the original publications []. This opens new avenues regarding the potential relationship between biological and recognition activity and structural features. Based on this paradigm, Kharel et al. showed, after an extensive evaluation of G4-forming oligonucleotides with distinct features, that the biological output depends critically on their topology, with only parallel G4s efficiently repressing mRNA translation [].

Different strategies may be employed to improve the efficacy of aptamers. For AS1411, structural polymorphism was an issue [], as it may contribute to diverse protein interactions and cellular effects. Several structural modifications and derivatives have subsequently been explored to improve AS1411 folding, target recognition and biological activity [–]. A wide range of AS1411-based conjugation and nanodelivery strategies have also been developed, including small-molecule complexes/conjugates, imaging agents, and nanoparticle-based systems, as reviewed elsewhere [, ]. The non-covalent association with G4 ligands (acridines, phthalocyanines, or natural compounds) creates supramolecular complexes that achieve enhanced tumor selectivity and efficacy for small-molecule therapeutics in cancer models [–]. Otherwise, covalent conjugation with chemotherapeutics, imaging agents (indocyanine green; ICG) [–], and nanoparticles (liposomes, dendrimers, and gold nanoparticles) [, , –], and more recently with PROTACs [–], provides versatile platforms for targeted therapy and diagnostic applications (Fig. ).

Another strategy based on the G4 structure involves the use of G4 decoys. Decoy G4 oligonucleotides are engineered G-rich sequences designed to fold into stable G4 structures and act as “molecular sponges” for G4-binding proteins (G4BPs), leading to a rebalance of G4 homeostasis. Some examples are reported for HRAS and KRAS, two well-known oncogenes, where the MAZ sequestration deprived the promoter of an essential transcription factor, resulting in repressed oncogene transcription and causing a strong antiproliferative effect mediated by apoptosis [–].

Aptamers capable of forming an iM structure are much less common. A recent study investigates the artificial aptamer BV42, which binds strongly to influenza A virus hemagglutinin and unexpectedly retains its iM structure even at neutral pH []. Similarly to G4, the iM structures can also be engineered to be conjugated with mesoporous silica nanoparticles, allowing controlled cargo release based on the pH dependency of the tumor microenvironment, which results in opening and closing the pores and subsequent drug release [].

As an alternative to G4- and iM-based therapeutics, a distinct class of nucleic acid-based compounds, termed PPRHs, emerged as a promising therapeutic approach. PPRHs are single-stranded DNA oligonucleotides engineered to self-fold into a stable hairpin formed by two antiparallel polypurine tracts connected by a short thymidine loop (Table ). The two arms of the hairpin pair interact with each other through reverse-Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds, creating an intramolecular duplex whose bases remain geometrically accessible for interactions with chromosomal DNA []. Once folded, a PPRH recognizes a complementary polypyrimidine sequence (parallel orientation) in single- or double-stranded DNA and, in the latter, can invade the helix and pair with the polypyrimidine strand in the major groove via Watson-Crick base pairing, displacing the resident purine strand (further debated). The result is a triplex/strand-displacement complex, forming a D-loop, which locally remodels chromatin and can block factor binding or RNA polymerase progression, resulting in gene expression regulation (Fig. ) []. Depending on the location of the targeted sequence, PPRHs can be classified as Template-PPRHs, which target the template DNA strand, or Coding-PPRHs, which target the polypyrimidine stretch in the coding DNA strand.

An advantage of PPRHs is that they form a triplex structure in a pH-independent manner and can be observed at physiological pH under the influence of divalent cations like Mg2+, allowing their applicability to therapeutics, in contrast with polypyrimidine chains that require cytosine protonation. Additionally, PPRHs exhibit no immunogenicity and do not activate innate inflammatory responses, have increased half-life and stability and show the ability to inhibit gene expression at ten times lower concentrations when compared with siRNA or antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) []. A summary of their main advantages, disadvantages and mechanisms, together with a comparison with TFOs and G4 aptamers, is presented in Table .

PPRHs are versatile molecules and were initially developed as gene-silencing tools, with their activity against specific target genes subsequently evaluated in several cancer-related systems, both in vitro and in vivo []. They have also shown the capability to correct point mutations at endogenous genomic loci in mammalian cells, including different mutant CHO cell lines and to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication [, –]. Beyond its extensive application and in vitro validation, studies conducted in xenograft models of prostate cancer demonstrated a decrease in tumor volume, reduction in target gene and protein levels, as well as the inhibition of blood vessel formation, providing the first preclinical proof of principle of PPRHs as a new silencing tool for cancer gene therapy []. More recently, additional in vivo evidence demonstrated that PPRH can have synergistic behavior with trastuzumab antibody, leading to the reduction of tumor growth, while intranasal administration of a SARS-CoV-2-targeting PPRH protected K18-hACE2 mice from SARS-CoV-2 infection and reduced viral burden [, ].

Regarding cellular delivery, PPRHs are commonly introduced into cultured cells using cationic lipid-based transfection systems. In particular, DOTAP has been widely employed to form electrostatic complexes with the negatively charged phosphodiester backbone of PPRHs, facilitating cellular uptake []. Nevertheless, efficient and tissue-selective delivery remains an important limitation for their therapeutic translation.

An additional mechanistic feature was identified during the evaluation of PPRHs targeting the thymidylate synthase (TYMS) gene []. The Ciudad group showed that, in addition to binding to the polypyrimidine target sequence and displacing the resident purine strand, PPRH binding can promote G4 formation by the displaced G-rich strand, which may provide an additional mechanism contributing to transcriptional regulation []. This possibility was subsequently investigated in in vitro and cell-based studies targeting other oncogenes containing G4-forming motifs, including KRAS and MYC [–].

Having examined non-canonical nucleic acid structures separately as potential drug targets (see the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section) and as therapeutic agents (see the “Non-canonical nucleic acids as therapeutics” section), we return here to the central question posed at the beginning of this review: should these structures be regarded as drug targets, as therapeutics, or as both? The answer is not uniform across structural classes and depends on two largely independent axes that should be evaluated jointly: first, whether a given structure has been pursued predominantly as a target, as a therapeutic or both, and second, how far the evidence for each role has progressed along the hierarchy from biochemical feasibility to cellular validation, or regarding their clinical potential (Table ). Applying this dual framework across the six structures reveals a translational landscape that is not only heterogeneous but arguably distorted by uneven historical investment (recently analyzed by D. Monchaud in []) rather than by biological merit alone.

Comparative analysis of non-canonical structural classes across the target side (biochemical evidence, cellular validation, and clinical potential) and the therapeutic side

G4s are the only structure for which this duality is fully realized on both axes and have reached clinical stage from either direction. As a target, G4 was the only class for which purpose-designed, structure-directed compounds have reached clinical trials (CX-3543, CX-5461, APTO-253, and QN-302), yet none has completed the full process (“G-Quadruplex” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section). As a therapeutic agent, the G4-forming aptamer AS1411 similarly reached Phase II trials, but was ultimately discontinued, as well as the thrombin-binding G4 aptamer NU172, which followed the same trajectory. Taken together, G4-based strategies demonstrate that reaching clinical trials on both the target and therapeutic sides of the duality does not, by itself, resolve the translational bottleneck, which for this structure lies specifically at the efficacy stage rather than at biochemical or cellular validation.

The iM structures show an emerging but earlier-stage version of the same duality, and it remains unclear whether this reflects genuine biological limitation or simply a shorter research history. As a target, ligand development remains confined to biochemical and, in select cases, cellular characterization, with no compound having entered clinical trials (see the “i-Motif” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section). As a therapeutic scaffold, the artificial iM-forming aptamer BV42 has been validated not only in vitro but also in a mouse model. Both applications, however, remain constrained by the same underlying property that motivated this review’s discussion of iM biology: strict pH dependence, which limits BV42 activity to acidic microenvironments and raises equivalent physiological-relevance concerns for iM-targeting ligands.

Triplex-forming approaches illustrate that the target/therapeutic duality is not always symmetric within a single structural class. As a direct target, triplex formation via TFOs remains restricted to homopurine sequences, requires favorable pH for pyrimidine-motif triplexes and, as discussed in “Triplex” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section, is further limited by chromatin accessibility, with no TFO or triplex-stabilizing small molecule having reached clinical evaluation. As a therapeutic tool, however, PPRHs are the most translationally advanced example beyond G4, with efficacy demonstrated in vitro and in vivo in xenograft models, though they have not yet entered clinical trials (see the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic” section). This asymmetry is itself informative and suggests that engineering a structure into a therapeutic scaffold can outpace the development of ligands against that same structure as a target, a pattern the field has not yet exploited systematically.

Thus, from the six structures discussed in this review, only G4, iM and triplex have produced a drug-like candidate at all, while R-loops, Z-DNA/Z-RNA, and DNA junctions remain, at present, targets only, with no engineered therapeutic scaffold reported in the literature reviewed here, a gap that is rarely acknowledged.

In this way, R-loops remain confined almost entirely to the target side of duality and to its earliest evidentiary stages. No R-loop-specific small molecule has been reported, similarly to iM and triplex, and the existing strategies act indirectly through RNase H1 augmentation or TOP1 inhibition, producing systemic rather than locus-specific effects (see the “R-loops” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section). This is arguably the most underexplored structure of the six, not because it is less biologically important, but because the field still lacks some of the chemical tools available for G4s or triplexes.

Z-DNA occupies a distinctive position on the target side. While CBL0137 has completed a Phase I clinical trial (see the “Z-DNA/Z-RNA” subsection in the “Non-canonical nucleic acid structures as therapeutic targets” section), its effect cannot be securely attributed to a Z-DNA-mediated mechanism, since the molecule can interfere with other biological mechanisms. Treating this compound’s clinical progress as validation of the Z-DNA hypothesis therefore overstates what the data actually show.

DNA junctions represent the least advanced class among those considered here. Several compounds, including peptides, helicates, and synthetic ligands, have provided substantial biochemical evidence for junction recognition, but cellular validation still relies largely on indirect readouts and is further complicated by chromatin-dependent accessibility. Selectivity also remains a challenge, as cross-reactivity with G4 structures has been reported for some ligand families and up to now, no compounds specifically targeting DNA junctions have entered clinical evaluation.

Two conclusions follow from this comparison. First, translational maturity does not track structural characterization or biological plausibility since structures are supported by substantial mechanistic evidence, have generated clinical-stage compounds on both sides of this dual role, and even there, no compound has completed clinical development. This raises questions about the origin of that asymmetry: how much of the current disparity in translational maturity across structures reflects genuine biological or druggability differences? How much reflects uneven investment and screening effort across the field? It is also worth asking whether G4’s evidentiary lead over the other five classes is a genuine reflection of differential biological importance, or largely a decades-long head start in tool development that was not accompanied by the other structures? If this head start, rather than intrinsic superiority, explains G4’s lead, then the persistent framing of G4 as the “most druggable” non-canonical structure may be an artifact of research history rather than a biological verdict, and the question follows directly: whether structures currently limited to the target side, such as R-loops, Z-DNA/Z-RNA, or DNA junctions, could be engineered into therapeutic scaffolds, as has already been achieved for G4 and for triplexes?

Second, do the specific barriers limiting each structure differ enough that they warrant distinct research priorities rather than a uniform strategy? G4 and iM strategies are limited mainly by selectivity and, for iM, by physiological pH-dependence. Triplex and DNA-junction strategies are limited by chromatin context and delivery. R-loop strategies are limited by the absence of structure-selective molecules altogether, which raises a genuine open question: is this an intrinsic biophysical limitation of R-loops, or simply an unexplored opportunity that reflects under-investment rather than druggability? Z-DNA strategies are limited by an unresolved gap between clinical activity and mechanistic attribution, a gap that, as argued above, the field should stop treating as a minor caveat and start treating as a central unresolved problem.

Also, other questions cut across all six structures and deserve attention. First, as programmable tools such as CRISPR-based and oligonucleotide-conjugate systems mature, are they capable of bypassing the selectivity limitations that have constrained small-molecule ligands? Second, as structural crosstalk between folds, such as between G4 and R-loops, becomes increasingly documented, is the single-structure targeting a rational default strategy? Thus, nucleic acid therapeutic approaches will need to consider the mutual dependence between co-occurring structures at the same locus, since modulating one may unintentionally perturb the other, an interaction that current experimental designs are not built to detect. Accordingly, future strategies could deliberately exploit it, for example by designing ligands or oligonucleotide tools intended to perturb a co-occurring G4/R-loop section as an integrated functional unit. Taken together, the evidence assembled here does not support treating non-canonical structures as a single druggable category. G4 stands apart empirically, not necessarily biologically, and the remaining five structures require targeted investment in tools and selectivity strategies before their translational potential can be fairly assessed.

Beyond the structural and translational asymmetries discussed above, several emerging trends are likely to reshape this landscape in the near future. The rise of generative AI-based molecular design raises an open question that cuts across all six structures. Can these tools finally resolve the selectivity problem that has constrained G4 and iM ligand development for two decades, or will they simply generate larger numbers of candidates? Platforms such as AGAPE, built specifically to predict G4-ligand binding affinity, illustrate the promise of this approach; however, their predictive power is only as good as the available data to train them, and such data remains scarce or absent for iM, triplex, R-loops, Z-DNA, and DNA junctions. Additionally, and arguably more disruptive, the trend concerns the shifting balance between small-molecule ligands and programmable oligonucleotide therapeutics. Is the future of non-canonical structure-targeting more likely to lie in programmable oligonucleotide or CRISPR-based tools, which can be rationally designed against a specific sequence and structural context, rather than in small molecules whose selectivity depends on structure-recognition chemistry? If so, the field’s focus on small-molecule ligand optimization for G4 and iM may need to be complemented, rather than replaced, by a parallel investment in programmable, sequence-directed modalities for the remaining non-canonical structures.

This review provides an overview of non-canonical nucleic acid structures and explores their potential relevance from biochemical curiosities to possible therapeutic intervention approaches such as drug targets or therapeutic agents.

As drug targets, these structures provide potential leverage over biological processes (transcription, translation, replication, and genome stability), and their enrichment at oncogene promoters, telomeres, and disease-relevant loci makes them attractive intervention points, despite a lack of direct evidence of such structures in vivo. Yet, their relatively high prevalence (non-B DNA structures may represent over 10% of the human genome []) makes the targeting of a single genomic site difficult, if not impossible. A broad toolkit, ranging from small molecules, peptides, to L-RNA aptamers and CRISPR-based systems, can stabilize or resolve these folds to reprogram cellular pathways. Conversely, as therapeutic agents, structure-forming oligonucleotides (G4 aptamers, TFOs, PPRHs) use the same conformational features to confer selectivity and, in some designs, catalytic or degrader-like effects. Recent work extends beyond target recognition to include oligonucleotide conjugates for cell-specific silencing, aptamer-guided drug delivery, and theranostic platforms that pair imaging with therapy.

However, significant challenges remain. For non-canonical structures as drug targets, selectivity is the central barrier and to date, no G4 ligand has completed the full clinical trial process. For nucleic acid therapeutics, cellular uptake, biodistribution, and stability in biological fluids remain major translational challenges. Unmodified oligonucleotides are susceptible to nuclease degradation and rapid clearance, while cellular internalization does not necessarily ensure pharmacological activity because intracellular trafficking and endosomal sequestration can substantially limit access to cytosolic or nuclear targets [–]. Chemical modifications, ligand conjugation and delivery systems such as lipid- or polymer-based nanocarriers can improve stability, tissue distribution, cellular uptake and pharmacokinetic properties, although efficient delivery to specific tissues and long-term safety remain important challenges [–].

To answer the question posed in the title of this review, non-canonical nucleic acid structures can potentially function both as therapeutic targets and as therapeutic agents, although the strength of evidence and translational maturity vary substantially among structural classes. This duality, together with emerging technologies and integrative research strategies, may provide new opportunities for nucleic acid-based therapeutic development. However, further mechanistic validation, improved structural selectivity, robust demonstration of target engagement in biologically relevant systems, and advances in delivery will be required before the therapeutic potential of many of these approaches can be fully established. As our understanding of the biology of non-canonical nucleic acid structures improves and more precise tools for their detection and manipulation become available, their potential contribution to future therapeutic strategies can be more rigorously evaluated.

medicine.title: Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in conjoined twin spinal cord separation: a dual-configuration case series
medicine.abstract: Surgical separation of conjoined twins with fused caudal spinal cords requires identification of a safe neural cleavage plane, yet anatomical boundaries are often indistinct. Triggered electromyography (tEMG) has been used to determine nerve root ownership, and iterative subdivision with sequential stimulation has been reported in pygopagus twins, but the sequence and its endpoint have not been standardized. This study describes a tEMG-guided progressive fascicular subdivision approach to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in two conjoined twin configurations.We monitored two cases (pygopagus and ischiopagus) using multimodal intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, including tEMG, transcranial motor evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and free-running electromyography. A dual-twin color-coded electrode configuration enabled simultaneous independent mapping of both nervous systems. Progressive fascicular subdivision with re-stimulation of each bundle was performed until a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval was identified.Case 1 involved pygopagus twins with a fused conus medullaris at S2. Case 2 involved ischiopagus twins with syringomyelia involving both spinal cords and an anterior sacral meningocele. In both cases, progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval, which guided microsurgical separation. Motor function and anal tone were unchanged at 6-month follow-up.Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in both pygopagus and ischiopagus configurations, including one with complex intrinsic spinal cord pathology. This interval reflects absence of detectable somatic motor activation in the monitored muscles and does not exclude sensory or autonomic fibers; its value as an intraoperative reference requires validation in larger series.
medicine.text:
Conjoined twins represent a rare congenital anomaly resulting from incomplete embryologic division of a single fertilized ovum, with an estimated incidence of approximately 1 in 50,000 to 1 in 200,000 births and a female predominance of approximately 3:1 [, ]. Among the recognized configurations, pygopagus twins account for approximately 6 to 18% of cases and ischiopagus twins for approximately 6 to 11% [, , , ]. In both variants, separation surgery frequently involves the distal spinal canal. When the caudal spinal cords fuse within a shared thecal sac, identification of a safe neural cleavage plane becomes a critical step. Because anatomical boundaries are often indistinct on imaging and inspection, intraoperative functional information is essential to guide dissection and preserve motor, sphincteric, and autonomic function.

Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM) has been incorporated into surgical strategies for the separation of conjoined twins. Triggered electromyography (tEMG) is well suited for functional mapping because stimulating exposed neural tissue can identify nerve root ownership and cross-twin motor responses that are not apparent anatomically. Malhotra et al. [] demonstrated this principle in a pygopagus pair with fused spinal cords below S2, where tEMG-guided identification of root ownership during filum terminale separation. Cromeens et al. [] showed that stimulation at the inferior apex of a fused spinal segment revealed that both nerve roots at that level belonged to the same twin, prompting a shift in the cleavage trajectory from midline to an oblique orientation. Mahmoud et al. [] reported dual IONM monitoring in a pygopagus pair with a U-shaped fused spinal cord, using tEMG to confirm cross-twin responses and guide dissection toward a region producing no responses in either twin. In contrast, Ashari et al. [] monitored two pygopagus separations with motor and somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) without tEMG root mapping and reported postoperative motor deficits despite stable intraoperative recordings.

These reports show that tEMG can guide separation of fused caudal spinal cords [, , ]. However, the iterative sequence and its endpoint have not been standardized. Yokota et al. [] subdivided fused root bundles into progressively smaller units and stimulated them sequentially to locate the area of least tEMG activity in both twins. Building on that experience, the present report formalizes this sequence, in which each subdivision step is followed by re-stimulation of the resulting bundles, and defines its endpoint as a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval: no responses in any monitored channel in either twin. In addition, the IONM literature on conjoined twin separation remains largely limited to pygopagus anatomy [, , , , ], and IONM use in ischiopagus separation has been described only briefly [].

In this study, we describe the IONM strategy used to separate two conjoined twin pairs with fused caudal spinal cords: one pygopagus pair and one ischiopagus pair with severe intrinsic spinal pathology, including syringomyelia involving both spinal cords and anterior sacral meningocele. We present a tEMG-guided progressive fascicular subdivision approach to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval to guide separation of the neural elements.

We performed both procedures under multimodal IONM to evaluate neural function in each twin while allowing independent interpretation of activation patterns. A dedicated intraoperative neurophysiology technician was assigned to each twin in the pygopagus case, whereas individual technicians were assigned to each lower limb in the ischiopagus case to facilitate symmetrical electrode placement. All electrodes were color-coded to prevent channel misidentification, with red labels for Twin A and blue labels for Twin B. Electrode tracers indicated laterality, with black for left-sided muscles and white for right-sided muscles, and additional wire colors were used intraoperatively to identify segmental levels (Fig. ).

We placed subdermal needle electrodes bilaterally in two categories of muscle groups. In both twins, the pilot muscles used for continuous monitoring included the quadriceps, tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, abductor hallucis, and external anal sphincter. The adductor magnus, hamstrings, and extensor digitorum brevis were additional homologous muscles used to detect cross-twin motor responses. We inserted double sets of concentric needle electrodes into the external anal sphincter of each twin to assess sacral root activation. The configuration was mirrored symmetrically between twins to permit direct comparison of responses across corresponding channels (Figs.  and ). Each twin was monitored with a separate system that recorded its own pilot muscles and the co-twin’s overlap muscles, so cross-twin responses were time-locked to the stimulus; the other system simultaneously displayed free-running EMG of the co-twin’s pilot muscles.

A multimodal monitoring protocol included SSEPs, transcranial motor evoked potentials (TcMEPs), free-running electromyography (fEMG), tEMG, bulbocavernosus reflex monitoring (BCR), electroencephalography (EEG), and train-of-four (TOF) neuromuscular transmission monitoring. SSEPs were elicited by stimulation of the posterior tibial nerve at the ankle (35 mA, 0.2 ms, 2.7 Hz) and the ulnar nerve at the wrist (20 mA, 0.2 ms, 3.1 Hz), with cortical responses recorded at CPz-CP3/CP4 and CP3/CP4 referenced to Fz or CPz. TcMEPs were obtained using transcranial stimulation through corkscrew electrodes positioned at C1-M3 and C2-M4, delivered as a double-train stimulation with two conditioning pulses and five stimulating pulses (pulse width 0.075 ms, interpulse interval 3 ms, intertrain interval 10 ms), with recordings from upper extremity thenar and hypothenar muscles and from the lower extremity pilot and overlap muscle groups bilaterally in both twins, following a threshold-guided optimization protocol validated in the same pediatric population at this institution []. Both modalities served as continuous surveillance of the ascending sensory and descending motor pathways.

Triggered electromyography was the principal mapping modality used to evaluate sacral root ownership and detect overlapping innervation between the twins. Stimulation was delivered using a handheld flush-tip monopolar probe with a reference electrode placed adjacent to the operative field. Constant-current stimulation consisted of repetitive single pulses lasting 0.2 to 0.3 ms at 1 Hz. We increased current intensity from 0.1 mA to a maximum of 5 mA using an ascending stimulation method until compound muscle action potentials (CMAP) were observed in the monitored muscle groups. Stimulation intensities are reported in the figure legends. A structure was considered tEMG-silent when stimulation up to 5 mA from each system produced no CMAP in either twin and no free-running EMG activity, tested immediately after an adjacent bundle had responded with the same system and settings (positive control). Train-of-four was 4/4 before monitoring, and we did not give neuromuscular blockers after induction.

During microsurgical exposure of the fused caudal neural elements, we applied tEMG to individual roots to determine their functional distribution. Activation confined to the muscles of the stimulated twin was interpreted as isolated innervation, whereas synchronous responses recorded in the co-twin’s homologous muscles were classified as cross-twin motor responses, consistent with overlapping innervation. In regions where cross-twin motor responses were recorded and a clear anatomical cleavage plane could not be determined, the intermingled sacral nerve roots of the cauda equina within the shared thecal sac were progressively subdivided into smaller root bundles under microscopic visualization, with re-stimulation of each isolated fascicle using the same parameters to reassess its functional contribution. We repeated this process iteratively until stimulation produced no electromyographic responses in either twin across all monitored channels. At this interval, the fused cord tissue that produced no tEMG responses was coagulated and divided. Because tEMG assesses only somatic motor activation in the monitored muscles, this interval does not exclude sensory, autonomic, or other functional fibers.

Six-month-old female pygopagus twins presented for surgical separation. Preoperative spinal MRI revealed a shared thecal sac with bilateral spinal cord tethering, a fused low-lying conus medullaris terminating at S2, a small central filum terminale lipoma, and a fibrous band bridging both coccyges (Fig. ). No distinct anatomical cleavage plane between the spinal cords was identified.

TcMEPs were stable and reproducible bilaterally in both twins after induction of total intravenous anesthesia and acquisition of baseline recordings. Lower extremity SSEPs were low in amplitude and inconsistently reproducible. The bulbocavernosus reflex was absent in Twin A at baseline and remained absent throughout the procedure.

Following midline incision and dural opening, the fused conus medullaris and cauda equina were exposed. tEMG mapping was initiated prior to any neural dissection. Stimulation of the left S2 root of Twin A elicited ipsilateral responses in gastrocnemius and abductor hallucis and cross-twin responses in the hamstrings and extensor digitorum brevis of Twin B, consistent with overlapping innervation at S1-S2 (Fig. A). Stimulation of the right S2 root of Twin B produced an ipsilateral response in abductor hallucis and a cross-twin response in the extensor digitorum brevis of Twin A, consistent with reciprocal overlap at the same segmental level (Fig. C). The pattern of cross-activation was bidirectional but not symmetric, with a broader overlap observed from Twin A’s root than from Twin B’s, suggesting that the shared territory did not align with a simple midline boundary.

We initiated progressive fascicular subdivision because these findings showed functional overlap without a clear anatomical boundary. Under microscopic visualization, the intermingled sacral roots were divided into progressively smaller bundles, with re-stimulation of each isolated fascicle after each subdivision. With successive subdivisions, the zone of cross-activation progressively narrowed. We ultimately identified a region in which stimulation produced no electromyographic responses in either twin across all monitored muscles, defining a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval that guided microsurgical separation of the conjoined spinal cords (Fig. B, D).

TcMEPs remained stable throughout the procedure without deviation from baseline, and fEMG showed no sustained neurotonic activity. At 6 months of follow-up, neither twin showed new motor deficits or changes in anal tone on clinical examination relative to preoperative status. Postoperative MRI showed no new abnormalities. Urodynamic studies were not performed.

Twenty-one-month-old female ischiopagus twins presented for surgical separation. Preoperative spinal MRI showed a shared thecal sac with cord tethering and a beaded syrinx extending approximately 3.7 cm within Twin A’s spinal cord and approximately 2.3 cm within Twin B’s spinal cord. Twin B exhibited a low-lying conus medullaris terminating at S3, leftward sacral angulation, and an anterior sacral meningocele with herniation of the meningeal sac into the presacral space. A segment of the spinal cord extended toward the anterior sacral meningocele and was tethered to its wall (Fig. ). Imaging did not identify a distinct anatomical cleavage plane between the neural elements.

Stable baseline TcMEPs and SSEPs were obtained from both twins after induction of total intravenous anesthesia. A 20-cm midline incision, equally distributed between both twins, exposed the shared dural sac. Following dural opening, the continuity of the neural elements and the absence of reliable anatomical landmarks prevented identification of individual cauda equina structures by inspection alone.

We initiated mapping with tEMG by stimulating identifiable sacral root bundles. Stimulation of the right S2 root of Twin A elicited an ipsilateral response in abductor hallucis and a cross-twin response in the extensor digitorum brevis of Twin B, consistent with overlapping sacral root contribution between twins (Fig. A). Stimulation of the left S2 root of Twin B produced the reciprocal pattern, with an ipsilateral response in abductor hallucis and a cross-twin response in the extensor digitorum brevis of Twin A, consistent with reciprocal overlap at the same segmental level (Fig. B). These findings demonstrated overlapping sacral innervation across both twins. Because these findings did not delineate a clear cleavage plane, we initiated progressive fascicular subdivision.

Under microscopic visualization, we divided the intermingled sacral roots into progressively smaller bundles, and we re-stimulated each isolated fascicle after subdivision. On the Twin A side, early subdivisions produced responses confined to Twin A channels without cross-twin activation (Fig. A, B), followed by a tEMG-silent interval with no responses in either twin across all monitored channels (Fig. C). On the Twin B side, subsequent subdivisions again produced responses confined to Twin B channels without cross-twin activation, involving the abductor hallucis and, in one subdivision, the external anal sphincter (Fig. D, E), followed by a second tEMG-silent interval that completed definition of the separation boundary and guided microsurgical separation of the conjoined spinal cords (Fig. F). Additional tethering was encountered where each cord adhered to the wall of the anterior sacral meningocele. We released these attachments by microdissection, and stimulation of the meningocele wall produced no tEMG responses.

Near the end of the procedure, Twin B developed significant intraoperative desaturation requiring anesthetic and physiological adjustments. This event was accompanied by EEG suppression and loss of TcMEPs and SSEPs in Twin B, whereas recordings from Twin A remained stable. Preservation of signals in Twin A supported a systemic physiological disturbance rather than primary neurological injury in Twin B. Following correction and hemodynamic stabilization, TcMEPs and SSEPs in Twin B recovered toward baseline. Both spinal cords and thecal sacs were separated with reconstruction of individual dural compartments, and at 6 months of follow-up neither twin showed new motor deficits or changes in anal tone on clinical examination relative to preoperative status. Postoperative MRI showed no new abnormalities. Urodynamic studies were not performed.

This report describes a triggered electromyography-guided strategy based on progressive fascicular subdivision to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval during surgical separation of fused caudal spinal cords in conjoined twins. IONM has previously been used to identify sacral root ownership and guide dissection, and iterative subdivision with sequential stimulation has been described []. The present cases refine this sequence and formalize its endpoint.

Early surgical series [, , , ] established the feasibility of separating twins with caudal spinal involvement but provided limited neurophysiological detail, and Fieggen et al. [, ] clarified the anatomical basis of shared neural elements in pygopagus and ischiopagus twins.

These cases make three specific contributions to the literature. First, they formalize a stepwise mapping methodology based on tEMG stimulation, progressive fascicular subdivision of the intermingled sacral roots, and iterative re-stimulation of each isolated bundle until a tEMG-silent interval is identified in both twins. Defining this interval explicitly provides a reportable electrophysiological endpoint that complements anatomical inference. Malhotra et al. [] established the principle of tEMG root mapping in pygopagus twins. Cromeens et al. [] provided the most detailed prior account of tEMG-guided surgical decision-making, showing that absent IONM responses together with a small dorsal cleft helped define the superior aspect of the separation plane, while sequential tEMG stimulation of roots at the inferior apex assigned root ownership and shifted the trajectory from an intuitively midline to an oblique course. Mahmoud et al. [] guided dissection toward a region producing no responses in either twin, but did not describe a structured subdivision sequence: the region of bilateral silence was identified through stimulation of anatomically accessible root bundles rather than through iterative fascicular subdivision with re-stimulation of each isolated fragment. The methodological contribution of the present cases therefore lies not in observing bilateral electrical silence alone but in formalizing the operative sequence used to generate, interrogate, and confirm that endpoint. Yokota et al. [] described the closest prior approach, subdividing root bundles into progressively smaller units and stimulating them sequentially to separate the roots along the boundary of least tEMG activity in both twins. The present cases adopt the same principle but define the endpoint as the absence, rather than minimization, of bilateral responses (Table ).

In contrast, the deficits reported by Ashari et al. [], despite stable TcMEPs and SSEPs, highlight the limitations of pathway surveillance alone when direct functional neural mapping is required.

Second, Case 2 demonstrates the applicability of the same mapping strategy in an ischiopagus configuration complicated by severe intrinsic spinal cord pathology. The existing IONM literature on conjoined twin separation is largely restricted to pygopagus anatomy [, , , , ]. In the present study, syringomyelia involving both spinal cords, a conus terminating at S3, sacral angulation, and an anterior sacral meningocele with presacral herniation made anatomical inference particularly unreliable. Rodriguez-De-Velasco et al. [] described ischiopagus separation with IONM assistance but did not detail a comparable neural mapping methodology. The identification of a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in Case 2 therefore supports using tEMG-guided progressive fascicular subdivision in settings where intrinsic spinal cord pathology obscures anatomical boundaries and increases the value of an electrophysiologically defined endpoint.

Third, the same mapping sequence was applied in both pygopagus and ischiopagus configurations within the same institution, suggesting that it may not be configuration-specific, although two cases cannot establish this.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. The evidence base consists of two cases, supporting a conceptual framework rather than a validated protocol. Reproducibility and generalizability will require confirmation in larger series. Cross-twin responses were obtained at 0.92 to 1.1 mA, which makes current spread through the shared cerebrospinal fluid less likely, although this cannot be fully excluded with monopolar stimulation. Follow-up was limited to 6 months, urodynamic studies were not performed, and continence cannot yet be reliably assessed at these ages; long-term bowel, bladder, and sexual function therefore remain to be determined, and the neurophysiological correlates of autonomic preservation in this population remain incompletely defined. In addition, the absence of bulbocavernosus reflex responses at baseline in Twin A of Case 1 precluded its use as a monitoring endpoint in that twin, illustrating the limitations of individual modalities in the presence of pre-existing sacral pathology. Finally, the intraoperative desaturation in Case 2 illustrated the value of independent dual-twin monitoring, since preserved signals in Twin A suggested a systemic rather than neurological cause.

Future reports should systematically document the number of fascicular subdivision steps required to reach the tEMG-silent interval, the stimulation intensity and controls used to confirm it, and long-term outcomes across motor, sphincteric, and autonomic domains.

Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval that guided microsurgical separation of fused caudal neural elements in two anatomically distinct conjoined twin configurations, one with complex spinal cord pathology. This interval reflects the absence of detectable somatic motor activation and should be interpreted together with anatomical findings and other monitoring modalities. Its reliability as an intraoperative endpoint requires confirmation in larger series.

medicine.title: Hemodynamic Challenges After Paraganglioma Resection in Fontan-Palliated Adult With Fontan-Associated Liver Disease
medicine.abstract: Chronic hypoxemia in cyanotic congenital heart disease is associated with increased risk of pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), particularly among patients with single-ventricle physiology.A 26-year-old man with unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect and extracardiac Fontan palliation, and Fontan-associated liver disease presented with hypertensive crisis, with imaging evidence of PPGL. The patient underwent robotic right adrenalectomy and nodule resection complicated by high-volume chylous ascites for several weeks.Chronic hypoxemia in cyanotic congenital heart disease, particularly univentricular physiology, is a well-established driver of PPGL. Existing guidelines mandate preoperative α-blockade and volume expansion for functional PPGL, but this approach is not tailored to Fontan physiology.We present a rare case of operative disruption of retroperitoneal lymphatics superimposed on Fontan-associated systemic venous and lymphatic congestion. Right heart catheterization, cautious α-blockade with volume expansion, and multidisciplinary perioperative management are essential to balance catecholamine blockade against the risks of venous congestion, lymphatic failure, bleeding, and thrombosis.
medicine.text:
Chronic hypoxia in cyanotic congenital heart disease (CHD) is an established driver in the development of pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL). Patients with univentricular heart disease, including Fontan-palliated patients, form one of the largest affected groups.

Although Fontan PPGL resection has been reported, management of catecholamine blockade in a patient with elevated Fontan pressures, mechanical atrioventricular (AV) valve anticoagulation, and Fontan-associated liver disease remains insufficiently described. Standard guidelines mandate preoperative α-blockade for functional PPGL, yet passive pulmonary perfusion in Fontan physiology depends on systemic venous pressure, making the preload-depleting effects of α-blockade potentially catastrophic. We report a case of PPGL in a Fontan-palliated patient and discuss perioperative management strategies.

A 26-year-old man with right atrial isomerism, heterotaxy, asplenia, situs inversus, and unbalanced AV septal defect (right ventricular dominant, double outlet right ventricle, pulmonary stenosis) presented with palpitations and hypertension. Surgical history included bidirectional Glenn palliation at 1 year of age, fenestrated extracardiac tunnel Fontan with mechanical AV valve replacement and epicardial pacemaker implantation at 10 years of age, and fenestration closure in 2023 for stroke. Postclosure Fontan pressure was 10 mm Hg with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of 7 mm Hg and resting oxygen saturations of 92%-94%. The patient also developed Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD), type 2 diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1C 6.6%), and secondary polycythemia (hemoglobin of 16 g/dL).

Three years later, the patient presented with diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, and systolic blood pressure in the 170s-200s, requiring intravenous medications.

The patient was started on carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily. Plasma metanephrine and normetanephrine were 0.17 (normal 0-0.5 nmol/L) and 16.95 nmol/L (normal 0-0.89 nmol/L), with normetanephrine urine excretion of 5,546 μg/d (normal 81-667 μg/d). Hemoglobin increased to 20 g/dL. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography demonstrated a DOTATATE-avid 2.4-cm enhancing right para-aortic and 3.4-cm right adrenal nodule, concerning for PPGL. He was admitted for perioperative optimization before surgical resection.

On admission, vital signs showed heart rate 60 beats/min, blood pressure 101 of 42 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 94% on 2 L/min oxygen supplementation. Right heart catheterization () showed PCWP of 10 mm Hg and a moderately elevated Fontan pressure of 17 mm Hg, notably higher than at fenestration closure years prior. Doxazosin was incrementally uptitrated to 16 mg twice daily; carvedilol was continued at 12.5 mg twice daily. Home diuretic was held to permit volume expansion. The patient underwent volume expansion with approximately 3 L of crystalloid, 3 g of sodium daily, and 3 L of targeted oral intake. Adequacy of α-blockade was assessed using Roizen criteria.Table 1Hemodynamic Assessment at Baseline, Before Operative Intervention, and After Operative InterventionBaselinePreoperativePostoperativeFontan pathway pressures, mm Hg Mean Fontan tunnel pressure101710 Mean SVC pressure101610 Mean IVC pressure101610Pulmonary artery pressure, mm Hg Mean PA pressure101610Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, mm Hg LPCWP10103 RPCWP10103Hepatic pressures, mm Hg Hepatic vein pressure101810 Hepatic wedge pressure112114 Transhepatic gradient134Oxygen saturations, % Fontan saturation606263 IVC saturation625966 SVC saturation625764 PA saturation626363Cardiac performance Cardiac output (Qs), L/min2.84.82.8 Cardiac index, L/min/m21.62.61.5IVC = inferior vena cava; LPCWP = left pulmonary capillary wedge pressure; PA = pulmonary artery; RPCWP = right pulmonary capillary wedge pressure; SVC = superior vena cava.

Once adequate volume expansion and Roizen criteria were achieved, the patient underwent robotic right adrenalectomy without complication and was transferred to the cardiothoracic intensive care unit for hemodynamic monitoring. A Jackson-Pratt drain was placed because of intraoperative ascites. Hypertension resolved, and antihypertensives were weaned. Home diuretic was restarted, and heparin-to-warfarin bridging was initiated for the mechanical AV valve (goal international normalized ratio: 3.0-3.5).

Pathology of the resected masses confirmed paraganglioma. On postoperative day 3, he developed hypotension from high-volume drain output and was transferred to the cardiac intensive care unit. Fluid analysis showed elevated triglycerides consistent with chyle (), prompting a low-fat diet, medium-chain triglycerides, and octreotide. Fecal α-1-antitrypsin testing was slightly positive at 0.87 mg/g. In the setting of large-volume chylous loss and fluid shifts, the patient developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Repeat catheterization 1 week postoperatively showed Fontan pressure decreased from 17 to 10 mm Hg. He continued to have 1-2 L of lymphocyte-predominant drain output daily, managed with albumin repletion, and was transitioned to nil per os diet with total parenteral nutrition.Table 2Fluid Analyses From Peritoneal Drain: First set of Analyses (#1) Performed on Postoperative Day 3; Second Set of Analyses (#2) Performed on Postoperative Day 10 After Dietary Modification and ResuscitationTriglyceride Serum #1, mg/dL176 Ascites #1, mg/dL126 Serum #2, mg/dL111 Ascites #2, mg/dL117Albumin Serum #1, g/dL3.5 Ascites #1, g/dL2.4 Serum #2, g/dL3.0 Ascites #2, g/dL1.9

This case illustrates a distinctive hemodynamic management challenge in Fontan physiology in the perioperative period. Univentricular heart disease constitutes the largest diagnostic group among CHD-associated PPGL, with a median age at diagnosis in the late 20s. The increased prevalence of PPGL in CHD is often driven by gain-of-function somatic mutations in EPAS1, the gene encoding HIF-2α responsible for chromaffin cell tumorigenesis. An increase in hemoglobin was observed in the preoperative period, which may reflect ongoing HIF-2α pathway activation from hypoxemia. Genetic testing for EPAS1 and related pseudohypoxia pathway mutations was not yet performed but could be pursued in all patients with Fontan and newly diagnosed PPGL., As a result, this patient was referred for outpatient genetic testing.

Roizen criteria assess adequacy of preoperative α blockade via close monitoring of in-hospital blood pressure and rhythm. Guidelines recommend a high-sodium diet and liberal fluid intake to prevent postresection vasoplegic hypotension, but this may warrant individualization in Fontan physiology. Systemic venous hypertension, nonpulsatile pulmonary blood flow, and low-cardiac output state define the Fontan circulation, and volume loading beyond already-elevated Fontan pressures can risk worsening hepatic congestion and sequelae of FALD. Although no formal cutoff exists for PPGL resection specifically, a Fontan pressure ≥15 mm Hg is generally associated with poor outcomes and increased mortality. Our patient's Fontan pressure had increased from 10 to 17 mm Hg, and additional volume expansion pre-PPGL resection may increase vulnerability to hemodynamic compromise and lymphatic failure. Conversely, inadequate expansion risks postresection vasoplegia without a subpulmonary ventricle to compensate. We suggest preprocedural right heart catheterization is essential in patients with Fontan undergoing PPGL resection to guide safe limits for α-blockade and volume expansion. Forgoing continuous pulmonary arterial catheter monitoring may have left our patient vulnerable to excessive volume expansion, possibly contributing to postoperative chyloperitoneum.

Ascites characterization is diagnostically complex, as Fontan-associated hepatic congestion, surgical lymphatic disruption, and protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) produce overlapping fluid profiles. Ascites triglycerides of 126 and 117 mg/dL fall below the traditional 200 mg/dL threshold for chylous ascites but exceed the revised cutoff of ≥81 mg/dL recently proposed as 95% sensitive and specific for chylomicron-positive chylous ascites in patients with portal hypertension. In Fontan physiology, hepatic congestion produces a high serum-ascites albumin gradient and high-protein ascites even without chyle. Borderline or modestly elevated fluid triglycerides do not exclude a chylous component. Serial fluid sampling may be necessary to capture the evolving effusion, as dietary fat intake and lymphatic stress can change over time.

The chylous ascites was most likely multifactorial. High-volume chylous ascites likely resulted from retroperitoneal lymphatic injury during surgery, superimposed on chronic Fontan-related lymphatic congestion and heterotaxy-associated lymphatic abnormalities. Chronically elevated central venous pressures in the Fontan circulation impair lymphatic drainage, and PLE develops in 5%-12% of post-Fontan patients, manifesting with ascites, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated fecal α-1-antitrypsin., PLE can be unmasked or precipitated by surgical stress. The mildly elevated fecal α-1-antitrypsin is inconclusive against established PLE but may support retroperitoneal surgical lymphatic disruption superimposed on chronic Fontan congestion and FALD. Octreotide and medium-chain triglycerides remain first-line for chylous leak. Propranolol has also been used as treatment for chylous effusions in infants. Surgical and interventional approaches remain last resort but often necessary therapies for persistent chylous leaks in congenital heart patients.

The resulting low venous pressure state from peritoneal volume loss likely contributed to the development of hypoxic respiratory failure and subsequent decompensation. Cardiac index fell from 2.6 to 1.5 L/min/m2 with a decrease in PCWP to 3 mm Hg, consistent with reduced preload from large-volume chylous and ascitic losses in an already preload-dependent system (). Postoperative hypotension in this setting is similarly multifactorial. Hypotension after PPGL resection occurs in an estimated 32%-44% of patients,, likely as a consequence of abrupt catecholamine withdrawal, adrenoceptor down-regulation, residual α-blockade, and contracted circulating plasma volume. This risk may be somewhat attenuated with selective α-1 blockade, as used in our patient. Literature surrounding the experience with PPGL resection in Fontan physiology is limited to case reports,, ,  with a recent three-patient adult Fontan series reporting similarly labile perioperative hemodynamics. Our case adds to this sparse literature and underscores that postoperative hypotension, although expected, is particularly dangerous as it is superimposed on a single ventricle circulation in which regulation of hemodynamics is already compromised.

The mechanical AV valve adds anticoagulation imperatives that conflict with the hemorrhagic risks of major abdominal surgery in FALD. Mechanical AV valves carry high thromboembolic risk, requiring an elevated international normalized ratio goal and perioperative heparin bridging. Our patient's mean prosthesis gradient increased from 3 to 4 mm Hg (2024) to 5 to 6 mm Hg (2026), raising concern for early valve dysfunction. Simultaneously, FALD-related coagulopathy, portal hypertension, and ascites elevate bleeding risk. Both thrombosis and hemorrhage are poorly tolerated in Fontan physiology.

Long term, many patients with Fontan are considered for heart transplantation. Invasive hemodynamics supported significant FALD, with a preoperative hepatic wedge pressure of 21 mm Hg and a transhepatic gradient that persisted postoperatively (4 mm Hg) despite reduction in Fontan pressure, suggesting fixed structural liver disease. Combined heart-liver transplant (CHLT) remains a strong consideration given progressively elevated Fontan pressures, FALD, a rising valve gradient, limited right ventricular function, and postoperative lymphatic complication. In adult patients with Fontan with a FALD score ≥2, defined by the presence of cirrhosis, varices, splenomegaly, or the need for repeated paracenteses, CHLT is associated with improved survival compared with isolated heart transplantation; however, higher FALD scores are associated with increased posttransplant mortality. Five- and 10-year survival rates following CHLT in patients with Fontan are approximately 73%, though early morbidity is substantial, with high rates of mechanical circulatory support, renal replacement therapy, and bleeding. It is difficult to diagnose this patient with recalcitrant ascites given the postoperative nature of the fluid buildup; nonetheless, this may represent a progression toward a more severe form of liver disease in which transplantation may be indicated. Referral decisions require careful hemodynamic and hepatic staging, and early multidisciplinary engagement of advanced heart failure, hepatology, and transplant teams is foundational to appropriate longitudinal management. The current hospitalization, although acute in its presenting problem, is also an opportunity to formally stage FALD, obtain genetic testing for EPAS1, and initiate the longitudinal transplant evaluation process.

PPGL resection in a patient with Fontan with FALD and a mechanical AV valve is a unique clinical scenario with several competing management imperatives. Postoperative chylous ascites requires careful differentiation between a reversible surgical complication and chronic Fontan lymphatic failure signaling elevated Fontan pressures exacerbated by volume overexpansion. Standard PPGL volume-loading protocols must be individualized against elevated Fontan pressures, potentially best guided by preprocedural right heart catheterization and pulmonary artery catheter monitoring.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Incidental Hepatocellular Carcinoma on Explant Pathology in Patients With Fontan Circulation After Heart–Liver Transplantation
medicine.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is an increasingly recognized complication of Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD), yet diagnosis remains challenging. We describe 4 patients with Fontan circulation in whom HCC was identified incidentally on explant pathology following combined heart–liver transplantation (CHLT). All patients underwent transplantation for Fontan circulatory failure and had hepatic lesions identified on surveillance imaging that were indeterminate for HCC with normal alpha-fetoprotein levels. Explant pathology revealed well- or moderately differentiated HCC in all cases. Among the 3 patients who survived transplantation, none have experienced recurrence to date. These cases highlight the limitations of current surveillance strategies in a subset of patients with FALD referred for CHLT. Further studies are needed to develop imaging criteria and biomarkers specifically validated for FALD-HCC.
medicine.text:
Despite excellent survival for single ventricle anatomy repair, the Fontan circulation (FC) introduces a host of end-organ sequelae, including Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD). FALD encompasses a spectrum of hepatic pathology, including liver fibrosis and cirrhosis, as a universal response to elevated central venous pressures and relatively low cardiac output that can progress over time. Among the most serious complications of FALD is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), an increasingly recognized cause of morbidity and mortality in individuals with FC with a cumulative incidence of 8.5% at 30 years post-Fontan operation. Median aged at diagnosis is 31 years, but has been reported in a patient as young as 12 years.

Early detection of HCC is particularly important as increasing numbers of patients with advanced FALD and Fontan circulatory failure are being considered for combined heart–liver transplantation (CHLT), but effective surveillance and diagnostic schemas have not been established. Conventional surveillance in individuals at risk for HCC, which includes biannual liver ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein(AFP), does not have proven efficacy in FC and has not been universally adopted. Imaging-based diagnosis of HCC by application of Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) criteria on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) is confounded by the presence of benign focal nodular hyperplasia-like lesions in the setting of congestive hepatopathy and is not recommended., At present, definitive diagnosis of HCC in the FC can only be made by histopathology.

The workup for CHLT in those with Fontan circulatory failure and associated FALD is comprised of a comprehensive liver evaluation, which includes cross-sectional abdominal imaging and AFP and is repeated annually once listed. We describe 4 patients with FC who were followed at our centers and who had incidental HCC (iHCC) diagnosed on explant pathology following CHLT. Clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings preceding transplantation, as well as posttransplant outcomes, are reviewed.

A 30-year-old man with tricuspid atresia status postlateral tunnel Fontan at 25 months of aged with conversion to an extracardiac conduit at 8 years of aged for protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) and subsequent pacemaker implantation for sinus node dysfunction was referred for transplant evaluation for recurrent PLE. CT performed 6 months before transplantation demonstrated cirrhotic liver morphology and multiple small enhancing lesions on the arterial phase in the right and left hepatic lobes without washout or pseudocapsule (). The nodules were overall stable in both size and number compared with the only prior cross-sectional abdominal imaging performed 13 months earlier.
