Arterially hyperenhancing lesions were defined as hepatic nodules demonstrating hyperenhancement relative to the surrounding liver parenchyma during the arterial phase of contrast-enhanced CT or MRI.

Explant liver pathology revealed a 2.0 cm moderately differentiated HCC in the right lobe directly adjacent to a radiographically indistinguishable benign nodule (). He is now 6 years posttransplant without recurrence.

The nearly indistinguishable radiographic characteristics of coexistent malignant and benign lesions in this case highlight the limitations of LI-RADS, an imaging-based schema, for the diagnosis of HCC in this study group. Major features of LI-RADS that favor malignancy include enhancing capsule, nonperipheral washout on portal venous or delayed phase, and threshold growth (defined as ≥50% size within 6 months), none of which were present in these lesions. Given stability in size, normal AFP, and indeterminate radiographic features, these lesions were serially monitored, and the definitive diagnosis was made only after CHLT.

A 38-year-old woman with tricuspid atresia status post–right atrium–to–pulmonary artery Fontan at aged 3 with subsequent conversion to a lateral tunnel at aged 21, history of atrial arrhythmia despite conversion, PLE, pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction, and esophageal varices, had multiple hyperenhancing liver lesions on CT over several years. She was referred for CHLT due to progressive cyanosis due to pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, progressive volume overload, and FALD cirrhosis.

Thirteen months before transplantation, CT imaging demonstrated multiple arterial phase hyperenhancing hepatic lesions with heterogeneous imaging characteristics, including a large 5.9 × 4.2 cm caudate lesion without washout, a 2.5 × 2.1 cm inferior right hepatic lobe lesion with subtle partial central washout, a 1.5 × 1.4 cm mildly hyperenhancing right hepatic lobe lesion demonstrating subtle washout, and a 2.1 cm left hepatic lobe lesion with washout thought to represent a regenerative or dysplastic nodule (). The lesions had been surveilled yearly by CT over the prior 9 years with no significant interval changes. AFP was 3.6 ng/mL before transplant. A percutaneous ultrasound-guided biopsy performed 8 years earlier of a lesion identified in the left lobe was negative for malignancy.

At transplantation, explant pathology revealed a 2.5 cm well-to-moderately differentiated HCC in the left lobe correlating to the nodule seen in segment 2 of the left lobe (). Explant pathology also demonstrated a hepatic adenoma in the caudate lobe corresponding to the largest lesion observed on pretransplant CT imaging. She remains under regular outpatient surveillance without recurrence 7 years posttransplant.

There was prolonged (∼9 years) radiographic stability before the eventual diagnosis of HCC, which raises the question of tumor biology in the setting of FALD and, in this particular case, a distinct phenotype of extreme indolence. We acknowledge a bias, however, in that patients with Fontan circulation undergo comparably intensive longitudinal imaging surveillance, allowing clinicians to observe hepatic lesions over many years. In contrast, for most patients with suspicious nodules in the setting of other chronic liver disease who are ultimately diagnosed with HCC, long-term serial imaging data are not available, because the diagnosis can be made radiographically using the LI-RADS schema and confounding nodules are not usually present.

We do not know if the left hepatic lobe nodule biopsied 8 years before transplant is the same nodule seen on serial imaging or the nodule ultimately found to be HCC, as the procedure was performed at an outside institution. Regardless, it is noted that biopsy of a representative or dominant lesion may provide reassurance when pathology is benign, but does not preclude HCC in a coexisting nodule or the development of HCC in the future.

A 38-year-old woman with tricuspid atresia and normally related great arteries status post–right atrium–to–pulmonary artery Fontan at aged 3 with subsequent conversion to a nonfenestrated extracardiac Fontan at aged 26 underwent CHLT for Fontan circulatory failure and advanced FALD with portal hypertension and uncontrolled ascites requiring multiple large-volume paracenteses.

Approximately 4 months before transplant, CT imaging demonstrated a 5-mm arterially enhancing lesion in the caudate lobe without washout or correlation on the venous or delayed-enhanced images, favoring a hepatic shunt or regenerative nodule (). AFP was 7.2 ng/mL from 2.4 ng/mL over the preceding 3 years. CT performed 3 years earlier showed no suspicious hepatic lesions.

Explant pathology revealed a 1.0 cm moderately differentiated HCC in the left lobe with lymphovascular and capsular invasion. Her postoperative course was complicated by graft failure requiring repeat liver transplantation 2 weeks after initial transplant. She ultimately died during the admission from transplant-related complications.

In contrast to the previous cases, the hyperenhancing lesion seen on imaging before transplant was not found to be HCC. This case more closely resembles the pattern of iHCC seen in the non-Fontan study group, in which tumors may evade detection because of their small size––the sensitivity of cross-sectional imaging increases for HCC ≥2 cm. These patients generally experience favorable HCC-specific outcomes after transplantation, due to the small size and early stage.

Notably, despite the small tumor size, explant pathology demonstrated lymphovascular and capsular invasion, features associated with more aggressive tumor biology. Risk of recurrence is higher with small-vessel vascular invasion (and poor differentiation). It is therefore conceivable that transplantation in this patient occurred during an early stage of tumor development.

A 26-year-old woman with heterotaxy syndrome (polysplenia) unbalanced atrioventricular canal to the right, subaortic stenosis, aortic coarctation, bilateral superior vena cava with interrupted inferior vena cava to an azygous continuation, status post staged palliation culminating in fenestrated extracardiac Fontan at 21 months of aged and revision at aged 13, had multiple arterially enhancing lesions with venous hypoenhancement in the right, left, and caudate lobes on yearly CT and magnetic resonance imaging scans dating back 7 years (, ). Given their stability over time, the lesions were favored to represent benign nodules. Serial annual AFP measurements never exceeded 3.7 ng/mL.

She was referred for transplant after developing right chylothorax and heart failure. Explant liver pathology revealed 5 foci of well-differentiated HCC in the right, left, and caudate lobes with the largest viable tumor measuring 5 cm. She is now 2 years posttransplant without recurrence.

The differential diagnosis of multiple foci of HCC includes intrahepatic spread from a single primary tumor or the de novo development of multiple primary tumors within a cirrhotic and chronically congested liver. The stability of the lesions over time and the absence of other features suggestive of aggressive tumor biology favor the latter, raising the possibility that the unique hepatic environment of FALD promotes the development of multiple independent malignant foci.

Although speculative, genetic predisposition, particularly given this patient's underlying heterotaxy syndrome, could be an underlying factor. Germline pathogenic variants have been reported in 11%-14% of patients with non-Fontan HCC, and future studies incorporating molecular and genetic characterization may help clarify the mechanisms underlying multifocal HCC in FALD.

We present 4 cases of iHCC identified on explant pathology following CHLT. All patients were referred primarily for cardiac transplantation because of Fontan circulatory failure but underwent CHLT given advanced FALD. All had hyperenhancing arterial phase hepatic lesions previously identified on surveillance imaging and pretransplant evaluation. None of these lesions were categorized as LI-RADS 5 (“definite HCC”), AFP levels remained within the normal range, and all were well or moderately differentiated on explant pathology.

Despite intensive clinical surveillance of this patient study group, these cases emphasize the inadequacy of relying on imaging and AFP alone for the detection of HCC. Not only are LI-RADS features unable to discriminate benign nodules from malignant nodules even when coexistent in the same patient, but we also demonstrate that the rate of HCC growth in the FC can be extremely indolent, with radiographic stability up to 9 years, suggesting a favorable prognosis. Furthermore, we show in 1 case that indolent HCC can be multifocal and posit a genetic predisposition for this tumor behavior. In contrast, the 1 de novo iHCC diagnosis of a small ∼1 cm HCC lesion not seen on cross-sectional imaging 4 months prior was the only case in which there was vascular invasion, consistent with aggressive tumor behavior.

Our findings are broadly consistent with reports of iHCC in non-Fontan transplant study groups, in which occult tumors have been identified on explant pathology despite pretransplant surveillance as well. The prevalence of iHCC at our 2 centers is 8.2% (4/49) and is comparable to reported prevalence estimates ranging from 4.2% to 40%, likely reflecting differences in patient study groups, surveillance practices, and diagnostic criteria. Similar to our cohort, AFP levels are frequently normal, tumors are often small and well differentiated, and posttransplant recurrence rates are low.,

This case series of iHCC in patients with FC undergoing CHLT highlights the diagnostic challenges of HCC in this study group. Normal AFP levels, coexistent benign arterially enhancing nodules, and radiographic stability of nodules ultimately found to be HCC were notable in the setting of comprehensive transplant evaluation. These findings underscore the limitations of current surveillance strategies in the Fontan study groups as a whole and support the need for imaging criteria and biomarkers specifically validated for FALD-HCC. Future studies on genomics and molecular drivers of HCC in the FC to elucidate tumor biology are urgently needed.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Network architecture of sleep, biomarkers, and cognition: Rapid eye movement sleep latency as a cross‐domain connector
medicine.abstract: Sleep disturbances are linked to Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRD) pathology and cognitive decline, but how sleep architecture, biomarkers, and cognition are organized within a conditional dependence framework remains unclear.We studied 98 adults spanning normal cognition (NC; n = 21), mild cognitive impairment (MCI; n = 34), and clinically diagnosed AD dementia (n = 43) using overnight polysomnography, plasma phosphorylated tau181 (p‐tau181), neurofilament light chain (NfL), brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), amyloid‐β positron emission tomography (PET), and multidomain cognitive testing. A regularized Gaussian graphical model was used to characterize conditional associations and identify cross‐domain connectivity among sleep, biomarkers, and cognition.The 17‐variable network contained 26 edges, with significantly denser within‐domain than cross‐domain connectivity (40.5% vs 9.6%; p < 0.001). Direct sleep‐cognition connections were sparse. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep latency had the highest bridge strength (0.387), directly connecting the sleep domain with NfL, amyloid‐β PET, and BDNF. Plasma p‐tau181 was the only biomarker directly connected to global cognition. Exploratory mediation analyses were consistent with indirect associations involving p‐tau181 in three of five cognitive domains.Sleep architecture and cognition were conditionally linked primarily through biomarker nodes. REM sleep latency and plasma p‐tau181 may represent key cross‐domain connectors linking sleep architecture, neurodegeneration, and cognition across the AD continuum.
medicine.text:
Sleep disturbances are common in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRD), and increasing evidence links alterations in sleep architecture to amyloid‐β (Aβ) and tau pathology as well as cognitive decline., , , ,  However, the extent to which sleep‐cognition associations are independent of the included biomarker measures remains unclear. Previous studies have often tested prespecified associations between selected sleep measures, biomarkers, or cognitive outcomes, whereas fewer studies have modeled sleep architecture, biomarker measures, and cognitive performance within the same conditional association framework.,  A central unresolved question, therefore, is whether sleep and cognition remain directly connected after biomarker measures are included in the same model, or whether their association is better represented by shared connections with biomarker nodes., , , ,

Conventional regression estimates the independent association between one exposure and one outcome after covariate adjustment. In contrast, network analysis estimates conditional associations among all variables simultaneously, allowing identification of bridge‐nodes and system‐level organization that cannot be inferred from pairwise regression models. Building on this framework, recent methodological advances in network analysis modeling provide an opportunity to address this gap by simultaneously characterizing conditional relationships across multiple domains.,  In a Gaussian graphical model, each edge represents the association between two variables after conditioning on all other variables in the network.,  This framework, therefore, can help distinguish direct conditional associations from associations that may be explained by shared connections with other variables. In addition, bridge centrality can identify variables that connect otherwise distinct measurement domains. Applied to sleep and AD, this approach may clarify which sleep features are most closely linked to biomarker variation and which biomarkers are most closely linked to cognitive performance, without imposing directional or causal assumptions.

A biologically plausible rationale for applying this network framework is that different components of sleep architecture appear to relate to distinct aspects of ADRD pathophysiology, rather than serving as a single nonspecific marker of poor sleep.,  Slow‐wave sleep (SWS, stage N3) has been most consistently linked to amyloid‐related pathology. Experimental and human imaging studies consistently support a role for SWS in glymphatic clearance, amyloid accumulation, and hippocampus‐dependent memory consolidation., ,  Beyond SWS, growing evidence suggests that rapid eye movement (REM) sleep provides complementary information regarding neurodegenerative processes. REM sleep is thought to reflect the functional integrity of brainstem and basal forebrain cholinergic circuits that are particularly vulnerable during neurodegeneration. Prospective epidemiologic studies have shown that reduced REM sleep is associated with an increased risk of incident dementia, while observational studies have reported associations between REM sleep alterations and biomarkers of neurodegeneration, including tau pathology and neuroaxonal injury, although these relationships remain less well established than those observed for SWS and amyloid pathology., , ,  Together, these observations suggest that SWS‐ and REM‐related measures may capture complementary aspects of neurodegeneration biology, providing a rationale for evaluating their conditional relationships with biomarkers and cognition within an integrated network framework.

In this study, we integrated polysomnography (PSG) sleep measures, plasma and imaging biomarker measures, and multidomain cognitive assessments in a clinical sample spanning normal cognition (NC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD. We aimed to (1) characterize the conditional association structure linking sleep architecture, biomarker measures, and cognitive performance, ; (2) identify cross‐domain connector nodes using bridge centrality; and (3) examine, through exploratory mediation analyses, whether specific biomarkers statistically accounted for indirect sleep–cognition associations.,

We conducted a cross‐sectional analysis within a clinically characterized sample of older adults spanning the AD continuum, including individuals with NC, MCI, and AD dementia. Participants were consecutively recruited from a tertiary neurology clinic. Clinical and cognitive assessments were completed at the initial visit, followed by blood collection; overnight polysomnography and amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) were performed within one month after blood collection. Clinical diagnostic classification was established at the initial visit, with participants categorized as NC, MCI, or clinically diagnosed AD dementia according to National Institute on Aging–Alzheimer's Association (NIA‐AA) criteria,, ,  as detailed in our previous work. Following diagnosis and enrollment, participants underwent standardized clinical, PSG, neuropsychological, and biomarker assessments. Key exclusion criteria included major neurological disorders other than AD, untreated primary sleep disorders, severe psychiatric disorders, and current use of antipsychotic or sedative‐hypnotic medications. Antidepressant use was permitted and accounted for as a covariate in the analyses. Participants with a prior diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) or a previously documented Apnea–Hypopnea Index (AHI) > 15 events/h were excluded at enrollment. However, study‐night AHI was not used as a post‐enrollment exclusion criterion, and some participants therefore had previously unrecognized elevations in AHI on the study PSG. The study was approved by the clinical research ethics committee of China–Japan Friendship Hospital, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment.

The source cohort for the present study comprised 128 participants and was the same source cohort described by Jin et al. The primary network analysis required complete data for all variables included in the 17‐node network. Of the 128 participants, 98 had complete data for all required variables and were included in the primary complete‐case analysis. The remaining 30 participants were not included in the primary network because of missing data for one or more required variables, predominantly neuropsychological test scores. Variable‐level missingness and comparisons between participants included and not included in the primary analysis are presented in Tables  and . Because the study was an analysis of a fixed existing cohort, no a priori sample‐size calculation was performed. We conducted a model‐based Monte Carlo recovery analysis using the exact precision matrix from the fitted 17‐node network as the data‐generating model. For candidate sample sizes of 75, 98, 125, 128, 150, and 200, 1000 datasets were generated at each sample size and analyzed using the same correlation estimation and EBICglasso procedure (γ = 0.50) as in the primary analysis. Performance was evaluated using the correlation between estimated and generating‐model edge weights and edge sensitivity and specificity.

We included variables from three predefined measurement domains: sleep architecture, biomarker measures, and cognitive performance. Sleep architecture was assessed using overnight PSG, including total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, REM sleep latency, and proportions of light sleep (N1 + N2), SWS, and REM sleep. The biomarker domain included Aβ PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) and plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 181 (p‐tau181) as AD pathology‐related biomarkers, neurofilament light chain (NfL) as a nonspecific marker of neuroaxonal injury, and brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) as a neurotrophic factor., , ,  Fasting blood samples were collected at approximately 8:00 AM after participants were instructed to avoid strenuous exercise. Plasma p‐tau181, NfL, and BDNF were measured in duplicate using the Quanterix single‐molecule array (Simoa) platform with the p‐tau181 V2 Advantage, NF‐Light Advantage, and BDNF Discovery kits, respectively, and reported in pg/ml. The p‐tau181 was considered an AD pathology‐related biomarker, NfL a marker of neuroaxonal injury, and BDNF a neurotrophic factor. Amyloid PET was performed using 18F‐florbetapir (18F‐AV45) on a GE Discovery Elite scanner. A 20‐min acquisition was initiated approximately 50 minutes after tracer injection. The cortical composite SUVR was calculated as the mean uptake across the frontal, temporal, and parietal cortices, anterior and posterior cingulate cortices, and precuneus, normalized to whole‐cerebellar uptake. Amyloid positivity was defined as a cortical composite SUVR ≥ 1.11.

Cognitive and affective performance was summarized into five cognitive domains and one affective symptom composite. Global cognition was assessed using the Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE). Language ability was derived from the Boston Naming Test and Verbal Fluency Test. Executive function was assessed using the Trail Making Test Part B, backward digit span, and Stroop interference accuracy. Attention was derived from the Trail Making Test Part A, forward digit span, and Stroop time, and visuospatial ability was derived from the Clock Drawing Test. Affective symptoms were represented separately as a neuropsychiatric symptom composite derived from the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Hamilton Anxiety Scale. Cognitive test scores were standardized as z‐scores and aligned such that higher values indicated better performance. Domain‐specific composite scores were calculated as the mean of available standardized test scores within each domain and then re‐standardized before network analysis. The affective symptom composite was calculated and standardized using the same approach.

Rather than imposing a priori directional assumptions, we estimated a Gaussian graphical model (GGM), in which nodes represent variables and edges represent partial correlations after conditioning on all other variables. This approach enables identification of direct statistical dependencies that may reflect underlying biological or functional pathways. To improve interpretability and reduce spurious associations, we applied regularization using the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (graphical LASSO) with extended Bayesian information criterion (EBIC) model selection (γ = 0.5). A value of γ = 0.5 was selected as a conservative choice to favor sparser and more interpretable networks, reducing the likelihood of spurious edges in the context of a modest sample size., ,

To quantify the relative importance of nodes within the network, centrality indices including strength, closeness, betweenness, and expected influence were calculated. Expected influence was included to account for both positive and negative edge weights. To further identify nodes linking different domains, bridge centrality metrics were computed based on predefined communities corresponding to cognitive, biomarker, and sleep variables. Bridge strength and bridge expected influence were used to identify nodes that connect otherwise distinct domains.

The robustness of the network was evaluated using bootstrap procedures. Edge accuracy was assessed via nonparametric bootstrap with 3000 resamples to estimate confidence intervals for edge weights. Centrality stability was examined using case‐dropping bootstrap, with correlation stability (CS) coefficients used to quantify robustness. CS coefficients are reported for centrality measures, with values above 0.25 considered acceptable, and values above 0.5 indicating good stability. Prior to model estimation, all variables were standardized and inspected for distributional properties. Given the use of rank‐based correlations in network estimation, strict multivariate normality was not required.

The primary network was estimated without covariate residualization. In an expanded covariate‐adjusted sensitivity analysis, each network variable was residualized for age, sex, education, apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 status, body mass index (BMI), antidepressant use, and AHI. Because AHI was unavailable for two participants, the complete‐AHI expanded network included 96 participants. A secondary expanded network median‐imputed the two missing AHI values and included all 98 participants. Network topology, edge‐weight correspondence, and bridge‐centrality rankings were compared with the primary network. We evaluated consistency between primary and adjusted models using edge‐weight correlations and visual comparison of network topology.,  To assess the robustness of findings across levels of granularity, we repeated analyses using individual cognitive test scores instead of domain composites. Finally, as an exploratory hypothesis‐testing complement to the descriptive network analysis, we conducted bootstrapped mediation analyses using structural equation modeling. These analyses were intended to test whether the observed sleep–biomarker–cognition pattern was statistically compatible with indirect associations. Indirect paths from the sleep variable identified as the primary cross‐domain connector (i.e., the node with the highest bridge strength linking sleep and biomarker domains) to five cognitive domains through each biomarker p‐tau181, NfL, amyloid‐β (Aβ) PET, and BDNF were tested with bias‐corrected confidence intervals based on 1000 bootstrap samples, adjusting for age, sex, and education. For significant indirect effects, we additionally calculated the proportion‐mediated as the indirect effect divided by the total effect. In additional analyses of potential correlates of REM sleep latency, we examined antidepressant use, AHI, and whole‐night SWS percentage. Antidepressant users and nonusers were compared using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test and a linear model adjusted for age, sex, education, BMI, clinical diagnosis, and whole‐night SWS percentage. Associations of AHI and whole‐night SWS percentage with REM sleep latency were assessed using Spearman correlations and multivariable linear models, adjusting for age, sex, education, BMI, clinical diagnosis, and antidepressant use; the SWS model used the same covariates. AHI was examined as a continuous measure and in sensitivity analyses restricted to participants with study‐night AHI ≤ 15 events/h and, more strictly, AHI ≤ 5 events/h.

To formally test whether conditional associations were concentrated within measurement domains, we compared within‐domain and cross‐domain edge densities using Fisher's exact test and compared absolute edge weights using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test. To verify that bridge‐node rankings were not artifacts of the EBIC tuning parameter, we estimated networks at γ = 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.0 and compared bridge strength rankings across specifications. To assess whether complete‐case analysis biased results, given that excluded participants were enriched for AD diagnoses (70% vs. 44%), we performed multiple imputation of missing cognitive test scores (m = 20, predictive mean matching; mice package), estimated the network on each imputed dataset, and compared pooled bridge strength rankings to the primary analysis. Because MMSE (Global Cognition) shares item‐level construct overlap with domain‐specific cognitive composites and could inflate bridge centrality through within‐community leakage, we additionally estimated the network after excluding this node from the cognitive community.

All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.2) using established packages for network estimation and validation, including bootnet, qgraph, networktools, and mgm. Network visualization employed force‐directed layouts to facilitate interpretation of system structure.

Of the 128 participants in the source cohort, 98 had complete data for all variables required for the primary network analysis (mean age 70.9 ± 9.7 years; 55.1% female; 43 AD dementia, 34 MCI, 21 NC). Participant characteristics are presented in Table . Participants with AD dementia showed lower cognitive performance and higher levels of AD pathology‐related biomarkers, including higher plasma p‐tau181 concentrations and higher Aβ PET SUVR values. No significant differences were observed across groups in age, sex, or sleep macro‐architecture measures. TST, sleep efficiency, REM sleep percentage, and REM latency were comparable across diagnostic categories. Biomarker differences were most pronounced between the AD group and the MCI and NC groups, whereas Aβ PET SUVR and NfL distributions overlapped between MCI and NC participants.

Demographics, lifestyle, and clinical characteristics of participants.

Note: Values are presented as *Mean (SD), #Median (IQR), or n (%).

Values in bold font indicate statistical significance at the 0.05 level (p < 0.05).

Abbreviations: Aβ PET, amyloid‐β positron emission tomography; AD: Alzheimer's disease; APOE4: apolipoprotein ε4 allele; BMI: body mass index; MCI: mild cognitive impairment; MMSE: Mini‐Mental State Examination; NC: normal cognition; NfL, neurofilament light chain; p‐tau181, plasma phosphorylated tau181; BDNF, brain‐derived neurotrophic factor; REM, rapid eye movement. SOL, sleep onset latency; SWS, slow‐wave sleep; TST, total sleep time.

Across sample sizes of 75, 98, 125, 128, 150, and 200, the median edge‐weight correlations were 0.894, 0.920, 0.936, 0.937, 0.946, and 0.959, respectively. The corresponding median sensitivities were 0.538, 0.577, 0.577, 0.615, 0.615, and 0.654, and the median specificities were 0.982, 0.982, 0.973, 0.973, 0.973, and 0.964. Within this simulated range, both the primary complete‐case sample (n = 98) and the multiply imputed sample (n = 128) showed high overall edge‐weight recovery and specificity. These findings support the adequacy of the available sample for recovering the broad sparse network pattern.

Network modeling revealed a structured framework comprising three domains: sleep architecture, biomarker measures, and cognitive performance (Figure ). Within‐domain connectivity was strong, particularly among cognitive measures and among sleep parameters, whereas direct connections between sleep and cognition were minimal after accounting for all variables. Cross‐domain edges predominantly linked sleep to biomarkers and biomarkers to cognition, with few direct sleep‐cognition edges surviving regularization. The network contained 26 non‐zero edges: 17 within‐domain (nine cognition‐cognition, two biomarker‐biomarker, six sleep‐sleep) and nine cross‐domain edges. Within‐domain edge density (17/42 possible, 40.5%) was significantly higher than cross‐domain density (9/94, 9.6%; Fisher's exact p < 0.001), and within‐domain edges were substantially stronger (median |r| = 0.223 vs. 0.053; Wilcoxon p < 0.001; Table ). Among the nine cross‐domain edges, four connected biomarker and sleep nodes, three connected sleep and cognitive/affective nodes (Affective symptoms‐N1+N2 sleep percentage [partial r = 0.053], visuospatial ability‐REM sleep latency [partial r = −0.018], and affective symptoms‐REM sleep latency [partial r = 0.010]), and two connected biomarker and cognitive nodes (Tables  and ). The complete edge list with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals is provided in Table . This pattern indicates that, within this system, the statistical association between sleep and cognition is largely accounted for by shared relationships with biomarker variables.

Examination of cross‐domain edges revealed a consistent pattern: sleep variables were conditionally associated with biomarker variables, and biomarker variables were conditionally associated with cognitive variables, whereas direct sleep‐cognition associations were sparse. Among sleep nodes, REM sleep latency showed the strongest cross‐domain connectivity with biomarker nodes (Table ), while biomarker nodes showed broader conditional associations with the cognitive domain.

Centrality analyses indicated that several nodes occupied prominent positions within the network (Figure ). Node strength, reflecting the sum of absolute edge weights, was highest for Global Cognition (1.11), Sleep Efficiency (0.93), N1+N2% (0.91), and p‐tau181 (0.90), indicating dense connectivity within their respective domains. Expected influence, which preserves edge sign, was highest for p‐tau181 (0.76), TST (0.61), and NfL (0.58). REM sleep latency ranked lower on overall centrality measures (strength = 0.50), as it had relatively few overall connections despite linking different network domains; this distinctive role is better captured by bridge centrality. Closeness and betweenness centrality did not meet acceptable stability thresholds (CS coefficients < 0.25).

Bridge centrality analyses quantified the cross‐domain role of each node (Figure ). REM sleep latency had the highest bridge strength of any node (0.387), exceeding the next sleep node (N1+N2%, 0.053) by more than sevenfold. Its cross‐domain edges connected to NfL (partial r = 0.134), Aβ PET (r = 0.119), and BDNF (r = −0.105). These edges were retained as non‐zero by the graphical LASSO penalty, indicating conditional associations that survived regularization. Percentile‐based 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) were wide (NfL: [0.000, 0.239]; Aβ PET: [0.000, 0.246]; BDNF: [−0.220, 0.000]), indicating limited edge‐level precision. Because graphical LASSO produced zero estimates in a proportion of the bootstrap samples, zero occurred at one endpoint of each interval. Among biomarker nodes, NfL (bridge strength = 0.164), Aβ PET (0.120), and BDNF (0.105) all contributed to cross‐domain connectivity, primarily through their edges to REM sleep latency. However, only p‐tau181 retained a non‐zero edge with the cognitive domain (global cognition‐p‐tau181: partial r = −0.068, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.154, 0.000]), despite having the lowest overall bridge strength among the biomarker nodes (0.068). This dissociation suggests that while multiple biomarkers contribute to cross‐domain connectivity, p‐tau181 occupies a unique position as the only biomarker node directly coupled to cognitive performance in this conditional independence framework. Although individual edge‐weight estimates had wide confidence intervals at this sample size, REM sleep latency retained the highest bridge‐strength rank across the prespecified sensitivity analyses, although the ordering of other nodes was not fully preserved (see the Robustness and Sensitivity Analyses section).

Additional analyses did not identify statistically significant associations of REM sleep latency with antidepressant use, AHI, or whole‐night SWS percentage. Median REM sleep latency was 159.0 min (interquartile range [IQR], 78.5–206.8) among antidepressant users and 123.0 minutes (IQR, 79.5–219.5) among non‐users (Wilcoxon rank‐sum test, p = 0.656). Antidepressant use was not significantly associated with REM sleep latency after adjustment for age, sex, education, body mass index, clinical diagnosis, and whole‐night SWS percentage (p = 0.393). Among 96 participants with available AHI data, AHI was not correlated with REM sleep latency (Spearman ρ = −0.026; p = 0.802), and the association remained nonsignificant after covariate adjustment (p = 0.285). Results were also nonsignificant among participants with AHI ≤ 15 events/h (n = 38; p = 0.222) and AHI ≤ 5 events/h (n = 11; p = 0.841), although the latter analysis was limited by the small sample. Whole‐night SWS percentage was not correlated with REM sleep latency (ρ = 0.065; p = 0.528; n = 98), and the association remained nonsignificant after covariate adjustment (p = 0.145). Detailed estimates are presented in Table  and Figure .

To complement the descriptive network with a hypothesis‐testing framework, we conducted bootstrapped mediation analyses testing indirect associations from sleep to cognition through each biomarker, adjusting for age, sex, and education. Based on the network results, we selected REM sleep latency, the sleep node with the highest bridge strength (0.387; next highest: N1+N2%, 0.053), as the predictor for exploratory mediation analyses. All four biomarkers were examined as candidate intermediate variables. REM sleep latency was significantly associated with Aβ PET SUVR (path a = 0.337, p = 0.006) and BDNF (a = −0.288, p = 0.003). Associations with p‐tau181 (a = 0.305, p = 0.068) and NfL (a = 0.361, p = 0.110) were in the expected directions but did not reach statistical significance. Significant indirect associations were observed through p‐tau181 for global cognition (indirect effect = −0.094, 95% CI −0.232 to −0.020; proportion‐mediated = 86.0%), language (−0.057, −0.167 to −0.003; proportion‐mediated = 102.1%, reflecting a near‐zero direct effect) and visuospatial ability (−0.068, −0.203 to −0.005; proportion‐mediated = 43.6%), but not for executive function or attention. The indirect association from REM sleep latency to global cognition through Aβ PET SUVR was also significant (−0.069, 95% CI −0.185 to −0.000; proportion‐mediated = 62.3%), but no significant indirect effects through Aβ PET were observed for the other four cognitive domains. Neither NfL nor BDNF showed significant indirect effects for any cognitive domain (Figure ; Table ). These findings provide complementary evidence of indirect REM latency–cognition associations involving p‐tau181 in selected cognitive domains. The proportion‐mediated estimates should be interpreted cautiously because several total effects were small or had confidence intervals crossing zero.

To evaluate the stability of the network estimates, case‐dropping bootstrap analyses with 3000 resamples yielded CS coefficients of 0.520 for node strength and expected influence (Figure ) and 0.133 for bridge strength (Figure ). Closeness and betweenness showed insufficient stability (CS coefficients < 0.25) and, therefore, were not interpreted as primary findings. The 3000‐resample nonparametric edge bootstrap also yielded wide confidence intervals for several edge estimates (Figure ; Table ).

In the expanded‐adjusted network of 96 participants with complete AHI data, network variables were residualized for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, BMI, antidepressant use, and AHI. The network contained 25 nonzero edges and was highly consistent with the primary network (edge‐weight r = 0.996), with REM sleep latency retaining the highest bridge‐strength rank (bridge strength = 0.312). After median imputation of the two missing AHI values, the analysis of all 98 participants yielded similar results (24 nonzero edges; edge‐weight r = 0.996), and REM sleep latency remained the top‐ranked bridge node (bridge strength = 0.311; Table  and Figures ).

To assess whether the top bridge ranking of REM sleep latency depended on analytic choices, we repeated the analysis across EBIC tuning parameters, multiply imputed datasets, alternative node inclusion, and individual cognitive measures. REM sleep latency also remained the top‐ranked bridge node across all tested EBIC tuning parameters (γ = 0.25–1.0), all 20 multiply imputed datasets, analyses excluding global cognition from the cognitive community, and the test‐level network using individual cognitive measures. Across multiply imputed datasets, its median bridge strength was 0.262 (2.5th–97.5th percentiles, 0.192–0.311). Rankings of other nodes, particularly NfL, varied across specifications; thus, the overall rank ordering was not fully preserved (Tables  and Figures ).

In this cross‐sectional study of individuals across the AD continuum, we examined the relationships among sleep architecture, biomarker measures, and cognitive performance when all variables were considered together. Our findings indicate that few associations between sleep and cognition remained in this joint model. In addition, REM sleep latency showed the strongest associations with the included biomarkers among the sleep measures, whereas plasma p‐tau181 was the only biomarker associated with global cognition.

A substantial literature has linked disturbed sleep to cognitive decline.,  However, most prior studies examined sleep–cognition associations using conventional regression approaches that adjusted for demographic covariates but did not consider all the included biomarker measures together. It therefore remains unclear whether the sleep‐cognition association reflects a direct relationship or if it is largely accounted for by shared or intermediary relationships with ADRD pathology. Our network analysis extends this question beyond conventional regression approaches by estimating the conditional association structure among all sleep, biomarker, and cognitive variables simultaneously. This pattern may have several biological interpretations, including that altered sleep architecture and cognitive impairment represent parallel manifestations of underlying neurodegenerative pathology and that their observed association is partly explained by shared relationships with biomarker‐defined disease processes. However, these findings do not establish a specific directional pathway.,

Among all sleep variables, REM sleep latency showed the strongest associations with the included biomarkers, a finding that was stable across covariate‐adjusted and test‐level network specifications. This result extends epidemiological evidence that reduced REM sleep predicted incident dementia and is consistent with our prior observation that prolonged REM latency was associated with elevated amyloid and tau burden. In the present study, the joint network did not retain a direct REM sleep latency–p‐tau181 edge. Instead, REM sleep latency was directly associated with Aβ PET, BDNF, and NfL, whereas p‐tau181 was the only biomarker directly associated with global cognition. Thus, the present study distinguishes the biomarkers most directly associated with REM sleep latency from the biomarker most closely related to cognitive performance.

The neurobiological plausibility of this finding rests on the known vulnerability of REM‐generating circuits to early AD pathology. REM sleep onset is regulated by brainstem nuclei, including the locus coeruleus (LC), and the basal forebrain cholinergic system, structures that accumulate tau pathology at Braak stages 0–I, often decades before cortical involvement.,  Degeneration of LC noradrenergic neurons not only disrupts REM regulation but also impairs norepinephrine‐mediated facilitation of glymphatic clearance, potentially accelerating amyloid and tau accumulation., ,  The basal forebrain cholinergic system, which regulates both REM sleep and cortical arousal, is similarly vulnerable to early AD pathology and shows atrophy proportional to amyloid burden. REM sleep latency, therefore, may serve as a functional readout of the integrity of these circuits, which is a physiological signal that reflects subclinical neurodegeneration before it manifests as cognitive impairment. Importantly, other sleep parameters, including TST, sleep efficiency, and SWS proportion, did not show comparable associations with the included biomarkers, despite well documented associations between SWS and tau burden. This dissociation suggests that in a system conditioning on all variables simultaneously, the unique information linking sleep to AD pathology is concentrated in REM‐related timing rather than in overall sleep quantity or NREM‐specific features.

On the biomarker side, NfL, Aβ PET SUVR, and BDNF were each associated with REM sleep latency. In contrast, p‐tau181 was the only biomarker associated with global cognition, suggesting that it may be more closely related to cognitive performance than the other included biomarkers.,  In the AT(N) framework, amyloid pathology is considered an upstream initiating event, whereas tau pathology more closely tracks clinical disease stage. The exploratory mediation analyses provided complementary evidence. p‐tau181 showed significant indirect associations between REM sleep latency and global cognition, language, and visuospatial ability. Aβ PET SUVR showed a significant indirect association only with global cognition, whereas NfL and BDNF showed no significant indirect effects (Figure ). Together with the network finding that p‐tau181 was the only biomarker directly associated with global cognition, these results highlight a potential role of tau‐related pathology in the relationship between REM sleep latency and cognition.

The clinical relevance of the p‐tau181–cognition association extends beyond disease staging. Plasma p‐tau181 is scalable, minimally invasive, and increasingly validated for predicting cognitive decline and conversion to dementia across diverse cohorts., ,  If replicated in longitudinal studies, these findings support further investigation of combined physiological and molecular markers for characterizing sleep‐related neurodegenerative processes. NfL and BDNF did not directly connect to cognition, consistent with their distinct biological roles: NfL is a nonspecific marker of neuroaxonal injury, whereas BDNF is a neurotrophic factor. Nevertheless, their conditional edges with REM sleep latency, together with the Aβ PET edge, indicate that the cross‐domain position of REM sleep latency extended beyond AD‐specific pathology to measures of amyloid pathology, neuroaxonal injury, and neurotrophic function.

Several limitations should be considered. The observational design precludes causal inference, and the cross‐sectional nature limits the assessment of temporal ordering among sleep, biomarker, and cognitive variables. The sample was deeply phenotyped, but modest in size (n = 98, 17 variables). Although no standard power calculation exists for regularized network models, the correlation stability coefficient for node strength and expected influence was 0.52, which is above the recommended threshold of 0.50 for reliable interpretation. However, edge‐level precision was limited, as reflected in wide bootstrap confidence intervals, and bridge strength showed limited stability (CS coefficient = 0.133), indicating that conclusions about the relative importance of individual variables in connecting the three domains should be interpreted cautiously.

Additionally, listwise deletion excluded 30 participants (23.4%), who had lower education, lower MMSE scores, and a higher proportion of AD diagnoses than those retained, potentially underrepresenting individuals with advanced cognitive impairment. Multiple imputation sensitivity analyses preserved the top ranking of REM sleep latency, although the relative ordering of biomarker nodes varied across imputed datasets. Moreover, the use of plasma biomarkers, although clinically scalable, may provide less direct measures of central pathology than cerebrospinal fluid or tau PET. Antidepressant exposure was available only as a binary indicator, without information on medication class, dose, treatment duration, or timing of administration; residual medication‐related confounding therefore cannot be excluded. In addition, sleep measures were derived from clinical sleep reports, and raw PSG signals and epoch‐level hypnograms were unavailable. Although whole‐night SWS percentage was available, the retained data did not include SWS duration within the first NREM cycle. We therefore could not calculate the proportion of this cycle spent in SWS or examine its association with REM latency.

Future studies incorporating epoch‐level PSG data should examine this relationship and determine whether cycle‐specific SWS proportions and other sleep‐cycle characteristics reveal additional cross‐domain relationships with biomarkers and cognition. Moreover, REM sleep latency may be phase dependent; however, measures of bedtime and circadian phase markers were unavailable. Future studies incorporating these measures are needed to clarify the influence of circadian phase on REM sleep latency and its associations with biomarkers and cognition. Finally, the sample was recruited from a single tertiary center in China. REM sleep latency norms and plasma p‐tau181 levels may vary across ancestries and laboratory platforms; replication in ethnically diverse, community‐based samples is needed.

When sleep, biomarker, and cognitive measures were considered together, direct associations between sleep architecture and cognitive performance were limited. Among the sleep measures, REM sleep latency showed the strongest sleep‐biomarker associations, whereas plasma p‐tau181 was the only biomarker directly associated with global cognition. Together, this pattern highlights the complementary information provided by physiological sleep measures and molecular biomarkers for characterizing relationships among sleep, neurodegenerative pathology, and cognitive impairment.
