medicine.title: Successful Repair of Giant Aortic Aneurysm With Severe Aortic Regurgitation in Fontan Patient
medicine.abstract: Progressive aortic root dilation in patients with Fontan circulation requires vigilant monitoring to ensure timely surgical intervention.A 41-year-old patient with Fontan circulation (tricuspid atresia, large ventricular septal defect, situs inversus totalis) presented on NYHA functional class II. Echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed severe aortic regurgitation with 8.1-cm ascending aortic aneurysm and impaired function. He underwent a modified Bentall and bilateral Cabrol procedure using 30-mm tube graft, 27-mm mechanical valve, and coronary conduits. Despite a challenging postoperative course requiring temporary intra-aortic balloon pump, he recovered well with improved ventricular function.Aortic root dilation is a recognized late complication in single-ventricle physiology. This is the first report of surgical repair of a giant aortic aneurysm with severe regurgitation and impaired function in mirror-image Fontan anatomy. This case highlights how modified graft techniques overcome extreme surgical constraints.A modified Bentall-Cabrol procedure can successfully repair giant aneurysms in Fontan anatomy.
medicine.text:
A 41-year-old male patient with Fontan circulation was admitted electively to undergo a surgical repair of severe aortic root and ascending aorta (AAo) dilation and severe aortic regurgitation (AR). Physical examination revealed a single second heart sound, to and fro murmur, mild hepatomegaly, finger clubbing, and chronic venous insufficiency in the lower limbs with prominent varicose veins. Preoperatively the patient was in NYHA functional class II.

The patient’s underlying anatomy was tricuspid atresia with pulmonary stenosis and situs inversus totalis. He underwent a Blalock-Taussig shunt at the age of 5 years, Glenn procedure at the age of 10, and then fenestrated Fontan completion at the age of 29. Soon after, he required a device closure of the fenestration and 8 months later he underwent conversion of the intracardiac Fontan to an extracardiac conduit because of baffle leaks and overall restrictive pattern of the flow from the inferior vena cava to the pulmonary artery. He received medication consisting of spironolactone 25 mg daily, a beta blocker (bisoprolol 1.25 mg daily), angiotensin receptor blocker (losartan 50 mg daily), loop diuretics (furosemide 40 mg daily), warfarin, and a proton pump inhibitor (esomeprazole).

A transthoracic echocardiogram was performed before surgical repair and revealed situs inversus/dextrocardia, single ventricle with left ventricular morphology, extracardiac Fontan baffle on the left, aortic valve with severe regurgitation, mitral valve without regurgitation, common atrial chamber, large ventricular septal defect, impairment of systolic function (ejection fraction [EF] 40%) of the single ventricle, and stenosis of the pulmonary valve and main pulmonary artery. His aortic root measured 7.3 cm, the aortic valve annulus measured 3.7 cm and the AAo 8.1 cm. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with T wave inversion in V5 and V6 leads. Oxygen uptake on cardiopulmonary exercise testing was 24 mL/kg/min. Twenty-four-hour tape monitoring detected premature supraventricular and ventricular contractions and tachycardia runs. His hemoglobin before surgery was 17.6 g/dL, the hematocrit was 53.5%, and the B-type natriuretic peptide level was 410 pg/mL (normal range <100 pg/mL). The cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the findings of aortic root, and AAo dilation of maximum diameter 8.1 cm. AR was calculated at 40%. Aortic arch and descending aorta were measured of normal diameter (). Single-ventricle end-diastolic volume was calculated at 484 mL and end-systolic volume at 264 mL. EF was calculated 45.4%. Abdominal ultrasound presented fatty acid liver disease and liver fibrosis. The liver elastography was consistent with chronic hepatic disease with heterogeneous parenchyma, stage IV fibrosis (15.5 kPa, F4 category). The Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs detected superficial and deep varicose veins. No obstruction of lower limb arteries or veins was detected.

The patient was referred for surgical repair. At first, we performed femoral arterial and venous cannulation. The cardiopulmonary bypass was initiated after the cannulation. Cooling to reach 23 degrees Celsius was completed and careful re-sternotomy (fourth time) and cardiac arrest were established. The known dextrocardia and a massive dilation of the aortic root and ascending aorta were revealed under the sternum. After the cardiac arrest and the dissection of aortic aneurysm, we found that the coronaries were markedly adherent in their anatomic positions so the direct and safe transfer to the conduit was unfeasible because of extreme tension and distortion risk. Therefore, the procedure was modified and the patient underwent modified Bentall and Cabrol procedures, which consist of root and ascending aorta replacement with a tube graft, reimplantation of the coronary arteries by using expanded polytetrafluorethylene vascular grafts, and an aortic mechanical valve. The aortic annulus was more than 37 mm with a dysplastic aortic valve. A 30-mm composite valve-bearing graft with a 27 aortic bileaflet valve was anastomosed to the aorta after the aneurysmal aortic root/aortic valve and aneurysmal ascending aorta were excised. The coronaries were reimplanted to the graft via separate 2 × 7-mm expanded polytetrafluorethylene tube interposition grafts (modified Cabrol technique) (, , and ).

Rewarming and restarting of the heart followed. The patient came off cardiopulmonary bypass with hemodynamic instability, requiring significant inotropic support, thus an intra-aortic balloon pump was placed. The cross-clamp and bypass times were 156 and 237 minutes, respectively. Meticulous hemostasis was completed, the sternum was left open, an epicardial bipolar VVI temporary pacemaker was placed, and the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit.

As far as perioperative anticoagulation strategy in this patient is concerned, oral warfarin was discontinued 5 days preoperatively. Therapeutic bringing was initiated 3 days before the surgery, when the international normalized ratio (INR) was below the target range, using subcutaneous enoxaparin (60 mg twice daily) with the final dose administered 24 hours before sternotomy to ensure adequate surgical hemostasis. Postoperatively, unfractionated heparin was initiated once initial hemostasis was confirmed hours after the surgery. No loading dose was given. The initial infusion rate was at 20 units/kg/h with activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) target of 60 to 80 s. The APTT was monitored every 4 hours initially until stable anticoagulation was achieved and then every 6 hours. Bridging to warfarin started when there was therapeutic APTT and the patient was clinically stable and had started oral feeding. The target INR range was 2.5 to 3.5. The bridging with heparin was continued until the INR was in therapeutic range for 2 consecutive days.

In the early postoperative period, the patient experienced severe hypokinesia of the anterior wall of the single ventricle and bilateral pleural effusions, mainly on the left, and required high doses of inotropes. His chest was closed on the third postoperative day, he was extubated on the fifth postoperative day and the intra-aortic balloon pump was removed the day after. Despite the rocky postoperative course, he was discharged in good condition on the 15th postoperative day with good cardiac function (echocardiographic EF 55%), mechanical aortic valve with only mild regurgitation, and aortic velocity of 2.3 m/s.

Three years after the procedure, in the last follow-up appointment, the patient is doing well, classified as NYHA functional class I-II and has good function of the single ventricle. The patient also underwent coronary computed tomography angiography, which showed a calcium score of 0, no stenosis or other abnormalities of the repaired coronaries, and the AAo maximum diameter is at the level of the coronaries that measures 4.1 cm, whereas at the level of anastomosis it measures 3.5 cm ( and ,  and ).

Congenital heart diseases, such as transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, and single-ventricle palliations, are associated with aortic dilation., Enlargement of the Fontan aorta is a commonly seen phenomenon. In a study of 235 participants with Fontan circulation, normal size of the aortic root was described in only 25% of the patients, whereas only 20% of patients with Fontan circulation had AAo dimensions within normal limits. The prevalence of severe (z-score ≥6.0) aortic root or AAo dilation is 8.5% and 22%, respectively. Only 4.9% of the studied population presented severe dilation in both sites. Kim et al identified the main risk factors of severe aortic root and AAo dilation in patients with Fontan circulation being older age at Fontan, male gender, high mean blood pressure, and left ventricular morphology. In our case, all of the preceding factors were present. However, the vast majority (96%) of the studied Fontan population presented only mild or less AR, with the larger aortic dimensions exhibiting higher grades of AR, such as our patient.

Aortic medial degeneration has been identified as a cause for dilation in patients with congenital heart diseases, including Fontan physiology. The pathophysiology of such dilation includes intrinsic factors and secondary factors, due to volume overload, or a combination of both. A study by Niwa et al on 88 patients with congenital heart disease with 10 different anomalies revealed that all of them had some degree of medial degeneration.

Life-threatening conditions associated with Fontan aortopathy have been described in the literature. A 26-year-old man with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and significant aortic root dilation of 78 mm presented with aortic dissection after the Fontan procedure. The same condition was observed in another 34-year-old Fontan patient with tricuspid atresia and dilated aortic root of 48 mm and ascending aortic aneurysm (60 × 57 mm). These cases underscore the critical role of well-timed surgical repair of aortic dilation in Fontan patients.

Our case is unique due to the underlying Fontan anatomy, situs inversus totalis and giant aortic root, and ascending aorta dilation of 81 mm complicated by severe AR. To our knowledge, this is the first such described case that was successfully managed with modified Bentall and Cabrol operations.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: How ICU Teams Can Engage With Healthcare Leaders to Transform the Practice of Critical Care Medicine Through ICU Liberation
medicine.abstract: The ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle is a quality improvement (QI) tool designed to optimize pain, sedation, and delirium management in critically ill patients, to facilitate ventilator weaning and early mobility in patients, and to increase patient and family engagement in care. Increasing bundle performance is associated with improved ICU patient outcomes and reduced healthcare costs. Support for bundle implementation and sustainability efforts by healthcare system leaders is the strongest determinant of bundle performance. This narrative review outlines strategies that ICU teams can use to secure the necessary executive support for their bundle implementation and sustainability efforts to improve their bundle performance.Medline and PubMed databases. Search terms included critical care, ICU liberation, ABCDEF bundle, ICU outcomes, QI, implementation, patient safety, healthcare leadership, and administrative harm.Peer-reviewed clinical trials, systematic reviews, observational studies, and narrative reviews (English only, from January 1990 to June 2025) focusing on the clinical and economic impacts of the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle and the role of healthcare leadership in improving bundle performance.Data were narratively aggregated without new statistical meta-analyses.Leadership strategies that support bundle performance include: executive sponsors engaging with ICU teams, developing an executive pitch, making a compelling business case for bundle implementation, and aligning the bundle with healthcare system strategic initiatives. Healthcare leaders should prioritize patient safety, teamwork, and family engagement in the ICU and provide the necessary information technology and QI resources to support data-driven bundle performance efforts.The ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle offers a synergistic, patient-centered framework to improve ICU patient care and outcomes and reduce healthcare costs for all ICU patients. Executive support for the bundle significantly improves bundle performance by ICU teams. ICU teams must partner with healthcare executives to get the necessary resources for their bundle implementation efforts.
medicine.text:
The principal goals-of-ICU care are to stabilize critically ill and injured patients and to prevent and treat organ dysfunction to improve survival. Over a decade ago, the standard of care for the sickest ICU patients was deep sedation, physical restraints, bed rest, and full ventilatory support until they clinically improved. Patients were rarely able to participate in their care actively, and families had limited access to their loved ones in the ICU. These treatment strategies were intended to allow patients to “heal” before peeling back these layers of support.

But we now know that this approach is associated with a higher incidence of delirium, acquired muscle weakness, and ventilator dependency in ICU patients, which can prolong ICU and hospital stays and increase the risk of iatrogenic complications and death in patients (–). ICU survivors often suffer from long-term physical and cognitive dysfunction and mental illness, known as post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) (–). Patients with PICS often experience significant physical and cognitive deficits and mental health issues, have poor quality-of-life scores, and are more likely to be discharged to a skilled nursing or rehabilitation facility and have shorter life spans (, ).

The Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) has published a series of clinical practice guidelines to improve patient care and outcomes for all ICU patients and to prevent PICS in ICU survivors (–). SCCM developed a bundle of evidence-based best practices known as the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle to help translate these guideline recommendations into clinical practice (Fig. ) (). The focus of this bundle is to optimize pain, sedation, and delirium management in patients to wean patients faster from mechanical ventilation, mobilize patients sooner, and increase ICU patient and family engagement in care. The ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle is designed to transform care delivery to “all” critically ill and injured patients and requires a collaborative, interprofessional, patient-centered, and team-based approach to care.

Several large multicenter studies have shown that bundle performance is associated with significant improvements in patient outcomes across diverse ICU patient populations, including both mechanically ventilated and nonmechanically ventilated patients (–). Increasing bundle performance is associated with significant reductions in the duration of mechanical ventilation, lengths of stay, deep sedation, restraint use, delirium, ICU readmission rates, hospital mortality, and skilled nursing facility (SNF) discharge rates for patients (Fig. ). Bundle performance also has a dose-response effect on ICU outcomes, with greater than 60% bundle performance levels resulting in accelerated improvement in these outcomes (Fig. , A and B) (, ).

Bundle performance also significantly reduces healthcare costs. One study demonstrated a 24% net reduction in ICU costs and a 30% net reduction in hospital costs following only partial bundle implementation (). In another study, bundle implementation was associated with significant improvement in mechanical ventilation and lengths of stay, resulting in a net institutional cost savings of $4.3 million (U.S. dollars) over 5 years (). A third study showed that high bundle adherence (> 60%) was cost-effective and improved ICU survivors’ quality-of-life post-discharge ().

The “value proposition” of the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle is that high bundle performance improves ICU patient outcomes while also significantly reducing healthcare costs across diverse ICU patient populations. But tangible support by healthcare system leaders is key to successful bundle implementation and sustainability efforts by ICU teams.

A recent SCCM survey of ICU liberation practices showed that strong leadership support, allocation of the necessary educational, technical, and financial resources, and alignment of the ICU liberation bundle with institutional strategic goals were the strongest determinants of higher bundle performance across all bundle elements (). Here, we outline several strategies for how ICU teams can effectively engage with hospital and healthcare system leaders to help them achieve and sustain a high level of ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle performance.

Despite the clinical and economic benefits, most ICUs have yet to fully implement the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle. A pre-pandemic worldwide survey of ICU liberation practices demonstrated moderate progress toward full bundle adoption, with 57% of respondents having implemented the bundle but with significant variability in individual bundle element compliance (). The COVID-19 pandemic had devastating effects on bundle implementation efforts worldwide. Because of safety concerns, resource limitations, and staffing shortages, care for critically ill patients during the pandemic commonly reverted to the ICU practice patterns of more than a decade before—deep sedation with benzodiazepines, paralysis, prolonged mechanical ventilation and bed rest, and increased restraint use, with limited family access to patients (–). An international point-prevalence study conducted during the first year of the pandemic showed that bundle performance had significantly decreased across ICUs compared with pre-pandemic levels, with overall bundle performance rates of less than or equal to 1% in both COVID and non-COVID ICU patients (). Ongoing staffing shortages, a loss of senior ICU staff with bundle expertise, newly hired staff with little knowledge of the bundle, staff burnout, competing quality improvement (QI) efforts, a lack of leadership support, and rising healthcare costs have all helped to perpetuate these ICU practices in the post-pandemic era ().

A more recent international survey of both ICU providers and leaders showed that bundle adoption remains below pre-pandemic levels, with significant variability in individual bundle element compliance (). Common barriers to bundle compliance include a lack of leadership and staff buy-in for the bundle, ICU staffing shortages, poor interprofessional team (IPT) communication around the bundle, and a lack of bundle education. Of these barriers, a lack of leadership buy-in and support for bundle implementation and sustainability efforts was the “most significant barrier,” reducing the odds of individual bundle element compliance by approximately 40–60%. By contrast, “strong” leadership support for the bundle, aligning the bundle with healthcare system strategic goals, was associated with a two- to three-fold increase in the odds of compliance across “all” bundle elements.

The failure of healthcare system leaders to prioritize and support bundle implementation and sustainability efforts can cause significant “administrative harm.” Administrative harm refers to harm caused by administrative processes, policies, and decisions that detract from or create unnecessary barriers to providing high-value care (). Administrative harm is an often overlooked yet common issue in healthcare that affects both patient outcomes and healthcare workers’ well-being. Complex interventions like the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle that require multidisciplinary engagement and cooperation are particularly prone to the impacts of administrative harm. Either through acts of “commission” (i.e., supporting processes that create barriers to bundle performance) or acts of “omission” (i.e., a failure to prioritize and support bundle performance efforts), administrative decisions can negatively impact successful bundle implementation and sustainability. ICU teams and hospital administrators must work collaboratively to make a compelling business case for ICU liberation, to facilitate bundle performance, and to overcome the negative impacts of administrative harm on ICU patient outcomes ().

In the wake of the pandemic, a lack of leadership support remains a significant barrier to bundle adoption, even as ICUs continue to experience an increased demand for critical care services, and healthcare systems worldwide remain ill-prepared to meet the challenges of future pandemics and other disasters (–). Knowing how to engage hospital leaders effectively empowers ICU teams to gain executive backing for bundle implementation efforts, driving better bundle performance, longevity, and team resilience. Best practices by healthcare system leaders to support bundle performance include: 1) healthcare executives directly engaging with multidisciplinary ICU teams; 2) promoting a robust safety culture and a collaborative work environment; 3) supporting a continuous learning environment in ICUs by providing sufficient information technology (IT) and QI resources for electronic health record (EHR) integration and extraction of bundle and outcome metrics, and data analytics for ongoing bundle performance measurement and benchmarking; and 4) prioritizing ICU patient and family engagement in care (, , –).

Direct engagement with ICU teams by healthcare system leaders is vital for the success of bundle implementation and sustainability efforts (). Healthcare executives have the authority and means to prioritize and allocate needed resources for complex QI initiatives like the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle. “Executive sponsors” working directly with ICU teams help to ensure that teams have the necessary resources and strategic guidance needed for their bundle implementation and sustainability efforts ().

Healthcare leaders who routinely practice “in-person executive rounding” in their ICUs can directly engage frontline staff and help them overcome barriers to their bundle implementation and sustainability efforts (, ). Executive rounding fosters more open communication and real-time feedback between healthcare administrators and staff. It enables administrators to gain a first-hand understanding of the daily challenges that frontline ICU staff face, which better informs their decision-making about resource allocation. It allows hospital administrators and staff to work collaboratively to identify and solve problems early on. Executive sponsors can also facilitate interdepartmental communication, collaboration, and care coordination around bundle implementation efforts. Engagement by administrators demonstrates to ICU staff that administrators care about them, and they value their input, which can improve staff morale, job satisfaction, and retention. Finally, executive rounding fosters a culture of continuous QI, which aligns with the goals of a continuous learning organization ().

Executive sponsors can also help ICU leaders develop an effective “executive pitch” to hospital leadership to make a compelling “business case” for investing in their bundle implementation efforts (Table ) (, , –). An executive sponsor can help ICU leaders shape an executive pitch by aligning the clinical needs of ICUs with important C-suite metrics like financial return, risk reduction, and strategic initiatives. Examples of how to align the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle with healthcare system priorities: 1) reduce ICU and hospital length of stay, which can increase hospital throughput and bed availability, and decrease delays in patient admissions, transfers, and discharges; 2) reduce SNF discharge rates for ICU survivors, which can reduce the risk of hospital readmissions for these patients; 3) reduce duration of mechanical ventilation, which can reduce preventable harms like ventilator-associated events; and 4) reduce ICU-acquired weakness, which can reduce fall risks in these patients. All of these potential benefits can translate into an improved return-on-investment for hospitals and healthcare systems. Executive sponsors can connect ICU leaders with financial and accounting staff to help make an effective business case for ICU liberation efforts.

Strategies for Creating an Effective ICU Liberation Executive Pitch

LOS = length of stay.

The ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle improves patient safety by reducing preventable harms associated with poorly controlled pain, deep sedation, delirium, prolonged mechanical ventilation, immobility, and a lack of patient and family engagement in care. Over a quarter century ago, the Institute of Medicine’s report entitled “To Err is Human: Building a Safer Health System” highlighted the importance of prioritizing patient safety in healthcare to reduce preventable patient harms and to improve outcomes (). This spawned an entire patient safety movement in healthcare that initially achieved real improvements in making healthcare safer for patients. Yet a recent study by Bates et al () suggests that healthcare systems have failed to sustain those initial gains in patient safety. This is due in part to the fact that patient safety is no longer a top priority in many healthcare systems. In 2017, patient safety was ranked as one of the top five concerns by healthcare executives who responded to the American College of Healthcare Executives’ annual survey (). In more recent years, patient safety as a priority has been replaced by workforce and financial challenges, addiction management, access to care, and governmental regulation (). In 2022, the National Steering Committee for Patient Safety in the United States published “The National Action Plan to Advance Patient Safety” (, ). This report included 17 actionable and practical recommendations for healthcare systems to advance patient safety in their organizations, focusing on: 1) culture, leadership, and governance; 2) patient and family engagement; 3) workforce safety; and 4) creating a continuous learning system. A strong safety culture has been shown to be an important determinant of bundle performance (). Healthcare executives must once again make patient safety a top priority in order to successfully implement and sustain complex QI efforts like the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle. They should also shift their focus from making bad ICU patient outcomes “never events” to maximizing bundle performance in order to “minimize” these bad outcomes.

High-quality patient care, favorable patient outcomes, and staff performance and well-being all depend on strong collaborative healthcare teams operating in healthy work environments that prioritize patient safety (–). This is particularly true when performing a complex clinical intervention like the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle. A statewide survey of ICU physician and nursing leaders in Michigan showed that strong leadership support for a robust safety culture and collaborative teamwork around the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle were strongly associated with higher levels of bundle performance (). There was also a significant dose-response effect between the level of interprofessional collaboration by ICU teams and overall bundle performance—the greater their level of collaboration, the better their bundle performance. Yet Pun et al () have demonstrated that ICU teamwork and the level of collaboration in work environments vary considerably between ICUs ().

Successful execution of the bundle requires consistent and effective IPT communication, collaboration, and care coordination around the bundle (, –). A systematic review showed that a lack of IPT care coordination is a significant barrier to bundle performance (). Daily IPT rounding in the ICU can help facilitate team communication and create a shared understanding of bundle-related patient goals and priorities for patient care (, ). ICU teams that conduct daily in-person IPT rounds achieve a higher degree of bundle performance than ICU teams that do not round daily (, ).

The structure and quality of IPT rounds can also influence bundle performance. Goal-oriented patient care discussions improve IPT communication efficacy better than data-oriented discussions on rounds. The use of goals-of-care checklists that include the bundle elements can help integrate the bundle into the daily ICU care plan, improve bundle performance, clinician satisfaction, and patient outcomes (–). Previous surveys have shown that the use of goals-of-care checklists is strongly associated with a higher degree of bundle performance (). Stollings et al () have published a review of evidence-based best practices for conducting effective IPT rounds to improve ICU liberation bundle performance. Healthcare leaders who help teams overcome barriers to staff participating in daily IPT rounds (i.e., staff availability, workflow reorganization, etc) can help teams improve their bundle performance.

A data-driven approach to bundle performance helps ICU teams improve care at the bedside in real-time, to measure their bundle performance over time, and to link bundle performance to relevant clinical outcomes. Bundle performance and outcomes data are also essential for benchmarking ICUs’ performance and for sustaining their bundle performance long-term. Healthcare systems can leverage bundle performance and outcomes data to spread the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle across the entire healthcare system enterprise (, ). Bundle performance also has a dose-response effect on improving ICU patient outcomes; above a 60% bundle performance threshold, outcome improvements accelerate (, ).

Achieving and maintaining a high level of bundle performance is a hallmark of a high-reliability organization (HRO) (). Joint Commission International defines a high reliability healthcare system as one that prioritizes consistent excellence in quality and safety across all services maintained over long periods of time (). HROs must make significant investments in IT and QI infrastructure and personnel to rapidly achieve and maintain high levels of bundle performance (). Insufficient allocation of IT and QI resources can negatively impact bundle performance by creating data bottlenecks, workflow disruptions, and analytical blind spots for frontline staff charged with bundle implementation (, ). Healthcare system leaders can help ICU teams achieve and maintain a high degree of bundle performance by allocating sufficient IT and QI resources to help drive data-driven bundle implementation and sustainability efforts.

IT integration of bundle-related metrics into the EHR facilitates bundle integration into the daily ICU workflow. It ensures that all ICU patients receive the appropriate bundle elements in a timely fashion. Extraction of aggregated patient, ICU, and healthcare system bundle performance data from EHR systems can also facilitate continuous QI efforts around the bundle. Brown et al () assessed the impact of EHR bundle integration on bundle performance and ICU outcomes in eight ICUs over a 15-month period. In four ICUs, staff were given bundle-related education and data literacy training. Weekly bundle performance reports were extracted from their EHR and shared with the staff. Staff in the other four ICUs had access to the same bundle metrics, but received no additional bundle education or training or bundle performance reports. In the intervention ICUs, bundle compliance more than doubled and was sustained throughout the study period, including during the first 3 months of the COVID-19 pandemic. By contrast, the control group ICUs showed no significant improvement in bundle compliance over time, and bundle compliance actually decreased during the 3-month pandemic period. Full bundle compliance was also strongly associated with fewer days of mechanical ventilation, decreased ICU and hospital mortality, and higher rates of patient discharges to home. SCCM has developed a standardized set of bundle performance metrics, collectively referred to as the ICU liberation minimum data set (). SCCM has partnered with several EHR manufacturers in the United States, including EPIC (EPIC, Verona, WI), CERNER (Oracle Cerner, Kansas City, MO), and others, to integrate these bundle metrics into their standard ICU platforms and to create bundle performance metrics reports. Healthcare executives play a key role in allocating sufficient IT resources to integrate bundle performance and outcome metrics into their ICU EHR systems.

Ongoing leadership support for ICU liberation QI efforts is a key driver for sustained bundle performance. Complex ICU QI projects often achieve initial success only to wane over time as project champions move on, staff turnover erodes unit knowledge, and new QI initiatives compete for staff time and other scarce resources. Creating a bundle “Control Plan” using the lean six sigma DMAIC methodology (i.e., define, measure, analyze, improve, and control) enables high-performing ICU teams to sustain their bundle performance over time (). An effective control plan includes: 1) a robust stakeholder communication plan; 2) updated unit and departmental policies that codify the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle into clinical practice; 3) bundle education and competency plans for new and existing staff; and 4) a data monitoring plan that includes specific bundle process and outcome measures, data sampling timeframes and performance targets, and identifies specific individuals responsible for monitoring bundle performance data. The use of control charts to statistically analyze bundle performance and outcomes over time can help ICU teams identify when observed changes in bundle performance and outcomes are due to either normal, random variation or to changes in the system that result in significant improvements (or deterioration) in bundle performance and outcomes (, ). Healthcare leaders can help to accelerate and sustain bundle performance by ICU teams by allocating sufficient QI resources and expertise to help teams analyze, interpret, and benchmark their bundle performance and outcomes data.

Successful bundle implementation and sustainability are further supported by a strong culture of “continuous learning” within a healthcare system. A recent report by the National Academy of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine entitled, “Crossing the Global Quality Chasm: Improving Health Care Worldwide,” defines a “Learning Health Care System as an organization that uses continuous cycles of learning and reflection to inspire growth and development, involving all stakeholders—staff, managers, executives, clinicians, patients, communities, and others—in that enterprise” (). Healthcare leaders who foster a continuous learning culture help to reinforce the development and execution of a data-driven control plan to sustain bundle performance.

A strong commitment to patient and family engagement is a defining element of high-quality critical care, with known benefits for patients, care teams, and family members. Family engagement increases patient safety, decreases the risk of ICU delirium, improves collaborative decision-making, and reduces patient suffering (–). ICU families can also experience long-term psychologic effects associated with the care of their loved ones, including anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and complicated grief (). Strong family engagement can lessen the morbidity of critical illness for both patients and their families (, ).

Family participation in ICU Team rounds, a top recommendation of the SCCM’s “ICU Guidelines for Family Centered Care,” helps to improve communication between patients, families, and ICU team members, and can help to ensure that the goals of care for each patient are in alignment with the care plan (, ). Participating in ICU rounds can help families to understand the rationale for various bundle-related interventions (e.g., spontaneous awakening trial, spontaneous breathing trial, early mobilization, etc). Families can also help to facilitate bundle delivery by directly participating in patient care activities for their loved one, including reorienting and reassuring patients, familiarizing the ICU environment for patients, assisting with grooming and simple care activities to reduce delirium, and coaching patients during their ventilator weaning and mobility efforts. Healthcare leaders can help ICU teams to value, prioritize, and incorporate family engagement into their ICU liberation practices.

ICU care is the most expensive form of healthcare, and the demand for critical care services continues to grow worldwide. The “Value Proposition” of ICU liberation is that higher performance of the ABCDEF bundle improves ICU patient care and outcomes and reduces healthcare costs by optimizing pain, sedation, and delirium management, to facilitate ventilator weaning and early mobilization of critically ill patients, and to increase patient and family engagement in care (). Unlike other ICU QI initiatives, ICU liberation applies to every ICU patient every day. Few evidence-based interventions have the potential to significantly improve outcomes for all critically ill patients, helping patients return to their previous lives and not just survive but thrive (). But ICU liberation is more than a QI initiative; it helps to transform the practice of critical care medicine by making it safer, more collaborative, data-driven, and patient- and family-centered. ICU liberation also allows hospitals and healthcare systems to transition from volume-based to value-based care, achieving the triple aim of lower healthcare costs, improved patient outcomes, and enhanced ICU population health.

Healthcare leaders can play a significant role in helping ICU teams successfully implement and sustain their performance of the ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle. Effective leadership strategies that help to support bundle performance include: Executive sponsors directly engaging with ICU teams, helping them to develop an effective executive pitch and a compelling business case for bundle implementation, and aligning the bundle with healthcare system strategic initiatives. Healthcare leaders should also prioritize patient safety, teamwork, and family engagement in the ICU and provide the necessary IT and QI resources to support data-driven bundle performance efforts. These strategies can help to accelerate improvements in bundle performance by ICU teams and build ICU resiliency even in the face of external threats and increased demands for ICU care ().

medicine.title: Matrine‐Loaded Macrophage Membrane‐Functionalized Liposomes Suppress Macrophage Dll4‐Dependent Vascular Smooth Muscle Cell Senescence and Improve Plaque Stability‐Associated Features
medicine.abstract: Macrophage inflammation and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) senescence contribute to atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability. We investigated whether matrine‐loaded macrophage membrane‐functionalized liposomes (M‐DTLPs) suppress macrophage Dll4‐dependent signaling, reduce VSMC senescence, and improve plaque stability‐associated features in experimental atherosclerosis. Non‐targeted liposomes (NTLPs), macrophage membrane‐functionalized liposomes (DTLPs), matrine‐loaded non‐targeted liposomes (M‐NTLPs), and M‐DTLPs were evaluated. Formulation properties, matrine loading, long‐term stability, release, macrophage uptake, Dll4 loss‐of‐function and overexpression rescue, VSMC senescence, plaque burden and composition, plaque‐macrophage localization, pharmacokinetics, and systemic safety were assessed in vitro and in atherosclerosis‐prone mice. DTLPs and M‐DTLPs retained nanoscale size, low polydispersity, spherical morphology, macrophage membrane‐associated F4/80 and CD68 signals, and sustained matrine release. Membrane‐functionalized formulations showed enhanced uptake by M1 macrophages. M‐DTLPs reduced macrophage Dll4 and VSMC HES1, p21, and p16; Dll4 knockdown reproduced these effects, whereas Dll4 overexpression partially reversed the M‐DTLP response. M‐DTLPs also reduced SA‐β‐galactosidase positivity and SASP‐related IL‐6 and IL‐1β while increasing EdU incorporation. In vivo, M‐DTLPs reduced lesion and lipid burden, increased collagen and ACTA2‐positive plaque area, increased fibrous‐cap thickness, reduced necrotic‐core area, and decreased ACTA2/p21 double‐positive VSMCs. M‐DTLPs showed greater plaque‐associated and CD68‐associated localization than M‐NTLPs, while major pharmacokinetic parameters remained comparable between the two liposomal matrine formulations. No overt biochemical, histological, body‐weight, or serum‐lipid safety signal was observed. M‐DTLPs combine macrophage membrane‐functionalized delivery with matrine pharmacology to suppress a Dll4‐dependent macrophage‐to‐VSMC senescence program and promote a plaque phenotype associated with greater structural stability in preclinical atherosclerosis.
medicine.text:
Atherosclerosis is a lipid‐driven inflammatory disease of the arterial wall and remains a major pathological basis for myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and peripheral arterial disease (Libby et al. ). Plaque progression reflects reciprocal interactions among retained lipoproteins, immune cells, endothelial cells, and VSMCs. VSMCs are plastic, disease‐responsive cells that can support fibrous‐cap integrity or adopt lesion‐associated states that contribute to progression (Basatemur et al. ). Senescent VSMCs lose reparative capacity and are associated with plaque‐vulnerability features, including impaired collagen‐rich cap integrity (Wang et al. ). The macrophage‐VSMC interface is therefore a biologically relevant site at which inflammatory signaling can influence plaque structure (Xue et al. ).

Delta‐like ligand 4 (Dll4) is a canonical Notch ligand induced in activated macrophages and can amplify inflammatory macrophage programs (Fung et al. ). Dll4‐Notch blockade attenuates atherosclerosis and metabolic inflammation in hyperlipidemic mice (Fukuda et al. ). More recently, palmitic acid exposure in Type 2 diabetes was linked to plaque vulnerability through macrophage Dll4 signaling and VSMC senescence (Wang et al. ). Together, these observations support testing whether selective reduction of macrophage Dll4 activity can modify VSMC senescence and plaque composition.

Matrine is a quinolizidine alkaloid from Sophora species with anti‐inflammatory activity in vascular and macrophage‐related settings. In VSMCs, matrine has been associated with reduced inflammatory responses and improved lipid‐metabolic disturbance through pathways that include NF‐κB regulation (Wang et al. ), and it can suppress adhesion‐molecule expression in activated VSMCs (Liu et al. ). Systemic matrine, however, lacks intrinsic cellular selectivity. Macrophage‐oriented nanomedicine provides a route for preferential delivery to inflammatory vascular sites and has shown efficacy in experimental atherosclerosis (Gao et al. ).

We therefore developed matrine‐loaded liposomes functionalized with macrophage‐derived membrane vesicles. The membrane‐functionalized formulations were designated DTLPs and M‐DTLPs. F4/80 and CD68 were used as macrophage membrane‐associated markers to verify membrane incorporation. We examined formulation properties, macrophage uptake, Dll4‐dependent macrophage‐VSMC signaling, VSMC senescence, plaque composition, in vivo localization, pharmacokinetics, and safety. Free matrine and matrine‐loaded non‐targeted liposomes were included in the therapeutic comparisons to distinguish matrine pharmacology, liposomal delivery, and macrophage membrane functionalization.

NTLPs were prepared by thin‐film hydration followed by size standardization. The lipid phase contained 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphocholine (DSPC), cholesterol, and dioleoylphosphatidylethanolamine (DOPE) at a molar ratio of 49:21:30; DSPE‐PEG2000 was included at 5 mol% of total phospholipid. Lipids were dissolved in chloroform, rotary evaporated at 50°C, vacuum dried, and hydrated to a total lipid concentration of 10 mmol/L. For matrine‐loaded cores, matrine was present during hydration at 50 μg/mL. The suspension was probe‐sonicated at 100 W for 15 min and sequentially extruded through 400‐, 200‐, and 100‐nm polycarbonate membranes, with at least 10 passes through each membrane. M‐NTLPs were produced by the same procedure without macrophage membrane fusion. For membrane functionalization, primary mouse macrophages were harvested as described below; membrane material was isolated by hypotonic disruption, mechanical homogenization, and differential centrifugation and converted to vesicles by sonication and extrusion. Membrane protein was quantified by BCA assay and mixed with liposomal cores at a membrane‐protein‐to‐total‐lipid mass ratio of 1:1. The mixture was bath‐sonicated at 42 kHz and 100 W for 2 min and co‐extruded 15 times through a 200‐nm membrane to generate DTLPs or M‐DTLPs. Unfused membrane was removed by centrifugation at 10,000g for 30 min at 4°C. Unencapsulated matrine was removed by centrifugal buffer exchange with three phosphate‐buffered saline washes. Final formulations were stored at 4°C and used under matched buffer conditions. F4/80 and CD68 were treated as macrophage membrane‐associated retention markers, not as two independent targeting ligands.

Hydrodynamic diameter and polydispersity index (PDI) were measured by dynamic light scattering, and zeta potential was measured by electrophoretic light scattering on a Malvern Zetasizer platform. Vesicle morphology was examined by transmission electron microscopy. F4/80 and CD68 retention was assessed by immunoblotting and fluorescence detection in macrophage membrane input, NTLPs, DTLPs, and M‐DTLPs. Matrine was quantified by HPLC after removal of unencapsulated drug. Encapsulation efficiency was calculated as 100 × (encapsulated matrine/input matrine), and drug loading was calculated as 100 × (encapsulated matrine/total mass of the recovered matrine‐loaded formulation). Short‐term colloidal stability was assessed at 0 and 24 h. Long‐term stability at 4°C was evaluated at 0, 1, 3, and 6 months by particle size, PDI, zeta potential, matrine retention relative to baseline, and encapsulation efficiency. Release studies were performed at 37°C in phosphate‐buffered saline and serum‐supplemented phosphate‐buffered saline for 72 h, with released matrine quantified chromatographically.

Primary macrophages were obtained from the peritoneal cavities of C57BL/6 mice. Mice received 3 mL sterile 3% Brewer thioglycollate intraperitoneally; 4 days later, the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 8 mL ice‐cold phosphate‐buffered saline. Recovered cells were centrifuged at 300g for 5 min, resuspended in Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium (DMEM; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific) containing 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin, plated for 2 h at 37°C with 5% CO2, and washed to remove nonadherent cells. Primary mouse aortic VSMCs were isolated from thoracic aortas after removal of adventitia and endothelial lining, minced, and digested with collagenase Type II (1 mg/mL) plus elastase (0.5 mg/mL) at 37°C for 1 h. Cells were filtered through a 70‐μm strainer, centrifuged at 300g for 5 min, initially expanded in DMEM with 20% fetal bovine serum, and maintained for experiments in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin; passages 3–6 were used. M1 polarization used lipopolysaccharide (100 ng/mL) plus recombinant interferon‐γ (20 ng/mL) for 24 h, whereas M2 polarization used interleukin‐4 (20 ng/mL) plus interleukin‐13 (20 ng/mL) for 24 h. M1 and M2 phenotypes were verified by iNOS/CD86 and ARG1/CD206 immunofluorescence, respectively (Figure ). For uptake studies, macrophages were seeded at 2 × 105 cells per well in 6‐well plates and exposed to DiO‐labeled NTLPs, DTLPs, or M‐DTLPs at 5.0 μg/mL total lipid for 24 h at 37°C. Dose‐ranging experiments evaluating 1.0, 5.0, and 10.0 μg/mL over 24 h identified 5.0 μg/mL as the working concentration because it produced a robust uptake signal while preserving cellular tolerance. Cells were washed three times with phosphate‐buffered saline before flow‐cytometric or confocal analysis. Intracellular trafficking in M1 macrophages was assessed with LysoTracker and DAPI, and DiO‐LysoTracker colocalization was quantified by Pearson correlation coefficient.

M1 macrophages were exposed to NTLPs, DTLPs, or M‐DTLPs at 5.0 μg/mL for 24 h. Macrophage‐VSMC signaling was then examined in a non‐contact Transwell system using 0.4‐μm‐pore inserts. VSMCs were seeded in the lower chamber and macrophages in the insert at matched densities of 4 × 104 cells/cm2 (1:1 seeding ratio). After formulation exposure, macrophages were washed to remove extracellular liposomes and co‐cultured above VSMCs for 24 h, permitting exchange of soluble mediators without direct cell–cell contact. Macrophage Dll4 and VSMC HES1, p21, and p16 were analyzed in their respective compartments. For Dll4 loss‐of‐function, macrophages received a Dll4‐targeting siRNA or non‐targeting siRNA control before M1 polarization; knockdown was verified by immunoblotting before the Transwell experiment. For rescue, M1 macrophages were transfected with a Dll4 expression construct or matched empty vector before M‐DTLP treatment, and restoration of Dll4 was confirmed by immunoblotting. Dll4 immunofluorescence used an anti‐Dll4 antibody from Abcam (Cambridge, UK), and immunoblotting used antibodies to Dll4 (Proteintech Group, Wuhan, China), HES1 (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), p21, p16, and β‐actin, with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies and chemiluminescent detection.

VSMC senescence was evaluated using complementary molecular and functional endpoints. SA‐β‐galactosidase‐positive cells were quantified from fixed acquisition fields; p21 and p16 were measured by immunoblotting; proliferation was assessed by EdU incorporation; and the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype was assessed by IL‐6 and IL‐1β concentrations in VSMC culture supernatants. For each independent culture, multiple microscopic fields were averaged to yield one biological replicate. The same endpoints were evaluated after macrophage Dll4 knockdown and Dll4 overexpression rescue. For in vivo confirmation, VSMC‐associated senescence was assessed by ACTA2/p21 double immunofluorescence in aortic‐root plaques and expressed as the proportion of ACTA2‐positive cells that were also p21‐positive.

Eight‐week‐old male ApoE−/− mice on a C57BL/6J background (B6/JGpt‐Apoe

em1Cd82
/Gpt, strain T001458; GemPharmatech, Nanjing, China) were acclimatized for 1 week and then maintained for 16 weeks on a Western‐type high‐fat diet (D12079B; Research Diets, New Brunswick, NJ, USA) containing 42% of energy from fat and 0.15% cholesterol. Mice were block‐randomized by baseline body weight to NTLPs, DTLPs, free matrine, M‐NTLPs, or M‐DTLPs (n = 6 per group for efficacy and safety experiments). Six mice were included in each efficacy and safety group, consistent with prior laboratory studies using the same ApoE−/− plaque‐histology model and endpoints; no formal prospective power calculation was performed. Formulations were administered by tail‐vein injection at weeks 4, 8, and 12 after initiation of the high‐fat diet. Liposomal groups received 10 mg/kg total lipid; matrine‐containing groups were dose matched at 0.5 mg/kg matrine equivalent, and unloaded controls received the corresponding lipid dose. Body weight was recorded every 2 weeks from week 0 to week 16. Investigators performing lesion morphometry and image quantification were masked to group allocation. No animals were excluded after randomization. At week 16, mice were anesthetized with inhaled isoflurane (3% induction and 1.5%–2.0% maintenance in oxygen); adequate depth was confirmed by loss of the pedal withdrawal reflex. Blood was collected under deep anesthesia, mice were euthanized with 5% isoflurane, death was confirmed by cessation of respiration and heartbeat, and the arterial tree was perfused with phosphate‐buffered saline before tissue collection. Animals were monitored daily for general condition, mobility, grooming, food and water access, and signs of distress; predefined humane endpoints included sustained loss of more than 20% body weight, severe respiratory distress, persistent recumbency, or inability to access food or water.

Whole aortas were stained en face with Oil Red O to quantify plaque area. Aortic‐root sections were used for Oil Red O measurement of lipid‐positive plaque area, Sirius Red and Masson trichrome assessment of collagen, and hematoxylin and eosin analysis of fibrous‐cap thickness and necrotic‐core area. Fibrous‐cap thickness was measured at the thinnest cap overlying the necrotic core, and necrotic‐core area was expressed relative to total plaque area. VSMC content was evaluated by ACTA2 immunofluorescence, and VSMC‐associated senescence by ACTA2/p21 double immunofluorescence. Separate plaque immunofluorescence assessed Dll4, CD68, and DAPI; CD68‐positive plaque area, Dll4 fluorescence intensity within CD68‐positive regions, and Dll4‐CD68 Pearson correlation coefficients were quantified using identical acquisition and threshold settings across groups. For each mouse, multiple sections or fields were averaged before statistical analysis so that the animal, rather than the image field, was the experimental unit.

For biodistribution, DiD‐labeled M‐NTLPs and M‐DTLPs were administered intravenously to separate mice. Whole‐body fluorescence was recorded at 1, 4, 12, and 24 h with identical acquisition settings. At 24 h, the heart, liver, spleen, kidney, and aorta were imaged ex vivo, and organ fluorescence was normalized to tissue weight. Aortic en face Oil Red O/DiD imaging was used to compare plaque‐rich and non‐plaque vascular regions and to calculate the plaque‐to‐non‐plaque fluorescence ratio. Plaque sections were analyzed for DiD association with CD68‐positive macrophages and for directional Manders overlap with CD68, ACTA2, and CD31. For pharmacokinetics, free matrine, M‐NTLPs, and M‐DTLPs were administered as a single intravenous dose at 0.5 mg/kg matrine equivalent. Plasma was sampled over 24 h and matrine quantified by reverse‐phase HPLC. Noncompartmental analysis provided terminal half‐life, AUC0–24, and systemic clearance. Biodistribution and pharmacokinetic experiments were analyzed independently of the 16‐week efficacy cohort.

Systemic tolerability was assessed in the five efficacy groups over the 16‐week study. Body weight was measured every 2 weeks. Endpoint serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, chloride, creatine kinase, creatinine, potassium, and sodium were measured after the final treatment interval. Liver, kidney, spleen, lung, and heart were examined by hematoxylin and eosin staining for overt treatment‐associated injury. Serum total cholesterol, LDL‐C, HDL‐C, and triglycerides were measured at the same endpoint to determine whether the plaque phenotype was accompanied by major systemic lipid changes.

Data are presented as mean ± SD unless otherwise stated. For cell experiments, n denotes independent biological cultures; repeated microscopic fields or technical wells were averaged within each culture before analysis. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test and homogeneity of variance with the Brown‐Forsythe test. Two‐group comparisons used unpaired two‐tailed Student t‐tests. For multiple groups, one‐way analysis of variance was followed by Sidak's multiplicity‐adjusted test for pairwise comparisons; safety and serum‐lipid panels used Dunnett's test with M‐DTLPs as the reference group. Longitudinal body‐weight and whole‐body fluorescence data were analyzed by two‐way repeated‐measures analysis of variance with treatment, time, and treatment‐by‐time terms; a Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied when the sphericity assumption was not met. Long‐term formulation stability was analyzed by repeated‐measures analysis with baseline as the reference. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Figure annotations are defined as ns, not significant; *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; and ***p < 0.001.

Three related formulations were evaluated: NTLPs, macrophage membrane‐functionalized DTLPs, and matrine‐loaded macrophage membrane‐functionalized M‐DTLPs (Figure ). Dynamic light scattering showed narrow, overlapping particle‐size distributions, while hydrodynamic diameter, PDI, and zeta potential remained comparable among formulations (Figure ). Transmission electron microscopy showed predominantly spherical vesicles (Figure ). F4/80 and CD68 signals were enriched in DTLPs and M‐DTLPs relative to NTLPs, with no material difference between the two membrane‐functionalized formulations, supporting retention of macrophage membrane‐associated proteins after fusion (Figure ).

M‐DTLPs showed consistent matrine loading and high encapsulation efficiency (Figure ). Particle size and PDI remained unchanged after 24 h (Figure ), and longer‐term follow‐up showed preserved particle size, PDI, zeta potential, matrine retention, and encapsulation efficiency over 6 months (Figure ). Matrine release was gradual over 72 h in both phosphate‐buffered saline and serum‐containing medium (Figure ). M1 and M2 polarization were validated by iNOS/CD86 and ARG1/CD206 staining, respectively (Figure ). Flow cytometry showed substantially greater uptake of DTLPs and M‐DTLPs than NTLPs in M1 macrophages, while uptake differences were smaller in M0 and M2 macrophages (Figure ). Confocal microscopy of M1 macrophages showed abundant intracellular DiO signal and greater DiO‐LysoTracker colocalization with DTLPs and M‐DTLPs than with NTLPs (Figure ).

M1 polarization increased macrophage Dll4 compared with M0, whereas NTLPs and unloaded DTLPs produced little change in the M1‐associated Dll4 signal. M‐DTLPs reduced macrophage Dll4 and were accompanied by lower VSMC HES1, p21, and p16 (Figure ). Dll4 knockdown in M1 macrophages reproduced the molecular effect of M‐DTLPs, reducing Dll4 together with VSMC HES1, p21, and p16 (Figure ). Functionally, both Dll4 knockdown and M‐DTLP treatment reduced VSMC SA‐β‐galactosidase positivity and IL‐6/IL‐1β while increasing EdU incorporation (Figure ). Conversely, macrophage Dll4 overexpression during M‐DTLP treatment partially restored Dll4 and VSMC HES1, p21, and p16 and partially reversed the SA‐β‐galactosidase and EdU responses (Figure ). These loss‐of‐function and rescue findings support a Dll4‐dependent contribution to the anti‐senescent effect of M‐DTLPs.

Five‐group efficacy comparisons distinguished unloaded particles, free matrine, non‐targeted liposomal matrine, and macrophage membrane‐functionalized liposomal matrine. En face Oil Red O staining showed the lowest aortic plaque burden with M‐DTLPs, with progressive improvement from free matrine to M‐NTLPs and then M‐DTLPs (Figure ). Cross‐sectional Oil Red O showed the same direction for lipid‐positive plaque area (Figure ). Sirius Red demonstrated greater collagen‐positive plaque area after matrine treatment, with the strongest response in M‐DTLPs (Figure ); Masson trichrome provided concordant collagen findings (Figure ). Hematoxylin and eosin analyses showed greater fibrous‐cap thickness and smaller necrotic‐core area in M‐DTLP‐treated plaques (Figure ). ACTA2‐positive plaque area increased across matrine‐containing formulations and was greatest with M‐DTLPs (Figure ). ACTA2/p21 double immunofluorescence showed a lower proportion of senescent‐marker‐positive VSMCs with M‐DTLPs (Figure ). In parallel, plaque CD68‐positive area remained broadly comparable across groups, whereas Dll4 fluorescence within CD68‐positive regions and Dll4‐CD68 colocalization decreased progressively with matrine‐containing formulations and were lowest with M‐DTLPs (Figure ).

Whole‐body fluorescence declined over time after both M‐NTLP and M‐DTLP administration, with broadly similar systemic signal trajectories (Figure ). Ex vivo imaging showed substantial liver and spleen signal for both formulations, while aortic fluorescence was greater with M‐DTLPs (Figure ). En face aortic imaging demonstrated greater DiD signal in Oil Red O‐positive plaque regions after M‐DTLP administration and a higher plaque‐to‐non‐plaque fluorescence ratio than with M‐NTLPs (Figure ). Within plaques, M‐DTLPs showed greater DiD colocalization with CD68‐positive macrophages and a higher DiD‐CD68 overlap coefficient (Figure ). Cell‐type comparison showed the strongest DiD overlap with CD68, lower overlap with ACTA2, and no material increase in overlap with CD31 (Figure ). These findings support preferential plaque‐macrophage localization rather than absolute macrophage specificity. Pharmacokinetic analysis showed prolonged terminal half‐life and greater systemic exposure, with reduced clearance, for both liposomal matrine formulations relative to free matrine; M‐NTLPs and M‐DTLPs remained comparable for these major parameters (Figure ).

Body weight increased similarly across NTLP, DTLP, free matrine, M‐NTLP, and M‐DTLP groups during the 16‐week observation period, with no treatment‐associated divergence (Figure ). Endpoint serum AST, potassium, sodium, ALT, chloride, creatine kinase, and creatinine were broadly comparable among groups (Figure ). Hematoxylin and eosin staining of liver, kidney, spleen, lung, and heart did not reveal overt treatment‐associated tissue injury (Figure ). Serum total cholesterol, LDL‐C, HDL‐C, and triglycerides were also comparable across groups (Figure ), arguing against a major systemic lipid‐lowering explanation for the plaque‐composition changes.

This study integrates formulation, cellular, mechanistic, plaque, biodistribution, pharmacokinetic, and safety data to evaluate matrine‐loaded macrophage membrane‐functionalized liposomes in atherosclerosis. The formulation preserved nanoscale liposomal characteristics, retained macrophage membrane‐associated markers, and showed preferential uptake by inflammatory macrophages. M‐DTLPs reduced macrophage Dll4, attenuated downstream VSMC HES1 and senescence markers, improved multiple plaque stability‐associated structural features, and showed no overt systemic toxicity signal under the tested conditions. These observations are consistent with prior studies showing that VSMC phenotypic modulation is a major determinant of atherosclerotic plaque composition and fibrous‐cap biology (Shankman et al. ; Wirka et al. ).

The mechanistic experiments strengthen the interpretation of the macrophage Dll4‐VSMC senescence link. Dll4 knockdown in M1 macrophages reproduced the molecular and functional effects of M‐DTLPs, whereas Dll4 overexpression partially reversed them. This bidirectional manipulation supports a Dll4‐dependent component of the response. HES1 changed concordantly in VSMCs, but HES1 itself was not directly manipulated; accordingly, the data support a Dll4‐dependent macrophage‐to‐VSMC signaling program without claiming that the complete Dll4‐HES1 pathway has been exhaustively established. This interpretation is consistent with established roles of Dll4‐Notch signaling in macrophage activation (Nakano et al. ).

The senescence phenotype is supported by several independent readouts. In addition to SA‐β‐galactosidase staining, M‐DTLP treatment reduced VSMC p21 and p16, lowered SASP‐related IL‐6 and IL‐1β, and increased EdU incorporation. The in vivo ACTA2/p21 double‐immunofluorescence analysis further links the senescence signal to VSMCs within plaques. These findings are consistent with prior evidence that VSMC senescence can compromise reparative capacity and contribute to vulnerability‐associated plaque architecture (Wang et al. ).

The five‐group efficacy design clarifies the relative contributions of matrine, liposomal delivery, and macrophage membrane functionalization. Free matrine improved plaque‐related readouts compared with unloaded controls, M‐NTLPs produced a larger effect than free matrine, and M‐DTLPs produced the strongest overall plaque phenotype. Importantly, M‐NTLPs and M‐DTLPs had similar major pharmacokinetic parameters, arguing that the additional efficacy of M‐DTLPs is not explained simply by longer systemic matrine exposure. The data therefore support an added delivery advantage associated with macrophage membrane functionalization. The direction of the matrine effect is also consistent with prior evidence that matrine suppresses ROS‐dependent inflammatory signaling in ox‐LDL‐stimulated macrophages (Zhou et al. ).

The in vivo localization data also refine the targeting interpretation. Both liposomal formulations accumulated strongly in liver and spleen, consistent with expected reticuloendothelial handling of nanoparticles. Against this background, M‐DTLPs showed greater aortic signal, higher plaque‐to‐non‐plaque fluorescence, and greater DiD association with CD68‐positive plaque macrophages than M‐NTLPs. Cell‐type overlap analysis further favored CD68 over ACTA2 and CD31. These findings support preferential plaque‐macrophage localization, while avoiding the stronger claim of absolute macrophage specificity in the absence of receptor‐blocking experiments. Prior nanomedicine studies have likewise demonstrated lesion‐directed nanoparticle delivery to plaque macrophages and therapeutic modulation of plaque inflammation (Flores et al. ; Fredman et al. ; Tang et al. ).

The plaque findings extend beyond lipid and collagen surrogates. M‐DTLP treatment was associated with a thicker fibrous cap, a smaller necrotic core, greater ACTA2‐positive plaque area, increased collagen, and fewer ACTA2/p21 double‐positive VSMCs. Together, these structural features define a plaque phenotype associated with greater stability. Nevertheless, plaque rupture, thrombosis, intraplaque hemorrhage, and long‐term clinical events were not directly measured, so the conclusions are intentionally framed around stability‐associated features rather than definitive plaque stabilization.

Several limitations remain. The membrane‐fusion platform is supported by retention of macrophage membrane‐associated proteins and preferential plaque‐macrophage localization, but the molecular determinants responsible for that preference have not been resolved and receptor‐blocking or competition experiments were not performed. HES1 changed downstream of macrophage Dll4 manipulation but was not itself directly perturbed. The study did not include a dose–response efficacy series, direct intraplaque matrine concentration‐time profiling, plaque rupture or thrombosis endpoints, female cohorts, additional disease models, or large‐animal validation. These questions, together with longer‐term efficacy and chronic toxicology, remain priorities for translational development.

M‐DTLPs combine macrophage membrane‐functionalized delivery with matrine pharmacology to suppress macrophage Dll4‐dependent VSMC senescence, improve plaque composition and structural stability‐associated features, and preferentially localize to plaque macrophages in preclinical atherosclerosis. These findings support further mechanistic and translational evaluation of macrophage membrane‐functionalized matrine nanotherapy.

medicine.title: Cancer‐Related Worries of Grandparents of Children With Cancer and Survivors: Mixed‐Methods Findings From the Multicenter GROKids Project
medicine.abstract: Grandparents of children with cancer may experience considerable emotional distress, including cancer‐related worries. However, little is known about the prevalence, nature, and longitudinal course of these worries.This study (a) examined the prevalence, nature, and longitudinal changes of cancer‐related worries among grandparents within 2 years following their grandchild's cancer diagnosis and into survivorship and (b) explored associations with information received, socio‐demographic, and clinical characteristics.Using a mixed‐methods design, we conducted a multicenter cohort study of grandparents of children diagnosed with cancer, recruited from eight pediatric oncology centers in Switzerland, with assessments at 3‐, 6‐, 12‐, and 24‐months postdiagnosis (T1–T4). In a complementary cross‐sectional study, grandparents of survivors were recruited (TCCS). Cancer‐related worries were assessed with an adapted Worry and Anxiety Questionnaire (WAQ), including an open‐ended question. Prevalence was calculated as the proportion reporting worries. Changes over time were analyzed with multilevel models and t‐tests, and associations with univariable regression analyses. Free‐text responses were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.Forty‐one grandparents of newly diagnosed children (T1–T4) and 133 grandparents of survivors (TCCS) participated (mean ages 68 and 72 years; 61% and 60% female, respectively). At T1, all grandparents reported worries. Although WAQ total scores declined over time (p < 0.001), 84%–88% still reported worries during treatment and 75% in survivorship. Qualitative analyses indicated that worry content shifted from survival and treatment initially to recurrence and long‐term consequences later. Receiving more medical information and lower education were associated with lower WAQ total scores (p < 0.05).Cancer‐related worries are common among grandparents, often persist into survivorship, and shift in focus over time. Timely medical information provision may help reduce worries, and healthcare teams could encourage parents to involve grandparents in family discussions.
