central nervous system

Worry Anxiety Questionnaire

When a child is diagnosed with cancer, the impact is felt across the entire family, including the grandparents [, , , , , , , ]. Research has shown that grandparents experience increased distress and a lower quality of life shortly after the diagnosis [, , , , , , ]. Despite these challenges, grandparents often remain important sources of emotional and practical support for the family [].

Qualitative studies have identified cancer‐related worries as an important part of grandparents' experiences [, ]. These worries often center around the grandchild's health, including fear of cancer recurrence, long‐term effects, or death. Grandparents may also be concerned about the well‐being of the parents, healthy siblings, or their own ability to support the family [, ]. However, quantitative evidence on the prevalence of worries, changes over time, and predictors remains limited.

Grandparents generally report good long‐term adjustment on generic outcomes such as psychological distress, with levels comparable to the general population [], yet cancer‐related worries may persist. Persistent worries have also been documented among survivors of childhood cancer (CCS) [] and their parents [], even years after diagnosis. Although such worries may represent a normal response to severe illness, persistent or severe worries may negatively impact quality of life and daily functioning in grandparents, as reported in parents of CCS [].

Contextual factors, such as an individual's role within the family and access to information and support, may be relevant for understanding differences in cancer‐related worries. Grandparents occupy a distinct position within the family system: they are emotionally invested yet typically have limited involvement in medical decision‐making and less direct access to healthcare professionals [, , ]. As a result, they may have fewer opportunities to obtain information about their grandchild's condition, which may contribute to uncertainty and persistent cancer‐related worries.

Among CCS [] and in the general population [], unmet information needs have been associated with greater health‐related worries. Having access to adequate information may help alleviate such worries. However, little is known about how the receipt of information influences cancer‐related worries among grandparents of children with cancer. Understanding the prevalence and course of these worries, as well as factors associated with them, may help identify grandparents who experience persistent or severe worries and inform strategies to support them.

This study (a) examined the prevalence, nature, and longitudinal changes of cancer‐related worries among grandparents within 2 years following their grandchild's cancer diagnosis and into survivorship and (b) explored associations with information received, socio‐demographic, and clinical characteristics.

This analysis is part of the multicenter mixed‐methods GROkids Project on the acute and long‐term psychosocial consequences in grandparents of children with cancer. We used data from the longitudinal cohort of grandparents of newly diagnosed patients and cross‐sectional data of grandparents of CCS. Detailed study procedures were reported elsewhere [].

For the cohort study, we enrolled families of children aged ≤ 18 years who were newly diagnosed with cancer and undergoing treatment in Switzerland. Parents received a study information sheet and a contact form, which they completed and returned to the study team. After receiving the contact form, grandparents were contacted separately by post and were sent an information sheet, informed consent form, and a prepaid return envelope. Grandparents completed questionnaires at four timepoints: T1 (3 months), T2 (6 months), T3 (1 year), and T4 (2 years).

For the cross‐sectional study, we enrolled families of CCS diagnosed 3–11 years earlier, with at least 2 years since treatment completion. This timeframe was selected to extend the assessment beyond the first 2 years after diagnosis, covered by the longitudinal cohort, into longer‐term survivorship. Parents or CCS received the same study information sheet and contact form, which they returned to the study team. Upon receipt, grandparents were contacted by post and received the study information sheet, informed consent form, and a prepaid return envelope. Grandparents completed a single questionnaire (TCCS).

Follow‐up reminders were sent after 4 weeks, and telephone calls were made when necessary. To support cohort retention, greeting cards were sent to grandparents on major holidays, and regular study updates were provided. Participants were recruited between October 2020 and March 2023, with follow‐up continuing until December 2024 [].

Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Ethics Committee Northwest and Central Switzerland (EKNZ 2020‐01409), and all participants provided written informed consent.

Cancer‐related worries were assessed using the Worry Anxiety Questionnaire (WAQ) [] at T1–T4, and among CCS‐grandparents (TCCS). It included quantitative and one qualitative open‐ended question. The first item of the original questionnaire (“What subjects do you worry about most often?”; free‐text answer) was slightly adapted (“Are you worried about your grandchild who was diagnosed with cancer? If yes, what specific worries do you have?”; free‐text answer) to specifically capture cancer‐related worries. Responses to this question, as well as the subsequent quantitative questions of the WAQ, were interpreted as reflecting cancer‐related worries, given the explicit reference to the grandchild's cancer diagnosis in the adapted first question. For Items 2–6, participants rated their responses on a 5‐point Likert scale (e.g., 1 “not at all” to 5 “very severely”), which were recoded into a 0–8 scale []. The items assessed the following aspects: the excessiveness (Item 2) and frequency (Item 3) of worries in the past 2 weeks, difficulty controlling worries (Item 4), physical symptoms related to worries, including restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbances (Items 5a–f), and the interference of worries with daily life (Item 6).

The WAQ total score (possible range 0–80) was calculated by summing Items 2, 3, 4, 5a–f, and 6 []. Scores were calculated if ≥ 6 of 10 items were completed. Any missing items were imputed using the participant's median; if fewer than six items were completed, the total score was set to be missing. The WAQ total scale showed very good internal consistency at all time points (Cronbach's α = 0.87–0.89).

The severity of cancer‐related worries was assessed using individual WAQ items on excessiveness, frequency, difficulty controlling worries, and negative impact on family life. For interpretation, responses were considered indicative of severe worry when grandparents reported “severe/very severe” or “frequent/very frequent” worries.

Because no quantitative studies have yet examined cancer‐related worries in grandparents of children with cancer, a range of socio‐demographic and clinical characteristics was explored. Information received was included as a potentially relevant target for intervention.

At all timepoints, grandparents' receipt of cancer‐related information was assessed using the Grandparents Information Needs Questionnaire [, ]. The measure covered 14 domains: nine medical (cancer type, treatment, treatment goals, side‐effects, disease progression, relapse, survival chance, late effects, palliative care) and five psychosocial (family communication, parental support, support for grandchildren, self‐support, peer support) domains. For each domain, participants indicated whether they had received information (yes/no). We summed the 14 binary items to provide a descriptive summary of the breadth of information received across domains (range: 0–14, with higher scores indicating that information had been received across more domains) [].

We examined the associations between cancer‐related worries and the following socio‐demographic characteristics: grandparents' gender (female vs. male), age (years; continuous), education level (high vs. low/medium), language region (German vs. French/Italian), monthly income (> 6000 Swiss francs [CHF] vs. ≤ 6000 CHF, corresponding to the median income), number of grandchildren (continuous), and the grandchild's gender (female vs. male).

We examined the associations between cancer‐related worries and the following clinical characteristics: the grandchild's age at diagnosis (years; continuous), diagnosis type (leukemia/lymphoma vs. central nervous system [CNS] tumor, and other diagnoses), and whether the grandchild experienced a relapse (yes vs. no).

Additionally, for grandparents of CCS, we included two survivorship‐specific variables: whether grandparents reported late effects in the grandchild (yes vs. no), and time since diagnosis (years; continuous), which ranged from 3 to 11 years in this group.

Quantitative analyses of prevalence, changes in WAQ total scores, and associated factors were based on closed‐ended questionnaire items. These analyses were conducted with IBM SPSS Statistics version 28.0 (IBM Corp, New York, US). All statistical tests were two‐tailed, with p‐values < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

Qualitative analyses of the nature of worries and changes in their nature over time used the open‐ended question (WAQ Item 1). Free‐text responses on this item were analyzed using Microsoft Excel for Microsoft 365 version 2507 (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, US).

Descriptive statistics were used to assess the prevalence, nature, and severity of cancer‐related worries. Specifically, we examined: (1) the presence of worries (Item 1; yes/no); (2) the average level of cancer‐related worries based on the WAQ total score; (3) the nature of worries (categorized from free‐text responses to Item 1); and (4) the severity of worries, based on the distributions of severity‐related individual items, i.e., excessive worries, frequency of worry, difficulty controlling worries, and negative impact on family life.

The free‐text responses were analyzed using qualitative content analysis []. Responses in German, French, and Italian were translated into English using DeepL Translate (DeepL SE, Cologne, Germany) and verified by team members fluent in the respective languages. One researcher (AM) coded the participants' responses and grouped the codes into overarching categories and subcategories of worries. An inductive approach was used, in which categories and subcategories were derived from the data rather than predefined. A research assistant checked the coding, and a third researcher (PFR) reviewed disagreements. Frequencies for each category and subcategory were summarized in a table.

Longitudinal changes in WAQ total scores during the first 2 years after diagnosis (T1–T4) were analyzed using a linear multilevel model with a random intercept to account for within‐person correlations. Time was included as a categorical independent variable, and the WAQ total score as the continuous dependent variable. We compared WAQ total scores of grandparents 3 months after diagnosis (T1) with those of CCS (TCCS) using an independent samples t‐test. Changes in the nature of worries over time were assessed by tabulating the qualitative categories of worries at T1–T4 and TCCS.

Univariable linear regression models were fitted to examine associations between WAQ total scores (continuous dependent variable) and the number of domains in which information was received at each time point, as well as socio‐demographic and clinical characteristics at T1. Each predictor was entered separately, and no multivariable models were fitted. Analyses were conducted separately in the cohort and cross‐sectional samples of grandparents.

Participant characteristics of grandparents shortly after diagnosis and in survivorship are presented in Table . For the cohort study (T1–T4), a total of 158 families were identified as eligible and approached. Contact information was provided for 85 grandparents from 30 families. Of those 85 grandparents, 41 (48%) from 20 families provided informed consent and completed the WAQ at least at one time point. A total of 13 families had more than one grandparent participating.

In the cross‐sectional study (TCCS), pediatric oncology divisions identified 1188 eligible families of CCS. Of those identified families, 86 families provided contact information for 225 grandparents. Of those 225 grandparents, 148 provided informed consent, and 133 (59%) from 66 families ultimately completed the WAQ. A total of 45 families had more than one grandparent participating.

In both studies, all grandparents for whom contact information was provided were subsequently approached by the study team.

At 3 months postdiagnosis (T1), all participating grandparents reported cancer‐related worries about their grandchild. Although this percentage gradually declined over time, most grandparents continued to report worries during treatment and survivorship: 88% at T2, 79% at T3, 84% at T4, and 75% at TCCS (3–11 years postdiagnosis).

Most grandparents reported low levels of worry severity across all time points, with the majority indicating that they rarely or never experienced excessive cancer‐related worries, had little difficulty controlling their worries, and perceived little or no negative impact of worries on family life (Figure ; detailed percentages are provided in Supplementary Appendix ). Nevertheless, a subgroup reported more severe worries in the early phase after diagnosis (T1–T2). For example, at T1, up to 44% reported frequent or very frequent worries, 18% experienced severe difficulty controlling their worries, and for 24% worries had a severe or very severe impact on family life. These proportions gradually declined over time, and in the survivorship phase (TCCS), only 8% reported frequent or very frequent worries, none reported difficulty controlling their worries, and 4% reported a severe or very severe negative impact on family life.

Multilevel analyses revealed a significant decrease in cancer‐related worries (WAQ total scores) over time (p < 0.001). Estimated marginal mean WAQ scores declined from M = 21.86 at T1 to M = 16.96 at T4 (Supplementary Appendix ). An independent samples t‐test showed that mean WAQ scores were significantly lower among grandparents in long‐term survivorship (M = 17.78) compared to those at T1 (p < 0.001).

Qualitative content analysis of open‐ended questions revealed a wide range of cancer‐related worries reported by grandparents over time (Table ). Worries about the health and well‐being of the grandchild were most prevalent, reported by 74% at T1 and 57% at TCCS. Within this category, worries about survival and prognosis were common early on (56% at T1), alongside worries about short‐term side effects of treatment (21% at T1). These health‐related worries decreased during treatment and follow‐up, with 16% of grandparents being concerned about survival at T4 and only 4% at TCCS. However, fear of cancer recurrence increased from 0% at T1 to 28% at T4. In survivorship, it was the most frequently reported concern (42% at TCCS), followed by the worry of long‐term health consequences (10% at TCCS).

Types of cancer‐related worries over time based on open‐ended responses from worried grandparents (any worry about grandchild: yes).

Note: Percentages reflect the proportion of worried grandparents mentioning the respective category or subcategory at each timepoint. Numbers in parentheses indicate absolute counts. Subcategories do not sum up to the total number of the main category, as some instances were only coded at the main category level when no specific subcategory could be identified. Also, grandparents could report multiple worries. T1–T4 represent measurement points at 3‐, 6‐, 12‐, and 24‐months postdiagnosis, respectively. TCCS refers to the survivorship phase, 3–11 years after diagnosis.

Grandparents also reported psycho‐emotional worries about the grandchild, such as emotional well‐being, coping, and trauma, although at lower rates (10%–29% across T1–T4 and TCCS). Worries related to the grandchild's future, including uncertainty, independence, and family planning, were reported by about 5%–25% of grandparents across time points. Education and employment worries (0%–9%) and worries about the grandchild's relationships (2%–9%) were reported less frequently. A few grandparents expressed worries about the well‐being of the child's parents or siblings, as well as their own well‐being (0%–8%).

Among grandparents in the 2 years following diagnosis (T1–T4), receiving medical information across more domains was significantly associated with lower cancer‐related worries (WAQ total scores) (β = −0.20, p = 0.024), whereas receiving psychosocial information across more domains was not associated with worries. In contrast, among CCS‐grandparents (TCCS), no significant associations were found between the number of medical or psychosocial domains in which information was received and WAQ total scores (Table ).

In univariable multilevel models with repeated measures (T1–T4), education level was the only variable significantly associated with WAQ total scores (Table ). Grandparents with low/medium education levels reported lower WAQ total scores than those with high education levels (β = −0.61, p = 0.028). No significant associations were found for grandparents' gender, age, language region, monthly income, diagnosis type, relapse status, grandchild's age at diagnosis, grandchild's gender, or the number of grandchildren. At TCCS, regression analyses likewise showed no significant associations between WAQ total scores and socio‐demographic or clinical characteristics, including time since diagnosis and presence of late effects.

This study presents the first longitudinal, mixed‐methods investigation of cancer‐related worries among grandparents of children with cancer, from shortly after diagnosis into long‐term survivorship. We found that cancer‐related worries were common among grandparents, although they declined over time. Receiving medical information in the first 2 years after diagnosis was associated with lower levels of worry.

Cancer‐related worries were highly prevalent in the first 6 months after diagnosis (88%–100%), and three quarters of grandparents still reported them in survivorship. These findings are consistent with qualitative studies identifying such worries as an important aspect of grandparents' experiences [, ]. In our study, however, most grandparents did not report excessive or uncontrollable worries or severe negative impact on family life, suggesting that worries often remained at a manageable level.

Although a subgroup of grandparents experienced (very) frequent (44%) or difficult‐to‐control (18%) worries shortly after diagnosis, these proportions decreased over time. From a stress–coping perspective, this pattern may reflect the gradual development of coping strategies and the use of social support in response to ongoing uncertainty []. Decreasing worries may also reflect cognitive re‐appraisal as uncertainty diminishes over time. Increased clarity and predictability gained through knowledge and experience over time may shift appraisals from threat toward a more manageable interpretation []. Comparable adaptation processes have been described in caregivers of children with cancer [, , , ].

Grandparents expressed a wide range of worries, of which health‐related concerns were most common. The content of worries changed over time: shortly after diagnosis, survival and treatment effects were the main focus, while later concerns centered on recurrence and long‐term consequences. This shift from immediate concerns to long‐term uncertainty is consistent with findings among CCS and their parents, who continue to report health‐related worries years after treatment [, , ].

Receiving medical information across more domains was associated with fewer cancer‐related worries during the first 2 years after diagnosis, whereas receiving psychosocial information was not. This finding is consistent with the observation that grandparents' worries were predominantly medical in nature. In addition, recent findings from the GROKids cohort showed that psychosocial information was generally rated as less important than medical information []. Qualitative data further indicated that medical information helped grandparents reduce uncertainty and feel more prepared for what to expect []. In survivorship, however, no significant associations were observed with receiving information. A possible explanation is that, as worries become less severe over time, grandparents may feel less dependent on information to manage them. Thus, the provision of comprehensive medical information may be particularly important shortly after diagnosis, when worries are more prominent and severe.

Socio‐demographic and clinical characteristics were generally poor predictors of cancer‐related worries. The only significant association was observed for education: grandparents with low/medium education levels reported lower levels of worry than those with higher education levels, in contrast to findings among parents [, ]. This discrepancy may reflect differences in access to information. Higher‐educated grandparents may understand medical information better but often depend on second‐hand information and, unlike parents, lack direct interactions with clinicians to clarify questions. This may leave them with greater uncertainty.

No significant associations were observed for gender, age, income, cancer type, relapse, or late effects. Similarly, a systematic review reported no strong associations between socio‐demographic and medical characteristics and cancer‐related worries []. This suggests that cancer‐related worries may reflect a more universal emotional response, not confined to specific socio‐demographic or clinical subgroups.

Cancer‐related worries may partly reflect objective medical risks among CCS, including late effects such as secondary neoplasms [, , , ]. However, in our study, grandparents' worries were not associated with clinical factors such as diagnosis, relapse, or late effects. This suggests that worries may also reflect subjective perceptions and emotional responses rather than medical risks alone [, ].

A major strength of this study is its longitudinal design, which enabled us to examine changes in cancer‐related worries over time. Combining quantitative and qualitative data provided a more comprehensive understanding of grandparents' worries. In addition, recruiting grandparents from Italian‐, French‐, and German‐speaking regions of Switzerland increased sample diversity and may support the generalizability of the findings across language regions, although no differences in worry levels were observed across these regions. Despite these strengths, several limitations should be considered.

First, sample sizes in the longitudinal cohort were modest at individual time points (N = 32–39), despite nationwide, multicenter recruitment to maximize enrollment potential. The limited sample size may have reduced statistical power and precluded more complex analyses, such as multivariable regression to adjust for multiple covariates and multilevel modeling to account for clustering of grandparents within families.

Second, our two‐step enrollment strategy, which relied on families to provide contact details of grandparents, may have introduced selection bias. Participating grandparents may have been more involved in the family or more concerned about the grandchild's health. Conversely, grandparents experiencing the most severe worries may have avoided participation because completing a questionnaire on cancer‐related concerns felt too confronting. As a result, the findings may either overestimate or underestimate the true prevalence of worries, although these opposing mechanisms may have partly balanced each other out. Furthermore, differences between respondents and nonrespondents, including educational attainment, could not be assessed. The observed association between education and cancer‐related worries should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

Third, generalizability to other cultural and healthcare contexts may be limited. This study was conducted in Switzerland, where family structures are marked by close intergenerational ties [] and childhood cancer survival rates are among the highest in Europe []. These factors may influence grandparents' worries: close family involvement could heighten concerns, whereas high survival rates may reduce fears of death compared with settings with lower survival rates.

Finally, the questionnaire was adapted to specifically ask grandparents about worries regarding their grandchild with cancer, rather than general worry. This focus may have increased the reporting of concerns []. Moreover, although the question explicitly referred to the grandchild's diagnosis, we cannot rule out that grandparents interpreted the question more broadly. They might also have reported general concerns about their grandchild, resulting in an overestimated prevalence of cancer‐related worries. In addition, the WAQ does not provide validated cut‐off points for classifying worry severity. Therefore, we relied on individual item responses (i.e., excessive worries, frequency, difficulty controlling worries, negative impact on family life) to describe severity. While these items provide a reasonable approximation, the absence of validated thresholds limits interpretability.

Our results highlight the need to acknowledge and address cancer‐related worries among grandparents. In particular, receiving medical information was associated with fewer worries in the first 2 years after diagnosis, underlining the importance of timely, comprehensive medical information. Information resources could cover medical aspects, such as treatment, late effects, and cancer recurrence. In addition, they could provide guidance on accessing support services, as grandparents often do not use formal psychological support because few services target them or they are unaware of available options [].

Including grandparents in family‐centered psycho‐educational interventions may help reduce cancer‐related worries. Such programs are typically delivered by multidisciplinary teams, with nurses, social workers, and psychologists playing central roles, in line with psychosocial standards of care in pediatric oncology []. However, given the limited psycho‐oncology resources in most pediatric oncology centers and the limited availability of formal structures targeting grandparents, direct professional support may not always be feasible. In these cases, healthcare teams could encourage parents to involve grandparents in family discussions and provide information booklets where available [], helping grandparents receive essential information. A tailored printed booklet has been shown to be feasible and acceptable, and was positively evaluated by most grandparents [].

Parent and family organizations may consider offering peer support to help grandparents manage their worries and maintain their supportive role within the family. As grandparents' worries were not clearly associated with clinical characteristics, interventions should address not only clinical information but also acknowledge grandparents' subjective experiences and support their ability to cope with uncertainty.

Although some worries persisted during survivorship, including the fear of cancer recurrence, worries were generally more severe and frequent during the early phase after diagnosis. This suggests that information provision and psychosocial support are particularly important during this initial period.

Future research should explore which strategies and intervention formats are most effective in reducing grandparents' cancer‐related worries, both in terms of information provision and psychosocial care to make sure this important group is not overlooked in survivorship care.

Cancer‐related worries are common among grandparents of children with cancer and often persist in long‐term survivorship, although their prevalence and severity generally decrease over time. Receiving medical information in the first 2 years after diagnosis was associated with fewer cancer‐related worries, highlighting the importance of timely and comprehensive information provision. Tailored educational and psychosocial support may help grandparents cope with their worries and sustain their important supportive role within the family.

medicine.title: Can a 3D Printed Chondrograft Implant Offer a Solution for Full Thickness Cartilage Lesions in an Equine Preclinical Model?
medicine.abstract: Articular cartilage defects have limited ability to heal resulting in fibrocartilage that is functionally and structurally inferior to hyaline cartilage. The aim of this study was to validate the Chondrograft Implant for full thickness cartilage lesion treatment, assessing its ability to fill the defect and support repair tissue engraftment. Bilateral 15 mm diameter cartilage defects were created on the lateral trochlear ridge of the femur in 12 skeletally mature horses. One defect was treated with the implant while the contralateral limb was an empty control defect. Horses were exercised starting at week 4 and study end points were at 36‐weeks for 4 horses and 52‐weeks for 8 horses. Lameness examinations were performed every 4 weeks and arthroscopic recheck surgeries were performed at 12‐weeks. Post‐mortem evaluation included macroscopic appearance, MRI, histology and biomechanical testing. Clinical, ICRS, MRI and gross morphology outcomes were compared between groups using parametric or non‐parametric tests as appropriate. Mechanical stiffness was compared between groups using two‐way ANOVA with Tukey's post‐hoc. There was no difference in lameness between control or treated limbs (p > 0.5). The 12‐week arthroscopy showed treated defects had significantly improved fill (99% vs 42%, p < 0.0001) and ICRS scores (11.3 ± 1.1 vs 4.1 ± 3.1, p < 0.0001). Endpoint ICRS grade at 52‐ weeks was significantly better in the treated defect compared to the control defect scoring (3.75 ± 2.25 vs 9.125 ± 2.25, p = 0.0005). Biomechanical testing revealed significantly improved repair tissue stiffness in treated defects compared to controls (p < 0.0001). Chondrograft implants resulted in excellent defect filling with biomechanical function similar to normal healthy articular cartilage.
medicine.text:
Articular cartilage is a highly specialized connective tissue with the critical role of providing a surface of minimal friction for joint motion as well as absorbing biomechanical forces [, ]. Due to its low cellularity, poor vascularity and sparse innervation, articular cartilage has a limited ability to repair following damage [, ]. Defects typically heal with the formation of fibrocartilaginous repair tissue, consisting predominantly of type I collagen which has inferior mechanical and functional properties to that of hyaline cartilage [, ]. This results in the initiation of a self‐sustaining inflammatory cascade which upregulates both inflammatory mediators and degradative enzymes, ultimately leading to progressive joint deterioration [, ]. Therefore, the development of a treatment for cartilage lesions that enables restoration of the joint surface with a tissue biomechanically identical to articular cartilage is highly sought after. To date, no such treatment exists.

There are a multitude of treatments available for cartilage defects which includes both those targeted at improving symptoms and those aimed at slowing or reversing the progression of the cartilage damage. An area of rapidly advancing treatments in the human field of cartilage repair is the production of implants to fill the cartilage defects. Metallic implants with various designs specifically manufactured to match the contour of commonly affected regions have been developed [, , ]. Despite patients reporting a reduction in pain and improved function in the short term, 47% of patients receiving implants required a revision surgery due to continued lesion progression []. Alternate implants utilize synthetic polymers or cell‐based scaffolds to mimic the structure and mechanical properties of native articular cartilage. An implant consisting of a collagen type I/III scaffold infiltrated with matrix‐induced autologous chondrocytes has been tested within the equine model and has also shown some promising results in human clinical patients [, ]. However, the repair tissue still has inferior biomechanical properties compared to normal articular cartilage despite improved gross healing and histological scores [, , ]. Synthetic polymer implants have shown success in clinical studies with excellent patient outcomes and return to athletic activity rates [, , ].

Chondrograft (Nanochon, Washington DC) is a porous, cylindrical implant made from a nylon based composite polymer. The material has an inherent nano‐microstructure that mimics aligned collagen fibers and the device is further 3D printed into a microporous structure to enhance tissue integration at the cartilage‐implant interface. In the present study we utilize the horse to validate the use of Chondrograft for the treatment of full thickness cartilage defects in humans. The horse was chosen as a translational pre‐clinical model due to its widely accepted similarities to humans for the assessment of cartilage repair. The articular cartilage thickness of the human medial femoral condyle is typically between 1.5 and 2 mm thick, similar to the horse which on average is 1.65–2.65 mm thick, making comparisons between the two species highly translational [, , ]. Additionally, the size of the horse and relative ease of joint arthroscopy makes arthroscopic follow‐up examinations and assessment of cartilage repair possible [].

The objective of this study was to validate the use of the implant for the treatment of a full thickness cartilage lesion, assessing its ability to fill the defect and support the engraftment of repair tissue in subchondral bone and surrounding cartilage. The first hypothesis was that the implant would provide immediate fill of the full thickness cartilage defect and incorporate into the repair tissue at both 36‐and 52‐week timepoints, revealing superiority to the untreated empty control defects. The second hypothesis was that the implant treated defects would have biomechanical stiffness more similar to healthy articular cartilage compared to untreated, empty control defects.

Twelve skeletally mature horses, aged 2–4 years were enrolled. This cohort included 7 mares and 5 geldings, with bodyweights ranging between 290 kg and 420 kg. Horses were excluded if they possessed a lameness exceeding a grade 1/5 following the American Association of Equine Practitioners (AAEP) grading scale, abnormalities of the stifle joint on radiographs or palpable effusion of the stifle []. Each horse underwent bilateral stifle arthroscopy in which a full thickness (approx. 2 mm depth), 15 mm diameter cartilage defect was created within the lateral trochlear ridge of the femur. One limb was randomly assigned to the treatment group and the other limb served as a control. The experimental protocol was approved by the IACUC at Colorado State University (protocol #3171).

30 min prior to induction all horses received pre‐operative antibiotics (Cefazolin 11 mg/kg intravenous (IV), Gentamicin 6.6 mg/kg IV) and an anti‐inflammatory medication (Phenylbutazone 1.1 mg/kg IV). After induction of general anaesthesia, horses were placed in dorsal recumbency. A standard arthroscopic approach to the femoropatellar joint was performed and the joint explored to ensure no abnormalities were present. The arthroscope remained in position throughout the procedure to visualize defect creation and filling. A mini arthrotomy was created over the lateral aspect of the joint, and utilizing a coring cylinder, a 15 mm diameter defect was created on the lateral trochlear ridge of the femur. The defect was created on the flattest surface on the axial aspect of the ridge. A curette was used to remove the entirety of the calcified cartilage exposing the subchondral bone and creating a small, flat surface at the base of the defect. The limb that was randomly assigned to the treatment group received an implant. Utilizing gas arthroscopy, the defect was dried thoroughly and then filled with fibrin glue. Autologous fibrinogen was made in the laboratory utilizing blood collected from each horse prior to surgery as previously described []. The fibrin glue was delivered in a duploject syringe to concurrently administer the autologous fibrinogen and bovine plasma thrombin (Thermofisher, Waltham, MA) into the defect. The implant was then immediately positioned into the defect so that it was flush with the cartilage surface, with the fibrin glue being utilized for fixation. A single Poly‐l‐lactide (PLLA) pin (Arthrex Trimit Pin, Arthrex, Naples, FL) was then used to secure the implant in place, and more fibrin glue was placed over the top to further seal the surface. The fibrin glue was allowed to dry for 5 min and then the joint was filled with saline. After removal of the arthroscopic instruments, the mini arthrotomy incision was closed in 5 layers (joint capsule, deep fascia, superficial fascia, subcutaneous tissue, skin) and the arthroscopic portal incision was closed with simple interrupted skin sutures. The control limb underwent the same procedure with the exception that the defect was left empty. Horses were confined to stalls for the first 27 days of the study, following which an exercise schedule was initiated and continued to the end of the study period (Supporting Information Table ). An outline of the study protocol is shown in Figure .

Horses underwent a full lameness examination performed by an ACVSMR boarded specialist at week 0 (baseline), followed by every 4 weeks until the study endpoint. Lameness was scored utilizing the AAEP lameness scale and femoropatellar joint effusion was assessed on a 0–3 scale (0 = negative, 3 = severe).

At 12‐weeks post defect creation and placement of implants a second look arthroscopy was performed to allow assessment of the repair tissue. The volume of the defect filled with repair tissue and the area of defect filled with repair tissue were estimated visually by 3 observers. The area of defect fill was estimated by the surface area of the 15 mm defect that was covered with repair tissue/implant (2D measurement). The volume of defect fill included the depth of repair tissue/implant filling the defect in addition to the surface area covering (3D measurement). Area and volume fill were selected as outcome measures because the implant was designed to achieve immediate and complete defect fill. These parameters enabled quantitative subjective assessment of implant‐mediated defect coverage and filling and facilitated comparison with the extent of spontaneous repair tissue ingrowth observed in control defects. Additionally, the International Cartilage Repair Society (ICRS) grading scale was used to evaluate the quality of the repair tissue for both control and treated defects [] (Supporting Information Table ).

The study endpoint was at the 36‐week timepoint for 4 horses, and the 52‐week timepoint for 8 horses, horses were randomly assigned to each timepoint. At this time the horses were humanely euthanized with Pentobarbitol Sodium (Beuthanasia‐D, Merck Animal Health) administered at 86 mg/kg IV. Limbs were disarticulated at the level of the coxofemoral joint. All stifle joints underwent MRI (Siemens MAGNETOM Trio Tim Scanner, Siemens Medical, Erlangen, Germany) utilizing the following sequences: Sagittal Dixon, Transverse PD, Transverse PD fat supressed, Transverse T2 DESS, Transverse T1W FSE, Dorsal T1 vibe and T2 map. MRI's were graded by a board‐certified radiologist utilizing the Magnetic Resonance Observation of Cartilage Repair Tissue 2.0 (MOCART) grading scheme [, ] (Supporting Information Table ) in addition to quantitative measures for T2 relaxometry, T2 cartilage mapping and synovial thickening/effusion.

Arthroscopy of the femoropatellar joints was performed following the post‐mortem MRI. The defects were scored arthroscopically in the same manner as the 12‐week second look arthroscopy, utilizing the ICRS grading scheme in addition to estimates of volume and area of the defect filled with repair tissue. The stifle joint was then opened fully exposing the lateral trochlear ridge. The defect was again scored following the same grading scheme utilized for the arthroscopic assessment at endpoint. Any additional observations were noted which included visible changes to the joint including the synovial membrane, defect firmness, attachment of the implant to the surrounding cartilage, attachment of the implant to the underlying bone and level of the defect repair.

Non‐destructive biomechanical indentation testing was performed on the lateral trochlear ridge at the site of each defect and surrounding cartilage. This included testing the repair tissue inside the defect and tissue adjacent to the defect giving a total of 15 indentation sites per sample (Figure ). Each test site was indented to a depth of 100 µm using a 0.8 mm diameter spherical indenter over a period of 1 s. The structural stiffness (N/mm) was calculated for each test site.

The cartilage defects and the underlying subchondral bone were harvested and fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin. Tissue blocks were prepared from osteochondral blocks 10 mm proximal and distal to the defects, the patella and the defect itself. The slides were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) or safranin O fast green. Slides were scored according to the ICRS II cartilage repair scoring system and the modified O'Driscoll scoring scheme giving individual scores for each parameter and a total sum score for each slide as previously described [, ] (Supporting Information Tables  and ). Histological sections were also stained for Type II Collagen immunohistochemistry (IHC). The MsαCollagen, type II antibody (II‐II6B3, Developmental studies hybridoma bank, Iowa) was utilized for staining following the protocol outlined in the supplementary methods. From the IHC slides, the type II Collagen‐positive tissue was measured using Nikon Elements Basic Research software attached to a Nikon Eclipse 80i microscope with a Nikon DS‐Ri2digital camera. Type II Collagen was reported as the percentage of positive Type II Collagen repair tissue in the total defect area in the control group, in the treatment group the defect area occupied by the implant was not included in the measurement. Similarly, the percent fill in the defects with any tissue was measured using the same software, microscope and camera.

Lameness and effusion grades were assessed for normality, following which a Mann‐Whitney test was performed at key timepoints (12, 36, and 52 weeks). Data relating to the ICRS scores and necropsy gross morphology scores were assessed for normality, following which a t‐test was used to compare groups when parametric data was present, and a Mann‐Whitney test was performed for non‐parametric data.

For MRI imaging, descriptive statistics for quantitative assessments were calculated by treatment group and timepoint. This included the mean, standard deviation, median and range. Quantitative and qualitative assessments were visualized using dot plots, showing all data points by treatment group and time point.

To assess the results of the mechanical testing, a two‐way ANOVA with Tukey's post‐hoc test was performed to determine statistical significance for stiffness comparing treatment groups and location with a significance level of 0.05. Natural log transformations were applied to the data to meet normality and equal variance assumptions.

Bilateral full thickness cartilage lesions on the lateral trochlear ridges of the femur were successfully created in all 12 horses. In all treated chondral defects the implant was positioned to the authors' satisfaction and held in place with a single PLLA pin and fibrin glue. No intra‐operative complications were encountered.

Mean (+/− Stand. Dev.) lameness and effusion scores are shown in Supporting Information Table  (Figure ). Lameness in both control and treated groups was mild with no significant difference between groups identified at key timepoints 12, 36, or 52 weeks (p values: 0.38, 0.97, and 0.71 respectively). Similarly, there was no significant difference between groups in terms of joint effusion (p > 0.05).

The 12‐week arthroscopic examination allowed for a second look at the healing defects. The arthroscopy revealed that the treated defects had a greater mean area of 99.17 ± 1.95% filled with implant or repair tissue, compared to 45.83 ± 33.7% in the untreated defects (p < 0.0001). When assessing the volume of the defect filled with implant or repair tissue, treated defects had a greater mean volume of defect filled 97.75 ± 5.79%, compared to 41.17 ± 27.58% in the untreated defect (p < 0.0001) (Figure ). The implant appeared to be non‐undulating with moderate to good cartilage attachment. The total ICRS scores for implant treated groups was 11.25 ± 1.13 compared to 4.08 ± 3.09 in the control group (p < 0.0001). The complete scores are outlined in Table .

Arthroscopic scores for horses at the 12‐week second look arthroscopy. Scores include the total international cartilage regeneration society (ICRS) score. p‐value is evaluating the mean differences between treated versus control groups.

Based upon the MOCART 2.0 scoring system, the treated group had a greater volume of defect filling, more complete integration into adjacent cartilage, more continuous articular surface of the implant/repair tissue and more normal signal density compared to the control group. The average MOCART score of the treated group was 74.58 ± 15.29, compared to 47.08 ± 18.88 in the control group (p = 0.0008) (Figure ). There was no difference between groups when evaluating quantitative variables for cartilage mapping (36‐weeks p = 0.2, 52‐weeks p > 0.99) and synovial thickening/effusion (36‐weeks p = 0.28, 52‐weeks p > 0.99) (Figure ). There was also no significant difference when assessing T2 relaxometry (Supporting Information Table ).

Arthroscopic examination of the treated defects revealed the surfaces were smooth to slightly undulating in 8/12 treated defects, and moderately undulating surfaces in 4/12 treated defects (33%). There was an approximately 1.5 mm round indentation in the center of the implant where the PLLA pin was placed. The control defect repair tissue had a severely undulating surface in 4/8 defects at the 52‐week timepoint, and a moderately undulating surface in 4/8 defects at the 52‐week timepoint and 4/4 defects at the 36‐week timepoint. All defects lacked filling at the center at both 36‐and 52‐week timepoints. At the 52‐week timepoint in 4/8 defects the central hole in the repair tissue was greater than 50% of the defect diameter with subchondral bone visible. There was no evidence of changes to the opposing cartilage surface of the patella caused by the implants in the treated defects. At 36‐weeks the treatment group had a significantly higher mean defect area fill with either implant or repair tissue of 100 ± 0.5%, as compared to the control group area fill of 87 ± 7.9% (p = 0.029). The treated defects also had a greater mean defect volume fill of 99 ± 2.5%, compared to the control group of 88 ± 8.9% (p = 0.057). At 52 weeks the area of defect fill was 96 ± 8.6% in the treated group, compared to 53 ± 29% in the control group (p = 0.0005). Similarly, the volume of defect fill was 94 ± 8.6%, compared to 53 ± 26% in the control group (p = 0.0005). Both the area and volume of the defect filled with repair tissue decreased from the 36‐week to the 52‐week timepoint in the control group (36‐weeks area 87%, volume 88%, 52‐weeks area and volume 53%). The area and volume filled by repair tissue/implant also decreased in the treatment group between the two timepoints but to a lesser extent than the control group (36‐weeks area 100%, volume 99%, 52‐weeks area 96% and volume 94%). The total ICRS score at 36 weeks was greater in the treatment group, 10.75 ± 1.5 as compared to the control group 7 ± 2.45 (p = 0.086)(Table ). At the 52‐ week timepoint the ICRS score continued to be higher in the treated group, with the control defect scored at 3.75 ± 2.25 and the treatment group scored at 9.125 ± 2.25 (p = 0.0005).

Gross morphological assessment revealed no evidence of synovitis, generalized inflammation, infection or incisional dehiscence in any of the joints. Representative arthroscopic and gross images of control and treated defects along with the corresponding histology are shown in Figure . Peri‐defect deterioration was present in one of the treated joints, compared to 5 of the control joints. Incongruency of the joint surface was identified in three of the control joints, and both incongruency of the joint surface and peri‐defect deterioration was present in two control joints. In one control joint a small, focal, radiating cartilage crack was noted adjacent to the defect.

In four (33%) of the treated defects, implant material was observed outside the defect and attached to the synovium. In three of these cases a portion of the implant's top layer had separated from the implant, while the remainder stayed well adhered to the defect (Horse #6, #7 and #8). In these implants several strands appeared to have separated originating at the hole where the pin had been placed to secure the implant (Figure ). At the 12‐week arthroscopies horse #6 showed some implant displacement with repair tissue overgrowth, horse #7 showed an intact implant with ideal positioning and horse #8 showed mild delamination. All 3 of these horses were in the 52‐week endpoint group. In one case (Horse #1), the majority of the implant material was found adhered to synovium at the 36‐week necropsy, however there was no gross evidence of synovitis surrounding the adhered implant. In this case, the defect had filled almost completely with repair tissue around the remaining portion of the implant (area 99%, volume 95%). At the 12‐week arthroscopy this horse was noted to have an intact implant.

Indentation testing identified that the treated defects were significantly stiffer than the control defects for both the central repair region (4.41 ± 4.14 vs 0.47 ± 0.50, p < 0.001) and peripheral repair regions (6.29 ± 4.23 vs 0.43 ± 0.35, p < 0.001) at the 36‐week timepoint, and for the central repair region at the 52‐week timepoint (4.87 ± 6.45 vs 1.46 ± 1.78, p = 0.022) (Figure ). The implant/repair tissue in the treated defect was not statistically different in stiffness to adjacent cartilage (p = 0.35), or distant cartilage (p = 0.8) at the 36‐week timepoint. Conversely, the stiffness of the repair tissue in the control defects were 1.81 and 2.29 N/mm lower than normal adjacent cartilage and distant cartilage to the defect respectively at the same timepoint (p < 0.001).

At both the 36‐week and 52‐week timepoints, Modified O'Driscoll scoring revealed the treated defect group had an improved score compared to the control defect group, with a significant difference at the 52‐week timepoint (36‐week − 14.5 vs 14.8, p = 0.1 and 52‐week − 15.6 vs 12.5, p = 0.02) []. At the 52‐week timepoint surface characteristics and structural integrity scores were consistently improved in the treated defect compared to control defects (1.4 vs 0.7 and 1.1 vs 0.4 respectively) (Figure ). The mean scores for patellar cartilage directly opposing the defect in the treated joints were significantly higher (better) compared to the control limb (25.3 vs 24.0, p = 0.02). This was primarily due to small superficial horizontal laminations at the cartilage surface with associated chondrocyte clustering seen in the control limb patella.

Arthroscopic ICRS scoring at endpoint. Horses 1–4 were evaluated at a 36‐week endpoint. Horses 5–12 were evaluated at 52‐week endpoint. p‐value is evaluating the mean differences between treated versus control groups for all horses.

ICRS scoring revealed that the treated defect group was not significantly improved compared to the control defect group at the 36‐week timepoint (32.3 vs 28.8, p = 0.1). However, at the 52 week timepoint the improvement of the treated defect was statistically significant (35.3 vs 25.9, p = 0.0005). At the 36‐week time point there was decreased type II collagen in the treated group compared to the control group. (12.1% vs 28.2%, p = 0.0001). Type II collagen content was similar between the treated and control group at the 52‐week time point (10.7% vs 8.6%, p = 0.36) (Figure ). Histology scores are outlined in Table .

Modified O'Driscoll histology scores, ICRS histology scores and Type II immunohistochemistry (IHC) percentage within the repair tissue at the study endpoints. p‐value is evaluating the mean differences between treated versus control groups for all horses.

This study evaluated the use of the Chondrograft implant for the treatment of full thickness cartilage defects within a horse pre‐clinical model. In concordance with our first hypothesis, the implant successfully filled a full thickness cartilage defect and enabled ingrowth of repair tissue throughout the implant pores. Our second hypothesis that the implant treated defects will be biomechanically superior to control defects was also confirmed. At the 52‐week timepoint, the implant/repair tissue filled on average 96% of the defect area compared to controls in which repair tissue filled on average 53% of the defect. Additionally, the control defect group had a much larger standard deviation representing increased individual variability in the repair tissue fill between horses. At the 12‐week timepoint a substantial portion of this difference in fill (implant 99% vs control 46%) originates from the fact that the implant instantaneously filled the entire defect whereas repair tissue ingrowth is a prolonged process. This is illustrated by the improvement in repair tissue fill in the control defects between the 12‐week arthroscopy and the 36‐week endpoint, where the area fill had increased to a mean of 87%. Interestingly, the repair tissue fill of the control defects markedly decreased to 46% in the horses at the 52‐week endpoint. A potential explanation for this decline is prolonged exercise and repetitive mechanical loading of biomechanically inferior repair tissue resulted in chronic degeneration and progressive loss of defect fill. This marked decline was not seen in the treated defects, even when delamination of the implant occurred. However, it should be noted that there was increased evidence of implant delamination at the 52‐week endpoint (3 horses, 38%) as compared to the 36‐week timepoint (1 horse, 25%), which could potentially be due to wear and tear of the implant over time. A later timepoint > 52 weeks would be needed to further investigate this, however in the cases of delamination the defect fill remained high due to the infill of repair tissue at the implant/cartilage interface.

The immediate filling of the defect in addition to the implant properties aided in the creation of a smooth joint surface in 8/12 treated defects. This helps to prevent the development of lesions on the opposing cartilage surface which can form secondary to the chondral defects []. Previously evaluated implants for cartilage defects have been found to produce lesions on the opposing cartilage surface, believed to be due to the increased stiffness of the implant compared to the surrounding cartilage in addition to implant protrusion [, , ]. The implant and repair tissue was 0.015–0.058 N/mm stiffer than the normal surrounding cartilage in the current study, however this difference was not statistically significant. The similar biomechanical properties of the implant to normal cartilage not only aids in the restoration of the joint surface but also helps to prevent concomitant lesions of the opposing cartilage.

Restoring appropriate mechanical function to the repair tissue represents a key objective of successful cartilage repair. The implant evaluated in the current study does not biodegrade over time; instead, repair tissue grows into and integrates the implant into the defect site. As a result, the mechanical properties provided by the implant are expected to remain stable over time. While the implant treated defects had biomechanical stiffness slightly higher than surrounding healthy cartilage, this increase was minimal and did not show signs of being detrimental at either timepoint. In contrast, repair tissue formed in control defects was significantly less stiff than native articular cartilage, consistent with what has been previously documented with fibrocartilage repair tissue. In the current study there was evidence of significantly worse cartilage degeneration of the patella directly opposing the defect in the control limb as compared to the treatment limb at both the 36‐ and 52‐week timepoints, which over time would likely progress resulting in further joint deterioration. This is similar to what is observed following microfracture of cartilage defects, where fibrocartilage production appears to have good short term clinical results, however, has a high long term lesion progression and failure rate [, ].

The ICRS scoring system was utilized to assess the repair tissue at both the 12‐week second look arthroscopy and the 36‐ or 52‐week study endpoint. This scoring system is validated for use in the assessment of cartilage repair techniques and enabled quantitative assessment of the repair tissue in the current study []. The overall ICRS score in the treated defect group at the 12‐week arthroscopic follow‐up was 11.25 ± 1.13, which was significantly improved compared to the control defect group which was 4.08 ± 3.09. At the 36‐week end point the ICRS scores for the repair tissue had improved from the 12‐week timepoint to 7 ± 2.45, however at the 52‐week end point the scores were markedly lower at 3.74 ± 2.25. The ICRS scores for the treated group remained similar at all timepoints assessed scoring 10.75 ± 2.25 at the 36‐week endpoint and 9.125 ± 2.53 at the 52‐week endpoint. A previous study reporting arthroscopic ICRS scores following cartilage repair techniques including microfracture (ICRS score 9.0 ± 1.8) and Matrix‐Assisted Chondrocyte Implants (MACI)(ICRS score 10.7 ± 1.3) reported scores lower than those obtained in the current study utilizing the implants []. MACI is a cartilage repair technique that involves the use of a porcine collagen type I/III scaffold that is infiltrated with autologous chondrocytes. Fibrin glue is used to secure the implant within the cartilage defect, similar to the method described in the current study. MACI has been evaluated within the equine preclinical model and is frequently utilized in people with chondral defects > 1 cm in diameter [, ]. Some long‐term clinical studies show significant improvements in pain and function as assessed by the Tegner and Lysholm scores starting 6‐months post‐operatively []. While 74% of patients reported either good or excellent results, 18.5% had recurrent pain and required further treatment [, , ]. A major challenge associated with biological implants such as MACI is the limited ability to generate repair tissue that is identical to the healthy articular cartilage. While repair tissue is improved in treated defects compared to controls, experimental studies suggest the repair tissue produced in MACI treated defects is mechanically inferior to naïve articular cartilage, with reduced GAG and collagen type II [, , ]. A key benefit of the implant in this study is that it does not rely on innate cartilage healing, instead, the 3D printed implant has biomechanical and structural properties that mimic articular cartilage and further, the repair tissue integrates into the implant. This approach minimizes the impact of individual variability in healing, offering a more consistent and reliable outcome than current biological therapies for cartilage repair. Type II collagen is the predominant collagenous component of articular hyaline cartilage and is therefore commonly used as a marker of hyaline or hyaline‐like cartilage formation. In contrast, fibrocartilaginous repair tissue typically contains a greater proportion of type I collagen and lower levels of type II collagen. Consequently, increased type II collagen content is generally associated with the formation of higher‐quality, more hyaline‐like repair tissue. At the 36‐week endpoint the type II collagen was significantly higher in the repair tissue within the control defect as compared to the repair tissue surrounding the implant (28.2% vs 12.1%, p = 0.0001). This is to be expected since the implant was occupying the majority of the defect in the treated defect with limited repair tissue ingrowth. At the 52‐week endpoint there was not a significant difference between the treated and control defects (8.9% vs 10.7%, p = 0.36). However, a key advantage of utilizing an implant to fill the defect is the reduced reliance on endogenous formation of high‐quality repair tissue, thereby potentially mitigating the requirement for robust type II collagen production to restore the articular surface.

In the current study the implant became readily incorporated into the surrounding cartilage, evidenced by the MOCART MRI and ICRS scores. The incorporation into surrounding cartilage is important to help reduce biomechanical and structural deterioration of the repair tissue over time due to exposure to shear forces [, ]. In clinical cases, MACI implant failure was associated with non‐integrated areas and implant fibrillation highlighting the importance of good integration with the surrounding cartilage for clinical success [, ].

Osteochondral allografts (OCA's) represent another frequently utilized option for cartilage repair with predictable patient reported improvement and over 75% of cases reliably returning to athletic activity. They enable reconstruction of the articular surface using healthy donor cartilage and subchondral bone with good graft survivability of 82% at 10 years post‐operatively []. Osteochondral grafts can either originate from the same patient (autograft) or another donor (allograft) and there are unique challenges associated with both. Autografts have limitations in the size of the cartilage defect that can be grafted in addition to the potential for donor site morbidity [, ]. Challenges associated with allografts include a lack of tissue donors, difficulties preserving grafts to enable off the shelf availability and the potential for infectious disease spread [, , , ]. These limitations represent benefits of the implant, with off‐the‐shelf availability, and no biological components that represent infectious disease risk. Other off‐the‐shelf implants developed for cartilage repair include Aragonite and Biocartilage (Arthrex, Naples, Florida) [, , ]. The aim of use for both implants is to enhance the regeneration of articular cartilage, improving the quality and mechanical properties of repair tissue. Although repair tissue was improved compared to untreated or microfracture controls, the repair tissue resulting from both of these implants or biologic paste does not regenerate to normal cartilage and was associated with abnormal bone growth in some instances [, , ].

While the horse is a well‐established preclinical model for the study of cartilage defects it does have some limitations in terms of the feasibility of replicating post‐operative care. Humans can be restricted to non or partial weight bearing on the operated limb following surgery to minimize loads on the implant immediately following placement, whereas the horse must recover from surgery and be instantly fully weight bearing. In 3 cases the implant showed delamination of the superficial fibers and in 1 case the majority of the implant had been dislodged from the defect and was found adherent to the synovium. It is likely that these failures occurred as the loads of the equine stifle exceeded the ultimate shear strength and/or tensile strength of the fibrin sealant and the PLLA pin leading to a breakdown and partial delamination of the implant. Despite the implant separation in these cases, the lameness and effusion scores of these horses were similar to the cohort with intact implants. Furthermore, the mean ICRS scores were similar to the scores for the intact implants and improved when compared to the control defects. This suggests that benefits of the implant persist, even in the face of implant delamination. Furthermore, the synovial tissue around the adhered implant fibers showed minimal to no evidence of an inflammatory response.

Limitations of this study include the use of PLLA pins to hold the implants in place. In the 4 cases where delamination and fraying of the implant superficial fibers occurred, it consistently began at the location of the pin placement. Further development of this implant by removing the need for a PLLA pin to secure it in place will likely reduce the risk of implant delamination and fraying and also improve the ease of implant placement. Additionally, the role of the fibrin glue in providing growth factors encouraging repair in the treated group may have contributed to the improved healing in the treatment group since the fibrin glue was not used to fill the control defects. Similarly, placement of the PLLA pin into the medullary cavity may have facilitated the influx of endogenous growth factors into the defect, potentially contributing to repair. However, because the implant occupied the majority of the defect created by the drill to place the pin, newly formed repair tissue that was influenced by these growth factors, represented only a small proportion of the defect and therefore contributed minimally to the overall defect scores. A greater concern regarding the use of the pin is the potential for long‐term adverse effects on the subchondral bone, as has been increasingly reported in recent studies assessing microfracture [, ]. Challenges associated with the lack of objective scoring mechanisms for some outcome variables were encountered and measures involving the visual estimation of defect volume and area of fill may have a margin of error. Where possible established scoring schemes were utilized. The use of an implant also introduces an element of bias during the scoring of variables as assessors could not be blinded as to the treatment group. Finally, the use of an empty defect as a control represents a limitation of the study. Current gold standard treatments such as microfracture, MACI and OCA's result in improved repair tissue compared to empty defects and so would represent a more clinically relevant comparison to the treatment group.

In conclusion, Chondrograft implants result in excellent defect filling and good integration to the surrounding cartilage, with biomechanical function similar to normal healthy articular cartilage. The implant appears to be a viable option to improve cartilage defect healing however, further optimization of this implant is ongoing so that both pin placement and fibrin glue will not be necessary to secure the implant to the subchondral bone. The Chondrograft implant appears to be a promising option for chondral defect repair of the knee and its evaluation in human patients may be considered.

medicine.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels
medicine.abstract: Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse’s contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.
medicine.text:
Perceptual decision-making is widely thought to involve a process of evidence integration over time (). An extensive body of research has successfully linked these integration computations to multiple neural decision signals in various species (; ; ; ; ) revealing a neural decision architecture that includes both effector-selective motor preparation signals and motor-independent signals that appear to reflect integration operations at an intermediate processing level (; ; ; ). Such neural decision processes have mainly been studied in the context of tasks requiring immediate judgements about a single continuously presented stimulus. However, in many real-life situations a decision-maker is afforded only a short glimpse of a relevant evidence source and it is uncertain whether and when they will receive an additional glimpse, as, for example, when evaluating an object among moving traffic that may be intermittently occluded. This scenario has begun to be studied using an intermittent-evidence task (), which we refer to as ‘gaps task’, in which up to two short pulses of noisy evidence for a certain motion direction are presented separated by a variable temporal gap, with a behavioural response required after a delayed cue. Previous studies using this task or variants of it have found that both evidence pulses are utilised, but not fully or equally (; ; ; ), and although a general information leakage account could be ruled out based on the absence of any decline in accuracy with gap duration, the neural underpinnings of the task, including the functional roles of effector-selective and motor-independent processes in handling and maintaining the intermittent evidence, and how such information underutilisation can arise, have remained unclear.

In humans, two neurophysiological signatures of decision formation can be utilised alongside behavioural data to gain insight into mechanisms underlying perceptual tasks (). First, spectral activity in the beta band (13–30 Hz), long observed to decrease over motor cortex with preparation of a contralateral limb (; ), has been found in decision tasks to build at an evidence-dependent rate, reaching a threshold level contralateral to, and coincident with, the executed action (; ; ; ; ; ). Motor beta dynamics have also been shown to reflect decisions and choice biases in humans (; ; ; ; ; ) and non-human primates (; ; ), highlighting its role as a key marker of decision-related activity. Second, a centroparietal positivity (CPP) in the human electroencephalogram (EEG) has been found to exhibit similar evidence-dependent buildup dynamics in conventional perceptual tasks with continuous stimuli such as random dot motion, but with an earlier latency; it begins building at a stimulus-aligned onset time, rises at a rate that scales with evidence strength, and peaks at the time of action choice when immediate execution is allowed (; ; ). Signals with similar dynamics have been observed in multiple brain regions including the parietal cortex intracranial recordings (; ; ), bearing some overlap with regions identified in functional imaging studies (; ; ). In contrast with motor preparation signals, the CPP exhibits evidence-integration dynamics even when no motor output is required (). In delayed-response tasks where actions are deferred until some time after the perceptual choice is made, the CPP peaks at decision commitment and falls back to its baseline level (; ; ), whereas relative motor preparation reflected in motor beta lateralisation (MBL) sustains until action execution (; ; ; ; ). These findings are consistent with the CPP tracking an intermediary, motor-independent evidence integration process that is continuously fed to downstream motor preparation, where a sustained representation of the DV is maintained after commitment is reached, until a response is made.

More recently, a few studies have highlighted that the CPP can behave differently in expanded judgement tasks, where evidence is presented as a series of discrete tokens that need to be integrated rather than as a continuous, noisy stream. In these tasks, centroparietal signals exhibit transient token-evoked positivities that scale with the immediate evidence, rather than tracking the evolution of an ongoing decision variable (DV) across tokens (; ; ). MBL, meanwhile, tracks the evolving decision variable across discrete tokens over multiple seconds, by stepping up or down according to the evidence in each token and sustaining in between them (; ; ). These findings again point to the operation of an intermediary decision process reflected in the CPP – one that can be flexibly configured to compute different quantities depending on the nature of the task.

The Gaps task, like expanded judgement tasks, involves temporally disparate pieces of information, but it holds key distinctions that demand dedicated investigation. In expanded judgement tasks, tokens typically bear little or no perceptual noise, but the overlap of the underlying generative distributions means they often provide conflicting information (e.g. ; ; ; ; ; ). The nature of the stimuli thus encourages appraisal of each token as a distinct object, potentially explaining the transient pattern of CPP activity. In contrast, the Gaps task involves pulses of evidence that are perceptually noisy but always indicate a consistent motion direction (), thus appearing as glimpses of the same object rather than a series of individual objects. Only one study has examined neural signatures of decision formation in this intermittent evidence context: using EEG,  showed that the CPP exhibits an evoked positivity after each pulse that appears to decay during the gap, suggesting a local processing role. However, how these pulse-evoked activities relate to the computations underpinning an ongoing decision, interact with motor preparation to determine choice, and relate to any information underutilisation, has not been examined.

In this study, we recorded EEG during the Gaps task () in two experiments with slightly different settings for the variable temporal gaps to ensure generality of findings. Our primary goal was to characterise the dynamics of the CPP and MBL in the context of this intermittent evidence task, and functionally relate them to behavioural indices of integration across tokens. We found that participants based their choices on both pulses but with a weaker influence of pulse 2, and coherence-dependent weightings on choice were mirrored in the magnitude of transient pulse-evoked CPPs. These patterns could be explained by a decision architecture where the CPP conducts two separate rounds of evidence accumulation, continuously feeding the accumulating evidence within each pulse to a downstream motor process indexed by MBL. MBL in turn tracks a continuous representation of the state of the overall DV, sustaining without loss of information throughout the gap and between the final evidence and the response. Our behavioural and modelling results indicated that participants engaged in a bounded accumulation process, so that evidence samples within each pulse were only integrated while the DV encoded in MBL had not yet reached the bound. Additionally, given the dynamic structure of the task involving evidence onsets and offsets, we explored the dynamics of attention, as indexed by occipital alpha signals, and these were suggestive of a key role in filtering out irrelevant dot-motion, and in modulating the weight of pulses on choice.

In this study, participants engaged in a motion direction discrimination task where, on most trials, two pulses of partially coherent dot motion (indicated by yellow dot colour) were separated by variable temporal ‘gaps’ in which motion was random, and thus uninformative (indicated by blue dot colour; ). Though coherence could differ, the direction was always consistent between the two pulses, so that they would be construed as two glimpses of the same evidence source. Our two experiments (Exp. 1: N = 22; Exp. 2: N = 21) differed only in the delays separating the two pulses. In both experiments, coherence levels were titrated for each participant using a staircase procedure aiming for an average 70% accuracy following a single evidence pulse. High (Exp. 1: M = 44.73%, SD = 12.64%; Exp. 2: M = 33.04%, SD = 13.41%) and low (Exp. 1: M = 26.75%, SD = 7.74%; Exp. 2: M = 19.82%, SD = 8.04%) coherences were then set to be, respectively, 25% higher and 25% lower than the staircase-estimated coherence (see Methods), and small adjustments were made between blocks if performance substantially changed ().

As expected, participants’ accuracy scaled with motion coherence and number of pulses. In one-pulse trials, participants were more accurate in the high coherence compared to the low coherence trials (, Exp. 1: β1 = 0.33 ± 0.05, p < 0.001; Exp. 2: β1 = 0.43 ± 0.06, p < 0.001, ). There was a further benefit in accuracy from the second pulse when present, indicated by sensitivity to coherence in both the first (, Exp. 1: β1 = 0.26 ± 0.06, p < 0.001; Exp. 2: β1 = 0.31 ± 0.05, p < 0.001) and second (, Exp. 1: β2 = 0.16 ± 0.06, p = 0.001; Exp. 2: β2 = 0.06 ± 0.04, p = 0.015) pulses. When both pulses in a two-pulse trial were the same coherence, participants performed better compared to one-pulse trials, exhibited both in high and low coherence trials in Experiment 2 (, Exp. 2: β1 = 0.16 ± 0.08, p = 0.047; β3 = 0.02 ± 0.08, p = 0.784), but only significantly so in high coherence trials in Experiment 1 (, Exp. 1: β1 = 0.21 ± 0.07, p = 0.013; β3 = 0.16 ± 0.07, p = 0.019). However, they did not perform as well as expected from a perfect accumulator (), estimated using performance in one-pulse trials to predict expected accuracy in two-pulse ones (see ; see Methods).

The fact that the regression coefficients for the second pulse were smaller than those estimated for the first one indicates that participants’ choices were guided more strongly by the first piece of evidence they received.
