medicine.title: Mechanical Hemolysis After Fontan Fenestration Closure
medicine.abstract: Mechanical hemolysis following transcatheter device closure is uncommon and is typically associated with a residual high-velocity shunt. Hemolysis after Fontan fenestration closure has not been previously reported.A 7-year-old boy with single-ventricle physiology underwent elective transcatheter Fontan fenestration closure, complicated by hematuria the following day. Laboratory evaluation confirmed nonimmune intravascular hemolysis. Echocardiography demonstrated a well-positioned device without residual shunt but with an atrioventricular valve regurgitant jet directed toward the device. Conservative management was pursued, with biochemical surveillance, folic acid, and iron supplementation. Device removal was not required.Device-related hemolysis is classically attributed to residual shunting. Described herein is hemolysis caused by regurgitant jet collision with a nonendothelialized device. Conservative management is appropriate in stable patients, as given expected resolution with device endothelialization.Hematuria after Fontan fenestration closure should raise suspicion for mechanical hemolysis, even without residual shunt. Early recognition is essential in Fontan patients and warrants earlier supportive intervention given limited cardiopulmonary reserve.
medicine.text:
A 7-year-old boy (weight: 18 kg) was referred for elective transcatheter Fontan fenestration closure. The underlying anatomy comprised dextrocardia, atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance, ventricular septal defect, mitral valve hypoplasia with a hypoplastic left ventricle, and pulmonary atresia. Staged palliation included a neonatal modified Blalock-Thomas-Taussig shunt, bidirectional cavopulmonary connection at 7 months of age, and extracardiac Fontan completion at 4 years of age. Long-term anticoagulation with warfarin was discontinued 72 hours preprocedure and bridged with low–molecular-weight heparin. There was no family history of coagulopathy or glomerular disease.

At the time of catheterization, the baseline oxygen saturations were 88% to 92% on room air. The echocardiogram demonstrated a patent fenestration (mean gradient: 4 mm Hg), mild to moderate atrioventricular valve regurgitation, and normal ventricular systolic function.

Cardiac catheterization was performed under general anesthesia with systemic heparinization (activated clotting time: 220 seconds) and prophylactic antibiotics. Baseline hemodynamics demonstrated a cardiac index of 2.6 L/min/m2 and a pulmonary/systemic flow ratio of 0.8:1, Fontan pressure of 13 mm Hg, transpulmonary gradient of 5 mm Hg, and pulmonary vascular resistance of 2.3 WU⋅m2. During test occlusion of the fenestration, the systemic oxygen saturation increased to 98% (pulmonary/systemic flow ratio: 1:1), with stable Fontan pressure (13 mm Hg) and no significant decrease in the cardiac index (4% decrease from baseline). The fenestration was successfully closed with a 5-mm Amplatzer septal occluder (Abbott) ( and ). Total procedural contrast volume was 6 mL/kg. There was no instrumentation of the urinary tract.

The patient was observed overnight, remaining afebrile and hemodynamically stable. After initially passing clear urine, he developed painless discoloration of the urine on postprocedural day 1, prompting further evaluation.

The postprocedural examination was unremarkable. The patient's vital signs were normal (heart rate: 90 beats/min, blood pressure: 100/70 mm Hg [83rd percentile], oxygen saturation: 95% on room air, afebrile). There was no murmur, no jaundice or petechiae, and no abdominal tenderness or vascular access site hematoma.

The differential diagnosis included anticoagulation-related hematuria, renal or urinary tract pathology (including contrast-associated renal injury), and intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria. Given the recent device implantation, procedure-related mechanical hemolysis was considered an important diagnostic possibility.

Initial laboratory testing demonstrated a normal coagulation profile, hemoglobin, platelet count, and renal function. Hemolysis screen was consistent with intravascular hemolysis. Screening for autoimmune pathology was negative. Results are outlined in , and trend over follow-up is demonstrated in .Table 1Hematologic and Hemolysis Work-Up at PresentationInvestigationResultNormal RangeHemoglobin119 g/L112-141 g/LMean corpuscular volume64.3 fL77.6-91.0 fLPlatelet count238 × 109/L203-431 × 109/LInternational normalized ratio1.20.9-1.2Serum creatinine39 μmol/L34-61 μmol/LLactate dehydrogenase1,485 U/L197-281 U/LC3-complement0.92 g/L0.90-1.68 g/LC4-complement0.19 g/L0.10-0.34 g/LHaptoglobin<0.1 g/L0.30-2.00 g/LPlasma free hemoglobinPositiveUnconjugated bilirubin22 μmol/L<7 μmol/LReticulocyte count158 × 109/L42-70 × 109/LDirect antiglobulin (Coombs) testNegativeG6PD activityNormalPeripheral blood smearOccasional schistocytesLaboratory investigations demonstrated compensated intravascular hemolysis characterized by elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1,485 U/L), undetectable haptoglobin (<0.1 g/L), positive plasma free hemoglobin, elevated unconjugated bilirubin (22 μmol/L), and reticulocytosis (158 × 109/L). Direct antiglobulin testing was negative, G6PD activity was normal, and peripheral blood smear showed occasional schistocytes.G6PD = glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Hematologic and Hemolysis Work-Up at Presentation

Laboratory investigations demonstrated compensated intravascular hemolysis characterized by elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1,485 U/L), undetectable haptoglobin (<0.1 g/L), positive plasma free hemoglobin, elevated unconjugated bilirubin (22 μmol/L), and reticulocytosis (158 × 109/L). Direct antiglobulin testing was negative, G6PD activity was normal, and peripheral blood smear showed occasional schistocytes.

G6PD = glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Urine analysis was positive for red blood cells, and microscopy demonstrated the absence of red blood cells, confirming hemoglobinuria rather than hematuria. Renal ultrasound excluded a structural renal anomaly.

The postprocedural echocardiogram demonstrated a well-positioned fenestration occluder without residual shunt. There was mild to moderate atrioventricular valve regurgitation (unchanged from the preintervention assessment). The high-velocity regurgitant jet was directed at the device, with localized flow acceleration identified on color Doppler ( and , ).

The diagnosis of hemolysis secondary to regurgitant jet impact on the fenestration occluder was established.

Hemoglobinuria was resolved within 48 hours. Given clinical stability, conservative management was adopted with serial clinical and biochemical surveillance. Folic acid supplementation (5 mg daily) was initiated to support increased erythropoietic demand, and oral iron therapy was added 2 weeks later in response to declining ferritin levels. One isolated episode of hemoglobinuria occurred in the week after discharge, with no further recurrence during follow-up.

At 46 days postprocedure, the patient remained clinically stable. Hemoglobin reached a nadir of 81 g/L before demonstrating early recovery. Biochemical markers of hemolysis had stabilized (). These findings supported continuation of conservative management, consistent with the expected trajectory of resolution with device endothelialization.

Device closure of Fontan fenestrations is considered a safe and effective procedure, with low morbidity and mortality. Clinically significant hemolysis after transcatheter device closure in children is rare, occurring in about 0.1% to 3% of cases, most commonly following patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect closure, where a high-velocity peridevice shunt causes mechanical red cell fragmentation., To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of mechanical hemolysis following Fontan fenestration device occlusion.

In contrast to previously reported cases of hemolysis, no residual shunt was identified in this patient. Additionally, the Fontan circulation has low-velocity, passive flow, making shear stress–related hemolysis from residual shunting unlikely. We propose that the mechanism in this case is distinct, caused by a high-velocity regurgitant jet directed at the device, with localized flow acceleration seen on color Doppler. In the context of a single ventricle physiology, the regurgitant jet reflects systemic pressures, generating greater shear stress at the device surface than equivalent regurgitation in a biventricular circulation. This is analogous to the mechanism described by Hwang et al, in which hemolysis occurred in the absence of a residual shunt, driven by a high-velocity pulmonary stenosis jet directed at a nonendothelialized patent ductus arteriosus occlusion device. This is a conceptually similar but anatomically distinct scenario.

A key vulnerability in this case is the limited cardiopulmonary reserve associated with the Fontan physiology. In the absence of a subpulmonary ventricle, Fontan flow is passive and cardiac output cannot be augmented effectively during periods of increased demand. Consequently, moderate anemia may result in clinically important symptoms at hemoglobin levels that would be well tolerated in biventricular physiology. This warrants earlier initiation of supportive therapy and lower threshold for reintervention in this population.

Management of device-related hemolysis in children is generally conservative when hemolysis resolves within weeks to months. Mild to moderate cases can be managed with folic acid and iron supplementation to support erythropoiesis, alongside measures to minimize renal injury from hemoglobinuria, including adequate hydration. In more severe or persistent cases, red blood cell transfusions may be required while awaiting spontaneous resolution with device endothelialization. If the hemolysis is intractable or life-threatening, invasive interventions to retrieve the device may be necessary. These include deploying additional devices or coils to eliminate residual jets or, in extreme cases, performing surgical retrieval and repair. In this case, conservative management was adopted given the clinical stability and early resolution of hemoglobinuria, consistent with prior reports of spontaneous resolution following device endothelialization, documented as late as 81 days postimplantation.

For patients with atrioventricular valve regurgitation undergoing Fontan fenestration closure, careful intraprocedural echocardiographic assessment of the relationship between regurgitant jet and intended occluder position should be performed before device release. Identification of a jet directed toward the device may enable repositioning or alternative device selection to mitigate hemolysis risk. Awareness of this mechanism should also lower the threshold for early postprocedural hemolysis screening in at-risk patients.

Mechanical hemolysis can occur after Fontan fenestration device closure even in the absence of a residual shunt, with atrioventricular valve regurgitant jet impact on a nonendothelialized device representing a previously unreported mechanism. Early recognition is particularly important in Fontan patients, in whom moderate anemia may result in disproportionate symptoms given limited cardiopulmonary reserve. Intraprocedural echocardiographic assessment of the regurgitant jet direction before device release may reduce risk in susceptible patients.

medicine.title: Catheter-Based Selective Pulmonary Artery Digital Subtraction Angiography and Microvascular Reserve Quantification in Fontan Patient
medicine.abstract: Fontan circulation allows univentricular congenital heart physiology to survive. Pulmonary microvascular images are poorly described in live patients during follow-up.A 25-year-old man with a diagnosis of tricuspid atresia status after extracardiac fenestrated Fontan surgery performed at 3 years of age, followed by fenestration device closure a year later, and with a history of hemoptysis at 9 years of age. Follow-up was performed through cardiac catheterization with selective pulmonary artery (PA) digital subtraction angiography (DSA). A decreased percentage of microvascular reserve associated with increased D-dimer suggested in situ thrombosis, and thromboprophylaxis was switched from aspirin to direct oral anticoagulation.We focus on catheter-based PA DSA microvascular reserve percentage, cardiopulmonary exercise test, and D-dimer quantification to generate evidence of in situ microvascular thrombosis.Catheter-based PA DSA revealing reduced microvascular reserve may identify in situ microvascular thrombosis and offer a novel pathophysiological insight in patients with Fontan circulation during follow-up.
medicine.text:
A 25-year-old man diagnosed with tricuspid atresia, ventricular septal defect, and pulmonary stenosis underwent an extracardiac fenestrated Fontan procedure performed at 3 years of age. During routine follow-up evaluation, he presented with dyspnea on exercise, which was quantified through a cardiopulmonary exercise test.

Bidirectional right Glenn anastomosis was performed at 9 months, followed by an extracardiac fenestrated Fontan procedure at 3 years of age. The fenestration was device-closed a year later. His medication includes eplerenone, candesartan, and aspirin. Hemoptysis secondary to a bronchial artery fistula at 9 years of age required catheter embolization, and aspirin was discontinued. After an uneventful follow-up without recurrence of hemoptysis, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin was added at age 21.

In a patient with Fontan circulation and worsening functional class, ventricular systolic dysfunction, significant atrioventricular valve insufficiency, and increased pulmonary vascular resistance should be ruled out.

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing showed a peak oxygen consumption (VO2) of 14.87 mL/kg/min, 35% of predicted; a weight of 92 kg, a height of 177 cm, a body mass index of 29.4 kg/m2, a peripheral O2 saturation of 89%, a hemoglobin of 15.9 g/dL, a D dimer of 0.53 μg/mL, and a pro-B-type natriuretic peptide of 295 pg/mL. A color Doppler transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a competent atrioventricular valve. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an ejection fraction of 51%, and T2-weighted lymphangiography observed type 3 distribution.

After informed consent was obtained, a routine follow-up cardiac catheterization depicted a transpulmonary gradient of 4 mm Hg and a pulmonary vascular resistance index of 1.7 WU/m2. Furthermore, a selective pulmonary artery digital subtraction angiography (PA DSA) with microvascular reserve percentage quantification was obtained through selective right and left inferior lobar PA angiography (pump injection using iodine contrast 25 mL at 15 mL/s at 7 frames per second during induced apnea).

Postprocessing was performed with a DICOM file. After capillary frame identification and polygonal study area delimitation, we developed an overimposed 10-mm cell grid, adjusted to the catheter diameter. Visual and artificial intelligence (AI) contrast quantification (using Claude Sonnet 4.6 [Anthropic]) were performed through gray scale as follows: visual quantification 0 = white, 1 = gray, 2 = black, and AI quantification prompt threshold (Claude Anthropic scale) >160 = 0 = white, 80 to 160 = 1 = gray, and <80 = 2 = black. Microvascular reserve percentage of each lung base was obtained as follows: the real score aggregate was divided by the ideal score aggregate (total cell number x 2), and the index obtained was multiplied by 100 ( and  respectively).

Three different microvascular reserve percentage severity scores were arbitrarily established: mild >66%, moderate 66%-33%, and severe <33%. D-dimer cutoff point was set above 0.50 μg/mL.

We included in the visual summary a 14-year-old control case diagnosed with a double-inlet univentricular heart showing right ventricular morphology who received a Fontan procedure performed at 4 years of age. Her investigations showed a peak VO of 17.9 mL/kg/min (predicted 52%); peripheral saturation of 90%, a hemoglobin of 15.2 g/dL, a D-dimer of 0.28 μg/mL, and a pro-B-type natriuretic peptide of 18 pg/mL. A color Doppler transthoracic echocardiogram showed a competent atrioventricular valve, and a cardiac MRI reported an ejection fraction of 70%, and T2-weighted lymphangiography showed a type 3 distribution. Cardiac catheterization reported a transpulmonary gradient of 7 mm Hg and a pulmonary vascular resistance index of 2.79 WU/m2.

According to the cardiopulmonary exercise test, the maximum VO2 and predicted percentage were decreased, with mild cyanosis and increased D-dimer levels above the 0.50 μg/mL cutoff. We added visual and AI microvascular reserve percentage quantification at the right selective inferior lobar PA (48%/59%) and left selective inferior lobar PA (31.9%/31.8) to get a deep Fontan function phenotype ( and , respectively).

Visual and AI methods were useful tools for follow-up evaluation of this patient, with cell number score aggregation; AI was faster than visual.

This finding may confirm our hypothesis that in situ thrombosis might be the most likely explanation for microvascular reserve percentage of <66%.

Apixaban thromboprophylaxis instead of aspirin, sacubitril/valsartan instead of candesartan, and eplerenone continuation were ordered together with cardiopulmonary exercise rehabilitation.

At 1 year follow-up he maintains a regular life activity, his peripheral O2 saturation increased to 94% and there were no new episodes of bleeding. Cardiopulmonary rehabilitation, a hypocaloric diet, and his described cardiac medications are maintained.

Fontan circulation includes a nonpulsatile flow and is characterized by a chronically increased systemic venous pressure and low cardiac output. This procedure, developed in parallel by Dr Kreutzer in Argentina and Dr Fontan in France, allows a variety of univentricular hearts to survive complex congenital heart diseases. This surgical procedure improves oxygen saturation, although during follow-up it exposes these patients to a variety of complications such as circulatory failure, ventricular dysfunction, atrioventricular valve regurgitation, refractory arrhythmia, protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, and extensive collateral circulation. Based on the American Heart Association guidelines, we previously reported 7 Fontan patients' functional phenotypes according to echocardiography, cardiac MRI, and transpulmonary gradient: 3 showed normal Fontan function, and 4 showed Fontan failure (one of them with protein-losing enteropathy and another with plastic bronchitis, both with a competent atrioventricular valve, preserved ejection fraction, type 3 T2-MRI lymphangiectasia, and a transpulmonary gradient >6 mm Hg).

Then, we raised the hypothesis that pulmonary vascular disease was the most probable cause of the Fontan failure phenotype.

Previous studies show that hematological factors and hemodynamic abnormalities increase the risk of pulmonary thrombosis, as the systemic venous flows passively through the PA. For this reason, the morbidity in adults with congenital heart disease increases, and a Fontan circuit thrombus may often be silent, but rarely innocent.,

We describe an adult patient with Fontan circulation showing a decreased cardiopulmonary exercise test, increased D-dimer, and normal vascular resistance in whom we developed a method to study the pulmonary microvascular structure through selective PA DSA.

In this case report, the microvascular reserve percentage severity was arbitrarily assigned, and the decision to initiate anticoagulation was based primarily on clinical suspicion because of an increase in the D-dimer cutoff level. Further research studies including a larger number of patients will be necessary to confirm the usefulness of this method to confirm this hypothesis.

Catheter-based selective PA DSA with microvascular reserve percentage quantification may be useful in patients with Fontan circulation during follow-up, suggesting in situ thrombosis as the likely cause of a decreased cardiopulmonary exercise test in patients with cyanosis and worsening functional class. Further research will be necessary to corroborate our hypothesis.

medicine.title: Capillary brain‐derived p‐tau217 for remote triaging of Alzheimer's disease pathology: Clinical performance in a CLIA/CAP‐certified laboratory
medicine.abstract: Expanding access to Alzheimer's disease (AD) blood biomarker testing through capillary collection beyond clinic‐based venipuncture could enable earlier biological triage, specialist referral, and timelier initiation of disease‐modifying therapies. Prior attempts to measure phosphorylated tau at amino acid 217 (p‐tau217) in capillary blood have not achieved the diagnostic accuracy required for triaging.This was a cross‐sectional diagnostic validation study (January 2025–April 2026) across six US sites. Adults aged ≥ 50 years with cognitive concerns were recruited, including a community‐based sample (N = 180) and specialty memory/research clinic sample with available amyloid positron emission tomography (PET; N = 64; total N = 244). Same‐day paired capillary (Tasso upper‐arm device) and venous samples were shipped ambient overnight and processed at a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)/College of American Pathologists (CAP)‐certified laboratory via proprietary capillary‐to‐assay workflow. Samples were measured using the BD‐pTau217 singleplex assay on the NULISA platform.Among 244 participants (mean age 64.3 [standard deviation 11.9] years; 153 female [62.7%]; 51 Black [20.9%]), capillary and venous brain‐derived p‐tau217 (BD–p‐tau217) correlated (R = 0.93, ρ = 0.73; both P < 0.001), with concentration‐dependent bias on Bland–Altman analysis. In the PET‐confirmed cohort (N = 64), capillary BD–p‐tau217 yielded area under the curve (AUC) 0.959 (95.7% sensitivity, 83.3% specificity; positive predictive value [PPV] 93.6%, negative predictive value [NPV] 88.2%), meeting Global CEO Initiative on Alzheimer's Disease (CEOi) low‐specificity and Alzheimer's Association guideline triage thresholds. Across the full cohort at 26% amyloid prevalence, against a composite reference standard, AUC was 0.959 (90.5% sensitivity, 89.0% specificity; PPV 74.0%, NPV 96.4%), meeting CEOi high‐specificity triage thresholds.Capillary BD–p‐tau217 met clinical performance standards for remote AD triage, to our knowledge the first capillary p‐tau217 test to meet these standards, suggesting it may support triage of patients for further diagnostic evaluation, including specialist referral and confirmatory testing.
medicine.text:
Blood‐based biomarkers, particularly plasma phosphorylated tau at threonine 217 (p‐tau217) collected by intravenous (IV) puncture, have emerged as highly accurate tools for supporting Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis among individuals with cognitive impairment. Despite these advances, several structural barriers limit timely access to biomarker‐based diagnosis. Approximately 92% of individuals with mild cognitive impairment go undetected in primary care due to limited clinician awareness and insufficient diagnostic infrastructure, precluding access to biological workup and disease‐modifying treatment. Patients also frequently delay presenting to clinical settings. For example, in a recent European survey, the average time between symptom onset and first primary care visit was 15.2 months, driven largely by stigma and fear of diagnosis. Furthermore, nearly half of individuals presenting to memory clinics, primary care‐ or specialty‐based, are suspected not to have AD and related dementias as the underlying etiology (42.5% and 45.9%, respectively), highlighting the potential of biological triaging to concentrate specialist capacity for those with confirmed AD pathology. Introducing biomarker testing at the point of first concern can inform etiology, improve referral quality, and support timely initiation of disease‐modifying therapies and lifestyle interventions, which are more effective when introduced at earlier disease stages., ,

Capillary blood collection enables at‐home sampling and lowers the barrier to biomarker testing, allowing individuals to proactively seek biological insight into their cognitive health outside clinical settings. Fingerprick dried blood spot approaches have shown initial success for measuring AD biomarkers,,  though collection failure rates of 15% to 25% have been reported when collected by a professional and 23% of participants in a self‐administered study did not complete the test kit. In addition, accuracy of dried plasma spot p‐tau217 for amyloid pathology has ranged from area under the curve (AUC) 0.66 to 0.86, which is insufficient for a triage test.,  The Tasso device, which collects capillary blood from the upper arm via an automated lancet, has shown 96% collection success and 86% comfort in self‐collection in an underrepresented cohort. However, previous studies have shown weak to moderate correlations between Tasso‐ and IV‐collected p‐tau217., ,

A potential concern is that capillary collection, unlike venipuncture, may add peripheral p‐tau217 to samples, as the lancet injures the densely innervated dermis, where nerve fibers contain tau and phosphorylated tau. To limit this, we selected a brain‐derived p‐tau217 (BD‐pTau217) assay, which excludes high‐molecular‐weight peripheral tau isoforms,  and shows high accuracy for amyloid pathology.

Capillary collection using the Tasso device for BD–p‐tau217 testing can facilitate patient‐friendly, remote sampling, but rigorous analytical and Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)/College of American Pathologists (CAP) validation is essential to enable disclosure of results to patients. We designed this study around three complementary evaluations. First, to assess analytical performance, we evaluated the correlation and agreement between capillary and venous BD–p‐tau217 across the full cohort (n = 244). Second, to assess clinical performance, we compared venous (IV) and capillary (Tasso) BD–p‐tau217 measurements against amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) confirmation as the reference standard in the clinical cohort (n = 64). Third, to assess real‐world fit for purpose, we evaluated overall diagnostic accuracy across the full cohort against a composite reference standard (amyloid PET where available, venous BD–p‐tau217 otherwise), at an amyloid prevalence reflecting community‐based screening populations. Clinical performance was assessed against pre‐specified acceptance criteria for triaging tests from the Global CEO Initiative on Alzheimer's Disease (CEOi) and Alzheimer's Association guidelines. ,

This was a multi‐site study evaluating capillary BD–p‐tau217 measurement using the Tasso device, with paired capillary and venous samples collected from each participant. The study comprised two complementary cohorts and recruitment took place across six geographically distinct US sites between January 29, 2025 and April 14, 2026. A clinical performance cohort (N = 64) was recruited from two specialty memory clinics, Memorial Healthcare in Owosso, Michigan and Wake Forest University Alzheimer's Disease Research Center in Winston‐Salem, North Carolina, where participants had clinically determined amyloid PET status available. A community fit‐for‐purpose cohort (N = 180) was recruited through community screening events targeting adults aged ≥ 50 years with self‐reported cognitive concerns; individuals aged 40 to 49 years were also eligible, resulting in a cohort aged ≥ 40 years of whom 80% (N = 144) were aged ≥ 50 years, reflecting the intended‐use population for remote capillary testing. Community events took place in Chicago, Flint, Dearborn, and Coldwater. All participants provided written informed consent. The study was approved by Sterling Institutional Review Board (protocol number 12951).

Paired capillary and venous blood samples were obtained from all participants on the same day. Capillary blood was collected from the upper arm using the Tasso+ device (Tasso, Inc.) into BD serum microtainers by trained study personnel following a standardized protocol. Venous blood was collected by standard phlebotomy in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes. To simulate remote collection conditions, both sample types were shipped overnight at room temperature, with processing initiated within 24 hours of collection and stored at −80°C. A subgroup of participants (N = 20) additionally performed unsupervised capillary self‐collection using the same Tasso+ device with BD microtainer tube after observing a professionally performed collection and receiving written and video instructions.

Pre‐analytical stability was assessed in capillary samples shipped at room temperature and received within 24 hours, following a design adapted from Verberk et al. Samples used for pre‐analytical experiments were not part of the performance analyses. For delayed processing, samples (N = 7) were held at room temperature until processing at 24, 48, or 72 hours after collection. For freeze–thaw stability, samples (N = 3) were processed at 24 hours, stored frozen, and subjected to up to three freeze–thaw cycles. Recovery was calculated relative to the 24‐hour timepoint and first cycle, respectively, with mean recovery as the acceptance criterion for a triaging test (75%–125%).

Capillary serum samples were processed using a proprietary, patent‐pending protocol prior to analysis. Venous samples were centrifuged at 1800 x g for 10 minutes. BD–p‐tau217 was quantified at AccessDx (Houston, TX), a CLIA‐certified and CAP‐accredited central laboratory, using a commercial BD–p‐tau217 immunoassay (Singleplex BD‐pTau217, Alamar Biosciences), in singlicate. All study samples followed an identical handling protocol and underwent no more than one freeze–thaw cycle before measurement and were not diluted. Inter‐assay coefficients of variation between different days and between different operators as well as intra‐assay coefficients of variation (CVs) of duplicated measurements of capillary samples were assessed using clinical samples at low, medium, and high concentrations, resulting in 9.4%, 12.6%, and 7.3%, respectively, with the highest CVs observed at the lowest concentrations (≈ 0.2 pg/mL). Samples were measured with operators blinded to amyloid PET status.

Amyloid PET imaging was performed using [1
8F]florbetapir (n = 38), [1
1C]PiB (n = 22), or [1
8F]florbetaben (n = 4) following established acquisition protocols. Scans were visually rated by experts blinded to clinical and biomarker information and classified as amyloid positive or amyloid negative using standard criteria. Where available, quantitative measures were also recorded: standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR; N = 21) and Centiloid values, calculated with MIM software (N = 37). For analyses requiring a binary amyloid status, visual read was used as the reference standard; quantitative measures were used in supplementary analyses.

Correlation between paired capillary and venous BD–p‐tau217 was assessed with Pearson and Spearman coefficients (n = 244). As chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a potential confounder of plasma p‐tau217 concentrations, a supplementary correlation analysis was performed excluding participants with CKD (n = 234). Agreement between capillary and venous BD–p‐tau217 was assessed by Bland–Altman analysis on log‐transformed values, as differences were non‐normally distributed and increased with concentration. Results are reported as the mean capillary/venous ratio with 95% limits of agreement (LoA), and proportional bias was tested by regressing the log ratio on the log mean. As pre‐specified in the validation plan, capillary and venous cutoffs were derived from Youden‐optimal receiver operating characteristic (ROC) cutpoints in the amyloid PET–confirmed subgroup (n = 64). Capillary and venous areas under the curve (AUCs) were compared using the paired DeLong test. Acceptance criteria were defined before analysis based on Alzheimer's Association clinical practice guidelines and CEOi recommendations: capillary BD–p‐tau217 was considered acceptable as a triaging test if it achieved ≥ 90% sensitivity and ≥ 75% specificity (low‐specificity triaging test) and as a high‐specificity triaging test if specificity was ≥ 85%.,  In the full cohort (n = 244), capillary BD–p‐tau217 was evaluated against a composite reference standard (amyloid PET where available, venous BD–p‐tau217 otherwise) to achieve sufficient amyloid prevalence (26% amyloid positivity) for stable positive predictive value (PPV) estimation at a community level. Venous BD–p‐tau217 was used as the reference for participants without amyloid PET because venous plasma is the established matrix for blood‐based AD biomarker testing, and its validity against amyloid PET was first verified in the PET‐confirmed subgroup (see Results); amyloid status in these participants was assigned using the PET‐derived venous cutoff. Measuring both matrices with the same assay ensured that any differences reflected the collection method rather than assay‐specific variation. A sensitivity analysis was repeated excluding the PET‐confirmed participants. BD–p‐tau217 concentrations were compared by amyloid status using the Mann–Whitney U test. Professionally collected and self‐collected samples were compared within person using Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests. Statistical significance was set at two‐sided α = 0.05. Analyses used Jamovi (version 2.3.28.0) and R in RStudio (version 2026.01.0+392), with the pROC package for ROC analyses and DeLong tests and ggplot2 for visualizations.

Code used for the statistical analyses reported in this article is available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Proprietary analytical pipelines used at the CLIA‐certified clinical laboratory are not available for redistribution.

A total of 244 participants were enrolled across six US sites (Table ; mean age 64.3 years, standard deviation 11.9; 62.7% female; 20.9% Black). Of these, 180 were recruited through community‐based cognitive screening events (mean age 60.3 years, 65.6% female, 25.6% Black) and 64 from a specialty memory clinic or Alzheimer's Disease Research Center with available amyloid PET status (mean age 75.4 years, 54.7% female, 7.8% Black). Amyloid‐positive participants more frequently reported a family history of AD compared to amyloid‐negative participants (46.0% vs. 26.5%) and comorbidity profiles differed between cohorts, with cardiovascular and metabolic conditions more prevalent in the community cohort. The memory clinic/research center subgroup was older and less ethnically diverse than the community cohort, reflecting the broader age range addressed by community cohort recruitment and known challenges in reaching ethnically diverse populations through specialty memory clinic settings.

Capillary and venous BD–p‐tau217 were correlated (R = 0.93, ρ = 0.73, both P < 0.001, Figure ) in the total cohort, and correlations were consistent across the six collection sites (R = 0.85 to 0.95, Figure  and Table  in supporting information). The highest IV BD–p‐tau217 value (IV 12.38 pg/mL; Tasso 7.24 pg/mL) was observed in an amyloid PET–positive participant with a Centiloid value of 174, consistent with high amyloid burden, and CKD as a co‐morbidity. Because CKD may confound plasma p‐tau217 concentrations, a supplementary analysis excluding participants with CKD (n = 234) yielded comparable results (R = 0.87, ρ = 0.73, both P < 0.001, Figure  in supporting information). Capillary concentrations were on average higher than venous concentrations (mean ratio 1.79, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.59 to 2.01; LoA 0.29 to 10.88; Figure ), with significant proportional bias (P < 0.001): capillary values were higher than venous at low concentrations and lower at high concentrations. Findings were unchanged after excluding participants with CKD (ratio 1.81; LoA 0.30 to 10.91; Figure ).

In the 64 participants with amyloid PET confirmation (46 amyloid positive, 18 amyloid negative), both venous and capillary BD–p‐tau217 differentiated amyloid PET–positive from amyloid PET–negative participants. Venous BD–p‐tau217 concentrations were higher in amyloid PET–positive than amyloid PET–negative individuals (+895%, 9.95‐fold increase, P < 0.001, based on average concentration, Figure ). Classification against amyloid PET status yielded an AUC of 0.989 (95% CI 0.972 to 1.000), with 93.5% sensitivity and 100% specificity (PPV 100%, negative predictive value [NPV] 85.7%, Figure ). Venous BD–p‐tau217 also correlated with quantitative amyloid measures, where available (SUVR: Pearson R = 0.78, Spearman ρ = 0.83, N = 21; Centiloid: Pearson R = 0.60, Spearman ρ = 0.73, N = 37; both P < 0.001; Figure  in supporting information). Together, these findings support the use of venous BD–p‐tau217 as a reference standard for participants without amyloid‐PET imaging. Capillary BD–p‐tau217 concentrations were higher in amyloid PET–positive than amyloid PET–negative individuals (+337%, 4.4‐fold increase, P < 0.001, Figure  in supporting information). Classification against amyloid PET status yielded an AUC of 0.959 (95% CI 0.910 to 1.000), with 95.7% sensitivity and 83.3% specificity (PPV 93.6%, NPV 88.2%, Figure ). Capillary and venous AUCs did not differ significantly (DeLong P = 0.15; Figure ). Capillary BD–p‐tau217 correlated with SUVR (Pearson R = 0.81, Spearman ρ = 0.76, N = 21) and with Centiloid values (Pearson R = 0.60, Spearman ρ = 0.73, N = 37; both P < 0.001; Figure ).

Capillary BD–p‐tau217 was higher in amyloid‐positive than amyloid‐negative individuals (+370%, 4.7‐fold increase, P < 0.001, Figure ) and differentiated amyloid‐positive from amyloid‐negative individuals with an AUC of 0.959 (sensitivity 90.5%, specificity 89.0%; PPV 74.0%, NPV 96.4% at 26% observed prevalence) against a composite reference standard (amyloid PET where available; n = 64, venous BD–p‐tau217 otherwise; n = 180, Figure ). In a sensitivity analysis excluding the PET‐confirmed participants, diagnostic accuracy was directionally unchanged (AUC 0.970, sensitivity 94.1%, specificity 92.6%), although amyloid prevalence in this subgroup was substantially lower (7.8%) than the 26% observed in the full cohort. In the sensitivity analyses excluding all 10 participants with CKD, the AUC was 0.956, with 91.4% sensitivity and 85.2% specificity (Figure ).

Capillary Tasso samples remained stable within 75% to 125% recovery for up to 48 hours at room temperature (n = 7; mean recovery 88.7%, Figure  in supporting information) and across three freeze–thaw cycles (N = 3; mean recovery 94.1%, Figure ). Within‐person BD–p‐tau217 concentrations did not differ significantly between professionally collected and self‐collected capillary samples (N = 20), with a collection success rate of ≈ 90%.

Expanding access to blood‐based AD biomarkers at scale requires collection methods that complement clinic‐based venous sampling and enable remote and community testing. However, prior efforts to measure p‐tau217 in capillary blood have not achieved the diagnostic accuracy required for triaging. We therefore used a BD–p‐tau217 assay to limit peripheral tau contribution. Measured in a CLIA/CAP‐certified laboratory, capillary BD–p‐tau217 met the objectives of our three‐part evaluation. First, capillary and venous BD–p‐tau217 correlated, with a concentration‐dependent bias. Higher capillary values at low concentrations likely reflect imprecision near the limit of detection, at which a small serum–plasma offset yields large relative differences. As peripheral nerves also contain small tau isoforms, a small peripheral contribution cannot be excluded. This bias did not compromise diagnostic accuracy against amyloid PET (AUC 0.959 vs. 0.989 venous; DeLong P = 0.15). Second, in the PET‐confirmed cohort, capillary BD–p‐tau217 met the CEOi low‐specificity and Alzheimer's Association guideline criteria for a triaging test (sensitivity ≥ 90%, specificity ≥ 75%),,  with specificity (83.3%) just below the CEOi high‐specificity threshold (≥ 85%). Third, across the full cohort at community‐representative amyloid prevalence, capillary BD–p‐tau217 met CEOi high‐specificity triaging thresholds against the composite reference standard (sensitivity 90.5%, specificity 89.0%). To our knowledge, this is the first study demonstrating that capillary blood collection can support a p‐tau217 test meeting established criteria for a triaging test.

A recent preprint reported only a moderate correlation between Tasso and venous BD–p‐tau217 (R = 0.53), measuring EDTA plasma with a 120‐plex NULISA panel after immediate processing. We used serum, a singleplex assay, and 24‐hour ambient shipment. These methodological differences likely explain the discrepancy in performance and underline that capillary performance should be validated for each specific collection and analytical workflow.

Like all blood biomarkers, capillary BD–p‐tau217 is intended to support, not replace, comprehensive clinical evaluation. Appropriate clinical implementation requires integration with cognitive assessment, assessment of other factors that impact cognition (e.g., depression, sleep), consideration of pretest probability, and access to structured clinical follow‐up to mitigate risks of misdiagnosis and unintended harm. Both cohorts in this study were enriched for individuals >50 years old with cognitive concerns and often a family history of AD, reflecting a population with elevated pretest probability. Accessible capillary testing addresses a distinct bottleneck: the entry point into the diagnostic pathway. By enabling biological triage before or alongside a primary care visit, capillary BD–p‐tau217 can identify individuals most likely to benefit from specialist referral, ensuring that limited neurology capacity is directed toward those with confirmed biological signal. When an elevated result is followed by neurologist evaluation and confirmatory testing, and presence of AD pathology is established, this pathway may include consideration of approved disease‐modifying therapies, enrollment in clinical trials, or lifestyle‐based risk factor management.

A key strength of this study is the recruitment of community‐dwelling individuals predominantly aged ≥ 50 years with cognitive concerns, reflecting the intended‐use population for remote capillary BD–p‐tau217 testing. In addition, recruitment was conducted across six geographically distinct US sites, with their inherent variability in staff, demographics, and sample handling logistics, enhancing generalizability of our findings and supporting real‐life feasibility. Furthermore, the community cohort included substantial representation of populations historically underrepresented in AD biomarker validation studies (25.6% Black), addressing a recognized gap in the generalizability of plasma p‐tau217 thresholds derived in predominantly White research cohorts. Last, the feasibility of unsupervised collection at scale was supported by including a self‐collection mode in our study.

This study has several limitations. Because recruitment focused on the community‐based intended‐use population rather than memory clinics, amyloid PET confirmation was available in only 64 participants, and quantitative amyloid measures (Centiloid or SUVR) were available in a subset of those. The PET‐confirmed subgroup was older and less ethnically diverse than the broader community cohort, limiting direct generalizability of the PET‐derived cutoff to younger and more diverse populations. In addition, the cutoff was derived in 46 PET‐positive and 18 PET‐negative participants and requires confirmation in larger cohorts. In the community cohort, amyloid status was inferred from venous BD–p‐tau217 rather than direct PET imaging; this is inherent to community‐based recruitment outside specialist clinical settings.

Future prospective longitudinal follow‐up of capillary BD–p‐tau217–positive participants through the diagnostic and care pathway will generate real‐world evidence of clinical utility, downstream diagnostic yield, and impact on therapeutic decision making. Independent external validation in demographically diverse prospective cohorts is needed to establish generalizability of performance across populations. Prospective triage studies should quantify the proportion of specialist consultations resulting in confirmed AD pathology and actionable treatment decisions when pre‐stratified by capillary BD–p‐tau217, demonstrating the clinical value of biological triage at the point of first concern.

In conclusion, capillary blood collection using the Tasso device provides accurate measurement of BD–p‐tau217, meeting CEOi and Alzheimer's Association guideline thresholds for triaging of amyloid pathology. By enabling biological triaging ahead of specialist referral, this approach has the potential to reduce diagnostic delays and concentrate memory care capacity on individuals with a high likelihood of underlying AD pathology.
