medicine.title: Adapting patient experience measurement to care trajectory in a multidisciplinary brain metastases program: a quality improvement evaluation
medicine.abstract: Patient experience is a core dimension of oncology care quality, but cognitive burden, emotional distress, and complex care trajectories in brain metastases populations may limit traditional survey approaches. This study evaluated the feasibility and interpretability of a locally developed, self-administered patient experience survey administered after initial brain-directed intervention within a multidisciplinary brain metastases program.We conducted a prospective quality improvement evaluation of a patient experience survey administered on tablets at follow-up visits two to three months after initial consultation. Eligible participants were new patients seen in a multidisciplinary brain metastases clinic. Descriptive statistics characterized response patterns, including agreement rates, “not applicable” responses, and missing data. Reasons for non-completion were categorized descriptively.Among 70 eligible patients, 41 completed the survey (59%). Overall ratings were high, with most respondents reporting that they were always treated with courtesy and respect and always received the best care possible. Communication and decision-making items showed high agreement. Treatment-dependent items showed reduced applicability, including explanations of medication and treatment impact on daily activities, with substantial “not applicable” responses. A subset strongly disagreed with items addressing clarity of results and functional impact. Open-ended responses were generally positive despite structured disagreement.Surveys administered after brain-directed intervention yielded high overall experience ratings but revealed variation in domain applicability, which may reflect treatment exposure and position along the disease trajectory. As a single cross-sectional administration of an instrument without formal psychometric validation, these findings primarily inform survey feasibility and design; trajectory-informed assessment strategies warrant prospective evaluation.
medicine.text:
Brain metastases are the most common intracranial malignancy in adults. They outnumber primary brain tumors and occur in 10–30% of patients with advanced systemic cancer [, ]. The clinical course is defined by neurologic complexity, compressed treatment timelines, and a rapidly evolving prognostic landscape. Care delivery requires coordination across neuro-oncology, neurosurgery, radiation oncology, medical oncology, and supportive services—a demand that has driven the development of dedicated multidisciplinary brain metastases programs at academic centers [, ]. These programs have demonstrated improvements in time to treatment, treatment decision quality, and care coordination; however, patient experience as a dimension of quality in this population remains poorly characterized [].

Patient experience is a core dimension of healthcare quality, increasingly recognized alongside clinical outcomes and safety as an essential target for measurement and improvement []. Patient experience refers to patients’ reports of what occurred during their care, such as whether goals were discussed or next steps were explained, whereas patient satisfaction reflects an evaluation of care relative to personal expectations; the two constructs are related but distinct, and the present evaluation focuses on experience. In oncology, patient experience surveys assess critical domains such as communication, shared decision-making, care coordination, and access to care, all of which influence treatment satisfaction, trust, and engagement []. However, the validity and interpretability of these measures depend heavily on their alignment with a patient’s stage in the care journey []. This issue is particularly relevant for patients with brain metastases, a population that remains understudied despite growing interest in patient-centered oncology care. Unlike many cancer populations in which patient experience instruments were developed and validated, patients with brain metastases often present during periods of diagnostic uncertainty, complex treatment planning, and substantial cognitive and emotional burden. Consequently, standard patient experience surveys—particularly when administered early in the course of care—may inadequately capture their priorities and experiences, raising concerns about whether existing measurement frameworks are appropriately aligned with the unique clinical circumstances and care trajectories of this population.

In this study, we evaluated the implementation of a self-administered, in-clinic patient experience survey within a multidisciplinary brain metastases program at an academic medical center. Our objective was to characterize response patterns, assess the relevance of survey items during early care encounters, and evaluate the interpretability of patient-reported experience data collected during this phase of care. Findings were used to identify opportunities to improve coordination, communication, and access within our clinical operations and to inform a more responsive strategy for measuring patient experience. This evaluation was conducted as a pilot and is intended to offer other multidisciplinary programs a practical starting point for developing their own patient experience surveys.

This was a prospective quality improvement evaluation conducted within a multidisciplinary brain metastases (BMETS) program at an academic medical center. The BMETS program operates as a co-located multidisciplinary clinic held one day per week, in which patients are evaluated by specialists across neuro-oncology, radiation oncology, stereotactic radiosurgery, neurosurgery, and palliative care during a single visit. Same-day neuroimaging is frequently obtained, with direct access to neuroradiology for real-time imaging review. A dedicated nurse coordinator facilitates patient flow and ensures appropriate specialist encounters throughout the visit. Each clinic concludes with a multidisciplinary brain metastases conference in which the treating team reviews cases collectively to align on treatment recommendations.

Eligible participants included new patients seen in the BMETS program between March 24, 2025, and October 29, 2025. Surveys were administered at the second or third clinic visit, following initial brain-directed intervention including stereotactic radiosurgery, whole-brain radiation, surgical resection, and repeat imaging.

The survey instrument was developed by the BMETS program clinical team and included domains related to communication, shared decision-making, treatment understanding, care coordination, and overall care experience (Supplementary Appendix 1). Items assessing communication and shared decision-making were rated on a five-point ordinal scale ranging from “not at all” to “completely,” with an additional “not applicable” response option. Items assessing overall care experience were rated on a frequency scale ranging from “never” to “always.” Example items assessed personal goals, quality of life, understanding of treatment recommendations, and communication of next steps. One open-ended prompt captured patient perspectives on the most difficult aspects of care and opportunities for improvement. The instrument was developed for program-level quality improvement and has not undergone formal psychometric evaluation (e.g., reliability, construct validity, or cognitive testing); findings are therefore intended to inform survey feasibility and design rather than to establish measurement validity. The survey was administered by the BMETS nurse coordinator or a medical assistant on a tablet once the patient was roomed, prior to the provider encounter. Eligible patients were identified by the nurse coordinator during a clinic review prior to each visit. Responses were collected electronically using Qualtrics XM (Qualtrics, Provo, UT, USA) and exported for descriptive analysis. The complete survey instrument is provided in Supplementary Appendix 1.

Survey responses were summarized using descriptive statistics. For each item, we examined response distributions, overall agreement rates, “not applicable” responses, and missing data. Reasons for non-completion were categorized descriptively based on clinical and operational factors. Given the quality improvement design and modest sample size, analyses were descriptive and intended to inform program-level insights rather than test hypotheses. This project was conducted as a quality improvement initiative and did not qualify as human subjects research requiring oversight by the institutional review board.

Of 70 eligible patients, 41 completed the survey (59%; Fig. ). Reasons for non-completion (n = 29) included transition of care or second opinion evaluation (n = 8), logistical barriers related to clinic workflow (n = 6), including patients who had left the clinic prior to survey administration or instances in which a staff member was unavailable to administer the survey, death prior to survey opportunity (n = 4), clinical deterioration or hospice discussions (n = 3), cognitive impairment (n = 2), language barriers (n = 2), refusal (n = 2), and non-response or blank survey (n = 2). All 70 eligible patients were accounted for within these completion and non-completion categories. The sample was predominantly non-Hispanic White (37/40, 93%) and female (63%), with a median age range of 60–69 years (Table ).

Overall experience ratings were high across several domains. Among respondents, 38 of 41 (93%) reported always being treated with courtesy and respect, and 37 of 41 (90%) reported always receiving the best possible care. Agreement (strongly or somewhat agree) was similarly high for discussion of personal goals (35/41, 85%), quality of life (35/41, 85%), reasons for not pursuing treatment (30/40, 75%), and involvement in decision-making (34/40, 85%). Several treatment-dependent and process-oriented items demonstrated higher rates of “not applicable” responses. The highest proportion of “not applicable” responses was observed for medication explanation (21/41, 51%), followed by impact of treatment on daily activities (11/41, 27%), communication of next steps (9/41, 22%), explanation of results (8/41, 20%), and contacting the team (7/41, 17%). Among respondents who provided ratings for these items, agreement levels were more variable than those observed in communication-related domains.

A subset of respondents selected “strongly disagree” for several items, including treatment impact on daily activities, clarity of results explanation, communication of next steps, contacting the team, and involvement in decision-making. Overall, response distributions differed across survey domains. Communication and decision-making items demonstrated higher agreement rates and lower proportions of “not applicable” responses, whereas treatment-dependent items showed greater variability in response patterns.

Open-ended responses were provided by 12 participants. These responses were reviewed descriptively and reflected generally positive feedback regarding the care experience. No formal qualitative analysis was conducted.

This study demonstrates both the feasibility and the limitations of using a locally developed, self-administered, in-clinic patient experience survey within a multidisciplinary brain metastases program. Although overall experience ratings were high across most domains, substantial variation in the applicability of specific survey items revealed important challenges in measuring patient experience in this population. The observed pattern of responses is consistent with the possibility that the relevance of individual experience domains shifts across the disease trajectory with changes in diagnostic certainty, treatment exposure, symptom burden, and care needs; because the survey was administered at a single time point, however, this interpretation is hypothesis-generating rather than demonstrated. Notably, domains related to treatment delivery, longitudinal care coordination, and supportive services were frequently rated as not applicable, suggesting a possible mismatch between survey content and the timing of assessment. These findings suggest that a single cross-sectional survey administration may not capture the full breadth of the patient experience for individuals with brain metastases. A longitudinal and stage-specific approach to measurement, with survey domains tailored to distinct phases of care, merits evaluation.

The divergence in response patterns across domains followed a consistent pattern. Items assessing communication, shared decision-making, and courtesy generated consistently high agreement. Treatment-specific items, including medication explanation, impact on daily activities, clarity of results, and communication of next steps, generated disproportionate “not applicable” responses alongside strong disagreement from the same patients. One possible explanation is that, for a subset of patients, the relevant clinical episodes had not yet stabilized or had already evolved beyond the measurement moment. Patients surveyed two to three months post-intervention may simultaneously be managing treatment effects, adjusting systemic therapy, and awaiting restaging imaging, conditions under which items about functional impact or care planning have no stable referent. Alternatively, some patients may misconstrue “not applicable” to mean no impact or that they did not experience any deficits, particularly among populations with lower health literacy, older adults, and when survey items are cognitively complex []. A generic “not applicable” option may conflate true inapplicability with response avoidance or uncertainty; item-specific applicability language (e.g., specifying the relevant treatment or encounter) may reduce this ambiguity in future survey iterations. For patients with brain metastases, where clinical status can shift substantially within weeks, a fixed survey window captures a cross-section of a moving target. To minimize the risk of measurement error from inconsistent interpretation of survey response choices, best practices recommend the use of screening questions and skip patterns to establish applicability before assessing the degree of impact or impairment [].

A second, related problem is the mismatch between how experience is captured and when it is captured. Cross-sectional measurement asks patients to rate their current state; retrospective measurement asks them to evaluate a prior period of care. These two modes can diverge, with discrepancies greatest when the recall window does not correspond to a clinically stable period []. Administering a retrospective survey in the clinic, while patients await scan results and specialist recommendations, may compound this. The emotional state at the moment of administration may shape responses to all structured items, and assessment timing and context may shape how patients integrate and translate their care experience.

Attribution is an interpretive challenge specific to multidisciplinary programs. When patients are evaluated by neuro-oncology, medical oncology, radiation oncology, neurosurgery, and palliative care within a single visit, survey responses conflate experiences across providers and encounters. It is not clear from a standard patient experience instrument which discipline or interaction patients are evaluating, or whether the ratings reflect the integrated program experience, a single dominant encounter, or the overall emotional valence of the visit. Prior work in multidisciplinary cancer care has demonstrated that attention to psychosocial needs—more than operational efficiency or coordination metrics—most strongly predicts patient satisfaction, and that this effect operates at the program level rather than being attributable to individual providers [, ]. In brain metastases, where prognostic information is often delivered in the same encounter as an experience survey, the emotional weight of that conversation may shape responses to all structured items, regardless of domain.

Among the 29 patients who did not complete surveys, the documented reasons, including death, clinical deterioration, hospice discussions, and cognitive impairment, reflect a clinical reality of this population. In most oncology patient-experience research, non-completion is treated as a logistical problem, thereby introducing selection bias []. In brain metastases, it identifies the patients with the most compressed trajectories and the highest symptom burden—those with arguably the greatest stake in goal-concordant, values-aligned care. Their systematic exclusion from patient experience data highlights the boundaries of what this measurement approach can capture in this population.

These findings have practical implications for multidisciplinary programs that use patient experience data for quality improvement. Survey domains may vary in their trajectory-dependence: communication, respect, and shared decision-making items appeared broadly applicable in our sample and may provide a stable foundation for measurement at any visit. Treatment-specific items may be more appropriately assessed at clinically stable time points after treatment effects have been experienced and integrated. A staged approach, in which different domains are administered at phase-appropriate intervals, may generate more interpretable and actionable data than a single fixed administration [].

The context of administration may matter as much as the timing. Surveys completed in the clinic while patients await scan results and specialist recommendations are administered under conditions of heightened anxiety that may compress and homogenize structured responses. Telephone-based administration at a neutral timepoint—separated from the clinical encounter—represents a meaningful methodological adjustment that may improve both response quality and the candor of patient feedback. Finally, patients too ill to complete surveys represent the population most in need of care that aligns with their values and goals. Integrating brief caregiver proxy assessments or structured narrative capture at supportive care touchpoints may extend the reach of patient experience measurement to this otherwise invisible population [, ].

This study was conducted at a single academic center with a small sample, limiting generalizability, and a larger, multicenter cohort would be needed to characterize patient experience in brain metastases more representatively. This evaluation was designed as a pilot quality improvement project rather than a definitive study; its value lies in offering other programs a practical starting point for developing their own surveys and in providing an early signal of where standard measurement approaches may fall short in this population. The survey instrument was locally developed and has not undergone formal psychometric validation, which limits comparability with standardized measures and means that our findings speak to survey feasibility and design rather than measurement validity; the local design did, however, allow inclusion of shared decision-making and care coordination domains specific to brain-directed intervention that standard instruments do not address. Survey completion was incomplete and influenced by clinical and logistical factors, introducing potential selection bias. Reasons for non-completion were systematically documented, transforming a source of selection bias into a substantive finding about the population that this measurement approach cannot reach. Because the survey was administered once, at follow-up visits, and administration time points were not compared, the observed differences in item applicability cannot be attributed to survey timing. Finally, the absence of longitudinal follow-up data precludes drawing conclusions about how patient experience evolves across the care trajectory; staged measurement designs spanning care transitions represent a natural next step for this work.

Patient experience surveys administered following brain-directed intervention in a multidisciplinary brain metastases program yielded high overall experience ratings but revealed variation in domain applicability, which may reflect the dynamic, multi-phasic nature of this disease trajectory. Communication- and relationship-oriented domains were consistently applicable, whereas treatment-dependent items yielded high rates of “not applicable” responses even at post-intervention visits. These findings suggest that standard patient experience measurement frameworks may be poorly aligned with the needs of the brain metastases population, and that staged, trajectory-informed measurement strategies warrant evaluation as a means to generate interpretable and actionable quality improvement data. Based on these findings, our program has initiated pilot testing of telephone-based survey administration at a neutral time point, separate from the clinical encounter, and at different time points throughout patients’ journeys to generate more interpretable and actionable patient experience data in this population. Such an approach could improve the interpretability, relevance, and actionability of patient-reported experience data, ultimately enhancing the ability of multidisciplinary brain metastases programs to identify unmet needs and guide quality improvement efforts.

medicine.title: Association of Walch glenoid morphology and fracture patterns in proximal humeral fractures
medicine.abstract: Proximal humeral fracture (PHF) assessment focuses on fracture pattern, bone quality, and patient factors, whereas glenoid morphology—central to biomechanics in glenohumeral arthritis and instability—is overlooked. We hypothesized that glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B (posterior decentring) is independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving PHFs.This single-centre, retrospective cohort study analysed 919 patients with a PHF and shoulder computed tomography (CT). Two blinded shoulder-subspecialized orthopedic trauma surgeons independently classified all cases; agreement was quantified with Cohen’s κ. Fractures were classified by the Neer and AO/OTA systems and glenoid morphology by the Walch classification. The primary outcome—tuberculum involvement (Neer IV/V)—was analysed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis.The cohort comprised 919 patients (72.6% female; median age at trauma 69 years). The Walch distribution in this CT-selected cohort was type A 42.7%, B 54.4%, C 2.7%, and D 0.2%; osteoarthritis was present in 59.5%. Walch agreement was moderate (κ = 0.53), with disagreement concentrated at the A1↔B1 decentring boundary (p < 0.001). Walch type B was independently associated with tuberculum involvement (adjusted OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56–2.74; adjusted RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.17–1.45; both p < 0.001) and with greater AO/OTA fracture complexity (adjusted ordinal OR 1.60, p < 0.001). Female sex was independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05–1.97, p = 0.023); age and osteoarthritis were not significant.In this CT-selected study population, glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B was independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving proximal humeral fractures. The association was statistically robust but clinically modest (AUC 0.62), and Walch type B morphology represented one of several correlates of fracture pattern rather than a standalone predictor. Glenoid morphology may therefore be worth recording during CT and fracture-pattern assessment; these hypothesis-generating findings are not sufficient to modify current treatment algorithms, but support the inclusion of glenoid parameters in future risk models and prospective studies.Level III retrospective cohort study prognostic study.
medicine.text:
Proximal humeral fractures (PHFs) are among the most common fractures of the upper extremity and rank as the third most frequent fragility fracture in the elderly, with an incidence that continues to rise as populations age [, ]. Nationwide registry data document both an increasing fracture incidence and a marked shift toward operative treatment, including a disproportionate growth in shoulder arthroplasty for geriatric fractures [, ]. Management remains contentious and must be individualized: non-operative treatment and osteosynthesis by locking-plate or intramedullary fixation are generally preferred in younger patients, whereas reverse total shoulder arthroplasty has become the treatment of choice in elderly patients with poor bone stock or complex fracture patterns [, –]. Clinical decision-making relies on the Neer and AO/OTA classifications, which categorize fractures by fragment number, displacement, articular involvement, and dislocation [, ]. These systems provide a common descriptive language, but their interobserver reliability is only fair to moderate and varies widely across studies (κ ≈ 0.21–0.67), and the 2018 AO/OTA revision did not consistently improve agreement; their value for guiding treatment selection or predicting outcome remains limited [–]. This suggests that factors associated with fracture behaviour may extend beyond the descriptive parameters these systems capture.

In glenohumeral osteoarthritis and instability, glenoid morphology is a recognized morphological parameter relevant to joint biomechanics, surgical strategy, and clinical outcome [–]. The Walch classification, developed for the osteoarthritic shoulder, describes glenoid wear and version; type B morphology denotes posterior decentring of the humeral head with posterior glenoid erosion and increased retroversion, progressing from posterior subluxation (B1) to a biconcave glenoid (B2) [–]. Even in the absence of established arthritis, a pre-osteoarthritic, posteriorly subluxated configuration (B0) can be identified, indicating that posterior decentring is a structural trait rather than merely an end-stage degenerative finding []. Biomechanically, posterior glenoid bone loss and retroversion displace the humeral head posteriorly and concentrate load eccentrically across the posterior glenoid, thereby altering force transmission across the glenohumeral joint [, ]. These altered loading patterns are a plausible mechanism for the posterior instability and component-loosening risks associated with type B glenoids [].

Despite this established role in degenerative and unstable shoulders, glenoid morphology is absent from every contemporary PHF classification, each of which is constructed exclusively from the humeral segments and their displacement [–]. This omission is potentially relevant, because glenoid morphology is a plausible modifier of the vector and distribution of force transmitted to the proximal humerus during a fall, and local load distribution—alongside bone quality—has been associated with where and how the proximal humerus fails [–]. The evidence linking bone properties to fracture pattern is itself mixed: lower local bone quality has been associated with more complex fracture configurations in some cohorts but not in others, suggesting that fracture morphology is multifactorial and may be associated with loading patterns rather than by bone density alone [, ]. To date, only two surgically treated cohorts have related pre-existing glenohumeral pathomorphology—advanced osteoarthritis and cuff-tear arthropathy—to PHF morphology [, ]; whether Walch glenoid morphology is associated with the fracture pattern in a CT-imaged fracture population not restricted to surgically treated patients or to a specific glenohumeral pathology has, to our knowledge, not been examined.

The Neer system organizes fractures into six categories (types I–VI) defined by anatomical location, displacement, and associated dislocation; these categories are descriptive and do not constitute a strictly ordinal severity scale [, ]. Within this scheme, Neer types IV and V denote patterns involving the greater and/or lesser tuberculum, which carry distinct clinical importance: the tuberosities are the osseous footprints of the rotator cuff, and their fracture and displacement disrupt the cuff force couple, complicate anatomical reduction and stable fixation, and adversely affect functional outcome [, ]. We therefore defined tuberculum involvement (Neer type IV or V) as a single, clinically anchored binary outcome and examined its association with glenoid morphology using multivariable binary logistic regression, complemented by a secondary multinomial analysis across the full Neer spectrum to examine whether the association extends beyond the binary outcome definition and by a separate ordinal analysis of AO/OTA fracture type to characterise overall fracture complexity as a distinct construct.

The aim of this retrospective cohort study was to determine whether Walch glenoid morphology is associated with tuberculum involvement in acute proximal humeral fractures. We hypothesized that posteriorly decentred Walch type B morphology is independently associated with tuberculum involvement (Neer IV/V) after adjustment for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis status.

This was a single-centre, retrospective cohort study conducted at a university-affiliated level-I trauma centre. The study was designed and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement []. The analytic plan—including the a priori designation of the primary hypothesis, the primary exposure and outcome, and the confounder set—was fixed before the inferential analyses were performed. The study was approved by the Hannover Medical School Research Ethics Committee (protocol code 10801_BO_K_2023; approval date 9 March 2023) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Consecutive patients presenting with a proximal humeral fracture and available shoulder computed tomography (CT) with three-dimensional reconstructions were identified from the institutional records for the period between October 2016 and February 2023. Cases with radiographically evident glenoid injury and cases with previous surgery of the glenoid were not eligible. DICOM files were uploaded to the Visage imaging workstation (Visage® 7.1 Enterprise Imaging Platform, Visage Imaging, Inc.). For each case, date of birth, sex, date of trauma, and age at the time of trauma (derived from the interval between date of birth and date of trauma) were recorded. The patient selection process is summarized in Fig. . Because CT with three-dimensional reconstruction was a prerequisite for inclusion, the resulting cohort represents a selected in-hospital population rather than the full spectrum of proximal humeral fractures presenting to emergency care; the implications of this selection step are addressed in Sect. “”.

The dataset provided for analysis comprised 919 cases. Data integrity was verified prior to analysis: there were no missing values in any variable, no duplicate patient identifiers, no implausible age values, and no cases in which the trauma date preceded the date of birth. All classification codes were valid for both raters. Consequently, no cases were excluded at the analysis stage, and the full sample of 919 cases entered all analyses. Because the dataset was complete, no imputation of missing data was performed.

Three established classification systems were applied to each case: the Walch classification of glenoid morphology in the three-dimensional CT-based modification by Bercik et al. [] (subtypes A1, A2, B1, B2, B3, C, D) [, ]; the Neer classification of proximal humeral fractures (types I–VI) []; and the AO/OTA classification of proximal humeral fractures (groups A1–C3) []. The Bercik modification does not include the pre-osteoarthritic, posteriorly subluxated B0 configuration [] as a separate category; B0 was therefore not recorded separately, and cases with a B0 configuration were assigned to subtype B1. Because the primary exposure was defined by the presence or absence of posterior decentring (Walch B versus non-B; Sect. “”), this assignment did not affect the dichotomous exposure classification. In addition, the presence of glenohumeral osteoarthritis was recorded as a binary variable (present versus absent), based on established radiographic criteria, with a Kellgren-Lawrence grade of > 2 defined as ‘present’ and a grade of < 2 defined as ‘absent’ []. Representative axial CT images of each Walch subtype are shown in Fig. .

All 919 cases were independently classified by two orthopedic trauma surgeons with subspecialty expertise in shoulder surgery, who were blinded to one another’s assessments. No consensus reading was performed. To preserve a single, internally consistent analytic dataset, the classifications of Rater 1, a senior attending shoulder surgeon, served as the basis for all descriptive, univariate, and multivariable analyses, whereas the classifications of Rater 2 were used exclusively to quantify interrater reliability and to provide an independent cross-rater replication of the primary model.

All analysis variables were derived and fixed prior to any statistical testing.

Tuberculum involvement was defined as a binary variable, coded 1 for Neer types IV or V and 0 for all remaining Neer types (I, II, III, VI).

Walch B morphology (posterior decentring) was defined as a binary variable, coded 1 for Walch subtypes B1, B2, or B3 and 0 for the remaining subtypes (A1, A2, C, D).

The Walch classification was additionally aggregated into the four principal classes A, B, C, and D for subtype-resolved analyses.

The AO/OTA classification was operationalized in two ways: (i) as a nine-level ordinal severity rank (A1 = 1 through C3 = 9, with increasing rank reflecting increasing fracture complexity), used for non-parametric group comparisons; and (ii) as the three-level ordinal AO type (A < B < C), used for ordinal regression.

Age at trauma (continuous), sex (female versus male), and osteoarthritis (present versus absent) were considered as potential confounders.

All analyses were performed in Python 3.12 (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA) using the pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, and scikit-learn libraries. Two-sided p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

The distribution of the continuous variables (age, age at trauma) was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test and visually inspected by Q–Q plots. Both age (W = 0.970, p < 0.001) and age at trauma (W = 0.966, p < 0.001) departed significantly from normality; continuous variables are therefore summarized as median and interquartile range (IQR) and were compared using non-parametric methods.

Continuous variables are reported as median (IQR); categorical variables are reported as absolute and relative frequencies.

Agreement between the two raters was quantified using Cohen’s κ for the nominal Walch and Neer classifications and weighted Cohen’s κ with quadratic weights for the ordinal AO classification. Reliability was additionally computed for the dichotomized exposure (Walch B) and outcome (tuberculum involvement). 95% confidence intervals (CI) for κ were obtained by bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations). κ values were interpreted according to the benchmarks of Landis and Koch []. To test the a priori hypothesis that interrater disagreement is concentrated at the A1↔B1 boundary—where posterior decentring is most difficult to adjudicate in the fractured shoulder—all discordant Walch cases were dichotomized into A1↔B1 disagreements versus all other disagreements, and the observed proportion was tested against the null expectation of an equal contribution from each of the 21 possible disagreement pairs (p = 1/21) using an exact one-sided binomial test.

The primary univariate association between Walch B morphology and tuberculum involvement was assessed using the χ² test, with the crude odds ratio (OR) and its 95% CI derived from the 2 × 2 table; the minimum expected cell frequency was verified to justify the χ² approximation. The distribution of Walch subtypes across Neer types was examined using the χ² test on the full 7 × 6 contingency table, with standardized residuals used to identify cells contributing disproportionately to the association; because several cells had low expected frequencies, this global test was interpreted descriptively. The association between Walch B morphology and AO complexity (ordinal rank) was tested using the Mann–Whitney U test, with the rank-biserial effect size r reported; differences in AO complexity across the four principal Walch classes were tested using the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s post-hoc comparisons under Bonferroni correction.

Each candidate covariate was screened for its association with both the outcome and the exposure. Variables associated with both at a liberal threshold of p < 0.20 were retained as confounders in the multivariable model, consistent with established epidemiological practice for confounder identification.

The primary model was a multivariable binary logistic regression of tuberculum involvement on Walch B morphology, adjusted for the retained confounders (age at trauma, sex, osteoarthritis). Prior to fitting, multicollinearity was assessed using the variance inflation factor (VIF), with VIF < 5 considered acceptable. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% CI are reported for all model terms. Model performance was evaluated using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, McFadden, Cox–Snell, and Nagelkerke pseudo-R², the likelihood-ratio test against the null model, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).

Three pre-specified secondary models were fitted. First, the primary logistic model was repeated with the full Walch subtype as a categorical predictor (reference A1) to determine whether the effect was specific to the B subtypes. Second, a multinomial logistic regression of the complete Neer classification (I–VI; reference Neer I) was fitted to confirm that the effect was not an artefact of the binary outcome definition. Third, an ordinal logistic regression was fitted to assess whether Walch B morphology was associated with a general fracture-severity gradient; because the nine-level AO model failed to converge owing to sparse cells, the three-level AO type (A/B/C) was used, and the proportional-odds assumption was examined by comparing coefficients across threshold-specific binary logistic models.

The robustness of the primary estimate was examined through a series of pre-specified subgroup exclusions, each targeting a specific potential source of bias. First, Neer VI fracture-dislocations were excluded to address a potential circularity between exposure and outcome: because Walch type B is defined by posterior humeral head decentring and Neer VI denotes fracture-dislocation, an acute traumatic dislocation could in principle be misclassified on post-traumatic CT as pre-existing posterior subluxation, spuriously inflating the association. Second, the rare Walch D subtype was excluded to confirm that the estimate was not distorted by unstable coefficients arising from its very small cell count, and both exclusions were additionally applied in combination. Third, the analysis was restricted to patients without osteoarthritis to test whether the association held independently of degenerative change (the osteoarthritis term, being constant in this subgroup, was removed from the model). Finally, the primary model was re-estimated using the fully independent classifications of Rater 2 (cross-rater replication) to verify that the finding was not driven by the assessments of a single observer. Because the outcome was common, a modified Poisson regression with robust (HC1) variance estimation was additionally fitted to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRR); a log-binomial model was fitted as a specification check and yielded the same estimate.

The primary hypothesis test was not adjusted for multiplicity, having been specified a priori as the single primary comparison. All secondary and exploratory p values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.

During the preparation of this study, the large language model Claude (Anthropic, 2025) was used in a supportive capacity for two methodological tasks: (i) assistance with the development, debugging, and verification of the Python code used for the statistical analyses described above, and (ii) assistance with the generation and formatting of data visualisations. In all cases, the authors independently verified the correctness of the generated code, the plausibility of the statistical output, and the accuracy of the visual representations against the source data. The final analytic decisions, the interpretation of all results, and the scientific conclusions remain entirely the responsibility of the authors.

The cohort comprised 919 patients. The median age at trauma was 69 years (IQR 58–80; range 19–97); the median age at data collection was 79 years (IQR 66–88). The cohort was predominantly female (667/919, 72.6%; male 252/919, 27.4%). Glenohumeral osteoarthritis was present in 547 patients (59.5%) (Table ). The age distribution of the cohort is shown in Fig. .

Interrater agreement was moderate for the nominal Walch (κ = 0.53, 95% CI 0.49–0.57) and Neer (κ = 0.59, 95% CI 0.55–0.63) classifications, and almost perfect for the ordinal AO classification using quadratic-weighted κ (κw = 0.81, 95% CI 0.77–0.85). Dichotomisation improved the reliability of the clinically decisive variables: agreement on tuberculum involvement was substantial (κ = 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.72), whereas agreement on the dichotomized Walch B exposure remained moderate (κ = 0.52, 95% CI 0.46–0.57) (Table ).

Of 336 cases in which the two raters disagreed on the Walch classification, 71 (21.1%) were A1↔B1 disagreements, a proportion substantially exceeding the 4.8% expected under a uniform distribution across all possible disagreement pairs (exact binomial test, p < 0.001). This confirms the a priori expectation that the principal source of interrater disagreement is the adjudication of posterior decentring in the fractured shoulder.

Tuberculum involvement occurred in 360 of 500 Walch B cases (72.0%) versus 226 of 419 non-B cases (53.9%). The association was highly significant (χ² = 31.41, df = 1, p < 0.001; minimum expected cell count 151.8), corresponding to a crude OR of 2.20 (95% CI 1.67–2.89).

The distribution of Walch subtypes across Neer types differed significantly (χ² = 135.83, df = 30, p < 0.001); because several cells had low expected frequencies (minimum 0.13), this global test is interpreted descriptively. Analysis of standardized residuals showed that Walch A1 was strongly overrepresented among Neer I fractures (standardized residual + 6.18) and that Walch B2 was markedly underrepresented among Neer I (− 4.14) and overrepresented among Neer V fractures (+ 2.17), consistent with a shift towards tuberculum-involving patterns in the presence of posterior decentring (Fig. ). Among Neer VI fracture-dislocations, the proportion of Walch B cases (30/61, 49.2%) did not differ materially from the overall Walch B rate (54.4%), arguing against a systematic distortion of the morphology assessment by the dislocation pattern.

Walch B morphology was associated with greater AO fracture complexity (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.001), although the effect size was small (r = 0.15); the shift was driven by a higher proportion of AO type B fractures in the Walch B group (56.4% vs. 41.3%) at the expense of type A fractures (23.0% vs. 40.6%). Across the four principal Walch classes, AO complexity differed significantly (Kruskal–Wallis H = 22.03, p < 0.001); in post-hoc testing, only the comparison between classes A and B reached significance after Bonferroni correction (p < 0.001), with all other pairwise comparisons non-significant.

All three candidate covariates satisfied the confounder criterion (association with both exposure and outcome at p < 0.20) and were retained: age at trauma (p = 0.004 with outcome; p < 0.001 with exposure), sex (p = 0.002; p = 0.014), and osteoarthritis (p = 0.020; p < 0.001). Multicollinearity was negligible (all VIF < 1.7).

In the primary multivariable logistic regression, Walch B morphology remained independently associated with tuberculum involvement after adjustment for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis (aOR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56–2.74, p < 0.001). Female sex was modestly associated with the outcome (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05–1.97, p = 0.023), whereas age at trauma (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.99–1.02, p = 0.262) and osteoarthritis (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.71–1.44, p = 0.951) were not (Table ). Notably, the univariate association of osteoarthritis with the outcome did not persist after adjustment, indicating that the association between glenoid morphology and tuberculum involvement is not explained by coexisting osteoarthritis.

The model fitted the data adequately (Hosmer–Lemeshow χ² = 9.20, p = 0.326) and was significant against the null model (likelihood-ratio χ² = 41.71, df = 4, p < 0.001), with pseudo-R² values of 0.035 (McFadden), 0.044 (Cox–Snell), and 0.061 (Nagelkerke) and an AUC of 0.62. Because tuberculum involvement was frequent in this cohort (63.8%), the adjusted odds ratios reported here must not be read as risk ratios: at an outcome prevalence of this magnitude, the odds ratio overestimates the corresponding relative risk. Taken together, the pseudo-R² values and the AUC indicate that Walch morphology and the covariates jointly account for approximately 6% of the variance in tuberculum involvement and discriminate only weakly between individual patients. In the modified Poisson model, the adjusted risk ratio for Walch B morphology was 1.30 (95% CI 1.17–1.45, p < 0.001; Table ).

When the full Walch subtype was entered as a categorical predictor (reference A1), the association was confined to the decentring subtypes B1 (aOR 1.98, 95% CI 1.33–2.93, p < 0.001) and B2 (aOR 2.40, 95% CI 1.57–3.67, p < 0.001). Subtypes A2 (aOR 1.07, p = 0.777), B3 (aOR 1.18, p = 0.649), and C (aOR 0.54, p = 0.156) were not significantly associated with the outcome; the estimate for the rare Walch D subtype was uninterpretable owing to quasi-complete separation (n = 2, both tuberculum-positive). The absence of a significant effect for B3 is most plausibly attributable to its small sample size (n = 41) rather than to a true null association.

In the multinomial regression of the full Neer classification (reference Neer I), Walch B morphology was associated with significantly increased odds of Neer III (OR 4.07, 95% CI 2.17–7.66), Neer IV (OR 3.97, 95% CI 2.37–6.65), Neer V (OR 5.15, 95% CI 2.84–9.32; all p < 0.001), and Neer VI (OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.22–5.01, p = 0.012), but not of Neer II (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.77–3.08, p = 0.228). Relative to minimally displaced fractures (Neer I), Walch B morphology was therefore associated with increased odds of all displaced patterns (Neer III–VI) but not of the anatomical-neck pattern (Neer II). The association was not confined to tuberculum-involving fractures, but was most pronounced for Neer V and, together with Neer IV, applied to the majority of this cohort (586/919). This also confirms that the primary finding is not an artefact of the binary outcome definition (Fig. ).

In the ordinal regression of AO type, Walch B morphology was associated with greater overall fracture severity (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.24–2.07, p < 0.001). However, the proportional-odds assumption was not satisfied for the Walch B term (nor for sex or osteoarthritis), so this estimate is reported as a descriptive summary measure rather than as a structurally interpretable parameter.

The primary estimate was robust across all sensitivity analyses (Table ; Fig. ). Excluding Neer VI fracture-dislocations (aOR 2.15), excluding the rare Walch D subtype (aOR 2.09), restricting to cases without osteoarthritis (aOR 2.51, with the constant osteoarthritis term removed), and excluding both Neer VI and Walch D (aOR 2.18) all yielded estimates consistent with the primary model, with all confidence intervals excluding unity and all p < 0.001.

Cross-rater replication using the fully independent classifications of Rater 2 reproduced the association (aOR 1.87, 95% CI 1.39–2.51, p < 0.001); the difference between the rater-specific point estimates was small (ΔOR = 0.20), indicating that the finding is not driven by the classifications of a single observer, notwithstanding the moderate reliability of the Walch classification.

After Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons, all principal secondary findings—including the subtype effects for B1 and B2, the multinomial associations for Neer III–VI, the Walch-subtype × Neer distribution, and the AO complexity comparisons—remained statistically significant; the non-significant subtype terms (A2, B3, C, D) likewise remained non-significant after correction.

This study shows a statistically robust but clinically modest, independent association between glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B and tuberculum involvement (Neer types IV and V) in a CT-selected hospital cohort of proximal humeral fractures. After adjustment for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis, Walch type B morphology was associated with a near-doubling of the odds of tuberculum involvement (adjusted OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56–2.74, p < 0.001). The association persisted across every sensitivity analysis and was reproduced when the fully independent classifications of the second rater were substituted (adjusted OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.39–2.51; ΔOR 0.20). A secondary multinomial analysis localized the association to the displaced fracture patterns: relative to minimally displaced fractures (Neer I), Walch B was associated with significantly increased odds of Neer types III, IV, V, and VI, but not of the anatomical-neck Neer type II pattern; the association was most pronounced for the tuberculum-involving Neer V pattern. In a separate ordinal analysis, Walch B was additionally associated with a higher AO/OTA fracture type (adjusted OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.24–2.07, p < 0.001); because the proportional-odds assumption was not satisfied, this estimate is interpreted descriptively and represents overall fracture complexity as a construct distinct from the primary tuberculum-involvement outcome [, ]. Two features of this estimate require emphasis. First, tuberculum involvement was common in this cohort (63.8%); at such an outcome prevalence an odds ratio systematically overestimates the corresponding risk ratio, so an adjusted OR of 2.07 must not be equated with a doubling of risk (adjusted risk ratio 1.30, 95% CI 1.17–1.45). Second, the model accounted for only approximately 6% of the variance in the outcome (Nagelkerke pseudo-R² 0.061) and discriminated weakly at the individual-patient level (AUC 0.62). Walch type B morphology was therefore one of several factors correlated with tuberculum involvement in the analysed patient group rather than a standalone predictor of fracture pattern.

Within the adjusted model, female sex was independently associated with tuberculum involvement (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05–1.97, p = 0.023), whereas age at trauma (OR 1.01, p = 0.262) and osteoarthritis (OR 1.01, p = 0.951) were not. Age, which was associated with the outcome in unadjusted screening, lost significance after adjustment, consistent with confounding by correlated factors rather than an independent effect of chronological age. Notably, osteoarthritis—although associated with Walch B morphology at the group level—was not independently associated with tuberculum involvement once glenoid morphology was modelled. This dissociation raises the possibility that the association between glenohumeral degeneration and fracture pattern is carried primarily by glenoid geometry—increased retroversion, biconcave or posteriorly eroded B-type glenoids, and posterior humeral head decentring—rather than by generalized changes in bone quality. Because no mediation analysis was performed, this remains a plausible mechanism rather than an established explanation; it is, however, consistent with the conflicting evidence on whether bone density itself relates to fracture complexity [, , –].

The absence of a significant effect for Walch types C and D most plausibly reflects limited statistical power. For Walch type C (n = 25), a non-significant trend toward lower odds of tuberculum involvement was observed (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.23–1.27, p = 0.156), which is hypothesis-generating and warrants verification in adequately powered cohorts. For Walch type D (n = 2), quasi-complete separation rendered the estimate uninterpretable, precluding any conclusion regarding this rare morphology.

A legitimate concern is whether posterior humeral head decentring on post-traumatic CT reflects a pre-existing chronic glenoid abnormality or an acute, trauma-induced dislocation—an ambiguity that could introduce circularity, given that Walch type B is defined by posterior subluxation and Neer type VI denotes fracture-dislocation. Three considerations argue against such an artefact. First, Walch B was not overrepresented among Neer VI fracture-dislocations: its prevalence in this subgroup (49.2%, 30/61) did not exceed the cohort-wide rate (54.4%) and did not differ from that in Neer I–V fractures (54.8%; χ² = 0.51, p = 0.474). Second, excluding all Neer VI cases left the association essentially unchanged (adjusted OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.59–2.91, p < 0.001). Third, glenoid morphology is described independently of fracture as a structural trait, and cases with evident glenoid injury or previous glenoid surgery were not eligible; a fracture-induced alteration of glenoid morphology is therefore unlikely. Together, these results indicate that the Walch B–tuberculum involvement association is not an artefact of misclassifying acute dislocation as pre-existing posterior subluxation. The present analysis examines the coexistence of glenoid morphology and acute fracture pattern; whether, and by what mechanism, glenoid morphology contributes to the fracture pattern is not addressed here and cannot be inferred from these data.

Mechanically, posteriorly eccentric glenoids impose asymmetric load across the posterior rim [–, ]; cadaveric data show that even modest posterior bone loss produces measurable posterior humeral head translation and altered joint contact []. Although these alterations have been characterized chiefly in the contexts of instability and arthroplasty [], their contribution to acute fracture mechanics is unestablished. The present finding is therefore best interpreted as hypothesis-generating: alterations in glenohumeral geometry consistent with Walch type B were associated with, but not shown to cause, the fracture pattern produced by an external load. These are plausible mechanisms rather than established explanations, by analogy with bone-mechanics observations at other anatomical sites in which pre-existing deformity is accompanied by altered stress distribution and failure mode [, ]. Prospective biomechanical work, using finite-element or cadaveric fracture modelling, would be required to test whether these plausible mechanisms in fact link retroversion, altered joint mechanics, and fracture pattern.

Risk-factor models for proximal humeral fractures have centred on osteoporosis, advanced age, and fall mechanism, but the type and energy of trauma and the patient’s musculoskeletal history may also be associated with fracture occurrence and pattern [, ]. Chronic, activity-related adaptations of the shoulder—for example altered humeral retroversion and capsular laxity in overhead athletes—are one plausible source of such variation [, ]. None of these variables was recorded here; future work should capture trauma mechanism, activity history, and previous shoulder injury (Sect. “”).

Plain radiographs remain the initial triage tool, but reliable identification of glenoid subtype and quantification of posterior wear require computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction []. Three-dimensional analysis, validated for arthroplasty planning [, ] and applied to fracture assessment [, ], measures fragment translation and rotation that two-dimensional radiographs systematically underestimate []. Conventional systems such as the Neer classification address only the humeral side and do not encode glenoid morphology []. Reporting a fracture pattern without a standardized glenoid descriptor therefore omits a potentially relevant morphological variable and a possible confounder for outcome studies. Three-dimensional CT additionally allows the Walch subtype to be adjudicated despite post-injury distortion [, ].

Because neither treatment nor outcome was analysed in this study, the following considerations are contextual: they are derived from the existing arthroplasty literature rather than from the present dataset. Posterior glenoid wear complicates glenoid preparation and guidewire positioning when arthroplasty is selected; the arthroplasty literature shows that posterior wear increases version error, component malposition, and subsequent loosening with standard techniques [, ], and that comparable difficulties arise for reverse arthroplasty []. Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is mechanically less dependent on a congruent native glenoid and an intact rotator cuff than hemiarthroplasty or internal fixation [, ]. Where posterior bone loss and retroversion must be addressed in arthroplasty, options include augmented glenoid components [], eccentric reaming (generally limited to retroversion < 15–20°) [, ], structural bone grafting [], and navigation or patient-specific instrumentation []. These considerations are reproduced here only to indicate why glenoid morphology is worth recording; neither they nor the present findings imply that Walch type B morphology should currently influence treatment selection.

Prospective evaluation is the appropriate next step. Future prospective cohort or registry studies should record the Walch classification together with the treatment actually delivered and the resulting outcomes, so that it can be tested directly whether Walch type B morphology predicts reoperation, malunion, loss of reduction, or inferior patient-reported outcomes. Such data—and not a cross-sectional association with fracture morphology—would be required before glenoid morphology could reasonably enter a treatment algorithm.

Current proximal humeral fracture practice and research largely overlook the glenoid. These data suggest that a simple glenoid-morphology modifier, recorded from standardized CT using validated three-dimensional criteria, may be worth evaluating in prognostic models and in the stratification of clinical trials. Incorporating a Walch-based modifier—including the Bercik three-dimensional modification—into prospective PHF registries [, ] would allow this to be tested (Sect. “”). Because the association observed in the present CT-selected cohort is statistically robust but clinically modest, its immediate implication is methodological rather than therapeutic: glenoid parameters should be recorded in future studies and risk models, not used to modify current treatment algorithms.

Several limitations apply. The retrospective, observational design precludes causal inference, and the temporal sequence between glenoid morphology and fracture cannot be established without pretraumatic imaging, which is not practically obtainable. Statistical power was limited for the rare Walch types C (n = 25) and D (n = 2), whose estimates are correspondingly unstable. The pre-osteoarthritic B0 configuration was not recorded as a separate category but was assigned to subtype B1 (Sect. “”); the subtype-resolved estimate for B1 therefore includes any cases with a B0 configuration, and an association specific to B0 cannot be derived from these data. Important variables were unavailable—trauma mechanism and energy, prior sporting and occupational activity, and previous shoulder injury—any of which could confound or modify the observed associations [, ]. Inclusion required CT, which introduces a selection bias that is probably more consequential than a simple imaging-availability effect and is therefore considered separately below.

The requirement for CT with three-dimensional reconstruction deserves closer scrutiny, because it is likely to have shaped the cohort in a directional rather than a random manner, so that the true extent of selection is probably underestimated. In routine practice, cross-sectional imaging is obtained when a fracture is considered for surgery, when the pattern appears complex, or when radiographs leave the morphology ambiguous; it is frequently omitted when a fracture is minimally displaced, low-energy, and unambiguously suitable for non-operative treatment, particularly in older or comorbid patients in whom the imaging result would not change management. Minimally displaced and low-energy fractures are therefore systematically underrepresented here, as are patients whose comorbidity precluded operative treatment from the outset. Of the 1410 patients initially screened, 359 were excluded solely because the requisite CT was unavailable (Fig. ), which quantifies the scale of this selection step. The analytic cohort should accordingly be understood as a selected hospital cohort comprising (a) surgically considered, (b) complex, or (c) morphologically ambiguous fractures, rather than as a representative sample of all proximal humeral fractures presenting to emergency care. Two consequences follow. First, the observed Walch distribution—type B in 54.4%—cannot be transferred to an unselected fracture population: a broader, radiograph-based cohort containing a higher proportion of minimally displaced injuries would plausibly show a lower proportion of type B glenoids and a lower prevalence of tuberculum involvement. Second, because both the exposure and the outcome are enriched in this cohort, the magnitude of the association may not be reproduced in an unselected population; whether it would be attenuated, preserved, or accentuated cannot be determined from these data. External validation in a consecutive, imaging-unselected cohort is therefore required before either the observed distribution or the effect size is generalised.

Classification reliability is a further consideration. All cases were classified independently by two blinded raters; interobserver agreement was moderate for the Walch (κ = 0.53) and Neer (κ = 0.59) systems and almost perfect for the AO/OTA system (quadratic-weighted κ = 0.81), values consistent with the fair-to-moderate ranges reported for these classifications [, , , ]. Agreement improved for the clinically decisive dichotomies (tuberculum involvement κ = 0.67; dichotomized Walch B κ = 0.52). The residual Walch disagreement was concentrated at the A1↔B1 boundary—the distinction of pure posterior decentring from a centred glenoid—which accounted for a disproportionate share of all discordant cases (21.1%; p < 0.001), whereas structurally evident osseous defects were more readily adjudicated [, ]. Such morphological ambiguity introduces predominantly non-differential classification variability that would, if anything, attenuate rather than inflate the measured association; that the effect nonetheless persisted under cross-rater replication (OR 1.87, p < 0.001) argues against a spurious finding. Because each rater assessed exposure and outcome on the same images, observer-expectation bias cannot be entirely excluded, although the concordance of the two independent raters’ adjusted estimates makes a substantial contribution from this source unlikely.

In the investigated cohort, glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B was independently associated with tuberculum-involving (Neer IV/V) and, secondarily, with more complex proximal humeral fractures, and this association was statistically robust but clinically modest, remaining stable across extensive sensitivity testing and independent cross-rater replication. Glenoid morphology—currently absent from all proximal humeral fracture classifications—therefore represents an anatomical factor that may be worth recording during CT assessment and fracture-pattern evaluation. Because Walch type B morphology accounted for only a small proportion of the variance in fracture pattern and discriminated weakly at the individual-patient level, it should be regarded as one of several correlates rather than a standalone predictor, and these findings do not support any change to current treatment algorithms. As CT was required for inclusion, the observed prevalence of Walch type B morphology and the magnitude of its association with fracture pattern apply to this selected cohort and require external validation in an imaging-unselected population before they can be generalised. Prospective studies incorporating a standardised glenoid-morphology descriptor—recorded alongside the treatment delivered and the resulting outcomes—together with dedicated biomechanical work, are needed to confirm these associations and to test their prognostic and therapeutic relevance.

medicine.title: Challenges of Fontan Completion in Bilateral Bidirectional Glenn
medicine.abstract: Bilateral bidirectional Glenn (BDG) anatomies present a distinct challenge for Fontan completion, with bilateral superior caval inflow creating competitive flow dynamics that impair balanced hepatic flow delivery.A 3-year-old with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and bilateral BDG underwent patient-specific computational surgical planning before Fontan completion. Six virtual surgical options, including an extracardiac conduit (ECC) and Y-graft variants with and without bilateral superior vena cava (SVC) bridging, were evaluated, with hepatic flow distribution (HFD) and power loss as primary endpoints.Although its baseline HFD was unbalanced, the ECC demonstrated the most consistent HFD response across simulated physiological states. By contrast, Y-graft performance was highly sensitive to arm placement. Bilateral SVC anastomosis improved HFD but introduced low-velocity stagnant flow, raising concerns for thrombosis.In bilateral BDG Fontan planning, computational modeling revealed nonintuitive flow interactions not predictable from anatomy alone. The ECC was selected for surgical robustness, whereas SVC bridging warrants further investigation.
medicine.text:
A 3-year-old child with a history of hypoplastic left heart syndrome and bilateral superior vena cavae (SVCs) was referred for modeling in preparation for Fontan completion. The patient had undergone a stage 1 Norwood procedure followed by bilateral bidirectional Glenn (BDG) anastomoses, with recurrent arch obstruction necessitating surgical augmentation at the time of the Glenn procedure and moderate tricuspid insufficiency. She was maintained on an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and aspirin in the interstage period.

The central question for this patient was operative: Given the bilateral BDG anatomy with constrained intrathoracic geometry, which Fontan configuration would provide the most favorable combination of hepatic flow splits and hemodynamic efficiency. Compared with patients with a unilateral SVC, bilateral SVCs create symmetric inflows that directly compete with inferior vena cava (IVC)-derived hepatic flow in the central pulmonary arteries, making balanced hepatic flow delivery substantially more difficult and in turn leading to higher rates of pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) and related complications., ,

Considering these concerns and restricted retrocardiac space (), an extracardiac conduit (ECC) and bifurcated Y-graft were considered. Although the ECC represents a conventional approach, the Y-graft was considered as an alternative, with theoretical advantages of directing individual conduit limbs toward the left and right pulmonary arteries (LPA, RPA) to circumvent routing difficulties and overcome known challenges of uneven pulmonary flow distribution (PFD) in bilateral BDGs. Given the inability to resolve this question through clinical judgment alone, preinterventional computational surgical planning was pursued to compare hemodynamic performances across candidate configurations.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with phase-contrast velocity mapping was performed, enabling reconstruction of the patient’s preoperative baseline anatomy () and time-averaged vessel flow information (). IVC flow represented 41.9% of the total systemic venous return, with the remaining split between left and right SVCs (32.7%, 25.4%). The baseline PFD demonstrated preferential right-sided flow, with a split of 35.9/64.1% between the LPA/RPA.Table 1Patient-Specific Time-Averaged Flow Rates Derived From Phase-Contrast CMRIVesselTime-Averaged Flow Rate (L/min)% of Systemic Venous ReturnPFD (%)IVC0.98641.9–Left SVC0.76932.7–Right SVC0.59725.4–LPA0.415–35.9RPA0.739–64.1CMRI = cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; IVC = inferior vena cava; LPA = left pulmonary artery; PFD = pulmonary flow distribution; RPA = right pulmonary artery; SVC = superior vena cava.

Candidate surgical options were iteratively generated by the clinical and engineering teams, ensuring surgical feasibility for each option before computational evaluation (). For each, time-averaged inflow conditions were prescribed at the IVC and SVCs, and outflow conditions at the LPA/RPA were prescribed to match the baseline PFD. Computational fluid dynamics simulations were performed for each option according to well-established surgical planning procedures. Simulations were performed using the baseline PFD, and with prescribed PFDLPA ratios ranging from 20% to 80% to evaluate the sensitivity of each option against postoperative physiological variations. For each simulation, hepatic flow distribution (HFD) and power loss (PL) were calculated. HFD was quantified by tracking IVC-derived blood through the Fontan pathway via passive scalar transport, thus providing a direct measure of hepatic flow to each lung. PL was quantified by calculating the net fluid energy dissipated across the Fontan circulation, thus representing the energetic efficiency of each option. Results were jointly reviewed by the multidisciplinary team to promote consistency in model construction, interpretation, and clinical decision-making.

The first iteration involved direct comparisons between the Y-graft and ECC configurations (). Option 1 implemented a 20 mm ECC anastomosed at the right-SVC–pulmonary artery junction with baffle curvature tuned to respect surrounding structures. Option 2 featured a Y-graft with a 20 mm base and flared 14 mm arms (preserving cross-sectional area across the Fontan). The left Y-arm was positioned between the bilateral BDG, whereas the right Y-arm was positioned lateral to the right SVC. Based on the surgical team's input, Option 3 was modified to shift each Y-arm leftward by 5 mm.

Collision-induced flow disturbances preferentially directed IVC flow toward the RPA for Options 1 to 3 (), resulting in unbalanced HFD at the baseline PFD with Option 2 performing significantly worse (HFDLPA = 2.3%) compared with Options 1 and 3 (10.5%, 10.0%). As the PFD ratio was varied, Option 1 resulted in the most consistent HFD splits, whereas Option 3 exhibited unstable HFD behavior (). PL values remained low across all 3, demonstrating energetically efficient options. The unbalanced HFD across these options prompted a second iteration of simulations.

In the second iteration, the potential for a bridge anastomosis consolidating the bilateral SVCs (modeled as a 10 mm conduit) was explored as a means to minimize flow collision and achieve symmetric hepatic flow. Options 4-6 repeated the ECC, Y-graft, and shifted Y-graft configurations with the bilateral SVC anastomosis incorporated ().

The bridging vein substantially improved hepatic flow splits (), with HFDLPA increasing to 56.6%, 48.3%, and 71.2% at the baseline PFD for Options 4-6, respectively. Options 4 and 6 provided the most consistent HFD across the simulated physiological range, whereas Option 5 exhibited nonmonotonic behavior (). PL for all options was modestly elevated compared with the first iteration, reflecting additional hydraulic resistance of the bridging vein. Although promising, flow visualization of the bridging vein identified areas of low-velocity, stagnant flow along the superior wall of the anastomosis, representing a potential substrate for thrombosis.
