Following multidisciplinary review, the surgical team selected the nonbridged ECC (Option 1) for Fontan completion. The primary rationale was the robustness of the ECC compared with the Y-graft, which did not provide sufficient hemodynamic advantages in this anatomy. Although Options 4-6 improved hepatic flow balance, low-velocity stagnant flow regions within the bridging vein raised concern for thrombosis. The combination of surgical robustness and thrombosis risk thus favored the ECC option.

The patient underwent Fontan completion with an 18-mm fenestrated ECC and tricuspid valve repair. Her postoperative course was complicated by chylothorax treated with a fat-free diet and diuretic therapy, and she was discharged on postoperative day 10 in good condition. At the most recent follow-up 2 weeks later, she was doing well with oxygen saturations of 96%. An echocardiogram showed patent bilateral BDG and Fontan baffles, mild tricuspid insufficiency, and normal single right ventricular function.

This case demonstrates that bilateral BDGs create unique competitive flow dynamics at the cavopulmonary junction, rendering balanced hepatic flow difficult to achieve. A key practical finding is the sensitivity of Y-graft performance to conduit arm positioning, with the leftward shift in Option 3 producing nonmonotonic HFD behavior because of additional flow collisions. Additionally, the Y-graft is intrinsically a more complex surgical choice featuring 3 anastomoses, thus necessitating longer bypass time, potential for implementation variation, and other complex factors. By contrast, the ECC demonstrated consistent behavior characterized by uneven baseline HFD and increasingly balanced hepatic flow across the simulated PFD range. Importantly, although balanced hepatic flow is desirable, the exact HFD threshold required to prevent PAVM development or optimize long-term outcomes remains unknown. In this patient, whose the left lung received 35.9% of pulmonary flow pre-Fontan, the clinical team reasoned that the HFD afforded by the ECC may prove sufficient, particularly given its trajectory toward improved balance in physiological states where left-sided pulmonary flow increases postoperatively. Combined with its established robustness, this consistency reinforced the team’s decision to select Option 1.

The bilateral SVC anastomosis also represents a notable finding for patients with BDGs, despite its potential drawbacks. Consolidating the bilateral SVCs fundamentally alters flow interactions at the cavopulmonary junction, resulting in improved hepatic flow in all configurations. These findings align with previous studies that have illustrated the effects of neo-innominate bridging modifications in restoring balanced hepatic flow. To overcome the consequences of geometric transition between the dual SVCs, tapered/flared bridge geometries or angled anastomotic orientations may be explored to create smoother connections and minimize low-flow zones. Should PAVM development occur over time, revisiting this strategy remains a viable future option.

From a broader perspective, computational surgical planning may be most valuable in anatomically complex cases where hemodynamic outcomes are difficult to predict from anatomy alone, including bilateral SVCs, interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, and patients with a failing Fontan. In its current form, the paradigm evaluates only a subset of factors that determine optimal hemodynamics. Future multiobjective frameworks that consider hemodynamics alongside material, surgical, and anatomical constraints will be needed for optimized designs. For instance, fluid-structure interaction modeling can enable conduit mechanical behavior analysis alongside flow performance, accounting for both material properties and deformations from adjacent structures such as a dilated/reconstructed aorta. Similarly, physics-based structural analyses can inform access for future percutaneous interventions such as pulmonary artery dilatation/stenting or conduit fenestration. Four-dimensional flow cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may also play a critical role in reducing simulation uncertainty and providing in vivo validation of predicted hemodynamics. Finally, broader clinical translation will require implementation across both scientific and patient-care communities. It is our hope that in the future, both collaborative and federated learning methods will enable surgical planning to reach more patients with single-ventricle physiology.

This case demonstrates unique flow interactions between competing dual SVCs and IVC-derived hepatic flow in bilateral BDG Fontan completion. The ECC emerged as the most consistent among the various configurations evaluated, whereas bilateral SVC anastomosis may serve as a future HFD optimization strategy with appropriate refinement to avoid thrombogenic flow. Together, these findings underscore the role of computational surgical planning as a preoperative planning tool in complex anatomies.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Leadless Transatrial or Transconduit Pacing in Fontan Circulation
medicine.abstract: Epicardial or transvenous pacing strategies may be suboptimal in certain patients with Fontan requiring permanent pacing. Leadless pacing offers an alternative, but experience in complex Fontan anatomy remains limited.We report 3 patients with Fontan who underwent transatrial or transconduit leadless pacemaker (LP) implantation. One patient with a lateral tunnel Fontan and sinus node dysfunction underwent successful placement of an AVEIR AR (Abbott) LP in the pulmonary venous atrium. Two patients with Fontan circulation and complete heart block with prior epicardial pacing systems underwent implantation of a Micra AV (Medtronic) LP in the systemic ventricle, with longer follow-up than in prior reports.This case series demonstrates leadless pacing in the pulmonary venous, atrial, and systemic ventricular chambers in Fontan circulation, including atrial AVEIR AR implantation and extended follow-up of ventricular Micra AV pacing. These approaches may expand pacing options in selected patients with Fontan when conventional strategies are limited, although long-term outcomes remain unknown.
medicine.text:
Patients with Fontan physiology are at increased risk of requiring permanent pacing for sinus node dysfunction (SND), complete heart block (CHB), and/or electromechanical dyssynchrony. Epicardial pacing systems require repeat operative intervention and are at high risk of lead failure because of high pacing thresholds or lead fractures. Transvenous approaches to atrial pacing may be an option for certain patients with a lateral tunnel Fontan; however, they may be limited by the accessibility of viable atrial tissue because of scar and/or pathway stenosis or baffle leaks requiring stenting. Transpulmonary artery atrial leads may offer an alternative for transvenous atrial pacing, although this strategy may be precluded by left pulmonary artery stenosis requiring stenting.

Leadless pacemaker (LP) implantation offers a promising alternative when traditional pacing options are limited. LP implantation is generally well tolerated, although it may be associated with access-site complications because of the large-bore femoral access required, device-associated thrombus with an increased risk of stroke, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. Concern has been raised regarding worsening atrioventricular valve insufficiency following LP implantation in the biventricular heart, attributed to injury to the valve leaflets or entanglement in the subvalvular apparatus, although findings have been ultimately reassuring.

Although leadless atrial pacing has recently been described in patients with Fontan, published experience remains sparse. Prior reports include implantation of an Abbott AVEIR VR device in the pulmonary venous atrium and an AVEIR AR device within the Fontan tunnel of an atriopulmonary Fontan; reports of an AVEIR AR device in the pulmonary venous atrium are limited. Prior reports of ventricular LP implantation in Fontan have demonstrated follow-up of less than 1 year., ,  We present 3 cases of LP implantation in patients with Fontan physiology to expand the limited existing literature, including the first published report of atrial pacing using an Abbott AVEIR AR Atrial LP in the pulmonary venous atrium of a patient with Fontan, as well as longer-term follow-up of ventricular pacing with a Medtronic Micra AV LP.

A 34-year-old man with hypoplastic left heart syndrome status post (s/p) lateral tunnel Fontan presented with exercise intolerance because of SND and desaturation in the setting of known baffle leaks. Atrial pacing was indicated to manage sinus pauses and maintain atrioventricular synchrony. The preprocedural echocardiogram was notable for a mildly dilated systemic right ventricle with normal systolic function, mild tricuspid insufficiency, and mild neoaortic insufficiency. An initial electrophysiology (EP) study demonstrated extensive scar within the lateral tunnel without a target for transvenous pacing. The need for left pulmonary artery stenting precluded a transpulmonary artery lead. Epicardial pacing was not pursued because of a prior history of pericarditis; thus, leadless atrial pacing was felt to be his best option.

During the initial EP study, access to the pulmonary venous atrium was achieved via a transbaffle puncture using a curled radiofrequency wire (VersaCross, Baylis). Following voltage and activation mapping, ablation of a cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent circuit was performed using a STSF Force/irrigated ablation catheter (Biosense Webster, Inc.). Two days later, the team reaccessed the previously created fenestration and performed serial dilation to allow advancement of the 26-F Abbott AVEIR sheath into the systemic atrium. The Abbott AVEIR AR LP was initially deployed at the base of the left atrial appendage; however, there was suboptimal injury current and high thresholds. The LP was then deployed deep in the left atrial appendage with good capture thresholds (, ) without phrenic nerve stimulation. Following LP deployment, the large transbaffle puncture was partially occluded with a 20-mm Amplatzer Septal Occluder. His immediate postprocedural course was complicated by atrial tachycardia requiring amiodarone. Two months later, a covered stent was placed in the lateral tunnel Fontan to occlude baffle leaks because of persistent cyanosis and to decrease the risk of paradoxical embolism following a new diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. At the 4-month follow-up, his device interrogation revealed 73% atrial pacing with a predicted longevity of >14 years (). Ventricular function and atrioventricular valve insufficiency remained unchanged on the postprocedural echocardiogram. He remains on apixaban without concern for thromboembolic complications at the most recent follow-up.

A 55-year-old man with double-inlet left ventricle (LV) s/p extracardiac Fontan, SND, CHB, and Fontan-associated liver disease complicated by chronic hepatitis B presented with recurrent syncope because of intermittent loss of capture without a ventricular escape in the setting of rising pacing thresholds. The patient had a hybrid Medtronic Percepta cardiac resynchronization therapy pacemaker (CRT-P) pacing system that included 2 epicardial ventricular leads and a transpulmonary artery atrial lead. Most recently, he underwent a lengthy epicardial lead revision 7 months prior, complicated by mediastinitis. The preprocedural echocardiogram was notable for a normal-sized LV with normal systolic function, mild right atrioventricular valve insufficiency, trivial left atrioventricular valve insufficiency, and mild aortic insufficiency. The decision was made to pursue leadless ventricular pacing because of concern about inadequate epicardial pacing sites.

Following failure of radiofrequency to perforate the conduit using a (VersaCross; Baylis) coiled radiofrequency wire, transconduit access was obtained with a Brockenbrough 2 transseptal needle (Medtronic) with a SafeSept guidewire (Pressure Products, Inc). Subsequent serial dilations allowed advancement of the 24-F Micra delivery sheath into the pulmonary venous atrium, across the right systemic atrioventricular valve, and into the single LV. A Micra AV (Medtronic) LP was first deployed in the posterolateral LV with inadequate capture at 3 volts. The LP was successfully redeployed in a more anterior/rightward apical position with improved capture thresholds (, ). During the procedure, the patient experienced significant systemic desaturation because of a right-to-left shunt through the right atrial access site, confirmed with transesophageal echocardiography. The puncture site was closed with a 6-mm Amplatzer Septal Occluder, with improvement in saturation. His procedure was complicated by femoral vascular access-site infection requiring incision and drainage and oral antibiotics. His Micra AV was programmed to VDD 80-120 beats/min at the time of discharge. His prior Percepta (Medtronic) CRT-P remained programmed atrial paced, atrial sensed, inhibited 85-110 beats/min. His ventricular function and atrioventricular valve insufficiency remained unchanged on the postprocedural echocardiogram.

At >2 years postimplantation, his device continued to display >90% tracking and a >10-year predicted longevity (). He was managed with low-dose aspirin and clopidogrel because of an increased risk of bleeding in the setting of his liver disease, without concern about thromboembolic complications during the follow-up period. More than 2 years postprocedure, the patient developed advanced heart failure symptoms and elected to transition to hospice care before his death.

A 44-year-old woman with tricuspid atresia s/p atriopulmonary Fontan and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome s/p ablation complicated by CHB presented with early battery depletion of her epicardial Medtronic Percepta CRT-P generator because of high capture thresholds. She had known chronically elevated epicardial pacing thresholds previously requiring multiple epicardial lead revisions. Leadless ventricular pacing was pursued because of concern about inadequate epicardial pacing sites. Preprocedural echocardiogram was notable for normal-sized LV with normal systolic function, trivial mitral insufficiency, and trivial aortic insufficiency.

Transbaffle access was achieved with radiofrequency application followed by serial dilation to allow advancement of the 24-F Medtronic delivery sheath into the systemic atrium, across the mitral valve, and into the LV. A Medtronic Micra AV LP was initially deployed in the posterolateral LV, then again more apically without effective capture at maximum output. The LP was finally deployed at the septal base of the anteroseptal papillary muscle with effective capture (, ). Following implantation, saturations remained at baseline at approximately 90% without supplemental oxygen; thus, the transbaffle puncture site was not occluded. She was noted to have a decrease in hematocrit from 45% to 31% attributed to unrecorded procedural blood loss without associated symptoms. Her device was programmed ventricular paced, dual-chamber sensed, dual response 70 beats/min before discharge. Her existing epicardial device was reprogrammed to ventricular paced, ventricular sensed, inhibited response 50 beats/min. Her ventricular function and atrioventricular valve insufficiency remained unchanged on the postprocedural echocardiogram.

One week after her procedure, she presented with shortness of breath and decreased saturations and underwent transfusion for presumed symptomatic anemia despite hematocrit unchanged from discharge. At the 6-week follow-up, saturations had improved, anemia had resolved, and there was no detectable residual baffle leak by transthoracic echocardiography. Because of easy bruising on apixaban, she was later transitioned to low-dose aspirin and clopidogrel. She subsequently presented to an outside hospital for acute influenza and experienced an embolic stroke immediately following intravenous medication administration. Although this was attributed to a paradoxical air embolism, anticoagulation was transitioned to warfarin.

At 18 months after implantation, device interrogation displayed >70% atrial tracking and a >10-year predicted longevity (). Approximately 21 months after device implantation, the patient underwent surgical reconstruction of her left pulmonary artery at an outside center, which was complicated by postoperative bleeding and the need for tracheostomy. The patient was reported to be deceased 3 months following her operation.

LP provided an effective and less invasive pacing strategy for 3 complex patients with Fontan in whom transvenous or epicardial approaches were prohibitively high-risk or not feasible. Existing reports of leadless pacing in patients with Fontan remain limited to isolated case reports and small series with short-term follow-up. Our experience adds 1 patient with successful systemic atrial pacing using the AVEIR AR LP and 2 patients with ventricular LP demonstrating stable device performance beyond 18 months, expanding the available follow-up in this population.

Several procedural considerations emerged from these cases. Transconduit or transatrial access can be achieved safely using standard transseptal equipment, although large-bore sheath passage may require serial dilation. Closure of the iatrogenic puncture site should be considered in patients with significant postprocedural right-to-left shunting through the access site. In our series, 1 patient required immediate device closure for worsening hypoxemia, whereas another experienced transient desaturation and anemia after an unclosed puncture with eventual spontaneous resolution. These observations suggest that intraprocedural hemodynamic assessment under anesthesia may underestimate the clinically relevant residual shunting in the postprocedural period.

Despite previously published concerns that LP implantation may worsen systemic ventricular function through electromechanical dyssynchrony or increase atrioventricular valve regurgitation from device-related mechanical interaction with or injury to the valve apparatus, we did not observe clinically significant changes during the follow-up period.

Thromboembolic risk remains an important consideration following implantation of intracardiac devices in the pulmonary venous atrium or systemic ventricle in Fontan circulation. Long-term warfarin remains the standard for transvenous leads placed inadvertently or intentionally via a transatrial approach into the LV. In contrast, no long-term anticoagulation is required with the leadless (WiSE CRT, EBR Systems) device because of its small size and woven polyester jacket, which promotes endothelialization and prevents clot formation. Although our patients received uncoated metallic LPs, these devices likely endothelialize and have a much smaller surface area for collect thrombus compared with transvenous leads. Ultimately, the optimal antithrombotic strategy after LP implantation in patients with Fontan remains unknown and is further complicated by the multiple comorbidities in this population. All patients were maintained on systemic anticoagulation and/or dual antiplatelet therapy without device-related thromboembolic events during follow-up, although 1 suffered a likely air embolus during a subsequent hospitalization. Our patients were poor candidates for anticoagulation with warfarin and/or direct oral anticoagulants to varying degrees.

The principal limitation of this report is the small sample size and limited follow-up duration. In addition, 2 patients subsequently died of complications of advanced Fontan physiology unrelated to their pacing systems, underscoring the high comorbidity burden in this population. Nevertheless, these cases demonstrate that leadless pacing can provide a durable pacing strategy in selected patients with Fontan limited conventional options and support further study of long-term outcomes in this growing population.

Leadless pacing provided an alternative strategy for 3 complex patients with Fontan in whom conventional epicardial or transvenous systems were high-risk or not feasible, with stable electrical performance during the follow-up period. These cases highlight important procedural considerations for LP implantation, including selective closure of iatrogenic access sites when clinically significant shunting occurs. Larger studies are needed to define long-term outcomes and optimal antithrombotic strategies in this population.

medicine.title: Towards alpha-blockade–free surgery for pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma: experience from a newly established adrenal center
medicine.abstract: Pheochromocytomas are rare catecholamine-secreting tumors for which surgical resection is the definitive treatment. Traditionally, preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade is strictly recommended. However, recent evidence has questioned its necessity. In this study, we report our experience with pheochromocytoma surgery at a newly established adrenal center without prior specialization in adrenal surgery.From May 2022 to May 2026, 18 patients (14 female, 4 male; median age 63.1 years, interquartile range (IQR) 46.2–70.1) with catecholamine-producing tumors (15 pheochromocytomas and 3 paragangliomas) underwent surgical resection in our institution. Seventeen patients did not receive any preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade, whereas one patient underwent surgery while already receiving phenoxybenzamine therapy initiated by the referral physician prior to admission. Intraoperative management included general anaesthesia, central venous access, and invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring. Urapidil and/or nitroglycerin were used as the primary antihypertensive agents. Data were prospectively collected and retrospectively analyzed, including patient demographics, preoperative metanephrine and normetanephrine secretion, intraoperative treatment of hypertension and hypotension, and postoperative outcomes.The median operative time was 49.5 min (IQR, 30–90). Sixteen procedures were performed minimally invasively (15 retroperitoneoscopic and one laparoscopic), and two by open approach. Partial adrenalectomy was performed in seven cases. Histology confirmed chromaffin cell tumors in all cases, with a median tumor size of 4.0 cm (IQR 3.15–5.15). Median peak intraoperative systolic blood pressure was 195 mmHg (IQR, 166–200). For intraoperative blood pressure control, urapidil was administered to 4 patients (22.2%), nitroglycerin to 3 (16.7%), and both agents to 3 (16.7%). The remaining 8 patients (44.4%), did not require pharmacological treatment. Ten patients (55.6%) had a maximum intraoperative noradrenaline requirement < 0.2 µg/kg/min, 5 (27.8%) required intermediate doses of 0.2–0.4 µg/kg/min, and 3 (16.7%) required high doses > 0.4 µg/kg/min. Median postoperative hospital stay was 2 days (IQR, 2–3). Two patients developed transient atrial fibrillation. No major complications or mortality occurred.Our results support the feasibility of alpha-blockade-free surgery for pheochromocytoma, even in centers with limited prior experience in pheochromocytoma surgery. Education of the anaesthesiology team, structured perioperative protocols, and close interdisciplinary collaboration appear to be important for ensuring safe perioperative management.
medicine.text:
Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) are rare catecholamine-producing tumors with an incidence of approximately 0.6 cases per 100,000 person-years. The 2022 World Health Organization (WHO) classification defines PPGLs as neuroendocrine neoplasms arising from chromaffin cells. Approximately 80–85% of pheochromocytomas originate from the adrenal medulla, while about 15–20% arise from extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue []. Approximately 30% of pheochromocytomas and up to 40% of paragangliomas are hereditary [–]. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment and nowadays is commonly performed using minimally invasive retroperitoneoscopic or laparoscopic techniques. Historically, adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma was considered a high-risk procedure, with perioperative mortality rates reported to be as high as 40–45% [–]. Over the latter half of the twentieth century, perioperative mortality declined dramatically to below 3% [–]. This remarkable improvement has been attributed to advances in anaesthetic management, refinements in surgical techniques, earlier diagnosis through improved biochemical and imaging modalities, and the widespread adoption of preoperative α-adrenergic blockade [, ]. Preoperative α-adrenergic blockade was subsequently introduced as the standard of care for patients undergoing pheochromocytoma resection and remains recommended by most international clinical practice guidelines [, ]. Despite its widespread acceptance, this recommendation has largely been based on historical experience rather than high-quality prospective evidence. In the past decade, this long-standing paradigm has been critically re-evaluated. In particular, Groeben et al. demonstrated that patients undergoing adrenalectomy with and without preoperative α-adrenergic blockade experienced comparable perioperative outcomes under contemporary anaesthetic and surgical management [, ]. These findings challenged the general routine of α-blockade and raised the debate regarding its necessity.

We therefore aimed to evaluate the safety and feasibility of α-blockade-free adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma and to assess whether outcomes reported by highly specialized, high-volume referral centers can be reproduced in a newly established adrenal surgery program.

From May 2022 to May 2026, 18 patients with catecholamine-producing tumors (15 pheochromocytomas and 3 paragangliomas) underwent surgical resection at our institution, which had no previous specialization in adrenal surgery. Preoperative diagnostic workup included biochemical assessment of plasma metanephrine and normetanephrine levels and cross-sectional imaging using computed tomography (CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for tumor localization and surgical planning. Preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade was not administered. The decision to omit routine preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade was established as an institutional strategy following interdisciplinary agreement between the surgical and anesthesiology teams. This approach was applied consistently throughout the study period, with the exception of one patient in whom phenoxybenzamine therapy had already been initiated by the referring endocrinologist. In this patient phenoxybenzamine treatment had already been initiated before referral and continued until surgery at a dosage of 60 mg per day. Patients were admitted either on the day before surgery or on the day of surgery. Routine preoperative intravenous volume expansion was not performed.

Perioperative anaesthetic management followed the institutional anaesthetic protocol. General anaesthesia was induced intravenously with propofol, remifentanil, and rocuronium, followed by endotracheal intubation. Anaesthesia was subsequently maintained using one of two techniques. Total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) consisted of continuous infusions of propofol and remifentanil, whereas volatile anaesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane in combination with sufentanil. In both groups, ventilation was performed using an oxygen–air mixture with an inspired oxygen fraction (FiO₂) of approximately 0.5. The choice of anaesthetic technique was at the discretion of the attending anaesthesiologist. Continuous invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring was performed via an arterial catheter. Central venous access was established through the internal jugular vein using a triple-lumen catheter. Anesthetic agents were administered using standard weight-based dosing and titrated according to individual clinical requirements. Intraoperative blood pressure was managed individually without a predefined mean arterial pressure target. Urapidil and/or nitroglycerin were administered as continuous infusions when required. Detailed information on individual drug dosages and intraoperative fluid administration was not consistently available due to the retrospective study design.

Patient positioning was determined by the surgical approach, with supine positioning for transabdominal procedures (laparoscopic or open) and prone positioning for the posterior retroperitoneoscopic approach. For posterior retroperitoneoscopic adrenalectomy, patients were positioned prone, and the retroperitoneal space was established using a balloon-free, three-port technique with CO₂ insufflation. After identifying the upper pole of the kidney, the adrenal gland was approached from its posterior aspect. Dissection was performed along the upper pole of the kidney using an energy device. Whenever feasible, arterial feeding vessels were identified and divided first to reduce tumor blood supply, while the adrenal vein was identified and sealed during progressive dissection rather than routinely ligated early. In cases of partial adrenalectomy, the tumor was dissected from the surrounding adrenal parenchyma while preserving the remaining gland.

For transabdominal laparoscopic and open procedures, patients were positioned supine. These approaches were selected for large tumors requiring wider surgical exposure. Open access was obtained through an upper abdominal laparotomy extended laterally to form an inverted L-shaped incision. Following mobilization of the adjacent organs, the tumor and its vascular attachments were progressively exposed. Feeding vessels were individually identified and controlled, and the tumor was carefully separated from surrounding structures, avoiding capsular disruption. En bloc resection of adjacent organs was performed when required by tumor involvement. For the assessment of intraoperative hemodynamic stability, baseline systolic arterial pressure, maximum intraoperative systolic arterial pressure, and the lowest intraoperative mean arterial pressure were recorded. Intraoperative hemodynamic management focused on the rapid control of blood pressure fluctuations, particularly during tumor manipulation and following tumor resection. Hypertensive episodes were treated with titrated intravenous urapidil and/or nitroglycerin according to the individual hemodynamic response. A continuous noradrenaline infusion was routinely established for all patients following tumor resection. The infusion rate was individually titrated according to arterial pressure and hemodynamic requirements. Noradrenaline support was subsequently reduced and discontinued by the attending anaesthesiologist once adequate hemodynamic stability had been achieved during the postoperative period. Postoperative complications were classified according to the Clavien–Dindo classification. Morbidity and mortality were assessed within 30 days after surgery. Routine postoperative follow-up was performed, although long-term outcomes were not included in the present analysis.

18 patients (14 female, 4 male; median age 63.1 years (IQR, 46.2–70.1)) with catecholamine-producing tumors (15 pheochromocytomas and 3 paragangliomas) underwent surgery at the center without previous specialization in adrenal surgery. Preoperative characteristics of the study cohort and the preoperative secretion values are summarised in Tables  and , respectively. Isolated metanephrine secretion was observed in 1 patient (5.6%), isolated normetanephrine secretion in 5 patients (27.8%), and combined metanephrine and normetanephrine secretion in 10 patients (55.6%). In 2 patients (11.1%), preoperative metanephrine and normetanephrine levels were within the reference range. Most patients were symptomatic: 15 patients had arterial hypertension, and 3 patients had​ suffered from diabetes mellitus.

Preoperative characteristics of the study cohort

The median duration of surgery was 49.5 (IQR: 30–90) min. Sixteen procedures were performed using minimally invasive techniques, including one laparoscopic adrenalectomy combined with distal pancreatectomy for metastatic pheochromocytoma and 15 retroperitoneoscopic operations. One patient with a 10 cm paraganglioma underwent primary open surgery. In one additional case, conversion from laparoscopic to open surgery was required due to strong tumor adherence to the liver and a tumor size of 13.5 cm. Partial adrenalectomy was performed in 7 patients. There was no need for blood transfusions in any patients. The median maximum intraoperative systolic blood pressure was 195 mmHg (IQR 166–200), while the median maximum diastolic blood pressure was 95 mmHg (IQR 80–110). 10 of 18 patients (55.6%) had a systolic BP > 180 mmHg. The median lowest intraoperative systolic blood pressure was 100 mmHg (IQR 90–110); three patients had a documented systolic pressure lower than 80 mmHg. For intraoperative blood pressure control, urapidil was administered to 4 patients (22.2%), nitroglycerin to 3 patients (16.7%), and both agents to 3 patients (16.7%). The remaining 8 patients (44.4%), including three patients with paragangliomas, did not require pharmacological treatment for intraoperative blood pressure control. 10 patients (55.6%) had a maximum intraoperative noradrenaline requirement < 0.2 µg/kg/min, 5 (27.8%) required intermediate doses of 0.2–0.4 µg/kg/min, and 3 (16.7%) required high doses > 0.4 µg/kg/min. In 16 patients, the noradrenaline support was discontinued in the operating theatre. One patient who had received preoperative alpha-blockade required prolonged postoperative noradrenaline support and was admitted to the ICU without evidence of organ dysfunction. All the other patients were admitted postoperatively to the recovery room. Only one patient required low-dose noradrenaline support in the recovery room, which was gradually weaned and discontinued after 1 h, after which the patient was transferred to the regular surgical ward. Two patients developed postoperative atrial fibrillation, which resolved following a single administration of a beta-blocker in each patient (Clavien–Dindo Grade II). No further antiarrhythmic treatment or anticoagulation was required. One of these patients was monitored overnight in the intensive care unit (ICU). One additional patient who underwent open surgery was admitted to the ICU for one day postoperatively for routine observation. The median postoperative hospital stay was 2 days (IQR: 2–3 days). One patient with metastatic pheochromocytoma underwent simultaneous pancreatic tail resection and developed a grade B pancreatic fistula, which was managed conservatively without additional intervention (Clavien–Dindo Grade I​). No Clavien–Dindo grade IV or V complications or 30-day mortality occurred. The median tumor size was 4.0 (IQR 3.15–5.15), range 2–13,5 cm). Chromaffin cell tumors were confirmed by final histopathological examination in all patients. One patient with metastatic disease had a Ki-67 proliferation index of 15%. The present study demonstrates that surgical resection of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas without routine preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade is feasible in a center without prior specialization in adrenal surgery. Despite the absence of routine preoperative alpha-blockade, no major cardiovascular complications or perioperative mortality occurred. Although intraoperative vasopressor support was frequently required, the maximum noradrenaline dose remained below 0.2 µg/kg/min in more than half of the patients. According to the dose categories proposed by Pölkki et al., only three patients (16.7%) required high-dose noradrenaline (> 0.4 µg/kg/min) []. In 16 patients, noradrenaline support could be discontinued in the operating room. Only the patient who received preoperative phenoxybenzamine developed prolonged arterial hypotension requiring continued noradrenaline support and postoperative ICU admission for one day. These findings suggest that the omission of preoperative α-adrenergic blockade reduces the risk of clinically relevant postoperative hypotension and the subsequent need for vasopressor support, potentially allowing patients to be safely managed on a peripheral ward.

For more than five decades, routine preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade has been regarded as the cornerstone of perioperative management for pheochromocytoma and remains recommended by current international guidelines. However, these recommendations are largely based on historical experience from an era characterized by open surgery, limited intraoperative monitoring, and the absence of modern short-acting vasoactive drugs []. In recent years, increasing evidence has challenged the need for this practice. Groeben et al. demonstrated that surgery performed without routine alpha-blockade is associated with comparable intraoperative hemodynamic control and no increase in major perioperative complications, questioning the evidence supporting mandatory pharmacological preparation []. Moreover, Groeben et al. reported for the closed case series no difference in maximal intraoperative systolic arterial pressures and hypertensive episodes above 250 mm Hg []. Subsequently, the international PHEO Initiative, including 1,860 patients from 21 experienced endocrine centers, demonstrated substantial variability in perioperative management while maintaining an overall cardiovascular complication rate of 5% and a mortality rate below 1%, regardless of the considerable differences in perioperative protocols []. More recently, Holscher et al. prospectively implemented a protocol omitting the traditional escalation of preoperative alpha-blockade despite current guideline recommendations and reported that this strategy could be safely adopted without compromising perioperative outcomes []. Collectively, these studies suggest that perioperative management of pheochromocytoma is evolving away from mandatory preoperative α-blockade.

The principal novelty of the present study is not the omission of preoperative alpha-blockade itself but the successful implementation of this strategy in a hospital without previous expertise in adrenal surgery. An important aspect of establishing this strategy was the close collaboration between the surgical and anesthesiology teams from the beginning of the adrenal surgery program. Before implementation, a joint meeting between the heads of both departments was held to review the available literature, particularly studies reporting perioperative management without routine preoperative alpha-blockade, and to agree on a common management strategy. Particular emphasis was placed on familiarizing the anesthesiology team with the specific hemodynamic challenges of pheochromocytoma surgery, including perioperative hypertensive episodes and hypotension following tumor removal. The perioperative management strategy included continuous invasive arterial pressure monitoring, central venous access, and the availability of rapidly titratable intravenous antihypertensive agents and vasopressors. This structured interdisciplinary approach facilitated the introduction of surgery without routine preoperative alpha-blockade into a newly established adrenal surgery program. To date, virtually all published series supporting modified perioperative management protocols have originated from high-volume endocrine referral centers with extensive institutional experience. Consequently, it has remained uncertain whether such protocols could be safely introduced in hospitals that are establishing an adrenal surgery program. Our experience suggests that successful implementation depends less on institutional adrenal case volume than on meticulous multidisciplinary preparation. Unlike the protocol described by Groeben et al., which primarily relied on sodium nitroprusside for the treatment of intraoperative hypertension [, ], our institution used urapidil or nitroglycerin as the first-line antihypertensive agent for intraoperative management. The use of urapidil as a possible hypotensive agent in pheochromocytoma surgery was already described by Holzer et al., in a study comparing the preoperative use of urapidil to phenoxybenzamine []. In our study, despite this difference in pharmacological management, perioperative outcomes were comparable, suggesting that successful implementation of an alpha-blockade-free strategy is unlikely to depend on a specific vasoactive drug. Rather, the availability of a rapidly titratable intravenous antihypertensive agent appears to be the critical determinant. This observation has important practical implications, as urapidil and nitroglycerin are widely available and routinely used throughout Europe, whereas sodium nitroprusside is unavailable or only rarely used in many countries because of concerns regarding cyanide toxicity and limited commercial availability [].

Current guidelines emphasize close postoperative monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, and blood glucose following PPGL resection because of the risks of hemodynamic instability and hypoglycemia []. However, recommendations regarding the required level of postoperative care vary. For example, the 2025 Japan Endocrine Society guideline specifically recommends postoperative ICU management []. Reflecting current practice in Germany, a recent Delphi consensus of the German Society of Endocrinology (DGE) and the Surgical Working Group for Endocrinology of the German Society for General and Visceral Surgery (CAEK/DGAV) reported that approximately 60% of expert centers routinely admit patients to an intensive care or intermediate care unit after PPGL surgery, highlighting substantial variability in postoperative management []. Similarly, a bi-national multicentre study from Australia and New Zealand including 223 patients found that 77% were admitted to a high-dependency or intensive care unit postoperatively. Despite comparable demographic and tumor characteristics between patients managed in the ICU and those treated on the surgical ward, the proportion of ICU admissions varied significantly between centers, further highlighting the heterogeneity of postoperative management strategies []. Routine postoperative ICU admission was not part of our institutional practice. Planned ICU admission was undertaken in two patients undergoing open surgery. One additional patient required unplanned ICU admission due to new-onset tachyarrhythmia absoluta, which resolved with conservative management. Our results are also consistent with the current trend toward individualized perioperative management. Recently, Araujo-Castro et al. demonstrated comparable postoperative outcomes in normotensive and hypertensive pheochromocytoma patients in a large international multicenter study, supporting the concept that perioperative risk is determined by multiple patient- and tumor-related factors rather than blood pressure status alone [].

The present study has several limitations. Its retrospective design, limited sample size, and lack of a control group preclude direct comparison with patients receiving conventional alpha-blockade. Furthermore, the retrospective design limited access to detailed information on anaesthetic drug dosages and intraoperative fluid management. The present study represents the initial experience of a single institution and therefore cannot establish superiority over current guideline-recommended management. Nevertheless, our study demonstrates the feasibility of implementing an alpha-blockade-free perioperative management in a newly established adrenal surgery program and provides practical information regarding the organizational requirements necessary for its successful introduction.

In conclusion, our experience demonstrates that surgery for PPLGs without routine preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade can be successfully implemented in a center without previous expertise in adrenal surgery. The success of this approach appears to depend less on institutional case volume than on structured multidisciplinary collaboration, standardized perioperative protocols, and modern anaesthetic management. These findings may facilitate the broader adoption of individualized perioperative strategies beyond traditional high-volume endocrine centers.

medicine.title: Admission CONUT Score is Associated With Recovery From Postoperative Urinary Retention After Hip Fracture Surgery
medicine.abstract: To evaluate whether the admission Controlling Nutritional Status score is associated with recovery from postoperative urinary retention before discharge after hip fracture surgery.This retrospective single‐center cohort included 90 patients with postoperative urinary retention after hip fracture surgery. Recovery was defined as discontinuation of clean intermittent catheterization before discharge with a postvoid residual urine volume ≤ 200 mL. Scores were categorized as < 3 or ≥ 3. Firth penalized logistic regression assessed recovery before discharge. A sensitivity analysis also treated the score continuously. Additional analyses used cumulative incidence functions and cause‐specific Cox regression, treating discharge without recovery as a competing event.Fifty‐eight patients (64.4%) recovered. Recovery proportions were 94.4% (34/36) and 44.4% (24/54) in patients with scores < 3 and ≥ 3, respectively (p < 0.001). A score ≥ 3 was associated with lower odds of recovery (adjusted odds ratio 0.045, 95% confidence interval 0.008–0.172, p < 0.001) and a lower cause‐specific recovery hazard (adjusted hazard ratio 0.37, 95% confidence interval 0.21–0.65, p < 0.001). An Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≥ 2 was also associated with lower recovery odds (adjusted odds ratio 0.176, 95% confidence interval 0.048–0.562, p = 0.002). Among recovered patients, median recovery times were 8–7 days, respectively (p = 0.371).A higher admission Controlling Nutritional Status score was associated with a lower likelihood of recovery from postoperative urinary retention before discharge. Prospective validation is needed before using the score to guide postoperative bladder management.
medicine.text:
Hip fracture in older adults is associated with substantial mortality, loss of independence, and functional decline [, ]. Postoperative urinary retention (POUR) is a common complication [] that may require catheterization and interfere with early mobilization [].

Previous studies have examined POUR incidence, risk factors, catheter management, and recovery after hip fracture surgery. Skelly et al. found that intermittent catheterization led to an earlier return to satisfactory voiding than indwelling catheterization []. Johansson and Christensson examined urinary retention and catheter management []. Japanese studies by Tobu et al. and Higashikawa et al. evaluated POUR risk factors and functional impairment [, ]; Tobu et al. also reported recovery after short‐term intermittent catheterization []. Other studies examined perioperative retention, functional outcomes, and catheter‐removal timing [, , ]. Tantigate et al. identified anticholinergic use, pre‐existing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), and impaired early mobilization as risk factors []. Recovery after established retention has also been studied through a standardized trial‐without‐catheter programme [] and orthogeriatric co‐management in Japan [].

Malnutrition and impaired muscle health are common after hip fracture []. A higher Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score, calculated from serum albumin, total cholesterol, and total lymphocyte count, has been associated with postoperative complications in this population []. Poor nutritional status and reduced physiological reserve may also be relevant to recovery of bladder emptying.

POUR is multifactorial, involving bladder dysfunction, comorbidities, medication use, anesthesia, and other perioperative factors [, ]. Although recovery after POUR has been studied, the association with admission nutritional status remains less well characterized. We therefore evaluated whether the admission CONUT score was associated with recovery before discharge among patients who developed POUR after hip fracture surgery.

This retrospective single‐center cohort study included consecutive patients who developed POUR after hip fracture surgery at Nagasaki Rousai Hospital, Japan, between January 2020 and April 2024. Clinical and laboratory data were extracted from electronic medical records.

Patients were excluded if they had pre‐existing neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, an indwelling urinary catheter before admission, or missing data required to calculate the CONUT score or assess recovery from POUR.

POUR was defined according to our institutional protocol as inability or difficulty in spontaneous voiding with a postvoid residual urine volume (PVR) ≥ 300 mL after removal of the indwelling urinary catheter. Recovery from POUR was defined as successful discontinuation of clean intermittent catheterization before hospital discharge, with a PVR ≤ 200 mL after spontaneous voiding. Patients who continued to require clean intermittent catheterization at discharge or had a PVR > 200 mL were classified as not having recovered.

PVR was measured after an attempt at spontaneous voiding using a portable bladder scanner (BladderScan BVI 6100; Verathon Inc., Bothell, WA, USA).

The CONUT score was calculated from serum albumin, total cholesterol, and total lymphocyte count measured at admission. Albumin contributes 0, 2, 4, or 6 points; cholesterol and lymphocyte count each contribute 0–3 points. The total ranges from 0 to 12, with scores of 0–1, 2–4, 5–8, and 9–12 conventionally indicating normal, mild, moderate, and severe nutritional impairment, respectively []. Patients were categorized as CONUT < 3 or ≥ 3, using a threshold previously applied in a urological perioperative study []. This is not an established threshold for recovery from POUR.

Recorded variables included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), fracture type, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS), hypertension, diabetes mellitus, reduced renal function, catheterization duration, use of medications for LUTS before treatment for POUR, and length of stay. Catheterization duration was the interval from surgery to first catheter removal. Reduced renal function was an admission estimated glomerular filtration rate < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. Admission ECOG PS was obtained from medical records and categorized as < 2 or ≥ 2.

Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, and categorical variables as number and percentage. Groups were compared using Student's t‐test or the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the χ
2 test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate.

The primary outcome was recovery from POUR before discharge. Firth penalized logistic regression was used because only two patients with CONUT < 3 did not recover, raising concerns about sparse‐data bias [].

Univariable analyses evaluated age, sex, BMI, ECOG PS ≥ 2, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, reduced renal function, catheterization duration, use of medications for LUTS, and CONUT ≥ 3. Fracture type was described but not modeled. Individual CONUT components were not entered separately. Length of stay was excluded because it was a post‐baseline variable potentially influenced by recovery.

The multivariable model included age, sex, BMI, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and CONUT ≥ 3 based on clinical relevance, regardless of univariable statistical significance. Age and BMI were continuous variables.

A sensitivity analysis replaced the CONUT category with the continuous score in the multivariable Firth model.

In additional time‐to‐event analyses, follow‐up began at treatment initiation for POUR and ended at documented recovery or discharge. Discharge without recovery was a competing event for in‐hospital recovery. Cumulative incidence was estimated using the Aalen–Johansen method []. Cause‐specific Cox regression included age, sex, BMI, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and CONUT ≥ 3; patients left the risk set at discharge without recovery. A sensitivity analysis used continuous CONUT. Tied recovery times were handled using the Breslow method. Recovery times among recovered patients were also compared using the Mann–Whitney U test.

Odds ratios (ORs), cause‐specific hazard ratios (HRs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. An OR > 1 indicated higher odds of recovery before discharge; an HR > 1 indicated a higher instantaneous recovery rate among patients still hospitalized and unrecovered.

Descriptive analyses and group comparisons used EZR version 1.68 []. Firth regression used JMP Student Edition version 18 (JMP Statistical Discovery LLC, Cary, NC, USA). Time‐to‐event analyses used Python version 3.11 (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA). Tests were two‐sided, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Nagasaki Rousai Hospital (approval number: 04014). The requirement for written informed consent was waived because of the retrospective observational design, and information regarding the study was disclosed using an opt‐out approach.

ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with language editing, literature organization, document preparation, and code for statistical consistency checks during manuscript revision. The final statistical analyses were independently repeated and verified by the authors. No patient‐level observations were generated.

Of 715 patients who underwent hip fracture surgery, 102 developed POUR. Twelve were excluded: six with pre‐existing neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, three with an indwelling catheter at admission, and three with missing data. The analysis included 90 patients (Figure ), of whom 58 (64.4%) recovered before discharge and 32 (35.6%) did not. There were 36 patients with CONUT < 3 and 54 with CONUT ≥ 3 (Table ).

Baseline characteristics according to the CONUT score at admission.

Abbreviations: CONUT, controlling nutritional status; ECOG, Eastern cooperative oncology group; LUTS, lower urinary tract symptoms.

Patients with CONUT ≥ 3 were older (87.2 ± 7.9 vs. 82.7 ± 8.6 years, p = 0.012) and had a lower BMI (19.7 ± 2.8 vs. 21.4 ± 3.8 kg/m2, p = 0.020). Sex, fracture type, ECOG PS, comorbidities, catheterization duration, LUTS medication use, and length of stay did not differ significantly (Table ).

Recovery before discharge occurred in 34/36 patients (94.4%) with CONUT < 3 and 24/54 patients (44.4%) with CONUT ≥ 3 (p < 0.001; Figure ).

In univariable Firth analyses, ECOG PS ≥ 2 and CONUT ≥ 3 were associated with lower odds of recovery (OR 0.262, 95% CI 0.091–0.682, p = 0.004; and OR 0.058, 95% CI 0.011–0.199, p < 0.001, respectively; Table ).

Firth penalized logistic regression analyses of factors associated with recovery from postoperative urinary retention.

Abbreviations: BMI, body mass index; CI, confidence interval; CONUT, controlling nutritional status; ECOG, Eastern cooperative oncology group; LUTS, lower urinary tract symptoms; OR, odds ratio.

These associations persisted after adjustment (ECOG PS ≥ 2: adjusted OR 0.176, 95% CI 0.048–0.562, p = 0.002; CONUT ≥ 3: adjusted OR 0.045, 95% CI 0.008–0.172, p < 0.001). Age, sex, and BMI were not significantly associated with recovery.

In the continuous‐CONUT sensitivity analysis, each 1‐point increase was associated with lower odds of recovery (adjusted OR 0.435, 95% CI 0.288–0.600, p < 0.001; Table ).

Sensitivity analysis using the CONUT score as a continuous variable.

Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; CONUT, controlling nutritional status; ECOG, Eastern cooperative oncology group; OR, odds ratio.

Among the 58 recovered patients, median recovery time was 8 days (interquartile range 5–12) overall, 8 days (6–12) with CONUT < 3, and 7 days (5–11) with CONUT ≥ 3 (p = 0.371; Table ). Cumulative incidence of in‐hospital recovery was lower with CONUT ≥ 3 (Figure ). In the adjusted cause‐specific Cox model, CONUT ≥ 3 was associated with a lower recovery hazard (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65, p < 0.001; Table ). The continuous‐CONUT analysis also showed an association (HR per 1‐point increase 0.71, 95% CI 0.62–0.82, p < 0.001).

Recovery outcomes according to admission CONUT category.

Note: Values are n (%) or median [interquartile range].

Abbreviation: CONUT, controlling nutritional status.

Multivariable cause‐specific Cox regression analysis of in‐hospital recovery from postoperative urinary retention.

Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; CONUT, controlling nutritional status; ECOG, Eastern cooperative oncology group; HR, hazard ratio.

In this cohort of patients with POUR after hip fracture surgery, higher admission CONUT was associated with lower odds of recovery before discharge. Associations were also observed in the continuous‐CONUT and cause‐specific Cox analyses. The comparison of observed recovery times was restricted to patients who recovered; it neither describes recovery in the whole cohort nor establishes equivalence between groups.

Previous studies have addressed POUR incidence, risk factors, management, and recovery [, , , , , , , , , , ]. Skelly et al., Cheng and Chin, and the Japanese orthogeriatric study evaluated catheter management or care pathways rather than admission nutritional status [, , ]. The present study examines admission CONUT in relation to recovery before discharge after established POUR. Differences in management and recovery definitions preclude direct comparison of recovery rates.

Malnutrition is associated with sarcopenia, reduced muscle strength, and diminished physiological reserve [, ]. Reduced detrusor contractility can contribute to incomplete bladder emptying []. Frailty is also associated with LUTS []. CONUT may therefore reflect frailty, sarcopenia, or impaired activities of daily living rather than a direct effect of nutritional status on bladder recovery. ECOG PS does not fully measure these conditions, so adjustment for it cannot exclude this explanation.

ECOG PS ≥ 2 was associated with lower odds of recovery in the primary model. Recovery after hip fracture has been associated with baseline function and other patient factors [, ], and comprehensive geriatric care can improve functional outcomes []. However, ECOG PS was not statistically significant in the continuous‐CONUT Firth analysis or the categorical‐CONUT cause‐specific Cox model. Its association should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

The cutoff of 3 has precedent in a urological perioperative study [], but it is not an established threshold for POUR recovery. It also divides the conventional mild‐impairment category of 2–4 []. The continuous analysis reduces reliance on this dichotomy but does not validate the threshold. CONUT combines albumin, cholesterol, and lymphocyte measurements []. Acute illness and inflammation may also affect these measurements, so we interpret the score as a possible marker of broader vulnerability rather than a purely nutritional measure.

Several limitations warrant emphasis. The retrospective single‐center design and small sample limit causal inference and generalizability. Firth regression reduces sparse‐data bias but does not resolve selection bias or residual confounding. Baseline LUTS severity, cognitive impairment, pre‐fracture mobility and activities of daily living, frailty, sarcopenia, anesthesia type, opioid exposure, and detailed perioperative medication use were unavailable. These factors may have substantially influenced the associations. Recovery was assessed only during hospitalization, and longer stays provide more opportunity to recover. The competing‐risk analysis describes in‐hospital recovery in the presence of discharge without recovery, but cannot remove the effects of discharge practices or establish recovery after discharge. The findings concern recovery after POUR onset, not POUR occurrence. PVR and catheterization requirements, rather than routine urodynamics, defined the outcome, leaving the underlying mechanism uncertain. Catheter management was not fully standardized and may have depended on the clinical course and physicians' decisions. Finally, acute illness and inflammation can affect CONUT; the association does not establish that nutritional intervention improves bladder recovery.

The CONUT score can be calculated from routinely available laboratory data. Clinical use requires prospective validation with frailty and functional assessments and follow‐up after discharge. Although nutritional screening and individualized support are recommended in geriatric care [], their effect on recovery from POUR remains unknown.

In conclusion, higher admission CONUT was associated with a lower likelihood of recovery from POUR before discharge after hip fracture surgery. Prospective validation is needed before using CONUT to guide postoperative bladder management.

Tomohiro Matsuo: data curation, formal analysis, writing – review and editing. Hidenori Ito: data curation, investigation, writing – review and editing. Ryoichi Imamura: writing – review and editing. Hideki Sakai: writing – review and editing, supervision.
