The requirement for written informed consent was waived because of the retrospective observational design, and information regarding the study was disclosed using an opt‐out approach.

The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

medicine.title: Transpulmonary Atrial Pacemaker Implantation in Fontan Circulation With Bilateral Glenn
medicine.abstract: Patients with Fontan circulation frequently develop atrial arrhythmias and sinus node dysfunction. Atrial pacing is challenging because conventional transvenous access is limited by complex Fontan anatomy.A 20-year-old man with dextroisomerism, bilateral Glenn anastomoses, and Fontan circulation presented with symptomatic sinus node dysfunction and recurrent supraventricular tachycardia. A transpulmonary transvenous approach achieved endocardial atrial lead implantation with excellent pacing parameters. Despite optimized medical therapy, heart failure progressed, and the patient died during transplant evaluation.This case highlights the technical feasibility of transpulmonary endocardial atrial pacing as an alternative to repeat epicardial surgery in selected patients with Fontan circulation. Careful procedural planning, multimodality imaging, and individualized assessment of long-term anticoagulation are important considerations. Despite arrhythmia control, optimized therapy and restoration of atrioventricular synchrony may not prevent heart failure progression, which may be irreversible.Transpulmonary endocardial atrial pacing is a feasible alternative in carefully selected Patients with Fontan circulation. Sudden cardiac death risk stratification remains limited in this study group.
medicine.text:
A 20-year-old patient with complex congenital heart disease and Fontan circulation presented with symptomatic sinus node dysfunction (SND) and recurrent supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). He had previously undergone catheter ablation of atrioventricular (AV) re-entrant tachycardia associated with twin AV nodes, with initial procedural success but subsequent arrhythmia recurrence. With progressive systemic ventricular dysfunction, a repeat electrophysiological study was performed. Following the first rapid atrial pacing train, spontaneous ventricular fibrillation (VF) developed, requiring brief resuscitation and defibrillation. The procedure was aborted, and the patient recovered without neurologic sequelae or evidence of end-organ injury.

The patient had dextroisomerism, dextrocardia, an unbalanced complete AV canal with hypoplasia of the left ventricle, double-outlet right ventricle, and persistent left superior vena cava ( and ).

He underwent staged single-ventricle palliation, including neonatal systemic-to-pulmonary shunt, bilateral bidirectional Glenn anastomoses at 6 months of age, and extracardiac Fontan completion at 6 years.

During adolescence, he developed SND with alternating sinus and junctional escape rhythms, associated with sustained and nonsustained SVT despite antiarrhythmic therapy.

An electrophysiology study performed via trans baffle access demonstrated twin AV nodes and dual AV node physiology. Atypical atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia was inducible, and radiofrequency ablation of the inferior node eliminated tachycardia inducibility.

Despite initial improvement, sustained SVT recurred during follow-up, with an arrhythmia burden of 14%. Escalation of medical therapy was limited by symptomatic bradycardia.

A repeat electrophysiology study was performed. Following the first burst pacing protocol, the patient developed low cardiac output with spontaneous degeneration into VF. Defibrillation and advanced resuscitation restored sinus rhythm, and the procedure was terminated. Coronary angiography showed no filling defects, and the patient recovered without neurologic sequelae or end-organ injury.

Serial echocardiograms before the procedure demonstrated progressive decline in systemic right ventricle systolic function. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a systemic right ventricular ejection fraction of 30% and indexed end-diastolic volume of 140 mL/m2, without myocardial fibrosis, consistent with advanced ventricular remodeling.

Guideline-directed heart failure (HF) therapy and systemic anticoagulation were initiated because of Fontan physiology and ventricular dysfunction.

Atrial pacing was indicated to treat symptomatic bradycardia, restore AV synchrony, facilitate HF therapy, and suppress SVT consistently triggered by junctional beats.

Epicardial and transvenous pacing strategies were evaluated with the multidisciplinary team and family. Given the patient's anatomy, multiple previous sternotomies, the need to preserve future surgical access for potential heart transplantation, and the existing indication for long-term anticoagulation, a transpulmonary transvenous atrial pacing approach was selected.

The procedure was performed under general anesthesia. Vascular access was obtained through the left femoral vein (11-F sheath) and left internal jugular vein (6-F sheath). Intravenous heparin was administered to maintain an activated clotting time >250 seconds throughout the procedure.

Left Glenn angiography through the jugular access delineated the pulmonary arteries and their relationship with the systemic atrium (). Simultaneously, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) from the Fontan circuit provided real-time visualization of the left pulmonary artery and systemic atrium.

A 90° LAMP transseptal sheath and a Brockenbrough needle (Abbott) were used. The needle was manually straightened, preserving only a slight distal angulation to enhance directional control. Under combined fluoroscopic and ICE guidance, a controlled puncture was performed from the left pulmonary artery into the systemic atrium (, , and , ).

A 0.014-inch Whisper guidewire was advanced into the atrium, with intracavitary position confirmed by ICE and fluoroscopy. The dilator was then advanced over the needle and guidewire into the atrium and then exchanged over a 0.035-inch Advantage guidewire for a coronary sinus delivery sheath (Attain Command 6250VIC, fixed curve; Medtronic).

An active fixation lead (Tendril 2088 TC, 65 cm) was deployed in the systemic atrium using manually shaped stylets to aid in the pacing site selection ( and ). Stable fixation was achieved, with excellent pacing parameters (P-wave amplitude >13 mV, capture threshold 0.25 V at 0.4 milliseconds, and lead impedance 1,420 Ω).

A short intracavitary lead loop was created to minimize tension at the fixation site before tunneling to a prepectoral pocket and connected to a pacing generator (Astra; Medtronic).

The procedure was completed without immediate complications. Apixaban was initiated 3 hours later. Chest radiography confirmed stable lead position, and device interrogation showed stable lead parameters without significant arrhythmia recurrence at 4-month follow-up ().

Despite optimized medical therapy and rhythm control, HF progressed, requiring 2 hospitalizations for decompensation. Pulmonary or systemic embolic events were not evident clinically or on imaging. Heart transplant evaluation was initiated, but he unfortunately died suddenly at home before its completion.

In Fontan physiology, atrial arrhythmias and SND contribute to clinical deterioration because loss of AV synchrony impairs ventricular filling, reduces cardiac output, and increases cavopulmonary pressures., ,  These effects are amplified in patients with systemic ventricular dysfunction, in whom atrial pacing may restore AV synchrony and improve hemodynamics.

In our patient, recurrent SVT occurred in the setting of dextroisomerism and twin AV nodes, a substrate associated with complex arrhythmias and lower ablation success rates. After VF complicated repeat electrophysiological testing, further invasive intervention was considered high risk, favoring atrial pacing and medical optimization.

Permanent pacing in Fontan circulation has traditionally relied on epicardial leads, requiring repeat thoracic surgery and showing less favorable lead performance and higher pacing than endocardial systems.,  Avoiding additional sternotomy is particularly relevant in young patients because it may complicate future heart transplantation. Contemporary endocardial pacing systems are MRI conditional, facilitating serial ventricular assessment.

The transpulmonary approach provides an alternative route to the systemic atrium. Careful preprocedural imaging is essential to define the spatial relationship between the pulmonary artery and the systemic atrium, select the optimal puncture trajectory, and anticipate anatomical constraints. Atrial leadless pacing in patients with Fontan circulation has been reported only in a limited number of cases and has primarily involved atrial tissue accessible from the Fontan pathway. Pacing parameters may therefore be more favorable in patients with lateral tunnel Fontan anatomy, where atrial tissue may be incorporated into the pathway, unlike in our patient with an extracardiac Fontan. Given the patient's anatomy, our institutional experience, and the available technology, a transpulmonary approach was considered the most appropriate strategy for achieving stable atrial pacing.

Intraprocedural guidance with angiography and ICE was fundamental for safe transcatheter puncture, guidewire advancement, and lead deployment. Alternative tools, including 3-dimensional mapping and computed tomography or MRI integration, may further facilitate the procedure.

Endocardial pacing in Fontan circulation requires careful consideration of thromboembolic risk because intracardiac hardware is introduced into an already prothrombotic circulation. Current guidelines recommend antithrombotic prophylaxis in adults with Fontan circulation and recognize transvenous pacing systems as a potential additional thromboembolic risk factor, although the magnitude of this risk and the extent to which it is mitigated by antithrombotic therapy remain uncertain. Observational data suggest a numerically higher thrombotic burden in patients with Fontan circulation with transvenous pacing leads, whereas antiplatelet and/or anticoagulant therapy has been associated with lower thrombotic risk.

Evidence specifically addressing anticoagulation after transpulmonary endocardial lead implantation is limited, and neither the optimal agent nor duration of therapy has been established. In our patient, who had no documented atrial fibrillation, flutter, or previous thromboembolic event, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction and the introduction of an endocardial lead exposed to the systemic circulation favored long-term anticoagulation rather than antiplatelet therapy alone. Vitamin K antagonists remain the most established strategy; however, observational studies and meta-analyses suggest that direct oral anticoagulants may provide comparable thromboembolic protection and bleeding risk in selected Patients with Fontan circulation, although definitive comparative evidence remains unavailable.,  Apixaban was selected after individualized assessment, considering the anticipated difficulty of maintaining a therapeutic international normalized ratio and our institutional experience with patients with Fontan circulation with systemic leads through a fenestration and biventricular patients with left ventricle endocardial leads treated with direct oral anticoagulants. Evidence supporting a specific anticoagulant for patients with transpulmonary endocardial leads remains lacking.

Primary prevention with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was also considered. Evidence supporting ICD benefit in single-ventricle patients, particularly those with a systemic right ventricle, remains limited. In the absence of syncope, ambulatory ventricular arrhythmias, myocardial fibrosis, or high-risk estimates using current adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) risk models (PREVENTION-ACHD and Spanish ACHD Network), pacing alone was selected as the initial strategy while HF therapy was optimized. Subcutaneous ICD screening confirmed that this device remained a feasible future option in combination with the pacing system. During the patient’s subsequent hospitalizations, there were no clinical or imaging findings suggestive of pulmonary or systemic thromboembolism, and both episodes were attributed to progressive HF. His death at home was preceded by symptoms suggestive of HF decompensation, without desaturation or focal neurologic deficits. Although pulmonary or systemic embolism could not be excluded at the time of death, an arrhythmic mechanism also remains possible.

In our setting, where transplant waiting times are generally short for adult patients, primary prevention ICD is frequently deferred when the estimated risk is not high.

To our knowledge, this is the first reported case in South America of transpulmonary atrial pacemaker implantation in a patient with Fontan circulation. Although the procedure successfully restored AV synchrony and controlled recurrent atrial arrhythmias, it did not alter the course of advanced Fontan HF. This case illustrates both the feasibility of this technique and the limitations of current risk stratification tools in this study group and the need for collaborative studies to narrow knowledge gaps regarding sudden death prediction and primary prevention ICD indications.

In carefully selected patients with Fontan circulation, transpulmonary endocardial atrial pacing is a feasible alternative to epicardial lead implantation, providing favorable lead performance and longevity. Successful implementation requires meticulous procedural planning, multimodality imaging, multidisciplinary decision-making, and individualized assessment of long-term anticoagulation, as the optimal antithrombotic agent and duration remain uncertain. This case also highlights the limitations of current sudden cardiac death risk stratification in patients with single-ventricle physiology.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: An Acute Coronary Event in a Patient With Fontan Circulation During Pregnancy
medicine.abstract: There is a growing number of adults living with Fontan circulation who are pursuing pregnancy.We report a case of a woman with Fontan physiology and pregnancy who had sudden onset chest pain, ST-segment changes, and troponin elevation with coinciding echocardiographic and magnetic resonance imaging changes consistent with myocardial injury from likely paradoxical coronary embolism.Patients with Fontan circulation are at increased thrombotic risk, which is further exacerbated by pregnancy. However, there are limited data regarding appropriate thromboprophylaxis in these patients, especially because there is also a significant bleeding risk.This case highlights the complexity of decision-making regarding diagnosis of coronary events in patients with Fontan circulation, as well as challenges determining ideal thromboprophylaxis in these patients during pregnancy.
medicine.text:
A 27-year-old woman with double-inlet left ventricle {S,L,L}, transposed great arteries, pulmonary stenosis, and bilateral superior venae cavae (SVCs) with the left SVC draining to the left atrium and a bridging vein, who was palliated with a 20-mm extracardiac fenestrated Fontan (), had been clinically well since her Fontan operation. She had normal left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) at her last clinic appointment 3 years earlier. Her home medications included aspirin 81 mg and lisinopril 10 mg daily. She was not using contraception. She presented with sudden onset sharp midsternal chest pain radiating to her back associated with left hand paresthesia, nausea, and vomiting.

On exam, her heart rate was 79 beats/min, blood pressure 142/98 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 84% in room air (at her baseline); she had no murmur, gallop, or peripheral edema.

The patient initially underwent a bidirectional Glenn operation with ligation of her main pulmonary artery and patent ductus arteriosus at 5 months of age before Fontan palliation at age 2. Additional history was significant for an incidental thrombus found in her main pulmonary artery stump during her Fontan operation. She had no other personal or family history of clotting disorders, and no thrombophilia work-up had been pursued.

The differential diagnosis of chest pain with troponin elevation and ST-segment changes is broad in a young woman with Fontan physiology. The first concern is a thromboembolic etiology because of the increased risk of clot in the Fontan pathway and subsequent pulmonary embolism or paradoxical embolism across the Fontan fenestration or, in this patient’s case, through her left SVC to her common atrium and coronary arteries. Other possibilities include myocarditis and less common etiologies such as nonembolic coronary complications (ie, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, coronary vasospasm, myocardial infarction), Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and aortic dissection.

Laboratory evaluation was notable for an initial high-sensitivity troponin T of 14 ng/L (upper limit of normal 19), which increased to a peak of 521 ng/L on repeat measurement 15 hours after presentation (). She had a normal N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide of 34 pg/mL. Electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in anterior leads and ST-segment depression in inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated new mildly decreased LVEF and isolated posterior apical wall akinesis with a focal hinge point in wall motion without any visualized thrombi within the Fontan pathway ().

Incidentally, serum human chorionic gonadotropin was mildly elevated at 19 mIU/mL, which on repeat testing increased to 34 mIU/mL over 48 hours, consistent with early pregnancy.

She was started on empiric treatment for an acute coronary event with aspirin 162 mg, heparin infusion, and sublingual nitroglycerin. To further assess for Fontan pathway thrombus, pulmonary embolism, and coronary artery pathology, a cardiac computed tomography angiography was performed with cardiac and early arterial acquisition to visualize the aorta and coronary arteries and delayed acquisition to ensure contrast opacification of the inferior vena cava to ensure enhancement of the Fontan pathway. This showed no obvious coronary obstruction, coronary emboli, or Fontan thrombus. The coronary artery distribution corresponded to the morphologic ventricle it supplied, with the left circumflex and left anterior descending coronary arteries originating from the anterior-facing sinus and coursing rightward to the right-sided left ventricle, and the right coronary artery originating from the posterior-facing sinus and coursing leftward to the hypoplastic left-sided right ventricle (). This is the most common arrangement of coronary arteries in patients with {S,L,L} double-inlet left ventricle. Because of these imaging findings coupled with improving ST-segment changes and symptoms, cardiac catheterization was not pursued.

Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging was performed, but no gadolinium was given because of pregnancy, and showed mildly reduced LVEF of 41%, elevated native T1 of 1,214 milliseconds and T2 of 57 milliseconds in the mid to distal inferior walls, consistent with diffuse myocardial fibrosis and myocardial edema, respectively. Because no gadolinium was administered, it was not possible to assess for late gadolinium enhancement or scar. No thrombus or obstruction was seen, although the wall motion abnormality was also seen on this study (, ).

Based on these studies, it was felt that the most likely etiology of her symptoms was coronary embolism, resolved with heparin, originating from a venous thrombus that embolized to her coronaries via her fenestration or left SVC-to-atrium connection. Myocarditis could not be excluded as a cause of acute myocardial injury, though focal wall abnormality would be more consistent with a coronary artery etiology. Anticoagulation was started with enoxaparin, lisinopril was stopped because of her pregnancy, and metoprolol succinate was started for her reduced ventricular function. Subsequent testing showed improving troponin and no additional electrocardiogram changes, and she was discharged after 3 days of observation. Extensive counseling was provided regarding the risks of an unplanned pregnancy in the setting of cyanosis and with a likely acute coronary event, and she chose to continue the pregnancy upon discharge, with a presumed gestational age of 3 weeks, 5 days.

After discharge, she presented to the maternal-fetal medicine clinic for evaluation at 9 and 13 weeks estimated gestational age. During these visits, she was noted to have small amounts of vaginal bleeding. At 22 weeks of gestation, she was emergently admitted to the hospital with large-volume vaginal bleeding due to placental abruption with spontaneous abortion. She underwent emergent dilation and evacuation with intraoperative blood loss of 4 L. She was intubated, briefly on inotropic support with phenylephrine, resuscitated with fluids and blood products, and managed in the surgical intensive care unit postoperatively. She recovered without additional complications. On discharge, anticoagulation was changed to rivaroxaban, which she continues indefinitely.

An echocardiogram performed 1 month after initial discharge demonstrated improvements in LVEF and wall motion abnormalities. Repeat CMR with gadolinium performed 8 months after presentation showed late gadolinium enhancement consistent with scar in the area that previously demonstrated increased extracellular volume and myocardial edema (elevated T1 and T2 mapping) without ongoing elevation in T2 mapping. Additionally, cardiac catheterization showed a dilated left SVC draining into the coronary sinus and calculated Qp:Qs of 0.5:1. Because of this large right-to-left shunt and its likely contribution to cyanosis, which further increases her risk of paradoxical emboli and pregnancy loss, the left SVC was device-occluded. Her postprocedure saturation increased to 91%-95%.

Since this intervention, she clinically reports no cardiac symptoms or bleeding complications. She remains on rivaroxaban and metoprolol and has had a copper intrauterine device placed for contraception.

We present what is most likely an acute coronary event due to thromboembolism in a patient with Fontan circulation. Although CMR with gadolinium can show both the sequelae of a coronary thrombotic event in the form of dense myocardial fibrosis with endocardial late gadolinium enhancement as well as features of myocarditis with myocardial inflammation and increased extracellular volume, gadolinium is contraindicated in pregnancy; this limited cross-sectional imaging in this case to computed tomography and noncontrast CMR.

Patients with Fontan circulation have passive pulmonary blood flow and thus an increased thrombosis risk. Previous studies have shown a high burden of Fontan circuit thrombi, many of which are clinically silent. Thus, it is recommended that all patients with Fontan circulation take antiplatelet or anticoagulant medications, although there continues to be ongoing debate about which agent should be the standard treatment. This risk of thrombosis is further heightened in pregnancy,, which may have contributed to this presentation. Current guidelines recommend an individualized approach to antiplatelet and anticoagulant management during pregnancy, with prophylactic enoxaparin recommended in select patients., This hesitation against using multiple agents is likely because of the increased bleeding risk in this patient group, with up to 35% of patients having bleeding complications during pregnancy, which are more common than thrombotic complications in pregnant patients with Fontan circulation.,

We report a case of possible coronary embolus in the early stages of pregnancy in a patient with Fontan circulation who then developed placental abruption. This case highlights the challenges of diagnosing coronary events in this patient group, as well as the challenge of balancing the risk of thrombosis and bleeding in pregnant patients with Fontan circulation.

medicine.title: VA-ECMO Bridge to Transplant in Acute Fontan Circulatory Failure
medicine.abstract: Little is known about strategies for managing adults with Fontan circulation who require temporary mechanical circulatory support.A 33-year-old woman with Fontan circulation presented with syncope and was found to have Fontan conduit stenosis with low cardiac output. The patient developed hemodynamic collapse during catheter-based intervention, necessitating veno-arterial extracorporeal circulatory membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) cannulation. She was supported by VA-ECMO and was successfully bridged to heart transplantation after 11 days of support.In a patient with acute Fontan circulatory failure, temporary mechanical support with VA-ECMO and a Fontan-tailored approach to ramp trial and weaning studies ultimately led to informed clinical decision-making and bridge to successful heart transplant.VA-ECMO can be used for temporary mechanical circulatory support in acute Fontan failure. Patients with Fontan circulation on VA-ECMO require careful management, with a thoughtful approach to hemodynamics given the circuit’s unique physiology.
medicine.text:
A 33-year-old woman with Fontan circulation presented with a syncopal episode. Her physical exam was notable for dextrocardia with normal S1, single S2, and no murmurs. Oxygen saturation was 92%. She had no edema.

The patient was born with an unbalanced complete atrioventricular (AV) canal defect with double outlet right ventricle and dextrocardia. She underwent staged palliation with bidirectional Glenn, extracardiac fenestrated Fontan, and anomalous pulmonary vein repair at age 10 (delayed combined repair following relocation to the United States). The fenestration was closed 5 months later. Ten months after the initial procedure, she underwent stenting of the Fontan baffle. Her history includes 3 prior pregnancy losses; she has no living children. Comorbidities include mild developmental delay and anxiety.

In a patient with Fontan circulation presenting with syncope, the differential diagnosis includes low cardiac output, Fontan pathway obstruction (conduit or baffle stenosis, thrombus), dehydration, tachyarrhythmia, sinus node dysfunction, and vasovagal events. Pathway obstruction and low-output failure were prioritized given her clinical history.

Echocardiogram showed a common AV valve with severe AV valve regurgitation, severe systemic right ventricular dysfunction, and limited Fontan baffle assessment. Cardiac catheterization performed for syncope work-up revealed an elevated Fontan pressure (16 mm Hg) and an undersized Fontan stent with a 2-mm Hg gradient between the inferior vena cava and branch pulmonary artery (). Systemic ventricular filling pressures were normal, but the patient had low cardiac output, with a cardiac output of 2.3 L/min and a cardiac index of 1.6 L/min/m2 (normal ≥2.2 L/min/m2). Transpulmonary gradient (TPG, defined as mean pulmonary artery pressure minus pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) was 5 mm Hg.

Given the catheterization findings, the patient was scheduled for balloon angioplasty of the Fontan conduit as a bridge to advanced therapies. The procedure was complicated by conduit rupture into the right atrium (). She had a brief cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation achieved, and the conduit was sealed with covered stent placement (). Following this event, she developed myocardial stunning with a further decline in systemic ventricular systolic function, contributing to deteriorating hemodynamics and worsening hypoxia. Notably, her TPG increased from 5 to 15 mm Hg. The decision was made to initiate veno-arterial extracorporeal circulatory membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support with cannulation during the catheterization procedure with multidisciplinary input from adult congenital heart disease, heart failure, and cardiothoracic surgery teams. She was then transferred to the cardiovascular intensive care unit. She was intubated and started on inhaled nitric oxide and vasopressor support. VA-ECMO flows were maintained around 2.7 L/min—approximately half her calculated expected cardiac output—reflecting a deliberate low-flow strategy intended to optimize central venous pressure while preserving native ventricular ejection. Transplant evaluation was expedited, and she was listed United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) Status 1 for single-organ heart transplantation (HT) after extensive multidisciplinary assessment. Her combined class I and II calculated panel reactive antibody was 92%, which put her in the highly sensitized category. Her liver disease was thought to be because of chronic passive congestion, and not cirrhosis, as she had no splenomegaly, no significant fibrosis, normal platelet count, and only trace ascites. Thus, she did not meet criteria for liver transplantation.

She was extubated 2 days after VA-ECMO cannulation, and vasopressors were weaned over the following days. She remained supported by a milrinone infusion. She subsequently underwent right heart catheterization with a formal VA-ECMO weaning trial for United Network for Organ Sharing transplant status renewal (). While she demonstrated stable hemodynamics during stepwise reduction of VA-ECMO flows, a 2-minute clamp trial produced a drop in mean arterial pressure by 10 mm Hg, an increase in TPG from 4 to 6 mm Hg, and a decrease in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure—signifying an inability to provide adequate pulmonary blood flow through the cavopulmonary circuit. This pattern reflected recurrent Fontan circulatory failure: the same physiology that had precipitated VA-ECMO initiation.Table 1Fontan Weaning Trial HemodynamicsVA-ECMO FlowMAPTPGPCWPBaseline 2 L/min9548Wean 1.5 L/min6757Clamp trial62 (transient 50)66MAP = mean arterial pressure; PCWP = pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

Fontan Weaning Trial Hemodynamics

The patient underwent heart transplant after 11 days on VA-ECMO. Fortunately, she had no donor-specific antibodies. Eleven months after the transplant, she continues to do well without readmission. She has preserved graft function.

The indication for intervention on the Fontan conduit was not in question: cardiac catheterization demonstrated a hemodynamically significant stenosis, elevated Fontan pressure, and a low-output state. Catheter-based intervention was complicated by conduit rupture, precipitating the acute decompensation described below. The focus of this case is 2-fold: 1) the decision to choose VA-ECMO for support once circulatory collapse occurred; and 2) management of VA-ECMO in patients with Fontan circulation.

In adult patients with Fontan palliation, there is limited evidence on the use of temporary mechanical circulatory support for acute Fontan failure in comparison to systemic ventricular failure, and no device has been designed specifically for Fontan physiology. Existing right ventricular support options remain limited. This matters because Fontan circulation depends on passive, nonpulsatile pulmonary blood flow, and its primary mode of failure is often not ventricular pump failure alone but insufficient transpulmonary flow through the cavopulmonary connection. VA-ECMO remains the predominant readily available option for acute mechanical rescue in Fontan circulatory collapse—there is no temporary support modality that restores subpulmonary ventricular function. Published experience reflects this challenge: use is rare, and reported mortality and complication rates are high, with little procedural guidance tailored to this population.

In this case, the decision was made to use VA-ECMO when the patient experienced persistent hypoxemia and circulatory failure because of sudden decline in systemic ventricular function from postarrest stunning, accompanied by a sudden rise in TPG. Using low flows in this patient (around half of the expected cardiac output) improved the patient’s condition by optimizing central venous pressure, minimizing the rise in ventricular afterload, and supporting pulmonary perfusion. In standard cardiac physiology, flow-ramp assessment during VA-ECMO weaning balances competing hemodynamic forces—increased afterload from retrograde aortic flow vs decreased preload from venous drainage. In patients with Fontan circulation, using the lowest effective VA-ECMO flow that maintains adequate end-organ perfusion is even more critical, given the increased risk of stasis and thrombosis when native ventricular output is suppressed by high flows. Monitoring arterial pulsatility is particularly important in this study group to ensure that the native systemic ventricle continues to eject.

Typically, VA-ECMO weaning trials focus on balancing hemodynamics and support reduction, guided by changes in mean arterial pressure. In patients with Fontan circulation, we suggest that a more informative indicator is the change in transpulmonary gradient. In this case, the TPG increased sharply from 5 mm Hg at baseline to 15 mm Hg at the time of postarrest myocardial stunning. This marked the transition from compensated to decompensated Fontan physiology more clearly than any single chamber filling pressure at the time of arrest. With the VA ECMO wean, the TPG gradient increased whereas pulmonary capillary wedge pressure decreased. Only the TPG predicted a decline in mean arterial pressure, suggesting that this is the superior marker for assessment of compensation, contrasting standard biventricular anatomy criteria.

In a patient with acute Fontan circulatory failure, temporary mechanical support with VA-ECMO and a TPG-guided approach to ramp trial and weaning studies ultimately led to rescue from a potentially catastrophic situation, informed clinical decision making, and a bridge to successful heart transplant.
