medicine.title: Sex-dependent spatial organization of microgliosis tracks synaptic pathology in the demyelinated superior colliculus
medicine.abstract: Visual impairment is a common and clinically salient manifestation of Multiple Sclerosis (MS), yet pathology across visual system structures remains incompletely defined. Although the optic nerve, lateral geniculate nucleus, and visual cortex have been extensively studied, involvement of the superior colliculus (SC), a key visual processing hub, remains unclear. Here, we combined human postmortem tissue analysis with functional assessment and spatial mapping in the MS-relevant cuprizone (CPZ) mouse model to define how demyelination and secondary injury are organized within the SC. Postmortem SC tissue from donors with MS revealed myelin loss, including focal demyelinated lesions. In mice, CPZ impaired visual function and induced widespread SC demyelination without detectable neuronal loss or axonal degeneration. In male mice, although diffuse demyelination was accompanied by widespread microgliosis, atlas-based mapping uncovered a previously unrecognized spatial organization: a discrete high-microgliosis compartment with a stereotyped location and shape in every CPZ-treated mouse. This compartment did not correspond to canonical SC maps and was not explained by baseline microglial or myelin differences or by variability in local demyelination severity. Instead, high-microgliosis regions showed increased synaptic elimination, suggesting that secondary synaptic pathology may contribute to spatial organization of microgliosis beyond diffuse myelin loss alone. Prolonged CPZ exposure expanded the high-microgliosis compartment stereotypically, whereas withdrawal produced spatially ordered partial resolution with persistence of a high-microgliosis core and partial visual recovery. Former high-microgliosis territories showed partial restoration of synaptic density despite myelin recovery comparable to persistent high-microgliosis regions. In contrast, female CPZ-treated mice developed widespread SC demyelination and microgliosis without comparable compartmentalization, demonstrating sex-differential organization of microglial reactivity. Together, these findings identify the human SC as a site of demyelinating injury in MS and establish the CPZ-treated mouse SC as a sex-sensitive in vivo framework for investigating spatially patterned microglial reactivity, synaptic pathology, and incomplete resolution of microgliosis after demyelination.
medicine.text:
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease of the central nervous system (CNS) in which demyelination, neuroinflammation, and neurodegenerative processes converge to disrupt neural circuit function and ultimately drive irreversible disability [, , ]. Visual dysfunction is among the most common and clinically salient manifestations of MS, often presenting early in the disease course [, , , , ]. Accordingly, the visual system has become a key model circuit in MS research, as its well-defined anatomy enables quantitative readouts to track dysfunction over time and, in some settings, relate early injury to subsequent disability [, , , , ].

Historically, visual symptoms in MS have been closely linked to inflammatory demyelination with associated axonal loss in white matter tracts, most prominently exemplified by optic neuritis—an acute inflammatory demyelinating attack of the optic nerve that typically presents with subacute, often painful, monocular vision loss [, ]. However, visual impairment is also common in the absence of a clinical history of optic neuritis, and the severity of dysfunction is often not explained by focal white matter lesion burden within the affected circuit [, , , , ]. These observations have motivated efforts to identify additional drivers of visual disability beyond white matter damage alone [, , ].

A growing body of evidence implicates gray matter pathology as a major contributor to disease severity and progression in MS [, , , ]. For instance, cortical abnormalities, including atrophy and neuronal injury, have been repeatedly associated with clinical disability and progressive disease features [, , , , , , ]. Subcortical gray matter structures are also prominently affected [, , , ]. In particular, thalamic atrophy and microstructural abnormalities correlate with neurological impairment across disease stages [, , , ], supporting the concept that integrative gray matter hubs may be especially vulnerable in MS [, , ]. Within the visual system, pathology has been documented at multiple gray matter nodes, including the primary visual cortex and the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the visual thalamus [, , , ]. In the visual cortex, cortical thinning, lesion burden, and functional reorganization have been linked to visual processing deficits, whereas imaging and postmortem studies of the LGN have identified structural injury associated with visual impairment [, , , ]. Together, these findings indicate that visual disability in MS reflects distributed injury across multiple gray matter nodes within the visual pathway.

At the cellular level, synaptic pathology has emerged as an early and functionally relevant form of gray matter injury in MS and MS-relevant models [, , , , , , , ]. Human postmortem studies, synaptic PET imaging, and preclinical models have identified synaptic loss or dysfunction across several CNS regions [, , , , , , , ]. In the visual thalamus, our prior work showed that loss of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) synaptic inputs to the dorsal LGN can occur early, precede detectable neuroaxonal damage, and correlate with visual acuity decline in MS-relevant mouse models []. We further found that reactive microglia engulf RGC synapses, establishing microglia-associated synapse loss as a potential substrate of circuit dysfunction in MS []. Consistent with this concept, previous work using the cuprizone (CPZ) model of demyelination, one of the most widely used MS-relevant models [, , ], has reported altered subcortical visual circuit function together with synaptic loss and microgliosis in the LGN []. Thus, synaptic pathology and microglial reactivity are increasingly recognized as important features of MS-relevant gray matter injury. However, how these pathologies are spatially organized within affected visual system structures remains poorly understood.

The superior colliculus (SC) is a key yet comparatively understudied node in mammalian visual circuitry, particularly in the context of neurodegenerative disease [, , , ]. It integrates multisensory inputs to direct orienting and defensive behaviors and exhibits a conserved laminar organization, with superficial layers receiving dense, topographically mapped visual input and deeper layers integrating multimodal sensory and motor-related information to support visuomotor transformations [, , ]. Recent advances have provided a refined understanding of SC microcircuits, genetically defined cell types, and proposed functional subdivisions that map onto distinct behavioral repertoires, including orienting, arrest, and escape-like responses [, , , ]. This highly organized heterogeneous architecture makes the SC well-suited for asking whether demyelination-associated pathology follows established anatomical, functional, or connectivity-based maps, or instead reveals disease-associated spatial organization not predicted by canonical SC structure. Although the SC has been implicated in several neurological disorders characterized by disrupted visual processing and sensorimotor integration, including Parkinson's disease, where altered SC-dependent visual responses have been reported in de novo patients [, , , ], systematic neuropathological characterization of the SC in MS or MS-relevant models has not been performed.

To address this gap, we integrated analysis of postmortem human SC tissue with functional testing and atlas-registered spatial mapping in the CPZ mouse model, which provides a controlled system to investigate CNS-intrinsic responses to oligodendrocyte loss and subsequent repair after toxin withdrawal [, , ]. We identify SC demyelination in postmortem tissue from donors with MS and show that CPZ induces widespread SC demyelination and visual dysfunction in mice while preserving neuronal and axonal densities. In male CPZ-treated mice, despite diffuse myelin loss and widespread microgliosis, atlas mapping identified an unexpected, discrete high-microgliosis (HG) compartment with highly stereotyped location and shape. This compartment did not correspond to established anatomical, functional, or connectivity-based SC maps and was not explained by baseline regional differences or local demyelination severity. Instead, HG regions showed synaptic loss and increased microglial engulfment of synaptic material. The compartment expanded reproducibly during prolonged CPZ exposure and incompletely resolved after withdrawal, leaving a persistent core, whereas former high-microgliosis territories showed partial restoration of synaptic density. Notably, the corresponding female cohort showed diffuse SC demyelination and microgliosis but lacked the stereotyped spatial pattern observed in males, demonstrating that microglial reactivity organization varies by sex. Together, these findings identify the human SC as an MS-relevant site of injury and establish the CPZ-treated mouse SC as a sex-sensitive in vivo framework for investigating spatially patterned microglial reactivity, synaptic pathology, and incomplete microgliosis resolution after demyelinating injury.

De-identified human postmortem brain specimens containing the SC were provided as non-human-subjects research/exempt under institutional policy. Samples were obtained from the University of Michigan Brain Bank (Michigan Medicine) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) NeuroBioBank (Bethesda, MD, USA). The cohort comprised 12 donors total: 6 male donors and 6 female donors. Control tissue was obtained from 6 donors (5 male, 1 female) without diagnosed neurological disease. MS tissue was obtained from 6 donors (1 male, 5 female) with progressive MS. Donor characteristics are summarized in Table .

Male and female wild-type C57BL/6J mice (The Jackson Laboratory; stock no. 000664; Bar Harbor, ME, USA) were used for all experiments. Mice were housed on a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle with food and water ad libitum and were 8 weeks at the start of experiments. All animal procedures were approved by the local Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines for animal welfare.

Cuprizone-mediated demyelination was induced by feeding mice powdered rodent chow (LabDiet 5001; PicoLab) containing 0.2% (w/w) cuprizone (bis(cyclohexanone)oxaldihydrazone; Sigma-Aldrich, C9012-25G) for 6 or 9 weeks. Chow was provided ad libitum and replaced regularly throughout the experiment. CPZ chow was prepared fresh at each change by thoroughly mixing cuprizone powder into powdered ground chow. Control mice received the same powdered chow without CPZ. For recovery experiments, mice were treated with 0.2% CPZ for 6 or 9 weeks followed by return to standard rodent chow (CPZ withdrawal) for either 1 week or 3 weeks before tissue collection. During experimentally induced demyelination and recovery, the mice were monitored daily, and body weight was measured twice weekly.

After diet administration, mice were euthanized with a lethal intraperitoneal dose of Avertin (2,2,2-tribromoethanol) and transcardially perfused with 0.1 M phosphate buffer (PB) followed by glyoxal fixative (9% glyoxal, 8% acetic acid in 0.1 M PB). Brains were dissected and post-fixed in the same glyoxal fixative for 4 h at 4 °C, cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in 0.1 M PB at 4 °C until equilibrated, embedded in a 1:1 mixture of 30% sucrose/0.1 M PB and O.C.T. compound (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and coronally cryosectioned at 10 µm for immunostaining. Sections were collected to sample the SC at three rostro-caudal levels: anterior (SC-A; Bregma − 3.15 to − 3.50), central (SC-C; Bregma − 3.51 to − 3.86), and posterior (SC-P; Bregma − 3.87 to − 4.22) (see Figure ). Sections were blocked and permeabilized for 2 h at room temperature in 10% normal goat serum (MilliporeSigma) with 0.3% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) in 0.1 M PB. Primary antibodies were diluted in blocking solution and incubated overnight at room temperature: mouse anti-APP (clone 22C11; MilliporeSigma, MAB348; 1:200, RRID:AB_94882), rabbit anti-CASPR (abcam; ab34151, 1:1000, RRID:AB_869934), rat anti-CD45 (clone IBL-3/16; Bio-Rad, MCA1388; 1:100, RRID:AB_321729), rat anti-CD68 (clone FA-11; Bio-Rad, MCA1957; 1:1000, RRID:AB_322219), rabbit anti-cleaved caspase-3 (R&D Systems; MAB835, 1:1000, RRID:AB_2243951), rat anti-Clec7a (InvivoGen, mabg-mdect; 1:200, RRID:AB_2753143), mouse anti-MAG (clone 513; MilliporeSigma, MAB1567; 1:100, RRID:AB_11214010), chicken anti-MAP2 (EnCor, CPCA-MAP2; 1:1000, RRID:AB_2138173), chicken anti-NeuN (MilliporeSigma, ABN91; 1:1000, RRID:AB_11205760), rabbit anti-neurofilament 200 (MilliporeSigma, N4142; 1:1000, RRID:AB_477272), rabbit anti-PLP (clone EPR23504-106; Abcam, ab254363; 1:500, RRID:AB_3095302), rabbit anti-P2RY12 (AnaSpec, AS-55043A; 1:2000, RRID:AB_2298886), and guinea pig anti-VGluT2 (Synaptic Systems, 135 404; 1:2000, RRID:AB_887884) (also summarized in Table S2). After washing, sections were incubated with species-appropriate Alexa Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 2 h at room temperature, washed, and mounted with Vectashield containing DAPI for nuclear counterstain (Vector Laboratories).

RNA in situ hybridization was performed using the RNAscope platform (ACDBio, Newark, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, SC-containing cryosections from control and CPZ-treated mice were processed with RNAscope pretreatment reagents, including Protease III incubation for 30 min at 40 °C, followed by rinses in RNase-free water. Sections were hybridized for 2 h at 40 °C with pre-validated RNAscope probes targeting Mm-Tnf (ACDBio, 311081, NM_013693) and Mm-Il6 transcripts (ACDBio, 315891, NM_031168.1). Following probe hybridization, signal amplification and detection were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After RNAscope detection, sections were immunostained against P2RY12 to identify microglia as described above, and sections were mounted with Vectashield containing DAPI for nuclear counterstain (Vector Laboratories).

Human postmortem brain tissue was dissected and formalin-fixed at autopsy. Tissue blocks containing the SC were identified, paraffin-embedded, and sectioned at 10 µm. For IHC, sections were deparaffinized and rehydrated through graded alcohols, using our established protocols []. Antigen retrieval was performed by heating slides to 80 °C in 10 mM Tris–EDTA for 30 min in a Coplin jar, followed by 45 min incubation at room temperature. Subsequent blocking, antibody incubations, washes, and mounting were performed as described for mouse tissue immunostaining. Myelin was detected using rat anti-MBP (clone 12; MilliporeSigma, MAB386, 1:500, RRID:AB_94975) and rabbit anti-PLP (clone EPR23504-106; Abcam, ab254363, 1:500, RRID:AB_3095302) (see also Table ).

Quantification of myelin (PLP, MAG, MBP), axonal/neuronal markers (NF200, MAP2), and microglial markers (P2RY12, Clec7a, CD45) was performed on coronal sections sampling three rostro-caudal SC planes (SC-A, SC-C, SC-P; Figure ). For each animal, two sections per rostro-caudal plane were immunostained and imaged on a Zeiss LSM900 laser-scanning confocal microscope equipped with 405, 488, 561, and 640 nm lasers using ZEN Blue (v3.9; Zeiss). For each section, 20 × tiled images spanning the entire SC were acquired, with acquisition settings held constant across samples within an experiment. Image analysis was performed in Fiji/ImageJ (NIH; v1.52k). Quantification was conducted blinded to experimental condition and followed published approaches with minor modifications []. Briefly, images were background-subtracted and thresholded using a single strategy per marker within an experiment. Thresholds were determined from representative images from each condition using the IsoData method (8-bit images; threshold range 85–255), and the same background subtraction and threshold parameters were then applied to all images for that marker within the experiment. Regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to the whole SC and to superficial vs. intermediate/deep layers of the SC were delineated using DAPI or relevant immunostained proteins (see above) together with reference to the mouse brain atlas []. The HG compartment was defined as a contiguous area of elevated Clec7a signal, defined as the threshold above the mean of the whole SC in the same section after background subtraction. For each ROI, immunoreactivity was quantified as the percent area occupied by threshold-positive signal in the resulting binary mask using the ‘analyze particles’ function. Values from each hemisphere and both sections were averaged to generate a single value per animal for each rostro-caudal plane.

Density of synaptic inputs was assessed by quantifying VGluT2 immunoreactivity in sSC and idSC, and by comparing HG vs. adjacent LG regions within each layer. For each animal, 1–2 non-overlapping 63× fields of view were acquired per hemisphere in each region (sSC–HG, sSC–LG, idSC–HG, idSC–LG) from two sections, yielding 6–8 fields of view per region per animal (1–2 fields × 4 hemispheres) and 12–16 fields of view per layer per animal. Images were collected on a Zeiss LSM900 laser-scanning confocal microscope using identical acquisition settings across groups within an experiment. For each field of view, a z-stack comprising three optical sections spaced at 1 µm was acquired, resulting in 18–24 single-plane images per region per animal (6–8 fields × 3 planes) and 48–96 single-plane images per animal across all four regions. Image analysis was performed blinded to experimental condition in Fiji/ImageJ. Single z-planes were background-subtracted and thresholded using a single thresholding strategy per experiment, as described above. Regions of interest were delineated for sSC and idSC based on DAPI morphology and atlas reference, and HG regions were defined by contiguous areas of high Clec7a immunoreactivity. VGluT2 signal was quantified as percent area occupied by threshold-positive puncta using the ‘analyze particles’ function. Values were averaged across z-planes and fields of view for each hemisphere and then across hemispheres to generate a single VGluT2 density value per animal for each region (sSC–HG, sSC–LG, idSC–HG, idSC–LG).

Cellular (NeuN, CD45high, cleaved caspase-3), paranodal (CASPR), axonal (APP), and RNAscope signals were quantified from single-plane confocal images acquired with identical imaging settings across groups within each experiment. For each animal, single-plane 20 × tiled images or 63 × micrographs were acquired from two sections at each of three SC rostro-caudal levels (SC-A, SC-C, SC-P) using a Zeiss LSM900 laser-scanning confocal microscope. Regions of interest corresponding to sSC and idSC were delineated based on DAPI morphology and atlas reference. Positive signals were manually counted in Fiji/ImageJ by an investigator blinded to treatment. For CD45+ cells, only CD45high, round cells consistent with infiltrating peripheral immune cells were counted, excluding CD45low ramified microglia. Counts were normalized to ROI area to obtain densities (cells, paranodes, or APP+ counts per mm2). Values from both sections and both hemispheres were averaged to generate a single density value per animal for each rostro-caudal level and layer. For RNAscope analyses, Tnf and Il6 puncta were quantified from matched SC regions. Total cytokine signal was quantified within SC regions of interest, and microglia-associated cytokine puncta were quantified within P2RY12+ microglial regions in LG and HG compartments. Values were normalized to control or LG regions as indicated in the figure legends.

Microglial synaptic engulfment was quantified as previously described [, , ]. Briefly, two SC-containing sections per mouse were immunostained for VGluT2, P2RY12, and CD68 and imaged on a Zeiss Observer spinning-disk confocal microscope equipped with 405, 488, 594, and 647 nm diode lasers using ZEN Blue software (Zeiss). Based on the gliosis mapping described above, high-magnification fields of view (63 ×) were selected per animal in HG regions and in adjacent low-microgliosis LG regions. Within each field, microglial cells were imaged. Z-stacks were acquired with approximately 50 optical sections at 0.18 µm step size using identical acquisition settings across groups within an experiment. Image processing and quantification were performed blinded to treatment in Fiji/ImageJ and Imaris (Bitplane). Three-dimensional surfaces were generated for microglia (P2RY12) and lysosomes (CD68), and VGluT2 signal contained within CD68+ volumes inside microglial boundaries was quantified. For each animal, engulfment values were averaged to obtain compartment-specific measures for HG and LG regions within the SC.

Visual function was assessed in awake, freely moving mice 1 day prior to cuprizone administration (baseline) and after 3, 6, 9, 6 + 1, 6 + 3, or 9 + 3 weeks of treatment, as indicated in the figures. Visual acuity scores were measured using the OptoMotry system (CerebralMechanics) as previously described, with no prior training required [, ]. In brief, mice were placed on an elevated platform in the center of a four-walled chamber surrounded by computer monitors displaying visual stimuli. Animals were exposed to a virtual rotating cylinder of vertical sine-wave gratings (rotation speed 12°/s, 100% contrast) at varying spatial frequencies (cycles/degree), which elicit reflexive head-tracking movements when visible []. Behavior was recorded with an overhead camera and scored by a trained observer blinded to treatment. Visual acuity score was defined as the highest spatial frequency that reliably evoked head tracking and was determined by systematically increasing spatial frequency until the animal no longer responded.

To generate spatial overlap heatmaps of the HG compartment, Clec7a and P2RY12 immunostaining were performed on mouse SC sections and whole-SC tiled images were acquired. Tiled images were aligned to an anatomically matched coronal reference section from the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas using the Fiji/ImageJ plug-in BigBrainWarp [, ]. After alignment, HG regions were delineated on the transformed images by manually tracing contiguous areas of elevated Clec7a signal, defined as the threshold above the mean of the whole SC in the same section after background subtraction. HG masks from individual animals were then exported and overlaid in a common atlas space to generate an overlap heatmap, in which each pixel value reflected the percentage of animals exhibiting HG at that location. Heatmaps were visualized as total extension (present in ≥ 1 animal), region present in most animals (> 75% overlap), and core region present in all animals (100% overlap).

Binary masks of HG compartments were exported from Fiji and analyzed in Python. For each mask, the outer boundary was extracted and represented as an ordered polygonal contour, which was then resampled to 360 points distributed evenly along the contour. To compare two compartments (e.g., across timepoints), we computed point-to-point correspondences by testing all circular shifts of the 360-point ordering and selecting the shift that minimized the overall boundary mismatch (summed Euclidean distances across all sets of points), thereby accounting for small indexing offsets introduced during contour sampling. Distances were then calculated between matched boundary points and converted from pixels to µm using the image scale. To obtain signed boundary change (expansion vs. retraction), displacement vectors were projected onto the local outward direction defined by the centroid-to-boundary vector at each point (positive values indicate outward expansion; negative values indicate inward retraction). For visualization, signed distances were smoothed using a moving-average window of five points. Quantifications were performed on unsmoothed values.

Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) from at least three independent biological replicates per group. Statistical analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 10 and 11 (GraphPad Software). For comparisons between two groups, two-tailed unpaired or nested Student’s t tests were used unless otherwise indicated. For within-animal repeated-measures comparisons (e.g., baseline vs. post-treatment optomotor testing, or HG vs. LG areas), two-tailed paired t tests were used. For comparisons among multiple groups with a single independent variable, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test was used. For non-parametric comparisons among multiple groups, Kruskal–Wallis test was used. Non-significant results are reported as ns (p ≥ 0.05). Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (*), p < 0.01 (**), p < 0.001 (***), and p < 0.0001 (****).

To first interrogate whether the SC is impacted in MS, we assessed myelin in postmortem SC from donors with MS compared to control specimens from donors without neurological disease (Table ). Confocal imaging of myelin basic protein (MBP, Fig. ) and myelin proteolipid protein (PLP, Figure ) revealed a loss of myelin in the SC in MS compared to controls. Regions of markedly reduced MBP immunoreactivity, consistent with focal demyelinated lesions, were identified in five of six MS samples. These regions showed lower myelin density than controls or normal-appearing gray matter (NAGM) in MS and varied in location and extent across the SC (Fig. , Figure ). These data extend previous evidence of demyelination throughout the visual circuit in MS, including the optic nerve, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, and visual cortex [, , , , , , , , , , , , ]. In addition, degeneration of the SC and other midbrain tectal structures has been documented in other neurological conditions, such as progressive supranuclear palsy, Parkinson's disease, and Lewy body dementia [, , , , , , , , , , ].

To provide a first comprehensive assessment of pathology in the SC in an MS-relevant setting, we utilized the CPZ mouse model of demyelinating disease, one of the most widely used preclinical models of MS [, ]. Mice were fed 0.2% (w/w) CPZ for 6 weeks—a commonly used regimen that produces robust gray matter demyelination (Fig. a) [, , , , ]—and compared to control mice on a standard rodent diet without CPZ. To maintain continuity with most CPZ paradigms, and to model the more severe MS disease course and greater disability accumulation prevalent in males with MS [, , , , ], we focused our initial analyses on male mice. As expected [, ], male CPZ-treated mice exhibited a moderate reduction in body weight compared to controls (Fig. b). Optomotor testing also revealed a marked reduction in visual acuity following CPZ treatment (Fig. c), evidence for clear visual system dysfunction in these mice. We, therefore, next assessed hallmark MS pathologies, including demyelination, neuroaxonal degeneration, and inflammation within the SC.

In line with previous work describing mouse SC organization into defined layers [, ], we found different densities in myelinated axons at baseline, with intermediate/deep layers (idSC) showing relatively higher densities compared to the superficial layer (sSC) (Figure ). Consequently, SC layers were analyzed separately in subsequent experiments. In addition, because CPZ pathology is spatially heterogeneous and has been reported to vary with anatomical level along the rostro-caudal (anterior–posterior) axis in other regions, most prominently described for the corpus callosum [, , ], we separately quantified pathology in anterior (SC-A, Bregma − 3.15 to − 3.5), central (SC-C, Bregma − 3.51 to − 3.86), and posterior (SC-P, Bregma − 3.87 to − 4.22) coronal planes of the SC (Figure ). We first interrogated changes in myelin by immunolabeling SC-A, SC-C, and SC-P sections for paranodal marker contactin-associated protein (CASPR, Fig. d) and myelin sheath proteins myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG, Fig. e) and PLP (Figure ). Quantification of all markers revealed widespread demyelination across all rostro-caudal SC planes following CPZ compared to controls (Fig. di, ei and Figure ). Across planes, myelin loss appeared more significant in sSC than idSC, which may reflect layer-specific susceptibility or differences in baseline myelin density that can influence quantitative sensitivity and dynamic range in immunofluorescence-based measurements [].

We next tested whether pronounced demyelination leads to neuronal cell death or axonal degeneration in the SC of these mice. Quantification of immunolabeled neuronal nuclei (NeuN) and microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2, Fig. a and Figure  b) to assess neuronal density, and neurofilament 200 (NF200) (Fig. b) to assess axonal densities, revealed no detectable differences in either sSC or idSC layers of SC-A, SC-C, and SC-P sections following CPZ treatment compared to controls. To independently corroborate these findings, we also assessed cleaved caspase-3 and amyloid precursor protein (APP) in adjacent sections, revealing no detectable apoptotic cells or APP+-axonal pathology across the SC, respectively (Figure a, b). Because RGC axons project through the optic tract toward retinorecipient targets, including the SC, we additionally assessed APP and NF200 in the optic tract from the same cohort (Figure c). Similar to the SC, CPZ-treated mice showed no induction of APP-positive axonal pathology and no detectable reduction in optic tract NF200 density compared to controls. Together, these analyses demonstrate that widespread demyelination occurs across SC layers and the rostro-caudal axis without the induction of neuronal cell death or axonal loss. These data are consistent with published work using comparable CPZ treatment regimens, showing pronounced demyelination across the brain with preserved neuroaxonal integrity [, ].

Widespread CPZ-induced demyelination in other brain regions is typically accompanied by diffuse, pronounced local inflammation, with reactive microgliosis among the earliest detectable secondary responses to myelin injury [, ]. To determine whether broad SC demyelination is similarly associated with widespread microglial activation, we immunolabeled adjacent SC-A, SC-C, and SC-P sections for the homeostatic microglia marker purinergic receptor P2Y12 (P2RY12) and the disease-associated microglia marker Clec7a (Figure a, b). Quantification of confocal images revealed a robust reduction in P2RY12 immunoreactivity and a concomitant increase in Clec7a signal in CPZ-treated mice compared to controls, consistent with widespread reactive microgliosis and a shift away from a homeostatic state to a disease-associated phenotype (Figure S6ai, bi). These changes were present in both sSC and idSC layers and across SC-A, SC-C, and SC-P planes, indicating broad microglial activation throughout the SC along the rostro-caudal axis.

Consistent with this, tiled images spanning the full SC corroborated P2RY12 downregulation and Clec7a induction across all rostro-caudal planes (Fig. ai, aii, full SC ctrl vs. CPZ). Despite this widespread response, closer inspection of full-SC tiles revealed a discrete high-microgliosis compartment (HG) in which microglial alterations were especially pronounced (Fig. a, orange outlines). This subregion was most clearly delineated by markedly elevated Clec7a relative to the remainder of the SC in CPZ-treated mice and showed concomitantly lower P2RY12 compared to other less affected SC regions (Fig. a, graphs on gray background, SC vs. HG). The HG compartment stereotypically spanned both sSC and idSC, comprising a large core within the ventro-lateral idSC with a slimmer lateral-to-medial neck region extending along the dorsal border of the sSC. Consistently, separate within-animal comparisons of high- vs. low-microgliosis regions in each layer identified substantially larger changes in the idSC than the sSC (ΔP2RY12: − 9.1% to − 23.8% in sSC vs. − 34.5% to − 58.2% in idSC; ΔClec7a: 1.343–2.983-fold in sSC vs. 26.81–55.51-fold in idSC), and confirmed that heightened microgliosis occurred in subareas of both layers in CPZ-treated animals (Figure a, b).

Immunostaining for the broad immune marker CD45 yielded consistent results, showing increased CD45 immunoreactivity in typically CD45low microglia in CPZ-treated mice compared to controls, with further elevation within the HG compartment (Figure a). CD45 staining also enabled assessment of CD45high round cells consistent with infiltrating peripheral cells, distinguishing them from CD45low, ramified microglia. In line with published work describing minimal to no peripheral immune cell recruitment in the CPZ model [, ], we observed no evidence for accumulation of CD45high round cells across SC layers or planes (Figure b), consistent with SC microgliosis and HG compartment formation being primarily organized by CNS-intrinsic cues in this model. To further determine whether this CNS-intrinsic response was accompanied by inflammatory cytokine expression, we performed RNAscope for Tnf and Il6, encoding pro-inflammatory cytokines TNFα and IL-6, in the same tissue. In line with previous observations in the CPZ model [, , , ], CPZ treatment increased overall Tnf and Il6 mRNA signal in the SC compared to controls (Figure c, d). Moreover, within CPZ-treated tissue, Tnf and Il6 puncta were enriched in P2RY12+ microglia within HG regions compared to LG regions (Figure cii, dii). Together with the CD45, P2RY12, and Clec7a data, these findings support the interpretation that the HG compartment exhibits heightened microglial reactivity with inflammatory features while remaining consistent with a predominantly CNS-intrinsic response in the CPZ model.

Notably, the HG compartment was present in all male CPZ-treated animals and appeared with strikingly consistent shape and location within the SC (Fig. b, see individual SC-C–HG regions for all eight CPZ-treated male animals). To map this compartment while accounting for potential sample distortion during tissue preparation, we used the Fiji plug-in BigBrainWarp to align full-SC confocal tiles to the corresponding coronal section from the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (Figure c) [, ]. Using these atlas-aligned masks, we generated an overlap heatmap of HG regions across animals, distinguishing the total extension of the affected region (present in ≥ 1 animal), the region affected in most animals (> 75% overlap), and the core region affected in all animals (100% overlap) (Fig. c, d). Projection of this heatmap onto established anatomical SC maps [, , ] showed partial yet incomplete overlap with superficial and intermediate/deep layers, and thus no clear alignment with these anatomical boundaries (Fig. e, left). Likewise, comparison with proposed functional SC subdivisions [], including areas relevant to vision, as well as arrest, turning, and triggering behaviors, revealed no clear correspondence (Fig. e, right). We also observed only limited overlap with known SC connectivity maps [, ], including, but not limited to, key inputs from retina, ventral LGN, and V1, S1, and M1 cortical areas, as well as relevant outputs to the dorsal and ventral LGN and zona incerta, without a clear match to specific input or output territories (Fig. f). Together, these analyses suggest that the characteristic shape and location of the HG compartment are not readily explained by selective vulnerability of currently defined anatomical, functional, or connectivity-based SC subregions.

To assess whether differences in microglial state at baseline could explain HG compartmentalization after CPZ, we next projected the average > 75% HG region (present in the vast majority of CPZ-treated animals) onto BigBrainWarp-aligned tissue from matched control mice and assessed P2RY12 and Clec7a expression (Figure d, e). In controls, the projected LG and HG regions showed uniform microglial tiling with consistently high P2RY12 expression and largely absent Clec7a immunoreactivity (Figure di, ei), suggesting no baseline differences in these markers and no evidence for microglial compartmentalization within healthy animals.

Because CPZ induces demyelination [, ], and our initial analyses were performed at the level of whole sSC and idSC layers, we next reanalyzed MAG and PLP immunoreactivity in HG and adjacent LG areas of CPZ-treated mice to test whether subregional differences in myelin loss might explain HG compartmentalization (Fig. a and Figures a, a). Unexpectedly, quantification of MAG (Fig. ai, Figure a) and PLP (Figure ai) revealed no differences in myelin between HG and LG within either layer, suggesting comparable myelin loss in HG vs. LG regions after CPZ. Likewise, projection of the average > 75% HG region onto BigBrainWarp-aligned control tissue showed comparable baseline myelin levels across layers and rostro-caudal planes (Figure b). Together, these findings suggest that neither baseline myelin content nor the degree of CPZ-induced demyelination is sufficient to explain the observed compartmentalized HG microgliosis module in the SC.

An emerging, underappreciated pathology in MS and MS-relevant models is the disruption of neural circuits via the loss of synaptic terminals [, , , ]. Our previous work identified early synapse loss in the dorsal LGN as a functionally relevant pathology that can precede neuroaxonal degeneration across multiple preclinical MS models []. We, therefore, immunostained adjacent SC-A, SC-C, and SC-P sections against synaptic inputs using vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGluT2) (Fig. b, Figure  b), and observed markedly reduced VGluT2+-synaptic density in HG regions (average Δ-30.1%) of both sSC and idSC compared to adjacent LG regions of the same layers in CPZ-treated mice (Fig. bi, Figure bi). These differences were not explained by pre-existing regional variation in synaptic baseline density, as projection of the > 75% HG region onto control tissue revealed comparable VGluT2+ synaptic density between projected HG and adjacent projected LG regions across layers and rostro-caudal planes (Figure c). Thus, CPZ-induced secondary synaptic injury, rather than baseline synaptic architecture or local demyelination severity per se, most closely aligned with the HG compartment across the SC (Figure d).

To further probe the relationship between compartmentalized microglial reactivity and synaptic loss, we next assessed microglia-mediated engulfment of VGluT2+ terminals (Fig. c). We co-immunolabeled microglia using P2RY12 and lysosomal marker CD68, together with VGluT2. Quantification revealed increased CD68+ phagolysosomes and a robust induction of microglial engulfment of VGluT2+ inputs in the SC of CPZ-treated mice compared to controls (Fig. ci), with VGluT2+-synapse engulfment further elevated within HG regions compared to adjacent LG areas (Fig. cii). Together, these data support a tight link between microglial reactivity and synaptic pathology that may govern the extent and spatial patterning of secondary injury subsequent to initial myelin loss.

To interrogate the dynamics of HG compartment formation, we extended CPZ treatment in a separate cohort of mice to 9 weeks (9wk) (Fig. a). Given the high consistency of HG across rostro-caudal planes in the 6-week cohort, we focused subsequent analyses on central SC planes (Figure ). After 9 weeks of CPZ, we immunolabeled microglia using P2RY12 and Clec7a (Fig. b), delineated HG regions in each animal (Fig. c), and generated overlap heatmaps (Fig. d) defining the total extension (present in ≥ 1 animal), the region present in most animals (> 75% overlap), and the core region present in all animals (100% overlap). Similar to 6 weeks, the HG compartment at 9 weeks exhibited a strikingly consistent shape and location, spanning both sSC and idSC and comprising a bulky core in the ventro-lateral-to-medial idSC with a substantial lateral-to-medial neck region extending along the dorsal sSC (Fig. c, d). Compared to 6 weeks, the 9-week cohort showed a marked expansion of the HG compartment (total extension: 1.67-fold, > 75% overlap: 2.19-fold, core: 5.23-fold) (Fig. dii), suggesting that not only the initial shape and localization of the HG compartment but also its expansion after prolonged CPZ exposure is highly stereotyped.

To validate and characterize this expansion, we projected the 6- and 9-week atlas-aligned > 75% HG masks onto 9-week tissue to distinguish newly emerged HG regions (9 weeks only), HG regions present at 6 weeks that persisted at 9 weeks (6/9-week overlap), and remaining LG tissue (Fig. e). Quantification of Clec7a (Fig. f) and P2RY12 (Fig. g) confirmed heightened microgliosis in newly emerged regions (9 weeks only) relative to LG areas, with sustained gliosis in the persistent HG compartment (6/9-week overlap). In line with HG tracking secondary synaptic pathology, VGluT2+-synaptic density was reduced by 26.28% in newly emerged HG regions compared with LG areas—similar to the average reduction observed at 6 weeks (Δ−30.1%)—whereas HG regions already present at 6 weeks and maintained through 9 weeks exhibited a larger decrease (Δ−37.13%), consistent with cumulative synaptic injury during prolonged CPZ exposure (Fig. h). To further characterize HG expansion, we generated wind plots for both brain hemispheres, comparing 9-week vs. 6-week cohorts (Fig. i, j). This analysis revealed a consistent and highly directed extension of the total HG compartment—originating from the ventro-lateral idSC core and dorsal sSC neck—predominantly toward the brain midline (Fig. k). Directionality analyses also suggested that the > 75% HG and core regions expanded preferentially medially, with additional dorsal and ventral spread, consistent with growth from a stable core rather than emergence from multiple independent foci. Of note, lateral expansion was more limited, likely constrained by the proximity of the HG compartment to the lateral SC tissue border.

Because the CPZ model is widely used to study repair after toxin withdrawal [, ], we next asked whether HG microgliosis resolves in a stereotyped manner after CPZ cessation. We treated an additional cohort of male mice with CPZ for 6 weeks, followed by 1 week of CPZ withdrawal (6 + 1 week), allowing for recovery (Fig. a). After 1 week of withdrawal, mice showed no further decline in visual acuity but also no recovery at this early repair timepoint (Fig. b). To contextualize this stabilization, we longitudinally assessed optomotor responses in an independent cohort maintained on a CPZ diet beyond 6 weeks (Figure a). In these mice, visual acuity declined progressively during continued CPZ exposure (Figure b), supporting the interpretation that early withdrawal coincides with cessation of progressive visual decline. We next immunolabeled microglia using P2RY12 and Clec7a (Fig. c), delineated HG regions for each animal (Fig. d), and generated overlap heatmaps in the recovery cohort (Fig. e) as above. Following 6 weeks of CPZ and 1 week of recovery (6 + 1 week), the HG compartment remained highly stereotyped but was largely restricted to the ventro-lateral idSC, with a persistent core and loss of the dorsal sSC neck region in all but one animal (Fig. d). Compared to 6-week CPZ, heatmaps showed a pronounced reduction in HG extent (total: Δ−36.1%; > 75% overlap: Δ−62.1%; core: Δ−25.8%; Fig. ei). Together, these data suggest that HG resolution is also spatially patterned. To validate this, we projected the 6-week and 6 + 1-week atlas-aligned > 75% HG masks onto 6 + 1-week tissue to distinguish resolved HG territory (6 weeks only) from persistent HG regions (6/6 + 1-week overlap) (Fig. f). Quantification of Clec7a and P2RY12 across the remaining HG core, adjacent peri-core regions, and distal tissue (Fig. g) revealed sustained high Clec7a and low P2RY12 in the core with graded normalization with increasing distance from the core, consistent with an “outside-in” resolution pattern of microgliosis (Fig. h). Wind-plot analyses comparing 6 + 1-week to 6-week cohorts (Fig. i, Figure c) showed robust reduction of the total and > 75% HG territories preferentially across medial and dorsal directions, whereas the core exhibited comparatively little net change and mixed local expansion and retraction (Fig. j, Figure S11d), consistent with a relative persistence of the core during early recovery.

To test whether the remaining HG core resolves with longer recovery, we treated a final male cohort of mice with 6 weeks of CPZ followed by 3 weeks of recovery (6 + 3 weeks) (Fig. k). These mice showed improved visual acuity compared to 6-week CPZ mice (Fig. l). Likewise, visual acuity partially recovered after withdrawal in the cohort maintained on a CPZ diet for 9 weeks, demonstrating that visual dysfunction retains the capacity for recovery even after prolonged toxin exposure (Figure b). We again immunolabeled microglia using P2RY12 and Clec7a (Fig. m), delineated HG regions (Fig. n), and generated overlap heatmaps (Fig. o) in the 6 + 3 cohort. As in the 6 + 1-week cohort, the residual HG compartment remained stereotyped and largely confined to the ventro-lateral idSC, persisting as a prominent core across animals (Fig. n, o). Comparison of HG extent between 6 + 3-week and 6 + 1-week cohorts revealed no further reduction in total, > 75% overlap, or core regions (Fig. oi–q). Consistently, quantification of Clec7a and P2RY12 across core, adjacent peri-core, and distal regions (Fig. r) confirmed sustained high Clec7a and low P2RY12 in the core with graded normalization with distance, suggesting persistent smoldering microgliosis centered around a stable HG core even after prolonged CPZ cessation. Together, these recovery paradigms show that early HG resolution coincides with stabilization of visual function, whereas longer withdrawal permits partial visual recovery despite persistence of the HG core in the SC.

We next asked whether this spatially patterned resolution of microgliosis was accompanied by recovery of myelin and synaptic pathology. Quantification of MAG immunoreactivity in central SC sections from 6-week CPZ, 6 + 1-week, and 6 + 3-week cohorts showed increased myelin density after CPZ withdrawal compared to 6-week CPZ, consistent with early remyelination across the SC (Figure e, ei). We then compared persistent HG regions with former high-microgliosis (fHG) regions after 1 and 3 weeks of recovery to determine whether tissue exiting the HG state showed differential recovery. fHG regions were defined as atlas-aligned territories included in the 6-week CPZ–HG compartment that no longer met HG criteria based on Clec7a/P2RY12 mapping after recovery. MAG immunoreactivity did not differ between HG and fHG regions at either recovery time point (Fig. s, si and Figure f, fi), suggesting comparable local myelin density after withdrawal-induced remyelination. In contrast, VGluT2+ synaptic density was significantly higher in former HG regions compared with persistent HG regions after both 1 and 3 weeks of recovery, with average increases of 12.1% and 19.6%, respectively (Fig. t, ti and Figure g, gi). Thus, CPZ withdrawal was associated with early SC remyelination, while spatial resolution of high-microgliosis identity was more closely associated with recovery of synaptic pathology than with regional differences in local myelin density.

Because sex-dependent differences in CPZ pathology and microglial responses have been reported [, , ], we finally asked whether HG compartment formation in the SC was conserved in female mice. 8-week-old female C57BL/6 J mice were treated with the same 6-week CPZ paradigm used for the male cohort and analyzed using the same spatial mapping workflow (Fig. a). CPZ-treated females showed mild body-weight reduction (Fig. b) and significant visual impairment by optomotor testing (Fig. c). In the corpus callosum (CC), a canonical CPZ-affected region, MAG and Clec7a quantification showed no detectable difference in CC demyelination or microgliosis between female and male CPZ-treated mice (Fig. d, e), indicating similar overall CPZ responsiveness across sexes, which is in line with published data in the CC [, ]. We next assessed whether microgliosis was similarly organized within the SC of the same mice. Female CPZ-treated mice showed widespread SC demyelination and broad microglial reactivity (Fig. f, g). However, unlike males, females did not develop a highly stereotyped HG compartment; instead, areas of elevated microgliosis were small, sparse, and variable across animals (Fig. h, i). Atlas-aligned overlap analysis confirmed markedly reduced spatial convergence of areas of elevated microgliosis in females compared to males, including a near absence of > 75% overlap territory (reduced by 56.1-fold compared to males, Fig. h–j). Given the small size of elevated-microgliosis regions, regional analyses were limited; nevertheless, MAG immunoreactivity and VGluT2+ synaptic density did not differ between elevated- and low-microgliosis regions in females (Fig. k–l). Together, these findings reveal sex-dependent spatial organization of the glial response to CPZ, with a distinct synapse-associated HG compartment emerging predominantly in the male SC.

Here, we identify the human SC as an MS-relevant site of gray matter injury by showing that it can harbor demyelination in MS, including focal lesions, thereby extending MS visual system pathology to an understudied visual and visuomotor hub [, , , ]. Although the small human cohort precludes conclusions about prevalence or clinical significance and does not establish whether the CPZ-defined high-microgliosis compartment and its synaptic and sex-dependent features are present in human MS, the human findings motivated spatially resolved characterization of the SC in the CPZ model. In male mice, we identified a highly reproducible high-microgliosis module that exhibited stereotyped expansion and incomplete resolution without conforming to established anatomical, functional, or connectivity-based SC maps. During recovery, former HG territories showed partial restoration of synaptic density, whereas persistent HG regions retained greater synaptic pathology despite comparable local myelin recovery. By contrast, female mice developed diffuse SC demyelination and microgliosis without comparable compartmentalization, indicating that the spatial organization of microglial reactivity differs by sex under the conditions tested. The CPZ-treated SC, therefore, provides a tractable in vivo framework for investigating how biological context, local tissue cues, and cellular interactions regulate the induction, propagation, persistence, and resolution of spatially organized microglial reactivity and secondary circuit injury.

The CPZ paradigm provides a controlled system to dissect CNS-intrinsic cellular responses and secondary pathology following demyelinating injury [, ]. Consistent with extensive CPZ literature showing robust and temporally defined demyelination across white and gray matter regions, including the corpus callosum, cortex, hippocampus, and subcortical sensory networks [, , , , , , , ], we found widespread SC demyelination across superficial and intermediate/deep layers and along the rostro-caudal axis. These findings extend the spatial map of CPZ pathology to the SC and indicate that it is broadly susceptible to CPZ-induced myelin loss. Consistent with the oligodendrocyte-targeted nature of CPZ toxicity and similar to other brain regions [, ], SC demyelination occurred without detectable reductions in neuronal and axonal densities or evidence of increased apoptotic cells or axonal pathology. Although these data support preservation of overt neuroaxonal integrity, they do not exclude more subtle forms of axon–myelin unit dysfunction. For instance, the observed reduction in CASPR-positive paranodes indicates disruption of paranodal organization, which may impair conduction or axon–glia interactions even in the absence of detectable axonal loss []. Moreover, APP immunostaining detects only a subset of axonal transport disturbances and may not capture milder transport defects, mitochondrial dysfunction, or ultrastructural injury [, , , ]. The persistence of synaptic pathology and HG microgliosis without APP-positive axonal pathology, therefore, suggests that synaptic injury and microglial reactivity can occur before, or independently of, overt axonal stress detectable using the markers applied here.

Functionally, we identified impaired optomotor response in CPZ-treated mice, followed by stabilization and partial recovery after CPZ withdrawal. Prior studies using acute dLGN slice recordings and visual evoked potentials have shown that CPZ disrupts visual system function, including impaired subcortical visual circuit activity, delayed visual conduction, and reduced visual evoked potential amplitudes during demyelination and recovery [, , , , ]. Our findings extend this work by demonstrating impairment of the optomotor response, a non-invasive, training-free behavioral measure of visual function []. Longitudinal analysis of an independent cohort showed progressive optomotor response decline during 9 weeks of continued CPZ exposure and partial recovery after subsequent withdrawal. Considered together, the recovery paradigms indicate that early partial HG resolution coincides with stabilization of visual function, whereas longer withdrawal permits partial optomotor response recovery despite persistence of the HG core in the SC. However, this temporal association does not establish that HG resolution in the SC directly drives functional recovery, because the optomotor response depends on distributed visual-motion and visuomotor pathways, including the accessory optic system and downstream motor circuits [, , , ]. Optomotor response testing, therefore, serves as a useful behavioral complement to electrophysiological readouts of integrated visual and visuomotor dysfunction in CPZ-treated mice rather than a region-specific functional measure.

In line with the well-established microglial response to CPZ-induced demyelination [, ], diffuse myelin loss was accompanied by widespread microgliosis across SC layers and rostro-caudal planes, reflected by markedly reduced P2RY12, increased Clec7a immunoreactivity, and induction of pro-inflammatory cytokine transcripts. Unexpectedly, heightened reactivity within this broad response organized into a stereotyped HG compartment that occupied a consistent location in all male CPZ-treated mice and spanned portions of both superficial and intermediate/deep SC layers. Atlas-aligned overlap heatmap projections of HG regions onto established SC maps showed no clear correspondence with canonical anatomical, functional, or input–output maps [, , ]. Baseline projection analyses also did not reveal pre-existing differences in the microglial markers, and HG vs. adjacent LG regions showed comparable myelin densities after CPZ. Together, these findings argue that HG compartmentalization is not readily explained by baseline microglial marker heterogeneity, local myelin architecture, or demyelination severity alone. Instead, it appears to represent a reproducible spatial module of heightened microglial reactivity shaped by the disease-induced local tissue context.

Consistent with this interpretation, a defining feature of the HG compartment was its association with synaptic pathology. While myelin measures were comparable between HG and adjacent LG regions, VGluT2+ synaptic density was markedly reduced within HG territories, with more pronounced loss in persistent HG regions during prolonged CPZ treatment. CPZ also increased CD68+ phagolysosomal content and enhanced engulfment of VGluT2+ synaptic material, with engulfment further elevated in HG regions. In line with previous findings [, , , , , , , ], these results extend evidence that synaptic pathology can emerge early in MS-relevant settings and may contribute to circuit dysfunction before overt neuroaxonal loss. However, the present data do not establish whether microglial reactivity causes synaptic loss, whether synaptic injury enhances microglial reactivity, or whether both reflect a shared upstream cue independent of the degree of demyelination. Rather, they identify a tight spatial coupling between microglial reactivity and synaptic injury within a reproducible gray matter compartment. To our knowledge, such a spatially discrete microgliosis module not explained by local demyelination severity has not previously been described in the CPZ model.

VGluT2 labels a prominent excitatory synaptic population in retinorecipient visual circuits, including RGC and other subcortical glutamatergic inputs, and provides continuity with prior LGN work identifying early VGluT2+ RGC-associated synapse loss in MS-relevant models [, , , ]. Given the dense retinal and subcortical excitatory input to the mouse SC, VGluT2 provides a biologically meaningful readout of excitatory synaptic integrity in this structure [, , ]. However, VGluT2 does not capture the full diversity of SC synapses, including VGluT1+ corticocollicular inputs, inhibitory synapses, or neuromodulatory terminals [, , ]. Thus, the present data demonstrate HG-associated loss of VGluT2+ excitatory terminals but neither establish nor exclude broader synaptic remodeling. Such remodeling remains plausible given evidence of diverse synaptic alterations in MS and MS-relevant models [, , , , , ]. Additional synaptic markers, circuit tracing, and functional studies will be required to define the synaptic specificity of HG-associated pathology.

Beyond these local mechanisms, pathology propagated through connected circuits may also contribute to the spatial organization of microgliosis. Recent work has shown that focal demyelination of projecting axons can induce retrograde microglial reactivity, synaptic engulfment, and transient synapse loss in connected gray matter, with resolution linked to remyelination []. In this study, however, the HG compartment did not clearly correspond to any single established SC connection and extended beyond its ventro-lateral core into superficial layers and additional territories during prolonged CPZ exposure. Moreover, persistent and former HG regions showed comparable local myelin recovery but differed in synaptic density, although this does not exclude demyelination or remyelination elsewhere along connected projections. Thus, connectivity-dependent signaling may contribute to HG formation without fully explaining its spatial organization and dynamics. Together, these studies suggest complementary levels of pathological organization; projection injury may induce secondary pathology in connected gray matter, while local synaptic, glial, and tissue-specific cues may further pattern that response. Direct circuit tracing and pathway-specific perturbation will be required to define the contributions of individual SC inputs and outputs.

The temporal behavior of the HG compartment further supports its interpretation as a microgliosis module with stereotyped dynamics. With prolonged CPZ exposure, HG regions expanded reproducibly from a stable ventro-lateral core into adjacent territories rather than appearing as independent reactive foci. After CPZ withdrawal, HG regions partially retracted in a spatially ordered manner, with apparent normalization beginning at the periphery, while a residual core persisted. Overall SC MAG density increased after CPZ withdrawal, consistent with remyelination across the SC. However, persistent HG and former high-microgliosis regions showed comparable myelin density at both 1 and 3 weeks of recovery, whereas VGluT2+ synaptic density was significantly higher in former HG regions than in persistent HG regions. This increase was evident after 1 week and became more pronounced after 3 weeks of recovery. These findings are consistent with partial restoration of synaptic density in territories that exited the HG state and support the idea that persistent HG regions represent microenvironments in which microglial reactivity and synaptic pathology remain coupled. However, whether the increase in VGluT2 density reflects functional synaptic restoration remains to be determined.

The female cohort further demonstrates that stereotyped HG compartmentalization is not an inevitable consequence of CPZ-induced demyelination or diffuse microgliosis. Despite widespread SC demyelination and microglial reactivity, female mice showed sparse, spatially variable areas of heightened microgliosis without the synapse-associated organization observed in males. Thus, under the conditions tested, HG compartmentalization represents a sex-differential rather than universal response to CPZ-induced demyelination. Comparable corpus callosum pathology supports overall CPZ responsiveness in both sexes, although variation in toxin metabolism, injury kinetics, or SC-specific tissue responses cannot be excluded. The mechanisms underlying this difference remain unknown but may involve sex-dependent differences in microglial state, hormonal context, or local tissue responses to demyelination [, , , , , ]. Studies across additional ages, strains, and demyelinating models will be needed to determine the generality of the phenotype, while spatial profiling of male and female SC tissue may help identify factors that permit or restrict HG formation.

Although the persistent core should not be directly equated with chronic active MS lesions [, ], its reproducibility provides a tractable system for studying CNS-intrinsic mechanisms of microglial propagation and incomplete resolution [, , , ]. The proximity of HG and LG territories enables spatially controlled comparisons of local synaptic, glial, inflammatory, and tissue-specific cues. This is of particular interest, because microglial reactive states are believed to arise from the integration of heterogeneous local molecular cues and cellular interactions, yet their spatiotemporal distribution in most models can vary markedly across animals and even within a single brain region, making where and when they occur difficult to predict and complicating in situ mechanistic dissection. The clear association with VGluT2+ synaptic loss and recovery suggests that local synaptic activity, terminal-specific vulnerability, or synaptic tagging pathways may help define HG territories [, , , , , , , ]. Astrocyte–microglia interactions, localized inflammatory cues, cellular stress, myelin debris handling, and extracellular matrix alterations may also shape regional susceptibility and persistence [, , , , , , ]. Future studies using the CPZ-treated SC to compare HG and LG regions through spatial transcriptomics or proteomics, circuit tracing, and targeted microglial perturbation should help identify factors governing HG induction, expansion, persistence, and resolution. Moreover, because the HG compartment extends into superficial SC layers, posterior cranial-window approaches could enable longitudinal comparisons of microglial behavior, synaptic remodeling, and circuit integrity across adjacent HG and LG microenvironments without tissue aspiration or penetrating lens implantation [, , ]. As a laminated midbrain structure, the SC offers a distinct neuroanatomical context from the more commonly investigated neocortex, complementing deep imaging studies of cortical pathology in MS.

Several limitations should be considered. First, although the CPZ model is useful for studying CNS-intrinsic demyelination, microglial reactivity, and repair, it does not reproduce the full autoimmune and peripheral immune complexity of MS. Thus, the HG compartment should be interpreted as a model of spatially organized microglial reactivity after demyelinating injury rather than as a direct equivalent of chronic active MS lesions. Second, microglial characterization remains marker-based and supports inflammatory features of the HG compartment, but does not define the full molecular diversity of HG and LG microglia. Third, our neuroaxonal and synaptic analyses exclude overt neuroaxonal loss and identify loss of a major excitatory synaptic population, but do not rule out subtler axon–myelin unit dysfunction, ultrastructural damage, or alterations in other synaptic classes. Fourth, the mechanisms underlying the sex-dependent organization of microgliosis remain unresolved. Finally, the human postmortem cohort lacks detailed clinical, treatment, lesion stage, and functional visual data. Accordingly, these data show that the SC can be affected by demyelinating pathology in MS, but do not establish prevalence, clinical significance, or whether human microglial/synaptic patterns in the SC resemble the CPZ-defined HG module. Future spatial transcriptomic, proteomic, ultrastructural, and functional studies will be required to define HG-associated molecular states, cellular interactions, and consequences.

Together, these findings establish the SC as an MS-relevant structure and identify, in male CPZ-treated mice, a previously unrecognized, spatially stereotyped module of microglial reactivity within a defined visual circuit. The HG compartment tracks synaptic pathology rather than local demyelination severity and exhibits reproducible expansion and incomplete resolution. Former HG territories showed partial restoration of synaptic density, whereas persistent HG regions retained greater synaptic pathology despite comparable local myelin recovery. Conversely, female mice developed widespread SC demyelination and microgliosis without comparable compartmentalization, indicating that HG organization differs by sex under the tested conditions rather than being an inevitable consequence of demyelination. By enabling spatially precise comparisons of regions that differ in microglial reactivity, synaptic integrity, and recovery dynamics within the same circuit, this model provides a platform to define how local cues and cellular interactions govern the induction, propagation, persistence, and incomplete resolution of microglial reactivity. More broadly, the mouse data support the concept that spatially organized microglia–synapse interactions may shape early secondary circuit injury and offer insight into persistent innate immune mechanisms with potential relevance to MS and related neurodegenerative diseases.
