medicine.title: Pericyte PDGFR‐β deficiency contributes to Aβ pathology through impaired glymphatic transport and altered AQP‐4 localization
medicine.abstract: Pericyte platelet‐derived growth factor receptor‐β (PDGFR‐β) signaling maintains neurovascular integrity, but its role in glymphatic function is unknown. We investigated whether pericyte PDGFR‐β deficiency is associated with glymphatic dysfunction and altered aquaporin‐4 (AQP‐4) localization in Alzheimer's disease (AD).Glymphatic trafficking was assessed by fluorescent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tracer injection. Meningeal lymphatic drainage was blocked by deep cervical lymph node (dcLN) ligation. Pericyte coverage, AQP‐4 expression/localization, and basement membrane components were analyzed by immunofluorescence and western blot. Pericyte‐conditioned medium was used to examine the effects of pericyte‐derived factors on astrocytic AQP‐4. The AQP‐4 facilitator TGN‐073 was administered to assess functional rescue. Blood–brain barrier integrity, microvascular density, and cerebral blood flow were also evaluated.DcLN ligation impaired amyloid beta clearance and spatial memory. Both APP/PS1 and Pdgfr‐β+/− mice exhibited pericyte loss and glymphatic dysfunction, with Pdgfr‐β+/− mice additionally showing reduced perivascular AQP‐4 expression, accompanied by decreased laminin‐α2/β1. In vitro, pericyte‐derived factors promoted AQP‐4 expression. TGN‐073 partially improved small‐molecule CSF tracer distribution in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice. Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice displayed exacerbated AD‐like pathology.PDGFR‐β deficiency compromises basement membrane integrity and AQP‐4 localization, impairing glymphatic transport and accelerating AD pathogenesis. The PDGFR‐β pathway may represent a novel therapeutic target for enhancing waste clearance.
medicine.text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the accumulation of amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain.,  The clearance of Aβ from the brain is a critical process in maintaining brain homeostasis and preventing the development of AD pathology.  The glymphatic system, a brain‐wide paravascular pathway, has emerged as a key player in the clearance of interstitial solutes, including Aβ. The system relies on the regulation of aquaporin‐4 (AQP‐4) channels in astrocytes.

Pericytes are mural cells that wrap around capillaries and contribute to the regulation of cerebrovascular function.  Pericytes secrete extracellular matrix components, such as laminin and fibronectin, which help to stabilize the vascular basement membrane and provide structural support to the endothelial cells. ,  These extracellular matrix components also influence the distribution and function of AQP‐4 channels in astrocytes. , ,  AQP‐4 is predominantly localized to the endfeet of astrocytes that surround blood vessels, forming a continuous and functional interface with the perivascular space.  This strategic localization of AQP‐4 facilitates the efficient exchange of water and solutes between the interstitial fluid and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which is essential for the proper functioning of the glymphatic system. ,

Platelet‐derived growth factor receptor‐β (PDGFR‐β) is a key receptor involved in pericyte survival and function.  Deficiency or dysfunction of PDGFR‐β has been shown to lead to pericyte loss.  In this study, we investigated the effects of pericyte PDGFR‐β deficiency on glymphatic function and Aβ pathology in a mouse model of AD. We hypothesized that loss of PDGFR‐β in pericytes is associated with impaired glymphatic clearance and exacerbated Aβ pathology, potentially involving changes in AQP‐4 localization. To test this hypothesis, we used APP/PS1 transgenic mice, which develop Aβ deposition and cognitive deficits, and Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, which exhibit reduced pericyte coverage due to PDGFR‐β haploinsufficiency. In these models, we evaluated glymphatic function, pericyte coverage, AQP‐4 expression, and Aβ pathology. Our results provide new insights into the contributions of pericytes and PDGFR‐β signaling to AD pathogenesis.

The APP/PS1 mice used in the experiment were purchased from Nanjing Institute of Biomedicine (Cat# N000175), and Pdgfr‐β+/− mice were purchased from Cyagen biosciences (KOCMS210421RT3). The APP/PS1 mice were crossed to the Pdgfr‐β+/− to generate the wild type, Pdgfr‐β+/−, APP/PS1, and Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice used in the present study. The genotype of the mice was identified at 1 month of age, after which they were housed separately (with a maximum of four littermates per cage), with only male mice included in the experiment. The mice were bred and housed in an animal facility, maintained in air‐conditioned rooms at 20°C to 22°C with a light period of 12 hours. This study was conducted in accordance with the recommendations for the ethical treatment of laboratory animals of the Ministry of Science and Technology of the People's Republic of China. All animal experiments were approved by the experimental animal ethics committee of Lanzhou University.

For glymphatic system assessment, APP/PS1 mice were administered a 3% solution of Cascade Blue–conjugated dextran (3 kDa, Thermo Fisher Scientific, D7132) into the striatum, lateral ventricle (LV), and cisterna magna (CM). In contrast, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice received a mixture of 2.5% tetramethylrhodamine (TMR)–conjugated dextran (70 kDa, Thermo Fisher Scientific, D1818) and FAM‐labeled human β‐amyloid (1–42) (4.8 kDa, QyaoBio) into the hippocampus, LV, and CM. For two‐photon detection, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice received 2.5% TMR‐conjugated dextran (70 kDa, Thermo Fisher Scientific, D1818) or TMR‐conjugated dextran (3 kDa, Thermo Fisher Scientific, D3308) into the CM.

The Cascade Blue–conjugated dextran and 3‐kDa dextran were selected to track bulk CSF flow and small‐molecule clearance, whereas the 70 kDa was used to assess macromolecular transport. The FAM–Aβ1
−
42 was used to directly monitor Aβ peptide clearance. , , ,

Intrahippocampal injections targeted the dentate gyrus (DG) region (coordinates: 2 mm lateral, −2.16 mm posterior, −2 mm ventral relative to bregma). Intrastriatal injections were aimed at the caudate putamen (coordinates: 2.8 mm lateral, −0.6 mm posterior, −3.5 mm ventral relative to bregma). Intraventricular injections were targeted to the right LV (coordinates: 1.2 mm lateral, −0.5 mm posterior, −2.5 mm ventral relative to bregma). Anesthetized mice were mounted in a stereotaxic frame, and fur was removed from the skin above the skull using depilatory cream. A midline incision was made to expose the skull. A small burr hole was drilled at the specified medial/lateral and anterior/posterior bregma coordinates using a stereotax‐mounted drill. The drill was then replaced with a 10 µl Hamilton syringe fitted with a glass micropipette, which was loaded into a syringe pump and backfilled with fluorescently labeled dextran or a dextran/hAβ(1–42) mixture. The needle tip was slowly lowered through the burr hole into the brain tissue until it reached the target depth. The needle was left in place for 5 minutes prior to the start of infusion. Infusions were performed for 5 minutes, with a final volume of 1 µl for the hippocampus and striatum (0.2 µL/min), and 2 µl for the LV (0.4 µL/min). The needle was left in place for an additional 5 minutes after the infusion to minimize diffusion of the tracer along the needle track. After 60 minutes, transcardiac perfusion with formaldehyde was performed under anesthesia, and brain tissues and deep cervical lymph nodes were collected.

Tracer infusions were performed as previously described. ,  Briefly, a 30‐gauge needle was connected to a 10‐µl Hamilton syringe via PE‐10 tubing. The tubing was first filled with mineral oil and then backfilled with the tracer solution immediately prior to injection. Mice were anesthetized and head‐fixed in a stereotactic frame, with the neck skin depilated using a depilatory cream. An incision was made along the midline of the neck muscles to expose the atlanto‐occipital membrane covering the CM. The mouse head was positioned at a 120‐degree angle to its body. The needle was inserted into the CM until the bevel of the needle tip passed through the atlanto‐occipital membrane, and then secured with tissue adhesive. The tracer was infused into the CM at a rate of 1 µl/minute for 5 minutes, resulting in a total volume of 5 µl (1 µL/minute). After successful injection, the syringe was removed but the tubing connected to the needle was left in place to prevent tracer leakage along the needle track. After 60 minutes, transcardiac perfusion with formaldehyde was performed under anesthesia, and brain tissues and deep cervical lymph nodes were collected.

The dynamics of CSF tracers within the brain were visualized through a cranial window using an advanced two‐photon laser scanning microscope (Nikon AX R MP). The cranial window surgery was performed 3 days before the imaging to allow for recovery. A 4 mm diameter craniotomy was precisely executed over the prefrontal cortex, located 1.0 mm lateral and 1.0 mm posterior to the bregmatic point, with careful attention to prevent dural rupture. After the craniotomy, the dura was coated with artificial CSF and sealed with a 3 mm diameter glass coverslip. Custom metal head‐fixation plates were then attached to the mice's skulls to ensure stable imaging conditions. Prior to the imaging session, a CM cannulation was carried out. Subsequently, 5 µL of a CSF tracer was administered to the mice. To visualize the vascular system, 0.1 mL of a blood–brain barrier (BBB)‐impermeable fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)–dextran solution (with a molecular weight of 2000 kDa; 1% in saline, FD2000s, Sigma‐Aldrich) was injected via the retro‐orbital vein. Imaging of the cortical layers was conducted from the pial surface to a depth of ≈ 65 µm using a 25 × objective lens with a numerical aperture (NA) of 1.05 and water immersion. For exciting the fluorescent tracers, two lasers were used: a Chameleon Discovery NX (Coherent), which was tuned to 1040 nm for the Texas Red (TMR) tracer, and 980 nm for the FITC dye. Emission filters were selected to capture signals within the 604 to 650 nm range for Texas Red and 495 to 540 nm for FITC. Dual‐channel acquisition was used, with one channel tracking the tracer movement (TMR) and the other visualizing the vascular system (FITC), both at a pixel resolution of 512 × 512 for high‐definition imaging. The cortex was scanned in a stepwise manner, with 2 µm increments in the z axis, from the surface to 65 µm below, at 10‐minute intervals throughout the experiment. Image analysis was performed post‐acquisition using Image J software.

For quantitative analysis, autofluorescence was removed from each animal by subtracting the signal at 0 minutes, and background subtraction was performed on the images. Uniform thresholding was applied using Image J, and the mean fluorescence intensity over time after thresholding was calculated. The fluorescence intensity of the supra‐threshold pixels within the entire field of view (prefrontal cortex) was calculated.

For APP/PS1 mice, Cascade Blue–conjugated dextran was injected into the striatum, LV, and CM. After transcardial perfusion and fixation, 25‐µm thick coronal sections were prepared. Sections were imaged using an Olympus BX53 fluorescence microscope. Regions of interest (ROIs) including the cortex, hippocampus, and striatum were defined based on Nissl staining. Using Image J software, the tracer‐specific color channel was background subtracted by measuring the mean fluorescence intensity in an ROI placed outside the tissue section, followed by uniform thresholding. The fluorescence intensity within each ROI was then calculated. Three sections containing the hippocampus and cortex (−1.50 to −2.50 mm relative to bregma) and three sections containing the striatum (0.00 to −1.00 mm relative to bregma) were imaged per animal, and the fluorescence intensity was averaged across these sections.

For Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, TMR‐labeled 70 kDa dextran and FAM‐Aβ1
−
42 were co‐injected into the hippocampus, LV, and CM or TMR‐labeled 30 kDa/70 kDa dextran were injected into the CM. After perfusion and fixation, 25‐µm coronal sections were prepared. Nuclei were stained with 4′,6‐diamidino‐2‐phenylindole (DAPI). Whole‐section images were acquired using a PanoBrain slide scanner (Meca Scientific) and stitched. ROIs covering the entire section, cortex, and hippocampal subregions (DG and CA1) were delineated based on the DAPI channel. To assess tracer coverage, the color channel corresponding to the tracer was separated in Image J, background subtracted using an ROI outside the tissue section, uniformly thresholded, and the mean fluorescence intensity was measured. For hippocampus injection, 10 sections evenly distributed between +0.00 mm and −3.15 mm relative to bregma were selected per animal and averaged. For LV and CM injection, 10 sections between +1.00 mm and −6.00 mm relative to bregma were averaged. For TGN‐073 treatment, three hippocampal sections (−1.50 to −2.50 mm relative to bregma) and three lateral ventricle sections (+1.00 to −0.00 mm relative to bregma) were imaged per animal, and the mean values were averaged.

Brain tissues collected from mice were immediately fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde solution (4% PA). The tissues were then immersed in a 20% sucrose solution for 72 hours, followed by transfer to a 40% sucrose solution for an additional 72 hours. Subsequently, the tissues were embedded and frozen in Optimal Cutting Temperature (O.C.T.) compound. Sections of 25 mm thickness were generated using low‐profile blades on a Thermo Scientific Cryotome E cryostat. For immunostaining, all samples were processed, sectioned, stained, imaged, and analyzed together under the same conditions and settings to ensure consistency. Brain sections were permeabilized and blocked in 10% donkey serum (in 0.3% Triton X‐100) at room temperature (RT) for 1 hour. The sections were then incubated with primary antibodies diluted in 1% donkey serum in phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS) for 1 hour at RT (Table ) followed by overnight incubation at 4°C. After primary antibody incubation, sections were washed three times with PBS and incubated with appropriate secondary antibodies (Table ) for 1 hour at RT. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. Finally, cover slips were sealed with 30% glycerin.

Antibody table.

Abbreviations: IF, immunofluorescence; WB, western blot.

To quantitatively evaluate perivascular AQP‐4 polarization, three complementary image analyses were performed on immunofluorescence images of brain sections stained for AQP‐4, the endothelial marker CD31, and DAPI. Confocal images were acquired under identical acquisition settings (Zeiss, LSM 900).

Perivascular ROIs were manually delineated within 5 µm from the vessel wall, whereas parenchymal ROIs were defined as adjacent areas located > 10 µm away from any visible vessel. The mean AQP‐4 fluorescence intensity was measured in each ROI, representing perivascular and parenchymal AQP‐4 expression, respectively. The AQP‐4 polarization index was calculated as the ratio of perivascular to parenchymal AQP‐4 fluorescence intensity.

A straight line was randomly drawn perpendicular to the vessel wall, and AQP‐4 fluorescence intensity was recorded from the vessel wall outward to a distance of 40 µm. The resulting fluorescence intensity–distance curves were plotted to compare the spatial distribution of AQP‐4 around the vasculature.

The Pearson correlation coefficient between AQP‐4 and CD31 signals was calculated using the Coloc2 plugin in ImageJ to assess the degree of AQP‐4 association with cerebral vessels.

Mice were anesthetized and secured on the operating table in a supine position. The neck skin was shaved and disinfected with iodine tincture. A longitudinal incision was made from the mandible to the sternum using a surgical blade. Under a dissecting microscope, the muscles and fascia were carefully separated along the trachea using blunt forceps. The deep cervical lymph nodes (dcLNs) are located beneath the sternothyroid muscle. The afferent and efferent vessels of the bilateral dcLNs were ligated with 8‐0 nylon sutures, and the skin was sutured. In the sham group, mice underwent only the exposure surgery of the bilateral dcLNs without any ligation. After recovery from anesthesia, the animals were returned to their cages and fed for 1 week, followed by the Aβ injection experiment.

Lyophilized Aβ1–42 (China Peptides) was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and then diluted in PBS (pH 7.4) to achieve a final concentration of 0.5 mM. The Aβ1–42 peptides were incubated with PBS at 4°C for 24 hours and subsequently stored in aliquots at −80°C to prepare the oligomer solution. For intracerebral injection, 1 µl of Aβ1–42 solution (500 µM) was injected into the DG of the hippocampus of 4‐month‐old c57bl/6 mice. Briefly, the mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and secured in a stereotactic frame with a mouse adaptor. A small burr hole was drilled in the skull, and the Aβ1‐42 solution was injected into the DG (coordinates: 2 mm lateral, −2.16 mm posterior, −2 mm ventral relative to bregma) using a glass capillary with an outer diameter of ≈ 70 µm mounted on a 5 µl Hamilton syringe. The injection was performed in 0.2 µl increments over 1‐minute intervals, followed by a 5‐minute waiting period before removing the needle to allow for adequate dispersion of the Aβ1–42. The vehicle‐operated group was subjected to identical surgery and injected with the vehicle. Behavioral experiments were conducted 2 months after Aβ1–42 injection. After the completion of the behavioral tests, brain tissues were collected.

To prepare mouse brain vascular pericyte‐conditioned medium (MBVP‐CM), MBVP pericytes were cultured to ≈ 80% confluence. The culture medium was then replaced with serum‐free medium (SFM). After 48 hours of incubation, the conditioned medium was collected and centrifuged at 2000 × g for 5 minutes to remove cellular debris. The supernatant was mixed with fresh SFM at a 1:1 ratio to obtain MBVP‐CM. The medium was used immediately or stored at −80°C for subsequent use. HA1800 astrocytes were seeded in 24‐well plates and cultured until reaching 80% confluence. After 24 hours, the medium was replaced with SFM or MBVP‐CM. After 24 hours of incubation, HA1800 cells were fixed with 4% PA and subjected to immunofluorescence staining for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, an astrocytic marker) and AQP‐4. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. Fluorescence images were acquired using a confocal microscope (Zeiss, LSM 900). The mean fluorescence intensities of GFAP and AQP‐4 were quantified by Image J. All experiments were performed in at least three independent replicates.

The open‐field test was conducted in a white box measuring 50 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm. The central area was defined as a 16.7 cm × 16.7 cm square. Each mouse's movement within the box was recorded for 5 minutes. Parameters such as moving time, moving distance, freezing time, and time spent in the center were analyzed using a video tracking system (TM‐vision, Chengdu Techman Software Company, Limited).

The novel object recognition (NOR) test was performed to assess object discrimination and spatial memory. Mice were habituated to the testing environment (45 cm length × 30 cm width × 20 cm height) for 10 minutes on three consecutive trials, with 60‐minute intertrial intervals. The testing procedure consisted of three sessions, each separated by a 60‐minute intertrial interval. In the sample phases 1 and 2 (10 minutes each), two identical cubes were presented. In the retrieval phase (10 minutes), one cube (the “remote” object) and one cylinder (the “recent” object) were presented. The discrimination index (DI) was calculated as follows: DI = 100% × time spent with the remote object/total time spent with both objects.

For the Morris water maze (MWM) text, a white circular pool with a diameter of 150 cm and a depth of 50 cm was used (TM‐vision, Chengdu Techman Software Company, Limited). The pool was divided into four quadrants. Water was added to submerge the platform 1 cm below the surface, and the water temperature was maintained at RT (22°C). Non‐toxic, white, powdered tempera paint was added to the water and mixed thoroughly to obscure the submerged platform from view. Four distinct flags were placed around the pool to enhance visibility. Mice were transferred from their housing facility to the behavior room and allowed to acclimate for at least 30 minutes before testing. For each trial, the mouse was gently placed into the water facing the edge of the pool. If the mouse found the platform within the 60‐second cutoff, it was allowed to remain on the platform for 5 seconds before being returned to its home cage. If the mouse failed to find the platform, it was placed on the platform for 20 seconds before being returned to its home cage. Path length, escape latency, and time spent in each quadrant were tracked. Each mouse underwent four trials per day for seven consecutive days. On day 8, the platform was removed, and path length, number of platform crossings, and time spent in the platform quadrant were recorded for each mouse.

Tissue extracts were prepared using radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer. After electrophoresis, proteins were transferred onto a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane (Immobilon‐P membrane, Millipore) at 120 volts for 1 hour. The membrane was blocked with 5% skim milk in Tris‐buffered saline with Tween 20 (TBST) for 1 hour at RT. The membrane was then incubated with primary antibodies diluted in 5% skim milk in TBST overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with appropriate secondary antibodies (Table ) for 1 hour at RT. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence assay kit (Chemiluminescent HRP substrate, Millipore). Data were analyzed using ImageJ software.

Brain slices containing the dorsal hippocampus were selected based on the mouse brain atlas and mounted on slides. The slices were stained with a 0.5% solution of methanol Congo red (Sigma, C6277) for 20 minutes, followed by differentiation in alkaline ethanol (2% potassium hydroxide dissolved in 80% ethanol) for 10 seconds. The slices underwent gradual dehydration with alcohol, clearing with xylene, and sealing with neutral gum.

BBB integrity was assessed by Evans blue extravasation and immunoglobulin G (IgG) immunostaining.

Mice were injected with 3% Evans Blue (Solarbio, IE0280) via the tail vein at 4 µL/g body weight. One hour later, mice were anesthetized and transcardially perfused with saline at a flow rate of 10 mL/min for 5 minutes. After decapitation, brains were removed. The tissues were homogenized in DMSO at 100 mg/mL, incubated at 60°C for 24 hours, and centrifuged at 1740 g for 10 minutes at 4°C. The fluorescence of the supernatant was measured using a spectrophotometer (excitation 620 nm; emission 680 nm). Evans Blue content was expressed as fluorescence intensity per milligram of tissue.

Brain sections containing the hippocampus were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 20 minutes at RT, washed three times with PBS, and then incubated with Cy3‐conjugated goat anti‐mouse IgG for 2 hours at 37°C. After three washes with PBS, blood vessels were labeled with CD31. Sections were counterstained with DAPI (Sigma‐Aldrich, D9542) for 10 minutes, mounted with an anti‐fade medium, and coverslipped. Images were captured using a confocal microscope (Zeiss, LSM 900).

Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and head fixed on a stereotaxic frame. The skull was exposed, and the bone over the right primary somatosensory cortex barrel field (S1BF; 3 mm lateral from the midline) was thinned using a drill. A laser Doppler flowmetry probe was placed over the barrel cortex, with two measurement points per animal ≈ 0.5 mm apart; the values were averaged for statistical analysis. Cerebral blood flow (CBF) was measured using a laser Doppler system (Perimed, PF6000), and data were recorded.

Data analyses and graph generation were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.5.1 software. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Differences between two groups were analyzed using unpaired Student t tests, whereas differences among three groups were assessed using one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For comparisons involving two independent variables, two‐way ANOVA was used. Non‐parametric tests were applied when data did not exhibit a normal distribution. All statistical tests were two sided, and a P value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The glymphatic system drains metabolic waste products, including Aβ, from the CSF to the cervical lymph nodes via meningeal lymphatic vessels, thereby accomplishing central nervous system waste clearance.  To evaluate whether blocking cerebral lymphatic drainage by bilateral dcLN ligation impairs brain Aβ elimination and cognitive performance, we ligated the dcLNs of 4‐month‐old C57BL/6J mice and injected oligomeric Aβ1–42 into the DG. Cognitive and memory functions were assessed 2 months later using the MWM and NOR tests (Figure ). MWM data showed that escape latencies progressively decreased across training days in all groups, suggesting successful acquisition of the hidden‐platform location (Figure ). From day 5 onward, however, Sham‐Aβ animals that received intra‐DG Aβ1–42 exhibited significantly longer latencies than Sham‐vehicle controls. Mice subjected to bilateral dcLN ligation plus Aβ1–42 injection (Ligation‐Aβ) displayed even earlier and more pronounced deficits, with latencies exceeding those of Sham‐vehicle mice from day 4 and surpassing Sham‐Aβ values on day 6 (Figure ). During the subsequent probe trial, Ligation‐Aβ mice spent less time in the target quadrant and crossed the former platform position fewer times than Sham‐Aβ animals (Figure ). Swimming speed and open‐field locomotor activity (distance travelled and time mobile) did not differ among groups, confirming that dcLN ligation and intra‐DG Aβ1–42 administration did not impair motor function (Figure  in supporting information). After the MWM test, the NOR test was conducted to corroborate the observed learning and memory alterations. Sham‐vehicle and Sham‐Aβ mice spent significantly more time exploring the novel than the familiar object, suggesting intact recognition memory (Figure ). In contrast, Ligation‐Aβ animals showed no preference, exhibiting equivalent exploration times for both objects (Figure ). DI quantification revealed a significant reduction in both Aβ‐exposed groups relative to Sham‐vehicle controls; moreover, DI in Ligation‐Aβ mice was further decreased compared to Sham‐Aβ animals (Figure ). Collectively, the MWM and NOR data suggest that dcLN ligation exacerbates the memory dysfunction induced by DG Aβ1–42 administration. Moreover, the experimental treatment did not affect the body weight of mice (Figure ). After completion of behavioral testing, we assessed the impact of impaired CSF drainage on Aβ clearance after dcLN ligation. Immunofluorescence staining revealed persistent Aβ deposits within the hippocampal DG of both Sham‐Aβ and Ligation‐Aβ mice; however, the residual Aβ burden was markedly lower in Sham‐Aβ animals compared to Ligation‐Aβ littermates (Figure ). Microglial density did not differ between the two groups (Figure ). These findings indicate that dcLN ligation impairs Aβ1–42 elimination and underscore the essential role of intact glymphatic flow in cerebral Aβ1–42 clearance.

We further investigated whether the increased Aβ deposition in the brains of APP/PS1 mice is associated with impaired glymphatic clearance. To address this question, we delivered the CSF tracer Cascade‐blue–conjugated dextran (3 kDa) into the LV and striatum of 15‐month‐old mice. Previous work has established that CSF outflow peaks during natural sleep or anesthesia and is suppressed in the awake state.  Therefore, mice were kept under continuous anesthesia after tracer injection to ensure a uniform arousal state and allow completion of CSF clearance. One hour later, the residual tracer signal in the periventricular region of the LV and in the striatum was quantified; lower residual levels indicate more efficient clearance of the tracer from the brain. After LV injection, APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significantly higher amount of tracer retained in the periventricular region of the ipsilateral LV and a significantly lower amount of tracer detected in the contralateral side compared to wild‐type (WT) mice (Figure  and Figure  in supporting information). After striatal injection, APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significantly higher level of residual tracer in the striatum compared to WT mice (Figure  and Figure ). Because CSF clearance is contingent upon CSF inflow, we next asked whether influx is also compromised in APP/PS1 mice. Cascade‐blue–conjugated dextran (3 kDa) was infused into the CM and allowed to circulate for 1 hour under continuous anesthesia before brain dissection and imaging. Influx volume was markedly reduced in APP/PS1 mice relative to WT mice (Figure ). Thus, both CSF inflow and clearance assays converge on the same conclusion: glymphatic circulation is impaired in APP/PS1 mice. Multiple independent reports have indicated that pericyte loss and/or degeneration is present in the hippocampus and cortex of human AD subjects.  Pericytes perform various functions, including maintaining the integrity of the BBB, regulating capillary blood flow, and contributing to glymphatic drainage.  Therefore, we sought to determine whether the impairment of glymphatic system circulation in APP/PS1 mice is related to pericyte loss. Immunofluorescence analysis of pericyte expression in the brains of 15‐month‐old APP/PS1 mice revealed a significant reduction in PDGFR‐β–positive pericytes compared to WT mice (Figure ). These results suggest that glymphatic system circulation dysfunction and pericyte loss are present in APP/PS1 mice.

Defective PDGFR‐β signaling has been shown to lead to pericyte dysfunction. Consequently, the Pdgfr‐β knockout mouse model has been widely used to investigate pericyte deficiency. ,  Western blot (WB) results showed that with aging, PDGFR‐β expression in the brains of Pdgfr‐β+/− mice was significantly downregulated (Figure ). At 12 months of age, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice exhibited a significant reduction in pericytes (Figure ). To determine whether pericyte loss was a key factor affecting glymphatic circulation and Aβ clearance, we injected a mixture of TMR‐labeled dextran (70 kDa) and FAM‐labeled hAβ (4.8 kDa) into the hippocampus, LV, and CM of 12‐month‐old Pdgfr‐β+/− mice. One hour after hippocampal injection, results showed that both TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ spread faster in the brains of WT mice, as evidenced by significantly increased deposition of TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ in the DG region at the injection site in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice compared to WT mice, while significantly reduced in the CA1 region (Figure  and Figure  in supporting information). In the dcLNs, WT mice showed minimal amounts of TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ, whereas Pdgfr‐β+/− mice showed almost no detectable CSF tracers (Figure  in supporting information). After 1 hour of LV injection, results showed that TMR‐dextran accumulated extensively around the ventricles (lateral, third, and fourth ventricles) and vessels, while FAM‐hAβ spread throughout the brain parenchyma (Figure  and Figure  in supporting information). Compared to WT mice, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice retained more TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ in the brain (Figure ), and WT mice had a significant amount of TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ around the vessels (Figure ). These tracers are believed to diffuse from the ventricles into the brain parenchyma, exchange with the interstitial fluid (ISF), and accumulate around the vessels for transport via the glymphatic system to the dcLNs. In the dcLNs, the accumulation of TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice was also significantly reduced compared to WT mice (Figure ). After 1 hour of injection into the CM, TMR‐dextran lymphatic influx was primarily observed in the cranial base and vessels of the cortex, with Pdgfr‐β+/− mice showing significantly lower influx of TMR‐dextran compared to WT mice (Figure  and Figure  in supporting information). The glymphatic influx of FAM‐hAβ was primarily observed in the sensory cortex, and similarly, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice showed much lower influx of FAM‐hAβ compared to WT mice (Figure  and Figure ). Likewise, in the dcLNs, the accumulation of TMR‐dextran and FAM‐hAβ in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice was significantly reduced compared to WT mice (Figure ). These results indicate that the glymphatic system circulation is significantly impaired in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, as evidenced by reduced Aβ clearance from brain tissue, slowed CSF–ISF exchange, and decreased glymphatic fluid flow to the dcLNs. These results suggest that pericyte loss is associated with impaired glymphatic function.

AQP‐4 is an important water channel protein predominantly expressed on astrocytes in the central nervous system, especially concentrated around blood vessels and the ventricles. AQP‐4 is responsible for water transport between the ISF and CSF, and its expression on astrocytic endfeet plays a crucial role in maintaining normal glymphatic function, facilitating the clearance of metabolic waste, such as Aβ.  Given the critical role of AQP‐4 in glymphatic system function, we further investigated whether the glymphatic circulation impairment in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice is related to AQP‐4 expression. Immunofluorescence double staining of AQP‐4 and the endothelial marker CD31 was performed (Figure ). In WT mice, AQP‐4 exhibited strong perivascular enrichment and extensive colocalization with CD31, reflected by a high Pearson correlation coefficient (Figure ). In contrast, Pdgfr‐β± mice showed a significantly reduced AQP‐4/CD31 colocalization, suggesting disrupted AQP‐4 polarization at the vascular endfeet. The mean AQP‐4 fluorescence intensity distribution curve along the distance from the vessel luminal midline further demonstrated that the sharp perivascular AQP‐4 peak observed in WT vessels was markedly attenuated in Pdgfr‐β+/− vessels (Figure ). Quantitative analysis revealed that the total AQP‐4 fluorescence intensity, perivascular AQP‐4 intensity, and the perivascular‐to‐parenchymal ratio (Figure , and Figure  in supporting information) were significantly decreased in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, indicating that pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling is essential for maintaining AQP‐4 distribution at the perivascular astrocyte endfeet.

To further determine whether pericyte loss and AQP‐4 mislocalization precede glymphatic dysfunction, we examined 7‐month‐old Pdgfr‐β+/− mice and WT littermates. At this age, NG‐2–positive pericyte fluorescence intensity was significantly reduced in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice (Figure  in supporting information), indicating pericyte loss. AQP‐4 immunostaining further revealed reduced AQP‐4–CD31 colocalization (Pearson coefficient) and attenuated perivascular AQP‐4 fluorescence peaks along the vessel lumen in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, whereas total AQP‐4 intensity was unchanged. The perivascular‐to‐parenchymal AQP‐4 ratio was reduced in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (Figure ). Notably, CM injection of TMR‐3 kDa dextran in 7‐month‐old mice showed no significant genotypic difference in tracer distribution across the lateral ventricle and hippocampus (Figure ). Collectively, these findings show that pericyte loss and AQP‐4 mislocalization occur early, whereas glymphatic dysfunction emerges later. This temporal difference partially supports the possibility that impaired glymphatic transport is a downstream consequence of pericyte loss and AQP‐4 mislocalization.

To further investigate whether pericyte‐derived soluble factors can directly regulate astrocytic AQP‐4 expression and localization, we treated HA1800 astrocytes with conditioned medium derived from pericytes (MBVP‐CM). Cells were incubated with SFM or MBVP‐CM for 24 hours (Figure ). Immunofluorescence staining showed that in SFM‐treated HA1800 cells, AQP‐4 displayed a punctate pattern, whereas MBVP‐CM treatment resulted in a more uniform distribution of AQP‐4 along the plasma membrane and cell processes (Figure ). Quantitative analysis demonstrated that MBVP‐CM significantly increased AQP‐4 fluorescence intensity compared to SFM treatment, whereas GFAP fluorescence intensity was not significantly altered (Figure ). These findings provide in vitro evidence that pericyte‐derived factors can modulate AQP‐4 expression and distribution in astrocytes.

To further investigate whether the impairment of glymphatic system circulation in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice is associated with AQP‐4 dysfunction, we administered the AQP‐4 facilitator TGN‐073 via intraperitoneal injection 30 minutes before injecting the CSF tracer into the CM. TGN‐073 binds to AQP‐4 and induces conformational changes in the AQP‐4 protein structure, which increases the water channel diameter of AQP‐4, thereby enhancing glymphatic transport.  To test whether TGN‐073 can regulate glymphatic activity by modulating AQP‐4 function, we used two‐photon microscopy to continuously monitor the effect of TGN‐073 on glymphatic flow in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice (Figure ). The results showed that, compared to the WT–Vehicle group, the WT–TGN group exhibited an increased distribution of CSF tracers in the brain parenchyma, including both the large molecule TMR‐70 kDa dextran and the small molecule TMR‐3 kDa dextran (Figure  and Figures  in supporting information). However, compared to the Pdgfr‐β+/−–Vehicle group, the Pdgfr‐β+/−–TGN‐073 group showed an increased distribution of only TMR‐3 kDa dextran, whereas TMR‐70 kDa dextran distribution showed no significant change (Figure  and Figures ). Similarly, 1 hour after tracer injection, compared to the WT–Vehicle group, the WT–TGN‐073 group showed a significant increase in both TMR‐3 kDa and TMR‐70 kDa dextran in the dcLNs (Figure  in supporting information). However, compared to the Pdgfr‐β+/−–Vehicle group, the Pdgfr‐β+/−–TGN‐073 group showed an increase in the distribution of only TMR‐3 kDa dextran (Figure ). To assess the differential effects of TGN‐073 on the distribution of CSF tracers in WT and Pdgfr‐β+/− mice, we calculated the ratio of the increase in fluorescence intensity of brain tracers in the 0 to 50 minutes post‐injection, after TGN‐073 administration. Results for TMR‐3 kDa dextran showed that the fluorescence intensity ratio in WT mice was significantly higher than in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice starting at 10 minutes and lasting until 30 minutes, suggesting a stronger facilitative effect of TGN‐073 on the small molecule tracer in WT mice (Figure ). For TMR‐70 kDa dextran, the fluorescence intensity ratio in WT mice was only significantly higher than in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice at 10 minutes, suggesting a stronger facilitative effect of TGN‐073 on large molecule tracers in WT mice and a more pronounced effect on small molecule tracers (Figure ). To further quantify the dynamic impact of TGN‐073 on CSF tracer distribution, we calculated the area under the curve (AUC) of the fluorescence intensity ratio for tracers in the brain of WT and Pdgfr‐β+/− mice from 0 to 50 minutes post‐injection. The AUC ratio was significantly higher in WT mice, further confirming that TGN‐073 has a stronger facilitative effect on CSF tracer distribution in WT mice (Figure  and Figure ). These results further support the conclusion that the impairment of glymphatic system circulation in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice is associated with AQP‐4 dysfunction and reduced expression. Brain‐slice histology corroborated the in vivo two‐photon findings. One hour after tracer injection, coronal sections spanning the lateral ventricle and hippocampus (Bregma +1 to 0 mm and −1.5 to −2 mm) were examined. Compared to the WT–Vehicle group, the WT–TGN‐073 group exhibited a marked increase in both TMR‐3 kDa and TMR‐70 kDa dextran fluorescence (Figure ). Similarly, Pdgfr‐β+/−–TGN‐073 brains showed higher dextran loads relative to the Pdgfr‐β+/−–Vehicle group (Figure ). Consistently, the brain‐slice data revealed that TGN‐073 potentiated CSF influx more robustly in WT mice than in Pdgfr‐β+/− littermates (TMR‐3 kDa: 50.65% vs. 31.26%; TMR‐70 kDa: 51.78% vs. 33.88%; Figure ). We further observed that (taking the hippocampus as an example), the small‐molecular tracer (3 kDa) rapidly entered the brain along the perivascular space and subsequently diffused into the interstitial parenchyma, whereas the large‐molecular tracer (70 kDa), although likewise flowing in via the perivascular route, remained largely confined to this compartment with restricted diffusion into the surrounding tissue (Figure  in supporting information). Previous studies have shown that pericytes interact with the dystrophin‐associated protein complex (DAPC) by secreting Laminin‐211, which anchors AQP‐4 to the astrocytic endfeet.  The DAPC complex is a multiprotein complex that includes α‐syntrophin (SNTA1), dystrobrevin (DTNA), dystrophin (DMD), and dystroglycan (DAG1; Figure ). Therefore, we used WB to examine the protein levels of laminin‐α2, laminin‐β1, SNTA1, and DAG1 in the brains. The results showed that, compared to WT mice, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice exhibited a significant downregulation of laminin‐α2, laminin‐β1, and SNTA1 expression in the brain (Figure ). These findings suggest that pericyte damage is associated with reduced laminin–α2/β1 expression, which may contribute to the decreased perivascular AQP‐4 expression in Pdgfr‐β+/− mice.

Previous results showed that APP/PS1 mice, an AD model, exhibit concomitant pericyte loss and glymphatic circulation impairment (Figure ), and that pericyte deficiency is associated with glymphatic dysfunction (Figure ). We therefore asked whether pericyte deficiency accelerates AD pathological progression in APP/PS1 mice. To address this question, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice were crossed with APP/PS1 mice to generate APP/PS1 mice with pericyte deficiency (Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice). Open field testing showed that pericyte deficiency did not affect locomotor function in mice (Figure  in supporting information). In contrast, MWM analysis revealed that Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice exhibited pronounced impairments in spatial learning and memory. Compared to APP/PS1 mice, Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice displayed a significantly prolonged escape latency, along with a marked reduction in both the time spent in the target quadrant and the number of platform crossings (Figure ). In the NOR test, Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice showed a significantly reduced preference index for the novel object compared to APP/PS1 mice (Figure  and Figure ), suggesting that pericyte deficiency further exacerbates cognitive deficits in APP/PS1 mice. Next, we evaluated the impact of pericyte deficiency on Aβ and phosphorylated Tau (p‐tau, AT8) pathology in APP/PS1 mice. The results showed that, compared to APP/PS1 mice, Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significant increase in both the number and area of Aβ plaques, as well as a marked increase in p‐tau–positive area (Figure  and Figure ). The number of NeuN‐positive neurons was also significantly reduced (Figure ). Together, these results suggest that pericyte loss promotes Aβ and p‐tau accumulation and accelerates neuronal loss in APP/PS1 mice. We next assessed neuroinflammation by immunofluorescence staining for GFAP (an astrocytic marker) and allograft inflammatory factor 1 (Iba‐1, a microglial marker). The area of GFAP‐positive astrocytes was comparable between APP/PS1 and Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice (Figure  in supporting information). In contrast, the number of Iba‐1–positive microglia was significantly increased in Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice compared to APP/PS1 mice (Figure ), indicating that pericyte deficiency enhances microglial activation without overtly altering astrocytic gliosis. To further explore the mechanisms by which pericyte deficiency influences AD pathological progression, we assessed AQP‐4 expression in Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice. AQP‐4 mediates metabolic waste clearance by regulating glymphatic circulation. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that, compared to APP/PS1 mice, Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice exhibited a significant reduction in perivascular AQP‐4 expression, whereas the area of GFAP‐positive astrocytes remained comparable between the two groups (Figure  and Figure ). The decrease in AQP‐4 may lead to glymphatic dysfunction, thereby further impairing Aβ clearance efficiency. Collectively, these results indicate that pericyte deficiency markedly exacerbates AD pathological progression in Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice, as evidenced by aggravated cognitive impairment and increased Aβ and p‐tau pathology. Moreover, pericyte deficiency leads to reduced perivascular AQP‐4 expression, which may diminish Aβ clearance by compromising glymphatic system function. Moreover, pericyte deficiency leads to reduced perivascular AQP‐4 expression, which may diminish Aβ clearance by compromising glymphatic system function. Given the established roles of pericytes in maintaining BBB integrity and regulating CBF, we also examined cerebrovascular integrity and perfusion. , ,  Endogenous IgG and Evans Blue extravasation were markedly increased (Figure  in supporting information), and CD31‐positive microvascular density was significantly reduced (Figure ), indicating aggravated BBB disruption and structural vascular injury. Laser Doppler flowmetry further demonstrated a significant decrease in CBF in Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice (Figure ). The accelerated AD pathological progression in Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice is therefore not solely attributable to AQP‐4 downregulation–induced glymphatic dysfunction, but also involves impaired cerebrovascular integrity and reduced perfusion.

In this study, by evaluating glymphatic system function and AQP‐4 expression in APP/PS1 and Pdgfr‐β+/− mouse models, we reveal a critical role for pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling in maintaining brain glymphatic homeostasis. Our findings suggest that loss of pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling is associated with reduced laminin–α2/β1 expression and decreased perivascular AQP‐4 localization, which may contribute to impaired CSF circulation and exacerbated AD‐related pathology in APP/PS1 mice. These findings provide novel mechanistic evidence, from the perspective of perivascular cell–cell interactions, linking glymphatic dysfunction to the progression of AD pathology.

The glymphatic system constitutes a major pathway for the clearance of metabolic waste from the brain, including Aβ. ,  Our data show that APP/PS1 mice exhibit impaired glymphatic circulation accompanied by pericyte loss, consistent with prior reports implicating glymphatic dysfunction in AD. ,  These observations further support a close association between compromised glymphatic function and the progression of AD pathology. Mechanistically, the glymphatic system facilitates the exchange between CSF and ISF, thereby promoting the removal of Aβ and other metabolites. When this system is disrupted—as observed in APP/PS1 mice—Aβ clearance is impeded, which may in turn accelerate its cerebral accumulation and exacerbate downstream neurotoxicity.

Glymphatic function is tightly regulated by multiple factors, including neurotransmitter tone, sleep–wake state, hemodynamic forces, and the expression and polarized localization of AQP‐4. For instance, the higher noradrenergic tone associated with wakefulness is generally linked to reduced glymphatic activity, whereas during sleep, norepinephrine exhibits rhythmic fluctuations that are coupled to vasomotion/CSF dynamics to coordinate glymphatic clearance. ,  Adenosine has also been shown to enhance glymphatic flow by activating A2A receptor signaling and thereby promoting AQP‐4 polarization.  In addition, hemodynamic drivers such as arterial pulsatility, vasomotion, and respiratory movements provide essential forces that propel glymphatic transport. , ,  Among these modulatory components, AQP‐4 is regarded as a central molecular determinant of glymphatic function: it is highly enriched in astrocytic endfeet, and both its expression level and polarized distribution directly influence the efficiency of glymphatic flux. ,  By facilitating exchange between CSF and ISF, AQP‐4 augments glymphatic transport and may consequently exert protective effects in neurodegenerative conditions such as AD. ,  In AD, loss of AQP‐4 polarization or reduced expression has been repeatedly documented; such alterations are expected to impair convective fluid transport and waste clearance efficiency, thereby further compromising glymphatic function.

Pericytes play an indispensable role in sustaining glymphatic function through PDGFR‐β–dependent signaling. In the present study, Pdgfr‐β+/− mice exhibited pronounced glymphatic impairment accompanied by a marked reduction in perivascular AQP‐4 expression and polarized localization, suggesting that intact PDGFR‐β signaling is critical for maintaining glymphatic homeostasis. Mechanistically, pericyte injury was associated with reduced expression of multiple extracellular matrix proteins within the basement membrane (particularly laminin‐211), which may disrupt the anchoring and polarization of AQP‐4 on astrocytic endfoot membranes. These results provide new experimental evidence that pericytes support glymphatic function, at least in part, by modulating astrocytic organization at the neurovascular interface. Consistent with this notion, disrupted pericyte–astrocyte crosstalk has been implicated as a key contributor to the initiation and progression of AD pathology. , , ,  Clinically, elevated levels of the pericyte marker PDGFR‐β have been detected in the CSF of individuals with early cognitive impairment, suggesting that pericyte dysfunction may represent an early indicator of cognitive decline in humans. ,  Moreover, transcriptomic analyses of post mortem AD brains have revealed substantial alterations in vascular–astrocytic interactions and widespread transcriptional remodeling, with many vascular changes localized to pericytes, further underscoring the pivotal role of pericytes in AD pathophysiology. ,

Pericytes are critical for maintaining astrocytic function, in particular by tightly regulating AQP‐4 expression at astrocytic endfoot membranes. ,  In transgenic mouse models lacking pericytes, AQP‐4 expression at astrocytic endfeet adjacent to capillaries is markedly reduced, resulting in impaired astrocyte polarization. ,  The expression and proper localization of AQP‐4 depend on α‐syntrophin, a membrane‐associated scaffolding protein. Accordingly, pericyte‐deficient mice exhibit decreased α‐syntrophin levels, which in turn leads to aberrant AQP‐4 targeting and distribution. , , ,  Beyond this intracellular anchoring machinery, pericytes also contribute to the basement membrane microenvironment by secreting multiple laminin subunits (e.g., laminin‐α2, ‐γ1, and ‐β1) that assemble into laminin‐211, a matrix component essential for vascular stability and glymphatic transport. , ,  Laminin‐211 interacts with the dystrophin–glycoprotein complex on perivascular astrocytes, thereby facilitating the anchoring of AQP‐4 at astrocytic endfeet. ,  This pericyte–astrocyte coupling is therefore pivotal for preserving glymphatic integrity, given the central role of the glymphatic system in clearing parenchymal waste. Consistently, studies using PDGF‐B signaling–deficient mouse models further suggest that disruption of the PDGF‐B/PDGFR‐β axis leads to pericyte loss, AQP‐4 depolarization, and impaired glymphatic function, highlighting the importance of pericyte–astrocyte interactions in maintaining glymphatic system homeostasis. ,  In our results, treatment with MBVP‐CM significantly increased AQP‐4 expression in HA1800 astrocytes, providing direct evidence that pericyte‐derived soluble factors can modulate AQP‐4.

Our results indicate that either Aβ overexpression alone (APP/PS1 mice) or partial Pdgfr‐β haploinsufficiency (Pdgfr‐β+/− mice) is sufficient to elicit a reduction in pericyte coverage. Notably, pericyte loss was more pronounced in the double‐transgenic Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice and was accompanied by a markedly accelerated progression of AD‐like pathology, further underscoring the critical contribution of pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling to AD pathogenesis. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of pericyte integrity in shaping AD pathology and highlight the pericyte PDGFR‐β pathway as a promising subject for future studies aimed at developing AD therapies.

Our data are consistent with the “two‐hit” vascular hypothesis of AD, whereby vascular injury (modeled by pericyte deficiency) and Aβ converge in parallel to drive disease pathogenesis and progression.,  However, the aggravated phenotype observed in Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice cannot be attributed solely to impaired glymphatic clearance. Pericytes are multifunctional cells that maintain BBB integrity, regulate CBF, and support cerebrovascular stability., ,  Consistent with these roles, we found that pericyte deficiency in APP/PS1 mice exacerbated BBB disruption, reduced microvascular density, and decreased CBF. In addition, Pdgfr‐β+/−/APP/PS1 mice displayed a significant increase in Iba‐1–positive microglia, indicating an enhanced neuroinflammatory response, while GFAP‐positive astrocyte area remained unchanged. These vascular and inflammatory alterations may independently contribute to Aβ deposition and behavioral deficits, independent of AQP‐4–dependent glymphatic dysfunction. Intriguingly, when intracellular Aβ accumulation exceeds the capacity of pericytes to clear Aβ, it can trigger pericyte death, which may contribute to pericyte degeneration and loss in AD. , ,  This suggests a vicious cycle in which Aβ‐induced pericyte injury impairs multiple vascular functions, including Aβ clearance, BBB maintenance, and blood flow regulation, further accelerating Aβ accumulation and neuronal loss. Although previous studies have shown that activation of PDGFR‐β signaling can restore BBB function, ,  whether such activation can also counteract the glymphatic deficits and microvascular abnormalities observed in our models remains to be determined.

Collectively, our study identifies pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling as a critical regulator of glymphatic function and a key factor in restraining AD‐like neurodegenerative pathology. This effect is mediated, at least in part, through the modulation of basement membrane composition and the maintenance of polarized AQP‐4 distribution along perivascular spaces. These findings elucidate the role of vascular–glial interactions in AD pathophysiology and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how vascular–glial interactions influence AD progression.

Our study provides robust evidence that pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling is critical for maintaining perivascular AQP‐4 localization and glymphatic clearance, and that its disruption exacerbates AD‐like pathology and cognitive impairment. Nevertheless, several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, our data are largely associative and do not directly establish a causal link among pericyte PDGFR‐β signaling, AQP‐4 redistribution, and glymphatic dysfunction. Future studies using inducible, pericyte‐specific deletion of Pdgfr‐β or targeted manipulation of AQP‐4 will be necessary to test causality. In addition, although our in vitro and pharmacological rescue experiments support a role for AQP‐4, whether PDGFR‐β–dependent signaling specifically controls AQP‐4 polarization in vivo remains to be determined. Second, Pdgfr‐β haploinsufficiency in our model is constitutive, which may induce developmental adaptations that could influence the adult phenotype. Although our data clearly show that pericyte deficiency aggravates AD pathology through multiple vascular and neuroinflammatory mechanisms, future work using inducible, pericyte‐specific depletion models will help distinguish developmental versus acute contributions of pericyte loss. Finally, AQP‐4 redistribution appears to be an early consequence of pericyte PDGFR‐β deficiency, whereas the reduction in glymphatic transport observed at older ages likely reflects a later, multifactorial process; future longitudinal studies with intermediate time points will be necessary to define the precise causal sequence.

medicine.title: Telehealth Access, Quality, and Cost in Veterans Health Administration Primary Care Clinics
medicine.abstract: This cross-sectional study examines variation in Veterans Health Administration primary care telehealth use and associations with access, quality, utilization, and cost.
medicine.text:
The Veterans Health Administration (VHA) was an early adopter of telehealth to expand primary care access. Most prior work examined individual telehealth use, yet clinic-level integration reflects modifiable organizational decisions and varies widely.,, One prior analysis of facility-level telehealth uptake across all outpatient care found mixed associations with utilization, spending, and quality, but this study combined clinical specialties and predated the postpandemic era. We describe VHA clinic-level variation in primary care telehealth use, identify characteristics associated with this variation, and examine associations with access, quality, utilization, and costs.

We conducted a cross-sectional study of a national sample of 909 VHA primary care clinics, including VA Medical Centers (VAMCs) and community-based outpatient clinics (CBOCs) in fiscal year (FY) 2024. The exposure was the clinic-level proportion of total primary care encounters delivered via synchronous telehealth (sum of telephone and video encounters divided by total primary care encounters), categorized into quartiles, using previously published primary care encounter definitions. Patients were aggregated to their VA Primary Care Management Module assigned clinician and care team’s clinic site. Patient characteristics were computed among all patients paneled to each clinic’s clinicians. Data sources included the VHA Corporate Data Warehouse, Primary Care Management Module, and Health Economics Resource Center average cost. Outcomes were patient-reported access via survey (eMethods in ), electronic quality measures (diabetes control, blood pressure control, statin therapy and adherence, colorectal cancer screening), utilization, and per-veteran VHA cost. All measures were aggregated and compared at the clinic level among veterans paneled to each clinic.

Race and ethnicity, drawn from self-report supplemented by administrative data via a validated algorithm, were included to characterize populations served. Utilization and cost comparisons were repeated within strata defined by urbanicity and clinic type (VAMC vs CBOC). Differences across quartiles were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test for continuous variables and Fisher exact test for categorical variables (2-sided, P < .05). Analyses used SAS Version 9.4 (SAS Institute) and R version 4.5.1 (R Project for Statistical Computing). This study was designated nonresearch and exempt from institutional review board evaluation by the VHA Office of Primary Care. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline.

In this cross-sectional sample of 909 VHA primary care clinics serving 5.91 million veterans (mean 6348 veterans per clinic), the clinic-level mean (SD) age of veterans was 64.5, (3.6) years, with 90.5% male and 53.1% urban-residing patients; 680 (81.1%) were CBOCs and 121 (18.9%) were VAMCs (). The mean (SD) proportion of primary care encounters delivered via telehealth was 36.4% (13.8% [N = 7 712 221]), with 32.3% (6 950 543) of all encounters delivered by telephone (). Primary care telehealth proportions ranged from 19.0% (6.2 percentage points [pp]) in quartile 1 (271 clinics) to 53.9% (7.4 pp) in quartile 4 (213 clinics) (). Compared with the lowest quartile, highest-quartile clinics more often served urban veterans (61.5% vs 43.9%; P < .001), were more often VAMCs than CBOCs (31.9% VAMCs vs 5.2% VAMCs; P < .001), had higher full time equivalent of primary care clinicians (10.4 vs 5.7; P < .001), served veterans who lived closer to the clinic (15.7 vs 19.2 miles; P < .001) and of higher neighborhood socioeconomic status decile (4.72 vs 4.35; P = .002), but were similar in age, sex, race and ethnicity, and chronic-condition prevalence ().

Abbreviations: CBOC, community-based outpatient clinics; ED, emergency department; VA, Veterans Affairs; VAMC, Veterans Affairs Medical Centers; VHA, Veterans Health Administration.

Other race includes those who identify as multirace or as other.

Access and quality were similar across quartiles. Total primary care encounter count did not differ across quartiles. Specialty (highest telehealth quartile: 4.52; lowest: 4.20), emergency (highest: 0.32; lowest: 0.18), and inpatient utilization (highest: 1.63; lowest: 1.57) and per-veteran cost (highest: $18 162; lowest: $14 664) were higher in the highest telehealth quartile, but most differences were no longer significant after stratifying jointly by urbanicity and clinic type. Residual differences occurred mainly within urban CBOCs.

In this national cross-sectional study of VHA primary care clinics, we found that most VHA clinics used telehealth for a significant share of primary care encounters, predominantly by telephone, and that substantial variation exists across clinics. The predominance of telephone use may reflect team-based encounters (eg, nurse and pharmacist contacts) captured in the denominator. Clinics providing the highest proportion of telehealth served veterans residing in urban settings, living closer to primary care, and of a slightly higher socioeconomic status. These clinics were more often VAMCs rather than CBOCs and had larger primary care clinician staffs, indicating that variation reflects clinic structure and local implementation alongside patient case mix. Clinics differed little in access and quality, whereas modestly higher utilization and costs among high-telehealth clinics, particularly urban CBOCs, may reflect differences previously documented for urban and VAMC-based care (eg, case mix, clinic structure) rather than telehealth itself., A key limitation is that this cross-sectional study measures telehealth use and outcomes concurrently; therefore, associations are descriptive, not causal. Causal inference can be addressed in future work with longitudinal quasi-experimental designs. Primary care telehealth policies should account for substantial clinic-level variation and the organizational and geographic contexts in which telehealth is implemented.

medicine.title: Imaging-Guided Ventricular Tachycardia Ablation in an Adult Patient With Fontan Circulation
medicine.abstract: Ventricular arrhythmias are an emerging cause of late morbidity in adults with Fontan circulation, yet catheter ablation strategies in this anatomically complex population remain poorly defined.A 25-year-old woman with tricuspid atresia palliated by total cavopulmonary connection presented with sustained ventricular tachycardia. Cardiac magnetic resonance showed circumferential subendocardial fibrosis in the right ventricular outflow tract. Imaging-guided catheter ablation was performed. The cardiac magnetic resonance–defined scar was targeted, abolishing local abnormal ventricular activities. The patient remained arrhythmia-free at the 12-month follow-up.Multimodality imaging facilitated a substrate-based ablation strategy by overcoming the anatomical and hemodynamic constraints inherent to single-ventricle physiology.Multimodality imaging is essential for ventricular tachycardia substrate characterization in Fontan patients. Right ventricular outflow tract fibrosis may represent the arrhythmogenic substrate even within the rudimentary right ventricle.
medicine.text:
A 25-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with palpitations and dyspnea of sudden onset in the context of an abdominal infection. On admission, her heart rate was 220 beats/min, blood pressure was 100/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 85% on room air. Physical examination revealed no audible murmurs, bilaterally preserved breath sounds without crackles or wheezing, and severe worsening abdominal pain. Peripheral perfusion was preserved.

The patient had complex congenital heart disease comprising tricuspid atresia with a consequently rudimentary right ventricle, ventricular septal defect, and secundum atrial septal defect. She had undergone staged single-ventricle palliation, culminating at the age of 3 years in a total cavopulmonary connection with a 16-mm extracardiac Gore-Tex conduit. Her subsequent course was complicated by sick sinus syndrome with an adequate junctional escape rhythm as well as extracardiac conduit stenosis requiring stent implantation and coil embolization of venovenous collaterals 9 years earlier. There was no prior history of documented sustained arrhythmia.

In a patient with complex congenital heart disease presenting with a sustained, regular, wide-complex tachycardia, the main differential diagnosis included ventricular tachycardia (VT) and intra-atrial re-entrant tachycardia or focal atrial tachycardia with rate-related aberrant conduction, particularly prevalent in patients after Fontan palliation.

A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) showed a sustained regular wide-complex tachycardia (QRS duration: 149 ms) with left bundle branch block morphology and fusion beats, consistent with VT (). The morphology was suggestive of an exit site within the outflow region of the rudimentary right ventricle.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrated a dominant systemic left ventricle with preserved systolic function, no significant valvular regurgitation, and an unobstructed Fontan pathway. Right heart catheterization revealed mildly elevated Fontan pressures (mean Fontan pressure: 17 mm Hg; end-diastolic pressure: 12 mm Hg), with no residual collaterals or fenestration.

Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) demonstrated circumferential subendocardial fibrosis in the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) of the rudimentary right ventricle (), consistent with a potential arrhythmogenic substrate. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) confirmed Fontan anatomy with a patent extracardiac tunnel stent, no atrial appendage thrombus, and a small residual communication between the caudal-dorsal aspect of the tunnel and the atrium.

Initial management comprised urgent electrical cardioversion with restoration of sinus rhythm and initiation of sotalol 40 mg twice daily as well as targeted antimicrobial treatment of the abdominal infection. Sotalol was preferred over amiodarone in view of the patient's young age and the anticipated long duration of therapy. The initial dosage was chosen conservatively given the patient's underlying sick sinus syndrome. She continued to experience symptomatic palpitations despite sotalol treatment, therefore catheter ablation was scheduled.

The procedure was performed under general anesthesia. Two ultrasound-guided punctures of the right common femoral vein were obtained, and, under TEE guidance, the Fontan conduit was punctured immediately below the stent to gain access to the common atrium (). High-density electroanatomical mapping of the dominant systemic left ventricle was performed with an HD Grid X catheter (Abbott). The rudimentary right ventricle was reached through the ventricular septal defect, although catheter maneuverability was limited. Additional retrograde access via the right common femoral artery enabled adequate mapping of the RVOT, which was feasible only with a TactiFlex SE catheter (Abbott).

VT was induced by burst pacing (cycle length: 240 ms) and was hemodynamically poorly tolerated (systolic blood pressure dropped to 75 mm Hg); the tachycardia was terminated by overdrive pacing. Substrate mapping identified a low-voltage area in the mid to distal RVOT, colocalized with the scar. Local abnormal ventricular activities and late potentials extending up to 75 ms beyond the QRS were recorded. Radiofrequency ablation was delivered at these sites, achieving complete abolition of the abnormal electrograms (, ). Postprocedural programmed stimulation induced only short runs of nonsustained VT. Postprocedural TEE excluded pericardial effusion or other complications.

Following the procedure, the electroanatomical map was merged with the preprocedural performed CT and CMR using ADAS3D (Medical SL) (). Post hoc analysis demonstrated that the scar identified on CMR corresponded to the scar detected on the electroanatomical map and represented the target for ablation.

Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement was discussed in detail by the heart team. Although VT in a single systemic ventricle carries meaningful sudden death risk, the index VT had been hemodynamically tolerated and had occurred in the setting of an acute, potentially reversible systemic illness (abdominal infection); the poorer tolerance of induced tachycardia was attributed to the vasodilatory effect of general anesthesia. Device options were nevertheless reviewed in view of the patient's anatomy: An extravascular ICD with substernal lead was precluded by the previous median sternotomy, and a conventional transvenous ICD was deemed undesirable because the lead would have required retrograde aortic placement in the systemic ventricle. The remaining feasible options as surgical epicardial leads, preserving antitachycardia pacing, or a subcutaneous ICD, accepting the higher risk of conscious shocks in the absence of antitachycardia pacing, were reserved for future consideration. Given complete substrate modification with acute noninducibility, implantation was deferred as an individualized decision, with residual risk explicitly acknowledged and discussed with the patient and a surveillance plan comprising clinical review with 12-lead ECG and ambulatory rhythm monitoring.

The patient was discharged on postprocedure day 3 in stable clinical condition. At the 12-month follow-up, she remained asymptomatic, with no documented recurrence of VT on serial ECG and ambulatory rhythm monitoring.

Although the Fontan palliation relieves cyanosis and prolongs survival, it results in profound alterations in cardiac physiology and circulatory hemodynamics. Arrhythmias are a frequent and clinically important complication after Fontan palliation, and they contribute substantially to long-term morbidity and mortality., Supraventricular arrhythmias predominate, yet ventricular arrhythmias are reported in approximately 3% to 12% of patients and are considered a leading presumptive mechanism of sudden cardiac death in this population. Their prevalence rises with time from palliation and parallels the development of systemic ventricular dysfunction. The underlying substrates are heterogeneous and include surgical scar, rudimentary ventricle, and diffuse interstitial fibrosis driven by chronic preload abnormalities, pressure or volume overload, hypoxemia, and progressive ventricular remodeling.

CMR with LGE has become a cornerstone for identifying the arrhythmogenic substrate in this population. In Fontan patients, LGE is detectable in a substantial proportion of cases and correlates with adverse ventricular remodeling, reduced exercise capacity, and ventricular arrhythmias. As illustrated by our case, the LGE distribution is not confined to surgical scars: Circumferential subendocardial enhancement in the rudimentary right ventricle and RVOT likely reflects fibrosis arising from long-standing abnormal loading and preoperative hypoxia rather than direct surgical injury, supporting a wider concept of substrate beyond incisional scar.

Catheter ablation in the Fontan circulation is technically challenging because of restricted vascular access, complex spatial relationships between the systemic venous baffle and the cardiac chambers, and frequent hemodynamic intolerance of induced VT. Preprocedural imaging in the present case identified the arrhythmogenic substrate and guided safe access and ablation strategy. Transbaffle puncture under TEE guidance, combined with retrograde aortic access, was required to reach the RVOT. A substrate-based strategy targeting low-voltage areas, late potentials, and local abnormal ventricular activities was preferred over conventional activation mapping given the poor hemodynamic tolerance of the tachycardia.

Contemporary expert consensus documents on arrhythmia management in adult congenital heart disease recommend referral of these patients to centers with combined expertise in congenital heart disease and electrophysiology and endorse multimodality imaging integration as a key step in substrate-based ablation in single-ventricle hearts.,,

Published experience with VT ablation after Fontan palliation is scarce, and the substrates described differ from ours. Miyamoto et al localized a re-entrant Purkinje-related tachycardia at the inferior septum of a hypoplastic left ventricle in double-outlet right ventricle, and Park et al targeted a His-Purkinje circuit by cryoablation to avoid atrioventricular block. In both studies, a conduction-system circuit was identified during tachycardia. Our case is complementary: The target was a preprocedurally defined region of LGE in the rudimentary RVOT, and multimodality imaging was used to plan access and confirm colocalization with the low-voltage region.

This single case permits no inference about efficacy. The clinical tachycardia was neither activation mapped nor entrained, so the link between the ablated substrate and the clinical circuit remains inferred, resting on colocalization of the low-voltage region with the CMR-defined scar and a compatible exit morphology. Follow-up was limited to 12 months, and durability and long-term sudden death risk are unknown.

Catheter ventricular ablation is feasible in patients with a Fontan circulation when supported by preprocedural multimodality imaging. Integration of imaging with the electroanatomical map enables targeted, substrate-based ablation despite the anatomical and hemodynamic constraints of single-ventricle physiology.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Junctional Rhythm Associated With Multilevel Flow Reversal in a Well-Functioning Fontan Detected by 4-Dimensional Flow
medicine.abstract: Flow reversal in Fontan circulation is highly associated with Fontan circulatory failure and adverse hemodynamics.A 12-year-old boy with hypoplastic left heart syndrome with an extracardiac fenestrated Fontan circuit underwent routine cardiovascular magnetic resonance surveillance. Phase-contrast and 4-dimensional flow imaging demonstrated late-systolic-to-early-diastolic flow reversal throughout the Fontan circuit and across the fenestration. The patient had no Fontan pathway obstruction, significant atrioventricular valve regurgitation, or ventricular dysfunction. Electrocardiography demonstrated a junctional rhythm (JR).JR is common after Fontan palliation and causes atrioventricular dyssynchrony. This case highlights chronic JR as a potential cause of multilevel flow reversal despite otherwise favorable Fontan anatomy and preserved ventricular function, expanding the differential diagnosis of flow reversal in patients with Fontan circulation.Advanced flow imaging may provide unique mechanistic insights into rhythm-related hemodynamic disturbances and improve the interpretation of Fontan flow patterns.
medicine.text:
A 12-year-old boy with hypoplastic left heart syndrome with a Fontan circuit presented for routine follow-up in the single ventricle/Fontan clinic. He was asymptomatic and remained physically active, participating in regular exercise and recreational activities without limitation. He denied chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or dyspnea. Physical examination was unremarkable, with a resting transcutaneous oxygen saturation of 93% on room air without edema or other signs of Fontan failure. As part of routine surveillance, cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging was performed.

The patient was postnatally diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (mitral atresia/aortic atresia) and underwent staged single-ventricle palliation consisting of neonatal balloon atrial septostomy, Norwood-Sano palliation with a 6-mm right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery (PA) conduit at 1 week of age, bidirectional Glenn with Sano takedown at 6 months, and extracardiac fenestrated Fontan completion using a 20-mm polytetrafluorethylene conduit with a 4-mm fenestration at 4 years of age.

His postoperative course was notable for the development of an intermittent junctional rhythm (JR) following the Fontan procedure. Electrophysiology evaluation was performed, and given his hemodynamic stability and absence of rhythm-related symptoms, conservative management with ongoing surveillance was recommended. The accelerated JR persisted after Fontan completion and remained present at the time of the current evaluation.

Electrocardiogram: Accelerated JR, heart rate: 90 beats/min ().

Exercise testing: Chronotropic insufficiency with JR predominance and intermittent sinus conversion.

CMR was performed on a 1.5-T scanner using standard 2-dimensional (2D) cine steady-state free precession and ferumoxytol-enhanced 3-dimensional inversion recovery balanced steady-state free precession angiographic sequences. The patient was awake, spontaneously breathing, and remained in JR throughout the study. Quantitative flow measurements in the superior vena cava (SVC), inferior vena cava (IVC), and branch PAs were obtained using free-breathing 2D phase-contrast (PC) imaging. Ferumoxytol-enhanced 4-dimensional (4D) flow CMR was additionally performed to comprehensively evaluate flow patterns throughout the Fontan circulation, including across the Fontan fenestration.

CMR demonstrated unobstructed, uniform Glenn and Fontan pathways, a patent Fontan fenestration, patent branch PAs, and an unrestrictive interatrial communication ( and ). The systemic right ventricle exhibited mildly depressed systolic function (ejection fraction 42%) without regional wall motion abnormalities, and trivial atrioventricular valve regurgitation (AVVR). Cine imaging confirmed retrograde atrial activation with atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve (). Pulmonary blood flow (PBF) distribution was balanced between the left and right PAs (45% and 55%, respectively). Despite these otherwise favorable findings, PC imaging demonstrated late-systolic-to-early-diastolic flow reversal within both PA branches, the SVC, and IVC, with subsequent 4D flow imaging confirming these abnormalities (, ). Flow across the Fontan fenestration was predominantly right-to-left, accounting for approximately 10% of cardiac output, with brief diastolic flow reversal (). This net right-to-left shunting was consistent with the mildly reduced resting oxygen saturation of 93%.
