The differential diagnosis of multilevel flow reversal in Fontan circulation includes conditions associated with adverse Fontan hemodynamics, such as elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, ventricular systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction, significant AVVR, Fontan pathway obstruction, and a substantial aortopulmonary collateral burden. These were excluded by careful review of the CMR and clinical data. Rhythm-related hemodynamic disturbances, particularly those resulting in atrioventricular (AV) dyssynchrony, should also be considered.

In the setting of preserved hemodynamics and absence of rhythm-related symptoms, a conservative approach was adopted. Aspirin and lisinopril were continued, and no immediate electrophysiologic intervention was pursued. The patient remained under longitudinal surveillance, with pacemaker implantation reserved for the development of symptoms or clinically significant hemodynamic consequences of AV dyssynchrony.

The patient remains clinically stable with preserved functional capacity (NYHA functional class I). Routine follow-up was continued without any intervention.

This case demonstrates an uncommon mechanism of multilevel flow reversal in Fontan circulation attributable to chronic JR rather than traditional markers of adverse Fontan hemodynamics.

In the Fontan circulation, PBF occurs in the absence of a subpulmonary ventricle and is driven by respiration and cardiac cycle–related pressure changes within the pulmonary venous atrium, which are transmitted retrogradely through the pulmonary vascular bed and influence flow throughout the Fontan pathway. Peak PA flow occurs during late systole to early diastole, corresponding to the early diastolic filling of the systemic ventricle. As a result, ventricle and AV valve performance and coordinated atrial contraction and relaxation, play critical roles in determining PBF patterns and overall Fontan hemodynamics.

Previous studies have associated late-systolic-to-early-diastolic pulmonary flow reversal with adverse hemodynamic features, including ventricular dilation, elevated v-waves, and significant AVVR. In contrast, the present case demonstrated only mild ventricular dilation, mildly depressed systolic function, trivial AVVR, and unobstructed Fontan pathways. The diffuse distribution of flow reversal throughout the Fontan circuit argues against a focal anatomical lesion and supports a circuit-wide hemodynamic mechanism.

In our case, cine imaging demonstrates that atrial contraction occurs against a closed AV valve. The resulting rise in atrial pressure may be transmitted retrogradely through the pulmonary veins and Fontan pathways, generating transient adverse pressure gradients that interrupt and briefly reverse forward flow. In Fontan circulation, where PBF is passive and highly sensitive to pressure fluctuations, the hemodynamic consequences of AV dyssynchrony may be amplified, producing the observed pattern of multilevel flow reversal.

Although retrograde flow associated with JR has previously been reported in patients with Fontan circulation, the present case extends those observations through a comprehensive characterization of flow patterns using both quantitative 2D and 4D flow CMR. Although 2D PC imaging provides accurate flow quantification at predefined locations, 4D flow CMR enables simultaneous assessment of time-resolved flow throughout the Fontan circulation within a single acquisition. In the present case, 4D flow imaging demonstrated temporally concordant flow reversal involving the SVC, IVC, both branch PAs, and the Fontan fenestration, supporting the concept of a circuit-wide hemodynamic disturbance rather than isolated vessel-specific abnormalities. Notably, the demonstration of transient diastolic flow reversal across the Fontan fenestration, which directly communicates with the common atrium, provides additional mechanistic support for retrograde transmission of elevated atrial pressure resulting from AV dyssynchrony. The visualization of fenestration flow is unique to 4D flow and was not possible with 2D flow alone. Interestingly, pre-Fontan CMR performed during sinus rhythm demonstrated exclusively antegrade flow in the SVC and branch PA () without evidence of flow reversal. This examination was performed under general anesthesia with positive-pressure ventilation. Although direct comparison is limited by the interval since Fontan completion and the markedly different physiological and respiratory conditions between the examinations, including differences in anesthesia and ventilation, these findings are directionally consistent with a contribution of chronic JR and AV dyssynchrony to the current flow abnormalities.

JR is a frequently encountered bradyarrhythmia in patients with Fontan circulation and commonly reflects underlying sinus node dysfunction (SND). Maintenance of sinus rhythm is critical for preserving efficient Fontan hemodynamics because loss of effective atrial contribution to ventricular filling and consequent elevations in atrial pressure may lead to low cardiac output and worsening venous congestion. Furthermore, the underlying SND may contribute to chronotropic incompetence and impaired exercise capacity.

Bradyarrhythmia is recognized as an important and potentially modifiable risk factor for Fontan failure. The 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Rhythm Society guidelines recommend electrophysiology evaluation of patients with Fontan circulation and symptomatic SND and device programming strategies that maximize atrial pacing. However, the management of chronic JR in otherwise asymptomatic patients with Fontan circulation remains less well defined. A recent multicenter congenital cardiology survey demonstrated substantial agreement in contemporary clinical practice, with most clinicians regarding JR as a benign finding in asymptomatic patients and recommending pacing primarily for symptom development or in conjunction with other cardiac surgery. In contrast, Alnoor et al reported acute invasive hemodynamic improvement with atrial pacing in 7 patients with Fontan and JR, suggesting earlier intervention may be beneficial in selected asymptomatic patients. However, these findings were based on a small cohort, and long-term outcome data are lacking. Importantly, recent work using respiratory-resolved 5-dimensional flow magnetic resonance imaging has demonstrated substantial respiration-driven variation in caval and PA flow energetics in patients with Fontan circulation. Future studies integrating rhythm and respiratory-resolved flow assessment are needed to better define the hemodynamic consequences of JR in Fontan circulation and guide patient selection for atrial pacing, particularly among patients with adverse flow patterns despite otherwise favorable Fontan anatomy and ventricular function.

This case highlights that chronic JR and AV dyssynchrony may mimic adverse Fontan hemodynamics despite otherwise reassuring clinical and imaging findings. Recognition of this mechanism using advanced flow imaging may improve interpretation of abnormal Fontan flow patterns and provide additional physiological information when considering longitudinal management strategies.

JR can result in multilevel flow reversal throughout the Fontan circulation even in the absence of advanced ventricular dysfunction or structural abnormalities. Comprehensive, single-acquisition 4D flow CMR was instrumental in recognizing the circuit-wide nature of this pattern. Recognition of rhythm-related flow abnormalities is essential for accurate interpretation of CMR findings and appropriate clinical decision-making.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: A Comprehensive Review on the Medicinal Attributes of Tetrazole Derivatives
medicine.abstract: The tetrazole moiety's unique bioisosteric properties and broad spectrum of pharmacological activities have made the heterocycle an important scaffold in medicinal chemistry. The nitrogen‐rich five‐membered tetrazole ring exhibits distinctive electronic and physicochemical characteristics and serves as an efficient bioisostere of carboxylic acid and related functional groups. This results in improved target interactions, metabolic stability, and pharmacokinetic profiles. The chemists have been intrigued by the diverse and fascinating properties of the tetrazole moiety, and extensive scientific studies have been conducted to integrate the tetrazole scaffold into various bioactive molecules, including complex frameworks. These modifications are believed to improve the biological activity, receptor‐binding affinity, selectivity of biological response, metabolic stability, and pharmacokinetic properties of the developed lead candidate(s). The advantages of tuning the physicochemical properties, metabolic stability, and ease of structural modification associated with integrating this privileged scaffold into the core structures of various hit/lead compounds provide an excellent foundation for developing new small‐molecule therapeutics to combat human ailments. This review highlights recent advances in the development of tetrazole‐based small heterocyclic molecules/drugs and their medicinal properties against several diseases, including anticancer, antitubercular, antifungal, and antidiabetic activities. The associated molecular pathways have been discussed in the extensive literature. Further, various synthetic strategies, structure–activity relationships and in silico studies employed in the development of physiologically active lead compounds have been compiled. Through this review, the authors aim to provide a broad perspective and valuable insights for researchers, inspiring novel approaches and accelerating the development of tetrazole‐based therapeutic agents with rich biological implications.
medicine.text:
Heterocyclic compounds account for the essential scaffold of organic compounds, as they are bestowed with an excellent pharmacological profile (Katritzky ; Al‐Mulla ; Eftekhari‐Sis et al. ). Numerous biological molecules, including haemoglobin, DNA, RNA, vitamins, hormones, etc., contain these ring structures as building blocks (Rulhania et al. ). Nitrogen‐containing heterocycles like triazoles, tetrazoles, imidazoles/benzimidazoles, pyrimidines, and quinolines exhibit tremendous therapeutic implications (Baranwal et al. ; Kabir and Uzzaman ). Researchers are currently interested in the astonishing chemistry of nitrogen‐containing heterocycles due to their abundance in naturally occurring bioactive compounds (Kumar and Narasimhan ; Mermer et al. ).

Tetrazoles are one of the important heterocyclic organic compounds having four nitrogen, one carbon, and two hydrogen atoms and are found to be a member of a class of five‐membered tethered aromatic rings (Neochoritis et al. ; Henary et al. ). Tetrazoles exhibit unique physicochemical properties as evidenced by their weak basicity, high nitrogen content, good thermal and chemical stability, and high enthalpy of formation.

Tetrazoles are frequently employed in SAR‐driven medicinal chemistry analogue syntheses, as metabolism‐resistant isosteric substitutes for carboxylic acids (Ostrovskii et al. ; Bonandi et al. ). These are a well‐known bioisostere of the carboxylic acid moiety, which has the capacity to mimic the carboxylic acid group in certain drug molecules to produce favourable pharmacokinetic changes (Malik et al. ; Biot et al. ). Carboxylic acids' low lipophilicity can limit the pharmacological agent's ability to cross biological membranes, and their metabolic instability can result in idiosyncratic toxicity and rapid elimination due to low bioavailability or rapid biotransformation (Bredael et al. ). Unsubstituted tetrazoles are moderately strong NH acids, where pK
a values lie in the range of 4 to 5, depending on the electronic properties of the substituent at the 5th position of the tetrazole ring (Boraei ). The presence of an electron‐withdrawing group at the 5th position decreases the electron density on the tetrazole ring, thereby weakening the hydrogen‐nitrogen bond, leading to easier ionisation and therefore lower pK
a values. Substituents such as CF3 and NO2 markedly enhance acidity, with reported pK
a values of 1.70 and −0.83, respectively (Trifonov et al. ). Electron‐donating groups reduce acidity by destabilising the anion and favouring the 1H‐tautomer. Additionally, bulky substituents at the ortho position on aryl rings hinder solvation of the 1H‐tautomer, increasing the proportion of the 2H tautomer and indirectly influencing its acidity (Trifonov and Ostrovskii ). It is noteworthy that tetrazoles also serve as a precursor for the synthesis of a wide range of nitrogen‐bearing heterocycles, such as 1,3,4‐oxadiazole, via the Huisgen method (Zou et al. ). It involves the loss of molecular nitrogen during the rearrangement reaction.

There have been extensive studies carried out regarding the tautomeric existence of tetrazoles, utilising various characterisation techniques (Katritzky and Lagowski ; Butler ). Through various analyses and assessments carried out, the melting point of the tetrazole molecule was found to be around 156°C–157°C. Tetrazole exists in a crystalline form in its natural habitat (Cherfi et al. ; Bhalla et al. ). The X‐ray diffraction study revealed that the tetrazole molecule remains in the 1‐H form in the solid state (Goddard et al. ). Analysis of dipole moments derived from microwave spectroscopy of gaseous tetrazole and its deuterium‐substituted counterparts enabled the researchers to infer the simultaneous presence of both 1‐H and 2‐H tautomeric forms in the gas phase (Krugh and Gold ). In simple words, 1‐H isomer dominates in crystalline form, whereas 2‐H form dominates mostly in the gaseous phase. It was observed that both the tautomers coexist in solution, and as the solvent's polarity increases, so does the population of the most polar 1‐H form (Chermahini et al. ). The tetrazole ring is π‐deficient due to the presence of the pyridine‐like nature of nitrogen. Tetrazoles exist in equilibrium between 1H‐ and 2H‐tautomeric forms, and electrophilic reactions such as alkylation and acylation may occur at either N1 or N2 positions depending on the reaction parameters. Tetrazole's structural properties were elucidated using X‐ray diffraction data. While 2‐H tetrazole exists in monoclinic form, 1‐H tetrazole crystallises in triclinic form (Figure ) (Chermahini et al. ; Katritzky et al. ; Balabin ).

Tetrazoles do not exist in nature. They are odourless, crystalline white to light yellow powder that melts between 1550°C and 1570°C. It is soluble in water, ethyl acetate, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and dimethylformamide (DMF) (Al‐Hourani et al. ). Another peculiarity of these compounds is that they contain the largest number of nitrogen atoms among stable monocyclic heterocycles due to the explosive character of pentazole compounds even at low temperatures (Pokatilov et al. ). The first publicly known synthesis of a tetrazole derivative was reported by Swedish chemist J. A. Bladin in 1885 at the University of Uppsala (Benson ). Tetrazole is a well‐known multifaceted pharmacophore, a prominent pharmaceutical scaffold and an exceptional heterocyclic compound with a broad range of pharmacological perspectives, such as analgesic (Rajasekaran and Thampi ), antiviral (Hutchinson and Naylor ; Mikolaichuk et al. ; Shiryaev and Klimochkin ), antimalarial (Gao, Chang, et al. ; Kalaria et al. ; Tukulula et al. ), antibacterial (Gao, Xiao, and Huang ; Rahi et al. ), antifungal (Wang et al. ; Łukowska‐Chojnacka et al. ), antiparasitic (Wani, Bhat, Azam, Choi, et al. ; Wani, Bhat, Azam, Lee, et al. ; Faria et al. ), anticancer (Zhang et al. ; Dhiman et al. ; Kumar et al. ; El‐Sayed et al. ), antihypertensive (Wu et al. ; Choi et al. ), antiallergic (Calogiuri et al. ), antiulcer (Hayao et al. ), antihyperlipidemic (Adak ). Tetrazoles have also been used in certain commercial sectors like agriculture, as herbicides, fungicides, etc. (Chen, Huang, et al. ).

The therapeutic efficacy of tetrazoles and their derivatives was found to be enhanced, and their toxicity reduced, when combined with other potential moieties (Mishra and Singh ). Conjugation of tetrazole with the triazole framework demonstrated potent antimicrobial and antitubercular activities. It is important to note that combining 5‐phenyl tetrazoles with other heterocyclic moieties is a well‐established approach for developing drug‐like compounds, enabling new pharmacological profiles and enhanced activity. Therefore, a single molecule with multiple pharmacophores, each with a distinct mode of action, may be useful in cancer therapy (Bhatt ). Literature studies revealed that thiotetrazoles have stronger activating properties than comparable five‐substituted tetrazoles employed in DNA and RNA synthesis and exhibit remarkable antihypertensive activity (Kaplancikli et al. ). Research efforts by the scientific community have led to the design and development of various tetrazole hybrids, such as tetrazole‐azole, tetrazole‐quinoline/quinolone, tetrazole‐pyridine, and tetrazole‐pyrimidine, which exhibit a wide range of therapeutic activities, including antifungal (Vandecruys et al. ) activity, and are used clinically. Oteseconazole is a tetrazole‐quinoline antifungal mainly used to prevent recurrent yeast infections. The antifungal activity is mediated by the selective inhibition of the fungal enzyme CYP51, which is essential for the synthesis of ergosterol, a critical component of the fungal cell membrane (Sobel and Nyirjesy ; Vandecruys et al. ; Jäger et al. ). Tetrazole derivatives have also been found to be efficient loop diuretics (Ukrainets and Bereznyakova ), such as azosemide (Ferraroni et al. ; Watanabe et al. ; Ukrainets and Bereznyakova ). These are generally used to treat conditions such as hypertension and oedema by inhibiting the reabsorption of sodium and chloride ions. This thereby increases the salt‐water excretion from the body. There are certain derivatives which are also employed as opioid analgesics, primarily used for anaesthesia during surgery (Khanage et al. ). One such example is alfentanil. They typically act via the μ‐opioid receptor in the brain, spinal cord, and other regions (Janssens et al. ; Paulino et al. ; Reitz ). Tetrazole derivatives are also effective antihypertensives, primarily acting by blocking angiotensin II, which causes blood vessels to tighten (Lawson et al. ). Some important tetrazole‐based antihypertensives include olmesartan, candesartan cilexetil, and losartan (Scott and McCormack ; Al‐Majed et al. , ; McClellan and Goa ; Easthope and Jarvis ). Cilostazol belongs to the group of tetrazole‐quinolinone drugs that have vasodilating properties. It typically works by inhibiting PDE3, thereby increasing cAMP levels and resulting in vasodilation (Kherallah et al. ; Robless et al. ). Tetrazole‐containing broad‐spectrum cephalosporin antibiotics are clinically used to treat skin infections and other lung, bone, joint, and urinary tract infections. Cefazolin is one of the many tetrazole‐based derivatives clinically used for this purpose (Bergeron et al. ; Kirby and Regamey ; Zappala et al. ). Derivatives containing tetrazole have potential antibacterial activity, and some, such as cefmenoxime and cefoperazone, have been used to treat bacterial infections in clinical practice, inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis and ultimately leading to bacterial death. The tetrazole‐oxazolidinone hybrids tedizolid and tedizolid phosphate are the most notable examples of other tetrazole‐based drugs. They achieve the desired pharmacological effect by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, thereby producing a bacteriostatic effect. They have already been introduced into clinical use to treat acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections caused by a range of bacteria, highlighting the potential of tetrazole scaffolds for developing new antibacterial agents (Megha et al. ). The study by V. H. Bhaskar and P. B. Mohite found that the nature and position of the substituent attached to the tetrazole ring significantly affect biological activity. For example, the presence of 4‐NO2, 4‐OH, and 4‐Cl in the phenyl ring at the fifth position of the pyrazoline ring of synthetic compounds containing a tetrazole moiety is responsible for the observed increase in the antibacterial, analgesic, and anti‐inflammatory activity (Bhatt ). Tetrazole derivatives have potential as anti‐tubercular agents due to their unique physicochemical profile, including enhanced lipophilicity, which enables them to cross the plasma membrane (Dalal and Mekky ). Therefore, these drugs represent successful examples of how incorporation of the tetrazole moiety can enhance target affinity, metabolic stability, aqueous solubility and pharmacokinetic behaviour without compromising safety or efficacy. For instance, the high selectivity of oteseconazole for fungal CYP51 and the potent angiotensin II receptor antagonism exhibited by losartan, olmesartan, and candesartan demonstrate that the tetrazole ring can enable precise interactions with a wide range of biological targets. The pictorial representation of various FDA‐approved drugs bearing a tetrazole scaffold is shown in Figure .

Due to their promising nature from a medicinal perspective, tetrazoles and their several derivative‐based drugs are currently in various phases of clinical development. VT‐1598 is one among the many such drugs that are currently in Phase I of clinical trial, being screened for the condition coccidioidomycosis. The trial is being done to study the safety and pharmacokinetics of the said drug. Similarly, BMS‐962212 is in Phase I of a clinical trial to evaluate the drug's safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics in the context of thrombosis. MK‐0354 is currently in Phase II for clinical efficacy and tolerability analysis in dyslipidemia. It is worth noting that the drug SCO‐101 is being tested for both colorectal cancer and pancreatic adenocarcinoma. SC‐101 is in Phase I/II clinical trials to assess safety and tolerability in pancreatic cancer, and in a Phase II trial for patients with metastatic colorectal cancer. An active study of UM171 in high‐risk hematologic malignancies is underway, with the drug in Phase II. HM30181 is in Phase II of a clinical trial safety study against tumours. A study to assess the safety and efficacy of MK8245 in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus is in Phase II of its clinical trial. The remarkable structural versatility and favourable physicochemical properties of the tetrazole scaffold have garnered considerable attention from both academia and the pharmaceutical industries. Ongoing research has led to the development of tetrazole‐based FDA‐approved drugs with considerable therapeutic relevance. These research efforts have continued through patent filings worldwide. These patents encompass diverse structural modifications, synthetic protocols, and therapeutic applications, reflecting the broad utility of tetrazole derivatives in modern‐day drug discovery. Collectively, the patent landscape highlights ongoing innovation aimed at enhancing biological activity, selectivity, pharmacokinetic profile and intellectual property value of tetrazole‐containing molecules. A representative compilation of patents on tetrazole derivatives, with distinct applications across diverse fields, is presented in Table .

There are several ways to make tetrazoles, but most employ azides as starting materials or reaction intermediates (Nasrollahzadeh et al. ). Starting materials for the synthesis of substituted tetrazoles include amines, cyano compounds, amides, alcohols and aldehydes, and aryl diazonium salts (Maji et al. ; Vishwakarma et al. ). The [3 + 2] cycloaddition of azides and organic nitriles is a common method for synthesising tetrazoles (Ojeda‐Carralero et al. ). Numerous strategies, such as electrochemical methods that exploit the interaction between azides and hydrazones to form tetrazoles, are being developed as new routes for producing this heterocycle (Manwar et al. ). But there are certain limitations in their synthetic processes. The main issue is regioselectivity when simultaneous functionalisation is performed. As tetrazole exists in two tautomeric forms, alkylation or arylation can occur at different nitrogen atoms mainly, N1 or N2, which leads to two regio‐isomeric products. However, other limitations include the use of strong Lewis acids and toxic metal catalysts, as well as the in situ generation of highly toxic and explosive hydrazoic acid when inorganic azides are used in the synthetic procedure (Uppadhayay et al. ). As the importance and efficacy of tetrazoles grew, several sustainable methods for their synthesis were also developed alongside. Two major methods for creating tetrazole compounds and derivatives are modern and green synthesis methods. While the latter category aims to reduce environmental impacts and improve sustainability, the former group uses ultrasound or microwave irradiation to accelerate the cycloaddition reaction (Prabhu et al. ).

Over the past decade, extensive research has yielded approximately 5000 publications reviewing the therapeutic potential of tetrazole‐based compounds across multiple disease domains. Numerous comprehensive reviews have been published addressing specific therapeutic applications: Popova et al. () conducted a mini‐review on the potential anticancer properties of tetrazole derivatives, while Gao, Chang, et al. () compiled the current status of tetrazole hybrids for antibacterial activity. A study on recent progress in nitrogen‐rich energetic materials based on the tetrazole skeleton was carried out by Chen, Lu, et al. (), whereas a mini‐review was published by Maruthamuthu et al. (), compiling the chemistry and biological significance of imidazole, benzimidazole, benzoxazole, tetrazole, and quinazolinone nuclei. The strategic modifications of the tetrazole core at N‐1, N‐2, and C‐5 positions through hybridisation with diverse heterocyclic moieties have generated various lead compounds exhibiting desired pharmacological properties against multiple disease‐causing pathways, with several advancing to preclinical and clinical development stages (Jaiswal et al. ). Despite tremendous progress being witnessed in the medicinal and therapeutic potential of tetrazole derivatives, very limited literature is available on the various pharmacological potential of tetrazole derivatives; however, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive review has systemically integrated the potential aspects of tetrazole derivatives alongside structure–activity relationships and mechanistic insights within a unified framework. Although reviews on synthetic strategies are available, the medicinal chemistry section, with particular emphasis on antitubercular, anticancer, and neuroprotective activities, is unavailable (Maji et al. ). Thus, the present review fills this critical gap by systematically compiling tetrazole‐based derivatives reported since 2015, with particular emphasis on their pharmaceutical properties and molecular scaffolds, and is supported by SAR analysis, molecular docking studies, and the patent landscape. The literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including Web of Science, ScienceDirect, PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, to ensure comprehensive coverage. Several keyword combinations were utilised, including tetrazoles, tetrazole derivatives, heterocycles, heterocyclic compounds, drug discovery, antiviral, anti‐tubercular agents, antimicrobials, anticancer, anti‐depressant, and anti‐inflammatory activity. Database searches were supplemented with Google Patents and ClinicalTrials.gov to identify patented innovations and ongoing clinical investigations. Only peer‐reviewed research articles, reviews, and relevant books were considered, while applying exclusion criteria for poor quality, inaccurate data, and limited relevance to the review's scope. EndNote Reference Manager Software was employed to manage references and eliminate duplicates, ensuring systematic organisation of the compiled literature. This review compiles approximately 30 research papers that focus on the compound of interest's diverse therapeutic potential. We believe this comprehensive review will serve as a valuable resource for medicinal chemists and drug discovery researchers seeking to exploit the tetrazole scaffold to develop next‐generation therapeutics against several diseases, while providing critical insights into rational design strategies, mechanistic understanding, and future optimisation directions.

Ni et al. designed and synthesised a series of 31 novel albaconazole hybrids, including eight tetrazole‐based derivatives, and evaluated their in vitro antifungal potential against seven common fungal strains. The study revealed that replacing the triazole rings with the tetrazole moiety resulted in significantly enhanced antifungal activity. The rationale behind this work is the albaconazole, which is a broad‐spectrum triazole antifungal, but is limited by CYP3A4 inhibition. Modifications of this structure by appropriate substitution at the 7th position, alteration of nitrogen positions in the quinazoline scaffold, and tetrazole replacement of the triazole ring to reduce CYP450 inhibition and improve safety. Among the synthesised compounds, 1a emerged as the most potent antifungal agent, exhibiting remarkable MIC values < 0.008 μg/mL against 
Candida albicans
 and Cryptococcus neoformans, and 2 μg/mL against 
Aspergillus fumigatus
. All tetrazole hybrids demonstrated high potency against 
C. albicans
 and 
C. tropicalis
 with MIC values of < 0.008 μg/mL. In contrast, incorporation of phenylpyrazolopyridazinone moiety linked with albaconazole sidechain leads to a marked reduction in antifungal potential, with no observable effect against 
A. fumigatus
 (MIC > 64 μg/mL). Notably, compound 1a exhibited the highest potency among the reference drugs. SAR analysis revealed that tetrazole retains potency and improves safety, while the presence of a halogen at the 7th position enhances activity against 
A. fumigatus
. However, triazole analogues and phenylpyazolopyridazinone derivatives exhibited poor antifungal activity. These findings clearly indicate that substitution with a tetrazole ring significantly enhanced antifungal potency (Figure ) (Ni et al. ).

Basireddy et al. reported the design, synthesis, and antimicrobial evaluation of pyrazolopyrimidine‐based 1,2,3‐triazole‐linked tetrazole hybrids, developed through a rational molecular hybridisation approach. All synthesised derivatives were screened for antibacterial (Gram‐positive and Gram‐negative), antifungal, and antitubercular activities. Among the series of synthesised derivatives, compound 2a exhibited broad‐spectrum antibacterial activity against Gram‐positive strains (
Staphylococcus aureus
 and 
Staphylococcus epidermidis
) and the Gram‐negative strain (
Klebsiella pneumoniae
), but showed no significant activity against 
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
. The observed MIC50 values were 4.93, 5.84, and 7.72 μg/mL, respectively. Compound 2b also demonstrated notable antibacterial potency, with MIC50 values of 6.15 μg/mL (
K. pneumoniae
), 5.02 μg/mL (
S. aureus
), and 5.53 μg/mL (
S. epidermidis
). Further antifungal studies revealed that compound 2b showed promising antifungal activity, with an MIC50 of 4.24 μg/mL against Fusarium oxysporum. Compounds 2h and 2a exhibited potent activity against Aspergillus niger, with MIC50 values of 4.12 and 5.45 μg/mL, respectively. Additionally, compound 2e demonstrated moderate inhibitory potential against both fungal strains, with MIC50 values of 7.50 and 9.43 μg/mL, respectively. The antitubercular evaluation revealed that compounds 2a and 2b exhibited excellent activity against 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
, with MIC50 values of 1.10 and 0.98 μg/mL, respectively. Molecular docking studies further supported the in vitro studies by indicating that compound 2a exhibited strong binding affinity within the active site of the 
M. tuberculosis
 target protein. Key interactions included π–cation interactions with Arg44(A) and Arg45(A), amide–π electrostatic interaction with Gly43(A), and multiple π–alkyl interactions involving Arg67(A), Arg44(A), Arg45(A), and Ala126(A) (×2), primarily contributed by the pyrimidine, triazole, and tetrazole moieties. Furthermore, the oxygen atom of the sulfonyl linker participated in dual hydrogen‐bonding interactions with Gly96(A) and Thr46(A), while the nitrogen atoms of the pyrimidine and tetrazole rings formed hydrogen bonds with Gln98(A). Additional hydrogen‐bonding interactions were observed between the triazole and pyrazole rings and Arg45(A) and Gln68(A), further stabilising the ligand–protein complex. Moreover, the synthesised hybrids met key drug‐likeness criteria and exhibited favourable ADME profiles, suggesting promising pharmacokinetic properties and potential bioavailability. SAR studies finally revealed that the presence of hydroxyl substituents developed the strongest antifungal potency. While bulky or electron‐withdrawing groups diminished the potency (Figure ) (Basireddy et al. ).

Obiad et al. developed a green synthetic strategy to prepare tetrazole‐based hybrids and assessed their antimicrobial activity against 
C. albicans
, 
C. glabrata
, and 
C. parapsilosis
. Among the synthesised compounds, derivative 3b emerged as the most potent antifungal candidate, exhibiting approximately threefold greater activity against 
C. glabrata
 than fluconazole with a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 0.98 μg/mL. The same compound also demonstrated promising activity against 
C. parapsilosis
, with an MIC of 15.6 μg/mL. 3a displayed an MIC of 7.4 μg/mL against 
C. albicans
, which was comparable to the reference drug fluconazole. Overall, the synthesised tetrazole hybrids exhibited broad‐spectrum antifungal activity. In addition, these compounds showed notable antibacterial efficacy against the Gram‐positive bacterium Enterococcus faecalis, with MIC values ranging from 1.2 to 31 μg/mL, comparable to those of azithromycin. Molecular docking studies targeting sterol 14α‐demethylase from 
C. albicans
 revealed that compound 3b established key interactions within the active site, including a hydrogen‐bond acceptor interaction with Ser378, hydrogen‐π stacking interactions with the heme group, and both hydrogen‐bond and π‐H interactions with Ser506, resulting in a binding energy of −8.74 kcal/mol. Furthermore, ADME predictions indicate that the synthesised compound with Jorgensen's Rule of Three has only a major deviation from Lipinski's Rule of Five. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis suggested that the sulfonamide moiety is crucial for potent antifungal and antibacterial activity, while the incorporation of an isoxazole substituent contributed to balanced antifungal efficacy. In contrast, simple benzimidazole‐tetrazole analogues exhibited weak antimicrobial activity, emphasising the importance of incorporating extended pharmacophoric features to enhance biological activity (Figure ) (Obiad et al. ).

Li et al. reported the design, synthesis, and fungicidal evaluation of a novel series of phenyloxadiazole‐fused tetrazole derivatives. The incorporation of the phenyloxadiazole scaffold into the tetrazole framework was based on its well‐ established biological significance in agrochemical research. Among the synthesised compounds, derivative 4a exhibited the most potent antifungal activity against CDM, with an EC50 of 1.78 mg/L. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies revealed that the introduction of small electron‐withdrawing substituents at the 4‐position of the phenyl ring markedly enhanced fungicidal activity, as demonstrated by compounds 4b and 4c, which had EC50 values of 5.16 and 5.15 mg/L, respectively. In contrast, bulky substituents at the para position resulted in reduced activity, whereas appropriately sized substituents at the 2‐ position contributed positively to antifungal potency. To further elucidate the observed SAR trends, a Comparative Molecular Field Analysis (CoMFA) model was established, demonstrating excellent predictive capability (q
2 = 0.791 and r
2 = 0.982), thereby validating its robustness. Guided by the COMFA counter maps, three additional derivatives (8d–8f) were designed and synthesised, yielding improved fungicidal activities with EC50 values of 1.43, 1.52, and 1.77 mg/L, respectively. Collectively, these findings provide valuable insight into the structural features governing antifungal activity and establish a reliable theoretical basis for the rational optimisation of phenyloxadiazole‐tetrazole derivatives as promising fungicidal candidates. Overall, the SAR investigation suggested that electron‐withdrawing substituents at the 3‐position significantly enhanced biological activity, while bulky or halogen substituents at the 2‐position were also favourable for improving fungicidal efficacy, with bulky groups at this position contributing to increased potency (Figure ) (Li et al. ).

Narkedimilli and co‐workers reported the rational design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of a library of benzo[d]oxazole‐linked triazolyl–tetrazole hybrids for antimycobacterial and antibacterial activity. The design strategy involved the hybridisation of dual heterocyclic hybrids combining benzo[d]oxazole, 1,2,3‐triazole and tetrazole moieties. All synthesised compounds exhibited variable potency, with MIC50 values ranging from 3.0 to 44.9 μg/mL against Gram‐negative bacteria and from 1.8 to 41.4 μg/mL against Gram‐positive strains. Among the Gram‐negative organisms, particularly 
P. aeruginosa
, compounds 5a and 5b demonstrated the most potent inhibitory activity, with MIC50 values of 3.0 and 3.8 μg/mL, respectively, surpassing the standard gemifloxacin (MIC50 = 5 μg/mL). Against 
Acinetobacter baumannii
, compound 5b exhibited an MIC50 of 5.1 μg/mL, comparable to moxifloxacin (5.0 μg/mL). In the case of 
K. pneumoniae
, compound 5d, bearing a trifluoromethyl substituent, showed an MIC50 of 7.4 μg/mL. For Gram‐positive bacteria, compound 5b showed notable activity against 
S. epidermidis
 (MIC50 = 3.0 μg/mL), comparable to that of moxifloxacin. Additionally, compounds 5a and 5c exhibited promising activity against 
S. aureus
, with MIC50 values of 1.6 and 3.2 μg/mL, respectively. Importantly, compound 5a demonstrated significant antitubercular activity against 
M. tuberculosis
 H37Rv, with an MIC50 of 3.0 μg/mL, exceeding that of standard drugs such as streptomycin and rifampicin. While compound 5d showed the 2nd‐highest inhibitory potency, with an MIC50 of 5.8 μg/mL against the same strain. Molecular docking studies against PDB ID 1EA1 revealed that compound 5a exhibited a binding free energy of −8.26 kcal/mol. It formed multiple π‐alkyl interactions with residues LeuA:321 (×2), CysA:396, ValA:434, and AlaA:256. Additionally, hydrogen bonding interactions were observed with ArgA:96 via the tetrazole moiety and with HisA:259 through the phenyl ring of the benzo[d]oxazole scaffold. Further stabilising interactions included a π–σ interaction with LeuA:32 and a π–lone‐pair interaction with MetA:433. Moreover, these compounds met key drug‐likeness criteria and exhibited favourable ADME profiles, suggesting promising pharmacokinetic properties and potential bioavailability. SAR studies highlighted that hydroxy and electron‐donating substituents enhanced antibacterial potency, whereas nitro and chloro substituents reduced activity (Figure ) (Narkedimilli et al. ).

Acar Cevik and colleagues designed and synthesised a series of tetrazole‐S‐alkyl‐piperazine hybrids and investigated their antifungal potential against clinically relevant Candida species, including 
C. albicans
, 
Candida krusei
, and 
C. parapsilosis
. The molecular design was inspired by clinically used azole antifungal agents, such as fluconazole and voriconazole, with the objective of targeting sterol 14α‐demethylase (CYP51) in Candida species. The incorporation of the tetrazole ring as a bioisosteric replacement for carboxylic acid functionality was intended to improve hydrogen‐bonding capability, aqueous solubility, and target affinity. Furthermore, the piperazine moiety was introduced to enhance physicochemical properties, while the thioether linker was employed to increase lipophilicity, improve drug‐like characteristics and contribute to antimicrobial activity. Among the synthesised derivatives, compounds 6a and 6b exhibited the most pronounced antifungal activity, comparable to that of fluconazole. Biological evaluation revealed that most compounds effectively inhibited the growth of 
C. parapsilosis
, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values ranging from 15.625 to 31.25 μg/mL, whereas moderate activity was observed against 
C. krusei
, with MIC values ranging from 39.0 to 62.6 μg/mL. Notably, compounds 6a and 6b displayed superior activity against 
C. krusei
, exhibiting MIC values of 7.81 and 3.90 μg/mL, respectively.in contracts, the synthesised derivatives generally showed lower potency against C. albicans. Molecular docking studies using the crystal structure of CYP51 (PDB ID: 5TZ1) validated the docking protocol, yielding a root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.4278 A°. Inactivity of a reliable binding model. The glide score ‘g’ of the evaluated compounds ranged from −5.743 to −8.390 kcal/mol, with compound 6a exhibiting the highest binding affinity (glide score 8.390 kcal/mol). The enhanced binding of compound 6a was attributed to hydrogen‐bond interactions with Ser378 and π‐cation interactions with Hem601, Tyr118, and His377. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis demonstrated that the incorporation of bulky hydrophobic substituents, particularly a cyclohexane group attached to the 4− position of the piperazine ring, significantly improves antifungal activity, as exemplified by compounds 6a and 6b. In addition, aromatic halogen substituent derivatives exhibited enhanced binding affinity, accompanied by lower MIC values, whereas the introduction of polar heteroaryl substituents resulted in diminished antifungal potency. Moreover, the presence of a methylene spacer between the piperazine and phenyl rings further enhanced biological activity, highlighting its favourable contribution to the overall antifungal profile of this series (Figure ) (Acar Cevik et al. ).

Nakada et al. conducted a high‐throughput screening of a library comprising 22,400 tetrazole hybrids to identify antifungal agents active against 
C. neoformans
. Two active hits were identified, one of which contained a tetrazole scaffold and demonstrated significant inhibitory activity. This compound was selected for further investigations owing to its high selectivity toward Cryptococcus species over Candida. Guided by in silico modelling, a series of novel derivatives were designed and synthesised. Among these compounds, 7a and 7b, incorporating a pyridine moiety, exhibited potent antifungal activity against 
C. neoformans
. Notably, compound 7a displayed superior activity against C. gattii compared to 7b, suggesting that halogen substitution enhances target binding interactions while contributing to species‐selective antifungal activity. Time‐kill kinetic studies performed at concentrations of 0.1 and 1.0 μg/mL, compared with amphotericin B (0.5–8.0 μg/mL), revealed that these tetrazole analogues exert a fungistatic mode of action. In addition, in vitro cytotoxicity studies in A549 lung cancer cells revealed an ED50 of approximately 100 μM and ED50/IC50 ratios > 1000, indicating substantially greater selectivity than amphotericin B (ratio approx. 40). Furthermore, mechanistic investigations suggested that the lead compound coordinated with Zn2+, implicating metal chelation as a possible contributor to the antifungal mechanism. In contrast, phenyl analogues lacking pyridyl moiety failed to exhibit Zn2+ chelation, underscoring the critical role of the pyridine‐tetrazole hybrid framework in mediating metal binding and antifungal efficacy (Figure ) (Nakada et al. ).

Bourhou et al. synthesised novel bis(arylidene‐2‐[(tetrazol‐5‐yl)]alkane) derivatives and evaluated their antibacterial and antifungal activities against four bacterial strains (
Listeria innocua
, 
Escherichia Coli
, 
P. aeruginosa
, 
S. aureus
) and four fungal strains (
C. albicans
, 
Rhodotorula glutinis
, Geotrichum candidum, 
A. niger
). The evaluation was carried out using gentamicin and cycloheximide as positive antibacterial and antifungal references, respectively, and DMSO as a negative reference. All the synthesised compounds exhibited measurable antimicrobial activity, although generally lower than the standard. Among them, compound 8a exhibited maximum antifungal efficacy with 13.45, 12.65, 14.75, and 11.25 mm activity against G. candidum, C. albicans, R. glutinis
, and A. niger, respectively. These findings indicated that converting parent nitrile compounds into tetrazole derivatives significantly enhances antifungal activity. Notably, compound 8a exhibited consistent inhibition without selective inactivity. In silico studies against biotin protein ligase, S. aureus, revealed that all the derivatives interacted through hydrogen bonding, electrostatic, and Vander Wall's contact with the active site. Further SAR analysis highlighted that spacer length affects the activities. Longer chains (n = 6) have stronger antifungal activity, while the presence of the tetrazole ring is essential for the activity (Figure ) (Bourhou et al. ).

The tetrazole ring itself plays a pivotal role in antimicrobial activity, as its removal resulted in a marked loss of potency. Incorporation of tetrazole into pyridine, triazole, oxadiazole, benzo[d]oxazole, pyrazolopyrimidine, and albaconazole frameworks significantly enhanced antibacterial, antifungal, and antitubercular activities. Small electron‐withdrawing substituents, particularly at the para‐position of the aromatic rings, improved antifungal activity, whereas bulky para‐substituents generally reduced potency. In contrast, larger substituents at the ortho position were beneficial in certain series. Cyclohexyl‐containing piperazine derivatives, trifluoromethyl‐substituted analogues, and tetrazole‐bearing albaconazole hybrids demonstrated superior antimicrobial activity due to improved lipophilicity and stronger target interactions. Enhanced activity was consistently associated with increased hydrogen bonding, π‐ interactions and favourable ADME properties. The visual representation is shown below in Figure .

Vellaiyan et al. synthesised and evaluated a series of flurbiprofen‐tethered 1,2,3‐triazole–tetrazole hybrids as potential anticancer agents. The rationale for this synthetic scheme was based on the clinically validated flurbiprofen scaffold, a propionic acid‐derived NSAID known to interact with COX enzymes and to be metabolised via CYP2C9. In this hybrid framework, the tetrazole moiety was incorporated as a bioisostere of the carboxylic acid group to enhance metabolic stability and lipophilicity, while the triazole linker was introduced to facilitate hydrogen bonding, π‐stacking interactions and steric adaptability. The synthesised compounds were evaluated for cytotoxic activity against a panel of human cancer cell lines, including HepG2, HuH7, MCF‐7, and T‐47D, using the MTT assay. Among the series, compound 9a, bearing a nitrophenyl tetrazole moiety, exhibited the highest antiproliferative activity, with IC50 values of 1.89 μM against HepG2 cells and 1.66 μM against MCF‐7 cells, outperforming the reference drug doxorubicin in certain assays. Structure–activity relationship analysis revealed that the presence of electron‐withdrawing groups, particularly –NO2 and –Cl, on the phenyl ring significantly enhanced the anticancer potency, which was attributed to its improved binding interactions within the CYP2C9 active site. Molecular docking studies further substantiated the experimental findings by demonstrating that compound 9a established multiple hydrogen bonds and π‐π stacking interactions with various key amino acid residues, including Arg80, Cys418, and Ser412, within the binding pocket. These interactions contributed to its strong binding affinity and its highest potency by increasing hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic stabilisation. Furthermore, ortho‐ and para‐substitutions favoured optimal orientation within the active site, facilitating more favourable ligand‐receptor interactions. The strong correlation between the in vitro cytotoxicity and in silico docking results identified compound 9a as a promising lead for further development and structural optimisation. Overall, the study highlights the therapeutic potential of triazole–tetrazole hybrids as selective and potent scaffolds for anticancer drug design, as shown in Figure  (Vellaiyan et al. ).

Reddy et al. designed and synthesised a novel series of indole–tetrazole‐based aromatic amides and assessed their anticancer efficacy through both in vitro and in silico investigations. The molecular hybridisation strategy integrated indole, tetrazole, and amide pharmacophores to exploit their reported anticancer properties, enhanced lipophilicity, and favourable drug‐like stability, respectively. Among the developed derivatives, compound 10a, bearing a para‐cyanophenyl substituent, emerged as the most potent candidate. It exhibited predominant cytotoxicity against MCF‐7 (breast), A549 (lung), and SKOV3 (ovarian) cancer cell lines, with IC50 values of 4.15, 3.54, and 5.22 μM, respectively, outperforming the activity of standard drug etoposide. In a tubulin polymerisation inhibition assay, compound 10a demonstrated an IC50 value of 0.34 μM, representing more than a threefold increase in potency over the reference inhibitor, combretastatin A‐4. SAR analysis highlighted the crucial role of electron‐withdrawing substituents, such as the cyano group, which remarkably enhanced biological activity by strengthening molecular interactions with the target protein. However, dihalogenated analogues exhibited comparatively lower potency, following the activity trend Cl > F > Br. Molecular docking studies further confirmed strong tubulin binding, thereby correlating with in vitro potency. The docking of the compounds against α‐, β‐tubulin (PDB ID: 1SA0) revealed the highest binding energy of −9.45 kcal/mol, with a strong hydrogen‐bond interaction with ASN329 for compound 10a. Furthermore, in silico ADMET prediction confirmed favourable pharmacokinetic characteristics, including high intestinal absorption (93%), metabolic compatibility, absence of AMES toxicity, and compliance with all five major drug‐likeness criteria. Collectively, these findings underline compound 10a as a promising lead scaffold for future anticancer drug development targeting tubulin polymerisation (Figure ) (Reddy et al. ).

Olejarz et al. designed and synthesised a series of tetrazole hybrids and evaluated their anticancer potential through comprehensive biological and computational studies. The study was based on the structural modification of 3,3′‐dimethoxybenzidine, a carcinogenic precursor of azo dyes, into tetrazole‐containing derivatives with potential therapeutic applications. Incorporation of the tetrazole moiety was intended to improve lipophilicity, bioavailability, and metabolic stability, while structural modification of the benzidine scaffold aimed to minimise toxicity and enhance anticancer activity. The target compounds were synthesised via thiourea intermediates, followed by cyclisation using sodium azide and HgCl2. Among the synthesised derivatives, compound 11a, bearing a benzyl substituent, emerged as the most potent analogue. It exhibited pronounced cytotoxicity against HeLa and SW620 cancer cell lines with IC50 values of 20.3 and 21.3 μM, respectively, while demonstrating low toxicity toward normal HaCaT keratinocytes, resulting in a favourable selectivity index of 1.98. Flow cytometric analysis further confirmed that compound 11a predominantly induced late‐stage apoptosis in cancer cells, with minimal effects on normal cells. Although cisplatin and doxorubicin displayed superior selectivity indices in HeLa and SW620 cells compared with the reference drugs. Molecular docking studies demonstrated that compound 11a possessed a high binding affinity towards the Bcl‐2 protein, comparable to that of the co‐crystallised ligand and established stable hydrogen bonding and π‐π interactions with key amino acid residues in the Bcl‐2 binding site. Furthermore, in silico toxicity assessment predicted low mutagenicity and acceptable acute toxicity relative to cisplatin and doxorubicin. ELISA assays revealed that compound 11a reduced IL‐6 production by more than 30% in HTB‐140 cells and approximately 28% in SW620 cells. To further elucidate the mechanism of action, western blot analysis was performed using compound 11b, bearing a 2‐phenylethyl group, in HeLa and SW620 cell lines. The results demonstrated a marked downregulation of Bcl‐2 protein expression in both cell lines, providing strong mechanistic evidence for apoptosis induction through Bcl‐2 inhibition. Concluding the findings, it was established that compound 11b emerged as the most convincing mechanistic lead while compound 11a emerged as the most potent tetrazole hybrid. These results highlight compound 11a as a selective and promising anticancer lead targeting Bcl‐2, with potential anti‐inflammatory effects as well (Figure ) (Olejarz et al. ).

Manwar et al. followed a [3 + 2] cycloaddition of azide‐nitrile for the synthesis of two series of substituted aryl tetrazoles (12 and 13) and screened them for anticancer activity. Among the synthesised analogues, compound 13a exhibited the most potent cytotoxic activity against the MDA‐MB‐231 cell line with an IC50 value of 69.99 μg/mL, while compound 12a was identified as the most potent cytotoxic agent against the HT‐29 cell line with an IC50 value of 86.73 μg/mL, respectively. Structure–activity relationship analysis revealed that both the nature and position of substituents on the aromatic ring, as well as the substitution on the acetamide nitrogen, markedly influenced the cytotoxic activity. The presence of electron‐withdrawing substituents at the para position of the benzene ring enhanced cytotoxicity. Moreover, ortho substitution on acetamide improved selectivity. These experimental findings were further substantiated by in silico studies, which showed that compound 12a demonstrated strong binding affinity for the active site of the 5FI2 receptor, with a binding free energy of −9.09 kcal/mol. Authors also pointed out that compound 12a formed key hydrogen bonds with LEU A:226 and GLY A:229, whereas 13a displayed hydrophobic interactions with a variety of amino acid residues. The superior binding profile of compound 1a was consistent with its pronounced cytotoxic activity against HT‐29 cells. Results of the density functional theory (DFT) analysis revealed that compound 12a possessed the highest dipole moment and remarkable hyperpolarizability among the evaluated derivatives. All these findings collectively indicate that compound 12a has significant potential as a lead compound for further structural optimisation aimed at enhancing its potency towards the 5FI2 receptor (Figure ) (Manwar et al. ).

A series of tetrazole hybrids have been synthesised via multicomponent Ugi reactions, and their prospective anticancer properties were studied and reported by Prabhu et al. The molecular design incorporated a tetrazole core, as a cis‐amide bioisostere, to enhance metabolic stability and mimic peptide bonds, while the sulfonamide moiety was introduced owing to its well‐established role as a pharmacophore in kinase inhibitors and anticancer agents. Among the compounds tested, 3a, bearing a chlorine substituent at the para position, emerged as the most promising analogue against ER‐positive MCF‐7 cells, with moderate potency against triple‐negative MDA‐MB‐231 cells. Functional assays, including colony formation and Hoechst staining, demonstrated that 14a induced G1‐phase cell‐cycle arrest and apoptosis. A strong binding affinity of 14a towards CDK6 was revealed by molecular docking analysis, with a Glide score of −7.4 kcal/mol. A specific interaction with the Val101 residue, along with notable affinity for Erα, was also observed, providing direct evidence of its dual‐targeting potential. Furthermore, pharmacophore analysis matched the experimentally observed cytotoxicity in MCF‐7 cells. SAR analysis suggested that electron‐withdrawing substituents play a crucial role in modulating the anticancer activity, but chlorine at the para position optimises binding to CDK‐6. Moreover, the biological investigations demonstrated that compound 14a significantly inhibited cell invasiveness in a time‐dependent manner, supporting its ER‐dependent antiproliferative and anti‐invasive activity. Additionally, ADME profiling using the QikProp module of Schrödinger software displayed that six of the synthesised compounds possessed favourable drug‐like properties, thereby highlighting their potential for further development as anticancer agents (Figure ) (Prabhu et al. ).

The antiproliferative activity of tetrazole derivatives is strongly influenced by the nature of aromatic substituents and the pharmacophore attached to the tetrazole nucleus. Electron‐withdrawing groups such as cyano, nitro and chloro consistently enhanced cytotoxicity by improving electronic interactions with biological targets. Hybridisation of the tetrazole scaffold with indole, triazole, aromatic amides, flurbiprofen and benzyl‐containing moieties significantly improved antiproliferative activity against multiple cancer cell lines. Compounds capable of forming multiple hydrogen bonds, π‐π stacking, and hydrophobic interactions with proteins such as tubulin, CDK‐6, CYP2C9, and Bcl‐2 exhibited superior activity. Additionally, these structural modifications promoted apoptosis, induced cell‐cycle arrest, reduced cancer cell invasion, and provided favourable pharmacokinetic profiles, indicating that tetrazole‐based molecular hybridisation is an effective strategy for developing potent anticancer agents (Figure ).

Labib et al. reported the design, synthesis, and anti‐inflammatory evaluation of four series of novel tetrazole‐based derivatives. The molecular design strategy involved replacing the sulfonamide SO2NH2 pharmacophore of celecoxib with a tetrazole ring to retain the acidic functionality required for hydrogen‐bonding interactions while potentially improving the pharmacological profile. In addition, diverse central scaffolds, including chalcone, isoxazole, pyrazole, and N‐acetylpyrazoles, were incorporated to investigate their influence on COX‐2 inhibitory activity and selectivity. Most of the synthesised derivatives exhibited potent and selective COX‐2 inhibition, with IC50 values ranging from 0.039 to 0.31 μM. Among them, compounds 16b, 16c, 17b, 17c, 18b, and 18c demonstrated the highest anti‐inflammatory activity, whereas compounds 17c and 18c displayed remarkable COX‐2 selectivity indices (SI = 297.67–317.95), surpassing that of celecoxib (SI = 282.22). The in vivo anti‐inflammatory evaluation further corroborated these findings, with 16c and 18c showing 30%–42% and 28%–40% inhibition of carrageenan‐induced paw oedema, respectively, together with pronounced suppression of prostaglandin E2 (81%–82%) and plasma protein binding comparable to that of celecoxib. Cytokine profiling revealed that trimethoxy‐substituted analogues (16c, 17c, 18c) were more effective than their dimethoxy counterparts in reducing TNF‐α and IL‐6 levels, with compound 18c exhibiting activity comparable to celecoxib. However, ulcerogenic assessment showed that compound 18b exhibited the highest gastric toxicity (UI = 0.55), a finding further supported by histopathological examination, which revealed severe mucosal damage, whereas the remaining derivatives induced only mild lesions. Molecular docking studies revealed that compound 18b possessed the strongest binding affinity toward COX‐2 (−16.20 kcal/mol) and formed key hydrogen‐bond interactions with residues His90, Tyr385, and Ser530 within the enzyme active site. SAR analysis highlighted the critical role of methoxy substitution, where trimethoxy analogues consistently outperformed dimethoxy and monomethoxy derivatives in COX‐2 inhibition, selectivity, and anti‐inflammatory activity. The tetrazole ring provided acidic functionality for H‐bonding. Five‐ membered heterocycles, isoxazole and pyrazole, have improved fit compared to the chalcone scaffold, thereby contributing to enhanced inhibitory potency, as shown in Figure  (Labib et al. ).

Chaban et al. designed and synthesised two series of thiadiazole‐tetrazole hybrids (19 and 20) and evaluated their anti‐inflammatory potential through in vivo and in silico studies. The molecular design was based on incorporating a tetrazole ring, a well‐established bioisostere of the carboxylate group, linked to a 2‐aminothiazole scaffold, a privileged pharmacophore in medicinal chemistry. The anti‐inflammatory activity of the synthesised compounds was assessed using the carrageenan‐induced rat paw oedema model at an oral dose of 50 mg/kg, with ibuprofen serving as the reference standard. Among the synthesised derivatives, compound 19a exhibited pronounced anti‐inflammatory activity, producing 40.5% inhibition of paw oedema, which was comparable to that of the standard drug ibuprofen. Additionally, compounds 20a, 20b, and 20c demonstrated significant inhibition of oedema, with inhibition values of 41%, 44.8%, and 40%, respectively. Molecular docking studies further revealed that compound 20b possessed the highest binding affinity towards the COX‐2 active site, with a binding free energy of −11.03 kcal/mol. The ligand established key hydrogen‐bond interactions with Tyr335, Leu352, and Arg513, together with hydrophobic contacts involving Val532, Leu352, and Ala527, supporting its binding profile. SAR analysis indicated that sulfanyl‐linked tetrazole derivatives consistently exhibited superior anti‐inflammatory activity compared with their aryltetrazolyl counterparts, suggesting that the sulfanyl linker enhances binding affinity within the COX‐2 active site. Furthermore, the presence of lipophilic substituents such as isopropyl, dimethyl and benzyl groups contributed to enhanced anti‐inflammatory efficacy, whereas the introduction of halogen substituents generally resulted in diminished activity. Overall, these findings identified thiadiazole–tetrazole hybrids as promising lead scaffolds for further development of selective COX‐2 inhibitors with improved therapeutic potential (Figure ) (Chaban et al. ).

Altıntop and coworkers reported a three‐step synthetic protocol for the preparation of a novel series of tetrazole–hydrazone derivatives and evaluated their anti‐inflammatory potential by assessing COX inhibition. The molecular design was based on the hybridisation of tetrazole and hydrazone pharmacophores to exploit their reported anti‐inflammatory properties and to generate compounds with enhanced COX‐inhibitory activity. The synthesised derivatives were subsequently screened for COX‐1 and COX‐2 inhibition using an in vitro colourimetric assay. Among the twelve synthesised compounds, 21a and 21b emerged as the most potent inhibitors of COX‐1 and COX‐2, respectively. Compound 21a inhibited COX‐1 by 40.88%, while compound 21b exhibited 42.38% inhibition of COX‐2, relative to the reference inhibitors SC‐560 and rofecoxib, respectively. SAR analysis revealed that the substituent at the N1‐position of the tetrazole ring plays a decisive role in modulating isoenzyme selectivity. Incorporation of the 1‐methyl‐1H‐tetrazole moiety favoured selective COX‐1 inhibition, whereas replacement with the sterically bulkier 1‐phenyl‐1H‐tetrazole group shifted the inhibitory profile toward COX‐2 selectivity, suggesting that increasing steric bulk at the N1‐position favours selective COX‐2 binding. Furthermore, the nature of the benzylidene substituent markedly influenced biological activity. Derivatives bearing piperidinyl or morpholinyl substituents displayed superior COX inhibitory activity, whereas incorporation of imidazolyl or triazolyl groups resulted in diminished potency (Figure ) (Altıntop et al. ).

Tetrazole derivatives demonstrated potent anti‐inflammatory activity primarily through selective inhibition of COX‐2. SAR studies revealed that trimethoxy‐substituted analogues exhibited significantly greater COX‐2 inhibition and selectivity than mono‐ or dimethoxy derivatives, while also producing greater suppression of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF‐, IL‐6. Structural modification at the N1 position of the tetrazole ring significantly influenced enzyme selectivity, with increased steric bulk shifting activity from COX‐1 toward COX‐2 inhibition. Furthermore, molecular hybridisation with hydrazone and thiadiazole scaffolds enhanced anti‐inflammatory efficacy by increasing hydrogen‐bonding and hydrophobic interactions with key COX‐2 residues, thereby improving potency and selectivity. The schematic representation is given in Figure .

Oulouş et al. reported the design, synthesis, and characterisation of a novel series of pyrazole–tetrazole hybrids, which were evaluated for their vasorelaxant and α‐amylase inhibitory activities. The molecular design was based on the hybridisation of pyrazole and tetrazole pharmacophores connected via a methylene linker, while systematic variation of substituents on the tetrazole ring was employed to investigate steric and electronic effects on biological activity. All synthesised compounds exhibited moderate to significant vasorelaxant activity (26%–67%) in isolated rat aorta assays, with verapamil and carbachol serving as reference standards. Among the series, compound 23a demonstrated the highest vasorelaxant effect, with an E
max of 67.67%, compared with verapamil (E
max of 91.62%) and carbachol (E
max of 85.52%). Molecular docking studies within the binding pocket of the voltage‐gated L‐type calcium channel further supported the experimental findings, revealing that compound 23a possessed a binding energy of −91.7 kcal/mol, compared with −108.27 kcal/mol for verapamil. The compound established key interactions with the amino acid residues Leu652 and Asn649, suggesting a favourable binding mode. Furthermore, the synthesised compounds were evaluated for their α‐amylase inhibitory activity with IC50 values ranging from 0.128 to 0.361 mg/mL. Notably, compound 22a exhibited the most potent inhibitory activity (IC50 = 0.128 mg/mL), which was comparable to that of the reference inhibitor acarbose (IC50 = 0.121 mg/mL). SAR studies revealed that incorporating an isopropyl substituent on the pyrazole ring enhanced lipophilicity, thereby improving the pharmacokinetic profile. Moreover, the nature of the side chain significantly influenced biological activity; for example, pyridyl, benzyl, and methyl groups conferred vasorelaxant, α‐amylase, and moderate dual activity, respectively, as shown in Figure  (Oulous, Dip, et al. ).

Fadaly et al. reported the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of two series of novel vicinal diaryl pyrazole derivatives incorporating tetrazole and urea pharmacophores. The design strategy was based on hybridisation, integrating the key structural features of celecoxib, losartan and captopril into a single scaffold. The Y‐shaped pyrazole core was derived from the celecoxib framework, while the tetrazole moiety served as a carboxylate bioisostere, and the urea linker provided additional hydrogen‐bonding interactions that contributed to angiotensin‐converting enzyme (ACE) suppression. The synthesised compounds exhibited promising ACE‐inhibitory activity, with IC50 values ranging from 0.078 to 7.422 μM, compared with perindopril (IC50 = 0.048 μM). Among the series, compounds 24a and 24b exhibited the highest inhibitory potency, with IC50 values of 0.078 and 0.094 μM, respectively. Based on their potent in vitro activity, these compounds were further evaluated for antihypertensive efficacy using the L‐NAME‐induced hypertension model. Treatment with perindopril and compound 24a significantly reduced systolic blood pressure by 18.6% and 20.7%, respectively, whereas compound 24b did not produce any significant antihypertensive effect. Furthermore, serum nitric oxide (NO) levels were markedly elevated following treatment with perindopril, 24a, and 24b, increasing by 159.8%, 345.8%, and 183.2%, respectively. All three treatments also attenuated inflammatory responses, as evidenced by reduced expression of NF‐κB p65 (−0.34, −0.62, and −0.22 fold) and p38‐MAPK (−0.45, −0.53, and −0.24 fold) for perindopril, 24a, and 24b, respectively. Histopathological examination further confirmed that perindopril and compound 24a effectively ameliorated L‐NAME‐induced cardiac tissue damage. Toxicological evaluation of the lead compounds (24a and 24b) demonstrated that liver and kidney function biomarkers (AST, ALT, ALP, and creatinine) remained within normal physiological limits, indicating a favourable safety profile. Furthermore, molecular docking studies revealed that the active compounds adopted binding conformations within the angiotensin II receptor comparable to those of losartan. Notably, the tetrazole ring engaged in hydrogen bonding with Thr358A, while the phenyl–tetrazole moiety occupied an extended region of the receptor binding pocket within the docking grid, thereby contributing to stable ligand–receptor interactions. SAR analysis indicated that the presence of bulky para‐substituted aryl groups enhanced lipophilicity and oral bioavailability while promoting dual ACE‐inhibitory and antihypertensive activities. These findings were further corroborated by both in silico molecular docking studies and in vitro biological evaluations (Figure ) (Fadaly et al. ).

Singh et al. reported the design and synthesis of a series of tetrazole‐containing 1,5‐benzothiazepine hybrids, which were evaluated for angiotensin‐converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitory activity through both in silico and in vitro studies. Hybridisation of tetrazole, a bioisostere of the carboxylate, and 1,5‐benzothiazepine, a cardiovascular modulator with ACE‐inhibitory potential, underlies the design strategy. All synthesised compounds exhibited IC50 values ranging from 7 to 38.3 μM and demonstrated significantly higher ACE inhibitory activity than the reference drug Captopril (IC50 = 56.3 μM). Among the series, compound 25b emerged as the most potent inhibitor, with an IC50 value of 7 μM. Molecular docking studies performed against human ACE (PDB: 1UZF) further supported its strong binding affinity (−9.65 kcal/mol), revealing key hydrogen bonding interactions with Gln245 and a carbon–hydrogen bond with Ser319. The tetrazole ring provides multiple hydrogen‐bond donors/acceptors. Additionally, compound 25b exhibited stabilising π‐alkyl interactions with residues Val343 and His347, as well as interactions involving Glu340, His477, and His317. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis indicated that tetrazole‐bearing 1,5‐benzothiazepines substituted with methoxy (25a) and chloro groups (25b) at the para position displayed enhanced ACE inhibitory activity. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the potential of tetrazole–benzothiazepine hybrids as promising scaffolds for the development of effective ACE inhibitors (Figure ) (Singh and Suman ).

Tetrazole derivatives displayed promising cardioprotective activity through ACE inhibition and vasorelaxant effects. Incorporation of tetrazole into pyrazole, benzothiazepine, diaryl pyrazole, and biphenyl scaffolds markedly improved antihypertensive activity. Para‐methoxy and para‐chloro substituents on aromatic rings enhanced ACE inhibitory potency, whereas ortho‐positioning of the tetrazole ring on biphenyl analogues increased lipophilicity and biological activity compared with corresponding carboxylic acid analogues. Strong hydrogen‐bond interactions with catalytic ACE residues, together with π‐alkyl interactions, contributed significantly to enzyme inhibition (Figure ).

Sartans, or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), constitute an important class of antihypertensive agents characterised by a common basic pharmacophoric framework comprising a biphenyl moiety bearing a tetrazole group, typically at the ortho position (Sörgel et al. ). These agents exert their antihypertensive effects primarily through selective antagonism of the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor, thereby inhibiting the physiological actions of angiotensin II (Schramm et al. ). Activation of AT1 receptors promotes vasoconstriction, stimulates aldosterone secretion, and increases sodium and water retention, collectively contributing to increased vascular resistance and blood pressure. Blockade of AT1 receptors consequently produces vasodilation and reduces aldosterone‐mediated fluid retention, thereby lowering blood pressure (Georgiou et al. ). Most sartans are administered orally and are available as conventional tablet formulations, with some agents also available as oral suspensions or sachets. Their pharmacokinetic profiles may vary considerably, with reported half‐lives ranging from approximately 2 to 24 h, depending on the individual drug. Losartan, the first marketed sartan, was introduced in 1995 (Bhardwaj ). It exhibits potent and selective antagonism at the AT1 receptor, with an IC50 of approximately 20 nM for inhibition of angiotensin II binding. However, several structurally diverse ARBs, such as valsartan, candesartan, and irbesartan, were developed and introduced into clinical use (Ladhari et al. ). Structural modifications of the prototypical sartan scaffold have generated both heterocyclic and non‐heterocyclic AT1R antagonists. For example, zolasartan is a chlorinated, non‐peptide AT1R antagonist containing an imidazole ring, whereas abitesartan and valsartan lack the imidazole ring characteristic of losartan and instead incorporate amino acid‐derived structural elements (Vyas and Ghate ; Adams and Trudeau ). Valsartan exhibits potent AT1 receptor antagonism, while irbesartan possesses a relatively prolonged duration of action compared with losartan and valsartan. Fimasartan represents another non‐peptide antagonist developed for the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. In clinical studies, administration of higher doses of fimasartan (360 mg/day) was associated with an increased incidence of dizziness and headache in a small number of patients; other reported adverse effects included diarrhoea, syncope and cold feet extremities (Pradhan et al. ).

The continued development of structurally diverse sartans has contributed to their extensive clinical application in the management of hypertension and related cardiovascular disorders. From a structural perspective, the biphenyl‐tetrazole pharmacophore and its modifications have played an important role in modulating receptor affinity, pharmacokinetic properties, and duration of action. Beyond the clinically established sartans, extensive research has focused on the structural modification of the tetrazole‐biphenyl scaffold to develop novel AT1R antagonists with improved antihypertensive activity and optimised pharmacological properties. Representative biphenyl‐based tetrazole derivatives with remarkable antihypertensive properties reported in the literature are summarised below.

Bayannavar et al. reported the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of four series of triazolyl–biphenyl hybrids for angiotensin‐converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition. The novel biphenyl‐triazole scaffolds were designed with ortho‐substituents to mimic pharmacophores in sartans. Among the sixteen evaluated compounds, derivatives 26a–d and 27a–d, bearing a tetrazole moiety, exhibited notable ACE inhibitory activity, with inhibition values of 67.45% and 67.50%, respectively. Importantly, tetrazole‐containing analogues demonstrated superior activity compared to their non‐tetrazole counterparts. Notably, compound 26a exhibited enhanced ACE inhibition (84% at 50 μg), surpassing that of the standard Lisinopril. Results of molecular docking studies against human ACE (PDB ID: 1O86) revealed that compound 26a formed multiple hydrogen‐bonding interactions within the ACE active site, involving key residues such as Tyr520, Lys511, Ala356, and Arg522. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis indicated that ortho‐substitution of the tetrazole ring on the biphenyl scaffold significantly increased lipophilicity (approximately 10‐fold) compared to corresponding carboxylate analogues, thereby enhancing biological activity. Moreover, the triazolone moiety serves as a hydrogen‐bond acceptor, stabilising ligand‐enzyme interactions. Furthermore, compound 26d demonstrated strong binding affinity, forming up to 9 hydrogen bonds within the ACE active site and achieving a high docking score (−10.81 kcal/mol), indicating a stable enzyme–inhibitor complex as represented in Figure  (Bayannavar et al. ).

Sanket Parshuram Zanjad and co‐workers designed and synthesised a series of diamino acid‐functionalised biphenyl tetrazole derivatives and evaluated their antihypertensive activity using a renovascular hypertensive rat model. The molecular design strategy involved incorporating the tetrazole moiety, owing to its favourable lipophilicity, metabolic stability, and hydrogen‐bond‐accepting capability, into the biphenyl scaffold, which is present in established antihypertensive agents such as losartan, valsartan, and telmisartan. Furthermore, functionalisation with diamino acids was employed to enhance aqueous solubility and biocompatibility, and to potentially facilitate targeted delivery. The synthesised derivatives were evaluated in vivo by measuring the reduction in systolic blood pressure relative to the control group. Among the tested derivatives, compounds 28a, 28b and 28c exhibited pronounced antihypertensive activity, producing reductions in systolic blood pressure of 33.67, 34.74 and 35.58 mmHg, respectively, compared with 42.77 mmHg for telmisartan. SAR analysis indicated that the incorporation of hydrophobic amino acids such as Ala, Phe, and Leu favoured antihypertensive activity, presumably through favourable interactions within the AT1R binding pocket, whereas the introduction of flexible, small, or polar amino acids resulted in reduced activity. The tetrazole moiety was found to be essential for maintaining activity, while incorporation of isonipecotic acid linker provided conformational rigidity and optimal spatial separation between the biphenyl and amino acid substituents, as shown in Figure  (Zanjad et al. ).

Masood et al. designed, synthesised, characterised, and biologically evaluated a series of ester derivatives based on 2‐(N‐((2‐(2H‐tetrazole‐5‐yl)‐[1,1‐biphenyl]‐4yl)‐methyl) pentanamido)‐3‐methyl butanoic acid. The design strategy was based on structural modification of valsartan, an established antihypertensive agent, through esterification with various phenolic moieties to modulate lipophilicity, absorption, and enzyme‐binding interactions. The synthesised compounds were subjected to in vitro studies for their antioxidant activity, urease inhibition, and antibacterial assay.
