Among the tested compounds, 29a exhibited the highest antioxidant and urease inhibitory activities, whereas all derivatives were inactive against the evaluated Gram+ and Gram‐ bacterial strains. Antihypertensive activity was subsequently assessed using an in vivo rat model, in which compound 29a reduced systolic blood pressure to 69.21 mmHg, compared with 82.41 mmHg for valsartan (Figure ). Furthermore, compound 29a demonstrated the highest inhibition of phenylephrine‐induced contraction (76.4%) in an isolated aorta assay. SAR analysis suggested that the simultaneous presence of methoxy and aldehyde substituents contributed to enhanced antihypertensive activity. In contrast, the incorporation of electron‐donating and electron‐withdrawing groups preferentially enhanced antioxidant and urease inhibitory activities, respectively (Masood et al. ).

The reported derivatives retain the core biphenyl‐tetrazole pharmacophore of clinically approved sartans (losartan, valsartan, candesartan, olmesartan) while modifying the terminal moiety to alter target selectivity or potency. In the triazole/triazolone series (26a–d, 27a–d), the sartans' imidazole/carboxylate head‐group was replaced with a triazolone or diphenyl‐triazole ring, shifting activity from AT1 antagonism toward ACE inhibition; ortho‐tetrazole substitution increased lipophilicity ~10‐fold over carboxylate analogues, and para‐methoxy/bromo substitution gave the strongest ACE inhibition, with 26a surpassing lisinopril. The diamino‐acid derivatives (28a–c) retained the AT1 ‐directed mechanism but introduced a piperidine‐isonipecotic acid linker bearing hydrophobic amino acids (Ala, Phe, Leu) to improve solubility and biocompatibility; this series showed antihypertensive activity but fell short of telmisartan, reflecting a trade‐off between drug‐likeness and potency. The most conservative modification, valsartan‐ester (29a), esterified the parent's carboxylic acid with a methoxy/aldehyde‐substituted phenol and, notably, exceeded valsartan's own antihypertensive efficacy and vasorelaxant activity (Figure ).

Hung et al. designed, synthesised, and evaluated two series (30 and 31) of novel theophylline derivatives fused with a tetrazole moiety for their anti‐Alzheimer's potential. Theophylline (methylxanthine), a CNS‐active, blood–brain barrier‐permeable scaffold, has previously been reported to possess acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition and anti‐amyloid properties. The hybridisation of theophylline core linked to tetrazole‐bearing phenyl derivatives via alkylamide or alkylester linkers aimed to bridge CAS and PAS of AChE gorge, exploiting π‐π stacking with aromatic residues. The compounds were evaluated for their anti‐Alzheimer's potential by monitoring the extent of AChE inhibition. Among the 17 derivatives investigated, compound 30a emerged as the most potent AChE inhibitor, with an IC50 of 15.68 μM, and exhibited moderate inhibitory activity against β‐secretase (BACE‐1). However, it was noted that the theophylline hybrids exhibited poor performance over the BACE‐1 target. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation studies revealed that the synthesised derivatives bind rigidly with the AChE active site, where the binding was predominantly stabilised by van der Waals interactions, involving π‐π stacking and side‐chain contacts. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies demonstrated that AChE inhibitory activity was significantly influenced by substitution at the 4th position of the phenyl ring, with the 4‐bromo substituent conferring the highest activity. In contrast, increasing the linker length to five or six carbon atoms reduced AChE inhibition, while introducing an electron‐donating methoxy (OCH3) group further decreased AChE inhibitory potency. Furthermore, shifting the tetrazole from the N‐2 to the N‐1 isomer did not enhance the activity, and conversion of the alkylamine linker to an alkylester linker likewise failed to improve the inhibitory potential. Moreover, the optimal linker length of 4 carbons displayed potent activity. Molecular docking studies further revealed that the lead compound formed favourable π‐π stacking interactions with key activity‐site residues, including Tpr86, Tpr286 and Tyr341, with docking scores ranging from −14 to −19 kcal/mol. Moreover, rules indicating favourable drug‐likeness and oral bioavailability thereby support their potential as promising anti‐Alzheimer's agents (Figure ) (Hung et al. ).

Dansena et al. proposed a novel strategy for the design and synthesis of tetrazole‐thiazole‐based pharmacophores for AD treatment. The rationale behind this design strategy is to merge pharmacophoric features into a single scaffold to achieve multi‐target activity. Both the tetrazole and thiazole moieties are known for their AChE inhibitory activity, and the choice of an amide linker is due to its flexibility, which allows simultaneous binding at the catalytic active site and the peripheral anionic site of AChE. Among all the synthesised compounds, 30a exhibited the most potent inhibitory activity, with an IC50 of 6.02 μM, indicating mixed‐type AChE inhibition. The compound effectively chelated Cu2+, Zn2+, and Fe2+ ions, indicating its potential to modulate metal‐induced neurotoxicity. Molecular docking studies revealed that the binding energy of 32a was −51.3645 kcal/mol, compared with the reference donepezil (−56.8743 kcal/mol). Interactions with residues such as Tyr341, Tyr124, Tyr337, Trp86, His447, Phe338, and Arg296 validated the compound's high docking score. In addition, in silico ADME and toxicity predictions indicated that 32a exhibits acceptable drug‐likeness and moderate tolerability, thereby highlighting its potential as a lead compound for further anti‐Alzheimer's drug development. The SAR studies indicate that halogen substitution confers moderate inhibitory activity. However, the introduction of para‐nitro at the thiazole‐linked phenyl ring, along with ortho‐hydroxy group on the tetrazole phenyl ring, significantly enhances inhibitory potency. Further mechanistic studies suggested that compound 32a acted as a mixed‐type inhibitor, binding both PAS and CAS. Lineweaver‐Burk plots, moreover, confirmed the dual‐binding nature (Figure ) (Dansena et al. ).

The neuroprotective activity of tetrazole derivatives largely depends on aromatic substitution and hybrid scaffold design. Para‐bromo substitution on the phenyl ring enhanced acetylcholinesterase inhibition, while simultaneous incorporation of a para‐nitro group on the thiazole‐linked phenyl ring and an ortho‐hydroxyl group on the tetrazole phenyl ring significantly increased anti‐Alzheimer activity. An optimal four‐carbon linker favoured effective binding to both the CAS and PAS of AChE, while longer alkyl chains diminished activity. Further, incorporation of complementary heterocycles such as theophylline and thiazole afforded multitarget‐directed ligands with enhanced AChE inhibition and metal chelating ability, thereby improving their neuroprotective potential (Figure ).

Ostrovskii et al. reported the design, synthesis, and antidiabetic evaluation of non‐annulated polynuclear tetrazole hybrids. The molecular design was based on the incorporation of a tetrazole ring, a well‐recognised bioisostere of carboxylate and cis‐amide functionalities, to enhance metabolic stability and hydrogen‐bonding capacity. The hybridisation strategy involved conjugating the tetrazole moiety with diverse heterocyclic frameworks to achieve multitarget pharmacological activity. In addition, the acetamide linker was introduced to provide conformational flexibility and appropriate polarity, thereby facilitating favourable non‐covalent interactions within enzyme‐binding pockets. The compounds were synthesised using 2‐(5‐phenyl‐2H‐tetrazol‐2‐yl)acetyl chloride as a versatile acylating agent and were developed to target key mechanisms involved in type 2 diabetes, particularly α‐glucosidase inhibition and PPAR‐γ modulation. Among the synthesised derivatives, compound 33a emerged as the most promising candidate, with a probability (P

a
 = 0.751) of inhibiting α‐glucosidase activity as assessed by PASS software. SAR studies suggested that the tetrazole moiety contributes significantly to biological activity by providing enhanced hydrogen‐bonding capacity and metabolic stability, while the acetamide linker enables efficient conjugation with additional heterocyclic pharmacophores. Molecular docking studies further supported these findings, with compound 33a exhibiting strong binding affinity toward the PPAR‐γ receptor (−8.8 kcal/mol), followed by compound 33b (−7.8 kcal/mol). The favourable binding was attributed to multiple non‐covalent interactions mediated by tetrazole and pyrimidine/triazole fragments within the receptor‐binding site. In vivo evaluation using an adrenaline‐induced hyperglycaemia model in rats demonstrated that compound 33a significantly reduced blood glucose levels, with efficacy comparable to metformin. At a dose of 100 mg/kg, compound 33a reduced blood glucose concentration to 8.00 mmol/L after 2 h, compared to 8.60 mmol/L for metformin at 300 mg/kg. However, in a separate mouse model, compound 33a showed comparatively weaker activity, with a blood glucose level of 35.83 mmol/L, whereas metformin exhibited a level of 28.93 mmol/L under similar conditions. Despite this variation in in vivo efficacy, the synthesised tetrazole hybrids also demonstrated promising anti‐obesity potential, indicating that further optimisation and scaffold repurposing may represent a valuable direction for future research. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of polynuclear tetrazole hybrids, particularly compound 33a, as promising candidates for further development as antidiabetic agents (Figure ) (Ostrovskii et al. ).

Oulouş and coworkers reported the design, synthesis, and antidiabetic evaluation of tetrapodal pyrazole–tetrazole hybrids, which were assessed for their α‐amylase inhibitory activity. All synthesised derivatives demonstrated IC50 values ranging from 7.7 × 10−4 to 11.10 × 10−4 mg/mL, compared to the standard acarbose (IC50 = 26.10 × 10−2 mg/mL). Among the series, compound 34d emerged as the most potent inhibitor, with a significantly lower IC50 value (11 × 10−4 mg/mL). Molecular docking studies further corroborated the experimental findings by demonstrating strong binding of compound 34d within the α‐amylase active site (PDB ID: 1OSE), with a high binding affinity (up to −128.05 kcal/mol). The ligand established key interactions with the catalytic residues Asp197, Glu233, and Asp300, in addition to hydrogen‐bonding and hydrophobic interaction involving Tyr151, His201, Lys200, Ile235, and Leu162, thereby contributing to enhanced binding stability within the enzyme active site. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis indicated that the presence of an isopropyl substituent in compound 34d plays a crucial role in enhancing α‐amylase inhibitory activity, most likely by promoting favourable hydrophobic interactions and improving the conformational fit of the ligand within the enzyme‐binding pocket owing to its branched structure. In contrast, the incorporation of a hydroxylated side chain reduced inhibitory potency, suggesting the increased polarity destabilises the enzyme‐ligand complex. Furthermore, the influence of N‐substitution on biological activity followed the order: isopropyl > propyl > aromatic > hydroxylated. Collectively, these findings highlight compound 34d as a promising lead scaffold for the development of potent α‐amylase inhibitors to manage type 2 diabetes mellitus (Figure ) (Oulous, Cherif, et al. ).

Min He et al. reported the design and synthesis of three libraries (35, 36, and 37) of 2,5‐disubstituted furan hybrids incorporating imidazole, triazole, and tetrazole moieties, which were evaluated as α‐glucosidase inhibitors for the treatment of type II diabetes. The design strategy employed a furan nucleus as the central scaffold because of its electron‐rich aromatic character, which provides a suitable framework for structural modification. The incorporation of azole moieties, including imidazole, triazole, and tetrazole, was based on their well‐established α‐glucosidase inhibitory potential, with the nitrogen‐rich heterocycles expected to enhance hydrogen‐bonding interactions and electronic conjugation, thereby improving enzyme‐binding affinity. Among the tetrazole‐containing derivatives, compound 37a exhibited the highest potency, with an IC50 value of 4.6 μM, outperforming the standard Acarbose. Kinetic studies revealed that acarbose acts as a competitive inhibitor (K
i = 557.2 μM), whereas compound 37a exhibits non‐competitive inhibition with a significantly lower K
i of 5.1 μM. Safety evaluations in HEK293, RAW264.7, and HepG2 cell lines indicated that compound 37a has a favourable toxicity profile, supporting its potential for further development. Molecular docking analysis demonstrated that compound 37a forms key hydrogen‐bonding interactions with residues Asp69, Arg442, and Asp215 within the active site of the enzyme (PDB ID: 3AJ7). Structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies highlighted that the presence of an electron‐withdrawing group, particularly a 2‐chloro substitution on the aryl ring, enhances inhibitory activity. Moreover, the position of halogen substitution was found to influence biological activity, following the trend ortho > meta > para. Additionally, compounds 37a and 36a exhibited minimal cytotoxicity towards HEK293 and HepG2 cell lines. Overall, these findings identify compounds 36a and 37a as promising and safe α‐glucosidase inhibitors, providing valuable scaffolds for further optimisation in antidiabetic drug development (Figure ) (He et al. ).

Selvarasu et al. reported the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of a series of 1‐aryl‐N‐tosyl‐1H‐tetrazole‐5‐carboxamide hybrids as potential antidiabetic agents. The design strategy was based on the incorporation of the tetrazole ring, a well‐established bioisostere of carboxylic acids, to improve bioavailability and metabolic stability. The acidic 5H‐tetrazole proton facilitates facile reaction with isocyanates, enabling the construction of diverse carboxamide derivatives. Furthermore, the introduction of the tosyl group was intended to increase the steric bulk, lipophilicity, and hydrogen‐bonding capability, while the carboxamide linkage contributes to scaffold stabilisation and mimics the key pharmacophoric features of sulfonamide‐based therapeutics. The synthesised compounds were assessed for their α‐glucosidase inhibitory potential using in vitro enzymatic assays. Among the series, compound 38a exhibited the highest potency against both α‐amylase and α‐glucosidase, with IC50 values of 59.38 and 50.76 μM, respectively, outperforming the reference drug acarbose. In vivo studies further supported these findings, where treatment with compound 38a in diabetic rats restored normal pancreatic architecture, including well‐defined acini and a normal number of islet cells. This observation was further validated by molecular docking studies, which revealed that compound 38a adopts a favourable binding orientation within the α‐glucosidase active site. The ligand established stable hydrogen‐bonding interactions with Asp960, Asp964, and Ser806, as well as π–π stacking interactions and hydrophobic contacts with Ala805, Met804, Trp812, and Ile881, thereby enhancing binding stability. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis indicated that the incorporation of an electron‐withdrawing group on the aryl ring, particularly trifluoromethyl (‐CF3) and nitro (‐NO2) substituents, significantly enhances inhibitory activity by strengthening interactions of the tetrazole moiety within the enzyme's catalytic pocket. Collectively, the favourable binding affinity and optimal binding orientation of compound 38a underscore the therapeutic potential of tetrazole‐based carboxamide hybrids as promising best in vivo efficacy, highlighting tetrazole‐based carboxamides as promising α‐glucosidase inhibitors for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (Figure ) (Selvarasu et al. ).

The tetrazole ring is the key pharmacophore responsible for enhancing antidiabetic activity by improving metabolic stability and hydrogen‐bonding interactions. Hybridisation with nitrogen‐containing heterocycles and incorporation of amide linkers further enhanced target binding and biological activity. Groups that are electron‐withdrawing in nature, particularly ‐CF3 and ‐NO2, enhanced enzyme inhibition, while moderately hydrophobic substituents such as isopropyl resulted in superior activity by promoting favourable hydrophobic interactions within the binding site (Figure ).

Mousa et al. reported the synthesis of a library of tetrazole–quinoline hybrids derived from quinaldic acid and evaluated for their antioxidant and antimicrobial activities. The design strategy was based on the pharmacological significance of the quinoline scaffold, which is well recognised for its antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. The quinoline nucleus also serves as a rigid aromatic heterocyclic framework, providing an effective platform for the introduction of structurally diverse substituents. Among the synthesised derivatives, compound 41a, bearing a 4‐bromophenyl substituent, demonstrated the highest antioxidant activity, exhibiting 61.4% DPPH radical scavenging at 100 μg/mL with an IC50 value of 59.61 μg/mL. In comparison, the reference antioxidant, ascorbic acid, displayed 91.2% radical scavenging at the same concentration with an IC50 of 6.38 μg/mL, indicating that compound 41a possessed moderate antioxidant efficacy. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis revealed that lipophilic electron‐withdrawing substituents, particularly the bromine atom in 41a, contribute significantly to enhanced antioxidant activity. Conversely, analogues containing nitro (41d) and hydroxyl (41f) substituents exhibited comparatively weaker or inconsistent antioxidant effects, suggesting that the nature of the substituent plays a critical role in modulating activity. In addition to its antioxidant potential, compound 41a exhibited remarkable antimicrobial activity. It demonstrated MIC values of 12 μg/mL against 
S. epidermidis
 and 15 μg/mL against 
Escherichia coli
, demonstrating activity comparable to the standard ampicillin (12 μg/mL against both strains). Furthermore, compound 41a displayed antifungal activity against 
C. albicans
, showing an MIC of 24 μg/mL, corresponding to approximately twofold lower potency than the standard drug metronidazole. Molecular docking studies further validated the experimental in vitro results by demonstrating favourable binding of compound 41a within the active sites of the target proteins. The compound exhibits strong binding affinities, with a docking score of −9.7 kcal/mol against 
S. epidermidis
, −9.1 kcal/mol against 
E. coli
, and −9.6 kcal/mol against Candida. Docking analysis revealed that the ligand established stable interactions through hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic contacts, and π‐π stacking with key amino acid residues, including Lys447, Trp207, and Asn121 (Mousa ). Collectively, these findings suggest that halogen substitution, particularly the incorporation of a bromine atom, plays a pivotal role in enhancing biological activity by strengthening ligand‐target interactions, thereby corroborating the experimental and computational results and validating the enhanced biological activity as determined by docking studies (Figure ).

Muhammed and co‐workers reported the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of a series of pyrrole‐3,5‐dione‐tethered tetrazole derivatives as potential urease inhibitors. The pyrrole‐2,5‐dione scaffold was selected for its well‐established pharmacological significance, while incorporating the tetrazole moiety, a recognised bioisostere of carboxylic acids, was intended to enhance binding affinity and improve metabolic stability. The synthesised compounds were evaluated in vitro for urease‐inhibitory activity, and most exhibited greater potency than the reference inhibitor, thiourea. Among the series, compound 42b containing a para‐nitro substituent, exhibited the highest activity with an IC50 value of 4.325 μM. Enzyme kinetic studies demonstrated that compound 42b functions as a non‐competitive inhibitor, with a ki value of 2.062 μM. Structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis revealed that electron‐withdrawing substituents, particularly the para‐nitro (‐NO2) group, play a crucial role in enhancing urease inhibitor activity by strengthening enzyme‐ligand interaction through favourable electronic effects. Interestingly, compound 42a, bearing an electron‐donating N, N‐diethylamino substituent, also exhibited considerable inhibitory activity (IC50 = 9.313 μM), which may be attributed to increased lipophilicity and favourable interactions within the hydrophobic regions of the enzyme. In contrast, compound 42b, possessing a hydroxyl substituent, exhibited comparatively lower activity (IC50 = 18.28 μM), suggesting that enhanced hydrophilicity may adversely affect binding affinity. Molecular docking studies further supported the non‐competitive mode of inhibition by demonstrating that the ligands preferentially bind to peripheral or allosteric regions of the enzyme. Notably, compound 42b formed hydrogen‐bonding interactions with the amino acid residues Val831, Asn131, and Arg132, along with a π‐cation interaction involving Lys128, collectively contributing to an improved hydrogen‐bonding network and hydrophobic stabilisation within the binding site. Furthermore, compounds exhibiting weak docking interactions correspondingly showed reduced in vitro inhibitory activity, indicating good agreement between the computational and experimental findings. In addition, ADMET and Pass predictions suggested favourable drug‐like characteristics, including low predicted toxicity and potential penetration into the central nervous system (CNS) (Figure ) (Muhammed Aziz and Ali Hassan ).

Tetrazole has emerged as a versatile and clinically validated heterocyclic motif in contemporary medicinal chemistry. Its ability to function as a bioisosteric replacement for carboxylic acid and other polar functionalities makes it particularly useful in medicinal chemistry. Together with its distinctive ionisation behaviour, hydrogen‐bonding capacity, and electronic properties, the tetrazole moiety can influence both the molecular recognition and the physicochemical properties of the lead compounds. The clinical success of tetrazole‐containing angiotensin II receptor blockers, including losartan, valsartan and irbesartan, provides an important demonstration that appropriate integration of the tetrazole core can contribute to receptor recognition, metabolic stability and favourable pharmacokinetic behaviour. Beyond antihypertensive agents, the broad range of pharmacological activities reported for tetrazole‐containing compounds further illustrates the adaptability of this scaffold across diverse therapeutic areas. A detailed analysis of the reported literature indicated that the biological activity of substituted tetrazole moiety is strongly dependent on the molecular environment surrounding the tetrazole ring. Variation in the N‐substitution, attachment position, linker architecture, aromatic or heteroaromatic substitution, and incorporation into hybrid scaffolds can substantially alter their potency, selectivity, physicochemical properties, and pharmacokinetic behaviour. For example, substitution of the tetrazole core at N‐1 position with cyclohexylpiperazine through a thioether linker afforded compounds with remarkable antifungal potency, while introduction of the thioether moiety contributed towards enhanced lipophilicity. Similarly, incorporation of the tosyl group at N‐1 position of the tetrazole‐5‐carboxamide core increases the steric bulk, lipophilicity, and hydrogen‐bonding capacity, thereby improving the antidiabetic activity simultaneously. In addition, N‐1‐linked tetrazole derivatives bearing indole, triazole, and flurbiprofen moieties demonstrated enhanced metabolic stability, while the addition of triazole linker increases the lipophilicity. Some of the reported tetarzole derivatives as disscused in the manuscript displayed superior anticancer potency as compared to the reference drugs doxorubicin and combretastatin by engaging in multiple binding interactions such as hydrogen bonding, π‐π stacking, and hydrophobic contacts, with various biological targets such as CDK6, tubulin, Bcl‐2, and CYP2C9 etc. Incorporation of hydrophobic amino acids, including Ala, Phe, and Leu, through an isonipecotic acid linker attached to the 5‐th position of the tetrazole core enhances the solubility and biocompatibility while retaining the AT1R activity. Furthermore, fusion of a methylxanthine moiety with an N‐2‐linked tetrazole resulted in notable blood–brain‐barrier permeability and remarkable anti‐Alzheimer's activity. However, substitution at the N‐3 position has been less explored during the studies. Overall, para‐substitution with an aryl ring bearing electron‐withdrawing groups, along with moderate‐to‐high lipophilicity imparting moieties such as cyclohexyl, isopropyl, or halogenated groups, was frequently associated with highly potent, metabolically stable, drug‐like lead compounds. However, enhanced in vitro potency alone should not be considered sufficient evidence of therapeutic potential. A considerable proportion of reported tetrazole derivatives remain at the preclinical stage, and their pharmacokinetic behaviour, safety, target selectivity, and in vivo efficacy warrented further investigations.

Despite these encouraging results, several activity‐specific studies remain essential for translating the therapeutic potential of these tetrazole hybrids into viable drug like candidates. Furthermore, one of the principal challenge for future tetrazole‐based drug discovery is to achieve an appropriate balance between target engagement and drug‐like properties. Although the ionisable and polar nature of tetrazoles can be advantageous for molecular recognition, it may simultaneously influence membrane permeability, solubility, absorption, tissue distribution, and oral bioavailability. While inappropriate substitution may sometimes introduce metabolic or off‐target liabilities. Early assessment of these, would help identify liabilities before compounds have been progressed to later stages of clinical development. For antimicrobial leads, biological studies involving resistant‐strain profiling, in vivo infection models, and biochemical target validation should be undertaken to confirm their spectrum of activity, potency and target selectivity. Similarly, promising anticancer candidates require appropriate optimization of selectivity indices, protein estimation assays, xenograft studies, target‐specific biochemical or cellular assays, and in vivo efficacy models to confirm their proposed mechanisms derived from computational studies. Building on the structural and mechanistic insights compiled in this review, future perspectives in medicinal chemistry should also place greater emphasis on translating promising structural and biological findings into well‐characterised drug candidates. Structure‐based approaches, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics, structural biology, and free energy calculations together with AI‐ML‐assisted prediction of activity and ADMET profiles, may facilitate more rational prioritisation of tetrazole chemotypes for synthesis and biological investigations. In parallel, development of greener, more scalable synthetic methodologies, along with improved impurity profiling, and careful assessment of process‐related safety parameters should be critically monitored for their clinical development. Further, exploration of under‐investigated substitution patterns and rational hybridization with established pharmacophores will further expand the medicinal utility of tetrazole derivatives in diverse therapeutic areas. Ultimately, integration of medicinal chemistry and computational chemistry, with pharmacology, ADMET optimization, and sustainable synthetic protocols is essential for translating the broad biological potential of tetrazole derivatives into clinically relevant therapeutics. This review is expected to be of utmost interest to the scientific community, as it emphasises the effective utilization of the diverse therapeutic potential of reported tetrazole derivatives and explores new strategies to overcome challenges involved in lead optimization and their clinical translation.

medicine.title: Apolipoprotein E genotype, PET and MRI biomarkers, and vascular risk: A multi‐modal investigation of memory performance in US POINTER
medicine.abstract:
The apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is a key genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the etiology of impairment in non‐carriers is less understood.We used regression and mediation models to test the cross‐sectional relationships among APOE genotype, positron emission tomography amyloid and tau, vascular risk factors, and episodic memory within the US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk ancillary imaging dataset of non‐demented older adults.In our cohort (N = 880), APOE ε4 carriers showed higher global amyloid, higher meta‐temporal tau, smaller hippocampal volume, poorer memory, and a stronger relationship between amyloid and tau standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR; ∆β = 0.22, p < 0.001). Tau predicted memory (p < 0.01) and partially mediated the APOE–memory association. In a stratified analysis, higher Framingham Heart Study risk score (FHS; p = 0.022) and not tau SUVR (p = 0.1) were associated with memory among APOE ε4 non‐carriers, whereas tau SUVR (p = 0.048) but not FHS risk score (p = 0.55) was associated with memory amongst APOE ε4 carriers.Drivers of cognitive performance appear to be specific to APOE ε4 carrier status, emphasizing the need to identify alternative, or contributing, disease mechanisms among non‐carriers.
The US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk (U.S. POINTER) cohort is composed of older adults at elevated risk of cognitive decline and cardiovascular disease burden.Further multimodal neuroimaging data was collected through the POINTER Imaging ancillary study.At baseline evaluation, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 genotype was significantly associated with amyloid and tau pathology, hippocampal atrophy, and poor episodic memory performance.
APOE ε4 genotype stratification analysis showed significant associations of Framingham cardiovascular risk score and smoking status with memory in non‐carriers only.Etiological pathways of dementia may differ in contributive strength to cognitive deterioration within this at‐risk cohort.
medicine.text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the predominant etiology of cognitive impairment and dementia and one of the leading contributors to global mortality and disability., , ,  The amyloid cascade hypothesis, which positions amyloid beta (Aβ) deposition as the critical upstream initiator of tau pathology and neurodegeneration, has historically defined AD research, providing the mechanistic basis for recent anti‐amyloid immunotherapies., , ,  Of note, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is widely recognized as the strongest genetic risk factor for late‐onset AD (LOAD) in some populations,,  as its isoform‐specific effects span Aβ aggregation and clearance, neuroinflammation, and lipid homeostasis., ,

APOE ε4 non‐carriers, however, constitute ≈ 75% of the general population and account for an estimated 33% to 50% of clinically diagnosed AD dementia cases, depending on ancestry and study cohort. Transcriptomic analyses indicate that AD pathogenesis in non‐carriers may also engage immunological and cardiovascular pathological pathways in addition to the amyloid‐driven pathology, a pattern further supported by genome‐wide association studies identifying immune and vascular susceptibility loci beyond the APOE region.,  Therefore, the extent to which biological mechanisms may drive cognitive decline in non‐carriers, especially in the preclinical stages of AD, remains incompletely understood.

Additionally, some degree of vascular comorbidity is the second most common pathology among patients with AD, with extensive neuropathological evidence implicating additive or synergistic contributions of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk burden to cognitive loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)‐based measures of white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), infarcts, and cerebral microbleeds generally display brain changes conferred by cerebrovascular processes, with WMHs as a specific, well‐supported marker of small vessel disease., , ,  These biomarkers are often associated with vascular risk factors, such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia, that may additively contribute to both CVD and dementia risk. However, the role of the APOE ε4 genotype within this framework has been less studied., , , , , , ,

To examine the impact of the APOE ε4 genotype on a more representative population, we assessed cross‐sectional differences by APOE ε4 genotype from participants of the US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk (US POINTER) randomized clinical trial. This study enrolled a diverse cohort of unimpaired older adults at elevated risk for cognitive decline due to family history, limited weekly physical activity, and elevated cardiometabolic risk, with multimodal neuroimaging and vascular data. Our goal was to evaluate (1) whether the APOE ε4 genotype is more likely to be associated with a “canonical AD” phenotype of reduced episodic memory performance, hippocampal atrophy, and elevated amyloid and tau positron emission tomography (PET); (2) whether the relationships among these measures differ by APOE genotype, and if so; (3) do vascular factors also differ in their association with cognition by APOE genotype.

Our study draws from participants of the POINTER Imaging study, an ancillary study of the US POINTER clinical trial. The parent trial evaluated whether two multidomain lifestyle interventions produce differential outcomes in cognitive trajectories over a 2‐year period.,  Participants were 60 to 79 years of age, led a sedentary lifestyle, followed a suboptimal diet, and carried an elevated risk for future cognitive decline based on these cumulative factors, with additional well‐recognized risk markers including CVD, a family history of memory impairment, and ethnoracial background. Participants were also free of meaningful cognitive impairment, which was operationalized as a modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (mTICS) score > 32, a global Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score of ≤ 0.5, and a CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR‐SB) score of ≥ 1.,

To reduce bias across demographic subgroups, mTICS scores were adjusted to account for age, education, and race/ethnicity, specifically +3 points for participants from minoritized ethnoracial backgrounds with a maximum adjustment of +5 points. Adjusted scores were capped at 50. Other criteria excluded individuals with significant neurological, psychiatric, or peripheral organ system diseases; recent or active alcohol/substance abuse; regular use of medications that may alter cognition; and assisted living or nursing home status. Under exceptional circumstances, such as an unreliable study partner, central review could approve enrollment of such individuals whose CDR‐SB score was ≥ 1. Further eligibility criteria have been delineated in a separate study.

Enrollment into the US POINTER trial and POINTER Imaging study opened in May 2019 and August 2020, respectively, with both trials completing recruitment in March 2023. Beginning August 2020, every newly randomized US POINTER participant without contraindications to MRI or PET imaging was invited to enroll in the POINTER Imaging study. Data used in preparation for this article were obtained from the US POINTER database on November 19, 2025. The POINTER Imaging study was composed of 1052 participants. Of these individuals, 172 were missing complete exposure or outcome data at the time of baseline evaluation, resulting in 880 individuals for our analysis.

All demographic information, including age, sex, ethnoracial group, and years of education, was obtained by self‐report. Physical measures, such as body mass index (BMI) and blood pressure, were measured by standard protocols. Standardized questionnaires were used to self‐report past medical history, while laboratory values, including hemoglobin A1c and cholesterol, were assessed from specimens that were collected after 10‐hour fasting.
APOE genotyping was performed for subsequent participant classification into APOE ε4 non‐carriers or APOE ε4 carriers with at least one ε4 allele. Of our total sample, 20 participants were APOE ε2/ε4 carriers. Because US POINTER aimed to reflect the diversity of the general population, we included these individuals in our analyses and classified them as APOE ε4 carriers.

Baseline cognition was assessed with the POINTER‐modified Neuropsychological Test Battery (PmNTB). This comprised the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test, Story Recall, and Visual Paired Associates for the episodic memory composite score; Number Span, Verbal Fluency, and Trail‐Making Test for the executive function composite score; and Trail‐Making Test, Part A and Digit Symbol Substitution Test for the processing speed composite score. Each sub‐score from these individual tests was converted to z scores using means and standard deviations derived from the full set of US POINTER baseline values. These z scores were then averaged to create the composite scores for episodic memory, executive function, and processing speed, with further scoring details previously reported in the parent study. For the purposes of our study, we used episodic memory performance to better evaluate aging trajectories that were susceptible to AD onset. We used the CDR‐SB score rather than global CDR because of its greater sensitivity to subtle cognitive changes.

By design, the US POINTER cohort is at higher risk for CVD. Prevalent CVD was defined by participant self‐report of any of the following: myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, congestive heart failure, uncontrolled arrhythmia, uncontrolled angina, cardiac surgery (stent placement, angioplasty, bypass, or valve replacement), or thromboembolic events (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or transient ischemic attack). Overall risk was indexed using the Framingham Heart Study (FHS) CVD risk score, an established estimator of the 10‐year probability of a major cardiovascular event, in which higher scores reflect greater risk. The FHS risk score is computed from age, sex, systolic blood pressure, current antihypertensive medication use, BMI, current smoking status, and history of diabetes. This score was calculated for our POINTER Imaging sample using available data, including participants who self‐reported prevalent CVD. Thus, our analysis focuses on the FHS risk score measure to operationalize prospective CVD risk.

T1‐weighted structural MRI was acquired on Siemens 3T platforms (Tim Trio, Magnetom, Verio, Skyra, or Prisma Fit) using a three‐dimensional magnetization rapid gradient echo (3D MPRAGE) sequence harmonized to the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) 3 protocol (repetition time [TR] = 2300 ms, echo time [TE] = min full echo, voxel size = 1 mm isotropic, and field of view = 256 mm). Cortical and subcortical parcellation was performed with FreeSurfer v7.1. Our hippocampal segmentation method uses a standard atlas‐based diffeomorphic approach with the minor modification of label refinement. We further modified this approach to include the European Alzheimer's Disease Consortium–ADNI harmonized hippocampal masks to assure standardization across cohorts. Hippocampal volume was then residualized by total cranial volume (TCV) to adjust for head size differences. Fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery images were also acquired (resolution = 1 × 1 × 1.2 mm, [TR] = 4800 ms, [TE] = 300 to 450 ms, inversion time = 1550 to 1800 ms, echo train length = 100 to 250 ms) and used with T1 MPRAGE to produce segmented WMH volumes, according to established protocol. All WMH volumes were residualized by TCV, although WMH volumes were natural logarithm transformed prior to residualization to normalize variance.

Aβ PET was acquired with [18F]florbetaben (FBB) and tau PET with [18F]MK6240. Image acquisition was performed on GE Discovery MI or ST, Siemens Biograph mCT 40 or Vision, or Phillips Gemini TF scanners. Participants received ≈ 8 mCi of FBB or 5 mCi of MK6240, with imaging performed from 90 to 110 minutes post‐injection across four 5‐minute frames. Pre‐processing followed the ADNI‐derived multisite harmonization pipeline used by the POINTER Imaging core analysis labs.,  Fully pre‐processed images were retrieved from the Laboratory of Neuro Imaging (LONI) and intensity‐normalized using the whole cerebellum (FBB) or inferior cerebellar gray matter (MK6240) as the reference region. Tracer‐specific regions of interest (ROIs) were sampled from FreeSurfer parcellations of each participant's native‐space T1 MRI. Global cortical FBB, meta‐temporal MK6240, and entorhinal cortex MK6240 standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) were computed by published methods., ,  The meta‐temporal ROI was used as the primary tau biomarker region in our analyses due to its established efficacy in capturing transitions between Braak stages. Full acquisition parameters and processing details have been previously reported.

We characterized all demographic, biomarker, and cognitive outcomes by APOE genotype using standard descriptive statistics of analysis of variance and Pearson chi‐squared test for the full dataset. All analyses were performed using the R statistical package version 4.5.0. Multivariate linear regression was used to assess associations among APOE genotype, global FBB amyloid, meta‐temporal and entorhinal cortex tau MK‐6240, hippocampal volume, WMH, peripheral vascular risk factors, and cognitive domain scores. Interaction terms were tested for APOE ε4 genotype x amyloid and APOE ε4 genotype x FHS risk score. We implemented parametric and non‐parametric mediation analysis using linear regression to predict episodic memory at baseline evaluation using the R mediation package 4.5.1. This package implements previously established methods and recommendations., , ,  In addition to the estimation of causal mediation effects, the software also allows researchers to conduct sensitivity analysis for certain parametric models. All analyses were adjusted for potential confounding variables of age, sex, education, ethnoracial group, and CDR‐SB. We tested for multicollinearity in models including FHS risk score and covariates of age and sex using variance inflation factors, which remained ≤ 2.

Our cohort consisted of 880 cognitively unimpaired older adults with a mean age of 68.4 ± 5.2 years, of whom 539 were female (61%), 250 (28.4%) were APOE ε4 genotype carriers, and 258 (29%) were amyloid positive. Subject characteristics for the whole group and stratified by APOE ε4 genotype are shown in Table . Univariate analysis found that APOE ε4 carrier participants had significantly higher global FBB amyloid (p < 0.001) and meta‐temporal tau MK6240 (p = 0.008), as well as poorer episodic memory performance (p = 0.019), than APOE ε4 non‐carrier participants. APOE ε4 genotype was not associated with participant age, sex, education, FHS risk score, CDR‐SB, or ethnoracial group. Mean raw hippocampal volumes and raw WMH volumes were smaller among APOE ε4 carriers, although these differences did not reach significance.

We further investigated whether the APOE ε4 genotype was associated with amyloid, meta‐temporal tau, hippocampal volume, and WMH in the full cohort (Table ). In linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, education, race/ethnicity, and CDR‐SB, we found that APOE ε4 genotype remained significantly associated with three biomarkers at baseline evaluation: greater amyloid (β = 0.10, 95% confidence interval [CI: 0.08, 0.12], p < 0.001) and meta‐temporal tau (β = 0.04, 95% CI [0.02, 0.06], p < 0.001) and smaller hippocampal volume (β = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.32, −0.04], p = 0.010). We also note that participants who self‐identified as Black had significantly lower overall amyloid (β = −0.05, 95% CI [−0.08, −0.02], p = 0.003) and tau burden (β = −0.04, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.01], p = 0.018), but significantly smaller hippocampal volumes (β = −0.28, 95% CI [−0.47, −0.09], p = 0.004). We next tested whether there was an APOE ε4 genotype x amyloid interaction in predicting meta‐temporal tau using a linear regression model. We found a significant interaction (β = 0.223, 95% CI [0.103, 0.343], p < 0.001; Table ), with both amyloid and tau quantified as continuous values with mean‐centered amyloid SUVR values. Greater amyloid burden was associated with greater tau among APOE ε4 carrier participants (β = 0.42, 95% CI [0.34, 0.51], p < 0.001). In contrast, greater amyloid burden was associated with less pronounced meta‐temporal tau in APOE ε4 non‐carrier participants (β = 0.20, 95% CI [0.11, 0.29], p < 0.001). These associations were significantly different when comparing APOE ε4 carrier to the APOE ε4 non‐carrier group (∆β = 0.22, p < 0.001; Figure ) using a Wald t test comparison.

We then looked at the independent baseline association of each biomarker with cognitive performance for the entire group (Table ). In individual linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, education, race/ethnicity, CDR‐SB, and APOE ε4 genotype, only meta‐temporal tau was significantly associated with worse episodic memory (β = −0.56, 95% CI [−0.94, −0.19], p = 0.003). Amyloid burden, hippocampal volume, and WMH were not significant predictors of memory performance at baseline. We also looked at the associations between (1) WMH and executive function (p = 0.521) and (2) WMH and processing speed (p = 0.113) based on evidence showing stronger effects of vascular contributions on these cognitive domains.,  Neither of these relationships were significant. Because meta‐temporal tau was the sole significant biomarker predictor of memory performance, we examined whether it accounted for the cross‐sectional association between APOE genotype and episodic memory using path‐analytic mediation with bootstrapped confidence intervals (k = 500 resamples). APOE genotype was associated with greater tau burden (β = 0.038, 95% CI [0.016, 0.061], p < 0.001), which in turn was associated with worse episodic memory (β = −0.563, 95% CI [−0.938, −0.189], p = 0.003). The indirect effect of APOE genotype on memory through tau was β = −0.201 (bootstrapped 95% CI [−0.048, −0.004]), consistent with partial mediation accounting for 10.8% of the total effect (Figure ). The direct effect of APOE genotype on memory remained significant after adjustment for tau (β = −0.180, 95% CI [−0.318, −0.053], p < 0.001) but was slightly attenuated relative to the total effect (β = −0.201, 95% CI [−0.339, −0.071], p < 0.001).

In a parallel analysis, substituting meta‐temporal tau for entorhinal tau, a brain region important to memory and one of the earliest regions affected by tauopathy in AD, the indirect effect accounted for 19% of the total effect (indirect β = −0.038, bootstrapped 95% CI [−0.073, −0.011]; Figure ). The direct effect remained significant (β = −0.162, 95% CI [−0.297, −0.026], p = 0.032) relative to the total effect (β = −0.200, 95% CI [−0.332, −0.058], p = 0.004), again with most of the association unaccounted by the tau pathway. To confirm that these effects were consistent in a preclinical AD stage, we reran mediation analyses in the amyloid‐positive subset of our cohort (Figure  in supporting information), and the results were essentially unchanged.

Previously, Harrison et al. demonstrated that vascular risk was related to brain structure, but not to amyloid or tau, and contributed to memory independently of AD pathology in the POINTER Imaging baseline study. We subsequently examined whether the APOE ε4 genotype modified the relationship between vascular risk and episodic memory. In linear regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, education, race/ethnicity, CDR‐SB, and APOE ε4 gene dosage (none, heterozygote, homozygote), FHS risk score was significantly associated with episodic memory performance (β = −0.006, 95% CI [−0.010, −0.001], p = 0.020; Table  in supporting information). The effect of APOE ε4 gene dosage on episodic memory also remained significant for both heterozygotes (β = −0.133, 95% CI [−0.263, −0.002], p = 0.046) and homozygotes (β = −0.397, 95% CI [−0.735, −0.059], p = 0.022). Conversely, in separate models, FHS risk score was not associated with executive function or processing speed when treated as independent variables using the same predictors. The APOE ε4 gene dosage x FHS risk score interaction was not significant when predicting episodic memory in a separate model adjusting for covariates (p = 0.1).

We performed an exploratory stratified analysis by APOE ε4 carrier status identical to those previously reported by Harrison et al. (Table  in supporting information). FHS risk score (β = −0.006, 95% CI [−0.011, −0.001], p = 0.022) was significantly associated with episodic memory performance among APOE ε4 non‐carriers, but not APOE ε4 carriers, whereas meta‐temporal tau SUVR (β = −0.656, 95% CI [−1.306, −0.006], p = 0.048), but not FHS risk score, was significantly associated with episodic memory among APOE ε4 carriers. We also sought to examine whether component vascular risk factors of the FHS score might explain cognitive variance among non‐carriers. In genotype‐stratified models adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, CDR‐SB, and amyloid and tau PET, we observed that smoking history (β = −0.152, 95% CI [−0.271, −0.032], p = 0.013) was the only component variable significantly associated with worse memory performance in individual linear regressions for non‐carriers (Table  in supporting information). These stratified estimates describe associations within APOE ε4 non‐carriers and do not constitute evidence that associations significantly differ by genotype.

The well‐established association between APOE ε4 genotype and LOAD risk has been substantiated by isoform‐specific studies of APOE–Aβ interactions.,  Yet the classical amyloid cascade, even when amplified by APOE,,  may not fully account for dementia risk in APOE ε4 non‐carriers., ,  Here, we determined the effects of APOE ε4 genotype on the associations among neuroimaging biomarkers, vascular risk, and cognition in the POINTER Imaging study, a cohort selected for increased risk of CVD and cognitive decline. Across the full cohort, we confirmed significant associations of APOE ε4 genotype with higher amyloid, higher tau, smaller hippocampal volume, and poorer episodic memory performance, consistent with prior evidence that APOE ε4–related genetic susceptibility is biologically expressed even in preclinical and prodromal stages. Because amyloid is thought to facilitate tau aggregation and spreading in traditional AD pathophysiology,,  we extended this framework by showing that APOE ε4 genotype carrier status moderates the baseline cross‐sectional association between amyloid and tau. This suggests that amyloid‐positive APOE ε4 carriers in this cohort had a more advanced expression of the canonical AD trajectory than non‐carriers,, ,  likely facilitated by tau expression. The smaller amyloid–tau associations first observed in the parent study by Harrison et al. and interpreted as indicating overall less AD pathology may therefore reflect pathological heterogeneity as a cause of reduced episodic memory performance (either additively or independently), because among APOE ε4 carriers, the AD canonical pathway appears strong.

Our mediation analyses demonstrated that meta‐temporal and entorhinal tau partially accounted for the APOE genotype–memory association by 10.8% and 19%, respectively. The stronger entorhinal effect is consistent with evidence that the entorhinal cortex is an early site of tau accumulation closely tied to memory outcomes. These significant effects were sustained for amyloid‐positive participants (n = 258), concurrent with the biological definition of AD.,  Together, these findings support tau burden as a potential marker linking APOE ε4 carrier status to lower memory performance, plausibly through APOE‐related exacerbation of Aβ‐triggered neurotoxicity and tau hyperphosphorylation, confirming our hypothesized AD canonical pathway for APOE ε4 carriers., ,  The direct effect of APOE genotype on memory, however, persisted after tau adjustment, indicating that this AD pathway does not fully account for memory. It remains uncertain how distinct APOE isoforms regulate neurotoxic gain or loss of function, including cell death, synaptic failure, or cerebrovascular dysfunction, in downstream neurodegeneration,, ,  or even their relationships with amyloid and tau.

Among our selected biomarkers (hippocampal and WMH volumes, amyloid and tau PET SUVR), only meta‐temporal tau burden significantly predicted memory performance. This aligns with growing recognition of tau PET as a more robust indicator of cognitive decline. The absence of significant associations of amyloid, hippocampal volume, or WMH with memory likely reflects the preclinical phase of this cohort. Unlike tau pathology, amyloid burden alone may not fully explain AD severity as an upstream process, while neuronal injury leading to measurable atrophy may be too subtle to capture earlier disease‐related change., ,

Because POINTER was selectively enriched for CVD, we sought to determine whether the composite FHS score and component risk factors were associated with cognition. Vascular processes are thought to contribute to cognitive impairment and dementia,, ,  and our prior work showed that FHS risk score was associated with episodic memory. Like Harrison et al., FHS risk scores remained significantly associated with episodic memory when added to the model containing amyloid and tau PET measures (Table ). Episodic memory scores were also significantly worse in both APOE ε4 homozygotes and heterozygotes. Given conflicting evidence on interactive associations between FHS risk and amyloid burden on tau accumulation and cognitive outcomes,,  we tested an APOE ε4 gene dosage x FHS risk score interaction on episodic memory, which was not significant. Due to the pleiotropic nature of APOE ε4 and its sustained effect in all our models, we performed exploratory analyses stratified by APOE ε4 genotype. Here, we evaluated possible differences among identical predictors of episodic memory performance within carriers and non‐carriers separately (Table ). We also examined independent associations of FHS risk score components with episodic memory within carriers and non‐carriers using the same models (Table ). Although we show FHS risk score significantly predicted memory in APOE ε4 non‐carriers, we interpret this cautiously due to a lack of a significant interactive effect. Vascular‐metabolic injury arguably occupies an important etiological role, but the parallel pathways of cognitive aging through amyloid and vascular pathology may not necessarily be independent due to intrinsic genetic risk alone. Rather, APOE ε4 heterogeneity may shift toward amyloidosis as a more dominant pathological contributor to cognitive performance in carriers. Conversely, cognitive decline for the APOE ε4 non‐carriers may manifest through a broader set of non‐amyloid or mixed pathologies, but these remain more difficult to detect, particularly in non‐impaired individuals., , , , , ,

The absence of significant associations between vascular risk factors and episodic memory among APOE ε4 carriers certainly does not exclude cerebrovascular disease in this group. Instead, APOE ε4–associated vascular injury may operate through mechanisms not captured by the vascular markers examined here. For example, APOE ε4 carriers show accelerated blood–brain barrier breakdown in the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe, both regions central to episodic memory, which can be detected in cognitively normal individuals and predicts subsequent cognitive decline independently of amyloid and tau status. This has been mechanistically linked to an APOE ε4–driven cyclophilin A‐MMP9 cascade in pericytes that degrade proteins, alongside reductions in cerebral blood flow and glucose uptake reported in non‐demented carriers.,  Crucially, this pathway is not captured by FHS risk score, smoking status, or MRI WMH measures. Other MRI measures may be better suited to detect preclinical vascular contributions to memory in APOE ε4 carriers and should be investigated in future baseline and longitudinal settings. Similarly, FHS risk score has been associated with cognitive impairment even after adjusting for PET measures of AD and MRI measures of vascular brain injury, likely reflecting systemic processes such as inflammation or toxic angiogenesis.,  How these downstream effects interact is not yet clear, as there is no current standard for demonstrating the additive effects of cerebrovascular disease and AD pathology.

These findings may have implications for the design and interpretation of future dementia prevention trials. The parent US POINTER trial reported that the structured‐intervention benefit on global cognition was consistent across APOE ε4 carriers and non‐carriers. Similarly, the Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) found no significant interaction between APOE ε4 genotype and intervention arm on its neuropsychological composite, although point estimates within APOE ε4 carriers were nominally larger. We note, however, that a longitudinal, multimodal intervention study for dementia in Japan did find a significant benefit of intervention on cognition for APOE ε4 carriers (p = 0.035), whose participants, unlike those of POINTER and FINGER, were already diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment. Therefore, multidomain interventions may operate through different biological mechanisms across APOE ε4 groups and disease stages. Further longitudinal biomarker modeling of our POINTER imaging cohort should be conducted to evaluate whether the strength of pathological pathways differs by APOE ε4 carrier status, particularly if vascular or cardiometabolic mechanisms are relevant among non‐carriers. This may better elucidate the comprehensive impact of hybrid lifestyle intervention programs.

Several strengths support our findings. US POINTER is currently one of the largest ethnoracially diverse cohorts of cognitively unimpaired older adults at risk for cognitive decline, recruited through community engagement at geographically distinct sites. The POINTER Imaging study further provides harmonized multimodal phenotyping, including PET, MRI, and vascular measures, with APOE genotyping. Studying this group at a pre‐symptomatic stage reduces the risk that the associations between biomarkers and cognitive outcomes are confounded by overt impairment, addressing the need to understand early disease indicators for the general population.

Inclusion of participants from different ethnoracial backgrounds also identified unique findings worthy of further research. For example, participants who self‐identified as Black/African American had lower amyloid and tau burden, and yet smaller hippocampal volume, higher FHS risk score, and overall worse memory, despite no significant difference in APOE ε4 prevalence compared to other ethnoracial groups, indicating the potential influence of mixed pathologies as previously reported. This should be interpreted in the context of broader social determinants of health, as previous studies suggest that AD and related dementias disparities may reflect compounded consequences of socioeconomic disadvantages, including neighborhood deprivation, chronic disease, and reduced medical access. This further speaks to the need for larger, more nuanced study cohorts representative of the US aging population in health care and research.

Our study is not without limitations. First, our cross‐sectional analyses cannot establish temporal ordering among neuroimaging biomarkers, vascular risk, and memory. Second, US POINTER participants were pre‐selected for elevated CVD risk and within a compressed range of cognitive function, which may introduce bias, attenuate our observed associations, and limit generalizability to lower risk older adults. Finally, the main study aims focused on WMH volume as the measure of vascular brain injury. Diffusion tensor imaging measures of fractional anisotropy or free water, both known to be associated with vascular brain injury in non‐impaired cohorts,,  might further elucidate subtle differences related to vascular risk factors.

As the field explores risk and protective factors that can identify disease earlier within at‐risk populations, understanding the biological substrate of APOE ε4 genotype–specific effects will offer a more robust translation of AD heterogeneity into clinically meaningful prevention and intervention strategies.

medicine.title: Metabologenomic assessment of biosynthetic capabilities in the genus Salinibacterium: untapped bioactive chemistry produced by marine strain AL4.1 isolated in the Chilean Patagonia
medicine.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance represents one of the most critical global public health challenges. Increasing evidence suggests that rare actinomycetes can harbour novel biosynthetic diversity to produce antimicrobial compounds. This work explores the capabilities for the biosynthesis of antimicrobial natural products of Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1, in contrast with those of Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6, through a comparative metabologenomic approach. Comparative bioactivity tests using both Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 revealed antimicrobial bioactivity of crude extracts from strain AL4.1 against Staphylococcus aureus. Liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry was performed on the tested samples, allowing for metabolite dereplication as well as identification of bioactivity-associated features. This revealed the presence of potential aromatic polyketides structurally related to known bioactive compounds such as phloretin, for which bacterial production had not been reported to date, as well as other potentially novel alkaloids and peptides. The genomes of both strains were sequenced and mined for their biosynthetic capabilities and further compared to those of other Salinibacterium strains with available genomic data. Phylogenomic studies suggested that both strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 could represent potentially new species. A mainly phylogeny-dependent distribution of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) was observed, emphasizing the presence of a widely distributed type III polyketide synthase BGC, which could be linked to the bioactive compounds. These results suggest that Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 can produce novel bioactive natural products, and the genus Salinibacterium holds relevant and underexplored biosynthetic potential.

The genomic data of Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 and Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6 generated and analysed for this study have been deposited at DDBJ/ENA/GenBank under BioProject accession numbers PRJNA1357017 and PRJNA1357379, respectively. The MS datasets generated and analysed for this study can be found in the MassIVE database under ID MSV000099771. Feature-based molecular networking analysis is publicly available at the GNPS2 platform under TaskID 6be1aa7edfe34b7c9b117190e94db4a5. Bioactivity-based molecular networking analysis was performed using the freely available R script provided by the authors: https://github.com/DorresteinLaboratory/Bioactive_Molecular_Networks/blob/master/Bioactive_Molecular_Networks_v1.1_MZmine2.r. All other relevant data and protocols can be found within this article and its supplementary figures and tables.

Overuse and misuse of antibiotics during the last decades have contributed to an accelerated emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in pathogenic bacteria []. Consequently, it is currently estimated that antimicrobial-resistant infections contribute to nearly 5 million deaths every year []. This has resulted in the consideration of AMR as one of the main threats to global public health by international organizations, as well as in the development of programmes and strategies to tackle it [, ]. Unsurprisingly, finding novel antibiotics that can effectively act against resistant pathogens has been pointed out as a key aspect within these strategies [], for which it becomes instinctive to recur to natural products (NPs), as historically, most antimicrobial agents have been generated either from these or their derivatives [, ].

Remarkably, almost two out of every three of these naturally derived antibiotics are produced by members of the phylum Actinomycetota, a diverse bacterial group with outstanding metabolic capabilities [, ]. Nonetheless, finding novel drugs even from these prolific producers continues to be challenging, since traditional bioprospecting approaches present major drawbacks such as severe rediscovery rates, challenging isolation of new producers and low production []. Thus, a steady development of novel strategies that draw upon the application of innovative approaches to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks has been observed in recent years. Among such approaches, integrative multi-omics methodologies have been proven efficient for tapping into novel borders of NP diversity and their potential for drug discovery [, ].

Moreover, expanding the study of microbial diversity into underexplored environments has also pushed the boundaries for the discovery of novel NPs, highlighting the biosynthetic potential of marine actinomycetes, as they hold chemistry that allows them to thrive in environmental conditions highly contrasting to those of terrestrial settings [, ]. Additionally, recent studies have suggested that ‘rare’ actinomycetes, i.e. those within the phylum Actinomycetota but outside the genus Streptomyces, represent a promising source of novel compounds despite being comparatively understudied [, ]. Metabologenomics has been used to link cryptic biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) with metabolite families in rare actinomycetes [–], though marine isolates have received less attention [].

Among these rare actinomycetes, the genus Salinibacterium was first described in 2003 with the species Salinibacterium amurskyense [] and to date comprises five other species, namely Salinibacterium xinjiangense [], Salinibacterium hongtaonis [], Salinibacterium metalliresistens [], Salinibacterium sedimenticola [] and Salinibacterium soli [].

Even though several species have been described, bioprospecting of antimicrobial NPs from this genus has been limited to date. Studies from two independent bioprospecting campaigns have tested crude extracts derived from Salinibacterium strains against ESKAPE (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter species) pathogens, a group of multidrug-resistant bacteria associated with healthcare-associated infections, yet no positive results were observed in any of them [, ]. Nonetheless, a third study reported growth inhibition through the cross-streaking method and concentrated supernatants from Salinibacterium spp. against bacterial pathogens relevant in aquaculture [].

Within this context, the present work takes a comparative metabologenomic approach to explore the biosynthetic capabilities for antimicrobial NP production of Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1, in contrast with those of Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6, both isolated from the Chilean coasts of the South Pacific Ocean, from two sites ~1,650 km apart. Additionally, such capabilities were further compared with those of other strains within the genus at the genomic level, giving evidence of the yet untapped biosynthetic potential they hold.

Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 was isolated from a 390 m depth marine sediment sample collected on 21 October 2014 near Wellington Island, in Magallanes, Chile (48° 53′ 5.94″ S 74° 25′ 41.28″ W), kindly handed to our team by Dr Silva with the Chilean programme ‘Cruceros de Investigación Marina en Áreas Remotas’ (CIMAR). After being stored for 5 years at −80 °C, the sample was thawed and directly plated in 0.5× M1 medium supplemented with artificial sea water, as well as with nalidixic acid (25 mg ml−1) and cycloheximide (100 mg ml−1), and incubated at room temperature.

For molecular identification of strain AL4.1, DNA extraction was achieved through thermal lysis in accordance with a simplified protocol [], and the obtained genomic DNA was used as a template for 16S rRNA gene PCR amplification with universal primers 27F and 1492R as previously described []. PCR product was then quantiﬁed and analysed for integrity with an agarose gel electrophoresis, to be later submitted for puriﬁcation and sequencing to Macrogen Inc. (Seoul, Korea). The obtained sequence was manually curated and used as a query for a blast alignment [, ] against NCBI’s 16S rRNA sequence database, allowing genus-level identification.

blast alignment of the 16S rRNA gene was also performed against Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6 from our collection, isolated and identified during a previous bioprospecting campaign [] from a shallow marine sediment sample from Diego Portales Beach, in Valparaíso, Chile (33° 2′ 0.10″ S 71° 35′ 41.18″ W).

Both strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 were cultured in tryptic soy agar (TSA) medium at 30 °C for 5 days for morphological characterization.

A preliminary qualitative screening was performed to identify strains with antibacterial potential, revealing a time-dependent antibacterial activity of extracts derived from strain AL4.1 against S. aureus. Given the limited number of antimicrobials bioprospecting studies involving the rare actinomycete genus Salinibacterium, a standardized follow-up assay was performed to determine whether the bioactivity observed for strain AL4.1 was strain specific or also present in Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6, another isolate from our collection for which no antibacterial activity had been previously reported.

Seed cultures for both strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 were obtained by inoculating a loopful of fresh biomass into a 250 ml baffled flask with 50 ml of tryptic soy broth medium, incubated for 48 h in an orbital shaker at 30 °C under continuous shaking at 200 r.p.m. Subsequently, 1 ml of seed culture was used to inoculate cultures of each strain in 250 ml baffled flasks with 50 ml of R5A medium [], having three biological replicates for each of the three extraction times at days 3, 5 and 7 of incubation, per strain. Cultures were also incubated in an orbital shaker at 30 °C under continuous shaking at 200 r.p.m., until their determined time of extract preparation. Two negative control blanks consisting of 50 ml of uninoculated culture media in 250 ml baffled flasks were also subjected to the same conditions until day 7.

For metabolite extraction, cultures were centrifuged at 5,000 r.p.m. for 10 min, and the biomass pellets were discarded. Remaining supernatants were transferred to separatory funnels and extracted twice using ethyl acetate (EtOAc) HPLC grade in a 1 : 1 ratio (v/v). Organic phases were concentrated under reduced pressure using a rotary evaporator at 35 °C. The resulting concentrates were divided into two aliquots prior to complete solvent removal in a vacuum concentrator, designated for bioactivity testing and liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, respectively. Dried crude extracts were weighed to determine extraction yield and stored at −20 °C until further use.

Antimicrobial activity of the extracts was tested as previously described [] with slight modifications. Tests were performed against the model strain S. aureus NBRC 100910T (STAU), which was cultured in a test tube with 5 ml of Luria–Bertani (LB) medium and incubated in an orbital shaker at 37 °C and continuous shaking at 200 r.p.m. for 24 h. The culture was then adjusted to an OD600 of 0.2 before surface spread inoculation of LB agar plates (150×15 mm; ~25 ml per plate).

Dry bacterial extracts derived from EtOAc were dissolved in methanol in distilled water (50 : 50, v:v) to a final concentration of 5 mg ml−1 and an additional dilution of 1 mg ml−1 (based on dried crude extract mass per volume). Antibacterial activity was evaluated through a drop diffusion assay under sterile conditions. LB agar plates were spread inoculated using a cotton swab with 200 µl of standardized bacterial suspension (OD600=0.2) of the model strain and allowed to dry. A 10 µl drop of each extract was applied onto the inoculated agar surface and allowed to completely evaporate before incubation. All assays were performed using three independent biological replicates per extract. Methanol in distilled water (50 : 50, v:v) and uninoculated growth medium extract were used as negative controls. Additional triplicates for medium extract and chloramphenicol were also obtained as negative and positive controls, respectively. Plates were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h, after which the visible inhibition zone diameter (IZD, mm) was manually measured. No correction for the diameter of the applied drop was performed, as inactive samples did not produce measurable growth inhibition.

Analyses focused on pre-specified comparisons between each bacterial extract (AL4.1 and VpJ6 at each time point) and the blank control. The positive control (chloramphenicol) was included as a reference for relative activity. The Wilcoxon test revealed no detectable systematic difference between internal and additional negative controls (uninoculated growth medium extracts); therefore, data were deemed comparable and pooling was done to improve estimation of baseline variability.

Effect sizes were calculated using two complementary metrics. Absolute inhibition was expressed as the difference in mean IZD between each extract and the blank control (Δ vs blank). Relative activity was expressed as the percentage of the mean IZD of the positive control (% vs positive control). These measures provide interpretable estimates of inhibition magnitude relative to baseline and to a standard antimicrobial agent.

Uncertainty in effect size estimates was assessed using nonparametric bootstrap resampling. For each comparison, 10,000 bootstrap replicates were generated by sampling with replacement from both the extract and the corresponding reference distribution (blank or positive control). Effect sizes were recalculated for each replicate, and 95% confidence intervals were obtained from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting bootstrap distributions. This approach avoids assumptions of normality and is appropriate for small sample sizes.

Statistical comparisons between each extract and the blank control were performed using the two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Given that comparisons were limited and defined a priori, P values were not adjusted for multiple testing and are reported as descriptive measures of evidence against the null hypothesis.

To attempt to identify metabolites linked to the observed activity, all samples in the antimicrobial bioactivity assays were analysed using a Thermo Scientific Vanquish ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 120 mass spectrometer. Dry blank and bacterial extracts were reconstituted in acetonitrile at 1 mg ml−1 with 10 µM glycocholic acid as an internal standard. Two microlitres of each sample was injected into an Accucore Vanquish C18 UHPLC column (1.5 µm, 100×2.1 mm) kept at 40 °C with water (0.1% formic acid) (A) and acetonitrile (0.1% formic acid) (B) as mobile phases. All used solvents were MS grade. Chromatographic separation was achieved at 0.200 ml min−1 using the following gradient: 0–1.5 min (20% B), 1.5–7 min (20–100% B), 7–17 min (100% B), 17–20.1 min (100–20% B) and 20.1–25 min (20% B). Before injection of experimental samples, a pool of media blanks was injected for the detection of blank-associated signals, and the data was used to create an exclusion list through Iterative Optimized Data Acquisition with default parameters as described in []. MS data were acquired with data-dependent acquisition (DDA) in positive ionization mode from 200 to 3,000 m/z, with mild trapping, the aforementioned exclusion list and higher-energy collisional dissociation normalized collision at 15, 20 and 30%. Electrospray ionization parameters were set to 3.5 kV for spray voltage, 45 l min−1 sheath gas flow, 15 l min−1 auxiliary gas flow, 5 l min−1 sweep gas flow, ion transfer tube at 350 °C and vaporizer at 400 °C.

Raw files were converted to mzML format using msConvert within the ProteoWizard toolkit [], and the resulting files were preprocessed applying the processing wizard tool of the mzmine platform v4.6.1 [], using the UHPLC, Orbitrap and DDA instrumental setup, in accordance with the acquisition procedure, as well as the feature list blank subtraction module with default parameters for culture media blank removal []. Comprehensively, vendor centroiding was enabled and mass detection was performed using the ‘factor of lowest signal’ algorithm with noise factors of 5.0 (MS¹) and 2.5 (MS²), followed by chromatogram building (ADAP) over 0.3–30.0 min, requiring ≥4 scans, a minimum consecutive intensity of 10,000, a minimum feature height of 50,000 and an m/z tolerance of 0.002 Da (10 p.p.m.). Chromatograms were smoothed using a Savitzky–Golay filter (5-scan window). Features were deconvoluted using the minimum search algorithm (chromatographic threshold 0.9; ≥4 scans; peak duration 0–1.5 min; minimum height 50,000), and MS/MS spectra were associated using a precursor tolerance of 0.01 Da (10 p.p.m.) and a retention time tolerance of 0.05 min. Isotope grouping was performed with 0.0015 Da (3 p.p.m.) m/z and 0.04-min retention time tolerances (max charge 2), retaining the most intense isotope and preserving features with MS/MS data; isotope patterns were annotated for H, C, N, O and S. Features were aligned using the join aligner (0.0015 Da/5 p.p.m., 0.1 min; m/z weight 3, RT weight 1), followed by blank subtraction (features present in ≥1 blank removed), filtering (≥10% sample presence), gap filling (0.002 Da/10 p.p.m., 0.1 min, ≥2 scans) and duplicate removal (7.5×10⁻⁴ Da/1.5 p.p.m., 0.035 min). Resulting files were automatically exported using the ‘Export molecular networking files’ option and used for further analyses.

Representative total ion chromatograms (TICs) were also generated and used to visually compare metabolite profiles between bioactive, non-bioactive and medium control extracts.

For initial annotation, visualization and identification of potential bioactivity-associated features in our non-targeted MS data, a bioactivity-based molecular networking (BBMN) approach [] with slight modifications was followed.
