The feature quantification table (iimn_gnps_quant.csv), pre-processed spectra (iimn_gnps.mgf) and metadata files obtained previously from mzmine, together with the raw data files (.mzML), were uploaded to the Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking (GNPS2) platform [] and used as input for the feature-based molecular networking (FBMN) workflow (SERVER:2025.02.12;WORKFLOW:2025.01.24) []. Molecular networks were generated using a precursor ion mass tolerance of 2.0 Da and a fragment ion tolerance of 0.5 Da. Edges were established based on a cosine similarity score ≥0.7 with a minimum of 6 matched fragment ions. The network topology was further constrained by retaining the top 10 most similar neighbours per node (topK=10) and limiting the maximum molecular family size to 100 nodes. Spectral library matching was conducted against all GNPS public libraries using a cosine score threshold of 0.7 and a minimum of 6 matched peaks, retaining only the top match per query spectrum. Analogue search was enabled with a maximum precursor mass shift of 1,999 Da. Spectra were filtered prior to networking using a window filtering approach, and precursor ion filtering was applied to remove signals around the precursor m/z. No normalization was applied to feature intensities prior to analysis. Features annotated by spectral library matching as common laboratory contaminants (e.g. phthalates, polyethylene glycols, siloxanes and fatty acid amides) were filtered out. Features with high-confidence spectral matches to public spectral libraries (GNPS) (cosine score ≥0.7 and manual inspection of fragmentation patterns) were assigned as level 2 (Putatively Annotated Compounds) annotations in accordance with the Metabolomics Standards Initiative (MSI) guidelines [].

The previously obtained quantification feature table was then modified with the respective bioactivity values for its use in the calculation of a bioactivity score, using the Pearson correlation between feature intensity across samples and the bioactivity level associated with each sample as previously described []. The networks obtained through FBMN were then exported and visualized using Cytoscape v3.10.3 [], and the results from the bioactivity score calculation were then mapped into it. Nodes with a Pearson correlation value r>0.90 and a Bonferroni-corrected P value <0.03 were defined as highly bioactivity-correlated, defining a node size of 80 for these, in contrast with a size of 50 for the rest of the nodes. Moreover, nodes were coloured by source, and GNPS-annotated ones were highlighted with green outlines.

Further annotation of the highly bioactivity-correlated features was achieved through SIRIUS v6.1.1 [], which allowed for initial molecular formula identification, as well as application of CSI:FingerID for structure search [] using the COSMIC workflow []; CANOPUS for systematic compound chemical classification [] based on ClassyFire []; NPClassifier for NP class annotation []; and MSNovelist for de novo structure generation [], all with default parameters unless specified otherwise and with the versions available via the SIRIUS web services at the time of analysis (August 2025). Features with ClassyFire and NPClassifier classifications with a probability P≥0.5 were assigned as level 3 (Putatively Characterized Compound Classes) annotations in accordance with the MSI guidelines. Features lacking reliable spectral matches or confident class predictions were classified as unknown (MSI level 4).

To improve annotation robustness and ease of visualization, features were filtered based on bioactivity correlation and network connectivity. Thus, the FBMN component with the most interconnected highly bioactivity-correlated features was prioritized for downstream analyses. Features lacking reproducibility across biological replicates or showing inconsistent ionization patterns were excluded. The prioritized component was visualized in Cytoscape v3.10.3 [], nodes were coloured by sample activity, those of SIRIUS-classified features were highlighted with blue outlines and those with a GNPS library spectral match, as well as a SIRIUS classification, were highlighted with magenta outlines. Previously obtained level 3 hierarchical annotations for the prioritized highly bioactivity-correlated features were plotted to contextualize chemical diversity.

MS/MS spectra of features of interest were queried against publicly available bacterial datasets to identify recurrent matches using microbeMASST []. Spectral similarity was evaluated using the following parameters: minimum cosine similarity of 0.8, at least three matched fragment ions, precursor m/z tolerance of 0.05 Da and fragment ion tolerance of 0.05 Da. Analogue search was enabled to capture structurally related spectra with differing precursor masses, restricting results to a precursor m/z window of ±10 Da. Resulting matches were filtered based on spectral similarity and manually inspected to confirm consistency of key fragment ions. Spectral occurrences across independent bacterial datasets were recorded and used to support the microbial distribution of the detected features.

To explore their phylogeny and attempt to find a biosynthetic basis for the observed differential bioactivity, the genomes of the Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 were sequenced through Illumina technology. The genomic DNA of Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 was extracted using a Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega Corporation, Madison, WI, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The obtained genomic material was later tested for concentration and contamination using a NanoDrop Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.), for quantification using a Qubit Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.) and for integrity with an agarose gel electrophoresis, eventually being stored at 4 °C until sent for sequencing. Strain’s AL4.1 genome was sequenced at Macrogen Inc. (Seoul, South Korea), the library was prepared using a Nextera XT DNA kit and paired-end sequencing was accomplished using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 Sequencing System according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). As for strain’s VpJ6 genome, it was sequenced at SeqCoast Genomics LLC (New Hampshire, USA), using the Illumina DNA Prep tagmentation kit (#20060059) with Illumina Unique Dual Indexes. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NextSeq2000 platform using a 300-cycle flow cell kit to produce 2×150 bp paired reads. A PhiX control (1–2%) was spiked into the run to support optimal base calling. Read demultiplexing, read trimming and run analytics were performed using DRAGEN v4.2.7 [], an on-board analysis software on the NextSeq2000. Paired-end raw reads for both genomes were then provided for further analysis.

Adapter removal and trimming were achieved using Trimmomatic v0.39 [], setting the ILLUMINACLIP parameter for the NexteraPE-PE adapters, with 2 seed mismatches, a palindrome clip threshold of 30 and a simple clip threshold of 10. The SLIDINGWINDOW parameter was also used to perform a sliding window trimming, with a window size of 4 and a minimum quality of 15. LEADING and TRAILING parameters were set to a value of 3, and the minimum read length was set to 36 bp. Both resulting paired and unpaired pre-processed reads were employed for a de novo assembly by Unicycler v0.5.1 [] using default parameters, and annotations of gene functions were accomplished applying Prokka v1.14.6 [] with default parameters.

The resulting draft assemblies were subjected to QUAST v5.3.0 [] and compleasm v0.2.6 [], a reimplementation of BUSCO [] based on miniprot [], using the Micrococcales lineage, for quality assessment. A graphic representation of the genomes was generated through GenoVi v0.2.16 [], which integrates DeepNOG [] to annotate the corresponding Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COGs) [] categories for each identified gene.

For a general genome-based taxonomic classification of both AL4.1 and VpJ6 Salinibacterium strains, assemblies were submitted to the Type (Strain) Genome Server (TYGS) [, ] which, briefly, determines a set of the closest type strain genomes via MASH [] intergenomic relatedness and 16S rDNA gene sequences and then performs pairwise genomic comparisons via Genome blast Distance Phylogeny (GBDP) [], to then use the resulting intergenomic distances for phylogenetic inference. The obtained genome-based tree was visualized and annotated using tvBOT [].

Moreover, to further evaluate these relationships, all-vs-all blast-based average nucleotide identity (ANIb) values were calculated using the AL4.1 and VpJ6 strains genomes and those of the type strains from each species in the Salinibacterium genus: S. amurskyense DSM 16400 (GCF_002797685.1), S. hongtaonis CGMCC 1.16371 (GCF_003065485.1), S. sedimenticola SYSU T00001 (GCF_026094475.1), S. metalliresistens H3M29-4 (GCF_029211225.1), S. soli WY-16 (GCF_030580675.1) and S. xinjiangense CGMCC 1.05381 (GCF_900230175.1), using the JSpecies Web Server (JSpeciesWS) [].

Genome mining of BGCs was performed using standalone antiSMASH v7.1.0 [], with all extra parameters on. Resulting antiSMASH gbk files from Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 were converted into FASTA format through the ‘bio’ Python package and used as input for the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database’s Resistance Gene Identifier (CARD’s RGI) [] in ‘loose’ mode. Results from CARD’s RGI, along with antiSMASH gbk files, were then used as input for pre-trained machine learning classiﬁers to predict antibacterial activity []. Available species-level taxonomic data from previously obtained microbeMASST spectral matches was used to search the antiSMASH database v5 [] to look for the presence of shared or homologous biosynthetic genes in species from which the datasets of the spectral matches were derived.

Detailed comparisons of the architecture of type III polyketide synthase (T3PKS) BGCs from Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6, as well as that of strain AL4.1 and those of Micromonospora tulbaghiae CNY-010 and Micromonospora auratinigra DSM 44815, were performed using clinker v0.0.31 [] through the CompArative GEne Cluster Analysis Toolbox (CAGECAT) []. AntiSMASH-derived gbk files corresponding to the predicted T3PKS BGCs were used as input. Protein translations were automatically extracted and aligned using clinker’s default global alignment algorithm with a minimum amino acid identity cutoff of 30%. Default parameters were used unless otherwise specified. The resulting comparative visualization was generated using clustermap.js [], with gene arrows coloured according to homologous gene groups and shaded links representing pairwise protein homology between clusters. Cluster orientation and vertical spacing were adjusted for ease of visualization, and annotated product labels are displayed for genes within the BGC of strain AL4.1.

To expand the comparative genomic study to the genus level, all Salinibacterium (TaxID 235888) genome assemblies deposited in RefSeq [] as of 4 July 2024 were downloaded using the NCBI Datasets command line interface [], together with their respective metadata. Atypical genome assemblies were excluded using the --exclude-atypical flag. The resulting 38 assemblies were then filtered according to their reported CheckM v1.2.2 [] values, keeping only those with a completeness >95% and contamination <5%, yielding a total of 37. These assemblies were then manually inspected to dereplicate those that corresponded to the same type strain from different collections, selecting the best assemblies for further analysis. The remaining 34 assemblies were then subjected to a second round of quality control applying compleasm v0.2.6 [], using the Micrococcales lineage and filtering for genomes with completeness >85% and redundancy <10%. All assemblies, including the two produced for this study, complied with the defined quality standards and thus conformed the final dataset for all further comparative genomic analysis (Table S1, available in the online Supplementary Material). The 36 genome assemblies in the final dataset were annotated using Prokka v1.14.6 [] with default parameters.

Further comparative phylogenomics and a more detailed positioning within the Salinibacterium genus of strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 were achieved through phylogenetic orthology inference using OrthoFinder v2.5.5 [], from which a rooted species tree was constructed via STAG [] and STRIDE [], using all protein annotations from the assemblies in the previously defined dataset. Microbacterium lacticum DSM 20427 (GCF_006716815.1) was used as an outgroup, being the type strain/species/genus of the Microbacteriaceae family, to which the Salinibacterium genus belongs. Furthermore, DIAMOND [] was used for sequence search, MAFFT [] for sequence alignment and FastTree [] for tree inference. The resulting species tree was visualized and annotated with the previously downloaded metadata using tvBOT [].

Genome mining of BGCs was performed for the remaining 34 assemblies in the Salinibacterium dataset using standalone antiSMASH v7.1.0 [], with all extra parameters on for consistency. All BGCs identified in the dataset were then used for the construction of similarity networks using BiG-SCAPE v1.1.9 [], with a cutoff of 0.3, pfam v37 [], the -mix parameter on and including the MIBiG database v3.1 []. Resulting BGC similarity networks were analysed and annotated using Cytoscape v3.10.3 []. CORASON-derived, multi-locus phylogenetic trees automatically generated from the BiG-SCAPE run were inspected to evaluate the evolutionary relationships of BGCs within gene cluster families (GCFs) of interest.

Isolated colonies of strain AL4.1 grown in TSA were circular, smooth, with low convexity and strong yellow pigmentation (Fig. S1). The partial 16S rRNA gene sequence of strain AL4.1 showed a similarity of 99.86% against that of S. amurskyense KMM 3673T, allowing it to be placed within the Salinibacterium genus. In addition, 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity of 100% between strain AL4.1 and Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6, previously isolated by our group from the coasts of Valparaiso [], prompted to include strain VpJ6 for parallel analysis.

Comparative bioactivity between the crude extracts derived from both strains against S. aureus NBRC 100910T (STAU) () showed that absolute inhibition zones against S. aureus for AL4.1-derived extracts at days 3 and 5 (Δ=2.5–3.8 mm), as well as all VpJ6-derived extracts (Δ=−1.2–2.5 mm), were comparable to the negative control. Relative activity compared to the positive control for these same samples was 0–13%, overall indicating absence of substantial antibacterial activity. In contrast, AL4.1 extracts obtained at day 7 produced a distinct absolute inhibition [Δ=14.1 mm (12.3–16)] and relative activity (39% [–]), suggesting a time-dependent production of antibacterial compounds. While the observed activity was not retained at (1 mg ml−1), these results should not be interpreted as a dose–response relationship due to the nature of the applied method.

Visualization of representative TICs from bioactive (AL4.1 – day 7), non-bioactive (VpJ6 – day 7) and medium control extracts (R5A), showed slightly distinct metabolic profiles (Fig. S2). FBMN networks are comprised of 4,318 nodes linked by 4,399 edges (Fig. S3a), distributed into 323 components (i.e. individual networks) and 2,076 (48%) singletons. Of all the nodes, only 754 (17.46%) were annotated by FBMN spectral similarity, out of which 45 were filtered out as contaminants, while the remaining 709 (16.42%) can be found in Table S2. Of the total 4,318 nodes, 256 are derived exclusively from strain AL4.1 and 104 exclusively from strain VpJ6, while the rest of them are produced by both strains (Fig. S3b).

BBMN analysis revealed 134 highly bioactivity-correlated nodes (Pearson correlation r>0.90 and Bonferroni-corrected P value <0.03). Component 28, consisting of 97 nodes, was identified as that with the most interconnected highly bioactivity-correlated nodes (36), accounting for 37% of its composition. Among the 36 highly bioactivity-correlated nodes within component 28, 15 had FBMN spectral matches (Table S3, a). Among these, detailed inspection of metrics revealed only the one corresponding to feature 4546 as highly confident (a), with a cosine score of ~0.89, six shared peaks and a Δ mass of ~6.96 Da, corresponding to Phloretin, for which a mirror plot can be observed in (b).

SIRIUS-based hierarchical NPClassifier and ClassyFire MSI level 3 annotations were obtained for 102 of the highly bioactivity-correlated nodes (Table S4); however, focus was given to those pertaining to component 28 (c, d). Remarkably, pathway-level NPClassifier annotations were obtained for 31 out of the 36 highly bioactivity-correlated nodes within component 28 (c), where ‘alkaloids’ and ‘amino acids and peptides’ were the most abundant, representing 16 and 10 nodes (~52% and ~32%), respectively. Only nine out of the previous 31 nodes achieved superclass-level annotations, being ‘tryptophan alkaloids’ the most frequent. No confident NPClassifier class-level annotations were achieved for any of the highly bioactivity-correlated nodes within component 28. Moreover, superclass-level ClassyFire annotations were also obtained for 31 out of the 36 highly bioactivity-correlated nodes within component 28 (d), where ‘organic acids and derivatives’, ‘benzenoids’ and ‘organoheterocyclic compounds’ were the most abundant classifications, accounting for 10, 9 and 9 nodes (~32%, ~29% and ~29%), respectively. As for the ClassyFire annotations beyond superclass, these could reach either the class, subclass or level 5, yet the most specific classification was variable for each of the 31 nodes. At the class level, the most frequent classifications were ‘carboxylic acids and derivatives’, ‘indoles and derivatives’ and ‘phenols’, with 9, 8 and 6 representatives, respectively. Out of the 15 nodes achieving level 5 classification, 9 correspond to ‘amino acids and derivatives’, followed by ‘3-alkylindoles’, with 2 representatives.

Features 3583, 3585, 4048 and 4546 were prioritized given their GNPS spectral matches to known bioactive compounds, platyphyllenone, phloretin, iprovalicarb and phloretin, respectively. However, no relevant matches were found for feature 3583. The corresponding results for the three remaining features can be found in Table S5. For feature 3585, there were eight matches, six of which correspond to Micromonospora species. For feature 4048, three matches, all of which correspond to the Alternaria genus. And for feature 4546, seven matches, five of which correspond to the Marinobacter genus and one to a Streptomyces species. The remaining matches all correspond to the Bacteria superkingdom.

According to QUAST results, the draft genome assembly produced by Unicycler for strain AL4.1 consists of 4 contigs (≥500 bp), with an N50 of 1,944,804 and an L90 of 2, a G+C content of 61.8% and a total length of 2.86 Mb. As for the draft genome assembly for strain VpJ6, obtained through the same method, it consists of 6 contigs (≥500 bp), with an N50 of 1,833,351 and an L90 of 3, a GC content of 61.65% and a total length of 2.67 Mb. Further statistics for both assemblies can be found in Table S6. Compleasm results indicate a completeness of 94.23% and a redundancy of 0% for the genome assemblies of both strains AL4.1 and VpJ6.

DeepNOG annotation performed through GenoVi (Fig. S4) identified a total of 3,055 genes in AL4.1’s genome, grouped into 23 categories according to the COG classification, indicating that 719 of them are involved in cellular processes and signalling, 584 in information storage and processing and 1,359 in metabolism. The remaining 393 of the predicted coding DNA sequences(CDSs) are poorly characterized, giving evidence of the strain’s novelty potential. As for VpJ6’s genome (Fig. S5), a total of 2,901 genes were identified and grouped into the same 23 COG classification categories, indicating that 717 of them are involved in cellular processes and signalling, 560 in information storage and processing and 1,243 in metabolism, while the remaining 381 of the predicted CDSs are poorly characterized.

Among the series of results delivered by TYGS, a whole-genome sequence-based phylogeny is provided (Fig. S6), where the included Salinibacterium species appear non-monophyletic. Their placements occur in distinct parts of the tree among lineages of Leifsonia, Rhodoglobus, Homoserinimonas, Microcella and Agromyces, and deeper intergeneric relationships show limited support. In this reconstruction, the Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 are placed with S. amurskyense DSM 16400T, the type species of the genus Salinibacterium. According to the TYGS identification based on digital DNA–DNA hybridization (dDDH; formula d4), the values with respect to S. amurskyense are 48.5% for strain AL4.1 and 68.4% for VpJ6 (Table S7). The first value is below the 70% species threshold [], whereas the second is borderline.

As for the all-vs-all ANIb values (Table S8), most of these ranged between ~70 and 76%. In contrast, AL4.1 showed ~92% ANIb against VpJ6 and S. amurskyense, whereas the value between strain VpJ6 and S. amurskyense exceeded 95%. Based on ANIb, dDDH and the TYGS genome-based tree, both strains are consistent with possible new species within Salinibacterium, yet VpJ6 lies at the species boundary. Additional analyses will be required for both before any formal assignment.

For strains AL4.1 and VpJ6, antiSMASH predicted the presence of four and three BGCs, respectively (Fig. S7), none of which were fragmented. For both strains, one BGC of betalactone type, one of T3PKS type and one of terpene type, while only for strain AL4.1, an additional one ofribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified peptide (RiPP) type (Table S9). The T3PKS-type BGCs of both strains, as well as the RiPP type of strain AL4.1, all showed probabilities above 0.6 for producing compounds with antibacterial activity (Table S9).

BGCs with probabilities above 0.6 for producing compounds with antibacterial activity included the RiPP type from strain AL4.1 and the T3PKS type from both strains. However, since no RiPP-like molecules were identified among the highly bioactivity-correlated features, we performed a detailed comparison of both T3PKS BGCs. This allowed us to evaluate whether genomic differences could account for strain-specific metabolite production (a) and explain the differential activity. This highlighted the rather limited number of genes shared between the two BGCs, half of which correspond to all the genes reported for BGC0000282 from MIBiG, involved in the biosynthesis of 2-methoxy-5-methyl-6-(13-methyltetradecyl)-1,4-benzoquinone and the precursor 2-methoxy-5-methyl-6-alkyl-1,4-benzoquinone (b).

To further support a potential link between the T3PKS BGC of strain AL4.1 and the bioactive metabolites, we compared this cluster with T3PKS BGCs from antiSMASH database entries of M. tulbaghiae CNY-010 and M. auratinigra DSM 44815, for which high-confidence MicrobeMASST matches were obtained for feature 3585 (c). This comparison revealed >30% sequence identity between the core biosynthetic genes of these clusters, including NNJCELAO_01703 within the AL4.1 T3PKS BGC. This core biosynthetic gene in AL4.1 (NNJCELAO_01703) is annotated as a chalcone/stilbene synthase, and its genomic context, including adjacent genes encoding a methyltransferase (NNJCELAO_01704) and an oxidoreductase (NNJCELAO_01705), is consistent with the biosynthetic logic of chalcone-like and other aromatic polyketide scaffolds (a).

Although feature 3585 showed a GNPS spectral match to phloretin, manual inspection indicated limited spectral agreement. In contrast, feature 4546, also annotated as phloretin (d), achieved higher-confidence annotation (MSI level 2). Notably, both features are part of FBMN component 28, suggesting that this may represent a family of structurally related metabolites.

Moreover, the highest-ranking structure prediction with the best CSI:FingerID score (−24.097), exact confidence score (0.994) and normalized SIRIUS score (1.0) (Table S10) was also examined in detail, corresponding to N-acetyltryptamine (e). Such predicted structure corresponds to node 3226, a highly bioactivity-correlated (r=0.986635875) singleton with an m/z of 203.118 and a retention time of 7.284 min, classified by NPClassifier as ‘alkaloids>tryptophan alkaloids>simple indole alkaloids’ and by ClassyFire as ‘organic acids and derivatives>carboxylic acids and derivatives>carboxylic acid derivatives>carboxylic acid amides>N-acetyl-2-arylethylamines’ (Table S4).

The tree resulting from the phylogenetic orthology inference for the 36 Salinibacterium strains in the dataset can be observed in (a), where the respective isolation sources for each strain have been annotated, and branches of the four identified clades (I, II, III and IV) have been distinctively coloured to facilitate visualization.

Clade I, the outermost and coloured orange, is the one with the least number of strains, comprised of merely two, and represents the most distal branch relative to the other clades. Clade II, coloured in purple, includes S. hongtaonis CGMCC 1.16371T and S. sedimenticola SYSUTT00001T, the latter being the only marine-derived strain within this clade. Together with clade I, these two clades include ~89% of the Salinibacterium strains in the dataset isolated from non-marine, non-terrestrial environments (yellow background). As for clade III, coloured in red, it contains all the terrestrial-derived strains, S. metalliresistens H3M29-4T isolated from contaminated soil [], S. soli WY-16T isolated from mud [] and S. xinjiangense CGMCC 1.05381T, isolated from frozen glacial soil []. Regarding clade IV, coloured in green, it contains ~82% of the marine strains in the dataset, including S. amurskyense DSM 16400T [], which appears closely related to the strains AL4.1 and VpJ6.

AntiSMASH genome mining of the 36 Salinibacterium strains in the dataset revealed a total of 146 BGCs, classified into five types, being the type others the most abundant with 50 BGCs, followed by terpenes with 40 and PKSother with 34, while only 14 were classified as RiPPs and 8 as nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) (b). Out of the total 146 BGCs, 16 were located at contig edges and might therefore be fragmented. These BGCs were grouped into 51 GCFs according to BiG-SCAPE clustering results, yet only 23 (~45%) of these are not singletons (GCFs conformed by a single BGC) when clustered by class weights (a) and only 21 (~41%) when clustered by mix weights (c).

Among these, the largest GCF is FAM_02555, with 26 BGCs belonging to the classification of others. Moreover, this GCF is grouped into a gene cluster clan (GCC), a second layer of clustering to group GCFs, together with FAM_02544, forming CLAN_2555 with 34 BGCs. Such GCC is the most widely distributed within the dataset, spanning three out of the four different clades of the phylogenomic tree, and all isolation sources, and is sub-classified by antiSMASH as a betalactone. The next largest GCF is FAM_02559, with 19 BGCs and belonging to the classification of terpenes. This GCF, together with FAM_02537, forms CLAN_2559, the second largest in the analysis with 24 BGCs. Moreover, FAM_02559, in contrast to FAM_02555, seems to have a phylogeny-dependent distribution, being exclusively present in all strains from clade IV of the phylogenomic tree. Similarly, FAM_02558 of type PKSother and composed of 14 BGCs is the third largest and is also widely distributed within clade IV, with only five exceptions in the outermost subclades. This GCF, together with three of the five previous exceptions, conforms CLAN_2558 under mix weights. The fourth largest GCF is FAM_02579, with barely five BGCs, representing a big leap from the previous largest GCFs. This GCF comprises PKSother-type BGCs and is exclusively present in S. xinjiangense and closely related strains from clade III. As for the rest of the GCFs, there are 3 with 4 members, 2 with 3 members and 12 with only 2 members, most of them showing a phylogeny-dependent distribution.

It is relevant to note that among these GCFs, those of type NRPS are the least common, being present only in some strains of clades II and III. The next least common GCFs are those of type RiPP, absent in clade I and sparsely distributed along the rest of the clades. Such observations suggest that the genus Salinibacterium might not be particularly prolific at producing peptide-related NPs. However, it is also relevant to recall that the RiPP-type BGC of Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 showed high probabilities for the biosynthesis of antibacterial compounds (Table S9), and it groups with barely three other BGCs, suggesting novelty potential worth further investigation.

Out of the BGCs shared between both Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6, only the ones of type other and terpene group into the same GCF when clustered by class weights (a), yet those of type PKSOther also group into CLAN_2558 when clustered by mix weights (c). Given that this particular GCC is the one where the T3PKS BGC from strain AL4.1 deemed as a plausible producer of the highly bioactivity-correlated features is located, a detailed inspection of the CORASON-derived phylogenetic tree of CLAN_2558 was also performed. Comparative analysis of gene cluster architectures showed a highly conserved core region, comprising a set of syntenic genes shared across most members of the clan. In contrast, flanking regions displayed higher variability, including gene insertions, deletions and rearrangements. These differences were translated into two distinct clades, only partially consistent with the genome-based phylogeny, one of which, interestingly, contained the BGCs of both AL4.1 and VpJ6 strains, although distant. The only BGC grouping closely to that of strain AL4.1 were those from strains NK8237 and NG253.

Rare marine actinomycetes represent an underexplored resource for bioprospecting of potentially novel bioactive compounds. The two Salinibacterium strains presented in this study, AL4.1 and VpJ6, show morphological characteristics and genomic features similar to those previously reported for other species within the genus, like S. xinjiangense [], S. hongtaonis [], S. sedimenticola [] and S. metalliresistens []. Carotenoids have been previously associated with yellow pigmentation in other members of the family Microbacteriaceae [, ] and have also been shown to confer resistance to environmental stressors such as freeze-thaw cycles and solar radiation in Antarctic heterotrophic bacteria []. A similar role might be hypothesized for strains in this study, particularly AL4.1, given the proximity of its isolation site to Antarctica.

Differential bioactivity assays demonstrated consistent growth inhibition against S. aureus from extracts derived from strain AL4.1 cultured in R5A medium at day 7. Even though such activity was not retained at the 1 mg ml−1 dilution, compound diffusion, physicochemical properties and interactions of crude extract components with the agar matrix often result in this threshold-dependent behaviour [, ]. A single previous report of bioactivity from Salinibacterium isolates described growth inhibition against Aeromonas hydrophila through the cross-streaking method from Salinibacterium sp. C3W3, as well as growth inhibition against Photobacterium damselae subsp. piscicida from cell-free supernatants of Salinibacterium strains C3W3 and C2W9 cultures. Nonetheless, even though crude extracts from these strains’ cultures were also tested, no activity was reported for those []. Therefore, this study represents the first report of bioactivity from crude extracts derived from a member of the genus Salinibacterium against a model strain of a high-priority pathogen () [].

This study also provides the first insight into the chemical diversity and bioactive potential of metabolites produced by a member of the genus Salinibacterium. BBMN analyses revealed the presence of 134 highly bioactivity-correlated features in the active extracts, including a high-confidence spectral match within component 28 to phloretin (4546), a compound previously reported for specific antimicrobial activity against S. aureus, consistent with the antibacterial profile observed for our extracts []. Yet, it is relevant to note that, so far, the natural production of this compound has been reported exclusively in plants, not in bacteria. Although further structural characterization will be required for confirmation, its MS/MS cosine similarity score (0.886472) suggests the presence of dihydrochalcone-like metabolites.

SIRIUS-based classifications of 31 highly bioactivity-correlated features within component 28 (c) revealed a predominance of classes widely recognized for their antimicrobial activities such as alkaloids [–], tryptophan alkaloids, particularly relevant in marine-derived compounds [], and amino acids and peptides [–]. However, no evident direct relationship could be observed for these class annotations and the BGCs identified in the genome of Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1, suggesting that a substantial fraction of the metabolome of strain AL4.1 may arise from either uncharacterized or highly divergent biosynthetic pathways. This highlights both the limitations of current genome mining and metabolite annotation frameworks, as well as the potential for novel chemistry within this strain. Noteworthy, the highest-ranking SIRIUS/CSI-FingerID annotation for a highly bioactivity-correlated feature (CSI:FingerID score: −24.097; exact confidence score: 0.994; normalized SIRIUS score: 1.0) corresponded to N-acetyltryptamine (e), a compound reported from Bacillus and Streptomyces strains, with activity against several clinically relevant bacteria [–]. Overall, these classifications and annotations suggest that metabolites produced by Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 may include compounds responsible for the observed antibacterial activity.

Since no genomic or metabolomic data are available for the Salinibacterium strains previously reported to display bioactivity [], only the data derived from the differential assays in this study were used to explore potential links between BGCs and highly bioactivity-correlated features. At first glance, the RiPP-type BGC appeared to be the most plausible candidate for the observed activity given its probabilities above 0.6 for producing compounds with antibacterial activity (Table S9) and exclusive presence in strain AL4.1, from which bioactive samples are derived. However, the m/z values and classifications for the highly bioactivity-correlated features do not suggest the presence of RiPP-like molecules, which typically exhibit larger molecular sizes [, ]. Detailed inspection of the RiPP-type BGC in strain AL4.1 did not reveal a recognizable precursor peptide [], preventing further structural predictions or direct comparison with the detected features.

The comparison of the T3PKS-type BGCs from both strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 (a) revealed that only six genes are shared between both BGCs, representing less than 20% of their total gene content, suggesting that the remaining 80% could contribute to the biosynthesis of different metabolites. This observation is consistent with component 28 of the molecular networks (a), which includes features detected in samples from both strains and therefore may reflect shared substructures [].

Notably, three of the six shared genes show high similarity to those of BGC0000282 from MIBiG (a), reported to biosynthesize the precursor 2-methoxy-5-methyl-6-alkyl-1,4-benzoquinone (b) []. Based on this, it was hypothesized that the orange-highlighted substructures (d) of phloretin could derive from this precursor. While canonical plant chalcone synthase genes were not identified in the genome of strain AL4.1, the core biosynthetic gene within this T3PKS BGC annotated with chalcone/stilbene synthase domains (score: 384; E-value: 8.6e-117), as well as additional genes coding for tailoring enzymes, is known to generate similar scaffolds [, ]. Moreover, given the shared presence of homologous T3PKS core genes among Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1, M. tulbaghiae CNY-010 and M. auratinigra DSM 44815, it is plausible that these organisms encode related biosynthetic pathways capable of producing aromatic polyketides.

Taken together, the co-occurrence of metabolite features within component 28 displaying similarity to phloretin-like structures, microbeMASST matches to other bacteria and conserved T3PKS biosynthetic genes provides converging, albeit indirect, evidence supporting a link between the predicted biosynthetic capacity of strain AL4.1 and the observed metabolites. While this association remains strictly putative, it establishes a mechanistically grounded hypothesis connecting genomic potential to metabolomic observations.

In the case of phloretin, a high-value dihydrochalcone applied in agriculture, medicine, food and cosmetics, several synthetic biology efforts have been made to achieve its production in either yeast [–] or bacteria [, ], still facing the challenge of low titres. Thus, the insights this work provides towards the characterization of a possible native bacterial biosynthetic pathway for a structurally related compound could be beneficial to such efforts.

Although the synthesis of N-acetyltryptamine, annotated among the highly bioactivity-correlated features (e), could originate from primary metabolism, the presence of a tryptophan decarboxylase gene in the genome of strain AL4.1, known to convert tryptophan into tryptamine [], together with an N-acetyltransferase (NNJCELAO_01719) located within the PKS BGC, may provide a plausible biosynthetic route for this compound.

Nonetheless, it is acknowledged that antiSMASH-based BGC prediction is dependent on rule-based detection, and consequently, highly divergent or atypical biosynthetic architectures may not be recognized through this approach, potentially leading to an underestimation of total biosynthetic capacity [, ]. In principle, this could limit the comprehensiveness of correlations between genomic predictions and bioactive metabolite features if undetected BGCs contribute to the observed activity. However, the reported associations are internally consistent and not systematically biassed within the scope of the analytical framework, though additional studies will be required to confirm them.

Regarding the comparative taxonomic assessment of Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6, the TYGS genome-based tree (Fig. S6) shows that both strains group with S. amurskyense. dDDH values to S. amurskyense were 48.5% for AL4.1 and 68.4% for VpJ6 (Table S7), with the former falling below and the latter approaching the 70% species delineation threshold []. Consistently, ANIb values (Table S8) were ~92% for AL4.1 vs S. amurskyense and above 95% for VpJ6 versus S. amurskyense, the latter exceeding the commonly used ANI cutoff for species boundaries [–]. ANIb values ~92% are lower than typically observed among conspecifics [] but, in cases of ecological or genomic differentiation, have been interpreted as indicative of distinct species [, , ]. Together, dDDH, ANIb and phylogenetic data suggest that both strains likely represent novel Salinibacterium lineages, although strain VpJ6 lies near the species boundary and further analyses will be needed before formal classification.

The TYGS-based phylogeny also highlights polyphyly within Salinibacterium (Fig. S6), consistent with previous findings by Gtari et al. [], who proposed the reclassification of S. soli and S. metalliresistens into Antiquaquibacter and S. hongtaonis and S. sedimenticola into Homoserinimonas, leaving S. amurskyense and S. xinjiangense within Salinibacterium. Our phylogenomic analysis (a) supports this subdivision, with these same species forming distinct clades and exhibiting clear differences in BGC distributions. Interestingly, S. xinjiangense and S. amurskyense do not group together in our dataset. The species S. xinjiangense groups instead with S. soli and S. metalliresistans, a pattern consistent with AAI relationships reported by Gtari et al. []. This observation suggests that the taxonomic placement of S. xinjiangense warrants further evaluation.

From the biosynthetic perspective, the average of 4.1 BGCs per genome observed in our Salinibacterium dataset is within the range observed for other rare actinomycetes with similar genome size such as Micrococcus and Agrococcus []. The distribution of BGCs across the Salinibacterium dataset varies considerably between and within clades II and III, depending on the BGC type. In contrast, in clade IV, where strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 are located, the distribution shows a stronger dependence on phylogeny (a, c), a pattern previously observed in other Actinomycetota genera, such as Salinispora [], Rhodococcus [] and Saccharopolyspora []. Nonetheless, it is also relevant to note that FAM_02555 and FAM_02544 form a GCC (CLAN_2555) that spans three of the four clades of the phylogenomic tree, something less frequently observed if the recent reclassifications are considered, given the relatively higher levels of variance in biosynthetic diversity that have been previously observed at the taxonomic rank of family []. As for the distribution and phylogeny of BGCs similar to the T3PKS BGC deemed as plausibly responsible for the biosynthesis of highly bioactivity-correlated compounds in strain AL4.1, this suggested that chemical diversity in these BGCs is likely driven by accessory gene variation rather than core scaffold changes. Additionally, its phylogenetic placement suggests that the BGC of strain AL4.1 could represent a distinct evolutionary variant, potentially associated with unique metabolic outputs among the Salinibacterium genus. However, comparative metabolomic studies including diverse strains will be key for the better understanding of the observed genomic capabilities.

Thus, our findings provide evidence that Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 produces likely novel NPs with antimicrobial bioactivity against S. aureus, a high-priority pathogen. These NPs display characteristics consistent with alkaloids and peptides, and their biosynthesis could be partially explained by a T3PKS BGC, which will be the focus of subsequent studies for experimental corroboration. The broad and phylogeny-dependent distribution of this BGC among other Salinibacterium strains suggests that this genus possesses relevant and underexplored biosynthetic potential for the production of bioactive NPs. Phylogenetic orthology inference supports the recent taxonomic reclassification of S. soli, S. metalliresistens, S. hongtaonis and S. sedimenticola into other genera but indicates that the placement of S. xinjiangense within Salinibacterium should be further evaluated. Moreover, the data suggests that strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 represent potentially novel species, although the overall genome relatedness indexes for VpJ6 fall near species delineation thresholds; therefore, additional analyses are required before formal taxonomic assignment. Collectively, the data and results presented here advance our understanding of the genomic and metabolomic diversity of rare actinomycetes and highlight the biotechnological potential of Salinibacterium as a source of new bioactive compounds.

medicine.title: Drug–Carrier Interactions in PEGylated Liposomal Doxorubicin‐Associated Renal Toxicity: A Systems‐Level Analysis of Complement–Coagulation Crosstalk
medicine.abstract: PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) is widely used in cancer therapy, yet rare cases of renal‐limited thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) have been reported, characterized by glomerular endothelial injury and microvascular thrombosis. The mechanisms underlying this distinct nephrotoxicity remain poorly understood, particularly the potential contribution of drug–carrier interactions. Here, we developed an integrated multi‐layer network toxicology framework to systematically investigate PLD‐associated renal injury. By integrating doxorubicin‐associated targets, carrier‐associated complement pathways, nephrotoxicity‐associated genes and renal injury‐responsive transcriptomic signatures, we identified 98 computationally derived candidate genes and constructed a mechanistic interaction network. Enrichment analyses highlighted complement activation and complement–coagulation crosstalk, while transcriptomic data indicated endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory activation and oxidative stress. PTGS2 and SERPINE1 were prioritized as candidate molecular convergence nodes linking inflammatory and prothrombotic signalling, and molecular docking and dynamics analyses supported in silico interactions between doxorubicin and these proteins. Immune‐related transcriptional signature analyses further indicated enrichment of gene programs associated with macrophage, neutrophil and dendritic‐cell signatures in renal injury. These findings suggest a candidate dual‐hit model in which doxorubicin‐induced intracellular stress and carrier‐associated complement activation may converge toward endothelial injury as well as inflammation–coagulation crosstalk, potentially contributing to PLD‐associated renal TMA.
medicine.text:
Breast cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, and anthracyclines, particularly doxorubicin, remain a cornerstone of systemic chemotherapy despite their dose‐limiting toxicities [, , , ]. PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD), the most clinically established liposomal formulation, was developed to improve pharmacokinetics and reduce the systemic toxicity of free doxorubicin, and is now widely used for the treatment of breast and ovarian cancers as well as other solid tumours [, , , , , ]. However, accumulating clinical evidence has identified a distinct and underrecognized adverse event associated with PLD‐renal‐limited thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), characterized by glomerular endothelial injury, microvascular thrombosis, and progressive renal dysfunction [, , , , ]. Unlike conventional doxorubicin nephrotoxicity, which is primarily driven by oxidative stress and tubular epithelial cell injury, PLD‐associated renal TMA exhibits a unique endothelial‐centered pathological phenotype, suggesting that its nephrotoxicity arises from mechanisms beyond the intrinsic toxicity of doxorubicin alone [, ].

PLD is a composite nanomedicine consisting of an active cytotoxic agent (doxorubicin) encapsulated within a PEGylated liposomal carrier. While doxorubicin is known to induce intracellular stress responses, including oxidative damage and inflammatory activation [], the PEGylated liposomal carrier, though generally considered biologically inert, has been shown to activate the complement system [, ]. Excessive complement activation leads to the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC), which can directly damage vascular endothelial cells and trigger downstream inflammatory and coagulation cascades [, ]. Importantly, certain molecular intermediates, such as SERPINE1, are positioned at the interface of these processes, functioning both as regulators of coagulation and as targets of doxorubicin []. These observations raise the possibility that PLD‐associated renal TMA arises from a coordinated interplay between drug‐induced intracellular stress and carrier‐associated immune activation. However, the respective contributions of the active drug and PEGylated liposomal carrier, as well as their potential interactions, have not been systematically delineated. Whether PLD nephrotoxicity primarily originates from the encapsulated cytotoxic agent, the PEGylated liposomal carrier, or their mechanistic interaction remains unresolved. In particular, it remains unclear whether PLD‐induced nephrotoxicity reflects independent parallel effects or a convergent mechanism that amplifies endothelial injury. Addressing this gap is critical for advancing our understanding of nanomedicine safety and for improving risk stratification in clinical practice.

In this study, we hypothesized that PLD‐associated renal toxicity may reflect the convergence of two mechanistically distinct processes: doxorubicin‐associated intracellular stress and carrier‐associated complement activation. To investigate this possibility, we developed an integrative systems‐level framework combining network toxicology, renal injury transcriptomics, protein–protein interaction analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations and immune‐related transcriptional signature analysis. Rather than assuming that either the drug or carrier alone accounts for PLD‐associated renal injury, we sought to identify molecular pathways that may connect these two toxicity layers and converge on endothelial and thrombotic injury. This approach allowed us to propose a putative dual‐hit model centered on complement–coagulation crosstalk and to identify candidate molecular mediators that warrant experimental validation.

Given that the direct cytotoxic effects of PLD are primarily attributable to doxorubicin, in silico toxicity prediction was performed to characterize its intrinsic nephrotoxic potential. The canonical SMILES structure of doxorubicin was obtained and submitted to ProTox‐3.0 and ADMETlab 3.0. Outputs from both platforms were integrated to evaluate toxicity endpoints, including organ toxicity, oxidative stress liability and predicted renal risk.

To capture conserved molecular features of drug‐induced kidney injury, the RNA‐seq dataset GSE145085 was retrieved from the GEO database. Due to the lack of PLD‐specific transcriptomic datasets, this dataset, based on a cisplatin‐induced acute kidney injury (AKI) model, was used as a surrogate transcriptional injury background to identify shared renal stress‐response programs rather than to define PLD‐specific transcriptional signatures. The dataset included 8 human kidney samples (control n = 4; cisplatin‐treated n = 4; Table ). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using the DESeq2 package in R (v4.5.2), with thresholds set at |log2FC| > 1.0 and adjusted p < 0.05. Results were visualized using volcano plots to illustrate global transcriptional alterations.

To capture the composite nature of PLD, targets were defined from two complementary sources. (1) Doxorubicin‐associated targets (drug‐driven layer): candidate targets were collected from SwissTargetPrediction, SEA, STITCH, CTD, SuperPred and PharmMapper, restricted to 
Homo sapiens
, and standardized using UniProt. Redundant entries were removed to generate a high‐confidence drug target set. (2) PEGylated liposomal carrier‐associated targets (carrier‐driven layer): as PEG does not directly bind protein targets, its effects were modelled using manually curated complement‐related genes from published literature [, ], which constitute the carrier‐associated target set. Accordingly, complement‐related genes were compiled to represent carrier‐associated immune activation. These two target layers were subsequently integrated to construct a unified PLD composite target system, enabling systematic analysis of drug–carrier interactions.

Disease‐related targets were retrieved from GeneCards, OMIM, Open Targets and TTD using keywords including thrombotic microangiopathy, acute kidney injury and nephrotoxicity. To improve specificity, only genes with relevance scores ≥ 10 (GeneCards) and ≥ 0.1 (Open Targets) were retained. All targets were standardized and merged to construct a comprehensive nephrotoxicity‐associated gene set.

To identify key mediators of PLD‐induced nephrotoxicity, intersecting genes among PLD composite targets, nephrotoxicity‐associated targets and DEGs from GSE145085 were defined as candidate targets. These candidates were submitted to the STRING database (confidence score ≥ 0.4, 
Homo sapiens
) to construct a protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, which was visualized and analysed using Cytoscape (v3.10.0).

Functional annotation was conducted using the DAVID platform, including Gene Ontology (GO) analysis across biological processes (BP), cellular components (CC) and molecular functions (MF), as well as KEGG pathway enrichment. Significantly enriched terms (p < 0.05) were visualized using bar plots, bubble plots and Sankey diagrams []. Particular attention was given to pathways related to complement activation, endothelial injury and inflammation–coagulation coupling.

To dissect respective contributions of drug‐ and carrier‐associated targets, we analysed four gene sets comprising doxorubicin‐associated targets, carrier‐associated complement‐related targets, full PLD composite targets and PLD composite targets after removal of manually curated carrier‐associated complement‐related genes (including two genes shared with drug‐derived targets). These gene sets were subjected to GO‐BP and KEGG enrichment analysis using the clusterProfiler package in R (v4.5.2). A permutation test (1000 permutations) was implemented in R to assess whether the substantial overlap between carrier‐associated genes and complement‐cascade (hsa04610) genes was attributable to random chance. The background gene universe for permutation testing comprised all annotated human gene symbols retrieved from the org.Hs.eg.db database.

Key regulatory genes were identified using the CytoHubba plugin in Cytoscape, applying six algorithms (Degree, Betweenness, Closeness, Bottleneck, MNC, Radiality) []. The top‐ranked genes from each method were intersected to obtain consensus hub genes, minimizing algorithm‐specific bias.

To evaluate direct interactions between doxorubicin and hub proteins, molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina []. Protein structures were obtained from the RCSB PDB database (resolution ≤ 2.5 Å), preprocessed using PyMOL. ITGAM was excluded because it acts as a receptor with no documented direct ligand‐binding evidence, whereas SERPINE1 was retained based on prior validation as a doxorubicin target []. Binding energies ≤ −5 kcal/mol were considered indicative of stable interactions. Binding conformations were visualized using PyMOL and Discovery Studio.

To evaluate the stability of drug–target interactions, 10‐ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted for the PTGS2–doxorubicin and SERPINE1–doxorubicin complexes using GROMACS (v2022.3) [, ]. The Amber99SB‐ILDN force field was applied, and systems were solvated in a TIP3P water model under periodic boundary conditions. Simulations were performed at a constant temperature of 300 K and pressure of 1 atm. Trajectory analyses included root mean square deviation (RMSD) to assess overall structural stability and root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) to evaluate residue‐level flexibility.

To characterize pathway‐level perturbations, GSEA was conducted using clusterProfiler, with KEGG gene sets (c2.cp.kegg_medicus.v2026.1). Significant pathways were defined as |NES| > 1.0, adjusted p < 0.05 and q < 0.25.

To characterize alterations in the immune microenvironment, ssGSEA was performed using the GSVA package (v2.4.9) based on MSigDB C7 immunologic signature gene sets. The relative abundance of 28 immune cell‐associated transcriptional signatures was quantified as previously described []. Differences in immune‐associated transcriptional programs between groups were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test, while associations between immune‐related signatures and hub genes were evaluated using Spearman correlation analysis. Importantly, these analyses were interpreted as relative enrichment of immune‐related transcriptional programs rather than direct evidence of immune cell infiltration, given the organoid‐based transcriptomic context. This computational analysis enables the systematic characterization of potential PEG‐triggered immune‐relevant transcriptional perturbations and their interplay with doxorubicin‐associated signalling, offering computational support for the hypothesized dual‐hit mechanism.

Unless otherwise specified, all statistical analyses were performed using R (v4.5.2). Continuous variables were analysed using nonparametric methods when appropriate. Between‐group comparisons of immune‐related features were performed using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test, and correlations among immune features were assessed using Spearman correlation analysis. For functional enrichment analyses, p values for all enriched pathways were adjusted using the Benjamini‐Hochberg method unless otherwise specified. In transcriptomic analyses, multiple‐testing correction was applied when appropriate, and adjusted p values were used to control the false discovery rate. All statistical tests were two‐sided unless otherwise specified, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

To define the composite nephrotoxicity landscape of PLD, we first evaluated the intrinsic renal toxicity of its pharmacologically active component, doxorubicin. In silico toxicity prediction using ProTox‐3.0 and ADMETlab 3.0 consistently classified doxorubicin as a toxicity class III compound with a predicted LD50 of 205 mg/kg (Figure ; Table ). Both platforms further predicted a high probability of nephrotoxicity (0.80 and 0.99, respectively), supporting doxorubicin as the primary source of intracellular toxic stress within the PLD system.

Nephrotoxicity prediction results of doxorubicin.

To establish a disease‐relevant molecular context for subsequent integrative analyses, we next characterized the transcriptomic landscape of renal injury using the GSE145085 dataset. Differential expression analysis identified 6132 DEGs, including 2846 upregulated and 3286 downregulated genes (|log2FC| > 1, adjusted p < 0.05). Principal transcriptomic alterations clearly distinguished injured kidneys from controls (Figure ), indicating extensive molecular reprogramming associated with renal injury and providing a general renal injury background for downstream systems analyses.

Given that PLD is a composite nanomedicine comprising both an active drug and a PEGylated liposomal carrier, we integrated drug‐derived targets, carrier‐associated complement‐related targets, nephrotoxicity‐associated genes and injury‐responsive DEGs to construct a PLD‐related toxicity network. A total of 265 PLD‐related targets and 6952 nephrotoxicity‐associated genes were compiled, yielding 98 overlapping candidate genes following intersection analysis (Figure ). Protein–protein interaction analysis revealed a highly interconnected network consisting of 98 nodes and 527 edges (Figure ). Notably, this integrated network simultaneously captured drug‐associated intracellular stress pathways and carrier‐associated complement signalling, providing a systems‐level framework for hypothesis generation regarding candidate drug‐ and carrier‐associated contributions in general renal injury.

To characterize the molecular features associated with the carrier‐associated toxicity of PLD, functional enrichment analyses were performed on the 98 overlapping candidate genes. GO analysis consistently identified complement activation, membrane attack complex (MAC) assembly, and complement‐mediated immune responses as the most significantly enriched biological processes (Figure ), indicating complement activation as a candidate upstream process in PLD‐associated nephrotoxicity. Consistent with these findings, cellular component enrichment highlighted complement complexes, membrane rafts and extracellular vesicles, whereas molecular function analysis revealed significant enrichment of complement binding, serine protease activity and C5a receptor signalling.

KEGG pathway analysis further demonstrated robust enrichment of the complement and coagulation cascades, accompanied by inflammatory signalling pathways and the p53 pathway. Moreover, complement signalling occupied a central position connecting immune activation with coagulation‐related pathways, suggesting that carrier‐associated complement activation may contribute to a cascade leading to endothelial injury and subsequent inflammation–coagulation coupling. Together, these findings support complement activation as a computationally predicted, carrier‐associated candidate process within the composite nephrotoxicity of PLD.

Pathway signatures associated with doxorubicin, the PEGylated liposomal carrier and the integrated PLD formulation were compared across four predefined target sets. These included doxorubicin‐derived, carrier‐associated, the full PLD composite and the carrier‐depleted PLD targets. Two genes, including the hub gene SERPINE1 and CFD, overlapped between the drug‐ and carrier‐associated sets. Owing to their small count, these genes were not analysed as an independent subset. Functional enrichment revealed distinct pathway profiles for each component (Figure ). Complement and coagulation cascades were exclusively enriched in carrier‐associated and full PLD composite sets, whereas drug‐derived and carrier‐depleted PLD sets lacked such signatures. GO‐BP analysis yielded consistent results, with complement activation terms restricted to carrier‐associated sets. Notably, in separate background contexts, SERPINE1 was associated with apoptosis‐ and inflammation‐related terms in the doxorubicin‐associated gene set, whereas it was enriched together with complement cascades in carrier‐associated ones. A 1000‐iteration permutation test confirmed non‐random enrichment of complement pathways in carrier‐associated genes (empirical p < 0.001). These results indicate carrier‐associated enrichment of complement‐related signatures. Given the literature‐based curation of carrier‐associated gene sets, this study provides computationally predicted pathway features without definitive evidence for in vivo pathogenic causality.

To identify the key molecular mediators linking the drug‐ and carrier‐derived toxicity pathways, topological analysis of the PPI network was performed using six independent cytoHubba algorithms, yielding seven consensus hub genes (Figure , Table ). To further prioritize these hubs for experimental validation, molecular docking was conducted between doxorubicin and these hub proteins (Table , Figure ). Structural analysis revealed extensive hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions within the binding pockets, indicating favourable ligand–protein recognition. Among these candidates, PTGS2 and SERPINE1 were prioritized as representative nodes based on their network centrality, functional relevance to inflammation/coagulation pathways, and favourable docking results (−12.2 and −9.8 kcal/mol, respectively, the top two among tested hubs). Notably, SERPINE1 was also found to be present in both drug‐ and carrier‐associated target sets, supporting its candidacy in linking drug‐carrier interactions. Although these two genes were not necessarily the highest‐ranked genes across all individual topological algorithms, they were selected as representative candidates based on the combined criteria described above.

Molecular docking results (binding energy).

PTGS2 and SERPINE1 were further selected for 10‐ns molecular dynamics simulations based on their binding energies. These short‐timescale simulations were performed to assess the initial stability of the docking poses rather than to capture large‐scale conformational transitions. Both the PTGS2‐doxorubicin and SERPINE1‐doxorubicin complexes rapidly reached equilibrium and maintained stable RMSD trajectories (~0.22 nm) throughout the simulations, with the protein–ligand complex and protein‐alone RMSD overlapping closely, indicating minimal ligand‐induced conformational changes. Ligand RMSD fluctuated within a narrow range, showing favourable binding poses (Figure ). RMSF analysis demonstrated limited residue fluctuations within the binding regions (Figure ), while system energy remained stable over time (Figure ). Collectively, these simulation results support local structural stability of both complexes in silico. Taken together, these findings suggest that PTGS2 and SERPINE1 are representative candidate nodes that may link carrier‐associated complement signatures with doxorubicin‐induced intracellular stress. While the docking and MD results support potential interactions between doxorubicin and these proteins, these computational observations do not establish direct causality but rather propose a testable hypothesis for how drug‐carrier interactions might converge on shared molecular targets. Further experimental validation is required to confirm this proposed connection.

To further characterize the downstream transcriptomic programs associated with the proposed dual‐hit hypothesis, GSEA was performed using the renal injury transcriptomic dataset. Significant enrichment was observed in pathways associated with endothelial barrier dysfunction, including tight junction–actin signalling (NES = 2.28), together with inflammatory signalling, particularly the JAK–STAT pathway (NES = 1.98) and oxidative stress responses, including KEAP1‐NRF2 signalling (NES = 2.03) (all adjusted p < 0.05; Figure ).

Among these signatures, endothelial barrier‐related alterations were prominent and accompanied by enrichment of inflammatory and stress‐response programs. These findings indicate that endothelial, inflammatory and oxidative‐stress‐related transcriptional responses are associated with the renal injury background represented by GSE145085. However, because the dataset was not generated from PLD‐treated tissue or a PLD‐specific renal model, these results should be interpreted as general renal injury‐associated signatures and not as direct evidence of PLD‐specific endothelial injury or inflammation‐coagulation coupling.

To evaluate immune‐related transcriptional programs associated with renal injury, ssGSEA was performed using the GSE145085 dataset. Compared with controls, the renal injury group exhibited significant enrichment of pathways associated with CD8+ T‐cell differentiation, CD4+ T‐cell activation and dendritic cell activation (Figure ), indicating broad alteration of innate‐ and adaptive‐immune‐related transcriptional programs. These findings suggest that complement activation is associated with broad changes in immune‐associated transcriptional programs rather than isolated innate immune activation.

Analysis of immune cell‐related gene signatures further showed significantly elevated signature scores for macrophages, neutrophils and activated dendritic cells in injured kidneys (all p < 0.05; Figure ; Figure ), consistent with the inflammatory‐like transcriptional profile predicted by the enrichment analyses. Correlation analysis suggested that PTGS2 was positively associated with NK cells and memory B cells, whereas SERPINE1 correlated with CD8+ T cells and Th2 cells. In addition, ITGAM exhibited strong associations with dendritic cells and NKT cells (Figure ), linking hub genes to complement‐associated immune‐related transcriptional signatures but does not establish direct interactions with or recruitment of the corresponding immune‐cell types. Collectively, these findings indicate that renal injury was accompanied by alterations in immune‐related transcriptional signatures. These correlations connect complement‐linked gene signatures with drug‐associated inflammatory transcriptomic signals and provide hypothesis‐generating support for the proposed dual‐hit mechanism. Given the organoid‐based experimental context and the lack of a physiological immune compartment, these results should be considered hypothesis‐generating evidence of immune‐related transcriptional perturbation rather than direct evidence of immune‐cell infiltration or PLD‐specific immune remodelling.

PLD has been widely adopted in oncology due to its reduced cardiotoxicity and improved pharmacokinetics compared with conventional doxorubicin. However, accumulating clinical evidence indicates that PLD induces a distinct form of renal injury, renal‐limited thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), characterized by endothelial damage and microvascular thrombosis, thereby limiting its clinical utility. The mechanistic basis underlying this toxicity has remained poorly defined. In the present study, we propose an integrative, multi‐layered framework to generate a hypothesis regarding a previously underappreciated dual‐hit mechanism, in which doxorubicin‐driven intracellular stress and PEG‐mediated complement activation may converge toward endothelial injury. This work, to our knowledge, provides the first computational framework of the composite nephrotoxic signatures associated with the active drug and nanocarrier components in PLD.

A central insight from this study is that PLD‐associated nephrotoxicity cannot be explained by the canonical mechanisms of conventional doxorubicin alone. Traditional doxorubicin‐induced kidney injury is largely attributed to oxidative stress, tubular apoptosis and fibrosis []. In contrast, our results consistently highlight the potential role of complement activation and inflammation–coagulation crosstalk in PLD‐associated injury models. This shift in pathogenic paradigm reflects the composite nature of PLD, in which the PEGylated liposomal carrier introduces an additional, immunologically active layer of toxicity. Specifically, PEGylated liposomes are known to activate the complement system, leading to the formation of membrane attack complexes (MAC) and direct endothelial injury [, ]. Our enrichment and immune‐related gene signature analyses support this carrier‐driven process, suggesting a potential role for complement activation as an upstream contributor in PLD‐induced TMA. Within this framework, PTGS2 and SERPINE1 emerge as key molecular nodes linking drug‐ and carrier‐associated effects. PTGS2, a critical regulator of inflammatory responses, promotes prostaglandin E2 production, thereby increasing vascular permeability and compromising endothelial barrier integrity []. Although PTGS2 upregulation has been reported in conventional doxorubicin nephrotoxicity, it is typically considered secondary to oxidative stress []. In contrast, our network topology and structural analyses suggest that under PLD conditions, PTGS2 may function as a primary downstream effector of complement‐driven inflammation, rather than a passive bystander. This distinction highlights a context‐dependent functional shift driven by the presence of the PEGylated liposomal carrier.

SERPINE1, a master regulator of fibrinolysis, represents another critical node bridging inflammation and coagulation. By inhibiting tissue‐type and urokinase‐type plasminogen activators, SERPINE1 suppresses fibrinolysis and promotes thrombus persistence []. Elevated SERPINE1 levels have been closely associated with microthrombus formation and acute kidney injury severity [, , ]. In the context of PLD, our findings suggest that SERPINE1 I ntegrates doxorubicin‐induced intracellular signalling with complement‐mediated coagulation activation, thereby acting as a molecular link in the dual‐hit hypothesis. Given that dysregulated fibrinolysis is a hallmark of TMA [], SERPINE1 likely plays a role in driving microvascular thrombosis downstream of endothelial injury. Importantly, our data suggest a possible sequence in which carrier‐associated complement signatures may be linked to endothelial damage and subsequently propagate two interconnected processes. First, complement activation promotes immune cell‐associated transcriptional changes. The identification of ITGAM (CD11b), a key component of complement receptor 3, as a hub gene suggests a functional link between complement signalling and leukocyte adhesion or migration []. Consistent with this, transcriptomic and ssGSEA analyses supported significant enrichment of inflammatory pathways (e.g., JAK–STAT signalling) and higher scores for macrophage‐ and neutrophil‐associated transcriptional signatures [, ]. These transcriptional signatures may further amplify inflammation through cytokine release, reinforcing PTGS2 activation. Second, complement activation interacts extensively with the coagulation system []. Through upregulation of SERPINE1, this interaction shifts the hemostatic balance toward impaired fibrinolysis and microthrombus formation. Together, these processes result in a continuing interaction among complement activation, immune recruitment, inflammatory signalling and coagulation dysregulation, ultimately culminating in glomerular endothelial injury and TMA.

At a broader level, this study expands the current conceptual understanding of nanomedicine‐associated nephrotoxicity. Conventional toxicological evaluations generally attribute nanodrug toxicity exclusively to the pharmacological activity of loaded compounds while regarding delivery carriers as biologically inert. Our findings raise the possibility that the PEGylated liposomal carrier actively reshapes the pathogenic landscape through immune activation. Whether the resulting drug‐carrier interaction is merely additive or represents an emergent effect remains speculative and cannot be determined using the current computational framework. This has important implications for the safety evaluation of nanomedicines, emphasizing the need to consider carrier‐induced immunological effects alongside pharmacological activity. From a translational perspective, the identification of the candidate complement–PTGS2–SERPINE1 crosstalk suggests potential pathways for therapeutic intervention. These molecules warrant further experimental investigation to evaluate their role as therapeutic targets for mitigating endothelial injury and inflammation–coagulation coupling [, ]. In addition, these molecules may serve as potential biomarkers for early detection and risk stratification of TMA in patients receiving PLD.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study used a computational framework based on publicly available transcriptomic data from a cisplatin‐induced acute kidney injury model (GSE145085), which provided a general renal injury background for hypothesis generation; future studies with PLD‐specific datasets and models that include a physiological immune compartment will be needed to refine these findings. Second, complement‐related genes were pre‐specified in the carrier target set, and sensitivity analyses confirmed this selection bias; consequently, complement activation cannot be independently established as an initiating event. Third, direct comparative studies between free doxorubicin, empty PEGylated liposomal carriers and PLD are required to substantiate the proposed drug‐carrier interactions. Future studies incorporating exposure‐specific models and mechanistic experiments will be essential to validate and refine the proposed framework.

This study presents a hypothesis‐generating computational framework for investigating potential drug‐ and carrier‐associated contributors to PLD‐related renal injury. The analyses identified complement‐related enrichment in the carrier‐associated target set and highlighted PTGS2 and SERPINE1 as candidate nodes implicated in inflammatory and coagulation‐related processes. Transcriptomic analyses from a cisplatin‐induced renal injury model further suggested endothelial stress and immune‐related transcriptional signature changes; however, these findings are not PLD‐specific and should be interpreted as signature‐level perturbations rather than direct evidence of immune‐cell infiltration. Overall, the results support a testable dual‐hit model in which doxorubicin‐ and carrier‐associated molecular signatures may converge on endothelial injury and inflammation‐coagulation crosstalk. Future experimental studies should prioritize direct comparisons of free doxorubicin, empty PEGylated liposomal carriers and PLD to investigate their relative contributions and establish the specificity and causal relevance of these molecular signatures.
