medicine.title: Cardiac CT in a Criss-Cross Heart With Double-Outlet Right Ventricle Guiding Single-Ventricle Palliation
medicine.abstract: Criss-cross heart with double-outlet right ventricle (DORV) and dual discordance is a rare phenotype challenging the conventional echocardiographic segmental characterization.An infant with prenatally diagnosed complex congenital heart disease had functionally univentricular physiology, severe pulmonary stenosis, and large septal defects. Echocardiography suggested double-inlet left ventricle with transposed great arteries but incompletely defined segmental anatomy and pulmonary arteries. Electrocardiographically gated cardiac computed tomography (CT) angiography established criss-cross atrioventricular relationships with clockwise ventricular rotation, straddling tricuspid valve, DORV from a mildly hypoplastic morphologic right ventricle, severe subpulmonary/pulmonary annular obstruction, confluent pulmonary arteries, single coronary artery pattern, and patent ductus arteriosus, supporting staged single-ventricle palliation.CT provided the segmental and vascular roadmap for staged palliation.Criss-cross heart with DORV and dual discordance frequently precludes biventricular repair, directing single-ventricle planning. CT is pivotal pre and postoperatively, defining pulmonary artery eligibility for cavopulmonary connection and confirming the substrate for Fontan completion.
medicine.text:
A 6-month-old infant with known complex congenital heart disease, following bidirectional Glenn palliation as part of a staged single-ventricle pathway, was referred for pediatric cardiology reassessment. At clinical examination, the infant was in good general condition, conscious, afebrile, and hemodynamically and respiratorily stable. The skin and mucous membranes were cyanotic and erythematous, with normally represented subcutaneous tissue. The pharynx was normally colored, and no palpable lymphadenopathy was detected.

Pulmonary examination revealed bilaterally present vesicular breath sounds, with wheezing, rales, and pre-existing upper airway secretions. Oxygen saturation was 86%. Cardiovascular examination showed rhythmic heart sounds, a heart rate of 138 beats/min, blood pressure of 106/66 mm Hg, a grade III/VI systolic murmur at the left parasternal border, and bilaterally present femoral pulses.

The abdomen was soft, elastic, and nontender on superficial and deep palpation. The patient had 2 semiconsistent stools, no vomiting, preserved oral intake, and physiological urination. The liver and spleen were not palpable. External genitalia were appropriate for age and sex. There were no signs of meningeal irritation or focal neurological deficits.

Anthropometric assessment documented a birth weight of 3,500 g and a current weight of 5,930 g.

A complex cardiac malformation was identified prenatally on serial fetal echocardiography; the pregnancy was otherwise complicated by threatened preterm labor and fetal left-sided ureterohydronephrosis. Postnatal echocardiography established functionally univentricular physiology with double-inlet left ventricle, double-outlet right ventricle with transposed great arteries, pulmonary valve stenosis, straddling and malformed tricuspid valve, and septal defects. A dynamic subpulmonary/right ventricular outflow gradient was noted, limiting pulmonary overcirculation. Oral propranolol was initiated to prevent hypoxic spells, but was temporarily withheld during a period of stable saturations. At an extended cardiac-surgical-interventional colloquium (including an international team), surgical intervention was deferred pending periodic reassessment. During a subsequent admission at 2 months of age, recurrent hypoxic spells with oxygen saturations falling to approximately 40% prompted reintroduction of propranolol and performance of electrocardiographically (ECG) gated cardiac computed tomography (CT) angiography, because echocardiography could not accurately delineate the pulmonary artery branches. CT confirmed confluent, adequately sized pulmonary arteries, a critically narrowed subpulmonary outflow tract (0.2-0.3 cm) and hypoplastic pulmonary annulus (0.6 cm), and further defined the segmental anatomy suggesting criss-cross heart arrangement, a single coronary artery pattern, and a patent ductus arteriosus (). Preoperative N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was elevated at 559.8 pg/mL. After clinical stabilization, the infant was discharged and thereafter scheduled for surgery. The international colloquium weighed biventricular against single-ventricle repair; the ventricular and valvar anatomy was judged unsuitable for 2-ventricle repair, favoring the single-ventricle pathway. At approximately 3.5 months of age, she underwent bidirectional cavopulmonary (Glenn) anastomosis with pulmonary trunk ligation, under cardiopulmonary bypass, with delayed sternal closure the following day ( and ); the postoperative course was complicated by transient ventricular systolic dysfunction, a postintubation laryngeal syndrome, a self-limited febrile episode, and transient electrolyte disturbances. Anticoagulation with warfarin was initiated at discharge and continued at home.

Extracardiac findings included dysmorphic features with whole-exome sequencing ongoing, bilateral intracranial intraventricular hemorrhage undergoing cystic transformation, and grade III-IV left hydronephrosis.

The central diagnostic problem was the segmental anatomy itself rather than a list of competing diseases. Postnatal echocardiography established a functionally univentricular malformation with transposed great arteries and pulmonary stenosis, identifying a double-inlet left ventricle, but the ventricular topology required further characterization (specifically whether this represented a true double-inlet arrangement or an atrioventricular-discordant criss-cross heart), and the origin of the great arteries required clarification. ECG-gated cardiac CT angiography confirmed the criss-cross arrangement with clockwise ventricular rotation, straddling of the tricuspid valve, and double-outlet right ventricle with mild hypoplasia, and precisely defined the level and severity of pulmonary obstruction. Equally important was determining whether pulmonary blood flow was duct-dependent; because it was not, emergency intervention was not needed. These findings collectively precluded biventricular repair, directing management toward a single-ventricle pathway.

Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with an intermediate QRS axis, heart rate of 110 beats/min, and normal intervals, without conduction abnormality. Holter monitoring confirmed sinus rhythm throughout, with a mean rate of 138 beats/min, sinus tachycardia during periods of agitation, and supraventricular and ventricular ectopic burden each below 1%; no sustained arrhythmia or conduction disturbance was detected. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed post-Glenn univentricular anatomy and guided warfarin dose adjustment, with international normalized ratio maintained within the therapeutic range throughout the admission.

The postoperative ECG-gated cardiac CT angiography performed before the current admission confirmed a patent superior cavopulmonary anastomosis without filling defect, mild decalibration of the superior vena cava proximal to the anastomosis, confluent pulmonary artery branches of normal caliber, and a ligated pulmonary trunk (). The underlying segmental anatomy was unchanged: atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance in a criss-cross arrangement, a 1.3 cm perimembranous ventricular septal defect with inlet extension, double-outlet right ventricle with a mildly hypoplastic morphologic right ventricle, a free subaortic outflow tract, and a single coronary artery with a retro-aortic and retro-pulmonary right coronary course. A right aortic arch with mirror-image branching, kinking of the right subclavian artery, a small diverticulum at the former ductal ampulla, and 2-3 small aortopulmonary collaterals bilaterally were also noted.

Cranial ultrasound showed stable cystic lesions at both choroid plexuses without mass effect; neurological assessment documented mild improvement in generalized hypotonia, with neurodevelopmental follow-up and whole-exome sequencing ongoing.

Full blood count demonstrated a compensated erythrocytosis with microcytosis—a pattern consistent with chronic cyanosis and concurrent iron deficiency—alongside mild lymphopenia and peripheral eosinophilia; hemoglobin was 15.0 g/dL and platelet count was within normal limits.

During the current admission, warfarin dosing was adjusted to target an international normalized ratio of 2-3, maintaining values within the therapeutic range. Propranolol and spironolactone were continued unchanged. No acute cardiac intervention was required.

The infant was discharged in stable condition on propranolol, spironolactone, and warfarin, with oxygen saturations of 75%-85% at rest and approximately 80% during feeding. An intercurrent rotavirus gastroenteritis was managed conservatively. Neurodevelopmental follow-up for the intracranial intraventricular hemorrhage and genetic work-up remain ongoing. Fontan completion is anticipated subject to favorable pulmonary vascular assessment, with continued nephrological and neurodevelopmental surveillance given the extracardiac comorbidities.

We present a case of criss-cross heart, a rare malformation arising from abnormal rotation of the ventricular mass about its long axis, producing crossing atrioventricular inflow streams and a horizontalized ventricular septum. In this patient, ECG-gated cardiac CT angiography showed clockwise ventricular rotation and the horizontalized, end-systolic-flattened interventricular septum suggested right ventricular pressure overload.

Cross-sectional imaging is particularly helpful for defining atrioventricular segmental situs and alignment., Criss-cross heart is associated with a wide spectrum of segmental combinations and associated malformations, including double-outlet right ventricle, transposition of the great arteries, ventricular hypoplasia, and pulmonary outflow tract obstruction., This particular combination of criss-cross architecture with a double-outlet right ventricle and simultaneous atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance is among the most complex segmental arrangements and often precludes biventricular repair, favoring a single-ventricle approach., Biventricular repair was not pursued here because the mildly hypoplastic right ventricle, the straddling tricuspid valve, and the severely obstructed subpulmonary outflow precluded a satisfactory 2-ventricle separation.

Echocardiography remains the first-line imaging modality, but in this infant the crossing connections, horizontal septum, and critically the pulmonary artery branches and extracardiac vasculature could not be fully resolved. ECG-gated cardiac CT angiography provides comprehensive segmental and vascular assessment and is increasingly central to diagnosis and surgical planning in complex congenital heart disease, particularly when echocardiographic windows are limited and detailed extracardiac vascular mapping is required., The single coronary artery pattern with a retro-aortic and retro-pulmonary course identified on CT carries direct surgical relevance, as it requires consideration during cannulation and myocardial protection planning.

Progression along the single-ventricle pathway depends on favorable pulmonary vascular physiology and suitable pulmonary artery anatomy, with confluent and adequately developed pulmonary arteries supporting cavopulmonary connection. The bidirectional cavopulmonary (Glenn) anastomosis is the standard intermediate stage, usually performed at 3-6 months of age, increasing effective pulmonary blood flow and unloading the single ventricle ahead of Fontan completion. In this infant, Glenn anastomosis was performed at 3.5 months, within the standard window, driven by recurrent hypoxic spells despite propranolol, with CT-confirmed pulmonary artery anatomy providing the necessary anatomical prerequisite. Postoperative CT confirmed the anatomical substrate expected to support the next stage. The extracardiac findings—intraventricular hemorrhage, hydronephrosis, and the as-yet uncharacterized genetic syndrome—did not alter the immediate surgical pathway but will require careful longitudinal assessment given their potential implications for neurodevelopmental outcome and Fontan candidacy. Three-dimensional reconstructions and printed or virtual models derived from CT data further improve comprehension of criss-cross anatomy and surgical planning.

In this infant with a rare criss-cross heart, double-outlet right ventricle and functionally univentricular physiology, multimodality imaging combining echocardiography with ECG-gated cardiac CT angiography enabled an accurate segmental diagnosis and, above all, an assessment of the pulmonary arteries that echocardiography could not provide, directing the infant appropriately along a single-ventricle palliative pathway.

When echocardiography suggests double-inlet left ventricle but atrioventricular-valve morphology, ventriculoarterial alignment, or pulmonary artery anatomy remain incompletely defined, early CT should guide surgical strategy.

Postoperative CT confirmed anastomotic patency and pulmonary artery confluence, supporting staged Fontan planning.

medicine.title: Fontan-Associated Liver Disease
medicine.abstract: Evaluating Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) remains challenging, as elastography reflects passive congestion and standard biochemistry often remains normal. We explore transient hepatic metabolic reserve exhaustion during hemodynamic and dietary stress.An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy who had undergone Fontan completion presented for routine evaluation coinciding with an unusually large mixed meal. Dried blood spot amino acid profiling by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry revealed marked hypercitrullinemia (188.9 μmol/L) with elevated ornithine and arginine, whereas shear-wave elastography peaked at 18.1 kPa and systemic ventricular ejection fraction transiently fell to 52%; standard liver biochemistry remained normal. Amino acids normalized within 5 days, with partial recovery of liver stiffness and ejection fraction at 3-month follow-up.Hemodynamic impairment combined with acute dietary stress can transiently exhaust hepatic metabolic reserve before conventional biochemical tests turn abnormal.Dried blood spot amino acid profiling is a promising noninvasive tool to unmask subclinical metabolic reserve exhaustion in Fontan-associated liver disease when standard liver enzymes are normal.
medicine.text:
A 10-year-old boy with a functionally single ventricle of left ventricular morphology, tricuspid atresia, hypoplastic right ventricle, transposition of the great arteries, and a ventricular septal defect presented for a routine follow-up evaluation after Fontan completion.

The patient reported no clinical symptoms. On physical examination, there were no signs of heart failure or hepatic congestion (no peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, jaundice, or hepatomegaly); oxygen saturation was 96%-97% on room air.

During this scheduled visit, which coincided with an unusually large mixed meal at a family celebration—despite strict parental dietary supervision—the patient accidentally consumed excessive food. Concurrent hemodynamic and metabolic alterations were identified for the first time in this asymptomatic patient.

Congenital heart disease was diagnosed prenatally at 18 weeks of gestation. The patient underwent staged surgical palliation:•Balloon atrial septostomy at 1 month of age;•Damus–Kaye–Stansel procedure with a Sano shunt and atrial septectomy at 1.5 months of age;•Bidirectional cavopulmonary anastomosis (bidirectional Glenn) at 8 months of age;•Nuss procedure for pectus excavatum repair at 2 years and 4 months of age;•Extracardiac nonfenestrated Fontan procedure with total cavopulmonary connection using an extracardiac conduit, combined with a redo Nuss procedure, at 3 years and 11 months of age.

Balloon atrial septostomy at 1 month of age;

Damus–Kaye–Stansel procedure with a Sano shunt and atrial septectomy at 1.5 months of age;

Bidirectional cavopulmonary anastomosis (bidirectional Glenn) at 8 months of age;

Nuss procedure for pectus excavatum repair at 2 years and 4 months of age;

Extracardiac nonfenestrated Fontan procedure with total cavopulmonary connection using an extracardiac conduit, combined with a redo Nuss procedure, at 3 years and 11 months of age.

The patient remains under regular outpatient pediatric cardiology follow-up and receives ongoing acetylsalicylic acid therapy.

Longitudinal follow-up included serial dried blood spot (DBS) amino acid profiling by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (since 2015) and echocardiographic evaluation following the Fontan operation (since 2019). All echocardiographic assessments and liver stiffness measurements were performed by a single operator using the same equipment. Between 2019 and 2024, parameters remained stable: systemic (morphologically left) ventricular ejection fraction (EF), assessed by the modified biplane Simpson method, was 60%-65% (). Subsequent longitudinal studies during the acute event and follow-up evaluation were likewise performed by the same operator using the same device.

Inborn errors of metabolism, specifically congenital urea cycle disorders, were considered unlikely based on the following:•A 10-year history of stable fasting amino acid profiles both before and after the acute episode;•Spontaneous normalization of laboratory parameters within 5 days without specific targeted therapy;•A normal urinary organic acid profile (without excretion of orotic acid and with a preserved alpha-ketoglutaric acid level, arguing against exhaustion of the alternative ammonium-binding pathway);•Clear temporal synchrony with acute hemodynamic impairment (systemic ventricular EF 52%) and peak liver parenchymal stiffness (18.1 kPa).

A normal urinary organic acid profile (without excretion of orotic acid and with a preserved alpha-ketoglutaric acid level, arguing against exhaustion of the alternative ammonium-binding pathway);

Clear temporal synchrony with acute hemodynamic impairment (systemic ventricular EF 52%) and peak liver parenchymal stiffness (18.1 kPa).

These findings suggest secondary transient exhaustion of hepatic metabolic reserve triggered by venous congestion and acute dietary stress, rather than a primary genetic etiology.

DBS amino acid profiling performed on November 6, 2025, demonstrated marked elevation of citrulline to 188.9 μmol/L (reference range: 6.042-44.61 μmol/L), with mild elevations of ornithine to 317.0 μmol/L (reference range: 27.66-298.1 μmol/L) and arginine to 57.0 μmol/L (reference range: 2.55-55.80 μmol/L). Mild increases were also observed in valine (311.0 μmol/L; reference range: 58.09-267.9 μmol/L) and glycine (470.6 μmol/L; reference range: 90.75-414.7 μmol/L), whereas all other quantified amino acids remained within their respective reference ranges. All DBS samples were analyzed in duplicate, and internal quality control results met predefined acceptance criteria. Shear-wave elastography performed on November 11, 2025, demonstrated a liver stiffness of 18.1 kPa, corresponding to the range of advanced fibrosis (METAVIR F3) in patients without Fontan circulation. Repeat DBS amino acid profiling performed the same day demonstrated complete normalization of the amino acid profile.

Transthoracic echocardiography performed on November 13, 2025, demonstrated a transient decrease in systemic ventricular EF to 52%.

Serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, creatinine, total protein, and albumin remained within their respective reference ranges throughout the observation period. Gamma-glutamyl transferase was chronically elevated independent of the acute event. The lowest platelet count (220 × 109/L) was recorded at the time of peak liver stiffness. No evidence of portal hypertension was identified.

No specific pharmacological or interventional treatment was administered during the acute episode. Management consisted of dietary counseling to avoid excessive dietary nitrogen load and close clinical follow-up.

Repeat DBS amino acid profiling performed 5 days later demonstrated complete normalization of the amino acid profile, and subsequent scheduled testing remained normal. One month later, urinary organic acid analysis was normal, including normal α-ketoglutaric acid levels and the absence of orotic acid.

At follow-up on February 13, 2026, systemic ventricular EF had partially recovered to 56%, while liver stiffness had decreased to 13.0 kPa without specific therapy. Oxygen saturation remained stable at 96%-97% throughout cardiology follow-up ().

Fontan palliation remains the standard surgical approach for patients with functionally or anatomically single-ventricle physiology. With improving long-term survival, an increasing number of patients reach adolescence and adulthood; however, most ultimately develop Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD), a progressive chronic hepatic disorder driven primarily by persistent systemic venous congestion., , ,

Assessing FALD severity remains challenging. Liver stiffness measured by elastography reflects not only fibrosis but also passive venous congestion, whereas conventional liver biochemical tests may remain normal despite disease progression. Recent multiomics studies suggest that disturbances in amino acid and energy metabolism may precede routine biochemical evidence of hepatic dysfunction.,

This case demonstrated a marked, transient elevation of citrulline accompanied by moderate increases in ornithine and arginine, occurring concurrently with transient hemodynamic deterioration and peak liver stiffness. In contrast, conventional liver biochemical tests remained within the reference range. These transient metabolic alterations may reflect a temporary reduction in hepatic metabolic reserve, a systemic consequence of Fontan physiology that underscores the importance of long-term multidisciplinary follow-up. In this context, hepatic metabolic reserve refers to the liver's capacity to maintain effective ureagenesis during acute metabolic stress.

Although elastography is a mainstay of FALD monitoring, it reflects passive venous congestion in addition to fibrosis and does not directly assess hepatocellular functional reserve. Concurrently, multiomics studies suggest that disturbances in amino acid and energy metabolism, together with transcriptomic reprogramming of hepatocytes, may precede abnormalities in conventional liver biochemical tests. Nevertheless, assessment of hepatic metabolic reserve is not currently integrated into standard FALD surveillance, and the clinical significance of transient alterations in urea cycle intermediates during acute metabolic stress remains largely unexplored.,

The observed temporal relationship suggests that acute hemodynamic impairment may have transiently reduced hepatic metabolic reserve. Under these conditions, an acute dietary nitrogen load may have exceeded the liver's capacity to maintain effective ureagenesis, resulting in transient accumulation of urea cycle intermediates. Biological plausibility for this mechanism is supported by Vilstrup et al, who demonstrated that impaired hepatic function requires higher plasma amino acid concentrations to achieve equivalent rates of urea synthesis following an amino acid load.

Despite extensive research on structural and histological alterations in FALD, we found no previous reports describing transient hypercitrullinemia associated with acute venous congestion after Fontan palliation. Current consensus recommendations acknowledge that conventional liver biochemical tests (alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and bilirubin) have limited sensitivity for detecting early functional hepatic impairment, whereas elastography primarily reflects passive venous congestion.,

The principal value of this observation is the generation of a clinically testable hypothesis. If confirmed in prospective studies, serial DBS amino acid profiling by LC-MS/MS may complement current FALD surveillance by providing additional insight into hepatic metabolic reserve and the liver's capacity to adapt to acute dietary challenge.

The principal limitation of this report is its single-patient design, which precludes establishing a definitive causal relationship between the observed metabolic, hemodynamic, and hepatic changes.

The exact protein content of the meal consumed during the family celebration could not be quantified, precluding identification of the dietary threshold that may have triggered the observed metabolic response.

Molecular genetic testing (eg, whole-exome sequencing) was not performed; therefore, subtle heterozygous variants associated with urea cycle disorders cannot be completely excluded. However, the patient's stable 10-year clinical course and the close temporal association with acute hemodynamic changes strongly support a functional rather than inherited basis for the observed biochemical phenotype.

Blood ammonia was not measured because the metabolic abnormalities were identified during routine outpatient evaluation in an asymptomatic patient. Nevertheless, the absence of encephalopathy, together with normal glutamine, glutamate, and α-ketoglutaric acid levels and the absence of urinary orotic acid, indirectly argues against clinically relevant impairment of ammonia detoxification.

Histological confirmation of FALD was not obtained because liver biopsy is not part of routine surveillance in pediatric patients after Fontan palliation.

This case generates a novel, clinically testable hypothesis that transient alterations in urea cycle intermediates may reflect a temporary reduction in hepatic metabolic reserve in FALD, even when conventional liver biochemical tests remain within the reference range. Whether serial LC-MS/MS amino acid profiling using DBSs can serve as a reliable biomarker of functional hepatic reserve warrants further investigation in prospective multicenter studies.

The clinical and laboratory datasets generated and analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request, subject to patient confidentiality protocols.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Recalibration of Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring Devices on Serial Catheterization in Adults With Fontan Circulation
medicine.abstract: There are limited data on long-term accuracy of invasive hemodynamic monitoring (IHM) in patients with nonpulsatile Fontan circulation (FC).In a retrospective review of 20 patients with FC and CardioMEMS IHM implanted (2015-2025), simultaneous IHM and invasive mean pulmonary artery pressure measurements were available during 6 repeat catheterizations in 6 patients. IHM readings were nearly all lower than invasive measurements, with the absolute difference ranging from 1 to 10 mm Hg.There are limited reports of recalibration data with IHM, and to our knowledge this is the first report of simultaneous IHM and invasive measurement in adults with FC. IHM accuracy is important with FC as small pressure differences can greatly affect physiology.IHM can provide outpatient pulmonary artery pressure measurements in patients with FC. Because we find discrepancy in device measurements in our cohort, we recommend recalibration with each hemodynamic catheterization in this population.
medicine.text:
With more patients living to adulthood with Fontan circulation (FC), there are an increasing number of patients who are developing Fontan circulatory failure (FCF). Because of the unique physiology of FC, with reliance on passive pulmonary blood flow and the presence of a single ventricle, there are many modes of FCF in addition to the range of physiologies seen in acquired heart failure. In adults living with acquired heart failure, use of invasive hemodynamic monitoring (IHM) with implanted devices, such as the CardioMEMS HF system (Abbot), has shown significant reduction in heart failure hospitalization in large randomized trials. Although studies to date have not shown an impact on heart failure hospitalization with IHM in patients with FCF, use of this device is increasing in some centers., Furthermore, although data are limited, pulmonary artery (PA) pressure readings on IHM in patients living with FC may better predict development of Fontan-associated liver disease as well as be associated with decreased survival. Importantly, because patients with FC do not have a subpulmonic ventricle, small variations in PA pressure can affect cardiac output and systemic organ function. Therefore, in addition to the trends seen in PA pressure over time, the accuracy of PA pressure reports of IHM can be integral to guide medical therapy. However, there are extremely limited reports of sensor accuracy over time in the acquired heart failure population, and no recommendations for device recalibration in these patients. Within the Fontan population, recalibration rates have been reported, although data on simultaneous IHM and invasive hemodynamic readings have only been specifically reported in 2 pediatric patients. Here we report early data after IHM implantation in adults with FC who underwent repeat catheterization with recalibration and describe accuracy of the device readings compared with directly measured hemodynamics.

Between 2015 and 2025, a total of 20 patients with FC had placement of a CardioMEMS device for IHM. Of these, 8 patients underwent repeat catheterization with device recalibration, and 6 had simultaneous device and invasive mean PA pressures recorded (). Patient data for these 6 patients, including underlying anatomy and location of insertion of the device, are summarized in . The post recalibration follow-up period was a median of 27.9 months (range 1.8-41.4), and median total follow-up time from IHM insertion was 5.11 years (range 2.13-7.98) to heart transplantation or death. At last follow-up, 5 patients (83%) were alive, 1 of whom had a heart transplant, and 1 (17%) died. In the patient undergoing transplantation, IHM was recalibrated posttransplantation with catheterization reporting similar transcatheter and IHM measurements, although simultaneous pressures were not reported.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported experience of longitudinal follow-up and recalibration of IHM and report of simultaneous pressures by IHM and cardiac catheterization in adult patients with FC. Although IHM is potentially a useful tool in managing this growing patient population, its utility depends on the accuracy of reported measurements over time. We found that IHM device readings often were lower than invasively measured mean PA pressure, which has the potential to falsely reassure adult congenital heart disease providers regarding patient clinical status. This adds to the limited data regarding accuracy of these devices over time. In the adult biventricular heart failure population, there are 2 studies reporting follow-up invasive hemodynamic measurements 60 days after IHM placement. One of these reports 16 patients with a mean device reading 1.6 mm Hg below invasive mean PA pressure measurement. In a separate report of 12 patients with acquired heart failure, systolic PA pressure was 6.2 mm Hg higher and diastolic PA pressure was 1.6 mm Hg lower by IHM measurement than invasive measurement. The CardioMEMS user manual also cites data of 80 patients with follow-up catheterization with difference in mean PA measurement up to 10 mm Hg. Specifically in the Fontan population, a pediatric case series of patients with FC included 2 patients who underwent repeat catheterization with IHM in place 6 months after implantation; one of these had a device reading 2 mm Hg below the simultaneous invasive measurement and the other exactly matched the invasive measurement. Together, these reports suggest that there is potential for device readings to become inaccurate (or “drift”) over time, although the degree to which this can occur and other factors affecting IHM device readings have yet to be determined. Although a small difference in biventricular circulation may not change management, with the passive pulmonary blood flow found in the FC, this small degree of change may affect clinical care. As such, IHM should not be used in isolation to manage volume status in patients with FC, but as an adjunct to clinical exam, history, weight changes, and laboratory values.

As more centers adopt the use of IHM in patients with FC, a prospective study of IHM devices in adults with FC is needed to evaluate device accuracy over time with data from the same patients in repeat catheterization. Future studies in this field will likely require multicenter collaboration, such as through ACTION (Advanced Cardiac Therapies Improving Outcomes Network), which has a registry for IHM use in pediatric patients and those with CHD. As our study is retrospective in nature, there is potential for selection bias in which patients were clinically deemed to warrant repeat catheterization with possible device recalibration, which may limit generalizability of these results. However, IHM still has the potential to provide longitudinal data, evaluating changes in physiology over time, but the data must be accurate to be used for effective changes in management.

Although IHM has the potential to evaluate longitudinal changes in Fontan physiology and assist with clinical management, due to discrepancy in follow-up invasive measurements compared with IHM reports in this series of patients, caution should be taken in interpretation of absolute measurements without additional studies. With this in mind, we recommend routine recalibration when a cardiac catheterization is performed for any indication and to consider repeat catheterization if IHM pressures do not match the clinical situation.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Clinical and hematological characterization and carrier status awareness in a colombian cohort of sickle cell trait: a multicenter study
medicine.abstract: Sickle cell trait (SCT) has traditionally been categorized as a benign carrier state; however, isolated reports and case series have nonetheless described rare complications overlapping with those seen in sickle cell disease (HbSS). The strength and consistency of these associations remain incompletely characterized. In this context, public health institutions like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have emphasized the need to expand research on SCT.To characterize the clinical and hematological profile of HbAS carriers compared with HbAA individuals and to assess carrier status awareness within a Colombian cohort.A descriptive and analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 400 adult volunteers from the Pacific and Atlantic Afro-descendant regions. Genotypes were confirmed via high-precision liquid chromatography (HPLC) and rs334 SNP sequencing. Clinical data were retrieved through structured interviews and medical record reviews. Hematological parameters and comorbidities were compared between HbAS and HbAA individuals using robust statistical analysis.A significant genotype unawareness was identified, with 45.9% (95%CI: 37.3%–54.8%; n = 56/122) of HbAS carriers being uninformed of their status prior to screening. Serious clinical events were documented predominantly in the HbAS group: Osteomyelitis and atypical diaphyseal femoral osteonecrosis occurred only in carriers (3.3% vs. 0.0%, Fisher´s exact p = 0.016). Neurovascular events; showed a higher prevalence in heterozygous individuals (5.7% vs. 0.9%, p = 0.013). The vast majority of HbAS carriers presented at the time of this project, percentage of HbS 36–40%. Regarding hematological parameters, HbAS individuals exhibited lower mean levels of RDW (12.2 ± 0.7% vs. 13.4 ± 1.3%, p = 0.017), platelets (260 ± 56.4 × 109/L vs. 308.2 ± 95.8 × 109/L, p = 0.003), and white blood cell count (6.1 ± 1.5 × 109/L vs. 7.4 ± 1.8 × 109/L, p = 0.026) compared to non-carrier individuals (HbAA).These findings suggest that HbAS may not be uniformly benign, as uncommon but clinically notable vaso-occlusive and osteonecrotic events were observed in a minority of carriers, alongside statistically detectable but subclinical hematological differences and a substantial gap in genotype awareness. Given the cross-sectional design and the small number of severe events, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to clarify their clinical significance and to inform screening and monitoring strategies in high-prevalence populations.
medicine.text:
Sickle cell trait (SCT) is characterized by the presence of one normal allele and one mutated allele that affects hemoglobin synthesis (HbAS; HBB: c.20 A > T, rs334, 11p15.4) (Ashorobi et al. ; Márquez-Benitez et al. ). Although individuals with SCT are traditionally considered asymptomatic, it is more accurate to say their symptoms are less evident than those observed in homozygous HbSS patients, which has contributed to their underrepresentation in research (Bernal et al. ; Grant et al. ). This presumed asymptomatic status has resulted in only 16% of HbAS carriers being aware of their condition (Grant et al. ; Kisakye et al. ). Such lack of awareness not only has been associated with a higher probability of risk of transmitting the mutation to future generations but also the likelihood of experiencing clinical complications when exposed to triggering conditions such as hypoxia, low temperatures, stress, acidosis or dehydration (Ashorobi et al. ; Grant et al. ). By 2050, the number of live births with SCT is projected to reach 404,200 people (Bucknor et al. ).

While HbAS has historically been classified as a benign carrier state with normal life expectancy, growing epidemiological and clinical evidence over the last decade suggests a more nuanced spectrum. Under specific physiological stressors; such as severe hypoxia, dehydration, or strenuous physical exertion or in the presence of overlapping genetic and environmental modifiers, HbAS individuals may exhibit a infrequent clinical events overlapping with microvascular or vaso-occlusive phenomena (Gupta and Kumar ). However, the mechanistic causality and the absolute risk of these clinical manifestations remain a subject of active debate and require rigorous phenotypic characterization in diverse populations.

In this context, public health institutions like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) since 2011, have emphasized the need to expand research on SCT (Bucknor et al. ). This is driven by the fact that reported clinical associations vary significantly in their strength of evidence. On one hand, associations between HbAS and conditions such as renal medullary carcinoma, renal papillary necrosis, or venous thromboembolism are relatively well-established (Olaniran et al. ; Zhang et al. ). On the other hand, systemic vaso-occlusive phenomena, chronic kidney disease, exertional rhabdomyolysis, splenic infarction, and certain pregnancy-related or musculoskeletal complications—such as atypical diaphyseal osteonecrosis occupy a much more controversial and emerging space in current literature (Hulsizer et al. ; Pavitra et al. ).

Rather than defining a definitive causal syndromic association, these observations emphasize the heterogeneity of the HbAS phenotype and challenge the notion of SCT as a uniformly benign condition.

In Colombia, the issue is complicated even further by the uneven distribution of SCT, showing a greater prevalence in populations residing along the Atlantic and Pacific Coasts regions historically underrepresented in national clinical research (Fong et al. ; Márquez-Benítez et al. ).

To date, the clinical, hematological, and genotype-awareness characteristics of HbAS carriers remain largely undocumented outside of isolated case reports, limiting the ability to contextualize these global controversies within a well-characterized local population.

Therefore, this study aims to address this gap by describing the clinical history, hematological profile and biological markers observed in a group of adult heterozygous individuals (HbAS) compared with HbAA individuals in Colombian regions with a high prevalence of hemoglobinopathies.

A descriptive and analytical cross-sectional study was conducted to characterize the clinical and hematological phenotypes of SCT (HbAS) carriers compared with non-carrier Individuals (HbAA). Non-probabilistic sampling design by convenience in a sample of subjects from the Colombian Atlantic and Pacific coast.

This design was selected to identify clinical complications in a population where such findings are historically underreported, therefore, the sample is not intended to be representative of the entire Afro-descendant population of Colombia.

This study adheres strictly to the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines (see Online Resource ).

The primary independent variable was the presence of the heterozygous HbAS genotype. The clinical profile was evaluated through a multidimensional approach, including clinical history and comorbidities.

Pathological antecedents were categorized as major vascular or systemic events documented in the medical records, including pneumonia, events overlapping with microvascular features (e.g., stroke, osteonecrosis), and obstetric or inflammatory complications. Comorbidities were defined as chronic non-communicable diseases, such as systemic arterial hypertension and Type 2 diabetes, verified through clinical history or ongoing pharmacological treatment.

Age and sex were treated as primary independent variables for the descriptive and comparative characterization of the cohort. Furthermore, all hematological parameters were adjusted and analyzed according to biological sex, recognizing the physiological variations in hemoglobin concentration and red blood cell indices.

All participants underwent a dual-stage diagnostic protocol to ensure maximum precision. Initial screening for hemoglobin “S” variants was performed using High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC). Subsequently, HbAS was confirmed through Sanger sequencing of the rs334 single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), (HBB: c.20 A > T; p.Glu6Val; 11p15.4) (Díaz-Matallana et al. ).

Based on genotypic confirmation, participants were classified into three groups: heterozygous HbAS, HbAA and other hemoglobin variants. Following genotype classification, participants underwent evaluation of clinical history and biological markers, including complete blood count (CBC) and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels. The integrated methodological workflow, from recruitment to molecular confirmation, is summarized in Fig. .

Whole blood samples from each patient were stored under controlled conditions, with appropriate temperatures maintained for each component, ensuring strict quality control during preservation.

Generation IV hemogram analyses were performed using the Advia 2120i (USA). The blood cell count included hematocrit, hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, red blood cell distribution width, platelet count, mean platelet volume, and total leukocyte count. Reticulocyte counts were obtained through the instrument’s fluorescence channel.

All hematological tests were conducted following prior equipment calibration and internal quality control procedures, which incorporated low, medium, and high concentration controls for each analyte. Each sample was analyzed in duplicate to ensure measurement reliability.

Determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using the Ultra Genesys analyzer (Trinity Biotech, USA). The analysis included the study of HbA, HbS, HbF, and HbA2, determined by retention times, chromatographic patterns, and relative percentages.

The HPLC technique allowed for the evaluation of HbF, HbA, HbA2, and HbS levels, considering retention times and percentage concentrations, as detailed below (Pecker and Naik ):

The p.Glu6Val mutation in the β-globin chain of hemoglobin was identified through rs334 SNP analysis, following the protocol described by Sograh Fatima and Al Musaaed . The procedure was carried out as follows:

The “salting out” protocol was used for whole blood samples according to Koshy et al. (), (Koshy et al. ).

PCR amplification: Performed using the following protocol: Promega Kit (Go Taq® DNA polymerase 1 U; 1X buffer, 0.8 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 1 µM primers) in a 30 µL volume.

The products were generated using the Axygen® Maxy Gene™ THERM-1000 thermal cycler (Union City, CA, USA) with the following cycling parameters: 1 cycle at 94 °C for 5 min, 30 cycles at 94 °C for 20 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, followed by 1 cycle at 72 °C for 20 min. The amplicons were verified on 1% agarose gel.

Sanger sequencing was performed on the ABI PRISM® 3730XL Genetic Analyzer (96 capillaries).

As a validity and reliability criterion, DNA was processed according to quality, concentration, and purity standards assessed by spectrophotometry (NanoDrop 2000 C). Repeatability (2–3 replicates) and amplification reproducibility were also considered.

In each PCR reaction, positive control and negative control were included to assess the assay’s performance and potential contamination.

For the alignment of multiple DNA sequences and electropherograms, Finch TV and Geneious Prime were used.

All laboratory analyses were performed following strictly standardized protocols to ensure analytical validity and reproducibility.

For hemoglobin variant quantification via HPLC, the system was calibrated using Hemoglobin Controls (levels 1 and 2) to ensure the precision of retention times and area percentages for HbA, HbS, and HbF peaks. Any run failing to meet the manufacturer’s resolution criteria was repeated.

Analytical instruments were calibrated according to manufacturer specifications. Internal quality controls encompassing low, medium, and high concentration levels were meticulously implemented. Hematological parameters were analyzed in duplicate to ensure intra-assay precision and minimize technical variance.

For molecular genotyping, DNA concentration and purity were assessed via spectrophotometry prior to amplification. Each PCR and sequencing run included validated positive and negative controls to monitor assay performance and preclude cross-contamination. A subset of samples (10%) was randomly selected for reanalysis to confirm inter-assay reproducibility.

All data was recorded and managed using REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), hosted at Universidad de La Sabana. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Group comparisons between HbAS (heterozygous) and HbAA (wild-type) controls were conducted using Student’s t-test for independent samples. Categorical variables, including clinical history manifestations and the rate of unrecognized carrier status, were presented as absolute frequencies and percentages (n, %) and compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for small cell counts (< 5), as appropriate.

Hematological parameters with sex-specific physiological reference ranges (hemoglobin and hematocrit) were stratified and analyzed separately by sex.

Unadjusted Odds Ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (95%CI) were calculated to evaluate the strength of association for clinical events exhibiting statistically significant differences. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.

All statistical procedures were performed using SPSS version 21.0.

The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the Universidad de La Sabana (Session No. 75, May 22, 2019). All procedures were conducted in strict accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (2013 revision) and applicable national regulations, specifically Resolution 8430 of 1993 from the Colombian Ministry of Health.

Classified as a minimal-risk study, all participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment, following a detailed explanation of the study objectives and procedures. To ensure participant privacy and data protection, each individual was assigned a unique alphanumeric identification code. All sensitive information was handled according to the confidentiality standards established in Article 15 of the Colombian Constitution, ensuring that personal and genetic data remained anonymized throughout the research process.

A total of 400 volunteer Individuals were recruited and met all inclusion criteria. The mean age of the participants was 32.0 ± 17.1 years. Table  shows the sociodemographic characteristics of the total recruited population.

In these specific cases, Sanger sequencing served as the definitive diagnostic tool, identifying the pathognomonic adenine to thymine substitution (A > T) at the rs334 locus on chromosome 11. No relevant clinical history was recorded among the heterozygote carriers identified in this screening (56/122).

Analytical comparison revealed that clinical manifestations associated with vaso-occlusive phenomena were significantly more frequent in HbAS carriers than in HbAA controls. Specifically, neurovascular events and acute vaso-occlusive crises showed a significantly higher prevalence in heterozygous individuals (5.7% vs. 0.9%, p = 0.013; unajusted OR = 6.45, 95% CI: 1.31–31.64).

Due to the low absolute event rate (n = 9 total events), multivariable adjustment was not performed to prevent model overfitting; thus, this association should be interpreted with caution as unadjusted.

Furthermore, atypical skeletal complications were documented exclusively within the HbAS cohort (3.3% vs. 0.0%, Fisher’s exact p = 0.016).

Regarding hematological parameters, HbAS individuals exhibited significantly lower mean levels of RDW than HbAA individuals (12.2 ± 0.7% vs. 13.4 ± 1.3%, p = 0.017), platelets (260 ± 56.4 × 109/L vs. 308.2 ± 95.8 × 109/L, p = 0.003), and white blood cell count (6.1 ± 1.5 × 109/L vs. 7.4 ± 1.8 × 109/L, p = 0.026) compared to non-carrier controls.

Notably, major clinical events traditionally associated with homozygous disease were identified in specific HbAS carriers (stroke, facial paralysis, vaso-occlusive and femoral diaphysis osteonecrosis).

To ensure diagnostic accuracy and exclude the possibility of compound heterozygosity, participants with severe clinical events underwent rigorous phenotypic and molecular validation. HbS/beta-thalassemia was excluded by the presence of a significant HbA fraction (> 40%), while HbS/beta+-thalassemia was ruled out based on normal HbA₂ levels (< 3.5%) and an HbA/HbS ratio greater than 1.0.

Finally, the absence of additional peaks in HPLC and the molecular confirmation of the rs334 mutation via Sanger sequencing confirmed a simple HbAS genotype, ruling out other structural variants such as HbC or HbE.

A 52-year-old female carrier (HbS: 36.3%; HbA/S ratio: 1.34) presented with a history of ischemic stroke and facial paralysis. Her records indicated a critical episode at age 29, characterized by pulmonary sepsis that triggered a vaso-occlusive crisis.

At the time of this investigation, the patient’s CBC parameters and HbF levels were within normal limits, the HbS value was 36.3%. HPLC analysis (Fig. ) and rs334 SNP sequencing confirmed a simple HbAS genotype.

The A/S genotype was confirmed by rs334 (SNP, HBB: c20A > T, 11p15.4p. Glu6Val mutation.

The A/S genotype was confirmed by rs334 (SNP, HBB: c20A > T, 11p15.4p. Glu6Val mutation.

A 63-year-old male carrier was diagnosed with femoral diaphysis avascular necrosis at age 26 via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as secondary to clinical manifestations of leg pain and gait impairment.

A thorough review of his clinical history ruled out common AVN risk factors, such as chronic glucocorticoid use, HIV, autoimmune diseases, hepatitis, alcohol dependence, obesity, hyperlipidemia, trauma, or thromboembolic events. Interestingly, he reports a family history of sickle cell anemia (HbSS).

At the time of this study, the CBC parameters and HbF levels were within normal limits, the HbS level for this patient was 36.9%.

As shown in Fig. , HPLC confirmed a profile consistent with simple heterozygosity. Hypertension was subsequently diagnosed at age 54.

No additional fractions were identified that would suggest structural variants other than hemoglobin S. The presence of and HbA fraction greater than 40% and an HbA₂ level within the normal range rule out a pattern compatible with HbS-β⁰-thalassemia (absence of HbA) or HbS-β⁺-thalassemia (marked reduction in HbA accompanied by elevated HbA₂) and other variants.

The A/S genotype was confirmed by rs334 (SNP), HBB: c.20 A > T, 11p15.4p. Glu6Val mutation.

This study aims to describe the clinical history present within a group of heterozygous patients, without establishing causal associations between the presence of the SCT and the onset of clinical events.

A finding of significant public health importance in this work is that 45.9% (56/122) of the HbAS individuals were unaware of their carrier status until their participation in this study. This lack of awareness not only increases vulnerability when exposed to triggering factors (hypoxia, acidosis, infections, among others) but also hinders reproductive counseling, underscoring the importance of strengthening newborn screening programs and early detection strategies in high prevalence regions, and is especially relevant when this knowledge could drastically transform birth-control and family planning related decisions. Strengthening these programs would not only reduce the incidence of homozygote presentations, but would also allow patients to make informed decisions over their healthcare (Bernal et al. ; Pecker and Naik ).

On the other hand, the mean age at diagnosis of the mutation in heterozygotes (26 ± 15.6 years) is consistent with biological mechanisms, as the presence of a normal allele delays symptom onset (Brandow et al. ).

Our findings are consistent with those reported by Vargas-Hernández et al. (), who also documented symptomatic manifestations in HbAS carriers in Colombia. However, there are notable differences between populations. While their study gathered participants from high-altitude regions, our cohort was obtained exclusively from coastal areas in the Caribbean and Pacific at sea level. Documenting major clinical events in this low-altitude cohort raises the possibility that altitude alone may not account for the observed clinical spectrum in HbAS carriers. However, whether these manifestations are modulated by genetic background, comorbidities, or diagnostic delays remains unconfirmed and requires further prospective investigation.

To date, no direct association or concurrent pattern between these clinical events and sickle cell trait (HbAS) has been definitively established, primarily due to methodological constraints such as small sample sizes and cross-sectional study designs. Nevertheless, several consensus reviews and clinical guidelines such as Tsaras et al. (), have described clinical manifestations in HbAS individuals that are co-present or overlap with features typically observed in homozygous individuals (Ambrosino et al. ; Tsaras et al. ; Vargas-Hernández et al. ).

In this study, we identified documented clinical manifestations such as diaphyseal femoral osteonecrosis, ischemic stroke, facial paralysis, pulmonary sepsis and other vaso-occlusive phenomena.

Notably, the clinical manifestations in our two critical cases occurred before 35 years of age, reflecting an early onset of events in these individuals. The case of diaphyseal femoral osteonecrosis reported here represents an extraordinarily rare observation, with no prior documented cases in Colombia describing such an atypical involvement of the femoral diaphysis in an HbAS individual. Literature indicates that avascular osteonecrosis is primarily observed in homozygous patients, with an estimated prevalence of approximately 20%, typically affecting the femoral head, femoral condyles, and humeral head (Gulghane et al. ; Leandro et al. ; Ouederni et al. ; Severyns and Gayet ).

Globally, very few isolated cases have been documented in individuals with SCT, including proximal tibial diaphyseal infarction in a compound heterozygote with persistent HbF (Alnaqbi ), humeral head necrosis in a 25-year-old female (Banait et al. ), and femoral head necrosis in a 27-year-old female (Brown et al. ). Although osteonecrosis is frequently associated with trauma, thrombosis, or corticosteroid therapy in the general population (Shah et al. ), the patient in our study presented with no documented exposure to these classic risk factors or predisposing conditions.

Within our cohort, no statistically significant differences were observed in the prevalence of chronic comorbidities such as hypertension (p = 0.161) or type 2 diabetes mellitus (p = 1.000). Although the lack of statistical significance precludes establishing an association in this population, hypertension remains a parameter of interest, as previous literature has highlighted it as a potential comorbidity in HbAS carriers (Bucknor et al. ; Olaniran et al. ; Pinto et al. ; Zhang et al. ). To overcome the cross-sectional limitations of our study, larger prospective cohorts or well-powered longitudinal studies tracking chronic vascular indicators are needed to clarify whether subtle, long-term cardiovascular risks differ between HbAS carriers and non-carrier controls.

Analysis of medical records revealed statistically significant differences in the frequency of osteoarticular (p = 0.016) and vaso-occlusive/neurological (p = 0.013) complications between groups. These differences were primarily driven by sporadic events in the HbAS group including vaso-occlusive crisis, osteonecrosis, facial paralysis, and ischemic stroke manifestations that were not documented in HbAA individuals.

Although the sickle cell trait is classically defined as an asymptomatic condition, our observations align with literature describing severe complications in carriers under extreme physiological stress (Ambrosino et al. ; Tsaras et al. ; Vargas-Hernández et al. ). Notably, our retrospective review of medical records identified an HbAS female patient who was initially hospitalized for pulmonary sepsis and subsequently developed a vaso-occlusive crisis during her clinical course. Furthermore, the documented ischemic stroke warrants particular attention due to its early onset. Ischemic stroke in individuals under 30 years of age is exceptionally rare in the general population, where young-adult strokes are frequently classified as cryptogenic in the absence of conventional risk factors (Zhang et al. ).

Although the reductions in leukocyte (p = 0.026) and platelet (p = 0.003) counts reached statistical significance in HbAS adults, mean values for both parameters remained within normal physiological reference ranges. Consequently, these findings represent statistically detectable differences of uncertain clinical significance, which may reflect normal biological variation or population-specific characteristics.

Interestingly, these observations align with reports by Reiner et al. (), who noted that while standard hematological counts in HbAS individuals remain within reference limits, carriers display a statistically significant shift toward lower leukocyte values. Additionally, literature evaluating cellular immune subsets has described variations in T-cell subpopulations in HbAS carriers, leading some authors to hypothesize a state of relative immunological quiescence or tolerance in this population (Mikhaylova et al. ; Reiner et al. ).

Various hypotheses in the literature address variations in inflammatory responses among sickle cell trait carriers, historically linked to evolutionary adaptations against severe malaria (Ferreira et al. ). Several studies have proposed potential modulating pathways in HbAS individuals, including the induction of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and carbon monoxide generation as potential regulators of systemic inflammation (Mikhaylova et al. ; Shah et al. ), as well as altered endothelial cytoadherence influencing acute-phase responses (Lansche et al. ). However, because specific cellular or inflammatory biomarkers were not measured in our study, these proposed mechanisms remain speculative in the context of our cohort.

Similarly, although our study did not evaluate platelet activation markers or gaseous mediators, the lower mean platelet count observed in the HbAS group (p = 0.003) highlights an area of ongoing scientific interest. Previous investigations have suggested that interactions between hemoglobin variants and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) might influence nitric oxide bioavailability and platelet dynamics (Straub et al. ; Wood et al. ). Nevertheless, dedicated functional assays are required to determine whether these physiological pathways account for the subtle hematological variations observed in our population.

Taken together, these literature-reported findings suggest that the observed hematological differences in HbAS carriers do not constitute cytopenias, but rather subtle physiological variations that warrant further exploration (Tetteh et al. ). Whether these differences reflect population-specific adaptations or controlled inflammatory profiles remains to be validated. Future large-scale longitudinal studies integrating direct measurements of oxidative stress, endothelial function, and immunological markers are necessary to establish the true clinical and biological relevance of these hematological variations.

Various studies have described clinical history in HbAS individuals that was historically classified as characteristic of homozygous patients (Pinto et al. ; Naik et al. ; Sanders ; Niebuhr et al. ; Verma et al. ; Resurreccion et al. ; Dawudi et al. ).

In this regard, Supplementary Table  (see Online Resource 2) provides a structured summary of selected studies that identified clinical complications of SCT, as reported by various authors and the expert panel of the Italian Clinical Society (Pinto et al. ).

The descriptive and cross-sectional design prevents the establishment of causal relationships between the HbAS genotype and the identified clinical events. In addition, because participants were recruited through family screening of individuals with a known family history of SCD and through self-referral of individuals seeking diagnostic testing or reporting clinical concerns, the cohort is likely enriched for symptomatic or family-affected carriers relative to the broader HbAS population.

A limitation of this study is the gender distribution asymmetry observed between groups (p = 0.040), characterized by a higher female representation within the control group (HbAA). However, this phenomenon aligns with established health-seeking behavior patterns in regional community-based studies. To mitigate potential confounding effects, hematological variables were analyzed using sex-adjusted reference values to ensure the validity of the comparative results.

Finally, while a robust diagnostic protocol was used (HPLC and rs334 SNP identification), the potential presence of co-inherited alpha-thalassemia was not evaluated, which is a known genetic modifier particularly prevalent in Afro-descendant populations that could influence hematological variability in some sickle cell carriers. Further studies should incorporate alpha-globin gene deletion analysis to better characterize SCT carriers in Colombian coastal regions.

This study provides descriptive evidence regarding the clinical profile of individuals with sickle cell trait, suggesting that this genotype does not always follow an entirely asymptomatic course, although the low frequency of severe events and the cross-sectional design preclude establishing causal inferences.

The documentation of uncommon severe clinical events, such as ischemic stroke and atypical diaphyseal femoral osteonecrosis in young HbAS carriers, underscores the importance of maintaining clinical vigilance.

The finding that 45.9% of carriers were unaware of their status prior to this study highlights a critical historical gap in public health detection. This high proportion of undiagnosed individuals likely stems from the fact that screening for hemoglobinopathies was only incorporated into national health guidelines in Colombia starting around 2016 without leaving older generations without routine early detection.

Finally, prospective longitudinal studies are needed to better characterize the clinical spectrum of HbAS in the Colombian population.

medicine.title: Junctional Rhythm and Atrial Ectopy Presenting as Chronic Abdominal Pain in Fontan Circulation
medicine.abstract: Rhythm disturbances may contribute to clinically significant hemodynamic compromise in patients with Fontan circulation, even without overt Fontan failure.A 32-year-old woman with double-inlet left ventricle and total cavopulmonary connection presented with years of debilitating abdominal pain resulting in marked functional limitation. Extensive abdominal, hepatic, lymphatic, and cardiac investigations failed to identify a cause. Holter monitoring demonstrated predominant junctional rhythm and frequent atrial ectopy, whereas cardiopulmonary exercise testing revealed heart rate–dependent restoration of sinus rhythm with suppression of atrial ectopy. Invasive assessment showed that temporary atrial pacing suppressed ectopy and improved Fontan hemodynamics. Following AAIR pacemaker implantation, abdominal pain resolved completely and functional capacity improved.This case illustrates that rhythm-related hemodynamic compromise may present with atypical extracardiac symptoms despite reassuring conventional investigations.Chronic abdominal pain in patients with Fontan circulation may reflect arrhythmia-related hemodynamic compromise despite apparently stable Fontan physiology.
medicine.text:
A 32-year-old woman with a total cavopulmonary connection (TCPC) was referred for evaluation of longstanding abdominal pain. The symptoms had developed gradually over several years and progressively worsened, resulting in marked functional limitation and social withdrawal. Following an uncomplicated salpingectomy, the abdominal pain became more severe, prompting extensive diagnostic evaluation. She reported no edema, syncope, or overt symptoms of heart failure.

The patient was born with double-inlet left ventricle and tetralogy of Fallot physiology. She underwent staged palliation culminating in a fenestrated lateral tunnel. She had longstanding sinus node dysfunction with intermittent junctional rhythm.

Additional history included inferior vena cava thrombosis requiring long-term anticoagulation with warfarin.

Potential causes of abdominal pain in a patient with Fontan circulation included:•Fontan-associated liver disease•Protein-losing enteropathy•Splanchnic venous congestion related to Fontan physiology•Gastrointestinal pathology•Arrhythmia-related hemodynamic compromise

Fontan-associated liver disease

Protein-losing enteropathy

Splanchnic venous congestion related to Fontan physiology

Gastrointestinal pathology

Arrhythmia-related hemodynamic compromise

Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated preserved single-ventricle systolic function (ejection fraction approximately 60%), competent atrioventricular valves, and unobstructed TCPC.

Gastroscopy was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound identified multiple hypervascular hepatic lesions. Further evaluation, including liver magnetic resonance imaging, serologic testing, and biopsy, confirmed benign focal nodular hyperplasia without evidence of clinically significant Fontan-associated liver disease. Dynamic contrast magnetic resonance lymphangiography excluded lymphatic abnormalities and protein-losing enteropathy.

Holter monitoring confirmed predominant junctional rhythm (65.8%) and a high burden of atrial ectopy (31.4%) (). Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) demonstrated preserved exercise capacity (peak oxygen uptake 26.9 mL/kg/min) but revealed junctional rhythm with frequent atrial ectopy at lower heart rates, with resumption of sinus rhythm during exercise.

In the absence of an alternative explanation for the patient’s symptoms, the observed rhythm abnormalities were hypothesized to contribute to impaired hemodynamics. Therefore, diagnostic right heart catheterization with temporary atrial pacing was performed. The patient demonstrated a slow junctional rhythm of approximately 45 beats/min with frequent atrial premature beats occurring in bigeminy. A temporary pacing lead was positioned in the lateral tunnel to assess the hemodynamic effects of atrial pacing. Temporary atrial pacing at 60 beats/min suppressed atrial ectopy and improved invasive hemodynamics, with a reduction in mean TCPC pressure from 15 to 13 mm Hg and an increase in systemic ventricular systolic pressure from 92 to 104 mm Hg ().

The hemodynamic improvement observed during temporary atrial pacing suggested that slow junctional rhythm and frequent atrial ectopy were important contributors to the patient’s symptoms. Therefore, permanent atrial pacing was pursued.

The feasibility of transvenous atrial pacing depends largely on Fontan anatomy. In patients with a lateral tunnel Fontan, atrial tissue within the tunnel permits relatively straightforward transvenous lead implantation. In contrast, pacing in patients with an extracardiac conduit Fontan is more challenging because the conduit lacks atrial myocardium and may require access through existing fenestrations, transpulmonary puncture, or limited residual atrial tissue.,

An AAIR pacemaker was implanted via the left subclavian vein. The lateral tunnel was mapped using a steerable delivery catheter to identify the site with the highest atrial sensing amplitude. An active-fixation lead was positioned in the superior aspect of the lateral tunnel () with satisfactory sensing and a pacing threshold of approximately 1.0 V. The device was programmed in AAIR mode with a lower rate limit of 65 beats/min.

At follow-up, the patient reported complete resolution of abdominal pain. She resumed an active lifestyle and started exercising regularly.

Pacemaker interrogation confirmed a persistent need for atrial pacing, with no significant atrial arrhythmias detected. When pacing was temporarily inhibited, the intrinsic atrial rate was approximately 45 beats/min, closely matching the native rhythm observed during invasive assessment.

Maintenance of optimal Fontan hemodynamics is essential to prevent progressive Fontan failure. In the absence of a subpulmonary ventricle, pulmonary blood flow depends on passive venous return and is highly sensitive to disturbances affecting preload, pulmonary vascular resistance, ventricular function, valve competence, and atrioventricular synchrony.

Sinus node dysfunction and junctional rhythm are common complications after Fontan palliation. Junctional rhythm may impair Fontan hemodynamics through loss of atrioventricular synchrony, retrograde flow within the Fontan circuit, increased atrial pressures, and reduced ventricular preload. Consistent with this mechanism, recent echocardiographic studies have demonstrated impaired cardiac output, worsening diastolic function, and pulmonary venous flow reversal during junctional rhythm, whereas atrial pacing improves these parameters by restoring atrioventricular synchrony rather than increasing heart rate. In our patient, frequent atrial ectopy may have further aggravated this hemodynamic inefficiency.

Extensive evaluation excluded structural abnormalities of the Fontan circuit, ventricular dysfunction, lymphatic abnormalities, and clinically significant Fontan-associated liver disease. The most striking observation was the apparent relationship between rhythm and symptoms. Temporary atrial pacing suppressed atrial ectopy and was associated with more favorable Fontan hemodynamics, whereas permanent atrial pacing resulted in complete and sustained symptom resolution. Given the dependence of the Fontan circulation on low systemic venous pressures, subtle rhythm-related hemodynamic impairment may have resulted in hepatic or splanchnic venous congestion, providing a plausible explanation for the patient’s chronic abdominal pain. Although a direct causal mechanism cannot be proven, the temporal relationship between rhythm optimization, hemodynamic improvement, and symptom resolution strongly supports this hypothesis. Interestingly, review of prior electrocardiograms and serial CPET data demonstrated longstanding junctional rhythm and atrial ectopy, predating the onset of abdominal symptoms by many years. Because these findings had remained stable over time, their potential hemodynamic significance had not previously been considered. This observation suggests that the clinical consequences of arrhythmias in patients with Fontan circulation may depend not only on their presence but also on their cumulative hemodynamic effects over time.

Rhythm disturbances may represent an underrecognized and potentially reversible cause of morbidity in patients with Fontan circulation. This case highlights the importance of considering rhythm-related hemodynamic compromise in patients with Fontan circulation presenting with unexplained symptoms despite apparently stable Fontan physiology, absence of structural abnormalities, and reassuring findings on conventional imaging and CPET.
