medicine.title: Molecular Profiling for Precision Medicine in Adrenocortical Carcinoma: Real-World Data From the French Network ENDOCAN-COMETE
medicine.abstract: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare tumor with poor prognosis. Precision medicine and molecularly matched treatment (MMT) represent a new opportunity in oncology.We conducted a retrospective study of patients with advanced ACC within the French ENDOCAN COMETE network from 2009 to 2022 who have been providing access to molecular profiling (MP). We investigated the benefits of the MMT strategy in terms of response according to RECIST, median progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and growth modulation index (GMI).We enrolled 78 patients with ACC who underwent MP of the primary tumor in 41 patients. Most patients had metastasis at diagnosis, with at least one GRAS criterion. P53 alteration and activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway were the most frequent genetic alterations. No mutations were found in 20.5% of patients' tumors. The microsatellite instability phenotype was present in two cases. The median OS from the date of first metastasis was 33.3 months (95% CI, 24.7 to 56.2) with most patients receiving platinum-based chemotherapy and mitotane as first-line therapy. Twelve patients were treated with MMT as a second- or third-line therapy. An objective response rate was observed in two patients with a complete response under immunotherapy. The median PFS with MMT was 2.5 months. The mean GMI was 1.02, above 1.3 in three patients (4%).Molecular alteration–based precision medicine is associated with potential antitumor benefits in a limited subset of patients with ACC.
medicine.text:
Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare tumor originating from the adrenal cortex, with fewer than 200 cases reported annually in France. The prognosis of patients with ACC is generally poor, with a survival rate of <15% at metastatic stage at 5 years. In advanced stages, the first-line systemic therapy recommended is mitotane alone or in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy based on the results of the FIRM-ACT study., After mitotane and platinum-based chemotherapy, no other drugs or combinations have reported either a response rate of 15% or a median progression-free survival (PFS) longer than 6 months.- Moreover, the clinical benefits of early inclusion in clinical trials for patients with metastatic ACC have been suggested in a retrospective study. Therefore, recent guidelines recommend to consider molecular profiling (MP) for all patients and participation in clinical trials as a second-line option.

Several -omics studies have highlighted the molecular pathways involved in ACC tumorigenesis and have attempted to identify the prognostic role of molecular classifications. Most ACC harbors genetic alterations, the most frequent genes involved in the TP53-cell cycle and Wnt-β-catenin pathways., Challenging the implication of the dysregulated IGF2-IGF1R pathway in ACC tumorigenesis, a phase III randomized-controlled trial (GALACCTIC, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT00924989) was conducted comparing linsitinib, an oral IGF1 receptor inhibitor, with placebo. Linsitinib was ineffective, suggesting that this alteration was not the main driver in most patients with ACC.

In oncology, MP based on the most frequently altered genes in metastatic cancers with a potential therapeutic impact is expected to be implemented for treatment and to improve the quality of care. In prospective studies including various solid tumors, MP allows to identify molecular alterations in 40%-90% of cases, translating into 10% to 25% of patients receiving molecularly matched treatment (MMT).- Recently, a simplified targeted-NGS approach to characterize the mutational profiles in patients with ACC was performed with promising results. Despite these findings, no MTT has been validated for the ACC.

To rationalize and structure this new approach based on molecular alteration, molecular tumor boards (MTB), tools like the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets (ESCAT), and molecular-based basket trials have been set up.

Although experts recommend MP for patients with advanced ACC, the benefits of MMT remain unknown in this rare cancer.

Therefore, we conducted this retrospective multicenter study in the French network ENDOCAN-COMETE to describe the access and results of MMT in patients with advanced ACC.

The medical files of unresectable or advanced ACC (stage III or IV) followed up between 2009 and 2022 in seven centers of the French network ENDOCAN-COMETE were retrospectively reviewed by one investigator (SL, MD MS). Patients with MP of their tumors as part of various research programs were included in this study. The patients' clinical and molecular characteristics were prospectively collected from each center. Follow-up was conducted in accordance with the current European Network for the Study of Adrenal Tumors (ENSAT) recommendations. The following parameters were recorded: clinical and pathologic features, prognostic parameters (GRAS criteria for grade, resection status, age, tumor syndrome, and hormonal secretion), and treatment details (drugs, line of treatment, mitotane maintenance, type of MT, imaging response according to RECIST 1.1 criteria, PFS, and molecular analyses). Clinical characteristics were collected at the time of diagnosis, metastatic stage, and MTB presentation/MTT therapy.

The following parameters were retrospectively collected: date of MTB, NGS panel used, results, therapeutic proposal, number of previous treatment lines, and in case of MMT during the disease time course: molecule, duration of treatment, and response according to RECIST 1.1.

All patients signed informed consent for MP analysis.

Molecular profiles were obtained from biopsies of different sites, including primary, mets, or liquid biopsies. If multiple MP was performed in one patient, the one that led to MMT was selected for this study.

The six different panels used, covering 82-523 oncogenes, are summarized in Appendix Table A. Among them, only three included microsatellite instability (MSI)/tumor mutational burden (TMB) status determination. MSI is defined by the ESMO as length variability in microsatellite regions because of deficient DNA mismatch repair and TMB as the number of somatic mutations per megabase of the interrogated genomic sequence.

MP in local MTB were reviewed. The actionability of each MA was classified based on the ESCAT classification. The primary objective was to assess the clinical applicability of ACC MP in clinical practice. Our first end point was to describe MMT results in terms of tumor response according to RECIST 1.1, median PFS, median overall survival (OS), and growth modulation index (GMI). GMI is defined as the ratio of time to progression (TTP) under MMT (TTPn, eg, oriented treatment line) to TTP under the treatment received before MMT (TTPn-1). A GMI ≥1.3 is considered a relevant clinical benefit, meaning TTPn is at least superior by 30% as compared with TTPn-1. Because of the large variety of molecules studied, we assessed the clinical benefits for each patient. Based on previous literature,,,, any drug providing ORR >15%, median PFS >6 months, or GMI >1.3 could constitute preliminary signal of interest.

The secondary objective was to characterize MAs in patients with ACC, and our second end point was to describe and classify MA according to prevalence, to report the incidence of MTT and MP in patients with ACC, molecular pathway, and ESCAT, and to describe the rate of inclusion in basket trials.

All statistical analyses were conducted using R software v4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with the following packages and versions: summarytools v1.0.0 for generating tabular summaries of quantitative and qualitative variables, survival v3.5.7 and survminer v0.4.9 for survival analyses, including Kaplan-Meier estimates and visualization, and tidyverse v2.0.0 for data wrangling and visualization. Oncoplots were generated to visualize mutational landscapes, prioritizing genes with recurrence ≥1%, and annotated with clinical metadata (eg, actionability, MSI status, and tissue of origin) using maftools v2.16.0.

This study was exploratory and did not test the prespecified hypotheses. Quantitative variables (eg, tumor size, Weiss score, and Ki-67 index) were summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median (IQR). Qualitative variables (eg, histologic subtype and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status) are reported as frequencies and percentages.

Survival end points were analyzed as follows: PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and comparisons between groups were performed using log-rank tests. The median follow-up time was calculated using the reverse Kaplan-Meier method, which treats patient censoring (eg, loss to follow-up) as the event of interest to account for incomplete follow-up data.

Reproducibility was ensured by fixing random seeds and archiving the analysis codes, input files, and session information in a public repository.

From 2009 to 2022, we included 78 patients with advanced ACC who underwent a tumor MP during their disease time course, including 42 patients with stage I to III disease at initial diagnosis and 36 patients with synchronous metastasis. All patients were characterized according to mENSAT-GRAS criteria, including 43 (55.1%) patients older than 50 years and 66 (85.7%) patients with hormonal secretion excess; Ki67 index was equal or higher than 20% in 51 (65.4%) patients. Seventy-seven patients (98.7%) had at least one unfavorable GRAS factor. Patients with metachronous metastatic disease had a mean time from localized to metastatic disease of 2.25 months (95% CI, 0.5 to 5.5). The clinical and pathologic characteristics of the patients are summarized in Table .

Patients' and Tumors' Characteristics (n = 78)

Fifty-nine metastatic patients (77.6%) were treated up-front with first-line platinum-based chemotherapy and mitotane, eight patients (10.5%) received platinum-based chemotherapy without mitotane, five (7%) mitotane alone, and four patients (5.3%) received other treatments (two cabozantinib, one cyclophosphamide-adriamycine-vincristine, one protocol). PFS under platinum-based chemotherapy (with or without mitotane) as first line was 4.1 months (95% CI, 3.6 to 5.2).

MP was performed on the primary tumor in 41 patients of total patients (53.9%), on the metastasis in 24 patients (32%), and liquid biopsy in 11 patients (14%).

Most frequent MA occurred in TP53 (26 patients, 33%), CTNNB1 (12 patients, 15%), RB1 (10 patients, 13%), and NF1 (six patients, 8%; Table ). The most frequently altered pathways were p53 pathway in 39 patients (50%) and Wnt pathway in 15 patients (19%). MSI status was found in 2 of 18 patients (11%) analyzed. MP did not reveal any mutations in 23 patients (29.5%; Fig ).

Main Molecular Alterations According to the Pathway Involved and the ESCAT Tiers

The median follow-up was 68.1 months (min: 30.3, max: 116.9) from the primary diagnosis. OS from the time of metastasis was 33.3 months (95% CI, 24.7 to 56.2; Fig A). In this cohort, the availability of MMT was not associated with a significant improvement in OS (P = .7; Fig B).

Twelve patients of 78 (15.4%) received targeted therapy based on MMT, including two patients with MSI tumors, one patient with PRMT5 alteration, one patient with FGFR alteration, one patient with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 alteration, three patients with MEK alteration, one patient with poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase alteration, and one patient with EZH2. MMT was administered in the second- and third-line settings in 7 (58.3%) and five patients (41.7%), respectively. Most patients had a Ki-67 ≥ 20% (n = 10/78, 83.3%) and/or at least one adverse GRAS factor (n = 11, 91.7%). Eight patients (67%) had a secretory syndrome and were treated with mitotane before MMT.

The therapies used were trametinib (three patients), everolimus (one patient), niraparib-dostarlimab combination (one patient), durvalumab-tremelimumab combination (one patient), trastuzumab-lapatinib combination (one patient), cypep-1 (one patient), futibatinib (one patient), phase I immunotherapy (LY3300054, one patient), phase I PRMT5 inhibitor (GSK204653, one patient), and phase I EZH2 inhibitor (GSK 2816128, one patient; Table ). MTT was administered as a compassionate program or in protocols in 5% and 7% patients, respectively.

Disease control rate was achieved in 3 of 12 patients (25%), including one complete response, one partial response, and one stable disease. Nine patients had progressive disease at the first evaluation, including one death. The reasons for MMR discontinuation were progression in eight patients (66.6%), toxicity in two patients (16.6%), death (unknown origin) occurring in one patient, and unknown reason in one patient. PFS of the MMT population was 2.5 months and 3.0 months for the previous line. The mean GMI was 1.02 (95% CI, 0.09 to 3.15) and was above 1.3 in 3 patients (25%) who received futibatinib, durvalumab-tremelimumab, and cypep-1. Regarding the patients with MSI ACC, only one responded. The individual clinical benefits for each of the 12 patients who underwent MMT are summarized in Figure .

To our knowledge, this multicenter study reported, for the first time, real-world data on the impact of precision medicine on the management of ACC by including 78 patients with advanced ACC followed from 2009 to 2022 within the French ENDOCAN-COMETE network.

MP is now recommended in the latest French guidelines for ACC workup, and NGS is increasingly being used in clinical practice routine., Moreover, patients with such a rare cancer were showed to benefit from national tumor board with experts of the ENDOCAN-COMETE network.

Forty-five patients (57.7%) had an OS of 24 months, reflecting a potential bias toward better prognosis disease, which allows time window for phase I enrollment.

The most frequently altered cellular pathways were the p53 and Wnt/β-catenin pathways as found in the literature.- However, to date, no US Food and Drug Administration–approved treatment targets these pathways. Most p53 mutations vary with no targetable means. Drugs targeting these pathways are currently in the early phases of development, with no approval. However, in vivo inhibition of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway using tegavivint, a Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor, reduced tumor growth, leading to ongoing phase I/II trials for the treatment of recurrent or refractory solid tumors (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04851119).

Only 15% of patients with MP received a MMT in our cohort, this rate being similar to other studies on precision medicine.,, Nine different classes of drugs were used with compassionate programs or phase I dedicated trials. Two best responses were observed. One complete response was obtained with durvalumab (anti–PDL1) plus tremelimumab (anti-cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 [CTLA4]) in a MSI patient, with alteration within both p53 and Wnt/B-catenin pathways, suggesting that these alterations may not systematically affect negative immunotherapy response. Although therapies targeting PD-1/-L1 and CTLA4 are increasingly recommended in many tumors, their role in ACC remains to be investigated. Several prospective trials- have investigated the safety and efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) in 10-50 evaluable patients with ACC: Objective response rates ranged from 6% to 23% and median PFS from 1.8 to 4.5 months. In addition, PDL1 immunostaining or the presence of adverse events were reported as potential predictors of response in a recent retrospective study. Although discouraged in most patients, prolonged responses have been reported in several studies, in contrast to cytotoxic chemotherapy or multikinase inhibitors, making this class of drugs the least disappointing in patients with ACC. Finally, no definitive predictive role was assigned to the loss of MMR proteins or TMB. In our study, MSI was identified in 2 of 18 patients (11%). One patient achieved a complete response, the best observed in our cohort, whereas the other experienced progressive disease under PD-L1 blockade, and no definitive conclusion can be drawn. cypep-1, either alone or in combination with pembrolizumab (anti–PD-1), showed promising results in our study based on its oncolytic peptide properties. This treatment led to a partial response in one patient, representing our second-best clinical outcome. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors were the most commonly used MTT in our population. Unfortunately, no response was observed, but one patient experienced stable disease under treatment with an FGFR inhibitor. One recent phase II study reported a 16% objective response rate and 6-month median PFS with cabozantinib in a selected population of advanced ACC, with an illustrated prolonged OS of 23.9 months. In a more aggressive population of patients, one retrospective study reported an 18% objective response rate and 4-month median PFS with the same agent, suggesting limited efficacy of MKI in this population of patients. No predictor of response has emerged in combination with ICI; the Cabaten trial reported 8% ORR and a median PFS of 2.9 in patients with ACC. Although disappointing again, the prolonged duration of 11.4 months for responders remains a small light in the dark. The role of mitotane, which induces CYP3A4 expression and has a prolonged half-life, should be investigated. Indeed, most of the lines preceding MMT include this. The systematic measurement of mitotane plasma concentration should be recommended in future MMT trials and, more generally, in all studies of TKI. In line with this comment, Campbell et al reported lower cabozantinib levels in patients with ACC although all patients started therapy when a low plasma level of mitotane was achieved below 2 mg/L and after 6-month withdrawal of mitotane for some of them. Therefore, we suggest that the development of new drugs for patients with ACC with potential drug-drug interactions with mitotane should favor antibodies or drug evaluation before mitotane exposure.

In conclusion, 3 of the 78 screened patients benefited from a molecular match-targeted therapy strategy. One patient with MSI benefited from this strategy under ICI. Our study confirms the predominance of p53 and Wnt/β-catenin pathway alterations in ACC tumorigenesis, which are not yet targetable. ICI, rather than multikinase inhibitors, provides benefits in a few patients.

medicine.title: Genomic Correlates of Chemoradiation Response in Locally Advanced Cervical Cancer: Implications for Precision Oncology
medicine.abstract: Locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC) accounts for a major healthcare burden in low‐ and middle‐income countries, where five‐year overall survival remains below 75% despite concurrent chemoradiation therapy (CCRT) as the curative standard. Treatment response is highly variable, yet clinical management is largely uniform. This review synthesizes current evidence on the genomic correlates of CCRT in LACC, spanning alterations in PIK3CA, PTEN, TP53, KRAS, ARID1A, and APOBEC‐driven mutational signatures. These pathways offer biologically coherent explanations for radioresistance, but the strength and maturity of supporting evidence vary considerably, and evidence for most markers remains prognostic rather than treatment‐predictive. No single genomic marker yet supports routine clinical use, and genome‐only models omit complementary contributions from the tumor microenvironment, hypoxia, cancer stem cell biology, and clinicopathological or imaging‐derived parameters. We further discuss the translational gap between genomic discovery and clinical implementation, with particular attention to population representation and resource constraints in high‐burden settings. Prospective, population‐inclusive genomic trials are urgently needed to translate these findings into equitable precision radiotherapy for patients with LACC worldwide.

Cervical cancer ranks among the top ten causes of cancer‐related death in women worldwide. In 2022, GLOBOCAN reported 662,044 new cases and 348,709 deaths related to cervical cancer [, ]. These figures are projected to rise by 17.8% by 2030 and may exceed one million annual cases by 2050 if current trajectories persist []. The burden falls disproportionately on low‐ and middle‐income countries, which account for 84% of incident cases and up to 90% of cervical cancer‐related mortality []. This inequity is driven by limited screening and vaccination infrastructure, delayed diagnosis, restricted treatment access and high‐risk factors including HIV‐mediated immunosuppression, multiparity, and early sexual debut.

This disparity has a direct clinical consequence: the majority of patients in low‐resource settings present with locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC), defined as FIGO 2018 stage IB3–IVA [, ]. While LACC accounts for approximately 37% of all cervical cancer presentations globally, this proportion may reach up to 90% in resource‐limited settings [, ]. Despite concurrent chemoradiation therapy (CCRT) as the curative standard, outcomes remain poor, with reported five‐year disease‐free survival and overall survival rates of 68% and 74%, respectively [, ]. Without prompt diagnosis and treatment, progression to metastatic disease carries a dismal median survival of approximately 7 months [].

These statistics expose a critical gap: treatment response in LACC is highly variable, yet clinical management remains largely uniform. Emerging genomic evidence may offer a path forward. Next‐generation sequencing (NGS) has enabled high‐throughput molecular profiling at scale, and landmark work by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), characterizing 228 primary cervical cancers and identifying 43,324 somatic mutations, has revealed recurrent alterations in PIK3CA, TP53, KRAS, and PTEN with potential to impair apoptosis and enhance DNA damage tolerance [, ].

This review addresses this translational gap by consolidating current evidence on the molecular landscape of LACC to define actionable biomarkers for treatment stratification and individualized clinical decision‐making.

For the purposes of this review, we define “precision radiotherapy” as the use of genomic and molecular biomarkers to inform radiotherapy‐specific clinical decisions in selecting appropriate candidates for dose escalation or de‐escalation, adaptive radiotherapy planning, biologically‐guided target volume delineation, and radiogenomic‐informed combination with systemic or immunotherapy agents. While the discussion that follows is centered on genomic and molecular correlates, chemoradiation response in LACC is multifactorial as it is also shaped by the tumor microenvironment, cancer stem cell biology, hypoxia, clinicopathological factors, and imaging‐derived parameters.

The pathogenesis of cervical cancer is predominantly driven by persistent infection with high‐risk HPV. HPV is a small, non‐enveloped double‐stranded DNA virus belonging to the family Papillomaviridae. More than 200 HPV genotypes have been identified, of which approximately 14 are classified as high‐risk for cervical carcinogenesis. Among these, HPV 16 and 18 are known as the most oncogenic subtypes and are detected in 70% of cervical cancers. In contrast, other types of HR‐HPV contribute to the remaining HPV‐associated cervical cancer, while low‐risk HPV (LR‐HPV) types are rarely implicated [, , , ]. Persistent HR‐HPV infection drives E6‐mediated p53 degradation and E7‐mediated pRb inactivation. Together they promote genomic instability, excessive cell proliferation, and malignant transformation [, ]. The same checkpoint losses extend to mitotic fidelity: centrosome amplification is proposed to follow a biphasic pattern over the course of carcinogenesis, with E6 and E2 predominating in early centrosome accumulation, before E7 becomes the dominant driver of centrosome overduplication in more advanced lesions, while E6 sustains a permissive environment for this accumulation through continuous relaxation of p53‐dependent checkpoint control [].

Concurrent chemoradiation therapy (CCRT), consisting of external‐beam radiation with cisplatin, followed by brachytherapy, remains the curative‐intent standard for LACC []. Treatment efficacy is primarily mediated through the induction of DNA double‐strand breaks (DSBs), compounded by cisplatin‐induced DNA crosslinking and replication stress, ultimately resulting in mitotic catastrophe and tumor cell death. However, clinical outcomes remain heterogeneous, likely reflecting interactions between treatment deliveries, the microenvironment, and genomic pathways that influence DNA damage response (DDR) signaling, cell cycle checkpoint integrity, oncogenic survival pathways, and immune evasion mechanisms.

As illustrated in Figure , these axes are functionally interconnected. Subversion of p53 and pRB by HPV oncoproteins can impair DSB repair fidelity, force aberrant S‐phase entry, and induce replication stress. Concurrent PIK3CA and KRAS mutations, most commonly through PIK3CA alterations and less frequently KRAS mutations, may further sustain pro‐survival signaling and attenuate radiation‐induced apoptosis. In parallel, alterations affecting tumor suppressor genes and chromatin remodeling regulators may reinforce oncogenic transcription programs and adaptive treatment resistance. Hypoxia‐driven signaling activity promotes angiogenesis and reshapes the tumor microenvironment [, , ]. Collectively, the co‐alteration of these genomic markers may contribute to the depth and durability of treatment response in LACC.

The therapeutic cytotoxicity of CCRT is fundamentally mediated through the induction of DNA DSBs, which, when unresolved, precipitate mitotic catastrophe and tumor cell death []. However, persistent HR‐HPV infection imposes a state of chronic genomic stress on the cervical epithelium even before treatment initiation, thereby critically preconditioning the tumor's DNA repair machinery. The oncoproteins E6 and E7 activate ataxia‐telangiectasia‐mutated (ATM) and ATM and Rad3‐related (ATR) DNA damage repair pathways []. HPV‐positive cells have been reported to demonstrate persistent ATM pathway activity with increased expression of phosphorylated ATM (pATM), Chk2, NBS1, and BRCA1 []. In parallel, E7‐induced replication stress activates ATR/Chk1 signaling and recruits DDR proteins to viral replication sites [], which further promotes replication stress tolerance and sustained viral replication.

Resolution of DNA strand breaks predominantly proceeds through two competing pathways: the high‐fidelity homologous recombination (HR) pathway and non‐homologous end‐joining (NHEJ) pathway [], with alternative end‐joining pathways becoming important when there is repair impairment [].

HPV oncoproteins can compromise HR fidelity and NHEJ, consequently increasing reliance on the highly error‐prone microhomology‐mediated end joining (MMEJ) pathway [, ]. PARP1, which coordinates both single‐strand break repair and NHEJ, represents another actionable mediator of radioresistance in cervical cancer []. However, HPV positivity alone does not establish a clinically actionable HR‐deficient phenotype as genotype, pathway activation, and functional repair capacity are not interchangeable [, ].

PIK3CA mutation is among the more extensively studied genomic correlates of CCRT outcomes in LACC. Activating mutations, particularly E542K and E545K, have been associated with adverse outcomes in retrospective cohorts. McIntyre et al. reported an adverse overall survival rate association in stage IB/II but not III/IVA disease [], while Lachkar et al. reported adverse adjusted survival associations in stages IIIB‐IVA []. Both findings suggest the association is not restricted to a single disease state. A third cohort, from Wang et al. adds a caveat rather than further confirmation; it associated reduced response with PIK3CA alterations, but combined mutation and amplification, precluding a mutation‐only interpretation of the response estimate []. Taken together, these remain associations within treated cohorts, not proof of differential benefit from CCRT.

Constitutive PI3K/AKT activation can support radiation resistance phenotype through enhanced DNA repair via DNA‐PKcs‐mediated NHEJ and HR activation, suppression of apoptosis, persistent mTORC1‐driven autophagy suppression, and cell‐cycle dysregulation favoring the radioresistant S phase, thus providing a biological rationale that requires clinical validation [, ].

PTEN loss further amplifies aberrant PI3K signaling through sustained AKT/mTOR activation and may influence immune suppression [, ]. In a 69‐patient outcome subset of a heterogenous cervical cancer cohort, PTEN mutation was associated with shorter progression‐free survival, whereas the overall survival difference was not significant []. Mutation, copy‐number loss, and protein loss should therefore be distinguished, and these findings do not establish a definitive CCRT predictor []. FBXW7 alterations frequently co‐occur with PIK3CA mutations and further exacerbate tumor aggressiveness through impaired degradation of oncogenic substrates. This has been associated with shorter survival and higher recurrence [, ]. Collectively, PIK3CA activation, PTEN loss, and FBXW7 co‐alteration within this pathway provide plausible therapeutic targets, but their clinical evidence and tissue‐specific immune effects should not be treated as equivalent.

RAS/MAPK pathway activation can also promote treatment resistance by attenuating radiation‐induced apoptosis and enabling escape from cell‐cycle arrest via ERK‐mediated phosphorylation of apoptotic regulators and cyclin D1/CDK‐driven G1‐S progression [, , ]. KRAS mutations, more prevalent in cervical adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous subtypes, were associated with recurrence in a surgical cohort whereas their relevance to CCRT‐specific response remains less certain [].

Enhanced replication stress tolerance and cooperation with the PI3K/AKT signaling provide a mechanistic rationale for further study []. Persistent RAF/MEK/ERK signaling synergistically crosstalks with PI3K signaling to enhance tumor adaptability under therapeutic stress. Furthermore, emerging evidence also suggests MAPK pathway activation may suppress interferon‐mediated immune responses, thereby contributing to immune evasion and reduced anti‐tumor surveillance []. It is important to note that the aforementioned interferon work used pancreatic models and also identified adaptive cell‐state changes after prolonged pathway inhibition, thus requiring caution when extrapolating to cervical cancer.

HPV‐driven disruption of the G1 checkpoint, via E6‐mediated p53 degradation and E7‐mediated pRb inactivation, renders LACC disproportionately reliant on S and G2/M checkpoints during CCRT []. Although TP53 mutations are relatively more frequent in HPV‐negative disease and a subset of locally advanced tumors, in some variants, TP53 mutations produce a stable gain‐of‐function p53 proteins that further impair DNA damage response, enhance genomic instability, and contribute to chemoradiotherapy resistance in a retrospective LACC cohort [, ].

A bioinformatics study identified CDK1 and CCNA2 among genes that are significantly upregulated in cervical cancer, with overexpression associated with advanced stage and poorer survival []. Translating this toward therapy, the CDK inhibitors SNS‐032 and AT7519 demonstrated preclinical efficacy in reducing tumor growth and metastasis in cervical cancer models [], though no clinical trials have followed. The furthest this strategy has progressed clinically is WEE1 kinase inhibition, targeting the same G2/M checkpoint strategy, and its trial has reached phase I: an adavosertib (AZD1775)‐CCRT trial enrolled ten patients; nine were patients with cervical cancer; however, it was halted early due to toxicity []. Despite strong biological rationale, cell‐cycle‐targeting strategies remain largely preclinical in cervical cancer, and this early clinical experience does not validate a genomic treatment‐selection strategy.

Epigenetic dysregulation shapes CCRT outcomes in LACC across transcriptional, DDR, and immune axes. ARID1A loss, occurring in 7%–26% of cervical cancers [] and enriched in advanced disease, disrupts the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin‐remodeling complex, impairing nucleosome positioning and transcriptional accessibility required for efficient HR repair and replication fork stability, potentially creating synthetic vulnerability to DNA‐damaging therapies [, , ]. Beyond HR impairment, ARID1A also contributes to replication stress sensing and ATR‐mediated checkpoint activation; loss of its function due to mutation or deletion may attenuate ATR signaling and downstream CHK1‐dependent S‐phase checkpoint responses []. This chromatin disorganization also promotes genomic instability and creates a context of increased dependence on compensatory epigenetic repression pathways, including EZH2/PRC2‐mediated H3K27 trimethylation, with therapeutic implications remain investigational []. Reported ARID1A frequencies vary across cohorts and assays; the wide prevalence range should not be interpreted as a pooled LACC prevalence. Cervical YAP‐dependency experiments support a preclinical therapeutic rationale rather than a validated prediction of radiosensitivity []. It should be underlined that this evidence differs from the retrospective CCRT associations for PIK3CA.

Beyond individual driver mutations, the cumulative genomic imprints of DNA damage and repair processes, or the mutational signatures, offer a systems‐level readout potentially relevant to treatment response in cancer, including LACC. Signatures reflecting defective repair pathways may carry therapeutic implications, but a genomic defect does not directly measure current repair capacity or radiosensitivity [, ].

APOBEC‐associated mutational signatures, particularly the APOBEC3, dominate the cervical cancer mutational landscape. TCGA characterization of 228 primary cervical cancers identified APOBEC mutagenesis as a defining genomic feature of the disease [], with subsequent cohort data detecting APOBEC signatures in 46% of squamous cell carcinomas []. APOBEC3 enzymes generate SBS2 and SBS13, which are COSMIC‐defined mutational patterns characterized predominantly by C>T and C>G substitutions within TpCpN trinucleotide contexts, respectively. These signatures are induced by viral infection and are associated with higher mutation burden [, ]. Zhang et al. reported that high APOBEC3 levels in cervical cancer tissues have a significant association with decreased OS and are an independent predictor of survival []. Despite its established role as a hallmark of cervical cancer genomics, further studies are needed to clarify the extent to which it influences treatment response and long‐term clinical outcomes.

The genomic alterations discussed capture a static, single‐region snapshot of tumor biology at diagnosis, whereas radioresistance emerges dynamically over the course of fractionated chemoradiation. Several non‐genomic processes that evolve during treatment are not reflected in a pretreatment mutation panel, yet interact with the pathways described earlier. Tumor hypoxia limits oxygen‐dependent fixation of radiation‐induced DNA damage and can co‐occur with, rather than substitute for, genomic drivers of radioresistance: combined imaging‐ and gene‐based hypoxia biomarkers have been shown to improve prediction of chemoradiotherapy failure beyond either modality alone, independent of intratumour heterogeneity [].

Cancer stem cell populations exhibit enhanced DNA repair capacity and quiescence‐mediated radioresistance that can be further amplified under hypoxic conditions, operating largely independent of driver mutation status []. An immunosuppressive microenvironment, reflected in altered myeloid and cytotoxic lymphocyte populations, can modulate treatment response through pathways overlapping with the antigen presentation and PD‐L1 regulation underlying the immunotherapy trials [, ]. Notably, on‐treatment circulating neutrophil counts and hematological indices, already captured through routine monitoring, have been independently associated with chemoradiation outcome in LACC [, ].

Clinicopathological and imaging‐derived parameters, tumor volume, nodal burden, and functional/hypoxia‐sensitive imaging, capture further aspects of this evolving biology that a one‐time genomic panel cannot, representing a pragmatic, resource‐appropriate complement to molecular profiling in settings where these are already collected as part of routine care []. Treatment‐related technical factors, namely the overall treatment time, delivered dose and brachytherapy quality, further modulate outcomes independent of tumor biology itself, underscoring that technical execution of CCRT remains as consequential as its biological determinants [].

The genomic landscape of LACC provides a research framework for patient stratification, treatment failure prediction, and combination strategy rationalization (Figure ).

Genomic profiling identifies biologically distinct subgroups, yet their use in treatment selection requires validation. PIK3CA mutation and PTEN loss have emerged as the most consistently evidenced markers of inferior response [, , , ]. Among 82 evaluable patients with LACC treated with radical chemoradiotherapy, PIK3CA mutations that were identified in 23% of pre‐treatment samples were associated with worse OS, particularly in FIGO stage IB/II disease []. Conversely, a cohort of 771 surgically resected cervical cancers associated PIK3CA mutation with improved relapse‐free survival []. These findings illustrate why prognosis must be distinguished from prediction of treatment benefit. Differences in stage, histology, adjuvant therapy, selection, and endpoints prevent a causal comparison between the surgical and CCRT cohorts. An adverse association within a CCRT‐treated cohort does not establish a CCRT‐specific predictive biomarker; differential benefit requires more evidence in genomic‐guided treatment outcomes, ideally from randomized studies.

Although cervical cancer harbors a range of recurrently mutated genes across key oncogenic pathways, the therapeutic landscape remains strikingly underdeveloped. The majority of agents listed carry no FDA approval in cervical cancer, with indications predominantly borrowed from breast, renal, or hematological malignancies, and the cervical‐specific evidence base is largely confined to early‐phase trials, many of which have been terminated prematurely or demonstrated only modest activity (Table ). This means that while the biological rationale for pathway‐targeted treatment is well established, clinical translation remains nascent and fragmented.

Genomic profiling provides a biological framework for investigating radiotherapy intensity and systemic therapy combinations. Tumors with intact DDR capacity or activated oncogenic signaling may benefit from dose escalation or addition of pathway‐targeted radiosensitizers, including inhibitors against PI3K or PARP, while those with HR deficiency or high genomic instability may achieve durable control at standard radiotherapy approaches []. Comprehensive exome analysis of 430 cervical carcinomas identified frequent deletions in ATM and ATR pathway genes, with preclinical evidence supporting enhanced chemoradiation response through ATM or CHK1 inhibition [], though clinical translation in LACC remains nascent. The existing evidence base is largely preclinical or observational; no genomically stratified radiotherapy dose‐modification trial has yet been completed in LACC, thus creating a gap that urgently requires a prospective design.

These concepts are complemented by parallel advances in radiotherapy delivery, despite the maturity of evidence varying considerably across techniques. At the established end, a randomized trial of intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) demonstrated reduced gastrointestinal toxicity without a demonstrated survival advantage [], while EMBRACE‐I established MRI‐guided adaptive brachytherapy (IGABT) as a personalization approach with 92% five‐year local control []. IGABT is itself a form of adaptive radiotherapy planning, and a combination of imaging‐ and gene‐based hypoxia biomarkers offers an early template for biologically‐guided target delineation []. At the investigational end, MRI‐guided adaptive external‐beam radiotherapy and particle therapy remain far earlier in development: available data are limited to a five‐patient MR‐linac boost planning study, planning proton evidence, and a three‐patient early safety report combining carbon‐ion therapy with durvalumab [, , ]. None of these findings establish superiority over modern photon CCRT plus IGABT, nor justify routine replacement brachytherapy []. Several remain resource‐intensive and are not yet widely accessible in LMIC settings. Nonetheless, where available, they offer a practical substrate onto which genomic stratification could eventually be layered, and their more limited availability elsewhere reinforces the case for context‐adapted, bridging strategies.

Radiotherapy exerts important immunomodulatory effects, including induction of immunogenic cell death, upregulation of PD‐L1 expression, and remodeling of the tumor microenvironment, thereby providing a strong rationale for combining radiotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibition. The landmark KEYNOTE‐A18 trial established that pembrolizumab added to CCRT significantly improved 24‐month progression‐free survival in high‐risk LACC (68% vs. 57%, HR 0.70, p = 0.002), leading to FDA approval in 2024 covering FIGO 2014 stages III‐IVA. Updated analyses further demonstrated a 33% reduction in mortality risk []. In contrast, the CALLA trial, which evaluated durvalumab with CCRT in 770 patients and did not meet its primary endpoint, with benefit observed only in the PD‐L1‐high subgroup [], therefore illustrating that unselected patient populations may dilute the efficacy signal of radio‐immunotherapy combinations. Notably, neither trial incorporated molecular stratification based on PIK3CA status, mutational burden, DDR signature, or APOBEC activity [, ]. Correlative analyses could test whether these features improve future treatment selection.

The divergent outcomes of KEYNOTE‐A18 and CALLA can be interpreted, cautiously, through the genomic mechanisms discussed above, without assuming these mechanisms explain the difference. Radiation‐induced cGAS‐STING activation and type I interferon signaling link DNA damage to immune priming [], while PIK3CA and PTEN alterations shape the tumor‐immune landscape, with PIK3CA mutation associating with an inflamed but exhausted T‐cell state [], and PTEN loss with immune evasion, albeit with tissue‐variable myeloid effects rather than a uniform M2 phenotypes []. APOBEC mutagenesis may generate candidate neoantigens whose immunogenicity depends on intact antigen presentation []. A PD‐L1‐high state may mark an inflamed, checkpoint‐dependent tumor, offering a plausible explanation for why durvalumab's benefit in CALLA was confined to this subgroup while pembrolizumab, which also blocks PD‐L2, benefited an unselected KEYNOTE‐A18 population; differing trial populations, schedules, and follow‐up preclude firm attribution [, ]. These mechanisms generate testable hypotheses rather than establish genomic causation or drug‐class superiority.

The central paradox of precision radiotherapy in LACC is that the disease burden is highest precisely where genomic‐guided care is least accessible. As illustrated by the tiered evidence framework from genomic profiling to equitable LMIC implementation (Figure ), bridging this gap is not a secondary consideration; it is the defining challenge of the field.

Most current biomarker studies remain retrospective, single‐institution, and reliant on hotspot sequencing of individual genes rather than composite pathway‐level signatures, including transcriptomic profiling capturing pathway activity downstream of individual mutations. Evidentiary maturity also differs by biomarker: PIK3CA has comparatively stronger retrospective CCRT associations, PTEN evidence is less treatment‐specific, and APOBEC remains exploratory; WEE1 inhibition has reached early clinical testing. However, this does not establish biomarker‐guided clinical utility.

No single genomic marker has yet demonstrated sufficient predictive accuracy for routine clinical adoption in LACC, while clinicopathological, imaging, and hematological parameters offer an already‐available complementary signal while pathway‐integrated genomic panels mature.

Furthermore, the genomic foundation of current biomarkers rests predominantly on TCGA and Western‐derived cohorts. Yet HPV subtype distribution, driver mutation frequencies, mutational signatures, and co‐existing environmental exposures differ substantially across ancestries and geographic regions. Transportability should therefore be tested in Sub‐Saharan African, Southeast Asian, or Latin American populations, which are the same populations bearing the brunt of global cervical cancer mortality. Therefore, prospective, multi‐center validation of pathway‐integrated biomarker panels, which incorporate common mutations, mutational signatures, and population‐specific validation, is still a critical unmet need.

Implementation barriers compound this further. Next‐generation sequencing infrastructure, bioinformatics capacity, and trained personnel remain scarce across high‐burden settings. Even where genomic sequencing is available, turnaround times, tissue preservation standards, and reimbursement pathways rarely support clinical decision‐making within treatment windows.

For LMIC specifically, a clinically grounded bridge strategy is both necessary and achievable. Routine hematological and nutritional parameters are already collected at every treatment visit and carry meaningful prognostic signals, yet remain inconsistently applied to surveillance decisions in practice. For example, neutrophil‐to‐lymphocyte (NLR) information may reflect systemic immune activation and correlates with survival and progression of cervical cancer across the CCRT course []. Hemoglobin level also influences tumor oxygenation, with values < 13 g/dL being associated with hypoxia‐driven resistance and higher treatment failure, whereas the obtained information can also provide albumin levels, where lack of it also predicts inferior survival and reduced complete response likelihood [].

Integrating these into structured, locally validated surveillance models, informed by existing knowledge of regional reproductive health patterns, healthcare‐seeking behavior, and community‐level risk factors, represents a pragmatic approach that can run in parallel with, rather than waiting for, genomic infrastructure development.

Future progress requires deliberate course correction. Large, regionally representative cohorts from Africa, Asia, and Latin America are essential to define population‐specific radiosensitivity profiles and actionable genomic targets, with LMIC institutions embedded as equal partners rather than sample sources. Precision radiotherapy in LACC will only fulfill its promise if its evidence base reflects the patients it is meant to serve. The correlates summarized in Figure  are a starting point toward the goal that still requires prospective validation.

LACC remains a disease of inequitable outcomes, and genomic evidence may contribute to improving treatment selection. Recurrent alterations in PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/MAPK, DDR, cell cycle, and epigenetic regulators contribute to a molecularly heterogenous disease, alongside microenvironmental, clinical, and treatment‐related factors. Mutational signatures extend this further, offering systems‐level records of mutagenic processes that single‐gene markers cannot capture.

Translating this evidence into equitable, population‐relevant precision radiotherapy, particularly across LMICs, requires prospective validation of clinical utility alongside access to high‐quality curative treatment.
