medicine.title: Smart Responsive Textiles for Chronic Wound Management: From Sensing to Closed‐Loop Therapeutics
medicine.abstract: Chronic wounds affect tens of millions of patients worldwide, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Conventional wound dressings mostly serve as passive protection and exudate management but cannot continuously monitor the changes in the wound microenvironment and respond to pathological signals to deliver therapy. This review offers a critical discussion on smart responsive textile systems embedded with wound monitoring and triggered therapeutic delivery. pH‐, temperature‐, enzyme‐ and glucose‐responsive materials are of particular interest, as they respond to clinically relevant changes associated with infection and impaired healing. Textile engineering strategies, including electrospinning, dipcoating, layer‐by‐layer assembly, weaving, and 3D printing, are discussed in the context of functional integration, scalability, mechanical performance, and drug delivery capability. Open‐loop, semi‐closed‐loop and fully autonomous closed‐loop architectures are compared based on the sensing strategy, actuation mechanism, user involvement, and technology readiness. Major barriers to clinical translation are also reviewed, such as sensor stability, biofouling, sterilisation, shelf life, manufacturing reproducibility, regulatory classification, cost‐effectiveness and the limited availability of robust clinical evidence. Overall, responsive textile dressings represent a promising route toward personalised and adaptive wound management; however, substantial advances in integrated validation, scalable manufacturing, and clinical evaluation are required before fully autonomous systems can achieve routine clinical use. Distinctively, this review links biomarker selection, responsive‐material mechanisms, textile integration, closed‐loop architecture and translational readiness within a unified framework, enabling direct identification of the key scientific and engineering bottlenecks that currently limit clinical adoption.
medicine.text:
Chronic wounds, including diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), venous leg ulcers (VLUs), pressure injuries (pressure sores) and non‐healing surgical wounds, are a growing global health crisis. Chronic wounds affect an estimated 40 million patients worldwide, with prevalence increasing due to ageing populations, increasing diabetes, and the obesity epidemic [, ]. In the United States alone, chronic wound care costs > $100 billion annually, more than the economic burden of many common cancers [, ]. Serious clinical consequences: infection, osteomyelitis, sepsis, amputation. An amputation of the lower limb due to diabetes occurs every 30 s in the world, and 85% of them are preceded by a chronic foot ulcer []. The mortality rate at 5 years after major lower extremity amputation is 50%–70%, worse than for many malignancies [].

Besides the clinical burden, chronic wounds cause a considerable psychological and socioeconomic burden for the patients. Chronic pain, malodorous exudate, social isolation, depression, loss of productivity, and reduced quality of life are almost universal among patients with non‐healing wounds []. Carer burden is another consideration, as family members often help with dressing changes, wound monitoring, and transport to clinic visits.

Conventional wound dressings, including gauze, films, foams, hydrocolloids, hydrogels and alginate‐based materials, primarily provide protection, moisture management and exudate absorption [, , ]. Although these functions are essential for wound care, conventional dressings generally cannot continuously assess changes in the wound microenvironment or adjust treatment in response to evolving pathology. Consequently, dressing replacement and therapeutic intervention are often based on predefined schedules or clinical observation rather than real‐time wound status []. This limitation creates a strong rationale for responsive systems capable of combining wound monitoring with condition‐dependent therapeutic action.

A paradigm shift is underway: from passive dressings to responsive (or “smart”) textiles that actively monitor wound biomarkers and deliver therapy only when needed [, ]. Normal wound healing progresses through four overlapping phases, haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling (Figure ), whereas chronic wounds frequently exhibit persistent inflammation, elevated protease activity, microbial biofilms and impaired tissue regeneration (Figure ). A responsive textile integrates three core functions: (1) sensing of pathological parameters (e.g., elevated pH, temperature, or protease activity); (2) processing of sensor data to determine whether intervention is required; and (3) actuation, on‐demand release of therapeutic agents (antibiotics, growth factors, anti‐inflammatory drugs, or analgesics) [, ]. The integration of these functional components within a smart textile dressing is illustrated in Figure , while Figure  demonstrates the proposed threshold‐triggered therapeutic response, in which detected changes in the wound microenvironment initiate condition‐dependent drug delivery.

This closed‐loop paradigm mimics biological feedback systems, potentially transforming chronic wound management from reactive to proactive, from one‐size‐fits‐all to personalised, and from episodic to continuous []. The analogy to the smartphone versus the landline telephone is apt: one is interactive and intelligent; the other is passive and limited. Responsive textiles do not replace conventional dressings for simple acute wounds but offer transformative potential for complex, chronic, and high‐risk wounds [].

Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on wound sensors, responsive polymers, hydrogel dressings or wearable electronics as separate topics, this review integrates these areas within a single structure–process–function–translation framework. The central contribution is to connect clinically relevant wound biomarkers with responsive polymer mechanisms, textile manufacturing routes, closed‐loop therapeutic architectures and technology‐readiness considerations. Particular emphasis is placed on the compatibility between sensing triggers and polymer responses, the trade‐offs among fabrication methods, the progression from open‐loop to autonomous systems, and the translational barriers that determine whether laboratory concepts can become clinically deployable wound dressings. Section  discusses the chronic wound microenvironment and clinically relevant biomarkers targeted by diagnostic systems. Section  critically analyses the pH‐, temperature‐ and enzyme‐responsive polymers that constitute the functional basis of smart textiles. Section  compares five textile‐manufacturing strategies for incorporating these responsive materials into wearable wound‐care platforms. Section  reviews open‐loop, semi‐closed‐loop and fully closed‐loop therapeutic systems. Section  provides a technology readiness assessment of the individual components and the integrated platforms. Section  outlines the main challenges in clinical translation including regulatory routes, manufacturing scalability, stability, cost‐effectiveness, reimbursement and end‐user acceptance. Finally, Section  discusses future directions and priorities for clinical adoption.

Normal wound healing progresses through overlapping haemostatic, inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases involving coordinated immune‐cell activity, extracellular‐matrix deposition, angiogenesis and tissue remodelling [].

In contrast, chronic wounds fail to progress through this sequence in an orderly manner and commonly remain in a persistent inflammatory state characterised by excessive protease activity, microbial burden, biofilm formation, impaired tissue regeneration and altered physicochemical conditions [, ] These changes create a dynamic wound microenvironment containing measurable biochemical and physical signals that can be exploited for smart wound monitoring and responsive therapy [, ].

pH, temperature, protease activity and glucose have emerged as practical targets for smart textile sensing [, ]. Four wound parameters: Importantly, these parameters are different aspects of wound pathology and should not be considered interchangeable or as specific markers for infection.

Normal healing wounds are acidic (5.5–6.5), which supports antimicrobial activity (through direct inhibition of pathogens and activation of host defence peptides); regulates protease activity (MMPs are optimally active at neutral to alkaline pH); and promotes fibroblast proliferation and migration []. In contrast, infected or chronically inflamed wounds are alkaline (pH > 7.5) due to bacterial metabolism (production of ammonia and other alkaline metabolites) and the host inflammatory response []. Alkaline pH induces biofilm development, increases MMP activity (which degrade ECM and growth factors), and inhibits fibroblast function []. A shift from acid to alkaline pH is a reliable early marker of infection and often precedes the development of visible clinical signs of infection (erythema, warmth, and purulence) by 24–48 h [].

Wound‐surface temperature is influenced by local perfusion, inflammation, anatomical site, ambient conditions and the thermal properties of the dressing. Consequently, a single absolute temperature threshold is difficult to apply across patients and wound locations. Local temperature elevation is more appropriately interpreted relative to a patient‐specific or anatomical reference, such as the contralateral site or the wound's longitudinal baseline [, ]. Persistent temperature asymmetry has been investigated particularly in diabetic‐foot monitoring, where a sustained local increase relative to the corresponding contralateral site may indicate inflammatory activity and increased risk of tissue breakdown []. However, temperature elevation is not specific to infection and should therefore be interpreted together with other clinical or biochemical indicators rather than used as a stand‐alone diagnostic criterion [].

Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP‐2 and MMP‐9, are zinc‐dependent endopeptidases, which are necessary for ECM remodelling in normal wound healing. Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) tightly regulate the levels of MMPs during normal healing. The ratio of MMP‐9 to TIMP‐1 is approximately 1:1 []. Chronic wounds are characterised by persistently elevated MMPs (MMP‐9 > 50 ng/mL, compared to < 10 ng/mL in normal healing) and an MMP‐9/TIMP‐1 ratio of 10:1 or greater []. Excess MMP activity degrades ECM proteins (collagen, fibronectin, and laminin), growth factors (VEGF, PDGF, and EGF), and their receptors, creating a hostile proteolytic environment that prevents progression from inflammation to proliferation [].

In patients with diabetes mellitus, high glucose concentrations in wound exudates are associated with poor healing outcomes, increased risk of infection, delayed angiogenesis, and impaired neutrophil function []. The normal wound glucose concentration is 2–5 mM, like that in the interstitial fluid. In poorly controlled diabetic patients (HbA1c > 8%), wound glucose concentrations can exceed 10 mM []. Monitoring glucose levels at the wound may allow for individualised glycaemic management, which may improve healing outcomes even if systemic glucose control is suboptimal []. Table  summarises these four biomarkers, including their normal ranges, pathological thresholds, sensing modalities, and response times.

Wound biomarkers for smart textile sensing: Normal ranges, pathological thresholds, sensing modalities, and response times.

Abbreviations: FRET, Förster resonance energy transfer; GOx, glucose oxidase; MMP, matrix metalloproteinase; PBA, phenylboronic acid; RTD, resistance temperature detector.

Each biomarker can be detected using multiple sensing modalities, with trade‐offs among sensitivity, response time, cost, and ease of integration into textiles [].

The simplest and most studied colorimetric pH sensors are for wound applications. pH‐sensitive dyes (bromothymol blue, transition range pH 6.0–7.6; phenol red, pH 6.4–8.0; or litmus, pH 4.5–8.3) are immobilised on textile fibres by physical adsorption, covalent grafting, or encapsulation in sol–gel matrices []. Dyes change colour when exposed to wound exudate (e.g., bromothymol blue: yellow at pH < 6.0, green at pH 7.0, blue at pH > 7.6), providing a visual readout to patients or clinicians. Colorimetric sensors are low cost, do not require electricity, and are easy to fabricate. However, they provide only semi‐quantitative information and require user interpretation [, ]. Electrochemical pH sensors based on polyaniline (PANI)‐coated electrodes allow for quantitative, continuous and real‐time pH monitoring with high sensitivity []. PANI is capable of changing its conductivity and redox state with the pH, allowing for electrical readout that could be integrated with a microprocessor for automated decision‐making.

Resistive temperature sensing in smart textiles can be achieved using either thermistors or resistance temperature detectors (RTDs), but these are distinct sensor classes. Thermistors are typically semiconductor‐based devices whose electrical resistance changes strongly and non‐linearly with temperature; negative‐temperature‐coefficient (NTC) thermistors are commonly used for compact, continuous temperature monitoring. RTDs, in contrast, usually employ metallic sensing elements whose resistance changes more linearly and predictably with temperature. Both approaches can be integrated into flexible or textile platforms, although their sensitivity, linearity, calibration requirements, and fabrication methods differ []. Thermochromic fibres provide a power‐free alternative by changing colour with temperature, but they are generally less quantitative than electronic resistive sensors [].

The most specific approach for MMP detection is the Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET)‐based peptide sensor. A peptide substrate with the MMP cleavage sequence (e.g., GPLGMHGK for MMP‐9) is tagged with a fluorophore (donor) and a quencher (acceptor) at opposite ends []. In the intact state, the donor and acceptor are close together, and the fluorescence is quenched. Cleavage of the peptide by MMPs results in separation of the donor and acceptor and emission of fluorescence []. The fluorescence intensity is directly proportional to MMP activity. FRET peptides can be covalently attached to textile fibres for on‐wound MMP monitoring. Alternatively, wound exudate can be sampled and studied ex situ using ELISA or gelatin zymography, but the process is not continuous and requires laboratory equipment [].

Glucose oxidase (GOx) is the most commonly used enzyme for glucose sensing. GOx catalyses the oxidation of glucose to gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2): glucose + O2 → gluconic acid + H2O2 []. H2O2 can be detected electrochemically (amperometry) or colorimetrically (peroxidase and a chromogenic substrate) []. GOx‐based sensors are highly specific for glucose and have been widely used in continuous glucose monitors for diabetes management. Phenylboronic acid (PBA)‐based sensors provide a sensor alternative that is enzyme‐free [, ]. PBA interacts with diols (e.g., on glucose molecules) through reversible covalent bonds, leading to a change in fluorescence, conductivity, or swelling that can be detected []. PBA sensors are more stable than GOx sensors (no enzyme degradation) but less specific (they also bind fructose and other diols) [].

Bacterial biofilms, structured communities of bacteria embedded in a self‐produced matrix of EPS (polysaccharides, proteins, and extracellular DNA), are a major characteristic of chronic wounds. Biofilms are present in about 80% of chronic wounds versus 6% of acute wounds []. Biofilm EPS protects bacteria from antibiotics (up to a 1000‐fold increased tolerance compared to planktonic bacteria), host immune responses, and environmental stresses []. The EPS also contributes to the alkaline pH and high protease activity observed in chronic wounds. Figure . The central wound diagram shows labels for the biofilm layer and EPS, with cellular components (neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts, and new blood vessels) annotated around the periphery [, ].

Biofilm detection is still a challenge for smart textiles. Indirect methods are monitoring pH (biofilms create alkaline microenvironments), temperature (biofilm metabolism creates heat), and protease detection (biofilms produce proteases) []. Direct biofilm sensors are under development [, ], using lectin‐coated fibres that bind EPS polysaccharides or DNA probes that hybridise with gene sequences specific to biofilms.

Chronic wounds are also biologically heterogeneous, and this heterogeneity can complicate both sensing and responsive therapy. The wound microbiome may contain mixed bacterial communities with different metabolic activities, biofilm‐forming capacities, and protease profiles, meaning that a single biomarker may not reflect microbial burden consistently across patients or wound types []. Host immune responses add further variability because neutrophil activity, macrophage phenotype, inflammatory cytokines, and host‐derived proteases can alter pH, temperature, and enzyme activity independently of bacterial infection. Biofilms are similarly heterogeneous in thickness, composition, oxygenation, and extracellular polymeric substance density, which may create spatial gradients across the wound bed. These factors can reduce sensor specificity, delay penetration of therapeutics, and produce uneven stimulus‐responsive release. Strategies to address these limitations include multimodal sensing, spatially distributed sensor arrays, biofilm‐targeted recognition elements, and patient‐specific or longitudinal baselines rather than reliance on a single universal threshold.

The clinical relevance of pH, temperature, and protease‐related biomarkers was established in Section . This section therefore focuses on how responsive polymers translate these wound‐associated changes into physicochemical responses such as ionisation, swelling, collapse, network cleavage, and controlled therapeutic release []. The suitability of each polymer system depends not only on stimulus sensitivity but also on response direction, kinetics, mechanical stability, and compatibility with textile integration.

pH‐responsive polymers contain ionisable weak acidic or basic functional groups whose protonation state changes with environmental pH, resulting in variations in chain charge density, hydration, conformation, network permeability and swelling behaviour []. Figure  illustrates this mechanism. These physicochemical changes can be exploited to regulate therapeutic loading and release. However, pH responsiveness should not be interpreted automatically as a sharp infection‐specific ON/OFF transition. The clinically useful response window depends on the effective pKa of the polymer within the network, copolymer composition, crosslinking density, ionic strength, local wound chemistry and interactions between the polymer and therapeutic cargo. Consequently, the suitability of a pH‐responsive material for wound management depends not only on whether it responds to pH, but also on whether the direction and magnitude of that response correspond to the intended wound‐state transition.

PAA is one of the most widely investigated anionic pH‐responsive polymers for biomedical and drug‐delivery applications. It contains carboxylic acid (—COOH) groups that undergo progressive deprotonation to —COO− as environmental pH increases relative to the effective pKa of the polymer network []. Increasing ionisation produces electrostatic repulsion between neighbouring negatively charged groups, promoting chain expansion, hydration and increased network permeabilit [, , , ]. At lower pH, protonation reduces charge density and electrostatic repulsion, favouring a comparatively more compact and less hydrated network. Importantly, this behaviour does not mean that native PAA provides a sharp switch specifically between a normally healing wound and an alkaline chronic or infected wound. Because the carboxylic groups of PAA may already be substantially ionised within the physiologically relevant wound‐pH range, its swelling generally changes progressively rather than remaining completely collapsed at pH 5.5–6.5 and becoming suddenly swollen only above pH 7–7.5. Therefore, PAA should be considered a tunable pH‐responsive platform rather than an inherently infection‐selective molecular switch. A narrower response window can be engineered by adjusting copolymer composition, crosslink density and local microenvironment or by introducing ionisable groups whose effective pKa lies closer to the desired therapeutic trigger range.

Chitosan is a naturally derived polysaccharide obtained by deacetylation of chitin and contains primary amino groups with an apparent pKa of approximately 6–6.5 [].

Its pH response occurs in the opposite direction to that of anionic weak‐acid polymers such as PAA. Under acidic conditions, protonation of —NH2 groups to —NH3
+ increases polymer charge density, hydration and swelling or solubility, whereas increasing pH causes deprotonation, reduced electrostatic repulsion and generally lower swelling or network contraction [].

Protonated chitosan can additionally exhibit antimicrobial activity through interactions between its positively charged groups and negatively charged bacterial cell surfaces.

Consequently, chitosan alone should not be described as a straightforward alkaline‐infection‐triggered swelling and release system, because its intrinsic swelling response is greater under acidic rather than alkaline conditions. Its value in smart wound dressings instead lies in its biocompatibility, antimicrobial properties and ability to form polyelectrolyte complexes, multilayer structures and composite networks in which its inverse pH response can be combined with other functional materials to regulate permeability and therapeutic release.

Other ionisable polymers may offer response windows that can be more closely aligned with wound‐relevant pH changes. Poly(methacrylic acid) (PMAA), for example, exhibits pH‐dependent ionisation that can be tuned through copolymerisation and network design, while histidine‐containing polymers and appropriately designed amine‐containing polymers provide additional routes for shifting the effective transition range []. Rather than assigning a universal infection threshold to a particular polymer class, the clinically relevant parameter is therefore the experimentally measured transition behaviour of the complete polymer network under wound‐like conditions [, , ].

Therapeutic agents can be incorporated into pH‐responsive systems during fabrication, for example by mixing the drug with the polymer or precursor solution before polymerisation, crosslinking or electrospinning, or after fabrication through swelling and loading from a drug solution []. Drug release may subsequently be altered by pH‐induced changes in network hydration, pore size, polymer–drug interactions or degradation. However, release kinetics cannot be generalised solely from the nominal identity of the responsive polymer. They depend on polymer composition, effective network pKa, crosslinking density, drug molecular size and charge, polymer–drug interactions, ionic strength and the magnitude and duration of the pH change. Accordingly, reported release fractions and response times should be interpreted for the specific formulation and experimental conditions rather than treated as universal values for PAA‐ or chitosan‐based wound dressings [].

Overall, the suitability of a pH‐responsive polymer for smart wound therapy should therefore be evaluated according to three linked criteria: the location of its effective response window relative to clinically relevant wound pH, the direction and magnitude of its structural response, and whether that response produces a therapeutically useful change in drug transport. This distinction is particularly important when pH‐responsive materials are incorporated into multimodal or closed‐loop wound systems, where an incorrectly assigned response threshold could lead to premature, delayed or inappropriate therapeutic activation.

Temperature‐responsive polymers exhibit a lower critical solution temperature (LCST), below which they are hydrated and swollen, and above which they dehydrate and collapse []. Figure  illustrates this mechanism.

Poly(N‐isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) is the gold standard temperature‐responsive polymer for biomedical purposes. PNIPAM has an LCST of approximately 32°C in aqueous solution, remarkably close to wound surface temperature (33°C–35°C) []. Below the LCST, PNIPAM chains are extended and hydrated with water molecules that hydrogen bond to amide groups (—NH—CO—) along the polymer backbone. The left panel of Figure  shows extended polymer chains with water molecules (H2O) and hydrogen bonds representing the swollen and hydrated state encapsulating the encapsulated drugs []. Above the LCST, hydrogen bonds break, water molecules are expelled and the polymer chains collapse into compact, globular conformations. Figure , right panel, illustrates collapsed polymer chains (tight spirals) extruding drug molecules, represented by dotted expulsion lines. Above the row, a small sigmoidal graph plots swelling ratio versus temperature with the LCST indicated by a vertical dashed line [].

Tuning LCST for wound infection detection. The LCST of pure PNIPAM (32°C) is below normal wound temperature (33°C–35°C), meaning pure PNIPAM would be collapsed (triggered) even in a healthy wound []. To raise the LCST to the infected wound range (38°C–40°C), PNIPAM is copolymerized with hydrophilic monomers (e.g., acrylamide, N,N‐dimethylacrylamide) or hydrophobic monomers (e.g., N‐tert‐butylacrylamide) to adjust the balance of hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions [, ]. For example, poly(NIPAM‐co‐acrylamide) with 10–20 mol% acrylamide exhibits an LCST of 37°C–39°C, enabling triggering specifically upon wound pyrexia [, ].

Applications in wound healing PNIPAM‐based hydrogels, nanofibers and coatings loaded with antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin and gentamicin) or growth factors (e.g., VEGF and PDGF) release their cargo only when the wound temperature exceeds the LCST []. This allows for therapy on demand during inflammation related to infection. PNIPAM has limitations, including slow response (minutes to tens of minutes), hysteresis (the swelling/collapse transition is not perfectly reversible), and potential toxicity of degradation products (isopropylamine) [].

Other temperature‐sensitive polymers. Poly(N‐vinylcaprolactam) (PVCL) has an LCST of 32°C–38°C (tunable) and is more biocompatible than PNIPAM because it does not produce toxic degradation products. Elastin‐like polypeptides (ELPs) are recombinant protein polymers that contain a pentapeptide repeat (VPGXG) and have sharp LCST transitions and are fully biodegradable, but their high cost prohibits them from widespread use [].

Enzyme‐responsive polymers incorporate peptide sequences that are specific substrates for wound‐relevant proteases, particularly MMP‐2 and MMP‐9 []. Figure  illustrates enzyme‐responsive drug release mediated by protease‐cleavable polymer networks.

In a typical design (Figure ), a hydrophilic polymer backbone (e.g., poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) or poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)) is crosslinked with short peptide sequences that are cleavable by target proteases []. The left panel (Figure , labelled “Low MMP activity – Intact crosslinks, drug retained”) shows an intact hydrogel network: polymer chains connected by red crosslinker bars labelled “MMP substrate peptide”, with drug molecules trapped in the network pores []. When MMPs are present at elevated levels (as in chronic wounds), the enzymes (represented by scissors icons) cleave the peptide crosslinks, causing network degradation and drug release []. In the right panel “Elevated MMPs (chronic wound)—Crosslinks cleaved, network degrades, drug released”, crosslinks are cleaved, the network degrades and drug molecules escape [].

The peptide sequence determines the specificity of the enzyme‐responsive systems. For MMP‐2 and MMP‐9, the optimal cleavage sequence is GPLGMHGK (with cleavage occurring between the glycine and leucine residues) []. Other sequences include GPQGIFGQ (cleaved by MMP‐1, MMP‐8, and MMP‐13) and GPLGVRGK (MMP‐2). The peptide crosslinker concentration (typically 1–10 mM in the hydrogel), crosslinking density (higher density = slower degradation), and pore size all influence release kinetics [].

Enzyme responsive systems have a high specificity for pathological protease activity and directly respond to the biochemical signature of chronic wounds. And since MMPs are increased in chronic wounds but not in normal healing (after the initial inflammatory phase), enzyme‐responsive systems can differentiate between physiological and pathological inflammation []. However, limitations include (1) high cost of custom synthesis of peptides (~$100–500 per gram); (2) limited stability of peptides in wound exudate, which contains multiple proteases that may cleave non‐specifically; (3) slow degradation kinetics (hours to days); and (4) difficulty in tuning the threshold (i.e., the MMP concentration required for release) [].

Other enzyme targets. Beyond MMP‐2 and MMP‐9, several other wound‐relevant proteases may be exploited for responsive sensing or therapeutic release. Neutrophil elastase is elevated during persistent inflammation and can serve as a marker of excessive inflammatory activity, although its presence is not specific to bacterial infection. Plasmin participates in fibrinolysis and tissue remodelling, but its physiological role in normal repair may limit its value as a stand‐alone pathological trigger []. Bacterial proteases, including collagenases and other secreted proteolytic enzymes, may provide greater infection specificity because they originate directly from microbial activity; however, their expression varies considerably among bacterial species, strains, and biofilm states []. Accordingly, enzyme‐responsive systems based on these targets must balance substrate selectivity against biological variability, cross‐reactivity with host proteases, and the need for clinically meaningful activation thresholds. Combining enzyme sensing with a second biomarker may therefore provide greater robustness than relying on a single protease trigger [].

Recent advances have produced dual‐responsive and triple‐responsive polymers that require multiple pathological signals to trigger drug release, reducing false positives [].

Copolymers or interpenetrating networks containing PAA and PNIPAM respond to both pH and temperature []. Importantly, the two components respond in different physical directions. Increasing pH promotes progressive deprotonation and swelling of PAA‐rich domains, whereas PNIPAM is hydrated and swollen below its lower critical solution temperature (LCST) and undergoes dehydration and collapse above the LCST []. Therefore, alkaline pH and elevated temperature do not simply cause both components to swell simultaneously. The net release behaviour depends on how these two responses are coupled within the network. AND‐like behaviour can arise only when the material architecture is designed so that low release occurs under each single‐trigger condition and substantially greater release occurs when both triggers are present. Such behaviour should therefore be demonstrated experimentally rather than inferred solely from the presence of two responsive polymers [].

Systems responsive to pH, temperature, and a third stimulus (e.g., glucose or MMPs) have been reported []. For example, a PNIPAM‐co‐PAA‐co‐PBA terpolymer responds to pH, temperature, and glucose, enabling triggered release in diabetic wounds with infection (both hyperglycaemia and elevated pH are required) [].

Host‐guest chemistry using cyclodextrin (host) and adamantane (guest) enables reversible, tunable responses []. Inclusion complexes (guests inside the host cavity) can be disrupted by competitive binding (e.g., small molecules present in wound exudate) or by changes in pH or temperature. These systems offer rapid, reversible transitions but require careful design to avoid premature release []. Table  provides a comparative overview of responsive polymer classes, highlighting their triggering mechanisms, swelling behaviour, response times, drug‐loading capacities and key limitations for wound‐dressing applications.

Comparison of responsive polymer classes for wound dressing applications.

Note: From a translational perspective, dip‐coating and weaving offer the strongest manufacturing scalability, whereas electrospinning and LbL assembly provide greater control over fibre morphology or coating architecture but are more difficult to scale reproducibly. Three‐dimensional printing offers the highest spatial customization but currently has lower throughput. Electrospinning is therefore most suitable when nanoscale morphology and drug loading are priorities, while dip‐coating or weaving may be preferable when manufacturing speed, robustness and integration with existing textile infrastructure are dominant considerations.

To translate responsive polymers into functional wound dressings, integration with textile substrates is necessary. Figure  shows five manufacturing strategies (1–5 in the figure) from laboratory techniques (electrospinning and layer‐by‐layer assembly) to industrially scalable processes (dip‐coating and weaving) and advanced additive manufacturing methods (3D printing) []. A decision tree at the bottom of Figure  assists in method selection according to application priorities [].

Electrospinning produces non‐woven nanofibre mats with high surface‐area‐to‐volume ratios and tunable fibre morphology, making it particularly attractive for wound dressings that combine drug delivery, sensing and extracellular‐matrix‐mimicking structures [, ]. Fibre formation results from electrohydrodynamic stretching of a charged polymer jet, while fibre diameter and morphology depend strongly on solution properties and processing conditions.

A critical advantage of electrospinning for smart wound dressings is the ability to fabricate core‐shell fibres using coaxial needles []. Two polymer solutions are delivered through concentric needles: the shell solution (responsive polymer, e.g., PAA or PNIPAM) and the core solution (drug, e.g., vancomycin or VEGF) [, ]. This configuration protects the drug from the external environment (preventing degradation) and ensures that drug release occurs only when the responsive polymer shell undergoes a conformational change (swelling or collapse) []. Core‐shell fibres can also be used to encapsulate two different drugs in separate compartments or to create gradient release profiles [].

(1) Electrospun nanofibre mats provide a high surface‐area‐to‐volume ratio, which is advantageous for drug loading, sensor immobilisation and interfacial interactions. The absolute specific surface area varies substantially with fibre diameter, porosity, polymer composition and measurement method and should therefore be considered formulation‐dependent []. (2) ECM‐mimicking architecture since the nanofibre diameter and morphology are comparable to native collagen fibrils (50–500 nm) []. (3) Versatility. A wide range of synthetic and natural polymers can be electrospun (PAA, PNIPAM, chitosan, polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(lactic‐co‐glycollic acid) (PLGA), gelatin, collagen, and silk fibroin) []. (4) Co‐spinning of multiple polymers and drugs in a single step.

Traditional single‐needle electrospinning has a very low throughput (0.1–1 g/h per needle); thus, it is not feasible for mass production []. Needleless electrospinning systems, including rotating‐electrode and wire‐based configurations, can generate multiple jets simultaneously and provide substantially higher productivity than conventional single‐needle systems []. However, needleless systems are less suitable for coreshell fibres and require accurate control of solution properties and process parameters []. Other limitations are solvent compatibility (many responsive polymers are soluble only in organic solvents, which can be toxic) and residual solvent in the final product (extensive drying is required) [, ].

Dip‐coating is a simple and scalable approach for functionalising existing textile substrates with responsive polymers [, ]. Continuous processing is compatible with roll‐to‐roll manufacturing, making this method attractive for large‐area wound‐dressing production. However, coating performance depends strongly on polymer–fibre interactions, solution rheology, withdrawal conditions, drying and the architecture of the textile substrate.

In simple dip‐coating, responsive polymers may adsorb onto textile fibres through van der Waals interactions, hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions. Although physical adsorption is straightforward, insufficient interfacial bonding may lead to non‐uniform coatings or leaching during use []. Surface pretreatments such as cold plasma can introduce reactive groups, including —OH, —NH2 and —COOH, thereby improving coating adhesion and durability. Coating characteristics are governed by coupled process variables including withdrawal speed, solution viscosity and concentration, number of coating cycles, substrate wettability and drying conditions. In the viscous‐drag regime described by Landau–Levich behaviour, increasing withdrawal speed generally increases the amount of liquid entrained on the substrate and can therefore increase wet‐film thickness, although the final coating also depends on drainage, evaporation and solution rheology []. Higher polymer concentration can increase coating add‐on but may also raise viscosity and reduce uniformity. Multiple dipping cycles can increase coating thickness, although at the expense of processing time and material use. Drying temperature should be sufficient to remove solvent while avoiding degradation of the responsive polymer or incorporated therapeutic agent, with moderate temperatures commonly preferred [].

Advantages include low cost; scalability to roll‐to‐roll manufacturing (hundreds of meters per minute); compatibility with existing textile manufacturing infrastructure; and applicability to a broad range of responsive polymers. Limitations: Uniform coating of complex textile architectures (e.g., thick non‐wovens, 3D spacer fabrics) can be difficult; leaching is possible due to physical adsorption; coating thickness is in the micrometre range (not nanometre precise) [].

Layer‐by‐layer (LbL) assembly involves sequential adsorption of oppositely charged species onto the textile surface, allowing multilayer coatings to be constructed with comparatively precise control over composition and thickness [, ]. Repeated deposition cycles enable responsive polymers, therapeutic agents and nanoparticles to be incorporated in defined sequences, providing greater control over interfacial structure and release behaviour than conventional bulk coating [].

LbL assembly relies on electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged polymers []. When the textile fibre (which may have a native surface charge or be plasma‐pretreated to introduce charged groups) is dipped into the polycation solution, the positively charged polymer adsorbs onto the negatively charged fibre surface []. Excess polymer is removed in the rinse step, leaving a single monolayer of polycation. Dipping into the polyanion solution then deposits a negatively charged polymer layer onto the polycation layer via electrostatic attraction []. Repeating the cycle builds up a multilayer coating with nanometre control over thickness (each bilayer is typically 1–10 nm) [].

Responsive polymers can be used as the polycation (e.g., chitosan, which is positively charged at acidic pH) or polyanion (e.g., PAA, which is negatively charged at alkaline pH) []. Drugs can be incorporated in several ways: (1) as a component of the polyelectrolyte (if the drug is charged), (2) as an intercalated layer between polyelectrolyte layers, or (3) encapsulated within nanoparticles that are then deposited via LbL []. By controlling the number of bilayers, the order of deposition, and the choice of polyelectrolytes, sophisticated release profiles (e.g., pulsed release, sequential release of multiple drugs) can be achieved [].

Advantages: nanometre control over coating thickness and composition; ability to incorporate multiple drugs and responsive polymers in defined spatial arrangements; mild aqueous processing conditions (no organic solvents, no high temperatures), preserving drug activity; and durable coatings due to multiple layers []. Limitations: very slow processing (hours to days to build enough bilayers, as each requires 10–30 min of dipping and rinsing); not currently suitable for high‐throughput manufacturing; requires precise control of solution pH and ionic strength to maintain optimal charge density [, ].

Woven architectures enable sensing, drug delivery, and electrical functionality to be spatially integrated through the use of different functional yarns within a common textile structure [, ].

This provides greater control over the location of individual functions than uniform surface coating and can support mechanically robust multilayer or modular dressing designs.

Yarns can be functionalised before weaving by: (1) coating the yarn with responsive polymers (via dip‐coating, LbL, or electrospinning directly onto the yarn), (2) using inherently conductive yarns (e.g., silver‐coated nylon, stainless steel fibres, carbon nanotube (CNT)‐incorporated yarns) for sensing, or (3) weaving drug‐loaded reservoir yarns (hollow fibres filled with drug solution, or solid fibres impregnated with drug) [, ].

Advantages: weaving is highly scalable (industrial looms operate at 500–2000 picks per minute, producing meters of fabric per minute); woven textiles are mechanically durable and can support repeated handling or laundering in non‐wound‐contact components; however, direct wound‐contact layers generally require controlled sterility and are more appropriately designed as single‐use or replaceable components; spatial patterning of functions is straightforward (different yarns can be placed in specific positions); and mechanical properties (tensile strength, tear resistance) can be tailored by yarn choice and weave pattern []. Limitations: woven fabrics have limited stretch and conformability (compared to knits), which may be problematic for wounds on mobile body sites (e.g., foot ulcers on the plantar surface); the minimum pore size (approximately 50 μm) is larger than electrospun nanofibers, which may affect cell infiltration and wound fluid transport []. Accordingly, reusable smart‐textile architectures may be more clinically realistic when reusable sensing/electronic modules are physically separated from a disposable sterile wound‐contact layer.

Three‐dimensional printing enables localised deposition of responsive hydrogels, sensors and therapeutic reservoirs onto textile substrates [, ]. Compared with conventional coating methods, additive manufacturing provides greater spatial control over material placement and may enable customised dressing geometries and region‐specific therapeutic loading.

Robocasting (or direct ink writing, DIW) is the most used 3D printing method for textile functionalisation. A shear‐thinning hydrogel (a material that flows when pressure is applied but solidifies when the pressure is removed) is extruded through a nozzle (diameter 100–500 μm) and deposited layer‐by‐layer onto the textile []. The adhesion of the printed hydrogel to the textile fibres is achieved by mechanical interlocking and covalent bonding with reactive hydrogels. Other 3D printing technologies include fused deposition modelling (FDM) for thermoplastic polymers (less common for responsive hydrogels) and stereolithography (SLA) for photocurable resins [].

The primary advantage of 3D printing is spatial control: sensors can be printed at one location, drug reservoirs at another, and different drug concentrations in different regions of the same dressing []. This enables patient‐specific geometries, a dressing can be printed to match the exact size and shape of an individual patient's wound (e.g., as determined by 3D wound scanning) []. Multiple drugs can be printed in gradient patterns to address spatially varying wound pathology (e.g., higher antibiotic concentration at the wound edge where biofilms are most prevalent) [].

The present printing resolution (100–500 μm) is far larger than electrospun nanofibers (50–1000 nm), which restricts the capability of creating ECM‐mimicking architectures []. The material palette is limited to shear‐thinning, fast‐gelling hydrogels (e.g., Pluronic F127, gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA), and alginate) []. The printing rate is slow (usually 1–10 cm2/min) and therefore not practical for mass production []. Adhesion between printed hydrogel and textile substrate can be poor, requiring surface pretreatment or adhesive interlayers [].

No single fabrication method is optimal for all responsive wound‐dressing applications. Electrospinning is advantageous when nanoscale fibres, high surface area or core‐shell drug reservoirs are required, whereas dip‐coating is more appropriate for scalable modification of existing textile substrates. LbL assembly provides superior control over thin multilayer coatings but is comparatively slow, while weaving enables spatial integration of multiple functional yarns and improved mechanical robustness. Three‐dimensional printing offers the greatest geometric and spatial flexibility but currently faces limitations in throughput and printable material selection. Accordingly, fabrication‐method selection should balance therapeutic function, manufacturing scalability, coating precision, mechanical requirements and the desired level of patient‐specific customization [].

From a translational perspective, dip‐coating and weaving offer the strongest manufacturing scalability, whereas electrospinning and LbL assembly provide greater control over fibre morphology or coating architecture but are more difficult to scale reproducibly. Three‐dimensional printing offers the highest spatial customization but currently has lower throughput. Electrospinning is therefore most suitable when nanoscale morphology and drug loading are priorities, while dip‐coating or weaving may be preferable when manufacturing speed, robustness, and integration with existing textile infrastructure are dominant considerations.

The goal of this field is a fully autonomous closed‐loop textile that senses wound state, processes the information, and delivers therapy without external intervention. Figure  presents four architectures of increasing complexity, with technology readiness levels (TRLs) ranging from TRL 3–4 (fully closed‐loop) to TRL 7–8 (open‐loop) [].

The dressing senses the wound state and provides a readout (typically a colour change), but the user (patient or clinician) must decide whether to intervene []. Figure , illustrates this architecture. The wound dressing contains a colorimetric pH sensor (a circle changing from yellow to purple) that indicates infection when the colour changes []. The user sees the colour change, manually applies antibiotic cream from a separate tube, and then reapplies or replaces the dressing. There is no automated feedback from sensor to actuator [].

The Wound Sense pH‐indicating dressing (developed by researchers at the University of Manchester, now in preclinical development) uses bromothymol blue‐immobilised gauze that changes from yellow (pH < 6.0) to green (pH 7.0) to blue (pH > 7.5) []. In a clinical study of 35 patients with chronic leg ulcers, the colour change accurately identified infection (defined by clinical criteria plus wound culture) with 89% sensitivity and 78% specificity. However, because the dressing does not deliver therapy autonomously, the clinical benefit depends on user recognition and response, a limitation in settings with low health literacy or limited access to care [].

Figure , lists pros: “✓ Simple, no electronics, no power needed” and cons: “✗ Requires user compliance, delayed response”. TRL: 7–8 (open‐loop pH‐indicating dressings are nearing commercial entry, with several products in the pipeline).

Semi‐closed‐loop systems integrate electrochemical sensors into the dressing and transmit data wirelessly to an external device (e.g., a smartphone), but the user still confirms drug release []. Figure , shows this architecture: the dressing contains electrochemical sensors (interdigitated electrodes—comb‐like structures for pH and temperature) and iontophoresis electrodes (two parallel rectangles) []. A wireless icon (curved arcs) connects the dressing to a smartphone. On the phone screen, the user sees “pH: 7.6 | Temp: 38.1°C | Release drug?” with a “YES” button []. When the user confirms, a voltage is applied to the iontophoresis electrodes, driving charged drug (e.g., gentamicin, which is positively charged) from the reservoir into the wound [].

pH is measured by open‐circuit potential with a working electrode coated with polyaniline and a reference electrode (e.g., Ag/AgCl). Temperature is measured using a thermistor (resistance changes with temperature) []. Iontophoresis: application of a small electric current (usually 0.1–0.5 mA/cm2, < 3 V) to drive charged drug molecules through the skin or wound bed. The drug reservoir, usually a hydrogel containing the drug in ionic form, is positioned between the skin and the electrode [].

A team at Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH) developed a semi‐closed‐loop dressing with PEDOT:PSS‐coated fabric for pH sensing and iontophoretic gentamicin delivery []. In a porcine wound infection model (n = 6 pigs, 4 wounds per pig), the system detected infection (pH > 7.5) with 95% accuracy within 2 h of bacterial inoculation and, upon user confirmation via smartphone, reduced bacterial burden by 3.5 log units within 24 h. The iontophoresis step operated at 0.2 mA for 2 h, corresponding to a nominal charge requirement of approximately 0.4 mAh per treatment. The practical power‐source requirement would be higher once losses associated with control electronics, voltage conversion and battery discharge characteristics are considered; therefore, battery capacity and dimensions should be selected on the basis of the complete system power budget rather than inferred from the iontophoresis current alone [].

Figure  lists pros: “✓ User in control, easier regulatory pathway (device with manual override)” and cons: “✗ Requires external device, still user‐dependent” []. TRL: 5–6 (semi‐closed‐loop systems have been validated in large animal models but not yet in humans) [].

Fully closed‐loop systems integrate sensing, processing, decision‐making and therapeutic actuation within the dressing, with minimal or no user intervention []. True autonomous operation additionally requires an onboard or self‐sustaining power source; systems that depend on externally supplied NFC power should instead be considered externally powered closed‐loop systems rather than fully autonomous devices. Representative example to date, a fully closed‐loop dressing has not been reported in humans, but a proof‐of‐concept system was demonstrated in vitro by []. Such early systems often consist of flexible electrochemical sensors (e.g., pH sensors based on polyaniline‐coated electrodes), temperature sensors (thermistors), microcontrollers (e.g., ATtiny85 or other low‐power chips), drug‐loaded responsive polymer reservoirs and thin‐film batteries. In a typical setup, the microcontroller reads the sensor data and activates therapeutic release when predefined decision criteria are met, for example when a validated pH threshold or combination of biomarker thresholds is exceeded []. However, current systems have major limitations including short battery life (~48 h), limited drug payload capacity, and lack of in vivo validation. These challenges need to be addressed prior to clinical translation.

Figure  lists pros: “✓ Autonomous, rapid response, complex logic (AND gates)” and cons: “✗ High technical barrier, regulatory challenge (combination product), power management” []. TRL: 3–4 (fully closed‐loop systems have been demonstrated only in vitro or in small animal models at the proof‐of‐concept level) [].

One of the key challenges in smart wound dressings is avoiding false positives, triggering drug release when only one biomarker is transiently abnormal, but infection is not present (e.g., a temporary pH elevation due to a dressing change or transient fever) []. AND‐gate logic systems address these issues by requiring both pH > threshold and temperature > threshold (or other combinations) to trigger release []. Figure , shows this architecture.

The dressing consists of two sensors; one is a pH sensor (circle marked “Input A: pH > 7.5”), and the other is a temperature sensor (thermometer icon marked “Input B: T > 37.5°C”). Both sensors are connected to a small logic gate symbol (AND gate, a D‐shaped icon with two inputs and one output). The AND gate output controls the actuator (drug release mechanism, shown as a spray or dots coming out).

Note: AND‐gate logic requires both predefined biomarker conditions to be satisfied before therapeutic activation. This may improve specificity compared with single‐trigger systems, although the stricter decision criterion can reduce sensitivity when only one clinically relevant biomarker exceeds its threshold. This logic can be implemented in hardware (using a simple microcontroller) or in materials (using dual‐responsive polymers, as discussed in Section ) [].

Combining two independent wound‐state signals may improve decision specificity by reducing therapeutic activation caused by an isolated abnormal biomarker. However, AND‐gate logic introduces an important diagnostic trade‐off []. Requiring both inputs to be positive may reduce false‐positive activation, but it can also increase false‐negative decisions if only one biomarker becomes abnormal, if one sensor fails to detect a true change, or if the biomarkers respond at different times during wound deterioration []. Therefore, AND‐gate logic should not be assumed to improve overall diagnostic performance automatically. Its clinical value depends on the sensitivity and specificity of the individual sensors, the correlation between the selected biomarkers [, ]. The prevalence of the target condition, and the relative consequences of false‐positive and false‐negative therapeutic activation.

For clinical evaluation, such decision architectures should therefore be assessed using standard diagnostic metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis may also be useful when continuous sensor outputs are converted into decision thresholds. These metrics should be reported together with the assumed disease prevalence and any correlation between biomarkers because both factors influence apparent diagnostic performance [].

A dual‐responsive PAA‐b‐PNIPAM copolymer system was designed by Zhang et al. []. The polymer experienced a coil‐to‐globule transition only when both pH > 7.5 and temperature > 38°C, releasing 65% of encapsulated vancomycin within 12 h []. At pH > 7.5 but temperature < 38°C, only 12% release was seen; at temperature > 38°C but pH < 7.5, only 8% release was seen. This result shows good AND‐gate logic on the materials level without requiring electronic components [, ]. In high‐risk wounds, the preferred decision rule may therefore differ according to whether the clinical priority is to minimise unnecessary drug release or to avoid missed pathological events.

Pros: “✓ AND‐gate logic reduces false positives and more specific targeting of infection.” Cons: “✗ requires dual sensors or dual‐responsive polymers, more complex to fabricate.” TRL: 3–4 (AND‐gate systems have been demonstrated in vitro but not in vivo) []. Engineering demands increase as smart dressings progress from open loop to autonomous systems. Semi‐closed‐loop platforms require reliable wireless communication with external readers, while fully closed‐loop systems must integrate low‐power sensing, processing, actuation, and power management. Data security and clear user interfaces are also important when wound data are transmitted to smartphones or clinical systems. Key failure modes include sensor drift, communication loss, power depletion, and unintended drug release. Therefore, autonomous systems should incorporate fail‐safe controls, dose limits, and detection of abnormal sensor behaviour to maintain safe operation [].

The roadmap in Figure  illustrates a progressive transition from component development and sensor integration toward preclinical validation, clinical evaluation, regulatory submission and eventual market entry. The sequence emphasises that advances in materials alone are insufficient for translation; progress requires coordinated development of sensing, manufacturing, clinical evidence and regulatory strategy. The projected milestones should therefore be interpreted as indicative development targets rather than fixed predictions.

Despite encouraging preclinical progress, several barriers must be overcome for clinical adoption []. Figure  presents a comprehensive analysis of these barriers across four panels (a–d).

Figure  a presents a harmonised roadmap for clinical adoption from 2025 to 2035. Component development and early integration activities dominate the 2025–2028 research phase, followed by preclinical validation and clinical translation between approximately 2028 and 2032. An initial regulatory‐guidance milestone is anticipated around 2028, while the first commercial open‐loop wound‐dressing products may emerge around 2029. Early first‐in‐human evaluation of more integrated closed‐loop systems may begin around 2030, although progression will depend strongly on safety, manufacturing reproducibility, and regulatory classification. Clinical validation and regulatory submission are expected to continue through the early 2030s, with commercial entry of fully closed‐loop systems remaining a longer‐term possibility around 2035. These dates should be regarded as indicative milestones rather than firm predictions because development rates will vary among technologies and regulatory pathways.

Regulatory classification of smart wound dressings depends on their intended use and primary mode of action (PMOA). In the United States, the FDA Office of Combination Products assigns the lead regulatory centre according to the PMOA []. Device‐led products may follow the 510(k), De Novo or PMA pathway depending on predicate availability and risk, while drug‐led combination products may follow an NDA‐based pathway. Early FDA Q‐Submission is therefore important to clarify classification and evidence requirements [].

In the European Union, classification is governed by the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR 2017/745), including specific considerations for devices incorporating medicinal substances []. Biocompatibility should be evaluated according to ISO 10993, while appropriate sterilisation validation and shelf‐life assessment are also required for wound‐contacting smart textiles [].

Beyond the United States and European Union, regulatory requirements vary across jurisdictions. In the United Kingdom, smart wound dressings are regulated through the MHRA under the applicable UK medical‐device framework, with classification determined by intended purpose, risk, and device characteristics. In China, medical devices are regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), and products incorporating sensing, drug delivery, or combination‐device functions may require additional technical and clinical evidence depending on their classification. These jurisdictional differences can affect classification, clinical‐evidence requirements, registration strategy, and time to market. Accordingly, global translation of smart wound dressings will require early regulatory planning tailored to the intended market rather than assuming that a single approval pathway is universally applicable.

The economic value of a smart wound dressing depends on the total incremental treatment cost over the complete episode of care and the probability and cost of adverse events that are avoided. For a single avoided outcome, the break‐even absolute risk reduction is:
ARRBE=ΔCcourse−ScareCevent

This formulation shows that the break‐even threshold cannot be determined from the price of one smart dressing alone. The analysis must specify how many disposable dressings are used during the treatment period, whether sensing or electronic components are reusable, the replacement frequency of wound‐contact components, and the corresponding cost of conventional care. Similarly, avoided amputation and hospitalisation should not be combined into a single risk‐reduction value unless their individual probabilities and costs are explicitly defined.

Figure  therefore presents the economic framework as a sensitivity analysis rather than claiming a single universal break‐even threshold. Net savings vary according to the incremental course‐level cost, the probability of avoiding major complications and the assumed cost of those complications. Because the modelled treatment horizon is only 6 months, annual discounting has little influence on the result and is not applied in this illustrative analysis. Definitive cost‐effectiveness estimates will require prospective clinical data on dressing utilisation, treatment duration, nursing‐resource use, complication rates and patient outcomes.

Translational barriers differ in both severity and tractability. Regulatory uncertainty and manufacturing scalability represent major constraints because they directly determine the feasibility of clinical development and reproducible production. Reimbursement [], stability and the lack of robust clinical evidence further influence adoption, whereas user acceptance becomes increasingly important as systems move from controlled studies into routine wound care []. The severity scores shown in Figure  represent the authors' qualitative assessment based on the reviewed literature rather than a formally validated expert‐elicitation scale.

Machine learning (ML) models trained on wound images (smartphone photographs) and continuous sensor data (pH, temperature, MMP activity over time) can predict healing trajectories and personalise treatment []. For example, a CNN trained on 2000 images of wounds was able to accurately predict 91% of the DFUs that would heal in 12 weeks. The sensor data (e.g., 7‐day pH trend) improved prediction accuracy to 96% []. An intelligent dressing incorporating tinyML could, in principle, personalise decision thresholds to patient‐specific baseline behaviour and temporal biomarker trends rather than relying on a single universal pH cutoff. Such adaptive approaches may improve individualisation but require rigorous clinical validation to avoid both undertreatment and unnecessary therapeutic activation []. This approach may lead to undertreatment (missed infections) and overtreatment (exposure to unnecessary antibiotics).

Power supply remains a major challenge for autonomous closed‐loop dressings. Three approaches are under investigation:

TENGs convert mechanical energy (body movement, wound deformation) into electricity via contact electrification and electrostatic induction. Textile fibres coated with triboelectric materials (e.g., polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and nylon) generate voltage pulses (10–100 V) and current (1–100 μA) upon movement. Limitations: low output power (microwatts to milliwatts) and wound dressings on immobile patients (e.g., bedridden patients with pressure ulcers) may not generate enough movement [].

Biofuel cells use enzymes (e.g., glucose oxidase and laccase) to generate electricity from biochemical energy in wound exudate (glucose and lactate). The theoretical power density is approximately 100 μW/cm2, sufficient for low‐power sensors but not for iontophoretic drug delivery (which requires milliwatts). Short operational lifetime (hours to days due to enzyme deactivation) remains a critical limitation [].

Power is supplied by an external transmitter (e.g., a smartphone or a dedicated charger) placed in the vicinity of the dressing through an NFC coil integrated into the textile. This technique is already used in continuous glucose monitors (e.g., FreeStyle Libre) and cochlear implants []. The dressing contains a receiving coil and a capacitor, making an LC circuit that resonates at the same frequency as the transmitter (usually 13.56 MHz for NFC). Advantages include no need for a battery, dressing can be completely sealed (no electrical connections in contact with wound exudate), and power can be supplied on demand (e.g., when the clinician or patient brings the transmitter close to the wound) []. Limitations: The dressing is not autonomous without the transmitter, and the patient must remember to charge the dressing at intervals.

Synthetic biology provides a radically different approach: genetically engineered bacteria embedded in textile fibres that sense wound biomarkers and produce therapeutics on demand. 
E. coli
 Nissle 1917 (a probiotic strain) has been engineered to sense acyl‐homoserine lactones (AHLs, quorum‐sensing molecules produced by 
P. aeruginosa
) and produce the antimicrobial peptide pyocin S5 []. When encapsulated in a hydrogel fibre and placed on a wound, the bacteria produce pyocin only when the density of 
P. aeruginosa
 reaches a threshold. In vitro proof‐of‐concept “living bandages” have been demonstrated, demonstrating a 4‐log reduction of 
P. aeruginosa
 growth within 24 h of quorum sensing detection.

(1) Bacterial containment: the engineered bacteria should not escape the dressing and colonise the patient. Solutions include encapsulation within a semi‐permeable membrane with pore size < 0.2 μm (which prevents bacteria passage but allows nutrients and therapeutics to diffuse) []. (2) Viability during storage. Bacteria must be alive in the dressing during storage on the shelf. Lyophilization (freeze‐drying) with trehalose as a cryoprotectant has shown promising results, with > 50% viability after 6 months at room temperature. (3) Biosafety and regulatory approval: live bacterial products are under strict regulatory requirements (like probiotics or live biotherapeutic products).

Besides pH, temperature, MMPs, and glucose, other wound biomarkers are being studied for incorporation into smart textiles:

In the near term, development should prioritise reliable integration of two or three clinically informative biomarkers with a single well‐controlled therapeutic output, rather than maximising the number of sensing and actuation functions. Such systems should first demonstrate reproducible operation in wound exudate, stable performance during clinically relevant wear periods, and clear improvement over single‐parameter monitoring before more complex autonomous architectures are pursued. These advanced actuation strategies should therefore be evaluated not only for therapeutic efficacy but also for wound‐specific safety, particularly in patients with neuropathy, ischaemia, impaired sensation or active infection.

The most realistic translational opportunities are: (i) validated open‐loop or semi‐closed‐loop dressings using a small number of clinically relevant biomarkers; (ii) scalable textile integration using manufacturing routes such as dip‐coating, electrospinning or weaving; and (iii) modular systems in which the wound‐contact layer is disposable while sensing or communication electronics are reusable where appropriate. Progress should be evaluated through predefined milestones including sensor accuracy in wound exudate, stability over the intended wear period, reproducible therapeutic dosing, large‐animal validation and early human‐factors testing. Fully autonomous multi‐actuator systems and living textiles remain important longer‐term directions but require substantially greater evidence of safety, reliability and regulatory feasibility.

This review has examined the convergence of responsive polymer chemistry and textile engineering that enables smart wound dressings for chronic wound management. Key findings include:

Biomarker targets are well‐defined. pH, temperature, MMPs, and glucose are clinically relevant, technically accessible, and have established normal/pathological thresholds (Section ).
Mechanisms of responsive polymers are well known. pH‐responsive polymers (PAA, chitosan), temperature‐responsive polymers (PNIPAM), and enzyme‐responsive polymers (MMP‐cleavable peptides) have been well characterised with tunable thresholds and release kinetics (Section ).
Multiple textile integration methods exist. Electrospinning, dip‐coating, LbL assembly, weaving, and 3D printing each offer distinct advantages and limitations; method selection depends on application priorities (Section ).
Closed‐loop systems are feasible but not yet clinical. Open‐loop (TRL 7–8) and semi‐closed‐loop (TRL 5–6) systems are near commercial entry; fully closed‐loop autonomous systems remain at the proof‐of‐concept stage (TRL 3–4) (Section ).
Regulatory and manufacturing barriers dominate. Regulatory pathway uncertainty (no FDA guidance as of 2026), manufacturing scalability, and stability/shelf life are the highest‐severity barriers (Section ).

Smart textiles are not the only approach to responsive wound care. Comparison with alternatives helps contextualise their advantages:

Electronic patches such as flexible printed circuit board (PCB) based sensors. Electronic patches are more mature than smart textiles, with a number of commercial products (e.g., Leaf Healthcare patient monitoring system). Advantages include better sensor accuracy, an established manufacturing base and current regulatory pathways (Class II devices). Drawbacks include less comfort, less breathability (non‐porous), pressure injury from rigid electronics and non‐washability. Smart textiles are familiar (patients are used to fabric dressings), breathable, conformable and easy to replace [].

Injectable hydrogels (e.g., MMP‐responsive PEG hydrogels) can be delivered to the wound bed to create an ECM‐mimicking architecture and for on‐demand drug delivery [, ]. Benefits: Can fill irregular wound geometries, can deliver drugs deep into tissue, minimally invasive for delivery. Disadvantages: Cannot be removed or adjusted after injection; non‐removability may complicate wound assessment; injection may cause additional tissue trauma. Smart textiles are noninvasive, removable and adjustable.

Systemic (oral or intravenous) antibiotics are often included in the current standard of care for infected wounds. Benefits: Established, inexpensive and widely available. Disadvantages: microbiome disruption (risk of Clostridioides difficile infection), antibiotic resistance selection pressure, absence of localisation (high systemic doses needed to reach therapeutic wound concentrations), and adverse effects (nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity). Smart textiles deliver antibiotics locally and on demand, greatly reducing systemic exposure [].

Several critical questions remain unanswered:

Optimal trigger thresholds. What is the best pH level to activate antibiotic release? A pH value around 7.5 is frequently used as an experimental decision threshold, but clinically relevant wound pH spans a broader and overlapping range, and no single cutoff has been established as universally diagnostic of infection. In contrast, some non‐infectious conditions (e.g., alkaline antiseptic exposure) may cause transient pH > 7.5. Multi‐parameter (AND‐gate) logic may be needed, but rigorous clinical studies to determine optimal thresholds are lacking [].
Long‐term stability. How long can responsive polymers maintain function under wound exudate conditions (proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), biofilms, temperature fluctuations)? Most studies report stability over days to weeks; clinical use requires stability over weeks to months. Accelerated stability testing (e.g., 40°C/75% relative humidity for 6 months) is needed to predict shelf life.
Patient preferences. Do patients prefer autonomous closed‐loop systems (no user control) or systems that alert them and require confirmation? Preferences may vary by age, health literacy, and prior healthcare experiences. Human factors studies are urgently needed.
Cost‐effectiveness in real‐world settings. Will payers (Medicare and private insurance) reimburse for smart dressings without definitive RCT evidence of cost savings? The revised break‐even framework demonstrates that cost‐effectiveness depends on the incremental cost of the complete treatment course, the probability and cost of avoided complications, and potential reductions in healthcare‐resource use. Robust estimates therefore require prospective clinical and health‐economic data rather than a single assumed risk‐reduction threshold.Biological heterogeneity and biofilm validation. Future validation should test smart dressings in polymicrobial and spatially heterogeneous biofilm models rather than relying only on single‐species planktonic systems. Such models should also account for host inflammatory responses that may alter biomarker levels independently of microbial burden.

This review has several limitations. First, most cited studies are preclinical (in vitro, small animal models). Large animal (porcine) data are sparse, and human data are very limited. Second, the review emphasises polymer‐based systems; electronic wound monitoring devices (e.g., impedance‐based sensors, ultrasound‐based sensors) are covered only briefly. Third, although the review discusses major regulatory considerations in the United States, European Union, United Kingdom and China, detailed country‐specific approval requirements are beyond its scope and may vary according to product classification, intended use and combination‐product status. Fourth, the review does not provide a formal meta‐analysis of drug release kinetics or clinical outcomes, as the heterogeneity of study designs precludes quantitative synthesis.

Responsive polymer textiles provide a paradigm shift in chronic wound management, from passive barriers to active, smart therapeutic platforms. The scientific basis is established within the fields of responsive polymer chemistry (pH‐, temperature‐, and enzyme‐responsive systems) and textile engineering (electrospinning, dip‐coating, LbL, weaving, 3D printing). Proof‐of‐concept closed‐loop systems have been shown in vitro and in small animal models. Open‐loop pH‐indicating dressings are approaching commercialisation (TRL 7–8) and may reach patients in 2–3 years. Semi‐closed‐loop systems with external readers remain at an intermediate stage of development and may reach clinical translation in the early 2030s, whereas fully closed‐loop autonomous systems remain at proof‐of‐concept stages and are unlikely to achieve commercial availability before approximately 2035.

The remaining challenges are mostly translational, including regulatory path clarification, scalability of manufacturing, stability/shelf‐life enhancement and demonstration of cost‐effectiveness. Overcoming these barriers will require interdisciplinary collaboration between polymer chemists, textile engineers, wound care clinicians, regulatory specialists, health economists and patient advocates. Continued investment and collaboration could see the first autonomous smart wound dressing in patients' hands within the next decade, revolutionising care for the 40 million patients worldwide who suffer from chronic wounds.

This study does not include any human concerns, animal tests, or sensitive data. Therefore, ethical approval was not necessary. All study techniques were followed in accordance with applicable guidelines and regulations.
