medicine.title: Pelvic osteotomy in classic bladder exstrophy and cloacal exstrophy: a systematic review and qualitative evidence synthesis with separate clinical pathways
medicine.abstract: To synthesise evidence on pelvic osteotomy in classic bladder exstrophy (CBE) and cloacal exstrophy (CE), with separate interpretation of their reconstructive pathways.PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus were searched to 9 September 2026. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data. MINORS and Cochrane RoB 2 assessed methodological limitations. Findings were synthesised qualitatively in separate CBE/bladder-exstrophy, CE and mixed-cohort strata.Thirteen studies were included: nine addressing CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported, three CE-specific studies and one mixed cohort. One was a pilot randomised trial; the remainder were observational. CBE studies described osteotomy-assisted primary closure and selective mobilisation when approximation was difficult, without establishing superiority over closure without osteotomy. CE studies described osteotomy within complex primary or repeat reconstruction involving staging, fixation and immobilisation. In one CE cohort, unadjusted closure success was 77.6% with osteotomy versus 41.7% without, but the association did not persist after adjustment. No technique showed consistent superiority. Evidence for independent improvements in continence, pelvic-floor anatomy or gait was insufficient; functional findings from CBE were not extrapolated to CE.CBE and CE require distinct interpretation. Osteotomy should be planned together with postoperative stabilisation and immobilisation to protect the reconstruction. Osteotomy selection in CBE depends on pelvic mechanics; CE requires specialist planning of pelvic mobilisation and stabilisation. Referral to experienced multidisciplinary centres should be prioritised. The proposed framework is conceptual, requires validation and cannot replace specialist expertise.
medicine.text:
Classic bladder exstrophy (CBE) and cloacal exstrophy (CE) are distinct clinical entities within the exstrophy–epispadias complex (EEC). CBE involves the lower urinary tract and anterior abdominal wall together with an open anterior pelvic ring, pubic symphyseal diastasis, external rotation of the hemipelves, shortening of the anterior pelvic segment, and altered acetabular orientation. Displacement and orientation of the pelvic-floor musculature further distinguish CBE from normal anatomy [–]. CE involves additional complex visceral and musculoskeletal abnormalities and is often associated with more severe pelvic deformity and wider pubic diastasis [, ]. Their reconstructive requirements and functional prognosis should therefore be considered separately.

In CBE, separation and external rotation of the hemipelves can increase the tension required to approximate the bladder, abdominal wall and pelvic floor. Osteotomy is used to increase pelvic mobility and facilitate pubic approximation, particularly when the pelvis is non-malleable or reconstruction is delayed []. In CE, pelvic mobilisation is considered within a more complex reconstructive pathway involving staging, fixation and postoperative immobilisation, including after failed closure [, , ]. Selective osteotomy strategies described in CBE should not be extrapolated to CE; even within CBE, use varies across patients and centres [, , ].

The orthopaedic component of exstrophy reconstruction has evolved considerably. Posterior iliac osteotomy was historically used to mobilise the pelvic ring, while anterior innominate and oblique osteotomies subsequently enabled correction through an anterior approach and avoided some of the logistical limitations associated with posterior exposure. More recent modifications, including mini-open anterior osteotomy and bilateral obturator osteotomy, have sought to achieve sufficient pelvic mobilisation while limiting additional surgical exposure and morbidity [, , , ]. The Y-pelvic osteotomy has also been described as a technical modification combining elements of anterior and posterior release; however, the available report is primarily technical and does not provide sufficient clinical outcome data to constitute comparative evidence []. Consequently, contemporary osteotomies should not necessarily be regarded as competing procedures, but rather as different strategies intended to address varying degrees and patterns of pelvic deformity.

The clinical role of pelvic osteotomy has also been influenced by changing reconstructive practice. Primary bladder closure was traditionally undertaken during the neonatal period, when the pelvis was considered more malleable. More recent population-level data demonstrate a shift toward delayed primary reconstruction, and pelvic osteotomy is used more frequently in patients undergoing closure beyond the first days of life []. In CBE, a large comparative institutional series demonstrated that pelvic osteotomy can be performed during both newborn and delayed closure, although outcomes differed according to osteotomy type, timing, centre, and patient characteristics []. In CE, where the pelvic deformity is generally more pronounced, osteotomy, staged reconstruction, fixation, and postoperative immobilisation have been associated with closure success in retrospective cohorts [, ]. More recent evidence further suggests a role for repeat osteotomy during secondary closure after failed reconstruction, although these findings remain observational and susceptible to confounding by surgical era, centre experience, immobilisation protocol, and case complexity [].

Importantly, successful approximation of the pelvic ring does not necessarily imply restoration of normal pelvic function. The only randomised study identified in the contemporary evidence base compared complete primary repair with and without anterior innominate osteotomy and found no significant between-group difference in most postoperative pelvic-floor magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measurements, although posterior bladder-neck position was closer to normal in the osteotomy group []. Long-term gait studies likewise demonstrate persistent alterations in pelvic, hip, knee, trunk, and foot biomechanics after bladder exstrophy reconstruction, with inconsistent differences between patients treated with and without osteotomy [, , ]. At the same time, measurable biomechanical deviations do not invariably translate into clinically limiting functional impairment, and recent observational data suggest that satisfactory functional or quality-of-life outcomes may coexist with residual pelvic deformity [, , ]. These findings emphasise the distinction between anatomical correction, mechanical support of reconstruction, and long-term functional recovery.

Despite decades of clinical experience, the evidence informing pelvic osteotomy in bladder exstrophy remains difficult to interpret. The condition is rare, surgical strategies have evolved substantially over time, individual centres employ different indications and immobilisation protocols, and contemporary evidence encompasses randomised imaging data, retrospective comparative cohorts, surgical case series, administrative database studies, and gait analyses. Moreover, the outcomes of interest extend beyond successful bladder closure to include recurrent exstrophy, prolapse, fistula formation, urinary function, pelvic morphology, gait, orthopaedic morbidity, and quality of life. Direct comparison between osteotomy techniques is therefore inherently limited, and the clinical relevance of individual procedures depends on pelvic morphology and reconstructive context rather than technical characteristics alone.

This systematic review evaluates the clinical evidence on pelvic osteotomy while maintaining separate interpretations for CBE and CE. CBE studies, including publications using the broader term bladder exstrophy, are distinguished from CE-specific studies and from a mixed cohort without separable phenotype-specific outcomes. The review addresses indications, techniques, closure outcomes, pelvic anatomy, function and complications within these strata. The Exstrophy Osteotomy Decision Framework (EODF) was developed as an author-derived conceptual synthesis with separate clinical pathways. It structures multidisciplinary discussion and identifies variables for prospective validation; it is not a validated treatment guideline.

This systematic review and qualitative evidence synthesis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement []. The review protocol was developed a priori but was not prospectively registered. Before study selection, the protocol defined the review question, eligibility criteria, information sources, search strategy, screening process, data extraction procedures, methodological quality assessment, and approach to evidence synthesis.

The review was designed to address the following clinical question:

What is the current evidence regarding the role, indications, and outcomes of pelvic osteotomy in bladder exstrophy reconstruction, and how do different osteotomy strategies relate to reconstructive, urological, and orthopaedic outcomes?

Eligibility was defined according to the Population–Intervention–Comparator–Outcome (PICO) framework.

Population (P): Patients with classic bladder exstrophy (CBE) or cloacal exstrophy (CE). Studies including broader exstrophy–epispadias complex populations were eligible when data relevant to bladder or cloacal exstrophy could be reliably identified.

Intervention (I): Pelvic osteotomy performed as part of bladder or cloacal exstrophy reconstruction, including posterior iliac, anterior innominate, oblique, combined anterior–posterior, mini-open anterior, bilateral obturator, and other modified pelvic osteotomy techniques. Studies examining reconstruction without osteotomy were also eligible when they provided clinically relevant information regarding the role of osteotomy or served as an osteotomy comparator.

Comparator (C): Where available, eligible comparators included reconstruction without pelvic osteotomy, different osteotomy techniques, different timing strategies, single-stage versus multi-stage reconstruction, patients treated with versus without osteotomy, and historical or institutional comparison groups.

Outcomes (O): Studies were required to report at least one clinically relevant predefined outcome. Primary reconstructive outcomes included successful bladder closure, bladder dehiscence, recurrent exstrophy, bladder prolapse, vesicocutaneous fistula formation, and need for reoperation. Secondary urological and anatomical outcomes included urinary continence, bladder capacity or growth, bladder-neck position or support, pelvic-floor morphology, pubic diastasis, and pelvic alignment. Orthopaedic and functional outcomes included acetabular orientation, gait, hip or lower-extremity function, quality of life where related to reconstructive outcome, and osteotomy-related or overall postoperative complications.

Original peer-reviewed clinical studies published in English were eligible, including randomised trials, prospective or retrospective observational studies, comparative cohort studies, cross-sectional functional studies, and clinical case series.

Studies were excluded from the formal evidence set if they were editorials, expert opinions, commentaries, conference abstracts, animal or cadaveric studies, isolated case reports or institutional series involving fewer than three patients, or publications without extractable postoperative clinical outcome data. Publications in languages other than English were also excluded.

Publications describing anatomy, imaging, biomechanics, or operative technique without extractable postoperative clinical outcomes were not included in the formal evidence set. Selected publications of this type were nevertheless retained as contextual literature when necessary to describe pelvic morphology, biomechanical principles, or the technical evolution of pelvic osteotomy. Such publications were not included in methodological quality assessment or used as outcome evidence.

A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase (Elsevier), and Scopus from database inception to 9 September 2026. The search combined controlled vocabulary, including Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and Emtree terms where applicable, with free-text terms relating to bladder exstrophy, cloacal exstrophy, the exstrophy–epispadias complex, pelvic osteotomy, and pelvic reconstruction.

The complete database-specific search strategies, search dates, and numbers of records retrieved are provided in Supplementary Table . The electronic search identified 268 records in PubMed/MEDLINE, 541 in Embase, and 537 in Scopus before deduplication. Reference lists of eligible studies were additionally screened to identify potentially relevant publications not retrieved by the database search.

All records retrieved through the electronic search were imported into reference-management software and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the predefined eligibility criteria. Publications considered potentially eligible by either reviewer underwent full-text assessment.

Full-text eligibility was independently assessed by the same two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion and consensus; a third reviewer was available for unresolved cases. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. When potentially overlapping cohorts from the same institution were identified, the most comprehensive dataset was retained for a given clinical outcome, and duplicate datasets addressing the same population and outcome were excluded. Separate reports from the same institution were retained only when they contributed distinct clinical scenarios, non-overlapping populations, or outcomes not reported in the more comprehensive dataset. The study-selection process was summarised using a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram [] (Fig. ).

Data were independently extracted by two reviewers using a standardised extraction framework. For each included study, the following information was collected where available: study characteristics, including first author, year of publication, country, institution, and study design; patient characteristics, including sample size, age, exstrophy phenotype, timing of reconstruction, and primary versus redo closure; pelvic characteristics, including pubic diastasis, pelvic rigidity or flexibility, and acetabular or other reported pelvic morphology; surgical variables, including osteotomy technique, reconstructive strategy, staging, and postoperative immobilisation; and clinical outcomes, including closure success, dehiscence, prolapse, fistula formation, reoperation, urinary outcomes, pelvic-floor findings, postoperative pubic approximation, gait, functional outcomes, quality of life, and complications.

Where outcome definitions differed between publications, the definitions used by the original study authors were retained rather than retrospectively standardised.

Methodological quality was assessed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by consensus.

Non-randomised studies were evaluated using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomised Studies (MINORS) []. The eight-item MINORS instrument was applied to non-comparative studies, with a maximum score of 16, and the 12-item instrument was applied to comparative studies, with a maximum score of 24.

Randomised controlled trials were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [], evaluating bias arising from the randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcomes, and selection of the reported result.

Methodological quality was not used as an exclusion criterion. Because MINORS does not provide formally validated categorical thresholds for study quality, individual domain scores and total scores were retained for transparent interpretation.

Formal meta-analysis was not undertaken because substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity was present across the included studies. Sources of heterogeneity included exstrophy phenotype, patient age, timing and type of reconstruction, primary versus repeat closure, pelvic morphology, osteotomy technique, postoperative immobilisation, outcome definitions, comparator selection, and duration of follow-up.

A structured qualitative synthesis was performed. Findings are presented in three strata: (A) CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported by the original authors, (B) CE-specific cohorts, and (C) a mixed cohort without separable phenotype-specific outcomes. This descriptive presentation is not a formal subgroup analysis. Within each stratum, findings were organised by closure, timing, anatomy, function and complications. Aggregate mixed-cohort results were not attributed to either phenotype. No pooled or head-to-head comparison between CBE and CE was performed.

Particular attention was given to study design and methodological limitations when interpreting associations. Given the predominance of retrospective and non-randomised evidence, associations between osteotomy use and clinical outcomes were not interpreted as evidence of independent causal effects.

Following qualitative synthesis, recurring anatomical, biomechanical, and clinical variables reported across the included studies were integrated into the Exstrophy Osteotomy Decision Framework (EODF).

The framework first distinguishes CBE from CE and prioritises assessment by an experienced multidisciplinary exstrophy team. Separate pathways consider pelvic morphology, diastasis, malleability, prior surgery, anticipated closure tension and postoperative stabilisation. The CBE pathway allows discussion of selective osteotomy; the CE pathway addresses the more complex requirements for mobilisation, staging and stabilisation without importing the CBE pathway for closure without osteotomy.

The EODF is an author-derived, evidence-informed conceptual synthesis. It has not undergone prospective clinical validation, formal consensus development or evaluation of clinical impact. It is neither a guideline nor a validated prediction rule and cannot establish competence to undertake exstrophy reconstruction or replace referral and specialist judgement.

The systematic search identified 1,346 records across the three electronic databases: 268 from PubMed/MEDLINE, 541 from Embase, and 537 from Scopus. After removal of 709 duplicate records, 637 unique records underwent title and abstract screening. Of these, 573 were excluded, leaving 64 reports sought for full-text retrieval. Eight reports could not be retrieved, and 56 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility.

Forty-three reports were excluded after full-text assessment: 16 because of an ineligible study design or publication type, 12 because they did not provide extractable postoperative clinical outcome data, seven because of an ineligible population or intervention, five because they represented overlapping patient cohorts from the same institution, and three because the sample size did not meet the predefined eligibility threshold. Thirteen studies fulfilled all eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative evidence synthesis (Fig. ). No randomised trial directly comparing different pelvic osteotomy techniques was identified. One pilot randomised controlled trial compared complete primary repair performed with versus without anterior innominate osteotomy [].

The 13 studies comprising the formal evidence set were published between 2014 and 2026 and differed substantially in study design, population, reconstructive strategy, and outcome assessment. One study was a pilot randomised controlled trial [], six were non-randomised comparative studies [–, , , ], and six were non-comparative observational studies or clinical series [, , –, ]. Individual exstrophy cohorts ranged from 15 to 286 patients, although some publications reported closure events rather than unique patients and several institutional series covered long treatment periods.

Nine studies evaluated CBE or patients described more broadly as having bladder exstrophy [–, , –, ]. Where the original report used the broader label, phenotype classification was retained as reported rather than assuming that every patient had confirmed CBE. Three studies focused exclusively on CE [, , ]. One mixed cohort included 17 patients with bladder exstrophy and two with CE; its aggregate outcomes could not be reliably separated by phenotype []. These groups are presented separately throughout the synthesis.

The osteotomy techniques represented in the formal evidence set included posterior iliac, anterior innominate, combined anterior–posterior, oblique iliac, mini-open anterior, and bilateral obturator osteotomies. Considerable heterogeneity was also present in postoperative stabilisation, including external fixation, Buck’s or Bryant’s traction, and spica casting. Consequently, direct comparison between osteotomy techniques was limited by differences in case selection, reconstructive protocol, immobilisation, surgical era, and institutional experience. The single randomised study, reported by Aboul Ela et al. [], was judged to be at high overall risk of bias using RoB 2. The principal concern was missing outcome data: four of the 12 infants allocated to the osteotomy group developed bladder dehiscence before the planned 3-month postoperative MRI and were therefore excluded from the imaging comparison, whereas no corresponding loss occurred among the eight infants allocated to reconstruction without osteotomy. Additional concerns related to insufficient reporting of sequence generation and allocation concealment, inability to blind the intervention, absence of reported assessor blinding for MRI measurements, and lack of a prospectively registered analysis plan. Consequently, the primary postoperative MRI comparison was effectively based on eight patients per treatment arm.

Among the six non-randomised comparative studies, MINORS scores ranged from 10 to 14 of 24 (median, 12). None reported a prospective sample-size calculation or blinded endpoint assessment. Control groups were generally internal and non-randomised, and baseline equivalence was incompletely demonstrated. Several studies included patients treated over multiple decades, introducing important potential confounding by surgical era, institutional practice, osteotomy selection, and postoperative immobilisation. Prospective data collection was clearly documented in only one comparative study []. Detailed MINORS item-level scoring for the comparative studies is presented in Table .

The six non-comparative studies achieved MINORS scores ranging from 6 to 12 of 16 (median, 8). Prospective data collection was documented in two studies [, ], while blinded or otherwise unbiased endpoint assessment was generally absent. No non-comparative study reported prospective sample-size calculation, and complete reporting of loss to follow-up was uncommon. The administrative database study by Fendereski et al. [] was additionally limited by reliance on diagnostic and procedural coding without access to operative records. Detailed MINORS item-level scoring for the non-comparative studies is presented in Table .

Overall, methodological limitations prevent causal attribution of outcomes to osteotomy technique or immobilisation. Associations were interpreted descriptively. Table  presents the RoB 2 assessment of the pilot randomised trial.

The largest study of osteotomy-assisted primary closure in CBE was reported by Khandge et al. [], who evaluated 286 patients undergoing pelvic osteotomy during primary reconstruction, including 186 newborn and 100 delayed closures. Overall closure success was 75.2% (215/286), with a reported success rate of 68.3% (127/186) among newborn closures and 88.0% (88/100) among delayed closures. Outcomes varied substantially by treating centre: overall success was 96.3% at the authors’ institution compared with 62.1% among patients operated on at outside institutions. Bladder dehiscence was reported in 12.4% of newborn closures and 3.0% of delayed closures.

Among patients for whom the osteotomy type was available, no statistically significant difference between combined, posterior iliac, and anterior innominate approaches was demonstrated in the newborn subgroup, with reported closure success rates of 80.0%, 60.8%, and 71.4%, respectively. In delayed closures, corresponding success rates were 100%, 72.4%, and 93.8%, with a significant between-technique difference reported in the original study. However, the marked differences between the authors’ institution and outside hospitals, together with non-randomised procedure selection, limited attribution of these differences to osteotomy technique alone [].

Three smaller single-arm studies evaluated more targeted osteotomy techniques during CBE or bladder exstrophy reconstruction as reported. Giordano et al. [] reported 18 patients treated with bilateral oblique pelvic osteotomy and found no bladder-closure failure, abdominal wound dehiscence, or recurrent exstrophy during follow-up. Abol Oyoun et al. [] treated 28 infants with bilateral mini-open Salter-like anterior osteotomy followed by spica casting; complete tension-free pubic approximation was achieved in all patients, with no reported wound dehiscence, wound infection, nerve palsy, or perioperative haemorrhage. Faraj et al. [] reported 17 children requiring bilateral obturator osteotomy because pubic approximation could not be achieved without undue tension during radical soft-tissue mobilisation; no bladder dehiscence occurred during a median follow-up of 34 months, and no neurovascular, infectious, gait-related, or penile vascular complication was reported.

These series demonstrate technical feasibility and favourable closure outcomes for several contemporary osteotomy approaches but do not provide controlled evidence establishing equivalence or superiority between techniques.

The relationship between timing and osteotomy use in CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported was evaluated from two complementary perspectives.

In the Khandge et al. CBE cohort [], all included patients underwent osteotomy, allowing comparison between newborn and delayed closure but not evaluation of whether osteotomy itself was required at either age. Mean pre-closure pubic diastasis was 4.05 cm in the newborn group and 4.54 cm in the delayed group. At the authors’ institution, osteotomy was considered in patients older than 72 h, those with pubic diastasis greater than 4 cm, or those with a non-malleable pelvis on examination under anaesthesia; these criteria represented an institutional protocol rather than prospectively validated thresholds.

At a broader health-system level, Fendereski et al. [] identified 149 patients undergoing primary bladder exstrophy closure between 2012 and 2023 in the Epic Cosmos database. The overall median age at closure was 54 days. Whereas median age at closure was within the first week of life during four of the first five study years, it was at least 2 months during six of the final seven years, demonstrating a temporal shift toward delayed primary closure. Pelvic osteotomy was coded synchronously with closure in 52 patients (35%); 44 of these 52 osteotomies (85%) occurred in patients undergoing delayed closure. Nevertheless, only 44 of 94 patients (47%) undergoing closure after 7 days of age had a synchronous osteotomy code. Because the database did not provide sufficiently granular operative information and outcomes were not stratified according to validated osteotomy exposure, these data describe contemporary practice patterns rather than the effectiveness of osteotomy.

CBE imaging and bladder-exstrophy radiographic studies did not show that osseous approximation consistently restores normal pelvic-floor anatomy [, , ].

In the randomised pilot study by Aboul Ela et al. [], 20 infants with CBE undergoing complete primary repair were allocated to anterior innominate osteotomy (n = 12) or repair without osteotomy (n = 8). Four patients in the osteotomy group developed bladder dehiscence before postoperative MRI, leaving eight evaluable patients in each arm. Among those completing imaging, the pre-to-postoperative changes in most pelvic-floor MRI measurements did not differ significantly between groups. Posterior bladder-neck distance was the only reported measurement that was closer to normal anatomy in the osteotomy group. Thus, the trial did not demonstrate generalised MRI normalisation of pelvic-floor anatomy attributable to anterior osteotomy, although interpretation is substantially constrained by differential loss of one third of the randomised osteotomy arm.

Radiographic studies demonstrated substantial early reduction of pubic diastasis but also persistent or recurrent separation during growth. In the Giordano et al. series [], median preoperative pubic diastasis was 35.6 mm and was reduced to approximately 7 mm after oblique osteotomy and closure. Partial recurrent diastasis developed during the first 6 months, after which measurements stabilised; median diastasis at 2 years was 23.6 mm. All osteotomies united radiographically, without nonunion or pelvic asymmetry.

Abol Oyoun et al. [] likewise achieved complete intraoperative symphyseal approximation in all 28 infants. At a mean follow-up of 4.78 ± 3.09 years, interpubic and interischial distances increased with growth, including a strong correlation between interpubic and interischial distances (r = 0.833, p < 0.0001). These findings are consistent with continued pelvic growth and partial widening after initial reconstruction rather than permanent maintenance of complete pubic apposition.

Three studies of CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported used quantitative gait analysis [, , ]. They identified persistent kinematic abnormalities relative to control or normative data, while the independent contribution of osteotomy remained uncertain. These findings do not establish gait outcomes in CE.

Petrarca et al. [] evaluated 19 patients with bladder exstrophy, including six who had undergone pelvic osteotomy and 13 who had not, together with 25 healthy controls. All patients were independent walkers and none reported clinically limiting gait abnormalities or restrictions in daily activities. Nevertheless, instrumented gait analysis demonstrated alterations involving the trunk, pelvis, hip, knee, and foot, with reduced kinetic parameters compared with controls. The pattern of compensatory movement differed between osteotomy and non-osteotomy subgroups: patients treated with osteotomy demonstrated greater trunk and pelvic retroversion, pelvic rotation, hip adduction, and knee flexion, whereas different compensatory deviations predominated in those managed without osteotomy.

Broström et al. [] compared 15 children with bladder exstrophy with 19 controls using three-dimensional gait analysis. The exstrophy cohort demonstrated greater external foot progression, increased hip adduction during stance, greater knee valgus during swing, and lower ankle push-off power. Within the exstrophy cohort, children with a history of osteotomy showed greater knee valgus during much of stance, whereas pelvic and hip kinematics were less clearly differentiated by osteotomy status.

Bakır et al. [] evaluated 27 patients aged 12–33 years, including five with previous osteotomy. Compared with the non-osteotomy subgroup, those with previous osteotomy demonstrated greater posterior pelvic tilt (− 12.1 ± 3.5° vs. −7.8 ± 2.9°, p = 0.01) and greater pelvic obliquity during swing (5.4 ± 2.1° vs. 2.7 ± 1.4°, p = 0.02). Mean residual pubic diastasis was numerically smaller after osteotomy (68.6 ± 24.4 mm vs. 81.4 ± 20.9 mm) but the difference was not statistically significant. Pubic diastasis correlated with several trunk and pelvic rotation parameters. Despite these measurable abnormalities, participants did not report limitations in daily activities, school attendance, or recreational participation.

Taken together, these gait studies consistently identified persistent biomechanical deviations after reconstruction but did not demonstrate that osteotomy restores normal gait. Conversely, the presence of measurable gait deviations was not consistently associated with clinically apparent functional disability. No CE-specific instrumented gait study was included.

In CBE or bladder-exstrophy series, reported orthopaedic morbidity was generally low, but small samples and incomplete adverse-event reporting limit estimates of uncommon complications. These rates should not be assumed to apply to CE.

In the largest CBE osteotomy cohort, Khandge et al. [] reported orthopaedic complications in five of 286 patients (1.7%), with no clinically meaningful difference between newborn and delayed reconstruction. Reported events included superficial pin-site infection, transient nerve palsy/foot drop, and hardware-related injury; only one patient required operative treatment, and the transient neurological deficit resolved without long-term sequelae.

No wound infection, nerve palsy, major haemorrhage, or other orthopaedic complication was reported in the 28-patient mini-open anterior osteotomy series []. Similarly, Faraj et al. [] observed no neurovascular obturator injury, infection, clinically evident gait abnormality, or abnormal ossification during a median follow-up of 34 months. Giordano et al. [] reported normal osteotomy union in all evaluated patients, with no infection, leg-length discrepancy, lower-limb axis abnormality, walking difficulty, or pain at the osteotomy site.

The randomised study by Aboul Ela et al. [] represents an important exception to the otherwise favourable complication reporting: bladder dehiscence occurred before 3-month follow-up in four of 12 infants randomised to osteotomy and in none of eight allocated to repair without osteotomy. Because of the pilot sample size, baseline imbalance, and high risk of bias, this finding cannot establish increased risk attributable to osteotomy, but it should not be omitted from the synthesis.

The three CE-specific studies addressed primary closure and complex reclosure [, , ]. Their results are presented separately from CBE because of different anatomy, reconstructive complexity and associated management. All three were retrospective reports from the same referral-centre database, with possible residual participant overlap and substantial centre and era effects.

Haney et al. [] evaluated 122 patients undergoing primary CE closure. In unadjusted analysis, successful closure occurred in 77.6% of procedures performed with any osteotomy compared with 41.7% without osteotomy (p = 0.007). Success rates differed according to osteotomy approach, reaching 90.0% after combined osteotomy, 76.2% after posterior osteotomy, and 60.9% after anterior osteotomy (univariate p < 0.001). Multistage reconstruction was also associated with greater closure success than single-stage reconstruction (77.4% vs. 45.7%; p = 0.001). Importantly, however, osteotomy itself was not independently associated with closure success in the multivariable model (p = 0.473), and osteotomy type likewise did not remain significant after adjustment (p = 0.272). In contrast, postoperative immobilisation remained independently associated with closure outcome in the multivariable analysis (p < 0.001). These findings indicate substantial confounding by era, institutional practice, staging, and stabilisation strategy.

Heap et al. [] examined 59 CE closure procedures in 56 patients selected because closure had been performed without osteotomy and/or conventional pelvic or lower-extremity immobilisation. Overall, 37 of 59 closure procedures (63%) ultimately failed. Failures consisted of bladder dehiscence in 14 cases, prolapse in 19, and both dehiscence and prolapse in four. Most procedures (93.2%) were performed without osteotomy. Lower-extremity immobilisation alone was used in 43 of 59 procedures, of which 37% were successful. Median pre-closure pubic diastasis was 6 cm (interquartile range, 4.8–8 cm), and the median number of closure attempts was two. Because only four procedures included osteotomy and treatment strategies were heterogeneous, the study primarily describes outcomes in a selected cohort lacking conventional biomechanical stabilisation rather than providing a balanced direct comparison of osteotomy versus no osteotomy.

The importance of pelvic mobilisation was also examined in secondary CE reconstruction. Crigger et al. [] evaluated 35 secondary closures, of which 19 were successful and 16 failed. Primary and repeat osteotomy were associated with secondary closure success, whereas secondary closure without osteotomy was more frequently associated with failure (p = 0.02). Combined vertical and transverse anterior innominate osteotomy was more frequently represented among successful secondary closures, whereas posterior iliac osteotomy alone was more frequently observed among failures (p = 0.02). Buck’s traction combined with external fixation was likewise associated with successful closure, whereas spica casting was more frequent among failed procedures (p = 0.02). Closure success also differed substantially by institution (p = 0.0016), reinforcing the likely influence of centre-specific expertise and management protocols.

Among CE patients studied by Heap et al. [], 31 of 56 patients (55.4%) achieved more than 3 h of daytime dryness according to the study definition of social continence. However, all socially continent patients emptied through a catheterisable outlet or equivalent reconstruction rather than demonstrating continence attributable to pelvic reconstruction alone. These data therefore provide limited information regarding a direct relationship between osteotomy and urinary continence.

No included study established an independent effect of osteotomy on long-term urinary continence in either phenotype. The CBE pilot trial assessed pelvic-floor imaging rather than long-term continence [], whereas the CE continence data arose from patients with catheterisable or reconstructed outlets [].

Kurniawan et al. [] reported 19 children, including 17 with bladder exstrophy and two with CE. The following aggregate findings are retained as mixed-cohort evidence and are not assigned to either phenotype.

Kurniawan et al. [] reported a median pubic approximation percentage of 78.5% in 19 children following innominate osteotomy. Older age at surgery correlated with greater postoperative diastasis (r = 0.469, p = 0.043) and a lower pubic approximation percentage (r = − 0.770, p = 0.009). However, this was a small, heterogeneous single-centre cohort without a non-osteotomy control group.

Kurniawan et al. [] reported a mean postoperative Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 score of 97.2 ± 1.6 among 19 children who had undergone pelvic osteotomy. The authors identified associations between age at surgery, postoperative diastasis, pubic approximation, and functional outcome; however, the absence of a matched non-osteotomy comparator and the small heterogeneous cohort precluded attribution of high quality-of-life scores to osteotomy itself. The absence of separable phenotype-specific estimates also prevents conclusions about CE quality of life.

Kurniawan et al. [] reported skin irritation in two of 19 patients and pin-tract infection in two of 19. These findings emphasise that the type of postoperative stabilisation contributes to morbidity in addition to the osteotomy itself. Because the cohort was mixed, these event counts cannot define a phenotype-specific complication rate.

In CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported, osteotomy was used during newborn and delayed closure; institutional selection incorporated diastasis and pelvic malleability [, ]. These studies do not establish that osteotomy is required at a particular age. In CE, the evidence concerns complex primary reconstruction and reclosure, with osteotomy closely linked to staging, fixation and immobilisation [, , ]. CE findings do not establish an osteotomy indication for CBE reclosure.

The available evidence did not establish a single osteotomy technique as superior across all reconstructive settings. Differences in reported closure rates between posterior, anterior, combined, oblique, mini-open, and obturator approaches were derived from non-randomised populations with substantial differences in age, phenotype, centre, surgical era, indication, and postoperative stabilisation. In CE cohorts in particular, osteotomy choice frequently co-varied with staging strategy, external fixation, traction, and institutional experience [, ].

The EODF therefore begins with separate CBE and CE pathways. Within each, it considers reconstructive history, age, diastasis, pelvic malleability, anticipated approximation tension and stabilisation. The framework assigns no validated numerical threshold and no universally preferred technique. Referral and multidisciplinary review precede technical selection.

The findings support separate clinical interpretations. In CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported, osteotomy-assisted primary closure was feasible in newborn and delayed settings, and small series described pelvic mobilisation when approximation remained difficult [, , , ]. These observations do not establish superiority over closure without osteotomy. In CE, retrospective studies associated aspects of osteotomy, staging and immobilisation with primary or repeat closure outcome, but independent osteotomy benefit remained uncertain [, , ]. The indications and reported outcomes of these two populations should not be treated as interchangeable.

No single osteotomy technique showed consistent superiority within either evidence stratum. Differences between approaches were confounded by anatomy, prior surgery, era, centre and stabilisation strategy [, , –, ]. The CBE pilot trial did not demonstrate generalised pelvic-floor normalisation [], and the bladder-exstrophy gait studies found persistent biomechanical deviations [, , ]. These functional findings cannot be generalised to CE, for which comparable evidence was lacking.

Accordingly, pelvic osteotomy should be interpreted primarily as a context-dependent mechanical intervention within a broader reconstructive pathway, rather than as an isolated procedure independently determining long-term urological or orthopaedic outcome.

The biomechanical rationale for osteotomy is compelling. The exstrophy pelvis is widened and externally rotated, increasing the distance across which the bladder, abdominal wall, and pelvic floor must be approximated. By mobilising the pelvic ring, osteotomy can facilitate medial displacement of the pubic bones and reduce tension on the reconstructed soft tissues.

For CBE, Khandge et al. reported osteotomy-assisted closure in newborn and delayed reconstruction, but their cohort contained no group treated without osteotomy []. The study therefore informs feasibility and treatment context rather than the independent effectiveness of osteotomy.

For CE, Haney et al. reported higher unadjusted closure success with osteotomy, but the association did not persist after multivariable adjustment, whereas immobilisation remained significant []. Heap et al. described frequent failure in a selected cohort lacking osteotomy and/or conventional immobilisation [], and Crigger et al. reported associations with osteotomy and stabilisation during reclosure []. These CE-specific observations concern a bundled reconstructive strategy; they cannot isolate the effect of osteotomy or establish superiority of a particular immobilisation method.

Osteotomy creates pelvic mobility, while fixation and postoperative immobilisation help maintain the achieved approximation during soft-tissue healing. Osteotomy alone should not be assumed to provide the postoperative stability required for healing. The osteotomy and stabilisation plan should therefore be considered together, with the method tailored to phenotype, pelvic mechanics and reconstructive complexity [–]. Comparisons based solely on osteotomy versus no osteotomy may obscure these linked interventions; the available observational data do not establish a universally superior immobilisation method.

In CBE, age has traditionally served as a surrogate for pelvic malleability. The observational evidence suggests that age should be interpreted alongside anatomy and the technical requirements of closure, rather than as an isolated indication.

Khandge et al. showed that osteotomy can be performed during both newborn and delayed CBE closure, while institutional indications incorporated not only age but also pubic diastasis and pelvic malleability []. Fendereski et al. demonstrated a contemporary shift toward delayed primary closure, yet fewer than half of delayed closures in their administrative cohort were accompanied by a synchronous osteotomy code [].

These CBE and bladder-exstrophy findings support considering diastasis, malleability, previous surgery and anticipated tension in addition to chronological age. Administrative patterns of osteotomy use do not establish which patients can safely undergo closure without osteotomy.

In CE, the included reclosure study addressed previously operated, complex anatomy []. Its associations should inform specialist discussion of CE reconstruction and should not be transferred directly to CBE reclosure. No included study defines a universal age, diastasis or rigidity threshold for either phenotype.

An anatomy- and mechanics-informed approach is therefore a conceptual organising principle, with phenotype-specific assessment and specialist judgement remaining essential.

The evolution of pelvic osteotomy should not be interpreted as a hierarchy of competing procedures. Rather, the available techniques provide different degrees and patterns of pelvic release.

In CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported, anterior, posterior, combined and oblique techniques have been used; mini-open anterior and obturator approaches have also been described in selected series [, , , ]. In CE, the comparative reports primarily concern anterior, posterior or combined osteotomy in complex primary or repeat reconstruction [, ]. The CBE series of more limited approaches do not establish their adequacy for CE.

The contemporary series describing these newer techniques report favourable early closure and complication profiles [, , ]. However, their small, non-comparative design precludes conclusions regarding equivalence or superiority. Absence of failure in a highly selected cohort of 17 or 28 patients cannot establish that a technique performs better than an established procedure, nor can such series reliably detect uncommon complications.

Likewise, higher closure success reported with combined osteotomy in selected cohorts should be interpreted cautiously [, , ]. Technique selection was strongly linked to anatomy, centre, surgical era, and immobilisation strategy, creating substantial confounding by indication and treatment period.

Technique selection should therefore address the mobility needed for the individual reconstruction within the relevant phenotype. The available evidence does not validate a hierarchy of limited, intermediate and extensive release or justify choosing a technique solely from historical closure percentages.

The CBE imaging and bladder-exstrophy gait evidence distinguishes anatomical approximation from restoration of normal function. Equivalent CE-specific functional evidence was not available.

The randomised pilot study by Aboul Ela et al. found no significant between-group difference in most postoperative pelvic-floor MRI measurements after complete primary repair with versus without anterior osteotomy; only posterior bladder-neck position was closer to normal in the osteotomy group []. Interpretation is limited by high risk of bias, particularly differential loss of four of 12 patients from the osteotomy arm following bladder dehiscence before postoperative MRI. Nevertheless, the study does not support the assumption that bony correction alone normalises pelvic-floor anatomy.

The gait literature leads to a similar conclusion. Petrarca et al., Broström et al., and Bakır et al. consistently identified persistent alterations in trunk, pelvic, hip, knee, or foot biomechanics after reconstruction [, , ]. Some parameters differed between patients treated with and without osteotomy, but these comparisons are highly susceptible to confounding by indication because patients selected for osteotomy may have had more severe baseline deformity.

Objective gait deviations did not consistently translate into clinically limiting disability in the bladder-exstrophy cohorts [, , ]. CBE or bladder-exstrophy radiographic series showed initial reduction followed by partial widening of the pubic gap during growth [, ]. The mixed-cohort findings [] are reported separately and cannot establish a CE-specific relationship between anatomy and function.

These findings argue against using radiographic pubic approximation or technically successful closure as surrogates for long-term function. Future assessment should distinguish reconstructive stability, anatomical correction, gait biomechanics, urinary function, and patient-reported outcome, as these domains may evolve independently.

The theoretical relationship between pelvic reconstruction and urinary continence is biologically plausible. Medialisation of the pelvic ring may improve the relationship between the bladder neck and pelvic-floor structures, potentially creating more favourable conditions for subsequent continence reconstruction.

For CBE, the randomised MRI study was not designed to test long-term continence []. For CE, the continence outcomes reported by Heap et al. involved catheterisable or reconstructed outlets and could not be attributed to osteotomy []. Neither evidence stratum establishes an independent continence benefit.

Continence in bladder exstrophy is multifactorial and depends on bladder capacity and compliance, outlet reconstruction, subsequent continence procedures, catheterisable channels, neurological factors, and long-term bladder development. Pelvic osteotomy should therefore not be presented as a continence procedure in itself.

The mechanical rationale for facilitating closure is better supported than an independent long-term urinary benefit, but the magnitude of benefit remains uncertain within each phenotype.

The main limitation is weak causal evidence within both phenotype strata. The CBE pilot trial was small and at high risk of bias []. Comparative observational studies had non-randomised allocation, incomplete baseline equivalence and substantial centre and era effects. The CE-specific evidence comprised three retrospective reports from one referral database, and no CE-specific randomised, pelvic-floor MRI or instrumented gait evidence was included. Small non-comparative studies could neither rank techniques nor reliably quantify uncommon harms.

Confounding by indication, centre and era is substantial. More complex pelves may receive more extensive osteotomy. Outcomes differed between specialist institutions and outside hospitals in the CBE and CE datasets [, ], but these associations do not isolate the effects of surgical volume, case mix, referral patterns or perioperative resources. Many cohorts also span decades during which staging, fixation and care changed together. No validated annual case-volume threshold or formal definition of a Centre of Excellence can be derived from these data.

Consequently, favourable outcomes associated with a particular osteotomy cannot reliably be attributed to that technique alone.

Future prospective multicentre research should analyse CBE and CE separately, distinguishing primary closure from reclosure. Standardised reporting should cover anatomy, malleability, indication and technique, fixation and immobilisation, centre experience, complications, closure definitions, continence, gait and patient-reported outcomes. Mixed cohorts should provide separable phenotype-specific estimates. The EODF additionally requires reproducibility testing, external validation and assessment of clinical impact before clinical recommendations can be based on it.

Because randomisation may be impractical in many reconstructive scenarios, carefully designed multicentre observational cohorts incorporating propensity-based or other causal-inference methods may provide the most realistic path toward stronger evidence.

Three-dimensional imaging and patient-specific modelling may also enable objective characterisation of pelvic deformity and ultimately permit decision-making based on measurable morphology rather than chronological age alone.

The present review also has limitations at the review level. The protocol was developed a priori but was not prospectively registered, and eligibility was restricted to English-language peer-reviewed publications, introducing potential language and publication bias. Formal assessment of publication bias was not considered informative because of the small number of studies, marked heterogeneity of designs and outcomes, and the absence of a quantitative meta-analysis. Despite explicit management of overlapping institutional cohorts during study selection, residual participant overlap across reports from high-volume referral centres cannot be completely excluded. Finally, the heterogeneity of exstrophy phenotypes, reconstructive strategies, osteotomy techniques, immobilisation protocols, outcome definitions, and follow-up precluded statistically meaningful pooling and necessarily limited the review to qualitative synthesis. Separating the presentation by phenotype improves clarity but does not remove within-stratum heterogeneity, referral bias or uncertainty in reports labelled only as bladder exstrophy. Aggregate findings from the mixed cohort cannot resolve phenotype-specific outcomes. Searches ended on 9 September 2026; later publications were not assessed.

CBE and CE should enter separate planning pathways. In CBE, the included studies describe selective osteotomy according to anatomy, pelvic mobility and anticipated closure tension; they do not prove that omission is safe for every apparently malleable pelvis [, , , ]. In CE, the greater reconstructive complexity warrants explicit specialist planning of pelvic mobilisation, staging and postoperative stabilisation [, , ]. The CBE pathway for considering closure without osteotomy is not a default option for CE, although the observational evidence also cannot establish a universal mandatory technique.

Referral of primary and repeat exstrophy reconstruction to experienced multidisciplinary Centres of Excellence should be prioritised whenever feasible. The institutional differences in CBE primary closure and CE reclosure reinforce this clinical priority, while remaining subject to case-mix and referral confounding [, ]. Such care requires coordinated paediatric urological and orthopaedic expertise together with perioperative resources for fixation, immobilisation and follow-up. The evidence reviewed does not define a numerical annual-volume threshold or prove that volume alone explains outcome differences.

Geographic, socioeconomic and health-system barriers may limit transfer. Where transfer is not feasible, early consultation and shared planning with a specialist centre should be sought, with explicit assessment of the local team and resources required for safe care. The EODF can structure that discussion by identifying the phenotype, previous reconstruction, pelvic mechanics and stabilisation plan. It cannot substitute for specialist training, justify complex reconstruction in an inadequately resourced setting or be assumed to improve outcomes in lower-volume practice.

Figure  presents separate CBE and CE pathways with referral and multidisciplinary review before technical planning. The framework organises concepts already used in specialist practice; its contribution is explicit presentation rather than a new proven treatment strategy. It is author-derived, has not undergone formal consensus development or prospective validation, and assigns neither numerical cut-offs nor a preferred osteotomy. Its clinical impact remains untested.

In CBE or bladder exstrophy as reported, pelvic osteotomy can facilitate mobilisation and pubic approximation during primary reconstruction. Selection should consider pelvic morphology, malleability, prior surgery and anticipated closure tension. The evidence does not establish a universally required age threshold or superiority over closure without osteotomy.

In CE, retrospective studies concern more complex primary and repeat reconstruction in which osteotomy, staging, fixation and immobilisation are closely linked. These findings support specialist assessment of the complete mechanical reconstruction plan but do not establish the independent effect of osteotomy or a universally superior technique. CBE treatment options and functional outcomes should not be extrapolated to CE.

Neither evidence stratum establishes that osteotomy independently improves long-term continence, normalises pelvic-floor anatomy or restores normal gait. Functional evidence is particularly limited for CE. Reported associations remain vulnerable to selection, centre and era effects, and mixed-cohort outcomes cannot provide phenotype-specific estimates.

Experienced multidisciplinary centres should be the preferred setting for primary and repeat exstrophy reconstruction whenever referral is feasible. In both pathways, the operative plan should address postoperative stabilisation and immobilisation as well as pelvic mobilisation. The EODF provides separate CBE and CE pathways for discussion and research; it is an unvalidated conceptual framework and cannot replace specialist judgement or the required infrastructure.

Prospective multicentre studies with separate CBE and CE analyses are needed to test osteotomy selection, stabilisation strategies and patient-centred outcomes, and to determine whether the proposed framework has clinical value.

medicine.title: The Evidence Journey in Patient‐Centered Medicine Development: Reflections on Recent Publications in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics
medicine.abstract: This Commentary highlights the evidence journey in patient‐centered medicine development: inter‐disciplinary innovations in quantitative methods for Probability of Success enabling rigorous decision‐making; decentralized clinical trials and implementation research enabling patient‐focused medicine development and deployment; and real‐world evidence, enabled by high‐quality data and advanced analytics, transforming decision‐making by regulators and health technology assessors. Multidisciplinary, cross‐sector collaboration and patient input are essential throughout the medicine lifecycle.
medicine.text:
Evidence on a medicine's quality, safety and efficacy/effectiveness is necessary to enable registration and inform its use in clinical practice. This Commentary highlights recent contributions published in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics relating to the evidence journey in the patient‐centered clinical development of medicines (Figure ).

Inter‐disciplinary innovations in quantitative methods for Probability of Success (PoS) are enabling rigorous decision making in clinical medicine development, thereby increasing the odds of regulatory approval and patient access, and enhancing sustainability of pharmaceutical research and development

In medicine development, late‐phase failures are most expensive in terms of costs and time. Moreover, patients enrolled in a late‐stage confirmatory trial are effectively not within the pool of potential participants for trial(s) of other investigational agent(s) in development for the same indication in the same timeframe. This makes it a responsibility in medicine development to prioritize progression of the most promising programs into pivotal clinical trials based on the totality of evidence.

Quantitative methods that explicitly incorporate available earlier phase and external data to forecast PoS enable principled decision making, including phase II to III go/no‐go decisions. PoS assessment is an opportunity for collaboration and intersectional innovation between the disciplines of clinical pharmacology, pharmacometrics, biostatistics, real‐world evidence, and data sciences. Two complementary scoping reviews by Cetinyurek Yavuz et al. and Jiang et al. review PoS methods to inform phase II to III go/no‐go decisions focusing on, respectively, (i) confirming efficacy and (ii) subsequent decision making in the medicine lifecycle. Efficacy‐based PoS methods with varying levels of complexity, depending on the extent of evidence available (e.g., single or multiple phase II trials from the same or different development program and with(out) data on the same endpoint) are available to developers. Beyond evaluating efficacy in a single phase III trial, different PoS definitions can be considered, including significance in multiple phase III trials, obtaining regulatory approval, market access/payer approval, return of investment, and outperforming competitors. Additionally, PoS calculations have been used to optimize clinical trial design and portfolio management, among others by informing sample size planning, interim analyses, and extended data collection in phase II trials. Interestingly, both reviews found that real‐world evidence (RWE), including evidence generated using data from routine clinical practice and registries, is hardly incorporated in PoS methods, despite the potential to identify the optimal target population, and provide additional evidence on efficacy and safety. Emerging approaches that make use of artificial intelligence/machine learning, the incorporation of patient preferences and RWE in future research will further optimize PoS calculations and accelerate medicine development through efficient use of all available data.

Decentralized clinical trials and implementation research are enabling patient‐focused medicine development and deployment, maximizing representativeness and adoption of emerging technologies like pharmacogenomics across diverse patient populations

Enrolling participants representative of the target population is needed to establish whether a medicine's benefit/risk as evaluated in clinical development translates into clinically meaningful outcomes and facilitates patient access. In medicine development and deployment, representativeness across many dimensions, including demographics, genetics, socioeconomic determinants of health, and healthcare system‐related factors, may affect successful implementation and subsequent population health outcomes.

Novel approaches to delivering clinical trials, such as decentralized clinical trial (DCTs) have the potential to, among others, reach a more diverse population compared with conventional approaches by bringing the clinical trial to the participant instead of the participant to the site. A series of recent tutorials detail “lessons learned during setup, regulatory submission, and conduct of RADIAL.” The RADIAL trial was designed to evaluate the impact of a methodological intervention (i.e., different levels of decentralization, including activities such as remote visits) on the feasibility and acceptability of DCTs. To ensure trial relevance and increase feasibility, input from patient representatives with lived experience was actively solicited through a Patient Expert Panel and a broader stakeholder panel. Experience with RADIAL suggests that clear communication on the trial relevance (in relation to the burden for sites and participants) may be particularly warranted for proof‐of‐concept clinical trials intended to evaluate trial methods, when the primary objective is not (directly) the evaluation of therapeutic benefit.

Next to increasing trial accessibility, capturing clinically relevant endpoints on how a patient survives, functions, or feels will ensure that a clinical trial is truly patient‐centric. In the context of rare diseases, clinical trial design is frequently impeded by a lack of well‐defined clinically meaningful endpoints because the natural history of disease is understudied. Poorly characterized natural history may furthermore challenge defining the target population, biomarkers, and external controls. Through the “totality of evidence” perspective, Chen et al. discuss potential approaches tailoring trial design to rare diseases, including prospectively planned adaptive designs, sequential multiple assignment randomized trials, unequal randomization ratios, and single‐arm trials with external controls. Real‐world data may furthermore be used to identify patients, targeting specific sites, thereby increasing trial feasibility and potentially broadening representativeness.

As we move to precision medicine, there is an increasing need to ensure the implementation of practice recommendations, including those for pharmacogenetic testing. Implementation trials intend to address barriers and facilitators to clinical implementation of evidence‐based interventions. These trials play an important role in establishing the usefulness of an intervention beyond medicine approval. Investigators of the PREPARE implementation trial share lessons learned for future implementation trials in an article by Guchelaar et al. PREPARE was a cluster‐randomized controlled crossover trial of a 12‐gene panel covering 50 variants with implications for the treatment with 39 medicines. The trial compared the effect of pharmacogenetic‐guided prescribing vs. treatment as usual on patient‐reported adverse drug reactions. The pragmatic design allowed for evaluating broad pharmacogenetic testing across healthcare systems in Europe. Nonetheless, imbalances between arms occurred due to the introduction of additional sites with varying treatment patterns after crossover and changing guidelines over time. Additionally, recruiting a diverse patient population proved challenging. Lessons from the RADIAL and PREPARE trials can help address these issues prospectively in future proof‐of‐concept and implementation trials, thereby advancing patient‐centered medicine development and deployment.

Real‐world evidence, enabled by high‐quality data and advanced analytics, is transforming decision making by both regulators and health technology assessors, ultimately enabling broad access to medicines globally

Beyond randomized controlled trials (RCTs), evidence frameworks are evolving to define the fit‐for‐purpose evidence required for regulatory and clinical decision making. Recent advances including the target trial emulation framework and incorporation of the estimand framework have improved the robustness and reporting transparency of observational studies. Explicitly defining the clinical question and emulating RCT components including the intervention, comparator, eligibility, outcome, and intercurrent events can help mitigate bias and may facilitate the integration of evidence from RCTs and RWE.

The use of detailed individual case safety reports and electronic healthcare databases to characterize a medicine's safety profile is well established. The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS, currently consolidated into the FDA Adverse Event Monitoring System, AEMS) holds data of individual case safety reports reported by the pharmaceutical industry and “members of the public” (including patients and healthcare professionals) and is frequently used for pharmacovigilance studies. Khouri et al. have cautioned that the broad availability of adverse event repositories, whether or not in combination with artificial intelligence tools, has led to an increase in low‐quality studies on false‐positive associations. Specifically, the authors caution against misinterpreting safety signals identified through disproportionality analyses as evidence for causality. The 10‐step guide on how to study FAERS data by Potter and colleagues is a useful tool to address these concerns and appropriately evaluate safety signals.

Recent publications describe how RWE has also been used to support regulatory decision making on medicines' efficacy profile. For example, Candore et al. have reported on the use of RWE for efficacy by reviewing submissions of 15 products to regulatory and health technology assessment (HTA) organizations from North America, Europe, and Australia, and Asano et al. have described the PDMA perspective on eight cases in which efficacy evaluations included external control arms. Across these articles, we find that RWE to study medicine efficacy has been used for regulatory decision making across geographical regions, albeit to a limited extent. RWE has been used primarily in medicines with an orphan designation when an RCT is considered infeasible and mostly using dedicated registries. International initiatives on the use of RWE to inform decision making on the medicine's effectiveness, including the ICH E23 guideline, will be important to move toward global regulatory harmonization.

After a medicine is registered, broad patient access and appropriate implementation, considering differences in healthcare systems and routine medical practice settings, ensures the medicine's potential can be maximized. Recently, Emond and colleagues have discussed case studies in which regulatory and downstream HTA evidence needs are not aligned. Divergence stems from, among others, a lack of patient‐centered, clinically relevant primary outcomes in confirmatory trials, and the use of small or uncontrolled trials. Policy solutions include pricing agreements reflecting uncertainty, and outcome‐based contracts, which require the incorporation of high‐quality RWE. Although evidence standards of medicines addressing unmet needs in (ultra)rare diseases may require different approaches to evidence generation, the evidence needs of all involved stakeholders, including regulators, health technology assessors, and prescribers, should be considered.

Several overarching patterns can be distilled from the articles highlighted in this commentary. First, the need for multidisciplinary, cross‐sector collaboration is apparent throughout the medicine lifecycle. Many of the highlighted papers originated from public‐private collaborations, demonstrating that advancing patient‐centered medicine development and employment requires collaboration across academia, industry, regulators, patients, and healthcare professionals. Relatedly, there is a need to share experiences across stakeholders. This is exemplified by the scoping reviews on PoS methods,,  tutorials on trial design and delivery,,  and discussion of regulatory and HTA decision making., ,  Global regulatory harmonization positioning the use of RWE and considering downstream decision making will be important moving forward. Throughout the medicine's lifecycle, it will be essential to incorporate patient input, ensuring broad access to medicines that are developed to serve those who need them.

The ideas outlined in this commentary and the highlighted articles published in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics nicely align with the scope of the American Society for Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics' Development, Regulatory & Outcomes network (https://www.ascpt.org/Member‐Services/Networks‐and‐Communities/Development‐Regulatory‐Outcomes). This network's activities take place across the discovery, development, regulation, and utilization continuum with a strong emphasis on scientific innovation, regulatory science, and clinical implementation. By bridging these fields and working together, we can ensure that advances in therapeutics translate into meaningful health benefits for all populations.
