As Deputy Editor‐in‐Chief and Editor‐in‐Training for Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics, Karthik Venkatakrishnan and Amos J. de Jong were not involved in the review or decision making processes for this work. Generative artificial intelligence was used to assist with an initial categorization of key articles, refining the text, and drafting the Figure. The authors retain full responsibility for the ideas and final content of this manuscript.

medicine.title: Functional outcomes in pediatric colorectal surgery: a predictor-based analysis of Hirschsprung disease and anorectal malformation in a resource-limited setting
medicine.abstract: Long-term fecal continence and bowel habit outcomes remain a significant challenge in pediatric colorectal surgery. This study evaluated long-term functional bowel outcomes in patients treated for Hirschsprung disease (HD) and Anorectal Malformations (ARM) using the standardized Rintala Bowel Function Score, identifying key clinical predictors of favorable outcomes.A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at St. Paul’s Hospital Millennium Medical College, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, among children who underwent definitive surgical repair for HD and ARM between January 2018 and December 2022. Functional bowel outcomes were evaluated using the Rintala Bowel Function Score (0–20 scale), with a score ≥ 17 defined as a clinically favorable outcome. Multivariable logistic regression was utilized to assess predictive factors.A total of 136 patients were included: 94 with HD and 42 with ARM. In the HD cohort, the presence of associated congenital anomalies and colonic excision proximal to the splenic flexure were major negative predictors of bowel function, reducing the probability of a favorable outcome from 66 to 22% (p = 0.007) and from 75 to 28% (p = 0.008), respectively. In the ARM cohort, 100% of patients with low-severity malformations achieved favorable outcomes compared with 54.5% of those with high/intermediate-severity malformations (p = 0.004).While anatomical severity appears to be an important factor influencing bowel function outcomes in ARM, associated systemic anomalies and the extent of colonic excision were also associated with poorer bowel function in children with HD. These findings highlight the potential importance of structured, long-term postoperative follow-up, with particular attention to children at higher risk of functional bowel problems.
medicine.text:
Hirschsprung disease (HD) and anorectal malformations (ARM) are major congenital colorectal disorders requiring specialized surgical management during infancy and childhood. Advances in operative techniques including transanal and laparoscopic-assisted pull-through procedures for HD and posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP) for ARM have markedly improved survival and anatomical reconstruction [–]. However, anatomical correction does not necessarily guarantee normal long-term bowel function. Children frequently experience persistent constipation, fecal soiling or incontinence, obstructive symptoms, and recurrent Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC), all of which adversely affect quality of life, social participation, and psychological well-being [–]. Systematic assessment of functional outcomes has therefore become an essential component of contemporary pediatric colorectal care.

Postoperative bowel function is influenced by a complex interaction of disease-specific, anatomical, surgical, and developmental factors. In HD, functional outcomes depend on the extent of aganglionosis, length of resected bowel, residual proximal colonic dysmotility, internal anal sphincter dysfunction, postoperative obstructive symptoms, HAEC episodes, timing of diagnosis and repair, and coexisting anomalies [, ]. In ARM, outcome is strongly tied to initial anatomical configuration, including malformation type and level, sphincter complex and pelvic musculature development, sacral anatomy, and associated spinal or urological defects [–]. Although children with less complex malformations frequently achieve satisfactory continence, those with complex defects remain at high risk for severe constipation, soiling, and fecal incontinence, reflecting interactions among anatomical severity, associated conditions, surgical factors, and postoperative management rather than operative technique alone [, –].

Associated congenital anomalies are particularly influential. ARM frequently co-occurs with genitourinary, vertebral, spinal, and cardiac defects, whereas HD is associated with chromosomal and syndromic conditions, notably Down syndrome [, –]. These coexisting abnormalities can impair neuromuscular development, pelvic floor function, and intestinal motility, compounding long-term bowel dysfunction—an association particularly vital to define where routine multidisciplinary follow-up is unavailable.

In resource-limited settings like Ethiopia, these management challenges are amplified by delayed presentation, restricted surgical access, financial and geographical barriers, inconsistent follow-up, and a lack of structured bowel-management programs. Predictors identified in high-resource systems may not fully capture the impact of late diagnosis and constrained post-discharge care, yet published data from such regions remain scarce.

Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate bowel function following definitive surgical repair of HD and ARM at a tertiary pediatric surgical center in Ethiopia and identify clinical and anatomical factors associated with favorable outcomes. Specifically, we evaluated the relationship of age at assessment, clinical presentation, anatomical severity, extent of colonic excision, and associated congenital anomalies with long-term bowel function measured by the Rintala bowel function score (Rintala BFS).

This single-center, retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted in the Pediatric Surgery Unit of St. Paul’s Hospital Millennium Medical College (SPHMMC) in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Eligible participants were children who underwent definitive surgical repair for Hirschsprung disease (pull-through procedure) or anorectal malformation (anoplasty/PSARP) at SPHMMC between January 2018 and December 2022, were aged ≥ 3 years at the time of evaluation, and were at least 6 months post-definitive surgery. Patients were excluded if their medical charts were missing or contained ≥ 15% unavailable study data, or if caregivers could not be contacted for the evaluation.

Eligible cases were identified from clinical and operative records. Data were collected through medical chart reviews and structured parental interviews (conducted either in-person during outpatient clinic visits or by telephone) administered by three trained physicians using a standardized questionnaire. The Rintala Bowel Function Score and recorded age represented the child’s status at the cross-sectional study assessment date rather than at a fixed postoperative interval.

Ethical approval was granted by the SPHMMC Research Directorate (approval number: PM23/112), and the study was conducted in accordance with international ethical standards for research involving human participants.

Bowel function was assessed using the Rintala Bowel Function Score, a widely used seven-item standardized measure of bowel function in children following colorectal surgery []. The Rintala BFS assesses the ability to hold back defecation, awareness of the urge to defecate, frequency of defecation, fecal soiling, fecal accidents, constipation, and social impact related to bowel dysfunction. The total score ranges from 0 to 20, with higher scores indicating better bowel function. Consistent with commonly used definitions in the pediatric colorectal literature, a Rintala BFS of ≥ 17 was considered a favorable bowel function outcome, whereas a score of ≤ 16 was considered an unfavorable outcome.

The primary outcome variable was bowel function categorized according to the Rintala BFS as favorable (≥ 17) or unfavorable (≤ 16). In addition, the total Rintala BFS was analyzed as a continuous outcome in the assessment of the relationship between age and bowel function.

For HD, the principal explanatory variables included associated congenital anomalies, clinical presentation, history of postoperative Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, and extent of colonic resection. Associated congenital anomalies were recorded as a binary variable and included documented cardiac, renal, gastrointestinal, chromosomal, or other congenital abnormalities. Clinical presentation was categorized according to the timing of presentation, distinguishing neonatal presentation from presentation after the neonatal period. The extent of colonic resection was categorized according to whether the resection extended proximal to the splenic flexure.

For ARM, explanatory variables included ARM anatomical severity, associated congenital anomalies, and age at the time of bowel function assessment. ARM severity was categorized as low or high/intermediate according to the anatomical level and type of fistula. Low ARM included perineal and vestibular fistula, whereas high/intermediate ARM included recto urethral fistula, rectovesical fistula, and cloacal malformations. Associated congenital anomalies were recorded separately based on the documented clinical diagnosis.

Demographic and clinical variables, including age at Rintala BFS assessment and sex, were obtained from medical records. Postoperative clinical information, including constipation, enterocolitis, and fecal incontinence, was obtained from the medical record and parental interview where applicable.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient demographics. Continuous variables (such as age and total Rintala BFS) were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U tests due to non-normal distributions. Categorical outcomes were compared using Chi-square or Fisher’s Exact tests.

Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed separately for each cohort to calculate Odds Ratios (OR) and 95% Confidence Intervals (CI) for achieving a favorable bowel outcome (≥ 17). Linear regression was used to evaluate the correlation between age at follow up and total bowel score. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. All analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.

During the study period from January 2018 to December 2022, 155 children underwent definitive surgical treatment for Hirschsprung disease or anorectal malformation at SPHMMC. Eight patients were younger than 3 years at the time of assessment and seven had undergone definitive surgery within the preceding 6 months; these 15 patients were excluded. The remaining 140 patients were eligible for data collection. Among these, one patient’s medical chart was unavailable and three patients had incomplete charts and/or were inaccessible by telephone for completion of the assessment. A total of 136 patients were therefore included in the final analysis, comprising 94 children with HD and 42 with ARM (Fig. ).

The age at definitive surgical intervention ranged from 7 months to 6 years in the HD group, with a median of 1.8 years (IQR, 1.1–3.2), and from 1 day to 7 years in the ARM group, with a median of 2 years (IQR, 1.2–2.8).

The median age at the time of bowel function assessment was 4.0 years (IQR, 3.5–5.0) for children with HD and 3.45 years (IQR, 3.1–3.95) for children with ARM. The overall age range was 3–10 years.

In the HD group, 71 (75.5%) patients were male and 23 (24.5%) were female, whereas the ARM group included 23 (54.8%) males and 19 (45.2%) females (Table ).

Among the HD patients (N = 94), the presence of associated congenital anomalies emerged as a major factor associated with long-term functional impairment. Patients without associated anomalies achieved a median Rintala BFS of 17 (IQR 14–19), with 66% achieving a favorable outcome, whereas those with associated anomalies had a significantly lower median Rintala BFS of 11 (IQR 8–15), with only 22% achieving a favorable outcome. On multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, presentation, and surgical extent, the presence of associated anomalies remained an independent negative predictor, reducing the odds of achieving a favorable bowel outcome by 85% (adjusted OR [aOR]: 0.15, 95% CI: 0.04–0.60, p = 0.007) (Table ).

The extent of colonic excision was another critical factor associated with long-term bowel function in HD. Patients who underwent colonic excision distal to the splenic flexure achieved a median Rintala BFS of 17 (IQR 13–20), with 75% achieving a favorable outcome, compared with a median score of 10 (IQR 6–14) and a favorable outcome rate of 28% among those with colonic excision proximal to the splenic flexure. On multivariable analysis, colonic excision proximal to the splenic flexure was independently associated with significantly lower odds of a favorable outcome (aOR: 0.14, 95% CI: 0.03–0.58, p = 0.008) (Table ).

Among the ARM patients (N = 42), the anatomical configuration of the initial defect was the dominant factor dictating long-term functional status. In the low-severity subgroup, 100% of patients achieved a favorable outcome with a median Rintala BFS of 18 (IQR 17–19), whereas 54.5% of patients in the high/intermediate-severity subgroup achieved a favorable outcome, with a wider score distribution and a median score of 17 (IQR 14–19). To resolve quasi-complete separation resulting from the 100% success rate in the low-severity group, Firth’s penalized likelihood logistic regression was applied, confirming that low anatomical complexity was strongly and independently associated with higher odds of favorable long-term continence (aOR: 18.52, 95% CI: 2.14–412.50, p = 0.004) (Table ).

Linear regression models assessing the relationship between age at follow-up and total continuous Rintala BFS demonstrated relatively flat trajectories in both HD (B = 0.32, 95%CI: –0.29 to 0.93, p = 0.293) and ARM (B = 0.18, 95%,CI: –0.46 to 0.82, p = 0.575) patients (Table ).

The clinical management of long-term bowel dysfunction in pediatric colorectal patients requires a clear understanding of underlying prognostic factors []. Our study demonstrates that although children with Hirschsprung disease and anorectal malformations both experience postoperative bowel dysfunction, the factors associated with unfavorable functional outcomes differ fundamentally. In HD, the extent of colonic resection and presence of associated anomalies were paramount, whereas in ARM, anatomical severity was the dominant determinant. These findings align with the understanding that postoperative bowel function reflects both surgical adequacy and intrinsic neuromuscular and anatomical characteristics [, ]

In HD, the primary pathology is the absence of enteric ganglion cells within the distal bowel. Following resection of the aganglionic segment and pull-through of innervated colon, most children achieve satisfactory function []. However, our finding that colonic excision proximal to the splenic flexure was associated with poorer functional outcomes is biologically plausible and consistent with literature showing that extensive resection impairs function. Removing a substantial length of normoganglionic colon reduces reservoir capacity and alters stool transit, increasing constipation and soiling risks. Although the lower proportion of favorable outcomes in this subgroup highlights considering resection extent during follow-up, the limited sample size requires cautious interpretation and confirmation in larger cohorts.

Associated congenital anomalies also appeared to influence functional recovery in HD. Children without associated anomalies achieved markedly higher rates of favorable outcomes than those with coexisting conditions, supporting reports of compromised bowel function in syndromic HD, particularly Down syndrome []. Contributing mechanisms include generalized hypotonia, impaired pelvic floor coordination, developmental delay, and toilet-training difficulties. However, this association should not be viewed purely as a direct anomaly effect; co-occurring neuromuscular traits, disease severity, and barriers to long-term care also contribute. Consequently, children with syndromic HD require earlier individualized bowel-management plans and multidisciplinary developmental support [].

The pattern observed in ARM was different. In these patients, bowel function was shown to be associated with the anatomical severity of the malformation. Children with low-severity defects (e.g., perineal fistulas) generally possess well-developed pelvic floor structures and a preserved sphincter mechanism [], explaining the 100% favorable outcome rate observed in this subgroup consistent with studies showing near-normal continence after low-complexity repairs []. Conversely, intermediate- and high-severity malformations frequently involve sacral dysgenesis, sphincter hypoplasia, and disrupted anorectal sensation []. Poorer outcomes in these higher-severity groups reinforce that intrinsic anatomical substrates remain a principal determinant of continence post-reconstruction, as documented in long-term ARM cohorts [, ].

These disease-specific patterns carry direct practical implications. In HD, outcome is heavily influenced by disease extent, retained colonic length, and systemic conditions; in ARM, initial anatomy and sacral/pelvic floor preservation impose stronger constraints. Postoperative management cannot rely on an assumption of spontaneous recovery. Instead, early risk stratification based on diagnosis, anatomical complexity, resection extent, and associated anomalies should guide targeted, proactive bowel-management interventions.

Notably, developmental age at follow-up and presentation type were not significantly associated with favorable bowel outcomes. This indicates that postoperative dysfunction does not spontaneously resolve with chronological age alone. This observation suggests although functional recovery can progress during childhood with structured treatment, physiological maturation without active intervention is insufficient for achieving continence [, ]. While these cross-sectional findings do not imply that bowel control never improves with age, they emphasize that awaiting passive maturation without active management is clinically inadequate.

At our institution, children undergoing definitive repair for HD or ARM receive outpatient clinical follow-up to evaluate bowel habits, with persistent symptoms managed using dietary modification, laxatives, or enemas. However, systematic long-term follow-up presents substantial challenges. Unlike specialized colorectal centers in high-resource settings, access to multidisciplinary bowel-management clinics, standardized bowel diaries, and specialized irrigation equipment remains limited. Consequently, the transition from successful surgical reconstruction to sustained functional recovery is frequently compromised by inconsistent follow-up or delayed treatment.

These contextual factors directly interact with clinical risk factors. Children with extensive HD, associated anomalies, or complex ARM require prolonged, intensive bowel management. Yet, these families face the greatest barriers to repeated hospital visits, including geographic distance, transportation costs, financial hardship, and lost caregiver income. Limited access to sustained care amplifies the functional impacts of high-risk anatomy. Thus, resource-limited environments should not be viewed separately from clinical predictors, as constrained post-discharge care directly modifies the ability of high-risk children to achieve optimal functional recovery.

In Ethiopia, where families travel long distances to reach tertiary centers, maintaining regular follow-up is particularly difficult, and specialized irrigation supplies are scarce. These barriers delay the recognition and treatment of constipation, risking fecal retention, progressive megacolon, overflow soiling, and severe social morbidity [–]. The poorer outcomes observed among high-risk patients reflect both intrinsic disease severity and systemic difficulties in delivering prolonged supportive care.

Given the substantial socioeconomic toll of chronic fecal incontinence including family financial strain, social stigma, and school absenteeism [, ] a proactive, front-loaded approach to postoperative care is essential. Caregiver education, dietary counseling, structured laxative therapy, and early habit monitoring should begin during the immediate postoperative period. Establishing standardized, locally sustainable bowel-management pathways will help bridge the gap between surgical success and functional recovery, though prospective multicenter studies are needed to evaluate their long-term efficacy in low-resource settings.

This study has several limitations. Its retrospective design and reliance on parental recall for the Rintala questionnaire may have introduced recall bias and limited assessment of temporal relationships. Although the overall sample size was adequate for a single-center cohort, subgroup sizes were small after stratification by diagnosis, anatomical severity, extent of colonic resection, and associated anomalies, limiting the precision of subgroup estimates. Follow-up was also heterogeneous, with relatively short follow-up for some patients, and a single assessment may not capture changes in bowel function over time. Finally, the single-center setting may limit generalizability. Larger prospective multicenter studies with standardized and longer-term follow-up are needed to validate these findings.

Long-term functional bowel outcomes appear to be associated with different clinical factors in children with HD and ARM. In HD, greater extent of colonic excision and the presence of associated congenital anomalies were associated with less favorable bowel function outcomes, while in ARM, anatomical severity appeared to be an important factor influencing long-term continence. The lack of a clear association between developmental age and improvement in bowel function scores suggests that spontaneous improvement with increasing age should not be relied upon alone, and highlights the potential value of early, structured, and individualized bowel management and long-term postoperative follow-up.
