medicine.title: The human microbiome in non-communicable diseases: Mechanistic insights into dysbiosis, systemic inflammation, and precision therapeutics
medicine.abstract: The human microbiome contributes to immune regulation, metabolic homeostasis, epithelial barrier integrity, and inter-organ communication. This review integrates evidence from gut, oral, skin, and cervicovaginal microbiomes, focusing on epithelial barrier dysfunction, altered microbial metabolite signaling, innate immune activation, inflammatory signaling, immune dysregulation, and host–microbe interactions across non-communicable diseases and microbiome-based therapeutic approaches in these contexts. Collectively, current evidence suggests that dysbiosis may represent not only a disease-associated microbial signature but also a potential mechanistic contributor to disease development and progression, although substantial interindividual and disease-specific variability remains. Microbiome-based diagnostics, fecal microbiota transplantation, personalized nutrition, and microbial therapeutics show considerable translational potential; nevertheless, causal relationships and clinical efficacy remain insufficiently established for several applications. Future research should therefore prioritize rigorously designed interventional and longitudinal studies integrating multi-omics profiling with host genetics and immune phenotyping to establish causal mechanisms, identify reproducible biomarkers, and support the development of precision microbiome-based therapeutic strategies.
medicine.text:
The human host and its indigenous microbiota form an integrated ecological system in which host physiology is inseparable from microbial contributions. The gastrointestinal tract harbors more than 100 trillion microorganisms whose collective genomes encode approximately 3 million genes, substantially exceeding the roughly 23,000 genes present in the human genome []. Colonization by these microbial communities plays a critical role in immune maturation and in maintaining host homeostasis by balancing environmental antigen exposure with appropriate immune responsiveness. In genetically vulnerable individuals, disruption of this balance could impair immune, metabolic, and antimicrobial defense functions []. Beyond immune modulation, the gut microbiome contributes to the digestion of dietary substrates that would otherwise be indigestible to the human host. Dietary fiber intake can shape microbiome diversity and functional capacity by modulating fiber-degrading microbial pathways and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, thereby influencing host metabolic and inflammatory responses, although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely characterized [,]. Advances in culture-independent, high-throughput sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene have substantially expanded the characterization of the human microbiota beyond the limitations of conventional culture-dependent approaches. The 16S rRNA gene contains nine hypervariable regions (V1–V9) that facilitate bacterial taxonomic identification and community profiling without the need for cultivation. Using such molecular approaches, approximately 2,172 human-associated microbial species representing 12 phyla have been identified, with more than 93% belonging to the major phyla Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes. These analyses have also enabled the detection of less abundant or previously underrecognized taxa, including Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila) []. Microbiota composition develops dynamically and age-specifically over the life course; gestational age at birth influences microbial colonization. Preterm infants exhibit lower bacterial numbers and reduced abundance of Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium compared to full-term infants [,], early antibiotic exposure further disrupts colonization patterns []. By adulthood, compositional variability decreases, and Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, and Actinobacteria become more abundant than in adolescence, a pattern associated with increased Clostridium and Bifidobacterium, which can be linked to endocrine changes [,]. Microbial communities are highly compartmentalized according to anatomical niche. The skin harbors site-specific microbial populations enriched in taxa such as Actinobacteria, Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium, and Staphylococcus spp. The oral microbiome is predominantly composed of Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Actinobacteria, although their relative abundances vary substantially among individuals. In contrast, the vaginal microbiome generally exhibits lower microbial diversity and is frequently dominated by Lactobacillus spp []. Among these niches, the gut harbors the largest and most metabolically active microbial community, dominated by members of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, and Proteobacteria, and plays a central role in host metabolism, immune regulation, and systemic homeostasis []. Geographic origin is an independent determinant of microbiome composition, especially in the gut; Western populations show Firmicutes-enriched profiles, whereas non-Western and fiber-rich-diet populations show Prevotella/Bacteroidetes-enriched profiles, with African populations exhibiting a high level of gut microbial diversity [,]. Inter-site communication occurs through interconnected microbial–host axes, including the gut–skin, gut–brain, and gut–heart axes, where microbial metabolites, immune mediators, and host signaling pathways facilitate bidirectional interactions between microbial communities and distant organs [,]. Microbial dysbiosis can arise in response to multiple host and environmental factors, including antibiotic exposure, dietary habits, genetic background, mode of delivery at birth, and industrialized lifestyles. Such alterations in microbial community structure and function may disrupt metabolic homeostasis and immune regulation, thereby contributing to the development or progression of metabolic, dermatological, periodontal, neurological, cardiovascular, and oncological disorders [,]. Rather than treating these associations as a catalog of independent disease processes, this review organizes the mechanistic evidence around six convergent pathways-intestinal barrier dysfunction, microbial metabolites, innate immune activation, inflammatory signaling, immune dysregulation, and microbial-host interactions-that recur across diverse non-communicable diseases and provide the conceptual foundation for microbiome-based precision therapeutics as shown in .

A structured literature search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. No lower publication-date threshold was imposed, and studies published from database inception through 31 August 2026 were considered. Search strategies combined free-text keywords including “human microbiome,” “microbiota,” “dysbiosis,” “gut microbiome,” “oral microbiome,” “skin microbiome,” “cervicovaginal microbiome,” “non-communicable diseases,” “intestinal barrier dysfunction,” “microbial metabolites,” “short-chain fatty acids,” “TMAO,” “immune activation,” “inflammatory signaling,” “host–microbe interactions,” “microbiome therapeutics,” “fecal microbiota transplantation,” “probiotics,” “phage therapy,” and “precision microbiome medicine.” Boolean operators (AND/OR) were applied to refine retrieval. Peer-reviewed human, clinical, epidemiological, and mechanistically relevant experimental studies were included, whereas duplicate, non-peer-reviewed, and out-of-scope publications were excluded. Priority was given to studies providing strong mechanistic, clinical, or translational evidence.

The human microbiome is a complex ecological community of bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses that maintains dynamic symbiotic relationships with the host. The host provides nutrients and a stable physicochemical environment, and the resident microorganisms contribute to the digestion of dietary substrates, the production of bioactive metabolites, the maintenance of epithelial barrier integrity, and the maturation and regulation of host immunity [,]. Resident microbiota can also contribute to colonization resistance by producing ribosome-synthesized antimicrobial peptides, particularly bacteriocins, which may inhibit competing microorganisms through mechanisms including membrane disruption and interference with essential cellular processes [,]. A study of thuricin CD, produced by Bacillus thuringiensis, reported that it was purified and demonstrated potent in vitro activity against clinical Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) isolates. Similarly, bacteriocin 21, produced by Enterococcus faecalis, enhanced intestinal niche competition and promoted clearance of vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) in a mouse model [,]. Disruption of these protective functions can significantly increase host susceptibility to pathogen colonization and infection. Studies investigating host–microbe interactions indicate that certain bacterial infections may influence cardiovascular disease through direct or indirect molecular interactions with host genes and signaling pathways, extending beyond mechanisms mediated solely by microbial metabolites. Escherichia coli O157:H7 (E. coli O157:H7) gene interaction network analysis revealed human and bacterial gene pathways linked to host defense, bacterial survival, and processes related to cardiovascular disease, suggesting possible molecular targets for comprehending pathogen-associated CVD []. Similarly, in vivo administration of a single dose of clindamycin can cause persistent alterations in the murine intestinal microbiota and increased susceptibility to C. difficile colitis, highlighting the critical role of an intact gut microbiota in maintaining colonization resistance [].

Dysbiosis is not a single microbial state but encompasses several overlapping alterations, including the depletion of beneficial taxa, the expansion of pathobionts, and the loss of microbial diversity. Loss of beneficial organisms such as Bifidobacterium may reduce the availability of protective metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) []. Conversely, the expansion of facultative pathobionts, particularly members of the Enterobacteriaceae, can increase exposure to microbial-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) and can activate inflammatory pathways, including toll-like receptor signaling (TLR-4) []. Reduction in α-diversity may further weaken ecological competition and colonization resistance, thereby increasing susceptibility to pathogen expansion [,]. Dietary composition also represents another major determinant of intestinal microbial diversity, as experimental consumption of a high-fat and high-sugar diet altered the intestinal microbial community and was associated with changes in the relative abundance of major bacterial groups, which include Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes []. Early-life exposures can also influence microbiome assembly; for example, cesarean delivery can disrupt maternal-to-infant transmission of Bacteroides strains and increase colonization by opportunistic hospital-associated organisms, like Enterococcus, Enterobacter, and Klebsiella, as demonstrated by longitudinal metagenomic analysis of 596 infants []. Similarly, formula feeding reduces exposure to human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), which normally selectively support beneficial Bifidobacterium species, thereby influencing early microbial development [].

Infectious, pharmacological, and psychological exposures can further modify host-microbe interactions []. Acute gastrointestinal infections may produce persistent changes in microbial composition, epithelial barrier function, and mucosal immunity and are associated with an increased risk of post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome (PI-IBS). Meta-analytic evidence indicates approximately a fourfold increase in IBS risk following infectious enteritis, with severe infection, antibiotic exposure, and psychological distress acting as additional risk factors [,]. Psychological stress can also influence microbial composition and intestinal barrier function by activating the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. Experimental evidence demonstrates that microbial colonization directly regulates this stress-response system, as seen in an in vivo study with germ-free mice exhibiting exaggerated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and corticosterone responses to restraint stress, which were further normalized when followed by colonization with Bifidobacterium infantis, indicating that microbial exposure during early life contributes to appropriate HPA-axis development [].

The gut–brain axis provides a mechanistic example of how these microbial perturbations can extend beyond the intestine. This bidirectional neuroendocrine network integrates neural, endocrine, immune, and metabolic signals through the enteric and autonomic nervous systems (ANS), the HPA axis, and the central nervous system (CNS). Microbial metabolites, including SCFAs and tryptophan-derived compounds, can influence enteroendocrine, immune, neuronal, and blood–brain barrier functions [,]. In gnotobiotic mice, removing the gut microbiota increased c-Fos expression in sympathetic neurons outside the gut. In contrast, adding SCFA-producing bacteria reduced this neuronal activation. Further tracing experiments showed that gut microbes can influence the brain through a gut-vagus-brainstem-sympathetic pathway, suggesting that the microbiota can regulate the nervous system through this circuit []. Together with the HPA-axis findings described above, these observations demonstrate that alterations in the microbiota can influence both autonomic and neuroendocrine stress pathways. Aging and medication can also play a role; age-associated changes in intestinal physiology, immune function, and motility are accompanied by alterations in microbial composition, which include reductions in beneficial taxa and expansion of facultative anaerobic organisms such as members of the Proteobacteria []. Similarly, medication exposure can produce a similarly substantial change. In a population-based analysis of 1,815 individuals, proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) use was associated with alterations in approximately 20% of detected bacterial taxa and enrichment of the oral-associated microorganisms, including Enterococcus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and E. coli []. These findings illustrate that microbiome composition is shaped not only by disease but also by common environmental, developmental, behavioral, and pharmacological exposures.

Although the gut is the best-characterized microbial ecosystem, host-microbe interactions also occur across other epithelial and mucosal surfaces, where microbial communities contribute to tissue-specific barrier integrity and immune homeostasis. The oral microbiome, comprising hundreds of microbial taxa, is dominated by commensal genera including Streptococcus, Actinomyces, Veillonella, Rothia, and Neisseria, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic approaches []. Disruption of this community is associated with the expansion of periodontal pathogens, as evidenced by DNA hybridization studies that identified increased abundance of the periodontal “red complex” organisms, including Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, and Treponema denticola (T. denticola), at diseased periodontal sites []. Importantly, experimental evidence from Agathobacter rectalis (A. rectalis) indicates that oral dysbiosis can influence distant tissues; oral administration of P. gingivalis to mice induced intestinal dysbiosis and barrier dysfunction, accompanied by increased endotoxemia and dissemination of bacterial DNA to the liver, providing experimental support for an oral-gut-liver microbial axis []. The skin microbiome similarly exhibits strong anatomical niche specificity, with sebaceous sites enriched in Cutibacterium, moist regions enriched in Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus, and dry sites supporting more diverse environmental-associated communities []. Resident microorganisms also contribute directly to barrier defense, as human skin-derived Staphylococcus epidermidis (S. epidermidis) isolates produce phenol-soluble modulins and antimicrobial molecules that inhibit Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) growth, biofilm formation, and colonization, demonstrating that commensals can actively protect the epithelial surfaces against pathogens []. Similarly, in the cervicovaginal tract, reproductive age determines the vaginal communities, which are primarily dominated by Lactobacillus spp. and can be classified into distinct Community State Types (CSTs) that reflect different ecological configurations []. Lactobacillus-dominated communities contribute to mucosal homeostasis by maintaining an acidic vaginal environment, producing antimicrobial metabolites, and modulating host immune responses. Conversely, reduction in Lactobacillus abundance has been associated with HPV acquisition and persistence and cervical disease progression [].

These findings further illustrate how disruption of site-specific microbial communities can alter epithelial and immune homeostasis. Importantly, host-microbe interactions are not merely descriptive associations but can be therapeutically manipulated. Computational analysis of host-pathogen interactions at the molecular scale has revealed host proteins that could regulate intracellular bacterial infection. In silico analysis of the BAG3 interactome revealed interactions with host and pathogen proteins implicated in Legionellosis, tuberculosis, salmonellosis, shigellosis, and pertussis. Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase 8 (MAPK8), Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase 14 (MAPK14), Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase 1 (MAPK1), Heat Shock Protein Family D Member 1 (HSPD1), Nuclear Factor Kappa B Inhibitor Alpha (NFKBIA), Toll-Like Receptor 2 (TLR2), and Ras Homolog Family Member A (RHOA) were identified as possible therapeutic targets []. Similarly, in a clinical trial, patients with metastatic melanoma who were refractory to anti-PD-1 therapy responded to responder-derived fecal microbiota transplantation combined with reintroduction of anti-PD-1 treatment, resulting in significant clinical responses in a subset of patients, demonstrating that modification of the intestinal microbiota can enhance responsiveness to cancer immunotherapy. This provides clinical evidence that microbiome composition can function as a modifiable determinant of therapeutic efficacy and establishes a mechanistic bridge between microbial ecology, host immunity, and precision therapeutics [,].

To protect the host, the microbiome maintains a single-cell-thick epithelial barrier and its overlying mucus layer, preventing bacterial translocation into the circulation. The mucin-degrading commensal A. muciniphila contributes to mucus-layer turnover by utilizing mucin as a nutrient source, a process associated with the maintenance of mucus thickness and intestinal barrier function []. Several Lactobacillus species and strains can strengthen intestinal barrier function by increasing or restoring tight junction proteins, including claudins, occludin, and Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1), although the underlying signaling mechanisms are strain-specific and context-dependent []. Butyrate-producing bacteria such as Bifidobacterium strengthen these junctions and reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS) in colonocytes [,]. When intestinal barrier integrity is compromised, intestinal permeability may increase, a phenomenon often described informally as “leaky gut;” however, intestinal permeability is the more established physiological and experimental measure of barrier dysfunction. This enhanced permeability facilitates the translocation of MAMPs, including lipopolysaccharide (LPS), peptidoglycan, and flagellin, from the intestinal lumen into the systemic circulation. These microbial components activate pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs), thereby promoting systemic inflammatory responses that may contribute to pathological processes across multiple organ systems []. This loss of barrier integrity is a recurring feature across non-communicable diseases (NCDs). In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), genome-wide association studies have identified susceptibility loci involving genes that regulate microbial sensing, autophagy, immune signaling, and epithelial barrier homeostasis, including nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2), autophagy-related protein 16-like 1 (ATG16L1), and interleukin-23 receptor (IL23R) []. In genetically susceptible individuals, alterations in these pathways can impair mucosal barrier function and dysregulate immune responses to the commensal gut microbiota, thereby promoting chronic intestinal inflammation []. Similarly, in type 2 diabetes, alterations in the gut microbiome include reductions in several SCFA-producing bacteria, such as members of the Faecalibacterium and Roseburia genera. A reduction in butyrate-producing microbes may weaken epithelial barrier function, increase intestinal permeability, and facilitate the translocation of bacterial products such as LPS, which can contribute to inflammatory signaling in metabolic tissues []. This is also seen in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: the portal vein directly connects the intestine to the liver, but when the gut barrier is compromised, hepatocytes are continuously exposed to endotoxins and toxic microbial by-products [,]. This can also be understood as part of an oral–gut–liver axis in which swallowed oral pathogens, particularly P. gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), colonize the gut, compromise intestinal barrier integrity, and translocate to the liver via portal and systemic circulation []. Dysbiosis may also increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, and impaired intestinal barrier function may increase the systemic exposure to LPS and other microbial products, which may be a driving factor in vascular and endothelial inflammatory signaling []. Experimental studies have demonstrated that oral administration of P. gingivalis can alter the composition of the gut microbiota and modulate the intestinal trimethylamine (TMA)–trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) metabolic pathway, thereby providing further evidence of a functional oral–gut microbial axis. In heart failure, intestinal hypoperfusion and congestion may compromise gut barrier function, while clinical studies have demonstrated depletion and alteration of the core intestinal microbiota []. A parallel “leaky mouth” phenomenon has been described in periodontitis, a chronic polymicrobial infection in which periodontal epithelial damage allows bacterial components and inflammatory mediators to enter the bloodstream, a mechanism implicated in the association between periodontal disease and depression and anxiety []. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by immune-mediated damage to the central nervous system. Alterations in the gut microbiota, including reduced abundances of Bifidobacterium spp. and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (F. prausnitzii), have been reported in individuals with MS, although findings have varied across study cohorts []. Similarly, in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors and interests, gastrointestinal symptoms including constipation, diarrhea, and abdominal pain are frequently reported, and increased intestinal permeability has also been described in subsets of affected individuals . Beyond the gut, periodontal oral pathogens, including P. gingivalis, T. denticola, and F. nucleatum, have been linked to blood–brain barrier disruption, providing an additional route by which oral dysbiosis may contribute to neuroinflammatory disease [].

Anaerobic fermentation of dietary fiber by the gut microbiota produces SCFAs, primarily acetate, propionate, and butyrate, with total concentrations reaching approximately 70–140 mM in the proximal colon []. SCFAs provide a substantial proportion of the energy required by colonic epithelial cells, with butyrate serving as a major energy substrate for colonocytes and also modulating gene expression through inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs) [], SCFAs can additionally activate FFAR2/GPR43 and FFAR3/GPR41 on enteroendocrine cells, promoting PYY and GLP-1 secretion and thereby contributing to the regulation of satiety and glucose metabolism []. Propionate is largely taken up by the liver, where it serves as a gluconeogenic precursor and can also modulate hepatic lipid and glucose metabolism, including the suppression of cholesterol synthesis in experimental models [], while butyrate activates G-protein-coupled receptor 109A (GPR109A) on colonic macrophages to promote an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype and induces forkhead box P3-positive regulatory T cells (Foxp3+ regulatory T-cell) differentiation [], making SCFAs central mediators of both local mucosal protection, systemic, metabolic and immune homeostasis [].

Healthy colorectal homeostasis is associated with beneficial gut bacteria such as A. muciniphila and the butyrate-producing F. prausnitzii, whose metabolites can influence intestinal epithelial metabolism and homeostasis []. While F. prausnitzii-derived butyrate can inhibit histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) and promote forkhead box P3 (Foxp3) expression, thereby maintaining the Th17/Treg — T helper 17 cells / regulatory T cells (Th17/Treg) balance and supporting intestinal immune homeostasis []. In obesity, alterations in gut microbial composition and function have been associated with an increased capacity for dietary energy harvest, although the frequently reported elevation in the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio is not consistently observed across human studies []. In experimental models, gut microbiota-mediated suppression of fasting-induced adipose factor (FIAF) can increase lipoprotein lipase activity and promote triglyceride storage in adipose tissue []. In rodents, increased microbial acetate production has also been shown to activate the parasympathetic nervous system, increase ghrelin secretion, and promote hyperphagia and metabolic dysfunction []. Gut dysbiosis can contribute to hypertension, characterized by persistently elevated blood pressure and reduced abundance of acetate- and butyrate-producing bacteria, and experimental studies indicate that SCFAs regulate vascular tone and blood pressure through receptors such as GPR41. In GPR41-deficient mice, loss of this signaling was associated with isolated systolic hypertension, supporting a role for SCFA–GPR41 signaling in blood-pressure regulation. More broadly, SCFA signaling through receptors such as GPR41 contributes to vascular regulation, and disruption of the gut microbiota–SCFA axis may therefore contribute to vascular dysfunction and impaired blood-pressure control [,].

A second major microbial metabolite axis involves TMAO. Gut bacteria metabolize dietary phosphatidylcholine, choline, and L-carnitine to TMA, which is subsequently oxidized in the liver by flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3) to form TMAO [,]. Elevated TMAO has been associated with platelet hyperreactivity, increased thrombotic potential, vascular inflammation, and a greater risk of major adverse cardiovascular events. In heart failure, higher circulating TMAO concentrations have also been associated with disease severity and mortality []. Elevated TMAO can also promote platelet hyperreactivity, thrombotic potential, and vascular inflammation, and higher plasma TMAO is independently associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events [,,,]. Atherosclerosis is also associated with alterations in gut microbial composition, including enrichment of Collinsella and depletion of butyrate-producing genera such as Roseburia and Eubacterium in patients with symptomatic disease; however, the causal contribution of these specific taxa to TMAO-mediated atherogenesis remains incompletely defined []. Larger metagenomic studies have identified enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae, including Klebsiella spp. and Enterobacter, in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, although the mechanistic contribution of these taxa to TMAO production and cardiovascular pathology remains to be established []. In heart failure, elevated TMAO correlates with disease severity and mortality []. A similar conclusion can also be drawn from the oral-gut-heart axis, in which oral dysbiosis may also influence the TMA–TMAO axis. In ApoE−/− mice, experimental periodontitis induced by oral P. gingivalis increased circulating TMAO, altered the gut microbiota, increased hepatic FMO3 expression, and aggravated atherosclerotic lesions, suggesting that oral inflammation may promote cardiovascular pathology [].

A third important microbial metabolite pathway involves tryptophan metabolism. Under physiological conditions, gut microbes influence tryptophan availability and serotonergic signaling. During systemic inflammation, bacterial products such as LPS and pro-inflammatory cytokines can enhance indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) activity, promoting the conversion of tryptophan to kynurenine and potentially reducing its availability for serotonin biosynthesis []. Enhanced kynurenine pathway activity can alter the balance of neuroactive metabolites, including 3-hydroxykynurenine and quinolinic acid, potentially contributing to neuroinflammation, excitotoxic signaling, altered HPA axis activity, and impaired neuroplasticity. These changes may contribute to neuroinflammation, excitotoxic signaling, altered HPA-axis activity, and impaired neuroplasticity, processes that have been implicated in the pathophysiology of depressive disorders. An analogous shift from the serotonin to the kynurenine pathway in Alzheimer’s disease generates neurotoxic quinolinic and kynurenic acid that impair synaptic function and promote neurodegeneration []. The clinical relevance of serotonergic signaling is also evident in disorders of gut–brain interaction such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), in which serotonergic neuromodulation can influence visceral sensation, gastrointestinal motility, and central pain processing. Accordingly, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have shown modest benefits for abdominal pain and some global IBS symptoms in clinical trials, although their efficacy is less consistent than that of tricyclic antidepressants, and current guidelines do not recommend SSRIs as routine first-line pharmacological therapy for IBS [,]. In autism spectrum disorder (ASD), propionic acid (PPA), an SCFA produced by several gut bacteria including members of Clostridium, has been investigated as a potential microbiota-derived mediator of neurobehavioral abnormalities. Experimental studies indicate that elevated propionic acid (PPA) exposure can alter mitochondrial and cellular metabolism, promote neuroinflammatory responses, and produce social and behavioral abnormalities in animal models, although a causal role for PPA in human ASD remains unestablished [,].

In nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, certain hyperalcohol-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) strains generate endogenous ethanol sufficient to trigger fatty liver disease upon transplantation into mice []. Microbial conversion of choline to trimethylamine may also alter hepatic phosphatidylcholine availability and lipoprotein metabolism, providing another potential link between gut microbial metabolism and hepatic steatosis [].

Gut microbial β-glucuronidases can deconjugate estrogen glucuronides, potentially increasing enterohepatic estrogen reabsorption []. In cervical cancer, alterations in gut and cervicovaginal microbiome composition have been associated with clinical outcomes, although the mechanistic contribution of microbial estrogen metabolism remains uncertain []. In colorectal cancer, distinct microbial genotoxins and metabolites can contribute to epithelial damage. pks-positive E. coli and other Enterobacteriaceae produce colibactin, which induces DNA cross-links and double-strand breaks, while cytolethal distending toxin produced by certain Gram-negative bacteria causes DNA strand breaks [,]. Sulfate-reducing bacteria such as Desulfovibrio produce hydrogen sulfide, which has been implicated in inflammatory and genotoxic processes in colorectal disease, although its effects are concentration and context-dependent []. In gastric carcinogenesis, nitrate-reducing bacteria may contribute to the formation of carcinogenic N-nitroso compounds as gastric acidity decreases. In oral squamous cell carcinoma, dysbiotic oral microbial communities have similarly been associated with tumor-promoting inflammation and altered microbial metabolism. Candida albicans can metabolize ethanol to acetaldehyde, while other oral bacteria also contribute to acetaldehyde production; these microbial metabolites may promote DNA damage and disrupt cellular homeostasis [].

Early microbial exposure is a critical driver of maturation of the host’s innate immune system, including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and NOD-like receptors (NLRs), calibrating inflammatory pathways so that the immune system does not overreact to self-antigens or benign environmental triggers [,]. When intestinal permeability increases, LPS derived from Gram-negative bacteria binds the TLR4/MD-2 complex on macrophages, adipocytes, and other cells, activating the MyD88-dependent cascade. In mice, a high-fat diet increased circulating LPS concentrations approximately two- to threefold, while chronic LPS infusion reproduced several metabolic abnormalities associated with high-fat feeding, including insulin resistance and weight gain []. Persistent low-grade exposure to microbial products such as LPS may therefore contribute to chronic inflammatory signaling and metabolic dysfunction, including insulin resistance and adipose-tissue inflammation; associations with vascular and neuroinflammatory disorders are also increasingly recognized, although their causal contribution in humans remains incompletely defined [].

This pattern-recognition step recurs as the initiating event across NCDs. In gastric carcinogenesis, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) virulence factors CagA and VacA drive early innate activation and IL-8-mediated chemoattraction of inflammatory cells [,]. In experimental models of Alzheimer’s disease, LPS can activate microglial TLR4/CD14 signaling and promote neuroinflammatory responses, while altered TLR4 signaling can influence microglial Aβ clearance and amyloid pathology []. LPS has been detected within Aβ plaques in AD patients’ brains, and microbial products such as curli fiber from E. coli and FapC from Pseudomonas can cross-seed Aβ and α-synuclein aggregation [,]. The periodontal keystone pathogen P. gingivalis provides an independent oral route to AD pathology: its DNA and gingipains have been detected in AD brains, where gingipain burden correlates with tau and ubiquitin pathology, and in mice, oral P. gingivalis infection causes brain colonization, neuroinflammation, and increased Aβ1–42 production, effects that are reduced by gingipain inhibitors [,].

Similarly, in Parkinson’s disease, gut dysbiosis, including alterations in SCFA-producing bacteria and enrichment of potentially pro-inflammatory taxa, has been associated with intestinal and systemic inflammatory changes that may influence α-synuclein pathology. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice, gut microbiota was required for microglial activation, neuroinflammation, α-synuclein pathology, and motor deficits, while antibiotic treatment reduced these phenotypes and microbiota recolonization restored them []. On healthy skin, S. epidermidis can modulate keratinocyte innate immunity through TLR2-dependent signaling; its lipoteichoic acid suppresses excessive TLR3-dependent inflammatory responses following skin injury, helping maintain controlled cutaneous inflammation []. In acne vulgaris, specific Cutibacterium acnes lineages are differentially associated with acne, with phylotype IA1 and several ribotypes enriched in affected follicles []. These strains can stimulate innate immune signaling in sebocytes and keratinocytes, including TLR2-dependent inflammatory pathways and inflammasome activation, contributing to IL-1β production and inflammatory lesion formation []. In rosacea, Demodex-associated Bacillus oleronius stimulates TLR2-mediated responses and cathelicidin (LL-37) production, and abnormal LL-37 processing generates pro-inflammatory fragments responsible for vascular dilation, erythema, and neutrophil recruitment. In atopic dermatitis, S. aureus can become highly dominant in lesional skin, with loss of microbial diversity and marked expansion during disease flares. S. aureus virulence factors, including proteases and toxins, can impair epidermal barrier function and stimulate keratinocyte and immune-cell inflammatory responses, contributing to disease exacerbation []. In type 2 diabetes, metabolic and inflammatory signals can activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in pancreatic islets, promoting IL-1β maturation and contributing to β-cell dysfunction and loss []. In oral squamous cell carcinoma, bacterial products can engage TLR2/TLR4-dependent innate immune pathways, contributing to chronic inflammatory signaling within the tumor microenvironment [], and in OSCC-associated dysbiosis more broadly, bacterial metabolites disrupt complement pathways and promote recruitment of tumor-associated macrophages, providing an innate route to immune evasion [].

After being activated, Toll-like receptors (TLRs) initiate downstream signaling cascades. There are two major adaptor proteins utilized by TLRs: myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88), which is used by all TLRs except TLR3, and Toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain-containing adaptor-inducing interferon-β (TRIF), which is utilized by TLR3 and TLR4. The MyD88-dependent pathway is engaged following TLR4 activation and promotes nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation through the sequential recruitment of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain-containing adaptor protein (TIRAP), also known as MyD88 adaptor-like (MAL), interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4 (IRAK4), interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 1 (IRAK1), tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), and transforming growth factor-β-activated kinase 1 (TAK1), resulting in the production of pro-inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). In turn, TLR4 also initiates the TRIF-dependent pathway through Toll-like receptor 4-associated adaptor protein (TRAM), leading to the activation of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) and inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa B kinase ε (IKKε), phosphorylation of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), and subsequent production of type I interferon [,]. These interconnected pathways link microbial dysbiosis to chronic inflammation and the development of non-communicable diseases ().

TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling has been implicated in the development of insulin resistance. In experimental models of type 2 diabetes and obesity, TLR4 activation can promote inflammatory signaling in hepatic, adipose, and skeletal muscle tissues, thereby interfering with insulin-receptor signaling and downstream PI3K–Akt pathway activation. However, evidence from human intervention studies remains less conclusive, indicating that the contribution of TLR4 signaling to human insulin resistance requires further clarification [,].

In obesity, changes in the intestinal microbiota and intestinal barrier dysfunction contribute to increased endotoxemia, which in turn leads to adipose tissue low-grade inflammation [,]. Indeed, in humans, an association between circulating LPS levels and expression of inflammatory genes in adipose tissue was observed, while in vitro studies demonstrated adipose tissue’s responsiveness to LPS. Altogether, these findings may serve as the basis for understanding how endotoxemia may contribute to adipose tissue dysfunction, although the extent to which this pathway is causal in human obesity remains to be established [].

In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), bacterial byproducts like LPS may engage TLR4 on Kupffer cells, thus initiating inflammatory and fibrotic responses that are characteristic of the condition []. In parallel, it has been suggested that the oral microbiota may play a role in the pathogenesis of MASLD, since there is a reported association between periodontitis and MASLD in population studies []. In particular, P. gingivalis -induced periodontitis exacerbated MASLD in murine models while increasing the levels of endotoxins in circulation, supporting the concept of a link between oral inflammation and liver disease []. In patients with MASLD, the presence of P. gingivalis DNA in saliva has been associated with greater liver stiffness measured by magnetic resonance elastography, providing additional evidence for a potential relationship between this oral microorganism and liver disease []. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that oral bacteria may be linked to liver inflammation and fibrosis in MASLD, though further studies are needed to establish causality.

In cardiovascular diseases, LPS can bind to TLR4 on the surface of vascular endothelial cells, thus initiating an inflammatory response that promotes atherosclerosis. In particular, LPS has been shown to increase the production of interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-8 (IL-8), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), as well as the expression of the adhesion molecules vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) in human coronary artery endothelial cells in a Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)-dependent manner. Therefore, LPS can be considered to promote vascular inflammation by inducing a pro-inflammatory endothelial cell phenotype []. In endothelial cells, LPS signaling mostly occurs through the MyD88-dependent pathway, with the TRIF-dependent pathway playing a lesser role than in macrophages [].

In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) can be detected years before the diagnosis of RA, potentially serving as biomarkers for the condition or informing early intervention. Indeed, the appearance of ACPAs precedes clinical manifestations of RA, while studies in humans also demonstrated the presence of ACPA+ B cell clones as well as citrulline-specific T cells in the lungs, supporting the notion of the mucosal innate- and adaptive-immune response playing a role in RA initiation []. Furthermore, the detection of secreted ACPAs in serum was associated with lung involvement, potentially identifying a subset of RA patients who may benefit from closer follow-up for pulmonary manifestations []. While these studies support the concept of mucosal immunity being involved in RA initiation, they do not establish the lung or oral mucosa as the exclusive sites of ACPA generation.

In gastric carcinogenesis, H. pylori infection increases interleukin-1β (IL-1β) production, which suppresses gastric acid secretion and can lead to atrophy. In particular, both H. pylori and IL-1β down-regulate the parietal cell hydrogen-potassium adenosine triphosphatase (H+/K+-ATPase) expression in human gastric epithelial cells, thus demonstrating that H. pylori can affect the function of parietal cells through inflammatory mechanisms []. In turn, IL-1β has been shown to suppress Sonic Hedgehog expression in parietal cells likely through a decrease in gastric acid secretion, thus affecting the normal epithelial turnover []. Finally, H. pylori infection can affect the gastric stem cell niche, leading to NF-κB activation and glandular remodeling, thus providing evidence for the link between this chronic infection and gastric cancer [].

In oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), oral microbes such as F. nucleatum can engage TLRs on tumor cells, thereby promoting tumorigenesis by creating an inflammatory microenvironment. In particular, TLR4, as well as its downstream adaptor molecule MyD88, are upregulated in OSCC tumor tissues compared to normal oral mucosa with variable levels depending on the degree of tumor differentiation. Specifically, stimulation of OSCC cell lines with LPS resulted in the activation of NF-κB/p38 MAPK pathways, leading to increased secretion of IL-6, IL-8, and VEGF, while suppression of TLR4 inhibited these effects, suggesting that LPS engagement of TLR4 can contribute to OSCC progression []. Overall, oral bacteria are involved in OSCC pathogenesis, which is supported by a scope review published in 2024 that analysed 13 studies and 1,677 participants []. In particular, individuals with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) had altered proportions of oral bacteria compared with healthy controls; notably, F. nucleatum and Prevotella intermedia were enriched in OSCC-associated samples, while broader alterations in Fusobacterium, Prevotella, and Porphyromonas were also observed []. Altogether, these findings support an association between alterations in the oral microbiota and OSCC, although it remains unclear whether specific bacterial species or combinations of microbial species are directly responsible for tumorigenesis. In addition, increased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) engagement of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) can activate downstream nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling and promote the production of pro-inflammatory mediators, providing a plausible inflammatory mechanism linking bacterial exposure to OSCC progression []. However, the precise mechanisms linking LPS–TLR4–NF-κB signaling to oxidative DNA damage or to the silencing of specific tumor-suppressor genes, such as CDKN2A or CDH1, have not been firmly established; therefore, such mechanistic interpretations should be approached with caution.

In colorectal cancer, biofilms formed by F. nucleatum, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF), and pks+ E. coli can be found in colorectal carcinomas, with various molecular and anatomical characteristics attributed to each of the bacteria. In particular, an analysis of 1,697 colorectal cancer tissues demonstrated that F. nucleatum was more commonly found in tumors located in the proximal colon, mismatch repair-deficient tumors, BRAF V600E-mutated tumors, CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP+) tumors, and tumors with increased tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, while pks+ E. coli was associated with APC mutated tumors []. In addition, ETBF and pks+ E. coli can cooperate to induce tumorigenesis, invade the mucosa, and cause DNA damage, thus contributing to colorectal cancer development []. Together, these findings indicate that F. nucleatum, ETBF, and pks-positive E. coli may contribute to colorectal carcinogenesis through distinct organism-specific mechanisms rather than through a single shared pathway. The evidence presented here particularly supports cooperative effects of ETBF and pks-positive E. coli involving inflammatory signaling, mucosal invasion, and DNA damage [].

In cervical carcinogenesis, vaginal microbiota is comprised of various bacteria that can be classified into six community state types (CST). CST IV is characterized by lower abundance of Lactobacillus spp. and higher alpha-diversity, while it is also associated with worse prognosis across the spectrum of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated diseases from healthy state to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive cancer []. Additionally, cervical microbiota can affect the host’s cytokine response to the infection, potentially determining the outcome of infection and the development of CIN []. CST IV, characterized by Lactobacillus depletion and greater bacterial diversity, is associated with HPV persistence and increasing CIN severity. Primary studies have shown that CST IV was more prevalent in women with persistent high-risk HPV infection and in those with more severe CIN, whereas Lactobacillus-dominated communities, particularly Lactobacillus crispatus, were associated with HPV clearance and regression []. However, these studies establish associations rather than demonstrating that CST IV directly causes HPV persistence or cervical carcinogenesis. Evidence for a direct gut microbiome–cervical cancer pathway remains limited; therefore, proposed mechanisms should be considered exploratory rather than established.

Commensal microbes influence adaptive immunity by regulating immune-cell responses to antigens, including the induction of regulatory T-cell differentiation and anti-inflammatory pathways. For example, B. fragilis produces polysaccharide A (PSA), which promotes regulatory T-cell responses and IL-10 production, thereby contributing to intestinal immune homeostasis []. Dysbiosis can disrupt these regulatory mechanisms and contribute to inappropriate immune activation [].

Similarly, there are associations between the microbiome and autoimmune diseases. For example, rheumatoid arthritis is considered to be a prototypical autoimmune disease driven by mucosal immune activation, possibly oral []. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease characterized by loss of peripheral immune tolerance, production of autoantibodies against nuclear antigens, complement activation, and immune-complex deposition in target organs, particularly the kidneys, skin, joints, and central nervous system. Studies in patients with SLE and lupus-prone mice have reported gut microbial dysbiosis, including reduced alpha diversity and alterations in the relative abundance of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, Faecalibacterium, Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Ruminococcus gnavus (R. gnavus). Increased R. gnavus abundance has been associated with greater disease activity and renal involvement, although microbial patterns vary among studies []. Additionally, in humans, decreased gut bacterial diversity and increased R. gnavus abundance were associated with overall disease activity and renal manifestations of lupus [,]. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by neuroinflammation and demyelination [,]. The microbiome has been implicated in MS pathogenesis, and transfer of microbiota from MS patients to germ-free mice resulted in more severe experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis than in mice that received microbiota from healthy controls [,]. In treatment-naïve patients with MS, alterations in the abundance of B. fragilis and Bifidobacterium have been reported, both of which have been implicated in immune regulation []. Additionally, alterations in oral microbiome, including decreased alpha diversity and reduced abundance of Gram-positive bacteria, and increased abundance of Prevotella, P. gingivalis, and F. nucleatum have also been associated with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS). These alterations, along with decreased salivary hypotaurine levels and disruption of oral microbe-metabolite networks, were attributed to impaired immune defense in patients with RRMS and implicated in altered myelin-specific immune responses []. However, because these human findings are primarily observational, causal relationships remain to be established. More interventional studies are needed to confirm the causal relationships in humans. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is an immune-mediated disease that includes Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) in which gut microbiome dysbiosis is a well-established contributor in pathogenesis. IBD patients also tend to have fewer microbial species, fewer beneficial species and a higher proportion of potentially pro-inflammatory species, such as Proteobacteria and Enterobacteriaceae []. These changes may lead to dysregulation of microbial metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and tryptophan-derived metabolites, which could affect the integrity of the epithelial barrier and the regulation of the mucosal immune system []. Importantly, experimental evidence indicates that dysbiosis may be a cause of intestinal inflammation in the context of IBD, besides being a result of it. The transfer of microbiota from Crohn’s disease patients to germ-free mice triggered spontaneous colonic inflammation, along with an increase in the abundance of R. gnavus and the activation of inflammatory pathways, such as NF-κB signaling []. In addition, fecal microbiota obtained from individuals who subsequently developed Crohn’s disease induced more severe colitis when transferred into germ-free mice than microbiota from matched healthy siblings, suggesting that disease-associated microbial alterations may precede the onset of clinically apparent Crohn’s disease []. Therefore, IBD dysbiosis could be a mechanism of disease by altering interactions between the epithelium and microbes and by inducing inappropriate mucosal immune activation.

There have been reports of changes in the oral and gut microbiome in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but the direction and biological relevance of these associations are still unclear. A primary study of children with ASD identified significant alterations in oral microbial communities, including reduced diversity in dental plaque, increased abundance of Proteobacteria, Streptococcus, and Haemophilus, and reduced abundance of Prevotella, Selenomonas, Actinomyces, Porphyromonas, and Fusobacterium []. Analysis of saliva from 180 children further identified differences in transcriptionally active microbial taxa between children with and without gastrointestinal disturbances []. Moreover, there was less diversity in community structure in 45 children with ASD than in 45 healthy controls in the gut, but the changes in individual taxonomic groups were not as consistent []. The study results indicate that these microbiomes are different in multiple body sites with ASD, but these are preliminary observational studies and do not answer the question as to whether microbiome changes contribute to the development of ASD, or if they are a secondary consequence of gastrointestinal issues, dietary changes, medication use, oral-health differences, or behaviors associated with oral diseases. Therefore, ASD should not be classified as a typical autoimmune disorder, but rather a neurodevelopmental disorder with microbiome and immune dysfunction.

Changes in host immunity have a close connection to oncogenesis, and dysbiosis of the microbiome may play a role in tumor development by causing chronic inflammation, genotoxicity and decreasing tumor immune surveillance. In the case of colorectal cancer (CRC), several microbial mechanisms have been experimentally proven. In ApcMin/+ mice, colonization with ETBF induces colitis and colorectal tumor formation, which is prevented by inhibition of IL-17 or IL-23 signaling, suggesting that ETBF activates epithelial STAT3 and triggers a Th17/IL-17-dominated inflammation []. BFT-induced IL-17 signaling then leads to the activation of NF-κB and STAT3 in colonic epithelial cells and induces chemokine expression which drives the recruitment of pro-tumorigenic myeloid cells []. Another way in which microbes evade the immune system is by the presence of F. nucleatum. Its Fap2 adhesin inhibits the activity of NK cells and tumor-infiltrating T lymphocytes by binding to the inhibitory receptor TIGIT, which promotes immune escape of tumors [] Furthermore, pks-positive E. coli is a genotoxin, causing DNA damage and mutational changes associated with CRC, and was found in larger quantities in the tumor tissue of early-stage CRCs compared to matched normal mucosa []. In the oral cavity, dysbiosis has also been correlated with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), and specific oral bacteria have been shown to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment. Experimental studies have demonstrated that P. gingivalis infection leads to upregulation of PD-L1 expression on dendritic cells via the Akt–STAT3 signaling pathway, which in turn subverts CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity, including the production of interferon gamma, perforin, and granzyme B, and exacerbates the progression of oral tumors. These findings suggest that oral microbial dysbiosis may contribute to cancer progression through the combined effects of chronic inflammatory signaling, modulation of antitumor immunity, and impaired immune surveillance rather than through the action of a single bacterial species alone [,]. The cervicovaginal microbiome is also altered in cervical cancer, with a change in the predominant community state type of the bacteria population (Lactobacillus). In the large observational analysis of 15,607 cervicovaginal samples, communities where L. crispatus, Lactobacillus gasseri, and Lactobacillus jensenii were abundant were associated with reduced prevalence of bacterial vaginosis, high-risk Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and abnormal cervical cytology, while Lactobacillus iners in combination with anaerobic bacteria was more often found in communities with high prevalence of high-risk HPV and abnormal cytology. In addition to Lactobacillus dominance, the functional properties of individual Lactobacillus species could affect vaginal ecology and the risk of ongoing HPV infection and cervical epithelial abnormalities.
