Mechanistic pathways linking human microbiome alterations to non-communicable disease.

Dietary supplements such as prebiotics and probiotics have inconsistent effects among individuals, partly due to inter-individual variation in microbiome composition and host physiology []. n a longitudinal multi-omics study, 61 healthy adults were monitored for nine consecutive days, revealing substantial interindividual variation in microbiome composition and metabolism that was influenced by gut physiology and environmental factors []. Individual responses have also been observed during probiotic interventions. Among 120 patients receiving probiotic adjuvant therapy for gout, 54 were classified as responders and 66 as non-responders, with distinct baseline microbiome and metabolomic profiles enabling prediction of treatment responsiveness []. Longitudinal microbiome datasets have also been analyzed using interpretable machine-learning approaches to identify time-dependent microbial biomarkers associated with disease outcomes []. Microbiome-based models have demonstrated the ability to predict individual glycemic responses to specific foods []. Furthermore, an 18-week randomized controlled trial involving 347 participants showed that a personalized nutrition program incorporating microbiome data, postprandial glucose and triglyceride responses, and health history produced greater improvements in triglycerides, body weight, and waist circumference than standard dietary advice []. According to this the future therapeutic strategies should integrate multi-omics data, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, and metabolomics with host immune and genetic signatures to better predict individual treatment responses []. Recent clinical evidence supports this concept, as baseline metagenomic and plasma/fecal metabolomic signatures predicted response to neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 immunochemotherapy in 44 patients with non-small-cell lung cancer, with microbial and metabolomic models achieving AUCs (Area under the curve) >0.85 [].

FMT has progressed from conventional donor-stool transplantation toward more standardized microbiota-based therapeutics, with the strongest clinical evidence available for in recurrent C. difficile infection (rCDI). In a phase III clinical trial, an oral microbiota-based therapy reduced recurrence from 39.8% to 12.4% at 8 weeks of treatment []. In another randomized trial involving 73 patients with mild to moderate ulcerative colitis, steroid-free remission was achieved in 32% of patients receiving donor FMT compared with 9% receiving autologous FMT []. Also, FMT in hepatic encephalopathy (HE), which is characterized by a loss of brain function due to a damaged liver that can no longer filter toxins from the blood, reduced recurrent episodes of HE but no improvement in cognition was observed, as per a phase II double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial []. Similarly, in anti-PD-1-refractory melanoma, FMT from immunotherapy responders combined with checkpoint blockade provided a clinical benefit in 6 of 15 patients via enhancement of CD8+T-cell activation, and reduced interleukin-8 (IL8) expression in myeloid cells []. Defined microbial consortia represent an important alternative to whole-stool FMT. High-dose VE303, an oral live biotherapeutic containing eight defined bacterial strains, reduced recurrent C. difficile infection to 13.8%, compared with 45.5% in the placebo group . A 2025 experimental study further demonstrated the potential of synthetic microbiomes by designing a 37-strain consortium (sFMT1) that suppressed C. difficile in vitro and in gnotobiotic mice, with competitive nutrient utilization through Stickland fermentation identified as an important mechanism of colonization resistance []. FMT is also being investigated for neurological disorders. However, a randomized trial involving 45 patients with Parkinson’s disease found no clinically meaningful improvement compared with placebo despite sustained modification of the gut microbiome []. Thus, neurological and autoimmune applications remain investigational. Future studies should focus on disease-specific phase II/III trials, donor–recipient matching, durable engraftment, functional biomarkers, defined microbial consortia, and long-term safety.

The microbiome is increasingly being investigated as a noninvasive source of biomarkers for early disease detection and risk stratification across NCDs. Evidence is particularly strong for colorectal cancer (CRC). A pooled analysis of 3,741 stool metagenomes from 18 cohorts identified reproducible species- and strain-level microbial signatures and achieved an average AUC of 0.85 for CRC prediction, supporting the potential utility of gut microbiome profiling for noninvasive screening []. Similarly, a four-year longitudinal study integrating metagenomics and metabolomics identified baseline alterations in microbial composition and circulating metabolites in individuals with impaired glucose tolerance who subsequently developed diabetes, and the combined model predicted disease progression with an AUC of 0.87 [].

Similarly, the oral microbiome may serve as a noninvasive biomarker for CRC risk. A prospective analysis of three US cohorts identified associations between specific oral taxa and distal colon and rectal cancers, suggesting potential for site-specific CRC risk stratification []. The vaginal microbiome also shows potential as a biomarker of cervical disease risk. A prospective cohort of 731 women followed for one year found that persistent high-risk HPV infection was associated with increased microbial diversity and reduced Lactobacillus abundance, suggesting potential utility for monitoring HPV persistence and cervical health []. In a separate longitudinal study of 49 cervical cancer survivors, Prevotella-dominant, high-diversity vaginal microbial communities were associated with post-treatment HPV persistence and subsequent cancer recurrence. The skin microbiome remains an emerging platform for biomarkers. A 2025 pilot study of 58 participants identified cancer-associated skin microbial profiles using NGS and machine learning, achieving an F1 score of 0.943, although larger longitudinal cohorts are required for validation []. Collectively, these findings support gut, oral, vaginal, and skin microbiomes as complementary sources of minimally invasive biomarkers, while emphasizing the need for standardized sampling, diverse reference populations, multi-omics integration, and prospective clinical validation. Recent findings also show that multimodal Artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches can be integrated into heterogeneous molecular, pathological, imaging, and clinical data to improve cancer risk prediction, prognostic assessment, treatment-response prediction, and better precise treatment decision-making [].

Future research should move beyond broad descriptions of dysbiosis toward the identification of specific microbial strains, metabolites, and molecular pathways that can be therapeutically manipulated along the microbiota–gut–brain axis. Causal evidence is already emerging from neurodegenerative disease models. In α-synuclein-overexpressing mice, gut microbiota was required for motor deficits, microglial activation, and α-synuclein pathology, whereas microbiota depletion attenuated these phenotypes; conversely, recolonization and administration of microbial metabolites promoted neuroinflammation and motor dysfunction, supporting a functional role for the microbiota in Parkinson’s disease [,]. Strain-specific interventions provide an additional therapeutic rationale. Administration of the butyrate-producing Agathobaculum butyriciproducens improved cognitive performance, reduced amyloid-β deposition and microglial activation, and attenuated neuroinflammation in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease []. More recently, A. rectalis supplementation improved cognitive impairment and reduced microglial activation in APP/PS1 mice, with bacterial butyrate implicated in modulation of the Akt/NF-κB pathway, further supporting metabolite-producing commensals as candidate next-generation psychobiotics []. Evidence is also emerging for stress-related neuropsychiatric disorders, as Lactiplantibacillus plantarum D-9 alleviated anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in stressed mice while modifying tryptophan metabolism, hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal-axis activity, and inflammatory signaling []. Importantly, this preclinical evidence is beginning to translate into controlled human studies. Bifidobacterium breve CCFM1025 significantly improved depressive symptoms in patients with major depressive disorder and altered gut microbial tryptophan metabolism and serotonergic pathways, providing early clinical evidence for a strain-specific psychobiotic effect []. More recently, the 2026 PRODG randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial evaluated adjunctive Lactobacillus helveticus and Bifidobacterium longum in 58 adults aged ≥60 years with moderate unipolar depression receiving standard antidepressant treatment. Probiotic supplementation was associated with greater overall improvement in depressive and anxiety symptoms, increased serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and increased fecal abundance of the supplemented strains; however, the probiotic group did not demonstrate an additional quality-of-life benefit, the group-by-time interaction for symptom trajectories was not significant, and attrition exceeded 50%, indicating that the findings should be interpreted as preliminary rather than definitive clinical evidence []. Collectively, these findings provide a rationale for developing defined microbial consortia, engineered psychobiotics, and microbiota-derived metabolite therapies according targeting short-chain-fatty-acid signaling, tryptophan metabolism, bile-acid pathways, microglial activation, neuroinflammation, and the HPA axis. However, translation will require larger, adequately powered randomized trials with standardized psychiatric outcomes and integrated longitudinal microbiome, metabolomic, inflammatory, and neurotrophic profiling to determine whether microbial changes are causal, reproducible, and clinically meaningful. The substantial interindividual variability of the human microbiome further suggests that future gut–brain therapeutics should move toward strain-specific, mechanism-guided, and patient-stratified interventions rather than one-size-fits-all probiotic approaches.

Bacterial taxa dominate microbiome research, but the phageome, mycobiome, and virome regulate community structure, predator–prey dynamics, horizontal gene transfer, immune tone, and interkingdom crosstalk in ways still poorly resolved. In IBS, fecal virome sequencing has revealed reduced viral diversity and altered Caudovirales-dominated composition associated with changes in the bacterial microbiome, although causality has not been established []. Alterations in the intestinal fungal microbiome have also been associated with visceral hypersensitivity in patients with IBS, while experimental studies in maternally separated rats provide mechanistic evidence of mast cell activation and degranulation []. Dedicated clinical trials targeting the IBS mycobiome or virome remain lacking. A primary human colonoid monolayer model now enables ex vivo study of phage translocation across intact, mucus-covered colonic epithelium, providing a mechanistic platform for future work []. A five-phage cocktail targeting IBD-associated K. pneumoniae effectively reduced pathobiont abundance and attenuated intestinal inflammation in colitis-prone mice. Subsequent evaluation in an 18-participant phase 1 clinical trial demonstrated a favorable safety profile and sustained phage persistence, providing an important translational link between preclinical mechanistic evidence and human safety data; however, its clinical efficacy remains to be established []. An AIEC-targeting three-phage cocktail reduced AIEC burden in LF82-colonized CEABAC10 mice and targeted AIEC in Crohn’s disease ileal biopsy homogenates, providing preclinical support for phage therapy in Crohn’s disease []. The subsequently developed seven-phage EcoActive cocktail was evaluated preclinically and subsequently advanced to a Phase 1/2a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03808103), which is currently active but not recruiting, with results not yet publicly available. Beyond the gut, phages targeting Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans kill 99% of biofilm-embedded cells in vitro, though periodontal clinical validation is lacking []. On the skin, a bacteriophage-derived chimeric endolysin selectively eliminated S. aureus in vitro, in reconstituted human epidermis, and in a murine infection model while largely preserving S. epidermidis []. However, a clinical trial in about 100 patients with atopic dermatitis found that topical endolysin was well tolerated but did not reduce the need for corticosteroids []. In the vaginal environment, a Gardnerella-targeting endolysin disrupted biofilms and reduced viable Gardnerella in ex vivo samples while preserving L. crispatus []. In parallel, Lactin-V, a live biotherapeutic containing L. crispatus CTV-05, significantly reduced recurrence of bacterial vaginosis in a phase 2b randomized controlled trial []. However, clinical evidence for phage- and endolysin-based therapies in BV remains limited, with efficacy still requiring validation in clinical trials. Realizing the therapeutic potential of phage-, endolysin-, and mycobiome-directed approaches will require integrated multi-omics studies and randomized clinical trials while addressing challenges such as phage resistance, horizontal gene transfer, immune activation, and unintended depletion of beneficial taxa.

Synthetic biology is increasingly enabling the development of programmable microbiome therapeutics in which engineered microorganisms can sense disease-associated signals, produce therapeutic molecules, remodel microbial metabolism, or selectively target pathogenic populations. Early proof-of-concept studies showed that engineered Lactococcus lactis (L. lactis) producing interleukin-10 (IL-10) could attenuate experimental intestinal inflammation, thereby demonstrating the feasibility of genetically modified bacteria as localized delivery systems for immunomodulatory molecules []. This strategy subsequently progressed to human investigation with the genetically modified L. lactis strain L. lactis-Thymidine-dependent strain 12 (LL-Thy12), which was engineered to secrete human IL-10 and incorporating a thymidine-dependent biological containment strategy, evaluated in a phase I clinical trial in patients with Crohn’s disease; the study provided preliminary evidence for clinical feasibility and biological containment, although subsequent development highlighted the difficulty of translating safety and target engagement into robust clinical efficacy []. In 2026, an engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 strain carrying the tetrathionate-utilization (ttr) operon was shown to exploit tetrathionate generated during intestinal inflammation, thereby gaining a selective fitness advantage within inflamed tissue; EcN:ttr demonstrated improved therapeutic efficacy in DSS-induced and Muc2−/− mouse models and also showed efficacy in a porcine model of colitis, providing an important preclinical bridge toward clinical translation []. In parallel, synthetic biology and CRISPR-Cas technologies are expanding microbiome engineering beyond the introduction of therapeutic strains toward precision elimination or modification of defined bacterial populations. Engineered bacterial vectors have achieved highly selective depletion of antibiotic-resistant E. coli and clearance of Citrobacter rodentium in murine models, illustrating the possibility of targeting specific pathogens or resistance determinants while minimizing the collateral disruption associated with conventional antibiotics []. CRISPR-Cas platforms are now being investigated more broadly for targeting bacterial virulence factors, antibiotic-resistance genes, and disease-associated microbial functions, although delivery, intracellular activity, off-target effects, horizontal gene transfer, and persistence of the editing machinery remain major translational challenges []. Beyond genetic editing, engineered bacteria are being developed as metabolic bioreactors capable of degrading harmful metabolites or producing therapeutic compounds; clinical programs involving engineered E. coli Nissle strains for phenylketonuria have provided evidence that genetically programmed bacterial metabolism can generate measurable pharmacodynamic effects in humans, although durable efficacy remains an important challenge []. Collectively, these advances suggest that future microbiome engineering will increasingly focus on sense-and-respond, disease-responsive, metabolically programmable, and self-limiting microorganisms, rather than constitutively engineered probiotics. Integration of CRISPR editing, synthetic gene circuits, biosensors, metabolic engineering, genetic biocontainment, and patient-specific multi-omics profiling could enable therapeutic strains to be tailored to individual microbial and host environments []

Pharmacomicrobiomics is emerging as an important component of precision medicine because the gut microbiome can bidirectionally influence drug disposition, efficacy, and toxicity, while pharmaceutical agents can themselves alter microbial community structure and function. A landmark systematic analysis demonstrated that 176 of 271 orally administered drugs were chemically modified by at least one of 76 representative human gut bacterial strains, with microbiome-encoded enzymes capable of directly altering intestinal and systemic drug metabolism in vivo []. Individual microbial pathways can have clinically important consequences; for example, Eggerthella lenta can inactivate the cardiac drug digoxin through the cardiac glycoside reductase system, while bacterial β-glucuronidases can reactivate the irinotecan metabolite SN-38 in the intestinal lumen and contribute to dose-limiting gastrointestinal toxicity [,]. Conversely, drugs can reshape the microbiome, with metformin, proton-pump inhibitors, antibiotics, and laxatives among the medication classes most strongly associated with altered gut microbial composition and function []. Importantly, the magnitude and direction of these interactions vary between individuals because microbial community composition, functional gene content, diet, disease state, and concomitant medications differ substantially among patients. The Microbiome-Derived Metabolism (MDM)-Screen developed by Javdan et al. demonstrated that subject-specific gut communities exhibit distinct drug-metabolizing capacities and identified microbiome-encoded enzymes responsible for individual drug transformations, providing a framework for patient-specific pharmacomicrobiomic profiling []. The microbiome may also influence pharmacodynamic response through host immunity; in melanoma, distinct gut microbial profiles were associated with response to anti-PD-1 therapy, while experimental and translational studies identified A. muciniphila and other taxa as contributors to improved checkpoint-blockade efficacy []. These findings support a future in which microbiome composition and functional capacity are integrated with pharmacogenomic, metabolomic, and clinical data to predict drug exposure, toxicity, and treatment response and to guide microbiome-informed dosing or adjunctive microbiome modulation. However, routine clinical implementation remains limited by the high interindividual variability in microbial metabolism, temporal instability of the microbiome, polypharmacy, diet-related confounding, insufficient standardization of biomarkers, and the difficulty of establishing causal relationships between microbial features and clinical pharmacokinetics. Future studies should therefore move from taxonomic associations toward function-based pharmacomicrobiomics, integrating metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics, microbial enzyme profiling, and prospective pharmacokinetic trials to identify actionable microbiome–drug interactions and determine when targeted microbial modulation can safely improve therapeutic efficacy or reduce toxicity.

The microbiome plays a fundamental role in the maturation and regulation of host immunity from early life onward, and its disruption has been associated with inflammatory, metabolic, allergic, and malignant diseases. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, and tryptophan-derived indoles, influence regulatory T-cell differentiation, epithelial barrier integrity, macrophage and dendritic cell function, and mucosal immune signaling, thereby providing mechanistic links between microbial ecology and long-term disease susceptibility [,,]. The first 1,000 days, encompassing preconception, pregnancy, infancy, and early childhood, may represent an especially important period because microbial colonization and immune development occur simultaneously and are influenced by delivery mode, breastfeeding, diet, antibiotic exposure, and other environmental factors. Prospective birth cohorts provide evidence supporting this concept: the KOALA Birth Cohort linked specific early-life microbial patterns with subsequent atopic manifestations and showed associations between early antibiotic exposure and recurrent wheeze, while contemporary prospective studies have further linked cesarean-associated microbial perturbations with increased childhood asthma risk []. The potential for intervention has also been tested clinically. Randomized trials of maternal or early-life probiotic supplementation have reported reductions in infant eczema or atopic eczema in some populations, although results have been inconsistent across strains, populations, and intervention schedules, emphasizing that probiotic effects are highly context- and strain-dependent []. More recent randomized evidence, including the multinational NiPPeR trial incorporating probiotics with other nutritional components from preconception through pregnancy, illustrates both the promise and complexity of preventive microbiome-oriented interventions, with several maternal and perinatal outcomes affected but no improvement in the primary glycemic endpoint []. These findings suggest that early-life microbiome modulation could become a preventive strategy for immune-mediated disease, but the current evidence is stronger for immune and allergic outcomes than for long-term prevention of major non-communicable diseases such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or cancer. Accordingly, future prevention trials should prospectively follow mother–infant cohorts for many years and integrate longitudinal microbiome sequencing, metabolomics, immune phenotyping, dietary exposures, antibiotic history, and host genetics rather than relying on single early-life microbiome measurements. The long-term goal is therefore not simply to increase microbial diversity, but to identify specific microbial functions and developmental windows that causally promote durable immune resilience, and then test these targets in adequately powered randomized trials before incorporating microbiome-based prevention into public-health recommendations.

The synthesis of evidence presented in this review indicates that the human microbiome contributes to metabolic, epithelial, immune, and inflammatory homeostasis across the gut, oral cavity, skin, and cervicovaginal ecosystems. Localized dysbiotic alterations may serve not only as disease-associated markers but, in specific contexts, as mechanistic contributors to non-communicable diseases by disrupting epithelial barriers, activating innate and inflammatory pathways, causing immune dysregulation, and altering interorgan communication. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, TMA–TMAO, and tryptophan-derived metabolites, represent important mediators linking microbial activity to host physiology. Microbiome profiling therefore has considerable translational potential for disease-risk stratification, biomarker development, personalized nutrition, and microbiome-directed therapeutics. However, substantial interindividual variability, the predominance of observational and cross-sectional evidence, and the limited causal validation available in humans currently restrict clinical translation. Future studies should prioritize longitudinal multi-omics approaches and well-designed interventional trials to establish reproducible causal relationships and identify clinically actionable microbiome-based strategies.

medicine.title: Access to systemic anti-cancer treatment in mesothelioma: a systematic review of inequities in treatment access and decision-making
medicine.abstract: To synthesise evidence on factors influencing access to and uptake of systemic anti-cancer treatment (SACT) for people with mesothelioma, an incurable cancer, with a focus on inequities in treatment pathways and decision-making within supportive oncology care.An integrative systematic review with narrative synthesis (PROSPERO: 603309) was conducted. APA PsycInfo, ASSIA, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, PubMed Central, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for English-language publications between 1 January 2008 and 18 October 2024. Eligible studies included empirical research and reproducible reviews reporting factors affecting access to or receipt of SACT among individuals with mesothelioma.The search yielded 716 records, of which 18 met inclusion criteria. Four interrelated themes were identified: (1) demographic characteristics; (2) information provision and decision-making; (3) clinical and disease-related factors; and (4) healthcare system and structural factors. An overarching theme of intersectionality demonstrated how social, clinical and organisational influences interact to shape treatment access and decision-making.Access to and uptake of SACT in mesothelioma is shaped by complex, interacting patient- and system-level factors, resulting in persistent inequities in treatment pathways. As SACT is typically delivered with palliative intent in this population, these findings highlight its role within supportive oncology care and the importance of equitable access, shared decision-making and consistent information provision across services.
medicine.text:
Mesothelioma is a rare, aggressive, and life-limiting cancer, most commonly affecting the pleura (lining of the lungs), but it can also arise in the peritoneum (lining of the abdomen) or other anatomical sites [, ]. It is almost exclusively caused by asbestos exposure and has a long latency period typically of 30–50 years []. The United Kingdom (UK) has the highest recorded incidence of mesothelioma worldwide, with approximately 2,700 new cases annually [, ]. Incidence in Europe is predicted to increase by 30.4% by 2040, and by up to 46.9% in North America, 57.1% in Oceania, and 72.0% in Africa []. Mesothelioma predominantly affects older people and men. The higher incidence among men reflects historical patterns of occupational asbestos exposure, particularly in industries such as construction, shipbuilding and mining []. The long latency period of the disease and bans on asbestos use contribute to the higher incidence among older populations [].

Mesothelioma remains incurable, with poor outcomes and around 60% of patients dying within a year of diagnosis []. The disease is characterised by rapid progression, unpredictable deterioration, and a high symptom burden including difficult-to-manage pain [, ]. In addition to physical impacts, it is associated with substantial psychosocial and emotional burden for patients and families [, –], alongside complex informational, legal and financial challenges due to its industrial cause. These factors necessitate highly coordinated, multidisciplinary care and comprehensive support.

With no curative treatment options, systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT) is typically delivered with palliative intent to slow disease progression, reduce symptoms, improve quality of life and extend survival []. In the UK, SACT is recommended as first-line treatment by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) []. Current options include chemotherapy and immunotherapy. The introduction of nivolumab plus ipilimumab following the CheckMate 743 trial represented the first major therapeutic advance in over a decade [, ]. CheckMate 743 was a phase III randomised trial comparing first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab with platinum-based chemotherapy and demonstrated improved overall survival with immunotherapy, establishing this combination as a first-line treatment option []. Surgical approaches were previously considered for selected patients. However, guidance from the British Thoracic Society (BTS) recommends against surgery for disease control in malignant pleural mesothelioma []. More recently, the phase III MARS2 trial demonstrated worse survival and quality of life outcomes with extended pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy compared with chemotherapy alone, challenging the role of radical surgery in the management of pleural mesothelioma []. Nevertheless, variation in international practice and debate surrounding the role of surgery persists [, ].

Despite these advances, access to SACT remains inconsistent. National Mesothelioma Audit data indicate that only 40% of patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma receive chemotherapy, with similar findings across successive audits []. This has led to recommendations that multidisciplinary teams with chemotherapy rates below 60% in performance status (PS) 0–1 patients review potential barriers to treatment access [].

Broader oncology research has identified inequities in access to cancer treatment are influenced by socioeconomic status [–], geography [, ], age [, ] and hospital involvement in clinical trials []. These findings raise concerns about similar disparities in mesothelioma care.

A national research prioritisation exercise identified mesothelioma patient experiences of treatment and decision-making as key research priorities []. Together with audit data [], this highlights the need to better understand barriers and facilitators influencing access to SACT in mesothelioma. This systematic review therefore aimed to identify and synthesise international evidence on barriers and facilitators affecting access to and uptake of SACT among mesothelioma patients. To our knowledge, this is the first review to focus on this issue in this population.

An integrative systematic review approach was used to synthesise evidence from qualitative and quantitative studies, following Whittemore and Knafl []. The review was conducted in accordance with guidance from the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination [] and reported in line with PRISMA guidelines []. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024603309). The review was guided by the research question: “What are the barriers and facilitators influencing access to and uptake of systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT) for mesothelioma patients?”.

The Mesothelioma UK Research Centre PPI Panel contributed throughout the review, including input into the protocol, interpretation of findings and ongoing feedback during the review process. The panel comprises people with personal experience of mesothelioma, including patients and carers.

A systematic search was conducted across seven databases: APA PsycInfo, ASSIA, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, PubMed Central, Scopus, and Web of Science. The search combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text terms related to three topics:MesotheliomaSystemic Anti-Cancer Therapy (e.g., “systemic anti-cancer therapy”, “chemotherapy”, “immunotherapy”, “SACT”)Access, uptake, and patient experience (e.g., “patient experience”, “treatment patterns”, “access to care”, “decision-making”, “disparities”, “equity”)

Searches were limited to English-language studies published between 1 January 2008 and 18 October 2024. Reference lists of included studies were also hand-searched to identify additional relevant studies. Table  reports search inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Table 1Search inclusion and exclusion criteriaInclusion criteriaExclusion criteriaEmpirical research (any design) or reproducible reviews reporting on access to, uptake of or decision making about SACTNon-empirical publications or studies not reporting on access to, uptake of or decision-making about SACT (e.g. studies focused solely on the epidemiology or biology of mesothelioma, general experiences of living with mesothelioma, or other treatments such as surgery)Human studiesNon-human studiesPublished from 2008 to date of searches (Oct 2024)Published prior to 2008English languageNon-English languageFocused on people with mesothelioma, including studies reporting the experiences or perspectives of family members, carers or healthcare professionals where these provided information relevant to patients’ access to, uptake of or decision-making about SACTStudies not focused on people with mesothelioma, or reporting family members’, carers’ or healthcare professionals’ experiences or perspectives without providing information relevant to patients’ access to, uptake of or decision-making about SACTPeer reviewed literatureGeneral discussion, theses, editorials, conference proceedings, commentary/opinion pieces, news articles, book chapters, case reports or literature review without replicable methodStudies with participants aged 18 years and overStudies with participants under age 18

Search inclusion and exclusion criteria

Two reviewers (JD and BT) independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (CG). The process was documented using a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram Fig. .

Methodological quality was assessed using the appropriate Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklist [] according to study design. One reviewer (JD) completed all appraisals, with 20% independently checked by a second reviewer (BT). Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Given the aim of providing a comprehensive synthesis of a limited evidence base, all studies meeting inclusion criteria were included regardless of quality, with appraisal used to inform weighting of results.

Data were extracted by one reviewer (JD) using a structured extraction form, with 50% checked for accuracy by a second reviewer (BT). Extracted data included: (1) publication details; (2) country of study; (3) research aim/objectives; (4) study design; (5) population characteristics, including sample size, age, sex, type of mesothelioma and participant group (patients, family members and carers or healthcare professionals), where reported (6) data collection methods; (7) key findings relevant to review question and (8) limitations. An integrative review approach was used to synthesise findings from diverse study designs. Narrative synthesis and inductive thematic analysis were conducted, involving iterative coding, development of conceptual categories, and identification of patterns across studies. A reflexive approach was maintained throughout the synthesis process, with regular discussion between reviewers to challenge interpretations and minimise bias.

The database searches yielded a total of 716 articles. After removing 117 duplicates, 599 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 383 were excluded based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, resulting in 216 articles for full-text retrieval. One article could not be retrieved, leaving 215 full-text articles assessed for eligibility. Following full-text screening, 198 articles were excluded. Seventeen articles met the inclusion criteria. An additional article was identified through hand-searching the reference lists of included articles, bringing the total number included in the final review to 18.

Study characteristics and key findings are presented in Supplementary Table . The review included 18 studies comprising quantitative (n = 15), qualitative (n = 1), and mixed-methods designs (n = 2). Studies were conducted in the UK (n = 3), Australia (n = 4), the USA (n = 6), the Netherlands (n = 1), Italy (n = 1), Canada (n = 1) and Belgium (n = 1). One study included data from multiple countries (Belgium, Netherlands and the UK) (n = 1).

All studies focused on individuals with mesothelioma and/or their family members and carers or healthcare professionals involved in mesothelioma care. Most studies were limited to malignant pleural mesothelioma (n = 16), with two including additional subtypes [, ]. The terms sex and gender were used inconsistently across the included studies and were frequently conflated; for clarity, the term sex is used in this review when referring to participant characteristics. Where reported, study populations were predominantly male. Mean or median participant age ranged from 68 years [] to 78 years []. Only one study included both chemotherapy and immunotherapy [], with the remaining studies (17/18) focused on chemotherapy. Consequently, findings primarily reflect chemotherapy-based SACT.

Overall, the methodological quality of included studies was moderate. Most studies demonstrated clear alignment between aims and design, appropriate recruitment strategies [e.g. –], and consideration of potential confounding factors [e.g. , ]. The majority provided sufficiently detailed descriptions of treatment variables and analysis, supporting the credibility of findings across the evidence base. Common limitations frequently related to specific CASP domains that were insufficiently addressed or not fully applicable to the study designs. Other limitations concerned the statistical precision of results [e.g. ], unclear generalisability [e.g. , , ], and insufficient discussion of clinical implications [e.g. , , ]. A small number of studies [, ] provided limited detail on recruitment processes, raising potential concerns regarding selection bias. Given these limitations, findings should be interpreted with appropriate caution. Tables A-C in Supplementary Information  present critical appraisal results for all included studies a) cohort studies b) cross-sectional studies and c) qualitative studies using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklists.

Four main themes were identified: (1) demographic and participant characteristics, (2) information and decision-making factors, (3) clinical and disease-related factors, and (4) healthcare system and structural factors. These are presented with associated sub-themes in Table . An overarching theme of intersectionality describes how these factors interact to shape access to and uptake of SACT.

Factors influencing access to and uptake of SACT identified across included studies

Older age consistently emerges as a significant barrier to accessing and receiving SACT among mesothelioma patients, with chemotherapy uptake declining as age increases [–, , –]. Definitions of older age were largely defined as above 75 or 80 years of age [, , –]. Patients aged ≥ 75 years are particularly underrepresented among those receiving SACT, [] and those opting for active symptom control rather than SACT tend to be significantly older (74.4 vs 68.4, p < 0.001) [].

Age also appears to influence treatment intensity. Danese et al. [] reported a decreasing average age across successive lines of chemotherapy and Linton et al. [] found patients over 80 years were less likely to complete three chemotherapy cycles than those under the age of 80.

Evidence regarding the influence of sex on SACT uptake is mixed. One study reported no significant association between sex and chemotherapy uptake [], whereas others found that female patients were less likely to receive chemotherapy [, ]. Bibby et al. [] further observed that female participants more frequently opted for active symptom control compared with males.

One study found that patients with higher BMI were significantly more likely to receive SACT compared to those with normal weight, as defined by the BMI tool [].

Patient choice plays a significant role in the uptake of SACT, even among individuals with good performance status. Schmid et al. [] reported that 44% of patients with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 0–1 declined treatment due to personal preference. Similarly, a survey of 78 patients reported that, although most patients (65%) expressed a preference for chemotherapy, a proportion remained uncertain (12%) or opted against treatment (17%) []. Qualitative findings suggest such reluctance is often driven by a desire to preserve quality of life, perceived limited benefit, fear of side effects, and prior negative experiences with chemotherapy [, ]. In one study, participants considered the potential impact of chemotherapy on quality of life to outweigh its benefits, even when well-informed about associated risks and advantages [].

The quality and availability of information were rarely addressed in the literature, with only two studies explicitly exploring this factor. Most participants (approximately 80%), in a study capturing patient and carer perspectives, reported receiving sufficient information to make informed decisions regarding chemotherapy uptake []. Clinicians, particularly nurses, emphasised the importance of education and clear information in influencing the feasibility and acceptability of chemotherapy [].

Clinicians play a critical role in shaping treatment decisions. While many patients and carers perceived decision-making as patient-led, a substantial proportion described shared decision-making or strong clinician influence []. Clinicians themselves reported high levels of involvement, with around 90% of doctors and over half of nurses reporting moderate-to-high involvement in supporting patients with treatment decision making []. Notably, 70% of doctors identified therapeutic nihilism (i.e. skepticism about treatment benefit) as a key barrier to recommending chemotherapy [], suggesting clinician perceptions may contribute to lower SACT uptake.

Family involvement was identified as an influence on treatment decision-making in one study []. Peer support from individuals with lived experience was also perceived as helpful in navigating treatment choices. Notably, 7% of participants reported wishing to speak with another patient about chemotherapy decisions but lacked the opportunity, highlighting the potential value of peer support in decision-making [].

Performance status (PS), most commonly assessed using the ECOG scale, is consistently associated with receipt of systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT) in mesothelioma. Across multiple studies, patients with good PS (ECOG 0–1) were significantly more likely to receive treatment, whereas those with poor PS (ECOG ≥ 2) were less likely [, , ]. Some clinicians reported delaying treatment in asymptomatic patients with good PS, opting to wait until symptoms emerged []. However, rapid disease progression sometimes led to PS deterioration before treatment could commence [].

Symptom burden and its management may influence treatment decisions, although findings are mixed. Qualitative evidence suggests that effective patient education and symptom management, particularly for breathlessness, pain and psychological distress, may enhance treatment feasibility and acceptability []. In contrast, an observational study found no significant differences in symptom profiles between patients receiving first-line chemotherapy and those managed with active symptom control [].

The influence of tumour histology on treatment decisions remains inconclusive. Several studies report that patients with epithelioid mesothelioma are more likely to receive SACT than those with biphasic or sarcomatoid subtypes [, , ], whereas one reported no significant association between histology and treatment uptake []. Treatment type may also vary by histology, with chemotherapy more frequently offered to patients with epithelioid or unspecified histology, while immunotherapy more commonly used in non-epithelioid cases [].

Evidence regarding disease stage and treatment uptake is conflicting. Some studies suggest that patients with later stage disease are less likely to receive chemotherapy or immunotherapy [], particularly if the disease progresses rapidly [, ]. However, other studies report higher use among patients with later-stage disease, potentially due to urgent need for intervention or greater symptom burden and an intention to reduce pain [, ]. In contrast, other observational studies [, ] found no clear association between stage and receipt of SACT.

Comorbidities appear to be a relevant, though inconsistently reported, factor in the uptake and continuation of SACT. Several studies indicate that lower comorbidity burden facilitates both initiation and continuation of treatment, with patients more likely to receive first-line chemotherapy [] and proceed to subsequent lines []. However, this association is not universal; one large-scale study found no significant link between comorbidity scores and receipt of systemic therapy []. Furthermore, findings from Barsky et al. [] suggest that lower comorbidity burden does not necessarily translate into higher treatment uptake.

Limited access to mesothelioma-specific clinical expertise is reported as a clear barrier to treatment. In one study, conducted in Australia and New Zealand, 44% of doctors identified lack of specialist services in rural or regional areas as a barrier to chemotherapy, while 58% of nurses cited limited clinician knowledge as a key obstacle []. National data from Italy similarly pointed to regional differences in specialist access as a contributor to variations in treatment uptake [].

Delayed diagnosis emerged as a structural barrier in one study. Survey findings showed 74% of nurses (n = 14) based in Australia and New Zealand identified prolonged time from symptom onset to diagnosis as a factor limiting access to chemotherapy [].

Timely referral to oncology services appears critical to treatment uptake. In an Australian and New Zealand study, nearly half of surveyed physicians and over 60% of nurses reported that failure to refer patients to a medical oncologist limited access to chemotherapy []. This is supported by UK data showing that 47% of patients who declined SACT had not been reviewed by an oncologist prior to their decision [], suggesting missed or delayed referral may directly restrict treatment uptake.

Geographic variation in SACT access is well-documented both within and between countries. In England and Wales, treatment rates for mesothelioma patients varied significantly across cancer networks, ranging from 47 to 78% overall and from 46 to 71% among those with good performance status []. Clinician perceptions echo these disparities, with 84% of nurses in Australia identifying treatment coordination, particularly in rural settings, as influencing feasibility and acceptability of chemotherapy []. Regional inequities were also reported in Italy, where chemotherapy uptake ranged from 28 to 71% []. Cross-national comparisons further illustrate this variability, with chemotherapy usage reported at 60% in Belgium, 41% in the Netherlands, and 37% in England []. These differences suggest that healthcare infrastructure, resource allocation, and regional policies influence treatment access.

Across the included studies, access to SACT was shaped by interacting influences spanning demographic, clinical, decision-making and healthcare system factors. These were rarely reported in isolation, with most studies identifying multiple co-occurring barriers, as presented in Table .

For example, older age, consistently associated with lower SACT uptake, was frequently reported alongside poorer performance status, together limiting treatment eligibility [, ]. Clinical factors, such as symptom burden, were also described alongside structural issues including delayed diagnosis, limited access to specialist services, and non-referral to oncology, particularly in rural or regional settings [, ]. In qualitative studies, clinician attitudes and therapeutic nihilism interacted with patient preferences, symptom burden, and quality-of-life considerations in shaping treatment decisions [].

Collectively, these findings indicate that variation in SACT uptake reflects the combined effect of multiple, overlapping influences across patient, clinical, and healthcare system levels. While not always explicitly examined, the co-occurrence of these factors suggests interaction effects, whereby combined influences have a greater impact than any single factor alone.

This systematic review synthesised international evidence on barriers and facilitators influencing access to and uptake of SACT for people with mesothelioma. Reduced access to SACT was associated with overlapping demographic, clinical, informational, and system-level disadvantages, including older age, female sex, poorer performance status, limited access to specialist expertise, and reduced likelihood of oncology referral. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous, with some findings inconsistent across studies.

The findings suggest that barriers to SACT co-occurred. This is consistent with recent evidence that co-occurring patient barriers amplify disadvantage [] and highlights the value of considering how different influences across the patient pathway may combine to shape treatment eligibility, feasibility, and acceptability.

Older age (often > 75 years) consistently emerged as a barrier to SACT uptake [–, , –], however chronological age alone cannot fully explain variation in treatment access []. Rather, age may reflect underlying factors such as performance status, comorbidity burden and perceptions of treatment benefit and tolerability. Evidence from other cancer populations, including non-small cell lung cancer [] and prostate cancer [], suggests that age itself may disproportionately influence clinician decision-making, highlighting the potential for age-related bias and the need for more individualised assessment frameworks.

Our review also suggests that female patients are less likely to receive SACT [, ]. This disparity is not explained by biological factors in the included literature and may instead reflect variation in clinician recommendation or patient preference, consistent with evidence that gender shapes treatment decision making in mesothelioma []. Similar patterns have been reported in other cancer populations, such as breast [] and gastroesophageal cancers [], further supporting the role of non-clinical factors in shaping treatment uptake. The predominance of male participants across the included studies is also consistent with the epidemiology of mesothelioma, which disproportionately affects men [].

Clinical factors also played a role in determining access to SACT, although their influence was not always consistent. The impact of tumour histology, stage of disease, and symptom management on treatment decisions was inconclusive [, , ]. This indicates variability in clinical interpretation and practice. In contrast, performance status emerged as a more consistent clinical determinant of access to SACT [, , ]. However, good performance status alone did not guarantee access to SACT. Decisions were also shaped by patient preference and clinician judgement, including the tension between initiating treatment early and waiting for symptom progression [] against the risk of rapid deterioration []. These findings show that clinical eligibility, while necessary, is insufficient to explain variation in SACT uptake without consideration of broader decision-making influences.

Decision-making surrounding SACT was further influenced by informational factors and the dynamics of clinician-patient interactions. Patient choice impacted treatment decisions with some patients declining treatment when clinically eligible [], often due to uncertainty about benefit and a desire to preserve quality of life [, ]. Nevertheless, refusal of treatment does not necessarily reflect fully informed choice. Qualitative evidence highlights the influential role of clinician opinion, peer support and concerns regarding the adequacy and balance of information provision [, ]. Therapeutic nihilism among clinicians emerged as a barrier to treatment recommendation, with some clinicians identifying doubt regarding the value of chemotherapy in mesothelioma [].

The limited exploration of information provision and communication processes within the mesothelioma literature represents an important gap. Across rare cancer populations, information needs are often unmet [], with patients reporting difficulties accessing disease-specific, tailored information to support treatment decision-making []. Rare cancer patients commonly seek information on treatment options, side effects and decision-making support, yet report that available information does not meet their needs as it is overly generic or lacking detail []. Limited health literacy and challenges in appraising online information may further compound these issues. In this context, clinicians and specialist nurses play a critical role in supporting informed treatment decisions. However, variation in access to specialist expertise may influence patients' ability to make informed choices, potentially contributing to differences in treatment uptake.

In addition to individual and decision-making factors, structural barriers played a critical role in shaping access to SACT. Delayed diagnosis and failure to refer patients for oncology review emerged as critical points at which access to SACT could be lost [, ]. Geographic variation in SACT uptake further highlights inequities in care delivery that are unexplained by patient or disease characteristics alone [, ]. Such disparities are consistent with wider rare cancer literature, which identifies fragmented care pathways, limited specialist expertise [, ] and a lack of high-quality evidence [] as barriers to optimal treatment and timely referral [, ].

These findings align with current policy priorities in England and internationally. The 2026 National Cancer Plan for England [] identifies rare cancers as a key contributor to cancer mortality and highlights variation in access to specialist and innovative treatments. Similarly, Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan [] recognises inequalities in access to cancer treatment across Europe and the importance of improving access to specialist services for people with rare and complex cancers. At a global level, the World Health Organisation’s Global Status Report on Cancer [] also highlights persistent inequalities in access to cancer services and the need for more equitable, patient-centred care. Mesothelioma exemplifies these challenges, reinforcing the relevance of these findings to address inequities in access to SACT in cancer care.

Taken together, the findings of this review highlight that barriers to SACT access are compounding rather than discrete, consistent with recent evidence that patient barriers to SACT interact to amplify disadvantage []. Notably, social determinants of health, including socioeconomic status, ethnicity, health literacy, and social support, were largely absent from the mesothelioma literature despite strong evidence from other cancer populations linking these factors to treatment access [–]. This represents a key evidence gap and limits a full understanding of inequities in SACT access.

This review has several limitations. The evidence base was predominantly observational and heterogeneous, with some findings inconsistent or inconclusive. Few studies were specifically designed to examine access to or uptake of SACT, with relevant findings often reported as secondary outcomes. Interpretation is further complicated by the frequent delivery of SACT alongside other treatment modalities, reflecting real-world practice but limiting the ability to disentangle factors influencing access to SACT specifically. In addition, the definition and availability of SACT have evolved over time and vary across settings. Almost all studies reflect chemotherapy-based treatment, whereas contemporary practice increasingly includes immunotherapy following changes in clinical guidance in the UK and internationally, including recommendations from the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in 2021 [], European Society for Medical Oncology [] and the American Society of Clinical Oncology []. This temporal and contextual variation contributes to heterogeneity across the evidence base. Furthermore, some sub-themes were informed by a small number of studies and should be interpreted with caution. Finally, although structured search processes with replicable methods were used, some relevant studies may have been missed, including non-English language publications due to resource constraints.

Improving access to SACT for mesothelioma patients will require coordinated interventions across clinical and system levels. Priorities include timely diagnosis, early oncology referral, and equitable access to mesothelioma-experienced multidisciplinary teams. Proactive oncology assessment and ongoing review would help ensure that treatment options are reviewed regularly throughout the disease trajectory. Addressing therapeutic nihilism through clinician education and evidence-informed guidance may support more balanced, patient-centred treatment discussions. Investment in mesothelioma clinical nurse specialist roles may further enhance information provision, symptom management, shared decision-making, and care coordination, while facilitating access to peer support for patients navigating complex treatment pathways.

This review highlights the need for robust, prospectively designed studies examining barriers and facilitators to SACT access in mesothelioma. Future research should prioritise prospective and intervention-based designs, incorporate patient-reported experiences and evaluate strategies aimed at reducing inequities in access to and uptake of treatment. Notably, the evidence base is heavily weighted towards chemotherapy, with only one study including immunotherapy. This represents a significant gap, particularly given the increasing use of immunotherapy in mesothelioma care. Further research is therefore needed to understand access to, and uptake of, immunotherapy to treat mesothelioma and how this may introduce new or differing inequities in treatment pathways.

Access to and uptake of SACT among people with mesothelioma is shaped by intersecting demographic, clinical, informational, and healthcare system factors. Addressing these disparities will require earlier referral pathways, equitable access to specialist multidisciplinary teams and enhanced patient-centred decision making. Understanding the cumulative nature of these barriers is essential for developing targeted interventions to improve equity in mesothelioma care.

medicine.title: Metabolic syndrome and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic links and precision prevention (Review)
medicine.abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD), however, the majority of previous studies regard MetS as an isolated risk factor and focus on single pathways, lacking systematic understanding of combined effects among multiple metabolic components. The present review systematically summarizes the multifaceted mechanisms by which MetS promotes AD pathology, including insulin resistance and cerebral energy dysregulation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation and glial cell activation, vascular dysfunction and dysregulation of the renin-angiotensin system, as well as the central convergent signaling pathway involving glycogen synthase kinase-3β. The present review further highlights emerging regulatory mechanisms involving the gut-brain axis, epigenetic reprogramming, sex differences and hormonal effects and senescent microenvironment. By emphasizing the peripheral-central crosstalk and interactive amplification of MetS components, the present review aimed to position AD as a central manifestation of systemic metabolic disorders in the brain and propose a multi-domain precision strategy integrating lifestyle intervention, metabolic drug repurposing, gut microbiota regulation, anti-aging therapy and biomarker-guided subtype classification for intervention against MetS-associated AD.
medicine.text:
Metabolic syndrome (MetS) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), major global public health challenges, are widely acknowledged by the academic community to have a complex, bidirectional promoting association (,). MetS comprises a cluster of interconnected risk factors associated with cardiovascular disease and diabetes, including abnormal glucose metabolism, elevated blood pressure and triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and obesity (particularly central obesity) (). Its pathogenesis may involve defects in adipocyte differentiation and increased visceral fat, triggering reactive oxygen species (ROS) production via nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate oxidase activation, leading to oxidative stress. This decreases levels of anti-inflammatory adiponectin, and increases the release of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, IL-6, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL), culminating in inflammation and thrombosis (). AD is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive memory loss and dementia, with pathological hallmarks including amyloid Aβ deposition, neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), neuronal loss, synaptic dysfunction and brain atrophy; AD is influenced by various factors such as genetics, aging, hypertension and diabetes (,).

MetS and its components are risk factors for the development of AD. A prospective cohort study showed that individuals with MetS have a 25% higher risk of dementia, with the risk increasing alongside the number of MetS components (). Other research has linked MetS and its components with an increased risk of young-onset dementia (). In addition, a predominantly USA-based cohort of patients with subclinical MetS showed a higher probability of developing neurocognitive decline, AD and associated dementias, with an even higher risk when cerebral small-vessel disease was present (). How MetS influences AD requires further investigation. Current research is often limited to single pathways or late-stage interventions, failing to elucidate the cascade from systemic metabolic disturbances to brain injury and lacking an integrated preventive and therapeutic perspective encompassing risk prediction, early intervention and precision treatment.

To overcome the aforementioned limitations, the present review aimed to outline the pathophysiological mechanisms of MetS-driven AD and propose precise strategies ranging from basic lifestyle interventions to metabolic drugs that improve AD pathology, including targeted therapies to provide new insights for breaking the cycle between MetS and AD and achieving early prevention and treatment of AD.

Insulin is a key hormone regulating glucose, lipid and protein metabolism, modulating blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake, enhancing glycogen and lipid synthesis and inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipolysis (). When insulin sensitivity or signal responsiveness declines, IR develops (). IR is classified into primary and secondary types based on its pathogenesis: Primary insulin resistance results from genetic defect with compensatory hyperinsulinemia and cannot be fully reversed by weight loss. Secondary IR is caused by acquired factors such as obesity (particularly visceral obesity), adipose tissue hypoplasia or dysfunction, excessive secretion of glucagon, hyperglycemia and certain medications, with obesity being the most common cause (). Adipose tissue dysfunction (excessive lipolysis, inflammation, hypoxia and macrophage infiltration) serves a key role in the onset and progression of obesity-associated IR (), which is a crucial pathological basis for the impact of MetS on the central nervous system.

In the central nervous system, insulin and insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-1/2 signaling are key for brain energy metabolism, synaptic plasticity and cognitive function (). Expression of insulin, IGF-1/2 and their receptors is notably reduced in the brain tissue of patients with AD, particularly in the hippocampus and hypothalamus (). Disrupted insulin signaling promotes the activation of the Aβ precursor protein/Aβ pathway, increasing Aβ production. Excess insulin competitively inhibits insulin-degrading enzyme, impairing Aβ clearance and accelerating amyloid plaque formation (). In the absence of overt peripheral metabolic abnormality, local brain IR can directly impair synaptic transmission and nural plasticity by decreasing the expression and phosphorylation levels of glutamate receptor subunits (). Furthermore, IR induced by a high-fat diet (HFD) leads to abnormal palmitoylation of the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolep ropionic acid receptor subunit Glutamate receptor subunit GluA1 via activation of the forkhead box O3a signaling axis, hindering its membrane surface transport, thereby inhibiting long-term potentiation and impairing learning and memory function () ().

Previous studies have confirmed that oxidative stress precedes Aβ deposition and NFT formation () and impaired energy metabolism occurs before cognitive deficit in early AD (), suggesting that oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction may be early drivers of the AD pathological cascade. Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to an imbalance in the electron transport chain and ROS production (). MetS contributes to decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity and membrane potential and excessive ROS production through multiple pathways, including impaired glucose use, inhibited insulin signaling, disordered fatty acid metabolism, a positive feedback loop between inflammation and ROS and compromised mitophagy (,). ROS and mitochondrial damage reinforce each other, leading to an energy crisis, accelerated Aβ and τ pathology, activation of neuroinflammation and ultimately contributing to AD development.

ROS promotes oxidative modification of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) protein. Mitochondrial energy deficit upregulates the β-secretase activity of β-site APP cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) activity, making oxidized APP protein more susceptible to cleavage by β-secretase, leading to increased Aβ production (). ROS inhibits serine/threonine-protein phosphatase 2A and activates glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β), promoting τ hyperphosphorylation and NFT formation (). Mitochondria are trafficked to synaptic compartments within neurons to sustain neuronal growth and development. Mitochondrial damage leads to neuronal energy crisis, subsequently decreasing synaptic plasticity (). This effect on synaptic memory is associated with interactive regulation involving the cAMP response element-binding protein/regulator of calcineurin 1 pathway (,). Damaged mitochondria release mitochondrial DNA and ROS as damage-associated molecular patterns, thus activating the NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 inflammasome, and producing IL-1β and TNF-α, which exacerbate Aβ and τ pathology (,). These interconnected steps form a cycle from MetS to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to Aβ/τ pathology, neuronal death, cognitive decline and ultimately manifesting as AD.

Silent information regulator 2-like protein 3 (SIRT3) is a NAD+-dependent deacetylase primarily localized in mitochondria that serves important roles in cellular metabolism, energy homeostasis, oxidative stress, autophagy and cell survival (). As the most abundant mitochondrial deacetylase expressed in the nervous system, SIRT3 regulates electron transport chain activity, stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and enhances antioxidant capacity (). In MetS models, blood glucose, fatty acids and inflammatory signals inhibit SIRT3 expression or activity, leading to mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation, increased ROS and accelerated mitochondrial metabolic dysregulation (,), rendering neurons more vulnerable to Aβ and τ pathology, and accelerating AD progression.

MetS is not a static condition but a dynamic state of bodily disturbance accompanied by inflammation. This inflammation disrupts peripheral and central immune homeostasis, particularly microglial function, and converts metabolic crisis into pathological catastrophe in the brain, driving the onset and progression of AD ().

Obesity, the primary pathological phenotype of MetS, represents a chronic stress state in adipose tissue (,). Adipocyte hypertrophy or local hypoxia induces macrophage infiltration, prompting the coordinated release of pro-inflammatory adipokines and forming a local 'inflammatory storm' (). Damaged adipose tissue secretes TNF-α and IL-6, inducing persistent low-grade chronic inflammation (,). Monocytes are recruited to adipose tissue and polarize into pro-inflammatory M1-type macrophages, releasing IL-1β, IL-18 and ROS, thus continuously amplifying inflammatory signals (). Metabolic abnormality and inflammatory responses exhibit a positive feedback association: Inflammatory factors such as TNF-α interfere with insulin receptor substrate tyrosine phosphorylation, inhibiting insulin signal transduction and exacerbating IR (,). Hyperglycemia and free fatty acids activate classical inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB (), forming a vicious cycle where metabolic abnormalities induce inflammation, and inflammation exacerbates metabolic disorder.

Against a backdrop of sustained systemic inflammation, peripheral inflammatory signals affect the central nervous system through multiple routes. Inflammatory factors can directly enter the brain when the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is compromised. With an intact BBB, peripheral inflammation activates brain endothelial cells, 'transducing' the inflammatory signal to the central nervous system (,). Microglia chronically exposed to inflammatory stimuli become hyperactivated, polarizing into a neurotoxic disease-associated phenotype (). In AD, hyperactivated microglia exhibit three aspects of dysfunction: i) Impaired phagocytic clearance, which decreases Aβ clearance efficiency; ii) sustained release of ROS and pro-inflammatory factors damaging neurons and synapses; and iii) aberrantly enhanced synaptic pruning, which non-selectively engulfs functional synapses (,). Microglia can transform into an anti-inflammatory phenotype under specific microenvironments; therefore, regulating microglial phenotypic balance, rather than simply inhibiting their activation, is a potential therapeutic strategy for MetS-associated AD ().

Inflammatory factors released by microglia (such as IL-1β and TNF-α) activate astrocytes, shifting them from a supportive phenotype to a pro-inflammatory state, impairing metabolic and nutritional support for neurons and secreting inflammatory mediators (). Activated astrocytes typically form a 'glial barrier' around Aβ plaques, potentially hindering pathological protein clearance and enhancing plaque neurotoxicity. Sustained inflammatory signaling activates inflammasomes through dysregulated autophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction, driving neurodegeneration ().

Systemic metabolic disturbance and chronic inflammation associated with MetS persistently activate RAS, disrupting cerebrovascular homeostasis and promoting neurodegeneration. RAS comprises renin, Ang, Ang-converting enzyme (ACE) and Ang II (), functionally divided into the classical axis [ACE-Ang II-Ang II type 1 receptor (AT1R)], mediating vasoconstriction, inflammation and oxidative stress, and the protective axis [ACE2-Ang-(-)-Mas], promoting vasodilation and anti-inflammation. These two axes maintain dynamic balance under physiological conditions, however, in the context of MetS, visceral fat expresses and releases nearly all RAS components via autocrine and paracrine mechanisms (,). Adipocyte hypertrophy and hypoxia in obesity enhance the production of renin, ACE and Ang II (). Simultaneously, high levels of free fatty acids and ox-LDL induce the overexpression of AT1R and increase Ang II generation by activating the chymase pathway in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, amplifying classical RAS axis activity in endothelial cells and macrophages (,).

Persistent overactivation of RAS is associated with cognitive decline (). In brain tissue of patients with AD, the expression of ACE, Ang II and AT1R is enhanced, and elevated cerebrospinal fluid ACE levels are associated with the degree of Aβ deposition (). Mechanistically, Ang II upregulates BACE1 () and γ-secretase activity (), thus promoting Aβ generation, and promotes abnormal τ phosphorylation via GSK-3β activation (). At the vascular level, sustained vasoconstriction and decreased nitric oxide bioavailability mediated by Ang II cause chronic cerebral hypoperfusion, impair lymphatic system function and compromise Aβ clearance (). Additionally, Ang II-induced oxidative stress and inflammation disrupt tight junctions in cerebrovascular endothelial cells (), leading to structural and functional damage to the BBB, facilitating the entry of peripheral inflammatory factors and neurotoxic substances into the brain parenchyma, hindering Aβ efflux to the periphery and further exacerbating neuroinflammation and plaque deposition (). As excessive RAS activation contributes to cognitive decline, RAS inhibition may improve cognitive function in selected populations. For instance, brain-penetrating ACE inhibitors can slow AD progression (), and RAS modulation delays the conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to AD (). Nevertheless, these beneficial effects are strongly modulated by host factors such as genetic background. Cognitive protection conferred by ACE inhibitors is only observed in individuals without the APOE ε4 allele (ApoE4) (). Notably, MetS-associated RAS imbalance does not act on the vascular system in isolation, but mutually amplifies the chronic inflammatory state, activates glial cells and induces brain IR, thus promoting AD development along the 'metabolic-vascular-immune axis' (). Therefore, RAS should be considered as a key pathological node in AD rather than a single therapeutic target ().

GSK-3 is a multifunctional serine/threonine kinase, which was initially named for its role in glycogen metabolism (). GSK-3 has two primary isozymes, with GSK-3β associated with body metabolism and brain development (). GSK-3β is primarily involved in the Wingless (Wnt)/β-catenin, NF-κB and phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B pathways (,) and acts as a downstream effector of the insulin signaling Akt pathway. IR inactivates Akt, leading to GSK-3β hyperactivation (). The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is a key regulatory network for maintaining the function of neurons, oligodendrocytes and microglia (). Under inflammatory conditions, hyperactivated GSK-3β promotes microglial polarization towards a pro-inflammatory phenotype, releasing inflammatory factors () and induces vascular inflammation, disrupts the BBB and Aβ clearance and promotes mitochondrial dysfunction triggering neuronal apoptosis (-).

GSK-3β is a key enzyme mediating AD pathology (). As one of the most important τ protein kinases in the body, activated GSK-3β can directly phosphorylate τ protein at multiple sites (), causing τ to detach from microtubules and aggregate into NFTs. Furthermore, GSK-3β modulates γ-secretase activity, promoting the production of the more aggregation-prone Aβ42 (). Notably, Aβ oligomers activate GSK-3β (), creating a cycle. ApoE4 exacerbates AD-like pathology in mice with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) by upregulating GSK-3β activity (). Lithium can inhibit GSK-3β activity, and lithium treatment prevents pathological changes and memory loss in AD and aging wild-type mice (). Furthermore, traditional Chinese medicine formulas, such as Danggui Shaoyao San, serve as GSK-3β inhibitors, participating in reducing AD risk both in vitro and in vivo (,). In summary, GSK-3β is one of the most direct molecular bridges connecting peripheral metabolic disturbance and central nervous system pathology ().

The gut-brain axis refers to the bidirectional signaling pathway between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system. Bidirectional signals exist between the gut and the brain, interacting through neural, hormonal and immune regulation. Within this axis, the brain regulates intestinal motility and secretory functions via the autonomic nervous system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, thereby altering the gut microbial environment (,). Conversely, the gut GM serves a dominant role through the enteric nervous system, the vagus nerve and its metabolites (short-chain fatty acids) (). Therefore, the GM is associated with maintaining normal energy metabolism in the brain, and GM dysregulation may increase the risk of neurodegenerative disease. HFD induces GM imbalance in mice and exacerbates cognitive dysfunction in AD mouse models (). Chen et al (), by studying germ-free 3xTg mice, found that GM imbalance exacerbates AD pathology, potentially through induced chronic inflammatory mechanisms. GM imbalance, by enriching pro-inflammatory bacteria such as Bacteroidetes, activates the CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein β/asparagine endopeptidase pathway and polyunsaturated fatty acid-associated neuroinflammation, thus promoting Aβ deposition, τ phosphorylation and microglial activation, worsening AD pathology. Furthermore, GM dysregulation may promote AD development by altering intestinal function, microbial metabolite synthesis and secretion, as well as compromising the integrity of BBB ().

Epigenetics refers to reversible modifications that regulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence; epigenetic modification is a key factor in AD pathogenesis, involving dysregulations in histone modifications, DNA methylation and non-coding RNAs (). Maternal HFD can confer susceptibility to MetS across generations via epigenetic mechanisms, affecting offspring neurodevelopment (). Fusco et al () reported maternal metabolic abnormality decreases offspring histone H3K9ac and H3K4me3 modifications through gametic mechanisms, thereby inhibiting hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression, leading to impaired synaptic plasticity and memory in the offspring. Furthermore, previous studies (-) have found altered methylation levels of multiple genes in the AD brain, particularly genes associated with Aβ metabolism and τ phosphorylation such as APP, BACE1 and microtubule-associated protein τ (MAPT). The APP gene promoter region is demethylated under AD pathology, leading to APP upregulation and increased Aβ deposition (). Simultaneously, BACE1, the key enzyme cleaving APP to produce Aβ, is upregulated by modifications such as hypomethylation, further accelerating Aβ deposition (). MAPT gene is also induced, leading to additional τ protein phosphorylation (). The aforementioned studies indicate that epigenetics directly regulate AD-related gene expression and impair synaptic function, thus triggering neurodegenerative lesions.

Epigenetic modifications require metabolic substrates. Metabolic disturbance directly alters the pool sizes of key metabolites in cells, thereby affecting epigenetic modification levels ().
