The 7 cases spanned earlier-stage presentations to advanced Fontan circulatory failure. Cases 1 and 2 were late presentations with high-pressure or low-output physiology. Case 1 had long-standing severe AVVR while Fontan pressure remained 12-13 mm Hg for years; replacement was performed only after central venous pressure (CVP) rose to 19 mm Hg with AVVR-RF 71% and marked ventricular dilatation. AVVR and end-diastolic volume (EDV) decreased postoperatively, but CVP improved only to 15 mm Hg, and pulmonary vascular resistance index remained elevated. Case 2 underwent replacement after systemic ventricular dysfunction had already developed (AVVR-RF 63%, EDV 217% of normal, EF 31%); recovery was prolonged, with discharge on postoperative day 87, but the patient achieved sustained clinical recovery and remains a long-term survivor.

Cases 4, 5, and 7 represented established Fontan circulatory failure in which pressure was modified by output, therapy, or shunt-related flow. Case 4 had severe common AVVR with AVVR-RF of 32%, low-output arrhythmic decompensation, and intensive diuretic therapy without marked CVP elevation; after replacement, tachyarrhythmia resolved, diuretics were discontinued, and echocardiography showed no significant residual AVVR. Case 5 had recurrent AVVR after systemic tricuspid valve repair, worsening to 45%, with ascites, hemoptysis, positive 99mTc-albumin scintigraphy despite preserved serum albumin (≥4.5 g/dL), indicating subclinical enteric protein loss, and systemic-to-pulmonary collateral flow (SPCF) burden during bosentan exposure; bosentan was discontinued before replacement, and postoperative CMR showed AVVR <5% and EDV 102% of normal. Case 7 had AVVR-RF of 28% with portosystemic-shunt–related high-output physiology, elevated Fontan pressure, and tadalafil exposure; tadalafil was discontinued preoperatively, AVVR decreased to 9% after replacement, and high-output physiology persisted but was clinically stabilized.

Cases 3 and 6 were the earlier-stage presentations. Case 3 underwent replacement when CVP had begun to rise to 14 mm Hg and CMR showed AVVR-RF of 57% with EDV 120% of normal, before overt end-organ injury; the postoperative stay was 25 days. Case 6 underwent replacement before marked Fontan pressure elevation, based on AVVR-RF of 37%, ventricular enlargement, and early pump dysfunction despite CVP of approximately 9 mm Hg, followed by discharge on postoperative day 37.

Catheterization provided the pressure-resistance context, whereas CMR quantified AVVR severity, ventricular volume, and flow burden ( and ,  and ). Preoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was not routine because it generally required general anesthesia; 4-dimensional cardiac CT was used for valve morphology and repairability. Intraoperative TEE reassessed repairability and guided repair vs replacement. EF was interpreted cautiously because it varies with loading conditions and imaging timing after volume unloading. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging was available only in cases 1 and 2: absent in case 1 and present as layered subendocardial and midwall septal enhancement in case 2, precluding systematic assessment.

SPCF and high-output burden were interpreted as modifiers rather than a single unifying mechanism. Preoperative pulmonary vasodilator therapy was used in cases 5 and 7 and was discontinued before replacement when excessive SPCF burden or high-output burden was recognized. Case 7 primarily reflected portosystemic-shunt-related high-output physiology, whereas case 1 had unilateral pulmonary blood flow with anatomically expected collateral burden, and case 2 had substantial relative flow burden in the setting of low systemic output.

All patients underwent systemic AV valve replacement after multidisciplinary discussion. Mechanical prosthetic valves were implanted in all cases, and valve type and size are listed in . In clinical practice, valve intervention was considered when substantial AVVR coexisted with progressive ventricular dilation or dysfunction, rising Fontan pressure, or refractory clinical deterioration, and transplantation was considered when severe ventricular dysfunction appeared unlikely to recover after valve intervention, as in the single transplanted patient (EF 20%); other patients were managed medically with continued surveillance. Repair was preferred when a durable result appeared achievable; replacement was favored when valve morphology, prior repair failure, recurrent regurgitation, clinical instability, or intraoperative assessment suggested that durable repair was unlikely.

Postoperative course varied as summarized in . Cases 1, 2, 4, and 5 had prolonged or complicated courses, whereas cases 3 and 6 had the shortest postoperative stays and less complicated courses (25 and 37 days, respectively). Case 7 required management of bleeding and anticoagulation while high-output physiology persisted. At last follow-up, 6 patients were alive. Case 1 lived independently and worked for many years after replacement but died suddenly at 35 years of age; the mechanism was unknown.

This series offers 4 practical observations based on paired pre- and postoperative physiological assessment. First, systemic AVVR after Fontan completion should be interpreted as a physiological burden, not merely an anatomical valve lesion. In patients with elevated Fontan pressure, paired catheterization showed that systemic AV valve replacement can reduce CVP ( and ). This has not been clearly demonstrated after Fontan completion. Regurgitant severity alone is likewise insufficient: Among 700 post-TCPC patients, 38 had AVVR-RF ≥20% without post-TCPC valve surgery, including 8 with AVVR-RF ≥30%. Serial CMR in cases 5 and 6 suggests that substantial AVVR may precede physiological deterioration (). Because most operated patients had already reached Fontan circulatory failure, practice may have favored late intervention; some unoperated patients with substantial AVVR may represent earlier-stage candidates. Thus, substantial AVVR appears necessary but insufficient; ventricular function and Fontan pressure should guide candidacy and timing.

Second, CVP is informative but insufficient. Cases 4 and 5 showed that low output, aggressive diuresis, altered loading conditions, or flow burden can dissociate measured CVP from overall AVVR-related circulatory stress, despite clinical manifestations such as ascites or hemoptysis. In case 4, outpatient diuretic treatment likely contributed to deceptively low preoperative Fontan pressure. Therefore, elevated or rising CVP may indicate advanced hemodynamic burden, but absence of marked CVP elevation should not reassure clinicians when CMR demonstrates substantial regurgitant-volume burden or when clinical deterioration is evident.

Third, CMR may help translate adult mitral regurgitation principles into decision-making for AVVR after Fontan completion, although adult thresholds should not be directly applied to Fontan physiology., , ,  In Fontan circulation, CMR-derived AVVR-RF, indexed regurgitant volume, indexed EDV, systemic and pulmonary flow indexes (QsI and QpI), and SPCF can characterize a regurgitant-volume-flow phenotype that complements catheter-derived pressure-resistance data. Postoperative recovery tended to be longer in patients with lower preoperative EF and larger ventricles, whereas AVVR-RF showed no comparable ordering (). Although no threshold can be derived from 7 patients, this pattern parallels adult primary mitral regurgitation, in which surgery is recommended before EF falls to ≤60%, and suggests that ventricular function may be more informative than regurgitant severity alone when assessing disease stage. Reduction in indexed AVVR amount was accompanied by a reduction in indexed EDV (), consistent with reverse remodeling after volume unloading.,

Fourth, SPCF or high-output burden may modify AVVR-related volume loading and its response to therapy. Serial CMR may be important when pulmonary vasodilators are used, because pulmonary vascular unloading may coexist with unintended collateral-flow or high-output volume loading. SPCF decreased markedly after bosentan withdrawal in case 5 (0.94-0.31 L/min/m2, with systemic flow index increasing from 1.92 to 2.46 L/min/m2). During this interval, AVVR-RF increased (), and diuretic therapy was unchanged; only after replacement could tolvaptan be discontinued, with marked reduction of ascites. By contrast, high-output physiology persisted in case 7 despite AV valve replacement and ventricular unloading. This provides a plausible mechanism for some of the heterogeneity observed in this case series.

These observations do not imply that a specific CVP, AVVR-RF, EF, or other CMR parameter should define surgical timing. Rather, high-pressure cases show that replacement can improve venous pressure after AVVR-associated decompensation, whereas cases 3 and 6 suggest a potential earlier-stage window for intervention during a rising-pressure or CMR-defined phase, before advanced venous-pressure elevation or overt circulatory failure. Rather than a decision algorithm, they support a conceptual framework weighing 5 domains together: CMR-derived regurgitant burden, ventricular size and function, catheter-derived Fontan pressure and resistance, output and collateral or high-flow burden, and end-organ status with repairability. A formal comparison of medical therapy, surgery, and transplantation was not attempted: Operated and currently unoperated groups differ in observation period and ascertainment, unoperated patients may still proceed to surgery, and only 1 patient underwent transplantation, so retrospective comparison would be dominated by selection bias, confounding by indication, and time-dependent bias. This framework requires multicenter validation.

Limitations include the retrospective single-center design, small sample size, heterogeneous anatomy, inclusion of only 7 of 12 isolated post-TCPC replacements with available preoperative post-TCPC CMR, lack of a nonoperative control group, and variable availability and timing of postoperative CMR. The CMR cohort did not include all 871 patients with Fontan circulation and cannot provide population-level estimates of significant AVVR prevalence. TEE and late gadolinium enhancement were not systematically acquired. Catheter-derived and CMR-derived flows are not interchangeable in Fontan physiology. SPCF estimates are method-dependent, and causality between pulmonary vasodilators, SPCF/high-output physiology, and AVVR progression cannot be proven.  and  are descriptive, and postoperative length of stay is a crude recovery index. Preoperative EF, ventricular size, and age covaried, precluding attribution to any single factor.

In patients after Fontan completion, systemic AVVR can create a potentially modifiable hemodynamic burden across different stages of Fontan circulatory failure. Paired data in this series show that AV valve replacement can markedly reduce AVVR and ventricular volume burden, and lower Fontan pressure in patients with elevated preoperative CVP. However, neither AVVR severity nor CVP alone is sufficient to define candidacy, because low output, aggressive diuresis, SPCF, or high-output physiology may mask or modify the hemodynamic burden. Integrated CMR and catheterization may help characterize disease stage and inform patient selection, although the optimal criteria and timing for intervention remain uncertain.

medicine.title: Carbonization of traditional Chinese medicines: processing strategies, chemical-material transformations, pharmacological activities and clinical applications
medicine.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) processing (Paozhi) is a critical pharmaceutical practice for enhancing the safety, efficacy, and clinical applicability of herbal medicines. Carbonization constitutes a distinctive processing strategy involving controlled thermal treatment that carbonizes the external surfaces while preserving the essential medicinal properties. This transformation not only modifies traditional indications but also expands clinical applications, particularly in the management of hemorrhage, chronic diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disorders and toxin-related conditions. Despite extensive empirical use, the material basis and mechanistic underpinnings of carbonized TCMs remain poorly defined. This review systematically synthesizes current advances in carbonization techniques, chemical and structural transformations and associated pharmacological activities. Emerging evidence indicates that carbonization induces coordinated multi-scale alterations, including the conversion of phytochemical constituents, the formation of porous carbon architectures and the generation of nanoscale carbon-based materials such as carbon dots. These physicochemical transitions are closely linked to bioactivities, including hemostatic effects, gastrointestinal mucosal protection, anti-inflammatory responses, antimicrobial activity and adsorption-related toxin mitigation. Accordingly, carbonized TCMs can be reconceptualized as a unique class of therapeutics arising from the interplay between chemical transformation and carbon-based structural evolution. By integrating traditional processing theory with contemporary insights from phytochemistry, pharmacology and materials science, this review identifies characteristic chemical transformation patterns and potential quality markers, summarizes emerging pharmacological mechanisms and proposes a carbon dot- and porous carbon-based material framework to better understand the therapeutic properties and quality characteristics of carbonized TCMs. Such an integrated perspective provides a foundation for process standardization, quality control and the modernization of evidence-based clinical applications.
medicine.text:
Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) processing, known as Paozhi, is widely used to modify crude herbal materials in order to improve safety, enhance efficacy and refine clinical applications [–]. Among these approaches, carbonization (Tan-Yao) represents a distinctive category in which herbs are subjected to controlled thermal treatment, leading to partial carbonization while preserving their internal bioactivity. These preparations are traditionally used for the management of hemorrhage, chronic diarrhea and gastrointestinal disorders, which remain clinically relevant in multiple therapeutic contexts [].

The use of carbonized materials in medicine dates back over two millennia; however, historical descriptions are largely empirical and lack mechanistic interpretation []. Modern pharmacopoeial inclusion, such as the listing of 27 carbonized TCMs in the 2025 edition of the Pharmacopoeia of the People’s Republic of China (ChP), highlights their continued clinical importance []. Despite this long-standing use, the scientific basis underlying carbonization-induced changes and their contribution to therapeutic effects remains insufficiently defined.

From a processing perspective, the efficacy and consistency of carbonized TCMs depend critically on precise thermal control. Both excessive carbonization (leading to ashing) and insufficient processing can compromise activity. The goal of processing is to achieve partial carbonization while retaining bioactive constituents, thereby balancing transformation and preservation. Recent studies suggest that the therapeutic properties of carbonized TCMs arise from coordinated changes in both chemical composition and material structure. Chemically, thermal treatment induces the transformation of small molecules, including flavonoids, tannins and 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF), as well as alterations in inorganic components [–]. Structurally, carbonization may generate porous carbon-like matrices with increased surface area, which may enhance adsorption of toxins and contribute to mucosal protection.

At the pharmacological level, accumulating evidence indicates that carbonized TCMs exert therapeutic effects through multiple pathways. Hemostatic activity involves vasoconstriction, platelet activation, coagulation cascade modulation and inhibition of fibrinolysis []. In addition, their adsorption properties and anti-inflammatory effects may contribute to gastrointestinal protection and toxin adsorption-related applications. These features may underlie their clinical utility in conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, chemotherapy-induced diarrhea and functional gastrointestinal disorders, where current therapeutic options may present limitations in efficacy or tolerability [, ]. Comparative studies between raw and carbonized herbs have demonstrated substantial differences in both composition and pharmacological properties. For example, carbonized Sanguisorbae radix and Schizonepetae herba exhibited enhanced hemostatic activity, altered tannin/flavonoid profiles, and the formation of carbonized structures or carbon dot-like nanostructures compared with their corresponding raw materials [–].

However, the reproducibility and standardization of carbonized TCMs remain major challenges. The properties of carbonized products are strongly influenced not only by processing parameters, such as heating temperature, duration and equipment type, but also by the intrinsic variability of the raw herbal materials, including species origin and harvesting season. In current practice, reproducibility is primarily controlled through standardized processing procedures defined in pharmacopeias, together with endpoint characteristics such as color, texture, odor and selected chemical markers. However, these approaches remain insufficient to fully capture the complex chemical and structural changes induced by carbonization. Although modern analytical approaches, including chromatographic fingerprinting, electronic sensory systems and carbon structure characterization, have been introduced to improve quality control, no universally accepted standard currently exists for defining the optimal degree of carbonization or ensuring batch-to-batch consistency. Nevertheless, several key questions remain unresolved. It is still unclear which chemical or structural features are primarily responsible for the therapeutic effects of many carbonized TCMs, whether carbon dots are genuine active substances, and how processing-induced changes correlate with clinical efficacy and safety. In addition, the lack of standardized processing protocols and systematic toxicological evaluation further limits mechanistic interpretation and clinical translation.

Despite growing interest, current research remains fragmented, with limited integration of processing science, material characterization, pharmacological mechanisms and clinical evidence. To address this gap, this review systematically summarizes recent advances in carbonized TCMs, covering processing technologies, physicochemical properties, compositional changes, pharmacological activities and clinical applications. By integrating traditional knowledge with modern scientific evidence, this work aims to provide a clearer framework for understanding carbonized TCMs and to support their standardization and evidence-based clinical use.

A comprehensive literature search was conducted using PubMed, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data databases. The search terms included combinations of “carbonized traditional Chinese medicine”, “charred herbal medicine”, “Tan-Yao”, “carbonization processing”, “炭药”, “炒炭”, “carbon dots” and related terms. Publications from database inception to March 2026 were considered. Both English- and Chinese-language studies were included to ensure broad coverage of historical records, pharmacopeial standards, phytochemical analyses, pharmacological studies and emerging materials-related research on carbonized TCMs. This review primarily included studies focusing on processing technologies, chemical and structural transformations, pharmacological activities, material characterization and clinical applications of carbonized herbal medicines. Conference abstracts lacking sufficient experimental details, duplicate publications and studies unrelated to medicinal carbonization processing were excluded. As the available evidence remains heterogeneous and mechanistic studies are still emerging, this work was conducted as a narrative review with a scoping perspective rather than a systematic review.

Historically, carbonized TCMs were prepared by manual stir-frying or calcination. Since the 1980s, industrialization has shifted this process toward standardized and mechanized production. Modern systems, including drum roasters and electromagnetic heating devices, enable more uniform heat transfer and reduce variability associated with manual operation [, ]. Microwave-assisted processing has recently emerged as an alternative approach. By enabling rapid volumetric heating, this technique shortens processing time by 30–50% compared with conventional methods [, ].

In parallel, process optimization has increasingly relied on multivariate experimental designs, such as orthogonal arrays and response surface methodology, to systematically define key parameters, including temperature, duration, rotation speed, and material loading (Table ).

Optimization of carbonized TCM processing technologies

“–” The specific processing equipment information was not clearly reported in this study

Stir-frying remains the most widely used method for producing carbonized TCMs (Fig. ). The desired endpoint is typically characterized by a blackened surface and a partially preserved interior, reflecting controlled surface carbonization. In modern practice, processing conditions are optimized using integrated criteria, including visual characteristics, chemical markers and bioactivity (e.g., hemostatic assays). For example, a systematic study on Sanguisorbae radix charcoal optimized the carbonization process based on hemostatic efficacy and comprehensive chemical characterization. The results showed that stir-frying at 250°C for 14 min produced material consistent with the ChP appearance characteristics and exhibited significantly enhanced coagulation and blood adsorption activities compared with the raw material and over-carbonized products. In particular, ellagic acid content and powder color difference values showed strong correlations with the hemostatic effect, suggesting their potential utility as processing and quality control markers for Sanguisorbae radix charcoal [].

Effective carbonization generally requires temperatures above 200°C, although optimal duration varies depending on material properties such as texture and moisture content [, , ]. Notably, significant variations in optimal stir-frying temperature and time for the same herb have been reported in different studies, such as those in Scutellariae radix. These discrepancies may be due to differences in herb origin, slice specifications, stir-frying equipment and evaluation indicators—some studies focused on hemostatic activity, while others prioritized active ingredient retention, leading to deviations in the selection of optimal parameters. Future studies should unify evaluation standards to reduce experimental heterogeneity. This processing method has been widely applied in industrial production. Modern manufacturing commonly employs automated electromagnetic stir-frying machines or rotary drum-type processing equipment with electric or gas heating systems. These devices enable precise temperature control and bidirectional stirring, while some systems are additionally equipped with flue gas exhaust functions to improve process stability and operational safety.

Calcination involves heating under limited-oxygen conditions to induce pyrolysis without combustion. This approach is particularly suitable for lightweight or porous materials such as Junci medulla and Nelumbinis folium that are difficult to process by stir-frying [, ]. In modern practice, traditional mud- or bamboo-sealed calcination has been largely superseded by TCM calcination furnaces, which offer precise regulation of temperature and atmospheric conditions. For example, tilting calcining pots and programmable calcining furnaces have been widely used in pharmaceutical enterprises for the production of carbonized TCM decoction pieces. Optimization focuses on temperature, duration, and the packing density (material-to-container volume ratio), utilizing carbon yield and morphological integrity as primary indices. For instance, the optimal calcination protocol for Junci medulla charcoal entailed heating at 250°C for 15 min (3 g/L load), while Nelumbinis folium charcoal required a lower temperature of 140°C for 20 min to maximize extract content and hemostatic activity [, ].

Sand-heating uses sand as a heat-transfer medium to ensure uniform heating and prevent localized overheating. This method is particularly suitable for dense or structurally sensitive materials. It also reduces smoke generation and improves processing conditions. Optimization typically focuses on the sand-to-material ratio, temperature and agitation. Under optimized conditions, this method enables rapid carbonization while retaining a relatively high level of bioactive constituents []. Nevertheless, its substitutability still requires further validation. Currently, due to limitations in applicable varieties, sand-heating carbonization remains mainly at the laboratory or pilot-scale research stage.

Baking employs controlled oven heating to achieve stable and uniform carbonization. It is particularly suitable for heat-sensitive materials that require precise temperature control. Studies have shown that optimized baking conditions can enhance hemostatic activity, with efficacy strongly dependent on temperature–time combinations [, ]. Baking carbonization is an emerging carbonization method mainly at the laboratory stage, and further studies involving additional carbonized TCM varieties are still needed to evaluate its applicability and rationality.

Microwave-assisted carbonization generates heat internally through electromagnetic interactions, enabling rapid and energy-efficient processing. This method is especially advantageous for thermolabile materials. Careful control of microwave power and exposure time is essential, as these parameters directly influence both chemical retention and structural formation. Optimized conditions can improve both bioactive compound preservation and adsorption capacity. For example, moderate microwave-assisted carbonization of Sophorae fructus increased both the content of kaempferide and the adsorption capacity of the processed product, whereas excessive heating resulted in a decline in kaempferide content []. Similarly, microwave-assisted carbonization of Gardeniae fructus retained higher levels of geniposide and tannins compared with traditional processing while maintaining comparable hemostatic activity []. Although microwave-assisted carbonization demonstrates advantages in energy efficiency and processing speed, its application remains largely confined to laboratory-scale or pilot-scale studies due to challenges related to penetration uniformity, equipment standardization and scale-up validation.

Although various carbonization techniques have been developed, process control during carbonized TCM production remains less systematically discussed than processing methods themselves. Traditionally, the endpoint of carbonization has been judged mainly by empirical indicators, including color change, odor, smoke intensity and texture. These sensory criteria are practically useful but highly operator-dependent and difficult to standardize, particularly during scale-up production.

Recent studies have attempted to introduce process analytical technology (PAT)-oriented approaches to quantify and control the carbonization process []. Temperature is one of the most critical process parameters. Non-contact infrared thermometry has therefore been introduced into stir-frying equipment to continuously monitor both the heating surface and material temperature, allowing dynamic regulation of heating power, drum rotation, feeding and discharging. Thermal analysis has also been used to define characteristic temperature ranges and mass-loss stages during carbonization, providing a basis for selecting appropriate processing temperatures [].

In addition to temperature control, visual and spectral monitoring methods have been explored for endpoint evaluation. Colorimetric sensing can convert traditional color descriptions into objective parameters such as L*, a* and b* values. For example, in the stir-frying of Sanguisorbae radix, color parameters were significantly correlated with changes in marker constituents, suggesting that colorimetry may serve as a rapid or online surrogate indicator of processing degree []. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIR) combined with chemometric models has also shown promise for process quality control of carbonized TCMs []. In carbonized Typhae pollen, Fourier transform (FT)-NIR combined with gradient-based discriminant analysis was used to distinguish different carbonization degrees and to identify qualified products during processing [, ]. During heating, monitoring smoke evolution or flue gas composition may therefore provide additional information on dehydration, pyrolysis and over-carbonization. However, compared with temperature, color and NIR-based approaches, standardized methods for smoke or flue gas monitoring in carbonized TCM processing are still limited.

Overall, current process control of carbonized TCMs is moving from subjective endpoint judgment toward quantitative and sensor-assisted monitoring. However, most available approaches still focus on individual indicators, such as temperature, color or spectral features. Integrated control systems that link critical process parameters with chemical transformation, carbon structure evolution, adsorption capacity and pharmacological activity remain insufficiently established. Future studies should develop multidimensional PAT frameworks combining real-time temperature monitoring, machine vision or colorimetry, NIR spectroscopy, volatile/smoke analysis and chemometric or artificial intelligence-based feedback control to improve reproducibility and define scientifically grounded carbonization endpoints.

Quality assurance is essential for ensuring the safety and consistency of carbonized TCMs. Current regulations are primarily based on the ChP, supplemented by regional processing standards issued by provinces such as Sichuan, Zhejiang and Beijing. In addition to the 27 carbonized TCMs officially included in the 2025 edition of the ChP, several additional varieties are documented in provincial standards, reflecting regional clinical practices and local medicinal traditions. These systems define evaluation criteria based on macroscopic features, identification methods (e.g., microscopy, TLC), and basic physicochemical parameters (e.g., moisture, ash, extractives) (Table ) [].

Quality standards of carbonized TCMs in the ChP (2025 edition)

“–” The corresponding quality standard items are not clearly specified in the 2025 edition of the ChP.

However, the assessment of carbonization degree remains largely qualitative. The ChP descriptions rely heavily on subjective organoleptic indices, encompassing chromatic characteristics (e.g., Nelumbinis rhizomatis nodus charcoal: “blackish-brown exterior, brownish interior”) textural properties (e.g., Platycladi cacumen charcoal: “brittle and easily fractured”), and olfactory/gustatory profiles (e.g., Schizonepetae herba charcoal: “scorched aroma”; Mume fructus charcoal: “sour with slight bitterness”). The inherent ambiguity of such qualitative descriptors denotes a lack of quantifiable metrics, resulting in significant variability in thermal control parameters across different manufacturers. For example, an analysis of 12 commercial batches of Platycladi cacumen charcoal from different regions revealed substantial variability in carbonization degree, impurity levels and flavonoid contents. Most batches showed evidence of over-carbonization relative to ChP criteria, while quercetin content varied markedly from 0.03–0.72 mg/g, highlighting the challenges of reproducibility and endpoint control in carbonized TCM production [].

Regarding chemical characterization, the majority of monographs still depend on qualitative TLC, with quantitative assays established for only a fraction of varieties. For instance, the ChP specifies that in Rhei radix et rhizoma charcoal, the content of total and free anthraquinones must not be less than 0.90 and 0.50% respectively; similarly, Zingiberis rhizoma charcoal requires a minimum 6-gingerol content of 0.050%. Crucially, a significant number of carbonized TCMs including Dryopteridis crassirhizomatis rhizoma, Cirsii herba, Imperatae rhizoma and Celosiae cristatae flos continue to utilize identification standards derived from their raw counterparts. This practice disregards the specific chemical transformations (e.g., component degradation or generation) induced by carbonization, rendering the quality control specific to the “charcoal” form inadequate. While basic purity parameters (e.g., moisture, total ash, acid-insoluble ash) are mandated for some entries, comprehensive testing requirements remain absent for more than half of the listed varieties. As a result, current quality systems do not adequately reflect the unique chemical characteristics of carbonized products.

Furthermore, regulatory coverage remains incomplete. The ChP currently encompasses less than one-third of the carbonized TCMs traditionally employed in clinical practice, leaving widely prescribed items such as Gardeniae fructus charcoal, Lonicerae japonicae flos charcoal and Crataegi fructus charcoal without unified national standards. Although recent studies have proposed potential quality markers, such as 5-HMF, melanoidins, oxidized tannins and inorganic components, these indicators have not yet been incorporated into official specifications.

Traditional quality assessment of carbonized TCMs relies heavily on sensory evaluation, including color, odor and taste. While effective in practice, this approach is subjective and lacks reproducibility. To address these limitations, modern quality control increasingly integrates analytical technologies, including biomimetic sensing, spectroscopy, chromatography and pharmacological evaluation (Fig. ). These approaches enable quantitative characterization of both chemical composition and functional activity.

Biomimetic systems, such as electronic eye, nose and tongue, translate sensory attributes into measurable signals. These technologies convert subjective sensory evaluation into reproducible, data-driven metrics, supporting process control and standardization.

Color analysis (e-eye) quantifies changes during carbonization using standardized color parameters (L* for lightness, a* for the red-green axis and b* for the yellow-blue axis). These parameters correlate with both processing degree and chemical composition, and can serve as non-destructive quality indicators []. Generally, increasing degrees of carbonization correlate with a progressive decline in lightness (L*), while a* and b* values exhibit material-specific trajectories that align with processing intensity. For instance, during the processing of Angelicae sinensis radix, the gradual visual transition from light yellow–brown to deep black is quantitatively reflected by decreasing L*, b* and total color difference (ΔEab*) values []. In Sanguisorbae radix, significant negative correlations between chromatic parameters and processing time have been established; specifically, a ΔEab* value exceeding 18 serves as an objective endpoint indicator, aligning with the morphological criteria of the ChP []. Critically, these colorimetric parameters extend beyond phenotypic characterization, serving as predictors of chemical composition and bioactivity. In Typhae pollen, the degradation of typhaneoside and isorhamnetin-3-O-neohesperidoside correlates positively with L*, b* and Eab* values []. Similarly, in Lonicerae japonicae flos, the reduction of flavonoids (luteoloside, rutin) and chlorogenic acid derivatives parallels changes in lightness and yellowness []. Furthermore, specific chromatic ranges can pinpoint optimal efficacy; in Cirsii japonici herba carbonisata, samples falling within defined ranges of L* (36.36–40.05) and a* (6.97–7.56) exhibit maximal levels of the hemostatic flavonoids pectolinarigenin and linarin, coinciding with peak coagulation activity []. These findings validate the utility of chromatic parameters as non-destructive surrogates for quality control.

E-nose technology employs sensor arrays to create holistic fingerprints of volatile components, utilizing pattern recognition algorithms to discriminate between processing stages. During the carbonization of Platycladi cacumen, sensors targeting aromatics (W1C), amines (W3C) and short-chain alkanes (W5C) show intensified responses, while alcohol/ketone-sensitive sensors (W2S) decline. This shift quantitatively reflects the attenuation of fresh herbal fragrances and the accumulation of pyrolysis-derived roasted notes, offering objective criteria for defining processing endpoints []. Similarly, in Moutan cortex charcoal, chemometric integration with support vector machine (SVM) models identified nitrogen oxides, short-chain alkanes and sulfides as principal differential odor constituents, enabling accurate quality prediction across different carbonization stages [].

E-tongue systems simulate human gustatory perception to profile attributes such as sourness, saltiness, astringency and bitterness. Carbonization typically simplifies the taste profile while enhancing specific therapeutic flavors. In Platycladi cacumen charcoal, the astringency-to-aftertaste ratio escalates dramatically (from 2.23 to 30.8), indicating the thermal degradation of macromolecular tannins into small-molecule polyphenols. Concurrently, increased saltiness and diminished bitterness likely reflect the release of inorganic cations and the volatilization of bitter principles, respectively []. For Crataegi fructus charcoal, a marked attenuation in acidic response aligns with the decomposition of organic acids, while enhanced saltiness and bitterness correlate with the liberation of inorganic ions and the formation of Maillard reaction products [].

Collectively, biomimetic sensory technologies enable the multidimensional, quantitative characterization of key quality attributes, transforming ephemeral experiential judgments into reproducible, quantitative metrics. These methodologies hold significant potential for process optimization and standard formulation, effectively bridging the gap between traditional pharmaceutical wisdom and contemporary analytical rigor. Despite their promising applications, biomimetic sensing technologies such as e-nose and e-tongue still face limitations in reproducibility and transferability. Variations in sensor materials, environmental humidity and temperature, signal preprocessing, and model calibration may affect inter-instrument and inter-laboratory consistency. Therefore, further standardization of sensor systems, data preprocessing protocols, and validation procedures is still required to improve the reproducibility of biomimetic sensing technologies.

Spectroscopic methods, particularly NIR and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), provide rapid and non-destructive assessment of carbonization. During thermal processing, characteristic spectral changes associated with O–H, C–H and carbohydrate-related absorption bands reflect dehydration, decomposition of polysaccharides and phenolic constituents, and progressive carbonization of herbal materials. In studies of Typhae pollen charcoal and Rhei radix et rhizoma charcoal, NIR spectral variations were successfully correlated with different carbonization stages and processing degrees [, ]. In a dynamic study on the carbonization of Typhae pollen, FTIR spectroscopy revealed progressive weakening of hydroxyl-associated absorption bands and aromatic carbon-related signals during carbonization, indicating dehydration, thermal degradation and evolution of aromatic carbon systems [].

Combined with chemometric or machine learning models, spectroscopic techniques enable improved discrimination and quality evaluation of carbonized TCMs. For instance, an SVM model developed using NIR spectra from 186 batches of Typhae pollen charcoal achieved classification accuracies exceeding 93% under tenfold cross-validation, with performance evaluated on an independent test set []. A convolutional neural network trained on multi-preprocessed spectral features from 166 samples of Typhae pollen charcoal achieved a recognition accuracy of approximately 95.4% on the validation/test dataset, although the relatively limited sample size may still affect model generalizability []. These advances suggest that spectroscopy-based intelligent analysis may provide promising tools for rapid process monitoring and quality assessment of carbonized TCMs.

Chromatographic techniques, including high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC–MS), remain essential for chemical profiling and identifying transformation pathways []. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS) and GC-ion mobility spectrometry (GC-IMS) analyses further reveal substantial changes in volatile components during carbonization, including the degradation of terpenoids and the formation of furans, aldehydes and other Maillard reaction-related products []. Together, these techniques provide complementary information for understanding chemical transformations and improving quality evaluation of carbonized TCMs.

Pharmacological evaluation is critical for linking quality to therapeutic efficacy. Centered on their traditional hemostatic efficacy, contemporary research has established a comprehensive bioassay framework integrating in vitro screening, in vivo validation, and multidimensional correlation analysis.

In vitro assays focus on critical mechanisms including the coagulation cascade and platelet function, offering rapid, high-throughput screening suitable for process monitoring. The classical coagulation panel, including prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), thrombin time (TT) and fibrinogen (FIB) serves as a fundamental diagnostic metric. Evidence indicates that the degree of carbonization significantly modulates these parameters, with both excessive and insufficient processing failing to optimize hemostatic activity [–]. Consequently, quantitative correlation analysis between coagulation indices and processing variables provides data-driven guidance for production optimization []. Additionally, platelet aggregometry assesses functionality via collagen-induced turbidity changes [].

In vivo models are essential for validating efficacy in complex physiological environments. The tail amputation model remains the most widely adopted approach for direct quantification of bleeding time and blood loss []. For internal hemorrhage, standardized liver or spleen injury models are employed to assess hemostatic intervention []. Furthermore, specific disease models offer targeted insights. For example, statin-induced cerebral hemorrhage in zebrafish provides a high-throughput phenotypic screen [, ], while dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis models enable the simultaneous assessment of hemostasis, anti-inflammatory activity and mucosal healing []. However, these models cannot fully recapitulate human coagulation physiology or the differences in hemostatic effects among types of bleeding; therefore, their relevance to clinical hemostasis requires further verification.

Multidimensional correlation analysis synthesizes biological efficacy data with chemical fingerprints and colorimetric parameters using multivariate statistics. These “spectrum-effect” or “appearance-effect” models demonstrate that the hemostatic activity of carbonized TCMs typically arises from multi-component synergy rather than single-compound action. Studies indicate that specific component ratios or combinations of peak areas exhibit stronger correlations with pharmacodynamic indices than individual markers [, ]. While mathematical modeling linking colorimetric data to biological potency promises rapid, non-destructive quality assessment, colorimetric measurements remain susceptible to instrumental variables [, ]. Therefore, a standardized protocol necessitating cross-validation with chemical profiling and bioassays is essential for quality control.

The therapeutic properties of carbonized TCMs are likely associated with multiple interconnected components, including residual native constituents retained, newly generated transformation products formed during thermal processing, and physicochemical properties of the resulting carbonized matrix. The relative contribution of these components is highly dependent on the degree of carbonization, making process control and reproducibility particularly challenging. Current control strategies mainly rely on standardized processing procedures defined in pharmacopeias, together with endpoint characteristics such as color, texture, odor and selected chemical markers. However, conventional single-marker approaches are often insufficient to fully reflect the complex compositional and structural changes occurring during carbonization.

Therefore, comprehensive analytical approaches are increasingly required for the evaluation of carbonized TCMs. Chemical characterization commonly includes HPLC/UPLC fingerprinting, LC–MS-based compositional analysis, GC–MS analysis of thermal degradation products and quantitative determination of representative constituents. Structural and material characterization methods, including scanning electron microscopy (SEM)/transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), are also increasingly applied to evaluate carbon structure evolution, porosity and surface properties. In addition, functional assays related to adsorption capacity, coagulation activity and pharmacological efficacy are increasingly recognized as important complementary approaches for quality evaluation.

Despite these advances, unified standards integrating chemical, structural and functional characteristics have not yet been established, and defining optimal carbonization endpoints remains a major challenge for the standardization and reproducibility of carbonized TCMs.

Carbonization of TCMs involves a series of thermally driven reactions, typically occurring at 180–250°C. Because different compounds vary in structure and thermal stability, they undergo distinct patterns of degradation, transformation or retention during processing (Table ). These reactions not only reduce or redistribute original constituents, but also generate new compounds that may contribute to pharmacological activity (Fig. ). Together, these changes define the characteristic chemical profile of carbonized TCMs.

Chemical composition changes during carbonization

* Disappeared compounds; † indicates compounds newly formed through thermal reactions during carbonization and absent or present only at trace levels in the raw herbs

Glycosides are among the most common constituents in TCMs and include flavonoid glycosides, anthraquinone glycosides, saponins and iridoid glycosides. Because glycosidic bonds are generally heat-sensitive, carbonization often promotes their cleavage into aglycones and sugar moieties. Under controlled conditions, this process may lead to depletion of glycosides together with relative enrichment of more thermostable aglycones, whereas excessive heating can cause further degradation of both forms.

Flavonoid glycosides are the most extensively studied group in carbonized TCMs. In many herbs, carbonization causes a marked decrease in glycosides and a corresponding increase in their aglycones. For example, in Platycladi cacumen, glycosides such as quercitrin and isoquercitrin decrease substantially after carbonization, whereas aglycones including quercetin and rhamnetin increase significantly [, ]. A similar pattern has been reported in Sophorae flos, where rutin is thermally degraded into quercetin and rutinose, leading to reduced rutin content and increased quercetin levels [, , ]. Comparable changes have also been observed in Nelumbinis folium charcoal, in which quercetin enrichment is associated with degradation of hyperoside, quercitrin and isoquercitrin [, ]. In Scutellariae radix, carbonization promotes conversion of baicalin and wogonoside into baicalein and wogonin respectively [, ]. Overall, these findings indicate that flavonoid glycosides are highly susceptible to thermal cleavage, whereas their aglycones are more likely to be retained or enriched under controlled carbonization.

Anthraquinone glycosides show a similar transformation pattern, although with distinct pharmacological consequences. In raw Rhei radix et rhizoma, conjugated anthraquinones such as sennosides A–D are major contributors to laxative activity. During carbonization, these glycosides are extensively degraded, whereas free anthraquinones (including emodin, chrysophanol, aloe-emodin and rhein) become relatively enriched [, ]. This compositional shift is closely associated with reduced cathartic activity and the emergence of the altered therapeutic profile of carbonized Rhei radix et rhizoma [, ]. A comparable transformation has been reported in Rubiae radix et rhizoma, where cleavage of anthraquinone glycosides increases the levels of aglycones such as xanthopurpurin and 6-hydroxyrubiadin [, ].

Saponins and iridoid glycosides also undergo pronounced thermal transformation. In Sanguisorbae radix, pyrolysis of the glucose moiety in ziyuglycoside I leads to the formation of ziyuglycoside II []. Some triterpene aglycones, such as tormentic acid and ursolic acid, are relatively heat-stable and can be largely retained under moderate processing conditions []. By contrast, iridoid glycosides often show poor thermal stability. Compounds such as gardenoside, geniposide and catalpol undergo rapid and often irreversible degradation during carbonization, resulting in a marked decline in total iridoid content [–].

Overall, conversion of glycosides to aglycones represents one of the most common chemical events during carbonization. The relative enrichment of aglycones under optimized carbonization conditions likely contributes to enhanced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and hemostatic activities, providing a crucial chemical basis for the modified pharmacological profiles of carbonized TCMs.

Tannins are a major class of polyphenols widely present in hemostatic TCMs. They are broadly classified into hydrolysable tannins and condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins), which exhibit distinct thermal stability and transformation pathways during carbonization.

Hydrolysable tannins contain ester linkages between phenolic acids (e.g., gallic acid or ellagic acid) and polyols. These ester bonds are thermally labile and readily undergo hydrolysis and pyrolysis during carbonization. As a result, small phenolic acids (primarily gallic acid and ellagic acid) are released and may further undergo secondary reactions such as cyclization or condensation to form derivatives (e.g., sanguisorbic acid dilactone) []. This process leads to a decrease in total tannin content, accompanied by enrichment of low-molecular-weight phenolics with strong antioxidant and protein-precipitating properties. This transformation is consistently observed across multiple materials. For example, in Sanguisorbae radix and Granati pericarpium charcoal, total tannins decrease markedly, while gallic acid and ellagic acid increase significantly [, ]. Similar increases in gallic acid have been reported in Mume fructus, Moutan cortex, and Scutellariae radix charcoal, and these changes are associated with enhanced astringent and hemostatic effects [–].

Condensed tannins, in contrast, are composed of flavan-3-ol units linked by C–C bonds, which confer greater thermal stability. However, at temperatures above ~ 200°C, these polymers undergo gradual depolymerization and oxidation, generating monomeric units (e.g., catechin derivatives) and smaller phenolic compounds such as protocatechualdehyde. For instance, in Sanguisorbae radix charcoal, total proanthocyanidins decrease sharply, while protocatechualdehyde increases substantially [].

Taken together, carbonization drives a shift from macromolecular tannins to low-molecular-weight phenolics. Under optimized conditions, partial retention of tannins maintains astringent and hemostatic functions, while newly formed phenolic acids contribute additional antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. This dual transformation provides an important chemical basis for the therapeutic properties of carbonized TCMs.

Polysaccharides, including starch, cellulose, pectin and heteropolysaccharides, undergo extensive thermochemical transformation during carbonization. These processes include glycosidic bond cleavage, depolymerization, dehydration, decarboxylation, caramelization and Maillard reactions, leading to the formation of a wide range of products from small molecules to polymeric structures.

At early stages, thermal cleavage of glycosidic bonds results in depolymerization into oligosaccharides and monosaccharides. With continued heating, hexoses (glucose, fructose) preferentially dehydrate to form 5-HMF, whereas pentoses (xylose, arabinose) are the primary precursors for furfural formation during thermal processing. These intermediates may further degrade into small carbonyl compounds (e.g., aldehydes and ketones) or participate in condensation reactions [].

Simultaneously, interactions between reducing sugars and amino compounds drive Maillard reactions, while dehydration and polymerization processes contribute to caramelization. These pathways ultimately generate high-molecular-weight products such as melanoidins and caramel-like pigments, which are closely associated with the characteristic color and aroma of carbonized materials. In Crataegi fructus, Imperatae rhizoma and Rhei radix et rhizoma, carbonization leads to a marked decrease in water-soluble polysaccharides, accompanied by a significant increase in 5-HMF [–]. In Angelicae sinensis radix, reduced tryptophan levels during processing correlate with increased 5-HMF formation, highlighting the involvement of Maillard reactions between polysaccharides and amino acids [].

Notably, 5-HMF has emerged as a representative marker of carbonization. Beyond serving as an indicator of thermal transformation, it exhibits multiple pharmacological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective and cardiovascular protective effects []. These findings suggest that polysaccharide degradation and subsequent reactions contribute not only to physicochemical changes but also to the bioactivity of carbonized TCMs.

Organic acids are widely distributed in fruit-derived TCMs and contribute to sour taste, digestive regulation and antidiarrheal effects. During carbonization, their profiles are substantially altered through processes such as thermal degradation, decarboxylation, oxidation, ester cleavage and molecular rearrangement.

Low-molecular-weight aliphatic acids, such as citric acid, are particularly heat-sensitive and are readily degraded during processing. Accordingly, their levels decrease markedly in carbonized products such as Crataegi fructus and Mume fructus charcoal [, ]. Aromatic organic acids exhibit more complex transformation patterns. Compounds such as caffeic acid and ferulic acid generally decrease during carbonization due to oxidative degradation. This trend has been observed in multiple materials, including Artemisiae argyi folium, Imperatae rhizoma, Angelicae sinensis radix and Cimicifugae rhizoma, reflecting the sensitivity of phenolic acids to high-temperature oxidation.

In addition, many organic acids exist in esterified forms that are susceptible to thermal cleavage. For example, rosmarinic acid in Schizonepetae herba can be converted into caffeic acid under heating [], while chlorogenic acid in Cirsii japonici herba decomposes into caffeic acid and quinic acid []. Isomerization reactions are also common. In Lonicerae japonicae flos, carbonization induces acyl migration among chlorogenic acid derivatives, leading to reduced levels of chlorogenic acid and isochlorogenic acid A, alongside increased formation of their isomers, including neochlorogenic acid and cryptochlorogenic acid [, ].

Overall, organic acids undergo coordinated processes of degradation, transformation and redistribution during carbonization. These changes reduce excessive acidity while generating structurally diverse derivatives, thereby contributing to both improved sensory properties and modulation of gastrointestinal activity.

Alkaloids are nitrogen-containing compounds with diverse structures and potent biological activities. During thermal processing, many alkaloids exhibit relatively poor thermal stability and may undergo demethylation, oxidation, degradation, hydrolysis or volatilization reactions depending on their structural characteristics. These transformations can substantially alter their pharmacological and toxicological properties.

In isoquinoline alkaloid–rich materials such as Phellodendri cortex and Phellodendri amurensis cortex, berberine undergoes site-specific O-demethylation to form berberrubine [–]. Structurally, this transformation converts a methoxy group of berberine into a phenolic hydroxyl group in berberrubine, thereby altering the polarity of the molecule, ionization state, protein-binding behavior and intestinal absorption characteristics []. Compared with berberine, which exhibits extremely low oral bioavailability, berberrubine shows improved intestinal absorbability and higher systemic exposure. Berberrubine is also one of the major phase I metabolites of berberine and berberine-derived metabolites, including berberrubine and berberrubine conjugates, contribute substantially to the in vivo disposition and pharmacological profile of berberine []. Berberrubine has been reported to retain several activities associated with berberine, including anti-inflammatory, metabolic-regulating, anti-ulcerative colitis, antithrombotic and antiepileptic effects [, ]. In DSS-induced ulcerative colitis, berberrubine at 20 mg/kg showed protective effects comparable to berberine at 50 mg/kg, mainly by preserving intestinal barrier integrity, regulating tight junction proteins and mucins, and suppressing inflammatory damage []. In metabolic models, berberrubine showed stronger in vivo glucose- and lipid-lowering effects than berberine []. Berberrubine differs from berberine in its pharmacokinetic properties and may also exhibit altered safety characteristics, although systematic comparative toxicological data remain insufficient. Although berberrubine formation supports the chemical basis for activity modulation during carbonization, direct evidence linking this specific transformation to the overall therapeutic effects of carbonized Phellodendri cortex remains insufficient.

Additionally, some alkaloids are thermally unstable and undergo substantial degradation or volatilization during carbonization. For example, the content of aporphine alkaloids in Nelumbinis folium, including nuciferine and related compounds, decreases markedly after carbonization [, ]. Similarly, arecoline in Arecae semen, a low-molecular-weight and volatile alkaloid, is readily lost during heating []. The reduction of arecoline content may attenuate its excessive parasympathomimetic activity and gastrointestinal stimulation, which is consistent with the traditional clinical application of carbonized Arecae semen for reducing irritation while maintaining therapeutic efficacy.

Current evidence indicates that alkaloid transformations during carbonization are highly structure-dependent and may influence bioactivity through changes in molecular structure and thermal stability. However, direct evidence linking specific alkaloid transformation pathways to the therapeutic effects of carbonized TCMs remains limited and requires further systematic investigation.

Volatile oils are key bioactive components in aromatic TCMs, mainly composed of monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes and aromatic aldehydes or ketones. Due to their low boiling points and high reactivity, these compounds are highly susceptible to evaporation, thermal degradation and oxidation during carbonization.

In Artemisiae argyi folium, monoterpenes such as eucalyptol and thujone are significantly reduced after carbonization, while non-volatile phenolic derivatives increase [, ]. Similarly, in Schizonepetae herba and Schizonepetae spica, monoterpene ketones (e.g., pulegone and menthone) decrease markedly, reflecting the loss of volatile fractions during heating [, , ]. Phthalides in Angelicae sinensis radix decrease during carbonization, accompanied by increased formation of thermal products such as 5-HMF []. In Toxicodendri resina, volatile aromatic hydrocarbons and carbonyl compounds are largely eliminated, contributing to reduced toxicity [].

Overall, carbonization drives a transition from volatile, stimulatory constituents to more stable and less irritant compounds. This shift is closely associated with a functional change from dispersing and activating effects toward astringent and hemostatic properties.

Inorganic elements, including calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc and potassium, are intrinsic components of TCMs and exist in diverse chemical forms. During carbonization, these elements undergo changes in chemical state, binding form and distribution, which can influence their solubility, bioavailability and biological activity.

Thermal processing can convert organically bound elements into more stable inorganic forms. For example, calcium oxalate (CaC2O4) may decompose into calcium carbonate, magnesium in chlorophyll can transform into magnesium oxide or carbonate, and organic iron complexes may be converted into iron oxides []. These transformations can alter their chemical reactivity and potential biological roles.

Carbonization leads to substantial loss of organic matrix, resulting in a general concentration effect of inorganic mineral elements in TCM residues. In several carbonized TCMs, calcium content or extractability increases significantly. For instance, in Shihui San, calcium levels increase markedly after carbonization, with some components showing several-fold enrichment []. Similar trends have been observed in Celosiae cristatae flos and Crataegi fructus charcoal [, ]. These changes are functionally relevant. Calcium ions play a central role in the coagulation cascade (Factor IV), and their increased availability may contribute to the enhanced hemostatic effects of carbonized TCMs. Overall, the redistribution and transformation of inorganic elements represent an important, yet often underappreciated, component of their effective substance basis.

Several studies suggest that structurally related compounds may undergo similar transformation pathways during carbonization under controlled thermal conditions. For example, O-glycosides are often thermally degraded into corresponding aglycones, tannins may degrade into smaller phenolic acids such as gallic acid, and reducing polysaccharides can undergo dehydration and Maillard-type reactions to generate 5-HMF and melanoidin-like products. Organic acids, volatile oils and alkaloids experience thermal decomposition, resulting in an overall reduction (Table ). In addition, calcium oxalate is converted to calcium carbonate under high-temperature conditions, thereby increasing the availability of releasable calcium ions. These observations suggest that certain classes of structurally related compounds may follow similar thermal transformation pathways during carbonization.

Representative chemical transformations during carbonization of TCMs

In addition to chemical transformations, carbonization induces substantial changes in the physical structure of TCMs, which play a critical role in their therapeutic function. At the microscale, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) reveals that many carbonized herbal materials develop porous bulk carbon-like architectures, including honeycomb-like, sponge-like or lamellar architectures. These features are associated with cell wall collapse, decomposition of mineral inclusions (e.g., calcium oxalate) and partial preservation of vascular frameworks [, , ]. The resulting increase in specific surface area may enhance adsorption capacity toward biomolecules, toxins or exudates. Several studies have reported positive correlations between adsorption capacity and hemostatic activity, suggesting that porous structural features may partially contribute to local therapeutic effects [, ]. In addition to porous bulk architectures, carbonization also generates heterogeneous amorphous carbonized residues composed of incompletely characterized organic and mineral-derived materials. These residues may contribute to adsorption, thermal stability or surface reactivity, although their precise composition and biological functions remain insufficiently defined. Current evidence suggests that carbonized TCMs represent complex multicomponent systems rather than uniform carbon materials.

More recently, isolated carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as a distinct category of nanoscale carbon-based materials identified in several carbonized TCMs. CDs are nanosized (< 10 nm) fluorescent carbon nanoparticles enriched with surface functional groups and generally exhibiting favorable biocompatibility []. They have been isolated from several carbonized TCMs, including Scutellariae radix charcoal and Mume fructus charcoal and exhibit biological activities comparable to their parent materials [, , ] (Fig. ). In contrast to porous bulk carbon structures primarily associated with adsorption-related properties, CDs are proposed to exert biological effects through nanoscale interfacial interactions, redox modulation and signaling regulation. In several studies, herbal-derived CDs demonstrated hemostatic, anti-inflammatory, wound-healing and organ-protective activities [–]. In addition, CDs can be generated from herbal precursors under hydrothermal conditions, supporting the hypothesis that they arise from thermal decomposition and carbonization-induced molecular reassembly processes [] (Table ). Although hydrothermal synthesis using raw herbal materials is frequently employed to generate “herbal CDs” for comparative studies, it remains unclear whether these hydrothermally generated nanoparticles are structurally and functionally equivalent to CDs naturally formed during traditional carbonization processes. The physicochemical environments involved in hydrothermal treatment and high-temperature stir-frying carbonization differ substantially in terms of temperature profiles, oxygen availability, reaction kinetics and matrix complexity. Notably, the lattice spacings reported for TCM-derived CDs vary considerably (0.17–0.393 nm). Spacings near 0.21 nm are generally considered consistent with graphitic carbon domains, whereas larger values may reflect defective carbon structures, surface functionalization, heteroatom incorporation or measurement variability. In particular, unusually large lattice distances reported for certain CDs, such as SHC-CDs (~ 0.393 nm), remain insufficiently understood and require further structural validation. Moreover, many currently reported TCM-derived CD studies still lack standardized nanoparticle characterization, including detailed size distribution analysis, zeta potential measurements, quantum yield reproducibility and batch-to-batch consistency evaluation, which limits mechanistic interpretation and reproducibility across studies.

Although CDs formed during carbonization are increasingly recognized as functional components, the precise mechanisms linking their physicochemical properties to biological activity remain to be fully elucidated. CDs isolated from different carbonized herbs commonly exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hemostatic and mucosal protective activities, which may be associated with their nanoscale structures and abundant surface functional groups. CD preparations derived from carbonized TCMs may contain co-extracted or surface-adsorbed small molecules, including flavonoids, phenolics, tannin degradation products and Maillard reaction products. However, current evidence remains insufficient to determine whether these biological effects arise predominantly from the intrinsic nanomaterial properties of CDs, from retained or transformed small-molecule constituents associated with their surfaces, or from synergistic interactions between these factors. In traditional decoction systems, the therapeutic effects of carbonized TCMs are therefore more likely mediated through a complex interplay between nanostructural characteristics, surface chemistry, and bioactive phytochemicals.

Although preliminary studies suggest potential biomedical applications of carbonized TCM-derived CDs, systematic toxicological evaluation remains limited. Current short-term in vitro studies and acute toxicity experiments in small animals suggest that CDs may exhibit relatively favorable biocompatibility and short-term safety profiles. Nevertheless, comprehensive data regarding their long-term biodistribution, metabolic fate, immunogenicity, reproductive toxicity and chronic safety are still lacking. Furthermore, no standardized regulatory framework currently exists for evaluating or approving CD-based preparations derived from carbonized TCMs. Therefore, substantial additional work will be required before clinical translation can be realistically considered.

Taken together, carbonization can be understood as a process involving coordinated chemical transformation and multiscale structural reorganization. Porous bulk carbon architectures, amorphous carbonized residues, and isolated carbon dots may each contribute differently to the physicochemical and pharmacological properties of carbonized TCMs. This emerging multilevel framework provides a more integrated perspective for understanding their effective substance basis and therapeutic activities.

Carbonized TCMs occupy a distinctive therapeutic niche, particularly in hemostasis, gastrointestinal mucosal protection, adsorption-related toxin mitigation and tissue repair. Despite their long clinical use, an unclear effective substance basis and poorly defined mechanisms have limited their modernization and broader application. Recent interdisciplinary studies have begun to clarify their pharmacological actions from both chemical and structural perspectives (Table ).
