Hemostasis is a tightly regulated process involving vasoconstriction, platelet activation, coagulation cascade activation and inhibition of fibrinolysis. Disruption of this balance leads to bleeding disorders [, ]. Increasing evidence indicates that carbonized TCMs exert hemostatic effects through coordinated modulation of these processes (Fig. ).

Activation of the coagulation cascade is a central mechanism. Carbonized TCMs are commonly evaluated using standard coagulation parameters (PT, APTT, TT, and FIB), which reflect different pathways. Several carbonized TCMs, including Nelumbinis rhizomatis nodus [], Rubiae radix et rhizoma [] and Celosiae cristatae flos [], significantly shorten both PT and APTT, indicating activation of both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. Platycladi cacumen charcoal and Artemisia frigida charcoal exerted their effects primarily through the intrinsic pathway [, ]. Some effects are linked to specific constituents. For example, vitamin K-like components in Cirsii japonici herba carbonisata promoted the synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X []. In addition, multiple carbonized TCMs increased fibrinogen levels, accelerating fibrin formation and stabilizing clots [, , ].

Platelet activation is closely associated with calcium signaling. Carbonization often increases the availability of inorganic calcium, which acts as a key cofactor (Factor IV) in coagulation and enhances platelet activity []. In addition, carbonized TCMs can regulate vascular and platelet signaling mediators. The balance between thromboxane B₂ (TXB₂) and 6-keto-prostaglandin F1α (6-keto-PGF1α) is critical for vascular tone and platelet aggregation. Moutan cortex charcoal, Nelumbinis rhizomatis nodus charcoal, and Zingiberis rhizoma charcoal restored this balance in hemorrhagic models, thereby improving hemostatic function [, , ].

Stabilization of formed clots is equally important. Some carbonized TCMs inhibited fibrinolysis by modulating the plasminogen system. The ethanol fraction of Zingiberis rhizoma charcoal prolonged euglobulin lysis time, indicating reduced fibrinolytic activity []. Similarly, the aqueous extract of Nelumbinis rhizomatis nodus charcoal reduced fibrin degradation products []. At the molecular level, modulation of the tissue-type plasminogen activator (t-PA) / plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) balance contributes to reduced fibrin breakdown, further stabilizing clots.

Current evidence suggests that the hemostatic effects of carbonized TCMs may involve coordinated chemical, physical and subtractive mechanisms. The carbonization of Platycladi cacumen converted flavonoid glycosides into aglycones (e.g., quercetin and kaempferol), which have been shown to markedly suppress simvastatin-induced cerebral hemorrhage in zebrafish []. Similarly, elevated quercetin in Nelumbinis folium charcoal and newly generated pectolinarigenin in Cirsii japonici herba carbonisata are correlated with procoagulant activity, highlighting the role of flavonoids in modulating coagulation factor activity [, ]. Characterized by polyphenolic structures, tannins facilitate hemostasis by precipitating proteins to form insoluble complexes, effectively sealing injury sites []. Tannins in Moutan cortex charcoal and Imperatae rhizoma charcoal significantly promoted platelet aggregation [, ]. In Sanguisorbae radix charcoal, constituents such as ellagitannins and ellagic acid show a strong positive correlation with hemostatic efficacy []. A combined molecular-docking and network-pharmacology analysis identified 5-tetradecenoic acid and 1-monolinolein as potential hemostatic constituents of Moutan cortex charcoal. These predictions were subsequently supported by an in vitro coagulation screening assay. However, their proposed interactions with coagulation-related targets, including SERPINC1, FVIII, FX, FII and FXII, remain computational predictions and require further direct experimental validation []. Additionally, coniferaldehyde in Crataegi fructus charcoal and 3-epi-betulinic acid in Nelumbinis rhizomatis nodus charcoal act as specific hemostatic agents [, ]. As a pivotal cofactor, calcium accumulates substantially during the carbonization of herbs like Crataegi fructus, Sanguisorbae radix and Celosiae cristatae flos, thereby directly fueling the coagulation cascade [, , ]. The formation of typical honeycomb or sponge-like porous carbon structures (e.g., in Sanguisorbae radix charcoal and Crataegi fructus charcoal) significantly enhances the physical adsorption of blood cells and clotting factors, accelerating thrombus formation via a physical mechanism [, ]. Isolated CDs derived from Platycladi cacumen charcoal and Mume fructus charcoal have demonstrated hemostatic and anti-inflammatory activities in several experimental assays, suggesting that nanoscale carbon materials may represent additional bioactive components generated during carbonization [, ]. However, whether these CDs contribute measurably to the overall therapeutic efficacy of whole carbonized herbal medicines remains unclear. Crucially, carbonization can degrade compounds that interfere with coagulation. For instance, nuciferine, a thermolabile alkaloid with potential anticoagulant effects, is degraded during processing, amplifying the net procoagulant activity of Nelumbinis folium charcoal []. This highlights that therapeutic efficacy arises not only from the enrichment of beneficial constituents but also from the pyrolytic removal of counteractive components.

Although these experimental models provide useful preliminary evidence regarding the hemostatic potential of carbonized TCMs, several translational limitations should be acknowledged. Commonly used models, including zebrafish thrombosis models and rat tail-amputation assays, primarily evaluate simplified aspects of coagulation or bleeding control and may not fully recapitulate the complexity of human hemostasis, vascular injury, inflammatory responses or clinical bleeding disorders.

Compared with the relatively well-characterized hemostatic effects of carbonized TCMs, current evidence supporting other pharmacological activities, including wound healing, antidiarrheal, anti-ulcer and antibacterial effects, remains comparatively preliminary. Most available studies are limited to in vitro assays, small-animal models or exploratory mechanistic analyses, and the active substance basis underlying these activities has not yet been systematically established. Nevertheless, emerging evidence suggests that carbonization-induced chemical transformation and structural remodeling may contribute to broader therapeutic properties beyond hemostasis.

Carbonized TCMs promote wound healing through coordinated regulation of inflammation, angiogenesis and tissue regeneration. Experimental studies showed that extracts of carbonized TCMs, including Sanguisorbae radix and Typhae pollen charcoal, significantly accelerated wound closure and improved collagen remodeling []. These effects are associated with enhanced fibroblast proliferation, extracellular matrix deposition and neovascularization. Material-based applications further highlight their regenerative potential. For example, nanofiber membranes loaded with Crinis carbonisatus promoted wound repair by supporting cell proliferation and vascular formation []. Artemisia frigida charcoal enhanced gastric ulcer healing through upregulation of angiogenic factors such as VEGF and bFGF []. At the nanoscale, carbon dots derived from carbonized Mume fructus (CMF-CDs) have been reported to exhibit wound-healing–related bioactivities in several experimental models. These nanomaterials were reported to promote wound repair-associated processes by inducing M2 macrophage polarization, enhancing angiogenesis, and stimulating collagen deposition. Mechanistic studies suggest that CMF-CDs may modulate the inflammatory microenvironment by reducing excessive reactive oxygen species generated during cellular metabolism []. Overall, wound healing effects arise from integrated anti-inflammatory, pro-angiogenic and pro-regenerative mechanisms, potentially involving both small molecules and carbon-based nanostructures.

The antidiarrheal effects of carbonized TCMs are mediated through a combination of physical adsorption, mucosal protection, and modulation of gastrointestinal motility. The porous structure formed during carbonization enables adsorption of intestinal gases, toxins, and inflammatory mediators, thereby reducing mucosal irritation. This structural mechanism complements chemical effects. For example, Crataegi fructus charcoal and nano-components from Granati pericarpium charcoal significantly reduce diarrhea severity and delay onset in animal models [, ].

In addition, carbonization generates bioactive compounds that directly regulate intestinal motility. Citri reticulatae pericarpium charcoal may reduce gastrointestinal motility through downregulation of circulating serotonin. Zingerone, formed during thermal processing of ginger, inhibits spontaneous smooth muscle contraction in a dose-dependent manner, indicating a direct myogenic effect independent of neuronal ion channels []. However, the mechanistic basis of the antidiarrheal effects of carbonized TCMs remains insufficiently characterized, and current evidence mainly derives from animal models and indirect pharmacodynamic observations.

Carbonized TCMs exhibit protective effects against gastrointestinal ulceration through coordinated regulation of inflammation, oxidative stress and epithelial barrier function.

In ulcerative colitis models, carbonized TCMs modulate inflammatory signaling and oxidative injury. For example, Rhei radix et rhizoma charcoal alleviates colonic inflammation through the combined action of anthraquinones, gallic acid and 5-HMF, which regulate inflammatory pathways and reduce oxidative stress []. Similarly, CD-enriched fractions derived from Sanguisorbae radix charcoal were reported to suppress the TLR4/MYD88/NF-κB pathway and mitigate oxidative damage []. Barrier protection is another key mechanism. Carbonized Linderae radix enhanced epithelial repair by preserving tight junction integrity and promoting mucosal regeneration, with increased expression of MUC2 indicating improved mucus barrier function. Mechanistic analyses indicated that the therapeutic effects of carbonized Linderae radix are preferentially mediated through inflammation- and apoptosis-related signaling pathways, including MAPK, PI3K-Akt and IL-17 [].

In gastric ulcer models, carbonized TCM–derived nanomaterials also show significant efficacy. For instance, carbon dots from Glycyrrhizae radix et rhizoma and Atractylodis macrocephalae rhizoma reduce mucosal injury, suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, TNF-α), and enhance anti-inflammatory signaling via IL-10 [, ]. Although these findings suggest therapeutic potential in gastrointestinal mucosal protection, most current studies remain exploratory and further validation of active substance basis and long-term efficacy is still required.

Sanguisorbae radix charcoal retained membrane-disrupting effects against Trichophyton rubrum while acquiring a novel ability to inhibit 1, 3-β-d-glucan synthesis, thereby disrupting fungal cell wall integrity. Concurrently, carbonization reduced cytotoxicity toward HaCaT keratinocytes, substantially improving the therapeutic index against dermatophytes. This enhanced antifungal activity may be associated with a cumulative 454.74% increase in five core bioactive compounds including gallic acid, methyl gallate, pyrogallol, ellagic acid and protocatechualdehyde relative to the unprocessed herb []. Furthermore, elevated levels of ziyuglycoside II in Sanguisorbae radix charcoal suppressed the growth of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) by inhibiting nucleic acid synthesis, underscoring its potential against drug-resistant pathogens []. In modern material applications, nanofiber membranes incorporating Crinis carbonisatus have demonstrated significant inhibition of S. aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, effectively reducing wound bacterial loads and accelerating the healing process []. These findings indicate that antibacterial activity may involve combined contributions from transformed bioactive compounds and carbonized structural features.

Carbonization induces substantial changes in the chemical composition and micro/nanostructure of TCM materials, including the degradation and transformation of native constituents, enrichment of carbon-rich fractions, and formation of porous carbonized architectures and carbon dots. These alterations are believed to collectively contribute to the pharmacological activities of carbonized TCMs. Among them, the relationship between carbonization-induced structural evolution and hemostatic activity has been investigated most extensively, while other activities such as wound healing, anti-ulcer, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial effects are still largely supported by studies on crude extracts. Current evidence suggests that these activities may arise from the synergistic effects of transformed small molecules, polyphenol-rich macromolecular fractions and carbonized nanostructures, although the precise active substances and structure–activity relationships remain insufficiently clarified.

Current evidence does not yet permit a definitive assignment of individual pharmacological effects to small-molecule, porous-carbon or CD/nanoscale drivers. Most studies have evaluated crude extracts, isolated compounds, or nanocomponents separately in different experimental models, without directly comparing these material fractions or quantifying their relative contributions to the activity of the whole carbonized preparation. Although selected small molecules and isolated CDs have demonstrated pharmacological activities, these findings do not establish that they are the principal active substances in the corresponding whole medicines. Similarly, the proposed contribution of porous-carbon structures is based mainly on material characterization and adsorption-related observations rather than direct causal evidence. Table  therefore summarizes the experimentally reported pharmacological evidence without assigning definitive driver categories. Comparative fractionation, component-depletion and reconstitution experiments, and standardized structure–activity studies will be required to establish the relative contributions of these chemical and material features.

Carbonization of herbal materials at high temperatures may generate potentially harmful compounds that warrant safety consideration. These include polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and thermal processing-derived substances such as acrylamide and 5-HMF, all of which have documented toxicological concerns [–]. Although most studies of carbonized TCMs focus on pharmacological efficacy, the presence and levels of these contaminants are highly dependent on raw material quality, processing temperature and duration. Therefore, explicit monitoring and risk assessment of these compounds are essential to ensure the safety of carbonized herbal products, particularly for clinical or dietary use.

Carbonized TCMs remain widely used in contemporary clinical practice, particularly in hemorrhagic disorders and gastrointestinal diseases. Their continued inclusion in the ChP and their presence in multiple classical and modern formulations underscore their therapeutic relevance. Representative preparations such as Heye Wan, Zhihong Changpi Wan, and Changweining Pian have demonstrated clinical efficacy in contemporary practice. However, the currently available clinical evidence is derived predominantly from expert experience, traditional practice records, small observational studies, and limited single-center clinical reports, rather than rigorously designed randomized controlled trials. Therefore, existing clinical observations should primarily be interpreted as exploratory or experience-based evidence supporting the continued empirical use of carbonized TCMs in specific therapeutic contexts.

Allergic purpura is a small-vessel vasculitic disorder involving the skin and multiple organ systems. In a comparative clinical study involving 80 pediatric patients with allergic purpura, Liangxue Duotan Decoction improved hemorheological and coagulation parameters and the cure rate was 95.9% in the Liangxue Duotan Decoction group versus 82.5% in the ketotifen group (p < 0.05) []. The formulation included several carbonized herbs, such as Rehmanniae radix charcoal, Cirsii japonici herba carbonisata, Cirsii herba charcoal, Scutellariae radix charcoal, and Rubiae radix et rhizoma charcoal, which are traditionally used for cooling blood and controlling bleeding. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is clinically characterized by thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding. Professor Jiageng Li has emphasized the empirical use of charcoal medicines for hemostatic intervention in this condition based on syndrome differentiation. According to expert-opinion–based clinical practice, acute cases are commonly treated with Scutellariae radix charcoal, Typhae pollen charcoal, Sanguisorbae radix charcoal, Sophorae flos charcoal, Platycladi cacumen charcoal and Trachycarpi petiolus charcoal, whereas chronic cases are more frequently managed using carbonized Zingiberis rhizoma and Artemisiae argyi folium preparations []. However, these applications are supported mainly by traditional clinical experience rather than controlled clinical trials.

Gastrointestinal bleeding represents one of the most common clinical applications of carbonized TCMs. In a comparative clinical study involving 90 patients with bleeding gastric ulcer, the rate of successful hemostasis was 96% in the micronized Rhei radix et rhizoma charcoal group versus 86% in the endoscopic topical norepinephrine-spray group (p < 0.01) []. Small observational clinical studies have also reported that Shihui San combined with Xiexin Tang or proton pump inhibitors improved symptom control in respiratory and gastrointestinal bleeding. In colorectal conditions, Tiexian Wutan Yin has been applied in exploratory clinical settings for hematochezia associated with rectal cancer []. In addition, a single case report described improvement of persistent upper gastrointestinal bleeding caused by portal hypertensive gastropathy following integrative treatment involving carbonized Rhei radix et rhizoma, Rubiae radix et rhizoma, Sanguisorbae radix and Schizonepetae herba [].

Carbonized TCMs are also extensively used in gynecological hemorrhagic disorders, including dysfunctional uterine bleeding, endometriosis-associated bleeding, cesarean scar defect–related bleeding and threatened abortion []. Renowned TCM doctor Guangji Song’s representative formula Zhibengling contains 17 medicinal components, including 11 carbonized herbs []. Similarly, renowned TCM doctor Zhaoling You has reported the empirical use of carbonized Dryopteridis crassirhizomatis rhizoma, Sanguisorbae radix, Lonicerae japonicae flos and Scutellariae radix in the treatment of previous cesarean scar defect–associated bleeding, emphasizing simultaneous hemostatic and anti-inflammatory management [].

Overall, current clinical applications of carbonized TCMs in hemorrhagic disorders are broadly consistent with their experimentally proposed procoagulant, platelet-regulating, antifibrinolytic and adsorption-related pharmacological mechanisms. Although carbonized TCMs have demonstrated clinical utility in hemorrhagic disorders, their application should be individualized according to syndrome differentiation and the patient’s specific clinical condition. In clinical practice, prescription strategies are adjusted dynamically based on therapeutic response and laboratory findings, and different carbonized herbs may be substituted or combined according to changing disease manifestations, reflecting the principle of “same syndrome, different treatment” in traditional Chinese medicine.

Chronic diarrhea is one of the most common gastrointestinal symptoms and may arise from multiple conditions, including chronic enteritis, intestinal tuberculosis, chemotherapy-related intestinal injury, irritable bowel syndrome and malabsorption syndromes. Based on clinical experience, renowned TCM doctor Jinjie Shao reported the use of modified Sishen Wan supplemented with carbonized Mume fructus and Crataegi fructus in patients with chronic diarrhea following esophageal cancer surgery and chemotherapy, aiming to strengthen gastrointestinal function while exerting astringent and antidiarrheal effects. Similarly, Banxia Xiexin Tang combined with carbonized Mume fructus and Crataegi fructus has been empirically applied for chronic diarrhea after cholecystectomy []. In a clinical observational study involving 33 patients with chronic diarrhea, the Jianpi Wan combined with carbonized herb group delivered a 93.9% cure rate, substantially exceeding the 74.2% cure rate of Jianpi Wan combined with conventional astringent herbs (p < 0.05) []. Crohn’s disease represents one of the major refractory inflammatory bowel disorders in modern clinical practice. Renowned TCM doctor Yan Zhao has reported the empirical use of carbonized Aurantii fructus immaturus, Scutellariae radix, Phellodendri chinensis cortex, Mume fructus and Rhei radix et rhizoma in patients with Crohn’s disease, aiming to achieve anti-inflammatory and adsorption-related mitigation of intestinal toxins while minimizing gastrointestinal irritation. Modern studies suggest that carbonized materials may contribute to antidiarrheal effects through adsorption-related mechanisms. Porous carbon structures generated during carbonization may adsorb intestinal gases, bacterial toxins and inflammatory substances, thereby reducing mucosal irritation, decreasing excessive gastrointestinal motility, and alleviating diarrhea symptoms [].

Ulcerative colitis is a chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder mainly affecting the colon and rectum. In a clinical observational study involving 30 patients with active ulcerative colitis, oral administration combined with retention enema therapy using Gegen Qinlian Wutan Tang (containing carbonized Angelicae sinensis radix, Crataegi fructus, Schizonepetae herba, Mume fructus, and Sanguisorbae radix) delivered a 93.3% cure rate, substantially exceeding the 66.7% cure rate of sulfasalazine enteric-coated tablet monotherapy (p < 0.05). The treatment was also associated with significant reductions in serum TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-8 levels, suggesting potential anti-inflammatory activity [].

Applications of carbonized TCMs in renal-related disorders have been reported mainly for hematuria and chronic kidney disease–associated complications. In a clinical observational study involving 50 pediatric patients with glomerular hematuria, modified Wucao Wutan Tang containing Crinis carbonisatus, Trachycarpi petiolus charcoal, Sanguisorbae radix charcoal, Cephalanoplosi herba charcoal, and Platycladi cacumen charcoal significantly improved hematuria symptoms []. In addition, Professor Jianguo Xie has reported the empirical use of Liuwei Dihuang Tang combined with carbonized Cephalanoplosi herba, Rubiae radix et rhizoma, Imperatae rhizoma and Nelumbinis rhizomatis nodus for hematuria associated with acute or occult nephritis []. Carbonized TCMs have also been explored in chronic renal failure–associated complications. In a clinical observational study involving 80 patients with chronic renal failure characterized by “kidney deficiency and turbid toxin syndrome,” retention enema therapy using Sitan Tang combined with colonic dialysis significantly improved renal function indicators []. Carbonized herbal materials may contribute both through systemic absorption of herbal constituents and through direct adsorption of intestinal uremic toxins after colonic administration.

Due to their astringent, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial and hemostatic properties, carbonized TCMs may facilitate wound contraction, reduce local inflammation, and promote tissue repair, thereby contributing to improved healing outcomes in chronic or refractory ulcerative conditions []. In a clinical observational study involving 50 pediatric patients with oral ulcers, Junci medulla charcoal was reported to accelerate ulcer healing and alleviate inflammatory symptoms []. In an observational dermatological study involving 86 patients with corticosteroid-dependent dermatitis oral modified Shihui San combined with lesion-localized vitamin C microneedle injection yielded a total effective rate of 93.0%, markedly outperforming the control oral therapy consisting of cetirizine hydrochloride capsules and vitamin C tablets, which produced a total effective rate of only 72.1% (p < 0.05) []. Professor Jianguo Xie has reported the empirical use of carbonized Gardeniae fructus and Lonicerae japonicae flos in the treatment of acne and refractory oral ulcers, particularly in combination with heat-clearing and anti-inflammatory herbal therapies []. These applications are considered to involve both anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects.

Overall, carbonized TCMs retain a central role in hemostatic therapy while demonstrating expanding applications in gastrointestinal, renal and dermatological conditions. Current clinical applications of carbonized TCMs remain supported primarily by practice-based evidence and exploratory clinical observations, highlighting the need for more rigorous and standardized clinical evaluation. In addition, variability in carbonization procedures, formulation composition and concomitant therapies complicates reproducibility and cross-study comparison. Therefore, current clinical evidence should be interpreted cautiously, and larger multicenter randomized controlled studies will be required to more rigorously establish efficacy and safety.

Recent advances have substantially improved the scientific understanding of carbonized TCMs, transforming them from empirically derived preparations into mechanistically interpretable therapeutic systems. Controlled carbonization induces coordinated chemical transformations and structural reorganization, leading to the formation of bioactive small molecules (e.g., flavonoid aglycones, phenolic acids and 5-HMF) together with functional carbon-based structures, including porous matrices and carbon nanomaterials. These changes collectively underpin their pharmacological effects. The relative contribution of these components is strongly influenced by the degree of carbonization and processing conditions. However, precise control of these factors remains difficult due to variability in raw herbal materials and the lack of standardized carbonization protocols.

Progress in analytical technologies has further enabled this transition. The integration of biomimetic sensing, spectroscopic methods and chromatographic techniques allows dynamic monitoring of the carbonization process and supports the establishment of quantitative quality indicators. In parallel, spectrum–effect relationship analysis provides a framework linking physicochemical characteristics to biological activity. Pharmacological studies demonstrate that carbonized TCMs act through multiple mechanisms, including modulation of coagulation, platelet function, fibrinolysis, inflammation, mucosal barrier integrity and adsorption-related toxin mitigation. Together, these findings provide a modern scientific basis for their traditional clinical use.

Beyond validation of traditional practices, carbonization has also emerged as a strategy for generating new therapeutic functionalities. The application of carbonization to previously unprocessed materials has shown promising results in gastrointestinal and renal protection [, , ]. In addition, the discovery of carbon dot–like nanomaterials derived from carbonized TCMs has opened a new avenue linking traditional medicine with nanotechnology [, ]. These materials exhibit diverse bioactivities and highlight the importance of structural evolution in addition to chemical transformation [, , ].

Despite these advances, several critical challenges remain. Firstly, current quality control systems rely heavily on sensory evaluation or limited chemical markers, which are insufficient to capture the integrated “process–composition–efficacy” relationship. Second, mechanistic studies often focus on individual components or isolated pathways, lacking a systems-level understanding of multi-component and multi-target interactions. Third, the relationship between micro/nano-structural features and pharmacological activity remains poorly defined. Fourth, clinical applications are still largely confined to traditional indications, with limited high-quality evidence for broader use in modern disease contexts. Finally, the lack of international and multi-center clinical trials limits the global translational application of herb carbonization. Additionally, the absence of harmonized nomenclature for herbs poses a significant barrier—specifically, the inconsistency between the Latin names of Chinese materia medica and their botanical scientific names in the literature, which leads to confusion in data integration, cross-study comparison and academic communication.

Future research should focus on establishing a more integrated and quantitative framework. In quality control, data-driven approaches combining process parameters, chemical profiles and bioactivity should be developed, with machine learning facilitating the identification of combinatorial quality markers. Multi-omics technologies may further elucidate system-level mechanisms, particularly in hemostasis, mucosal repair and immune regulation. Interdisciplinary integration with materials science and nanomedicine is expected to clarify structure–activity relationships and enable the development of new functional biomaterials. In clinical research, well-designed trials are needed to define the role of carbonized TCMs in modern therapeutic areas, including inflammatory bowel disease and other refractory conditions. Standardizing herb nomenclature and promoting international multi-center clinical trials are essential to enhance the credibility and applicability of research findings on TCM carbonization.

In summary, carbonization drives simultaneous chemical transformation and structural evolution, forming a distinctive therapeutic system with integrated biological functions. Integrating traditional knowledge with modern science will advance mechanistic understanding and quality standardization, and expand the clinical potential of carbonized TCMs in contemporary medicine.

medicine.title: Emergent connections: a community-based model for advancing social connection among immigrant older adults with disabilities
medicine.abstract: Social isolation is an urgent public health concern, especially for older immigrants who face heightened barriers to social participation due to disability, structural health inequities, and limited access to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. This study presents a programmatic model that explains how social connection and sustained participation can be fostered through accessible, culturally responsive, and participatory design.This community-engaged case study examines a national virtual program serving Spanish-speaking older adults, many of whom have sensory disabilities and chronic illnesses. A thematic and comparative analysis was conducted using qualitative interviews with 10 older adults with vision impairment, program documents, and consultation with program leadership. This led to the identification of a programmatic model, the Emergent Connections Platform.The emergent connections platform strengthens loosely connected social networks among older adults who share cultural and lived experiences through three pillars. The first is cultural, linguistic, and physically accessible infrastructure. Second, shared governance cultivates member leadership and program co-creation. Third, a flexible structure allows for evolution in response to member needs and innovations. These pillars collectively create pathways for individuals to engage, lead, and strengthen their communities.Advancing a more inclusive democracy requires sustained investment in accessible, community-led initiatives that support the leadership and innovation of marginalized older adults. This calls for moving toward models that position older adults as co-creators of programs and services. Doing so cultivates social connection through leadership, reciprocity, and a sense of belonging within a broader social fabric.
medicine.text:
National public health authorities are calling increased attention to the public health crises of loneliness and social isolation. The U.S. Surgeon General declared social disconnection a public health crisis in 2023 and called for a national strategy to rebuild social infrastructure. A 2024 national poll revealed that nearly 30% of U.S. adults aged 50 to 80 reported feeling socially isolated, and 33% experienced loneliness (). Robust epidemiological evidence has consistently linked social isolation with adverse health outcomes and increased mortality risk (). For instance, a meta-analysis of 70 prospective studies found that social isolation was associated with a 29% greater risk of premature death from all causes (). Additionally, social isolation is a well-documented risk factor for poor mental and physical health, including depression, anxiety (; ), cognitive decline (; ; ), and the progression of chronic conditions (; ). A scoping review by  examining 128 studies published between 2000 and 2013 found only two studies without a negative association between social isolation and health.

Older adults with visual impairments are especially vulnerable to social isolation due to mobility challenges, reduced access to information, and difficulty engaging in social, cultural, or recreational activities (; ; ). Some research shows that Latine older adults have a greater risk of developing blindness and visual impairment (; ). This is partly due to a lifetime of low-paying, physically demanding, and irregular labor that diminishes their health, as well as systemic health disparities related to incidence and access to treatment (; ; , ). Latine adults are less likely to have access to an eye doctor, more likely to report being unable to afford eyeglasses, and less likely to receive necessary vision care than non-Hispanic white adults (). Yet, despite this growing acknowledgement of the risks of social isolation and the disproportionate vulnerability of immigrant older adult populations and people with disabilities, there remains a lack of targeted interventions for non-English-speaking older adults.

To address this gap, this study examines how cultural, linguistic, and structural program features shape sustained social and civic engagement among Spanish-speaking older adults with blindness and low vision. Using data from the national virtual program Well-Connected Español (WCE), a new model to foster social connection was identified: the emergent connections platform, which shows how social networks among immigrant older adults are actively produced and sustained despite linguistic exclusion and disability-related barriers. Furthermore, the study shows how accessibility infrastructure, member-led governance, and flexible programming operate as interdependent mechanisms that enable participation and collective engagement beyond the program. Overall, the study analyzes how these conditions shape social ties, cultivate leadership and innovation, and sustain civic participation among immigrant older adults with vision impairment.

Various reviews of the literature on loneliness and social isolation among older adults find key indicators that interventions should address, such as size and structure of social networks, frequency and quality of social contact, social engagement, and social support (; ; ). In a scoping review,  identified nine intervention types ranging from one-to-one contact and group activities to service delivery models and media-based programs. Similarly,  outlined four broad approaches based on an integrative review of literature from 2008–2021: intergenerational initiatives, age-friendly communities, community-based group physical activities, and technology-mediated social connection.

However, a systematic review further found that existing interventions often lack specificity in addressing the needs of socially disadvantaged older adults, including those marginalized by race/ethnicity, language, geographic location, and disability (). Within this broader population, the experiences and needs of immigrant older adults remain especially underexamined in aging research, particularly regarding social isolation, loneliness, and culturally responsive interventions (). Immigrant older adults may share some challenges experienced by other socially disadvantaged older adults, such as lower socioeconomic status, having a disability, and reduced social capital (). However, migration-related experiences and cultural contexts create additional and distinct barriers to social connection and service access (). These barriers include language barriers, restricted eligibility for services and benefits, disrupted family and social networks following migration, discrimination, fear of deportation, and limited access to culturally and linguistically responsive services (; ; ; ; ).

have been one of the very few to develop a typology specifically focused on culturally relevant social support models that combine formal and informal support for immigrant populations. Their study identified four types of interventions to support immigrants: dyadic models that connect individuals to services through culturally informed mediators, social network interventions that strengthen support provided by trusted community leaders, and mutual aid approaches such as professionally led support groups and peer-led self-help groups that foster connection, reciprocity, and resilience. Community-based strategies further extend support through social justice-oriented collective action aimed at challenging structural inequities, redistributing power, and promoting empowerment and advocacy.

These typologies are especially useful because they highlight that social connection is a multidimensional process shaped by social position, cultural context, and life-course transitions. The convoy model of social relations (; ) further illustrates how social networks evolve over time, with individuals relying on different forms of support as their circumstances change. In later life, social convoys become smaller as opportunities to form new relationships decrease (), a process that may be accelerated by migration, disability, illness, or caregiving demands. Consequently, interventions that recognize the dynamic and culturally embedded nature of social support may be better positioned to strengthen social connection among diverse aging populations.

This study employed a community-engaged case study design to examine the core dimensions of the WCE model. This design enabled an examination of how WCE promotes culturally relevant social support among non-English-speaking older immigrants with sensory disabilities and how the model compares to others described in the literature. WCE was selected as the case for this study because it represents a rare, information-rich example of a national, linguistically and culturally responsive virtual program serving a hidden population. Spanish-speaking Latine immigrants, many of whom are older adults living with visual impairment, physical disability, or other functional limitations, are often underrepresented in empirical studies due to intersecting barriers related to language, disability, immigration status, and social isolation. This made it a particularly well-suited organization to partner with, offering insights into how programs can facilitate connection and participation among a structurally marginalized and hard-to-reach population.

Launched in 2019 to address social isolation among older Spanish-speaking adults, WCE serves those at greatest risk of isolation, including individuals who are homebound, geographically isolated, living with disabilities, or limited by language and/or technology. The program offers over 40 classes and groups accessible by telephone or video conferencing. WCE operates through a peer-led model that emphasizes connection and reciprocity. Members participate in program governance through an Advisory Council, serving one-year terms to ensure participant perspectives guide program decisions. Members also facilitate groups and receive onboarding, training, and mentorship, while program managers lead monthly support groups that address group dynamics, technology use, and participant needs. Program staff provide additional layers of support by moderating educational groups, facilitating Advisory Council meetings, offering technical assistance, and hosting community programming such as holiday celebrations and prayer services. The program’s leadership is uniquely positioned to provide culturally competent support, as staff members are bilingual, bicultural, and members of the communities they serve.

WCE is part of a larger nonprofit organization, Front Porch, committed to supporting older adults through senior living communities, community services, virtual programming, and other innovative initiatives. The program is supported through the nonprofit’s operating resources and philanthropic funding. In addition, the program benefits from the administrative, technological, and programmatic infrastructure needed to support its ongoing implementation. This broader organizational backing has helped sustain the program since its inception.

Recruitment began in April 2023 following Institutional Review Board approval. To be eligible to participate in the study, WCE members needed to be age 60 and older living in California. The requirement to reside in California was included to allow for examination of how members engaged with one another across both virtual programming and shared geographic proximity beyond the online platform. Recruitment was conducted through an established partnership with WCE and began with a virtual presentation, “Historias con valor,” delivered by the PI on April 5, 2023, as part of the “Health and Life” series. The session shared prior findings on Latine older adults’ civic participation and introduced the current study, inviting WCE members to participate in qualitative interviews. WCE staff then facilitated recruitment by sharing study information with interested members and providing a list of individuals who opted in and consented to being contacted. Recruitment continued through this opt-in process until early September, with participants self-selecting into the study and later disclosing their participation to WCE staff.

In total, 14 older adults participating in WCE were recruited and completed all data collection and member checking. Since this study’s focus is on understanding the factors that facilitate connection and participation among older adults with visual impairment, data are drawn from a sub-sample (n = 10) of participants who self-disclosed having visual impairments during the interviews.  illustrates demographic characteristics of the ten participants included in this sample. All participants were immigrants with visual impairment; the average age was 68. Most participants were female (n = 6), lived with family (n = 8), had some college education (n = 6), and were born in Mexico (n = 6). Four participants owned their home, and only three participants were married.

Participants’ demographics (N = 10).

Data collection included a brief demographic questionnaire, followed by an in-depth semi-structured interview focused on community engagement over the prior 12 months with specific focus on involvement in the WCE program, and lastly, an in-depth life course interview broadly focused on life course experiences that shaped community involvement. Each interview lasted 1.5 to 2 hr and was conducted by phone in Spanish, recorded with consent, and transcribed. Data triangulation was achieved through additional sources including program documents (e.g., catalogs from Fall 2022–Fall 2023, informational sheets, and the 2022 impact report), attendance at WCE programming, and ongoing consultations with the program director (second author). These sources provided firsthand understanding of the program structure, supported cross-validation of emerging interpretations, and added context and nuance to participants’ experiences and the groups they joined or led. Ongoing conversations with the program director also enabled the PI to track the program’s development from 2022 to 2025.

Data derived from the demographic questionnaire, prior 12-month community engagement interview, and life course interview were integrated into chronological narratives spanning participants’ lives from childhood through later life using a narrative crafting approach. The narratives were developed through an iterative process of engaging closely with participants’ stories, removing repetitive details, reordering excerpts to create a coherent flow, and adding brief contextual transitions (). The chronological narratives, incorporating participants’ experiences from childhood to the present day, were then returned to participants for review and verification 8–10 months after data collection ended. To ensure accessibility, the principal investigator read the narratives aloud by phone for participants who requested it, while others reviewed them with assistance from family members or through assistive technology. These follow-up conversations provided opportunities for clarification, correction, and elaboration, and captured changes in participants’ engagement, leading to additional data on the development of some of their initiatives. This member check process concluded about a year after the data collection phase, strengthening the temporal depth of the analysis.

Using narratives from later life (age 60 and older), a thematic analysis was conducted to examine the experiences of older adults with vision impairment in WCE and how the program fosters connection and engagement. Analysis began with open coding of interviews, focusing on experiences of participation following vision loss and on program-related and external factors that facilitated or constrained engagement. Descriptive codes during this phase included blind community network, lack of information, safety, language, felt excluded, losing sight, technology, informal initiative, instrumental support, in-person meet-ups, etc. This initial coding situated WCE within each participant’s broader social network, revealing how the program intersected with, or compensated for other forms of support.

In the second analytic phase, codes were grouped into broader categories capturing key dimensions of the program, as well as unanticipated outcomes of participation. These categories were refined through iterative comparison across interviews and data sources to identify recurring patterns and relationships. These are some examples of the emerging codes during this phase; barriers to participation included child codes such as structural, linguistic, safety, and transportation. Well-connected spinoffs included in-person meet-ups, braille classes, instrumental support, and leadership process included codes for formal leadership WC, WC facilitator, WC opportunities, and participation from home, including technology, video conferencing groups, and safety. Program materials and facilitator training curricula were analyzed concurrently to contextualize participants’ accounts and to identify intended program structures, values, and mechanisms of support. Preliminary analysis of participant narratives generated initial interpretations of how the program functioned in practice, which informed further conversations with the program director to clarify program design, implementation decisions, and adaptations over time. This iterative process allowed participant experiences to be used as a lens for understanding both the intended structure of the program and how participants experienced it, which helped to conceptualize the program model.

In the third phase, a comparative analysis was conducted to examine the relationship between the social support typology proposed by  and the program model identified through this case study. Drawing on thematic analysis of participant interviews, the first author’s observations of the program, revision of program documents, and discussions with the program director and staff, the first author systematically compared the defining characteristics of each typological model with the intervention elements that emerged from the analysis. This process enabled the identification of areas of conceptual alignment, overlap, and divergence, providing an interpretive framework for understanding how the program related to established models of social support for immigrant populations. The analysis revealed that the configuration of WCE program features could not be fully explained by any single existing model. Instead, the program incorporated elements that cut across multiple forms of social support while also demonstrating unique features not captured in prior typologies. This analysis led to the conceptualization of a new social support program model, the emergent connections platform.

Findings from this analysis revealed key dimensions of participants’ experiences and program engagement in WCE. Reflecting unique programmatic features of the newly identified model, the emergent connections platform (). These are, an accessible infrastructure; a design centered on members’ capacity to share, lead, and support; and an adaptable program structure. These features operate together to lower barriers to participation while creating conditions for sustained engagement and member-driven innovation within and beyond the program.

One of the foundational pillars of an emergent connections platform is the presence of infrastructure that is culturally, linguistically, and physically accessible to the community it serves. In the case of WCE, this meant designing a system that met the needs of Latine, Spanish-speaking, immigrant older adults, many with visual impairments. As a fully remote program that engages older adults with visual impairments, technological access was a central concern. Therefore, WCE designed Abiento, a conferencing system featuring name recognition, simplified two-digit access codes, automated call-in reminders, automatically scheduled phone calls, and bilingual customization. Most participants expressed appreciation for the telephone-based format, which eliminated the visual navigation barriers inherent in screen-based platforms. This is particularly important for those with limited tech literacy, vision impairments, or mobility constraints.

For participants who are blind or have low vision, the phone-accessible design addressed the challenges of traveling to physical locations. Despite being connected only through voice, some participants emphasized that the experience felt like being in-person. Maité, a 60-year-old Mexican woman who lost her sight completely in 2015, shared:Well-Connected facilitates my participation and that of others by connecting us through Zoom or by telephone. They provide us with a code to call in, or they send us the link to connect. Before each season, we have to register for the classes. They send us a calendar by USB, printed, and in braille, so we can see what classes we want to take… One chooses the class, and at the time of the class, they connect us through a telephone call, or we can connect ourselves with the link they send us…. For me, it’s almost like being in person with the other participants, it’s really wonderful…. If the classes were in person, it would be difficult for me because of transportation and because of my disability. I’m going to be honest, walking alone in the streets makes me very nervous because of the insecurity.

Maité’s experience illuminates how thoughtful design choices like automated calls, audio-based participation, and information in multiple formats (USB, printed, and braille) can reduce barriers that might otherwise exclude older adults with disabilities from meaningful social engagement.

Moreover, this model attends to the linguistic and cultural relevance of the population served. Since the program is co-designed and co-led by and for the Latine community, members and program staff see themselves as part of one community. This shared cultural identity fosters an environment where trust, belonging, and meaningful participation can flourish. Members expressed, “We feel like a family. If someone has a problem or we’re feeling sad, we get together, we talk, we vent because you’re talking to people who’ve been through the same situations you’re going through right now” (Ermina). Over half of participants emphasized that this cultural alignment is especially critical for non-English-speaking immigrant older adults who often experience disconnection and discrimination when navigating formal service systems. One older man from Peru, Emilio, shared observations about a local organization:90% of the programs are in English and 20% in Spanish perhaps, because they have trainers who are bilingual or Spanish-speaking…. Even the bulletins they send are in English. I say, “English in a Latino community? Who’s going to understand English?” Seriously. That fact is very concerning. When I tell them we need people who speak Spanish, they say, “We’re trying, we’re looking, we’re working on it….” I think that suddenly what’s needed most is for…the person in charge, the CEO, to be someone Latino. Someone who has more awareness of the need, who sees the Latino community, who sees that, “Yes, they really need it,” but since there isn’t that force, it doesn’t matter much to them.

I say, “English in a Latino community? Who’s going to understand English?” Seriously. That fact is very concerning. When I tell them we need people who speak Spanish, they say, “We’re trying, we’re looking, we’re working on it….” I think that suddenly what’s needed most is for…the person in charge, the CEO, to be someone Latino. Someone who has more awareness of the need, who sees the Latino community, who sees that, “Yes, they really need it,” but since there isn’t that force, it doesn’t matter much to them.

Similarly, another participant shared that the Latino community is overlooked.There’s always discrimination, even when they say there isn’t…. Recently I went to an event, but it was only in English, so my niece went to help translate, it was purely for the güeros, not for Latinos…. I’ve been participating there for about 10 years; it wasn’t pleasant to feel that there’s no equality. I keep going, but only with the Spanish group because they teach us a lot for daily life and the person who leads the group is a very good person and we get along well.

In contrast, WCE centers Spanish language, Latine cultural references, and culturally grounded ways of relating. All staff are bilingual and Latine, fostering relational values such as respeto, confianza, and reciprocidad through culturally affirming programming. Activities reflect participants’ interests and heritage, such as Bible study, music, sharing migration stories and vision loss experiences, gardening, and exchanging home remedies and recipes. This affirms cultural identity and fosters meaningful social connection. One example is “From Your Kitchen to Your Palate,” a session facilitated by Ermina, a 60-year-old Mexican participant:We share recipes and cook virtually…talked among ourselves to see what we could share…. We thought of an activity related to grandma’s memories…and we decided to focus on food… Our classmates are from different countries, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Colombia. Sometimes we ask them if they want to share some recipes. There are between 6 and 15 people in the group…we feel good, we all participate, laugh… I’ve shared three of my mom’s recipes. One of them is her recipe for cream enchiladas… When I shared that recipe with the group…I was back in that moment when my mom made them, and that delicious smell came to me; I savored them.

We share recipes and cook virtually…talked among ourselves to see what we could share…. We thought of an activity related to grandma’s memories…and we decided to focus on food… Our classmates are from different countries, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Colombia. Sometimes we ask them if they want to share some recipes. There are between 6 and 15 people in the group…we feel good, we all participate, laugh… I’ve shared three of my mom’s recipes. One of them is her recipe for cream enchiladas… When I shared that recipe with the group…I was back in that moment when my mom made them, and that delicious smell came to me; I savored them.

A second pillar of the emergent connection platform is its member-driven design, where participants share, lead, and co-create the program. Leadership is cultivated over time through relational support and inclusive practices that position older adults as active contributors rather than passive recipients. This structure positions members as contributors whose lived experiences, interests, and skills are integral to the community’s growth and vitality. Through structured opportunities for leadership development and social engagement, it facilitates expansion of participants’ social networks. However, unlike social network interventions that focus on mobilizing recognized community leaders, WCE develops peer leaders within a virtual platform.

The program’s design creates opportunities for all members to contribute. A 67-year-old woman from Mexico, Alicia, shared how she encouraged another member to participate more:A lady, the mother of a participant, she’s 92 years old now, and she wasn’t participating in any group. I told him, “Your mom can participate,” and he said, “Yes, my mom, but she forgets now.” I told him, “She can do what she can do. Nobody’s going to force her, it’s voluntary.” Now, the lady is very active, very happy, and that fills me with so much joy, because she’s leading the Holy Rosary and we’re helping her.

A lady, the mother of a participant, she’s 92 years old now, and she wasn’t participating in any group. I told him, “Your mom can participate,” and he said, “Yes, my mom, but she forgets now.” I told him, “She can do what she can do. Nobody’s going to force her, it’s voluntary.” Now, the lady is very active, very happy, and that fills me with so much joy, because she’s leading the Holy Rosary and we’re helping her.

Rafael, the son, shared that his mother also co-facilitates a music group, where she helps to request the songs from Alexa and can remain engaged in the community despite being blind and having dementia.

Participants are invited to lead sessions based on their interests, facilitate one-time events, co-facilitate discussions, and start new groups. The range of activities and topics that can be proposed is broad enough to allow people with various abilities and interests to have the opportunity to lead. This fosters self-efficacy, skill-building, and a deepened sense of purpose and belonging. Participants shared a sense of freedom to create new groups/classes and get involved as much as they wanted to. For example, Rafael, a 68-year-old Mexican man who is deaf and blind, specifically joined Well-Connected to facilitate a class on immigration experiences. This led to another class, two events outside of WCE, and plans for a new class. He said, “The fact that Well Connected gives us the freedom to decide what we want to teach also helped facilitate my participation and that of others.” Rafael shared his experience of being the first blind person to facilitate a group.I was the first blind facilitator. From there I started bringing in more blind participants. Now there are many blind people there. Well-Connected has been able to facilitate that I and other people like me can participate because they give us confidence. They trusted me and invited me to facilitate classes and also others…they supported us to be able to do it. There are quite a few blind people there who have great abilities, who inspire you.

I was the first blind facilitator. From there I started bringing in more blind participants. Now there are many blind people there. Well-Connected has been able to facilitate that I and other people like me can participate because they give us confidence. They trusted me and invited me to facilitate classes and also others…they supported us to be able to do it. There are quite a few blind people there who have great abilities, who inspire you.

However, without building capacity into the program’s design, leadership roles would likely only be taken up by those already confident or positioned to do so, like Rafael. The theorized model addresses this gap by embedding leadership opportunities into the structure of the program. In the case of WCE, this approach allows members to progress through different roles in the program, from participant to co-facilitator and lead facilitator, at their own pace, with support and encouragement from staff and peers. Members are encouraged to assume leadership roles by other members and staff. For example, peers who need to step down from a facilitator role or need help with a group may ask another member to take over or co-lead, or encourage them to facilitate a class. Alicia shared her experience of stepping into a leadership role when her friend could no longer continue:I’m the facilitator through my friend. We were a small group of friends, she lived in San Francisco and called me when she was already very sick, and asked me if I could become the facilitator, because she couldn’t do it anymore…. The coordinator called me, and told me, “The current facilitators can’t do it anymore.” When I introduced myself to the group [the first time], I told them my condition and said I needed help, because I can’t read the Holy Rosary book…. Everyone said yes, and right now we’re doing very well, everyone is participating… I feel very happy to be able to contribute like this, even if it’s by phone…. That I’m in a community, in a group…It makes me very proud of myself.

I’m the facilitator through my friend. We were a small group of friends, she lived in San Francisco and called me when she was already very sick, and asked me if I could become the facilitator, because she couldn’t do it anymore…. The coordinator called me, and told me, “The current facilitators can’t do it anymore.” When I introduced myself to the group [the first time], I told them my condition and said I needed help, because I can’t read the Holy Rosary book…. Everyone said yes, and right now we’re doing very well, everyone is participating… I feel very happy to be able to contribute like this, even if it’s by phone…. That I’m in a community, in a group…It makes me very proud of myself.

Alicia’s example illustrates how WCE’s peer-to-peer structure creates space for collaborative leadership, where facilitators can acknowledge their needs and rely on group support to fulfill their roles. Other times, WCE staff directly ask members if they would like to facilitate a class. This was the case for Nieves, a 63-year-old woman from Colombia with low vision.At first, I didn’t know what I was going to do, nor what it meant to be a facilitator. All I knew was that I had been a teacher. As they say, it’s by getting involved that you learn. I decided to start teaching a class on gratitude…[later] I invented the “talking about everything a little bit” class. It’s an opportunity for people to express themselves and say what they feel, what’s happening to them…The class wasn’t really a class, but rather a group, but not a support group.

At first, I didn’t know what I was going to do, nor what it meant to be a facilitator. All I knew was that I had been a teacher. As they say, it’s by getting involved that you learn. I decided to start teaching a class on gratitude…[later] I invented the “talking about everything a little bit” class. It’s an opportunity for people to express themselves and say what they feel, what’s happening to them…The class wasn’t really a class, but rather a group, but not a support group.

This distinction is important. Like a support or self-help group, her class is peer-led and grounded in mutual support, but the topics are broad enough that it does not always center on a problem. The catalog description for this group was: “Join our group and share whatever you would like. This is a conversation group where the goal is to have a good time and share.”

This leadership structure enables continued growth and evolution in a way that remains rooted in the needs and strengths of members. The emergent nature allows participants to continue imagining new ways to participate, new topics and experiences to share, and new opportunities to support each other. Throughout the interviews, most participants shared plans for future groups and classes they hoped to facilitate, reflecting an ongoing sense of agency and possibility. As one participant expressed, “We don’t have an idea yet of when the program will be. Maybe in two more seasons, when I feel stronger, more confident to do things and have a project.” This forward-looking orientation exemplifies how WCE’s structure cultivates not only current leadership, but also the conditions for future leadership to emerge.

The third pillar of the emergent connection platform is its capacity to foster mutually transformative dynamics, reciprocal processes through which members and the program adapt and grow in response to one another. Rather than functioning according to a static service delivery program model, an emergent connections platform is adaptive, constantly evolving with members’ interests, needs, contributions, and relational dynamics. Similarly, members evolve as their social networks expand and their sense of self-efficacy grows. These dynamics are evident in WCE, where members formed enduring social networks while initiating in-person meetups, translating materials into braille, and launching braille classes within and outside the program. As participants’ lives are expanded through connection and support, the program is simultaneously reshaped through their innovation and participation.

Unlike dyadic models that strengthen personal support systems primarily through culturally matched intermediaries who connect immigrants to formal services, WCE cultivates peer-to-peer relationships within a structured virtual environment. These connections expand participants’ social support networks and create opportunities for members to both receive and provide emotional and instrumental support, fostering relationships that often persist beyond the structured environment. For example, as Juan, a 75-year-old man from Guatemala, described, participation offered a form of collective care and addressed their social isolation:I decided to sign up to participate, and above all to have communication with other people. Sometimes it’s like a form of therapy, because you’re alone or want to listen to someone or receive support from other people who are in the same situation [have visual impairment].

I decided to sign up to participate, and above all to have communication with other people. Sometimes it’s like a form of therapy, because you’re alone or want to listen to someone or receive support from other people who are in the same situation [have visual impairment].

This sense of connection creates a foundation for deeper engagement and expanding support. Exemplifying this, Ernesto, a 61-year-old-man from Peru, described assisting a friend he met through Well-Connected who was facing kidney dialysis:I have a friend I met through Well-Connected who is now on dialysis…. I had to get involved with the hospital, contact them and tell them what was happening, because he had language barrier problems…. When I heard about his situation, I got involved because it made me a little sad that he was alone here. Like there was no one to support him, so I had to get involved…talk with the nurse, talk with the social worker and everything, and kind of put a little more pressure on them so they could help him better. He was in a shelter…. I was looking for contacts…so he could find a place to live. Because he couldn’t be on the kidney waiting list if he was in a shelter. He had to be in a house…. He achieved it, so he’s satisfied. Waiting for one of these days…he might get a call to receive a kidney…. With the little one has, you have to help.

Members also coordinate support for individuals outside the WCE network. Ernesto recounted sending a cane, a talking clock, and adaptive drinking aids to someone in need:We’ve communicated with people from Well-Connected, and outside of Well-Connected. Two weeks ago, I sent a man…some things that could help him. The information about this person came to me through someone from Well-Connected, although the man who received it is not a member of this group.

We’ve communicated with people from Well-Connected, and outside of Well-Connected. Two weeks ago, I sent a man…some things that could help him. The information about this person came to me through someone from Well-Connected, although the man who received it is not a member of this group.

He described the process of checking whether the recipient would be comfortable accepting help before sending items, noting this was his first time organizing such assistance. This reciprocal dynamic enables older adults and those undergoing physical transitions to find purpose as valuable members of a community where they can receive and offer support.

Beyond one-to-one support, participants have created new opportunities to engage their new WCE community outside of the program. Viviendo con Alegría (Living with Joy) is an in-person meetup in San Francisco initiated by WCE members. Rafael, who initiated the gatherings and has been living in the U.S. for 22 years, shared:Back in Mexico I always organized events… [but this] was my first time organizing something like this here in the United States. It was something new and a bit difficult, but I went around knocking on doors…until I found the people who did help me…. The planning process was challenging since I had to handle all the coordination by phone, securing a venue and arranging for people to contribute food…. The entire effort was voluntary and community-driven, with each person sharing a dish at the gathering…. Saturday June 25, 2022, was the first time we met. We met at a church in the Mission, because another WCE member belonged to that church and spoke with the pastors to help us host it there…. We were 22 people. Many couldn’t go because of transportation or because they got sick, but it was a lot of fun.

Carolina, a 74-year-old participant from Mexico, shared her experience, revealing how these gatherings brought members and program staff together in community, transcending the typical service provider-recipient dynamic:We’ve now met twice in the Mission… People volunteer to bring something. I’ve brought 40 or 50 chicken flautas both times. I buy them at a restaurant and take them there so everyone can take two or three flautas. One woman makes pozole and other people bring traditional things from different places, pupusas, flautas, cochinita. Both times my sister drove me and went with me. I introduced her to everyone there…we give each other a handshake, a hug. It’s a great pleasure to be able to meet each other. For me it was a great blessing, because I met the directors of Well-Connected and many facilitators whom we already knew by voice. Others joined us by phone. They’d call from Santa Barbara and communicate, “What are you doing now? What are you eating?” and I felt my heart swell.

Program staff attended the first gathering primarily as guests, as members assumed leadership in securing the location, food, and other logistics. Their second event received greater support from WCE staff who facilitated meeting location and other members who helped to co-organize. As part of this event, members contacted Telemundo, a major Latino news channel, to conduct an interview and promote WCE. Rafael reflected, “In the second event… Well-Connected got more involved, I knew more people who could help, and I didn’t struggle as much.”

The second major project that members initiated was the development of a braille class specific to their community’s needs. Many participants shared that existing organizations serving the blind in California lacked programs in Spanish, making it extremely difficult to access the training necessary to adapt to vision loss. Recognizing this gap, Well-Connected members created their own solution: teaching each other braille in Spanish virtually. The project evolved through multiple stages of member initiative and programmatic response. Lazaro, a 62-year-old man from Mexico, first proposed the idea after a conversation with a friend from the program:He asked me if I knew braille, I told him yes, he says, “Why don’t you share braille here with Well-Connected?” I told him, “I don’t know how it could be done in a virtual way.” After some time thinking about how I could do it…we communicated with Well-Connected, and the program accepted…. I ended up facilitating the classes alone because my friend was still a beginner in braille. Now I teach braille at intermediate and advanced levels in Spanish through Well-Connected. I use the same system that a great teacher taught me…. I spend hours preparing classes and writing lessons to make it easier for students. Last week I sent material to a man and just to send him the material took three hours. Previously I had to prepare 31 pages for four students. For those four students I spent approximately three hours for each of them or more…. People tell me they want to pay me to teach them braille, but I never accept anything because I was taught for free…. Buying materials to teach the class is something I do on my own…. I don’t have money to spare. When you give something or a part of what you need yourself, you feel more satisfaction.

As the class grew, Lazaro asked Maité, a 60-year-old Mexican woman, to join as co-facilitator, given her braille knowledge. Despite her initial nervousness about teaching in a group setting, Maité felt responsible for carrying out the lesson: “I have to be able to do this, they need me, he needs me, and the others who are learning do, too.” As the WCE braille class progressed, members began asking if she could meet with them outside of class to practice braille. Eventually, she decided to extend the class beyond WCE through WhatsApp to offer additional practice. At the time of our interview, she met with a group of students weekly for 1–2 hr by phone to practice outside of WCE.

Initially, the braille class relied on standardized lessons from the Hadley Institute for the Blind. However, these materials were only available in English. Recognizing this language barrier was a significant obstacle for members, Maité expressed her desire to find someone who could cover the material costs so that Lazaro could create Spanish-language lessons. During the member-check a year after our interview, in 2024, Maité shared that they had addressed this barrier directly by developing original lesson materials, drawing inspiration from the English-language Hadley Institute books and requesting support from WCE to print materials.During the semester we met…with the director of Well-Connected, it’s something that’s done with all the facilitators. And we told him if they could help us print the material in braille and he found a printer in San Francisco, and they print it for us in braille there. The company does it for free. Twelve students enrolled and they all received the material. We plan to keep doing it this way now. It gives me so much satisfaction and joy when I hear a student who was having difficulty, be able to understand and learn. I feel very excited and it helped me a lot to show myself that I’m capable of leading, even though I can’t see, if I set my mind to it.

And we told him if they could help us print the material in braille and he found a printer in San Francisco, and they print it for us in braille there. The company does it for free. Twelve students enrolled and they all received the material. We plan to keep doing it this way now.
