I feel very excited and it helped me a lot to show myself that I’m capable of leading, even though I can’t see, if I set my mind to it.

Due to the member’s initiative, WCE is now the only national program offering braille classes in Spanish. Since this is a highly needed resource for the Spanish-speaking community, WCE has opened these classes to people of all ages. This initiative to adapt and expand braille classes exemplifies how members catalyze programmatic expansion within an emergent model. While this initiative resembles community-based strategies, the members did not frame their participation as a tool for social activism and systemic change. Instead, they viewed this social support principally as practical aid, serving as a pathway to empowerment and greater autonomy.

This study expands empirical research on interventions addressing social isolation among marginalized communities, particularly older adults with vision impairment (VI) and non-English speakers, by examining how technology-supported platforms can foster meaningful social connection. While prior studies on social support models emphasize increasing social contact or delivering structured programming (; ), this study’s findings highlight a different mechanism. The identified model is a dynamic process that reduces participation barriers, cultivates reciprocal peer networks and leadership, and creates opportunities for members to innovate and shape the evolution of the program. These findings are consistent with prior research demonstrating that interventions are more likely to produce beneficial outcomes when older adults are engaged as active participants rather than passive recipients of services, particularly when interventions provide purposeful activities and meaningful functional roles that enable contribution, reciprocity, and meaningful engagement (; ). Extending this work, our findings suggest that participatory approaches may be particularly valuable for marginalized older adults because they not only increase engagement but also enable participants to exercise agency, contribute expertise, and co-create social environments that support sustained connection and participation within and outside the program.

Findings from this study also contribute to the growing literature on technology-supported approaches to addressing social isolation among older adults (; ), including emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-based interventions. Several types of (AI)-based interventions have been developed, such as social robots, telepresence systems, and smart home devices, with current research demonstrating their potential to reduce loneliness and depressive symptoms (). However, less attention has been given to how technology can foster sustained social connectedness, reciprocal peer relationships, and meaningful community participation. A scoping review of AI technologies designed to support older adults’ social connectedness found that only one prior study, conducted in Japan, developed an intervention specifically aimed at increasing social participation through remote volunteer work (). Moreover, existing interventions developed in the United States have rarely focused explicitly on strengthening social connectedness or considered how cultural and linguistic diversity shapes opportunities for participation ().

Our findings extend this emerging literature by highlighting the importance of technology-supported platforms that build relational infrastructure and position older adults as active contributors, leaders, and members of an interconnected community. The platform reframes older adults as active agents within a community network through an organizational structure that engages members as experts and leaders who can contribute knowledge, organize activities, and support peers. This accessibility is particularly significant for individuals experiencing vision loss, who may encounter substantial environmental and logistical barriers to participating in traditional community activities (). Lowering the barriers to access broadens who can participate and ensures that individuals vulnerable to isolation are able not only to join but also to contribute and lead.

In addition, the platform expands participants’ social support networks by connecting individuals with others who share language, culture, and lived experiences. Social networks have long been understood as webs of relationships through which individuals are embedded in patterns of reciprocity, emotional closeness, and interaction (; ; ). Participation in such networks is strongly associated with increased access to social support (), comprising caring relationships that provide emotional, informational, and practical assistance. Consistent with this literature, participants described how the platform connected them with peers who understood their experiences with vision loss, migration, language barriers, and aging.

Prior research suggests that support is particularly effective when it comes from individuals who share relevant social or experiential similarities, as this fosters empathic understanding and trust (). The emergent connections platform cultivates conditions for members to identify shared interests, propose new initiatives, and develop programming with logistical support from the organization. In doing so, it incorporates several intervention strategies previously identified in the literature on social isolation () but restructures them within a participatory framework in which older adults engage in collective problem-solving and program co-creation. This emergent structure provides opportunities for members to develop agency, mastery, and purpose while strengthening the collective capacity of the group.

These dynamics resonate with the concept of convivencia, rooted in Latin American traditions, which describes a sense of collectivity and solidarity that emerges through shared experiences, values, and opportunities for mutual exchange and co-creation (; ). Convivencia emphasizes not only social interaction but also the relational processes that sustain community life, including agency, trust, collaboration, and belonging (; ). The emergent connections platform reflects these dynamics by enabling participants to engage with one another frequently, supporting each other in practical and emotional ways. Through these interactions, participants develop not only social ties but also a sense of shared belonging and interdependence that sustains engagement over time and across changing physical circumstances. Prior research suggests that individuals often feel most connected when they experience a sense of purpose, reciprocity, and being needed within a network (). By creating a space where older adults can actively support others and contribute their skills, the platform fosters relationships characterized by mutual care rather than one-directional assistance.

While this study makes an important contribution to research on interventions addressing social isolation among marginalized older adults, it has several limitations. First, the Latine population is highly diverse, and cultural values, migration histories, and expectations regarding services may vary across communities in ways not captured in this study. Additionally, immigration or documentation status can shape individuals’ access to services and their experiences with service providers. However, given the sensitive political climate surrounding immigration in the United States, this information was not collected to protect participants and encourage participation.

Second, participants self-selected into the study. This may introduce selection bias, as they may be more likely to report positive experiences with the program and may not capture the experiences of those who discontinued involvement or encountered barriers to sustained engagement. Although the purpose of this study was to identify and conceptualize an emerging intervention model rather than evaluate program effectiveness, this selection process limits the range of perspectives represented. However, the trustworthiness of the findings was strengthened through triangulation across participant interviews, observations of the program, program materials, and ongoing discussions with program leadership and staff. Future research should examine the experiences of nonparticipants, individuals who disengage from the program, and those reporting less favorable experiences to further refine and test the framework. Lastly, the program examined in this study operates within a larger national organization and benefits from the funding, infrastructure, and technological capacity of a well-established nonprofit. Programs with similar technological and accessibility supports may be more difficult to implement in smaller organizations or local contexts with fewer resources. These structural and contextual factors may limit the transferability of the findings to other organizational and geographic settings.

This study highlights the potential of emergent, participant-driven programs as a potential intervention for addressing social isolation amongst marginalized older adults. Organizational support plays a critical role in sustaining these initiatives by providing technological infrastructure, facilitation, and logistical coordination. At the same time, the model produces a cyclical dynamic in which member initiative drives program adaptation, while program flexibility strengthens members’ capacity to lead and contribute. The relational networks that emerge within this environment stand in contrast to dominant models of social service provision, which are often structured around top-down systems of assistance. By foregrounding reciprocity, participation, and collective agency, the theorized model offers an alternative approach to addressing social isolation that is anchored in co-creation and reciprocity.

medicine.title: The emerging functional landscape of piRNAs in ocular health and disease
medicine.text:
Ocular diseases encompass a diverse spectrum of pathologies affecting key structures of the eye, including the retina, lens, optic nerve, and cornea (). Many of these conditions remain leading causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. Vision depends on highly specialized, metabolically demanding tissues, particularly photoreceptors and the retinal vasculature, which together enable phototransduction and sustain the energetic needs of the neurosensory retina (). Disruption of these systems, whether through photoreceptor degeneration or vascular dysfunction, underlies major vision-threatening diseases, including diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, retinopathy of prematurity, and subretinal fibrosis (). Because retinal neurons, vascular cells, and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) are continuously exposed to metabolic, oxidative, and environmental stress, maintaining retinal homeostasis requires tightly regulated gene expression programs.

Consistent with this, many ocular diseases are associated with alterations in gene expression programs that govern cellular identity, stress responses, and tissue homeostasis (). Among the regulatory mechanisms of these processes, small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs) have emerged as important contributors to ocular development, tissue homeostasis, and disease (). Although they do not encode proteins, sncRNAs exert broad control over gene expression through transcriptional, posttranscriptional, translational, and epigenetic mechanisms, influencing processes such as differentiation, cellular stress adaptation, and disease-associated signaling pathways ().

Among the diverse sncRNAs, piRNAs represent a unique, relatively underexplored class. Initially identified in the germline as guardians of genomic integrity, piRNAs function by associating with PIWI proteins to silence transposable elements (TEs) and protect genomic stability (, ). This activity is mediated through the formation of the piRNA-induced silencing complex (piRISC), which directs sequence-specific regulation of target transcripts. Although piRNAs were initially thought to function exclusively in germline cells, subsequent studies demonstrated their work in diverse somatic tissues (, ). In these tissues, piRNAs were reported to regulate gene expression through various mechanisms including DNA methylation, chromatin remodeling, and posttranscriptional control (). Consistent with these broader functions, piRNAs have been implicated in a range of human diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disorders, and neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease (). More recently, advances in high-throughput sequencing and computational analysis have enabled the identification of piRNA expression profiles in ocular tissues, providing early evidence that PIWI-piRNA pathways may also function in the eye ().

Most of these findings are in the early stages, and it is not yet known exactly how specific piRNAs or PIWI proteins influence ocular health. Addressing this knowledge gap is significant because differential gene-regulatory networks are central to angiogenesis, fibrosis, oxidative stress responses, and cellular stress adaptation, which are hallmarks of many vision-threatening diseases. A better understanding of piRNA-mediated gene regulation may uncover novel molecular mechanisms underlying ocular disease and identify new opportunities for biomarker discovery and therapeutic intervention. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of piRNA expressions and functions in potential eye tissues, with a focus on their emerging roles in angiogenesis and fibrosis. We also discuss the potential of piRNAs as biomarkers and therapeutic targets to guide future research directions in ocular health.

Unlike miRNAs, piRNAs currently lack a unified nomenclature across major databases, and the same piRNA sequence may therefore be represented by different identifiers across studies and repositories (). Species-specific abbreviations are commonly incorporated into piRNA identifiers; for example, hsa denotes Homo sapiens, mmu denotes Mus musculus, and rno denotes Rattus norvegicus (). An identifier such as hsa-piR-22032, for example, is used by piRNAdb for a human piRNA and is cross-referenced to several alternative identifiers in other piRNA databases. Numerical components of piRNA identifiers are generally database-specific accession or sequential identifiers and should not be interpreted as indicating evolutionary families, functional classes, or genomic clusters (, ). Because piRNA identifiers and annotations can differ across repositories, cross-referencing multiple databases and reporting the piRNA nucleotide sequence, species, genomic coordinates when available, and the source database in addition to the database-specific identifier can improve reproducibility and reduce ambiguity in piRNA identification.

Cross-species interpretation of piRNA studies also requires particular caution. In contrast to many protein-coding genes and miRNAs, individual mature piRNA sequences generally show limited conservation among mammalian species, whereas the genomic locations and organization of subsets of piRNA-producing loci can show substantially greater conservation (). Early comparative analyses demonstrated conservation of the genomic locations of several piRNA clusters among mouse, rat, and human despite limited conservation of individual piRNA sequences (). More recent comparative studies of mammalian pachytene piRNAs similarly demonstrated that piRNA-producing loci can retain conserved synteny and structural characteristics across placental mammals even though their underlying piRNA sequences are poorly conserved (, ). Therefore, when a piRNA-associated phenotype is identified in mouse or rat models, the presence of a sequence-equivalent or syntenically related human piRNA should be established before assuming direct translational relevance. Ideally, cross-species interpretation should consider nucleotide sequence, genomic location or synteny, expression pattern, and functional validation in human cells or tissues rather than relying on similarity in piRNA numerical identifiers alone.

Several publicly available resources can be used to verify piRNA sequences, nomenclature, genomic coordinates, piRNA-producing clusters, and related annotations (). Because individual piRNAs may be assigned different identifiers across repositories, cross-referencing multiple databases and reporting the nucleotide sequence and genomic location, when available, can improve reproducibility and reduce ambiguity in piRNA identification.

PIWI-family proteins are evolutionarily conserved across animals, although their number, nomenclature, expression patterns, and biological functions vary among species. Humans express four PIWI-family members (PIWIL1–PIWIL4), whereas distinct homologs have been characterized in commonly used animal models. The major PIWI proteins identified in humans and representative animal models, together with their principal reported functions, are summarized in .

The PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathway is an evolutionarily conserved small RNA system that plays essential roles in preserving genome integrity and regulating gene expression (, , ). Initially characterized for its role in transposable element (TE) repression, the pathway is now recognized as a broader RNA-guided regulatory network that functions through transcriptional, epigenetic, and posttranscriptional mechanisms, with additional roles in translational regulation (, , , ). piRNAs arise from diverse genomic loci, including TE-rich clusters, intergenic regions, pseudogenes, and, during development, protein-coding genes (, , ). Long precursor transcripts are exported to specialized cytoplasmic compartments associated with nuage, a perinuclear, membraneless germ-cell granule enriched in RNA-processing factors, and mitochondrial membranes (), where the RNA helicase MOV10L1 promotes precursor binding and remodeling, the endonuclease Zucchini/PLD6 mediates endonucleolytic cleavage, and the resulting pre-piRNAs are loaded onto PIWI proteins. Their 3′ ends are subsequently trimmed by the 3′-to-5′ exonuclease PNLDC1 and 2′-O-methylated by the RNA methyltransferase HENMT1, generating mature 24–32-nucleotide piRNAs (, ). In many animals, primary piRNAs also initiate the ping-pong amplification cycle. Antisense piRNAs bound to PIWI proteins recognize and cleave complementary TE transcripts, generating the 5′ ends of sense secondary piRNAs (, ). These secondary piRNAs are loaded onto a partner PIWI protein and can reciprocally cleave antisense precursor transcripts, producing additional antisense piRNAs. This reciprocal cleavage amplifies piRNA populations and generates the characteristic 10-nucleotide overlap between the 5′ ends of sense and antisense piRNAs (, , ). In Drosophila, PIWI-directed cleavage can also initiate downstream Zucchini-dependent phased processing, thereby increasing the diversity and abundance of piRNAs produced from a precursor. In mammals, secondary piRNAs produced through this pathway can promote MIWI2 loading and contribute to nuclear transposon silencing in fetal germ cells (, ) ().

Mature piRNAs associate with PIWI proteins to form effector complexes that recognize target RNAs through sequence complementarity and coordinate multiple regulatory outcomes (, , ) (). In the cytoplasm, PIWI-piRNA complexes cleave complementary TE transcripts, thereby reducing transposon expression while reinforcing piRNA production through secondary amplification (, , ). In the nucleus, PIWI proteins promote durable transcriptional silencing through species-specific epigenetic mechanisms, including piRNA-directed de novo DNA methylation in mammalian fetal male germ cells and recruitment of chromatin-modifying machinery that establishes H3K9me3-enriched heterochromatin in Drosophila (, , , , ). Beyond direct TE repression, PIWI-piRNA pathways can influence endogenous gene expression: PIWI-dependent chromatin changes at TE insertions may alter the expression of neighboring genes (), whereas selected cellular mRNAs can be regulated directly through piRNA-guided deadenylation and decay, endonucleolytic turnover, or translational control (). These findings also demonstrate that the targets, biological importance, and molecular mechanisms of non-TE piRNA functions differ among species, developmental stages, cell types, and individual transcripts (, , ).

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a progressive disease of the central retina and a leading cause of irreversible vision loss among older adults worldwide (, ), which predominantly affects the macula, the central region of the retina responsible for precise and detailed vision (). Clinically, AMD progresses through early, intermediate, and late stages, with late AMD classified as dry (atrophic) or wet (neovascular) AMD (nAMD) (). Dry AMD is characterized by drusen accumulation, RPE dysfunction, and geographic atrophy (, ). On the contrary, nAMD is characterized by choroidal neovascularization (CNV), vascular leakage, and scar formation (, ).

The disease begins long before drusen are clinically noticeable, with some of the earliest changes occurring in the RPE, a cell layer that depends on metabolic resilience, polarity, and a strong capacity to cope with oxidative stress (, ). Because the RPE is highly metabolically active and constantly exposed to oxidative damage, prolonged stress places a significant burden on its mitochondrial function, which is key for maintaining cellular homeostasis (, ). As mitochondrial dysfunction progresses, energy production declines and cellular stress increases, causing the RPE to reprogram its transcriptional and metabolic state (). Under sustained metabolic and mitochondrial stress, the RPE may either maintain its epithelial identity or move toward inflammatory, degenerative, or angiogenic phenotypes (). Recent studies suggest that this transition is regulated not only by classical signaling pathways but also by epigenetic regulators and posttranscriptional regulatory systems, which may also contribute to retinal stress response (, , , ).

Direct evidence for the role of piRNAs in ocular AMD-related biology remains limited but important. Karpagavalli et al. () identified 266 piRNAs in human retina and RPE datasets and showed that 261 piRNAs were associated with PIWIL4/HIWI2 in ARPE-19 cells. Their in silico/computational analysis linked these piRNAs to pathways involved in intracellular trafficking, circadian regulation, and oxidative stress responses. Several piRNAs, including piR-hsa-26131, piR-hsa-11361, and piR-hsa-11360, were predicted to interact with regulatory RNA networks involving miRNAs and long non-coding RNAs. These findings support the presence of a PIWI-associated piRNA pathway in retinal and RPE cells; however, most predicted piRNA-target relationships have not yet been functionally validated in AMD models.

More direct functional evidence comes from an experimental choroidal neovascularization (CNV) model. In a laser-induced CNV mouse model, PIWIL4 expression was increased, and PIWIL4 knockdown reduced angiogenic activity, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secretion, and VEGFR2 phosphorylation (). This suggests that PIWIL4-associated pathways may contribute to VEGF-driven neovascularization. However, because the specific disease-driving piRNAs and their direct targets remain incompletely defined, this evidence should be interpreted as early mechanistic support rather than proof of an established piRNA therapeutic target in AMD ().

Direct studies of PIWI-piRNA interactions in AMD are limited; thus, nonocular models offer indirect mechanistic insight into pathways relevant to AMD. In luminal breast cancer, piR-823 was enriched in ALDH-positive cancer stem cell populations from MCF-7 cells and detected in patient tumors. Gain- and loss-of-function studies showed that piR-823 promotes cell proliferation, colony formation, mammosphere growth, and expression of the stemness markers OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG. In MCF-7 xenografts, piR-823 knockdown reduced tumor growth. Mechanistically, piR-823 increased DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B expression and DNA methylation, leading to Wnt/β-catenin activation (). This shows that piRNAs may help maintain pathological cell states through epigenetic changes, rather than merely serving as passive markers.

Li et al. () also showed that piRNA-823, carried by extracellular vesicles (EVs) in multiple myeloma, can influence endothelial cell behavior. When piRNA-823 was introduced into these cells, it led to more cell growth, tube formation, and invasion, as well as elevated levels of VEGF, IL-6, and ICAM-1. This also resulted in increased tumor growth in xenograft models (). These results suggest that piRNAs can influence endothelial activation and proangiogenic signaling, which are important in neovascular AMD. Other studies suggest that piR-651 promotes cell growth in A549 lung cancer cells and xenograft models by driving cell-cycle progression through cyclin D1 and CDK4 (). In another study, piR-932, found in epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-enriched breast cancer stem cells, was suggested to interact with PIWIL2 and be associated with methylation-based repression of Latexin (). These findings support the idea that piRNAs control cell-state changes through epigenetic regulation ().

piRNAs and PIWI proteins with roles relevant to ocular disease

AMD, age-related macular degeneration; ARPE-19, human retinal pigment epithelial cell line; CNV, choroidal neovascularization; DR, diabetic retinopathy; HIF-1α, hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha; ICAM-1, intercellular adhesion molecule 1; IL-6, interleukin 6; JAK2, Janus kinase 2; mTOR, mechanistic target of rapamycin; OIR, oxygen-induced retinopathy; PI3K, phosphoinositide 3-kinase; PIWI, P-element-induced wimpy testis; PIWIL, PIWI-like; piRNA, PIWI-interacting RNA; RPE, retinal pigment epithelium; ROP, retinopathy of prematurity; STAT3, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3; VEGF, vascular endothelial growth factor; VEGFR2, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2.

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus and remains a major cause of vision loss worldwide (, ). Chronic hyperglycemia damages the retinal neurovascular unit by inducing oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, and progressive breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier (). These metabolic disturbances produce early structural abnormalities, including pericyte dropout, endothelial cell degeneration, and basement membrane thickening, which together lead to the formation of acellular capillaries and increased vascular permeability characteristic of nonproliferative DR (NPDR) (, ). As capillary nonperfusion worsens, retinal hypoxia induces a strong upregulation of VEGF and other proangiogenic mediators, resulting in the pathological neovascularization that defines proliferative DR (PDR) and substantially contributes to vision loss (, ).

Emerging evidence indicates that piRNA expression is altered in DR (). Chen et al. () identified 30 differentially expressed piRNAs in the aqueous humor of patients with PDR, demonstrating that piRNAs are detectable in human ocular fluids and dynamically regulated in diabetic retinal disease, although the functional role of these differentially expressed piRNAs remains largely underexplored. Similarly, Yu et al. () reported 79 differentially expressed piRNAs in retinal tissues from a mouse model of PDR, with pathway enrichment analyses linking these piRNAs to angiogenesis- and proliferation-related signaling pathways. Together, these studies suggest that piRNA dysregulation accompanies diabetic retinal injury and is associated with molecular programs involved in neovascularization. However, these profiling studies remain descriptive and do not establish whether altered piRNAs are causal drivers, adaptive responses, or downstream markers of retinal damage.

Mechanistic evidence supporting a functional role for piRNAs in retinal angiogenesis has begun to emerge but remains limited. In an experimental retinal neovascularization model, Yu et al. () adopted studies from a cancer model to demonstrate that piR-1245, acting through PIWIL2, regulates the JAK2/STAT3 pathway and modulates hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and VEGF expression, thereby promoting pathological angiogenesis. This adopted study provides functional evidence that a specific piRNA-PIWI axis can influence hypoxia-driven angiogenic signaling in the retina. Although this model is not restricted to DR, the pathway is highly relevant to PDR, where retinal hypoxia and VEGF signaling are central drivers of pathological neovascularization.

In tumor-associated endothelial models, piR-823 has been shown to promote endothelial activation by increasing VEGF, IL-6, ICAM-1, and CXCR4 expression, leading to enhanced endothelial proliferation, migration, and tube formation (). In vascular injury models, piRNA DQ614630 has been associated with endothelial apoptosis and dysfunction under oxidized LDL-induced stress (). These findings do not directly establish a role for piRNAs in DR, but they support the broader possibility that piRNAs may regulate endothelial activation, inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and vascular remodeling, all of which are central features of diabetic retinal disease.

piRNAs could be relevant to earlier stages of DR, although direct evidence is currently lacking. Pericyte dysfunction is a key initiating event in diabetic retinal microvascular injury. A study by Suo et al. () showed that METTL3-mediated m6A methylation was increased under diabetic stress, impaired pericyte function, and contributed to diabetes-induced retinal vascular complications in animal models. Although this does not demonstrate a piRNA-mediated mechanism, it supports the broader concept that RNA-based regulatory pathways may contribute to early diabetic retinal vascular injury ().

In summary, current evidence suggests that piRNAs are altered in DR and may be linked to angiogenesis, proliferation, and cellular stress pathways. However, most findings remain descriptive, and the causal roles of individual piRNAs in diabetic retinal pathology require further validation.

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a developmental disorder of the retinal vasculature that arises from disruption of the tightly regulated program of postnatal vascularization in preterm infants and remains a leading cause of childhood blindness worldwide (). Distinct from diabetic retinopathy, which involves the degeneration of a preexisting vascular network, ROP is characterized by a fundamental failure of normal vascular development followed by a subsequent phase of aberrant vascular repair ().

The pathogenesis of ROP follows a strict biphasic progression. In the first phase (vaso-obliteration), the transition of a preterm infant from the relatively hypoxic intrauterine environment to a hyperoxic extrauterine environment exacerbated by supplemental oxygen leads to the suppression of HIF-1α (, ). This molecular downregulation precipitously reduces the expression of VEGF and other essential survival signals, resulting in apoptosis of existing endothelial cells and the arrest of physiological retinal vascularization (, ).

As the infant matures and is removed from the oxygen incubator, the metabolic requirements of the developing neural retina increase, leading to a profound oxygen deficiency within the extensive avascular peripheral zones. This metabolic demand triggers the second phase (vasoproliferation), marked by the stabilization of HIF-1α and a compensatory, yet dysregulated, surge in proangiogenic mediators, primarily VEGF (, ). During this phase, neovascularization occurs not as a functional intraretinal network, but as fragile, disorganized vessels that breach the internal limiting membrane and extend into the vitreous (). These pathological vessels are prone to hemorrhage and are frequently accompanied by myofibroblast-rich fibrovascular membranes (). The subsequent contraction of these membranes generates significant tractional forces, which can lead to retinal detachment and permanent blindness (, ). This biphasic framework initial vaso-obliteration followed by hypoxia-driven neovascularization is consistently recapitulated in the murine oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) model, which remains the gold standard for investigating ROP mechanisms (). Evidence suggests that piRNAs may regulate hypoxia-driven angiogenesis in ROP. Using an in vitro and in vivo oxygen-induced retinopathy models, Yu et al. () investigated piR-1245 in retinal neovascularization. Hypoxia increased piR-1245 and PIWIL2 expression in human retinal endothelial cells, whereas piR-1245 knockdown reduced cell proliferation, migration, and tube formation. It also suppressed JAK2/STAT3 signaling and decreased HIF-1α and VEGF expression. In mice, piR-1245 reduction attenuated pathological retinal neovascularization. These findings indicate that piR-1245 promotes retinal angiogenesis through the PIWIL2-associated JAK2/STAT3/HIF-1α/VEGF pathway.

Direct evidence linking piRNAs to ROP remains limited. ROP involves oxygen-driven vascular loss followed by hypoxia-induced angiogenesis; thus, piRNA-PIWI networks may regulate both phases. Profiling piRNA expression during retinal vascular development and validating their targets in endothelial and glial cells are needed to clarify their role ().

Subretinal fibrosis is a pathological process in which cells in the subretinal space produce excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) and form contractile scar tissue. It develops in advanced neovascular retinal diseases, including nAMD, PDR, and severe ROP (, ). Fibrosis arises when RPE cells, endothelial cells, pericytes, and infiltrating mesenchymal-like cells undergo EMT or EndMT (). These transitions increase α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), collagen I, collagen III, and fibronectin, which accumulate and contract within the subretinal space (), leading to irreversible photoreceptor degeneration and permanent vision loss (). Although the contribution of non-coding RNAs such as microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs to fibrotic remodeling has been increasingly recognized, the role of PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) in subretinal fibrosis remains largely unexplored.

Several independent lines of evidence show that piRNAs regulate core fibrotic pathways in other organs. In systemic sclerosis, dermal fibroblasts show significant upregulation of piR-32364, likely driven by intrinsic TGFβ signaling; experimental overexpression of piR-32364 in normal fibroblasts is associated with a significant reduction in COL1A1 mRNA and protein levels, suggesting a direct piRNA-mediated effect on collagen regulation (). In cardiac fibrosis, a cardiac-abundant and fibroblast-specific piRNA (CFRPi; piRNA000691) is upregulated in pressure-overloaded mouse, pig, and human hearts. CFRPi directly promotes fibroblast activation, collagen I expression, α-SMA induction, and ECM deposition. Knockdown of CFRPi attenuates fibrosis and reverses systolic and diastolic dysfunction in mice (). Mechanistically, CFRPi was suggested to suppress apelin (APLN), a cardioprotective peptide, and activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, establishing a piRNA-driven profibrotic signaling axis ().

No study has directly linked piRNA expression or function to subretinal fibrosis. Future research should identify piRNA expression patterns in fibrotic retinal tissues, assess PIWI protein levels in key cell types, and validate piRNA-PIWI targets in pathways regulating EMT, EndMT, and extracellular matrix accumulation. These studies will determine whether piRNAs drive fibrosis or reflect ongoing retinal injury.

Ocular tumors represent a diverse family of rare neoplasms that develop within the structures of the eye, including the retina, the uvea (iris, ciliary body, and choroid), the conjunctiva, and the vitreous (). The two most common eye tumors are retinoblastoma, which affects children, and uveal melanoma, which affects adults (, ). Despite the current advances in local tumor control through radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and surgical interventions, a significant percentage of patients develop metastatic disease, underscoring the urgent need for novel molecular targets and biomarkers (). Although miRNAs and lncRNAs have been relatively well studied in ocular malignancies such as uveal melanoma and retinoblastoma (, ), the investigation of piRNAs in ocular tumors remains in its early stages ().

Two key studies have established the importance of PIWI-piRNA pathway in ocular tumor biology. Sivagurunathan et al. () demonstrated that the PIWI-like protein HIWI2 is aberrantly overexpressed in retinoblastoma cells and that its silencing leads to downregulation of OTX2, G2-M cell cycle arrest, reduced PCNA levels, decreased p16 expression, and altered VEGFR2 levels, collectively suggesting that HIWI2 plays a role in retinoblastoma progression. Also, a study from Kneitz et al. () showed that piRNA expression is dysregulated in melanoma, with distinct piRNA expression profiles distinguishing high-grade uveal melanoma from lower-grade melanoma subtypes and normal tissue in fish models. Furthermore, the piRNA pathway components PIWIL1, PIWIL2, and Tudor are expressed in pigment cell tumors at varying levels depending on tumor type ().

These findings, although derived from cell line experiments and animal models, suggest that piRNA dysregulation may be a shared feature of ocular tumorigenesis across different tumor types. The broader context of non-coding RNA research in ocular tumors, including extensive work on miRNAs (, ), and lncRNAs in uveal melanoma and retinoblastoma, provides a foundation within which piRNA research can be advanced in ocular biology (). The epigenetic characterization of ocular tumors, including DNA methylation profiling and the recognition that epigenetic mechanisms play critical roles in ocular development and disease further supports the biological plausibility of piRNA involvement in ocular tumorigenesis (, ).

There are unique characteristics of piRNAs that make them an attractive candidate as biomarkers for ocular disease.
1) piRNAs can be detected in diverse biofluids, including serum, plasma, saliva, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (, ). piRNAs are remarkably stable in serum and biofluids; unlike siRNA and miRNA, which are easily and rapidly degraded by nucleases, endogenous mature piRNAs naturally carry a 3′ terminal 2′-O-methyl group, which contributes to their intrinsic biological stability (). Balaratnam et al. () compared the stability of a piR-FTH1 oligonucleotide bearing a 3′ 2′-OMe modification with an unmodified counterpart in a serum degradation assay. Both RNAs were incubated in fetal bovine serum at 37°C and sampled over time. The unmodified piR-FTH1 was fully degraded within 30 min, whereas the 3′ 2′-OMe piR-FTH1 remained intact for at least 8 h. These findings underscore the protective effect of 3′ 2′-O-methylation against serum RNases and highlight the utility of 2′-position modifications for enhancing the pharmacological durability of small RNAs.2) piRNAs also function as extracellular signaling molecules carried by EVs. The vesicle lipid membrane protects piRNAs from enzymatic degradation and enables their transport between tissues. In the ocular surface, EVs carry small RNAs that regulate corneal repair and immune responses. Cancer studies show that EV-associated piRNAs remain biologically active, promote tumor growth and spread, and serve as stable biomarkers. Their detection in circulating EVs from human body fluids further supports their diagnostic and biological relevance. These findings identify EV-associated piRNAs as protected, mobile regulators with potential roles in ocular repair and disease ().

piRNAs can be detected in diverse biofluids, including serum, plasma, saliva, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (, ). piRNAs are remarkably stable in serum and biofluids; unlike siRNA and miRNA, which are easily and rapidly degraded by nucleases, endogenous mature piRNAs naturally carry a 3′ terminal 2′-O-methyl group, which contributes to their intrinsic biological stability (). Balaratnam et al. () compared the stability of a piR-FTH1 oligonucleotide bearing a 3′ 2′-OMe modification with an unmodified counterpart in a serum degradation assay. Both RNAs were incubated in fetal bovine serum at 37°C and sampled over time. The unmodified piR-FTH1 was fully degraded within 30 min, whereas the 3′ 2′-OMe piR-FTH1 remained intact for at least 8 h. These findings underscore the protective effect of 3′ 2′-O-methylation against serum RNases and highlight the utility of 2′-position modifications for enhancing the pharmacological durability of small RNAs.

piRNAs also function as extracellular signaling molecules carried by EVs. The vesicle lipid membrane protects piRNAs from enzymatic degradation and enables their transport between tissues. In the ocular surface, EVs carry small RNAs that regulate corneal repair and immune responses. Cancer studies show that EV-associated piRNAs remain biologically active, promote tumor growth and spread, and serve as stable biomarkers. Their detection in circulating EVs from human body fluids further supports their diagnostic and biological relevance. These findings identify EV-associated piRNAs as protected, mobile regulators with potential roles in ocular repair and disease ().

Detection of piRNAs in aqueous humor represents a significant advance for ocular biomarker development. Chen et al. () identified 30 differentially expressed piRNAs between PDR eyes and cataract control eyes in aqueous humor samples. This study demonstrated the piRNA expression profile of the aqueous humor of PDR eyes, suggesting that piRNAs may serve as potential biomarkers involved in the pathogenesis of PDR. Similarly, piRNAs have been linked to the pathogenesis of nAMD, where PIWIL4-associated piRNAs regulate VEGF-driven CNV (). The ability to detect piRNAs in ocular fluids supports their potential as noninvasive biomarkers and therapeutic targets for retinal vascular diseases. The anatomic compartmentalization of the eye provides a unique advantage for biomarker development, as ocular fluids can be sampled during routine clinical procedures such as intravitreal injections or cataract surgery ().

Building on their demonstrated stability in circulation and accessibility in peripheral biofluids, circulating piRNAs have attracted increasing attention as minimally invasive biomarkers for disease detection and monitoring. Studies across multiple diseases have shown that circulating piRNA expression profiles can distinguish diseased individuals from healthy controls, reflecting underlying pathological processes and highlighting their diagnostic potential (, ). Although studies investigating combined piRNA-based biomarker panels in ocular diseases are currently lacking, findings from other neurodegenerative disorders highlight their potential. Jain et al. () demonstrated that a combined miRNA-piRNA signature derived from CSF exosomes distinguished patients with Alzheimer’s disease from controls, and integration of this small-RNA signature with established CSF protein biomarkers increased the diagnostic performance to an AUC of 0.98. Given the shared features of neurodegeneration, inflammation, and cellular dysfunction observed in both Alzheimer’s disease and retinal disorders such as AMD, similar multimodal biomarker strategies may hold promise for improving the early detection, diagnosis, and monitoring of ocular neurodegenerative diseases.

Computational approaches have become essential for studying piRNAs, particularly in diseases where experimental validation is limited, and have accelerated biomarker discovery. High-throughput sncRNA sequencing helps identify piRNA expression profiles throughout the genome, whereas bioinformatic pipelines make it possible to analyze piRNA clusters and track their expression changes in different biological conditions (, ). Early tools such as PILFER showed that piRNA clusters can be found using sequencing data, which helped set the stage for annotating piRNAs across the transcriptome (). In addition to expression profiling, researchers have developed many machine learning and network-based methods to predict piRNA-disease associations. For example, early supervised learning models like iPiDA-sHN combined sequence features with disease semantic similarity to predict potential associations, demonstrating that computational inference of piRNA-disease links is possible (). However, these approaches are limited in capturing nonlinear relationships within sparse biological networks.

To address these limitations, graph-based deep learning models have been introduced. The iPiDA-GCN framework applies graph convolutional networks to heterogeneous piRNA-disease networks, integrating sequence similarity, disease semantic similarity, and known associations to learn low-dimensional representations of biological entities. This approach improves predictive performance by capturing complex topological relationships in biomedical networks and enabling link prediction in sparse interaction graphs (). Computational methods have been developed for RNA-RNA interaction prediction, which are relevant for inferring downstream piRNA regulatory mechanisms. Deep learning frameworks based on convolutional neural networks and multi-head attention mechanisms have been applied to predict piRNA-mRNA interactions directly from sequence data, demonstrating improved performance over traditional feature-based and thermodynamic models by capturing latent binding patterns in nucleotide sequences (). Collectively, these computational methods show that piRNA research now relies more on combining sequencing data, similarity networks, and deep learning. In studies of eye diseases, where tissue samples are scarce, these approaches help researchers choose which piRNAs to test in the laboratory and build networks linked to disease.

Although piRNA-based therapy has not yet entered clinical use in ophthalmology, emerging evidence from ocular neovascularization models suggests that PIWI-piRNA pathways may have therapeutic relevance in diseases characterized by abnormal angiogenesis, fibrotic remodeling, and pathological changes in cellular identity. The therapeutic interest in this pathway does not come from the idea that piRNAs should replace existing treatments, but from the possibility that selected piRNAs or their PIWI protein partners may regulate upstream or parallel molecular programs that contribute to disease persistence, treatment resistance, or tissue remodeling (, ).

This distinction is important for interpreting the current literature. Currently, ocular piRNA studies should be viewed primarily as target-discovery and mechanism-generating studies rather than evidence of established therapy. A piRNA cannot be considered a therapeutic target solely because it is differentially expressed in diseased tissue or ocular fluid. Therapeutic relevance requires stronger evidence that the piRNA has a causal role in disease biology, that its molecular target can be validated, and that modulating the piRNA or its PIWI partner produces a measurable benefit without disturbing normal retinal homeostasis ().

The eye provides a favorable setting for the development of nucleic acid-based therapies because local delivery can concentrate treatment within ocular tissues while reducing systemic exposure. Intravitreal, subretinal, and suprachoroidal routes are already used or actively investigated for posterior-segment therapeutic delivery, including gene- and RNA-based approaches (). This local accessibility has supported the clinical development of antisense oligonucleotides and other RNA-based strategies for inherited retinal diseases, showing that retinal gene expression can be modulated through sequence-directed therapeutics (, ).

This broader RNA-therapeutic landscape provides a useful foundation for future piRNA-directed approaches. In principle, disease-promoting piRNAs could be suppressed using antisense oligonucleotides, locked nucleic acid inhibitors, antagomir-like molecules, or other chemically modified oligonucleotides. Conversely, protective piRNAs could potentially be restored using synthetic piRNA mimics or vector-based expression systems. These strategies remain hypothetical in ocular disease, but they are conceptually supported by the broader progress of RNA therapeutics in ophthalmology.

Unlike conventional antisense or siRNA approaches, piRNA activity depends on several cellular factors. piRNAs function together with PIWI proteins, and their effects may vary according to which PIWI proteins are present, where the complex is in the cell, and how well the piRNA matches its target. Depending on these factors, piRNAs may regulate gene expression by degrading RNA, suppressing transcription, or promoting epigenetic silencing (). Therefore, future piRNA-directed therapy will require more than identifying a disease-associated piRNA. It will require defining the active piRNA-PIWI complex, the relevant ocular cell type, the direct molecular target, and the biological consequence of modulating that axis ().

Delivery will be central to the success of any future piRNA-based ocular therapy. The optimal route would depend on the target disease, anatomical compartment, and cell type. Intravitreal delivery may be better suited for inner retinal cells, retinal vascular endothelial cells, and vitreoretinal disease processes, whereas subretinal delivery may be more appropriate for photoreceptors and the RPE. Suprachoroidal delivery is also being explored as a route for accessing the choroid and outer retina, which may be relevant for diseases involving the RPE-choroid interface ().

Potential delivery platforms include chemically modified oligonucleotides, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, viral vectors, and extracellular vesicle-inspired systems. Chemically modified oligonucleotides may improve nuclease resistance and tissue retention, whereas nanoparticle and extracellular vesicle-based systems may improve cellular delivery and cargo protection. Viral vectors could support sustained expression but would require careful dose control and long-term safety evaluation (, ). These delivery considerations are especially important for piRNAs because PIWI-piRNA pathways may influence gene expression at multiple regulatory levels, including transcript stability and epigenetic regulation ().

Safety remains a major barrier to piRNA-directed therapy. Because piRNAs may regulate multiple targets and may participate in chromatin-level gene regulation, inappropriate modulation could produce unintended effects on gene expression (). Potential risks include off-target transcript regulation, immune activation, altered epigenetic programming, disruption of normal retinal homeostasis, and interference with endogenous PIWI-piRNA functions. These risks are especially important in the retina, where highly specialized neurons, vascular cells, glia, and RPE cells must maintain precise gene-expression programs for long-term visual function. Therefore, piRNA-based interventions require rigorous target validation, precise dosing and delivery, and careful assessment of retinal toxicity, structure, and function before clinical application.

Despite significant advances in identifying piRNA dysregulation across a wide spectrum of ocular diseases, our understanding of the biological functions and therapeutic potential of the PIWI-piRNA pathway in the eye remains incomplete. Many current findings are largely correlative, and critical questions regarding the cellular origins, molecular targets, and mechanistic contributions of piRNAs to ocular physiology and pathology remain unresolved. Addressing these knowledge gaps will require rigorous functional studies, improved bioinformatic pipelines, single-cell and spatial transcriptomic approaches, and validation in clinically relevant models. The key outstanding questions and future research priorities that must be addressed to advance the field of ocular piRNA biology are summarized in .

Outstanding research questions and knowledge gaps in ocular piRNA research

Most studies report altered piRNA expression in ocular diseases, but the direct molecular targets of these piRNAs and many computationally predicted piRNA-target relationships remain experimentally unvalidated. Functional confirmation through direct target validation, together with loss- and gain-of-function studies, is needed to establish causal roles and molecular mechanisms.

The cell type-specific origin and actions of piRNAs within ocular tissues remain poorly defined because bulk sequencing approaches cannot distinguish cellular sources and targets.

The expression patterns, localization, isoform diversity, and disease-stage specificity of PIWI proteins in the eye require comprehensive characterization.

Current piRNA annotations may include misclassified small RNAs or degradation products, highlighting the need for stringent bioinformatic and experimental validation.

The clinical translation of piRNA-based biomarkers and therapeutics is limited by small patient cohorts, methodological variability, delivery challenges, and unresolved safety concerns.

Comparative studies are needed to determine whether PIWI-piRNA regulatory mechanisms identified in ocular tissues are conserved across other neural, vascular, and fibrotic systems.

PIWI, P-element-induced wimpy testis; piRNA, PIWI-interacting RNA.

The study of piRNAs in ocular biology remains at an early stage, but growing evidence suggests that PIWI-piRNA pathways may participate in regulatory processes relevant to retinal disease. Although first defined by their role in genome defense, piRNAs are now detected in the retina, RPE, ocular fluids, and models of neovascularization, raising the possibility that they influence angiogenesis, oxidative stress responses, fibrosis, and cell-state transitions in the eye.

The greatest value of piRNA research in ophthalmology lies in mechanism discovery. Most existing studies are descriptive, and the functional significance of piRNA expression changes remains unclear. Determining which piRNAs are biologically active, which PIWI proteins they require, which ocular cell types they operate in, and which targets they regulate will be essential for establishing whether they contribute to disease progression or simply reflect cellular stress.

This distinction is critical for translational applications. piRNAs show potential as biomarkers because of their stability and detectability in biofluids, and they may eventually offer therapeutic opportunities in diseases driven by aberrant angiogenesis, fibrosis, or metabolic stress. However, their clinical utility will depend on rigorous validation, improved annotation, disease stage-specific analysis, and careful evaluation of delivery and safety.

Overall, piRNAs represent an underdeveloped but promising frontier in ocular research. Defining how PIWI-piRNA networks function in retinal and ocular tissues may reveal new layers of gene regulation that shape disease onset, progression, and treatment response, ultimately informing future strategies for diagnosis, monitoring, and targeted intervention.

medicine.title: Successful Fontan Completion in a 36-Year-Old
medicine.abstract: Fontan palliation is commonly completed at 2-4 years, but delays may occur due to medical optimization and, rarely, loss to follow-up.A 36-year-old woman with tricuspid atresia status post–bidirectional Glenn presented with significant exercise intolerance and hypoxemia. She had lived over 2 decades with Glenn physiology and successfully carried 2 pregnancies. The patient ultimately underwent fenestrated Fontan completion with significant functional improvement.This case represents an exceptionally prolonged duration of Glenn physiology, demonstrating that this palliation can be highly durable in select patients with favorable anatomy and hemodynamics. Fontan completion in this patient resulted in meaningful functional improvement, though it remains a temporizing measure that carries substantial risks and potential long-term morbidity.Glenn palliation can be durable in select patients. Fontan completion may meaningfully improve function well beyond the conventional 2-to-4-year age window, and timing should be patient-specific.
medicine.text:
A 36-year-old woman established care at our adult congenital heart disease clinic. She was born in the Soviet Union and carried the postnatal diagnosis of tricuspid atresia type 1B (normally related great arteries with pulmonary outflow obstruction). She had undergone 3 palliative procedures. These included a Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt at 8 months of age and a second unspecified shunt palliation at 9 years, both in Moscow. This was followed by a bidirectional Glenn procedure in Paris, France, at 13 years of age.

Following her Glenn procedure in 1999, she did very well with no substantial symptoms through 2020. She moved to the United States, had 2 children in 2008 and 2009, and remained an active bike rider.

In 2021, she experienced progressive functional decline beginning with an admission to a regional hospital in Florida for Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of an unspecified location. She recovered with 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotic therapy, but thereafter reported ongoing chest discomfort, hypoxemia, and fatigue. Five months later, she was diagnosed with a non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction of uncertain chronicity. Cardiac catheterization suggested ischemia in the right coronary artery distribution, but no interventions were undertaken. Three months later, she presented with dyspnea and worsening hypoxemia, and was found to have bilateral pulmonary emboli. Cardiac catheterization at that time demonstrated preserved cardiac output of 3.5 L/min, Glenn pressure of 10 mm Hg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 7-8 mm Hg, and pulmonary vascular resistance of 1.7 Wood units x m2. She was started on apixaban without significant improvement in her symptoms. There were subsequent discussions regarding Fontan completion vs transplant evaluation, but she moved before completing this work-up and eventually settled in Chicago.

At her Adult Congenital Heart Disease clinic visit in 2023, she presented with NYHA functional class IV heart failure symptoms, including baseline fatigue, exercise intolerance, orthopnea, and desaturations to below 60% with minimal activity. She was unable to walk 10 steps without severe fatigue. Her symptoms prevented her from working. She had visible cyanosis, digital clubbing, and mild tachypnea. Her saturation at rest was 69%. Medications included metoprolol for substantial ventricular ectopy burden and sildenafil.

Given her symptoms, her case was presented at a multidisciplinary cardiovascular surgical conference to determine management: Fontan completion or heart transplantation.

She had no significant comorbidities, including no synthetic liver or renal dysfunction.

Her laboratory workup was largely unremarkable aside from secondary erythrocytosis, with a hemoglobin of 18 g/dL.

A cardiac catheterization was notable for a cardiac output of 4.1 L/min with a pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratio of 0.41. She had reassuring Glenn and branch pulmonary artery pressures of 6 mm Hg. Transpulmonary gradient on sildenafil was 3 mm Hg, and pulmonary vascular resistance was 2.9 Woods units x m2. Her left ventricular end-diastolic pressure was 10 mm Hg. There were no significant aortopulmonary collaterals (APCs) or veno-venous collateral vessels seen, nor was there clear evidence of pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, despite having lived with Glenn physiology for over 2 decades. Of note, despite a pulmonary artery still in anatomical continuity with her Glenn circulation, there was no visible antegrade pulmonary blood flow on left ventriculogram. The atrial septum, pulmonary veins, and aortic arch were unobstructed.

Exercise stress test was notable for a submaximal effort (respiratory exchange ratio of 1), a severely depressed peak VO2 of 11.9 mL/kg/min, and desaturations to <50% at peak exercise.

Cross-sectional imaging, both computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, was completed and demonstrated a patent Glenn pathway. Her left ventricle (LV) was mildly dilated and had mild systolic dysfunction (LV ejection fraction was 44%). She also had inferior and inferolateral LV wall thinning with late gadolinium enhancement involving approximately 25% of her cardiac mass, consistent with suspected prior right coronary artery territory infarct.

After extensive multidisciplinary discussion, she was determined to be an acceptable candidate for Fontan completion. Despite a substantial myocardial scar, she demonstrated only mildly depressed global left ventricular function. Her ventricular filling pressures and Glenn pressures were reassuring. The patient herself voiced ongoing preference for Fontan completion. A formal transplantation evaluation was deferred, and she was scheduled for Fontan completion.

A fenestrated extracardiac Fontan procedure was completed via repeat sternotomy with a 24-mm expanded polytetrafluoroethylene conduit with a 5-mm fenestration. Despite no antegrade pulmonary blood flow on catheterization, a small residual opening was noted on direct visualization, prompting division and oversewing of the main pulmonary artery to limit ventricular volume loading and to improve circulatory efficiency. Finally, she underwent branch pulmonary arterioplasty using bovine pericardium. Cardiopulmonary bypass and cross-clamp times were 336 and 157 minutes, respectively. Postoperative systolic function was mildly depressed on epinephrine at 0.05 μg/kg/min and inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm. She received multiple blood product transfusions intraoperatively but achieved good hemostasis by the end of the case.

Her postoperative course was largely uncomplicated, consisting of mild bilateral pleural effusions that resolved with diuresis. She was extubated on postoperative day (POD) 1, and her chest tubes were removed on POD 3. A 6-minute walk test was completed 1 week after her Fontan procedure, at which time she walked 1,200 feet without rest, and her saturations had improved to 80%-85% with a nadir of 63% during activity. There was no evidence of significant end-organ dysfunction, and she was discharged on POD 13.

She was referred for outpatient cardiac rehabilitation but did not complete any sessions within our system due to loss to follow-up and insurance difficulties before moving out of state. Over the next 6 months, her baseline saturations increased from the low- to mid-80% range to the high-80% range, with desaturations to the mid-70% range during ambulation. She reported improved exercise tolerance, walking up to 3 hours at a time, and baseline comfort. She developed persistent lower extremity edema, managed with loop and thiazide diuretics.

At 2 years post-Fontan completion, repeat cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a mildly dilated LV and severely depressed LV ejection fraction (31%), with 39% of Fontan flow shunting through the fenestration. She also had worsening APC burden, with a ratio of pulmonary to systemic blood flow around 1.5. An oral heart failure regimen was initiated, with lisinopril, spironolactone, and empagliflozin added to metoprolol and sildenafil. She remains on rivaroxaban for thrombosis prophylaxis. Medication side effects impacted adherence, ultimately leading to discontinuation of lisinopril.

Despite her depressed systolic function, she remains asymptomatic, able to walk without significant limitation, and is working part-time as a server in a restaurant. Her baseline saturations remain primarily in the high-80% range.

Optimal timing of Fontan completion remains under investigation. The operation is typically performed at 2-4 years, but recent literature suggests similar outcomes with completion as early as 18 months. Despite these findings, the median age at Fontan completion has increased to about 3.4 years in recent decades.

Long-term durability of Glenn physiology is poorly described. This case demonstrates an exceptionally prolonged period living with Glenn physiology, extending into the fourth decade of life. It suggests that in patients with favorable anatomical and hemodynamic characteristics, Glenn circulation may remain well tolerated for much longer than anticipated. A systemic LV, absence of significant mitral or aortic regurgitation, and limited collateral burden likely contributed to this patient's long-term survival and relatively preserved functional status. Notably, she did not have evidence of pulmonary arteriovenous malformations despite presumed minimal-to-absent hepatic venous flow to the pulmonary circulation for over 2 decades.

Because she underwent Fontan completion in mid-adulthood, she avoided many of the end-organ complications commonly observed in prolonged Fontan physiology. She survived her Fontan operation with minimal perioperative complications and had a reasonable functional outcome. She experienced significantly improved activity tolerance but has not returned to her pre-2021 baseline. Her subsequent decline in ventricular function occurred in the setting of significant inferolateral myocardial injury, suggesting ischemia contributed to both her initial clinical deterioration and ongoing systolic dysfunction. Despite worsening systolic function and APC burden, her filling pressures remain low.

The durability of her Fontan physiology remains uncertain. Fontan palliation was offered with the hope that it would provide some symptomatic improvement and postpone the need for transplant without compromising future transplant candidacy. Close ongoing cardiac and end-organ surveillance is paramount but remains challenging in the setting of frequent relocations and insurance interruptions.

Importantly, this case should not be interpreted as support for routine Fontan deferral, as delayed Fontan completion has been associated with higher rates of transplantation and death. Rather, it highlights the potential durability of Glenn physiology in select patients and reinforces the importance of an individualized approach to Fontan timing.

This case highlights the potential durability of Glenn physiology in patients with favorable anatomical and hemodynamic characteristics. It also underscores the heterogeneity amongst patients with single-ventricle physiology, emphasizing the importance of individualized decision-making regarding Fontan timing rather than reliance on a uniform age-based approach.

The authors have reported that they have no relationships relevant to the contents of this paper to disclose.

medicine.title: Chromatin dynamics secondary to dexamethasone exposure identifies 67 genes linked to elevated IOP and primary open-angle glaucoma
medicine.abstract: Steroid-induced elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is a risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). IOP is regulated by trabecular meshwork (TM). We have generated genome topology, epigenome, and expression profiles of three independent nonglaucomatous human TM cell strains before and after dexamethasone treatment, which serves as a model for investigating increased IOP. We integrated dexamethasone-induced alterations in chromatin landscape with genetic variants linked to IOP and POAG in genomewide association studies. Our studies uncover regulatory role of 103 noncoding lead variants and identify 67 gene targets that potentially contribute to steroid-induced IOP and POAG risk.
medicine.text:
Glaucoma is a heterogeneous group of chronic multifactorial optic neuropathies that lead to irreversible blindness, affecting nearly 80 million individuals worldwide (). The disease manifests a complex clinical etiology, resulting in loss of retinal ganglion cells and damage to the optic nerve. Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the most prevalent subtype that accounts for over 80% of glaucoma in United States () and is characterized by increased resistance to aqueous humor (AH) outflow without anatomical changes to the iridio-corneal angle (). The key POAG risk factors include genetic susceptibility, age, large vertical cup-to-disc ratio, and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP); the latter being the only known modifiable element (–). Current treatment options for POAG are limited, with primary focus on slowing disease progression by reducing IOP via surgical or pharmacological intervention ().

Both POAG and IOP are highly heritable; over 40% of POAG patients have a family history (). Genomewide association studies (GWAS) have uncovered 226 IOP (–) and 359 POAG (, ) associated risk loci, with a significant overlap between the two (). IOP and POAG risk variants colocalize near genes involved in regulation of cell adhesion (ANGPT1, FERMT2, IGF1), reactive oxygen species mitigation (TXNRD2, KLF5), actin skeleton organization (AFAP1, GAS7, SPTNB1, ANTXR1), and lipid metabolism (ABCA1, PLCE1, DGKG). However, nearly all lead GWAS variants and those in linkage disequilibrium (LD) are localized in the noncoding genome (). Variants in cis-regulatory elements (CRE) can potentially modify the expression of distal genes. Regulatory effects are further modulated by tissue- and disease-specific epigenetic states and 3D chromatin architecture. Therefore, understanding the links between genetic variants and pathogenesis requires investigations into the relevant biological context ().

IOP is determined by the balance between AH production and its outflow. Trabecular meshwork (TM), a mesenchyme derived smooth muscle-like tissue, primarily regulates AH outflow resistance and is critical for maintaining IOP (). Prolonged use of glucocorticoids, a common treatment for ocular diseases, elevates IOP in approximately 40% of general population and 92% in patients with POAG by inducing widespread transcriptional changes in genes that are preferentially expressed in TM, leading to reduced phagocytosis, increased actin reorganization, and formation of cross-linked actin networks (, ). Dexamethasone-treated TM cells have been used to investigate how these drugs act to increase IOP and glaucoma risk in steroid-responsive individuals (–). Here, we leverage this model system to decipher the gene regulatory networks associated with IOP and POAG susceptibility and to understand the influence of GWAS identified noncoding variants. We create a comprehensive promoter-centered genome topology map, with epigenetic landscape and transcriptional profiles, of three independent primary human TM cell strains before and after treatment with dexamethasone. Our analyses of multiomic datasets identify altered 3D genome topology and epigenetic landscape of TM expressed genes as well as transcription factor (TF) hubs associated with IOP-mimicking conditions. Integrations of chromatin looping and CREs with IOP and POAG GWAS variants have uncovered candidate genes and signaling pathways that contribute to IOP elevation and POAG risk. Our studies thus provide a genetic basis and targets for therapies of these debilitating conditions.

We captured the transcriptome (total RNA-seq) alongside genomewide identification of histone marks for transcriptionally active (H3K27ac, H3K4me1/2/3) and repressed regions (H3K27me3/H3K9me3), chromatin accessibility (), and CTCF binding of three primary human TM cell strains from healthy donor eyes expressing juxtacanalicular region marker genes ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S1A). Comparison to tissue-based scRNAseq () revealed our primary TM cells express transcriptional signatures associated with juxtacanalicular, fibroblast-like TM, and Schlemm’s canal-associated cell populations, retaining key TM-related features in culture. Genes enriched for activating histone modifications exhibit higher expression, whereas repressing marks are localized primarily to genes showing low expression (SI Appendix, Fig. S1B). Based on chromatin accessibility, CTCF binding, and active/repressive histone marks, we identified 13 epigenetic states () (). The regions classified as active promoters are concentrated in 5’UTRs or near transcription start sites (TSS). Enhancers are found diffusely across the genome, whereas markers for active transcription are elevated across gene bodies and especially near the 3’-region of genes ().

Our analysis uncovers 1,768 super-enhancers (SEs), which overlap genes enriched for canonical TM cell functions including extracellular matrix organization, cell adhesion, TGFβ response, and actin filament assembly ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S1C). These regulatory regions are also associated with high gene expression ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S1D) and 58.3% overlap a gene promoter. A comparison of these TM SEs with 1.17 million SEs from 1,739 human samples () reveals that the average TM SE is present in less than 15% of non-TM samples (SI Appendix, Fig. S1E). Few TM SEs appear nearly universal; e.g., the SE overlapping the cell cycle gene SEPTIN9 is present in 1,603 samples (92.1%) including TM (). Notably, 31.5% TM SEs are detected in <5% of other tissues; e.g., the SE over LMX1B, linked to actin cytoskeleton maintenance (), is observed in 36 samples reflecting specificity of its regulatory action ().

We performed promoter capture Hi-C (pc-Hi-C) () and identified 30,375 loops; of these, 26,495 (87.2%) loops overlap promoters including key TM genes, such as MYOC (). We then evaluated the specificity of these promoter-centered contacts by comparing to promoter-centered loops from 20 human tissues (). Notably, 23.1% of promoter loops identified in TM cells were not detected in any other tissues examined (). For example, FBLN1, a highly expressed gene encoding a major component of extracellular matrix (), has several promoter-centered loops detected only in TM (). In contrast, only 12.9% of TM promoter loops are observed in at least half of the tissues. We identify 611 genes that share TM promoter loops with 15 or more tissues, and these genes are enriched for constitutive functions such as cell cycle regulation, protein polymerization, and organelle organization (SI Appendix, Fig. S1F). For example, promoter–promoter contact between RBX1, a gene regulating the protein turnover () and the histone acetyltransferase () EP300, is detected in 16 of the 20 tissues examined ().

Chromatin contacts are frequently anchored by CTCF (). We show that 6,536 promoter loops are associated with at least one CTCF-bound foot and 4,837 genes possess CTCF-anchored promoter loops in all three TM samples (). These genes were enriched for pathways such as growth, organelle localization, and actomyosin organization (SI Appendix, Fig. S1G).

Multiomics framework provides insights into regulation of TM genes. We specifically highlight the chromatin context of fibronectin-1 (FN1; ), a component of TM extracellular membrane (). The FN1 gene is highly expressed in TM and localized to compartment A. Its promoter is enriched in activating histone marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me3) and deficient in repressive marks (H3K27me3 and H3K9me3). The active transcription of FN1 is consistent with the H3K36me3 peak. We also uncover 35 promoter-interacting loops, many of which contact a SE located ~200 kb upstream of TSS.

Treatment of TM cells with dexamethasone (dex), a glucocorticoid commonly used to mimic IOP elevation in vitro (, ), results in 3,423 differentially expressed genes and accounts for ~13% of the total variation in expression ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S2 A and B). Dex’s effect is mediated via glucocorticoid receptors (GR) and over half (51.4%) of putative GR target genes () are differentially expressed following the treatment (SI Appendix, Fig. S2C). Glucocorticoid treatment increases IOP in approximately 40% of individuals, i.e., “steroid responders” (). The strains used here are derived from steroid-responsive individuals as indicated by comparison of dex-induced expression changes to published transcriptomes of dex-treated TM cells from responder and nonresponder donors () (SI Appendix, Fig. S2D).

We identify 4,152 expressed enhancer RNAs (eRNAs; SI Appendix, Fig. S2E) with 51 differentially expressed after dex treatment (SI Appendix, Fig. S2F). Curiously, dex augments the expression of a predicted eRNA and its proximal gene ALOX15B (SI Appendix, Fig. S2G), which generally shows decreased expression in optic nerve and brain astrocytes ().

Histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, and CTCF binding demonstrate widespread epigenetic alterations following dex treatment (). Genomewide, 25.8% of peaks are lost, including 2,628 overlapping gene promoters and SEs (SI Appendix, Fig. S2H). We observe a significant reduction of H3K4me2 marks that are associated with tissue-specific TF binding at enhancers and edges of promoters (). In contrast, dex-treated cells exhibit elevated CTCF, H3K36me3, and H3K4me1 binding that are linked to chromatin insulation, active transcription over gene body, and promoters, respectively.

The number of H3K27ac and H3K27me3 peaks remain relatively stable at active enhancers and repressors, respectively. Yet, changes in distribution of these marks coincide with altered expression patterns. Genes showing lower expression after dex treatment tend to reside near regions shifting toward a repressive epigenetic state (i.e., gain of H3K27me3 and/or loss of H3K27ac), whereas those presenting higher expression are colocalized with activating epigenetic changes (i.e., gain of H3K27ac and/or loss of H3K27me3; ). For example, the FKBP5 locus, a functional regulator of the GR complex (), is enriched for activating epigenetic marks, concurrently gaining H3K27ac and losing H3K27me3 (). FKBP5 and other genes at this locus demonstrate significantly increased expression following dex treatment. In contrast, significant reduction in expression of five genes at the genomic region ~1 Mb away is associated with the loss of multiple H3K27ac peaks (). Large scale chromatin reorganization at the FKBP5 locus in response to glucocorticoid treatment has been reported in mouse and human macrophages ().

We further annotated enhancers based on the activation state; 8,342 enhancers are present in both treatment groups and active in at least one (). Approximately 10% of these enhancers switch between an active and nonactive state after treatment. Dynamic enhancers overlap genes that are enriched for ECM organization, actin morphology, cell adhesion, and Rho GTPase signaling (); all known to regulate IOP in TM cells (–). We note the gain of H3K27ac peaks and switch to an active state for two primed enhancers at a POAG locus near ATP10A (), which exhibits increased expression after dex treatment of TM cells ().

Over one-third of TM SEs (37.8%) are gained or lost following dex treatment (). Gained SEs are enriched for apoptotic genes, whereas lost SEs are for genes associated with cytoskeletal and cell binding functions. Complementary analysis of H3K27ac occupancy (Dataset S1) broadly supports these binary classifications: 146 of 181 gained SEs (80.7%) show increased H3K27ac following dex treatment, whereas 47 of 76 lost SEs (61.8%) have decreased occupancy. Donor-blocked GLM testing identifies 68 SEs with differential occupancy at nominal P < 0.05 and 29 at FDR < 0.05, including 16 gained and 13 lost SEs.
