For example, a lost SE located near HGF shows significantly reduced H3K27ac occupancy (; log2FC = −0.57, FDR = 0.015) and reduced expression after dex treatment (log2FC = −1.20, FDR < 0.001) and mediates protective effects of TM stem cells to reduce TGF-β2-induced oxidative stress and fibrotic responses, suggesting that reduced HGF-associated enhancer activity may attenuate endogenous protective signaling (). Conversely, a gained SE overlapping RHOB promoter and gene body shows significantly increased H3K27ac occupancy (; log2FC = 0.67, FDR = 0.007) and enhanced expression (log2FC = 1.10, FDR < 0.001). RHOB is induced by norepinephrine in TM cells and implicated in reduced TM phagocytosis and permeability and in nocturnal IOP elevation, suggesting this locus potentially relevant to dex-induced outflow dysfunction ().

Dex-induced transcriptome changes can be mediated, at least in part, by remodeling of chromatin compartments and promoter-interacting loops. We identified significant shifts in 493 regions (50 kb width) primarily toward heterochromatic B compartment (). Though only 0.7% of the total, these dynamic regions appear to be hotspots for transcriptomic and epigenetic changes (). Windows moving toward euchromatic A compartment reveal high gene expression, along with increased H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K36me3 signals, as well as a decrease in H3K27me3 marks. In contrast, shifts toward B compartment correspond to lower gene expression and reduced marks for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3. Both classes of compartments exhibit lower levels of H3K4me2 (SI Appendix, Fig. S3A), suggesting that overall signal for this mark is lower after dex treatment.

One dynamic region includes ZBTB16, a Zn-finger TF that interacts with histone deacetylase and dramatically increases expression in TM cells with dex treatment (). A shift from B to A compartment and in chromatin landscape at the ZBTB16 gene region coincides with augmented transcription from <1 CPM in control samples to >150 CPM (). We observe increased signals for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K36me3, and H3K4me3 as well as emergence of multiple enhancers and a SE overlapping the gene body. Furthermore, we detect the loss of looping upstream of ZBTB16 likely due to the appearance of a TAD boundary (SI Appendix, Fig. S3B). Notably, dex treatment of kidney podocytes similarly leads to the emergence of a SE that overlaps ZBTB16 driving increased acting filament synthesis and improving cytoskeletal stabilization ().

In TM cells, dex treatment alters 23,397 promoter-interacting loops, including 1,350 loops that interact with SEs and 557 with promoters of TFs (), which can serve as gene networks hubs for steroid-induced IOP elevation and POAG risk. Three TFs corresponding to activating promoter loop changes (i.e., gain of loops to enhancers or loss of loops to repressors) exhibit higher expression, whereas 19 TFs showing lower expression show gain of loops to repressors and/or loss of loops to enhancers (). Next, we assessed whether changes in the expression of TFs correspond to changes in TF binding using ATAC footprinting (). Many TFs have dramatically altered binding scores after dex (); these include CEBP, JUN, and FOS family proteins (). The expression of CEBPD increases concurrently with the gain of contact between the promoter and an intronic SE, loss of contact with intergenic repressors, and a shift toward A compartment (). In contrast, AP-1 constituent TFs have reduced contact with distal CREs and exhibit lower expression (), possibly due to the loss of an enhancer rich region upstream of JUN following the dex treatment (). Interestingly, 177 genes with CEBPD bound promoters specific to dex are enriched for MAPK signaling and extracellular matrix organization (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 C and D). In contrast, JUN-bound promoters of 438 genes specific to control samples are enriched for regulation of WNT and RAP1 signaling, and interleukin 18 (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 E and F).

We performed separate enrichment analyses for gene sets exhibiting changes in transcription, epigenetic marks, compartmentalization, or distal contact patterns, and intersected these analyses to distinguish biologically meaningful units altered across multiple levels of regulation (). Integrated multiomic analyses reveal concordant epigenetic and transcriptional changes in genes associated with key TM functions including focal adhesion, actin cytoskeleton, ECM structure, and fibronectin binding (). TNF and AGE-RAGE signaling are the two pathways most consistently identified across these analyses ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S4 A and B).

Coordinated downregulation of TNF signaling is evident with corresponding changes in epigenome marks of multiple TFs and their gene targets (). Expression of the gene encoding iTAP (FRMD8), which is required to initiate TNF signaling (), is reduced by 25% (FDR = 0.004), gaining a repressive mark directly over the promoter region after dex (SI Appendix, Fig. S4C). We also note that promoter interacting loops observed exclusively in the dex treated samples contact the genomic region including rs1346, a lead SNP identified in POAG GWAS (SI Appendix, Fig. S4C) (, ).

Dex response results in ~30% lower expression of the NFKB1 gene encoding NFkb and twofold higher expression of the NFKBIA gene encoding its inhibitor. The regulatory mechanisms orchestrating these changes appear diverse. Enhanced expression of NFKBIA may be driven by distal enhancer CREs gained in regions of loop contact to the promoter as well as by the activation of an enhancer directly over its TSS (). In contrast, repression of NFKB1 coincides with a local shift to heterochromatic B compartment after dex (). Expression of CREB5, encoding another TF in this pathway, is reduced by almost 50%, possibly due to reduced contact with an upstream enhancer region (SI Appendix, Fig. S4D).

Downstream regulatory targets of these repressed TFs include inflammatory cytokines such as LIF and IL6 (, ). LIF expression is reduced over 80% and coincides with deactivation of enhancers directly over the TSS region, loss of contact between the promoter and an upstream cluster of active enhancers, and loss of a SE directly overlapping the gene in control conditions (). We further note that the lost SE contains rs9614165, a lead SNP for POAG (). Changes in the IL6 gene are similar; its expression is reduced by 88% and a SE in contact with the promoter region via looping is lost in response to dex (SI Appendix, Fig. S4E). Additional regulatory targets include VCAM1; this gene encodes a cell adhesion molecule, and its expression is decreased ~70% () as the locus shifts toward B compartment, loses distal enhancers and exhibits reduced looping to an upstream CRE near POAG lead SNPs () (, ).

We also identify changes in the TNF target gene, PTGS2 (also called COX2) (). PLA2G4A and the adjacent PTGS2 both encode enzymes necessary for prostaglandin synthesis () and their expression is significantly reduced following dex treatment. The locus containing these genes shifts from A to B compartment, and PLA2G4A loses a CRE near its promoter post–dex treatment. The PTGS2 gene encoding an enzyme that catalyzes arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2 () loses a distal SE connected to the promoter region by looping. This reaction is negatively correlated with the conversion of arachidonic acid into hydroperoxy eicosatetraenoic acids by ALOX15B (). TSS region of ALOX15B loses a repressive mark and gains an enhancer while augmenting expression from <0.1 CPM in control to >2.5CPM after dex treatment (SI Appendix, Fig. S4F). Prostaglandin H2 is further converted to PGF2a catalyzed in part by the product of AKR1B1 () and the expression of this gene is reduced by ~25% (). Analogs of PGF2a are used frequently to treat elevated IOP underscoring the importance of changes in this biosynthetic pathway for glaucoma pathogenesis.

We then sought to connect promoter loops and SEs with lead GWAS variants identified for IOP (, ) and POAG (, ) as well as respective LD variants (). For each, we identify loops connecting gene promoters to either lead GWAS SNPs or variants in LD in each of our three chromatin loop sets [i.e., resource (); control; and dex-treated ( and )]. We identify 29 target genes associated with 23 lead IOP variants and 57 target genes linked to 46 POAG lead variants through contacts with gene promoters. ( and Dataset S2). Of these, 19 target genes are shared between the IOP and POAG analyses. Target genes for these lead variants are enriched for pathways such as vesicle-mediated transport, Toll-like Receptor, MAPK, and Hippo signaling. The promoter for LRIG1 forms extensive loops with a region >300 kb away that contains SNPs identified in both IOP and POAG GWAS datasets (). Next, we assess the tissue-specificity of loops connecting lead SNPs to gene promoters in comparison to publicly available pc-Hi-C data from 20 tissues (). Only one SNP-promoter loop is detected in most tissues (rs1782976-APP), whereas over half are enriched in TM cells (IOP: 55.2%; POAG: 52.6%;  and SI Appendix, Fig. S5A). For example, the SNP rs17752199 is proximal to PKHD1 but forms long range contacts with the promoter of TFAP2B (). In mice, a deletion from intron 2 to the 3’UTR of Pkhd1 reduces Tfap-2b expression and results in elevated IOP and RGC death (). We therefore hypothesize that disruption of chromosomal architecture interferes with TFAP2B expression in human TM.

To evaluate whether the candidate IOP and POAG associated variants identified through promoter-looping analyses have measurable regulatory effects, we compared these with expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) datasets from GTEx cultured fibroblasts and retina tissue (, ). For each candidate SNP, we assessed whether the same genomic variant was reported as an eQTL. We also evaluated whether the eQTL-associated gene corresponded to the promoter target identified by our chromatin looping analysis. Among the 23 IOP lead variants involved in candidate variant–promoter interactions, 13 overlap the eQTLs in cultured fibroblasts and seven overlapped eQTLs in retina (Dataset S3). Of the 13 variants supported by cultured fibroblast eQTL data, three show concordant target gene associations; i.e., the eQTL associated gene matches the promoter target identified by pc-HiC. In the retina eQTL dataset, no eQTL-associated gene matched the promoter targets identified by chromatin looping.

Among the 46 POAG lead variants involved in variant–promoter interactions, 22 overlap eQTLs in cultured fibroblasts and 14 with eQTLs in the retina (Dataset S3). Of the 22 variants supported by cultured fibroblast eQTL data, five show concordant target-gene associations. One of the 14 variants supported by retina eQTL data shows a concordant variant–gene association.

The concordance among variant overlap, eQTL association, and promoter targeting provides additional support for a regulatory role of the proposed IOP and POAG causal variants. Candidate variants without detectable eQTL support may nevertheless be functional since QTL effects may be cell-type specific, context-dependent, or undetectable in datasets with limited sample size.

We further examined allele-specific chromatin accessibility at candidate IOP and/or POAG variants (Dataset S4). Twelve variants were heterozygous with at least five allele-informative reads and sufficient coverage for formal testing. rs2105587, connected to PRSS23 by pc-Hi-C, demonstrates significant allelic imbalance in TM1 (370 A:246 C; FDR 9.3 × 10−6). The imbalance is detected separately in control (232 A:147 C; FDR = 3.0 × 10−5) and dex-treated cells (138 A:99 C; FDR = 0.040), but the allelic proportions do not differ between conditions (FDR = 0.96). Complementary CUT&Tag analysis (Dataset S4) identifies H3K4me1 imbalance in TM2 at rs3120976 near MAT1A (FDR = 0.015) and rs4689872 near AFAP1 (FDR = 0.015).

Allele-specific expression was assessed using heterozygous transcribed variants within genes putatively linked to IOP or POAG lead SNPs by chromatin looping (Dataset S4). In COL4A1 linked to rs61963301 the alternate allele fraction was reduced from 0.55 to 0.31 after dex treatment in TM2 (FDR = 0.0042). Similarly, IL34 in the target gene assigned to rs12598456 decreased in TM3, from 0.60 to 0.31 (FDR = 0.0166). These findings provide exploratory evidence of allele-sensitive regulation at selected POAG-associated loci.

We ascertained nine IOP and 18 POAG lead SNP overlapping loci that change compartments after dex treatment; these include five SNPs identified in both IOP- and POAG-GWAS. For example, the region containing EMCN and the lead SNP rs1501086 switches from A to B compartment in response to dex treatment and the EMCN gene has reduced expression by approximately half (). EMCN is a marker gene for endothelial cell types () and inhibits focal adhesion between cells and ECM (), pointing to a potential role in regulating AH outflow in TM tissue.

Next, we identified SEs overlapping with a maximum of 15 IOP and 23 POAG associated lead variants (). On average, SEs containing SNPs are tissue-enriched; just 6.4% of non-TM samples () share SEs overlapping IOP lead variants and 9.4% with POAG lead variants ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S5B). For each SNP, we quantify changes in histone, ATAC, and CTCF peaks within 5 kb regions ( and SI Appendix, Fig. S5C). Lead SNPs near JAG1 and LMX1B reside in TM specific SEs and are colocalized with extensive epigenetic changes induced by dex treatment. JAG1 maintains promoter loops to an A compartment region ~500 kb away containing a SE observed in just 0.8% of non-TM samples. The distal SE region contains lead SNPs identified in both IOP and POAG studies and gains H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peaks for both after the addition of dex (). We similarly detect multiple lead IOP SNPs near LMX1B () and identify a SE overlapping the gene promoter, which is present in just 0.2% of non-TM samples. After dex, the SE locus shows higher H3K4me1 and CTCF binding consistent with a change in promoter regulation. LMX1B encodes a LIM-homeodomain protein required for TM formation (). In humans, LMX1B mutations cause nail-patella syndrome (), a disease linked to elevated risk of glaucoma (), whereas heterozygous Lmx1b mutations result in elevated IOP and glaucoma in mice ().

POAG susceptibility is associated with elevated IOP and hundreds of noncoding genetic variants. There is an unmet need to integrate POAG and IOP associated variants in the noncoding genome to expression of the coding genome and identify potential causal genes, as reported in other complex traits (, ). Our dex-treated TM cells directly capture glucocorticoid-induced TM dysfunction and are a good model of elevated IOP; even though this system does not directly model POAG, it provides useful insights into underlying mechanism. Our study highlights the importance of elucidating cell-type specific transcription regulatory modules, identifying CREs and promoter-centered chromatin contacts unique to TM. In elevated IOP-mimicking conditions, we uncover highly orchestrated and dysregulated changes across genome architecture, epigenetic landscape, transcription factor hubs, and transcriptional patterns including those in disease associated genes. For example, we uncover regulatory mechanisms likely controlling TM specific MYOC transcriptional circuits in homeostasis and steroid-induced dysregulation; mutations in this gene are associated with 2 to 4% of adult-onset POAG and 10% juvenile open angle glaucoma (). Intriguingly, multiple genes required for arachidonic acid (AA) metabolism undergo coordinated changes including ALOX15B, which mediates the inflammation reducing effect of glucocorticoids by increasing the biosynthesis of specialized mediators (). Yet, TM inflammation has been hypothesized to contribute to POAG pathogenicity () in apparent contrast to increased anti-inflammatory activity driven by elevated ALOX15B expression after dex. Recent results from rat glaucoma models have demonstrated that the IOP lowering effects of the glaucoma drug Latanaprost are both mediated by ALOX15B upregulation and PTGS2-driven prostaglandin synthesis pathway (). Our studies uncover widespread downregulation of this key pathway in elevated IOP-mimicking conditions and reveal regulatory hubs likely underpinning this pathogenic repression.

Footprinting analysis has allowed mapping of dynamic DNA–protein binding of CEBPD and JUN. Effector genes of CEBPD, predicted to have increased binding after dex, are enriched for those associated with extracellular organization, caspase activity, MAPK signaling, and eicosanoid metabolism; the latter two terms are also among the top pathways in our multiomic analyses consistent with widespread changes across transcriptional, epigenetic, and topological levels. Prostaglandin analogues are widely used as the first line of treatment for POAG; reducing IOP by increasing the AH outflow through conventional and unconventional pathways (, ). Pathways that gain SEs post treatment also identify apoptotic signaling, suggesting a potential role of the gain of CEBPD binding in regulating pathways associated with increased IOP.

Genes predicted to have reduced JUN binding are enriched for integrin function, adherens junction organization, and cell surface receptor signaling pathway. Focal adhesions which involve integrins remodel the extracellular matrix, resulting in cross-linked actin network (CLANs) formation in glaucoma (). Integrins interact with receptors for advanced glycation end-products (RAGEs) to regulate the level of glycosylated proteins in podocytes (). AGE-RAGE signaling was one of the top pathways identified by our multiomic analysis in dex treated TM cells. AGEs are the result of high glucose, oxidative stress, and advanced age; all of these have been implicated in vision loss, where they mediate crosslinking of extracellular matrix proteins (). Single-cell RNA-seq of TM derived from aging macaque eyes have ascertained a cluster enriched for AGE-RAGE signaling pathway (). These results therefore direct to association of AGE-RAGE to glaucomatous conditions.

GWAS have discovered genetic loci linked to POAG and IOP. Our study builds on these findings by uncovering specific target genes for disease-associated loci. More than half all promoter–SNP loops we identified are not observed in any of 20 tissues previously examined by pc-Hi-C, thereby exposing novel targets. We have identified MIR760 gene as the target gene for BCAR3 locus and the lead variant rs7525880 that are associated with POAG (). MIR760 is downregulated in human primary TM cells treated with either TGFβ1 or TGFβ2 (). Additionally, MIR760 is downregulated in glaucoma tissues, when compared with their expression levels in controls (). We have also identified FZD4 gene as the candidate target for POAG GWAS locus TMEM135 and the lead variant rs2513214 (). FZD4 belongs to frizzled receptors family and its stimulation can activate both Wnt/β-catenin canonical and Wnt/Ca2+ non canonical pathways (). FZD4 is upregulated in TM cells subjected to cyclic mechanical stretch as compared to control cells (). We have shown that Wnt signaling pathway is broadly enriched for epigenetic changes following dex treatment in TM cells. TGFβ and Wnt signaling pathways are reported to be crucial for maintaining TM homeostasis and regulating IOP ().

SEs harboring POAG lead variants are also rarely detected in non-TM samples. We have connected multiple SNPs residing in a SE to JAG1, which encodes a canonical ligand for NOTCH receptor that mediates downstream functions in development, homeostasis, and repair. Intriguingly, JAG1 plays a key role in kidney fibrosis (), a condition similar to the fibrosis observed in glaucoma (). Additionally, the expression of JAG1 and Notch receptors progressively decline with increasing stiffness of TM cells, a condition that mimics glaucoma (). We hypothesize that the variation in JAG1 regulation at this SE may contribute to IOP changes in TM cells and therefore to glaucoma risk.

In sum, our high-resolution promoter-centered chromatin contact map and epigenetic signatures have provided unique insights into TM specific gene regulation. Through noncoding genome annotation and physical contact mapping, we have also uncovered candidate genes associated with elevated IOP- and POAG-like pathogenesis in dex treated TM cells. We however appreciate that experimental validations are required for the new target genes identified here. Further investigations would be necessary to examine 3D chromatin architecture of donor TM tissue from controls and glaucoma patients. Owing to heterogeneity in cellular composition of TM, single-cell studies including single cell Hi-C will help in delineating cell type specificity of chromatin contacts.

TM cells treated with dex offer a useful in-vitro system to mimic elevated IOP and TM dysfunction but do not directly model POAG. Investigations using cells from POAG patients would provide additional insights. The TM cells we used were grown in 2D culture; therefore, TM tissue or 3D culture systems will be valuable since the TM in vivo consists of distinct layers and sheet-like structures. We need to validate the identified target genes as well. Additional experiments utilizing mechanical stress or alternative stimulants may reveal conserved mechanisms associated with POAG. Our experiments were performed on bulk samples at a single time point; therefore, single-cell analyses and time-course experiments would provide more precise spatiotemporal relationships between structural changes and gene expression.

A detailed description of experimental design and analyses is provided in the SI Appendix, Supplementary Materials and Methods. Briefly, we isolated human TM cells from deidentified healthy donors. The use of these tissues was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Duke University School of Medicine (IRB Protocol ID: Pro00120553) and was conducted in compliance with Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) guidelines and the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki. We performed promoter capture Hi-C, total RNAseq, CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag, and ATACseq of TM cells. Next, we treated cells with dex and repeated the multiomic analysis to identify epigenetic, topological, and transcriptomic changes associated with glucocorticoid treatment (GSE301525) (). Finally, we integrated these data with GWAS to identify putative gene targets for variants associated with elevated IOP and POAG.
