medicine.title: Reactive molecular dynamics insights into oxidation-induced degradation of ofloxacin and toxicity assessment of its transformation products
medicine.abstract: The persistence and bioactivity of fluoroquinolone antibiotics in aquatic environments pose significant ecological and public health risks. In this study, the degradation mechanisms of ofloxacin (OFX) upon oxidation, such as by cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) treatment, were investigated using reactive molecular dynamics simulations within the density functional tight-binding framework, and the associated detoxification behavior was evaluated using quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR)-based toxicity assessment. Atomic oxygen (O), a dominant CAP-generated reactive species, was employed as a model oxidant to elucidate molecular-scale transformation pathways. Two oxidation regimes, corresponding to low and high (plasma) oxidation doses, were examined: non-consecutive and consecutive O atom impacts. Non-consecutive oxidation primarily induces isolated hydroxylation and hydrogen abstraction events, resulting in limited structural disruption and minimal reduction in predicted toxicity. In contrast, consecutive O atom exposure triggers cumulative oxidation characterized by repeated hydroxylation, hydrogen abstraction, heterocyclic ring opening, molecular fragmentation, and in one of the five simulated sequences, defluorination. Cleavage of the C–F bond proceeds via an indirect, multistep mechanism involving electronic redistribution and structural relaxation. QSAR-based toxicity predictions reveal a progressive detoxification trend under consecutive oxidation: whereas early intermediates retain toxic and mutagenic characteristics, advanced-stage products exhibit markedly reduced acute aquatic toxicity, lower bioconcentration potential and, where predictable, suppressed mutagenicity. Where it occurs, defluorination eliminates the pharmacophoric functionality of OFX and facilitates subsequent oxidative fragmentation. These findings demonstrate that sustained oxidative exposure is essential for effective (plasma-driven) detoxification of fluoroquinolone antibiotics and provide atomistic insights for optimizing (plasma-based) advanced oxidation processes in wastewater treatment.
medicine.text:
Antibiotics are among the most widely used pharmaceutical compounds worldwide. Due to their low biodegradability, a considerable fraction of the administered antibiotics dose is excreted unmetabolized and subsequently released into aquatic environments, where these compounds can persist for extended periods. This persistence promotes the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and poses potential risks to both ecosystems and human health. In particular, exposure to antibiotic-contaminated water has been associated with adverse biological effects, including endocrine disruption. Consequently, the effective removal of antibiotics from wastewater has become a critical challenge for environmental protection and public health.

Based on their chemical structures and mechanisms of action, antibiotics can be classified into several major groups, including β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, macrolides, and aminoglycosides. Among these, fluoroquinolones are extensively prescribed due to their broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and clinical efficacy. However, incomplete metabolism results in substantial environmental discharge, with approximately 70% of the administered dose being excreted and entering wastewater streams.

Ofloxacin (OFX), a representative fluoroquinolone antibiotic, is frequently detected in wastewater and surface water, raising significant ecological concerns. This issue is particularly pronounced in rapidly developing regions, such as China. Reported OFX concentrations in wastewater treatment plant effluents and river surface waters reach approximately 780 ± 130 ng L−1 and 74 ± 15 ng L−1, respectively. The widespread occurrence of OFX is largely attributed to its poor biodegradability, as only about 10% of the compound undergoes metabolic transformation, while most of the remaining fraction is directly discharged into the environment.

Conventional techniques for OFX removal, including adsorption, photocatalysis, membrane filtration, and biological treatment, have been extensively investigated. Although adsorption using materials such as activated carbon and graphene-based sorbents can partially remove OFX, and photocatalysis enables its oxidative degradation under light irradiation, these methods often suffer from limited efficiency, incomplete mineralization, or high operational costs. Similarly, membrane filtration and biological treatment face challenges related to membrane fouling and low biodegradation rates, respectively. These limitations have motivated the development of advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) and hybrid technologies for antibiotic removal.

Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has recently emerged as a promising AOP for water treatment due to its ability to generate a wide spectrum of reactive species under ambient conditions. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of CAP in degrading fluoroquinolone antibiotics, including OFX. For example, Nguyen et al. reported significant degradation of OFX and other antibiotics in hospital wastewater using CAP, while Sarangapani et al. showed that CAP treatment not only degraded OFX but also substantially reduced its biological activity, producing less harmful byproducts. These findings highlight the potential of CAP as an environmentally friendly and cost-effective technology for wastewater treatment.

In addition to CAP, other AOPs such as heat-activated persulfate oxidation and magnetic CuFe2O4-assisted peroxymonosulfate systems, have demonstrated high efficiency in OFX degradation, with reported mineralization and reductions in the toxicity of transformation products. Despite these advances, the molecular-level mechanisms underlying OFX oxidation, particularly under CAP treatment, remain insufficiently understood.

Atomistic simulations can help address this gap. Conventional fixed-topology molecular dynamics (MD) cannot describe bond breaking or formation, whereas reactive MD enables these processes to be investigated using empirical reactive force fields or quantum-mechanically based methods such as density functional tight binding (DFTB). Here we adopt DFTB-based reactive MD (DFTB-MD). DFTB is an approximate density functional theory (DFT) method that explicitly treats electronic structure while typically offering an approximately two-orders-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to DFT. Its computational efficiency and reported performance in predicting hydrogen-binding energies, proton affinities, and proton-transfer barriers make it useful for exploring reactive pathways. Unlike empirical reactive force fields, it provides an explicit electronic-structure description of the reacting system. DFTB also supports a spin-polarized treatment of open-shell species, including ground-state triplet O(3P). Reactive DFTB-MD has previously been applied to plasma-induced oxidation of oligosaccharides, amino acids, and the β-lactam antibiotic amoxicillin, in the latter study, O atoms were identified as key species driving ring opening and fragmentation.

Herein, we combine reactive DFTB-MD simulations with quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR)-based toxicity predictions to investigate OFX degradation and link atomic-level oxidative pathways with the predicted toxicity of the resulting transformation products. Atomic O is selected as a representative reactive oxygen species (ROS) for modeling direct oxidative pathways under CAP treatment. We compare two regimes representing isolated and cumulative oxidative exposure: 100 independent non-consecutive O-atom impacts on intact OFX and five sequences of 20 consecutive impacts, with each impact acting on the product of the preceding step. Specifically, we (a) identify reactive sites and dominant initiation channels and relate their selectivity to DFT-computed X–H bond dissociation energies, which also serve to benchmark DFTB3 for this system; (b) trace how cumulative oxidation leads to heterocyclic ring opening, fragmentation, and C–F bond cleavage; and (c) use T.E.S.T. to predict acute aquatic toxicity, bioconcentration factor, developmental toxicity, and mutagenicity for the selected transformation products, examining whether detoxification is associated with specific structural changes rather than molecular size reduction alone. To our knowledge, this is the first reactive MD study of fluoroquinolone degradation under CAP-relevant conditions and the first to examine how isolated versus cumulative oxidative exposure shapes both degradation pathways and predicted detoxification. Together, these analyses provide mechanistic insight into plasma-driven OFX degradation and its potential for detoxification, with possible relevance to other AOPs.

In this study, reactive MD simulations were performed based on the density functional tight-binding (DFTB) method using the DFTB+ package. To accurately describe interatomic interactions, the “3ob-3-1” parameter set, developed for the DFTB3 framework and validated for organic and biomolecular systems, was employed. All DFTB3 calculations were performed self-consistently (SCC-DFTB3), with a maximum of 300 SCC cycles and a self-consistent-charge convergence tolerance of ≈1 × 10−5 e (DFTB+ default), together with Fermi–Dirac electronic smearing at an electronic temperature of 1000 K to aid SCC convergence (distinct from the 300 K thermostat temperature governing the nuclear dynamics). An empirical hydrogen-bonding damping correction (damping exponent = 4.0) was applied to improve the description of X–H interactions, which is particularly relevant given that H-abstraction represents a dominant reaction channel in this study, and dispersion interactions were accounted for using an empirical Lennard–Jones correction based on universal force field (UFF) parameters. All simulations employed spin-polarized (collinear) DFTB, initialized with two unpaired electrons consistent with the O(3P) + closed-shell OFX entrance channel; the total spin was subsequently allowed to relax during the trajectory to capture spin changes associated with radical formation and quenching. A minimal valence basis (s orbitals for H; s,p orbitals for C, N, O, and F) was used, consistent with the 3ob-3-1 parameter set, and Γ-point-only k-point sampling was applied given the large (30 Å3) simulation cell. To model the interactions between CAP and OFX, atomic O was selected as the impinging reactive species, representing the dominant ROS generated during CAP treatment. This choice is directly supported by our previous combined computational-experimental study of oligosaccharide oxidation. In that study, O-atom-only DFTB-MD simulations of cellotriose predicted specific oxidation products, including products resulting from hydroxyl group addition (+16 Da) and lower-mass di- and monosaccharide fragments resulting from glycosidic bond cleavage. These products were independently confirmed by high-resolution mass spectrometry of cellotriose treated with a CAP jet. This product-level agreement between simulation and experiment demonstrates that O-atom-driven chemistry alone can reproduce the dominant oxidative degradation pathways observed experimentally, even though a real CAP-liquid system contains a broader mixture of reactive species. The choice of O is further supported by two complementary lines of evidence. First, systematic screening of nine CAP-generated RONS (O, OH, HO2, H2O2, O3, NO, NO2, NO2−, NO3−) against a model antibiotic showed that only O and OH induced bond-breaking and bond-forming reactions. O reacted through H-abstraction mechanisms essentially identical to those of OH and behaved as two OH radicals within a single collision. These findings support the selection of O as both the most reactive species among those tested and a representative single-species proxy for the RONS cocktail. Second, isotope-labeling experiments showed that plasma-generated O atoms cross the gas–liquid interface and react directly with dissolved organic compounds without first forming OH through reaction with water, supporting the availability of aqueous O atoms as an independent reactive species.

An O-only model is therefore representative of the fast, direct oxidative pathways captured within the ∼200 ps trajectory window of each simulation (see below), predominantly involving H-abstraction, hydroxylation, and radical addition/elimination reactions. However, it does not capture (i) synergistic effects arising from the simultaneous presence of multiple RONS, which experimental studies suggest can enhance degradation beyond that achieved by any single species alone, or (ii) slower reaction channels involving less reactive RONS (e.g., H2O2, O3, NO2−, NO3−) that may become relevant on timescales beyond those accessible in these simulations. The consecutive O-atom impact simulations (see below and Section 3.2) partially address the cumulative and sequential nature of oxidative exposure by subjecting the same molecule to repeated O-atom impacts. However, potential contributions from other RONS, acting independently or synergistically with O, remain outside the scope of this single-species framework and warrant investigation in future work.

The simulations were performed without an explicit aqueous environment. This is a deliberate model boundary. The model isolates the intrinsic chemical reactivity of O(3P) toward the OFX framework (the site selectivity, elementary reaction steps and bond energetics of direct O-atom attack) independent of solvent effects. This choice is chemically justified for the oxidant studied here. Isotope-labeling experiments with 18O2-fed plasma showed that more than 90% of the oxidized products of a dissolved aromatic probe (phenol) incorporated the plasma-derived 18O. This demonstrates that O atoms entering the liquid react directly with the solute rather than first converting to OH radical through reaction with water. Consistent with this, Car–Parrinello MD simulations indicate that O atoms are stable in liquid water, with an energy barrier of about 10 kcal mol−1 for reaction with the solvent, and DFTB-MD simulations showed that triplet O remains unreacted in bulk water over 10 ps. The reaction lifetime of O(aq) with a dissolved aromatic compound at sub-millimolar concentration has further been estimated at about 50 ns. The chemically decisive step in solution is therefore a direct, bimolecular encounter between an O atom and the solute. This is precisely the event captured by the present simulations, in which O-atom attack on OFX occurred within 15 ps in all trajectories (median 3.9 ps; see reaction analysis below).

The simulation model of the OFX molecule is shown in , where the piperazinyl ring, quinolone core, and oxazinyl ring are indicated in yellow, green, and blue, respectively. The piperazinyl moiety is known to play a critical role in the degradation behavior of fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

To prepare the molecular structure for the simulations, the initial structure of OFX was obtained from the PubChem database (National Institutes of Health, National Center for Biotechnology Information) and subsequently optimized in the gas phase at the density functional theory (DFT) level using the ORCA quantum chemistry program. The optimization employed the B3LYP hybrid exchange–correlation functional and the 6-311G* basis set, with a neutral singlet electronic state (charge 0, multiplicity 1) and tight SCF convergence criteria. The resulting DFT-optimized structure provided the starting geometry for both the bond dissociation energy calculations and the subsequent preparation of the reactive DFTB-MD simulations.

As a complementary analysis, X–H bond dissociation energies (BDEs) were calculated to relate the site selectivity of H-abstraction-the most frequently observed reaction mechanism in this study (see Section 3)-to bond strength and to benchmark DFTB3 against DFT. The calculations considered all 11 H-bearing sites of OFX (C1–C5, C8, C13, C16, C17, C18 and the carboxylic O–H site), collectively accounting for all 20 H atoms in the molecule (see ). For each site, one H atom was removed, and the resulting doublet radical was fully reoptimized at the unrestricted B3LYP/6-311G* level, followed by harmonic frequency analysis. All optimized radicals were confirmed to be local minima, with no imaginary frequencies and negligible spin contamination (〈S2〉 = 0.753–0.760). Electronic bond dissociation energies were calculated as De = E(R˙) + E(H˙) − E(RH), and the corresponding values at 298 K, D298, were obtained by including zero-point and thermal corrections. For CH2 and CH3 groups, a single representative H atom was removed, and the resulting radical was fully reoptimized. The same quantities were calculated at the DFTB3/3ob-3-1 level using the Hamiltonian settings employed in the reactive MD simulations.

For the reactive DFTB-MD simulations, the DFT-optimized OFX molecule was placed at the center of a cubic simulation box with dimensions of 30 Å × 30 Å × 30 Å, providing sufficient space for interactions with an incoming O atom. Periodic boundary conditions were applied in all three spatial directions. The OFX structure was then energy-minimized at the DFTB3 level using the conjugate gradient algorithm, followed by thermalization (or equilibration) at 300 K for 700 ps in the canonical (NVT) ensemble using the Berendsen thermostat with a coupling constant of 100 fs. Equilibration was assessed by monitoring temperature and total energy fluctuations (see Fig. S1 in the SI). A time step of 0.5 fs was used throughout all simulations.

The Berendsen thermostat (see above) was used both during equilibration and throughout all production trajectories, and was coupled to all atoms, including the impinging O atom; overall translation of the system was removed at every step. The production runs were not switched to the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble. The Berendsen scheme suppresses kinetic-energy fluctuations and does not rigorously sample the canonical ensemble, and it can transfer kinetic energy into motions without a restoring force (the “flying ice cube” effect). For the equilibrated OFX configurations, this artifact is absent: the instantaneous temperature was 290–297 K, and only 0.7–3.2% of the kinetic energy resided in center-of-mass translation and overall rotation, at or below the equipartition value of 4.3% (Table S1 in the SI).

The translation of the impinging O atom relative to OFX is, however, such a motion without a restoring force. We therefore examined the O-atom velocities directly in all 100 non-consecutive trajectories. The O atom was launched with a thermal velocity (mean kinetic energy 0.033 eV, consistent with 300 K). While the system temperature remained at 300 K, its kinetic energy increased progressively during the approach, reaching on average 0.18 eV (median 0.15 eV; 90th percentile 0.32 eV) shortly before contact with OFX. The thermostat therefore does not drain the kinetic energy of the projectile; instead, it moderately accelerates it, so that collisions occur at somewhat super-thermal energies. These energies are small compared with the heat released by the reactions themselves, which transiently raises the temperature of the whole system to a median of ∼540 K. Moreover, trajectories propagated without any thermostat (NVE), in which no such acceleration occurs, yielded the same reaction pathways. The effect may, however, increase the reactivity of the more strongly bound sites and thereby contribute to the weak dependence of site selectivity on bond strength (Section 3.1). Stochastic thermostats such as Andersen or Langevin dynamics, which do not exhibit this artifact, are recommended for future studies.

With a well-equilibrated model system established, we proceeded to investigate the bond-breaking and bond-formation processes and degradation pathways of OFX. A total of 200 DFTB-MD impact simulations were conducted, comprising 100 independent non-consecutive impacts and five sequences of 20 consecutive impacts. For the non-consecutive simulations, the final configuration from equilibration was used as the starting structure for all 100 trajectories. For the consecutive simulations, five configurations (A–E), sampled at equally spaced time points within the final 100 ps of equilibration, were used to initiate the five impact sequences. The non-consecutive and consecutive simulations represented isolated and cumulative oxidative exposure, respectively.

Specifically, in the non-consecutive impact simulations, each trajectory started from an intact OFX molecule, allowing the interaction between a single O atom and pristine OFX to be evaluated independently. In contrast, the consecutive impact simulations involved sequential O atom impacts on OFX molecules that had already undergone structural modification, enabling the investigation of progressive degradation pathways. At the start of each simulation, a single O atom was randomly positioned at least 7 Å away from the OFX molecule to avoid any initial close-contact interaction. The velocity direction of the incoming O atom was randomly assigned, and its initial kinetic energy was set to correspond to room temperature (300 K). Non-consecutive trajectories were propagated for a target duration of 200 ps (4 × 105 MD steps), whereas each consecutive impact was simulated for 50 ps (1 × 105 MD steps), both under the NVT ensemble. These durations were sufficient to capture key chemical events, including hydrogen (H) abstraction, hydroxylation, ring opening, bond cleavage, and molecular fragmentation, with every trajectory extending well beyond the completion of its reactive events (see below).

To facilitate systematic interpretation of the obtained degradation pathways, a structured labeling scheme was adopted. In the non-consecutive impact simulations, 19 distinct reaction mechanisms were identified and sequentially labeled as R1–R19, where “R” denotes an independent single-impact reaction event originating from pristine OFX.

In contrast, the consecutive impact simulations involved progressive oxidation sequences starting from five different initial molecular configurations to ensure structural diversity. Each configuration was assigned a letter identifier (A–E), and the consecutive oxidation intermediates generated within each sequence were labeled sequentially (i.e., A1–A20, B1–B20, C1–C20, D1–D20, and E1–E20). Indeed, 20 consecutive DFTB-MD simulations were performed for each configuration. In this nomenclature, the letter designates the initial configuration set, whereas the numerical index represents the oxidation stage within that specific consecutive pathway. This classification clearly differentiates between independent single-impact reactions and multistep progressive degradation sequences, thereby facilitating systematic comparison of mechanistic evolution and toxicity trends. The 50 ps duration of the consecutive impacts is supported by the temperature evolution of the corresponding trajectories (Fig. S2 in the SI). Reactive events produce short temperature spikes from the heat released in exothermic steps. In configuration A, all such events occurred within the first ∼34 ps of each impact, with no further events in the remaining ∼16 ps. After each event, the temperature returned to the 300 K range within about 1 ps, and all 20 impacts ended at ∼300 K. Each impact therefore starts from a thermalized structure, so no separate re-equilibration step was required between successive impacts, and no excess energy accumulates over the series.

Bond formation and cleavage were identified by visual inspection of the trajectories in Jmol and cross-checked against the temperature and energy records of the DFTB+ output. To make this criterion quantitative, bonds were also assigned automatically in every saved frame (every 0.1 ps). Two atoms were considered bonded when their separation, evaluated under the minimum-image convention, was below 1.2 times the sum of their covalent radii. A change in the bond network was counted as a reaction only if the new bonding pattern persisted for at least 1 ps, which filters out transient encounters and vibrational fluctuations. The results are insensitive to these parameters: varying the distance factor between 1.15 and 1.25 and the persistence time between 0.5 and 2 ps changes the median first-reaction time by at most 0.3 ps and leaves its maximum unchanged. The automated analysis agrees with the visual inspection and the temperature record. All 100 non-consecutive trajectories are reactive, and in 96 of them the temperature maximum within the first 20 ps coincides, to within 1 ps, with the structurally detected first reaction.

All first reactions occurred within 14.7 ps (median 3.9 ps; 91% within 10 ps; Fig. S3 in the SI). Every trajectory continued for at least 12 ps after its last bond change. After each reaction, the temperature returned to 294–301 K (median 299 K), and the bond network then remained unchanged; we take this combination as the steady-state criterion. Among the 78 trajectories longer than 50 ps, only one showed a bond change after 20 ps (a secondary C–C cleavage at 44.8 ps). The simulated durations therefore capture the reactive phase of every trajectory.

To evaluate the environmental implications of OFX degradation, QSAR analysis was conducted using the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Toxicity Estimation Software Tool (T.E.S.T.), version 5.1.2.0. This software predicts toxicological and physicochemical endpoints directly from molecular structure using internally calculated molecular descriptors and multiple statistical modeling approaches.

Molecular structures obtained from the DFTB-MD simulations were exported as MDL MOL files and imported into T.E.S.T. for batch toxicity prediction. Following any trajectory step that resulted in molecular fragmentation, only the largest resulting fragment was submitted to T.E.S.T. for toxicity prediction at that and all subsequent steps. The 3D geometries of these transformation products were obtained directly from the DFTB3/3ob-3-1 level of theory used throughout the reactive MD simulations (Section 2.1), consistent with the Hamiltonian governing the bond-breaking and bond-formation events themselves. We note that this level of theory has limited direct bearing on the resulting toxicity predictions: T.E.S.T.’s QSAR models (hierarchical, single-model, nearest-neighbor, and group-contribution methods, combined via the consensus approach) are built exclusively on two-dimensional, topology-based molecular descriptors, including E-state indices, connectivity and constitutional descriptors, molecular fragment counts, and related graph-theoretical properties and explicitly do not incorporate three-dimensional (x, y, z) coordinate-based descriptors. Consequently, what determines the T.E.S.T. predictions is each transformation product's correct molecular connectivity (bonding pattern and functional groups), which was faithfully captured from the DFTB3-level structures, rather than the specific level of theory used for any further geometric refinement. The consensus modeling approach was employed, which integrates hierarchical clustering, single model, nearest neighbor, and group contribution methods. The consensus prediction represents the averaged output of applicable models within their defined applicability domains, thereby improving robustness and minimizing model-specific bias. Default applicability domain constraints were retained to ensure reliability of predictions. When a compound fell outside the applicability domain, the corresponding endpoint was reported as “N/A”.

Four environmentally relevant endpoints were selected to provide a multidimensional assessment of ecological and health risks associated with OFX and its transformation products. Acute aquatic toxicity was evaluated as the 48 h LC50 for Daphnia magna, representing the concentration (mg L−1) causing 50% mortality after 48 hours of exposure. The bioconcentration factor (BCF) was included to estimate the bioaccumulation potential of degradation intermediates in aquatic organisms. Developmental toxicity was assessed to evaluate the potential interference with normal organismal development, reflecting chronic and reproductive hazards. Mutagenicity was predicted to assess the genotoxic potential of intermediates based on Ames test-related QSAR models.

For the binary endpoints (developmental toxicity and mutagenicity), the classification labels were taken directly from the T.E.S.T. consensus output, which applies the software's built-in cut-off at a predicted value of 0.5. The selection of these four endpoints was guided by their regulatory and environmental relevance for pharmaceutical contaminants undergoing plasma-induced advanced oxidation. Acute toxicity and bioaccumulation address immediate and long-term ecological hazards, while developmental toxicity and mutagenicity capture chronic and genetic hazard dimensions. Together, these parameters provide a complementary set of hazard indicators for evaluating detoxification trends under consecutive and non-consecutive oxidative degradation pathways. Because the aquatic assessment is restricted to a single trophic level (invertebrates), toxicity toward fish and primary producers was not evaluated; the predictions therefore describe relative hazard trends along the degradation pathways rather than a full ecological risk assessment.

Because the reliability of the reaction-mechanism statistics reported in Section 3 below depends on the underlying sampling design, we assessed it separately for the non-consecutive and consecutive datasets, which differ fundamentally in structure.

For the non-consecutive simulations, each of the 100 trajectories is an independent, identically distributed single-impact event on pristine OFX, so the resulting reaction-mechanism frequencies are multinomial sampling outcomes. We evaluated the adequacy of n = 100 using 95% Wilson score confidence intervals together with a nonparametric bootstrap (20 000 resamples); the two methods agree closely (see  below, and Fig. S4 in the SI). The dominant reaction class (H-abstraction-initiated pathways, 91% of trajectories) has a 95% CI of [84%, 95%], confirming that this majority finding is well resolved at n = 100. The most frequent individual mechanism (reaction 1, 15%) carries correspondingly wider uncertainty (95% CI [9%, 23%]), and mechanisms observed only once (∼1%) should be read as evidence that a given pathway is chemically accessible rather than as a precise probability estimate. A sample-size sensitivity analysis (Fig. S4 in the SI) shows that this level of precision is essentially unimprovable without disproportionate computational cost: resolving individual rare-pathway frequencies to comparable precision would require sample sizes an order of magnitude larger than is feasible for DFTB-MD.

The consecutive simulations follow a different sampling logic and require a different treatment. Each of the five initial configurations (A–E) is a single, sequentially dependent trajectory of 20 impacts, in which each step is conditioned on the product of the previous one; the unit of independent replication is therefore N = 5, not 100, and trajectory-level bootstrap resampling is not statistically appropriate here. This design reflects a deliberate trade-off: the consecutive dataset was built to probe whether sustained, cumulative oxidation drives a qualitative outcome – progressive detoxification and, ultimately, defluorination – rather than to establish quantitative reaction probabilities, and expanding N further was not computationally tractable given the cost of 20 sequential production trajectories per configuration. We therefore assess this dataset by direct reproducibility across the five independent configurations: all five independently reach the same qualitative endpoint, classification as non-harmful (LC50 > 100 mg L−1) by the final oxidation stage, despite substantial quantitative variability (121.8–2918.6 mg L−1). This five-for-five agreement supports the robustness of the detoxification trend reported in Section 3.2.2 at the qualitative level, while N = 5 affords comparatively limited power to resolve its precise magnitude – a limitation we state explicitly rather than imply a false precision.

Accordingly, we limit our quantitative claims: percentages and confidence intervals are reported only for the well-resolved, aggregate-level and high-frequency outcomes established above, while single-occurrence pathways and consecutive-impact trends are described qualitatively.

For each non-consecutive DFTB-MD trajectory, the initial position of the impinging O atom was drawn from a uniform distribution within the 30 × 30 × 30 Å simulation box, with the draw rejected and repeated if the resulting distance to the OFX molecule's center of mass was less than 7 Å. The O atom's initial velocity was assigned independently along each Cartesian axis, yielding a mean launch speed of ≈6.27 Å ps−1, close to the theoretical Maxwell–Boltzmann mean speed for atomic O at 300 K (6.30 Å ps−1). Because velocity direction was assigned independently of position, the O atom was not aimed at OFX, and no formal impact parameter is defined for this launch scheme. Each trajectory was propagated for the full 200 ps regardless of the outcome of any early encounter; combined with the NVT thermostat and periodic boundary conditions, this allows an O atom that does not react immediately to continue diffusing, including through periodic re-entry and potentially react at a later point within the same 200 ps window. The reaction-mechanism frequencies reported in  therefore represent the eventual outcome over this full 200 ps window rather than a first-encounter probability.

To assess whether this sampling scheme introduces a directional bias, we analyzed the actual initial position and velocity-direction vectors used across the 100 non-consecutive trajectories (Fig. S5 in the SI). A Rayleigh test for a net preferred direction was non-significant for both position (R̄ = 0.070, p = 0.687) and velocity direction (R̄ = 0.091, p = 0.480). However, because the cubic simulation box lacks spherical symmetry, uniform-in-volume position sampling is expected to show a higher-order (octahedral) bias favoring the box's 8 corner directions over its 6 face-normal directions once the sampled radius exceeds half the box width (15 Å), a regime capturing roughly half of all accepted position draws. A shape-diagnostic statistic sensitive to this specific pattern confirmed a significant corner-favoring bias in the position sampling (observed mean = 0.778 vs. isotropic expectation = 0.831; z = −5.51, p < 0.0001), but no significant bias in the velocity-direction sampling (observed mean = 0.847 vs. 0.831; z = 1.61, p = 0.107).

A box-frame bias of this kind would only translate into biased sampling of OFX's molecular surface if the molecule's orientation within the box were fixed across trajectories. We therefore examined the orientation diversity of the five independent starting configurations used to seed the non-consecutive simulations (20 trajectories per configuration; Section 2.1). The angle between each configuration's principal molecular axis was computed for all 10 configuration pairs, giving a mean pairwise angle of 51.0 ° – well within the expected range for five independently, randomly oriented axes (Monte Carlo null distribution: 57.3° ± 6.8°; observed value at the 16th percentile; Fig. S6 in the SI). Consequently, although the position-sampling scheme exhibits a real, quantifiable directional bias in the fixed box frame, this bias is not expected to translate into a systematic over- or under-sampling of specific OFX functional groups at the ensemble level, since the corner-favoring directions correspond to different molecular sites across the five independently oriented configurations. We nonetheless note this as a methodological improvement for future studies: initial O-atom positions could instead be sampled directly on a spherical shell (e.g., via a Fibonacci-sphere scheme) to eliminate this box-geometry artifact at the source.

Reactive MD simulations were performed to investigate the degradation mechanisms of OFX upon interaction with O atoms. Using a non-consecutive simulation strategy, a total of 100 independent DFTB-MD trajectories were analyzed, leading to the identification of 19 distinct reaction mechanisms. These mechanisms are summarized in  and provide insight into the primary pathways involved in the oxidative degradation of OFX. As shown in , the dominant class of reaction pathways (91%, reactions 1–11) [95% CI: 84–95%] is initiated by H-abstraction from the OFX molecule. In the majority of these cases (90%, reactions 1–10), H-abstraction is followed by OH group formation. In one less frequent pathway (reaction 11), the reaction progresses further, resulting in the release of both H2O and CO2 molecules, indicative of a more advanced degree of molecular fragmentation.

In addition to H-abstraction-driven processes, alternative reaction pathways are observed in 9% of the simulations (reactions 12–19). These pathways involve various bond formation and bond cleavage events, including C–O–C linkage formation and C–C bond dissociation, which contribute to structural modification of the OFX molecule. Notably, a subset of these reactions (4%) leads to the formation of epoxide-like intermediates, suggesting oxidation routes distinct from simple hydroxylation.

Because the reactive sites carry different numbers of equivalent H atoms, raw event counts do not directly reflect intrinsic site reactivity. We therefore normalized the frequency of each single-site H-abstraction channel (reactions 1–10) by the number of H atoms at the corresponding site (n(H)) and related it to the X–H BDE (Table S2 and Fig. S7 in the SI). Per-H reaction frequency decreases significantly with increasing BDE (Spearman ρ = −0.88, p < 0.001; Poisson regression, p < 0.001), and a log-linear dependence describes the data well (residual deviance 3.9 on 9 degrees of freedom). This dependence is, however, far weaker than thermodynamic control of the form k ∝ n(H)·exp(−ΔE/kT) would imply. The fitted slope (−1.5 ± 0.5 eV−1) is about 26 times smaller than the value of −38.7 eV−1 expected at 300 K, and Boltzmann weighting would assign about 90% of all abstractions to the weakest bond (C17), compared with the observed 6.7%.

The data instead reveal two regimes. The seven C–H bonds adjacent to N or O (C1–C5, C16, C17; De = 4.05–4.34 eV) react with statistically indistinguishable per-H frequencies (5.4% on average; χ2 = 0.79, p = 0.99), although Boltzmann weighting would predict a variation of about five orders of magnitude across this range. Reactivity decreases only for the stronger bonds, namely the C18 methyl group, the carboxylic O–H and the vinylic C13–H (De = 4.45–4.98 eV; 2.0–3.3% per H), and no abstraction occurs from the aromatic C8–H bond (De = 5.26 eV). This behavior is characteristic of a highly reactive radical for which abstraction from weak bonds is fast relative to its encounter with the molecule. The product distribution is then governed by the number and accessibility of H atoms rather than by bond strength, which becomes selective only for bonds from which abstraction is substantially disfavored. A similarly low selectivity is well established for OH radical, which reacts with most organic compounds at near-diffusion-controlled rates.

DFTB3 reproduces the B3LYP BDEs with a mean absolute error of 0.12 eV (2.8 kcal mol−1), a root-mean-square deviation of 0.15 eV and no systematic bias (mean signed error +0.01 eV), with Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients of 0.93 and 0.96, respectively (Fig. S8 and Table S2 in the SI). The largest deviations occur for C18 (+0.32 eV) and C13 (−0.21 eV). Importantly, both methods yield the same separation between the weaker α-heteroatom C–H bonds and the stronger X–H bonds, and the dependence of per-H frequency on BDE remains significant when DFTB3 BDEs are used instead (p = 0.004). The site-selectivity analysis is therefore insensitive to the level of theory, supporting the adequacy of DFTB3 energetics for describing the reactions studied here. Returning to the observed reaction pathways, their coexistence highlights the complex and competitive nature of plasma-induced oxidation processes. Among all identified mechanisms, the most frequently observed reaction (15%) corresponds to the formation of an OH group following H-abstraction from the C1 methyl group (reaction 1). Normalized per H atom (5.0%), however, C1 is no more reactive than the other α-heteroatom sites; its higher raw frequency reflects its three equivalent H atoms. This observation indicates that hydroxylation represents a predominant initial modification pathway, likely altering the physicochemical properties of OFX and influencing its subsequent reactivity. The molecular details of this hydroxylation mechanism are shown in . The incoming O atom initially abstracts a H atom from the C1 methyl of the piperazinyl ring (red arrow). This process generates a transient OH radical and a C-centered radical site on the OFX. Subsequent recombination of the OH radical with the C-centered radical site (green arrow) forms an OH group at C1, which persisted unchanged for the remainder of the trajectory. The heat released by this recombination is dissipated by the thermostat within about 1 ps, after which the temperature returns to ∼300 K (Section 3.2.1).

In addition to the dominant hydroxylation pathway described above, several alternative oxidative transformation routes are identified under non-consecutive O atom impact conditions. The oxidants in experimentally studied advanced oxidation systems differ fundamentally from the atomic O simulated here.

Persulfate- and peroxymonosulfate-based processes are dominated by solvated ˙OH and SO4˙−radicals, which differ from atomic O in electrophilicity, steric demand and diffusion behavior. Nevertheless, several of the transformations identified here (hydroxylation, decarboxylation, ring transformation and defluorination) have also been reported experimentally for OFX in such systems. This convergence does not validate the specific mechanisms simulated here. Rather, it indicates that these transformations reflect intrinsic structural weak points of the fluoroquinolone skeleton, which are attacked by chemically distinct oxidants. A degree of mechanistic kinship is nevertheless expected at the level of the primary steps: in our previous study, O atoms and OH radicals reacted with amoxicillin through the same H-abstraction and OH-addition mechanisms.

One such alternative pathway is the decarboxylation-like transformation illustrated in . In this pathway, an O atom attacks the carboxyl-containing region of OFX and initiates H-abstraction from the carboxylic acid group, producing an OH radical and promoting electronic polarization around the neighboring C11–C12 fragment. This local polarization weakens the C11–C12 bond and facilitates a decarboxylation-like elimination process, resulting in the release of CO2. Subsequently, the generated OH radical abstracts the H atom from C13, leading to H2O formation and generation of a locally unsaturated quinolone intermediate. As a result, π-electron redistribution and bond rearrangement occur around the C11–C13 region, increasing local structural strain within the quinolone core. This mechanism corresponds to reaction 11 of .

The steps of this pathway are well separated in time and do not proceed as a single thermally driven cascade. In the trajectories following this route, CO2 was released within 0–1.6 ps of the initial H-abstraction, accompanied by only a modest transient temperature rise (peak 340–412 K). The subsequent H-abstraction that yields H2O occurred 1.8–13 ps later, after the system had fully re-thermalized (median temperature 301–312 K in the preceding picosecond). The decarboxylation is thus a prompt follow-up reaction of the carboxyl radical formed by H-abstraction, occurring faster than vibrational energy relaxation in liquid water would remove the released energy. The dehydration step, by contrast, is a separate reaction taking place at 300 K. This pathway indicates that isolated O atom impacts can induce not only hydroxylation but also radical-mediated decarboxylation, dehydration, and local electronic reorganization. Decarboxylation has likewise been identified as an important OFX transformation route in experimental studies of radical-driven oxidation, albeit with different oxidants (see above). Although this pathway involves both decarboxylation and subsequent dehydration steps within the same trajectory, all reactive events originate from a single externally impinging O atom; the OH radical produced during the initial H-abstraction acts as an in situ secondary reactive species. We therefore classify this reaction as a single-impact (non-consecutive) cascade.

Furthermore, as shown in , non-consecutive O atom impacts can trigger additional oxidation pathways involving localized O addition to unsaturated C centers, intramolecular bond rearrangement, and the formation of strained cyclic intermediates. In  (reaction 12), the incoming O atom attacks the electron-rich C10–C11 unsaturated region of the quinolone core. Due to the adjacent carbonyl functionality, this site is electronically activated, and O atom addition induces local π-electron redistribution within the aromatic scaffold. Consequently, a C10–O–C11 epoxide-like intermediate is formed, eventually leading to the breakage of the C10–C11 bond. The formation of the three-membered cyclic ether (C10–O–C11) introduces considerable angle strain and locally disrupts conjugation, thereby destabilizing the quinolone core and increasing its susceptibility to subsequent oxidative transformations, such as ring expansion.

In , the O atom adds to the fluorine-bearing carbon (C7), disrupting the aromaticity of the ring. This is followed by a 1,2-shift of the F atom to the neighboring carbon (C6) and formation of a C7O carbonyl group (reaction 13). This rearrangement does not involve homolytic cleavage of the C–F bond, as the F atom is never released. It corresponds to the fluorine analogue of the NIH shift, a 1,2-migration of ring substituents that accompanies the oxidation of aromatic rings by O-atom-transfer oxidants and has been observed experimentally for fluorine during the oxidation of fluorobenzenes. The pathway occurred in a single non-consecutive trajectory (1%) and, independently, in one consecutive sequence (D3, Section 3.2.1). Its energy barrier was not characterized, and the accuracy of DFTB3/3ob-3-1 for this specific rearrangement has not been benchmarked against higher-level methods, so its occurrence should be interpreted qualitatively. The susceptibility of the C–F-containing region is nevertheless consistent with experimentally reported defluorination pathways of OFX in peroxymonosulfate-assisted oxidation systems.

This observation suggests that local perturbation of the fluorinated moiety may precede deeper oxidative C–F bond cleavage under sustained oxidation conditions. Defluorination of OFX has also been reported experimentally in peroxymonosulfate-assisted oxidation, indicating that the C–F-containing region is a structural weak point susceptible to attack by different oxidants. In , an O atom adds across the C11–C13 unsaturated bond, forming a second epoxide-like C11–O–C13 intermediate. Similar to the pathway in , this reaction interrupts local π-delocalization and generates a strained cyclic structure. The associated bond reorganization modifies the electronic structure of the quinolone fragment and may weaken neighboring bonds, thereby facilitating further oxidation in subsequent reaction steps.

Taken together, the pathways shown in  and  demonstrate that non-consecutive O atom impacts can induce a broader range of oxidative transformations than simple hydroxylation alone. These include radical-mediated decarboxylation, dehydration, O addition, intramolecular rearrangement, fluorine-associated electronic redistribution, and epoxide-like intermediate formation. From a chemical perspective, these reactions reveal multiple competing reactive sites within OFX. From a physical perspective, they reflect localized electron-density redistribution, disruption of conjugation, and accumulation of structural strain within the molecular framework.

Overall, non-consecutive O atom interactions with OFX reveal diverse oxidation pathways, predominantly governed by H-abstraction and subsequent hydroxylation, but also involving O insertion, bond rearrangement, and strained cyclic intermediate formation. Despite this mechanistic diversity, most reactions remain localized and do not lead to extensive fragmentation of the OFX scaffold. The quinolone core and overall molecular architecture are largely retained after non-consecutive oxidative events, indicating that non-consecutive O atom impacts (corresponding to a low plasma oxidation dose) are insufficient for deep degradation or effective detoxification of OFX. These observations underscore the need for consecutive oxidation, corresponding to a high plasma oxidation dose, in which cumulative O atom impacts can drive more extensive structural disruption and progressive toxicity reduction, as discussed in Section 3.2 below.

As discussed in the previous section, a total of 19 independent reaction mechanisms (R1–R19) were identified under non-consecutive O atom interactions with the OFX molecule (). The resulting oxidation products were evaluated for their environmental risk profiles using the QSAR protocol described in Section 2.2. Four key endpoints are considered, and the predicted values are summarized in  and Table S3 of the SI.

The predicted LC50 values, representing 48 hours acute toxicity toward Daphnia magna, show substantial variation among the identified reaction mechanisms (). Based on commonly used LC50 classification thresholds, four pathways (R11, R17, R18, and R19) are categorized as toxic (LC50 < 10 mg L−1). A larger group, including the OFX molecule and pathways R1–R10, R12–R14, and R16, falls into the harmful category (LC50 between 10 and 100 mg L−1), while only pathway R15 exhibits an LC50 value exceeding 100 mg L−1 and is thus classified as non-harmful. These results suggest that non-consecutive O atom interactions (corresponding to a low plasma oxidation dose) are generally insufficient to significantly reduce the acute aquatic toxicity of OFX and, in some cases, may lead to the formation of intermediates with increased toxicity. Predicted BCF values also vary considerably across the reaction pathways (). The parent OFX molecule exhibits a moderate BCF value (∼3.5), while pathway R11 shows the highest predicted accumulation potential. In contrast, pathways R12–R17 yield products with reduced BCF values, indicating a potentially improved environmental profile with respect to bioaccumulation. Developmental toxicity predictions reveal that all structures exhibit values above 0.5 (), indicating that none of the oxidative pathways appreciably reduces the embryotoxic potential of OFX. Mutagenicity predictions further demonstrate that the majority of oxidation products retain genotoxic characteristics (). Specifically, 13 oxidation products, including R1–R10, R12, and R15, as well as the original OFX molecule, exceed the mutagenicity threshold of 0.5 and are classified as mutagenic, whereas seven pathways (R11, R13, R14, R16, R17, R18, and R19) are predicted to be non-mutagenic.

Overall, although limited detoxification is observed in isolated cases such as R15, the majority of oxidative transformation pathways generated under non-consecutive O atom impacts retain or, in some cases, amplify toxicological risks. These findings indicate that more extensive, multistep oxidative processes, i.e., consecutive O atom impacts corresponding to a high plasma oxidation dose, are required to achieve effective environmental detoxification of fluoroquinolone antibiotics such as OFX (see Section 3.2).

In contrast to the non-consecutive impacts, the consecutive impact strategy was designed to simulate sustained plasma exposure (i.e., a high plasma oxidation dose) by sequentially introducing O atoms to previously oxidized OFX structures. For each of the five distinct initial configurations (A–E series), 20 consecutive DFTB-MD simulations were performed, resulting in a total of 100 trajectories. This multistep approach enabled the observation of progressive structural evolution beyond isolated oxidation events. Across the trajectories, the dominant mechanisms include repeated O addition (hydroxylation), H-abstraction, ring opening, C–C and C–N bond cleavage, defluorination, and fragmentation into small molecules such as CO2 and H2O; together, these results support a cumulative O atom-driven degradation mechanism under consecutive O atom exposure. The complete reaction sequences for the five initial configurations are presented in Fig. S9–13 of the SI.

The multi-step cascades reported below are not artifacts of local energy accumulation. All production trajectories were propagated under continuous coupling to a 300 K heat bath (Berendsen thermostat, τ = 100 fs) applied to every atom (Section 2.1). Exothermic reaction steps produce short temperature spikes (median peak ∼540 K in the non-consecutive trajectories), but these decay within about 1 ps, after which the temperature returns to 294–301 K. In the consecutive series, every impact likewise ends at ∼300 K, so no excess heat accumulates from one impact to the next (Fig. S2 in the SI). Most successive events within an impact are separated by several picoseconds, with full return to 300 K in between. Moreover, trajectories propagated without any heat bath (NVE), in which all reaction heat is retained, yielded the same reaction pathways as the thermostatted simulations. Because the outcome is the same whether reaction heat is removed within ∼100 fs or retained entirely, the reported pathways are not products of transient heating.

For comparison with experimental oxidation systems, the reported OFX degradation pathways vary depending on the oxidants and treatment conditions. For example, Wang et al. reported that OFX degradation in a Cu–Fe oxide/persulfate system proceeded through four reaction pathways: carbonylation, decarboxylation, demethylation, and hydroxylation. In another study, OFX degradation in a BiVO4–polydopamine-modified carbon felt/peroxymonosulfate system was found to involve acetylation, decarboxylation, and defluorination pathways. Because these systems are dominated by solvated ˙OH and SO4˙− radicals, their pathways cannot be compared one-to-one with the O-atom chemistry simulated here. The recurrence of decarboxylation, hydroxylation and defluorination across these different oxidants nevertheless identifies the carboxyl group, the piperazinyl ring and the fluorine-bearing region as the principal structural weak points of OFX. The present DFTB-MD simulations reveal that, under consecutive O atom exposure, OFX degradation is governed by a cumulative O atom-driven mechanism in which repeated oxidative events progressively destabilize the molecular framework; see .

The A configuration in  provides a representative example of progressive oxidative degradation. Initial hydroxylation occurs on the oxazinyl moiety (A1), indicating that early-stage oxidation is not exclusively confined to the piperazinyl ring. Subsequently, in intermediate A2, oxidative destabilization of the piperazinyl ring is initiated. The introduction of OH groups at the piperazinyl moiety weakens the local C–N bonds and increases the structural flexibility of the side chain, rendering it more susceptible to further oxidative attack. In the transition from A2 to A3, an incoming O atom attacks the OH group formed in A1, abstracting two H atoms and leading to the formation of an H2O molecule. In intermediate A4, a subsequent O atom attacks the same reaction site, regenerating an OH group. This repeated hydroxylation process reflects the cumulative nature of plasma-induced oxidation, whereby consecutive O attacks progressively destabilize the molecular framework. Further degradation leads to the formation of intermediate A5, in which the piperazinyl ring becomes increasingly susceptible to oxidative C–N bond cleavage. At this stage, the integrity of the piperazinyl ring is significantly compromised, setting the stage for ring-opening reactions. In the final step (A6), a newly generated O atom attacks the piperazinyl ring, triggering ring opening through H-abstraction at the C1 position and resulting in the formation of an OH radical. Simultaneously, oxidative attack at the C18 position promotes fragmentation of the molecular skeleton, yielding small molecules such as CO2, H2O and CH2O. These reactions represent advanced oxidation and partial mineralization of the OFX molecule. The subsequent degradation pathways (A7–A20) following A6 are further detailed in Fig. S9 of the SI.

Similar progressive oxidation trends were observed for the B, C, and E configurations, where repeated O atom incorporation leads to cumulative destabilization of heterocyclic fragments and stepwise fragmentation. Detailed mechanistic pathways for these configurations are provided in Fig. S10, S11 and S13 of the SI. Although structural variations exist among the initial configurations, the dominant mechanistic theme across all series remains sequential hydroxylation and H-abstraction leading to structural simplification.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reported by Zhu et al. further support the preferential reactivity observed in the present simulations. Their analysis demonstrated that the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of OFX is primarily localized on the piperazinyl substituent, rendering it highly susceptible to electrophilic radical attack by species such as SO4˙−, HO˙, and atomic O. In contrast, the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) is concentrated on the quinolone core, favoring nucleophilic interactions. This orbital distribution is fully consistent with the DFTB-MD results, in which initial and successive oxidative events frequently target the piperazinyl moiety, ultimately leading to ring opening and structural destabilization.

Among the consecutive pathways, the D configuration reveals a mechanistically critical transformation: defluorination. The reaction sequence is schematically illustrated in . Starting from the intact OFX molecule, electrophilic O atom addition initially occurs at the electron-rich piperazinyl moiety, forming the first hydroxylated intermediate (D1). Subsequent O atom incorporation in D2 proceeds on the oxazinyl ring, demonstrating that consecutive O atoms promote parallel oxidation across multiple molecular regions rather than acting at a single functional site. In D3, O atom addition to the fluorine-bearing carbon of the quinolone core is followed by a 1,2-shift of the F atom to the neighboring carbon, the same NIH-shift-type rearrangement observed in the non-consecutive pathway of . This behavior is consistent with the fluorine relocation observed in the non-consecutive impact pathway shown in , suggesting that the C–F containing region is particularly sensitive to O atom-induced electronic rearrangement.

Following this initial rearrangement, further oxidative transformations progressively destabilize the molecular framework, ultimately leading to defluorination in D8. Further hydroxylation in D4 predominantly targets the oxazinyl fragment, increasing local bond strain around heteroatoms. In D5 and D6, repeated O atom incorporation into both the piperazinyl and oxazinyl moieties amplifies conformational instability and electronic perturbation. In D7, sequential H-abstraction from the piperazinyl ring results in H2O formation and generation of a C-centered radical, markedly enhancing molecular reactivity. Finally, in D8, additional hydroxylation combined with structural relaxation induces intramolecular bond reorganization that destabilizes the fluorine-containing fragment and leads to cleavage of the C–F bond with release of an FH species. Subsequent chain reactions promote opening of the piperazinyl ring and further structural fragmentation (see Fig. S12 in the SI). These results indicate that defluorination does not occur via direct substitution but rather through an indirect, cumulative mechanism involving sequential O addition, H-abstraction, electronic redistribution, and structural relaxation. Cleavage of the C–F bond represents a pivotal transition in OFX degradation, as it disrupts the pharmacophoric functionality responsible for antibacterial activity and facilitates subsequent oxidative fragmentation and mineralization into simpler, less persistent products. Importantly, comparative toxicity analysis (Table S7 of the SI) shows that the transition from D7 to D8 is accompanied by a pronounced reduction in predicted molecular toxicity, highlighting that defluorination not only deactivates OFX biologically but also mitigates its environmental hazard.

Overall, the consecutive impact simulations show that continued O atom exposure drives OFX degradation through a cumulative and hierarchical oxidation process, progressing from hydroxylation and ring destabilization to fragmentation and defluorination.

All 20 oxidation intermediates generated under consecutive O atom impact conditions were evaluated for each configuration (e.g., A1–A20) using the QSAR protocol described in Section 2.2. Full QSAR-based toxicity predictions for products formed from consecutive O atom impacts in each configuration (A–E) are provided in Tables S4–S8 of the SI. Here the focus is on the A configuration. Comparable overall trends were also observed for the B–E configurations, particularly the progressive reduction in acute aquatic toxicity and bioconcentration potential at advanced oxidation stages, although the magnitude of detoxification varied depending on the initial molecular configuration. Because each intermediate represents a progressively oxidized state of its predecessor, this approach enables systematic analysis of how sustained plasma-driven oxidation affects the environmental risk characteristics of OFX.

The predicted trends for configuration A are summarized in  and Table S4 of the SI. Acute toxicity profiles, based on 48 h LC50 values for Daphnia magna, exhibit a clear improvement compared to those obtained under non-consecutive O atom exposure (). Most oxidation products, including the parent compound OFX and intermediates A1–A5, A7–A9, A11–A12, and A15–A17, are classified as “harmful” (LC50 between 10 and 100 mg L−1). Notably, only four pathways (A6, A10, A13, and A14) fall into the “toxic” category (LC50 < 10 mg L−1), while late-stage intermediates A18, A19, and A20 display LC50 values exceeding 100 mg L−1 and are therefore categorized as “not harmful”. These results indicate that deeper oxidation under consecutive O atom interactions gradually reduces the acute toxicity of OFX.

The predicted BCF values further support this detoxification trend (). While OFX and intermediate products (A1–A10) exhibit non-negligible bioaccumulation potential, with BCF values generally below 3 and clearly lower than that of A11, the latter shows the highest predicted bioaccumulation risk. In contrast, most advanced oxidation products, particularly A18 through A20, display substantially reduced BCF values that often fall below critical thresholds. These results indicate that sustained oxidation not only reduces acute toxicity but also diminishes the bioaccumulation potential of OFX degradation products, which is a key requirement for environmentally sustainable wastewater treatment technologies.

Developmental toxicity predictions reveal that most oxidation intermediates retain scores above the threshold value of 0.5, indicating persistent embryotoxic potential during the early and intermediate stages of degradation (). However, a clear decreasing trend is observed for later-stage intermediates, particularly A19 and A20, which exhibit values falling below the toxicity threshold. In addition, intermediates A13–A18 show a gradual reduction in developmental toxicity compared to the parent compound, suggesting partial mitigation of embryotoxic effects. Although several of these products remain classified as toxic, the observed downward trend reflects a progressive attenuation of developmental toxicity as oxidation proceeds.

Mutagenicity predictions further elucidate the detoxification potential of consecutive oxidative degradation (). Intermediates exhibiting mutagenicity scores above the threshold value of 0.5 include the parent compound OFX, as well as intermediates A1–A5, A8–A10, and A15–A17, indicating the persistence of genotoxic characteristics during the early and intermediate stages of oxidation. In contrast, intermediates A6, A7, A12, A18, and A20 display mutagenicity scores below 0.5 and are therefore classified as non-mutagenic, suggesting partial elimination of genotoxic potential upon deeper oxidation. For intermediates A11, A13, A14, and A19, mutagenicity predictions are not available due to limitations related to the applicability domain of the QSAR model. Despite these gaps, the overall trend clearly demonstrates that extended, consecutive oxidation substantially reduces mutagenic potential, with later-stage intermediates for which predictions were available showing a higher likelihood of genotoxicity elimination (mutagenicity could not be predicted for several late-stage intermediates; see Section 2.2).

Because only the largest fragment was submitted to T.E.S.T. following a fragmentation event, we assessed whether the detoxification trend described above reflects genuine structural change rather than a trivial reduction in molecular size. Across all 100 largest-fragment intermediates from the five independent configurations (A–E), molecular weight and LC50 are significantly but only moderately correlated (log-linear R2 = 0.18, p < 0.0001; Fig. S14A in the SI), indicating that molecular weight alone accounts for a minority of the variation in predicted toxicity. Residual analysis, the deviation of each intermediate's predicted toxicity from the value its molecular weight alone would suggest, reveals a specific, reproducible structural basis for this remaining variation. Intermediates carrying reactive electrophilic groups (hydroperoxides, peracids, epoxides, or imines/aldehydes formed immediately following fragmentation) are consistently predicted to be more toxic than their size alone would suggest, whereas intermediates in which these reactive groups have resolved to stable carboxylic acid or alcohol functionalities are predicted to be substantially less toxic, even when the aromatic core remains extensively oxidized overall (Fig. S14B in the SI). This pattern held independently across multiple configurations and was not associated with defluorination, which occurs in only one configuration (D) and showed no significant relationship with predicted toxicity when tested at its actual point of occurrence. These results indicate that the QSAR-predicted detoxification trend tracks specific reactive-electrophile chemistry rather than simple molecular size reduction.

Overall, the toxicity assessment confirms that consecutive O atom impacts are significantly more effective than isolated, non-consecutive oxidation events in achieving meaningful detoxification of OFX. This detoxification is attributable to specific reactive-electrophile chemistry rather than a trivial molecular-weight effect (see above). Although early oxidation steps may generate intermediates with comparable or even elevated toxicological risks, sustained oxidative processing leads to progressive reductions in acute toxicity, bioaccumulation potential, developmental toxicity, and mutagenicity. These findings highlight the critical importance of prolonged and cumulative oxidative exposure, such as that provided by CAP or other AOPs, in transforming fluoroquinolone antibiotics from persistent, biologically active pollutants into environmentally benign species.

The present simulations describe intrinsic O-OFX reactivity without an explicit aqueous environment, and several solvent-related effects therefore remain outside their scope. These include dielectric screening of charge-separated and polar intermediates and transition states; solvent-mediated proton transfer through the hydrogen-bond network, acid–base equilibria, and hydrolysis of oxidized intermediates; and hydrogen bonding between water and OFX, which may alter H-abstraction barriers at polar sites. In addition, OFX is modeled in its neutral, non-zwitterionic form, whereas its zwitterionic form predominates in aqueous solution near neutral pH. Secondary reactive species generated in the liquid, such as –OH, are likewise not represented. These omitted effects may alter energy barriers and the relative contributions of competing pathways. Accordingly, the reported reaction frequencies should be interpreted as outcomes under the modeled conditions rather than as aqueous-phase product yields.

Heat removal is represented approximately through coupling to a thermostat at 300 K, although this does not reproduce the microscopic dynamics of energy transfer to water. In the NVE trajectories examined, the same reaction pathways were observed without a heat bath, supporting their robustness with respect to thermostat coupling within the tested conditions. A comprehensive treatment of the remaining solvent effects is beyond the computational scope of the present study. Implicit solvation could account for part of the dielectric response but would not explicitly represent water-mediated proton relays or hydrolysis; its application would also require validation for the present DFTB3 parameterization and reactive protocol. Explicit solvation would substantially increase the computational cost, especially for the independent-impact ensemble and consecutive-impact sequences considered here. Our previous DFTB-MD study of amoxicillin, a molecule of comparable size to OFX, estimated that an aqueous system containing approximately 870 water molecules would require about 440 days of computation per 200 ps impact trajectory. Although this estimate is specific to the computational setup considered in that study, it illustrates the challenge of combining explicit solvation with extensive reactive-trajectory sampling.

Nevertheless, previous applications of this approach identified reaction classes, including hydroxylation, ring opening, and fragmentation, which were consistent with experimental observations for plasma-treated aqueous cellotriose and amoxicillin. This agreement supports the potential aqueous relevance of the intrinsic pathways identified here, but does not directly validate the OFX-specific pathways or their relative frequencies. Extending the framework to explicitly solvated OFX systems is therefore an important direction for future work.

This study elucidates the degradation and detoxification mechanisms of OFX under CAP treatment or other AOPs, by integrating reactive DFTB-MD simulations with QSAR toxicity assessment. By explicitly distinguishing between non-consecutive and consecutive O atom impacts (corresponding to low and high (plasma) oxidation doses, respectively), it reveals how the continuity of oxidative exposure governs both structural evolution and environmental risk reduction.

Non-consecutive O atom interactions predominantly induce isolated hydroxylation and H-abstraction events, resulting in limited structural disruption and negligible improvement in predicted toxicity. In contrast, consecutive oxidation triggers cumulative molecular destabilization characterized by repeated hydroxylation, H-abstraction, heterocyclic ring opening, fragmentation, and a mechanistically critical defluorination step. Cleavage of the C–F bond proceeds through an indirect, multistep pathway driven by electronic redistribution and structural relaxation, rather than direct substitution. Toxicity analysis demonstrates a clear progressive detoxification trend under sustained oxidation. While early intermediates retain toxic and mutagenic characteristics, advanced-stage products exhibit reduced acute aquatic toxicity, lower bioaccumulation potential, and suppressed mutagenicity. Defluorination emerges as a pivotal transformation linking structural degradation to environmental risk mitigation.

Overall, these findings establish a mechanistic framework connecting consecutive oxidation, C–F bond cleavage, and progressive detoxification of fluoroquinolone antibiotics. The results provide atomistic insight essential for optimizing (plasma-based) AOPs aimed at efficient removal and risk reduction of persistent pharmaceutical contaminants in wastewater.

Otamurot Rajabov: writing – original draft, methodology, validation, investigation, visualization, formal analysis, data curation. Davronjon Abduvokhidov: writing – original draft, methodology, investigation, formal analysis, data curation. Annemie Bogaerts: writing – review and editing, supervision, data curation. Maksudbek Yusupov: writing – original draft, validation, supervision, data curation, project administration, funding acquisition, conceptualization.
