medicine.title: From efficacy to effectiveness in gynecologic oncology: social determinants, therapeutic transportability, and biological weathering
medicine.abstract: Precision therapeutics have improved outcomes in gynecologic oncology, but their population-level impact depends on both biological efficacy and reliable treatment delivery. Randomized controlled trials establish causal effects under defined conditions; real-world evidence characterizes implementation and transportability while introducing distinct confounding and measurement challenges. This contextual narrative review integrates pivotal and updated therapeutic studies with clinical, social and translational evidence available through September 2026. Progression-free survival and overall survival are distinct endpoints, whereas effectiveness concerns benefit in routine care; cross-study interpretation requires aligned populations, treatment strategies, follow-up and estimands. The benefits of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors and immunotherapy are examined separately by molecular subgroup and treatment setting. Financial hardship, geographic access, caregiving and health-system constraints can affect initiation, tolerable exposure and continuity. We use the proposed term “social discontinuation” for treatment disruption with a material social contribution, while distinguishing clinical reasons and patient preference. Biological weathering provides plausible links between cumulative adversity and inflammatory, neuroendocrine, epigenetic and immune phenotypes. Human epidemiological associations, translational findings and experimental mechanisms support different inferences; mediation through treatment delivery remains distinct from biological modification of treatment effect. Priorities include justified broader eligibility, prospective social-needs and exposure measurement, responsive symptom management, navigation and hybrid care. Automated extraction and prediction tools require external validation, fairness assessment and prospective clinical-impact evaluation. Integrating randomized and real-world evidence can identify remediable barriers without diminishing the clinical value of effective therapies.
medicine.text:
Molecularly directed treatments have changed gynecologic oncology. First-line maintenance with the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor olaparib prolonged progression-free survival (PFS) in ovarian cancer with a BRCA1/2 mutation. Lenvatinib–pembrolizumab improved survival in previously treated advanced endometrial cancer, and mirvetuximab soravtansine established an effective biomarker-selected option in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. These advances make reliable delivery of effective therapy an increasingly consequential clinical objective.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the strongest foundation for causal therapeutic evaluation. Randomization minimizes measured and unmeasured confounding in expectation; predefined endpoints, standardized treatment strategies, prospective toxicity ascertainment and prespecified biomarker analyses support interpretable, and reproducible evaluation. Observational adjustment offers different protections and cannot recreate randomization simply through greater sample size. Efficacy describes benefit under specified conditions; effectiveness concerns benefit under routine-care conditions. Pragmatic randomization can evaluate the latter, so these questions are not synonymous with particular data sources.

Internal validity concerns the credibility of the study estimate. Generalizability and transportability concern extending inference to a target population, with transportability particularly relevant when study and target populations differ. An endpoint is also distinct from an estimand: the latter specifies the population, treatment comparison, outcome, handling of intercurrent events and population-level summary. Thus, trial PFS, overall survival (OS) and routine-care effectiveness require related but different interpretations.

Social determinants of health (SDOH) can influence access, treatment initiation, tolerable exposure, supportive care and continuity. Biological weathering adds a plausible, incompletely validated account of how cumulative adversity may become biologically embedded. This review connects these implementation and biological perspectives while preserving the complementary roles of randomized and real-world evidence (RWE).

This contextual narrative review was organized around therapeutic transportability rather than exhaustive treatment enumeration. Targeted searches and citation tracing used PubMed-indexed publications, primary journal reports and official regulatory or policy documents available through September 14, 2026. Search concepts combined ovarian, endometrial or cervical cancer with PARP inhibition, immunotherapy, real-world outcomes, eligibility, treatment persistence, financial toxicity, geographic access, social determinants, allostatic load, stress signaling and implementation. Methodological searches addressed estimands, transportability, endpoint ascertainment, mediation, and prediction.

Pivotal randomized trials and mature follow-up reports were prioritized for therapeutic effects. Comparative observational studies informed routine-care associations; prospective human and patient-reported studies informed social exposures and delivery. Experimental studies were included when they tested a relevant mechanism, with species and setting distinguished from human clinical evidence. Original methodological publications and authoritative guidance informed interpretation. Conference-only updates were identified as such and were not treated as equivalent to complete peer-reviewed reports.

Selection favored direct relevance to the stated claim and sufficient information on population, treatment setting, comparator, endpoint and follow-up. Secondary news accounts, duplicate reports and unrelated-cancer estimates presented as gynecologic findings were excluded from the evidentiary basis. Reviews supported orientation rather than substitution for available primary therapeutic evidence.

Synthesis considered confounding, selection, measurement and missing-data limitations, consistent with established bias domains. Biological evidence was separated into human epidemiology, human translational association and experimental mechanism. No pooled effect estimate, formal certainty score or systematic-review completeness claim is made. This purposive approach can overlook relevant studies and should be interpreted as a critical conceptual synthesis rather than a treatment guideline.

PARP inhibitors have produced substantial benefits in appropriately selected populations. SOLO1 evaluated olaparib after platinum response in newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer with a BRCA1/2 mutation: the PFS hazard ratio (HR) was 0.30 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.23-0.41). Seven-year estimated OS was 67.0% versus 46.5%; the OS HR was 0.55 (95% CI, 0.40-0.76). This clinically important descriptive separation did not meet the prespecified significance threshold; time to subsequent treatment also favored olaparib.

PAOLA-1 tested olaparib added to bevacizumab, not olaparib monotherapy, and established a PFS benefit concentrated in homologous recombination deficiency (HRD)-positive disease. Final OS was not significantly improved overall, whereas the prespecified exploratory HRD-positive subgroup supported benefit; comparable benefit was not established in HRD-negative disease. PRIMA demonstrated niraparib-associated PFS improvement in a higher-risk population, including beyond HRD-positive disease. Its final overall-population OS HR was 1.01 (95% CI, 0.84-1.23). ATHENA-MONO’s 2026 follow-up supported sustained rucaparib PFS benefit, with OS still interim.

These findings favor agent-, biomarker-, and setting-specific decisions, particularly in homologous-recombination-proficient disease. HRD-positive populations include tumors without a BRCA1/2 mutation, and genomic-scar definitions and clinical eligibility should be specified when discussing their expected benefit. Current US prescribing information limits first-line niraparib maintenance to HRD-positive advanced ovarian cancer; historical enrollment criteria do not define today’s indication. Hematologic toxicity, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms and uncommon myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia require individualized discussion and monitoring.

NOVA established PFS benefit with niraparib after platinum-sensitive recurrence; its final report did not establish an OS difference. SOLO2 demonstrated PFS benefit with olaparib in BRCA1/2-associated recurrent disease, followed by numerically longer OS without conventional statistical significance. ARIEL3 established rucaparib PFS benefit, while final analyses found no significant OS advantage despite persistent benefit in time to second progression or death. These populations differ from patients now recurring after first-line PARP inhibition.

PFS benefit can matter through delayed progression and subsequent treatment, even when OS superiority is unproven. Its surrogacy for OS requires context-specific validation. OS also reflects subsequent therapy, crossover where permitted, post-progression survival, competing mortality and power. Post hoc SOLO2 findings raise concern about subsequent chemotherapy outcomes after olaparib, but selection among patients who progressed and received chemotherapy limits causal interpretation. They motivate sequencing research rather than establish that resistance cancels earlier benefit. Treatment discussions should also distinguish remaining progression-free from remaining symptom- and treatment-free. A longer interval before recurrence may be valuable while maintenance itself imposes toxicity and monitoring demands. The appropriate judgment integrates those tradeoffs with patient priorities rather than using OS significance as the sole definition of effectiveness.

RUBY demonstrated PFS benefit from dostarlimab with carboplatin–paclitaxel followed by maintenance, subsequently supported by an OS advantage. NRG-GY018 established pembrolizumab–chemotherapy PFS benefit in separately evaluated mismatch repair-deficient and mismatch repair-proficient cohorts. The 2025 peer-reviewed OS analysis was immature; a 2026 conference update reported further follow-up and subsequent-therapy analyses and remains separately identified as abstract-level evidence.

KEYNOTE-775 established lenvatinib–pembrolizumab PFS and OS benefits after prior platinum therapy, including in mismatch repair-proficient disease, with substantial toxicity and frequent dose modification. Five-year results published in 2026 support durability. Prior checkpoint inhibitor exposure was excluded, making contemporary post-immunotherapy sequencing a distinct evidence question. Barbi et al.’ retrospective dosing study found an age-adjusted association between lower starting lenvatinib doses and poorer PFS; clinician-selected dosing and nonsignificant unadjusted comparisons support prospective evaluation rather than causal attribution.

KEYNOTE-826 established pembrolizumab–chemotherapy benefit in persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, including programmed death-ligand 1-positive disease, confirmed by final OS follow-up. KEYNOTE-A18 separately demonstrated OS benefit with pembrolizumab added to chemoradiotherapy in high-risk locally advanced disease. Disease setting, prior treatment, biomarker eligibility and functional status determine applicability. Poor survival in frailer treated cohorts can reflect baseline prognosis and competing risks, even when treatment remains beneficial.

The efficacy-effectiveness gap describes potential divergence in benefit across trial and routine-care conditions because of population, exposure, supportive-care, access and competing-risk differences. It identifies transportability or implementation questions, not invalidity of the randomized estimate. Worse absolute survival can coexist with a preserved relative treatment effect; similar medians likewise need not imply equivalent effects. Hazard ratios depend on follow-up and changing risk-set composition, further limiting cross-study numerical comparisons.

Three comparisons should be separated: outcomes among treated patients, effects of initiating competing treatment strategies, and effects under specified sustained-exposure strategies. The first can describe a care gap without identifying its cause; the latter two require an appropriate comparator and explicit handling of treatment changes. A routine-care cohort with more competing mortality may have shorter survival despite a similar relative anticancer effect. Conversely, similar survival can conceal differences in baseline prognosis. The clinical question is therefore which benefit would be achieved by comparable strategies in the target population, not whether two published curves overlap.

Trial progression commonly follows prespecified imaging schedules and Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, whereas real-world PFS can rely on clinician documentation, radiology abstraction, treatment-change proxies or incomplete scan dates. Comparative interpretation requires aligned populations, molecular composition, treatment lines, comparators, time origins, endpoints and estimands. Treatment discontinuation and subsequent therapy must be handled consistently with the question being estimated.

RWE is not uniformly less favorable: the Unicancer cohort associated PARP maintenance after platinum-sensitive recurrence with longer PFS and OS than observation, subject to residual confounding. A single-arm first-line niraparib electronic health record cohort describes routine-care outcomes but cannot quantify benefit lost relative to PRIMA. RWE additionally informs comorbidity, sequencing, persistence and long-term care. Its comparative estimates require attention to confounding by indication, selection, informative censoring, missingness and outcome or treatment-line misclassification.

Performance-status, organ-function and comorbidity restrictions may underrepresent routine-care populations. Some protect safety; others warrant intervention-specific reassessment, as recommended by the American Society of Clinical Oncology–Friends of Cancer Research performance-status working group. Gynecologic trial research also documents incomplete demographic reporting and unequal representation. These limitations principally affect external applicability, while randomization protects inference within the enrolled population (). A patient excluded for impaired organ function presents a different benefit—risk question from one unable to attend a distant trial center. Separating safety-driven eligibility from participation barriers helps identify whether additional pharmacologic evidence, recruitment support or both are needed.

Medication adherence encompasses initiation and implementation; persistence describes continued treatment before discontinuation. Dose intensity concerns delivered dose per unit time; it differs from the proportion of prescribed doses taken. Appropriate prescribed reduction can support persistence rather than indicate failure. PRIMA’s prospectively introduced weight- and platelet-based starting dose improved hematologic tolerability without apparent efficacy loss, although starting-dose strategies were not randomized against each other.

Exposure analyses should record prescribed and received doses, interruption, re-escalation and reasons for change. Frailty, toxicity and early progression can influence both dosing and outcomes; a single final-dose category obscures this time ordering. Clinically appropriate treatment adaptation should therefore be distinguished from avoidable underexposure.

Protocolized monitoring is a component of effective treatment delivery. Randomized electronic symptom monitoring improved patient-reported outcomes and reduced emergency visits across advanced solid tumors. The GAP70+ cluster-randomized trial showed that geriatric assessment-guided management reduced serious treatment toxicity in older adults. These interventions support responsive, tolerable care; their populations and endpoints delimit extrapolation to individual gynecologic regimens. We propose evaluating the entire response pathway: who reviews a reported symptom, how quickly clinical assessment occurs, and whether a treatment adjustment or practical assistance follows. Collecting symptoms without capacity to respond should be distinguished from delivering a tested supportive-care intervention.

We use the proposed term social discontinuation for interruption, avoidable exposure loss or premature cessation to which financial, geographic, caregiving, logistical or access constraints materially contribute. Financial distress and care avoidance provide an empirical rationale, but this construct is not a validated oncologic endpoint.

Operationalization should separate initiation failure, temporary interruption and permanent cessation, combining patient-reported barriers with pharmacy and clinical records. Progression, contraindications, toxicity and informed preference require separate documentation, while allowing concurrent social contributions. Preference alone should not be relabeled nonadherence. Prospective adjudication, reproducibility testing and assessment of responsiveness to support are necessary before using the construct for benchmarking.

For research, we suggest recording the immediate clinical reason and the contributory social circumstance as separate fields, together with the patient’s account and the support offered. An interruption for fatigue may reflect appropriate toxicity management, lack of access to timely reassessment, or both. Denominators should distinguish everyone offered treatment from those who initiated it. This proposed classification would allow intervention studies to examine preventable disruption without penalizing clinically justified cessation or patient choice.

Financial toxicity includes material hardship and distress rather than drug price alone. Patient surveys document cost-coping strategies; development of the Comprehensive Score for Financial Toxicity provided a patient-reported assessment framework. In gynecologic oncology, financial distress has been associated with poorer quality of life and delaying or avoiding care. Across oral anticancer therapies, higher out-of-pocket costs were associated with prescription abandonment or delayed initiation.

Insurance interacts with employment, cost-sharing and provider networks. US gynecologic cancer data describe insurance churn and non-employment; Medicaid could protect lower-income households against financial hardship. Consequently, a universal payer hierarchy is less informative than identifying specific coverage gaps and connecting patients with benefits advice, medication assistance and relevant community resources. A practical assessment should be repeated when employment, insurance or treatment changes, because an affordable initial prescription does not establish sustainable access throughout maintenance. Reported hardship should trigger a discussion of feasible support rather than an inference about willingness to continue treatment.

National workforce studies describe geographically uneven gynecologic specialist availability, with subsequent spatial analysis confirming disparities in potential accessibility. Distance alone incompletely measures transport availability, appointment capacity, referral delays and household travel costs. Centralizing complex procedures and decentralizing appropriate follow-up need not be competing objectives. Shared-care networks should be evaluated for timely referral, procedural quality and continuity rather than location alone. A useful implementation model separates the functions requiring specialist facilities from those deliverable locally, while defining responsibility for laboratory review, symptom escalation and treatment decisions. Geographic-access measures can then be paired with completed referrals and patient-reported travel burden, making the target for service redesign more specific than a rural–urban category.

Population-based uterine cancer analyses demonstrate differences in subtype distribution and survival across racialized groups. Residual disparities in an equal-access military system indicate that common coverage does not exhaust the relevant explanatory pathways. Race is a social construct, not a tumor mechanism; ancestry, structural racism, lifetime environment, stage, treatment and sampling require distinct consideration.

Molecular profiling has identified differences in histologic composition, molecular subtypes and therapeutic targets between sampled populations. Such findings support inclusive research, not deterministic attribution of biology to racial identity. Intersectionality considers overlapping social positions and systems of disadvantage; statistical synergy or an “exponential” mortality effect requires additional evidence rather than following from the framework itself.

Weathering connects cumulative adversity with multisystem physiological dysregulation. Allostatic-load research associated composite physiological measures with later health outcomes, while population studies described racialized differences in age patterns. In ovarian cancer, prospective observational research associated social attachment with survival. Together these findings justify investigation of biological embedding without establishing a drug-selection biomarker ().

The 3 evidence levels answer different questions. Population epidemiology identifies patterns of exposure and outcome; human translational studies examine associated molecular or physiological states; experiments manipulate selected mechanisms. Confidence in one level does not transfer automatically to another. In particular, an experimentally causal stress pathway may remain untested as the mediator of a measured social disparity or as a modifier of randomized treatment benefit.

The hypothalamic—pituitary—adrenal/glucocorticoid-receptor pathway is distinct from sympathetic/catecholamine—adrenergic signaling. Thaker et al. demonstrated adrenergic stress-related tumor growth and angiogenesis in an ovarian carcinoma mouse model. Sloan et al. identified stress-associated macrophage recruitment and metastasis in experimental breast cancer. These are mechanistic findings within their respective models, not direct tests of socioeconomic deprivation in patients.

Endogenous glucocorticoid signaling promoted dysfunctional CD8-positive T-cell states in experimental tumors, with related human associations. Local steroid production and receptor biology matter: circulating stress measurements cannot automatically identify the same tumor-level mechanism.

Human ovarian cancer research associated psychosocial measures with interleukin-6, while human leukocyte studies linked perceived social isolation with transcriptional differences. Powell et al. combined experimental social stress with human translational observations to implicate adrenergic myelopoiesis in inflammatory expression patterns. Disease burden, infection, medication exposure and reverse causation remain important. Inflammaging denotes age-associated inflammation, not every inflammatory state accompanying disadvantage.

Stress-related leukocyte telomere associations support biological plausibility but do not establish mediation of gynecologic treatment failure. Endometrial tumor methylation differences across racialized groups similarly require attention to ancestry, subtype, cell composition, stage and sampling. Cross-sectional tumor comparisons cannot reconstruct a complete longitudinal social exposure or assign PAX8 expression or CCNE1 amplification a social cause. Exposure definitions and molecular sampling also need to distinguish peripheral blood from tumor tissue and treatment-naïve from treated specimens.

Experimental β2-adrenergic signaling can strengthen myeloid-derived suppressor-cell function. In mouse studies, adrenergic signaling also impaired effector T-cell phenotypes and checkpoint-inhibitor activity. These findings support specific candidate mechanisms; regulatory T cells, fibroblasts and checkpoint-related changes should not be assembled into one proven human adversity-to-resistance pathway.

A prognostic marker identifies outcome risk; a predictive marker identifies heterogeneity in treatment effect, preferably demonstrated through a treatment-by-marker interaction in randomized data. Social adversity may affect outcomes through access and exposure even when pharmacologic efficacy is unchanged. Establishing that mediated delivery pathway is different from showing biological effect modification, and causal mediation itself requires adequate control of exposure—mediator—outcome confounding.

Prospective studies should combine repeated social assessments, inflammatory or neuroendocrine biomarkers and paired tumor samples with treatment comparisons and detailed exposure records. Their purpose is to determine which pathway operates, when, and for whom. Temporal ordering is central: disease progression can worsen financial strain and stress biomarkers, while treatment toxicity can alter both medication exposure and inflammation. Analyses should prespecify whether treatment delivery is an intermediate variable, a competing explanation or part of the treatment strategy being compared. Intervention studies that resolve transport or cost barriers can test delivery mechanisms directly, without requiring proof of a tumor-intrinsic weathering pathway. Until clinically validated interaction evidence emerges, weathering markers remain investigational rather than tools for withholding effective therapy.

An actionable assessment records transport, housing, food, medication affordability, language, caregiving and patient priorities. “Not assessed,” “not disclosed,” and “no identified need” should remain distinguishable; area deprivation and diagnostic codes are incomplete substitutes for patient-level information. We propose a closed-loop workflow: confirm the need, agree on a response, assign responsibility and document referral completion or unresolved barriers.

Guevara et al. demonstrated technical feasibility of extracting SDOH information from electronic health records using language models. Clinical utility requires separate evaluation of referral completion and treatment continuity. Sparse documentation may reflect limited questioning, unequal disclosure opportunities or absent services rather than absence of need. Extraction systems therefore inherit documentation gaps; their outputs should not be treated as direct measurements of every patient’s social circumstances. Human review, patient confirmation, uncertainty flags, privacy protection and appropriate access controls are essential safeguards when documented information is converted into decision support.

Model complexity should match the prediction task. Adequate sample size, transparent reporting and independent validation are necessary for regression and machine-learning models alike. Bias appraisal should examine participant selection, predictors, outcome definitions and analysis. Discrimination alone is insufficient: calibration and decision-analytic net benefit clarify whether acting on predictions is useful.

Obermeyer et al. demonstrated how a cost-based proxy for clinical need introduced racial bias. Oncology models likewise require scrutiny of historical labels, nonrandom missingness, dataset shift and subgroup errors. A model that accurately predicts underuse could still reinforce it if used to restrict therapy. Validation should therefore examine the proposed action as well as the score: a threshold that triggers additional navigation has different consequences from one that limits referral. Performance should be reassessed after workflow or population changes, and evaluation should include referral uptake, staff workload and unintended exclusion alongside statistical accuracy. Prospective impact evaluation should test supportive responses rather than assume that prediction itself improves survival.

Pandemic-era ambulatory data showed differences in telemedicine access by language, age and socioeconomic conditions. A gynecologic surveillance program demonstrated feasible local–specialist visits and reduced travel burden, supporting hybrid care while leaving active-treatment safety, scalability and survival equivalence to further evaluation. Local examination, accessible technology and in-person escalation remain integral (). Hybrid pathways should accommodate people unable to use video or complete digital questionnaires, with interpreter access and alternative contact routes. Reducing long-distance travel can still leave local transport, privacy and caregiver needs unresolved; these belong among implementation outcomes rather than being assumed away.

Navigation improved later care timeliness in a multicenter intervention program, particularly where usual-care delays were greater. A separate randomized community-health-worker intervention reduced acute care use in advanced cancer. These studies support testing defined navigation and symptom-response functions, rather than assuming any navigator deployment improves gynecologic survival.

Medicare introduced community health integration and principal illness navigation payments in 2024, subject to service and billing requirements. As of 2026, G0136 describes standardized physical activity and nutrition assessment rather than a general SDOH-screening service. Financing therefore requires jurisdiction- and year-specific verification, alongside adequate referral capacity.

Pragmatic designs can randomize navigation, symptom support or hybrid delivery while maintaining consent, safety and reliable outcome ascertainment. The PRECIS-2 framework links eligibility, delivery, follow-up and analysis choices to intended applicability. Broader eligibility should remain intervention-specific; representation should be assessed against a defined target population rather than enrollment diversity alone.

Trials should prospectively record social needs, changing exposure and multiple reasons for interruption, selecting stratification variables according to the hypothesis rather than requiring every social domain as a stratum. Comparative post-marketing studies should align eligibility, treatment assignment and time zero through target-trial specification. Classifying patients by whether they ever received maintenance can otherwise introduce immortal-time bias.

Residual confounding, informative censoring and time-varying treatment changes warrant sensitivity analyses. Transportability additionally requires adequate population overlap and measurement of relevant effect modifiers. The research agenda should separately test whether support improves delivery and whether exposure-related biology modifies therapeutic effects. Success in the former is clinically valuable regardless of the latter.

An informative next step would randomize a defined support package within an otherwise consistent treatment pathway, measuring initiation, interruption, patient-reported symptoms and clinically justified dose modification before examining longer-term outcomes. An embedded translational study could separately prespecify a biomarker interaction. This design would distinguish improvement in the ability to receive treatment from modification of its biological effect, while retaining a transparent causal contrast. For both randomized and observational evaluations, the primary analysis should specify whether treatment discontinuation is included in the strategy’s total effect or addressed through a hypothetical sustained-treatment question. Reporting both without distinguishing their assumptions can obscure rather than explain an implementation gap.

Precision therapeutics have improved gynecologic cancer care, but population-level impact also depends on access, tolerable exposure, supportive care and continuity. Therapeutic transportability connects randomized evidence with heterogeneous clinical contexts while preserving the causal value of well-conducted trials. Social discontinuation offers a proposed implementation construct; biological weathering provides a plausible but incompletely validated mechanistic framework. Progress requires clinically justified inclusive eligibility, prospective social and exposure measurement, rigorous RWE and direct evaluation of barrier-reducing interventions. The objective is precision treatment that is both biologically appropriate and reliably deliverable.

medicine.title: Global Burden, Development-Related Inequalities, and Projections of Brain and Central Nervous System Cancer, 1990-2050: Implications for Cancer Control
medicine.abstract: Brain and central nervous system (CNS) cancers require specialized care. Evidence linking temporal trends, development-related disparities, and future patient volumes is needed for surveillance and service planning.This composite ecological study integrated GLOBOCAN 2022, Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023), Human Development Index (HDI) data, health-system indicators, and population projections. Estimated annual percentage changes (EAPCs) quantified 1990-2023 trends, with segmented regression assessing slope changes. Population-weighted slope, relative, and concentration indices quantified HDI-related inequality; models adjusted HDI associations for universal health coverage (UHC) and physician density. Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) models projected age-standardised rates and counts to 2050, with temporal holdout testing for 2016-2023.GLOBOCAN estimated 321,731 new cases and 248,500 deaths in 2022. In GBD 2023, global age-standardised incidence was stable on average over 1990-2023 (EAPC, 0.032%; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.005 to 0.070), whereas mortality declined (-0.216%; 95% CI, -0.262 to -0.170). Segmented models identified slope changes around 1998 for incidence and 2000 for mortality. Recorded incidence and mortality were concentrated toward higher-HDI countries; concentration indices were 0.214 (95% CI, 0.146-0.269) and 0.157 (95% CI, 0.097-0.218), respectively. Adjustment for physician density attenuated the HDI coefficients by 55.7% for incidence and 54.1% for mortality, but both remained positive. By 2050, posterior median annual counts were approximately 605,000 incident cases (95% uncertainty interval [UI], 292,000-1,213,000) and 351,000 deaths (168,000-692,000).Stable average age-standardised incidence and declining mortality, with historical slope changes, coexist with a projected rise in absolute burden. Cancer control strategies should distinguish improvements in case ascertainment from changes in underlying risk and use projections as conditional planning estimates.
medicine.text:
Brain and central nervous system (CNS) cancers are a heterogeneous group of malignant tumours with a clinical burden that is disproportionate to their incidence. Diagnosis usually requires cross-sectional imaging, specialist pathology, and increasingly molecular classification; treatment may involve neurosurgery, radiotherapy, systemic therapy, rehabilitation, and palliative care.- Population estimates are therefore shaped not only by disease occurrence but also by the capacity to detect, classify, treat, and register cases.

Global studies have established marked variation by geography, age, sex, and development level.- Since the release of GBD 2021 and GLOBOCAN 2022, several analyses have extended these descriptions to country trends, specific age groups, formal inequality measures, and projections through 2035-2050.- The 2025 GBD 2023 cancer forecast, which includes brain and CNS cancer among its cancer groupings, provides an important methodological benchmark.

 Rates and forecasts differ because populations, source systems, projection assumptions, and terminal years are not identical.

The remaining question is not simply whether the global burden is large. Two interpretive problems are more consequential for cancer control. First, GLOBOCAN and GBD are often placed side by side as if they were interchangeable measurements, although they use different data inputs, estimation procedures, and consistency constraints.,,- Second, comparisons across development strata are frequently based on unweighted group means. Such comparisons do not quantify the absolute and relative gradient across the full population distribution and may encourage an overly literal reading of low rates in settings with limited diagnostic and registry capacity.

This distinction matters for CNS cancer because an undiagnosed tumour cannot enter a cancer registry, and an incompletely investigated death may not be assigned to CNS cancer. Higher recorded incidence in high-development settings may reflect biological, demographic, diagnostic, and registration processes operating together. Conversely, low recorded incidence in lower-development settings cannot be assumed to indicate low underlying occurrence. Broader transitions in human development affect both cancer patterns and the capacity to measure and control them.

 Formal population-weighted inequality measures can describe the distribution of recorded burden, but they cannot by themselves separate ascertainment from disease risk.

A second planning problem is the divergence between age-standardised rates and absolute workload. Population growth and ageing can increase the number of patients requiring imaging, surgery, radiotherapy, rehabilitation, and end-of-life care even when the age-standardised incidence rate is stable. Projections based on age-specific counts are therefore useful for service planning, provided that they are presented as conditional forecasts rather than predictions of future policy, technology, or survival.

We integrated GLOBOCAN 2022, GBD 2023, country-level Human Development Index (HDI) data, and Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) projections. Our objectives were to describe the contemporary burden, estimate temporal and sex-specific trends, quantify population-weighted development-related inequality, and project global rates and absolute counts to 2050. Each database was assigned a source-specific role; numerical estimates were not pooled or treated as direct validation of one another.

We conducted a composite ecological study comprising a 2022 cross-sectional description, a longitudinal trend analysis for 1990-2023, a country-level development-related inequality analysis, and a Bayesian age-period-cohort forecast for 2024-2050. GLOBOCAN 2022 described incidence, mortality, five-year prevalence, regional patterns, and country-level HDI gradients., GBD 2023 supplied annual global and location-specific age-standardised rates and age-specific counts., UNDP supplied 2022 HDI values,

 and WPP 2024 supplied age-specific population projections.

 Reporting followed the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER).

Analyses were separated by objective: GLOBOCAN for contemporary cross-sectional burden, GBD for longitudinal trends and BAPC inputs, UNDP for country development ranking, and WPP for future population denominators (). The analytic units were countries/territories or aggregated age-year cells, not individual participants. Consequently, participant recruitment, eligibility sampling, and sample-size calculation were not applicable. The HDI inequality analysis used the 185-country/territory GLOBOCAN 2022 set because its outcomes were GLOBOCAN incidence and mortality estimates. The broader 204-country/territory GBD set was used for longitudinal analyses and did not define the inequality-analysis denominator.Table 1.Data sources and analytic rolesSourceYearsPrimary role in this studyGLOBOCAN 2022/GCO Cancer Today2022Cross-sectional incidence, mortality, prevalence, regional patterns, and country-HDI gradientsGBD 2023 Results1990-2023Annual age-standardised rates, EAPC trends, and age-specific BAPC inputsUN World Population Prospects 20242024-2050Future age-specific population denominators for BAPC projections and medium/high/low demographic scenariosUNDP HDI data2022Country-development ranking for correlation, SII, RII, and concentration-index analysesWorld Bank World Development Indicators2018-2022UHC and physician-density ascertainment-proxy sensitivity analyses

Data sources and analytic roles

The GLOBOCAN Cancer Today category ‘Brain, central nervous system’ covers malignant neoplasms of the meninges, brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves, and other CNS sites corresponding to ICD-10 C70-C72. The GBD 2023 extract used cause 477, Brain and central nervous system cancer, which is mapped principally to primary malignant CNS sites (ICD-10 C70-C72; ICD-9 191-192). Non-malignant or uncertain-behaviour tumours and secondary CNS metastases are outside this cancer cause. GBD integrates cancer-registry incidence and cause-of-death sources; non-specific or implausible causes of death (‘garbage codes’) are redistributed within the GBD cause-of-death framework before final cause-specific estimates.,

Outcomes were incident cases, deaths, five-year prevalent cases where available, and age-standardised incidence and mortality rates per 100,000 population. The source category combines biologically and clinically heterogeneous tumours, including gliomas, meningeal malignancies, embryonal tumours, ependymal tumours, and other rare entities. Because neither GLOBOCAN nor the extracted GBD cause series provided comparable country-year histological strata, all analyses concern the aggregate malignant CNS category and cannot attribute trends or inequalities to particular molecular or histological subtypes.

We defined the EAPC as the average annual percentage change in an age-standardised rate over the modelled interval. The primary analysis fitted ordinary least squares to lnrate = α + β × year and calculated EAPC = 100 × (e^β − 1), with 95% CIs from the standard error of beta. Because serially ordered rates can be autocorrelated, we repeated the global analysis using Prais-Winsten regression with an estimated AR(1) error. We also fitted continuous one-break segmented log-linear models, selecting the break year from 1995-2018 by minimum Bayesian information criterion (BIC), and compared BIC with the single-slope model. GBD marginal 95% UIs describe estimation uncertainty for individual years, but the released extract did not provide the joint across-year covariance required to propagate upstream GBD uncertainty through either trend regression. Location-level EAPC classifications were therefore treated as exploratory and were not adjusted for multiple testing.

Country-level associations between HDI and age-standardised incidence or mortality were assessed using Pearson correlations after graphical assessment of approximate linearity and Spearman correlations as a rank-based sensitivity measure. Among the 185 GLOBOCAN countries/territories, 175 had matched 2022 HDI values and constituted the primary complete-case inequality sample. Ten locations lacked observed HDI values (Supplementary Table S8B). These were French Guiana, French Polynesia, Guadeloupe, Guam, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Martinique, New Caledonia, Puerto Rico, Réunion, and Somalia. For inequality metrics, countries were ordered by HDI and assigned the population-weighted fractional rank Ri = (Ci - 0.5 × Pi)/ Ptotal. Weighted linear regression of ASR on Ri> 
SII=y^(1)−y^(0);RII=y^(1)/y^(0)
. The concentration index was twice the population-weighted covariance of ASR and rank divided by the weighted mean ASR.- Ninety-five percent intervals used 2,000 country-level bootstrap samples; countries were resampled with replacement, and population weights were renormalised within each replicate. The bootstrap was unstratified and did not constrain the population share of HDI strata to remain fixed across replicates. Additional sensitivity analyses (i) excluded zero-ASR countries, (ii) removed each complete-HDI country in turn, and (iii) used 50 stochastic regression imputations for the 10 missing HDI values. For imputation, we fitted a ridge-stabilised linear regression of observed HDI on log population and one-hot indicators for UN region, World Bank income group, and WHO region (alphabetically first category as reference), without cancer outcomes. Each imputation drew regression coefficients from their estimated multivariate normal distribution and added an independent normal residual draw; predicted HDI values were truncated at plausible bounds of 0.35 and 0.98 to prevent stochastic extrapolation beyond the international HDI range. Sensitivity estimates were summarised by their mean and 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across the 50 completed data sets rather than by Rubin-rule standard errors.

As an exploratory ascertainment-proxy sensitivity analysis, we linked the 2022 World Bank UHC service coverage index and the most recent physician-density observation available during 2018-2022 (physicians per 1,000 population)., Separate country-level ordinary least-squares models regressed incidence or mortality ASR on HDI plus one proxy, with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. HDI coefficients were expressed per 0.1-unit increase; the UHC coefficient was scaled per 10 points. These proxies were not incorporated into the primary inequality indices because they were ecological, strongly correlated with HDI, and did not directly measure cancer-registry completeness or neuro-oncology diagnostic access.

We fitted BAPC models to global age-specific incidence and death counts with corresponding population denominators using BAPC and INLA., Historical population denominators for 1990-2023 came from GBD, and WPP 2024 supplied 2024-2050 populations. Age, period, and cohort effects were each specified as intrinsic second-order random walks (RW2), each with rank deficiency 2. BAPC set constr=TRUE explicitly for age; period and cohort used INLA’s default constr=TRUE, and no user-specified rankdef value was supplied. These constraints support prediction, but age, period, and cohort components were not interpreted as separately identifiable causal effects. Each structured precision used a log-Gamma prior with shape 1 and rate 5 × 10-5 (log0 = 4; ΛM = FALSE). An independent and identically distributed overdispersion term used ln γ(1, 0.005), also with initial log-precision 4. Counts followed a Poisson likelihood. We compared age-only, age-period, age-cohort, and full APC specifications using the deviance information criterion (DIC).

Age-standardised rates and total counts were generated from one common set of 2,000 joint latent-Gaussian posterior draws per outcome obtained with inla.posterior.sample under single-thread execution (incidence base seed, 20260804; mortality base seed, 20261804; batch seed equal to the base seed plus the first draw index). The same draws generated , Supplementary Table S4, 2023 and 2050 totals and intervals, draw-level percentage changes, decomposition terms, and WPP scenarios. Percentage changes from 2023 to 2050 were calculated within each draw before summarisation. Let C(r,p) = sum_a r_a p_a denote the total count from age-specific rates r and populations p. For each draw, the symmetric demographic component was D = 0.5{[C(r2023, p2050) - C(r2023, p2023)] + [C(r2050, p2050) - C(r2050, p2023)]}; the rate component was R = 0.5{[C(r2050, p2023) - C(r2023, p2023)] + [C(r2050, p2050) - C(r2023, p2050)]}. Thus, D + R exactly equalled C(r2050, p2050) - C(r2023, p2023) in every draw. Posterior means were reported for the additive reconciliation because component-wise posterior medians need not sum exactly. The primary forecast used the WPP medium variant; WPP low and high variants were applied to the same posterior age-specific 2050 rates as a demographic sensitivity analysis. Ages 85-89, 90-94, 95-99, and 100+ were aggregated as 85+ to match the BAPC input structure.

For temporal validation, models were refitted using 1990-2015 data and used to predict 2016-2023. We generated 2,000 joint posterior draws and compared posterior medians with observed annual age-standardised rates and counts. Prespecified metrics were mean absolute percentage error, root mean squared error, mean error, and empirical 95% interval coverage. Calibration plots, annual residuals (predicted minus observed), and predicted-versus-observed plots are presented in Supplementary Figure S1 and its source-data sheet.

Data preprocessing and frequentist analyses used Python 3.13.14 with pandas 2.3.3, NumPy 2.5.0, SciPy 1.18.0, and Matplotlib 3.11.0. BAPC analyses used R 4.5.1, BAPC 0.0.37, INLA 25.10.19, and Epi 2.65. Country names and ISO3 codes were harmonised before source linkage; age groups were standardised to 18 five-year groups (85+ open interval), and source-specific units were converted to counts or rates per 100,000 as appropriate. Full software, source-file, preprocessing, age-aggregation, unit-conversion, and seed specifications are reported in Supplementary Table S12. Two-sided P values below .05 were considered statistically significant, but location-level multiple comparisons were exploratory. Comparisons across sex, HDI group, or region were descriptive; substantial overlap of source uncertainty intervals was not interpreted as definitive evidence of a difference. This study used only public, aggregated, de-identified data and involved no participant recruitment, individual-level records, or human tissue. Ethics approval and informed consent were therefore not required.

GLOBOCAN estimated 321,731 new cases, 248,500 deaths, and 1,199,313 five-year prevalent cases worldwide in 2022. The global ASIR was 3.47 per 100,000 and the ASMR was 2.59 per 100,000. Males accounted for 54.0% of incident cases and 56.3% of deaths. Europe had the highest continental ASIR (5.57) and ASMR (3.93), whereas Africa had the lowest ASIR (1.86) and ASMR (1.64). Very high-HDI countries had an ASIR of 4.85 and ASMR of 3.29, compared with 1.56 and 1.38 in low-HDI countries (, , and Supplementary Tables S1-S2).Table 2.Key quantitative findingsDomainEstimateGLOBOCAN 2022 global counts and prevalence321,731 new cases; 248,500 deaths; 1,199,313 five-year prevalent casesGLOBOCAN 2022 global ratesASIR 3.47 per 100,000; ASMR 2.59 per 100,000GBD incidence trendASIR 4.29 to 4.41; EAPC 0.032% per year (95% CI, -0.005 to 0.070)GBD mortality trendASMR 3.17 to 2.98; EAPC -0.216% per year (95% CI, -0.262 to -0.170)HDI inequalityIncidence SII 4.23 (95% CI, 3.00-5.13), RII 4.72 (2.59-9.56), and concentration index 0.214 (0.146-0.269); mortality SII 2.30 (1.45-3.24), RII 2.82 (1.84-4.86), and concentration index 0.157 (0.097-0.218)BAPC projection for 2050Posterior median 605,000 new cases (95% UI, 292,000-1,213,000) and 351,000 deaths (168,000-692,000)Trend sensitivityPrais-Winsten EAPC: incidence 0.061% (95% CI, -0.035 to 0.158); mortality -0.192% (-0.330 to -0.054). Key quantitative findings

In GBD 2023, the global both-sex ASIR changed from 4.29 per 100,000 in 1990 to 4.41 in 2023. The primary EAPC was 0.032% per year (95% CI, -0.005 to 0.070; P = .104), indicating stable incidence on average over the full period. The ASMR declined from 3.17 to 2.98 per 100,000, with an EAPC of -0.216% (95% CI, -0.262 to -0.170; P < .001). Prais-Winsten sensitivity estimates were 0.061% (95% CI, -0.035 to 0.158) for incidence and -0.192% (-0.330 to -0.054) for mortality. Segmented regression favoured one-break models over a single slope (the segmented model reduced BIC by 28.4 for incidence and 47.2 for mortality): incidence rose before 1998 (EAPC, 0.474%; 95% CI, 0.342-0.607) and declined slightly thereafter (-0.049%; -0.084 to -0.015), whereas mortality changed from 0.242% (0.148-0.335) before 2000 to -0.350% (-0.385 to -0.315) thereafter. Thus, autocorrelation adjustment preserved the primary classification, while segmented models showed that the 34-year average masked temporal structure (, Supplementary Tables S6-S7).

Among 175 countries/territories with complete HDI linkage, HDI was positively associated with ASIR (Pearson r = 0.664; Spearman rho = 0.672; both P < .001) and ASMR (Pearson r = 0.581; Spearman rho = 0.601; both P < .001). Incidence inequality estimates were SII 4.23 (95% bootstrap CI, 3.00-5.13), RII 4.72 (2.59-9.56), and concentration index 0.214 (0.146-0.269); mortality estimates were SII 2.30 (1.45-3.24), RII 2.82 (1.84-4.86), and concentration index 0.157 (0.097-0.218). Fifty-imputation analyses of all 185 countries produced closely similar point estimates (incidence SII 4.21, RII 4.70, concentration index 0.214; mortality SII 2.30, RII 2.81, concentration index 0.157). Excluding zero-ASR countries and leave-one-country-out analyses did not materially change the direction or magnitude (Supplementary Tables S3 and S8).

In exploratory ascertainment-proxy models, the UHC index was highly correlated with HDI (r = 0.912). After UHC adjustment (n=175), the HDI coefficient per 0.1-unit increase was 0.933 cases per 100,000 (95% CI, 0.514-1.353) for incidence and 0.529 deaths per 100,000 (0.200-0.859) for mortality; the UHC coefficient was not independently associated with either outcome. Physician density was also correlated with HDI (r = 0.793). In physician-density models (n=167), HDI coefficients remained positive but were attenuated by 55.7% for incidence (adjusted beta, 0.414; 95% CI, 0.089-0.740) and 54.1% for mortality (0.274; 0.027-0.522); physician density was independently positive for both outcomes. These exploratory results are compatible with ascertainment contributing to the recorded HDI gradient but do not isolate that mechanism (Supplementary Table S8).

The posterior median global ASIR was 4.46 per 100,000 in 2050 (95% UI, 2.14-8.88) and the ASMR was 2.41 (1.15-4.77). Posterior median annual counts were approximately 605,000 incident cases (95% UI, 292,000-1,213,000) and 351,000 deaths (168,000-692,000). Draw-level posterior percentage changes from 2023 were 58.1% (95% UI, -23.9% to 217.1%) for incidence and 32.9% (-36.2% to 162.1%) for mortality. Based on posterior means, the total projected increase was 254,292 incident cases (204,771 from demographic change plus 49,521 from rate change) and 105,448 deaths (144,898 from demographic change minus 39,450 from rate change). These additive mean-based decompositions are distinct from differences between separately reported posterior medians. Under WPP high versus low population variants, posterior median 2050 counts ranged from 594,000 to 616,000 for incidence and 346,000 to 356,000 for mortality. The full APC model had the lowest DIC for both incidence (8152.9; delta DIC versus age-cohort, 10.0) and mortality (7833.4; delta DIC, 33.6) (Supplementary Tables S4 and S9-S10).

In the temporal holdout analysis, models trained through 2015 produced 2016-2023 ASR MAPE values of 1.54% for incidence and 1.51% for mortality. ASR RMSE values were 0.078 and 0.050 per 100,000, respectively. Count MAPE values were 0.58% and 0.64%. Empirical 95% interval coverage was 100% for incidence ASRs and counts, 87.5% for mortality ASRs (7 of 8 years; one annual interval missed), and 100% for mortality counts. Residual plots showed mild negative incidence residuals in 2020-2022 and no marked nonlinear pattern for mortality, although only eight holdout years limited calibration assessment (Supplementary Figure S1 and Supplementary Tables S5A-S5B).

This composite ecological analysis yielded four findings relevant to cancer surveillance and service planning. In 2022, brain and CNS cancer caused almost as many deaths as new diagnoses. From 1990 to 2023, global age-standardised incidence was stable on average and mortality declined, although segmented analyses identified changes in slope. Recorded rates were concentrated in higher-HDI settings, and absolute numbers were projected to rise substantially by 2050, chiefly because of demographic change. Sensitivity analyses supported the direction of these findings but also reinforced that they are conditional estimates from modelled aggregate data.

Recent studies based on GBD 2021 and GLOBOCAN 2022 have already described the international burden of CNS cancer and forecast further growth in absolute case numbers.- Kim and colleagues used GLOBOCAN 2022 and projected a 32.9% increase in adult cases by 2050 under constant incidence rates.

 Other GBD 2021 analyses reported substantial geographic heterogeneity and projected continued burden through 2035 or 2036., A study restricted to adults aged 20-64 years also projected increasing case numbers to 2050.

 The 2025 GBD 2023 cancer forecast extends this forecasting agenda across cancer groupings, including deaths, YLLs, and DALYs, and derives incidence using forecast mortality-to-incidence ratios.

 The official forecasts and our BAPC projections used different forecasting frameworks and population assumptions. Their estimates should therefore be interpreted as complementary projections rather than directly interchangeable results or independent validation.

The present study differs in three respects. It uses the complete GBD 2023 annual series through 2023, separates the analytic roles of GLOBOCAN and GBD, and quantifies the population-weighted HDI gradient with slope, relative, and concentration indices and bootstrap uncertainty. It also derives projected totals and changes from joint age-specific posterior draws rather than applying a crude population multiplier. The draw-level median increase of 58.1% in incident cases from 2023 to 2050 is not directly comparable with projections restricted to adults or based on constant rates. Such differences reinforce that projections should be interpreted with attention to age range, baseline year, source system, and model structure rather than ranked as competing point forecasts.

The 2022 GLOBOCAN and 2023 GBD/BAPC totals should not be interpreted as a single sequential series. The fitted GBD/BAPC 2023 medians were 382,614 incident cases and 264,127 deaths, approximately 18.9% and 6.3% above the GLOBOCAN 2022 totals. These differences cannot be attributed to any single component using the available aggregate data. The relative contributions of reference-year differences, source coverage, redistribution, smoothing, and internal consistency constraints cannot be quantified or decomposed. GLOBOCAN is designed for contemporary international cancer comparisons and selects country-specific estimation strategies, whereas GBD constructs internally consistent longitudinal series using different data integration, covariates, smoothing, and redistribution procedures. We therefore assigned the sources different analytic roles and did not pool or calibrate their totals (Supplementary Table S11).

The stable average incidence and overall mortality decline mask historical slope changes, and neither pattern can be assigned to a single mechanism. Better imaging and registration can increase observed incidence, while advances in surgical safety, radiotherapy, molecular classification, systemic treatment, and supportive care may improve outcomes for selected patients.- Changes in cause-of-death certification and GBD input data can also affect mortality estimates. The decline in age-standardised mortality should therefore be read as a population-level surveillance pattern, not as evidence of uniform survival gains across countries or tumour subtypes.

Males had higher incidence and mortality in both contemporary and longitudinal estimates, consistent with registry reports and epidemiological reviews.- Potential explanations include sex-linked genetic and hormonal biology, differential occupational exposure to ionising radiation or other carcinogens, diagnostic pathways, and sex differences in histological composition or survival. None can be separated in these aggregate data, and higher male mortality may reflect both incidence and post-diagnosis survival. The observed sex contrast is therefore ecological and should not be interpreted as a causal individual-level effect.

Established or debated risk-factor evidence likewise does not justify attributing the ecological time trends to exposure change. Therapeutic or high-dose ionising radiation is an established risk factor for CNS tumours.

 Large mobile-phone studies, including INTERPHONE, have not provided a consistent causal explanation and remain vulnerable to recall and selection bias

; a 2024 systematic review found moderate-certainty evidence that mobile-phone radiofrequency exposure likely does not increase the risk of the most investigated adult brain tumours.

 Allergic conditions have shown inverse observational associations with glioma, but causality is uncertain.

 Population ageing strongly affects counts, yet period/cohort extrapolation cannot anticipate future structural shifts in diagnosis, tumour classification, treatment, environmental exposure, or registration.

The aggregate outcome also obscures subtype-specific trajectories. Glioblastoma, lower-grade diffuse gliomas, malignant meningeal tumours, embryonal tumours, and other CNS malignancies differ in age distribution, molecular drivers, lethality, and diagnostic requirements. A stable aggregate ASIR could therefore coexist with opposing subtype trends. Future surveillance should report comparable histological and molecular strata when registry completeness permits.

The positive HDI gradient is the most easily misinterpreted result. Very high-HDI countries had more than three times the recorded incidence rate of low-HDI countries, and the population-weighted concentration index was positive for both incidence and mortality. These are inequalities in recorded, modelled burden rather than direct evidence that development causes CNS cancer. HDI covaries with imaging access, neuropathology, cancer registration, death certification, population age structure, health-care access, and potentially exposure patterns. The physician-density sensitivity models attenuated the HDI coefficients by approximately 54%-56%, supporting the plausibility of an ascertainment contribution, whereas UHC adjustment caused little attenuation. Because both proxies are broad ecological measures, strongly correlated with HDI, and not direct measures of CNS diagnostic or registry completeness, they neither quantify nor eliminate residual ascertainment bias. GBD covariates and spatiotemporal smoothing may reduce random gaps but cannot remove all systematic under-ascertainment.

The incidence gradient was larger than the mortality gradient across the SII, RII, concentration index, and grouped HDI comparisons. This pattern and the physician-density sensitivity are compatible with stronger development dependence in diagnostic ascertainment than in death attribution, but neither proves that mechanism. Multiple imputation of the 10 missing HDI values, exclusion of zero-ASR countries, and leave-one-out analyses showed that the result was not driven by the linkage pattern or a single influential country. Residual confounding, proxy measurement error, collinearity, temporal mismatch in physician-density observations, and source-model dependence remain substantial.

The projection converts rate patterns into a service-planning question. Approximately 605,000 new patients and 351,000 deaths were projected for 2050 under continuation of the modelled age, period, and cohort structure and the WPP medium population path. The draw-level changes had wide intervals that included decreases, so the medians should not be described as inevitable. On the posterior-mean scale used for the additive decomposition, the total increases were about 254,000 cases and 105,000 deaths; population growth and ageing contributed about 205,000 cases and 145,000 deaths, while rate change contributed about 50,000 cases and offset about 39,000 deaths. Posterior means were used because component-wise posterior medians are not additive. Low/high WPP variants changed 2050 medians modestly relative to the much wider epidemiological posterior uncertainty.

Incident cases and deaths capture only part of the clinical workload. GLOBOCAN estimated almost 1.2 million people living within five years of a brain or CNS cancer diagnosis in 2022. This population includes patients receiving active treatment, people undergoing surveillance imaging, and survivors living with neurological, cognitive, endocrine, or functional consequences. Five-year prevalence cannot be translated directly into clinic visits or workforce requirements, but it broadens the planning frame beyond newly diagnosed patients. Rehabilitation, seizure management, neurocognitive assessment, caregiver support, and survivorship or palliative pathways should be considered alongside operative and radiotherapy capacity.

Planning priorities differ by surveillance context. In countries with mature registries, the central task may be maintaining timely multidisciplinary care as populations age. In settings with limited imaging and neuropathology, investment in diagnostic access and registry completeness may initially increase recorded incidence. Such an increase should not automatically be interpreted as prevention failure; it may represent improved case finding. Specialist referral and treatment capacity also depend on access to essential medicines and functional primary-care noncommunicable-disease platforms., Cancer control programmes should therefore pair capacity expansion with indicators of diagnostic timeliness, pathology coverage, treatment access, and registry completeness rather than evaluate progress from modelled incidence alone.

Projection uncertainty widened with the forecast horizon, especially for age-standardised rates. The BAPC results should be used as conditional planning estimates, not deterministic forecasts. Although the full APC specification was favoured by DIC and short-term holdout errors were small, one of eight mortality intervals missed its observed value. The model cannot foresee future changes in classification, diagnostic diffusion, treatment, environmental exposures, or registry systems; nor does it propagate upstream GBD draw covariance that was unavailable in the extracted series.

The study has several strengths. It assigns distinct roles to two major estimation systems rather than pooling their totals, uses the complete annual GBD 2023 series, combines absolute and relative population-weighted inequality measures, explores health-system proxies, reports draw-level posterior changes, compares nested BAPC structures, tests WPP population variants, and evaluates short-term temporal prediction. The reporting package follows GATHER and supplies source data for Supplementary Figure S1.

The limitations are equally important. GLOBOCAN and GBD are modelled systems whose estimates depend on registry coverage, vital statistics, covariates, redistribution, and smoothing. GBD marginal UIs and serial covariance were not propagated through trend regressions. HDI, UHC, and physician density are broad national measures; UHC and physician density were highly correlated with HDI, physician observations spanned 2018-2022, and neither directly measured imaging, neuropathology, or registry completeness. Adjustment for survival, genetic, occupational, or environmental factors was not possible. The 10 missing HDI values were imputed only in sensitivity analysis. Pearson correlations may be affected by nonlinearity despite graphical review, while multiple location-level EAPC tests were exploratory and unadjusted. Aggregating ages 85+ may conceal oldest-old heterogeneity. BAPC intervals were wide, one mortality holdout interval missed, and the model assumes historical structure continues. The broad cause category precluded subtype analysis, and ecological associations cannot support individual-level causal inference.

Brain and CNS cancer showed stable average global age-standardised incidence and declining mortality over 1990-2023, with evidence of historical changes in slope. Segmented analyses indicated increases followed by declines, with changes around 1998 for incidence and 2000 for mortality. Recorded rates also showed substantial development-related inequality, and annual case and death counts may increase by 2050. These findings support strengthening imaging, neuropathology, registration, multidisciplinary treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative capacity while distinguishing true epidemiological change from ascertainment and source-model effects. The projections should guide scenario planning and be updated as new registry, GBD, and population data become available.
