medicine.title: Chromosome-Scale Genome Assembly and Annotation of the Goldenrod Gall Fly, Eurosta solidaginis (Fitch) (Diptera: Tephritidae)
medicine.abstract: Eurosta solidaginis is a plant-parasitic insect that develops from egg to adult inside of a spheroid gall it induces on the stem of goldenrod plants (Solidago spp.). E. solidaginis is widespread across North America, with a geographic distribution that extends from Southern Canada to Texas and the Southern U.S. and from the Atlantic coast to the Great Plains and includes scattered populations reaching the West coast. The natural history, ecology, and physiology of E. solidaginis are well-documented, and its overwintering physiology, multitrophic interactions, and ecological speciation have been well-studied. Surprisingly, genomic resources are restricted to an incomplete scaffold-level genome assembly lacking protein-coding gene annotation. To advance understanding of the physiology, gall-forming, and population structure of E. solidaginis, we sequenced and assembled the genome of a single pupa using PacBio HiFi sequencing and Hi-C chromatin proximity sequencing technology. Here, we present a fully annotated, chromosome-level de novo assembly of the 1.9 Gb genome, spanning five autosomes and the sex chromosomes. The assembly has a contig N50 of 3.7 Mb and a scaffold N50 of 289.3 Mb, and 96.5% of expected Diptera Benchmark of Universal Single-Copy Orthologs in the genome found in single copy. We annotated 14,223 identified protein-coding genes, identifying 96.2% of Benchmark of Universal Single-Copy Orthologs in the protein set found in single copy. The 18,293 bp mitochondrial genome was assembled and subsequently annotated separately. Even though there are 400 to 450 gall-inducing tephritid species, this is the second high-quality, chromosome-level genome assembly of a gall-forming fly in the family, and the third freeze-tolerant dipteran genome.
medicine.text:
The goldenrod gall fly, Eurosta solidaginis (Fitch) (Diptera: Tephritidae), is a univoltine insect distributed broadly in North America, from Southern Canada to Texas and the Southern U.S. and from the Atlantic coast to the Great Plains, with scattered populations reaching the West coast. E. solidaginis is tightly associated with its perennial Solidago spp. host plant, inducing prominent spheroid stem galls (; ). Adult flies emerge in late spring, do not feed, and live for about two weeks (). During their adult stage, they mate and females insert eggs into the center of newly growing Solidago stem buds (). Eggs hatch after 7 to 10 d and the larvae burrow into the stem, secreting saliva that induces the plant to surround it in a round gall. The larva uses this gall tissue as food and the gall structure as shelter (). Gall size typically reaches its maximum in late summer, while larvae continue feeding and growing (). Prior to winter, the larva chews an exit tunnel that reaches close to the gall surface, then molts into a prepupa, and enters diapause when the plant senesces. Warming spring temperatures trigger pupation and adult eclosion at the end of winter (). E. solidaginis galls host a community of inquilines and parasitoids, and the system has become a classic example for studying stabilizing selection on gall sizes as a result of tri-trophic interactions involving herbivores, plants, and natural enemies (; ; ; ), as well as host preference, gall induction, host-associated genetic divergence (, ; ; ; ), and freeze tolerance (; ; ; ; ; ).

A fragmented scaffold-level reference genome for E. solidaginis was released in 2023 (National Center for Biotechnology [NCBI]: GCA_029619165.1; 49,048 scaffolds, N50 = 46.9 kb). Fragmented genomes are of limited utility for mapping adaptive loci and exploring structural variations such as repetitive elements and inversions necessary for population and evolutionary genomics as they do not present the assembly in context to chromosomes, may contain assembly orientation error, and contain a level of assembly gaps. Here, we present a chromosome-scale genome assembly for E. solidaginis, one of the first for a galling tephritid fly. We extracted high-molecular-weight (HMW) DNA from a single adult male and sequenced it to 21× using PacBio HiFi, and a Hi-C library preparation and sequencing from a second adult male from the same collection. We assembled using HiFiASM v0.19.3-r572 (), yielding 569 scaffolds, including six chromosome-scale pseudomolecules assigned to five autosomes and the putative X chromosome. This assembly structure is consistent with the diploid chromosome number of 2n = 12 commonly reported in Tephritidae (), including species in the same subfamily, Tephritinae (). We annotated the genome using NCBI Eukaryotic Genomic Annotation Pipeline v10.3. We assembled a contiguous 18,293 bp mitochondrial genome using the MitoHiFi v3.2 pipeline (), with the Procecidochares utilis mitochondrial genome (NCBI RefSeq accession: NC_020463.1) as a reference. Mitochondrial reads were then identified by mapping the mitochondrial genome assembly and excluded from the nuclear genome assembly. This high-quality genome assembly will be an asset for future genomic investigations of E. solidaginis, and for comparative genomic investigations of ecology, evolutionary biology, physiology, and plant–insect interactions.

In total, 50 Gb of raw PacBio HiFi reads were generated from a single Eurosta solidaginis adult male, resulted in an estimated 21× genome coverage. The total haploid assembly size is estimated at 1.86 GB based on k-mer analysis with GenomeScope v2 (k-mer = 21, k-cov = 21; ). Analysis of primary assembly completeness of the genome using Diptera (odb 10) s revealed 96.8% of expected genes found in single copy, 25.1% duplicated, 1.0% fragmented, and 2.2% missing out of the expected 3,285 Diptera orthologs (). After duplicate purging and placing contigs to putative chromosomes, the final genome size was 1.9 GB. Removing the duplicate contigs increased single-copy orthologs from 71.7% in the primary assembly to 96.5% and reduced the duplicate genes from 25.1% to 1.4% in the final scaffolded assembly (). The assembly is 35% larger and more intact than the most recently published E. solidaginis genome in NCBI (assembly ID: GCA_029619165.1): nearly 43,000 fewer scaffolds and N50 increased from 46.9 kb to 289 Mb. GC content of our E. solidaginis assembly (37.5%) is comparable to the other Diptera species assemblies. The Hi-C contact map showed six prominent interaction blocks along the diagonal, with stronger contacts within than between the six major scaffolds (), supporting our interpretation of them as chromosome-scale pseudomolecules. After scaffolding, our final assembly comprised 569 scaffolds including the six chromosome-scale pseudomolecules assigned to the five autosomes and a putative X chromosome, and 563 unplaced scaffolds ( and ). Comparative analysis with a publicly available chromosome-scale assembly for Zeugodacus cucurbitae (NCBI RefSeq accession GCF_028554725.1) revealed strong correspondence between the five autosomes of the two species, along with several links between the Z. cucurbitae X chromosome and the putative X chromosome of E. solidaginis, supporting our chromosomal assignment (). We did not assess chromosome-end completeness by telomeric repeat screening because the telomere sequence motif in Diptera is largely unknown and is not conserved in Diptera (). Thus, the presence or absence of this motif would not be a reliable indicator of chromosome-end completeness in E. solidaginis.

Summary of E. solidaginis genome assembly and annotation metrics

The NCBI Eukaryotic Genomic Annotation Pipeline predicted 21,190 genes and pseudogenes, of which 17,839 were genes (6,614 of which had variants), giving rise to 42,847 predicted transcripts. We identified 3,351 nontranscribed pseudogenes, but no evidence of transcribed pseudogenes. Windowmasker () estimated that 61.4% of the genome was composed of repetitive elements. Benchmark of Universal Single-Copy Ortholog (BUSCO) analysis of the predicted gene set using “protein” mode was performed against the Diptera odb10 dataset (containing 3,285 genes; ; ). Our final annotated protein set had 97.6% complete BUSCOs, 96.5% of which were single copy, with 1.4% of genes duplicated, 1% fragmented, and 1.4% missing. Thus, the completeness of the annotated gene set closely matches the genome, validating the quality of genome assembly and gene predictions. We report the genome assembly and annotation metrics in .

We assembled the mitochondrial genome with a total size of 18,293 bp and annotated its 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNAs (tRNAs), 2 ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs), and the D-loop control region, where the order and orientation of the gene structure are shown in .

We present a high-quality, chromosome-level reference assembly with associated annotation. Combining long-read HiFi sequencing with Hi-C data yielded a highly contiguous 1.9 GB genome assembly, with a scaffold N50 of 289.3 Mb and a BUSCO score of 96.5% complete single copy and 1.4% duplicated orthologs. The annotation includes 21,190 predicted genes, providing a resource for future research on the unusual biology of Eurosta solidaginis across several subdisciplines.

E. solidaginis galls were collected from Koffler Scientific Station, King City, Ontario, Canada, in November 2022. Galls were dissected, and larvae were reared in room temperature until its pupae stage. Pupae were flash frozen using liquid nitrogen at the onset of eye pigmentation (when the eyes first began to turn red) and stored at a −80 °C freezer upon shipment. Samples were shipped overnight on dry ice to the United States Department of Agriculture-Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS)-Tropical Pest Genetics and Molecular Biology Research Unit, USA.

HMW genomic DNA was extracted from the whole body of a single male using the Qiagen MagAttract HMW DNA Kit (Qiagen, Hilden Germany), following protocol for the fresh or frozen tissue. The extracted DNA was quantified using the dsDNA Broad Range Qubit assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) and the fluorometer function of a DS-11 Spectrophotometer and Fluorometer (DeNovix Inc, Wilmington, Delaware, USA). DNA purity was assessed using the UV-Vis spectrometer feature of the DS-11, which measured Optical Density (OD) 260/230 and 260/280 ratios. After isolation, DNA underwent a 2.0 Solid-Phrase Reversible Immobilization (SPRI) bead clean-up, and the HMW DNA was sheared to a mean size of 20 kb using the Diagenode Megaruptor 3 (Denville, New Jersey, USA). The size distribution of the post-sheared DNA was analyzed with the Genomic DNA 165 kb Kit on the Femto Pulse System (Agilent Technologies, Inc., Santa Clara, California, USA). Post-shearing size distribution was assessed using the Genomic DNA 165 kb Kit of the Femto Pulse System (Agilent Technologies, Inc, Santa Clara, California, USA). The sheared DNA served as input for the preparation of a Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) SMRTBell library, which was prepared using the SMRTBell Express Template Prep Kit 2.0 (Pacific Biosciences, Menlo Park, California, USA).

The prepared library was bound and sequenced at the USDA-ARS Tropical Pest Genetics and Molecular Biology Research Unit in Hilo, HI, on two PacBio 8M SMRT Cells on a Sequel IIe system. To target HiFi reads, the library was sequenced using a 30-h movie time, and raw subreads were converted to consensus HiFi data by processing with circular consensus sequencing (CCS) to call a single high-quality consensus sequence for each molecule, using a 99.5% consensus accuracy cutoff using the SMRTLink v8.0 software.

Concurrent with the PacBio HiFi library preparation and sequencing, a Hi-C library was prepared from a second male from the same collection. Flash-frozen tissue was ground in 1× phosphate-buffered-saline (PBS) solution to disrupt cell tissue and then fixed in 2.4% formaldehyde. After the cross-linking, the reaction was quenched with 2.5 M glycine, and the fixed nuclei were pelleted. Following cross-linking, cells were lysed, and chromatin was digested using the enzymes DdeI and DpnII (New England Biosciences, Ipswich, Massachusetts, USA). Following chromatin digestion, digested ends of the DNA were repaired and filled in with nucleic acids and a biotin-14-dATP. The proximal DNA fragments were then ligated and cross-links were reversed. After cross-link reversal, the resulting DNA was purified twice using SPRI beads. Following the SPRI bead purification, biotin from the ends that failed to ligate was removed, followed by another SPRI-based purification. The sample was then sheared to a mean peak of 400 to 450 bp using a Diagenode Bioruptor Pico. Following fragmentation, SPRI beads were used to size select the sample to remove both small and large fragments and the sample was enriched for ligated contacts by pulling down the biotin ligated products with MyOne Streptavidin C1 beads. Following biotin enrichment, the sample was repaired and dA-tailed and prepared for sequencing by ligating adapters using the NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit followed by the Element Biosciences Adept Library Prep Kit (Element Biosciences, San Diego, California, USA). Resulting Hi-C libraries were sequenced on one flow cell of an Element Biosciences Aviti system to 100× coverage of the genome size. Raw sequence files were demultiplexed and converted to standard fastq format using Bases2Fastq.

Total RNA extraction was performed on 11 E. solidaginis samples representing different life stages and adult body parts: the head, thorax, and abdomen from one male and one female (a total of six samples), two larvae samples, and three pupae samples. Adult flies were collected in 2022, larvae and pupae were collected in 2023, all at Koffler Scientific Station, King City, Ontario, Canada (44.03016, −79.52773). Total RNA of 11 samples were extracted using the Zymo Research Direct-zol-96 MagBead RNA kit. Following RNA isolation, the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module protocol was used for poly A selection. NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit was used to prepare RNA-seq libraries targeting a final library size of 300 to 600 bp. The resulting RNA-Seq library was sequenced as part of a barcoded pool on one 2 × 150 sequencing kit for the Element Biosciences Aviti system.

To increase representation of key genes associated with cold tolerance, RNAseq data were also included from larvae collected from galls in London, Ontario, Canada (43°00′N, 81°15′W) in 2012 and 2013. To obtain diverse gene expression profiling, larvae were exposed to −12 °C for 2 h, and then warmed to 5 °C for 0, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, or 360 min. Individual samples were flash frozen until RNA extraction using TRIzol (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Five pooled individuals from each treatment were then purified using the RNAeasy Lipid Tissue Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The quality and concentration of RNA were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 Spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, DE, USA) and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). cDNA libraries for sequencing were constructed using the Illumina TruSeq RNA Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and quality was again checked with the Bioanalyzer. The resulting cDNA libraries sequenced as 50 bp single-end reads at the University of Utah's Microarray and Genomic Analysis Shared Resource. All raw RNA-seq reads are available under Sequence Read Archive (SRA) accession no. from SRX25264716 to RX25264735 (BioProject PRJNA1029130).

PacBio Sequel IIe HiFi and Element Aviti Hi-C sequencing of E. solidaginis produced sufficient data for a highly contiguous contig assembly with chromosomal resolution. All contigs were taxonomically classified using BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) against nucleotide and protein databases and visualized with Blobtools. The genome assembly was performed using HiFiASM v0.19.3-r572 () as a diploid assembly which resulted in a primary and alternate assembly. Following assembly, the primary and alternate assembly served as the input to the PurgeDups v1.2.6 pipeline (). The resulting primary purged assembly was scaffolded using the YaHS v1.2a.2 pipeline (). Briefly, paired 150 bp reads sequenced from a Hi-C library were mapped to the primary purged assembly using bwa-mem2 v2.2.1 (). Duplicate artifacts were removed using Picard (http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/), and the YaHS pipeline created a chromatin contact matrix from the mapping of proximity ligated pairs that it used to order and orient contigs, placing contigs into a single chromosome when there are contacts between them and identifying chromosomal boundaries when there is a significant lack of contacts. The HiC contact matrix was visualized in Juicebox for manual Hi-C editing (), making minor manual edits to fix erroneous translocations and inversions as suggested in the Juicebox documentation.

Genome size based on Kmer distribution was assessed from CCS reads using GenomeScope v2.0 (). Assembly metrics for the contig assembly were assessed using BBtools stats.sh. Duplicate levels were assessed using Kmer Analysis Toolkit () and a BUSCO Diptera ortholog database version 10 (odb) in “genome” mode. Assembly quality values as determined by parity in relation to the Kmer profile of the CCS reads were determined using YAK. The Blobtools pipeline was used to identify nonarthropod contigs and to visualize the assembly. Results of the Blobtools pipeline were summarized using blobblurb (https://github.com/sheinasim/blobblurb). The CCS reads were mapped back to the assembly and unmapped reads were extracted and run through the MEGAN metagenomics pipeline for cursory metagenomic analysis of opportunistic metagenomic sequences.

Syntenic chromosomes with a chromosome assembly of the melon fly Z. cucurbitae were identified using Diptera odb 10 BUSCOs annotated in genome mode in both the Z. cucurbitae and E. solidaginis assemblies. Record name and positions for each BUSCO identified in single copy in both assemblies were visualized in R using the package Rideogram (; ).

All potential copies of the mitochondrial genome were identified and annotated using the MitoHiFi v3.2 pipeline (). The publicly available mitochondrial genome of Procecidochares utilis (NCBI RefSeq accession: NC_020463.1) was employed as a reference for sequence alignment through the blastn function of BLAST+ (). Contigs with high-scoring alignments containing the entire mitochondrial genome were removed from the main assembly before submission to allow for manual annotation and separate submission.

A total of 763,755,318 RNA sequencing reads from pooled transcriptome data including pooled larvae, pooled pupa, adult head, abdomen, and thorax were used for genome annotation through the NCBI Eukaryotic Genomic Annotation Pipeline v10.3. This pipeline was chosen to ensure consistency and standardization in annotation methods with other closely related species. Repeats were identified and masked using WindowMasker (). Following gene annotation, the estimate of the completeness of the gene set was calculated by performing a BUSCO analysis on the annotations in “protein” mode. A description of the RNA sequencing reads is available on the NCBI annotation release (GCF_040869045.1-RS_2024_08, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/refseq/annotation_euk/Eurosta_solidaginis/GCF_040869045.1-RS_2024_08/).

medicine.title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models
medicine.abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human–animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.
medicine.text:
Chickens and pigs are not only essential sources of animal-derived protein in human nutrition but also valuable models in research fields such as immunology, infectious diseases, cancer, and developmental biology. In recent years, pigs have emerged as the most important translational model organism, bridging preclinical research and human trials []. They are used in various biomedical research fields such as diabetes [], cancer [], or cognitive and behavioral research []. Compared to rodents, they offer many significant advantages. Of particular importance are their relatively long life span, which enables longitudinal studies, as well as the closer resemblance to the human pathophenotype []. The similarity in size, physiology, and anatomy supports the advancement of surgical research and additionally attributes great translational value to the pig []. This also includes the field of xenotransplantation, driven by the critical shortage of human donor organs, for which the pig is considered the most suitable donor species []. As a result, the demand for genetically modified (GM) pigs has increased significantly over the past decade. Similarly, chickens have gained substantial importance as complementary model organisms in both basic and applied research. GM chickens play a central role in developmental biology [], where they have enabled fundamental discoveries in embryogenesis and tissue differentiation. They have provided key insights into immunology [,] and mechanisms of disease resistance [,], contributing to both veterinary and human health research. Compared to mammalian models, chickens offer unique experimental advantages, including easy access to the developing embryo and cost-effective large-scale studies. In addition, they serve as efficient bioreactors for the production of recombinant proteins in ovo [], further increasing their biotechnological and translational value. Taken together, valuable models for biomedical and translational research have been established using chickens and pigs. Nevertheless, the efficiency and safety of generating such models could be greatly improved by advancing delivery tools for these species [].

CRISPR/Cas9 and Cre recombinase are widely used genome engineering tools that have been substantially refined in recent years. Innovations such as catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9), base editors, and transcriptional modulators (CRISPRa/i) have expanded the range of possible genetic modifications beyond simple gene disruption []. These technologies now form the foundation of state-of-the-art strategies for generating GM animals. In pigs, the historical lack of fully functional germline-competent embryonic stem (ES) cells necessitated gene targeting in somatic cells, a technically demanding and inefficient approach []. This limitation significantly restricted the generation of GM pigs until the introduction of CRISPR/Cas9, which enabled direct and more efficient genome editing. Today, GM pigs are typically produced either by microinjection of genome-editing tools into zygotes or by modifying somatic cells followed by somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) []. A comparable challenge existed in chickens, where ES cells also failed to contribute to the germline. This obstacle was overcome through the possibility to cultivate and manipulate germline-competent primordial germ cells (PGCs), thereby allowing precise genome engineering, including targeted knock-ins and knock-outs [,]. Currently, genetic modification in chickens relies predominantly on the editing of PGCs []. Although these approaches are well established, they remain labor-intensive and time-consuming, particularly due to the need to breed founder animals, and they may result in unintended genotypes []. To better comply with the 3R principles and accelerate research timelines, there is a growing demand for efficient, safe, and rapid in vivo delivery systems for genome engineering tools []. These strategies might allow more precise and time-efficient generation of modified animals, as they might enable the refinement of existing animal models while reducing the need to generate new ones. While these approaches do not eliminate the need for embryo production and microinjection, they have the potential to improve genome editing efficiency greatly, thereby increasing the proportion of successfully edited embryos. This may reduce the number of surplus animals required in accordance with the 3R principles to generate the desired genotype and contribute to more efficient production of genetically modified animals.

Virus-like particles (VLPs) are self-assembling nanostructures ranging from 20 to 200 nm in size, with broad applications in therapeutics, vaccines, and diagnostics []. In mouse models, VLPs have been successfully used as protein delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools such as CRISPR/Cas9 and Cre recombinase not only in vitro but also in vivo [,]. Importantly, VLP-based delivery has proven particularly effective for the in vivo editing of immune cells, demonstrating the feasibility of targeting key components of the immune system with high efficiency []. While this delivery system is well established in mice, there is no evidence of the effectiveness of genome engineering using VLPs in livestock species such as pigs and chickens. In this study, we systematically evaluated a repertoire of these nanostructures including Cre and Cas9 VLPs in these species. We demonstrated that in both pigs and chickens, VLPs provide an efficient platform to deliver genome editing tools and fluorescent proteins in vitro in cells and organoid systems, ex vivo in organ cultures and additionally in ovo in chicken. The use of this technology will advance the development of genetically modified livestock models, contributing to disease prevention and improved animal health according to the One Health approach.

The first goal was to test the transduction efficiency of VLPs on porcine primary kidney fibroblasts (pKDNFs), chicken DT40 cells, as well as chicken primordial germ cells (PGCs) by delivery of fluorescent proteins. pKDNFs, DT40 cells and PGCs were transduced with VLPs packaged with superfolder (sf) GFP. As early as 24 h post-transduction, FACS analysis and fluorescence microscopy showed that nearly all somatic porcine and chicken cells (>90%) were successfully transduced ( and ). After 48 h, only a slight decrease in the fluorescence of sfGFP signal in pKDNFs was visible. Additionally, VLPs carrying the red fluorescent protein mCherry transduced pKDNFs and DT40 cells with efficiencies comparable to those of sfGFP VLPs ( and ). Given that PGCs are known to be difficult to transfect, varying VLP volumes were evaluated in PGCs. It was found that 20 µL VLPs reached comparable results to 5 µL VLPs on somatic cells (,  and ).

To test the functionality of Cre VLPs on pKDNFs, we used cells from a dual-fluorescent reporter pig [], where successful recombination excised a loxP-flanked stop (LSL) cassette containing the mTomato gene, and thereby activating downstream eGFP expression as an easy and direct readout. Cre VLPs produced strong expression of eGFP 48 h post-transduction ( top), indicating successful excision of the LSL cassette. We extended this study to evaluate VLPs in a non-mammalian vertebrate, the chicken. To assess the efficiency of Cre VLPs in chicken, IghKO DT40 cells—a chicken B cell lymphoma line in which the immunoglobulin heavy chain (Igh) gene is disrupted [] —were used. Transduction of these cells with Cre VLPs was expected to result in recombination of the IghKO repair template cassette and simultaneous excision of eGFP. Accordingly, fluorescence microscopy revealed that Cre VLPs resulted in only a minor detectable eGFP signal in any transduced group after 24 h, which indicated efficient recombination and consequently, loss of eGFP expression ( top; ). Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that 24 h post-transduction, a significant decrease in eGFP-positive cells was observed in the group transduced with 20 µL Cre VLPs. Similarly, after 72 h a significant decrease was also observed in the group transduced with 10 µL compared with the control ().

To test Cre VLPs on a more complex in vitro system, we investigated their functionality on porcine colonic organoids from the same reporter pig. Transduction protocols for human and murine organoids [] were adapted and optimized for porcine organoids leading to efficient recombination caused by Cre VLPs. Strong eGFP expression was evident after 48 h ( bottom). As a more elaborate avian ex vivo culture system, tracheal organ cultures (TOCs) from JH-KO chickens [] were used. Similar to the principle described above, VLP-mediated delivery of Cre led to recombination and consequent loss of eGFP signal. A decrease of eGFP fluorescence in the VLP-treated TOCs was visible 48 h after transduction ( bottom). To further assess the tissue penetrance and distribution of VLP-mediated recombination, tissue sections of the treated TOCs were analyzed, revealing more pronounced Cre-mediated recombination in the outer tissue layers compared with the inner layers ().

For further analysis of Cre VLP efficiency on livestock cells we compared VLPs to commercially available tatCRE, a delivery system of Cre using the cell-penetrating tat peptide. Therefore, porcine fibroblasts derived from a dual-fluorescent reporter pig and chicken IghKO DT40 cells were used to cover both mammalian and non-mammalian organisms. Fluorescence microscopy as well as flow cytometry showed successful recombination for both Cre VLPs and tatCRE in either of the used reporter systems, with pKDNFs expressing GFP and DT40 cells losing GFP signal over time, respectively (). For both species, a stronger recombination-mediated change in fluorescence was detected when Cre VLPs were used compared to tatCRE-treated cells. However, strong toxic effects were observed for primary porcine cells, as seen in their shrinking morphology. Here, GFP expression was only observed for cells that survived tatCRE treatment (). This toxicity was not observed for the DT40 cell line ().

To assess whether the baboon envelope (BaEV) glycoprotein enhances transduction of porcine cells as it is the case for other species [], Cre VLPs were produced with varying ratios (3:0, 2:1, 1:2, 0:3) of vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein (VSV-G) and BaEV. The distinctly pseudotyped VLPs were used to transduce reporter pKDNFs and in the recommended ratio of 1:2 VSV-G:BaEV, the transduction efficiency was strongly decreased and resulted in less eGFP signal while the ratio of 3:0 VSV-G:BaEV showed the best result (). Consequently, all experiments in this study were conducted using VSV-G only.

Lastly, to quantify protein content in the VLPs and determine the optimal amount of VLPs for transduction, three distinct batches of Cre VLPs were analyzed through ELISA and additional functional tests on reporter pKDNFs (). Based on a positive correlation, 5–10 µL of Cre VLPs with a concentration of 2.55 U/µL were used in the experiments.

After Cre VLP functionality was proved in a fluorescent reporter system, organoids from pigs that carry latent mutations in the oncogene KRAS and the tumor suppressor gene (TSG) TP53 [,] were established. The oncogenic mutations KRASG12D and TP53R167H are silenced by a LSL cassette in the first intron of the gene. Organoids were transduced with Cre VLPs and grown in culture for up to 46 days. From day 24 in culture, we observed a change in the organoids’ morphology from a branched, differentiated to a cystic and proliferative architecture (, , and ) indicating activation of the silenced mutations. Recombination PCR was performed to assess excision of the LSL cassette in both genes. As early as day 5, recombined TP53R167H () and KRASG12D () alleles were detectable, with increasing intensity over time. By day 26, the LSL cassette was no longer amplifiable, indicating complete excision. For KRAS, loss of the WT band suggested loss of heterozygosity at DNA level. To evaluate transcriptional consequences, RNA was converted to cDNA and allelic expression was quantified. For both TP53 () and KRAS (), WT and mutant transcripts were still detectable at later time points (day 20 and day 26, respectively). Together, these data demonstrate that VLP-mediated Cre delivery enables stable activation of latent oncogenic alleles in porcine organoids and drives their phenotypic transformation.

As a next step toward genome editing in livestock, Cas9 VLPs were applied to pKDNFs targeting different TSGs to generate single knockouts (SKOs). Forty-eight hours after transduction, inference of CRISPR edits (ICE) analysis of isolated gDNA revealed high editing efficiencies, with insertion and deletion (INDEL) rates of 80–98% and corresponding knockout (KO) scores of 70%–98% (). To achieve even higher KO scores more consistently, different multiplexing strategies were evaluated (). Inclusion of two gRNAs targeting two different genes in a single VLP batch (multiplexing strategy 1, MPS1) markedly reduced editing efficiency in both analyzed loci and showed a bias towards one gRNA (). In contrast, co-transduction with two separately produced VLP batches, each containing one gRNA targeting a different locus (MPS2), resulted in editing efficiencies comparable to SKOs for both genetic loci and was therefore used for subsequent experiments (). Furthermore, using MPS2, dual targeting of IL-10 with flanking gRNAs achieved INDEL and KO scores of up to 100% in pKDNFs, with ICE analysis confirming complete excision of the target region (, , and ). MPS2 was further applied to porcine organoids, multiplexing Cas9 and Cre VLPs simultaneously. Five days after transduction, ICE analysis showed an INDEL score of 81% for B2M, comparable to a SKO, while simultaneous Cre activity and successful recombination was confirmed by strong eGFP expression (, , , and ). Finally, multiplexed Cas9 VLPs targeting IL-10 were microinjected into in vitro fertilized porcine oocytes ( and ). After 7 days in culture, 66.6% of blastocysts were edited, with INDEL rates of 94%–100% and KO scores of 61%–100% (). In one blastocyst, 100% KO was achieved, with 98% of edits resulting from dual gRNA-mediated excision, as confirmed by ICE analysis ().

To evaluate Cas9-mediated genome editing in chicken cells via VLPs, the B2M locus was targeted. MHC-I surface expression on adherent HD11 cells and in the bursa of embryonic day (ED)19 embryos was analyzed by flow cytometry following transduction with Cas9 VLPs. A pronounced reduction in mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was observed in HD11 cells at 48 h and 72 h post-transduction (). Furthermore, gene editing in chicken PGCs achieved a mean INDEL frequency of 20% at 72 h post-transduction ( and ). For in ovo delivery, B2M-targeting VLPs were injected intravenously into ED12 chicken embryos (). Gene editing was assessed seven days later (ED19). A significant decrease in surface MHC-I expression was detected in the bursa (), whereas reduced MHC-I expression in PBMCs was observed in a subset of embryos (), indicating tissue-specific editing efficiencies. Additionally, VLP-treated and untreated bursae were stained for MHC-l expression (). Notably, all analyzed bursi (9/9; 100%) exhibited detectable gene editing, with 7/9 reaching INDEL frequencies >10% (), underscoring the robustness of the in ovo VLP delivery.

To enable epigenome editing, a plasmid for expression of a Gag-dCas9 fusion protein was cloned using the plasmid for Gag-Cas9 expression as template for site-directed mutagenesis. dCas9 VLPs were used to test a passive demethylation approach proposed by Sapozhnikov and colleagues []. Therefore, intron four in TP53 was targeted, since a highly methylated internal promoter (P2) is located in this region. Two established gRNAs were used to target several CpG islands of interest (). Multiplexed dCas9 VLPs led to a demethylation frequency of up to 21% in pKDNFs after 6 days (). CpGs 2 and 3 showed the highest demethylation rate because they are targeted by both gRNAs simultaneously, and the results align with the predicted demethylation window. The use of dCas9 VLPs including only gRNA1 led to less demethylation, even after a prolonged transduction period of 15 days ().

In this study, we establish VLP-mediated delivery as an efficient platform for transferring diverse cargoes into cells from multiple livestock species. Through optimization of VLP production, we generated a versatile panel that performed robustly across in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo systems. This approach addresses key barriers that have limited the translation of genome engineering technologies from model organisms to livestock, including inefficient delivery of genome editing tools, with important implications for model refinement, scalability, and ethically responsible research avoiding time-consuming germline breeding strategies for the generation of transgenic lines.

Efficient VLP production for livestock applications required systematic optimization of Gag and VSV-G expression in producer cells compared to murine and human systems [,]. The recruitment of envelope glycoproteins such as VSV-G by Gag during virion formation is a complex process that remains incompletely understood. Current evidence indicates that no single Gag domain mediates this process, but rather that VSV-G and other envelope proteins are recruited at lipid-rich assembly and budding sites []. Higher levels of VSV-G expression in producer cells increase its incorporation into virions and can enhance transduction efficiency by up to 55-fold in vitro []. Implementing these adjustments enabled robust transduction of porcine and chicken cells, organoids, organ cultures, and oocytes, underscoring the need for species-specific optimization when adapting VLP technologies to livestock.

Reporter VLPs carrying sfGFP or mCherry efficiently transduced porcine and avian somatic cells as well as PGCs without detectable toxicity. In addition to serving as process controls, these reporters enabled cell sorting and rapid verification of successful delivery, particularly in PGCs, where transduction efficiencies approached completeness, while electroporation yielded lower and more variable editing rates []. Although cellular viability was not quantitatively assessed in this experiment, the cells maintained a healthy morphology and continued to proliferate throughout the observed period, with no apparent signs of cytotoxicity, suggesting that the VLP transduction did not cause substantial cellular toxicity under the tested conditions.

Building on the validated functionality of Cre VLPs in samples from a dual-fluorescent reporter pig [], we achieved robust activation of latent oncogenic mutations via efficient excision of LSL cassettes in organoids derived from oncopigs [,]. For these studies, we employed a porcine model of familial adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer (CRC) [], that additionally harbors silenced KRASG12D and TP53R167H mutations and established organoids from polyp biopsy material. Cre-mediated recombination consistently induced a phenotypic transition from branched, differentiated architectures to cystic, highly proliferative morphologies that were maintained over extended culture periods. Notably, comparable structural differences were also observed between human patient-derived organoids from healthy and tumor tissue, respectively []. We hypothesize that activation of KRASG12D and TP53R167H—orthologous to key driver mutations in human CRC—triggers oncogenic signaling cascades and downstream transcriptional reprogramming, ultimately promoting enhanced proliferation. Future studies should delineate the affected pathways in greater detail and assess autologous reimplantation of edited organoids to accelerate in vivo disease modeling [].

In avian systems, Cre VLPs enabled rapid genome engineering in both chicken IghKO DT40 cells and TOCs. This approach provides a practical mean to evaluate disease-resistance genes ex vivo [], complementing earlier mouse-based demonstrations of VLP utility in organ cultures [] and offering particular value for species in which stable genetic modification remains technically challenging. Although recombination was also detected in the deeper tissue layers, it was less pronounced than in the superficial layers. The partial recombination observed in these deeper regions suggests that increasing the VLP concentration and extending the exposure time may enhance VLP penetration and recombination throughout the tissue. In addition, pseudotyping with alternative envelope proteins could potentially improve VLP penetration into tracheal tissue and thereby enhance recombination in the deeper layers [].

For further efficiency assessment of Cre VLPs, we performed a comparison to the commercially available tatCRE, in which Cre is fused to a protein transduction domain derived from HIV, the 11 aa peptide tat []. tatCre induced efficient, however, lower, recombination in both porcine and avian reporter systems, although using higher concentrations than for Cre VLPs. This suggests a superiority of the entry mechanism used by Cre VLPs—receptor-dependent clathrin-mediated endocytosis [,]—compared to the tat peptide, which enters the cell via receptor-independent lipid raft-mediated macropinocytosis []. In addition, during tatCRE treatment, toxic effects were observed on primary porcine cells indicated by their change in morphology, leading to unwanted selection of fitter cells. These findings as well as the additional removal steps required for tatCRE, highlight the advantages of VLP-based delivery system.

To benchmark particle inputs, Cre content in VLP preparations was quantified by ELISA and showed a positive correlation with functional activity. In contrast, Cas9-mediated editing was highly dependent on sgRNA design and target context, necessitating functional pre-testing. Accordingly, we report VLP volumes that consistently performed in pigs and chickens rather than absolute protein loads across all preparations.

While VSV-G confers broad tropism through interaction with the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), which is widely expressed on the surface of most cell types [,], pseudotyping with the BaEV glycoprotein resulted in reduced efficiency in pigs compared with mice and humans [], highlighting the importance of species-specific optimization. BaEV utilizes the neutral amino acid transporter ASCT1 as a receptor in human and murine cells. Although this receptor is highly conserved across mammalian species [], differences in receptor expression levels or compatibility may exist between murine, human, and porcine cells, potentially limiting viral entry in the latter. Future studies should therefore explore alternative envelope glycoproteins to achieve improved tissue or cell-type specificity in pigs and chickens [].

Although our findings are currently limited to primary cells and organoids, they provide proof of principle for VLP-mediated Cre delivery in chicken- and porcine-derived systems and establish a basis for future in vivo studies. If successfully translated in vivo, this approach could eliminate the need for breeding Cre driver lines with loxP-containing animals, thereby reducing breeding efforts, surplus animals, and experimental timelines. Although commercially available chicken lines carrying loxP-based reporter systems exist (e.g., the Chameleon line []), there are currently no commercially available Cre-expressing chicken lines, largely due to the associated phenotypic burdens observed in constitutive Cre expression []. In pigs, several loxP-based disease models have been established [,] that require tissue-specific activation by Cre recombinase. However, only a limited number of Cre driver lines are available, such as the PTF1A-Cre line []. Importantly, PTF1A expression is not strictly restricted to the target organ (pancreas), which may result in off-target recombination and unintended disease phenotypes. In addition, breeding strategies to generate the required transgenic animals are time-consuming and require large numbers of animals. The future application of Cre VLPs in ovo and in vivo could overcome the need for a Cre-expressing transgenic line and thereby drastically reduce the number of animals required for breeding strategies that combine Cre and loxP lines.

Cas9 VLPs enabled robust SKOs in pKDNFs and organoids. Of the two multiplexing strategies evaluated, combining separate single gRNA VLP batches (MPS2) maintained high editing efficiencies across multiple loci and supported complete fragment deletions using dual gRNA strategies targeting a single locus. In contrast, packaging two gRNAs into a single VLP batch (MPS1) reduced overall editing efficiency and introduced biased gRNA usage. We hypothesize that co-expression of two gRNAs in producer cells leads to competition for Cas9 binding during ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly. Differences in gRNA stability or affinity for Cas9 may result in preferential formation of one RNP species [], which is subsequently enriched during VLP packaging. In addition, the limited cargo capacity of VLPs may further contribute to the observed reduction in editing efficiency, as distinct RNP complexes compete for incorporation into particles. Consequently, MPS2 facilitates the generation of combinatorial genotypes required for modeling CRC consensus molecular subtypes [–] and other multigenic disease states in livestock.

Microinjection of multiplexed Cas9 VLPs into the perivitelline space of porcine oocytes yielded a high proportion of efficiently edited blastocysts, thereby potentially simplifying the generation of new genetic lines. The lower blastocyst development rate observed following IVF compared with parthenogenetic activation is likely attributable to the inherent biological variability and technical limitations to porcine IVF, including variable fertilization efficiency, sperm quality, and polyspermy [–], rather than to VLP exposure. In comparison to conventional pronuclear injection—which is technically challenging in porcine oocytes []—VLP delivery circumvents the need for pronuclear targeting through biological transduction and may reduce risks associated with vector-encoded nucleases, such as off-target editing and mosaicism []. Although in silico off-target analysis predicted no or only few potential off-targets for the gRNAs used in this study (), more comprehensive investigations will be required to reliably assess the occurrence of off-target editing and mosaicism. Relative to our previous workflows employing DNA vectors or RNP complexes [], Cas9 VLP microinjection increased the proportion of edited blastocysts, underscoring its practical advantages for establishing genetically engineered livestock lines. Notably, no toxicity was observed in porcine cells, organoids, or oocytes, supporting further exploration of direct in vivo administration, pending appropriate safety evaluation of the immunogenic potential of VLPs.

In chicken cells, B2M targeting with Cas9 VLPs induced a rapid reduction in MFI and thereby in MHC-I expression in HD11 cells within 24–48 h. In ovo injection at ED12 resulted in reduced MHC-I expression in the bursa and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Remarkably, all analyzed bursi (100%) exhibited detectable gene editing, demonstrating the robustness of this approach in ovo. Consistent with the flow cytometry data, representative immunofluorescence staining of bursa sections confirmed reduced MHC-I surface expression in the bursa. The intensity of MHC-I staining varied between individual bursi, which may reflect variability in the efficiency of in ovo injection and subsequent VLP delivery. The relatively high variability observed in the PBMCs 7 days post-injection is likely attributable to technical challenges associated with in ovo vascular injections, including the difficulty of accurately targeting small and fragile embryonic blood vessels, which may result in variable delivery efficiency and occasional embryo loss. Collectively, these findings establish VLP-mediated delivery as a flexible platform for investigating immune and developmental gene function in avian systems, complementing prior in ovo VLP vaccine applications [] and extending the utility of VLPs beyond mammalian models. Notably, the high transduction efficiency (>98%) achieved in PGCs using sfGFP-VLPs enables broad opportunities for the generation of new GM chicken lines. Additionally, gene editing efficiency in PGCs reached approximately 20% 72 h post-transduction, indicating sustained Cas9 activity and selective persistence of edited cells in this population.

Multiplexed dCas9 VLPs supported a targeted passive demethylation strategy [] at the internal TP53 promoter P2 in porcine cells, achieving greater than 20% reduction at CpG sites using overlapping gRNAs over a six-day period. Delivery of a single gRNA resulted in markedly weaker effects, underscoring the advantage of multiplexing for efficient epigenome editing. Follow-up studies will assess the consequences of targeted demethylation on expression of relevant TP53 isoforms. In a porcine osteosarcoma model, Niu and colleagues reported that methylation levels at CpGs 2 and 3 within P2 differ by approximately 30%–40% between osteoblasts derived from healthy and diseased animals, correlating with increased expression of an oncogenic TP53 isoform driven by this promoter []. Based on these findings, the in vitro demethylation levels (>20%) achieved in our system could induce a more moderate, yet biologically relevant activation of isoform expression in vivo, thereby providing a suitable platform to investigate its functional consequences. Nevertheless, this hypothesis needs to be proven by future in vivo work. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dCas9 VLP–mediated demethylation extends the application of CRISPR technologies in livestock beyond genome editing towards targeted epigenetic modulation.

Finally, although constitutive Cas9- or Cre-expressing livestock lines represent valuable resources [,,], their generation requires extensive breeding and frequently results in unwanted genotypes. Beyond embryo genome editing, VLPs may also enable future applications in both germline and somatic genome engineering. In the in ovo model, direct VLP delivery could facilitate immunological and developmental studies and through targeted pseudotyping of primordial germ cells, may ultimately provide a strategy for generating stable genetically modified avian lines. Furthermore, tissue-specific in vivo delivery of VLPs in genetically modified pig models could enable flexible somatic genome editing, for example, by accelerating colorectal tumor development through local introduction of additional driver mutations. Together, these potential applications further highlight the versatility of VLP-based genome editing and its potential to support the 3R principles [].. This strategy enables inducible or stage-specific genetic perturbations throughout the animal’s life span [], thereby supporting more refined and flexible experimental designs.

In summary, our results establish VLP-mediated delivery as a safe, rapid, and effective platform for genome and epigenome manipulation across porcine and avian cell lines, organoids and in ovo models. By demonstrating transient and multiplexed delivery of Cre, Cas9, and dCas9 in diverse experimental settings, our study provides a stepwise validation of the technology from in vitro to ex vivo and in ovo settings. This progression provides a basis for exploring future in vivo applications, where VLP-mediated delivery may enable more efficient and targeted gene editing. Importantly, the systematic evaluation and optimization of the platform in non-animal and intermediate models supports the principles of the 3Rs, potentially helping to reduce animal use and avoid unnecessary in vivo experimentation. Collectively, these findings position VLP-based delivery as a practical tool to accelerate functional genetic studies in livestock cultures, with possible application in agricultural and biomedical research.

The mutations D10A and H840A disable Cas9’s cutting ability [], and they were introduced into the plasmid using NEBuilder HiFi DNA assembly. Potential off-targets with 0, 1, or 2 mismatches for all cloned sgRNAs were determined using CasOFFinder (http://www.rgenome.net/cas-offinder/) (). Off-targets with 3 or more mismatches were neglected, given that earlier studies reported an absence of off-target cleavage by VLP-delivered Cas9 at this mismatch level [].

Protocols for production of Cre and Cas9 VLPs were adapted from recent publications [,]. Briefly, 4 × 106 HEK293-FT cells were seeded into a Corning 10 cm dish (Sigma, Darmstadt, GER) and were transfected on the following day using Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER) or Viafect (Promega, Madison, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. For producing Cre VLPs, a mixture of Gag-Pol (8.1 µg), VSV-G (3 µg) and Gag-Cre (5.1 µg) was transfected. For producing Cas9 VLPs or dCas9 VLPs, a mixture of Gag-Pol (8.1 µg), VSV-G (3 µg), Gag-Cas9 or Gag-dCas9 (5.1 µg) and sgRNA-SUPERBLADE (13.2 µg) was transfected. For producing sfGFP-/mCherry VLPs, a mixture of Gag-Pol (8.1 µg), VSV-G (3 µg) and Gag-sfGFP or Gag-mCherry (5.1 µg) was transfected. Visible syncytia formation indicated successful co-transfection of all plasmids 24 h to 48 h after transfection (). 48 and 72 h after transfection, VLPs were harvested by removing the supernatant and were stored at 4 °C. To purify and concentrate the VLPs, the supernatant was centrifuged at 5,500g for 12 h at 4 °C or ultracentrifuged at 50,000g for 2 h 15 min at 4 °C and the resulting VLP pellet was resuspended in cold PBS. The purified VLPs can be stored short-term at 4 °C and long-term at −20 °C or −80 °C.

To quantify the protein content in the VLPs, ELISA was performed as previously described []. For quantification of the Cre amount in VLPs, the following antibodies were used: primary antibody anti-Cre recombinase (D7L7L) XP Rabbit mAb #15036 (Cell Signaling, USA) at a concentration of 19 ng/mL, secondary antibody Goat anti-rabbit IgG-HRP #4030-05 (SouthernBiotech, Birmingham, USA) at a concentration of 23.75 ng/mL. For quantifying the Cas9 amount in VLPs, the following antibodies were used: primary antibody mouse monoclonal IgGiK anti-Cas9 AB (7A9-3A3) (Cell Signaling, USA) at a concentration of 0.4 µg/mL, secondary antibody mouse IgGk BP-HRP sc-516102 (SantaCruz, Dallas, USA) at a concentration of 40 ng/mL. Three batches of distinctly produced Cre and Cas9 VLPs were measured and tested for functionality. For consistency of the experiment, typically 5–10 µL Cre VLPs and 10–20 µL Cas9 VLPs were used. It should be noted that the efficiency of all VLPs varies depending on the transduction of pig or chicken cells, which is why each batch was tested on the respective target cells to ensure maximal reliability and performance.

To test VLPs on pKDNFs, 150,000 cells were seeded in a 12-well plate. On the following day, medium was changed and 5–20 µL VLPs were added. Analysis was conducted starting 24 h post-transduction at distinct time points.

For Cre VLPs, pKDNFs from a dual fluorescent reporter pig were used [], which switch from mTomato to eGFP expression upon Cre-mediated recombination. Cells were transduced with 10 µL Cre VLPs and fluorescence microscopy (ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA) was conducted after 24, 48, and 72 h.

To compare Cre VLPs with commercially available tatCRE (Merck #SCR508, Darmstadt, GER), pKDNFs were additionally treated with 20 µL tatCRE for 6 h according to the manufacturer’s instructions. This corresponds to 200 U (4 µM Cre protein). In parallel, 5 µL Cre VLPs (12.75 U, as determined by ELISA) were applied. As Cre content in VLPs was quantified by ELISA and tatCRE units are based on the manufacturer’s functional reporter assay, the respective U values should not be considered directly equivalent. Cells were analyzed 48 h post-transduction by flow cytometry (Attunes NxT, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER) as well as fluorescence microscopy (ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA).

To test Cas9 VLPs, 20 µL were applied to the cells. Forty-eight hours post-transduction, cells were detached and gDNA isolated using QuickExtract DNA Extraction Solution (Biosearch Technologies, Petaluma, USA). PCR amplified a 200–700 bp region around the target locus (sequences in ). The product was checked for correct size on an agarose gel and subsequently sent for Sanger sequencing (Eurofins Genomics, Ebersberg, GER). Sequencing results were analyzed for the percentage of INDELs using the online ICE analysis tool by Synthego (https://ice.editco.bio).

To test reporter VLPs, 5 µL sfGFP-VLPs or 10 µL mCherry VLPs were added to the cells. sfGFP or mCherry expression was analyzed 24 and 48 h after transduction using fluorescence microscopy (ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA) and Flow cytometry (Attunes NxT, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER).

For demethylation, pKDNFs with high methylation levels at the target locus were used. 300,000 cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and transduced every second day with 20 µL of dCas9 VLPs for up to 15 days. Cells were harvested after 1, 3, 6, and 15 days for methylation analysis as described below, with remaining cells reseeded for continued treatment.

To test Reporter VLPs, 1 × 106 DT40 cells were seeded in a 12-well plate. The next day, 5 µL of sfGFP VLPs or 10 µL of mCherry VLPs were added to the medium. For PGCs, 125,000 cells were seeded in a 12-well plate and 5, 10, or 20 µL sfGFP VLPs were applied. Fluorescent protein expression was analyzed 24 h and 48 h after transduction using fluorescence microscopy (ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.3, San Diego, USA) and Flow cytometry (Attunes NxT, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER).

Chicken IghKO DT40 cells [] were used to test Cre VLPs in chicken suspension cells, as they exhibit an eGFP cassette flanked by loxP sites. 65,000 cells were seeded in a 12-well plate and on the next day 5, 10, and 20 µL Cre VLPs were added. eGFP expression was analyzed 24, 48, and 72 h after transduction using Flow cytometry (Attunes NxT, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER) and fluorescence microscopy (Discover ECHO Revolve v7.2.3, San Diego, USA).

To compare Cre VLPs with commercially available tatCRE (Merck #SCR508, Darmstadt, GER), DT40 cells were additionally treated with 20 µL tatCRE for 6 h according to the manufacturer’s instructions. This corresponds to 200 U (4 µM Cre protein). In parallel, 20 µL Cre VLPs (51 U, as determined by ELISA) were applied. As Cre content in VLPs was quantified by ELISA and tatCRE units are based on the manufacturer’s functional reporter assay, the respective U values should not be considered directly equivalent. Cells were analyzed 48 h post-transduction by flow cytometry (Attunes NxT, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER) as well as fluorescence microscopy (ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA).

To evaluate B2M Cas9 VLPs, 250,000 adherent chicken HD11 cells [] were seeded in 12-well plates and transduced the following day with 10 µL Cas9 VLPs. Cells were harvested 48 and 72 h post-transduction using PBS/EDTA and stained for flow cytometry with mouse anti-chicken MHC-I primary antibody (2.5 µg/mL) and IgG-APC secondary antibody (2 µg/mL). Data were acquired on an Attune NxT flow cytometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, Germany). For PGCs, 125,000 cells were seeded per well in 12-well plates, and cell pellets were collected after 48 and 72 h to assess gene editing. gDNA from HD11 cells and PGCs was isolated using the ReliaPrep Blood gDNA Miniprep System (Promega, Madison, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Gene editing was verified by PCR using FIREPol DNA Polymerase Mastermix (Solis Biodyne) with an annealing temperature of 60 °C and a 30 s elongation time; chicken B2M primers are shown in . PCR products were size-verified by agarose gel electrophoresis and subjected to Sanger sequencing (Eurofins Genomics, Ebersberg, Germany). INDEL frequencies were quantified using the TIDE web tool (https://tide.nki.nl).

Permission for taking biopsies from pigs was issued by the government of Upper Bavaria, Germany (ROB-55.2-2532.Vet_02-23-82). Experiments were performed according to the German Welfare Act and European Union Normative for Care and Use of Experimental Animals. Porcine colonic organoids were established from a biopsy of either normal mucosa or a polyp from a pigs’ colon as described before [] with adaptations to the protocol. Briefly, the tissue was minced and washed five times with PBS containing 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin. The tissue pieces were digested using preheated 10 mg/mL collagenase P (Sigma, Darmstadt GER) for 1 h at 37 °C. Afterwards, the tissue was resuspended in cold AIM V (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER) and the crypts were released mechanically by shaking for 30 s. The suspension was passed through a 100 µm cell strainer to remove unwanted residues. The crypts were pelleted for 5 min at 400g and plated in a prewarmed 24-well plate with Matrigel (Corning, New York, USA) with a density of 200–400 crypts per well. After 20 min at 37 °C, organoid growth medium (human) (OGM, Stemcell Technologies, Vancouver, CAN) with 10 mM Thiazovivin (Sigma, Darmstadt, GER) and 100 µg/mL Primocin (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Darmstadt, GER) was added. After 10 days in culture, Thiazovivin and Primocin were removed from the medium. To passage organoids, the medium was aspired, and the domes were dissolved with 1 mL cold PBS. The samples were pelleted and resuspended in cold PBS. The organoids were dissociated using a 25 G syringe and incubated with gentle dissociation reagent (Stemcell Technologies, Vancouver, CAN). The cells were again centrifuged and plated as described above.

Protocols for transduction of organoids with VLPs were adapted from previous publications []. Briefly, organoids were dissociated and centrifuged for 5 min at 400g. The pellet was resuspended in 500 µL OGM with Thiazovivin. The suspension was distributed to a 96-well plate with 100 µL per well and VLPs were added. The plate was then centrifuged at 200g and room temperature for 3 h and then incubated for 3 h at 37 °C. Finally, the suspensions were mixed, briefly centrifuged and plated again.

To test Cre VLPs, porcine colonic organoids were transduced with 5 µL of Cre VLPs. In case of a fluorescence readout, eGFP expression was analyzed 24, 48 and 72 h after transduction using fluorescence microscopy (ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA). In case of activation of latent oncogenic mutations, DNA and RNA were extracted from the organoids using the Qiagen Mini Kit following the manufacturer’s instructions. One dome of organoids was dissociated, centrifuged and resuspended in 350 µL lysis buffer. Concentrations of DNA and RNA were measured, and the samples stored immediately at −20 °C and −80 °C, respectively. DNA was submitted to recombination PCR and RNA to pyrosequencing, which is described below. Furthermore, the morphology of the organoids was assessed until 46 days after transduction.

To test Cas9 VLPs, porcine organoids were transduced with 20 µL of Cas9 VLPs. After 5 days, DNA was extracted and analyzed for INDELS as described above.

pKDNFs with high methylation levels in the desired promoter 2 (P2) region of TP53 were transduced with dCas9 VLPs. gDNA was extracted prior to and after transduction using QuickExtract DNA Extraction Solution (Biosearch Technologies, Petaluma, USA) and concentration was measured using FastGene NanoSpec Photometer (Nippon Genetics, Dueren, GER). For bisulfite conversion, the EZ DNA Methylation-Direct Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, USA) was used according to the manufacturer’s protocol starting from step 2. 400 ng gDNA were converted per sample. The reagents from the PyroMark PCR kit (Qiagen, Hilden, GER) were used to amplify the target region using 3 µL of CT-converted DNA as input. After confirmation of successful PCR, pyrosequencing was conducted using PyroMark Q48 Advanced CpG reagents on a PyroMark Q48 Autoprep instrument (Qiagen, Hilden, GER). The TP53 CpG Methylation assay was designed using PyroMark Assay Design 2.0 software (Qiagen, Hilden, GER).

To verify the activity of Cre delivered by VLPs, a PCR across the LSL cassette in intron one of both KRAS and TP53 was conducted. Isolated gDNA of wildtype and VLP-transduced organoids was used. GoTaq G2 DNA Polymerase (Promega, Walldorf, GER) was used for amplification and the following cycle conditions were set: 3 min 95 °C, then 40 cycles of 45 s, 95 °C, 45 s, 59 °C, 90 s, 72 °C followed by 5 min at 72 °C.

To prove that the latent mutations were activated and expressed by VLP delivered Cre, the proportion of wildtype (G) and mutant (A) KRAS and TP53 alleles was assessed. Therefore, RNA of wild-type and VLP-transduced organoids was isolated, and cDNA was synthesized using the LunaScript RT Master Mix Kit (NEB) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. cDNA was diluted (1:3) and the desired loci amplified with the PyroMark PCR kit (Quiagen, Hilden, GER). PCR fragments were checked on an agarose gel before submitting them to pyrosequencing. KRAS and TP53 allelic quantification assays were designed using PyroMark Assay Design 2.0 software (Quiagen, Hilden, GER) and pyrosequencing was conducted using the PyroMark Q48 Advanced CpG reagents on a PyroMark Q48 Autoprep instrument (Quiagen, Hilden, GER).

Oocytes were prepared and submitted to microinjection as described before [,]. Briefly, oocytes were isolated from prepubertal gilts (Vion SBL Food GmbH, Landshut, Germany) and maturated in vitro. The zygotes were either in vitro fertilized or submitted to parthenogenesis. In the first case, successfully maturated zygotes were determined visually, and deep-frozen sperm was thawed, prepared, and assessed for viability. Sperm was transferred to the zygotes and incubated in a triple-gas incubator at 38.5 °C for 7 h. Afterwards, the zygotes were washed and selected for the presence of two polar bodies indicating successful fertilization. The fertilized embryos were submitted to microinjection, where approximately 10 pL of VLPs were injected into the perivitelline space []. Embryos were cultivated for 7 days until blastocysts developed for the assessment of targeting efficiency. For parthenogenesis, following microinjection oocytes with polar bodies were submitted to activation by applying a 43 V DC current for 80 µs. Fused oocytes were washed and incubated with 5 µg/mL Cytochalasin B to prevent extrusion of the second polar body. After 3 h, activated oocytes were washed and cultivated for 7 days.

To assess the impact on embryo development, different dilutions of VLPs were injected into zygotes prior to parthenogenesis (). Subsequently, VLPs were injected into zygotes that were in vitro fertilized (). To analyze gene editing efficiencies, blastocysts were transferred into a PCR tube containing 12 µL embryo lysis buffer and incubated at 65 °C for 1 h followed by 95 °C for 10 min. Subsequently, the lysate was used as template for ICE analysis as described above.

TOCs were prepared as described before [] from embryonated JH-KO chicken eggs [] (TUM Animal Research Center, Freising, GER) that exhibit an eGFP cassette flanked by loxP sites. According to European regulations, interventions and treatments involving chicken embryos are not classified as animal experiments and are even recognized as a replacement method under the 3Rs principle. In accordance with Article 14 of the German Animal Welfare Ordinance (TierSchVersV), ethical approval is only required if chicken embryos are used at a developmental stage before hatching and are intended to survive beyond hatching. Therefore, terminal procedures such as organ harvesting prior to hatching do not require ethical review or authorization as animal experiments. Briefly, eggs were embryonated until ED20, embryos were decapitated, and the tracheae were removed. The tracheae were cut into 0.8 mm rings and transferred into a falcon holding 300 µL TOC Medium (Medium 199 with Hanks’ salts, 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin, 1% Glutamaxx). Ten µL Cre VLPs were added into a falcon containing n = 3 TOCs in medium. eGFP expression was analyzed 48 h after transduction using fluorescence microscopy (Discover ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA). In a second experiment, the TOCs were embedded in Cryomolds containing OCT Tissue Tek (Sakura Finetek, Torrance, USA), frozen on dry ice and cut into 7 µm sections, with 100 µm trimmed between consecutive sections. Images were acquired using flouresence microscopy (Discover ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA).

Wild-type eggs (White Leghorn, TUM Animal Research Center, Freising, GER) were collected and stored up to 3 weeks at 16 °C. For in ovo experiments, eggs were incubated at 37.8 °C, after 7 days the eggs were candled and infertile or dead eggs were removed. Fifty µL VLPs were injected into a blood vessel on ED 12 as described before []. On ED 19 blood was collected again in ovo, subsequently the embryo was decapitated and bursi were collected. PBMCs were isolated from blood using Histopaque (Sigma, Darmstadt, GER) and consequently were stained for flow cytometry analysis using primary mouse-anti-chicken MHC-I antibody (Clone F21-2; 2.5 µg/mL; Biozol #SBA-8345-01, Hamburg, GER); and secondary goat-anti-mouse IgG-APC (0,5 µg/mL; Biozol #SBA1031-11L, Hamburg, GER). Bursi were strained through a cell strainer, density centrifugation using Histopaque (Sigma, Darmstadt, GER) was performed and subsequently resulting cells were stained for flow cytometry as described before. gDNA was isolated from bursa cells using ReliaPrep Blood gDNA Miniprep System Kit (Promega. Madison, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. gDNA was analyzed for CRISPR edits as described above. In a second experiment, bursi were embedded in Cryomolds containing OCT Tissue-Tek (Sakura Finetek, Torrance, USA), frozen on dry ice and sectioned into 7 µm sections, with 200 µm trimmed between consecutive sections. Sections were stained using primary mouse-anti-chicken MHC-I antibody (Clone F21-2; 2.5 µg/mL; Biozol #SBA-8345-01, Hamburg, GER); and secondary goat-anti-rabbit IgG-AF568 antibody (0.01 mg/mL; Fisher Scientific #0.348.072, New Hampshire, USA). Flourescence images were acquired using ECHO flourescence microscope (Discover ECHO Revolve Version v7.2.2, San Diego, USA).
