medicine.title: Sex-specific mechanisms and therapeutics in heart failure: translating biology into personalized care
medicine.abstract: Sex is one of the most consistent, yet clinically underexploited, determinants of heart failure (HF) phenotype, mechanism, and outcome. Building on landmark reviews and the 2024 scientific statement of the Heart Failure Association, which documented well-recognized phenotypic differences but noted that their mechanisms remain only partially defined, this review examines how sex differences in HF arise and how firmly they should guide practice. Epidemiologically, female predominance in HF with preserved ejection fraction (EF) is age- and menopause-dependent rather than lifelong. Mechanistically, sex-divergent hormonal signalling, autonomic tone, coronary microvascular dysfunction and myocardial fibrosis often produce similar phenotypes through different mechanisms: microvascular dysfunction is similarly prevalent in both sexes but linked to fibrosis in women and atherosclerotic risk factors in men, and oestradiol regulates collagen synthesis in opposite directions in female and male cardiac fibroblasts. Clinically, comorbidities carry divergent prognostic weight by sex. Graded against the strength of evidence, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors show established sex-neutral efficacy, whereas the greater benefit of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism in women rests on subgroup signals that await confirmation. Natriuretic peptide concentrations are substantially sex-dependent, yet diagnostic thresholds remain sex-neutral, although sex-specific calibration is methodologically achievable. Women remain underrepresented in HF trials and less often referred to specialized care. HF is therefore best understood as a sex-differentiated syndrome whose frameworks were built largely around male-pattern disease. Sex-calibrated trial enrolment, sex-specific biomarker and EF thresholds, and stratification by menopausal stage are concrete next steps towards personalized care.
medicine.text:
Heart failure (HF) affects an estimated 55.5 million adults worldwide, and its global prevalence has more than doubled since 1990. In 2021, 29.2 million males (51.7%) and 27.3 million females (48.3%) were living with HF, a near-parity in case counts that masks substantial regional variation and a profound divergence in phenotype by sex. US prevalence is projected to reach 8.5 million by 2030. Within this burden, sex is one of the most consistent, yet clinically underexploited, determinants of phenotype, trajectory, and outcome. This review adopts the two-phenotype classification of the 2026 ESC guidelines [heart failure with reduced EF (HFrEF), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <50%; heart failure with preserved EF (HFpEF), LVEF ≥50%], which discontinued the heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) category because of its pathophysiological and therapeutic overlap with HFrEF; findings from studies using the earlier three-category classification are reported in their original terminology. This position is not universal: a contemporaneous Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) scientific statement argued that HFmrEF should be retained as a distinct, clinically actionable phenotype.

Men more frequently present with HFrEF of ischaemic aetiology, whereas women more frequently present with HFpEF, hypertension, diastolic dysfunction and valvular disease as underlying causes. This split is consistent globally: ischaemic heart disease remains the leading cause of HF in men, whereas in women its contribution is markedly lower, often comparable to or below that of hypertensive heart disease. After acute coronary syndrome treated with percutaneous coronary intervention, men had a higher 5-year risk of new-onset HFrEF than women in a propensity-matched analysis of 3334 patients (17.9% vs 14.8%, HR 1.22, 95% CI 1.03–1.44), with the divergence emerging within the first year. Women with HF are also older, have a higher ejection fraction (EF), and report a greater symptom burden at presentation, which complicates both diagnosis and outcome comparison.

The asymmetry is most pronounced in HFpEF. Among Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 years or older hospitalized with HF, female sex was independently associated with preserved systolic function (adjusted risk ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.63–1.78). This female predominance is, however, age-dependent: across the full adult age range, women younger than 50 years were 6% to 28% less likely than men to be hospitalized with HFpEF, and female predominance emerged only with advancing age, suggesting that its drivers, discussed in Sections 2–5, are age- and likely menopause-related. In a Japanese cohort of 2824 patients with HFpEF, the male proportion declined progressively from 75.6% at age 54 years or younger to 49.5% at 85 years or older (); the same cohort showed age-dependent differences in mode of death, discussed in Section 6.

The divergence extends to lifetime risk. In pooled data from Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) and the Cardiovascular Health Study, women had a higher lifetime risk of HFpEF than of HFrEF (10.7% vs 5.8%), whereas men had comparable lifetime risks of both (12.6% each), indicating that female predisposition to HFpEF is a lifetime-scale phenomenon rather than a cross-sectional prevalence pattern.

Sex also interacts with race. Black adults carry the highest HF burden, with roughly 2.5-fold higher hospitalization rates than White adults, earlier onset, and higher mortality; African American women have the highest HF prevalence of any race-sex subgroup, with a hospitalized presentation skewed more towards HFrEF than that of White women, whose excess burden is concentrated in HFpEF. Sex-specific HF biology therefore cannot be considered in isolation from other demographic modifiers.,

Outcome data add a further layer of complexity. Women with HF lose more life-years relative to sex- and age-matched population life expectancy than men after an index hospitalization, despite a generally higher EF and, in some subtypes, a more favourable short-term prognosis. In a UK primary care cohort of over 55 000 patients, women were diagnosed about 5 years later than men and had a 14% lower age-adjusted mortality (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.84–0.88), yet survival improved more in men over 2000–2017 (annual mortality reduction 2.9% vs 1.4%, interaction P < .001). A Swedish nationwide study spanning 1987–2014 (>700 000 patients) likewise found that the mortality gap relative to the general population has not narrowed equally by sex. Across three independent populations, women thus have lower age-adjusted mortality, yet lose more life expectancy and have seen slower improvement over time (). This paradox indicates that sex-specific mechanisms, and not merely sex-stratified prevalence, warrant dedicated synthesis.

Three independent cohort studies converging on the sex-differentiated outcome paradox in heart failure

Despite this evidence, sex has historically been underused as an analytic axis in HF trials: women remain underenrolled relative to their share of the HFpEF population, and sex-stratified analyses have often been underpowered, post hoc, or omitted. Recent trials and their subanalyses (Section 7) have begun to close this gap, but translation of sex-specific mechanistic insight into clinical decision-making remains inconsistent.

This review builds on a substantial body of prior synthesis. Landmark reviews established the clinical and pathophysiological landscape of sex differences in HF and why women are overrepresented in HFpEF,, addressed sex and gender as complementary determinants of HF, and, most recently, examined sex-related similarities and differences in response to HF therapies. The 2024 scientific statement of the Heart Failure Association of the ESC consolidated this knowledge into a society position on presentation, diagnosis, and management, while noting that the mechanisms behind the well-recognized phenotypic differences remain only partially defined. This review takes that gap as its starting point and adds four elements. First, it moves from documenting whether sex differences exist to examining how they arise, linking mechanism to clinical phenotype within a single framework. Second, it explicitly grades the evidence, distinguishing established sex-neutral effects from subgroup signals and unresolved questions. Third, it treats sex as a life-course variable modified by age and menopausal status rather than as a static category. Fourth, it addresses translation: sex-specific calibration is methodologically achievable, and the remaining barrier is clinical implementation, now within the two-phenotype classification of the 2026 ESC Guidelines.

We conducted a narrative synthesis of the literature on sex-specific mechanisms and therapeutic responses in HF. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for articles published between January 2018 and June 2026, with emphasis on studies from 2023 onwards reflecting recent sex-differential subanalyses of major HF trials; earlier landmark studies were included where foundational. Search terms combined ‘heart failure’ with ‘sex differences’, ‘sex-specific’, ‘oestrogen’, ‘androgen’, ‘autonomic nervous system’, ‘microvascular dysfunction’, ‘myocardial stiffness’, ‘SGLT2 inhibitors,’ and related terms. Reference lists of key reviews and trial subanalyses were hand-searched. Articles were selected on the basis of relevance, methodological quality, and recency, with priority given to large randomized trials, sex subanalyses, and mechanistic studies with translational relevance. This review follows the SANRA recommendations for narrative reviews.

Oestrogen exerts its cardioprotective effects primarily through two nuclear receptor subtypes, ERα and ERβ, both expressed in cardiomyocytes. Experimental evidence indicates that ERβ plays the dominant cardioprotective role in the failing heart: ERβ knockout models show increased mortality and exacerbated left ventricular remodelling after injury, while ERβ-selective agonism improves cardiac contractility and reduces fibrosis in models of pressure-overload HF, whereas ERα-selective activation does not replicate this benefit. Clinically, premenopausal women have consistently lower HF incidence and mortality than postmenopausal women and age-matched men, a difference long attributed to endogenous oestrogen's cardioprotective signalling, though the precise translational mechanism—and how it might be pharmacologically exploited—remains incompletely defined. This cardioprotective signal may be phenotype-specific rather than uniform across HF subtypes. In the MESA cohort, a higher testosterone-to-oestradiol ratio and lower oestradiol levels were associated with increased risk specifically of HFrEF, but not of HFpEF, in postmenopausal women—the HF subtype more commonly seen in older women—suggesting that declining oestradiol during menopause may differentially affect the vascular and cardiac remodelling pathways that lead to HFrEF vs HFpEF, rather than uniformly elevating HF risk across phenotypes.

Testosterone’s cardiac effects are more contested than oestrogen's and appear dose- and context-dependent. Physiological testosterone, acting through the androgen receptor, supports contractility and cellular energy metabolism, and low endogenous testosterone in men is associated with adverse cardiac remodelling and increased HF risk. Conversely, testosterone can also promote pathological hypertrophy and fibrosis via androgen receptor-mediated genomic pathways, particularly at supraphysiological concentrations, and animal models show testosterone enhancing early post-infarction remodelling while oestrogen protects against it in the same setting. This dual character—protective at physiological levels, harmful in excess or in specific remodelling contexts—distinguishes androgen signalling from the more uniformly protective role attributed to oestrogen and helps explain why androgen-based therapeutic strategies in HF have not translated as cleanly as hoped. This sex-divergence in androgen effects was directly tested using Mendelian randomization, which allows causal rather than merely associative inference. Using sex-specific genetic variants predicting testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin levels in over 425 000 UK Biobank participants, genetically predicted pro-androgenic profiles in women were causally associated with adverse markers of left ventricular structure and function typically associated with HFpEF and HF more broadly, whereas evidence of a comparable causal effect in men was substantially weaker. This asymmetry is notable: it suggests that androgen excess may be mechanistically more consequential for HF risk in women than in men—the inverse of the intuitive assumption that androgens matter primarily in male cardiac physiology—and adds genetic, causally anchored support to the more equivocal observational evidence discussed above ().

Rather than a gradual, chronological accumulation of risk, cardiovascular risk factors in women show a distinct acceleration around the perimenopausal period—an inflection driven by ovarian ageing rather than age alone. The American Heart Association's 2020 scientific statement on the menopause transition formalized this evidence, documenting that lipid profiles, visceral adiposity, blood pressure, and vascular function all worsen disproportionately during this window, independent of chronological ageing. This transition period is increasingly recognized as a critical opportunity for cardiovascular risk assessment and early intervention in women, rather than a symptomatic phase to be managed in isolation from cardiovascular health.

Early enthusiasm for hormone replacement therapy (HRT) as cardioprotective was reversed by the Women's Health Initiative and related trials, which found increased cardiovascular events with HRT initiation in older, more distant-from-menopause populations. Subsequent age-stratified reanalysis gave rise to the ‘timing hypothesis”: HRT initiated within 10 years of menopause onset or before age 60 is associated with reduced coronary heart disease and all-cause mortality, while initiation later—when vascular disease may already be established—shows neutral or harmful effects, potentially through destabilization of existing atherosclerotic plaque. This timing-dependence is central to understanding why HRT trial results have appeared contradictory across the literature, and it has direct relevance for how sex-specific HF risk should be counselled across the menopausal transition rather than treated as a fixed, age-independent exposure. Real-world evidence introduces further nuance to the timing hypothesis specifically for HF outcomes. A large retrospective cohort analysis of Taiwan's National Health Insurance Database found that hormone therapy use showed no significant association with HF risk, regardless of the presence or severity of menopausal symptoms. This contrasts with the more optimistic coronary heart disease outcomes seen in age-stratified randomized controlled trial reanalyses, suggesting that the cardioprotective signal from HRT timing may not translate uniformly to HF-specific endpoints—an important caveat given this review's focus on HF rather than cardiovascular disease broadly. Sex hormones therefore shape HF risk in sex-divergent and sometimes counterintuitive ways, from ERβ-mediated cardioprotection to a disproportionate harm of androgen excess in women, yet hormone therapy has not shown HF-specific benefit ().

A robust body of evidence shows that men and women differ systematically in autonomic cardiac control. Women show a relative predominance of vagal (parasympathetic) modulation despite typically higher resting heart rates, while men show comparatively greater sympathetic tone—a pattern documented across heart rate variability (HRV), muscle sympathetic nerve activity, and plasma catecholamine studies. This sex-based autonomic balance is not merely a resting-state curiosity; it has been proposed as a physiological substrate for some of the sex differences in cardiovascular risk and arrhythmia susceptibility observed across the HF spectrum (.).

The most comprehensive quantification of this comes from a meta-analysis pooling 172 studies and nearly 300 000 participants, which confirmed that women show significantly higher HRV indices consistent with vagal dominance, alongside a lower mean R-R interval, across the healthy adult population. This sex difference in HRV persists across age groups, though its magnitude attenuates with advancing age and menopausal status, suggesting a hormonal contribution layered on top of an underlying sex-based autonomic architecture.

These autonomic differences carry direct clinical relevance. Sex differences in β-adrenergic receptor responsiveness have been linked to relative cardioprotection in females, and given the well-established relationship between sympathetic overactivation and both arrhythmogenesis and mortality in cardiovascular disease, this autonomic asymmetry is a plausible contributor to the sex differences observed in arrhythmia susceptibility and sudden cardiac death risk. Clinically, subgroup analyses of HF trial data suggest a somewhat more favourable beta-blocker response in women compared with men, in contrast to renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, where treatment benefit appears more consistently demonstrated in men—a divergence that may partly reflect the underlying autonomic and receptor-level sex differences discussed above, though trial data remain limited by historical underenrollment of women. However, this mechanistic and observational picture should be weighed against the strongest available quantitative evidence: a systematic meta-analysis pooling 25 randomized controlled trials and over 100 000 HFrEF patients found no statistically significant sex-treatment interaction for either beta-blockers or renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASi), for all-cause mortality or the composite of mortality and HF hospitalization. This suggests that while autonomic and receptor-level sex differences provide biological plausibility for differential drug response, the aggregate randomized-trial evidence does not yet support treating beta-blocker or RASi efficacy as meaningfully sex-differentiated in clinical practice—a distinction this review revisits in Section 7.

Men more frequently develop obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease, whereas women disproportionately present with coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) in the absence of obstructive disease. This is not simply a diagnostic curiosity: among patients referred for coronary angiography, excess cardiovascular risk in women relative to men was found to be associated specifically with severely impaired coronary flow reserve (CFR) rather than obstructive disease—meaning the standard angiographic workup systematically underdetects the pathology driving risk in women.

Direct evidence links impaired CFR to future HFpEF hospitalization. In a prospective cohort of patients undergoing evaluation for suspected coronary disease, those with both impaired CFR and elevated diastolic filling pressures (E/e′) had a more than five-fold increased risk of HFpEF hospitalization compared with patients with diastolic dysfunction alone—an adjusted annualized HFpEF hospitalization rate of 14.6% vs 2–3% in other subgroups. This establishes CMD not as a bystander finding but as an independent, quantifiable contributor to HFpEF risk that compounds the effect of diastolic dysfunction rather than merely correlating with it.

The structural basis for this risk was demonstrated in an autopsy-based study comparing myocardial tissue from HFpEF patients, hypertensive patients without HF, and controls: HFpEF hearts showed significantly reduced coronary microvascular density alongside increased myocardial fibrosis, independent of epicardial coronary artery disease severity or hypertension history, with fibrosis inversely correlated with microvessel density. This provided the first direct histological evidence that microvascular rarefaction and interstitial fibrosis are coupled processes in HFpEF, rather than fibrosis being a downstream consequence of macrovascular ischaemia alone.

A cardiac MRI study directly comparing sex-stratified predictors of reduced myocardial perfusion reserve found that traditional atherosclerotic risk factors (diabetes and hyperlipidaemia) predicted impaired perfusion in men, while in women, perfusion impairment instead correlated with left ventricular mass index and native T1 relaxation times—markers of hypertrophy and diffuse fibrosis rather than classical risk-factor burden. This suggests CMD arises through mechanistically distinct pathways by sex: a risk factor-driven atherosclerotic pathway in men vs a structural/fibrotic pathway more characteristic of women—directly relevant to how CMD screening and risk stratification should be interpreted differently by sex rather than applying a single unified threshold. This sex divergence in CMD's underlying biology extends beyond structural imaging correlates to the molecular level. In the prospective multinational PROMIS-HFpEF study, CMD (defined as CFR <2.5) was similarly prevalent in men and women with HFpEF (77% vs 70%, P = .27)—indicating no meaningful sex difference in CMD burden itself—yet proteomic profiling identified substantially different circulating biomarker correlates of CFR by sex, with minimal overlap between the proteins independently associated with CMD in men vs women. This reinforces the conclusion that CMD in HFpEF is not a single, sex-uniform pathophysiological entity: while its prevalence is comparable across sexes, the molecular pathways driving it appear substantially distinct, with direct implications for how sex-tailored diagnostic biomarkers or therapeutic targets for CMD might eventually be developed.

A recent narrative synthesis frames CMD as the vascular-to-myocardial disease axis in HFpEF, incorporating hormonal, immune-metabolic, and myocardial-vascular coupling mechanisms. Taken together, impaired CFR predicting HFpEF hospitalization, autopsy-confirmed microvascular rarefaction coupled to fibrosis, and sex-divergent pathways to CMD position CMD as a shared endpoint reached through sex-specific routes, fibrosis-linked in women, and risk factor-linked in men, in contrast to the macrovascular atherosclerosis that dominates male-pattern HFrEF ().,

Titin is a major determinant of cardiomyocyte passive stiffness, with alternative splicing producing a more compliant N2BA and a stiffer N2B isoform. In HFpEF, increased cardiomyocyte stiffness has been linked to altered titin phosphorylation, providing a cellular mechanism of diastolic dysfunction that is distinct from extracellular matrix fibrosis., Emerging evidence suggests that female hearts may exhibit greater titin-related stiffness, in contrast to the fibrosis-driven stiffness more characteristic of men. Titin also contributes to genetic susceptibility: titin variants are the most frequently identified mutations underlying HF, although their penetrance is likely shaped substantially by inflammatory and autoimmune mechanisms.

Extracellular matrix remodelling is also strongly influenced by sex and hormonal status. Although women tend to show greater overall myocardial stiffness under pressure overload, men have generally shown a greater whole-myocardial fibrotic response than premenopausal women. Experimental studies indicate that oestrogen signalling contributes to this difference in a sex- and context-dependent manner. In cardiac fibroblasts, 17β-oestradiol reduced collagen I and III expression in female-derived cells, and collagen condensation in engineered tissue derived from them, whereas opposite effects were observed in male-derived cells, reflecting differences in ERα- and ERβ-mediated signalling (). Under pro-fibrotic stimulation, however, ERβ activation can suppress myofibroblast transition and collagen production., Thus, the effect of oestrogen on cardiac fibrosis cannot be described as uniformly anti- or pro-fibrotic, but depends on sex, receptor context and the underlying profibrotic stimulus.

Importantly, this balance changes with ageing. Loss of ovarian oestrogen after menopause is associated with increasing inflammation, extracellular matrix deposition, and myocardial stiffness in women, providing a plausible mechanistic link to their increasing susceptibility to HFpEF with advancing age. A study of fibroblasts from endomyocardial biopsies of patients with HF further suggests that sex differences involve not only the amount of fibrosis but also the pathways through which fibroblasts become activated: male cells show broader TGF-β-associated extracellular matrix remodelling, whereas female cells, particularly in HFrEF, may exhibit a more inflammatory and collagen-producing phenotype. These observations support the concept that similar increases in myocardial stiffness may arise through different cellular mechanisms in women and men, raising the question of sex-stratified anti-fibrotic strategies, which current evidence does not yet resolve. Epicardial adipose tissue may provide an additional link between metabolic disease and myocardial stiffness, particularly in obesity-related HFpEF. Adipose-derived inflammatory mediators and microvascular dysfunction can promote interstitial fibrosis and elevated filling pressures, although reported sex differences in epicardial adiposity remain dependent on the imaging method used.,, Notably, echocardiographic epicardial fat thickness has been associated with haemodynamic signs of pericardial constraint in women but not in men, although the sex interaction was not statistically significant; it nonetheless offers a concrete pathway linking epicardial adiposity to elevated filling pressures in women.

Sex differences in myocardial stiffness are detectable before symptomatic HF develops. In a post hoc analysis of the PARABLE trial in patients with asymptomatic pre-HFpEF (stage B), women had higher left ventricular end-diastolic stiffness, filling pressure, effective arterial elastance and systemic vascular resistance, together with lower total arterial compliance, than men, after adjustment for age, hypertension, diabetes, obesity and vascular disease, and despite a lower burden of diabetes and coronary artery disease. These findings suggest that sex differences in cardiomyocyte stiffness, extracellular matrix remodelling, and ventricular–arterial coupling converge on a common physiological consequence in women: higher diastolic filling pressures and greater arterial load. At the organ level, sex-specific remodelling trajectories are less settled. Under pressure overload, both sexes initially develop concentric hypertrophy, but the classic view that women remain concentric while men progress to eccentric hypertrophy has been challenged by hypertensive and population cohorts in which women showed more abnormal, often eccentric, left ventricular geometry, and body-size indexing may have confounded earlier comparisons.,

Sex differences in myocardial stiffness thus arise at the level of titin, fibroblasts and adipose tissue, are modulated by age and menopausal status and are detectable before symptoms, identifying the pre-HFpEF stage as a potential, as yet untested, window for sex-specific screening or intervention ().

Sex-related phenotypic divergence is most extensively characterized in HFpEF, reflecting both its larger research base and the female predominance discussed in Section 1; this section also considers the more limited evidence for sex-differentiated phenotyping within HFrEF, particularly by aetiology. Across comorbidities, a recurring pattern emerges: the same condition can carry different risk and prognostic weight in women and men ().

Despite a lower overall comorbidity burden, women with cardiometabolic HFpEF show a similar metabolic syndrome profile: in a UK Biobank cardiac magnetic resonance study, men more often accumulated two to three cardiometabolic comorbidities and women one to two, despite comparable metabolic derangement, and latent class analysis identified sex-associated subgroups differing in body composition, lipid biomarkers, and resting cardiac output. A lower comorbidity tally in women may therefore not indicate lower cardiometabolic risk, and comorbidity-based risk tools calibrated on male-predominant patterns may underestimate risk in women.

Diabetes shows the most robust sex-differential signal. In a meta-analysis of 47 cohorts comprising over 12 million individuals, diabetes conferred a greater excess relative risk of incident HF in women than in men, most pronounced for type 1 diabetes (pooled relative risk 5.15 vs 3.47; women-to-men ratio 1.47) and smaller but significant for type 2 diabetes. The asymmetry is not explained by glycaemic control alone and has been attributed to sex-divergent vascular, inflammatory, and possibly diagnostic-delay mechanisms, suggesting that diabetic women may warrant closer HF surveillance. The link between diabetes and outcome also varies with age: in a Japanese HFpEF cohort, poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c > 7.0%) independently predicted sudden cardiac death in patients aged 64 years or younger (adjusted hazard ratio 4.26, 95% CI 1.45–12.5) but not in older patients, in whom HF-related death predominated. The mechanisms underlying this age-dependent association remain uncertain (Section 1).

The prognostic effect of obesity once HF is established, the so-called obesity paradox, also appears to differ by sex, but the direction of the difference is unresolved. In a pooled analysis of two Korean registries, higher body mass index was associated with lower 1-year mortality in men but not in women, consistent with an earlier single-centre study. In contrast, in a large international cohort with advanced systolic HF, overweight conferred a survival benefit in women, whereas overweight or obese men had higher adjusted mortality, with a significant sex-by-BMI interaction. A large Taiwanese cohort found no obesity paradox in either sex across EF categories. These discrepancies may reflect differences in fat distribution, muscle mass, fitness, and population characteristics in body composition that were not consistently measured, rather than a settled biological effect.

Frailty, more prevalent in women with HF, shows an unresolved sex-specific prognostic role. In a NHANES-based cohort of 958 patients with HF, frailty independently predicted cardiovascular mortality in women, whereas an earlier elderly outpatient cohort found that frailty predicted mortality and readmission in men but not in women. Among 103 patients with concurrent chronic kidney disease and HF, female sex was associated with frailty (P = .021), and frailty with markedly worse health-related quality of life, the outcome these patients themselves prioritized over survival or avoidance of hospitalization.

Nutritional risk, at the opposite end of the body composition spectrum from obesity, also shows a sex-divergent prognostic pattern. Among 234 patients hospitalized with acute HFpEF, a higher NRS-2002 nutritional risk score was associated with a roughly 11.6-fold increase in the odds of in-hospital mortality per unit increase in men but not in women. Together with the frailty findings discussed above, this suggests that cachexia and related body composition derangements are active contributors to HF pathophysiology whose prognostic weight differs between sexes, such that sex-neutral thresholds may misestimate risk.

Cardiorenal interaction is similarly not sex-neutral: women hospitalized for acute HF more often develop worsening renal function during decongestion, with a disproportionately higher subsequent risk of cardiovascular death and rehospitalization (Section 7).

Iron deficiency shows a bidirectional sex pattern. In a chronic HF cohort followed for a median of 84 months, absolute iron deficiency was twice as prevalent in women as in men (30.1% vs 14.6%), whereas functional iron deficiency was more prevalent in men (16.6% vs 9.3%); in each sex, the less prevalent subtype carried the greater prognostic weight, functional iron deficiency predicting adverse outcomes in women and absolute iron deficiency in men. Because intravenous iron trials such as FAIR-HF and AFFIRM-AHF used a single, sex-neutral definition of iron deficiency, sex-stratified analyses of existing and future trial data are warranted. The pattern is also context-dependent: in a separate cohort, the female predominance of iron deficiency was significant in chronic but not acute HF, and prevalence varied more than six-fold depending on which of three common definitions was applied, a threshold sensitivity paralleling the NT-proBNP calibration problem discussed in Section 8.

Atrial fibrillation shows a sex-differentiated prognostic signature within HFpEF. Women with atrial fibrillation-associated HFpEF had the most abnormal left ventricular geometry and diastolic function of any subgroup and were the only group in which atrial fibrillation independently predicted adverse cardiovascular outcomes (hazard ratio 2.7), whereas men carried intermediate, less differentiated risk. Atrial fibrillation may therefore identify a distinctly high-risk HFpEF phenotype in women, which warrants evaluation of whether rhythm or rate control strategies should be tailored by sex.

Within HFrEF, sex-differentiated prognosis appears aetiology-dependent. Among 7487 patients with HF, cumulative mortality in HFrEF with ischaemic cardiomyopathy was higher in men than in women, whereas mortality in non-ischaemic HFrEF was similar between sexes. Women in both subgroups were older, with higher EF and smaller left ventricular diastolic dimensions, yet sex was not an independent predictor of mortality after adjustment for aetiology and these covariates. The male disadvantage thus concentrates in the ischaemic pathway, consistent with the oestrogen-mediated protection against post-infarction remodelling (Section 2) and the male predominance of obstructive epicardial coronary disease (Section 4), and it begins early: men also face a higher risk of new-onset HFrEF after acute coronary syndrome (Section 1).

Standard HF diagnostic frameworks were developed predominantly in cohorts with male-pattern disease. Because normal female hearts have a higher EF than male hearts, a fixed EF cut-off (lower limit of normal 61% in women vs 55% in men on cardiac magnetic resonance) may capture women with more advanced remodelling relative to their own physiological baseline than men captured by the same threshold, a bias built into the diagnostic criteria rather than into disease biology, with consequences for trial enrolment, phenotyping and the therapeutic responses discussed in Section 7. Further evidence from a Swiss cohort of 5824 patients with HF indicates that the prognostic significance of LVEF varies according to sex and follow-up duration, supporting the need to consider sex when interpreting EF as a marker of disease severity.The same principle applies at the molecular level: in a blood-based multi-omic study differentiating HFpEF from HFrEF, distinct transcriptomic and proteomic panels were required to achieve comparable diagnostic accuracy in men and women. Across comorbidities and diagnostic tools alike, the same finding can carry different weight in women and men, so sex-neutral thresholds, from iron indices to EF and biomarker panels, risk misclassifying patients of one sex ().

Among the major HF drug classes, SGLT2 inhibitors show the most consistent sex-neutral efficacy and therefore provide a reference point for evaluating the more heterogeneous evidence below. In the EMPEROR-Preserved trial, empagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization to a similar degree in both sexes (hazard ratio 0.81 in men vs 0.75 in women, P for interaction = .54), although women in the placebo arm had a lower baseline risk. A pooled patient-level analysis of DAPA-HF and DELIVER confirmed this consistency across the full EF spectrum: women had better adjusted outcomes regardless of treatment arm (adjusted HR for cardiovascular death 0.69), while the relative effect of dapagliflozin did not differ by sex. A meta-analysis of four trials spanning HFrEF and HFpEF reached the same conclusion. SGLT2 inhibitors are therefore among the few HF drug classes with a trial-confirmed sex-neutral efficacy profile (). Because most women in these trials were postmenopausal (mean age 66–72 years), however, this consistency cannot establish whether efficacy is independent of oestrogen status, and evidence in premenopausal women is lacking.

Sex-specific therapeutic response in heart failure by drug class and strength of evidence

ACEi, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; ARB, angiotensin receptor blocker; ARNI, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor; EF, ejection fraction; HF, heart failure; HFpEF, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; HFrEF, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; MRA, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; RCT, randomized controlled trial; SGLT2, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2.

In contrast, sacubitril-valsartan shows a sex-differential signal that is most evident in HFpEF. In the prespecified sex subgroup analysis of PARAGON-HF, which narrowly missed its primary endpoint, the reduction in HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death was greater in women than in men, a divergence proposed to have contributed to the borderline overall result. The signal was not uniform across outcomes: women had greater reductions in HF hospitalization but smaller improvements in patient-reported health status. Across the EF spectrum, a pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF (HFrEF) and PARAGON-HF showed that the benefit of sacubitril-valsartan diminished with increasing EF in both sexes but extended to a higher EF range in women than in men. One proposed explanation, discussed in Section 6, is that a uniform EF cut-off, applied to women whose normal EF is higher, may enrich trial populations for women with more advanced remodelling relative to their own physiological baseline; their greater benefit may then reflect a diagnostic threshold that is not sex-calibrated rather than a fundamentally different drug response.

Sex differences in autonomic and β-adrenergic signalling (Section 3) provide a plausible basis for differential beta-blocker response, and trial subgroup analyses suggest a somewhat more favourable response in women, whereas angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) benefit has been demonstrated more consistently in men within historically male-dominated HFrEF populations. However, a meta-analysis of 25 randomized trials including over 100 000 patients with HFrEF found no significant sex–treatment interaction for either class. This divergence most likely reflects the limited power of individual trial subgroups: sex-differentiated efficacy for these classes remains a plausible hypothesis rather than a practice-changing finding.

A secondary sex-stratified analysis of the TOPCAT trial found that spironolactone's effect on the primary composite outcome in HFpEF differed by sex, with a more pronounced benefit in women than in men.

Loop diuretic therapy shows a clinically meaningful sex asymmetry in practice. Among 6545 patients hospitalized for acute HF (40% women), women received lower loop diuretic doses (furosemide-equivalent dose through Day 5: 200 vs 240 mg intravenously) and lost less weight, with a slightly lower diuretic response per unit dose, despite similar symptom improvement. They were nevertheless more likely to develop worsening renal function during decongestion (adjusted hazard ratio 1.24), and when it occurred, it carried a disproportionately higher risk of 180-day cardiovascular death and rehospitalization than in men. Lower doses therefore did not protect women against renal injury, and sex-specific decongestion strategies warrant prospective investigation rather than extrapolation from male-predominant dosing conventions.

Obesity-related HFpEF, the phenotype most closely linked to the inflammatory-metabolic pathway discussed in Section 5, has become a direct target of incretin-based therapy., In a prespecified pooled analysis of STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM (1145 patients, 49.7% women), women had higher body mass index, higher C-reactive protein and worse symptoms at baseline, despite a higher EF and less atrial fibrillation. Semaglutide 2.4 mg reduced body weight more in women than in men (−9.6% vs −7.2%, P for interaction = .006), yet improved the KCCQ Clinical Summary Score (P for interaction = .94), 6-minute walk distance and the hierarchical composite endpoint to a similar degree in both sexes. This dissociation between a sex-differential weight effect and a sex-neutral symptomatic benefit suggests that the benefit is not simply proportional to weight loss. The finding should not be generalized to the whole class: in a meta-analysis of six trials (24 781 patients), earlier GLP-1 receptor agonists evaluated in broader diabetic populations had a neutral effect on cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization in both sexes.

Myosin-targeted therapies show sex-differential signals in both directions of modulation. In GALACTIC-HF (n = 8232), sex did not modify the effect of the cardiac myosin activator omecamtiv mecarbil (P for interaction = .68); although women reached higher plasma concentrations at equivalent dosing, they had fewer serious adverse events, including ventricular arrhythmias. In a post hoc analysis of the DIG trial, the calcium-dependent inotrope digoxin was associated with higher all-cause mortality in women but not in men; an inotrope acting directly on myosin rather than on calcium handling may therefore be better suited to women, a hypothesis that remains to be tested. In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a distinct entity that can present with HF-like symptoms, the myosin inhibitor mavacamten produced more than twice the symptomatic improvement in women compared with men in EXPLORER-HCM (KCCQ-CSS 14.8 vs 6.1 points, P for interaction = .026). Whether sex-divergent excitation–contraction biology consistently shapes the response to both myosin activators and inhibitors (mavacamten, aficamten) remains an open question for future research.

Sex differences in body composition, renal clearance and volume of distribution mean that identical doses can produce different plasma exposures, but whether this justifies sex-specific dosing remains contested. A post hoc analysis of BIOSTAT-CHF found that women with HFrEF had the lowest risk of death or HF hospitalization at about half the ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker doses associated with the lowest risk in men. This was not replicated in CHARM, which found no sex difference in achieved candesartan dose or in the dose–outcome relationship, nor in HEAAL, where higher-dose losartan improved outcomes in both sexes. The optimal-dosing question therefore remains unresolved, and the frequently cited ‘half the dose’ finding should not be regarded as settled.

Treatment patterns also differ across healthcare systems. In contrast to the female underuse of guideline-directed therapy commonly reported in Western cohorts, a Taiwanese cohort of 12 428 hospitalized patients found higher use of every major drug class in women than in men, associated with lower long-term all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in women, mainly in HFpEF and HFmrEF. Female underuse may therefore reflect healthcare-system and referral dynamics rather than sex biology (Section 9).

Women experience adverse reactions to HF medications more often than men and account for up to two-thirds of drug-induced QT prolongation and torsade de pointes, partly through sex-hormone effects on repolarization. Sex-specific pharmacology is therefore a matter of risk minimization as well as efficacy, and both dimensions remain limited by the persistent underrepresentation of women in HF research. Across drug classes, only SGLT2 inhibitors have established sex-neutral efficacy; the apparent advantages of other therapies in women rest on subgroup signals, and sex-specific dosing remains unresolved ().

Women generally have higher circulating NT-proBNP concentrations than men, including among individuals without established cardiovascular disease, although this sex difference varies with age and may not persist in the oldest age groups. In a large general-population reference cohort, median NT-proBNP concentrations in women were 1.7- to 2.4-fold higher than in age-matched men before age 60—for example, 51 pg/mL vs 21 pg/mL under age 30, and 66 pg/mL vs 38 pg/mL at ages 50–59—with a moderately elevated NT-proBNP (≥125 pg/mL, the universal definition of heart failure's corroborating threshold) roughly 9-fold more likely in women than men after adjustment, even in the complete absence of classical cardiovascular risk factors. This is not confined to healthy populations: in a large HF outpatient cohort, NT-proBNP levels were higher in women than men across every body-mass-index category studied, with women showing NT-proBNP cut-offs for risk prediction ∼30% higher than men's regardless of BMI. The clinical consequence is direct: applying a single, sex-neutral NT-proBNP threshold—as most current guidelines and the universal HF definition do—will systematically flag more women as biochemically abnormal at any given level of true cardiac dysfunction, or conversely, may under-flag men relative to their own risk, since the same absolute number carries different diagnostic weight depending on the expected sex-specific baseline. Despite this well-documented divergence, no major guideline has yet adopted sex-specific NT-proBNP cut-offs for either diagnosis or risk stratification, a discrepancy between the strength of the evidence and current clinical practice that represents one of the clearer near-term opportunities for sex-specific personalization discussed in this review (). Recent diagnostic accuracy research has evaluated age-adjusted NT-proBNP thresholds in the community, including analyses stratified by sex and body mass index. Such studies provide a practical framework for evaluating subgroup-calibrated diagnostic thresholds, although age-based calibration should not be conflated with evidence supporting sex-specific thresholds.,

A complementary rather than replacement biomarker strategy may offer a more immediate path forward than awaiting sex-specific recalibration of natriuretic peptides. Soluble ST2 (sST2), a biomarker of myocardial fibrosis and mechanical stress, is reported to be largely unaffected by sex, age, BMI, renal function, atrial fibrillation, anaemia, or HF aetiology—in direct contrast to NT-proBNP's substantial sex-dependence—while retaining independent prognostic value in both acute and chronic HF. This sex-invariance is not entirely uncontested in narrower populations (one study in kidney transplant candidates found sST2 correlated with male sex). A serial proteomic study in stable HFrEF patients similarly found IL1RL1 (the gene encoding the ST2 receptor) to be significantly higher in men than women at baseline, independent of clinical characteristics—a direct measurement that further complicates the sex-neutrality claim in this specific population, even as the weight of evidence in broader, more heterogeneous HF cohorts continues to support sST2's relative sex-invariance. Combining sST2 with NT-proBNP—reflecting two mechanistically distinct pathways, natriuretic stretch response vs fibrotic-inflammatory remodelling—has been proposed to offer more balanced, less sex-confounded risk stratification than either biomarker alone, though this combined approach has not yet been adopted into major HF guidelines and its specific value for correcting sex-based misclassification has not been directly tested.

Beyond single biomarkers, the same calibration question applies to composite HF risk scores more broadly. As discussed in Sections 6 and 7, sex differences in body composition, renal clearance, comorbidity clustering, and baseline EF all feed into most contemporary risk-prediction models, yet the majority of widely used HF risk scores were derived and validated in cohorts with substantial male overrepresentation, particularly in the HFrEF literature predating the SGLT2 inhibitor era. The NT-proBNP evidence above provides a concrete, quantifiable example of a broader pattern: a single-threshold approach calibrated on a mixed-sex population without accounting for the systematic baseline offset between sexes risks misclassifying risk in a sex-differential way even when the underlying biomarker or model performs well on average.

A concrete counter-example demonstrates that sex-specific calibration is achievable in practice, even if not yet applied to natriuretic peptide thresholds. The American Heart Association's PREVENT equations—the current primary-prevention risk model recommended for estimating cardiovascular disease risk, including HF specifically—are explicitly sex-specific, deriving separate risk equations for men and women from a derivation cohort of over 3.2 million individuals. External validation demonstrated good discrimination in both sexes, with a C-statistic of 0.79 in women and 0.76 in men, suggesting that sex-specific model architecture does not come at the cost of predictive performance in either sex. That such calibration has been implemented for a general cardiovascular risk tool but not yet for HF-specific biomarker thresholds such as NT-proBNP illustrates that the barrier to sex-specific risk stratification in HF is not technical or methodological, but one of clinical translation and guideline uptake.

The unmet needs below follow directly from the four contributions outlined in the Introduction: where mechanisms are now understood well enough to be tested clinically, where therapeutic evidence remains at the level of subgroup signals, where menopausal stage modifies the effect of sex, and where calibration is ready for clinical translation.

Despite three decades of regulatory and professional-society attention, women remain persistently underrepresented in the HF trials that shape guideline-directed therapy. In a systematic analysis of the 33 HFrEF randomized controlled trials that demonstrated significant mortality or hospitalization benefit and subsequently influenced the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guidelines, women comprised only 23.2% of the pooled 104 972 participants (participation-to-prevalence ratio 0.58, against a benchmark of 0.8–1.2 considered adequate representation)—meaning the evidence base underlying current first-line HFrEF therapy was generated in a population that systematically underrepresents the sex making up roughly half of the real-world HFrEF patient population. This is compounded by a documented—though, as discussed in Section 7, not universally replicated—dosing consequence: some observational analyses have reported that women obtain optimal clinical benefit from ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers at lower doses than men, though this finding has not been consistently confirmed across major trial reanalyses; regardless, guideline-recommended target doses remain uniform across sexes, derived predominantly from male-dominated dose-finding cohorts.

This underrepresentation is not confined to the research setting; it extends into routine clinical practice through disparities in access to specialized care. A scoping review of sex-based differences in referral to outpatient HF clinics—settings associated with improved guideline-directed therapy uptake and outcomes—found consistent evidence that women are less likely than men to be referred to specialized HF care, independent of disease severity. This referral gap compounds the trial-enrolment gap described above: women are simultaneously underrepresented in the evidence base that defines optimal HF care and less likely to be routed towards the specialized settings where that evidence-based care is most consistently delivered—a dual disadvantage that trial-design reforms alone would not fully address.

The mechanistic and therapeutic-response evidence synthesized across this review—sex-divergent hormonal signalling (Section 2), autonomic tone (Section 3), microvascular pathophysiology (Section 4), myocardial stiffness mechanisms (Section 5), sex-specific comorbidity clustering (Section 6), differential drug response (Section 7), and biomarker calibration (Section 8)—collectively makes the case that HF is not one disease with a uniform sex-neutral treatment algorithm, but a sex-differentiated syndrome whose current diagnostic and therapeutic frameworks were built predominantly around male-pattern disease. The concrete, near-term precision-medicine opportunities emerging from this evidence include prospective, adequately powered dose–response studies to resolve whether sex-informed dosing for RAAS-modulating and beta-blocker therapy would improve outcomes—a question Section 7 shows remains genuinely open rather than settled; sex-specific NT-proBNP thresholds for diagnosis and risk stratification; and diagnostic EF thresholds that account for the systematic difference in normal female vs male EF rather than applying a single fixed cut-off across both sexes.

Three priorities follow directly from the gaps identified across this review. First, future HF trials—particularly in HFrEF, where underrepresentation is most severe—should adopt enrolment targets calibrated to disease-specific sex prevalence rather than convenience-based recruitment, with mandatory prespecified sex-subgroup reporting as a condition of publication and guideline citation, not an optional secondary analysis. Second, mechanistic research should move beyond documenting the existence of sex differences (the primary focus of the literature synthesized in Sections 2–5) towards testing whether sex-specific dosing, thresholds, or treatment algorithms derived from these mechanisms actually improve outcomes—the observational and mechanistic evidence base is now substantial, but prospective, sex-stratified interventional trials testing sex-tailored strategies remain rare. Third, given that many of the sex differences discussed throughout this review are modulated by menopausal status rather than chronological age alone (Section 2), future trial design and biomarker interpretation should stratify by reproductive/menopausal stage where feasible, rather than treating ‘female’ as a single homogeneous category across the adult lifespan.

medicine.title: Gut Stem Cell Secretome Therapy Promotes Durable Neuroprotection and Functional Recovery After Stroke
medicine.abstract: Stroke causes rapid neuronal death and gut barrier disruption in the acute phase, with persistent cognitive-affective impairment in the chronic phase. We previously showed that transplants of intestinal epithelial stem cells ameliorated the acute and chronic impairment of stroke. The current study tested the efficacy of a cell free strategy, specifically, the secretome of intestinal epithelial stem cells.Middle-aged male and female rats underwent middle cerebral artery occlusion or sham surgery and received intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome from healthy sex-matched adult or control media. Behavioral assays (social interaction, novel object recognition and Barnes maze), gut histology, markers of gut permeability, serum cytokines were performed at acute and chronic time points. Group differences were assessed by two-way ANOVA.In the acute phase, vehicle-treated stroke animals displayed histopathological changes in the gut including villus blunting, loss of goblet cells, increased markers of gut permeability and elevated systemic inflammation. In the chronic phase, stroke resulted in cognitive/affective changes including social withdrawal, recognition memory and spatial memory deficits. In middle-aged males, three doses of IESC secretome treatment 4h/24h/48h after stroke restored mucosal architecture, goblet cells and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase. Cognitive and social outcomes, tested 4+ weeks after stroke, were significantly improved compared to vehicle-treated stroke animals. However, in middle-aged females treated with the same regimen of intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome, gut architecture was not restored and inflammatory cytokines remained elevated. Long term cognitive impairment was only partially improved in this group. Proteomic analysis of the secretome revealed a largely shared core of proteins between males and females with sex differences in pathway level regulation. Subsequently, another cohort of middle-aged females was administered four doses of secretome 4h/12h/24h/36h after stroke. This regimen restored gut architecture and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase, and improved long term cognitive outcomes.Collectively, these studies underscore the therapeutic potential of IESC secretome and the importance of tailoring post stroke therapy by demographics such as biological sex. These data further support the hypothesis that gut ‘repair’ is tightly associated with long-term improvement in stroke outcomes.
