N heterocycles, while the peak at 818.49 cm−1 was assigned to the characteristic breathing mode of triazine units in g-C3N4. A broad band absorption in the 3150–3500 cm−1 region corresponds to the stretching vibration modes of terminal NH groups. The FTIR spectra of both the SrFe12O19 MNPs and 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite show the characteristic peaks of metal–oxygen stretching vibrations at around 460–630 cm−1. In addition, the lower intensity of the g-C3N4 characteristic peaks in the nanocomposite is due to the low g-C3N4 concentration. However, the peaks around 3400 and 1600 cm−1 are attributed to the stretching and bending vibrations of the adsorbed water on the hexaferrite NPs, respectively. These results indicate that the 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite heterostructure is well-obtained.

XPS investigations were performed to assess the chemical and surface electrical configuration of the as-synthesized SrFe12O19 MNPs, 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite, and 2D g-C3N4 material (). The XPS survey spectra of SrFe12O19 and g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 confirm the presence of C, N, Sr, Fe, and O elements (). The deconvoluted high-resolution C 1s spectrum is shown in (). The peak at 284.2 eV reflects the sp2 C–C bonds in the CN structure. The peaks at 285.9 and 288.3 eV are the characteristic peaks of [C]3–N and NC–N or sp2-bonded carbon in the nitrogen aromatic system, respectively.  displays the deconvoluted spectrum of N 1s with binding energies (BE) at 398.6, 399.7, and 401.1 eV, assigned to the C–NC bond, N–[C]3, and C–NHx (sp2 hybridized nitrogen in triazine unit), respectively. The distinctive doublet of Sr2+ (Sr 3d5/2 and Sr 3d3/2) is responsible for two peaks in the XPS spectrum of Sr 3d in SrFe12O19 at BEs of 133.08 and 134.68 eV ().

The high-resolution XPS spectra of the Fe 2p regions of the 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite reveal two spin–orbit doublets at BEs of approximately 710 and 720 eV, which correspond to the Fe 2p3/2 and Fe 2p1/2 core-levels, respectively. Additionally, there are two additional peaks at BEs of approximately 719 and 732 eV, attributed to shakeup satellites (). As a result, the BEs of the 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 peaks (ΔE ≈ 13.5 eV) and the satellite peaks closely match the reported values for Fe3+.

Three peaks in the BE region of 529–534 eV can be seen in the deconvoluted spectrum of O 1s (). The lattice oxygen in the metal–oxygen bond is responsible for the peak at a BE of around 530 eV, while the adsorbed O− or O22− species at BEs of around 531.5 eV are linked to the intrinsic oxygen vacancies on the surface. Notably, the slight shift in the Sr 3d and O 1s corresponding peaks of hexaferrite could be explained by the coordination environment of the SrFe12O19 MNPs after their deposition on the 2D g-C3N4 material.

At neutral pH, zeta potential measurements were conducted to assess colloidal stability, particle size, surface charge, and photocatalyst interactions with the pharmaceuticals. When photocatalyst particles are dispersed in solution, their surface charge can affect system stability and the adsorption or interaction of polar or non-polar reactant layers, as well as the resulting photocatalytic activity. As a result, photocatalyst nanoparticles with opposing surface charges would be able to greatly boost the adsorption capacity and hence improve the photocatalytic performance of the target pollutant with their specific electric charge. In addition, dispersion increases with stronger negative or positive zeta potential, which also improves stability and colloidal properties due to electrostatic repulsion. The zeta potential analysis measurement of the g-C3N4 nanosheets is about −32.4 mV (), whereas the g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite had a surface charge of −30.6 mV in deionized water. In general, a zeta potential value of more than ±30 mV is thought to result in enough repulsive force to improve physical colloidal stability. According to zeta potential data, the colloidal suspensions of the as-synthesized nanomaterials have a net negative surface charge in aqueous solutions, which promotes good colloidal stability over an extended period. The as-synthesized g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite reveals an average particle size of approximately 264.8 nm (). In contrast, the average sheet size of pure g-C3N4 is about 1382 nm. This could be explained by the reduced nanosheet size after the decoration of the g-C3N4 surface by SrFe12O19 MNPs.

The optical properties of the as-synthesized 2D g-C3N4, SrFe12O19 MNPs, and 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite were determined using UV-DRS (). The visible light absorption edge of pure g-C3N4 is at about 440 nm, corresponding to the intrinsic bandgap absorption. The SrFe12O19 reveals a maximum visible light absorption edge at about 800 nm. Compared to g-C3N4, the absorption range in the visible region widens following the introduction of SrFe12O19 MNPs into the 2D g-C3N4. Furthermore, the bandgap energies were calculated based on Tauc plots ((αhv)2 = A(hv − Eg)) (). The Eg values of the pure g-C3N4 and M-type hexaferrite SrFe12O19 are about 2.70 and 1.46 eV, respectively. In contrast, the Eg edge of the hybrid nanocomposite g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 is at about 1.60 eV. The results of the optical response indicate that the preparation of the heterostructure g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 can significantly improve the optical absorption properties and enhance the conversion efficiency of solar light, which is beneficial for enhancing the photocatalytic activity.

The morphology, size, and shape of pure and decorated M-type SrFe12O19 MNPs on 2D g-C3N4 were studied using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (). The FESEM images show a uniform distribution of SrFe12O19 MNPs with interconnected spherical-like shapes and a size range of about 25–55 nm. Moreover, the TEM image of the g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite shows densely grafted SrFe12O19 MNPs on the surface of the 2D g-C3N4 sheets, indicating the successful decoration of g-C3N4 sheets with SrFe12O19 nanoparticles.

The N2 adsorption–desorption isotherm curves of SrFe12O19 MNPs and the 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite are shown in . According to the IUPAC classification, the isotherms of the hexaferrite MNPs may be assigned to type II for both SrFe12O19 and g-C3N4/SrFe12O19. Additionally, the BET surface areas of the obtained nanomaterials were found to be 24.91 and 176.53 m2 g−1 for SrFe12O19 and g-C3N4/SrFe12O19, respectively. This confirms the good dispersion of MNPs on the g-C3N4 sheets, with significant defects in the overall porous structure.

The photocatalytic performance of the prepared nanomaterials was evaluated for the degradation of tetracycline (TC) as an APC model substrate in an aqueous solution. Prior to photodegradation, the batch experimental setup was kept in the dark for 60 min to achieve an adsorption–desorption equilibrium. This step is essential for distinguishing the contribution of adsorption from that of photodegradation and ensuring that any decrease in concentration under irradiation is primarily due to photocatalytic activity.

As seen in , employing SrFe12O19 MNPs and 2D g-C3N4 as photocatalysts results in a moderate photodegradation efficiency for tetracycline. This limited activity can be attributed to the rapid recombination of electron–hole pairs and to restricted light absorption in certain regions of the spectrum. The degradation of the antibiotic is significantly enhanced when both nanomaterials are combined as the 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite. Furthermore, the contribution of direct photolysis of TC remains negligible, confirming that the degradation observed is primarily catalytic.

The as-synthesized g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 reveals the highest degradation efficiency of 73% in 180 minutes. This significant improvement reflects the presence of a synergistic effect between the two semiconductor phases within the heterostructure. This higher photocatalytic efficiency can be attributed to improved light absorption, accelerated photogenerated charge separation during photocatalysis, and the high surface area of the 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite compared with those of the pristine nanomaterials (SrFe12O19 MNPs and 2D g-C3N4). In particular, the interface between g-C3N4 and SrFe12O19 promotes the directional transfer of electrons and holes, which reduces their recombination and increases the formation of reactive oxygen species (˙OH and ˙O2−), responsible for the degradation of tetracycline.

The effect of the catalyst concentration on the antibiotic removal efficacy has also been examined (). An initial catalyst concentration of 0.2 g L−1 reveals a modest degradation efficiency of about 32%. Meanwhile, as the catalyst concentration increases to 0.4 g L−1, an optimum photocatalytic degradation of 64% is obtained in 2.5 h. Beyond 0.4 g L−1, stable photocatalytic degradation was observed, which is explained by particle collision and agglomeration with increasing adsorbent dosage, resulting in a decrease in the available specific surface area for adsorption.

illustrates the effect of the catalyst concentration on the degradation efficiency of tetracycline. A significant increase in the degradation rate is observed when the concentration increases from 0.2 to 0.4 g L−1, reaching a maximum of approximately 64%, which can be attributed to the increase in the number of available active sites and to greater production of reactive species under irradiation. Conversely, beyond this optimal concentration, a decrease in efficiency is observed at 0.6 and 0.8 g L−1. This decrease can be explained by screening effects limiting light absorption, as well as particle agglomeration at high concentrations, which reduces the active surface area and promotes the recombination of electron–hole pairs.

Since pH affects adsorption and pollutant dissociation, its effect on the photocatalytic degradation of TC was investigated (). It was observed that the change in the pH of the reaction medium affected the rate of TC photocatalytic degradation. The results show that the degradation rate increases gradually as the pH rises, from approximately 15% at pH 2.5 to nearly 55% at pH 10. This low efficiency in a strongly acidic environment can be attributed to the protonation of the photocatalyst surface as well as to the dominant cationic form of tetracycline, which limits favorable electrostatic interactions and the generation of reactive species. At neutral pH (pH ≈ 7), a significant improvement in degradation is observed (∼48%), suggesting conditions more favorable to the production of oxidizing radicals. Under basic conditions, maximum efficiency is achieved, which can be explained by the increased formation of hydroxyl radicals (˙OH) and by the predominance of anionic forms of TC (pKa ≈ 3.3; 7.7; 9.7), facilitating their interaction with the active species generated on the catalyst surface. These results confirm that pH plays a decisive role in the photocatalytic process, with alkaline conditions generally being more favorable for the degradation of antibiotics.

To shed more light on the optimization of the reaction conditions, the effect of tetracycline concentration was studied (). The initial TC concentration ranged between 10−4 and 10−5 mol L−1. At the lowest concentration, g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite degraded over 95% of the TC molecules. With increasing initial TC concentration, a consistent decline in the degradation efficiency is observed. At relatively low initial TC concentrations, the abundance of available photocatalytic active sites relative to the number of TC molecules favors efficient degradation. In contrast, at higher initial concentrations, the number of TC molecules increases relative to the available active sites, limiting their accessibility and reducing photocatalytic performance. Moreover, the increased concentration of TC molecules can hinder light absorption by the photocatalyst, further contributing to the slower degradation rate.

Radical scavenging experiments have been carried out to pinpoint the contribution and function of the main reactive species in the photocatalytic degradation of TC led by g-C3N4/SrFe12O19. For the analysis, various sacrificial substances, including benzoquinone ([BQ] = 1 mmol L−1), tertiary butyl alcohol (TBA 2% (v/v)), and triethanolamine ([TEA] = 1 mmol L−1), are used as scavengers of the superoxide radical (˙O2−), hydroxyl radical (˙OH), and holes (h+), respectively. The impact of the scavengers on the nanocatalyst photodegradation effectiveness is shown in . The investigation revealed that BQ reduces the percentage of degradation from 86% to 7%, suggesting that ˙O2− is the main contributing species in the total degradation process. In contrast to BQ, the addition of TEA and TBA results in a modest suppressing effect. The analysis is further supported by the location of the band edge potential, indicating that the production of ˙O2− is possible, as previously mentioned, and that this is the main active species responsible for the indirect photodegradation of TC.

Stability and reusability represent the main factors that determine the suitability of a photocatalyst for use in terms of sustainability and the circular economy. The hybrid g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 photocatalyst was recovered by simple separation using an external magnet for further runs. The photocatalytic degradation efficiency of TC remains fairly stable at 95, 90, 84 and 81% over 4 consecutive runs (). The XRD spectrum shows that the identity of the recovered hybrid 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocatalyst remains stable with no significant modification (). The SEM image of the recovered photocatalyst () shows a uniform distribution of nanoparticles with no obvious change in the morphology compared with the fresh photocatalyst (). The material, with excellent stability and recoverability in diverse media, may have potential applications in photocatalysis.

Total organic carbon (TOC) measurement was used to track the kinetics of total tetracycline mineralization in the aqueous phase. As shown in , a significant reduction in TOC was effective from the early phases of irradiation to 90% mineralization after 24 h. Thereafter, with a prolonged reaction time of 72 h, almost total tetracycline mineralization of 95% is achieved, with the disappearance of all photoproducts that are obtained at the start of the photocatalytic process (95% degradation within 3 h). This confirms that the as-prepared 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite is highly effective for total mineralization of APCs and other organic contaminants.

The scope and limitations of the as-developed nanocatalytic heterojunction system, 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19, were further investigated in the photodegradation of APCs and other organic contaminants under optimized conditions. All organic pollutants were removed with good to excellent degradation efficiency: tetracycline 95%, sulfamethazine 68%, mefenamic acid 50%, and malachite green 93.5% (). Moreover, tetracycline is known for its relatively slow degradation under photocatalytic conditions, primarily due to its stable structure and resistance to oxidative attack. However, the catalyst's negative charge may improve the degradation rate by enhancing adsorption, allowing more effective interaction with reactive oxygen species (ROS). The negatively charged catalyst will predominantly attract the positively charged form of tetracycline, facilitating adsorption. Once adsorbed onto the surface, photogenerated ROS can degrade the antibiotic via oxidative mechanisms. Meanwhile, sulfamethazine and mefenamic acid carry a negative charge, which will lead to electrostatic repulsion with the negatively charged catalyst. The repulsion between the catalyst and these APC molecules may limit their adsorption, which reduces the overall photocatalytic degradation efficiency. On the other hand, a negatively charged catalyst enhances the photodegradation of malachite green due to the strong electrostatic attraction between the cationic dye and the negatively charged catalyst surface, leading to better adsorption. This increased adsorption brings more dye molecules in proximity to ROS, which break down the dye molecular structure. As a result, malachite green undergoes efficient degradation, making negatively charged catalysts particularly suitable for the photocatalytic removal of cationic dyes.

illustrates the potential charge separation, migration, and degradation processes inside the hetero photocatalyst. As shown in , both SrFe12O19 MNPs and 2D g-C3N4 are photoactivated when exposed to visible light, producing holes and electrons in their respective valence and conduction bands. Based on the normal hydrogen electrode (NHE), SrFe12O19 and g-C3N4 have conduction band (CB) potentials of +0.85 and −1.12 eV, while the measured valence band (VB) potentials were +2.31 and +1.58 eV, respectively. Therefore, the photogenerated electrons from g-C3N4 can be transferred to the CB of SrFe12O19 due to the more negative CB energy of 2D g-C3N4 compared with that of SrFe12O19 MNPs.

In contrast, the high positive VB energy of SrFe12O19 compared to g-C3N4 resulted in the recombination of the SrFe12O19 photogenerated holes with those of g-C3N4, leading to the transfer of photogenerated electrons to the VB of g-C3N4. The potential of O2/˙O2− (−0.33 eV) is more negative than the CB potential of SrFe12O19 (+0.85 eV); thus, the adsorbed oxygen molecules cannot be reduced to ˙O2− by the CB electrons of SrFe12O19. The formation of ˙OH cannot be directly attributed to the VB holes of g-C3N4 because its VB potential (+1.58 eV) is less positive than the standard redox potentials of OH−/˙OH (+2.40 eV) and H2O/˙OH (+2.72 eV). Therefore, the generation of ˙OH through direct oxidation of OH− or H2O by g-C3N4 VB holes is not thermodynamically favorable based on the reported band potentials. Accordingly, this pathway has been excluded from the proposed mechanism ().

The radical-scavenging experiments provide additional evidence regarding the reactive species involved in the photocatalytic degradation. The degradation efficiency decreased from 86% to 7% in the presence of benzoquinone (BQ), indicating a major contribution of ˙O2− radicals. The addition of tert-butanol (TBA) decreased the degradation efficiency from 86% to 40%, demonstrating the involvement of ˙OH, while triethanolamine (TEA) decreased the degradation efficiency to 35%, confirming a significant contribution of photogenerated holes.

These results cannot be satisfactorily explained by a conventional type-II mechanism because the electrons remaining on the SrFe12O19 CB would lack sufficient reduction potential for O2 activation. Therefore, considering both the experimentally determined band positions and the radical-scavenging results, an S-scheme charge-transfer mechanism provides a more consistent interpretation of the observed photocatalytic behavior. Hence, a reasonable process of carrier separation in the system can be explained and is presented in . After the formation of the inner electric field, photoexcited electrons in the CB of SrFe12O19 are prone to recombination with holes in the VB of g-C3N4, and S-scheme structure composites are formed, which promote electron accumulation in the CB of g-C3N4 and hole accumulation in the VB of SrFe12O19, possessing sufficient potential to readily form ˙O2− and ˙OH. This inhibition results in the availability of e−/h+ pairs in the CB of g-C3N4 and the VB of SrFe12O19, which enhances charge transfer at the g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 interface. So, the electrons in the CB of g-C3N4 react with O2 to form superoxide radicals, while holes in the CB of g-C3N4 oxidize OH− to ˙OH radicals. These holes, superoxide radicals and hydroxyl radicals interact with the complex structures of an antibiotic to break it into intermediates.

The electrons in the g-C3N4 CB possess sufficient reduction potential to reduce dissolved O2 to ˙O2−, which is consistent with the inhibition observed in the presence of BQ. Meanwhile, the highly positive holes in the SrFe12O19 VB have substantially stronger oxidation ability and can contribute to pollutant degradation and, depending on the interfacial/surface reaction environment, to ˙OH generation. The involvement of ˙OH and h+ is also supported by the inhibition observed upon the addition of TBA and TEA, respectively.

Finally, excess ˙O2− will react with H+ to form ˙HO2, and proceed to form ˙OH. The resulting separation of photogenerated electrons and holes facilitates their participation in reactions with reactants adsorbed on the surface of the g-C3N4/SrFe12O19. This leads to significantly enhanced photocatalytic performance due to the internal electric field formed at the interface, inducing the selective recombination of low-energy charge carriers while preserving the high redox potential electrons in the CB of g-C3N4 and holes in the VB of SrFe12O19. In addition, the charge transfer of the S-scheme structure is demonstrated indirectly by the production of ˙O2− and ˙OH, because such powerful redox ability can only be obtained in an S-scheme system.

As seen in , the photocatalytic efficiency of the developed g-C3N4 (5 wt%)/SrFe12O19 (95 wt%) photocatalyst is superior to those of other reported hexaferrite/g-C3N4 composites. It should be noted that a comparison of efficiencies and apparent rate constants of the degradation process should be considered cautiously since the reported data involve different pollutants, different catalyst amounts, different radiation conditions, and different initial concentrations of the pollutants and reaction times. Moreover, the developed photocatalyst composition differs significantly from several other reported materials where g-C3N4 acts as the main component and the hexaferrite was used only as a minor component. Therefore, the obtained photocatalytic efficiency shows that a relatively small amount of g-C3N4 can contribute to the photocatalytic efficiency of a SrFe12O19-rich nanocomposite due to a more effective charge separation and transfer process. Thus, the present approach shows the possibility of using SrFe12O19 as the main photocatalytically active component with g-C3N4 as an interfacial and dispersing material. This combination of photocatalytic activity, high hexaferrite content and magnetic recoverability highlights the potential of the developed composite for recyclable photocatalytic applications.

In conclusion, a simple approach was used for the successful preparation of a hybrid 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite. Pristine 2D g-C3N4 and SrFe12O19 MNPs, as well as the hybrid nanocomposite, were characterized using advanced techniques, i.e. XRD, FTIR, XPS, SEM, TEM, UV–DRS, and Zetasizer analysis. The resulting nanocomposite reveals a good degradation efficiency for tetracycline, as a model active pharmaceutical contaminant (APC), and a high magnetic recoverability over a number of cycles. Additionally, based on band structure analysis and photocatalytic performance, the enhanced activity of the 2D g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite can be attributed to an S-scheme heterojunction mechanism. Upon visible-light irradiation, the interfacial internal electric field between the two semiconductors facilitates the selective recombination of low-energy charge carriers, ensuring the conservation of high-energy electrons in 2D g-C3N4 and strongly oxidative holes in SrFe12O19 MNPs. The as-developed magnetic g-C3N4/SrFe12O19 nanocomposite could be used as a potential photocatalyst in APC and wastewater treatment processes thanks to its high activity, long-term durability, and easy magnetic recoverability.

medicine.title: Cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and neurodegeneration biomarkers in the diagnosis and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a multicohort observational study
medicine.abstract: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS.We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses including an external ALS cohort (n = 153).Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82–0.88), which increased to 0.90 (0.88–0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 [2.17–7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36–1.92]).Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical management of ALS.This study was primarily supported by JST SPRING (JPMJSP2125). A complete list of funding organisations is provided in Acknowledgements.
medicine.text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterised by progressive motor neuron loss. Current diagnostic criteria rely heavily on clinical observations,, which can be ambiguous and often require prolonged follow-up, contributing to diagnostic delays. Median survival is 2–5 years, but the clinical progression varies substantially. Reliable biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis are urgently needed, both to guide clinical management and to improve clinical trial design.

Fluid biomarkers, measured in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or blood, are well established in some neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's disease; AD), and have also been studied in ALS. Previous studies have demonstrated the high diagnostic and prognostic value of neurofilament light chain (NfL) in ALS., , ,  Some studies have reported modest alterations of AD-related fluid biomarkers in ALS, including phosphorylated tau (e.g., pTau181 and pTau217),, ,  glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP),, ,  and amyloid-β 42 (Aβ42)., , ,  However, it remains unclear whether these biomarkers can complement NfL in diagnostic or prognostic models. It is also uncertain whether the observed alterations in AD-related markers reflect AD co-pathology or can occur in ALS in the absence of AD. Only a few studies have incorporated Aβ status into their analyses, reporting plasma pTau elevations irrespective of Aβ status, or increased plasma GFAP levels in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup. The collective profile of AD-related biomarkers, especially in CSF, remains to be characterised in the context of overlapping ALS and AD. Given that the prevalence of AD pathology increases with age and influences biomarker levels even without symptoms,,, ,  disentangling AD-related processes is important both for accurate interpretation of fluid biomarkers and for understanding heterogeneity in ALS. Although rare neuropathological reports have suggested increased cognitive impairment in patients with motor neuron disease and concomitant AD pathology, the prognostic relevance of AD co-pathology in ALS remains uncertain, and in vivo data examining this interaction are limited.

To address these knowledge gaps, this study has three objectives: (i) to assess how the presence of AD co-pathology (i.e., positive CSF Aβ status) is associated with distinct biomarker profiles and clinical characteristics cross-sectionally and longitudinally in ALS; (ii) to determine whether additional CSF biomarkers improve diagnostic accuracy beyond NfL; and (iii) to evaluate how different fluid biomarkers add prognostic value to established clinical features in predicting disease progression, both for clinical practice and clinical trial development. Throughout our analyses, we sought to incorporate non-linear associations captured by machine learning (ML) approaches and to develop clinically interpretable frameworks. Following examples from the AD field, we developed a two-cutoff diagnostic strategy to enhance the use of biomarkers beyond simple cut-offs, while maintaining a clinically intuitive workflow.

We included patients with ALS and disease controls (DC) who had baseline CSF samples collected at Nagoya University Hospital. The diagnosis of ALS was established according to the revised El Escorial criteria (REEC) by at least two neurologists and neurophysiologists. The DC group consisted of (i) ALS mimics, defined as patients who were initially suspected of ALS but received an alternative diagnosis (e.g., myopathy and cervical spondylosis) after thorough investigation or follow-up; and (ii) patients with other neurological disorders that were clinically distinct from ALS, including Parkinson's disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), and idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). All participants underwent CSF sampling, along with standardised clinical assessments including routine blood tests. Sex was recorded as reported in the clinical records at baseline.

Patients with ALS who provided informed consent were enrolled in a prospective longitudinal cohort at Nagoya University, which started in 2013. For the present analysis, we included all consecutive participants with available baseline CSF samples enrolled between January 2013 and September 2024. At baseline, assessments included the revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R),, diagnostic classifications according to the REEC, pulmonary function tests, and cognitive screening using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Frontal Assessment Battery (FAB)., Longitudinal clinical data, including ALSFRS-R, were collected every six months through in-person visits or structured telephone interviews until death or censoring. When follow-up information could not be obtained, at least two additional contact attempts were made at different time points. If these attempts were unsuccessful, the case was censored at the date of the last confirmed contact. Edaravone and riluzole use were coded as binary variables indicating whether each patient had received the medication during follow-up.

Patients who provided separate informed consent specifically for genetic analysis underwent genetic testing. Pathogenic variants in major ALS-associated genes (e.g., SOD1, TARDBP, FUS, VCP, TBK1, and C9orf72) were assessed by whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing as part of established external sequencing projects.
C9orf72 repeat expansions were confirmed by repeat-primed PCR or long-read sequencing. APOE genotype was obtained from sequence-derived allelic calls at rs429358 and rs7412.

CSF samples were collected via lumbar puncture, aliquoted, and stored at −80 °C until analysis. Samples were transported from Nagoya University to Lund University under strict temperature control, and all assays were conducted at Lund University. We quantified the following CSF biomarkers: NfL, GFAP, Aβ peptides (Aβ38, Aβ40, and Aβ42), and phosphorylated tau (pTau181, pTau217). NfL and GFAP were measured using the Simoa Neurology 2-Plex B Assay (N2PB, Quanterix). Aβ38, Aβ40, and Aβ42 were measured on the MSD platform using the V-PLEX Aβ Peptide Panel 1 (6E10) Kit (Meso Scale Diagnostics). pTau181 and pTau217 were quantified using non-commercial MSD immunoassays developed by Lilly Research Laboratories (capture antibodies: IBA406 and IBA493, respectively; detector: SULFO-TAG-4G10-E2), as previously described., Catalogue and lot numbers for commercially available assays are provided in the . Aβ peptides were analysed from first-thaw aliquots, while other analytes were measured from aliquots that had previously been thawed once. To ensure inter-plate comparability, each plate included identical internal quality control (QC) samples. QC samples were assayed in duplicate for Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217. Plate-to-plate variation was corrected by normalising concentrations to the corresponding QC samples for each analyte. Study samples were measured in singlicate, and sample allocation was stratified to balance diagnostic subgroups across plates. The mean QC-based inter-plate coefficients of variation were 11.8% for Aβ38, 5.7% for Aβ40, 8.8% for Aβ42, 6.1% for pTau217, 18.3% for pTau181, 12.1% for GFAP, and 9.5% for NfL. The corresponding intra-plate coefficients of variation, derived from duplicate QC measurements, were 2.7% for Aβ38, 2.8% for Aβ40, 2.4% for Aβ42, 5.1% for pTau217, and 9.0% for pTau181. All assays adhered to the manufacturers' analytical procedures.

To enable cross-cohort bridging, all plates contained reference CSF samples from the Swedish BioFINDER cohort (NCT03174938). The CSF Aβ42/40 ratio threshold for Aβ positivity (0.077) was derived from the BioFINDER cohort, where it was validated against Aβ positron emission tomography (PET). In addition, given the potential role of Aβ40 as a reference marker for Aβ peptides, the Aβ38/40 ratio was evaluated as an index of relative Aβ peptide balance.

Routine blood test results, including creatinine (Cr), creatine kinase (CK), albumin (Alb), and cystatin C (CysC), were analysed by routine clinical chemistry methods at Nagoya University Hospital.

Pairwise correlations between baseline clinical characteristics and biomarker levels were assessed using Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients. Pearson correlations were used for biomarker–biomarker associations after log-transformation, whereas Spearman correlations were used for associations between biomarkers and clinical variables, as clinical variables included ordinal and non-normally distributed measures (e.g., MMSE). Differences among diagnostic groups were evaluated using Wilcoxon or Kruskal–Wallis tests, applying Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR) correction. Associations between cognitive scores (MMSE, FAB) and CSF Aβ42/40 were analysed using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and years of education.

Diagnostic performance was quantified by the area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). Individual biomarkers were first evaluated in isolation, followed by simple additive logistic regression models combining NfL with one additional biomarker. Generalised linear regression models (GLMs) and ML classifiers incorporating all measured fluid biomarkers were then evaluated within a nested 5-fold cross-validation framework repeated 10 times.

We additionally evaluated a two-step, NfL-first diagnostic strategy, reserving multivariable testing for cases not clearly classified by NfL alone: (i) NfL was applied in the first step using prespecified operating criteria of 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity to define an intermediate-NfL zone (i.e., “grey zone”); and (ii) patients within the grey zone were further classified by ML models using all other measured fluid biomarkers. The entire procedure was implemented within the same cross-validation framework. NfL thresholds corresponding to these operating criteria were derived in each training set and applied to the corresponding held-out test set. We then trained ML models on grey-zone cases within the training set and applied them to grey-zone cases in the corresponding held-out test set. Further details are provided in the  section below.

Two prognostic outcomes were defined: (a) the rate of functional decline, quantified from longitudinal ALSFRS-R trajectories; and (b) time to death or tracheostomy.

ALSFRS-R trajectories were analysed using linear mixed-effects (LME) models with random intercepts and slopes. Time × biomarker interaction terms were evaluated to determine each biomarker's association with ALSFRS-R decline. To examine potential modifying effects on NfL, we also assessed models including time × NfL × other CSF biomarker interaction terms. Continuous biomarker values and covariates were standardised to z-scores before constructing interaction terms in the LME models. Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIFs). For survival analyses, Cox proportional hazards models were employed. Entry time was defined as the date of the baseline visit, and participants were followed until death/tracheostomy or censoring. NfL × other biomarker interactions were also evaluated in the Cox models. Kaplan–Meier curves with log-rank tests were used to compare survival across relevant subgroups defined by biomarkers.

For both slope and survival outcomes, all models were evaluated as (i) unadjusted, (ii) adjusted for age and CSF NfL, and (iii) adjusted for core clinical features. For graphical presentation, NfL was categorised into tertiles, whereas it was modelled as a continuous standardised variable in the LME and Cox analyses. All multivariable analyses were performed using complete-case data. Core clinical features were defined based on prior literature and data availability in the cohort: age; vital capacity (percent predicted, %VC); baseline disease progression rate (ΔFS, calculated as [48—baseline ALSFRS-R] divided by [months from symptom onset to baseline]); site of symptom onset (bulbar vs spinal); and baseline REEC classification (definite vs others).,, In LME models, all covariates were specified with time interaction terms. In additional exploratory sensitivity analyses, the primary LME models were compared with models including the same core clinical covariates without covariate × time interactions; time × NfL × age and time × NfL × APOE ε4 status terms were also added separately to assess whether the time × NfL × CSF biomarker interaction remained after accounting for these additional potential effect modifiers. Subgroup analyses stratified by CSF Aβ status were also conducted for both slope and survival analyses.

To assess the consistency of the subgroup survival findings, we also analysed an independent ALS cohort from Bologna, Italy. The dataset included baseline CSF Aβ42/40, CSF NfL, survival data, and the core clinical covariates; CSF NfL was measured on the Simoa SR-X platform using the NfL Advantage Assay (Quanterix), and CSF Aβ42 and Aβ40 were measured using Lumipulse G β-Amyloid 1–42 and 1–40 assays (Fujirebio). Aβ positivity was defined according to the reported cut-off (CSF Aβ42/40 < 0.068), applied a priori. Cox subgroup analyses stratified by Aβ status were performed in the Bologna cohort, using the same covariates as in the Nagoya cohort, followed by cohort-stratified pooled analyses allowing cohort-specific baseline hazards. NfL was log-transformed and z-scored within each cohort. Given the available data structure, the Bologna cohort contributed only to the Aβ subgroup survival analyses.

For prediction-oriented analyses, individual ALSFRS-R slopes were calculated using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. Based on previous literature, we included patients with ≥3 valid assessments,, and required ALSFRS-R ≥20 at baseline., Assessments beyond the 24-month window after baseline were excluded to focus slope estimation on a clinical trial–relevant period and limit the influence of floor effects in advanced stages., To evaluate how well these simplified measures of individual functional decline could be predicted from baseline clinical and biomarker data, and whether ML improved prediction beyond conventional GLMs, we used these slopes as outcomes for GLMs and ML models. Sensitivity analyses were repeated after removing the baseline ALSFRS-R criterion, relaxing a minimum requirement of ≥2 ALSFRS-R assessments, or both.

We developed ML models for diagnostic classification and regression of individual ALSFRS-R slopes. To identify biomarkers that consistently contribute to predictive performance across different algorithmic architectures, we evaluated Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), support vector machines (SVM), and k-nearest neighbours (KNN), alongside GLMs using the same covariates. To ensure unbiased estimation and fair comparison across algorithms, all models were trained, hyperparameter-tuned, and evaluated using the same nested 5-fold cross-validation framework, as described below.

We first randomly partitioned the dataset into five non-overlapping folds, stratified by diagnostic group for classification analyses. In each outer loop, four folds (80% of the data) were used for model training and the remaining fold (20%) for testing. This procedure was repeated across all five outer loops, ensuring each participant was included in the test set once, thereby yielding one out-of-fold predicted value per participant. We then pooled out-of-fold predictions across outer loops to calculate cross-validated performance estimates (e.g., AUC and R2).

Hyperparameters were optimised within each training set using inner 5-fold cross-validation, with no use of outer test-fold data for model fitting or tuning. Where applicable, predictors were centred and scaled within each training fold. The optimal hyperparameter configuration was selected by maximising AUC for classification analyses and minimising root mean squared error for regression analyses. For XGB, the number of boosting rounds was determined by early stopping within the training set, with a maximum of 2000 rounds. In regression analyses, additional XGB parameters were explored using a small random search with time and iteration limits, and the best configuration was refit on the full training fold. For GLMs, no hyperparameter tuning was conducted, but model fitting was performed using the same outer folds as other algorithms.

Diagnostic performance metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV) and prognostic performance metrics (cross-validated R2 for slope prediction) were calculated based on pairs of out-of-fold predicted values and observed outcomes. To assess the robustness of performance estimates to data partitioning, we repeated the nested cross-validation procedure 10 times with different random 5-fold partitions. For each task, we selected the algorithm with the highest median performance across all 10 repeats (AUC for classification and R2 for regression) for detailed visualisation. Confidence intervals for diagnostic metrics were estimated by participant-level bootstrap; prognostic R2 variability was summarised across cross-validation repeats.

For the two-step diagnostic approach, we derived diagnostic performance metrics for each classification stage within the same repeated nested 5-fold cross-validation structure. In Step 1, NfL-based rule-in and rule-out cutoffs targeting 95% specificity and 95% sensitivity, respectively, were determined within each training set and applied to the corresponding test set, immediately assigning ALS or non-ALS labels to cases outside the cutoffs. Only cases with intermediate NfL values proceeded to Step 2. In Step 2, ML models were trained within the grey-zone subgroup in the training set (including selection of model-specific decision thresholds targeting 95% specificity) and then applied to grey-zone cases in the test set. Performance metrics based on out-of-fold predictions were summarised separately for (i) Step 1 rule-in and rule-out classifications, (ii) Step 2 Grey-zone classifications, and (iii) the overall two-step strategy. Grey-zone AUC reflects discrimination among grey-zone cases only, whereas the overall AUC was calculated from pooled final predictions across all cases.

Model interpretability was assessed using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values. To ensure representativeness, SHAP beeswarm plots and confusion matrices were generated from a representative repeat with overall model performance closest to the median across repeats. Additionally, mean absolute SHAP values, normalised as relative contributions within each algorithm, were summarised across all repeats to evaluate the consistency of feature importance across models.

We evaluated how NfL-based enrichment would reduce the required sample size for ALS clinical trials, using the same complete-case dataset as above (see  section). Patients were stratified by baseline CSF NfL, and the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of individual ALSFRS-R slopes were calculated within each subgroup. Assuming a treatment effect corresponding to an X% reduction in the absolute value of the mean slope (Δ = X% × |μ|), the standardised effect size was defined as Cohen's d = Δ/σ. Required total sample sizes (α = 0.05, power = 0.80) were computed using two-sample t-test-based power analysis under equal allocation and compared between all-comers and NfL-enriched subgroups (the upper 50% and top quartile) to quantify the relative sample-size reduction achievable through enrichment.

We also examined an outcome-adjustment approach. Crude sample-size requirements were calculated using two-sample t-test power analysis assuming Δ = 1–6 points over 24 weeks, α = 0.05, and power = 0.80, with an SD of 6.0 derived from the 24-week ALSFRS-R change assumption in the edaravone phase III trial. Adjusted sample sizes were estimated as: Nadjusted = Ncrude × (1 − R2), where R2 was obtained from cross-validated GLMs including baseline prognostic covariates.

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.5.0 using the packages lme4, caret, xgboost, and fastshap.

This study was conducted in accordance with the 2024 Declaration of Helsinki, and clinical data and biospecimens were used in accordance with the consent procedures approved for each study protocol. The Nagoya cohort study was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine (Nos. 2013–0035, 2015–0041, and 2022–0155) and complied with the applicable Japanese governmental ethical guidelines for medical research involving human subjects. Written informed consent was obtained from all prospectively enrolled participants. Retrospective use of existing clinical data and/or stored biospecimens was conducted under an opt-out procedure approved by the ethics committee. Study information, including instructions for opting out, was publicly available on the institutional website. The BioFINDER study (NCT03174938) was approved by the Regional Ethical Committee in Lund (No. 2016/1053), and the Bologna cohort study by the Ethics Committee of Area Vasta Emilia Centro (CE-AVEC 17151–17152); written informed consent was obtained from all participants in both studies.

The funders of the study had no role in study design, data collection, statistical analysis, results interpretation, or writing of the report.

A total of 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease controls (DCs), including 71 mimicking conditions (e.g., myopathy and cervical spondylosis), were included in the study (). Age and sex distribution were comparable between groups. Detailed disease categories and their baseline characteristics are described in . Most patients in the ALS cohort presented with spinal-onset, and baseline ALSFRS-R scores were consistent with early-to-mid stage. Ten patients classified as ‘suspected’ at baseline were later confirmed as having ALS and were retained in the analysis. The prevalence of Aβ positivity was similar between the ALS (14% [37/264]) and DC group (13% [21/164]; ). Across both groups, Aβ-positive individuals were older and had lower MMSE scores (). Among patients with ALS who consented to APOE genotyping, 20% (39/196) were APOE ε4 carriers, and Aβ positivity was more frequent in carriers than in non-carriers (28% [11/39] vs 11% [17/157]; age-adjusted odds ratio 3.40 [95% CI 1.35, 8.46]).Table 1Baseline characteristics of patients with ALS and disease controls.CharacteristicALSn = 264DCn = 164Age at baseline67 (58, 73)66 (53, 73)Sex (female)103 (39%)68 (41%)BMI at baseline21.1 (19.2, 23.3)22.1 (20.1, 24.5)Bulbar onset61 (23%)NAALS-associated genetic mutation No known pathogenic variant179 (68%)NA Pathogenic variant16 (6.1%) Genetic testing not performed69 (26%)ALSFRS-R at baseline42 (39, 44)NADisease duration at baseline, months12 (8, 22)NAREEC classification at baseline Suspected10 (3.8%)NA Possible51 (19%) Probable, laboratory supported51 (19%) Probable114 (43%) Definite38 (15%)%VC at baseline93 (76, 107)NAΔFS at baseline0.46 (0.25, 0.86)NAMMSE at baseline28 (26, 29)29 (26, 29)FAB at baseline15 (13, 17)15 (13, 16)APOE haplotype ε2 carrier11 (5.6%)NA ε3 homozygote146 (74%) ε4 carrier39 (20%)Aβ status (positive)37 (14%)21 (13%)Aβ, amyloid-β; ALS, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; ALSFRS-R, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale–Revised; APOE, apolipoprotein E; BMI, body mass index; ΔFS, disease progression rate from symptom onset to baseline; FAB, Frontal Assessment Battery; MMSE, Mini-Mental State Examination; REEC, revised El Escorial Criteria; %VC, percent predicted vital capacity.Median (Q1, Q3); n (%).DC (disease controls): ALS mimics (n = 71), CIDP (n = 31), MSA (n = 25), PD (n = 24), and iNPH (n = 13). Baseline biomarker concentrations across disease groups, stratified by Aβ status, are summarised in  and . Patients with ALS had elevated CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, Aβ38/Aβ40, pTau181, and pTau217 compared to DCs. In contrast, GFAP and Aβ42/40 ratios were comparable between groups. In analyses restricted to Aβ-negative individuals, CSF NfL and Aβ38/40 were markedly increased in ALS compared with DCs, while pTau181 and pTau217 showed smaller but statistically significant increases (). This pattern remained consistent when DCs were further stratified into detailed diagnostic subgroups, except for Aβ-negative MSA ().

Pairwise correlations among baseline biomarkers and clinical characteristics are summarised in . Most biomarkers showed moderate correlations with age (|r| ≈ 0.2–0.5). After adjustment for age, no significant sex differences were observed across fluid biomarkers, except for higher Cr (P < 0.001) and the Cr/CysC ratio in males (P = 0.011). Patients with known ALS-associated pathogenic variants (n = 16) were significantly younger than non-carriers (median 55 [IQR 48–59] vs 67 [59–73]; P < 0.001), but no fluid biomarkers differed significantly after FDR correction.

NfL was correlated with core clinical features, including ΔFS and %VC (|r| ≈ 0.2–0.4). A lower Aβ42/40 ratio was moderately correlated with higher pTau181 and pTau217 levels (|r| ≈ 0.3–0.5), and weakly correlated with worse MMSE and FAB scores in the ALS cohort (ρ ≈ 0.15, both P < 0.05; ). Although the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup showed largely preserved cognitive function (MMSE median 27 [IQR 24–28]; ), the association between Aβ42/40 and MMSE remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, and years of education (). Notably, Aβ38/40 did not correlate with Aβ42/40 within either the ALS or DC groups, suggesting that these measures may reflect distinct processes.

Diagnostic performance of fluid biomarkers is shown in . When each biomarker was evaluated individually in the full dataset, NfL showed the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.84, 95% CI 0.80–0.88), whereas Aβ38/40 (AUC = 0.67), CK (AUC = 0.66), pTau181 (AUC = 0.58), and pTau217 (AUC = 0.57) achieved modest performance (A). CK lacked specificity when compared with ALS mimics (note that 37% [26/71] of these had myopathic conditions). In contrast, the Aβ38/40 ratio showed less variation than CK across control groups (). Nonetheless, in comparison with DCs, adding any single biomarker to NfL in GLMs did not improve discrimination beyond NfL alone (B).

ML classifiers trained on all measured CSF biomarkers, blood creatinine, and CK, achieved high cross-validated diagnostic performance (C). RF and XGB models achieved AUCs of 0.90 (95% CI 0.88–0.92), exceeding that of NfL alone (0.85 [0.82–0.88]). These performance differences were consistent across 10 nested cross-validation repeats, with RF achieving the highest median AUC (). Feature-importance analyses using the representative RF model identified NfL, CK, and Aβ38/40 as the top three contributors (D). Across all evaluated algorithms and repeats, NfL remained the dominant feature, with Aβ38/40 and CK consistently ranked among the top contributors (E). These results indicate that while NfL remains the dominant diagnostic marker, additional biomarkers may provide complementary information that cannot be captured by simple additive models.

Building on the dominant diagnostic performance of NfL, we evaluated a clinically relevant two-step framework applying two cut-offs based on prespecified operating criteria. When a single NfL cut-off defined by 95% sensitivity or 95% specificity was applied, substantial risk of misclassification remained: 68% (178/262) of patients with ALS fell below the high-specificity cut-off (false negatives), and 54% (80/149) of DCs exceeded the high-sensitivity cut-off (false positives; A). In contrast, applying both 95% sensitivity and specificity cut-offs simultaneously defined cases with grey-zone NfL values, and separated these from cases with clearly high or low NfL values (B). Patients falling within this grey-zone proceeded to additional biomarker testing, allowing progressive refinement before final classification (C). We examined this framework by applying ML classifiers to the grey-zone cases.

Under the nested cross-validation structure, NfL cut-offs corresponding to 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity were derived in each training fold and applied to the held-out test set. Across 10 repeated 5-fold cross-validations, the rule-in and rule-out NfL thresholds averaged approximately 6600 ± 1900 pg/mL and 770 ± 50 pg/mL, respectively, with grey-zone cases accounting for 58 ± 1% of all patients (note that this percentage is dependent on the proportion of ALS and controls in the cohort). Grey-zone cases were subsequently analysed using ML classifiers incorporating all measured fluid biomarkers except NfL.  summarises the variability of NfL thresholds, patient assignment, and diagnostic performance across all repeats and models. Among the evaluated algorithms, the RF model achieved the highest median overall AUC across 10 repeats and was therefore selected as the representative model for visualisation. Within the grey-zone cases, the RF model achieved moderate discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.77), while maintaining high overall PPV (∼90%) across the entire diagnostic strategy (B and ). CK, GFAP, and Aβ38/40 were the top three contributors in this model (D).

As predictive values vary with disease prevalence, we further simulated hypothetical ALS prevalence scenarios (). Applying two NfL cut-offs and ML classifiers to the grey-zone cases yielded more stable classification performance than dichotomising at a single NfL cut-off (e.g., Youden index-maximised), across varying prevalence settings. This advantage was particularly evident at moderate ALS prevalence levels (15–30%).

From the ALS cohort, 218 patients with at least two ALSFRS-R measurements were included in the LME slope analysis. Core clinical features, such as age, ΔFS, and %VC, but not sex, were associated with faster ALSFRS-R decline (). Importantly, CSF NfL remained a significant predictor of faster decline after adjustment for these variables, with a standardised effect size comparable to ΔFS and %VC. No other fluid biomarker provided additional prognostic value beyond age and NfL. Individual ALSFRS-R trajectories coloured by baseline ΔFS (A), NfL (B), and %VC () illustrate heterogeneous patterns of functional decline and are consistent with the prognostic relevance of these factors.

Given the dominant prognostic value of NfL, we further examined its interaction with other CSF biomarkers. Both Aβ38/40 and Aβ42/40 showed significant interactions with baseline NfL in longitudinal models of ALSFRS-R decline, after adjustment for core clinical features (). The association between higher NfL and faster progression was more pronounced in Aβ-positive patients (C). In exploratory sensitivity analyses, the Aβ38/40 × NfL × time and Aβ42/40 × NfL × time interaction terms remained robust in unadjusted models, models including the core clinical covariates without covariate × time interactions (), and models additionally including either age × NfL × time or APOE ε4 × NfL × time interaction terms (all P < 0.01). Across these sensitivity analyses, the binary Aβ status interaction estimates were also broadly consistent with the primary estimate shown in , with modest attenuation in some models; the corresponding estimates (β [95% CI]) were −0.45 [−0.95 to 0.04], −0.47 [−0.96 to 0.02], −0.36 [−0.76 to 0.03], and −0.38 [−0.86 to 0.09], respectively (n = 218, except for the APOE ε4 model [n = 172], based on complete-case analysis). Subgroup analyses stratified by Aβ status showed a broadly similar pattern, although small subgroup sizes limit the interpretation of these binary comparisons ().

We next evaluated how well baseline clinical and biomarker data predicted individual ALSFRS-R slopes across models, using the cross-validated R2 between observed and out-of-fold predicted slopes. In the primary analysis of 180 patients with ≥3 ALSFRS-R assessments, sequential inclusion of core clinical features (e.g., age, ΔFS, %VC) in GLMs increased cross-validated R2 to approximately 0.13–0.14 (D). Adding CSF NfL further improved model performance (ΔR2 ≈ 0.06), and inclusion of interaction terms of NfL with other biomarkers provided a modest additional gain (ΔR2 ≈ 0.03). ML models incorporating all core clinical features and fluid biomarkers did not outperform GLMs that included NfL × other biomarker interactions. While NfL, ΔFS, and %VC consistently contributed to these ML models, predictions tended to deviate substantially in cases with extremely rapid functional decline (). Sensitivity analyses including patients with ≥2 ALSFRS-R assessments yielded comparably modest predictive performance: the NfL × Aβ38/40 and NfL × Aβ42/40 interaction models yielded cross-validated R2 of approximately 0.20–0.22, while ML models yielded values of approximately 0.12–0.19 ().

Survival analyses were also conducted to assess consistency across outcome measures. Among 250 patients in the ALS cohort with available survival data, 150 events were observed, and the median survival from the baseline visit was 33.9 months (95% CI 28.5–39.5). Cox proportional hazards models adjusting for core clinical features showed that higher CSF NfL was associated with shorter survival, supporting its prognostic relevance (). Sex was not significantly associated with survival. Consistent with the ALSFRS-R functional decline analyses, a significant interaction between NfL and Aβ42/40 was observed for survival (). In subgroup analyses, the HR for NfL was higher in patients with Aβ-positive ALS (HR 4.38 [2.13–9.03]) than in those with Aβ-negative ALS (HR 1.72 [1.40–2.11]), after adjustment for core clinical features (A and B).

To assess the consistency of the Aβ-stratified survival findings, we further analysed an independent cohort from Bologna, Italy (n = 153, 102 events; median survival 25.6 months). This cohort showed baseline characteristics comparable to those of the Nagoya cohort, including the proportion of Aβ-positive cases (22/153, 14% vs 37/250, 15%) and APOE ε4 carrier status (). Although the small sample size limited the statistical power of the Bologna cohort alone, the direction of the association was consistent with that observed in Nagoya (). In cohort-stratified pooled analyses, the association between NfL and survival was stronger in Aβ-positive ALS (HR 4.02 [2.17–7.45]) than in Aβ-negative ALS (HR 1.62 [1.36–1.92]; C; ). This trend is visualised in Kaplan–Meier curves showing poorer survival with higher NfL tertiles, most pronounced in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (D and E; ).

To evaluate the biomarker's potential utility for improving clinical trial efficiency, two complementary sample size simulations were explored: (1) enrichment strategy selecting participants within the top NfL quantile and (2) outcome adjustment strategy using cross-validated R2.

Sample size simulations suggested that baseline NfL-based enrichment could reduce the total number of participants required to detect a given treatment effect on the ALSFRS-R slope. Assuming a 40% treatment effect, restricting enrolment to the upper 50% (≥ median NfL) or upper quartile reduced the required sample size by 21% and 34%, respectively (A), although this approach would require a larger screening population.

A complementary approach is to retain all participants and adjust for baseline covariates rather than restrict enrolment. In this simulation, using cross-validated R2 values and assuming treatment effects of 2.4–3.6 points on the ALSFRS-R over 24 weeks, adjustment for baseline CSF NfL alone reduced the required sample size by ∼10%, whereas adjustment for core clinical features achieved a larger reduction of ∼14%. Their combined inclusion provided additional benefit, achieving a ∼20% reduction (B). Further inclusion of the CSF NfL × Aβ42/40 interaction term provided only a modest additional gain, reducing the required sample size by up to 22%.

We evaluated CSF biomarkers to optimise the diagnostic and prognostic work-up of ALS. NfL remained the most informative marker across analyses, consistent with previous studies, but other markers also showed discriminative value, suggesting potential relevance to the pathophysiological mechanisms of ALS. Moreover, Aβ status modified the association between baseline NfL and subsequent functional decline. This finding indicates that AD co-pathology may modulate disease progression and contribute to clinical heterogeneity in ALS. Collectively, integrating multiple high-performing fluid biomarkers that represent distinct pathological processes may refine diagnostic and prognostic assessments in ALS.

Aβ42/40, phosphorylated tau, and GFAP are core biomarkers in the biological definition of AD, reflecting cerebral Aβ deposition (and, to a minor degree, tau pathology) and astrogliosis., In ALS, prior studies summarised in systematic reviews have reported heterogeneous findings for these markers, potentially reflecting inconsistent control group definitions, age distributions, biofluid types (CSF vs blood), assay platforms, and unaccounted AD co-pathology., Only a few studies represent early attempts to address AD co-pathology in ALS, focussing primarily on plasma GFAP and pTau isoforms in ALS cohorts., To address these gaps, we evaluated CSF biomarkers while minimising AD-related confounding by stratifying patients by CSF Aβ42/40 status. The resulting Aβ-positive prevalence (∼14% at a median age of 67 years) aligned with epidemiological expectations and prior studies., Additionally, the observed APOE ε4 carrier frequency in our ALS cohort and the associated odds of Aβ positivity were consistent with prior population-based estimates.,, Importantly, although most patients with Aβ-positive ALS have preserved cognitive scores (median MMSE: 27 [IQR 24–28]), lower Aβ42/40 was associated with worse MMSE after adjustment for age, sex, and years of education. These findings suggest that, even in the context of ALS, a reduction in Aβ42/40 may reflect coexisting early or preclinical AD-related pathology, in line with the established interpretation of reduced Aβ42/40 in the AD continuum. Stratifying by Aβ status thus enabled us to distinguish biomarker alterations primarily driven by ALS from those influenced by coexisting, including early-stage, AD pathology.

CSF pTau181 and pTau217 were elevated in ALS compared to DCs, even within the Aβ-negative subgroup. While blood pTau elevation in ALS has been consistently reported, possibly attributable to peripheral origins,, ,  findings for CSF pTau have been inconsistent. Earlier meta-analyses,, largely lacking age-matching and Aβ status stratification, suggested that CSF pTau181 levels in ALS were similar to or slightly lower than in neurological controls. In contrast, our age-balanced and Aβ-stratified analyses demonstrated significantly higher CSF pTau181 and pTau217 in ALS than in DCs, although the absolute differences were modest. Among Aβ-negative DC subgroups, MSA cases alone had higher pTau181 levels than ALS. These observations underscore the need for well-characterised control cohorts incorporating rigorous age matching and Aβ stratification. Pathologically, how pTau elevations relate to neurodegenerative changes in ALS remains unclear. Neuropathological studies have not demonstrated an ALS-specific tau aggregation pattern in the brain; instead, tau pathology in ALS has been reported as age-related, resembling primary age-related tauopathy or typical AD patterns accompanied by Aβ pathology.,, In our cohort, the prevalence of CSF Aβ positivity was similar in ALS and DCs, arguing against an increased propensity for AD co-pathology in ALS. Longitudinal fluid biomarker and PET studies will be essential to disentangle these ALS–Aβ–Tau relationships.

Regarding CSF GFAP, consistent with prior studies,, the levels were comparable between ALS and DCs. Additionally, CSF GFAP levels did not differ by Aβ status within the ALS cohort. Given the limited sensitivity of CSF GFAP to early AD-related change,, and the relatively preserved cognition observed in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup, this result appears reasonable. The primary relevance of GFAP may lie in elucidating the influence of astroglial co-pathology, rather than in direct clinical application.

Importantly, the ALS cohort exhibited distinct alterations in CSF Aβ peptides. Previous meta-analyses reported higher CSF Aβ42 levels in ALS than in neurological disease controls, though without adjustment for Aβ40. We confirmed these findings after stratification by Aβ status, and further observed elevated CSF Aβ38, Aβ40, and the Aβ38/40 ratio independent of Aβ status. In AD, shorter Aβ species such as Aβ38 are relatively protective, whereas longer forms such as Aβ42 are aggregation-prone and neurotoxic., ,  The increased Aβ38/40 ratio despite comparable Aβ42/40 levels may suggest altered Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) processing in ALS rather than a uniform elevation of Aβ peptides. Experimental studies have reported APP upregulation preceding motor neuron loss in a mouse model, and clinical studies suggest that APP-related Aβ dynamics in ALS diverge from canonical AD patterns., Taken together, Aβ-related pathways may represent an ALS-relevant biological axis distinct from AD. Indeed, Aβ-related measures contributed to diagnostic ML models and later emerged as modifiers of the NfL–progression relationship.

In ALS research, evidence for diagnostic biomarkers that complement NfL remains limited. Prior studies often lacked internal validation and relied on comparisons against healthy controls, potentially inflating performance estimates. We addressed these gaps by applying comprehensive diagnostic modelling approaches, evaluating all models using the same 5-fold cross-validation framework. ML models incorporating additional biomarkers improved the diagnostic performance beyond NfL (AUC ≈ 0.90), suggesting non-linear contributions from secondary analytes. Although CK and Aβ38/40 consistently contributed to these models, the modest performance gain suggests that further improvement may require integrating complementary, non-redundant information. Given the biological heterogeneity of ALS, achieving substantially higher diagnostic performance against clinically relevant disease mimics may be inherently challenging. Further gains will require ALS-specific information that is not captured by markers of general neurodegeneration, potentially extending beyond fluid biomarkers alone.

The dominant but not definitive diagnostic value of NfL warrants careful consideration in clinical practice. Reliance on a single cut-off carries substantial misclassification risk. Thus, we propose a two-cutoff framework that introduces a grey zone. In this approach, clearly low or high NfL values can guide immediate decisions, while grey-zone cases enriched for ALS risk should undergo careful follow-up and targeted testing with other modalities (C). This workflow enables dynamic diagnostic refinement over time and better reflects real-world clinical reasoning. We piloted this framework by applying ML classifiers to the NfL grey-zone subgroup using other fluid biomarkers. Although discretising NfL inevitably involved some loss of information, the rule-in/out misclassification was reduced compared with a single-cutoff dichotomisation. Importantly, while this approach reduces overall diagnostic error, a small number of patients with ALS who have very low NfL levels may still be misclassified at the first step. Such patients, however, are more likely to follow a slowly progressive course, allowing a longer window for diagnostic observation.

Future multimodal work, ideally in prospective cohorts including all patients with suspected ALS, should integrate imaging and neurophysiological tests to better reflect clinical practice. For example, electromyography features reflecting lower motor neuron involvement and structural MRI findings such as motor cortex atrophy could complement biomarker-based grey-zone assessment., The choice of biofluid matrix also warrants further study. Although CSF allows simultaneous evaluation of co-pathologies (e.g., Aβ42/40 and α-synuclein seed amplification assays) with less systemic confounding, its invasiveness and procedural demands limit scalability and longitudinal sampling. While biomarkers such as NfL correlate across blood and CSF,, head-to-head comparisons are needed to establish their relative clinical utility. Future research should quantify the performance gap between blood and CSF biomarkers when integrated with co-pathology assessments. Additionally, prevalence-specific implementation is essential. The high ALS prevalence in our study population (64%) naturally increased PPV, decreased NPV, and broadened the grey zone. Achieving such a high pre-test prevalence in clinical practice would require substantial triaging prior to biomarker testing. While cut-off derivation in this study was methodologically independent of disease prevalence, and model performance remained robust across a range of simulated ALS prevalences, optimal clinical implementation will still require calibration to the intended diagnostic context and pre-test probability.

In prognostic analyses, CSF NfL strongly predicted ALSFRS-R decline and survival, consistent with prior studies., While Aβ-related measures alone were not associated with disease progression as main effects, both interaction and subgroup analyses suggested effect modification: the relationship between baseline NfL and subsequent functional decline varied by Aβ-related measures. Biologically, this may indicate that AD co-pathology (as reflected by reduced Aβ42/40) or altered APP processing (as suggested by reduced Aβ38/40) modifies clinical vulnerability at a given level of neuroaxonal injury. Interestingly, lower levels of soluble APP fragments (sAPPα and sAPPβ) in CSF have been reported to be associated with faster ALS progression. Additionally, neuropathological studies and experimental ALS models have shown that increased APP expression or dysregulated APP processing is associated with neuronal injury and impaired axonal transport., Taken together, these findings support the hypothesis that altered APP metabolism may represent one aspect of neuroaxonal vulnerability and contribute to prognostic heterogeneity in ALS.

Notably, the apparent modifying effect of AD co-pathology status was observed primarily in patients with high NfL levels, whereas no clear effect was observed among those with lower NfL levels. One hypothesis-generating interpretation is that when ALS-related neuroaxonal injury is limited, as reflected by lower NfL, there is insufficient disease activity to drive measurable functional decline, leaving little scope for additional pathology to modify the clinical course. AD co-pathology may act primarily as a modifier of disease progression rather than an independent driver, becoming clinically relevant in ALS only once a substantial level of neuroaxonal damage is present.

At present, predicting individual disease progression remains challenging due to clinical heterogeneity in ALS. Although ΔFS is an established prognostic marker, it does not reliably predict subsequent individual progression on its own. In line with this, even models incorporating NfL and core clinical features, including ΔFS and %VC, yielded modest cross-validated R2 (≈0.20) for predicting subsequent ALSFRS-R slope. Additionally, ML regressors did not outperform GLMs once an interaction between NfL and AD-related biomarkers was included. This performance ceiling may reflect both the limited sample size, which restricts ML complexity, and intrinsic properties of the outcome itself. Since ALSFRS-R decline often flattens in advanced stages and follows non-linear patterns,, the OLS-derived slope may oversimplify progression. However, given the approximate linearity of ALSFRS-R decline over typical clinical trial windows, slope-based analyses will remain essential in clinical trials.

In this context, it is crucial to develop prognostic models that are comparable across cohorts. In our cohort, combining NfL with %VC and ΔFS improved model performance, indicating that each captures complementary aspects of disease progression. Novel biomarkers should likewise be evaluated based on how much they complement NfL and core clinical features. To enhance comparability across studies, future studies should incorporate a standard set of established covariates (e.g., age, %VC, ΔFS),, and report standardised performance metrics (e.g., R2, concordance index, AIC) to clarify the incremental prognostic value of novel biomarkers. Such harmonisation will also support future clinical trial design.

Considering the current limitations of granular, individual-level prediction of ALSFRS-R trajectories, prognostic stratification by expected progression rate may represent a more feasible and clinically relevant application, with potential benefits for both trial efficiency and communication with patients. Our sample size simulation suggested that NfL may be useful for this purpose, consistent with a previous study. In our simulations, enriching for participants with high NfL values increased the mean rate of ALSFRS-R decline and thereby reduced the required sample size, albeit at the cost of increased screening burden and reduced generalisability. Given that the association between NfL and functional decline may differ by Aβ status, incorporating Aβ status could further refine prognostication, particularly in older cohorts. As an exploratory strategy, prioritising enrolment of Aβ-negative participants might improve trial efficiency, as Aβ-positive ALS cases are relatively rare, biologically complex, and may exhibit greater NfL-dependent variability in progression, making treatment-effect estimates less stable. Alternatively, Aβ status could be incorporated as a stratification factor.

Another approach to improving trial efficiency is to adjust outcomes for predefined prognostic markers rather than restrict eligibility., Unlike the enrichment approach, covariate adjustment preserves broad inclusion, which is particularly important in rare diseases, and is encouraged by regulatory guidance. Our analysis showed that NfL, ΔFS, and %VC provide comparable prognostic value, highlighting the need to discuss how best to incorporate these variables. Options include using one as the sole adjustment factor, combining multiple predictors, or using specific variables (e.g., %VC) as inclusion criteria. Developing consensus on covariate selection and biomarker integration will be essential to translate these predictors into practical trial design frameworks.

This study has several notable strengths. First, we systematically characterised CSF biomarkers and clinical characteristics while explicitly accounting for Aβ status. This approach enabled us to assess biomarker differences according to Aβ status and examine their associations with disease progression. Second, the study included a large ALS cohort profiled with well-validated CSF biomarker assays,, and the direction of the Aβ-stratified survival associations was consistent across two independent cohorts. Third, we rigorously assessed diagnostic and prognostic relevance across analytical frameworks, including machine-learning models.

Several limitations should also be acknowledged. External validation for the diagnostic modelling was not feasible because comparable multi-analyte CSF datasets were unavailable. This limitation was mitigated through rigorous internal cross-validation, yielding consistent findings across multiple analytical frameworks. Sex-specific model performance was not evaluated, given the limited sample size for further sex stratification, particularly within the cross-validation framework and the Aβ-positive subgroup; sex was not significantly associated with functional decline or survival. The sample-size simulations assumed equal treatment effects across subgroups and no attrition. These analyses were intended as illustrative demonstrations rather than formal trial designs. In addition, biologically defined AD cases were not included in the cohort, and the dataset therefore lacked an internal positive control for AD pathology. Nonetheless, the Aβ42/40 threshold was adopted a priori from the independent BioFINDER cohort using a rigorous bridging approach within the same assay framework. Concordance with APOE ε4 carrier status, consistency across dichotomous and continuous Aβ42/40 analyses, and findings from the Aβ subgroup analyses in the independent cohort further supported the observed associations.

This study highlights the potential complementary value of amyloid-related fluid biomarkers in ALS. While NfL was the most informative marker for both diagnosis and prognosis, CSF Aβ38/40 provided additional discriminative value to NfL, and Aβ status, reflecting AD co-pathology, modified the association between baseline NfL and subsequent functional decline. Personalised diagnosis and prognostication incorporating fine-grained assessment of co-pathology may help refine patient stratification and clinical trial design in ALS.
