medicine.title: Decoding adenomyosis: integrative insights from genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational analyses
medicine.abstract: Adenomyosis is an oestrogen-driven, inflammatory uterine disorder characterised by endometrial glands and stroma in the myometrium resulting in abnormal bleeding, pain, and poor reproductive outcomes. Multiple contributors to its pathogenesis and pathophysiology have been identified over the years using a variety of experimental approaches and technologies, with gaps in integrating these approaches into a comprehensive paradigm of adenomyosis pathobiology. This review provides integrative insights from recent studies focused on genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational approaches. These demonstrate that select genes are causally linked to adenomyosis and that genomic and epigenetic mechanisms promote the enhanced oestrogen and diminished progesterone signalling and associated inflammation that are pathognomonic of the disorder, supported by orthogonal validation including novel 3D in vitro cell models. In addition, advanced computational tools, including AI-driven platforms that integrate multiomics data, reveal promising therapeutic candidates for mitigating disease progression and symptoms and improving fertility and pregnancy success.
medicine.text:
Adenomyosis is an oestrogen-driven disorder characterised by endometrial glands and stroma in the myometrium. This ectopic location results in myometrial inflammation, smooth muscle hyperplasia, uterine enlargement, fibrosis, and neuroangiogenesis–impacting uterine function and well-being of those affected., ,  Adenomyosis occurs in 20%–34%, ,  of reproductive age women, although pelvic imaging reveals disease in adolescents and postmenopausal women. Common symptoms include dysmenorrhoea, pelvic pain, abnormal uterine bleeding, as summarised by Vannuccini and colleagues in Series Paper 1, and infertility and poor pregnancy outcomes as discussed by Chapron and colleagues in Series Paper 4. Current therapies to relieve pelvic pain and abnormal uterine bleeding include analgesics, antifibrinolytics, contraceptive steroids, GnRH analogues, and progestin-containing intrauterine systems. Their efficacies and side effects vary among patients, and hysterectomy is curative but precludes fulfilling pregnancy goals. Thus, there is a significant unmet need for novel drug discovery to mitigate adenomyosis-related symptoms and improve reproductive outcomes. We posit there is an opportunity to leverage rapidly developing technologies to deepen understanding of the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of this common, debilitating disorder to achieve these clinical goals.

Adenomyosis pathogenesis derives mainly from invasion of endometrial basalis into the myometrium due to repetitive endometrial–myometrial junction (EMJ) trauma and repair, de novo metaplasia, and “outside-in” invasion of ectopic endometrium (EcE) into the myometrium. Risks of developing the disorder include uterine surgery, multiple pregnancies, and endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) exposures, and a possible genetic predisposition. Notably, adenomyosis has some features in common with endometriosis: both are inflammatory, oestrogen-driven disorders that share KRAS, PIK3CA, ARID1A, FBXW7, PPP2R1A and PIK3R1 somatic mutations in eutopic endometrial basalis and functionalis and lesion epithelial cells.,,, Clinically, they commonly co-occur and result in severe dysmenorrhoea and heavy menstrual bleeding.,,

Adenomyosis pathophysiology comprises enhanced oestrogen signalling (“oestrogen dominance”) diminished progesterone signalling (“progesterone resistance”), and local and systemic inflammation. Altered steroid hormone receptor promoter methylation and other epigenetic modifications result in impaired PGR and ESR1 signalling and enhanced ESR2 signalling. Adenomyosis lesions in the myometrium and the eutopic endometrium (EuE) of adenomyotic uteri exhibit enhanced oestrogen signalling due to high local expression of CYP19A1 (encoding aromatase) and decreased HSD17β2 (converts E2→E1). Collectively, these result in high intra-cavitary and intra-lesional E2 that drive proliferative (lesion growth) and inflammatory, angiogenic, and fibrotic processes,, (). This oestrogen-dominant environment also increases myometrial hypercontractility via activation of tissue injury and repair (TIAR) and inflammation which further stimulate E2 production in a feedforward loop., Moreover, extra-pituitary prolactin (PRL) and PRL signalling mediate adenomyosis disease development, pain, and progression in animal models, and a prolactin receptor (PRLR) monoclonal antibody inhibits these effects and reduces pelvic pain in endometriosis patients. In addition, the oxytocin receptor (OTR) is abnormally elevated in adenomyosis uteri, contributing to hyperperistalsis and dysmenorrhoea. In this second paper of the Series, we aim to summarise rapidly evolving genetic, multiomic and integrative computational analyses and 3-dimensional validation platforms that are advancing insights into these processes and novel drug discovery for disease progression, symptom management,,, and improving pregnancy success., The first, third, and fourth papers of the Series on adenomyosis focus on tailored management of abnormal uterine bleeding and pain, potential biomarkers for improving diagnosis and treatment, and adenomyosis-related infertility, respectively.,,

Genetic studies reveal association between catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) 158 G/A heterozygous genotype with increased adenomyosis risk in Asian populations (). Also, specific allelic distributions in several oestrogen-metabolising enzymes are significantly associated with increased adenomyosis risk, including frequencies of the C/T genotype of CYP1A1, the C allele and C/A and C/C genotypes of CYP1A2, and the C/T genotype of CYP19 (). These data link genetic factors influencing oestrogen signalling pathways to adenomyosis risk, supporting functional connections between steroid hormones, their receptors, and adenomyosis pathogenesis and pathophysiology.

Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), a key enzyme in prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) biosynthesis, is crucial in TIAR and the microtrauma feedforward loop. The −1195G > A variant in the promoter region of the gene encoding COX-2 (PTGS2) is associated with increased risk of adenomyosis (). Notably, celecoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor, significantly reduced the depth of infiltration into the myometrium and fibrosis in a murine model of adenomyosis. Uterine tissues from mice treated with celecoxib had decreased expression of aromatase and lower concentrations of oestrogen. In human adenomyosis lesions, levels of proteins of the oestrogen signalling pathway (ERβ, CYP19A1, HSD3β2, HSD17β1 and StAR) positively correlate with the levels of COX-2 and downstream enzymes in PGE2 biosynthesis (mPGES-1, mPGES-2, cPGES), and PGE2 receptors (EP2, and EP4)–linking PGE2 and oestrogen pathways in adenomyosis ().

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is a key modulator of neuroangiogenesis, and VEGF gene polymorphism linkage with adenomyosis risk has yielded conflicting results. One study found association of the −2578A and −1154A alleles with decreased risk compared to the −2578C and −1154G alleles, respectively (). In contrast, frequency of the A allele of VEGF −2578 C/A gene polymorphism was greater in infertile women with versus without adenomyosis. These discrepancies likely reflect divergent study designs and cohorts, and potential confounding effects of comorbidities.

Epithelial somatic mutations in eutopic endometrial basalis and functionalis and adenomyotic lesions display KRAS as the major driver with mutational frequencies of 34%–37.1% in affected cases.,, The KRAS mutation G12C autonomously activates the KRAS/MAPK signalling pathway promoting cell survival. Other somatic mutations include PIK3CA (12.2%), ARID1A (12.1%) and FBXW7 (9.8%) (). In adenomyosis, an oligoclonal disorder, KRAS mutations are linked to progesterone resistance. Moreover, aberrant activation of CTNNB1 (β-catenin) promotes adenomyosis through epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and cell proliferation. Notably, a specific allelic mutation c.110C- > T in the CTNNB1 gene was identified in two cases of diffuse adenomyosis ().

Whole-exome sequencing of laser microdissected samples revealed shared somatic mutations between multiple adenomyotic lesions and matched EuE, supporting a model of clonal expansion from an ancestral clone, consistent with a dominant clonal landscape with relatively limited clonal diversity in adenomyosis lesions. This contrasts with the greater clonal heterogeneity and more prevalent independent mutational events observed in endometriosis lesions.

Study of somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs) has identified chromosome 1q gain as the recurrent SCNA shared across multiple adenomyotic lesions, indicating a restricted SCNA landscape in adenomyosis (), compared with the diversity in SCNA patterns reported in endometriosis. The occurrence of whole genome doubling (WGD) events was associated with an early onset of adenomyosis (before 40.5 years of age) in contrast to no association observed in endometriosis. Despite this progress in research regarding genetic susceptibility and somatic mutations, currently genome-wide association studies specifically targeting adenomyosis remain limited.

Epigenetic alterations contribute to the pathogenesis of adenomyosis, including DNA methylation, histone and m6A modifications, and non-coding RNAs.

Abnormal expression of deoxyribonucleic acid methyltransferases (DNMTs) has been reported in adenomyosis., DNMT1 and DNMT3B immunoreactivity was increased in EcE (, ). DNMT1 expression in EuE correlates with heavier menses and DNMT3B in ectopic lesions correlates with dysmenorrhoea severity. Moreover, DNMT3A expression is markedly reduced in ectopic and EuE. DNMT1 overexpression drives promoter hypermethylation and downregulation of KL (encodes Klotho, an anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative protein and co-receptor of fibroblast growth factors) and PPARG (encodes PPARγ), and increased p16 and p21 expression, thereby linking aberrant DNA methylation to epithelial senescence in lesions. Hypermethylation of the PR-B promoter contributes to impaired progesterone signalling in adenomyosis. Histone modifications alter chromatin and nucleosome dynamics and gene expression and play a role in adenomyosis pathobiology. HDACs (histone deacetylases) 1, 2 and 3 are upregulated in endometrium and lesions of adenomyosis patients, and HDAC2 immunoreactivity in EuE correlate with dysmenorrhoea severity (, ). HDAC type and protein expression depend on extent of disease and degree of fibrosis., Downregulation of eutopic endometrial HDAC3 in women with adenomyosis-associated heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) impairs NF-κB signalling and inflammation. Furthermore, high expression of lysine-specific histone demethylase 1A (KDM1A, (LSD1)), targets histone and non-histone proteins in adenomyosis lesions. Silencing KDM1A in vitro limits cell motility, invasiveness, and proliferation of both eutopic and ectopic endometrial stromal cells, suggesting that KDM1A could be a potential therapeutic target (, ).

EuE of patients with adenomyosis versus controls exhibit reduced global m6A RNA methylation and differential expression of key m6A regulators., Among the latter were writer METTL3 (methyltransferase-like 3), eraser FTO (fat mass and obesity-associated protein), ZC3H13 (zinc finger CCCH-type containing 13), and reader YTHDC1(YTH domain containing 1), (, ). In addition, increased IGF1 and DDT (D-dopachrome tautomerase) expression significantly correlated with decreased METTL3 expression, implicating METTL3-depedent m6A loss in enhanced epithelial proliferation and cell migration in adenomyosis, (, ).

Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including miroRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and circular RNAs (circRNAs) regulate epithelial invasion, EMT, oestrogen-sensitive proliferation, inflammatory signalling, and immune polarisation and promote progesterone resistance in adenomyosis (, ). Potential non-coding RNA and other biomarkers are summarised by Merino-Pérez and colleagues in Series Paper 3.

Animal models suggest that EDCs promote epigenetic reprogramming of cells in both the endometrial and myometrial compartments involving steroid hormone signalling and inflammation. Dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), phthalates, and bisphenols (BPA, BPS) alter DNA methylation marks and histone modifications resulting in persistent inflammatory and oestrogen-dependent signalling (, ). A murine model demonstrated that in utero TCDD (2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin) exposure alters adult steroid responses and contributes to transgenerational development of adenomyosis (, ). These observations suggest possible prevention of adenomyosis and ameliorating molecular dysregulations, if translatable to humans.

Adenomyosis lesions express abnormal DNMTs, HDACs, KDM1A and m6A regulators that respond to nutrient availability, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cytokines, suggesting diet and inflammation may regulate the epigenome in adenomyosis pathophysiology (, ). Notably, anti-inflammatory diets and anti-oxidant supplements are emerging as beneficial non-hormonal approaches in endometriosis patients,; perhaps, similar strategies may be trialed for patients with adenomyosis.

Hdac3 inhibition in mouse models promotes inflammation, increased uterine bleeding, and impaired endometrial repair in the setting of fibrosis. In contrast, in vitro, HDAC3 suppression in human endometrial epithelial cells from highly fibrotic lesions impairs NF-κB signalling, underscoring the impact of fibrosis in drug response. A 2022 review by Guo details therapeutic candidates for adenomyosis in the context of pathophysiology and nuances of disease extent, degree of fibrosis, and associated symptoms.

The histone demethylase KDM1A has promise in cancer therapy and myelofibrosis. As silencing KDM1A inhibits cell motility, invasion, and proliferation of eutopic endometrial stromal cells and ectopic stromal cells, KDM1A may be a therapeutic candidate to minimise adenomyosis disease progression.

In addition to dysregulated steroid hormone action, factors such as PRL signalling, immune dysregulation, cell state transitions, fibrosis, angiogenesis and neuroangiogenesis promote the adenomyosis phenotype.,

A transgenic mouse model of PRL overexpression or pituitary transplantation in the uterus both result in an adenomyosis phenotype. Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of adenomyosis lesions from in women revealed PRLR-expressing ECM-high epithelial and inflammatory fibroblast subclusters, underscoring a role for PRLR in ECM remodelling and inflammation. Moreover, PRL enhanced proliferation and suppressed apoptosis of the ECM-high epithelial population in vitro, suggesting it may increase disease burden and enhance survival in vivo. PRLR is also expressed in nociceptors in female-selective pain syndromes. HMI-115, a monoclonal antibody inhibiting PRLR, markedly reduced adenomyosis progression in mice and ameliorated endometriosis-associated pain in a phase 2 trial in women. These data support targeting PRLR as non-hormonal therapeutic approach for adenomyosis symptoms, needing further investigation.

Local and systemic immune dysregulation prevail in adenomyosis patients, with shifts in the balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory signalling. Early studies reported increased macrophages and γδT cells, aberrant HLA expression, increased T helper 17 (Th17) cells and decreased regulatory T cells (Tregs) in the circulation, and broad alterations in cytokines and other inflammatory-related factors in endometrium and disease lesions. Uterine natural killer (uNK) cell abundance is high (≥300/mm2) in patients with adenomyosis, although its relevance to symptoms and/or pregnancy success is unclear. A population of exhausted natural killer group protein 2A (NKG2A) + CD8+ T-cells in EuE and lesions has been identified, and their abundance correlates with disease severity, likely driven by overexpression of the NKG2A ligand HLA-E and interleukin-15 (IL-15) in glandular epithelial cells. A 2025 integrated analysis of endometrial microarray, bulk RNA-seq and single cell RNA-seq datasets identified metabolic reprogramming and decreased anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage abundance. Taken together, altered immune cell abundance and features in the endometrium and lesions are consistent with chronic inflammation possibly contributing to lesion persistence and impaired reproductive function. However, there remains controversy in the literature about cell-type abundance (uNK, M2 macrophage) and relationship to symptoms and pregnancy outcomes that warrants further study.

Abnormal immune activation, hormonal imbalance, EMT, and fibrosis pathway activation (FMT and smooth muscle metaplasia, SMM) comprise mechanisms underlying fibrotic remodelling in adenomyosis disease progression. Inflammation in adenomyosis is closely associated with TIAR within the EMJ, EuE and ectopic myometrial lesions. The disease microenvironment comprises elevated monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL1β), interferons (IFN-α, IFN-γ), and other immune mediators that trigger multiple signalling pathways. Included are NF-κB, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), NOTCH, cGAS-STING, and TGF-β/Smad signalling pathways,,–interconnecting cascades that promote inflammation-related fibrogenesis ().

Neuro-immune-fibrosis crosstalk has emerged as a prominent feature of adenomyosis. Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-positive nociceptors within fibrotic adenomyosis lesions in patients and murine models support nociceptive nerve ablation to relieve fibrosis and disease. CGRP inhibitors are in clinical use for migraine headache management and reduce disease burden and pain in a mouse model of endometriosis. By analogy, these non-hormonal therapies await further study in adenomyosis disease burden, fibrosis, and associated pain.

Integrated multi-omics combined with experimental verification identified PI3K/AKT signalling as central to myometrial fibrosis in adenomyosis. AKT/GSK-3β and sphingosine kinase/sphingosine-1-phosphate/sphingosine-1-phosphatereceptors (SphKs/S1P/S1PRs) also contribute to fibroblast activation, ECM accumulation, and lesion progression.

Adenomyosis lesions and associated EuE are characterised by prominent vascularity and angiogenesis, with increased microvessel density in lesions and increased immature α-SMA negative microvessel and lymphatic vessel densities in both tissues versus controls. In a mouse model, treatment with axitinib, an inhibitor of VEGF-R2 and angiogenesis, markedly reduced disease severity. Overexpression of Talin 1 cytoskeletal protein (regulating integrin activation) in cultured adenomyosis-derived stromal cells enhanced their proliferative response to E2 and stimulated secretion of angiogenic factors promoting in vitro angiogenesis, implicating intra-lesional integrin-cytoskeleton signalling in E2-stimulated cell growth and angiogenesis. Collectively, the hyperestrogenic microenvironment promotes and angiogenesis involving VEGF, HIF-1α and downstream pathways including NF-κB.

Neuroangiogenesis is closely associated with angiogenesis, and adenomyosis lesions exhibit high expression of neurogenic factors [nerve growth factors (NGFs), synaptophysin (SYN), microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2)], and inflammatory mediators [IL-1β, corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and urocortin (Ucn)]., This neurogenic-inflammatory network has been implicated in associated pain and HMB in adenomyosis patients. Increased levels of neuropeptides and neurotransmitters in adenomyotic lesions by immunohistochemistry included NK1R (substance P receptor), RAMP1 (receptor activity modifying protein 1), CRLR (calcitonin receptor like receptor), and ADRB2 (adrenergic β2 receptor), and reduced α7nAChR (α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor), with lesional ADRB2 levels correlating positively with dysmenorrhoea severity. These observations support a model wherein neuroangiogenesis, sensory neuropeptides, and sympathetic noradrenergic signalling promote lesion growth, fibrosis, inflammation, and pain, while loss of cholinergic anti-inflammatory signalling via α7nAChR removes a potential dampening on disease progression.

Steroid hormone responsive uterine compartments relevant to adenomyosis pathogenesis include the EMJ, comprising the basalis and lower functionalis endometrium and the sub-endometrial inner myometrium, all of Mullerian origin. Recent single-cell transcriptomics, coupled with computational strategies including trajectory inference (for dynamic cell state transitions), cell–cell communication analysis (ligand-receptor pairs and enriched pathways), network-based pathway inference (mechanic signalling), and multi-omics data integration, have built comprehensive single-cell atlases of adenomyosis lesions and matched eutopic tissues, foundational to adenomyosis pathogenesis and pathophysiology.,, ,

Single-cell RNA-seq of eutopic and ectopic tissues from adenomyosis patients compared to control endometrium reveal transcriptional programs involved in cell motility, proliferation, angiogenesis, inflammation, and cancer processes, consistent with collective migration and invasion of endometrial-derived cells into the myometrium. In a study of three subjects with diffuse adenomyosis in the proliferative phase identified 11 cell types in EuE and 13 in lesions, with markedly increase fibroblast-like cells, SMCs, and neurons not detected in matched endometrium. Pseudotime trajectory revealed mesenchymal–epithelial transition (MET) in EuE, while lesion fibroblast-like cells transitioned in two divergent paths: ECM-producing fibroblasts and SMCs. Together, these observations support dynamic mesenchymal and epithelial transitions, expansion of fibroblast-like and SMCs (and neurons), and acquisition of pro-migratory, pro-angiogenic, pro-fibrotic, and inflammatory phenotypes that promote endometrial invasion into and remodelling of the myometrium in adenomyotic uteri. Moreover, WNT signalling contributed to EMT mediated through differential expression of secreted frizzled-related proteins from fibroblast-like cells, opening promising avenues for targeted drug discovery. scRNA sequencing adenomyosis lesions and eutopic (functionalis) endometrium of cases and controls in the secretory phase identified five major cell types, including ECM-high epithelial cells and an inflammatory fibroblast subcluster with high PRLR expression, as noted above.

Spatial transcriptomics revealed spatial features of ectopic endometrial penetration into the myometrium in 2025. Integrating spatial transcriptomics with bulk RNA-seq deconvolution, and scRNA-seq, a pseudo-spatial continuum from the endometrial invagination site to deep ectopic lesions was defined. At the invagination front, SFRP5+ epithelia were identified that informed clustering and pathway activity inference and IHH as a candidate promoting endometrial proliferation and angiogenesis. During progression into the myometrium, ESR1 + SMCs facilitated invasion by creating migratory tracts via collagen degradation. In deeper lesions, gene set activity scoring and RNA velocity analysis further suggested CNN1 + stromal fibroblasts undergo FMT in response to profibrogenic signals inferred from ligand-receptor interactions in lesion, thus driving fibrosis of the adenomyotic foci. In 2026, another spatial transcriptomics study further revealed that the adenomyosis lesion transcriptome more closely resembles endometrial basalis than functionalis and is enriched in olfactory signalling, dysregulated oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis, and chronic inflammation. Furthermore, in silico drug screening identified candidates that reversed lesion chronic inflammation pathways.

While the above sequencing studies comprise huge datasets, given heterogeneity in study design, cohort composition, sequencing platforms, and analytical pipelines, future studies warrant re-evaluating the reproducibility of key inferred biological pathways across studies., Quality control parameters often vary across datasets, and batch effect correction methods can themselves introduce variability, generating both false-positive and false-negative signals. Differences in adenomyosis diagnostic criteria, menstrual cycle timing at sampling, and tissue collection techniques may also contribute to variation in reported conclusions. Further refinement holds promise to enrich drug discovery and prognostics for adenomyosis symptoms and responses, disease progression, and recurrence.

The eutopic endometrial proteome differs between adenomyosis and controls and between two subtypes defined by ultrasound criteria in a 2025 study of subjects with internal adenomyosis of the junctional zone (JZ)/inner myometrium, subjects with external adenomyosis (in outer myometrium without JZ alteration), as well as 18 healthy controls. Compared to controls, both internal and external lesions showed enrichment of biological processes related to innate immune response. However, external adenomyosis was characterised by more pronounced immune and inflammatory signatures; whereas, internal adenomyosis was associated with pathways involved in cell migration and apoptosis. Complementing these data, an integrated analysis of adenomyosis proteomics and metabolomics identified proteins and signalling networks linked to myometrial fibrogenesis and activated PI3K/AKT signalling in myofibroblasts. In vitro inhibition of PI3K/AKT significantly reduced the production of fibronectin and collagen by cultured primary myofibroblasts from adenomyosis lesions, suggesting this pathway as a potential target for antifibrotic therapy.

Notably, a 2025 study integrated the first high-coverage, quantitative lipidomic atlas of human myometrium, quantifying 317 lipid species in 38 women with adenomyosis and 65 controls. Among these, 83 lipid species were markedly altered in adenomyosis, mapping to metabolic pathways related to inflammation, cell migration and immune dysregulation. Further analysis revealed a diagnostic signature of a five-lipid panel comprising hexosylceramide (HexCer), lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), cholesterol ester (CE), and two triacylglycerol (TAG) species that distinguished adenomyosis from controls with high accuracy and clearly discriminated between lesions and adjacent myometrium. Another metabolic dataset of 1100 lipid species from 22 patients with adenomyosis and 22 controls, consistently identified elevated levels of acylcarnitines and lysophosphatidylcholines in cases. These lipidomic data provide valuable insights into dysregulated lipid features that impact disease pathophysiology and hold promise for future biomarker development to enrich imaging and histologic diagnoses.

In 2025, the reproductive tract microbiome has emerged as a potential contributor to adenomyosis and related uterine disorders, also summarised by Merino-Pérez and colleagues in Series Paper 3. An endometrial microbiome study identified Citrobacter freundii, Prevotella copri, and Burkholderia cepacia as candidate microbial biomarkers for adenomyosis, although their pathogenic significance and clinical utility require further validation in larger cohorts.

Three-dimensional in vitro physiomimetic models are increasingly invoked in adenomyosis research.,, , ,  Endometrial organoids have been used to investigate adenomyosis-related endometrial receptivity, implantation failure, and pregnancy disorders, as discussed by Chapron and colleagues in Series Paper 4. A floating endometrial organoid model comprising co-cultured epithelial and stromal cells enabled study of epithelial-stromal interactions within a single, differentiated 3D structure. An endometrial assembloid model integrating epithelium with matched patient-derived stromal fibroblasts and SMCs isolated from eutopic and ectopic endometrium, generated an endometrium-like structure comprising three compartments: E-cadherin + epithelial cells, COL1A1+ stromal cells, and α-SMA + SMCs. ScRNA sequencing of hormonally-treated assembloids revealed that ectopic epithelial cells display a luminal-dominance, glandular-deficient phenotype under progesterone treatment. This was associated with ectopic stromal reorganisation (loss of BMP4+ and accumulation of CRYAB + IL15+ cells) consistent with impaired BMP-mediated stromal-epithelial signalling and enhanced WNT signalling. Another study of epithelial-stromal assembloids revealed impaired adenomyosis-related endometrial receptivity, including progesterone-resistance, reduced stromal compartment LIF and HOXA10 expression, and epithelial cells without pinopode formation.

Numerous therapeutic candidates have been identified through single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and other multi-omics,,,, as noted above.  shows discovery advances with clinical applications,,,,,,, ,  including de novo drug development to reduce HMB and subendometrial myometrial contractility and improve dysmenorrhoea scores and frozen embryo transfer (FET) success rates. As many pathways are shared by other inflammatory, fibrotic, and pain disorders, drug repositioning is another approach for adenomyosis target discovery (). Targeted therapies found in emerging approaches for adenomyosis.

Drug development should aim for stratification by specific disease sub-types (focal, diffuse, adenomyoma, outside-in), age, cycle phase, and comorbidities. As adenomyosis derives from EuE and often is contiguous with the uterine cavity, intrauterine drug delivery is a potential option, along with systemic approaches. Current therapeutic candidates focus on mainly adult surgical cohorts,,,,, highlighting the need to expand the pipeline of drug discovery and delivery to adolescents who may have different needs than adult women, as discussed in Series Paper 1.

The future portends a vast expansion of publicly available and newly generated multi-omics data, electronic health record (EHR) data across diverse populations, and multimodal digital imaging, live surgical data transformation, and “wearables” and other real-world data. Further research, using tools of artificial intelligence, such as large language model (LLM)-based chatbots and generative AI-enabled “digital twins”, is needed to integrate these vast datasets and decode adenomyosis pathobiology through multidisciplinary teams pioneering advanced technologies and computational approaches and engaging all stakeholders including those affected by adenomyosis. The goal of constructing a patient-in-silico model (“digital twin”) of disease features, risk factors, past, current and simulated therapies, and prognosis is to inform the clinical team and the individual patient to select an optimal treatment plan. The cycle would be repeated as new patient data become available, with synchronisation of the patient and her digital twin. These future directions are anticipated to enrich diagnostic accuracy and develop personalised therapeutics, prognostics, and care pathways to improve reproductive outcomes and overall health and well-being of patients with adenomyosis across the lifespan and across generations.

In summary, this review has assessed multi-dimensional technologies and experimental and computational approaches to decode adenomyosis that enrich the knowledge base generated in the recent past. Key features include how genetic susceptibility, somatic mutations, epigenetic alterations, hormonal imbalance, immune dysregulation, cell state transitions, fibrosis, angiogenesis, neuroangiogenesis, dysbiosis, and mechanisms of tissue injury and repair converge to establish a chronically inflamed, hyperestrogenic uterine microenvironment in patients with adenomyosis. Genetic variants and widespread epigenetic reprogramming drive progesterone resistance, oestrogen dominance, inflammation, impaired endometrial function, and adenomyosis lesion initiation and progression. High order molecular analyses and multi-omics platforms identify actionable pathways and candidate biomarkers to accelerate drug discovery, and advanced 3D in vitro models enable discovery of cell type- and compartment-specific pathways and validation of drug candidates. Moreover, emerging microbiome and environment-immune data underscore adenomyosis as a systemic rather than a purely localised uterine disorder, which may be preventable.

While this review has revealed major advances in research on adenomyosis pathogenesis and pathophysiology and accompanying caveats, outstanding questions remain. We offer the following in the context of leveraging big data (molecular, genetic, multiomic, EHR, imaging) and the increasing power of AI applied to making “precision medicine” a reality for patients with adenomyosis. Some outstanding questions include:•How can we translate current and forthcoming knowledge driven by advances in developed and future technologies and models of similar disorders into actionable paradigms for individualisation of care with, e.g., medical digital twin models, and what resources are needed?•What biomarkers of disease diagnosis, stratification, and developmental trajectories will be in our future adenomyosis “toolbox”?•Can we tailor mono- and multi-therapeutics with minimal side effect profiles and superior outcomes to current therapies for symptom management and improved fertility, pregnancy outcomes, and quality of life?•Can we develop prognostics tailored to the individual for disease impact on outcomes, progression, recurrence, rare malignant transformation, and prevention?•What will effective medical approaches will there be for cure of adenomyosis beyond surgery?•How can equitable care for patients with symptomatic adenomyosis be realised in the future?

medicine.title: SnS-modified platinum electrode for electrocatalytic hydrazine oxidation: mechanistic insights and electrochemical sensing
medicine.abstract: Hydrazine (HZ) is a highly toxic and carcinogenic chemical widely used in industrial, agricultural, and pharmaceutical applications, making its rapid and reliable determination essential for environmental monitoring and public health protection. In this work, a Pt/SnS-modified electrode was developed as an electrochemical sensing platform for sensitive HZ detection. Tin sulfide (SnS) particles were synthesized via a hydrothermal method and immobilized onto a Pt surface using a thin PTFE binder layer. The morphology and chemical composition of the modified electrode were characterized by SEM, EDX, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, and XRD confirming the successful formation of the SnS catalyst. Electrochemical investigations revealed that the Pt/SnS electrode exhibited enhanced electrocatalytic activity toward HZ oxidation in alkaline medium compared with bare Pt, producing more than a twofold increase in oxidation current and improved HZ adsorption. Chronoamperometry and convolution potential sweep voltammetry indicated an overall four-electron oxidation process to nitrogen, while kinetic analysis suggested an irreversible multistep oxidation mechanism with an apparent anodic electron-transfer coefficient (β) of 0.30–0.32. Differential pulse voltammetry enabled HZ determination over two linear concentration ranges of 5–35 µM and 50–3500 µM, with a limit of detection of 2.68 µM and a limit of quantification of 8.13 µM. The sensor further exhibited good operational stability, reproducibility, selectivity against common interfering species, and satisfactory recoveries of 81.0–99.3% for simulated industrial water samples. These results demonstrate that the Pt/SnS-modified electrode is a prospective electrochemical sensing platform for HZ detection, while the mechanistic electrochemical studies provide fundamental insight into its potent electrocatalytic performance.
medicine.text:
Hydrazine (N2H4) is an inorganic compound, widely used in chemical industries, pharmaceuticals, corrosion inhibitors, antioxidants, catalysts, polymer manufacturing, emulsifiers, pesticides, insecticides, herbicides, dyestuffs, and explosives. Owing to its high hydrogen content (12.5 wt%) and carbon-free oxidation products, hydrazine (HZ) has also attracted considerable interest as a promising fuel for alkaline direct HZ fuel cells. Despite these advantages, HZ is highly toxic, carcinogenic, and environmentally hazardous even at low concentrations. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) classifies HZ as a probable human carcinogen (group B2), while the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) considers HZ a potential occupational carcinogen. High-level HZ exposure can affect the central nervous system and may irritate the eyes, nose, and throat; it can also damage the lungs, liver, and kidneys. Consequently, the development of rapid, sensitive, and reliable analytical methods for HZ determination is of considerable importance for environmental monitoring, industrial process control, and public health protection.

Several analytical techniques, including spectrophotometry, chromatography, fluorescence spectroscopy, chemiluminescence, and capillary electrophoresis, have been employed for HZ determination. Although these methods generally provide satisfactory analytical performance, they often require sophisticated instrumentation, laborious sample preparation, skilled operators, and relatively high operational costs. In contrast, electrochemical sensing has emerged as an attractive alternative owing to its simplicity, rapid response, low cost, high sensitivity, portability, and suitability for on-site monitoring. The analytical performance of electrochemical sensors, however, strongly depends on the electrocatalytic properties of the electrode material.

Platinum (Pt) is one of the most effective electrocatalysts for HZ oxidation because of its excellent electrical conductivity, chemical stability, and intrinsic catalytic activity. Nevertheless, bare Pt electrodes often suffer from surface poisoning by adsorbed intermediates, which restrict their analytical performance. To overcome these limitations, numerous Pt-based composite electrodes have been developed by incorporating transition metals, metal oxides, sulfides, phosphides, and carbon-based materials to enhance catalytic activity and improve electron-transfer kinetics.

Semiconductor–metal composites have attracted considerable attention for chemical sensing because of their catalytic and structural properties. Among these materials, tin sulfide (SnS) has emerged as a promising semiconductor owing to its low toxicity, earth abundance, chemical stability, layered crystal structure, and favorable electronic properties. The presence of sulfur atoms introduces highly polarizable surface sites capable of interacting strongly with adsorbed molecules, while tin provides additional catalytic centers for surface reactions. When integrated with Pt, SnS is expected to modify the electronic structure of the Pt surface through interfacial electronic coupling, thereby optimizing the adsorption strength of HZ and its reaction intermediates. Such synergistic interactions can facilitate charge transfer, increase the density of electrochemically active sites, and promote the oxidation kinetics of HZ. Furthermore, a thin polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) binder offers excellent chemical resistance and mechanical stability, enabling firm immobilization of SnS particles on the Pt surface without significantly hindering electrolyte accessibility or long-term electrode stability.

Although several Pt-based composite electrodes have been reported for HZ oxidation, studies employing Pt/SnS heterostructures remain scarce, and the fundamental role of SnS in promoting HZ electrooxidation has not been adequately elucidated. In particular, mechanistic investigations correlating catalytic enhancement with electron-transfer kinetics and analytical sensing performance are limited. Establishing such relationships is essential for the rational design of efficient electrochemical HZ sensors.

Recent developments in chemical sensing highlight the importance of integrating appropriate sensing materials with effective transduction strategies and reliable analytical validation. For example, biogenically synthesized CuO- and Fe3O4-based electrochemical biosensors have demonstrated the relevance of nanomaterial design, selectivity, and matrix testing in pesticide detection. Beyond conventional electrochemical configurations, advances in field-effect-transistor (FET) sensors and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) integration offer potential routes toward miniaturized and portable sensing systems. Recent work on Ti3C2Tx/CuO-based extended-gate FET sensors has further highlighted the influence of charge-carrier transport in the electronic transducer on sensing performance. Although these platforms employ different analytes and sensing architectures, they illustrate the broader shift toward sensor designs that consider material properties, interfacial interactions, electronic readout, and practical validation together.

In this work, a Pt/SnS-modified electrode was fabricated by immobilizing hydrothermally synthesized SnS particles onto a Pt substrate using a PTFE binder. The morphology, composition, and chemical states of the modified electrode were characterized by SEM, EDX, Raman spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The electrocatalytic behavior toward HZ oxidation was systematically investigated using cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, differential pulse voltammetry, and convolution potential sweep voltammetry. Particular emphasis was placed on evaluating the electrode as an electrochemical sensor for HZ through determination of its sensitivity, selectivity, detection limit, and practical applicability in simulated industrial water samples, while mechanistic electrochemical analyses were performed to elucidate the origin of its enhanced sensing performance.

Hydrazine hydrate (N2H4·H2O), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) solution were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Analytical-grade hydrazine hydrate was used to prepare solutions in deionized (DI) water with a resistivity of approximately 18 MΩ·cm. Electrochemical measurements were performed using an Autolab potentiostat (PGSTST 128N, The Netherlands) and a WaveDriver 10 instrument (Pine Research Instrumentation, USA) in a conventional three-electrode configuration. A Pt electrode with a geometric surface area of 0.0314 cm2 and a Teflon-protected body was used as the working electrode. A Pt wire and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode containing saturated KCl served as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. All potentials are reported versus Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl).

SnS was synthesized by dissolving 5 mmol of SnCl2·2H2O in 15 mL of DI water under magnetic stirring until a homogeneous solution was obtained. Thiourea (4.5 mmol) was then added, and the mixture was stirred for an additional 30 min. The resulting solution was transferred to a 100 mL Teflon-lined autoclave and heated at 200 °C for 24 h. After the autoclave had cooled naturally to room temperature, the resulting precipitate was collected by centrifugation at 6000 rpm, washed with absolute ethanol and DI water using a vortex mixer, and dried at 60 °C for 2 h. The dried product was subsequently used to modify the Pt electrode.

The Pt electrode was mechanically polished on a lapping pad using alumina powder with a particle size of 0.3 µm in a figure-eight motion until a clean surface was obtained. The polished electrode was then sonicated for 20 min at 25 °C in a cleaning medium containing 0.5 M H2SO4 and acetone to remove surface contaminants. Electrochemical cleaning was subsequently performed by cycling the electrode in 0.1 M H2SO4 between 0.2 and +1.5 V versus Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl) at a scan rate of 0.1 V s−1 until successive cyclic voltammograms became stable and reproducible.

To prepare the catalytic ink, 1 mg of the synthesized SnS catalyst was mixed with a 5 wt% PTFE solution diluted with ethanol. A 6 µL aliquot of the resulting ink was drop-cast onto the cleaned Pt electrode (geometric surface area = 0.0314 cm2) using a micropipette. The modified electrode was then heated in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 10 min. PTFE served as a binder to immobilize the SnS particles on the Pt surface.

Electrochemical measurements were performed in a conventional three-electrode cell using the Pt/SnS electrode as the working electrode, a Pt wire as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl) as the reference electrode. Linear polarization curves were recorded in 0.1 M NaOH under N2-saturated conditions, both in the absence and presence of hydrazine (HZ). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted in 0.1 M NaOH containing 2 mM HZ at an excitation potential of −0.35 V. The effect of HZ concentration was investigated by cyclic voltammetry (CV) following successive additions of HZ to 0.1 M NaOH. The influence of scan rate on mass transport was examined by CV in 10 mL of 0.1 M NaOH containing 1.5 mM HZ, using scan rates ranging from 0.01 to 0.4 V s−1. N2 gas was used to maintain an inert atmosphere during the electrochemical measurements. Data analysis and graphical presentation were carried out using SigmaPlot v.10 and OriginPro 2025b.

The surface morphology and elemental composition of the synthesized material were examined using scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM–EDX; SmartEDX, ZEISS, Germany). Raman spectra were recorded using an Ava Raman spectrometer equipped with a 785 nm laser (Avantes, The Netherlands). Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns were recorded using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 Å). Le Bail fitting of the PXRD pattern was performed using TOPAS 3 (Bruker AXS) to evaluate the crystalline phase and refine the lattice parameters. The chemical states of the synthesized material were investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) using a Kratos Axis Ultra spectrometer equipped with a delay-line detector (DLD) and an Al Kα radiation source (1486.6 eV). Open-circuit potential (OCP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were performed using an Autolab potentiostat (PGSTST 128N, The Netherlands).

The morphology and composition of the synthesized SnS catalyst were characterized by SEM, EDX, and Raman spectroscopy. Representative SEM micrographs recorded at magnifications of 3000× and 100 00× () reveal a relatively uniform distribution of SnS particles with micrometer-sized features over the sample surface. The EDX spectrum () confirms Sn and S as the principal constituent elements, with atomic percentages of 68.1% and 31.9%, respectively. Although the measured Sn/S ratio deviates from the ideal 1 : 1 stoichiometry of SnS, the elemental analysis confirms the presence of Sn and S as the major constituents. Further structural confirmation was obtained from Raman spectroscopy. As shown in , a characteristic Raman band centered at 320 cm−1 is assigned to the Ag vibrational mode of SnS, which is in good agreement with previously reported values for crystalline SnS, thereby confirming the successful synthesis of the sulfide phase.

The electrochemical characteristics of the catalyst surface were first investigated by linear polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. To probe the interaction between HZ molecules and the electrode surface, linear polarization curves were recorded in 0.1 M NaOH in both the absence and presence of HZ.  compares the polarization behavior of pristine Pt and Pt/SnS electrodes under identical experimental conditions. The open-circuit potential (OCP) values revealed the difference in responses for the pristine Pt and Pt/SnS electrodes following the addition of HZ. For pristine Pt, the OCP shifted from −0.712 V in blank 0.1 M NaOH to −0.692 V after HZ addition, corresponding to a positive shift of 20 mV. In contrast, the OCP of the Pt/SnS electrode shifted from −0.159 V to −0.629 V, corresponding to a negative shift of approximately 470 mV. This substantially larger potential displacement indicates that the open-circuit electrochemical equilibrium of the modified electrode was more strongly perturbed by the introduction of HZ under the conditions investigated. The observed potential shift is interpreted as evidence of a pronounced interfacial response to HZ addition on the SnS modified Pt in comparison to the bare Pt electrode.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was employed to investigate the interfacial impedance characteristics of bare Pt and Pt/SnS electrodes in 0.1 M NaOH containing 2 mM HZ. The experimental Nyquist plots (shown in ) were fitted using the equivalent circuits presented in the inset of , and the corresponding fitting parameters, estimated errors, and goodness-of-fit statistics are summarized in Table S1.

The impedance spectrum of bare Pt was fitted using a circuit comprising the solution resistance (Rs), a constant-phase element (CPE) in parallel with a branch containing the resistance (Rp) and Warburg diffusion element (W). The fitted values of (Rs) and (Rp) were 116.42 Ω and 20.760 kΩ, respectively, with a χ2 value of 0.063293. In comparison, the Pt/SnS spectrum required a more complex equivalent circuit containing two resistive-CPE elements connected in series after the solution resistance. The fitted parameters were Rs = 123.68 Ω, Rp = 19.889 kΩ, and R1 = 15.550 kΩ, with a χ2 value of 0.063193.

Notably, the principal fitted resistance parameter (Rp) decreased by approximately 4.2% following SnS modification, from 20.760 to 19.889 kΩ. Although this modest decrease cannot be interpreted as a definitive reduction in the overall charge-transfer resistance because the two electrodes were fitted using different circuit topologies, it indicates that the principal resistive contribution (Rp) is comparable for the two electrodes and is slightly lower for Pt/SnS. The additional R1 ‖ CPE element in the Pt/SnS model indicates an additional relaxation contribution associated with the modified electrode. This contribution may be related to the SnS/PTFE-containing surface layer or an additional interfacial process; however, its precise physical origin cannot be uniquely established from the present impedance data.

The chemical composition and oxidation states of the synthesized SnS catalyst were further investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The survey spectrum () confirms the presence of Sn, S, and O as the major constituent elements of the catalyst. The high-resolution Sn 3d spectrum () exhibits two characteristic peaks centered at 487.9 eV and 496.3 eV, corresponding to the Sn 3d5/2 and Sn 3d3/2 spin–orbit components, respectively, which are characteristic of Sn species in SnS. These two peaks are separated by approximately 8.4 eV, in good agreement with previously reported values for SnS. The deconvoluted S 2p spectrum () displays a well-defined doublet with binding energies of 163.6 eV and 164.7 eV, assigned to the S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2 states of sulfide (S2−) in SnS, respectively. In addition, a distinct peak at 169.7 eV is attributed to oxidized sulfur species, which likely originated from partial surface oxidation of the catalyst upon exposure to air.

To further examine possible surface transformation during alkaline electrochemical operation, the SnS catalyst was characterized by XPS after completion of the electrochemical sensing experiments. The O 1s spectrum (given in Fig. S1) exhibits two components at measured binding energies of 531.65 and 532.51 eV, corresponding to corrected binding energies of 530.59 and 531.45 eV, respectively. The lower-binding-energy component at 530.59 eV is assigned to surface-bound hydroxyl groups (Sn–OH), oxygen-deficient lattice coordination sites, or surface-terminating oxygen species associated with the SnS surface. The component at 531.45 eV is attributed to physisorbed/chemisorbed ambient water (H2Oads). These features indicate the presence of oxygen-containing surface species after exposure to the alkaline electrolyte; however, the O 1s spectrum does not show a distinct component that can be unambiguously assigned to a separate SnO phase. Therefore, the post-electrochemical XPS results do not provide direct evidence for substantial conversion of SnS into SnO.

The crystalline phase of the synthesized tin sulfide material was investigated by X-ray diffraction (XRD). As shown in Fig. S2(A), the experimental diffraction pattern was compared with simulated patterns of α-SnS (Pnma), β-SnS (Cmcm), π-SnS (P312), SnS2 (P3̄m1), and Sn2S3 (Pnma) to evaluate the phase assignment and identify possible secondary phases. The experimental reflections show good agreement with the simulated pattern of orthorhombic α-SnS, supporting its assignment as the predominant crystalline phase in the synthesized material. No detectable characteristic reflections attributable to β-SnS, π-SnS, SnS2, or Sn2S3 were observed in the experimental pattern, indicating that these phases were not detected within the sensitivity of the XRD measurement. Furthermore, Le Bail fitting of the room-temperature XRD pattern yielded an Rwp value of 0.2108 and a goodness-of-fit value of 1.11 (Fig. S2(B)). The refined lattice parameters were a = 11.1850(6) Å, b = 3.9849(5) Å, and c = 4.3145(3) Å, consistent with the orthorhombic α-SnS structure. Overall, the agreement between the experimental diffraction pattern, the simulated α-SnS pattern, and the refined lattice parameters provides additional crystallographic evidence supporting the assignment of the synthesized material to α-SnS.

The electrocatalytic activity of the Pt/SnS electrode toward HZ oxidation was evaluated by cyclic voltammetry (CV) in 0.1 M NaOH. As shown in , the Pt/SnS electrode recorded in the absence of HZ (dashed line) exhibits only a negligible background current over the investigated potential window, indicating that the modified electrode does not undergo significant faradaic processes in the supporting electrolyte.

Upon the addition of HZ, the bare Pt electrode exhibits an oxidation wave with an onset potential of approximately −0.83 V (vs. Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl)), followed by a relatively sharp anodic peak centered at −0.77 V. Although HZ oxidation is initiated at a comparatively lower overpotential on the pristine Pt surface, the oxidation current reaches a maximum of only 0.81 mA cm−2 before decreasing rapidly at more positive potentials. Such behavior suggests that the catalytic activity of bare Pt is not sustained over a broad potential range. In contrast, the Pt/SnS electrode displays a substantially different voltammetric response. The oxidation process begins at approximately −0.65 V, followed by a broad anodic wave centered near −0.34 V. Despite the slightly more positive onset potential, the modified electrode produces a notably higher peak current density of approximately 1.8 mA cm−2, corresponding to more than a twofold enhancement compared with the bare Pt electrode. Moreover, the broad oxidation wave extends over a wider potential region without the abrupt current decay observed for pristine Pt, indicating that the catalytic surface remains active throughout the oxidation process.

Here, the enhanced oxidation current and sustained catalytic response demonstrate that immobilization of SnS on the Pt surface considerably improves the electrocatalytic performance toward HZ oxidation. The improved activity is consistent with the formation of additional catalytically active interfacial sites and more favorable adsorption and activation of HZ on the Pt/SnS interface. These observations agree well with the pronounced OCP shift and the kinetic analyses presented in the subsequent sections. The larger oxidation current together with the negligible background current recorded in the blank electrolyte provides a higher signal-to-background ratio, which makes the Pt/SnS electrode a viable candidate for conducting sensitive electrochemical HZ detection. Moreover, to establish the most suitable candidacy as a substrate for SnS modification, Pt was compared with other commonly used electrode materials in identical experimental conditions. As shown in Fig. S3, Au/SnS exhibits an HZ oxidation peak at −0.252 V with a low peak current density of only 0.286 mA cm−2, while GC/SnS produces no well-defined oxidation peak. The superior electrochemical response of Pt confirms its suitability as the substrate for SnS modification.

presents the concentration-dependent cyclic voltammograms recorded for the electrocatalytic oxidation of HZ at the Pt/SnS electrode. As the HZ concentration increased, the oxidation peak current increased monotonically, demonstrating good electrocatalytic response of the modified electrode toward HZ. Simultaneously, the oxidation peak shifted slightly toward more positive potentials with increasing HZ concentration, suggesting that a progressively higher overpotential is required to sustain the oxidation process at elevated analyte concentrations. This behavior can be attributed to increased surface coverage of adsorbed species and the accompanying concentration overpotential requiring for HZ oxidation. The difference between the peak potential and the half-peak potential (ΔEp) remained within the range of 0.040–0.048 V, which is characteristic of an irreversible electrode process. Moreover, the relatively small ΔEp values indicate rapid heterogeneous electron-transfer kinetics and efficient charge transport at the Pt/SnS interface despite the irreversible nature of the oxidation reaction. To gain further insight into the reaction kinetics, the kinetic order (γ) with respect to HZ concentration was determined from the concentration-dependent voltammograms using the following .1log j = log k + γ log[HZ]where, j is the oxidation current density, k is the apparent kinetic rate constant, and γ is the kinetic order of the reaction.  shows the plots of log j versus log[HZ] obtained at applied potentials of −0.40, −0.45, and −0.50 V. The corresponding kinetic orders were determined to be 1.03, 1.05, and 1.07, respectively. The values close to unity demonstrate that the electrocatalytic oxidation of HZ follows first-order reaction kinetics with respect to HZ concentration over the investigated potential range. The observed first-order behavior indicates that the oxidation rate is directly proportional to the HZ concentration in solution. Such linear concentration dependence is particularly advantageous for electrochemical sensing because the oxidation current changes proportionally with analyte concentration, enabling straightforward calibration.

At this point, it was important to evaluate the number of electron transfer involved to predict the oxidized product generated due to HZ oxidation reaction at Pt/SnS electrode. For this purpose, chronoamperograms (CAs) of 2 mM HZ in 0.1 M NaOH solution were recorded systematically by stepping the potential by 50 mV from −0.6 to −0.2 V. It was observed that the data received at potentials less negative than −0.6 V matched well with the well-known Cottrell equation shown as .2where, j = current density (mA cm−2), n = electron number, C = concentration of analyte (mol cm−3), D = diffusion coefficient expressed as cm2 s−1 which is 1.4 × 10−5 in the present case),t = time (s).

The apparent number of electrons transferred during hydrazine oxidation was estimated from the slope of the current density versus t−1/2 plot (given as inset of ) obtained from the chronoamperometric data at −0.45 V. The calculated electron number was approximately 3.71, which is close to the theoretical value of four electrons for the overall oxidation of hydrazine to nitrogen. Assuming nitrogen as the final oxidation product, the corresponding net reaction in alkaline medium can be proposed as per following .3N2H4 + 4OH− → N2 + 4H2O + 4e−

The effect of scan rate on HZ oxidation provides important insights into the underlying electrochemical mechanism.  presents the CVs of 1.5 mM HZ in 0.1 M NaOH recorded over a scan rate range of 0.01–0.4 V s−1. As the scan rate increases, the peak current (jp) increases systematically, accompanied by a noticeable positive shift in the peak potential (Ep).

A linear relationship between jp and the square root of the scan rate (ν1/2) is observed (R2 = 0.95), as shown in , suggesting that the overall process is diffusion-controlled. However, further kinetic analysis reveals deviations from ideal behavior. Specifically, the difference between the peak potential and half-peak potential (|Ep −Ep/2|) increases progressively with scan rate, as illustrated in , due to the continuous anodic shift of Ep at higher scan rates.

For the HZ oxidation reaction, the magnitude of (|Ep −Ep/2|) increases considerably from 60 mV to 170 mV with increasing scan rate. Such pronounced variation is characteristic of an irreversible electrochemical process. Moreover, this deviation indicates that the reaction kinetics do not strictly follow classical Butler–Volmer equation behavior. Instead, it suggests the involvement of complex, multi-step electron transfer processes.

In such case, convolution potential sweep is the most convenient tool to study the electron transfer process where all the data points are used from the original CV to carry out analysis. Furthermore, it is also used to study the kinetic and thermodynamic behavior of electron transfer processes. The convolution current I(t) was calculated from the voltammetric response using the integral transformation as per following .4where, i(u) represents the experimentally obtained current at time u. The transformation of the voltammetric data resulted in a characteristic sigmoidal curve as shown in  (dotted line), which is a hallmark of diffusion-controlled electrochemical processes. At sufficiently positive potentials, the convolution current reaches a steady-state plateau corresponding to the limiting convolution current (Il). The limiting convolution current is expressed by the following .5Il = nFAC√Dwhere n is the number of electrons transferred, F is the Faraday constant, A is the electrode area, C is the bulk concentration of HZ, and D is its diffusion coefficient. The limiting current (Il) was found nearly independent of scan rate (see ) and exhibited an average value of approximately 4.66 × 10−4 A. This behavior is advantageous for the accurate determination of n, provided that the background capacitive current is properly corrected. By considering a diffusion coefficient value of 1.4 × 10−5 cm2 s−1 (ref. ) and an electrode surface area of 0.0314 cm2, the number of electrons transferred was calculated to lie in the range of 3.71–3.83. These values are close to 4, indicating a four-electron (4e−) transfer process for HZ oxidation, which is consistent with previously reported results.

The potential-dependent heterogeneous rate constant, k(E) (also expressed as khet), for an irreversible process can be evaluated from , which is shown in .6where Il is the limiting convolution current (4.66 × 10−4 A), It is the time-dependent convolution current, and it is the cyclic voltammetric current. In , the increase in ln khet with applied potential (E) indicates that the heterogeneous electron transfer process at the electrode surface is strongly potential-dependent. The apparent transfer coefficient (βapp) was subsequently determined from the slope of the ln khetvs. E plots by linear regression within a narrow potential window, according to .7

In , the transfer coefficient (β) is observed to vary within a narrow range of 0.30–0.32 over the potential window of −0.75 to −0.45 V at different scan rates. The consistently low value of β (<0.5) suggests that the electron transfer process might be highly asymmetric and kinetically sluggish in the forward direction. Such behavior is typically indicative of a rate-determining step (RDS) involving the formation of a reactive intermediate species rather than a direct concerted electron transfer. In particular, a β value considerably lower than 0.5 implies that the transition state might be closer to the reactant side, with the involvement of a slow initial electron transfer step that may lead to the generation of a radical intermediate (˙N2H4). This observation indicates a multi-step electron transfer mechanism in which the formation of the intermediate is slower than the subsequent oxidation steps.

HZ oxidation at the Pt/SnS electrode proceeds via heterogeneous electron transfer steps coupled with surface adsorption phenomena. As per our previous calculation, the overall oxidation involves a four-electron transfer process. In alkaline media, this reaction is likely preceded by a chemical pre-adsorption step, where HZ molecules accumulate near and partially adsorb onto the electrode surface. The imposed waiting time prior to measurement facilitates this pre-accumulation, enhancing surface coverage and promoting interfacial reactions. Based on these observations, the oxidation mechanism at the Pt/SnS interface can be proposed as a sequence of chemical and electrochemical steps. Initially, HZ interacts with the catalyst surface in the presence of hydroxide ions, leading to partial dehydrogenation and the release of the first electron as shown in .8*N2H4 + OH− → *N2H3 + H2O + e−

This is followed by a second electron transfer step that might generate a highly reactive radical intermediate ().9

The formation of this radical species is kinetically slow, consistent with the low β values obtained from CPSV analysis. Once formed, the radical intermediate undergoes rapid subsequent oxidation steps due to its high reactivity, leading to the formation of molecular nitrogen ().10

The final steps are expected to be significantly faster, as radical species readily undergo oxidation. Overall, this plausible mechanistic pathway highlights that HZ oxidation at the Pt/SnS electrode is governed by a multi-step kinetic pathway.

To evaluate the feasibility of the Pt/SnS electrode as a cost-effective and reliable electrochemical sensor for HZ quantification in aqueous media, differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) measurements were performed at room temperature in 0.1 M NaOH containing various concentrations of HZ (5–3500 µM). The corresponding DPV responses are presented in . The Pt/SnS-modified electrode exhibited a concentration-dependent increase in oxidation peak current, revealing two distinct linear concentration ranges of 5–35 µM and 50–3500 µM, as shown in . The calibration curve for the lower concentration range was described by the equation y = 4.2 × 10−5x − 9.9 × 10−5, with a correlation coefficient (R2) of 0.9932. For the higher concentration range, the linear equation was y = 4.3 × 10−6x + 6.4 × 10−4, with an (R2) value of 0.9924. Here, x represents the HZ concentration (µM), and y represents the oxidation peak current (mA). The corresponding slopes were 4.2 × 10−5 and 4.3 × 10−6 mA µM−1 for the lower and higher concentration ranges, respectively. Based on the geometric electrode area of 0.0314 cm2, the corresponding current–density-normalized sensitivities were 1.34 × 10−3 and 1.37 × 10−4 mA cm−2 µM−1, respectively. The limit of detection (LOD) was calculated using the slope of the lower-concentration calibration curve and the standard deviation of five blank measurements according to  and .11SD = SE × N12where SD is the standard deviation, SE is the standard error of the blank measurements (1.527 × 10−8 A), N is the number of blank measurements (5), and b is the slope of the lower-concentration calibration curve (4.2 × 10−8 A µM−1). Based on these equations, the LOD of the Pt/SnS electrode for HZ detection was determined to be 2.68 µM. Similarly, the limit of quantification (LOQ) was calculated using .13

The LOQ of the Pt/SnS electrode was calculated to be 8.13 µM, indicating its capability for quantitative HZ determination above this concentration within the lower linear range. The two distinct linear ranges demonstrate the concentration-dependent analytical response of the Pt/SnS electrode over a broad concentration interval. The Pt/SnS electrode exhibits comparable performance to that of previously reported noble metal-based electrodes for HZ detection, as summarized in .

As summarized in , the Pt/SnS electrode exhibits a competitive analytical performance compared with previously reported noble-metal-based HZ sensors. Its sensitivity in the lower concentration range (1337.6 µA mM−1 cm−2) exceeds those reported for PdNPs-EDAC/GCE (403.7 µA mM−1 cm−2) and GO/CTS/Pt/GCE (104.6 µA mM−1 cm−2). Its LOD of 2.68 µM is also lower than those of several reported electrodes, including GO/CTS/Pt/GCE, Nano-Au/Ti, and Pd/BMWCNTs. Although some comparative sensors achieve lower LODs or higher sensitivity, the Pt/SnS electrode offers a favorable combination of sensitivity and an extended upper linear range reaching 3500 µM. These comparisons establish Pt/SnS as a prospective and competitive alternative for electrochemical HZ detection.

The electrochemical stability of the Pt/SnS electrode toward HZ oxidation was evaluated by continuous cyclic voltammetric cycling in 3 mM HZ dissolved in 0.1 M NaOH at a scan rate of 0.1 V s−1. As shown in , after 50 consecutive CV cycles, the 51st cycle retained a peak current density of 1.40 mA cm−2, compared with an initial value of 1.52 mA cm−2, corresponding to a current retention of 92.1%. Moreover, the oxidation peak potential exhibited only a slight positive shift from −0.34 V to −0.33 V. The minimal loss in current response and negligible peak potential shift indicates good electrochemical stability and good resistance of the Pt/SnS electrode to surface deactivation during repeated HZ oxidation.

To further assess the stability and reproducibility of the Pt/SnS electrode, additional experiments were performed to examine the effect of storage time and electrode-to-electrode variation. For storage stability, cyclic voltammograms for 2 mM HZ oxidation were recorded using the same Pt/SnS electrode after storage periods of 0, 3, 6, 30, and 54 h under otherwise identical experimental conditions (). The oxidation response remained well preserved throughout the investigated storage period (). The onset potential (Eonset) and peak potential (Ep) remained identical in CVs recorded in the period 0 to 6 h. The onset potential varied only slightly from −0.65 V at 0 h to −0.66 V at 54 h, while the peak potential changed from −0.34 to −0.36 V. The corresponding peak current density decreased from 0.89 to 0.75 mA cm−2, corresponding to approximately 84% of the initial response. These relatively small changes in the electrochemical response indicate that the Pt/SnS electrode retained its catalytic activity over the investigated storage period.

The reproducibility of the electrode fabrication was further evaluated using four independently prepared Pt/SnS electrodes under identical experimental conditions ( and ). The independently fabricated electrodes exhibited closely comparable onset potentials ranging from −0.65 to −0.67 V and peak potentials ranging from −0.34 to −0.36 V, while the peak current densities varied between 0.83 and 0.89 mA cm−2. The relatively small variation in both potential and current response demonstrates good electrode-to-electrode reproducibility of the Pt/SnS fabrication procedure. Together, the storage-stability and independent-electrode measurements provide additional evidence that the observed HZ oxidation response is reproducible under the experimental conditions employed in this study.

The selectivity of the Pt/SnS electrode toward HZ oxidation was evaluated in the presence of 13 potential interfering species, including FeSO4·7H2O, FeCl3·6H2O, CH4N2O (urea), ascorbic acid (AA), NH2OH·HCl, NH4OH, KNO3, CuSO4·5H2O, NiSO4·6H2O, NaCl, KHCO3, Na2CO3, and glucose. Transition metal ions (Fe2+, Fe3+, Cu2+, and Ni2+) were selected because they may be present in industrial wastewater and can interact with the electrode surface or participate in competing electrochemical processes. Inorganic salts (NaCl, KNO3, KHCO3, and Na2CO3) were included to assess the influence of electrolyte composition and ionic strength on the HZ oxidation response. Nitrogen-containing compounds (urea, NH2OH, and NH4OH) were selected because of their chemical characteristics or potential coexistence in HZ-containing industrial streams, whereas glucose and ascorbic acid were included as representative organic species that may interfere with electrochemical measurements.

The bar graph in , showing the HZ oxidation peak current densities extracted from the CVs in Fig. S4, illustrates the variation in the electrochemical response following the addition of each interfering species at 3 mM. The current-retention values ranged from 85.48% to 132.47%, with an average of 105.51% across the 13 tested species (Table S2). However, the average response masks species-dependent effects. FeCl3·6H2O, NH2OH·HCl, NaCl, and KHCO3 produced positive current deviations of 21.37%, 19.53%, 32.47%, and 21.74%, respectively, whereas CuSO4·5H2O and NiSO4·6H2O decreased the current response by 14.52% and 13.11%, respectively. For a quantitative assessment, a current-retention interval of 90–110% was adopted as a study-specific screening criterion, corresponding to a deviation of ±10% from the HZ-only response. Seven of the 13 tested species fell within this interval, while the remaining six exceeded it, indicating that the influence of individual interferents cannot be considered negligible in all cases.

As shown in Fig. S4, the HZ oxidation peak potential remained nearly unchanged in the presence of the tested species, and no additional redox peaks were observed within the investigated potential range. Nevertheless, the observed changes in peak current demonstrate that interference may occur even in the absence of additional redox peaks. It should also be noted that these experiments were conducted using CV with 3 mM HZ and 3 mM of each interfering species.

To assess the practical applicability of the Pt/SnS electrode for HZ determination in complex matrices, recovery experiments were performed using simulated dye and pharmaceutical industry samples spiked with 3 mM HZ. The analytical results are summarized in . The Pt/SnS electrode exhibited satisfactory analytical performance in the investigated real samples, with recoveries ranging from 81.00% to 99.33%. The dye industry samples showed good recoveries of 97.33% for sample-1 (predominantly containing Alizarin red) and 99.33% for sample-2 (predominantly containing methylene blue), indicating that these dye constituents exerted minimal interference on the electrochemical oxidation of HZ. Similarly, the pharmaceutical sample-2 (predominantly containing fexofenadine hydrochloride) exhibited a high recovery of 96.66%, confirming the reliability of the proposed sensor in pharmaceutical matrices. In contrast, the sample-1 (predominantly containing acetaminophen) showed a comparatively lower recovery (81.00%), suggesting that certain excipients or active pharmaceutical ingredients may partially suppress the HZ oxidation current through matrix effects or competitive adsorption on the electrode surface. Nevertheless, the sensor maintained a distinct HZ oxidation response, enabling successful quantification even in this comparatively challenging matrix.

Average concentration obtained from three independent measurements using the Pt/SnS electrode.

Relative standard deviation (RSD) of three independent measurements.

Recovery (%) = (obtained concentration/added concentration) × 100.

The precision of the proposed sensing platform was further demonstrated by the low relative standard deviation (RSD) values, which ranged from 0.05% to 0.29%, indicating good repeatability and high measurement precision. The combination of high recoveries and low RSD values confirms that the Pt/SnS electrode possesses good accuracy, precision, and robustness for HZ determination in complex industrial and pharmaceutical samples, highlighting its potential for practical environmental and industrial monitoring applications.

A Pt/SnS-modified platinum electrode was successfully fabricated by immobilizing hydrothermally synthesized SnS particles onto a Pt substrate using a thin PTFE binder layer. Structural characterization by SEM, EDX, Raman spectroscopy, PXRD, and XPS provided evidence supporting the formation of the SnS-containing material. Electrochemical studies demonstrated that SnS modification enhanced the HZ oxidation response, producing more than a twofold increase in oxidation current relative to bare Pt while maintaining good operational stability. Kinetic investigations using cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry, and convolution potential sweep voltammetry indicated that HZ oxidation proceeds through an irreversible multistep pathway involving an overall four-electron transfer to form nitrogen, with an apparent transfer coefficient (β) of approximately 0.30–0.32. This behavior suggests a kinetically slow initial electron-transfer step followed by more rapid oxidation of intermediate species. The enhanced catalytic response is attributed primarily to favorable HZ adsorption and activation at the Pt/SnS interface. The electrode enabled HZ determination over two linear concentration ranges of 5–35 µM and 50–3500 µM, with a limit of detection of 2.68 µM and a limit of quantification of 8.13 µM. Interference and recovery experiments using simulated industrial samples provided an initial assessment of analytical applicability, although the variation in responses indicates that further matrix-specific validation is required. Future development could explore miniaturization through smaller-area or thin-film Pt electrodes, screen-printed electrode designs, and optimized SnS loading to reduce noble-metal consumption. Integration with a portable potentiostat and compact electronic readout could facilitate on-site hydrazine monitoring, although these approaches require further investigation and experimental validation. Overall, this study provides mechanistic insight into HZ electrooxidation at the Pt/SnS interface and establishes a foundation for the further development of practical electrochemical hydrazine sensors.

The authors declare no competing financial interest.

medicine.title: Advancing NTM research with citizen science
medicine.abstract: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) is a generic term for the >200 species of environmental mycobacteria. NTM are ubiquitous, but there is extensive variation in the distribution of individual species. In a recent article published in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, Wilsey et al. describe how community-based citizen science efforts helped map the distribution of NTM in Hawai’i (R. N. Wilsey, L.-H. Ding, S. N. Dawrs, C. K. Raulerson, et al., Appl Environ Microbiol 92:e00269-26, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.00269-26). Mycobacterium chimaera, an opportunistic pathogen and the leading cause of NTM pulmonary disease in Hawai’i, was among the most common species isolated.
medicine.text:
In a recent article published in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, Wilsey, Ding, Dawrs, and colleagues present the results of a remarkable study that combined community-based citizen science efforts with laboratory-based culture and genomic analyses ().
