During a 5-year sampling campaign, a network of volunteers, including many high school and university students, collected >2,300 environmental samples from the islands of Hawai’i, O’ahu, Maui, and Kaua’i. Sampling included dirt from gardens and natural areas, dust from indoor and outdoor locations, water from streams, and biofilms from household plumbing (e.g., kitchen sinks, bathroom showerheads). Nearly one-quarter of all samples were culture-positive for nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). The isolates included Mycobacterium species known to be opportunistic human pathogens (e.g., Mycobacterium chimaera and Mycobacterium abscessus) as well as numerous potentially novel taxa.

Studies investigating the environmental distribution of NTM date back to at least the 1950s (, ). Much remains to be discovered about how the environment shapes NTM populations, but various factors, including the moisture content of soil as well as the pH and mineral content of soil and water, have been associated with the prevalence of certain species (, ). In the 1980s, a series of papers describing the epidemiology of NTM in the continental United States revealed that NTM species are not evenly distributed. There is a geographic bias, such that different species are more likely to occur in different regions (). International surveys confirm that the distribution of NTM varies between countries and across continents (, ). Because NTM infections result from environmental exposures, rather than person-to-person transmission, species distribution has implications for human health.

Globally, organisms of the Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) are the leading cause of pulmonary disease due to NTM. However, a comprehensive review of the global epidemiology of NTM pulmonary disease indicates that, in some jurisdictions, other species (esp. Mycobacterium kansasii, Mycobacterium xenopi, and members of the Mycobacterium abscessus-chelonae group) are isolated more frequently than MAC (). Even within MAC, there is variation. In the Americas, M. avium tends to be most common, whereas studies from China, South Korea, and Australia report more Mycobacterium intracellulare.

In Hawai’i, M. chimaera is the most common MAC species (). M. chimaera is infamous for its role in a global outbreak of illness associated with contaminated heater-cooler units due, in part, to persistence in disinfection-resistant biofilms (). In the current study, M. chimaera was recovered from 40% (238/590) of lung samples and 8% (56/700) of environmental samples. Although it was recovered from soil and natural water samples, most of the Hawai’ian isolates were from household plumbing, including biofilms from showerheads and sinks. Sequence analysis indicates that the M. chimaera strains circulating in Hawai’i represent distinct regional lineages, now designated Pacific Island Circulating Clusters 1 and 2. These are genomically unrelated to the heater-cooler strain.

Overall, environmental sampling revealed that rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) are more prevalent than slowly growing species. Three RGM were widespread. Mycobacterium porcinum (an RGM of the Mycobacterium fortuitum complex), M. chelonae, and M. abscessus were isolated from 13.9%, 11.3%, and 10.9% of environmental samples, respectively. These RGM were also frequently recovered from respiratory samples, representing 5.0%, 20.0%, and 1.5% of lung isolates, respectively. The relatively high prevalence of these organisms in both environmental and clinical samples highlights how the distribution and abundance of an opportunistic pathogen influences the relative risk of infection.

The extensive sampling associated with this project also enabled the research team to look for “hotspots,” geographic regions where samples were more likely to be culture-positive for NTM. Of the six hotspots initially identified, the elevated NTM positivity rate was statistically significant for two regions: Kahului on Maui and the Hilo and Hawaiian Paradise Park on Hawai’i Island. A third region, Puhi in southeastern Kaua’i, didn’t achieve statistical significance for all NTM but was significant as a hotspot for M. chimaera.

In most jurisdictions, NTM infections are not considered “notifiable diseases.” However, by providing evidence that environmental diversity does mirror clinical prevalence, this study demonstrates that NTM should not be ignored by public health. Just as households are encouraged to protect themselves from mosquito-borne pathogens by eliminating sources of standing water, reminders to clean or replace faucets and showerheads fouled by biofilms could help households reduce exposures to NTM. Similarly, it’s routine to provide public health alerts warning of high Escherichia coli levels in recreational waters. Why not notify the public about environmental NTM hotspots? To achieve the robust sampling required for identification of such hotspots, jurisdictions could follow the Hawai’ian example and engage citizen scientists. Not only is this an effective way to collect incredible data, but it raises awareness of environmental microbiology and provides aspiring researchers with an accessible, and much-needed, introduction to scientific principles.

medicine.title: When does a funnel become a trap? A Gömböc-inspired model of protein folding landscapes
medicine.abstract: The protein folding problem remains a fundamental challenge in biophysics. While energy landscape theory resolves Levinthal's paradox through funnel-shaped landscapes, the quantitative effects of landscape ruggedness on folding kinetics are not fully understood. We introduce a computational model inspired by Gömböc, a convex 3D shape with one stable equilibrium and one unstable equilibrium, as an analogy for protein folding landscapes. Using a tunable ruggedness parameter, we simulate “folding” across multiple ruggedness conditions (r = 0 and r = 10−8 to 10−3), spanning five orders of magnitude in the positive-r regime. At minimal ruggedness (10−8), the model achieves 83% success in reaching native-like states. Increasing the ruggedness to 10−7–10−5 reduces the success rate to 25–39%, reflecting landscape trapping as an analog for kinetic trapping in physical folding. Benchmarking against the TPR1 domain via Rosetta and AlphaFold3 reveals native-like coverages of 77% and 90%, respectively, showing qualitative correspondence with the Gömböc model's success rates at low ruggedness. These findings suggest that the Gömböc-inspired model captures essential features of folding landscape quality and may serve as a useful heuristic for comparing foldability across different systems, bridging mathematical topology with protein biophysics.
medicine.text:
The protein folding problem, which involves understanding how a linear amino acid chain consistently folds into its native three-dimensional structure, has captivated biologists, chemists, and physicists for decades. Anfinsen's thermodynamic hypothesis posits that the native structure represents the global free energy minimum under physiological conditions. However, this principle alone cannot explain the remarkable speed and reliability of folding in vivo. Levinthal's paradox suggested that a random search for a stable configuration in the conformational space would require astronomical timescales, yet many proteins would fold in milliseconds or less.

The energy landscape theory of protein folding provides a conceptual framework for resolving this paradox. According to this theory, proteins fold on funnel-shaped energy landscapes where the native state sits at the global minimum, and the landscape's topography, particularly its ruggedness, determines folding kinetics. A perfectly smooth funnel enables rapid, deterministic folding, whereas excessive ruggedness creates kinetic traps that slow folding and increase the probability of misfolding.

However, natural proteins are not perfectly smooth; they exhibit varying degrees of landscape ruggedness resulting from evolutionary pressures, including the need to avoid aggregation, accommodate functional dynamics, and navigate cellular environments. Understanding how ruggedness quantitatively affects folding outcomes is therefore essential for both basic science and applications in protein design and disease modeling.

The concept of “frustration” in protein folding captures this ruggedness, the extent to which interactions conflict with each other, creating local energy minima that can trap folding intermediates. Minimally frustrated proteins have landscapes dominated by the native funnel, whereas highly frustrated proteins exhibit multiple competing minima. Experimental studies have shown that frustration is unevenly distributed in protein structures, with some regions showing higher frustration than others.

In this study, we introduce a computational model inspired by Gömböc, a convex three-dimensional shape with exactly one stable and one unstable equilibrium point, as an analogy for protein folding landscapes.

The Gömböc (pronounced goemboets) was discovered by Hungarian scientists Gábor Domokos and Péter Várkonyi in 2006. It is the first known convex 3D shape made of homogeneous material, which is monomonostatic, i.e., it has just one stable and one unstable point of equilibrium, a property long thought impossible. It has been proven that such a 2D shape is impossible; however, monomonostatic bodies can exist in higher dimensions. The shapes of 3D monostatic convex homogeneous bodies are somewhat close to a sphere, although the exact shape is elusive and hard to visualize, describe, and identify; the minimal number of faces for monomonostatic polyhedra might be very large. These unusual properties gave rise to the name Gömböc, a character in Eastern Europe fairy tales (compared with the Slavic “Kolobok”) and an elusive, almost spherical, bread-like being. Gömböc-like shape capsules have also been manufactured and implemented in biomedical research and drug delivery.

The mathematical curiosity of the Gömböc provides a powerful analogy for protein folding: the shape always returns to its unique stable position when perturbed, just as a well-evolved protein consistently refolds to its native state. However, the pathway involved depends on how it is perturbed, mirroring the multiple folding pathways observed in proteins.

The unique stability properties of Gömböc make it an ideal metaphor: like a well-evolved protein, it has a single, well-defined native state but can approach it through multiple pathways. By systematically varying a ruggedness parameter across several orders of magnitude, we map the relationship between landscape topography and folding outcomes, identifying optimal regimes and paradoxical behaviors. Note that Gömböc reaches its stable equilibrium relatively slowly in comparison with the departure from the unstable equilibrium. This process is similar to protein unfolding being approximately two orders of magnitude faster than folding.

Our computational model () captures this essence while incorporating key biophysical features of real proteins: chain connectivity, excluded volume, local steric constraints, and long-range interactions that can create frustration. By systematically tuning a ruggedness parameter, we explore the continuum from perfectly smooth funnels to extremely rugged landscapes, providing quantitative insights into how landscape topography determines folding outcomes.

The conformational space of proteins is multidimensional. While the original Gömböc is a 3D shape, it can be generalized to higher dimensions via mathematical induction by revolving an n-dimensional Gömböc in the (n + 1)-dimensional space around a line that connects two equilibria. The resulting n + 1 shape is a Gömböc because any point on its surface, other than the original equilibria, belongs to the n-dimensional Gömböc and, therefore, is not an equilibrium point.

Long molecules, such as polymers, are often modeled by random 3D chains in space; however, simplified models are often 2D chain models; the latter tend to capture the most significant characteristics of the former. An ideal chain has an average end-to-end distance proportional to the square root of the number of segments (the scaling exponent of 0.5). A chain without self-intersection is called a chain with excluded volume. These chains have scaling exponents of 3/5 (or 0.588 based on elaborate scaling arguments) in 3D and 3/4 in 2D.

Protein conformations were represented as closed, two-dimensional chains consisting of N = 48 discrete points (vertices) in the plane, yielding a flattened coordinate vector of length 96. This representation abstracts the polypeptide backbone as a continuous, closed chain with fixed segment connectivity but variable bond angles and positions.

We constructed the target (‘native’) conformation as a two-dimensional analog inspired by Gömböc, a convex 3D shape with exactly one stable and one unstable equilibrium. In this analogy the native conformation corresponds to the unique stable equilibrium of the Gömböc, while the unstable equilibrium is represented conceptually by the high-energy, disordered or randomly initialized chain conformations from which optimization begins; these starting states are unstable with respect to the native basin and spontaneously evolve toward it under the energy gradient (when the landscape is sufficiently smooth). Our 2D representation captures the essential property of a unique global energy minimum while remaining computationally tractable, although it does not fully satisfy the mathematical definition of a Gömböc.

Like the 3D Gömböc shape, which is close to a sphere, the equilibrium chain was assumed to be a perturbed ring (). The native chain was constructed via multiharmonic Fourier synthesis with incommensurate frequencies to ensure aperiodicity.

The 2D closed chain model used in this study is the constructed native conformation (target shape) generated via multiharmonic Fourier synthesis with asymmetry perturbation, representing a Gömböc-like convex contour with a single pronounced global energy minimum. This 2D analog captures the essential property of a unique stable state while enabling computation of the free energy landscape.

A base polar function r(θ) was supplemented with Cartesian polynomial shear to break the radial symmetry, yielding a unique, smooth, asymmetric target shape analogous to a protein's native state. The native shape was parameterized as follows:r(θ) = C0 + C1 sin θ + C2 sin(k1θ + φ) + C3 cos(k2θ),where θ ∈ [0,2π) is uniformly sampled at N points (endpoint excluded). The coefficients C0 = 1.0, C1 = 0.20, C2 = 0.12, C3 = 0.08, k1 = 2.8, k2 = 4.5, and φ = 0.5 were selected empirically to generate a mildly asymmetric, near-circular convex contour that possesses a single pronounced global energy minimum while remaining free of self-intersections and of radial symmetry that would produce degenerate minima. These values yield a shape qualitatively reminiscent of a 2D projection of a Gömböc-like body. Cartesian coordinates were computed viax = r(θ)cos θ, y = r(θ)sin θ

To break the radial symmetry and ensure a unique global energy minimum, we apply a coordinate transformation that shifts the x-coordinate of each point on the basis of its y-coordinate:x ← x + 0.12y2 − 0.04y3, y ← y

The quadratic term (0.12y2) introduces a symmetric lateral deformation, whereas the cubic term (0.04y3) breaks up asymmetry. Only the x-coordinate is modified to preserve the overall convexity and prevent self-intersection. The y-coordinate remains unchanged, ensuring that the perturbation is minimal and that the shape remains close to the original ring.

The non-dimensional potential energy function E comprises seven additive terms designed to balance the native attraction, geometric constraints, and tunable frustration:E = Enat + Econf + Erep + Elocal + Ebond + Erug + Efrust

The energy function integrates the following terms: the native attraction energy Enat, which drives folding via a quadratic root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) potential near the native state. Confinement energy (Econf to prevent expansion; steric repulsion energy Erep to avoid self-intersection; local geometry energy Elocal to maintain approximately 114.6° bond angles; bond restraint energy Ebond to preserve segment lengths; random ruggedness energy Erug, which introduces local energy variations via stochastic perturbations according to the following equation:where N = 48 (number of points), so 2N = 96 coordinates; xi parameters are the flattened coordinates of the current conformation; Ni(0,1) are independent standard normal random variables; r is the ruggedness parameter with c = 0.01 and k = 20; and frustration energy Efrust, which penalizes nonnative long-range interactions for residue pairs separated by at least five positions along the chain according to the following equation:where M is the set of long-range residue pairs whose current distance deviates significantly from the native distance, and where dij is the Euclidean distance between two points (residues) i and j on the chain with α = 15. Both Erug and Efrust are scaled by the same tunable ruggedness parameter r. Scaling both terms by a single control parameter simultaneously modulates the amplitude of stochastic local noise and the strength of non-native long-range penalties. This design choice permits systematic exploration of landscape roughness while preserving the relative balance between the two sources of frustration; independent scaling of the two terms would introduce an additional free parameter without altering the qualitative conclusions of the study. This model belongs to the class of structure-based (Gō-like) models, in which the energy function is constructed with explicit knowledge of the target native conformation.

The numerical optimization generates folding trajectories via deterministic gradient-based minimization, which employs a two-stage hybrid strategy to balance global exploration and precise local convergence. In Stage I, the conjugate gradient method was applied for 2000 iterations with a gradient tolerance of 10−3, which was chosen for its efficiency in navigating the initial high-energy regions of the landscape. Stage II utilized the Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) algorithm for 6000 iterations with a stricter gradient tolerance of 10−6, ensuring accurate convergence near local minima. A total of 700 independent folding experiments were conducted across seven ruggedness conditions (n = 100 per condition), with simulations terminating upon convergence (gradient norm < 10−6) or after reaching the 10 000-step iteration limit. The model is pattern-reproducible but not bit-reproducible: without a frozen noise field, reruns give different individual trajectories but the same ensemble statistics. The trajectories were classified into six outcome categories on the basis of final RMSD values: perfect (≤0.12), success (≤0.20), good (≤0.30), near-native (≤0.40), misfolded (≤0.55), and poor (>0.55). The energy drop was also recorded to differentiate successful native state recovery from optimizer trapping (analogous to kinetic trapping in physical folding):ΔE = Einit − Efinalwhere Einit and Efinal are the potential energies at the start and end of the simulation, respectively. Computationally, all simulations were implemented in Python 3.9.12, leveraging NumPy 1.21.5 for numerical arrays and SciPy 1.7.3 for optimization routines, while visualizations were created via Matplotlib. The calculations were performed on a standard workstation (Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM), with the full ensemble requiring approximately 4 CPU-hours of computational time.

The Rosetta modeling suite (version 2020.03) was used to perform parallel ab initio folding simulations on a well-characterized protein domain. The TPR1 domain of the Hop adaptor protein (PDB ID: 1ELW, chain A) was selected as the test system, a 118-residue domain solved by X-ray diffraction at 1.60 Å resolution. The MPI-parallelized ab initio relax application was employed to generate 2500 independent decoys across 24 physical cores. The key simulation parameters included increased cycle amplification (cycles = 10) to enhance conformational sampling, radius of gyration reweighting (Rg = 0.5 Å) to bias toward compactness, and balanced secondary structure weights (0.5) for the helix and loop. Following the centroid-based sampling stage, all-atom relaxation was performed via the fast relaxation protocol to refine the local geometry. Folding outcomes were assessed by plotting Rosetta energy scores against the Cα RMSD relative to the native structure, and the lowest-energy decoys (top 1.0%, corresponding to 25 structures) were extracted for visual inspection. To characterize the topography of the energy landscape, all 2500 decoys were clustered via the Rosetta cluster application with a 3.0 Å RMSD radius, grouping similar conformations and revealing the density of states across the folding funnel.

The AlphaFold (AF3) server was used to provide a contemporary benchmark for protein structure prediction and to assess the folding landscape of the TPR1 domain via the AF3 model. The generated protein structure was evaluated by measuring the overall confidence score (pTM) and per-residue confidence, which were assessed via the predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT). The predicted aligned error (PAE) plot was used to analyze expected position errors between residues within the same structural domain, with values typically less than 5 Å confirming the integrity of the TPR fold. Finally, the generated structures were aligned against the experimental X-ray crystal structure to calculate RMSD values via PyMOL software.

The Gömböc-inspired computational model clearly reveals a transition in folding behavior as landscape ruggedness increases (). Protein conformations are represented as closed two-dimensional chains with a tunable ruggedness parameter (r) in the energy function. While the true Gömböc is a 3D convex body with a single stable and unstable equilibrium, our 2D analog captures the essential feature of a unique, stable native state with multiple accessible folding pathways, serving as a conceptual rather than geometric analogy.

Gömböc model: fraction with RMSD ≤ 0.4 (dimensionless, normalized). The results are not directly comparable to the reference data.

Reference metrics for qualitative comparison only: pLDDT = AF3 per-residue confidence score averaged over all residues (0–100); coverage = percentage of Cα atoms aligned within 1.0 Å RMSD after structural alignment.

At zero ruggedness (r = 0.0), the landscape acts as a near-perfect funnel, yielding an average energy drop of 129.5 ± 21.7 arbitrary units, convergence in 21 optimization steps, and a 93% success rate in reaching native-like states (RMSD ≤ 0.4). This behavior mirrors minimally frustrated, efficient folding akin to an ideal Gömböc returning to its stable equilibrium (). A slight increase to r = 10−8 reduces the energy drop to 123.9 ± 23.9 units, extends the number of steps to 47, and decreases the success rate to 83%, maintaining near-ideal behavior. However, further escalation to r = 10−7 sharply impairs the outcome: the energy drop decreases to 67.0 ± 20.7 units, the number of steps increases to 63, and success further decreases to 39%, as stochastic energy fluctuations begin to disrupt the gradient-based optimization pathway. At r = 10−6 and 10−5, this noise dominates the landscape, yielding modest energy drops (14–17 a.u.) over just 6 to 10 steps, with success rates falling to 25–26% (). Higher ruggedness (r = 10−4) yields even smaller energy changes (2.2 ± 5.9 a.u.) and fewer steps (4), with success rates plateauing and showing a slight recovery to 33% at the highest ruggedness. However, the stochastic noise at extreme ruggedness values (10−4 and 10−3) causes the gradient-based optimizer to terminate prematurely; thus, the apparent recovery in the success rate is merely an artifact of the baseline probability that a random initial conformation happens to fall within the near-native RMSD threshold. This algorithmic failure at intermediate ruggedness (r = 10−7 to 10−6) functionally mimics the kinetic trapping described by Porebski et al., who reported that the rugged folding landscapes of functional proteins render them susceptible to misfolding and aggregation.

The present Gömböc-inspired model complements our earlier topological bioscaling analysis of Trp-cage folding, in which the chain was shown to pass through fractional-dimensional intermediate states (1 ≤ D ≤ 1.92) whose stability is controlled by interaction energy. Together, the tunable ruggedness parameter r and the fractal scaling approach provide a quantitative bridge between monomonostatic topology and the dimensional properties of native state recovery under optimization.

Overall, our results quantitatively demonstrate how even minute increases in landscape ruggedness dramatically degrade folding efficiency, shifting from rapid, high-fidelity convergence to severe landscape trapping and misfolding. This is similar to how Gömböc is fragile and sensitive to a slight change of its shape.

Rosetta ab initio folding simulations generated 2500 independent decoys for the TPR1 domain, revealing a characteristic funnel-shaped energy landscape with a well-defined global minimum (). The TPR1 domain is a critical component of the Hsp70/Hsp90-organizing protein (Hop), where it serves as a scaffold by binding directly to the C-terminal EEVD motif of Hsp70. This interaction facilitates the transfer of client proteins from Hsp70 to Hsp90, coordinating their maturation and folding. Consistent with this well-folded, minimally frustrated system, the lowest-energy decoys (after outlier removal) achieved scores near −350 REU at Cα RMSD values of 0.7–1.1 Å relative to the experimental structure; the lowest-energy structure in the cleaned set has E = −350.14 REU and RMSD = 0.822 Å. Analysis revealed a clear energetic gap of ∼30–40 REU between native-like conformations (RMSD < 2.0 Å) and misfolded structures, indicating a minimally frustrated folding landscape dominated by a single, deep funnel (). The top 1.0% of the decoys (n = 25) achieved RMSD values below 1.5 Å, confirming that the TPR1 domain is a well-behaved, efficient folding system.

Favorable energetic contributions included attractive van der Waals interactions (Eattr ≈ −730 REU), backbone hydrogen bonding (Ehbond ≈ −86 REU), and favorable electrostatic interactions (Eelec ≈ −230 REU), balanced by steric repulsion (Erep ≈ 75 REU) and solvation effects (Esol ≈ 510 REU). The outlier removal (3.8% of decoys) substantially improved the energy-RMSD correlation from r = 0.434 to r = 0.699 (p < 0.001), a 60.9% increase revealing the underlying funnel topology (Fig. S1A–F). The clean dataset (n = 2404) presented RMSD values ranging from 0.526 to 12.472 Å (mean 2.379 ± 2.392 Å) and energies ranging from −350.140 to −245.833 REU (mean: −322.132 ± 14.458 REU). The energy gap between the lowest-energy structure and the second lowest-energy structure (E = −350.131 REU, RMSD = 0.803 Å) was ΔE = 0.009 REU, indicating that multiple distinct conformations near the native state have similar energies (). The energy functions used in the Rosetta protocol are based on Anfinsen's hypothesis, in which the native state corresponds to a unique, low-energy, thermodynamically stable conformation. One-way ANOVA across RMSD tertiles revealed highly significant energy differences (F = 752.43, p < 0.001), confirming that the TPR1 domain is a robust benchmark for comparison with the Gömböc-inspired model.

The AF3 predictions for the TPR1 domain exhibited exceptionally high confidence, with an overall pTM score of 0.91 and per-residue pLDDT values ≥90 for >95% of the residues, indicating “very high” confidence.

The PAE plot revealed predominantly low expected position errors (most values <5 Å, with a maximum of approximately 14 Å), confirming a single, well-defined structural fold without domain-swapping or alternative conformations. High-confidence AF3 predictions (pLDDT ≥ 90) with a uniform PAE plot are characteristic of well-folded, minimally frustrated systems, as frustrated proteins often exhibit conformational heterogeneity reflected in lower prediction confidence or alternative domain arrangements. These results support the classification of the TPR1 domain as a minimally frustrated system suitable for benchmarking the Gömböc-inspired model.

A quantitative comparison of structural prediction accuracy revealed that AF3 substantially outperformed Rosetta in alignment with the experimental reference (). In this analysis, accuracy benchmarking tests confirmed superior protein structure prediction by AlphaFold compared with established physics-based ab initio methods, including Rosetta. The best AF3 alignment achieved an RMSD of 0.3 Å with 90% atom coverage, whereas Rosetta's optimal alignment yielded 0.43 Å RMSD at 77% coverage. AF3 also demonstrated greater consistency (RMSD range: 0.30–0.49 Å) than Rosetta did (0.43–0.72 Å). AF3 alignments began at 0.45 Å RMSD versus 1.26 Å for Rosetta, indicating inherently closer proximity to the native conformation.

Collectively, these results establish AF3 as a more accurate predictor for this target, achieving sub-0.5 Å RMSD values approaching the experimental resolution. These data were close to the 0.5 Å RMSD benchmark reported for the Trp-cage protein folded by AlphaFold2. The residual differences between the predicted models and the experimental X-ray structure (RMSD 0.3–0.7 Å) can be attributed to several factors: (i) the finite resolution of the experimental structure (1.60 Å), (ii) the absence of crystal-packing contacts in the computational models, (iii) differences in the treatment of side-chain rotamers and solvent, and (iv) the fact that both Rosetta and AF3 sample an ensemble of near-native conformations rather than a single crystallographic snapshot.

A direct comparison between Rosetta/AF3 alignment coverage and Gömböc-inspired model success rates reveals a compelling parallel. AF3 achieved 90% coverage at 0.30 Å RMSD, whereas Rosetta achieved 77% coverage at 0.43 Å RMSD, qualitatively corresponding to Gömböc success rates at low ruggedness: 93% (r = 0.0) and 83% (r = 10−8), respectively. The success rate of the Gömböc-inspired model decreased sharply to 26–39% at higher ruggedness values (r = 10−7 to 10−6), which is characteristic of highly frustrated landscapes where folding becomes trapped (analogous to kinetic trapping in physical folding). These findings suggest that the ruggedness parameter captures essential features of folding landscape quality, with qualitative correspondence between model success rates and prediction method performance. However, further validation of diverse protein targets and explicit physical units is needed to establish a model as a quantitative predictor.

In this study, we introduced a computational model inspired by Gömböc, a convex shape with a single stable equilibrium, to investigate how landscape ruggedness influences protein folding landscape optimizability. By systematically varying a ruggedness parameter across multiple conditions (r = 0 and r = 10−8–10−3, spanning five orders of magnitude in the positive-r regime), we demonstrated a sharp transition from efficient, funnel-dominated folding to trapped, misfolded states analogous to kinetically trapped intermediates. At minimal ruggedness, the model achieved 93% success in reaching native-like conformations, showing qualitative correspondence with the high-accuracy predictions of AF3 (90% native-like coverage) for the TPR1 domain. In contrast, increasing the ruggedness by as little as a factor of 10−7 reduced the success rate to 39%. While the metrics differ, this degradation in optimizability is broadly consistent with the lower native-like coverage achieved by Rosetta (77%) compared with AF3 (90%) for the minimally frustrated TPR1 domain.

These findings suggest that the Gömböc-inspired model captures essential features of folding landscape quality. Unlike conventional Gō models that encode only native contacts, the present formulation combines a monomonostatic (single-stable-equilibrium) geometric target with an explicit, tunable Efrust that penalizes non-native long-range distances and a stochastic ruggedness term Erug that injects local energy noise. The sharp degradation of success rate with increasing r demonstrates that the optimizability of the landscape depends critically on the interplay between the unique stable native basin (the Gömböc-like property) and the strength of competing interactions; when r is negligible, the funnel dominates, and the model recovers the native state with high fidelity, whereas even minute ruggedness introduces kinetic traps analogous to those observed in frustrated proteins. The correspondence between model success rates and the performance of state-of-the-art structure prediction methods, despite differing metrics and dimensionalities, indicates that the ruggedness parameter may serve as a useful heuristic for comparing foldability across different systems. By bridging mathematical topology with protein folding biophysics, this approach offers a scalable platform for exploring the effects of frustration, evolutionary design principles, and the limits of foldability.

Future work will extend the model to three dimensions, incorporate sequence-specific effects, validate diverse protein targets, and explore its applicability to intrinsically disordered proteins and aggregation-prone systems.

The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.

medicine.title: Integration of an FDA-Authorized Digital Autism Diagnostic Tool Into an Outpatient Developmental Pediatrics Workflow: Preliminary Quality Improvement Study
medicine.abstract: Long wait times and specialist shortages delay autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis, often beyond the period when early intervention is most effective. Digital diagnostic tools may help increase diagnostic capacity by supporting clinicians in delivering timely autism evaluations within routine outpatient care.This study aimed to conduct a preliminary assessment of the integration of a digital autism diagnostic device (Canvas Dx) into an outpatient developmental pediatrics workflow, including a descriptive evaluation of agreement between device outputs and specialist clinical diagnoses and an exploration of clinician and caregiver experience.A single-center, prospective quality improvement study evaluated the implementation and performance of Canvas Dx in a specialty developmental pediatrics clinic. Canvas Dx is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–authorized digital ASD diagnostic device approved for use in children aged 18 to 72 months with caregiver or health care provider concern for developmental delay. Eligible children were consecutively prescribed Canvas Dx during the study period and completed the assessment as part of routine clinical care. Device diagnostic outputs were compared with the final specialist clinical diagnoses. Clinician and caregiver feedback was collected to explore their experience with the assessment process and perceived workflow impact via poststudy surveys that captured both structured quantitative questions and open-ended qualitative questions.A total of 28 children were included (mean age 52.2, SD 13.8 months; 7/28, 25% female), with an autism prevalence of 67.9% (19/28) based on specialist diagnosis. The device generated a determinate result for 22 (78.6%) participants. Among participants with determinate device results, sensitivity was 94.1% (95% CI 73%-99%) and specificity was 80% (95% CI 37.6%-96.4%). Positive predictive value was 94.1% (95% CI 73%-99%), and negative predictive value was 80% (95% CI 37.6-96.4%) when compared with specialist diagnosis. These estimates were imprecise, particularly for specificity and negative predictive value, because of the small number of participants without an ASD diagnosis. Clinicians reported improved insights and ease of use during evaluation visits, and caregivers reported high satisfaction with the assessment process.This preliminary quality improvement assessment demonstrates the feasibility of integrating Canvas Dx into a routine outpatient developmental pediatrics workflow and provides initial descriptive data on agreement with specialist diagnostic determinations and clinician and caregiver experience. Given the small sample size and resulting imprecision of diagnostic performance estimates, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and used to inform larger prospective evaluations of diagnostic performance and workflow impact.
medicine.text:
The prevalence of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has steadily increased over the last 2 decades [], while there is simultaneously a shortage of specialists trained to diagnose ASD [-] This has contributed to an average age of diagnosis that is later than the optimal period [] for young children to receive the intensive behavioral intervention that contributes to optimal long-term outcomes [,]. Long wait times for ASD diagnostic evaluations remain a significant challenge across the United States, with recent studies reporting waits of several months to more than 1 year [-]. At the time this project was conducted, internal clinic waitlist data maintained by the Division of Neurodevelopmental Pediatrics at Children’s National Hospital indicated that wait times for autism diagnostic evaluations exceeded 12 months. There is thus an urgent need for improved processes to establish ASD diagnoses in a timely fashion so that families of young children with ASD can access appropriate intervention services [].

Canvas Dx is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–authorized diagnostic device that can support the diagnosis or ruling out of ASD in children with developmental delay or other ASD-specific concerns between 18 and 72 months of age []. This project assessed the impact of incorporating the Canvas Dx system into the workflow of outpatient developmental pediatrics clinics at Children’s National. The system was used with 28 consecutive patients who met the criteria for the Canvas Dx system’s indications for use, as determined by the division’s intake coordinator on initial contact with referred families.

Canvas Dx is a prescription-only, FDA-authorized software-based diagnostic aid intended to support clinicians in diagnosing or ruling out ASD in children aged 18 to 72 months who have concerns about developmental delay []. The device combines information from 3 independent sources, including a caregiver questionnaire, a treating clinician questionnaire, and a standardized clinical analysis of caregiver-uploaded home videos, within a locked machine learning algorithm to generate a positive, negative, or indeterminate result for autism. To support clinical interpretation, contextual information, including a detailed developmental profile that maps observed behaviors to the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [Fifth Edition]) diagnostic criteria for ASD and summarizes strengths and challenges across key developmental domains, is also generated to help inform clinical decision-making and intervention planning. For participants receiving an indeterminate result, the report also includes a predefined indeterminate category (low, moderate, or high). The low, moderate, and high categories are defined by prespecified algorithmic thresholds designed to stratify ASD likelihood among children for whom the device cannot generate a definitive positive or negative result. The thresholds were selected during device development to provide the clearest separation in ASD likelihood within the indeterminate population, with higher categories representing progressively greater likelihood of ASD. These evidence-based categories were established using an independent development dataset (n=261; autism prevalence 26.8%; 34% female). Within this development dataset, 5% of children classified as low indeterminate, 25% classified as moderate indeterminate, and 35% classified as high indeterminate received a specialist-confirmed ASD diagnosis, supporting the intended risk stratification across categories []. Data inputs and outputs are summarized in .

Evidence supporting Canvas Dx includes results from a prospective, double-blinded, multisite pivotal clinical trial that demonstrated high agreement between Canvas Dx outputs and blinded specialist diagnoses, with consistent performance across sex, race and ethnicity, and socioeconomic status []. Subsequent real-world studies have demonstrated that Canvas Dx maintains accuracy outside of investigational settings and can substantially reduce the time to ASD diagnosis compared with traditional specialty referral pathways [,].

In a prospective observational study integrating Canvas Dx into a primary care diagnostic workflow, for example, use of the system was reported to be feasible for clinicians and acceptable to families, while compressing the diagnostic timeline by several months relative to nearby specialty centers []. A larger real-world case series further demonstrated strong diagnostic performance across diverse practice settings, with determinate outputs produced for most cases and median ages for positive results occurring well before the national average age of ASD diagnosis in the United States []. To date, most published evaluations of Canvas Dx supporting its clinical validity, real-world effectiveness, and potential system-level benefits have focused on primary care setting integration [,]. In contrast, the present study provides a preliminary examination of its potential applicability within a specialty diagnostic pathway.

This quality improvement project was designed as a preliminary assessment to characterize real-world use of Canvas Dx and generate descriptive data to inform future larger-scale evaluation.

The primary objective was to preliminarily characterize agreement between Canvas Dx determinate outputs and standard clinical autism diagnoses made by developmental pediatrics specialists in a routine outpatient clinical setting and to generate descriptive diagnostic performance estimates to inform future larger-scale evaluation.

The secondary objective was to explore clinician and caregiver experience with Canvas Dx and perceived workflow impact associated with incorporating the system into outpatient developmental pediatrics practice.

This single-center, prospective quality improvement study preliminarily evaluated the implementation of Canvas Dx in a specialty developmental pediatrics clinic and descriptively characterized its diagnostic performance compared with specialist clinical diagnosis.

This preliminary quality improvement project was reviewed by the Children’s National Hospital Institutional Review Board (IRB), which determined that the project was exempt from full IRB review because it met the criteria for a quality improvement initiative intended to improve clinical processes and patient care. The project did not involve experimental interventions. Because the project was determined to be exempt, the IRB determined that formal informed consent was not required. All data used for analysis were deidentified prior to analysis and reporting. Participant privacy and confidentiality were protected in accordance with institutional policies and applicable ethical standards, and no individually identifiable information was included in the study results. Participants did not receive financial compensation for participation in this quality improvement project.

The project took place within an outpatient developmental pediatrics clinic affiliated with Children's National Hospital in Washington, DC.

Participants were enrolled and data were collected between May and September 2025 as part of routine clinical care. Participants included children aged 18 to 72 months with caregiver or health care provider concern for developmental delay who met the device’s indications for use. The complete Canvas Dx indications for use are included in . Children were referred from primary care to the developmental pediatrics clinic for evaluation of a range of developmental concerns, including but not limited to suspected ASD. Consistent with the Canvas Dx indications for use, eligibility was based on the presence of broad developmental concerns rather than an ASD-specific referral; therefore, children were not excluded if suspicion of ASD was not the primary reason for referral. Eligibility was determined during intake prior to clinic visits.

No formal sample size target or power calculation was established because this was a time-limited quality improvement project rather than a prospectively powered diagnostic accuracy study. Enrollment was determined pragmatically by the number of eligible patients meeting the device indications for use who presented during the implementation period and by the limited number of device licenses available for the project. Accordingly, the resulting sample was intended to provide preliminary descriptive data to inform future larger-scale evaluation. Participant flow through the study is summarized in .

Caregivers completed the Canvas Dx app-based questionnaire and uploaded short home videos of their child prior to the clinic visit. Clinicians completed the Canvas Dx clinical questionnaire. The reference standard clinic visit consisted of a comprehensive, approximately 1-hour, in-person developmental evaluation conducted by a board-certified developmental pediatrician. The evaluation included a caregiver interview, review of developmental and medical history, direct clinical observation of the child, review of available records, and any additional developmental assessments deemed clinically appropriate. Following completion of the evaluation, the developmental pediatrician integrated all available clinical information to determine whether the child met DSM-5 criteria for ASD or another neurodevelopmental condition.

The primary outcome measured was diagnostic agreement between the digital diagnostic device and specialist clinical diagnosis. Secondary outcomes included clinician- and caregiver-reported experience with the device.

The specialist clinical diagnosis was categorized as ASD or non-ASD based on the developmental pediatrician’s final clinical determination. Canvas Dx generated 1 of 3 possible outputs: positive for ASD, negative for ASD, or indeterminate. For participants receiving a determinate Canvas Dx result, agreement was defined as a positive Canvas Dx result with a specialist diagnosis of ASD or a negative Canvas Dx result with a specialist diagnosis of non-ASD. Discordance was defined as a positive Canvas Dx result with a specialist diagnosis of non-ASD or a negative Canvas Dx result with a specialist diagnosis of ASD.

Clinician and caregiver experience with Canvas Dx was assessed using brief surveys administered following use of the device. Surveys measured secondary outcomes including satisfaction and comfort with the assessment process, perceived ease of use, acceptability, time burden, confidence in the diagnostic result, and willingness to recommend the approach. The complete caregiver and clinician survey instruments are provided in  and .

Caregivers were asked whether they were comfortable using the Canvas Dx device for their child’s evaluation (yes or no). Five additional items assessed whether the device worked without problems, whether instructions for recording the child were easy to follow, whether the caregiver could use the device independently, willingness to recommend the device to other families, and trust in the diagnosis received from the health care provider. These items used a 5-point Likert response scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Time burden was assessed by asking caregivers how much time they spent completing Canvas Dx tasks, with categorical response options. Optional open-ended questions invited caregivers to describe what they liked and did not like about the device and provide additional feedback.

Clinicians were asked whether they were comfortable using Canvas Dx as part of their patient’s evaluation (yes or no). Five additional items assessed whether the platform worked without difficulties, ability to use it without assistance from the Canvas Dx team, confidence in the diagnosis received from Canvas Dx, perceived usefulness of the assessment summary, and willingness to recommend this type of evaluation to other health care providers. These items used a 5-point Likert response scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Clinicians were also asked whether they reviewed the full Canvas Dx report and whether they would consider continuing to use Canvas Dx in clinical practice (yes or no). Optional open-ended questions solicited feedback regarding the report, reasons for continued use, comparison with other diagnostic tools, and additional experiences with Canvas Dx.

Descriptive analyses and diagnostic performance calculations were conducted using Python (version 3.12; Python Software Foundation). Diagnostic agreement and determinate versus indeterminate outcomes were summarized using counts and percentages. Given the preliminary nature of this quality improvement study and the small sample size, no inferential statistical testing was performed.

Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were calculated among determinate cases, with 95% CIs calculated using the Wilson score method. Indeterminate results were excluded from these calculations because they do not represent positive or negative diagnostic classifications, but rather cases in which the algorithm abstains from making a diagnostic call because of uncertainty.

The abstention mechanism allows the system to acknowledge uncertainty and avoid overconfident classification when evidence is insufficient [,]. Analyzing abstention cases separately is consistent with prior evaluations of Canvas Dx [,] and reflects the intended behavior of an abstaining classifier, for which diagnostic accuracy metrics describe performance only when the algorithm issues a classification, while the determinate rate provides complementary information regarding the frequency of abstention.

Responses to quantitative clinician and caregiver survey items were analyzed descriptively. Categorical responses were summarized using frequencies and percentages, and Likert-scale responses were summarized by the distribution of responses across response categories. Given the small sample size and exploratory nature of these secondary outcomes, no inferential statistical testing was performed.

Open-ended clinician and caregiver survey responses were analyzed using an inductive qualitative content analysis approach [,]. Responses were reviewed in their entirety, and meaningful units of text were identified and assigned descriptive codes. Related codes were then grouped into broader descriptive categories reflecting recurring aspects of clinician and caregiver experience with Canvas Dx. Caregiver and clinician responses were analyzed separately because the survey questions and perspectives differed between groups. Responses provided in Spanish were translated into English for analysis, with the original responses retained for reference. Given the small number and brief nature of the open-ended responses, the analysis was intended to provide descriptive context regarding participant experience rather than to achieve thematic saturation. One researcher performed the initial coding and category development, and a second researcher independently assigned the source responses to the established categories, with no discrepancies identified.

A total of 28 children meeting the indications for use were consecutively enrolled in the quality improvement project (mean age 52.2, SD 13.8 months). Seven (25%) were female, and 21 (75%) were male. Autism prevalence according to the reference standard specialist diagnosis was 67.9% (19/28). There were no missing data for the primary diagnostic accuracy analyses. Participants represented a racially and ethnically diverse cohort, with the largest groups identifying as Black and not Hispanic and as other and Hispanic. The distribution of participant race and ethnicity is presented in .

Self-reported race and ethnicity of participants enrolled in the developmental pediatrics quality improvement study (N=28)a.

aPercentages are based on total sample size (N=28) and may not sum to 100% due to rounding. Race and ethnicity categories are reported as provided by participants or caregivers.

The device generated a determinate result (positive or negative for autism) for 22 (78.6%) of the 28 participants. Among participants with determinate results, the device demonstrated strong agreement with specialist clinical diagnoses. Of the 17 participants who received a specialist-confirmed autism diagnosis, 16 also received a positive autism result from the device, corresponding to a sensitivity of 94.1% (16/17; 95% CI 73%-99%). Of the 5 participants who were determined by specialists not to meet the criteria for autism, 4 also received a negative result from the device, yielding a specificity of 80% (4/5; 95% CI 37.6%-96.4%).

The positive predictive value of the device was 94.1% (16/17; 95% CI 73%-99%), with 16 of 17 participants who screened positive receiving a specialist-confirmed ASD diagnosis. The negative predictive value was 80% (4/5; 95% CI 37.6%-96.4%), with 4 of 5 participants who screened negative confirmed as not having ASD.

A total of 6 indeterminate results were received (6/28, 21.4%). Four (66.7%) were high indeterminate, 2 (33.3%) were moderate indeterminate, and none were low indeterminate. Autism prevalence within the indeterminate group was 33.3% (2/6). Both high indeterminate cases were confirmed as having autism by a clinician. More than half (4/6, 66.7%) of the participants with indeterminate results had reported co-occurring conditions. For indeterminate cases, global developmental delay was reported for 33.3% (2/6), language disorder was reported for 16.7% (1/6), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder was reported for 16.7% (1/6).

Of the 6 clinicians who participated in the pilot, 5 were board-certified developmental-behavioral pediatricians, and 1 was a nurse practitioner. Four (66.7%) of the participating clinicians completed poststudy feedback surveys regarding their experience using Canvas Dx as part of the diagnostic process. All 4 indicated that they were comfortable using Canvas Dx as part of their patients’ evaluations. All 4 agreed or strongly agreed that the site worked without difficulties, that they were able to use the site without assistance from the Canvas Dx team, that they were confident in the diagnoses their patients received from Canvas Dx, and that they would recommend this type of evaluation to other health care providers. Responses regarding the usefulness of the assessment summary were more variable: 2 clinicians strongly agreed that it was useful, 1 agreed, and 1 strongly disagreed. All 4 clinicians reported that they had read the full Canvas Dx report and that they would consider continuing to use Canvas Dx in their clinical practice.

Inductive qualitative content analysis of clinician free-text responses identified 4 primary descriptive categories: value of structured clinical information, value of naturalistic behavioral information, perceived clinical and access value, and limitations. Clinicians described the Canvas Dx report as organized and clinically informative, including its structured presentation of behaviors and symptoms and organization according to DSM-5 criteria. One clinician described the report as “well organized,” noting that it “highlighted behaviors and symptoms appropriately” and “provided relevant information for care management.” Another noted, “I appreciated the breakdown of response by DSM-5 criteria.”

Clinicians also described the value of naturalistic behavioral information, particularly the ability to review videos of children outside the clinical environment. One clinician reported, “I really liked having videos of the patients in their home or other comfortable setting to see before I met the family.” Perceived clinical and access value included convenience for families, parent involvement, confirmation of clinical impressions, and the potential to improve access to autism diagnosis and intervention. One clinician noted that Canvas Dx “allows the parents to be involved in the diagnostic process, which often helps with acceptance of the diagnosis.”

The qualitative analysis also identified several individual limitations or concerns. One clinician reported difficulty with 2-factor authentication due to inconsistent cellular service. The same clinician described uncertainty regarding the incremental impact on their own diagnostic decision-making, noting that although Canvas Dx provided confirmation of their clinical impression, it did not necessarily change their diagnostic decision. The clinician also suggested that the tool may have greater value for less specialized health care providers seeking to provide an earlier diagnosis. Additionally, one clinician expressed concern regarding the report template’s requirement to assign a level of support need, indicating that this feature may be limiting in certain clinical contexts.

In total, 15 (55.6%) of the 27 participating caregivers returned their postassessment feedback survey regarding their experience using Canvas Dx as part of their child’s diagnostic evaluation. One caregiver was the parent of twins who completed the survey once for her 2 children. All respondents (15/15, 100%) reported that they were comfortable using the Canvas Dx device, as indicated by affirmative responses to a binary yes or no item assessing overall comfort with the platform.

Overall ease of use and functionality were rated highly. For the statement “The Canvas Dx app worked fine without problems,” 86.7% (13/15) of caregivers selected “strongly agree,” while the remaining 13.3% (2/15) selected “agree.” Similarly, 93.3% (14/15) strongly agreed that the directions for recording their child were easy to follow, with one caregiver (6.7%) selecting “agree.” With respect to independent use, 86.7% (13/15) of respondents strongly agreed that they could use the app without assistance, and 13.3% (2/15) agreed. When asked whether they would recommend the app to other families, 86.7% (13/15) of caregivers strongly agreed and 13.3% (2/15) agreed. Using an adapted net promoter score (NPS) calculation in which “strongly agree” responses were categorized as promoters and “agree” responses as passives, the resulting NPS was 87, reflecting a high willingness to recommend the device among respondents. Caregivers also reported favorable perceptions of efficiency. Ten (66.7%) respondents indicated that completing the questionnaire and recording and uploading 2 home videos took less than 15 minutes, while 5 (33.3%) caregivers reported completion times of 15 to 30 minutes. No participants reported requiring more than 30 minutes to complete the process, suggesting low time burden for most families. Caregivers also reported high levels of trust in the results their child received from the health care provider at the clinic visit, with 86.7% (13/15) strongly agreeing and 13.3% (2/15) agreeing with this statement.

Inductive qualitative content analysis of caregiver free-text responses identified ease and simplicity of completing the assessment as the primary descriptive category. All 6 caregivers who responded to the question regarding what they liked about Canvas Dx described aspects of ease of use, including the simplicity and practicality of the device, clarity of instructions, or ease of recording and uploading videos. Representative comments included, “It is very easy and practical,” “I liked that the instructions are very well explained,” and “Videos were easy to record or upload.” Additional open-ended comments reflected trust and appreciation for the assessment process, including “Overall, there is great confidence in how it works” and “I am very grateful for being shown the device.” No negative aspects of the Canvas Dx device were identified in caregiver open-ended responses.

In this preliminary quality improvement project evaluating the integration of Canvas Dx into a specialist autism diagnostic workflow, Canvas Dx determinate results showed a high level of agreement with specialist clinical diagnoses. However, the small sample size, particularly the small number of participants without an ASD diagnosis, resulted in wide CIs and limited the precision of diagnostic performance estimates. Accordingly, these findings should be considered preliminary and descriptive rather than confirmatory. They provide initial evidence to inform larger studies evaluating Canvas Dx performance within our specialist developmental pediatrics workflows. While subgroup sample sizes were too small to support meaningful comparisons of diagnostic performance across sex, race, and ethnicity, the study cohort was demographically diverse and included substantial representation of participants identifying as Black or African American (non-Hispanic), a population historically underrepresented in clinical research [,] and disproportionately affected by delayed diagnosis. Equitable representation across demographic groups is a critical consideration for digital diagnostic tools intended for broad clinical deployment [], as it supports their potential to contribute to more consistent and timely identification across populations that have traditionally faced barriers to care.

Of the 6 participants who received an indeterminate result, autism prevalence was lower than in the positive subset, and a majority had documented co-occurring developmental conditions, including global developmental delay, language disorder, or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Although the small number of indeterminate cases precludes firm conclusions, the observed co-occurrence of developmental conditions among these children warrants further investigation into whether phenotypic complexity may be associated with indeterminate outputs. The ability to return an indeterminate result rather than forcing classification in ambiguous cases is consistent with the device’s abstention-based responsible AI framework [,].

Beyond diagnostic performance, clinician and caregiver feedback indicated generally positive experiences with Canvas Dx, including satisfaction, perceived ease of use, and acceptability within the clinical workflow. Qualitative content analysis of clinician feedback identified perceived value of structured clinical information and naturalistic behavioral information as key categories, including the structured presentation of DSM-5 criteria and the ability to review videos of children in naturalistic settings prior to in-person visits. Caregivers also reported high levels of comfort with the assessment process and found the platform easy to use and time efficient. Consistent with these quantitative findings, qualitative content analysis of caregiver feedback identified ease and simplicity of completing the assessment as the primary descriptive category. These findings suggest that the assessment can be completed with minimal burden on families and is acceptable for use within routine clinical care. Caregivers also expressed a strong willingness to recommend the tool to others, further supporting its overall acceptability.

The largest real-world Canvas Dx study to date did not report on caregiver or clinician experience []. However, findings from our study related to clinician and caregiver acceptability mirror those reported in the study by Sohl et al [], in which Canvas Dx was integrated into a primary care workflow. In that study, both health care providers and families reported ease of use, and device results showed agreement with the final clinical diagnosis. The present project extends those findings to a specialist diagnostic context and demonstrates similarly favorable perceptions of device workflow integration and clinical accuracy.

Notably, the proportion of children receiving a determinate result in the current project was higher than that reported in both the Sohl et al [] and Salomon et al [] studies. This difference may reflect variation in population characteristics, referral patterns, clinical setting, or implementation workflow. The higher determinate rate observed here suggests that in certain clinical contexts, the device may be able to provide actionable diagnostic support for a substantial majority of patients. Further comparative evaluation across care settings would be valuable to better understand the factors that influence device performance in different contexts.

More broadly, the present findings contribute to a growing literature evaluating alternative approaches to traditional autism diagnostic pathways. Primary care–based diagnostic models, telehealth assessment, remote behavioral observation, and digital approaches have increasingly been evaluated as strategies to expand diagnostic capacity and facilitate more timely autism evaluation [-]. A 2023 scoping review of ASD diagnosis in US primary care settings identified studies evaluating diagnostic accuracy, time to diagnosis, specialty wait times, and clinician comfort with diagnosis, supporting the feasibility of expanding diagnostic evaluation beyond traditional pathways []. Within specialty settings, investigators have evaluated fast-track and stratified diagnostic models designed to better allocate specialist resources and reduce time to diagnosis []. Collectively, these studies reflect increasing efforts to move beyond a uniform, resource-intensive diagnostic pathway toward approaches that match the intensity of assessment to individual clinical needs []. The present study contributes to this literature by providing preliminary evidence regarding the integration of an FDA-authorized digital diagnostic device into an existing specialty developmental pediatrics workflow.

These findings have several implications for future clinical evaluation and implementation. First, the preliminary diagnostic performance estimates observed among determinate cases, particularly for sensitivity and positive predictive value, suggest that the device may be particularly useful in supporting accurate identification of ASD, with the potential to facilitate more timely access to appropriate intervention. However, given the small sample size and resulting imprecision of these estimates, particularly for specificity and negative predictive value, larger studies are needed to more precisely characterize diagnostic performance and potential clinical impact. Second, the abstention mechanism appears to appropriately flag cases with phenotypic complexity, reinforcing rather than replacing clinician expertise. Third, the integration of structured caregiver-reported data and home-based video provides clinicians with insight into child behavior in naturalistic settings, which may enhance diagnostic confidence and family engagement.

From a workflow perspective, clinician feedback from this preliminary quality improvement project suggests that the device can be incorporated into routine evaluation processes without substantial technical barriers, although these findings should be confirmed in larger implementation studies. Caregiver feedback suggests low time burden and high user satisfaction, perceived ease of use, and acceptability, which are critical components for sustained adoption.

This project has several limitations. Although all eligible patients were enrolled consecutively, the small sample size resulted in wide CIs around estimates of diagnostic accuracy, limiting the precision of these estimates. Accordingly, the diagnostic performance findings should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Because specialists were not blinded to the Canvas Dx result, diagnostic independence between the index test and reference standard was not maintained. This may have introduced incorporation bias [] and should be considered when interpreting the diagnostic accuracy estimates. However, this workflow reflects the intended real-world clinical use of Canvas Dx as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for specialist clinical judgment. Only 4 of the 6 clinicians participated in the survey, which limits the generalizability of health care provider experience findings. Additionally, caregiver survey completion was 56%, raising the possibility of response bias. It is plausible that caregivers with more polarized experiences may be most likely to complete the survey [], potentially inflating or deflating satisfaction metrics. Given the uniformly positive caregiver responses observed, positivity bias cannot be excluded, and the survey findings should therefore be interpreted as descriptive of respondents rather than representative of all participants. Future studies with larger samples and higher response rates will be important to validate these findings. The study was conducted within a single implementation context, and findings may not generalize to other geographic regions, practice types, or patient populations.

Because diagnostic accuracy analyses were limited to participants receiving determinate results, overall system performance must be interpreted in light of the abstention rate. While the abstention mechanism reflects responsible AI design, future research should continue to examine the characteristics of children who receive an indeterminate output and best-practice protocols for making accurate diagnostic decisions in this group.

In this preliminary quality improvement project, Canvas Dx demonstrated high observed concordance with specialist diagnostic determinations among children receiving determinate results and was well accepted by both clinician and caregiver users. The device’s ability to provide structured behavioral insights, incorporate naturalistic videos, and integrate into routine workflow suggests potential for meaningful clinical utility. However, given the preliminary nature of this study, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory and require confirmation in larger-scale evaluations. Collectively, these findings suggest that Canvas Dx has the potential to support routine ASD diagnostic workflows and provide a foundation for larger implementation studies. In the context of persistent specialist shortages and prolonged wait times for ASD evaluation, further evaluation of technologies that may help streamline diagnostic pathways is warranted.

medicine.title: Multidomain determinants of perivascular spaces indicate early cerebrovascular vulnerability in individuals at risk of Alzheimer’s disease
medicine.abstract: Perivascular spaces (PVS) are MRI-visible markers of cerebrovascular and glymphatic function, but their regional determinants in preclinical Alzheimer’s disease (AD), regarding sex and AD biomarkers, remain poorly understood.We studied 1199 cognitively unimpaired ALFA study participants (aged 54–65 years), genetically enriched for AD risk, with CSF biomarker phenotyping in 296 participants. PVS were automatically quantified in basal ganglia, centrum semiovale, hippocampus, and midbrain on 3T MRI. Counts were modeled using Poisson or negative binomial regression, adjusting for demographics, cardiometabolic, lifestyle, and genetic factors, with effect modification by sex and amyloid/tau (AT) status.PVS showed marked regional specificity. Centrum semiovale PVS were associated with age, male sex, and cardiometabolic factors, whereas hippocampal and midbrain PVS were more closely related to AD biomarker status and sleep or psychological measures. Men exhibited higher centrum semiovale burden while women showed higher counts in hippocampus, midbrain, and basal ganglia. Associations were stronger in amyloid-positive individuals with concurrent tau pathology. Polygenic scores for lipid and metabolic traits contributed modestly to regional PVS variation.PVS burden is associated with multidomain determinants in preclinical AD with regional, sex-specific, and biomarker-dependent patterns, supporting PVS as accessible MRI markers for risk stratification and precision prevention.“Early Identification of Markers in Alzheimer’s Families/ALFA (ALFA Cohort)” (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02485730). Registration number: NCT02485730.
medicine.text:
Perivascular spaces (PVS) are small, fluid-filled compartments that surround penetrating blood vessels in the brain and play a central role in interstitial fluid drainage, metabolic waste clearance, and neuroimmune regulation.– Once considered incidental findings, enlarged or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-visible PVS are now recognized as markers of cerebrovascular and glymphatic dysfunction and are increasingly studied in the context of brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD).,

Quantitative MRI assessment of PVS provides a non-invasive window into cerebrovascular and glymphatic integrity.– Emerging evidence suggests that PVS burden exhibits marked regional heterogeneity across the brain, reflecting distinct pathophysiological mechanisms that may underlie PVS enlargement in different anatomical regions.– Increased PVS burden, particularly in the basal ganglia, may serve as an early imaging marker of vascular dysfunction and impaired brain clearance, processes increasingly linked to AD pathogenesis.,–

PVS burden is already considered a core neuroimaging feature of cerebral small vessel disease,, and several studies have reported associations with cerebrovascular risk factors,

 Aβ and tau pathology,, and neuroinflammatory mechanisms., However, most existing evidence derives from general population samples or clinical cohorts with established cerebral small vessel disease or symptomatic neurodegeneration. Consequently, the determinants of PVS burden during the preclinical stages of AD, when cerebrovascular and clearance dysfunction may still be modifiable,

 remain poorly understood.

Current evidence suggests that PVS burden reflects the combined influence of demographic factors, vascular and metabolic health, lifestyle and environmental exposures, and genetic susceptibility.,, Advanced age and male sex have consistently been associated with higher PVS burden, along with hypertension and obesity.,,,, More recent evidence implicates environmental exposures,

 sleep disturbances,, and neuropsychiatric symptoms, in glymphatic and cerebrovascular dysfunction. In parallel, genetic studies indicated that PVS burden is partly heritable and shares genetic architecture with cardiometabolic traits and AD-related pathways., Yet, how these multidomain determinants shape regional PVS burden, and whether their effects differ by biological sex or AD biomarker status, remains largely unexplored.

Sex differences in vascular aging, lipid metabolism, hormonal regulation, sleep architecture, and neuroinflammatory responses may critically modify perivascular vulnerability, particularly in midlife. Likewise, the presence of early AD pathology, as defined by CSF Aβ and tau biomarkers, may alter the relationship between systemic risk factors and perivascular integrity. Understanding how sex and biomarker stage interact with multidomain risk factors is essential to disentangle early cerebrovascular and clearance dysfunction from downstream neurodegeneration and to identify tractable targets for prevention.

In this study, we examined demographic, cardiovascular, lifestyle/environmental, and genetic determinants of PVS burden across 4 brain regions, in 1199 cognitively unimpaired participants aged 54–65 years from the ALFA (ALzheimer and FAmilies) study, a cohort genetically enriched for AD risk. We further investigated whether these associations varied by sex, CSF Aβ status, and amyloid/tau (AT) biomarker classification in a nested biomarker subsample of 296 individuals. We hypothesized that PVS reflect the cumulative impact of genetic vulnerability and modifiable risk exposures, and that these effects are region- and stage-specific revealing early cerebrovascular vulnerability potentially influencing early AD pathology.

A schematic overview of the study design is presented in .

Participants were drawn from the ALFA study, a single-site, prospective cohort of 2743 CU individuals aged 45–74 years recruited in Barcelona, Spain, and designed to characterize early biological changes in the preclinical stage of AD.

 Most participants are first-degree descendants of patients with AD dementia (86% with a parental history of dementia and 48% with parental AD onset before age 75), resulting in an elevated prevalence of APOE-ε4 carriers and higher polygenic susceptibility to AD., At the parental-cohort level, exclusion criteria included cognitive impairment (Mini-Mental State Examination < 26, Memory Impairment Screen < 6, Time-Orientation < 68, or semantic fluency < 12), Clinical Dementia Rating scale > 0, major neurological or psychiatric disorders, relevant medical conditions affecting cognition, including brain injury, and a family history suggestive of autosomal dominant AD.

 For the present analyses, we further restricted the sample to participants with available 3T structural MRI, genotyping, and comprehensive clinical and lifestyle assessments, additionally excluding those with structural brain lesions or poor MRI quality, yielding a final analytic sample of 1199 participants, aged 54–65 years. A nested cohort of 296 participants had available CSF biomarker profiling that was used for biomarker-stratified analyses. The ALFA study protocol was approved by the Independent Ethics Committee Parc de Salut Mar Barcelona and conducted in accordance with the Spanish Law 14/2007 on Biomedical Research (Ley 14/2007 de Investigación Biomédica) and a written informed consent was obtained for each participant.

Brain MRI data were acquired on a 3T scanner (Ingenia CX, Philips, Amsterdam, Netherlands) using the harmonized ALFA imaging protocol, which was identical for all participants., The protocol included high-resolution 3D T2-weighted Turbo Spin Echo (TSE) sequence (voxel size 1 × 1 × 1 mm, repetition time/echo time (TR/TE): 2500/264 ms, flip angle = 90°), a 3D T1-weighted Turbo Field Echo (TFE) sequence (voxel size 0.75 × 0.75 × 0.75 mm, TR/TE: 9,90/4.6 ms, flip angle = 8°) and a 3D T2-FLAIR sequence (TSE, voxel size 1 × 1 × 1 mm, TR/TE/TI: 5000/312/1700 ms). All MRI scans underwent routine visual quality assessment by a trained neuroradiologist. Participants with insufficient image quality or clinically relevant incidental findings were excluded prior to downstream image processing.

 Preprocessing steps included denoising, bias field correction, and spatial normalization. T1-weighted images were processed using the FreeSurfer (v6.0) recon-all pipeline to extract cortical and subcortical regions.

 Regional brain volumes used for sensitivity analyses were derived from FreeSurfer (v7.1.1)

 outputs: hippocampal and midbrain volumes were extracted directly from segmentation files, basal ganglia volume was computed as the sum of caudate, putamen, and pallidum, and centrum semiovale volume was approximated using total cerebral white matter volume.
