PVS burden was automatically determined from the T2-weighted images using a weakly supervised convolutional neural network., Regional PVS counts were obtained bilaterally for the basal ganglia, centrum semiovale, hippocampus, and midbrain. Regional PVS counts were averaged across hemispheres.

In its original validation study, the algorithm achieved detection performance approaching human inter-rater agreement, when evaluated against expert point-wise manual annotations in an independent population-based cohort across the same four anatomical regions.

 Its robustness to common imaging confounders was subsequently assessed using attention maps verifying that the network accurately discriminates PVS from other markers of cerebral small vessel disease, including white matter hyperintensities and lacunar infarcts. Even in scans with extensive white matter hyperintensity burden or basal ganglia lacunar infarcts, segmented PVS showed minimal overlap with these lesions.

Demographic variables included age, sex, years of education, family history of AD, and age of AD onset in first-degree relatives. Cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors were assessed through standardized clinical evaluations, including body mass index (BMI), systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure, resting heart rate, and serum lipid profiles (total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol). Cardiovascular dementia risk was quantified using the Cardiovascular risk factors, Aging and Incidence of Dementia (CAIDE) score,

 which integrates age, sex, education, BMI, SBP, DBP, total cholesterol, and physical activity (CAIDE-I), with an extended version that also incorporates APOE-ε4 carriership (CAIDE-II).

 Smoking status was assessed using standardized questionnaires (current, former, or never), along with other lifestyle determinants information, physical activity (MET·hour/week), sleep duration (hour/day), and self-reported symptoms of anxiety and depression.

 Exposure to particulate matter (PM2.5) air pollution was estimated with 2009 ESCAPE LUR models in Barcelona, based on seasonal measurements at 40 sites and geographic predictors.

 Participants’ 2013–2014 addresses were geocoded to assign annual exposures, limited to stable residents (⩾3 years).

Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples and genotyped using the Illumina NeuroChip array.

 Quality control followed established protocols,

 variants with call rate < 95%, minor allele frequency < 0.01, and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium p-value < 10−6 were excluded. Samples with call rate < 98%, sex mismatch and excess heterozygosity were also excluded. Imputation was performed via the Michigan Imputation Server

 using the Haplotype Reference Consortium Panel (HRC r1.1 2016). APOE genotypes were defined by rs429358 and rs7412,

 and categorized as ε4 carriers and non carriers, as well as their ε4 genetic load (0/1/2 alleles). Polygenic risk scores (PRS) were computed in PRSice-2 using clumping and p-value thresholding,

 and were standardized to z-scores. PRS were derived for AD (AD, Aβ42, p-tau), cardio- and cerebrovascular diseases (hypertension, ischemic stroke, cerebral small vessel disease), metabolic traits (BMI, body fat index (BFI), HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol), sleep quality (insomnia, sleep duration), and neurological and psychiatric disorders (anxiety, major depressive, social interaction and isolation, stress), as well as pathway-specific mechanisms previously implicated in AD (amyloid, immune, external stimuli signaling, cholesterol efflux, complex lipoprotein metabolism).

Regional PVS counts were inspected for distributional properties. Vuong’s non-nested test was applied to assess whether zero-inflated models provided a statistically superior fit over their standard counterparts. Model selection was further guided by log-likelihood values and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Based on these diagnostics, Poisson models were selected for basal ganglia and hippocampus regions, while negative binomial models were used for centrum semiovale and midbrain regions.

Each determinant domain (demographic; cardiovascular and metabolic; lifestyle, environmental factors and mental health; genetic) was analyzed separately, using generalized linear models adjusted for age, sex, and intracranial volume.

Results were reported as rate ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals. False discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied within each domain to account for multiple comparisons. Effect modification by sex, Aβ status, and AT biomarker classification (A−T−, A+T−, A+T+) was examined through stratified models and interaction terms in the pooled sample to formally evaluate subgroup differences. Aβ positivity (A+) was defined as CSF Aβ42/40 < 0.071.

 The selection of these three stratification variables was predetermined according to previous knowledge. Sex was included in line with the growing recognition of sex as a biological variable in biomedical research,

 and because sex differences have been reported affecting AD risk factors and disease progression,

 specifically in PVS burden.

 CSF Aβ and AT biomarker status were included to test whether determinants of PVS burden differ across biologically distinct stages of the preclinical AD continuum, consistent with prior evidence that PVS burden tracks with both amyloid and tau pathophysiology., Tau positivity (T+) was defined as CSF p-tau >24 pg/mL. A−T+ participants were excluded to filter out individuals who may not be within the AD continuum.

As a sensitivity analysis, all models were additionally adjusted for the volume of the corresponding anatomical region to account for potential confounding by regional brain size.

All analyses were performed in R version 4.3.1.

The study sample included 1199 CU participants (64% women) from the ALFA cohort, with a median age of 59.4 years. Sample characteristics are summarized in .

Participant characteristics in the full sample and CSF biomarker subsample, stratified by sex, Aβ status, and AT biomarker group.

N: Sample Size; AD: Alzheimer’s disease; CSF: cerebrospinal fluid; PM2.5: Particulate Matter; SBP: Systolic Blood Pressure; DBP: Diastolic Blood Pressure; HDL: High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol; LDL: Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol; BMI: Body Mass Index; CAIDE: Cardiovascular risk factors, Aging and Incidence of Dementia; PVS: Perivascular Spaces; IQR: Interquartile Range.

Variables include demographic, cardiovascular and metabolic, lifestyle and genetic factors, and regional PVS counts. Continuous variables are shown as median (IQR) and categorical variables are presented as n (%). P-values were obtained using the Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variables, and the χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate. Sample size varies across variables due to missing data. The CSF biomarker subsample includes participants with available CSF amyloid and tau measurements.

Bold values indicate p < 0.05.

Detailed estimates for all models are shown in  and Supplemental Table 1.

Higher PVS counts were significantly associated with older age and male sex, consistent with previous literature. Each additional year of age corresponded to a ~1%–2% increase in centrum semiovale PVS counts (95% CI = 1.073–1.213, pFDR = 3.48 × 10−5), independent of sex. Men exhibited higher PVS counts than women in the centrum semiovale (95% CI = 0.505–0.644, pFDR = 5.07 × 10−19), whereas women showed higher PVS counts in the other regions (95% CI = 1.356–1.586, pFDR = 5.13 × 10−21 in the hippocampus; 95% CI = 1.120–1.323, pFDR = 1.77 × 10−5 in the midbrain; 95% CI = 1.065–1.257, pFDR = 0.002 in the basal ganglia). Years of education, as a proxy for cognitive reserve, was not significantly associated with PVS counts in any region ().

Higher DBP was nominally associated with increased PVS counts at the centrum semiovale (95% CI = 1.015–1.169, p = 0.015), while elevated LDL cholesterol levels (95% CI = 0.851–0.975, p = 0.007) and total cholesterol levels (95% CI = 0.867–0.995, p = 0.037) were associated with lower hippocampal-PVS burden. In contrast, higher BMI was associated with reduced basal ganglia PVS counts (95% CI = 0.897–0.973, pFDR = 0.012; ).

Higher physical activity was associated with reduced centrum semiovale PVS counts (95% CI = 0.831–0.971, pFDR = 0.033). Other lifestyle factors and psychological variables, including smoking, sleep duration, and anxiety or depression showed nominal trends or region-specific trends but did not survive multiple comparison corrections ().

PRS for BMI and PRS for HDL cholesterol were significantly associated with lower centrum semiovale PVS counts (95% CI = 0.878–0.990, pFDR = 0.043; 95% CI = 0.866–0.979, pFDR = 0.030, respectively), while the HDL cholesterol PRS was associated with lower hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 0.930–0.999, p = 0.045). A PRS for insomnia was also associated with lower hippocampus-PVS counts (95% CI = 0.923–0.991, pFDR = 0.030; ).

Following the pronounced sex-based disparities observed in PVS counts across all regions, we conducted sex-interactions and stratified analyses to identify specific differences between women and men (, Supplemental Figure 1).

A significant interaction with the PRS for HDL cholesterol was observed in the midbrain (pFDR = 0.015), suggesting sex-specific lipid-related genetic influences on perivascular integrity (Supplemental Table 2). Nominal interactions were also found for BMI and PRS for complex lipoprotein metabolism pathway in the basal ganglia (p = 0.025, p = 0.041, respectively), PRS for p-tau in the midbrain (p = 0.037), and PRS for amyloid pathway in both the centrum semiovale (p = 0.027) and midbrain (p = 0.025).

Sex-stratified analyses showed that, in men, higher PRS for HDL cholesterol was significantly associated with greater midbrain PVS counts (95% CI = 1.025–1.170, pFDR = 0.027), consistent with the interaction effect noted above. Higher BMI was significantly associated with lower PVS counts in the basal ganglia (95% CI = 0.817–0.946, pFDR = 0.007; Supplemental Table 3).

In women, PVS counts were not significantly associated with any of the determinants that showed significant sex-interaction terms. However, other significant and nominal associations were observed, predominantly in the centrum semiovale PVS count. Age showed a positive association with greater PVS burden (95% CI = 1.085–1.292, pFDR = 3.20 × 10−4). A higher PRS for HDL cholesterol was associated with reduced PVS counts (95% CI = 0.809–0.964, pFDR = 0.017; Supplemental Table 4).

Psychological and behavioral factors showed significant interactions with Aβ status, including sleep duration (pFDR = 0.044) and depressive symptoms (pFDR = 0.022) in the hippocampus (, Supplemental Figure 2, Supplemental Table 5). Anxiety also showed a nominal interaction in the centrum semiovale (p = 0.025). Other nominal interactions were observed between Aβ status and several vascular and lifestyle determinants. Specifically, interactions were found for SBP (hippocampus, p = 0.027) and PM2.5 air pollution exposure (basal ganglia, p = 0.048). Within the genetic domain, a nominal interaction was found for cholesterol efflux AD pathway PRS (p = 0.047) in the midbrain.

Aβ-stratified analyses showed that, in Aβ+ individuals, female sex remained a robust determinant of PVS burden, presenting a significantly lower centrum semiovale-PVS counts (95% CI = 0.343–0.749, pFDR = 0.003) and higher hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 1.171–1.958, pFDR = 0.009). Among lifestyle factors, physical activity was associated with reduced centrum semiovale-PVS burden (95% CI = 0.599–0.917, pFDR = 0.031), whereas longer sleep duration was associated with higher hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 1.051–1.345, pFDR = 0.031). Increased PM2.5 exposure (95% CI = 1.057–1.583, pFDR = 0.042) was also linked to greater centrum semiovale-PVS burden. In the genetic domain, APOE-ε4 carriership and ε4 heterozygosity were significantly associated with greater hippocampal PVS burden (95% CI = 1.086–2.018, pFDR = 0.046; 95% CI = 1.097–2.050, pFDR = 0.046, respectively; Supplemental Table 6).

In Aβ− individuals, sex-related differences were consistent, with female sex being associated with lower centrum semiovale and higher hippocampal and midbrain PVS counts (95% CI = 0.410–0.783, pFDR = 0.003; 95% CI = 1.089–1.602, pFDR = 0.026; 95% CI = 1.104–1.699, pFDR = 0.022, respectively). Within the vascular domain, increased SBP was associated with higher hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 1.106–1.811, pFDR = 0.033), while LDL cholesterol was associated with lower PVS counts in the hippocampus (95% CI = 0.803–0.955, pFDR = 0.028). Distinct genetic associations emerged in Aβ− individuals. PRS for anxiety and stress were negatively associated with hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 0.824–0.985, pFDR = 0.044 for both), while PRS for major depressive disorder was positively associated with midbrain PVS counts (95% CI = 1.047–1.285, pFDR = 0.019). PRS for insomnia showed a negative association with midbrain PVS counts (95% CI = 0.797–0.972, pFDR = 0.022; Supplemental Table 7).

Nominal interactions were observed between CSF-determined AT biomarker classification and several vascular, lifestyle, and psychological determinants. These findings suggest that the influence of systemic and behavioral factors on PVS burden may vary across AD biomarker stages (, Supplemental Figure 3, Supplemental Table 8). Nominally significant interactions (A+T− vs A−T−) were found for heart rate in the centrum semiovale (p = 0.044), SBP in the hippocampus (p = 0.035), ambient PM2.5 exposure in the basal ganglia (p = 0.034), and anxiety in the centrum semiovale (p = 0.010). In addition, significant interactions emerged (A+T+ vs A−T−) for sleep duration (p = 0.012) and depressive symptoms (p = 0.006) in the hippocampus, and the cholesterol efflux AD pathway PRS (p = 0.04) in the midbrain. Smoking status also showed nominal interactions with both former smoking in the centrum semiovale (p = 0.010) and current smoking in the midbrain (p = 0.011).

AT-stratified analyses showed that, in participants without evidence of amyloid or tau pathology (A−T−), female sex remained a consistent determinant, and was associated with lower centrum semiovale PVS counts (95% CI = 0.410–0.783, pFDR = 0.003), and higher PVS counts in the hippocampus (95% CI = 1.089–1.602, pFDR = 0.026) and midbrain (95% CI = 1.104–1.699, pFDR = 0.022). Within the cardiovascular and metabolic domain, increased SBP was associated with higher hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 1.106–1.811, pFDR = 0.033), whereas higher LDL cholesterol levels were associated with lower hippocampal PVS burden (95% CI = 0.803–0.955, pFDR = 0.028). Within the genetic domain, several PRS showed region-specific associations. In the midbrain, higher genetic risk factor for depressive disorder was associated with increased PVS counts (95% CI = 1.047–1.285, pFDR = 0.019), while higher genetic risk factor for insomnia was associated with lower PVS counts (95% CI = 0.797–0.972, pFDR = 0.022). In the hippocampus, higher polygenic risk for anxiety and stress-related disorders were associated with lower PVS counts (95% CI = 0.824–0.985, pFDR = 0.044 for both; Supplemental Table 9).

In individuals with abnormal amyloid but normal tau (A+T−), demographic determinants were significantly associated with regional PVS counts, while vascular determinants exhibited a nominal significance. Sex remained a strong predictor, with female sex associated with higher hippocampal PVS counts (95% CI = 1.126–2.016, pFDR = 0.032; Supplemental Table 10).

In participants with both amyloid and tau pathology (A+T+), distinct associations emerged. Sex remained a significant predictor, with female sex associated with lower centrum semiovale-PVS counts (95% CI = 0.193–0.703, pFDR = 0.013). Strong effects were also observed for former smoking, associated with higher centrum semiovale-PVS counts (95% CI = 2.378–15.910, pFDR = 0.003) and sleep duration, associated with higher hippocampal counts (95% CI = 1.079–1.762, pFDR = 0.05; Supplemental Table 11).

When additionally adjusting for the volume of the corresponding anatomical region, the results were largely consistent with the primary analyses. In some cases, the magnitude of the associations became stronger after volume adjustment, including the higher PVS burden in females in the hippocampus, midbrain and basal ganglia, and the positive association between age and centrum semiovale PVS. Others were modestly attenuated but remained statistically significant (Supplemental Tables 12–22).

In this large cohort of CU individuals at increased genetic risk for AD, we identified multidomain determinants of PVS burden across distinct brain regions. Demographic, cardiovascular, lifestyle/environmental, and genetic factors contributed differentially to regional PVS variation, with several associations moderated by sex, amyloid status, and AD pathology stage. These findings highlight the complexity of PVS determinants and support their potential as early MRI markers of cerebrovascular vulnerability in preclinical AD.

The centrum semiovale emerged as the most consistently affected region across demographic and genetic domains, reinforcing prior evidence that MRI-visible PVS in this region are closely linked to the accumulation of Aβ pathology, which is a hallmark of the AD continuum.,,, In contrast, the basal ganglia showed a different etiological profile, showing a strong association with BMI, which is maintained in the men-stratified analysis, consistent with its sensitivity to hypertensive arteriopathy.,, The hippocampal and midbrain PVS burden showed distinct patterns, with associations more tightly linked to AD biomarkers and psychiatric or sleep-related factors, suggesting that PVS burden in these regions may be less related to traditional vascular mechanisms, and potentially more to glymphatic or neuroinflammatory processes.,, The hippocampus, in particular, is known to be highly sensitive to sleep-related changes in Aβ accumulation, potentially caused by disruptions of perivascular drainage.

 This spatial pattern supports the notion that distinct perivascular mechanisms operate across vascular and limbic territories, reflecting the interplay between hemodynamic stress, metabolic demand, and clearance pathways.,,,, Together, these results point to regional specificity in the mechanisms underlying PVS counts, vascular and hemodynamic influences in white-matter regions such as the centrum semiovale and basal ganglia, and non-traditional vascular factors, possibly involving clearance or inflammatory processes, in limbic regions such as the hippocampus and midbrain.

Age was a robust determinant of PVS counts, but its effects were region-specific. Advancing age was significantly associated with greater PVS burden only in the centrum semiovale, whereas no significant effects were found in the basal ganglia, hippocampus, or midbrain. This finding differs from large population-based studies, which reported age-related PVS increases across all regions, particularly in the basal ganglia., The narrower age range and younger mean age of the ALFA cohort could likely explain this regional restriction, as white-matter PVS tend to appear earlier in life, while basal ganglia PVS emerge later with cumulative vascular injury.

 Our results therefore suggest that centrum semiovale perivascular alterations may represent early manifestations of vascular stress in midlife, potentially preceding the deeper basal changes seen in older or clinically affected populations.

Sex also emerged as a consistent determinant of PVS burden. Men exhibited higher PVS counts in the centrum semiovale, whereas women showed higher counts in the other three regions. This pattern aligns partially with previous large-scale imaging studies that found higher centrum semiovale and midbrain PVS counts in men,, higher hippocampal PVS counts in women,, and varying results for basal ganglia PVS counts.,– These differences may reflect earlier, sex and AD-specific influences of vascular and hormonal factors in our younger, healthier sample that are not yet detectable in general population samples. Notably, the predominance in hippocampal and midbrain burden in women may reflect greater vulnerability of estrogen-responsive regions, as post menopauseal declines in estradiol are known to impair neuroinflammatory regulation, mitochondrial function, sleep architecture, and glymphatic clearance

 while the stronger centrum semiovale effects in men may correspond to higher vascular stiffness and blood pressure profiles. Notably, the presence of more PVS in the hippocampus of women is in line with their higher lifetime risk of AD and hypotheses that suggest greater depositions of Aβ in the hippocampus and cortical tissues, as pointed by others.

Sex-stratified analyses further supported the existence of sex-specific biological pathways influencing PVS burden. The most robust interaction was observed between sex and the PRS for HDL cholesterol in the midbrain, suggesting that genetic variation in lipid metabolism affects perivascular integrity differently in men and women. In men, a higher PRS for HDL cholesterol was associated with greater midbrain PVS counts, whereas in women, a higher PRS for HDL cholesterol predicted lower centrum semiovale PVS burden. These results point toward distinct regulation of lipid transport and cerebrovascular homeostasis, consistent with prior evidence linking estrogen, lipid metabolism and vascular function.,

Cardiovascular risk factors were key contributors to PVS burden, supporting the close relationship between vascular health and perivascular function.,, Blood pressure emerged as the main cardiovascular risk factor. Both SBP and, in particular, DBP were positively associated with PVS counts in the centrum semiovale and midbrain. This finding is consistent with previous evidence from the general population, which suggests that DBP is a particularly sensitive determinant of PVS and may directly influence perivascular fluid exchange more than SBP.

 These effects persisted after adjustment for age and sex, and remained consistent after stratification by AD biomarkers, indicating that vascular factors contribute to perivascular enlargement independently of amyloid or tau pathology. Interestingly, while previous studies reported that cardiovascular risk factors were most strongly associated with hippocampal PVS,

 we did not observe significant associations in the main-analysis in this region. However, in amyloid-specific models, we showed a nominal interaction between SBP and amyloid status in the hippocampus, with higher SBP associated with greater hippocampal PVS burden in Aβ− individuals. The overall lower blood pressure levels in ALFA, could be partly accounting for these weaker and regionally restricted associations. In addition, our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that vascular dysfunction and impaired arterial pulsatility hinder glymphatic clearance, leading to solute accumulation and PVS dysfunction.,

Lifestyle and mental health factors further modulated PVS burden with region-specific patterns. We observed a significant interaction between depression and Aβ status for hippocampal PVS, suggesting that depressive symptoms confer additional burden in an amyloid-dependent manner. Greater physical activity was associated with reduced centrum semiovale PVS burden, and this association persisted in Aβ+ individuals. In addition, longer sleep duration was related to higher hippocampal PVS burden in biomarker-positive participants. These observations may relate to literature linking disturbed sleep with impaired glymphatic clearance., In the main analysis, an insomnia PRS was associated with lower hippocampal PVS, whereas no consistent genetic effects for sleep-related traits were observed, suggesting that sleep’s influence on perivascular function is primarily behavioral or environmentally mediated rather than genetically determined in a cohort of middle-aged at-risk individuals for AD. Smoking and air pollution also contributed to PVS burden. Former smoking was associated with higher centrum semiovale burden in A+T+ participants, while PM2.5 exposure showed AT-dependent associations, reinforcing the notion that chronic systemic inflammation and vascular stress contribute to PVS enlargement.,–

Genetic factors also played an important and independent role in shaping PVS burden. PRS for metabolic traits, especially BMI and HDL cholesterol, were linked to lower PVS counts in the centrum semiovale. These associations contrast with expectations based on vascular risk but are consistent with the complex and sometimes paradoxical relationships reported between BMI and cerebrovascular or neurodegenerative outcomes,, which have been partly attributed to the inherent limitations of BMI as an indirect proxy for adiposity.

 In support of this heterogeneity, previous work

 also reported opposite effects of BMI across regions (higher hippocampal PVS with manual counts but lower with total counts), a pattern that may reflect anatomical, methodological, or population-specific differences. A similar inverse association between total cholesterol and PVS burden was also reported in the basal ganglia,

 suggesting that the counterintuitive direction we observed in our hippocampal analysis may not simply be cohort-specific, but instead reflect complex biological relationships that cannot be resolved with the present cross-sectional data. It should also be noted that PRS capture an individual’s aggregate genetic liability rather than the phenotype itself, and the correspondence between genetic- and phenotypic-level findings should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Distinct genetic signatures were also evident for some biomarker stages. In participants without amyloid or tau pathology, psychiatric and sleep-related PRS (anxiety, depression, insomnia) showed associations with hippocampal and midbrain burden, whereas in Aβ+ individuals, APOE-ε4 became more prominent in the hippocampus, with higher PVS counts associated with both ε4 carriership and single-allele load, corroborating general population-based findings, where dose-dependent associations between APOE-ε4 allele count and hippocampal PVS burden were detected.

 In those within the A+T+ group, no PRS signal survived FDR correction. These shifts suggested that different genetic mechanisms predominate along the AD continuum, from psychological pathways in the earliest stages,– to APOE-related influences once amyloid is present, although larger stratified datasets will be needed to draw firmer conclusions.,

Overall, the sex-stratified associations were the most consistent of the three stratification schemes, likely reflecting, at least in part, the larger subgroup size and the substantial existing evidence for sex differences in lipid regulation and cerebrovascular/glymphatic physiology in AD.,,– Associations involving sex remained evident across all biomarker-defined groups, although their magnitude and regional distribution varied across stages of the AD continuum. The Aβ- and AT-stratified findings, by contrast, should be considered more exploratory given the smaller subgroup sizes. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, this is among the first studies to examine multidomain determinants of regional PVS burden across CSF-defined biomarker stages, and we therefore believe these analyses provide a valuable hypothesis-generating framework for future studies in larger, adequately powered cohorts.

The observed findings have several implications for early detection and prevention. PVS burden, which is now measurable on standard MRI via automated methods, may serve as a low-cost biomarker capturing the cumulative impact of vascular, lifestyle, and genetic risk in preclinical AD. The identification of modifiable factors highlights concrete prevention targets. Furthermore, the differential effects by sex and biomarker stage suggest that strategies to preserve cerebrovascular health should be tailored to individual risk profiles, integrating biological sex and AD biomarker status., This aligns with emerging precision medicine approaches aimed at delaying or preventing symptomatic conversion.

This study has several strengths. It leverages the well-characterized ALFA cohort, a deeply phenotyped, biomarker-enriched sample of CU adults in midlife, providing a unique opportunity to investigate early cerebrovascular alterations. The use of a fully automated, reproducible quantification pipeline for PVS ensures objective and region-specific assessments, improving sensitivity compared to visual scales. Integrating multidomain risk profiling allowed us to disentangle independent and interacting determinants of PVS burden in unprecedented detail. Importantly, additional sensitivity analyses adjusting for the volume of the corresponding anatomical regions yielded highly consistent results, supporting the robustness of the primary findings and indicating that the observed associations were not driven by differences in regional brain volume. The large sample size and harmonized imaging and biomarker protocols enhance internal validity and comparability with other AD research preclinical initiatives. Nonetheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and limits interpretation of temporal relationships between PVS burden, making it impossible to determine whether PVS burden precedes or follows early AD-related changes. Moreover, PVS were assessed as structural MRI markers, and no direct measures of perivascular fluid flow or glymphatic clearance were available; therefore, interpretations regarding glymphatic function should be considered hypothesis-generating. While the automated quantification reduces subjectivity, it remains sensitive to scanner-specific variability and technical artifacts, warranting replication across diverse populations and imaging platforms. Although we corrected for multiple testing, some associations remained at nominal significance and should be interpreted as exploratory. Furthermore, the genetic analyses are constrained by current PRS methods, which do not fully capture rare variants or gene-environment interactions that may influence PVS. In addition, stratified genetic analyses, particularly those involving APOE-ε4 homozygotes, were limited by small subgroup sample sizes, which may have reduced power to detect associations and contributed to marginal or non-significant effects. Finally, the ALFA cohort is genetically and demographically enriched for AD risk and relatively homogeneous in terms of ancestry, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to the general population. The individuals analyzed in this study are on average younger, more highly educated, and in better cardiovascular health than population-based samples in which PVS have previously been studied.,, The elevated familial and genetic loading for AD in this cohort, reflected in a substantially higher proportion of APOE-ε4 carriers than expected in the general population, may also modify the determinants of PVS burden identified here. Replication in more demographically diverse, including individuals without a family history of AD and of non-European ancestry, will therefore be necessary to determine whether the regional, sex-specific, and biomarker-dependent patterns we observed generalize beyond genetically at-risk, midlife populations.

Future work should examine longitudinal trajectories of PVS burden in relation to AD biomarker progression, cognitive performance, and clinical outcomes. Integrating PVS with other markers of CSVD, such as white matter hyperintensities, could help disentangle shared and distinct vascular pathways contributing to impaired brain clearance. Combining MRI-based PVS measures with complementary glymphatic proxies, including diffusion tensor-imaging-based analysis along the perivascular space (DT-ALPS),

 and fluid biomarkers of neuroinflammation, vascular injury, and metabolic stress could clarify mechanistic pathways linking vascular and glymphatic dysfunction to AD risk. Intervention studies targeting vascular and lifestyle risk factors are essential to determine whether interventions on those risk factors can modify PVS trajectories and reduce subsequent cognitive decline. Ultimately, integrating perivascular imaging metrics into multimodal biomarker frameworks may refine risk stratification and accelerate the development of personalized prevention strategies in AD.

medicine.title: Facile fabrication of Ag-doped α-Fe2O3 with enhanced ethanol gas sensing performance
medicine.abstract: The development of high-performance ethanol sensors represents a critical imperative for ensuring operational safety in industrial settings, enabling rigorous environmental monitoring, and safeguarding public health. In this work, Ag-doped α-Fe2O3 sensing materials were fabricated via a facile chemical precipitation route. At the optimum temperature of 200 °C, the sensor exhibited a response of 17.5 to 100 ppm ethanol, with rapid response and recovery times of 13 s and 9 s. Compared to pristine α-Fe2O3, the response value increased by 6.5-fold, while the device also exhibited superior selectivity and long-term stability. Ag doping generates abundant active catalytic sites on the α-Fe2O3 surface, enhancing ethanol adsorption and oxidative degradation. The resultant Ag/α-Fe2O3 heterointerface further optimizes charge transport and mobility, delivering markedly improved gas-sensing performance.
medicine.text:
With the accelerating advancement of modern industrial manufacturing and the transportation sector, ethanol, serving as both a critical chemical feedstock and a clean-burning fuel, has seen widespread adoption in chemical synthesis, energy production, and pharmaceutical applications. Nevertheless, its intrinsic volatility and flammability introduce significant safety hazards throughout the entire lifecycle encompassing processing, storage, distribution, and end-use. Consequently, the development of high-performance ethanol sensors constitutes a pivotal imperative for safeguarding industrial operations, enabling robust environmental surveillance, and ensuring public health protection. Among various gas sensors, metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) sensors have been widely adopted owing to their salient advantages, including high sensitivity, compact form factor, low fabrication cost, and seamless compatibility with integrated-circuit platforms.

α-Fe2O3 is an n-type semiconductor with a bandgap of 2.2 eV, offering the merits of low cost, excellent chemical stability, and nontoxicity. Despite its favorable gas-sensing performance, α-Fe2O3 typically necessitates elevated operating temperatures and exhibits sluggish response kinetics, thereby constraining its applicability in portable and low-power devices. Noble metal functionalization represents a highly effective approach for enhancing the gas-sensing performance of MOS-based gas sensors. Liu et al. showed that the enhanced ethanol-sensing performance arises from the synergistic effect of the porous α-Fe2O3 structure, the superior catalytic activity of Au nanoparticles, and Schottky barrier formation at the heterointerface. The optimal sensor exhibited a response value of 17.4 toward 100 ppm ethanol at 300 °C. Cheng et al. synthesized Pd-doped α-Fe2O3 porous nanotubes (PNTs). The 3.0 wt% Pd-doped α-Fe2O3 PNT sensors exhibited superior ethanol-detection performance at 240 °C. The response and recovery times are 8 s and 30 s, respectively. The improvement in sensing performance is primarily attributed to the pronounced sensitization effect of the incorporated Pd components. Ag is considerably more cost-effective than Au, Pt, and Pd, rendering it highly favourable for practical device applications. In addition, Ag exhibits pronounced catalytic spillover activity toward ethanol oxidation. Crucially, Ag readily forms a Schottky contact with α-Fe2O3, thereby modulating the surface electron depletion layer; this simultaneously enhances the gas response and lowers the operating temperature. Mirzaei et al. prepared Ag@α-Fe2O3 core–shell heterostructure nanoparticles by the sol–gel method. The sensor exhibited a relatively low response of 6 to 100 ppm ethanol vapor at 250 °C, with response and recovery times of 5.5 s and 16 s, respectively. This improvement stems from the increased specific surface area, which provides abundant active sites, while Ag nanoparticles introduce chemical and electronic sensitization to lower activation energy and promote interfacial charge transfer for efficient ethanol detection. Jia et al. also reported that the sensors based on Ag/α-Fe2O3 microspheres showed a higher response to ethanol than to other gases. At 240 °C, the response to 50 ppm ethanol was approximately 11.2. The incorporation of Ag functioned as an active catalyst, generating additional active sites that are considered essential for enhancing sensing sensitivity. Prior related studies have predominantly examined relatively high temperatures. Furthermore, owing to the early publication dates of these works, investigations into sensing performance remain incomplete, for example, studies examining the influence of humidity on performance and stability are still lacking. In this study, Ag/α-Fe2O3 composites were synthesized via a facile chemical precipitation route and employed as sensing materials for ethanol gas sensors. The sensor based on 2 wt% Ag/α-Fe2O3 exhibited markedly improved gas-sensing performance, delivering a response of 17.5 to 100 ppm ethanol and rapid response/recovery dynamics (13 s/9 s) at 200 °C. It also showed superior selectivity, insensitivity to humidity, and exceptional long-term stability.

FeSO4·7H2O (4 mmol) and Na2SO4·10H2O (0.3 mmol) were dissolved in 50 mL of deionized water and stirred at room temperature until a clear solution was obtained. Subsequently, 0.06 M CH3COONa solution was added, and the mixture was allowed to react under continuous stirring for 24 h. The resulting precipitate was collected by centrifugation and washed alternately with deionized water and absolute ethanol several times to remove residual ions. After drying at 100 °C for 12 h, FeOOH powder was obtained. Finally, the as-prepared FeOOH was calcined at 500 °C for 2 h to yield brownish-red α-Fe2O3 powder.

FeOOH powder (0.1 g) was ultrasonically dispersed in 100 mL of deionized water for 30 min to achieve complete exfoliation. Subsequently, 0.5 mL, 1 mL, 2 mL, and 3 mL of 0.1 mol per L AgNO3 standard solution were added dropwise to the dispersion to fabricate Ag/α-Fe2O3 gas-sensitive materials with nominal Ag doping levels of 0.5 wt%, 1 wt%, 2 wt%, and 3 wt%, denoted as S1, S2, S3, and S4, respectively. The mixtures were stirred at room temperature for 12 h to ensure complete reaction, then centrifuged and repeatedly washed with deionized water and ethanol. The resulting precipitates were dried at 100 °C for 12 h and subsequently calcined at 500 °C for 2 h to yield Ag/α-Fe2O3 composites with varying Ag contents. A schematic illustration of the synthesis procedure is presented in .

X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku D/Max2550, Tokyo, Japan) measurements were performed using Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å) over a 2θ range of 15°–80° to characterize the crystal structures of the as-synthesized Ag/α-Fe2O3 composites. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, Hitachi SU8010, Japan) was performed at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV to observe the microstructural morphology, coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for micro-area compositional analysis. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI 5000 Versaprobe) equipped with Al-Kα excitation (hν = 1486.6 eV, ΔE = 0.85 eV) was employed to determine the elemental composition and chemical valence states.

As shown in , an appropriate amount of the sample powder was dispersed in deionized water to yield a homogeneous slurry, which was then uniformly coated onto the surface of an Al2O3 ceramic tube using a fine-tipped brush. No organic or inorganic binder was applied during this procedure. The ceramic tube (length: 4 mm; outer diameter: 1.35 mm; inner diameter: 1 mm) was pre-patterned with a pair of Au electrodes at both ends. After drying at 160 °C for 10 h, the tube assembly, including the integrated heater, was welded onto a pedestal. This mild heat treatment enhances the physical contact between adjacent sensing particles and stabilizes the sensing film, without triggering phase transition or grain growth of the material. No film peeling or cracking occurred after heating. Before measurement, the sensor was aged at 180 °C for 48 h.

The gas-sensing performance was assessed using a WS-30B gas-sensing test system (Henan Weisheng Electronic Technology Co., LTD, China). The measurement circuit consists of the sensor resistance RS, load resistance RL, and supply voltage VC. The sensor resistance was calculated from the output voltage Voutput across RL using the following equation:1

During testing, the target analyte in liquid form was introduced into the evaporation via syringe and vaporized thermally. The relationship between the injected liquid volume and the resulting gas concentration was established as follows:2where Vx (mL) denotes the injected liquid volume, V (mL) the test chamber volume, C (ppm) the target gas concentration, M (g mol−1) the molar mass of the liquid, d (g cm−3) its density, and p the liquid purity. TR (°C) and TB (°C) represent the ambient temperature and the test chamber temperature, respectively.

In this work, the sensor response S was defined as: S = Ra/Rg, where Ra is the sensor resistance in air and Rg is the sensor resistance upon exposure to the target gas. All measurements, encompassing response/recovery kinetics, repeatability, and long-term stability, were performed under strictly identical experimental conditions.

All samples were preliminarily screened via gas-sensing measurements, and only the best-performing sample (S3) was selected for detailed characterization by XRD and XPS. As shown in , the XRD patterns of the pristine α-Fe2O3 and sample S3 (2 wt% Ag/α-Fe2O3) are presented. The α-Fe2O3 phase exhibits a hematite structure with a typical hexagonal lattice. The diffraction peaks observed at 24.24°, 33.26°, 35.8°, 40.99°, 49.53°, 54.13°, 57.6°, 62.54°, and 64.09° correspond to the (012), (104), (110), (113), (024), (116), (018), (214), and (300) crystallographic planes, respectively, which are in good agreement with the standard card (JCPDS: 89-0597). In addition to the characteristic peaks of pristine α-Fe2O3, the S3 composite displays distinct diffraction peaks attributable to Ag nanoparticles (JCPDS: 99-0094) at 38.3°, 44.5°, and 64.63°, indexed to the (111), (200), and (220) planes. Phase analysis reveals that the characteristic diffraction peaks of S3 show no significant shift relative to those of pristine α-Fe2O3 nanoparticles, indicating that Ag nanoparticle incorporation does not perturb the crystal structure of α-Fe2O3. The distinct diffraction peaks corresponding to both α-Fe2O3 and Ag phases coexist without any detectable impurity reflections, providing robust evidence for the successful synthesis of a highly crystalline Ag/α-Fe2O3 composite. XRD patterns were analyzed quantitatively using MDI Jade 6. Following background subtraction and Kα2 stripping, instrumental broadening was corrected using an IPC (instrument profile calibration) file derived from a silicon standard. High-intensity representative diffraction peaks were fitted with the pseudo-Voigt function to extract the FWHM and associated fitting uncertainties. Crystallite sizes were estimated via the Scherrer equation with a shape factor of K = 0.89. The Scherrer-calculated coherent-scattering crystallite-domain sizes of α-Fe2O3 and Ag/α-Fe2O3 were 216 nm and 193 nm, respectively. It should be noted that the resulting Scherrer values correspond to coherent scattering domains rather than actual physical particle sizes. Appropriate Ag suppresses grain growth, yielding smaller crystallites and a greater number of grain boundaries that scatter X-rays and weaken the diffraction peaks. This provides additional surface-active sites and gas adsorption channels, thereby facilitating the adsorption and desorption of target gas molecules.

SEM images of α-Fe2O3 doped with varying molar ratios of Ag composites are presented in . All Ag/α-Fe2O3 composites exhibit well-defined hierarchical nano-flower-like architectures.  show the SEM image and corresponding EDS elemental mapping image of sample S3, which visually confirm the homogeneous spatial distribution of Ag, Fe, and O across the composite structure. Ag is uniformly dispersed in the composites. Na2SO4 and CH3COONa were employed as precursors during synthesis. The resulting powders were thoroughly washed with deionized water and ethanol several times, followed by high-temperature calcination to remove residual soluble ionic species. No crystalline Na-containing phases were detected in the XRD patterns. EDX measurements across multiple regions exhibited negligible Na signals. It should be noted that EDX is a surface-sensitive, semi-quantitative technique, and trace Na below its detection limit cannot be entirely ruled out. Nevertheless, any such potential trace Na residue, if present, would not affect the structural and gas-sensing performance conclusions of this work. Quantitative ICP-OES characterization will be performed in future work to further verify this.

To elucidate the chemical nature of the α-Fe2O3 and S3 composites, XPS was conducted to determine the surface elemental composition and valence states. As shown in , the survey spectrum exhibits distinct characteristic peaks corresponding to Fe, O, Ag, and C elements. The presence of C is ascribed to ubiquitous hydrocarbon contamination from the instrument, while the absence of additional impurity peaks confirms the high purity of the as-synthesized material.  presents the high-resolution Fe 2p spectrum of α-Fe2O3. Two dominant peaks are observed at binding energies of 723.7 eV and 710.1 eV, which are assigned to the spin–orbit split Fe 2p1/2 and Fe 2p3/2 orbitals, respectively. The peak separation of 13.6 eV is consistent with the characteristic signature of Fe3+. Additionally, prominent satellite peaks at 718.5 eV and 725.9 eV arise from electronic excitation of Fe3+, exhibiting excellent agreement with the standard Fe2O3 reference spectrum. The O 1s high-resolution spectrum of α-Fe2O3 is displayed in . Three deconvoluted peaks at binding energies of 531.9 eV, 530.6 eV, and 529.1 eV correspond to adsorbed oxygen (OC), oxygen vacancies (OV), and lattice oxygen (OL), respectively. Their relative contents are quantified as 8.34%, 18.05%, and 73.61%.

illustrates the Fe 2p spectrum of the S3 composite. Characteristic peaks at 723.3 eV and 709.8 eV are attributed to Fe 2p1/2 and Fe 2p3/2, respectively. Peaks at 723.3 eV and 709.8 eV indicate the presence of Fe2+, while those at 712.1 eV and 725.5 eV confirm Fe3+. Satellite peaks associated with Fe3+ are observed at 725.5 eV and 718.0 eV. The O 1s high-resolution spectrum of S3, shown in , reveals three well-resolved peaks at 532.4 eV, 531.1 eV, and 529.5 eV, corresponding to OC, OV, and OL, respectively. Their respective contributions are 16.11%, 32.57%, and 51.32%. Compared with pristine α-Fe2O3, the S3 composite exhibits a significantly elevated concentration of OC and OV, which provide abundant active sites for the adsorption and surface reactions of target gas molecules. The synergistic effect between OC and OV facilitates surface redox processes, thereby substantially enhancing gas-sensing performance. displays the high-resolution Ag 3d spectrum, where characteristic peaks at 373.6 eV (Ag 3d3/2) and 367.6 eV (Ag 3d5/2) confirm the successful incorporation of metallic Ag into the composite. As evidenced by the XPS data presented in , Ag doping effectively modulates the distribution of surface oxygen species in the α-Fe2O3-based sensing material.

To elucidate the gas-sensing potential of Ag/α-Fe2O3 composites, a systematic evaluation of the sensing performance was conducted on pristine α-Fe2O3 and S1–S4 composite sensors. All sensors were initially exposed to 100 ppm ethanol over an operating temperature range of 80–300 °C (80, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300 °C), with the corresponding results illustrated in . For metal oxide semiconductors, the operating temperature determines the type of surface adsorbed oxygen species and the reaction kinetics between ethanol and adsorbed oxygen. Below 80 °C, the sluggish surface redox reaction yields a negligible sensing response. Above 300 °C, excessive thermal desorption of surface oxygen reduces active sites, while high temperature may also cause grain sintering and higher power consumption. Therefore, the 80–300 °C range was selected to identify the optimal operating temperature of Ag/α-Fe2O3 to ethanol. It is noted that low-temperature (<80 °C) sensing performance was not systematically characterized in this work and will be investigated in follow-up studies. The sensor response exhibited a characteristic volcano-shaped dependence on operating temperature, arising from the interplay between surface adsorption kinetics and the thermally competitive redox reaction mechanisms. The Ag/α-Fe2O3 sensor achieved its optimum operating temperature at 200 °C, which was therefore adopted for subsequent measurements. Notably, this represents a 50 °C reduction compared to the optimal temperature of 250 °C for pristine α-Fe2O3. This shift can be attributed to the superior catalytic activity of Ag, which accelerates the redox reaction between α-Fe2O3 and ethanol. Furthermore, Ag incorporation lowers the activation energy barrier for ethanol oxidation, enabling efficient gas–solid reactions at reduced temperatures and consequently decreasing the sensor's optimal operating temperature. As shown in , the dynamic response curves of α-Fe2O3 and Ag/α-Fe2O3 composite (S1–S4) sensors to ethanol were recorded at 200 °C over a concentration range of 5–100 ppm. It can be observed that the response values of both sensor types increase progressively with rising ethanol concentration. This behavior is attributed to the enhanced interaction between adsorbed ethanol molecules and the surface-active sites of the sensing material at higher concentrations, resulting in a more pronounced modulation of electrical resistance. Notably, the S3 (2 wt% Ag/α-Fe2O3) sensor exhibited the highest gas-sensing response of 17.5, representing a ∼6.5-fold enhancement over the pristine α-Fe2O3 (2.7). The limit of detection (LOD) is defined as the minimum gas concentration discernible by a gas sensor. The LOD can be calculated according to the equation:3where RMSnoise denotes the root mean square of the baseline noise and slope represents the sensitivity (i.e., the slope of the response curve). The LODs are determined to be 0.33 ppm and 0.076 ppm for the α-Fe2O3 and S3 sensors, respectively, indicating that the S3 sensor exhibits superior detection sensitivity with a markedly lower detection limit.

As shown in , the response and recovery characteristics of pristine α-Fe2O3 and Ag-loaded α-Fe2O3 sensors were evaluated at 200 °C. Both the response and recovery times to ethanol exhibit a non-monotonic trend, initially decreasing and subsequently increasing with rising Ag doping content. Notably, the S3 sensor demonstrated the optimal performance, with response and recovery times of 13 s and 9 s, respectively. This marked improvement is primarily attributed to the catalytic activity of Ag nanoparticles. Specifically, the formation of a Schottky barrier at the Ag/α-Fe2O3 interface facilitates interfacial electron transfer, while hybridization between the d-orbitals of Ag and the C–O bonds of ethanol molecules promotes chemisorption of the target gas. Additionally, Ag catalysis lowers the activation energy of surface redox reactions. However, at higher Ag loadings, the response and recovery times increase again, which can be ascribed to the surface shielding effect induced by excessive Ag nanoparticles. This effect diminishes the density of exposed active sites on the α-Fe2O3 surface and reduces the concentration of oxygen vacancies, thereby compromising sensing kinetics. The repeatability of gas sensors serves as a critical performance indicator for evaluating response consistency across successive measurements under identical operating conditions, thereby directly governing the reliability and reproducibility of detection data. As evidenced by the repeatability test results presented in , the S3 sensor exhibits favorable repeatability performance.

As shown in , selectivity tests were conducted on the S3 sensor at 200 °C against a suite of VOC analytes, including ethanol, ammonia, n-butanol, acetone, ethylene glycol, and isopropanol. The results indicate that the S3 sensor exhibits a significantly enhanced response to ethanol compared with other VOCs, thereby validating its superior ethanol selectivity.  illustrates the 30 day stability assessment of both pristine α-Fe2O3 and S3 sensors toward 100 ppm ethanol at 200 °C, demonstrating that both sensing materials retain favorable long-term stability.  presents a comparative analysis of the ethanol-sensing performance of the S3 sensor against previously reported works. The S3 sensor demonstrates a markedly enhanced ethanol response at a lower operating temperature, underscoring its considerable promise as a low-power solution for ethanol detection.

Res./Rec. time – response/recovery time.

When Ag-doped α-Fe2O3 is employed for ethanol gas sensing, its fundamental mechanism remains rooted in the semiconductor surface reaction governed by the oxygen chemisorption model. XPS O 1s characterization confirms the coexistence of adsorbed oxygen (OC), oxygen vacancies (OV), and lattice oxygen (OL) on the material surface, and the synergistic interplay between OC and OV dominates the enhanced sensing performance. As an n-type semiconductor with a bandgap of 2.1 eV, α-Fe2O3 derives its electrical conductivity primarily from the free electrons supplied by oxygen vacancies (OV). These OV serve as preferential active sites for oxygen adsorption and ionization, promoting the generation of chemisorbed oxygen species. Upon operation at 200 °C in air, atmospheric O2 molecules adsorb onto the α-Fe2O3 surface and capture free electrons (e−) from the conduction band, yielding chemisorbed oxygen species, primarily O−, which exhibits maximum reactivity at this temperature ( and ). This electron withdrawal engenders an electron-depleted layer at the particle surface, which functions as a potential barrier impeding interparticle electron transport and thereby elevating the overall resistance of the material. Upon exposure to ethanol, ethanol molecules diffuse to the α-Fe2O3 surface, acting as a reducing agent, undergo redox reactions with the chemisorbed O− species (). These reactions consume surface-adsorbed oxygen and release electrons back into the conduction band. The reinjected electrons partially screen the space charge within the depletion region, leading to a marked thinning of the electron depletion layer and a consequent decrease in resistance. The noble metal Ag exhibits notable catalytic activity toward ethanol redox reactions. Ag doping increases the concentration of OV in α-Fe2O3, further promoting the formation of reactive OC. It effectively reduces the activation energy of the reaction, facilitates the cleavage of C–H and O–H bonds, and thereby enhances both the reaction kinetics and sensing response.4O2(gas) → O2(ads)5O2(ads) + e− → O2−(ads)6O2−(ads) + e− → 2O−(ads)7C2H5OH(ads) + 6O−(ads) → 2CO2(gas) + 3H2O(gas) + 6e−

Furthermore, interfacial contact between Ag and α-Fe2O3 induces pronounced electronic modulation. Considering the work functions of α-Fe2O3 (5.9 eV) and Ag (4.72 eV), electrons spontaneously transfer from Ag to α-Fe2O3 upon heterojunction formation. This charge redistribution lowers the surface work function and facilitates the adsorption and activation of ambient oxygen species. Meanwhile, the establishment of a Schottky barrier at the Ag/α-Fe2O3 heterointerface reshapes the electron transport pathway and accelerates carrier dynamics during gas-sensing reactions. Although direct KPFM measurement of the interfacial potential barrier is not conducted in this work, the formation of such Schottky contact between metallic Ag and n-type α-Fe2O3 has been well documented in previous literature, and the corresponding sensing mechanism is illustrated in . Beyond electronic sensitization, Ag surface decoration introduces abundant extra active sites on α-Fe2O3, which promotes the adsorption and desorption of ethanol molecules. In addition, the inherent affinity of Ag toward ethanol effectively suppresses competitive adsorption of interfering gases (e.g., ammonia and acetone), contributing to improved selectivity. Benefiting from these synergistic effects, the ethanol sensing response of Ag-modified α-Fe2O3 composites rises with increasing Ag loading. Nevertheless, excessive Ag incorporation drastically decreases the baseline resistance of the composite, which results in oversaturated charge carriers and weakens the barrier modulation effect at the interface. In addition, severe aggregation of overloaded Ag nanoparticles may induce surface shielding of α-Fe2O3, which blocks the exposure of surface-active sites and impedes the contact between ethanol molecules and the oxide substrate. Collectively, the combined electronic and chemical sensitization endows the S3 sensor with optimal ethanol-sensing performance.

In summary, this work presents a facile chemical precipitation synthesis of Ag-doped α-Fe2O3 composites for high-performance ethanol sensing. At an optimal 200 °C, the sensor achieves a response of 17.5 to 100 ppm ethanol with fast kinetics (13 s/9 s), alongside excellent selectivity, reproducibility, and long-term stability. The performance enhancement stems from Ag/α-Fe2O3 synergy: Ag nanoparticles catalyze ethanol oxidation and enrich surface-active oxygen, lowering the reaction barrier and promoting interfacial charge transfer, while the Schottky heterojunction optimizes carrier transport and suppresses recombination, amplifying conductivity modulation. Optimal Ag loading maximizes these dual benefits; excess deposition occludes active sites and degrades sensitivity.

Ying Chen: writing – original draft, writing – review and editing, conceptualization, data curation, formal analysis, funding acquisition, methodology, resources. Ximeng Zong: data curation, formal analysis.

There are no conflicts to declare.

medicine.title: The evolution of image-guided ablations for thyroid disorders: a historical review
medicine.abstract: Over the past four decades, the management of thyroid nodules and selected thyroid malignancies has progressively shifted from surgery-centered approaches toward image-guided minimally invasive treatments (MITT). What began in 1985 with ultrasound-guided percutaneous ethanol injection evolved into a range of energy-based techniques, including laser ablation (LA), radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA), and high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU).This historical review aimed to reconstruct the major milestones in the development of image-guided thyroid ablation. A systematic PubMed literature search and predefined selection criteria were used to identify seminal studies, first clinical applications, major technological innovations, comparative studies, guideline-defining publications, and landmark long-term follow-up studies. Overall, 43 milestone papers were included for qualitative historical analysis. The evolution of thyroid ablation can be divided into five phases: conceptual origins (1985–1999), birth of the thermal procedures’ era (2000–2006), methodological standardization (2007–2012), oncologic consolidation and comparative evidence (2013–2018), and final codification by means of international guideline endorsement and long-term validation (2019–2025). Recent 10-year follow-up studies have confirmed the durable efficacy of MITT for benign nodule management and their sustained oncologic control in low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma. Image-guided thyroid ablation has transitioned from experimental innovation to an evidence-based, guideline-supported therapeutic domain, representing a paradigm shift toward precision medicine, organ preservation, and minimally invasive endocrine oncology.
medicine.text:
The main objectives of modern medicine are to improve the cost-effectiveness and safety profile of diagnostic and therapeutic procedures and to minimize their potential adverse effects on patients’ quality of life []. For these reasons, over the past forty years, the treatment of thyroid nodules and cancer—traditionally based on surgery—has evolved substantially driven by the advances in the field of image-guided minimally invasive procedures [, ].

This evolution began with the first experimental percutaneous injections in the endocrine neck. Driven by technological innovation, these initial approaches progressed to a series of modern, energy-based, therapeutic techniques for treating functional disorders and benign and malignant thyroid nodules. These methods are currently routinely employed with a wide range of indications and include percutaneous ethanol injection, laser, radiofrequency, and microwave ablation, and—to a lesser extent—high-intensity focused ultrasound. These techniques were comprehensively defined by their pioneers as image-guided ablations [, ].

It is a common observation that as medical procedures become commonplace, the memory of their origins and the evolution that led to their clinical application tends to fade. The objective of this historical review is to reconstruct the major milestones leading to the development and clinical implementation of image-guided ablation techniques for thyroid diseases. So, we will trace the evolution from initial experimental concepts to the diverse range of methods employed in current practice.

This study was designed as a historical review aimed at reconstructing the major milestones in the development of image-guided thyroid ablation. A systematic literature search and selection methodology was adopted to provide a structured and reproducible framework for the identification of relevant milestone publications. The literature search and study selection process followed the principles of the PRISMA 2020 statement, where applicable to the historical nature and objectives of the present review [].

The research was conducted using the terms “thyroid ablation” with “ethanol,” “laser” (LA), “radiofrequency” (RFA), “microwave” (MWA), and “high-intensity focused ultrasound” (HIFU). A total of 1922 studies were found on PubMed: 197 on percutaneous ethanol injection (PEI), 272 on LA, 989 on RFA, 372 on MWA, and 92 on HIFU. Further refinement was done by selecting the articles that were the earliest to describe the different techniques, their employment in clinical practice, and their innovation progress. The primary screening yielded a total of 136 articles: 48 studies for PEI, 31 for LA, 31 for RFA, 17 for MWA, and 9 for HIFU to include in the review.

Records were screened to identify publications potentially relevant to the historical development of each technique. Duplicate records and studies addressing aspects already represented by earlier milestone publications, without introducing a relevant technical, clinical, or methodological advancement, were excluded. The search and screening process was independently performed by two authors, and the study selection process is summarized in Fig. .

Milestone papers were defined a priori as studies fulfilling at least one of the following criteria: (1) first description of a thyroid ablation technique; (2) first clinical application in humans; (3) major technical innovation influencing subsequent practice; (4) first comparative study between techniques or versus surgery; (5) publication of consensus statements or clinical guidelines; (6) landmark long-term follow-up studies significantly influencing clinical adoption. Disagreements regarding study selection were resolved by consensus between the two reviewers.

ChatGPT and Grammarly were employed during manuscript preparation, mainly to support language editing, enhance clarity and coherence, and improve the overall readability of the text.

Finally, 43 studies were selected: 3 studies for PEI, 10 for LA, 15 for RFA, 7 for MWA, and 8 for HIFU.
