Imaging characteristics of normal developmental and anatomical variants

In infants younger than 4 months of age, a low attenuation focus in the anterior otic capsule, extending into the petrous apex toward the petrous occipital fissure, is commonly observed []. This hypoattenuating focus represents a normal developmental finding related to incomplete mineralization of the bone or cartilage and should not be mistaken for an abnormality in young children. In adults, however, similar low attenuation around the otic capsule should raise concern for otosclerosis, which is rare in childhood [, ].

The subarcuate (petromastoid) canal is a small bony passage that connects the posterior cranial fossa to the mastoid antrum. It carries the subarcuate artery and a dural sleeve, and courses horizontally in the temporal bone, parallel to the IAC and through the loop of the superior semicircular canal []. A prominent subarcuate canal, defined as greater than 2 mm or larger than the vestibular aqueduct, is a normal variant in pediatric patients on CT, and should not be mistaken for a fracture (Fig. ). It typically narrows and elongates to the adult form by approximately 5 years of age [, ].

The cochlear cleft, characterized by pericochlear curvilinear CT hypoattenuation lateral to the apical turn of the cochlea, is an anatomical variant associated with younger age that should not be mistaken for a fracture (Fig. ). It has been reported in up to 41% of pediatric patients and is located in the middle part of the otic capsule, close to the fissula ante fenestram region [, ]. Post-mortem studies have shown that it consists of fatty marrow spaces, reflecting incomplete or delayed endochondral ossification of the space between the endosteal and periosteal layers of the otic capsule [, ]. Its incidence decreases with age [].

An aberrant course of the petrous segment of the internal carotid artery (ICA) is a rare anatomic variant in which the ICA passes through the tympanic cavity without a separating bony plate, presenting as a vascular mass within the tympanic cavity on otoscopic inspection. It results from a congenital malformation in which the ICA enters the middle ear posterolateral to the normal petrous carotid canal due to agenesis of the first embryogenic segment of the ICA [, ]. The diagnosis of an aberrant ICA is critical because improper surgery or treatment can lead to massive hemorrhage [, ]. On axial CT, it appears as a tubular structure crossing the middle ear from posterior to anterior at the level of the cochlear promontory, rejoining the horizontal petrous ICA. On coronal CT, it is seen as a soft tissue density overlying the cochlear promontory (Fig. ). Key imaging features include enlargement of the inferior tympanic canaliculus, absence of the vertical segment of the petrous carotid canal, and absence of the bony plate separating the carotid artery from the middle ear []. An aberrant ICA may be mistaken for a lateralized ICA, which is instead an incidental normal petrous ICA anatomical variant in which the genu of the vertical and horizontal segments is located posterolateral to its normal position and protrudes into the anterior mesotympanum []. A lateralized ICA is associated with a thinned or dehiscent lateral wall of the petrous ICA canal, typically near the basal turn of the cochlea. In addition, in contrast with the aberrant ICA, the vertical segment of the petrous carotid canal is preserved and there is no enlargement of the inferior tympanic canaliculus [].

Petrous apex effusions, or trapped fluid, represent simple fluid accumulation within the petrous apex air cells without signs of acute infection [, ]. They typically develop following middle ear or mastoid infection, which leads to mucosal edema, obstruction of the communicating air channels between the middle ear and apical air cells related to adhesive fibrosis, with resultant entrapment of residual fluid [, ]. They are considered one of the most common petrous apex imaging findings and is found in approximately 1% of all cranial MRI studies [, ]. They have been described as “leave alone” lesions, referring to incidental findings that do not require treatment, biopsy, or follow-up imaging []. However, some patients may present with indolent infections, hearing loss, headache, facial spasm, or positional vertigo; in such cases, imaging follow-up or surgical drainage may be required if conservative management fails [, ].

On CT, effusions may be distinguished from mass lesions by the preservation of normal trabecular architecture and lack of bone remodeling []. On MRI, they are typically hypointense on T1WI, but in cases of high protein content the signal may appear intermediate or hyperintense (Table ). The differential diagnosis in such cases includes asymmetric pneumatization that can be easily excluded with fat-suppressed sequences, cholesterol granuloma, and mucocele. On T2WI, effusions are hyperintense and show no enhancement on post-contrast sequences (Fig. ) [, , ].

Imaging characteristics of inflammatory lesions

Cholesterol granulomas are the most common lesions of the petrous apex in adults but are rarely encountered in children, particularly before adolescence []. They occur in patients with a pneumatized petrous apex and chronic otitis media and are considered to be a sequela of chronic inflammatory disease [, ]. The classic theory attributes their development to insufficient aeration of the petrous apex air cells, resulting in negative pressure, air resorption, mucosal edema, hemorrhage, neovascularization, and repeated hemorrhage. This leads to inflammation, tissue breakdown, and cholesterol accumulation, which elicits a foreign-body reaction and gradual expansion due to bone remodeling and resorption. An alternative hypothesis proposes that excessive pneumatization exposes bone marrow, leading to hemorrhage. This, in turn, causes obstruction of the apical drainage pathways, blood degradation, a foreign-body reaction, and ultimately cyst formation with progressive bone expansion [, , ]. Lesions arising from the petrous apex may disseminate in several directions, most commonly posterolaterally toward the mastoid segment, IAC, or middle ear. In some cases, they may also involve adjacent structures including the clivus, cerebellopontine angle, and middle cranial fossa []. Symptoms are variable and generally result from mass effect and compression of nearby neurovascular structures. Hearing loss is the predominant clinical manifestation, followed by vertigo and headache, while less common presentations include tinnitus, otalgia, diplopia, trigeminal neuralgia, and facial spasm [].

On CT, cholesterol granulomas typically appear as expansile, sharply defined lesions with cortical thinning, trabecular destruction, and central low attenuation [, , ]. On MRI, they demonstrate high signal intensity on both T1- and T2WI, and FLAIR due to blood degradation products and cholesterol content, and lack restricted diffusion on DWI (Fig. ) []. A characteristic peripheral low signal rim on T2WI may be present due to hemosiderin deposition [, ]. Their large size and associated bony gaps caused by bone remodeling and expansion may be mistaken for bone destruction; however, the absence of enhancement on post-contrast images helps distinguish them from malignant lesions [–]. Mild peripheral enhancement may occasionally be seen due to an inflammatory response, but there is no central enhancement to indicate solid tissue [, ]. The differential diagnosis includes asymmetric petrous apex pneumatization, mucocele, and petrous effusions as described earlier, and petrous apex aneurysm due to the bright appearance on TOF MRA [, ].

Cholesteatomas can be congenital or acquired. Congenital cholesteatomas account for up to 5% of all cholesteatomas and most commonly arise in the petrous apex and the middle ear, and rarely in the mastoid []. They originate from ectopic rests of embryological epithelial tissue in the petrous apex, forming cysts lined by stratified squamous epithelium. Progressive desquamation leads to accumulation of keratinized debris, resulting in inflammation, cyst enlargement, and gradual bone resorption []. Congenital cholesteatomas typically occur in children and young adults and present as a whitish mass behind an intact tympanic membrane []. Acquired cholesteatomas more frequently arise in the tympano-mastoid region and may extend into the petrous apex []. They develop later in life, usually in the setting of chronic otitis media or Eustachian tube dysfunction, leading to tympanic membrane retraction or perforation [].

Congenital cholesteatomas are slow-growing lesions and may be asymptomatic for years []. Bone erosion is less common than in acquired cholesteatomas, tends to occur later in the disease course, and is generally less extensive [, ]. However, the disease is locally invasive and may lead to significant complications, including hearing loss, facial or abducens nerve palsy, trigeminal neuralgia, and headache [, ].

On CT, cholesteatomas appear as non-enhancing, hypodense, expansile soft tissue lesions that cause variable degrees of bone destruction [, ]. On MRI, they are hypointense on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, and do not enhance following contrast administration []. Gadolinium contrast is not required for cholesteatoma imaging evaluation unless complications, such as meningitis or ear infection, are suspected []. DWI is particularly useful, as cholesteatomas demonstrate marked diffusion restriction, helping differentiation with inflammatory processes in the same location (Fig. ) []. Non-echo-planar DWI should be acquired for the detection of small and recurrent cholesteatomas [, , ].

Petrous apicitis refers to suppurative inflammation of the pneumatized petrous apex, usually occurring as an extension of middle ear or mastoid infection [, , ]. Due to the close proximity of the petrous apex to the trigeminal ganglion within Meckel’s cave and the abducens nerve within the Dorello canal, these structures are commonly involved, resulting in the classic Gradenigo triad of otomastoiditis, deep facial pain, and lateral rectus palsy [, , ]. Facial nerve paralysis and vertigo/sensorineural hearing loss secondary to vestibulocochlear nerve involvement may also occur [].

In patients with petrous apicitis, CT demonstrates opacification of the petrous apex air cells and mild osseous expansion in the early stages, progressing to trabecular breakdown and aggressive bone destruction in the later stages [, ]. MRI typically shows T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of the pneumatized petrous apex mucosa (Fig. ). Because of the proximity of the petrous apex to the brain, complications such as abscess, meningitis, and thrombophlebitis may occur and are best detected on MRI [, ]. Ring-enhancing lesions with diffusion restriction suggest abscess formation, whereas heterogeneous marrow enhancement in a non-pneumatized petrous apex is suggestive of osteomyelitis []. Petrous apex osteomyelitis is more frequently encountered in adults and is uncommon in children [].

Meningiomas are the most common intracranial tumor in adults; however, they are rarely found in children and tend to demonstrate more aggressive or even malignant behavior in the pediatric population [, ]. Pediatric presentation is usually syndromic and commonly associated with genetic disorders such as neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) or Gorlin–Goltz syndrome [, ]. Petrous apex meningiomas can be either dural-based (petroclival and CPA) or, rarely, intraosseous [, , ]. CPA meningiomas arise from the dura along the posterior surface of the petrous apex and may extend into the IAC. Petroclival meningiomas originate from the medial aspect of the petrous bone and extend over the petrous apex or into Dorello’s canal [, ].

Four imaging patterns of petrous apex involvement have been described: (1) pseudoinvasion, in which petroclival meningiomas appear to invade the petrous apex because of the variable appearance of the apex, its thin cortical shell, and volume-averaging effects, although true invasion is absent; (2) hyperostosis with sclerosis of the petrous apex; (3) true invasion of the cortical and trabecular bone with obliteration of the marrow space and pneumatized air cells; and (4) intraosseous meningiomas, which are rare and may mimic a primary or metastatic bone tumor [, ].

CT and MRI demonstrate a dural-based extraosseous mass typically hyperdense on CT, iso- to hypointense on T1WI, and iso- to hyperintense on T2WI []. Hyperostosis may demonstrate low attenuation on both T1- and T2WI [, ]. Intense homogeneous enhancement and the presence of a dural tail are characteristic imaging features on MRI (Table ) [, ].

Imaging characteristics of benign and malignant lesions

Schwannomas are benign lesions that arise from the Schwann cells of the nerve sheaths and may occasionally affect the petrous apex. Petrous apex schwannomas most commonly arise from the V, VII, and VIII cranial nerves, resulting in osseous remodeling and expansion of the petrous apex [, ]. In children, they are rare and are typically associated with syndromic conditions such as NF2 [].

On CT, schwannomas appear as well-circumscribed, expansile, isoattenuating lesions, and enhance after contrast administration. On MRI, they are iso- to hypointense on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, and demonstrate marked enhancement on post-contrast images [, ]. Larger schwannomas may show cystic degeneration, hemorrhage, and fluid–fluid levels, findings that may suggest the diagnosis []. Trigeminal schwannomas are rare and typically present in patients between the fourth and sixth decades of life []. They arise from the Meckel’s cave or the cisternal segment of the nerve and may extend in any direction along the nerve, causing expansion of the neural foramina and superior indentation of the petrous apex. In contrast to facial and acoustic schwannomas, trigeminal schwannomas more frequently demonstrate prominent cystic components [, ]. Facial nerve schwannomas account for approximately 0.8% of all petrous lesions []. They typically arise from the geniculate ganglion and result in expansion of the geniculate fossa and facial nerve canal []. Vestibulocochlear nerve schwannomas originate around the vestibular nerve in the IAC and appear on imaging as enhancing masses filling or expanding the IAC, with possible progressive extension into the CPA or the labyrinth []. Rarely, primary intraosseous schwannomas may originate from the deep petrosal nerve [].

Paragangliomas (PGL) arising from the jugular fossa may occasionally erode the medial margin of the fossa, invade the occipital bone, and involve the adjacent petrous bone [, ]. They may occur sporadically or as part of a familial syndrome. Hereditary paragangliomas typically present earlier in life than the sporadic lesions, as part of the hereditary paraganglioma–pheochromocytoma (PGL-PCC) syndrome, and are commonly multiple, affecting different sites and recurring over time [, –]. When these features are present, or there is a family history of PGLs and PCCs, hereditary PGL-PCC syndrome should be strongly suspected and molecular genetic testing should be performed [].

Contrast-enhanced MRI is considered the modality of choice []. However, contrast-enhanced CT offers greater sensitivity for lesions smaller than 1 cm and provides superior spatial resolution and anatomical delineation []. On CT, paragangliomas typically appear as hypervascular soft tissue masses producing a characteristic “moth-eaten” pattern of bone erosion with enlargement of the jugular foramen due to tumor infiltration along the Haversian canal system [, ].

On MRI, paragangliomas demonstrate avid enhancement and may show multiple flow voids []. On T1WI, they may have a typical “salt and pepper” appearance caused by the prominent intratumoral vasculature [, ]. The hyperintense “salt” foci likely represent areas of intratumoral hemorrhage, whereas the hypointense “pepper” component (also evident on T2WI) corresponds to flow voids produced by high-velocity blood flow within feeding vessels []. Because paragangliomas demonstrate avid uptake on 18FDG PET scan, they may be mistaken for aggressive or malignant lesions. However, the location at the jugular foramen, the marked hypervascularity, and the presence of additional paragangliomas in the head and neck region should suggest the diagnosis [].

Chondromyxoid fibromas (CMFs) are rare, benign, slow-growing cartilaginous bone tumors characterized by chondroid, myxoid, and fibrous differentiation []. They typically arise in the metaphyses of long bones, whereas skull base and temporal bone involvement is exceedingly rare, with only a few cases reported originating in the petrous and sphenoid bone [, ]. CMFs most commonly present in adolescents and young adults; however, temporal bone lesions tend to present later in life [–]. Only a few cases have been reported in the pediatric population [–]. Clinical manifestations depend on the involvement of adjacent cranial nerves and may include tinnitus, otalgia, hearing loss, or facial nerve palsy [, ].

On CT, CMFs appear as well-defined, lobulated soft tissue masses with sclerotic rims and scalloped margins. Intratumoral calcifications have been reported in most of the skull base CMFs and may aid the diagnosis [, ]. On MRI, they are typically hypointense on T1WI, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2WI, and usually demonstrate contrast enhancement []. The differential diagnosis includes myxoid chondrosarcomas, which may demonstrate similar MRI characteristics but typically exhibit a more infiltrative growth pattern with aggressive bone destruction []. Chordomas usually demonstrate greater extraosseous extension than CMFs and may be easily differentiated on immunochemistry []. In the mastoid region, CMFs may mimic a facial nerve schwannoma; however, the presence of intratumoral calcifications may favor CMFs, as they are less commonly seen in facial nerve schwannomas [].

Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is an aggressive malignant childhood tumor arising from skeletal muscle or primitive undifferentiated mesenchymal tissue [, ]. It accounts for about 3–5% of all childhood malignancies and is the most common soft tissue sarcoma []. RMS demonstrates a bimodal age distribution that varies by histological subtype. The embryonal subtype, which accounts for approximately 70% of cases, typically affects younger children and is associated with a better prognosis, whereas the alveolar type, comprising about 15% of cases, is more common in adolescents and is linked to a poorer prognosis []. Approximately 36% of RMSs arise in the head and neck region, with about 7% involving the temporal bone []. They usually involve the external auditory canal, middle ear cavity, and facial nerve, but may extend medially into the petrous apex []. Clinical presentation may mimic chronic otitis media with blood-stained aural discharge, aural polyps, and hearing loss; patients may also present with facial nerve palsy []. On CT, RMS appears as an aggressive soft tissue mass associated with osseous destruction []. On MRI, RMS appears iso-hypointense on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, demonstrates variable contrast enhancement, and the majority of lesions show restricted diffusion [, –]. On imaging, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) may have a similar appearance; however, RMS more often presents as a solitary destructive lesion, whereas LCH and metastases are frequently multiple [, ].

Ewing sarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant bone tumor that mainly affects children and adolescents and represents the second most common primary bone tumor in this population []. In pediatric patients, it accounts for approximately 6–9% of all malignant bone neoplasms []. Skull involvement is reported in about 1–6% of cases, and petrous bone involvement is very rare [–].

On CT, Ewing sarcoma typically appears as an expansile lesion with aggressive bone destruction, a characteristic periosteal reaction, and enhancing soft tissue components. On MRI, it is typically hypo- to isointense on T1WI, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2WI, demonstrates diffusion restriction, and shows significant, heterogeneous contrast enhancement [, , ].

LCH is a lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by proliferation of mature eosinophils and Langerhans cells and typically affects children between 5 and 15 years of age []. The temporal bone is the most common skull base site of involvement, with the mastoid and petrous apex most frequently affected [, ].

On CT, LCH lesions demonstrate a typical lytic, “punched-out” appearance with beveled edges due to asymmetric erosion of the inner and outer cortices, without sclerosis of the margins [, ]. Unlike metastatic neuroblastoma, there is no associated periosteal reaction [, , ]. Erosion of the bony labyrinth and ossicular chain may occur [, ]. On MRI, lesions are typically isointense to muscle on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, with surrounding bone marrow and soft tissue edema, and may demonstrate restricted diffusion (Fig. ) [, , ]. Marked enhancement is seen after contrast administration on both CT and MRI [].

Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilaginous tumors that arise from remnants of enchondral cartilage along skull base synchondroses []. At the petrous apex, they most typically originate at the petroclival and petrosphenoidal synchondroses and most commonly present in the second or third decade of life with headache, sixth cranial nerve palsy, and hearing loss [, ]. They are more common than their benign counterparts, but similar to chondromas, they are associated with several syndromes, including Ollier disease, Maffucci syndrome, Paget disease, and osteochondroma [].

These tumors are locally invasive and, on CT, appear as expansile lobulated masses that cause destruction of the petrous apex []. The internal matrix architecture depends on the amount of the chondroid tissue, and characteristic chondroid matrix calcifications produce the classic “rings and arcs” appearance in approximately 50% of cases [, , , , ]. On MRI, chondrosarcomas typically demonstrate low to intermediate signal intensity on T1WI, depending on the calcifications within the mass, and markedly high signal intensity on T2WI relative to the brain []. Post-contrast images show variable enhancement [].

Chordomas are rare malignant tumors derived from remnants of embryonic notochord tissue and may occur anywhere from the skull base to the sacrum []. Skull base chordomas are typically midline lesions arising from the spheno-occipital synchondrosis of the clivus, which may extend laterally and involve the petrous apex [, , ].

Pediatric chordomas account for approximately 5% of all chordomas and are typically more aggressive, with a broader spectrum of clinical presentations and a higher rate of metastasis [, ]. On CT, they appear as locally destructive soft tissue masses and calcifications are often evident and may represent residual bone trabeculae [, ].

On MRI, chordomas are hypointense on T1WI, markedly hyperintense on T2WI, and have variable ADC values, but typically lower than those of chondrosarcoma []. Following contrast administration, they show variable enhancement and may exhibit a characteristic “honeycomb” appearance due to enhancing internal septations []. Chondroid variants of chordoma may mimic chondrosarcomas; however, the enhancing internal septations and the absence of the typical “rings and arcs” pattern help in the differential diagnosis []. In general, chondrosarcomas are more lateral, have higher ADC, and are even less frequent in children. A recent paper published by Tian et al. graded chordomas into three groups based on the tumor-to-pons signal intensity ratio and suggested that this ratio may have diagnostic and potential therapeutic significance [].

Endolymphatic sac tumors (ELSTs) are rare, aggressive tumors arising from the proximal rugose portion, also known as the intermediate segment, of the endolymphatic sac, located between the IAC and the jugular foramen []. These lesions are typically centered along the posterior wall of the temporal bone and may extend into the petrous bone and CPA []. They are usually sporadic; however, when associated with von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome, they occur at a younger age, may be bilateral, and show a female predominance [–].

On CT, ELSTs typically appear as retrolabyrinthine soft tissue masses with aggressive bone destruction (Fig. ). Small, irregular calcifications are commonly present and represent residual bone fragments []. Intratumoral bleeding is frequent, resulting in variable signal intensity on both T1- and T2WI. Following contrast administration, ELSTs demonstrate avid, nodular enhancement due to their rich vascularity. In lesions larger than 2 cm, signal voids from high-flow vessels are commonly observed []. Both paragangliomas and ELSTs are hypervascular lesions that may demonstrate internal hemorrhage and permeative bone destruction. However, a retrolabyrinthine location, association with VHL syndrome, and absence of flow voids in smaller lesions favor the diagnosis of ELST [, ].

Neuroblastoma is the most common tumor diagnosed in the first year of life, with familial cases accounting for approximately 1–2% of all cases []. Metastases to the temporal bone are rare; however, they represent the most frequent petrous bone metastases in children []. The imaging appearance depends on the characteristics of the primary tumor but typically demonstrates lytic lesions with associated bone destruction and an aggressive periosteal reaction []. On CT and MRI, they appear as multiple, well-defined, enhancing soft tissue masses associated with osseous destruction [, ].

Fibrous dysplasia is a genetic disorder of bone proliferation and maturation characterized by replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue []. It can be monostotic, polyostotic, craniofacial, or syndromic (e.g., McCune-Albright syndrome) [, ]. The polyostotic form typically presents in younger children and involves the temporal bone []. Temporal bone involvement may present with conductive hearing loss due to external auditory canal stenosis and the involvement of the petrous bone is quite rare and usually spares the otic capsule [, –]. On MRI, fibrous dysplasia appears as an expansile bone lesion that is hypointense on T1WI, demonstrates heterogeneous signal intensity on T2WI, and shows variable post-contrast enhancement. CT is considered diagnostic and demonstrates an expansile lesion in the medullary space with a characteristic ground-glass matrix and usually preserved cortex [, ] (Table ). Occasionally, lucent areas with thin sclerotic margins may be observed [, ]. Paget disease may have a similar appearance, but it typically occurs in adults [].

Aneurysmal bone cysts (ABCs) are rare, benign, tumor-like lesions that typically affect children and young adults under 20 years of age. They are characterized by blood-filled cavities that progressively expand and destroy bone and are thought to result from vascular malformations []. ABCs occurring in the temporal bone are uncommon, and lesions arising from the petrous portion of the temporal bone are exceedingly rare []. On CT, they appear as expansile, multilobulated, “bubbly” lesions with internal septations and fluid–fluid levels within the cavities. MRI demonstrates similar findings to those on CT [, ].

Petrous apex meningoceles are rare, cystic lesions that represent focal herniation of the dura from the posterolateral wall of Meckel’s cave into the petrous apex []. They are thought to result from chronically or intermittently increased intracranial pressure transmitted into Meckel’s cave through a patent porus trigeminus [, ]. They may be bilateral and may be associated with Usher syndrome and Neurofibromatosis type 1 [, ]. Petrous apex meningoceles are typically incidental findings in adults and rarely require intervention. However, they are frequently symptomatic in children, presenting with CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea [, ].

On CT, they appear as lobulated, cystic lesions causing smooth expansion of the petrous apex and enlargement of the porus trigeminus []. On MRI, they typically follow CSF signal intensity on all sequences. High-resolution coronal T2WI is particularly useful for demonstrating communication with Meckel’s cave []. CT or MR cisternography may help identify the site of the osteodural defect in cases of CSF leak [].

Petrous ICA aneurysms are extremely rare lesions, particularly in children, and are most frequently of the fusiform type [, ]. Congenital ICA aneurysms are usually seen at a younger age, whereas acquired/pseudoaneurysms may be post-traumatic, mycotic, or post-radiation and can occur at any age []. Although usually asymptomatic, these aneurysms may enlarge and compress adjacent neurovascular structures, leading to cranial nerve palsies, Horner syndrome, and sensorineural hearing loss [, , –].

CT demonstrates expansion of the walls of the petrous artery canal or even dehiscence of its bony walls. Following contrast administration, a mural thrombus may be identified; however, embolic events are rare [, ]. On MRI, signal intensity is variable and depends on flow dynamics or the presence of intraluminal thrombus. CT and MR angiography are both diagnostic and are essential for lesion characterization (Fig. ) [, ].

Imaging features often overlap, making careful interpretation essential.

Knowledge of age-related anatomy and normal variants helps avoid misdiagnosis.

CT and MRI provide complementary information and should be integrated for accurate lesion characterization.

A structured imaging approach helps narrow the differential diagnosis and supports clinical management and surgical planning. Correlation with clinical findings and multidisciplinary discussion improves diagnostic confidence and patient care.

medicine.title: RE1 silencing transcription factor is reduced in endometriosis, and uterine deletion in mice alters progesterone responsiveness
medicine.abstract: Endometriosis is a common disease in women characterized by altered steroid hormone signaling, infertility, and pelvic pain. RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST) is a candidate regulator of steroid hormone signaling in gynecologic disease, but a role in endometriosis pathophysiology remains unexplored. To fill this knowledge gap, our study utilizes human endometrial and endometriotic tissues coupled with a conditional knockout mouse model for uterine Rest deficiency. We show that REST is significantly reduced in eutopic and ectopic endometrial tissue from women with endometriosis and that deletion from mouse uterine tissue recapitulates clinical characteristics in women with endometriosis including progesterone resistance, subfertility and pelvic pain. These findings will further guide future research to understand impaired steroid signaling in the pathophysiology of endometriosis.
medicine.text:
Endometriosis is an estrogen-dependent disease that affects approximately 10% of reproductive-age women, or 190 million worldwide, not including the estimated 6 million who are suspected to go undiagnosed (, ). The disease is characterized by the ectopic presence of tissue containing endometrial stroma and glands outside of the uterus which can develop into superficial or deep infiltrating lesions. Aberrant steroid hormone signaling, specifically progesterone (P4) resistance, is implicated in the advancement of disease pathophysiology at the level of both the ectopic endometriotic lesion and the eutopic endometrium ().

For example, patients with endometriosis exhibit altered expression levels of several endometrial P4 target genes (–) which may be due to abnormal expression and/or function of P4 receptors (PGR), PGR-A and PGR-B (–), as well as inflammation, genetic abnormalities, and epigenetics (–). The inability of eutopic endometrium and ectopic endometriotic tissue to properly respond to P4, leading to hyperestrogen action and inflammation, promotes proliferation and survival of the ectopic tissue and the onset of endometriosis-associated symptoms.

Clinical manifestations of the disease that cause many patients to seek medical evaluation include infertility and pelvic pain (–). For endometriosis-associated infertility, poor oocyte quality, impaired embryo implantation, and P4 resistance are implicated as contributing factors, yet the precise mechanisms remain poorly understood (, , , ). In patients with endometriosis, pelvic pain does not always correlate with stage or severity of the disease (, ). However, aberrant P4 response and concurrent overexpression of estrogen receptor-β (ESR2) results in excessive inflammation and sensitization (, , ). This pro-inflammatory environment brought on by P4 resistance in the tissue could contribute to manifestation of pain symptoms experienced by patients.

P4 resistance is a central mechanism in endometriosis and can influence endometriosis-associated fertility challenges and pelvic pain through promotion of aberrant steroid hormone signaling and increased estrogen activity. These characteristics can also drive lesion survival through blunted P4 responsiveness and inflammation. However, the exact molecular mechanisms and pathways leading to P4 resistance in disease tissue have yet to be fully elucidated. As such, a critical gap in knowledge remains as to why eutopic endometrium and ectopic endometrial-like tissue from patients with endometriosis exhibit altered P4 responsiveness.

Although P4 resistance is well documented in endometriosis pathophysiology, the molecular mechanisms driving physiological changes in the tissue that promote an altered P4 response are not fully understood, limiting the identification of potential new biological targets for treatment. Recent evidence suggests the neuron-restrictive silencer factor/RE1-silencing transcription factor (NRSF/REST) may play a crucial role in steroid hormone responsiveness in reproductive tissue and the transcriptional regulation of P4 target genes, contributing to uterine pathology (–).

REST is a transcriptional repressor that inhibits neuronal gene expression in non-neuronal tissues but can also act as an enhancer of gene transcription (, ). REST functions in the nucleus and binds to highly conserved RE1 elements in target genes (, ). Recent ChIP-seq data support a direct relationship between REST and PGR signaling with observed RE1 sites in roughly 200 REST target genes in close proximity to PGR-A and PGR-B binding sites (, ). The loss of functional REST protein in uterine leiomyoma has been associated with an abnormal response to steroid hormones, enhanced estrogen signaling, and a disruption in PGR signaling resulting in altered expression of genes containing both REST and PGR target sequences (). Furthermore, coimmunoprecipitation experiments revealed interaction between REST and PGR, and genes containing both REST and PGR target sequences showed aberrant expression in a REST knockout mouse model (), suggesting an epigenetic influence of REST in the regulation of P4 target genes that share both REST and P4 response elements. Additionally, altered expression of these REST-PGR target genes coincided with enhanced ER-α (ESR1) signaling, which supports an overall dysfunctional sex steroid regulation in the tissue (). Further, the loss of REST protein, but not transcript expression in uterine leiomyoma tissue promotes aberrant expression of REST and P4 target gene (, , ). These findings support REST as a key modulator of steroid hormone signaling, with presence of REST necessary for full P4 responsiveness. Whether a similar REST-dependent mechanism contributes to P4 resistance in endometriosis remains unexplored.

To fill this knowledge gap, we first characterized the expression of REST protein in endometriosis utilizing a robust, well-characterized number of human specimens. Next, we investigated how reduction in uterine REST protein influenced eutopic and ectopic endometriotic tissue by assessing fertility and pelvic pain symptomology often associated with endometriosis using a novel Rest-deficient mouse model. Additionally, we investigated loss of REST protein in endometriotic-like lesion survival in vivo. These studies are an essential step to begin to determine whether REST/regulation of REST could be examined as a potential therapeutic target for endometriosis treatment.

Previous studies have demonstrated aberrant expression of REST in human cell lines and tissue, implicating REST in steroid hormone signaling and tumor pathogenesis including breast cancer and uterine leiomyoma. Currently, there are no published studies that have investigated REST expression in the setting of endometriosis, a disease characterized by progesterone resistance. We first aimed to characterize the subcellular localization and expression pattern of REST protein in human endometriosis by immunohistochemical assessment of ectopic endometriotic lesion tissue and matched eutopic endometrium from patients with confirmed endometriosis (N = 16 overall; n = 7 proliferative; n = 9 secretory) and then compared REST expression to eutopic control tissue from patients without endometriosis (N = 15 overall; n = 7 proliferative; n = 8 secretory) (SI Appendix, Table S1) in specimens obtained from the proliferative () and secretory ().

Immunohistochemical analysis revealed predominant nuclear localization of REST protein expression in glandular epithelium and endometrial stroma of eutopic endometrium tissue collected from control patients from both the proliferative (black arrows, ) and secretory (black arrows, ) stages of the menstrual cycle. In contrast, nuclear REST expression in glandular epithelium and stroma was reduced or absent in ectopic lesion and eutopic endometrial tissue from patients with endometriosis, independent of menstrual cycle stage (). Quantitative H-Score (Histological Score) analysis confirmed that nuclear REST expression was significantly lower in ectopic endometriosis lesion tissue (Glands: proliferative, P = 0.0002; secretory, P = 0.0377. Stroma: proliferative, P < 0.0001; secretory, P = 0.0011) and matched eutopic endometriosis endometrium (Glands: proliferative, P < 0.0001; secretory, P = 0.0001. Stroma: proliferative, P < 0.0001; secretory, P < 0.0001) as compared to nuclear REST expression in the glandular epithelium and stroma of control eutopic endometrium (). Additionally, in control samples, nuclear REST expression was significantly higher compared to cytoplasmic expression in both the glandular and stromal (Glands: proliferative, P = 0.0306; secretory, P = 0.0311. Stroma: proliferative, P < 0.0001; secretory, P = 0.0006), unlike in endometriosis eutopic endometrium where nuclear REST expression was significantly reduced relative to cytoplasmic in glands alone (proliferative, P = 0.0158; secretory, P = 0.0134). Nuclear REST expression in ectopic endometriotic lesion tissue of glands (proliferative, P = 0.0656; secretory, P = 0.0568) and eutopic (proliferative, P = 0.1495; secretory, P = 0.2459) and ectopic (proliferative, P = 0.2020; secretory, P = 0.6329) tissue in stroma trended lower compared to cytoplasmic expression but overall was not significant. No differences were observed between proliferative and secretory phases of the menstrual cycle within either group. These findings demonstrate abnormal subcellular localization with reduced nuclear expression of REST in both eutopic and ectopic endometriotic tissue which may suggest loss of REST function as a nuclear transcription factor. To evaluate the impact of loss of REST expression in both eutopic endometrial tissue and ectopic endometriotic tissue we next utilized a mouse model with conditional deletion of Rest expression.

Rest fl/fl mice () were mated to Pgr Cre/+ mice to generate a Rest fl/fl Pgr Cre/+ (Rest d/d) line, in which the expression of Cre recombinase is under the control of progesterone receptor (PGR) promoter action. Rest knockout at the transcript and protein levels were respectfully confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blot (SI Appendix, Fig. S1). Fertility was assessed by conducting breeding trials using 2-mo-old female Rest d/d mice (n = 8) that were mated with wild-type C57BL/6 males of proven fertility. As a control group, Rest fl/fl female mice (n = 9) were also mated with wild-type C57BL/6 males with two females of each genotype per cage with the same male. After the first round, when pups were weaned from the dams, each mother was remated. After 3 rounds of consecutive mating (approximately 4-mo in duration), the total number of litters and pups were calculated for both genotypes. After 3 breeding cycles (SI Appendix, Table S2), Rest fl/fl female dams produced a total of 248 pups across 26 litters, with 96% of females having successful parturition and birth of viable offspring. However, Rest d/d female dams only produced 57 pups in total across 11 litters. The duration of each mating round did not differ between genotypes (). However, compared to Rest fl/fl control females, Rest d/d females exhibited a significant decrease in total number of litters per breeding round and the litter size per dam from the first round of breeding to the subsequent second and third rounds (). The proportion of dams with litters decreased from round 1 to round 2, with only 1 out of 8 dams in round 2 producing pups and remained low in round 3 (2 out of 8 dams, SI Appendix, Table S2). In contrast, Rest fl/fl dams maintained a stable average litter size across all mating rounds ( and SI Appendix, Table S2). Across all consecutive rounds of mating, Rest d/d dams produced significantly smaller litter sizes compared to Rest fl/fl dams in the same round (). Due to PGR expression in the mammary glands, we investigated if loss of REST affected lactation and feeding in KO females by assessing body weight of the pups. The average litter weight of the two genotypes (Rest fl/fl = 10.22 grams; Rest d/d = 9.35 grams) was not statistically different between genotypes (). A decline in successful pregnancy in Rest d/d females is consistent with subfertility, suggesting that loss of REST in eutopic uterine tissue may contribute to impaired fertility. We do not believe that the reduction in fertility was due to compromised ovarian steroid action and/or impact on the endometrium as females of both genotypes exhibit normal estrous cycles (SI Appendix, Table S3). Further, assessment of uterine tissue at the termination of the breeding trial in females of both genotypes revealed an approximate fourfold increase in uterine wet weights in the Rest d/d mice compared to controls () which was characterized by the presence of large endometrial glandular cysts (), indicative of unopposed estrogen action.

To determine if the uterine alterations observed in the Rest d/d mice develop independent of mating and pregnancy, we evaluated gross morphology of virgin female mice of both genotypes. Rest d/d mouse uteri displayed hallmarks of unopposed estrogen action in the tissue including an increased uterine wet weight and distended, fluid-filled uterine horns as compared to the uteri of control mice at all ages (). Histological assessment using hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed no structural abnormalities in Rest control mice () from 6 to 12 mo of age. In contrast, Rest d/d uteri where characterized by enlarged cystic glands (defined as glands with a diameter greater than 500 μm) in the endometrium with loss of a clearly define uterine lumen by 12 mo of age (). These phenotypic differences in the absence of uterine Rest expression are evidence of a hyperestrogenic effect and possible P4 resistance which was consistently observed in Rest deficient females at 6-, 9-, and 12-mo of age.

To determine if loss of REST expression impacted steroid effects on the uterus we examined uterine genes associated with E2 and P4 signaling in mice of both genotypes in response to steroid treatment. Rest  d/d mice exhibited a hyperestrogenic phenotype in response to E2 treatment alone () and in combination with P4 (). Comparison in the ability of P4 to repress the effect of E2 on uterine wet weight gain revealed that while concurrent administration of E2 with P4 reduced uterine wet weight in Rest fl/fl females (), P4 was unable to induce a similar suppression of E2 stimulated uterine wet weight gain in Rest d/d females ().

To evaluate if the altered E2 and P4 responsiveness impacted known E2 () and P4 () regulated genes, we assessed expression at 0 h, 6 h, and 24 h post–steroid treatment. In response to E2, Lif expression was increased in mice of both genotypes with Rest d/d females exhibiting significantly higher levels compared to controls at 6 h post E2 administration (). In contrast, while E2 stimulated Timp1 expression in mice of both genotypes (), there was no difference in the level of induction between genotypes unlike the induction of Lif. Last, expression of the validated REST target gene, Mmp24 was significantly higher in Rest deficient females but unaffected by E2 treatment ().

Evaluation of known P4 uterine target genes () revealed alteration in induction in some but not all genes. More specifically, progesterone receptor (Pgr), a target gene upregulated in the human eutopic endometrium in patients with endometriosis during the early secretory stage, showed a significant increase in expression 6 h after E2 + P4 treatment in both Rest fl/fl and Rest d/d uterine tissue. Notably, Rest d/d Pgr levels were significantly higher compared to Rest fl/fl, with fold-changes of 4.8 and 3.2 respectively (), a similar pattern documented in the endometrium of patients diagnosed with endometriosis as relative to healthy controls. Secreted phosphoprotein-1 (Spp1), a glycoprotein implicated in regulation of the immune response, had significantly lower expression compared to control mice after steroid hormone treatment at 24 h (8.8- and 19.8-fold-change, respectively; ), consistent with downregulation in human endometriosis. However, mucin-1 (Muc1) expression, while differentially expressed, was elevated in Rest d/d compared to controls at 6 h (8.6- and 2.5-fold-change, respectively) and 24 h (7.5- and 1.1-fold-change, respectively) after treatment (), differing from the reduction seen in human endometriosis (). Mmp9 expression, which is typically suppressed by P4, was significantly higher in Rest d/d mice at 24 h post steroid treatment (). Similar to E2 treatment, treatment with E2 + P4 did not influence Mmp24 expression but again, there was highly significant up-regulation of its expression in Rest d/d uteri in all groups compared to Rest fl/fl tissue (). These observations may be interpreted to suggest that in the absence of REST, impaired regulation of P4 responsive genes is selective, and not a global effect. These findings indicate that loss of uterine REST in our mouse model is associated with impaired regulation of select E2 as well as P4 responsive genes, similar to P4-regulated gene expression documented in the endometrium of patients diagnosed with endometriosis.

To investigate if REST deficiency in endometriotic lesion tissue impacts lesion dynamics, we utilized a well-established experimental model of endometriosis (, ), Endometrial fragments from donor mice with Rest fl/fl or Rest d/d genotypic backgrounds were injected into the peritoneal cavity of wild type C57BL/6 female recipient mice to induce development of ectopic endometriotic-like lesions (SI Appendix, Fig. S2). Ten days after induction of disease, all mice were subjected to P4 treatment, Von Frey filament testing, vaginal balloon distention, and tissue harvest as outlined in . In recipient mice harboring Rest fl/fl endometrial tissue, P4 treatment significantly increased withdrawal threshold relative to recipients of Rest fl/fl tissue treatedwith placebo (), indicating a higher tolerance for mechanical pressure and lower mechanical sensitivity (–). In contrast, Rest d/d recipients show a moderate trend of increased threshold when treated with P4 but overall was not significant between the placebo and P4 treated groups (P = 0.0864), suggesting a resistance to the effects of P4 treatment for mechanical allodynia in association with endometriosis. Recipients of Rest d/d tissue exhibited lower withdrawal thresholds when compared to Rest fl/fl of the same treatment. This was observed under both treatment conditions, placebo and P4 injections, indicating heightened mechanical sensitivity. On day 15, vaginal hyperalgesia was assessed using graded vaginal balloon distensions (VBD) to measure the visceromotor reflex (VMR), a validated indicator of endometriosis-associated vaginal sensitivity in rodents (, , ). In our model, no difference was observed in visceromotor reflex, whether between treatments and/or genotype of donor tissue, overall () or individual pressures of balloon distension (), with uterine REST deficient tissue and P4 treatment having minimal effect on displays of vaginal sensitivity.

Survival and growth of endometriotic lesions are supported by aberrant expression of P4 responsive genes and uninhibited E2 activity. However, it is well established that pain severity experienced by patients with endometriosis does not correlate to disease severity (, ). All mice subjected to VBD were killed humanly and endometriotic-like lesions were excised from surrounding tissue in the abdominal cavity. One lesion was observed in each mouse which developed on the peritoneal wall at the site of tissue transfer. Lesion size was recorded (mm3) with representative images displayed in .

Rest fl/fl endometrial tissue lesions treated with P4 were significantly smaller relative to placebo (average 1 mm3 vs. of 3 mm3), unlike Rest d/d endometrial tissue lesions which did not significantly differ in size between placebo and P4 treated groups (average 7.16 mm3

Rest d/d; ). Placebo treated Rest d/d lesions exhibited a significantly higher percentage of Ki67-positive cells compared to all other groups, indicating increased cellular proliferation in these endometriotic-like lesions (). This reduction in size of the Rest-deficient endometriotic-like lesions was not associated with alterations in steroid receptor expression as the genotypic background of fragments and/or P4 treatment had no significant effect on nuclear expression of ER-alpha in the glandular epithelium or stroma of the endometriotic-like lesions across all groups (). Progesterone treatment significantly reduced epithelial cell PGR protein expression in Rest fl/fl P4-treated mice compared to placebo-treated mice (). In contrast, P4 had a lesser effect on epithelial cell PGR protein expression in Rest d/d lesions (). A similar observation was made for nuclear PGR protein staining in the lesion stroma, with a nonsignificant trend toward lower PGR expression in the P4 treated groups compared to placebo groups in both Rest fl/fl and Rest d/d tissue (P = 0.1436 and P = 0.0580, respectively; ).

Endometriosis is a chronic estrogen-dependent disease characterized by aberrant steroid hormone signaling, particularly impaired progesterone (P4) responsiveness, which contributes to lesion development and persistence. Although P4-based therapies are widely used clinically, many patients exhibit incomplete or variable responses, highlighting a limited understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying P4 resistance in endometriosis. Previous studies have demonstrated dysregulation of P4 target genes in the endometrium of women with endometriosis (). Altered PGR isoform ratios, inflammation, and epigenetic mechanisms have all been proposed to disrupt P4 signaling, although the underlying molecular pathways remain unclear (). Infertility and chronic pain are among the most common symptoms reported by patients, yet their presentation varies. This variability may reflect differences in hormone responsiveness that influence disease presentation, progression, and treatment response.

RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST) has emerged as a candidate regulator of steroid hormone signaling through its interaction with PGR and coregulation of P4-responsive genes. Given that reduced REST expression has been reported in uterine leiomyoma and breast cancer, we hypothesized that REST is similarly reduced in endometriosis and contributes to impaired P4 responsiveness and lesion persistence. To test this, we characterized REST expression in human endometriosis tissues and used a uterine-specific Rest knockout mouse model to investigate its role in fertility, hormone responsiveness in the uterine tissue, endometriotic-like lesion development, and pain-related phenotypes.

Our study identifies loss of nuclear REST protein as a feature of both eutopic endometrium and ectopic endometriotic lesions when compared to healthy control endometrium. In human endometriosis tissues, REST protein was markedly reduced in the nucleus and mislocalized to the cytoplasm in both eutopic and ectopic tissue. Cytoplasmic retention of REST may contribute to functional loss by promoting ubiquitination-mediated degradation (, ). The mechanism which contributes to retention of REST within the cytoplasm, subsequent ubiquitination and resulting protein degradation was not explored but may involve a REST-interacting LIM domain protein (RILP) (, ). These findings support REST as a potential regulator of P4 responsiveness in endometriosis. However, elucidating the mechanisms underlying REST protein loss in endometriosis will also be important, beginning with assessment of RILP expression in endometriotic tissues. Targeting these processes may provide therapeutic opportunities to restore REST function.

Using our conditional uterine Rest knockout, loss of REST resulted in progressive subfertility, supporting a role for REST in reproductive function. Although Rest knockout females retained partial fertility during early breeding cycles, reproductive success declined over time compared with control females, which maintained consistently high fertility across all cycles. Because PGR is also expressed in the ovary, we cannot exclude potential ovarian contributions, including altered steroid production. However, as mice of both genotypes exhibited normal 4 to 5 d estrous cycles, we do not believe that E2 or P4 production was compromised in the Rest-deficient mice. This, coupled with the fact that uterine steroid responsiveness was altered in the Rest d/d mice when identical amounts of exogenous E2 or P4 were given to mice of both genotypes would suggest that steroid signaling pathways contributed to the observed phenotype, not differences in endogenous E2 or P4 levels. Nevertheless, the phenotype is consistent with the subfertility frequently associated with endometriosis and supports the utility of this model for studying endometriosis-associated reproductive dysfunction.

At the tissue level, Rest deficiency produced a hyperestrogenic uterine phenotype and reduced P4-mediated suppression of estrogen-driven uterine growth. Importantly, this phenotype does not suggest complete P4 resistance, but rather a blunted or diminished responsiveness to P4. This distinction is critical, as it more closely resembles the partial P4 insensitivity observed clinically in endometriosis. Our study is a step forward in identifying pathways involved in the characterization of endometriosis associated subfertility, which can lead to better diagnostic measures for fertility outcomes in endometriosis patients.

Consistent with studies showing dysregulation of P4 target genes in women with endometriosis (), uterine Rest loss selectively altered expression of some P4-responsive genes in mouse tissue. This selective effect suggests that REST functions as a context-dependent transcriptional regulator, likely through interaction with PGR at shared regulatory elements. Notably, impaired P4 responsiveness occurred despite preserved PGR expression, indicating that P4 resistance can develop independently of receptor abundance. Loss of REST did not significantly alter PGR transcript levels, further supporting a role for REST in epigenetic or coregulatory control of P4 target gene expression. These findings are consistent with previous reports demonstrating blunted P4 signaling responsiveness despite minimal differences in PGR expression between eutopic endometrium from women with and without endometriosis (). We also observed alteration in expression of the E2 target gene Lif, but not, Timp-1 in Restd/d mice treated with E2. This observation is in accord with recent findings that Rest deficiency is associated with altered E2 signaling pathways and much like P4 indicates that REST may function in an epigenetic or coregulatory role for transcription of select E2-regulated genes independent of changes in Esr1 expression.

Our lesion data further support this interpretation. Er-α and Pgr expression were unchanged in endometriotic-like lesions derived from Rest-deficient tissue. However, lesion size and proliferation remained largely unaffected by P4 treatment compared with lesions from control mice. Thus, endometriotic-like tissue receptor expression alone in this model was insufficient to drive an effective biological response to P4 treatment in the absence of REST. This suggests that REST may facilitate proper PGR transcriptional activity, potentially through chromatin remodeling or coregulatory complex formation, and influence tissue P4 responsiveness. Similar observations have been reported in other hormone-dependent systems where steroid receptor expression remains stable despite altered downstream signaling (–, ).

Pain-related outcomes only partially correlated with lesion characteristics. Mechanical sensitivity of the hind paw was highly responsive to P4 treatment, with respect to REST expression. Conversely, vaginal sensitivity remained consistent, regardless of Rest expression or P4 treatment. It is important to note that the visceromotor response of all groups in this study was consistent with our previous publications of either endometriosis induction () or early life stress/vaginal inflammation (, ), indicating significant visceral hyperalgesia. These observations suggest that while the P4 treatment was sufficient to reduce hind paw allodynia (secondary measure of pain), it may not have been sufficient to reduce primary measures of hyperalgesia, regardless of its effect on the lesions themselves. This dissociation is consistent with clinical observations that lesion burden does not necessarily correlate with pain severity and suggests that REST may differentially influence somatic and visceral pain pathways. Variability in P4 responsiveness associated with REST expression may also contribute to differences in pain phenotypes. Additional studies incorporating inflammatory analyses alongside REST expression and pain assessments will be important to clarify these relationships.

Collectively, these findings support a model in which loss of uterine Rest results in a blunted P4 signaling responsiveness, persistent estrogenic activity, and enhanced lesion survival. This framework also raises the possibility that REST contributes to the heterogeneity observed in endometriosis symptoms and treatment responses.

Considerations when interpreting the results from this study include variability in human endometriotic lesion type, anatomical location, and duration each lesion has been present in the pelvic cavity may contribute to differences in REST expression and were not fully stratified. Although the conditional knockout model provides important mechanistic insight, it does not fully recapitulate the complexity of human endometriosis, including systemic immune influences, environmental factors, and lesion heterogeneity. Future studies should include broader characterization of P4-responsive genes within REST-dependent transcriptional networks beyond the scope of this work. In addition, some endometriotic-like lesion cross-sections lacked well-defined glandular structures, which may affect interpretation of immunohistochemical analyses. Lesions were evaluated at a single time point (2 wk following experimental induction), limiting assessment across different stages of lesion establishment and progression.

Assessment of pain-like behavior also revealed limited and modality-specific effects. The absence of changes in vaginal sensitivity may reflect model limitations or suggest that REST primarily influences specific nociceptive pathways. Clinically, these findings raise the possibility that REST status could serve as a biomarker for P4 responsiveness or treatment stratification. If REST contributes to variability in hormone responsiveness, it may help explain why some patients respond poorly to P4-based therapies and endometriosis present with a variation in fertility and pain symptomology. Integrating REST into broader models of endometriosis pathophysiology, including immune, inflammatory, and neurogenic pathways, will also be important for understanding symptom heterogeneity. Overall, our findings support a model in which loss of REST promotes blunted P4 responsiveness, persistent estrogenic activity, and enhanced lesion persistence, key features underlying endometriosis pathophysiology and clinical variability. More advanced translational models may help determine whether restoring REST function can rescue P4 responsiveness and limit disease progression.

All studies conducted using human and mouse tissues were respectively approved by the University of Kansas Medical Center Institutional Review Board and Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Further details for experiments using human and mouse tissues are provided in the SI Appendix.

Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and all use of human tissues was performed in accordance with Institutional Review Board (IRB)-approved study protocols (IRB00000161) at the University of Kansas Medical Center. All human endometrial tissue specimens were collected at the University of Kansas Medical Center by trained surgical professionals in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology. Eutopic and ectopic endometrial tissue specimens were collected from consenting women with confirmed laparoscopic endometriosis who presented with pelvic pain following failed previous endometriosis treatment and undergoing surgical removal of endometriotic lesion tissue. Control eutopic endometrial tissue specimens were collected from women with pain but no laparoscopic evidence of endometriosis. For some experiments, archived endometrial and endometriotic lesions tissue blocks were retrieved from the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine for immunohistochemical localization studies. Patients who reported the use of hormones and/or birth control were excluded. Information on stage of menstrual cycle (Proliferative or Secretory) was based on patient’s medical records and histological assessment. Grouping was done on basis of stage of menstrual cycle (Proliferative vs. Secretory). Additional patient characteristics were noted including age, presence of leiomyoma, adenomyosis, and/or polyps, and stage of endometriosis (Stage I/II vs. Stage II/IV) as identified by pathology reports (SI Appendix, Table S1).

RNA was isolated, cDNA synthesized and mRNA levels examined in mouse tissues by qRT-PCR analysis. Further details for experiments using human and mouse tissues are provided in the SI Appendix.

Protein was isolated and subjected to Western blot for mouse uterine tissue while proteins were localized in human mouse tissues by immunohistochemical localization. Further details for experiments using human and mouse tissues are provided in the SI Appendix.

All other experimental details are provided in the SI Appendix.
