medicine.title: Heart failure beyond cardiology: a primary care perspective on the 2026 ESC guideline
medicine.abstract: No abstract
medicine.text:
The 2026 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of heart failure (HF) extend well beyond an update of treatment recommendations. They simplify ejection-fraction phenotypes to HFrEF and HFpEF, introduce stages A to D, emphasize prevention and early recognition, and propose a community-based diagnostic pathway. They also explicitly involve generalists in multidisciplinary and long-term HF care. These changes move the HF agenda upstream, outwards from the hospital, and across professional boundaries.

As a general practitioner with specialist expertise in cardiovascularcare, I welcome this direction. It recognizes that improving HF care cannot be achieved in cardiology clinics alone. Yet it also exposes a significant gap between these ambitions and their translation into everyday practice. Primary care serves largely unselected patient populations, often managing multimorbidity and competing healthcare needs, with limited access to diagnostic investigations, rather than focusing on a single disease pathway. Extending HF care towards general practice is therefore not merely a change of location: it requires evidence about whom to investigate, which services are needed, and how responsibilities can be shared across care settings without increasing fragmentation.

This Viewpoint raises three related questions. Upstream, what does identifying people at risk of HF add to existing cardiometabolic prevention? Outwards, what constitutes a safe and efficient diagnostic pathway before specialist referral? And across professional boundaries, how can specialist HF expertise be incorporated into whole-person care?

Stage A identifies people at risk of HF, which involves individuals with risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and chronic kidney disease. These common risk factors are already central to cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic prevention and are associated with multiple disease trajectories, of which HF is only one. Why, then, classify this broad population as being at risk of HF specifically? The original universal definition of HF acknowledged the limited uptake of Stage A terminology and uncertainty about progression to symptomatic disease. Unless this classification changes risk assessment, clinical management, or patient outcomes, the priority in primary care should remain better management of shared risk factors rather than introducing another confusing, disease-specific label.

Stage B (pre-HF) raises a more consequential question because it makes asymptomatic cardiac abnormalities an explicit target for intervention. Certain abnormalities warrant treatment, but systematically identifying them in the community would require decisions about who should receive natriuretic peptide testing, echocardiography, and subsequent follow-up. The guideline does not establish a validated case-finding strategy for selecting individuals from the much larger cardiometabolic-risk population. At scale, even selective testing could substantially increase investigations and referrals. The evidence is promising but incomplete. STOP-HF reduced a composite of asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction with or without HF and cardiovascular hospitalization, but increased cardiac investigations and did not significantly reduce HF alone. PONTIAC found benefit among 300 selected patients with diabetes and elevated NT-proBNP, before the widespread use of sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors for prevention. The RED-CVD trial showed increased detection of HF, atrial fibrillation, or coronary disease from 3% to 8% through proactive assessment of high-risk primary care patients, but whether this translate into better patient-outcomes is not yet established. Systematic case-finding for stage B is therefore not yet ready for widespread implementation in primary care. Future trials should compare targeted case-finding with contemporary preventive care, measuring symptomatic HF, hospitalization, downstream testing, patient burden, healthcare resource use and costs rather than diagnostic yield alone.

The ESC guideline introduces age-adjusted NT-proBNP thresholds above which chronic HF is considered more likely: 125, 250, and 500 pg/mL for patients aged under 50, 50–74, and at least 75 years, respectively. These are not stand-alone rule-out cut-offs: clinical suspicion may justify further assessment below them, particularly in patients with obesity or possible HFpEF. Higher thresholds improve specificity and reduce referrals, at the price of lower sensitivity. A UK diagnostic accuracy study involving 155 347 patients demonstrates this trade-off. Importantly, a threshold is also a service rule. Dutch general practice guidance uses a fixed NT-proBNP threshold of 125 pg/mL, with an abnormal electrocardiogram providing another route to echocardiography, while the UK guideline (NICE) recommends specialist assessment at 400 pg/mL and prioritizes values above 2000 pg/mL. A symptomatic 78-year-old with NT-proBNP of 300 pg/mL might therefore follow different diagnostic routes across these systems. The relevant outcomes include timely confirmation, missed HF, avoidable imaging and referral, and access for patients whose symptoms remain concerning despite lower peptide levels.

Assay choice and service access add complexity. General practitioners may receive test results for BNP rather than NT-proBNP from local laboratories, although the ESC age-adjusted thresholds apply to NT-proBNP. In our Amsterdam primary care study of 15 234 patients tested for suspected HF, NT-proBNP had better diagnostic performance than BNP, while individualizing thresholds using readily available characteristics offered only modest gains. An international Heart Failure Association survey found that 34.3% of respondents reported no community access to NT-proBNP testing and 40% lacked a pathway from an abnormal result to echocardiography and cardiology assessment. A test threshold cannot be evaluated independently of availability, waiting times, communication of results, and safety-netting. Prospective pragmatic studies should therefore compare complete diagnostic pathways rather than biomarker thresholds alone.

The ESC rightly calls for multidisciplinary, patient-centred HF care. Yet the guidelines necessarily frame collaboration around HF, whereas primary care must organize care around the person. In a Dutch primary care population aged 55 years or older, ∼98% of people with HF had multimorbidity. Parallel pathways for HF, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease may each improve disease-specific processes while collectively adding appointments, monitoring, and conflicting advice. The starting question is not who owns each HF task, but who coordinates the patient’s care. Shared records, explicit responsibility for medicines and deterioration, rapid access to specialist expertise, and a clear route back after referral matter more than a simple transfer of tasks.

Care models must also reflect how health systems differ. Dutch general practitioners coordinate specialist access and provide much chronic disease care, whereas patients in Germany can directly consult many office-based specialists. Studies in the Netherlands and Sweden suggest that patients managed predominantly in primary care are often older, have more comorbidities, and are more likely to have HFpEF than cardiology-managed populations., These are partly different clinical populations, not merely the same population treated in different locations. Of 19 multidisciplinary HF trials in a systematic review, only six recruited in the community and only two both recruited there and involved patients’ own primary care professionals. We need collaborative models designed and evaluated with community clinicians and patients from the outset, using outcomes that include quality of life, continuity, treatment quality, unplanned care, and workload as well as HF events.

The 2026 ESC guideline is right to move HF care upstream into prevention, outwards into the community, and across professional boundaries. But its wider ambitions require a wider evidence base: whom to investigate, which community diagnostic sequences work, and how to integrate HF treatment into the care of people with multiple conditions. These questions are health-system dependent and should be studied where care is delivered. As the scope of HF guidelines extends into general practice, primary care should help define the evidence and contribute to guideline panels from the outset, not merely deliver recommendations developed elsewhere.

medicine.title: Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid
medicine.abstract: Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated (n = 61), particularly CTX-M-15 (n = 53). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species (n = 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboring blaCTX-M-15 within a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-risk Escherichia coli clones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface.Wildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-risk Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli lineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely related K. pneumoniae ST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.
medicine.text:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among Enterobacterales (particularly Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter spp.) represents a major threat to human and animal health (, ). Resistance to expanded-spectrum cephalosporin (ESC) antibiotics is mainly driven by extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) and plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamases (pAmpC) (, ), which are frequently carried on mobile genetic elements that facilitate horizontal gene transfer and the dissemination of multidrug resistance ().

In the context of One Health, the epidemiology of ESBL- and pAmpC-producing Enterobacterales is shaped by multifaceted interactions among humans, domestic animals, wildlife, and the environment (). Antimicrobial use in human and veterinary medicine may select for resistant bacteria that subsequently spread through direct contact, food chains, water, and environmental contamination (). Consequently, ESC-resistant Enterobacterales are now widely detected not only in clinical settings but also in livestock, companion animals, food products, and natural ecosystems, reflecting the interconnected nature of resistance dissemination ().

Wildlife is increasingly recognized as an important component of the environmental ecology of AMR. By occupying the interface between natural and human-impacted environments, wild animals may acquire, maintain, and disseminate resistant bacteria across ecosystems. ESBL- and AmpC-producing Enterobacterales have been reported in numerous wild bird and mammal species worldwide, with migratory birds potentially contributing to long-distance dissemination of epidemic lineages and resistance genes (, ). Zoos represent another important interface where exotic animals, humans, and the environment interact, potentially facilitating the dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria through animal exchanges and conservation programs (). ESBL- and AmpC-producing Enterobacterales have been detected in zoo animals in several countries, with reported prevalences ranging from 12% to 32% (, ).

Despite growing evidence from Europe and Asia, genomic surveillance of ESC-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife remains limited in North Africa. In Algeria, studies have reported clinically important resistance genes, including blaNDM-5 and mcr-1 genes, in migratory birds and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales in wild boars (, ). However, the occurrence, population structure, and dissemination of ESBL- and pAmpC-producing Enterobacterales in wildlife remain largely unexplored (, ).

Here, we combined large-scale sampling with whole-genome sequencing to investigate the prevalence, genomic diversity, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-resistant Enterobacterales recovered from free-ranging and captive wild animals in Algeria. We further assessed the distribution of epidemic clones and resistance plasmids to better understand the role of wildlife in the environmental dissemination of ESC resistance within a One Health context.

Between October 2021 and June 2023, a cross-sectional survey was conducted in six Algerian provinces to investigate the occurrence of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) in wildlife. A total of 1,899 samples were collected from free-ranging wild animals (n = 1,521), captive animals housed in six zoological parks (n = 365), and zoo workers (n = 13) (; ) (). Free-ranging wildlife samples consisted primarily of freshly voided feces collected from migratory, sedentary, and breeding birds, together with terrestrial and marine wildlife (). Captive animal samples included feces from birds (n = 136), mammals (n = 195), and reptiles (n = 21), as well as environmental samples comprising enclosure water (n = 7) and food (n = 6) ().

Numbers of samples collected from the different ecological niches in Algeria and distribution of OXA-48-producing and ESC-resistant Enterobacterales

Results are from Mehidi et al. ().

pAmpC, plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase; ESBL, extended-spectrum β-lactamase; ESC-R Enterobacterales, extended-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales.

The zoos were chosen according to their geographic location (eastern, central, western Algeria). Across all participating zoological parks, antimicrobial agents were used exclusively for therapeutic purposes under veterinary supervision.

Fresh fecal samples from wild birds were collected using sterile swabs, while approximately 1–5 g of freshly voided feces from wild mammals were collected in sterile containers. Fresh fecal samples of captive animals were collected immediately after defecation, early in the morning, and before routine cleaning of each enclosure to minimize environmental contamination. Sampling was performed only once per enclosure to avoid duplication, and the number of fecal samples collected was limited to the number of animals present, with a maximum of five samples collected from enclosures containing five or more animals. For fish and sea urchins, intestinal contents were aseptically collected after dissection. For animals housed in tanks, such as crocodiles, fecal sampling was replaced by water sampling. Three water samples of approximately 500 mL each were collected from each tank before the addition of disinfectant, and additional environmental water samples were collected where applicable. Fresh excreta, and environmental water samples were collected using sterile containers. Between 50 and 100 g of food samples were collected using a sterile spoon and transported in a sterile container. Rectal peri-anal swabs from zoo workers were self-collected using Amies transport swabs (Oxoid, Algeria).

Samples were transported at 4°C and processed within 24 h at the Laboratory of Microbial Ecology, University of Bejaia. Fecal samples were enriched in 5 mL of Trypticase Soy Broth (TSB; Fluka, USA) supplemented with cefotaxime (8 μg/mL) and vancomycin (32 μg/mL), food samples (25 g) were homogenized in 225 mL antibiotic-supplemented TSB, and 50 mL of collected water was added to 50 mL of antibiotic-supplemented TSB. Samples were incubated for 18 h at 37°C. After enrichment, the samples were diluted 1:10, and 200-μL aliquots were plated onto MacConkey agar containing cefotaxime (8 μg/mL) and incubated for 18–24 h at 37°C. One representative colony per morphotype was selected and identified by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (MALDI Biotyper, Bruker, Hamburg, Germany).

Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by disk diffusion and broth microdilution using Sensititre panels (Thermo Fisher Scientific, France), which included 47 antimicrobial agents of clinical and veterinary relevance () (). Results were interpreted according to EUCAST clinical breakpoints (https://www.eucast.org/clinical_breakpoints) and the CASFM Veterinary Committee recommendations (https://www.sfm-microbiologie.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/CASFM_VET2021.pdf), where appropriate.

Susceptibility testing for 35 representative ESC-R Enterobacterales

EUCAST breakpoints are used unless indicated.

MIC interpretation according to EUCAST guidelines. unless specified: gray shading: resistant; underlined values = susceptible with high dosing; white: susceptible.

2016 E. coli isolate from Pigeons of Bejaia region.

Clavulanate at fixed concentration of 2 µg/mL; avibactam at fixed concentration of 4 µg/mL; tazobactam at fixed concentration of 4 µg/mL; relebactam at fixed concentration of 4 µg/mL; vaborbactam at fixed concentration of 4 µg/mL.

No current breakpoints in EUCAST guidelines.

Veterinary breakpoints were used (https://www.sfm-microbiologie.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/CASFM_VET2023.pdf).

Breakpoints for E. coli and C. koseri were used.

Tetracycline MIC ≤ 4 µg/mL for wild-type isolates.

E. coli breakpoints for uncomplicated urinary infections.

A dash (–) indicates that no EUCAST clinical breakpoint is available for the corresponding antibiotic.

Presumptive ESBL production was assessed by the double-disk synergy test using cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, and amoxicillin-clavulanate disks. Confirmation was performed using the ESBL NDP test and the NG-Test CTX-M MULTI lateral flow immunochromatographic assay (NG Biotech, France), which detects the five major CTX-M groups (groups 1, 2, 8, 9, 25), as previously described ().

Genomic DNA was extracted using the PureLink Genomic DNA Mini Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Sequencing libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra DNA Library Preparation Kit (NEB, Boston, MA, USA) with dual-index adapters and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 platform (2 × 150 bp). One representative K. pneumoniae ST17 isolate O100C1 was additionally sequenced using Oxford Nanopore MinION technology to obtain a complete plasmid sequence ().

Reads were assembled using CLC Genomics Workbench v12 (Qiagen). Genome assemblies were analyzed using the bioinformatics pipeline of the French National Reference Center for Antibiotic Resistance. The resistome was determined using an in-house script and an in-house reference database. The default thresholds were set at 80% sequence identity and 80% coverage. Sequence types (STs) were assigned according to the Achtman multilocus sequence typing (MLST) scheme. Genome assemblies were analyzed using an in-house BLASTn-based script, whereas raw reads were analyzed using ARIBA v2.14.6. MLST schemes were periodically updated using mlstdb v1.1.1. Plasmid incompatibility groups were determined using PlasmidFinder (https://genepi.food.dtu.dk/PlasmidFinder/). Virulence scores for K. pneumoniae isolates were determined using Kleborate (). Mutations within the quinolone resistance-determining regions (QRDRs) of gyrA, gyrB, parC, and parE were identified by comparison with the reference genomes of K. pneumoniae MGH78578 and E. coli MG1655 (, ). The ftsI and mrdA genes, encoding PBP3 and PBP2, respectively, were extracted from each genome assembly using BLASTn. Nucleotide and translated protein sequences were aligned using AliView software and the MUSCLE program (version 1.0.0.0). Contigs carrying carbapenemase genes were compared with reference plasmid sequences retrieved from GenBank to characterize their genetic environments and assess plasmid relatedness.

To investigate the dissemination of the predominant lineage, all publicly available K. pneumoniae ST17 genomes (n = 991) and their corresponding metadata were retrieved from Pathogenwatch (https://pathogen.watch/), and analyzed alongside the 27 ST17 genomes generated in this study. Core genome MLST (cgMLST) analysis was performed using chewBBACA (https://github.com/B-UMMI/chewBBACA) () with the scheme scgMLST629_S (629 loci) () downloaded from the Pasteur Institute and adapted for use with chewBBACA (). Allele calling at 95% sequence identity produced a cgMLST phylogenetic tree. The β-lactamases from these genomes were identified using ABRicate (https://github.com/tseemann/abricate) with the NCBI database. Phylogenetic relationships and associated metadata were visualized using Microreact (https://microreact.org/project/2WtTuCa6ovAQGXNUf2hnGW-st17) while publication-quality trees were generated with iTOL (Fig. 3 and 4).

Differences in ESC-R-E carriage rates between host groups were compared using Fisher’s exact test. A two-sided P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using online Medcalc software (https://www.medcalc.org/en/calc/fisher.php).

A total of 1,899 samples were collected between 2021 and 2023, including 1,521 samples from wild animals, 365 samples from captive animals, and 13 rectal swabs from zoological park staff (; ) (). Growth on cefotaxime-containing selective media was observed for 303 samples (16.0%), with higher recovery rates among captive animals (198/365, 54.2%) than free-ranging wildlife (105/1,521, 6.9%). Following antimicrobial susceptibility testing, 73 samples yielded expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) (3.9%). Seven isolates producing OXA-48-like carbapenemases had previously been characterized () and were not included in subsequent analyses focused on ESC resistance mediated by ESBLs and cephalosporinases.

The remaining 66 ESC-R-E isolates were obtained mainly from captive animals (47/365, 12.9%), followed by free-ranging wildlife (18/1,521, 1.2%) and one zoological park worker (1/13, 7.7%) (; ). These isolates belonged predominantly to Klebsiella pneumoniae (n = 33), Escherichia coli (n = 29), and, less frequently, Klebsiella quasipneumoniae (n = 2) and Enterobacter hormaechei (n = 2) ().

The seven previously characterized OXA-48-producing isolates were recovered from both free-ranging wildlife (n = 5; four E. coli and one K. michiganensis) and captive animals from the El Aouana Boudjeblida zoological park in Jijel (n = 2; E. coli) () (). In addition, two ESBL-producing isolates recovered from pigeons in Bejaia in 2016 (E. coli and K. pneumoniae) were included in subsequent comparative genomic analyses to investigate persistence of resistance lineages over time.

All 66 ESC-R-E isolates displayed a positive ESBL NDP test, confirming the presence of a cefotaxim hydrolyzing enzyme. The NG-Test CTX-M MULTI assay identified CTX-M enzymes in 61 isolates, whereas the remaining five isolates displayed a cephalosporinase phenotype.

Whole-genome sequencing confirmed that CTX-M enzymes were the dominant mechanism of ESC resistance. Among the 61 CTX-M-producing isolates, CTX-M-15 was predominant (n = 53), followed by CTX-M-27 (n = 5), CTX-M-1 (n = 1), CTX-M-2 (n = 1), and CTX-M-55 (n = 1) (; ). The two historical pigeon isolates from 2016 also carried blaCTX-M-15 (; ).

Plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamases were identified in four isolates, including blaCMY-145 (n = 2) and blaCMY-141 (n = 1) in E. coli, and blaDHA-1 in K. quasipneumoniae subsp. Quasipneumoniae (; ). Species-specific chromosomal β-lactamase genes were also detected, including blaSHV in all K. pneumoniae isolates, blaOKP-A and blaOKP-B variants in K. quasipneumoniae isolates, and blaACT variants in both E. hormaechei isolates.

All ESC-R-E isolates exhibited multidrug-resistant phenotypes, with resistance mainly involving penicillins, third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, aztreonam, aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones (). In contrast, most isolates remained susceptible to carbapenems, except for the previously characterized OXA-48-producing isolates () (). All isolates remained susceptible to eravacycline, and all but one isolate were susceptible to colistin and the newly available β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations tested.

Whole-genome analysis revealed a marked predominance of a single K. pneumoniae lineage. Among the 35 Klebsiella spp isolates recovered, 27 belonged to K. pneumoniae ST17, and all carried blaCTX-M-15 (; ). ST17 isolates were detected across multiple geographic locations and host species, including captive mammals and birds, free-ranging wild birds, and one zoological park worker.

Most ST17 isolates originated from captive animals (22/27), particularly from zoological parks in Algiers and Jijel. Four isolates were recovered from free-ranging birds in the Bejaia region, while one isolate was obtained from a zoo worker. The close genetic relatedness among these isolates, together with their occurrence in different host categories, indicates circulation of a highly conserved ST17 lineage within wildlife-associated and zoological environments.

The ST17 isolates carried the capsule locus KL25 and O locus O5 but lacked major virulence-associated determinants, resulting in a Kleborate virulence score of 0 (). The short genetic distances observed within the ST17 cluster were consistent with recent diversification from a common ancestor rather than multiple independent introductions.

Other Klebsiella lineages were identified but occurred at lower frequency. ST29 isolates producing CTX-M-15 were recovered from a wild cattle egret and a captive fennec fox sampled approximately 240 km apart, suggesting circulation of related clones across geographically separated environments. Both possessed the capsule locus KL19, O locus O1, and the ybt14 yersiniabactin locus, corresponding to a Kleborate virulence score of 1 (). Additional STs, including ST219, ST323, ST348, ST584, and the high risk ST307, were detected sporadically and reflected greater diversity within the Klebsiella population. Of note, ST348 was identified in a Pigeon from 2016.

Isolates belonging to Klebsiella quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae and Klebsiella quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae formed distinct branches clearly separated from the K. pneumoniae clusters, as expected. (). The K. quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae ST2010 isolate produced DHA-1 and was recovered from a Barbary ground squirrel (Atlantoxerus getulus) in the Oran Zoo, while K. quasipneumoniae subsp. similipneumoniae ST414 isolate, produced CTX-M-15 and was obtained from a migratory white stork (Ciconia ciconia) in Bejaia.

BlaOXA-48 -producing strains formed a distinct but phylogenetically restricted cluster (). These included isolates from a black-headed gull (Chroicocephalus ridibundus; ST88), a Barbary macaque (Macaca sylvanus; ST2674), and a common house martin (Delichon urbica; ST1621). Four ST13 isolates formed a highly homogeneous subcluster, consistent with recent clonal dissemination. Three isolates from yellow-legged gulls (Larus michahellis) carried the ybt17 (ICEKp10) and clb3 loci (Kleborate virulence score = 2), whereas one isolate from a black-headed gull harbored ybt10 (ICEKp4) without clb (score = 1). The remaining OXA-48 producers lacked these virulence determinants (score = 0). A nearby ST2787 isolate clustered with this group (; ). Despite belonging to different STs, OXA-48-producing strains showed strong phylogenetic relatedness, suggesting recent emergence through plasmid-mediated acquisition of blaOXA-48 within established lineages rather than independent clonal expansion.

Overall, the phylogeny indicates polyclonal dissemination of ESBL-producing Klebsiella strains, contrasting with the more recent clonal or oligoclonal emergence of OXA-48 producers. These findings highlight the role of wildlife and anthropized environments in the circulation and evolution of antibiotic-resistant Klebsiella within a One Health framework.

To investigate the genetic basis underlying the successful dissemination of CTX-M-15-producing K. pneumoniae ST17, hybrid genome sequencing was performed on representative isolate O100C1. The complete genome consisted of a 5,157,420-bp chromosome and three circular plasmids. The largest plasmid, designated pO100C1, was a 212,580-bp IncFIB(K) plasmid carrying a multidrug resistance region containing blaCTX-M-15 together with additional resistance determinants, including blaOXA-1, blaTEM-1, catB3, qnrS1, sul1, dfrA12, aac (3)-Iia, aph (6)-Id, aph(3″)-Ib, aadA2, aac(6′)-Ib-cr, and mph(A) genes (). The plasmid also contained multiple insertion sequences and transposable elements, including the ISEcp1- blaCTX-M-15 -Tn3 module, suggesting acquisition and mobility of the resistance region.

To determine whether the genetic environment of blaCTX-M-15 was conserved among ST17 isolates, Illumina contigs carrying blaCTX-M-15 from the remaining ST17 isolates were compared with pO100C1. All isolates contained sequences corresponding to the same multidrug resistance region, including the ISEcp1- blaCTX-M-15 -Tn3 module and adjacent resistance-associated elements. Furthermore, read mapping against the complete pO100C1 sequence demonstrated coverage across the entire plasmid backbone in all ST17 isolates, indicating the presence of highly related IncFIB(K)-like plasmids within this lineage (data not shown).

The evolutionary relatedness of pO100C1 was investigated by comparison with publicly available IncFIB(K) plasmids from K. pneumoniae collected from different geographical regions, time periods and human clinical settings. The closest match was plasmid pGN4146-1, recovered from a human isolate in Guatemala in 2020 (215,412 bp; GenBank accession CP142061.1) (), which shared 99.99% nucleotide identity across the entire plasmid sequence. Another highly related plasmid, p1_6Gaza2023, recovered from a ST225 bloodstream isolate in Gaza in 2023 (209,339 bp; GenBank accession CP165004.1) (), shared 99.99% nucleotide identity across 96% of the pO100C1 sequence. These highly conserved plasmid backbones demonstrate that the IncFIB(K) plasmid lineage carrying blaCTX-M-15 gene is not restricted to a single bacterial sequence type and has circulated across geographically distant human and animal-associated settings.

Other IncFIB(K) plasmids associated with ST17 isolates, including pIso00199_01 from Ghana in 2016 (221,581 bp; GenBank accession CP095141.1) () and pKp2177_1 from Norway in 2008 (182,204 bp; GenBank accession CP075592.1) (), displayed lower overall similarity but retained conserved plasmid regions and resistance-associated modules. Comparative analysis using Clinker and Proksee confirmed that pO100C1, pGN4146-1, and p1_6Gaza2023 shared a highly conserved backbone organization, including the ISEcp1- blaCTX-M-15 -Tn3 region, whereas pIso00199_01 and pKp2177_1 represented more divergent variants of the same plasmid family ().

Our findings indicate that CTX-M-15 dissemination among K. pneumoniae ST17 in Algeria is associated with both expansion of a successful bacterial lineage and circulation of a conserved IncFIB(K) plasmid backbone. The detection of closely related plasmids across human isolates from different continents and a wildlife-associated isolate from Algeria suggests long-term maintenance and international dissemination of this resistance platform across diverse ecological settings.

K. pneumoniae ST17 is considered a globally distributed, opportunistic MDR lineage that is particularly associated with healthcare settings and neonatal intensive care units (). To place the Algerian K. pneumoniae ST17 isolates into a global context, a cgMLST analysis was performed using 991 publicly available ST17 genomes together with the 27 ST17 genomes generated in this study (). The global ST17 population showed extensive geographic diversity and was predominantly composed of human-associated isolates. The Algerian ST17 isolates formed a highly related cluster, consistent with recent local expansion within wildlife-associated and zoological environments.

Despite their local clustering, the Algerian isolates were genetically related to ST17 isolates recovered from human sources across different continents, indicating that the lineage shares a common global population structure. Together with the identification of closely related IncFIB(K)-CTX-M-15 plasmids, these findings support the circulation of successful K. pneumoniae ST17 lineages across diverse ecological compartments, including human, captive animal, and wildlife-associated settings ().

Whole-genome phylogenetic analysis of the 29 ESBL/AmpC-producing Escherichia coli isolates revealed substantial genetic diversity, with isolates distributed among six phylogroups (A, B1, B2, C, D, and F) (; ). Phylogroup A was predominant (12/29), followed by phylogroups D (8/29) and F (6/29), whereas phylogroups B1 and C were less frequently represented. The phylogenetic structure reflected multiple patterns of dissemination, including localized expansion of successful lineages and the independent acquisition of resistance determinants among genetically diverse backgrounds.

Several clonal groups were repeatedly detected across different hosts and geographic locations. The ST38 lineage (n = 6; phylogroup D) was identified in both captive and free-ranging animals from Bejaia, Jijel, and Setif. Five isolates carried blaCTX-M-15, whereas one carried blaCTX-M-27. Despite variation in ESBL content, these isolates formed a closely related cluster, supporting dissemination of a common genetic background associated with multiple resistance determinants (; ). Importantly, a CTX-M-15-producing isolate recovered from pigeons in Bejaia in 2016 clustered with the ST38 isolates identified in the present study, suggesting persistence of this lineage in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems over several years. These findings indicate that the dissemination of CTX-M-15-producing E. coli in Algeria involves not only acquisition of resistance genes but also the maintenance and spread of successful bacterial lineages adapted to diverse ecological settings.

The CTX-M-27-producing ST457 lineage (n = 4; phylogroup F) was exclusively recovered from captive mammals housed in zoological parks located in Bejaia and Oran, separated by approximately 642 km. These isolates formed a compact phylogenetic cluster, supporting interregional dissemination potentially driven by animal movements, zoo management practices, or shared environmental sources. Additional recurrent lineages included ST10, identified among captive animals at the Oran zoological park, and ST540, detected in a wild boar and a yellow-legged gull from Bejaia. The presence of different ESBL variants (CTX-M-15 and CTX-M-279) within closely related ST540 isolates highlights the contribution of horizontal gene transfer to resistance diversification.

Several internationally recognized high-risk clones were also identified. The ST361 lineage (n = 3; phylogroup A) provided another example of inter-host distribution. Two CMY-145-producing isolates were recovered from yellow-legged gulls in Bejaia. The third isolate, producing CTX-M-15, originated from a Barbary ground squirrel (Atlantoxerus getulus) at the Oran zoological park. Despite differences in β-lactamase content and host origin, these isolates were closely related, illustrating the ability of successful E. coli lineages to acquire diverse resistance determinants across ecological settings (). Two additional high-risk clones, ST167 and ST410, although these were represented by single isolates were identified ().

Several sporadic clones belonging to distinct phylogroups further highlight expanded genetic diversity. These isolates belonged to diverse sequence types, including ST1303, ST1722, ST1727, ST2334, ST354, ST5708, ST6448, and ST7937, recovered from different captive and free-ranging hosts. Their phylogenetic separation suggests multiple independent introductions of resistant E. coli lineages rather than expansion of a single dominant clone. Together, these findings demonstrate that ESBL-producing E. coli circulating in Algerian wildlife-associated environments comprise a genetically diverse population shaped by both clonal dissemination and repeated acquisition of mobile resistance determinants (; ).

Because amino acid insertions in PBP3 (e.g., YRIN and YRIK) in E. coli have been associated with reduced activity of aztreonam/avibactam and, in some isolates, decreased susceptibility to cefiderocol, particularly when combined with additional resistance mechanisms such as β-lactamase production or porin alterations, PBP3 sequences were analyzed. Three isolates carried these insertions: one ST410 isolate harbored the YRIK insertion together with the A413V substitution, while two ST361 isolates carried the YRIN insertion in combination with the Q227H, E349K, and I532L substitutions. The most common PBP3 variant, detected in 14 of 29 isolates, comprised the D149E and I332V substitutions (; ).

To assess the relationship between animal-associated ESBL-producing isolates and carbapenemase-producing E. coli, genomes available from a previous project (PRJNA1242567) () were incorporated into the phylogenetic analysis. Several carbapenemase-producing lineages, including ST38, ST131, ST227, ST540, and ST1135, clustered near ESBL-producing animal isolates, suggesting shared genetic backgrounds and the potential for resistance diversification through acquisition of mobile β-lactamase genes. These observations further support the role of wildlife-associated and anthropized environments as interconnected settings where successful E. coli lineages and resistance determinants can circulate. Of note the ST38 isolate that produced OXA-48 without CTX-M-15 clustered very closely to the CTX-M-15 producing isolates ().

Overall, the phylogenetic analysis revealed a complex population structure encompassing localized clonal expansion, interspecies transmission, and interregional dissemination across phylogroups A, B1, B2, C, D, and F. These findings underscore the importance of wildlife, zoological parks, and other anthropized environments as interconnected ecological reservoirs driving the evolution and dissemination of multidrug-resistant E. coli within a One Health framework.

Two isolates belonging to the Enterobacter cloacae complex were identified during this study. The first isolate, Enterobacter hormaechei subsp. steigerwaltii ST88, was recovered from a Senegal parrot (Poicephalus senegalus) housed at the Algiers zoological park and carried the β-lactamase gene blaLAP-2 (). The second isolate, Enterobacter hormaechei subsp. hormaechei ST269, was isolated from bat guano collected in Bejaia, and carried the β-lactamase gene blaCTX-M-15. Although uncommon in this collection, these isolates demonstrate that β-lactamase-producing members of the E. cloacae complex circulate across distinct wildlife-associated environments, including captive animals and free-ranging wildlife ().

The emergence of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) in wildlife and captive animals highlights the increasing complexity of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dissemination beyond healthcare and agricultural settings. Although ESBL-producing Enterobacterales have been extensively studied in humans, livestock, and companion animals (), their ecology in wildlife remains insufficiently characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In this study, ESC-R-E were detected in both free-ranging wildlife and captive animals in Algeria, with markedly higher carriage rates (P-value < 0.05) among captive animals (13.5%) than free-ranging wildlife (1.6%). These findings suggest that zoological environments, where animals, humans, and anthropogenic inputs intersect, may represent important ecological compartments for the maintenance and circulation of clinically relevant resistance determinants.

CTX-M enzymes were the predominant mechanism of ESC-R, consistent with their global expansion among human, veterinary, and environmental Enterobacterales. In Algeria, previous studies have reported ESBL- and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales in wildlife and domestic animals, including detection of clinically important genes, such as blaCTX-M-15 and blaOXA-48 (, ). Our findings extend these observations by demonstrating that CTX-M-producing Enterobacterales circulate across multiple wildlife-associated settings and involve diverse bacterial hosts. The widespread presence of blaCTX-M-15 genes is highlighted by their occurrence in various Enterobacterales species, including E. coli (n = 29), Klebsiella sp. (n = 35), and E. hormaechei (n = 2).

Unlike what was shown for the 29 OXA-48-like producers (), where 13 were E. hormaechei subsp. hoffmannii isolates, belonging to ST145 (11 isolates) and ST286 (two isolates), here only one E. hormaechei subsp. steigerwaltii ST88 producing LAP-2 β-lactamase and one E. hormaechei subsp. hormaechei ST269 producing CTX-M-15 were found. Of note, these STs are rare in clinical settings.

The predominance of CTX-M-15-producing K. pneumoniae ST17 was one of the most notable findings of this study. Unlike what was found for OXA-48 producers with 4/9 STs belonging to ST13 (), here 27 of the 34 K. pneumoniae isolates belonged to ST17, and all carried blaCTX-M-15. ST17 has been reported worldwide, predominantly from human clinical settings, and is increasingly recognized as a successful multidrug-resistant lineage responsible for hospital outbreaks, prolonged intestinal colonization, and increasingly, hypervirulence (). Classical ST17 strains are generally not considered “hypervirulent” in the traditional sense like K1-ST23 strains (). However, many ST17 (>53%) isolates carry yersiniabactin siderophore loci, capsule loci such as KL25, and O-antigen type O5, known to enhance colonization and pathogenicity (). Here, the ST17 clone carries the KL25 and the O5 capsular loci but lacks the yersiniabactin siderophore, suggesting lower virulence.

The high genetic similarity of Algerian ST17 isolates recovered from captive animals, free-ranging birds, and a zoo worker suggests circulation of a conserved lineage within a shared ecological context. The genomic success of this ST17 lineage appears to be supported by acquisition and maintenance of a conserved IncFIB(K) plasmid carrying blaCTX-M-15. Comparative analyses demonstrated that the plasmid identified in this study belongs to a globally distributed IncFIB(K) plasmid family associated with CTX-M-15-producing K. pneumoniae (, ). The high nucleotide identity observed with plasmids recovered from human isolates from geographically distant regions indicates that this resistance platform has circulated internationally for several years. The conservation of the ISEcp1-blaCTX-M-15-Tn3 resistance module despite variation in accessory plasmid regions suggests that this element represents a stable platform for dissemination of ESBL resistance among successful K. pneumoniae lineages.

In contrast to the predominance of a single K. pneumoniae lineage, ESBL-producing E. coli isolates displayed substantial population diversity. Nevertheless, several internationally distributed high-risk clones were identified, including ST38, ST167, ST361, and ST410. These lineages are frequently associated with multidrug resistance and acquisition of clinically important β-lactamase genes, including blaCTX-M-15 and carbapenemase determinants (). Two ST361 and one ST410 had 4 AA insertions in PBP3, which may lead to reduces susceptibility to cefiderocol and aztreonam/avibactam (). Indeed, for isolate ST361 O108B7 and isolate ST410 O100E9, aztreonam/avibactam MICs of 4 and 16 µg/mL were found respectively. The detection of these clones in wildlife-associated environments suggests that successful human-associated lineages may circulate beyond clinical settings and interact with diverse ecological compartments.

Among these lineages, ST38 was particularly notable because it was detected across different hosts and geographic locations and has previously been associated with extensive acquisition of resistance determinants, including blaOXA-48 gene (, ). In this study, CTX-M-producing ST38 isolates were recovered from both captive and free-ranging animals, indicating circulation of this lineage in Algerian animal-associated environments. Whether these isolates represent recent introductions from anthropogenic sources or long-term maintenance within environmental compartments remains unknown and requires longitudinal genomic surveillance. Importantly, a closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST38 isolate was already detected in pigeons from the Bejaia region in 2016, suggesting persistence of this lineage in Algerian wildlife-associated environments over time. Of note, in a previous study, one ST38 producing OXA-48 isolate was already found but displayed a different resistome without blaCTX-M genes.

Wild species, adaptable to diverse environments, move between natural habitats and human-modified areas, increasing direct and indirect interactions with humans and livestock (). Although wildlife is increasingly recognized as an important component of the AMR ecology, the precise contribution of wild and captive animals to human exposure remains difficult to quantify, particularly in LMICs (). Wild animals may acquire resistant bacteria through contact with contaminated environments, food chains, human activities, or other animals, while migratory species may contribute to long-distance movement of resistance determinants. The trafficking of wild animals from regions with high MDR prevalence to less affected areas further exacerbates this phenomenon (). Zoological parks represent additional interfaces where animal exchange, human contact, and environmental contamination may facilitate persistence and circulation of resistant bacteria.

Overall, this study demonstrates that ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, including internationally successful K. pneumoniae ST17 and E. coli high-risk clones, circulate in wildlife-associated and zoological environments in Algeria. The detection of conserved resistance plasmids and bacterial lineages shared with human-associated populations highlights the interconnected nature of AMR dissemination across ecological compartments. Integrated One Health surveillance combining genomic epidemiology of humans, animals, and environmental sources will be essential to better understand transmission pathways and to design effective strategies for limiting the spread of antimicrobial resistance.

K. pneumoniae ST17 contributes substantially to the global burden of multidrug-resistant infections, although susceptible isolates lacking acquired resistance determinants have also been described (). Our findings further support the central role of plasmid-mediated evolution in the ecological success of this lineage. Comparative genomic analyses indicate that the blaCTX-M-15 carrying plasmid identified in the representative ST17 isolate belongs to a family of closely related IncFIB(K) plasmids that has circulated internationally for at least 15 years. While some members of this family remain nearly identical despite their recovery from different continents, others display more divergent plasmid architectures while retaining a highly conserved multidrug resistance module centered on the ISEcp1-blaCTX-M-15-Tn3 transposition unit. This observation suggests that diversification has mainly resulted from the acquisition, loss, and rearrangement of accessory regions rather than extensive modification of the resistance backbone. Such an evolutionary pattern is consistent with previous comparative genomic studies showing that IncF plasmids possess conserved conjugative backbones while acting as dynamic platforms for homologous recombination and horizontal acquisition of accessory resistance determinants, thereby promoting their persistence and dissemination among successful K. pneumoniae lineages (). Furthermore, the identification of this IncFIB(K) plasmid lineage in a captive wild mammal, together with the occurrence of closely related ST17 isolates in captive animals and a zoo keeper, extends its known ecological distribution beyond the human clinical setting and supports the hypothesis that zoological environments may constitute overlooked reservoirs contributing to the long-term maintenance and international dissemination of both the ST17 lineage and its associated epidemic IncFIB(K) plasmids within a One Health framework.

medicine.title: Design, click synthesis, and biological evaluation of novel uracil-1,2,3-triazole hybrids as dual EGFR/CDK1 inhibitors: antiproliferative activity, mechanistic insights, and in silico studies
medicine.abstract: A novel series of uracil–1,2,3-triazole hybrids was designed, synthesized, and evaluated as dual EGFR/CDK1 inhibitors to target cancer cell proliferation and survival. Synthesis was initiated via the nucleophilic substitution of 2-chloro-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-pyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (3) with sodium azide, yielding the key intermediate 4. Subsequent copper-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloadditions (CuAAC) with various terminal alkynes and 1,3-dicarbonyls afforded the target triazole analogues 6a,b, 8a–c, and 10b,c. In vitro antiproliferative screening against a panel of four human cancer cell lines (MCF-7, HT29, PANC1, A549) and one normal cell line (Vero) identified compound 10a as a potential candidate. Compound 10a exhibited potent dual inhibitory activity, with IC50 values of 0.082 µM and 0.131 µM for EGFR and CDK1, respectively; it was about 2.4-fold less potent than erlotinib against EGFR but about 4.8-fold more potent than roscovitine against CDK1. Mechanistically, 10a induced significant G0/G1-phase cell-cycle arrest (74.89% versus 60.04% in control) and increased apoptotic cells (early plus late apoptosis, 13.55% versus 1.16% in control) in HT29 cells, accompanied by upregulation of Caspase-3 and BAX, with a rise in Bcl-2 whose significance remains to be established. Molecular docking predicted that 10a can occupy the ATP-binding pockets of both EGFR and CDK1, and normal-mode analysis (iMODS) suggested that the docked complexes are structurally plausible. Computational ADMET profiling, however, flags several liabilities for 10a, including predicted hepatotoxicity, low predicted oral absorption and a short predicted half-life. These findings highlight the uracil–triazole scaffold, specifically compound 10a, as a promising starting point for the development of targeted dual EGFR/CDK1 anticancer therapeutics.
medicine.text:
Researchers have recently shown a great deal of interest in 1,2,3-triazoles and their derivatives. That is related to the utility of the former molecules in a variety of synthetic methods and have a wide range of possible pharmacological effects, including anticancer, antibacterial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory, anti-Alzheimer, antidiabetic, anti-oxidant activities.

Protein kinases, such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and the cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) including CDK1, play critical roles in cancer progression and drug resistance, and efforts have been made to regulate their activity in the treatment of cancer. The regulation of a number of important protein kinases, including the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and the cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) such as CDK1, is important for cancer progression and therapeutic resistance and has been targeted for cancer treatment. Single-target anti-cancer drugs can effectively treat the disease in the beginning, but their clinical efficacy is soon curtailed by drug resistance and cellular pathway compensation. The challenges have been overcome with a high likelihood of success by employing multi-targeting therapy. This will take the form of simultaneous inhibition of multiple kinase pathways by using hybrid molecular scaffolds to target EGFR and CDK networks simultaneously, successfully suppressing multiple, overlapping aspects of tumor growth and survival at once. In conclusion, multi-kinase inhibition provides a more powerful, long-lasting and effective anticancer effect than single-target inhibitors. Recent EGFR-inhibitor studies continue to highlight both the therapeutic value and the resistance liabilities of this target.

The hybrid compound I () was the most effective and highly antiproliferative hybrid with 50% growth inhibition concentration (GI50) of 25 nM. Furthermore, compound I was a very potent inhibitor of the EGFR enzyme with an IC50 of 73 nM and seemed to be a good candidate to efficiently induce apoptosis in cancer cells.

It was found that compounds IIa and IIb () were among the most potent synthesized agents; compound IIb particularly emerged as a potent antiproliferative agent, and a dual inhibitor of both EGFR and BRAFV600E. This compound has been identified as a potent inhibitor of the cell cycle of cancer cells at the G1 phase by biological analysis, which helps to inhibit the growth of tumor cells. In the study on pyrimidine-benzotriazole derivatives, III () was proved to be the most promising and potent multi-kinase inhibitor. The molecular docking study revealed that the triazole group within III was crucial to form the critical hydrogen bond and favorable π–π interaction with the ATP binding pockets of CDKs. This allowed the compound to attain strong CDK inhibitory activities in the nanomolar range. In addition, in vitro and in vivo studies showed that III was highly inhibitory to the proliferation of cancer cells, colony formation and cell cycle progression. It was also able to significantly inhibit the growth of human tumor cells with a daily oral administration of 20 mg kg−1 in an SiHa xenograft mouse model without apparent toxicity. 1,2,4-Oxadiazole linked 1,2,3-triazole IV () was reported as potent modulator of the EGFR/PI3K/mTOR signaling cascade. Compound IV proved to be one of the most active derivatives in the evaluation against A549 lung cancer and Caco-2 colon cancer cell lines. Compound IV was found to be the most effective inhibitor of PI3K, mTOR and EGFR and to cause strong upregulation of the tumor suppressor protein p53 in A549 cells. It also showed high levels of multi-kinase inhibition and high levels of activation of p53 in the Caco-2 cell line. In addition, molecular docking studies showed that compound IV has a higher binding affinity to the EGFR active site compared to the gefitinib reference drug, in agreement with its proposed mechanism of action. Compound V () was found to be the most active derivative. It showed notable antiproliferative activity against breast, liver, and colon cancer cell lines with IC50 values of 5.1, 5.02 and 6.6 µM, respectively.

Interestingly, compound V was the most active towards EGFR (IC50 = 0.25 µM) showing equipotency with the reference drug erlotinib. In addition, it exhibited as the highest in vivo anti-tumor activity in mice, demonstrated by molecular modeling of its docking inside the proper and stable active site of EGFR. Interest report indicated that compound VI () exhibited high cytotoxicity in breast cancer (MCF-7) and lung cancer (A549) cell lines with IC50 value of 6.70 µM and 20.49 µM respectively, higher than the standard agent lapatinib. This was followed by the induced fit docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation of 300 ns which also demonstrated the high stability of B-4 with EGFR within a biomimicking environment, confirming that compound VI as a potent targeted EGFR inhibitor and apoptosis inducer. The selenium nanoform of pyrimidine derivative, compound VII (), proved to be the best dual inhibitor in this series. It showed an outstanding anti-proliferative effect in various cell lines (MCF-7, HepG-2, A549 cells) and was more than 93% effective than its non-nano equivalent. Highly active in inhibiting CDK1 with an IC50 of 0.47 µM, enzymatically. The pyrimidine core was found to be well docked in the ATP binding pocket of CDK1 through molecular docking. These results give a very pertinent structural context to consider the introduction of pyrimidine or new uracil scaffolds into dual-acting anticancer drugs.

Aly et al. described the design, synthesis, and antiproliferative activity of uracil-based compounds and also 1,2,3-triazoles as possible dual inhibitors of EGFR and BRAFV600E.

The design strategy used in this study is based on a binary-target inhibition approach, combining structural elements of two clinically validated kinase inhibitors roscovitine (a CDK1 inhibitor) and erlotinib (an EGFR inhibitor) in the same chemical scaffold that can simultaneously bind to both the CDK1 and EGFR active sites (). The purine core was simplified from roscovitine to maintain CDK1 recognition and its flexible hydroxymethyl-linker side chain was modified, maintaining key hydrogen-bonding interactions. The quinazoline-aniline pharmacophore necessary for binding with the EGFR was retained in erlotinib as a bioisosteric framework, and systematic substitution at the terminal aryl/heteroaryl group was performed to optimize the binding affinity and selectivity. The two pharmacophoric fragments were then merged together and elaborated to produce five different series (I–V; compounds 3, 4, 6a,b, 8a–c, and 10a–c; respectively) containing different groups that were structurally different to investigate different bioisosteric replacements and effects of substituents at the point of hybridization. The rational hybridization strategy aimed to result in dual acting antiproliferative compounds that were capable of blocking both cell-cycle progression by inhibiting CDK1 and proliferative signaling by inhibiting EGFR with the aim of achieving binary-function inhibition.

This study outlines a two-step synthetic pathway for the preparation of 2-azido-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (4) starting from 6-amino-1,3-dimethyl-pyrimidine-2,4(1H,3H)-dione (1). The overall scheme demonstrates the functionalization of a pyrimidine core, a common scaffold in medicinal chemistry, to introduce an azide group, which is a versatile handle for further chemical modifications, particularly in biorthogonal reactions such as click chemistry.

The initial step involved the reaction of 6-amino-1,3-dimethylpyrimidine-2,4(1H,3H)-dione (1) with 2-chloroacetyl chloride (2). This reaction was carried out under mild conditions, specifically in dimethylformamide (DMF) using an ice bath for 2 h (). The product obtained from this reaction was 2-chloro-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (3). This transformation is a classic example of N-acylation, where the amino group of compound 1 acts as a nucleophile, attacking the carbonyl carbon of 2-chloroacetyl chloride (2), followed by the elimination of hydrogen chloride. The use of an ice bath suggests that the reaction is exothermic or that side reactions are minimized at lower temperatures, ensuring selective acylation of the primary amine. The resulting chloroacetamide derivative (3) serves as a crucial intermediate, possessing an electrophilic chlorine atom that can be readily displaced by various nucleophiles. In the second step, the chloroacetamide derivative (3) was subjected to a nucleophilic substitution reaction with sodium azide (NaN3). The reaction was performed in DMF at 90 °C for 2 h, yielding 2-azido-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydro-pyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (4) in 75% yield (). This reaction proceeds via an SN2 mechanism, where the azide anion displaces the chloride ion from the α-carbon of the acetamide moiety. The introduction of an azide group is a significant synthetic maneuver. Azide functionalities are well-known for their utility in click chemistry. This makes compound 4 a valuable building block for synthesizing more complex molecules, including potential pharmaceutical agents or biochemical probes.

Subsequent synthesis of novel triazole-linked hybrid compounds 6a,b was achieved via a Copper(i)-catalyzed Azide–Alkyne Cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction, commonly known as Click Chemistry. This highly efficient and regioselective reaction serves to connect the pyrimidine-2,4-dione scaffold, previously functionalized with an azide group of 4 (), with the prepared alkyne-substituted benzoxazole and benzimidazole derivatives 5a,b. The key transformation in this scheme is the CuAAC reaction of 2-azido-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydro-pyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (4) with 5a,b. The reaction was performed in dimethylformamide (DMF) at room temperature for 20 h, utilizing sodium ascorbate and copper(ii) sulfate (CuSO4) to generate the active copper(i) catalyst in situ.

The azide group of 4 and the terminal alkyne group on compounds 5a,b are ideal partners for this [3 + 2] cycloaddition. The reaction proceeds with high regioselectivity, exclusively forming the 1,4-disubstituted 1,2,3-triazole ring. This triazole linkage acts as a stable and rigid linker between the two pharmacologically relevant moieties: the pyrimidine-2,4-dione and the benzoxazole/benzimidazole/benzothiazole systems. The characterization data, including 1H NMR, 13C NMR, mass spectrometry, and elemental analysis, confirmed the chemical structures of our new synthesized compounds 6a,b. All spectral data for synthesized products 6a,b clarify that they are formed from one molecule of terminal alkynes 5a,b and one molecule of 4 without any elimination. For example, 1H NMR spectral data of compound 6a was identified as 2-(4-((benzo[d]oxazol-2-ylthio)methyl)-1H-1,2,3-triazol-1-yl)-N-(2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydro-pyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide revealed seven singlet signals at δH = 3.18, 3.31, 4.71, 5.76, 8.06, 8.42, 10.58 ppm due to the two methyl groups, SCH2, NCH2, CH-5, triazole CH5 and NH groups, respectively. The 13C NMR spectrum revealed represented signals at δC = 26.6, 27.6, 29.7, 58.4, 89.0, 125.7, 141.3, 158.1, 161.5, 163.6, 189.4 ppm corresponding to 2 CH3, SCH2, NCH2, C-5, triazol C-5, triazol C-4, C-6, 2CO, 4CO and NHCO, respectively.

Then we sought for the preparation of novel 1,2,3-triazole derivatives 8a–c from uracil-containing azide precursor 4 and various alkyne derivatives 7a–c (). The starting material, 2-azido-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (4), features of uracil core substituted with an acetamide bearing an azide group. This azide functionality is crucial for the subsequent cycloaddition reaction. The reaction proceeds with the treatment of azide 4 with dimethyl but-2-ynedioate (DMAD) and its analogues 7a–c under reflux conditions in acetone.
