illustrates the synthesis of novel 1,2,3-triazole derivatives 10a–c featuring uracil moiety. This transformation involves the reaction of 2-azido-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydro-pyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (4) with various 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds 9a–c. The reactions were conducted in ethanol at 50 °C, in the presence of triethylamine (Et3N) as a base. Three different 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds were employed to demonstrate the versatility of this reaction. For compound 9a, pentane-2,4-dione (acetylacetone) was used, leading to the formation of product 10a. When ethyl acetoacetate (9b) was reacted with azide 4, compound 10b was obtained. Similarly, the reaction of ethyl benzoylacetate (9c) with azide 4 yielded compound 10c. The general structure of the triazolo–pyrimidine-acetamide derivatives 10a–c indicates the successful formation of the 1,2,3-triazole ring. The structures for all obtained products are fully consistent with their spectral data including 1H NMR, 13C NMR spectrum, mass spectrometry, in addition to and elemental analysis. To confirm our results, we choose compound 10a, which was assigned as 2-(4-acetyl-5-methyl-1H-1,2,3-triazol-1-yl)-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide. Mass spectrometry and elemental analysis for compound 10a indicate that it has the molecular formula of C13H16N6O4 with m/z 320, which indicate that it is the result of a combination between one molecule of 2-azido-N-(1,3-dimethyl-2,6-dioxo-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyrimidin-4-yl)acetamide (4) and one molecule of acetyl acetone (9a) with the elimination of one molecule of H2O. The 1H NMR spectrum for compound 10a showed seven singlet signals with chemical shifts at δH = 10.50, 8.00, 5.79, 3.34, 3.30, 3.10 and 2.26 ppm, which were assigned as NH, H-5triazol, CH2, NCH3, COCH3, NCH3 and CH3, respectively. The four methyl groups were further confirmed from their 13C NMR spectrum, which gave signals at δC = 29.7 (NCH3), 27.7 (NCH3), 26.9 (COCH3), and 10.0 ppm (CH3). The reactions under both types of conditions are regioselective, and the regioselectivity of this type is consistent with the precedent reported by Zeghada et al.

The proposed mechanism for the formation of compounds 10a–c through catalyzation of triethylamine (Et3N) during the condensation of an azide compound 4 with active-methylene 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds 9a–c, was based on an initially abstracting of the acidic methylene proton of the 1,3-dicarbonyl compound by Et3N to afford the resonance-stabilized enolate A. The carbon-centered enolate attacks the terminal electrophilic nitrogen of azide 4 with a proton transfer and tautomerization then generate a conjugated intermediate containing the three azide-derived nitrogen atoms and the two carbon atoms that become C4 and C5 of the triazole ring to form the cycloadduct 12. Et3N would then promote the subsequent proton-transfer and elimination steps. These dehydration reactions would then proceed in three steps: (i) a protonation at the keto carbonyl oxygen atom of 12, which corresponds to the most basic centers, (ii) an E1 elimination of water at the hydroxy group of the protonated intermediate 13, and (iii) a proton elimination at the vicinal C5 carbon atom of the formed intermediate 14 to re build the C4–C5 double bond of the enol, thus yielding the final 1,2,3-triazoles 10 ().

MTT assay was used to assess the viability of human cancer cell lines (MCF7, HT29, PANC1 and A549 cells) and the normal Vero cell line after 48 h incubation at the concentration tested. The synthesized compounds (3, 4, 6a,b, 8a–c and 10a–c) were tested for their in vitro anti-proliferative activity against four human cancer cell lines (MCF-7, HT29, PANC1, A549 cells) and one normal cell line (Vero cells) by cell viability assay, where doxorubicin was used as a reference drug ( and ). The results showed a wide range of cytotoxicity for the derivatives tested. Compound 3 turned out to be the most remarkably potent compound, showing broad-spectrum activity with a very high inhibition of cell viability in all cancer lines (e.g., 7.64% and 3.98% viability in MCF-7 and HT29 respectively). At the single screening concentration, compound 3 reduced PANC1 and A549 viability more than doxorubicin did. Moderate anti-proliferative profiles were observed in derivatives 6b, 8c and 10a with significant activity against PANC1 and MCF-7, respectively. On the other hand, the anti-cancer activity of compounds such as 8b and 10c was very low, with 10c showing an unfavorable anti-cancer activity in regards to normal Vero cells (6.23% viability). The overall average suppression of cancer cell viability across the four tested tumor lines, indicating the general descending order of potency of the synthesized compounds is: 3 > 6b > 8c > 10a > 10b > 8a > 4 > 6a > 10c > 8b.

Half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) is one of the most important parameters used to assess the cytotoxic activity of potential anti-cancer drugs; the lower the concentration of the drug required to inhibit the growth of half the population, the more potent the drug will be in terms of antiproliferative activity. The synthesized derivatives (3, 4, 6a,b, 8a–c, and 10a–c) were tested for their in vitro antiproliferative activity against four human cancer cell lines (MCF-7, HT29, PANC1, and A549) along with the normal Vero cell line, using doxorubicin as a standard chemotherapeutic drug standard. The results are summarized as half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50 in µM) in  and . Overall, the compounds showed a wide range of cytotoxicities. Compound 3 was the most effective broad-spectrum agent with relatively low IC50 values of 30.88, 74.89, 24.22 and 21.25 µM on the MCF-7, HT29, PANC1 and A549 cell lines, respectively. Notably, it was highly effective against PANC1 and A549 cells (IC50 = 24.22 and 21.25 µM), approaching the potency of doxorubicin (11.18 and 16.21 µM). In addition, a notable activity was found for compound 10c against the colon cancer cell line HT29 (IC50 = 9.38 µM) approaching the potency of doxorubicin (IC50 = 5.91 µM). It is interesting to note that 10c showed a much more favorable safety profile with low toxicity towards normal Vero cells (IC50 = 103.48 µM) as compared to doxorubicin (IC50 = 39.43 µM), giving a Vero/HT29 selectivity index of about 11, compared with about 7 for doxorubicin. Moderate to weak activities were also found with other derivatives, compounds 10a, 8c and 10b with moderate inhibition against MCF-7. In contrast, 8b was the least active against the cancer panel, and had high safety margins on normal Vero cells (IC50 > 190 µM), in addition to 4 and 8a. The general descending order of antiproliferative activity for the synthesized series is (based on the average IC50 values obtained on the four cancer cell lines): 3 > 6b > 10a > 10b > 10c > 8c > 6a > 8a > 8b > 4.

In vitro inhibitory activity of tested compounds 3, 10a, and 10c was studied using the standard reference drug erlotinib () that inhibits the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). As depicted in the data, all of the evaluated compounds exhibited good anti-EGFR activity with IC50 values in the sub-micromolar range. Compounds 10a was the most effective inhibitor of the series with an IC50 value of 0.082 ± 0.002 µM, approximately 2.4-fold less potent than the reference drug erlotinib with an IC50 value of 0.034 ± 0.001 µM. Compound 3 also demonstrated strong inhibitory activity with an IC50 of 0.116 ± 0.003 µM, compound 10c had the lowest relative activity of the three test compounds with an IC50 of 0.189 ± 0.005 µM. The results indicate that 10a is a sub-micromolar EGFR inhibitor, although less potent than erlotinib, and is presented as a starting point for structural optimization rather than as an equipotent EGFR agent.

Synthetic compounds were found to be EGFR inhibitors and also tested against Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 1 (CDK1) with roscovitine as the reference compound (). To the credit of the three compounds tested 3, 10a, and 10c, all showed better inhibitory activity against the CDK1 enzyme than did the reference compound. As in the previous work, compound 10a was found to be the most active derivative in this assay, with an excellent IC50 value of 0.131 ± 0.004 µM, approximately 4.8-fold more potent than roscovitine (IC50 = 0.624 ± 0.029 µM). Compound 3 also showed outstanding activity with IC50 value of 0.163 ± 0.000 µM. Moreover, all the least active compound in this series, 10c (IC50 = 0.463 ± 0.017 µM) was able to beat the reference drug. These results indicate sub-micromolar CDK1 inhibition across the series, with 10a the most active member. As only a single wild-type enzyme was tested, these data do not establish selectivity or cellular CDK1 inhibition.

The expression of important apoptotic markers (Caspase-3, Bcl-2 and BAX) were also analyzed in order to elucidate the underlying apoptotic mechanisms of the tested compounds in HT29 cells. IC50 and fold change of casp-3, BcL2 and BAX for 1,2,3-triazole/pyrimidine-2,4-dione hybrids 3, 10a, and 10c were as shown in  and . It was found that compound 10c is the most potent modulator among the agents tested to the assay as well as showed significant dose-dependent upregulation of these proteins. At its IC50 concentration (9.38 µM), 10c increased both the pro-apoptotic enzymes Caspase-3 (3.02-fold) and BAX (2.47-fold) when compared with the untreated control. Apparent is that this pro-apoptotic signal was accompanied by a 16.67-fold increase in the protein Bcl-2, which is anti-apoptotic, the origin of which is unknown; it may reflect a compensatory survival response, but oxidative stress was not measured. Compounds 10a and 3 also induced Caspase-3 and BAX less strongly: 1.92- and 1.93-fold for 10a at its IC50 (88.74 µM), and 1.79- and 1.89-fold for 3 at its IC50 (74.89 µM). Overall, caspase-3 was the most consistent apoptotic marker across compounds, with 10c the strongest inducer. Because Bcl-2 rose more than BAX, the BAX/Bcl-2 ratio (calculated from the mean values) decreased relative to control for all three compounds (for 10c from about 85 to about 13), so an intrinsic-pathway mechanism cannot be inferred from these markers; caspase activity and cleaved-caspase or PARP immunoblots are required.

The results indicated that compound 10a was associated with accumulation at the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle, with the proportion of cells in the G0/G1 phase increasing to 74.89%, compared to 60.04% in untreated control cells. The S-phase fraction decreased to 19.66% and the G2/M fraction to 5.45%, compared to 31.49% and 8.47%, respectively, in the control group. Consistent with this, compound 10a is associated with proliferation through G0/G1 accumulation. Because CDK1 mainly governs G2/M progression, G0/G1 accumulation is more consistent with suppression of EGFR-driven G1 progression ( and  and ).

The impact of compound 10a on cell death was evaluated through flow cytometry analysis, focusing on both apoptotic and necrotic stages in HT29 colorectal cancer cells. The results indicated that compound 10a induced cell death, with 3.61% of cells in the early apoptosis stage and 9.94% in the late apoptosis stage, giving 13.55% apoptotic cells in total. By comparison, untreated control cells exhibited minimal apoptosis, with only 0.91% in early apoptosis and 0.25% in late apoptosis, giving 1.16% apoptotic cells in total (3.76% when necrotic cells are included). Furthermore, necrosis was found to be higher in cells treated with compound 10a, with 3.87% of cells entering necrosis, compared to 2.60% in the control group. Thus, 10a increased the apoptotic fraction about 12-fold relative to control (13.55% versus 1.16%), with a smaller increase in necrosis (3.87% versus 2.60%) ( and  and ).

Molecular docking was used to predict plausible binding modes of compound 10a within the ATP-binding sites of EGFR (PDB: 1M17) and CDK1 (PDB: 4YC6). The docking protocol was first validated by redocking the co-crystallized ligands, erlotinib for EGFR and roscovitine for CDK1. The redocked poses reproduced the crystallographic conformations with heavy-atom RMSDs of 1.20 Å and 1.57 Å, respectively, both below the 2.0 Å threshold commonly used to judge pose reproduction ( and  and ).

Heavy-atom RMSD of the redocked co-crystallized ligand. C-Docker energies are per-residue interaction contributions (kcal mol−1). Length is the interaction distance in Å.

At the EGFR site, erlotinib gave an S score of −8.99 kcal mol−1, with a hydrogen-bond donor interaction to MET742 (3.56 Å) and a π–H interaction with CYS773 (3.75 Å). Compound 10a scored −6.64 kcal mol−1 and was predicted to retain the MET742 hydrogen-bond donor contact (4.00 Å) and to form a hydrogen-bond acceptor interaction with CYS773 (3.14 Å). It also made π–H contacts with LEU694 (4.36 Å) and CYS773 (4.60 Å). Its heavy-atom RMSD of 2.94 Å relative to the erlotinib pose indicates that 10a occupies a partly different region of the pocket than erlotinib, although it contacts the same key residues.

At the CDK1 site, roscovitine gave an S score of −7.23 kcal mol−1, with a hydrogen bond to ASP146 (2.91 Å), a π–H interaction with LYS130 (3.48 Å) and a π–π stacking interaction with HIS162 (3.97 Å). Compound 10a scored −6.78 kcal mol−1 and formed two hydrogen-bond donor contacts with ASP146 (3.21 Å and 3.31 Å), mirroring the hydrogen-bonding pattern of roscovitine, together with a π–H interaction with VAL18 (4.34 Å). Its heavy-atom RMSD of 1.70 Å relative to the roscovitine pose indicates a broadly similar binding orientation.

Docking scores are predictive only. The weaker EGFR score for 10a (−6.64 versus −8.99 kcal mol−1) is consistent with its weaker enzymatic inhibition (0.082 versus 0.034 µM for erlotinib). The CDK1 scores of 10a and roscovitine are close (−6.78 versus −7.23 kcal mol−1), whereas the enzyme assay shows about 4.8-fold greater potency for 10a (0.131 versus 0.624 µM). The docking model therefore does not explain the CDK1 potency difference, and the predicted binding modes require experimental confirmation.

Normal mode analysis (NMA) was performed with the iMODS server on both docked complexes (EGFR–10a and CDK1–10a). NMA models collective, low-frequency motions within an elastic-network approximation; it is not a molecular dynamics simulation and does not sample conformational ensembles over time. The molecular mobility and the structural dynamics of the docking complexes were calculated by using iMODS. iMODS is an online server that offers simple and flexible tools for the analysis of crucial dynamics, such as Eigen values, Variance, Covariance maps, B-factors and Elastic networks. The input files were the PDB files that were docked and submitted to the server and all parameters were left default until the results were displayed. iMODS uses Normal Mode Analysis (NMA) in combination with the coordinates of the docked complexes, to assess both the molecular motion and the structural flexibility of the biological macromolecules. The molecular motion and deformability are shown as colored arrows in every panel of , with two clusters showing the directionality of NMA motion for both the EGFR–compound 10a and CDK1–compound 10a complexes. Interestingly, the CDK1–compound 10a complex has a distinct large red arrow, suggesting a more prominent conformational motion at the global level than in the EGFR complex with more localized conformational motions of its domains. Each residue (Cα atom) in the protein chain is shown to be distorted in a unique manner, with the colored hinges indicating the distinct nature of the distortions that contribute significantly to the deformability of the complex (). In the case of the EGFR–compound 10a complex, the deformability values are fairly low and are relatively uniform for most of the residues (atom indices 0–260) with modest peaks generally located between residues 50–100 and 150–200. In contrast, the CDK1–compound 10a complex shows significantly stronger and more abundant deformability peaks throughout the sequence (from atom indices 0–320), indicating that compound 10a confers greater conformational flexibility on CDK1 as a whole. The server calculated the eigen values of 9.434286 × 10−6 for the EGFR–compound 10a complex and 1.313036 × 10−4 for the CDK1–compound 10a complex (). Compared with the EGFR complex, the first normal mode for the EGFR–compound 10a complex has a considerably lower eigenvalue, indicating that the overall structure of the complex is more flexible. The higher value for the CDK1–compound 10a signifies a more rigid and more restricted molecular system in the lowest mode. Furthermore, the individual variance contributions of the normal modes are shown in , where it is seen that the variance of each individual mode is inversely proportional to the eigenvalue. The first few modes of the low frequency modes contribute the largest percentage of variance (purple bars), and the cumulative variance (teal bars) quickly reaches 100% percent by the 6–8 modes, indicating that the most important modes of motion are well captured in the first few modes. The structural stability of docked molecules is shown in the B-factor plot () that compares the fluctuations observed in NMA with the B-factors from the experimental PDB structures (grey). The NMA-predicted B-factors for the EGFR–compound 10a complex show several large peaks, which are generally in good agreement with the crystal structures' experimental B-factors, indicating that the binding of compound 10a does not significantly alter the native flexibility profile of EGFR. In the case of the CDK1–compound 10a complex, the B-factors of NMA are larger, especially in the loop regions (residues 40–80 and 130–170). The PDB experimental data is similar, but less pronounced, as these regions of CDK1 are known to be dynamic, making it difficult to collect experimental data on them. C-Covariance Matrix: This is a colored display of correlated motions (red), uncorrelated motions (white) and anti-correlated motions (blue) in the covariance matrix (). The correlation map for the EGFR–compound 10a complex shows that there are several large off-diagonal blocks of red color for the positive correlations, while there are large blocks of blue color for the anti-correlation. This indicates that the structural domains of EGFR move in an opposite but coordinated fashion when compound 10a binds to it. However, the diagonal-dominant red pattern of the 10a covariance map suggests more localized domain-specific correlated motions, and correlates more strongly with the bilobal architecture of CDK1. The elastic network model () signifies that the Cα atoms of the docking protein are connected by elastic springs of varying strength, with darker grey spots corresponding to stronger and firmer springs between pairs of atoms. The contact map for the EGFR–compound 10a complex reveals a widespread network of strong contacts, especially in the central active site region (residues 100–200), which is a reflection of the structural rigidity of the compound 10a at the active site region. The elastic network shows tight firm contacts around the N terminal lobe (0–100) and weaker, but still important contacts around the C terminal lobe (101–299) in the case of the CDK1–compound-10a complex. This is typical of the contact distribution observed within the CDK1 kinase pocket, and shows that compound 10a can be stably docked in the CDK1 binding pocket of both target proteins. Together, the NMA results indicate that the docked complexes are mechanically plausible in the normal-mode approximation. Stability over time was not assessed; a conventional MD simulation of at least 100 ns is required for that purpose and is listed as future work.

The identification of a promising therapeutic candidate requires not only potent biological activity but also favorable pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles, collectively described as ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) properties. In recent years, several computational platforms have been developed to predict these parameters and facilitate early-stage drug discovery. Among these, ADMETlab 3.0 has emerged as a widely utilized and reliable web-based tool for evaluating the pharmacokinetic behavior of potential anticancer agents.

Accordingly, the ADMET profile of compound 10a was assessed using ADMETlab 3.0. The radar plot indicates that 10a satisfies several drug-likeness rules (no Lipinski violations and no PAINS alerts), but it also shows several liabilities. However, the predicted topological polar surface area (TPSA ≈ 120.88 Å2) is high, which is generally associated with limited passive membrane permeability.

The predicted log P (−0.234) is low and predicted aqueous solubility (log S −1.442) is moderate. The predicted HIA and bioavailability score are both 0.0, Caco-2 permeability is weak (−4.945), and the predicted half-life is short (about 1.07 h). Importantly, the predicted hepatotoxicity (DILI 0.969; hepatotoxicity 0.612) is high and must be regarded as a serious liability. These in silico predictions do not establish a favorable pharmacokinetic profile; they identify the properties that future analogues must address ( and ).

This series of C-4′ triazole-substituted uracils delineates a clear relationship between structural modification, cellular fate, and dual EGFR/CDK1 inhibition. The chloroacetamide precursor, compound 3, exhibited aggressive, broad-spectrum cytotoxicity with only moderate enzymatic inhibition. This profile is consistent with, but not proven to arise from, nonspecific reactivity of the electrophilic chloroacetamide group; thiol reactivity and kinome selectivity of 3 were not measured, so compound 3 is treated here as a synthetic intermediate and mechanistic reference rather than a lead. Converting the azide into triazoles 6a,b narrowed this activity spectrum. The benzimidazole derivative 6b was more active than its benzoxazole analogue 6a, aligning with established trends in triazole-based kinase inhibitors although the structural basis for this difference was not examined.

The ester-functionalized triazoles 8a–c exhibited diminished potency (IC50 > 60 µM). A plausible explanation is that the polar ester groups increase the topological polar surface area and limit membrane permeability; this was not tested directly.

The most significant findings emerged from the 1,3-dicarbonyl derivatives. The 4-acetyl-5-methyl motif in 10a was the most active motif in this series, yielding sub-micromolar IC50 affinities for both EGFR (0.082 µM) and CDK1 (0.131 µM). Docking suggests that this substituent may engage the hinge region of the ATP pocket; this has not been verified experimentally. Replacing the 5-methyl group with a 5-ethoxy group (10b), or exchanging the 4-acyl for a 4-benzoyl aryl system (10c), severely compromised enzymatic activity. Interestingly, 10c demonstrated unexpected cytotoxicity selectivity against HT29 cells (IC50 = 9.38 µM) while sparing normal Vero cells (IC50 = 103.48 µM). The basis of this HT29 selectivity is unknown; it may reflect differences in cellular uptake, metabolism or target expression, and was not investigated further.

While 10a demonstrates highly potent enzymatic inhibition, its moderate antiproliferative IC50 values (58–150 µM) may reflect pharmacokinetic barriers, such as restricted passive diffusion, active P-glycoprotein efflux, or competition with high intracellular ATP concentrations. The G0/G1 accumulation and apoptosis observed in HT29 cells occur at micromolar concentrations close to the cellular IC50 and are consistent with, but do not demonstrate, engagement of EGFR or CDK1 in cells; compound stability, solubility and intracellular exposure were not measured.

The cytotoxic activity of the twelve synthesized uracil derivatives was assessed against A549 (lung adenocarcinoma), MCF-7 (breast adenocarcinoma), PANC-1 (pancreatic carcinoma), and HT-29 (colorectal adenocarcinoma) cell lines, alongside the non-tumorigenic Vero cell line as a normal cell reference, using the MTT colorimetric assay, with doxorubicin serving as the positive control. Cells were seeded at 1 × 105 cells per mL (100 µL per well) in 96-well plates and incubated at 37 °C/5% CO2 for 24 h to establish confluent monolayers. Following medium removal and washing, serial two-fold dilutions of each compound in RPMI-1640/2% FBS were added in triplicate for 48 h. MTT solution (5 mg mL−1 in PBS; BioBasic Canada Inc., 20 µL per well) was then added, and after 4 h of incubation, the formazan crystals were dissolved in DMSO (200 µL) and absorbance was recorded at 560 nm (ref. 620 nm). Cell viability was expressed as a percentage relative to untreated controls, and IC50 values were derived from dose–response curves using [GraphPad Prism. 8]. Morphological examination was performed in parallel to corroborate quantitative findings, with apoptosis identified by nuclear condensation and fragmentation, and necrosis by nuclear swelling and chromatin flocculation.

The inhibitory activity of the synthesized uracil derivatives against wild-type EGFR kinase was evaluated using the EGFR Kinase Assay Kit (BPS Bioscience, Cat. #40321) in a luminescence-based 96-well format, with erlotinib as the positive control reference inhibitor. Reaction mixtures (50 µL per well) were assembled by combining 5× kinase assay buffer (6 µL), ATP (500 µM, 1 µL), PTK substrate poly(Glu : Tyr 4 : 1) (50×, 1 µL), and water (17 µL), followed by the addition of 5 µL of each test compound solution. Reactions were initiated by the addition of recombinant EGFR (wild-type, 1 ng µL−1, 20 µL) and incubated at 30 °C for 40 min. Blank wells received 1× kinase assay buffer in place of enzyme. Kinase-Glo MAX luminescence reagent (Promega, 50 µL per well) was then added, and after 15 min at room temperature in the dark, luminescence was recorded using a microplate reader. Residual kinase activity was calculated relative to the enzyme-only control, and IC50 values were derived from dose–response curves using [GraphPad Prism.8]. All samples were tested in duplicate.

The inhibitory activity of the synthesized uracil derivatives against CDK1/CyclinB1 was evaluated using the CDK1 Assay Kit (BPS Bioscience, Cat. #79597) in a luminescence-based 96-well format, with roscovitine serving as the positive control reference inhibitor. Reaction mixtures (50 µL per well) were assembled by combining 5× kinase assay buffer 1 (6 µL), ATP (500 µM, 1 µL), 10× CDK substrate peptide 1 (5 µL), and distilled water (13 µL), followed by the addition of 5 µL of each test compound solution. Reactions were initiated by the addition of recombinant CDK1/CyclinB1 enzyme (∼1.0 ng µL−1, 20 µL) and incubated at 30 °C for 45 min. Blank wells received 1× kinase assay buffer in place of enzyme, and blank values were subtracted from all readings. Kinase-Glo MAX luminescence reagent (Promega, 50 µL per well) was then added, and after 15 min at room temperature in the dark, luminescence was recorded using a microplate reader set to luminescence mode. Residual CDK1 activity was calculated relative to the enzyme-only control, and IC50 values were derived from dose–response curves using [GraphPad Prism.8]. All samples were tested in duplicate.

The intracellular expression levels of the pro-apoptotic proteins Bax and Caspase-3, and the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2, were quantified in compound-treated HT-29 and MCF-7 cells using commercially available sandwich ELISA kits, following a common cell preparation protocol. Briefly, cells were seeded at 1 × 105 cells per mL (2 mL/plate) in 3.5 cm tissue culture plates and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h to form confluent monolayers, after which the growth medium was replaced with DMEM supplemented with 2% FBS containing two concentrations of each test compound (IC50 and IC50/10), with PBS-treated plates serving as controls. After 24 h of compound exposure, cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, detached by trypsinization, pelleted by centrifugation at 1000×g for 5 min, washed three times in pre-cooled PBS, resuspended in fresh PBS, and lysed by sonication; cellular debris was removed by centrifugation at 1500×g for 10 min and the clarified lysates were assayed immediately. For ELISA quantification, 100 µL of each standard or sample lysate was added to the designated wells of the 96-well plate and incubated for 80 min at 37 °C, followed by three washes with 1× wash solution (200 µL per well). Biotinylated detection antibody (100 µL per well) was then added and incubated for 50 min at 37 °C, followed by three washes, and Streptavidin-HRP working solution (100 µL per well) was subsequently added and incubated for 50 min at 37 °C, followed by five washes. TMB substrate solution (90 µL per well) was added and the plate was incubated for 20 min at 37 °C in the dark, after which the reaction was terminated by the addition of stop reagent (50 µL per well), converting the blue color to yellow. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader, and protein concentrations (ng mL−1) were interpolated from the respective standard calibration curves. Results were expressed as fold-change relative to untreated control cells.

HT29 cells were prepared using the COULTER DNA PREP Reagents Kit (PN 6607055) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Cells were first permeabilized with DNA PREP LPR solution (comprising nonionic detergents, saline, and stabilizers, with <0.1% potassium cyanide and <0.1% NaN3), and subsequently stained with DNA PREP Stain, consisting of propidium iodide (50 µg mL−1) and RNase Type III-A (4 KU per mL). DNA content was measured by flow cytometry using 488 nm excitation, with fluorescence emission collected between 560 and 680 nm, allowing the cell population to be resolved into G0/G1, S, and G2/M phases based on single-parameter DNA histograms. Prior to analysis, the instrument was calibrated with 10 µm Flow-Check Fluorospheres to maintain a half-peak coefficient of variation of ≤2% in the red fluorescence channel. All procedures were carried out at room temperature (20–25 °C), and reagents were stored at 2–8 °C between uses.

Docking was performed with MOE (2014.2) in standard-precision (SP) mode, and the S score reported in  is the Glide docking score in kcal mol−1. C-Docker energies were calculated and visualized in Discovery Studio Visualizer.

Compound 10a was drawn in ChemDraw (v22.2.0) and converted to 3D with LigPrep in Maestro (v13.4). Tautomers and ionization states were generated with Epik, and the structure was energy-minimized with the OPLS4 force field.

Crystal structures of EGFR (PDB: 1M17) and CDK1 (PDB: 4YC6) were obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank. Each structure was processed with the Protein Preparation Workflow (OPLS4): hydrogens were added and hydrogen-bond networks optimized, water molecules and heteroatoms other than the co-crystallized ligand were removed, and only the chain containing the bound ligand was retained. Restrained minimization was then performed with OPLS4.

Receptor grids were generated with the Glide grid module, centred on the co-crystallized ligand in each structure.

The docking protocol was validated by redocking erlotinib into 1M17 and roscovitine into 4YC6. Heavy-atom RMSDs between the redocked and crystallographic poses were calculated; values below 2.0 Å were considered successful reproduction ().

Flexible-ligand docking was performed in Glide SP mode, with Epik state penalties added to the docking score and penalties applied to non-cis/trans amide bonds. Partial-charge cutoff and van der Waals scaling for ligand atoms were 0.15 and 0.80, respectively. The top-scoring pose for each compound was retained for interaction analysis, which was performed in Discovery Studio Visualizer. Interactions were classified as hydrogen bonds (donor or acceptor), π–H, or π–π contacts, and distances are reported in .

Pharmacokinetic, physicochemical, drug-likeness, and toxicity properties of the most active compounds were predicted using the ADMETlab 3.0 online platform (https://admetlab3.scbdd.com/). Parameters related to absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity, and medicinal chemistry profiles were evaluated to estimate the druglikeness and pharmacokinetic behavior of the investigated compounds.

A series of uracil–1,2,3-triazole hybrids was successfully synthesized in this study via three click chemistry routes and were characterized completely by spectroscopic and analytical methods. Biological evaluation revealed that compound 3 is the most-broad antiproliferative agent and compound 10c is the most selective against the HT29 cell line of colon cancer, while compound 10a is the most potent dual EGFR/CDK1 inhibitor in the series, approximately 2.4-fold less potent than erlotinib against EGFR and about 4.8-fold more potent than roscovitine against CDK1. ELISA quantification of apoptosis markers showed that the active hybrids, and in particular 10c, upregulate Caspase-3 and BAX together with a larger rise in Bcl-2, so the apoptotic mechanism remains to be established. The findings show that the target compounds are associated with G0/G1 cell-cycle accumulation and increased apoptosis; these phenotypic observations are consistent with, but do not establish, dual EGFR/CDK1 targeting in cells. Molecular docking predicts that compound 10a can occupy the ATP sites of both EGFR and CDK1, and normal-mode analysis supports the structural plausibility of these complexes; experimental confirmation is required. Additionally, compound 10a shows several predicted pharmacokinetic and safety liabilities, including hepatotoxicity risk, low predicted oral absorption and a short half-life, which must be addressed in optimization. These results collectively suggest that the uracil–triazole hybrid scaffold is a viable chemical platform to develop dual-kinase targeted anticancer therapeutics, as compound 10a is a promising lead compound for further optimization, more comprehensive mechanistic studies, and in vivo evaluation.

medicine.title:
Cumulative barriers to healthcare access as a marker of health system
failure: evidence from a national study of people with diabetes in
Brazil
medicine.abstract:
To evaluate healthcare access barriers and their cumulative association with
clinical and economic outcomes among Brazilians with diabetes, focusing on
the primary care context and health inequalities.A weighted survey (n = 1843) was conducted in 2024 using a structured
questionnaire. The sample was weighted to match the Brazilian National
Health Survey, ensuring representativeness of public health system users. A
cumulative barrier score (0–8) was analyzed using Poisson regression
adjusted for sociodemographic and clinical variables.The primary barriers identified were difficulty scheduling appointments
(47.4%), medication unavailability (42.6%), and lack of supplies (39.4%).
The mean barrier score was 4.13 (standard deviation 2.80). A consistent
dose-response pattern showed that a higher cumulative barrier burden was
associated with increased emergency department visits, higher out-of-pocket
expenditures, and a greater prevalence of chronic complications (adjusted
prevalence ratio 1.05 per additional barrier; 95% confidence interval
1.04–1.07; p < 0.001). These impacts were more
pronounced among low-income individuals and those with type 1 diabetes.Healthcare access barriers are highly prevalent in Brazil and are
cumulatively associated with adverse clinical and economic outcomes. This
cumulative burden serves as a pragmatic marker for identifying high-risk
individuals and informs public health strategies to reduce health
inequalities and improve care delivery in primary care settings.
medicine.text:
Diabetes mellitus (DM) is one of the most prevalent chronic conditions worldwide and
poses significant challenges to health systems due to its high prevalence,
therapeutic complexity, and risk of complications. In 2023, over 540 million adults
were estimated to be living with DM globally, with projections indicating a
continued increase, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (). In Brazil, DM prevalence exceeds
10% of the adult population, representing a major public health concern that
requires effective prevention and management strategies (). Despite advances in care organization, including
primary health care expansion and provision of free medications and supplies through
the Unified Health System, structural inequalities in treatment access persist,
especially among socioeconomically vulnerable populations (,).

Multiple factors hinder access to DM care, including the unavailability of
medications and supplies, long waiting times, shortages of healthcare professionals,
financial constraints, and geographic barriers. These obstacles compromise
continuity of care and treatment adherence, increasing the risk of microvascular and
macrovascular complications such as retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and
cardiovascular events (-).

International evidence suggests that these barriers rarely occur in isolation;
instead, they tend to accumulate and interact, amplifying their impact on healthcare
utilization, direct costs, and clinical outcomes (). In Brazil, although inequalities in access to care
and medications have been described, national research evaluating the cumulative
impact of these barriers from a health systems perspective, particularly in primary
care, remains limited (,).

Given that primary health care is the main entry point and care coordinator for
individuals with DM, understanding how multiple barriers combine and influence
clinical and economic outcomes is essential for informing public policies and
strengthening healthcare delivery systems (,,).
Therefore, we aimed to identify and quantify barriers to DM treatment access in
Brazil and to evaluate their cumulative effect on clinical and economic outcomes
using a nationally representative, weighted sample, focusing on primary care.

This national cross-sectional study was conducted between July 1 and August 22, 2024,
to evaluate healthcare access barriers among adults (≥18 years) with
self-reported, physician-diagnosed DM. Participants from all five regions of Brazil
were recruited via an online structured questionnaire administered through the
Qualibest platform. After excluding incomplete or inconsistent responses, 1843 valid
questionnaires were available for analysis. Post-stratification weights based on
sex, age group, and region, according to the 2019 National Health Survey, were
applied to ensure the sample’s national representativeness of public health system
users. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and Brazilian regulations
(Resolution No. 466/2012). Institutional Review Board approval was obtained, and
written informed consent was secured from all participants.

Data were gathered with a 46-item closed-ended questionnaire encompassing
sociodemographic, clinical, and healthcare access factors. Clinical variables
included DM type, disease duration, comorbidities, and self-reported glycated
hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels. Healthcare access barriers were measured across
predefined domains, such as appointment scheduling, waiting times, healthcare
professional availability, financial barriers, and access to medications and
supplies. A cumulative barrier score was calculated by summing reported barriers for
each participant (range: 0–8). For analysis, the score was considered as both a
continuous variable and categorized into three levels: low (0–3 barriers), moderate
(-), and high (8 barriers). Main
clinical and economic outcomes included: experiencing multiple barriers (≥4),
high direct monthly healthcare expenditures (≥BRL 500.00 per month),
emergency service use in the prior 12 months, poor glycemic control (self-reported
HbA1c ≥8%), and at least one chronic DM-related complication (retinopathy,
neuropathy, nephropathy, diabetic foot, myocardial infarction, or stroke).

Descriptive analyses used weighted means and standard deviations (SD) for continuous
variables and frequencies/proportions for categorical variables. Associations
between cumulative barrier scores and study outcomes were evaluated using Poisson
regression with robust variance, yielding adjusted prevalence ratios (PR) and 95%
confidence intervals (CI). Models were hierarchically adjusted for sociodemographic
(sex, age, race/ethnicity, education, region, insurance status) and clinical
variables (DM type, duration, comorbidities, current treatment). Effect modification
was explored via interaction terms with key variables (e.g., income, DM type). All
analyses incorporated sampling weights and were conducted using R software (v.
4.3.0), with statistical significance set at < 0.05.

The weighted sample consisted of 1843 individuals with DM. Most participants were
female (58.3%), and the largest age groups were 30–59 (41.8%) and 65–74 (26.3%).
Most lived in the Southeast (46.7%) and Northeast (26.1%); 75.7% did not have
private health insurance. Type 2 DM was most common (74.6%). Sociodemographic and
clinical data are detailed in .

Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of the study population (n =
1843)

The most frequent barriers were difficulty scheduling appointments (47.4%),
medication unavailability in public pharmacies (42.6%), and limited access to
supplies (39.4%). Other barriers included transportation difficulties, financial
constraints, and long waiting times, indicating predominantly structural access
limitations (). The mean
cumulative barrier score was 4.13 (SD 2.80), with approximately one-third reporting
six or more barriers. In adjusted analyses, the absence of private insurance and
lower monthly income were strongly linked to a higher burden of barriers
(≥4). Individuals with type 1 DM and those with multiple comorbidities also
reported more barriers, indicating that both social and clinical vulnerability
increase access limitations ().

Prevalence of healthcare access barriers among individuals with diabetes (n =
1843)

Factors associated with multiple healthcare access barriers (≥4
barriers) among individuals with diabetes

A clear dose-response relationship was found between the cumulative number of
barriers and adverse outcomes (). Those with more barriers had higher emergency service use,
greater out-of-pocket healthcare expenditures, worse glycemic control (HbA1c
≥8%), and a higher prevalence of chronic complications. Each additional
barrier was independently associated with increased chronic complication prevalence
(adjusted PR 1.05; 95% CI 1.04–1.07; p < 0.001), supporting the
cumulative burden effect (). 
illustrates the dose-response relationship between the number of reported healthcare
access barriers (categorized as low, moderate, and high burden) and the adjusted PR
for high direct healthcare expenditures, emergency department use, poor glycemic
control (HbA1c ≥8%), and chronic complications. Estimates incorporate
post-stratification weights to ensure national representativeness.

Association between cumulative healthcare access barriers and clinical and
economic outcomes

Additionally, the impact of cumulative barriers varied by subgroup. Stronger
associations with adverse clinical and economic outcomes were seen among individuals
without private insurance, those with lower income, and patients with type 1 DM,
highlighting disproportionate effects on vulnerable populations.

This national study found a high burden of healthcare access barriers among adults
with DM in Brazil, with most participants reporting multiple concurrent limitations.
There was a consistent dose-response pattern: more barriers were associated with
higher healthcare utilization, higher direct out-of-pocket costs, and greater
prevalence of chronic complications. These data reinforce that barriers to care
often accumulate, amplifying their combined impact on health system functioning and
clinical outcomes. Our results are consistent with previous research linking limited
healthcare access to worse glycemic control and more complications in people with DM
(-).

While many prior studies focused on individual barriers, this study advances
understanding by adopting a cumulative approach. This aligns with established social
vulnerability and cumulative disadvantage frameworks, illustrating how multiple
structural and organizational barriers interact to exacerbate health inequalities
(-). The observed associations with
healthcare utilization are consistent with evidence that reduced primary care access
increases reliance on emergency services and overall healthcare costs (-). The greater barrier burden among those without
private insurance, with lower income, and with type 1 DM, along with stronger
associations with adverse outcomes, underscore the interplay of clinical complexity
and social determinants in DM care in Brazil (-). In
particular, the higher burden in type 1 DM may reflect the ongoing, intensive need
for access to insulin, specialized supplies, and multidisciplinary care, all
especially sensitive to systemic failures.

From a clinical and organizational perspective within primary care, these findings
suggest that assessing cumulative access barriers may offer a pragmatic supplement
to traditional risk stratification. Identifying individuals with high barrier
burdens can guide targeted interventions and individualized care planning,
especially in resource-constrained settings. Although the cumulative barrier score
used assumes equal weighting of domains, it remains a practical measure of overall
access burden in real-world conditions.

Some methodological considerations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional design
limits causal inference; reverse causality is possible, as those with more severe
disease may experience more barriers and require more healthcare. Use of
self-reported data may introduce measurement bias, particularly in clinical
variables such as HbA1c and complications. Online recruitment may have caused
selection bias, as participation required digital literacy and internet access,
potentially underrepresenting populations with the highest levels of socioeconomic
vulnerability and the most severe access barriers, possibly resulting in
conservative estimates. Future longitudinal studies could better assess causal
pathways, and additional research is needed to determine which barrier combinations
most affect outcomes, and whether reducing cumulative burden can yield measurable
health and cost benefits.

In summary, integrating assessment of access barriers into routine primary care could
enhance identification of high-risk patients. At the system level, strategies to
reduce structural barriers (e.g., improving medication availability and care
coordination) are essential for more efficient resource use and better outcomes,
particularly in socially vulnerable populations.

medicine.title: Mapping human genetic associations to drug targets in valvular heart disease: an integrative evidence synthesis
medicine.abstract: Valvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum.We retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741).We identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability.This genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies.Limburg Clinical Research Centre of UHasselt, Jessa and ZOL; British Heart Foundation; National Institute for Health and Care Research; UK Research and Innovation; European Research Council; Horizon Europe.
medicine.text:
Valvular heart disease (VHD), encompassing stenosis or regurgitation of the aortic, mitral, tricuspid, or pulmonary valves, is a significant public health issue, affecting approximately 74 million individuals across the globe. VHD causes significant cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide. In 2019, the Global Burden of Disease Study reported an estimated annual 164,000 deaths due to non-rheumatic VHD and 306,000 deaths due to rheumatic heart disease. Heart valve dysfunction can lead to haemodynamic alterations that manifest as chamber dilation and/or myocardial hypertrophy, secondary to volume or pressure overload. Without timely intervention, these changes can lead to heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation (AF), thromboembolic phenomena, and sudden cardiac death.,

Severe VHD disease is managed with surgical or transcatheter valve replacement or repair procedures in specialised centres., In the setting of global population ageing, morbidity and health care–associated costs attributed to VHD continue to rise, emphasising the critical need to identify molecular targets for pharmacological intervention.

Currently, there are no available medical therapies to prevent or slow the progression of VHD. Denosumab and Alendronic acid have failed on a randomised controlled trial to slow the progression of aortic valve (AV) calcification in patients with calcific aortic stenosis (AS). Similarly, statins, in isolation,, or in combination with ezetimibe, had no benefit on the progression of AS. A systematic review of randomised controlled trials showed that anti-inflammatory agents, namely corticosteroids, were ineffective at reducing the risk of heart valve lesions with acute rheumatic fever. Consequently, the latest World Health Organisation guideline for the management of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease does not endorse these agents.

Efforts to develop effective therapies remain hindered by incomplete understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenesis. The availability of low-cost sequencing platforms, and progress of statistical tools to generate inferences from genomic data, accelerated knowledge accumulation on the genetic associations of a multitude of common diseases, namely AS, mitral valve prolapse (MVP), and tricuspid valve disorders. Furthermore, information on bioactive molecules with drug-like properties, including protein sequencing, functional information and druggability status, is now available as open-source through the ChEMBL and Open Targets platforms. These tools offer substantial potential to advance holistic understanding of the molecular landscape of VHD, by improved identification of risk-associated genes and pathogenic molecular pathways. Moreover, they support the strategic prioritisation of emerging signalling pathways and distinct molecular targets for drug development and subsequent validation in clinical trials.

We have recently developed an evidence synthesis approach to cross-link publicly available data on genetic associations, drug targets and clinical evidence on drugs to accelerate identification of potential drug targets and drug repurposing opportunities. Among patients with AF, we were able to identify 613 unique drug compounds targeting 68 targets identified from known AF genetic associations. Of these, 21 of the drugs were present in guidelines for AF management, validating the discovery power of the approach. Furthermore, several drug repurposing opportunities were identified.

We aimed to apply our previous evidence synthesis approach and identify drugs targeting genes or associated pathways involved in the pathophysiology of VHD, utilising a combination of different bioinformatics platforms, and to describe the existing evidence support for the use of such drugs.

The study protocol was registered on PROSPERO: 2025 CRD420251071741. In brief, we searched and extracted evidence from publicly available databases in three steps according to the methodology described by Kukendrarajah et al:(i)Identification of genetic variants for VHD using the NHGRI-EBI Catalogue of human genome-wide association studies (GWAS Catalogue) and Ensembl;(ii)The annotated genes from the previous stage were run through the Open Targets platform to find potential drug targets. This step aimed to identify drugs interacting with the annotated genes, or encoded proteins thus providing insights for drug development;(iii)Confirmation and validation of the association between the identified drugs in stage ii and VHD was obtained through structured searches and review of evidence from MEDLINE and the ClinicalTrials.gov

Identification of genetic variants for VHD using the NHGRI-EBI Catalogue of human genome-wide association studies (GWAS Catalogue) and Ensembl;

The annotated genes from the previous stage were run through the Open Targets platform to find potential drug targets. This step aimed to identify drugs interacting with the annotated genes, or encoded proteins thus providing insights for drug development;

Confirmation and validation of the association between the identified drugs in stage ii and VHD was obtained through structured searches and review of evidence from MEDLINE and the ClinicalTrials.gov

We performed manual searches on GWAS Catalogue and Ensembl on the 15th of July 2026 utilising the following expressions: “valvular heart disease”, “heart valve disease”, “aortic valve disease”, “aortic valve stenosis”, “aortic stenosis”, “aortic valve calcification”, “mitral valve disease”, “mitral valve prolapse”, “mitral stenosis”, “tricuspid valve disease”, “tricuspid regurgitation”, and “rheumatic heart disease”.

The annotated genes obtained from the previous search were run through the Open Targets Platform on the 15th of July 2026: individual genes were queried one by one.

Finally, each of the identified drugs was run through the MEDLINE data base and ClinicalTrials.gov on the 15th of July 2026 for existing clinical on VHD effects providing support to the findings. The structured search strategy used for MEDLINE was: “[drug name]” AND (“mitral” OR “aortic” OR “Tricuspid” OR “pulmonary” OR “heart” OR “rheumatic”) AND (“valve” or “valvular”). On ClinicalTrials.gov (“mitral” OR “aortic” OR “Tricuspid” OR “pulmonary” OR “heart” OR “rheumatic”) AND (“Valve” OR “Valvular”) was entered in the “Condition or disease” field and the drug name in the “Intervention/treatment” field.

For Stage (i) we utilised genome wide association studies (GWAS) or other study designs available within the GWAS Catalogue or Ensembl EMBL-EBI providing information on genetic variants associated with VHD.

For stage (iii) we included published randomised controlled trials (RCTs), RCT protocols available on ClinicalTrials.gov, observational studies (case–control, drug safety registries) and laboratory studies providing information on the identified drugs and their impact on valvular heart disease. Evidence from clinical and laboratory studies on the identified drugs was classified according to three categories: (1) therapeutic potential, (2) preclinical and mechanistic cardiovascular effects, and (3) adverse cardiovascular effects.

Eligibility criteria for studies informing the third step of our approach were determined based on the population, intervention, comparison, and outcome (PICO) approach. The population of interest was: patients with VHD, or patients who are at risk VHD. Drugs identified in step ii were the intervention, and the comparator was any active comparator, or placebo, or standard treatment. Studies with no available comparator were also considered eligible.

The primary outcomes of interest were: a) development of VHD, defined as a composite, or any of the following individual components: AS, aortic regurgitation (AR), mitral regurgitation (MR), MVP, mitral stenosis (MS), and tricuspid regurgitation (TR); b) progression of VHD, as a composite or any of the abovementioned individual components, assessed as per each manuscripts protocol. Secondary outcomes included: heart failure hospitalisations, need for VHD intervention, and all-cause mortality.

This evidence synthesis used only publicly available, non-identifiable data from published studies and databases and did not involve direct participant recruitment or access to identifiable individual-level data. Therefore, institutional ethics approval and informed consent were not required.

We utilised the approach developed by Kukendrarajah et al. We systematically identified all genes associated with VHD, determined which existing drugs target these specific genes and summarised the available evidence regarding the efficacy of these drugs for treating VHD.

In Stage (i), information on genetic variants was extracted from the GWAS Catalogue and Ensembl. The GWAS Catalogue is a curated database of published GWAS linking genetic variants to human traits and diseases. It provides standardised, structured data on associations between genetic markers and complex phenotypes, along with study metadata. Ensembl is a genome browser and annotation platform, that can also provide information on phenotypes and associated genetic variants. Information on the original GWAS publication identification, sample size, chromosomal region, author reported and mapped/annotated genes was extracted. The original publications informing the findings on GWAS Catalogue and Ensembl were screened for data of interest from expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) and colocalisation, that could pinpoint further causal genes or drug targets of interest.

In Stage (ii) we extracted data from the Open Targets platform. This is an open-source database integrating >20 different public data sources with available data drug compounds and targets, diseases, phenotypes, and genetic associations. For each annotated gene in Stage i we extracted information on the location of the encoded proteins (subcellular location, and whether or not these are present in the heart), function/gene ontology, tractability and available drugs. For each drug, information on phase of development (I to IV), action type (agonist, antagonist, inhibitor, etc), drug target(s), disease/indication, status of drug development (N/A, completed, recruiting, withdrawn from market, discontinued) and presence of black box warnings was extracted.

Finally, for Stage (iii) we extracted information from studies identified via MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov: main study characteristics, patient populations, sample sizes, reported effect of the identified drugs (beneficial, neutral or harmful), maximum level of available evidence/type of available evidence, and effect estimates, and quality of evidence.

Microsoft Excel was utilised for data management. All searches and data extraction were conducted independently by SMF and RP, and any discrepancies were resolved with the help of a third referee (AC), when required.

The Cochrane's Risk of Bias V1 was utilised for RCTs providing evidence for VHD outcomes on drugs linked to targets, the Newcastle Ottawa-Scale was utilised for the appraisal of case–control studies, and the quality of genetic studies (Q-Genie) tool was used for Mendelian randomisation studies. Quality assessment was done by two researchers (RP & SMF), and disagreements between the two were resolved by consensus or via a third party (AC).

Data were extracted and reported in tables as per Kukendrarajah et al. No formal data synthesis/meta-analyses was conducted.

To prioritise targets, we applied a prespecified exploratory 10-point matrix spanning genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability. Mendelian randomisation, colocalisation, fine-mapping, and plasma pQTL evidence each scored 1.5 points; eQTL and disease-relevant cell-type expression each scored 1 point; and tractability scored 2 points for an existing drug, 1 for tractability evidence alone, and 0 otherwise. Mendelian randomisation and colocalisation were weighted highest for their complementary causal evidence, and plasma pQTLs above eQTLs given their closer proximity to pharmacological modulation.,, , , ,  The score was intended for hypothesis-generating ranking, not causal or clinical prediction.

Identified drugs were classified into three evidence tiers: therapeutic potential (at least one RCT with a pre-specified valve endpoint, or Mendelian randomisation evidence implicating the drug target in VHD, in a compound at phase ≥3); preclinical/mechanistic support (animal or cell-based data only, no valve-specific clinical endpoint); and safety signal (documented adverse cardiovascular effect with no countervailing therapeutic signal in VHD).

To further characterise the pathways associated with the identified targets, we conducted an exploratory, post-hoc Reactome analysis. Using the Reactome platform, we performed pathway identifier mapping, over-representation analysis, and expression analysis on the target list.

Analyses were descriptive. Results are presented as counts and percentages where appropriate, and effect estimates were reported as provided in the source studies. No formal meta-analysis was undertaken and no pooled effect estimates were calculated. The exploratory 10-point prioritisation matrix was used for hypothesis-generating ranking and was not intended as a statistical prediction model.

The funders had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, writing of the report, or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.

Our searches on GWAS Catalogue and Ensembl identified 1464 genetic associations, corresponding to 844 unique genetic variants, respectively (). Detailed information on cohort composition with detail on ethnicity and continent/country, as well as the genetic variants, directionality of effects (with effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals), with location, genetic annotation and reference of the GWAS is present in the Data Supplement. The majority of the cohorts included in this evidence synthesis were of European ancestry.

Of the 582 candidate genes identified in Open Targets Platform, 431 (74%) had tractability information. Of these, 51 genes had linked compounds (): 388 distinct pharmacological agents; 273 in phase 3/4 of clinical development. Of the 380 druggable genes with no linked drug compounds, 42 had high protein expression in the heart ( and ), underscoring a substantial gap between genetic discovery and therapeutic development. Proposed molecular pathways linked to annotated genes with available opportunities for drug repurposing.

Infiltration of circulating lipoproteins and their enzymatic cargo — including Lp-PLA2 (linked to LDL) and autotaxin (carried by Lp(a)) — is facilitated by shear stress-mediated endothelial injury

Hydrolysis of lysophosphatidylcholine by autotaxin yields lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), which activates NF-κB in VICs, driving osteoblastic gene expression and calcification

Interaction between Lp(a) oxidised phospholipids (OxPL) and VICs upregulates IL-6, amplifying the inflammatory microenvironment

Stimulation of adhesion and migration of macrophages secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines; OxPL-mediated TLR4 activation sustains NF-κB signalling

Promotion of VIC osteogenic differentiation via upregulation of RUNX2, BMP2, and ALPL; OxPL antibody blockade abrogates these effects

ABL1, a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, activates MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT signalling cascades, promoting VIC and vascular cell proliferation, survival, and migration

Downstream activation of mTOR-HIF1α promotes metabolic reprogramming; ABL kinases also facilitate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) relevant to VIC myofibroblast activation

ABCC9 encodes SUR2, the regulatory subunit of K-ATP channels; K-ATP channel activity regulates smooth muscle and VIC resting membrane potential, stress responses, and mechanosensing

Altered ABCC9 function may dysregulate intracellular signalling cascades governing VIC responses to haemodynamic stress in valve disease

SUR2/K-ATP channels modulate cardiomyocyte and vascular protection against ischaemic stress and inflammatory remodelling

ADAMTS5 is one of the most abundant proteases secreted by cardiac fibroblasts; it cleaves the chondroitin sulphate proteoglycan versican in the cardiac ECM

Accumulation of uncleaved versican in Adamts5-deficient mice impairs cardiac function and reduces cell–cell communication proteins; versican and versikine accumulate in ischaemic heart failure

β-1 adrenergic receptor stimulation (see ADRB1) increases versican expression, while β-blocker treatment reduces ECM versican deposition

GWAS implicated the ADAMTS protease family in cardiovascular diseases; ECM proteoglycan fragments generated by ADAMTS5 can act as DAMPs activating innate immune responses

β-1 adrenergic receptor (ADRB1) stimulation increases versican expression in cardiac fibroblasts; β-blocker treatment attenuates versican accumulation and reduces overall ECM deposition in ischaemic heart failure

Adrenergic signalling modulates cardiac fibroblast activation and collagen turnover, influencing valve ECM homoeostasis

Serum amyloid P component (APCS) is an acute-phase protein that activates complement and modulates innate immune responses; elevated APCS levels are associated with increased cardiovascular risk

APCS binds to chromatin, fibronectin, and other ECM components, potentially modulating ligand availability and inflammatory cell recruitment in valve tissue

SAP binds fibronectin, collagen, and laminin, influencing fibril organisation and protecting ECM components from enzymatic degradation

APOB encodes the main structural protein of LDL particles; rare protein-disrupting APOB variants conferring lifelong lower LDL-C are associated with substantially reduced risk of aortic stenosis

Higher LDL-C promotes lipid infiltration into valve interstitial tissue, oxidative modification, and subsequent VIC activation

Oxidised APOB-containing lipoproteins (oxLDL, Lp(a)) trigger TLR4 and NF-κB-mediated pro-inflammatory and pro-osteogenic cascades in VICs, upregulating RUNX2 and BMP2

CACNA1C encodes CaV1.2, the cardiac L-type Ca2+ channel; calcium influx through CaV1.2 activates calcineurin/NFAT and downstream RUNX2, driving osteogenic differentiation of VICs

CACNA1C genetic variants are associated with calcific aortic valve disease; CaV1.2 signalling regulates cell cycle progression and VIC mechanosensing responses to haemodynamic stress

CDK6 directly phosphorylates NF-κB p65 at Ser536, amplifying NF-κB transcriptional activity and inflammatory gene expression; CDK6 inhibition (PD332991/palbociclib) suppresses TNF-induced NF-κB activation and cytokine production

Aberrant CDK6 expression in diseased tissue contributes to chronic inflammation through NF-κB–dependent upregulation of cytokines and adhesion molecules

CDK8 is a transcriptional kinase of the Mediator complex that regulates super-enhancer-driven inflammatory gene programmes via NF-κB and STAT pathways

COL4A2 encodes type IV collagen α2, a critical component of vascular basement membranes; disruption of collagen IV network integrity impairs basement membrane function and promotes ECM disorganisation

ELN (elastin) is the primary structural protein of the ventricularis layer of the aortic valve; elastin fragmentation and disorganisation are hallmarks of AS progression

Reduced elastin content correlates with greater valve calcification and stiffening; elastin loss activates VIC myofibroblast differentiation and promotes osteogenic reprogramming

ENPP3 belongs to the ENPP ectonucleotidase family and hydrolyses extracellular nucleotides including ATP; the closely related family member ENPP1 is the primary generator of extracellular pyrophosphate (PPi), a potent inhibitor of calcium phosphate crystal deposition, and reduced PPi in aortic VICs is associated with acquisition of a calcifying profile

Dysregulation of ENPP-family nucleotide hydrolysis may alter the PPi/phosphate balance in the valve microenvironment, potentially influencing mineralisation

ENPP3 hydrolyses extracellular ATP on basophils and mast cells, limiting ATP-mediated inflammatory activation; adenosine generated by downstream nucleotide catabolism modulates macrophage inflammatory responses through A2A and A2B receptors, and purinergic tone may influence the valve inflammatory microenvironment

ESRRG (ERRγ) is an orphan nuclear receptor that activates genes involved in mitochondrial energy transduction and fatty acid oxidation in cardiac cells

ERRγ suppresses fibroblast activation gene programmes, maintaining VIC quiescence and limiting pro-fibrotic and pro-calcific responses

ESRRG induces cardiac hypertrophy via GATA4 activation; ERRα/γ double knockout disrupts cardiac maturation with persistent fibroblast signatures and VIC activation markers

FADS1 encodes Δ5 desaturase and FADS2 encodes Δ6 desaturase, the rate-limiting enzymes in ω-6 PUFA synthesis; the rs174547 variant at the FADS1/2 locus is associated with reduced AS risk (OR 0.91 per C allele)

Genetically elevated arachidonic acid (AA) levels and a higher AA:linoleic acid ratio are causally associated with increased aortic valve calcification via Mendelian randomisation

AA promotes VIC pro-inflammatory arachidonate cascade (COX-2/prostaglandins, leukotrienes), contributing to valvular inflammation and calcification; FADS1 expression is higher in calcified versus non-calcified valve tissue

FGF23 is the primary phosphaturic hormone regulating phosphate and vitamin D metabolism; Mendelian randomisation supports a causal effect of elevated FGF23 on CAVS risk

FGF23 augments phosphate-induced vascular calcification by promoting osteoblastic differentiation through ERK1/2 phosphorylation; FGF-23 and PTH are independently associated with aortic valve calcification extent in CKD patients

FGF23-FGFR signalling promotes cardiac fibrosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, and myofibroblast activation through paracrine mechanisms independent of renal effects

FN1 (fibronectin 1) is overexpressed in calcified aortic valve tissue; fibronectin is a core ECM glycoprotein secreted by VICs that promotes myofibroblast differentiation, valve thickening, and fibrosis

FN1 acts as a scaffold for growth factor binding and VIC adhesion; overexpression in calcified regions correlates with progressive ECM stiffening and osteogenic reprogramming

Soluble fibronectin fragments act as DAMPs, activating TLR4-NF-κB innate immune responses in valve endothelial and interstitial cells, amplifying the pro-calcific inflammatory milieu

FTO is an m6A RNA demethylase that modulates gene expression post-transcriptionally FTO variants are associated with aortic valve stenosis in a sex-specific manner with heterozygote advantage.

FTO suppresses STAT3 activation through m6A-dependent post-transcriptional regulation of pro-inflammatory interferon-stimulated gene expression; reduced FTO function may therefore augment STAT3-driven transcription of pro-inflammatory genes relevant to valve inflammation and calcification

HMGB1 is a DAMP that, once secreted, activates TLR4→JNK MAPK→NF-κB signalling, inducing high-level pro-inflammatory cytokine production in VICs; both HMGB1 and TLR4 are overexpressed in calcified aortic valves

TLR4 knockdown or JNK/NF-κB inhibition markedly reduces HMGB1-induced cytokine release and VIC mineralisation

HMGB1-TLR4-NF-κB axis upregulates osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP, osteocalcin) in VICs, promoting osteoblastic differentiation and calcium nodule formation

HMGB1 activates RAGE and NF-κB pathways to induce VEGF expression, promoting neovascularisation within valve lesions, which is associated with disease progression

HMGCR encodes HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis; Mendelian randomisation confirms HMGCR inhibition (statins) reduces LDL-C and is associated with protection against aortic vascular disease
