The main molecular mechanisms underlying CAVD are illustrated in .

The early phase of aortic valve disease features endothelial dysfunction and subendothelial lipid infiltration, progressing to inflammation, fibrosis and calcification.

Endothelium-dependent vasomotion is impaired early due to dysregulated endothelial nitric oxide (NO) synthase and increased nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate oxidase–derived reactive oxygen species in the valvular microenvironment. NO produced by valvular endothelial cells (VECs) maintains valvular homoeostasis by paracrine regulation of valvular interstitial cells (VICs). Indeed, it has been shown that endothelial-derived NO inhibits RUNX2 dependent calcification, at least in part by NOTCH1 activation. Studies have also demonstrated that NO depletion upregulates dipeptidyl peptidase-4 expression in VICs, disrupting autocrine insulin-like growth factor-1 signalling and promoting CAVD progression. Remarkably, a RCT showed that ataciguat reactivation of oxidised soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), the primary receptor for NO, slowed AV calcification, by reducing BMP2 signalling in VICs.

Endothelial dysfunction, triggered by shear and mechanical stress, promotes the uptake of lipids, which is linked to an inflammatory reaction that serves as a key initiating mechanism in the pathogenesis of CAVD. Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and Lipoprotein (a), Lp(a), are key risk factors for CAVD, with Lp(a) also accelerating disease progression.,,, Lp(a) is implicated in AS via its covalently linked oxidised phospholipids. In CAVD, the expression and activity of lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2 (Lp-PLA2) are upregulated, facilitating the conversion of oxidised phospholipids bound to Lp(a) into lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC). LPC is subsequently processed by autotaxin (secreted by VICs) to generate lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), which strongly promotes osteoblastic transition. Lp(a) interaction with ApoC-III promotes mitochondrial stress, increasing proinflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-6) and BMP-2 in VICs. Oxidised lipoproteins also increase ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 promoting the adhesion and migration of immune cells. These immune cells, particularly macrophages, secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), which promote endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT). Profibrotic effects are also mediated by local increase angiotensin II by infiltrated immune cells and increased angiotensin-converting enzyme originating from both LDL particles and VIC., Macrophage-released extracellular vesicles (EVs) also contribute to the progression from micro to macrocalcifications, by providing a scaffold for nucleation of calcium-phosphate crystals., ,  Sortilin, a multiligand sorting receptor linked to LDL metabolism, promotes EV-mediated calcification by promoting the incorporation of the tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP, encoded by ALPL) into extracellular vesicles. Once released, annexin-1 facilitates aggregation of EVs within the extracellular matrix (ECM), particularly in collagen-rich areas.

Finally, activated VICs (and infiltrated mast cells) contribute to neovascularisation through the secretion of pro-angiogenic factors such as Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) A, promoting further uptake of lipoproteins and immune cells.,

HMGCR encodes HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol biosynthesis; Mendelian randomisation confirms that HMGCR inhibition lowers low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and confers protection against aortic vascular disease, although randomised trials have failed to slow progression of established AS, suggesting additional pathways sustain the disease beyond LDL lowering., Similarly, PCSK9 mediates lysosomal degradation of LDL receptors, elevating circulating LDL-C; loss-of-function PCSK9 variants are associated with lower calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) prevalence, and PCSK9 inhibition reduces CAVS risk via LDL lowering and modest Lp(a) reduction. Notably, PCSK9 is expressed in calcified aortic valves and VICs upregulate its secretion under pro-osteogenic stimuli, with neutralising antibody treatment reducing in vitro VIC calcium accumulation independent of LDL-receptor effects.,, APOB, encoding the main structural protein of LDL particles, complements these findings: rare protein-disrupting APOB variants conferring lifelong lower LDL-C are associated with substantially reduced AS risk, and oxidised APOB-containing lipoproteins trigger TLR4/NF-κB-mediated pro-osteogenic cascades in VICs.

The Δ5-and Δ6-desaturase enzymes, encoded by FADS1 and FADS2 respectively, are central to polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism by catalysing conversion of linoleic acid (LA) to arachidonic acid (AA) and α-linolenic acid to eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). Genetic variations, within FADS1 and FADS2, have been linked to altered plasma levels of AA and LA. Mendelian randomisation suggest a potentially causal link between higher plasma AA, the product of the ω-6 pathway, and AS, with increased plasma ω-6 fatty acids associated with valve calcium.

The IL6 locus at 7p15.3 achieved genome-wide significance, with rs1800795, located in the promoter region of IL6, emerging as the most probable causal variant. This variant is associated with elevated expression of IL6 antisense RNA, modulating IL6 transcription. IL-6 upon binding to its receptor complex, activates JAK/STAT3 pathway and promotes transcription of pro-inflammatory and osteogenic genes (RUNX2, BMP2, ALPL), which play a central role in VIC activation and osteogenic transformation., Downstream activation MAPK and PI3K-Akt pathways promote cell survival, proliferation, and inflammatory mediator release.

CDK6 gene polymorphisms have also been associated to AS., The proposed pathophysiologic role of CDK6 in AS is linked to inflammation, via NF-κB p65 subunit phosphorylation, enhancing NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory gene expression that promotes VIC osteogenic transformation via RUNX2 signalling.,

The FTO gene encodes an m6A RNA demethylase that catalyses the removal of methyl groups from N6-methyladenosine residues on mRNA, thereby influencing transcript stability and translation. Recent evidence suggests that FTO modulates proinflammatory interferon-stimulated gene expression via transcription factor STAT3, establishing a potential link between epitranscriptomic regulation and valvular inflammation.

High-Mobility Group Box 1 (HMGB1) rs181753401 was identified as a locus associated with AS. as a locus associated with AS. During cell stress, injury, or death, HMGB1 translocates from the nucleus to the extracellular space and acts as an inflammatory mediator with cytokine-like properties. It binds to cell surface receptors such as TLR4, triggering the release of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that play a key role in VIC activation.

The main molecular mechanisms underlying mitral valve prolapse (MVP) due to myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) are illustrated in .

TGF-β signalling plays a pivotal role in the development and progression of MMVD., Under pathological conditions, TGF-β promotes transformation of quiescent VICs into activated myofibroblasts form (aVICs), which are responsible for ECM remodelling and fibrosis. In addition to VIC activation, TGF-β signalling induces EndMT, a process where VECs lose their endothelial characteristics and acquire mesenchymal traits. This transition further amplifies the pool of activated cells contributing to ECM disruption. This altered ECM is characterised by increased glycosaminoglycan accumulation, fragmented collagen, and disorganised elastin fibres, which contributes to the thickening and deformity of valve leaflets, hallmark features of myxomatous degeneration. TGF-β signalling can foster an inflammatory microenvironment by recruiting pro-inflammatory macrophages and driving immunogenic ECM remodelling, mirroring mechanisms seen in CAVD.

From a molecular point of view, TGF-β operates through both canonical and non-canonical pathways. The canonical route involves phosphorylation of Smad2/3 proteins, which then form complexes with Smad4 and translocate to the nucleus to regulate gene expression linked to fibrosis and cellular activation. Non-canonical pathways, including MAPK (ERK, JNK, p38) and PI3K/AKT signalling, also modulate cellular responses and often interact with the Smad-dependent mechanisms, enhancing the overall impact of TGF-β signalling.

BMPs are important members of the TGF-β superfamily and may also be involved in MMVD progression., ,  BMP activates canonical and non-canonical pathways. The canonical pathway is characterised by phosphorylation of intracellular Smad1, Smad5, or Smad8 proteins, which then form complexes with Smad4. These complexes translocate to the nucleus, where they regulate the transcription of genes involved in ECM production, cell proliferation, and myofibroblast differentiation. BMPs also activate non-canonical pathways, including MAPK cascades such as ERK, JNK, and p38, which further influence cellular behaviour and interact with Smad-dependent mechanisms.

Among the genes identified in GWAS, CTGF is the only one with available opportunities for drug repurposing. CTGF is a key regulator of fibrotic processes, known for its ability to activate myofibroblasts and drive ECM protein remodelling. TGF-β and BMP signalling pathways stimulate CTGF transcription, amplifying the fibrotic response and CTGF is markedly upregulated in human myxomatous mitral valves compared to non-myxomatous counterparts, underscoring its role in disease progression and structural degeneration.,

The main molecular mechanisms underlying rheumatic valve disease are illustrated in .

The pathogenesis of acute rheumatic fever and its progression to rheumatic heart disease is primarily driven by repeated infections with Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus (GAS). Two main immunopathogenic mechanisms have been proposed to explain how GAS infection leads to tissue damage. The first is the well-established theory of molecular mimicry, in which streptococcal antigens, particularly the M protein, share structural similarities with host cardiac proteins. This antigenic resemblance triggers an autoimmune response in which antibodies and T cells directed against the pathogen also target host tissues. The second, more recent theory involves the formation of neo-antigens. In this model, GAS penetrates the endothelial barrier and deposits M protein within the subendothelial collagen matrix, specifically binding to the CB3 region of type IV collagen. This interaction generates novel antigenic structures that elicit an autoimmune response against collagen.

Both mechanisms initiate a cascade of immune events beginning with the production of autoreactive antibodies, including anti-endothelial cell antibodies (AECA), and autoreactive CD4+ T cells., ,  AECA contribute to endothelial activation, upregulating adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1, which facilitate the infiltration of immune cells into cardiac tissue., ,  Complement activation follows, leading to cell lysis and further tissue injury. In damaged regions, structural proteins such as collagen, laminin, keratin, and tropomyosin are released and presented by antigen-presenting cells, including resident dendritic cells, monocyte-derived antigen-presenting cells, valvular fibroblasts, and endothelial cells aberrantly expressing MHC class II molecules., ,  This antigen presentation drives the expansion of autoreactive T-cell populations and promotes epitope spreading, broadening the immune response over time., ,

Among the genes identified in GWAS, cholecystokinin B receptor (CCKBR) and RHD are the only ones with available opportunities for drug repurposing. The molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. However, CCKBR is known to activate key intracellular signalling pathways, including the MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT cascades, and to modulate transcription factors such as NF-κB and CREB1, which play a key role in regulating cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, anti-apoptotic responses, and inflammatory signalling, all of which are central to the pathogenesis of chronic valvular inflammation and fibrosis.

Statins have been formally tested for AS progression, but four dedicated Phase 3 RCTs failed to demonstrate a significant effect on haemodynamic progression or clinical events,, , , and a trial in bicuspid aortic valve patients was similarly neutral. Attention has shifted to PCSK9 inhibitors, which lower LDL-C more potently and additionally reduce Lp(a). A post-hoc analysis of the FOURIER trial (n = 27,564) found evolocumab was associated with a potential reduction in AS events after the first year of treatment. Three Phase 3 RCTs now directly evaluate AS progression with PCSK9 inhibitors: alirocumab or evolocumab combined with atorvastatin; a PCSK9 inhibitor–statin combination in mild-to-moderate AS with cardiovascular disease or hypercholesterolaemia; and the PICASO trial evaluating tafolecimab. Among Lp(a)-targeting oligonucleotides, Pelacarsen is being evaluated in a Phase 3 RCT directly assessing AS progression in mild-to-moderate calcific AS, with additional cardiovascular outcome trials ongoing., Olpasiran showed a favourable AS safety profile across Phase 1 and dose-finding RCTs,, and a Phase 3 cardiovascular outcomes trial is underway, with post-hoc valve analysis a future possibility. Inclisiran is being evaluated in the Phase 3 ALFA trial in patients with moderate or severe aortic calcification, though without a dedicated valve endpoint.

Ziltivekimab is being assessed in the Phase 3 trials, ,  across inflammatory heart failure and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease populations; none specifies valve endpoints, but IL-6/IL-6R signalling is mechanistically relevant to AS-related inflammation and calcification. Additional IL-6R-targeting agents (levilimab, sarilumab, satralizumab, tocilizumab, and vobarilizumab) may also be relevant, and Mendelian randomisation data suggest genetically proxied tocilizumab is associated with reduced AS risk. The haemodynamic stress pathway has also been clinically explored: the BLAST trial evaluated bisoprolol for AS progression in mild-to-moderate AS with hypertension but was terminated before completion.

Preclinical data provide supporting evidence for several candidates. In vitro, pravastatin reduced myofibroblast activation and calcific nodule formation in valvular interstitial cells, suggesting pathway-specific anti-calcific effects not captured in clinical statin trials., Imatinib and becaplermin both target PDGF-B signalling, with imatinib partially reversing valve abnormalities in a murine PROX1-deficiency model. Conversely, nilotinib promoted VIC calcification and osteogenic activation experimentally, and a case report described rapid AS progression under nilotinib therapy, an important safety consideration for patients requiring tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.,

A summary of pharmaco-therapeutic randomised controlled trials evaluating medical therapies for primary VHD progression is provided in .

As an exploratory assessment of the complementary value of pathway-based analysis, the identified genetic targets were additionally analysed using Reactome for identifier mapping, pathway over-representation, and expression analysis. This generated thousands of pathway and interactor outputs and highlighted additional candidate therapeutic agents not captured by the primary pipeline, including icosapent ethyl, which is currently being evaluated in a randomised controlled trial for its ability to slow aortic valve calcification in patients with moderate aortic stenosis. Detailed curation and interpretation of these outputs were beyond the scope of this study; the complete results are provided as .

Quality appraisal of the clinical evidence is available as .

Despite decades of research, no pharmacological therapies have been shown to prevent or slow the progression of primary valvular heart disease. Management remains largely dependent on surgical or transcatheter valve replacement, and the pipeline for disease-modifying medical therapies is strikingly sparse.

To address this gap, we applied a genetics-informed evidence synthesis framework integrating data from the GWAS Catalogue, Ensembl, Open Targets, Reactome, MEDLINE, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Of 844 unique variants, 582 candidate genes were identified, of which 431 (74%) were druggable, yet only 51 had linked drug compounds, leaving 380 (88%) without active therapeutics. This marked attrition, from genetic association to drug availability, is the central finding: it maps the translational frontier of VHD pharmacology and identifies a substantial pool of genetically supported targets for future development. Hese findings highlight three hypothesis-generating areas for further investigation: (a) genetically supported targets currently lacking active compounds; (b) existing drugs that may warrant further evaluation as repurposing candidates; and (c) cardiovascular safety signals associated with some target-linked drugs that should be considered in future mechanistic and clinical studies.

Beyond the 51 genes with linked compounds, 42 druggable candidate genes encode proteins highly expressed in the heart but without associated therapeutics, representing a group of targets warranting further investigation. An important proportion of the identified drugs were originally developed as antineoplastic agents, reflecting an inherent bias in Open Targets toward well-characterised, already-drugged pathways. Nevertheless, 273 of 388 drugs are in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development and widely used clinically, making real-world evidence generation through electronic health records a practical next step. For agents in earlier development, VHD incidence and progression should be incorporated as pre-specified endpoints in future trials.

Among the drugs with clinical evidence of therapeutic potential, pelacarsen stands out as the most advanced candidate, with an ongoing Phase 3 trial directly evaluating whether Lp(a) lowering can slow the progression of calcific aortic stenosis; olpasiran represents a closely related option with existing cardiovascular outcome data. The strongest repurposing opportunities are concentrated in aortic stenosis, particularly around the Lp(a)/LPA and IL-6/IL-6R pathways. Evidence for myxomatous mitral valve disease, rheumatic heart disease, and tricuspid phenotypes remains more limited and mechanistically distinct, warranting independent investigation.

This study extends the evidence synthesis approach previously described by our group for atrial fibrillation, where 21 identified compounds were already present in management guidelines, confirming its generalisability across disease areas with available GWAS data. Genetic association with a disease-relevant pathway is a necessary but not sufficient criterion for repurposing candidacy; safety profile and the quality of clinical evidence must all be weighed alongside genetic support. Drugs with compelling genetic rationale but a prohibitive adverse cardiovascular profile are retained but not proposed as repurposing candidates.

Several limitations merit explicit discussion. This work represents a structured prioritisation of existing evidence to guide future drug development in VHD and was not designed for independent biological discovery or validation. GWAS signals identify statistical associations, not causal genes; mapping variants to the nearest gene without systematic fine-mapping can be misleading. To mitigate this, we integrated available functional data, fine-mapping, eQTL, plasma pQTL, colocalisation, and Mendelian randomisation results. Cell-type-specific expression in valvular cells is incompletely captured by bulk-tissue datasets. The Open Targets platform reflects a pharmacological landscape weighted toward oncology and inflammation; drug availability should not be conflated with biological relevance to VHD. Most available GWAS captured disease susceptibility rather than progression; a multi-trait GWAS on aortic valve function and progression has now been incorporated. Phenotypic misclassification and ancestry bias may have influenced gene prioritisation; study-level details are provided in the supplement. Sex-disaggregated genetic association and drug-response data were not consistently available across the source datasets, and no sex-based analyses were therefore performed. Consequently, this study could not assess potential sex-specific differences in genetic associations, target prioritisation, therapeutic effects, or adverse cardiovascular signals. The prioritisation matrix was exploratory: its prespecified weights were not derived from VHD-specific outcomes, and partly overlapping evidence sources may not be statistically independent. Rankings should therefore be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. Furthermore, the prioritised targets and pathways were not subjected to independent biological validation, and the predominance of genetic and clinical evidence for AS limits the generalisability of these findings to other valvular phenotypes, for which the evidence base was substantially more limited. Finally, the exploratory Reactome analysis generated thousands of additional pathway and interactor outputs that were beyond the scope of curation in this study; systematic human curation of these findings represents an important direction for future work to further expand the therapeutic landscape identified here.

This genetics-informed evidence-synthesis approach identified 14 drugs with clinical evidence of therapeutic potential and 8 with preclinical cardiovascular support for VHD, while 380 of 431 druggable targets (88%) remain without linked compounds, highlighting substantial untapped therapeutic potential. Drug repurposing opportunities were predominantly concentrated in aortic valve disease and aortic stenosis, whereas evidence for myxomatous mitral valve disease, rheumatic valve disease, and tricuspid phenotypes was more limited. Most available drugs targeting the annotated genes were originally developed as antineoplastic agents, further highlighting the lack of therapies specifically designed for valvular disease. Further research is needed to bridge this translational gap, clarify the role of the identified drugs, and improve understanding of the molecular pathways underlying the distinct forms of VHD.

medicine.title: Late pacemaker lead perforation in acute myopericarditis: a case report
medicine.abstract: Although myocarditis can be associated with ventricular wall thinning, aneurysm, and free wall rupture, late pacemaker lead perforation in myopericarditis is previously unreported.A 71-year-old man with a dual-chamber pacemaker placed 7 years prior presented with acute myopericarditis 2 months after atrial fibrillation ablation, left ventricular ejection fraction of 52%, and small pericardial effusion. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) revealed focal late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) of the basal inferolateral wall of the left ventricle. Diffuse, circumferential pericardial LGE was present around the left and right ventricle with small effusion. One month later, he returned with worsening chest pain, decompensated heart failure, moderate pericardial effusion, and effusive-constrictive physiology. Echocardiography identified a new pacemaker lead perforation. Following device revision, he was discharged on colchicine, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and empagliflozin. On follow-up, ejection fraction normalized, and constrictive physiology and cardiac inflammation resolved.Late lead perforation is a rare complication of myopericarditis and should be considered in patients who re-present with progressive pericardial effusion and decompensation after initial improvement.
medicine.text:
Inflammatory myopericardial syndrome (IMPS) is the initial term of overlapping myocarditis and pericarditis syndromes described in the 2025 European Society Guideline until a final diagnosis is made. This reflects that inflammation of the myocardium (myocarditis) and pericardium (pericarditis) can evolve along a clinical spectrum from pericardial-dominant to myocardial-dominant presentations.,

Although cases of pericardial tamponade from myocardial wall rupture in myocarditis have been reported, these events are typically described in patients with ventricular aneurysm formation or severe giant cell myocarditis., While small pericardial effusions are common in myocarditis and may reflect a component of pericardial inflammation consistent with IMPS, progressive pericardial effusion in the absence of malignancy, connective tissue disease or tuberculosis is uncommon. Development of new, late lead perforation 7 years after implantation following initial improvement has not been previously reported.

A 71-year-old man presented to the emergency department with pericarditis-like chest pain 2 months after atrial fibrillation ablation. He has a past medical history of atrial fibrillation status post pulmonary vein isolation (6 years prior) and superior vena cava isolation with cavotricuspid isthmus ablation (2 months prior). He also had a history of sick sinus syndrome status post dual-chamber pacemaker implantation (7 years prior), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnea. His CHA2DS2-VASc score (C: congestive heart failure, H: hypertension, A2: Age ≥ 75, D: diabetes, S2: stroke or transient ischemic attack, V: vascular disease, A: age 65–74, Sc: sex category female) was 2 (age and hypertension), reflecting his thromboembolic risk, and his HAS-BLED (H: hypertension, A: abnormal renal and/or liver function, S: stroke history, B: bleeding history or predisposition, L: labile international normalized ration, E: elderly (age > 65), D: medication usage predisposing to bleeds or alcohol use) score was 2 (age and concomitant medication predisposing to bleeding), reflecting his bleeding risk. Device interrogation demonstrated atrial pacing 55% of the time and right ventricular (RV) pacing 9% of the time, with the underlying rhythm demonstrating sinus node dysfunction and atrial pacemaker dependence. His home medication regimen included acetaminophen as needed, atorvastatin daily, docusate sodium, dofetilide 500 mcg every 12 hours, a multivitamin, and rivaroxaban 20 mg daily.

His initial electrocardiogram (EKG) demonstrated diffuse ST-segment elevations, most prominent in the anterolateral leads (). Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 69.0 mg/L (reference range <5.0) and elevated high-sensitivity Troponin T, peaking at 29 ng/L (normal ≤15). Invasive coronary angiography revealed only mild non-obstructive coronary artery atherosclerosis. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed a small, uncomplicated pericardial effusion without constriction (see , ). Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging revealed LVEF 52%, focal late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in the basal inferolateral wall in a non-ischemic mid-myocardial pattern, diffuse pericardial LGE, and small pericardial effusion (). Right ventricular myocardial LGE was difficult to separate from the circumferential pericardial LGE. He was diagnosed with acute myopericarditis and discharged on colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily and a tapering course of ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily.

One month later, he returned with worsening pericarditic chest pain radiating across the chest and into the jaw, accompanied by dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination showed elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral rales, and pitting edema; blood pressure was 149/76 mmHg and heart rate 60 beats/min. The differential diagnosis included heart failure due to progressive myocarditis or constrictive pericarditis, with pacemaker malfunction and recurrent atrial arrhythmia considered less likely.

Chest radiograph demonstrated interstitial pulmonary edema and small bilateral pleural effusions without evidence of significant lead malposition (). The N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was elevated at 1632 pg/mL (baseline 108 pg/mL during prior admission), and his weight was increased by 5 kg. His CRP remained elevated at 30.8 mg/L. His EKG demonstrated normal voltage without electrical alternans, with interval improvement in the previously noted ST-segment changes, and troponin levels remained within the normal range.

Repeat TTE showed ejection fraction 50%, moderate pericardial effusion (up to 1.7 cm), and no diastolic right ventricular collapse. Constrictive physiology was present with mild inspiration related interventricular septal shift, significant mitral and tricuspid inflow variability with inspiration, annulus reversus, and diastolic expiratory flow reversal in hepatic vein. A pacemaker lead tip was seen moving in and out of the RV apex diagnostic of RV lead perforation (red arrows, ; , ). The inferior vena cava (IVC) collapsed ∼70% with inspiration. Cardiac computed tomography confirmed RV pacemaker lead perforation with hemopericardium (; , ). Device interrogation showed RV lead thresholds had risen from a previously elevated 2.8 V at 1.2 ms to 6.5 V at 1.2 ms, consistent with perforation.

A multidisciplinary team involving cardiovascular surgery, electrophysiology, general cardiology, and the patient discussed management options, ultimately proceeding with RV lead extraction by electrophysiology in the operating room with cardiac surgery available if sternotomy became necessary. The patient underwent uncomplicated RV lead extraction with simultaneous dual-chamber pacemaker implantation and septal RV lead placement, performed during the same procedure given his pacemaker dependence. Follow-up TTE 48 hours post-procedure showed no pericardial effusion and chest radiograph showed proper lead positioning (). He remained on an ibuprofen taper and completed 6 months of colchicine therapy.

At 3-month follow-up, repeat TTE demonstrated improvement in LVEF to 61%. Previously observed constrictive physiology had resolved, with normalization of IVC respiratory collapse and resolution of interventricular septal shift, respiratory inflow variation, annulus reversus, and hepatic vein expiratory flow reversal. CMR at 3 months showed only mild pericardial delayed LGE with normal T2 imaging and parametric mapping values. At 6 months, CMR showed further improvement in LGE with only minimal pericardial enhancement ().

Not previously reported, we present a rare case of a 71-year-old male who developed acute myopericarditis and subsequently returned one month later with late RV pacemaker lead perforation occurring seven years after device implantation, and decompensated heart failure with effusive-constrictive physiology. Notably, CMR obtained at the time of myopericarditis diagnosis demonstrated basal anterolateral myocardial and diffuse, circumferential pericardial LGE including overlying the pacemaker lead, indicating myocardial and pericardial involvement. On this study, the distal RV was sub-optimally visualized due to pacemaker artefact, limiting differentiation between RV myocardium and pericardium; however, RV pericardial LGE was present. While the precise mechanism of lead perforation cannot be established, we hypothesize that inflammation-related myocardial and/or pericardial tissue friability may have contributed to perforation in the setting of a lead with chronically elevated thresholds, potentially reflecting pre-existing lead-related susceptibility.

Pacemaker lead perforation with subsequent pericardial effusion, as seen in our case, is rare, occurs in only 0.1–0.8% of cases, and is most often seen early after initial implantation. Late perforation after first few months of implantation is rarer still, with few cases reported. Predisposing factors for perforation include temporary leads, active fixation leads, older age and low body mass index., Perforation with subsequent acute pericarditis is often reported. However, acute myopericarditis preceding perforation has not been reported. In our patient, both CMR and TTE completed during his initial presentation did not have evidence of lead perforation.

Diagnosing lead perforation can be challenging given its variable clinical presentations. Although chest x-ray is often the simplest initial tool to reveal macro-dislodgment, but can underappreciate subtle lead migration, as in our case. In patients with cardiac devices presenting with pericardial effusion, our practice is that TTE should carefully assess each lead tip position and examine all echocardiographic views carefully. In our patient, the lead perforation was seen in the apical three-chamber view on TTE. Chest computed tomography was confirmatory for the pacemaker lead perforation. Of note, acutely rising pacemaker lead thresholds may indicate potential lead displacement., Given atrial dependence and confirmed lead perforation, immediate lead extraction with simultaneous replacement was pursued rather than deferring intervention until resolution of the myopericarditis.

Management in our case included treatment for each individual component, i.e. effusive-constrictive pericarditis and myocarditis. The patient was discharged on standard pericarditis treatment, but a prolonged colchicine course of at least 6 months. NSAIDs were used after shared decision-making and close supervision to avoid further heart failure. The effusive-constrictive physiology was favoured to be contributing more to the decompensated heart failure rather than LVEF 52%, and this supported the more aggressive pericarditis treatment. Corticosteroids were avoided due to comorbidities and patient preference. The patient tolerated NSAIDS well and responded favorably. For the myocarditis component, he received limited goal-directed medical therapy with the sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor empagliflozin per patient preference. He subsequently had recovery of LV function.

This case illustrates that late lead perforation is a rare complication of myopericarditis and should be considered in patients who re-present with progressive pericardial effusion and decompensation after initial improvement.

Tyler Canova, MD, is a second-year Internal Medicine resident at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN. Originally from Akron, OH, he completed his undergraduate studies at The Ohio State University before earning his medical degree from The University of Toledo College of Medicine. His professional interests include general cardiology, cardiovascular imaging, interventional cardiology, and critical care cardiology, with plans to pursue fellowship training in cardiology. He has been actively involved in cardiovascular outcomes and imaging research, with various projects focused on coronary artery disease, cardiogenic shock, and structural heart disease. He additionally enjoys teaching and caring for critically ill patients.

medicine.title: Metal–organic frameworks for antibiotic removal from water and wastewater
medicine.abstract: The persistence of antibiotics in aquatic environments has emerged as a critical environmental challenge due to their extensive use, incomplete metabolism, and continuous release from municipal, hospital, and industrial sources. Their accumulation in water and wastewater systems fosters antimicrobial resistance, disrupts ecosystems, and poses severe risks to public health. Conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon and zeolites often fall short in terms of selectivity, regeneration, and adsorption capacity, necessitating innovative alternatives. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), with their tunable porosity, high surface areas, adjustable chemical functionalities, and structural diversity, have attracted significant attention as next-generation adsorbents for antibiotic removal. This review provides a comprehensive discussion of the occurrence and impacts of antibiotics in aquatic systems, followed by a critical evaluation of the adsorption performance of pristine MOFs, MOF derivatives, and MOF-based composites. Emphasis is placed on synthetic methodologies, purification/activation strategies, and mechanistic insights underlying antibiotic–MOF interactions. Furthermore, the study highlights the regeneration potential of MOFs for sustainable applications, compares their performance with conventional adsorbents, and identifies the persisting challenges in stability, scalability, and selectivity. Finally, knowledge gaps and future directions are outlined, focusing on defect engineering, hybrid frameworks, and other critical factors governing efficient application in real wastewater treatment to accelerate the translation of laboratory studies into practical deployment. By consolidating advances and challenges, this work positions MOFs as promising candidates for addressing the global threat of antibiotic pollution in water and wastewater.
medicine.text:
Water pollution has become a major global issue, raising concerns about its effects on human health, environmental quality, and the ecosystem. The presence of dangerous substances in water bodies in the ecosystem has a great impact on human health, contributing to a decline in life expectancy, an increase in hormonal disorders, and the emergence of new diseases and infections. The economic and industrial sectors pay a large amount for water treatment in order to make it usable. Improved water quality is achievable by avoiding the dumping of dangerous waste, reducing pollution, minimizing the release of hazardous chemicals and materials (halving the proportion of wastewater to be treated), and increasing recycling and safe reuse globally. To date, several pollutants that are responsible for the contamination of water and wastewater have been identified, with antibiotics being one of the leading contaminants.

The increase in population, coupled with rising life expectancy, the emergence of new pandemics, livestock development, large-scale manufacturing, and the overuse of antibiotics, has resulted in increased antibiotic consumption globally. Various studies have reported the presence of over 200 types of antibiotics, used in human and veterinary medicine and agriculture, in water bodies such as drinking water, soil, vegetables, groundwater, municipal sewage, and sludge, contributing to antibiotic resistance and ecological impacts. Antibiotics are categorized into tetracyclines (TCs), sulfonamides (SAs), β-lactams (β-LAs), macrolides (MLs), aminoglycosides (AGs), and quinolones (QNs) based on their distinct chemical structures and mechanisms of action. However, the two antibiotics commonly found in wastewater and widely used in human and veterinary medicine to control bacterial diseases are tetracyclines (TCs) and sulfamethoxazole (SMZ). They are difficult to be metabolized by human and animal digestive systems and are excreted into the environment, thereby promoting the emergence of TC- and SMZ-resistant bacteria.

Hospital risk assessments also reveal that antibiotic wastewater contributes significantly to environmental toxicity; therefore, there is an urgent need to treat antibiotic-containing wastewater using efficient methods. Various techniques have been employed to treat antibiotic wastewater, including ultrafiltration, ultraviolet treatment, chlorination, distillation, chemical transformation, biological treatment, and low-frequency ultrasonic radiation. However, these traditional approaches are associated with drawbacks, including excessive reagent use, high energy consumption, low efficiency, and difficulty in controlling microbial growth.

To mitigate these limitations and further enhance antibiotic removal from wastewater, there is a need for advanced, highly efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable methods. Recently, membrane separation technology has been proven to be effective and has been widely adopted to improve water quality due to its specific advantages, such as ease of integration, high separation efficiency, compact design, flexibility, and outstanding performance. Another effective technique is adsorption for the removal of antibiotics from wastewater. This technique is preferred over many other techniques because it poses a low risk of forming toxic by-products, it interacts with target pollutants, and has a high surface area. However, it is also associated with a peculiar problem, whereby its efficiency can be affected by the composition of the aqueous environment, the type of adsorbent used and its properties. Porous materials, such as nanocomposites, nanoparticles, clays, graphite oxide, activated charcoal, foams, zeolites, and ceramics, have diverse applications due to their high specific surface area and rapid diffusion through their pores, enabling the effective removal of antibiotic pollutants.

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are crystalline porous coordination networks assembled from metal ions or metal-containing secondary building units interconnected by organic linkers. As a versatile class of coordination materials, MOFs have attracted considerable attention for the removal of antibiotics and other pharmaceutical contaminants from wastewater. Their effectiveness is primarily associated with their high porosity and specific surface area, well-defined and tunable pore architectures, and abundance of accessible adsorption sites. Unlike many conventional porous adsorbents, the modular nature of MOFs enables the pore size, framework composition, surface functionality, and local coordination environment to be systematically tailored. Such structural flexibility can regulate molecular transport and accessibility while promoting selective host–guest interactions with target antibiotic molecules. In particular, control over pore dimensions can enhance adsorption specificity by favouring contaminants with appropriate molecular size and geometry. These combined features of high porosity, structural tunability, and readily adjustable surface chemistry have established MOFs as promising platforms for the selective capture and removal of antibiotics from contaminated water ().

This review discusses the significance and uniqueness of MOFs compared with conventional adsorbents, highlighting their extensive specific surface area, versatile surface chemistry, and controlled pore size. It also examines the persistent threat posed by antibiotics in wastewater and various methods for synthesizing MOFs and MOF derivatives as adsorbents for removing antibiotics from water. Furthermore, the review critically analyzes the compositional features of MOFs responsible for their enhanced performance and highlights the mechanisms underlying MOF adsorption for the removal of antibiotics from wastewater. Finally, this study addresses the regeneration of MOFs for antibiotic sorption, as well as the theoretical studies that explain their enhanced performance as sustainable alternative adsorbents for antibiotic removal from water or wastewater.

Antibiotics are indispensable in modern medicine and veterinary practice, but their extensive use and subsequent release into the environment have raised growing concerns about their environmental distribution, ecological impacts, and contribution to antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotics are classified into various categories based on their chemical structures: glycopeptides, polymyxins, aminoglycosides, macrolides, oxazolidinones, β-lactams, quinolones, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, and streptogramins. Among these, tetracyclines, sulfonamides, and macrolides are widely used in both human and veterinary medicine for safeguarding animal health and diagnosing and treating infectious diseases in humans. Penicillin, a representative of the β-lactam class, is one of the earliest and most recognized antibiotics, including naturally occurring penicillin G, the extended-spectrum penicillin piperacillin, and aminopenicillins such as ampicillin.

The most frequently detected antibiotics in effluents, sewage sludge, sediments, soils, and food products are sulfonamides, macrolides, and quinolones. Their widespread occurrence has made antibiotic pollution a serious environmental concern, particularly in rivers and seas, where antibiotics can bioaccumulate in aquatic organisms, reducing biodiversity. In addition, their persistence in the environment threatens food chains, disrupts soil decomposition, endangers both aquatic and terrestrial organisms, and accelerates the development of bacterial resistance.

Antibiotic contamination has been detected in soil, water bodies, and sewage. Given its detrimental effects on human health and ecosystems, including the induction of bacterial resistance that undermines the efficacy of infection treatments, effective mitigation is critical. Drug-resistant bacteria can reach humans and animals through contaminated water or food prepared using contaminated water, disrupting the gut microbiota and causing a range of health problems. Identifying contamination sources is therefore essential for preventing the entry of antibiotics into humans and ecological systems.

Municipal wastewater is a major reservoir of pharmaceuticals due to inadequate treatment and the improper disposal of antibiotics by consumers. The primary inputs include industrial operations (e.g., slaughterhouses and poultry facilities) and household waste (). Antibiotics consumed by humans and animals are excreted, and subsequently enter wastewater treatment plants. While some antibiotics undergo chemical or physical transformations during treatment, many persist, depending on the treatment processes employed.

Antibiotics from the main classes of tetracyclines, β-lactams, quinolones, macrolides, and sulfonamides are frequently detected in activated sludge, sewage, digested sludge, and effluents, acting as pseudo-persistent pollutants. Municipal wastewater also harbors diverse microorganisms, enhancing the emergence of drug-resistant organisms, including commensals, pathogens, and environmental bacteria. Although wastewater contains other contaminants, such as heavy metals, pesticides, and endocrine disruptors, the spread of drug-resistant pathogenic bacteria remains a primary concern.

Hospital wastewater contains a complex mixture of pharmaceutical residues, disinfectants, organic halogens, radioisotopes, contrast agents, heavy metals, cytostatic drugs, and laboratory chemicals (). Several of these, particularly cytostatic and antineoplastic agents, are environmentally hazardous due to their mutagenic, teratogenic, and carcinogenic properties. As a result, hospital effluent constitutes a significant reservoir for antibiotic-resistant bacteria and resistance genes.

Conventional wastewater treatment methods are often insufficient to remove these compounds, allowing toxins to partially or completely enter the environment. Assessing the contribution of hospitals to overall pharmaceutical loads is challenging because many medications are also widely used by the general population. Ongoing studies are investigating hospitals as potential reservoirs of multidrug-resistant bacteria. Hospital wastewater is estimated to contain approximately 25% antibiotics, with resistance gene quantities ranging from 0.4 to 1.8 log units higher than in municipal wastewater. Common antibiotics detected include enrofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, oxolinic acid, ofloxacin, norfloxacin, sulfapyridine, trimethoprim, and metronidazole.

In many developing countries, antibiotic overuse and misuse, facilitated by over-the-counter availability, contribute to environmental contamination. Antibiotics enter surface and groundwater through runoff, wastewater discharges, and effluents from livestock operations. Rainfall and irrigation exacerbate this process, transporting antibiotics into aquatic systems and making runoff a dominant pathway for environmental contamination.

The application of manure, pesticides, and fertilizers further increases the risk of antibiotic resistance genes entering water bodies. Seasonal factors such as precipitation, snowmelt, nutrient load, and stream velocity also influence the concentration and distribution of antibiotics. Antibiotics with higher solubility spread more rapidly in the environment, intensifying their impact.

Direct discharge of untreated effluents from healthcare facilities worsens this issue. Similarly, improperly discarded solid antibiotics may leach into groundwater or nearby surface waters during rainfall events ().

Slaughterhouse wastewater is a significant source of resistant bacteria due to the clinical use of antibiotics in livestock, which contributes to their environmental dissemination. The misuse of antibiotics in animal husbandry, along with growth-promoting practices, has accelerated the development of antimicrobial resistance in livestock-associated bacteria. Slaughterhouse effluents often contain high levels of lipids, proteins, organic matter, pathogens, and veterinary pharmaceuticals, making them globally hazardous. Drugs such as oxytetracycline and procaine penicillin G, commonly used in cattle in Central African countries, are excreted in animal feces and urine, ultimately reaching wastewater systems.

Hospitals commonly release a wide range of therapeutic agents, including contrast media, analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs, laxatives, and antibiotics. Among these, antibiotics are the most significant contributors, entering municipal sewage systems and persisting through various stages, such as digested sludge, activated sludge, and ultimately urban biosolids. When not fully removed during water treatment, these compounds pose substantial risks to aquatic ecosystems. Studies have reported the presence of antibiotics not only in wastewater effluents but also in lakes, rivers, groundwater, and even drinking water. Sulfonamides, tetracyclines, and macrolides are particularly prevalent in swine effluent, with recorded concentrations of 324.4, 388.7, and 72 µg L−1, respectively. At sub-inhibitory levels, these antibiotics facilitate the gradual emergence of resistance within bacterial populations, enabling resistance to spread across communities. At higher concentrations, they are directly toxic to aquatic organisms, impairing growth, organ development, reproduction, and survival, thereby disrupting ecological balance.

Furthermore, macrolides and sulfonamides have been shown to inhibit algal growth and photosynthetic activity, causing structural damage to plant cells and reducing carbon dioxide fixation rates. Such disruptions to primary producers can cascade through ecosystems, amplifying the ecological consequences of antibiotic pollution.

MOFs constitute a rapidly evolving class of porous crystalline materials that distinguish themselves from conventional adsorbents, such as activated carbon, zeolites, and silica gels, through their exceptional tunability. Structurally, MOFs are constructed from inorganic nodes (metal ions or metal–oxo clusters) connected by organic linkers, forming extended networks with highly ordered and customizable architectures. Unlike traditional adsorbents, which are often constrained by fixed pore structures and limited surface chemistry, MOFs exhibit a modular design principle. This modularity allows researchers to carefully adjust pore size, shape, and surface functionality simply by varying the choice of metal centers or organic linkers. As a result, MOFs can be rationally tailored to meet the demands of highly specific adsorption processes, whether for gas storage, separation, catalysis, or pollutant capture.

The metal node, more accurately described as the metal ion or metal–oxo secondary building unit, plays a decisive role in determining framework connectivity, crystal-growth direction, particle shape, pore architecture, and surface chemistry. Differences in metal-ion radius, oxidation state, coordination number, geometry, hydrolysis rate, and metal–ligand bond strength can produce MOFs with markedly different morphologies, including nanoparticles, rods, plates, cubes, and polyhedral crystals, even when closely related organic linkers are employed. Highly connected clusters, such as Zr-based secondary building units, generally yield rigid and hydrolytically stable frameworks, whereas metal centers with lower connectivity may form more flexible structures that undergo pore opening or “breathing”. These structural differences regulate pore volume, aperture dimensions, defect concentration, external surface roughness, and the proportion of adsorption sites accessible to antibiotic molecules. The metal center also directly influences adsorption: activation may expose coordinatively unsaturated Lewis-acidic sites that can bind the amino, carbonyl, carboxylate, hydroxyl, and sulfonamide groups of antibiotics. Consequently, changing the metal node can alter both mass transfer and binding affinity, as demonstrated by the substantially different adsorption capacities reported for structurally related Fe-, Al- and Cr-containing MIL-101–NH2 frameworks. Thus, adsorption performance depends not simply on the nominal BET surface area but on the combined effects of accessible porosity, water stability, particle morphology and the chemical affinity of the exposed metal sites.

The organic spacer provides a complementary level of structural and chemical control because its length, rigidity, denticity, connectivity, planarity, and substituent groups determine the separation and orientation of adjacent metal nodes. Longer and more rigid linkers can enlarge cavities and increase internal surface area, whereas excessively flexible or elongated spacers may promote framework interpenetration, pore contraction or structural collapse during activation. Linker geometry also governs framework dimensionality and crystal habit: linear ditopic ligands commonly generate channels or layered structures, while trigonal and multitopic ligands favour highly connected cage-like networks. These effects determine whether an antibiotic can enter the pore system, diffuse through interconnected channels and approach the available binding sites; pores that are smaller than the hydrated or aggregated antibiotic species may remain inaccessible despite a high measured surface area.

In addition, aromatic spacers promote π–π interactions with the conjugated rings of ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, tetracycline and sulfamethoxazole, while functional groups such as –NH2, –OH, –COOH and –SO3H introduce hydrogen-bonding sites and modify hydrophilicity, acid–base behaviour and pH-dependent surface charge. Electron-donating or electron-withdrawing substituents further regulate the electronic compatibility between the linker and the antibiotic, thereby affecting adsorption strength and selectivity. Therefore, effective antibiotic adsorption requires the coordinated selection of the metal node and organic spacer so that pore apertures match the molecular dimensions of the target compound, transport resistance is minimized, and multiple interactions, including pore filling, metal coordination, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, hydrophobic association and π–π stacking, operate synergistically.

One of the most outstanding advantages of MOFs is their pore-size tunability, which spans from sub-angstrom dimensions to several nanometers, far exceeding the relatively narrow pore-size range of zeolites (0.3–2 nm) and the less controllable porosity of activated carbons. This flexibility provides MOFs with superior selectivity and adsorption performance. For instance, MOF-74 exhibits a CO2 uptake capacity of approximately 5.5 mmol g−1, significantly outperforming zeolites under similar conditions (2–3 mmol g−1). Such performance is attributable to both the optimized pore dimensions and the functionalized adsorption sites within the MOF framework, which can be engineered to interact strongly and selectively with target molecules.

Another defining characteristic of MOFs is their exceptionally high surface area, which frequently exceeds 5000 m2 g−1, with some ultraporous frameworks such as NU-110 achieving values as high as 7000 m2 g−1. By comparison, activated carbons typically offer surface areas of 1000–2335.9 m2 g−1, while zeolites rarely exceed 800 m2 g−1. The enormous accessible surface area of MOFs, coupled with their open and well-defined framework, translates into markedly higher adsorption capacities for gases and vapors. This advantage is particularly evident in hydrogen storage, where MOFs demonstrate gravimetric capacities of up to 9 wt% at cryogenic temperatures, surpassing the 5 wt% capacity achievable with activated carbons. Moreover, MOFs allow the chemical functionalization of their pore walls to introduce specific interactions such as Lewis acid–base interactions, hydrogen bonding, or π–π stacking, which are difficult to incorporate in the rigid lattices of zeolites or the amorphous networks of carbons. This functional versatility is crucial for challenging separations, such as differentiating structurally similar hydrocarbons or selectively removing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from complex gas mixtures.

Beyond their structural advantages, MOFs have overcome one of their early limitations (stability). Conventional wisdom once considered MOFs fragile compared to the robust frameworks of zeolites; however, recent advances, particularly in zirconium-based systems such as UiO-66, have yielded materials with outstanding stability under moisture, acidic, and thermal stress. These materials not only withstand harsh operating conditions but also maintain their crystallinity and porosity after prolonged use. Furthermore, the regenerability of MOFs is another distinguishing advantage: they can undergo multiple adsorption–desorption cycles with minimal performance loss. This contrasts with activated carbons, which often suffer from pore blockage, irreversible adsorption, or structural collapse during regeneration.

The exceptional porosity and tunable chemistry of MOFs make them appealing adsorbents for antibiotic removal, but their hydrolytic stability is a major challenge for effective wastewater treatment, as water can hydrolyze metal–ligand bonds, leading to framework degradation, pore collapse, and reduced adsorption performance. Among the reported materials, UiO-66 is one of the most water-stable MOFs due to its highly connected Zr6O4(OH)4 secondary building units and strong Zr–carboxylate interactions, which result in excellent hydrolysis resistance and structural stability over multiple adsorption–desorption cycles. However, the conventional solvothermal synthesis of UiO-66 often involves costly zirconium precursors, organic solvents such as DMF, and energy-intensive activation, thereby increasing production costs. Recent advances, such as water-based hydrothermal synthesis, continuous-flow processing, and the use of recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET) as a source of terephthalate, have greatly enhanced the scalability and economic viability of UiO-66, confirming its potential for large-scale applications. In addition, the hydrolytic stability can be significantly improved by judiciously choosing high-valent metal nodes (such as Zr4+, Al3+, and Cr3+), using hydrophobic linker functionalization, employing defect engineering and post-synthetic modifications, and preparing MOF/polymer or MOF/carbon composites, which enhance structural resilience while maintaining adsorption performance in practical aqueous environments.

The combination of tunable structure, ultrahigh surface area, functional versatility, and enhanced durability positions MOFs as next-generation adsorbents that can outperform conventional materials in a wide spectrum of applications. Their adaptability enables fine-tuning of adsorption processes for environmental remediation, industrial separations, energy storage, and beyond. Importantly, the ability to design MOFs at the molecular level ensures that their performance can be continually optimized, bridging the gap between laboratory innovation and large-scale deployment.

The synthesis of novel MOFs has drawn considerable attention, particularly through the design of innovative organic ligands and the optimization of conditions that promote metal–ligand coordination. The characteristics of ligands, including the length and orientation of connecting units, size, chirality, and geometric compatibility with metal ions, play a decisive role in determining the structure and properties of MOFs. A wide range of synthetic strategies have been reported, including hydrothermal synthesis, solvothermal methods, microwave-assisted techniques, sonochemical processes, electrochemical synthesis, and mechanochemical approaches, in addition to traditional trial-and-error experimentation ().

The hydrothermal method promotes the self-assembly of MOFs from soluble precursors within sealed autoclaves at 80–260 °C under autogenous pressure (). Reaction conditions, particularly cooling rates, strongly influence crystal quality. Although widely adopted in zeolite synthesis, this method has become an important approach in MOF research. Reactions may require several days, similar to solvothermal approaches, while diffusion-based crystallization can take several weeks.

Mechanochemical synthesis () involves applying mechanical force to induce chemical transformations in the absence of solvents. Traditionally applied in metallurgy and mineral processing, this method has been extended to inorganic chemistry and pharmaceutical manufacturing. In MOF synthesis, milling or grinding, often using automated ball mills or simple mortar-and-pestle setups, facilitates reactions among poorly soluble precursors such as metal oxides, hydroxides, and carbonates, thereby generating little to no solvent waste. While often described as “solvent-free,” purification may still require small amounts of solvent. The main limitation of this batch-processing method is its relatively low scalability. Nevertheless, mechanosynthesis is considered environmentally sustainable and cost-effective, aligning with green chemistry principles. Three main approaches are employed: (a) solvent-free grinding (SFG): eliminates solvents entirely. (b) Liquid-assisted grinding (LAG): introduces minimal amounts of solvent to improve molecular mobility, increasing speed and adaptability. (c) Ion- and liquid-assisted grinding (ILAG): combines small amounts of solvent and salts to promote structural control in targeted MOF synthesis.

In particular, LAG has demonstrated advantages, accelerating reactions through enhanced mobility of reactants and occasionally directing structural outcomes. ILAG extends this principle, enabling the synthesis of pillared-layered MOFs and highlighting the influence of ions and solvents on framework formation.

Electrochemical synthesis has been scaled to industrial MOF production due to its advantages over solvothermal methods (). It eliminates unwanted anions (e.g., nitrates) from metal salts, reduces reaction temperatures, and allows the rapid in situ generation of metal ions at electrode surfaces. This localized ion generation minimizes bulk crystallization and reduces the risk of crack formation in MOF films during cooling, which is common in solvothermal synthesis due to mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion. Moreover, the ability to fine-tune parameters such as voltage and type of applied signal offers greater control over synthesis compared to thermal methods.

The solvothermal method, typically employing standard electric heating, is one of the most common approaches for synthesizing MOFs. In this process, metal precursors and organic ligands are dissolved in a solvent and sealed within a reaction vessel, where crystallization occurs under controlled temperature and self-generated pressure for a defined period (). The crystallinity and yield of MOFs strongly depend on both the choice of solvent and reaction parameters. Solvents such as acetonitrile, acetone, methanol, N,N-diphenylformamide, and N,N-diethylformamide are frequently used due to their high solubility. Solvent mixtures are often employed to overcome solubility limitations of the starting materials. Typical solvothermal synthesis is conducted at 60–220 °C, with upper limits reaching 250 °C. Reaction times range from several hours to a few days, after which the vessel is cooled to room temperature, and the product is isolated, washed, and dried. Open-system modifications of solvothermal synthesis have also been explored, requiring fewer instruments and making the process more accessible. This method has been particularly effective for the synthesis of MIL-series MOFs, improving nanoscale morphology, crystallinity, and product yield. However, its scalability in commercial applications is limited by the large quantities of fine particles generated during synthesis, which hinder industrial viability.

Microwave-assisted synthesis enables rapid heating of precursor solutions, facilitating the formation of nanoscale metal crystals within an hour (). Although not yet widely applied to the synthesis of crystalline MOFs, this technique offers precise control over particle size and morphology, providing a rapid and energy-efficient alternative to conventional heating. A key limitation is the frequent formation of non-crystalline products, though this characteristic can still provide uniform seeding conditions. Successful crystallization typically requires highly saturated solutions, with solubility increasing at elevated temperatures, followed by crystal formation during cooling.

Sonochemistry employs high-frequency ultrasound (20 kHz to 10 MHz) to generate cavitation, microjets, and localized extreme conditions that promote chemical reactions (). These effects can clean surfaces, disperse particles, and enhance solubility, while also driving bond cleavage, radical generation, and high-energy molecular transformations. Sonochemistry is well established in organic and nanomaterial synthesis and has recently been applied to MOF synthesis. Its main advantages are rapid reaction rates, energy efficiency, environmental sustainability, and scalability at ambient temperatures.

Comparatively, different synthetic techniques () yield MOFs with varying porosities and surface areas. Mechanochemical methods, for example, have been used to synthesize MOF-74 with porosity comparable to that of solvothermal products, despite avoiding toxic solvents and reducing waste generation. Similarly, IRMOF-3 synthesized mechanochemically retained high porosity and crystallinity after solvent exposure and activation, demonstrating the strong influence of organic linker properties on final MOF performance. Ultimately, the choice of synthesis method depends not only on structural requirements but also on sustainability considerations, with mechanochemical routes offering clear advantages for environmentally responsible synthesis.

The practical deployment of MOFs in wastewater treatment requires synthesis methods capable of moving beyond milligram- or gram-scale laboratory preparation while preserving crystallinity, accessible porosity, and batch-to-batch consistency. Scale-up should therefore not be assessed solely by whether a larger reaction vessel can be used. More relevant criteria include space-time yield, product yield, solvent and energy consumption, heat and mass transfer, reproducibility, reactor safety, ease of continuous operation and downstream requirements for washing, solvent exchange and activation. From this perspective, conventional hydrothermal and solvothermal synthesis remain highly versatile, but they are not necessarily the most attractive routes for large-scale manufacturing. Increasing the volume of sealed batch reactors can produce larger quantities, yet non-uniform temperature and concentration gradients become increasingly important as reactor dimensions increase. Moreover, prolonged heating, high solvent inventories and pressure-rated equipment increase both capital and operating costs. These limitations are especially important when high-boiling organic solvents such as DMF are employed. Consequently, simply enlarging a solvothermal batch reactor is not the most efficient path to industrial production, even though the method remains valuable for MOFs whose formation requires tightly controlled crystallization conditions. Reviews of MOF manufacturing similarly identify flow chemistry, mechanochemistry and electrochemistry as principal routes with strong scale-up potential.

Continuous-flow synthesis is currently one of the most convincing approaches for large-scale MOF manufacturing because reactor volume can be decoupled from total production capacity. Precursors are continuously introduced, crystallization occurs under controlled residence times and temperature, and the product is continuously withdrawn, thereby improving heat and mass transfer and reducing batch-to-batch variability. Schoenecker et al. demonstrated a flow-through crystallization strategy for UiO-66-NH2, establishing that continuous processing could retain the desired phase and porosity while providing a rational route to scale-up. Notably, Rubio-Martinez et al. scaled continuous MOF production by more than two orders of magnitude and reported aluminum fumarate production at 5.6 kg h−1, corresponding to a space-time yield of approximately 97 159 kg m−3 day−1, without requiring substantial re-optimization of the small-scale reaction conditions. These results illustrate an important engineering advantage of continuous operation: scale-up can be achieved by increasing flow rate, reactor dimensions, or by using parallel reactors rather than simply enlarging a batch autoclave.

Microwave-assisted synthesis can also be scaled up when combined with a continuous-flow reactor design. Conventional batch microwave synthesis is rapid and energy-efficient at the laboratory scale, but microwave penetration depth, non-uniform electromagnetic fields, and difficulties in heating large reaction volumes can restrict direct scale-up. Continuous-flow microwave reactors alleviate many of these constraints by processing comparatively small volumes continuously while maintaining rapid and homogeneous heating. Taddei et al. demonstrated the continuous-flow microwave synthesis of UiO-66, MIL-53(Al) and HKUST-1 at multigram scale within minutes, achieving high space-time yields and demonstrating the feasibility of this approach for intensified production. Therefore, microwave synthesis should not simply be classified as poorly scalable; rather, batch microwave synthesis is limited in scale, whereas continuous-flow microwave processing is substantially more promising for high-throughput manufacturing.

Mechanochemical synthesis has similarly evolved from a laboratory-scale grinding method into a credible continuous-production strategy. The major attraction is its very low solvent requirement, which can substantially reduce solvent purchasing, recovery and disposal costs relative to conventional solvothermal routes. Although ordinary mortar grinding and batch ball milling are inherently limited in throughput, continuous twin-screw extrusion (TSE) has changed the scalability outlook. Crawford and co-workers demonstrated the continuous preparation of commercially relevant HKUST-1, ZIF-8 and Al-fumarate frameworks by single- and twin-screw extrusion, reaching kilogram-per-hour production rates while using little or no solvent. The activated products retained surface areas and pore volumes comparable to those of materials obtained through conventional solvent-based synthesis. More recent assessments likewise identify TSE as particularly attractive because screw speed, feed rate, temperature, residence time and mechanical shear can be controlled independently, allowing continuous production and straightforward process intensification. Mechanochemistry, therefore, has limited scalability in conventional batch milling and substantial scalability when implemented through continuous extrusion.

Electrochemical synthesis is another strong candidate for industrial production, particularly because metal ions can be generated directly from sacrificial metal electrodes, reducing the need for metal salts and their associated counterions. The process can operate under relatively mild thermal conditions and can potentially be integrated into continuous reactors. Commercial interest in this route is well established; electrochemical production has historically been associated with the scale-up of HKUST-1-type materials. More recent work by Vehrenberg et al. demonstrated continuous steady-state HKUST-1 electrosynthesis for as long as 60 h using periodic polarity reversal to reduce electrode passivation. A maximum production rate of 1.83 mg h−1 cm−2 was achieved, substantially exceeding that of conventional direct-current operation. Nevertheless, electrochemical synthesis is not universally applicable to all MOF chemistries, and electrode passivation, reactor architecture, electrical energy requirements and electrode-area-to-reactor-volume ratio remain important scale-up considerations.

By comparison, sonochemical and conventional hydrothermal methods currently have less evidence supporting their use for industrial-scale MOF production. Sonochemistry offers rapid nucleation and potentially low bulk operating temperatures, but scale-up is complicated by non-uniform cavitation fields, attenuation of ultrasonic energy with reactor volume, and the need to maintain comparable acoustic intensity throughout large vessels. Accordingly, scaling up ultrasonic flow cells may be more realistic than simply enlarging vessels. Hydrothermal and solvothermal synthesis are technologically mature and can certainly be operated at kilogram scale, but long residence times, high solvent inventories, and pressure/temperature requirements can reduce their economic attractiveness relative to intensified continuous processes. Spray-drying is another emerging strategy because atomization enables rapid heat and mass transfer and continuous powder formation; seed-mediated spray-drying has, for example, been demonstrated for UiO-66 and other MOFs. However, spray-drying remains less widely validated across MOF families than continuous-flow or extrusion.

Therefore, no single synthesis route can be designated universally optimal for MOF scale-up, because framework chemistry strongly determines suitable precursors, solvents, nucleation kinetics and activation requirements. Nevertheless, the available evidence places continuous-flow synthesis, continuous mechanochemistry/twin-screw extrusion and electrochemical synthesis among the most credible manufacturing routes, while continuous-flow microwave processing provides a particularly attractive intensified option for MOFs that crystallize rapidly. Conventional hydrothermal/solvothermal methods remain valuable where high crystallinity and precise phase control are paramount, but their solvent, energy and pressure requirements reduce their attractiveness for commodity-scale adsorbent production. For wastewater applications, scale-up assessment should additionally include downstream washing and activation, solvent recovery, shaping into mechanically robust particles or monoliths, and the ability to reproducibly produce water-stable MOFs. Thus, an industrially relevant synthesis route must optimize not only MOF yield and crystallinity, but also space-time yield, environmental footprint, manufacturing cost, and adsorbent processability.

The physicochemical properties of MOFs are intimately linked to their adsorption performance; consequently, comprehensive characterization is indispensable for correlating structural features with antibiotic removal efficiency. Because adsorption depends on pore accessibility, surface chemistry, crystallinity, particle morphology, defect concentration, and framework stability, no single analytical technique can adequately characterize MOFs. Instead, complementary characterization methods are routinely employed before and after adsorption to elucidate structural evolution and identify the dominant adsorption mechanisms. In particular, powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), scanning and transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), nitrogen adsorption–desorption analysis, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), Raman spectroscopy, and zeta potential measurements constitute the principal techniques used to evaluate MOF adsorbents. Together, these analyses verify successful synthesis, assess structural integrity after activation, monitor framework stability during adsorption–desorption cycles, and provide evidence for interactions between antibiotics and adsorption sites. Since the adsorption efficiency discussed throughout this review depends strongly on the framework architecture, systematic characterization is essential to understand why certain MOFs exhibit superior adsorption capacities despite having similar surface areas or pore volumes.

Powder XRD remains the primary technique for confirming phase purity and crystallinity because each MOF possesses a characteristic diffraction fingerprint. Comparison of experimental and simulated diffraction patterns verifies successful framework formation, while changes in peak position or intensity after adsorption provide valuable information on structural stability or framework distortion. For example, the excellent hydrolytic stability of UiO-66 is commonly demonstrated by the retention of its diffraction peaks after repeated adsorption–desorption cycles, whereas Cu-based HKUST-1 may exhibit peak broadening or diminished crystallinity following prolonged exposure to water because of partial hydrolysis of Cu–carboxylate bonds. Electron microscopy complements PXRD by revealing particle size, crystal morphology and surface texture. SEM is particularly useful for identifying cubic, octahedral, rod-like or polyhedral crystals, whereas TEM provides detailed information on internal porosity, crystal defects and lattice ordering. For example, previous studies have highlighted that modifying the Zn : Co ratio in Zn/Co-ZIF/chitosan composites effectively altered particle size and surface texture, thereby influencing active-site distribution and tetracycline adsorption, illustrating the importance of morphological characterization in understanding adsorption behaviour.

The porous nature of MOFs is primarily evaluated using nitrogen adsorption–desorption measurements, from which the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area, pore volume and pore-size distribution are obtained. These parameters govern the accessibility of adsorption sites and strongly influence molecular diffusion within the framework. Nevertheless, as demonstrated by several studies, adsorption performance cannot be explained by surface area alone because frameworks with lower BET values may outperform more porous analogues owing to stronger host–guest interactions. Consequently, spectroscopic techniques are required to identify the chemical nature of these interactions.
