In addition, hydroxyl groups (–OH), which are common in antibiotics like tetracyclines, can interact with metal centers through their oxygen atoms, while carboxyl groups (–COOH) in penicillins and cephalosporins can also donate electron density to metal ions. Moreover, sulfur-containing groups, such as those in sulfonamides, can serve as donors in metal–ligand coordination. These interactions are not only specific but also significantly enhance the binding strength of the antibiotic–MOF complex, as coordinate-covalent bonds formed between the metal and functional groups are generally more robust and stable than weaker non-covalent interactions. This characteristic enables MOFs to effectively capture and retain antibiotics, even under complex environmental conditions.

The robustness of the metal–ligand complexes formed between MOFs and antibiotics hinges on several crucial factors, including the charge and coordination geometry of the metal ion, the nature of the functional groups of the antibiotic, and the overall structure of the MOF. Metal ions with higher charges, like Fe3+ or Al3+, are particularly successful in forming stable complexes due to their enhanced ability to polarize the electron-rich functional groups of antibiotics. This polarization boosts the electron donation from the functional groups of antibiotics, resulting in stronger and more durable metal–ligand interactions. Additionally, the coordination geometry of the metal ion, whether tetrahedral, octahedral, or another configuration, can affect the binding strength and selectivity. The overall architecture of the MOF, which encompasses the size and arrangement of its pores, along with the density of functional groups, also significantly influences the adsorption capacity and selectivity for various antibiotics. Thus, metal–ligand coordination within MOFs presents a highly efficient and selective approach for antibiotic adsorption, which can be utilized in fields such as environmental cleanup, wastewater treatment, and targeted drug delivery systems.

The effectiveness of metal–ligand coordination in the adsorption of antibiotics onto MOFs is shaped by several critical factors, each impacting the strength and selectivity of the interactions. A vital factor is the type of metal ion at the center of the MOF. Different metal ions display diverse coordination preferences that determine which functional groups of antibiotics can successfully interact with the metal center. For example, metal ions like Zn2+ and Cu2+ are particularly adept at coordinating with electron-rich nitrogen and oxygen atoms commonly found in antibiotics such as aminoglycosides and β-lactams. These metal ions typically form stable coordination bonds with the heteroatoms in the functional groups of the antibiotics, facilitating effective adsorption. Conversely, metal ions like Fe3+ and Al3+, due to their higher positive charge, create stronger coordination bonds with both nitrogen and oxygen donors, making them particularly efficient at interacting with antibiotics containing carboxyl or amino groups, such as penicillins and cephalosporins.

Beyond the selection of the metal ion, the geometry and coordination environment of the metal center are crucial to the adsorption process. The coordination geometry, whether it is octahedral, tetrahedral, or another configuration, determines the availability of binding sites on the metal center for antibiotic molecules. Metal ions with greater coordination numbers, capable of accommodating multiple ligands, provide several binding sites for functional groups of antibiotics, thereby enhancing the overall adsorption capacity of the MOF. This feature is particularly significant for improving the retention of larger or more complex antibiotics, where multiple interactions may occur simultaneously. The coordination environment of the metal ion also impacts the bond strength of its interaction with the antibiotic, as the spatial arrangement of ligands surrounding the metal ion affects its ability to coordinate with the functional groups of the antibiotic.

Steric hindrance and the size of the antibiotic molecules further affect the efficiency of metal–ligand coordination. Antibiotics with large or sterically hindered functional groups may have trouble approaching the metal center, which can diminish their capacity to effectively coordinate with metal ions. In contrast, smaller, more flexible antibiotics with easily accessible lone pairs on heteroatoms (such as nitrogen, oxygen, or sulfur) can readily interact with the metal center, thereby improving the overall adsorption efficiency. The flexibility of antibiotics also enables them to adjust their conformation to better align with the coordination sites of the metal, facilitating stronger interactions. Therefore, the size and flexibility of antibiotics are important factors to consider when optimizing MOFs for antibiotic removal or selective targeting.

Thus, the electronic characteristics of the functional groups of antibiotics play a significant role in the strength of metal–ligand coordination. Functional groups of antibiotics that possess higher electron density or increased polarity, such as carbonyl (–CO) or sulfonate (–SO3−) groups, are particularly effective in donating electron density to metal ions, thereby enhancing the coordination interaction. This increased electron donation strengthens the coordination bond and results in a more stable antibiotic–MOF complex. Electronegativity is crucial here, as highly electronegative groups can better polarize the metal–ligand bond, leading to more robust adsorption. As such, the electron density and polarity of the functional groups of antibiotics significantly affect the efficiency and selectivity of metal–ligand coordination in MOFs, underscoring their importance in optimizing these materials for targeted antibiotic removal in environmental and biomedical contexts.

van der Waals forces are individually weaker than coordination or electrostatic interactions but can contribute to adsorption through cumulative contacts between the antibiotic and the framework. Their contribution becomes more relevant when antibiotics contain hydrophobic or aromatic domains and when the MOF presents complementary non-polar surfaces. These interactions generally operate synergistically with hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction and π–π interactions rather than acting as the sole determinant of antibiotic uptake.

For instance, MOFs like ZIF-8 (zeolitic imidazolate framework-8) and UiO-66, which feature hydrophobic alkyl and aromatic linkers, provide optimal conditions for the aromatic rings of sulfonamides to establish strong van der Waals interactions. Besides these hydrophobic interactions, the sulfonate group in sulfonamides can also engage in metal–ligand coordination with the metal nodes of the MOF, further enhancing the strength of the antibiotic–MOF complex. This collaboration among van der Waals forces, metal–ligand coordination, and possible hydrogen bonding mechanisms significantly boosts the adsorption efficiency, indicating that these MOFs are promising candidates for antibiotic delivery systems.

In a similar vein, tetracyclines, which also feature aromatic ring structures, can participate in van der Waals interactions with the hydrophobic regions of MOFs. The non-polar regions of tetracycline molecules can align with the hydrophobic organic linkers found within MOFs, optimizing the interaction between the antibiotic and the MOF structure. The hydrophobic nature of tetracycline molecules, combined with their ability to form π–π stacking interactions, further enhances the adsorption capacity of MOFs, thereby improving the retention and controlled release of antibiotics. Thus, the combination of van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonding, and metal coordination ensures that MOFs can effectively engage with a diverse array of antibiotics, amplifying their potential in drug delivery and environmental applications ().

van der Waals forces are important intermolecular interactions that arise from electrostatic attractions between permanent or transient dipoles. They are commonly classified into: London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole interactions (Keesom forces), and dipole-induced dipole interactions (Debye forces). These interactions can contribute significantly to the adsorption of antibiotics onto metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). Although these forces are individually weak, their combined effects are crucial for stabilizing the antibiotic–MOF complex, especially when they act synergistically with stronger interactions, like hydrogen bonding or electrostatic forces.

London dispersion forces, also termed dispersion forces, occur due to instantaneous dipoles that are formed by momentary changes in electron distribution. These temporary dipoles can induce corresponding dipoles in nearby molecules, leading to weak attractive interactions. Dispersion forces hold particular significance when both the antibiotic and the MOF surface are either nonpolar or weakly polar. In the context of MOFs, these forces become important when the organic linkers or the MOF surface contain hydrophobic groups such as alkyl chains or aromatic rings. Antibiotics containing hydrophobic functional groups, like nonpolar alkyl or aromatic rings, can interact with these hydrophobic segments of the MOF via dispersion forces, enhancing the stability of the antibiotic–MOF complex.

Dipole–dipole interactions interactions (Keesom forces) occur when the electron density of the MOF surface induces a temporary dipole in the antibiotic molecule, particularly when the antibiotic is somewhat polar. When a polarizable antibiotic approaches the MOF surface, the electron cloud within the molecule shifts to align with the electric field produced by the MOF surface. This interaction creates an attractive force that further solidifies the adsorption process. The significance of Keesom forces is most pronounced when the antibiotic molecule can undergo distortions in its electron cloud, facilitating a stronger interaction with the MOF surface. Overall, these van der Waals forces, including dispersion and induced dipole interactions, function together to enhance the antibiotic–MOF complex, especially when the antibiotic includes both hydrophobic and polar features, each engaging in distinct types of interactions with the MOF surface to maximize the adsorption process.

van der Waals interactions in the adsorption of antibiotics onto MOFs are crucial, especially for antibiotics that contain hydrophobic regions or aromatic structures. Hydrophobic antibiotics, including sulfonamides, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones, exhibit strong van der Waals interactions with MOFs, particularly when the MOF structure contains hydrophobic or non-polar regions. These interactions mainly arise from London dispersion forces and are particularly important when the MOF surface contains abundant non-polar organic linkers like alkyl chains, aromatic rings, or benzene derivatives. The attraction between the non-polar regions of the antibiotic and the hydrophobic surfaces of the MOF promotes a robust and stable bond, which is vital for effective adsorption and retention of the antibiotic within the MOF structure. This effect is especially noticeable for antibiotics that contain significant hydrophobic regions, which can engage with the hydrophobic sites or non-polar groups on the MOF surface.

The relationship between hydrophobic antibiotics and hydrophobic MOF surfaces exemplifies how van der Waals forces can greatly enhance the adsorption process. The structural features of the MOF, especially the type of its organic linkers, play a key role in facilitating these interactions. The non-polar groups present in the MOF create an optimal environment for hydrophobic antibiotics, where van der Waals forces can amplify the adsorption mechanism. Nonetheless, the entire adsorption process often involves a complex interplay of various intermolecular forces. Although van der Waals forces are relatively weak on their own, their collective impact becomes considerable when paired with stronger interactions, such as hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and π–π stacking interactions. For example, a hydrophobic antibiotic might interact with the MOF through both van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonding, leading to a synergistic effect that bolsters the stability and strength of the antibiotic–MOF complex. In numerous MOFs, the presence of both hydrophobic and polar groups fosters an environment in which van der Waals forces collaborate with other adsorption mechanisms, enhancing the overall efficiency and stability of the adsorption process.

Therefore, van der Waals interactions, particularly between hydrophobic antibiotics and hydrophobic MOF surfaces, are a critical aspect of the adsorption mechanism. When these forces are combined with other stronger interactions, they play a significant role in the stability and effectiveness of the antibiotic–MOF complex, thus enhancing the performance of MOFs in drug delivery and environmental remediation applications. The varying nature of these interactions highlights the intricacy and efficacy of the adsorption process, where multiple forces can act synergistically to optimize the retention and release of antibiotics.

The surface area and porosity of MOFs are crucial factors influencing the strength and degree of van der Waals interactions during the adsorption of antibiotics. MOFs that possess high surface areas and significant pore volumes provide various opportunities for antibiotics to engage with the framework, thereby increasing the instances of van der Waals interactions between the antibiotic molecules and the MOF surface. The structural attributes of the MOF, particularly the dimensions, shapes, and distribution of pores, greatly impact the effectiveness of antibiotic interactions with the MOF through van der Waals forces. Together, these elements enhance the overall adsorption process, allowing for more effective retention of the antibiotic within the MOF matrix.

MOFs with substantial surface areas, such as MIL-101(Cr) and UiO-66, highlight the significance of high accessible surface area in promoting numerous van der Waals interactions between antibiotics and the MOF surface. The large quantity of available interaction sites within these frameworks enables a considerable increase in the number of antibiotic molecules that can be adsorbed. Besides van der Waals interactions, additional forces such as hydrogen bonding or metal–ligand coordination may also contribute, further boosting the adsorption efficiency and capacity. Consequently, MOFs with high surface areas can deliver exceptional performance in terms of antibiotic loading and stability, making them excellent candidates for drug delivery applications.

In contrast, porosity is essential for determining the accessibility of the MOF to antibiotic molecules, especially those with hydrophobic regions. Larger pores not only enhance the accessibility of these hydrophobic sites but also facilitate the accommodation of larger antibiotic molecules, thus amplifying the number and strength of van der Waals interactions. By creating a suitable environment for antibiotics with hydrophobic functional groups, MOFs with optimized porosity can greatly enhance the efficiency of the adsorption process. The combination of high surface area and finely tuned porosity allows MOFs to serve as highly effective platforms for the adsorption and controlled release of antibiotics, promoting their use in various therapeutic and environmental applications.

Desorption and reusability are critical factors that determine the practical applicability of MOFs. The economic feasibility of regeneration depends largely on the cost of regeneration agents. The choice of a desorption technique is influenced by both the nature of the adsorbed contaminants and the intrinsic properties of the MOF.

Pressure-swing regeneration, as well as thermal or solvent-based techniques, may induce the release of antibiotics from MOFs. Microwave irradiation accelerates desorption through localized heating; however, careful control is required to prevent overheating and structural degradation of the MOF. Vacuum regeneration, while often time-consuming, enhances desorption by reducing pore pressure. Electrochemical regeneration enables precise control of desorption kinetics via electrochemical reactions, but it requires specialized equipment and appropriate electrode configurations. The efficiency and cycle time can be further optimized by integrating multiple regeneration approaches, either sequentially or simultaneously. The direct integration of regeneration techniques into MOF-based adsorption systems allows continuous operation without requiring removal of the adsorbent. In situ methods, such as backwashing or cyclic regeneration, can reduce downtime and enhance process efficiency in filtration applications.

Several physicochemical parameters also govern the desorption of contaminants from MOFs (). Adjusting the solution pH significantly influences adsorption and desorption behavior; certain metal contaminants adsorb rapidly at specific pH values and can subsequently be released following a change in pH. Similarly, modifying the ionic strength can alter MOF–pollutant interactions; for instance, added salts promote desorption by competing with contaminants for available active sites. Elevated temperature increases molecular mobility, thereby facilitating contaminant release, while solvent exchange can also enhance desorption. Competitive adsorption using molecules with higher affinity enables the displacement of adsorbed species.

Chemical agents, including chelating, reducing, and oxidizing agents, can interact with bound pollutants to release them from MOFs. Ultrasonic waves disrupt MOF-contaminant interactions, thereby accelerating desorption, while electrochemical treatments desorb charged species under an applied electric field or potential.

Experimental studies have highlighted the effectiveness of these strategies. Elsherbiny et al. regenerated Zn(BDC) using sodium hydroxide, achieving 99.7% efficiency after five cycles, with FTIR and PXRD analyses confirming the structural stability of the MOF. Nguyen et al. regenerated MOF-808 with acetone containing 2% HCl over four cycles, observing only a 5% decline in adsorption capacity and surface area, enabling at least three reuse cycles. Jiang et al. investigated the regeneration of UiO-66 after metronidazole adsorption by calcination at 300–600 °C. While calcination at 600 °C transformed UiO-66 into ZrO2, calcination at 300 °C for 4 h preserved its structural integrity and resulted in a 92.7% recovery rate. FTIR spectra confirmed the decomposition of metronidazole at higher temperatures. Subsequent adsorption experiments at 12.5 mg L−1 and 30 °C verified the reusability of UiO-66.

Although MOFs demonstrate significant promise as sustainable materials for antibiotic adsorption, several barriers still impede their large-scale application. Future research on MOF-based adsorption should focus on enhancing adsorbent stability, selectivity, and overall performance. However, much of the current literature is still restricted to batch experiments employing single-contaminant synthetic solutions, leaving several crucial gaps unaddressed. Issues such as antibiotic-specific selectivity, the effects of competing ions, and the performance of MOFs in real or complex wastewater remain insufficiently studied. Similarly, fixed-bed investigations, which are essential for understanding dynamic adsorption behavior, are still limited. For practical deployment, comprehensive evaluations of the mechanical strength and long-term durability of MOFs under real-world operating conditions are necessary. The challenges of handling low antibiotic concentrations in authentic water samples, as well as the presence of multiple coexisting pharmaceuticals, also require further study. Equally important are environmental and waste-management considerations, including monitoring potential metal-ion leaching, developing effective regeneration strategies for column-scale operation, and ensuring the safe disposal of exhausted MOFs. A critical transition from laboratory-scale batch studies to column experiments is needed to address operational challenges such as head loss, flow rate optimization, and channeling. Moreover, computational and modeling tools, including design-of-experiments approaches and artificial neural networks, remain underutilized in optimizing MOF adsorption processes. Finally, the economic aspects of large-scale MOF production have received little attention; systematic studies on manufacturing costs are essential to assess the feasibility and promote the sustainable development of this technology. These challenges and their corresponding solutions are discussed below.

A less frequently acknowledged limitation in the current literature is the absence of standardized experimental conditions for comparing MOF adsorbents. Reported capacities are obtained using widely different antibiotic concentrations, sorbent dosages, pH values, temperatures and contact times, while some studies report fitted Langmuir capacities and others report experimental equilibrium uptake or percentage removal. Consequently, apparent differences among materials may reflect variations in experimental design as much as differences in intrinsic adsorbent performance. This problem is amplified when dissimilar antibiotic molecules are compared, because molecular size, charge state, aromaticity and coordination ability determine which MOF functionalities become advantageous. Although high adsorption capacities remain useful indicators of sorbent potential, they should therefore not serve as the sole basis for identifying superior materials. Earlier critical work has proposed preferential adsorption metrics, effective surface-area metrics and other normalized performance descriptors precisely because conventional capacity comparisons can obscure the underlying structure–mechanism–performance relationships. Future studies should adopt standardized benchmark concentrations, report equilibrium and kinetic capacities separately, quantify adsorption at environmentally realistic concentrations and include standard tests for hydrolytic stability, metal leaching, regeneration, selectivity and fixed-bed breakthrough. Establishing such datasets would permit statistically meaningful comparisons and substantially improve the predictive value of MOF structure–property–performance relationships.

A major knowledge gap lies in the long-term structural stability of MOFs when exposed to water and wastewater matrices containing diverse ions, organic matter, and fluctuating pH. Some MOFs can undergo degradation under aqueous conditions, thereby reducing their adsorption efficiency. For example, MOF-74 undergoes structural degradation upon exposure to humidity or water due to hydrolysis or ligand dissociation. Future research should focus on designing hydrolytically stable MOFs or protective composites that preserve their structural integrity while maintaining high adsorption performance. Engineering inherently water-stable frameworks or applying post-synthetic modifications and hydrophobic coatings will be essential to maintain adsorption performance and longevity.

The regeneration of MOFs after antibiotic adsorption remains poorly studied compared to their initial adsorption performance. Efficient and sustainable desorption methods are necessary to ensure multiple cycles of use. Currently, harsh solvents or energy-intensive methods are often used, limiting practical feasibility. Future studies should develop green, low-cost regeneration strategies while maintaining adsorption capacity and framework stability.

Although the studies discussed above confirm that MOFs can simultaneously capture antibiotics and coexisting contaminants, the available evidence remains scarce compared with the extensive literature based on single-solute systems. Importantly, observations from binary mixtures should not automatically be extrapolated to authentic wastewater containing dozens of organic and inorganic species. Future research should therefore employ multicomponent matrices containing environmentally relevant concentrations of antibiotics, heavy metals, nutrients, dissolved organic matter and background electrolytes and should quantify both individual and overall removal efficiencies. Particular attention should be directed toward determining whether coexisting species produce competitive, independent or synergistic interactions during adsorption and how such interactions influence framework stability, selectivity and regeneration. Continuous-flow experiments using real municipal, hospital, pharmaceutical and livestock wastewater are especially necessary to establish whether multifunctional MOFs retain their performance under realistic hydraulic and fouling conditions. Mechanistic methods such as XPS, two-dimensional correlation FTIR spectroscopy, operando spectroscopy and molecular simulations should further be employed to identify changes in adsorption-site occupation and pollutant speciation within mixed systems.

Despite impressive laboratory-scale performance, the scalability of MOF synthesis for industrial wastewater treatment is still limited by high costs, high energy consumption, and the use of toxic organic solvents. Translating laboratory success to large-scale application is hindered by high costs, reliance on toxic solvents, and batch-based synthesis methods. Emerging scalable synthesis techniques, such as microwave-assisted solvothermal synthesis, bio-inspired methods, mechanochemical milling, spray-drying, flow chemistry, and high-pressure homogenization, offer promising alternatives that merit further development and optimization to make MOFs more industrially feasible.

Another important knowledge gap concerns the potential ecotoxicity and environmental risks of MOFs themselves when used in large-scale applications. Leaching of metal ions or degradation products into water systems may pose risks to aquatic life and human health. Therefore, comprehensive environmental risk assessments, including life-cycle and toxicity studies, should accompany future MOF development to ensure environmental compatibility and regulatory compliance.

MOFs are rarely applied as part of integrated water treatment systems. In practice, adsorption alone may not be sufficient, and coupling MOFs with other processes such as photocatalysis, membrane filtration, or advanced oxidation could enhance removal efficiency. More research is required to evaluate synergistic effects and optimize hybrid systems incorporating MOFs for the removal of antibiotic pollutants.

The efficiency of MOF-based adsorption is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. The effect of water chemistry parameters (e.g., ionic strength, dissolved organic matter, pH and temperature) on antibiotic adsorption by MOFs is still not well documented. These factors can significantly alter adsorption kinetics and capacity. Systematic investigations are necessary to assess MOF performance under diverse environmental conditions to ensure applicability in real-world scenarios. Controlled lab studies need to be complemented by evaluations across a range of realistic environmental variables, leading to the creation of MOFs that maintain high performance under varying conditions.

MOFs are often tested against a limited range of model antibiotics, while the real-world problem includes diverse classes such as sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and β-lactams. The selective adsorption of MOFs for different structural classes of antibiotics is poorly understood. Future research should design functionalized MOFs tailored for specific antibiotic groups to maximize removal efficiency. Researchers should also prioritize MOF tuning for class-specific selectivity and broad-spectrum removal, guided by molecular structure–adsorption relationships.

Introducing structural defects into porous materials such as MOFs is a powerful strategy to enhance their adsorption performance. Defects such as missing linkers, missing nodes, or open metal sites can create additional adsorption sites and increase pore accessibility, thereby improving uptake capacity and selectivity for target molecules. For instance, vacancy engineering can expose coordinatively unsaturated metal centers, which serve as high-affinity binding sites for gas molecules or contaminants. Additionally, controlled disorder may introduce microenvironments that favor specific interactions, such as hydrogen bonding or π–π stacking, thereby further improving adsorption behavior. However, while these benefits are significant, excessive or poorly controlled defect introduction can undermine the structural integrity and long-term stability of the framework. A key challenge in defect engineering lies in optimizing the type, concentration, and spatial distribution of defects to achieve a functional balance between enhanced adsorption and mechanical robustness. Approaches such as modulator-driven synthesis, post-synthetic modification, or thermal treatment can help fine-tune defect profiles without compromising crystallinity. Going forward, a deeper understanding of defect–property relationships, supported by advanced characterization and computational modeling, will be essential to harness defect engineering as a precise and scalable tool in materials design for adsorption applications.

Although some studies employ DFT and molecular dynamics simulations to study adsorption, computational modeling remains underutilized in predicting MOF–antibiotic interactions. Machine learning approaches could accelerate the discovery of new MOFs by predicting adsorption capacity and stability from structural features. Expanding computational tools will bridge the gap between theoretical design and experimental validation.

The incorporation of MOFs into the circular economy remains underdeveloped. Future prospects also involve integrating MOFs into a circular economy framework. Instead of disposal, possibilities like repurposing antibiotic-loaded MOFs for the corresponding applications or regenerating them within circular systems could substantially reduce environmental footprints. Future research should design MOFs not only for performance but also for reintegration into sustainable frameworks. Research on sustainable end-of-life strategies for MOFs is scarce but essential to minimize environmental footprints and align with global sustainability goals.

MOFs exhibit substantial potential for antibiotic adsorption because their pore architecture, metal nodes and linker chemistry can be systematically tailored to regulate molecular accessibility and host–guest interactions. The adsorption process is rarely governed by a single mechanism; rather, pore filling, electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, π–π interactions and coordination with exposed metal sites frequently operate concurrently. Among the materials evaluated in this review, Mn-PBO/GO exhibited the highest reported adsorption capacity, reaching 1183.56 mg g−1 for ciprofloxacin. Nevertheless, such maximum capacities should not be interpreted as an absolute ranking of adsorbent quality because they originate from studies conducted under different concentrations, pH values, dosages and equilibrium conditions. A more informative comparison is obtained from structurally related materials examined against the same adsorbate. In the isostructural MIL-101(M)–NH2 series, for example, MIL-101(Fe)–NH2 showed the highest adsorption capacity of 607.3 mg g−1 for Rocephin, compared with 413.7 mg g−1 for MIL-101(Al)–NH2 and 281.9 mg g−1 for MIL-101(Cr)–NH2. Its superior performance despite the higher BET surface area of the Al analogue demonstrates that adsorption cannot be predicted from BET surface area alone; the chemical identity of the metal node, accessibility of adsorption sites and strength of antibiotic–framework interactions are equally decisive.

Collectively, the literature therefore does not support a simple hierarchy in which the MOF with the largest surface area or highest qmax is automatically the most suitable antibiotic adsorbent. Instead, performance emerges from a multidimensional relationship involving accessible porosity, metal-node chemistry, linker functionality, antibiotic speciation, aqueous stability and regeneration behaviour. Several high-capacity composites remain insufficiently evaluated for metal leaching, mechanical durability, low-concentration adsorption and repeated regeneration, whereas more robust Zr- and Fe-based frameworks may provide a more credible compromise between adsorption efficiency and operational stability. The field should consequently progress beyond the pursuit of record capacities under optimized single-solute batch conditions toward standardized head-to-head benchmarking, environmentally relevant concentrations, multicomponent and real wastewater matrices, continuous-flow and fixed-bed studies, long-term regeneration, metal-leaching assessment and life-cycle evaluation. Only through such application-oriented validation can it be established whether the molecular tunability that makes MOFs scientifically attractive can be converted into a technically and economically meaningful advantage over established wastewater-treatment adsorbents.

medicine.title: Seed Amplification Assay–Based Detection of Alpha-Synuclein Aggregates Outperforms Immunohistochemical Analysis in the Intestinal Mucosal Biopsies of Parkinson’s Disease and Multiple System Atrophy Participants
medicine.abstract: To determine whether an α-synuclein (α-Syn) seed-amplification-assay (SAA) detects seeding-competent aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies, differs by gastrointestinal region, registers pathology more frequently than immunohistochemistry (IHC), and associates with Parkinson’s disease (PD) diagnosis, disease duration or severity.This cross-sectional, proof-of-concept diagnostic accuracy study analyzed duodenum, ileum, and sigmoid biopsies from PD participants, age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), plus exploratory multiple system atrophy (MSA) subtypes [parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar (MSA-C)]. Ileal and sigmoid PD and HC biopsies were assessed using proteinase K-resistant phospho-Ser129 IHC. SAA-positivity was evaluated against clinical and biological measures.In PD, SAA detected seeding-competent α-Syn aggregates with high observed specificity (97.5–100%) and region-dependent sensitivity (18/37, 48.65% in ileum and 36/56, 64.29% in sigmoid). Sigmoid SAA positivity increased significantly with PD disease duration (40.00% at <5 years, 73.33% at 5–10 years, and 93.75% at >10 years), independent of motor severity, whereas ileal positivity remained stable across disease stages. In 37 paired sigmoid biopsies, SAA detected α-Syn aggregates 2.8-fold more frequently than IHC. Sigmoid seeding activity was detected in all five MSA-P, but not in two MSA-C. IHC did not detect aggregates in any MSA.In PD, α-Syn SAA detected seeding-competent α-Syn-aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies with high observed specificity, moderate sensitivity, and approximately 2.8-fold higher detection rate than IHC in sigmoid. Positive SAA in MSA patients supports GI involvement across synucleinopathies. SAA detection in PD differed by intestinal region and disease duration, supporting further validation of intestinal SAA as a PD biomarker.Alpha-synuclein (α-syn) seed-amplification-assay (SAA) is highly accurate in cerebrospinal fluid and skin, but collection requires a dedicated invasive or minor surgical procedure and is not collected at population scale.Four previous studies have reported α-syn seeding activity in gastrointestinal biopsies, with sample sizes of 7–23 patients, single anatomical regions, and widely varying positivity rates.Immunohistochemistry for α-syn in mucosal biopsies is limited by sparse, unevenly distributed pathology, the absence of a standardized scoring system, and its inability to establish whether detected aggregates are seeding-competent.Whether gastrointestinal seeding activity varies by anatomical region, disease duration, disease severity or severity of motor and GI symptoms is unknown.In the largest gastrointestinal α-Syn SAA series to date (96 participants), biopsies obtained during routine endoscopy identified PD with 97.50-100% specificity and moderate sensitivity (48.65% ileum, 64.29% sigmoid).Sigmoid SAA-positivity was duration dependent, rising from 40% at <5 years to 94% beyond 10 years (adjusted OR 2.82 per 5 years), and disease duration was the only independent correlate once H&Y stage was included in the model.Constipation, intestinal inflammation, and sigmoid mucosal dysbiosis tracked PD severity but did not distinguish sigmoid SAA-positive from SAA-negative participants.Ileal SAA-positivity was constant across disease duration and severity, indicating that positivity was not uniform along the gastrointestinal tract.In the identical PD participant’s sigmoid tissue, SAA identified α-Syn pathology in 28 of 37 patients compared with 10 of 37 by proteinase K-resistant phospho-Ser129 immunohistochemistry.Sigmoid SAA-positivity was detected in 5 of 7 participants with MSA, with positive cases confined to the parkinsonian subtype (MSA-P) and negative cases to the cerebellar subtype (MSA-C).Strain typing by α-Syn SAA enables differentiation of PD from MSA cases using sigmoid biopsies.Colonoscopy is already performed at scale in the age group at-risk of PD, so mucosal biopsies are an accessible matrix for α-Syn seeding assays and for biomarker-based enrichment of clinical trials.Because yield depends on both sampling site and disease duration, prospective validation against cerebrospinal fluid must specify region and stage; a negative result from a single site cannot currently exclude PD.

medicine.title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
medicine.abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV- associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.Adults over 50 years of age comprise a rapidly growing proportion of both HIV treatment and prevention populations, yet the biological effects of aging on antiretroviral drug disposition remain poorly understood. We demonstrate that aging, sex, and HIV status differentially alter proteins and pathways involved in antiretroviral transport, activation, and nucleotide homeostasis, with the most pronounced effects occurring in colorectal tissue, providing a mechanistic foundation for future studies of HIV therapeutics in aging populations.

medicine.title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease
medicine.abstract:
Background
Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. 
Methods
We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity.
Results
A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099. The mitigation of degenerative neuropathology was linked to targeted inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2 and complemented by reduced levels of gliosis in astrocytes and microglia in the SN. Single-microglia segmentation analysis suggested URMC-099 treatment preserved dynamic effector state switching in microglia to enhance autophagic flux to reduce the overall burden of pathologic aSyn. Transcriptomic analysis of a complementary in vitro microglia model corroborated the retention of a homeostatic-like effector state with URMC-099 treatment that was unique to MLK3/LRRK2 dual inhibition.
Conclusions
Unilateral injection of low dose AAV-haSyn successfully resulted in a lateralized model of early, progressive PD. Dual inhibition of aberrant MLK3 and LRRK2 activity with once-daily i.p. URMC-099 therapy significantly mitigated the development of PD pathology and progression in an early manifest phenotype. Our results present a potential mechanism of therapeutic action dependent on the dual inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2. This presents a novel therapeutic modality that may be beneficial to a broad population of etiologic PD patients.
