psychology.title: Beyond symptom severity: Prognostic information from subjective person‐specific problem networks in young people
psychology.abstract: Person‐specific network models are increasingly proposed to support personalized assessment and psychotherapy, but it remains unclear whether the information they contain is prospectively informative in young people. We tested whether characteristics derived from a brief perceived causal network (PECAN), particularly its perceived relational structure, provided prognostic information about subsequent psychopathology beyond baseline symptom severity.Participants were 361 children, adolescents, and young adults assessed by self‐report or parent‐report. At baseline, participants selected personally relevant problems, rated their severity, and indicated how they perceived these problems to be related. Psychopathology was assessed with the pediatric symptom checklist (PSC‐D) at baseline and approximately 4, 8, and 12 weeks later. Linear mixed‐effects models examined prospective associations of PECAN characteristics with psychopathology. Exploratory post hoc analyses additionally examined problem breadth, defined as the number of personally relevant problems selected.Global characteristics of perceived problem relations showed little consistent incremental prognostic information beyond baseline psychopathology and problem breadth. Mean perceived causal strength and maximum normalized weighted outdegree were not associated with subsequent psychopathology, while an inverse association with network density emerged only in self‐report and was not robust across sensitivity analyses. In exploratory analyses, greater problem breadth was associated with higher subsequent psychopathology in both self‐report and parent‐report, and these associations remained essentially unchanged after adjustment for conventional PSC‐D symptom breadth.The first prospective evaluation of PECANs provided limited support for incremental prognostic information contained in global perceived relational characteristics. Exploratory analyses nevertheless identified problem breadth as a potentially informative compositional characteristic of personalized problem representations. These findings suggest that different components of person‐specific models should be evaluated separately and highlight the need for confirmatory replication before they inform personalized clinical decisions.
psychology.text:
Person‐specific models of psychopathology are increasingly proposed as a basis for personalized assessment and psychotherapy, including individualized case conceptualization and the identification of potentially relevant treatment targets (Bringmann, ; Burger et al., ; von Klipstein et al., ; Wright & Woods, ). The relevance of such personalization is also supported in young people: a recent meta‐analysis of randomized trials found a small but significant advantage of personalized over standardized psychological interventions in adolescents, while also highlighting substantial heterogeneity in how personalization was implemented (Li et al., ). Young people are a particularly important population in which to evaluate person‐specific approaches because many mental disorders first emerge during childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood, making this a critical period for early assessment and intervention (Solmi et al., ). Person‐specific representations may be especially relevant during this period because psychological difficulties can be heterogeneous and may change substantially across development. Person‐specific network approaches represent one potential route toward such personalization because they conceptualize psychopathology as a system of interacting problems while allowing the configuration of that system to be characterized at the level of the individual (Borsboom, ; Bringmann, ). Such representations may preserve clinically relevant heterogeneity that is obscured when individuals are summarized by diagnostic categories or aggregate symptom scores, as individuals with similar overall symptom severity can differ substantially in the particular problems contributing to that severity (Fried & Nesse, ; Sonuga‐Barke, ).

As person‐specific networks move toward clinical applications, establishing the validity of the information they provide becomes increasingly important. Their use for personalization rests on one fundamental empirical assumption: characteristics captured by these models should contain information relevant to subsequent clinical course. Initial evidence from statistically estimated person‐specific longitudinal networks is promising but limited. In adults receiving psychotherapy for chronic depression, person‐specific symptom‐network characteristics improved prediction of treatment outcome beyond conventional baseline characteristics, with pairwise symptom associations contributing particularly strongly (Schumacher et al., ). A reanalysis of the same data supported incremental information from symptom associations beyond changes in symptom severity (Schumacher et al., ). A smaller proof‐of‐concept study likewise found prospective associations between idiographic network characteristics and depression outcomes 6 months later (Cusack et al., ). Together, these findings suggest that person‐specific network information may be prospectively informative, but available evidence is based primarily on networks estimated from intensive repeated assessments.

Perceived Causal Networks (PECANs) offer a substantially lower‐burden approach to constructing person‐specific networks (Klintwall et al., ; Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). Rather than estimating relations statistically from repeated measurements across days or weeks, individuals construct a network within a single assessment by selecting psychological problems they consider personally relevant, rating their current severity, and indicating whether and how strongly they perceive these problems to influence one another (Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). The resulting network therefore represents the individual's subjective understanding of their difficulties rather than statistically established or objectively causal relations. At the same time, evaluating PECANs in young people raises a specific developmental question because the method requires both recognition of personally relevant difficulties and judgments about how these difficulties influence one another. These components may not be equally accessible across development. This raises the possibility that the compositional and relational components of PECANs may also differ in their validity. Previous PECAN‐CA research found that older age and better understanding of symptom and network concepts were associated with more reliable network representations and greater feasibility (Vogel, Fromm, et al., ).

Previous research supports several prerequisites for investigating the prospective validity of PECANs. In adults, PECANs were highly individualized and showed good immediate reliability (Klintwall et al., ), while the child and adolescent adaptation demonstrated good feasibility and reliability for several characteristics (Vogel, Fromm, et al., ). Young people with similar social‐anxiety presentations also rated their personalized PECANs as more representative than randomized or prototypical disorder representations (Vogel et al., ). These findings suggest that PECANs can efficiently capture person‐specific differences that respondents recognize as representative of their difficulties. Whether such differences also contain information about subsequent psychopathology, however, remains unknown.

A particularly demanding benchmark for evaluating such information is current psychopathology. Baseline symptom severity is itself strongly prognostic: in more than 11,000 young people, current symptoms predicted transition into the highest psychopathology‐risk group one year later with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.84 (Hill et al., ). For a personalized representation to provide meaningful additional prognostic information, it therefore needs to capture characteristics of an individual's difficulties that are not already contained in overall symptom severity.

Importantly, PECANs contain two conceptually distinguishable layers of personalized information. First, the selection of problems characterizes the composition of an individual's difficulties, including their breadth—that is, how many different problems are considered personally relevant. Second, the perceived relations characterize how these selected problems are subjectively organized as a network (Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). As illustrated in Figure , young people with comparable levels of aggregate psychopathology may therefore construct personalized representations that differ both in the breadth and composition of selected problems and in how these problems are perceived to be connected.

This distinction allows a more specific question than whether a person‐specific network as a whole is prognostically informative: where within the representation does prospective information reside? Personalized problem selection may preserve heterogeneity that is lost in aggregate scores. Previous longitudinal research provides indirect evidence that higher psychiatric symptom counts in adolescence and difficulties spanning multiple problem domains are associated with poorer subsequent outcomes (Vander Stoep et al., ; Verhulst & van der Ende, ), while greater transdiagnostic symptom diversity has been associated with higher distress and lower well‐being (Kennedy et al., ). However, these approaches generally do not separate breadth from overall symptom burden. The relational component of a PECAN may, in turn, provide additional information about how an individual's problems are perceived to reinforce or influence one another. Whether either component carries prospective information beyond conventional symptom severity has not previously been tested.

The present prospective study therefore provided, to our knowledge, the first test of the prognostic information contained in Perceived Causal Networks, examining whether such brief person‐specific representations are prospectively informative across childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood. Using both self‐ and parent‐report, we assessed PECANs at baseline and psychopathology approximately 4, 8, and 12 weeks later. We used a hierarchical approach to distinguish information contained in personalized problem composition from information contained in relational network structure. The preregistered analyses focused on characteristics of the perceived relations among problems. Exploratory post hoc analyses additionally examined problem breadth, the number of problems identified as personally relevant, as a compositional characteristic associated with subsequent psychopathology beyond baseline symptom severity. Relational characteristics were subsequently evaluated after accounting for both baseline psychopathology and problem breadth.

Data were obtained from a completed longitudinal study conducted between January and August 2026 examining person‐specific representations of psychological problems in children, adolescents, and young adults. Participants were recruited through postal mailings distributed to households, a university outpatient psychotherapy clinic, schools, and social media. Depending on age, assessments were completed either by young people themselves or by a parent reporting on their child. Parent reports were obtained for children and adolescents aged 6–17 years, whereas self‐reports were obtained from adolescents and young adults aged 14–21 years. Self‐ and parent‐report data were analyzed separately because each PECAN represents the respective informant's subjective representation of the young person's problems.

At baseline (T1), participants completed a PECAN assessment and the Pediatric Symptom Checklist (PSC‐D). As in previous PECAN studies, a second PECAN assessment was administered shortly thereafter to evaluate short‐term reliability (Klintwall et al., ; Vogel, Fromm, et al., ). At this second assessment, the problems selected during the initial PECAN were retained, and participants repeated the assessment of perceived relations among these problems. Psychopathology was reassessed approximately 4, 8, and 12 weeks later (T2–T4). Reliability analyses were based on participants with sufficient repeated PECAN data. The assessment schedule is summarized in Figure .

The original dataset comprised 723 baseline records. Records were excluded because of duplicate participation, consent or data‐use issues, age or informant ineligibility, incomplete baseline participation, or prespecified response‐quality criteria. Detailed participant flow and reasons for exclusion are shown in Supporting Information : Figure S1.

The final analytic sample comprised 361 participants, including 255 self‐reports and 106 parent reports. All participants had selected at least three problems and provided sufficient baseline data to derive the relevant PECAN characteristics. The original sample size was informed by an a priori power analysis indicating that approximately 62 participants were required to detect an association of r = 0.35 with 80% power at α = 0.05; recruitment targets were increased to accommodate attrition.

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (2025‐JGU‐psychEK‐S072). Written informed consent was obtained from legal guardians or directly from adolescents where they were considered capable of providing informed consent; assent was obtained from minors where applicable. The analyses and data‐quality procedures were preregistered on AsPredicted (No. 269,512). Reporting followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline; the completed checklist is provided in the Appendix S1.

Perceived Causal Networks are person‐specific representations of psychological problems and their perceived relations (Klintwall et al., ; Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). Participants selected 3–7 personally relevant problems from a 24‐item transdiagnostic problem pool. The pool was developed as a clinically and developmentally informed set of candidate problems intended to provide broad coverage of psychological difficulties relevant to children and adolescents while remaining suitable for use in a community‐based sample. HiTOP served as a conceptual framework for broad transdiagnostic coverage rather than as a formal one‐to‐one mapping of individual problems onto HiTOP spectra. The pool additionally included developmentally relevant interpersonal, school‐related, behavioral, and health‐related difficulties that may be salient to young people and parents but are not fully represented by conventional symptom categories. Short problem labels were accompanied by informant‐adapted explanatory descriptions intended to facilitate comprehension. The range of 3–7 problems was chosen to provide a minimally informative relational representation while maintaining feasibility and reliability, consistent with previous PECAN‐CA findings (Vogel, Fromm, et al., ). The problem list covered internalizing, externalizing, attentional, behavioral, cognitive, interpersonal, somatic, and health‐related difficulties and is provided in Supporting Information : Table S1.

For each selected problem, participants rated current severity from 0 (no distress) to 10 (extreme distress). Perceived relations were subsequently elicited for each selected problem. Participants were instructed to consider: “If this difficulty gets worse, which other difficulties also get worse?” and “What else can this difficulty lead to for you?” They then indicated which of their other selected problems were influenced by the focal problem. For each endorsed relation, participants rated its strength from 1 to 10, with the endpoints labeled “very low influence” and “very strong influence.” The resulting PECAN is therefore a directed, weighted representation of participants' subjective understanding of how their problems influence one another rather than evidence of objective causal effects.

The core PECAN network‐construction component—selection of personally relevant problems, severity ratings, and ratings of perceived relations—was timed electronically. Completion time was calculated by summing the corresponding page‐level completion times; values exceeding 30 min were excluded from timing descriptives as likely interruptions.

We derived characteristics corresponding to three complementary aspects of the individualized problem representation: 
Problem breadth
 was the number of problems selected as personally relevant (range 3–7). All selected problems contributed to this count irrespective of their subsequent severity rating, because problem selection and current severity were treated as distinct components of the personalized representation. 
Problem intensity
 was indexed by mean severity across selected problems. Summed PECAN severity, used in preregistered concurrent analyses, combined breadth and intensity and was therefore not interpreted as a breadth‐independent intensity measure. Three characteristics summarized 
problem relations
. Mean perceived causal strength was the average strength of endorsed relations. Network density was the proportion of all possible directed relations that were endorsed. Weighted outdegree was the summed strength of outgoing relations for each problem, normalized by its maximum possible value, 10 (k − 1); the maximum normalized weighted outdegree across problems was retained.

General psychopathology was assessed using the 17‐item German Pediatric Symptom Checklist (PSC‐D; Dippel et al., ) in corresponding self‐ and parent‐report versions. Items are rated from 0 (never) to two (often), yielding total scores from 0 to 34. The total score was used at baseline and as the primary follow‐up outcome; internalizing and externalizing subscales were examined exploratorily. Self‐report PECAN characteristics were related to self‐reported PSC‐D scores and parent‐report characteristics to parent‐reported scores.

The German PSC‐D has been validated in children and adolescents up to age 17 (Dippel et al., ). Because the self‐report sample also included young adults aged 18–21 years, central self‐report analyses were repeated after restricting the sample to the age range covered by the German validation. The PSC‐17 has previously been used in samples including participants up to age 21 (Doupnik et al., ).

Internal consistency of the PSC‐D total score was evaluated separately by informant and measurement occasion.

Self‐ and parent‐report data were analyzed separately throughout. Unless otherwise stated, continuous PECAN predictors were standardized within informant group, effect estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals, and two‐sided statistical tests were evaluated at α = 0.05.

Following previous PECAN studies (Klintwall et al., ; Vogel, Fromm, et al., ), short‐term reliability was assessed using within‐person Spearman correlations for weighted directed relations and absolute‐agreement intraclass correlation coefficients for weighted outdegree. For relation‐level reliability, participant‐specific Spearman correlations were calculated between the complete weighted relation vectors of the two PECAN assessments, with absent relations represented by zero; the median correlation and a bootstrap 95% confidence interval were used as summary measures. Outdegree reliability was quantified using a two‐way absolute‐agreement, single‐measure ICC [ICC(A, 1)].

Concurrent associations between PECAN characteristics and baseline PSC‐D psychopathology were examined separately by informant. Pearson correlations were used as primary estimates, with Spearman correlations examined as rank‐based sensitivity analyses. Mean severity across selected problems was examined as the breadth‐independent indicator of problem intensity. The preregistered analysis using summed PECAN severity was additionally retained; because this score combines the number and severity of selected problems, it was interpreted as an indicator of combined problem breadth and intensity rather than problem intensity alone. Mean perceived causal strength and network density were examined as characteristics of problem relations. Their joint associations of causal strength and density with baseline psychopathology were additionally examined using standardized linear regression models.

The central analyses examined whether baseline person‐specific characteristics provided prognostic information beyond baseline psychopathology. All available PSC‐D observations at T2–T4 were analyzed jointly using linear mixed‐effects models with participant‐specific random intercepts. Models included baseline PSC‐D total score and follow‐up time, coded 0, 1, and 2 for T2, T3, and T4, respectively. Continuous PECAN predictors were standardized within informant group.

Analyses followed a hierarchical approach (Figure ). Problem breadth, indexed by the number of selected problems, was first examined after adjustment for baseline PSC‐D and follow‐up time. Problem breadth had not been specified as the central prognostic construct in the preregistration and was therefore treated as an exploratory post hoc characteristic of the personalized problem representation. Characteristics of problem relations, mean perceived causal strength, network density, and maximum normalized weighted outdegree, were subsequently examined in separate models additionally adjusted for problem breadth. Maximum normalized weighted outdegree was likewise added post hoc as an exploratory relational characteristic.

Incremental model fit associated with problem breadth was evaluated using likelihood‐ratio tests and changes in Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Benjamini–Hochberg false‐discovery‐rate correction was applied across the three relational characteristics separately within each informant group. Problem breadth was treated as a distinct conceptual test and was therefore not included in this correction.

The preregistered prospective analysis plan included longitudinal trajectory models and baseline‐adjusted prospective analyses, with the latter originally framed as sensitivity analyses. We emphasize the baseline‐adjusted models in the present manuscript because they most directly address whether PECAN characteristics provide prognostic information beyond current psychopathology. The preregistered trajectory analyses are reported in the Supporting Information : Table S5. All analytic refinements relative to the preregistration—including the post hoc examination of problem breadth and maximum normalized weighted outdegree—are summarized in Supporting Information : Table S2. Detailed supporting analyses are reported in Supporting Information : Table S3 (retest reliability), Table S4a,b (concurrent associations), Table S6a–c (sensitivity analyses), Supporting Information : Table S7 (attrition analyses), and Supporting Information : Table S8 (exploratory subscale analyses).

Sensitivity analyses examined robustness to source subsample, follow‐up availability, conventional PSC‐D item breadth, response quality, and restriction of self‐report analyses to ages 14–17 years. Pediatric Symptom Checklist item breadth was defined as the number of baseline items endorsed at least sometimes (>0). Internalizing and externalizing PSC‐D scores were examined as exploratory secondary outcomes. Further details are provided in Supporting Information : Table S8.

A post hoc sensitivity analysis examined whether the prognostic association of problem breadth depended on including selected problems with very low current severity. The central models were therefore repeated using a severity‐qualified breadth score counting only selected problems rated ≥2 on the 0–10 severity scale. This threshold was used as a reviewer‐motivated robustness check rather than as a validated clinical cutoff.

The final analytic sample comprised 361 participants, including 255 self‐report and 106 parent‐report participants. Self‐report participants were 14–21 years old (M = 18.14, SD = 1.69), whereas young people represented in the parent‐report sample were 6–17 years old (M = 10.14, SD = 3.07). Baseline PSC‐D scores averaged 9.49 (SD = 5.71) in self‐report and 11.67 (SD = 5.55) in parent‐report. For descriptive context, both mean scores were below the screening threshold of 15 established for the original PSC‐17 (Gardner et al., ). This threshold indicates a positive psychosocial screen rather than a diagnostic or clinical severity classification. German norms distinguishing normal, subclinical, and clinical ranges have not yet been established for the PSC‐D and are currently under development (Dippel et al., ). Participants selected on average 4.42 (SD = 1.68) and 4.30 (SD = 1.54) personally relevant problems, respectively. Mean problem intensity was 7.40 (SD = 1.86) in self‐report and 6.67 (SD = 1.86) in parent‐report. Further baseline characteristics are presented in Table . Internal consistency of the PSC‐D total score was acceptable to good across measurement occasions in both self‐report (Cronbach's α = 0.729–0.835) and parent‐report (α = 0.756–0.783). The core PECAN network construction took on average 3.96 min (SD = 3.08; median = 3.26; IQR = 1.78–5.20) among 332 participants with usable timing data.

Baseline sample and PECAN characteristics.

Abbreviation: PECAN, perceived causal network.

Follow‐up PSC‐D data were available for 231 participants at T2, 179 at T3, and 172 at T4. Overall, 235 participants (65.1%) contributed at least one follow‐up assessment, including 161 self‐report participants (63.1%) and 74 parent‐report participants (69.8%); 163 participants completed all four assessments.

Follow‐up availability was associated with several baseline characteristics, including problem breadth in the parent‐report sample and, for T4 availability, in the self‐report sample. Additional associations were observed for baseline psychopathology, age, characteristics of problem relations, and source subsample. Primary mixed‐effects models incorporated all available follow‐up observations rather than requiring complete cases.

Short‐term reliability of weighted problem relations differed between informants. Median within‐person Spearman correlations between the two PECAN assessments were high in self‐report (median ρ = 0.984, 95% CI [0.763, 1.00]) and moderate in parent‐report (median ρ = 0.518, 95% CI [0.402, 0.645]). Weighted outdegree showed ICCs of 0.785 (95% CI [0.718, 0.837]) in self‐report and 0.732 (95% CI [0.684, 0.773]) in parent‐report; thus, the preregistered ICC threshold of 0.80 was not reached in either informant group. Detailed reliability analyses are reported in Supporting Information : Figure S2 and Table S3.

Concurrent associations with baseline psychopathology differed across characteristics of the person‐specific representation. Summed PECAN severity, which combines problem breadth and intensity, was positively associated with baseline PSC‐D scores in both self‐report (r = 0.589, p < 0.001) and parent‐report (r = 0.262, p = 0.007). In contrast, mean severity across selected problems showed no positive association with baseline PSC‐D scores in self‐report (r = −0.121, p = 0.054) or parent‐report (r = −0.167, p = 0.088).

Characteristics of perceived problem relations showed small inverse concurrent associations with psychopathology. Mean perceived causal strength was negatively associated with baseline PSC‐D scores in both self‐report (r = −0.186, p = 0.003) and parent‐report (r = −0.257, p = 0.008). Network density was negatively associated with PSC‐D scores in self‐report (r = −0.211, p < 0.001), but not in parent‐report (r = −0.088, p = 0.370). In models including both relational characteristics, causal strength and density retained independent associations in self‐report (β = −0.144, p = 0.023; β = −0.176, p = 0.005, respectively), whereas only causal strength remained associated in parent‐report (β = −0.249, p = 0.011; density: β = −0.050, p = 0.602). Full concurrent analyses are provided in Supporting Information : Table S4a,b.

Problem breadth provided prognostic information beyond baseline psychopathology in both informant groups. As expected, baseline PSC‐D strongly predicted subsequent psychopathology (self‐report: b = 0.61, 95% CI [0.52, 0.70], p < 0.001; parent‐report: b = 0.60, 95% CI [0.49, 0.71], p < 0.001). After adjustment for baseline PSC‐D and follow‐up time, greater problem breadth was associated with higher PSC‐D scores across T2–T4 in self‐report (b = 1.23, 95% CI [0.67, 1.79], p < 0.001) and parent‐report (b = 1.48, 95% CI [0.78, 2.17], p < 0.001).

Thus, individuals who identified a broader range of problems as personally relevant showed higher subsequent psychopathology even when they had comparable levels of psychopathology at baseline. A 1‐SD increase in problem breadth corresponded to approximately 1.68 additional selected problems in self‐report and 1.54 in parent‐report. Expressed per additional selected problem, this corresponds to approximately 0.73 higher PSC‐D points in self‐report and 0.96 higher PSC‐D points in parent‐report.

Adding problem breadth improved model fit beyond models containing baseline PSC‐D and follow‐up time alone in both self‐report (ΔAIC = −15.50; ΔBIC = −11.51; likelihood‐ratio p < 0.001) and parent‐report (ΔAIC = −13.32; ΔBIC = −10.11; likelihood‐ratio p < 0.001).

In contrast to problem breadth, characteristics of perceived problem relations provided little consistent additional prognostic information. After adjustment for baseline PSC‐D, follow‐up time, and problem breadth, mean perceived causal strength was not associated with subsequent psychopathology in either self‐report (b = 0.39, 95% CI [−0.03, 0.82], p = 0.071) or parent‐report (b = −0.39, 95% CI [−1.09, 0.31], p = 0.275). Maximum normalized weighted outdegree was likewise not associated with subsequent PSC‐D scores (self‐report: b = −0.26, 95% CI [−0.68, 0.15], p = 0.216; parent‐report: b = −0.38, 95% CI [−1.15, 0.40], p = 0.338).

Network density showed an inverse association with subsequent psychopathology in self‐report (b = −0.59, 95% CI [−1.07, −0.11], p = 0.017), but not in parent‐report (b = −0.38, 95% CI [−1.13, 0.38], p = 0.328). The self‐report density association was at the Benjamini–Hochberg false‐discovery‐rate threshold across the three relational characteristics (q ≈ 0.050) and was therefore interpreted cautiously. Overall, relational characteristics did not show a consistent pattern of incremental prognostic associations across informants. The network‐density associations are illustrated in Figure .

The association between problem breadth and subsequent psychopathology was robust across sensitivity analyses. Estimates were essentially unchanged after additional adjustment for the number of baseline PSC‐D items endorsed at least sometimes (self‐report: b = 1.22, 95% CI [0.66, 1.77], p < 0.001; parent‐report: b = 1.53, 95% CI [0.83, 2.22], p < 0.001). Perceived Causal Network problem breadth was moderately associated with PSC‐D item breadth in self‐report (r = 0.61) and more weakly in parent‐report (r = 0.39), indicating overlap but not equivalence between personalized problem breadth and breadth of symptom endorsement on the conventional measure.

The problem‐breadth association was also unchanged when only selected problems with severity ratings ≥2 were counted (self‐report: b = 1.27, 95% CI [0.72, 1.83], p < 0.001; parent‐report: b = 1.48, 95% CI [0.78, 2.17], p < 0.001). Only 18 of 1584 selected problems (1.1%) had severity ratings below this threshold.

Adjustment for source subsample likewise produced little change in the problem‐breadth estimates (self‐report: b = 1.25, 95% CI [0.66, 1.85], p < 0.001; parent‐report: b = 1.47, 95% CI [0.77, 2.18], p < 0.001), with similar results when source‐by‐time interactions were included. Excluding participants with a Response Speed Index >2 likewise produced little change in the central findings.

Restricting self‐report analyses to participants aged 14–17 years left 22 participants with data available across all measurement occasions (T1–T4). Despite the small sample, problem breadth remained positively associated with subsequent psychopathology (b = 1.51, p = 0.045). In contrast, the inverse density association observed in the full self‐report sample was not reproduced in this age‐restricted analysis (b = 0.34, p = 0.529), further indicating limited robustness of the relational characteristics.

The preregistered trajectory analyses similarly provided little evidence that baseline characteristics of problem relations were consistently associated with differential change in psychopathology over time. An inverse time‐by‐density association emerged in self‐report but was not robust across sensitivity analyses or reproduced in parent‐report. Preregistered trajectory analyses are reported in Supporting Information : Table S5; sensitivity analyses, including response‐speed and age‐restricted analyses, are reported in Table S6a–c; attrition analyses are reported in Supporting Information : Table S7; and exploratory subscale analyses are reported in Supporting Information : Table S8.

The present study addressed a foundational question for the use of person‐specific networks in personalized assessment and psychotherapy: which information contained in an individual's network is prospectively informative beyond conventional symptom severity? To our knowledge, this is the first prospective evaluation of Perceived Causal Networks. The central finding was that the relational component of PECANs showed little consistent incremental prognostic information. Mean perceived causal strength and maximum normalized weighted outdegree were not associated with subsequent psychopathology, and the inverse association observed for network density in self‐report was neither reproduced in parent‐report nor robust across sensitivity analyses. Thus, the aspects of PECANs most directly reflecting their network structure did not consistently predict subsequent psychopathology beyond baseline severity and problem breadth. In contrast, exploratory post hoc analyses indicated that problem breadth—the number of problems considered personally relevant—was prospectively informative in both self‐ and parent‐report. This pattern suggests that the most consistent prognostic information in the present study resided in the composition of the personalized problem representation rather than in its perceived relational structure.

This distinction reflects two conceptually different components of PECANs: individuals first define which problems constitute their personalized representation and subsequently specify relations among them (Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). The present findings suggest that, within this brief single‐assessment format, these components do not contribute equally to prospective information. The distinction between compositional and relational information is also important when considering the validity of PECANs. Respondents may be able to reliably identify and prioritize the problems they experience while having more limited insight into how these problems influence one another (Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). Accordingly, reproducibility of perceived causal relations should not be interpreted as evidence that these relations correspond to causal processes operating over time. Although the endpoints of the causal‐strength scale were verbally labeled, ratings were not anchored to concrete frequencies, situations, or external reference points. Individual differences in scale use may therefore have contributed to between‐person differences in relational characteristics based on edge strength. Future work should examine alternative causal phrasings and more concrete or comparative anchors, compare subjective relations with EMA‐derived temporal relations, and test whether clinician‐assisted elicitation, integration of empirical prior knowledge, or combination of information across informants improves the validity of relational judgments (Scholten et al., ; Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). The marked difference in relation‐level reliability between self‐ and parent‐report should also be interpreted cautiously because informant perspective was confounded with age: self‐reports were obtained from adolescents and young adults, whereas parent reports predominantly represented younger children and adolescents.

Several non‐mutually exclusive explanations may account for the association with problem breadth. First, breadth may capture a compositional aspect of psychopathology not fully represented by aggregate severity. Identical sum scores can correspond to markedly different symptom profiles (Fried & Nesse, ), and a broader personally relevant problem repertoire may reflect a more multifaceted or less circumscribed presentation. This interpretation is consistent with longitudinal findings linking higher symptom counts and difficulties spanning multiple domains to poorer subsequent outcomes (Vander Stoep et al., ; Verhulst & van der Ende, ). The present study extends this work by showing that personalized problem breadth remained prospectively informative even when baseline psychopathology was held constant.

Importantly, the breadth association also remained essentially unchanged after additional adjustment for the number of PSC‐D items endorsed at baseline. Perceived Causal Network problem breadth was therefore related to, but not interchangeable with, conventional symptom breadth. One possible explanation is that personalized problem selection captures difficulties that fall partly outside the content of a brief fixed‐item questionnaire. Perceived Causal Network allowed participants to select from a broad transdiagnostic range of problems informed by HiTOP (Kotov et al., ), whereas the PSC‐D comprises 17 fixed items (Dippel et al., ). At the same time, the present findings do not establish that personalized selection is necessary to recover this information. A more comprehensive fixed transdiagnostic assessment might capture similar breadth. Accordingly, the present breadth finding should not be interpreted as evidence that personalization itself accounts for the incremental prognostic information. The effect may partly reflect the broader or different content sampled by the PECAN problem pool relative to the PSC‐D. Direct comparisons will therefore be important for determining whether the observed signal reflects personalization itself, broader content coverage, or both.

Problem breadth may additionally reflect how individuals perceive and prioritize their difficulties. PECANs do not simply record endorsement of predefined symptoms; respondents identify which problems they consider personally relevant (Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). Breadth may therefore capture the perceived salience or scope of an individual's difficulties before any relational network is constructed. Because PECAN characteristics and PSC‐D outcomes were obtained from the same informant, shared reporting tendencies cannot be excluded. Informant agreement in young people varies with factors such as problem salience and observability (Karver, ). Nevertheless, the replication of the breadth association across self‐ and parent‐report is noteworthy given the different perspectives from which young people's difficulties were represented.

The comparatively limited prognostic information contained in relational characteristics is equally relevant for evaluating person‐specific networks. Previous studies in adults have suggested that statistically estimated person‐specific symptom relations can contribute to prediction of psychotherapy outcome and later symptom course (Cusack et al., ; Schumacher et al., , ). These findings differ from the present pattern, but the approaches capture fundamentally different forms of person‐specific information. Statistically estimated longitudinal networks derive relations from repeated within‐person observations, whereas PECAN relations represent respondents' subjective perceptions of how their problems influence one another within a single assessment (Klintwall et al., ; Vogel, Blanken, et al., ). The present results should therefore not be interpreted as evidence against relational approaches more generally.

Moreover, our analyses summarized relational organization using global characteristics such as mean perceived causal strength, density, and maximum outdegree. Global summary characteristics may not fully capture the aspects of relational organization most relevant to the network hypothesis (Bringmann, ; Cusack et al., ). Relevant information may instead reside in particular relations, local structures, or the identity of specific highly connected problems. Idiographic network characteristics can vary substantially depending on symptom selection and observation period (Cusack et al., ), and a relation that is clinically meaningful for one individual need not translate into a prognostically informative global network statistic across individuals. Future studies should therefore compare alternative representations of relational structure rather than interpreting the present null findings as a definitive test of the prognostic relevance of network organization. The inverse density association observed in self‐report was not reproduced in parent‐report or the age‐restricted sensitivity analysis and should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Overall, the present results indicate limited incremental prognostic value of the global relational characteristics examined here rather than an absence of potentially meaningful relational information within PECANs.

These findings are relevant to personalized assessment and psychotherapy in young people. Personalized interventions show a small advantage over standardized approaches in adolescents, although implementation varies considerably (Li et al., ). Person‐specific networks represent one possible route to such personalization and are increasingly proposed for case conceptualization and treatment targeting (Bringmann, ; Burger et al., ; Vogel, Blanken, et al., ; von Klipstein et al., ; Wright & Woods, ). The present study addresses one prerequisite for these applications—prospective validity—and suggests that simple problem breadth may carry more consistent information than global relational characteristics. Direct comparisons with previous PECAN studies are difficult because assessment formats and timing definitions differed. The original online PECAN required a median of 22.7 minutes including immediate retest items, whereas the interviewer‐guided PECAN‐CA procedure required approximately 29 minutes on average including 10 minutes of psychoeducation (Klintwall et al., ; Vogel, Fromm, et al., ). The present estimate of 3.26 minutes refers only to the core network‐construction component and to relatively small networks constrained to 3–7 selected problems. The resulting networks were therefore deliberately brief representations rather than exhaustive mappings of participants' difficulties. Accordingly, the present completion time should not be interpreted as a direct reduction relative to earlier PECAN estimates. Nevertheless, such brief completion raises the question of how much reflection participants devoted to perceived causal relations. The substantial short‐term consistency of relational ratings, particularly in self‐report, argues against an explanation based solely on careless responding, but does not establish the validity of these judgments.

Several limitations should be considered. First, problem breadth was intentionally constrained to between three and seven selected problems as part of the PECAN procedure. The present measure therefore captures variation in the breadth of an individual's prioritized problem representation rather than an exhaustive count of all psychological difficulties. Although problem labels were accompanied by informant‐adapted explanatory descriptions, comprehension of the individual problem terms was not formally assessed in the present study. This is relevant because previous PECAN‐CA findings suggest that understanding of symptom and network concepts may affect the reliability and feasibility of the resulting representations (Vogel, Fromm, et al., ). Second, PECAN characteristics and PSC‐D outcomes were assessed from the same informant, leaving open the possibility of shared perception or reporting effects. Replication using cross‐informant, clinician‐rated, or functional outcomes would provide stronger evidence of external validity. Third, follow‐up participation declined across the 12‐week study period and was associated with some baseline characteristics. Although the mixed‐effects models incorporated all available follow‐up observations and the central breadth association was robust across multiple sensitivity analyses, bias due to informative missingness cannot be excluded. Fourth, the follow‐up period was relatively short, and the findings therefore concern short‐term course rather than longer‐term developmental or treatment outcomes.

Finally, the present study examined incremental prognostic associations rather than developing and externally validating an individual‐level prediction model. The findings demonstrate that problem breadth contains information about subsequent psychopathology beyond baseline severity, but they do not establish predictive accuracy, decision utility, or benefit from network‐informed treatment selection for individual patients. Likewise, the limited findings for relational characteristics cannot exclude prognostic or therapeutic value contained in specific relations, local network structures, or alternative representations of relational information. Independent replication in larger longitudinal and clinical samples, longer follow‐up periods, and ultimately prospective evaluations of network‐informed clinical decisions will be required to establish which components of person‐specific networks are most useful for personalized psychotherapy.

Across childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood, a brief person‐specific assessment contained prospective information beyond conventional baseline psychopathology in both self‐ and parent‐report. Importantly, this information was not distributed uniformly across components of the personalized network. Exploratory analyses indicated that the most consistent signal was contained in problem breadth: young people whose representations encompassed a broader range of personally relevant difficulties showed higher subsequent psychopathology despite comparable baseline symptom severity. In contrast, global characteristics of perceived relational structure provided little consistent additional information beyond problem breadth. These findings provide a first prospective evaluation of PECANs and underscore the importance of evaluating compositional and relational components of person‐specific models separately. Confirmatory replication is needed before either component is used to inform personalized clinical decisions.

psychology.abstract: Clinical research on psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) has expanded substantially in recent years, particularly for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depressive disorders. Contemporary studies have generally evaluated psychedelic administration within controlled therapeutic settings that include psychological support, preparation, and integration. However, variability in clinical response and methodological challenges have highlighted the importance of individual, relational, and contextual factors, often described as “set and setting,” in understanding therapeutic outcomes. The role of psychotherapy and the broader therapeutic context therefore remains an important area of investigation.This scoping review aimed to map the contemporary evidence on PAT, characterize the clinical and psychotherapeutic approaches used with psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, and DMT, summarize reported clinical and safety findings, and identify methodological, mechanistic, ethical, and implementation considerations across existing protocols.A structured search of PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov was conducted on 23 February 2026. Sources published or publicly available between January 2020 and November 2025 were eligible. The review included peer-reviewed and relevant non-peer-reviewed sources addressing psychedelic-assisted interventions, including primary clinical studies, reviews, clinical trial registrations, regulatory documents, and other relevant contextual sources. Records were managed using Zotero and screened against predefined Population, Concept, and Context criteria. Findings were synthesized descriptively according to source type and evidence domain.The mapped evidence was most developed for MDMA-assisted therapy in PTSD and psilocybin-assisted interventions for depressive disorders. Randomized clinical trials reported reductions in PTSD and depressive symptoms following MDMA- and psilocybin-based interventions, respectively, while emerging clinical evidence also investigated LSD-based treatment for generalized anxiety disorder. Evidence for DMT-assisted therapy remained comparatively preliminary, with several available sources consisting of trial registrations or industry-reported information. Across the literature, preparation, supervised psychedelic administration, and integration were common therapeutic components, although the structure and intensity of psychotherapy varied substantially. Functional unblinding, expectancy effects, heterogeneity of psychotherapeutic approaches, and limitations in long-term safety data were recurring concerns. Ethical issues included informed consent during altered states of consciousness, therapist competence and boundaries, cultural considerations, and equitable access.PAT represents a rapidly developing area of clinical research, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous across compounds, indications, therapeutic models, and levels of evidential maturity. Future research should improve the standardization and reporting of psychotherapeutic interventions, strengthen methods for assessing blinding and expectancy, establish consistent long-term safety monitoring, and develop robust ethical and equity frameworks. Clear distinction between peer-reviewed clinical findings and preliminary or contextual evidence will also be essential as PAT research progresses toward broader clinical implementation.
psychology.text:
After decades of limited regulatory activity, interest in combining psychedelic compounds with structured psychotherapy has re-emerged as a major focus of psychiatric research. Recent phase 2 and 3 clinical trials have reported therapeutic benefits of psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) for several psychiatric conditions, although the evidence base remains heterogeneous and methodological limitations continue to complicate interpretation. Among the most advanced areas of research is MDMA-assisted therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). In a multisite phase 3 trial, participants receiving MDMA-assisted therapy showed significantly greater reductions in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms than those receiving therapy with placebo (). Psilocybin has also demonstrated antidepressant effects in controlled clinical studies. In a randomized clinical trial, a single 25-mg dose administered with psychological support produced greater reductions in depressive symptoms than an active placebo, with benefits observed during follow-up ().

Contemporary PAT protocols generally combine several stages of psychological support, including preparatory sessions, supervised drug administration, and subsequent integration sessions. These components are intended to establish therapeutic rapport, support participants during the acute psychedelic experience, and help them incorporate experiences or insights into everyday life. However, the specific nature, intensity, and theoretical orientation of psychotherapy vary considerably across studies. In MDMA-assisted therapy, for example, treatment protocols have incorporated a therapeutic approach emphasizing participant-led emotional processing and an “inner healing intelligence” framework. For classic psychedelics such as psilocybin and LSD, proposed therapeutic mechanisms include alterations in emotional processing, cognitive flexibility, self-related processing, and patterns of brain network activity. Associations between aspects of the acute subjective experience and subsequent clinical outcomes have also been reported, although these relationships do not by themselves establish causality.

Despite promising clinical findings, important methodological challenges remain. The pronounced subjective effects of many psychedelic compounds can compromise treatment blinding, allowing participants and therapists to infer treatment allocation. Functional unblinding may therefore contribute to expectancy effects and complicate the interpretation of both self-reported and clinician-rated outcomes. Public expectations surrounding psychedelic treatments may further influence participants’ experiences and treatment perceptions (; ). Regulatory guidance has consequently emphasized the importance of trial designs capable of more clearly characterizing the contributions of the investigational drug, psychotherapy, treatment context, and expectancy effects ().

Research on PAT has expanded beyond PTSD and depressive disorders to include anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, and psychological distress associated with serious or life-threatening illness. Emerging studies have also examined applications in other populations and therapeutic contexts, although the evidence remains preliminary in several of these areas (; ). Alongside the expanding clinical literature, ethical and practical questions have become increasingly important. These include the adequacy of informed consent in the context of altered states of consciousness, standards for therapist training and professional conduct, management of therapeutic boundaries, equitable access to treatment, and appropriate consideration of Indigenous knowledge and cultural contexts ().

Amid this rapidly evolving clinical and regulatory landscape, this scoping review maps the evidence on psychedelic-assisted therapy involving psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, and DMT, with particular attention to clinical outcomes, proposed mechanisms, safety, therapeutic approaches, methodological challenges, and ethical considerations. It examines common principles and important differences across existing treatment protocols and identifies areas in which further research is needed to strengthen the evidence base and inform safe, equitable, and scientifically rigorous clinical development.

This study was conducted as a scoping review to map the available evidence on psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT), characterize the types of evidence available, and identify major clinical, therapeutic, methodological, mechanistic, safety, and ethical considerations within the field. The review was informed by established scoping-review methodology and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines ().

The review was structured using the Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework. This approach was selected because the objective was to map a broad and heterogeneous body of evidence rather than to estimate the comparative effectiveness of a specific intervention. Consistent with scoping-review methodology, the review considered multiple types of evidence sources, including primary research, secondary literature, clinical trial records, regulatory documents, and other relevant publicly available sources.

Eligibility criteria were defined according to the PCC framework.

Population: The review considered evidence concerning human participants receiving, or being studied in relation to, psychedelic-assisted interventions. Relevant populations included individuals with psychiatric or psychological conditions such as major depressive disorder, treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety disorders, and substance use disorders. Evidence involving healthy participants was also considered where it provided relevant information on therapeutic mechanisms, safety, expectancy, psychotherapy, or methodological issues related to PAT.

Concept: The concept of interest was psychedelic-assisted therapy involving psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, or DMT in conjunction with psychotherapy, psychological support, preparation, integration, or related therapeutic procedures. Evidence addressing clinical outcomes, therapeutic models, safety and adverse events, mechanisms of action, methodological challenges, expectancy and blinding, and ethical considerations was also considered.

Context: The review encompassed clinical and research settings in which psychedelic-assisted interventions were investigated or delivered, as well as relevant regulatory and therapeutic-development contexts. This included structured psychotherapy settings, clinical trials, ongoing registered studies, regulatory frameworks, and other sources documenting the development or implementation of PAT.

Sources published or publicly available between January 2020 and November 2025 were eligible. The review included both peer-reviewed and relevant non-peer-reviewed sources to capture the breadth of evidence in this rapidly developing field. Peer-reviewed sources included primary clinical studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative and mechanistic reviews, and other substantive scholarly publications. Non-peer-reviewed sources included clinical trial registry records, regulatory documents, organizational reports, and company communications when they provided relevant information concerning ongoing research, trial design, regulatory developments, treatment protocols, or preliminary findings not yet available in peer-reviewed publications.

Sources were excluded when they focused exclusively on animal or preclinical research; examined pharmacological, molecular, or neurobiological effects without relevance to therapeutic psychedelic use; addressed recreational or non-clinical psychedelic use; were editorials, opinion pieces, news items, or commentaries without substantive relevance to the review objectives; were published in languages other than English; or fell outside the specified publication period.

Importantly, source inclusion did not imply equivalent evidential weight. During data charting and synthesis, sources were classified according to their type and evidential role. Peer-reviewed primary clinical studies were distinguished from secondary literature, registered clinical trials, regulatory documents, and industry-reported or other preliminary information. Findings from non-peer-reviewed sources were therefore presented as contextual, regulatory, ongoing, or preliminary evidence, as appropriate, rather than as established clinical findings.

The literature search was conducted using PubMed, PsycINFO, and Scopus to identify scholarly publications relevant to PAT. ClinicalTrials.gov was searched separately to identify registered and ongoing clinical studies and to capture information on the developing clinical research landscape.

Additional sources were identified through manual screening of the reference lists of included publications and relevant reviews. Regulatory and other publicly available sources identified during the search and reference-screening processes were also considered where they met the predefined eligibility criteria.

The selection of multiple source types was intentional because scoping reviews are suited to mapping heterogeneous evidence, including published research and relevant non-research sources, particularly in emerging fields where important developments may precede peer-reviewed publication.

Search strategies were developed using combinations of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms relating to psychedelic-assisted therapy, the compounds of interest (psilocybin, MDMA, LSD, and DMT), psychotherapy and psychological support, psychiatric and psychological conditions, clinical research, safety, mechanisms, and ethical considerations.

The searches were conducted on 23 February 2026. The date of the database search was distinct from the eligibility period, which was limited to sources published or publicly available from January 2020 through November 2025.

Database-specific search strings, search fields, Boolean operators, filters, and other search limits are provided in . The search strategies were adapted to the indexing system and syntax of each database. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were subsequently screened to identify additional eligible sources. The detailed reporting of the search strategy was intended to facilitate reproducibility, consistent with recommendations for scoping-review searches.

All records retrieved from the electronic searches were imported into Zotero reference manager, where duplicate records were identified and removed. The remaining records were screened by title and abstract against the predefined eligibility criteria. Potentially relevant records were subsequently assessed at the full-text or complete-record level, depending on the source type.

Two reviewers independently screened records during the title/abstract and full-text stages. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented and summarized in the PRISMA-ScR flow diagram ().

Because the review included different types of evidence sources, the selection process also recorded the source category of each included record. These categories included primary clinical studies, secondary scholarly literature, clinical trial registrations, regulatory documents, and industry or organizational sources.

Data were charted using a standardized approach. Information extracted from primary clinical studies included:author and year;study design and phase, where applicable;sample size and participant characteristics;psychedelic compound and dose;psychotherapy or psychological-support protocol;clinical indication;comparator or control condition;treatment setting;duration and follow-up;primary and relevant secondary outcomes;adverse events and safety findings; and.major methodological limitations.

For reviews and other secondary scholarly publications, data included the review type, scope, principal findings, and relevance to clinical, mechanistic, methodological, therapeutic, safety, or ethical questions.

For clinical trial registrations, regulatory documents, and industry or organizational sources, information was charted according to the purpose of the source, including intervention characteristics, trial design, regulatory considerations, study status, preliminary findings, or other relevant contextual information.

The source type and publication status were recorded for each included source to ensure that peer-reviewed clinical evidence could be distinguished from preliminary or contextual information during synthesis.

Given the heterogeneity of the included sources, interventions, therapeutic approaches, clinical populations, outcomes, and evidence types, findings were synthesized descriptively rather than through quantitative meta-analysis.

The evidence was organized into six broad domains:clinical outcomes and therapeutic effects;psychotherapy and therapeutic models;methodological considerations, including blinding and expectancy;mechanisms of action;safety and adverse events; and.ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations.

Primary clinical studies were presented separately from secondary literature and contextual sources. Clinical trial registrations, regulatory documents, and industry-reported findings were explicitly identified as such and were not treated as equivalent to peer-reviewed clinical results.

Where a secondary publication discussed primary studies that were also included in the review, the secondary source was used to provide context or interpretation rather than being counted as an additional independent clinical observation. This approach was used to minimize duplication and avoid overstating the amount of available clinical evidence.

No quantitative meta-analysis, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or GRADE assessment was undertaken. The purpose of the synthesis was to map the breadth and characteristics of the available evidence, identify areas of convergence and uncertainty, and highlight methodological, clinical, safety, ethical, and regulatory issues requiring further investigation. Key methodological, ethical, safety, and implementation findings identified across the evidence are summarized in .

As this study involved the synthesis of previously published or publicly available information and did not involve direct recruitment or interaction with human participants, institutional ethical approval was not required.

The evidence identified for the period January 2020 to November 2025 encompassed psychedelic-assisted interventions involving MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, and DMT across several psychiatric indications, particularly post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), major depressive disorder (MDD), treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and anxiety disorders. The evidence base comprised randomized clinical trials, open-label studies, follow-up analyses, reviews, methodological publications, clinical trial registrations, regulatory documents, and other contextual sources. These sources were considered separately according to their evidence type during data charting and synthesis.

The most developed clinical evidence concerned MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD and psilocybin-assisted therapy for depressive disorders. Evidence concerning LSD- and DMT-assisted interventions was comparatively limited and included both peer-reviewed clinical studies and preliminary or developmental sources. Across the clinical studies, psychedelic administration was generally accompanied by psychological support or psychotherapy, although the structure, intensity, duration, and theoretical orientation of the therapeutic component varied between studies. The characteristics and evidence types of the principal sources are summarized in .

Summary of clinical trials and reviews on psychedelic-assisted therapy (2020–2025).

Two multicenter phase 3 randomized trials evaluated MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD. The first trial included 90 participants with severe PTSD who were randomized to MDMA-assisted therapy or placebo with manualized psychotherapy. MDMA-assisted therapy produced a significantly greater reduction in clinician-administered PTSD symptoms than placebo-assisted therapy, with a between-group effect size of 0.91 for the primary CAPS-5 outcome. Functional impairment, assessed using the Sheehan Disability Scale, also improved significantly in the MDMA group ().

A subsequent phase 3 trial included 104 participants with moderate to severe PTSD and replicated the primary finding. The least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 score was −23.7 with MDMA-assisted therapy compared with −14.8 with placebo plus therapy (p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 0.7). Improvement in functional impairment was also greater in the MDMA group, although the effect was smaller than that observed for the primary PTSD outcome (). Seven severe treatment-emergent adverse events were reported across the two treatment groups, with no serious treatment-emergent adverse events or deaths during the trial.

Clinical studies of psilocybin-assisted therapy included both MDD and TRD populations. In a phase 2 randomized clinical trial involving 104 adults with MDD, a single 25-mg dose of psilocybin administered with psychological support was associated with rapid reductions in depressive symptoms, with treatment effects observed during follow-up through 6 weeks ().

In a larger randomized trial involving 233 participants with TRD, participants received a single 1-, 10-, or 25-mg dose of psilocybin with psychological support. The 25-mg group demonstrated greater improvement in depressive symptoms at 3 weeks than the 1-mg group, providing evidence of a dose-related difference in the primary efficacy outcome ().

The evidence also included the phase 2 randomized trial comparing psilocybin with escitalopram in 59 participants with MDD. Participants received two doses of psilocybin or a low-dose psilocybin control together with psychological support and 6 weeks of escitalopram or placebo. The primary between-group comparison on the QIDS-SR-16 at 6 weeks did not reach statistical significance, although several secondary outcomes favored psilocybin (). This study was therefore classified as a primary clinical trial rather than a mechanistic review.

Longer-term follow-up data were also identified from psilocybin development programs. These analyses provided information on persistence of treatment response beyond the primary trial endpoints but were based on subsets or follow-up cohorts and were therefore interpreted separately from the randomized primary analyses.

Evidence for LSD-based treatment was less extensive than that for MDMA and psilocybin. A phase 2b multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated a single dose of MM120 (lysergide) in 198 adults with moderate to severe generalized anxiety disorder. Participants were randomized to placebo or 25-, 50-, 100-, or 200-μg doses. The study identified a significant dose-related reduction in anxiety symptoms, with the 100-μg dose producing a substantial improvement at the primary four-week endpoint ().

The trial therefore provided peer-reviewed clinical evidence supporting further investigation of single-dose lysergide for generalized anxiety disorder. However, interpretation remains subject to the characteristics of the selected study population, the single-dose design, and the methodological challenges associated with maintaining blinding in psychedelic trials.

The evidence concerning DMT-assisted therapy was comparatively preliminary. The sources identified during the review included early-phase clinical research, trial-registration records, and industry-reported information concerning investigational formulations such as SPL026. These sources described the development of DMT-based interventions for depressive disorders, including studies examining single-dose administration with psychological support.

Because a substantial proportion of the available DMT evidence consisted of trial registrations or company-reported information rather than completed peer-reviewed clinical publications, these findings were classified as preliminary or contextual evidence. Consequently, claims concerning efficacy, durability, safety, or drug interactions were not treated as equivalent to findings from completed peer-reviewed randomized clinical trials.

Source verification also identified citation discrepancies in the previously assembled evidence base. In particular,  did not provide evidence concerning DMT or SPL026 and were therefore excluded from the DMT synthesis. The publication concerns a phase 1 investigation of PNT001, an anti-tau antibody, rather than a psychedelic intervention.

Difficulty maintaining treatment blinding emerged as a recurring methodological issue across the psychedelic literature. The pronounced subjective effects of psychedelic compounds may enable participants and therapists to infer treatment allocation, creating the potential for expectancy and performance effects. Methodological literature identified several approaches to addressing this problem, including more credible active comparators, prospective assessment of treatment-guessing and expectancy, and improved reporting of blinding integrity.

The review also identified literature examining the role of psychotherapy in PAT. The available publications described considerable variation in the amount, structure, and theoretical orientation of psychological support provided before, during, and after psychedelic administration. , for example, highlighted the relatively limited empirical literature examining psychotherapy as a distinct component of psychedelic-assisted treatment and emphasized the need for greater attention to psychotherapy processes and therapeutic models.

Regulatory sources identified during the review similarly emphasized methodological and safety considerations specific to psychedelic clinical trials. These included the effects of psychoactive treatment on blinding, appropriate safety monitoring, characterization of the intervention and therapeutic context, and the need for rigorous trial conduct and outcome assessment. Regulatory documents were treated as contextual evidence and were not used as evidence of clinical efficacy.

The mechanistic literature identified several proposed pathways through which classic psychedelics may contribute to therapeutic change. These included serotonin 5-HT2A receptor signaling, alterations in large-scale brain-network activity, changes in cognitive and emotional processing, and increased psychological flexibility. Reviews of classic psychedelics have described these mechanisms as interacting processes rather than as a single established pathway.

The therapeutic interventions accompanying psychedelic administration also varied considerably. Common elements included preparatory sessions before dosing, monitored support during the acute psychedelic experience, and post-session integration. However, the specific content, duration, therapist orientation, and degree of structure differed between studies.

For MDMA-assisted therapy, the therapeutic model was more explicitly standardized across the phase 3 program, whereas classic psychedelic studies showed greater variation in the nature of psychological support. The literature also identified therapist-related factors, therapeutic alliance, participant expectations, and the management of suggestibility as areas requiring further empirical investigation. At present, however, the available evidence does not establish that any single psychotherapeutic model or therapist-related factor is necessary or sufficient for clinical improvement.

Across the contemporary clinical studies identified in the review, commonly reported acute adverse events included headache, nausea, dizziness, transient anxiety, and temporary physiological changes such as elevations in blood pressure. The frequency and severity of adverse events varied according to compound, dose, clinical population, and study design.

The safety findings were obtained predominantly from controlled clinical settings involving participant screening, preparation, supervised administration, and post-session monitoring. Consequently, the observed safety profiles reflect the characteristics of these selected research populations and treatment conditions. The absence of a particular adverse event in individual studies was not interpreted as evidence that the event could not occur in other populations or under less controlled conditions.

Similarly, the available evidence was insufficient to establish the absence of longer-term psychiatric or cardiovascular risks. Many clinical trials excluded participants with conditions considered to increase the risk of adverse outcomes, and follow-up periods varied substantially between studies. Safety findings were therefore interpreted in relation to sample size, participant selection, duration of follow-up, and study design rather than as definitive estimates of population-level risk.

Challenging psychological experiences, including transient anxiety, fear, perceptual disturbances, or emotional distress, were also reported across the literature. Some publications proposed that appropriately supported challenging experiences may contribute to therapeutic processes. However, this interpretation remains provisional, and challenging experiences were not considered inherently therapeutic in the present synthesis.

Ethical considerations emerged as a recurring theme across the literature on psychedelic-assisted therapy. The reviewed sources identified several issues associated with the vulnerability of participants during altered states of consciousness and the intensive interpersonal nature of psychedelic-assisted treatment. Informed consent was therefore identified as an important consideration, particularly because participants may experience substantial changes in perception, cognition, emotional processing, and suggestibility during psychedelic administration.

The literature also emphasized therapist competence, professional conduct, and the maintenance of appropriate therapeutic boundaries. Particular attention was given to the potential vulnerability of participants to interpersonal influence during psychedelic experiences, including the ethical management of touch and other forms of physical or relational contact (; ; ). These findings highlighted the importance of appropriate therapist training, clearly defined professional boundaries, and procedures for responding to psychological distress ().

Cultural and equity considerations were also identified. The reviewed literature raised questions concerning the representation of diverse populations in psychedelic research, equitable access to emerging treatments, and the appropriate consideration of Indigenous knowledge and cultural contexts. Barriers related to treatment cost, availability of trained therapists, geographic access, and reimbursement were identified as potential factors affecting equitable implementation. Overall, the ethical findings indicated that safe translation of psychedelic-assisted therapy into broader clinical practice requires attention not only to pharmacological safety but also to informed consent, therapist competence, interpersonal boundaries, cultural context, and equitable access.

This scoping review mapped the rapidly expanding literature on psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) published or publicly available between 2020 and 2025. The evidence base varied substantially across compounds, clinical indications, study designs, and levels of evidential maturity. Peer-reviewed clinical evidence was most developed for MDMA-assisted therapy in PTSD and psilocybin-assisted interventions for depressive disorders, whereas the evidence for LSD- and DMT-assisted interventions was comparatively less extensive. The review also identified recurring methodological, psychotherapeutic, safety, ethical, and regulatory issues that influence interpretation of the emerging clinical literature.

The phase 3 MDMA trials provided relatively substantial controlled evidence concerning MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD. Both trials reported greater reductions in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms with MDMA-assisted therapy than with placebo-assisted therapy, accompanied by improvements in functional outcomes (, ). These findings are important because the trials used structured psychotherapy in both treatment conditions, allowing the clinical comparison to reflect the addition of MDMA within a defined therapeutic framework rather than a comparison between drug treatment and psychotherapy alone.

At the same time, the findings should not be interpreted independently of the methodological characteristics of psychedelic trials.
