The marked subjective effects of MDMA can compromise treatment masking and increase the likelihood that participants and therapists infer allocation. Consequently, expectancy and other nonspecific effects may contribute to observed between-group differences. Recent evidence syntheses have similarly identified concerns relating to blinding, heterogeneity of psychotherapy, and study quality within the MDMA literature.

The psilocybin literature showed a similarly expanding but heterogeneous evidence base. Randomized trials in MDD and TRD reported relatively rapid reductions in depressive symptoms following single-dose administration with psychological support (; ). However, results differed according to comparator, outcome measure, follow-up period, and study population. The trial comparing psilocybin with escitalopram, for example, did not demonstrate a statistically significant between-group difference on its prespecified primary outcome at 6 weeks, despite favorable findings on several secondary outcomes (). These differences highlight the importance of considering the complete outcome structure of individual trials rather than describing the psilocybin evidence as uniformly positive.

The evidence for LSD-assisted treatment was more limited but included a randomized phase 2b trial of MM120 in generalized anxiety disorder. The reported reduction in anxiety symptoms following a single administration provides a basis for continued clinical investigation, although the evidence remains constrained by the characteristics of the trial population, single-dose design, follow-up duration, and difficulties with maintaining treatment masking ().

DMT-assisted therapy remained at an earlier stage of development during the review period. Much of the available information concerning SPL026 originated from trial registrations and industry communications rather than completed peer-reviewed clinical publications. These sources are useful for mapping the development of the field, but do not provide the same evidential basis as independently published clinical results. Accordingly, claims regarding the efficacy, durability, safety, or interaction profile of DMT-based interventions should remain provisional until supported by adequately reported peer-reviewed clinical studies.

A central finding across the mapped literature was that PAT is not simply a pharmacological intervention. Most contemporary clinical protocols incorporate some form of preparation, support during psychedelic administration, and post-session integration. However, the nature and intensity of these components vary considerably between studies.

This variability creates an important challenge for interpreting clinical outcomes. When psychedelic administration and psychotherapy are delivered together, the observed treatment effect may reflect pharmacological effects, therapeutic processes, expectancy, the treatment environment, or interactions among these components. The available literature does not yet establish the relative contribution of each factor.

The evidence concerning psychotherapy itself also remains comparatively underdeveloped. Therapeutic approaches range from supportive and relatively nondirective models to more structured or integrative approaches. Differences have been reported in therapist training, session structure, preparation, integration, management of acute experiences, and the use of therapeutic techniques () similarly highlighted the limited empirical investigation of psychotherapy as a distinct component of psychedelic-assisted treatment. Further research should therefore evaluate psychotherapy processes explicitly rather than treating psychological support as a uniform intervention across trials.

Claims concerning particular therapeutic models should also be interpreted cautiously. The present evidence does not establish that directive approaches are superior to nondirective approaches, nor that a particular therapist stance or integration model is necessary for therapeutic benefit. Comparative studies that manipulate or systematically characterize these components are needed.

The mechanistic literature provides several plausible explanations for how psychedelic compounds may contribute to therapeutic change. Classic psychedelics such as psilocybin and LSD primarily exert their acute effects through serotonergic mechanisms involving the 5-HT2A receptor, with downstream changes in brain-network activity, perception, cognition, and emotional processing (). Proposed psychological mechanisms include increased cognitive flexibility, modification of maladaptive beliefs or priors, enhanced emotional processing, and changes in self-related processing.

These mechanisms should nevertheless be distinguished from demonstrated mediators of clinical outcome. Associations between the intensity or characteristics of the acute psychedelic experience and subsequent improvement do not establish that the experience itself causes therapeutic change. Expectancy, therapeutic alliance, contextual factors, and other components of the treatment environment may contribute simultaneously.

MDMA differs pharmacologically from classic serotonergic psychedelics and has been investigated in relation to emotional processing, social connection, fear responses, and trauma-related psychotherapy. Its effects may therefore interact with the therapeutic processes used in PTSD treatment. However, the relative contributions of pharmacological and psychotherapeutic mechanisms remain incompletely characterized.

Functional unblinding emerged as one of the most important methodological issues across the evidence base. The recognizable subjective effects of psychedelic compounds make conventional placebo-controlled designs difficult to maintain. Participants who correctly infer their treatment allocation may subsequently report outcomes differently, while therapists who know or infer allocation may alter their interactions with participants.

These concerns do not invalidate randomized trials, but they complicate interpretation of their effect estimates. Future studies should therefore incorporate prospective assessment of treatment-guessing, expectancy, and masking integrity. The development of more credible active comparators may also improve the interpretability of controlled trials, although no comparator completely reproduces the complex subjective and physiological effects of psychedelic drugs.

The regulatory literature has similarly recognized these challenges. The FDA’s 2023 draft guidance on psychedelic drug development specifically highlighted the distinctive effects of psychedelics on consciousness and the need to account for these characteristics in clinical trial design, including the role of psychotherapy, safety monitoring, dose–response assessment, and durability of treatment effects.

The contemporary clinical trials reviewed generally reported acute adverse events such as headache, nausea, dizziness, transient anxiety, and temporary cardiovascular changes. However, these findings should be interpreted in the context of intensive participant screening, controlled administration, trained supervision, and exclusion of individuals considered to be at elevated risk for certain psychiatric or medical complications.

Accordingly, the absence of particular serious outcomes in individual trials should not be interpreted as evidence that those risks are absent. Sample sizes remain relatively small for several compounds, follow-up durations vary, and trial populations may not represent the full range of patients who could eventually receive these interventions. A precise estimate of the frequency of rare serious adverse events also cannot be derived reliably by simply pooling heterogeneous studies without prespecified definitions and denominators.

Longitudinal pharmacovigilance will therefore be important as psychedelic interventions progress into larger and more diverse populations. Future research should use standardized adverse-event definitions, consistent reporting procedures, systematic assessment of psychiatric and cardiovascular outcomes, and sufficiently long follow-up to identify delayed or uncommon events.

Challenging psychological experiences require similar caution. Anxiety, fear, perceptual disturbances, or emotional distress during the acute psychedelic state may occur even under controlled conditions. Some authors have proposed that such experiences can form part of a therapeutic process when appropriately supported, but this remains an interpretive hypothesis rather than evidence that adverse experiences are intrinsically beneficial.

The transition from controlled research environments to broader clinical implementation raises ethical issues that extend beyond pharmacological safety. Participants undergoing altered states of consciousness may experience increased psychological vulnerability and heightened sensitivity to interpersonal and environmental cues. This places particular importance on informed consent, therapist competence, professional boundaries, appropriate management of touch and interpersonal contact, and clear procedures for responding to distress.

Therapist training is therefore likely to be an important component of safe implementation. However, the optimal content and duration of training remain incompletely defined. Training frameworks should be informed by empirical evidence concerning therapist competence, therapeutic alliance, management of acute psychological experiences, and integration rather than relying solely on consensus or professional tradition.

Equity is another important consideration. Existing clinical trials may not adequately represent the demographic and socioeconomic diversity of the populations who could ultimately seek PAT. Barriers related to cost, treatment availability, geographic access, therapist training, and reimbursement could affect who is able to benefit from emerging interventions. Future research and implementation frameworks should therefore consider representativeness during recruitment and accessibility during clinical translation.

Ethical implementation also requires attention to cultural context and Indigenous knowledge where relevant to the development and use of psychedelic practices. Such considerations should avoid treating Indigenous traditions simply as sources of therapeutic techniques while overlooking questions of cultural ownership, representation, benefit sharing, and historical context.

Developments occurring toward the end of the review period further illustrate the importance of interpreting psychedelic-assisted therapy within its regulatory and research-integrity context. In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a Complete Response Letter concerning the MDMA-assisted therapy application for PTSD. The regulatory response required deficiencies in the application to be addressed and requested an updated safety assessment, including additional information from clinical studies and adverse-event analyses. The FDA also stated that the product could not be legally marketed until the application received approval. These regulatory requirements highlight the distinction between promising clinical trial findings and the evidentiary and safety standards required for regulatory authorization ().

The MDMA literature also experienced important research-integrity developments in 2024. Three publications based on phase 2 randomized trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy were retracted following concerns regarding protocol violations at a study site. The retraction notices indicated that the violations had not been adequately disclosed and that affected data had not been removed from the analyses. These events do not by themselves determine the validity of the broader MDMA evidence base, particularly because subsequent phase 3 studies were conducted, but they demonstrate the importance of transparent reporting, adherence to approved protocols, appropriate handling of affected data, and independent scrutiny of clinical research findings. They also reinforce the need to distinguish individual study findings from the overall maturity of an evidence base.

Evidence for psilocybin also advanced to phase 3 evaluations in 2025. The COMP005 phase 3 trial of COMP360 psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression reported a statistically significant difference in the primary outcome at 6 weeks, with a mean difference of −3.6 points in change in MADRS scores between the 25-mg and placebo groups (p < 0.001) (). The trial sponsor additionally reported that an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board identified no unexpected safety findings or clinically meaningful imbalance in suicidal ideation between treatment groups. Because these findings were initially reported by the study sponsor, they should be interpreted as emerging phase 3 evidence pending consideration of the full peer-reviewed publication. The results nevertheless represent an important transition from earlier phase 2 evidence toward larger confirmatory trials ().

The translation of efficacy findings into routine clinical care remains a separate question from efficacy under controlled trial conditions. Recent evidence from the routine treatment of treatment-resistant depression suggests that outcomes observed in clinical practice may differ from those reported in highly selected and closely monitored research populations (). This distinction is particularly relevant for psychedelic-assisted therapy because implementation requires trained therapists, appropriate clinical infrastructure, careful participant selection, preparation and integration procedures, and systems for monitoring adverse psychological and physical effects. Accordingly, evidence from routine care should be considered alongside randomized trials when evaluating the practical generalizability of psilocybin-assisted treatment.

Several priorities emerged from the mapped evidence. First, adequately powered randomized trials with longer follow-up are needed across compounds and clinical indications, particularly for interventions that currently rely heavily on early-phase or non-peer-reviewed evidence. Second, future studies should more explicitly characterize the psychotherapeutic component, including preparation, therapist orientation, session structure, integration, and treatment fidelity.

Third, methodological studies should continue to address functional unblinding and expectancy through improved comparator conditions and prospective measurement of treatment beliefs. Fourth, safety monitoring should extend beyond acute dosing sessions and incorporate standardized long-term assessment of psychiatric, cardiovascular, and other clinically relevant outcomes.

Finally, studies should examine the interaction between pharmacological and psychotherapeutic components rather than treating PAT as a single indivisible intervention. Designs that can distinguish drug effects, psychological support, expectancy, therapeutic alliance, and contextual effects would provide a stronger basis for understanding how PAT produces clinical change.

This review has several strengths. It mapped both peer-reviewed and relevant non-peer-reviewed evidence, allowing the review to capture not only completed clinical studies but also ongoing trials, regulatory developments, and emerging evidence in a rapidly changing field. The use of the PCC framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting approach also provided a structure appropriate for a heterogeneous evidence base. In addition, the distinction between primary clinical evidence, secondary literature, and contextual sources reduced the risk of treating fundamentally different source types as equivalent.

Several limitations should nevertheless be considered. The search was restricted to English-language sources and covered a limited number of databases. The publication and availability window was restricted to January 2020 through November 2025, meaning that relevant earlier evidence and developments after the search period were outside the scope of the review. The search itself was conducted on 23 February 2026, but no sources published or publicly available after November 2025 were eligible.

The review also did not undertake a formal risk-of-bias assessment or GRADE evaluation. This was consistent with the scoping-review objective of mapping the evidence, but it limits the extent to which the review can make conclusions about comparative efficacy or certainty of treatment effects. Considerable heterogeneity existed across compounds, indications, sample sizes, outcome measures, psychotherapy protocols, and follow-up periods. In addition, overlap between primary studies and secondary reviews creates a possibility of repeatedly encountering the same underlying clinical evidence, although this was addressed during synthesis by distinguishing primary studies from secondary sources.

Finally, publication bias, sponsorship bias, and the inclusion of industry-reported information may have influenced the available evidence, particularly for compounds at earlier stages of clinical development. Non-peer-reviewed sources were therefore treated as contextual or preliminary evidence rather than as equivalent to peer-reviewed clinical findings. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the overall landscape mapped by the review.

The evidence mapped in this scoping review demonstrates substantial expansion of research into psychedelic-assisted therapy between 2020 and 2025, particularly for MDMA-assisted therapy in PTSD and psilocybin-assisted interventions for depressive disorders. Clinical evidence for LSD-assisted treatment in generalized anxiety disorder also emerged during the review period, whereas DMT-assisted interventions remained at an earlier stage of development and were represented substantially by preliminary or contextual sources.

The evidence does not yet support viewing PAT as a uniform therapeutic intervention. Clinical protocols differ in psychedelic compound, dose, psychological support, therapist approach, preparation, integration, outcome assessment, and follow-up. Methodological challenges, particularly functional unblinding and expectancy effects, further complicate interpretation of treatment effects. Important uncertainties also remain concerning long-term safety, the specific contribution of psychotherapy, and the generalizability of findings from highly selected clinical trial populations.

Future research should therefore move beyond demonstrating whether psychedelic interventions produce clinical change and examine how, for whom, and under what therapeutic conditions such effects occur. Greater standardization and transparent reporting of psychotherapeutic procedures, improved approaches to blinding and expectancy assessment, systematic long-term safety monitoring, and rigorous attention to informed consent, therapist competence, cultural considerations, and equitable access will be important for the responsible development of PAT.

Overall, the field has generated substantial clinical and methodological knowledge but remains characterized by important evidence gaps. Continued rigorous investigation will be necessary to determine the durability, safety, mechanisms, and generalizability of psychedelic-assisted interventions and to establish how emerging findings can be translated appropriately into clinical practice.

psychology.title: First-time voters in Türkiye: a thematic analysis from a political psychology perspective
psychology.abstract: Studies on young people’s participation in elections have largely focused on structural determinants, the formation of voting habits, or calculations based on rational choice. However, these approaches have limited scope when it comes to explaining how individuals experience and make sense of the moment they first become involved in electoral politics. To address this gap, this qualitative study is based on in-depth interviews with 26 young voters in Türkiye reflecting on their first voting experiences. The interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis with the support of MAXQDA, and the findings were interpreted through four analytical lenses: affective intelligence, social identity, cognitive dissonance, and political efficacy. The findings show that voting behavior is shaped not only by strategic considerations but also by how participants understand their political identities and perceive their ability to exert political influence. The study shows that casting a first vote is experienced as a psychologically meaningful moment of political self-understanding, extending accounts of youth political participation beyond structural conditions and strategic reasoning.
psychology.text:
This study examines how first-time voting is experienced and interpreted within the framework of political psychology. At a time when political disengagement, intergenerational divisions, and increasingly complex patterns of participation are becoming more pronounced, young people’s first encounters with electoral politics deserve closer attention. These experiences can be considered not only in terms of observable behavioral patterns but also through identity, cognition, and emotion. First-time voting is particularly important in this respect, as it represents an initial stage of direct participation through which individuals begin to position themselves in relation to the political system.

The existing literature on voting behavior has largely developed around three main research axes. Studies within the first axis highlight structural and developmental variables -such as resources, institutional arrangements, and life-cycle effects- in shaping electoral participation and voter preferences (; ; ). The second research axis conceptualizes voting behavior through rational choice models and limited information processing, focusing on decision-making mechanisms based on cost–benefit calculations and heuristic shortcuts (; ; ). The third strand, grounded in political psychology, examines how emotions, identity formation, and perceptions of political efficacy shape political behavior (; ; ; ).

However, these approaches fall short in explaining how individuals experience their first time voting and what kinds of meanings they ascribe to that experience. While structural and rationalist studies rely largely on survey data, aggregate indicators, and observable behavioral outcomes, most research in the field of political psychology employs experimental or large-sample quantitative designs. Although these approaches make important contributions to explaining the determinants of voting behavior, they reveal less about how individuals construct and interpret their first encounters with electoral participation through their own narratives. Moreover, recent studies in Türkiye have examined young voters in relation to digital political participation and the use of media for political information (; ). These studies provide important evidence on young voters’ participation and media practices, but they do not focus directly on how young people interpret and make sense of the experience of voting for the first time. In this regard, this study seeks to overcome the mentioned weaknesses in theory and methodology by examining participants’ accounts through perspectives from political psychology and a thematic analytical approach.

Based on participants’ experiences of voting for the first time in Türkiye, this study examines how this experience can be viewed as a significant step in the formation of individuals’ political identities and their future political behavior. By analyzing the memory and perception of the participants of this experience, one can understand the way how the participation in the election process is perceived by the individuals. Special emphasis will be put on the emotions like fear, uncertainty, hope, and determination. The study is not aimed at measuring turnout or partisan behavior of participants. It studies how emotions, political identity, cognitive assessments, and political efficacy are revealed in the accounts of participants’ first voting experience. Voting is therefore approached not merely as a behavioral choice between candidates or parties, but as an experience through which individuals interpret their relationship with politics and their own capacity for political influence. Participants’ narratives form the basis of the analysis and are interpreted through theoretical perspectives from political psychology. Within this target group, the study draws on interviews with 26 university students from six universities in Türkiye. Participants were selected through maximum variation sampling to reflect variation in academic field, gender, and electoral experience.

In the literature on voter participation, structural and developmental models -which have long sought to explain the phenomenon through resources, institutional arrangements and life-cycle-related effects- have gained prominence. , highlighting the importance of political efficacy for electoral participation, state that “internal efficacy usually refers to the degree to which people think they can influence the government or policy outcomes, while external efficacy indicates the extent to which citizens perceive a government to be responsive to their interests. Both forms of efficacy are expected to increase turnout” (p. 355). Within this framework, however, psychological variables are largely treated not as dimensions of individuals’ lived experiences but as predictors of electoral participation. Developmental explanations similarly emphasize that voting behavior stabilizes over time. As  states, “voting behavior is, in part, a gradually acquired habit” (p. 42).  further show that “when young adults leave home, the influence of their parents’ strong voting habits decreases while the weaker voting patterns among their peers have a greater impact” (p. 380). These studies therefore conceptualize first-time voting primarily in terms of structural conditions, political socialization and habit formation.

Recent research continues to show the importance of political socialization and electoral context during the early stages of participation. , using longitudinal data from newly eligible voters in the United Kingdom, found that childhood volunteering had little effect on turnout on average, but had a positive effect among young people whose parents were politically disengaged. , using data collected before, during, and after national elections in Germany, the Czech Republic, and Sweden, found that political engagement increased during election periods. In the German sample, this increase was particularly pronounced among less engaged young people and first-time voters. These studies show that early electoral participation develops in relation to both previous political socialization and the context in which young people encounter elections.

Rational choice models, on the other hand, treat voting behavior as a decision-making process in which costs and benefits are weighed.  argue that political participation should be theoretically explained rather than dismissed as irrational or inexplicable, stating that “the function of theory is to explain behavior and it is certainly no explanation to assign a sizeable part of politics to the mysterious and inexplicable world of the irrational” (p. 25). Subsequent work has emphasized bounded rationality in explaining voting behavior.  show that voters rely on “heuristic-based information processing” rather than exhaustive evaluation (p. 968). At the macro level,  observes that “the main factors that affect variations in turnout are institutional variables” (p. 111). While these approaches shed light on strategic reasoning and decision-making under conditions of limited information, they remain limited in explaining the emotional ambivalence and identity-related uncertainty that may accompany voting for the first time.

Political psychology addresses this limitation by bringing emotion and identity more directly into the analysis of political behavior.  argue that when anxiety signals novelty, “reliance on habits diminishes and the brain shifts to deliberative consideration of the new information” (p. 333).  further demonstrate that “anger, more than anxiety or enthusiasm, will mobilize” participation (p. 156). Alongside emotion, identity also shapes the meanings individuals attach to political events, actors and preferences. As  notes, “it is the meaning of American identity, not its existence, that determines its political consequences” (p. 130), showing that the political significance of identity depends on how that identity is understood.

In the context of young people’s political participation,  observe that young people often perceive “relatively few opportunities available for them to intervene effectively in formal political life” (p. 360).

Recent research in Türkiye has also examined the relationship between youth political participation and digital media. , based on interviews with 30 young members of political parties and civil society, examined social media as a motivation for political participation. , using survey data collected after the 2018 general election, found that offline political participation was related to sharing political views online and exposure to alternative political ideas.  focused on how Generation Z uses media as a source of political information, while  examined the digital political participation of 646 university students who were to vote for the first time in the 2023 general elections. More recent studies have also examined young voters’ perceptions of politicians’ social media use () and the relationship between social media use and political literacy among young voters ().

Within this framework, the study contributes to political psychology by addressing limitations in structural and rational models. It analyses participants’ narratives through a framework attentive to emotion, cognition and identity, thereby examining the psychological meanings associated with voting for the first time.

In addition to institutional and structural factors, individuals’ emotional orientations, cognitive evaluations and group affiliations also shape political behavior. Political psychology provides conceptual tools for examining these processes during moments of political entry such as voting for the first time. Rather than treating theory as a set of testable propositions or using these perspectives as predetermined coding categories, this study uses four perspectives -affective intelligence, social identity, cognitive dissonance and political efficacy- as analytical lenses for interpreting participants’ narratives. Their purpose here is not to repeat the literature review but to clarify how the inductively derived themes are interpreted at the level of meaning-making rather than prediction or measurement.

According to the affective intelligence perspective, emotions regulate attention when individuals face new or unfamiliar situations.  explain that “people have two distinct emotional systems: a dispositional system that incorporates people’s normal feelings about things and a surveillance system that manages their attention,” and that this surveillance system relies on emotions “most notably anxiety, fear, or uncertainty, to signal that something about the world is not routine and that conscious attention is necessary” (p. 324).  further distinguish between emotional states, noting that “Anger and enthusiasm, then, both lead us to take action” and that “we suspect anger and enthusiasm, more than fear or anxiety, are likely to push us to that choice” (p. 160).  similarly shows that “campaign ads can stimulate this pattern of behavior by cueing enthusiasm” (p. 398).

Social identity theory conceptualizes group membership as part of the individual’s self-concept.  defines social identity as “that part of an individual’s self-concept which derives from his knowledge of his membership of a social group (or groups) together with the emotional significance attached to that membership” (p. 69). Applied to partisanship,  argues that “partisan identification is an important social identity for many individuals” (p. 136).  further shows that sorting “has acted to increase the strength of political identities and has polarized mass political behavior” (p. 128).

Cognitive dissonance and motivated reasoning help explain how political commitments are maintained or adjusted after a choice has been made.  emphasize that “voting represents decisional commitment in that it is clearly a behavioral act in support of a candidate” (p. 523), indicating that electoral choice carries psychological weight beyond the immediate act of voting.  similarly demonstrate a “prior attitude effect such that attitudinally congruent arguments are evaluated as stronger than attitudinally incongruent arguments” (p. 755).

Political efficacy is examined here through participants’ perceptions of their capacity to understand politics and influence political outcomes rather than as a fixed personality trait.  define electoral efficacy as “the feeling that one’s vote is potentially decisive” (p. 311), linking participation to the belief that individual political action can matter. Similarly,  define internal efficacy as “beliefs about one’s own competence to understand, and to participate effectively in politics” (p. 1407).

In light of these discussions, the study approaches first-time voting as an experience shaped by emotion, identity, consistency-seeking and perceptions of political competence. These perspectives guide the interpretation of how participants narrate their first voting experiences and position themselves in relation to the wider political system. Voting for the first time is therefore considered not only as a choice at the ballot box, but also as a psychological and social experience through which individuals begin to define themselves politically.

The forms of political participation and perspectives on political processes among first-time voters play a significant role in shaping future democratic functioning and policy-making processes. For this reason, taking into account the experiences, expectations and political orientations of younger generations is of critical importance not only for the development of democracy but also for strengthening social progress. In this context, examining the voting behavior of young people can contribute significantly to both policy-making and the academic literature.

In line with this aim, the study addresses the following research questions:

RQ1. How do participants describe and make sense of their first voting experiences?

RQ2. Which emotional, social, and cognitive processes play a role in the formation of their voting decisions?

RQ3. How do participants perceive the extent to which political actors and the political system respond to their expectations and demands?

RQ4. In what ways is the voting experience related to their developing political identities?

RQ5. What kinds of expectations, concerns, and emotional orientations do they express regarding the political future?

This study uses a qualitative research design and reflexive thematic analysis to examine how individuals perceive and interpret their first voting experiences. The constructivist worldview forms the philosophical basis of the study. In constructivism, reality is regarded as a socially constructed phenomenon. From this perspective, knowledge is co-created between the researcher and participants through interaction and interpretation. Accordingly, this study sought to gain rich and in-depth insights into participants’ subjective experiences by engaging them in open-ended conversations and analysing the resulting data inductively. Reflexive thematic analysis was considered suitable for this purpose because it enables the identification and interpretation of patterns of meaning across participants’ accounts while recognizing the active role of the researcher in the analytical process (, ).

The main purpose of the study is to understand participants’ accounts through their own perspectives, without using any pre-determined theoretical categories in the coding process. Accordingly, the analysis process was conducted using an inductive, theme-based approach that took into account the contextual complexity specific to each participant’s experience. The theoretical perspectives outlined earlier were used at the interpretation stage rather than as a priori coding categories.

In this study, participants were selected using maximum variation sampling, one of the purposive sampling strategies. This sampling approach was chosen with the aim of highlighting, within as broad a framework as possible, the diverse experiences, perspectives and ways of making sense of the first voting experience among young voters. Care was taken to ensure that participants were diverse in terms of academic field, gender and electoral experience, with the aim of reflecting the variations within Generation Z in the research. The sample consists of individuals born between 1997 and 2003 who had experienced voting for the first time and were able to reflect on that experience. This age range allows participants to be classified within the demographic boundaries of Generation Z. Ensuring diversity among participants is important for examining the different motivations, tendencies and patterns in the voting behavior of young people belonging to this generation in a more comprehensive manner ().

Demographic information of participants.

The sample for this study consists of 26 participants studying in various academic departments at six different universities in Türkiye. Seventeen of the participants are women and nine are men. The interviews were conducted face-to-face between August 2023 and January 2024; during the data collection process, a semi-structured interview form was used, which allowed for the collection of in-depth data while maintaining thematic consistency among the participants. The interview guide covered participants’ understandings of Generation Z, their first voting experience, factors influencing their voting decisions, observations during the election process, expectations from politics and politicians, sources of political information, and their views on youth political attitudes and political responsiveness. Because the interviews were semi-structured, follow-up questions were used when necessary to clarify responses, obtain further explanation or examples, and explore issues raised by participants in greater depth. The complete interview guide is provided in .

Participants from other universities were interviewed in August 2023 while they were attending the summer school program at Manisa Celal Bayar University. Interviews with participants from Manisa Celal Bayar University continued in the following months.

The interviews were conducted without the participation of any third parties. No participants refused or withdrew from the study, and no repeat interviews were conducted. The interview form was pilot-tested with two individuals who met the inclusion criteria, and limited adjustments to the wording were made to enhance clarity and the flow of the discussion. The interviews lasted 30–40 min. With participants’ consent, all interviews were audio-recorded. The interviews were conducted jointly by the first and third authors. The first and second authors are male academics in the field of political science, while the third author is a female postgraduate student in the same field. All three researchers have experience in qualitative research.

The fact that some participants had voted in more than one election added analytical depth to the research. This made it possible to examine not only participants’ accounts of their first voting experiences but also their reflections on whether and how their perspectives had changed in subsequent electoral contexts. Although the study is not based on a longitudinal research design, participants with multiple electoral experiences were able to draw comparisons between their first and later voting experiences. These participants were not treated as a separate analytical group; rather, their later experiences provided an additional point of reference for interpreting their first voting experience.

The researchers’ academic backgrounds in political science and their shared academic interest in youth political participation were considered a positioning factor that needed to be taken into account throughout the research process. Although this positionality was seen as an opportunity that could foster sensitivity in the interpretation of participants’ narratives, it was also recognized that it could entail a risk of interpretative bias; consequently, reflexive awareness was maintained throughout the data collection and analysis processes. All interviews were conducted in the first author’s office at the Faculty of Economics and Administrative Sciences, Manisa Celal Bayar University. The office provided a quiet and private setting in which the interviews could be conducted without interruptions. Participants were informed that there were no “right” or “wrong” answers and were encouraged to express their views freely. Some participants from Manisa Celal Bayar University were acquainted with the researchers in an academic context, whereas participants from other universities had no prior relationship with the research team.

The collected data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Once the verbatim transcripts had been imported into MAXQDA 26, the texts were reviewed several times to support familiarization with the data, and the coding process was gradually refined in line with these repeated readings. Initial codes were developed inductively and closely related codes were subsequently grouped into descriptive categories. These categories were then examined in relation to broader patterns of meaning during the development of candidate themes, which were reviewed and refined through repeated movement between coded segments, individual transcripts and the dataset as a whole. This process enabled the analysis to move beyond the identification of individual codes toward the interpretation of broader patterns of meaning relevant to participants’ first voting experiences.  provides a concrete example of the coding process followed in this study.

Example of the coding and theme development process.

“Generation Z is a generation born into technology. This is the biggest difference between them and other generations.” (P4)

“First and foremost, the reason I voted was because it is my right as a citizen, and I felt that I had to use it.” (P8)

“I exercised my vote as my democratic right.” (P12)

In addition to the interview transcripts, field notes and analytical memos were kept on a regular basis to enable the tracking of analytical assessments that emerged during the data collection and coding process. These records helped the researchers to preserve the train of thought that emerged during the process and to pursue the interpretation process in greater depth.

The frequency figures and participant-based code matrices represent two different units of analysis. The frequency figures show the total number of coded segments; therefore, the same participant may contribute more than one coded segment to a particular code when the issue appears in different contexts within the interview. In contrast, the participant-based matrices indicate whether a code appears in each participant’s transcript; each participant is counted only once for a given code (shown as 1), regardless of the number of coded segments in that transcript. The resulting totals may therefore differ. These frequencies are presented descriptively and were not treated as indicators of the analytical importance of particular codes or themes.

Analytical rigor was supported through repeated engagement with the interview transcripts, analytical memoing, and ongoing reflection on the development of codes and themes. In line with the reflexive thematic approach, coding was not treated as a process aimed at establishing a single objectively correct interpretation of the data. Instead, the researchers’ interpretive role was acknowledged throughout the analysis.

The first and second authors engaged in iterative analytical discussions during the development and refinement of themes. These discussions were used to consider alternative interpretations, question emerging assumptions, and refine the boundaries and meanings of the themes rather than to establish inter-coder agreement. All stages of the analytical process were documented to support transparency and consistency between the research questions, the data and the final thematic structure.

Selected participants were contacted again during the analytical process to obtain their reflections on preliminary thematic interpretations. These responses were considered as an additional interpretive perspective rather than as confirmation of a single correct interpretation. Data collection concluded after 26 interviews, by which point later interviews were producing increasingly recurrent accounts. This was treated as a pragmatic indication of dataset adequacy rather than as evidence that all possible themes had been exhausted. Throughout the study, the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist was used as a basis to support the transparency of the reporting process, researcher reflexivity and analytical rigor (; see ).

This research was approved by the Manisa Celal Bayar University Social and Human Sciences Scientific Research and Publication Ethics Committee (Decision No: 2022/10; Ref. No: E.447045). All procedures were conducted in accordance with ethical guidelines for social science research. Given the political sensitivity of the topic, particular attention was paid to ensuring a voluntary and secure research environment. Prior to each interview, participants were informed about the purpose of the study, their right to withdraw at any time, and the confidentiality of their responses. Written and verbal informed consent were obtained.

Participants were assigned numerical identifiers (e.g., P1, P2), and identifying information was removed during transcription. Audio recordings and transcripts were stored in password-protected files accessible only to the research team. To reduce potential social desirability pressures, participants were reminded that participation was voluntary, that their responses would remain confidential, and that there were no right or wrong answers. Interviews were conducted in a quiet and private office setting.

As the data are based on self-reports relating to politically sensitive experiences, there is a possibility that social desirability may have influenced participants’ narratives. Although confidentiality, voluntary participation, and the absence of “right” or “wrong” answers were emphasized throughout the interviews, this possibility cannot be entirely ruled out. In reflexive thematic analysis, researchers’ perspectives form part of the interpretive process; accordingly, the themes presented in this study reflect an interaction between participants’ accounts and the researchers’ analytical engagement with the data.

The sample consisted entirely of university students, which limits the transferability of the findings to young people outside higher education. In addition, some participants from Manisa Celal Bayar University were acquainted with members of the research team in an academic context, and all interviews were conducted in the first author’s university office. This institutional proximity may have influenced how some participants expressed politically sensitive views, even though confidentiality and voluntary participation were emphasized throughout the interviews.

Because some participants were recalling first voting experiences that had occurred several years earlier, their accounts may also have been shaped by retrospective recall and subsequent electoral experiences. In future research, expanding the sample to include individuals outside the university context and examining the dynamics identified here through comparative, longitudinal or mixed-methods designs could enable a more detailed assessment of how the findings are shaped in different social and electoral contexts.

In this section, the analysis of data obtained from the interviews revealed that the participants’ experiences were organized around four main themes. The themes address the research questions in overlapping ways rather than corresponding to them on a one-to-one basis. Generational Self-Perception and Identity relates primarily to participants’ developing political identities and their orientations toward the future (RQ4 and RQ5). Psychological Dynamics of Political Engagement addresses how participants made sense of voting and the emotional, social, and cognitive processes involved in their decisions (RQ1 and RQ2). Political Information and Aspirational Orientations concerns both political information-seeking and participants’ expectations of political actors and the political system (RQ2, RQ3, and RQ5). Youth Expectations and Perceived Political Responsiveness relates most directly to participants’ perceptions of responsiveness and their expectations regarding the political future (RQ3 and RQ5). The first of these, Generational Self-Perception and Identity, focuses on the common characteristics through which Generation Z participants define themselves and how they ascribe meaning to their generational identity. Within this framework, the category Cognitive and Affective Representations of Generation Z reflects both the participants’ cognitive assessments and emotional orientations regarding their own generation. Participants’ narratives suggest that generational self-perception also provides a context for how they position themselves politically. When assessed from the perspective of social identity theory, belonging to Generation Z goes beyond a simple demographic definition for the participants. This sense of identity is related to how young people analyse the political world, access sources of political information and position themselves within a political context that also includes their expectations of the political system. Within this framework, the close relationship that this generation maintains with technology, their ability to adapt rapidly to change and the anxieties they harbor regarding their future are not merely labels that define this group. These characteristics also accompany how participants perceive themselves as a generation and interpret their political environment.

In the second theme, “Psychological Dynamics of Political Engagement”, participants’ accounts of voting for the first time are examined through the emotional, cognitive and social processes associated with political participation. This theme comprises two mutually reinforcing categories: “Perceived Political Agency and Internalized Civic Norms” and “Social Influence, Value Orientations, and Political Evaluations”. The first concerns how participants understand voting as a civic right, a form of political agency and a possible means of expressing demands for change. The second concerns how the social environment, personal and collective values, candidate-related evaluations and broader political considerations are reflected in participants’ voting preferences. When these two elements are considered together, the experience of voting for the first time cannot be assessed solely as an individual and rational cost–benefit analysis. Emotions such as hope, disappointment and anxiety—as embodied in the statements of the participants—also accompany political participation. In this context, voting decisions are described through a combination of deliberation, social influence, identity-related orientations and emotion.

The third theme of the study, “Political Information and Aspirational Orientations”, examines both how participants engage with sources of political information and what they expect from political actors and the political system. This theme is further divided into two categories. The first, “Media-mediated Political Learning and Information-Seeking”, focuses on the sources through which participants follow political developments and seek political information. The second, “Expectations, Needs, and Perceptions of Political Trust”, examines participants’ expectations concerning political representatives and broader social and political conditions, together with how these expectations relate to their perceptions of political trust and responsiveness. Considered together, these categories show that participants’ orientations toward politics are shaped both by the information environments through which they encounter politics and by their expectations concerning recognition, justice, freedom and the future.

The fourth theme, “Youth Expectations and Perceived Political Responsiveness”, focuses on young people’s expectations concerning a more responsive and inclusive political environment. The category “Demands for Responsive Representation” encompasses participants’ proposals regarding how political parties, candidates and representative mechanisms could establish more effective relationships with young people. This theme demonstrates how participants articulate expectations of being understood, represented and responded to by political actors and institutions. Their proposals concern not only practical political demands but also the conditions under which they believe political participation and change could become more meaningful.

presents the category Cognitive and Affective Representations of Generation Z under the theme Generational Self-Perception and Identity. The related views were organized into nine codes. Born into technology appeared in 15 coded segments, while Inquisitive, research-oriented, conscious (7) and Open-minded/innovative thinking (6) were also common in participants’ descriptions. Hopeful was coded in six segments, while Living with uncertainty and anxiety appeared in five. These accounts show that participants described their generation not only through technology and openness to change, but also through different emotional orientations toward the future. Other codes included Open to influence, changeable (4), Experiencing an economic crisis (3), More sensitive (2), and Freedom-seeking (2).

The participant-based coding matrix shown in  indicates that these characteristics appeared across different interviews rather than being limited to a small number of participants. Technology was a common reference point, but participants did not attach the same meaning to their generational position. Some associated it with greater awareness and political engagement, while others emphasized uncertainty or expressed optimism about the capacity of their generation to bring about change.

One participant linked technological familiarity with greater awareness of politics:

“Contrary to what is generally assumed, I think we are a more conscious generation, born into technology. Therefore, we follow current events, the past, and the future more closely. I think Generation Z is more conscious and more connected to civic duties and politics.” (P2)

Another participant emphasized uncertainty:

“Based on my close circle, we are an indecisive and excited generation that does not quite know what it wants or what it wants to do. I agree with the view that we came into the worst period. We are unlucky and indecisive.” (P3)

A more optimistic account associated the generation with the possibility of change:

“Generation Z represents a revolution for me compared with other generations. There are many differences in technology, communication and transportation that the previous generation did not have. This makes me think that this generation can change Türkiye. Generation Z is the generation with that opportunity.” (P18)

presents the category Perceived Political Agency and Internalized Civic Norms under the theme Psychological Dynamics of Political Engagement. Participants’ views were organized into five codes. Democratic right of citizenship was coded in 12 segments and Expectation of change/innovation in eight. Personal values and identity (4), Legitimate expression of dissent (3), and Freedom of thought (2) added different meanings to why participants considered voting important. Voting was therefore described not only as a civic right, but also as a means of expressing a political position, exercising individual agency, and seeking change.

The participant-based matrix shown in  reflects differences in how political agency was experienced. For some participants, voting combined civic responsibility with the possibility of expressing dissatisfaction. Others associated voting more directly with becoming an individual or with expectations that political change could occur.

One participant described both the legitimacy and the limits of individual voting:

“I voted out of civic awareness. Voting was the most legitimate way for me to express my reaction to issues I was uncomfortable with. It was my first time and I was excited. After voting, I realized that one vote has little effect. If there is going to be change in society, it has to be collective, not individual.” (P4)

Another gave voting a more personal meaning:

“I voted to feel that I was an individual.” (P17)

A different account connected voting directly with hope for political change:

“I still had some faith in democracy and I voted to change things. I thought change would happen. I was hopeful.” (P25)

“It was my first time voting. Voting for me was like looking for an option within a lack of options. I thought there should be a complete change. Seeing the same names repeatedly kept leading to the same things. I think this was helplessness.” (P10)

presents the category Social Influence, Value Orientations, and Political Evaluations under the theme Psychological Dynamics of Political Engagement. Influence of family (16) and Influence of social media (14) were frequently represented in the coded material. Social environment and Promises made by candidates were each coded in ten segments. Candidate characteristics, ideological orientations, nationalism and religion, economic conditions, and participants’ broader worldviews also appeared in their accounts. The interviews show that political preferences were related both to social influences and to participants’ own evaluations of candidates, values and political conditions.

The participant-based matrix shown in  indicates that these influences were distributed differently across participants. Family and social environment were important in some accounts, but participants also described later processes of questioning, candidate evaluation and exposure to political information. Value orientations were more decisive for others.

One participant described family as an early influence without treating it as fully determining later political views:

“Candidates’ promises and ideology have an effect, of course, but they do not completely change things. Family lays a certain foundation from childhood. But my views really took shape in my youth; if I had to put a number on it, family twenty percent, myself eighty percent.” (P14)

Another emphasized the evaluation of campaign promises and information encountered through media:

“I already had a political view, but I examined the candidates’ promises. The media is also important because it puts the positive and negative sides of each candidate in front of us. It makes it easier for us to see and question them. I tried to find more objective comments through the media.” (P20)

“Social media influences me and my friends in lasting and different ways. But when we look at our families, they are strongly attached to another party. We are first shaped by our families’ views, and then we can change through the influence of social media and politicians.” (P6)

A different account placed greater weight on established ideological and value orientations:

“I never saw the economy as a determining factor in my voting behavior. We are a Muslim country; religion, Turkism and nationalism affect me. I vote for whoever holds this view.” (P7)

presents the category Media-mediated Political Learning and Information-Seeking under the theme Political Information and Aspirational Orientations. Instagram-Twitter was coded in 22 segments, Various YouTube channels in 18, and Following television in eight. Digital platforms therefore occupied an important place in participants’ accounts of political information. The interviews also show that these platforms were used in different ways. Some participants followed an initial piece of content with further reading, while others moved between television, social media and YouTube or deliberately sought views different from their own.

The participant-based matrix shown in  indicates that social media and YouTube appeared across a broad part of the sample, while television remained part of some participants’ information environments. The accounts suggest that media use involved more than choosing a single platform; participants often described moving between sources and evaluating the information they encountered. The platform codes were based on sources mentioned by participants during the interviews rather than on a predefined list of social media platforms.

One participant explained how a short social media video could lead to further political information-seeking:

“I see a two-minute video and think, ‘that was a good speech.’ Then I get curious about the person and go to their social media account. I try to read their posts, their views on events, and the texts they write. I also try to learn about the ideologies they believe in.” (P1)

Another described moving between traditional and digital media:

“I use mass media, mainly news channels. But we follow things that are not shown on the news through social media. I follow Twitter or news sites. I also watch YouTube.” (P21)

A third account included an explicit attempt to encounter views beyond the participant’s own political position:

“I mostly follow Twitter because that is where most news first appears. I also follow Instagram, and sometimes television and radio. I want to follow news channels even when they do not reflect my own views because I want to see the other side. Sometimes I feel as if I am in an echo chamber because I end up following more people who share my own views.” (P24)

“I use Instagram and Twitter. I think following their own accounts rather than fan accounts is healthier, because fan accounts tend to go back to older events and present past mistakes more negatively. I think they should all be followed through their own accounts.” (P16)

presents the category Expectations, Needs, and Perceptions of Political Trust under the theme Political Information and Aspirational Orientations. Economic freedom was coded in 12 segments and Personal development/quality education in eight. Employment and individual freedom were each represented in seven segments, while justice and honest and ethical decision-making appeared in six. Other codes concerned security, meritocracy, transportation, accountability and participation, being understood, fulfillment of promises and political change. Participants’ expectations therefore included both material conditions and the way political institutions and representatives were expected to respond to citizens.

The participant-based matrix presented in  shows that these expectations were not concentrated in a single area. Economic conditions and education appeared alongside justice, freedom, accountability, security and communication. This variation is important for understanding political trust here as a perception related to several aspects of participants’ relationship with the political system rather than as a single attitude.

One participant focused specifically on transparency and accountability:

“They need to be more open. We want to see where the taxes we pay go. When we look for an answer to this question, we face various accusations. There should be an accountable, transparent and open structure.” (P5)

Another combined economic expectations with security, education and a desire for support from elected representatives:

“Generation Z wants economic comfort and prosperity. They want security, comfortable spaces and dormitories, and more educational opportunities. They want to know that the person who is elected stands behind them, protects them and is there for them.” (P8)

In another account, the focus was on justice, freedom, and political communication:

“I think they expect a just and free environment. I want us to be given a little more freedom. I also want the language used toward us to be softer because there is a real lack of communication.” (P22)

“At least, we expect to be in a better position than we are now, especially in terms of the economy and education. We expect things to change. We have serious problems with education, housing, and finding a job after graduation.” (P19)

presents the category Demands for Responsive Representation under the theme Youth Expectations and Perceived Political Responsiveness. Politicians should value and understand young people was coded in nine segments, Concerns about the future should be alleviated in seven, and Politicians should improve themselves in six. Participants also referred to opportunities to go abroad, equal living conditions, access to technology, education, basic needs, economic policies and opportunities for young people to participate in politics. These demands concerned both young people’s living conditions and the relationship they expected political actors to establish with them.

The participant-based matrix mentioned in  reflects the different forms that these demands took. Some accounts centered on employment, economic conditions and future uncertainty. Others focused on political communication, being listened to and creating more opportunities for young people to participate.

One participant connected future anxiety with unemployment and unequal opportunities:

“I think the reason Generation Z becomes depressed is completely related to unemployment and the economic situation. I will graduate next year, but I do not know what I am going to do. There is a need to ensure that everyone can live under equal conditions.” (P9)

Another focused on the style of political communication:

“My complaint is that they sometimes speak by shouting and raising their voices. I think it could be calmer. I know that my friends think the same way.” (P13)

A third account placed greater emphasis on listening and participation:

“They should listen to young people. They should adopt a participatory approach. A platform could be created for young people where their suggestions could be collected. The most important thing is that young people are listened to.” (P26)

“Personally, politicians should improve themselves. For example, do they read books? I think they speak too much in colloquial language, even at a lower level. They should focus more on English.” (P11)

As the research findings also show, for young voters, voting for the first time does not simply mean participating in the electoral process. According to data from the interviews, this first experience represents a process in which individuals assess how they position themselves within the political system, what emotions accompany their voting behavior, and whether the choices they ultimately make align with their perception of their own political reality. When approached from this perspective, the notion that the first voting experience is based solely on the resources available to voters in this group or on the strategic calculations they make is incomplete (; ). When the first election day arrives, the young voter begins to reflect on their political identity and enters a process of making sense of their choices in this arena, thereby beginning to question the nature of the direct or indirect relationship they have established with the political system.

During the research process, participants described their generation through expressions such as “born into technology”, “questioning” and “living with uncertainty”. These shared definitions suggest that generational belonging is not merely demographic but is also connected to common historical and socio-economic conditions. In line with social identity theory (; ; ), the findings indicate that generational identity may provide a shared point of reference for political self-positioning, even where strong party affiliation is absent.

According to the participants’ statements, emotions do not influence first-time voting in a single direction. Affective intelligence theory associates anxiety with greater attention to unfamiliar situations and links emotions such as anger and enthusiasm to political mobilization (; ). In this study, however, anxiety, hope, optimism and disappointment often appeared together and were closely tied to economic insecurity, distrust of institutions and limited political options. This suggests that the political effects of emotion depend strongly on the context in which these emotions are experienced.

In addition, when young voters determine their political preferences, they do more than simply express their support for a single candidate or party. They also seek to establish a connection between their choice and their own political stance. Within this framework, political information may be processed in a biased manner, serving to preserve individuals’ previous decisions and allegiances. Rather than evaluating new political developments impartially, individuals may interpret them through the lens of their existing beliefs and commitments (); such commitments may also influence their subsequent political evaluations (). The participant’s description of voting as “searching for an option within a lack of options” suggests that first-time voting may involve an effort to reconcile political preferences with a restricted set of electoral alternatives. In fact, such statements do not fundamentally indicate inconsistency. They also reveal the effort of political identities, which are still developing around the first voting experience, to find a balance with the electoral alternatives available within the existing system. In this context, voting for the first time can be understood as a process of political self-positioning in which individuals’ self-definition and political preferences mutually shape one another.

Although political efficacy remains visible within the research findings, it also appears to rest on relatively fragile ground. The classical distinctions in the literature between internal and external political efficacy concern individuals’ beliefs regarding their own political competence and the responsiveness of the political system to citizens’ expectations (; ). The fact that participants regard voting as a democratic right points primarily to an internalized civic norm rather than, by itself, to a perception of internal political efficacy. At the same time, participants’ assessments of whether their political actions can make a difference, together with references to systemic stagnation and limited responsiveness, reveal the conditional nature of political efficacy within their accounts. The act of voting is not only a reflection of efficacy but is itself involved in its negotiation. Among the participants, efficacy therefore appears as a dynamic perception rather than a fixed predictor of voting, shaped by context and by their electoral experiences.

The findings also have practical implications for political communication and youth engagement. Participants’ accounts suggest that engagement with young voters is related not only to election campaigns but also to access to political information, opportunities to express their concerns, and perceptions that political actors respond to their expectations. For political parties, public institutions, and youth-oriented civil society organizations, these findings point to the relevance of providing accessible political information and creating channels through which young people can express their priorities and receive responses. The findings also suggest that youth engagement should not be approached through a single communication platform, as participants described moving between social media, YouTube, television, and other sources when following political developments. This is consistent with recent research in Türkiye showing links between social media use, political participation, and political information among young people (; ). Recent qualitative research also shows that young voters evaluate not only the content of political communication on social media but also how politicians communicate through these platforms ().

To conclude, the presented data allows viewing the phenomenon of voting for the first time through the prism of being a psychological threshold experience rather than the start of the process of forming habits (). The creation of identity, emotional evaluation, consistency seeking, and judgment of efficacy form dimensions of a single experience. Furthermore, by using concepts from political psychology to interpret the themes developed through reflexive thematic analysis, this study shows how qualitative research can provide new insights into processes that have often been examined through surveys and experiments.

In order to expand research within this field in the future, the possible link between the identity associated with belonging to a specific generation and partisan perspective should be explored. In this case, the issue of emotional ambivalence in electoral processes and its connection to perceptions of political efficacy will be explored more thoroughly and the findings will be enriched. In addition, comparative research conducted in polarized political environment and contexts characterized by economic uncertainty will be helpful in assessing whether the findings are generational phenomena or peculiar only to the Turkish one.

Conceptualizing first-time voting behavior as a psychological threshold experience represents an important step in developing the theoretical basis of electoral participation. The aim of this research was to dispute the perception of first-time voting behavior either as something that simply becomes the start of a usual routine or as some kind of rational strategy. That is because first-time voting transcends both frameworks and appears to be an activity related to the formation of political identity, the evaluation of emotions and perceptions of political competence. In this particular case, voting among youth in the country under examination is closely intertwined with the political and economic situation. What is more, the construction of generational identity is directly linked with the feeling of economic uncertainty and distrust in institutions. Emotions that are triggered by such circumstances are not separate triggers that prompt voters to go to the polls. They are rather the result of the complicated combination of hopes and uncertainties, anxieties and sense of civic belonging.

This perspective reveals that the coexistence of a sense of civic duty and concerns about the responsiveness of the political system highlights how participation in electoral processes is shaped by current conditions. In this context, while participants may view voting behavior as valuable within democratic systems, their perceptions of the political impact of their votes remain closely linked to the responsiveness of the political system. By using reflexive thematic analysis within a political psychology framework, the present study complements research that has primarily examined voting behavior through survey research and quantitative measures by focusing on the meanings participants attach to their first voting experience. The fact that this study aimed to better understand how people position themselves politically the very first time they vote allows us to further examine how the first election experience may relate to future political involvement. Future research could follow the same people over many election cycles to learn more about how the perceptions that emerged in this study change over time. Thus, comparative research could be carried out in other democracies with political polarization or different kinds of political instabilities to find out whether the results of this study are unique for Türkiye or rather generational.

psychology.title: Cultural Adaptation of A Family-Based Intervention for Pediatric Chronic Symptoms in Latin America: A Content and Systems-Level Approach to the Development and Implementation of the Comfort Ability® Program – Español (CAP-ESP)
psychology.abstract: Pediatric chronic pain and related functional symptoms are prevalent, disabling, and require multidisciplinary intervention, inclusive of psychology. The Comfort Ability® Program (CAP) intervention aligns with evidence-based practice, offering patients and caregivers accessible, targeted education and skills training in a cognitive behavioral framework. The CAP intervention is a well-established and widely disseminated intervention with over 50 implementation sites in North America and Australia.This study describes the initial phase of culturally adapting the Comfort Ability® Program for Latinx families beginning with a Colombian population. Using a systems-level approach to cultural adaptation, this study (1) characterizes clinical needs and care gaps in Colombia, (2) identifies professional perspectives on culturally relevant factors, and (3) assesses health-system delivery considerations to inform implementation.A year-long, phased partnership between the USA-based CAP-Hub and an interdisciplinary behavioral health team in Medellín, Colombia (GROWTH) included: (a) bidirectional training/observership and first-pass Spanish translation of CAP materials; (b) a 6-hour multidisciplinary co-creation day in Colombia; and (c) capacity‑building activities including a hybrid professional/community Pain Education Day and targeted health-system and community outreach. Qualitative workshop data were analyzed via thematic analysis supported by Azure OpenAI GPT-5 with manual review and verification. Quantitative data were summarized descriptively.Thirty-nine healthcare leaders attended co-creation workshop (91.2% with prior pediatric chronic pain involvement); 34 completed post-workshop questionnaires. Pain Education Day reached 111 in-person and 209 virtual participants. Results underscore the need for interdisciplinary collaboration and will meaningfully inform intervention development.The initial phase of CAP-ESP cultural adaptation generated actionable cultural and system-level insights, established relationships, generated educational opportunity, and set the stage for pilot testing and implementation in Colombia.
psychology.text:
