Chronic pain (i.e., any pain that lasts longer than 3 months) such as headache, abdominal pain, muscle pain, joint pain, and nerve pain, along with related functional symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, and fatigue (henceforth referred to collectively as “chronic symptoms”) are common features of many pediatric diseases, illnesses, and injuries and are the current leading cause of disease burden and disability worldwide in adulthood. Due to their biopsychosocial complexity,,, the management of chronic symptoms such as persistent pain requires specialized multidisciplinary care inclusive of psychological interventions designed to target specific risk and resilience factors. Notably, of all treatment modalities for pediatric chronic symptoms (e.g., pharmacological, physical, psychological), psychological interventions based in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) have the strongest evidence base for reducing severity and improving physical, psychological, and social function, especially when provided as part of interdisciplinary care.

However, there are clear and alarming disparities in terms of who has access to this effective care and how this care is delivered., Chronic symptoms are known to be pervasively underdiagnosed and undertreated in marginalized communities due to a variety of individual, community, and system-level factors. Racially and ethnically minoritized groups are more likely to experience stereotyping, bias, racism, discrimination, and oppression, which all contribute to the etiology and maintenance of chronic symptom disparities.,, Additionally, individuals who have been historically, economically, and socially marginalized have far less access to comprehensive chronic symptom care, making the management of chronic symptoms even more challenging.,

Beyond physical suffering, there are significant economic disparities associated with chronic symptoms. For example, young adults with chronic symptoms are less likely to have a full-time job, less likely to have work associated with long-term career goals, significantly more likely to receive public assistance, are at increased risk of early parenthood, and have lower quality relationships with peers and romantic partners., These disparities are even more evident in minoritized populations. Because of this significant morbidity and robust evidence demonstrating the link between pediatric chronic symptoms and chronic symptoms in adulthood, there is a global call to action for improved comprehensive chronic symptom care in pediatrics that is impactful and accessible to all. With research demonstrating that Hispanic youth in particular may experience higher prevalence of chronic symptoms such as pain while having less access to empirically based psychological treatments, this population is in critical need of culturally congruent interventions embedded within accessible care models., In addition to these challenges facing minoritized Hispanic youth, within Latin America more broadly there is a need for increased pain management resources. Pain management in Latin America is challenged by a lack of pain education for providers alongside economic, social, and cultural challenges, resulting in a general lack of resources for pediatric pain patients., This study explores a multi-layered, comprehensive approach to adapting the Comfort Ability® Program, a widely disseminated family-based intervention rooted in cognitive behavioral therapy and evidence-based practice (EBP) for the treatment of chronic pediatric symptoms. This study serves as a first step toward improving access to evidence-based pain management care for families in Colombia, with an ultimate goal of working toward increasing access to this specialized care across Latin America and Hispanic populations more broadly.

Over the past 20 years extensive literature on cultural adaptation has emerged, highlighting both theoretical and practical approaches to modifying existing, research-supported interventions across varied populations and clinical settings. There is ongoing debate regarding the need to balance adherence to the fidelity an existing intervention and the need for the flexibility and modification to enhance adoption in new cultural contexts. While there is no agreed‑upon best model, there is general consensus regarding the need for careful evaluation and subsequent modification of (1) surface-level factors such as language (e.g., translation of text, modified metaphors, culturally relevant examples), (2) deeper-level factors such as intervention content (e.g., inclusion of cultural values or beliefs, expansion to include extended family), and (3) systems-level factors such as consideration of training models and healthcare systems (e.g., professional development needs, creation of referral pathways). Additionally, structured cultural adaptation processes that meaningfully engage in partnership with local systems, providers, and patients are known to significantly increase treatment effectiveness and decrease inequities in care., Schilling et al. provide a helpful framework of best practices for cultural adaptations of parent interventions, including centering the need for assessment of systems-level strengths and needs. Key steps within this framework include conducting needs assessments with the target population, engaging community stakeholders, and collecting data to inform both surface-level and deep-structure adaptations. These steps are essential for successful piloting and refinement of an existing intervention. Relatedly, conceptual frameworks on dissemination or “scaling-out” of existing interventions suggest that the amount of modification needed and the expectancy of benefit is influenced by the extent to which the population, delivery system, or both are sustaining change in the adaptation. In practice, there is a wide continuum across cultural adaptation outcomes with some interventions requiring little to no adaptation and others requiring substantial changes or even the need for an alternate, novel intervention altogether. Thus, it is imperative to approach cultural adaptation procedures with both the knowledge of existing adaptation approaches and with the capacity to evaluate systematically as the process unfolds, remaining open to a wide variety of factors that may enhance or impede adaptation and implementation.

Frustration with the gap between known effectiveness of targeted pediatric psychology intervention for patients with chronic pain and their families and the lack of access led to the creation of the first Comfort Ability® Program (CAP) intervention in 2010, at a large tertiary care center in the northeastern United States. The CAP intervention is a brief (12-hour) intervention for youth with chronic pain and their caregivers. It is rooted in cognitive behavioral therapy and provides targeted neuroscience education, an array of evidence-informed coping strategies, and teaches families how to generate functional recovery plans. It is also designed to reduce the stigma and biomedical biases known to impede initiation of psychological intervention and foster safe and supportive group engagement, all in accordance with best practices in biopsychosocial intervention.,

Iteratively developed and tested in collaboration with patient partners and interdisciplinary experts, the CAP intervention uses multimethod learning techniques to teach neuroscience pain education, provide hands‑on skills training with an array of evidence-based strategies, and teaches targeted caregiver training skills. The CAP intervention was designed for implementation with an intensive one-day format, reducing the likelihood that patients and families would receive only a partial “dose” of the intervention via attrition as seen in multi-session groups. It is delivered as a manualized, interactive intervention to help adolescents and their parents or caregivers learn how to manage chronic symptoms. Research demonstrates that CAP is a feasible intervention with demonstrated functional and psychosocial gains for both adolescents and caregivers. Originally begun as an intervention focused entirely on pediatric chronic pain, in 2023 the program underwent a significant revision based on updated science and identified clinical needs to expand its focus to chronic pain and related symptoms (e.g., nausea, fatigue, dizziness).

One of the unique aspects of the CAP implementation model in the pediatric psychology landscape is its dual focus on both content development and dissemination. Grounded in both Knowledge Mobilization, and the RE-AIM framework,, CAP has undergone an iterative process of content development and systems level procedural modifications based on feedback from a network of over 50 international CAP sites. Knowledge Mobilization focuses on the process of moving academic research into real-world settings where it can be effectively used to enhance practice or policy., RE-AIM focuses more specifically on how to ensure an intervention can reach the targeted population, evaluate its effectiveness, develop organizational support for delivering the intervention, ensure that the intervention is delivered with fidelity, and is sustainable., Using this framework within North America, CAP has responsively adapted to (1) private and public hospital settings, (2) developed diverse and systematic procedures for education and onboarding of intervention site directors and group leaders inclusive of psychologists, allied professionals working in pediatric health settings (e.g., social workers, physical therapists, nurses), and trainees (e.g., interns, residents, fellows), and (3) expanded consultation opportunities for administrative processes and co-development of novel clinical care pathway for new and existing CAP sites. In addition, previous publications outline the collaborative and systematic procedures associated both with the development of a content-level adaptation designed for patients with sickle cell pain (CAP-SCP) as well as a systems-level and cultural evaluation of CAP in an Australian context. Specifically, within the CAP-SCP adaptation, a careful analysis and co-creation with a multidisciplinary team with patient partners determined that there were substantial changes needed to the structure of the intervention delivery as well as content. The Australia co-creation event included collaboration between interdisciplinary professionals, patient partners, and healthcare executives to consider language, cultural similarities and differences, and healthcare system-level factors. In this instance, CAP was determined to be an excellent fit clinically, closing an imperative healthcare gap. However, additional work was needed to secure long-term sustainability within the universal health system.

The CAP intervention was designed to address many of the barriers to engaging in psychological interventions for pediatric chronic pain and has been successfully adapted to various settings and populations. However, to date it has not been available to Spanish-speaking families. This is highly problematic because, although Hispanic youth experience higher rates of chronic pain in comparison to their non-Hispanic peers, empirically based psychological treatments are underutilized in this population due to lack of access and insufficient attention to cultural relevance.,, As noted above, patients from developing countries (including those in Latin America) also face challenges due to the under-recognition of pediatric chronic pain and associated symptoms, limited financial resources for the development and implementation of culturally congruent pain assessment and management practices, lack of pain education and training for pediatric providers, and limited research on pain management., Given that language-specific, culturally adapted interventions have been shown to significantly increase treatment effectiveness and decrease inequities in care for populations from diverse backgrounds,, it is imperative that well-established interventions undergo a rigorous translation and cultural adaptation process that enhances access to care for underserved communities.

This article describes the exploration and initial phase of cultural adaptation for the Comfort Ability® Program Español (CAP-ESP), a multi-layered process of interdisciplinary collaboration, co-creation, and education in partnership with the CAP USA based hub (CAP-Hub) and Colombian partners. When complete, this adaptation process will include essential engagement and feedback from patients with lived experience and their caregivers. However, the initial phase of the adaptation, as outlined in this paper, focuses on engagement with local systems and multidisciplinary professionals. Specifically, the primary qualitative assessment aims of this project are to: (1) identify clinical need and gaps in care regarding multidisciplinary pediatric chronic symptom management in Colombia, (2) identify relevant cultural factors (e.g., concepts of pain, illness, family values, stigma regarding mental health), and (3) to learn about system-level differences (e.g., professional education and practice parameters) and health delivery system factors (e.g., clinical and referral pathways) that will inform intervention adaptation and implementation. Beyond the specific aims, an essential goal of this phase of the cultural adaptation process is to build capacity, laying the professional and system-level groundwork for collaboration on a formal implementation study. It is important to note that a cultural adaptation in Colombia is not expected to generalize to Latin America more broadly or to Hispanic youth in the US. However, a successful adaptation of CAP-ESP in Colombia may provide an effective roadmap for broader cultural and language adaptations. Moreover, lessons learned in this process will help to streamline the iterative process of adaptation in other healthcare and cultural settings.

A multi-layered, cross-cultural exploration of clinical care and system-level needs was developed in partnership with an evidence-based multidisciplinary behavioral health practice in Medellín, Colombia (GROWTH). Leaders of the Colombian team included coauthor EP (GROWTH co-founder, a bilingual neuropsychologist) who played a pivotal role in design and execution of co-creation and educational initiatives, and core members of her team including SG and IP, neuropsychologists, and JL, a Colombian palliative care physician. From the CAP hub, MV (a native Colombian and pediatric pain psychologist) led the adaptation process with support from AEH (bilingual pediatric psychologist with expertise in provider education and program development) and RC (CAP founder and director). The initial aim of this adaptation process is focused on healthcare systems and providers, a foundational step that is congruent with Schilling et al.’s framework. Moreover, starting the adaptation process with systems and providers ensures that there is a clinical need, can help to identify key organizational and cultural barriers within a system, and builds trust and stakeholder buy-in, an essential part of working cross-culturally in Latin America. This process aligns with Aarons et al.’s (2017) construct of “Type 1” scaling out, a type of scaling in which a target population (i.e. pediatric patients with pain and other chronic symptoms) is the same, but the intervention’s setting and delivery system is different. The CAP cross-cultural team (CAP-Hub and GROWTH) developed a phased project, unfolding over the course of 1 year, in which there was (1) opportunity for GROWTH to learn evidence-based practice in pediatric chronic symptom management as well as CAP-specific research and clinical intervention (pre-adaptation), (2) development and analysis of a cross-disciplinary co-creation day to broadly evaluate the need and potential fit of clinical, system, and intervention-specific component parts within the Colombian system, and (3) community outreach and professional development initiatives to lay the groundwork for pilot testing and future implementation, if deemed appropriate.

The CAP cultural adaptation process began by GROWTH sending two bilingual neuropsychologists to the United States for a 1-week training and observership program, embedding within the US-based CAP-Hub. During this time, GROWTH conveyed their belief that there was a clinical need for the CAP intervention in Colombia and that there was presently no access to routine psychosocial intervention for pediatric chronic pain and other symptoms. As a next step, GROWTH psychologists developed a first-pass translation of CAP materials into Spanish, and the CAP-Hub reviewed translations and facilitated graphic design of the new materials. Simultaneously, the GROWTH team helped plan and coordinate a 1-week visit to Colombia for the CAP-Hub team (including 5 pediatric psychologists and 1 program manager) during which there was joint leadership for the following three initiatives: (1) Multidisciplinary CAP co-creation workshop, (2) Professional Pain Education Day, and (3) Community and Health system outreach. These events, detailed below, are essential to the cultural adaptation process as they focus on creating a shared understanding of the system-level and clinical issues and help to build sturdy collaborations that foster the cultural adaptation process.

A co-creation workshop is a structured, participatory process where an array of invested people come together to collaboratively shape, refine, or adapt a program. Co-creation actively invites multiple perspectives into the design process, an especially powerful approach in the context of cultural adaptation, where local knowledge is foundational to a successful implementation. For this project, the co-creation workshop was specifically designed to help the team learn and reflect on the cultural values, relational norms, and healthcare practices across a variety of Colombian healthcare leaders and professionals, specifically as relates to treatment of pediatric chronic pain. It was also intended to build trust and familiarity in this relatively novel practice area. The workshop, held in Medellín, included structured individual and group-based activities.

The co-creation workshop was organized by the Colombian GROWTH partners. A list of potential participants was identified by the Colombian team invested in pediatric pain care and included local leaders with intimate knowledge of medical education, healthcare delivery professionals from public and private hospitals (both clinical providers and administrators), and community partners (e.g. school nurses). GROWTH partners personally invited all potential participants via WhatsApp or telephone call. Prospective participants were informed about the co-creation activity through a flyer that detailed the purpose of the event and how their contributions would be used. In accordance with local regulations and institutional policies, a formal consent process was not required for this event. However, to protect 235 participants, all questionnaire data was anonymous and no personal information (e.g., names) was collected by notetakers during discussions. At the start of the event, the purpose of the co-creation day was again explained and participants were reminded that engagement in the day was voluntary. In total, 45 professionals were invited to participate. All agreed to participate, though six were unable to attend on the day of the workshop due to scheduling conflicts. Therefore, there were 39 participants in total including two GROWTH representatives and six community participants. A gift bag – including a book, a Comfort Ability coping kit, and Spanish pain management resources – was provided as a thank you for participation. There was no additional compensation.

Data collected in each activity included individual questionnaire-based responses (quantitative and qualitative) and notes taken by a dedicated bilingual note taker during facilitated, multidisciplinary discussion groups of 8–10 professionals. The individual questionnaire, developed for this specific project, included open-ended questions and ratings for participants to complete at the start of each activity, before there was opportunity for group discussion. This strategy is based on a well-established qualitative research technique that helps to (1) reduce groupthink, (2) capture independent perspectives, (3) minimize the influence of dominant group participants, (4) promote reflection, and (5) provide complementary data. A copy of the questionnaire is attached as . The small group discussions were not recorded, but a bilingual note taker was present in each group to record data.

The co-creation workshop was 5-hours long and included the following 5 activities:
Activity #1: Building Cross-Disciplinary Connection. The goal of this activity was to create a warm, collaborative, working group. Participants were paired with a new acquaintance, and they interviewed each other using a set of structured questions that encouraged sharing about professional experiences, discussion of a change or innovation that had made a big impact in their work, and personal perspectives on what a successful collaboration might look or feel like to them.Activity #2: Preparing to Engage. The goal of this activity was to create a relaxed and open mind-set, a critical part of effective brainstorming. Participants engaged in a psychologist-led mindfulness practice. This activity provided both experiential knowledge of a practice commonly used in the treatment of chronic pain (and in the CAP intervention), and helped participants create an open and curious mind-set, preparing for discussion about clinical experiences and challenges.Activity #3: Evaluation of a Clinical Case Study. The goal of this activity was to learn how providers from different disciplines and different sectors of the healthcare system conceptualize a complex case of a young person with chronic pain. Group leader presented the case of “Gabriela,” a 14-year-old adolescent with chronic pain (see , Activity #3). Each participant individually responded to a series of questions regarding their familiarity and conceptualization of cases like Gabriela’s, reflected on how they might contribute to Gabriela’s care, and how they would advise the family. Following individual responses, the group was instructed to collaborate in an activity of “building a care path” for this patient; they used printed blocks to write out different steps in the care pathway and organized them into the “path” that a patient might take on the road to recovery. They were prompted to discuss how long it would take the family to navigate the pathway, what factors might make it go faster or slower, and what they thought would optimize the path. Individuals then had the opportunity to go around the room and view how other groups had envisioned pathways, followed by additional time for reflections and group discussion. Photographs of each group’s care pathway were taken to record the various responses.Activity #4: Pain and Culture. The goal of this activity was to understand participants’ view of pain from a cultural lens as this is known to influence clinical decision making, communication with patients, and can reveal training and support needs. For example, how symptoms are described (e.g., extent to which there is suffering and distress or the need for stoicism), who helps to treat symptoms (family, spiritual healers, doctors, friends), what symptoms may mean (e.g., punishment, bad luck, genetics), what treatment or relief looks like (e.g., prayer, acceptance, medication) all inform the language and approach for an intervention like CAP. In this activity, participants were asked to individually reflect on what family values or beliefs within Colombian culture were important to consider in Gabriela’s case, and to reflect on how these might be relevant in clinical care more broadly.Activity #5: Assessment of CAP Clinical Domains. The goal of this activity was to assess participants professional view of congruence/incongruence across CAP’s core clinical domains of functional recovery (i.e., school, sleep, activity). This activity unfolded in two parts, (1) participants individually rated (0–10) the level of concern a specific functional challenge (co-sleeping with a parent, missed school, discontinuation of sport) would raise for them professionally, (2) four key CAP intervention components were evaluated in small groups with participants allowed to self-select into groups based on their interest or professional experience. Written intervention content was shared with participants so they could review, explore, and react. Discussion groups were led by a CAP team psychologist, with translator available when needed. A designated notetaker (nonparticipating GROWTH staff) recorded group insights and questions.

The GROWTH and CAP-Hub collaboration determined that a Pain Education Day would help both professionals and the lay community to explore and understand the biopsychosocial approach to pediatric pain management. Additionally, it was hoped that this initiative would help lay the groundwork for a shared understanding of clinical issues as well as an opportunity to build relationships that could subsequently support the creation of new referral pathways and intervention implementation. Therefore, following the co-creation workshop (so as not to unduly influence participant feedback), the CAP-Hub hosted a 4-hour Pain Education Day, open to professionals and the lay community, that provided an overview of pediatric chronic pain and the role of psychology in multidisciplinary treatment.

The education day was delivered live in-person but was also transmitted virtually via live video feed and recorded. Lectures were delivered primarily in Spanish, with live translation available for the English lecture and discussion. The structured curriculum included an overview of the history and current understanding of pediatric chronic pain, an introduction to pain neuroscience, discussion regarding the role of behavioral health in the biopsychosocial model of care, and teaching regarding specific evidence-based interventions for adolescents and parents. The day finished with a panel discussion featuring three Latin American physicians from the CAP-Hub (two anesthesiologists and a psychiatrist specializing in chronic symptoms) discussing their perspectives on multidisciplinary work in the US. Throughout Pain Education Day an effort was made to highlight existing free resources readily available in Spanish for providers of all disciplines. Provision of this education aligns with the principles of community-engaged research by providing a direct benefit to participating services while setting the stage for a sustainable integration of the intervention into routine practice in the future.

During CAP-Hub visits in Colombia, a series of health system outreach events and media engagements were scheduled to further expand knowledge of healthcare delivery systems in the private and public sector, build local relationships, and provide support and education to the community. Site visits included meetings at local hospitals with clinical staff (i.e., social workers, psychiatrists, physicians, physical therapists) and hospital administration (i.e., hospital presidents, department leadership), as well as university meetings in the allied health field to build academic relationships and learn training models. Additionally, toward the goal of providing education to the community, the CAP-Hub team participated in three Spanish language podcasts and the GROWTH team was featured in a local paper, highlighting their co-creation work in the CAP adaptation process, and setting the stage for expanded clinical care in pediatric chronic symptom management (see  for links to Colombian media).

Analysis of qualitative feedback from the co-creation workshop participants was completed using thematic analysis in partnership with the study institution’s AI Resource Hub specialists. Our approach was mapped onto a well-established inductive thematic analysis framework, consistent with guidance that AI supports rather than replaces human judgment. Azure OpenAI GPT-5 was used to qualitatively evaluate thematic categories across the five co-creation workshop activities. The AI model was guided by an analytic prompt developed in collaboration with the institution’s AI experts and the CAP-Hub team. Current research states that if the prompt design framework is developed with researcher feedback and aligned with traditional qualitative methods, it enhances an AI-model’s effectiveness in qualitative analysis by improving context definition, methodological guidance, and data structuring. Toward this goal, three members of the CAP-hub team (AEH, RC, and SRM) jointly worked with the AI specialist to (1) familiarize the model; (2) develop activity-specific prompts specifying analytic tasks; and (3) define target structured outputs (themes, definitions, counts, quotes) and constraints to prevent fabricated content and quotes. Analysis was conducted separately for each activity to reflect the structure, content, and flow of the co-creation day. The AI model generated structured outputs in JSON format, including two to four attributed quotations per theme. These outputs were aggregated to examine thematic frequency and patterns within each distinct activity. To address ethical and quality-control considerations, CAP-Hub team members oversaw data analysis reviewing individual feedback, manually checking codes and themes across the full sample, and verifying the authenticity of quotations identified by the model.

The management of quantitative data from the co-creation and pain education day is descriptive in nature, including summation and means.

A total of 45 local leaders in healthcare were invited to participate in the co-creation workshop. All enthusiastically accepted the invitation, though six (13%) were unable to come on the day of the workshop due to scheduling conflicts. The final group included 39 participants. Participants came from a range of disciplines including psychology (n = 20), physical therapy (n = 9), nursing (n = 1), and medicine (n = 9 from pediatrics, neurology, palliative care, gastroenterology, nutrition). Participants’ years of professional experience ranged from 2 to 31 years, with the average length of time in practice as 13.8 years (SD 7.9 years). Almost all (91.2%, N = 31) of the participants had previous involvement in a pediatric chronic pain case, reflecting that these were indeed providers who had personal experiences related to patients with pediatric chronic pain in Colombia. Results described below highlight the feedback recorded in participants’ individual questionnaires submitted at the end of the workshop (N = 34). A short video of the co-creation and education events, including participant feedback, is also available in .

Within the knowledge and skills theme, attendees expressed a strong desire to deepen their understanding of chronic pain in children and adolescents, to learn evidence-based management strategies, and to gain practical tools and interventions they could directly apply in clinical practice. Many explicitly wanted to better understand and work with the Comfort Ability® Program, enhance their clinical care, and develop capacity for research and program implementation in their own settings.

The second theme emphasized context, culture, and holistic approaches that were congruent with Colombian culture. Participants highlighted the importance of adapting mind-body and pain management concepts to Colombian sociocultural context and the local health system. They underscored the need to incorporate holistic and multimodal perspectives on pain and consistently linked their learning goals to improving the quality, relevance, and impact of care for children with chronic symptoms and their families.

The third theme centered on cross disciplinary collaboration, building networks, and collective reflection. Attendees hoped to build and strengthen professional networks and communities of practice dedicated to pediatric pain, engage in interdisciplinary collaboration, and learn from the diverse perspectives and experiences of others. They also valued opportunities for critical reflection – to debate their own knowledge, identify blind spots and systemic issues, and jointly recognize challenges and gaps in current practice.

Together, these three themes illustrate participants’ strong focus not only on individual learning, but also for co-creating sustainable, contextually grounded, and collaborative approaches to pediatric pain care in Colombia. These results confirm that there is a basis for building intervention and suggest that there is capacity for a robust, culturally responsive implementation study of CAP.

During this activity, participants were asked to reflect and discuss their vision and perceived contributing factors to a successful collaboration. Identified themes were as follows: Communication (n = 9), emphasizing open, clear, and continuous information exchange among team members; Interdisciplinary Teamwork (n = 7) highlighting coordinated work across professional roles and disciplines as central to effective collaboration; and Family Involvement (n = 5) underscoring the importance of actively engaging caregivers and children in their care and decision-making processes. Participants also described successful collaboration as grounded in education and support (n = 3), with shared learning, guidance, and tangible assistance. Less frequently, but notably, respondents emphasized shared goals and trust (n = 2), such as aligned objectives, mutual confidence, and respect, and a positive emotional climate and validation (n = 2), characterized by empathy and a supportive relational environment.

In this mindfulness-based activity, 50% of the participants reported that they had practiced mindfulness before. After engaging in the relaxation exercise led by a CAP-Hub team member, 82.4% of participants reported a lower stress score (M = 3.37, SD = 1.97) compared to their stress level before the exercise (M = 5.87, SD = 1.53).

When asked to describe what roles they have played or could potentially play in a pediatric chronic pain case similar to the one presented, participants identified a diverse set of professional roles. They reported involvement in assessment and diagnosis, conducting comprehensive evaluations of cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and contextual factors (n = 12), and in intervention and treatment as providers delivering ongoing psychotherapeutic and other clinical care (n = 14). Roles also encompassed family support and counseling (n = 10), addressing caregivers’ emotional needs and family dynamics, and education and psychoeducation (n = 8), providing information about pain, treatment options, and coping strategies. In addition, participants emphasized interdisciplinary collaboration (n = 6) with other health professionals, therapeutic accompaniment (n = 5) through sustained emotional presence and support, prevention and functional maintenance (n = 4) to avert complications and promote daily functioning, and cultural sensitivity and relational dynamics (n = 4), explicitly integrating cultural context and relationship patterns into care.

Before processing the case with the other pediatric experts present and collaboratively creating a case formulation, attendees recorded their individual reflections and assessment of the case study. They most frequently emphasized emotional and psychological factors, highlighting anxiety, depression, and emotional distress (n = 18) as central drivers of the patient’s physical symptoms, and often raised the possibility of somatic symptom disorder (n = 7), with somatic complaints emerging in the absence of clear “organic causes.” Respondents also underscored the role of family dynamics and support (n = 6), noting family pressures, limited resources, and relational difficulties, and advocated for a multidisciplinary treatment approach (n = 5) integrating psychological, social, and medical interventions. Additional themes included learning disability and academic pressures (n = 4), where intellectual challenges and school demands were seen as exacerbating emotional and physical difficulties, and chronic pain and hypersensitivity (n = 5), describing amplified pain perception influenced by emotional and contextual factors. Finally, participants acknowledged uncertainty and diagnostic challenges (n = 4), given overlapping emotional, physical, and social contributors, and pointed to cultural and social considerations (n = 3), including family structure and societal expectations, as important contextual influences on the patient’s presentation and potential outcomes.

Another theme that participants highlighted was the role of the family both in the perception of pain and its treatment. For example, “We are a culture that places a lot of importance on the opinions of all family members,” and “families have very close bonds that impact care and support, either perpetuating symptoms or aiding improvement.” Finally, many participants commented about the high degree of stigma associated with psychology and mental health. Participants wrote,
“In Colombia psychology is still seen as a taboo,” “social patterns tend to keep the mental health of family members secret,” and “going to a psychologist or psychiatrist is ‘only for crazy people,’ [is] a belief we must work to change.”

Notably, through group discussion and written comments, participants also offered important insight regarding how their healthcare system affects access to pediatric pain care. Specifically, without a primary PCP or centralized records (neither of which are common in Colombia), both providers and families can feel lost and uncertain about a child’s diagnoses and may have difficulty implementing a cohesive functional rehabilitative plan. Additionally, providers shared that within Medellín’s healthcare system “pediatric” designation typically refers to patients up to the age of 14, a fact relevant that CAP’s target audience is 10–17-year-olds and their caregivers. Discussions also highlighted that health psychology is a nascent discipline in Colombia and that access to pediatric psychology (the most common profession for CAP intervention facilitators in North America and Australia) is nonexistent.

Participants independently rated their level of concern (1–5, “not at all” to “extremely”) if a patient reported difficulties across different areas of functioning that are addressed directly through the CAP intervention (i.e., school, peer engagement, activity, and sleep): “How concerned would you be if your adolescent patient (or their parent) reported that they were ….” Across all items, participants reported substantial concern, with the majority of ratings falling in the “moderate” to “extremely” concerned range. Concern was highest for indicators of school and social impairment. For “not able to complete homework” and “not able to attend school at all,” 16% were “moderate” and 81% “extremely” concerned. For “not able to do activities of daily living independently” and “missing out on activities with friends,” 29% rated “moderate” and 71% “extremely” concerned in both cases. Sleep disruptions were rated as key areas of concern as well: for “getting less than 7 hours of sleep per night,” 45% endorsed “moderate” and 36% “extremely” concerned, and for “sleeping too much and missing activities,” 36% and 58%, respectively. Taken together, these patterns underscore that local pediatric experts prioritize school engagement, daily functioning, social participation, and sleep as key areas of clinical focus, closely mirroring evidence-based pediatric pain approaches and supporting the conceptual alignment of the CAP intervention within the local context.

A total of 320 individuals participated in the Pain Education Day program, including 111 in-person attendees and 209 virtual registrants. The in-person group comprised a variety of professionals, including psychologists, physicians, and allied health professionals as well as caregivers, patients and other members of the lay community (see ). Virtual registrants represented a range of Spanish-speaking countries including Colombia (n = 109), the United States (n = 34), Peru (n = 16), Mexico (n = 8), Ecuador (n = 6), Uruguay (n = 6), Spain (n = 5), Costa Rica (n = 4) and Venezuela (n = 3), Boliva (n = 2), Puerto Rico (n = 2) and Argentina (n = 1).Table 4.Pain education day participants by profession categories.Professional RoleIn-Person ProgramVirtual ProgramTotalPsychiatry538Physician Roles(General Pediatrics, Pediatric Subspecialties, Anesthesia, Pain/Palliative, Physiatry/PM&R, Other)116273Psychology & Mental Health Providers3298130Allied Health Role(Physiotherapy, Occupation therapy, child life, music therapy, nutrition, prehospital care technology)161026Nursing6410Social work156Education/pedagogy/teaching055Administration/business/coordination167Students/Residents(Medical, Psychology, Other)71017Other professional roles11011Unknown31031Total participantsaccounted for111209320

Following this successful event, CAP staff were invited to present at numerous other events in Colombia on the topic of multidisciplinary pain treatment including a local hospital’s Grand Rounds and the Sociedade de Anestesiologia Regional Latino Americana (LASRA). Additionally, they were asked to host a Pain Education Day in Uruguay (livestreamed for an international audience) and with ongoing demand for additional education, they teamed up with GROWTH to provide a series of webinars for both local providers and those from other Spanish‑speaking countries. Recently, due to ongoing requests for education and outreach, a multidisciplinary, bilingual international outreach team was formalized (CAP-Global Outreach; CAP-GO) to extend this important work beyond this cultural adaptation project.

Consistent with consensus literature in cultural adaptation processes, the development of CAP-ESP is carefully unfolding as a collaborative, systems-level exploration of clinical need and health care practice infrastructure, along with evaluation of surface-level and contextual cultural differences that will shape intervention and implementation procedures. Adherence to these important factors will facilitate CAP’s goal of meaningfully embedding evidence-supported, family-based, clinical intervention for the management of pediatric chronic pain and functional symptoms in Colombia, while also setting the stage for adoption more broadly in Latin America. Congruent with Schilling et al.’s framework which centers systems-level needs as a critical part of a successful adaptation, this initial study has focused on gathering information and feedback from community stakeholders to inform surface-level and deep-structure changes that may be needed. Critically, the next phase of the adaptation process will include building patient and caregiver partnerships, ensuring that the CAP framework broadly targets the unmet need for psychological intervention for chronic pain and related symptoms, is a culturally acceptable approach, and meaningfully enhances access to care. Through this current in‑depth evaluation of healthcare systems and professional landscape (the foundation of Schilling et al. 2001 recommendations for best practices), we have learned many essential lessons that will help to shape the next phase of development.

Importantly, the CAP-Hub and GROWTH collaboration has been significantly strengthened through this one-year collaborative process. This relationship building is not a luxury in Colombian culture; warm, personal, face-to-face connection is foundational to collaboration and building trust in Latin America. Without this foundation, embedding a novel clinical intervention with healthcare systems-level implications would simply not be possible. This sturdy partnership has been the catalyst for every initiative in this cross-cultural adaptation process and will continue to be central in the pilot phase of development, and beyond. Relatedly, by making time for relationship building beyond GROWTH (e.g., Colombian hospital site visits, meetings with cross disciplinary professionals in the community, and engaging with local media), the CAP-Hub team has gained essential information that informs the cultural adaptation, even beyond the scope of the data captured and analyzed from the co-creation day. Therefore, what follows is an overview of data analysis, combined with relational learning that unfolded in parallel to this process, offering a dynamic perspective on cultural adaptation in alignment with our study aims.

Healthcare professionals consistently identified pediatric chronic pain as an important but underserved clinical need, characterized by limited specialized services, fragmented care pathways, and a need for interdisciplinary, evidence-based management. Very encouragingly, multidisciplinary professionals in Colombia unequivocally believe there is a need for a clinical intervention such as CAP to support pediatric patients who present with debilitating chronic pain and related symptoms and their families. Moreover, there is a shared cross-cultural understanding of the inherent complexity in helping these patients return to function and the need for coordinated multidisciplinary care. Across the Colombian healthcare system, there is presently no systematic way for families to obtain psychological intervention alongside physical therapy and medical intervention, and this is a clear and recognized gap in care. Toward the goal of closing this gap, specific considerations at the clinical, health-care systems-level, and professional educational landscape are reviewed.

Participants viewed culture as extending beyond language and ethnicity to include family relationships, beliefs about pain, stigma surrounding psychological care, and broader social expectations like school attendance. These factors were perceived as central to how children and families understand pain, seek care, and engage with treatment.

Cultural factors in Colombia may contribute to professionals being more likely to have a greater emphasis on a dichotomous explanatory model of chronic pain (i.e., biomedical vs. psychological), as opposed to a more unified biopsychosocial model. This may be in part to widespread acknowledgment of mental health stigma and a cultural context of pain and suffering that can influence patient and family engagement in care. While there was general congruence in the CAP-specific treatment targets (i.e., sleep, school, activity), Colombian professionals noted important differences in school‑related function. For example, in the US, school absenteeism/school avoidance is a common presenting issue for pediatric patients with pain and other. However, within the Colombian system, it is very unusual. Even when patients cannot attend class due to symptoms, they will go to school because it is not acceptable for them to remain at home.

One cultural component of CAP that was confirmed to be essential is its core focus on including family members in treatment for a child’s pain and other chronic symptoms. In North America, family attendance at CAP usually includes patients and their parents/primary caregivers. However, to align with core family values in Colombia – and Latin America more broadly – it is likely that CAP-ESP will be adapted to extend to include additional family such as grandparents, aunts, and uncles. Other clinical insights include the need for some surface-level modifications to language and metaphors, but with overall enthusiasm for the CAP intervention content and engaging, accessible materials. Overall, the cultural exploration with professionals suggests that there is strong alignment and that with some tailoring the CAP intervention is likely to be culturally compatible.

The goal of this aim was to understand and distinguish system-level barriers from cultural barriers. Results suggest that implementation challenges are likely to be driven primarily by health-system constraints – including fragmented care coordination, limited pediatric psychology services, and differences in professional roles – rather than disagreement with the intervention’s underlying approach.

There were numerous system-level insights that will help to inform implementation. For example, presently, in Colombia, pediatric care is split across two disparate systems. Up to age 14, patients are treated in the pediatric system, and beginning at age 15, they are treated within the adult system. This has significant implication for CAP, an intervention that targets patients ages 10–17. Thus, CAP will either need to be embedded in two systems, or new access/referral paths will need to be developed to route patients across systems.

Another critical systems issue is that there is no centralized medical record or primary care provider in Colombia. In many cases, this means that there is significant discoordination in care, with parents needing to navigate through the system independently. This challenge was clearly reflected in co-creation activity of building clinical care pathways. Across groups, no two pathways to care were similar. Additionally, there was little group consensus on how patients might be funneled through subspecialty providers or when and how they could access interventions such as physical therapy or psychological services. Notably, the clinical care pathway activity also highlighted that many families include spiritual and holistic healing as essential healthcare intervention, alongside or in lieu of evidence-based treatment. These challenges, while formidable, were recognized in the context of a health system that is actively evolving. Cross disciplinary professionals noted that this may be an ideal time to implement the CAP intervention, setting an example for coordinated, comprehensive care in pediatrics.

At a systems-level, it’s also essential to consider that pediatric psychology does not exist as a profession in Colombia. In contrast, in North America most CAP sites have pediatric psychologist who serves as program director in a pediatric hospital setting, and more broadly, there is cultural understanding that the pediatric psychology profession addresses the intersection of physical and mental health (i.e., specializing in the psychological aspects of illness and injury). While there are many trained professionals in Colombia who have the expertise and skills needed to deliver CAP, important consideration will need to be given to professional development for CAP leaders and referring providers.

Beyond the primary aims of this study, the CAP-Hub and GRWOTH teams were hoping to gain insight into the educational needs and responsiveness of professionals and the community. Based on the feedback in both the co-creation workshop and subsequent educational opportunities, there is a clear desire for more targeted education on the topic of pediatric chronic pain. As the co-creation workshop feedback noted, there are many misconceptions about pediatric chronic pain that need to be changed, and the high number of registrations at all educational events – along with ongoing requests for participation in additional education events – far exceeded the CAP-Hub team expectations and demonstrates an eagerness to learn and connect with other providers on this topic.

This preliminary exploration and cultural adaptation was limited to feedback from one city in Colombia (Medellín), the second largest city in the country and one that is known for its modernization. As such, it cannot be assumed to be representative of other Colombian cities and other parts of Latin America. As this adaptation process unfolds, additional work will be needed to determine if other regions can “borrow strength” from the work that has been completed, or if similar procedures will be needed to ensure cultural adaptation success. It also cannot be assumed that the 39 multidisciplinary healthcare providers who elected to participate in the co-creation day were representative of all local pediatric providers, and because of the use of contemporaneous notes rather than verbatim transcripts there may have been a loss of nuance information shared during the workshop. Additional stages of the adaptation will also need to include participants with lived experience to share their own perspective on the healthcare systems and family contexts that may influence the final programmatic adaptation. Finally, although there was careful attention to translation procedures, it is always possible that nuanced qualitative feedback may have been overlooked or misinterpreted.

Additionally, while the qualitative nature of this project provides rich data, it also introduces some notable limitations. For example, it can be inherently challenging to assess whether aims were objectively met because subjective data and sociocultural meaning are prioritized over the measurement of predefined outcomes in this phase of the cultural adaptation process. Moreover, we must acknowledge that even with transparency and reliance on proven qualitative research methodology, interpretation of qualitative data is inherently influenced by context and researcher reflexivity.

After completion of this first phase of the cultural adaptation process, the CAP-Hub and GROWTH team made modifications to the CAP intervention and, to date, have completed three pilot CAP interventions. Focus groups and in-depth interviews are currently being conducted with patient and caregiver participants on both their experience of the program content but also feedback on when and how a program such as CAP should be accessed, to continue deepening the cross-cultural understanding of healthcare systems from a patient perspective, further informing CAP implementation planning. Feedback from these pilot groups will inform additional cultural adaptation needs, with a goal of facilitating a robust implementation in Medellín by 2027. Lessons learned from this adaptation and implementation process, inclusive of clinical, system-level, and educational needs, will help to inform additional efforts to provide comprehensive care for pediatric chronic pain and related symptoms in Colombia, and more broadly across Latin America.

This article describes the first phase of culturally adapting the Comfort Ability® Program (CAP) intervention – a brief, manualized, CBT-informed, family-based treatment for pediatric chronic pain and related symptoms – for Spanish-speaking Latinx families in Colombia (CAP-ESP). This initial adaptation work demonstrates that culturally responsive implementation in Latin America necessitates much more than surface‑level adaptation; it requires deliberate systems-level planning, cross-disciplinary relationship building, and educational outreach to professionals and the lay community. A year-long collaboration between the CAP-Hub and an interdisciplinary psychology practice helped lay the groundwork for several key initiatives, including a co-creation day, pain education events, and opportunities for bidirectional learning about health care and educational systems. Collectively, these initiatives have generated practical guidance about cultural considerations as well as helped to highlight opportunities and challenges across various healthcare delivery systems. Importantly, these efforts have also served to strengthen relationships across institutions and disciplines, increased awareness of evidence-based pediatric pain management, and produced actionable priorities to refine CAP-ESP materials and implementation procedures. Pilot testing for CAP-ESP is currently underway, and next steps will include iterative refinement with patient and caregiver input, feasibility testing in Colombian clinical settings, and evaluation of implementation outcomes (e.g., acceptability, adoption, fidelity, and sustainability) alongside patient and family outcomes.

psychology.title: Why Patient-Reported Outcome Measures Have Not Reached Primary Eye Care: A Critical Narrative Review of the Targeting, Access, and Action Gaps
psychology.abstract: Eye care is shifting into community and primary care settings, yet patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) have not followed. Non-adoption is routinely attributed to clinician time, information technology, and absent guidance, explanations that are real but have not changed practice. This critical narrative review synthesises evidence across ophthalmic PROM psychometrics, implementation science, community eye care service evaluations, and primary eye care epidemiology, with every primary source verified against its PubMed record. We propose, as hypotheses requiring validation rather than as established findings, four structural gaps: instruments calibrated in hospital and surgical cohorts may mistarget milder community populations; in the only published implementation reporting uptake, patients with lower visual acuity were less likely to attempt a self-administered vision PROM, suggesting that non-completion may be informative rather than random; we identified no primary eye care study in which scores were returned to the consultation, the step at which benefit has been demonstrated in other specialties; and the high-volume community case mix remains largely unmeasured. Beneath these, we propose a fifth, cross-cutting funding gap, since we identified no routine reimbursement route for this activity, although the service and financing evidence available to us is predominantly from the United Kingdom. We set out a staged implementation route, the observations that would confirm or refute each proposed gap, and the strongest counter-argument to our own position, namely that non-adoption may be rational where instruments carry little decision-relevant information in mild disease.
psychology.text:
Globally, an estimated 43.3 million people were blind in 2020, with a further 295 million experiencing moderate or severe distance vision impairment and 510 million living with vision impairment from uncorrected presbyopia []. Much of this burden is avoidable, and much of it is managed, or ought to be managed, outside hospitals. Health systems in the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and elsewhere have accordingly moved substantial volumes of eye care into community optometry, shared-care schemes, and primary care-led services.

Patient-reported outcome measures are standardised instruments completed by patients to quantify symptoms, functioning, and health-related quality of life from their own perspective. In ophthalmology, they capture what visual acuity and intraocular pressure cannot: difficulty with night driving, glare, dependence on others, and the emotional consequences of losing sight [,]. Their value is not seriously disputed. A Cochrane review of 116 randomised trials involving 49,785 patients found that feeding PROM data back to clinicians and patients probably improves patient–clinician communication, rates of diagnosis and notation, and disease control, with smaller gains in quality of life [].

Yet in routine ophthalmic practice, adoption has stalled. A cross-sectional survey of ophthalmologists in the United Kingdom, Germany, and Switzerland found that only 31% of 112 respondents used PROMs at all, and use was concentrated in cataract services []. In primary eye care specifically, systematic collection is close to non-existent. The explanations usually offered, namely the consultation time, poorly designed information technology, and absent guidance on instrument selection, are well documented and undoubtedly contribute [,]. They are also, we argue, insufficient. These same barriers apply in oncology, psychiatry, and rheumatology, where PROM programmes have nevertheless been established at scale.

One finding from the European survey is particularly difficult to reconcile with the standard account: perceived usefulness did not predict adoption []. Clinicians who believed PROMs were valuable were no more likely to use them. If the obstacle were awareness, persuasion, or education, that relationship should hold. It does not. Something structural is intervening between belief and practice.

This review advances a different explanation, which we offer as a structured hypothesis rather than a demonstrated account. We propose that PROMs have failed to reach primary eye care for reasons rooted in measurement science, service design, and payment and that four specific gaps, namely targeting, access, action, and evidence, may each independently break the chain between instrument development and clinical benefit, while a fifth, funding, appears to act across all of them (). Throughout, we have sought to keep the strength of each claim proportional to the evidence behind it, and we flag explicitly where an argument rests on extrapolation from hospital populations, on a single study, or on evidence drawn from a single health system. We then set out the strongest case against our own argument, the observations that would distinguish the two accounts, and what would have to change, in what order, for the chain to close.

This is a critical narrative review, not a systematic review, and it makes no claim of exhaustive retrieval. The design was adopted deliberately, because of the nature of the literature. The question that we address, namely why an intervention with demonstrated benefit elsewhere has failed to establish itself in a particular setting, requires synthesis across bodies of work that share no common indexing vocabulary and would not be captured by any single reproducible search string. A systematic search restricted to studies reporting PROM use in primary eye care returns a small and heterogeneous set of reports, most of which are descriptive, and excludes precisely the psychometric and implementation evidence needed to explain the pattern. We use “critical narrative review” throughout in the sense defined by SANRA []: a non-systematic synthesis that states its search and selection methods transparently, appraises the evidence it cites, and distinguishes argument from demonstration.

We searched MEDLINE via PubMed up to June 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking from key papers and by targeted hand-searching of the reference lists of included reviews. Four domains were searched separately, because no single string spans them: (i) development and psychometric evaluation of vision-specific PROM instruments, with particular attention to Rasch analyses reporting item-to-person targeting; (ii) implementation studies and evidence syntheses concerning PROM adoption in routine care; (iii) service evaluations of community, optometry-led, and primary care-based eye services; and (iv) epidemiological data describing the primary eye care case mix. The principal concepts combined in each domain were, respectively, patient-reported outcome measures with ophthalmic and psychometric terms; patient-reported outcome measures with implementation, barrier, and facilitator terms restricted to reviews; optometry and primary eye care service terms with evaluation, referral, and commissioning terms; and ophthalmic disease terms with prevalence and population terms. The full search strings are given in .

Titles and abstracts were screened against the purpose of each domain rather than against formal eligibility criteria. For domain (i), we sought primary psychometric evaluations of named vision PROMs, prioritising those reporting person and item locations on a common scale; for domain (ii), we sought systematic reviews, umbrella reviews, and implementation studies reporting barriers, facilitators, or the effects of PROM feedback; for domain (iii), we sought evaluations of services actually delivering eye care outside the hospital, with reported activity or outcome data; and for domain (iv), we sought population-level estimates of the conditions presenting to such services. Records were retained when they contributed evidence bearing on one of the five proposed gaps, and systematic reviews, population-based studies, and primary psychometric analyses were preferred over narrative accounts and single-case reports. Thirty-three sources are cited.

Selection was iterative and purposive rather than protocol-driven, and no review protocol was registered, consistent with the narrative design set out in . The citation set should accordingly be read as evidence assembled in support of an argument and appraised as such, rather than as the complete retrievable evidence base on this question. The search strings in  are reported in full so that the yield can be reproduced and independently screened.

Because a central risk in work of this kind is that the argument and evidence become difficult to separate, we have adopted a consistent convention. Where a statement describes what a cited study directly observed, it is written as a finding and attributed to that study. Where a statement extends such a finding to a population, setting, or health system that the study did not examine, it is identified as an inference, an extrapolation, or a hypothesis, and the direction and basis of the extrapolation are stated. Table 2 records, for each proposed gap, the strength and provenance of the supporting evidence alongside the proposed response, and  sets out the specific points at which our argument depends on extrapolation rather than observation.

Citation verification. Every primary source cited in this review was checked against its PubMed record for authorship, journal, year, volume, and pagination before inclusion. We report this explicitly because reference inaccuracy is a growing and under-acknowledged problem in the review literature and because a review of this kind depends entirely on the accuracy of its sources. Assertions that could not be traced to a verifiable indexed record were removed rather than retained with approximate attribution.

Reporting standard. This review was prepared with reference to SANRA, the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles, which addresses the justification of importance and aims, a description of the literature search, referencing, a presentation of the evidence level, and a presentation of relevant endpoint data [].

Patient and public involvement. No patients or members of the public were involved in the conception, design, or drafting of this review. We consider this a substantive limitation given that our central argument concerns the mismatch between instruments and the patients asked to complete them, and we recommend that any programme following the route proposed in  be co-designed with patients from the outset.

Readers should weigh the findings accordingly. A purposive synthesis carries a real risk of selective citation, and we return to this in the limitations.

Any argument about measurement must begin with the population being measured and with a clear definition of the setting. Terminology here is not standardised across health systems, and a reviewer from one country may not recognise the arrangements of another.

Definition. By primary eye care, we mean the first point of professional contact for an eye problem, delivered outside hospital ophthalmology and without prior specialist referral. In the United Kingdom, this is predominantly community optometry, operating through General Ophthalmic Services sight testing and locally commissioned enhanced schemes such as Minor Eye Conditions Services; in Australia and Canada, independent optometric practice fulfils a comparable role; in the United States, optometry and primary care physicians share it; and in many low- and middle-income settings, the equivalent function sits with primary health facilities, ophthalmic clinical officers, and community outreach. What unites these arrangements is not the professional group or funding model but position in the pathway: undifferentiated presentations, unselected severity, and responsibility for deciding who needs onward referral.

Service evaluation data give a reasonably concrete picture. In a twelve-month evaluation of the Lambeth and Lewisham Minor Eye Conditions Scheme, 2123 patients accessed the service; the most common presenting reasons were red eye (36.7%), painful white eye (11.1%), and flashes and floaters (10.2%). Community optometrists managed 64.1% of patients without referral, and 18.9% were referred to hospital eye services, of which 89.2% were judged appropriate. First hospital attendances referred by general practitioners fell by 26.8% (95% CI −40.5% to −13.1%) relative to a neighbouring area without the scheme [].

Alongside this acute workload sits a large burden of chronic and refractive need. Dry eye disease has a reported prevalence of 5–50% depending on the definition applied, with symptoms and signs diverging substantially []. Uncorrected presbyopia affects an estimated 510 million people worldwide, and a further 295 million experience moderate or severe distance vision impairment [].

Hospital ophthalmology, by contrast, concentrates advanced and surgical disease: cataract waiting lists, low-vision clinic referrals, established macular degeneration, and glaucoma with measurable field loss. The instruments discussed in  were built in that second population.  sets the two case mixes against the availability of validated PROM evidence, and  maps the same relationship.

The definition above deliberately spans several health systems, but the evidence that we draw on is not evenly distributed across them, and that asymmetry affects how the framework should be read. The service-delivery and financing evidence in  and  is predominantly British, reflecting where community eye care has been most formally evaluated [,]. The access evidence in  comes from a single clinic in the United States []. The largest patient-reported effect sizes that we cite come from a low-resource setting in East Africa []. We therefore expect the five proposed gaps to differ in prominence between systems, and we set out that expectation here so that readers outside the United Kingdom can judge which parts of the argument transfer.

In publicly funded systems with commissioned community eye care, the targeting and action gaps are likely to dominate, because a delivery infrastructure already exists and the limiting factors are instrument performance and the absence of a defined route from score to decision. The funding gap takes the specific form of activity falling outside a fixed national fee, as the English that needs an assessment that we cite illustrates [].

In insurance-based systems, the funding gap would be expected to take a different form: the constraint is less the absence of any payment route than the absence of a billable code or quality incentive attached to patient-reported measurement, while the access gap may be compounded by variation in coverage. The United States screening programme that we cite was designed around a safety-net population for related reasons [].

In low- and middle-income settings, where primary eye care is often delivered by ophthalmic clinical officers or outreach teams, the evidence gap is likely to be the binding constraint, since few instruments have been developed or validated in these populations, and the access gap may be dominated by literacy and language rather than by digital exclusion. At the same time, the Zanzibar data indicate that interventions deliverable at this level produce the largest patient-reported gains in the literature that we reviewed [], which makes the measurement deficit more, rather than less, consequential.

We have not identified evidence that would allow these systems to be ranked empirically, and we present this comparison as a structured expectation to be tested rather than as a finding.

The instruments that dominate ophthalmic PROM practice were developed in populations with established, often advanced, disease. The NEI VFQ-25 was constructed from a cohort recruited across eleven university-based ophthalmology practices, comprising patients with age-related cataract, macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, primary open-angle glaucoma, cytomegalovirus retinitis, or low vision []. The VF-14 was derived from 766 patients undergoing the first cataract surgery []. The Impact of Vision Impairment questionnaire was evaluated in 314 first-time referrals to low-vision clinics []. Catquest-9SF was Rasch-scaled on 10,486 questionnaires drawn from the Swedish National Cataract Register and tested in a further 10,886, that is, on patients proceeding to surgery [].

These are appropriate development populations for the purposes that those instruments were designed to serve. The difficulty arises when the same instruments are transplanted into a population sitting substantially lower on the underlying disability continuum.

Rasch analysis makes targeting explicit: it places persons and items on a common logit scale, so that mismatch between item difficulty and person ability becomes measurable rather than assumed. Applied to the NEI VFQ, the results have been consistently unflattering. Pesudovs and colleagues found the NEI VFQ-39 and NEI VFQ-25 had good measurement precision but exhibited multidimensionality, misfitting items, suboptimum targeting of item difficulty to person ability, and dysfunctional subscales, twelve of them in the 25-item version []. Their conclusion was that the instrument is flawed as an overall measure and requires segregation into separate visual functioning and socioemotional scales. This was subsequently replicated in an independent Chinese cataract waiting-list cohort, where the original questionnaire was, in the authors’ words, once again found to be flawed [].

Lundström and Pesudovs reported that items were well targeted to preoperative participants, with a 0.34 logit difference between person and item means []. But a systematic review of thirteen Catquest-9SF validation studies across diverse populations, totalling 15,289 respondents, found significant mistargeting in nine of them, with a range of 0.66 to −2.04 logits and, in most studies, the tasks being easy relative to respondent ability [].

That last clause deserves emphasis. Mistargeting in the direction of items being too easy was observed in populations still sick enough to be on a cataract surgery waiting list. Primary eye care sees patients earlier and milder than that. We are not aware of evidence that targeting improves as severity falls, and the logic of the measurement model indicates that it should worsen; we therefore advance this as an inference rather than an observation, and  states the limits of that inference explicitly. No published Rasch analysis of a vision PROM in an unselected primary eye care population was identified.

Poor targeting is not an abstract psychometric complaint. It has three consequences that bear directly on whether a PROM can be useful in a community consultation ().

Ceiling effects. When most respondents can perform most of the tasks that an instrument asks about, scores compress at the favourable end of the scale. A patient with early cataract who reports no difficulty with any of nine daily activities is indistinguishable from a patient with no cataract at all.

Insensitivity to change. Longitudinal monitoring depends on the instrument being able to register deterioration. If a patient begins at the ceiling, meaningful early decline is invisible until it becomes severe, which is precisely when the instrument is no longer needed to detect it.

Inflated sample size requirements. Reduced measurement precision at the relevant end of the scale means that studies attempting to demonstrate a PROM-driven benefit in primary care need larger samples than equivalent hospital studies, making the evidence harder and more expensive to generate. This may partly explain why that evidence does not exist.

A related problem compounds this. Interpreting any PROM score requires knowing what magnitude of change is meaningful to a patient, yet minimal important differences in ophthalmic research remain inconsistently established []. Where estimates do exist, they are necessarily derived from the cohorts in which the instruments were developed, which, as set out above, are hospital and surgical populations; we record this as an inference from the development literature rather than as a separately evidenced finding. A clinician in a community setting therefore faces not only a score of uncertain precision but no reliable benchmark against which to judge it.

Braithwaite and colleagues reached a compatible conclusion in their review of PROM research in modern ophthalmology, noting considerable progress in cataract, glaucoma, medical retina, and low vision, alongside a paucity of useful tools for less common conditions, and proposing item banks administered by computer-adaptive testing as a route past the traditional limitations of fixed-form instruments []. Computer-adaptive testing is directly relevant here: by selecting items matched to each respondent’s estimated ability, it addresses targeting at the level of the individual rather than the cohort.

The second gap has received remarkably little attention, and we consider it the most consequential for the interpretation of existing data.

The clearest evidence comes from the only published implementation of PROMs in a primary eye care setting that reports full uptake data. Over two months, general health and functioning PROMIS surveys were offered to all patients attending an optometric clinic in Rochester, New York. Of 651 patients, 258 chose to attempt the survey and 193 completed it, in a mean time of 6.36 min with a range extending from 1.43 to 51.92 min []. Overall completion was therefore 29.6% of those attending.

The critical finding is not the completion rate but its distribution. In this cohort, patients with low visual acuity were significantly less likely to attempt the survey (p = 0.049) []. Younger patients were more likely to complete it. No other patient characteristic distinguished participants from non-participants.

The implication, if this finding generalises, is uncomfortable. A self-administered instrument designed to quantify the impact of poor vision would systematically under-sample patients with poor vision. On this reading, the attrition would not be random but informative, structurally correlated with the construct being measured, and mean vision-related quality-of-life scores derived from self-administered collection in community settings would be optimistically biased by an unknown margin. We emphasise the conditional form of this claim. It is an inference from one single-centre study of a general-health instrument, with a p-value of 0.049, in one United States optometry clinic; it has not been replicated, and it has not been demonstrated for any vision-specific PROM. We therefore advance it as a hypothesis rather than as an established property of community PROM data. It is directly testable, and  sets out the reporting standard that would test it.

The wider implementation literature is consistent with this. A systematic review with qualitative evidence synthesis of electronic PROM collection in older adults identified clinical conditions, socio-cultural factors, digital literacy, access to digital technology, and user interface design as the factors most salient to older patients, with 29 of 34 review findings graded at high or moderate confidence [].
