An umbrella review of 34 reviews found no consensus favouring paper or electronic administration, but identified offering both options as an important facilitator specifically to mitigate digital literacy bias [].

If this finding replicates, the practical conclusion is that assisted, large-print, audio, and interviewer-administered formats should be treated as the default design requirement for vision PROMs, not as an accommodation offered on request. An instrument that only the better-sighted can complete is not measuring what it claims to measure. We note that this recommendation follows from the hypothesis rather than from demonstrated bias and that it is, in any case, consistent with the independent evidence on digital exclusion among older adults cited above [,].

Even where PROMs are collected in eye care, the data are rarely returned to the encounter that generated them.

This matters because feedback is the mechanism of benefit. The Cochrane review of PROM feedback identified 116 randomised trials across psychiatry, primary care, oncology, and other disciplines, involving 49,785 patients []. It found moderate-certainty evidence that feedback probably improves quality of life (SMD 0.15, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.26), increases patient–physician communication (SMD 0.36, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.52), improves diagnosis and notation (RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.08), and improves disease control (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.41). A subsequent meta-analysis restricted to oncology found comparable improvements in health-related quality of life, communication, and one-year survival [].

Notably, the effects concentrate in communication, diagnosis, and notation, outcomes that arise from a clinician seeing a score and responding to it. Collection alone does not produce them. This is the step missing in eye care.

Where PROMs and patient-reported experience measures have been deployed in community eye services, the data have been analysed in aggregate for a service evaluation. A community-based glaucoma clinic in Cambridge administered a modified glaucoma patient-reported outcome and experience measure to 96 consecutive patients, finding that 96% reported the experience as comfortable and 93% judged it equivalent to what they would expect from hospital care []. These are valuable findings about the acceptability of community delivery. They are not, and were not designed to be, instances of PROM data altering an individual patient’s management.

We could identify no published study in primary eye care demonstrating a PROM score returned to a clinician during a consultation and used to modify a decision.  accordingly marks these two stages as “no evidence identified” rather than as zero, since they have not been evaluated in any study that we located. This is absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence, and the distinction matters: we are not reporting that such use was measured and found not to occur.

The European survey finding noted in the introduction bears repeating in this context: perceived usefulness did not predict adoption []. Clinicians are not failing to use PROMs because they doubt their value. They are failing to use them because the operational path from a completed questionnaire to a changed decision does not exist in most community services. Building conviction will not build that path.

Where a path has been sketched, it has been promising. A proposal to combine visual acuity with patient-reported outcome measures in an appropriateness and prioritisation tool for cataract surgery illustrates how patient-reported disability might reorder access on grounds other than acuity alone []. This remains a proposal requiring evaluation rather than established practice, but it is the right shape: a defined score, a defined threshold, and a defined consequence.

The fourth gap follows from the first three. Because instruments were built for hospital populations, because the patients most affected complete them least, and because collected data are not acted upon, there has been little incentive to generate evidence in the settings where most eye care now happens.

We suggest, however, that the field has been looking in the wrong place. The search for a global vision-related quality-of-life measure suitable for primary care has proved difficult for the psychometric reasons set out above. But there exists a category of patient-reported measurement that is brief, already validated, immediately actionable in a community consultation, and almost entirely neglected: measures of treatment administration and adherence.

A cross-sectional observational study in 136 Belgian community pharmacies assessed the eye-drop technique and patient-reported problems in 678 established eye-drop users with a mean age of 68.9 years []. Although 98.0% successfully instilled at least one drop, 14% required multiple attempts and only 3% performed every step correctly. Common deviations included touching the bottle to the eye or eyelid (40.7%), failing to close the eye afterwards (67.8%), and failing to perform nasolacrimal occlusion (94.7%). One in five ophthalmic suspensions was not shaken before use. Forty per cent of patients reported at least one problem with instillation, most often difficulty getting a drop into the eye (18.3%), too many drops emerging from the bottle (14.6%), or difficulty squeezing the bottle (12.2%). Roughly half recalled ever having received instruction in the technique.

Separately, patients whose adherence fell below 80% based on electronic monitoring and those scoring lower on a general glaucoma medication adherence self-efficacy scale were significantly more likely to have worse visual field defect severity [].

As an important qualification, these studies establish that the eye-drop technique and adherence are common, consequential, and remediable problems. They do not, on their own, establish that the patient-reported measurement of those problems performs well, because both relied substantially on observations rather than self-report: the technique was assessed via demonstration in the pharmacy study [] and via video recording with electronic monitoring of adherence in the glaucoma study []. The 40% figure for self-reported instillation problems is genuinely patient-reported; the 3% figure for perfect technique is observed. The gap between what patients report and what they do is precisely what is unknown here, and it matters: a self-reported technique measure that misses most of the errors that an observer would catch would be worse than useless. Validating brief self-reported technique and adherence items against observed performance in a community population is, in our view, the single most tractable and highest-yield study in this field.

Consider what this combination represents. A patient-reported measure that takes under two minutes, requires no visual acuity to complete, identifies a problem present in 40% of users, has an immediate and low-cost intervention available in any community setting, and is associated with the clinical outcome that matters. It satisfies every criterion that the vision-related quality-of-life instruments struggle to meet. It is also, as far as we can establish, almost never collected systematically in primary eye care.

A second underexploited area is refractive and presbyopic correction. In a population-based survey in Zanzibar, presbyopia prevalence was 89.2% with spectacle coverage of only 17.6%; at six-month follow-up, 93.6% of those given spectacles still had them, mean satisfaction was 89.5%, and correcting presbyopia produced an effect size of 2.90 based on visual function and effect sizes ranging from 1.15 to 3.90 across quality-of-life domains []. These are among the largest patient-reported effect sizes in the ophthalmic literature, generated by an intervention deliverable at the primary level.

Community screening programmes offer a further route. The Michigan Screening and Intervention for Glaucoma and Eye Health Through Telemedicine programme was designed to deliver glaucoma screening in a federally qualified health centre and a free clinic, combining telemedicine review with health coaching and the provision of low- or no-cost spectacles, with vision-related quality of life among its stated outcomes []. Programmes of this kind place patient-reported measurement in exactly the setting where the access gap bites hardest, and their evaluation deserves close attention.

The equity dimension deserves emphasis. Low vision identified in general practice has been shown to carry poor function and inadequate support: in three West Glamorgan practices, the mean NEI VFQ score among registered blind and partially sighted patients was 41.5%, and although 80% had received a social services visit, only a third remained in contact []. The psychosocial burden of macular degeneration is comparable to that of major chronic systemic illness [], and vision-related quality of life declines measurably with severity and the bilaterality of impairment, while generic instruments such as the SF-12 detect no difference at all []. Generic measures are insensitive here; vision-specific measures work, but only if the people with the worst vision can complete them, which returns us to the access gap.

A further obstacle appears to cut across the other four and may be the most powerful of all, although the evidence available to us is indirect and almost entirely British: little of the activity that we have described appears to be funded.

A needs assessment conducted across Leeds, Bradford, and Airedale, areas without a commissioned Minor Eye Conditions Service, recorded how patients presenting to optometry with minor eye conditions were actually paid for. Optometrists managed 75% of patients. But 53% of patients paid privately for the appointment, 9% were absorbed into a General Ophthalmic Services sight test, 19% were seen without charge through practitioner goodwill, and 19% received no consultation at all and were redirected to a pharmacy, general practitioner, or emergency department. Some 34% would otherwise have attended an emergency department [].

This is the economic context into which PROM collection is being proposed, at least in the United Kingdom. A community optometrist working to a fixed sight-test fee has, so far as we have been able to establish, no routine mechanism to bill for administering a questionnaire, for reviewing it, or for the additional consultation time that acting on it would require. We have not identified a published description of such a mechanism in any health system, but we note that the absence of a published description is weaker evidence than a documented absence, and that reimbursement arrangements may exist that are not reported in the indexed literature. Where enhanced activity has been commissioned and paid for, uptake has followed and outcomes have been demonstrable []. Where it has not, the work is either charged to the patient, absorbed as unpaid goodwill, or declined [].

We suggest that this offers a more parsimonious explanation than clinician attitudes for the finding that perceived usefulness does not predict PROM adoption []. A practitioner may hold PROMs in high regard and still be unable to perform unfunded work at volume. If that is correct, then the substantial literature devoted to clinician education, awareness, and engagement has been addressing a genuine but secondary constraint.  accordingly represents funding not as a fifth link in the chain but as the substrate on which all the others rest. We stress that this is a proposed explanation offered in competition with the attitudinal one and that the two have not been tested against each other.

Of the five proposed gaps, this is the one supported by the weakest and most geographically restricted evidence, and we advance it as a hypothesis rather than as a demonstrated mechanism. The reimbursement data that we cite describe minor eye condition consultations in three English areas, not PROM collection specifically, and no study has directly tested whether funding PROM activity increases it. That test is set out in . Any extension of this argument beyond the United Kingdom is an assumption on our part rather than a finding, and  sets out how we would expect the constraint to differ in insurance-based and low-resource systems.

A review that only marshals evidence for its own thesis is of limited use. We therefore set out the strongest position opposing ours, which we do not think is currently refutable.

The argument runs as follows. In a population with mild, early, or absent disease, a global vision-related quality-of-life score may genuinely carry very little decision-relevant information. If a patient with early cataract and 6/9 acuity reports no functional difficulty, the clinician has learned almost nothing that they did not already know from the history. On this reading, ceiling effects are not a defect of the instrument so much as an accurate reflection of a population that is, for the most part, functioning well. Clinicians may have arrived empirically at the conclusion that the measurement does not repay the time, and the failure of perceived usefulness to predict adoption [] would then reflect a gap between abstract endorsement and situated judgement rather than a structural blockage.

This position has real force, and two observations support it. First, PROM feedback effects in the Cochrane synthesis, while positive, were modest for quality of life (SMD 0.15) and concentrated in communication, diagnosis, and notation [], outcomes plausibly already achieved by a competent history in a low-complexity encounter. Second, most of the trials in that synthesis were conducted in populations with substantial symptom burden, where the prior probability of the questionnaire surfacing something unknown is far higher.

Our argument and the rational non-adoption argument make different predictions, and the distinction is empirically tractable.

If non-adoption is rational, then instruments targeted to mild disease, through item banks or computer-adaptive testing, should still fail to change decisions, because the information deficit lies in the population rather than the instrument. If our account is right, better-targeted instruments should surface actionable findings at a materially higher rate.

If non-adoption is rational, then eliminating the acuity-related response bias through assisted administration should not alter conclusions drawn from the data. If our account is right, assisted administration should shift observed mean scores downward and reveal unmet need concentrated in the previously missing respondents.

If non-adoption is rational, funding PROM collection should not increase it much beyond a token level. If the funding gap is real, reimbursement should produce a step change, as it has for other enhanced community eye services [,].

None of these has been tested. We regard that as the most important finding of this review: the field has been debating whether clinicians should use PROMs without having established whether, in this population, they would learn anything.

A further complication applies to longitudinal use in chronic eye disease. Patients adapting to progressive impairment may alter their internal standards, values, and conceptualisation of quality of life over time, the phenomenon of response shift []. A patient whose visual function has deteriorated may report unchanged or even improved quality of life because the frame of reference has moved. In slowly progressive conditions such as glaucoma and macular degeneration, which are increasingly monitored in community settings, this undermines the interpretation of serial scores in exactly the pathway where longitudinal PROM monitoring is most often proposed. Symptom- and task-specific measures are less vulnerable to this than global quality-of-life instruments, which is a further argument for the sequencing that we propose below.

The five gaps are not equally tractable. Two can be addressed with instruments that already exist; three require new measurement science, service redesign, and trials. We therefore propose a sequence rather than a programme, on the principle that early demonstrable wins are what sustain implementation effort (, ).

Several questions appear to us to be both answerable and consequential.

Does routine collection of eye-drop technique and adherence measures in community pharmacy or optometry, with a defined remediation pathway, improve adherence and slow field loss in glaucoma? This is testable now with existing instruments in a cluster-randomised design.

What are the psychometric properties of OSDI and DEQ-5 when administered in unselected primary eye care populations, and what are the minimal important differences in mild disease? Neither has been characterised in this setting.

How large is the acuity-related response bias in self-administered vision PROMs, and does assisted administration eliminate it? This requires only that studies report attempt and completion rates stratified by visual acuity, a reporting standard that we would urge journals to adopt.

Does returning a vision PROM score to a community optometrist before the consultation change referral decisions, and are those changes appropriate? The prioritisation literature suggests a mechanism []; no trial has tested it.

Do brief self-reported eye-drop technique items agree with the observed technique in a community population? Existing evidence for technique failure is largely observational [,], and the validity of a self-reported substitute is unestablished.

Does reimbursing PROM collection and the response within an enhanced service contract increase uptake, and by how much relative to education alone? This directly discriminates between the funding explanation and the attitudinal one.

The instruction to define thresholds with pre-agreed actions is easy to state and rarely operationalised.  illustrates what it would mean concretely for a community glaucoma pathway, using only measures that already exist.  is an illustration of a design principle and must not be read as a clinical guideline or as a recommendation for immediate use. None of the thresholds that it contains has been validated, the instruments have not been tested together as a protocol, the intervals are conventional rather than evidence-derived, and the allocation of professional responsibility reflects United Kingdom community optometry practice and would need to be reassigned elsewhere. It is offered as a worked example of what closing the loop would require and as a template for local calibration and prospective evaluation.

Two design features distinguish this from conventional PROM collection. Every measure has a named action and a named person responsible, so that a score cannot be recorded without a consequence being specified. And no measure requires good visual acuity to complete, which addresses the access gap at the level of protocol design rather than as an afterthought. A third feature is the explicit separation of patient-reported screening from the observed assessment. The first row is a patient-reported screen whose function is to identify who needs their technique watched; the observation is the action triggered by the screen, not part of the measure itself. This distinction matters because, as  notes, the published evidence for technique failure is largely observational, and the agreement between what patients report and what they do has not been established.

This review is purposive rather than systematic, and the risk of selective citation is real. We constructed an argument and then assembled evidence bearing on it; a differently constructed argument could be supported from the same literature. Readers should treat the five-gap framework as a hypothesis organising the available evidence rather than a finding established by it, and  sets out the principal competing account.

The targeting argument rests on extrapolation. This is the most serious weakness in our case, and we wish to state it plainly. The Rasch evidence that we rely on, namely Pesudovs and colleagues, its independent replication, and the Catquest-9SF synthesis [,,], is derived entirely from hospital, cataract surgical, and low-vision cohorts. We are not aware of any published Rasch analysis of a vision PROM conducted in an unselected primary eye care population. Our inference that targeting deteriorates further as severity falls is grounded in the internal logic of the measurement model and in the observed direction of mistargeting, but it is an inference and not an observation. A systematic extraction of person and item mean locations across published Rasch analyses, plotted against the severity of each development population, would test it directly, and we regard this as the highest-priority methodological study arising from this review.

Our verification procedure relied on a single bibliographic database. PubMed does not index all relevant literature, particularly optometric, health services, and grey literature, and service evaluations of community eye care schemes frequently appear in reports rather than indexed journals. Restricting citation to verifiable indexed records improves accuracy at some cost to coverage and probably under-represents non-anglophone and low-income-country experience.

Our evidence base is also geographically uneven, and the framework should be read with that in mind. The service-delivery and financing evidence is almost entirely from the United Kingdom [,], the access evidence from a single clinic in the United States [], and the largest patient-reported effect sizes from East Africa []. The five proposed gaps are therefore best supported in publicly funded systems with commissioned community eye care and least well supported in insurance-based and low-resource systems.  sets out how we would expect the framework to differ in those settings, but that section is an argued expectation rather than an evidenced finding, and we are not aware of comparative data that would test it.

Finally, the status of the five gaps should not be overstated. They are proposed explanations that organise the available evidence; they are not established causes, they have not been tested against one another, and their relative contribution is unknown. Each rests on evidence of differing strength, set out in , and the access and funding gaps, in particular, rest on single studies.  states the observations that would confirm or refute each of them.

Several claims rest on single studies. The access gap argument, in particular, derives its central evidence from one implementation study in one US optometry clinic []. That finding is biologically plausible, coheres with the wider literature on digital exclusion among older adults [], and, to our knowledge, has not been contradicted, but it has also not been replicated, and a single p-value of 0.049 is a slender foundation for an argument of this weight. Replication should be a priority.

Observational designs predominate throughout the evidence base, with the attendant risks of confounding and selection bias, although the assumption that observational studies systematically overstate effects relative to randomised trials is itself not well supported []. Finally, we have proposed a staged implementation route that has not been tested as a whole; its components differ considerably in the strength of evidence behind them, as  indicates.

Patient-reported outcome measures have not reached primary eye care, and the standard explanation, that clinicians lack time, systems, and guidance, does not fit the evidence. Clinicians who consider PROMs useful are no more likely to use them than those who do not.

We have proposed five structural gaps that, taken together, may account better for the pattern and which we advance as hypotheses to be tested rather than as demonstrated causes. The instruments were calibrated on populations that primary eye care rarely sees and appear liable to mistarget when moved. Self-administration may systematically exclude the patients with the worst vision, in which case the data that are collected would be biased in a direction that flatters. Collected scores are banked for audit rather than returned to the consultation, which is the only step at which benefit has been demonstrated elsewhere. Measurement development has tracked surgical pathways, leaving the most common reasons for attending a community eye service essentially unmeasured. And beneath all of these, we identified no funding mechanism for the work, which may explain, more economically than any account based on clinician attitudes, why conviction and practice have come apart, although the evidence for this is British and indirect.

We have also set out the strongest argument against our own position: that in a largely well-functioning population, a vision quality-of-life score may simply carry little decision-relevant information and that clinicians have worked this out. We cannot currently refute this, and the studies that would discriminate between the two accounts have not been done. That, rather than any of our five gaps, may be the most useful thing that this review has to say.

None of this argues against PROMs in primary eye care. It argues against continuing to approach them as a problem of persuasion. The most promising route begins not with a better quality-of-life instrument but with short, already-validated, immediately actionable patient-reported constructs, whether a patient can get a drop into their eye, whether they are taking their treatment, and what their ocular surface symptoms are doing, collected in formats that do not require good vision to complete, returned to a clinician who has a pre-agreed action, and evaluated properly. That is a smaller ambition than a comprehensive vision PROM programme. It has the considerable advantage of being achievable now.

psychology.title: Aligning Scope‐Holder Ergonomics With the Muscle Strain Profile of Therapeutic Endoscopy
psychology.abstract: No abstract
psychology.text:
To the Editor,

Nagano et al. report a motion‐optimized scope‐holder that, in an ex vivo model, lowered biceps brachii and trapezius activation, NASA‐TLX and procedure time []. The problem is real: 76.3% of French endoscopists report work‐related musculoskeletal disorders, and risk rises with cumulative workload []. We add two points: muscle selection and the nature of the load relieved.

The montage recorded biceps brachii, trapezius, and flexor carpi ulnaris, capturing the antigravity and postural cost of holding the scope, where the device performed best. Yet, the authors' previous study identified the pronator teres and extensor carpi radialis as the most activated muscles, trending higher during ESD []. Our ESD data concur: the left extensor carpi radialis exceeded 10% of maximal voluntary contraction for over 80% of dissection time []. Cervical posture and posterior neck muscle activity capture different aspects of strain: the authors recorded relatively low posterior neck activity [], whereas we found 42% more time in the neck‐flexion risk zone during dissection than colonoscopy [].

Second, flexor carpi ulnaris activity, the authors' proxy for dial manipulation and torque control, barely changed (p = 0.049 overall, non‐significant in both subgroups). Against the strong proximal effects, this suggests the holder relieves the carrying component of scope handling while leaving fine control intact. That distinction may matter: our ESD data point to sustained distal muscle loading as a potentially important source of strain, alongside gravitational load []. Consistently, benefit was clearest in novices and non‐medical participants, with no significant change in experts.

We commend the authors' motion‐capture‐derived design and disengageable articulation, which suit the alternating static and dynamic phases of ESD. Future work should record extensor carpi radialis and pronator teres activity, pair posterior neck EMG with cervical kinematics, and test the device during live dissection rather than a static marking task.

Antoine Debourdeau: conception and design of the correspondence (60%), interpretation and integration of the cited data (50%), drafting of the manuscript (70%), critical revision and approval of the final version (50%). Clara Yzet: conception and design of the correspondence (40%), interpretation and integration of the cited data (50%), drafting of the manuscript (30%), critical revision and approval of the final version (50%). Overall contribution: A.D. 60%, C.Y. 40%. Both authors approved the final version and agree to be accountable for all aspects of the work.

The authors have nothing to report.

This article is a Letter to the Editor and does not report any new study involving human participants or animals; ethics committee approval and prospective study registration were therefore not applicable. Data cited from our previously published studies were obtained in investigations that had received the required institutional ethics approval, as reported in those original articles.

The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

This article is linked to Nagano et al. papers. To view this article visit https://doi.org/10.1111/den.70209.

psychology.title: Fostering professional vision in clinical ward rounds through digital simulation-based learning with eye-movement modelling examples and personalised feedback: study protocol for four experimental studies
psychology.abstract: Clinical ward round communication is a core competency in medicine. Advanced professional vision (aPV)—comprising visual noticing and knowledge-based reasoning—is foundational to effective ward round performance. Eye movement modelling examples (EMMEs) represent a promising simulation-based approach to training aPV in medical students. This protocol describes four randomised experiments embedded within the EMMA learning environment examining design features of EMME-based training.Four pre-registered randomised controlled experiments with pre-test/intervention/post-test design. Studies 2a and 2b (October 2026–January 2027): parallel screening experiments; Study 2a: EMME-based learning with raw fixation visualisation versus attention map visualisation versus minimal control (same ward round videos without gaze visualisation) (pre-post design). Study 2b: video-based learning without EMME gaze visualisation, with textual versus graphical versus combined large language model (LLM)-generated feedback versus minimal control (pre-post design). Study 3 (Q2–Q3 2027): confirmatory 2×2 factorial (4 cells, n≈55 per cell) crossing the best visualisation (Study 2a) with the best LLM feedback (Study 2b). Study 4 (Q1-Q2 2028): EMME-based simulation with embedded prompts versus a priori prompts versus no prompts. Participants are randomly assigned via computerised allocation and are medical students in the clinical phase of their studies (third year onwards) at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) with no prior clinical ward round leadership experience. Study 2a: n=96; Study 2b: n=88; Study 3: n=220; Study 4: n=190 (all studies f=0.25, α=0.05, power=0.80, mixed split-plot Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)).Ethical approval was obtained from the Munich Technical University ethics committee (03/2026; grant code 2025-702 S-CT). Dissemination is planned in peer-reviewed journals in the areas of education psychology and medical education. Data of studies 2–4 will be made available following the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) principles () in the TUM Open Data Repository or OSF including metadata and persistent identifier (PID)/digital object identifier (DOI) assignment.The four studies will be pre-registered separately prior to participant enrolment at the Open Science Foundation (OSF) Registries (https://osf.io/registries). Registration numbers and dates will be inserted here upon receipt. Each study will be registered as a separate pre-registration entry, given their distinct hypotheses and designs.
psychology.text:
Clinical ward round communication is an essential component of inpatient care that is directly linked to patient outcomes.
 Core physician tasks during ward rounds include patient status assessment, clinical decision-making and empathetic patient communication.
 Despite its importance, ward round communication is frequently of suboptimal quality due to time pressure, team instability and communication failures.

Advanced professional vision (aPV) constitutes a critical prerequisite for effective ward round performance. aPV is conceptualised as a diagnostic capacity comprising (1) advanced noticing—the targeted, rapid and selective processing of task-relevant visual information and (2) advanced reasoning—the knowledge-based interpretation of observed events in relation to clinical and communicative goals.
 Expert physicians demonstrate distinct gaze patterns during ward rounds: they allocate fixations selectively to clinically salient targets (patients, monitors, team members), maintain extended visual fields and rapidly integrate visual with verbal information.
 Social gaze—directed at patients and team members—is particularly relevant for detecting emotional states and coordinating non-verbal communication.

Eye movement modelling examples (EMMEs) are instructional videos that overlay an expert’s real-time gaze trajectory onto task-relevant video footage, making otherwise covert perceptual strategies visible for learners. EMMEs function via three mechanisms: (1) guiding learner attention toward task-relevant scene elements; (2) visualising expert perceptual strategies; and (3) creating a vicarious first-person learning experience.
 Used as representational scaffolds, EMMEs have been shown to foster expert-like perception in medical imaging and professional vision in teacher education but have not been empirically tested for ward round communication.

The EMMA learning environment (EMMA-LE) integrates EMME-based simulation with LLM-generated feedback and knowledge activation prompts. Built on Moodle, it presents four authentic ward round cases, each comprising four phases (greeting/rapport, case status, decision-making, discharge). Each phase is anchored by at least two EMMEs with structured reflection tasks. Studies 2–4 test specific instructional design features of this environment.

The experimental studies described in this protocol build on Study 1 of Project C03, in which simulated ward round conversations were filmed with real doctors and trained actors as patients. During these simulations, the doctors‘ eye movements were filmed with mobile eye tracking. The resulting video material was the basis for producing the EMME-videos used in the later studies. Based on the Study 1 data, we identify expertise-specific gaze and communication patterns functional for ward round communication; these expert strategies inform the EMME stimulus material used in the studies described here. Building on this foundation, three unanswered design questions motivate the proposed studies: First, EMMEs differ in how gaze is visualised—raw fixations preserve spatial accuracy but may impose high cognitive load on novices; attention maps reduce informational density but may sacrifice detail.
 Second, LLM-generated feedback holds promise for personalised, scalable formative assessment of reflective texts, but it is unknown whether textual, graphical or combined feedback most effectively promotes aPV. Third, knowledge activation prompts support learners’ pre-knowledge activation prior to or during EMME viewing,
 but optimal timing of such prompts (a priori vs embedded) is yet untested. Studies 2–4 systematically address each question in controlled experimental designs.

Studies 2a and 2b first test gaze visualisation and LLM feedback in isolation and in parallel. On this basis, Study 3 subsequently crosses the most effective visualisation with the most effective feedback in a confirmatory 2×2 factorial design. This makes the interaction of both design features measurable and allows internal replication of the screening results.

Studies 2b and 3 include a minimal feedback control group receiving only word-count feedback (no content-based guidance), allowing isolation of LLM feedback effects from mere engagement effects. Study 2a includes a minimal control condition in which participants view the same first-person ward round videos without gaze visualisation, allowing isolation of gaze visualisation effects from effects of video exposure and perspective. These comparators were chosen to reflect realistic educational alternatives that might be used in standard medical curricula.

Studies 2a and 2b are screening experiments designed to identify the most effective visualisation and feedback formats for subsequent combined testing in study 3.

Study 4 includes a control group that views EMMEs without any additional textual cueing. This condition represents standard EMME-based learning and allows the effects of embedded and a priori prompts to be isolated while controlling for exposure to the same videos, reflection activities and feedback.

To determine whether simulation-based aPV training using EMMEs with raw fixation or attention map gaze visualisation leads to greater gains in advanced noticing and reasoning compared with a minimal control condition without gaze visualisation, and which of the two visualisation formats is more effective (pre-post design), in order to select the most effective visualisation format for Study 3.

To determine which format of LLM-generated feedback (textual vs graphical vs combined vs minimal control) on learners’ video-based reflective writing—presented without EMME gaze visualisation—most effectively promotes reflection quality and aPV (pre-post design), in order to select the most effective feedback format for Study 3.

To test, in a confirmatory 2×2 factorial design crossing the most effective gaze visualisation (Study 2a) with the most effective LLM feedback (Study 2b), the main and interaction effects of both design features on (a) written reflection quality during the intervention, (b) aPV from pre- to post-test and (c) diagnosing/intervening skill outcomes, including the comparison of LLM feedback with versus without EMME.

To determine whether embedded knowledge activation prompts (integrated into EMME videos) or a priori prompts (presented before each EMME) yield greater gains in aPV compared with EMME-based learning without prompts.

The study focuses on medical students, not clinical patients. No direct patient data are collected in Studies 2–4. Medical students served informally in the iterative design of the EMMA-LE during pilot testing (Study 1b) and their feedback informed EMME content and prompt design. A formal patient and public advisory board is not constituted for this study. Real patients consented to and participated in ward round filming for Study 1 EMME material only (governed by a separate protocol).

As shown in , all four studies share a within-between mixed (split-plot) design: group is the between-subjects factor (in Study 3, two crossed between-subjects factors with two levels each) and time is the within-subjects factor (two levels: pre-test, post-test). Studies 2a and 2b are conducted in parallel (October 2026 – January 2027); Study 3 commences after completion of both screening studies; Study 4 follows Study 3.

EMMA-LE, EMMA Learning Environment; EMME, Eye Movement Modelling Examples; LLM, Large Langauge Model.

All studies are conducted at the TUM Medical Faculty (Klinikum rechts der Isar, Munich, Germany). Data collection sessions occur in a computer laboratory within the TUM Medical Education Center, ensuring standardised hardware (desktop computers with high-resolution screens), eye-tracking setup (Tobii Pro or equivalent) and internet connectivity for the Moodle-based EMMA-LE. Remote data collection via personal devices is not planned for Studies 2–4 due to requirements for standardised eye-tracking.

Enrolled in the clinical phase of the TUM medical degree programme (third year or higher).

No prior independent leadership of clinical ward rounds.

Sufficient German language proficiency to engage with case materials and provide written reflections.

Normal or corrected-to-normal vision (required for eye-tracking validity).

Written informed consent obtained prior to any study procedure.

Current enrolment or prior participation in a ward round communication simulation course targeting the same competencies (eg, EMMA pilot).

Known visual impairment incompatible with eye-tracking calibration.

Participation in Study 1b of Project C03 (to prevent contamination of EMME stimuli familiarity).

Simultaneous enrolment in Studies 2a, 2b, 3 and 4 (each participant may only participate in one of the four studies).

The EMMA-LE is a digital environment; no clinical training sites are involved. Research assistants delivering sessions will receive standardised training (minimum 4-hour training session) covering participant reception, eye-tracker calibration, script delivery and protocol adherence. Only trained research assistants are authorised to conduct data collection sessions.

All treatment groups across Studies 2–4 work within the EMMA-LE. The environment presents EMME from three clinical ward round–patient cases, each covering four key phases: (1) greeting the patient and establishing rapport; (2) gathering information and summarising case status; (3) clinical decision-making and discussion of next steps; (4) summing up and discharge. Each phase is represented by at least two EMMEs (24 EMMEs total), each covering a clinically relevant 10–30 s sequence.

For each EMME, the learner workflow is: (a) watch an EMME video; (b) receive a guiding prompt (eg, ‘Why is this sequence relevant for clinical case management / team coordination / empathetic communication? Analyse the visual and verbal behaviour of the physician!’); (c) provide a written reflection (free text); (d) receive LLM-generated feedback; (e) optionally revise the reflection and receive updated feedback before advancing to the next EMME.

EMMEs are produced by having a leading physician wear a mobile eye-tracking device (eg, Tobii Pro Glasses 3) during a ward-round simulation. The physician interacts with a simulated patient (standardised patient or actor) and a nursing colleague. Scripts are developed from Study 1 findings and clinical expert input, each featuring elements related to the three ward-round key tasks. Four video/EMME cases are produced; three are used in the EMMA-LE for Studies 2–4 and one is reserved for pre/post-test measurement.

Treatment group 1 (raw fixations): EMMEs display the physician’s scan path as individual fixation circles with saccade lines overlaid in real-time on the ward round video footage.

Treatment group 2 (attention maps): EMMEs display a continuously updated heat-map-style attention overlay that smooths and aggregates fixation data, highlighting areas of sustained gaze without individual fixation circles or saccade paths. Attention maps are computed using a Gaussian kernel with sigma=1 degree of visual angle.

Control group (minimal control): Participants view the same first-person ward round video sequences without any gaze visualisation overlay, that is, not as EMMEs. All other elements of the EMMA-LE (cases, tasks, time on task) are identical to the treatment groups. This condition allows effects of gaze visualisation to be separated from effects of mere exposure to the video material and its perspective.

Study 2a follows a randomised three-group pre-post design (n=96). The central test is the pre-post gain in aPV under each visualisation format; the more effective format is carried forward to Study 3. Planned contrasts compare each visualisation format with the minimal control and the two visualisation formats with each other. Participants complete pre-test, EMME-based intervention and post-test as described in the Participant timeline.

All four study groups work with the same ward round video sequences presented without EMME gaze visualisation, so that the effect of LLM-generated feedback can be estimated independently of any visualisation effect (n=88; n=22 per group; randomised pre-post design). The most effective feedback format is carried forward to Study 3. Groups differ only in the type of LLM-generated feedback on their written reflections:

Group 1 (textual feedback): Participants receive content-focused textual feedback generated by a domain-trained LLM, informing them about aspects they correctly identified and aspects present in the expert solution that they have not yet addressed.

Group 2 (graphical feedback/reflection score): Participants receive a graphically displayed reflection score (0–100) calculated from text length, argument count and argument complexity via the LLM, presented graphically in the EMMA-LE interface.

Group 3 (combined feedback): Participants receive a combination of textual and graphical feedback (as described above) simultaneously.

Group 4 (minimal/control feedback): Participants receive only word-count feedback (eg, ‘Your reflection was 67 words long. The average student reflection is 112 words. The average expert reflection was 134 words. You can revise or proceed’.). No content evaluation is provided.

The LLM is trained on (a) existing textual data from medical students’ verbal reasoning on physician-patient communication videos; (b) pilot data from Study 1b on EMMEs; (c) expert reflective assessments (minimum 20 per EMME). Training uses 80/20 data split for training and validation, with supervised learning and fine-tuning optimised on expert-reference comparisons.

Study 3 crosses the most effective gaze visualisation from Study 2a (factor 1: best EMME visualisation vs no EMME visualisation) with the most effective LLM feedback format from Study 2b (factor 2: best LLM feedback vs minimal control feedback) in a fully crossed 2×2 between-subjects design (N≈220; n≈55 per cell):

Cell 1 (control): no EMME visualisation, minimal control feedback.

Cell 2 (feedback only): best LLM feedback from Study 2b, no EMME visualisation.

Cell 3 (visualisation only): best EMME visualisation from Study 2a, minimal control feedback.

Cell 4 (combined): best EMME visualisation and best LLM feedback.

This design makes the following effects measurable: (a) the effect of LLM-based feedback with versus without EMME (Cell 4 vs Cell 2); (b) the direct comparison of feedback versus visualisation effects (Cell 2 vs Cell 3); and (c) internal replications of the screening results for the best feedback (Cell 2 vs Cell 1) and the best visualisation (Cell 3 vs Cell 1). The analysis uses a split-plot ANOVA with two between-subjects factors (see the Statistical methods section).

All three groups access the same EMME cases with the most effective gaze visualisation identified in Study 2a, combined with the most effective LLM-based feedback identified in Studies 2b and 3. Groups differ in how knowledge activation prompts are provided:

Group 1 (embedded prompts): Brief textual cues appear as pop-up overlays at designated moments within the EMME video stream (eg, ‘In the next 10 s, pay attention to the nurse’s facial expression and gesture’). These prompts are derived from expert reflective comments and highlight specific communicative aspects.

Group 2 (a priori prompts): A single textual prompt is displayed before each EMME video begins (eg, ‘In the following video, pay attention to how the physician responds to the patient’s verbalised anxiety’). No prompts appear during video playback.

Group 3 (control—no prompts): Participants view EMMEs without any additional textual cueing. They receive the standard guiding reflection questions but no attention-directing prompts.

Intervention modifications for individual participants are not applicable in the educational experiment context. Participants may withdraw at any time without consequence. If technical failures (eg, eye-tracker malfunction, system outage) prevent completion of the intervention, we attempt to reschedule the session. If rescheduling is not feasible, the participant is excluded from per-protocol (PP) analyses but retained in intention-to-treat analyses.

To promote adherence, participants are informed about the structure and expected duration of the session before enrolment. Sessions are conducted in a standardised computer laboratory setting to minimise distractions. Research assistants are present throughout. Progress through the EMMA-LE is system-logged (timestamps, EMME completion, reflection length) to monitor engagement. Participants who complete fewer than 70% of EMME reflection tasks are flagged for sensitivity analyses.

No clinical treatments are involved. Participation in concurrent ward round simulation training specifically designed to foster the same aPV components tested in this study is not permitted during the study period. Participants who independently complete such training during the study interval should report this; their data will be handled in sensitivity analyses.

Measured during the diagnostic task (pre/post-test video clip, approximately 3 min) while participants’ eye movements are recorded. The following metrics are extracted for pre-defined areas of interest (AOIs: patient, team members, clinical documents, monitoring equipment):

Mean fixation duration on clinically relevant AOIs (milliseconds)—reflects depth of processing (a).

Time to first fixation on pre-defined clinically relevant events (saccade latency, milliseconds)—reflects processing speed (a).

Fixation dispersion/scan path coverage across the visual field (degrees of visual angle)—reflects breadth of visual field use (b).

Dwell time and fixation count within relevant AOIs—reflect sustained attention to key information (c).

Fixation count and dwell time on irrelevant AOIs; proportion of fixations on relevant versus irrelevant AOIs—reflect selective filtering (d).

Analysis metric: pre-to-post change scores for each eye-tracking metric and comparison of group means at post-test.

Measured via the pre/post-test diagnostic task: participants provide written responses to the open prompt ‘What did you observe for each participant?’ after watching the test video. Quality is assessed using a modified professional vision coding system (based on ) by trained research assistants (minimum two raters per response):

Criterion e: Extent to which reasoning addresses individual ward round participants (vs the situation as a whole)—scored 0–3.

Criterion f: Number and specificity of behavioural and gaze cues drawn from the scene—scored 0–3.

Criterion g: Degree to which cues are related to overarching goals of ward round communication, including differentiated description of patient emotional status—scored 0–3.

An overall Advanced Reasoning Score (0–9) is derived by summing criteria e, f and g. Interrater reliability is assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Cohen’s Kappa; minimum acceptable ICC=0.75.

Quantitative reflection quality score derived from participants’ final written reflections on each EMME (after potential revision), rated using the same coding system. This captures learning process quality and is used to examine within-intervention improvement trajectories.

Measured via validated questionnaire instruments provided by Project M (SHARP Collaborative Research Centre), administered at pre-test and post-test. Specific instruments to be determined in coordination with Project M; constructs include cognitive load, situational interest, self-regulated learning strategies and learning emotions.

Assessed via standardised scenario-based vignette responses (closed and open items) examining whether participants can identify diagnostic problems and suggest appropriate interventions in novel ward round scenarios. Items are developed in collaboration with Project C01.

No physical harms are anticipated from participating in an educational computer-based simulation study. Potential minimal harms include: (1) cognitive fatigue from 150-minute sessions (mitigated by structured breaks); (2) discomfort from the eye-tracking device (mitigated by calibration procedures and the right to withdraw). Participants are informed of their right to withdraw at any time. Any adverse events (eg, headache, eye strain) will be recorded by the supervising research assistant. Adverse event rates will be reported in all study publications.

provides an overview of the participant timeline across the studies, including enrolment, interventions, assessments and debriefing.

SHARP, Collaborative Research Center "Simulation-Based Learning in Higher Education: Advancing Research on Process Diagnostics and Personalised Interventions" (DFG CRC / TRR 419).

Studies 2a and 2b—Oct 2026 to Feb 2027.

Study 3—Q2–Q3 2027.

Study 4—Q1–Q2 2028.

Power analyses were conducted using G*Power 3.1 for a split-plot mixed ANOVA with between-subjects factor group (k groups) and within-subjects factor time (two levels: pre-test, post-test; cf. ). For Study 2a, power was calculated for the three planned pairwise contrasts on the Group×Time interaction (raw fixations vs attention maps; each visualisation format vs minimal control; Bonferroni-adjusted α=0.0167), assuming f=0.25 and a conservative pre-post correlation of r=0.30. This yields n=31 per group (n=93), rounded to n=96 (n=32 per group) for balanced block randomisation.

EMME, eye movement modelling examples; LLM, Large Language Model.

Sample sizes are inflated by 10% to account for anticipated attrition (non-completion of post-test or insufficient eye-tracking quality). Attrition-adjusted targets: Study 2a n=108, Study 2b n=97, Study 3 n=242, Study 4 n=209. For reporting, analyses will be conducted both on the full intention-to-treat sample and on the PP sample (participants completing≥70% of the EMMA-LE and both test sessions).

Participants will be recruited through multiple channels within TUM Medical Faculty:

Announcements in clinical semester courses and clerkship orientations.

Email distribution via the TUM Medical Faculty student mailing list.

Flyers posted at the clinical campus (Klinikum rechts der Isar).

Announcements via the official TUM medical student platform.

Interested students register via an online sign-up form. Eligibility is confirmed during a brief telephone or email screening. Informed consent is obtained in writing at the start of Session 1. Participants receive course credit or a small financial compensation (€15 per session) for participation as permitted by TUM ethical standards.

A computer-generated random allocation sequence will be produced by an independent statistician (Prof. Gollwitzer’s team) using R statistical software (the sample() function) prior to the start of data collection for each study. The allocation sequence will be generated independently for each study.

Randomisation is simple randomisation stratified by prior eye-tracking experience (yes/no) and study semester (early clinical=semesters 5–6; late clinical=semesters 7–10) to ensure balanced group composition. Block randomisation (block size=3 or 6 for Study 2a; block size=8 or 12 for Studies 2b and 3; block size=6 or 9 for Study 4) will be used to ensure approximate balance throughout recruitment. Block sizes are concealed from recruitment staff; details are documented in a separate sealed document.

Allocation is managed via a central computerised system (REDCap). Researchers conducting screening and enrolment do not have access to the allocation sequence. At the start of Session 1, after consent and pre-test completion, the research assistant enters the participant ID into REDCap, which reveals the allocated group condition automatically. Envelopes are not used.

The random allocation sequence is generated by the independent statistician and uploaded to REDCap. Research assistants who enrol participants do not have access to the sequence until after pre-test completion. The REDCap system implements allocation after pre-test completion, ensuring concealment during enrolment and pre-test administration.

Due to the nature of the educational interventions (participants interact with visibly different types of EMME feedback or prompts), full blinding of participants to their allocated condition is not feasible. The following blinding arrangements apply:

Participants: Not blinded to their group condition.

Research assistants administering sessions: Not blinded (must load correct EMMA-LE condition).

Outcome assessors (coders of written reasoning texts): Blinded to group allocation. All participant IDs are pseudonymised prior to coding.

Eye-tracking data analysts: Blinded to group allocation during metric extraction and primary analysis.

Data analysts (statisticians): Provided with coded group labels (A/B/C) rather than descriptive labels during primary analysis; unblinded for interpretation.

Reasoning texts are exported from REDCap after removing all identifiable metadata. Pseudonymised texts are distributed to coders in randomised order. Coders are trained on a separate coding dataset that does not include study participants. Eye-tracking files are labelled with participant IDs only; group labels are stored in a separate file not accessible to the eye-tracking analyst until after primary metric extraction.

Unblinding of outcome assessors is not required before primary analyses are complete. Unblinding of analysts occurs after the locked, pre-registered analysis plan has been executed. Any unplanned unblinding (eg, due to coder inference from content) is documented. Participants are fully debriefed regarding their group condition after completion of the post-test session.

Eye movements are recorded using Tobii Pro Fusion (or equivalent remote desktop eye-tracker, sampling rate≥120 Hz) during the pre- and post-test diagnostic task. Equipment is calibrated using a 9-point calibration routine; only participants achieving calibration accuracy<1.0 degree of visual angle are included in eye-tracking analyses. The diagnostic task video is presented full-screen at a standardised viewing distance of 65 cm. AOIs are pre-defined by two clinical experts and two educational psychologists prior to data collection, and their coordinates are fixed in the eye-tracking analysis software (Tobii Pro Lab or equivalent). AOI definitions and coordinates will be published in the pre-registration.

Key metrics extracted per AOI: mean fixation duration, time to first fixation, fixation count, dwell time, scan path length, fixation dispersion. Metrics are extracted using automated scripts in Python/Tobii API; output is reviewed by Dr Kosel.

Written reflections are submitted directly via the EMMA-LE (Moodle text entry fields). Texts are exported as CSV files with participant pseudonyms. Two trained research assistants independently code each text using the modified professional vision coding system, scoring criteria e, f and g on 0–3 scales. Rater training uses a separate, independently sourced set of medical student texts not from the study sample. Interrater reliability is assessed before each coding phase; if ICC<0.75, further training is provided before continuing. Final scores are computed as the average of two raters; discrepancies>1 point are adjudicated by a third rater.

Demographic questionnaire and M-Project instruments are administered via REDCap. Validated instruments include: cognitive load items (7-point Likert, validated for educational research contexts), situational interest (adapted from Renninger & Hidi), and self-regulated learning (adapted from MSLQ). Specific instruments will be finalised in coordination with Project M.

Time-stamped logs of participant interactions (EMME views, reflection submissions, feedback accesses, revision cycles) are automatically recorded by the learning platform. These support secondary analyses of learning process quality and adherence.

Participants who do not attend Session 2 (post-test) will be contacted once by email and once by phone within 48 hours. A rescheduling window of±2 days around the target post-test date is permitted. Participants who do not complete the post-test within this window are retained in Intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses with missing post-test data handled by multiple imputation (see Items 27b and 27c); last observation carried forward (LOCF) is used only as a sensitivity analysis. For missing eye-tracking data (calibration failure), participants are excluded from eye-tracking analyses only and retained in all other analyses.

All participant data are stored in REDCap hosted on TUM secure servers, complying with GDPR. Personal identifying information (name, email, student ID) is stored in a separate REDCap database linked to pseudonymised participant IDs; this linkage file is accessible only to the data manager (Katrin Brauer) and the PIs. Study data files (eye-tracking, coded texts, questionnaires) carry participant IDs only. Data backups are performed automatically daily. Raw eye-tracking files are stored on password-protected external drives in a locked laboratory. Data retention: 10 years from study completion, per TUM data management policy. Range checks are applied to all questionnaire data on entry. Double-entry verification is performed for a 10% random sample of coded reasoning texts.

Primary analyses are conducted in R (V.≥4.3). For each cluster of dependent variables (advanced noticing metrics; advanced reasoning score), a separate split-plot mixed ANOVA is computed with group (between) and time (within) as factors, and Group×Time interaction as the primary test of the experimental effect. F-statistics and partial η² effect sizes are reported. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons are conducted using Bonferroni correction. For Study 2a (three groups), planned contrasts will compare each visualisation format (raw fixations, attention maps) versus minimal control, and raw fixations versus attention maps (Bonferroni-adjusted α=0.0167). For Study 2b (four groups), planned contrasts will additionally compare: textual versus graphical, textual versus combined, graphical versus combined, and each active feedback versus control. For Study 3, the split-plot ANOVA includes two crossed between-subjects factors (visualisation: best vs none; feedback: best vs minimal control) and time as the within-subjects factor; the Visualisation×Feedback (× Time) interaction is the primary confirmatory test. Planned cell contrasts follow the pre-specified comparisons: Cell 4 versus Cell 2 (feedback with vs without EMME), Cell 2 versus Cell 3 (feedback vs visualisation) and Cell 2 versus Cell 1/Cell 3 versus Cell 1 (internal replications of the screening results).

Where multiple correlated dependent variables within the same aPV component are analysed, a multivariate ANOVA (MANOVA) will be performed first to control Type I error inflation, followed by univariate ANOVAs as follow-up.

For secondary outcomes (motivational-affective questionnaires, system log metrics), separate ANCOVAs will be run with pre-test values as covariates.

ITT population: All randomised participants with at least partial pre-test data. Missing post-test data imputed using multiple imputation (m=20) with predictive mean matching for continuous outcomes. Imputation assumes data are missing at random; the imputation model includes group, pre-test scores, the stratification variables and auxiliary variables related to dropout. Estimates are pooled using Rubin’s rules. Multiple imputation is the primary missing-data strategy; LOCF is used only as a sensitivity analysis (Item 27d).

PP population: Participants completing≥70% of EMMA-LE tasks and both test sessions with valid eye-tracking calibration. PP analysis is the primary analysis for advanced noticing outcomes; ITT is primary for advanced reasoning. This distinction reflects that eye-tracking outcomes cannot be meaningfully obtained or imputed for participants without valid calibration.

Sensitivity analyses: See Item 27d.

Missing questionnaire items: Single items within a scale are imputed using the participant’s mean on the remaining items of the same scale (if≤30% of items are missing for that scale). Scales with>30% missing items are excluded for that participant. Missing eye-tracking data due to calibration failure: excluded from eye-tracking analysis; retained in other analyses. Missing written reflection post-test data: multiple imputation as described above.

Pre-specified subgroup analyses:

Prior simulation experience (yes/no): tested as a moderator via Group×Time×Experience three-way interaction.

Study semester (early vs late clinical phase): tested as a moderator.

Gender: exploratory, given no prior evidence of gender differences (Section C03.7 of project proposal).

Sensitivity analyses: complete-case analysis; LOCF imputation; exclusion of participants with≥1 protocol deviation; analysis with alternative eye-tracking AOI definitions (wider vs narrower boundaries).

Given the low-risk educational nature of the studies and the absence of clinical endpoints or pharmacological interventions, a formal independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) is not constituted. Data safety oversight is performed by the SHARP Collaborative Research Centre steering committee, which receives annual progress reports from all projects. Any unexpected adverse events are reported to this committee and to the responsible ethics committee within 2 weeks of occurrence.

No formal interim analyses are planned, as the studies are brief (each study’s data collection spans approximately 4–6 months) and no safety concerns warrant early stopping. If systematic data collection errors or equipment failures are identified affecting≥20% of participants, the principal investigators and SHARP steering committee will convene to assess whether to continue, pause, or modify data collection.

Each doctoral researcher (DR#9 for Studies 2b and 3; DR#10 for Studies 2a and 4) conducts weekly quality checks on data completeness, eye-tracking calibration success rates, and coding progress. A monitoring log is maintained. Monthly meetings between the doctoral researchers and the PIs (Gartmeier, Seidel) include review of the monitoring log. Any protocol deviations are documented in a protocol deviation log with date, description, and action taken.

The project includes research on human subjects. Ethics approval has been obtained from the responsible ethics committee on 9 March 2026 (Ethikkommission der Technischen Universität München; grant code is 2025-702 S-CT). Studies 2–4 fall under this approval as experimental substudies of Project C03. Any new study components requiring additional ethics review (eg, modified EMME content featuring emotionally distressing scenarios) will be submitted for supplementary approval before implementation.

All important protocol modifications (changes to eligibility criteria, outcomes, analysis plan, or intervention procedures) will be: (1) documented in the protocol amendment log with date, description, and rationale; (2) reported to the responsible ethics committee; (3) updated in the trial registration record; (4) communicated to enrolled participants if they affect ongoing participation. Minor modifications (eg, minor wording corrections) are documented in the amendment log but do not require ethics committee notification.

Informed consent is obtained by trained research assistants at the start of Session 1. Participants receive a written information sheet (minimum 48 hours before the session, transmitted via email after registration) describing: study purpose, procedures, time requirements, data management, right to withdraw, and dissemination plans. Consent forms are signed in person at the start of Session 1. Participants under 18 years are excluded (not expected, given clinical semester enrolment requirements in Germany). Consent forms are stored separately from study data.

Participants are asked to provide optional consent for their data (pseudonymised reflective texts, aggregated eye-tracking metrics) to be used in: (a) cross-project analyses within the SHARP CRC; (b) future meta-analyses on EMME-based learning. Data sharing is conditional on separate optional consent; refusal does not affect eligibility for the primary study.

Participant names, email addresses and student IDs are stored in a separate encrypted REDCap database accessible only to the data manager and PIs. Study databases contain pseudonymised IDs only. Eye-tracking recordings showing participants’ faces are not collected (participants watch stimulus videos; the eye-tracker only records gaze coordinates). All data are stored on TUM General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)-compliant servers in Germany. The linkage file is destroyed 10 years after publication of final study results. All research assistants and doctoral researchers sign a data confidentiality agreement.

No physical harms are anticipated requiring post-trial care. Participants in the wait-list and control conditions are offered access to the full EMMA-LE after completion of the post-test, providing equivalent educational opportunity. All participants receive a debriefing document summarising the study rationale, hypotheses and their group condition. If studies reveal that a particular design feature is clearly superior, the superior design will be recommended for integration into the standard TUM ward round communication curriculum.

Results will be disseminated regardless of direction of findings. Planned dissemination activities include:

Publication of this study protocol prior to data collection in BMJ Open.

Pre-registration of all empirical studies in the project.

Publication of results in high-impact peer-reviewed journals in medical education and educational psychology.

Presentations at conferences such as The International Association for Health Professions Education (AMEE), Gesellschaft für Medizinische Ausbildung (GMA), European Association for Research in Learning and Instruction (EARLI), Americal Educational Research Association (AERA).

Results communicated to participants via a project newsletter at study completion.

Integration into SHARP project reports to the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) and to SHARP transfer and science communication activities

psychology.title: Effectiveness of a compassion‐based positive psychology group intervention for cardiac recovery: A multiple‐baseline single‐case experimental design study
psychology.abstract: Patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD) commonly experience mental health problems. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a group‐based compassion‐based positive psychology intervention (CB‐PPI) in patients with CVD.A multiple‐baseline single‐case experimental design with three phases (baseline, intervention, follow‐up) was used to examine the effectiveness of an eight‐week group CB‐PPI. Twelve participants completed weekly assessments of psychological wellbeing, anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, adaptive capacity, and positive skills. Multilevel analyses were conducted to compare outcomes during the intervention and follow‐up phases with the baseline phase. In addition, participants completed comprehensive questionnaires at baseline, post‐intervention, and two‐month follow‐up. Reliable changes and Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests were conducted.Compared with the baseline phase, significant improvements in weekly assessments were observed during the follow‐up phase for depressive symptoms, adaptive capacity, and positive skills. No significant effects were observed for anxiety symptoms and psychological wellbeing, and no significant differences were found between the baseline and intervention phases. Significant improvements in overall, emotional, and psychological wellbeing were found from pre‐ to post‐intervention, as well as in positive reframing and savouring. Psychological wellbeing significantly improved from pre‐ to two‐month follow‐up.This study provides preliminary evidence that a group‐based CB‐PPI may support patients with CVD in developing positive skills, enhance adaptive capacity, and improve wellbeing and depressive symptoms, although results are inconsistent across methods. However, more research is needed to confirm these findings, examine mechanisms of change, and establish the clinical utility of CB‐PPI in cardiovascular care.
psychology.text:
Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) comprise a broad range of disorders affecting the heart and blood vessels (World Health Organization, ). Mental illbeing, including depression and anxiety, is highly prevalent among patients with CVDs (Hare et al., ; Tully et al., ) and has consistently been associated with adverse clinical outcomes (Ma, ; Rutledge et al., ; Watkins et al., ). By contrast, positive mental health or mental wellbeing, including positive emotional, psychological and social functioning (Keyes & Waterman, ), has been linked to more favourable health outcomes in patients with CVDs (Arabadjian et al., ; DuBois et al., ; Salman et al., ), while evidence from the general population suggests that greater psychological wellbeing is linked to lower risk of developing mental illbeing (Keyes et al., ; Schotanus‐Dijkstra, ten Have, et al., ; ten Klooster et al., ; Wood & Joseph, ). Together, these findings underscore the critical importance of addressing both mental illbeing and wellbeing in the context of care of patients with CVDs.

Mental illbeing and wellbeing can be seen as distinct yet interrelated dimensions of mental health (Iasiello & van Agteren, ; Keyes, ; Westerhof & Keyes, ). Building upon this so‐called two‐continua model, the model of Sustainable Mental Health has been developed as a heuristic, balanced treatment approach (Bohlmeijer & Westerhof, ). This model posits that both mental illbeing and wellbeing are influenced by an individual's underlying adaptive capacity, defined as the ability to manage and adjust to personal challenges (Franken et al., ). Adaptive capacity are influenced by barriers and resources, specific behavioural, emotional and cognitive processes that can be conceptualized as factors that may influence a person's general capacity to adapt, instead of equivalents of this adaptive capacity itself. For example, barriers as avoidance‐oriented behaviour, less adaptive emotion‐regulation strategies, or maladaptive cognitive processes (e.g., negative repetitive thinking) may make it more difficult to respond flexibly to challenging situations, whereas resources encompass functional processes (e.g., use of personal strengths, positive reframing, supportive relationships, and self‐compassion) (Bohlmeijer & Westerhof, , ). Evidence for the model of sustainable mental health is emerging, suggesting that adaptive capacity is strongly associated with mental illbeing and mental wellbeing, and may be influenced by barriers such as repetitive negative thinking and resources such as self‐compassion and positive reframing (Kloos et al., ; Wang et al., ). This highlights the importance of balanced interventions that address not only dysfunctional processes but also strengthen positive psychological resources that foster adaptive capacity and mental health as key components of psychological adjustment in CVD care.

Positive psychology interventions (PPIs) aim to promote mental wellbeing through the development of positive behaviours, cognitions, feelings, and strengths (Schueller & Parks, ). Evidence suggests that PPIs can benefit individuals with a variety of clinical conditions (Carr et al., ; Chakhssi et al., ). In their meta‐analysis of 20 trials involving 1222 patients, Tönis et al. () found that PPIs significantly improved mental wellbeing and reduced mental illbeing among individuals with CVD. Five of these studies were conducted as part of the development and optimisation of the Positive Emotions after Acute Cardiac Events (PEACE) intervention during a 6‐year process (Huffman et al., ; Tönis et al., ). The 12‐week phone‐delivered PEACE interventions combined motivational interviewing with various PPIs (e.g., writing a gratitude letter, writing about a best possible future, performing acts of kindness, and savouring) (Huffman et al., ). Where PEACE consists of multiple PPIs, other studies included single PPIs, such as gratitude journaling (Redwine et al., ), a spiritual or religious intervention (Elham et al., ), and optimism or positive thinking (Ghodsbin et al., ; Mohammadi et al., ). In addition, it has been found that combining PPIs with compassion‐based interventions may be particularly effective in promoting mental wellbeing (Kraiss et al., ; Schotanus‐Dijkstra, Drossaert, et al., ; Wang et al., ).

Self‐compassion represents a particularly important psychological resource for adaptive capacity and mental health. It involves treating oneself with kindness, recognizing one's experiences as part of the shared human condition, and maintaining mindful awareness of negative thoughts and emotions (Neff, ). From a complementary perspective, self‐compassion has also been described as a flow of compassion directed toward oneself (Gilbert, ), encompassing sensitivity to personal suffering, efforts to prevent and alleviate it, and the exercise of wisdom and courage (Gilbert, ). Self‐compassion has been positively associated with mental wellbeing in the general population (Zessin et al., ), quality of life among older adults with CVD (Salehi et al., ), and lower levels of mental illbeing both in the general population (MacBeth & Gumley, ) and in patients with CVDs (Morgenroth et al., ). Furthermore, self‐compassion has been found to facilitate self‐regulatory resources (Biber & Ellis, ; Sirois, ) and has been linked to lower levels of subclinical CVD in midlife women, suggesting potential cardioprotective effects (Thurston et al., ). Studies investigating compassion‐based interventions for patients with CVDs have reported that patients showed improvements in emotion regulation (Bronsi et al., ; Izanloo et al., ) and reductions in anxiety and depression (Adibizadeh & Sajjadian, ), although evidence remains preliminary (Austin et al., ; Kılıç et al., ; Tönis et al., ).

Combining PPIs and compassion‐based interventions may offer a particularly powerful approach to improving mental health in patients with CVDs. Compassion‐based interventions help patients acknowledge and tolerate their suffering, while reducing self‐criticism, shame and feelings of isolation (Gilbert, ; Neff, ). By downregulating threat and fostering emotional safeness, compassion may create the psychological conditions necessary for patients to engage meaningfully with PPIs. In turn, PPIs can build on this foundation by cultivating positive emotions, meaning and personal strengths (Schueller & Parks, ). Thus, compassion may prepare the ground, and PPIs may help patients flourish. Therefore, this intervention primarily aims to enhance wellbeing, which is common for PPI research (e.g., Bolier et al., ; Chakhssi et al., ). Recently, a transdiagnostic compassion‐based positive psychology group intervention was developed, combining evidence‐based PPIs with compassion‐focused practices. In a randomized controlled trial, the intervention significantly improved mental wellbeing and personal recovery among individuals with bipolar disorder compared to treatment as usual, with effects maintained up to 12 months (Kraiss et al., ).
