The rationale of the intervention was adapted to fit patients with CVD, while the components (i.e., positive psychological skills targeted by the intervention, including self‐compassion, savouring, and gratitude) of the intervention were maintained. The intervention was previously tested in a separate cohort in a cardiology setting and a mixed‐methods case study (n = 1) in a general hospital demonstrated preliminary benefits, including increased self‐compassion and adaptive capacity 2 months after completing the intervention (Tönis et al., ).

The present study aims to further evaluate the effects of this compassion‐based PPI (CB‐PPI) in patients with CVD. To achieve this, a single‐case experimental design (SCED) was utilized, that enables intensive, prospective measurement within individuals across time, with participants serving as their own controls (Kazdin, ; Tate & Perdices, ). This design facilitates causal inference while requiring fewer resources than large‐scale trials and avoids withholding the intervention from participants (Kazdin, ; Tate & Perdices, ). SCEDs are within‐subject designs typically conducted with small groups of participants (Maric, ). In the current study, a multiple‐baseline study was conducted to examine the effectiveness of a compassion‐based positive psychology group intervention on psychological wellbeing (primary outcome), anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, adaptive capacity, and positive skills (i.e., gratitude, savouring, self‐compassion, and positive reframing) in patients with CVDs.

This study was approved by the Medical Ethical Committee Eastern Netherlands (NL82786.091.22). The Single‐Case Reporting Guideline in Behavioural Interventions 2016 (SCRIBE; Tate et al., ) was followed for reporting this study. A complete SCRIBE checklist is included in Appendix .

The current study employed a multiple‐baseline design, a subtype of SCEDs, to evaluate the effectiveness of a compassion‐based PPI on mental health in patients with CVDs. Weekly repeated measures were completed during a baseline, intervention, and follow‐up phase. The baseline phase served as the comparison phase, providing insight into levels of outcome measures prior to participating in the intervention (Kazdin, ), while the other two phases aimed to examine changes over time during and after the intervention.

Participants were eligible if they (1) were at least 18 years of age, (2) had a diagnosis of myocardial infarction, recent heart surgery, or heart failure with confirmed clinical stability, (3) demonstrated sufficient motivation to participate in the intervention and engage in home practice, and (4) had access to a device enabling completion of online questionnaires. Participants were excluded if they (1) experienced a mental illbeing, as indicated by severe depression or anxiety symptoms, (2) had a life expectancy of less than 2 years, (3) were receiving other psychological treatments during the planned CB‐PPI, or (4) were awaiting major medical intervention (e.g., surgery). Mental illbeing and motivation to participate were assessed by a healthcare psychologist involved in cardiac rehabilitation, whereas physical eligibility was assessed by a cardiologist or nurse specialist.

The target sample size was 14 participants divided across two groups. Sample size estimation was based on SCED power simulations (Ferron & Sentovich, ), indicating sufficient power (>.80) to detect large effects (Cohen's d ≥ 1.5) with at least 20 assessments per participant and a minimum of four participants. Comparably large effect sizes (e.g. d > 2.0) are not uncommon in SCED research (Levin et al., ). Including two groups also allowed for systematic replication, thereby improving external validity and generalisability. To account for attrition, the target sample size was set at seven participants per group.

Participants were referred by hospital‐based psychologists involved in cardiac rehabilitation at a general hospital in the Netherlands. Eligible participants received study information and were given 2 weeks to consider participation. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Participants in the first group were recruited between October 2023 and February 2024, and the intervention took place from March to May 2024. Participants in the second group were recruited between September 2024 and March 2025, and the intervention took place from April to May 2025.

Participants were randomly allocated to one of three different baseline lengths (i.e., 5, 6, or 7 weeks) using Sealed Envelope software (https://www.sealedenvelope.com/simple‐randomiser/v1/lists) employing block randomisation to ensure an even distribution of baseline lengths. Because the intervention was delivered in a group format, all participants within a group began the intervention on the same day, while their SCED baseline measures commenced at different time points.

The baseline phase of the first treatment group was extended by 1 week due to a delay in the intervention start. Similarly, a one‐week break occurred during the intervention phase of this group due to holidays, and an additional SCED measure week was added. One week prior to the intervention, participants completed a comprehensive online pre‐intervention questionnaire. Additional comprehensive questionnaires were administered immediately post‐intervention and 2 months post‐intervention (follow‐up). All weekly SCED measures and comprehensive questionnaires were administered via the questionnaire software Qualtrics.

The intervention, Living Well with Heart Disease, is a transdiagnostic, group‐based programme combining compassion‐based and positive psychology intervention (Kraiss et al., , ). It consisted of eight weekly, 2‐h, face‐to‐face sessions delivered at the hospital by two trained healthcare psychologists experienced in delivering this intervention to patients with CVDs. In the second treatment group, one facilitator discontinued participation after the second session due to medical reasons; consequently, the remaining sessions were delivered by a single psychologist.

Each session included a combination of psychoeducation, exercises, group discussion, and reflection. Sessions covered (1) introduction, (2) self‐compassion, (3) positive emotions, (4) dealing with anxiety, (5) goals and optimism, (6) strengths, (7) positive relationships, and (8) post‐traumatic growth. A detailed overview of session content is available in a previously published case study (Tönis et al., ).

Participants were encouraged to apply learned skills in daily life through homework assignments involving reading and practicing one to four exercises based on positive psychology, mindfulness, and self‐compassion. Participants received a Dutch version of the self‐help book Using positive psychology everyday, learning how to flourish (Bohlmeijer & Hulsbergen, ) and a workbook containing exercises, journaling space, and preparatory materials. A treatment diary was maintained by the psychologists to monitor treatment fidelity.

Two types of measures were used to evaluate the intervention effectiveness: (1) weekly SCED measures administered during the baseline (5–7 weeks), intervention (8 weeks), and follow‐up (8 weeks) phases, and (2) comprehensive questionnaires administered at baseline, post‐intervention, and follow‐up. The weekly SCED measures were selected to correspond conceptually with the comprehensive questionnaires.

Weekly SCED measures assessed psychological wellbeing, anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, adaptive capacity, and positive skills (i.e., gratitude, savouring, self‐compassion, and positive reframing), see Table  in Appendix  for the items. Psychological wellbeing was measured using the 6‐item subscale of the Mental Health Continuum—Short Form (MHC‐SF; Keyes et al., ; Lamers et al., ), anxiety symptoms with the 2‐item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD‐2; Donker et al., ), depressive symptoms with the 2‐item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ‐2; Löwe et al., ), and adaptive capacity with two items of the Generic Sense of Ability to Adapt Scale (GSAAS; Franken et al., ) with the highest factor loadings.

Positive skills were assessed using two items with high factor loadings from comprehensive questionnaires: gratitude (Short Gratitude, Resentment and Appreciation Test, Dutch translation, S‐GRAT‐NL; Jans‐Beken et al., ), savouring (Savouring Beliefs Inventory, SBI; Bryant, ), self‐compassion (Self‐Reassuring subscale of the Forms of Self‐Criticizing/Attacking and Self‐Reassuring Scale‐Short Form, FSCRS‐SF; Sommers‐Spijkerman et al., ), and positive reinterpretation (Coping Orientations and Problems Experienced inventory, COPE; Carver et al., ).

Mental wellbeing was assessed using the 14‐item MHC‐SF (Keyes et al., ; Lamers et al., ). Anxiety symptoms were measured with the 7‐item GAD (GAD‐7; Spitzer et al., ), depressive symptoms with the 9‐item PHQ (PHQ‐9; Kroenke et al., ), and adaptive capacity with the 10‐item GSAAS (Franken et al., ). All measures were validated in Dutch and demonstrated good psychometrics (Donker et al., ; Franken et al., ; Lamers et al., ; Zuithoff et al., ). Internal consistency at baseline was good for mental wellbeing (α = .91) including its three subscales (α > .82), as well as anxiety symptoms (α = .83), depressive symptoms (α = .83), and adaptive capacity (α = .89). Average scores were calculated for the MHC‐SF (including emotional, social and psychological wellbeing subscale) and the GSAAS, whereas sum scores were calculated for the GAD‐7 and PHQ‐9, with higher scores indicating higher levels of the respective constructs.

Positive reframing was assessed using the 4‐item positive reinterpretation and growth subscale of the COPE (Carver et al., ), savouring using the four positively worded items of the reminiscing subscale of the SBI (Bryant, ), and self‐compassion using the 8‐item self‐reassuring subscale of the FSCRS‐SF (Sommers‐Spijkerman et al., ). Sum scores were calculated for these measures, with higher scores indicating greater use of the respective skills. All measures were validated and satisfactory to good psychometric properties were found for the subscales (Bryant, ; Golay et al., ; Kloos et al., ; Sommers‐Spijkerman et al., ). Internal consistency at baseline was good for positive reframing (α = .83), savouring (α = .81), self‐compassion (α = .89).

Experiences with the intervention were evaluated with six items based on the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ‐8; Attkisson & Zwick, ). Participants were asked about their experiences with the quality of the intervention on a four‐point scale (i.e., from excellent to worse), as well as the satisfaction with the intervention, wish fulfilment, recommending the course to others, and experienced support in dealing with their situation on a scale from not at all (1) to totally (10). This data was descriptively analysed.

Primary intention‐to‐treat analyses were conducted using linear mixed‐effects models to examine intervention effects on the continuous outcomes psychological wellbeing, anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, adaptive capacity, and positive skills. Fixed effects included study phase (baseline, intervention, and follow‐up) and time within each phase. Study phase was dummy‐coded with the baseline serving as reference category. Time was centred at the start of the intervention or follow‐up phase, such that the first assessment in that phase was coded as zero. Consequently, model estimates for study phase represent differences between baseline and beginning of the intervention or follow‐up phase (Declercq et al., ). Separate models were run to compare baseline with intervention outcomes and baseline with follow‐up outcomes.

Random‐intercept and random‐slope models were specified to account for repeated measures nested within individuals, and model fit was compared using likelihood ratio tests. Random slopes were retained only when they significantly improved model fit. Restricted maximum likelihood estimation was used throughout. Per‐protocol analyses were also conducted, including participants who attended at least six of the eight sessions (Kraiss et al., ). In exploratory post‐hoc analyses, an interaction between phase and group was added to examine potential differences in intervention effects between groups. To quantify overall effect size across participants, between‐case standardized mean difference (BC‐SMD) was calculated (Hedges et al., ; Valentine et al., ), accounting for missing data, small sample sizes, repeated measures within individuals, and within‐ and between‐case variances. BC‐SMDs were interpreted as small (.20–.50), moderate (.50–.80) or large (>.80) (Cohen, ). Analyses of weekly SCED measures were conducted in R (version 4.4.1), using the nlme package (Pinheiro, ) for mixed‐effect modelling and the scdhlm package (Pustejovsky et al., ) for effect size estimation.

Exploratory post‐hoc analyses examining group‐by‐phase interactions were conducted by adding interaction terms to the primary mixed‐effects models. Differences in questionnaire scores between pre‐ and post‐intervention and between pre‐intervention and follow‐up at group level were examined using two‐sided Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests. These analyses were conducted in SPSS version 28.0.1. The Reliable Change Index (RCI; Jacobson & Truax, ) was calculated for each outcome between baseline and post‐intervention, baseline and follow‐up, as well as post‐intervention and follow‐up for individual changes (one‐sided). RCIs were based on reported Chronbach's alpha and standard deviation derived from Dutch studies with large sample sizes (Kloos et al., ; Tönis et al., ) following (Tönis et al., ).

The ggplot2 package (Wickham, ) in R was used to visualize weekly SCED measures for individual participants included in the per‐protocol analyses.

A total of 17 participants registered for the study, of whom 16 provided informed consent (one withdrew due to scheduling issues with work obligations) and 15 completed the pre‐intervention questionnaire including demographics. One participant only participated in the intervention but not in the study due to research obligations related to their specific CVD at inclusion. Three participants dropped out during the intervention for reasons including having already learned what they needed, unspecified reasons, and medical reasons. An overview of the response rate per participant is presented in Table  in Appendix . On average, the 12 randomized participants completed 17.2 weekly SCED measures (74.5%, range 2–25). No adverse events were reported.

The majority of participants were male (60%), with a mean age of 60.7 years (SD = 6.4, range: 48–73). Most were married or in a registered partnership (66.7%), with the remainder divorced (26.7%), or never married (6.7%). Regarding employment status, participants were employed (53.3%), retired (20%), receiving sickness benefits (20%), or acting as informal caregiver for a partner (6.7%). Education levels were higher professional education (46.7%), (pre‐)vocational education (46.7%), or academic education (6.7%).

The psychologists facilitating both groups maintained treatment diaries to document any deviations from the protocol, which was largely followed. Minor adjustments included using their own recordings with the same content for the audio exercises instead of the provided ones and rephrasing theoretical explanations to better match participants' needs. Based on prior experience, an additional activity was included in the final session, inviting participants to write a compassionate wish for the group members.

Analyses were repeated excluding participants who attended fewer than six of the eight intervention sessions (participants 106 and 204). Findings (Tables  and , Appendix ) were comparable with the intention‐to‐treat analyses. Visualizations of individual outcome trajectories of per‐protocol participants can be found in the appendix (Figures , Appendix ).

For the primary outcome psychological wellbeing, significant interaction effects between group and intervention phase (B = −.42, p = .026) and between group and follow‐up (B = −.55, p < .001) were found. This indicates that changes in psychological wellbeing and both the intervention and follow‐up periods differ significantly between the two groups.

Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests examined group‐level changes between pre‐ and post‐intervention, and pre‐intervention and follow‐up (Table ). Significant improvements from pre‐ to post‐intervention were observed for mental wellbeing (Z = −2.55, p = .011), emotional wellbeing (Z = −2.33, p = .020), psychological wellbeing (Z = −2.11, p = .035), positive reframing (Z = −2.05, p = .04), and savouring (Z = −2.06, p = .040). From pre‐intervention to follow‐up, significant improvements were found for psychological wellbeing (Z = −2.06, p = .039).

Outcomes assessed at baseline, post‐intervention, and two‐month follow‐up, along with the calculated RCIs, are presented in Table  in Appendix . Reliable change could be calculated for 10 participants from pre‐ to post‐intervention, 6 participants from pre‐intervention to follow‐up, and 7 participants from post‐intervention to follow‐up. From pre‐ to post intervention, reliable increases were observed in ability to adapt (n = 2), mental, emotional and social wellbeing (n = 1), self‐compassion (n = 2), and anxiety (n = 1), and reliable decreases in self‐compassion (n = 1) and anxiety (n = 2). From pre‐intervention to follow‐up, reliable increases were observed in ability to adapt (n = 1), mental, emotional and social wellbeing (n = 1), self‐compassion (n = 1), and anxiety (n = 1), and reliable decreases were observed in emotional wellbeing (n = 1), anxiety (n = 1), and depression (n = 2). From post‐intervention to follow‐up, reliable decreases were observed in emotional wellbeing (n = 1), anxiety (n = 1), mental and social wellbeing (n = 1), and positive reframing (n = 1), and a reliable increase was observed for self‐compassion (n = 1).

A total of 11 participants completed the questions on user experience. Overall, the quality of the course was rated as excellent by 9.1% of participants and as good by 90.9% of the participants. Furthermore, 18.2% of participants rated the quality as more than adequate, while 81.8% rated it as adequate.

Overall satisfaction with the intervention was rated at 7.8 (SD = .40, range: 7.0–8.0). The extent to which the intervention fulfilled participant's wishes was rated at 7.5 (SD = .82, range 6.0–9.0), willingness to recommend the course to other clients was rated at 8.5 (SD = .93, range = 7.0–10.0), and the extent to which the course helped participants better cope with their problems was rated at 7.8 (SD = 1.08, range = 6.0–9.0).

This multiple‐baseline single‐case experimental design (SCED) study examined the effects of an innovative group compassion‐based positive psychology intervention (CB‐PPI) in 12 patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD). Findings demonstrated significant improvements in depressive symptoms, adaptive capacity, and positive skills (gratitude, savouring, self‐compassion, and positive reframing) from baseline to follow‐up on weekly assessments. No significant changes were observed for anxiety symptoms and psychological wellbeing on weekly measures. Comprehensive questionnaires, however, indicated significant improvements in overall mental, emotional, and psychological wellbeing, as well as in positive reframing and savouring from pre‐ to post‐intervention, and in psychological wellbeing from pre‐intervention to follow‐up at group level. Therewith, these results were inconsistent across methods. At individual level, reliable changes following the intervention were observed across several outcomes, including ability to adapt, mental, emotional, and social wellbeing, self‐compassion, anxiety and depression. However, the direction and occurrence of reliable changes varied across these outcome measures and time points, with both reliable increases and decreases observed. Thus, the reliable change findings provide indications of individual‐level change but do not point to a consistent pattern of improvement across outcomes. Furthermore, user experiences showed that participants were positive about the intervention, which was evaluated as adequate and good.

CB‐PPI is a transdiagnostic group intervention combining positive psychology and compassion‐based approaches. The group CB‐PPI was specifically developed to enhance adaptation and promote positive mental health in individuals facing somatic or mental health challenges. Its effectiveness in improving positive mental health and personal recovery has been demonstrated in patients with bipolar disorder (Kraiss et al., ).

The present findings suggest that group CB‐PPI may enhance mental wellbeing in patients with CVD, although results were mixed. Significant improvements were observed on comprehensive questionnaire measures but not on weekly brief assessments of psychological wellbeing. Mental wellbeing is a key healthcare outcome, reflecting an individual's capacity to experience joy, meaning, and connectedness despite somatic or mental health conditions (Bohlmeijer & Westerhof, ). Higher mental wellbeing is consistently associated with reduced short‐ and long‐term risk of mental disorders (Keyes et al., ; Schotanus‐Dijkstra, ten Have, et al., ; ten Klooster et al., ; Wood & Joseph, ). Findings of the current study are consistent with prior research demonstrating the benefits of PPIs in CVD populations. For example, Huffman et al. () developed the PEACE programme, which combines gratitude‐, strengths‐ and meaning‐based exercises with motivational interviewing and reported improvements in psychological outcomes among patients with heart disease (Celano et al., ). In addition, a recent meta‐analysis by Tönis et al. () reported small to moderate effect sizes for mental wellbeing across twenty studies evaluating PPIs in CVD patients. In the current study, significant interaction effects of group were found for psychological wellbeing on the comparison between the baseline and intervention phase, as well as between baseline and follow‐up phase. These differences between groups in weekly psychological wellbeing may reflect variation in professional guidance, as the first group was led by two experienced psychologists, while the second group was led by only one due to unforeseen medical circumstances.

Weekly measures showed a significant reduction in depressive symptoms from baseline to follow‐up, aligning with prior studies on PPIs in clinical populations (Chakhssi et al., ), including those with CVDs (Tönis et al., ). PPIs may influence depressive symptoms through various pathways, such as positive reinterpretation related to themselves, an increase in adaptive capacity, a faster focus on positive events and a reduced focus on the negative ones, or a more positive view of oneself and thereby a reduction in negatively biased self‐referential thoughts (Bohlmeijer, ). However, these potential processes of change are theoretically driven and therefore require future empirical support.

In addition to mental health outcomes, this study examined potential mechanisms underlying CB‐PPI, including gratitude, savouring, self‐compassion, and positive reframing. Significant increases from baseline to follow‐up in weekly measures were observed for these skills, suggesting that participants developed these capacities through the intervention.

Savouring and gratitude can be seen as core components of PPIs and are specifically designed to enhance positive emotions (Bohlmeijer, ). Positive emotions are particularly relevant in the context of somatic illness, as they have been shown to buffer stress, improve coping, and promote psychological resilience in various samples (Folkman, ; Sewart et al., ). According to the broaden‐and‐build theory (Fredrickson, ), positive emotions broaden individuals' momentary thought–action repertoires and build enduring psychological, social, and physical resources. Upward spirals of positive emotions may foster engagement in adaptive coping, and adaptive coping may foster positive emotions (Fredrickson & Joiner, ). This indicates that upward spirals of positive emotions may help counterbalance illness‐related distress. Positive reframing (or reappraisal) reflects the capacity to reinterpret stressful or adverse experiences in a more constrictive or meaningful way, such as a learning opportunity (Lambert et al., ). Positive reframing has been found to be associated with resilience in a meta‐analysis (Stover et al., ) and may function as a moderator in the relationship between stressful situations and depressive symptoms (Riepenhausen et al., ; Troy et al., ). This skill is particularly relevant for individuals with CVD, who often face persistent uncertainty, functional limitations, and lifestyle changes. Research has shown that positive reappraisal as a coping strategy is associated with enhanced psychological health in chronic disease patients and illness self‐management (e.g., HIV patients; Finkelstein‐Fox et al., ).

Compared to earlier PPIs for patients with CVDs, CB‐PPI places a stronger emphasis on self‐compassion. Self‐compassion is particularly relevant in the context of severe somatic disorders such as CVDs, as it can promote self‐regulation by reducing defensiveness, self‐criticism, and emotional states that interfere with self‐regulation, while increasing engagement in self‐care, health‐promoting behaviours, and adherence to medical recommendations (Sirois et al., ; Sirois & Hirsch, ; Terry & Leary, ). Empirical evidence for compassion‐based interventions in CVD populations remains emerging but promising. Studies have reported improvements in emotion regulation (Bronsi et al., ; Izanloo et al., ) and reductions in anxiety and depression (Adibizadeh & Sajjadian, ), suggesting potential feasibility and psychological benefits, although systematic reviews indicate that the overall evidence is still limited and heterogeneous (Austin et al., ; Kılıç et al., ; Tönis et al., ). The present findings contribute to this growing literature by suggesting that self‐compassion may be a relevant mechanism of change within integrative interventions such as the group CB‐PPI evaluated in this current study.

The current study also demonstrated significant improvements in adaptive capacity in weekly measures from baseline to follow‐up. Adaptive capacity refers to the ability to respond flexibly to life events and daily challenges (Franken et al., ) and has been proposed as a core component of sustainable mental health (Bohlmeijer & Westerhof, ; Kloos et al., ; Wang et al., ). Within this framework, gratitude, savouring, self‐compassion, and positive reframing can be conceptualized as internal psychological resources that support adaptive capacity and mental wellbeing. Adaptive capacity is related to concepts such as sense of coherence (SoC) and general self‐efficacy (Surtees et al., ; Yang et al., ). SoC refers to a enduring but dynamic perception that life is comprehensible, manageable, and meaningful (Antonovsky, ). A strong SoC has been associated with better mental health outcomes (Posadzki & Glass, ), potentially as it enables faster adaptation when experiencing adverse events (Surtees et al., ). Similarly, general self‐efficacy, one's perceived capacity to successfully manage challenging situations is proposed to be linked to coping strategy use (Bandura, ) and found to be associated with better functioning, i.e., higher levels of quality of life (van Hof et al., ). Conceptually, adaptive capacity overlaps with these constructs, as all reflect the ability to effectively manage stress and maintain functioning under adversity.

Across outcomes, weekly measures predominantly showed improvements during the follow‐up phase rather than during the intervention phase. This pattern suggests that the benefits of group CB‐PPI may require time to consolidate and become manifest in daily functioning. This finding aligns with those of Nikrahan et al. (), who found significant between‐group differences at follow‐up but not at post‐intervention for depression, happiness and hope after a 6 week group PPI for patients with a cardiac disease. However, a systematic review on PPIs for patients with a CVD showed significant effects for distress and mental wellbeing at both post‐intervention and follow‐up (Tönis et al., ). Compassion‐focused interventions target the development of new affective and self‐regulatory capacities by strengthening the affiliative/soothing affect system and reducing self‐criticism and shame, a motivational and emotion‐regulation shift rather than a direct suppression of symptoms or enhancement of wellbeing (Gilbert, ). Because these underlying cognitive–affective systems are often underdeveloped, changes may require time and consolidated practice before becoming apparent (Gilbert & Procter, ). This can create a temporal lag between the initial training period and observable clinical outcomes. Additionally, early in training, increased awareness of difficult affect, such as grief, and fears of compassion can transiently elevate distress or slow immediate gains, even as the capacity for self‐soothing and self‐kindness begins to grow (Kirby, ). Over time, changes in affect regulation and self‐relating processes tend to become more stable and generalized, resulting in amplified improvements at follow‐up. Importantly for SCED designs, this pattern suggests that intervention effects may not peak during the intervention phase but may instead emerge during follow‐up, making longitudinal or repeated measurement essential for capturing the full course of change. Future research could further study the underlying mechanisms by directly assessing the three emotion regulation systems (i.e., soothing, threating, and drive system) using recently developed measures, such as the digital Three Circles Scale (Moloney‐Gibb et al., , ).

Furthermore, the current findings align with those of a mixed‐methods case study (Tönis et al., ), which reported a reliable increase in adaptive capacity and self‐compassion at 2 month follow‐up, after an initial decrease of adaptive capacity and mental wellbeing from pre‐ to post‐intervention. This indicates that interventions based on positive psychology and compassion may require time to consolidate in patients with CVD; however, the mixed findings of the timing of effects require further research on the specific timing of change.

First, SCEDs have limited external and internal validity due to the absence of a control group. Randomized controlled trials are recommended to more robustly evaluate the effectiveness of a group CB‐PPI in patients with CVD.

Second, participants could withdraw without providing a reason in line with ethical guidelines, limiting insights into dropout causes and potential barriers to participation. One participant discontinued after feeling sufficiently skilled, illustrating that withdrawal does not necessarily indicate negative outcomes. This finding aligns with the argument by Bente et al. () that adherence to newly acquired skills may be more important than adherence to the intervention itself, indicating that dropout is not always an indicator of a negative outcome of an intervention.

Third, follow‐up was limited to 2 months post‐intervention; longer‐term effects remain unknown. Future research should include extended follow‐up periods (e.g., 6 months or longer) to assess durability of effects.

This SCED provides preliminary evidence that CB‐PPI offered in a group format may support patients with CVD in developing positive skills such as gratitude, savouring, self‐compassion, and positive reframing, enhancing adaptive capacity, and reducing depressive symptoms. Findings on psychological wellbeing were mixed across outcome measures and time points. More research is needed to confirm these findings, clarify mechanisms of change, and determine optimal implementation in cardiovascular care.

psychology.title: Interventions to prevent suicide and suicidal thoughts or behaviours in the perinatal period: a global mixed-methods systematic review
psychology.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of maternal death during the perinatal period. While routine enquiry and identification is widely recommended, evidence on comprehensive interventions remains limited. This review evaluated global evidence on the effectiveness of interventions for perinatal suicide, associated thoughts and behaviours, and key implementation features.We conducted a mixed-methods systematic review using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. We searched eight databases and other sources from inception to December 3, 2025, for global evidence across all income settings without language restrictions. We included studies evaluating interventions, programmes or strategies reporting on our primary outcome: perinatal suicide or suicidal thoughts or behaviours (including ideation, self-harm, attempts) during pregnancy or one year after birth. Data were extracted and appraised for methodological quality. Meta-analysis was not possible due to clinical and methodological heterogeneity; data were synthesised using a convergent integrated approach. PROSPERO: CRD42025625903.We screened 27,045 records; 19 records representing nine studies were included: three randomised controlled trials, one secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial, one non-randomised controlled trial, one quasi-experimental study, one cross-sectional descriptive study, one economic modelling, and one qualitative study. Studies were conducted between 2011 and 2025 in North America, Europe and Asia and included 3613 participants from at risk or disadvantaged populations across eight studies, plus a simulated cohort of 1000. We found trials of indirect clinical interventions targeting parenting or attachment did not reduce suicidality, whereas task-shared behavioural activation psychotherapy targeting depressive drivers, was associated with an 80% reduction in odds of suicidal ideation at three months in a secondary trial analysis. System or community-level strategies in three trials and the modelling were associated with reduced suicide or suicidal ideation by integrating routine screening within multidisciplinary pathways that ensured immediate linkage to care. Informal or crisis support mechanisms facilitated immediate access and worked as protective buffers against self-harm in two feasibility and qualitative studies; faith practices helped counter barriers to formal care while helplines remained limited by them.Our results suggest that suicide prevention could be improved by embedding routine identification within coordinated health and community safety nets ensuring immediate linkage to care. Expanding evidence-based psychological care and task-sharing targeting depressive drivers of suicidality may help at-risk women receive timely support. Future research explicitly designed and powered for perinatal suicide prevention is needed.The 10.13039/501100000272National Institute for Health and Care Research.
psychology.text:
Suicide is a leading cause of mortality during pregnancy and in the first year after childbirth (the perinatal period), accounting for 20% of global postpartum deaths.,  It is also a leading cause of death among women of reproductive age, with 132,000 deaths of women aged 15–49 years occurring globally in 2023. Suicidal ideation, defined as thoughts of ending one's own life, affects an estimated 8% of individuals globally during the perinatal period,  and predicts later suicidal behaviour including attempted suicide and suicide. In the United States, suicidal ideation during the perinatal period increased by 100% between 2008 and 2018, with wide ethnic disparities including a disproportionate 700% increase among Black individuals. Sub-Saharan African countries face suicidal ideation rates of 15–33% among perinatal individuals, nearly triple those in Western Europe or Australia. Recent UK data further underscore this crisis, with a 55% increase in postpartum ideation reported since the COVID-19 pandemic., ,  Beyond the immediate loss of life, perinatal suicide carries a significant burden to families and societies, impacting child development and generating an intergenerational cycle of psychiatric morbidity. Addressing this public health crisis is central to Sustainable Development Goal 3.4, which aims to reduce premature mortality and promote mental health and wellbeing globally.

To date, research on perinatal suicide has historically focused on estimating prevalence and identifying risk factors. Mental disorders, including severe psychotic disorders and common mental disorders (e.g., depression and anxiety) are among the most common complications in childbirth, affecting nearly one in five perinatal individuals, and when poorly managed, are associated with worse outcomes. Although the presence of mental disorders is among the strongest predictors of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, risk is multifaceted and influenced by a range of interacting factors. These include trauma (e.g., childhood abuse, intimate partner violence, conflict), socioeconomic disadvantage (e.g., young age, poverty, low education, Black ethnicity), and psychosocial stressors (e.g., stress, social isolation, drug misuse, sleep deprivation, death of close person)., , , ,  While understanding the epidemiology and risk factors for perinatal suicide is essential, urgent public health action is needed to address what remains a leading contributor to maternal mortality. Advances in both pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments for perinatal mental disorders have improved identification and management of mental health disorders in the perinatal period. However, evidence on effective strategies to prevent suicide among perinatal populations remains limited and this has also been highlighted in England's latest suicide prevention strategy which includes pregnant women and new mothers as a priority group. Maternal health systems have a unique, often lost opportunity to intervene during pregnancy and the first year after childbirth, as women are in frequent contact with health services for both themselves and their children. And given the drivers for perinatal suicide extend beyond the presence of mental disorder alone, there is a need for targeted evidence-based, holistic approaches that also align with the World Health Organisation's guideline for integration of perinatal mental health into maternal and child health services.,

Suicide is frequently considered within a broader continuum of suicidal thoughts and behaviour, ranging from suicidal ideation and planning to suicide attempts and death. This continuum reflects the complex and interacting social, structural, and individual determinants that shape suicide risk over time. Suicide prevention frameworks often therefore adopt a public health approach, recognising the need for coordinated action across multiple levels, including universal population strategies, selective interventions for groups at increased risk, and indicated interventions for individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts or behaviours. Within these frameworks, outcomes such as suicidal ideation, self-harm, and suicide attempts represent earlier stages along the pathway to suicide and are therefore important targets for prevention research. Since suicide is a relatively rare outcome, research evaluating prevention strategies often examined this broader spectrum of suicidal thoughts and behaviours. However, it remains unclear how such prevention approaches have been applied within the perinatal period or how effective they are for this population. We therefore aimed to evaluate interventions, programmes, and strategies reporting prevention or reduction of suicide and suicidal thoughts or behaviours during the perinatal period, and identify key features associated with effective prevention and the reduction of inequalities.

A global mixed-methods systematic review was undertaken to assess the effect of existing interventions for prevention or reduction of suicide, and suicidal thoughts and behaviours (including suicidal ideation, self-harm, and suicide attempts) during the perinatal period (e.g., pregnancy to one year postpartum), and identify key features and components that might contribute to effective implementation. Anticipating a scarcity of trials directly addressing perinatal suicide and need to explore implementation factors, we followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological guidance for the conduct of mixed-methods systematic reviews, which allows for the combination of evidence from quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies into a single cohesive narrative considering limited evidence in this field. This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025625903) and followed PRISMA reporting guidelines.

In this global review, we assessed studies that reported any intervention on perinatal suicide or suicidal thoughts and behaviours. A preliminary search of PROSPERO, PubMed and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews found no existing or in progress such a review. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Global Health, PsycINFO, Web of Science, ASSIA, CINAHL and CENTRAL from inception to December 3, 2025. We did not include any country or language restrictions. Our search strategy combined a comprehensive list of maternal suicide and suicidality related terms (see ). We also hand-searched bibliography and reference lists of the studies identified and other reviews, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, relevant websites, national and international reports and guidelines and dissertations and thesis; Google Scholar, Open Grey, the ISRCTN registry, and the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry.

Studies were eligible if they evaluated an intervention, programme or strategy delivered during pregnancy or up to one year postpartum, and reported outcomes (whether primary or secondary) related to suicide or suicidal thoughts and behaviours. Given that suicide is a rare outcome in intervention studies, and is often conceptualised as a spectrum of thoughts and behaviours, we adopted a broad outcomes framework. Therefore, studies reporting on suicide, suicide attempts, self-harm or suicidal ideation were eligible for inclusion. Quantitative measures of these outcomes included event rates (e.g., incidence of self-harm, suicide), effect estimates (e.g., odds ratios, 95% CIs), and validated measures of suicidal ideation (e.g., scores >0 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS] Item 10 ‘The thought of harming myself has occurred to me’). For qualitative and mixed-methods evidence, outcome data comprised verbatim participant reports, implementation features, and perceived protective mechanisms against self-harm. Studies were included regardless of their study design; restricting the review to trials alone might have excluded potentially relevant studies (e.g., system/population-level, target trial emulation and economic modelling, which are valuable for projecting population-level impacts given the rarity of perinatal suicide as a primary outcome in traditional trials). We excluded studies if they only reported prevalence rates, studied risk factors without an intervention, presented no intervention or did not report on suicide or suicide thoughts or behaviours (see  for detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria). We did not include interventions targeting women before pregnancy or beyond one year postpartum, All records were uploaded to Covidence software and duplicates removed. Titles, abstracts, and full texts (including associated secondary and exploratory papers) were screened by two independent reviewers (CFT, YDE, KDB, AE) and discrepancies were resolved by consensus or referred to a third reviewer.

We developed and piloted a data extraction form covering six broad areas: 1) characteristics of study type and settings country, year, design including randomised trial, quasi or non-randomised trial, quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods, primary aim, setting (community, healthcare institutions, industry) and ethics; 2) the description of study participants, including inclusion and exclusion criteria, total numbers, mean age, ethnicity, timing, marital status, education and socio-economic status, pre-existing medical or mental health conditions and other lifestyle/health behaviours such us substance misuse, physical/sexual abuse or previous suicide attempts; 3) descriptions of interventions (and comparison if any) and its components such as what was provided, who provided it, how and where it was delivered, and the dosage or frequency; 4) description of outcome measures (effect size, numbers, percentages, quotes); 5) description of how the intervention may work (theory of change); 6) and descriptions of intervention challenges and strategies, with a blank field for other details that were deemed relevant to perinatal suicide. The data extraction form also integrated the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) to assess methodological quality of any study type concurrently with data collection. JBI and MMAT guidelines discourage the provision of numerical quality scores and instead recommend a narrative summary. The extraction template and raw extraction data are included in . Each extraction was carried out independently by two reviewers (CFT, YDE). A third reviewer (KDB) selected a random sample of extracted data to ensure accuracy and harmonisation.

After data extraction and appraisal, studies underwent further review to discuss the possibility of a meta-analysis to assess the effect of the interventions on maternal suicide and suicidality, but this was not possible given the significant heterogeneity in study designs, interventions and outcomes. We specifically evaluated the feasibility of performing a meta-analysis across four studies reporting suicidal ideation via EPDS Item 10., , ,  However, quantitative pooling was not possible due to substantial clinical, methodological, and design heterogeneity (see ). Therefore, we used the JBI's convergent integrated approach to synthetise findings across all study designs. This approach was chosen because both the quantitative data (effectiveness) and qualitative data (implementation processes) addressed our review objective: understanding what works and why. Consequently, data were not segregated into separate summaries, but integrated thematically based on similarity of meaning. Quantitative data regarding suicide and suicidal ideation and behaviour were extracted independently by two reviewers. To ensure comparability with qualitative evidence, we performed ‘qualitisation’, wherein numerical results were systematically converted into narrative, textual statements describing the intervention's effectiveness, while retaining all underlying numerical and statistical metrics (e.g., percentages, odds ratios, 95% CIs, p-values) to preserve complete data granularity. This process was supported by a data conversion table () which provides an audit trail mapping statistical results to these descriptive statements. Qualitative data, including implementation features, experiences and theories of change, were synthesised using thematic synthesis. Following the initial independent synthesis of the qualitative and qualitised quantitative streams, we integrated these data through a repeated, detailed examination of the pooled findings. We identified key categories based on similarity of meaning, allowing us to combine quantitative evidence of effectiveness with qualitative evidence regarding what works and why (implementation features and theory of change). These categories were finally aggregated into overall integrated findings to address the aim of the review (see synthesis matrix of this integration in ).

As this study is a systematic review of publicly available published literature, ethics approval and participant informed consent were not required.

The funder had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, writing of the report, or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.

The searches produced 27,045 records, of which 4594 were removed as duplicates. A total of 22,451 records were screened by title and abstract, and 97 full-text articles. Nineteen records representing nine studies were included., , , , , , , ,  All studies were published between 2011 and 2025 and represented a mix of high- and low-income settings and included a wide variety of methods. Three randomised controlled trials were conducted in Europe (Germany, the UK, France),, ,  one secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial in the US and Canada, one non-randomised controlled trial in Japan, one cross-sectional descriptive study in India; and three additional studies in the USA: one quasi-experimental cross-sectional study, a hypothetical economic modelling study and a qualitative study.
 summarises the search results and screening process,  reports the characteristics of included studies (detailed further in ), and a dedicated summary of studies reporting suicidal ideation via EPDS Item 10 is provided in . Eight studies included a total of 3613 participants, with an additional simulated cohort of 1000 individuals from the hypothetical economic model and often targeted at risk and disadvantaged populations. Three studies specifically included women based on clinical risks of severity: women discharged from a psychiatric mother and baby unit with severe illness (e.g., psychosis or bipolar disorder), women with scores greater than nine or ten on the EPDS indicating probable depression or high emotional distress,,  or women identified with clinically significant level psychopathology and bonding difficulties. Other studies focused on socioeconomic disadvantage, including Black and Latina women, low-income women eligible for Medicaid,  or women with multiple social risks such as low education, single parenthood, and immigrant status. The studies varied widely in intervention scope, provider, delivery method and its theory of change, as well as measurement and reporting of perinatal suicide and suicidality, and implementation features, but synthesis integration identified three broad categories based on how interventions were intended to work: 1) system or community level strategies, 2) clinical and digital interventions, and 3) informal or accessible crisis support systems. These categories served a pragmatic organisational purpose for this review, and rather than indicating mutually exclusive categories, they operated as complementary, integrated parts of the care pathway. While system or community strategies largely provided the essential architecture to reach and care for women, the clinical and digital interventions represented the therapeutic content itself.

Three studies (two trials and one quasi-experimental) evaluated system-level or community-wide strategies designed to identify women who scored highly on the EPDS with clear referral and management pathways., ,  These interventions aimed to improve identification of mental health risk thorough routine enquiry and defined referral and treatment pathway, and were underpinned by medical and public health models, hypothesising that increasing detection rates via universal enquiry would only reduce symptom severity and mortality risk if aligned with defined pathways to professional care. A comprehensive community-wide initiative in the US trained >500 health and social care providers in detection, enquiry and case ascertainment protocols while establishing a specialist clinic for complex cases which resulted in a statistically significant reduction in the frequency of women reporting suicidal thoughts (defined based on score >0 on EPDS Item 10) from 7.1% in the baseline cohort to 3.5% post-intervention. The Nagano trial in Japan, included a program integrating routine mental health screening by public health nurses, case management, and multidisciplinary clinical networks and found a significantly lower suicidal ideation (EPDS Item 10 > 0) in the intervention group compared to the control group (usual postnatal care with standard home visits without specific mental health screening protocols) at 3–4 months postpartum (4.3% vs 11.5% respectively; p = 0.014), although differences were not significant at 7–8 months (p = 0.111). Meanwhile, the economic modelling study of a US Medicaid population projected that routine EPDS use in outpatient settings followed by psychiatrist-mentored pharmacotherapy or interpersonal therapy would be cost-effective, potentially preventing 0.24 suicides per 1000 women compared to usual care. A key implementation finding across these studies was the importance of effective gatekeepers; screening was only successful when supported by a functional multidisciplinary network able to receive referrals, ensuring women identified as at risk did not fall through the net.

Three trials and a secondary analysis of a trial assessed clinical and digital interventions, including skills-based and psychotherapeutic approaches designed to address individual psychopathology and parenting needs., , ,  Unlike system- or community-level interventions, these were time-limited, curriculum-based programmes grounded in attachment theory, ecological models, or cognitive behavioural principles. Two trials focused on parenting and attachment skills: a 10-week attachment-informed group programme (Circle of Security-Parenting) delivered online and face-to-face by trained psychologists in the UK, and a high-intensity home-visiting programme (CAPEDP) by psychologists from pregnancy through the child's second birthday in France; and found no reductions in suicidality compared to the control group (standard care tailored to clinical needs, which could include e.g. home-based visits, psychiatric reviews, psychological therapies, parent–infant interventions). The UK trial reported 11 (3%) adverse events involving ‘self-harm or concerns about self-harm’, which were higher in the intervention group compared to treatment-as-usual (9 vs 2 respectively) and the France trial reported ‘no suicide attempts’ in either group. Similarly, a digital mindfulness and CBT application (‘mindmom’) monitored remotely by study staff to target pregnancy-related anxiety in Germany and reported no significant differences in suicidal ideation (EPDS Item 10 > 0) between the intervention and a control group receiving treatment-as-usual alongside a restricted version of the study app (limited to generic pregnancy reading) (6.3% vs 11.5%; χ2 = 2.49, p = 0.11). In contrast, the secondary analysis of the SUMMIT trial of task sharing and Behavioural Activation (BA), a psychotherapy targeting avoidance and hopelessness, significantly reduced suicidality: the odds of endorsing suicidal ideation decreased by 25% with each additional session (odds ratio [OR], 0.75; 95% CI, 0.58–0.96; p = 0.03) and by 80% at 3 months post randomisation (OR 0.20; 95% CI, 0.14–0.27; p < 0.001). The effect did not differ between specialist (psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers) and non-specialist providers (nurses, midwives, doulas) or between in-person and telemedicine delivery, though this trial was limited by the use of four active comparators (comparing specialists and delivery methods) without a non-intervention control group. Both specialist and non-specialist providers received the same competency-based training and were assessed by standardised assessments, with clear clinical safety and escalation protocols. Although attrition remained a challenge across this category, the digital mindfulness app saw a 38% dropout rate and the home-visiting programme reported 50% missing data by 18 months.,  Retention was high in the BA trial (91% analysed), suggesting that brief, focused psychotherapies delivered by non-specialists via telemedicine are acceptable. However, although task-sharing facilitates access, it should be embedded within escalation processes, as some non-responders with complex trauma required more intensive care.

Finally, two smaller studies (quantitative descriptive and qualitative) examined informal or accessible crisis support systems, designed to overcome barriers to mental health care and grounded in accessibility and biopsychosocial-spiritual frameworks, with one study suggesting that spiritual beliefs could actively support emotion regulation and function as cognitive tools preventing self-harm. In India, a 24-h mobile helpline managed by a psychiatric social worker for women with severe mental illness discharged from a mother-baby unit was found to be feasible and used specifically for “help to deal with suicidal ideation” during two of the 248 calls (0.8%). Implementation barriers to technology and gender inequalities were reported to be fatal a woman at risk died by suicide after being unable to access the helpline because she did not own a mobile phone, despite her family having the number. Qualitative findings from the USA identified faith as a perceived protective coping mechanism that may buffer suicide risk and support emotional regulation, particularly among women experiencing barriers to formal mental healthcare and African American and Latina mothers. Faith functioned both as an immediate coping strategy through prayer and as a protective mechanism through beliefs that suicide was contrary to God's will preventing self-harm (“I know if I was to hurt myself, I could not ask God for forgiveness”), while also providing sometimes rapid symptom relief (“There was never a day where that praying did not work… all of a sudden your spirit just lift up”).

Overall methodological quality across the included studies was variable. Among the three primary randomised controlled trials,, ,  all reported robust randomisation and allocation concealment procedures. Blinding of participants was not feasible due to the nature of the interventions (smartphone app or parenting group), though outcome assessor blinding was achieved in two trials.,  High attrition was a notable risk of bias, with 36%–50% missing data reported in the digital mindfulness and home-visiting trials.,  Across these three trials, suicidality was tracked solely as an adverse event or safety monitoring metric rather than a prespecified primary efficacy endpoint. Adherence was also variable; the parenting trial reported a mean attendance of 64% (6.4 out of 10 sessions). In the secondary analysis of the SUMMIT trial, participant blinding to intervention arm and outcome assessor blinding were both achieved and data completeness was high (91% analysed), but the reported 80% reduction in suicidal ideation (measured as a secondary outcome) was derived using available observed data rather than an intention-to-treat analysis. While it lacked a non-intervention control arm, a significant dose–response effect was established, with suicidality decreasing by 25% with each additional session attended.

Among the non-randomised study and the quasi-experimental study and the descriptive cross-sectional study, all included representative target samples, with suicidal ideation evaluated as a primary outcome in the non−randomised trial and a secondary outcome in the quasi-experimental study. However, methodological limitations included the absence of baseline data in an abstract-only report, potential temporal confounding due to seasonal variation in birth cohorts (potentially influencing depressive symptoms), and risk of non-response bias where 33% of the target population was lost to follow-up. The economic modelling study could not be formally appraised as its projections were based on a simulated hypothetical cohort derived from literature rather than empirical trial data. In contrast, the qualitative study, despite its small sample, it demonstrated methodological quality with clear coherence between the theoretical framework, data collection, and qualitative interpretation.

This global mixed-methods systematic review evaluated the effects of existing interventions on perinatal suicide and suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and identified key features associated with their implementation. Nine studies, using diverse methodologies and conducted in Europe, North America, and Asia between 2011 and 2025 were included. Target populations largely comprised of women with identifiable risk factors, defined by clinical severity (discharge from psychiatric units, positive scores for distress on psychometric scales) or by socioeconomic disadvantage (poverty, minority ethnic group, immigrant status). Across studies, three broad and complementary categories were identified: system or community-level strategies, clinical or digital interventions, and informal or accessible crisis support. System and community level strategies that combined routine enquiry with structured referral and management pathways showed potential for reducing suicidal thoughts or ideation. Clinical and digital interventions targeting more indirect factors such as attachment, parenting or birth anxiety showed limited effect, whereas targeted psychotherapies addressing depressive symptoms showed greater potential for reducing suicidal thoughts. Informal or accessible crisis support mechanisms, including mobile helplines and faith-based practices, provided immediate, accessible and culturally relevant forms of crisis management and self-harm reduction. The mechanisms by which these interventions were meant to work varied from early detection and referral to care, skills-based and psychotherapeutic approaches grounded in attachment, ecological, and cognitive behavioural theories, and improved emotional regulation and barriers to help-seeking.

The core component in system and community level strategies was not detection alone, but the integration of risk identification with structured referral and management pathways that ensured rapid access to care. These interventions showed the greatest potential for reducing suicidality when detection was embedded within a multidisciplinary safety net. The US community-wide initiative and the Japanese suicide prevention programmes established clear clinical networks linking trained gatekeepers (e.g., public health nurses, social workers) to specialist psychiatric care, reducing provider uncertainty and loss to follow-up among women at risk.,  The economic modelling similarly indicated that risk identification might only be lifesaving and cost-effective when linked to timely treatment initiation. These findings align with the concept of safety netting in health systems, which uses overlapping layers of clinical, social, and structural protection to prevent patients at high risk from falling through gaps in care; and reinforces evidence that a strong safety culture and active multidisciplinary feedback loops are vital to reduce maternity mortality. By shifting from routine enquiry and risk identification alone, to an integrated safety net, such approaches address siloed working, poor communication, and fragmented follow-up, all key contributors to perinatal suicide. This direction is reflected in NHS England's recent Maternal Care Bundle and the WHO perinatal mental health framework, both of which advocate integrated, community-based models with shared responsibility for risk management.,

Findings from the clinical and digital trials found a clear distinction in intervention targets. Standardised psychological interventions focussing on broader constructs, such as maternal sensitivity, anxiety, parenting or attachment (e.g., Circle of Security-Parenting, mindfulness, home visiting) did not reduce suicidal ideation. These programmes faced implementation challenges, including high attrition and suicide was indeed monitored only as an adverse event rather than addressed as a clinical outcome., ,  This aligns with evidence suggesting that indirect interventions without a specific, targeted suicide-prevention focus do not appear to independently reduce suicidal thoughts. However, the recent task-sharing and BA trial, which directly addressed avoidance and hopelessness, showed significant reductions in suicidal ideation. In contrast to the parenting and attachment focused interventions identified in this review, BA provides specific tools to disrupt the depressive cycle and may reduce suicide risk by increasing values consistent living and awareness of unhelpful behaviours. A recent review highlighted indeed the transdiagnostic potential of BA, emotion regulation, and cognitive restructuring as core mechanisms for perinatal mental health interventions. In the BA trial, non-specialists delivered the intervention as effectively as trained specialists, aligning with global evidence on the scalability of task-shared treatments for perinatal mental health including the Lancet Commission on Global Mental Health and WHO guidance on integrated perinatal mental health services., ,  And such competency-based training protocols are not limited to this single trial but are successfully leveraged across broader task-sharing platforms globally to build mental health capacity. These findings do not suggest that parenting or attachment based interventions are unimportant, but rather that interventions seeking to reduce suicidal thoughts may require an explicit focus on the mechanisms underpinning suicidality, alongside broader support for the mother-infant relationship.

An interesting finding of this review is the potential role of informal or accessible crisis support systems to bridging the gap to care for populations facing structural barriers, although evidence was limited to two smaller studies. Qualitative findings showed how faith and church participation could function as a protective mechanism to suicide among ethnic minority groups who may distrust formal systems. Several studies indicate a protective association between religiosity or spirituality and depression or suicide risk in the general population, partly mediated through social support, with emerging evidence suggesting lower perinatal anxiety and depressive symptoms among those engaging in faith practices.,  However, no studies have directly assessed this relationship or the impact of faith or organised religious participation on perinatal suicide. Similarly, the 24-h helpline shows the potential of using remote connections for crisis management, providing women had safe access to a mobile phone. However, if this support system is not readily accessible in a crisis, the protective mechanism fails. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence that faith-based practices are clinically effective interventions for reducing suicidality. Rather, they highlight the potential role of informal, culturally relevant coping and support mechanisms that may complement evidence-based clinical care, particularly for women facing structural barriers to accessing services.

This is to our knowledge, the first mixed-methods systematic review to synthesise global interventions, strategies and programmes to prevent perinatal suicide, and related thoughts or behaviours. The main strengths of the study include the robust JBI methodology, the inclusivity of diverse study designs, interventions and outcomes across diverse settings, despite no study from Africa or Latin America, and the integration of a large trial which provides high-quality evidence on task-sharing and BA. Statistical inter-rater reliability coefficients were not calculated as per JBI, and coding alignment was managed through parallel independent extraction and consensus with a third reviewer. The heterogeneity of study designs, interventions and reported outcomes was a limitation and made a meta-analysis impossible. The inclusion of an economic modelling study, while useful for projecting potential impacts, is a limitation as its findings are based on simulated hypothetical cohorts rather than empirical participant data. Only one study in this review evaluated a direct intervention specifically designed to target suicidal thoughts and behaviours. Suicide and related thoughts or behaviours were predominantly treated as secondary outcomes of depression or parenting studies, mostly measured via proxies indicators, such as the EPDS Item 10, rather than comprehensive suicide risk assessments such as the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale; and two studies explicitly assessed perinatal suicide as adverse events. Across the four studies evaluating suicidal thoughts via EPDS Item 10, a consistent positive trend emerged. While meta-analysis was not possible due to methodological and clinical heterogeneity, both targeted psychological therapies and structured system-level referral networks showed promise in reducing the proportion of women endorsing self-harm thoughts. Consequently, our findings need to be interpreted with caution even given encouraging results from the task-sharing BA trial. The secondary analysis of the task-sharing with BA trial lacked a non-intervention control arm, limiting our ability to rule out general improvement over time, but the effectiveness of the intervention was established in the parent SUMMIT trial. Combined with the clear dose–response relationship observed in our pooled data, where each additional session attended was associated with a 25% reduction in the odds of endorsing suicidal ideation, these findings support a treatment effect.

Given the focus within clinical guidelines for managing suicidal thoughts or behaviours on dialectical behavioural approaches, the absence of such approaches in the identified interventions is surprising.,  Our study complements a recent review of the acceptability and feasibility of interventions for perinatal suicidal behaviour, which primarily focused on pharmacological treatments and excluded non-peer-reviewed studies and those where suicide was a secondary outcome; it also highlighted the importance of whole-family, trauma-informed, integrated care models. We identified several planned or ongoing trials () but future research should prioritise interventions that directly target drivers of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, use validated suicide-specific outcomes, measures self-harm and suicide attempts as well as ideation, and evaluate care models that combine system interventions with multidisciplinary safety nets and access to community support. Given suicide is a rare outcome, target trial emulations and larger-scale population-based approaches might be appropriate to investigate the effectiveness of interventions on perinatal suicide reduction. Further research on informal coping mechanisms, such as faith or community support, are needed to build culturally relevant safety plans for suicide prevention.

In a recent Lancet correspondence, Dandona and colleagues argued that maternal suicide prevention should adopt a life-course approach, integrating mental health into routine maternal care, and extending support beyond the traditional postpartum period, and improving surveillance to reduce preventable deaths and their consequences for children and families. Echoing this, our review suggests that suicide prevention likely depends on integration of mental health services and coordinated action across multiple levels, combining health and community safety nets for early identification and referral with accessible, evidence-based psychological therapies that address key drivers of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, such as depression and hopelessness. Structured community and system-level interventions and targeted psychological therapies, including tasked-shared BA, look promising. Although the BA evidence is derived from a secondary analysis of a single trial, and its success in this review relies on structured, supervised collaborative care models within well-resourced trials, and its implementation in regions with differing legislative frameworks or scarcer mental health infrastructure requires careful adaptation. Within the broader public health framework, scalable solutions may lie in embedding prevention within coordinated maternity, mental health, and community systems, strengthening multidisciplinary safety nets and expanding culturally relevant, evidence-based psychological care to ensure that women identified at risk receive timely and effective support. To ensure these safety nets are effective, systems must account for structural barriers and recognise the value of informal community coping mechanisms in bridging gaps to formal care. Ultimately, suicide prevention must be recognised as a core maternal health priority, ensuring that women are supported as whole individuals beyond their parenting roles to improve outcomes for both the mother and the surviving child.

CFT, JS and AE designed the study. CFT, YDE, KDB, AE and JS selected studies for inclusion. CFT, YDE and KDB extracted data, assessed quality and verified the underlying data. All authors (CFT, YDE, KDB, SB, HRJ, CAW, JS and AE) contributed to the analyses and interpretation of the findings. CFT drafted the manuscript and all authors commented and approved the final version of this manuscript.

All data extracted and analysed are included within this article and its  files. No additional original data were generated.
