psychology.title: Prevalence and Associations for Use of Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) Among Paediatric Cancer Patients in Norway: A Cross-Sectional Survey
psychology.abstract: In Norway, 7,400 individuals diagnosed with childhood cancer before the age of 18 are alive today, facing lasting burdens from the disease and its treatment. This study investigates the prevalence of complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) use among children with cancer in Norway, based on parental reports. It also examines the types of CAM modalities used, their perceived effects, safety, and associated demographic and cancer-related factors. An online cross-sectional survey was conducted in 2021 in collaboration with the Norwegian Children’s Cancer Society. The study utilised a modified version of the International Questionnaire to Measure Use of Complementary and Alternative Medicine (I-CAM-Q), adapted for children with cancer. Data were collected from 95 mothers and 22 fathers, covering 117 children, using convenience sampling with a response rate of 17%. Nearly half (47%, n=55) of parents reported that their children used CAM during or after cancer treatment. Modalities included vitamin D supplementation (19%, n=22), music therapy (18%, n=21), art therapy (16%, n=19), psychotherapy (9%, n=10), and massage or aromatherapy (8%, n=9). Although 82% (n = 45) of parents of children using CAM reported benefits, 7% (n = 4) reported adverse effects associated with these modalities. CAM use was primarily motivated by the burden of adverse and late effects of cancer treatment, such as fatigue (p=0.004), worry or unrest (p=0.036), and memory or concentration difficulties (p<0.001). The findings suggest that non-verbal and creative forms of support, such as massage, music therapy, and art therapy, were highly valued in this national sample. Further research is needed to better understand the unmet needs and expectations of both parents and children and to improve the quality of life for children with cancer and their families.
psychology.text:
Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) encompasses medical and health practices,

 systems, and products that are not typically recommended during conventional medicine consultations.

 In Norway, practices are considered CAM if they are primarily offered outside the public healthcare system, even though some CAM modalities, like art therapy and music therapy, are offered at Norwegian hospitals for specific patient groups.

 These modalities are mainly offered at hospitals by healthcare personnel (HCP) who are dual-trained (e.g., areas a nurse and art therapist).

Childhood cancer is a rare disease, accounting for 1–4% of all cancers globally.

 The most common types of childhood cancers include neoplasms of the blood and lymphatic systems, embryonal tumours, as well as tumours affecting the brain, bones, and connective tissues.

 Advancements in treatment have significantly improved survival rates for many childhood cancers. However, global disparities in survival well known with survival probabilities exceeding 80% in high-income countries, whereas they remain around 30% in low-income countries., Cancer remains the second leading cause of death (after accidents) among European children aged 5–14.

 In Norway, childhood cancer is the leading cause of death among children over the age of one.

 According to the Norwegian Childhood Cancer Registry, 6,746 Norwegian children and adolescents were diagnosed with cancer between 1993 and 2025, with 212 new cases reported in 2025.

 The most common types are brain tumours (30%), leukaemia (25%), lymphoma (13%), bone cancer (5%) and neuroblastoma (4%).

 With a survival rate of 90%,

 7,400 individuals in Norway were alive by the end of 2025 after being diagnosed with cancer during childhood or adolescence.

 However, four out of five of these survivors experience negative long-term effects from the cancer or its treatment.

The high survival rates, prolonged treatment durations, and burden of adverse and long-term effects make the experience profoundly challenging for both patients and their parents., Common adverse effects during and shortly after treatment include anaemia, fatigue, infections, mucositis due to immunosuppression, malnutrition, nausea, vomiting, pain, and psychosocial challenges., To help their children cope with these challenges, many parents seek additional support beyond conventional medical care.,

Norway’s conventional healthcare system follows the Nordic welfare model, which strongly subsidizes conventional medical treatments offered within the official tax-funded healthcare system with treatment free of charge for children up to 16 years of age.

 However, some supportive modalities commonly reported for children with cancer, most notably art and music therapy,

 are also routinely provided within hospital-based paediatric oncology services and are therefore available free of charge to eligible patients.

 Psychotherapy in Norway is provided within the public healthcare system by licensed psychologists, but is also offered outside the official system by CAM providers such as Gestalt therapists and coaches.

Studies conducted between 1977 and 2015, comprising 61 studies of 7,219 children from 34 countries, report that the prevalence of CAM use, including traditional medicine, among children with cancer varies between 6% and 100%., The median estimated prevalence of use was 77% in low-income countries (LIC), 60% in lower-middle income countries (LMIC), and 47% in high-income countries (HIC).

 The most commonly reported modalities were supplements, dietary changes, visits to a traditional healer, and spiritual modalities. The rationale for use was that parents wanted to do everything possible for their child by boosting the immune system, improving general well-being, and treating adverse effects from conventional cancer treatment.

In Europe, knowledge about CAM use in paediatric cancer care is limited. Since 2018, only three studies in Europe have investigated CAM use in paediatric cancer patients.- The prevalence of use ranges from 47% in France

 to 56% in the Netherlands,

 with a notably high prevalence of 69.3% reported at a Swiss paediatric haematology-oncology centre.

 The most commonly used modalities across these countries were oral supplements and homeopathy.

In Norway, two earlier studies have examined CAM use among children with cancer. A 1992 study involving 31 children estimated CAM use to be between 30% and 60%, with herbal medicines, religious practices, and dietary supplements being the most commonly reported modalities.

 A 2007 qualitative study explored CAM use among 21 families of children with cancer, highlighting the use of herbs and supplements. This study found that parents were cautious about giving herbs and supplements to their children due to concerns about potential negative interactions with conventional treatments.

 Additionally, a 2016 Norwegian study reported that 5% of parents in the general population consulted a CAM provider for their children’s health problems annually. Furthermore, 15.7% of parents gave their children supplements, herbs, or natural health products.

Given the considerable time that has elapsed since the last Norwegian study was conducted, together with the limited sample sizes of existing studies, this study aimed to explore the current prevalence of CAM use among children in Norway diagnosed with cancer, based on parent-reported information. It also examines the types of CAM modalities used, their perceived effects and safety profiles, as well as the demographic and cancer-related factors associated with CAM use.

An online cross-sectional survey was conducted throughout 2021 in collaboration with the Norwegian Children’s Cancer Society, a nationwide organisation that provides guidance and support to families who currently have, or have previously had, children with cancer. The survey targeted 700 active members and utilised the Norwegian adaptation

 of the International Questionnaire to Measure Use of Complementary and Alternative Medicine (I-CAM-Q),

 which includes separate adaptations for cancer contexts

 and for paediatric populations.

To be eligible for inclusion, participants had to be at least 18 years old, and be a parent of a child diagnosed with cancer before the age of 18 within the preceding 30 years. Only one parent per child was eligible to participate in the study. Former paediatric oncology patients who were now adults were not invited to participate, nor were other informal caregivers, such as grandparents, family members, or friends, as the study focused exclusively on parents and their child with cancer.

Participants were recruited using convenience sampling,

 a non-probability method in which respondents are selected because they are readily available. The data collection followed Dillman’s survey method, which emphasizes tailored design to maximize response rates through clear communication, multiple contact attempts, and user-friendly survey formats.

 One week before the survey was distributed, the Norwegian Children’s Cancer Society sent an email to prepare participants for the upcoming survey. The survey itself was distributed via an invitation letter containing a link to the online questionnaire, which was designed and managed using Nettskjema.no.

 Additionally, two reminder emails were sent after the initial distribution to encourage participation. The invitation was further shared with all members through three editions of the organisation’s quarterly newsletter. The Norwegian Children’s Cancer Society had approximately 1,900 registered family members; about 700 were ‘active’ at the time of the study (as defined by the Society) and were expected to receive the invitation. Because the exact number of eligible members who actually received or saw the invitation is unknown (e.g., undeliverable emails, spam filters), the response-rate denominator was treated as an estimate.

The survey link was also shared on three separate occasions in 2021 via the Facebook pages of the 13 regional local chapters of the Norwegian Children’s Cancer Society. Additionally, the investigators partnered with the childhood oncology unit at the University Hospital of Northern Norway, where informational pamphlets were distributed to parents of hospitalised children. To further enhance outreach, the survey was promoted on the social media platforms of the National Research Centre in Complementary and Alternative Medicine in Norway (NAFKAM). The survey platform did not block duplicate submissions; the final dataset was screened for duplicate or implausible entries, and none were retained in the analytic sample. As an incentive to encourage participation, respondents were offered the opportunity to enter a lottery when completed the survey. Twelve gift cards, each valued at 1,000 NOK, were randomly awarded to participants.

The questionnaire used in the survey was adapted from the Norwegian version

 of the validated International Questionnaire to Measure Use of Complementary and Alternative Medicine (I-CAM-Q).

 The previously developed cancer-specific I-CAM-Q

 served as the basis for our instrument, which was then further refined using interviews with parents of children with cancer in Norway conducted two years prior to this survey,

 and an integrative review on the information and communication needs of parents of children with cancer regarding the use of CAM., The chief adviser for scientific development at the Norwegian Children’s Cancer Society reviewed the questionnaire and provided feedback, which was incorporated into the final version of the questionnaire.

The gender of the parents and children with cancer was determined by asking the parents to identify as a woman or man and to indicate whether their child was a girl or boy. The parents’ age at the time of the survey was obtained as a continuous variable. In the analysis, the parents’ age was categorised into three groups (26-40 years, 41-50 years, and 51-62 years), representing the age span of the parents. Level of parental education was recorded using six levels: primary education (up to 10 years), upper secondary education (from 11-13 years), lower levels at university/college (up to 4 years), higher levels at university/college (more than 4 years), and don’t know, and refuse to answer. These were merged into a measure with four categories; less than 13 years of education, college/university less than 4 years, college/university 4 years or more, and refuse to answer, as none of the parents answered “don’t know.” Household income was collected using the following categories: NOK <150,000, 150,000-250,000; 251,000-350,000; 351,000-450,000; 451,000-550,000; 551,000-750,000; 751,000-1,000,000; and more than NOK 1,000,000, don’t know, and refuse to answer. These were re-categorised into low (< NOK 550,000/USD 55,000), middle (NOK 550,000 – 1,000,000/USD 55,100-100,000), high household income (>NOK 1,000,000/>USD 100,000), and refuse to answer. None of the respondents checked “don’t know.” Other personal characteristics included location (city (more than 50,000 inhabitants), town (between 10,000 and 50,000), village (less than 10,000), rural area, don’t know, and refuse to answer).

The parents were asked about their child’s cancer diagnoses (leukaemia, lymphoma, neuroblastoma, bone cancer, Wilms tumour of the kidney, soft-tissue sarcoma, retinoblastoma, germ cell tumour, other, don’t know), and which treatment the child had received (chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy, stem cell/bone marrow transplantation, antibody treatment, cancer treatment with hormones, and/or other, and don’t know). Parents were further asked to mark adverse effects experienced by the child due to cancer treatment (i.e. weakened immune system, poor appetite) while the recurrence of cancer was assessed by asking if the child had cancer again after the first time (yes/no). The child’s age when diagnosed with cancer was asked as a continuous variable and then grouped into three categories (0-5 years, 6-10 years, and 11-16 years representing the age range of the children in the study). The survey inquired about the child’s age at the time of the study as a continuous variable. If the child was no longer undergoing treatment, the age at which the child entered remission was also requested. Additionally, parents were asked to confirm if the child was still alive (yes/no), and if not, to provide the age at which the child passed away.

A Likert scale was used to measure the child’s overall health (very good, good, neither good nor bad, bad, very bad), their health compared with other children the same age (better health, similar health, poorer health, don’t know), and the extent to which cancer treatment affected the child’s cognitive development (minimally, to some extent, very much, don’t know).

For analysis we collapsed categories to improve cell sizes and support meaningful comparisons. “Overall health” was grouped as very good/good, neither good nor bad, and bad/very bad. “Health compared with others” was grouped as better/similar health, poorer health, and don’t know. Three respondents (2.6%) did not answer the overall-health item because their child had died; these responses were treated as missing.

The questionnaire measured various CAM modalities used by the children with the following question: Has the child used any of the following to help reduce health challenges resulting from cancer diagnosis or treatment? (Please mark all that apply): Provider-based therapies (acupuncture, healing, homeopathy, massage/aromatherapy, psychotherapy, reflexology); natural remedies/dietary supplements (vitamins B, C, D, and E, turmeric garlic, blueberry extract, ginger), and self-care practices (meditation, music therapy (both listening/playing), art therapy (drawing), and yoga).

Psychotherapy in Norway is offered by both licensed health professionals (psychologists) and CAM providers (e.g., gestalt therapists).

 In this paper, psychotherapy is considered part of the CAM outcomes; however, the tables also include footnotes presenting percentages of CAM use excluding psychotherapy. Additionally, as art and music therapists are not licensed HCP in Norway, their practices are classified as CAM in line with the Norwegian Act regarding alternative treatment for diseases.

For each modality or category, respondents were asked whether they had used it to address specific symptoms, such as pain, fatigue, nausea, or vomiting. Respondents were also asked to indicate whether each care modality had any impact (yes/no) and, if it had, to specify the outcome as one of the following: symptoms cured, symptoms reduced, no change, or unsure. Furthermore, for each modality used, they were asked to report whether any adverse effects were experienced (yes/no). For self-care practices, parents were asked whether these practices were used for a specific reason (yes/no) and, if so, to indicate the reasons for use (e.g., maintaining a normal routine, helping the family focus on something else, taking a break from the illness/hospital, benefiting the child, or “I don’t know”). Parents were further asked whether the CAM modalities were used during active cancer treatment (while receiving cancer treatment, e.g., chemotherapy, radiotherapy, etc), after cancer treatment (once the child ended cancer treatment), and/or during palliative care (end-of-life care received while the child was in a terminal phase).

Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used to summarize the sample characteristics and the prevalence of CAM modalities among respondents. The prevalence of CAM use was compared across groups using the Pearson chi-square test for categorical variables with larger sample sizes, and Fisher’s exact test was applied for smaller sample sizes or sparse data. For continuous variables, independent-samples t-tests and Mann–Whitney U tests were conducted. Missing data were handled using a complete-case approach: observations with missing values on variables required for a given analysis were excluded from that analysis. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 28.0.1.0, with p-values <0.05 considered statistically significant.

A total of 117 responses were received from the survey, resulting in a response rate of 17%. The respondents were parents of children with cancer, reporting on their child’s use of CAM. Of 117 respondents, 21.4% (n=25) reported that their child was still undergoing cancer treatment at the time of survey completion. Among the 89 parents whose child had completed therapy and was alive at survey completion, the recall window ranged from 0–30 years: 60.7% (n=54) completed the survey within 0–5 years after the end of their child’s therapy, 22.5% (n=20) within 6–10 years, and 16.9% (n=15) more than 10 years after end of therapy. An additional 3 parents (2.6%) reported their child had died; timing of death was not recorded. The majority of respondents were mothers (81%, n = 95), with a mean parental age of 43 years (SD = 7.98) at the time of the study (). Most parents had attended university or college (71%, n = 83), and 43% (n = 50) had completed four or more years of university education. Similarly, 43% (n = 50) of parents reported a household income exceeding NOK 1,000,000 (USD 100,000) (). More than half of the participants (58%, n = 68) lived in cities or towns. Among the children with cancer, 52% (n = 61) were female, and 61% (n = 71) were diagnosed with cancer between the ages of 0 and 5. The overall age range of diagnosis spanned from 0 to 16 years (). The most commonly reported cancer diagnoses were leukaemia (53%, n = 62) and brain cancer (15%, n = 18) (). Most children underwent chemotherapy (94%, n = 110), surgery (37%, n = 42), and/or radiotherapy (27%, n = 32). Adverse effects from conventional cancer treatment were reported for all children (100%, n = 117). A median of 8 different adverse and late effects was reported (IQR = 7), with the number of complaints ranging from 1 to 22 per child. Most frequently reported were weakened immune system (73%, n = 85), poor appetite (70%, n = 82), nausea and vomiting (70%, n = 82), pain (68%, n = 78), and fatigue (61%, n = 71). Nearly half of the parents (47%, n = 55) reported that their child utilised various CAM modalities throughout their cancer journey. Specifically, 27% (n = 31) of children used natural remedies or supplements, while 21% (n = 24) received treatment from CAM providers. Similarly, 21% (n = 24) participated in self-care practices. The number of CAM modalities used ranged from one to five, with an average of 2.15 (SD = 1.11) modalities per child (). The most frequently used CAM modalities included vitamin D supplementation (19%, n = 22), music therapy (18%, n = 21), art therapy (16%, n = 19), psychotherapy (9%, n = 10), and massage or aromatherapy (8%, n = 9) (). Vitamin D supplementation was primarily used to address issues such as poor appetite, fatigue, and a weakened immune system. Activities such as drawing and playing music were adopted not only because they were familiar within the family and surrounding environment but also because they were perceived as beneficial to the child’s health. Psychotherapy was utilised to address concerns such as worry and psychological reactions, while massage and aromatherapy were primarily employed to alleviate pain. Psychotherapy can be considered CAM in Norway, depending on the provider’s qualifications. A sensitivity analysis was conducted to account for this classification and is presented at the bottom of . Among parents reporting their child’s CAM use, 82% (n=45) reported that the modality used had an effect. Among those who found the CAM modalities effective, 53% (n = 24) indicated they reduced symptoms, 11% (n = 5) reported symptoms were cured, and 36% (n = 16) did not specify how the modalities were beneficial. However, 7.3% (n = 4) reported that their child experienced adverse effects from the CAM modalities. These events were associated with psychotherapy (n = 1), reflexology (n = 1), vitamin D (n = 1), vitamin E (n = 1), and unspecified vitamins (n = 1) (). The time associated with CAM use varied, with 70% (n = 40) of children using CAM during cancer treatment and 80% (n = 44) using CAM post treatment and (). Parents who organized CAM treatment for their children were significantly more likely to do so if their child experienced specific symptoms, such as shortness of breath (71%, n = 15), worry (62%, n = 34), fatigue (58%, n = 41), and difficulties with memory and concentration (67%, n = 31), compared to children without these symptoms (p<0.05, ). Children who used CAM had a higher adverse/late-effects index than those who did not, although the difference was not statistically significant. Children who used CAM (n = 55) had a median of 8 adverse/late effects (IQR = 10, range 1–22), compared with a median of 7 (IQR = 6, range 2–18) in children who did not use CAM (n = 62). Mann–Whitney U = 1397.5, Z = −1.685, two-tailed p = 0.092 (Monte Carlo p = 0.088, 99% CI 0.083–0.094). The rank-based effect size was small (r = 0.16), indicating a small difference in distributions.

The study found that many parents (47%, n=55) actively sought CAM to mitigate the adverse and late effects experienced by their children during (70%), as well as after (80%) anti-cancer treatment. Parents reported using CAM to address symptoms including worry and shortness of breath, as well as fatigue and difficulties with memory and concentration. Among parents whose children used CAM, 82% (n = 45) reported that the therapies were beneficial. Adverse effects associated with these modalities were reported in fewer than 8% of cases.

The findings of our study are consistent with the prevalence rates of CAM use reported among children with cancer in other high-income countries.,,- Studies conducted in Switzerland,, France,

 the Netherlands,

 and the United States

 indicate that the use of CAM in paediatric oncology patients varies broadly, with reported rates ranging from 35% to 70%.

In this study, the most frequently used CAM modalities included vitamin supplementation, art and music therapy, psychotherapy, and massage/aromatherapy. The prominent use of vitamins resonates with findings from prior research,,, which consistently highlight vitamins as a commonly chosen CAM modality in children with cancer. For instance, Sanchez et al observed that vitamins were utilised by 15% of their study’s participants.

Vitamin D deficiency is widely recognised as the most common nutritional deficiency, and studies have shown that vitamin D deficiency is more prevalent in children with haematological malignancies compared to their healthy peers.- In the present study, vitamin D was provided for 19% (n=22) of children. It was primarily used to address issues such as poor appetite, fatigue, and a weakened immune system. The importance of vitamin D in cancer pathogenesis has gained increasing recognition for its positive effects on bone health and for strengthening the immune system.

 Guidelines recommend a daily intake of 10µg to 15µg for children under the age of 18.

 Vitamin D is found in many types of fish, with the highest concentrations present in fatty fish species such as salmon, trout, mackerel, halibut, herring, and plaice. However, the frequent difficulties children with cancer face in meeting their nutritional needs

 may have contributed to the use of vitamin D to address issues related to the child’s poor appetite.

In addition to addressing physical health, our research also highlighted the importance of emotional and psychological well-being and the need for such support. We found that 18% of the children engaged in music as a way to maintain a sense of normalcy and to offer a much-needed respite from their illness and hospital stay during cancer treatment., In a qualitative study conducted by the same research team,

 music was used to strengthen family relationships and allow the children to express their emotions. For example, a participant who was a music therapist at the hospital treated a little girl who stopped talking after surgery. During a music therapy session, a week after surgery, the music therapist and the girl were looking for the girl’s voice. They found the voice inside the guitar by playing lullabies. Having found her voice, the girl started to talk again. Moreover, music therapy has been documented to enhance the overall well-being of paediatric cancer patients as well as alleviate distress, anxiety, and pain., Although no previous studies have reported on the specific prevalence of music therapy among paediatric oncology patients, there is a consensus that music therapy is widely utilised in paediatric oncology globally., Similarly, 16% of the parents in this study reported using art therapy, such as drawing, for the same reasons as playing music. Drawing provides a natural form of expression for children who may struggle to verbally articulate their thoughts and feelings.

 It has been increasingly recognized as an effective treatment for reducing depression and anxiety in children with cancer., While detailed studies on the prevalence of art and music therapy in paediatric oncology are scarce, a recent study indicated that 5.2% of Norwegian somatic hospitals offer art and expression therapy to their patients.

 In the qualitative study mentioned above,

 modalities like play, psychodrama therapy, music, and virtual reality programmes were often used for stress management, to divert the attention of children from painful procedures, treatment regimens, and the burden of having a cancer diagnosis. At the hospital, children played to process emotions, and through role-play they coped with their situation. Using techniques such as role-play, the HCP helped children to process their emotions. The playroom was a safe space where patients and their parents could freely express their emotions without restraint. The notable prevalence of psychotherapy as a frequently utilised modality in this study may reflect a distinctive characteristic of the Norwegian context.,,,, Parents who sought psychotherapy for their children often did so to address concerns such as worries and psychological reactions. These findings align with existing literature, which highlights that children with chronic physical conditions, including cancer, face an increased risk of psychological challenges such as anxiety and depression.

 Children with cancer frequently endure persistent pain, often resulting in extended hospital stays.

 In the present study, massage and aromatherapy were used primarily to alleviate pain following the completion of cancer treatment. Most parents found these modalities beneficial for their children. This aligns with previous research demonstrating the effectiveness of massage and aromatherapy in reducing pain among paediatric cancer patients- using essential oils such as peppermint,

 lavender, orange, juniper berry, patchouli, and ylang-ylang.

Consistent with previous research,,, a significant proportion of parents (53%, n=24) reported a positive impact of CAM modalities on their children’s well-being. Notably, of the 55 participants, 82% (n = 45) found CAM beneficial, with 53% (n = 24) specifically reporting a reduction in the severity of symptoms related to cancer treatments. These findings are consistent with a Swiss study, in which 87% of parents reported benefits from their child’s CAM use. Specifically, 76% observed improvements in their child’s overall health, while 54% noted a reduction in adverse effects related to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Our findings also parallel those of Laengler et al,

 in which less than 8% of parents reported adverse effects from their child’s use of CAM. In the present study only four parents reported adverse effects attributed to their child’s CAM use, including muscle pain, headache and nausea, linked to psychotherapy, reflexology, vitamin D and vitamin E. These findings were observational; therefor, the study design does not allow for definitive causal inference. Future longitudinal research is required. A systematic review

 of observational studies reported that 58% of the included studies did not report adverse effects from CAM modalities. This lack of safety data is concerning because parents and HCPs need evidence on whether an intervention imposes additional physical or psychosocial burden on the child. Moreover, data on CAM use in paediatric brain tumour populations are limited. In adults, Armstrong et al reported CAM use by 34% of brain tumour patients.

 In the present study, 55.6% of children with brain tumours reported CAM use, making brain tumours the cancer type most commonly associated with CAM use. This finding is based on a small subgroup (n = 18) and should be interpreted cautiously. It may reflect greater morbidity and treatment intensity (e.g., surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, prolonged steroid use) and/or higher symptom burden in this group, which could confound the association.

 The intensity and complexity of these treatments may drive the search for additional supportive care options, like CAM, to alleviate the physical and psychological burden experienced by these young patients. From the literature, we know that cancer patients use CAM to strengthen the immune system, alleviate adverse effects from cancer treatment, give hope, and reduce stress., Parents of children with cancer provide CAM for their children to contribute to the child’s recovery (do everything possible for their child) and to offer a sense of hope., Results from unpublished data from Norway

 show that parents express interest in discussions about CAM and other supportive care approaches. These discussions focus on strategies to support their own well-being, as well as that of their children and families, by reducing anxiety, preparing healthy meals, and maintaining a normal daily routine.

The inclination of parents to seek CAM modalities for their children may be influenced by the presence of distressing symptoms and the constraints of available pharmacological interventions. Children with symptoms such as fatigue, nausea/vomiting, immunosuppression, anxiety, and concentration difficulties were more likely to use CAM than those without these symptoms. However, because the study is cross-sectional and subject to potential selection bias and confounding, we cannot determine temporality or causality (i.e., whether symptoms prompted CAM use or vice versa). The similar pattern observed in a recent Norwegian study of adult cancer patients

 provides external consistency and thus strengthens confidence in the robustness of this association across populations, although it does not address causality.

Particularly, fatigue stands out as a symptom that significantly impairs quality of life both during and post-cancer treatment. Given that pharmacological remedies are not routinely recommended for managing fatigue,

 parents and caregivers may be more motivated to explore non-pharmacological options that can offer symptom relief and enhance the overall well-being of their children.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) is a prevalent adverse effect that is typically managed with antiemetic medications. Despite the use of these drugs, control of CINV remains suboptimal and is often only partially achieved.

 Previous research has consistently identified immune system enhancement as one of the primary motivations for the use of CAM in paediatric oncology patients., The risk of late infections and the potential need for reimmunization among children with cancer are insufficiently described.

 Additionally, children undergoing cancer treatment commonly experience profound anxiety,

 with worry being cited as an especially troubling symptom.

 Despite the frequency and intensity of anxiety, it may be under-assessed and under-managed by healthcare providers.

 Compounding these challenges, many paediatric cancer patients also struggle with concentration, a symptom for which therapeutic options are notably scarce.

 In light of these unmet needs, CAM modalities such as music therapy, and acupuncture

 may offer valuable treatment avenues for these prevalent concerns.

When interpreting the findings of this study, it is essential to consider both its strengths and limitations.

A key strength of the present study is its exploration of CAM use among paediatric patients in Norway, a country with high socioeconomic status and an advanced healthcare system, where a marked divide exists between conventional medicine and CAM. Consequently, parents primarily seek complementary therapies outside the paediatric oncology wards where their children receive treatment. In contrast to the presently acknowledged integrative oncology paradigm, where evidence-based complementary medicine modalities are being provided 
within
 the oncology centre, the present study explores CAM use among children in a clinical setting where these modalities are utilised mostly 
outside
 the conventional treatment setting. The gap between the concepts of CAM and integrative oncology is far from semantic but reflects a scientific rigor, legitimacy, openness, and level of communication between healthcare professionals, patients, and their informal caregivers. The present findings may be relevant not only to Norway but also to other European countries, particularly those in Scandinavia, France, and Eastern Europe, where integrative oncology has not yet been widely adopted despite a growing body of evidence-based research. One possible barrier to integration is the classification of music therapy, art therapy, and certain forms of psychotherapy as CAM. In other countries, these modalities may instead be considered components of psycho-oncology or supportive care rather than CAM. The present study therefore contributes a perspective that has received limited attention in the integrative paediatric oncology literature. It describes a setting in which the integration of supportive modalities may be constrained despite potential facilitators, including parental openness and the availability of national resources. These findings may inform a gradual, evidence-informed process of recognising and integrating appropriate supportive modalities while maintaining scientific rigour.

One of the primary limitations is the relatively small sample size and low response rate, which undermine the generalisability of the findings. Despite efforts to reach respondents through various channels, the number of survey participants remained limited. This challenge is consistent with findings from other research on CAM use in paediatric cancer patients,, which reports a moderate median sample size of 75 participants across 28 studies.

 This limitation could be attributed to several factors, including the significant burden parents face in caring for a child with cancer while managing other responsibilities, as well as the anxiety and stress induced by the research process,

 particularly for parents who have lost their child to cancer.

Another limitation is the possibility that the survey link may have been distributed to parents of children with cancer who are not members of the Children’s Cancer Society. This could have further reduced the response rate among the intended target group, introducing some uncertainty about whether the data fully represent members of the Children’s Cancer Society. However, it is certain that all respondents are, or have been, parents of children with childhood cancer, ensuring that the study remains relevant to this population. Nevertheless, the findings of this study are based on a smaller and specific group of childhood cancer survivors in Norway, and as such, the percentages presented should be interpreted with caution. Future studies with larger and more diverse samples are needed to validate or challenge these findings. The study may also be subject to selection bias. Participation was voluntary and may have preferentially attracted parents who are more engaged in their child’s care or who have particularly strong experiences or opinions about supportive therapies, which could inflate estimates of CAM use and reported benefits. Notably, the questionnaire did not label “CAM” as a separate category in the instrument or participant information sheet; it was not CAM-specific but surveyed a broad range of supportive-care approaches, including non-CAM modalities (the non-CAM items are not reported here). This neutral framing likely reduced but did not eliminate CAM-specific selection and reporting bias. Consequently, the results should be interpreted with appropriate caution. However, non-response bias remains a concern, as parents who chose not to participate may differ significantly from those who did, potentially being less interested in CAM or facing greater time constraints. These factors could limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader population of parents of children with cancer. Although our recall window potentially extended up to 30 years, this risk is mitigated because most respondents reported much shorter intervals: of 117 parents, 67.5% reported contemporaneous or near-contemporaneous experience (0–5 years), while only 12.8% reported more than 10 years since end of therapy. Being diagnosed within the last 30 years is further not equivalent to being out of treatment for 30 years, many children experience prolonged or late effects and may receive ongoing care long after diagnosis. Our measures reflect CAM use across the cancer trajectory (during treatment, in the immediate aftermath, and in survivorship) which complicates simple interpretations of recall interval. Nevertheless, recall bias may have affected our findings: over long intervals parents can misremember or misreport their child’s CAM use and its effects. A cancer diagnosis is profoundly traumatic, and parents often vividly recall treatments and symptoms

; however, vivid memories can still be inaccurate, and peripheral details may be forgotten, so the perceived role or effectiveness of CAM could be either over- or underestimated.

Similarly, response bias could have influenced the findings, as participants may have provided socially desirable answers or exaggerated the benefits of CAM to align with perceived expectations or personal beliefs.

 However, efforts were made to minimize this bias by ensuring full anonymity of the respondents. Measurement bias is another potential limitation, as the reliance on subjective self-reports may not have fully captured the extent of CAM use or its outcomes. However, it is worth noting that the agreement between self-reported data and registered healthcare utilization is generally high,

 which lends some credibility to the findings.

A significant study limitation, which may impede generalization to other countries, is the CAM categorization adopted in the present study, especially the inclusion of psychotherapy and expressive arts like music and art therapy. These modalities may be regarded in other paediatric oncology settings as non-CAM, particularly when provided by the psycho-oncology unit embedded in the paediatric department or by the supportive/palliative care service. Nevertheless, these therapies often include mind-body therapies, such as relaxation and guided imagery, regarded within the complementary and integrative medicine scope of practice. Moreover, some of these expressive therapies are also regarded as part of leading integrative medicine, such as Anthroposophical medicine, with specialized branches of music, art, and movement (Eurythmy) modalities relevant in supportive cancer care.

 In the case of psychotherapy, it remains unclear whether the psychotherapy reported by respondents was delivered by a licensed psychologist (typically not classified as CAM) or by a psychotherapist operating outside of conventional healthcare. This ambiguity may have influenced the reported prevalence of CAM use. For example, nine individuals reported using psychotherapy without engaging in any other forms of CAM. To address this issue, the prevalence of CAM use excluding psychotherapy is presented in .

Emotional bias may also have influenced responses, particularly among parents who experienced significant emotional distress, such as those who lost a child to cancer, potentially affecting how CAM use and its perceived benefits were reported.

Another limitation is that parents were asked to relate and interpret their child’s association with CAM use, while not exploring the child’s direct perspective, at least with adolescents, and without referring to their own quality of life -related concerns and CAM experience. In contrast, present integrative oncology interventions in paediatric oncology, tend to focus not only on the sick child but on the parents’ self-perspective, experience, and quality of life -related concerns as reported by Gressel et al in Israel.

Despite these limitations, the study has several notable strengths. The findings regarding CAM use are consistent with those reported in earlier studies conducted in other high-income European countries,-,,, lending credibility to the results and ensuring criterion validity. Furthermore, although the sample size is small, it is comparable to the population of children diagnosed with cancer in Norway. For example, the distribution of cancer diagnoses in the sample, where leukaemia and central nervous system tumours are the most common, mirrors the national statistics.

 Similarly, the majority of children in the sample were diagnosed at age five or younger, which aligns with the broader Norwegian childhood cancer population, where cancer is more frequently diagnosed in children aged 0–6 years.

 Additionally, the symptoms most commonly reported in this study (weakened immune system, poor appetite, nausea/vomiting, pain, and fatigue) are consistent with those documented in the literature.,, Finally, this study represents the first nationwide investigation into CAM use among children with cancer in Norway.,

This study provides valuable insights into the use of CAM among paediatric cancer patients and their families. By acknowledging potential biases, the findings highlight the complexity of researching CAM use in this population and underscore the importance of interpreting the results in light of these limitations.

Using a symptom-focused lens of fatigue, anxiety, and worry, CINV, and cognitive concerns, we recommend integrating supportive CAM modalities such as music therapy, art therapy, psychotherapy, and massage within paediatric cancer centres. This implementation must, however, be guided by a formal risk-benefit evaluation for each modality.

 We also encourage routine, non-judgmental conversations about CAM and other supportive modalities in paediatric oncology settings. Keep in mind that clinicians do not need to be CAM experts to initiate these conversations.

Future research should aim to address these biases through more diverse sampling and strategies to minimize recall and response biases, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of CAM use in paediatric cancer care. Future work could be prospective and longitudinal, linking CAM use to patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and healthcare use, including adolescent self-reports. Moreover, the present study, with its focus on the parents, may be regarded in the broad context of the informal caregiver literature, while attending to the significant other’s or carer not only as a source of information but as a client that should be further explored in terms of their health-related concerns. While parents are often perceived as the most devoted informal caregivers, the present study may also suggest attending to their own needs and expectations within the parent-child dyad. In this regard, the present study may be meaningful not only as narrow-angle CAM research in a specific paediatric oncology environment in Norway but as a call for in-depth integrative oncology research in the adult setting while highlighting the role of the informal caregivers.

In this national parent sample, many families reported using CAM and supportive care modalities during and after treatment, mainly for symptom relief. Reported benefits were common, and adverse events were uncommon. Given the symptom burden and limited pharmacological options, it’s reasonable to explore evidence-informed supportive interventions and ensure open clinician-family communication about use, safety, and expectations.

psychology.title: Reward Prediction-Error Fidelity: a testable hypothesis linking reinforcement learning mechanisms to applied behavior analysis for autism and neurodevelopmental conditions
psychology.abstract: Applied behavior analysis (ABA) has developed an effective technology of reinforcement delivery, including Discrete Trial Training, Natural Environment Teaching, and token economies, largely on functional-behavioral grounds. Computational neuroscience has independently produced formal accounts of reinforcement learning centered on prediction errors and credit assignment. I propose a testable hypothesis connecting the two: the effectiveness of a reinforcement procedure depends on the quality of the learning signal that its delivery produces on each occasion, a property I term Reward Prediction-Error Fidelity (RPE Fidelity). The property is decomposed into four dimensions, temporal credit, contingency, prediction, and outcome value, each corresponding to a construct long studied in behavior analysis. Formalized within an actor-critic model with eligibility traces, the four dimensions enter the learning update multiplicatively, which implies that they cannot compensate for one another and that the effect of each depends on the others and on the learner’s history. The combination rule distinguishes the hypothesis from the separate behavioral constructs it draws on, and its dependence on learning history distinguishes it from steady-state quantitative models of reinforcement. I situate the hypothesis within an integrative framework, discuss its application to autistic learners, including differences in reward processing and volatility estimation and the role of learner assent, and compare it with procedural fidelity, quantitative behavioral theory, and alternative learning models, including attentional, timescale-invariant, successor-representation, and Bayesian accounts. I derive nine predictions, specifying for each the result that would favor the hypothesis and the result that would favor its strongest competitor, and outline a staged research programme compatible with single-case experimental designs.
psychology.text:
Reinforcement is one of the few constructs studied with comparable rigor at both the neurobiological and the behavioral level of analysis, yet the dialogue between these two literatures remains surprisingly limited in practice. Neuroscience has, over the past three decades, produced a detailed mechanistic account of how the brain represents and updates value, from the discovery of the dopaminergic reward prediction error to the cellular dynamics of eligibility traces and synaptic plasticity. Independently, applied behavior analysis (ABA) has developed, refined, and empirically validated a technology of reinforcement delivery (encompassing procedures such as Discrete Trial Training (DTT), Natural Environment Teaching (NET), and token economy systems) almost entirely on functional-behavioral grounds, with comparatively little explicit reference to the underlying neurobiology.

This separation is not merely an academic curiosity: it means that many long-standing ABA practice principles (the immediacy of reinforcement, the differential durability of intermittent versus continuous schedules, the value of pairing tangible and social reinforcers) are empirically well supported but rarely explained in terms of the mechanisms that produce them. Conversely, neurobiological findings on reward learning rarely engage with the applied, real-world contingency management systems in which reinforcement is most systematically and repeatedly deployed. This article addresses that gap by proposing a specific, testable hypothesis; it does not attempt an exhaustive review.

I propose the following hypothesis. The effectiveness of a reinforcement procedure depends on the quality of the learning signal produced by each delivery, beyond the identity of the reinforcer and adherence to the written protocol. I term this property Reward Prediction-Error Fidelity (RPE Fidelity) and decompose it into four dimensions: temporal credit, contingency, prediction, and outcome value. Each of these variables corresponds to a construct that behavior analysis has long studied, namely immediacy of reinforcement, response-reinforcer contingency, schedule arrangement, and motivating operations. The claim specific to this article concerns how they combine. When the four dimensions are formalized as terms of a single learning update (Section 2.3), they enter multiplicatively rather than additively. This implies that they cannot compensate for one another: a severe deficit in any one of them limits learning regardless of the others, and the effect of improving one depends on the level of the rest. The combination rule distinguishes RPE Fidelity from the separate behavioral constructs it draws on, its dependence on the learner’s history distinguishes it from steady-state quantitative models of reinforcement, and together they make the hypothesis testable in a discriminating way (Section 7.2). RPE Fidelity is also distinct from procedural fidelity: a procedure can be delivered exactly as written while producing a degraded learning signal.

The argument proceeds from neural and computational foundations to applied reinforcement procedures, competing models, and discriminating empirical predictions.

The neurobiological basis of reinforcement is largely attributed to phasic activity in midbrain dopamine neurons, particularly within the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which project to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and prefrontal cortex. The seminal work of  established that these neurons do not simply signal the occurrence of reward, but rather encode a reward prediction error (RPE): a bidirectional signal reflecting the discrepancy between expected and received outcomes. Dopamine neurons are activated above baseline when reward exceeds expectation, remain unchanged when reward is fully predicted, and are suppressed below baseline when an expected reward is omitted.

This RPE signal has since been characterized as a biologically plausible teaching signal, capable of adjusting synaptic strength until an organism’s internal estimate of value converges with actual outcomes (). More recent work has complicated this picture without overturning it: dopamine neurons show functional heterogeneity, and a purely scalar, unidimensional account of the RPE signal appears insufficient to capture the full range of dopaminergic responses observed across tasks and brain regions (; ; ). Recent single-neuron recordings add a further complication: at least part of what was traditionally interpreted as a pure learning signal may instead reflect ongoing regulation of behavioral performance and motor vigor, indicating that distinct dopaminergic subpopulations may encode parallel value functions (). Alternative accounts go further, proposing that mesolimbic dopamine conveys causal associations between events rather than prediction errors (; see Section 6.10). The present hypothesis therefore requires only that the RPE constitute one important computational mechanism through which dopaminergic signaling contributes to reinforcement learning. It does not require a unitary account of dopamine function.

The RPE hypothesis derives much of its explanatory power from its correspondence with formal computational models of learning developed independently in psychology and machine learning. The  model first formalized the notion that learning is driven by the discrepancy between predicted and actual reinforcement, a principle later generalized by temporal-difference (TD) reinforcement learning algorithms (), which extend this logic across sequences of states and predictions rather than single associative events. The convergence between the firing patterns of dopamine neurons and the error term of TD models is widely regarded as one of the more notable points of contact between computational neuroscience and behavioral theory, while the field continues to debate how completely this convergence generalizes given documented dopaminergic heterogeneity (Section 2.1); it nonetheless provides a principled, if partial, bridge between operant learning as conceptualized in ABA and its underlying neural implementation.

Operant learning requires the learner to estimate not only the value of situations but also which response to emit in them. I therefore formalize the hypothesis within an actor-critic architecture (; ), which has been proposed as a model of the functional division between ventral and dorsal striatum (; ). Consider a single teaching trial in which the target response a* is emitted in state s and followed, after k time steps, by the first stimulus that reliably signals reward, and then by the outcome o. For simplicity, the outcome is treated as terminating the trial, so that V(st + 1) = 0. The four dimensions of RPE Fidelity then correspond to specific terms of the model.

When the error is computed, the eligibility of a* is (γλ)k. Temporal Credit Fidelity is therefore defined by k, the delay between the target response and the first reliable reward signal, rather than by the delay to the primary reinforcer. This distinction is central in applied settings. Once a stimulus such as praise, a token, or a marker has acquired value through pairing, its onset itself generates a prediction error [δ = γ·V(smarker) − V(sprev)], so that conditioned reinforcers can bridge delays far longer than the cellular window described in Section 3.1 (). The window of approximately 0.3–2 s therefore constrains, at the synaptic level, the interval between the response and the first reliable value signal, not the interval between the response and a backup reinforcer.

The reward term is r = u(o)·m, where u(o) is the unconditioned value of the outcome and m ∈ [0,1] is the learner’s current motivational state with respect to it. Motivating operations () act on m: satiation and habituation lower it, deprivation raises it. Outcome Value Fidelity is thus defined by the product u(o)·m at the moment of delivery, not by nominal reinforcer preference.

Outcomes that occur in the absence of the target response are learned by the critic as value of the context c, which forms part of V(st) at the time of the outcome. Because the error following the target response is computed against this baseline, δ = r − V(c), noncontingent outcomes that raise V(c) reduce the error that follows a*, and therefore reduce the actor’s update. Contingency accordingly acts through the value of the context, not only through the representation of the response. In the Rescorla-Wagner model with the context treated as a competing cue, asymptotic associative strength corresponds to ΔP = P(O|R) − P(O|¬R) under the conditions analyzed by , which provides a formal link between Contingency Fidelity and the classic contingency literature on operant behavior (; ).

In this form, all four dimensions appear as factors of a single product: temporal credit through (γλ)k, outcome value through u(o)·m, contingency through ΔP, and prediction through αt and through the dependence of the realized error on the learner’s current expectation. The derivation makes its assumptions explicit. The product form holds when noncontingent outcomes are of the same kind and value as contingent ones and are not signaled by a distinct stimulus; when they are signaled, V(c) does not rise and the contingency factor tends toward P(O|R), which is the basis of Prediction 2. Three consequences follow from , .

First, non-compensation. The dimensions enter  as factors of a product, not as terms of a sum. If any factor approaches zero [a delay long enough that (γλ)k ≈ 0, a context that already predicts the outcome as well as the response does, a fully satiated learner, or exhausted associability], the update approaches zero regardless of the other factors. At the level of the learning update, the combination rule is therefore multiplicative; whether the observable ratings of the profile (Section 6.8) show the same structure remains an empirical question, because the mapping from dimensions to ratings is itself imperfect.

Second, interaction. Because the dimensions multiply, the effect of improving one depends on the level of the others; the cross-partial derivatives of  are nonzero. For example, increasing outcome value should produce a smaller gain when temporal credit is poor than when it is good. This property of the model is tested directly by Prediction 1.

Third, history dependence. V(c) and αt change with the learner’s history, so identical delivery conditions produce different updates at different stages of learning. As expected value approaches u(o)·m, δ shrinks; this is why Prediction Fidelity is defined relative to the stage of learning, and why the same reduction in predictability can impair acquisition yet support maintenance (Prediction 3).

The multiplicative structure of ,  is not specific to the actor-critic formulation. A product of an error term, an eligibility or salience term, and a learning rate is shared by error-driven learning rules generally, from the  model, in which the prediction error is scaled by salience parameters of the stimulus and the outcome, to three-factor synaptic learning rules (). The combination rule is therefore a robust property of the family of models on which the prediction-error account rests, not a consequence of a particular modelling choice. The hypothesis does not claim to introduce a new learning algorithm. Its claim is that the variables applied behavior analysis manipulates on each delivery are the arguments of this product, so that a structural property of error-driven learning becomes an empirical constraint on applied procedures, where it has not been tested and where practice recommendations typically address timing, contingency, schedule, and reinforcer value as separate considerations. Where the present formulation does depend on specific modelling choices, namely the absolute scaling of the eligibility trace, the role of context value in contingency, and the history dependence carried by V(c) and αt, these choices generate the predictions that distinguish it from alternative accounts (Predictions 2, 3, and 6–9).

Each dimension corresponds to a construct already studied in behavior analysis: delay of reinforcement (), response-reinforcer contingency (; ), schedule arrangement (), and motivating operations (). These constructs specify the effect of each variable, but not how the variables combine, nor how their effects change with learning history;  specifies both. The account also differs from  Mathematical Principles of Reinforcement, which likewise has a multiplicative structure and whose coupling coefficient plays a role analogous to the eligibility trace. The difference lies in the third consequence: the Mathematical Principles of Reinforcement primarily describe steady-state response rates, whereas  describes trial-by-trial acquisition and contains terms, V(c) and αt, through which learning history modulates the effect of identical delivery conditions. The discriminating tests between the two accounts therefore concern learning trajectories rather than asymptotic performance (Section 7.2).

– describe model-free learning. Sensitivity to contingency degradation and to outcome devaluation are, however, classic signatures of goal-directed control (), and instrumental behavior is thought to reflect an arbitration between the two systems that shifts with training (). The hypothesis does not require that ABA procedures be learned exclusively through model-free computation; it requires only that the delivery conditions captured by the four dimensions determine the quality of the experience from which both systems learn. The two systems nonetheless make different predictions about Outcome Value Fidelity, which provides an additional test. Under goal-directed control, a change in m (for example, satiation before a session) should alter responding immediately, before the devalued outcome is experienced; under model-free control, it should alter responding only after the outcome has been experienced and the error updated. Because goal-directed control tends to predominate early in training and habitual control after extended practice, this difference should itself depend on the stage of learning.

The formal account specifies what would have to be true of the underlying computation for the hypothesis to hold; it does not show that ABA procedures are implemented by this computation. Alternative learning models, including attentional, Bayesian, successor-representation, and retrospective causal accounts, treat some of the same dimensions differently and are compared with the present formulation in Section 6.10.

A central question in translating dopaminergic mechanisms into applied practice concerns the temporal window within which reinforcement remains behaviorally effective. At the cellular level, this question has been addressed through the concept of a synaptic eligibility trace. Using optogenetic stimulation of dopaminergic and glutamatergic inputs separately in striatal medium spiny neurons,  showed that dopamine promotes spine enlargement only within a narrow window, approximately 0.3–2 s after the preceding glutamatergic input, with the precise boundaries of this window set by the kinetics of cyclic AMP regulation in thin distal dendrites. This work, together with the behavioral correlate described by , provides a candidate cellular mechanism consistent with the well-established behavioral principle that reinforcement is most effective when delivered promptly after the target response, while also showing that this window is a range with a specific molecular basis rather than a single fixed threshold. As formalized in Section 2.3, this window constrains the interval between a response and the first stimulus that reliably signals reward, which in applied settings is frequently a conditioned reinforcer rather than the primary outcome.

This finding offers a candidate mechanism for what applied behavior analysts have long formalized as the immediacy principle: reinforcement delivered without delay following a target response is, in many paradigms, associated with stronger and more reliable learning than delayed reinforcement, a pattern consistent with the eligibility-trace window described above. As Section 3.2 details, this should not be read as a fixed biological threshold that transfers directly to instruction; the size of the delay effect depends on whether the learner has other information supporting correct attribution of the outcome to the response.

Complementing this cellular evidence, behavioral studies in humans confirm that the timing of reinforcement shapes not only the rate of acquisition but also the durability of what is learned. In a motor-skill learning task, delaying reward delivery by a few seconds altered the trajectory of learning: training with a short delay (1 s) produced continuous improvement in performance, whereas a long delay (6 s) produced high initial learning rates followed by an early plateau, lower performance at the end of training, and reduced overnight consolidation (). The authors motivated this comparison with earlier neuroimaging evidence that short and long reward delays preferentially engage fronto-striatal and hippocampal systems, respectively; the study itself did not measure neural activity, so this dissociation remains a plausible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

These findings should not, however, be read as establishing a fixed, universal delay threshold that transfers directly from single-synapse recordings to classroom instruction. A substantial literature on human causal learning shows that the detrimental effect of a response-outcome delay depends heavily on whether the learner has structural knowledge of the relevant timeframe:  found that providing cues to the trial structure significantly improved causal judgments in the presence of delay, and a follow-up study showed that the negative effect of delay on causal learning could be abolished entirely by a change in instructions alone (). These studies measured explicit causal judgments in adults, and whether the same effect holds for implicit operant learning, particularly in children who cannot report their expectations about timing, remains an open question. Analogous findings from the behavior-analytic literature on delay-of-reinforcement gradients () and temporal discounting (), which do concern operant behavior directly, show that delay effects are well documented independently of any neurobiological account. Together, this evidence indicates that temporal contiguity and correct credit assignment are related but dissociable: a response and its consequence can be separated by several seconds and still be attributed correctly if the learner has adequate information about the response-outcome relationship. I therefore treat reinforcement timing not as a fixed biological threshold to be imported directly into instructional design, but as one input, among others, to the temporal credit assignment problem formalized in Section 2.3.

Discrete Trial Training (DTT) typically pairs a discriminative stimulus, response, and reinforcer within a tightly controlled and immediate sequence, while Natural Environment Teaching (NET) often involves greater variability in the interval between response and reinforcement due to its embeddedness in naturalistic activity (). Rather than treating this as evidence that DTT is intrinsically better aligned with the eligibility-trace window than NET, which is not a necessary property of either technology, the more precise question is how well timing and contingency are controlled within each method on a given occasion. Framed this way, RPE Fidelity becomes a property of how a procedure is implemented on a specific trial, independent of which ABA technology is used.

Once a target behavior has been established, the schedule by which reinforcement is delivered becomes a critical determinant of both its strength and its resistance to extinction, as established in the classic behavior-analytic literature on schedules of reinforcement (). Continuous reinforcement (in which every instance of the target behavior is reinforced) produces rapid initial acquisition but yields responding that extinguishes quickly once reinforcement is withdrawn. Intermittent schedules, by contrast, particularly variable-ratio (VR) arrangements in which reinforcement follows an unpredictable number of responses, generate higher and more sustained rates of responding that are considerably more resistant to extinction.

This behavioral asymmetry, known as the partial reinforcement extinction effect, has well-established behavioral explanations, including frustration theory () and sequential theory (), which attribute it, respectively, to the conditioning of responding in the presence of anticipatory frustration and to learned associations between sequences of nonreinforced responses and subsequent reinforcement. Neurobiological findings are compatible with these accounts but do not replace them. Phasic dopamine responses to reward-predicting stimuli vary monotonically with reward probability, whereas a slower, sustained component of activity has been reported to covary with outcome uncertainty, which is maximal at a probability of 0.5 (). The interpretation of this sustained component remains debated: it has been argued that it may arise from averaging, across trials, prediction errors whose positive and negative values are coded asymmetrically, rather than from a distinct uncertainty signal (). Under either interpretation, the finding bears on the associability component of Prediction Fidelity (Section 2.3) rather than on the prediction error itself, and it concerns the informativeness of reinforcement rather than unpredictability as such; it should not be read as implying that unpredictability should be maximized (Section 6.4).

A pilot study in an elementary school classroom embedded variable-ratio contingencies within a token-based game, with the explicit aim of eliciting reward prediction errors, and reported increased student engagement (). The study did not measure prediction-error signals, so its results are compatible with, but do not demonstrate, the involvement of the mechanism proposed here.

More broadly, the token economy, in which tokens earned for target behaviors are later exchanged for backup reinforcers, is among the most extensively evaluated reinforcement-based classroom strategies. Meta-analyses report large effects in general and special education classrooms, moderated by components such as backup reinforcer type and exchange schedule (; ), although an evaluation against What Works Clearinghouse standards concluded that methodological weaknesses in the single-case literature prevented classifying token economies as a best practice ().

The practical relevance of this evidence is sharpened by a systematic review of 96 published token-economy studies, which found that only 19% (18 of 96 articles) provided replicable, complete descriptions of all primary procedural components (). Token economies are known to be effective on average, but the specific configuration of their parameters, the token production schedule, the exchange schedule, and backup reinforcer characteristics, is often left underspecified in the published literature. This is precisely the gap that a dimensional account such as RPE Fidelity is positioned to address: rather than asking only whether a token economy was used, it asks which specific configuration of timing, contingency, predictability, and value parameters was in place.

Beyond token economies, differential reinforcement procedures, in which reinforcement is delivered contingent on a specific, targeted response class while other responses are placed on extinction, represent a second major family of reinforcement-based classroom interventions. A recent systematic literature review of differential reinforcement in applied settings for individuals with autism found large to very large effects across seventeen studies, with differential reinforcement of alternative behavior and of low rates of behavior producing particularly strong outcomes (). A complementary systematic review focused specifically on skill acquisition, rather than behavior reduction, found that differential reinforcement conditions favoring independent responding over prompted responding produced faster skill acquisition across the studies reviewed (). Together, these findings extend the evidence base for reinforcement scheduling beyond token economies to the broader family of differential reinforcement procedures used routinely in DTT and NET.

Meta-analytic evidence supports the effectiveness of Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention for young autistic children, although the scarcity of randomized designs introduces uncertainty into these estimates (, ; ; ). Because the present hypothesis concerns the parameters of reinforcement delivery rather than the effectiveness of comprehensive programmes, studies that manipulate individual reinforcement parameters, such as those reviewed above, are more directly relevant to testing it.

The evidence in this section bears on the Outcome Value and Prediction dimensions: it concerns the conditions under which the value of a reinforcer, and of the activity it follows, changes as a result of reinforcement itself.

The same reward circuitry that supports reinforcement-based learning can, under certain conditions, undermine motivation once extrinsic reinforcement is withdrawn, a phenomenon described as the overjustification effect. When performance-based monetary reward was introduced for an intrinsically engaging task and subsequently removed, activity in the anterior striatum and prefrontal regions declined in parallel with voluntary task engagement (). A meta-analysis of 128 studies found that tangible rewards contingent on engagement, completion, or performance undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation, more strongly in children than in college students (; see also ), although later syntheses show that incentives and intrinsic motivation jointly predict performance and that the effect depends on how directly the incentive is tied to the behavior measured ().

Two findings qualify the relevance of this literature for applied behavior analysis. First, a quantitative review of 65 data sets from individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities found a mean effect that did not differ from zero, with outcomes consistent with overjustification only somewhat more likely for behaviors already occurring at high levels without extrinsic reinforcement (); the risk therefore concerns mainly behaviors that already occur spontaneously, which bears on target selection rather than on the use of reinforcement as such. Second, the type of reinforcer appears to matter: in a recent functional imaging study, both monetary and social rewards preserved neural intrinsic value after withdrawal, but only monetary reward reduced behavioral motivational drive (). This dissociation offers a partial rationale for the common practice of pairing tangible reinforcers with social praise, and bears directly on the treatment of social reward in Section 6.5.

The same unpredictability that makes variable-ratio schedules effective for establishing durable, extinction-resistant behavior (Section 4.1) is mechanistically related to reinforcement dynamics documented in the behavioral addiction literature, where both the variability and frequency of reward delivery contribute to the addictive potential of a reinforcer (). This is not a reason to avoid variable-ratio schedules in ABA practice, which remain well supported, but a reason to apply them deliberately and with planned fading once a skill is consolidated, rather than sustaining high variability indefinitely.

The evidence reviewed in Sections 2–5 spans cellular, computational, behavioral, and instructional levels of explanation. I organize it around a single principle: a reinforcement event supports learning to the extent that its delivery allows the learner to answer four questions. Two concern credit assignment in the strict sense: what produced the outcome (contingency), and when the relevant response occurred (temporal credit). Two concern the computations that operate on that attribution: how much the outcome differs from what was expected (prediction), and how much it is worth at that moment (outcome value). I refer to the degree to which delivery conditions support all four as learning-signal quality, and to its measurable counterpart as RPE Fidelity. Because prediction errors shrink as an association is learned, the aim of a well-designed procedure is not to sustain large prediction errors indefinitely, but to keep each reinforcement event informative at the current stage of learning.

RPE Fidelity is conceptually distinct from the well-established construct of procedural fidelity, also termed treatment integrity, which quantifies the extent to which an intervention is delivered as designed and written (). A reinforcement procedure can be delivered with high procedural fidelity while still providing a poor learning signal, for instance when its schedule has become fully predictable. This distinction corresponds to the difference between M0 and M3 in Section 6.10.

The Neurobehavioral Reinforcement Translation Framework (NRTF) organizes this evidence across six levels of analysis. It is intended as an integrative heuristic rather than as an independently validated model.
