In doing so, it builds directly on the critical review by Klassen and Klassen [], which identified persistent conceptual and measurement problems in this literature and called for more rigorous, domain-specific research; the present review will assess the extent to which those problems persist in the 2019 to 2026 literature.

The strengths of this protocol include adherence to rigorous JBI and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, preregistration on the Open Science Framework, a comprehensive search architecture across 6 prominent biomedical databases without geographic restrictions, dual independent screening and data extraction protocols using Covidence, and trilingual coverage (English, Portuguese, and Spanish). Limitations include restricting the primary search time frame to 2019 to 2026, which, although justified by recent curriculum reforms and postpandemic adaptations, risks omitting earlier foundational studies. To mitigate this, backward citation searching will be executed on all included studies. As an update of the earlier critical review by Klassen and Klassen [], this review is explicitly framed as a contemporary map of the field since 2019 rather than a comprehensive historical map. Furthermore, scoping reviews do not mandate formal risk-of-bias assessment, meaning that the overall methodological quality of primary studies will not be quantitatively weighted.

In accordance with JMIR Research Protocols standards, the findings of this review will be actively disseminated through multiple scholarly and operational channels: (1) publication of the completed review in an open-access peer-reviewed medical education journal; (2) presentation at national and international medical education conferences (eg, AMEE and Ottawa Conference); and (3) translation into an open-access executive summary distributed to medical school curriculum committees, deans of medical education, and student mental health task forces to inform evidence-based pedagogical design.

The summary of the current literature through this scoping review will aid in understanding not only self-efficacy among medical students but also which factors are associated with its construction. Furthermore, knowing the self-perception of students throughout their academic trajectory in higher education may serve as support in the development of new teaching strategies and adaptation of the current model. Thus, this study has practical applications in the teaching-learning context of the training of new medical professionals, which may reflect in better academic performance of these professionals and the development of modern curricula adapted to contemporary times.

This protocol for a scoping review establishes a rigorous methodological foundation to clarify how self-efficacy is conceptualized, quantified, and enhanced in undergraduate medical education. The resulting evidence map will serve as an essential resource for educational leaders seeking to design targeted interventions that bolster student confidence, clinical competence, and professional identity formation. The conclusions drawn will be strictly bounded by the descriptive, mapping nature of the scoping review methodology.

This protocol meticulously outlines a robust and systematic approach to conducting a scoping review on self-efficacy among medical students. By adhering to established methodological frameworks and incorporating rigorous search, selection, and data extraction strategies, this protocol ensures transparency and reproducibility. Ultimately, this detailed roadmap will enable a comprehensive mapping of existing literature and the identification of crucial knowledge gaps, thereby providing valuable evidence to inform and enhance educational strategies aimed at fostering self-efficacy and optimizing academic outcomes in medical education.

psychology.title: Graduate student publishing in the United States: Assessing differences by discipline, program rank, and student characteristics
psychology.abstract: Graduate students, especially those in doctoral programs, are often encouraged to publish their work before graduation. Although a growing literature examines graduate student publishing, many studies rely on faculty CVs or publication records, while survey studies are often limited to particular disciplines or institutions. Using data from a probability survey of graduate students in six natural, behavioral, and social science disciplines in the United States, this study examines rates and patterns of publishing among graduate students. We find that about 80% of students in their fifth year or greater year report having published at least one peer-reviewed article and about 20% report having published five or more. Graduate students in psychology have published the most articles, while those in sociology and political science published the least of the disciplines considered. Undergraduate research experience and plans to pursue a research-intensive tenure-track career are positively associated with graduate student publishing. The analysis does not find evidence of gender differences in publishing, but it does find that Black students have fewer articles than their White peers even after we account for other variables. By including current graduate students who have not published and those who may not pursue faculty careers, this study provides a broad assessment of how publishing varies across student and program characteristics.
psychology.text:
For a variety of reasons, faculty and administrators encourage graduate students to publish research before they graduate. Wilkins, Hazzam, and Lean [], for instance, surveyed tenured faculty and administrators (e.g., graduate directors) in business and management programs to ask their opinions about graduate student publishing. Every one of their respondents stated that graduate students should be publishing or at least trying to publish in peer reviewed journals, and some of the respondents’ programs required it to graduate. Similar studies of other fields have also found a growing emphasis on and pressures resulting from an expectation that graduate students should be publishing []. Responding to these pressures, many articles and books can be found providing advice to graduate students on how to publish research while also maintaining the other tasks and outcomes expected of a graduate student [–].

In part, the emphasis on graduate student publications is because those publications can help the profile and research productivity of faculty mentors and graduate programs. Perhaps less selfishly, publishing in graduate school is seen as an important mechanism for building students’ research and writing skills. Indeed, publishing has been found to be a key milestone in the development of students’ professional identity and confidence []. Publications can also serve as career currency [] and promote increased visibility in the field []. This is particularly true for those desiring an academic career, where having publications as a graduate student often serves as an indicator to search committees of a candidate’s potential future research productivity [–], although this evidence includes doctoral-specific research, such as Horta and Santos’s study of PhD holders working in Portugal, and there are some questions as to whether this indicator is valid []. Reliable information about graduate student publishing is therefore important for understanding more than an academic expectation. It can show when publication becomes part of students’ professional development, whether access to publication opportunities differs across disciplines and program settings, and whether disparities emerge before students enter the faculty labor market. It also provides a basis for assessing how closely the expectations placed on graduate students align with what students actually accomplish.

There has been some critique of the strong emphasis on graduate student publishing, either specifically or as part of a broader critique of academic publishing. Drawing on PhD students in mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macau, Horta and Li [] (see also []) argue that the focus on getting graduate students to publish leads them to see their research as commodities and devalue other aspects of their training and future career. Speaking more broadly about academic publishing, Hermanowicz [] argues that the proliferation of publishing expectations in academia has led to a watered-down and ritualized form of research in which everyone feels the need to produce publications even if they are not of particularly high quality (see also []).

Despite such critiques, the expectation that graduate students publish remains strong. A growing literature has examined doctoral and graduate student publishing []. The available evidence, however, remains fragmented across disciplines, institutions, national systems, and research methods. Studies based on faculty CVs exclude students who do not later enter faculty careers, while studies based on publication records cannot capture students who have not published [–]. Survey studies can capture nonpublishers and individual characteristics, but many rely on samples limited to a single discipline, institution, or nonprobability recruitment strategy [–]. These limitations make it difficult to estimate how common publishing is across the broader graduate student population or how publication activity varies across student and program characteristics.

In this study we use data from a probability survey of graduate students in U.S.-based programs across six natural, behavioral, and social science disciplines. We assess how many students have published peer-reviewed articles and how publication activity varies by discipline, program year, program ranking, and student characteristics. By surveying current graduate students, the study includes students who have not published and those who may pursue careers outside academia, two groups often absent from studies based on publications, faculty CVs, or samples of current faculty. This allows us to examine publication activity while students’ academic and career trajectories are still developing. Before discussing our data, measures, and analysis further, we begin by briefly discussing the context of graduate education in the U.S. and briefly reviewing insights from the largely faculty-focused research productivity literature before examining what is currently known about graduate student publishing specifically.

Publication expectations need to be understood within the structure of graduate education. In the United States, graduate education includes both master’s and doctoral programs. Master’s programs may be terminal or may provide a pathway into doctoral study, while some doctoral students also receive a master’s degree during their program []. Doctoral programs generally combine advanced coursework and supervised research culminating in a dissertation, although the sequence and specific requirements vary across disciplines, programs, and institutions []. This variation reflects the decentralized nature of U.S. doctoral education, which does not have a single national set of degree requirements.

This decentralized structure also means that publication expectations vary across U.S. graduate programs. Individual programs may encourage or require publication, but there is no uniform national publication requirement for receiving a doctorate. A recent study at one U.S. university, for example, found that fewer than 15% of the university’s departments had at least one degree program requiring scholarly publication before graduation, although previously published material appeared in 45% of the theses and dissertations examined []. In some other national systems, publication is tied more directly to degree completion. Quan and colleagues’ [] analysis of a representative sample of PhD programs at 164 Chinese universities found that publications indexed in the Science Citation Index were often required for graduation, with some programs also specifying the student’s authorship position. Kazakhstan provides another example of a publication requirement implemented at the national level []. These differences are important for interpreting publication rates because the institutional incentives facing students differ across higher education systems. The present study should therefore be understood as an analysis of students in U.S. graduate programs rather than as a universal account of graduate student publishing.

Scientific examinations of research productivity have, perhaps understandably, predominantly focused on faculty. This literature can be largely categorized into two subgenres, although these sometimes overlap and do not necessarily represent every study in this area. The first consists of studies examining larger trends and patterns in publishing across time, discipline, or type of institution. Such research, for instance, has consistently found that article productivity has been steadily increasing over time, spreading out more evenly across types of institutions, and in some cases coming at the expense of publishing books and other forms of dissemination [,].

Studies have also found significant differences in the number of research publications across disciplines or fields of study, although how these fields are operationalized varies across analyses []. Shin and Cummings [], for instance, found that faculty in engineering, medical and health sciences, and natural sciences publish more than those in the arts and humanities. Social science faculty did not significantly differ from those in the arts and humanities. However, a study of Norwegian researchers found a different pattern, with humanities and social science scholars publishing at a faster rate than peers in natural sciences, technology, and medicine []. The authors argue that these diverging patterns are a function of their study having a more complete record of publications than those typically used in previous research.

A second category of studies of research productivity has focused on assessing and understanding differences in publication rates by faculty demographics, such as their age, gender, and/or race or ethnicity. On gender, for instance, a number of single-discipline and multi-discipline studies have found that women have fewer publications than men on average [–], although this appears to vary by factors like discipline, rank, and cohort [,]. However, some studies have not found such gender differences or found that women publish more in at least some institutional contexts [], while other studies have found that the gender gap is removed when accounting for factors like individuals’ time for research, suggesting that the effect of gender is mediated through other variables []. Moreover, other studies have suggested that the presence of a gender gap in publishing depends on the metrics used [,].

Research looking at racial and ethnic differences in publishing have also tended to find disparities [,]. Looking at sociologists, for instance, Hermanowicz and Clayton [] found that Black and Latino/a faculty published fewer peer-reviewed articles on average as compared to White and Asian faculty, although the gaps varied somewhat depending on whether solo or co-authored articles was considered as well as the ranking of the institution.

None of these faculty-focused studies, of course, tell us directly about rates or patterns of graduate student publishing. There are some studies, though, that get at this issue—at least to some extent.

There have been a few methodological strategies for studying publishing among graduate students. Some studies have collected data from the curriculum vitae of current faculty and assessed which publications were completed before the individual entered a tenure-track career. Hatch and Skipper [] examined 500 social science vitae from faculty at research universities who finished their doctorates in the past five years. They found that, on average, these individuals had a little over four peer-reviewed publications before they graduated. This varied across disciplines, as psychology faculty published the most as graduate students (mean of 8.4) and political science students published the least (2.0), with sociology (3.9) and social work (4.7) in between those two. The authors also reported that, across all the disciplines, males published slightly more in graduate school than females (mean of 4.5 compared to 4.1), but their analysis did not assess whether this was statistically significant or independent of discipline and other variables.

In a similar study, Warren [] examined the CVs of faculty in top sociology departments to assess trends in the number of publications individuals have upon hire as a new assistant professor. This does not precisely represent publishing in graduate school, as some of these “upon hire” publications may have occurred during postdoctoral positions. However, this measure still serves as a useful proxy. The author’s analysis found that, in the most recent years considered (2015–2017), new assistant professors in top sociology departments had an average of just under five peer-reviewed articles. This average has trended upwards over the thirty years examined. Warren also considered gender differences in articles upon hire, but the pattern was not definitive, as in some years newly hired women published more articles on average and in others it was men that had published more. Studies using CVs of faculty obviously miss publishing by graduate students that do not enter the professoriate, as do surveys of current faculty that then identify publications produced by respondents before they received their PhD (e.g., []).

Beyond looking at faculty CVs, some research has extracted data from publications themselves []. For example, Garbati and Samuels [] examined a handful of journals in education, language studies, educational psychology, and literacy studies to assess the rate at which graduate students appeared as authors. They found that this occurred relatively rarely in their sample, as graduate students made up less than nine percent of all authors. Of course, utilizing journals comes with some weaknesses, as it provides limited information on the graduate students themselves (i.e., covariates) and students that have not published articles are obviously not going to be present.

Using a broader analysis of publication records, Larivière [] examined doctoral students’ participation in peer-reviewed publications in Quebec between 2000 and 2007. Doctoral students contributed to about one-third of Quebec’s publication output, with greater participation in the natural and medical sciences than in the social sciences and humanities. This demonstrates the scale of doctoral students’ contribution to published research. At the same time, studies based on publication records cannot capture students with no publications and provide limited information about students’ characteristics, motivations, or career goals.

Another strategy has been to track graduate student publications within a single institution. Pezzoni et al. [], for example, linked six engineering and natural science PhD student cohorts at the California Institute of Technology with publication data from Web of Science. Their analysis found that, across disciplines, students produced an average of.86 publications per year. This average was lower in biology (.65) and higher in chemistry (1.00) and physics (1.04). They also found that female graduate students tended to publish less than males, but this was dependent on the sex of their advisor.

Looking beyond data extracted from CVs or publication records, some research has taken a survey-based approach to measuring graduate student publishing. One advantage of this method is that it allows the researcher to collect measures that cannot be extracted from CVs (e.g., individual attitudes or behaviors). However, many of these studies have been limited in the scope and generalizability of their samples.

Roksa et al. [], for instance, surveyed a little over 300 PhD students in the biological sciences with a particular interest in how publishing varies by students’ demographic characteristics. Students were recruited by first contacting graduate program directors and department chairs and asking them to forward the survey to students. Their analysis found that White women, Black and Latino/a students published less than White men. These differences were independent of other variables. Of course, such single-discipline surveys preclude the ability to assess differences across disciplines, and the sampling in this study was not done on a probability-basis.

Similarly, Willis, Bridges, and Jozakowski [] conducted a population survey of psychology faculty in research universities in the United States. Graduate students were not an intentional part of their sample, but the researchers “encouraged faculty members to send the [survey] invitation to their colleagues and graduate students.” From the 240 graduate students that were forwarded the survey and responded, the authors found that the average number of peer reviewed articles was 2.86. This did not differ by sex, but it was significantly higher among White graduate students (3.42) compared to students of color (1.32). In a sample of graduate students who self-identified as Black, Baylor and Middleton [] report that the mean number of publications among the surveyed students was less than one. This study, however, is limited by a small sample size and the inability to make meaningful comparisons across disciplines.

Golde and Dore [] conducted a national U.S. survey of doctoral students across 11 disciplines and 27 institutions. They found that 73% of students were interested in publishing research findings, but only 52% felt confident doing so and fewer than 43% believed their program had prepared them to publish. The study also identified disciplinary differences in students’ opportunities to participate in ongoing research. Although the data were collected more than two decades ago, the study remains an important historical reference point for understanding doctoral students’ experiences with publishing.

More recent research continues to demonstrate the role of mentoring relationships in graduate student publishing. Li and Fernandez [], for instance, used survey data from doctoral students in Canada and found that more frequent research-focused interactions with advisers were associated with more first-author publications. More broadly, Mertkan and colleagues [] provide a systematic review of the relationship between predoctoral publishing and later academic careers.

Research orientation may also be relevant to publication activity. Although much of the evidence comes from faculty-focused studies, individuals who prefer conducting research over other tasks tend to be more productive [,]. Students may also pursue doctoral education for multiple, overlapping reasons. London and colleagues [] identified several motivations among engineering PhD holders in the United States, including career aspirations, prior academic experiences, the influence of other people, and intrinsic interests. Students may therefore value making a contribution to research while also pursuing career advancement or professional status. We consequently treat the importance of contributing to one’s discipline, the importance of having a high-status career, and students’ career preferences as related but distinct orientations rather than opposing motivations.

A couple broad conclusions can be drawn from the research reviewed above. First, publication activity is shaped by both students’ preparation and professional orientation and by the institutional and disciplinary settings in which they are trained. Although findings are not always consistent, research often identifies differences across disciplines and disparities associated with students’ gender, race or ethnicity, and other characteristics.

Second, the literature focused on graduate student publishing is larger than a primarily faculty-focused account might suggest, but important limitations remain. Studies based on faculty CVs exclude students who do not later enter faculty careers, while studies based on publication records cannot capture students who have not published and often provide limited information about students’ characteristics and goals. Surveys of current graduate students provide this information, but they have frequently focused on selected disciplines, institutions, or nonprobability samples. National context creates an additional source of variation because publication may be a formal completion requirement in some systems and primarily a professional or disciplinary expectation in others.

In this study we use a probability sample of graduate students in U.S. programs across six natural, behavioral, and social science disciplines. This design allows us to examine current students, including those with no publications and those who may not pursue faculty careers, while assessing differences across disciplines, program rankings, and student characteristics. We assess two questions:

(1) How does the rate of publishing peer-reviewed articles as a graduate student vary across disciplines and program ranks?

(2) Is there evidence of disparities in publishing as a graduate student by demographic indicators—such as gender and race or ethnicity—and do these remain when accounting for factors like career orientation and research preparation?

The data for this study come from a survey fielded in September and October of 2025 on a sample of graduate students in U.S. programs in six natural and social science disciplines—biology, physics, chemistry, psychology, sociology, and political science. Sampling for the survey took place in two stages. In the first stage, all graduate programs in these disciplines that were ranked by U.S. News & World Report were stratified into five quintiles. We used the full range of rankings for five of the disciplines, but for psychology we only used the top 200 programs. Our initial examination found that below this level many of the psychology programs were online, professionally-focused programs and distinct from higher ranked psychology programs. We randomly selected five programs within each discipline-quintile stratum to create a sample of 150 programs in total, or 25 per discipline.

In the second stage, we extracted student names and email addresses from the selected programs’ online graduate directories. If a program did not have such a directory, then it was replaced at random with another in the same stratum. This produced a student sample of 8,543 students.

We then invited these students through email to complete a survey programmed into Qualtrics. Students were provided with information regarding informed consent in the recruitment email and on the first screen in Qualtrics before choosing to participate. As an incentive, students were offered the opportunity to enter into a lottery for one of 100 $50 gift cards. The data collection for this study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at West Virginia University (Protocol #2405975847). Written documentation of consent was waived for this study given its online nature and the minimal risk involved to subjects. All subjects were provided the required information for consent in the recruiting email and on the first page of the survey and were told that proceeding with the survey implied their consent to participate.

In the end, we received 1,712 responses. A comparison of the respondents to the full student sample finds that chemistry students (25.9% of sample frame compared to 19.2% of the respondents) and physics students (22.1% of frame compared to 18.9% of respondents) are somewhat underrepresented in the respondents, while political science (12.3% of frame compared to 14.4% of respondents), psychology (16.4% of frame compared to 19.0% of respondents), and sociology (9.8% of frame compared to 14.8% of respondents) are somewhat overrepresented. The distribution of biology respondents is close to the sample frame (13.1% of frame compared to 13.4% of respondents). Our analysis includes a measure to account for disciplinary differences.

Our interest in this study is to assess patterns of publishing among graduate students. For this, we utilized an item on the survey that asked students, “How many peer-reviewed articles have you published, either by yourself or with coauthors?” Responses ranged from (0) 0 to (5) 5 or more. We note that the survey did not provide a definition or criteria for “peer-reviewed articles.” This could be seen as a limitation, as it could introduce some measurement error. However, the language and culture of peer-review publishing is strong enough in U.S. graduate programs that we do not see this a major issue.

We assess the associations between our outcome and a wide range of predictors. These predictors, however, can be grouped into three conceptual categories: (1) predictors measuring aspects of students’ characteristics; (2) predictors measuring students’ preparation for and professional orientation towards publishing; (3) predictors measuring disciplinary and programmatic cultures of the student’s graduate program.

As reviewed above, many studies have examined how researchers’ publishing productivity is associated with their demographic characteristics—such as their age, gender, or race or ethnicity. Given this, we include indicators of students’ age, gender, and race or ethnicity.

We also include some predictors that have not been considered as much or at all in productivity research, such as students’ socioeconomic background, sexual identity, their partnership and parental status, and whether they were born in the U.S. or not. Students’ socioeconomic status is measured with a scale representing students’ level of agreement with six statements. These statements were, (1) I usually had the latest toys, electronics, clothes, or other things I wanted when I was growing up; (2) Growing up, I often had to do without things I needed. (3) I attended a poor or economically disadvantaged high school; (4) I always received the medical and dental care I needed growing up; (5) My family often took out-of-town vacations when I was growing up; and (6) My family struggled to make ends meet when I was growing up. Responses for these statements ranged from (1) strongly disagree to (5) strongly agree. We coded the responses such that higher responses indicate a higher socioeconomic background and then combined them into a mean scale with a Cronbach’s alpha score of  .82.

Some research has pointed to the value individuals place on research as an important predictor of publishing productivity [,]. Given this, we include another group of predictors representing students’ preparation for and orientation towards conducting research and publishing. For instance, we asked students to rate how important “making an important contribution to my discipline” is to them, as well as how important “having a high-status career” is to them. Responses to these two items ranged from (1) not at all important to me to (4) very important to me.

We also asked students about their career goals with a question asking, “Setting aside all other considerations, which of the following careers would you most prefer after finishing your graduate program?” Possible responses were, (1) teaching-intensive tenure-track professor, (2) research-intensive tenure-track professor, (3) other type of career in academia (e.g., administration, research support), (4) career outside of academia (e.g., industry, government, nonprofit sector), (5) something else.

Lastly in this group, we include a measure asking students whether they participated in undergraduate research experiences. The question on the survey asked, “Did you participate in any research experiences while obtaining your bachelor’s degree? These are typically outside of class requirements and often lead to you presenting in oral or visual form at a conference or symposium.” Responses were (0) No and (1) Yes.

As discussed earlier, past research on productivity has noted variation across disciplines and institution types. Such variations could be attributed to factors such as the variation in the types of research being done, work styles (e.g., independent or collaborative), and productivity expectations or norms across disciplines and institutions. To account for such factors, we include indicators representing the discipline of the student’s graduate program, the quintile of the program’s ranking, and the type of program the student is in (i.e., doctoral, terminal M.A., or something else like a dual degree program). Note that the vast majority of our respondents are doctoral students.

All analyses were conducted in Stata/SE 18.0. Rather than remove cases with missing data on the measures above, we used multiple imputation through chained equations (m = 10) to utilize the full sample of 1,712 respondents. We begin by examining descriptive statistics for all of our dependent and independent measures. Because it is overdispersed (mean = 1.77, variance = 3.16), we utilize a negative binomial regression model to predict our outcome measure of how many peer-reviewed articles students have published. We present effects in the form of incidence rate ratios (IRRs). In this form, effects over 1.0 represent a positive effect for a predictor—that is, the predictor is associated with more published articles. Effects below 1.0 represent a negative effect, or an association with fewer published articles.

In our model we include a control measure for how many years the student has been in their program, since we would expect that students who have been in their programs longer would have more publications on average. Because our sample frame was constructed in late summer and early fall, we had few student respondents in their first year of their graduate program. Given this, we combined the first and second year students. So, this measure ranges from (1) first or second year to (5) sixth or more years. The regression model also adjusts the variance-covariance estimates for the clustering of students within graduate programs.

We recognize that our outcome measure is undoubtedly right-censored for at least some students given that it represents “five or more publications” and some students would have scored higher if they have more than five publications. As we discuss at the end of our results section, we also estimated a right-censored Poisson model that produced largely similar results with a few exceptions. However, this alternative model was not able to be analytically combined with our multiple imputation of missing values, so its sample size differs (N = 1,515).

Descriptive statistics for all of our measures are shown in . We can see that about one-third (33.6%) of the graduate students have not published a peer-reviewed article, while 21.3% have published one article, 14.6% have published two articles, 9.7% have published three, 5.9% have published four, and 14.6% have published five or more articles.

Note: N = 1,712.

presents the number of publications by a student’s year in their graduate program. For students in their first and second years, a little over half have no publications. This declines to just over 40% among students in their third year, just over 30% students in their fourth year, and 20% for students in their fifth, sixth or more years. Looking at the other end of the spectrum, we see that under 10% of students in their first or second years report having more than five articles. This increases to about 20% among students in their fifth year.

breaks the publication counts out by discipline. Here we see that political science has the highest overall percentage (52%) of students without any published articles. This is followed by sociology, with 41% of graduate students having not yet published an article. On the other hand, only 21% of psychology graduate students have yet to publish an article. Indeed, psychology graduate students are the most likely to have published five or more articles, with 29% reporting this response.

presents the publication counts by student gender identity. Comparing men and women, we do not find any immediately noteworthy differences. Thirty-four percent of men report no publications compared to 32% of women, and 15% of both men and women report having five or more publications. The non-binary or other gender identity group does show a bit more difference, with 43% of this group reporting no publications and only 11% reporting five or more.

compares publication counts across racial or ethnic groups. Looking at the percentage with no publications, we see that Black students are the highest at reporting no published articles, with 47% in this category. This is followed by Latino/a students at 39%. At the high end of publication counts, we see that White and East Asian students are the most likely to have five or more publications, with 16% in each of these groups reporting that number of articles.

Of course, none of the bivariate patterns seen in these figures account for other factors that may also be associated with these differences. To this end, we now turn to our negative binomial regression model predicting graduate students’ number of published articles. The results for this model are shown in . As to be expected, the number of years a student has been in their graduate program is positively and significantly associated (IRR = 1.21, p < .001) with the number of articles they have published.

Note: N = 1,712; *p < .05 **p < .01 ***p < .001; Incidence rate ratios presented; Variance-covariance estimates adjusted for clustering of cases within programs.

Looking at the research preparation and orientation predictors, we find that students who had a research experience as an undergraduate report more published articles than those who did not (IRR = 1.49, p < .001). We also find that, net of the other measures in the model, students who rate having a high-status career as important to them have more published articles (IRR = 1.05, p < .05) than those who say such a career is not important to them. On the other hand, students who rate making a contribution to their discipline as important to them do not significantly differ in the number of published articles compared to those who say such a contribution is not important to them. Taken together, these results show a positive association between publication counts and the importance students place on having a high-status career, while the measured importance of contributing to the discipline is not independently associated with publication counts. Because these orientations are not mutually exclusive, we do not interpret this pattern as evidence that career motivations displace a desire to make a scientific contribution.

The analysis also finds that students expressing a preference for a research-intensive tenure track career report more published articles (IRR = 1.31, p < .001) than those who say they prefer a teaching-intensive tenure track career. As we will discuss more later, the causality here could go both ways. That is, success in publishing could lead students to desire an academic research career, and that desire could also lead them to pursue publishing.

Turning to the predictors measuring different aspects of students’ characteristics, we do not find a significant difference between men and women but we do find a significant difference between men and non-binary students, with the latter reporting fewer publications (IRR = .75, p < .05). This full model obviously includes the full range of controls, some of which could be mediating gender differences. However, even if we estimate a simpler model that only accounts for years in program, discipline, program type, and program ranking quintile, we still do not find a significant difference in articles between men and women.

We do find, however, that Black graduate students report fewer published articles than their White peers (IRR = .69, p < .01) independent of the controls. We do not find significant differences by sexuality, parental status, or socioeconomic background. On the other hand, we do find independent associations for partnership status and age. Older students and those who are married report having published more articles than those who are younger or unmarried. The data do not allow us to identify the mechanisms behind these associations, and further research is needed to determine why age and partnership status are related to publication counts.

Finally, we turn to the findings for our predictors representing disciplinary and programmatic norms. Perhaps surprisingly, we do not find that students in terminal master’s programs significantly differ in their number of published articles compared to doctoral students. As suggested in , however, we do find significant independent differences across disciplines. Relative to biology graduate students, those in physics (IRR = .79, p < .05), sociology (IRR = .61, p < .001), and political science (IRR = .44, p < .001) have published fewer articles. Graduate students in psychology, though, have published more than those in biology (IRR = 1.30, p < .01). Looking at differences by the ranking quintile of the graduate program, we do not find significant differences except for students in the bottom quintile who, relative to those in the top quintile, have published fewer articles (IRR = .72, p < .01).

As noted in our analysis plan, because our outcome is right-censored, we also estimated a censored Poisson model. However, this model could not be analytically combined with the multiple imputation of missing values, so its analytical sample consists of 1,515 cases (228 right-censored). The findings for this model largely mirrored those in  with a couple notable exceptions. First, this model showed a significant difference between men and women, with women publishing less (IRR = .89 p < .05). Second, this model showed a significant difference between White students and Latino/Hispanic students (IRR = .75 p < .01) and South Asian students (IRR = .76, p < .01). Finally, this alternative model found a significant difference between students born in the U.S. and those born outside the U.S., with the former publishing more (IRR = 1.16 p < .01). These differences could be a function of the differences in sample size or the different treatment of the censoring. At the very least, this suggests that these particular differences are more sensitive to modeling choices, while the others appear more robust.

We synthesize and discuss these findings further in the next section.

The analysis above provides a broad, probability-based examination of graduate student publishing across six disciplines in the United States. Unlike studies based on faculty CVs or publication records, our sample includes current students with no publications and students who may not enter faculty careers. Our data show that by the time students approach the end of their graduate careers, about 80% will have published at least one peer-reviewed article, and a little over 20% will have published five or more articles. Additionally, graduate students who had research experience as undergraduates have more publications than those without similar experience. This may reflect the fact that students who enter graduate school with research experience are already familiar with the research process, even if they have not yet published. This familiarity may make it easier for students to become involved in others’ projects or begin their own research after entering graduate school. These findings suggest that undergraduate research opportunities may be valuable for developing research skills, although further research is needed to determine whether they contribute to future publications.

The process of publication can help graduate students develop skills used in academic research. Writing for publication, responding to peer review, and navigating the publication process provide students with experience that can be useful in academic careers. A record of research productivity can also be an advantage in the academic job market. Understanding differences in publication productivity can help programs identify ways to provide students with opportunities to develop research and publishing skills.

The publication rates identified in this study should be interpreted within the context of the U.S. graduate education system. Because U.S. doctoral education is decentralized [], and individual programs may establish their own publication expectations [], student publishing may reflect a combination of disciplinary practices, research and mentoring opportunities, program expectations, and anticipated career benefits. The rates should not be assumed to apply directly to systems in which students must meet formal publication requirements before receiving their degrees. In those settings, publication activity is also tied directly to degree completion [,].

Our results indicate that graduate students in psychology publish at a particularly high rate, while those in physics, sociology, and political science publish at lower rates. Golde and Dore [] report that students in psychology and other lab-based sciences have opportunities to take on roles in ongoing research projects. This provides them with a structured opportunity for co-authorship and publication that students in the humanities, for example, lack. The research lab model often used in psychology programs not only benefits graduate students, but can also provide opportunities for undergraduate students to get research experience.

Hatch and Skipper’s [] findings support this, noting that psychology faculty reported publishing the most when they were graduate students, compared with political science and sociology faculty. The apprenticeship model used in many psychology programs might be used in other disciplines to encourage co-authorship. A team structure may also provide opportunities for incoming graduate students to gain writing experience and observe the process of publishing academic work.

Mertkan et al. [] note that some programs have institutionalized publication expectations through graduation requirements, but even without an institutional policy, publishing is framed as a way to gain advantages in the academic job market. The proliferation of publishing among graduate students across disciplines is important, as academic jobs become more limited. Graduate students with a strong publication record are valued in the job market, as their record signals potential research productivity as a faculty member [,]. Our findings indicate that students who prioritize high-status careers publish more. A strong publication record may provide an advantage in the academic job market.

This aligns with previous research highlighting the advantages of publishing during graduate school. Höhmann [], for example, in a critical piece on demystifying the publishing process in graduate school, emphasizes that publishing as a student demonstrates academic potential, increases visibility, and offers an opportunity to learn about the writing process through peer review. However, graduate students who anticipate an academic career focused on teaching may be disadvantaged in the job market, as they are not publishing at the same rate. Future research should examine whether opportunities to develop publishing skills are particularly important for students pursuing teaching-focused academic careers.

Previous research has established a link between publishing early and often and future success []. As such, students who are encouraged to publish and experience early success may be inclined to continue on this trajectory. Students without that experience, or even those who fail to publish their work, may be discouraged from pursuing a research-intensive job. Alternatively, students who are motivated to pursue a research-focused career may also embrace the “early and often” strategy to make strides toward their goal. Our findings support this contention, where students who aspire to a research intensive tenure track career have published more articles than those who are interested in teaching. The findings also indicate that students who have not published by the end of their fifth year are not likely to do so. This finding suggests that early involvement in research and publishing may be worth further investigation, regardless of whether students have identified a career path.

Our analysis also finds that age and partnership status are associated with publication counts, but the data do not identify the mechanisms behind these relationships. These patterns may reflect differences in prior educational or professional experience, program circumstances, available support, or other factors not measured in the study. Future research should examine these possibilities before drawing conclusions about why older and married students publish more. These findings suggest that providing students at different life stages with opportunities to participate in research and develop publishing skills may be worth considering.

Notably, we do not find a statistically significant connection between making a contribution to the discipline and publishing. At the same time, students who place greater importance on having a high-status career publish somewhat more. This pattern suggests that career incentives may be one factor associated with graduate student publishing, but it does not indicate that students who publish more are less interested in making a scientific contribution. These motivations can coexist, and our measures do not capture the full range of reasons students may have for pursuing publication.

While we do not find significant gender differences in graduate student publishing, our analysis shows that Black students publish less, even after accounting for a wide range of measures, such as undergraduate research experiences and career preferences. Graduate programs would benefit from recognizing this inequality, and focus on inclusive practices in research groups and opportunities to co-author. Studies consistently find Black and Latino/a students published less than White and Asian students and faculty [,,]. While research indicates that new faculty members have an average of four publications [], Baylor and Middleton [] find a mean of less than one publication in their sample of Black PhD students at HBCU or PWI. Identifying the mechanisms underlying this gap should be of interest to both researchers and graduate programs.

Of course, our analysis is not without its limitations. Our outcome measure, for example, is a single item that focuses on overall peer-reviewed articles and does not distinguish between single-authored or co-authored articles, number of authors, co-author type (e.g., faculty or other graduate students), or other details that could provide some nuance to our findings. While our survey-based measures have advantages, self-reported publication numbers may also be subject to more measurement error—although this would primarily only be problematic if it is systematic across other variables in some way. Moreover, our data, while representing a range of disciplines, also does not include many that could be of interest. We also recognize that our data is cross-sectional in nature, which makes determining the causal nature of some associations difficult. In particular, it is not clear whether a student’s preference for a research career or the importance they place on having a high-status career is a predictor of or an outcome of publishing. It is likely to some extent both. That is, students with a preference for a research career place more emphasis on publishing, which leads them to publish research, which then further increases their interest in a research career. The sample is also limited to graduate students in U.S. programs. We therefore cannot determine how publication rates or their predictors differ in national systems with different doctoral structures or formal publication requirements. Comparative research is needed to determine which patterns identified here are specific to the U.S. context and which extend across graduate education systems.

Despite the limitations, our findings point to important policy implications. The differences in publication rates identified in our study raise questions about whether all graduate students have comparable opportunities to participate in research and publishing. The results indicate differences in publication rates across program rankings, with students in the bottom quintile publishing less than those in the top quintile. Doctoral programs are largely structured as apprenticeships, aiming to prepare students to become independent researchers. As a result, many students collaborate with faculty members on research projects; however, the quality of these relationships varies in the level of training provided, and students differ in how well they are prepared to conduct research during the program and after graduation [,]. If graduate programs want to strengthen these apprenticeship models, summer research programs focused on skill building for incoming students could be one approach to consider. These types of programs might be especially useful in lower-quintile programs, where students have lower publication rates.

In a national study of doctoral students in the arts and sciences, Golde and Dore [] note that fewer than half of students felt their program prepared them to publish. While programs may have an expectation for student publications, they may not have the structure in place to adequately prepare students for success. This may be especially true for programs without research labs. These programs, notably political science and sociology, which have relatively low rates of graduate student publications, might consider research groups as one possible way to provide students with additional research opportunities. The effectiveness of these programs should be evaluated in future research. Writing and publishing workshops and mentorship models could also be explored, particularly with attention to structural barriers that hinder publication productivity for people in minoritized groups.
