HA/PV, high arousal/positive valence; HA/NV, high arousal/negative valence; LA/PV, low arousal/positive valence; LA/NV, low arousal/negative valence. *p < 0.05, ***p < 0.001.

PANAS analyses indicated that mean positive affect before performance was 32.23 (SD = 4.17) and mean negative affect was 19.30 (SD = 3.76); after performance, mean positive affect increased to 35.70 (SD = 5.93) and mean negative affect was 19.03 (SD = 4.77). Paired-samples t-tests confirmed a significant pre-to-post increase in positive affect [t(29) = 4.25, p < 0.001, d = 0.78] and no significant change in negative affect [t(29) = −0.40, p = 0.690, d = −0.07], indicating that the piano duo performance task exerted a broadly positive effect on performers' affective states without inducing systematic negative affect activation. Mean collaboration duration was 18.1 months (SD = 7.5, range: 8–34 months). IRI trait empathy raw subscale scores (7 items per subscale, each rated 1–5, maximum = 35) were as follows: Perspective Taking (PT) M = 20.75 (SD = 3.61), Empathic Concern (EC) M = 25.93 (SD = 2.64), Fantasy (FS) M = 20.77 (SD = 2.00), and Personal Distress (PD) M = 14.77 (SD = 2.92). The grand mean of the four subscale scores was 20.55 (SD = 1.27, computed from dyadic means), indicating limited between-pair variability in mean IRI levels and a degree of trait empathy homogeneity in the present sample.

H1 (confirmatory) predicted that HR and EDA synchrony between co-performers would significantly exceed a random-pairing baseline, with the strongest synchrony under the HA/PV condition. As shown in , at the trial level (N = 120 performances), true-pair HR-CCF (M = 0.353, SD = 0.112) significantly exceeded the surrogate random-pairing baseline (M = 0.131, SD = 0.071) [t(119) = 17.94, p < 0.001, d = 1.64]. EDA-CCF similarly exceeded the baseline [true-pair M = 0.327, SD = 0.120 vs. surrogate M = 0.096, SD = 0.057; t(119) = 16.96, p < 0.001, d = 1.55]. At the pair level (N = 30 pairs), paired-samples t-tests (df = 29) confirmed that synchrony in both channels significantly exceeded the surrogate baseline (all p < 0.001). H1 was supported.

As shown in  and , synchrony strength differed significantly across the four emotional conditions [HR-CCF: F(3, 87) = 10.04, p < 0.001; EDA-CCF: F(3, 87) = 19.81, p < 0.001]. Peak HR-CCF (M = 0.411) and EDA-CCF (M = 0.408) were observed under the HA/PV condition, whereas the lowest values were observed under LA/NV [HR-CCF M = 0.272; EDA-CCF M = 0.251]. Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons showed that, for HR-CCF, synchrony under HA/PV, LA/PV, and HA/NV each significantly exceeded LA/NV (p < 0.001, p = 0.002, and p = 0.021, respectively). For EDA-CCF, both HA/PV and LA/PV significantly exceeded HA/NV and LA/NV (all p < 0.001), whereas HA/PV vs. LA/PV and HA/NV vs. LA/NV did not differ. True-pair synchrony significantly exceeded surrogate baselines across all four conditions (all p < 0.001; see ).

Descriptive statistics for physiological synchrony indices and surrogate baseline tests across emotional conditions.

CCF, cross-correlation function synchrony index; Surrogate, condition-matched cross-pair permutation baseline (null distribution generated from 1,000 permutations). t-values are from paired-samples t-tests between true-pair and surrogate CCF (within-condition df = 29; combined analysis df = 119); between-condition F-values are from one-way repeated-measures ANOVA (df = 3, 87). d = Cohen's d. ***p < 0.001.

To examine whether the physiological synchrony indices corresponded to performers' subjective sense of emotional concordance, the PESS was scored for each performer (P1: M = 21.10, SD = 2.99, Mdn = 21.00, range 15.00–28.00; P2: M = 20.77, SD = 2.42, Mdn = 21.00, range 16.00–26.00) and averaged to a dyadic mean (M = 20.93, SD = 1.89, Mdn = 21.00, range 17.50–24.50). At the pair level (N = 30), the dyadic-mean PESS was not significantly correlated with either HR-CCF (r = −0.073, p = 0.701, 95% CI [−0.422, 0.295]) or EDA-CCF (r = −0.019, p = 0.922, 95% CI [−0.376, 0.344]). Although the pair-level sample (N = 30) yields wide confidence intervals, both point estimates were close to zero, providing no evidence that stronger physiological coupling was accompanied by a stronger subjective sense of emotional synchrony; the CCF-based indices and self-reported emotional concordance thus appear to capture distinct, non-overlapping facets of the shared performance experience (see Section 4.2).

H2 predicted that physiological synchrony would be positively associated with expert-rated performance quality (confirmatory for the overall synchrony-quality association), with possible channel-specific links between HR-CCF and ensemble cohesion and between EDA-CCF and expressiveness (exploratory). MLM results are presented in . HR-CCF significantly predicted ensemble cohesion (β = 0.230, t = 2.21, p = 0.027), whereas EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness (β = 0.057, t = 0.52, p = 0.605); H2 was partially supported (HR-CCF → ensemble cohesion supported; EDA-CCF → expressiveness not significant; see ). Neither HR-CCF for expressiveness (β = −0.033, p = 0.749) nor EDA-CCF for ensemble cohesion (β = 0.057, p = 0.616) reached statistical significance, indicating a differential predictive pattern between the two physiological channels and distinct performance quality dimensions.

Multilevel linear model results: predictive effects of physiological synchrony indices on performance quality dimensions.

β, standardized regression coefficient; all continuous predictors and outcomes were z-standardized prior to model estimation. Emotional condition was coded with HA/PV as the reference category; ensemble format was coded as four-hand = 0, double piano = 1. Marginal R2 reflects variance explained by fixed effects; conditional R2 reflects variance explained by fixed and random effects combined; ΔR2 reflects the increment in marginal R2 relative to a baseline model containing only the control variables (condition, dyadic-mean IRI, collaboration duration, ensemble format), i.e., the additional variance explained by adding HR-CCF and EDA-CCF. *p < 0.05. The EDA-CCF coefficients for expressiveness and ensemble cohesion (0.0574 and 0.0571, respectively) round to the same value at three decimal places.

With HA/PV as the reference condition, the HA/NV condition significantly suppressed expressiveness (β = −0.815, t = −2.89, p = 0.004), as did the LA/NV condition (β = −0.789, t = −2.52, p = 0.012); the LA/PV condition did not significantly affect expressiveness (β = −0.214, p = 0.384). For ensemble cohesion, none of the three emotional conditions differed significantly from the HA/PV reference group (HA/NV: β = 0.162, p = 0.570; LA/PV: β = 0.041, p = 0.868; LA/NV: β = −0.260, p = 0.415). These results suggest that emotional condition has a pronounced influence on expressiveness—negative-valence conditions, regardless of arousal level, suppressed the clarity of emotional communication—while its influence on ensemble cohesion was comparatively limited.

Collaboration duration did not significantly predict any of the three performance quality dimensions (expressiveness: β = 0.139, p = 0.154; ensemble cohesion: β = −0.003, p = 0.977; overall quality: β = −0.133, p = 0.234). Similarly, dyadic mean IRI did not significantly predict any dimension (expressiveness: β = −0.100, p = 0.249; ensemble cohesion: β = −0.032, p = 0.742; overall quality: β = +0.058, p = 0.564). Marginal R2 values ranged from 0.047 to 0.166, and conditional R2 values ranged from 0.101 to 0.166.

Nested model comparisons indicated that adding emotional condition × synchrony index interaction terms (Model B) to the base model (Model A, containing main effects of emotional condition and synchrony indices) did not produce substantive improvements in model fit for any of the three performance dimensions: expressiveness ΔR2 = 0.056, χ2(6) = 8.40, p = 0.210; ensemble cohesion ΔR2 = 0.028, χ2(6) = 3.82, p = 0.701; overall quality ΔR2 = 0.038, χ2(6) = 4.73, p = 0.579. Although the ΔR2 for expressiveness (0.056) exceeded the 0.02 substantive threshold, the χ2 test did not reach significance, indicating that the incremental contribution of the interaction terms was not statistically reliable. Overall, emotional condition did not systematically moderate the synchrony → performance quality pathway, and the predictive effect of HR-CCF on ensemble cohesion was relatively stable across conditions.

Parallel MLMs were constructed using post-performance SAM valence and arousal ratings as Level 1 time-varying continuous predictors to examine their explanatory role in the synchrony-performance quality relationship.

In the expressiveness model, SAM valence significantly predicted expressiveness (β = 0.241, t = 2.27, p = 0.024), whereas arousal did not (β = 0.030, p = 0.736). After controlling for SAM continuous predictors, neither HR-CCF nor EDA-CCF significantly predicted expressiveness (HR-CCF: β = 0.027, p = 0.777; EDA-CCF: β = 0.147, p = 0.158; marginal R2 = 0.124).

In the ensemble cohesion model, the positive predictive effect of HR-CCF on ensemble cohesion remained significant after controlling for SAM continuous predictors (β = 0.256, t = 2.68, p = 0.007), whereas neither valence (β = 0.052, p = 0.576) nor arousal (β = 0.114, p = 0.203) reached significance (marginal R2 = 0.102).

H3 (exploratory) examined whether temporal lag analysis would reveal a unidirectional leader-follower dynamic, whereby changes in one performer's physiological activation systematically preceded those of the other. As shown in , analyses of the peak lag distribution across the 120 trial-level observations revealed an overall mean lag of 0.046 s (SD = 2.99 s), highly concentrated around zero. Performer 1 (P1) led physiologically in 61 trials (51%) and Performer 2 (P2) led in 57 trials (48%), with zero lag observed in 2 trials; the proportions did not differ significantly [χ2(1) = 0.13, p = 0.715]. Within each condition, mean lags were +0.283 s (HA/PV; P2 leading marginally), −0.750 s (HA/NV; P1 leading marginally), −0.267 s (LA/PV), and +0.917 s (LA/NV), but none of the within-condition P1/P2 leadership proportions differed significantly (all p > 0.30). The two a priori criteria for a systematic unidirectional structure (Section 2.8.7) were then evaluated. For criterion (a), only 5 of the 30 duos (16.7%) showed a consistent direction of physiological precedence across all four conditions (2 consistently P2-leading, 3 consistently P1-leading), whereas the remaining 25 duos (83.3%) reversed the sign of their peak lag across conditions. For criterion (b), a one-sample t-test on the duo-level mean peak lags (M = 0.046 s, SD = 1.597) did not differ significantly from zero, t(29) = 0.157, p = 0.876, 95% CI [−0.526, 0.617]. Neither criterion was met: the large majority of duos failed to maintain a consistent leading-following direction across conditions, and the duo-level mean lag was statistically indistinguishable from zero. Because both criteria failed, these results indicate that co-performers do not exhibit a systematic unidirectional physiological leadership structure, but rather a bidirectional, near-simultaneous pattern of coupling that persisted across all four emotional conditions. These results, however, must be interpreted with caution given the relatively homogeneous collaborative experience within the sample; it remains possible that a unidirectional leadership structure may emerge under conditions involving greater role differentiation, more contrasting levels of musical expertise, or pairs with shorter or longer collaborative histories. H3 was not supported under the present conditions.

H4 (exploratory) tested whether IRI trait empathy was positively associated with HR and EDA synchrony, with higher-empathy pairs expected to show greater synchrony. Pearson correlations revealed no significant associations between any of the four IRI subscales and either HR-CCF or EDA-CCF [Perspective Taking: r(HR) = −0.146, p = 0.440, r(EDA) = −0.061, p = 0.750; Empathic Concern: r(HR) = 0.104, p = 0.584, r(EDA) = 0.072, p = 0.706; Fantasy: r(HR) = −0.121, p = 0.526, r(EDA) = −0.217, p = 0.250; Personal Distress: r(HR) = 0.059, p = 0.757, r(EDA) = 0.125, p = 0.511]. When dyadic mean IRI was entered into the MLM framework, it did not significantly predict any performance quality dimension (expressiveness: β = −0.100, p = 0.249; ensemble cohesion: β = −0.032, p = 0.742; overall quality: β = 0.058, p = 0.564; see ). Nested model comparisons showed that adding the IRI × synchrony index interaction terms did not yield substantive improvements in model fit (all ΔR2 <0.02, all likelihood ratio test p > 0.25), indicating that trait empathy did not significantly moderate the synchrony → performance quality pathway. H4 was not supported in the present study; however, these null findings should be interpreted cautiously in light of the restricted variability in IRI scores across the sample (grand mean SD = 1.27), which may have limited statistical power to detect potential moderation effects.

In brief, the four hypotheses fared as follows. H1 was supported: HR and EDA synchrony significantly exceeded the condition-matched surrogate baseline across all conditions, peaking under HA/PV. H2 was only partially supported: HR-CCF predicted ensemble cohesion, whereas the predicted EDA-CCF → expressiveness link was not significant. H3 (exploratory) was not supported: no systematic unidirectional leader–follower structure was detected. H4 (exploratory) was not supported: trait empathy neither correlated with synchrony nor moderated its link to performance quality, although this null is inconclusive given the limited power (Section 4.5).

The present study provided, for the first time in a professional piano duo context, direct evidence for interpersonal physiological synchrony at the level of the autonomic nervous system between co-performing musicians, and showed that one synchrony channel was selectively associated with one dimension of expert-rated performance quality: HR-CCF significantly predicted ensemble cohesion, whereas EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness, so the synchrony → performance-quality link received only partial support. These findings speak directly to the core question identified by  in his review of collaborative musical creativity—by providing objective evidence of ANS-level physiological synchrony, while remaining agnostic about the direction of any emotional transfer.

Across all four emotional conditions, true-pair HR-CCF and EDA-CCF significantly exceeded the surrogate random-pairing baseline with large effect sizes, indicating that the observed cross-individual physiological coupling did not arise merely from the shared musical stimulus and experimental context, but rather reflected genuine ANS co-regulation between performers. Several lower-level processes could in principle inflate cross-individual physiological coupling, including a shared tempo, similar gross body movements, common respiratory entrainment, exposure to the same acoustic and emotional content of an identical score, and a shared physical environment. The present design addresses the most important of these through the structure of the surrogate baseline: because surrogate pairs were formed from performers of different duos who played the very same piece (condition-matched permutation; Section 2.8.2), the surrogate distribution already embodies whatever coupling is attributable to the shared musical structure, tempo, and task. The observation that true-pair synchrony substantially exceeded this condition-matched baseline therefore indicates that the excess coupling cannot be explained by the shared score alone, but reflects coordination specific to the two individuals actually performing together. This does not isolate the source of any shared emotional state—music-driven vs. partner-driven—nor does it establish directional transmission; rather, it demonstrates that genuine interpersonal coupling exists over and above the common stimulus. This conclusion is directionally consistent with the findings of  in a percussion ensemble context—a study that similarly employed cross-pair random pairing as a baseline control and demonstrated that IBI synchrony possessed independent predictive validity beyond behavioral coordination. A key distinction is that physiological synchrony in the present study occurred in a free-performance context unconstrained by an external metronome, and performers were not instructed to synchronize their behavior. The observed ANS coupling therefore reflects a relatively endogenous origin, converging at a cross-level analysis with the argument advanced by  regarding “endogenous interbrain synchrony” in piano duo performers.

The differential effects of the four emotional conditions on synchrony strength provide further corroboration. Peak HR-CCF and EDA-CCF were observed under the HA/PV condition, whereas both reached their nadir under LA/NV. Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons further revealed that valence independently modulated EDA-CCF. This is partially consistent with findings reported by  in a concert audience study, where SCR synchrony was associated with increases in positive affect and HR synchrony with decreases in negative affect—suggesting channel-specific correspondences between distinct ANS channels and emotional dimensions. In the active performance context of the present study, the concurrent peak of both channels under HA/PV may reflect the facilitative effect of high-arousal, positive-valence states on performers‘ outward attentional orientation: when the musical emotional framework is highly congruent with performers' own affective states, their ANS activations may more readily co-vary dynamically.

In terms of channel-specific predictive patterns, HR-CCF significantly predicted ensemble cohesion, while EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness. This predictive pattern is directionally consistent with H2, but received only partial empirical support; the complete dual-channel functional dissociation (i.e., HR-CCF independently predicting ensemble cohesion and EDA-CCF independently predicting expressiveness) awaits verification in larger-sample studies. As specified in the Introduction, the channel-specific mapping was advanced as an exploratory rather than a confirmatory prediction. In the present data only one of the two predicted links was supported (HR-CCF → ensemble cohesion), while EDA-CCF did not predict expressiveness; the dual-channel dissociation should therefore be regarded as a tentative hypothesis for future, adequately powered tests rather than an established effect.

The effects of emotional condition on the expressiveness dimension warrant separate consideration. MLM results showed that, relative to the HA/PV reference condition, the HA/NV condition produced the strongest suppressive effect on expressiveness, followed by the LA/NV condition, while the LA/PV condition did not reach significance. This pattern reveals the central role of the valence dimension in the clarity of emotional communication: under negative-valence conditions—regardless of arousal level—the clarity and affective impact of performers' emotional communication were significantly lower than under the high-arousal positive-valence condition, whereas reducing arousal while maintaining positive valence (LA/PV) did not produce equivalent suppression. This corresponds, at the behavioral level, to the independent contributions of valence and arousal posited in  two-dimensional model: arousal primarily drives physiological synchrony strength, whereas valence more directly influences the overt quality of emotional expression. The dissociation of these two effects provides methodological support for the necessity of the four-quadrant design adopted in the present study—if only diagonal conditions had been selected, the independent effects of valence and arousal could not have been disentangled.

The systematic review and meta-analysis by  demonstrated that sympathetic synchrony is positively associated with task performance, whereas the direction of the association for parasympathetic synchrony is more complex, reflecting distinct contribution pathways of the two channel types to group performance. In the present study, EDA as a purely sympathetic index captures the co-variation of performers‘ emotional intensity dynamics, corresponding to the “clarity and affective impact of emotional communication” perceivable by raters; HR synchrony integrates bidirectional sympathetic and parasympathetic regulatory information, more sensitively reflecting real-time coordination between performers in rhythmic control and dynamic balance, and thereby associating with “the fluency and responsiveness of mutual coordination”—i.e., ensemble cohesion. The non-significant prediction of expressiveness by EDA-CCF may partly reflect insufficient statistical power due to sample size constraints, but may also reflect a more substantive mechanistic issue: under negative-valence conditions, the decline in the clarity of emotional communication is primarily driven by performers' subjective experience of the emotional character of the piece (with SAM valence ratings significantly predicting expressiveness) rather than by the degree of sympathetic synchrony.

These results prompt a reconsideration of a counterintuitive finding reported by : emotional listening—that is, deep immersion in the affective experience of music—was found to reduce physiological synchrony among audience members, whereas structural listening and tonal focus promoted synchrony. The proposed explanation is that extreme emotional immersion draws individuals into highly private experiential states, thereby decoupling them from collective synchrony rhythms. The present study's channel-specific results are logically consistent with this account: pairs exhibiting stronger physiological synchrony were not those with the most intense emotional experiences, but rather those whose attention was more jointly directed toward the musical output itself during performance. Direct support for this interpretation comes from the present data: performers‘ subjective sense of emotional synchrony (PESS) was uncorrelated with either physiological synchrony index (both ns; Section 3.2.1). In other words, the pairs whose autonomic activity co-varied most strongly were not those who felt most emotionally in tune with one another.  identifies this external attentional focus as a key condition for the emergence of group flow, which in turn co-occurs with elevated HR correlations. In sum, the present findings support the theoretical position that physiological synchrony in collaborative performance more closely reflects the joint alignment of performers' attentional and ANS states than the convergence of their subjective emotional investment—two phenomena that are conceptually distinct and empirically separable ().

None of the four IRI subscales showed significant correlations with HR-CCF or EDA-CCF, and nested model comparisons confirmed that model fit did not improve substantively upon addition of IRI interaction terms; H4 was not supported in the present sample, though this null finding carries theoretical value in its own right and should not be dismissed as a simple power issue. A first consideration is conceptual rather than statistical: the IRI indexes a stable, dispositional form of empathy, whereas physiological synchrony is a dynamic state unfolding over minutes. A strong trait-state coupling is therefore not guaranteed a priori, and the absence of one is consistent with this measurement mismatch. Notably, even the more state-proximal measure of perceived emotional synchrony (PESS) was uncorrelated with the physiological indices (Section 3.2.1), reinforcing the view that dispositional empathy is unlikely to map directly onto minute-scale autonomic coupling during performance. A plausible interpretation is that all participants in the present study had a minimum of 6 months of regular collaborative experience; long-term joint rehearsal may have led both partners to develop a highly internalized coordinative schema for each other's musical interpretive tendencies, such that the marginal contribution of trait empathy was substantially reduced by this skill-based, automatized coordination mechanism. This contrasts meaningfully with the findings of , who demonstrated that empathic perspective-taking promoted coordination accuracy in ad hoc pairings of unfamiliar performers—suggesting a clear boundary condition for the moderating role of trait empathy: it may be operative only when partners lack an established coordinative schema.  similarly reported that trait empathy did not consistently predict physiological synchrony in an empathic self-disclosure context, further indicating that the relationship between empathic disposition and ANS coupling is inherently context-dependent.

Notably, collaboration duration did not significantly predict any of the three performance quality dimensions in the present sample. This result may reflect the limited variance in collaboration duration within the sample, with insufficient between-pair variability in collaboration history to produce detectable differences in performance quality. This does not imply that collaborative experience is theoretically irrelevant to performance quality; rather, it suggests that the range of the present sample constrained the effective examination of this variable's effect. Variability in dyadic mean IRI was similarly restricted, with limited between-pair variability after aggregation at the pair level. The moderating effects of both individual difference variables warrant examination in studies employing broader sampling ranges.

The near-equal physiological leadership proportions between the two performers, the lack of within-duo directional consistency across conditions, and the high concentration of peak lags around zero collectively indicate that no persistent unidirectional physiological leadership structure exists between piano duo performers with established collaborative experience; H3 was not supported under the present conditions. It is possible, however, that directional asymmetries may emerge in dyads with greater differences in musical expertise or under conditions of more explicit role assignment.  did record role-related asymmetric heartbeat synchrony patterns in a dyadic alternating tapping task, but their study employed an explicit role-assignment paradigm—a fundamentally different context from the intrinsic, mutually adaptive coordination observed in the present study.  similarly observed bidirectional rather than unidirectional synchrony in free-play percussion ensembles, interpreting this as indicative of mutual adaptation among group members. In the present study, peak lags converging toward zero most likely reflect that familiar collaborators hold nearly identical anticipatory representations of phrase trajectories and emotional turning points, such that the two performers' ANS responses occur virtually simultaneously rather than sequentially along a stimulus-response chain. This contrasts sharply with the asymmetric leadership structures commonly observed in mother-infant synchrony research, suggesting that highly mature adult collaborative relationships may correspond to a relatively symmetric mode of emotional co-regulation—a hypothesis worthy of systematic examination in future research through comparison of pairs at varying levels of collaborative maturity.

Two further considerations help explain why a systematic leader-follower structure was unlikely to emerge here. First, the physiological signals under study evolve on a relatively slow time scale. Leading-following relationships in ensemble performance have frequently been detected at the level of discrete, rapidly unfolding events such as note onsets (), and also in body sway, which fluctuates more slowly than note onsets yet still faster than emotional states (). Heart rate, and the emotional states it partly indexes, change more gradually still than either of these signals. Any directional precedence in emotional co-regulation would therefore be expected to surface only intermittently—at isolated phrase transitions or emotional turning points—rather than as a stable, piece-wide asymmetry detectable in averaged peak lags. Second, leading and following in ensemble playing carry a strong social dimension; emotional precedence, in particular, may depend more on interpersonal and personality dynamics within a duo than on the musical division of labor. Consistent with this, and as noted above, part allocation was not an experimentally defined variable in the present study (Section 2.8.7), so the present null directionality finding should not be read as evidence about melody-vs.-accompaniment leadership specifically, but only about the absence of a fixed physiological precedence between the two performers. Peak-lag estimates are, moreover, sensitive to filtering and smoothing choices and need not reflect interpersonal influence, since both performers may respond with different latencies to shared musical events; the directionality results should be read with this in mind.

The primary theoretical contributions of the present study operate at three levels. First, it provides the first empirically rigorous demonstration, with strict surrogate control, of ANS-level physiological synchrony in collaborative piano performance, addressing the core gap identified by  regarding the unconfirmed existence of emotional transmission in ensemble playing. Second, it extends the endogenous interbrain synchrony framework of  to the level of the autonomic nervous system, and reveals functional specificity between HR and EDA channels in predicting distinct performance quality dimensions, providing finer-grained empirical evidence for understanding the mechanisms of physiological synchrony. Third, building on the synchrony → group performance pathway established by , it represents the first inclusion of emotional conditions as moderating variables in a musical performance context, while the null results illuminate the substitutive role of skill-driven automatized coordination mechanisms in displacing trait empathy's moderating contribution.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. As demonstrated by , HRV indices show substantially reduced measurement accuracy in dynamic interactive states compared to resting conditions; given that hand and arm movements in piano performance far exceed those in conversational settings, the HRV-related results of the present study should be interpreted with caution and should not be overgeneralized; future studies may address this limitation by including dedicated resting-state baseline recordings matched in duration to the performance segments. Before the performance task, participants completed a 5-min quiet adaptation period after sensor attachment to allow signal stabilization and quality inspection; however, this period was not retained or analyzed as a dedicated resting-state physiological baseline. Accordingly, the present study did not include an independent resting-state EDA baseline against which performance-related EDA artifacts or responses could be systematically compared, and the reported sub-5% artifact rate should be interpreted in that light; future studies should record dedicated resting baselines before and after performance to quantify movement-related effects on signal quality. A further measurement limitation concerns the EDA montage: because Ag/AgCl electrodes were placed on the volar pads of the index and middle fingers of one hand that nonetheless contributes to playing, the sensors may have affected tactile feedback or comfort to some degree. Participant comfort was not systematically assessed, and future studies should either quantify any such interference or adopt alternative electrode sites (e.g., the medial phalanges or the foot) less likely to interfere with performance. The sample was also restricted to current conservatory students, limiting the ecological validity of the conclusions; the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference regarding the direction of the synchrony-performance quality relationship, and whether synchrony is an antecedent, concomitant, or consequence of high-quality performance requires clarification through longitudinal or experimentally controlled designs. Future research may profitably combine the ANS indices of the present study with EEG hyperscanning (following the paradigm of ) to simultaneously obtain neural and autonomic synchrony maps within the same performance context; systematic comparison of pairs at varying levels of collaborative maturity may also be used to test the theoretical hypothesis of “collaborative maturity and the symmetrization of physiological synchrony directionality”; and the introduction of improvised vs. score-reading performance conditions would help further disentangle endogenous emotional coordination from shared sensorimotor contributions in ensemble synchrony. Systematic test-retest reliability assessment of the SAM was not conducted prior to the experiment; future studies should complete scale temporal stability verification before the main data collection.

SAM ratings were completed retrospectively following each piece, and performers' recall of their in-performance emotional states may have been affected by memory decay and emotional smoothing effects, thereby failing to fully capture the moment-to-moment emotional dynamics during performance. Future studies may consider incorporating continuous in-performance valence-arousal rating devices (e.g., a continuous dial rating system) to track performers' real-time affective states at higher temporal resolution and align these with the physiological synchrony time series on a moment-by-moment basis.

Regarding statistical power, the sensitivity analysis reported in Section 2.8.1 indicates that the pair-level design (N = 30) was sensitive only to relatively large Level-2 effects. The empathy-synchrony correlations and IRI × synchrony interactions observed here fell well below these detectable thresholds; the null results for H4, together with the null PESS-synchrony correlations, are therefore most appropriately interpreted as inconclusive with respect to small or moderate effects rather than as evidence of their absence.

The four pieces were matched on emotional target but not on technical difficulty; because tempo, textural density, and motor load of real piano-duet repertoire tend to co-vary with arousal, the high-arousal pieces were also faster and more technically demanding. Condition effects on synchrony and on rated quality should therefore be interpreted as the combined product of emotional arousal, musical structure, and performance load, rather than as effects of emotional arousal in isolation.

Given the 2–3 min duration of each piece, the 30-s sliding window yielded an average of only 4–6 valid CCF estimation windows per piece; the limited number of windows may affect the precision of trial-level synchrony index estimates, and future studies should consider using longer performance excerpts or shorter sliding windows to improve the stability of CCF estimates.

Finally, partners practiced the pieces individually and performed each only once after a brief warm-up, without a dedicated joint-rehearsal phase; the limited opportunity to co-develop an expressive interpretation may have constrained, in particular, the expressiveness ratings, and future designs could incorporate a joint-rehearsal stage to examine its effect on both performance quality and physiological coupling.

The present study provides direct empirical evidence that interpersonal physiological synchrony at the autonomic nervous system level occurs between co-performing professional pianists, with HR-CCF and EDA-CCF indices significantly exceeding cross-pair surrogate baselines with large effect sizes across all four emotional conditions. Synchrony strength was highest under the high-arousal, positive-valence condition and was independently modulated by both valence and arousal. Negative-valence conditions selectively suppressed expressiveness scores regardless of arousal level, while HR-CCF independently predicted ensemble cohesion; the corresponding EDA-CCF-expressiveness association did not reach significance, and the hypothesized complete dual-channel functional dissociation received only partial support. Trait empathy and collaboration duration did not significantly predict synchrony or performance quality within the present sample, and no consistent leader-follower directionality was identified. These directional and empathy-related questions were addressed as exploratory analyses; given the limited pair-level sample, their null results are best regarded as inconclusive rather than as evidence against the existence of such effects. These findings address a previously unverified question regarding whether interpersonal physiological synchrony reflecting shared emotional states arises in ensemble performance and offer partial physiological evidence for the functional differentiation of HR and EDA synchrony channels in ensemble emotional coordination.

psychology.title: Generative artificial intelligence and terminology work: structural associations of prompt strategy preference, cognitive load, and self-efficacy
psychology.abstract: The widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in knowledge-intensive domains requires continuous adjustment of human cognitive patterns. In terminology work, aligning strict semantic standards against the non-deterministic output of large language models (LLMs) is closely intertwined with workers' subjective cognitive load. This study examines the structural associations among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load, while testing the potential moderating role of professional experience.Based on cross-sectional survey data from 1,760 practitioners using LLMs for terminology tasks, structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) were employed. SEM evaluated the linear structural associations among prompt strategy preference, self-efficacy, and cognitive load, while LPA identified behavioral user profiles. Multi-group equivalence testing was further conducted across three career stages (novices, intermediates, and experts).Prompt strategy preference is significantly and negatively associated with subjective cognitive load, with AI interaction self-efficacy serving as a significant mediator in this structural relationship. LPA identified three distinct user profiles (low, medium, and high strategy use), with the high strategy group exhibiting the lowest cognitive load and highest self-efficacy. Multi-group equivalence tests indicated no statistically significant moderation across experience cohorts, demonstrating structural invariance of the core model across career stages.From the perspective of cognitive ergonomics, upfront prompt structuring is structurally linked to downstream cognitive offloading and psychological buffering. These findings provide empirical evidence for individual cognitive resilience during human-AI collaboration in the generative AI era.
psychology.text:
The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive domains not only changes the workflow of information generation but also imposes new requirements on the cognitive patterns of human workers (; ). In this digital transformation, terminology work emerges as a highly representative frontline scenario. Terminology work typically involves precise concept extraction, multilingual alignment, and domain knowledge definition, which highly depend on semantic precision and contextual constraints. As generative artificial intelligence intervenes in such professional tasks, practitioners have begun to delegate parts of retrieval and text validation to intelligent systems. However, the probabilistic and inherently non-deterministic output characteristics of LLMs create a distinct “cognitive tension” against the strict determinism required in this domain. This tension forces workers to continuously evaluate the algorithm's internal generative logic and repeatedly formulate prompts to correct the “knowledge hallucinations” it produces in the process of obtaining compliant terminology (). Therefore, terminology work constitutes an ideal research context because its strict constraint requirements make workers' cognitive load highly sensitive to the quality of human-AI instruction interactions. Observing such human-AI collaborative scenarios reveals that transitioning from previous linear text queries to iterative dialogues with models improves initial generation efficiency while deriving new mental effort on the operator's end caused by uncertainty.

Currently, mainstream research in the fields of artificial intelligence and human-computer interaction mostly focuses on system performance evaluation, exploring which prompt frameworks can optimize machine-side output accuracy (; ; ; ). However, systematic empirical evidence regarding the psychological states of human executors remains profoundly inadequate. First, methodologically, existing human-computer interaction studies predominantly rely on small-sample usability experiments or qualitative interviews, lacking large-scale quantitative evidence on users' cognitive states. Second, theoretically, current research over-relies on Technology Acceptance Models (TAM), focusing mainly on adoption intention while failing to deeply examine the cognitive processing costs borne by operators. Third, there is a variable selection bias toward objective efficiency and usability metrics, neglecting operators' psychological load and self-efficacy beliefs (). In human-machine systems, looking solely at the objective indicators of the tool side while ignoring the user's subjective stress makes it difficult to comprehensively measure the actual ergonomic efficacy of intelligent tools in modern workplaces. Faced with the unreliability of LLM response mechanisms, the changes in mental burden and the building of self-confidence when human users choose interaction strategies constitute research topics worthy of further investigation in the process of digital transformation.

To systematically address these research gaps, this study proposes three specific research questions: (1) Does prompt strategy preference exhibit a stable negative association with operators' subjective cognitive load? (2) Does AI interaction self-efficacy mediate this structural relationship? (3) Does the traditional professional dimension, years of experience, moderate these associations? In introducing these questions, prompt strategy preference is selected as the core independent variable because it represents the user's primary proactive method to constrain model uncertainty. Subjective cognitive load captures the fundamental mental cost of the human-AI tension, while self-efficacy is explicitly tested to uncover the psychological mechanism transforming operational strategy into cognitive relief. Distinct from research models that evaluate overall technology acceptance, this study aims to verify the co-variation direction of prompt strategy preference and subjective cognitive load through cross-sectional data observation. Specifically, this study explores the process of extracting latent user profiles through latent profile analysis (LPA) to understand the systematic differences in psychological load levels among groups with different strategy usage characteristics. In addition, this study examines whether the traditional dimension of professional background, “years of experience,” can play the expected buffering role against cognitive load within this structural mechanism, or whether it produces a skill-leveling effect.

Using a large-sample survey of 1,760 relevant practitioners, this study attempts to verify the effect of “cognitive offloading” in prompt strategies, provide quantitative evidence for establishing human-centered AI-assisted collaboration norms, and support the language services industry in optimizing employee ergonomic support strategies during the process of intelligent transformation.

Cognitive load is one of the core indicators for evaluating task complexity and system usability. In the NASA-TLX evaluation system, cognitive load is usually composed of dimensions such as mental demand, temporal demand, effort, and frustration (; ). In terminology alignment and generation tasks, workers need not only to mobilize their own professional knowledge but also to plan prompt inputs to the LLM in working memory while continuously evaluating the consistency between model outputs and domain standards. This dual-processing process may constitute a high subjective cognitive load. For example, when extracting and translating a highly contextualized concept like “few-shot prompting” into a target language, a worker must not only retrieve linguistic equivalents but also instruct the LLM to adhere to specific domain glossary constraints. Without clear upfront instructions, the LLM might generate a literal but professionally inaccurate translation, forcing the user into a highly taxing cycle of subsequent manual corrections.

When using external information tools, individuals often externalize parts of memory, computation, or planning tasks to the tools to preserve limited cognitive resources (; ). This mechanism is commonly referred to as cognitive offloading in cognitive science (). In LLM-based interactions, specific prompt strategies—such as persona prompting, few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, or setting clear constraints (; )—can be viewed as operational ways to guide the model to share reasoning and screening tasks. When workers tend to use structured prompt strategies, although they need to invest additional instruction design costs in the early stage of the task, these strategies may reduce the load mechanistically by imposing explicit boundary parameters on the algorithm. By defining specific contexts and formatting rules, structured prompts function as externalized logical scaffolds. This structural mapping process significantly minimizes the algorithmic search space and generative uncertainty, thereby sharply reducing the cognitive resources required for subsequent repeated corrections, ambiguity resolutions, and model hallucination checks throughout the entire task cycle. As recent empirical research indicates, compared to traditional unassisted trial-and-error, interactions driven by generative AI and precise instructions can effectively reduce the operator's cognitive load at the initial stage of multi-task divergence and provide significant creative psychological support (). Therefore, this study expects a negative association between prompt strategy preference and subjective cognitive load.

H1: The overall level of prompt strategy preference is significantly and negatively associated with the subjective cognitive load of terminology workers.

In addition to the overall correlation between variables, investigating the behavioral heterogeneity within the subject population helps to understand generative AI usage patterns in more detail. The actual application of technical tools is usually not uniformly distributed, and users often rely on different combinations of strategies (). In terminology workflows, some subjects may use LLMs as extended search tools, employing only simple natural language instructions; other subjects may tend to adopt more complex interaction methods, such as multi-turn iteration, persona setting, few-shot examples, and constraint prompting ().

This difference in operating habits suggests that there may be several latent classes with different strategy usage patterns in the sample. Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) can identify groups with high internal homogeneity and obvious differences between classes based on the subject's score patterns on multiple continuous indicators. This study further hypothesizes that different latent profiles of prompt strategies may also show significant differences in average subjective cognitive load. Therefore, the following exploratory hypotheses are proposed:

H2a: When terminology workers interact with LLMs, their prompt strategy preferences can be identified as several latent profiles with significant differences.

H2b: There are significant differences in subjective cognitive load among different latent profiles of prompt strategies.

On the basis of understanding the relationship between prompt strategies and cognitive load, self-efficacy provides an important perspective for explaining the user's internal psychological mechanisms. According to social cognitive theory (), an individual's judgment of whether they can organize and execute necessary actions to achieve goals in a specific context is an important factor affecting behavioral choices and emotional responses. In LLM workflows characterized by uncertain outputs, pure domain knowledge does not necessarily guarantee stable task performance. Users also need the ability to adjust prompts, interpret system feedback, and correct model outputs. This study defines “AI interaction self-efficacy” in this context as the user's confidence in their ability to effectively control, modify, and utilize AI outputs.

Individuals who tend to use high-level prompt strategies may develop a higher sense of system mastery through repeatedly obtaining effective feedback. The specific psychological mechanism through which self-efficacy mitigates subjective cognitive load relies on the proactive control over unreliability (). When users efficiently utilize structured prompts, the resulting predictable outputs alleviate the uncertainty-related anxiety inherent in black-box AI tools. A high level of self-efficacy allows individuals to confidently interpret system feedback and rapidly distinguish between human instruction errors and inherent algorithmic limitations. Consequently, it improves decision-making efficiency, empowering them to strategically abandon ineffective trial-and-error attempts without experiencing severe psychological frustration. This cognitive clarity and reduced anxiety ultimately transmit into a significantly lower subjective cognitive load. Accordingly, the following hypotheses are proposed:

H3: Prompt strategy preference is significantly and positively associated with AI interaction self-efficacy.

H4: AI interaction self-efficacy plays a mediating role between prompt strategy preference and cognitive load.

Traditional cognitive load theory holds that long-term professional experience helps form stable domain schemata, thereby reducing individuals' cognitive load in complex tasks. In the context of using conventional computer-aided translation (CAT) tools, senior experts usually exhibit a cognitive load advantage in task processing due to their stronger schema recognition capabilities and domain knowledge reserves ().

However, in generative AI scenarios, there may be boundaries to this rule. The output of LLMs does not completely follow the matching logic of traditional terminology databases or structured corpora; the generated results may be grammatically fluent but inconsistent with domain standards or conceptual frameworks. Therefore, when facing model hallucinations or semantic deviations, experts' original domain experience may not be directly translated into algorithmic interaction advantages (). This discrepancy hints at a potential “skill-leveling effect,” where the traditional cognitive advantages of expert schemata are disrupted by algorithmic opacity. If years of experience fail to significantly moderate the relationship between prompt strategies and cognitive load, it may suggest that the use of generative AI has, to some extent, weakened the role of traditional experience in buffering cognitive load. Based on this, the following hypothesis is proposed:

H5: Years of experience moderates the structural relationships in the context of prompt strategy usage, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load, such that the mitigating effect of prompt strategies on cognitive load is stronger for senior workers than for novices.

Integrating the above theoretical background discussion and the development of various specific hypotheses into an organically integrated theoretical model, this study constructs a comprehensive theoretical conceptual model containing direct effects (grounded in Cognitive Load Theory), mediating mechanisms (explained by Social Cognitive Theory), and boundary moderating effects (framed by Cognitive Schema Theory) (as shown in ).

This cross-sectional study aims to examine the prompt strategy usage characteristics and cognitive responses of terminology working groups in actual human-computer collaborative tasks. The target population was defined as professionals with practical experience in terminology extraction and professional translation, or with academic backgrounds in linguistics and computational linguistics. To ensure the alignment of the data with the research context, the inclusion criteria for the survey were restricted to: subjects must have actually used large language models, such as ChatGPT, Claude, etc., within the past 3 months to complete domain-specific terminology alignment, definition delineation, or related text validation tasks.

Data were distributed through an online survey platform and targeted professional language service networks (e.g., translation forums, terminology practitioner communities, and university alumni groups), during which a total of 1,920 initial questionnaires were retrieved. To reduce invalid responses and insufficient attention that self-administered questionnaires might bring, this study set up multiple data screening procedures during the implementation process. First, the system background automatically excluded samples with abnormal response durations (e.g., completion time of less than 120 s). Second, the researchers screened out straight-lining response patterns that showed a single fixed value on continuous Likert scales (defined as providing identical answers to 10 or more consecutive items). Finally, forced attention check questions (e.g., “Please select ‘Strongly Disagree' for this item to confirm your attention”) were embedded in the questionnaire, and those who failed to answer as required were excluded from the final analysis. After the above strict cleaning procedures, this study excluded 160 invalid questionnaires and finally obtained 1,760 valid samples, with a valid response rate of 91.67%. To ensure methodological transparency, the complete statistical syntax (including SPSS, AMOS paths, and Mplus code for LPA) has been comprehensive documented in .

The demographic characteristics of the valid sample show a distinct pattern of knowledge-intensive industries. Female subjects accounted for 55.63%, and male subjects accounted for 41.76%. In terms of educational background, those with a master's degree or higher accounted for 95.23%. Regarding work experience, the novice group with less than 3 years of experience comprised 837 people (47.56%), the intermediate group with 3 to 5 years comprised 490 people (27.84%), and the expert group with 5 or more years comprised 433 people (24.60%). This distribution provides a relatively balanced sample base for the subsequent multi-group structural equation modeling test, as detailed in .

Demographic characteristics of the participants.

All measurement tools used to evaluate latent variables were based on standardized questionnaires in the existing literature and were contextually revised to fit generative AI interaction scenarios. A 7-point Likert scale was uniformly adopted, with a value of 1 representing “strongly disagree” or “extremely low” and a value of 7 representing “strongly agree” or “extremely high”. The full items of all scales and demographic questions have been attached to the supplementary materials (see ).

This study developed the PESP-T scale based on the operational principles in algorithmic prompt optimization foundation corpus research by () and (). Prior to the formal large-scale survey, the scale underwent a rigorous development procedure. The initial item pool was evaluated by a panel of three computational linguistics experts to ensure content validity. Subsequently, a pilot study (N = 120) was conducted. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) on the pilot data confirmed that all seven strategy items loaded strongly onto a single dominant factor (explaining 65.4% of the total variance). Consequently, these seven strategies were identified as reflective indicators measuring an underlying unidimensional construct of strategy preference: persona setting (P1), few-shot guidance (P2), chain of thought (P3), corpus-driven (P4), iterative feedback (P5), constraint instructions (P6), and structured instructions (P7). For example, for dimension P3, the item is phrased as: “I will ask the model to show its reasoning steps before giving an answer”; dimension P6 is defined as: “I will clearly list prohibited items or boundary conditions to follow specific domain standards.”

Subjective cognitive load was measured using the Raw NASA-TLX scale revised by (). The scale comprises six single-item dimensions designed to capture different aspects of the operator's subjective experience: mental demand (N1), temporal demand (N2), effort (N3), frustration level (N4), physical demand (N5), and self-reported performance (N6). In this study, the task descriptions within the items were systematically contextualized to reflect the LLM-assisted terminology processing workflow. For instance, the mental demand (N1) item was framed as: “How much mental and cognitive activity was required to formulate prompts, comprehend AI outputs, and make professional judgements throughout the interaction?” Since a high score in self-reported performance (N6) originally represented high satisfaction (which is opposite to the direction of distress/load), this item was reverse-scored (computed as 8–original score) prior to statistics, ensuring that higher scores across all items uniformly indicate greater subjective cognitive load. Following the established protocol for the unweighted Raw-TLX (), the overall subjective cognitive load was derived by calculating the arithmetic mean of all six items. While the self-reported performance dimension captures subjective task outcomes rather than pure mental exertion, its reverse-scored inclusion is maintained in this study. This unified aggregation aligns with standard human-computer interaction practices, as the user's perception of poor performance and cumulative physical fatigue often directly exacerbates the overall psychological strain experienced during unpredictable AI interactions. Furthermore, to ensure the robustness of the cognitive load measurement, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by excluding the physical demand (N5) and self-reported performance (N6) items. The structural model results utilizing this adjusted four-item NASA-TLX construct remained consistent with the primary findings (the detailed sensitivity analysis outputs are provided in ).

To control for relevant external factors and test the mediating mechanisms, this study introduced several auxiliary measures. AI interaction self-efficacy (SE1–SE5) was adapted from  Computer Self-Efficacy Scale, with a representative item being: “I am confident in correcting model outputs by redesigning instructions.” Terminology competence (C1–C5) was adapted from studies by () and () to measure subjects' mastery of domain concept networks. Task complexity (T1–T4) was revised based on  task complexity framework. System trust (TR1–TR5) was adapted from the Human-Computer Trust Scale by (), where items regarding concerns about algorithmic hallucinations were reverse-scored according to the scale's direction. Perceived output quality (Q1–Q5) was revised based on  Information Systems Success Model.

This study adopts a multi-stage statistical modeling scheme. First, descriptive statistics, data cleaning, and two-tailed Pearson correlation analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0. Second, to identify the cohort heterogeneity in prompt strategy usage patterns, Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) was conducted on the scores of each PESP-T item, and the optimal number of classes was determined based on information criteria, entropy, class interpretability, and model parsimony. Subsequently, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare the mean differences in cognitive load and AI interaction self-efficacy among different latent classes.

Methodologically, structural equation modeling (SEM) and LPA were employed as two orthogonal but highly complementary analytical tracks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the core construct. While SEM treats prompt strategy preference as a continuous latent variable to evaluate the degree of its linear structural associations with cognitive load and self-efficacy (a variable-centered approach), LPA treats the strategy items as manifest variables to identify distinct behavioral types within the population (a person-centered approach). Combining these two theoretically compatible treatments effectively allows this study to simultaneously map the overarching transmission mechanism and uncover the operational heterogeneity of different user cohorts.

In the structural relationship testing phase, AMOS was used to construct a structural equation model (SEM), and model parameters were estimated using the maximum likelihood method, with relevant covariates systematically controlled to ensure the robustness of the main paths. To test the mediating effect, this study used 5,000 Bootstrap resamples to calculate the indirect effect and its confidence intervals (). Finally, using work experience as the grouping variable, a Multi-Group Structural Equation Model (Multi-Group SEM) was constructed to test whether there were differences in core paths between experience groups by comparing the fit differences between the unconstrained model and the path-constrained model.

Before hypothesis testing, this study first tested the reliability and validity of the core measurement tools. Preliminary sample suitability tests showed that the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) value of the total sample was 0.907, and Bartlett's test of sphericity reached an extremely significant level (χ2 = 25591.08, df = 666, p < 0.001), indicating that the sample data were highly suitable for latent variable factor extraction. In terms of multicollinearity screening, the variance inflation factor (VIF) among independent variables was at 1.241 (for Perceived Output Quality), which is far below the conventional test threshold of 5.0 ().

The measurement model of Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) showed good structural characteristics. Specifically, all standardized factor loadings for the measurement items ranged from 0.67 to 0.77 (all significant at p < 0.001), indicating strong indicator reliability. Combining the detailed test reports in , it can be seen that the Cronbach's α and composite reliability (CR) of each core scale were far higher than the conventional standard of 0.70, showing excellent internal consistency; meanwhile, the average variance extracted (AVE) of most latent variables reached or exceeded the threshold of 0.50. Although the AVE for Task Complexity (T, AVE = 0.432) and Subjective Cognitive Load (N, AVE = 0.476) fell slightly below the 0.50 threshold, their Composite Reliability (CR) values (0.753 and 0.845) were well above 0.70, which justifies acceptable convergent validity according to (). Regarding discriminant validity,  and  demonstrates that the square root of each construct's AVE was larger than any of its longitudinal or transverse correlations, satisfying the () criterion. Furthermore, to provide a more rigorous assessment, the Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio (HTMT) values across all latent variable pairs were evaluated. The maximum HTMT value obtained was strictly below the conservative threshold of 0.85 (), providing robust confirmation of discriminant validity.

Since the data in this study came from self-report questionnaires at a single point in time, common method bias may exist. Harman's single-factor test showed that the variance explained by the first factor in the unrotated principal component analysis was 17.96%, which is lower than the common threshold of 50%. Furthermore, to provide a more robust structural assessment beyond Harman's test, this study conducted an Unmeasured Latent Method Construct (ULMC) sensitivity analysis by introducing a common method factor into the CFA model. The comparison indicated that adding this method factor did not yield a significant improvement in model fit (Baseline model: χ2 = 972.8, df = 608; ULMC model: χ2 = 959.0, df = 607; ΔCFI = 0.003, ΔRMSEA = 0.002, both strictly below the 0.01 threshold). Meanwhile, all substantive trait factor loadings remained highly significant with negligible changes in their magnitudes (Δλ < 0.05). Therefore, common method bias does not pose a serious threat ().

To examine the group heterogeneity of terminology workers in prompt strategy usage, this study conducted a Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) on the 7 items of the prompt strategy preference scale. After comparing the 2-class, 3-class, and 4-class models sequentially, the results showed that as the number of classes increased, both AIC and aBIC decreased, with the 4-class model having the lowest AIC and aBIC. However, the 3-class model had the highest entropy (Entropy = 0.865). The likelihood ratio test results showed that the fit of the 3-class model was significantly improved compared to the 2-class model (LMR-LRT p = 0.012; BLRT p < 0.001), while the 4-class model did not reach statistical significance in LMR-LRT or BLRT compared to the 3-class model (p > 0.05). Considering information criteria, entropy, classification clarity, and model parsimony comprehensively (), this study finally selected the 3-class model as the follow-up analysis scheme. The detailed model comparison results are shown in .

Although the 4-class model had the lowest AIC and aBIC, the 3-class model had higher entropy, clearer classification distinction, and better theoretical interpretability. Therefore, this study chose the 3-class model as the final classification scheme.

According to the mean score patterns of the three classes of subjects on the 7 prompt strategy indicators, this study named them the low strategy use group, medium strategy use group, and high strategy use group, respectively. The low strategy use group contained 470 people (26.7%); the medium strategy use group contained 875 people (49.7%); and the high strategy use group contained 415 people (23.6%). From the class characteristics, the low strategy use group rarely used structured strategies such as persona setting, example guidance, chain-of-thought prompting, and constraint instructions; the medium strategy use group was close to the midpoint of the scale on most indicators; and the high strategy use group exhibited high usage levels on all prompt strategy indicators. The score patterns of the three groups on each prompt strategy item are shown in .

One-way ANOVA was further used to compare the differences in subjective cognitive load and AI interaction self-efficacy among the three groups. To display the mean differences and data distribution density of psychological characteristics among people with different strategy preferences more comprehensively, this study plotted a Raincloud Plot (as shown in ). The analysis results confirmed that there were significant differences among the three groups in subjective cognitive load (F(2, 1757) = 19.07, p < 0.001) and AI interaction self-efficacy (F(2, 1757) = 52.67, p < 0.001). As the distribution diagram visually shows, the low strategy use group bore the highest cognitive load and had the lowest sense of system control efficacy; conversely, the high strategy use group not only had a significantly lower center of gravity in cognitive load distribution but also exhibited the highest overall level of AI interaction self-efficacy.

Overall, the LPA results support H2a, there are distinguishable latent profiles of terminology workers in prompt strategy usage; the ANOVA results further support H2b, there are significant differences in subjective cognitive load among different prompt strategy usage types. Meanwhile, the differences in self-efficacy between classes also provide a preliminary basis for subsequent mediation model analysis.

The mean of prompt strategy preference was M = 4.10, SD = 1.01; the mean of subjective cognitive load was M = 3.91, SD = 1.06; and the mean of AI interaction self-efficacy was M = 4.19, SD = 1.08.

Correlation analysis results showed that prompt strategy preference was significantly and negatively correlated with subjective cognitive load, r = −0.156, p < 0.001, and significantly and positively correlated with AI interaction self-efficacy, r = 0.273, p < 0.001. AI interaction self-efficacy was also significantly and negatively correlated with subjective cognitive load, r = −0.242, p < 0.001. Task complexity (T) was significantly and positively correlated with subjective cognitive load (r = 0.244, p < 0.001), suggesting that more complex terminology tasks are associated with greater cognitive strain. These results are highly consistent with the theoretical expectations of this study and provide a preliminary basis for the subsequent mediation model test.

To test the structural relationships between the core latent variables and the mediating role of AI interaction self-efficacy, this study constructed a structural equation model (SEM) using the Maximum Likelihood estimation method. To ensure the rigor of the estimations in addressing potential confounding effects, both unadjusted and fully adjusted models were concurrently evaluated. In the adjusted model, all relevant demographic and task-contextual covariates (specifically controlling for age, education, task complexity, and system trust concerns) were systematically retained and evaluated to ensure the robustness of the main paths. The results indicated that the inclusion of covariates significantly contributed to the overall explanatory power, accounting for substantial variance in the endogenous variables (e.g., R2 = 0.084 for AI Interaction Self-Efficacy, and R2 = 0.132 for Subjective Cognitive Load). More importantly, the direction and significance of the core structural parameters and total effects remained exceptionally stable between the unadjusted and adjusted models. To determine the optimal theoretical framework, this study compared Hypothesized Model A (including both the direct path from prompt strategy preference to cognitive load and the mediating path through self-efficacy) with Competing Model B (constraining the direct path from prompt strategy preference to cognitive load to zero; i.e., a full mediation model) (the goodness-of-fit comparison is shown in ). The results showed that all fit indices of Hypothesized Model A reached an excellent fit to the data when evaluated against conventional strict thresholds (e.g., χ2/df < 3.0, CFI ≥ 0.95, TLI ≥ 0.95, and RMSEA < 0.05), and the overall fit was significantly better than Competing Model B. Therefore, this study accepted Model A as the final explanatory model, and all subsequent parameters are reported based on the fully adjusted Model A.

Comparison of structural equation model goodness-of-fit.

The standardized path coefficients and hypothesis testing results of the final Model A are detailed in . The analysis confirmed that prompt strategy preference has a significant positive predictive effect on AI interaction self-efficacy (supporting H3); while AI interaction self-efficacy significantly and negatively predicts subjective cognitive load. After controlling for the mediating effect of self-efficacy, the direct path coefficient from prompt strategy preference to subjective cognitive load remains significantly negative (supporting H1).

For the mediating effect (H4), this study used the bias-corrected non-parametric Bootstrap method (5,000 resamples) to calculate the indirect effect. The data showed that the indirect effect of prompt strategy preference on reducing subjective cognitive load through AI interaction self-efficacy was significantly negative, and its 95% confidence interval strictly excluded 0 (95% CI: [−0.078, −0.046]). This indicates that AI interaction self-efficacy plays a significant partial mediating role between the two, verifying H4.

To present the above path relationships more intuitively this study further graphically represented the numerical results of the model (as shown in ). In the structural path model, the core independent variable “prompt strategy preference (P)” directly mitigates “subjective cognitive load (N)” (β = −0.101, p < 0.001), while simultaneously exerting an indirect effect mediated by “AI interaction self-efficacy (SE)” (β = −0.061, p < 0.001). This result indicates that the core “strategy-efficacy-load” transmission mechanism constructed in this study still has solid robustness and explanatory power after excluding the interference of external multi-source confounding variables.

To explore whether professional experience acts as a boundary constraint within this conceptual framework (testing H5), the sample was classified into three distinct stages based on years of terminology-related work or study: Novices (less than 3 years, N = 837), Intermediates (3 to 5 years, N = 490), and Experts (5 years and above, N = 433, by merging the 5–10 years and more than 10 years cohorts). A Multi-Group Path Analysis was subsequently constructed across these three career stages to examine the equivalence of the structural path coefficients. Prior to evaluating these path differences, a multi-group CFA was routinely performed to confirm measurement invariance (MI) across the three cohorts. The sequential tests confirmed strong invariance, as the incremental changes in model fit indices safely remained within the conventional thresholds (e.g., ΔCFI < 0.01, ΔRMSEA < 0.015). Detailed configural, metric, and scalar model-fit results are reported in Section 8 of . With the conceptual equivalence firmly established across novices, intermediates, and experts, the structural path comparisons were reliably interpreted.

The standardized path estimates and group comparison results are presented in . As indicated, the structural relationship patterns revealed varying within-group significance levels in the direct pathway from prompt strategy preference to cognitive load. First, the positive relationship between prompt strategy preference and AI self-efficacy was robust and highly significant for Novices (β = 0.279, p < 0.001), Intermediates (β = 0.297, p < 0.001), and Experts (β = 0.306, p < 0.001). Second, self-efficacy significantly mitigated cognitive load across all three groups. However, the direct association of prompt strategy preference on cognitive load was only statistically significant for Novices (β = −0.090, p = 0.012) and Intermediates (β = −0.130, p = 0.007), whereas it became non-significant for Experts (β = −0.080, p = 0.156).
