psychology.title: The construction and validation of the Rula wellbeing scale
psychology.abstract: Psychotherapy outcome research has traditionally emphasized symptom reduction, yet psychotherapy may also enhance eudaimonic wellbeing, including meaning, purpose, connectedness, and adaptive functioning. Despite growing interest in wellbeing as a treatment outcome, few ultra-brief measures are available for routine use in psychotherapy. The present series of studies developed and evaluated the Rula Wellbeing Scale (RWS), a four-item measure designed to assess core domains of eudaimonic wellbeing relevant to clinical practice.In Study 1, exploratory factor analysis was used to refine an initial 12-item pool, resulting in a unidimensional four-item solution assessing social connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation. In Study 2, confirmatory factor analysis in an independent non-clinical sample supported a single-factor structure, whereas a bifactor model was not supported. In both Study 1 & 2, the RWS demonstrated good internal consistency and expected associations with related constructs, including positive correlations with life satisfaction, flourishing, and global wellbeing, and a negative correlation with loneliness. In Study 3, the single-factor structure was replicated in a clinical sample of psychotherapy clients, and the scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency.As hypothesized, the RWS scores were negatively associated with depression and anxiety. Mean scores were also lower in the clinical sample than in the non-clinical sample, supporting sensitivity to differences in wellbeing across populations.Collectively, findings provide initial support for the RWS as a psychometrically sound, ultra-brief measure of eudaimonic wellbeing. The scale may have particular utility in psychotherapy and measurement-based care contexts where brief, practical, and conceptually meaningful assessment tools are needed.
psychology.text:
The RWS is a brief 4-item measure of eudaimonic wellbeing designed for use in psychotherapy. This measure is open access and free to use.It assesses domains often relevant to treatment progress, including connectedness, purpose, daily functioning, and emotion regulation.Findings support its reliability and validity across non-clinical and clinical samples.The RWS may be useful in measurement-based care when clinicians want to assess wellbeing alongside symptom change.

The RWS is a brief 4-item measure of eudaimonic wellbeing designed for use in psychotherapy. This measure is open access and free to use.

It assesses domains often relevant to treatment progress, including connectedness, purpose, daily functioning, and emotion regulation.

Findings support its reliability and validity across non-clinical and clinical samples.

The RWS may be useful in measurement-based care when clinicians want to assess wellbeing alongside symptom change.

Measurement-based care (MBC) is the prevailing method to assessing the effectiveness of psychotherapy process and outcomes (; ; ; ; ), providing important clinical and research data to understand how clients respond to treatment and benefit from care. Psychotherapy outcome research has traditionally treated symptom reduction as the primary indicator of effective treatment. Yet psychotherapy is also well positioned to promote meaning, purpose, connectedness, and fuller engagement with life (; ; ). Indeed, interventions designed to enhance wellbeing show relatively robust effects on wellbeing, whereas evidence for symptom reduction is more variable across intervention types and designs (; ; ; ). A review of positive psychology interventions across 41 countries and 347 studies produced small-to-medium improvements in wellbeing and strengths, alongside meaningful reductions in ratings of depression, anxiety, and stress with interventions effects sustained at three-month follow-up (). Thus, psychotherapy is increasingly conceptualized as having two parallel aims: alleviating distress and fostering wellbeing.

Eudaimonia is a dimension of wellbeing that is especially relevant to psychotherapy (; ). In contrast to hedonic perspectives, which emphasize pleasure, positive affect, and life satisfaction, eudaimonic perspectives emphasize meaning, self-realization, vitality, personal growth, purpose in life, and functioning in accord with valued goals (; ; ). This distinction matters clinically because people may experience some reduction in distress without necessarily regaining a sense of vitality, agency, direction, or coherence in how they are living. In clinical contexts, researchers emphasize that eudaimonic wellbeing can act as both a target of intervention and a valuable index of recovery, often complementing symptom-focused outcomes (; ; ; ). Nevertheless, symptom improvement and eudaimonic improvement should not be presumed to move in lockstep (e.g., ). Several reviews note that flourishing tends to integrate hedonic and eudaimonic components, yet scales and research designs vary in how they balance these dimensions; some measures emphasize eudaimonia explicitly, others mix hedonic and eudaimonic elements (; ; ). In short, eudaimonia represents a meaningful domain within a broader, multi-faceted conception of wellbeing relevant to mental health and psychotherapy (; ; ).

Some of the core tenets of MBC have traditionally included outcome monitoring and client feedback regarding the working alliance and responsiveness to treatment. Therapists who are responsive to their MBC feedback show reduced rates of deterioration and superior outcomes compared to those who do not (; ). Over the years, the utilization of ultra-brief measures has increased in an effort balance capturing important treatment data with practical constraints on the data collection process (e.g., time burden, workflow disruptions, inconsistent implementation; ). Although research and professional guidelines have endorsed MBC as a pathway to higher-quality care, there is a deeper concern that guidelines alone do not automatically translate into practice. This has led to calls for actionable, practice-ready guidelines that address barriers to implementation (e.g., time pressure, workflow disruption) in concrete ways rather than relying on broad recommendations (; ). This duality, robust evidence alongside uneven real-world adoption, creates a demand for streamlined, practical, and scalable measurement approaches that do not overburden clinicians or patients and still gather important feedback about treatment ().

Indeed, extensive research on psychological wellbeing has been conducted since its introduction by various scholars (e.g., ; ; ), and numerous measures have been developed to capture what it means to be psychologically well. In a recent review of measures of psychological wellbeing,  identified 135 instruments capturing various forms of psychological wellbeing across 49 review articles. The most commonly reported measures in reviews were the Satisfaction with Life Scales (SWLS; ) and the World Health Organization Quality of Life Brief Version (WHOQOL-BREF; ). Several scales were also adapted across different cultures and languages, including the Ryff Scales of Psychological Wellbeing (RPWB; ), the SWLS, the McGill Quality of Life Questionnaire (MQOL; ), and the WHOQOL-BREF. While measures introduced in these reviews have generally shown strong reliability and validity, because of their comprehensiveness and length, may not always be useful for repeated use in clinical settings.

Although ultra-brief measures such as the Outcome Rating Scale (ORS; ), the Patient Health Questionnaire–4 (PHQ-4; ), the Working Alliance Inventory–Brief 3 (WAI-B3; ), and the short-form Cultural Humility Scale (CHS-SF; ) have been developed to assess symptoms, alliance, and humility, few ultra-brief measures provide routine feedback on client wellbeing. One such attempt at an ultra-brief measure of wellbeing was the Rating of Outcome Scale (). The ROS is a three-item measure of wellbeing which initially demonstrated good reliability, validity, and responsiveness to change. Relative to the ORS, the ROS showed somewhat better concordance with outcomes and less oversensitivity to change, supporting its utility for routine outcome monitoring (). The ROS captured general wellbeing along three domains (e.g., internal, relational, task-functioning; ), representing a globalized and general psychological wellbeing as opposed to a eudaimonic wellbeing.

This study aimed to develop and test the reliability and validity of an ultra-brief wellbeing scale for use in psychotherapy. Informed by theories on eudaimonic wellbeing and MBC literature, we sought to develop a scale with both non-clinical and clinical samples (in psychotherapy) to examine its psychometric evidence for validity and reliability. Further, we plan to establish criterion-related validity via comparison with established psychological wellbeing, depression, and anxiety measures. Finally, we provide guidelines for determining reliable change and clinical cutoff scores. In doing so, the creation, validation, publication, and dissemination of the new Rula Wellbeing Scale (RWS) can address the gap between measuring symptom-reduction versus a holistic view of recovery through creating an ultra-brief open access scale that builds on extensive research in the field of wellbeing while prioritizing the realities of routine clinical care.

The initial sample (n = 475) was selected from a large practice-research network (PRN). From the initial sample, 14 participants were excluded due to invalid responses to any of the validity-check items (e.g., “If you are paying attention, indicate so by choosing response 2”). After screening the data for invalid responses, the analytic sample was n = 461 (see  for demographics). New clients who had not received any treatment were invited to participate in the study via email communications. Those who elected to participate completed an informed consent form and then completed the measures (see below). All participants were actively seeking mental health care, were 18 years old or older, and were not seeking medication treatment. The treatments were outpatient services provided by licensed therapists across the United States.

Sample demographics.

This question was not collected due a technical error.

RULA Wellbeing Scale (RWS) was tested in this study. See results for psychometric information. The initial item pool consisted of 12 items for the RWS measure designed by the authors to capture multiple theoretically derived domains of wellbeing, across four general domains: (1) social connection/relationships (e.g., I have felt connected to others), (2) daily functioning (e.g., I have been able to keep up with daily responsibilities, like work, school, tasks at home), (3) sense of meaning and purpose (e.g., I have felt a sense of purpose in my life), and (4), regulation (e.g., I have been able to manage my emotions). The scale was developed to assess core domains of eudaimonic wellbeing and adaptive functioning. Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale anchored as 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater wellbeing and adaptive functioning.

Initially, we sought out therapists within a large practice-research network to understand their opinions and needs in a new wellbeing measure. Based on their feedback and in conjunction with other existing measures, we developed a set of items that were vetted by three expert psychotherapy researchers who have extensive experience with MBC and the theory/practice of eudaimonic wellbeing. They provided open-ended responses to the items. The major theme from the experts was to be mindful of having items that assess various aspects of eudaimonic wellbeing (vs. focusing on a sub-set of items that might be more highly correlated but lack the clinical relevance).

Schwartz Outcome Scale (SOS-10; ). The SOS-10 is a single dimension, 10-item, brief measure of wellbeing from an intrapersonal and interpersonal perspective (). The SOS-10 utilizes a scale of 0 (Never) to 6 (All/Nearly all of the time) to evaluate the frequency with which respondents felt in accordance with the respective item (e.g., “I feel hopeful about my future.”, “I am able to handle conflict with others.”). The SOS-10 has shown excellent reliability (α = 0.96) across clinical and non-clinical populations. In the present study, the SOS-10 demonstrated excellent reliability, α = 0.94.

The Revised UCLA Loneliness scale – 3 items (UCLA-3; ; ) is a globally used, ultra-brief scale for measuring feelings of social isolation. The three-item scale has demonstrated satisfactory reliability and discriminant validity. The reliability coefficient in the current sample was acceptable, α = 0.77.

Satisfaction with Life Scale (SLWS; ) was used to measure global life satisfaction. The SWLS is a five-item self-report measure of cognitive evaluations of one’s life. Items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), with higher scores suggesting greater life satisfaction. Total scores are calculated by adding item responses. The SWLS has demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = 0.87), a unidimensional structure, and convergent validity with related wellbeing constructs (). In the current study, the SWLS demonstrated excellent reliability (α = 0.90).

Moments of Flourishing Experience Scale-16 (MFES-16; ) is a 23-item self-report measure of momentary, positive affect–based flourishing experiences. Items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale 1 (absolutely untrue of me) to 7 (absolutely true of me), with higher scores indicating greater flourishing. The MFES consists of four subscales: Calm & Self-Acceptance, Vitality, Generosity of Spirit & Gratitude, and Connection & Purpose (). The psychometric evidence shows a multidimensional structure with strong internal consistency for the total scale (α = 0.97) and subscales, as well as convergent and discriminant validity across clinical and general population (). The current study utilized the 16-item version of the MFES for brevity. The MFES-16 assesses flourishing across three factors (Positive Emotional Wellbeing, Positive Life Functioning, and Positive Interpersonal Relationships). The full-scale MFES-16 demonstrated excellent reliability (α = 0.93).

Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7; ). The GAD-7 is a brief clinical assessment of generalized anxiety disorder. Participants are asked to respond to questions about the frequency of anxiety symptoms in the last 2 weeks (). The scale uses 4-point Likert scale, from “0” (not at all) to “3” (nearly every day), and the total scores range from 0 to 21. The GAD-7 has established excellent reliability statistics (α = 0.92), with good test–retest reliability observed via intraclass correlations (r = 0.83; ). The GAD-7 demonstrated similarly excellent reliability ratings in the current study (α = 0.90).

Patient Health Questionaire-9 (PHQ-9; ). The PHQ-9 is a brief and widely used measure of depression severity. The PHQ-9 is a self-report measure utilizing a scale of “0” (not at all) to “3” (nearly every day) to assess the frequency with which respondents experience depression symptoms in the past 2 weeks (). The total scores range from 0 to 27. In its initial validation, the internal reliability of the PHQ-9 has been established as excellent across two clinical samples (α = 0.89, and α = 0.86). In the current study, the PHQ-9 indicated excellent (α = 0.87).

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) procedures were conducted using IBM SPSS Version 29.0 () to examine the latent structure of the initial item pool and to inform item selection for scale refinement. Because the goal of this phase of scale development was to identify latent constructs rather than simply reduce data, principal axis factoring was used as the extraction method. Given that domains of wellbeing were expected to be obliquely related rather than orthogonal, a direct-oblimin rotation was used.

Factor retention decisions were based on multiple criteria, including eigenvalues (>1), inspection of the scree plot, interpretability of the factor solution, and magnitude and pattern of factor loadings. Items were evaluated for retention based on conceptual relevance, primary factor loadings, and cross-loadings. In line with common recommendations for exploratory factor analysis in scale development, items with primary loadings of approximately 0.30 or higher and minimal cross-loadings (+/− 0.15; ) were considered for retention, although conceptual considerations and content coverage were also prioritized.

The dataset was examined for missing data. All variables were fully observed; therefore, no missing data analysis (e.g., Little’s MCAR test) was required. Examination of univariate outliers for scores showed that there were no cases in which skewness and kurtosis values were < |2| (). Additionally, survey responses were subjected to a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test of sampling adequacy (KMO = 0.922 indicating highest range of accuracy) and Bartlett’s test of sphericity (p = <0.001) to determine the appropriateness of further factor analyses, which suggests the data were appropriate to analyze.

Direct-oblimin rotation was used for the initial EFA, given it was expected that factors extracted would be correlated. Additionally, item retention was based on several criteria, including factor loadings ≥ 0.3, absolute factor loadings no greater than 0.3 on more than one factor, item cross-loadings no greater than |0.15|, item communalities ≥ 0.40, and interpretability of factors (). Eigenvalue analysis (eigenvalues ≥ 1) indicated the presence of 1 distinct factor. Items with low communalities and weak factor loadings were excluded. The final result was a unidimensional scale consisting of four items and a single-factor solution accounting for 59% of variance, with higher scores indicating stronger experiences of wellbeing across the following dimensions: connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation (see  for factor loading estimates).

Study 1 exploratory factor analysis (clinical sample).

n = 461, M, mean; SD, Standard Deviation.

To refine the initial 12-item pool resulted in the development of the RULA Wellbeing Scale (RWS) scale, which demonstrated promising construct validity and reliability. Given these results, we concluded that all items were accessing the same construct. We then calculated Pearson correlations between each retained item and each of the eight excluded items to examine the extent to which the four retained items represented content from the original item pool. All 32 correlations were positive and statistically significant (p < 0.001). The retained connectedness item was most strongly associated with experiencing happiness with others (r = 0.592), mattering to others (r = 0.575), and relationship satisfaction (r = 0.542). The daily-functioning item was most strongly associated with having fun (r = 0.506) and confidence in handling life’s challenges (r = 0.485). The retained purpose item was strongly associated with having a sense of direction (r = 0.813) and experiencing life as meaningful or significant (r = 0.791). Finally, the emotion-regulation item was most strongly associated with confidence in handling life’s challenges (r = 0.572). These correlations indicate that the retained items correspond meaningfully with conceptually related content from the original item pool while preserving coverage of distinct aspects of wellbeing.

Next, we examined how well the four retained items represented the original item pool by examining the relationship between the four-item RWS total and the total score of the eight excluded items. The two scores were strongly positively associated (r = 0.844; p < 0.001), indicating substantial correspondence (approximately 71% of shared variance) between the retained items and the broader content represented in the original pool. The four-item RWS total was also strongly correlated with the original 12-item total (r = 0.935; p < 0.001). However, since the four retained items are included in the 12-item total, this association was interpreted descriptively as evidence of a part-to-whole score correspondence rather than as an independent validity estimate.

Additionally, we examined the larger pool of items to reduce to 4 items, with a focus on overall clinical representativeness as well as following the expert advice to keep the items representative of the larger construct. Although the daily-functioning and emotion-regulation items had comparatively lower loadings, their loadings were adequate for retention, and they represented clinically important content not captured by stronger-loading items. Simply, we wanted at least one item per domain that reflects important milestones in clinical work. These four items included: “I have felt connected to others.”, “I have been able to keep up with daily responsibilities & routines (like work, school, or tasks at home).”, “I have felt a sense of purpose in my life.”, and “I have been able to manage my emotions.” The scale reliability was good (α = 0.79 especially for a four-item measure).

Based on these four items, consistent with our expectations, the RWS demonstrated a coherent and theoretically expected pattern of associations with the external validity measures (see ). Specifically, RWS scores were positively and strongly associated with other indicators of wellbeing and adaptive functioning, including the SOS-10 (r = 0.724), SWLS (r = 0.636), and the MFES-16 (r = 0.788), suggesting strong convergent validity. In contrast, RWS scores were negatively associated with loneliness (r = −0.466), anxiety (r = −0.704), and depression (r = −0.617), indicating that higher wellbeing as assessed by the RWS corresponds with lower psychological distress and social disconnection. Notably, the strongest associations emerged with conceptually proximal positive flourishing measure (MFES-16), whereas the association with loneliness was more moderate, which is consistent with the view that the RWS captures a broader eudaimonic wellbeing construct rather than merely the absence of psychological distress. Overall, this pattern supports the validity of the RWS as a brief indicator of eudaimonic wellbeing with meaningful, but not redundant, overlap with related constructs. For our next study, we tested the factor structure in a non-clinical sample as well as testing the associations between the RWS and other similar/different constructs.

Full-scale correlations with RWS.

**Correlation is significant at the <0.01 level. Study 1 n = 461; Study 2 n = 924; Study 3 n = 2,757; SWLS, Satisfaction with Life Scale; SOS-10, Schwartz Outcome Scale; UCLA-3, UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale; MFES-16, 16-item Moments of Flourishing Experience Scale; PHQ-9, Patient Health Questionnaire; GAD-7, Generalized Anxiety Disorder.

Participants were recruited using CloudResearch () survey participant recruitment platform. Research has shown that recruitment from cloud-sourced samples is often more diverse and outperforms pool participants on online attention checks, suggesting a higher level of attentiveness (; ). Nevertheless, the use of cloud-sourced samples in social science research presents several concerns and limitations. In particular, the potential for invalid data and misrepresentation necessitates the inclusion of screening questions designed to assess participant attentiveness (). In the present study, three validity checks were employed, and participation was restricted to individuals residing in the United States. The survey took approximately 10–15 min to complete. Upon completion, participants were paid $2.50 amount. From the initial sample (N = 950), 26 participants were excluded due to invalid responses to any of the validity-check items. The final sample consisted of 924 participants (see  for demographics).

RULA Wellbeing Scale (RWS) was established in Study 1 as a reliable measure of wellbeing in a single-factor solution. All four items were included in the present study. In the current study, the RWS demonstrated a good reliability coefficient of α = 0.83.

Schwartz Outcome Scale (SOS-10; ). The psychometric properties of the SOS-10 are described in Study 1. In the present study, the SOS-10 demonstrated an excellent reliability coefficient of α = 0.95.

The Revised UCLA Loneliness scale – 3 items (UCLA-3; ; ). The psychometric properties of the UCLA-3 are described in Study 1. The reliability coefficient in the current sample was good α = 0.83.

Satisfaction with Life Scale (SLWS; ). The psychometric properties of the SWLS are described in Study 1. In the current study, the SWLS demonstrated excellent reliability (α = 0.94).

Moments of Flourishing Experience Scale-16 (MFES-16; ) The psychometric properties of the MFES-16 are described in Study 1. In the current study, the MFES-16 demonstrated excellent reliability (α = 0.94).

The purpose of Study 2 was to test the model-fit of the 4-item, single-factor structure of the newly formed RWS with a non-clinical sample and to test the construct validity of the RWS with other measures of mental health. The fit of two different models was tested and compared, including a single-factor model and bifactor model. In the single-factor model items were specified to load onto the associated factor, and each of the four RWS items assessed four aspects of wellbeing. This model suggests that each of the RWS items are related to each other, but each constitutes a distinct feature of wellbeing loading onto a single factor. Conceptually, the bifactor model suggests that a general RWS factor shares variance with all four of the items, and that items with similar content share variance beyond the general factor ().

More specifically, study 2 tested the model fit of the single-factor structure, and a bifactor structure. CFA analyses were conducted using structural equation modeling (SEM) via AMOS version 29 (). Model fit was evaluated using multiple indices, including the comparative fit index (CFI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean residual (SRMR) to determine the adequacy of model-to-data fit. Recommended values for these fit indices have ranged from less (CFI ≥ 0.90; RMSEA ≤ 0.08; SRMR ≤ 0.10) to more conservative (CFI ≥ 0.95; RMSEA ≤ 0.06; SRMR ≤ 0.06; ). Notably, and given the low degrees of freedom associated with the model, RMSEA values were interpreted with caution, as RMSEA is known to be inflated and less reliable in models with very few degrees of freedom ().

Study 2 adhered to the same data screening and cleaning procedures outlined in previous studies (see above), with no noteworthy outliers, violations of normality, and with missingness qualified as MCAR. We utilized the same testing conventions as described in Study 1.

Two candidate models were tested (e.g., single-factor and bifactor). The single-factor was tested and observed to fit the data as follows: x2 = 67.271, p < 0.001, df = 2; CFI = 0.955; RMSEA = 0.185 (90% CI = 0.149, 0.225), and SRMR = 0.0391. These fit statistics demonstrate good fit to the data, with the exception of RMSEA. RMSEA can be less reliable and inflated in models with very few degrees of freedom (i.e., ultra-brief scales) and should be interpreted alongside the other fit statistics (). The bifactor model was also evaluated to assess dimensionality and test whether the RWS items simultaneously reflected a general wellbeing factor and more specific domains. However, the model was not identified (df = −2), and several parameters, including factor loadings and variances, were not estimable. These results indicate that the bifactor specification was not supported by the data, likely due to the small number of items relative to the model’s complexity. Given the absence of a stable solution and the lack of evidence for meaningful multidimensional structure, the bifactor model was not retained. Instead, the single-factor model was selected as the most parsimonious and empirically supported representation of the RWS.

Our results supported a single-factor model with four items. The highest loading on the general factor was 0.788 for Item 3 (“I have felt a sense of purpose in my life”) followed by Item 1 (“I have felt connected to others”; 0.733), Item 2 ([“I have been able to keep up with daily responsibilities & routines…]”; 0.733), and Item 4 (“I have been able to manage my emotions”; 0.729; see ). Items associated with connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation were included in this overall factor (see ). The RWS full-scale reliability was also supported in the CFA results (α = 0.832).

Standardized factor loadings: confirmatory factor analyses.

Study 1 n = 461; Study 2 n = 924; Study 3 n = 2,757; β, Standardized Factor Loading.

Finally, as we predicted, the RWS was significantly and negatively correlated with the UCLA three-item loneliness scale (r = −0.51, p < 0.001). Conversely, the RWS was observed to have significant and positively correlated relationships with the SWLS (r = 0.57, p < 0.001), SOS-10 (r = 0.85, p < 0.001), and the MFES-16 (r = 0.70, p < 0.001). The RWS was moderately and negatively related with loneliness ratings, and a reduced sense of connectedness with others, thus establishing some inverse associations with loneliness alongside convergent validity with measures of wellbeing and flourishing (see ).

The purpose of study 3 was to examine the validity and reliability of the RWS in a clinical sample. The current study includes responses from clients in outpatient treatment settings. The outpatient sample comprised individuals seeking psychotherapy via telehealth services in North America via a PRN. These clients were distinct from the sample in study 1. All clients in the clinical sample entered the treatment program, and research voluntarily. The current study seeks to offer more evidence of construct validity by including measures of pathology (anxiety and depression). We predict that the RULA will be inversely correlated with these measures.

A total of 2,757 participants in Study 3 were recruited from outpatient telehealth psychotherapy. See  for demographic information.

RULA Wellbeing Scale (RWS). The psychometric properties of the RWS were established in non-clinical populations in studies 1 and 2. In the current clinical sample, the reliability coefficient was observed to be acceptable (α = 0.70).

Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9; ). The psychometric properties of the PHQ-9 are described in Study 1. In the current study, the PHQ-9 indicated good reliability (α = 0.87).

Generalized Anxiety (GAD-7; ). The psychometric properties of the GAD-7 are described in Study 1. The GAD-7 demonstrated similar reliability ratings in the current study (α = 0.89).

The clinical sample had no noteworthy outliers, violations of normality, and no missingness to report. Study 3 offered further support for the reliability of the RWS in a clinical population, with acceptable internal consistency ratings for the full scale (α = 0.70). The highest standardized factor loading on the general factor was 0.666 for Item 3 followed by Item 1 (0.621), Item 4 (0.601), and Item 2 (0.534; see ). The single-factor was tested again and observed to fit to the data as follows x2 = 19.730, p < 0.001, df = 2; CFI = 0.990; RMSEA = 0.057 (90% CI = 0.036, 0.081), and SRMR = 0.017. These fit statistics demonstrate good fit to the data, suggesting the one factor model is appropriate. Similar to our prediction, the RWS was negatively correlated with the PHQ-9 (r = −0.634, p < 0.001) and GAD-7 (r = −0.518, p < 0.001). In other words, the RWS was moderately and negatively associated with both depression and anxiety ratings, which supports expected inverse associations with other measures of psychological disorders.

Because the intended use of the RWS includes psychotherapy and outcome-monitoring applications, it was important to establish benchmarks for clinical interpretation. Thus, we evaluated both a clinical cut-off, to distinguish individuals more similar to clinical versus non-clinical populations. The clinical cut-off point is the point in the distribution of both samples with the greatest divergence (minimal overlap). In doing so, therapists can understand relative to this norming sample if their clients’ functioning has shifted in a more functional range. We also calculated a reliable change index (RCI) score to assist therapists understand the minimum amount of change needed to conclude that score differences are unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone (cf. ). Establishing these values strengthens the scale’s applied relevance by supporting interpretation of both clinical status and meaningful change over time.

We utilized the non-clinical samples and only selected those who reported less distress on the PHQ-9 & GAD-7 (i.e., under 10) to ensure the non-clinical sample were not significantly distressed. We compared those participants with the combined clinical sample’s RWS scores. The RWS scores range from 0 to 16 and based on the clinical cut-off score the reliable difference between the clinical sample and the non-distress sample was estimated to be 12. This suggests those who score under 12 are more likely to resemble clinically seeking individuals. We also calculated the RCI, or how much change on the scale is needed to rule out measurement error. We utilized a pooled standard deviation, and reliability estimates across the samples to calculate the RCI. The RCI was estimated to be 2.27 (or for simplicity 2 or 2.5), indicating that change of approximately 2–2.5 points can be interpreted as reliable change.

The primary purpose of the present investigation was to develop and establish the psychometric properties of a new ultra-brief measure of eudaimonic wellbeing. Using robust non-clinical and clinical samples in North America, the 4-item RWS was developed. EFA procedures reduced the original 12-item pool to a 4-item single-factor solution with good internal reliability. Subsequent CFA procedures tested two candidate models, a single and bifactor solution, with data fitting the single-factor model more parsimoniously. The ultra-brief RWS efficiently evaluates eudaimonic wellbeing across four domains: connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation. Overall, the factor structure and reliability of the RWS, yielded robust psychometric properties across non-clinical and clinical samples.

Noteworthy differences in RULA mean scores were found between non-clinical participants in Study 2 and clinical samples in Study 3. Specifically, means for RWS total scores from clinical sample (M = 8.25, SD = 3.19) were generally lower than non-clinical sample (M = 12.89, SD = 3.81). Additionally, criterion-based validity was assessed across conceptually related measures. Convergent validity was established by comparing RWS with established positive psychology measures and measures of psychological distress.

The present series of studies aimed to develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the RULA Wellbeing Scale (RWS), an ultra-brief measure of eudaimonic wellbeing. The four items reflect a unified construct of wellbeing that integrates key domains of functioning, purpose, connection, and emotional regulation. The aim of this scale is to provide a free, open access, psychometrically sound clinical tool with low burden for clients and providers to support treatment planning and assess progress across treatment, promoting collaborative care.

Across three studies, we implemented a systematic, multi-phase scale development process to reduce the item pool, detect and establish the underlying latent structure, and evaluate the reliability and validity of the measure. This included the use of complementary exploratory and confirmatory factor analytic approaches, alongside tests of construct validity in both non-clinical and clinical samples. Collectively, these studies provide a comprehensive and methodologically robust foundation supporting the RWS as an ultra-brief, psychometrically-sound, and empirically grounded indicator of eudaimonic wellbeing.

In Study 1, exploratory factor analytic procedures were used to examine the underlying structure of an initial item pool designed to capture multiple theoretically-derived domains of wellbeing. Using principal axis factoring with oblique rotation, results supported a unidimensional structure, leading to the refinement of the scale from 12 items to a concise 4-item solution. This final structure demonstrated good internal consistency (α = 0.79) and conceptual coherence, with items reflecting key domains of wellbeing, including connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation.

Study 2 sought to confirm this structure and further evaluate the construct validity of the RWS in an independent non-clinical sample. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the single-factor model as the most parsimonious representation of the data, whereas a bifactor model was not empirically supported. Evidence of construct validity was demonstrated through expected associations with established measures of wellbeing and loneliness, indicating that the RWS reliably captures (α = 0.83) a general dimension of eudaimonic wellbeing that is related to, but distinct from, both positive functioning and social isolation.

Study 3 extended these findings to a clinical population of individuals engaged in outpatient psychotherapy. The single-factor structure was again supported, and the scale demonstrated acceptable reliability (α = 0.70). Consistent with theoretical expectations, RWS scores were negatively associated with measures of depression and anxiety, providing additional evidence of hypothesis-consistent associations with psychological distress in a clinical context. Notably, mean differences between clinical and non-clinical samples further supported the scale’s sensitivity to variations in eudaimonic wellbeing across populations. Finally, we established preliminary clinical interpretive benchmarks for the RWS, extending its utility beyond psychometric evaluation alone. Specifically, the clinical cut-off and RCI estimates suggest the scale may be useful not only for identifying individuals whose scores more closely resemble treatment-seeking populations, but also for detecting meaningful changes in wellbeing over time that are unlikely to reflect measurement error.

Our findings offer initial support for the RWS as a parsimonious and psychometrically-sound indicator of eudaimonic wellbeing. Notably, the emergence and replication of a single-factor structure across studies suggests that the construct assessed by the RWS may reflect a higher-order, integrative dimension of wellbeing that cuts across traditionally distinct domains assessed by the four items (e.g., connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation). This is consistent with theoretical perspectives that conceptualize mental health not as the absence of pathology, but as the presence of adaptive functioning and positive psychological processes that cohere into a unified experience of wellbeing (; ). At the same time, the significant and moderate associations observed with both measures of positive functioning (e.g., life satisfaction, flourishing) and indicators of distress (e.g., depression, anxiety, loneliness) suggest that the RWS occupies a meaningful position within this broader nomological network. In other words, the RWS captures a construct that is related to, but not reducible to, either domain alone. Perhaps most importantly, the brevity of the scale, coupled with its consistent performance across non-clinical and clinical samples, highlights its potential utility as a pragmatic tool for both research and applied settings, particularly in contexts where assessment burden may be minimized without sacrificing conceptual coverage.

This measure can provide an opportunity for routine outcome monitoring focused on clients’ sense of wellbeing. Symptom management is only one piece of the puzzle in mental health treatment. For example, a client may endorse decreased symptoms of depression on the PHQ-9 (), and may also report better sleep, less fatigue, and improved mood without necessarily endorsing an increased sense of wellbeing in their life (). That client may still report a sense of lacking or languishing that the clinician may be able to attend to help bolster the client to re-engage with meaningful values, connections, and activities. As such, we encourage mental health providers to utilize this measure alongside symptom-based measures to gain a fuller picture of clients’ overall psychological functioning. In doing so, this measure can be easily administered before every session to track progress, which is consistent with best practice guidance from APA (see ).

Our findings should be interpreted considering several limitations. First, although the single-factor model demonstrated strong CFI and SRMR values in Study 2, its RMSEA exceeded conventional benchmarks. Indeed, RMSEA can perform poorly in models with very few degrees of freedom (). Therefore, the collective pattern of fit indices should be considered rather than any single index. Nevertheless, replication across additional non-clinical samples is warranted. Second, internal consistency was lower in the clinical telehealth sample than in the development and non-clinical samples. Although coefficient alpha is influenced by sample characteristics and the small number of items, continued evaluation of score reliability across settings and populations is needed. Third, the RWS was moderately to strongly associated with depression and anxiety but is not intended to replace disorder-specific symptom assessment. It should instead be used alongside symptom measures when both distress and positive functioning are clinically relevant. Finally, test–retest reliability and longitudinal measurement invariance have not yet been established. Consequently, the proposed reliable-change benchmark should be regarded as preliminary pending direct longitudinal evaluation.

The RWS is a new ultra-brief measure of eudaimonic wellbeing designed for tracking clients’ progress throughout their course of psychotherapy. RWS consists of four items that evaluate four domains of eudaimonic wellbeing: connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation. In the present study, the RWS demonstrated good internal reliability across samples using only four items to assess eudaimonic wellbeing. The RWS can be efficiently administered and scored alongside other measures of symptomatology to balance deficit-focused understanding of mental health.

psychology.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education and graduate employability: cognitive engagement, self-efficacy, and career adaptability in the AI era
psychology.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used in higher education, but its contribution to graduate employability cannot be inferred from access to AI or frequency of use alone. This critical narrative review examines how AI-supported learning may relate to employability through processes discussed in educational psychology and career development. Searches of Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed covered database inception to 1 July 2026, with supplementary searches completed on 2 October 2026. The literature was synthesized interpretively and critically, with attention to the type of outcome measured and the extent to which findings support the proposed relationships. The synthesis focuses on cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, self-efficacy and motivational regulation, and career adaptability. Three tensions organize the discussion: capability augmentation and cognitive offloading, career agency and AI-related insecurity, and resource access and capability differences. Included studies report associations or short-term changes in outcomes such as engagement, AI literacy, self-efficacy, career adaptability, and perceived employability. Direct evidence linking AI-supported learning to later employment outcomes remains limited. The proposed framework should therefore be read as a set of theory-informed pathways for future testing, rather than as an established causal or temporal sequence. Implications for assessment, disciplinary AI literacy, career education, institutional support, and future research are discussed.
psychology.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially generative AI, is changing how university students search for information, receive explanations, draft and revise work, solve problems, and prepare for careers. These changes are often framed as questions of technological adoption or digital skill. A more consequential educational question concerns what AI changes in the learner: whether students remain cognitively engaged, regulate their learning, develop realistic beliefs about their competence, and use learning experiences to adapt to an uncertain future. Graduate employability provides an important distal outcome for this question because the value of higher education depends not only on what students can produce with technological assistance, but also on what they understand, can judge, can transfer, and can continue to develop after graduation.

Graduate employability is therefore treated here as a developmental rather than purely labor-market construct. Employability research has long moved beyond a checklist of disciplinary knowledge and generic skills toward relational and capital-based accounts that incorporate identity, psychological resources, adaptability, and the capacity to mobilize learning across contexts (; ; ). AI intensifies this shift because it changes both capability formation and the environment in which capabilities are evaluated. AI can extend access to feedback, information, rehearsal, and task support, while also making it easier to bypass the cognitive activity through which durable capability develops. It can increase confidence and career exploration, while simultaneously heightening perceptions of replaceability and uncertainty. It can widen access to educational resources, while differences in prior knowledge, AI literacy, institutional support, and access to high-quality tools may produce unequal learning gains (; ).

Educational psychology provides a useful framework for explaining why AI-supported learning can produce both beneficial and adverse outcomes. Cognitive engagement reflects the extent to which students invest effort in analyzing, evaluating, and constructing meaning during learning, and recent meta-analytic evidence suggests that generative AI can enhance cognitive engagement when it is used to support active learning, although over-reliance may produce disengagement and shallow processing (). Self-regulated learning further captures learners' capacity to plan, monitor, evaluate, and adapt their learning strategies, processes that remain particularly important when students interact with AI systems that can readily perform parts of a task on their behalf (; ). Self-efficacy represents students' perceived capability to manage academic demands and use available resources effectively; emerging evidence in higher education indicates that perceived AI capability, independent learning, and academic self-efficacy are closely interconnected (). Career adaptability extends these learning-related resources into the transition from university to work by enabling students to anticipate change, maintain a sense of control, explore alternative pathways, and sustain confidence under occupational uncertainty (; ). Taken together, these constructs suggest that the relationship between AI use and graduate employability is better understood as a developmental learning-to-employability pathway, in which the educational value of AI depends on whether its use strengthens cognitive engagement, self-regulation, efficacy beliefs, and adaptive career resources rather than merely improving task efficiency.

Existing reviews have provided strong syntheses of AI in higher education, AI literacy, employability, and institutional implementation, but the literatures remain fragmented across learning science, career psychology, graduate-capital perspectives, and labor-market change (; ; ; ). The contribution of the present review is not another thematic inventory of benefits and risks. It integrates three recurrent tensions-augmentation vs. cognitive offloading, career agency vs. AI-related insecurity, and resource democratization vs. capability stratification-with three educational-psychological mechanisms: cognitive engagement and self-regulation, self-efficacy and motivational regulation, and career adaptability. The review focuses on (1) how AI-supported learning changes these psychological processes, (2) how they help explain variation in graduate-employability outcomes, and (3) under what educational and contextual conditions AI-related resources are converted into sustainable capability rather than superficial performance.

Graduate employability refers to the developing capacity to secure, sustain, and progress in work by mobilizing personal resources within social, institutional, and labor-market contexts. It is therefore distinct from employment status alone (; ; ). In this review, AI literacy refers to the ability to understand AI capabilities and limitations, use AI appropriately, evaluate its outputs, and act responsibly (; ). AI literacy may be relevant to employability when students use disciplinary knowledge to assess whether AI-generated information is accurate, appropriate, and professionally relevant. This positions AI literacy as a potential resource for learning and work; it does not establish that AI literacy leads to employment or better employment outcomes.

Cognitive engagement refers to the mental effort learners invest in understanding and evaluating material (). Self-regulated learning involves planning, monitoring, and adjusting one's learning (). These processes are relevant to AI-supported learning because AI may change how learners distribute effort between themselves and the tool. Cognitive offloading occurs when mental work is delegated to an external resource. AI may reduce task demands, but learning may be hindered when it replaces learners' reasoning or checking. The implications depend on which tasks are delegated and whether learners evaluate the output (; ).  distinguishes automation from augmentation and discusses the potential complementarity of human intellect and AI. Applied to education, this perspective draws attention to whether students remain responsible for interpreting information, evaluating outputs, and making decisions. It provides a conceptual lens for this review, rather than evidence of improved graduate employment.

Academic self-efficacy refers to students' beliefs about their ability to complete academic tasks. AI self-efficacy concerns their perceived ability to use, understand, and critically evaluate AI. Both are beliefs about capability and should not be treated as evidence of demonstrated skill (; ). Motivational regulation refers to strategies for sustaining effort when motivation declines and is closely related to self-regulated learning ().

Career adaptability comprises psychosocial resources for responding to career tasks, transitions, and uncertainty. Its dimensions are concern, control, curiosity, and confidence. Career adaptability is a career-development resource, not an employment outcome (; ). The term career adaptability scale is used only when referring to the specific instrument.

The translation of AI-related resources into learning and career development may also depend on institutional conditions. In a study of administrative staff at Italian public universities,  examined human and relational barriers to AI-related institutional change, including issues concerning autonomy, competence, and relatedness (). As that study concerns university employees rather than students, it informs the institutional context of the framework only; it is not direct evidence about student learning or graduate employability. Together, these concepts inform a proposed account of how AI-supported learning may relate to graduate employability through learning, psychological, and career-development processes.  presents this conceptual account. The relationships shown are theoretical propositions and should not be interpreted as an established causal or temporal sequence.

This study adopted a critical narrative review to integrate research on the use of artificial intelligence in higher education and graduate employability, with a focus on the relationships among learning processes, psychological mechanisms, and career development. Given the interdisciplinary nature of the topic and the range of outcomes considered, we used an interpretive narrative synthesis rather than quantitative pooling. Through iterative reading of the relevant literature and theories, we identified three tensions: capability augmentation vs. cognitive offloading, career agency vs. AI-related insecurity, and resource democratization vs. capability stratification. These tensions informed the development of the proposed theoretical framework.

Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed were searched. The main search covered each database from its inception to 1 July 2026, with supplementary searches conducted through 2 October 2026. Priority was given to AI-related studies published in 2023 or later. Reference lists of relevant publications were also consulted to identify foundational theoretical work. The following Boolean search string was used across the databases, (“artificial intelligence” OR “generative AI” OR “generative artificial intelligence” OR ChatGPT OR “large language model” OR “AI literacy” OR “AI adoption”) AND (“higher education” OR university OR universities OR college OR colleges OR undergraduate OR undergraduates OR “graduate students”) AND (employability OR employment OR “career readiness” OR “career adaptability” OR “career development” OR “career guidance” OR “career decision making” OR “career commitment” OR “self-efficacy” OR “self-regulated learning” OR “cognitive engagement” OR “student engagement” OR motivation OR anxiety OR “perceived employability”).

All retrieved records were imported into EndNote for deduplication and then screened by title, abstract, and full text. Two authors (LYK and HHZ) conducted the screening, and disagreements were resolved through discussion. The final corpus comprised 46 publications; the selection process is summarized in .

The literature was read and compared iteratively in relation to the review questions, and themes were developed through this interpretive process. Evidence was first organized by the core constructs addressed, AI application context, study populations and disciplines, research designs, and outcome types. Recurring relationships, divergent findings, and contextual conditions were then compared across studies, leading to the development of five themes. For each theme, the number and types of relevant publications, study settings and populations, areas of convergence and divergence, and limitations related to study design are described. Methodological strengths and limitations are discussed descriptively, with consideration of study design, sampling, measurement, and follow-up. The synthesis also distinguishes between study populations and levels of analysis. Studies involving higher education students or graduates inform the discussion of individual-level learning, psychological, and career-related outcomes. Studies involving university faculty or staff, as well as institutional- and labor-market-level research, are considered evidence about the educational and institutional context. Findings from different populations and levels are not treated as equivalent.

English-language publications were considered if they addressed AI-related learning, psychological, career, or employment processes in higher education. Studies of students and recent graduates formed the core evidence; studies involving university staff, employers, institutions, or labor markets were included only as context relevant to graduate employability. Eligible sources included empirical studies, reviews, theoretical or conceptual papers, and relevant foundational literature. AI-related studies published from 2023 onward were prioritized, while foundational work could predate this period. Studies without substantive relevance and those focused solely on AI technical performance were excluded ().

Inclusion and exclusion criteria.

To distinguish among outcomes measured at different levels, the literature was grouped into four categories. Direct employment outcomes included employment status, time to employment, job quality, income, retention, and employer evaluations. Indirect career indicators included perceived employability, career readiness, career exploration, career decision-making, and career adaptability. These indicators reflect students' perceptions or resources relevant to career development, but do not directly measure whether graduates obtain jobs, secure higher-quality work, or perform effectively in the workplace. Proximal learning and psychological outcomes included AI literacy, engagement, self-regulated learning, self-efficacy, motivation, anxiety, and course-related performance. The fourth category comprised theoretical propositions concerning how AI-supported learning might relate to career development or employment through learning and psychological processes. Studies involving university employees, institutional policies, or implementation were treated as contextual evidence rather than direct evidence of student-level learning or graduate employment. Claims about employment outcomes are based only on studies that measured such outcomes directly. The characteristics of the included studies, including their designs, AI application contexts, and primary outcomes, are presented in .  summarizes how the themes relate to the proposed pathways.

Characteristics and principal findings of the included studies.

Synthesis matrix linking review themes, proposed pathways, and related findings.

Evidence for this theme comes primarily from conceptual frameworks and review studies of AI literacy, including discussions of its dimensions and assessment (; ; ). These studies generally describe AI literacy as encompassing more than the ability to operate AI tools. It also involves understanding AI capabilities and limitations, evaluating AI-generated outputs, using AI systems appropriately, and acting responsibly. The literature further emphasizes the role of disciplinary knowledge: students need to apply standards from their field to judge whether AI-generated information is relevant, accurate, and professionally appropriate.

These findings support viewing AI literacy and disciplinary judgement as potential resources relevant to employability. However, current evidence focuses mainly on conceptual definitions, educational competencies, and AI-related learning, it does not establish that higher AI literacy leads to higher employment rates, better job quality, or stronger workplace performance. Whether these capabilities translate into an advantage in recruitment or professional practice remains to be tested.

Research in this area includes reviews, cross-sectional studies, quasi-experimental studies, and longitudinal studies. A within-subjects longitudinal study found that student engagement and self-regulated learning increased during the AI-enhanced flipped-classroom phase, particularly agentic engagement and metacognitive regulation (). A quasi-experimental study in nursing education and other studies involving university students reported that structured AI activities may support higher-order thinking, AI literacy, task strategies, and self-evaluation (; ). In the study by Xu et al., 68 university students participated, but the difference in academic performance between groups was not statistically significant.

The findings point to the importance of task design. When students first develop their own ideas, evaluate AI-generated outputs, and explain their revisions, AI may support engagement and self-regulated learning. AI dependence, however, has been associated with weaker critical-thinking performance, and cognitive fatigue has been proposed as one possible explanation (). A three-wave study also linked students' ChatGPT use with procrastination and concerns about memory (). Reviews have described both the potential benefits of AI feedback and explanations and the risks of overreliance and shallow processing (; ; ; ).

AI may support learning when students remain responsible for reasoning, monitoring, and checking. When it replaces these activities, cognitive offloading may result. Intervention and longitudinal studies provide more information about learning processes than cross-sectional self-report studies, but they still mainly assess proximal learning outcomes.

Research on AI-related self-efficacy and motivation suggests that students' confidence is associated with their AI literacy, learning experiences, and perceptions of their ability to use AI. In higher education, perceived AI ability has been associated with academic self-efficacy and independent learning disposition (). A quasi-experimental study involving 200 undergraduate STEM students found that AI-assisted writing support was associated with higher intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy, with greater benefits among students with lower academic achievement (). Other studies included in this review have also reported associations among AI literacy, AI self-efficacy, motivation, and career commitment (; ; ).

These relationships may operate in both directions. Higher AI self-efficacy or literacy may encourage students to use AI more actively, while successful experiences with AI may, in turn, strengthen their self-efficacy. Prior academic preparation, digital skills, learning motivation, instructor support, and access to AI tools may also influence both AI use and self-efficacy. Existing correlational studies cannot establish the temporal order or direction of these relationships.

AI anxiety and perceived risk of replacement may undermine students' career agency. Studies have reported associations between AI anxiety and AI dependence, less favorable career decision-making, or lower career adaptability (; ). Students may experience AI as a resource for practice and learning, while also feeling greater uncertainty about their future. Self-efficacy also needs to be considered alongside demonstrated capability. Students may feel more capable when AI produces fluent content, even if they cannot independently explain or reproduce the reasoning behind it. AI anxiety may affect students' willingness to use AI and their career decisions, but it may also arise from unsatisfactory experiences with AI, lower AI literacy, or concerns about labor-market changes. Cross-sectional studies cannot determine whether anxiety precedes these behaviors, follows them, or changes alongside other factors. Current evidence does not point to a single role for AI-related confidence. Structured practice may support motivation and self-efficacy. Anxiety, dependence, or confidence based mainly on AI-generated outputs may weaken students' independent agency.

Career adaptability has been examined in relation to AI-related learning and career indicators. Research in business and management education has reported associations between AI literacy, perceived AI readiness, and career adaptability (). A study of Chinese university students also found an association between generative AI acceptance and perceived employability, with positive attitudes toward AI and career adaptability potentially contributing to this relationship (). Other studies have examined associations between AI anxiety, career decision-making, and career adaptability (; ).

These findings are based mainly on cross-sectional designs and self-reported measures. They show associations with career-related perceptions or resources, but do not establish whether AI-related learning precedes changes in career adaptability or perceived employability. The direction may also be reversed: students with greater career adaptability may be more likely to explore AI tools and career information. Prior career experience, field of study, institutional support, and labor-market conditions may also influence these relationships. The available evidence therefore does not establish that AI-related learning improves career entry, job quality, or workplace performance. Longitudinal studies following students beyond graduation and measuring employment outcomes directly are needed.

AI may broaden access to feedback, learning support, and career information, but access to tools does not necessarily lead to equivalent learning gains. Existing studies suggest that prior knowledge, AI literacy, confidence, language resources, access to AI tools, and institutional support may shape how students use AI and what they gain from it (; ). Students with stronger disciplinary knowledge and self-regulatory skills may be better equipped to evaluate AI-generated outputs, whereas those with weaker foundations may find it more difficult to identify inaccurate information that appears credible. Some studies have found that structured AI support may benefit lower-achieving students (), suggesting that AI could help narrow disparities. At the same time, reviews and student-profile studies indicate that the benefits may depend on students' existing resources and the support available to them.

Solid arrows represent theory-informed directional propositions; the dashed link to employment outcomes marks a proposed translation that remains untested. Dotted connectors indicate contextual moderation, and the return arrow represents a proposed feedback process. The figure should not be interpreted as an established causal or temporal sequence.

At the individual level, student–AI engagement varies in purpose, quality, and degree of reliance. Structured use involving independent reasoning, output verification, reflection, and revision may be associated with gains in AI literacy, disciplinary judgement, cognitive engagement, self-regulated learning, and confidence. Substitutive use may accompany cognitive offloading, shallow processing, or anxiety. These relationships may vary with prior competence, task design, and institutional support.

Proximal learning and psychological indicators are distinct from career-related indicators such as career adaptability, career readiness, and perceived employability. Much of the evidence linking these variables is cross-sectional or self-reported. Reverse direction and shared influences including prior competence, discipline, work experience, and institutional support remain plausible. Career-related indicators are also distinct from direct employment outcomes, including employment entry, time to first job, job quality, retention, and employer assessment. Their translation into such outcomes remains a hypothesis because longitudinal follow-up evidence is limited. Graduate and employer outcomes may inform future curricula and career support, although this feedback process also requires empirical testing.

AI literacy can be embedded within disciplinary learning rather than delivered mainly through generic tool workshops. Programmes can specify what responsible human AI performance means in their field, what can be delegated, what must be verified, which forms of evidence are required, and which decisions remain the learner's or professional's responsibility. Engineering and computing may emphasize validation, debugging, model limitations, and data reasoning; health and regulated professions require attention to safety, evidence appraisal, privacy, and accountability; humanities and social sciences may focus on source verification, interpretation, argument quality, authorship, and contextual sensitivity.

Assessment design can preserve cognitive agency by asking students to document revisions, verify claims, compare outputs, justify delegation decisions, explain errors, and defend their final work. In foundational courses, staged or partial AI use may be appropriate when students are still developing the knowledge needed to evaluate system outputs. In advanced courses, AI use can be incorporated into authentic tasks while disciplinary judgement remains visible.

A calibration cycle may help distinguish AI-supported performance from independently retained capability: students first attempt a task, use AI to extend or challenge their reasoning, verify the output against disciplinary evidence, and then complete an unassisted explanation or transfer task. Prompt histories, revision traces, verification decisions, and confidence ratings can inform feedback. Assessment research has similarly called for attention to learning processes and responsible AI use (), the DRIVE framework treats AI interactions as possible evidence of learning (), while the Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale aligns permitted AI use with intended learning outcomes ().

Career education can pair AI-supported occupational exploration with reflection on changing task requirements, transferable capabilities, and alternative career plans. Assisted and unassisted practice, together with comparison of confidence and performance, may help students assess which capabilities they can use independently. Institutions can also monitor differences in access, AI-related confidence and anxiety, disciplinary foundations, and guidance, then provide support responsive to students' needs. These are educational implications of the proposed framework; their effects on employment outcomes require evaluation.

The principal theoretical contribution of this review is to frame the relationship between AI-supported learning and graduate employability as a possible developmental process, rather than as a direct consequence of AI access, acceptance, literacy, or use. The framework proposes several relationships for further investigation. Cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning may be associated with whether AI-supported activity contributes to learning that can be retained beyond the immediate task. Self-efficacy and motivational regulation are included as psychological resources in the proposed framework. Career adaptability may be relevant to how students apply learning resources in career exploration and adjustment. These relationships are proposed pathways; the available evidence does not establish them as causal mechanisms or a confirmed temporal sequence. Broader reviews of higher education employability likewise distinguish educational activities, skill development, and labor-market outcomes (; ).

Recent reviews describe AI literacy as involving more than the operational use of AI systems, including the knowledge and competencies needed to understand and evaluate AI (). Studies included in this review report associations or changes in proximal outcomes such as engagement, self-regulated learning, and task performance following AI-supported activities (; ). However, these findings do not establish that AI-supported learning improves later employment outcomes. The literature on AI and self-regulated learning in higher education also identifies both potential support and challenges, indicating that outcomes may depend on the learning task and the guidance provided (). One possible interpretation is that AI may support learning when students retain responsibility for reasoning, monitoring, and checking outputs; this remains a proposition requiring further testing.

Positive perceptions of AI and concerns about its use or employment implications may coexist. Differences in prior competence, perceived control, AI-related anxiety, and perceived occupational change may help explain variation across students; current evidence does not establish a single, uniform effect. Similarly, career adaptability may be relevant to students' career development, but its role in linking AI-supported learning with employability remains uncertain. Studies of AI-related career outcomes have primarily examined career adaptability and perceived employability rather than actual employment outcomes (; ). Research on career adaptation among higher education students provides a broader context for considering these relationships, but does not demonstrate an AI-related employment effect ().

Direct evidence concerning employment status, job quality, or employer evaluations remains limited. Many studies instead measure perceived employability, career readiness, AI literacy, engagement, self-regulated learning, or other psychological and educational outcomes. These measures are relevant to employability research, but they should not be treated as equivalent to actual employment outcomes. Cross-sectional associations also leave the direction of relationships unresolved: for example, students with stronger career adaptability may be more likely to explore AI tools and career information. Prior competence, work experience, discipline, institutional resources, and labor-market conditions may also contribute to observed associations. Evidence about university employees, institutional policies, or implementation should therefore be interpreted as contextual evidence, rather than as direct evidence about student-level learning or graduate employment. Employment outcomes are shaped by more than students' learning experiences and psychological resources. Recruitment and workplace performance may also depend on disciplinary competence, communication, professional presentation, punctuality, teamwork, collaboration, leadership, prior experience, and employer expectations. These factors were not consistently measured in the studies reviewed. Positive self-reports of readiness or confidence therefore cannot establish that graduates demonstrate these competencies in recruitment or workplace settings.

The evidence base was unevenly distributed across publication years, countries, disciplines, and study designs. Of the 46 included publications, 24 were conducted in mainland China and 41 were published in 2025 or 2026. Classified by their primary study context, 26 were broad or multidisciplinary, or did not specify a discipline; eight focused on business or management; three on vocational or applied education; three on language-related fields; two each on nursing and STEM or engineering; and one each on teacher education and humanities or social sciences. Methodologically, 28 studies used cross-sectional surveys, 12 used intervention, quasi-experimental, or longitudinal designs, four were qualitative studies, and two analyzed documents or employment-related data. This concentration of recent research, Chinese settings, and cross-sectional surveys limits the transferability of findings across disciplines and national contexts. Only a small subset of studies reported employment status or employment rates, and only one followed graduates' employment status 6 months after a course.

Findings were not uniformly positive. AI anxiety was not significantly associated with career decidedness among students in English language teaching and English language and literature, although a weak negative association was found among translation and interpreting students (). AI anxiety did not significantly predict lifelong learning tendency among pre-service teachers, and self-efficacy did not significantly moderate the relationship between AI anxiety and career decisions in another study (; ). Other studies found no significant direct relationship between generative AI learning support and employability, or between continued intention to use AI and career-choice intention (; ). Results may therefore vary with discipline, task, prior achievement, and institutional context. For example, structured AI-assisted writing appeared to benefit lower-achieving students, whereas another study associated stronger prior quantitative skills with greater AI capital (; ). These findings suggest that prior competence, field of study, and institutional support may be relevant boundary conditions. Evidence concerning socioeconomic position, disability, language proficiency, and access to paid AI tools remains limited.

Future research should examine these proposed relationships over time. Longitudinal studies could follow students from AI-supported learning experiences through career preparation and into employment, measuring both intermediate outcomes and subsequent labor-market outcomes. Experimental and quasi-experimental studies could compare learning activities that require students to verify AI outputs, explain revisions, or complete later tasks without AI assistance. Interaction logs, revision histories, confidence accuracy calibration, independent error detection, and delayed transfer tasks may help distinguish perceived fluency from independently demonstrated capability. Studies should also account for alternative explanations, including prior achievement, work experience, discipline, institutional support, and labor-market conditions. Where feasible, outcomes should include career entry, job quality, employer assessments, and performance on authentic professional tasks. Cross-disciplinary and cross-cultural comparisons may clarify how professional norms, access to AI, and employment conditions shape these relationships.

Several limitations qualify this review. Its critical narrative design prioritized conceptual integration and did not include formal risk-of-bias scoring or quantitative effect estimation. The search was restricted to English-language publications indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed. Relevant studies in other languages or outside these databases may therefore have been missed. Backward citation tracking helped identify foundational work but may have favored established citation networks. Gray literature was not systematically searched, and publication bias could not be formally assessed. The evidence base is also changing rapidly, with 41 of the 46 included publications appearing in 2025 or 2026; future research may alter the current interpretation. Finally, direct evidence linking AI-supported learning to graduate employment remains limited, while employment outcomes are also shaped by economic, organizational, and labor-market conditions beyond the individual learning and psychological processes examined here.

AI adoption rates, prompt proficiency, and short-term task performance alone provide an incomplete account of AI's role in higher education. This review identifies cognitive engagement, self-regulated learning, self-efficacy, and career adaptability as learning-related and career-related resources that may be relevant to graduate employability. However, the available evidence, which mainly concerns proximal learning outcomes and self-reported career indicators, does not establish that AI-supported learning improves employment rates, job quality, or workplace performance.

The framework presents possible relationships for future investigation rather than an established causal or developmental sequence. AI-supported learning may contribute to resources relevant to employability when students retain responsibility for reasoning, monitoring, and verifying information and receive appropriate pedagogical and institutional support.
