This study explored how Arab women therapists in Israel experience and make sense of bodily phenomena in psychotherapy. The findings suggest that embodied awareness is not merely a professional skill acquired through formal training, but also an ongoing process shaped through personal experience, clinical practice, cultural meanings, and professional development. Participants described the body as a source of knowledge, attunement, and therapeutic understanding while simultaneously negotiating cultural, gendered, and professional expectations. The study extends prior discussions of embodiment beyond individual psychological processes to highlight sociocultural dimensions through which bodily awareness is developed and expressed. The findings contribute to a culturally informed understanding of psychotherapy by suggesting that embodiment may serve as not only a therapeutic resource but also a site where personal histories, professional identities, and cultural meanings intersect and are continuously negotiated.

psychology.title: Household work participation is associated with adolescent mental health through parent-child relationship and resilience
psychology.abstract: Adolescent mental health is a central concern in educational psychology and youth development. This study used data from a school-based survey on 1,152 junior middle school students in Xi’an, China and examined whether and how participation in household work was associated with adolescent mental health. We assessed a serial mediation model in which parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience were specified as potential mediators. Results revealed that household work participation was positively correlated with adolescent mental health, parent-child relationship, and resilience. Furthermore, household work participation was significantly associated with greater perceived closeness with parents and higher resilience, after adjusting for gender, grade, only-child status, academic performance, hukou status, school type, family structure, and parental education. Bootstrap mediation analyses indicated that the association between household work participation and mental health was consistent with an indirect-effects pattern that involved parent-child relationship, resilience, and their serial pathway. Among the indirect pathways, the resilience pathway accounted for the largest proportion of the total indirect effect. These findings suggest that household work may represent a meaningful family-based context associated with adolescent psychological well-being, greater perceived closeness with parents, and stronger psychological resources. This study contributes to research on adolescent mental health by highlighting the educational and developmental value of household work within family life.
psychology.text:
Adolescent mental health is fundamental for healthy development, educational adjustment, and long-term well-being. In the present study, better adolescent mental health is operationalized as lower levels of psychological distress, including depressed mood or difficulty cheering up, nervousness, restlessness, hopelessness, feelings that everything was an effort, and feeling that life was meaningless (). Mental health problems during adolescence warrant particular attention because they are closely related to adolescents’ emotional adjustment, school functioning, interpersonal relationships, and subsequent development. China has emphasized mental health education as an important component of quality-oriented education, with schools encouraged to support students’ psychological development, coping skills, and capacity to face setbacks (). Nevertheless, adolescent mental health remains a major public health and educational concern. The Report on National Mental Health Development in China (2019–2020) reported a 24.6% depression detection rate among Chinese adolescents (). Furthermore, the  emphasized the need to strengthen students’ mental health management and recognize the role of labor education in promoting holistic development.

Labor education is a shared responsibility of society, schools, and families. At the societal level, it is a necessary pathway for adolescent growth and an important component of moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic, and labor education (). At the family level, household work provides adolescents with opportunities to acquire everyday life skills, develop a sense of responsibility, and participate in family life (). At the school level, household work is closely connected with the broader goals of labor education as it helps students form positive attitudes toward labor, cultivate practical skills, and develop responsibility and autonomy (; ; ).

Beyond the specific policy context of labor education in China, household work can also be understood from the broader perspective of life education. Life education emphasizes learning through everyday living, respect for life, responsibility, and personal development, rather than evaluating activities simply in terms of whether they are pleasant or unpleasant. From this perspective, age-appropriate participation in household work may provide adolescents with opportunities to learn self-care, responsibility, cooperation, and engagement in family life. This broader perspective is also consistent with  LIFE framework, which emphasizes the developmental value of involving children in everyday responsibilities from an early age.

However, previous studies have shown considerable variation in children’s and adolescents’ participation in household work across family and social contexts (; ). Parents assume most of the household responsibilities in many families, which may reduce adolescents’ opportunities to develop self-care skills and experience meaningful family contribution (). Therefore, whether participation in household work is associated with adolescent mental health and the psychosocial mechanisms of such an association remain important questions.

Previous research has identified a wide range of individual, family, and school-related factors associated with adolescent mental health (; ; ; ). However, comparatively less attention has been paid to routine family practices that are repeatedly embedded in adolescents’ everyday lives. Household work participation represents one such practice. Unlike occasional educational activities, household work involves repeated participation in family responsibilities, practical problem solving, and interaction with parents. Therefore, household work participation may constitute an important everyday family context associated with adolescents’ psychological development.

Existing studies on household work have primarily examined life skills, learning, problem-solving, and other developmental outcomes (; ; ). Some evidence also suggests that the developmental implications of household work may depend on the family context in which it occurs. For example,  found that household work involvement was associated with problem-solving abilities among preschool children and that parental scaffolding moderated this association. These findings indicate that household work may be developmentally relevant and that family interaction may shape its developmental implications.

However, less is known about whether household work participation is associated specifically with adolescent mental health and through which psychosocial mechanisms. In particular, existing studies have generally not simultaneously examined parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience as sequential mediators linking household work participation with adolescent mental health (; ; ). Accordingly, the present study extends existing evidence by focusing on adolescent mental health and by examining parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience as potential relational and psychological pathways in a Chinese adolescent sample. Specifically, we examined two research questions: (1) Is household work participation associated with better adolescent mental health? and (2) Do parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience independently or sequentially mediate this association?

Previous studies have examined adolescent mental health from psychological, sociological, and educational perspectives. Psychological research has emphasized both individual, such as personality, self-esteem, emotion regulation, and psychological resources, and environmental factors, such as family relationships, parenting style, parents’ mental health, school climate, and academic pressure (; ; ; ; ; ; ). Similarly, sociological studies have highlighted the influence of family socioeconomic status, social networks, social support, and parent-child interaction (; ; ; ; ; ). Educational research has increasingly examined how labor education and everyday practical activities support students’ psychological development (; ; ).

Household work refers to unpaid domestic work performed by family members to meet household needs, including cooking, washing dishes, doing laundry, cleaning, and organizing the living spaces (; ; ). These activities are not merely routine tasks for adolescents. They can also be understood as family-based practical experiences that help them acquire life skills, develop autonomy, and internalize responsibility.

Several mechanisms may help explain the association between household work participation and adolescent mental health. First, household work may be associated with greater self-care capacity, which may reduce dependence on parents and improve adolescents’ perceived competence. Second, regular household work may contribute to healthy routines and lifestyle habits, associated with self-esteem, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being (; ; ). Third, household work may foster responsibility, persistence, and prosocial orientation, all relevant to positive personality development and mental health (; ).

Based on the mechanisms outlined above and prior evidence linking household work with adolescent adjustment and developmental outcomes (; ), the following hypothesis was proposed:

H1: Participation in household work would be positively associated with adolescent mental health.

Family systems theory suggests that family subsystems influence one another and jointly shape adolescent development (). Parent-child relationship is a core component of the family system and is formed through repeated interaction. Household work is an everyday domain in which such interactions can occur. When adolescents contribute to domestic work, parents may perceive them as more responsible and considerate, which may reduce conflict and enhance emotional closeness (; ; ). Thus, household work may provide a practical context for positive parent-child interaction.

Similarly, household work may also be associated with adolescent resilience. Resilience refers to an individual’s capacity to adapt positively when faced with stress, adversity, or developmental challenges (; ; ). It is shaped by both risk and protective factors, including self-efficacy, coping strategies, family environment, parenting style, and social support (; ; ; ; ,). Everyday prosocial activities and life skills may function as protective factors by increasing adolescents’ sense of competence, responsibility, and connectedness (). Since household work involves practical problem solving and family contribution, it may provide adolescents with opportunities to develop psychological resources relevant to coping with difficulties.

Therefore, the following hypotheses were proposed:

H2: Participation in household work would be positively associated with adolescents’ perceived closeness with their parents.

H3: Participation in household work would be positively associated with adolescent resilience.

Previous research has identified parent-child relationship quality and adolescent resilience as important predictors of adolescent mental health (; ; ). Supportive and emotionally close parent-child relationships provide adolescents with a sense of security, belonging, and trust; conversely, strained relationships may increase stress and undermine psychological adjustment (; ). Furthermore, positive parent-child relationships are associated with greater resilience and may provide adolescents with emotional support, behavioral guidance, and confidence when facing setbacks (; ; ).

Resilience is widely regarded as a protective factor for adolescent mental health (). Adolescents with higher resilience tend to adopt more adaptive coping strategies, maintain greater optimism, and exhibit better adjustment under stress (; ). In addition, resilience may buffer the effects of negative life events and reduce depressive symptoms (; ). These findings suggest that both parent-child relationship and resilience may serve as key pathways through which household work participation may relate to adolescent mental health.

Therefore, the following mediation hypotheses were proposed:

H4: Participation in household work would be positively associated with adolescent mental health through parent-child relationship.

H5: Participation in household work would be positively associated with adolescent mental health through adolescent resilience.

H6: Participation in household work would be positively associated with adolescent mental health through the serial pathway of parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience.

Data were drawn from the Family and School Life of Middle School Students survey, a school-based survey conducted by a research team at Xi’an Jiaotong University. The survey collected information on students’ family background, family learning, school life, and parent-child relationship. Participants were junior middle school students from nine schools of different types in Xi’an, China.

Students were recruited through the participating schools. After school administrators and teachers helped distribute the survey information, eligible students were invited to complete the questionnaire on a voluntary basis. Students were eligible to participate if they were enrolled in one of the selected junior middle schools and were able to complete the questionnaire independently.

Missingness across the variables included in the analyses was low at the item level, with the highest missing rate being 2.74%. Little’s MCAR test conducted on the core study variables in the full sample was non-significant (χ2 = 1.98, df = 6, p = 0.921), providing no evidence against the MCAR assumption for these variables. Under the complete-case criterion, 125 respondents with incomplete data on the variables used in the analyses were excluded, yielding a final analytic sample of 1,152, representing 90.21% of the original sample (N = 1, 277). Comparisons of excluded and retained respondents showed no significant differences in gender, grade, urbanicity, school type, paternal education, or maternal education (all p > 0.05); family structure differed between the two groups (χ2 = 40.58, p < 0.001) and was included as a covariate in all regression models.

Adolescent mental health was assessed using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6; ). The six items assessed feeling depressed or unable to cheer up, nervousness, restlessness or difficulty remaining calm, hopelessness, feeling that everything was an effort, and feeling that life was meaningless. Each item was rated on a 5-point frequency scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always) and was reverse-scored so that higher scores indicated better mental health. The six reverse-scored items were summed, yielding total scores ranging from 6 to 30. The Chinese K6 has demonstrated satisfactory reliability in previous research (; N = 8,289; Cronbach’s alpha = 0.84; test-retest reliability = 0.79). In the present sample, the scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.89).

Household work participation was measured using four behavioral items assessing washing clothes, cooking or helping with cooking, cleaning the home, and organizing or tidying one’s room. Each item was rated on a 5-point frequency scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). The four items showed acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.79), and principal component analysis supported a single-component structure, with a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) value of 0.70. A weighted composite score was calculated as 0.81 × washing clothes + 0.72 × cooking or helping with cooking + 0.86 × cleaning the home + 0.76 × organizing or tidying one’s room. The resulting score ranged from 3.15 to 15.75, with higher values indicating more frequent household work participation.

Parent-child relationship was assessed using a single self-report item: “How close is your relationship with your parents?” Responses were rated on a 5-point scale: 1 = not close at all, 2 = not very close, 3 = average, 4 = relatively close, and 5 = very close. Higher scores indicated greater perceived closeness with parents. The item was treated as a global indicator of adolescents’ perceived closeness with their parents and should not be interpreted as a multidimensional assessment of parent-child relationship quality. Previous methodological research suggests that single-item global measures can provide adequate validity for concrete and unidimensional constructs (; ). Because the construct was assessed using a single item, internal consistency indices such as Cronbach’s alpha were not applicable.

Adolescent resilience was measured using the 10-item Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-10). Each item was rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (never) to 4 (always), with total scores ranging from 0 to 40; higher scores indicated greater resilience. Previous validation research in a Chinese sample demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.91), 2-week test-retest reliability (r = 0.90), and a single-factor structure (). In the present sample, the scale demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.90).

Control variables were selected based on previous research indicating that adolescent mental health is associated with demographic characteristics, family socioeconomic and structural factors, school context, and academic pressure (; ; ; , ; ). Accordingly, the analyses controlled for gender, grade, only-child status, hukou status, paternal and maternal education, family structure, school type, and academic performance.

Paternal and maternal education were each converted into years of schooling: primary school or below = 6 years, junior middle school = 9 years, senior high school or secondary vocational school = 12 years, junior college = 15 years, bachelor’s degree = 16 years, and postgraduate education = 19 years. Family structure was classified into four categories: (1) nuclear family; (2) single-parent or reconstituted family; (3) extended family living with parents and grandparents; and (4) joint or skipped-generation family. School type was classified into elite, high-quality, and regular schools according to the classification used in the sampling design. Hukou status distinguished urban from rural household registration. Academic performance was measured using students’ self-reported class ranking from 1 (poor) to 5 (very good).

Analysis proceeded in three steps. First, Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated to examine bivariate associations between household work participation, parent-child relationship, resilience, and mental health. Second, multiple linear regression models with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors were estimated to examine whether household work participation was associated with mental health, parent-child relationship, and resilience, adjusted for control variables. The available analytic dataset did not retain school identifiers; therefore, school-level cluster-robust standard errors or multilevel models could not be estimated. Third, mediation analyses were conducted using ordinary least squares regression and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. A serial mediation model was assessed using PROCESS Model 6 in SPSS version 25, in which household work participation was specified as the independent variable, mental health as the dependent variable, and parent-child relationship and resilience as the sequential mediators. The coefficients displayed in  are standardized regression coefficients (β) estimated from the PROCESS Model 6 serial mediation model; they are path coefficients rather than Pearson correlation coefficients. The bivariate Pearson correlation coefficients are reported separately in .

Pearson’s correlations between household work, parent-child relationship, resilience, and mental health.

N = 1,152. ***p < 0.001.

All analyses treated higher mental health scores as indicating better psychological well-being. Bootstrap confidence intervals that did not include zero were interpreted as evidence of statistically significant indirect effects. Standardized regression coefficients (β) were additionally reported as measures of effect size.

To assess the potential influence of complete-case exclusion, additional missing-data sensitivity analyses were conducted. Excluded and retained respondents were compared on selected background characteristics, and the serial mediation model was re-estimated using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) on the full sample (N = 1, 277).

As a post hoc sensitivity check, statistical power for the indirect effects was evaluated conditional on the observed effect estimates (). Using the observed path coefficients from the N = 1,152 analysis as generating values, a Monte Carlo simulation with 3,000 replications was conducted. Because this analysis was conditional on the observed estimates, it was not interpreted as independent confirmation of sample-size adequacy.

The final analytic sample consisted of 1,152 students.

presents the Pearson’s correlation coefficients between the core variables. Mental health was positively associated with household work participation, parent-child relationship, and resilience. Furthermore, household work participation was positively associated with both parent-child relationship and resilience. These findings provide preliminary support for the proposed associations among the study variables.

presents the regression coefficients for the serial mediation model. All regression equations were adjusted for gender, grade, only-child status, academic performance, hukou status, school type, family structure, paternal education, and maternal education. Household work participation was positively associated with mental health in the total-effect model (b = 0.166, SE = 0.044, β = 0.110, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.080, 0.251]), and was positively associated with parent-child relationship (b = 0.073, SE = 0.009, β = 0.223, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.055, 0.091]) and resilience (b = 0.582, SE = 0.073, β = 0.210, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.438, 0.725]). Parent-child relationship was also positively associated with resilience (b = 1.957, SE = 0.226, β = 0.231, p < 0.001, 95% CI [1.513, 2.401]). These results were consistent with H1-H3.

Regression coefficients of the serial mediation model.

N = 1,152. HW, household work participation; PCR, parent-child relationship; RES, resilience; MH, mental health. b, unstandardized regression coefficient; SE, standard error; CI, confidence interval; β, standardized coefficient. The PCR equation included HW and the covariates; the RES equation included HW, PCR, and the covariates; the MH equation included HW, PCR, RES, and the covariates; and the total-effect equation included HW and the covariates. All models were adjusted for gender, grade, only-child status, academic performance, hukou status, school type, family structure, paternal education, and maternal education. Model fit was R2 = 0.090 for PCR, R2 = 0.261 for RES, R2 = 0.206 for MH, and R2 = 0.068 for the total-effect model.

Serial mediation analysis was used to examine the indirect associations of household work participation with mental health through parent-child relationship and resilience. In the outcome equation, parent-child relationship (b = 0.679, SE = 0.132, β = 0.147, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.420, 0.938]) and resilience (b = 0.191, SE = 0.017, β = 0.351, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.158, 0.224]) were positively associated with mental health, whereas the direct association between household work participation and mental health was not statistically significant (b = −0.022, SE = 0.042, β = −0.015, p = 0.604, 95% CI [−0.105, 0.061]).

As shown in , the total indirect effect was statistically significant (b = 0.188, SE = 0.025, β = 0.124, 95% bootstrap CI [0.142, 0.240]). All three specific indirect effects were significant: HW → PCR → MH (b = 0.049, SE = 0.013, β = 0.033, 95% bootstrap CI [0.027, 0.077]); HW → RES → MH (b = 0.111, SE = 0.019, β = 0.074, 95% bootstrap CI [0.076, 0.151]); and HW → PCR → RES → MH (b = 0.027, SE = 0.006, β = 0.018, 95% bootstrap CI [0.017, 0.040]). The indirect pathway through resilience accounted for the largest proportion of the total indirect effect (59.2%), followed by the parent-child relationship pathway (26.3%) and the serial pathway (14.5%). These findings were consistent with H4-H6.

Direct, indirect, and total effects of household work on mental health.

N = 1,152. HW, household work participation; PCR, parent-child relationship; RES, resilience; MH, mental health. Indirect effects were estimated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples with percentile 95% confidence intervals. A bootstrap confidence interval excluding zero was interpreted as evidence of a statistically significant indirect effect. All models were adjusted for gender, grade, only-child status, academic performance, hukou status, school type, family structure, paternal education, and maternal education. b, unstandardized coefficient; SE, standard error; β, standardized coefficient. The proportion of the total indirect effect was calculated as each specific indirect effect divided by the total indirect effect.

As a missing-data sensitivity analysis, the serial mediation model was re-estimated using FIML on the full sample (N = 1, 277). The focal path coefficients and indirect effects were substantively similar to those from the complete-case analysis (N = 1,152), with the total indirect effect estimated at 0.187 under FIML compared with 0.188 in the complete-case analysis.

As a post hoc sensitivity check conditional on the observed estimates, the Monte Carlo analysis yielded estimated power of 0.999, 1.000, and 1.000 for Ind1, Ind2, and Ind3, respectively, with an estimated power of 1.000 for the total indirect effect. These estimates are reported as conditional sensitivity information and should not be interpreted as independent evidence of sample-size adequacy.

This study examined the association between household work participation and adolescent mental health and assessed indirect associations through parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience. Adolescents who participated more frequently in household work tended to report greater perceived closeness with their parents, higher resilience, and better mental health. Significant indirect associations were observed through parent-child relationship, resilience, and their serial combination. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings represent statistical indirect associations and should not be interpreted as establishing temporal or causal mediation.

Our findings contribute to the literature by further clarifying the relevance of household work as an everyday family activity associated with adolescent mental health. Household work is meaningful in this context not simply because it involves routine tasks, but because it repeatedly engages adolescents in family responsibilities, practical problem solving, and interactions with parents. Previous research has already suggested that household work is related to adolescent adjustment, although the direction of this association may depend on the amount and context of the work. For example,  found that longer housework duration was associated with higher depressive symptoms among Chinese adolescents, particularly among rural adolescents. Similarly,  found that household work involvement was associated with problem-solving abilities among preschool children, with parental scaffolding moderating this association. Although their study focused on younger children and cognitive development, it likewise highlights the importance of family interaction in understanding the developmental relevance of household work. Thus, our findings should not be interpreted as suggesting that household work is uniformly beneficial. Rather, they extend previous work by indicating that the relational and psychological context surrounding household work-particularly adolescents’ perceived closeness with their parents and resilience-may be important for understanding its association with adolescent mental health.

We further highlight the role of parent-child relationship as an interpersonal mechanism. Household work may create opportunities for cooperation, communication, and recognition of each other’s contributions. Such cooperative family experiences may be associated with lower conflict and greater emotional closeness between parents and adolescents (; ). Consistent with previous evidence linking parent-child communication and relationship quality with adolescent mental health (), our findings suggest that adolescents’ perceived closeness with their parents may be an important interpersonal correlate linking household work participation with mental health.

Adolescent resilience emerged as the strongest indirect pathway. This finding is consistent with the view that resilience functions as a protective psychological resource for adolescents facing stress and developmental challenges (; ). Household work may provide adolescents with opportunities to practice persistence, problem solving, and responsibility in everyday family life. Such experiences may be associated with psychological resources relevant to resilience, which in turn is closely associated with adolescent mental health (; ; ).

The importance of relational context observed in the present study is consistent with findings from prior studies conducted in Western cultural settings. Research based on European American families has shown that the association between adolescents’ housework and adjustment is context-dependent. , for example, found that greater housework time was associated with more depressive symptoms among adolescents with low familism values or high parent-youth conflict about housework. Similarly,  highlighted the importance of mother-youth relationship quality in shaping how household responsibilities relate to adolescent well-being in low-income U.S. families. Together with the present findings, these studies suggest that household work itself may not be inherently beneficial or harmful; its psychological meaning may depend on the relational context in which it occurs. Our finding that parent-child relationship and adolescent resilience were involved in the indirect association therefore provides additional evidence that family interaction and psychological resources may be important for understanding when household work is associated with better adolescent adjustment.

The findings have practical implications for families, schools, and professionals involved in adolescent mental health promotion. Household work should not be viewed simply as additional tasks imposed on adolescents. Rather, age-appropriate household responsibilities may provide opportunities for family participation, cooperation, and the development of responsibility and competence. Viewed from a life-education perspective, such everyday responsibilities may also help adolescents learn to engage constructively with necessary aspects of daily life and family participation (). At the same time, the present findings should not be interpreted as evidence that assigning more household work necessarily improves mental health. For school counselors, family counselors, and other professionals working with adolescents, the relational context surrounding household responsibilities-including parent-child communication, perceived fairness, and the emotional climate in which household work is performed-may be relevant when understanding adolescents’ family experiences and psychological adjustment.

The findings also have implications for future research. First, longitudinal studies are needed to establish the temporal ordering among household work participation, parent-child relationship, resilience, and mental health. Second, future research should distinguish the frequency of household work from its qualitative characteristics, including whether participation is voluntary or compulsory, whether responsibilities are perceived as fair, and whether household work occurs in a supportive or conflictual family climate. Third, cross-cultural studies are needed to determine whether the associations observed in the present Chinese sample generalize to Western and other cultural contexts. Finally, future studies should use multi-informant and multidimensional measures of parent-child relationship and examine whether family relationship quality moderates the association between household work and adolescent mental health.

This study has several limitations. First, we used cross-sectional data, which limits causal inference. Although the serial indirect-effect model was theoretically grounded, the estimated indirect effects represent statistical associations and do not establish temporal or causal mediation. Longitudinal or experimental designs are needed to examine the proposed mechanisms more rigorously. Second, parent-child relationship was measured via a single self-report item. Future research should use validated multi-item scales and obtain information from both adolescents and parents. Third, the sample was limited to junior middle school students in Xi’an, China. Future studies should examine whether these findings can be generalized to other age groups, regions, and cultural contexts. In addition, because the data were collected at a specific historical time point, future studies using more recent and longitudinal data are needed to examine whether the observed associations remain stable across different educational and social contexts. In addition, although participants were recruited from nine schools, school identifiers were not retained in the analytic dataset, so school-level clustering could not be modeled. Future studies should retain school identifiers and include a larger number of schools to permit cluster-adjusted or multilevel analyses. Fourth, household work participation was measured according to frequency and type of activity. Future research should further distinguish between voluntary and compulsory participation, perceived fairness, parental expectations, and emotional climate in which household work is performed.

Participation in household work was positively associated with adolescent mental health. Furthermore, significant indirect associations were observed through parent-child relationship, resilience, and their serial pathway. These findings suggest that everyday household work may serve as a potentially relevant family-based context associated with adolescent psychological well-being. Overall, the findings highlight household work participation, perceived closeness with parents, and resilience as potentially relevant correlates of adolescent psychological well-being.

psychology.title: Safety and Usability of a Novel, Robotic Assistance System for Echocardiographic Examination
psychology.abstract: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is essential for modern cardiac diagnostics, yet it is difficult to access in remote areas. Remotely operated robotic-assisted ultrasound may enable access to services in rural and remote locations, while also improving ergonomics for the sonographer. This study evaluated the safety, usability and patient satisfaction of a novel robotic ultrasound assistance tool (RUAT).This open-label, single-site, single-arm clinical trial enrolled adult participants who had recently completed a standard manual echocardiogram. A trained sonographer performed a robot-assisted TTE from a dedicated workstation in the same room as the patient. Endpoints included safety measured by adverse events, technical and clinical usability, and patient satisfaction using surveys about the participants’ experience.The trial cohort (n=30; mean age 62.9 ± 17.5 years; 70% men) all successfully completed the robot-assisted TTE and the patient satisfaction survey. There were no adverse events or adverse device effects. The functional verification checklist supporting technical usability demonstrated an average usability rate of 96.9% (95% CI [98.9–100.0]), with a 100% rate across 10 of 12 metrics. The sonographer’s review of the acquired robotic images measured the clinical usability and 29 of 30 examinations met acceptable diagnostic standards (96.7%; 95% CI [88.1–100.0]). The mean participant satisfaction score was 8.3 out of 10, with 96.7% scoring ≥6.The RUAT demonstrated high technical and clinical usability, as well as high acceptance by participants. These findings indicate that robot-assisted TTE is a viable strategy to enhance remote access to TTE services.
psychology.text:
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) remains a cornerstone of modern cardiac imaging as the primary modality to guide therapeutic decision-making in patients with suspected or confirmed heart failure, valvular heart disease and coronary artery disease, cardiac arrhythmia, and for rapid acute assessment within emergency and critical care pathways., However, the application of TTE in rural and remote areas is constrained due to a lack of local specialised staff and services.–

Individuals living outside major metropolitan areas encounter barriers when they require diagnostic imaging and are often required to travel long distances for tests, which frequently delays diagnosis and treatment, leading to adverse cardiovascular outcomes.,,–

Collaborative robotic (COBOT) systems have emerged as a highly promising technological innovation. Advancements in robotic automation and telecommunication hardware allow robotic manipulators to hold and position standard ultrasound transducers securely on human subjects while being directed remotely by a trained sonographer. Early generation systems have demonstrated the basic technical feasibility of remote transducer positioning, although evidence of clinical implementation remains limited.–

For traditional TTE, the physical mechanics of image acquisition remain a primary challenge. When performing a traditional TTE, sonographers apply sustained static muscle loading, repetitive application of force and unsupported arm abduction, which places an immense physical burden on their bodies. As a result, up to 90% of cardiac sonographers live with pain and are prone to extensive sick leave and even premature retirement as a result of work-related musculoskeletal disorders. In addition, the unmonitored, subjective and sometimes high-force pressures applied by sonographers during a manual scan commonly result in chest wall discomfort for patients.

Recent advancements in COBOT frameworks offer a pathway to address these issues by allowing the sonographer to be removed from the physical delivery of transducer pressure. In replacing the manual manipulation of the probe by the sonographer with a workstation-guided graphical user interface, COBOT systems enable the sonographer to continue to use their highly developed fine motor skills without the muscular strain. The integration of internal force-torque tracking loops in the COBOT allows for quantifiable, regulated force parameters and enables the delivery of a pre-programmed force that is appropriate for the individual patient. Clinical data evaluating the technical usability and patient tolerability of these automated force regulation loops during human examination remain sparse.

This study aimed to formally evaluate the safety profile, technical and clinical usability, and participant acceptance of a novel robotic ultrasound assistance tool (RUAT).

The investigational device evaluated was the RUAT (RMI Oceania). The RUAT functions as a COBOT system that enables operators to steer an ultrasound transducer through remote-controlled operation of a robotic arm. The RUAT is compatible with commercially available ultrasound equipment (Aplio i900, Canon Medical Systems).

The system is divided into a remote patient system and a local sonographer workstation, which was connected via hardline Ethernet in this study. The remote patient system comprises the robotic arm, force sensor and proprietary probe holder and is monitored by specialised dual-camera tracking (a close-up probe positioning camera and a wide-angle patient camera). It also includes a screen to allow audiovisual communication between the patient and the operator, and emergency stop features including a hand-held buzzer for the patient and trolley-mounted stop button for the clinician. The sonographer’s workstation has a proprietary graphical user interface and is used to manipulate the ultrasound probe, define force limits and view the images streamed from the camera.

This study was conducted as a single-site, open-label, single-arm feasibility clinical trial in Australia at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital in Brisbane, Queensland. All participants provided written informed consent prior to screening and enrolment. Each participant had previously undergone a clinically indicated traditional TTE. Two sonographers were present in the same room as the participant for each robot-assisted TTE; one scanning sonographer to operate the RUAT via the dedicated remote workstation and one observing sonographer to ensure safety and to support the participant.

The study population comprised patient volunteers aged 18 or older, who had already undergone a clinically indicated traditional TTE. Major exclusion criteria included pregnancy, acute cardiac symptoms or highly restricted mobility that may have prevented the patient from lying down on their left-hand side for the duration of the procedure.

Before the trial started, three senior cardiac sonographers completed a novel robot-assisted TTE training programme, requiring completion of virtual environment modules and practical simulation using the RUAT with an ultrasound simulator. This allowed for familiarisation with the graphical user interface, the trajectories of the robotic arm and development of the fine motor skills required to adjust the probe using the controller.

Primary endpoints focused on evaluating safety, technical usability, clinical usability and patient-reported acceptance. Safety parameters included incidence of adverse events (AEs), serious adverse events, adverse device effects (ADEs) and serious adverse device effects from consent until 72 hours post-procedure. Technical usability was evaluated using a 12-item functional verification checklist completed by the observing sonographer during or immediately after each robot-assisted TTE procedure to log mechanical, electronic and software performance. Clinical usability was determined by the performing sonographer who assessed the diagnostic quality of robot-assisted TTE images. Sufficient diagnostic quality was defined as on-axis images that were suitable to form a clinical assessment. Participant experience and device acceptance were assessed using a satisfaction survey containing four subscales scored on a 10-point Likert scale (1 indicating extreme disagreement/dissatisfaction, 10 indicating perfect agreement/satisfaction).

The trial sample size was determined using exact single-proportion CI formatting. Assuming a robot-assisted TTE success rate of 80%, a sample size of 30 participants was calculated to provide a two-sided 95% CI width of 30.9% [61.4–92.3] using the exact Clopper-Pearson formula. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 or higher (SAS Institute).

Continuous demographic attributes, verification rates and satisfaction subscale parameters are expressed as either mean + standard deviation (SD) or median with interquartile range (IQR) and absolute minimum/maximum bounds. Categorical variables are reported as absolute counts and percentages. Two primary analysis sets were defined as the full analysis set (FAS), consisting of all enrolled participants meeting selection criteria, and the safety analysis set (SAS), comprising all subjects with any physical exposure to the RUAT device.

A total of 30 eligible participants were enrolled in the study (30% women, mean age 62.9 ± 17.5 years, mean weight 86.9 ± 18.8 kg, mean height 173.3 ± 12.2 cm). All 30 participants successfully completed a robot-assisted TTE and the 72-hour safety phase analysis, resulting in no early withdrawals, investigator-driven discontinuations or dropouts. The FAS and SAS were identical (n=30).

Safety outcomes were optimal across the study with no reported AEs or ADEs. None of the participants reported local thoracic skin injury, bruising, localised soreness or chest wall discomfort during the examination or within the 72-hour post-procedure window.

The 12-item functional verification metrics completed across the 30 procedures demonstrated a combined positive success rate of 96.9% (95% CI [98.9–100.0]). The system achieved >95% across nine out of the 12 technical indices, as shown in . Technical limitations were identified through Question 2 (‘Did the robotic arm move into home position when instructed?’), which recorded three negative outcomes (10.0% failure rate; 90.0% success; 95% CI [29.2–100.0]). Evaluation of clinical usability identified that robot-assisted TTE was of sufficient diagnostic quality to generate a qualitative or quantitative clinical assessment in 29 of the 30 cases, yielding a clinical adequacy success rate of 96.7% (95% CI [88.1–100.0]).

Subjective feedback from the participants demonstrated an overall mean score of 8.3 (SD 1.0) across all aggregated satisfaction evaluations on the 10-point scale, with individual entries ranging from a minimum score of 5.5 and a maximum of 10.0. Twenty-nine out of 30 participants (96.7%; 95% CI [88.1–100.0]) recorded an overall satisfaction score equal to or greater than 6.0; detailed analysis of the individual satisfaction subscales is provided in . Subscale 1 (procedural movement speed and comfort) and subscale 2 (safety perception during active transducer adjustments) achieved the highest scores, with a mean of 9.3 and 9.2, respectively. Comfort regarding physical chest wall compression (subscale 3) achieved a mean score of 8.2. Subscale 4 (Could you clearly see the video of the sonographer via the integrated screen?) was the lowest performing, recording a mean score of 6.3 and an absolute minimum score of 1.0 due to physical obstruction in the line of sight.

The primary focus of this clinical investigation was to evaluate the safety profile, technical and clinical usability, and patient-reported acceptance of a robot-assisted TTE. The study met its predefined success criteria across all major fields. The system demonstrated a strong safety profile, with no recorded adverse events or device-related complications. This safety profile confirms that integrating automated, internal force-torque tracking loops can enable safe robot-assisted TTE on humans while appropriately managing the physical interactions required during a TTE investigation. Sonographers selected the appropriate maximum force threshold required for each acoustic window per patient, which was determined by image quality and balanced with patient comfort.

Technical performance was high, with a combined success rate of 96.9%. The robotic manipulator tracking and probe positioning performed reliably in almost all cases, while the performance of the force sensor was 100%. Similarly, the clinical usability was also very high, with sonographers judging the tele-robotic images as meeting diagnostic requirements in 96.7% (29 out of 30) of the examinations. This success rate significantly exceeds the trial’s pre-specified minimum usability threshold of 80.0%. Initial home positioning failures in 10% of cases were resolvable via standard workstation resets without interrupting the overall robot-assisted TTE procedure or compromising patient safety.

In contrast to traditional TTE, a key finding in this research is the clinical and technical usefulness of the regulation of force applied by the RUAT system. Traditionally, sonographers performing manual scans will exert unmonitored and variable physical forces to optimise image acquisition. This increases when scanning technically difficult patients or navigating complex anatomical variations. During a manual scan, there is no feedback mechanism to measure force in real time, so excessive pressures can be maintained for a long time, which frequently results in chest wall discomfort, bruising to the patient and musculoskeletal pain for the sonographer.

The RUAT’s automated internal force-torque tracking loop is a significant advantage. For most of the trial cohort, a conservative default of 2 kg was applied to acquire diagnostic images in 96.7% of cases. This demonstrates that excessive and continuous force is not required when using this system. A 5 kg ceiling is a safety mechanism to prevent accidental overshoot by the operator or sudden surges in pressure when the patient moves. The ability to reduce pressure to as low as 1 kg while scanning sensitive anatomy, such as the suprasternal notch or subcostal windows, enables a nuanced control of the pressure applied by the RUAT system. This changes the model of scanning from unmonitored operator pressure to regulated and quantifiable force parameters. This precision explains the complete lack of soreness in the chest wall or skin injuries within the 72-hour safety window. This also provides a framework for future protocols for automated imaging where the force applied can be programmed.

This study demonstrates high levels of participant satisfaction with the procedure, indicating acceptance of the device, particularly in relation to the pressure applied by the probe. This will be particularly important when the technology is used for truly remote scanning where the sonographer and patient are in separate locations, benefiting patients who live in rural or remote locations and are currently required to travel long distances to undertake an echocardiogram. Lower satisfaction scores regarding the obscurity of the sonographer video (mean 6.3 ± 3.1) highlighted the practical limitation of the location of a fixed patient viewing screen by the bedside. Ensuring clear, uninterrupted audiovisual communication is important for reducing patient anxiety and maintaining high satisfaction, particularly when using these systems in fully remote and regional telecommunication networks where the sonographer is not physically in the room.

From a service access and equity perspective, robot-assisted TTE can enable diagnostic studies to be completed from centralised workstations, improving access to underserved, geographically isolated communities.,– Democratising access to cardiac imaging is likely to expedite diagnosis and the implementation of treatment strategies for patients in remote locations, which will improve cardiovascular outcomes. The successful validation of the RUAT system has potentially significant implications in improving service provision for patients in geographically isolated areas. In demonstrating that a sonographer can safely and effectively control the RUAT system from a workstation to acquire diagnostic-quality images in 96.7% of scans, this trial establishes a scalable model for decentralised cardiac care. This can help to enable sonographers based in centralised metropolitan locations to service a network of robotic systems positioned across rural locations and deliver specialised TTE across geographically distant locations much quicker than traditional outreach services. This capability assists in addressing the disparity in access to healthcare between urban and rural communities.

It is important to note the potential ergonomic value of RUAT technology for cardiac sonographers. Traditional TTE places a significant physical burden on operators, with up to 90% of sonographers experiencing work-related musculoskeletal disorders resulting in pain, extended sick leave and potential early retirement., This is attributed to sustained muscle loading and repetitive awkward scanning postures while performing diagnostic ultrasound in a clinical environment. The RUAT system fundamentally alters the biomechanical risk factors that have plagued sonographers for decades. The RUAT reduces the risk of occupational injury by removing prolonged abduction of the sonographer’s scanning hand, traditionally required for probe manipulation and pressure, and replacing it with an interface that can be guided from a workstation. The RUAT system removes the need for the physical delivery of angulation and force, allowing probe manipulation from a workstation, enabling the sonographer to use fine motor skills to operate the system but eliminating the physical burden. This allows the sonographer to operate from a more ergonomically sound posture and reduces the physical strain associated with traditional scanning, presenting a viable strategy for reducing musculoskeletal injuries. Ultimately, this system has the potential to significantly reduce the occupational injury rate among sonographers.

Considering the potential downstream effects of protecting the workforce, robot-assisted TTE may also increase capacity and prove to be an invaluable resource in the diagnosis and monitoring of conditions which require frequent check-ups to assess the effectiveness of guideline-directed medical therapies. Heart failure, in its many forms, is one of these. The use of echocardiography in the diagnosis and monitoring of heart failure is well established due to its ability to phenotype the diagnosis and longitudinally assess structural change., Laborante et al. discuss how technological advances in heart failure monitoring have enabled early intervention strategies to potentially prevent decompensation, and robot-assisted TTE would complement this strategy.

It is known that early and rapid uptitration of heart failure therapies improves patient outcomes and reduces readmission rates. The provision of more accessible serial TTE monitoring to provide updated assessments on filling pressures in patients with preserved ejection fraction, assess the authenticity of reverse remodelling and monitor responsiveness to guideline-directed medical therapy is a potential area of interest in future research into robot-assisted TTE.– The provision of services closer to home builds capacity for more personalised care plans, which is particularly important for older people, those with frailty and exacerbated symptoms where timely intervention may preclude further decompensation. As heart failure nurses become more common in primary care settings, robot-assisted TTE performed by a trained echocardiographer at a central location could be used to supplement clinical findings and be beneficial even in metropolitan centres. Further studies are required to look at the potential applications of robot-assisted TTE and evaluate its longer term impact.

There were several study limitations that require consideration when interpreting the findings. This investigation was designed as a single-site, single-arm feasibility trial with a modest sample size of 30 participants, limiting the ability to generalise the safety and usability findings across broader, unselected clinical populations. While the performing sonographer operated the system via a dedicated workstation, they were in the same room as the patient. This arrangement allowed for direct, verbal communication and may not reflect the technical and interpersonal dynamics of a long-distance regional telecommunications network. The RUAT was directly connected to the workstation via an Ethernet cable; therefore, this study aims to test the technology in its purest form, prior to introducing the potential limitations of network induced instability and latency issues, which may be experienced in truly remote applications.

This clinical trial demonstrates that robot-assisted TTE using a novel RUAT is safe, highly functional and clinically useful. It is also well tolerated by patients. Robot-assisted ultrasound represents a viable technological solution to improve echocardiographic access in geographically isolated populations, while simultaneously addressing occupational safety for sonographers by reducing the physical strain of prolonged manual positioning. Future trials should evaluate the clinical deployment of the system across large, distributed regional telecommunication networks in larger, unselected clinical populations.

psychology.title: Dance- and movement-based interventions for autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis
psychology.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulties in social communication, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and impaired adaptive functioning. Although behavioral and developmental interventions remain central to ASD management, the effects of dance- and movement-based interventions (DMIs) across different functional domains have not been fully clarified. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of DMIs on overall autism symptom severity, social communication/social responsiveness, and motor function in individuals with ASD.This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Eligible DMIs included formal dance/movement therapy or dance movement psychotherapy and other structured dance- or purposeful movement programs in which movement constituted a central therapeutic or rehabilitative component. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO were searched from inception to August 2026. Randomized and non-randomized controlled studies were not combined in the same primary meta-analysis. Randomized studies reporting sufficiently comparable outcomes were synthesized using standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) under random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE.Twelve controlled studies involving individuals with ASD were included and showed substantial variation in intervention format, comparator conditions, outcome measures, and risk of bias. Exploratory RCT-only meta-analyses included three studies for social communication/social responsiveness (n = 76; SMD = −0.68, 95% CI: −1.58 to 0.23; p = 0.15; I² = 72%) and three studies for motor function (n = 55; SMD = 2.04, 95% CI: −0.52 to 4.61; p = 0.12; I² = 92%); certainty of evidence was very low for both domains. Overall autism symptom severity was represented by one randomized trial (n = 30; SMD = −3.09, 95% CI: −4.19 to −1.99), resulting in low-certainty evidence and precluding pooling. Narrative synthesis identified potentially favorable signals in joint engagement, cooperative behavior, interpersonal synchrony, emotion inference, and gesture imitation, but these findings arose from small and heterogeneous studies.The current evidence base for DMIs is small, heterogeneous, and of low to very low certainty. Structured narrative synthesis suggests possible domain-specific benefits, whereas exploratory pooled estimates for social communication/social responsiveness and motor function remain inconclusive. DMIs may have potential as complementary interventions for ASD, but larger, methodologically rigorous randomized trials with standardized interventions and outcome measures are required.https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261495230, identifier CRD420261495230.
psychology.text:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent differences in social communication and reciprocal social interaction, together with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities (, ). Its presentation varies widely across individuals and across development, and the effects on daily life are equally variable. Current epidemiological estimates also point to a substantial public-health burden. The U.S. Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network identified ASD in 1 in 31 8-year-old children in 2022 (), while the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 estimated that 61.8 million people worldwide, or about 1 in 127, were on the autism spectrum (). In China, a nationwide study reported a prevalence of 0.70% among children aged 6–12 years (). The social and economic burden of ASD is substantial, including heightened family stress, reduced quality of life, and high costs of long-term care and educational support. These estimates differ across populations and surveillance methods, but they underscore the scale of ASD and the need to address the functional difficulties that accompany it.

Motor difficulties are one of these less visible but clinically relevant areas. They are not part of the core diagnostic criteria, yet systematic reviews and meta-analyses have documented differences in motor coordination, postural control, gross and fine motor skills, and early motor development (–). Such difficulties can affect play, physical activity, learning, and participation in everyday social situations. They may also intersect with social functioning. Most studies included in one systematic review reported an association between motor and social skills in ASD (), and atypical interpersonal motor synchrony has been described in social interaction (). For intervention research, motor outcomes therefore merit separate attention rather than being treated only as secondary behavioral measures.

Medication played a limited role in treating the core features of ASD and was used mainly for associated symptoms or co-occurring conditions (, ). Behavioral, developmental, communication, and social interventions remained central to care and could improve selected outcomes, although response varied considerably (, ). Some behavioral programs required intensive practice, sustained therapist or family involvement, or highly structured teaching (). For minimally verbal individuals, communication interventions that did not depend solely on spoken language, including augmentative and alternative communication approaches, were also investigated as alternatives or complements (). These differences in treatment demands prompted interest in complementary approaches that could engage participants through non-verbal interaction while addressing social and motor processes within the same activity.

For the purposes of this review, dance- and movement-based interventions (DMIs) were defined as a broad category of structured interventions in which dance or purposeful movement formed a central therapeutic or rehabilitative component, regardless of whether the program was delivered within a formal psychotherapy framework. Within this broader category, dance/movement therapy (DMT)—also termed dance movement psychotherapy (DMP) in some settings—is a formal psychotherapeutic approach in which movement is used to support emotional, social, cognitive, and physical integration (, ). Other DMIs evaluated in ASD included creative movement, inclusive community dance, and imitation- or synchronization-based programs (–). Across these formats, rhythm, body awareness, imitation, mirroring, and shared movement provided opportunities for participants to respond to another person’s actions and coordinate movement in real time (). Action-observation processes and embodied accounts of cognition have been proposed as possible explanations for such effects (, ), although the mechanisms of clinical change remain uncertain. The diversity of the field was reflected in controlled studies ranging from imitation- and synchronization-based work with autistic adults () to protocol-based DMP in children () and inclusive community dance programs ().

Despite the growing number of studies, the evidence remained difficult to compare. Earlier reviews reported possible benefits in social reciprocity, communication, body awareness, emotional expression, and sensorimotor functioning, but repeatedly noted small samples, heterogeneous interventions, and variable methodological quality (, , ). A 2022 meta-analysis of seven controlled studies found pooled effects favoring dance interventions for overall ASD symptoms and social interaction, but not empathy (). Reviews of physical activity more broadly have also reported improvements in social communication, although they combine exercise modalities that are not directly comparable with DMT or dance-based programs (). A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials in children and adolescents reported favorable effects on several social and behavioral outcomes (), but its search ended in March 2025, it excluded adults and non-randomized controlled designs, and motor function was not analyzed as a separate pooled domain. Evidence published after that search further broadened the field: one randomized trial examined synchronized group movement and prosocial behavior in young autistic adults (), while a longer-term controlled DMT study followed children for 11 months and assessed global symptoms, repetitive behaviors, and social responsiveness (). The main uncertainty is therefore no longer simply whether dance-related interventions can produce change, but whether effects are consistent across age groups and study designs, whether motor function shows a distinct intervention effect, and which additional outcomes can be meaningfully combined. The number of randomized studies identified in the present review was smaller than that reported in the recent meta-analysis by Jingyao et al. (), despite the later search date and broader age eligibility. This difference primarily reflects differences in search coverage and intervention eligibility rather than the search period alone. Jingyao et al. searched several Chinese databases, including CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP, and included a broad spectrum of dance activities, including standardized dance training and several Chinese-language or locally indexed studies. In contrast, the present review searched five international bibliographic databases and required dance or purposeful movement to constitute a predefined central therapeutic or rehabilitative component; general exercise, sports training, and recreational activities without a substantive dance/movement component were excluded. Accordingly, the two reviews captured partially different evidence bases. The present review extends the earlier synthesis by including adults and non-randomized controlled studies in the systematic review, separating randomized from non-randomized evidence in quantitative synthesis, evaluating motor function as a distinct outcome domain, incorporating studies published after the earlier search, and applying design-specific risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE.

We therefore conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled studies involving individuals with ASD across age groups and intervention formats. Eligible interventions included formal DMT and other structured dance- or movement-based programs, with usual care, wait-list, no-intervention conditions, and active comparators considered as controls. Given the limited number of randomized trials available in this field, we included controlled studies with different designs to characterize the current evidence base. Outcomes were organized into three prespecified domains: overall autism symptom severity, social communication/social responsiveness, and motor function. Quantitative pooling was undertaken when at least two randomized studies assessed sufficiently comparable outcomes; otherwise, findings were synthesized narratively and, where appropriate, individual study effect estimates were reported. Outcomes that were insufficiently comparable for quantitative pooling—including empathy and emotion inference, joint engagement, cooperative behavior, interpersonal synchrony, sensory and emotional measures, verbal and non-verbal communication, and neurophysiological outcomes—were summarized narratively. By examining these domains separately, we aimed to clarify where evidence is relatively consistent and where interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity. This domain-specific synthesis may help clinicians interpret the current evidence more cautiously and guide researchers in developing future trials with standardized interventions and outcome measures.

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement (). The review protocol was registered retrospectively in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD420261495230) ().

A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, Embase, and PsycINFO was conducted from database inception to 1 August 2026. Search terms combined concepts related to autism spectrum disorder and dance- or movement-based interventions. The core search strategy was: (Autis* OR “Autism Spectrum Disorder” OR Asperger* OR “Pervasive Developmental Disorder”) AND (“Dance Therapy” OR “Dance Movement Therapy” OR “Dance/Movement Therapy” OR “Dance Movement Psychotherapy” OR “Movement Therapy” OR “Creative Movement Therapy” OR “Dance Intervention” OR “Dance Activity”). Search syntax was adapted to each database. No language or publication-date restrictions were applied. Search reporting was guided by PRISMA-S recommendations ().

For each search, titles and abstracts were screened, and full-text versions of articles meeting the criteria were downloaded. The full texts were reviewed, and any reference articles not yet obtained were ordered and acquired.

Studies were eligible for inclusion in the systematic review if they met all of the following criteria: (1) participants had a diagnosis of ASD or an autism-spectrum condition established according to internationally recognized diagnostic criteria, including DSM-IV, DSM-5, ICD-10, or other validated diagnostic procedures reported by the original study (); (2) the intervention consisted of DMT, dance movement psychotherapy, creative movement, or another structured dance- or movement-based program in which intentional movement, expressive movement, rhythm, or interpersonal movement interaction represented a central therapeutic component. Interventions primarily involving general physical exercise, sports training, or recreational activities without a defined dance/movement component were excluded; combined interventions were eligible when the dance/movement component was predefined, distinguishable from other components, and accounted for a meaningful proportion of the intervention content; (3) the study used a controlled interventional design, including randomized controlled trials, randomized crossover trials, wait-list controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, or other prospective controlled designs, with a concurrent comparator; (4) the study reported measurable quantitative outcomes related to autism symptom severity, social or communicative functioning, motor performance, psychosocial functioning, or intervention-related neurophysiological changes.

Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: (1) participants did not have ASD, or ASD-specific data could not be separated from a mixed diagnostic sample; (2) dance or structured movement was not a substantive component of the intervention; (3) no clearly defined concurrent control or comparator group was included; (4) the report was a review, protocol, purely qualitative study, case report, uncontrolled case series, or conference abstract/other report with insufficient methodological or outcome information; or (5) the same or substantially overlapping participant sample was reported in more than one publication, in which case the report providing the most complete data for the relevant outcome was retained and related reports were not treated as independent studies.

For quantitative synthesis, studies were additionally required to provide sufficient numerical data for effect-size estimation and to report outcomes that were sufficiently comparable in both clinical construct and measurement domain. Randomized and non-randomized studies were not combined in the same primary meta-analysis. Where at least two randomized studies assessed sufficiently comparable outcomes, randomized studies were pooled using meta-analysis. Non-randomized controlled studies and outcomes that were not considered sufficiently comparable for pooling were retained in the systematic review and synthesized narratively.

Two authors (M.X. and X.X.) independently screened the literature, reviewed titles and abstracts, and assessed full-text articles for eligibility. Any disagreement regarding study inclusion was resolved through discussion and consensus, with adjudication by a third author (W.J.) when necessary. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded, and the study-selection process was summarized using a PRISMA flow diagram.

Data were extracted using a standardized form. Extracted items included first author, publication year, country or region, study design, sample size, sex distribution, participant age, intervention and comparator characteristics, intervention duration, outcome measures, and quantitative outcome data. For continuous outcomes, post-intervention means, standard deviations (SDs), and sample sizes were extracted. The quantitative data used in the meta-analyses were checked against the original reports. Particular attention was given to studies producing unusually large, standardized effect estimates to verify whether the extracted values represented SDs rather than SEs and whether endpoint values, rather than change scores or adjusted estimates, had been entered.

Outcomes were grouped according to conceptual similarity into overall autism symptom severity, social communication/social responsiveness, motor function, and other outcomes. When more than one measure within a study assessed the same domain, one measure was selected according to conceptual relevance and comparability with measures used in the other included studies, so that each study contributed no more than one effect estimate to a given meta-analysis. Outcomes that were not sufficiently comparable for quantitative pooling, including empathy and emotion inference, joint engagement, cooperative behavior, interpersonal synchrony, sensory and emotional measures, verbal and non-verbal communication, and neurophysiological outcomes such as functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS)-derived measures (), were synthesized narratively.

Risk of bias was assessed separately according to study design. Randomized studies were evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, whereas non-randomized controlled intervention studies were assessed using the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool ().

For RoB 2, risk of bias was assessed across five domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of the outcome, and bias in selection of the reported result. Overall judgments were categorized as low risk, some concerns, or high risk. For ROBINS-I, the domains included bias due to confounding, selection of participants, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, measurement of outcomes, and selection of the reported result. Overall judgments were categorized according to the ROBINS-I framework ().

Risk-of-bias assessments were performed at the outcome level where appropriate. Judgments were based on information reported in the original studies, and disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus.

All included studies were first synthesized narratively according to study design, participant characteristics, intervention components, comparator conditions, outcome measures, and risk-of-bias judgments. Meta-analysis was used as a secondary, exploratory synthesis when at least two randomized studies reported outcomes judged sufficiently comparable in clinical construct and measurement domain. Non-randomized controlled studies were not pooled with randomized trials and were retained in the narrative synthesis. Meta-analyses were performed in Review Manager (RevMan), version 5.4.1.

Because conceptually related outcomes were assessed using different instruments, effect sizes were expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The SMD was calculated as Hedges’ adjusted g, using the pooled within-study SD and a small-sample correction (). Post-intervention endpoint values were used, and random-effects models were applied because clinical and methodological variation across studies was anticipated ().

For crossover trials, first-period data before crossover were used when available to avoid double counting and potential carryover effects (); this approach was applied to Aithal et al. For multi-arm studies, only groups relevant to the comparison were entered, without duplicating participants within a meta-analysis.

Before pooling, the direction and conceptual meaning of each outcome measure were examined. For social communication/social responsiveness outcomes, higher scores indicated greater impairment, and negative SMDs therefore favored the intervention. For motor outcomes, higher scores were aligned to indicate better performance, such that positive SMDs favored the intervention. Differences in the constructs represented by the individual instruments were also considered when determining whether outcomes were sufficiently comparable for quantitative synthesis.

The social communication/social responsiveness meta-analysis included randomized studies assessing the SCQ, SRS-2 Social Communication and Interaction score, or ATEC social ability domain. The motor-function meta-analysis included randomized studies assessing gross motor performance, MABC-2 performance, or objective motor coordination. Because each individual instrument was represented by only one study, instrument-specific subgroup analyses were not considered statistically appropriate. After restriction to randomized evidence, only one randomized trial contributed data on overall autism symptom severity; therefore, a pooled meta-analysis was not performed for this domain, and the evidence was summarized narratively together with the individual study effect estimate.

Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test and quantified with the I² statistic (). I² values of approximately 0%-40%, 30%-60%, 50%-90%, and 75%-100% were interpreted as potentially unimportant, moderate, substantial, and considerable heterogeneity, respectively, while also considering the magnitude and direction of effects.
