Because considerable heterogeneity was observed in the motor-function analysis, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed by sequentially excluding each study to evaluate the stability of the pooled estimate.

A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Publication bias was not formally assessed because fewer than 10 studies contributed to each meta-analysis, making funnel-plot asymmetry tests unreliable in this setting ().

The certainty of evidence for the main outcome domains was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach (). Evidence was evaluated across the domains of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Certainty was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. Summary of Findings tables were generated using GRADEpro GDT for social communication/social responsiveness, motor function, and overall autism symptom severity.

A systematic literature search identified a total of 963 records from PubMed (n = 412), Web of Science (n = 276), Cochrane Library (n = 183), Embase (n = 59), and PsycINFO (n = 33). After removing duplicates, 780 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 728 records were excluded based on title and abstract review, and 52 reports were sought for retrieval. Twelve reports could not be retrieved, leaving 40 full-text reports for eligibility assessment. Of these, 28 were excluded because they were case studies (n = 3), non-intervention studies (n = 2), did not involve an eligible dance- or movement-based intervention (n = 3), included an ineligible study population (n = 4), or did not provide sufficient quantitative outcome information to meet the eligibility criteria (n = 16). Ultimately, 12 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the systematic review ().

The 12 included studies comprised eight randomized studies and four non-randomized controlled studies and included children, adolescents, and adults with ASD. Sample sizes were generally small, ranging from 14 to 57 participants, and intervention duration ranged from approximately 5 weeks to 1 year. Considerable variation was evident in participant age, study design, intervention format, comparator condition, treatment duration, and outcome assessment ().

Characteristics of the studies included in the systematic review.

Study characteristics include country or region, study design, intervention and control sample sizes, participant age, intervention and comparator characteristics, intervention duration, and reported outcomes or main findings.

The interventions differed substantially in their therapeutic orientation and movement components. Aithal et al. evaluated a protocol-based dance movement psychotherapy (DMP) program against standard care in children with ASD, whereas Mastrominico et al. examined a manualized DMT program emphasizing mirroring against a wait-list control in adults. Ma et al. compared DMT with rehabilitation training, while Mateos-Moreno and Atencia-Doña evaluated an intervention combining DMT with music therapy. Ren et al. used a parent–child intervention incorporating music therapy and DMT, compared with no intervention. These studies therefore differed not only in intervention content but also in the extent to which movement was embedded within a psychotherapeutic, rehabilitative, or multimodal framework.

Other studies used structured movement approaches that were distinct from formal DMT/DMP. Lindor et al. evaluated the AllPlay Dance program against a wait-list condition, whereas Cui et al. examined a structured dance/movement intervention against a control condition. Souissi et al. used a psychomotor dance/movement intervention, with motor coordination and gesture imitation among the principal outcomes. Chiang et al. evaluated caregiver-mediated joint-engagement training incorporating creative body-movement play. Dvir et al. directly compared synchronized with non-synchronized movement, thereby isolating interpersonal synchronization more specifically than studies using passive or wait-list controls. Similarly, Koehne et al. compared dance therapy with a control movement condition and focused on emotion inference, empathy, and interpersonal synchrony. Su et al. compared creative movement with general movement and sedentary play and additionally incorporated behavioral and fNIRS-derived outcomes. Thus, comparator intensity ranged from standard care, wait-list, or no intervention to rehabilitation and active movement-based comparators, which may have influenced the magnitude and interpretation of between-group effects.

Outcome assessment was similarly heterogeneous. Overall autism symptom severity was assessed using the CARS, ABC, and ECA-R, whereas social communication/social responsiveness was assessed using the SCQ, SRS/SRS-2, and the ATEC social ability domain. Other studies examined more specific interpersonal constructs, including joint engagement, cooperative behavior, social closeness, interpersonal synchrony, emotion inference, and empathy. Motor outcomes included MABC-2 performance, gross motor development, and objective motor-coordination measures, while additional outcomes included gesture imitation, sensory and emotional functioning, verbal and non-verbal communication, and fNIRS-derived cortical activation. These measures represent related but non-equivalent constructs; accordingly, outcomes were quantitatively pooled only when they were judged sufficiently comparable within a prespecified domain, while more distinct outcomes were retained for narrative synthesis. The contribution of each included study to the quantitative and narrative syntheses is summarized in .

Risk-of-bias assessments are summarized in . Among the randomized studies assessed using RoB 2, most outcomes were judged as having some concerns. The outcomes reported by Lindor et al. were judged to be at high overall risk of bias, primarily because of concerns related to deviations from the intended intervention and missing outcome data (). The remaining randomized studies were judged as having some concerns overall, most commonly because of limited reporting of the randomization process, outcome measurement, or selection of the reported result.

Among the four non-randomized controlled studies assessed using ROBINS-I, Ma et al. and Mateos-Moreno and Atencia-Doña were judged to be at serious overall risk of bias, with confounding representing the principal concern (, ). Koehne et al. and Chiang et al. were judged to be at moderate overall risk of bias. The domain-level judgments for both assessment tools are presented in . Taken together, these judgments indicate that the evidence base was affected by methodological limitations across both randomized and non-randomized studies, which were considered when interpreting the quantitative and narrative findings. Accordingly, favorable findings from individual studies, particularly those derived from small trials or non-randomized designs, were interpreted as signals of potential benefit rather than confirmatory evidence of efficacy.

Three studies (, , ) reported quantitative outcomes related to overall autism symptom severity, using the Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC) (), Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) (, ), and Revised Clinical Scale for the Evaluation of Autistic Behavior (ECA-R) (). However, only Ren et al. was a randomized controlled trial. Ma et al. and Mateos-Moreno and Atencia-Doña were non-randomized controlled studies and were therefore not pooled with the randomized evidence.

In Ren et al., the post-intervention CARS score favored the intervention group, with an SMD of −3.09 (95% CI: −4.19 to −1.99). The underlying endpoint data were rechecked against the original report and confirmed to represent post-intervention means with SDs rather than SEs, change scores, or adjusted means. Because only one randomized study contributed to this outcome domain, no pooled meta-analysis was performed.

The two non-randomized studies also reported changes in overall symptom measures following dance- and movement-based interventions. These findings were retained in the narrative synthesis rather than quantitatively combined with the randomized trial because of differences in study design and outcome measurement. Given the different study designs, outcome instruments, and risk-of-bias profiles, the directionally favorable findings across these studies should not be interpreted as independent confirmation of a common treatment effect.

Three studies (, , ) contributed data to the meta-analysis of social communication and social responsiveness. For the crossover study by Aithal et al., only first-period data were used. The analysis therefore included 36 participants in the intervention groups and 40 in the control groups. Outcomes were measured using the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) (), the Social Responsiveness Scale-2 Social Communication and Interaction (SRS-2 SCI) score (), and the social ability domain of the Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC) (). Ma et al. () also reported social-responsiveness outcomes but was not included in the primary meta-analysis because of its non-randomized design. Cui et al. assessed social responsiveness using the SRS; however, exact post-intervention group means and SDs were not reported in extractable numerical form. This outcome was therefore retained in the narrative synthesis rather than included in the social-function meta-analysis.

The random-effects meta-analysis yielded an SMD of −0.68 (95% CI: −1.58 to 0.23; p = 0.15), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 72%) (). The confidence interval crossed the line of no effect, and the pooled effect was not statistically significant. Negative SMDs favored the intervention because higher scores on the included measures represented greater social impairment.

Although these measures were considered sufficiently related to permit exploratory pooling within a broad social communication/social responsiveness domain, they are not interchangeable measures of a single construct. The substantial heterogeneity observed across the three randomized studies may therefore reflect differences not only in intervention effects but also in outcome measurement, intervention content, participant characteristics, and comparator conditions. Because each instrument was represented by only one study, construct-specific subgroup analyses were not feasible. Accordingly, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a broad summary of a heterogeneous evidence base rather than as a precise estimate of the effect of DMIs on a single social construct.

Three studies (, , ) contributed to the quantitative synthesis of motor function, comprising 27 participants in the intervention groups and 28 in the control groups. Motor outcomes were assessed using different measures, including the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 (MABC-2) (), the Test of Gross Motor Development-3 (TGMD-3) (), and an objective motor-coordination measure. SMDs were pooled using a random-effects model.

The pooled SMD was 2.04 (95% CI: −0.52 to 4.61; Z = 1.56, p = 0.12), with considerable heterogeneity (I² = 92%) (). The confidence interval crossed zero, and the pooled effect was not statistically significant. Positive SMDs favored the intervention because higher scores represented better motor performance. The underlying endpoint data for Cui et al. and Souissi et al. were rechecked against the original reports and were confirmed to represent post-intervention means with SDs rather than SEs or change scores.

Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses showed marked variation in the pooled estimate. Excluding Lindor et al. yielded an SMD of 3.17 (95% CI: 0.93 to 5.42; p = 0.005; I² = 78%). Excluding Souissi et al. yielded an SMD of 2.08 (95% CI: −2.28 to 6.44; p = 0.35; I² = 96%), whereas excluding Cui et al. yielded an SMD of 0.92 (95% CI: −1.20 to 3.04; p = 0.39; I² = 84%) (). Given that only three studies contributed to the analysis, these leave-one-out analyses were descriptive and should not be interpreted as establishing the robustness of the pooled effect.

The three studies also differed in intervention emphasis and motor-outcome definition, ranging from broader dance-based or psychomotor programs to measures of gross motor performance, MABC-2 performance, and objective motor coordination. Together with the very small study-level samples and considerable statistical heterogeneity, these differences limit the interpretability of the pooled SMD. The meta-analytic estimate should therefore be considered exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of a uniform motor effect across DMI formats.

Several additional outcomes were not quantitatively pooled because the available measures represented distinct constructs or were reported by only one or two studies. These included joint engagement, empathy and emotion inference, cooperative behavior, interpersonal synchrony, gesture imitation, sensory and emotional outcomes, verbal/non-verbal communication, and neurophysiological measures ().

Chiang et al. reported greater child-initiated supported and coordinated joint engagement in the intervention group at the 3-month follow-up (). Dvir et al. reported greater cooperative behavior at follow-up and greater social closeness with familiar peers after synchronized movement, whereas no clear between-group difference was observed for work-related stress. Koehne et al. reported improvement in emotion inference and movement-related synchronization outcomes, while empathic feelings did not show a corresponding improvement. Mastrominico et al. found no significant overall intervention effect on empathy.

Souissi et al. reported higher post-intervention scores for simple hand and arm gesture imitation in the intervention group, whereas post-intervention IQ did not differ significantly between groups. Su et al. reported changes in interpersonal synchrony and fNIRS-derived cortical activation following creative movement. Other sensory, emotional, language, and communication outcomes reported by Ma et al., Mateos-Moreno and Atencia-Doña, and Aithal et al. were retained as narrative evidence because they were not sufficiently comparable for quantitative synthesis.

Cui et al. reported significant post-intervention between-group differences in the SRS total score and its social domains following dance therapy, but the exact post-intervention means and SDs required for effect-size calculation were not available in numerical form. The SRS findings were therefore interpreted narratively. Taken together, these study-specific findings suggest that potential effects may be more apparent for selected domains of interpersonal coordination, engagement, or motor behavior than for broader constructs such as empathy or global autism-related functioning. However, because these outcomes were generally assessed in single small studies using different instruments and intervention formats, the apparent domain-specific pattern remains hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

The GRADE assessment is summarized in . The certainty of evidence for social communication/social responsiveness was rated as very low. Evidence was downgraded for risk of bias because one contributing randomized trial was judged to be at high risk of bias while the remaining trials had some concerns, for inconsistency because substantial heterogeneity was present (I² = 72%), and for imprecision because the 95% CI was wide and crossed the line of no effect. The certainty of evidence for motor function was also rated as very low because of serious risk of bias, considerable inconsistency (I² = 92%), and imprecision associated with the small sample size and wide confidence interval. For overall autism symptom severity, the certainty of evidence was rated as low. The evidence was based on a single small randomized trial with some concerns for risk of bias and was downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision () ().

This systematic review identified a small and clinically heterogeneous evidence base spanning multiple DMI formats, comparator conditions, age groups, and outcome constructs. Accordingly, the structured narrative synthesis provides the primary framework for interpretation, whereas the meta-analyses should be regarded as exploratory summaries of selected randomized evidence. After separating randomized from non-randomized evidence, pooled effects for social communication/social responsiveness and motor function were not statistically significant and were rated as very low-certainty evidence. For overall autism symptom severity, only one randomized trial was available, resulting in low-certainty evidence and precluding pooling. Narrative findings suggested potentially favorable changes in selected interpersonal and functional outcomes, but the magnitude, consistency, and generalizability of these signals remain uncertain.

Previous quantitative evidence has suggested that dance-based interventions may reduce overall autism-related symptom severity. Chen et al. reported a favorable pooled effect in a meta-analysis of controlled studies. However, the present review separated randomized and non-randomized evidence rather than combining different study designs in the same primary meta-analysis. Under this approach, only Ren et al. contributed randomized evidence for overall autism symptom severity, whereas Ma et al. and Mateos-Moreno and Atencia-Doña were retained in the narrative synthesis because of their non-randomized designs. Although the randomized trial showed a marked between-group difference in CARS scores, it included only 30 participants. The GRADE assessment therefore indicated low-certainty evidence, with downgrading for risk of bias and imprecision related to the single small trial. Consequently, the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether the observed effect is reproducible across populations, intervention formats, and measures of overall autism symptom severity.

Social communication and social responsiveness showed a more uncertain pattern than suggested by the original mixed-design analysis. When the primary meta-analysis was restricted to randomized studies, the pooled estimate remained in the intervention-favoring direction but was not statistically significant, and the certainty of evidence was rated as very low. This differs in strength from earlier meta-analyses that reported favorable effects of dance-based or related movement interventions on social outcomes (, ). Broader physical-activity reviews have also reported improvements in social communication and sociability in children and adolescents with ASD, although these reviews included intervention modalities that were not directly comparable with DMIs. Differences in the populations, comparator conditions, intervention content, and outcome definitions may partly explain the variation across reviews.

An additional source of uncertainty was the conceptual diversity of the measures included in the present social analysis. The SCQ, SRS-2 Social Communication and Interaction score, and ATEC social ability domain all capture aspects of social or communicative functioning, but they are not interchangeable measures of a single construct. The substantial heterogeneity observed across the three randomized studies may therefore reflect not only differences in intervention effects but also differences in what was being measured. The available evidence was therefore insufficient for construct-level comparisons.

Several features of DMIs provide plausible explanations for the direction of the social findings, although the present evidence cannot establish a specific therapeutic mechanism. Interpersonal synchrony has been described as atypical in ASD and has been proposed as a potential target for social intervention (). Dance- and movement-based programs commonly incorporate imitation, mirroring, rhythm, and shared movement, requiring participants to attend to another person’s actions and coordinate their own behavior within an interpersonal context. Findings from individual studies were compatible with this hypothesis: Koehne et al. reported changes in synchronization, movement reciprocity, and emotion inference, while Dvir et al. reported greater cooperative behavior following synchronized group movement. However, empathy outcomes were less consistent, and an earlier meta-analysis similarly found little evidence of improvement in empathy (). Improvements in observable coordination or social engagement should therefore not be assumed to represent broader changes in empathic functioning.

Motor function warrants particular attention because motor coordination, balance, motor planning, and related difficulties are frequently reported in individuals with ASD (–). In the present review, the pooled estimate was in the intervention-favoring direction but did not reach statistical significance, and the certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across the three randomized studies, and the leave-one-out analyses showed that the pooled estimate was sensitive to the inclusion of individual studies. In particular, although exclusion of Lindor et al. () resulted in a statistically significant pooled estimate, substantial heterogeneity remained, whereas exclusion of either Cui et al. () or Souissi et al. () produced estimates with confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. The motor findings therefore cannot be regarded as robust across study combinations.

The variability in motor effects may partly reflect differences in both intervention content and outcome measurement. The three studies assessed different aspects of motor performance, including gross motor skills, MABC-2 performance, and objective motor coordination, while intervention duration and therapeutic emphasis also differed considerably. The particularly large study-level effects reported by Cui et al. and Souissi et al. were rechecked against the original reports; the values used in the meta-analysis were post-intervention endpoint means with SDs rather than SEs or change scores. These large effects therefore did not appear to result from an extraction or variance-conversion error, but both studies involved small samples, which limits the precision and stability of their effect estimates.

The uncertain pooled motor finding should not be interpreted as evidence that structured movement interventions have no relevance to motor development in ASD. Evidence from the broader exercise literature has generally been more favorable. Recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses have reported improvements in motor and related functional outcomes following structured physical exercise or motor interventions in children with ASD (–). However, these findings cannot be directly extrapolated to DMIs because exercise and motor-training programs differ from DMT and related dance-based approaches in therapeutic rationale, intervention components, intensity, and intended outcomes. The contrast nevertheless highlights the need for future DMI trials to include validated motor measures as prespecified outcomes and to report intervention dose and motor-specific treatment components in sufficient detail.

The outcomes that could not be quantitatively pooled further illustrate the breadth and conceptual heterogeneity of the evidence base. Individual studies reported changes in joint engagement, cooperative behavior, interpersonal synchrony, emotion inference, gesture imitation, and movement reciprocity, but these constructs were assessed using substantially different methods. Chiang et al. () reported changes in joint engagement following a caregiver-mediated intervention incorporating creative body-movement play, while Koehne et al. and Dvir et al. examined interpersonal synchronization and related social outcomes. These findings indicate that movement-based interventions may influence specific forms of interpersonal engagement, but they should not be treated as interchangeable measures of a common social construct.

Empathy findings were less consistent. Mastrominico et al. () did not demonstrate a clear overall intervention effect on empathy, and an earlier meta-analysis similarly reported little evidence of improvement in this domain (). Su et al. () combined behavioral measures of interpersonal synchrony with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and reported intervention-related differences in cortical activation following creative movement. Such neurophysiological findings are of interest for hypothesis generation but remain preliminary and should not be interpreted as evidence of an established neural mechanism. More generally, the small number of studies assessing each of these outcomes and the substantial differences in measurement methods prevented defensible quantitative synthesis.

The breadth of the DMI construct remains an important interpretive consideration. Although all included programs used structured dance or movement as a central component, they differed substantially in therapeutic framework, delivery format, dose, comparator condition, and intended target. The pooled estimates should therefore not be generalized uniformly across all DMI formats. Future trials should report intervention components, therapist qualifications, theoretical framework, dose, and treatment fidelity more consistently to distinguish formal DMT/DMP from other structured movement-based approaches.

Taken together, the present findings support a cautious interpretation of DMIs as potential complementary approaches rather than established stand-alone treatments for ASD. The randomized evidence for social communication/social responsiveness and motor function remained uncertain and was rated as very low certainty, while the evidence for overall autism symptom severity was based on a single small, randomized trial and was rated as low certainty. The current evidence therefore does not establish that DMIs are superior to other physical, behavioral, or creative interventions, nor does it identify an optimal intervention format, intensity, frequency, or duration. Their potential value may lie in combining structured movement with opportunities for interpersonal coordination and non-verbal engagement, but larger and methodologically rigorous trials are required to determine whether these features translate into reproducible clinical benefits.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings. The number of studies contributing to each quantitative synthesis was small, and sample sizes were generally modest, which limited the precision of the pooled estimates and the feasibility of subgroup analyses. In addition, the included studies varied in participant characteristics, intervention formats, comparator conditions, and outcome measures, contributing to heterogeneity across analyses. Some methodological limitations were also identified in the primary studies, particularly in relation to incomplete reporting and the use of subjective outcome measures in some trials. In addition, Chinese-specific databases such as CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP were not searched, and therefore some locally indexed Chinese studies captured by previous reviews may not have been identified. Although the structured narrative synthesis helps clarify these sources of variation, it does not eliminate the limitations of the underlying evidence.

Despite these limitations, the present review strengthened the synthesis by separating randomized and non-randomized evidence, applying design-appropriate risk-of-bias tools, conducting sensitivity analyses, and formally assessing the certainty of evidence using GRADE. Future studies with larger samples, more standardized intervention reporting, and more consistent outcome measures will help clarify the magnitude and clinical relevance of the observed effects.

This systematic review identified a limited and heterogeneous evidence base for dance- and movement-based interventions across age groups. The structured narrative synthesis suggested potentially favorable signals in several domains, particularly interpersonal engagement and coordination, but these findings were derived largely from small studies using heterogeneous interventions and outcome measures. Exploratory RCT-only meta-analyses for social communication/social responsiveness and motor function were not statistically significant and were rated as very low-certainty evidence, while evidence for overall autism symptom severity was limited to a single small, randomized trial and was rated as low certainty. DMIs may have potential as complementary interventions for ASD, but current evidence is insufficient to establish consistent efficacy, identify an optimal intervention format, or determine which participants are most likely to benefit. Larger, methodologically rigorous randomized trials with standardized intervention descriptions and outcome measures are needed to clarify their clinical role.

psychology.title: Potential Impact of Breathing Practice on Brain and Mental Health in Rural Adolescents With Psychiatric Symptoms: Protocol for a Single-Arm Pilot Feasibility Trial
psychology.abstract: Mental health conditions (MHC), particularly depression and anxiety, are the leading contributors to youth disability globally. In the United States, there has been a steep increase in diagnosed MHC cases over the last decade. Adolescents in rural areas are disproportionately affected by the combination of limited access to mental health professionals and stigma around seeking care. Current treatment options, mainly psychotherapy and psychopharmacology, have shown modest effects. Prior research suggests associations between slow-paced deep breathing and autonomic function, cerebral perfusion, and stress regulation, supporting further investigation of structured breathing as a potential adjunctive approach for MHC management.This study aims to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, implementation appropriateness, and participant satisfaction of a digitally supported, breathing-based intervention for adolescents with mild-to-moderate anxiety and depressive symptoms. The study will assess recruitment, retention, intervention engagement, usability, and the feasibility of collecting physiological and patient-reported outcome data to inform the design of a future efficacy trial.We aim to recruit approximately 40 adolescent patients receiving care through the Mayo Clinic Health System from rural communities in northwestern Wisconsin and southeastern Minnesota. Participants will complete a 4-month structured breathing program delivered entirely online, supported by a mobile app for guided instruction and practice tracking. All participants will attend 2 in-person visits (baseline and 4 mo) for functional near-infrared spectroscopy, as participants will already be on-site, the baseline and final study assessments will be completed at these same visits. A subsample (n=10) will additionally undergo magnetic resonance imaging at these visits.This study was funded in October 2025, and data collection began in February 2026, with completion anticipated in late 2026. As of July 2026, 14 of the 40 (35%) planned participants have been enrolled. Analysis will follow completion of data collection, with results expected to be reported in early 2027.Adolescents with anxiety and depression are a particularly vulnerable group, often undertreated due to limited access to mental health care. The proposed breathing intervention is designed as an accessible and scalable approach that warrants feasibility evaluation in rural youth populations.
psychology.text:
Mental health conditions (MHC), particularly depression and anxiety, are the leading contributors to youth disability globally. In the United States, over 5.3 million adolescents aged 12 to 17 (20.3%) had a current diagnosis of MHC in 2023, representing a 35% increase since 2016 []. Adolescents in rural areas often experience more severe emotional problems than their urban peers, partly due to limited access to mental health professionals, including psychiatrists, therapists, and other supports []. In addition, rural youth face stigma that is uniquely shaped by cultural norms, which can discourage help-seeking for MHC []. Untreated depression and anxiety may culminate in a state of chronic stress, a key contributor to altered brain development and impaired self-regulation, subsequently increasing the risk of negative outcomes such as substance use, academic struggles, and delinquency [].

Adolescent anxiety and depression are currently treated using psychotherapy, psychopharmacology, or a combination of both. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most used pharmacotherapy to treat adolescent anxiety and depression; however, treatment response varies across individuals depending on factors such as diagnosis, symptom severity, and comorbidities, and many patients continue to experience residual symptoms despite treatment [,]. A 2022 meta-analysis of 34 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 6161 children and adolescents with major depressive disorder reported a small effect size of 0.12 []. Similarly, a 2019 network meta-analysis of 22 RCTs including 2623 youth with generalized, social, and separation anxiety disorders found that SSRIs increased treatment response compared to placebo (odds ratio 4.6, 95% CI 3.3‐7.5), though many patients continued to experience residual symptoms []. Alternatively, adolescents and families may express a preference for nonpharmacological treatment options. In one survey, parents (N=143) favored counseling and physical activity over medication for managing adolescent depression []. Another study surveying adolescents who had received both medication and counseling found that 31% reported little to no benefit from medication, and 44% reported minimal benefit from counseling alone []. These challenges underscore the urgent need for accessible, low-barrier, self-paced strategies to augment existing treatments and support emotional and physiological regulation, particularly for adolescents in underserved areas with limited access to evidence-based treatment.

Slow, deep-paced breathing has emerged as a promising yet underutilized self-regulatory practice for individuals with MHC, with prior research suggesting associations with autonomic function, cerebral perfusion, and stress regulation [-]. Building on this literature, the present study focuses on the feasibility of implementing a structured breathing-based intervention and the feasibility of collecting brain physiological measures in adolescents with clinical anxiety and depression. Prior studies indicate that slow-paced breathing is associated with cardiovascular and neurophysiological processes relevant to stress and emotional regulation [-]. Consistent with this rationale, mindfulness-related processes have also been associated with more adaptive cognitive emotion regulation in adolescents, further supporting investigation of self-regulatory interventions in this population []. Structured breathing has also been associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow, cerebral blood circulation, and brain metabolic processes [,].

Of particular interest is the prefrontal cortex, a brain region critically involved in emotional regulation, executive function, and autonomic control []. Altered structure and function of prefrontal circuits have been consistently implicated in both adolescent and adult anxiety and depression, particularly in relation to disrupted connectivity with limbic regions and reduced regulatory control over emotional and stress responses by the prefrontal cortex [,]. Prior work has shown that specific prefrontal subregions and their projection pathways may be disrupted in these conditions and may represent physiological systems relevant to evaluating breathing-based interventions [,]. Respiration-related fluctuations in blood-oxygen-level dependent signals and CSF dynamics, once considered physiological noise, are now detected via advanced functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and are increasingly understood to reflect meaningful interactions between breathing and brain physiology [,,,].

Our preliminary work [,] suggests that respiration is associated with autonomic balance, cerebral circulation, and CSF movement. These physiological systems provide a mechanistic rationale for evaluating structured breathing interventions and can be feasibly assessed in adolescents to inform the design of future mechanistic and efficacy trials. Accordingly, the present study is explicitly designed to evaluate feasibility, acceptability, and implementation appropriateness of structured breathing intervention in adolescents with physiological and psychological measures examined descriptively rather than as efficacy end points.

Specifically, this study assesses the feasibility of collecting functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data in the full sample and the feasibility, tolerability, and completion rates of MRI in a subsample of 10 adolescents, without prespecifying neurobiological efficacy hypotheses. These imaging modalities are included to evaluate participant burden, data quality, and procedural viability in a rural adolescent population and to inform the design of future fully powered trials.

Given the increasing mental health burden among adolescents and persistent barriers to care in rural communities, self-regulatory practices, such as structured breathing, warrant feasibility evaluation as adjuncts to conventional treatment. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the feasibility, acceptability, and satisfaction with a structured breathing-based intervention while also evaluating the feasibility of multimodal physiological data collection (fNIRS and MRI) in rural adolescents with anxiety and depression.

This project is grounded in an equity-oriented approach to serving diverse and underserved populations. Adolescents with anxiety and depression are a particularly vulnerable group, often undertreated due to limited access to pediatric mental health specialists, extended wait times, and transportation barriers—challenges that disproportionately affect low-income families.

Can a structured breathing-based intervention for rural adolescents be feasibly implemented and perceived as acceptable, appropriate, and satisfactory by adolescents while also supporting adequate digital engagement through a mobile app and the feasible collection of physiological (fNIRS), psychological, and neuroimaging (MRI; subsample n=10) data to inform the design of future larger-scale trials?

The study hypothesizes that a structured breathing-based intervention will be feasible, acceptable, and appropriate for implementation among adolescents, as demonstrated by successful recruitment and retention and favorable scores on the acceptability of intervention measure (AIM), intervention appropriateness measure (IAM), and feasibility of intervention measure (FIM). It is further hypothesized that adolescents will demonstrate adequate engagement with the mobile app, reflected in adherence metrics, sustained use over the intervention period, and favorable usability ratings that inform barriers and facilitators to digital delivery.

Exploratorily, the study expects that the collection of fNIRS and psychological data will be operationally feasible with acceptable data completeness and tolerability. Descriptive summaries of these measures will be used solely to estimate variability, assess data quality, and inform the design of adequately powered future trials, without testing clinical or neurobiological efficacy or prespecifying directional effects.

To assess the feasibility, participant satisfaction, acceptability, and implementation appropriateness of a structured breathing-based intervention among adolescents. Feasibility will be evaluated based on recruitment rates, retention through the final assessment, and the completion of study procedures. Participant satisfaction will be assessed using satisfaction surveys, including quantitative ratings and open-ended responses. Acceptability and implementation appropriateness will be evaluated using standardized implementation outcome measures, including AIM, IAM, and FIM.

Preliminary feasibility data from our prior adult healthy control study support the plausibility of this approach. In that study, the recruitment rate exceeded 80% among eligible individuals approached, and participant compliance with the breathing protocol was approximately 85%, based on self-reported practice logs and session attendance. While these findings are not intended to predict outcomes in adolescents, they provide supportive evidence for the feasibility and acceptability of the breathing intervention framework.

To evaluate intervention adherence, usability, and engagement using metrics collected through the mobile app platform. App-based data will be used to characterize adherence patterns, sustained engagement over time, and user interaction with intervention components. These data will inform the identification of barriers and facilitators to digital engagement and guide refinements to intervention delivery and technological infrastructure for future larger-scale trials. Usability will be assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS).

To assess the feasibility of collecting physiological and psychological data in the context of a structured breathing-based intervention, including measures of cerebral oxygenation and local tissue hemodynamics using fNIRS in the full sample and MRI in a subsample of participants, alongside validated mental health measures. Exploratory analyses will focus on feasibility indicators such as data completeness, participant tolerance, and procedural viability. Descriptive summaries will be used to examine variability and estimate preliminary effect sizes to inform the design and power calculations of future adequately powered trials. The study is not powered to test clinical, physiological, or neurobiological effectiveness or efficacy hypotheses.

This protocol adheres to the SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 () [] statement for reporting clinical trial protocols; relevant guidance from the CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2010 extension for pilot and feasibility trials [] was incorporated to align with the feasibility objectives of the study. The intervention is described according to the TIDieR (Template for Intervention Description and Replication) checklist () [] to facilitate complete reporting and reproducibility of the breathing intervention, including its rationale, procedures, instructor qualifications, mobile app functions, delivery format, practice progression, adherence monitoring, and permitted adaptations. Feasibility outcomes were informed by the framework proposed by Bowen et al []. and include assessments of acceptability, implementation, practicality, and demand using standardized implementation outcome measures (AIM, IAM, and FIM) [].

As a pilot feasibility study, this trial is not designed to evaluate intervention effectiveness but to determine whether a future definitive trial is warranted. Progression to a future RCT will be guided by predefined feasibility benchmarks, including recruitment of at least 75% of the planned sample within the recruitment period, retention of at least 80% through the 4-month follow-up, completion of physiological assessments (fNIRS and MRI, where applicable) in at least 80% of eligible participants, and mean AIM, IAM, and FIM scores of at least 4.0 on a 5-point scale. Adherence to the breathing intervention will also be summarized descriptively using app-based practice metrics. These benchmarks will guide interpretation of feasibility and identify aspects of the protocol requiring refinement before a future efficacy trial.

This is a single-arm, nonrandomized pilot feasibility study designed to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and implementation appropriateness of a structured breathing-based intervention for rural adolescents with mild to moderate anxiety or depression. The study will also assess the feasibility of collecting physiological and psychological measures to inform the design of future adequately powered trials. Approximately 40 participants will be recruited from Mayo Clinic Health System (MCHS) clinics serving rural communities in northwestern Wisconsin and southeastern Minnesota.

Participants must (1) be 12 to 17 years old, (2) have a clinical diagnosis of mild or moderate depressive disorder and/or an anxiety disorder, (3) be receiving care at one of 2 participating MCHS outpatient psychiatry clinics, and (4) must reside in rural areas as defined by Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) [] codes (RUCA codes 4‐10). RUCA codes provide a standardized method for classifying rurality based on population density, urbanization, and commuting patterns, thereby capturing individuals living in small towns and outlying rural communities.

Participants must be able to read and understand English, and both parental or guardian consent and adolescent assent will be required. Adolescents with co-occurring mild to moderate alcohol or drug use problems will be eligible, provided these conditions do not require immediate specialized treatment or crisis intervention.

Exclusion criteria include current suicidal ideation or self-harm behavior requiring immediate clinical intervention, as well as severe psychiatric comorbidities such as psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder with psychotic features, severe substance use disorders, or eating disorders. Participants with severe cognitive impairment that would interfere with study participation will also be excluded. These criteria are intended to ensure participant safety and the feasibility of study procedures within a pilot implementation framework.

Potential participants will be identified through review of existing medical records at participating clinics and approached by members of the study team following approved recruitment procedures. Interested adolescents and their parents or guardians will receive detailed information about the study activities, including participation in the intervention and assessment requirements at each study time point, prior to providing informed consent and assent.

The breathing intervention is reported according to the TIDieR checklist to ensure complete and reproducible reporting of all intervention components. The intervention does not have an official or commercial program name and was developed specifically for this study as a structured breathing-exercise intervention. This study will use a fully online, structured breathing practice protocol to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of delivering a breathing-based intervention to rural adolescents. The intervention combines guided virtual sessions with self-directed daily practice supported by a mobile app (). The breathing program itself is delivered entirely online; this includes the one-time preprogram orientation with the instructor, all training, and all practice sessions, as well as the mobile app, which is used for both guided instruction and adherence tracking. The only in-person contact occurs at the 2 study visits (month 0 and month 4). All participants attend these visits for fNIRS data collection; because they are already on-site, the baseline and final study assessments are completed at the same visits. A subsample (n=10) additionally undergoes MRI during these 2 visits.

All participants will receive the same instructional materials and structured progression to maximize intervention fidelity. The breathing practice emphasizes soft, gentle movements intended to promote relaxation and awareness of breathing mechanics. Exercises are designed to support gradual familiarization with paced breathing and with postural engagement in a manner suitable for beginners.

Participants will follow a structured practice progression, beginning with 15-minute sessions and gradually increasing to 30 minutes and then 36 minutes per session over the course of the program. Participants will be encouraged to engage in self-practice at least 3 times per week. The program is designed to be accessible and adaptable, allowing participants to follow instructional video content and practice at their own pace. The mobile app serves both instructional and adherence-monitoring functions by providing standardized guided breathing sessions, practice reminders, and automated recording of session frequency, duration, and completion.

Breathing instructors will be informed only of each participant’s first name and age to facilitate instruction and safety but will not be provided with any additional study-related information. No direct identifiers or research data will be shared.

Monthly virtual check-ins will be conducted by the study team to collect survey data and to support participant engagement. These check-ins are intended to facilitate data collection and monitor feasibility-related outcomes rather than deliver therapeutic content.

Upon completion of the study, participants may elect to continue participating in the breathing program independently of the research study.

Mobile app data will be linked to participants through the study-specific identification numbers, and no protected health information will be collected or stored in the app. The mobile app is not considered an intervention component but serves solely as a tool for tracking engagement and adherence. The app records timestamps indicating when participants initiate and complete breathing practice sessions. Log data are transmitted daily via Wi-Fi or a cellular connection, depending on participants’ settings, and are stored using study identification numbers without direct identifiers.

The app is designed for 2-fold purposes: compliance tracking and instructional purposes. Participants can use the app to follow along and guide their practice. It is instructional in nature and helps to provide clear instructions on the different poses and postures, as well as how long one is expected to hold each posture. Each time a participant logs into the app to follow along with the instructional video, it will show the study team when and for how long the participant followed the video and completed the practice. This is how the app will be used as a compliance tracker as well.

To support safe participation while allowing flexibility in scheduling, the intervention includes a one-time initial instructional session followed by 2 ongoing formats: daily self-guided practice and optional weekly live online sessions. All sessions are designed to accommodate varying time commitments and learning preferences.

Participants are required to attend an initial online instructional session before beginning self-guided practice. During this session, participants receive instruction on the breathing protocol, guidance on progressing through the recommended practice schedule, and instruction on use of the mobile app.

Initial supervised online session: This one-time, real-time online session allows participants to join a live breathing practice led by the instructors, thereby supporting learning and familiarity with the breathing practices through real-time instruction.

Daily self-practice sessions: Daily self-guided practice follows a structured protocol with session durations of 15, 30, or 36 minutes, delivered via standardized online instructional videos on a video-hosting platform. The breathing practice mobile app is used to track session completion and adherence. Participants who experience discomfort or scheduling barriers may temporarily reduce practice frequency or duration before resuming the recommended progression while maintaining participation in study assessments.

Optional weekly online sessions: Optional weekly real-time online sessions allow participants to join live breathing practice sessions led by the instructors.

Participants will complete 2 in-person study visits at baseline (day 0) and approximately 4 months (day 120) later. These visits will include the completion of study surveys and the collection of respiratory fNIRS data.

Following the baseline in-person visit, participants will attend an initial online breathing instruction session (approximately 60 min). This session will orient participants to the breathing practice protocol and provide instruction on the use of the mobile app. This session is instructional in nature and is intended to support safe and consistent participation rather than to deliver individualized therapeutic content. Participants will also complete 3 monthly online study visits (days 30, 60, and 90), during which study surveys and brief guided breathing check-ins will be completed. A scheduling window of up to 3 weeks before or after the planned study visits and survey time points will be permitted to minimize barriers to participation.

This flexibility applies to both in-person and online components of the study, including baseline and 4-month visits as well as monthly online visits. Participants are encouraged to communicate with the study team to identify convenient times for these monthly online visits. Participants are encouraged to maintain the practice on their own time and schedule, seeking a minimum of once per week for at least 30 minutes. The app acts as both an instructional device for the breathing practice and a way to track consistency and compliance.

This study was reviewed and approved by the Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board (IRB number 25‐012922). All caregivers and participants will provide informed consent and assent, respectively, prior to participation, and procedures are designed to minimize risk and protect confidentiality. Participant safety will be safeguarded by trained clinical research coordinators. Data will be stored securely in REDCap, accessible only to authorized study personnel, and curated in accordance with Mayo Clinic policies and National Institutes of Health (NIH) data-sharing guidelines. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations. Deidentified datasets may be deposited in an appropriate research repository consistent with Mayo Clinic policy and funder requirements.

Exploratory measures are included to assess the feasibility, tolerability, and data quality of collecting psychological and physiological data in the context of a structured breathing-based intervention. A stepwise feasibility approach will be used, with lower-burden measures implemented in the full sample and higher-burden neuroimaging procedures conducted in a subsample. Data from these measures will be used solely to evaluate procedural feasibility, estimate variability, and inform the design of future adequately powered trials; no clinical, physiological, or neurobiological efficacy hypotheses will be tested.

Participants will complete a series of self-report surveys assessing mental health symptoms, well-being, and feasibility-related outcomes. Surveys include the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Linear Analog Self-Assessment (LASA) for quality of life, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Self-Rated Abilities for Health Practices Scale (SRAHP), and an exit survey. Survey content may be simplified or omitted as necessary to reduce participant burden or eliminate redundancy.

Responses to the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 will be reviewed by a study psychiatrist (Drs Sharma and Bormann) after each study visit in accordance with the depression and anxiety management plan. Survey data will be collected and managed using REDCap.

Physiological data collection will follow a tiered feasibility strategy, with fNIRS implemented in the full sample as the primary physiological modality, followed by MRI in a smaller subsample to assess the feasibility of higher-burden neuroimaging procedures.

At designated in-person study visits, intake and month 4, participants may undergo the collection of basic physiological measures to assess the feasibility and tolerability of the monitoring procedures. These measures may include respiratory belts, pulse oximetry or photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiogram recordings using commercially available systems (eg, Biopac Systems, Inc; Obelab, Inc []). Specific modalities may be simplified or omitted if needed to reduce participant burden or address feasibility constraints.

fNIRS data will be collected using a portable, noninvasive system to assess the feasibility of measuring cerebral hemodynamic signals during study visits (). The device estimates relative changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin concentrations in superficial cortical regions, including the prefrontal cortex, by emitting near-infrared light at 2 wavelengths (approximately 780 nm and 850 nm) and detecting wavelength-specific changes in light absorption ().

fNIRS data will be used solely for feasibility-related purposes, including evaluation of signal stability, motion tolerance, participant comfort, and completeness of data acquisition. Data will be summarized descriptively to estimate variability and inform protocol refinement and sample size considerations for future studies. No mechanistic, physiological, or clinical efficacy hypotheses will be tested using fNIRS data in this study.

A subset of participants (n=10) will additionally undergo MRI scanning to assess the feasibility, tolerability, and logistical requirements of incorporating MRI procedures into future larger-scale trials. MRI acquisition will occur after completion of fNIRS assessments and will be conducted using a 3T MRI scanner at MCHS–Eau Claire during after-hours, with support from 2 trained MRI technologists.

The MRI protocol may include phase-contrast MRI for flow-related measures and echo-planar imaging, followed by T1-weighted and T2-weighted anatomical imaging. For T2 imaging, both brain and abdominal scans will be acquired, with the abdominal scan included to assess the feasibility of capturing respiratory-related anatomical movement. MRI-compatible physiological monitoring (eg, PPG and respiratory belts) will be used to evaluate the feasibility of concurrent physiological data acquisition within the scanner environment.

A head-coil mirror and screen-based cue presentation will be used to display breathing-related prompts during scanning. If participant fatigue, discomfort, excessive motion, or sleep occurs, the scan sequences may be abbreviated, simplified, or discontinued. Scan repetition will be limited by feasibility considerations rather than data optimization. Total scan time will not exceed 70 minutes.

All MRI sequences will be conducted under FDA nonsignificant risk guidelines, as verified by a magnetic resonance physicist. The imaging protocol may be modified within these guidelines to accommodate feasibility, safety, or participant tolerance considerations.

MRI data will be used exclusively to evaluate feasibility parameters, including recruitment into the MRI subsample, scan completion rates, participant tolerance, motion-related data quality, and procedural logistics. Data will be summarized descriptively to inform the design of future adequately powered trials. No neural, physiological, or behavioral efficacy hypotheses will be tested with MRI data in this study.

Our study includes a detailed adherence and compliance training program designed for the 4-month duration of the study.

Participant engagement: Participants will receive a report on their activity and will be asked to confirm whether there are any errors or updates needed. If a participant does not communicate with the study team for 5 days regarding their daily practice, the study team will send a reminder via their preferred contact method (eg, text message, telephone call, or email). This ensures ongoing engagement and addresses any participant concerns. For the breathing group, any feedback from the instructors will be relayed to the participants, and vice versa.

Emphasis on honest reporting: We encourage participants to report on their practice habits honestly and without any pressure. Self-practice is not mandatory, and there is no need to overcommit. The most important aspect of this study is that participants provide genuine feedback on their actual practice. The study seeks to understand natural compliance patterns, and we value honest, pressure-free reporting over strict adherence to practice frequency.

Potential adverse events (AEs) related to breathing practice, which involves light physical exercise, are generally minor and infrequent. Participants may experience dizziness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath, or headaches, particularly if they are new to breathing techniques or overexert themselves. Some individuals may report mild discomfort in the chest, muscle strain, joint discomfort, sleep problems, or increased anxiety during practice. Rarely, hyperventilation can occur, leading to tingling in the extremities or fainting. It is important to note that these events are typically transient and resolve quickly without lasting effects. Proper instruction and gradual introduction to breathing techniques can minimize the occurrence of these AEs. Participants must report any AEs to the study coordinator immediately and seek medical attention if necessary. In the S1_GHQ survey, we include a section to evaluate potential AEs of breathing practice.

The depression questionnaire (PHQ-9) responses are screened real-time by study coordinators. Any PHQ-9 total score of greater than 5 or any positive (ie, nonzero) response to the suicidal thoughts question (9) will be addressed promptly by the study coordinator by communicating with the study clinicians. Clinical psychiatric procedures for assessing and managing depression will be followed by the study physician psychiatrist (PS and NB).

Participants will receive US $50 for each in-person visit completed at baseline (0 d) and at 4 months (120 d). Additionally, during the monthly online survey and breathing-practice check-ins at 1 month (30 d), 2 months (60 d), and 3 months (90 d), participants will receive US $20 for each completed online survey. Participants who complete all study activities may receive up to US $160 in total compensation.

The primary outcomes of this study focus on implementation feasibility and acceptability and encompass three domains: (1) acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility of the breathing-based intervention; (2) recruitment and retention feasibility; and (3) participant satisfaction.

Acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility of the breathing-based intervention will be assessed using standardized implementation outcome measures, including AIM, IAM, and FIM.

Recruitment and retention feasibility will be evaluated by calculating the proportion of eligible adolescents who enroll in the study and the proportion of enrolled participants who are retained through the final study assessment.

Participant satisfaction will be assessed using satisfaction surveys, including quantitative ratings, open-ended survey responses, and the study exit survey.

Secondary outcomes focus on intervention engagement and digital delivery feasibility and include digital usability, engagement with the mobile app, adherence to the breathing practice, and caregiver-reported observations.

Digital usability and engagement will be assessed using app usability ratings and in-app analytics, including frequency of logins, session duration, and feature use.

Adherence and engagement will be assessed using breathing session attendance records, app-based adherence metrics, and completion rates of assigned breathing practice sessions.

Caregiver-reported observations of adolescent mood, behavior, emotional regulation, and engagement with care will be collected via caregiver-completed surveys. These data are intended to provide contextual information regarding feasibility and perceived relevance of the intervention rather than to assess clinical effectiveness.

Exploratory outcomes are included to assess the feasibility of collecting physiological and psychological data and to estimate variability to inform future trials. These outcomes are not intended to test efficacy or effectiveness.

The feasibility of assessing cerebral hemodynamic signals will be evaluated using fNIRS-derived estimates of relative changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin. Analyses will focus on data completeness, signal quality, and participant tolerance.

In a subset of participants (n=10), the feasibility of MRI data acquisition will be assessed using structural and functional MRI sequences as previously described. Outcomes will include scan completion rates, participant tolerance, and data quality. MRI data will be summarized descriptively and will not be used to test neural or clinical hypotheses.

The feasibility of collecting validated self-report measures of emotional and behavioral well-being will be assessed using the PHQ-9, GAD-7, GHQ, LASA, PSQI, MFIS, PSS, and SRAHP.

Descriptive pre-post summaries of validated psychological measures will be examined to estimate variability and inform power calculations for future trials. The study is not powered to test hypotheses or evaluate intervention effectiveness.

All primary and secondary outcomes will be summarized using descriptive statistics, including means, SDs, medians, proportions, and 95% CIs, as appropriate. Because this is a pilot feasibility study, the analytic focus is on estimation, variability, and data completeness, rather than hypothesis testing or formal statistical inference. Simple data visualizations (eg, pre-post plots, individual change trajectories, and distributional summaries) will be used to illustrate patterns and heterogeneity of responses. These summaries will inform the selection and prioritization of outcomes, including implementation, behavioral, and physiological measures, for future larger-scale trials.

For exploratory physiological and neuroimaging data, including fNIRS measures in the full sample and MRI data in a subsample of participants, analyses will focus on within-person descriptive changes from baseline to postintervention. Physiological recordings will be processed with standard preprocessing procedures to assess data quality, completeness, and signal stability. Summaries will characterize general patterns in cerebral oxygenation and basic physiological responses during study visits. These analyses are intended solely to evaluate the feasibility and interpretability of data collection procedures and to determine whether the observed variability suggests potential utility for inclusion in future studies; no efficacy or mechanistic hypotheses will be tested.

Qualitative feedback obtained from participants through open-ended survey responses will be analyzed using a brief thematic analysis approach. Two reviewers will independently review responses and identify common themes related to perceived benefits, challenges, acceptability, and overall impressions of the intervention. Any discrepancies will be resolved through discussion. Qualitative findings will be used to contextualize quantitative feasibility outcomes and to inform the refinement of the intervention and study procedures.

This study was funded in October 2025. Enrollment began in February 2026 and remains ongoing; as of manuscript submission (July 2026), 14 of 40 (35%) planned participants have been enrolled. Data collection is expected to conclude in late 2026. No interim analyses have been conducted; formal data analysis will commence after final data collection, with results anticipated for dissemination in spring 2027.

This pilot feasibility study is designed to determine whether a structured, app-supported deep-breathing intervention and multimodal physiological assessment protocol can be successfully implemented among rural adolescents with anxiety and depressive symptoms. We anticipate that the study will generate feasibility data regarding recruitment, retention, intervention acceptability, adherence, and the feasibility of collecting high-quality physiological and neuroimaging data. Rather than testing treatment efficacy, the primary contribution of this study will be to determine whether the intervention and study procedures are feasible and to generate estimates necessary for the design of a future adequately powered clinical trial. The results of this study will provide summaries of key feasibility outcomes and physiological and psychological data to inform the design and statistical planning of a subsequent fully powered trial. Accordingly, analyses will focus on recruitment and retention, intervention acceptability and participant satisfaction, adherence and digital engagement, and the data completeness, tolerability, and quality of multimodal data collection (fNIRS in the full sample and MRI in a subsample), rather than hypothesis testing. Outcomes will be summarized using descriptive statistics (means, SDs, medians, proportions, and 95% CIs, as appropriate). These findings will be used to refine study procedures, optimize assessment timing, and inform effect-size assumptions and sample-size calculations for future trials.

Although breathing-based interventions have been conducted to reduce anxiety, improve stress regulation, and enhance emotional well-being in adults [,], relatively few studies have examined their feasibility in rural adolescents, particularly using objective physiological measures alongside patient-reported outcomes. Furthermore, previous studies have rarely integrated portable neurophysiological assessments such as fNIRS. This study therefore addresses an important gap by providing feasibility data to inform the design of future effectiveness trials.

This project addresses two main priorities: (1) reducing health disparities and (2) enhancing population-based and value-based care in rural communities by evaluating the feasibility and acceptability of a low-burden, scalable breathing-based intervention for adolescents with anxiety and depression.

A major strength of the study is its integration of behavioral, psychological, and objective physiological measures while leveraging digital technology to support intervention delivery and adherence in a rural population. The inclusion of both portable neuroimaging (fNIRS) and MRI will also provide valuable information regarding the feasibility of collecting multimodal mechanistic data in this setting.

If feasibility benchmarks are achieved, future studies will expand recruitment across multiple rural health systems to generate a larger dataset and subsequently include suburban and urban settings to evaluate implementation across diverse populations and improve generalizability. Given the limited evidence on structured breathing interventions for adolescents living in resource-constrained rural communities, this work may provide the foundation for a future adequately powered multicenter RCT. Ultimately, this research may help determine whether a structured deep-breathing intervention can be feasibly implemented as a practical, low-burden adjunct to conventional care among rural adolescents.

As this is a pilot feasibility study, several limitations should be acknowledged. The single-arm design, relatively small sample size, and absence of a control group preclude conclusions regarding clinical effectiveness or neurobiological mechanisms. In addition, recruitment from rural outpatient psychiatry clinics within a single health system may limit the generalizability of the findings. The primary purpose of this study is to evaluate study procedures, participant engagement, and data collection processes that will inform the design of future adequately powered trials.

Study findings will be disseminated through presentations at regional and national scientific conferences, publications in peer-reviewed journals, and communication with participating clinical sites, community stakeholders, and participating families. The findings will also be used to guide the design and implementation of future multisite clinical trials evaluating structured breathing interventions for adolescent mental health.

This pilot study will evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of a structured breathing-based intervention for rural adolescents with anxiety and depression. Findings on recruitment, participant retention, adherence, intervention acceptability and satisfaction, and data completeness will inform the design of future adequately powered RCTs evaluating the clinical effectiveness of this intervention.

psychology.title: From spike to baseline: distance-collapse in Buddhist contemplative practice and durable wellbeing
psychology.abstract: Across contemplative traditions, the most experienced practitioners describe an endpoint in which devotion is no longer confined to particular times and places but becomes a continuous, featureless condition scarcely distinguishable from ordinary living. Positive psychology, approaching the same terrain from a measurement perspective, distinguishes fleeting hedonic states from durable eudaimonic wellbeing and finds that repeated contemplative states can consolidate into stable traits. What has been missing is a single structural account of the mechanism that carries the first into the second.This study proposes that contemplative maturation is, at root, the collapse of the separation between the practitioner and what the practice orients toward, a single distance parameter D whose fall toward zero generates the rest. As D → 0, the duration of each contact contracts and its frequency rises toward continuity; their product (the devotional throughput) acts as a compensatory trade-off rather than a conserved quantity; the amplitude of the sacred–profane oscillation falls to zero; and the baseline of consciousness rises to absorb it. The endpoint is a straight line, embodiment, in which the separation has vanished: one no longer visits the temple or performs the prayer but is the temple, is the prayer. The practitioner is flat relative to their own elevated baseline and elevated relative to the ordinary world.The argument is developed within the Liberation Mathematics program, joining a wave-mechanical description of practice to the Phenomenology Quotient (PQ) and Threshold Modulator (τ) constructs. Theravāda insight practice (the sustained observation of arising-and-passing, udaya–vaya, toward the unconditioned, asaṅkhata) provides the structural backbone; jhānic factor-dropping, equanimity (upekkhā), and the brahmavihāras supply the operational detail; and a cross-traditional comparison finds structurally analogous trajectories in dhikr, the Jesus Prayer, japa, and nembutsu.Durable wellbeing is a baseline phenomenon, not a peak phenomenon. Buddhist contemplative practice enhances wellbeing by shifting from amplitude-seeking into baseline elevation, a reading that recovers what the traditions have long described and yields falsifiable predictions about the affective signatures of long-term practice.
psychology.text:
An old and stubborn finding in the psychology of happiness, and an old and stubborn claim in the literature of contemplation, turn out to be the same observation seen from two sides. The psychological finding is that peaks do not last. The elation of a windfall and the devastation of an accident both fade over months, toward a level set largely before the event occurred; the famous comparison of lottery winners and people newly paralyzed found their settled happiness far closer than anyone expected (). Pleasures adapt. The treadmill returns us, with some reliability, to where we began (). Whatever durable wellbeing is, it does not seem made of high moments, because high moments are precisely the part of experience that erodes.

The contemplative claim is stranger and, on its face, almost disappointing. The practitioners a tradition most trusts (the ones it calls awakened, liberated, established) describe their condition not as a perpetual peak but as something close to invisibility. Nothing in the posture, nothing in the gaze, no performance of holiness. The Zen formula is exact in its flatness: before awakening, one carries water and chops wood; after awakening, one carries water and chops wood. The destination has no distinguishing feature. A tradition organized around the pursuit of extraordinary experience will, by its own internal logic, struggle to recognize the ordinary as its fulfillment.

Put the two together, and a single question falls out, which is the question of this study. If durable wellbeing is not a peak, and if the contemplative endpoint is not a peak either, what mechanism allows a practice that begins as a series of intense, bounded, special experiences to become a continuous and unremarkable way of being? How does a spike become a baseline? The traditions describe the destination and the journey with great care, but they do not describe the dynamics of the transformation in a form that connects to anything measurable. Positive psychology has the measurements (trait versus state, hedonic versus eudaimonic, the consolidation of repeated states into lasting dispositions) () but has not had a structural picture of why contemplative repetition should produce that consolidation rather than mere habituation (; ).

The proposal developed here is that the missing picture is a wave. A practice is an oscillation in consciousness; maturation is the controlled collapse of that oscillation into a straight line; and the straight line, correctly understood, is not the cessation of practice but its saturation, the point at which what was once a special act has become indistinguishable from being alive. The remainder of the study sets out the model (§3), shows that Buddhism has independently diagnosed the central error the model predicts (§4), reads Theravāda insight practice as the engine of the collapse (§5), adds the second, relational axis the model requires (§6), completes the account of embodiment with a cross-traditional comparison (§7), and then states the wellbeing thesis formally and exposes it to falsification (§8–§9).

The novelty is easily mistaken for a more familiar claim, so it had better be stated plainly. The claim is not that contemplative practice improves wellbeing, which is by now well established. It is the proposal that contemplative maturation can be described geometrically, and at its root as the collapse of a single separation parameter, the felt separation between practitioner and what the practice orients toward, from which the more familiar signatures (the rising baseline, the falling amplitude, the consolidation of state into trait) follow as consequences rather than causes. This furnishes a common explanatory architecture linking Theravāda insight practice, the state-to-trait transformation documented by contemplative neuroscience, and durable eudaimonic wellbeing. The contribution is the architecture, not the correlation.

A formal model of something as intimate as contemplative experience invites a reasonable suspicion, and it is best met at the outset. Husserl accused Galileo of covering the living world with a garb of ideas so successfully that the covering came to be mistaken for the thing covered ().
