The same risk attends any attempt to write consciousness as a curve. If the reader leaves believing a person’s awakening is an equation, the model will have harmed.

The position taken here is narrower and, I hope, harmless. The wave model, and the PQ and τ constructs it draws on, are offered as the skeleton of the phenomenon and not as the phenomenon itself, in the way an anatomical drawing describes the structure of a face without competing with the face, or a score describes a symphony without replacing the hearing of it. The mathematics is descriptive, not generative. It does not produce equanimity; it describes the shape of what is felt when equanimity arrives. Its practical value is recognition: a practitioner who understands that the quiet that follows years of sitting is a genuine baseline shift, and not fatigue or the loss of an earlier intensity, is more likely to trust it, return to it, and let it deepen. The formula scaffolds toward the building, and is meant to be taken down once the building stands.

The status of the equations needs a word, since their form invites one misreading and forecloses another. They are phenomenological models in the sense the term carries in systems ecology or population dynamics, compact descriptions of how quantities co-vary and tend toward limits, and not empirically fitted laws with calibrated constants; to write A ∝ D is to assert a direction and a limit, not a measured slope. Yet this is not the same as calling them metaphors, and the difference is testable. Each variable admits an operational proxy: the frequency ν and duration d of contemplative contact are directly countable by experience-sampling; physical and temporal distance are metric; and the amplitude A and baseline B have candidate physiological surrogates already in use, the phasic, event-evoked measure of a signal set against its tonic resting level, as when amygdala reactivity is read in an ordinary, non-meditative state (). One could therefore log these surrogates over months and plot a contemplative time-series much as a cardiologist plots an electrocardiogram, watching the tall, sparse spikes of early practice resolve into a higher, quieter line. The comparison is exact in one respect and misleading in another, and the difference is worth stating plainly: like the electrocardiogram, such a trace would be a model-laden projection that is nonetheless real and trackable; unlike it, the quantity it projects, the intensity of consciousness itself, has no single calibrated instrument so that the trace would plot surrogates of a latent variable rather than the variable directly. Read this way, the equations are a measurement program in waiting, falsifiable through their surrogates, rather than laws already fitted.

For this reason, the quantitative language throughout is deliberately light. The relations stated below are idealizations, heuristics for thinking about direction and limit, and not measured laws. Where the model touches data, it does so through predictions (§9), which is the only honest place for it to make contact.

On the word “sacred.” A second clarification concerns a word, and it earns the space. To speak of a sacred distance, and of a sacred–profane oscillation, is to borrow a vocabulary that a generation of critical scholarship has taught us to distrust: the category of the sacred, and its partition from the profane, is not a cross-cultural universal but a historically particular construction, shaped by Otto, Durkheim and Eliade and exported through the study of religion in ways later scholars have worked to denaturalize (; ; ; ). The caution bites harder here, since the tradition that supplies the backbone of the study has no sacred entity in the Western sense at all. It applies again to the tidy “Theravāda progression” invoked below, which recent scholarship reads as partly the artifact of a modern, reforming Buddhism rather than a timeless given (). I take these warnings seriously, and mean the term in none of the senses they indict.

What the distance parameter D measures is not proximity to a sacred object but the felt separation between the practitioner and whatever their tradition orients practice toward, the telos, or in Tillich’s functional idiom the object of ultimate concern (), whatever its content and by whatever name. It is a relation, not a substance; and it is one instance of a more general quantity this program employs, the distance of a state from the fixed reference whose reaching is its goal. The equilibrium-geometry of flourishing developed elsewhere in the program measures exactly such a distance in the space of wellbeing and names it, in Sanskrit, duratva, the distance of a life from the surface of balanced flourishing, whose collapse reduces avoidable suffering (). D and duratva are not the same distance: one is a relation along a single practitioner–object axis, the other a position in a four-coordinate wellbeing space. They are siblings under one parent (separation from a fixed reference, whose collapse is the telos) and, as §8 argues, they are coupled, the closing of D being one route by which a life reaches low duratva. The word sacred is kept below only as an occasional, flagged shorthand for this functional distance, never as a claim about a sacred realm.

One further word, on reality itself, since the phrase risks running two things together. What is meant throughout is the phenomenal sense of reality, the felt quality by which some contents strike us as more real than others, and not reality in the ontologist’s sense. That felt quality has a phenomenology of its own, from Jaspers’s early analysis of the sense of reality () to more recent work treating it as plural and metacognitively structured [Fortier’s taxonomy of the sense of reality ()] and to Losoncz’s account of heightened reality (). The collapse described here lives in that register: as D falls, the partition of felt reality into set-apart and ordinary things dissolves, until nothing is held as more real than the rest. Nothing is asserted about reality as the ontologist means it, which is also why sacred reality, where the phrase survives below, names a felt sense and not a posited thing.

Read functionally, the distance is not the property of religious lives only. Every life stands at some remove from its own equilibrium (the balanced, non-compensable flourishing the duratva model formalizes) whether or not it frames that remove in any religious vocabulary at all. The distance is a structural feature of being a self, not a devotional posture: what the traditions call liberation or salvation, what positive psychology calls durable wellbeing, and what a clinician calls recovery are different charts of one equilibrium, and contemplative practice is one well-mapped route toward it. One qualification guards the claim from overreach. Saying every life has such a distance does not mean every life seeks to close it; many orient toward acquisition or distraction, which the duratva model shows to increase the distance rather than reduce it. The reference is universal; the movement toward it is not. It is the distance, not the wish to be rid of it, that belongs to everyone.

Consider any repeated devotional or contemplative act, a period of seated meditation, say, or a recitation, a round of the rosary, a prostration. Before the act, attention rests at its ordinary level. During the act, something rises (a quality of presence, of contact, of consciousness brought to bear) and afterward it subsides. Repeated over days and years, the practice is therefore a periodic perturbation of consciousness, and can be written, with no pretense of precision, as.
ψt=Bt+At·gν t

where ψ(t) is the level of consciousness at time t, B is the baseline, the ambient level between acts, A is the amplitude of the rise the act produces, ν is the frequency with which the act recurs, and g is the shape of a single instance, whose width we may call its duration d. Four quantities, then, carry the whole argument: amplitude, frequency, duration, baseline. A first relation, established in the opening study of this program (), links two of them: as a practice is done more often, its instances grow shorter, so that the product d·ν, a kind of devotional throughput, often exhibits a compensatory trade-off, the one rising as the other falls. One does not need a 90-minute ceremony once a month and a single breath many times an hour to do different amounts; they can be the same amount distributed differently.

The decisive question is what maturation does to these quantities, and here the natural assumption is wrong. The natural assumption, the founding assumption of every tradition that equates depth with intensity, is that to advance is to raise the amplitude: a bigger experience, a higher peak, a more dramatic contact. This study claims the opposite. Mature practice lowers the amplitude. As the practice is repeated, A falls toward zero, ν rises toward continuity, d contracts toward the instantaneous, and the consciousness that the peaks used to concentrate does not vanish but becomes distributed through baseline functioning. The oscillation flattens; the mean rises to meet it; and the curve asymptotes to a horizontal line lying well above where it began ().

This reframing immediately resolves an apparent contradiction within the program. It is useful to define a Phenomenology Quotient, PQ = C(e)/C(g): the ratio of the consciousness brought to a particular event to the consciousness held as one’s general waking baseline. We characterize stable liberation, which we call Level 3, as the condition in which PQ remains permanently above one. Yet the present model says the endpoint has zero amplitude. The two are reconciled by noticing that they measure against different baselines. The amplitude of the practice-wave is, in these terms, the height of the C(e) spikes above C(g), roughly (PQ − 1) at the peak. As cumulative practice raises C(g) itself, the ratio C(e)/C(g) flattens toward one: every event is now met with the same fully deployed consciousness, so no event stands out as a spike. Measured against the practitioner’s own raised baseline, the curve is flat—PQ ≈ 1 everywhere. Measured against the ordinary, unraised baseline of the world, the same line stands permanently elevated—PQ > 1, the Level-3 criterion (). The liberated person is flat relative to the self and elevated relative to the world. There is no contradiction here, only two frames.

One further quantity must be kept distinct from amplitude, because the model needs two axes and not one. Amplitude concerns time: how sharply the sacred is set apart from the profane moment to moment. But practice also discriminates by object—it grants full consciousness to some things and persons and withholds it from others. We name this the Threshold Modulator, τ ∈ [0,1]: the pre-reflective permission a mind extends, before any deliberation, to constitute a given object at full depth. Ordinary τ is sharply selective. The flattening of amplitude is one collapse, the abolition of special moments; the equalization of τ toward one is a second, orthogonal collapse, the abolition of special objects. Embodiment, as §7 will argue, requires both ().  gathers the four wave-quantities, their direction under maturation, and the Buddhist practice that operates on each.

The four quantities of the practice-wave.

Maturation does not raise the peaks; it lowers amplitude, raises frequency, contracts duration, and lifts the baseline that absorbs them. Frequency and duration tend to trade against each other (a compensatory relation (d·ν), not a strict conservation law), and amplitude and baseline trade likewise, as consciousness once concentrated in the oscillation is redistributed into the mean.

If maturation lowers amplitude, then the most natural mistake a practitioner can make is to pursue amplitude, to take the height of the experience for the measure of its depth. This is the contemplative form of the hedonic treadmill. The seeker who chases ever more vivid absorptions, more flooding bliss, more spectacular openings, is doing on the cushion exactly what the windfall-chaser does in the market: maximizing a quantity that, by its nature, returns to baseline and must therefore be sought again at higher and higher intensity. It is an addiction to the steep part of the curve.

Remarkably, the Buddhist tradition diagnosed this error from the inside and built its correction into the architecture of practice. The classical map of meditative absorption in the Visuddhimagga is, read carefully, a program of deliberate amplitude reduction (). The first absorption still contains the coarse movements of applied and sustained thought; these are let go. It still contains rapture, pīti, the flood, the thrill, the very high-amplitude event a novice would take for the goal; this too is let go. It still contains pleasure, sukha, of a calmer kind; this, too, is let go. What remains at the fourth absorption is one-pointedness and equanimity, a state the texts describe as neither-pleasant-nor-painful—luminous, stable, and flat. The tradition does not treat the surrender of rapture as a loss. It treats it as the advance. The map runs from the spike toward the line.

The flattened wave is called upekkhā, equanimity, and it must not be mistaken for numbness. The two pull opposite ways. Numbness lowers the baseline, narrows consciousness, and refuses to feel. Equanimity raises it: consciousness so fully and evenly present that no part of experience needs to be spiked into salience or pushed out of awareness. It is zero amplitude at a high baseline, the affective signature of the straight line. This is also, stated in the vocabulary of wellbeing, the structural exit from the hedonic treadmill: not a better way to chase peaks, but the cessation of peak-chasing in favor of a raised and even ground. Where positive psychology observes that hedonic adaptation defeats the pursuit of high moments (; ), the contemplative tradition offers not a faster treadmill but a different floor.

Equanimity addresses amplitude. The second movement of the collapse is along frequency, and here Theravāda insight practice supplies not merely an example but the structural backbone of the whole account. The foundational instruction of the Satipaṭṭhāna teaching is to extend mindfulness across every posture and activity—walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating, and the humblest bodily functions are each named explicitly as occasions for awareness (). The ideal is not a long daily session but unbroken attention (), satata-sati: contact with the practice approaching continuity. In the terms of the model, ν rises toward the limit while each act of noting contracts to the momentary, the compensatory product d·ν spreading a once-bounded practice across the whole of waking life until there is no longer a marked instance to point to.

But the deepest reason to take Theravāda as the backbone is that its central practice is the observation of a waveform.

What follows is a reconstructed sequence, drawn from canonical and commentarial sources and from the modern insight-practice lineages that have shaped how they are read; I offer it as a model of a tendency the tradition makes available, not as an ethnographic account of Theravāda practice as a whole (). Insight meditation trains attention on udaya–vaya, the arising and passing away of phenomena, the ceaseless rise and fall that the tradition holds to be the fundamental texture of all conditioned things (). As concentration sharpens, what first appeared as solid, named objects resolves into finer and finer oscillations, until at the stage the commentaries call bhaṅga, the knowledge of dissolution, experience is met as a near-continuous shimmer of vanishing (; ). The practitioner is increasing the resolution of attention upon the wave (). The whole purpose of this exercise is to deliver the mind to that which does not arise and pass, the unconditioned, asaṅkhata, nibbāna, named throughout the canon precisely by its freedom from the rise-and-fall (; ; ).

One caution, lest the geometry be mistaken for a metaphysics. To represent asaṅkhata as a straight line is a claim about the geometry of attention, the cessation of the sacred/profane oscillation, and not a claim that the unconditioned is, ontologically, merely a flat line. In Buddhist thought, asaṅkhata is a far richer soteriological category than any diagram can carry; the line is its attentional signature, the shape awareness takes as it approaches what does not arise, and nothing more is asserted of it here.

The developmental shape this implies is more interesting than a simple fading, and worth drawing out. Maturation does not pass directly from oscillation to stillness; it first passes through an intensification. Early practice meets the world as sparse, slow, high-amplitude waves, a few salient events standing well clear of a dull baseline. As attention sharpens, the waves do not merely shrink; they multiply and quicken, until arising and passing are met as a dense, rapid shimmer, the stage the tradition marks as bhaṅga, the dissolution in which each thing is seen breaking up moment by moment (). Only then does the oscillation cease to be a distinct feature at all: the shimmer grows so fine and so continuous that it reads as a single unbroken level, and attention is delivered to the non-arising. These three phases (sparse oscillation, dense oscillation, baseline absorption) are the same arc the wave-quantities trace (low ν, then high ν, then ν continuous as A → 0) and the same arc a contemplative record would show across years (§7.2). The line is reached not by quieting the wave but by letting it become continuous: frequency rises to its limit before amplitude disappears into the baseline.

This gives the wave-to-line geometry a precise canonical home. The conditioned, saṅkhata, is the waveform, that which arises and ceases. The unconditioned, asaṅkhata, is the straight line, that which neither rises nor falls. The model’s central image is therefore not a metaphor imported into Buddhism but a restatement, in the language of oscillation, of the saṅkhata–asaṅkhata distinction the tradition places at its very center. Insight practice raises the frequency of observation of the conditioned wave until the practitioner touches what the wave was always moving through. The line is reached by attending to the oscillation, not by suppressing it.

A practice can flatten its amplitude and raise its frequency and still remain partial, because both of those collapses concern the temporal distribution of consciousness—they abolish special moments. They do not, by themselves, abolish special objects. A meditator may reach great evenness on the cushion and still extend full reality only to a narrow circle of persons and things, withholding it, below the level of choice, from the stranger, the inferior, the inconvenient. The relational filter, τ, may remain sharply selective even when the temporal wave has gone flat. This is the failure the tradition would call dry insight: clarity without warmth.

The remedy is the second axis of the collapse, and Buddhism trains it directly through the brahmavihāras (loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and again equanimity) whose defining instruction is extension without distinction: the radiation of goodwill to all beings, the friend and the stranger and the enemy received at the same depth, in every direction, without remainder. This is the equalization of τ toward one across all objects. It matters for wellbeing and not only for metaphysics. A consciousness that grants full reality to some and withholds it from most is, among other things, lonely and effortful; the steady labor of maintaining the filter is itself a low-grade suffering. Broadening awareness to receive experience without the constant work of selective admission is, as the contemplative-science literature has begun to document, associated with greater meaning and a more durable, less defended wellbeing (). This is more than philosophical inference: training in compassion and loving-kindness has been shown to raise positive affect lastingly and to shift the neural response to the suffering of others from distress toward affiliation (), while loving-kindness practice builds durable personal resources that in turn predict gains in life satisfaction (), the affective and motivational signature one would expect if the equalization of τ were a trainable change and not a figure of speech. Embodiment, then, sits at the corner where both collapses are complete: no special moments and no special objects, the sacred saturating time and object alike ().

It remains to say precisely what the straight line is, and how it differs from simply giving up. A wave requires a gradient, a difference between two levels, to travel between. The practice-wave oscillates because ‘in the sacred’ and ‘out of it’ are different states; the rise and fall is the mind moving across that difference. When the baseline has risen to meet the peaks, the gradient is gone: there is no longer a profane trough for the sacred crest to be distinct from, because every moment is now held at the level the crest once reached. The wave goes flat not because the practice was abandoned but because it has nowhere left to travel. The line is flat through saturation, not through cessation. This is the formal content of the old report that, for such a person, the temple and the self are no longer separable: the sacred has stopped being a place one goes to and a time one keeps, and has become the medium one lives in.

The same completion can be read a third way, not across time, as the flattening of amplitude, and not across objects, as the equalization of τ, but along the distance between the practitioner and the sacred. This third reading proves the deepest, for the other two follow from it, as §7.1 will make precise; to keep it distinct from the duration d, write this separation as D. Devotion begins in proximity: the sacred is a separate object, approached at set times and in set places, and the practice is the closing of a gap (D > 0). In the Buddhist idiom, this is the stage of access, upacāra—drawing near but not yet arrived. With maturation, the gap closes to juxtaposition: the sacred is no longer visited but continuously adjacent, a companion to every act—sati standing beside the whole of life, the prayer always at one’s side (D → 0, yet still two). The limit is superimposition: the practitioner and the practice come to occupy one place, no line can be drawn between them, and the boundary that made them two is gone (). One no longer prays; one is prayer. The grammar of the movement is the grammar of that collapse (from the transitive I pray to, through prayer accompanies me, to the bare copula I am prayer) which is the nembutsu’s jiriki giving way to tariki, restated in the language of distance.

The last station needs care, because superimposition is, in classical Indian thought, the very name of bondage: adhyāsa, the false overlay of the not-self upon the self, the rope mistaken for the snake. The terminus meant here is that error’s inverse and its undoing. Where bondage superimposes what is not there, embodiment is the limit at which two layers can no longer be told apart, the point the optics of the wave makes exact, since two identical waves perfectly in phase are indistinguishable from one. It is better, then, to name that limit coincidence, or identity: not two things overlaid, which could in principle be peeled apart, but a single figure where there seemed to be two. The graded vocabulary of the Indian traditions already marks the stations on the way—sāmīpya, nearness to the divine; sārūpya, the taking on of its very form; sāyujya, fusion with it, a ladder of decreasing distance that ends, as the model does, in coincidence. And superimposition is, spatially, nothing other than the vanished gradient of the wave: when the field of the sacred and the field of the self hold the same value at every point, no difference remains for an oscillation to cross. The straight line, the equalized τ, and the coincident figure are three faces of one event.

The clearest single ritual instance is the Pure Land practice of nembutsu, the recitation of the name of Amida Buddha. It begins as a counted, effortful act, repeated by deliberate will. In Shinran’s mature teaching, the recitation undergoes the transformation the model describes: it ceases to be something the practitioner does by their own power, jiriki, and becomes the spontaneous sounding of the name through them, tariki, the name saying itself, the doer dissolved into the deed (). The boundary between the one who practices and the practice has gone transparent; what remains is shinjin, the settled condition, continuous and unmarked. The recitation has become a baseline rather than an event.

The same collapse appears across traditions that did not borrow from one another (; ; ), the strongest evidence that it describes ritual as such, rather than the idiom of one school.  sets out the convergence. In each case a practice is inaugurated as a bounded, effortful, intermittent act of high amplitude and low frequency, and matures into something continuous, faint, and effortless, for which the tradition coins a specific name, and in each case that name marks the disappearance of the boundary between the practitioner and the practice.

The same waveform collapses across six independent traditions.

A bounded, effortful, high amplitude act matures into a continuous, faint, effortless condition with a tradition-specific name, and in every case the named endpoint marks the dissolution of the boundary between practitioner and practice. This convergence shows that the collapse describes the structure of repeated devotional practice.

Two clarifications guard this convergence against over-reading, for it would be a serious error to suggest that every contemplative path culminates in the same flat line. The model does not claim that all traditions value amplitude reduction, still less equally. Ecstatic and devotional currents—bhakti at its most rapturous, Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, Hasidic fervor, several tantric lineages—deliberately cultivate and retain high amplitude, and would rightly reject the suggestion that their summit is equanimity. The present account takes no quarrel with them. Its claim is narrower and conditional: to the extent that a tradition produces durable embodiment, a stable trait rather than a recurring state, its most established practitioners tend shift from episodic peaks toward a steadier baseline, whatever the amplitude of the peaks encountered along the way. Prizing the peak and exhibiting the baseline shift are not exclusive; a tradition may do both. The straight line described here is one well-attested terminus (paradigmatically, though not uniquely, the Buddhist one) and not the single destination of contemplative life.

The three readings of this section have circled a fourth thing without naming it, and it is not a reading at all, but the cause of the other three. Beneath the flattening of amplitude, beneath the equalization of τ, lies a single quantity whose decline generates them both: the distance between the practitioner and the sacred. Write it D, not the duration d of §3, but the separation the practice exists to cross. D need not be measured in meters. It may be physical (the kilometers to a temple), attentional (the effort required to summon remembrance), symbolic (the dependence on an external object or image), or existential (the felt distance from what ultimately matters); physical distance is only its most visible form. The whole of contemplative maturation can then be written as the monotonic decline of this one parameter, D → 0.

The typology is worth fixing at once: a single symbol covering four separations could otherwise be made to carry too much. Four distances can be told apart: a physical distance, the meters to a shrine or temple; a temporal distance, the interval between one contact and the next; an attentional distance, the effort a mind must spend to bring the sacred to mind; and an existential distance, the felt separation from what ultimately matters. The first three are surrogates; the last is primary. Existential distance is what liberation actually closes (dukkha, in one of its aspects, simply is this separation held open) and the other three are its outward and measurable shadows: as the existential gap narrows, the pilgrimage shortens, contact grows continuous, and remembrance ceases to cost effort. When the proportionalities that follow speak of D, they speak, strictly, of these measurable surrogates, through which the primary distance is tracked rather than observed directly.

Three relations tie the wave-quantities to D. They are structural proportionalities—statements of direction, in the heuristic spirit of §2, and not metric laws with units:
d∝D,ν∝1/D,A∝D

The baseline follows the complementary tendency:
B↑asD↓

As sacred distance contracts, less consciousness is concentrated into episodic peaks, and more is redistributed into the standing level of awareness itself. The rise of baseline is therefore the inverse expression of the decline of distance.

Under these proportionalities, reducing distance shortens individual contacts, increases their frequency, lowers their amplitude, and raises the baseline into which that amplitude is progressively absorbed.

The closer the sacred draws, the less time and effort a single contact requires, so duration falls with distance; the closer it is, the more often contact can be made, until contact is unbroken, so frequency rises as distance falls; and the amplitude of the sacred–profane swing scales with the separation, because the swing simply is the mind’s repeated travel across the gap. The linear form is chosen for conceptual transparency, not fitted precision: any monotonic relation (D2, log D, or another) would preserve the qualitative conclusions, since the argument turns only on the directions of change and on the single limit D → 0.  depicts the plots of the four quantities against a decreasing D.

Two consequences follow, and they recover by derivation what earlier sections had to assume or merely assert. First, the compensatory product d·ν, posited in §3 as a rough constancy of devotional throughput, is now explained rather than stipulated: if duration shrinks in proportion to D while frequency grows as its inverse, their product changes little with D, a compensatory trade-off rather than an exact conservation, since the reciprocal form is an illustrative choice and not a fitted law. What looked in §3 like a conserved throughput is really this trade-off, and it falls out of the distance collapse rather than having to be stipulated. Second, since amplitude scales with separation, its vanishing at the limit is automatic:
lim(D→0)A=0

The flattening of the wave, the whole burden of the preceding sections, is therefore not the primary event but the visible signature of a deeper compression. The straight line of §3 and the gradient-less saturation with which §7 opened are the same fact told twice: a wave requires two distinguishable regions and a distance between them, and at D = 0 there is no second region left to travel to. Amplitude collapse, baseline elevation, the contraction of duration, the rise of frequency, all four are consequences of the single decline of D. This reverses the descriptive hierarchy the study has so far presented: distance is the proposed organizing parameter, and the wave its observable expression.  reads a representative Buddhist progression in exactly these terms.

A representative Buddhist progression read as the decline of D, the felt separation from the practice-telos.

As the locus of the awakened condition moves from a distant, set-apart place to awareness itself, D falls toward zero while the duration of each contact contracts and its frequency rises toward continuity. The endpoint is not a place reached but a separation dissolved.

Two book-keeping quantities make the picture exact, and they must not be confused, since one collapses while the other is conserved. The first is the traversal volume, the product of the duration, frequency, and distance of a contact—.
V=d·ν·D

—a measure of the total reaching across the gap that a practice performs: the kilometers walked to the shrine, the hours given, the acts of crossing summed over a life. Under the proportionalities above it is not conserved but driven to zero, for its distance factor vanishes while the throughput d·ν that it multiplies stays roughly fixed:
lim(D→0)V=0

At the limit there is no separation left to cross and no act of crossing; the traversal volume is the very quantity embodiment eliminates. A mature practice does not preserve its total reaching—it abolishes it. What is conserved is a different object, and the two are easily mistaken for one another: not the traversing but the presence it carried. Writing E = ∫ C(t) dt for cumulative contemplative engagement (the total consciousness brought to a life, the area beneath the curve), embodiment leaves E roughly intact while V, D, d, and A fall and ν rises. The reaching collapses to nothing; the presence is conserved and merely redistributed, no longer gathered into occasional summits but spread across the whole of a life. The mountain becomes a plateau, a lasting condition Maslow distinguished from the transient peak (), and the peak becomes the ground. This is the exact content of the image of a sacred found within rather than traveled to: the distance has gone to zero, yet nothing of the devotion is lost.

Buddhism states the limit more starkly than any theistic tradition, because it has no deity to stand at a distance from. The separation that collapses is the felt distance between ordinary awareness and the awakened condition—first imagined as elsewhere, a future attainment reached by long effort, and progressively seen never to have stood at a distance at all. This is the force of Nāgārjuna’s claim that there is not the slightest difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa (): the distance between bondage and liberation is zero. One does not travel to awakening; awakening is the condition of the traveling. The refuge is not lodged in a place but carried in awareness itself, the same interiorization that other traditions render as the heart becomes the Kaʿba, the indwelling Christ, the Name residing within.

At the limit, the grammar of practice turns from the transitive to the copula. One no longer enters prayer; prayer becomes the mode in which life is lived. One no longer remembers the sacred; the sacred becomes the condition of remembering. The temple no longer occupies a place in space; awareness is the temple:
lim D→0,d→0,ν→∞ Practice=Being

And the wellbeing thesis deepens with it. Existential distance, the felt separation from what ultimately matters, is itself a mode of suffering; dukkha has, among its faces, exactly the structure of a gap not yet closed. To raise the baseline is, at root, to reduce that distance, and eudaimonic flourishing is the affective signature of a separation grown small. Embodiment, on this reading, is not the accumulation of experience but the elimination of distance.

One clarification protects this endpoint from a natural misreading, and the traditions are unusually explicit about it. The straight line is not the practitioner dissolving into what was sought; it is coexistence at zero distance, with experienced separation gone and no annihilation of lived embodiment. The Buddhist name for it is exact: saupādisesa-nibbāna, extinction with the substrate remaining (). The fires of greed, hatred and delusion are out. However, the person is not: the aggregates continue, the senses still register the pleasant and the unpleasant, and the awakened one walks and teaches for 45 years in that condition, the substrate falling away only at death. The affective form is put about as plainly as one could ask. Struck by a painful feeling, the arahant feels the bodily pain but not the second, mental arrow that ordinarily follows—pierced by one dart, not two (). The first arrow still lands; the second never does—amplitude-collapse in the canon’s own words, sensation remaining while the reactive swing above it goes flat. Nor is the result a serene withdrawal from the body’s decay: in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta the aged Buddha likens his body to a worn cart kept going with straps (), and dies not by any transcendent exit but of an ordinary illness after a lay follower’s meal, instructing that no blame attach to the giver. A worn-out mortal body and an unshaken awareness, neither fused nor fled: that is the line, lived. The tenth of the ox-herding pictures says the same pictorially, the one who has finished the search returns to the marketplace with open hands (). And the shape recurs outside Buddhism: the late Kṛṣṇa, his displayed power spent to nothing, at last simply is the sthitaprajña (unshaken in sorrow, uncraving in joy) that he had decades earlier only described, the sought drawn wholly inside the seeker (). In none of these is the endpoint an absorption into a void; it is an ordinary, mortal figure from whom the distance has simply gone.

This stillness is easily misheard, so let me be plain: it is not stasis. Events still arrive, the body still ages, relationships still change, new domains are still entered; what stops is the displacement of the ground beneath them. In the wave model this is low amplitude around a raised baseline; in the equilibrium model, small excursions and a fast return to the surface; in the liberation model, continued movement through the world with fixation on any achieved position falling toward zero. The Buddha’s first arrow without the second, and the late Kṛṣṇa who keeps acting while nothing he does hardens into a self, are comparable not because their traditions teach one doctrine but because both show the same shape—full contact with change, little residual seizure. What goes still is not the world but the machinery that once caught each wave and made a self of it.

The distance-collapse principle invites an obvious objection—that its central quantity is phenomenological, and so unmeasurable. The objection has less force than it first appears. Pain, stress, attentional load, and subjective wellbeing were each once thought inaccessible for want of an instrument, not for want of existence; what was missing was operationalization, not the phenomenon. The quantities marshaled in this study (amplitude A, baseline B, duration d, frequency ν, the threshold modulator τ, and the sacred distance D resolved in §7.1 into physical, attentional, and existential components) are candidates for the same treatment: each is tied to a behavioral, temporal, affective, or phenomenological dimension that can in principle be observed.

Two cautions keep the operationalization honest, and both bear on how D is handled. First, D is best treated not as a sum of its components but as a latent quantity estimated from them. Physical distance in meters, attentional distance as the effort or latency needed to re-establish contact, and existential distance as a rated felt-separation cannot simply be added: they carry different units, and any composite would require standardization and weighting before it meant anything. Second, the temporal aspect of separation is not independent of the model at all (the interval between one contact and the next is, by definition, the reciprocal of the frequency ν), so the temporal dimension is already carried by a primary variable and must not be double-counted inside D. With these provisos, the components of D and the wave-quantities together define a small panel of trackable indicators rather than a single elusive one.

That panel makes possible what one might call a contemplative record: a longitudinal profile assembled from repeated measurement of the panel—amplitude and baseline through phasic-versus-tonic physiological surrogates, frequency and duration through experience-sampling, the components of distance through the metric and rated indicators just named. Plotted across months and years rather than within a single sitting, such a record would resemble a physiological monitoring trace more than a list of isolated experiences (): the tall, sparse spikes of early practice giving way to a higher, quieter line as amplitude migrates into baseline and contact approaches continuity. As with the electrocardiogram invoked in §2, the resemblance is structural and not mechanistic. The record would no more diagnose awakening than an electrocardiogram diagnoses a life; its use would be humbler and real, to make developmental trends legible, to tell a genuine baseline shift from fatigue or the loss of an earlier intensity, and to register the stagnation or regression that subjective impression alone may miss.

The claim is that this license is stronger than a purely descriptive one and weaker than a metaphysical one. The quantities introduced here are not only ways of speaking about contemplative experience; they are candidate developmental variables whose trajectories, once operationalized and validated, could let contemplative maturation be monitored rather than merely attested. Whether the instruments can in fact be built is an empirical question this study does not settle. It settles only what they would have to measure.

A reviewer may reasonably ask what a validated instrument for the two least tangible quantities would look like, and the model is specific enough to answer. For D, the route is a latent-variable one: assemble a short battery of standardized indicators (a metric or rated physical-distance item; a re-engagement cost, meaning the latency and effort needed to return attention to the practice-object after interruption; and a brief felt-separation scale for existential distance), then test by confirmatory factor analysis whether they load on a single factor, as the distance-collapse reading predicts. Convergent validity would be their joint decline across a longitudinal sample; discriminant validity, their separation from a general mindfulness scale. For τ, the natural instruments are differential rather than absolute: a processing-depth or affective-response task that presents near and far others (kin, stranger, unfamiliar out-group) and measures the gap in attention, memory, or evoked response between them, with τ-equalization registering as the shrinking of that gap. Its neural counterpart is the narrowing of the differential amygdala and reward response across target categories already reported in compassion training (). Neither instrument exists in validated form; both are buildable with existing methods, and the predictions of §9 are framed so that building them would test the model rather than presuppose it.

A last point turns the record into a test rather than a description. What would set this account apart from its rivals is not a change in any single indicator but the way several move together. Habituation can lower affective amplitude without lifting the tonic baseline; attentional automatization can shorten the marked duration of practice without touching continuity of awareness; affect regulation can damp reactivity without producing the standing availability of attention. The distance-collapse reading predicts more than any of these alone: that as perceived separation falls, amplitude and marked duration contract together with rising continuity and an elevated baseline. Subjective and neural effort may fall alongside, but they are treated as a separate correlate, not identified with d; and τ, the relational filter, sits on its own axis and equalizes only under relational cultivation, so it is not carried in this bundle. Should these quantities fail to move together across a long record, the case for a single latent D weakens, and a family of partly independent processes fits better. That is the shape of a genuine test.

The predictions of §9 turn on the affective signatures of long-term practitioners, and that phrase needs unpacking, because the answer is not a count of years. Two things are being run together in the ordinary phrase, and the model needs them apart. One is exposure—how much practice a person has done, counted in cumulative years, lifetime hours, current frequency, and retreat or lineage history, and it is by exposure alone, with no outcome built in, that a long-term practitioner should be defined. The other is maturation, or stabilization: a structural condition in the equilibrium geometry the duratva model provides (), namely a life that holds low duratva within a band bounded away from zero (zero being the tradition’s limiting jīvanmukti, not an operational bar), that swings only a low amplitude of excursion from the surface, and that recovers the low value quickly when perturbed, the recovery rate that in the published model scales with vairāgya, non-seizure. Keeping the two apart matters, because long practice does not guarantee maturation: exposure and outcome can come apart, and only if they are defined separately does the prediction of §9 stay a prediction rather than a definition. Each maturation term is a measurement procedure with its threshold left open—position through a battery over the four coordinates, excursion through the phasic-versus-tonic surrogates proposed for A, recovery through a perturb-and-track design. The study offers how maturation would be located, not a number it can supply.

The pieces now assemble into a single claim about wellbeing. Hedonic wellbeing, in this picture, is amplitude: the height of pleasant events above baseline. It is by definition reversible, by definition adapting, by definition a Level-1 phenomenon in the stratification adopted here—real, available, and impermanent (; ). Eudaimonic wellbeing is baseline: the level of C(g) itself, the ground from which all events are met. It is durable precisely because it is not an event and therefore has nothing to adapt back from. The whole difference between the wellbeing that fades and the wellbeing that lasts is the difference between amplitude and baseline—between the spike and the line.

This is exactly the distinction that contemplative neuroscience has been converging on under the heading of altered traits. The thesis of that literature is that the lasting value of meditation lies not in the states it occasions but in the conversion of repeated states into stable traits (; ). The empirical signatures map onto the model with some precision. Long-term practitioners show changes that persist outside formal practice, in the ordinary resting condition, a baseline shift, not merely a taller spike: reduced amygdala reactivity measured in a non-meditative state is a change in B, not in C(e) (). Expert practitioners reach and sustain attentional states with markedly less effort than novices, the neural cost of concentration falling as expertise grows, the contraction of d, deliberate engagement giving way to effortless continuity (). Meta-analysis finds the largest and most reliable effects of practice in stable dispositional measures rather than transient ones (), and the broader literature on the neuroscience of mindfulness reads, throughout, as a literature about baseline reorganization (). The same convergence appears in the neuroscience and phenomenology of non-dual and “pure” awareness, where the deep baseline is described in terms of an even, non-reactive affect rather than heightened positive affect (; ; ). The motivational counterpart is equally familiar: self-determination theory’s account of internalization, in which a behavior moves from externally imposed to fully integrated regulation (), is the same trajectory seen from the side of the will, the practice ceasing to be something one is made to do and becoming something one is, which is internalization and embodiment described twice ().

The thesis can therefore be stated in a line. Buddhist contemplative practice enhances durable wellbeing by converting amplitude-seeking into baseline-elevation, by lowering the swing, raising and equalizing the ground, and contracting deliberate effort toward effortless continuity, so that what began as a series of special states becomes a settled trait. This is not a discovery laid over the tradition; it is the tradition’s own account of equanimity and the unconditioned, rendered in a vocabulary that connects to measurement.

Stating the thesis this way exposes a distinction that the wellbeing literature has tended to leave implicit, and that the present model lets us draw sharply. There are not two geometries of wellbeing but three, and they correspond exactly to the quantities of the practice-wave and the two axes of its collapse (). The first two are familiar. Hedonic wellbeing is amplitude: the height of pleasant events above the baseline, episodic and reversible by nature, and therefore the form that hedonic adaptation reliably erodes. Eudaimonic wellbeing is baseline: the elevation of C(g) itself, durable precisely because it is a trait rather than an event and so has nothing to adapt back from (; ).

Three geometries of wellbeing. Hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing are distinguished by the temporal axis alone (amplitude versus baseline).

Embodied wellbeing adds the second, relational axis, the equalization of τ, and is the form most easily overlooked, because it has neither the drama of the peak nor any visible mark of the raised ground.

The third form is the one this study makes explicit, and it is what embodiment in the full sense requires. A person may have a high and stable baseline (be, by every eudaimonic measure, flourishing) and yet still extend full reality only to a chosen circle, withholding it below the level of choice from the stranger and the inconvenient. Their wellbeing is durable but divided; the relational filter τ remains selective even though the temporal wave has gone flat. Embodied wellbeing is the conjunction of the brahmavihāras train (§6): a raised baseline that is also relationally even, full consciousness extended without the constant, low-grade labor of selective admission. Eudaimonia answers the temporal axis; embodiment completes the relational one as well. It is worth distinguishing this sense of embodiment, the even extension of awareness, from the somatic codification of practice into the body developed elsewhere in this program (; ): the two are complementary, the one relational and the other bodily. This is why the two collapses of §3 had to be kept distinct; the wellbeing taxonomy is their direct consequence.

A single illustration (offered as illustration, not as data) fixes why the embodied form is the easiest of the three to miss. Picture two people on a long retreat. The first is a gifted newcomer, 3 weeks in and luminous with rapture: her face shines, she is moved to tears by ordinary things, and everyone near her can feel that something is happening. The second has practiced for 40 years and is, to all appearances, unremarkable—he eats his rice, washes his bowl, answers a question briefly and without drama. By amplitude, the newcomer is plainly more advanced; she is having the larger experience. Measured by baseline and by τ, the order reverses. Her radiance will subside when the retreat ends and the conditions that produced it are withdrawn; his evenness will not, because it is no longer a state he is in but the ground he is. The counterintuitive consequence of this account, that the mature practitioner may appear less dramatic than the enthusiastic beginner, is not a paradox but the expected signature of a wave that has gone flat at a high level.

These three geometries can finally be drawn together with the wellbeing model the study has leaned on, closing the distance between the two. Represent a life as the duratva series δ(t), the moving distance of its state from the equilibrium surface, and the practice-wave of this study is that series read from the inside: its baseline B is the (inverse) mean level of δ, a life resting near the surface; its amplitude A is the amplitude of δ’s excursions away from the surface; and maturation, A → 0 with B raised, is δ settling onto a low, quiet level—small mean and small variance together. On this reading, the wave’s baseline and amplitude have natural dynamical analogs in the duratva series: baseline corresponds inversely to its long-run mean distance from equilibrium, amplitude to the size and variability of its excursions, and the damping of the wave to the rate at which a life returns toward the surface after a perturbation (). Two things follow. Because δ is a distance and so non-negative, an elated spike and a grief-spike register alike as excursions from equilibrium, not a defect but the duratva model’s own thesis, that seized elation raises avoidable suffering exactly as loss does, both flattened by the same vairāgya. And the contemplative collapse of D is, in these terms, one family of routes toward low, stable δ. It is not a single-axis intervention: different practices work on different coordinates—insight on Vidya, non-seizure practices on vairāgya, the brahmavihāras on relational reciprocity, grounded service (sevā) on Dhana, so what matures is not one coordinate but a life’s tendency to rebalance toward the whole surface. A life may also reach that surface by non-contemplative means, material sufficiency and relational reciprocity among them; contemplative practice is one well-mapped way into the wellbeing geometry, not a separate geometry. The claim is offered as a bridging hypothesis, testable through the co-variation of affective amplitude and duratva excursion, and not as an identity of the two constructs.

A guard against a predictable misreading is owed here. None of this reduces liberation to a psychological trait to be optimized. The raised baseline is a consequence of reduced seizure, not a quantity to be accumulated, and contemplative practice is neither necessary nor sufficient for flourishing on its own: material sufficiency, relational reciprocity, institutional security, and communal life remain non-compensable conditions of wellbeing in the wider duratva model, and the contemplative route presupposes the social world in which a life is held rather than replacing it. Nor is nirodha being rebranded as eudaimonic gain. The wellbeing signature is what cessation of reactive appropriation looks like from outside; it is not the point of the cessation.

A structural model earns its place only if it can be wrong. The following predictions follow from the account and are, in principle, testable with existing instruments for affect, attention, and wellbeing.

The limitations are real and should be stated plainly. First, the relations among A, ν, d, and B are offered as heuristics for direction and limit, not as measured laws; the compensatory trade-off between d and ν, in particular, is a descriptive regularity rather than a measured conservation law. Second, the PQ and τ constructs introduced here still lack validated measurement instruments; the model predicts what such instruments should capture, but the instruments have not been built. Third, the cross-traditional convergence of  is suggestive rather than probative—it shows a common shape, not a common cause, and the traditions differ in ways the table necessarily flattens. Fourth, and most important, the model describes the structure of the transformation and takes no position on the metaphysics of any tradition’s endpoint; that asaṅkhata can be described as a straight line is a statement about the geometry of attention, not a claim about what, if anything, lies beyond the conditioned ().

Falsifiable predictions of the wave-collapse account.

Prediction 1 distinguishes the model from a ‘bigger peaks’ account; Prediction 3 is the sharpest test, since a single-axis model would not predict the dissociation.

A further substantive limitation concerns the shape of the path rather than its endpoint. The model is stated as a smooth, monotonic decline of D toward zero, and real contemplative development is neither smooth nor reliably monotonic: practitioners report long plateaus, regressions, and frank distress, and a growing literature documents meditation-related difficulties ranging from transient destabilization to prolonged impairment (). Two things follow. First, the monotonic form is an idealization of the attractor, not a description of the trajectory; it says where sustained practice tends, not that every interval of practice moves there, and the predictions above concern long-run position and stability rather than step-by-step descent. Second, the model has room for the difficult phases rather than being embarrassed by them. The dense-shimmer stage of §5, the bhaṅga in which arising and passing are met at their finest resolution, is just where the tradition locates its most destabilizing territory, the dukkha-ñāṇas or “dark night” in the model’s terms; it is a regime of very high frequency reached before the baseline has risen to absorb it, a transitional spike and not the flat line. Adverse outcomes can be read, similarly, as characteristic failure modes: amplitude collapsing while the baseline stays low, which is the numbness of §4 and not equanimity, or a destabilized τ that derealizes self and world instead of equalizing regard (). The account does not claim that practice is uniformly safe or that the descent is painless. It names a direction and some ways the descent can go wrong.

The disappointment with which this study began—that the contemplative endpoint looks like nothing in particular, and that durable happiness refuses to be made of high moments—turns out to be the same fact stated twice, and the fact is structural. Wellbeing that lasts is a property of the baseline, not of the peaks; and the baseline is raised not by amplifying experience but by letting its oscillation flatten until what was concentrated in the peaks has been redistributed into the ground. Buddhist practice is, on this reading, an unusually explicit technology for that flattening: equanimity lowers the amplitude, insight raises the frequency of attention upon the conditioned wave until the unconditioned is touched, and the brahmavihāras equalize the relational filter so that the collapse extends across objects as well as moments. The resulting straight line is not the end of practice. It is practice become continuous, effortless, and invisible, the temple spread so evenly through a life that it can no longer be told apart from the living. Beneath even this lies the simplest statement the study can make, and the one it would put at its center: the flattening is the shadow of a vanishing distance (). Every quantity the model follows (amplitude, frequency, duration, baseline) moves as it does because the separation between the practitioner and the sacred closes toward zero. At zero there is no longer a sacred to travel to, only a sacred to be. In the end, wellbeing is more baseline than spike.

psychology.title: Peripheral β-Endorphin in Borderline Personality Disorder: Investigating Clinical Correlates and Longitudinal Changes During Psychotherapy
psychology.abstract: Borderline personality disorder is characterized by difficulties in regulating emotions and managing relationships and is frequently associated with self-injury. Research has suggested that endogenous opioids could play a role in this last aspect, but so far little is known. This study examined the blood levels of β-endorphin, the main endogenous opioid, in 49 patients with borderline personality disorder and 25 healthy individuals. It also explored whether these levels were related to clinical characteristics and changed during one year of psychotherapy. Before the therapy, β-endorphin levels were similar in patients and unaffected people and were not linked to self-injury or other clinical features. Levels of β-endorphin also did not change overall during the psychotherapy. However, patients who improved had lower β-endorphin levels at the beginning and showed an increase during the treatment, unlike those who did not improve. If confirmed, these findings suggest that β-endorphin levels may help identify patients who are more likely to benefit from psychotherapy. Further research involving larger groups of participants is needed to confirm these results and determine whether measuring β-endorphin could eventually help to guide treatment and to improve care for borderline personality disorder.
psychology.text:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a severe mental disorder characterized by emotion dysregulation, unstable identity, and disturbed interpersonal function.

The symptoms of BPD include acute dysfunctional behaviours, such as repetitive self-harm, chronic suicidal thoughts or attempts, aggressive outbursts and high sensitivity to rejection. Clinical manifestations of BPD can be extremely heterogeneous: patients may exhibit very different presentations, some predominantly showing heightened impulsivity, emotion dysregulation and affective instability, which attract more professional attention and urgency to intervene, whereas others present a clinical profile characterized by hyperarousal, emotion overmodulation and dissociative features. BPD symptoms first appear in early adolescence, peak in late adolescence and early adulthood and decline thereafter, and they can markedly vary both qualitatively and quantitatively over the life span. BPD is associated with a range of poor outcomes, including low occupational and educational achievement, lack of long-term close relationships and increased conflicts with partners, sexual risk-taking, and low levels of social support, leading to poor life satisfaction [].

Nonetheless, BPD is not as untreatable as previously thought. Psychotherapy represents the first-line treatment, and pharmacotherapy can be used as adjunctive treatment in specific situations. Different psychotherapeutic approaches have demonstrated efficacy in treating BPD patients []. Among these, metacognitive interpersonal therapy (MIT) and structured clinical management (SCM) have been tested as treatments for BPD in a randomized controlled clinical trial conducted by our research group (CLIMAMITHE project) [,]; the results showed that both therapies produced significant improvements in BPD symptomatology [].

From an etiopathogenetic perspective, the mechanisms underlying BPD are thought to result from a complex interplay of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors []. Among the biological processes implicated in the disorder, the most extensively investigated involve dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis [] and alterations in the oxytocin system [,,]. These systems play a central role in stress response, emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning, all of which represent core domains of impairment in BPD.

Another biological mechanism that is attracting increasing attention is related to the endogenous opioid system. Interest in this system stems from evidence indicating altered pain sensitivity and processing in patients with BPD []. These alterations have been particularly investigated in relation to non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), a core behavioural feature of BPD. NSSI consists of the deliberate and direct destruction of body tissue without suicidal intent and is thought to represent a maladaptive strategy for regulating intense negative emotional states and reducing aversive internal tension [,,,]. Most BPD patients report little or no pain during episodes of NSSI, and several studies have demonstrated reduced pain sensitivity in BPD patients who engage in NSSI compared with unaffected controls []. Specifically, BPD patients report less pain when exposed to thermal [,,], electrical [], mechanical and chemical stimuli []. Notably, lower pain sensitivity has been associated with higher levels of aversive internal tension and dissociative symptoms, suggesting a close relationship between altered pain processing and core symptoms of BPD [].

The mechanism proposed to underlie the reduced pain sensitivity observed in patients with BPD may involve a dysregulation of the endogenous opioid system, which may result from histories of trauma and chronic stress and/or from a genetic predisposition. Within this framework, NSSI may represent a maladaptive coping strategy aimed at stimulating endogenous opioid release [,]. Moreover, neuroimaging studies have demonstrated altered baseline μ-opioid receptor availability and abnormal endogenous opioid system activation during negative emotional states in individuals with BPD [].

β-endorphin is one of the major endogenous opioids and mainly acts as an agonist at μ-opioid receptors. It plays a key role in stress-induced analgesia and in the modulation of thermal pain perception. Interestingly, β-endorphin and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), the pituitary hormone involved in the stress response, share a common precursor, pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) []. A limited number of studies have reported reduced basal β-endorphin levels in individuals exhibiting NSSI. A study conducted in adults with cluster B personality disorders, most of whom had BPD, described lower central β-endorphin levels, measured in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), in patients with NSSI compared with those without []. In contrast, other studies performed in adolescents have examined peripheral β-endorphin levels, reporting lower plasma concentrations in individuals with NSSI compared with a control group [] and reduced plasma β-endorphin in female adolescents with NSSI compared with controls []. However, a more recent study, also involving adolescent participants, found no association between peripheral (plasma) β-endorphin levels and either NSSI or BPD symptoms []. Overall, knowledge in this field remains limited.

Based on these findings and the current gaps in the literature, the present study aimed to further elucidate the role of β-endorphin in BPD by investigating its peripheral serum levels in affected individuals and their possible associations with clinically relevant features, including NSSI and emotion dysregulation. We also aimed to explore whether psychotherapy, consisting of MIT and SCM, is associated with changes in β-endorphin concentrations and whether these changes are related to treatment outcomes. As an exploratory objective, we also examined whether baseline β-endorphin levels are associated with subsequent treatment outcomes, as a potential predictor of psychotherapy response.

BPD patients and unaffected volunteers (controls, CTRL) were enrolled in the framework of the CLIMAMITHE project (ClinicalTrials.org: NCT02370316), a randomized controlled clinical trial evaluating the effects of MIT and SCM on clinical, neuroimaging and molecular outcomes. The trial was carried out at two centres: IRCCS Istituto Centro San Giovanni di Dio, Brescia, Italy (site 1; coordinating centre); Third Center of Cognitive Psychotherapy, Rome, Italy—Scuola Italiana di Cognitivismo Clinico (SICC), Rome, Italy (site 2). Unaffected controls were recruited separately and included as a reference group. The complete description of the clinical trial protocol and clinical results have been previously published [,]. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the coordinating centre, IRCCS Istituto Centro S. Giovanni di Dio Fatebenefratelli, Brescia, Italy (Protocol No. 67/2014).

The inclusion criteria for patients were: (a) age between 18 and 45 years; (b) a diagnosis of BPD according to DSM-IV-TR; (c) signed informed consent. The exclusion criteria were: (a) a lifetime diagnosis of schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or bipolar disorder; (b) substance abuse or dependence in the 3 months before the enrolment; (c) organic mental syndromes, dementia or cognitive impairment; (d) relevant neurological signs; (e) in women, pregnancy or lactation; (f) concurrent psychotherapies. The inclusion criteria for CTRL were: (a) age between 18 and 45 years; (b) signed informed consent, whereas the exclusion criteria were any cognitive impairment or psychiatric/neurologic condition, including alcohol or substance abuse.

Within the overall CLIMAMITHE cohort, a subgroup of participants agreed to undergo blood sampling for molecular analyses; the present study included all BPD patients and CTRL with available serum samples, comprising 49 BPD patients and 25 age- and sex-matched CTRL. Blood samples from patients were collected at baseline (T0), after 6 months of treatment (T6), and at the end of treatment (after 12 months—T12), whereas CTRL were sampled at T0. Since some patients discontinued the clinical intervention, blood samples were available for 40 patients at T6 and 34 at T12.

The diagnosis of BPD was confirmed using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV-TR disorders I and II [,]. At baseline, patients and CTRL underwent a multidimensional evaluation to assess various clinical features by scoring: (a) emotional dysregulation through the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS) []; (b) BPD symptomatology through the Zanarini Rating Scale for borderline personality disorder (ZAN-BPD) []; (c) interpersonal functioning through the Inventory of Interpersonal Problems (IIP) []; in patients, this assessment was repeated at T6 and T12. At baseline, both patients and CTRL were also evaluated for the attachment style by the Attachment Style Questionnaire—Italian Version (ASQ) [] and childhood traumatic experiences by the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) [].

Patients were randomly assigned to two intervention groups: MIT [] and SCM []; among the 49 BPD patients enrolled, 25 underwent MIT and 24 SCM.

MIT is a cognitive behaviour-based psychotherapeutic approach aimed at increasing metacognitive abilities in order to improve personality functioning and promote better interpersonal relationships, following a goal hierarchy: (a) the assessment of symptoms, mental state, metacognitive functions, interpersonal problems, and emotion regulation skills; (b) intervention on the aspects that interfere with therapeutic alliance and/or threaten patient’s life (in particular, self-harming/suicidal behaviours); (c) intervention on symptoms that cause suffering to the patient; (d) intervention to promote integration of different mental states [].

SCM belongs to the group of generalist models for the treatment of BPD and has been used as a comparator treatment against which other specialized protocols could be tested in research studies []. Therefore, SCM did not originally represent a type of psychotherapy but has then evolved into a distinct set of organizational psychotherapy principles []. SCM reflects the “best general psychiatric treatment for BPD”, and it is intended to be used by generalist mental health clinicians with minimal additional training. SCM is tailored to BPD symptomatology and employs a supportive approach with case management and advocacy support, whose core elements include psychoeducation, problem-solving, explicit safety planning, medication review, and assertive follow-up if appointments are missed [,].

Both treatments consist of a weekly 50 min individual session and a 90 min group session (manualised metacognitive skill training in MIT and problem-solving in SCM), covering a period of about 6 months during the year of individual psychotherapy.

When needed, BPD patients received pharmacological treatment, prescribed following a standardized protocol based on relevant pharmacological guidelines. The pharmacological agents included antidepressants, antipsychotics, anxiolytics, and mood stabilizers. During the clinical trial, substantial stability of drug therapy was maintained. Detailed information on pharmacological treatment has been previously reported in the original clinical trial [].

Patients were classified as full responders if they showed a decrease of at least 25% in the DERS scores from T0 to T12 (corresponding to 36 points, i.e., a decrease of 1 score point for each of the 36 DERS items) and as partial responders if they showed a decrease of at least 12.5% (i.e., between 18 and 36 points). If the decrease was <12.5%, or if the DERS scores increased, they were classified as non-responders. These thresholds are those used in the original clinical trial [].

Peripheral venous blood samples were collected in the morning, after an overnight fast. Serum separation occurred after 1 h by centrifugation at 1680× g for 15 min. Serum samples were aliquoted and stored at −80 °C until the time of analysis.

β-endorphin concentrations were determined using the competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit for Beta-Endorphin CEA806Hu (Cloud-Clone Corp., Katy, TX, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. Although assays were performed in different batches, all samples from the same patient across different time points, together with matched controls, were assayed within the same batch. Each sample was assessed in duplicate. The kit detection range is 1.6–1000 pg/mL, and the minimum detectable dose is less than 0.7 pg/mL. The intra-assay variability, expressed as the coefficient of variation, was <10% and the inter-assay variability <12%.

The laboratory analyses were performed blinded to treatment response.

Data are described as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for continuous variables or as frequencies and percentages for categorical ones. For variables that were not normally distributed, data were additionally expressed as medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs). Gaussianity assumption for continuous variables was assessed by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk tests, combined with visual inspection.

Comparisons between groups for continuous variables were carried out through Student’s t-tests for normally distributed variables and Mann–Whitney tests for non-normally distributed ones; for categorical variables, chi-square tests were applied. Correlations were evaluated through Pearson’s r coefficient or Spearman’s ρ coefficient depending on data normality.

For the longitudinal evaluation of clinical scores and β-endorphin levels, generalized linear mixed models were applied by setting time (three time points: T0, T6, and T12), treatment type group (MIT vs. SCM) or response group (Responders vs. Non-responders) and time × treatment type group/time × response group interaction as fixed effects, while a subject-specific random intercept was included to account for repeated measurements within subjects. Post hoc pairwise comparisons were adjusted for multiple testing using the Bonferroni correction.

Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and statistical analyses were carried out by SPSS 26.0 and through R language v.4.3.2 with the package “glmmTMB” for GLMM. Graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism v.8.4.3.

Descriptive statistics for the demographic and clinical features of BPD patients (n = 49) and CTRL (n = 25) are shown in , along with the results of the corresponding statistical tests comparing the two groups. BPD patients and CTRL subjects did not differ significantly in terms of age or sex distribution (p = 0.273 and p = 0.800, respectively). As expected, patients scored significantly higher than controls on the DERS, ZAN-BPD, Inventory of Interpersonal Problems (IIP), and Attachment Style Questionnaire (ASQ). The only exception was the ASQ subscale “Relationships as Secondary” for which the difference approached statistical significance (p = 0.054).

No significant differences were observed between patients in the MIT and SCM treatment groups for all the variables analyzed.

Baseline β-endorphin levels were not normally distributed (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test: p = 0.003; Shapiro–Wilk test: p < 0.001); thus, non-parametric tests were applied.

When comparing BPD patients vs. CTRL, no significant differences in serum β-endorphin levels were detected (BPD: 145.8 ± 65.6 pg/mL (median = 130.9, IQR = 70 pg/mL), CTRL: 136.0 ± 47.7 pg/mL (median = 127.9, IQR = 59 pg/mL); p = 0.587) (A).

Moreover, β-endorphin concentrations did not correlate with disease severity, evaluated both by DERS and ZAN-BPD scales (p = 0.387 and p = 0.692, respectively), and with all the IIP and ASQ scores/subscores. In addition, β-endorphin levels did not significantly differ between patients receiving and not receiving psychotropic drugs (p = 0.725), nor between patients with or without a history of suicide attempt(s) (p = 0.936).

In light of the altered pain sensitivity reported in BPD and of the role of β-endorphin in pain perception, we also examined potential differences in its serum levels between patients who exhibited non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI, n = 23) and patients who did not (non-NSSI, n = 25; one patient was excluded from this analysis because of missing NSSI data). As shown in B, no significant difference was found between groups (NSSI: 151.7 ± 78.9 pg/mL (median = 144.5, IQR = 75 pg/mL), non-NSSI: 141.6 ± 53.0 pg/mL (median = 130.9, IQR = 69 pg/mL); p = 0.959).

Among the entire cohort of 49 patients who participated in the study, 36 completed the 12-month treatment period. Overall, psychotherapy significantly reduced patients’ symptomatology, as evidenced by significant decreases in both DERS and ZAN-BPD scores over the course of treatment (p = 0.004 and p < 0.001, respectively). The mean DERS scores were 124.3 ± 25.0 at T0, 111.6 ± 28.3 at T6 and 109.7 ± 26.6 at T12; the mean ZAN-BPD scores were 15.9 ± 4.5 at T0, 11.7 ± 4.2 at T6 and 8.9 ± 4.0 at T12.

In detail, seven patients out of 36 (19.4%) were classified as full responders, and eight (22.2%) as partial responders, whereas twenty-one (58.3%) were considered non-responders to psychotherapy. For subsequent analyses, a binary classification was adopted, combining full and partial responders into the responder group (RESP, n = 15) and comparing them with non-responders (NON-RESP, n = 21). The MIT and SCM groups were comparable in terms of the distribution of RESP and NON-RESP patients (p = 0.821).

Importantly, the RESP and NON-RESP groups did not significantly differ in demographic or clinical variables at baseline, including age, sex, alcohol or substance abuse, psychotropic medication use, presence of NSSI, and clinical scale scores ().

Concerning β-endorphin, a GLMM with a Gamma distribution and log link was fitted to account for the positively skewed distribution of the outcome; therefore, no direct log transformation of the raw data was applied. The model converged successfully, and diagnostics revealed no significant violations. Estimated marginal means were computed on the link scale and then back-transformed to the original response scale for interpretation.

Baseline β-endorphin concentrations did not differ significantly between the MIT and SCM groups.

Moreover, β-endorphin levels did not show significant changes over the treatment period (time effect: p = 0.616), nor was a significant time × treatment type interaction detected (p = 0.127) (estimated marginal means ± standard errors of the mean: MIT T0 = 133 ± 13.4 pg/mL, MIT T6 = 139 ± 14.0 pg/mL, MIT T12 = 128 ± 13.4 pg/mL; SCM T0 = 146 ± 13.4 pg/mL, SCM T6 = 144 ± 13.2 pg/mL, SCM T12 = 166 ± 15.6 pg/mL). The results are represented in A.

We subsequently explored whether β-endorphin levels differentially changed in relation to treatment response. Given the absence of significant differences between the MIT and the SCM groups, the entire sample was considered, taking into account the treatment response status.
