At baseline, β-endorphin concentrations significantly differed between the RESP and NON-RESP groups (p = 0.001), prompting further analyses of baseline β-endorphin as a potential predictor of treatment response (see the subsequent paragraph “Baseline β-endorphin as predictor of response to psychotherapy”).

When evaluating time × response interactions, a clear divergence emerged between RESP and NON-RESP patients (overall time × response interaction, p = 0.025), primarily driven by differences between the T0 and T12 assessments (adjusted p = 0.021). In particular, β-endorphin concentrations increased significantly in RESP patients from T0 to T12 (adjusted p = 0.016), whereas no significant variation was detected in NON-RESP patients over the same interval (adjusted p = 1.000).

The estimated marginal means ± standard errors were: RESP T0 = 111 ± 11.9 pg/mL, RESP T6 = 123 ± 13.2 pg/mL, RESP T12 = 140 ± 15.0 pg/mL; NON-RESP T0 = 168 ± 15.2 pg/mL, NON-RESP T6 = 156 ± 14.1 pg/mL, NON-RESP T12 = 157 ± 14.8 pg/mL. The results are represented in B.

We also tested possible correlations between changes, from T0 to T12, in β-endorphin levels and corresponding changes in clinical scale scores. No significant result was observed, either in the whole patients’ cohort (correlation with Δ DERS: p = 0.086; correlation with Δ ZAN-BPD: p = 0.593) or when considering the responder group only (correlation with Δ DERS: p = 0.841; correlation with Δ ZAN-BPD: p = 0.719).

Patients who responded to treatment exhibited significantly lower β-endorphin serum concentrations at T0 than non-responders (RESP: 113.53 ± 32.80 pg/mL (median = 102.6, IQR = 57 pg/mL), NON-RESP: 178.78 ± 80.05 pg/mL (median = 169.8, IQR = 116 pg/mL); p = 0.001), suggesting that lower baseline β-endorphin are associated with a more favourable treatment outcome (A).

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis also demonstrated that baseline β-endorphin levels discriminated responders from non-responders to psychotherapy with good accuracy, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.806 and showing statistical significance (standard error = 0.072; 95% CI: 0.665–0.948, p = 0.002) (B).

Although changes in β-endorphin concentrations during treatment did not correlate with changes in clinical severity, baseline β-endorphin levels positively correlated with Δ DERS scores, defined as DERS at T12—DERS at T0 (p = 0.040, r = 0.344) (C). Since lower Δ DERS values indicate greater improvement in emotional regulation (or a smaller worsening, if positive), this finding indicates that lower baseline β-endorphin concentrations were associated with a more pronounced clinical improvement in emotional regulation. No corresponding correlation was observed for Δ ZAN-BPD scores (p = 0.938).

In this study, we investigated the relationship between peripheral β-endorphin concentrations, clinical features and response to psychotherapy in patients with BPD. Baseline β-endorphin concentrations did not differ between patients with BPD and unaffected controls, nor were they associated with clinical severity measures, suicide attempts or NSSI. Moreover, psychotherapy was not accompanied by a significant overall change in β-endorphin concentrations across the entire cohort of patients. However, longitudinal analyses revealed a significant time × response interaction, indicating distinct trajectories according to treatment response. Specifically, β-endorphin levels increased significantly during treatment in responder patients, whereas they remained stable in non-responders.

A further relevant finding was that baseline serum β-endorphin emerged as a potential predictor of treatment response. In particular, responder patients exhibited lower β-endorphin concentrations at baseline than non-responders, and ROC analysis indicated good discriminatory ability in this exploratory analysis (AUC > 0.8). Consistently, lower baseline β-endorphin levels were associated with greater improvement in emotional regulation, as indexed by larger reductions in DERS scores over the course of treatment. By contrast, no correlation was found between changes in β-endorphin concentrations during treatment and either DERS or ZAN-BPD scores.

To our knowledge, this is the first study comparing peripheral β-endorphin levels between patients with BPD and unaffected controls. Previous studies have primarily investigated β-endorphin in relation to NSSI rather than BPD itself, leaving the question of whether altered β-endorphin represents a disorder-specific feature unexplored. We found no significant case–control difference and did not observe any association of baseline peripheral β-endorphin concentrations with baseline clinical symptoms, including NSSI. These findings suggest that peripheral β-endorphin levels are unlikely to represent a trait marker of BPD or to reflect the severity of its clinical manifestations.

With respect to NSSI, previous studies have yielded heterogeneous findings. In a study by Stanley and colleagues, adults with Cluster B personality disorders (mainly BPD, but also including antisocial, narcissistic and histrionic personality disorders) and a history of suicidal behaviour were stratified according to the presence or absence of repetitive NSSI. The authors found lower CSF concentrations of β-endorphin and met-enkephalin, another endogenous opioid, in individuals with NSSI compared with those without NSSI, suggesting a possible dysregulation of the endogenous opioid system in relation to self-injurious behaviours; however, the sample size was quite small (14 NSSI vs. 15 non-NSSI). Based on these findings, the authors proposed an opioid deficiency model, suggesting that reduced endogenous opioid tone may contribute to NSSI by increasing vulnerability to emotional distress and promoting self-injury as a mechanism to restore opioid homeostasis []. Similarly, two studies in adolescent populations reported reduced plasma β-endorphin levels in individuals exhibiting NSSI compared with controls, suggesting that reduced peripheral opioids may represent a biological correlate of NSSI, at least during adolescence. In particular, Van der Venne and colleagues investigated a relatively large cohort of female adolescents (94 with NSSI and 35 without NSSI). In addition to lower plasma β-endorphin concentrations, adolescents with NSSI showed increased pain thresholds and lower pain intensity ratings []. Cakin Memik and colleagues investigated a mixed-sex adolescent sample including 49 individuals with NSSI and 39 controls. Whereas lower plasma β-endorphin levels were observed in adolescents with NSSI compared with controls, no significant differences were found for met-enkephalin. Importantly, the authors highlighted that basal peripheral measurements may be influenced by several confounding factors and may not fully capture the dynamic changes in the endogenous opioid system. They suggested that repeated, time-dependent assessments of peripheral opioid neuropeptides in relation to NSSI episodes may provide a more accurate characterization of their involvement in self-injurious behaviours []. This consideration may also be relevant for interpreting our findings, as peripheral β-endorphin was assessed under basal conditions and not in temporal proximity to NSSI episodes or acute emotional states. Therefore, the absence of differences in basal β-endorphin levels between patients with and without NSSI does not exclude a possible involvement of opioid mechanisms in the regulation of self-injurious behaviours. More recently, Kao and collaborators also investigated plasma β-endorphin levels in adolescents (n = 53), examining possible associations with NSSI and BPD symptoms. In contrast to previous studies, no significant association was found between basal plasma β-endorphin concentrations and NSSI, nor with BPD symptoms []. These findings are consistent with our results, suggesting that peripheral β-endorphin levels may not reliably reflect the presence of self-injurious behaviours or borderline psychopathology. This is further supported by the study of Mürner-Lavanchy and colleagues, who applied a machine-learning approach to evaluate a panel of candidate biological markers, including β-endorphin, associated with NSSI in female adolescents. The strongest predictors of NSSI were low oxytocin, increased pain threshold and elevated leukocyte counts, whereas β-endorphin did not emerge as a relevant predictor [].

Concerning the longitudinal assessment of β-endorphin changes during psychotherapy, to our knowledge no previous study has investigated this aspect in patients with BPD. Although in the present study psychotherapy was not associated with an overall change in β-endorphin concentrations, we observed a significant time × response interaction, indicating divergent trajectories according to treatment response. Specifically, besides showing lower baseline β-endorphin concentrations than non-responders, responders exhibited a significant increase in β-endorphin levels from baseline to treatment completion, whereas non-responders displayed no significant change over time. Regarding the increase in β-endorphin levels observed exclusively among responders we hypothesize that clinical improvement may be associated with greater adaptability of the endogenous opioid system. This finding could indicate that some patients are more capable of engaging opioid-related mechanisms during psychotherapy, potentially facilitating therapeutic response. Conversely, the absence of such changes in non-responders may reflect reduced capacity for an adaptive modulation of the endogenous opioid system in response to psychotherapy. This speculative interpretation should be considered together with the possibility of a ceiling effect: higher baseline β-endorphin concentrations may limit the extent of further increases over time. Overall, the observed pattern could suggest that alterations in endogenous opioid system do not characterize patients with BPD as a whole but may instead reflect biological heterogeneity among patients, potentially associated with differences in psychotherapy outcomes. However, these mechanistic interpretations remain speculative and require further investigation. Nevertheless, the predictive value of baseline β-endorphin for treatment response should be considered preliminary, given the small subgroup sizes (15 responders and 21 non-responders) and the relatively wide confidence interval of the ROC analysis (0.665–0.948). Notably, no other baseline variable, including indices of initial symptom severity, showed a significant association with treatment response; thus, the ability of baseline β-endorphin levels to distinguish between responders and non-responders may be of particular interest, given that clinical characteristics did not appear to differentiate the two groups.

Some limitations should be considered when interpreting the study findings. First, the relatively modest sample size, particularly the smaller subgroups in the longitudinal and treatment response analyses, limits the statistical power and the generalizability of the observed results. Second, the analyses examining baseline β-endorphin levels as a potential predictor of psychotherapy response were exploratory, and all the analyses were conducted without a validation cohort and should therefore be interpreted cautiously. In addition, the baseline group comparisons and correlation analyses were exploratory and were conducted without adjustment for multiple testing. Although this approach was considered appropriate given the hypothesis-generating nature of these analyses, the number of comparisons performed increases the possibility of type I error. Larger independent cohorts are therefore required to clarify the role of peripheral β-endorphin in the mechanisms underlying response to psychotherapy in BPD and to determine whether its baseline levels may serve as a possible predictive biomarker of treatment outcome.

In conclusion, in the present study, peripheral β-endorphin levels did not appear to be associated with BPD diagnosis or specific clinical manifestations such as NSSI but were associated with response to psychotherapy. These findings suggest that peripheral β-endorphin may represent a potential candidate biological marker associated with psychotherapy response, rather than a stable trait marker of BPD. However, its possible role in treatment responsiveness and its predictive value for psychotherapy outcome remain preliminary and warrant further investigation in larger samples and independent validation cohorts.

psychology.title: Within-Conversation Sudden Changes in Expressed Suicide Risk during Crisis Counseling
psychology.abstract: Crisis counseling aims to reduce suicide risk within a single conversation. While recent studies suggest that suicide risk can change nonlinearly over time, few have examined moment-to-moment changes within brief conversations changes. This study investigated sudden shifts in the expressed suicide risk during crisis chats. Using 2,110,114 messages from 81,569 text-based crisis line chats, we adapted sudden gain and loss criteria from psychotherapy research to identify within-conversation sudden changes in suicide risk. A machine-learning model assessed message-level suicide risk expression. We compared expressed risk changes between the conversations with and without sudden shifts. Overall, sudden reduction in expressed risk occurred in 12.5% of chats, while 13.9% showed sudden elevation. Chats with sudden reduction demonstrated greater improvement at the end of the chat than those with sudden elevation or no sudden changes. This study supports and extends findings on the nonlinearity of suicide risk to a moment-to-moment scale.
psychology.text:
Suicide is a serious public health issue across age groups. Suicide rate increased by over 30% in the past 20 years. Over two thousand adolescents died by suicide in the U.S. in 2020 alone (). It was the second leading cause of death among adolescents and younger adults, and the ninth leading cause of death among adults. Older adults have the highest suicide rate among all age groups (). Crisis hotlines - both phone- and text-based - can be an effective means of accessible and immediate support (, ; ; ). Despite initial evidence for effectiveness, the effectiveness and the mechanisms of change of crisis hotlines remain understudied. Most outcome studies on crisis hotlines centered on pre- and post-conversation surveys, whereas within-conversation studies focus on quality auditing, not testing hypotheses about the process of care (; ).

There are two limiting factors of research in crisis hotlines: First, the one-time nature of crisis counseling needs alternative methods to reveal change processes within the session, compared to psychotherapy that can reveal change processes from session-by-session data. Second, the intense labor needed to conduct within-session evaluation makes it difficult to scale up. Most change process studies in psychotherapy research rely on progress monitoring over multiple sessions (; ), whereas crisis counseling typically necessitates key outcomes (e.g., imminent risk reduction) to occur over the course of a single conversation. Due to the anonymous nature of crisis hotlines, it can be very difficult to obtain outcome ratings from clients after a conversation has ended. In other contexts, studies on momentary therapy processes involve intensive coding. For example, motivational interviewing studies involve assessments of therapists’ use of skills at every talk turn (i.e., each therapist and client statement) and within-session micro-outcomes, such as increases in change language or motivation (; ; ). Crisis counseling studies also involve intensive within-session assessment. For example, studies of Safety Plan Interventions () demonstrated the effectiveness of brief, structured techniques ().  assessment of crisis hotlines involves crisis interventions and client risk factors. But these ratings are typically summed over a conversation. Less is known about how risk changes dynamically during a conversation. Regardless, intensive coding of conversations can be extremely costly and time-consuming. Even large-scale studies typically focus on single conversation summaries of content (e.g., did the client mention a plan during a conversation) rather than the unfolding of the process over time. While conversation summaries allow evaluations of the impact of the intervention, like whether a texter is less distressed, it prevents an analysis of the path that leads to these changes. Better characterizing the pathways by which suicide risk is reduced could enhance the delivery of crisis counseling.

Recent empirical studies suggest that changes in suicide risk are likely nonlinear, rapid, and difficult to predict. About 50% of the people who attempted suicide experienced a sudden but not progressive surge in suicide urges (; ). A study using ecological momentary assessment found that suicide risk fluctuated drastically within hours (). Veterans with suicide risk also transitioned in phases between low-intensity and high-intensity suicidal ideation rather than gradually (). In the domain of suicide prediction, suicide-related risk factors (; ; ; ) often had poor predictive validity for future high-risk episodes, such as attempts or death by suicide (). Less than 10% of people who reported suicidal ideation eventually made an attempt (). The difficulty in predicting how suicide risk changes complicates the understanding of change mechanisms in crisis counseling.

In response to the difficulty in predicting changes in suicide risk, research on nonlinear change in risk has gained attention. Suicide researchers have begun to conceptualize changes in suicide risk from a dynamical system perspective.  and  suggest that suicidal behavior is often an emergent phenomenon, arising from complex interactions between biopsychosocial factors (e.g., cognitions, affects, behaviors, physiology, environments), where different suicide risk levels represent different dynamics between these factors. For example, a person’s suicidal ideation may at first be triggered by guilt from failing at an important project, which then triggers long-dormant self-harming behaviors to escape the pain. The self-harm in turn adds to their guilt and shame, forming a vicious cycle that exacerbates their negative thought of “I’m a failure,” thus reinforcing their suicidal ideation. If a crisis intervention is applied to help distract them from negative thoughts or guilt, it may disrupt the vicious cycle that traps them at a high suicide risk state, leading to a transition to a low-risk state. This new, reduced risk state may be maintained if the client is able to regain access to helpful coping strategies that were once blocked from their mind in the highly suicidal state. While crisis intervention presents a key moment when there should be a shift in suicide risk, the path of change for suicide risk during a crisis counseling conversation is largely unexamined.

Outside of crisis counseling, sudden changes in symptoms - often called sudden gains and losses - have been observed in psychotherapy for decades.  first formulated their observations of sudden reduction in clients’ depressive symptoms between two contiguous sessions. Later studies on sudden gains suggest that this phenomenon is prevalent across different treatment approaches, client populations, and measures (; ; ; ; ; ). A meta-analysis showed that 14-62% of clients experienced at least one sudden gain over the course of their treatment (), which was correlated with better overall improvement (; ).

Sudden losses, on the other hand, were less studied than sudden gains but were also found in different psychotherapies and outcome measures, with occurrence rate varying widely from 3.0-38.8% (; ; ; , ; ; ). Associations between sudden losses and long-term treatment outcomes were mixed. Some found that sudden losses were associated with negative treatment outcomes (), while others found no such association (; ).

Sudden gain and loss research has focused entirely on between-session changes in symptoms over time, essentially large changes in symptoms between sessions that might be spaced by days or weeks. However, crisis counseling typically involves one conversation. There have been no studies of sudden gains or losses in suicide risk, despite some researchers arguing for a similar dynamical system perspective of suicidality (; ). Suicide risk research has historically focused on suicide-related factors and prediction of suicide over time. There has been limited attention to within-person momentary dynamics until recently (e.g., ). There are additional challenges with crisis counseling where the therapeutic process unfolds in minutes to hours and typically lacks follow-up sessions. The difference in format makes it difficult to operationalize sudden gains and losses in a way that is analogous to psychotherapy research. Therefore, despite the shared theoretical basis, the study of within-conversation sudden changes in suicide risk remains less studied. However, if it is possible to adapt the well-studied method of sudden gain/loss from traditional psychotherapy to crisis counseling, it may help better understand the mechanism of suicide risk changes, particularly during crisis counseling when suicide risk would be expected to be more dynamic.

The present study tested the presence of nonlinear changes in suicide risk during crisis counseling. We adapted the methods from the evaluation of sudden gains and losses in the general psychotherapy literature. Since this was one of the first studies to bridge sudden gain/loss research and crisis counseling research, we would use “sudden gain” and “sudden decrease in suicide risk,” as well as “sudden loss” and “sudden increase in suicide risk” interchangeably. As an exploratory analysis, we compared the descriptive characteristics of sudden gains and losses with those in traditional psychotherapy (e.g., ; ). We hypothesized that the clients who had sudden gains were associated with greater improvement at the end of a crisis conversation than those with sudden losses.

The current study was not pre-registered.

The analysis codes are publicly accessible at GitHub (https://github.com/XinY-Z/suddenChange.git). The dataset is not publicly accessible because clients did not provide consent to share the data with the public.

This study involved an analysis of existing data rather than new data collection. We reported how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, and all measures in the study.

The study has been approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Utah (IRB_00131153) and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki.

The data was collected as part of usual care from a text-based crisis counseling service based in the mountain west of the United States between 2017-2021, totaling 2.1 million messages. The service is available 24 hours per day, 7 days per week; it is primarily marketed to teens and young adults in Utah but is accessible to persons of all ages and can be used by persons outside the state. Clients gave assent to making their data available for research. The assent was included in the terms of service for the service’s text-based application. The dataset represented 81,569 crisis conversations, 38,595 unique client identification numbers, and 92 therapists. 65.3% of the clients used the service only once, 17.0% twice, 6.9% three times, and 10.9% four or more times. The median number of messages per conversation was 18, with a mean of 25.9 and standard deviation (SD) of 25.7, ranging from 1 to 593 messages. 95% of the conversations fell between 2 to 94 messages. Because the platform is anonymous, no client or therapist demographic information is available. However, therapists are all licensed or license-eligible clinical social workers with additional training in crisis counseling.

To permit efficient evaluation of the high volume of messages in our dataset, we previously trained a machine-learning-based assessment that captured expressed suicide risk in each message over the course of a crisis conversation (). We used a transformer-based language model (i.e., RoBERTa) that had been pre-trained on a large corpus of open-source text to understand general language (). We finetuned the model by continuing to train it to rate expressed suicide risk using 5,992 de-identified crisis conversations from the same text-based crisis counseling service as in the current study. This finetuning technique - tailoring foundational models to specific tasks - has been used to build a number of automated psychotherapy process measures, including therapists’ use of motivation interviewing skills (Atkins et al., 2014; Can et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2012), use of psychotherapy skills from various theoretical orientations (Mehta et al., 2022), and use of suicide risk assessment and interventions ().

Expressed suicide risk was assessed entirely from clients’ or therapists’ text messages. A team of therapists rated the level of a conversation as high or low risk based on the entire conversation, following the Suicide Risk Assessment Standards (). These text messages and suicide risk ratings were then used to train the automatic assessment model used in the current study. The model achieved an ROC AUC of 90.4% in identifying therapist-rated risk levels (). The trained model was then used to predict the suicide risk level of each message. Following the same method in the primary research (), we extracted the probabilities of classifying the message as high risk vs. low risk from the logistic output layer of our model, yielding a continuous proxy of expressed risk at message level. In their error analysis,  found that their RoBERTa-based model was able to capture expressed risk fluctuations from message to message, even though their model was trained on the conversation level. Examples include key phrases that indicate suicidal ideation or intent and clients’ premature termination of the session. This finding corroborated previous studies (e.g., ), suggesting that machine learning models may be able to learn the continuous latent representation of a construct from these binary labels.

We used the formula for identifying sudden gains from the criteria established by . Because no sudden gain studies have characterized change from moment to moment within a conversation, we adapted several aspects of the formula. The criteria were as following:

To reduce bias due to measurement error, reliable change index () is often used as a criterion for absolute changes in sudden gain literature (). The calculation of RCI relies on the test-retest reliability of a psychological scale, which did not apply to the message-level index measured by the machine-learning model. Instead, we used an empirical approach based on the standard deviation of the differences of the contiguous data points, similar to how  originally defined RCI (p. 14):

xi+1−xi⩾|1.96×sdiff|

where xi is the expressed suicide risk level (in probability) of message i, xi+1 is the expressed suicide risk level at the next message i+1, and sdiff is the standard deviation of the difference of the expressed suicide risk level between two contiguous messages. To qualify as a sudden gain or loss, the change in risk probability must be 1.96 times beyond sdiff in the entire dataset (i.e., 21.3% change in the probability of risk) to account for 5% Type I error. This helps reduce false positives due to random fluctuation in expressed suicide risk (i.e., noise).

The criterion for relative change is used in conjunction with the absolute change criterion to determine “meaningful changes,” especially for very high-risk clients where meeting the absolute change criterion does not mean their risk levels have become low. Conventionally, a relative change is set at 25% change from two contiguous sessions (). We also chose 25% as the criterion to determine sudden gains and losses, except that we used suicide risk of two contiguous messages, shown as follows:

xi+1−xi⩾|25%×xi|

where xi is the expressed suicide risk level (in probability) of message i, and xi+1 is the expressed suicide risk level at the next message i+1.

Stability of change is conventionally determined by a significant two-sample t-test between three pre-change and three post-change sessions (). Again, we followed this criterion except that we focused on pre-gain and post-gain messages. The mean risk levels of the three messages before (messages i−2, i−1, i) and after the sudden change (messages i+1, i+2, i+3) are significantly different, tested by a two-sample t-test. Crisis conversations with fewer than six messages could not conduct the t-test because of the insufficient number of messages. These conversations were kept in the analysis, but assumed to contain no sudden gains or losses. This decision likely yields a conservative estimate of sudden change rates.

A message must meet all three criteria (absolute change, relative change, stability of change) to be considered a sudden change in expressed suicide risk.

After sudden changes were identified, we summarized four descriptive characteristics from these sudden changes based on previous sudden gain and loss literature: occurrence rate, timing, magnitude, and reversal rate (). Occurrence rate refers to the percentage of clients who experienced at least one sudden change in suicide risk. Timing refers to when a sudden change occurs, characterized by mean, median, and standard deviation of the message number when the change happened. Magnitude refers to the amount of sudden change relative to the baseline level of the entire data in the unit of standard deviation. Reversal rate is the percentage of clients with an erosion of at least 50% of the improvement at any point following the improvement (). These descriptives were calculated separately for sudden gains and losses. The occurrence rate of chats with both sudden gains and losses was also calculated ().

We evaluated the criterion-related validity of the sudden gains and losses in expressed suicide risk by comparing it to the overall expressed risk reduction. Specifically, we conducted a Kruskal-Wallis test comparing the overall risk changes between the chats with sudden gains, with sudden losses, and with no sudden changes. The overall risk reduction was calculated by the difference of the mean risk level of the first three messages and the mean risk level of the last three messages in a crisis chat. To reduce the influence of measurement error that is more salient in momentary analysis, we took the average of three contiguous messages instead of relying on just one message. This goes in parallel with the three sessions used in the “stability of change” criterion of identifying sudden gains and losses in psychotherapy studies. We assessed the effect sizes using Hedge’s g following post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm-Bonferroni adjustment.

We found 10,210 (12.5%) crisis chats with at least one sudden gain (a decrease in risk). The median number of sudden gains per chats was 1, the maximum 3. The average magnitude of the sudden gains was 0.99 SD of the baseline expressed risk level. Out of the 10,210 chats with sudden gains, 2,377 (23.3%) exhibited at least 50% loss of the improvement in the expressed suicide risk (reversal). The median timing of sudden gains was at the 7th message (M = 11.1, SD = 12.4), while 95% of the sudden gains occurred between the 3rd and the 45th messages.

The occurrence rate of sudden gains in text-based crisis counseling was lower than the lower bound in traditional psychotherapy (14.3-62.2%; ). The magnitude of sudden gains was smaller but within the range in traditional psychotherapy (M = 1.51 SD, range = 0.75-2.14 SD; ). The distribution of timing suggests that sudden gains tended to occur early in a chat (median 7th message for sudden gains vs. median 18 messages in total), aligning with the previous study that a substantial proportion of sudden gains occurred early in the treatment (). The reversal rate was smaller but within the range in previous studies on traditional psychotherapy (M = 31.5%, range = 7.7-100%; ).

Sudden losses were found in 11,350 (13.9%) crisis chats. The median number of sudden losses in these chats was 1, the maximum 4. The average magnitude of the sudden losses was 1.11 SDs of the baseline expressed risk level. Out of the 11,350 chats with sudden losses, 7,620 (67.1%) exhibited at least 50% recovery from the elevation in the expressed risk. The median timing of sudden losses was at the 6th message (M = 8.5, SD = 8.2), while 95% of the sudden losses occurred between the 3rd and the 31st messages.

The occurrence rate of sudden losses fell within the range in the previous study on psychotherapy (3.0-26.5%; ; ; ). Sudden losses tended to occur early in a chat, which differs from the previous study where the majority of sudden losses occurred later in the treatment ().

We also found 2,146 (2.6%) crisis chats containing both sudden gains and losses, comparable to the proportion found in a previous study (4.5%; ). Out of these chats, 817 (38.1%) had losses following gains, and 1,329 (61.9%) had gains following losses. The gain-then-loss cases were similar to the reversal cases in the sense that deterioration occurred after gains but with slightly different clinical implications. The smaller number of gain-then-loss cases than reversal cases suggests that many sudden gain cases, if they later exhibited deterioration, deteriorated progressively rather than suddenly.

illustrates an example chat with a sudden gain in expressed risk. Our model captured the drop in expressed risk when the client confirmed to the therapist that “I will be okay tonight.”  illustrates an example chat with a sudden loss, when the client expressed having access to means for self-harm. In other chats, moments of sudden changes that the model captured include explicit expressions of suicidal ideation, a confirmation of being safe from self-harm, therapist’s expression of concerns about the client’s safety, and so on.

The baseline probability of high expressed risk in the first three messages across all the crisis chats was 50.6% (SD = 33.9%). At the end of the chat, the probability of high expressed risk in the last three messages was 42.3% (SD = 32.4%) on average, representing a significant overall reduction of 8.3% (SD = 30.6%, p < .001, Hedges’ g = 0.25, 95% CI [0.24, 0.26]) within crisis chats.

In chats with sudden gains, the mean probability of high expressed risk in the first three messages was 63.2% (SD = 27.8%), and 24.7% (SD = 21.5%) in the last three messages, representing a large overall reduction of 38.5% (SD = 32.1%, p < .001, Hedges’ g = 1.55, 95% CI [1.52, 1.58]). In chats with sudden losses, the average probability of high expressed risk in the first three messages was 25.4% (SD = 23.7%), and 51.4% (SD = 27.5%) in the last three messages, representing a medium overall deterioration of 25.9% (SD = 32.9%, p < .001, Hedges’ g = 0.72, 95% CI [0.69, 0.75]). In chats without sudden gains or losses, the average probability of high expressed risk in the first three messages was 52.3% (SD = 34.3%), and 43.8% (SD = 33.5%) in the last three messages, representing a significant overall reduction of 8.5% (SD = 24.0%, p < .001, Hedges’ g = 0.25, 95% CI [0.24, 0.26]). On average, sudden gains accounted for 48.9% of the maximum risk change in a chat (the highest risk level minus the lowest risk level). Sudden losses accounted for 58.6% of the maximum risk change in a chat.

Comparing the overall risk changes between the three groups, Kruskal-Wallis test indicated a significant difference, χ2(2) = 1.7 X104, p < .001. Post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests showed that all the three types of chats differed from each other, p < .001 (). The difference in the change of risk between the chats with sudden gains vs. no sudden gains or losses was large, Hedge’s g = 1.06, 95% CI [1.03, 1.09], and was much larger comparing sudden gains to chats with sudden losses, Hedges’ g = 1.98, 95% CI [1.95, 2.02]. Chats with sudden losses had less overall change in risk than chats with no sudden changes, Hedges’ g = −1.19, 95% CI [−1.22, −1.16]. These effect sizes are large in psychological research and are larger than previously found in traditional psychotherapy (Hedges’ g = 0.68, 95% CI [0.54, 0.81]; ).

Crisis counseling may be effective for reducing suicide risk, but studies on how expressed risk changes within a crisis conversation are scarce. Still, such studies are important for understanding the mechanisms of change in single-contact crisis counseling. The nonlinear nature of suicide risk changes () makes it difficult to predict its trajectory (). In this study, we adapted sudden gain and loss criteria from psychotherapy to the within-conversation sudden changes of expressed suicide risk. We used a large text-based crisis line database that was annotated by a previously trained RoBERTa risk assessment model.

We found that many descriptive characteristics of sudden gains and losses in our study were similar to those in traditional psychotherapy, with some key differences including the occurrence rate of sudden gains and the timing of sudden losses. The similarities in these characteristics across treatment modalities (i.e., crisis counseling vs. traditional psychotherapy) and time scales (i.e., within- vs. between-session) suggest that sudden gains and losses may be a more general phenomenon than previously considered. Dynamical system theory predicts the behaviors of a system (e.g., nonlinear changes) when it is structured in a certain way, regardless of what the components are (). It may be possible to find similar patterns if these symptoms are governed by a similar overarching mechanism. These interpretations are speculative, as the present study does not directly test mechanisms or dynamical system parameters.

However, the key differences we found such as occurrence rate of sudden gains and the timing of sudden losses suggest that their application to crisis counseling contexts also requires careful interpretation. In psychotherapy, sudden gains are typically observed across sessions over weeks or months and are often interpreted as reflecting relatively durable cognitive or affective reorganization. In contrast, the present study examines these phenomena within the much shorter time scale of a single crisis conversation, where changes in suicide risk may unfold over minutes. This difference in temporal resolution has important implications. First, sudden gains or losses observed in crisis counseling may be consistent with rapid affective or interpersonal regulation - potentially co-occurring with real-time therapist intervention - rather than the emergence of a new, stable psychological equilibrium. For example, sudden gains may occur when a therapist introduced a distress tolerance skill or validation for the client, or when the client expressed improvement (). Sudden losses may occur when a client disclosed a certain high-risk behavior with the therapist’s risk assessment (). Second, the high-frequency measurement used in the present study increases sensitivity to moment-to-moment fluctuations, which may inflate the detection of abrupt changes relative to session-level assessments used in psychotherapy research. Finally, because crisis conversations do not typically include extended follow-up, the persistence of post-change states cannot be evaluated, limiting our ability to determine whether these shifts represent transient de-escalations or more enduring transitions. Therefore, while the present findings extend the study of sudden gains and losses to a novel and clinically important context, they should be interpreted as reflecting acute, within-episode dynamics rather than directly analogous processes to those observed in longer-term psychotherapy. Application of dynamical system models for psychopathology is still at its early phase and needs more specific research ().

We found that the effect sizes in pre-post changes were large between the chats with sudden gains, with sudden losses, and without any sudden changes, and were larger than those found in traditional psychotherapy (; ). This means that sudden gains and losses may be stronger indicators for overall client outcomes in crisis counseling than in traditional psychotherapy. However, the discrepancy in effect sizes may be attributed to the brief nature of crisis intervention. The reversal rate of sudden gains was slightly smaller compared to that in traditional psychotherapy, perhaps because the clients could not be routinely monitored unlike traditional therapies. As a result, the effect size in our study may not reflect the clients who relapsed after the end of the chat. Another reason may be our focus on a much smaller time scale. Focusing on a larger time scale (e.g., per session or per day) would average out spikes of changes. For example, a client may express an acute increase of suicidal ideation when starting to process trauma in a session, and then decreased as the trauma is processed or the emotion is regulated towards the end of the session. This momentary spike could be undetected by pre- and post-session outcome monitoring, or be averaged out when analyzing session-by-session changes. Although process research on a larger time scale could be more robust to noise, it may also miss clinically meaningful moments (). Given the nonlinearity of suicide risk fluctuation (), capturing these momentary spikes of change in suicide risk has significant clinical importance. A third possible reason may be the regression to mean (). Clients who use the crisis service may have already been in certain physical or emotional crises. It is expected that their baseline symptom level would be higher than the clients at a regular mental health service. If crisis intervention is effective, their risk level may undergo a larger reduction to return to a normal level, resulting in larger overall changes at the end of the conversations.

The current study has several research and clinical implications. First, we found sudden gains and losses in expressed suicide risk at the within-conversation level in crisis counseling. This finding expands the previous finding on the nonlinearity of suicide risk to a much smaller time scale. Continued exploration of the nonlinearity of suicide and the associated modeling methods may lead to better understanding of the trajectories of suicide risk that were difficult to predict in the past (). Second, the current study is one of the first to bridge the sudden gains and losses in traditional psychotherapy and the nonlinearity of suicide risk. Despite the theoretical homology between the two nonlinear phenomena (; ; ), there have been no studies that compared the sudden gain/loss between crisis counseling and traditional psychotherapy. Our findings suggest the existence of nonlinear transitions in expressed risk that is consistent with dynamical system theory. Future research may consider testing more specific dynamical system-based hypotheses of suicide change in crisis counseling. For example,  tested the catastrophe model of suicide for the existence of multiple homeostases of risk level. In psychotherapy more broadly, Olthof et al., (2023) examined the association between early warning signals (statistical indicators prior to a critical transition in a dynamical system) and sudden gains/losses. These more specific approaches may provide better understanding of the association between the nonlinearity of within-conversation suicide risk and dynamical system model. Third, we showed that machine-learning models can help scale up momentary studies of crisis counseling considerably, with promises of addressing the labor demand that used to prohibit researchers from doing such research in mass. It is possible to train additional models to automate key process and outcome measures (e.g., motivational interviewing skills, suicide assessment skills, and suicide-related factors such as thwarted belongingness) that help better understand the mechanisms in the sudden gains and losses in expressed suicide risk.

The present study has several limitations. First, it should be noted that our indicator measured the expression of suicide risk rather than the suicide risk itself, because the indicator relied solely on what had been verbally expressed by clients or therapists to assess risk levels. It implies that a message may be rated as low-risk if it had not been expressed, even if the client is experiencing a high suicide risk. For example, a client may start the conversation with their concerns, only later revealing having thoughts of attempting suicide. In this case, the indicator could not assess the latent suicide risk when it was not yet expressed. This is a difficult problem to solve without self-report data from clients at the end of the chat. Future studies may consider cross-validating machine learning models with client self-report measures.

Second, we used an empirical approach instead of a reliable change index in identifying sudden gains and losses, because test-retest reliability was not available with machine learning models. In addition, the test-retest reliability could not be calculated when interventions were involved. This may have introduced differences in our findings compared to those in the sudden gain and loss literature. Although the applications of machine learning to psychotherapy research are rapidly growing (), there has not been a consensus on how to translate the reliabilities in machine learning into psychometric reliabilities. Recent studies have such as comparing human-machine reliability with human-human reliability using the same method (; ). Future studies may benefit from a continued exploration of ways to bridge the language, methods, and metrics between machine-learning and psychological research.

Third, despite the strong discriminative power of the RoBERTa model we used, it is still prone to potential errors - detecting risk when it is not there or vice versa. Transformer-based models such as RoBERTa take the advantage of the context around a word to make inferences, i.e., a word’s relations with other words or sentences (; ). When the size of the context was limited or different from which the model was trained, it may lead to reduced accuracy. However, the model may also have used certain phrases that are less sensitive to word contexts to make accurate inferences about risk level (e.g., “I’ll be okay tonight”, see ). Future studies may explore the possibility of adding weights to certain domain-specific and context-insensitive phrases during model training ().

Fourth, our dataset did not have other outcome variables to corroborate the criterion-related validity of the model’s indication of suicide risk. Although the model has a good to excellent ability in discriminating low- vs. high-risk conversations, having another within-conversation outcome variable can be helpful to further test the validity of the model’s within-conversation assessment of expressed suicide risk. However, the one-time and anonymous format of crisis counseling may lead to increased nonresponse rate in collecting such outcomes (). Observer ratings may still be needed to evaluate such within-conversation outcomes. An example can be change talks from motivational interviewing (e.g., ), which refer to clients’ expression of motivation or an action to initiate change. To accommodate the large volume of crisis counseling usage, it may be helpful to continue adopting machine learning techniques to automate these measures.

In addition to these limitations, we were unable to assess whether sudden gains and losses in expressed suicide risk differed by demographic variables, such as age. Factors that influence suicide risk can vary by ages (; ). For example, younger adults may be more vulnerable to social (e.g., isolation, bullying) and family stresses (e.g., domestic violence) whereas older adults could be more vulnerable to decreased cognitive abilities. These mechanistic differences may shift clients’ responsiveness to interventions, thus influencing the sudden gains/losses in crisis counseling. Future studies may consider using datasets from in-person crisis services (e.g., emergency departments, crisis service at student counseling centers, etc.), where client demographic information is more readily available.

We also did not assess the differences in sudden gains and losses before, during, and after covid-19 pandemic. Pandemic and the associated lockdown can lead to elevation in suicide-related factors such as isolation, loneliness, economic fallout, domestic abuse, stigma and fear (). These acute elevations could drive a shift in the population of the clients and the content of the crisis conversations during the pandemic. For example, a national study found higher rates of aged clients (50+ years old) and female clients using crisis lines, as well as a higher rate of anxiety (). It could be possible that the elevated distress in general led to fewer gains and more losses because the impact of the lockdown (e.g., unemployment in the aged population, death of loved ones) was not easily resolvable in a single crisis conversation. The other way may also be possible. Acutely elevated distress, such as feeling of isolation in adolescents, may be quickly ameliorated with the therapist’s timely empathy, resulting in more observation of gains. Our study is limited in that these demographic variables were unavailable. Future research should consider examining the moderating effect of pandemic on sudden gains and losses in expressed suicide risk.

Despite these limitations, our findings suggest that sudden changes were present at the within-conversation level in brief crisis counseling. Sudden changes were also associated with clients’ overall risk reduction in a conversation. These findings corroborated the nonlinear process of suicide risk changes and the feasibility of adapting sudden gain and loss literature to study this nonlinearity. The present study also demonstrated the use of machine-learning-based automatic measures for within-conversation moment-to-moment studies that were once difficult to scale up in proportion to the rapidly growing data volume in psychotherapy research.

psychology.title: Digital Phenotyping of Voice Biomarkers for Psychological States in College Students: Longitudinal Mobile App Study
psychology.abstract: College students face significant mental health challenges, yet traditional assessments often rely on in-person self-reports and long-form self-report survey approaches. The prevalence of smartphones and longitudinal digital phenotyping—using data from devices to rapidly monitor mental health processes—offers an opportunity to assess well-being using a nondisruptive, prevention-focused “light touch” approach via voice journaling and emoji-based expression. While voice biomarkers are associated with clinical anxiety and depression, little research has explored voice biomarkers’ relation to psychological predictors of mental health processes in young adults.This study aimed to explore the utility of smartphone-captured voice biomarkers as objective indicators of psychological predictors of affective states in college students.College students (N=289) used the Meet Pandora smartphone app for over 2 months. Approximately 3 times per week, participants responded to voice journal prompts, such as “Describe a place you like to visit.” Voice biomarkers were extracted from responses, and their association with concurrent psychological measurements (ie, voice journaling measured closest in time to psychology surveys) was modeled using multivariable, mixed-effects, covariate-adjusted (gender, baseline mental health diagnosis, prompt sentiment, foreign national status, and time) models. Random intercepts were included to control for baseline individual differences, and all analyses were adjusted for multiple comparisons.Associations were predominantly within students. On the 5-point daily affect scale (higher scores indicate more negative affect), negative affect was characterized by more utterances than usual (odds ratio [OR] 1.16, 95% CI 1.09‐1.23; adjusted P<.001) and less positive language (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.87‐0.97; adjusted P=.007), accompanied by reduced vocal energy and pitch: magnitude mean (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.78‐0.88), pitch mean (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73‐0.86), and root-mean-square energy (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85‐0.95; all adjusted P<.001), with harmonics-to-noise ratio and pitch variance showing the same pattern (both adjusted P≤.01). Among students who used more positive language than their peers on average, stress was lower (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50‐0.92; adjusted P=.049) and their self-regard was higher (adjusted P=.04).While speech and acoustic features did not predict weekly measures of loneliness or acceptance, they were associated with stress, self-regard, and daily affect fluctuations. More positive language was associated with lower stress and higher self-regard. These findings highlight the utility of high-frequency assessments via voice biomarkers as signals of affective changes in college students. This work highlights that brief vocal samples may be able to detect early, affect-specific signs of mental health risks in young adults, which has important implications for psychopathology prevention and improving well-being.
psychology.text:
The transition to college represents a critical developmental period characterized by increased independence, shifting social networks, and heightened academic and psychosocial demands. Thus, college transitions are inherently stressful [-]. As a result of uncertainty and other stressors, college students carry a substantial mental health burden. Recent data indicate 38% of students screen positive for moderate or severe depression and 34% for anxiety, with 13% reporting suicidal ideation in the past year []. In addition to these more severe diagnosable mental health problems, many students experience high levels of negative stress, loneliness, not feeling accepted, and negative affect that may impair functioning and progress to clinical disorders [,].

Early detection of negative mental health states represents a critical opportunity for timely, targeted, early intervention that can improve both mental health and academic outcomes [,]. Indeed, social isolation and loneliness increase the risk of depression and anxiety up to 9 years downstream [], and college students who report early and often that they do not belong tend to have higher depression at the end of a semester []. Early detection efforts can be particularly impactful in college populations because of stressful transitions these young people undergo during a developmental period when social hierarchies are unstable and affective states are more dynamic and context-dependent relative to older adults [].

Even though there is a great need for detecting risk for mental health problems in college students, traditional assessments are poorly suited to capturing early signals. Subpar detection can be traced to an overreliance on episodic, in-person evaluations when problems have already escalated to the point of concern and/or retrospective self-report measures administered infrequently and with questionable precision. Additionally, both standard approaches are limited by biases associated with subjective self-reported measurement []. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) research has demonstrated that momentary data collection substantially improves accuracy and ecological validity compared to retrospective reporting, but typical EMA methods disrupt daily routines by “pinging” individuals with prompts to complete self-reports []. Thus, “light touch” digital approaches that greatly reduce burdens on college students, but can also collect data in brief time windows, may be more acceptable and engaging to young people, a perspective supported by qualitative evidence [,].

Digital mobile devices may provide a low-burden, scalable means for assessing, and ultimately improving, college students’ mental health []. In addition to providing access to self-report questionnaires, mobile phones enable digital phenotyping through collection of multimodal data streams, including voice recordings through voice journaling. Voice-derived biomarkers such as prosodic, spectral, and temporal speech features have demonstrated utility in detecting and monitoring depression and anxiety [,]. More recent studies using mobile-collected speech data further support the feasibility of predicting mental health symptom severity in real-world populations to detect clinical conditions and estimate severity []. These findings suggest that vocal biomarkers may provide an objective and scalable marker of psychopathology. However, existing research has focused primarily on identifying or diagnosing clinical conditions, with limited attention to negative affective states or to young adult populations. This blind spot is particularly notable given that strong and volatile negative emotions predict the onset of mood disorders []. From a psychopathology prevention perspective, it is critical to identify the risk markers of a pending depressive or anxious episode.

Although prior work has examined the use of voice biomarkers in relation to individual mental health constructs, no study, to our knowledge, has evaluated their ability to predict multiple psychological state changes (eg, perceived stress, loneliness, perceived acceptance, and core affect) simultaneously within a college population. Also, while much research on core affect focuses on specific emotions as predictors of downstream outcomes [], advances in emotion science have emphasized understanding more basic underlying affective processes that contribute to the construction of emotional experiences []. That is, researchers frequently emphasize core affect—or low-level, consciously accessible affective feelings and neurophysiological responses []—states of valence (positivity vs negativity) and activation (high vs low) as proximal predictors of health-related outcomes []. The current work advances research at the nexus of mobile sensing, emotion, and affective states by focusing on identifying biomarkers associated with core affect as assessed via emoji usage.

To advance knowledge in identifying affective risk factors, the research reported here leveraged a mobile health platform, Meet Pandora (developed by Taehyung Cho), to collect high-frequency, multimodal data including ecologically relevant self-report and voice-derived features from college students in their daily environments. We evaluated whether these signals predict psychological state changes in stress, loneliness, acceptance, and core affect, with the goal of enabling earlier detection of mental health risk in this high-need population.

Participants were undergraduate students enrolled at a highly selective private Northeast US university and recruited through a university study portal. All research was approved by the site’s institutional review board, along with informed consent obtained from all participants. Two cohorts of students were recruited: (1) spring 2024 semester (Cohort 1, n=169) and (2) spring 2025 semester (Cohort 2, n=120). Data from both cohorts were integrated for analysis, with most self-report surveys and voice prompts being the same in both studies. Participants in Cohort 2 were offered a stress survey that was not available to the participants in Cohort 1, and Cohort 2 also had additional voice prompts that students were able to respond to ().

The Meet Pandora smartphone app, available on Android and Apple iOS operating systems, was used to collect data. After signing informed consent, per protocol, students were onboarded onto the app and were asked to review and accept Pandora Bio’s privacy policy. Additionally, before submitting any data on the app, they were prompted to enable the app to use the device microphone and were asked to opt in (check) other permissions for location data collection and use of their smartphone camera. Voice recordings were not collected passively and required the students to actively engage (click a button) to record. They were told that all data would be deidentified and that their identifiable data would not be shared. Meet Pandora facilitates frequent, low-burden self-report using formats such as voice journals, self-reports, and emoji-based representations of core affect. The tool collects data both actively through participant self-reports (validated instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire 8-item (PHQ-8), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7), and the Flourishing and Stress scales, as well as brief daily, weekly, and monthly self-reports), and passively through derived voice biomarkers, GPS data, and phone usage metrics ().

PHQ-8: Patient Health Questionnaire 8-item.

GAD-7: Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale.

Questions on acceptance and loneliness were administered to participants weekly. To measure acceptance, participants were asked, “How accepted do you feel by your friend group?” (1=not at all accepted and 5=strongly accepted). To measure loneliness, they were asked, “How often have you felt lonely?” (1=very slightly or not at all and 5=extremely). A high or low acceptance and loneliness dichotomous label was derived from participants’ responses, where a score of 3 (the midpoint) or higher was labeled as “high” acceptance or loneliness, and scores of 1 or 2 were labeled as “low.”

As part of the weekly survey, participants reported their stress by responding to the question “How much stress are you experiencing in your life right now? (1=none, 4=a moderate amount, and 7=an extreme amount).” An ordinal stress label was derived from participants’ responses by categorizing scores into 3 ranked groups: low (scores 1‐3), medium (score 4), and high (scores 5‐7). Notably, this stress measure was only included in the second study (n=120).

Another essential psychological state that was measured and derived is the participant’s self-regard []. As part of the weekly self-reports, participants were asked these four questions: “How accepted do you feel by your friend group?” “How often have you felt lonely?” “To what extent did you go out of your way to avoid one or more difficult situations?” and “Overall, how good or bad did you feel about yourself this week? (1=Extremely good to 7=Extremely bad).” A composite weekly self-regard score was derived in 2 ways. First, a weekly continuous self-regard score was derived by averaging z-score-scaled responses to the 4 questions (excluding observations for which at least one question was unanswered). Second, for interpretability, self-regard weekly state was derived as high or low self-regard using principal component analysis (PCA) and K-means clustering.

Participants also provided their affective states via emojis during daily prompts. Participants chose up to 3 out of 16 emojis to best represent how they felt in the moment. Available options (and their activation and valence categorization) were: Accepted (low activation and positive), Angry (high activation and negative), Annoyed (high activation and negative), Anxious (high activation and negative), Confused (low activation and negative), Contented (low activation and positive), Excited (high activation and positive), Fearful (high activation and negative), Happy (high activation and positive), Hopeful (high activation and positive), Lonely (low activation and negative), Proud (high activation and positive), Refreshed (low activation and positive), Relaxed (low activation and positive), Sad (low activation and negative), and Tired (low activation and negative; ). Because every participant’s daily entry included at least 1 and up to 3 emojis, the first emoji was treated as the primary indicator of their core affect and used to derive all subsequent daily affect labels. To evaluate broad daily affect states, a daily ordinal label was calculated to capture the net polarity of all emojis selected during a given self-report. This was computed by calculating the ratio of positive emojis to the total number of emojis entered, which was then mapped onto a standardized ordinal scale.

We also calculated valence by arousal interactions. The first emoji selected by participants was divided into 4 categories: high activation and positive, high activation and negative, low activation and positive, and low activation and negative. This classification system was created by intersecting the binary valence dimension (positive vs negative affect) with the binary arousal dimension (high vs low activation).

Voice biomarkers were derived from participant speech recordings to capture daily variation in vocal and linguistic behavior. We derived features that capture both how they speak and what they say. During the study, participants were prompted to provide a voice journal 3 times per week by responding to 1 of 50 available questions, such as “Describe the highs and lows of your day.” Questions were either positive or neutral, designed to prompt responses between 30 seconds and 2 minutes. Participants could choose a different question to respond to if they did not want to respond to the one initially surfaced to them. From the participants’ audio responses, features from 2 general categories were derived and measured: speech and acoustic. The description of all derived speech and acoustic features is shown in .

VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner.

HNR: harmonics-to-noise ratio..

RMS: root-mean-square.

Voice data entries were joined to each participant’s corresponding responses to weekly prompts to integrate the biomarker data with psychological labels (loneliness, acceptance, stress, and self-regard). To ensure temporal relevance leading up to the self-reported psychological states, a 7-day lookback window was applied. Daily voice biomarker data were linked to a weekly survey label only if the audio entry was recorded on the same day or within the 7 days immediately preceding that specific self-report. For analysis of voice and daily self-report, the voice and daily affect labels were joined if both data points were recorded on the exact same calendar day for each participant. This day-level alignment ensured that the vocal expressions being analyzed had direct correspondence to the participant’s self-reported affective state at that specific time.

To understand and remove outliers in the derived voice biomarkers, a large language model (LLM; Google Gemini 2.0 Flash) was used to examine every instance to identify physically impossible observations []. Based on the model’s output, 424 outliers were identified due to the presence of background noise.  includes chat history and prompts.  summarizes the removal criteria, which were implemented using R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing) code based on the criteria below.

In the multivariable mixed-effects modeling of voice biomarkers associated with loneliness, acceptance, stress, and daily emojis, a target feature removal was implemented to maximize data retention. For instance, if the mean pitch for a specific voice sample was physically impossible, only the mean pitch for that instance was removed, and the rest of the features for that sample were retained.

Criteria are not mutually exclusive; a single voice instance could fail more than one threshold (eg, low harmonics-to-noise ratio and an implausible pitch mean from the same noisy recording). The 424 total reflects unique instances removed for at least one criterion, not the sum of the individual counts above.

WPM: words per minute.

HNR: harmonics-to-noise ratio.

From participants’ daily voice journals, 16 features were extracted and derived. Prior to statistical modeling, a correlation analysis was conducted to assess voice feature multicollinearity. Magnitude variance, which measures the variance in volume, had a Pearson correlation of 0.92 with magnitude mean, and average spectral centroid, which measures the brightness and sharpness of the audio, had a Pearson correlation of 0.94 with zero crossing rate. Consequently, these 2 features were excluded from subsequent analysis. The feature correlation matrix is given in . Prior to modeling, voice biomarkers were standardized using the built-in scale() function in R to ensure a mean of 0 and a SD of 1, thereby ensuring the direct comparison of effect sizes across different features.

Because each voice sample was elicited by a prompt that varied in emotional sentiment (positive or neutral), the sentiment of the prompt is a potential source of variation in the voice biomarkers. For example, a positive prompt may elicit a faster speech than a neutral one, introducing variation in the voice biomarker that reflects the eliciting condition rather than the student’s underlying state. Therefore, we evaluated whether prompt sentiment was associated with voice biomarkers, and where it was associated, we adjusted for prompt sentiment to reduce measurement-related variability. Specifically, for each voice biomarker (feature), the model treated prompt sentiment as a binary value (positive or neutral) and was parameterized as follows:

where Prompt_Sentimentij denotes prompt sentiment for the ith observation from the jth student, Featureij represents the voice feature for observation i from participant j, uj is the student-level random intercept, and εij is the error term.

Voice biomarker features were also divided into 2 distinct groups: speech and acoustic features. Speech features are features that describe the temporal characteristics. Acoustic features describe the underlying physical properties of the voice, such as pitch mean, root-mean-square (RMS) energy, and magnitude. To control for the inflation of Type I errors from multiple comparisons, P values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate method within each feature group (speech and acoustic; ).

Weekly psychological states (acceptance and loneliness) were treated as binary (high vs low). Self-regard was modeled 2 ways: as a binary outcome (1=low self-regard and 0=high self-regard) and as a continuous z-score composite, on which higher scores indicate lower self-regard. Daily affect sentiment was treated as a 5-point affect scale, and stress was treated on a 3-point scale with higher numbers associated with higher stress. Valence and arousal derived from emojis as described earlier in the methods were coded as follows: valence was treated as 1=negative and 0=positive, while arousal was treated as 1=high activation and 0=low activation. The combination of valence and arousal was treated as 1=negative and high activation, with 0 used to denote 3 other categories (positive and high activation, positive and low activation, and negative and low activation).

Modeling the association between voice biomarkers and daily and weekly outcomes accounted for the repeated outcome measures over days or weeks, repeated voice biomarkers over weeks, the measurement-related variability introduced by the prompt sentiment, and potential confounders (ie, person-level features that are associated with both the outcome of interest and with the voice biomarkers). Each voice biomarker was first standardized and then represented in the model as person-level mean (between-person effect) and person-mean centered by subtracting the person-mean from the value at the given timepoint (within-person effect). Potential confounders that were included in all models include gender identity (male, female, or other), mental health diagnosis (yes or no), and foreign national status (yes or no). In addition to gender identity, mental health diagnosis, and foreign national status fixed effects, additional fixed effects included day number and voice biomarker (feature). Random effects for student (intercept) were also included to account for repeated measures. Consistent with the analysis of prompt sentiment, voice biomarkers were divided into two groups: speech and acoustic, and P value adjustments were made within each feature group.

In each model, the psychological state (acceptance, loneliness, stress, self-regard, or daily affect) served as the dependent variable, and a single voice biomarker served as the primary predictor, entered as both its person-level mean (between-student effect) and its person-mean-centered deviation (within-student effect). One model was fit per voice biomarker, each adjusted for the covariates described above and including a random intercept for student.

The model family was determined by the measurement scale of the outcome. Dichotomous outcomes (acceptance, loneliness, and the binary self-regard label) were fit as logistic mixed-effects models using glmer() in the lme4 package. Ordinal outcomes (weekly stress on a 3-point scale and daily affect on a 5-point scale) were fit as cumulative-link, proportional-odds mixed models using clmm() in the ordinal package. Continuous weekly self-regard was fit as a linear mixed-effects model using lmer() in the lme4 and lmerTest packages, with degrees of freedom and P values derived from the Satterthwaite approximation. All models were fit with the bobyqa optimizer, and 95% CIs were obtained from the fixed-effects estimates. Associations are reported as odds ratios (OR) for the logistic and ordinal models and as unstandardized regression coefficients for the linear model, in which the outcome is on a standardized (z-score) scale. The logistic parameterization is as follows and the parameterization for the ordinal stress and continuous self-regard outcome model is similar.

where Outcomeij denotes the binary outcome variable for the ith observation from the jth student, FeatureMeanj represents the mean of the feature for the jth student, and FeatureDiffij represents the feature difference of the ith observation from the mean for the jth student. Genderj represents the gender, Diagnosesj represents the diagnosis status of the jth student, ForeignNationalj represents the foreign national status of the jth student, PromptSentimentij represents the prompt the student j responded to at observation, i, DayNumberij represents the response day i of the jth student, and u0j is the student-level random intercept and εij is the error term.

The study was conducted under an institutional review board–approved study protocol at the University of Rochester. The University of Rochester Research Subjects Review Board (RSRB) provided approval for all data collection and data treatment procedures prior to the collection of any data with the RSRB approval number of 00011296. All participants signed informed consent and were enrolled in-person into the study. Participants were informed by the University of Rochester study coordinator that their participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw at any time. All participants were offered the opportunity to ask questions regarding informed consent. Before using the Meet Pandora app, at the time of onboarding, and following informed consent, the Meet Pandora privacy policy and terms and conditions of use were surfaced in the app, and students were asked to read and accept the terms and conditions. The privacy policy states that their data will not be identifiable and will not be shared beyond deidentified data used for research purposes. All participants were required to be 18 years or older at the time of enrollment. Age and gender characteristics are summarized in the paper.

Students (N=289) participated for an average of 49.40 days (SD 20.78, range 1‐101 days). The age and prevalence of mental health diagnoses are representative of a typical college-age population. The cohort is diverse with respect to sexual orientation, race, religion, and first-generation and international students and is skewed towards females (229/289, 79%).  contains demographic information.

In total, 281 of 289 (97.2%) students responded to 1 or more voice prompts throughout the study. A total of 2036 weekly self-reports were available for analysis. After accounting for missing values, 1330 (65.6%) of entries reported low loneliness, and 696 (34.4%) reported high loneliness. For acceptance, 1893 (93.7%) of entries reported high acceptance, and 128 (6.3%) reported low acceptance. Because the stress measure was only administered to the second cohort, 802 weekly self-reports included stress data. After accounting for missing values, 271 (34.7%) reported low stress, 189 (24.2%) reported medium stress, and 322 (41.2%) reported high stress. For weekly continuous self-regard measurements, 273 students had 1308 entries with a valid derivation. For the dichotomous label of weekly self-regard, 703 (53.8%) indicated high self-regard and 605 (46.2%) indicated low self-regard.

There were significantly more data for daily entries. For daily ordinal affect, there were 5687 entries with 1906 (33.5%) negative, 489 (8.6%) somewhat negative, 530 (9.3%) neutral, 620 (10.9%) somewhat positive, and 2142 (37.7%) positive affect. When categorized by the interaction of valence and arousal, 1810 (31.8%) of these daily entries reflected low-activation and negative states, 1506 (26.5%) low-activation and positive, 1462 (25.7%) high-activation and positive, and 909 (16%) high-activation and negative.

Percentages are based on the total sample.

LGBTQ+: lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and others.

For mental health diagnoses, participants were able to select more than one category; therefore, mental health diagnoses are not mutually exclusive, and cumulative percentages exceed 100%.

ADHD: attention-deficit-hyperactivity disorder.

When students refreshed the app in some instances, multiple entries per week were captured instead of one entry per week per protocol.

Five speech features returned statistically significant associations (adjusted P<.05) with positive prompt sentiment, suggesting that whether the prompt was positive or neutral introduced variation in speech features. Conversely, no acoustic features returned statistically significant results. Because prompt sentiment was shown to affect participants’ speech features, it was added as a controlling covariate in subsequent multivariable analyses. All subsequent models associating voice biomarkers with outcomes converged.  and  contain speech and acoustic features and their analysis results.

Analysis was based on 281 students with evaluable data. Odds ratios represent the odds of responding to a positive versus a neutral prompt per 1 SD increase in each feature. Higher words per minute and Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner score are associated with higher odds of having responded to a positive prompt. Higher number of utterances, utterances per minute, and duration are associated with higher odds of having responded to a neutral prompt.

VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner.

Analysis was based on 281 students with evaluable data. Odds ratios represent the odds of responding to a positive versus a neutral prompt per 1 SD increase in each feature. None of the acoustic features were associated with higher odds of being prompted by a positive prompt.

RMS: root-mean-square.

Self-regard was modeled in 2 ways, as a continuous outcome and as a dichotomous outcome.
