Inspection of the distribution of responses across Likert-scale responses for each of the outcomes indicated that dichotomization was necessary for loneliness and acceptance, and that collapsing to 3 categories was required for stress in order to estimate within-student and between-student associations (). While a sufficient number of state changes were not observed for modeling the association of voice biomarkers with a change in a student’s state of acceptance (results were not statistically significant), the majority of models converged in order to estimate the association of voice biomarkers with changes in a student’s feelings of loneliness and stress. State changes for each outcome are depicted in .

Neither speech nor acoustic features were associated with acceptance or loneliness. Among students who used more positive language than their peers on average, stress was lower (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50‐0.92; adjusted P=.049) and their self-regard was higher (adjusted P=.04). The dichotomous self-regard analysis also showed the finding of higher word count associated with lower within-person self-regard.  contains the acceptance, loneliness, stress, and dichotomous self-regard results.  contains the continuous self-regard results.

Analyses included 272 students (acceptance, loneliness), 113 students (stress), and 273 students (self-regard). Only features with at least one term reaching an adjusted P≤.05 are shown.

Acceptance (0=low and 1=high). No features were associated with acceptance.

Loneliness (0=high and 1=low). No features were associated with loneliness.

VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner.

Self-regard, continuous (lower=higher self-regard, higher=lower self-regard)

VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner.

All models evaluating the within-student and between-student associations of voice biomarkers with daily affect, measured by daily mood score, valence, arousal, and the combination of valence and arousal converged. See  for the daily affect results.

Speech features were associated with within-student negative daily affect, where a higher daily affect score was more negative. Specifically, a higher number of total utterances than usual was associated with negative daily affect (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.09, 1.23; adjusted P<.001). Additionally, a negative sentiment, measured by the Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner (VADER) sentiment score, was associated with negative daily affect both within-student (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.87-0.97; adjusted P=.007) and between students (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.98; adjusted P=.04).

Acoustic features also correlated with within-student negative daily affect. Decreased volume and physical energy than usual were associated with negative daily affect: RMS energy (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85-0.95; adjusted P<.001); magnitude mean (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.78-0.88; adjusted P<.001). Furthermore, lower average pitch (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.86; adjusted P<.001), pitch variance (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.83-0.97; adjusted P=.01), and harmonics-to-noise ratios (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85-0.97; adjusted P=.005) were significantly associated with lower daily affect.

Analyses included 280 students. Only features with at least one term reaching an adjusted P≤.05 are shown.

VADER: Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner.

RMS: root-mean-square.

HNR: harmonics-to-noise ratio.

No features were associated with arousal.

Models fit to the 2 dimensions of core affect (valence and arousal) [] demonstrated significant within-student associations with both speech and acoustic features, predominantly for valence but not for arousal. Consistent with the daily affect analysis, negative valence (1 vs 0 for positive valence) was significantly associated with students voicing a higher number of utterances (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.24; adjusted P=.003), a higher rate of utterances per minute than usual (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.05-1.21; adjusted P=.01), and by lower VADER sentiment scores than usual (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83-0.95; adjusted P=.007).

Within-student acoustic features demonstrated strong negative associations with valence. Consistent with the ordinal daily affect findings, when in a positive valence state, students voiced higher volume measured by magnitude mean (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77-0.89; adjusted P<.001), pitch, measured by pitch mean (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.71-0.86; adjusted P<.001), and energy, measured by RMS energy (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85-0.97; adjusted P=.03), and harmonics-to-noise ratio (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82-0.96; adjusted P=.03) compared to their usual. No voice features were associated with arousal states.

Treating high arousal negative valence versus the 3 other states (high arousal and positive valence, low arousal and positive valence, and low arousal and negative valence), only between-student utterances per minute were associated.

This study evaluated the utility of smartphone-captured speech and acoustic features as objective indicators of psychological states in college students. Principal findings indicate that voice biomarkers were associated with daily affect states, self-regard, and stress, but no reliable associations with loneliness or acceptance. These associations were predominantly within-student, describing how a student’s voice shifted as their own state changed over time. For self-regard and stress, only speech and linguistic features tracked these within-student shifts. Participants’ affect, derived via an ordinal label on a 5-point scale and via a binary valence label, exhibited consistent results, revealing that positive and negative core affects were characterized by a distinct speech and acoustic profile, dominated by the acoustic elements. Behaviorally, positive daily affect was associated with fewer total utterances, a lower rate of utterances per minute, and higher positive sentiment in the transcribed text. The arousal component of affect did not yield any reliable associations, while between-student utterances per min were associated with higher odds of reporting a high-activation negative state, the only reliable association observed for the valence-by-arousal interaction.

The observed discrepancy between the predictive ability of daily versus weekly models aligns with established literature on EMA and recall bias []. However, this difference is also driven by differences in statistical power: weekly models have fewer observations, hence fewer state changes with which to model within-student associations. When recalling contextualized emotion states such as loneliness, acceptance, stress, and self-regard over the course of a week, participants mentally aggregate and average their emotions over several days, introducing cognitive biases and inconsistencies to their responses. For instance, a high-intensity emotional experience on one day might have an outsized impact on a weekly recall in addition to temporal misalignment between the assessments. Because participants’ core affects naturally fluctuate throughout the week, the effect captured by a voice biomarker may not align with the retrospective psychological state reported each week. In contrast, daily emoji self-reports capture acute, in-the-moment affective states, and core affect in particular, which not only physically manifest in neurophysiological responses but also in the vocal biomarkers on the same calendar day of recording. This reinforces the foundational premise of EMA: capturing data in the moment reduces the cognitive biases inherent in retrospective surveys and reveals critical affective fluctuations that episodic reporting misses []. By pairing high-frequency voice biomarkers with high-frequency, low-burden self-reports like emojis, this study successfully uses EMA principles for modern digital phenotyping.

Our acoustic findings for negative valence are consistent with prior clinical research on vocal biomarkers. Negative daily affect was characterized by lower magnitude mean, lower pitch mean, reduced RMS energy, and lower harmonics-to-noise ratios. These features mirror lower, less energetic voice profiles classically associated with clinical depression and negative affect in previous research [,].

While several studies have demonstrated that the affective dimension of arousal is strongly encoded in acoustic features such as pitch and intensity [,], our study identified within-person associations for valence but not arousal. There are 2 explanations for this observation. First, valence and arousal were measured by a pictorial (eg, emoji-based) single momentary assessment, similar to the nonverbal self-report pictorial technique used in another study which found that arousal was more difficult to report and more error-prone []. Second, the evidence that arousal is strongly encoded in voice largely derives from posed, acted, or exaggerated portrayals and stimuli, which may be attenuated in a more natural setting as was studied here. Therefore, the null associations we observed for arousal may reflect both the measurement method and the natural setting rather than an absence of vocal arousal encoding.

The relationship between higher word count and low self-regard provides a unique behavioral phenotype. While previous studies [,] have linked clinical depression to decreased speech quantity, our findings suggest that in a college population, low self-regard may manifest behaviorally as over-explaining, or increased verbal load and processing during open-ended voice prompts, driving higher word count. This finding coheres well with research conducted on social media platforms that observes over-disclosure is tied to increased risk for mental health problems [].

Our finding that vocal biomarkers track within-person changes in daily affect has clinical relevance based on prior literature. Daily negative affect and affect dynamics have been shown to predict depression and anxiety symptoms in young adults [], and heightened affective instability has been shown to distinguish individuals with current depressive and anxiety disorders from those without []. Prior work has demonstrated that passive and active data collection using smartphones can predict clinically relevant states such as depressed mood among undergraduate college students with clinical depression []. Furthermore, deep learning models have been applied to longitudinal smartphone data to predict future anxiety symptoms []. These results position voice as a candidate signal within a broader set of biomarkers to passively assess mental health in young adults using smartphones.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting results from this study. First off, using smartphones to collect data introduces variability and noise in derived voice biomarkers due to hardware and contextual variability. Related to voice journaling used in this study, the sample size and design did not allow us to more directly assess the impact of cultural-linguistic diversity. Second, to promote engagement, abbreviated or derived psychological measures (such as the self-regard label and single-item emoji selections) were used rather than full-length, clinically validated diagnostic interviews. This approach assesses psychological states quickly without disrupting the participants’ day, which allows for a wealth of data that is less impacted by missingness, but lacks the diagnostic depth of traditional clinical assessments. Next, this study used an observational, correlational design. While mixed-effects modeling effectively isolated the impact of within-person fluctuations and controlled for individual baselines, and care was taken to control for multiple comparisons, direct causal inferences are not possible without accompanying experimental data. Lastly, in our conservative analytical approach, several biomarkers approached but did not meet statistical significance for their association with loneliness and acceptance. Future research would benefit from more tightly aligning the time scale between voice biomarkers and psychological constructs. A larger study with a longer follow-up period would increase statistical power and allow for the application of deep-learning models. Such a study could uncover additional novel associations, including the association between affective states, psychological states (self-regard, loneliness, acceptance, and stress), and mental health diagnoses.

This study demonstrates that smartphone-captured voice biomarkers can be an effective tool for monitoring changes in affective states. While voice biomarkers did not predict loneliness or acceptance evaluated at the weekly level, they were highly sensitive to weekly assessments of stress and daily fluctuations in affect and valence. The majority of associated voice features reflect how someone speaks (pitch and intensity, etc), not what they say (VADER sentiment). This study suggests that college student self-monitoring built on prosody rather than language could inform and nudge students to take the next step based on their own within-person affective changes while being less privacy-invasive than a tool that analyzes what was said. Furthermore, these voice features leverage an individual student’s changes from their own speaking rather than a comparison to other students, which furthers their perception of privacy when using such a tool. These findings underscore the importance of using high-frequency and low-friction measures such as emojis, short surveys, and voice journaling when conducting digital phenotyping, which confirms existing research []. Ultimately, this approach paves the way for the development of scalable, targeted interventions that act on precise mechanisms and are capable of reaching college students before symptoms escalate into clinical disorders.

psychology.title: Text Psychometrics: Assessing psychological constructs in text using natural language processing
psychology.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP). Yet when used to assess psychological constructs in text, they are generally not evaluated for the types of validity, reliability, and standardization typically expected from traditional questionnaires with rating scales. This study bridges that gap by proposing a framework for evaluating the psychometric properties of NLP-based psychological assessments (including LLMs-based ones), an area of research we refer to as Text Psychometrics. We first review different NLP methods, compare their ability to address key challenges in psychological research such as explainability, and outline ways of evaluating them on many desirable psychometric properties. Our goal is to describe most psychometric properties that may be of interest, especially for psychology and NLP researchers who are less familiar with psychometrics or psychometricians who are less familiar with NLP. We then illustrate the tradeoffs of different NLP methods through two empirical studies. Study 1 classifies thousands of crisis counseling conversations and Reddit posts into different types of mental health issues and introduces a novel method to evaluate text models for content validity—the extent to which a test captures the full range of expressions of a single construct. Study 2 examines prospective criterion validity by estimating how 49 known suicide risk factors predict imminent risk in crisis counseling conversations. We find that mentioning lethal means for suicide, the police, depressed mood, and anxiety in text as well as the texter writing more than the counselor characterize the conversations that end up needing an emergency service intervention for imminent suicide risk, which showcases the interpretability of the method that was used. In sum, NLP studies in psychology often rely on only a few validation metrics; here, we demonstrate the need for broader psychometric evaluation and, as a step towards Text Psychometrics, provide practical examples and future directions that can help researchers evaluate these models.
psychology.text:
Text data is ubiquitous: it is present in social media, direct messages, clinical interview transcripts, survey responses, electronic health records, and scientific documents. There are thousands of distinct well-studied constructs psychologists and social scientists might wish to quantify in text including emotions, moods, symptoms, attitudes, states, traits, and abilities, often through different dimensions such as valence, arousal, frequency, and severity (i.e., dimensions are a measurable axis a construct varies along) []. The goals of these assessments could be to screen for a health outcome, summarize a person’s experience, trigger an intervention, or use measurements as variables in subsequent models to further understand a psychological theory [,]. This can be used to make individual-level predictions, such as a suicide risk screening [], or to do large-scale public-health monitoring such as understanding how a pandemic might be affecting different psychiatric populations over time []. The traditional approach Psychometrics has taken to measure psychological constructs has heavily relied on rating scales (), alongside behavioral tasks, implicit motive assessments, and other types of data. Rating scales ask a rater to convert a subjective observation into a specific value, usually on an ordinal scale. Compared to rating scales, systematically measuring constructs from natural language itself can seem more complex or inexact. However, language has been shown to describe nuances and extremes with more detail and greater ecological validity than rating scales []. Natural language processing (NLP) offers many tools to quantify these constructs, and the recent growth in abilities of large language models (LLMs) –a subset of NLP models based on deep neural networks that have billions of parameters– shows promise for identifying constructs more reliably [,].

Comparing the utility of natural language and rating scales requires evaluating multiple desirable psychometric properties (e.g., comparing the predictive abilities of each), considering the trade-offs in the time it takes to produce scores (e.g., one-minute journaling entries may capture many more diverse symptoms across individuals than a one-minute screening tool), and assessing how well a researcher can measure a specific construct’s presence and severity. For instance, a person may not mention a specific symptom in an open-text response, but may nevertheless be experiencing it to a certain degree. If it is critical that a specific construct is explicitly captured, or if the individual has difficulty articulating their emotions (e.g., due to severe depression and/or alexithymia), it may be better assessed through a quick ordinal rating scale –though recent evidence indicates language models can actually outperform rating scales even for individuals with high alexithymia []. Conversely, natural language is the gold standard in scenarios where self-reported ratings are inadequate; for example, implicit motives or subconscious associations cannot be captured through rating scales, but they often are expressed in natural language or behavioral tasks. Furthermore, open-ended language provides crucial context—differentiation, for instance, normative sadness at a funeral compared to clinical depression—which rating scales often strip away.

Historically, the different types of validity, reliability, and standardization typically expected from questionnaires using rating scales [] are not normally carried out when evaluating NLP models for psychological measurement. Researchers would never publish scales without assessing these psychometric properties, but they do so for NLP and other behavioral or biological markers, which are also susceptible to poor psychometrics, a double standard that has been called the “psychometric bias” [].

NLP studies tend to validate models using a single –albeit important– approach: comparing text model outputs to human-coded labels or annotations taken as “ground truth” ([–]; see criterion validity in the section “”). For instance, humans may code or label sentences from Reddit for different emotions, and then a machine learning model can learn to predict human-coded emotions from patterns in language using a variety of methods []. Here, “training” (or “fitting”) a model means adjusting its internal parameters on a set of labeled examples so that its outputs come to match the labels; “inference” is then applying the fitted model to new text. This same approach— predicting human-coded labels— is also the main form of validation used in NLP benchmark leaderboards. Leaderboards allow users to compare and rank models evaluated on many datasets and tasks. For instance, the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark covers 8 tasks (e.g., text classification, summarization, semantic similarity), 58 datasets, and 112 languages [].

In NLP and machine learning, predictive ability is evaluated on new data than what the model was trained on in order to test generalizability. However, psychology often uses a different and controversial definition of “prediction” [–]. Correlating two variables or fitting a linear regression to the data and using the model to provide a predicted value of the dependent variable for a specific individual is not necessarily prediction for machine learning. In those cases, the model “observes” all the data to provide an estimate (i.e., within-sample prediction; see ). Prediction for machine learning is defined as fitting the model with certain data (i.e., allowing the model to learn the association between dependent variables and independent variables) and then predicting (i.e., “guessing”) the value of the dependent variable for new data the model did not use for any aspect of model fitting (i.e., test set/s) []. This is known as out-of-sample prediction and can be done via cross-validation (i.e., splitting the existing data into a training set the model learns from and a separate test set, held back and never seen during fitting, used only to score the model) or other resampling methods []. Association can be thought of as a broader term that can refer to (a) this out-of-sample prediction, (b) estimation of the dependent variable’s value for a specific data point using all data during model fitting (i.e., within-sample prediction or association), or (c) estimation of sample-level or aggregate coefficients (e.g., correlations, within-sample regression coefficients, and other within-sample associations). The latter two forms of association are often referred to as “prediction” in psychology, but these within-sample predictions do not imply out-of-sample prediction capabilities (i.e., generalizability); that is, the estimates one obtains from within-sample predictions may not generalize to other similar samples, and machine learning requires this be tested to claim “prediction.” Therefore, while it is common knowledge that correlation (or more generally, association) does not imply causation, it is less known among psychologists that correlation (or association) does not imply prediction. Moreover, many have stressed that prediction should be chosen over association in many psychology studies and related fields [–]. For instance, any clinical application would require a model to make accurate predictions on new individuals that arrive to the clinic; we simply would not know whether the within-sample predictions are accurate on new patients without proper out-of-sample testing (see also  of dataset shift in the section “”).

Given that the goal of many applications is to try to automate human language tasks, providing a model that generalizes and can predict new samples of human judgments the model has not encountered is understandably the main priority, but should not be the only priority. A single metric is likely not capable of capturing many aspects of validity. We will provide examples of how to evaluate many psychometric properties in the section “”. These can be validated through within-sample associations or out-of-sample predictions, with the latter providing a stronger claim of generalizability.

Our study aims to provide a framework for evaluating psychometric properties of NLP models and is structured as follows:

In the section “”, we argue why putting more focus on broader types of validation in NLP-based psychological assessments is important and we review the non-obvious shared history between psychometrics and NLP.

In the section “”, we review different NLP methods and how they can be used to assign a score to a text document (e.g., text classification) for psychological assessments. We also propose key constraints psychology researchers face when using NLP models (e.g., small datasets, the need for explainable and private models) and how to overcome them with different NLP model characteristics. We also introduce an improved method of text classification with embeddings we call “Construct-Text Similarity.”

In the section “”, we provide an overview of how psychometrics has evaluated the validity and reliability of psychological assessments and how these properties can be evaluated in text data.

In the section “”, we provide a use case and test these methods in detecting a diverse set of mental health issues including suicidal ideation, eating disorders, and physical abuse to compare methods (open-source and proprietary LLMs, lexicons, and embeddings methods) and observe their performance across constructs. We provide a novel way of quantitatively evaluating content validity in text, that is, whether a tool assesses most behaviors or expressions associated with the construct being measured.

In the section “”, we focus on a methodologically more challenging task, that of predicting which of a set of suicidal individuals is at high imminent risk, which is a scenario with several common constraints in clinical NLP: an imbalanced dataset; and the need for models that are trustworthy and explainable. We predict this using initial parts of the conversation to evaluate prospective criterion validity. We also demonstrate how to inform theory by estimating how predictive each variable is of the dependent variable (i.e., feature importance).

In the “” section, we systematically compare NLP methods on a subset of these desirable properties so researchers can decide which NLP method to use, given each method may respond better to the different constraints researchers may have. And we discuss open areas of research for Text Psychometrics.

We refer to Text Psychometrics as research into the validation of NLP-based (including LLM-based) psychological assessments derived from human text. This refers to a growing, interdisciplinary research community effort. In this study, we focus on supervised NLP approaches—that is, models trained to predict a known label or score (e.g., a diagnosis, a symptom severity rating). Agreeing upon a specific term may help highlight a critical gap: standard NLP research –while very broad and rich– primarily evaluates out-of-sample prediction of ground-truth labels. While very valuable, this misses the rigorous psychometric requirements (e.g., content validity, reliability, fairness) required for valid psychological assessments.

A related area of research uses NLP to improve the development and validation of rating-scale assessments, such as generating questionnaire items (e.g., [,]), which could also fall under Generative Psychometrics (if using LLMs) and under the more established ‘computational psychometrics’ [], which is much more broad in scope. A second related area of research is assessing the artificial psychological profiles of artificial intelligence (AI) models [], which has been referred to as AI Psychometrics or LLM Psychometrics [,]. We can distinguish this from Text Psychometrics in that the latter measures psychological properties in humans from their natural language or uses NLP to improve rating-scale assessments in humans. AI or generative psychometrics [] are viable terms but would not be a fitting label for these applications if using many NLP methods (e.g., lexicons, TF-IDF, sentence embeddings) that should not be considered intelligent or generative. Furthermore, AI methods in the distant future may not be called generative.

Independent of how researchers decide to name this type of research –and we are open to other options–, we hope this study will help consolidate efforts to taxonomize and standardize the evaluation of desirable properties of these NLP-based models in a broader sense than what has been done thus far. And there is a growing number of studies trying to improve the psychometric validation of text-based NLP models for psychological assessments [,,–]. Each study has focused on specific types of models and properties. [] demonstrated that an NLP model detecting paranoia from text data had good test-retest reliability (see the section “” for definitions), it correlated positively with clinical ratings of paranoia and correlated negatively with measures of anxiety and depression. [] evaluated different types of validity (face, convergent, divergent, content, predictive) of several text embedding models using synthetic natural language data. [] describe how to assess validity and reliability of NLP model bias such as gender bias. [] have demonstrated that automated evaluation of topic models using coherence metrics fail to capture human judgments. [] had annotators rate the degree of hate speech in text documents using an ordinal scale and then used item response theory and deep learning to build a model that outputs a debiased continuous measure of hate speech from text. We contribute to prior work by (1) describing how NLP and psychometrics have a shared history (the section “Bridging natural language processing and psychometrics, two fields with a shared history”), (2) describing traditional and more recent NLP methods and proposing desirable NLP model characteristics (the section “”), (3) proposing additional desirable psychometrics properties and methods for evaluating these properties in NLP models (the section “”), (4) evaluating a few of these properties across two studies (sections and), and (5) discussing open areas of research and future directions (the section “”).

Human language has played a central role in the historical development of psychometrics. For a brief overview of psychometrics and related methods including item-response theory, network analysis, and causal inference, see section A of  (“Brief history of psychometrics: from classical test theory to networks and causal inference”). In  we highlight key developments in psychometrics, NLP, and AI throughout history. Psychometrics has discovered key attributes humans have (e.g., states, traits, attitudes) often by collecting large lists of words associated with psychological traits. Since early in psychometric history, it was clear that just because we have different words for constructs and traits does not mean these words refer to different attributes; therefore, there was a need to discover the underlying independent and general constructs from all possible construct names []. Thurstone’s (1934) “The Vectors of Mind” [] suggested we can discover the key, non-redundant psychological traits by having individuals rate if they would describe someone with adjectives such as “friendly” or “cheerful.” Using factor analysis, he grouped words with similar ratings and was surprised to discover there were only five factors underlying personality. Factor analysis would return how much each word is associated with each factor (i.e., factor loadings). He proposed plotting each adjective as a vector of points in space in five dimensions whereby similar traits would point in the same direction; if they are anticorrelated they would be pointing in opposite directions; and if they are independent, then they would be orthogonal (p. 15). One could measure this using cosine angles from the center of the space. Allport, Odbert, and Cattell between the 1930s and 1950s took this approach and gathered such ratings on thousands of words, an approach that ultimately led to the Big five factors of personality [], which includes openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.

Lexicons (i.e., lists of words and phrases associate with constructs) have also been used to measure psychological constructs in text. The General Inquirer gathered thousands of words related to different constructs, but used the first commercial computers from the 1960s to automatically count the appearance of different words in corpora [] which later inspired the widely used Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) [] and many other lexicons [].

Not only was language key in developing psychometrics, psychometrics has also influenced NLP, although this is relatively unknown. About three decades after Thurstone’s (1934) address, vector space models by Salton and others in the 1960s and 70s took this factor analysis approach [], (without acknowledging Thurstone as far as we can tell) but vectorized words by counting how many times a word co-occurs with other words (dimensions of the vector) within small windows of text across different corpora [,]. This was used to find documents that were similar to a query in information retrieval systems (e.g., finding articles about a topic in libraries).

This approach, along with advances in deep learning and hardware capabilities, contributed to the explosion of vector semantics that came with the creation of the word2vec word embedding algorithm in 2013, which was able to better quantify aspects of the meaning of words in vectors (i.e., ordered lists of numbers that represent positions in a multidimensional space). Improving upon word embeddings led to current state-of-the-art transformer-based embeddings, which can encode aspects of sentence and document meaning. These embeddings from transformer models have a wide variety of uses including information retrieval, paraphrase detection, categorizing text, summarization, and keyword extraction []. The origins of vector semantics is often credited to hypotheses in linguistics from the 1950s from Harris (“If A and B have almost identical environments we say that they are synonyms” []) and Firth (“You shall know a word by the company it keeps” []): vector semantics captured a word’s meaning by counting which words it co-occurs with. However, we find factor analysis as previously described also had a large influence as well. We can add the following quote by Thurstone (1934) to the history of vector semantics: “each trait can be represented as a point on the surface of a ball. If two traits A and B tend to coexist, the two points will be close together on the surface of the ball.” ([] p. 14).

Conventional psychological assessments tend to provide either binary variables, (e.g., present vs. absent) or continuous scores reflecting severity or frequency of symptoms, which are aggregated for a final score via sum scores, averages, or more complex scoring models (e.g., weighted composites, factor scores from factor analysis, or latent trait estimates from item response theory). How can we assess psychological constructs from text data? NLP offers a diversity of methods. The overall pipeline might involve preprocessing the text data (e.g., tokenization, lemmatization), feature extraction (e.g., turning characters into quantitative information such as counts or embeddings) (In machine learning, ‘feature’ refers to ‘variables’, often independent variables), a specific model (e.g., logistic regression, a specific transformer-based LLM), and output type (e.g., binary, multinomial, ordinal, continuous). Deep learning models including LLMs tend to do any preprocessing within the model. (For more in depth introductions to machine learning, deep learning, and LLMs, see [–]).

A recurring question is what the “item” or unit of analysis is in text-based assessment. The input unit that receives a score is the document—a post, conversation, or response— analogous to a test administration, with the construct detector acting as the scorer. Sentences, phrases, and tokens are the finer granularities at which feature extraction operates for particular methods (e.g., construct-text similarity tokenizes into independent clauses). There is thus no fixed “item” analogous to a scale item. A separate, diagnostic notion of item appears later in our content-validity test sets (Section 5.4), where individual prototypical tokens are used to probe coverage.

If the output is categorical (binary or multinomial) then machine learning calls this task ‘classification’. If the output is ordinal or continuous, this is known as a ‘regression’ task in machine learning (not to be confused with the type of model such as linear regression or logistic regression). Classification varies between binary classification (one out of two possible answers is correct, “Does the text mention loneliness?”), multiclass (only one out of several answers is correct, outputs for all options sum to 1; e.g., “Does this text belong to the depression, anxiety, or healthy participant samples that do not overlap?”), and multilabel (more than one answer can be correct, output for each range from 0 to 1; e.g., “Which symptoms does the text mention?”). (For a more formal description of text classification, see section C of  (“Formal description of text classification”).). A regression task (i.e., predicting an ordinal or continuous output) could try to detect severity from text (e.g., total score of the PHQ-9 from a concurrent journal entry), frequency (e.g., how often the person felt sadness in the last two weeks), or the model’s confidence the symptom is present; however, some continuous outputs that might appear as confidence scores are often not well calibrated as actual probabilities [].

In machine learning, the “validity” of the output is mainly evaluated by comparing it to some ground truth or criterion –often a human judgement, and increasingly LLM evaluations []. If the output is categorical (binary or multinomial), the metrics used are classification metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, precision, accuracy, F1 score, ROC AUC, and inter-rater reliability (i.e., between human and model scores). If the output is ordinal or continuous, then common validity metrics are mean absolute error, mean squared error, R2, and inter-rater reliability. These are performance metrics evaluating agreement with a ground truth label, which can be seen as a partial assessment, but is itself an imperfect proxy for the underlying construct (i.e., the estimand); psychometrically valid psychological assessments reflect a broader claim than performance against any single ground truth (see the section “”).

A challenge when assessing mental health from existing retrospective text data is a person may have said “I am sad” and it is not clear how sad they are (i.e., the cardinality), since this could be a valid expression of mild and severe sadness. This ambiguity is a limitation of some static retrospective text, not of language’s expressiveness per se—in real-world dialogue, a clinician, for instance, can follow up with specific questions to resolve severity or frequency, potentially achieving even more granularity than standard rating scales. Therefore, one approach is to use text classification to try to detect whether the mention of a construct is simply present or absent in a binary way (e.g., does the text mention loneliness?). Multiple constructs that capture different severity levels in a binary way can be assessed (e.g., worry and panic).

We now describe multiple NLP methods and depict them in , which we illustrate using classification examples. Assessing cardinality (e.g., severity) is an alternative, and adapting these methods to ordinal or continuous assessments is straightforward from an NLP perspective by changing certain elements of the model (e.g., the loss function) and evaluation metrics (e.g., see []). Overall, we recommend using LLMs when feasible for improved predictive performance (see the section “” for an in-depth discussion), but we describe other commonly-used approaches as well.

These methods are best understood as combinations of choices at distinct layers of a pipeline rather than as interchangeable alternatives at a single level: (1) text representation / feature extraction (e.g., lexicon counts, embeddings, entailment scores, LLM-generated scores); (2) scoring or aggregation (e.g., summed counts, maximum cosine similarity); (3) a predictive model or decision rule (e.g., logistic regression, a gradient-boosted tree, a fixed threshold, or none in the zero-shot case, i.e., where the model is applied to a task with no task-specific training examples); and (4) the validation target against which the output is evaluated. The same tool can occupy several layers—an LLM can serve as representation, scorer, and model at once— which is why we describe methods by the pipeline stages they combine. Critically, psychometric validity is a property of the measurement outcome as a whole (the end-to-end output), not of any single internal component []; attributing a result to a particular component is a separate, complementary exercise that can be done by ablation (see the section “” and ).

Lexicons or dictionaries. Using lexicons is a traditional way of performing text classification []. Lexicons contain one or many constructs, each with an associated list of tokens (words and phrases) – which can be validated by domain experts – that are counted in a given document []. Higher counts indicate the construct is more likely to be present. Then these counts can be used as is or as variables in a statistical or predictive model (i.e., learning to weight specific counts to optimize prediction of some dependent variable), which would be highly interpretable and would avoid missing obvious, prototypical tokens (e.g., “anorexia” for eating concerns) that might be missed by a high-performing deep learning model []. Our construct-tracker package allows for using generative AI to automatically create the initial lexicon, which can then be validated by human experts []. This is useful when the goal is to detect a construct with a simple, interpretable baseline model and/or guarantee not missing certain phrases (e.g., flagging suicidal language) or as an initial screening of potentially relevant documents (For a tutorial on building or using existing lexicons, see: https://github.com/danielmlow/construct-tracker)

Rule-based linguistic variables. Many variables can be extracted that capture semantic, morphology, syntactic and discursive aspects of language based on rules or dictionaries (e.g., list of prepositions) and therefore do not require complex models to derive (for reviews, see [,]). Once extracted into variables, then a model can learn which ones characterize the presence of a given construct in text. These variables include part-of-speech tags—including the frequency of nouns, verbs, adjectives, and pronouns— and the ratio between them. A high prevalence of first-person singular pronouns (e.g., I, mine, my) can characterize speakers’ focus on others versus themselves, and a lower prevalence of nouns-verb ratio might indicate word-finding difficulties []. Measures of lexical richness, such as Honore’s statistic, quantify vocabulary diversity and repetition patterns. Syntactic complexity measures are derived from the length of clauses, and usage of dependent clauses, tree depth. Finally, discourse markers reflect the degree of cohesion and coherence in a speaker’s narrative; for instance, semantic coherence in discourse captures the semantic similarity between successive phrases to capture staying or going off-topic []. Together, these tend to capture cognitive processes (e.g., tangential speech in psychosis). They tend to not necessarily capture the mentions of psychological states such as loneliness directly but linguistic behavior that correlate with the presence of these types of constructs.

Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) is a common technique for identifying words and phrases in documents that characterize a dependent variable based on how frequently they appear in a given text relative to a larger corpus []. These scores can be used as variables in predictive models (e.g., see [] for words that characterize different mental health support groups on Reddit). Unlike lexicons, TF-IDF requires no expert input, making it data-driven, scalable, and domain-agnostic. However, as with lexicons, TF-IDF treats words independently and lacks semantic understanding. Furthermore, this data-driven approach that finds words that characterize a variable is likely to be dependent on the specific dataset used and might not generalize to other datasets. Other methods presented here (including lexicons and LLMs) have the advantage of detecting a broad coverage of words that are prototypical of a construct –if designed to do so– and not just associated in some way in a specific dataset [].

Unsupervised topic modeling (e.g., Latent Dirichlet Allocation or LDA, BERTopic) do not start from a deductive approach where we have certain constructs of interest like text classification does, but rather discover topics that are present in the text inductively. They group frequently co-occurring words into latent topics, which can subsequently be mapped to psychological constructs by subjectively interpreting the cluster of words or using automated methods []. This is data-drive and requires little preprocessing. However, one key limitation is that these approaches frequently yield low-coherence topic clusters marked by intrusions—words that are semantically unrelated to the rest of the cluster (e.g., “date” appearing among “kill,” “intrusive,” “thought”) [,]. Furthermore, the cluster can be interpreted as representing many different constructs. We suspect that many social scientists would prefer to begin by measuring very specifically-delineated constructs already known to be relevant to their domain (e.g., the extent to which participants discuss rumination or bullying), reserving data-driven, exploratory methods as exploratory approach aimed at surfacing potentially novel constructs. More recent embedding-based topic modeling approaches, such as BERTopic [], attempt to improve on this by combining document embeddings (dense numerical vectors that capture meaning rather than just word co-occurrence) with clustering algorithms to group semantically similar documents before extracting representative terms for each cluster, resulting in more semantically coherent topics than LDA. However, they remain unsupervised in the sense that the resulting topics are not guaranteed to correspond to constructs of a priori theoretical interest and may be too heterogeneous.

Supervised topic modeling (e.g., supervised LDA, supervised BERTopic) jointly infer latent thematic structure from word co-occurrence and fit a predictive model (e.g., regression) of that structure onto an observed outcome, so the topics are shaped to be predictive of the label as well as descriptive of the text. Supervised BERTopic clusters over sentence embeddings where label information is used to warp the embedding space (via supervised dimensionality reduction) before clustering, so documents sharing a label end up closer together and more separable into distinct topic clusters. Supervision optimizes topics to predict your outcome, not to be more internally coherent, and can even reduce standard coherence scores as a tradeoff [].

The remaining methods are generally carried out using deep learning methods. Rarely is training done from scratch on the target task (e.g., loneliness detection), given they generally require large datasets labelled for the target task; rather, pretrained models like BERT [] are trained on a very large corpus (the entire English Wikipedia and other sources) in a self-supervised manner (e.g., predicting masked words within the input) to generate rich, internal representations that quantify aspects of meaning of words and phrases. Then this model can be fine-tuned (i.e., adapted) for a specific task (e.g., detecting loneliness in text) on a smaller, annotated dataset (e.g., documents coded for loneliness or other constructs) by attaching a feedforward neural network []. Pretraining can also be done in a supervised manner by training to predict labels in large, publicly-available datasets (e.g., for named-entity recognition). Then these pretrained models can be fine-tuned for the target task, which should improve performance in comparison to using the target dataset to train the model from scratch.

Named-entity recognition classifies each token as a possible entity belonging to a category or ontology []. The presence or sum of entity types in a document would return similar results as text classification. The general approach is to train a model to output a probability for each entity type.

Natural language inference and textual entailment. This method can be used for text classification as well [–]. Entailment is inferring whether two sentences are a contradiction or an entailment (e.g., “Met my first girlfriend that way.” is a contradiction of “I didn’t meet my first girlfriend until later.”; “At 8:34, the Boston Center controller received a third transmission from American 11” is an entailment of “The Boston Center controller got a third transmission from American 11.”; []). In a classification setup, the document to be classified can be treated as the premise for which one can build a positive hypothesis using the template “this text is about <construct > ” as well as a negative hypothesis using other labels; []. Gretz et al (2023) [] fine-tune natural language inference models which output entailment and contradiction scores that serve for text classification.

Embeddings turn each text into a fixed-length numeric vector that captures aspects of its meaning. In supervised prediction, those vectors become the independent variables or features: texts already labeled for some construct (e.g., journal entries coded for depression severity), embed or vectorize each document with pre-trained embeddings, and train a model (e.g., logistic regression, a gradient-boosted tree) to map the embedding to the label. The model learns which directions and dimensions in embedding space are associated with the outcome (each one being relatively uninterpretable), and can then predict labels for new, unlabeled texts. Because embeddings encode semantic similarity, this can generalize better than exact-word methods like lexicons or TF-IDF (e.g., “worthless” and “unworthy” land near each other), at the cost of interpretability.

Fine-tuning deep learning models. Whereas traditional methods involve some preprocessing (e.g., lemmatization, data cleaning, and feature extraction), pretrained deep learning models like BERT allows for end-to-end prediction, taking raw data, skipping most preprocessing, and outputting a prediction []. However, this generally requires a substantial amount of labeled training data, at least in the thousands of samples (although new advances such as LoRA are improving this []).

Construct-text similarity. Since lexicons can miss important tokens that they do not have (e.g., a lexicon may have “suicide attempt” but miss “attempted suicide” or “tries to take ones life” if not in the lexicon), there is a method to find semantically similar tokens to the ones in lexicon using deep learning using relatively interpretable method called dataless classification [], similarity-based zero-shot text classification [] or sentecon [], among others. We introduce a more generalized version that has more parameters to choose from for each step, which we call construct-text similarity (which we expect will be a more transparent term for psychologists), as shown in Fig A in . This method works as follows: it first computes the similarity between a target construct representation (e.g., text embedding for the phrase “eating disorders” or for many tokens related to eating disorders or the average of all of these) and each token in a given document (e.g., text embeddings for phrases). It then takes a summary statistic as the final output (e.g., maximum between all construct and document embeddings). This approach produces a zero-shot output, meaning the method requires no training data. The construct can be the average of the text embeddings for a lexicon’s category, which means that it can capture much of what the lexicon captures and also similar words while a lexicon can only capture exact matches. The process of being able to capture similar words has been demonstrated to outperform lexicons []. It is a middle ground between interpretable lexicons which will miss similar words if not in the lexicon and standard supervised deep learning which is a black box and hard to explain. It can also combine counts (0 or N with semantic similarity if there is not an exact match). However, it does not learn the contextual cues or reasoning abilities found in the previously described deep learning models. The resulting score can be used as the output for zero-shot text classification. It was found to outperform the textual entailment approach in a zero-shot setting [], but not when textual entailment models were fine-tuned []. It is also more lightweight than deep learning methods because it can run more easily on standard CPUs (central processing units, the general-purpose processors in any computer), unlike deep learning, which often requires specialized GPUs (graphics processing units, hardware built to run the many parallel computations deep learning needs). This is especially beneficial for psychology researchers who may not have the expertise to work with GPUs. (For a tutorial on construct-text similarity, see https://github.com/danielmlow/construct-tracker/blob/main/tutorials/suicide_risk_lexicon_construct_text_similarity.ipynb.)

Large language models that generate text can be used for text classification (i.e., generating a score) by designing prompts to score whether certain constructs are present in a given document [,] –which can be considered LLM-assisted qualitative coding [,]. (For a tutorial on using LLMs to detect constructs in text and compare to human coders, see: https://github.com/childmindresearch/llm_tracker.) However, the best-performing models (e.g., the latest GPT, Gemini, Claude) tend to be proprietary [] and therefore require users to submit the prompt to a company’s server through a browser or API [], which may be infeasible if the data is highly sensitive. Another reason for submitting data to APIs are because generally for a fee, users can run inference or training quickly on cloud-based GPUs (e.g., OpenRouterAI, Replicate, Huggingface API, Microsoft Azure, Amazon Bedrock). Alternatively, users can download open-source LLMs (e.g., Gemma, Llama, Qwen, Mistral series). These tend to be smaller (e.g., 2B-70B parameters) and underperform their larger proprietary counterparts (with the exception of DeepSeek R1 which has 671B parameters [] and Llama-4 Maverick with 400B parameters []) and require considerable computational resources such as GPUs. Models can be quantized by reducing the precision of the weights for faster inference and fine-tuning while achieving similar performance [] which can lead lighter models to run on a personal computer’s GPU or CPU (e.g., using packages such as transformers, Ollama, GPT4All, llama cpp), which is likely to become very prevalent as models become smaller and more efficient and hardware capabilities improve. Leaderboards include Huggingface Open LLM leaderboard (https://huggingface.co/spaces/open-llm-leaderboard/open_llm_leaderboard#/) and the Chatbot Arena (https://lmarena.ai/) [].

Now that we have introduced several NLP methods, we highlight desirable NLP model characteristics as shown in . These tackle pragmatic constraints that psychology researchers often face. One is the limited availability of big training datasets, especially in clinical settings. This poses a challenge for fine-tuning standard supervised learning models such as BERT that require large datasets. A second challenge is the need for interpretable models to understand how a model is making predictions to increase trust that it is not biased []. Explainability methods also allow researchers to rank which variables are most predictive of a target variable, which can be used to advance scientific understanding of the variables or discover novel risk factors []. A third challenge is the need to keep sensitive data private, which currently limits the use of submitting data to cloud services to use existing proprietary generative AI models, although cloud-based data security may improve in the near future.

Given these constraints and NLP-model characteristics, researchers can choose different types of approaches to perform text classification, which we guide how to do in the section “”. Once an NLP model is trained using machine learning, different psychometric properties can be evaluated. There is not a one-size-fits-all method, and choosing a method will depend on these constraints and on evaluating multiple psychometric properties.

There are many desirable psychometric properties that we may want a psychological assessment tool to fulfill. Here we provide a concise outline of these properties with examples of how to evaluate them with text-based models. This list of properties is helpful for several reasons: first, to adapt the definitions of classical and modern psychometric concepts to fit the needs of current NLP and AI goals. And second, to inspire new types of analyses that might be less frequent among NLP researchers so they can validate their models more broadly and help link their intuitive analyses to concepts that already have a vast literature in psychometrics.

Causal validity. Ideally, a measurement is demonstrated to be valid when a measurement outcome (e.g., change in thermometer) is caused by an intervention on the target attribute (e.g., temperature) []. This causal effect can be estimated through randomized controlled trials or causal inference methods for observational data []. This causal perspective on validity might discard many types of so-called validity approaches listed here as necessary to prove validity; in particular, construct validity []. NLP example: evaluating the validity of an NLP model that measures state anxiety from text data: participants could be randomly assigned to a relaxation- or anxiety-inducing task and asked immediately after to write about their affect –a valid score from this NLP model would be lower after the relaxation task than the anxiety task.

Criterion validity. An instrument score is valid if it is associated with a criterion assumed or demonstrated to be valid []. The criterion is often a human or expert judgment but can also be a certain behavior or biological variable. Psychometrics has generally focused on within-sample associations, while NLP and machine learning focus on out-of-sample prediction. There are three types of criterion validity, depending on when the criterion and the instrument were assessed:

(a) Concurrent validity: The instrument’s score is associated with a more standard or previously validated questionnaire total score or questionnaire item that at face value is valid, assessed at the same time point, either through correlations or out-of-sample prediction. NLP example: Correctly classifying crisis counseling conversations as being about physical abuse given the counselor’s annotation (i.e., the criterion; demonstrated in the section “”).

(b) Prospective validity: Rating scales should be associated with future scores or future behaviors within the same person, which may require repeated measures. This will also depend on whether the construct is an episodically-changing trait or a persistent trait. Higher scores on a suicide risk assessment questionnaire should have a positive correlation with future suicide attempts. This is related to the study of dataset shift in machine learning (see ). This has been traditionally referred to as “predictive validity” []; however, given correlation is not prediction (see Prediction entry below), we use “prospective validity” instead. NLP examples: (1) Demonstrate baseline language patterns are associated with future PTSD symptoms []. (2) Predict whether a conversation will be annotated as an imminent risk by the counselor (better assessed towards the end of the session) from the initial 25% of the conversation (demonstrated in the section “”).

(c) Retrospective validity: Whether an instrument reflects past conditions or behaviors. For example, the score of a suicide risk assessment should correlate with lifetime suicidal thoughts and behaviors. NLP example: Train a model to detect language about depression and correctly identify which individuals had been diagnosed with a depressive disorder in the past, independent of current diagnosis.

Ecological validity. The assessment resembles real-world conditions vs. tightly controlled laboratory conditions. NLP example: Have participants journal by randomly prompting them during the day (i.e., ecological momentary assessment); social media data [].

Face validity. Whether a test appears to be valid for members of the target population based on a subjective judgment. For instance, individuals may not support the claim that the way they draw a person –a common projective assessment– clearly reflects their personality or mental health. If a math exam is clearly too hard for test-takers, then it will have low face validity. A scale assessing honesty may purposely try to have low face validity to avoid a social desirability bias. NLP example: The individuals being assessed could compare the construct being assessed (e.g., anxiety) with the question they were asked (e.g., “Describe what has been worrying you the most today,” which would have high face validity versus “Describe this picture of a forest” which may have low face validity). If the model is explainable (see ), they could assess the appropriateness of the explanation. For instance, if a model uses words from text like “bulimia” and “eating” to indicate eating and body image concerns but ignores “anorexia,” it may indicate low face validity []).

Construct validity. Some constructs such as pain, mood, attitudes, disability, and quality of life are not directly measurable and therefore do not have a clear gold-standard method of measurement []. Construct validation is thought to provide support that the measurement is measuring a given construct. A measurement score for a construct should not be highly associated with scores for unrelated constructs (discriminant validity) and associated scores for similar constructs (convergent validity). It can be demonstrated though a pairwise correlation matrix of related and unrelated scores or through prediction. Discriminant validity has a variety of methods []. If one of the two variables being associated is considered true (e.g., a gold standard), then the association would be a demonstration of criterion validity; when neither is, it is a demonstration of construct validity. A test can be similar to another, but they can both be invalid; therefore construct validity can be seen as an inferior form of validity than criterion validity with a gold standard, and there is good reason to suggest it does not assess validity properly []. NLP example: Among individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis, the NLP metric of semantic coherence was correlated with positive thought disorder severity (e.g., tangentiality and derailment) and the NLP metrics of complexity (sentence length and complementizer use) were correlated with negative thought disorder severity (poverty of speech and content) []. A type of construct validity is known-groups validity: When a test score discriminates between two groups known to differ []. NLP example: A valid measure of quality of life from natural language should likely differ between groups with and without chronic pain.

Content validity. The systematic examination of the test content by an expert to determine whether it covers a representative sample of the behavior to be measured []. A scale assessing depression should cover most common symptoms; however, depression scales perhaps should be expected to have low content validity given the dozens of diverse symptoms that are considered part of depression (i.e., heterogeneity [],). NLP example: Even though a classifier has relatively high performance on a test set, this does not guarantee it covers a representative sample of the behaviors of the construct being measured. A classifier can achieve higher performance detecting eating or body image concerns while missing “anorexia” if this token is relatively infrequent in the test set []. LIWC has low content validity for most mental health symptoms such as hopelessness or suicidal ideation. Content validity test sets compute the sensitivity of a given trained model on its ability to predict as positive a list of tokens that cover most types of instances of the construct (proposed in the current study).

Epistemic validity and clinical utility. Validity is often seen as a demonstration that a test measures what it intends to measure [,], independent of how it is being used []. However, a test may be used to inform a diagnosis or treatment plan or to determine the efficacy of a therapeutic or educational intervention. Aspects of how a score is interpreted and used in practice ethically or unethically are related to its epistemic validity [] (see also [],). Relatedly, determining whether a certain sensitivity and precision of a test is appropriate depends not on only their values but on how decisions will be made as a consequence of their values, their clinical utility. This can be quantified through a net benefit analysis which weighs potential benefits versus harms of a test, considering its true positive and false positive rates [–]. NLP example: Consider an NLP model that detects suicide ideation in the last clinical visit to determine whether their should be a follow-up; if the model has low precision, it might still lead to improved outcomes compared to not deploying it, a net benefit.

Cultural validity refers to the extent to which a construct, its operationalization, and its interpretation are appropriate and meaningful across different cultural contexts, reflecting both universal (etic) and culture-specific (emic) understandings of behavior and experience [,]. Without cultural validity, assessments risk incorporating unexamined cultural assumptions, leading to systematic mismeasurement, biased inferences, and reduced generalizability across populations. NLP examples: A model assessing depression from text may perform well on Western social media but misclassify culturally normative expressions of distress (e.g., somatic complaints or indirect emotional language) in non-Western or minoritized groups, indicating low cultural validity. Text-based variables highlighted as indicators of a target variable “flourishing” (e.g., autonomy- or achievement-focused language) may align with individualistic cultural values while ignoring relational or communal expressions of well-being, revealing culturally specific assumptions embedded in the model []. cover how text markers of depression change with race.

Fairness. Related to the concept of equivalence in psychometrics, a test should not unintentionally function differently for different groups (e.g., age, disability, gender, race, ethnicity, education level, sexual orientation) [], particularly if it is unknown to the test recipient. More broadly, fairness relates to evaluating whether discoveries (e.g., five dimensions of personality) generalize as universals beyond the socioculturally-narrow populations where they were tested []. NLP example: A model underpredicts the need for an intervention for a protected group. Metrics and algorithms exist to identify and mitigate bias []. Discovering social bias in LLMs is another active field of research given the data used to train models, while large in scale, may also be narrow socioculturally [].

Measures of uncertainty. Uncertainty can be considered as doubt about the validity of a measurement result and a dispersion of the values that could reasonably be attributed to the attribute being measured []. While standard deviations and confidence intervals can be estimated as average effects, individual predictions should also convey level of confidence as well as a lack of confidence when a model has not been trained on similar samples. Uncertainty methods for individual predictions include probabilities, prediction intervals, conformal sets, Monte Carlo dropout, ensembling, and Bayesian methods []. NLP examples: (1) If model predicts high risk with high uncertainty, do not deploy planned intervention and have expert inspect. (2) Generative AI models could provide confidence estimates and evidence that supports their opinions or inferences.

Standardization. Method by which a score’s test is interpreted by comparing a score to a representative sample (populational norms) on standardized scores (e.g., stanines, T scores; []). Lack of replication across studies can occur when different measurements of the same construct are done differently due to either different unstandardized research design or operationalization. NLP examples: (1) Leaderboards are ways of standardizing models’ criterion validity, public tokenizers can help standardize preprocessing. (2) Standards for feature extraction could be developed to rule out results across studies are not different due to differences in pipeline implementations or choices in parameters.

Unidimensionality. Whether the target construct to be measured is homogenous, that is, indicators measure the same thing (e.g., a specific type of insomnia) or whether it is heterogeneous and thus measures multiple things (e.g., depression [],). The amount of dimensions can be assessed through exploratory factor analysis (EFA), categorical principal component analysis loading plots, and item response theory []. If items or more specific constructs have strong associations to certain latent variables and not to others, then each latent variable can be seen as a homogeneous construct. These could still be grouped into a multidimensional scale (e.g., personality, job performance). A network approach does not need to assume latent variables and can assess dimensionality through community detection of observed variables. NLP example: The dimensionality of a lexicon can be assessed by encoding the tokens with embeddings and clustering, where the amount of clusters (i.e., construct dimensions) would have the highest average silhouette score. Embeddings could also be used in factor analysis. Variables of a trained model could also be evaluated similarly.

Reliability. The consistency of a measure depends on the condition under which it is evaluated (For an extensive overview of reliability in NLP, see []):

(a) Parallel-forms reliability and intra-method reliability. Consistency of responses of a given individual to two versions of the same questionnaire that use different items []. NLP example: If we consider trained models as individuals, slightly changing prompts to a generative AI LLM can result in very different performance [,,]. Testing sensitivity of a model to reinitializing random weights or parameters [,].

(b) Test-retest (across time). Measuring same individuals using same test across time points. When this is done by a same rater over time, it is called intra-rater reliability. As with prospective validity, this will depend on whether construct is expected to change (i.e., trait) or remain stable over time (i.e., state). NLP example: An NLP model detecting paranoia from text had good test-retest reliability over the course of several days using intra-class correlation [].

(c) Internal consistency (across items). Degree to which items measure the same thing []. The most widely-used Cronbach’s alpha is not recommended as it tends to underestimate reliability due to many unrealistic assumptions, such as assuming each item on a scale contributes equally to the total score (tau equivalence) []. A related, older method is split-half reliability, which correlates two halves of the items (typically with a Spearman–Brown correction); Cronbach’s alpha can be understood as the mean of all possible such split-half correlations. A measurement may have high internal consistency but not be unidimensional (a more stringent concept) if items are associated with multiple latent variables (see unidimensionality section above); for instance, a test measuring both depression and anxiety may yield a high internal consistency (since these tend to be correlated), but is not unidimensional. NLP example: The Suicide Risk Lexicon [] as a whole covers a diverse set of risk factors, but each of its 49 constructs could be evaluated for internal consistency by computing the average cosine similarity of each token’s embedding with a target label embedding representing the construct.

(d) Inter-rater (across raters). Consistency across different raters’ independent judgements as measured through absolute percentage agreement, Cohen’s Kappa, intra-class correlation (ICC) and other methods []. NLP examples: (1) Annotators judging whether to include tokens in a lexicon []. (2) Two distinct topic models could be both correct because of the subjective nature of categorization, topic models could be considered raters and reliability could be assessed through Rand Index [].

Which of these properties should be evaluated will depend on the goals of the study. Some of the properties we present may only demonstrate some expected property of a valid assessment, but not prove validity themselves (e.g., construct validity may not prove validity per se). (For further discussion on validity and measurement, see section B of  (“How to define measurement and validity?”).) Having said this, we expect researchers would want to evaluate most of these different properties depending on their application, but might only evaluate some of them (e.g., standardization) after more fundamental evaluation (criterion validity) is assessed.

Traditional psychometrics built on reflective latent-variable models assumes ordinal or continuous item responses, local independence, and one or more common factors. These are properties of that measurement model, not of text data per se, and they bind only when such a model is fit to text-derived variables (e.g., embeddings used in factor analysis; The section “”). Most of the framework above instead concerns supervised classification, whose relevant assumptions are those of predictive modeling: that the training sample is representative of the deployment population, that generalization is evaluated out-of-sample, and that the text–label relationship is stable across time and population (or that shifts are modeled; see  shift, Section 3.2). Given this, three clarifications follow. First, both structured elicitation (e.g., “Describe what has worried you most today”) and unstructured or social-media text are admissible; structured text raises the probability the construct is expressed and improves face and content validity, while unstructured text can raise ecological validity at the cost of control over whether the construct surfaces. Second, when a single text expresses multiple constructs (e.g., both anxiety and resilience), we do not partition variance across latent dimensions; constructs are scored independently through multi-label classification or separate binary models, so a document can score positive on several at once. Whether co-expressed constructs are correctly distinguished is then a discriminant-validity question that our content-validity test sets address directly, by checking that a construct’s prototypical tokens are detected by that construct’s model and not by others. Third, as noted in The section “”, the document is the scored unit; there is no fixed scale-item analogue, and the prototypical tokens of our content-validity test sets serve as a separate diagnostic notion of item.

The following two studies we performed demonstrate trade-offs of selecting a given NLP method as a function of the dataset, goal, and psychometric property that should be fulfilled. The studies try to assess variables related to psychological crises and mental health, tasks that highlight the need for models that are valid, explainable, and keep sensitive data private. In study 1, we compare predictive performance of a wide variety of NLP methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate why it is important to evaluate content validity, and we provide a novel way of doing so: evaluating whether a model trained to detect a construct can correctly classify highly prototypical and obvious words and phrases of said construct, as defined by experts. In study 2, we showcase a common scenario of class imbalance where the outcome of interest is rare. We predict the target variable –which is in the future– using increasingly larger segments of the crisis counseling conversation (i.e., prospective validity). In this high-stakes scenario, we use an interpretable method to avoid unknown bias and to understand which symptoms most predict future risk. In neither study, do we attempt to achieve a fully psychometrically validated model, which is beyond the scope of this study. We wish to simply showcase how to test different NLP models and evaluate a few psychometric properties of these models. Certain properties would require additional measures (e.g., convergent and discriminant validity) or repeated measures (e.g., test-retest reliability), which we do not have in these datasets.

Here, we present a use case to demonstrate how to train and validate these different types of NLP methods to detect a diverse set of psychological constructs in two datasets: (a) issues discussed during de-identified Crisis Text Line conversations, as annotated by the crisis counselor immediately following the conversation; and (b) similar types of issues from Reddit (described in the section “”). The semantic variety of issues –from suicide to bullying to gender/sexual identity– should allow us to evaluate the sensitivity of the models to these different types of constructs. Demonstrating that an NLP model can detect what counselors coded as the conversation happened is a form of concurrent criterion validity (that is, if we consider their judgment ground truth). However, our main goal is to demonstrate that while being able to predict a human-annotated label is key, high-performing models may or may not be capturing a representative set of expressions of the target construct (i.e., low content validity). To assess this, we introduce a novel way of evaluating content validity (see the section “”).

Crisis Text Line. Crisis Text Line is a nonprofit organization that provides free, 24/7, confidential mental health support for individuals in crisis who can begin a conversation with a trained, volunteer counselor via text messaging, WhatsApp, or webchat. Crisis Text Line users have been reported to be predominantly young (76% under the age of 25), female (79%), white (53%) and heterosexual (52%) []. We built several different datasets using Crisis Text Line data, containing de-identified crisis counseling conversations between individuals in crisis and counselors from the years 2017–2022.
