Years 2020 and 2021 were omitted to avoid symptoms and concerns that were prevalent during the Covid-19 pandemic. In  we show the distribution of the 13 most common types of issues as labelled by the counselors. We built balanced binary datasets (training set N = 4000, test set N = 600) where only one of these issues was present vs. a random selection of the remaining types of issues from a total of 52,270 unique conversations. We balanced the test set as well so that comparisons across methods and constructs reflect model’s ability to tell the two classes apart rather than differences in base rate; we evaluate performance under a realistic, imbalanced class distribution in Study 2. Binary models were used because multi-class classification could change radically depending on what constructs are chosen and we want to reflect a psychometric test that results in a single score. The sample size was chosen to test how increases in training set affects performance and we consider 4000 samples would be among the larger samples in clinical studies.

Reddit. Reddit is a widely-used forum, used by 22%, of U.S. adults []. It is organized into subreddits, many of which are lightly-moderated spaces for seeking and providing mental health support. Using the Python praw package (v7.8.1), we downloaded posts from 11 subreddits (4000 for training and 600 for testing for each subreddit), reflecting most of the Crisis Text Line issues (i.e., Depression, Anxiety, SuicideWatch, Lonely, SelfHarm, EatingDisorders, GriefSupport, Bullying, Addiction, AskLGBT, SexualAssault). Since these are public data, we can evaluate the performance of proprietary state-of-the-art LLMs in their ability to identify the subreddit of each post. Posts were from 2025, after each model’s training data cutoff date, so these samples were not in the model’s training data. This also allows us to evaluate how much our results change across two datasets, keeping constructs relatively constant. This dataset differs from Crisis Text Line in being a monologue (looking at just the post content), not a dialogue, and coming from a different population: while Reddit users also tend to be young, they are characterized by being less young (44% under 29 years old), mostly male, and with more Asian and Hispanic than White users []. Real world use for detecting subreddit of a post include: discovering language patterns and symptoms belonging to a mental health community and assigning posts to optimal subfora (if this were required).

We include interpretable methods (lexicons, similarity-based text classification) given psychologists commonly use models for high-stakes decisions or to advance the understanding of what predicts a given construct. And we also include zero-shot methods (construct-text similarity and generative AI) given the previously discussed challenges of obtaining computational resources and the moving target of constructs that might need to be assessed.

LIWC-22 lexicon. LIWC is a lexicon that counts the proportion of tokens related to 117 categories including semantic constructs (family, anger) and nonsemantic linguistic variables (1st person pronouns, unique words).

Suicide Risk Lexicon (SRL). this lexicon contains tokens (words and phrases) associated with 49 different risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) including direct self-injury, hopelessness, and discrimination []. It has been shown to surpass LIWC and offers higher content validity (i.e., more related constructs) than LIWC for language around psychological issues and imminent risk. Initial tokens were built using GPT-4 turbo and later validated by clinicians. Counts are normalized by document word count. For a tutorial, see: https://github.com/danielmlow/construct-tracker/blob/main/tutorials/suicide_risk_lexicon.ipynb.

LIWC-22 and SRL were trained using logistic regression. Hyperparameter tuning was done using Bayesian optimization using the scikit-optimize package on a 5-fold cross-validation of the training set. Hyperparameter tuning of the Ridge alpha parameter included values [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100].

Construct-Text similarity (CTS). We apply this method, as described in the section “”, twice: once by building the construct representation using only one prototypical token and again by using all prototypical tokens from the suicide risk lexicon as construct’s tokens; prototypical tokens are those that scored 3 out of 3 by all clinicians in how much they represent a given construct (e.g., “anorexia” is very prototypical of eating disorders while “didn’t eat much” is less so). We tokenize the document into independent clauses (with subject and predicate) to capture more minimal units of meaning than sentences separated by punctuation. We compute the maximum similarity to capture the document token with the highest similarity to any prototypical lexicon token. We then min-max scale the output of the cosine similarities between 0 and 1 to match the scale of other models.

Open-source LLM Gemma instruct models. Gemma 7B is an open-source generative LLM that was high-performing on multiple tasks involving reasoning, question-answering, math and science, and coding at the time of analysis []. Gemma 2B is a smaller version that is expected to underperform but can run efficiently on a personal CPU unlike its larger counterpart. These models were downloaded onto our private and secure computer cluster. We provided the prompt displayed in Fig B in . We did inference using Gemma 2B-it on a single NVIDIA GeForceGTX1080Ti GPU for 10 hours and Gemma 7B-it on a single QUADRORTX6000 for 16 hours.

Proprietary LLM Google Gemini 2.0 flash & OpenAI GPT-4o models. These models are among the highest performing models at the time of analysis (https://huggingface.co/spaces/lmarena-ai/chatbot-arena-leaderboard). Therefore, we used these for public Reddit data but not Crisis Text Line data. They also allow for a prompt that includes the entire codebook which reduces API requests considerably (see Fig C in ). We randomized the order of the constructs in the prompt for every submission to avoid an ordering bias. To encourage the model to select the most highly predicted tokens, the temperature—a parameter controlling output randomness or creativity that typically ranges between 0–1— was set to a low value of 0.1. If the output of LLMs did not contain a parseable JSON (approximately 3% of cases), random output scores (i.e., between 0 and 1) were generated.

In  we show the average and range of the performance of the different binary text classification models across the different types of issues in two datasets, summarized using ROC AUC, the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance will be ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative instance by the classifier (0.5 = random; 1 = perfect prediction). In both datasets, the SRL outperforms LIWC, which is expected given it actually captures more relevant constructs to mental illness (i.e., as higher content validity at face value). In the Crisis Text Line dataset, the CTS model—using just a single variable in a zero-shot fashion– surpasses LIWC and the Suicide Risk lexicon trained on 300 documents and matches LIWC trained on 4000 samples. In the Reddit dataset, the CTS models performed relatively well: they only marginally underperformed the lexicon models but used only one variable and did not require any training (i.e., zero-shot). The LLMs require no additional training data from the target dataset (e.g., Crisis Text Line, Reddit) and improve their performance likely as a function of parameter size and recent innovations in training which allow for larger training datasets (while model and training specifications are proprietary, GPT4o and Gemini 2.0 flash are likely larger than gemma 2–7b models; []).

To evaluate content validity quantitatively (albeit in a simple way), we introduce content validity test sets: lists of tokens judged by experts to be highly prototypical of the construct of interest. Prototypical tokens are those that first come to mind when thinking of a construct (“I’m a burden” or “I’m a nuisance” for burdensomeness) –given a specific definition– and have fewest variables in common with other constructs []. Prototypical tokens should not lead to many false positives where the person is not expressing the construct (e.g., “I’m anxious” for burdensomeness). While these tokens are likely to appear in a large enough test set, their relative frequency will be different, as depicted in . A random test set will evaluate a model’s ability to generalize to real, unseen data; while a content validity test set will answer the question: how many of the obviously prototypical tokens can the model detect? These lists can be obtained from publicly available lists made by experts (e.g., symptoms in DSM-5) or more rigorously by creating a lexicon and validating it with clinicians, as done with the Suicide Risk Lexicon (SRL; []) (We specifically used SRL tokens judged 3/3 by experts (srl_prototypes_v1-0) from construct-tracker package. For a tutorial, see: https://github.com/danielmlow/construct-tracker/blob/main/tutorials/suicide_risk_lexicon.ipynb). We would expect high-performing models to capture all prototypical tokens, especially those scored 3 out of 3 in clinician evaluations of prototypicality as we test here. Therefore, the metric of choice is sensitivity: out of the prototypical tokens how many can the model correctly predict? While traditional test sets include non-obvious positive cases making a perfect prediction of 1 very difficult, we expect all models to have a perfect sensitivity close to 1 in detecting obvious tokens, especially those built using SRL (SRL and CTS). These content validity test sets provide a model-agnostic method of evaluating content validity, which can also serve as an explainability tool (i.e., what information does the model capture?) []. evaluated content validity of text embeddings through probing experiments: text is encoded with a given embeddings model x (e.g., BERT) and with an interpretable feature f (e.g., sentence length); the embedding is assumed to contain the interpretable information if it can predict it, a common approach in explainable machine learning. However, this does not answer whether a model captures a representative set of prototypical expressions, which may be closer to the definition of content validity, and we try to demonstrate through our complementary approach, which unlike probing is dataset-independent and works for evaluating models and not just embeddings.

In  we show the average and range of the performance of the same binary text classification models as the section “” but now tested on lists of clinically-validated tokens that are highest on prototypicality (i.e., content validity test sets), computing the sensitivity for these tokens (i.e., content validity). Any misses are considered an obvious mistake. As expected, SRL-based models (SRL and CTS using prototypical SRL tokens) are able to capture the prototypical tokens except CTS (1 prototype) which has low performance. Evaluating the model just on out-of-sample prediction using metrics such as ROC AUC or F1 score (i.e., criterion validity) miss this lack of content validity. Surprisingly, gemma models perform extremely well on average, although much worse for some constructs. Unsurprisingly, the more recent and larger Gemini 2.0 flash and GPT-4o models perform very well on average.

In summary, from a Text Psychometrics standpoint, Study 1 shows that criterion validity and content validity can dissociate: several methods reached good criterion validity (ROC AUC > 0.75) on the held-out task yet missed many prototypical expressions of the construct (content-validity sensitivity < 0.80), a gap that a single performance metric would hide. The lexicon built for this domain (SRL) outperformed the general-purpose lexicon (LIWC) and, together with construct-text similarity using multiple prototypes, captured nearly all prototypical tokens, whereas construct-text similarity with a single prototype had high criterion validity but low content validity. The practical lesson is that evaluating only out-of-sample prediction is insufficient; our content-validity test sets provide a model-agnostic, dataset-independent way to check whether a model covers the range of a construct’s expressions.

The goal of this second use case is to present a more challenging NLP task: predicting a low-base rate phenomenon: whether the outcome of the conversation resulted in requesting an emergency services intervention, resulting in an imbalanced dataset. Furthermore, we will predict this outcome using earlier parts of the conversation, which is a form of prospective criterion validity. We show how different classification metrics improve as more messages are included. We finish by providing an algorithmic explanation (i.e., feature importance), that is, revealing which risk factors are most predictive of the outcome which can help inform theory.

During Crisis Text Line conversations analyzed, counselors assessed for suicidal thoughts, suicidal plans, access to means, and imminent 48-hour timeframe, in that order (see [] for more details). If a texter is determined to be at a high risk by the crisis counselor, the counselor will involve a supervisor. The supervisor evaluates whether the texter is in immediate danger and unable to create a safety plan or deescalate, in which case the supervisor may contact local emergency services. To better dissociate the likely highest risk group in the dataset, we created two groups: (a) suicidal desire without plans, means, or timeframe, and (b) cases where an emergency service intervention was initiated, which has all symptoms present and cannot be fully deescalated. Such models could speed up risk assessments (e.g., alert the supervisor earlier), give a second opinion to the counselor and supervisor, or, after appropriate validation, be used in a different setting where there is no counselor (e.g., social media). We balanced the training set by downsampling suicidal desire cases to the imminent risk sample size to avoid the model over-predicting values closer to the majority value, resulting in a training set of 3500 (half in each group). The test set included a total of 2358 cases, with 2152 suicidal desire cases without plans, means, or timeframe cases (91% of test set) and 206 emergency services intervention cases (9% of test set).

For this task, we wanted an explainable model to improve trustworthiness and so we could perform feature importance analysis to understand which risk factors are associated with imminent suicide risk needing an emergency service intervention. We chose CTS with all prototypical tokens given its high performance in the prior task in capturing constructs. We used all constructs from the Suicide Risk Lexicon as independent variables and trained a LGBMClassifier model. Hyperparameters [and values] tested for the LGBMClassifier were: num_leaves [,,], colsample_bytree [0.1, 0.5, 1], max_depth: [0,5,15], min_child_weight: [0.01, 0.001, 0.0001], min_child_samples: [,,].

In  we report predicting the outcome of the conversation resulting in an emergency service intervention as the conversation advances (computed on the quartiles of the number of messages across all participants of the training set: 25% = 28, 50% = 43, 75% = 64, 100% varies by conversation). Similar performance to using the entire conversation can be achieved with the first 3/4 of the conversation, which could help speed up potential alert systems that could be designed in the future, if the number of messages or duration of conversation could also be reliably predicted, to help supervisors make a decision. Whether this model is clinically useful (one of the psychometric properties we described), that is, whether these classification metrics are sufficiently high for a model to be deployed –in particular, models with a low precision, which is common in low-base rate phenomena such as suicide risk assessments []– could be evaluated quantitatively with a net benefit analysis, which should include weighing potential benefits versus risks of harm of emergency services interventions, which may vary across populations [–].

Understanding which variables are associated with suicide risk from a language perspective can help inform the theory of suicide risk: what risk factors should counselors pay particular attention to? To compute feature importance with the LGBMRegressor model, we calculated the improvement in the information gain (i.e., the splitting criterion) from using a given feature in a tree’s split (i.e., how much a given feature helps to reduce the error). Other methods include SHAP [], leave-one-feature out (especially when there is colinearity) (https://github.com/aerdem4/lofo-importance), and permutation feature importance.

In  we show the top 20 variables for predicting imminent risk with emergency service intervention. Mentions of lethal means for suicide (e.g., cutting), Other substance use & overdose (“overdose,” “pills”), and having the texter write more than the counselor were the most predictive variables for detecting the need for an emergency service intervention.

From a Text Psychometrics standpoint, Study 2 demonstrates prospective criterion validity under realistic class imbalance: an interpretable pipeline (construct-text similarity features from the Suicide Risk Lexicon feeding a gradient-boosted model) predicted a future emergency-service intervention from only the first portion of a conversation, with performance improving as more of the conversation was observed and near-complete performance reached by three-quarters of the conversation. Because the outcome is rare (9% of the test set), we report precision and PR AUC alongside ROC AUC, and note that whether such a model should be deployed is a question of clinical utility (net benefit) rather than discrimination alone. The interpretability of the method also let us recover which known risk factors were most predictive—lethal means, substance use and overdose, and the texter writing more than the counselor— showing that a psychometrically-motivated, explainable model can both predict and inform theory.

We have introduced Text Psychometrics as an important area of research to improve the validity and reliability of NLP methods being developed for psychological assessments in text data. We reviewed how to validate models that use NLP to assess psychological constructs in text through examples and through two original studies. In particular, we have provided a novel method for evaluating content validity using lexicons and expanded a similarity-based text classification method which we call construct-text similarity which is interpretable and lightweight. Next we help guide researchers in choosing the optimal NLP method given their research and dataset constraints.

In  and in the following discussion we provide a practical decision guide summarizing our qualitative analysis of the trade-offs of different NLP methods, as a function of different, key desirable properties.

The first point to make is that using an existing lexicon is rarely the optimal choice given it generally has lower predictive performance compared to other methods due to lack of incorporating contextual information and/or reasoning capabilities. We also argue it tends to lack content validity at face value since it does not generally capture the main target constructs of interest in any given study []; furthermore, when used to detect a given construct, the resulting model misses many prototypical tokens of the construct as shown with the content validity test sets (). Nevertheless, an advantage of using a widely-used lexicon like LIWC is to compare to prior findings so as to improve reproducibility and validation across diverse datasets. We argue creating this should be attempted (and is already being attempted) with LLM-based models, given all their advantages. Therefore, once widely-used LLM-based models are created for a given construct, there should be a balance between capturing constructs in slightly better ways with using existing well-validated models, to avoid the same issue of over-proliferation of under-utilized rating-scale assessments [].

An alternative is building one’s own lexicon, and one can have an LLMs generate a draft lexicon as a starting point []. This is likely to achieve improved performance (criterion validity) and higher content validity. Custom lexicons can be used directly without training a model (zero-shot) in the sense that one can count whether their tokens appear in a document without training a model, although it is unlikely to perform very well. It is better to train a model to learn how much to weigh these counts to detect the dependent variable. The main limitations with lexicons is they cannot match tokens that are similar to the ones they have (“suicide attempt” will not match “attempted suicide”) and they lack awareness of how a word’s context might be associated with the target variable (’not sad’,’very sad’,’sort of sad’), which explains their limited performance. Fine-tuning a deep learning model (e.g., BERT) overcomes this issue of context, which is one of the reasons why it tends to outperform lexicons, but requires substantially more training data and are black-boxes []. An intermediate approach between lexicons and fine-tuning a deep learning model is to use Construct-Text similarity, which is zero-shot, matches similar tokens, has high content validity, and is interpretable. However, it is also insensitive to context which will limit its predictive performance.

We also note that apparent interpretability of lexicons depends on reporting which tokens drove a construct; because individual matched tokens may not be prototypical of that construct (e.g., “cut” is less prototypical than “BPD” for borderline personality disorder) or may be shared by multiple constructs leading to a biased interpretation of what constructs are most important for prediction. Furthermore, interpretability of a method should always be assessed alongside its predictive performance: the closer a model performs to chance, the less relevant its explanation is for the target application.

Recent LLMs perform well zero-shot, can be fine-tuned for improved predictive performance, and can be requested to provide self-explanations of why they generated a certain result, which may or may not be truthful []. They may be sensitive to extremely large prompts (i.e., context windows) and can capture attempts at avoiding keyword detection (e.g., “s3lf harm3d yesterday” would be likely flagged as self harm). Open-source versions currently require substantial computational resources (GPUs, technical abilities) and tend to perform worse than proprietary versions []; however, a proprietary version requires users to submit their data to APIs, which may not be permitted for sensitive data. It is also challenging to make generative LLMs output deterministic results, which may create unforeseen errors and is particularly problematic in high-stakes scenarios. Other approaches (BERT-type models) can be used in these settings for deterministic results as an alternative or used alongside generative LLMs.

Overall, LLMs are already dominating other methods given their performance is extremely high on many types of tasks. For supervised text classification with enough labeled data, fine-tuned encoder models (e.g., BERT/RoBERTa) can match zero-shot generative LLMs [,]; generative LLMs are most advantageous in zero-shot settings (when limited training data is available or training is undesirable) and likely for many other NLP tasks. LLMs will gain even more traction once their size decrease in order to run more easily on personal computers and their self-explanations are deemed not only plausible, but also faithful (i.e., true) []. More mechanistic interpretability methods and understanding for LLMs are also being developed [,]. Lexicons or construct-text similarity might be prioritized over other deep learning approaches when (a) an interpretable model is preferred for high-stakes decisions or scientific inquiry (perhaps used in tandem with LLMs to guarantee capturing tokens an LLM might miss); and (b) when models that might result in higher predictive performance are challenging to train or use due to lack of labeled data, computational resources, or data-privacy requirements that forbid sharing data with a LLM API or cost (e.g., running LLMs for millions of electronic health records).

A complementary strategy is triangulation: when a finding replicates across methods with different assumptions (e.g., lexicons, embeddings, language models), confidence increases in the findings (e.g., as in [], where convergence across three complementary methods strengthened the substantive conclusion); when it appears with one method but not others, it can be treated with caution. Nevertheless, agreement across methods may, depending on the analyses and interpretation, be closer to a form of reliability than to validity: multiple methods may converge yet share the same bias—so triangulation should be paired with the validity checks in Section 4 (e.g., criterion and causal validity). Efforts to share and independently validate language-based models across labs [] can further support such convergence.

It is commonly thought that a biomarker (digital speech pattern, neural circuit, genetic marker) or behavioral marker (language sentiment) are objective because they can measure variables automatically, that is, they are more objective than any one human’s subjective opinion. However, can these markers be considered objective if they are predicting subjective variables such as a self-report questionnaire? A first consideration is that the target labels may come not from self-report but from the opinion of experts who provided the labels, who may use more objective criteria than nonexperts. The label may be a gold-standard that is relatively objective, such as a diagnosis of vocal-fold paralysis through video endoscopy []. A model that accurately predicts expert judgements could be more objective than most non-expert humans. Second, if a model is biased or unfair, such as one that unjustly uses proxies for race to grant or deny parole to incarcerated individuals [], it could in theory be improved or corrected through bias mitigation methods []. This model could end up being more objective than the average judge. Therefore, by increasing the amount of training datasets and correcting over time, a model might become more objective than the humans who provided annotations in any one of its training datasets. Self-supervised models such as generative AI LLMs achieve this even without an external criterion: it uses next-word prediction of the own training data on vast amounts of diverse corpora to allow models to gain rich representations useful in having better predictions than many humans in a variety of downstream tasks, especially when combined with reinforcement learning with human feedback []. While bias mitigation methods can reduce systematic errors in theory, it would be premature to conclude that corrected models are more objective than human judges; this claim requires empirical demonstration under controlled conditions, ideally using criterion labels that are themselves verifiably objective.

Nevertheless, given text-based measures often predict subjective target variables, it might be important to evaluate the validity of a text-based measurement beyond assessing its convergence to a subjective rating scale []. Several studies have compared text models to rating scales without having to train the text model to optimize the prediction of a self-report rating scale variable. One study [] took the pictures of facial expressions of different emotions done by actors (happy, sad, or contemptuous, taken as the ground-truth) and randomly assigned participants to either describe each expression with words or rate each stimulus using rating scales for the corresponding expression (e.g., 1 = low to 5 = high happiness). Then both types of responses (i.e., text versus rating scale) were used to predict the ground-truth emotion category and the text-based model showed higher performance. Therefore, these types of analyses allow text-based models to independently be compared to rating scales using criterion validity of a ground truth.

Another study [] first had one set of individuals write narratives about a series of internal states (e.g., depression, anxiety); these narratives are safely assumed to be about those states (ground-truth). Then, a second set of individuals read these narratives and were asked to evaluate them in two ways: by generating five descriptive words summarizing the text, and by assigning scores using relevant rating scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7). Finally, models were trained to predict the ground-truth states from either the semantic representations of the five descriptive words or the rating-scale scores. The text-based models (using the descriptive words) outperformed the rating scales in accurately detecting the emotional states.

Going forward, –as stated in the Introduction– choosing between natural language and rating scale assessments should weigh their many psychometric properties, assessment time, and whether assessing a given construct or its severity is needed. A person may not mention they are experiencing a symptom or may not clarify how severe a given symptom is, which could be evaluated with a specific rating scale or followup open-text question.

As NLP-based assessments improve, it might be possible for users to assess individuals without their consent. This could lead to spreading private information or rejecting individuals during jobs or insurance applications based on model predictions. European legislation has proposed individuals have a right to an explanation on high-stakes algorithmic decisions, which would make these malicious practices illegal []. As models become better, users may not doubt models’ outputs, which is especially problematic if we trust AI to evaluate AI (the section “Other NLP tasks”). If measurement is done via AI chatbots then all the known risks of generative AI hold: hallucinations; suicide encouragement; non-evidence-based medical recommendations; disinformation; illegal, toxic, and discriminatory content; leakage of personal information or copyrighted material from the training set; and plagiarism []. Standardized AI safety benchmarks are being used to assess LLMs []. Specific questions could be posed to a model to determine whether it will output harmful content such as suicide methods. Furthermore, training, fine-tuning, and particularly running inference with LLMs can produce a substantial impact on the environment, and reducing this impact is an active area of research [].

LLMs are known to suffer from small changes in the prompts, which can be evaluated more thoroughly (e.g., see [], who refer to this as a lack of consistency), which is similar to parallel forms validity or intra-method validity in psychometrics [].

We evaluated different types of models in predicting 13 types of issues. A comparison of these text classification methods (and potentially other methods) on multiple datasets from different domains (e.g., clinical, nonclinical, political) would be useful. While we cannot assume the results will hold exactly in other datasets, we do hypothesize a similar trend in other datasets given the discussed advantages and limitations of each approach (e.g., amount of training data needed, how content validity reflects capturing relevant constructs, the lack of context-sensitivity in some methods, reasoning abilities and general-domain knowledge of newer generative AI models).

To limit the scope of our study, we have focused on comparing text models to rating scale assessments. We have not compared text models to behavioral tasks, qualitative interviews, or other types of data often used in psychology and psychometrics, which would be important to explore in future work.

In this section, we discuss possible extensions to this type of research, beyond the specific use case of crisis counseling discussed above. These do not reflect any plans or opinions of Crisis Text Line.

In section A of  (“Brief history of psychometrics: from classical test theory to networks and causal inference”), we briefly reviewed factor analysis, item response theory, networks, and causal inference. Other multivariate modeling has been approached in psychometrics using MANOVA (independent regression models) and a series of path analyses such as structural equation models (which integrate confirmatory factor analysis into a path analytic framework), multidimensional scaling [], and moderator-mediator models [] that try to provide more insight into associations between variables. Future work could further explore how to combine these methods with text data; for instance, using embeddings instead of rating-scale responses for factor analysis.

Multiple methods could be applied to improve performance including few-shot or exemplar prompting (i.e., including multiple examples in the prompt with their correct labels), chain-of-thought prompting (i.e., instructing the model to provide a step-by-step explanation in the prompt before providing the answer), ensemble refinement (e.g., include multiple chain-of-thought responses through temperature sampling in the prompt for the final answer), sampling different hyperparameters (temperature, top-k, and nucleus), and fine-tuning using efficient methods such as QLoRA [,].

We focused on text classification, but there are many other NLP tasks that could also benefit from rigorous psychometrics. We briefly outline additional tasks and how they are currently validated. Many of these tasks and metrics can be evaluated before and after deployment.

NER: classification metrics can be used as well as more nuanced interpretability methods [].

Summarization and question-answering. Summarization has many applications such as creating artificial memories in generative AI chatbots so it can access information about a user or provide summaries of electronic health records to clinicians before they see a patient. Question-answering also returns a text which needs to be validated to some ground truth. Validation of these tasks involves comparing the similarity to a ground-truth (criterion validity), although recent approach are reference-free [].

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is an approach to improve generative AI giving them access to external databases []. Even though LLMs are originally trained on large corpora, they will likely not have information that is proprietary or novel and, therefore, can benefit from searching through new data using semantic textual similarity and other techniques. There are many metrics and benchmarks that evaluate different properties of the retrieved information []. Applying item-response theory (IRT) could help evaluate whether the system adapts appropriately to varying levels of question difficulty or ambiguity.

Chatbots. Evaluating the quality of a chatbot will require similar metrics as we have used, but also ethical considerations as well as metrics related to user engagement and conversation length. Fully automated chatbots likely pose serious risks in high-stakes scenarios such as crisis counseling. A desirable property for a chatbot could be long-term memory of the interactions with the user, which may help the system retrieve details of the user over time and over longer documents. Another may be to have a reliable personality [].

Agentic AI. AI agents can take human input via prompts in order to interact with a device and take actions. Examples include virtual assistants that can set an alarm; AI research assistants that can search for articles, analyze data, and draft manuscripts; and code assistants that can generate and test scripts []. They are typically evaluated using task completion metrics, benchmark suites (e.g., BabyAGI, AutoGPT), and qualitative human feedback on their goal achievement and adaptability. Incorporating psychometrics could enhance evaluation by modeling latent behavioral traits and tracking their evolution over time, task type, complexity, and novelty.

LLM-as-a-judge: AI evaluating AI for automated psychometrics. If AI is similar or better than humans at a given task, then AI could be the ground truth criterion we try to predict, perhaps to validate smaller, weaker, faster, or cheaper models. This is known as LLM-as-a-judge []. The gemma models we used incorporate this during training by having a larger, higher capability model express choose between responses it produces []. Models could choose the best hyperparameters of another model for training, suggest adjustments during training, suggest how to adapt trained models to new data, generate synthetic training data to improve measurement, continually monitor predictions once deployed, and run tests to improve predictions. It is feasible that AI could one day help demonstrate all the desirable properties we outlined in the section “” on its own. However, generative AI has been shown to carry different types of racial and gender biases [] as well as methodological biases [], which should be carefully evaluated and mitigated.

We have tried to organize and promote research into the validation of NLP-based (including LLM-based) psychological assessments derived from human-generated text. We first presented different types of validity and desirable properties that could be evaluated for text-based assessments. We then systematically compared a diverse set of models including lexicons, zero-shot construct-text similarity, and zero-shot generative AI on different desirable properties in their ability to predict different types of mental health issues and imminent suicide risk. We argue there is a hyperfocus on criterion validity (e.g., out-of-sample prediction of a gold-truth label). We introduced content validity test sets as a way to demonstrate whether models miss any key prototypical expressions of the target variable. This helps us demonstrate that some models can have good criterion validity (e.g., ROC > 0.75) but miss many prototypical tokens (e.g., content validity sensitivity < 0.80). In a second use case, we predicted the need for a future emergency service intervention (i.e., prospective criterion validity) and uncovered which risk factors most predicted the need for an emergency service intervention (e.g., lethal means for suicide more than depressed mood or hopelessness). We finish by providing a comparison of key desirable properties to select models depending on the constraints different researchers may have (). As an additional step towards Text Psychometrics, we hope this study will encourage broader validation of these promising NLP methods in psychology, medicine, and the social sciences, and we see much room for future work to extend it.

psychology.title: Neurophysiological changes following intensive Naikan therapy in a patient with recurrent depressive episodes later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder: A case report
psychology.abstract: Intensive Naikan therapy is a structured Japanese psychotherapy involving systematic reflection on interpersonal relationships; however, its neurophysiological correlates remain unclear. We herein report changes in resting‐state electroencephalography (EEG), the P300 event‐related potential, and standardized low‐resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA)–estimated source activity after intensive Naikan therapy.A 29‐year‐old man with recurrent depressive episodes and anxiety about family relationships and future employment underwent 7 days of inpatient intensive Naikan therapy. He was later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder after a hypomanic episode during the follow‐up. Assessments were performed before and after the intervention. Anxiety decreased on State–Trait Anxiety Inventory state and trait scores (42 to 20 and 30 to 20, respectively), and depressive symptoms remained minimal on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Beck Depression Inventory (4 to 3 and 0 to 0, respectively). Psychological measures suggested reduced self‐ and other‐blame and greater acceptance of family members. Resting‐state EEG showed a negligible change in peak alpha‐band global field power, whereas peak beta‐band global field power decreased from 5.13 × 103 to 2.84 × 103 µV2/Hz. During the auditory oddball task, P300 amplitude at Pz increased from 5.5 to 7.3 µV. sLORETA images were evaluated descriptively, without statistical comparisons or uncertainty estimations.Intensive Naikan therapy was temporally associated with reduced resting‐state beta activity and an increased P300 amplitude. These observations from a single uncontrolled case with multiple assessments are hypothesis‐generating and do not establish treatment efficacy, causality, or a treatment mechanism.
psychology.text:
Naikan therapy, a Japanese psychotherapy involving systematic reflection on interpersonal relationships, has been used to alleviate psychological distress and as an adjunctive intervention for psychiatric symptoms. Clinical studies have suggested its benefits for depressive and anxiety‐related symptoms.,  However, the cited evidence includes an uncontrolled pre–post study on 28 patients with anxiety disorders and a non‐randomized comparison of daily Naikan practice in 47 patients with depression, all of whom had received intensive Naikan therapy. These designs limit attribution of the reported benefits specifically to intensive Naikan therapy.

Only a few studies have examined physiological changes during Naikan therapy. Shiga serially recorded frontal electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, electromyography (EMG), and palm skin temperature in three participants during 7 days of intensive Naikan therapy. The findings obtained showed more sustained mid‐alpha activity, decreased EMG, and increased skin temperature, possibly reflecting relaxation and adaptation to the Naikan setting. Nevertheless, standardized pre–post EEG studies using quantitative measures, event‐related potentials, and source localization are limited.

We previously reported the clinical course and psychodynamic formulation of the present case, but not the neurophysiological findings. We herein present exploratory changes in resting‐state EEG, P300, and standardized low‐resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA)–estimated source activity before and after intensive Naikan therapy in a patient with recurrent depressive episodes who was later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder.

At the time of intensive Naikan therapy, the patient was a 29‐year‐old unmarried man with recurrent depressive episodes, anxiety about the future, and longstanding family‐related interpersonal difficulties, particularly involving his father. In his early 20s, he developed insomnia, loss of appetite, nausea, depressed mood, and anxiety. He initially received treatment for a somatoform disorder and was subsequently treated for depression.

Despite multiple antidepressant trials and repeated hospitalizations for recurrent symptoms and self‐harm, symptoms persisted, and he was referred to our hospital for consideration of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). At admission, depressive symptoms were mild, with a Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM‐D) score of 14 and a Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) score of 16. Depressive symptoms improved during inpatient rest and supportive listening, and ECT was not performed.

However, low self‐confidence and concerns about family relationships and future employment persisted. Consistent with these interpersonal difficulties, a personality assessment using the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) suggested low stress tolerance, difficulty expressing emotions appropriately, and passive‐aggressive tendencies (Supplement ). Since the psychosocial assessment indicated persistent family‐related difficulties, intensive Naikan therapy was initiated on hospital Day 40 after psychoeducation.

Intensive Naikan therapy was conducted for seven consecutive days (hospital Days 40–46) in a private room on the ward as an inpatient adaptation of the original Naikan method. The patient systematically reflected on significant others using three standard themes: (1) what he had received from the person, (2) what he had given to the person, and (3) the trouble and difficulties he had caused them. The procedure and concomitant medication are detailed in Supplement .

During the first several days, he was able to recall theme‐congruent episodes, although his descriptions were brief and non‐specific. His recollections from the mid‐phase onward became more concrete, particularly regarding his mother. He also increasingly described events from others' perspectives, including reframing his father's scolding as guidance intended to teach right from wrong. By the final day, he expressed a more agentic attitude toward his life. He acknowledged that he had not sufficiently confronted his illness and stated that he wanted to engage more actively in treatment and efforts toward social reintegration.

Intellectual functioning was assessed at admission using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale‐Revised.

After obtaining consent, clinical and psychological assessments were conducted before intensive Naikan therapy (Pre‐INT; hospital Day 36) and after the completion of intensive Naikan therapy (Post‐INT; hospital Day 50). Depressive and anxiety symptoms were assessed using HAM‐D, BDI, and State–Trait Anxiety Inventory. Interpersonal‐cognitive and coping‐related changes were evaluated using the Picture‐Frustration Study, Sentence Completion Test (SCT; Seiken adult version), and Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations. The SCT was reviewed descriptively by the treating psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist without formal scoring. Quantitative results are summarized in Table .

Clinical assessments and psychometric measures.

Abbreviations: ‐, not assessed; BDI, Beck Depression Inventory; CISS, Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations; FSIQ, Full Scale Intelligence Quotient; HAM‐D, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale; INT, intensive Naikan therapy; P‐F study, Picture‐Frustration Study; PIQ, Performance Intelligence Quotient; Pre‐INT, before intensive Naikan therapy; Post‐INT, after intensive Naikan therapy; S‐anxiety, state anxiety; STAI, State–Trait Anxiety Inventory; T‐anxiety, trait anxiety; VIQ, Verbal Intelligence Quotient; WAIS‐R, Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale‐Revised.

Imaggression refers to impunitive or non‐blame responses.

Resting‐state EEG, the P300 event‐related potential, and sLORETA source estimation were performed on hospital Days 35 and 49 (around 2:00 p.m., respectively), before and after intensive Naikan therapy, based on a previously published protocol. EEG was recorded using a 32‐channel DC amplifier (EEG‐2100 version 2.22J, Nihon Kohden Corp., Tokyo, Japan) with electrodes placed according to the international 10–20 system (Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4, C3, C4, P3, P4, O1, O2, F7, F8, T7, T8, P7, P8, Fz, Cz, and Pz). Recordings were conducted in a wave‐shielded and sound‐attenuated room. The sampling rate was 500 Hz, with a bandwidth filter of 0.16–120 Hz and a 60‐Hz notch filter. The reference electrodes were averaged ear electrodes, and electrode impedance was kept below 10 kΩ.

In resting‐state EEG, the patient lay on a bed with his eyes closed in a silent, darkened room for 5 min. EEG data for the resting‐state EEG analysis were segmented into consecutive 2‐s epochs. Epochs with voltage amplitudes exceeding ±200 μV were rejected. After rejection, 89 and 79 epochs were retained for Pre‐INT and Post‐INT recordings, respectively. These epochs were then imported into sLORETA software. Using the “EEG to cross spectrum” function, cross‐spectral matrices were computed over a frequency range of 1–20 Hz. Global field power (GFP) was calculated from 19 scalp electrodes, and the resulting GFP spectra were obtained. The alpha‐ and beta‐frequency ranges were defined according to the 2017 International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology (IFCN) terminology: alpha activity was defined as 8–13 Hz and beta activity as frequencies >13 Hz.

The P300 component was elicited using an auditory oddball paradigm. Standard tones of 1000 Hz were presented with a probability of 80% (n = 200), and target tones of 2000 Hz with a probability of 20% (n = 50). Auditory stimuli were presented binaurally through headphones. Each tone had a duration of 100 ms, with a rise/fall time of 10 ms and a variable interstimulus interval of 1.5–2.5 s. The patient was instructed to remain awake, keep his eyes open, fixate on a red circle displayed on a monitor, attend to the auditory stimuli, and press a button as quickly and accurately as possible in response to target tones. P300 data were analyzed using Vital Tracer and EPLYZER II (Kissei Comtec Co., Ltd., Nagano, Japan). EEG epochs of 700 ms were extracted, with a baseline period from −100 to 0 ms before stimulus onset. Epochs with voltage amplitudes exceeding ±50 μV were manually rejected. After artifact rejection, 41 and 39 artifact‐free target epochs were retained for the Pre‐INT and Post‐INT assessments, respectively, and were averaged offline to obtain the P300 waveform. P300 amplitude and latency were measured at Pz, where P300 amplitude is typically maximal. Within the 250–400‐ms time window after target stimulus onset, the positive maximum peak was identified.

In the source estimation, P300 waveforms were analyzed using the “EEG/ERPs to sLORETA” function in sLORETA software. Current source density (CSD) was estimated from the 19 scalp electrodes included in the analysis within the 250–400‐ms post‐target‐stimulus time window, corresponding to the period in which the P300 component was observed. The estimated CSD distribution was then visualized as sLORETA images.

Clinical, psychological, and neurophysiological findings from Pre‐INT to Post‐INT are summarized in Table , Figure , and Supplement . Anxiety decreased, while depressive symptoms remained minimal. Psychological measures suggested reduced blame‐related responses, decreased emotion‐oriented coping, increased problem‐oriented coping, and more accepting SCT narratives toward family members. Resting‐state EEG showed a negligible change in peak alpha‐band GFP, whereas peak beta‐band GFP decreased from 5.13 × 103 to 2.84 × 103 µV2/Hz (Supplement ). P300 amplitude increased at the Pz electrode from 5.5 to 7.3 µV (Figure ). sLORETA source estimates are presented descriptively in Figure .

The patient was discharged on hospital Day 53 after improvements in depressive and anxiety symptoms and more considerate interactions with family members. Approximately 1 year later, he experienced a hypomanic episode. Antidepressants were discontinued, mood stabilizers were optimized, and the diagnosis was revised to bipolar II disorder according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision, which was in use at that time. In the present study, the longitudinal diagnostic course was retrospectively reviewed and confirmed to meet the criteria for bipolar II disorder in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition. He subsequently returned to work.

In the present case, beta‐band GFP decreased, and P300 amplitude increased after intensive Naikan therapy, whereas the change in alpha‐band GFP was negligible. sLORETA images were evaluated descriptively. Anxiety and blame‐related responses decreased, and SCT narratives suggested greater acceptance toward family members, consistent with previous findings of reduced externalized blame and changes in empathy‐related indices after Naikan therapy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine P300 and sLORETA‐estimated source activity before and after intensive Naikan therapy. However, concomitant medication, inpatient care, sleep and vigilance, repeated testing, and the evolving diagnostic context preclude attributing these observations specifically to Naikan therapy.

The relative stability of alpha‐band GFP does not exclude differences in wakefulness or drowsiness during resting‐state EEG recordings between Pre‐INT and Post‐INT. The reduction in beta‐band GFP occurred alongside lower anxiety scores, whereas depressive symptoms were already minimal at Pre‐INT. For context, increased beta‐band power and decreased alpha1‐band power have been reported in generalized anxiety disorder. In a different clinical context, Higuchi et al. reported a relationship between frontal β1 activity and somatic concern in drug‐free subjects with at‐risk mental states. These findings raise the hypothesis that beta‐band GFP may be related to anxiety; however, this relationship was not established in the present case. A cross‐disorder review found marked overlap and within‐disorder variability in resting‐state EEG band‐power findings, as well as methodological heterogeneity. Accordingly, the beta‐band difference observed here is not sufficient to identify a specific clinical process. Although Shiga reported different physiological findings during intensive Naikan therapy in healthy participants, differences in the study design, measures, and clinical context preclude direct comparisons.

sLORETA images were evaluated descriptively for the P300 time window before and after intensive Naikan therapy. However, because this was a single‐case report and no statistical comparisons or uncertainty estimations were performed for sLORETA images, the results obtained cannot be interpreted as evidence of increased frontal cortical activity. With this caution in mind, the post‐intervention increase in P300 amplitude at Pz is a descriptive observation of unknown functional significance. P300 abnormalities have been reported in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder and, thus, are not unique to a single diagnosis. Treatment‐associated P300 changes have also been reported; however, methodological heterogeneity limits comparisons across studies. P300 amplitude is affected by attention, arousal, and stimulus/task parameters. Therefore, an amplitude increase alone does not identify a treatment‐specific effect or a particular cognitive improvement.

The later diagnosis of bipolar II disorder changes the diagnostic context in which these findings need to be interpreted. Possible contributions from a bipolar‐spectrum pathophysiology or illness‐related state variation cannot be distinguished from any potential effects of Naikan therapy. Therefore, these results cannot be generalized to patients with major depressive disorder. This case highlights the importance of a longitudinal diagnostic assessment when interpreting neurophysiological observations in patients with recurrent depressive episodes.

There are several limitations that need to be addressed. This was a single uncontrolled case. Changes across multiple measures in the same patient do not constitute the independent replication of a treatment effect. Furthermore, with only one pre‐intervention and one post‐intervention neurophysiological recording session, the stability and reproducibility of the observed differences remain unknown. Inpatient rest, supportive care, expectancy, and the passage of time cannot be separated from any potential intervention‐specific effects. Although EEG recordings were performed under conditions that were kept as consistent as possible, including the recording time and analytic procedures, the pre‐ and post‐intervention assessments were conducted on different days. Therefore, we cannot completely exclude the possibility that day‐to‐day variability or other uncontrolled factors (including sleep, vigilance, fatigue, and repeated exposure to the oddball task) may have contributed to the observed neurophysiological changes. Additionally, the patient received multiple psychotropic medications, including several benzodiazepine‐type agents (Supplement ). Benzodiazepine administration has been associated with increased EEG beta power and a reduced P300 amplitude. Although the regimen remained unchanged between Pre‐INT and Post‐INT, unchanged doses do not establish equivalent drug effects at both recordings. Therefore, medication‐related effects cannot be excluded, and their contribution to the observed pre–post differences remains unclear. Since it was not possible to retrieve behavioral response data during the P300 task, including the accuracy of button‐press responses to target stimuli, we were unable to investigate whether pre–post differences in task performance contributed to the observed P300 amplitude difference. Although the retained target‐epoch counts were similar (41 and 39), possible contributions from trial‐count differences or residual noise cannot be excluded. Detailed neuropsychological testing was also not available. Moreover, sLORETA provides an indirect low‐resolution estimate of cortical source activity.

This case illustrates neurophysiological changes before and after intensive Naikan therapy in a patient with recurrent depressive episodes later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder. Reduced beta‐band GFP and an increased P300 amplitude occurred alongside improvements in anxiety and interpersonal‐cognitive measures. These uncontrolled observations across multiple measures are descriptive and hypothesis‐generating, do not establish treatment efficacy, causality, or a treatment mechanism, and require replication.

Atsushi Furuichi treated the patient and drafted the manuscript. Yuko Higuchi conducted EEG recordings and analyzed EEG data, drafted the neurophysiological methods section, and critically reviewed and commented on the manuscript. Naohito Kaneko contributed to the analysis of EEG data. Tsutomu Takahashi critically reviewed and commented on the manuscript. All authors read and approved the final manuscript.

The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

Ethical review and approval were not required for this case report according to institutional policy.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this case report, including the clinical course, interventions, examinations, and accompanying clinical, psychological, neurophysiological, and medication data.
