psychology.title: Associated Factors for Long-Term Sick Leave or Reduced Work Capacity Due to Musculoskeletal Disorders Among Nursing Staff: An Exploratory Study
psychology.abstract:
What are the main findings?
•Over one-third of respondents are at high risk for Work Instability and therefore at an increased risk of long-term sick leave or reduced work capacity due to musculoskeletal disorders.•Older age of the nurses, shift work, lack of assistive equipment and moderate-to-poor ergonomic practices were identified as influencing factors.

What are the implications of the main findings?
•Having sufficient assistive devices and following good ergonomic practices can reduce the physical strain on nurses.•A combination of environmental and behavioral prevention measures is necessary to support nurses’ long-term health and work ability.
Background/Objectives: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are often the cause of long-term sick leave (LTSL) or reduced work capacity (RWC) among nurses. We therefore investigated the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs among nurses, as well as possible ergonomics-related influencing factors. Methods: The cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 using an online questionnaire. The study population consisted of nursing staff insured with the German Institution for Statutory Accident Insurance and Prevention in the Health and Welfare Services (BGW). The risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs was assessed using the German version of the Nurse—Work Instability Scale (Nurse-WIS). In addition, data relating to sociodemographic factors, health behaviour and workplace ergonomics were collected. The exploratory statistical analysis was descriptive, bivariate and multivariate. Results: A total of 501 nurses took part in the survey (mean age 45.5 ± 13.4 years; 86.2% female). A total of 36% of participants were identified as being at high risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. The following associated factors were identified for individuals at high risk: age group 50 to 59 (OR 2.8; p = 0.001), shift work (OR 1.6; p = 0.026), insufficient availability of ergonomic aids (OR 1.8; p = 0.004) and a subjective assessment of ergonomic working practices as moderate (OR 2.3; p < 0.001) or poor (OR 2.5; p = 0.033). Conclusions: The proportion of individuals at increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs was high in the study sample. To protect nursing staff at an early stage, healthcare facilities should ensure the availability of sufficient ergonomic aids and provide regular ergonomic training for staff.
psychology.text:
Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are one of the most common health problems in Europe, affecting millions of people in the workforce. Approximately 25% of European workers suffer from back pain and 23% from muscle pain []. Compared to other occupational groups, workers in the healthcare professions are particularly prone to MSDs [], with nursing staff facing a substantial risk []. The causes of MSDs include heavy lifting, performing repetitive tasks, maintaining poor postures for extended periods, and working despite fatigue or pre-existing injuries [,]. Additional risk factors include psychosocial stress and effort-reward imbalances []. This leads to reduced work ability among nursing staff, which continues to deteriorate with age []. The consequences include impaired health and quality of life for those affected, as well as a decline in the quality of care for patients [].

Ergonomics focuses on how tasks can be adapted to a person’s physical and mental resources without limiting their performance or well-being []. Teaching ergonomic principles is an integral part of nursing education programs to prevent the development of MSDs []. However, a recent review shows that the effectiveness of curricular interventions on ergonomics in nursing education is low []. In daily practice, there are difficulties in applying ergonomic knowledge to the daily work of nursing staff []. The failure to apply ergonomic principles leads to physical complaints, reduced job satisfaction, and absenteeism among nurses. This results in increased strain on nursing staff due to overtime, further staffing shortages, and unnecessary costs for the healthcare system []. These MSD-related periods of incapacity for work, reduction in working hours, and workforce withdrawal place an additional burden on a healthcare system that is already suffering from a shortage of healthcare workers [].

Incapacity for work is often preceded by a phase of work instability (WI). WI means that, in the period leading up to the actual incapacity for work, those affected are already experiencing increasing difficulty in coping with the demands of their daily work []. It has been shown that interventions implemented during the WI phase can prevent the loss of work capacity. Therefore, early identification of affected individuals is important [,,].

The Nurse—Work Instability Scale (Nurse-WIS) is a profession-specific instrument that appears capable of identifying nurses at risk for WI and therefore at increased risk for long-term sick leave (LTSL) or reduced work capacity (RWC) due to MSDs []. The predictive ability of the German version of the Nurse-WIS with regard to LTSL or RWC due to MSDs has so far been examined in two German longitudinal studies. These studies revealed moderate levels of specificity (76.7 and 63.4, respectively) and sensitivity (73.9 and 64.1, respectively) [,]. Given the predictive power of the Nurse-WIS, this questionnaire can be used in companies as a screening tool to identify employees at risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. It has been found that the risk of premature retirement increases with a history of previous periods of long-term sick leave []. The Nurse-WIS appears to be suitable for identifying individuals at risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs at an early stage and for initiating timely interventions. This could potentially prevent sick leave and early retirement, which would benefit not only those affected, but also patients and the entire healthcare system. Risk factors for MSD-related incapacity for work among nursing staff have been studied repeatedly [,,,]. However, job-related risk factors, especially ergonomics-related factors, for the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs among nursing staff have not yet been investigated.

Therefore, this exploratory study aims to answer the following questions:What percentage of nursing staff are at increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs?Which ergonomics-related factors are associated with an increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs?

What percentage of nursing staff are at increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs?

Which ergonomics-related factors are associated with an increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs?

The study was conducted as a cross-sectional survey using an online questionnaire developed specifically for this research. The data collection period was from May to September 2025.

The target group for the survey consisted of nursing staff and nursing trainees working in hospital and outpatient care settings. From a total of 21,000 insurance claims related to uncomplicated commuting accidents reported to the German Institution for Statutory Accident Insurance and Prevention in the Health and Welfare Services (BGW) in 2023 and 2024, 4000 nursing professionals were randomly selected and invited to participate in the online survey (a random sample of approximately 20%). Uncomplicated commuting accidents that are not subject to mandatory reporting occur predominantly by chance and are unlikely to be associated with musculoskeletal disorders before or after the accident. These insurance claims are therefore likely representative of the total number of nursing staff insured by the BGW. A commuting accident is not considered reportable if it results in no sick leave or sick leave not exceeding 3 days. Statutory accident insurers in Germany are only aware of their insured individuals once they report a work-related or commuting accident, or a suspected occupational disease. Therefore, it was not possible to randomly select the study population from the total group of all nursing staff insured by the BGW.

Insured individuals who met the inclusion criteria were invited by letter by the BGW’s liaison office to participate in the study. After excluding 643 individuals due to incorrect addresses, employment in occupational groups outside the target population, or having reached retirement age, a total sample of 3357 (83.9%) individuals remained. In the invitation letter, the recipients received the following information about the study: the purpose and procedure of the survey, the voluntary nature of participation, information on data protection, and the anonymous handling of their data without disclosure to third parties. Approval for the study was granted by the “Local Psychological Ethics Committee at the Center for Psychosocial Medicine” (LPEK) of the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf (UKE) (LPEK-0903).

To participate in the study, potential participants accessed the study website hosted on the UKE’s servers using an individual study ID via a QR code or link provided in the invitation letter. Before the survey began, participants actively gave their consent to participate based on the participation information and privacy policy. This consent could be withdrawn at any time during the survey without providing a reason. At the UKE, data collection and analysis were conducted in a pseudonymized manner, preventing the study ID from being linked to the BGW’s personal data by the participants. After four weeks, the BGW’s data protection office used the individual study IDs to identify individuals who had not yet participated in the survey at that time. The BGW’s data protection office sent these individuals a reminder letter inviting them to participate in the study.

Sociodemographic, health-related, occupational, and ergonomics-related data were collected. To assess the participants’ educational qualifications, they were asked about their high school diploma and professional qualifications.

Data on the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs were collected using the validated German version of the Nurse-WIS []. The questionnaire contains 30 statements that respondents are asked to rate as “Agree” or “Disagree.” A total score (0–30) is calculated from the responses, which is then classified into one of three risk categories: low (<10 points), moderate (10–19 points), or high (≥20 points). Individuals with a score of 20 or higher on the Nurse-WIS are at risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. The Nurse-WIS has proven to be a reliable prognostic tool for predicting the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs [].

We developed new questions regarding ergonomic knowledge specifically for this survey. To this end, five multiple-choice questions on various aspects of ergonomics were asked (). A total score was derived from the correct answers (0 = no knowledge, up to 10 = extensive knowledge). The score was dichotomized based on the median (scores below 8 points: low to medium knowledge; scores of 8 points or higher: high knowledge). To conduct a pretest regarding the difficulty level and comprehensibility of the questions, a member of the nursing team distributed the questionnaire to 20 licensed healthcare and nursing professionals at a university hospital. Using questions developed specifically for the survey, data were collected on participation in ergonomic training courses over the previous two years, the availability of ergonomic aids in the facilities, and their use by the participants. Participants’ subjective assessment of their own ergonomic work practices was also measured using a question developed specifically for the study: “Overall, how would you rate your own ergonomic work practices?” Participants rated their own ergonomic work practices on a six-point scale ranging from 1 (very good) to 6 (unsatisfactory). The newly developed questions have not undergone prior validation.

The outcome measure was the proportion of nurses who, according to the Nurse-WIS, were at high risk for LTSL due to MSDs. Independent variables included sociodemographic, health-related, occupational, and ergonomics-related data.

Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and proportions; continuous variables were presented as means with standard deviations. For further statistical tests, the variables “occupational group” and “setting” were combined. To investigate associations between dependent and independent variables, odds ratios (OR) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) were first calculated using univariate logistic regression analyses. From the univariate analyses, all variables with a p-value <0.25 were included in the baseline model for the multivariate logistic regression analysis []. Using the backward selection method, the multivariate models were then reduced to significant predictors []. The remaining covariates were checked for interaction and multicollinearity and, where confirmed, only one of the affected variables was included.

To investigate possible nonresponse bias, an analysis of nonrespondents was conducted using the random sample. The influence of age, gender, occupation, and setting on the response rate was examined. Data from the routine dataset were used for the nonresponder analysis. Significance tests (chi-square tests) were used to examine systematic differences. Data collection was conducted using the Unipark online platform, and subsequent data analysis was performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), Version 29 (IBM). The significance level was set at p < 0.05.

The response rate relative to the number of people originally contacted was 15.6%. Of the 523 data sets originally included, all cases with missing values for the following variables were excluded prior to analysis: age, gender, Nurse-WIS, assistive technology use, and subjective assessment of one’s own ergonomic work practices. After cleaning the data, 501 data sets were included in the analysis.

86.2% of the participants were female, and their mean age was 45.5 (SD: 13.4) years (). The average weekly working hours were 34.7 (SD: 9.9) hours, and the respondents had been employed in nursing for an average of 20.8 (SD: 13.4) years. Certified health and nursing professionals accounted for the majority of respondents at 59.8%, while 9.5% were certified geriatric care workers and 18.6% of the participants reported having a qualification as a nursing assistant. 52.9% reported having a secondary school diploma as their highest level of education. Slightly more than half of the participants (57.6%) worked in a hospital, 64% worked shifts, and 19.5% held a management position. Nearly half of the respondents (48.5%) were employed full-time. Just over 60% of the participants reported engaging in physical activity for less than two hours per week, and 25.4% were smokers. 34.5% were of normal weight, 1.2% were underweight, and a total of 61.2% fell into the overweight and obese Body Mass Index (BMI) categories. Two-thirds of the respondents had attended an ergonomic training course within the past two years. More than half of the respondents (56.5%) consider the supply of ergonomic aids at their respective facilities to be insufficient. When asked about their own use of available aids, 73.2% reported frequent use, 21.9% moderate use, and 5.0% rare or no use of these aids. The majority of respondents (67.1%) possessed a high level of ergonomic knowledge. Slightly less than half of the participants rated their own ergonomic work practices as good (47.7%) or moderate (46.9%). Only 5.4% of respondents rated their own ergonomic work practices as poor.

According to the Nurse-WIS, 22.8% of the overall group had a low risk, 41.7% had a moderate risk, and 35.5% of respondents had a high risk of MSD-related LTSL or RWC. No statistically significant differences were observed between women and men (p = 0.430) ().

In the bivariate analysis, the availability of ergonomic aids in the facilities and the subjective assessment of one’s own ergonomic work practices were found to have a statistically significant influence on classification into the highest risk category ().

Individuals who rated the assistive equipment resources at their current facility as insufficient had an increased OR of 1.9 (95% CI = 1.34–2.88) compared to individuals from facilities with sufficient resources. Increased ORs were also observed for nursing staff who rated their own ergonomic work practices as moderate or poor (OR 2.1; 95% CI = 1.43–3.10 and OR 3.0; 95% CI = 1.34–6.75, respectively). Women (OR 1.4; 95% CI = 0.81–2.46), individuals working shifts (OR 1.5; 95% CI = 0.99–2.16), smokers (OR 1.5; 95% CI = 0.98–2.24), and participants who engaged in physical activity for less than two hours per week (OR 1.4; 95% CI = 0.95–2.24) also had increased ORs compared to the respective reference group. The age of the respondents also influenced their classification into the highest-risk category of the Nurse-WIS. Here, nurses between 50 and 59 years showed the highest increase in risk, with an OR of 1.8 (95% CI = 1.00–3.14). However, the associations between the last five factors and the outcome were not statistically significant.

In the multivariate model, shift work, the availability of assistive devices at the workplace, the subjective assessment of one’s own ergonomic work practices, and age also had a statistically significant influence on the probability of a high risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs ().

Compared to individuals who rated their own ergonomic work practices as good, those who rated their own work practices as moderate or poor had elevated ORs (OR 2.3; 95% CI = 1.51–3.45; p < 0.001 and OR 2.5; 95% CI = 1.08–5.79; p = 0.033). Individuals working in facilities without adequate assistive devices had an OR of 1.8 (1.21–2.74; p < 0.001) compared to the reference group. The probability of falling into the high-risk category was also elevated for nursing staff working shifts compared to those who did not work shifts (OR 1.6; 95% CI = 1.06–2.44; p = 0.026). Age also represented a statistically significant associated factor: For individuals in the 50–59 age group, an OR of 2.8 (95% CI = 1.50–5.13; p = 0.001) was observed compared to the reference group.

The results of the non-responder analysis are presented in . Statistically significant differences in response rates were observed with respect to gender, age, occupational group, and setting. Men participated in the survey less frequently than women (10.1% versus 14.4%, p = 0.002). The lowest response rate was among insured individuals under 30 years of age (7.8%). Certified nursing staff participated more frequently than nursing assistants (14.6% versus 8.6%, p < 0.001). Hospital employees participated more frequently than those working in outpatient settings (15.6% versus 11.8%, p < 0.001).

The risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs, as well as associated factors, was analyzed in a sample of 501 nursing staff from outpatient and inpatient settings. In our study, 35.5% of respondents showed a high risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs according to the Nurse-WIS. No statistically significant differences were found between women and men. Shift workers, facilities with inadequate ergonomic equipment, individuals with moderate-to-poor ergonomic work practices, and older employees were identified as risk groups for LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. Contrary to expectations, the level of knowledge regarding ergonomic work practices had no significant influence on the outcome.

Our data confirm the findings of an earlier study from Germany, in which the proportion of nursing staff at increased risk for LTSL or RWC due to MSDs was 39.4%—only slightly higher than the 35.5% found in the current study []. In a study from Brazil, the proportion of respondents at high risk according to the Nurse-WIS was 30.6%, which is lower than in our study. It should be noted, however, that the Brazilian-Portuguese version of the Nurse-WIS has fewer items, so the comparability of the results is limited []. Compared to the results of Harling et al., our findings are significantly higher than the 23.7% [] and 23.3% [] observed in the high-risk group. In contrast to the present study, these two studies surveyed exclusively employees in long-term care for the elderly, which could explain the difference in the results. In our study, no statistically significant differences were observed between women and men. Thus, our results confirm those of an earlier study [].

To date, the literature has not examined factors associated with the Nurse-WIS. For this reason, the following comparisons cite studies that have examined factors associated with absence from work due to MSDs or illness. Our survey showed that the likelihood of a high risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs increases with age. Our study thus confirms the findings of two recent reviews that identified age as a significant risk factor for absence from work due to illness [,]. One reason for this is the increased prevalence of chronic conditions such as MSDs with advancing age [,]. This increased susceptibility can be explained by the loss of physical strength and reaction time that accompanies aging. This can lead to limitations in daily work life, such that affected individuals can no longer meet the demands of their jobs and their work ability declines []. Another factor that increases the risk of absence from work due to MSDs among older workers is psychosocial demands in the workplace as well as work-time-related exposures []. This increased vulnerability to chronic diseases is even more pronounced in physically demanding occupations among older workers. Heavy lifting (loads of 15 kg or more), pulling or pushing heavy loads, repetitive movements, and working with the upper body twisted or bent forward have an even greater impact on the risk of long-term sick leave among older workers compared to their younger colleagues [,]. This effect can also be observed in physically demanding care professions, where MSDs are common across all age groups. Garzaro et al. [] found a particularly marked increase in the prevalence of MSDs and, consequently, a decline in work ability among those aged 46 to 55 as well as among employees aged 56 and older. These findings were confirmed by our study, in which the group of respondents aged 50 to 59 showed the highest risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. However, the results of our study show a decrease in the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs in the age group ≥60 years, which contradicts the findings of the study by Garzaro et al. []. One possible explanation for the reduced OR in this age group is the healthy worker effect.

Our study identified shift workers as another group at increased risk for LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. Our findings thus confirm the results of earlier studies [,]. Previous publications have shown that this effect is further amplified with increasing age [,,]. In a prospective panel study from Germany, it was also observed that the introduction of flexible work schedules among employees aged 50 to 65 led to a reduction in the risk of absenteeism []. In contrast, in their study of male shift workers aged 50 to 59, Afsa & Giford found no significant increase in the risk of sick leave compared to individuals with fixed working hours []. In our sample, the vast majority of participants were female, which could explain the difference from the results of that study.

In our sample, there was a statistically significant association between moderate or poor ergonomic work practices, as well as a lack of assistive equipment, and an increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs according to the Nurse-WIS. However, no statistically significant association was found between an increased risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs and the level of ergonomic knowledge. These results suggest that it is not ergonomic knowledge alone, but rather the implementation of this knowledge by nursing staff in their daily work and the existing working conditions that can lead to a reduction in the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. Thus, our findings are consistent with other publications on this topic. Two recent reviews have shown that the consistent use of ergonomic techniques in patient care reduces the physical strain on nursing staff. This leads to a reduction in the risk of MSDs and, consequently, to a reduction in the risk of absence from work due to MSDs [,]. A precondition for ergonomic behavior in the workplace is the sufficient availability of ergonomic aids for transferring and mobilizing patients. In a review of biomechanical studies, manual patient transfers in particular were identified as a risk factor for pain in the lumbar spine, shoulders, and knees. The authors’ recommendations included not only “no-lift” strategies but also the use of assistive devices []. Wiggermann et al. [] observed that ergonomic practices in patient care are more likely to occur when sufficient assistive devices are available, when nurses are involved in planning the procurement of these devices, and when they are encouraged by their supervisors to use them. Furthermore, it was found that an adequate supply of assistive devices led to fewer nursing staff considering a job change. In their five-year follow-up study, Owen et al. [] observed a significant decrease in MSDs, back injuries, and absence from work due to MSDs following the implementation of an ergonomic program that included assistive devices, compared to a control group. In particular, the use of ceiling and floor lifts during patient transfers had a particularly strong impact on reducing MSDs, injuries, and absenteeism [,,]. Risor et al. [], on the other hand, found no significant reduction in MSDs or absence from work due to MSDs following the acquisition of assistive devices, even though participants in the intervention group reported using the devices daily in patient care. The authors speculated that the 12-month observation period may have been too short and that positive effects on health status and workplace absenteeism might only become apparent after several years. The lack of evidence in our study for a statistically significant influence of ergonomic knowledge on the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs following the Nurse-WIS confirms earlier findings that knowledge does not automatically lead to a change in behavior []. Several studies have observed that the regular knowledge transfer about ergonomic work practices through training sessions is not sufficient to ensure that ergonomic work practices are consistently implemented in everyday work. A combination of regular training sessions, positive changes in the working environment, and organizational support yielded the best results [,,,].

To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to focus on identifying risk groups for LTSL or RWC due to MSDs in the nursing profession. The early identification of individuals at risk allows for timely preventive and rehabilitative measures, which could help ensure that those affected remain healthy and continue working in the nursing profession for longer. However, several limitations should be taken into account when interpreting the results. Our study is a cross-sectional survey; therefore, no conclusions regarding causal relationships can be drawn. Furthermore, the results are based on subjective reports from participants, which were provided retrospectively over a 12-month period. This may lead to recall bias among the respondents. Although participants were selected at random, given the response rate of 15.6%, selection bias cannot be ruled out. This could be attributed to the fact that individuals affected by MSDs are more likely to participate in a survey on this topic than those not affected. The non-responder analysis revealed significant differences between responders and non-responders in terms of age, gender, occupation and setting. As these characteristics may be potentially associated with the occurrence of MSDs and the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs, it cannot be ruled out that the composition of the study population may have influenced the observed risk estimate. Certain groups may have been over- or underrepresented in the sample studied, meaning that the estimated risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs may not fully correspond to the risk of the underlying population. The results should therefore be interpreted with caution, particularly with regard to their generalizability. The lack of an effect of ergonomic knowledge could be due to the lack of variance in the responses. Since a large proportion of the respondents possessed extensive knowledge in the field of ergonomics, the values show a low degree of variation. This makes it statistically much more difficult to demonstrate significant correlations. It remains unclear to what extent this ceiling effect is attributable to the operationalization of ergonomic knowledge or to the sample’s high level of knowledge. Since the instrument is an objective knowledge test rather than a subjective assessment of ergonomic knowledge using a response scale, a ceiling effect would, to a certain extent, be inevitable if the sample possessed a high level of ergonomic knowledge. However, it is also possible that our instrument did not fully capture the sample’s total ergonomic knowledge. Furthermore, the questions relating to ergonomic knowledge and the use of ergonomic techniques in everyday practice were developed by the research team and had not undergone any prior validation. Additionally, the exclusively subjective assessment of one’s own working practices must be taken into account as a further potential cause of measurement bias. Due to a desire to conform to social norms, participants might rate their own working practices more highly than they actually are, in order to avoid any potential negative consequences of their statements. The results should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Future studies should focus on geriatric care, as very few caregivers from this field participated in our survey. Furthermore, future studies should include more men, young employees, and nursing assistants in order to extend the findings to the groups that were underrepresented in our study.

In addition, future research should address not only declarative knowledge regarding ergonomic issues but also questions concerning practical competencies, the quality and frequency of the application of ergonomic techniques, and the actual workload faced by nursing staff in their daily work. Another important issue is how to address the identified risk groups within organizations in order to prevent impending LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. We are currently unaware of any publications regarding a selection of specific preventive measures that have been recommended or evaluated for such identified risk groups. Future research should address this issue.

Overall, the results of this study show that just over one-third of the respondents are at high risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs according to the Nurse-WIS. The following factors were identified as associated factors: the age of the nursing staff, shift work, a lack of assistive equipment in the facilities, and a moderate-to-poor assessment of their own ergonomic work practices. In contrast, the level of knowledge regarding ergonomic behavior in everyday nursing practice had no statistically significant association with the outcome. These results suggest that it is not ergonomic knowledge alone, but rather the application of this knowledge in everyday nursing practice and under the prevailing working conditions in the facilities that appears to be relevant for reducing the risk of LTSL or RWC due to MSDs. Ergonomic work practices reduce the physical strain on nursing staff, which could lead to a reduction in MSDs and their negative consequences for those affected, patients, and the healthcare system. A combination of behavioral and situational prevention measures is recommended, which should address both organizational and individual factors in order to support nurses’ long-term health and work ability. Furthermore, as the study design does not allow any conclusions regarding a causal relationship, future studies should be conducted using a longitudinal design.

psychology.title: What Are the Most Central Parenting Behaviors in Interactions With Infants? A Network Analysis of the Coding Interactive Behavior Instrument
psychology.abstract: Parenting has repeatedly been shown to have an important role in child development, and valid instruments assessing parent‐child interaction quality are thus crucial for our understanding of parenting in child development. Network psychometrics is a novel approach to measurement validation in giving a more dynamic exploration of relations among relatively stable dispositions. The Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) instrument is a global rating system of parent‐child interaction quality, consisting of items averaged onto parenting composites. Studies have shown that these composites can be validated but are also liable to change due to contextual factors, making comparison across studies and contexts difficult. We investigate network analysis as an alternative to using these composites to understand parenting. The sample was 304 mother‐infant and 303 father‐infant dyads in a free‐play interaction coded with the CIB. The results showed similar network structures for both mothers and fathers, yielding closely linked clusters of items for sensitivity, affect, and intrusiveness. Configural and partial metric invariance was established between the two networks. We also found the item Acknowledging to be the most central parenting behavior in the networks. Our results illustrate how a network analysis provides important information on multidimensional constructs and informs our understanding of the central and core elements of parenting of infants.
psychology.text:
Parenting in infancy (birth‐12 months) may be considered the most intense caregiving stage but also the most influential stage for children's further cognitive and socioemotional development (e.g., Ainsworth et al. ; Bornstein ; Leerkes et al. ; Madigan et al. ). In particular, the quality of parent‐infant interactions and especially parental sensitivity (i.e., the parent's ability to notice, interpret, and act promptly and appropriately to the child's signals; Ainsworth et al. ) have consistently been demonstrated to be important for infant development (e.g., Cooke et al. ; Madigan et al. ). Consequently, valid instruments for the assessment of parenting behaviors and parent‐child interaction quality are imperative not only for understanding the role of parenting in infant development but also for identifying families in need of support and for monitoring changes following interventions aimed at promoting sensitive parenting.

Although observational measures are typically considered the “gold standard” for assessing interaction quality, systematic reviews have found that many of the existing observational instruments lack an empirical investigation of construct validity, for example, in the form of factor analyses to investigate an instrument's internal structure (Gridley et al. ; Lotzin et al. ). Construct validity is generally defined as the extent to which an instrument's items reflect the latent construct they are intended to measure (cf. Borsboom et al. ). Network psychometrics is a relatively new direction of test theory to investigate construct validity, focusing on how an instrument's items interconnect and ‐act to make up a construct (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ). One of the benefits of network psychometrics is also in its estimation of an item's centrality, that is, how central/influential an item is to the construct in question (Burger et al. ). The present study aims to examine the construct validity and core parenting behaviors of the widely used observational instrument Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB; Feldman ) in mother‐infant and father‐infant dyads using network psychometrics.

The CIB has been used for assessing caregiver‐child interaction quality in a wide array of contexts—for example, premature children (Feldman et al. ), mothers with depression (Feldman et al. ), children at socio‐emotional risk (Dollberg et al. )—and across different cultures (e.g., Europe, North America, South America; Feldman ). The CIB has been developed to code interactions in different ages (0–18 years) with a varying number of items depending on the age of the child. Studies using the CIB analyze the interaction quality on either item‐level (e.g., Cordes et al. ; Egmose et al. ; Steele et al. ) or composite‐level by taking the mean scores of selected items (e.g., Egmose et al. ; Feldman et al. ; van Huisstede et al. ). These composites are named based on theory and research in early social development, for example, a composite consisting of items relating to the parent's supportive presence and ability to acknowledge the child's signals is named parental sensitivity.

Despite the widespread use of the CIB, systematic reviews have identified few‐to‐no studies empirically investigating its construct validity using factor analyses (Lotzin et al. ). The lack of construct validity is also evident in its use. In her manual from , Feldman proposed six factors, with two focusing on parental behaviors (sensitivity and intrusiveness; see Supporting Information ). She was able to confirm this factor structure in a sample of 483 caregiver‐child dyads with the age range of the children remaining unclear (cited in Feldman ). However, some studies estimate parental factors other than the ones proposed by Feldman (), such as a parental Social Withdrawal construct (Feldman et al. ; Stuart et al. ). Further, when the same constructs are used, studies vary with respect to which items they include in the constructs. For example, some studies include the parental item Affectionate Touch in the sensitivity composite (Dollberg et al. ; Dollberg et al. ; Feldman et al. ; van Huisstede et al. ) whereas others do not (Cordes et al. ; Egmose et al. ; Feldman et al. ; Thompson‐Booth et al. ). From a theoretical perspective, Mesman and Emmen () have questioned the sensitivity construct used in the CIB system, since this construct includes items such as parental Positive Affect and Affectionate Touch, which are not comparable to Ainsworth et al. ’s () original definition of sensitivity. Instead, they argue that parental sensitivity and parental affect and warmth are related yet distinct dimensions of parenting behavior.

Since the publication of the previously mentioned reviews (Gridley et al. ; Lotzin et al. ), more studies have examined the construct validity of the CIB using confirmatory factor analysis. To the best of our knowledge, we are the only researchers who have examined the factor structure in dyads with infants. However, we were not able to confirm Feldman's factor model in a Danish sample of 419 mothers interacting with their 3‐months‐old infants in a free‐play situation, with the mothers either having a depression diagnosis (n = 236) or being at‐risk of depression (n = 183) (Stuart et al. ). Instead, we found support for a four‐factor model, with three parental factors. The first one was maternal sensitivity, which incorporated Feldman's () sensitivity and intrusiveness composites as well as other items. Further, we found two unique factors to the study, maternal social withdrawal and maternal controlling behavior. We then tried to replicate this factor structure with the fathers in their interactions with the infants (Stuart et al. ). However, this four‐factor model we found for mothers did not fit the father‐infant dyads. Instead, we found some support for a three‐factor model consisting of two parental factors paternal sensitivity and paternal positive affect. There were many similarities, but the different factor structures made it impossible for us to establish measurement invariance of the CIB between mothers and fathers. Evidence from studies involving older children similarly suggests that the CIB factor structure is not stable across developmental stages or interaction context. For example, Dutch studies of 18‐month‐old toddlers found different factor structures depending on whether interactions occurred during structured tasks (i.e., book reading and puzzle solving) or during free play (Krijnen et al. , ). Likewise, studies involving older children have generally failed to replicate Feldman's original factor structure or have identified similar factors with differing item loadings (Fahrer et al. ; Steenhoff et al. ). Together, these findings suggest that the organization of CIB behaviors may vary according to developmental stage, cultural context, and interaction context, consistent with theories of domain‐specific socialization proposing that important parenting behaviors may manifest differently across interactional domains (Grusec and Davidov ).

Based on these results, it seems as if the factor structure and the loading items are highly dependent on contextual factors, as we found different factor structures for mothers and fathers, and Krijnen et al. (),  ( found different results depending on the interaction context. Feldman () has also noted that other factors such as culture and child age can influence the CIB factor structure. This dependency, however, makes comparisons between studies challenging, as maternal sensitivity scores will always be calculated using different items depending on the sample. To overcome this, Feldman () suggests that core items exist, meaning that these items are essential across contexts. For example, the item Acknowledging must be a part of a sensitivity composite, and the item Overriding must be a part of an intrusiveness composite (intrusiveness refers to various interfering parenting behaviors where the child's signals are not adequately met but often overruled and can be seen as an opposite to sensitive caregiving; Hallers‐Haalboom et al. ; Wood ). However, this may prove challenging when both Acknowledging and Overriding load on the same composite, as is the case in the Stuart et al. () model. These core items are theory‐based and to the best of our knowledge, they have not yet been empirically supported. Thus, an empirical investigation of how the items interdepend on each other and whether it is possible to identify core items for measuring parent‐child interaction quality is needed.

Network psychometrics, also known as network analysis, is a combination of systems thinking and psychometrics to investigate constructs as a set of components and the relationship among those (Isvoranu et al. ). Compared to classical and modern test theory where items are theorized to be determined by a common latent construct, network psychometrics models each item in a mutually reinforcing network, thus offering a new conceptualization of why psychometric variables cluster together (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ). Within classical and modern test theory, it is assumed that the latent construct causes the item response, making the construct impossible to observe and test directly, whereas network psychometrics assume the item responses to cause the latent construct (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ). Using this approach, in the current study, we investigate how the components (different parenting behaviors) in a construct (parent‐infant interaction quality) are mutually connected rather than measure the construct as its own singular entity. The outcome of a network psychometrics analysis is thus a graph of how the items are connected. Figure  is a simplistic graph of how a network of some of the CIB items could be. In network analyses, the variables/items are also called nodes, and the connections (i.e., lines) are called edges. Some items have more edges: They are more densely connected, meaning that they are a central/core item. If one intervenes on that item, the majority of other items will also be affected due to the core item's many connections (Burger et al. ). In Figure , Acknowledging would be considered a central item, as it has four connections, while Depressed Mood only has one and would thus be considered less central. Further, in Figure  not all items are connected, meaning that they cannot all assess the same construct: Network psychometrics is thus also an approach to psychometrically validate an instrument and an indication of latent constructs that are determined by the interconnectedness of items (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ).

To our knowledge, no previous studies have investigated the construct validity of the construct parent‐child interaction quality as measured with the CIB using network estimations. As reviewed, the factor analyses of the CIB have yielded a different number of composites from study to study, and while differences exist of the items loading on the composites, there are also many similarities. For example, Acknowledging does seem to always be part of a sensitivity composite, as is in line with Feldman's () theory of core items. What seems to be the crucial challenge to the contextual stability of the CIB is the number of latent constructs, that is, the composites found in factor analyses. With network psychometrics, we move away from the latent construct focus that has been a staple of classical and modern test theory (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ; Isvoranu et al. ): As we are not able to directly measure/observe the latent construct—which is why we rely on multiple items to make up the construct—it may be more informative to focus only on how the observable items interrelate into clusters that are perhaps indicative of latent constructs. Our hope is that a network psychometrics analysis of the CIB can yield an understanding of important parenting behaviors during free‐play with their infants.

The present study thus investigates the network model of mother‐infant and father‐infant dyads using the CIB to measure interaction quality in an at‐risk sample of maternal postpartum depression and/or infant social withdrawal. The objective is to identify what parenting behaviors are most important for the interaction quality. Therefore, we focus only on the 18 items relating to the parent's behavior to identify core parenting items (Supporting Information ). In our previous factor analyses of the CIB, we were not able to compare the structures for mothers and fathers (Stuart et al. , ). As mentioned, the theory behind classical test theory and network psychometrics differs in their view of how items relate to each other. Thus, we want to investigate if core parenting behaviors do emerge independently of the context, which in the present study is parental gender. Thus, we will compare the network structures and the core items across mothers and fathers. Specifically, we investigate whether the two networks are measurement invariant by investigating for configural (i.e., do the items cluster together similarly in the two networks) and metric (i.e., are the strength of the item connections similarly both within and between the clusters) invariance.

The study is part of a larger project, The Copenhagen Infant Mental Health Project (CIMHP; Væver et al. ). In total, 607 families consented to participate. If both mother and father consented, we randomly selected the sex for the present study to ensure no dependency between the mothers and fathers. The sample size for this study was 304 mother‐infant dyads, and 303 father‐infant dyads. The majority of the mother‐infant dyads (65.5%) and father‐infant dyads (87.6%) were also included in the previous confirmatory factor analyses studies that validated the CIB (Stuart et al. , ). A public health visitor (employed by the municipality of Copenhagen) recruited participants during a routine visit throughout the first year postpartum. At the 2‐months postpartum visit (and possibly at later visits as well, if deemed clinically relevant), the health visitors routinely screen the mothers for depression with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS; Cox et al. ) and the infants for social withdrawal with the Alarm Distress Baby Scale (ADBB; Guedeney and Fermanian ). Families were invited to participate, if the mother scored above cut‐off, that is, 10, on the EPDS, and/or if the infant scored above cut‐off of 5 on the ADBB. The family was then offered a home visit by a clinical psychologist from the research team where written informed consent was obtained from the mothers and their partners. During the home visit, a five‐minute mother‐infant and three‐minute father‐infant interaction of free play was video recorded. The parents were instructed to play and interact with their child as they normally would. They could choose to use whatever toys they already had in the house if that was how they would usually play with their infants. The interaction orders were not counterbalanced but conducted in a manner that fitted into the family's schedule. Exclusion criteria were bipolar I disorder/psychotic disorder, severe intellectual impairment, recent suicidal ideation/attempt, present alcohol/substance abuse, and/or infant diagnosed with autism/early developmental delay. The project was approved by the local review board (Approval number: 2015‐10) and conducted in accordance with the 1975 Helsinki Declaration as revised in 2008 as well as national ethical guidelines. Table  shows the sample characteristics. While the sample was at risk of maternal postpartum depression (with 45.5% of the mothers meeting DSM‐5 criteria for depression) and/or infant social withdrawal (9.7% of the sample), it was also a very well‐resourced sample (i.e., living together, employed, high educational status). Although the sample included infants in the age range of 2–11 months, the vast majority (74.8%) were 2–3 months.

Parent‐infant interaction quality was coded using the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB; Feldman ) instrument. CIB is a global rating system for social interactions and was coded based on viewing 5 minutes of mother‐infant and 3 minutes of father‐infant free play interactions video‐recoded during the home visit. The measure consists of 33 items: 18 items that relate to the parent's behavior (e.g., “Acknowledging”), eight to the child (e.g., “Initiation”), five to the dyad (e.g., “Dyadic Reciprocity”), and two that represent the lead‐lag of the interaction, (i.e., “Child‐led” and “Parent‐led”). The items are scored from 1 (minimum level of the behavior) to 5 (maximum level of the behavior) with half‐point increases, resulting in a nine‐point scale. See Table  for short descriptions of the items included in the present study.

For the present study, six and four coders were involved in coding the mother‐infant and father‐infant videos, respectively. All coders were trained to agreement (minimum 85%) on 13 videos coded by Feldman's research team. One coder (2nd author) was considered the main coder, and she coded 20% of each individual coders' videos for reliability. The coders had no prior knowledge of the dyads. Reliability values were calculated for the entire CIMHP sample. For the mothers, 21.6% were coded with an inter‐rater agreement of 91.7%. For the fathers, 23.1% were randomly selected for reliability coding, with an inter‐rater agreement of 92.9%. Inter‐rater reliability was calculated based on an absolute agreement one‐way random effects model (Koo and Li ) and are presented in Table . For mothers, reliability was good‐to‐excellent on all items except on Elaborating, which was moderate (range of ICCs: 0.568–1). The same was the case for fathers, except it was Anxiety that showed moderate reliability (range of ICCs: 0.673–1).

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2. We used the qgraph package (Epskamp et al. ) to estimate the networks of the CIB items in mothers and fathers, separately. The bootnet package (Epskamp, Borsboom, and Fried ) was used to further investigate how stable the networks were (i.e., do they cluster together similarly and with the same number of connections) in a bootstrap procedure. Finally, to compare the two networks for mothers and fathers, we used the package NetworkComparisonTest (van Borkulo et al. ) and the EGAnet (Jamison et al. ) to establish measurement invariance.

As items are rated on an interval scale, we estimated a partial correlation network using a Spearman correlation matrix (due to the multivariate non‐normality; Isvoranu and Epskamp ), using graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (gLASSO; Friedman et al. ) regularization. After gLASSO regularization, we selected a network using Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC; Foygel and Drton ), with γ = 0.5. We visualized the network with blue edges (i.e., connections) indicating positive edge weights (i.e., associations), and red indicating negative edge weights. The bolder the edge is, the stronger its weight is. To assess the most central items in the networks, we used Strength, which is the summation of the absolute edge weights connected to a node (i.e., item), and Expected Influence, which is the summation of a node's positive edge weights without taking the absolute value. Strength, thus, functions as a proxy measure of each item's influence/importance in the network, while Expected Influence indicates which item has the greatest positive impact on the rest of the items in the network.

To estimate the stability of the connections between the items (edge weights), we used non‐parametric bootstrap estimation with resampling rows with replacement of 1000 samples. To estimate the stability of the centrality indices, we used case‐dropping subset bootstrap samples (n = 1000). We used the correlation stability (CS) coefficient to measure stability of centrality indices, with the CS threshold set at 0.7 (Epskamp, Borsboom, and Fried ). This reflects the maximum proportion of cases that can be dropped, so that in 95% of the samples, the correlation between the original calculated centrality indices and the centrality of the networks in the bootstrapped subsets is 0.7 or higher. Epskamp and colleagues (, ) recommend that the CS should be above 0.5 and not below 0.25 to be accurate in its interpretability.

Finally, we tested for configural and metric invariance in the overall connectivity between the networks of mothers and fathers, rerunning the analyses on the full sample. Configural invariance means that the same nodes have been identified in the same clusters for both groups. Metric invariance tests the equivalence of network loadings (i.e., the strengths of the items both within and between cluster community) across the two groups. The reported p‐values are two‐tailed and Bonferroni‐Holm adjusted and evaluated at a significance level of 0.05.

Before estimating the networks for mothers and fathers, we checked the stability of the items by bootstrapping the network for the entire sample. The items Affectionate Touch (P16) (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.49), Consistency of Style (P14) (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.5), and Negative Affect (P9) and Hostility (P10) (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.61) were unstable in their connections with the other items in the network across the 1000 bootstrap samples (e.g., they may have been more strongly connected to one cluster of items in some of the samples compared to others). Those items were then removed which improved the stability (CS(cor = 0.7) ≥ 0.88). The four items were thus excluded from all further analyses.

Figure  visualizes the relationships between the CIB parent items for mothers. The network consists of 14 nodes with a mean edge weight of 0.019. The network density was somewhat high with 55 out of 91 possible connections observed, that is, 60.4% of all possible connections. For fathers (Figure ), the 14 nodes had a mean edge weight of 0.028 and a slightly lower network density with 51 out of 91 possible connections observed, that is, 56.0% of all possible connections. While the network for fathers is less dense with fewer connections, the two networks are very similarly structured. As the EBICglasso algorithm is more sensitive to including false edges that are depicted as weak, we highlight some of the stronger connections that we find theoretically significant in the network. In the following, the hyphen sign: “‐” is used to represent network edges between the nodes.

Across the two networks, items theoretically indicating a sensitive parent are seen in the cluster of connections between Acknowledging (P3), Supportive Presence (P18), Appropriate Range of Affect (P13), and Resourcefulness (P15). Additionally, we also see a very strong connection between the intrusive forms of behaviors Forcing (P1)—Overriding (P2). These items are connected to the sensitivity cluster via Acknowledging (P3). Moreover, a strong connection exists between Elaborating (P5)—Imitating (P4), however, the two items are not a part of the sensitivity cluster but connected via Acknowledging (P3). There is also a cluster of affect‐related items in the strong connections between Depressed Mood (P8)—Positive Affect (P7), Positive Affect (P7)—Enthusiasm (P17), and Enthusiasm (P17)—Depressed Mood (P8). The connections between Depressed Mood (P8), Positive Affect (P7), and Enthusiasm (P17) are negative, and the link between Positive Affect (P7) and Enthusiasm (P17) is positive. This cluster is connected with the intrusiveness cluster via a negative connection between Depressed Mood (P8)—Overriding (P2). The affect cluster for both mothers and fathers is partially connected to the sensitivity cluster via a positive connection to Vocal Appropriateness (P11) and Appropriate Range of Affect (P15).

Figure  presents the centrality measures for mothers (upper) and fathers (lower). The bootstrap test showed the centrality measures to be stable for both mothers (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.75) and fathers (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.749). “Strength” indicates that the five most central items for mothers are Acknowledging (P3), Appropriate Range of Affect (P13), Enthusiasm (P17), Supportive Presence (P18), and Resourcefulness (P15). Regarding “Expected Influence”, the top five are Supportive Presence (P18), Appropriate Range of Affect (P13), Imitating (P4), Resourcefulness (P15), and Acknowledging (P3). For fathers, the top five according to “Strength” are Acknowledging (P3), Positive Affect (P7), Supportive Presence (P18), Resourcefulness (P15), and Appropriate Range of Affect (P13). The latter four were all very close in rank. For “Expected Influence” they are Supportive Presence (P18), Resourcefulness (P15), Enthusiasm (P17), Appropriate Range of Affect (P13), and Positive Affect (P7). To understand how stable the items were in their centrality, we conducted bootstrapped stability tests on the “Strength” of the parenting behaviors for mothers (Supporting Information : Figure S1) and fathers (Supporting Information : Figure S2). Stability above 0.7 was considered acceptable. For both mothers and fathers, we see that all of the identified top five most central items were very stable across the bootstrapped samples. However, the best‐performing items across samples were Acknowledging (P3), meaning that this parenting behavior was considered central across the different samples.

Finally, when comparing the two networks, the global strength test, that is, the overall level of connectivity, was not significant (p = 0.593). This indicates that there was no significant difference in how densely or strongly connected the items were in the network for mothers compared to fathers. The weighted adjacency matrices showed a rather large correlation coefficient (r = 0.85), indicating that the overall structure of the networks was very similar. Configural invariance was established, as all the items had a replication over 0.7 in their clusters across 1000 bootstrap samples (Figure ). The metric invariance test is presented in Figure . We were only able to establish partial metric invariance, as Depressed Mood (P8) failed to be invariant. All other items were invariant at the metric level. This indicates that the items are organized in the same clusters and have the same level of strengths in their connections within and between the clusters equally between mothers and fathers.

The aims of the present study were to examine the construct validity of the parenting items of the CIB in a Danish sample of mothers and fathers of infants using network psychometrics and to investigate measurement invariance between the networks for mothers and fathers. The sample was included based on screenings of maternal postpartum depression and/or infant social withdrawal, making the sample at‐risk. Previous studies have found postpartum depression to negatively affect the mother‐infant relationship quality (for a meta‐analysis, see Bernard et al. ). However, research has also found that other risk factors are necessary to observe these negative effects, meaning that postpartum depression in and of itself is not necessarily enough to have an observable impact (e.g., Crugnola et al. ; Kingston et al. ; Smith‐Nielsen et al. ). We also found that depression did not seem to significantly impact the relationship quality as measured with the CIB in the same sample as in the present study (Stuart et al. ), as well as no association between infant social withdrawal and parental sensitivity (Rudling et al. ). However, without a community control group, it remains unclear whether the identified behavioral networks generalize to community populations or reflect patterns specific to at‐risk families.

Preliminary checks indicated that most items were stable enough for network psychometrics, except for Negative Affect (P9), Hostility (P10), Consistency of Style (P14), and Affectionate Touch (P16). Both Negative Affect (P9) and Hostility (P10) had minimal variation, suggesting that these behaviors were infrequently observed. Despite most mothers being at risk for postpartum depression, the sample was well‐resourced in terms of educational attainment and relationship status, and the free‐play scenario may not have elicited enough distress to capture the range of parenting behaviors identified by the CIB (Joosen et al. ; Leerkes et al. ). Affectionate Touch (P16) was likely excluded due to weak correlations with the remaining items, possibly reflecting cultural norms in Northern Europe, where less physical closeness and touching is observed (Keller et al. ). Previous research also suggests that Affectionate Touch (P16) is unrelated to sensitivity and should not be included in the composite (Cordes et al. ; Stuart et al. ). The omission of Consistency of Style (P14) was less expected. It may be a challenge to validly assess the consistency of interaction style in 3–5 min of free play, but scores varied across participants (Table ) and it correlated with multiple CIB items (Supporting Information : Tables S3 and S4). Instead, its role as a broader descriptor of interaction quality may explain its instability. Bootstrapped networks assess whether each item maintains consistent connections and strengths. Consistency of Style (P14), which reflects the predictability and consistency of parental behavior throughout the interaction (Feldman ), may shift in relation to different behaviors across the bootstrapped samples. Cross‐validation of our networks is needed to clarify the role of these excluded items in parent‐child interaction quality.

Across both networks, item clustering was theoretically meaningful. Acknowledging (P3), Supportive Presence (P18), Resourcefulness (P15), and Appropriate Range of Affect (P13) all tap into behaviors of parents following the child's signals by adapting their own behavior (Feldman ). They thus formed a parental sensitivity cluster, aligning with Ainsworth et al.’s () original definition of sensitivity. Although affect is not part of Ainsworth's original definition (Mesman et al. ), Appropriate Range of Affect (P13) involves attuning to the child's emotional signals (Feldman ) which accords with the definition. Interestingly, Supportive Presence (P18) and Acknowledging (P3) were not as strongly connected directly for fathers as for mothers. Instead, Supportive Presence (P18) was more strongly connected with Resourcefulness (P15). Previous confirmatory factor analyses also support this sensitivity cluster (Krijnen et al. , ; Steenhoff et al. ; Stuart et al. , ).

Imitating (P4) and Elaborating (P5) formed a separate cluster, connected to the sensitivity cluster through Acknowledging (P3). However, these behaviors are not definite markers of sensitivity; their appropriateness may be context dependent–for instance, when the infant is alert and displaying signs of interest and engagement. It is also important to note that this cluster may be age‐specific, as Imitating (P4) is only coded when the infant is between 2 and 12 months. Although Feldman () included those two items in the sensitivity composites, other analyses associate them with paternal teaching behavior (Steenhoff et al. ) and maternal stimulation (Krijnen et al. , ). This network analysis suggests that sensitivity in parenting involves acknowledging the child's behavior, often through imitation and elaboration.

Another cluster tapped into the parent's affect with the items Positive Affect (P7), Enthusiasm (P17), and Depressed Mood (P8) being interlinked. For both mothers and fathers, the affect cluster was connected to the sensitivity cluster through the Vocal Appropriateness (P11) item. This connection, however, was weaker for fathers than for mothers. When coding this item, you rate both if the parent uses an appropriate tone of voice matched to the child's age, as well as the warmth in the tone (Feldman ). Vocal Appropriateness (P11) was thus not a central item in either of the clusters but could be what is termed a bridging item in network psychometrics: An item that bridges different constructs. The fact that we find affect and sensitivity to be distinct clusters align with previous research (Davidov and Grusec ; Mesman and Emmen ).

Intrusive parenting behaviors Forcing (P1) and Overriding—Intrusiveness (P2) also clustered together. Although some studies suggest Forcing (P1) is not inherently intrusive when interacting with infants, specifically (Feldman et al. ; van Huisstede et al. ), others group these behaviors (Dollberg et al. ; Feldman et al. ). In the present study, Forcing (P1) and Overriding (P2) were positively connected, indicating that physically moving/manipulating the child may increase the risk of disrupting the child's signals. Our network analysis thus supports Feldman's () proposed factor structure with an intrusiveness composite, although our cluster only contains two out of the five proposed items. Furthermore, Forcing (P1) showed very low stability across the bootstrap samples (Supporting Information : Figures S1 and S2), indicating that its position and strength in the networks is relatively uncertain. Despite our network structure aligning with previous research (Krijnen et al. , ; Mesman and Emmen ; Steenhoff et al. ; Stuart et al. , ), further validation is needed to assess their stability and generalizability.

Even though the two networks were overall similar, differences also emerged. The paternal network was less densely connected, with Depressed Mood (P8) being more strongly connected for mothers. This difference may be explained by sample characteristics and the at‐risk nature of the mothers. Another marked difference is that Acknowledging (P3) and Supportive Presence (P18) are not as strongly directly connected for fathers compared to mothers. However, both the global strength test and the weighted adjacency matrices indicated no significant structural differences. Previous research comparing mothers and fathers in their interaction with infants had mixed results, with some studies finding significant differences in sensitivity (Volling et al. ) or positive affect (van Berkel et al. ) and others finding no differences (e.g., Steenhoff et al. ). Meta‐analyses suggest no differences in mothers' and fathers' parenting behaviors (Deneault et al. ; Jiang et al. ). One explanation for these similarities may be fathers' increasing involvement in daily childcare over recent decades (Deneault et al. ). Greater time spent with children may enhance parents' ability to interpret infants' signals, leading to similar behaviors regardless of parent gender. The home setting may have also facilitated natural interactions, reducing parent gender differences (Bureau et al. ; Feldman and Bakermans‐Kranenburg ; Steenhoff et al. ). However, it remains important to explore specific parenting behaviors where mothers and fathers may diverge. Fathers tend to engage more in play than caregiving and favor physical play—especially with older children (Parke and Cookston ). It is also important to note that the observation context can play a role. A recent meta‐analysis found a significant difference in mothers' and fathers' sensitivity in play situations, although they did not find an overall effect of observation context (Deneault et al. ). Furthermore, studies found differing factor structures when the same mother‐infant dyads interacted in a free‐play versus structured setting (Krijnen et al. , ). As most children in our sample were 2–3 months old and we only examined interaction quality in a low‐stress free‐play situation, future research should investigate if our network structures can be replicated in other interactive contexts as well as with older children.

We established configural and partial metric invariance, indicating that item clustering and interconnections were similar for mothers and fathers. Although the top five central items differed for mothers and fathers, measurement invariance tests indicated that these differences were not statistically significant. Centrality plots (Figure ) further support this conclusion: Although Positive Affect (P7) only ranked in the top five for fathers, it remained influential for mothers in terms of strength. Overall, the network structures appeared similar, except for Depressed Mood (P8), where strength was not invariant. This finding may reflect the nature of our sample, with 45.5% of mothers meeting DSM‐5 criteria for depression and the remaining presenting subclinical levels of depression. Thus, Depressed Mood (P8) may differ between at‐risk mothers and fathers rather than across community samples in general. Future studies with more similar groups of parents are needed to clarify these differences in CIB parenting items.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate measurement invariance between mothers and fathers using the CIB. In our previous validation studies of the CIB using factor analysis, we did not test for measurement invariance due to differing factor structures for mothers and fathers (Stuart et al. , ). Interestingly, network analysis revealed partial invariance, suggesting that its results may be more generalizable compared to the many different factor structures found of the CIB. The clusters identified using network psychometrics align with the latent factors from factor analyses, and simulations indicate that network analysis is superior for detecting such clusters (Golino and Epskamp ). If the latent factors are more unstable compared to the network clusters, then that instability may explain why we were able to find partial invariance between mothers and fathers.

Despite the top five most central items differing between mothers and fathers, all of the items in the sensitivity cluster—Acknowledging (P3), Appropriate Range of Affect (P13), Resourcefulness (P15), and Supportive Presence (P18)—were consistently included across indices and groups. Acknowledging (P3), in particular, emerged as a core item, supported by the bootstrap stability tests (Supporting Information : Figures S1 and S2), where this item showed the highest stability across samples. Given that sensitivity is a key parenting behavior and predictor of child outcomes (e.g., Madigan et al. ; Rodrigues et al. ; Zeegers et al. ), it is not surprising that items in the sensitivity cluster were central in our study. This finding reinforced the idea that sensitive parenting is fundamental to parent‐child interaction quality. Our findings align with Feldman's () identification of Acknowledging (P3) as a core item in a sensitivity composite. Network analysis indicates that interventions aimed at improving parent‐child interaction quality should prioritize Acknowledging (P3), as changes in these items are likely to influence other parenting behaviors coded with the CIB.

We previously validated the CIB in the same sample using factor analysis, identifying four factors for mothers (maternal sensitivity, maternal social withdrawal, maternal controlling behavior, and child engagement) and three for fathers (paternal sensitivity, paternal positive affect, and child engagement) (Stuart et al. , ). Despite the similarities between the sensitivity factors and clusters–such as Acknowledging (P3) and Supportive Presence (P18) being indicators of sensitive parenting behaviors–the factor analyses also included negatively loading items like Overriding‐Intrusiveness (P2) and Anxiety (P12), which are not typically associated with sensitivity. In contrast, network analysis allows for visualizing item interdependencies while maintaining distinct, theoretically meaningful clusters. A limitation of factor analysis is in its assumption of item independence, meaning that it does not take into account how items may affect each other (Mulaik ).

The key difference between construct validation using factor and network analysis lies in causality: Factor analysis argues a latent construct causes item responses, whereas network analysis suggests item responses cause the latent construct (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ). The causal interpretation within factor analysis of the latent construct causing the observable behaviors can become vacuous if no theoretical and/or empirical investigation of the latent construct is possible; we may just overinterpret the factor model if our only evidence of a latent construct is the model fit (Christensen et al. ). With network models, the latent construct becomes transparent both theoretically and analytically from the distribution of the item clusters (Epskamp, Maris, et al. ). Moreover, network psychometrics identifies central/core items, such as Acknowledging (P3) which is a central item for both mothers and fathers. Identifying core behaviors can inform interventions by targeting those items with the greatest potential impact on the rest of the network. Researchers argue that network psychometrics provides a more dynamic approach to understanding psychological constructs (Christensen et al. ). However, future studies should replicate both our factor and network analyses to assess their strengths and applications in construct validation and intervention design.

The study has several limitations. The sample may not be generalizable, as the mothers were well‐resourced despite being at risk of postpartum depression. The network structure might differ in a less‐resourced at‐risk sample or a broader community sample. Additionally, we found only weak correlations between background factors (e.g., education, age) and CIB items, likely due to the sample's homogeneity. Feldman () also points out that the structure of the instrument is liable to change depending on the culture. We also only observed parents interacting with very young infants and in a free‐play situation, which may also limit the generalizability. Replication in other samples is necessary to assess the generalization of the results. The present study was a part of a larger project where fathers were not required for maternal participation. Another limitation is thus potential selection bias in the paternal sample. Due to practical considerations, the observation length differed between mothers (5 min) and fathers (3 min), which could have influenced the results. Although prior research suggests observation duration does not significantly impact comparing mothers' and fathers' sensitivity (Deneault et al. ) and even short interactions can be reliably coded (e.g., Beebe et al. ), future studies should standardize observation lengths to improve comparability. The small sample size may have also affected network estimation precision. Although the bootstrap tests indicated network stability, precision increases with over thousands of participants, and a sample of 500 is considered moderately large (Epskamp, Borsboom, and Fried ). Another limitation is that we only analyzed parenting items of the CIB, omitting child behaviors that contribute to interaction quality. Future studies should incorporate both parent and child behaviors in a network analysis to capture the bidirectional nature of interactions. Finally, as the study is cross‐sectional, network edges represent both within‐ and between‐subjects effects, limiting causal interpretation. Although the partial correlation networks can generate hypotheses about causal relations (Epskamp, Borsboom, and Fried ), future studies should investigate how different parenting behaviors interlink to understand the construct of parent‐child interaction quality.

In conclusion, this study is the first to apply network psychometrics to assess the construct validity of parent‐child interaction quality, providing new insights into the similarities and differences between mother‐infant and father‐infant interactions. Overall, parenting behaviors were largely similar, with configural and partial metric invariance being established. Although confirmatory factor analyses indicate CIB composites vary by context, our findings indicate that item interdependence remains stable across parent gender. Further, Acknowledging (P3) emerged as a core item of sensitive parenting for both mothers and fathers. If future studies validate these findings, network psychometrics could help refine parenting interventions by targeting the most influential behaviors to maximize improvements in parent‐child interaction quality.

psychology.title: Dual manipulation of individuals by non-invasive intelligent technologies and its risk governance: from the perspective of the Destiny Machine metaphor
psychology.abstract: The “Destiny Machine” metaphor reveals an ethical concern: big data and artificial intelligence, operating as a data-power social machine, manipulate individuals with pre-determinacy as the core logic. At cognitive-information and behavioral decision-option levels, this manipulation appears as cognitive manipulation by recommendation algorithms and decision-making manipulation by automated decision systems. To uncover its psychological mechanisms and ethical risks, this paper builds a framework integrating ethics and psychology.The Destiny Machine is transformed into an analytical tool with three dimensions: pre-determinacy, irresistibility, and concealment. Drawing on dual-process theory, automation bias, moral disengagement, and psychological reactance, it analyzes how non-invasive intelligent technologies psychologically manipulate individuals and shape their ethical risks, adopting the human-centered approach as the guiding principle for governance.Cognitive manipulation by recommender systems, typified by TikTok, leaves users unaware that their cognitive preferences are being systematically reshaped, keeping them imperceptibly immersed.
