If there is a significant difference at post-test between the experimental and control group the effect size will be calculated as partial η2p. When significant interactions occur, post hoc tests will be utilized to identify where the significant differences occurred.

An a priori power calculation was performed in order to determine the sample size needed. Using G*Power 3.1 with an expected moderate effect size (f = 0.25), alpha (0.05), and power (0.8) for the repeated measures Group × Time interaction, it was determined that 80 participants were needed.

The study had a total of 80 school-aged children that were randomly divided into two groups (the experimental group n = 40 and the control group n = 40). Each participant was able to complete both the baseline evaluation and the 12-week intervention. There were no dropouts due to physical or psychological discomfort, emotional distress, or side effects associated with the interventions.

Prior to the intervention, there were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in age, sex, SASC total score, fear of negative evaluation, social avoidance and distress, or any of the five peer-interaction dimensions (all p > 0.05), indicating comparable baseline characteristics ().

Baseline characteristics of participants.

A two-way (Group × Time) repeated measures analysis of variance with two levels of time (pre-post) and two levels of group (experimental-control), conducted on total social anxiety scores after completion of the 12-week treatment program, showed an extremely high level of statistical significance for both main effect of Time, F(1, 78) = 13.04, p = 0.0008 and the Group × Time interaction F(1, 78) = 68.42, p < 0.0001; partial eta squared = 0.467. In addition to these results, there was a highly statistically significant main effect of Time for Fear of Negative Evaluation F(1, 78) = 9.29, p = 0.003 and Social Avoidance and Distress F(1, 78) = 10.25, p = 0.002 and a highly statistically significant Group × Time interaction effect for both Fear of Negative Evaluation F(1, 78) = 54.76, p < 0.0001; partial eta squared = 0.413 and Social Avoidance and Distress F(1, 78) = 61.35, p < 0.0001; partial eta squared = 0.440. The significant interaction effects indicated that all participants demonstrated a decrease in their social anxiety symptoms over time but the reductions were larger in magnitude for those who received the active treatment compared to those in the standard physical education control group.

Post hoc analyses revealed that compared with children who participated in the standard physical education control condition during the same 12-week study period, children that received volleyball-based cooperative tactical team sports training exhibited larger gains on all of the posttest measures of social anxiety; therefore, it appears as though the specific nature of the program was directly related to its effect on reducing social anxiety.

These study results demonstrate that collective volleyball cooperative team tactics training positively impacted young children’s levels of social anxiety; particularly with respect to their fear of negative evaluation (i.e., social evaluative concerns) and their level of social (, ; ).

Descriptive statistics of social anxiety scores before and after intervention.

Peer interaction ability improved after the intervention, with greater improvement observed in the intervention group. Significant Group × Time effects were identified for all five prespecified peer-interaction dimensions: interaction initiative, peer acceptance, interaction coordination, interaction openness, and conflict resolution ability.

Descriptive comparisons showed that scores on each of the five peer-interaction dimensions increased from pre- to post-intervention in the experimental group. Although modest improvements were also observed in the standard physical education control group, post-intervention scores were higher in the experimental group across all five dimensions.

These findings suggest that the structured volleyball cooperative tactical training will improve young children’s peer interaction skills through repeated opportunities to communicate with each other, work together, coordinate roles, and resolve conflicts while (; ).

Descriptive statistics of peer interaction ability before and after intervention.

The mixed-design ANOVA demonstrated significant Group × Time interaction effects for interaction initiative (F(1, 78) = 57.84, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.426), peer acceptance (F(1, 78) = 62.17, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.443), interaction coordination (F(1, 78) = 55.93, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.418), interaction openness (F(1, 78) = 49.86, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.390), and conflict resolution ability (F(1, 78) = 51.72, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.399). These analyses therefore focus on the five explicitly defined peer-interaction dimensions rather than an additional overall composite.

The control group experienced modest improvements on a few scales; this could relate to overall physical activity involvement. The experimental group had greater increases in both affective/interpersonal aspects and thus demonstrated a higher level of effect than the control group from engaging in the cooperative-tactical training aspect of volleyball ().

Mixed-design ANOVA results for intervention effects on social anxiety and peer interaction ability.

There were no major side effects throughout the twelve week trial. Some children said they had some fatigue and minor muscle soreness for a short time after doing the workout. The soreness stopped after they rested and relaxed for a while after the workout. None of the participants suffered from major athletic injuries, emotional issues due to discomfort, or withdrew as a result of discomfort.

Children and their parents generally found the program to be very acceptable. This suggests that Collective Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training can be safely conducted with school-aged children as long as it is done under the direction of a qualified coach or other professional.

This research investigated the effects of a 12-week collective volleyball cooperative tactical training program with respect to social anxiety and ability to interact with peers by children who are 8–12 years old. Results indicated participants in this cooperative tactical volleyball intervention experienced a larger decline in their levels of social anxiety, and also experienced an improved level of peer interaction abilities compared to the participants in the standard physical education control group. Therefore, these results indicate that cooperative sport team training can be used as a viable school based method to promote the psychosocial growth of children.

Another major outcome from this study revealed that a large reduction in children’s social anxiety occurred when participating in collective volleyball cooperative tactical training. A child who has social anxiety may exhibit an excessive concern for being negatively evaluated by others; avoid interactions with other people due to fear of rejection or embarrassment; experience discomfort while communicating with other people socially. The children involved in the current program did not have to verbally discuss their thoughts or feelings with each other. They participated with other children on specific volleyball related tasks including passing, receiving, team work in small groups, and coordinating team tactics. Since these activities are based upon working together to accomplish a task and are less likely to be perceived as a source of judgment by peers compared to direct conversation or interaction, these types of activities can assist children to become accustomed to group participation (, , ).

The reduction of fear of peer disapproval can relate to the structure of a co-op setting. Traditionally, competition among young players is associated with a concern for the evaluation of their peers. In contrast, the volleyball tactics and team building that occurred in this study were based on cooperation; all children had to work together as a unit toward an end goal. The focus was on working collectively, sharing knowledge and expertise, and supporting one another. Children who experience repeated success while working within a positive supportive environment are less likely to have fears regarding how they will be perceived by other children (, , , ).

Children that have social anxiety will likely avoid new or unknown social interactions as a result of the lack of confidence when communicating interpersonally. As a child continues through volleyball cooperative training, they are exposed to multiple, consistent, and predictable ways to interact with peers during team-based activities such as calling for the ball, reminding teammates of actions needed, moving to assist other players on their team, and responding to the needs of the group. While interacting within this setting is active, it is generally less stressful than many other forms of social interaction. Through repeated, successful experiences with peers, children can become accustomed to being around others and reduce their tendency to avoid social interactions.

One of the primary results obtained from this study is an increase in students’ ability to interact positively with their peers as a result of participating in Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training. As compared to the Control Group, the Experimental Group demonstrated a significantly larger gain in taking the initiative to engage in peer interactions, being accepted by their peers, coordinating and facilitating peer interactions, expressing openness and receptivity during peer interactions, and resolving conflicts with other peers. All of these elements relate to developing students’ ability to form and sustain peer relationships in the classroom setting. In addition to reducing the occurrence of negative social–emotional responses, the data indicates that Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training can help foster positive interpersonal behaviors among students.

The development of an active interaction initiative among peers in this study could be due to the nature of the volleyball training. In all team based aspects of volleyball such as during cooperative passing and receiving or when children are completing various tactical assignments, they will need to make their intentions known verbally while asking for assistance from their teammates. This provides multiple opportunities for verbal communication; thus providing numerous opportunities for children to become increasingly comfortable initiating interactions. Unlike most forms of instructional content that teach social skills within a classroom setting, the nature of volleyball provides many instances where the children can interact with one another on a daily basis. These interactive experiences present the opportunity for children to demonstrate communication and complete task(s) by communicating—peer acceptance improved following intervention. The improvement in peer acceptance likely resulted from the team-based nature of the cooperative volleyball activities allowing children to feel both included and valued as part of a cohesive unit. Children who participate with their team are often rewarded through peer recognition of their contributions toward shared successes. By focusing on how the entire team works together toward common goals, this type of intervention promotes cooperation over competition and encourages inclusion of all participants (, , , ).

Children demonstrated an improvement in their interaction coordination and conflict management abilities. Children have to work together as a team when they participate in volleyball cooperative tactical training; each child has to be able to coordinate his/her own movement, make decisions about who will do what, adhere to the rules of the game, and adapt to the needs of the team. When participating in this type of training, there is always going to be some form of disagreement or mistake that occurs. However, by guiding them in problem solving using verbal communication and teamwork, these types of activities can lead children to develop more adaptable ways for interacting with others and manage conflicts.

When compared to standard physical education programs, a cooperative volleyball program that is designed specifically as a team will have a much more defined focus on how psychological elements are developed within teams. A standard physical education program may offer students an opportunity to engage in physical activity; may help improve their mood or overall physical fitness; however, it typically lacks intentional team communication, the use of cooperative strategies/tactics, mutual support among teammates, or a structured approach for developing groups based on roles. As such, when compared to the non-structured nature of a standard physical education program, this study was able to create a highly structured environment where all four aspects were built into the structure of the team’s training program. Therefore, it would be expected that the team participating in the cooperative volleyball program would show significantly higher gains than the team in the standard physical education program.

The theory of social learning states that a child develops their own social behavior based on what they see, do and experience with others. Social Learning Theory states that children develop their social skills by observing other people’s social behaviors, by copying or modeling those behaviors, by participating in those behaviors, and receiving feedback from the people around them. When working together during volleyball cooperative team tactics, children are able to observe positive peer interactions, copy good teamwork and communications, participate in team efforts and immediately get feedback from coaches and peers. Children will continue to repeat these experiences as they develop their ability to interact socially in an appropriate manner. Children who have success with their teammates, especially when it comes to being able to work together, will be more confident interacting with peers which will reduce their tendency to avoid social situations (, ).

From a school-based physical education context, this study indicated that using sport training as a means of promoting not only physical, but psychological and social development. Volleyball is commonly provided within schools, has minimal equipment requirements, and allows for adaptation to both physical and cognitive characteristics of children. With organization centered on cooperation and communication with peers during volleyball training, children’s social confidence and overall quality of peer relationships may be positively enhanced (, ).

The conclusions from this research will be beneficial for application. With respect to providing interventions to school aged children that are either mildly socially anxious or lack sufficient peer interaction experiences; there can be limitations as to how willing children are to engage psychologically. Sport based intervention is often an interactive way to playfully and non-stigmatized way for children to develop their interpersonal skills. Incorporating team based activities such as volleyball training into school PE programs could provide a natural and accepting environment for developing these skills. Additionally, it could be used to support the integration of body–mind type education into school environments.

The first limitation is that our sample size was somewhat limited. While we were able to use an appropriate number of participants (n = 80) for the intervention we have implemented, larger numbers will likely be needed to make our results generalize to a broader population. The second limitation is that our program was a 12-week one, and we did not collect data after those 12-weeks. Thus, it is difficult to say if the positive outcomes noted in this study would be sustained beyond completion of the program. The third limitation is that most of the information collected in this study came from self-report questionnaires. We suggest that in future studies, researchers could gather additional information about the social aspects of their subjects through teacher ratings, behavioral observations, parent reports or even qualitative interviews. A fourth limitation concerns expectancy and social desirability bias. Because the physical nature of the intervention made participant blinding impossible, children were aware of whether they were receiving cooperative volleyball training or standard physical education. Although questionnaires were administered anonymously in a quiet classroom by trained research assistants who were not involved in intervention delivery, this awareness may have influenced post-intervention self-reports, particularly if participants expected improvement or wished to respond favorably after taking part in the novel cooperative program. Future studies should combine self-report measures with blinded independent observer ratings, teacher or parent reports, and behavioral indicators of peer interaction. A fifth limitation concerns measurement validation. The study-specific 25-item peer-interaction questionnaire was informed by the broader ICQ framework and by published Chinese adolescent/youth adaptations, including psychometric validation of the Chinese ICQ-15 and a published 25-item shortened ICQ precedent (). However, the exact item set and domain labels used in the present study are not identical to those published instruments. Accordingly, the external validation evidence for ICQ-based measures cannot be assumed to validate the exact questionnaire used here. Although internal consistency was high in the present sample (Cronbach’s α = 0.91), internal consistency alone does not establish construct validity. Future studies should independently evaluate the factorial structure, convergent validity, test–retest reliability, and measurement invariance of the present form, or replicate the findings using a published externally validated peer-interaction instrument.

The study has shown some evidence that the training of volleyball cooperative tactics can help to reduce social anxiety and improve a child’s ability to interact with their peers. The program is especially important because it teaches the importance of working together, communicating, and achieving common goals. The most significant element of the training is not necessarily just getting children involved in an activity; it is how the training allows them to work cooperatively as a group.

This study found that a 12-week collective volleyball cooperative tactical training program was associated with reduced social anxiety and improved peer interaction ability in children aged 8–12 years. Compared with the standard physical education control group, the experimental group showed greater reductions in SASC total scores, fear of negative evaluation, and social avoidance and distress, together with greater improvements in interaction initiative, peer acceptance, interaction coordination, interaction openness, and conflict resolution ability.

The intervention offered children a supportive and natural opportunity for social interaction with their peers by way of working together in teams on offense and defense through such activities as cooperative passing; working in groups to complete both small group objectives and large group objectives; creating opportunities for children to coordinate tactics and work as a team.

Collective Volleyball Cooperative Tactical Training as a School-Based Model to Promote Student Mental Health (Social Development) through Physical Education can be safely implemented into schools. This type of training could assist in providing teachers and students alike with an opportunity to integrate child mental health promotion and social development education in their physical education programs. Future research will need to assess the collective volleyball cooperative tactical training’s longitudinal impact on student mental health and social development, as well as assess if it is effective across various educational environments and age groups.

psychology.title: The words of our inner worlds: emotional language use in mind-wandering and dream reports reflects mental ill-being
psychology.abstract: Do the words we use reveal how we feel? While much research has explored language use in social media, little is known about how the content of spontaneous thoughts and experiences, such as daytime mind-wandering and nighttime dreaming, reflects well-being, and ill-being. We analyzed 1 496 mind-wandering reports (N = 152) and 1781 dream reports (N = 172) using the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count. Participants also self-reported their well-being and ill-being. Linear mixed-effects models showed that ill-being (negative affect, anxiety, and depression symptoms) was associated with the use of negative tone and negative emotion words (including anxiety, anger, sadness words) in mind-wandering reports. Ill-being (specifically, negative affect) was also associated with greater use of anxiety words in dream reports. Well-being (eudaimonic well-being and peace of mind) was associated with the use of positive tone words in mind-wandering reports, but this association was not robust in sensitivity analyses. These findings indicate that the way people describe their feelings in reports of different conscious states reflects aspects of their mental health and may contribute to future diagnostic tools in psychology and psychiatry.
psychology.text:
Mental ill-being, including anxiety and depression, affects nearly 600 million people globally, yet mental health services remain critically underfunded worldwide (, ). This underscores the urgent need for reliable, scalable, and cost-effective diagnostic and prognostic markers for mental health. Recent research suggests that the language people use can effectively track and predict mental health outcomes (, ). For example, negative emotion words expressed in social media posts, personal communication, and clinical settings—assessed through tools like the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC; )—have been linked to symptoms of affective disorders (; ; , ; ; ; ). Furthermore, linguistic markers have been shown to track treatment progress in real-world therapeutic interactions (). However, it remains unclear whether emotional language in reports of spontaneous thoughts and experiences can serve as reliable markers of mental health.

Spontaneous thoughts and experiences, such as mind-wandering (or daydreaming) during wakefulness and dreaming during sleep, are mental states or sequences of mental experiences where thoughts or images flow freely, largely unconstrained by external stimuli or cognitive control (). Adults spend a third to half of their time engaged in mind-wandering (; ; ), and dreaming is a near-universal phenomenon during sleep (). As such, these experiences provide a largely unfiltered view of people’s inner lives and emotional states. While both mind-wandering and dreaming offer a unique window into mental well-being, the relationship between mind-wandering and dreaming is still debated. Some theories suggest a continuity between them, proposing that dreaming is an intensified form of mind-wandering (; ; ; ; ). According to the continuity perspective, mind-wandering, and dreaming share underlying mechanisms and reflect ongoing thoughts, concerns, and emotions that persist across waking and sleep states. For example, according to the dynamic framework of thought, conscious experiences exist on a continuum (from active wakefulness, to mind-wandering, to night-time dreaming) and differ from each other due to their various levels of constraint. The content and dynamics of mental states are constrained either deliberately via cognitive control or automatically via affective and sensory salience. In this view, mind-wandering is a form of spontaneous thought whose contents and transitions are more deliberately constrained than those of dreaming, but less so than those of ruminative, task-centric, creative, and obsessive thought. Dreams, then, are characterized by affect that is unconstrained by external stimuli (; ). Conversely, the discontinuity perspective proposes that dreaming involves different cognitive and emotional processes compared to mind-wandering (; ).

Although both mind-wandering and dreaming are marked by varying degrees of emotion and have been linked to mental well-being and ill-being (, , ; ), few studies have directly examined how emotional content in both states reflects mental health. Studying both mind-wandering and dreaming allows us to explore whether the emotional content of these experiences is similarly or differently associated with well-being and ill-being, providing insights into the continuity or discontinuity of our experiences across different states.

Mental health refers to not only the absence of mental ill-being but also the presence of mental well-being (; ). The umbrella term well-being encompasses both hedonic well-being (feeling good and being satisfied with one’s life), eudaimonic well-being (personal growth and a sense of purpose; ; ), and the more recently integrated concept peace of mind (inner peace and harmony; ; , ). In contrast, mental ill-being involves states of distress and dysfunction, typically manifesting as negative affect, anxiety, or depression (; ). Understanding how the emotional content of spontaneous thoughts and experiences reflects these aspects of well-being and ill-being may offer valuable pathways for understanding and assessing changes in mental health.

Research suggests that the content of spontaneous thoughts and experiences can reveal patterns of emotional language related to mental health. For example,  developed and used a text analysis software based on LIWC to analyze active emotion vocabularies expressed in stream-of-consciousness essays and blogs. They found that people with greater differentiation in negative emotion vocabularies showed higher levels of ill-being, whereas those with more differentiated positive emotion vocabularies exhibited lower levels of ill-being. Similarly, using LIWC to code naturally occurring, unprompted thoughts,  reported that rumination, a key feature of ill-being, was associated with more negative, past-oriented, and self-focused thoughts. Parallel findings in dream research show that negative affect expressed in dream reports correlates with anxiety, depression, and overall psychopathology (; ; ; ), while positive affect in dream reports has been linked to peace of mind (). Using graph analysis,  analyzed dream reports and transcribed interviews of schizophrenic, bipolar, and healthy individuals, finding that dream reports mirrored patients’ mental states more accurately than interviews. More recently,  applied LIWC to dream reports and found that the emotional language in these reports reflected participants’ mental distress during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Given how common mind-wandering and dreaming are in daily life, exploring their potential for monitoring mental health is crucial. If reports of spontaneous thoughts and experiences can reliably reflect well-being and ill-being, they could become valuable tools for assessing mental health. This could be especially impactful in clinical settings, offering scalable, and cost-effective tools to discreetly track mental health states and intervene in affect-related psychopathology. In this context, the growing field of digital psychiatry, coupled with linguistic analysis tools like LIWC, could harness these spontaneous reports as part of large-scale mental health solutions.

In this study, we investigated whether the emotional language in written mind-wandering and dream reports reflects well-being and ill-being. We hypothesized that (1) well-being measures (life satisfaction, domain satisfaction, positive affect, eudaimonic well-being, and peace of mind) would be positively associated with the use of positive emotion words in mind-wandering and dream reports, but negatively associated with the use of negative emotion words in these reports; (2) ill-being measures (negative affect, anxiety, and depression) would be negatively associated with the use of positive emotion words in mind-wandering and dream reports, but positively associated with the use of negative emotion words. Consistent with prior findings (), we expected peace of mind and anxiety to be the strongest predictors of positive and negative vocabularies, respectively.

To test these hypotheses, we analyzed the daily diary data collected in the UK and Australia over a 4-month period (July—November 2020; ). Briefly, participants first completed a questionnaire measuring various aspects of well-being and ill-being. After this, over the course of 2 weeks, participants completed two daily diaries. In the evenings, they engaged in a 10-min mind-wandering session and subsequently filled out a mind-wandering diary, reporting everything that went through their minds during the session. In the mornings, immediately upon awakening, participants filled out dream diaries, reporting their dreams from the previous night (see ). We applied LIWC to the 1496 mind-wandering reports from 152 individuals and 1781 dream reports from 172 individuals to examine how well-being and ill-being measures predicted the emotional language used in those reports (measured as relative word frequencies within emotion word categories). Based on principal component analysis, the main analyses were conducted using well-being and ill-being composites (calculated as the mean of standardized scores of its constituent measures).

This study analyzed data collected in the framework of a large international study, ‘The MIND Research Study’ (https://osf.io/su7mn/). Participants were recruited via press releases and advertisements in social media. A total of 1781 dream reports were collected from 172 participants (139 women, 25 men, 8 ‘other’; ages 19–78, M = 46.99, SD = 14.80 years), 64 Australian and 108 British. Additionally, 1496 mind-wandering reports were collected from 152 participants (123 women, 23 men, 6 ‘other’; ages 19–78, M = 48.42, SD = 14.71 years), 59 Australian and 93 British. Of the 172 participants who provided dream reports, 148 also provided mind-wandering reports, while four participants provided mind-wandering reports but no dream reports.

All data were collected online during 4 months (July to November 2020) via a website created for the purposes of this study. Participants were prompted to read through the study description and instructions and then received a unique participant ID to use throughout the study. After providing informed consent and confirmation of being at least 18 years old, participants completed a questionnaire containing demographic questions and a battery of scientifically validated well-being and ill-being scales (see Materials and Measures). Following this, they provided mind-wandering and dream reports daily for 14 days (see ). Participants received no reimbursement for participation. Ethical approval was obtained from the Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee and the Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee. The authors assert that all procedures contributing to this work comply with the ethical standards of the relevant national and institutional committees on human experimentation and with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975, as revised in 2008.

Mental well-being was conceptualized as consisting of hedonic well-being (life satisfaction, domain satisfaction, and positive affect), eudaimonic well-being, and peace of mind; ill-being as the presence of negative affect, and symptoms of anxiety and depression. Empirically validated well-being and ill-being scales were administered online in English.

The Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; ) was used to measure participants’ global life satisfaction. This well-validated and highly reliable scale is an established measure of life satisfaction (). The scale prompts participants to rate five statements (e.g. ‘I am satisfied with my life’) from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The summed five items provided the total score, with higher scores denoting higher life satisfaction. See  for descriptive statistics and internal consistency (Cronbach’s α) for this and all other well-being and ill-being measures.

Reliability and descriptive statistics of well- and ill-being measures (N = 176)

Note. Includes 172 participants with dream logs (of whom 148 provided mind-wandering logs) plus 4 participants who provided mind-wandering logs but not dream logs (152 participants with mind-wandering logs in total). Cronbach’s α was based on 172 participants for individual scales and 176 for the composite scores. IB = ill-being, WB = well-being. LIWC = Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count. N = number of participants. SWLS = Satisfaction with Life Scale. BBQ = Brunnsviken Brief Quality of Life Scale (BBQ). PANAS = Positive Affect Negative Affect Schedule. PA = positive affect. NA = negative affect. PWB = Ryff’s Scales of Psychological Well-Being. PoM-5 = Peace of Mind Scale. PHQ-9 = Depression scale from Patient Health Questionnaire. GAD-7 = Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale.

The Brunnsviken Brief Quality of Life Scale (BBQ; ) assessed participants’ satisfaction with major life domains. On this 12-item scale, participants were asked to rate how satisfactory (e.g. ‘I am satisfied with my learning: I have the opportunity and desire to learn new, exciting things and skills that interest me.’) and important (e.g. ‘Learning is important for my quality of life’) they currently considered six life domains (leisure time, view on life, creativity, learning, friends and friendship, view of self) to be, from 0 (do not agree at all) to 4 (agree completely). The total score was calculated by multiplying the satisfaction and importance rating for each domain, then summing their products.

Positive affect was measured via the ten positive emotion items (e.g. enthusiastic, proud, active) on the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS-PA; ), which is among the most used and highly validated measures of affect (). Negative affect was measured via the ten negative emotion items (e.g. scared, irritable, jittery) of PANAS (PANAS-NA). Participants rated to what extent (1: very slightly or not at all, to 5: extremely) they had experienced each of the twenty emotions within the past 2 weeks. The summed positive and negative emotion items yielded the scores on the positive and negative affect subscales, respectively.

Eudaimonic well-being was measured via the 18-item Psychological Well-Being Scale (PWB; ). The scale is subdivided into six subscales: autonomy (e.g., ‘I judge myself by what I think is important, not by the values of what others think is important.’), environmental mastery (e.g. ‘In general, I feel I am in charge of the situation in which I live.’), personal growth (e.g. ‘For me, life has been a continuous process of learning, changing, and growth.’), positive relations with others (e.g. ‘People would describe me as a giving person, willing to share my time with others.’), purpose in life (e.g. ‘Some people wander aimlessly through life, but I am not one of them.’), and self-acceptance (e.g. ‘I like most parts of my personality.’), with three items for each subscale. Participants rated their agreement with each statement, from 1 (strongly agree) to 7 (strongly disagree). The summed items provided the total score, with higher scores signifying greater eudaimonic well-being.

Inner peace and harmony were measured via the Peace of Mind Scale (PoM; ). The scale consists of seven items, two of which are reverse-scored. Participants indicated how often they felt inner peace and ease in their daily lives by rating each statement (e.g. ‘My mind is free and at ease’) from 1 (not at all) to 4 (all of the time) (unlike the original scale, the scale we used did not include the middle scale point alternative ‘often’). Previous studies have shown that, in Western samples, the two reverse-scored items load on a separate factor (, ). We performed a confirmatory factor analysis using the lavaan function () in R. As previously reported, the 2-factor PoM solution was a significantly better fit (CFI = .93, RMSEA = .139, SRMR = .057) than the 1-factor solution (CFI = .90, RMSEA = .161, SRMR = .067), χ2 = 19.986, P < .001. As such, we used the 5-item PoM (i.e. PoM-5), containing all non-reversed items, in our analyses.

Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9; ). The scale draws from the diagnostic criteria in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5; ). Participants indicated how frequently, over the past 2 weeks, they had been bothered by each of nine symptoms (e.g. ‘Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless’), from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day). The summed scores reflect the level of depression, with higher scores denoting more severe depression (scores 5, 10, 15, and 20 denote mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe depression, respectively).

Symptoms of anxiety were measured via the seven items on the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7; ). The measure is based on the first three (A, B, C) diagnostic criteria for generalized anxiety disorder in the DSM-5. Participants indicated how often they had been bothered by seven problems (e.g. ‘Feeling nervous, anxious or on edge’) over the past 2-week period, from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day). The summed scores reflect the level of anxiety, with higher scores implying more severe anxiety (scores 5, 10, and 15 represent mild, moderate, and severe anxiety, respectively).

Mind-wandering was first defined in the instructions to participants as ‘the contents that enter our mind when we are not engaged in or focused on any specific activity or task, or when such activities/tasks are sufficiently automatized. For example, our minds may wander when we go to bed in the evenings, while we brush our teeth, or while driving somewhere.’ For the mind-wandering task, participants were instructed to let their minds freely wander for a 10-min period each evening, ideally around the same time. They were encouraged to refrain from trying to control their thoughts, and to set a timer to avoid having to monitor the time. They were asked to perform this task in a quiet place free of disturbances, with their eyes open or closed. Promptly following the 10 min, participants were asked to write down, in as much detail as possible and without censoring any content, everything that had gone through their minds during the 10-min mind-wandering period. Finally, they rated on a 5-point scale (1: not at all, to 5: extremely) the extent to which they had experienced positive and negative affect during mind-wandering.

Participants were instructed to complete a dream log immediately upon awakening each morning, and to do so every day, including on mornings when no dream was recalled. They first indicated whether they remembered any dream experiences from the preceding night, choosing between recalling a dream including at least some of its content, believing they had dreamt but recalling nothing of it (a so-called ‘white dream’), or believing they had not dreamt. Those who reported recalling dream content were asked to report the dreams ‘exactly as [they had] experienced them,’ and to ‘report everything [they] remember (what happened, where, who was present, what [they] were thinking and feeling): no detail is too irrelevant or inconsequential to be reported.’ Participants were also asked not to censor the report or make the dream more structured, organized, logical, or complete than how they remembered it. Participants who woke during the night and recalled a dream were instructed to record it at that point rather than waiting until morning.

Upon enrolling in the study, participants received detailed instructions on how to remember and report their dreams, including keeping the log within reach, forming a pre-sleep intention to recall their dreams, remaining still upon awakening and mentally replaying the dream, briefly noting the main events in bullet points, and then writing down the report in full. No formal definition of ‘dream’ was provided. Participants relied on their everyday understanding of the term, guided by the content specification above. This was a deliberate choice, intended to avoid constraining which experiences participants judged reportable and thereby excluding fragmentary or thought-like experiences of theoretical relevance to the comparison with mind-wandering. Participants were asked to submit one dream per report and to re-open the reporting form for each additional dream from the same night. They were also asked to provide any waking commentary (such as contextualization of reported events) in brackets. Participants also rated on a 5-point scale (1: not at all, to 5: extremely) the extent to which they had experienced positive and negative affect during the dream. Although this study primarily focused on the analysis of narrative mind-wandering and dream reports, supplementary analyses were performed to examine the convergence between participants’ self-ratings of affect and corresponding LIWC emotional language categories.

The full reporting instructions for the mind-wandering and dream logs can be found on https://osf.io/su7mn/overview. Although participants were given clear instructions regarding when to perform the mind-wandering and dream tasks, there were no practical constraints set by the researchers on when they could complete the tasks and submit the reports within the data collection period. All mind-wandering and dream reports were collected in written form only.

First, all the mind-wandering and dream reports were pruned by two coders (NS and RB). The process involved marking and removal of all waking commentary not part of the actual experience from the reports. Waking commentary provided in brackets (as per instructions), as well as text that was clearly waking commentary but not provided in brackets, was removed. For example, in the following excerpts the italicized parts were removed: ‘(this is a small part of a longer dream, I suspect) I am in a classroom together with my husband…’ and ‘this was my second dream of the night. I was in a huge house which I owned…’ In cases where text in brackets was clearly part of the dream, that text was retained in the report. Reports that contained multiple separate dreams were separated so that each report contained only one dream.

Lemmatization was not implemented because LIWC already accounts for different forms of many words through the use of word stems marked with asterisks (). Stop-word removal was also not applied because, in standard LIWC dictionary analyses, words are retained and matched against the predefined dictionaries. Removing stop words could therefore remove words included in LIWC categories being analyzed. Stop-word removal is primarily relevant to other linguistic methods, such as meaning-extraction and open-vocabulary approaches. We therefore retained the original text, apart from pruning described above, to preserve comparability with LIWC’s standard dictionary-based scoring procedure.

Emotional language use was analyzed using the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC-22, v. 1.2.0) text analysis software (). The default internal LIWC-22 Dictionary (English) was applied. All words in the narrative reports directly associated with affect or emotion within LIWC-22 (i.e. all available affect-related categories) were analyzed. This involved the LIWC-22 ‘affect’ category (2999 words), with its subordinate categories ‘positive tone’ (e.g. well, new, love), ‘negative tone’ (e.g. bad, wrong, too much), and ‘emotion.’ Within ‘emotion,’ ‘positive emotion’ (e.g. good, happy, hope) and ‘negative emotion’ (e.g. bad, hurt, tired), and subcategories of the latter, ‘anxiety’ (e.g. worry, fear, nervous), ‘anger’ (e.g. hate, mad, frustr*), and ‘sadness’ (e.g. disappoint*, cry), were selected. Each category’s original vocabulary was used as-is, and hence no words or phrases were added to or removed from any of the categories. Because the umbrella categories ‘affect’ (first level) and ‘emotion’ (second level) did not contribute insights beyond those already provided by their subcategories, these were left out of the final analysis. Thus, seven subcategories were analyzed. In addition, word count was summarized using LIWC-22.

In LIWC-22, positive and negative tone categories reflect sentiment and contain words broadly associated with positive and negative emotion (happy, joy, sad, etc.), words associated with those emotions (beautiful, birthday, funeral, etc.), and selected modifiers (e.g. too much). More narrowly, the categories ‘Positive emotion’ and ‘Negative emotion’ only include true emotion labels and words that strongly suggest emotion (e.g. ‘laughter,’ which typically implies positive affect). ‘Negative emotion’ includes numerous undifferentiated negative emotion words, of which subsets are contained within the narrower categories of ‘anxiety,’ ‘anger,’ and ‘sadness’ (). The score in each category represents the respective percentage of affect or emotion words out of the total number of words in the report.

Statistical analyses were performed using R (v. 4.2.1; ). Mind-wandering and dream reports were analyzed separately as not all participants overlapped. Because most of the variables were non-normally distributed, Spearman correlations were conducted to examine the relationship between well-being and ill-being scales and LIWC-22 categories.

To avoid issues with multicollinearity between the various well-being and ill-being variables, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed based on standardized scale scores (scores were mean-centered and scaled to unit variance; see  and ). The first principal component showed a bipolar contrast between well-being and ill-being measures, while the second principal component reflected positive loadings across all eight scales. Based on the overall pattern of the loadings, the measures were grouped into theoretically defined well-being and ill-being composites. At the participant level, each individual scale score was standardized (z-scored), and the well-being and ill-being composite scores were calculated as the mean of the standardized scores of their respective constituent scales. The well-being composite consisted of SWLS, BBQ, PANAS-PA, PWB, and PoM-5, whereas the ill-being composite consisted of PANAS-NA, GAD-7, and PHQ-9. The resulting well-being and ill-being composite scores were moderately negatively correlated (r = −.47, P < .001). Participant-level composite scores were calculated and subsequently merged into both report-level datasets.

The emotional language outcome variables (i.e. LIWC-22 relative word frequencies within the specified categories) were continuous dependent variables that were positively skewed. We applied a square root transformation to the outcome variable to mitigate skewness. The transformed variable was then modeled using the lmer function from the lme4 package (). Although normality of residuals was not perfectly achieved, we used these models as our primary analysis because they are robust to non-normal residuals at these sample sizes and because they provide parsimonious and interpretable models. To verify that the distributional assumption did not affect our conclusions, we refitted all primary models as Tweedie generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) on the untransformed outcomes using the function glmmTMB from the R package glmmTMB (). We did not directly compare the two model families by information criteria, because they are fitted to different response scales and their likelihoods are therefore not comparable.

LIWC-22 categories (positive tone, negative tone, positive emotion, negative emotion, anxiety, anger, sadness) were level-1 outcome variables, whereas well-being composite score and ill-being composite score were level-2 fixed-effect predictors that were standardized before model estimation. To control for age (continuous variable), gender (categorical variable: woman, man, other), and country (categorical variable: Australia, United Kingdom), these variables were added as level-2 fixed-effect covariates in all models. Age was standardized before model estimation. Gender and country were entered as categorical factors using treatment (dummy) coding, with woman serving as the reference category for gender and Australia for country. To account for the nested data, participant-specific random intercept was included in all models. Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate correction (FDR; ) was then applied across the 28 focal tests of our hypotheses (2 predictors × 7 LIWC outcomes × 2 report types). Age, gender, and country were covariates and were not included in the FDR correction family because they were included to adjust the focal estimates rather than as hypotheses under test. As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the primary models after excluding reports containing fewer than 25 words, given that LIWC-based analyses have recommended a minimum length of 25 words for more stable percentage-based estimates (). The same 28-test FDR correction family was used in the sensitivity analyses.

In case a well-being or ill-being composite was a significant predictor of LIWC scores, we performed follow-up models in which we tested the particular well-being and ill-being variables that make up the respective composite as predictors. To avoid multicollinearity issues, each of these variables was entered separately in a model (together with the control variables age, gender, and country).

The original data contained 1767 mind-wandering reports and 2604 dream reports (). Because the subsequent analyses used multilevel models, participants who provided at least three reports of the respective report type were included in the analyses (; ). Following this criterion, participants provided an average of M = 10.35 dream reports (SD = 6.10, Mdn = 9.00, range = 3–32) and M = 9.84 mind-wandering reports (SD = 5.28, Mdn = 10.00, range = 3–40) during their participation in the study. Because the study allowed participants to submit multiple dream reports from the same night, some participants provided a relatively high number (>30) of dream reports over the 14-day period. Additionally, although the protocol specified a 2-week logging period, participants who wished to continue were permitted to do so for longer.  and  display the descriptive statistics and internal consistency (Cronbach’s α) of each well-being and ill-being scale and the associated composite variables, and of LIWC categories, respectively. The scores mirror the established normative values for each scale, indicating alignment with previous research.

To assess whether the distributional assumptions of primary models influenced our conclusions, we refitted all models as Tweedie generalized linear mixed models on the untransformed outcomes. All 28 focal tests were in the same direction and 27 of 28 reached the same conclusion after FDR (see ). The single exception was the association between well-being and positive tone in mind-wandering reports, which was not significant under the Tweedie models (adjusted p = .215, compared with .038 in the primary analysis). The associations between ill-being and negative emotional language use in mind-wandering reports and between ill-being and anxiety words in dream reports were unchanged.

Sensitivity analyses excluding reports containing ˂25 words (50 mind-wandering reports and 125 dream reports were excluded, leaving 1446 and 1656 reports, respectively) yielded a broadly similar pattern of findings (see ). In mind-wandering reports, the five ill-being associations remained significant after FDR correction. The association between well-being and positive tone no longer survived correction (adjusted p = .038 versus .137). In dream reports, the single association between ill-being and anxiety words that survived correction in the primary analyses was attenuated and no longer significant (B = 0.051 versus 0.041; adjusted p = .020 versus .082). Thus, the associations between ill-being and negative emotional language use in mind-wandering reports were robust to the exclusion of very short reports, whereas the weaker dream associations were not.

Taken together, the five associations between ill-being and negative emotional language use in mind-wandering reports were significant in the primary models, Tweedie models, and in sensitivity analyses. The association between ill-being and anxiety words in dream reports was also significant in both primary and Tweedie models but attenuated below significance when reports of ˂25 words were excluded. The association between well-being and positive tone in mind-wandering reports was significant only in the primary models and should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Follow-up models, in which we used the individual well-being and ill-being scales as separate predictors, revealed that in mind-wandering reports each of the three ill-being scales (i.e. negative affect, depression, anxiety) individually predicted the five negative-valence LIWC categories (negative tone, negative emotion, anxiety, anger, and sadness). The only exception was anger, where symptoms of depression did not reach significance (see ). Among the three ill-being measures, symptoms of anxiety, and negative affect were the strongest overall predictors. Of the five well-being scales, eudaimonic well-being and peace of mind predicted positive tone words after FDR correction. In dream reports, negative affect (but not symptoms of anxiety or depression) individually predicted the use of anxiety words (see ).

Additional analyses showed that self-rated affect was associated with corresponding LIWC emotional language scores at both the within- and between-person levels in both report types (all ps < .001; see ). This provides convergent evidence for an association between emotional language use and self-ratings of affect. Because participants provided a single overall rating of positive and negative affect for each episode, this convergence pertains to global affective tone rather than for discrete emotions.

We investigated whether the emotional language people use to describe spontaneous thoughts and experiences—such as mind-wandering and dreaming—reflects their mental well-being and ill-being. Our findings provide evidence for a link between ill-being and emotional language use and more limited evidence for a link with well-being. In particular, ill-being (characterized by negative affect, anxiety, and depression symptoms) was associated with negative tone as well as the use of negative emotion words, including anxiety, anger, and sadness, in mind-wandering reports. We also found an association between well-being (specifically eudaimonic well-being and peace of mind) and the use of positive tone words, although this association was weaker and did not hold in sensitivity analyses. In dream reports, the association between ill-being and emotional language use was weaker and limited to anxiety words. Although well-being did not predict the use of emotional words in our dream dataset, ill-being predicted the content of both mind-wandering and dream reports.

Overall, measures of self-reported negative affect over the past 2 weeks predicted negative word use across both mind-wandering and dream reports. Additionally, symptoms of anxiety and depression also predicted almost all aspects of negative word use in mind-wandering reports. Replicating previous work on analyses of clinical interviews (), our results showed that depression was linked to the use of sadness words, while anxiety was linked to a broad range of negative emotion words, but especially with anxiety words. These findings align with patterns observed in studies of social media texts where negative emotion words, particularly sadness, were positively associated with self-reported depression and anxiety (; ).

Our findings are also consistent with research on therapy transcripts and simulated telehealth psychiatric intake interviews, where higher depression scores were associated with the use of negative tone, negative emotion, anxiety, and sadness—but not anger—words (), with sadness words more closely related to measures of depression than anxiety (). Our observation that depression was associated with all negative emotion word categories except anger echoes earlier findings suggesting that anger word use increases as depression symptoms subside (). However, unlike in previous findings (), depression was not significantly associated with lesser use of positive emotion words. Together, these findings support the notion that the emotional language used in mind-wandering and dream reports indeed seems to reflect ill-being.

Our results suggest that reports of spontaneous experiences could be a useful tool for tracking mental ill-being, complementing other types of texts. For example, while social media conveniently provides vast amounts of texts produced by people, it also comes with challenges.  observed that socioeconomic, cultural, and regional variations may drive inconsistencies in the utility of such methods for predicting well-being from tweets. In addition, social media posts are subject to biases such as strategic self-presentation, with individuals more likely to share positive sentiments in public (). Initial findings also hint toward stronger associations between linguistic markers and measures of ill-being in private (rather than public; ) and informal (rather than formal; ) settings. Thus, analyzing the content of reports of spontaneous experiences, like mind-wandering and dream reports, which are less susceptible to these biases, may offer more accurate insights into mental health. The asymmetry we observed, with stronger and more robust associations for ill-being than for well-being, is consistent with this literature, in which linguistic markers have generally tracked ill-being more reliably than well-being.

More broadly, the present findings contribute to growing efforts to understand how affective experience varies across different states of consciousness. Research on affect has predominantly focused on active wakefulness, despite the fact that conscious experience extends across states characterized by markedly different relationships to external environment, including mind-wandering and dreaming (). Examining affect across these states may help identify which features of affective experience show continuity across waking and sleeping consciousness and which are state-dependent. The present finding that individual differences in ill-being are associated with emotional language not only during mind-wandering but also during dreaming is consistent with some degree of continuity in affective processes across conscious states, while differences in the strength and pattern of these associations point to potential state-dependent variation. Related work has similarly linked negative affect during both mind-wandering and dreaming to greater worry during wakefulness (), whereas dream fear has been associated with greater affect reactivity (). Examining how diurnal variation in affective processes () relates to affect during sleep may thus help elucidate a more comprehensive account of how emotional experience is organized across the day-night cycle and across different states of consciousness.

Theoretically, our findings align with the dynamic framework of thought (), suggesting that mind-wandering and dreaming are related but distinct states of consciousness, both reflecting affective states across the day-night cycle. The stronger association between ill-being and mind-wandering reports, as compared to dream reports, suggests that mind-wandering is more closely tied to real-time emotional and cognitive processes, particularly anxiety and negative emotions. In contrast, dreaming may reflect more enduring emotional themes, potentially shaped by memory consolidation processes during sleep that integrate and stabilize emotional experiences over time. Thus, while mind-wandering seems to reflect immediate emotional states, dreaming might instead engage broader, long-term emotional processing.

It is possible, however, that it is not the experiences per se that are different (i.e. more negative), but rather the way individuals describe them. For example, more anxious individuals may simply use more negative words when describing their (both daytime and night-time) experiences, compared to less anxious individuals. Indeed, trait-like individual differences have been suggested to underlie continuity between daytime and nighttime experiences (). Nevertheless, the language used in these reports, whether or not the experiences themselves are inherently more negative, appears to be an important indicator of ill-being.

Future studies could compare dream and mind-wandering reports with social media posts as predictors of mental health and examine other aspects of language that have been tied to variations in well-being (e.g. words related to loneliness, hostility, and I-language). Additionally, exploring the relationship between emotional language use and other markers of emotional well-being (e.g. alexithymia; ) and emotion regulation may provide further insight into how language reflects mental health.

Our findings should be considered in light of several limitations. The observed association between emotional language use and ill-being, and more modestly well-being, may partly reflect the context of data collection during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, when levels of ill-being were globally elevated (). Indeed, we did find that country predicted the use of negative emotion, anxiety, and anger words, albeit in opposite directions across the two report types. It would be interesting to further explore the relationship between emotional language use and mental health across a variety of contexts, countries, and cultures.

A further reason why ill-being predicted emotional language use more strongly than well-being may be the human tendency to express negative experiences relatively more explicitly and positive experiences more implicitly (, ), combined with the context-blindness of LIWC. Since LIWC plainly measures word frequencies regardless of context (e.g. negation, sarcasm, and metaphor), it cannot distinguish between the meaning of ‘I am sad’ and ‘I am definitely not sad’, or capture nuances in the meanings of ambiguous words such as ‘mad’ (e.g. ‘I feel mad at them’ and ‘they were madly in love’) (Pennebaker Conglomerates, n. d.). Thus, it may be that these constraints cause LIWC to bypass the more implicitly expressed positive emotions. This insensitivity to context constitutes a significant limitation inherent in bag-of-words methods such as LIWC, which highlights the need for more nuanced, context-sensitive tools in research using natural language processing.

The strong negativity bias in LIWC vocabularies may contribute to the same asymmetry. Since LIWC negative vocabularies contain significantly more words than the positive vocabularies do (e.g. 337 words in the ‘positive emotion’ category versus 618 words in the ‘negative emotion’ category), LIWC may capture negative content in the reports more effectively than it does positive content. This may also help explain why the association between well-being and positive tone was the least robust of our findings.

Similarly, the presence of modifiers in tone vocabularies (such as ‘too much’ in the negative tone vocabulary) may lead to ambiguous or erroneous sentiment characterization in some reports. For example, in the phrase ‘too much joy’, LIWC-22 would count ‘too much’ toward negative tone and ‘joy’ toward positive tone, without evaluating the meaning of the phrase as a whole. Thus, the resulting scores reflect the dictionary classifications of the constituent words or expressions rather than a context-sensitive interpretation of the phrase. The issue may be particularly relevant for shorter reports, in which individual dictionary matches have a greater influence on percentage-based LIWC scores. Consistent with this, excluding reports of ˂25 words attenuated the two weakest associations in our data, while leaving the associations between ill-being and negative emotional language use in mind-wandering reports unchanged. It should further be noted that, unlike the tone vocabularies, the emotion vocabularies used in the present study do not contain such modifiers and are therefore not affected by this particular issue. More generally, this illustrates a limitation intrinsic to closed-vocabulary approaches: valence is assigned at the level of the word rather than the phrase, so negation, intensification, and irony may not be adequately captured.

Over time, new linguistic approaches have evolved that extend and complement LIWC by automatically extracting content from large corpora of experience reports in increasingly potent and nuanced ways (for a review, see ). For example,  presented a tool for automatically scoring enormous sets of dream reports in line with a well-established manual coding system. This new method quickly extracts detailed insights about characters, interactions, and emotions, i.e. three highly informative dimensions of dream narratives, from large datasets, and allowed the researchers to analyze 24 000 dream reports to explore broader questions and find support for the continuity hypothesis. Moreover,  presented an unsupervised deep-learning framework that discovers dream themes and patterns in large-scale data without the use of scoring categories or pre-existing structures. The method aims to reflect the spontaneous nature of dreams more closely and with higher ecological validity and nuance than traditional, structured methods can. As such, it can be used to augment and balance traditional methods. In their study, analysis of over 44 000 dream reports yielded 217 topics grouped into 22 overarching themes. While most of these overlapped with traditional scoring categories, some new, previously undetected themes also emerged.

Broadly, studies using machine learning methods, including large language models (), offer promising alternatives to LIWC by capturing contextual nuances and reducing vocabulary-driven biases in emotion detection. While LIWC is a well-established tool in psychological research, recent advancements in AI technologies provide opportunities for complex lexical analysis that may increasingly be used to augment LIWC. These methods should be applied and compared in follow-up studies, in ways that respect known issues (such as inherent biases in the training data).

In this study, participants were asked to intentionally engage in mind-wandering, a process that differs from the unintentional mind-wandering often studied outside the lab, where participants are prompted randomly throughout the day (). This approach, commonly used in resting-state fMRI studies (), was chosen to ensure consistency with the dream reporting procedure. However, spontaneous thoughts emerging during intentional mind-wandering may differ from those arising unprompted. Although immediate sampling throughout the day might provide different insights (), the procedure used in this study ensured consistent reporting across both mind-wandering and dream experiences.

Relatedly, although participants were given instructions regarding when to perform the mind-wandering task and report their dreams, no practical constraints prevented them from performing the tasks at times other than those specified (i.e. dream reporting in the morning and mind-wandering in the evening). Time-of-day and circadian factors may influence both reported well-being and the content of conscious experiences (). Allowing participants some flexibility in scheduling the tasks was a deliberate choice. It accommodated individual chronotypes and the practical demands of home-based daily participation over 2 weeks, particularly given that data were collected during COVID-19 restrictions, when many participants were managing work, caregiving, and other responsibilities at home. Stricter enforcement would likely have reduced compliance and increased attrition. However, this flexibility leaves open the possibility that task and reporting times varied both within and between participants. Future studies could reduce this uncertainty by implementing more restricted reporting windows and recording the timing of both task completion and reporting more precisely.

In this study, timestamps indicating when the reports were submitted were automatically collected. However, these timestamps may not reflect when the experience was initially reported because participants were allowed to first write down their reports on paper or elsewhere before transferring them to the online reporting system. Thus, the interval between the initial recording of the experience and its online submission could vary. For this reason, we did not further analyze reporting times.

A few methodological challenges related to dream recall and reporting should be noted. Dream reports necessarily constitute a selective and potentially incomplete representation of dream experiences because they depend on what is attended to, encoded, retained, and subsequently recalled upon awakening. Dream memories may fade rapidly following awakening and may be further affected by interference and by the delay between the dream experience and its report (; ). In the present study, participants were instructed to take notes of their dreams immediately upon awakening, which should have reduced such memory effects. However, because the initial notes could be transferred into the online reporting system later, some dream content may nevertheless have been forgotten or modified during this process. Importantly, the dreams recalled upon spontaneous morning awakening are unlikely to constitute a random sample of all dream experiences occurring during the night. The most recent and affectively salient (especially negative) dream experiences may be particularly likely to be remembered in the morning, with recency being an especially important factor ().

Moreover, later-night rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep dreams tend to be more emotional than earlier-night REM dreams (). Thus, the emotional characteristics of dreams may themselves influence their likelihood of being recalled. Dream recall and reporting are also subject to substantial individual differences, including differences in attention to and interest in dreams, participant’s introspection and reporting skills, mind-wandering tendency, and trait differences in sleep patterns (; ; ). Taken together, dream reports analyzed here should not be regarded as a representative sample of all dream experiences occurring across the night.

It should further be noted that all reports were collected in written form. Compared with transcribed oral reports, written reports may involve a greater degree of reflective reconstruction and less immediate expression (). Several features of our procedure were designed to minimize such reconstruction: participants were instructed to write their reports immediately after the mind-wandering period and immediately upon awakening, not to revise their reports with later additions or conclusions or to make the experience more logical or complete than remembered, and to record any waking commentary in brackets so that it could be removed prior to analysis. Importantly, because both report types were collected using the same modality, reporting modality cannot account for the differences observed between mind-wandering and dream reports. Nevertheless, it is possible that oral rather than written reports would have yielded different results. Future studies could therefore collect reports in both oral and written form and directly compare the resulting findings.

Moreover, although gender was controlled for, the generalizability of the results is limited by the gender imbalance in the sample, as four out of five participants were women. Juxtaposing the language of women and men, previous work from large-scale studies suggests that text produced by women tends to contain more references to internal processes, social relationships, friendly interactions, emotions (especially positive), as well as more negations, while men’s language contains more associations to external and impersonal objects and processes, negative emotions, and tends to be colder and more hostile (; ; ; ). Given these patterns, it may be that a sample featuring predominantly men would produce different results, such as less emotionality overall—echoing the commonly reported higher rates of alexithymia in men ()—as well as a tendency toward more negative emotion words in particular. To clarify the potential impact of these tendencies on the relationship between emotional language use in reports of spontaneous experiences and mental health, future studies should aim toward greater gender balance.

Further relating to the sample, participants were not required to be native speakers of English and their first language or English proficiency was not recorded. The study was advertised and participants were recruited in Australia and the United Kingdom, both of which are home to populations with high levels of native or high-proficiency English speakers (; ). During data preparation, all reports were read in full and none were excluded on the grounds of English language proficiency or readability. Since participants were required to provide detailed free-form reports in English daily over a 2-week period, this requirement may have introduced a degree of self-selection favoring individuals comfortable with written English.

Finally, given the correlational nature of the study, no causal relationships are revealed from its results. However, future studies involving longitudinal designs may shed light on the direction of causality, elucidating whether, e.g. ill-being causes individuals to express themselves more negatively, or whether instead negative language use can contribute to ill-being (e.g. by providing conceptual frames that shape how experiences are constructed; ). Assessing well-being and ill-being over extended periods may provide insights into how changes in language use may correspond to changes in well-being and ill-being (e.g. among at-risk students or in therapeutic contexts). Longitudinal designs may also be beneficial due to their capacity to consistently capture experiences over time. While in this study, participants only rated their waking well-being and ill-being on one occasion (i.e. before commencing the 2 weeks of dream diaries and/or the mind-wandering task), longitudinal and more time-sensitive approaches (e.g. taking into account what time of the day or days of the week participants fill out the questionnaires) may reflect participants’ waking emotional experiences more accurately (). This may especially be the case as many women of reproductive age (who make up a large portion of the participants in psychological studies) experience significant fluctuations in mood throughout the month due to hormonal shifts (; ).

In conclusion, our study highlights the potential of analyzing emotional language in mind-wandering and dream reports as a tool for understanding mental health, particularly mental ill-being. Although mind-wandering reports appear more sensitive to these links, both types of spontaneous experience reports offer valuable insights that could inform the development of more effective prognostic and diagnostic tools in clinical settings. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify the causal relationships between emotional language use and mental health.

psychology.title: Professional practices, collective dynamics, and psychosocial aspects of sailors on a French warship
psychology.abstract: Warship crews live and work for extended periods in confined spaces, separated from their families and exposed to high operational demands. While psychosocial risks in naval and maritime work are increasingly documented, little is known about how sailors collectively organize, regulate, and adapt their daily activity aboard combat vessels. To our knowledge, no psychological study has documented collective activity in situ aboard a French warship.Document sailors’ professional practices, collective dynamics, and psychosocial aspects in situ during an eight-day embarkation aboard a French multi-mission frigate.This is a descriptive and qualitative study, of the experience report type, carried out in March 2026 during an eight-day embarkation aboard a French Navy European Multi-Mission Frigate taking part in a high-intensity exercise in the Atlantic. Data were collected through unstructured participant observation, from an observer-as-participant position. Inductive analysis drew on grounded theory and work psychology literature.Three mechanisms emerged. First, rank-based messes provided spaces for peer interaction, informal regulation, and the expression of tensions. Second, sailors used situational leeway to adapt their activity to operational constraints and develop practical solutions. Third, interactions between experienced and less experienced sailors supported the transmission of knowledge, practices, and norms, contributing to collective memory and professional continuity.These findings illustrate how professional practices, collective dynamics, and psychosocial aspects are intertwined in sailors’ daily activity aboard a French warship. Informal collective spaces, opportunities to adapt work activity, and the transmission of the professional genre between experienced sailors and newcomers support professional activity.
psychology.text:
In March 2026, a work psychology researcher conducted an eight-day field immersion aboard a French Navy European Multi-Mission Frigate (FREMM), as part of a broader research project on the integration of emerging technologies into naval work environments. However, it also provided an opportunity to examine the everyday social and collective dimensions of naval work. The adoption of such technologies cannot be understood solely in terms of technical or cognitive factors. It is also shaped by the collective dynamics and social conditions within which sailors work, coordinate their activities, and negotiate the demands of their environment.

Research on military collectives has traditionally focused on group cohesion, as a driver of performance under pressure (; ). More recent work has examined the stressors experienced by sailors and the importance of social resources in counteracting their effects (; ). However, few studies have examined the everyday practices through which collective activity is organized aboard operational vessels, where crews live and work together for extended periods, away from their families and friends. Sailors assigned to sea-going units are absent an average of 4 months per year, and some units experience even longer deployments (). How do sailors manage collective work under such conditions? How do they handle the tensions and conflicts that arise? Despite their relevance to understanding military work, these processes remain underexplored.

Work psychology offers a relevant theoretical and methodological framework for examining these dynamics.
