Concepts such as real activity and professional genre (; ) draw attention to the distinction between prescribed work and the activity that workers actually develop in practice. This perspective emphasizes the collective processes through which professionals transmit and transform occupational knowledge, coordinate their actions, negotiate ways of working, and develop situated responses to the problems encountered in real activity. Such approaches have been applied across a range of occupational settings, including healthcare, industry, and public services (). To our knowledge, however, they have never been mobilized to examine collective activity aboard combat vessels.

International studies on sailors’ health highlight the ambivalent role of onboard relationships, which are experienced both as a resource and as a source of tension. Among naval personnel, social tensions on board contribute to psychological strain; conversely, peer support emerges as a resource during deployment for dealing with these tensions (; ). Among merchant seafarers, resources such as good working relationships, fair workload distribution, and social support are associated with lower levels of anxiety and depression. By contrast, exposure to workplace violence increases this risk (). More broadly, onboard living and working conditions emerge as the strongest predictor of psychological well-being (). In France, available research has focused mainly on sailors’ health. In the French Navy,  described the difficulties of adapting to life on board, related to restricted living space, confinement, prolonged separation, and possible exposure to danger.  found that 54.1% of the 405 sailors surveyed, deployed aboard five surface ships, had taken at least one medication without a prescription during their mission. This finding suggests reliance on self-medication to cope with the constraints of deployment. Among civilian seafarers, studies have documented exposure to verbal aggression, sexual harassment, and potentially traumatic events (). Others have identified work strain, sleep constraints, isolation, and family separation among merchant Navy officer cadets ().

Taken together, these studies have improved knowledge of the stressors that sailors face and of the importance of resources, such as social support, in coping with them. Overall, they shed light on the psychosocial working conditions of sailors in both merchant and naval settings (; ; ). However, they have mostly addressed these issues through self-reported experiences, questionnaires, health indicators, individual adaptation capacities (), or specific psychosocial factors. Even the available qualitative work relies on sailors’ retrospective accounts collected in focus groups (), rather than on direct observation of how collective activity is organized, regulated, and adapted in situ aboard an operational warship. To our knowledge, no previous study has examined, through direct observation of everyday activity aboard a French Navy warship, how professional practices, collective dynamics, and psychosocial processes are articulated. The collective is not only a potential source of social support; it is also central to how naval work is organized, regulated, and adapted in practice. What remains less understood is not simply whether sailors experience these constraints, but how they collectively organize, regulate, and adapt their everyday activity in response to them.

The present brief report addresses this gap through an observational study informed by a work psychology and psychosocial perspective. Drawing on field observations collected during an eight-day embarkation aboard a French Navy European multi-mission frigate (FREMM), the study examines selected aspects of sailors’ everyday collective activity, with particular attention to how work is organized, negotiated, and adapted in practice. Rather than providing an exhaustive account of life aboard the vessel, it uses selected observations to illustrate how collective activity develops at the intersection of formal organizational prescriptions, the ways in which sailors appropriate rules and professional norms and situated interactions among crew members. The objective of this study is therefore to document sailors’ professional practices, collective dynamics, and psychosocial aspects in situ during an eight-day embarkation.

This is a descriptive and qualitative study, of the experience report type, based on an eight-day field immersion conducted in March 2026 during an exercise in the Atlantic Ocean. It draws on unstructured participant observations conducted by a work psychology researcher aboard a FREMM specializing in anti-submarine warfare. The FREMM, on which the researcher embarked, is organized around several functional areas, including the bridge for navigation and maneuvering, the operations center for combat operations, the hangar and flight deck, the engine rooms, the medical area, the information technology and digital systems area, the personnel management and logistics area, and the ship’s safety command post. In addition to these operational areas, the vessel includes spaces devoted to meals and collective gatherings, relaxation, rest, and maintenance-related activities. During working hours or watch periods, sailors occupy posts associated with their functional responsibilities; in more private or semi-private spaces, such as lounges and berthing areas, they tend to regroup with peers or colleagues of similar rank.

The immersion took place during a high-intensity exercise involving several French Navy forces, designed to refine sailors’ detection and artillery practices. Although the content of the exercise cannot be described in detail for confidentiality and national security considerations, it can be noted that it also included mandatory onboard safety drills designed to detect and address potential incidents, such as fire, leakage, flooding, or toxic contamination.

Access to the vessel was obtained through a formal embarkation request. The researcher, affiliated with the French naval academy, submitted a request to the Director of Officers, who facilitated contact with available vessels. The commanding officer of a FREMM agreed to host the researcher for an eight-day embarkation. The purpose of this embarkation was to observe sailors’ professional practices. Prior to the embarkation, the commanding officer informed the crew that a researcher would be onboard and that they were free to speak with her or not. All crew members were thus aware that the study was taking place.

During the embarkation, the researcher conducted unstructured participant observations. Her role was primarily observational, although she also engaged in informal interactions with crew members, corresponding to an observer-as-participant position (). She observed sailors’ professional practices during exercises and, when possible, asked them questions (only with the sailors who had spontaneously spoken to her beforehand) either during the activity or afterward about the behaviors, decisions, and adjustments they had made or were making. She observed and/or interacted informally with a large proportion of the crew, including personnel across ranks and status groups, such as officers, non-commissioned officers, senior non-commissioned officers, and enlisted sailors. The researcher carried out all these activities in order to better understand the sailors’ work environment but also to engage in interactions based, as far as possible, on mutual trust. Her role was therefore to become acculturated to this environment, to respect its rules and customs, in order to be accepted in return by the crew:

Whatever the researcher’s status on board, they are now ‘embarked’ in this unusual field, which nevertheless makes them, for a time, a participant in the place, its inhabitants and their destinations, even the most unexpected. They are first and foremost a civilian passenger who must comply with the daily constraints of military life. (, p.10).

This position implied a continuous presence in work and living spaces, without prior selection of observed situations. The researcher thus shared the crew’s daily life, took part in meals, attended exercises and debriefings, and engaged in informal exchanges with sailors who came to her spontaneously. Observations were conducted in all functional areas of the FREMM to which she had access, for example the bridge, the safety command post, and the engine rooms. Only the operations center and the information technology and digital systems area command post were not accessible to the researcher, as these areas were restricted to authorized personnel.

To track her observations, the researcher kept a field logbook. This tool enabled her to record what she perceived and heard about life on board over the eight-day immersion. Each evening, she revisited her daily notes, expanding them with reflexive comments, distancing herself from immediate impressions, and organizing them in a more systematic manner until theoretical saturation was reached. After the embarkation, she cross-referenced her field notes with the existing scientific literature. The resulting material covered a wide range of situations, including sailors’ activities at different posts, the general organization of the vessel, self-presentation strategies during debriefings, formal procedures, and everyday interactions on board. In terms of data analysis, the researcher adopted an inductive approach informed by grounded theory principles (; ). The analytical categories presented in the findings were not defined a priori; rather, they progressively emerged from the field notes through constant comparison across situations observed over successive days, including exercises, debriefings, meals, and informal interactions. Among the themes that emerged from these observations, the organization of collective life on board, and its effects on sailors’ work collectives, appeared particularly salient for two reasons. First, this focus was consistent with the researcher’s disciplinary orientation in work psychology and her socioconstructivist grounding, which conceptualizes work as situated activity embedded in a broader social and organizational context. Second, it resonated with the commanding officer’s interest in better understanding collective dynamics within the warship. The researcher therefore agreed to provide him with oral feedback on this issue, summarizing what she had observed and analyzed regarding the crew’s collective functioning on board. This feedback included both interpretive observations and practical suggestions.

The study complied with the Code of Ethics for Psychologists and the Declaration of Helsinki. The entire crew was informed by the FREMM’s commanding officer, prior to embarkation, of the researcher’s presence and the purpose of the study. In accordance with ethical considerations, the researcher only observed and engaged in informal interactions with sailors who came to her spontaneously to speak. No formal interviews were conducted, including on the theme of the collective onboard. Anonymity was guaranteed, and no sensitive data were collected.

Consistent with the inductive method (), this study does not seek statistical generalizability but offers a contextualized understanding of the observed dynamics. The findings presented in the following section draw on the researcher’s field logbook and on the scientific literature revisited after the embarkation. They do not claim to be exhaustive: they offer a situated reading of selected aspects of collective life onboard, based on observations conducted during the eight-day immersion.

Life at sea is characterized by constant proximity, a pronounced permeability between private and professional life, and separation from one’s shore-based social network, although this separation is no longer complete given the availability of digital communication tools. The crew therefore lives in a kind of social and spatial “bubble,” in which spaces and times devoted to formal work are closely intertwined with those dedicated to more informal interactions. In demanding work situations, family members and friends can ordinarily provide external resources for coping with occupational strain. At sea, however, these external resources are less readily available. Family and friends can help with emotional regulation when a conflict arises among sailors, but what about at sea, when those sources of support are far away? During an exercise conducted aboard the FREMM, the researcher observed tensions between crew members stemming from divergent views about the most appropriate strategy for carrying out the task. The researcher identified two spaces in which such tensions could be expressed and regulated. The first was formal: the post-exercise debriefing functioned as a structured feedback setting in which crew members could voice disagreements within a framework specifically designed for collective analysis. During these debriefings, contradictions were discussed collectively in order to make sense of unexpected events encountered during the exercise and to reconsider the activity with a view to improvement. The second space was more informal. In the evening, before meals, sailors gathered with peers of the same rank or hierarchical level for a moment of relaxation. These rank-based spaces, called “messes,” provided an opportunity to express emotions, release frustrations accumulated during the day in one’s functional role, and feel understood by others who shared similar constraints. Peers thus played an important role in listening, support, and the regulation of tensions. This organization into rank-based messes - a distinctive feature of large Navy vessels - and the peer role associated with them may therefore help transform tensions experienced at work into something that can be spoken about, shared, and ultimately worked through. Although the researcher did not directly observe such situations, the reverse process may also be considered: when tensions arise within the mess, among peers, formal work colleagues may in turn assume a regulatory function. This spatial and social differentiation may therefore be particularly important because it can partly substitute for the emotional and social support usually provided by family members when such support is less accessible at sea. On newer frigates, either recently delivered or still under construction, the organization of private spaces is expected to change, with some spaces being merged in favor of more functionally oriented layouts. A senior non-commissioned officer, questioned by the researcher in an informal discussion, expressed concern about this development. In his view, the merging of messes increases hierarchical proximity, as ranks become more mixed within the same private spaces, thereby reducing opportunities for free expression within rank-based collectives. For this sailor, the implications of this spatial reconfiguration were clear: without a dedicated “release valve” for expressing tensions, there may be a greater risk of animosity, unspoken resentment, and persistent conflict.

On board, other practices also contributed to creating spaces for creativity and social bonding, including humorous morning announcements, joke exchanges among colleagues, and video game sessions in the mess. These activities allowed crew members to relax and build interpersonal ties, but also to express themselves beyond formal procedures, produce shared cultural content, and play with the codes of everyday life on board. Like peer exchanges, these creative - or, more precisely, recreational - spaces appeared to function as resources for social bonding. For instance, the researcher heard, as did the rest of the crew, morning announcements from sailors on the bridge who used excerpts from well-known songs to present the day’s activities or to send a message to another sailor celebrating a birthday.

Creativity, however, was not limited to recreational forms of expression; it was also embedded in work activity itself. The researcher observed this practical creativity in sailors’ everyday work: “I do it this way; it’s easier,” “If I put it here, it will hold better,” or “Wait, normally we do it like this, but if you go this way, it will be faster and produce the same result.” Such ordinary adjustments help make work possible by facilitating action, arbitrating between constraints, and adapting prescribed procedures to situated demands. On the FREMM where the field immersion took place, the commanding officer trusted crew members and allowed them such leeway. Sailors were therefore able to use this flexibility to develop situated ways of working, imprinting a “signature” on their activity while collectively adapting to constraints and unexpected events.

Peer sailors - either of the same rank as the newcomer or of the rank to which the newcomer aspires - who had already been at sea for several months or years transmitted skills, gestures, postures, and practical tips to less experienced crew members. For example, the researcher observed a watch supervisor on the bridge teaching a mnemonic strategy to a midshipman to help her remember key information to report to the navigating officer, her hierarchical superior. The spaces in which this transmission occurs are often those in which collective work enables rules to be adjusted and mutual assistance among professionals to emerge. The construction of sailors’ experience is therefore inseparable from collective dynamics that support the transmission of practical knowledge, gestures, and norms. It may thus be particularly relevant to rely on peers who are positioned to sustain this transmission and to facilitate the organizational socialization of newcomers to the Navy.

The originality of this study lies in both its field setting and its methods of data collection and analysis. Regarding the field setting, researcher immersions aboard combat vessels remain rare. These 8 days spent aboard a FREMM during a high-intensity exercise made it possible to observe sailors’ real activity () as it unfolded, whereas existing studies rely mainly on questionnaires or retrospective accounts (; ). As for the analysis, the concepts of professional genre (; ) and work collective () had not, to our knowledge, previously been used to study collective life on board. Yet they make it possible to capture what sailors concretely do together, day to day, to keep their work going.

The work collective observed on board appeared to us to be relatively balanced. Peer relationships played a supportive role, and the commanding officer placed his trust in the crew by granting it situational leeway (). In addition, experienced sailors actively passed on the professional genre to newcomers. Research on military cohesion has mainly approached it as a lever for performance under pressure (; ). Our observations suggest that collective life on board cannot be approached solely from the perspective of performance. Research conducted among shipboard sailors points in the same direction, identifying socialization opportunities and peer support as important resources during deployment (; ). Our study adds to this work by showing how these resources are embedded in the everyday organization of collective activity. Three mechanisms emerge from our observations: the role of rank-based messes in regulating tensions among peers, the leeway that makes room for real activity, and the transmission of the professional genre from experienced sailors to newcomers. These mechanisms can be interpreted through the theoretical framework of work psychology.

The mess, as a compartmentalized space for relaxation and self-disclosure (), appears to function as a structural “release valve,” enabling tensions experienced at work to be verbalized, shared, and potentially worked through, thereby supporting recovery from work (). Studies conducted among United States Navy sailors identify camaraderie, moments of sociability, and organized social events on board as among their main means of coping with stress at sea (; ). Recreational activities and the role of music also constitute important resources (). The morning announcements set to songs and the video game sessions observed aboard the FREMM follow the same logic. Beyond the recreational function of collective events, onboard living and working conditions emerge as the strongest predictor of sailors’ psychological well-being (). The authors relate these conditions to the layout of living spaces, interpersonal relationships, and relaxation areas. Our observations suggest that the organization of space matters: by separating work areas from relaxation areas, and messes by rank, it makes these moments of regulation possible. Research on military groups, for its part, emphasizes the role of strong cohesion in mitigating the effects of isolation (; ; ). However, the present study provides a more nuanced perspective by examining the dialectic between cohesion and conflict. Although tensions and conflicts may be avoided or suppressed because they are experienced as uncomfortable and have been associated with adverse outcomes for well-being, including depressive symptoms and burnout (; ; ), our observations suggest that such tensions may also be part of the collective’s functioning and contribute to its regulation by reshaping interpersonal relationships and group dynamics, provided that they do not become persistent or destructive (). This distinction calls for a more dynamic and process-oriented understanding of collective life onboard, in which cohesion does not necessarily imply the absence of tensions or conflict. Rather, tensions may form part of the processes through which collective relations are negotiated and regulated. From this perspective, conflict should not be understood solely as a threat to be neutralized, but also as a potentially constructive process that, when expressed and regulated within dedicated spaces, may help clarify expectations, readjust roles, and ultimately support the collective’s capacity to work together under pressure.

The concept of “real activity” () and the situational leeway granted by the commanding officer () highlight the dialectical relationship between prescribed and real activity: prescribed activity shapes real activity, while real activity may, in turn, lead prescriptions to evolve. The observations collected aboard the FREMM illustrate this dialectic. The ordinary remarks of sailors such as “I do it this way; it’s easier,” “If I put it here, it will hold better” show that these adjustments are not mere deviations from the norm: they make work possible, arbitrate between competing constraints, and adapt procedures to the situated demands of action (). It is precisely in this gap between the prescribed and the real that the meaning of work develops. This perspective enables sailors to develop their “power to act” (), particularly when they benefit from situational leeway within the organization of work. The observations suggest that the commanding officer of the FREMM granted precisely the kind of leeway that allows sailors’ power to act to develop.

The development of the “power to act” facilitates the development of the “professional genre” (). The transmission of the “professional genre” () from experienced sailors to novices further sustains the collective memory of the trade and facilitates the organizational socialization of newcomers (). It allows them to avoid having to reinvent everything and to integrate into a collective already carrying implicit rules.  recommend developing peer mentoring, particularly during the first months on board; our observations show that it already exists informally. For example, observing a watch supervisor teach a midshipman a mnemonic strategy for remembering the information to be reported to the navigating officer provides a concrete illustration of this process. What is transmitted here is not merely a technique; it is also a way of relating to the profession - a way of carrying oneself, communicating, prioritizing, and coordinating with others. Such transmission presupposes spaces in which collective work enables professional rules and practices to be discussed and adjusted (). The mess, debriefings, and informal interactions that characterize life onboard constitute precisely such spaces. These observations are consistent with recent research on the psychosocial vulnerabilities of naval personnel (; ; ; ). Rather than contradicting these findings, the present study places them within the everyday organization of collective activity. Rank-based messes, situational leeway, and the transmission of the professional genre appear to function as collective resources that may mitigate—though not eliminate—the psychosocial strains identified in this literature.

Despite these contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the researcher’s position as an observer-as-participant () may have introduced several sources of bias, including social desirability on the part of sailors during interactions with the researcher and potential observer effects related to the researcher not being subject to the same disciplinary rules as the crew. Second, restricted access to certain areas of the ship, such as the operations center and information technology and digital systems area command post, may have limited the scope of the observations, particularly regarding collective work in “high-intensity” situations. Third, the study did not include formal interviews or focus groups specifically addressing the work collective, limiting our ability to examine participants’ own interpretations of the observed dynamics. Nevertheless, the study retains heuristic value. Few studies in psychology have gained access to an operational warship, and this eight-day immersion provides rare empirical material on sailors’ collective activity. The application of French and international work psychology concepts (e.g., “professional genre,” “real activity,” and “work collective”) to the context of the French Navy also offers a relatively underexplored perspective, as research on naval personnel has predominantly relied on surveys or retrospective accounts (; ). Furthermore, the inductive and qualitative methodology enables a contextualized understanding of the observed dynamics (see ).

This study set out to document sailors’ professional practices, collective dynamics, and psychosocial aspects in situ during an eight-day embarkation aboard a French multi-mission frigate. Three main findings emerged. First, collective life onboard cannot be reduced to cohesion; rather, it relies on differentiated spaces and roles through which tensions can be expressed and regulated. Second, the organization of work allows for situated adjustments that contribute to making activity meaningful, provided that sufficient situational leeway is granted by the chain of command. Third, the transmission of practical knowledge and professional norms between experienced sailors and newcomers supports the continuity of the trade and the socialization of new crew members. Taken together, these findings suggest that the psychosocial dimension of naval work is not an adjunct to operational effectiveness but one of the conditions that sustain it.

These findings also point to several implications for the organization of work onboard. Rank-based messes may be considered not only as spaces for rest and social interaction, but also as resources for collective regulation and should therefore be taken into account when designing future vessels. This is consistent with recent recommendations to improve onboard living conditions and to increase opportunities for social activities at sea (; ). Similarly, preserving opportunities for situational leeway may support the expression of real activity and enable crews to adapt their practices to the demands of specific situations. The role of experienced sailors, particularly senior non-commissioned officers, as carriers and transmitters of the professional genre could also be more explicitly acknowledged, both to support meaning at work and to facilitate the organizational socialization of newcomers, in line with calls to develop peer mentoring on board (). More broadly, these mechanisms may be relevant to the design of collective work in other confined and isolated environments.

These findings open several avenues for future research. Further observational studies combining in situ observation with interviews could examine whether similar mechanisms operate across different types of vessels and within other branches of the French armed forces. Longitudinal research could also examine how situational leeway, peer regulation, and the transmission of professional knowledge evolve over the course of a deployment or career. Finally, future research should investigate how emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, interact with these collective mechanisms and potentially reshape the organization, regulation, and transmission of work in naval environments.

psychology.title: Psychotherapeutic Care in Austria 2026–2040: An FTE-Calibrated Simulation of Workforce, Funding and Care Capacity
psychology.abstract: Background/Objectives: Psychotherapeutic care in Austria faces the transition introduced by the Psychotherapy Act 2024 (PThG 2024), an aging profession, and a need far exceeding publicly funded provision (potential capacity ≈669,000 vs. ≈199,250 publicly (co-)funded patients per year in 2022). Methods: We developed an FTE-calibrated Monte Carlo simulation (30,000 iterations per scenario, 2026–2040; anchors: 21 treatment hours/week, 13 units/patient/year) distinguishing potential, accessible, and fully funded capacity while treating supervised trainees as a separate, survey-anchored capacity line whose capacity rises with insurance funding, including the PThG 2024 transition (master’s entry 2026/27; the old pathway ends in 2038), a static robustness matrix at the 2023 capacity anchor (need 5–12%; intensity 13–40 units/patient/year) and weekly-hours-anchor sensitivities (21/15.8/13.3 h/week). Results: At 13 units/patient/year, the expansion scenario closes the median care gap from 2028 and the partial-funding scenario from 2032, largely by funding the services of trainees who are already treating under supervision; at 30 units/patient/year, even a full expansion covers only ≈30% of a 9% need at the 2023 anchor (≈49% with projected 2040 capacity); and under lower weekly-hours anchors, the gap closes later or not at all. The 2038 end of the old pathway produces a workforce-growth cliff: sustaining growth requires about 1500 master’s places per year with matching phase-3 places. Population needs dominate cost uncertainty (Spearman ρ up to 0.79) ahead of the activation rate; exploratory cumulative follow-on costs up to 2040 approximate €83/13/1 billion (A/B/C). Conclusions: Activating existing capacity—including trainees’ services, whose capacity line rests on a single unweighted survey and expert assumptions—is the dominant short-term lever; master’s and phase-3 places determine workforce growth after 2038; and in higher-intensity treatment scenarios, capacity expansion becomes indispensable.
psychology.text:
Psychotherapeutic care in Austria is at a structural turning point, where three developments overlap. First, the Psychotherapy Act 2024 (PThG 2024) fundamentally transforms professional training into a consecutive bachelor’s–master’s system followed by a specialist training phase []. Second, the existing profession is aging: of the 11,676 psychotherapists registered in the professional register in 2023, 27% were already over 65 years old []. Third—and this has been most clearly underestimated in the debate so far—the computed personnel capacity exceeds publicly funded care several times over.

Specifically, recent analyses [,] have shown that, at an empirical median of 21 treatment hours per week and 13 treatment units per patient per year, the theoretical total capacity is roughly 669,000 persons per year. In 2022, however, only about 199,250 persons received partially or fully publicly funded psychotherapy, while only about 96,500 persons received fully funded psychotherapy [,]. Against an estimated need or treatment willingness of 9% of the population (~805,000 persons in the insured reference population used throughout this model []), the gap between computed capacity and socially accessible care becomes evident.

This implies a fundamental conceptual shift: the central challenge of Austrian psychotherapeutic care is not primarily a workforce or recruitment problem but a funding, access, and structural problem. While reform-cohort models have traditionally focused on the number of licensed therapists, the present FTE-calibrated model shows that even a growing profession cannot provide the needed coverage of care without corresponding funding activation.

The health-economic relevance of this diagnosis is considerable. International evidence indicates that longer waiting times for psychotherapeutic treatment are associated with poorer treatment outcomes and with higher economic costs of care, although effect sizes vary across settings [,]. Chronic mental disorders in turn cause productivity losses, sick leave, and early retirement on an economically substantial scale [,]. Persons in training under supervision (old system: in Ausbildung unter Supervision, i.A.u.S.; new system: Psychotherapeut:innen in Fachausbildung unter Lehrsupervision, PiFALS; henceforth ‘supervised trainees’)—around 2799 in 2023 [] and about 3200 in 2025 ()—occupy a critical dual function: they are part of both the current care capacity and the future workforce reserve. Their services are currently not funded by statutory health insurance, so their funding, or lack thereof, acts on both dimensions simultaneously.

This paper integrates these empirical anchors for the first time into a consistent simulation model that renders the structural sensitivities of Austrian psychotherapeutic care up to 2040 transparent, differentiates three capacity levels—potential, accessible/partially funded, and fully funded—and models supervised trainees of the old and new training systems as a capacity line of their own.

As of 2023, 11,676 psychotherapists were registered in the Austrian professional register [,]. Of these, 8523 (73%) were under 65 years of age and 3159 (27%) were over 65. The study by Dinhof et al. [] provided the first empirically robust data on actual care activity: the median of weekly treatment hours was 21, which, at 45 working weeks per year, yielded an annual treatment capacity of 945 h per full-time-equivalent therapist. At the current value of 13 units per patient per year [], this corresponds to a computed capacity of 72.7 persons per therapist per year; the parallel social-insurance accounting reports an average of 13.8 units across all funding channels in 2022 [].

This FTE calibration is methodologically central because it shifts the model basis from headcount logic (‘how many therapists are registered?’) to capacity logic (‘how many persons can actually be treated?’). The underlying 13 treatment units per person per year reflect the current status quo. A systematic review of dose–response effects in routinely delivered psychological therapies reports optimal doses between four and 26 sessions, which varies with setting, clinical population, and outcome criterion, with 11 to 19 sessions typically needed for both reliable and clinically significant improvement []; depending on the clinical picture, 30 to 40 units per year serve as higher-intensity reference scenarios—adequate intensity varies substantially with the diagnosis, severity, treatment modality, and treatment goals. The model thus maps a best-case theoretical capacity at the current treatment intensity, and adjusting to higher treatment intensities reduces the theoretical capacity correspondingly.

The care figures for the reference year 2022 result from the funding channels reported by Dinhof et al. []: about 95,100 persons received fully funded psychotherapy through care associations and institutions and about 1400 through the ÖGK’s own psychotherapeutic facilities—combined together as ≈96,500 fully funded persons (≈1.1% of the total population)—while a further ≈102,750 persons received subsidized psychotherapy in private practice. Together, these three channels reach ≈199,250 persons through partially or fully funded psychotherapy in 2022, which Dinhof et al. [] also reported as a minimum figure. This quantity is not identical to the 370,389 persons counted under the broader psychosocial care definition of the social-insurance analysis [] and must not be substituted for it. This contrasts with a treatment willingness and epidemiological need of about 9% of the population []. Because publicly funded psychotherapy is an insurance benefit, all model calculations refer to the 8,942,791 persons entitled to benefits in Austrian social health insurance in the 2022 annual average [] rather than to the resident population of about 9.1 million; at 9%, this corresponds to an absolute need of roughly 805,000 persons per year (≈820,000 if referred to the resident population).

The difference between the computed capacity (669,000) and fully funded care (96,500) illustrates the scale of the funding gap: 86% of the potential psychotherapeutic capacity is not translated into socially accessible, fully funded care. Even when including partially funded services, care reaches only about 30% of potential capacity and only about 24% of epidemiological need. This discrepancy is the central structural finding that the present model attempts to quantify and project.

The PThG 2024 fundamentally replaces the Psychotherapy Act of 1990. In the new system, training is structured in three consecutive phases: (1) a six-semester bachelor’s program in psychotherapy, (2) a four-semester master’s program, and (3) a subsequent phase of specialist training under teaching supervision (phase 3) [,]. Full licensure occurs only after completion of all three phases. Neither the PThG 2024 nor the PTh-AAQV 2024 fixes a minimum duration for phase 3 in calendar years; both specify minimum contents and volumes instead (at least 2050 training hours in total, of which 1000 h of psychotherapeutic treatment, 400 h of theory, 200 h of teaching supervision and 200 h of self-experience) [,]. The effective duration of phase 3 is therefore not a legal constant but a model parameter, and the simulation varies this accordingly ().

In the old system, 5021 persons were still enrolled in the Fachspezifikum (method-specific training) in 2023 [], and 2799 persons were undergoing specialist training with teaching supervision []; completions in the old system reached 514 in 2023 []. The most recent training statistics (reference date 1 June 2025) show that the old pathway is still expanding ahead of its statutory closure: 5601 persons were enrolled in the Fachspezifikum, with 929 admissions, 624 completions, and 91 drop-outs in the 2024/25 reporting year; 3238 of the enrolled persons (57.8%) already held the status ‘in training under supervision’ (i.A.u.S.), which entitles them to treat patients under supervision, meaning that—as the training statistics note—they already contribute to psychotherapeutic care, although their services are not refundable by statutory health insurance []. The transitional provisions of the PThG 2024 fix the horizon of this pathway: admission to the old Fachspezifikum is inadmissible after 1 October 2030, and old-pathway training must be completed by 30 September 2038 (§§ 60(4) and 61(3) PThG 2024) []. Old-system completions will therefore end in 2038. In the new system, the master’s programs in psychotherapy are offered from the winter semester 2026/27; persons with an equivalent bachelor’s degree enter at the master’s level (about 500 places per year at public universities, a planning figure of the Federal Ministry communicated to the authors; and an estimated 500 at private universities); and specified professions—among which including psychiatrists and other physicians with a qualification in psychotherapeutic medicine, clinical and health psychologists, and music therapists—may enter phase 3 directly (§ 10 PThG 2024) [,]. Two provisions establish trainees as a policy lever from the outset: from 1 October 2026, persons in training under supervision are listed in the professional register with the addition ‘in specialist training under teaching supervision’, which makes them visible as providers of care, although the listing alone does not make their services an insurance benefit—§ 135(1)(3) of the General Social Insurance Act (ASVG, as amended by BGBl. I No. 145/2024) covers psychotherapy only by persons entitled to independent practice under § 22 PThG 2024 []; and the first licensures from the master’s route are expected from about 2030–2032, several years earlier than the first graduates of the full bachelor’s–master’s route.

The profession’s age structure points to a substantial retirement wave over the next 10 to 15 years. Therapists over 65 years old (3159 persons) continue to contribute to care capacity albeit with reduced weekly hours []. The model assumes a retirement/exit rate of about 3.5% per year (range: 2–5.5%), yielding a modeled exit figure of about 420 persons per year in 2026, rising with the growing stock to 832 persons per year in 2040 under Scenario A and 937 under Scenario C.

The model operates on five interlinked analytical levels. Level 1—Training policy: Decisions on training architecture, phase-3 capacities, and funding act on the future workforce with a time lag; the latency between a training decision and its licensure effect is modeled for the master’s-entry route of the new system as two years of master’s studies plus a variable phase-3 duration of two to five years (mode three), so that the first licensures arrive about four to seven years after entry—because phase 3 carries no statutory minimum length, this latency is drawn from a distribution instead of being fixed (). Trainees in phase 3 already treat patients under teaching supervision, so the care effect of a training decision precedes its licensure effect. Level 2—Workforce dynamics (FTE): The stock dynamics of licensed therapists, calibrated with the empirical FTE anchor of 945 treatment hours/year and the age-corrected value of 57.31 persons per registered therapist (72.69 per fully active therapist), define the potential care capacity. Level 3—Funding activation: The share of potential capacity translated into accessible (partially/fully funded) care depends on care structures, tariffs, statutory-insurance contracting, and the institutional integration of teaching supervision; this activation rate is the genuinely policy-sensitive lever. Level 4—Waiting time and chronification: The care gap (need minus accessible capacity) determines chronification risk via waiting times; this relationship is qualitatively documented but not empirically quantified in precise risk curves by waiting duration, so the model treats it as a sensitivity parameter in three variants. Level 5—Societal follow-on costs: Chronification, sick leave, and productivity losses generate monetizable follow-on costs that quantify the economic value of investing in accessible care.

The model’s central theoretical thesis is that funding activation—the share of potential FTE capacity converted into socially accessible care—is the dominant health-policy lever. The number of licensed psychotherapists is a necessary but not sufficient condition to cover the care needed. A policy focused exclusively on training numbers risks leaving already existing potential unactivated.

This is a deterministic–stochastic simulation model with probabilistic uncertainty analysis (Monte Carlo simulation, 30,000 iterations per scenario). The model is not a predictive forecasting model but a scenario model that represents structural sensitivities and ranges of possible developments under defined assumptions. The model logic follows discrete annual updates from 2026 to 2040. The source code is provided as  and the documentation as ; the outputs are provided as .

The model’s methodological foundation is FTE (full-time-equivalent) logic rather than pure headcount logic. The capacity calculation uses the empirically anchored value of 945 annual treatment hours per therapist (an upper-bound reading of capacity; see  and ) [] and 13 treatment units per patient per year []. Methodologically central is the distinction between a computed FTE capacity of 72.69 persons/year per fully active therapist and an age-corrected empirical capacity of 57.31 persons/year per registered therapist. The latter—derived from the ratio 669,121/11,676—is used in the model because it implicitly accounts for the reduced activity of therapists aged over 65. This empirical calibration avoids the overestimation trap that a pure FTE approach would create.

This yields the core formulas (, ): annual hours = 21 h/week × 45 weeks = 945 h/year; capacity per fully active therapist = 945/13 = 72.69 persons/year; and capacity per registered therapist (model value) = 669,121/11,676 = 57.31 persons/year. Potential capacity(t) = therapists(t) × capacity per registered therapist + trainee capacity(t), where trainee capacity(t) = [i.A.u.S.(t) + PiFALS(t)] × 72.69 × [f0 + (f1 − f0) × insurance-funding share of trainee services × ramp(t − 1)], with f0 = 0.60 in the current unfunded state and f1 = 0.90 under full insurance funding (modes; , ). Accessible capacity combines the activated share of the therapists’ capacity with the insurance-funded share of the trainee capacity: Accessible capacity(t) = therapists’ capacity × activation rate(t) + trainee capacity(t) × insurance-funding share of trainee services(t). Fully funded capacity(t) = therapists’ capacity × full-funding share(t) + activated trainee capacity × (full-funding share/activation rate)—the full-funding share of therapists’ capacity is defined relative to the potential capacity throughout (cf. ). In each Monte Carlo draw, the full-funding share is capped at the activation rate, so that fully funded capacity cannot exceed accessible capacity. Care gap(t) = need(t) − accessible capacity(t), which is bounded below at zero. Two distinct quantities must not be conflated at this point. The 13 treatment units per patient and year reported by Dinhof et al. [] are the empirically observed average of currently publicly funded psychotherapeutic care in Austria; this value estimates only the capacity that the existing system realizes. The 40 sessions per year used by Riess et al. [], by contrast, are a therapeutic reference value describing the intensity that adequate, guideline-oriented treatment of many mental disorders can require; it characterizes need but not delivered care. The model keeps the two apart: capacity is computed from the empirical 13 units, while treatment intensities of 20, 30, and 40 units are entered exclusively as sensitivity parameters in the robustness analysis (). This allows us to show how a higher clinical treatment intensity affects the computed capacity and care gap without altering empirical input data.

The model distinguishes three operationally separate levels of care capacity. Level 1—Potential capacity: As a theoretically available care capacity based on FTE calibration, potential capacity comprises licensed professionals and, as a separate capacity line, supervised trainees of both the old (i.A.u.S.) and new systems (PiFALS, phase 3), whose treatment capacity counts as potential whether or not it is insurance-funded, though its level does rise with funding (). Level 2—Accessible capacity: The share of potential capacity translated into actually usable care via statutory-insurance contracting, outpatient-clinic structures, partial funding, or self-payment constitutes the accessible capacity; for therapists, the activation rate varies by scenario, from 33% (Scenario A) to 82% (Scenario C), and for trainees, a separate parameter—the share of trainee services funded by statutory health insurance—is being phased in from 2027 onward (). Level 3—Fully funded capacity: The share of potential capacity provided to patients without financial co-payment (statutory health insurance, ÖGK quotas, free outpatient-clinic care) constitutes the fully funded capacity; this is the socially relevant core quantity for equity-oriented care planning.

The relationship between waiting times and the chronification of mental disorders is qualitatively supported by the literature, yet precise, validated risk curves by waiting duration are not available [,]. Two qualifications matter here: van Dijk et al. [] found no association between waiting time and the clinical course during the waiting period—the association they did report concerns the treatment outcome—and Catarino et al. [] modeled waiting time as a cost driver without estimating a waiting-time-dependent drop-out or persistence risk. The model therefore treats chronification as an explicit sensitivity parameter and runs three variants in parallel (); it takes the direction of the effect from the literature, and its magnitude is a scenario assumption in this study. The three variants are implemented as scenario-independent robustness runs (, ): within each variant, identical chronification and waiting-time parameters apply to all three scenarios, while the main model draws these parameters from scenario-specific distributions ().

All uncertain parameters are modeled as triangular distributions (minimum; mode; maximum) and drawn once per Monte Carlo iteration (). All parameters are sampled independently across iterations; conceptually related parameters (e.g., activation, trainee funding, full-funding share, and phase-3 capacity; outpatient-clinic expansion is not a separate parameter but part of the activation rate) are therefore uncorrelated within a draw, with one deliberate exception: the full-funding share is capped at the activation rate of the same draw (). If such parameters are, in fact, positively correlated, independent sampling understates the width of the resulting uncertainty intervals (and overstates it under a negative correlation); this simplification is acknowledged here. Throughout the study, reported intervals (95% and 80% PI, also termed uncertainty intervals in the figure captions) are percentile intervals of the simulated Monte Carlo distribution; they reflect propagated parameter uncertainties and are not repeated-sampling confidence intervals. The evidential status of each distribution—an empirically anchored value, official planning value, expert assumption, empirically informed assumption, or scenario-defining value—is classified in the notes for  and annotated per parameter in the source code (, Q1–Q5). The distributions common to all scenarios and the scenario-specific ones are listed in .

Scenario A—Status quo/underfunding: The current structures are continued, with a low activation rate (mean 33%), high self-payment share, and limited outpatient-clinic capacity, insurance funding of trainee services rising only to 15–50% (mode 30%; like all insurance funding of trainee services in the model, this presupposes a change in the legal or contractual framework;  and ), and 350–800 phase-3 training places per year. Scenario B—Transition/partial funding: Through the stepwise expansion of outpatient structures, partial funding of trainee services (40–85%, mode 65%), 800–1600 phase-3 places per year, and the partial expansion of statutory-insurance contracting, the activation rate rises to a mean of 58% and the full-funding share to 39% of potential capacity. Scenario C—Expansion/full funding: With near-complete insurance funding of trainee services (75–100%, mode 90%); 1300–2500 phase-3 places at universities, outpatient clinics and teaching practices; the substantial expansion of psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics; and a marked increase in publicly funded quotas, the activation rate reaches a mean of 82% with the full-funding share at 75% of potential capacity (equivalent to 92% of accessible capacity). Master’s places (about 1000 per year: 500 publicly funded places at public universities and an estimated 500 at private universities) and admissions to the old pathway are held at their current levels in all three scenarios; the effect of additional master’s places is examined separately (). The empirical anchors of the FTE calibration are summarized in .

The annual change in the stock of licensed psychotherapists follows the classical stock equation: PT(t+1) = PT(t) + completions(t) − retirements(t) − exits(t). Completions come from the old pathway (until 2038) and, from 2029/2031 onward, from phase 3 of the new system. The results are reported in .

Potential FTE capacity results from the stock multiplied by the age-corrected capacity per registered therapist (57.31 persons/year; ), a value that already embeds the reduced activity of therapists aged over 65 relative to the 72.69 persons/year of a fully active therapist, plus the capacity of supervised trainees. Capacity per trainee is the same for both training systems and depends on the funding for trainee services. In the current, unfunded state, it is set at 60% (range 50–70%) of a fully active therapist. This value is anchored on a stratified re-analysis of the authors’ member survey of December 2024 [] (): trainees under supervision (n = 638) reported 0.61 of the mean weekly free-practice hours (including administration), 0.70 of the mean total weekly hours (free practice plus institution), and 0.50 of the mean annual patients of listed psychotherapists (n = 2139); 40% of the trainees practiced psychotherapy as their sole occupation (listed: 67%) while 82% planned to expand their hours by 2030 (mean +12.6 h/week), i.e., the unfunded trainee is a part-time provider with unused capacity. Under full insurance funding, the capacity per trainee is assumed to rise to 90% (range 80–100%)—an expert assumption of the authors, as the obligation to attend supervision remains while theory training is completed—and, because a practice has to be built up, it follows the funding ramp with a lag of one year, expressed as capacity per trainee(t) = 72.69 × [f0 + (f1 − f0) × funding share × ramp(t − 1)] and applied to the entire treating trainee stock. With the scenario-specific funding shares, the effective factor therefore rises from 0.60 in 2026–2027 to about 0.70 (A), 0.79 (B), and 0.86 (C) by 2031 (medians); both f0 and f1 are part of the sensitivity analysis, and fixed funding-independent factors are examined in . Accessible capacity is the sum of therapists’ capacity multiplied by the scenario-dependent activation rate and trainee capacity multiplied by the share of trainee services funded by statutory health insurance. Trainee services are currently paid privately—under the current law, they are not an insurance benefit ()—so their insurance funding presupposes a change in the legal or contractual framework; the model therefore treats it as a policy measure that can take effect after the register listing of 1 October 2026, and the funding share is phased in linearly from zero in 2026 to its scenario value by 2030 (25% of the target in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029). In Scenario A, the activation rate is only 33% (corresponding to today’s reality of roughly 30% of all therapists holding an insurance quota or an outpatient-clinic position). In Scenario C, it rises to 82%, implying a comprehensive restructuring of the care landscape, with substantial insurance expansion and outpatient-clinic development.

The care gap is operationalized as the positive difference between need (treatment willingness × population) and accessible capacity: care gap(t) = max(0, need(t) − accessible capacity(t)).

The reform-cohort model distinguishes three groups simulated in parallel (): (1) persons in the old training system (Fachspezifikum), anchored on the training statistics from 2025 (5601 enrolled, 3238 of them i.A.u.S.) [], with admissions of about 950 per year until the statutory admission deadline of 1 October 2030, completions following the observed turnover of the pool (about nine years) until 2030 and accelerating thereafter, such that all remaining candidates complete by the statutory deadline of 30 September 2038 (§§ 60(4) and 61(3) PThG 2024)—the i.A.u.S. share of the pool is 57.8% until 2030 and rises to 100% by 2033 as the remaining candidates advance into the supervised-treatment phase; (2) master’s-entry cohorts of the new system from the winter semester 2026/27 onward—about 1000 per year (500 fixed places at public universities, 250–750 at private universities), with two years of master’s studies, followed by phase 3 (PiFALS) for a duration of two to five years and a lead time of 0.5–2 years before full treatment activity—supplemented by a small number of direct entrants to phase 3 under § 10 PThG 2024 (20–100 per year), with the completion rate of the new system () applied at the end of the master’s program; and (3) bachelor’s programs of the new system, currently offered only at private universities, whose graduates fill the same master’s places and are therefore not counted separately. Propaedeutic candidates who can no longer enter the old Fachspezifikum in time (about 30% switch to the master’s program, according to the authors’ assessment) compete for the existing master’s places and do not add throughput. Phase-3 training places (, places per year) multiplied by the phase-3 duration produces the number of simultaneously available places; candidates without a place wait in a first-in-first-out queue and are treated at 50% of the PiFALS capacity while waiting (500 of the 1000 required treatment hours can be completed outside a formal training place). This waiting time prolongs their training. The queue logic is adapted from the authors’ phase-3 decision model; all candidates who begin phase 3 complete it.

This structure implies two transition phenomena. The first is the familiar ‘reform dip’ in licensures between the end of the old pathway and the ramp-up of the new one; the second is a ‘transition cliff’ in 2038, when the old pathway’s completions and supervised trainees disappear within one to two years. Both are quantified in  and discussed in .

Societal follow-on costs comprise three additive components: follow-on costs(t) = waiting-time costs(t) + chronification costs(t) + productivity losses(t). This additive structure does not fully capture the interaction effects between components (e.g., chronification increasing sick leave).

Waiting-time costs cover the excess utilization of general practice, psychiatric emergency care, and psychotropic medication between care indication and treatment start. Based on the international evidence regarding excess costs and productivity effects of untreated and more severe mental disorders [,], the base costs of €2500/€5000/€9000 per untreated person and year are modeled (triangular; mode €5000) and multiplied by the scenario-specific waiting-time cost factor (), which corresponds to effective waiting-time costs of about €440–€710 per untreated person and month across the scenarios. Chronification costs arise because chronic mental disorders entail substantially higher lifetime costs; the model computes them as the product of the care gap, the chronification rate (variant-dependent), and an excess cost factor (triangular €4000/€10,000/€20,000 per chronified person and year, mean about €11,300; ). To orientate this, König et al. [] reported six-month excess costs of €6123 (severity level 1) to €31,883 (level 4) in 2019 euros, i.e., roughly €12,000 to €64,000 annualized; the mode and mean used here are deliberately set below the lower end of that range. Productivity losses follow the human-capital approach, where an employment rate of 58%, 24 sick-leave days/year, and a GDP contribution of €490 per working day imply about €6800 per affected person and year (24 × €490 ≈ €11,800 per affected employed person, weighted by the employment rate). Because only some people in the care gap incur losses of that magnitude, this value enters the model as an upper anchor. In contrast, the modeled productivity cost per person in the care gap is drawn from a triangular distribution of €1000/€3000/€7000 (). For context, in 2025, dependent employees in Austria recorded an average of 14.7 absence days per insured person, corresponding to about 4.0% of total working time []; the 24 days assumed here refer to persons with untreated mental disorders, whose absence durations exceed the population’s average.

To anchor the per-person cost parameters in Austrian empirical data, we cross-checked the model’s cost assumptions against the secondary-cost compilation by Seitz et al. [], who assembled per-patient primary and secondary annual costs for chronic pain patients with somatic symptom disorder in Austria (n = 106; 1-year follow-up after an 8-week integrated inpatient intervention) from Austrian statistical and tariff sources: €186 per sick-leave day, derived from an average of 35 million workdays lost per year at a total cost of €6.5 billion over 2006–2010 [,]; €3168 per hospital day in a public hospital (range: €2923–3401); €24 per medical examination and €10.1 per physician consultation billed to the social-insurance carriers; and average medication costs per patient [].

In that high-utilizer population, the total annual secondary costs per patient amounted to €147,689 before the intervention and €67,943 in the year after it—a reduction of €79,746 per patient per year, driven mainly by 24.3 fewer hospitalization days (−€76,919) and 64.5 fewer sick-leave days (−€11,980), although the expenditure on psychotherapy sessions increased (+€237) [].  sets these empirical anchors against the model’s per-person cost parameters.

Scenario A—Status quo/underfunding continues current structures. The activation rate remains at about 33%; only about 15% of potential capacity is provided fully funded. The care gap falls from about 418,000 persons/year in 2026 to about 287,000 in 2033—even the modest insurance funding of trainee services (30%) activates up to 84,000 persons/year of trainee capacity—before widening again to about 321,000 by 2040 as the old-system trainees complete and disappear (§ 60 PThG 2024). The new system delivers only about 580 licensures per year. Cumulative follow-on costs by 2040: €83 billion (95% PI: 37–143).

Scenario B—Transition/partial funding assumes a stepwise expansion of outpatient structures and partial funding of trainee services (65%). The activation rate rises to 58%, the full-funding share to 39% of potential capacity. The care gap falls from 249,000 (2026) to zero between 2032 and 2036—activated trainee capacity peaks at about 197,000 persons/year in 2032—and reopens to about 37,000 persons/year in 2040 after the old pathway ends (38% of runs show no gap in 2040); relative to Scenario A, this is an 88% reduction. Cumulative follow-on costs: €13 billion (95% PI: 1–51).

Scenario C—Expansion/full funding models the near-complete insurance funding of trainee services (90%), sufficient phase-3 training places, and a substantial expansion of psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics. The activation rate reaches about 82%, with the full-funding share at 75% of potential capacity (equivalent to 92% of accessible capacity). Accessible capacity exceeds the median modeled need from 2028; the care gap remains at a median of zero until 2040 (99% of runs show no gap in 2040). Cumulative follow-on costs fall to €1.3 billion (95% PI: 0–8), corresponding to avoided follow-on costs of roughly €82 billion versus Scenario A.

Timing these levers is decisive. Insurance funding of trainee services acts within one to four years, as trainees already exist and are already treating; the phase-3 and master’s pipeline acts on licensures after four to seven years; and the statutory end of the old pathway in 2038 removes both its completions and its trainees regardless of policy. Measures that expand phase-3 places and master’s places would therefore need to be in place well before 2038 if the workforce is to keep growing after the transition ().

presents the central three-level capacity model in the final year of 2040.

The figure visualizes the central structural finding of this study: the potential capacity exceeds need in every scenario in 2040 (Scenario A: 980,000 persons/year against a median need of about 647,000, i.e., 152%) because the licensed profession grows until 2038 and because the treatment capacity of supervised trainees counts as potential; yet in Scenario A, the accessible capacity (320,000) covers only 50% of need and fully funded capacity (152,000) covers only 23%. In Scenario B, the accessible capacity (603,000) reaches 93% of need, and fully funded capacity (412,000) reaches 64%. In Scenario C, accessible capacity (908,000) exceeds need (140%) and fully funded capacity (831,000) alone covers 129%.

This illustrates why a pure workforce policy remains insufficient: with the same professions and the same trainees, the three scenarios differ in 2040 by a factor of almost three in terms of accessible care. The difference between potential and accessible capacity is the policy-relevant activation margin, and in 2040, between 6.5% and 9% of potential capacity (88,000/69,000/84,000 persons/year in A/B/C) is the trainee capacity that depends on a single lever—the insurance funding of trainee services, which, in the model, raises the activated share and the capacity per trainee.

shows the cumulative follow-on costs from 2026 to 2040, with 80% and 95% uncertainty intervals per scenario.

The follow-on cost curves diverge strongly with the increasing projection horizon (medians and intervals in ).

It is worth noting the saturation dynamic in Scenarios B and C: because accessible capacity covers the median needs from 2028 (C) and 2032 (B), annual follow-on costs fall to zero from these points, and the cumulative cost curve flattens into a plateau; in Scenario B, the curve resumes a slight rise from 2037, which is when the old-system trainees have completed, and the gap reopens.

Even when accounting for the uncertainty intervals, the scenario ranking remains robust: the upper 95% bound of Scenario C (€8 billion) lies clearly below the lower 95% bound of Scenario A (€37 billion), and Scenario C is cheaper than Scenario A in 100% of simulation runs and cheaper than Scenario B in 94% of them (Scenario B cheaper than A in 99%; unpaired comparison of runs across scenarios). In the model, activation and full funding are associated with substantially lower societal follow-on costs than maintaining the status quo under every plausible parameter constellation.

visualizes the interplay of completions from the old system, completions from the new system, and retirements/exits (top row), as well as the stocks of supervised trainees in the old system, in phase-3 training places, and in the waiting queue (bottom row), across the three scenarios.

The graph shows that the old pathway, fed by about 950 admissions per year until 2030, delivers about 640 completions in 2026 followed by about 714 per year from 2030 to 2038—slightly above the 624 observed in 2024/25—before it ends under the transitional law (§ 60 PThG 2024). Completions from the new system begin with a few direct entrants in 2029, reach about 470–620 in 2031, and plateau at about 580/year in A, 740/year in B and 840/year in C from 2033; the differences between scenarios stem from the completion rate and, in Scenario A, from the phase-3 places, which become binding from 2030—about 1050 candidates are waiting for a place in 2040 (mean waiting time 0.7 years), whereas in B and C, the places suffice. The bottom row shows the trainee stocks: the old-system stock rises from about 3400 (2026) to a peak of about 4200 in 2032 and falls to zero by 2039, while the new-system phase-3 stock builds up from 2028 to about 1800/2400/2700 trainees (A/B/C) by 2031–2032—a level limited in A by places and in B and C by master’s intake.

The retirement line rises in all scenarios from about 420 (2026) to 830–940 per year (2040) as the stock grows; until 2038, completions exceed retirements everywhere, such that the licensed stock grows to 16,200–17,900 by 2038. From 2039, the picture reverses: without the old pathway, the new system’s 580–840 licensures per year fall short of retirements, and the stock declines by roughly 240–430 per year (C/A). The ‘retirement wave’ is therefore not the binding constraint of the transition decade; the binding constraint is the new system’s throughput after 2038.

shows the development of the annual care gap—operationalized as need minus accessible capacity—over 2026–2040, with 95% uncertainty intervals per scenario.

The three scenario curves show marked qualitative differences (medians in ); in 2040, 99% of Scenario C runs and 38% of Scenario B runs show no gap.

The most important clinical–structural result is the speed at which trainee funding acts: both B and C close the median gap within six years, without a single additional licensure, because they activate capacity that already exists. The wide uncertainty bands reflect the dependence of this result on the level of needs, the activation rate, and the assumed trainee capacity; however, they are tellingly asymmetric in favor of covering need, which is bounded below at zero.

quantifies the influence of the 17 uncertain model parameters on two endpoints—cumulative follow-on costs by 2040 and accessible capacity in 2040. In the figure, Spearman rank correlations computed within each scenario across its 30,000 Monte Carlo iterations are shown: positive values indicate increasing effects of higher parameter values, while negative values indicate decreasing effects (). We compute correlations within scenarios because the scenario-specific parameter distributions barely overlap; a correlation pooled across scenarios would measure scenario membership rather than parameter influence and is therefore not reported. We report two endpoints because the training-pipeline parameters affect the workforce and capacity with a lag and are therefore invisible in the cost endpoint, which is dominated by the years before 2032. The weekly-hours anchor enters this analysis through the capacity per therapist (FTE anchor): its distribution (50–68 persons/year per registered therapist, mode 57.31; ) corresponds to scaling the 21-h anchor by a factor of 0.87–1.19, i.e., to about 18–25 treatment hours/week per therapist at 13 units per patient per year. The alternative anchors of 15.8 and 13.3 treatment hours/week lie outside this range and reflect a different measure (activity-adjusted means instead of the published median); they are therefore analyzed as separate model runs rather than as sampled uncertainty (, ).

The sensitivity analysis yields five central insights. First, the choice of policy package dominates: cumulative costs differ between the scenarios by more than an order of magnitude, a between-scenario finding carried by the scenario comparison ( and ). Second, within every scenario, the assumed population need is the largest single source of cost uncertainty (ρ = +0.70/+0.74/+0.79), and its weight increases with the activation level; closing the gap does not buffer the system against need as it makes need the binding uncertainty, which is why the robustness analysis across need levels () is integral to the model rather than an appendix to it. Third, regarding costs, the activation rate is the strongest steerable parameter, followed by the FTE anchor, the retirement rate, and the insurance funding of trainee services; the clinical risk factors (waiting-time factor, chronification) matter only in the underfunded Scenario A (). Fourth, for accessible capacity in 2040, the ranking changes: after the activation rate, the retirement rate, and the FTE anchor, the pipeline parameters become visible (master’s places, completion rate, insurance funding of trainee services, lead time to full trainee activity, phase-3 duration; ); for the licensed stock in 2040, the retirement rate dominates (ρ ≈ −0.8), followed by master’s places, the completion rate, and, in Scenario A alone, by the phase-3 places, which bind there (). Fifth, the full-funding share does not influence costs or the care gap by construction (its non-zero correlations in Scenario C, −0.10 with costs and +0.14 with accessible capacity, arise only from its coupling to the activation rate through the consistency constraint): it defines the equity level of care (level 3) and must be read as a distributional, not an efficiency, parameter; likewise, the two trainee-capacity parameters—the unfunded level f0 (0.5–0.7 of a fully active therapist) and the fully funded level f1 (0.8–1.0)—have only small within-scenario correlations with costs and accessible capacity (|ρ| ≤ 0.03), even though they set the level of the trainee effect, as their uncertainty ranges are narrow relative to the need range. Their influence lies in the level of the results, not in their dispersion, which is why the trainee-capacity assumption is examined separately with fixed factors in .

The new system’s master’s intake is currently limited to about 1000 places per year (about 500 publicly funded places at public universities and an estimated 500 at private universities; ). To determine the intake at which the new system sustains the workforce after the old pathway ends, the master’s intake was varied from 1000 to 2500 places per year in all three scenarios, with all other draws unchanged (). Because phase-3 places are the second bottleneck, we ran each intake level twice: with the phase-3 places in the respective scenarios () and with phase-3 places scaled in proportion to the intake.

Three results follow. First, with proportionally growing phase-3 places, Scenario B closes the care gap durably with about 1500 master’s places per year, and Scenario C from the current intake; Scenario A—with today’s activation and trainee funding—does not close it at any intake examined (168,000 persons/year at 2500 places). Second, master’s places alone are not enough: with the phase-3 places of Scenario A held constant, an intake of 2500 produces a waiting queue of about 12,000 candidates in 2040 (mean waiting time 3.5 years), with a smaller licensed stock and a larger gap than the same intake with proportional phase-3 places ( and its notes). Third, with every additional 500 master’s places, the licensed stock in 2040 is raised by about 2000–3000 persons (A/B/C), i.e., the throughput needed to replace the old pathway’s 714 completions per year and to keep the stock growing after 2038 lies at roughly 1500 places per year, provided that the phase-3 places grow with it.

The results in , , , , , ,  and  rest on the assumption of a population need of up to 9% (range 5–9%, mode 7.5%) and a treatment intensity of 13 units per patient per year, with the latter matching the value on which the capacity anchor of Dinhof et al. is based []. Both assumptions are open to challenge: published Austrian estimates span a clinical need of about 13.8% of the population and a realistic treatment need of about 9% []—the four need levels examined here (5%, 7.5%, 9%, 12%) are therefore an explicit modeling choice spanning a deliberately low lower bound and an upper bound that includes subclinical burden and not a range taken from a single source—while Riess et al. [] used 40 sessions per year as a therapeutic reference value for guideline-oriented treatment; because adequate intensity varies with diagnosis, severity, treatment modality and treatment goals, 30 and 40 units per year are treated here as higher-intensity scenarios and not as a general benchmark.

To test the stability of the model results against these two central parameter assumptions, a systematic robustness matrix was computed—four need levels (5%; 7.5%; 9%; 12%) × four treatment intensities (13; 20; 30; 40 units) × three scenarios = 48 constellations—with each being deterministic and with additional Monte Carlo uncertainty (20,000 iterations) around the activation and funding parameters.

The capacity scaling follows a simple, transparent logic. Since theoretical total capacity (669,121 persons/year) is based on 13 units per patient per year, it scales inversely proportionally to treatment intensity: capacity(E) = 669,121 × (13/E). At E = 20 units, theoretical capacity falls to 435,000 persons/year; at E = 30, to 290,000; and at E = 40, to ~217,000. This deterministic reduction is mathematically necessary and cannot be compensated by activation. The matrix is a static analysis: it rescales the 2023 capacity anchor (669,121 persons/year: the theoretical capacity of the 11,676 licensed psychotherapists of 2023 at 13 units/patient/year, without trainee capacity) and applies fixed scenario activation shares to it (30%/57%/82% for A/B/C in the deterministic matrix, varied as triangular distributions in the Monte Carlo component; ) instead of using the dynamically projected workforce and trainee stocks of , , , , , ,  and ; the same intensities applied to the projected capacities of 2030 and 2040 are reported in  ().

In Scenario B, near-complete coverage (85%) is reached only at 5% need and 13 units.
