The graph makes the central robustness finding tangible: all three scenario curves fall markedly as treatment intensity rises. While Scenario C still achieves 68% coverage at 13 units, this value falls to 30% at 30 units and 22% at 40 units. The scenario difference (C–A) persists in absolute terms but shrinks relatively; at high treatment intensity, activation alone becomes an insufficient lever.

The absolute gap () grows monotonically with treatment intensity: in Scenario C, it rises from about 256,000 persons (13 units) to about 567,000 (30 units) and to about 627,000 (40 units). In absolute numbers, this gap is comparable to that of Scenario A at low intensity, highlighting treatment intensity as an underestimated model parameter.

The deterministic robustness matrix was complemented by a Monte Carlo component in which the scenario-specific activation and full-funding shares vary as triangular distributions (20,000 iterations per cell).  presents the resulting medians and 95% uncertainty intervals for coverage at 9% need.

The uncertainty intervals clarify three findings: (1) the scenario ranking is robust under all treatment intensities—the 95% uncertainty intervals do not overlap; (2) with rising treatment intensity, the absolute intervals narrow, reflecting the approach to a structural care shortage that parameter fluctuations can barely alter; and (3) even the upper bound of the 95% uncertainty interval of Scenario C at 30 units does not reach the 100% line.

presents coverage at two contrasting treatment intensities (13 units = current value; 30 units = higher-intensity scenario) across all need levels. Because capacity is proportional to the weekly treatment hours divided by the units per patient per year (capacity = 669,121 × (h/21) × (13/E)), a lower weekly-hours anchor acts like a higher treatment intensity: at 13 units per patient per year, the alternative anchors of 15.8 and 13.3 treatment hours/week are equivalent to about 17 and 21 units at the 21-h anchor (Scenario C, 9% need: about 51% and 43% coverage instead of 68%; for the dynamically projected model, see  and ).

The graph shows the model’s most important methodological asymmetry: at 13 units, Scenario C can computationally cover even higher need levels (123% at 5% need; 51% at 12% need). At 30 units, all three scenario curves remain permanently below the 60% line. The difference between the two treatment intensities is larger in every scenario than the difference between the scenarios themselves—a central finding for interpretation.

The capacity per supervised trainee is the least documented quantity of the model (). To test how far the results depend on it, the main model—in which the capacity factor rises with the insurance funding of trainee services from f0 ≈ 0.60 to at most f1 ≈ 0.90—was compared with four variants in which the factor is fixed at 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, or 0.9 of a fully active therapist, for both training systems and irrespective of funding, and with a counterfactual lower bound in which trainee services are never insurance-funded in any scenario (funding share zero; capacity per trainee stays at f0; this corresponds to the current legal situation, ), with all other draws unchanged (). The fixed factors bracket the survey-based unfunded level (0.50–0.70) from below (0.3) and reach the mode of the fully funded level (0.9), which lies above the effective factor of every scenario in the main model (at most 0.86); 0.3 represents a trainee treating about one day per week.

Four results follow. First, the scenario ranking and the qualitative conclusions do not depend on the trainee capacity: Scenario C closes the median care gap in every variant (from 2030 at a factor of 0.3, from 2028 at 0.7 and above), whereas Scenario A closes it in none (minimum gap 262,000 persons/year even at 0.9). Second, the timing of the closure in Scenario B is sensitive to the assumption: at a fixed factor of 0.3 or 0.5, the median gap in Scenario B does not close at all (minimum 46,000 and 29,000 persons/year); at 0.7, it closes by 2033; at 0.9, by 2031; and in the funding-dependent main model, by 2032—the closure in the partial-funding scenario therefore hinges on the capacity per trainee rising above today’s part-time level once trainee services are funded, which is precisely the mechanism the survey data suggest (82% of trainees plan to expand their hours). Third, the effect on cumulative costs is moderate relative to the scenario differences (). By 2040, the fixed-factor variants hardly differ because the old-system trainees have since completed and only the phase-3 stock of the new system remains. Fourth, the counterfactual without any insurance funding of trainee services marks the lower bound of the lever: cumulative costs rise to €96/31/3.9 billion (A/B/C), the gap in Scenario B never closes, and Scenario C closes it only by 2032 instead of 2028 (). The window of need coverage in the partial-funding scenario therefore exists only because trainee services become insurance-funded.

Weekly-hours anchor. Because potential capacity scales linearly with the weekly-hours anchor, the full simulation was re-run with the anchor set to 15.8 and 13.3 treatment hours/week (the activity-adjusted weighted means for both contracted and all listed practitioners from the authors’ weighted secondary analysis of the individual-level data of the ÖBVP member survey from December 2024 [];  and ), with the capacity triangle and the trainee module rescaled consistently. Under 15.8 h/week, the median care gap no longer closes in Scenario B (minimum ≈ 132,000 persons/year) and closes in Scenario C only from 2031 onward; under 13.3 h/week, it no longer closes, even in Scenario C (minimum ≈ 5500 persons/year in 2033; 66,458 in 2040), and cumulative follow-on costs rise to €103.7/39.5/7.5 billion and €113.5/53.2/15.7 billion (A/B/C) (). These runs hold the scenario activation shares constant across anchors (a one-factor sensitivity). Because the status-quo activation is calibrated on the observed reach, Scenario A falls below that reach at the lower anchors, and its cumulative costs there overstate the status-quo case; with the status-quo activation and full-funding shares rescaled by 21/h, so that Scenario A reproduces the accessible capacity of the 21-h main model, its cumulative costs are €86.5 billion (15.8 h/week) and €88.0 billion (13.3 h/week). The 21-h results should therefore be read as upper bounds on capacity ().

Treatment intensity at dynamically projected capacity. The static robustness matrix () evaluates the 2023 capacity anchor. Applying the four treatment intensities to the dynamically projected accessible capacity (medians) of 2030 and 2040 yields, for a 9% need, coverage of 104%/113% in Scenario C at 13 units/patient/year but only 45%/49% at 30 units/patient/year (). The closure of the median care gap under Scenario C at 13 units/patient/year and the low coverage at higher intensities are thus the same model logic evaluated at different treatment intensities and thus not a contradiction.

Separating the two trainee mechanisms. Holding capacity per trainee fixed at the unfunded level f0 while making trainee services financially accessible isolates the pure accessibility effect: cumulative follow-on costs in Scenario B fall from €31.0 billion (no trainee funding; ) to €15.7 billion compared to €13.1 billion in the main model, but the median gap then no longer closes completely (minimum ≈ 10,600 persons/year). The accessibility of existing trainee services thus carries most of the cost effect, whereas the complete closure of the Scenario B gap in 2032–2036 depends on the funding-induced rise in capacity per trainee from f0 toward f1 ().

Scenario-independent chronification and waiting-time variants. The three variants of  are implemented as separate runs in which identical chronification and waiting-time parameters apply to all three scenarios, while all policy parameters remain scenario-specific. The difference in cumulative follow-on costs between Scenarios A and C then ranges from €51.6 billion (conservative) over €62.2 billion (realistic) to €76.0 billion (pessimistic), as compared with €82.1 billion in the main model (). The scenario-specific coupling of the clinical–economic parameters thus accounts for roughly €20 billion of the A–C difference; the ranking of the scenarios is unaffected.

Sequential decomposition of the policy levers. Starting from Scenario A and cumulatively switching parameter groups to their Scenario C distributions (common random numbers) shows that activating the capacity of listed psychotherapists carries the largest single contribution: median cumulative follow-on costs fall from €83.4 to €3.5 billion, and the median gap closes by 2030. Insurance funding of trainee services advances closure to 2028 (−€1.4 billion); the training-capacity group raises the accessible capacity from ≈754,000 to ≈905,000 persons/year without further affecting the gap at 13 units/patient/year; and the clinical–economic parameters contribute the remaining −€0.8 billion (). Because the gap already closes at the first step under 13 units/patient/year, this ordering partly reflects the sequential design; at higher treatment intensities and after the 2038 transition, the capacity contribution of the training levers becomes decisive ( and ).

The robustness analysis sharpens the model’s main message in an important respect. At the current treatment intensity of 13 units per patient per year, activation is the dominant lever for closing the care gap. In the higher-intensity scenarios (30–40 units), the finding changes substantially: coverage of a 9% need in Scenario C falls from about 68% at 13 units/year to about 30% at 30 units/year at the 2023 capacity anchor () and remains below 50%, even with the projected 2040 capacity (), so that additional capacity expansion becomes indispensable. The trainee-capacity assumption, by contrast, changes the timing of the gap closure in Scenario B but not the scenario ranking (). Lower weekly-hours anchors shift the conclusion in the same direction, even at 13 units/patient/year (, ).

The policy consequence: Activation and funding policy remains the most important short-term lever—particularly because, once the legal and contractual conditions are in place, it takes effect without training latency. In the medium to long term, however, the model suggests that it would need to be complemented by substantial capacity expansion (more master’s places, more phase-3 places, more outpatient clinics) as treatment intensity moves from 13 units towards higher treatment intensities of 30+ units/patient/year.

The most fundamental result of this study is conceptual in nature and is further differentiated by the robustness analysis: the FTE calibration, with the empirical anchors of Dinhof et al. [] and Gruber et al. [], suggests that Austrian psychotherapeutic care—at the current treatment intensity of 13 units per patient per year—suffers primarily from insufficient activation of existing capacity and less from a shortage of psychotherapists in the narrow sense. This diagnosis changes, however, in the higher-intensity scenarios: at 30–40 units/year, activation becomes necessary but not sufficient; additional capacity expansion is therefore structurally required.

Even allowing for part-time work, private practice, and self-pay priorities, the contrast between the computed capacity and the 199,250 persons reached with partial or full funding in 2022 () suggests a substantial activation gap. The simulation indicates that, even with a stagnating profession, doubling the activation rate—from about 30% to about 60%—could markedly reduce the care gap, provided treatment intensity remains constant.

One policy implication of the model results—under the stated assumptions—is that a strategy relying exclusively on expanding training places, without addressing the funding and structural side in parallel, could end in an activation trap: growing therapist numbers without correspondingly growing socially accessible care. Both levers are complementary and necessary.

Persons in training under supervision (2799 in 2023 []; 3238 in 2025 []) occupy a system-critical dual function: they are simultaneously part of the current care capacity and the future workforce. A lack of funding for their services therefore acts as a damage multiplier on three levels: it withholds current care (unfunded trainees cannot deliver insurance-funded services in outpatient clinics), slows training (through self-funding pressure), and erodes the institutional base (outpatient clinics without trainee funding are not economically viable).

The model quantifies this lever for the first time. At the survey-anchored treatment capacity of 60% of a fully active therapist in the current unfunded state (), the roughly 3400 trainees of 2026 represent about 147,000 persons/year of potential capacity, 18% of the national total, rising to about 270,000–350,000 persons/year (25–30%) by 2032 when the old-system stock peaks; the phase-3 stock of the new system has built up and the capacity per trainee has risen with the phased-in funding. Funding their services activates this capacity within one to four years without a single additional licensure (). The survey data add a second mechanism to this lever: trainees today work part-time in psychotherapy (), so insurance funding not only activates existing services but raises the services per trainee—in the model, from 0.60 to up to 0.90 of a fully active therapist—and the robustness analysis shows that the closure of the gap in Scenario B depends on this rise (). Without insurance funding of trainee services, the gap in Scenario B would not close in any year (). Insurance funding of trainee services is accordingly a lever that acts on both sides of the dual role at once and, in the model, within one to four years; however, under the current law, trainee services are not an insurance benefit (). Its effect is, however, time-limited by the transitional law: the old-system trainees complete by 2038, and the lever then depends entirely on the size of the new system’s phase-3 stock.

Two transition effects need to be separated. The classical ‘reform dip’—a temporary shortfall of licensures between the end of the old pathway and the ramp-up of the new—is, in the model, short and shallow: master’s entrants are licensed from 2031, the old pathway continues to deliver about 714 completions per year until 2038, and the licensed stock grows in all scenarios until then. The consequential effect is the transition cliff of 2038 created by § 60 PThG 2024: within two years, the old pathway’s completions and its supervised trainees (about 4200 at the 2032 peak) disappear; from 2039, the licensed stock shrinks, the trainee capacity falls to about a fifth to a third of its peak; and, in Scenario B, the closed care gap reopens (). The FTE calibration nevertheless shows that the care effect of this cliff is far smaller than its workforce effect wherever activation is high: in Scenario C, the gap stays closed with a 99% probability in 2040; in Scenario A, it widens by about 34,000 persons/year—not primarily because of the cliff but because activation remains low.

This is an important finding for health-policy prioritization: the reform dip of the early 2030s has been overestimated in the debate so far. At the same time, two other quantities have been underestimated—the short-term activation and funding question and the throughput of the new system (master’s places, phase-3 places) needed after 2038 in the long term ().

In the FTE model, psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics emerge as a central structural component for the activation question. They combine phase-3 training capacity with care provisions in one integrated institution and enable trainee services to be publicly funded—thus, they become simultaneously care effective and training supportive. The model makes the phase-3 place a binding constraint in the status quo scenario: any expansion of the master’s intake without additional places lengthens the queue rather than the workforce (); in Scenarios B and C, the places suffice for the current master’s intake but not for an expanded one. Compared with physician-led psychosocial centers, which primarily offer psychiatric care with subordinate psychotherapy, psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics address the specific structural gap between the training and care systems.

Within the scenarios, the retirement rate correlates only moderately with cumulative follow-on costs but strongly with the licensed stock and accessible capacity in 2040 (). In the health-policy debate, the retirement wave is often portrayed as the central risk factor. The FTE-calibrated simulation shows a more differentiated picture, namely retirements act via the stock → potential capacity → accessible capacity → care gap → costs, and with each retired therapist removing more accessible capacity, the higher the activation rate becomes; in the underfunded Scenario A, most potential capacity is not activated in the first place, so retirements hardly show in the cost balance. Moreover, until 2038, completions exceed retirements in every scenario, so the stock grows despite the aging profession; the retirement rate becomes decisive only after the transition cliff, when the new system’s throughput has to cover it alone.

This does not mean retirements are unimportant. Their significance lies more in the capacity base, in the post-2038 dynamics, and in demographic time-criticality than in the absolute level of follow-on costs. Methodologically, this teaches us not to confuse sensitivity analyses with importance analyses: a parameter can be structurally time-critical without appearing dominant in the sensitivity correlation.

The modeled cumulative difference in follow-on costs of roughly €82 billion (Scenario A minus Scenario C, 2026–2040) corresponds to an average annual difference of about €5.5 billion—about 1.1% of Austrian GDP (€494 billion in 2024). These figures denote avoided downstream societal costs and not net savings: the incremental implementation costs of Scenarios B and C—additional insurance expenditure for psychotherapy, outpatient-clinic expansion, remuneration of supervised trainees, additional master’s and phase-3 training places, and supervision—are outside the model’s scope and would have to be netted against the avoided costs in a full economic evaluation. This order of magnitude is consistent with European estimates: the OECD and the European Commission put the total cost of mental ill-health at more than 4% of GDP across the 28 EU countries—over €600 billion in 2015—of which about 1.6% of GDP are indirect labor-market costs and 1.3% direct health expenditure [].

The cross-check against Austrian secondary-cost data (, ) indicates that the model’s per-person cost parameters are low relative to this clinically selected high-utilizer population: observed per-patient costs in the high-utilizer population studied by Seitz et al. [] exceeded the model’s per-person cost assumptions (€5000–18,000 in total) by one to two orders of magnitude. Because this comparison population is a clinically selected high-utilizer group and not directly representative of the heterogeneous population constituting the care gap, these figures do not establish a strict lower bound; the finding nevertheless replicates, at the micro level, the macro-level thesis of this study: expenditure on psychotherapeutic treatment is small relative to the secondary costs it avoids.

International benchmarking of the Austrian activation gap is methodologically difficult because few countries systematically publish comparable data on computed care capacity (FTE) and socially accessible care. Nevertheless, the literature offers structural indications. Germany: In the German statutory system, with needs-based planning performed by the regional associations of statutory health insurance physicians, care is steered via practice seats. The 2017 structural reform was intended to shorten waiting times. Still, a practice-based cohort study found the average wait for a first consultation unchanged at about three weeks, and the interval between first contact and the start of treatment increased from about 18 to 20 weeks []; this indicates a likewise relevant activation gap albeit differently structured: the bottleneck is less the activation of existing capacity than the cap on insurance-funded seats. Switzerland: With the change to the prescription model on 1 July 2022, psychological psychotherapy is publicly funded on medical prescription rather than under delegation. Official monitoring shows how quickly a structural reform propagates: expenditure on psychological psychotherapy rose from CHF 528 million (2021) to an estimated CHF 922 million (2024), i.e., by about 20% per year, while the supplied full-time equivalents grew by roughly 35% between mid-2022 and mid-2023 []. The Netherlands: The Dutch system combines mandatory health insurance with stepped care levels (basis-GGZ, specialist GGZ). It achieves comparatively broad access, albeit under strict indication rules and capped session numbers []. The United Kingdom (IAPT/NHS Talking Therapies): The Improving Access to Psychological Therapies program (since 2007; NHS Talking Therapies from 2023) set out to train more than 10,500 new therapists and, by 2018, was treating over 560,000 patients per year, with routine outcome data obtained for 98.5% of them []; what is methodologically interesting is its combination of workforce expansion (tiered therapist qualifications) with a high activation—and yet the typical treatment duration is short, which, in the terms of our model, corresponds to a low treatment intensity.

The international comparison suggests that Austria’s activation gap falls within a range typical of mixed systems but is structurally unfavorable. Structural reforms, such as the Swiss prescription model or the British IAPT, show that a substantial increase in the activation rate is possible within a few years, each with specific trade-offs: in Switzerland, there was a strong cost increase; in the UK, there was a reduction in treatment intensity. An Austrian reform would have to address these trade-offs explicitly.

Using 9% of the population as the upper need estimate (mode 7.5% in the triangular distribution) follows the treatment-willingness operationalization by Dinhof et al. []. This quantity differs conceptually from epidemiological need (12-month prevalence of mental disorders requiring treatment, typically estimated at 15–20% in Austria) and from actual care demand (clinical indication × treatment motivation × availability).

The robustness analysis across 5%, 7.5%, 9%, and 12% need () shows that the qualitative scenario ranking is stable across all need levels. The absolute care gap and coverage, however, are highly sensitive: at 5% need, Scenario C could computationally exceed 100% coverage at current intensity, whereas at 12%, this was only about 51%. The choice of need operationalization is therefore a politically and scientifically important prior decision that must be made transparent.

The simulation results suggest the following conditional policy implications; their estimated effects depend on the assumed parameterization and have not been prospectively validated. They are model-based hypotheses that require empirical validation. (1) Activation as the time-critical lever: At the current treatment intensity, activating existing capacity has the strongest short-term effect; in the higher-intensity scenarios, a parallel capacity expansion would be required. Within the model’s assumptions, this points to fair insurance tariffs (raised to professionally justified fee levels), statutory-insurance contracting with outpatient clinics (including trainee services once § 135 ASVG has been amended), regional care planning, and reduced bureaucratic access barriers. (2) Insurance funding of supervised trainees’ services: The model results suggest recognizing and funding trainee services as care services from the moment the register listing takes effect (1 October 2026), most directly by amending § 135(1)(3) ASVG and the corresponding provisions for other insured groups (); in the model, this funding is the lever that closes the care gap in the partial-funding scenario by 2032. (3) Expansion of psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics with phase-3 capacity: Outpatient clinics—as hybrid structures of care and training—are, within the model’s parameterization, a central structural component; the results suggest expanding these within spatial–regional care planning, endowed with publicly funded quotas, and certified as core institutions of phase-3 training. (4) A monitoring system for FTE availability: Austria so far lacks systematic reporting of treatment hours, age structure, and activation rates in psychotherapeutic care; we therefore recommend annual monitoring of psychotherapeutic care capacity by BMSGPK and/or GÖG that records not only the number of registered psychotherapists but also full-time equivalents, age structure, retirements, training capacity, the number of trainees in specialist training under teaching supervision, care sector, and funding status as preconditions for evidence-based workforce planning. (5) Master’s and phase-3 capacity of the new system: At the current master’s intake of about 1000 per year (about 500 publicly funded places at public universities and an estimated 500 at private universities), the new system’s licensures (about 580–840 per year) fall short of retirements after 2038 in every scenario, such that the licensed stock shrinks; about 1500 master’s places per year with proportionally growing phase-3 places at universities, outpatient clinics, and teaching practices are, in the model, the intake at which the workforce keeps growing after the transition cliff ()—phase-3 places without master’s places are as ineffective as master’s places without phase-3 places, whose absence lengthens training through waiting times and reduces long-term output. (6) Periodic workforce and care projections: The present model could serve as the basis for periodic (e.g., biennial) updated projections as further primary data become available. (7) Insurance expansion as a demand-side measure: A substantial increase in publicly funded psychotherapy quotas would be the most direct form of activation increase and could simultaneously reduce social inequality in access to care.

The model has several substantial limitations that must be discussed explicitly. The FTE anchor is an empirical median: The 21 treatment hours/week [] are an empirical median, not a legally defined full-time equivalent; actual variability in the profession is considerable (part-time work, multiple employment, private practice); the model maps the median assumption, not the distribution. A weighted secondary analysis of the individual-level data of the ÖBVP member survey from December 2024 [] (listed practitioners only, post-stratified to federal-register margins; ) yields, for the same profession, an activity-adjusted weighted mean of 13.3 h/week across all listed practitioners and 15.8 h/week among contracted practitioners. The two figures do not measure the same construct—a median against a weighted mean and elicited treatment hours against treatment time isolated from a reported activity mix—and neither is a correction of the other. Because potential capacity scales linearly with this parameter, the capacity levels reported here should be read as upper bounds until the two instruments are reconciled: under the lower anchors, the median care gap no longer closes in Scenario B (15.8 h/week), nor at 13.3 h/week, even in Scenario C, and the cumulative follow-on costs rise accordingly (). Treatment intensity of 13 units/patient: This figure reflects the current value [] and presumably underestimates the treatment intensity required for many clinical pictures; assuming 30 units/patient, theoretical capacity falls to about 290,000 persons/year—a different and more realistic magnitude of the activation gap. Chronification modeling: Despite the three-variant approach, quantitative chronification dynamics by waiting duration remain a central uncertainty; empirically validated risk curves are urgently needed. No regional differentiation: The model operates at national level; considerable regional differences (Vienna versus rural federal states; care density, transport links, outpatient-clinic density) are not represented. Quality dimensions: the model maps capacities quantitatively, not qualitatively; it does not consider modality-specific fit, treatment quality, differential effectiveness, or indication decisions. No system-adaptation dynamics: The model assumes that actors (patients, therapists, institutions) do not react to the evolving care gap; in reality, price, substitution, and political adjustment effects would occur. Sensitivity analysis as a correlation measure: The within-scenario rank correlations in  capture monotonic relationships but no interaction effects, and they describe parameter uncertainty within a policy package, not the effect of choosing between packages; extended variance-based sensitivity analyses (Sobol indices, EFAST) would be useful in follow-up work. Trainee capacity: The treatment capacity of supervised trainees in the current unfunded state (60%, range 50–70% of a fully active therapist) is anchored on a stratified re-analysis of a single unweighted member survey, with a 43.5% response rate, categorical answers converted to category midpoints, and respondents who are younger and more active than the profession as a whole [] (); its rise to 90% (range 80–100%) under full insurance funding, the one-year lag, and the equal treatment of old-system and phase-3 trainees are expert assumptions of the authors. Because the trainee line contributes 18% of potential capacity in 2026 and up to 30% in 2032, this assumption sets the trainee effect level and the timing of gap closure in Scenario B (). A longitudinal measurement of trainees’ treatment hours before and after the register listing of 1 October 2026 is the single most important calibration task (). Training pipeline: The master’s intake (500 public places as a ministerial planning figure, 500 private places as an estimate), the direct entrants under § 10, the phase-3 duration and the lead time to full trainee activity are planning assumptions rather than observed values; the accelerated completion of all old-system candidates by 2038 follows the law and not observed behavior; the queue model assumes no drop-outs while waiting; and the propaedeutic candidates who switch to the master’s program are assumed to compete for the existing places. Need operationalization: The 9% treatment-willingness value is based on [] and is a model assumption; actual clinical need, epidemiological need, and treatment willingness can diverge considerably. Secondary-cost anchoring: The cross-check against Austrian secondary-cost data () relies on a clinically selected high-utilizer population [] and on aggregate statistics with reference years 2006–2016; it indicates that the cost parameters are low relative to this specific population but is not a formal cost-of-illness validation for the average person in the care gap.

The present simulation identifies several priority research needs: an empirical FTE survey with full coverage and distribution analysis (not only the median) of weekly treatment hours in the Austrian profession and of persons in training under supervision, extending the cross-sectional survey re-analysis of  into a panel that observes trainees before and after the register listing of 1 October 2026; differentiated measurement of activation rates by sector (insurance quota, self-payment, outpatient clinic, teaching practice); validation of the chronification–waiting time relationship in Austrian data (longitudinal study); measurement of actual waiting times by care sector and region; a cost analysis of specialist training under teaching supervision (cost per training place, funding requirements, economic viability of outpatient-clinic structures); an evaluation study of existing psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics in Austria (care quality, cost efficiency, training integration); system-dynamics modeling with explicit feedback loops (price–quantity effects, substitution dynamics); extended variance-based sensitivity analyses (Sobol indices); a comparative study of activation rates and funding models in Germany, Switzerland, and the Netherlands; and an analysis of regional care density and its FTE activation rates.

The present FTE-calibrated simulation model suggests a differentiated finding: at the current treatment intensity of 13 units per patient per year, psychotherapeutic care in Austria is limited primarily by the insufficient activation of existing capacity into socially accessible, publicly funded care and less by a shortage of psychotherapists in the narrow sense. The computed personnel capacity of about 669,000 persons/year contrasts with fully funded care of only about 96,500 persons (2022). The robustness analysis sharpens this finding for higher treatment intensities: in the higher-intensity scenarios of 30–40 units per patient per year (adequate intensity varies with diagnosis, severity and treatment modality), activation becomes necessary but is not sufficient; additional capacity expansion is therefore structurally required. Fewer weekly treatment hours have the same effect: because capacity scales linearly with the hours each therapist treats per week, the survey-based anchors of 15.8 and 13.3 treatment hours/week instead of 21 act like about 17 and 21 units/patient/year at the 21-h anchor, and the median care gap then no longer closes in Scenario B, nor at 13.3 h/week, even in Scenario C (, ); the reported capacity levels are therefore upper bounds.

The central health-policy thesis of the model can be stated as follows: investments in public funding, in psychotherapeutic outpatient clinics, in the insurance funding of supervised trainees’ services, and in master’s and phase-3 capacities are, in the scenario comparison, structural measures with high leverage on access and avoided downstream societal costs, whose implementation costs lie outside the model’s scope ()—with the activation dimension dominant in the short term and parallel capacity expansion becoming necessary in the medium to long term as treatment intensity rises.

In the most favorable scenario (expansion/full funding) and under the 21-h weekly-hours anchor, the care gap can be closed by 2028, with avoided follow-on costs of roughly €82 billion versus the status quo by 2040. Even in the moderate scenario (partial funding), the gap closes from 2032 to 2036 and is reduced by about 88% by 2040, with avoided follow-on costs of about €70 billion—in both cases largely by funding the services of trainees who already treat under supervision who today mostly work part-time and have capacity to spare. This trainee-capacity line rests on a single unweighted member survey and on expert assumptions about capacity under full funding; it is the first calibration priority once post-reform data become available. The reform dip of the early 2030s is shallow in the FTE model; the decisive transition effect is the cliff of 2038, when the old pathway’s completions and trainees disappear and the new system’s throughput—about 1000 master’s places per year today (about 500 publicly funded places at public universities and an estimated 500 at private universities), and about 1500 needed with matching phase-3 places—decides whether the workforce keeps growing. The methodological lesson of this study is that workforce models without FTE calibration and without three-level capacity differentiation miss the actual health-policy lever.

Beyond care provision, these findings also inform national research and training policy. The Austrian University Development Plans (GUEP 2025–2030 and GUEP 2028–2033) [,] do not address psychotherapy specifically, but they set the framework objectives—interdisciplinary competence, lifelong learning and international collaboration—within which the new university-based psychotherapy training will have to be situated; this perspective should also inform the reading of OECD indicators that portray Austrian outpatient care as capable of improvement.

Methodologically, the reported figures are scenario simulations under explicit assumptions and not empirical forecasts. Their main function is to structure the problem, identify critical decision points, and estimate orders of magnitude. The most urgent next research step is to deepen the calibration—particularly regarding activation dynamics, the chronification–waiting time relationship, and regional care. Austrian psychotherapeutic care stands at a reform-driven crossroads; decisions in the coming years—especially the funding structure—will determine the care situation up to 2040 and beyond.

psychology.title: “Maa. She is Me”: Gendered Emotional Climate in the Making of Therapists in India
psychology.abstract: In contemporary India, gendered injuries such as affinal violence, son preference, and female feticide may endure within families as mental distress among women. Drawing on twelve months of ethnographic fieldwork at a postgraduate counseling psychology program in Bangalore, this paper examines how trainees’ gendered subjectivities are shaped by growing up within what I call a gendered emotional climate: the durable affective condition that forms as the emotional circumstances of a household, where structural violence is absorbed into kinship, recur and settle over the long arc of growing up. Through a person-centered account of a trainee whose path to becoming a counselor was inseparable from her mother’s history of abuse and chronic distress, I argue that counseling training functions as a form of repair of the emotional climate. It sets in motion the processing of the psychic afterlives of gendered injury and equips trainees to partially rework the gendered emotional climate in their natal households. Training-mandated self-work thus becomes inseparable from filial work. Rather than isolating the subject from family life, counseling may cultivate an ethic of self-making that remains embedded in kinship while partly reworking inherited emotional worlds. This finding has significant implications for clinical understandings of the relationship between gender justice and mental health in post-liberalization India.
psychology.text:
On a late winter afternoon, six of us walked back to campus after a hearty lunch, hustling through the narrow lanes crowded with students, rickshaws, and motorbikes in southern Bangalore. Someone among us said, “Would you want to end up like your mother?” It was common for us—mostly women in our twenties—to have witnessed our mothers or aunts sacrifice their aspirations to take on care responsibilities. Identifying with mothers came with the possibility of identifying with the psychic afterlives of their gendered experiences. The question lingered in the air, charged with ambivalence. Such ambivalence is not incidental to kinship but constitutive of it, since kin relations bind persons through compelling and often contradictory moral claims (Peletz, ). For Natasha, like many of her classmates, this question would become the fulcrum of her self-work—the introspective practice mandated by her postgraduate training in counseling psychology at St Mary’s University. Through her story, this article explores how becoming a counselor in urban India is a deeply relational project of self-making. For women, who comprised the majority of trainees enrolled in the program, the work of self-making was intertwined with filial work.

Since the 1991 economic liberalization, there has been a feminized expansion of counseling and therapeutic self-work in urban centers, where therapy is becoming a recognized practice among the elite and middle classes (Roy, 2025b). According to the erstwhile dean of psychology at St Mary’s, the number of counseling programs in India increased from one to 25 between 2000 and 2016. This made counseling a distinctly generational profession. The significance of this study lies in showing that, in contemporary India, interventions against gender injustice remain incomplete if they do not attend to the psychic afterlives of son preference, affinal vulnerability, and ordinary domestic violence as they are lived within families and carried into the making of future practitioners of care.

The psychological pressures of patrilineal kinship and son preference are everyday conditions of life in much of North India, especially rural Haryana, where Natasha’s mother grew up. Women’s mental distress is rarely a purely individual experience but is instead an “intersubjective” phenomenon deeply rooted in the domestic sphere and thus transmitted into the felt emotional climate of the household. A primary idiom of distress is “tension” (tenshun), which serves as a dimensional category mediating between external structural stressors—such as poverty, debt, or family conflict—and internal pathological states (Simpson, , 1–26; Weaver & Karasz, ). For many women, this “tension” reflects the crushing weight of affinal vulnerability, a precarious social positioning where a wife’s security in her husband’s home is contingent upon her ability to "adjust" to the demands of her in-laws (Chua, ). In the wake of violent events like female infanticide and feticide, the spectral traces of gendered wounds seep into the everyday, as the afterlives of violence often do (Chatterji & Mehta, ; Das, ).

Pinto observes that affinal vulnerability—the inherent precariousness of a woman’s position in her husband’s household—remains a primary site of mental health crises, leading some scholars to characterize hysteria in India as "the wife’s disease." In many North Indian contexts, in-marrying daughters-in-law are often perceived as potential threats to the moral coherence of the patrilineage, making them uniquely vulnerable to psychological distress or “madness.” Symptoms such as “chakkar” (giddiness), “dissociative stupors,” or “clenched teeth” are frequently read by clinicians as manifestations of agency gone awry within the family. For many women, madness is a manifestation of the fragility of kinship bonds, where the fear of persistent dislocation and the potential loss of children are woven into the normal, if heightened, stresses of marital life. Women are forced to inhabit a psychological space where freedom can bleed into abandonment, and care is often inseparable from constraint (Pinto, ). These psychological spaces are charged with emotional climates that persist over long periods. To the married woman, it could be most of her married life, and to her children, most of their life at home may be characterized by such a persistent climate of distress.

The domestic environment in India represents a unique “zone of social abandonment” for the severely mentally ill. Unlike the Western model, where abandonment most often manifests on the street, in India, disordered individuals are frequently “hidden” within the family home to preserve family honor (izzat) (Marrow & Luhrmann, ). As we see in Jhumpa Lahiri’s ( [1999]) prose, this confinement is often an extension of “kin-work,” where the family struggles to inhabit a damaged world of broken bonds. Antiviolence counseling in Northern India operates by seeking to reorder, rather than eliminate, the hierarchical dependencies and interconnections that define a woman’s position within her family (Kowalski, ). With few emotional outlets available, the child may serve as the object of the mother’s unfulfilled desires; this can cause the child to feel like a “savior” for the mother, potentially transforming the “good mother” into a “bad mother” who is perceived as overwhelming or devouring (Kakar, , 89–92). Many of the counseling trainees I met during fieldwork were admittedly predisposed to a savior role in interpersonal relationships.

Most trainees enrolled in counseling training programs in India are women. Sociologist Anne Gagnant de Weck observes that the vastly disproportionate number of women enrolling in psychotherapeutic training and practicing as therapists is driven by a complex interplay of cultural stereotyping, economic expectations, and the unique gendered tensions of India’s transitioning society, making counseling a feminized profession in the subcontinent. Psychology is widely stereotyped as a feminine pursuit, thus making it difficult for men, who must bear the breadwinner burden, to pursue it. Psychotherapy, being a highly flexible practice, allows women (often the trailing spouse in a heterosexual marriage) to continue practicing it even as they move to accommodate their husbands’ careers in other fields like engineering, medicine, and corporate establishments. When women attempt to claim personal autonomy, choice, or happiness, it frequently triggers intense moral panics and family conflicts. They find in psychotherapeutic concepts a vital “laboratory” and a vocabulary to negotiate their own desire for individual agency, make sense of emotional distress, and create a space of their own (Gagnant de Weck, ). Course-mandated self-work partially converts gendered injury among trainees into internal resources.

This paper focuses on the effects of such internal resources, developed through training, on the emotional climate of mothering in the natal households of future mental health practitioners. According to psychoanalyst Sudhir Kakar, the mother helps the infant “learn to deal with anxiety without feeling devastated, and to temper and manage the inevitable feelings of frustration and anger” (, 55); for this reason, he urges anthropologists and psychologists to attend not simply to discrete maternal acts but to the “total emotional climate, the gestalt, of mothering” (, 55–56). The “good mother” in an Indian setting is normatively expected to be a nurturing, fear-dispelling presence. Her “hallowed presence” provides life-giving reassurance to the child, forming a bedrock of basic trust in the environment. The emotional climate of mothering is thus the mother’s presence as a whole human being, rather than just a provider of physical needs such as feeding or weaning (Kakar, ). This formulation is useful because it shifts analytic gaze away from a distressed mother as an isolated source of psychic injury and toward the larger affective field in which mother and child come to inhabit one another’s worlds. It also draws attention to the transmission of gendered harm in the form of a long-term felt condition for children.

In this paper, I extend Kakar’s formulation of the dyadic emotional climate between mother and child to what I call a gendered emotional climate. It refers to the enduring affective condition in which the mother’s subordinate status in a patrilineal setting shapes the emotional circumstances of the child’s development. This framing acknowledges that the mother’s capacity to soothe her child is associated with her position and overall gender norms in the household. Gendered wounds are often lived as diagnosed and undiagnosed forms of mental distress in mothers within families in South Asia (Clarke et al., ; Das et al., ; Nayar & Mehrotra, ). Female counseling trainees who grew up in difficult emotional climates related to the devaluation of daughters often share the suffering of their mothers. For the daughter, the mother is a significant source of the predominant cultural norms of femininity.

Anthropological and sociological scholarship has long cautioned that the spread of psy-knowledge individualizes structural problems, pathologizes ordinary distress, and produces governable, neoliberal selves (Furedi, ; Illouz, ; Rose, ). In Indian debates, these worries (Gooptu, ) converge with Hindu-nationalist critiques of psy-disciplines as solvents of collective life (Aggarwal, ). These critiques have force, but they often target therapeutic discourse rather than the neoliberal structures within which it operates, and risk obscuring the ways psy-concepts can also enable subjects to name, rather than internalize, the harms those structures inflict (Funahashi, ; Kitanaka, ). Vorhölter () argues for a “more-than-critique-anthropology” in her ethnography of the emergence of psychotherapy in Uganda; this approach takes practitioners’ visions seriously as one valid analytical perspective among others. Besides Vorhölter, I follow Duncan () in treating psy-globalization as a dual process: globalizing psy-ideas are transformative for and transformed by the contexts they enter. They articulate with political–economic projects and, at the same time, open sites where those projects can be commented upon and reworked.

I argue that training reframes maternal suffering from individual maternal failure (as mental illness often gets framed) to the psychic consequences of gendered violence, both symbolic (Morgan & Björkert, ) and physical. During mandated “self-work,” which is a key part of training as a counselor, childhood emotional climate becomes both an object of interpretation and an inner resource for care with transformative potential. Trainees are offered a framework for understanding the mother’s actions as the effects of gendered suffering rather than individual failure. Training thus cultivates a therapeutic self by transforming gendered subjectivity into a capacity for listening, reframing, and relational repair among kin. After discussing the method and context of my study, I will discuss the climate of mothering that Natasha experienced as it emerged during training. Then I will discuss how she worked on herself in relation to her mother during the program. The program facilitated new emotional climates both within and beyond the classroom. Following this, I will demonstrate the salience of focusing on mother–daughter relationships in patrilocal and patrilineal contexts marked by volatile emotions as a possible means of changing the gendered emotional climate of mothering. I conclude with clinical implications of the concept of emotional climate beyond my immediate field site and policy recommendations to address female feticide and infanticide.

My primary ethnographic field site was the postgraduate counseling training program of a leading private university in Bangalore, which I refer to as ‘St Mary’s University’ (hereafter ‘St Mary’s’), managed by an indigenous congregation. I participated in pedagogical activities, such as classes, conferences, seminars, and therapy simulations, as any student enrolled in the program would. My research design was assessed by the Norwegian Data Protection Services (Sikt) as having a legal basis to possess personal data. According to Article 6(1)(e) of the General Data Protection Regulation, the legal basis of processing personal data was the data subject’s consent.

My position oscillated between an observer who participated and a participant who observed. I conducted semi-structured interviews with sixteen counseling trainees and a few trainers. I maintained confidentiality across these relationships, since my role shifted between confidant to students and collaborator with instructors. While this analysis draws on these interviews, it follows a person-centered ethnographic approach that privileges depth over representational coverage (see also Hollan ). Natasha’s trajectory is examined in detail rather than abstracted from the interviews because it offers a particularly rich window into the processes of self-work, relational repair, and reinterpretation of maternal suffering that recur across multiple interviews (of trainees like Anirudh, Snigdha, Roshni, and Yamini mentioned in this paper). Natasha’s retrospective narratives, part of which were her accounts of her mother, were my objects of analysis. These narratives were an effect of the program, as it helped her interpret her relationship with herself and her mother. I make no claim to her mother Sarika’s experience, to which I have no independent access. I conducted member checking with Natasha, a key contributor to the data presented in this paper. I also conducted interviews with counselors (graduates of St Mary’s and other programs in major cities) who had recently started practice.

Only four of the 57 trainees in the cohort identified themselves as men, while the rest were women. All trainees, barring two outliers (who were 25 and 26), were between 20 and 22 years of age. The gendered nature of training’s effects on counselors’ lives led me to examine the continuum between being a daughter and being a counselor. This focus on the daughter–counselor continuum reflects the feminized composition of the cohort; how the same self-work bears on the gendered subjectivities of the male trainees—their work as men—lies beyond the scope of this article. It is a limitation and promising direction I flag for future research. Further, training operates in the interpretive and relational register, while leaving the consequential material conditions of gender injustice almost unchanged.

I lived alone in a one-bedroom rental apartment close to campus during my year of fieldwork. Classmates from St Mary’s often dropped by. To most of them, who lived in paying-guest facilities, my place, admittedly, felt like “home,” where they could spend time with their friends from class, away from the watchful eyes of hostel wardens or the invasive presence of roommates. Sometimes we had extended discussions, parties, movie nights, or we cooked together. Living alone near campus enabled forms of intimacy and conversation that would not have been possible in the program’s formal spaces. My apartment became a site of fieldwork, where trainees often continued the reflective and relational exercises initiated in class. It let me live with the inner worlds of my interlocutors, which was key to my primary interest—self-making practices in counseling training. Opening my home to trainees allowed me to notice the self-work that happened beyond institutional settings.

I approached Natasha’s story as a person-centered (Hollan, ; Levy, ) subjective account situated in a moral and historical field. This approach enables a researcher to take the symbolic and psychic labor of self-making seriously—how people work through past injuries, not in isolation but with relational responsibility toward others. Rather than a Western import or a local distortion, therapy emerged as a site where gradual, recursive self-making unfolds. A person-centered approach to ethnography allows us to dwell on the contradictions that emerge in ethical experiments in everyday life, rather than collapsing them into normative theories of personhood. I understand the core assumption of this method as:“Recognizing the multiplicity of human conditions, we affirm that our subjectivities and the moral processes in which we engage are forever in flux—[…] As our worlds change, […] they remake our most intimate inner processes: emotion, cognitive style, memory, our deepest sense of self.” (Kleinman & Fitz-Henry, , 55)

“Recognizing the multiplicity of human conditions, we affirm that our subjectivities and the moral processes in which we engage are forever in flux—[…] As our worlds change, […] they remake our most intimate inner processes: emotion, cognitive style, memory, our deepest sense of self.” (Kleinman & Fitz-Henry, , 55)

Person-centered ethnography is thus a powerful technique to analyze a process as intimate as the interlocutor’s metamorphosis of self.

My unit of analysis is the self-work of a trainee, or the intentional process of discerning and reflecting upon one’s own thoughts, emotions, and behavioral patterns during training. In its attention to how practitioners are formed, mine is an ethnography of clinical training in the sense of Luhrmann (), whose concern is with what young clinicians learn to notice and how they come to notice it rather than with the validity of any particular mode of treatment. Any ethnographic exploration of subjectivity needs to be linked to gender (Good et al., ) under prevailing normative orders. In my fieldwork, the practice of self-work is improvised within constraints—specifically, a patrilineal kinship system and the symbolic violence of rejecting female children. This allows for both continuity and change.

Natasha read out of her reflective essay on family in a Professional Development (PD, or process development) class: “To understand who I am, we need to understand [...] my mother.” [emphasis mine] She urged us to picture her mother, Sarika, as “a woman rocking a summer dress in her fifties”—a bold sartorial choice for a Haryanvi woman living with her in-laws in North India. This image contrasts Sarika’s younger self, “shipped off” according to Natasha, as a teenager from her natal village to her affinal kin in New Delhi, into a conservative multigenerational Baniya household, where she endured years of physical and emotional abuse from the matriarch, her mother-in-law, until she, along with her husband and children, moved out of Natasha’s ancestral home only a few years ago. The mother-in-law’s grip persisted over the emotional climate in the ancestral home, and Sarika still bore traces of the abuse. However, she was able to begin altering her emotional climate as a mother. By this time, Natasha was an adult and intimately familiar with the complex relationship of a bride with the mother-in-law in a climate of son preference.

Marriage is central to the identity of women in South Asia, as singlehood and divorce continue to be taboo (Lamb, ). The transition from natal to affinal household is riddled with hurdles for a bride in a patrilocal system. Traditionally, it has been challenging for most brides to find allies in their mothers-in-law. Incorporated as the 'gift' from bride-givers to bride-takers, the in-marrying bride enters as subordinate to a mother-in-law whose seniority confers authority, owing her service and deference, thus producing durable affinal asymmetries (Dube, ; Karve, ; Vatuk, ). However, this relationship is fluid, strategic, and rooted in material circumstances rather than timeless norms (Vera-Sanso, ). For instance, per Natasha’s account, her mother, Sarika, was able to create a condition free of fear and subordination after moving out of her mother-in-law’s household; an emotional climate that had long stifled her and her dependents began to change. Leaving the house was a change in material conditions that was perhaps as effective as, or even more effective than, any reinterpretation that psychotherapy offered.

Sarika’s subjectivity was shaped by long-standing patriarchal norms and gendered violence, all of which seeped into Natasha’s and her siblings’ affective experience of their mother. Natasha’s emotional climate growing up was volatile. Her father and sister were a passing source of stability. After the sudden demise of Sarika’s brother when Natasha was in fourth grade, Sarika entered a prolonged period of grief, often withdrawing into herself. The memory of her mother crying uncontrollably upon the children’s return from school remains etched in her mind as a ‘core memory,’ shaping Natasha’s inner world. Natasha recalled this as a time when her mother “was not herself.” This observation, grounded in her training, was not merely descriptive. For Natasha, “self” is a term infused with meaning—both a psychological construct and a professional tool, as the self is the primary instrument counselors use. Her mother’s fractured sense of self deeply shaped her own; Natasha admittedly had an “anxious attachment style” that, in her opinion, impeded her success in romantic relationships.

Natasha was far from the favored child: her brother Shashank, born with a speech impairment, received greater affection from Sarika, while Natasha felt she had to earn her mother’s love. Her sister Koyel—who unwound with Natasha through “emergency dance parties” during challenging times—served as a quasi-maternal figure, someone she even once wished on Mother’s Day. Sarika would have birthed a girl child when she conceived for a third time if not for the forced termination of her fetus following sex determination, which is an illegal but existing practice in several regions, especially northern and northwestern India. Sarika managed to keep the sex of her fetus from affinal kin for the first three months of her fourth pregnancy. That is how she was able to carry Natasha to term. Natasha learned about her family’s history of female feticide as an adolescent when, in a fit of rage, her mother retorted, “I should have aborted you when I could.” The remark left Natasha with a lasting feeling of rejection. By the end of Natasha’s reflective essay on family, which recounted the above details, Sarika’s emotional climate of mothering had moved many in the training cohort to tears. Sarika was both Natasha’s primary object of identification and a sustained source of emotional wounding.

Natasha brought glimpses of her mother’s various experiences of gendered injury into the classroom by sharing that her mother had a neurotic personality. According to the counseling curriculum, neuroticism, a personality trait rather than a mental health condition, is described as a frequent inclination toward negative emotions like anxiety, hopelessness, and sudden mood fluctuations. Sarika’s distress was inseparable from her subordinate position within the kinship system. Much of her distress may have been a form of coping with personal grief in a hostile affinal ecology of son preference. Take this verse from a Haryanvi folk song celebrating son preference, for example: “Suhagan gaavein, putar khilavein (the married women who sing receive sons).” (Toor, ).

Natasha’s eyes beam when she recounts how her father gave up karate after his first daughter was born. His karate practice involved the risk of physical injury. Natasha’s relationship with masculinity has been rough despite sharing a healthy relationship with her father. When Natasha was eight, a man masturbated to her in public while she was returning from school with her mother by a rickshaw—unfortunately, not an uncommon form of sexual harassment in New Delhi. At 12, her cousin sexually harassed her. Her ex-boyfriend, during her first experience of romantic touch, “realized” he is asexual after their first act of physical intimacy. Hence, touch has been a complex subject for her. Self-aware as most trainees were, Natasha associated her own anxious attachment style with the contradictory forms of masculinity she had experienced. She “sabotaged” her romantic relationships in the past—a pattern she is working on in her current relationship with Suman Lokhande, a fellow trainee, who, Natasha believes, “is more empathic than” her. Natasha and Sarika had both experienced emotional challenges that took sustained, deliberate effort to be overcome (Fig. ).

Natasha was no exception among her cohort in terms of intergenerational wounds. The following is an excerpt from her peer Susan Aleyamma Cherian’s reflection:

Susan’s amma (mother), besides receiving differential treatment from Susan’s ammachi (paternal grandmother in this case, although the term is also used to address mother and maternal grandmother among Malayali), was depressed and had lost her parents early in her life. In her essay, Susan is explicit about how her amma’s distress had an impact on the relationship between them. All her life, Susan was cautious about sharing her “sad stories” with her amma so as not to aggravate her suffering or contaminate the prevailing gendered emotional climate that the household was accustomed to. She described her ammachi’s differential treatment of her mother “as usual in almost all Indian homes” (Fig. ). The persistent tension in this relationship is a common theme in South Asian tales and folklore. For instance, the lyrics of a Haryanvi folk song—sung on the festival Teej in the month of Saaman when married women sing and swing in groups awaiting their brothers’ kothli (gifts)—loosely translate to the following:Bed batade sasu reshmi ri— (Plait a silken rope, dear mother-in-law—)Aari ghalwade baag ke beech, (In the middle of the garden…)Baag jhulan heri jaan de ri. (…get it hung.)Kun je ghale teri jhool ne he (To swing in the garden, let me go!) […]Bed batadu bahu reshmi he— (Plait a silken rope I can, dear daughter-in-law—)Aaye ghalwadu mahal ke beech. (In the middle of the mansion, I can get it hung.)Baag jhulan ki to taal se he. (To swing in the garden, you cannot go!)Lal gaya pardes me he, (My dear son has gone to a distant land.)Aaye bahu log karenge takraar. (O daughter-in-law, people around will create a scene.)Baag jhulan ki to taal se he. (To swing in the garden, you cannot go!)(Toor, )

Bed batade sasu reshmi ri— (Plait a silken rope, dear mother-in-law—)

Aari ghalwade baag ke beech, (In the middle of the garden…)

Baag jhulan heri jaan de ri. (…get it hung.)

(Toor, )

Sarika was not simply the source of distress; she was herself immersed in and formed by a climate of subordination that exceeded her (Bourgois, , 284–285). In Natasha’s case, what mattered was not only Sarika’s speech, moods, or decisions taken in isolation, but the total emotional climate in which mothering took place: affinal violence, unresolved grief, son preference, sibling differentiation, sexual threat, and the everyday vulnerability of being a daughter in a patriarchal kinship order.

Following Jenkins (), emotion need not be treated as a process sealed within the 'box' of the psyche; it can instead be understood as an atmosphere that traverses the space and time of bodily longing, memory, gendered power relations, and psychic conflict. Feeling, in this view, is not only something that radiates outward from a bounded self, but a shared socioemotional space of power and position to which kin become attuned. This is why Natasha’s childhood is better understood not as life with a “difficult mother” but as life inside a gendered emotional climate in which her mother’s suffering, her grandmother’s authority, her father’s relative tenderness, her brother’s favored status, and the spectral presence of the aborted female foetus all coexisted and pressed upon her. As Wu () notes in the context of China, intimate feelings are inseparable from wider structures: what was lived as volatility or neuroticism within the family was intertwined with longer histories of patriarchy, affinal domination, and daughter devaluation.

On a November evening, Natasha and her peers, Anirudh, Snigdha, and Roshni, gathered in my living room. After cooking, dining, doing the dishes, and intermittently using the fan as the temperature fluctuated, we sat around my low round coffee table. The conversation drifted gradually toward marriage. Marriage was no longer a compulsion for most trainees, as it had been for their parents, especially their mothers. So, when relatives asked when Koyel would get married, their parents defended her. Natasha’s mum often said, “She is happy; how many of us can say that about our lives?” After recounting this, Natasha remarked that the generation before her “just got married because they had to and stayed married because they had to.” “All Indian families,” remarked Anirudh. What appear as low divorce rates in India are less signs of marital stability than outcomes of dense moral, economic, and gendered constraints that make leaving both difficult and consequential (Pinto, ). Together, the trainees were beginning to attune to feelings that eventually settled as shared feelings that pervaded their emotional climates in Bangalore. They recognized and named patterns of the reproduction of gendered injuries. Training signaled that subjects with some agency could transform the emotional climate around them.

Natasha and Snigdha shared that they were disturbed by their respective grandmothers' opinions. Both normalized domestic violence against wives by husbands. Natasha was uncomfortable with her dadi (paternal grandmother) eating from dadu’s (paternal grandfather’s) used plate after he had finished his meal. Natasha “protested a hundred times” against her dadi’s practice. Snigdha noted how when she first got her period, maa (meaning mother, a term she used to address her dadi) commanded her to maintain rules of purity and pollution, for instance, not to enter the kitchen when menstruating. Despite acting out of habitual disposition in matters concerning the self and the daughters-in-law, grandmothers were affectionate toward their grandchildren. The emotional patterns reproduced at specific spaces (Reckwitz, ), in this case, the patrilocal household, sustained both adoration and resentment in the gendered emotional climate of growing up.

The shift in thinking about family life, shaped by structural constraints, was consequential. It helped trainees see their mothers and grandmothers less as troubled individuals and more as inhabitants of a gendered emotional climate: the felt condition of constraint, grief, and subordination that patrilineal kinship produces inside domestic space. For Natasha, becoming a counselor involved confronting intergenerational family climates of violence and suffering. Like many of her classmates, Natasha reconfigured relational subjectivities intertwined with modes of kinship and care. She tapped into her potential to break the pattern, referring, among other things, to moral injuries to the gendered self (in this case, Natasha and her mother) in patrilocal emotional climates. Breaking the pattern here does not mean severing ties or breaking up families. It refers to the (partial) breaking of relationships between individuals. It breaks away not from family members but from ways of relating to them that sustain moral injuries, and what is an emotional climate if not a sustained mode of relating to the other?

Rather than merely learning therapeutic techniques, trainees are expected to undertake sustained self-work. Not only do these practices build skill, but they also cultivate specific ethical subjectivities characterized by empathy, reflexivity, and emotional regulation. At St Mary’s, trainees were theoretically trained in empathy and its various types, including additive and subtractive empathy. Instructors in their skills labs urged students to practice empathy in interactions with clients. The effects of self-work at St Mary's went beyond individual trainees. By naming the emotional climates of their upbringing—the volatility, the grief, the gendered silences—trainees began to alter those conditions, not only for themselves, but for the kin they carried into the room. The program facilitated new emotional circumstances, or climates, both within and beyond the classroom. These climates mattered because, sustained and repeated, they began to recompose the gendered emotional climate that trainees carried from their natal households. I foreground this durable change as the work of relational repair; more reflexive practice and more livable intimate lives follow from it as secondary effects. These effects were uneven but observable across the cohort.

In the PD batch I attended, Bella, an American instructor from Texas, said, “We wouldn’t be in this profession if we weren’t empathetic people.” The person-centered argument that counselors must be empathetic was implied, but trainees were taught how to express empathy as counselors to help heal clients. I understand this ineffable “effect”—not the feel of a single session but the durable affective baseline that sustained therapy works to shift—as emotional climate. Self-work emboldened Natasha to cultivate a self who would be open to the possibility of a romantic relationship with a man. Training is a moral laboratory (Mattingly, ) that lets Natasha try out new ways of being a daughter, this time with the possibility of becoming a therapeutic self. It is her renewed attempt at being her mother’s daughter, in turn creating a second chance at mothering for her mother. Their deeply moral and relational process of self-making, in the words of Veena Das (, 61), is “the limit at which the self separates into that which can be destroyed and that which must endure.” What does storying do for the trainees? A practitioner’s painful memories are not obstacles to care but its very medium (Chapman,  blurring of patient and healer that, in Natasha's case, extended to her mother.

Natasha’s self-work did not stop at the mother–daughter relation. While self-work did not dissolve the limits her family imposed on her sexuality, for instance, training gave Natasha a means to live within these constraints differently. Her intercaste relationship with Suman—kept hidden from her biological family, navigated through the borrowed domestic space of my apartment—represented a parallel practice of kinning (Howell, ), one in which the values learned in counseling replaced caste as the organizing logic of intimacy. Drawing boundaries here did not mean severing family ties but gradually choosing proximity to some relations and distance from others with an intentionality that training had made possible. Suman and Natasha delicately navigated the nuances of intimacy and the space between them.

Over years of therapy, Natasha partially reshaped her selfhood in the directions she wanted. She continues to negotiate her way toward the person she wants to be—the one most aligned with her vision of the future—and, as her training recommends, an authentic version of herself. For instance, she overcame her fear of men and went on to see a male therapist. It was a milestone in her personal journey to becoming a counselor. Her emotional climate around men who were not her father was warming up. She believed she could look back on her choice of a male counselor as evidence of practicing what she “preaches” when she would encourage a future client to overcome fears. Drawing parallels with confessional modes, trainees are required to articulate inner truths to supervisors and peers, rendering their emotional climates alterable. The measures of such self-cultivation may not conform to normative expectations of particular gendered, caste, or class relations. Thus, counseling training is not simply professional education; it is a unique disciplinary and ethical project that recognizes trainees as both long-term subjects and agents of relational repair.

Natasha proudly recounts how Sarika, who never attended college, has three children with postgraduate degrees. To Natasha, her siblings’ formal education is a step in the right direction. Despite early injuries, Natasha’s self-work was saturated with her mother’s presence. She wrote,“Maa. She is me. Or I am her. By some unexplainable science, we have the same heart.”

“Maa. She is me. Or I am her. By some unexplainable science, we have the same heart.”

This is not a description crafted over “a weekend of introspection” of what growing up in a gendered emotional climate does: it produces a self inseparable from the relational conditions of its formation. Neither was Natasha’s identification with Sarika an evidence of failed separation. As Martin () argues, the infant does come to develop a sense of being separate, but this differentiation is never final or complete; it remains a form of separateness constituted in relation to the caregiver. Natasha’s self-work thus did not require detaching from her mother so much as renegotiating the terms of that relation. Natasha and Sarika do not simply share memories or traits; they share an emotional climate to which they were both porous, one that women in patrilocality are especially susceptible to. This confluence between Natasha’s self and her mother’s self is generative. It shows that Natasha moves between unity and separation, drawing the boundaries of selfhood to varying degrees and in different contexts. Natasha’s therapeutic engagement did not aim to detach from Sarika but, in counseling terms, to ‘re-story’ their intertwined lives. Thus, it redrew how they related to each other, and how strongly the spectral traces of an unborn girl would resonate between them.

Natasha addressed the learned victimhood in her mother. To her, Sarika was at once an aspirational ideal and a cautionary tale. She respected her mother’s resilience despite the repeated hardships she endured. She explained to Sarika the possibilities within her kinship framework, considering her husband and mother-in-law, both of whom were placed higher in the kinship hierarchy than she was. She did not have to sever ties with her in-laws or lead a family life isolated from her sense of self. She learned to live with ambiguity, not by detaching from kinship, but by relating differently within it. If kinship is a practice, then it is both structured and structuring (Bourdieu, ; Lahire, ). The grammar of North Indian kinship is the structure, while a relationship’s evolving emotional dispositions are the forces that structure it.

A parallel pattern surfaced in my interview with Yamini, a 22-year-old trainee from Tamil Nadu. She described teaching her mother techniques she had learned in class. “I have literally trained my mother to be another counselor,” she said. Yamini also reported that her mother’s relationships with her own mother-in-law and husband had eased as her mother began considering others’ perspectives in ways she had not previously. The reach of this repair was confined to Yamini’s mother: “I've tried my dad…did not work. My sister…did not work. Grandfather is like an extreme level, can’t change him at all.” Yamini's mother, too, was unsettled rather than simply gladdened, telling Yamini, “I have changed so much because of you… I don't know whether I should be happy or sad about it.” The gendered emotional climate of mothering, then, could be reworked across regional kinship grammars, but this reconfiguration was uneven, and not always experienced as welcome by those it touched.

Repairing a gendered emotional climate does not mean dismantling the kinship structure that generated it. The present terms governing relations among household members vary depending on how one person addresses another, what can be said aloud, and, most importantly, what is classified as an individual member’s failing. It means durably reworking the relations and habits through which the emotional climate is sustained. Much of Sarika’s affliction, which was a symbol of a disordered kinship, was mitigated by reworking familial ties like pieces of a puzzle that fit within the board, not by isolating or trying to fit a piece into another puzzle altogether. Therapeutic repair is set in motion by reinforcing the value of care back into kin networks (Kowalski, ). Similarly, Natasha tried to rework her inherited wounds into future-oriented forms of care. Her emotional labor in this repair work was facilitated by course-mandated self-work, which included at least 10 sessions of personal therapy and various reflective exercises, such as journaling and instructor-assigned introspective dialogs. By addressing the fractures in her selfhood, Natasha addressed the fracture in her mother’s sense of self and their mutual network of kin. For instance, she psycho-educated her family about how to navigate lingering interpersonal feelings. As the self is relationally constructed (Csordas, ), so is its fracture and, in turn, repair.
