Despite the conceptual richness, critical structural weaknesses persist. This scoping review identified a pronounced ‘hourglass’ pattern of theoretical integration across the design lifecycle. This theoretical gap suggests that although system intent and outcome assessment are theoretically informed, the construction of system logic, data structures and testing protocols is frequently driven by pragmatic or ad hoc technical decisions. As Goode et al argued, the absence of a continuous theoretical thread undermines the alignment between identified user needs and the final technical artefact. The application stages and rationale illuminate this gap. During the design phase, frameworks, such as TDF, Technology Acceptance Model and systems thinking, were used to support user-centred design and enhance the usability, accessibility and appropriateness of reporting protocols and interfaces.
 The implementation phases benefited from the HFE and Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), which facilitated the understanding of contextual enablers and barriers.
 Behavioural theories further support the identification of social and psychological determinants that influence reporting behaviours.
 Evaluation and monitoring were most strongly represented by frameworks, such as Reason’s model, Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) and the Harm Susceptibility Model applied to assess reporting processes and risk patterns.

 Although these frameworks enhance retrospective analysis and learning, their dominant use in the evaluation stage reinforces the field’s reliance on explanatory rather than predictive approaches.

Behavioural theories were the most frequently represented theoretical approaches in HIRLs. In particular, the TPB and TDF confirm that incident reporting is primarily conceptualised as a human behavioural challenge rather than a purely sociotechnical one. Studies using these frameworks– moved beyond interface-level concerns to interrogate socio-psychological determinants. This emphasis aligns with Trifiletti et al, who argued that effective interventions must be grounded in a theory capable of explaining the mechanisms of behavioural change. Importantly, these findings reinforce the notion that the intention to report does not automatically translate into actual reporting behaviour, highlighting the need for system-level enablers and sustained user engagement. Moreover, the application of HFE, systems thinking and the SEIPS model is consistent with the sociotechnical perspective on patient safety.
 These frameworks conceptualise safety and performance as emerging from interactions among person, task, physical environment, technology and tools and the organisation of work rather than just resulting from individual-level factors.
 Their application supports a more holistic approach to HIRL design and implementation, ensuring that requirements extend beyond just user motivation. This includes system usability, accessibility, task alignment and organisational contexts, for example, governance, feedback mechanisms, resources and healthcare employee capacity building to act on effective reporting incidents.

In terms of level of integration, most of the included studies demonstrated the ‘Full Integration’ of TFs, applied philosophies and models indicating increasing methodological rigour and a move away from superficial theory application into HIRLs research.
 Hybrid approaches, such as combining HFE with CFIR, exemplified this maturation. However, 10 studies were classified as partially integrated and one study superficially integrated, highlighting the ongoing challenges in fully operationalising the theory. This observation aligned with concerns highlighted by Peerally et al regarding the implementation of patient safety tools without sufficient consideration of their underlying principles and contextual requirements.

This limitation is compounded by extreme fragmentation across the evidence base. Majority frameworks (20 of 28 studies) were unique models that were applied only once, preventing the development of shared, validated analytical tools. This fragmentation directly undermines analytical capacity and standardisation. Explanatory frameworks were the most frequently used in 10 studies, whereas predictive frameworks remained scarce in three studies, reinforcing a retrospective orientation towards understanding past events rather than predicting risk. Consequently, the lack of robust data collection and analytical tools limits scalability and generalisability, particularly given the strong focus on the evaluation of 12 studies and localised design interventions in seven studies ().

The strength of this scoping review includes the methods adhered via the rigorous guidance of the JBI and Arksey and O’Malley framework. A comprehensive search strategy encompassing academic databases, manual search using Google Scholar, grey literature and citation tracking was used. Although data extraction and synthesis were conducted by one reviewer (AAB), bias was reduced through regular debriefings with the research team (CAO’D and PB) and verification of a sample of extracted data. The theory underpinning each included study was identified and then mapped to Goode et al’s systems thinking framework and identified which parts of HIRLs development.

Nevertheless, this study has some limitations. The evidence base was geographically concentrated in the USA (25%) and the UK (17%), constraining global generalisability. Reporting cultures are deeply embedded in local, legal, professional and hierarchical contexts, meaning that Western models may not fully translate into other settings. In addition, reliance on academic publications may exclude internal healthcare industry design manuals and proprietary frameworks. The observed ‘middle-stage gap’ may also reflect reporting bias, whereby theoretical input during technical design was undertaken but insufficiently documented. Finally, the classification of integration levels inherently involves some subjectivity, despite the use of established criteria. In clinical practice, this review underscores the necessity of integrating multiple theoretical perspectives to address the psychological, organisational, technical and system-level determinants of incident reporting. The identified frameworks (see ) directly support user-centred design, targeted training, cultural change, resource allocation and continuous feedback mechanisms, demonstrating tangible real-world utility.

Future studies should prioritise bridging the theoretical gap across the design and testing phases of HIRLs. Studies must explicitly document how the HFE, Cognitive Task Analysis and systems thinking approaches inform technical specifications and data collection protocols. Thus, there is a clear need to move from explanatory models towards predictive approaches. Integrating behavioural theory with quantitative and machine learning techniques, such as k-nearest neighbour algorithms offers a pathway for transforming incident reporting from a retrospective function into a proactive early warning system.

Another interpretation around the use of theory is that there is no real consistency or even comment on which theories are best suited to this topic. The theories identified are broad and diverse, almost as if there is a ‘wild west’ approach to considering which theoretical underpinnings are potentially useful in this domain. Future researchers should begin to critically explore the utility and usefulness of underpinning theory in the design, implementation and evaluation of HIRLs over time.

It is also equally important to expand stakeholder inclusivity. Although pharmacists and nurses comprised the primary participant group of studies, the development of genuinely ‘high-level’ requirements necessitates active engagement from physicians, managers and administrative leaders, and other stakeholders. Finally, extending the research to low- and middle-income countries is essential for adapting and validating frameworks across diverse cultural and organisational contexts.

This scoping review provides a comprehensive and integrated map of the TFs, applied philosophies and models underlying the design, implementation and evaluation of HIRLs. Although the field demonstrates increasing methodological maturity and theoretical diversity, the persistent absence of theory during the core technical stages poses a substantial risk to system effectiveness. Addressing this ‘middle gap’ through lifecycle-based, predictive and context-sensitive theoretical integration is critical if HIRLs evolve from passive data repositories into dynamic engines of organisational learning, and sustained patient safety improvement.

psychology.title: From pseudo-haptic weight to product meaning: an integrative review of mediated perception, semantic activation, and judgment
psychology.abstract: Digital and immersive media increasingly allow people to inspect and manipulate products without receiving the forces that normally accompany physical handling. This creates a psychological problem: how does a digitally generated cue become a felt weight and then an abstract judgment? This integrative review synthesizes a bounded corpus of 56 publications across sensory and consumer psychology, haptic perception, embodied cognition, learned expectancy, semantic activation, and virtual-reality pseudo-haptics. A structured evidence audit separates cue generation, perceived weight, product-specific semantic activation, diagnostic inference, and downstream judgment, while distinguishing direct or near-direct quality evidence from value, preference, comfort, portability, stability, and other outcomes. Within this corpus, direct or near-direct weight-quality evidence is limited to a small subset, so favorable heavy or light effects should not be relabeled automatically as quality effects. The evidence does not support a general heavier-is-better rule. Heaviness can imply solidity, durability, quantity, or premiumness, whereas lightness can imply comfort, portability, user-friendliness, or, in some categories, advanced engineering. Embodied cognition explains why bodily weight experiences can transfer to abstract judgment but is not sufficiently specific to explain category-dependent reversals. Learned expectancy helps explain how prior knowledge can bias perceived heaviness, semantic activation explains how the same percept can make different concepts accessible across product categories, and haptic diagnosticity specifies when weight information is likely to be used. Integrating these accounts, the review uses product-specific weight semantics as an organizing construct for learned category knowledge linking heaviness or lightness to diagnostic attributes; a product-specific weight-quality schema is the narrower case in which those meanings inform perceived quality. Pseudo-haptic methods are theoretically useful because they can vary perceived weight while physical mass is held constant, allowing tests of sensation-to-meaning translation in mediated environments. The review develops a process model and research program that separates manipulation validity, perceived weight, semantic activation, diagnostic attribute inference, and causal effects on judgment.
psychology.text:
Consumers rarely evaluate products through vision and verbal information alone. Sensory marketing research conceptualizes sensory cues as inputs that shape perception, judgment, and behavior, including consumers’ self-generated inferences about abstract product properties such as sophistication and quality (). Related reviews of sensory package design and touch research likewise place haptic cues within product perception and judgment rather than treating them as merely design variables (; ). Haptic information is particularly important when product evaluation depends on material properties that cannot be fully inferred visually. , for example, identified texture, hardness, temperature, and weight as product attributes for which touch can be diagnostic, while  showed that physical examination is especially influential when preferences depend on material rather than geometric product properties. From this perspective, touch is not simply experiential enrichment; for many products, it is information.

Weight is a theoretically distinctive haptic cue because it has both a direct physical meaning and a learned symbolic meaning. A consumer can use weight to judge how heavy an object is, but the same cue can also imply density, capacity, sturdiness, abundance, premiumness, or technological inefficiency. Studies across food packaging, restaurant settings, product design, retailing, and advertising demonstrate that weight can migrate into evaluations that are not intrinsically about mass (e.g., ; ; ; ). At the same time, the direction of these effects is not uniform. A heavier wine bottle or restaurant menu may convey higher quality or premiumness, whereas a heavier-looking portable product can be evaluated less favorably because heaviness conflicts with portability (; ).

The question becomes more consequential as product evaluation moves online and into immersive media. Traditional e-commerce removes direct physical contact, and even immersive VR does not automatically reproduce forces consistent with an object’s apparent mass. Nevertheless, human-computer interaction (HCI) research has developed pseudo-haptic techniques that manipulate the relationship between users’ physical actions and the visual responses of virtual objects. Control-display (C/D) ratios, perceptible tracking offsets, altered rotational dynamics, and related techniques can make virtual objects feel heavier or lighter without changing their physical mass (; ; ; ).

These two literatures—consumer meaning of weight and technological simulation of weight—historically advanced largely in parallel, but that separation is now less complete.  show that VR control can change perceived product weight and product evaluation, with the preferred direction reversing between products for which heaviness is a positive versus negative attribute. More directly,  show that pseudo-haptically induced heaviness can affect scarcity valuation and purchase intention and can raise hedonic and utilitarian value for products in which greater weight is associated with higher value. These studies make a broad claim that “virtual weight affects product evaluation” insufficiently novel. The sharper question is how a virtual weight percept becomes a product-specific meaning—such as durability, stability, premiumness, portability, comfort, advanced engineering, or quality—and which of those meanings actually drives consumer judgment.

The resulting problem is psychological rather than primarily managerial. It is also a media-psychology problem because an interactive medium can alter the sensorimotor contingency through which a cue is delivered while leaving the represented product visually unchanged. The key explanatory sequence is how a digitally specified sensorimotor relation becomes a percept, how learned category knowledge changes the interpretation of that percept, and how the activated meaning enters judgment. Virtual product interaction is especially useful for this question because pseudo-haptic techniques can manipulate perceived weight without changing physical mass. The topic therefore sits at the intersection of perception, cognition, human-computer interaction, and media psychology, with product evaluation serving as a consequential judgment domain rather than as the theoretical endpoint.

This review has three aims. First, it separates claims that are often treated as interchangeable: whether weight is perceived, whether weight changes a judgment, whether a heavier or lighter state is preferred, whether that direction is quality-diagnostic, and which specific meaning carries the effect. Second, it compares the explanatory roles of embodied cognition, semantic activation, learned expectancy, and haptic diagnosticity instead of treating any one account as sufficient. Third, it develops a process-level account of pseudo-haptic weight in which virtual sensation can reactivate learned product knowledge. The central construct is product-specific weight semantics, defined as learned category knowledge about what greater or lower weight signifies for a focal product; product-specific weight-quality schema is treated as the narrower quality-focused case.

This article is an integrative, theory-building Review rather than a Systematic Review or quantitative meta-analysis. Its purpose is to connect literatures that have developed at different levels of analysis - physical and visual weight cues, haptic information use, abstract embodied effects, perceptual expectancy, digital compensation, and pseudo-haptic weight generation - and to identify where their explanatory claims converge or diverge. Accordingly, the review does not estimate an average effect size, make prevalence claims, or use the composition of the literature set as evidence that one direction of effect is more common.

Literature for this integrative review was identified primarily through iterative keyword-based searches in Google Scholar and Web of Science, conducted from approximately May to September 2026; the final search took place in September 2026. Terms were used individually and in combinations, including “weight perception,” “product weight,” “pseudo-haptic weight,” “virtual reality weight,” “haptic perception,” “consumer judgment,” “perceived quality,” “embodied cognition,” and “semantic activation.” Full texts were accessed through publisher and institutional resources; for some articles, Qingli Academic (青梨学术) provided by the author’s university was used as a full-text access route rather than as a separate bibliographic database. The aim was to assemble a theoretically relevant corpus, not to conduct an exhaustive or preregistered systematic review.

The bounded core corpus contains 56 published works represented in the reference list. A publication was retained for the core synthesis when it directly informed at least one link in the focal psychological sequence: (a) a physical, visual, observed, numeric, or virtual weight cue; (b) perceived heaviness or mass; (c) a product-specific semantic or diagnostic inference; (d) an abstract or product judgment; or (e) a pseudo-haptic technique capable of manipulating or validating perceived weight. Consumer studies were retained when weight functioned as an explanatory cue; human-computer interaction studies were retained when the manipulation or validation concerned perceived mass or weight; and mechanism studies were retained when they clarified embodiment, expectancy, semantic activation, haptic diagnosticity, or causal-process testing. Work focused only on physical load, generic motor effort, or immersive presence without a weight-perception link was outside the focal synthesis.

The corpus is intentionally purposive rather than exhaustive. Because it was not assembled as a preregistered systematic search, the review does not report PRISMA counts or imply that all eligible studies in every database were captured. This design choice is consistent with the theory-building objective but places a clear boundary on claims of completeness. The review therefore reports the selection logic and analytic framework used for the bounded corpus rather than retrospective search counts that cannot be verified.

Additional references are cited selectively where they provide contextual evidence for adjacent visual-semantic phenomena; these sources were not included in the structured coding or evidence-stream counts of the bounded 56-publication core corpus.

The synthesis uses a stage-based conceptual coding scheme. Each publication was coded by literature stream, weight type, direction or valence, whether perceived weight was measured, the status of the outcome with respect to quality, the primary mechanism lens, relevant boundary conditions, and the link in the proposed process that it could inform. Quality outcomes were separated into direct or near-direct quality evidence, quality-related proxies such as price, value, premiumness, preference, or general evaluation, other diagnostic attributes such as durability, stability, comfort, portability, density, or volume, and studies with no quality outcome. A separate claim-boundary code recorded what each study could not establish. This calibration step was used to prevent three recurrent inference jumps: from preference or value to perceived quality, from a product-by-weight reversal to semantic activation, and from a technically valid virtual-weight illusion to a consumer judgment mechanism. Within the bounded 56-publication corpus, four works were coded as direct or near-direct evidence involving quality; the remainder primarily informed proxies, other attributes, mechanisms, or methods. This count is descriptive of the selected corpus and is not an estimate of prevalence in the wider literature.  summarizes the four evidence streams used in the integration.

Four evidence streams in the bounded review corpus.

A recurring finding across consumer and sensory research is that weight becomes a cue for attributes that are not equivalent to physical mass.  manipulated the weight of otherwise similar bowls and found changes in perceived food density, liking, and expected price. In a related study,  showed that heavier containers increased expected satiety, perceived density, and expected fullness.  demonstrated that container weight can bias judgments of volume, implying that consumers use weight as a heuristic when other attributes are uncertain.

These effects also occur when multiple sensory cues are present.  showed that package weight interacted with color and fragrance intensity in shaping judgments of liquid bath soap, underscoring the fact that weight is embedded in a broader multisensory configuration rather than processed in isolation.  likewise found that cutlery weight, size, shape, and color altered taste- and value-related judgments, but the direction of the weight effect was expectation-dependent. Such findings are theoretically valuable because they show that a simple monotonic account of weight is inadequate.

Weight can also influence downstream economic responses.  found that packaging weight influenced flavor-related evaluations and, through those evaluations, desire and willingness to pay.  reported that heavier cutlery improved diners’ evaluations and willingness to pay in a realistic restaurant context.  moved beyond product evaluation and showed that haptic heaviness can influence preferences for combined versus partitioned pricing through processing ease. Collectively, these studies support a general proposition: consumers use weight as an inferential input to judgments that extend beyond weight itself.

Within the bounded corpus, the direct or near-direct weight-quality subset is small and heterogeneous.  documented a market-level association between wine-bottle weight and price and discussed weight as a possible extrinsic cue to price and quality.  linked heavier restaurant menus to more upscale impressions and higher expected service quality.  reported a broader economic association between product weight and inferred quality across narrowly defined varieties, with meaningful category exceptions.  provide the clearest consumer-level evidence in this subset, showing that heavier wine bottles were associated with higher perceived quality and price, with consumer knowledge or expertise acting as a boundary condition.

These studies differ in what they can establish. The bottle-weight evidence from  is correlational,  concerns inferred economic quality rather than an experimental consumer judgment, and  examine expected service quality in a restaurant context rather than perceived construction quality of the weighted object itself. They nevertheless show that consumers can encounter stable category regularities in which heaviness co-occurs with higher-end positioning, making learned weight-quality associations psychologically plausible without establishing a universal causal rule.

Other heavier-is-better findings are better treated as adjacent evaluative or value evidence rather than direct quality evidence. Very light mobile-phone variants can reduce appeal and value perceptions (); heavier cutlery can improve dining evaluations and willingness to pay (); and heavier packaging can alter flavor-related evaluations, desire, and willingness to pay (). These effects demonstrate that weight can migrate into consequential judgment, but they do not by themselves show that consumers perceived the focal product as higher in quality. The defensible conclusion is therefore conditional: heaviness can support quality-related inference when the category makes heaviness diagnostic of solidity, durability, abundance, premiumness, or another quality-relevant meaning.

Evidence for lighter-is-better is less numerous but theoretically decisive because it reveals that favorable lightness can arise for reasons other than quality.  showed that greater visually induced heaviness reduced evaluation in portability-oriented contexts.  found that increasing smart-glasses weight increased perceived heaviness and substantially reduced wearing comfort.  treated weight as a negative feature of portable chargers and showed that weight and size jointly shaped perceived weight, satisfaction, preference, and expected price, while also indicating that preference did not improve indefinitely as weight decreased.  likewise showed that lighter-looking products were judged more user-friendly, with perceived weight implicated in the effect. Together, these findings show that “lighter is better” often means more portable, comfortable, or user-friendly—not necessarily higher in perceived quality.

The importance of product meaning is also apparent in  location-effect research. Visual placement influenced perceived product heaviness, but evaluation depended on whether heaviness was a positive or negative attribute for the focal product.  reached a closely related conclusion using product shadows as a visual heaviness cue. These studies establish weight valence and product-specific desirability, but they do not imply that every positive or negative weight preference is a quality judgment. That additional inference must be demonstrated rather than assumed.

bring this category-dependence into VR marketing. Across seven VR scenario experiments, perceived control affected perceived product weight and product evaluation, and the preferred control condition depended on whether the focal product was classified as one for which heaviness was positive or negative. Importantly, their product pretest first measured how important weight was in evaluating 21 products and then asked whether consumers wanted the weight-salient products to be heavier or lighter. This procedure establishes weight salience and desired weight direction, not a weight-quality association. Although the paper discusses meanings such as quantity, durability, stability, smallness, and portability, those semantic meanings were not directly measured as the mechanism. This distinction creates a specific opportunity for research on what a virtual weight percept actually activates in memory.

The convergence of heavier-is-better, lighter-is-better, and reversal effects suggests that the most useful theoretical construct is not a global preference for heaviness or even a single weight-quality mapping. Consumers appear to hold product-specific weight semantics: learned category knowledge about what heaviness or lightness signifies for a focal product. The same preferred direction can arise from different meanings. A product may be preferred lighter because it is more comfortable or portable without being judged higher in quality, while a product may be preferred heavier because it contains more material or quantity rather than because its construction is better.

The distinction is psychological as well as terminological. Weight valence describes whether a heavier or lighter state is liked or preferred; weight diagnosticity describes whether weight is informative for a judgment; and semantic content describes what the cue is taken to mean. These dimensions can dissociate. A light product may be preferred because it is easier to carry even when lightness says little about build quality, while a heavy product may imply greater quantity without implying superior construction.

This review therefore uses product-specific weight semantics as the broader working construct and reserves product-specific weight-quality schema for the narrower subset in which greater or lower weight specifically signals higher quality. Both constructs should be treated as continuous rather than imposed as categorical labels. This distinction matters empirically. If a light-is-better product is valued because lightness means comfort or portability, perceived quality should not be forced into the model as the mediator. Conversely, if lightness activates advanced materials, engineering sophistication, or precision and those meanings increase perceived quality, then a genuine light-is-better weight-quality schema is present.

Importantly, product-specific weight semantics need not be activated only by cues that directly specify an object’s physical mass. Visual design features can also convey heaviness or lightness through spatial, semantic, and crossmodal correspondences. For example, the location of a product image on a package can alter perceived visual heaviness: images positioned lower, to the right, or in the bottom-right region are experienced as heavier, and package evaluations depend on whether heaviness is desirable for the focal product (). Visual weight can also be conveyed through typography and color. Heavier typefaces and visually heavier colors can activate weight-related associations that spill over into judgments of product healthiness and subsequent purchase intentions (). Likewise, congruence between visually light or heavy packaging colors and vertical product location can influence perceived visual heaviness, perceptual fluency, and product choice (). More broadly, the vertical placement of brand logos can activate spatially grounded meanings and alter brand preference, illustrating that packaging layout carries semantic information beyond literal visual content (). These findings broaden the present framework by showing that weight-related meaning can be activated even when no physical mass information is provided. Such indirect visual cues may therefore converge with, amplify, or conflict with pseudo-haptically induced weight perceptions in shaping product-specific semantic and diagnostic inferences.

summarizes the strongest supported inferences and the overextensions that the present review seeks to avoid.

Evidence calibration: what the existing literature supports - and what it does not.

Embodied-cognition research provides an important foundation for understanding why a tactile property can influence an abstract judgment.  showed that holding a heavier clipboard increased judgments of importance, monetary value, and cognitive elaboration.  similarly demonstrated that incidental experiences of weight, hardness, and roughness systematically influenced social judgments and decisions. In retail contexts,  found that heavier environmental haptic cues could enhance perceptions of retailer competence and affect downstream responses.

These studies establish a broad principle: bodily sensations can migrate into abstract cognition. However, they should not be treated as direct evidence that heavier products are perceived as higher quality. Importance is not quality; competence is not quality; monetary value is not necessarily quality. Treating these adjacent outcomes as interchangeable would overstate what the evidence shows.

For the present problem, embodiment is therefore best treated as a permissive account: it explains why a bodily state can enter higher-order cognition, but it does not uniquely predict which product attribute becomes accessible, when a weight cue will be ignored, or why the same heaviness percept can be favorable for one product and unfavorable for another.

provide a more precise mechanism for the present problem. Their studies showed that the effect of physical weight on psychological significance depends substantially on semantic activation. The implication is that weight does not necessarily exert a direct evaluative effect; instead, the physical cue can make weight-related concepts more accessible, and those concepts then shape judgment. This account is better suited than a generic “heavy means important” explanation for predicting why identical weight sensations can have different consequences across products.

Product research provides increasingly specific examples of this semantic logic.  showed that perceived weight helped connect color lightness to two different attribute judgments: darker products were seen as more durable, whereas lighter products were seen as more user-friendly.  similarly showed that visual gradient cues changed perceived weight and stability perception, with perceived weight functioning as an inferential route to stability. By contrast, the smart-glasses and portable-charger findings of  and  show that lightness can primarily imply comfort or portability. Taken together, these studies suggest that the theoretically relevant mediator is not “positive weight meaning” in the abstract but the specific semantic content made accessible for the focal product.

Semantic activation therefore supplies directional specificity that a generic embodiment account lacks. Its critical prediction is not simply that weight changes evaluation, but that the accessible concept should match the product-relevant meaning of the weight state and should statistically or causally account for the judgment when competing explanations are controlled.

Learned expectancy can also enter the process before downstream evaluation.  meta-analysis of size-weight and material-weight illusions supports accounts that combine conceptual expectations with bottom-up information.  further showed in immersive VR that prior material–weight expectations can bias perceived heaviness even when visual and tactile material cues are experimentally placed in conflict.  distinction between sensation and perception therefore remains important: the external cue must produce a perceptual experience, but that percept is interpreted through learned knowledge. For consumer research, the key extension is to test both where category knowledge alters perceived weight and what product meaning is activated after weight is perceived.

Expectancy operates at an earlier locus than semantic evaluation. Prior category or material knowledge can alter the experienced heaviness of an object before any explicit judgment about durability, comfort, or quality is made. This distinction prevents a common causal shortcut: a category difference in evaluation may reflect a change in the weight percept itself, a change in what the percept means, or both. A strong mechanism study should therefore measure perceived weight before testing downstream semantic interpretation.

Haptic diagnosticity addresses a different question: when is weight information likely to be used?  identify weight among attributes for which touch can be diagnostic, and  show that physical examination matters more when preferences depend on material properties.  similarly distinguishes sensation from perceptual interpretation in sensory judgment. These accounts explain selective reliance on haptic information, but diagnosticity alone does not specify the sign of the effect or the particular meaning activated. A cue can be highly diagnostic because it informs comfort, quantity, durability, or quality, and those meanings need not point in the same evaluative direction.

The four accounts are therefore complementary at the level of a process model, but they are empirically distinguishable because they locate the effect at different stages. Evidence that category or material expectations change reported heaviness before downstream semantic judgments would implicate learned expectancy. Evidence that perceived weight is comparable across conditions while category changes which attribute becomes accessible would favor semantic activation. Evidence that a weight effect strengthens when weight is relevant to the focal task or judgment, and weakens when it is not, would support a diagnosticity account. A more context-general shift from experienced heaviness to abstract importance or value would be more consistent with broad embodied transfer. The stage-specific framework therefore does more than combine labels: it assigns competing causal loci and yields falsifiable tests of perception, semantic accessibility, and diagnosticity.

compares these accounts and clarifies what each can and cannot explain in the proposed framework.

Comparison of psychological accounts of weight-based judgment.

These accounts are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Embodied cognition explains why bodily or sensorimotor weight experience can enter abstract cognition, including when the source of the sensation is incidental to the object being evaluated. Learned expectancy may affect the perceived weight itself; product-specific semantic activation specifies which category-relevant meaning becomes accessible; and diagnosticity governs whether that meaning is used in the focal judgment. Hence, a finding that portability or functionality is inferred from lightness does not, by itself, rule out embodied cognition. The competing possibilities concern the source, content, and judgmental use of the weight-related information, which should be tested separately.

An illustrative comparison may clarify the distinct yet potentially complementary roles of these mechanisms in weight-based judgment. For a smart device in a category where lightness is associated with advanced engineering or functional efficiency, visual or pseudo-haptic cues indicating lower weight may shape perceived heaviness through learned expectations and activate functionality-related meanings through product-specific semantic associations. When functionality is relevant to the evaluation task, these meanings may serve as diagnostic information and subsequently influence product evaluation or purchase intention. However, such inferences depend on category-specific associations; in other contexts, lightness may primarily indicate comfort or portability rather than superior quality. By contrast, holding a heavier clipboard has been shown to influence judgments of abstract importance (), without necessarily requiring an inference about the clipboard’s functional attributes. This finding is consistent with a broader embodied association between physical weight and abstract significance rather than a product-specific diagnostic inference. The two pathways should therefore be regarded as analytically distinguishable but potentially co-occurring. Although general embodied associations may contribute alongside semantic activation and diagnostic reasoning, their relative causal contributions remain to be established. Future research should separately assess the source of the weight cue, perceived weight, the accessibility of product-specific meanings, and the extent to which those meanings inform subsequent judgments.

Online product evaluation changes not only the amount of information available but also its sensory form.  showed that consumers with a stronger need for tactile input are less likely to purchase online, particularly when product evaluation depends on touch.  and  likewise demonstrate that touch matters most when haptic attributes are diagnostic. The implication is not that all online products suffer equally from touch deprivation; rather, digital environments selectively remove information that matters more for some products than others.

frame new digital technologies as sensory-enabling tools that can partially compensate for missing sensory inputs.  provide a consumer example in multisensory augmented reality: touch control rather than voice control increased willingness to pay through reduced mental intangibility and greater decision comfort, and congruent auditory feedback strengthened part of this process. The implication for VR retail is that immersive visualization alone does not solve the haptic problem and that the value of an additional sensory cue may depend on its congruence with the product interaction rather than on sensory richness per se.

Digital environments can communicate weight in several qualitatively different ways. Consumers can be told a numeric weight, infer weight from an image, observe another hand interacting with a product, imagine the bodily action of holding it, or experience an interaction that produces a felt discrepancy consistent with effort or resistance.  showed that gesture control and visual presentation can facilitate haptic and spatial imagery in virtual product experience, thereby reducing product uncertainty.  similarly found that 2D versus 3D product presentation changes size-related perception, with perceived weight playing a role in later value-related responses. These channels should not be assumed to be psychologically equivalent.

provide especially important evidence for the distinction between knowing and sensing. Across 11 studies, showing a hand holding a product improved confidence in weight judgments and affected evaluation, purchase intention, and choice. Notably, effects could persist even when numeric weight information was available. A number on a screen therefore does not necessarily substitute for a cue that allows consumers to mentally simulate weight.

Observed and device-mediated touch offer more direct routes to haptic compensation. , across images, GIFs, and VR, showed that observing a hand in physical contact with a product can generate a vicarious haptic effect that increases psychological ownership and product valuation through felt ownership of the virtual hand.  developed HAPshop and showed that technology-enabled haptic information can enhance spatial proximity, product elaboration, evaluation certainty, and purchase likelihood. Although neither stream isolates product weight as the sole cue, both demonstrate that digital haptic information can change consumer processing and valuation. The stronger question for pseudo-haptic weight is therefore not whether a digital cue can matter, but whether a simulated weight percept activates the same product-specific meanings learned from real-world experience.

Pseudo-haptics use cross-modal perceptual interactions to create touch-, force-, or resistance-like sensations without reproducing the full physical force itself (). For weight, a central implementation is the control-display (C/D) ratio.  showed that manipulating the relation between physical movement and displayed movement altered perceived mass during virtual object manipulation. The basic intuition is that when a user moves physically by a given amount but the virtual hand or object moves less, the visual–motor discrepancy can be interpreted as greater resistance or weight.

systematically developed C/D-ratio manipulation for immersive VR and generated reliable changes in perceived virtual-object weight while examining limits related to virtual-hand ownership.  subsequently showed that dynamically changing the C/D ratio can also simulate weight change and that an alternative hand-redirection method can improve embodiment. These studies are especially valuable for consumer research because the manipulation is software-based and can vary perceived weight while holding visual product appearance constant. At the same time, they make it important to separate a weight illusion from a broader change in how much control the user feels over the interface.

The methodological challenge is that a large visuomotor discrepancy may be perceived as lag, poor tracking, constrained control, or system malfunction rather than weight. This concern is particularly relevant in light of , who intentionally manipulated movement freedom and movement gain to alter VR control; the same family of visuomotor relations can therefore change both perceived weight and perceived control. Consumer studies should not treat a significant perceived-weight difference as sufficient evidence of a clean manipulation. Pretests should also assess perceived effort, latency awareness, frustration, usability, realism, sense of control or agency, and cybersickness, and the main study should use a mapping that produces weight differences without large unintended changes on these dimensions.

To isolate pseudo-haptic weight from interface-related confounds, empirical studies should use a two-stage calibration and validation procedure rather than adopting a fixed C/D ratio from prior research. First, a technical pretest should compare several control–display mappings and select the smallest mapping difference that reliably changes perceived weight while maintaining acceptable virtual-hand ownership, agency, usability, and realism and avoiding marked changes in perceived latency, task frustration, or cybersickness. No universal gain threshold should be assumed, because acceptable mappings depend on the device and task. Second, the main experiment should revalidate perceived weight and assess perceived effort, agency, usability, latency awareness, frustration, and cybersickness. If these competing measures are not affected by the manipulation, covariate-adjusted analyses may be reported as robustness checks. If they are themselves affected, simply controlling for them can obscure causal pathways; competing or parallel-process models, together with independent manipulations where feasible, should distinguish a perceived-weight route from agency or motor-friction routes to judgment.

demonstrated that deliberate, perceivable tracking offsets can induce weight perception without specialized force-feedback hardware.  extended pseudo-haptic mass display to object rotation, showing that altered rotational motion can communicate both total mass and mass distribution. These approaches broaden the behavioral vocabulary through which virtual weight can be expressed, which is useful for products that are rotated, inspected, or repositioned rather than simply lifted.

Multisensory extensions can further change the effective range of simulated weight.  combined C/D-ratio manipulation with electrical muscle stimulation and showed that multisensory feedback substantially expanded the range of weight that could be simulated. Yet more sensory feedback is not automatically better.  used dynamically adjusted C/D ratios to convey changing weight in a virtual mug and found that additional vibrotactile feedback did not further improve weight-change perception. This finding cautions against designs that confound weight with generic interaction richness.

provide a particularly useful validation benchmark. By comparing direct C/D-ratio manipulation, velocity restriction, and real lifting, they found that direct C/D control produced virtual weight impressions and lifting behavior closer to real-world lifting than the velocity-restriction method.  extend this validation strategy by analyzing objective kinematic features and subjective fatigue while comparing virtual pseudo-haptic lifting with real-weight lifting. Together, these studies suggest that consumer manipulation checks can be strengthened by supplementing self-reported heaviness with behavioral or kinematic indicators when feasible.

Cross-modal sound provides another route to weight perception.  showed that objects paired with higher-pitched sounds were perceived as lighter than those paired with lower-pitched sounds, whereas loudness did not produce the same pattern. In a VR dumbbell task,  likewise found that lowering the pitch of impact sounds, particularly lower-frequency components, increased perceived heaviness. Auditory pseudo-haptics are therefore a plausible robustness manipulation, but their suitability should depend on whether the product interaction naturally produces diagnostic sound. Recent work also extends virtual weight beyond near-field hand manipulation:  introduced RayFlex, a raycast-based pseudo-haptic technique for inducing weight perception during distant VR interaction. The expanding technique set confirms that virtual weight is technically tractable; the unresolved consumer question is which meaning the induced percept activates.

summarizes the major pseudo-haptic weight techniques and the construct-validity issues they create for psychological research.

Pseudo-haptic weight techniques and their relevance to psychological research.

The literature reviewed above now establishes four relatively strong conclusions. First, weight can influence product inferences and evaluation. Second, the direction of the effect depends on what weight means for the product category. Third, virtual systems can induce weight perception without changing physical mass. Fourth, recent consumer-oriented VR studies already show that virtual interaction and pseudo-haptic weight can affect product evaluation and purchase-related responses (; ). The remaining gap is therefore narrower: which learned product-specific semantics are activated by a virtual weight percept, when those semantics are specifically diagnostic of quality, and how that activation produces downstream consumer judgment.

This distinction matters because a virtual weight effect can arise for reasons that have little to do with learned product semantics. A heavier pseudo-haptic manipulation may increase effort, novelty, immersion, salience, frustration, or generalized substantiality. A directional reversal across products remains useful evidence against a simple main-effect explanation, but it is no longer sufficient by itself:  already demonstrate a product-type reversal, and  already show stronger value effects for products in which heaviness is associated with higher value. A stronger contribution must directly identify the semantic meaning that becomes accessible and show that this meaning, rather than generic effort or control, carries the effect.

Two recent studies are the closest existing consumer evidence.  show that VR control affects perceived product weight and evaluation, with the direction depending on whether heaviness is treated as a positive or negative product attribute. However, their pretest establishes weight salience and desired weight direction rather than a weight-quality mapping, their focal downstream measure is general product evaluation rather than perceived quality, and the proposed product meanings are not directly measured.  go one step closer to the present focal manipulation by directly using pseudo-haptics to modulate heaviness perception in virtual product evaluation. They report effects on scarcity valuation and purchase intention and stronger hedonic and utilitarian value for products in which greater weight is associated with higher value. Yet this study likewise does not establish product-specific semantic activation or perceived quality as the explanatory mechanism. Together, these papers substantially narrow the novelty space while leaving a clear mechanism gap.

A more defensible gap has five elements. First, product pretests should distinguish desired weight direction from weight-quality direction: wanting a product to be lighter or heavier does not necessarily mean that lightness or heaviness signals higher quality. Second, the specific semantic content of weight should be established independently—for example durability, stability, premium construction, quantity, portability, comfort, or advanced engineering—rather than inferred after the fact. Third, the pseudo-haptic manipulation should be explicitly designed to change perceived weight while minimizing changes in control, agency, latency awareness, frustration, or usability. Fourth, perceived quality should be focal only for products whose weight-quality association is empirically demonstrated; otherwise the appropriate mediator may be another diagnostic attribute. Fifth, the semantic mechanism should be measured close to the weight experience and, ideally, tested causally rather than only through a statistical mediation model. In this formulation, the contribution is not “VR weight affects consumers” or even simply “heavy versus light reverses by product,” but “pseudo-haptically felt weight selectively activates learned product-specific semantics, and quality-relevant semantic activation translates virtual weight into perceived quality and consumer response”.

Product-specific weight semantics can be defined as learned category knowledge about what greater or lower weight signifies for a focal product. These meanings may include durability, solidity, stability, quantity, premium construction, performance, portability, comfort, user-friendliness, or technological sophistication. Product-specific weight-quality schema is the narrower case in which those learned meanings make heaviness or lightness diagnostic of overall product quality. The distinction should be treated as empirical, not assumed. A product can be strongly light-is-better because consumers value comfort while showing little or no light-quality association.

The term product-specific weight semantics is not intended as a replacement for embodied cognition, expectancy, semantic activation, or cue diagnosticity, nor as a claim that a new cognitive architecture has already been validated. It is an organizing construct that makes the content of learned category knowledge explicit and measurable. Likewise, product-specific weight-quality schema is used as shorthand for an empirically demonstrable learned mapping between weight and quality, not as evidence for a validated latent scale. This narrower definition reduces the risk of relabeling comfort, portability, quantity, or value effects as quality effects.

More precisely, product-specific weight semantics denotes a learned representational knowledge structure, not a newly established perceptual mechanism. Once activated by a weight experience, this structure can support an active, context-sensitive inference. Category expectancy concerns how prior knowledge may shape anticipated or experienced heaviness; product-specific weight semantics specifies what that heaviness or lightness signifies for the product; and haptic diagnosticity concerns whether the resulting information is relevant enough to enter judgment. Need for Touch describes an individual difference in seeking or relying on haptic input (), not the category-specific semantic content of that input. Prior product expertise may sharpen learned associations (), whereas hedonic versus utilitarian goals or durability versus portability framing can determine which association becomes diagnostic. Central-versus-peripheral cue processing likewise concerns how extensively a cue is considered, rather than specifying the learned meaning of weight. These constructs can interact without being interchangeable.

This formulation makes the category role theoretically explicit and suggests a two-stage measurement strategy. At the first stage, product categories should be screened continuously for weight salience, desired weight direction, weight-quality direction, weight diagnosticity, quality versus price importance, context dependence, and the naturalness of exploring weight through handling. At the second stage, a smaller set of products should be tested under heavier-versus-lighter scenarios with open-ended associations collected before any researcher-provided semantic scale. This sequence allows the data to reveal whether a product is best described as Heavy→Quality, Light→Quality, Light→Comfort/Portability, quantity/value driven, context-dependent, or weight-neutral.

The proposed process model contains five stages. Real-world category experience provides the learning history; product-specific weight semantics represent the learned knowledge structure; a physical or pseudo-haptic interaction produces a perceived weight state; the perceived state activates a diagnostic meaning; and that meaning contributes to judgment. Perceived quality is included only when the activated meaning is empirically quality-relevant.  presents the model in stage form.

Stage-based integrative model of pseudo-haptic weight and product meaning.

The model preserves  distinction between sensory input and perceptual interpretation but makes the semantic stage more explicit. The pseudo-haptic manipulation is the sensory/interactivity cue; perceived weight is the perceptual state; product-specific semantic activation is the cognitive interpretation; a diagnostic attribute inference follows; perceived quality is focal only when the activated meaning is quality-relevant; and evaluation or choice is the downstream response. Product-specific weight semantics moderate the translation from perceived weight to meaning. This structure remains deliberately simpler than a model that simultaneously treats presence, tangibility, mental simulation, and need for touch as chained mediators.

A key implication is that category knowledge can enter twice: before evaluation, by biasing the weight percept through expectancy, and after perception, by determining which meaning is activated. Separating these loci is important because they imply different interventions and different falsification tests. A manipulation that changes semantic accessibility without changing perceived weight would support a post-perceptual mechanism; a category effect on perceived heaviness would indicate an earlier expectancy contribution.

The review makes four theoretical contributions. First, it introduces an explicit evidence-calibration principle into the weight literature by separating cue generation, weight perception, semantic interpretation, diagnostic attribute inference, perceived quality when relevant, and downstream judgment. This distinction changes what counts as evidence for the focal construct: a technically convincing weight illusion is not consumer-quality evidence, and positive effects on comfort, importance, quantity, competence, value, preference, or willingness to pay are not interchangeable with perceived quality. The structured coding of outcome type and claim boundaries makes these inferential limits visible rather than leaving them implicit.

Second, the review replaces a global heavier-is-better premise with a directional, category-contingent account. Weight desirability, weight diagnosticity, and weight-quality direction are analytically distinct. This distinction accommodates Heavy-to-Quality, Light-to-Quality, Light-to-Comfort/Portability, quantity/value, and weight-neutral patterns without assuming that one evaluative rule applies across categories.

Third, the review integrates existing psychological accounts by assigning them different causal loci and different empirical signatures. Embodiment explains how sensorimotor states can influence abstract cognition; expectancy predicts that learned knowledge can alter the perceptual experience itself; diagnosticity predicts when weight will be used as information; and semantic activation predicts which product meaning becomes accessible once a weight percept is available. The contribution is therefore not a competing grand theory but a process architecture that turns theoretical alternatives into discriminating tests.

Fourth, the review refines the bridge between psychological research on mediated perception and consumer-oriented HCI. Recent studies already show that virtual control or pseudo-haptic heaviness can change product evaluation, so novelty can no longer rest on demonstrating another virtual-weight effect. The stronger contribution is process-level: to establish when a digitally generated sensorimotor discrepancy recreates a psychologically meaningful weight percept, which learned category representation it activates, and whether that representation causally shapes judgment. In this sense, pseudo-haptics functions as an experimental method for studying sensation-to-meaning translation in mediated environments.

Proposition 1 (perceptual validity). A pseudo-haptic manipulation intended to represent greater versus lower weight should first produce a corresponding difference in perceived weight without a comparably large change in perceived latency, loss of control or agency, frustration, usability, or technical malfunction.

Proposition 2 (semantic selectivity). Once a weight percept is established, product-specific weight semantics should moderate which concept becomes accessible. The same perceived heaviness should therefore activate different diagnostic meanings across categories when those categories have different learned weight associations.

Proposition 3 (quality diagnosticity). Weight-congruent pseudo-haptic feedback should increase perceived quality only when an independent pretest demonstrates that the activated weight meaning is quality-diagnostic. When the relevant meaning is comfort, portability, quantity, or another attribute, that attribute rather than perceived quality should be the proximal judgment.

Proposition 4 (causal process). Effects of pseudo-haptic weight on downstream evaluation, choice, purchase intention, or willingness to pay should be carried by the sequence from perceived weight to product-specific semantic activation to the focal diagnostic judgment; experimentally changing the accessibility or diagnosticity of the meaning should alter the effect in the predicted direction.

The first empirical requirement is a two-round product pretest rather than an immediate choice of one “heavy” and one “light” product. In Round 1, approximately 25–30 real product categories should be screened. A practical design is to recruit roughly 180–200 participants and randomly assign each participant about 10 products to reduce fatigue. For each product, measures should distinguish familiarity, weight salience, desired weight direction, weight-quality direction, weight diagnosticity, quality importance, price importance, context dependence, and the naturalness of exploring weight by lifting or handling. The critical distinction is between “I want this product lighter/heavier” and “lighter/heavier means higher quality.” In Round 2, approximately 6–8 shortlisted products can be presented in randomized heavier-versus-lighter scenarios. Open-ended questions should first ask what characteristics the weight makes participants think of and why; only afterward should explicit semantic ratings and perceived-quality measures be administered. This procedure can identify Heavy→Quality and Light→Quality products while retaining Light→Comfort/Portability and weight-neutral products as theoretically informative boundary cases.

A separate technical pretest should establish heavy and light pseudo-haptic conditions.  provide the most direct C/D-ratio foundation,  extend the method to dynamic changes, and ,  provide useful real-weight and kinematic benchmarks. C/D ratio is therefore a strong primary candidate, but the exact mapping should be piloted rather than borrowed from a study whose goal was to manipulate control. The manipulation check should assess perceived weight and effort together with sense of control or agency, latency awareness, frustration, usability, realism, and cybersickness. Auditory pitch provides a credible alternative manipulation (; ), but it should be used only when the product action naturally generates diagnostic sound. The cleanest first study should use one validated method; method comparisons can be reserved for later robustness or product–manipulation-fit tests.

Operationally, the calibration study should document each tested gain mapping, the perceived-weight difference it produces, and the distributions of agency, ownership, usability, perceived effort, latency awareness, and adverse symptoms. Selection criteria for the main-study mapping should be specified before evaluating downstream product judgments. In the main study, both the weight manipulation check and potential interface-related alternative pathways should be reported. An apparent weight effect accompanied by substantial loss of agency should not be presented as an isolated weight-perception effect without additional evidence.

A clean first consumer experiment can cross product meaning (a pretested Heavy→Quality versus Light→Quality category) with pseudo-haptic weight (heavy versus light). Perceived quality should be the focal dependent variable only if the product pretests show a genuine weight-quality mapping in both directions. The expected pattern is a crossover interaction: heavy > light for Heavy→Quality products and light > heavy for Light→Quality products. However, this 2 × 2 should be treated as a necessary foundation rather than the sole novelty, because recent studies already demonstrate product-contingent virtual-weight effects. Where feasible, using more than one product exemplar per semantic direction or replicating the pattern across products will reduce the risk that a single stimulus drives the interaction.

The mechanism study should measure what becomes cognitively accessible immediately after the pseudo-haptic interaction and before asking for perceived quality. Open-ended thought listing is useful for discovering product-specific meanings without prompting participants, while a reaction-time semantic or evaluative priming task can test whether pretested target concepts become more accessible online. Target words should be drawn from the product pretest rather than assumed in advance—for example, durable, solid, stable, or premium for one category and portable, comfortable, advanced-material, or precise for another. Explicit semantic ratings can complement these measures but should not be the only evidence of activation. A subsequent experiment should strengthen mechanism evidence by manipulating the accessibility or diagnosticity of the proposed semantic meaning. Following the causal-chain logic articulated by , a series of experiments that both measures and experimentally changes the proposed process can provide stronger evidence than a single mediation analysis. For example, a usage goal or contextual prime could make durability versus portability more diagnostic. If the pseudo-haptic weight effect changes in the predicted direction when the relevant meaning is made more or less accessible, the semantic account becomes substantially more credible.

A concrete causal-chain paradigm could use a 2 × 2 × 2 between-participants design crossing pseudo-haptic weight (heavy vs. light), a pretested product-specific weight-quality schema (Heavy→Quality vs. Light→Quality), and the accessibility of a diagnostic goal (durability-focused vs. portability-focused). A perceived-weight measure would verify the manipulation; pretested thought-listing, semantic-accessibility measures, and distinct perceived quality and attribute judgments would then identify which meaning becomes active. The semantic account predicts a category-schema-dependent reversal that is strengthened, weakened, or redirected by the goal prime when it makes the relevant attribute more or less diagnostic. In contrast, a generic embodied-heaviness or effort explanation would more naturally predict a broader weight effect that is less sensitive to product-specific semantic fit. The critical evidence is not a statistical mediation alone: manipulating accessibility must causally alter the predicted product-relevant inference, while perceived-weight validity and competing agency and effort explanations remain separately assessed.

A subsequent study can distinguish objective knowledge from embodied perception.  show that numeric weight information does not necessarily eliminate the effects of imagery-evoking visual cues, and  report that actual weight information did not remove the effect of VR control on perceived weight. Future work can therefore compare numeric weight information, pseudo-haptic felt weight, and—where feasible—real physical weight while measuring the same semantic outcomes. If pseudo-haptic felt weight produces stronger or qualitatively different product-specific semantic activation than numeric information, the finding would show that “knowing” a product’s weight and “feeling” its weight are not psychologically interchangeable in digital sensory marketing.

Several moderators are plausible but should be introduced only after the core mechanism is established. Need for touch may amplify reliance on haptic information (; ), and product expertise may strengthen learned category associations (). Usage context may change which weight meaning is diagnostic: the same product can be evaluated under a portability goal, a durability goal, or a performance goal. Product–manipulation fit is another important boundary. Auditory impact cues are natural for products that are placed, struck, or dropped but less natural for products such as glasses, whereas C/D-ratio manipulations are most defensible when the task naturally involves lifting or moving. More broadly, multisensory congruence can shape consumer response (; ), and cross-modal auditory evidence shows that pitch can bias perceived weight (; ). These factors are promising extensions, but they should not be added simultaneously to the first mechanism test. In addition, alternative explanations should be measured rather than handled only rhetorically. Effort, novelty, immersion, perceived realism, control, and generic substantiality are particularly important because each can covary with pseudo-haptic manipulations and can influence evaluation independently of product-specific semantics.

A complementary source–target dissociation experiment could separate incidental embodiment from product-linked semantic inference. Participants would hold an unrelated heavy or light object in one hand while evaluating an otherwise identical target product with the other hand. The incidental load would be varied independently of the target’s own physical or pseudo-haptic weight, and the felt weight of the target, abstract importance, product-specific associations, and evaluation would be assessed separately. A general influence of the unrelated load on importance despite unchanged target-weight perception would be consistent with an incidental embodied pathway; a target-linked weight effect that selectively activates pretested durability, portability, or other functional concepts would support an additional product-specific semantic pathway. Both patterns may occur together, so their coexistence should be tested rather than ruled out a priori.

The applied implication is deliberately narrower than the theoretical contribution. In digital product environments, weight should be represented only when it is psychologically diagnostic for the category and when the chosen interaction makes the intended weight percept credible. A heavier or lighter pseudo-haptic state should not be treated as universally beneficial: its value depends on the meaning it activates, and a manipulation that is experienced as lag or loss of control can undermine the intended inference. For design, diagnostic congruence is therefore more important than simply increasing sensory richness.

This review has several limitations. First, it is an integrative synthesis of a bounded 56-publication corpus rather than an exhaustive systematic search. It is suited to theory construction and comparison, but it cannot establish the prevalence or mean magnitude of weight effects, and relevant studies may remain outside the corpus.

Second, direct evidence for weight-to-quality mappings is concentrated in a narrow subset of the bounded corpus. Only four publications were coded as direct or near-direct quality evidence, and even these differ in design and construct: they include market associations, inferred economic quality, expected service quality, and consumer perceived quality. Much of the strongest light-is-better evidence instead concerns comfort, portability, user-friendliness, satisfaction, or preference. The proposed distinction between product-specific weight semantics and weight-quality schema is therefore intentionally conservative and should be tested across a broader range of categories and usage contexts.

Third, product-specific weight semantics and the narrower weight-quality schema are working integrative constructs rather than validated scales. Their dimensionality, reliability, stability across contexts, and discriminant validity relative to haptic diagnosticity, expertise, and general product beliefs require direct empirical study.

Fourth, the evidence boundary between real and virtual weight remains incomplete.  and  connect virtual weight-related experiences to consumer responses, but the literature has not yet established that pseudo-haptically induced weight consistently reactivates the same semantic knowledge learned from physical product experience. Demonstrating that representational continuity - and separating it from generic effort, control, or novelty - is the central empirical challenge raised by this review.

Weight is a simple physical variable with multiple psychological meanings. Across the reviewed literature, perceived weight can inform density, quantity, stability, durability, comfort, portability, premiumness, value, and quality-related judgments, but no universal heavier-is-better rule is supported. What matters is the learned meaning that a weight state carries for the focal product and whether that meaning is diagnostic for the judgment being made.

Digital and immersive media make this problem theoretically useful because they separate physical mass from perceived weight. Pseudo-haptic techniques can generate a weight experience through visuomotor or cross-modal relations even when real mass is unchanged. The next step is therefore not to demonstrate another main effect of virtual heaviness. It is to identify the stage at which category knowledge enters, measure the specific meaning made accessible by the percept, and establish whether that meaning causally translates virtual sensation into judgment. Framed this way, pseudo-haptic weight provides a tractable model for studying how mediated sensory experiences reactivate real-world semantic knowledge.

psychology.title: Documenting symptom and context changes in individual case safety reports: a methodological perspective
psychology.abstract: Individual case safety report narratives support pharmacovigilance by preserving clinical chronology and contextual information. A possible information gap concerns how documented symptom changes, surrounding circumstances, and actions already taken are linked and attributed to their sources. Its frequency and consequences have not been established. This Perspective proposes a minimal representation of symptom trajectories, context, actions, subsequent responses, concurrent changes, and remaining uncertainty. A limited procedural inspiration is the repeated observation and revision of working hypotheses used in dynamic psychotherapy; this does not establish a new pharmacovigilance diagnostic method. The proposal builds on existing case processing, causality frameworks, quality assessment, and follow-up practice. Evaluation would first audit source records and processing histories, then compare the proposed representation with optimized routine narratives containing the same facts. An independently adjudicated reference would specify what the records support, without claiming to establish biological causality. The primary endpoint would be correct reconstruction of prespecified case information; unsupported conclusions, completion, and workload would be assessed separately. Additional questioning would require a later, distinct evaluation of information yield, nonresponse, recall, and questioning effects. Contextual information must not delay reporting or justify unsupported dismissal of a medicinal-product contribution. The representation warrants testing, including the possibility that good routine processing already provides equivalent practical information.
psychology.text:
Individual case safety reports (ICSRs) support the assessment of suspected adverse reactions to medicinal products. Their narratives help pharmacovigilance (PV) assessors reconstruct the clinical course and identify questions requiring clarification. The issue considered here is whether available accounts of symptom and context changes can be represented more usefully. Neither the frequency of a specific documentation gap nor a resulting systematic causal error is established by the evidence reviewed.

The practical proposal is to preserve six connected elements: each symptom’s course, explicitly documented context, an action or situation change that already occurred, the subsequent response, concurrent changes, and remaining uncertainty. For example, a record might describe dizziness and palpitations after dosing, several actions during a telephone call, and improvement in only one symptom. The documentation should preserve that sequence and distinguish a contemporaneous report from a later recollection. It should not replace either account with an inferred psychological explanation.

The question is whether making these relationships explicit improves reconstruction compared with well-performed routine processing. Both representations must contain the same medical and contextual facts, sources, and uncertainties. The proposed addition would be redundant wherever routine narratives already make the relevant relationships sufficiently clear. Evaluation therefore needs to test an incremental information benefit rather than assume one from a visually structured example. This Perspective develops the representation and a staged research approach. It reports no empirical evaluation and proposes no new regulatory data requirement.

The proposed gap is relational: individually present details may be difficult to connect to a particular symptom, time, or source. Conversely, an explicit sequence can preserve ambiguity when the documents do not support a reliable connection. Success would mean recovering what is documented more faithfully, including its limits, rather than producing a more confident account.

Routine PV already accommodates chronology, clinical course, concomitant treatment, dechallenge, and rechallenge. The International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E2B (R3) standard for electronic transmission of ICSRs provides narrative and assessment fields alongside structured data (). The proposal does not introduce temporal reasoning into an otherwise static system. Nor does adding narrative headings demonstrate that readers will make better decisions.

Reporting conventions also matter. ICH E2D (R1) distinguishes spontaneous reports, which imply causal suspicion for reporting purposes, from solicited reports requiring a causality assessment (). Suspicion is not proof of causation. Organized collection, including patient support programs, does not by itself guarantee complete or unbiased information. These source types should not be pooled as interchangeable observations in an initial evaluation.

The World Health Organization (WHO) already addresses context in vaccine safety.
