Its causality-assessment manual for adverse events following immunization, in the 2019 update, recognizes developments concerning immunization stress-related responses (). The dedicated manual describes a broader range of stress-related responses than anxiety alone (). These are important precedents, not validation of the present representation for general medicine reports. The narrower contribution proposed here is an explicit, source-attributed description of documented changes, tested against existing competent practice.

Quality and reporting research further constrain the claim. VigiGrade evaluates documentation completeness, not whether a suspected reaction was actually caused by a medicine (). Longitudinal presentation has also been developed for reviewing adverse drug events in clinical records (). Follow-up questionnaires are established tools: European Medicines Agency guidance addresses specific questionnaires requested by regulators and emphasizes proportionate information collection (). A recent qualitative study of ten experts likewise supports targeting consequential information gaps, but does not quantify the benefit of this proposal (). These approaches address different tasks. The proposed reconstruction test would complement completeness assessment by asking whether a reader can recover the documented relationships. It would not replace a quality instrument or establish a universal follow-up requirement.

Five processes should remain distinct: symptom occurrence, perception and reporting, information collection and processing, subsequent reconstruction or classification, and causal or signal assessment. Stimulated reporting concerns changes in reporting activity; notoriety bias can affect reporting patterns after safety alerts (). Expectancy-related symptoms, omitted narrative information, misclassification, and causal error are different problems. Their direction and magnitude require appropriate reference information and designs. Disproportionality measures are sensitive to several such mechanisms and do not establish incidence or individual causality (). A clearer narrative cannot be assumed to correct population-level reporting selection.

One procedural inspiration comes from intensive short-term dynamic psychotherapy (ISTDP). Its psychodiagnostic approach uses repeated observation of responses to interventions to revise working hypotheses and guide subsequent actions (; ). The transferable proposal here is limited to documenting sequences of symptoms, actions already taken, and subsequent changes. It does not ask PV personnel to apply psychotherapeutic pressure or challenge. Retrospective accounts remain recollections, not moment-to-moment observations. The clinical concept of a therapeutic window does not establish a validated PV assessment window; suitable conditions for any later information collection would need separate evaluation. This procedural origin neither validates psychological attribution of adverse events nor demonstrates diagnostic superiority in PV.

A dynamic description records relationships rather than merely adding labels such as “stress present.” It asks what was reported before and after an action, which symptoms changed, which persisted, and what else changed simultaneously. Repeated updates may revise the account as further evidence becomes available. An unchanged symptom is informative documentation, while an undocumented response is unknown. Neither should disappear when a summary emphasizes improvement. For case assessment, the resulting sequence could help locate a contradiction or identify a useful clarification: for example, whether the two symptoms actually followed different courses. An initially plausible interpretation may then remain open or require revision. These are proposed uses of the information, not demonstrated outcomes.

The distinction is especially important when several actions occur together. Less dizziness after sitting down, drinking water, and moving to a quieter room cannot isolate the contribution of any one change. Elapsed time, the medicine, other clinical processes, and contextual influences remain compatible explanations. A recorded temporal relationship is therefore a reconstruction target, not a causal test. Even accurate reporting of improvement does not establish why it occurred. The value of preserving the sequence must be demonstrated through readers' performance, including their ability to retain uncertainty and recognize unresolved medical questions.

specifies the six documentation elements. A trained case processor would assemble them from available intake records and follow-up material after necessary triage, or in parallel with timely reporting. The module is a proposed documentation structure, not a validated questionnaire or score. Context documentation must not delay acute care or required reporting, and these elements are not additional conditions for accepting a report.

A minimal source-attributed representation of documented changes.

For each element, preserve source identity and location, source actor, and the available precision of event and recording times; retain later processing separately. Distinguish direct observations, contemporaneous patient or third-party reports, and later recollections. Entries describe existing records and do not require additional patient questioning. The elements can be documented in the factual narrative field H.1 of the International Council for Harmonisation E2B (R3) standard, with reporter and sender interpretations distinguished in H.2 and H.4 (). Unknown elements do not delay reporting. Examples are synthetic and illustrate documentation, not diagnostic rules.

Each statement should retain its source identifier and location, the person providing the information, and the distinction between event time, original recording time, and later processing. Precision should not exceed the source: “after a few minutes” must not become a timestamp. A clinician’s measurement, a contemporaneous patient or third-party report, and a later recollection are different kinds of evidence. Unknown information, an explicitly denied feature, and a reported absence of change require separate descriptions. Conflicting accounts should remain attributable rather than being silently reconciled. Reporters would not be expected to learn the module or classify mechanisms. Case processors would need shared worked examples and rules for preserving ambiguity; a clinical assessor would still decide whether unresolved information warrants ordinary medical follow-up.

The factual sequence can be represented in E2B (R3) H.1, while reporter and sender interpretations remain distinguishable in H.2 and H.4; H.3.r accommodates sender diagnosis or reclassification (). This field mapping concerns technical accommodation, not regulatory endorsement of the proposed structure. Changes to coding or assessment should follow applicable procedures, with the supporting evidence and reason recorded. The module must not turn an inferred mechanism into a source fact or obscure a reporter’s causal suspicion.

illustrates the intended contrast using an entirely synthetic case. Optimized routine narrative B and explicit representation C share all facts. During a same-day call, the person reports initially unchanged dizziness and palpitations after several actions, followed by less dizziness but persistent palpitations. A noisy setting at onset is recalled only the next day. Measurements and later clinical outcomes remain undocumented in both versions. B is deliberately coherent; C adds organization rather than privileged clinical information. The shared reconstruction task asks which symptom improved and which remained unchanged; the later course of palpitations remains an open follow-up question. The illustration establishes neither an information benefit nor the cause of the symptoms. In a real case, unresolved medical concerns would continue to guide appropriate assessment and follow-up.

Evaluation should separate an audit of existing information, a controlled representation test, and any later intervention to collect additional information. A defensible first audit could sample adult spontaneous reports involving dizziness, palpitations, or dyspnea in a specified non-vaccine medicine setting and time period. Eligibility would include serious and nonserious reports without selecting presumed psychological cases. Random sampling should use case families, linking follow-ups and duplicates. Missing or inaccessible source records must remain visible in the sampling account.

Two independent coders would inventory relevant medical and contextual information in initial reports, actual follow-up records, and processing histories before examining final narratives. A third assessor would adjudicate disagreements; pre-adjudication agreement would also be reported. Audit outcomes would include the proportion of sampled case families with an assessable source-to-narrative chain and, within comparable chains, the proportion of relevant source facts omitted or altered. A final narrative alone cannot establish whether information was never requested, never received, or lost during processing.

The representation test would compare optimized routine narrative B with explicit representation C using the same source packet and factual content, including contextual details. Parity includes documented relationships, source attributions, and uncertainty, not merely isolated facts. Independent PV reviewers would check routine quality and factual parity before testing. Naturally clear relationships must not be removed from B to favor C. Length, layout, and preparation effort should be recorded, because the contrast evaluates a representation package rather than a pure effect of headings.

Assessors independent of the format authors would establish an adjudicated facts reference from the source packet before B and C were constructed. It would define what the records support, including source attribution, uncertainty, contradictions, and timing precision; it would not establish biological truth. Prespecified questions would address ordinary case-assessment needs, covering core medical facts as well as contextual relationships. Targets would be set independently of compliance with the proposed six-element structure. The scoring rubric would accept semantically equivalent answers, be pretested on separate cases, and be frozen before evaluation. It is a new measurement proposal requiring evaluation, not an already validated instrument.

Case-reader assignments would be randomized and balanced so that multiple readers assess each case in each format, while individual readers assess different cases in both formats. No reader would see two versions of the same case or linked case family. Training would be identical and order counterbalanced. Readers cannot be blinded to visible formatting; scoring of their answers should be masked to allocation where practicable. Cases used for training or rubric development would be excluded from testing.

The primary endpoint would be the proportion of prespecified factual targets correctly reconstructed in each case-reader assignment. The contrast would be C minus B, with cases weighted equally, reported in absolute percentage points with a confidence interval. Core medical targets would also be reported separately. Partial submissions retain credit for correct answers; unanswered targets and unstarted assignments contribute no successful reconstruction to this operational endpoint. Completion and accuracy among completed assignments would be reported separately. Technical data loss would be distinguished from noncompletion and examined through prespecified sensitivity analyses.

Analysis would account for both case and reader variation, following the general rationale for crossed random factors (). Targets within a case should not be treated as independent case replications. Sample-size planning would require a prespecified practically relevant difference, desired precision, and plausible variance components. A nonsignificant result would not establish equivalence. Secondary outcomes would include unsupported factual additions, unwarranted definitive causal conclusions, justified clarification questions, inappropriate context-based dismissal, preparation time, active reading time, and completion. For each error type, the denominator would be assessable case-reader assignments, counting assignments with at least one error; unavailable responses would be reported separately. Agreement between readers would describe reproducibility, not causal accuracy.

Clarification performance would distinguish coverage of independently identified information gaps from unnecessary questions. Cases without such gaps would have no coverage denominator, but their unnecessary questions would still count. A separate decision task would assess whether context alone prompted unsupported dismissal or downclassification against prespecified processing rules. This would measure behavior in an offline task, not observed patient harm. Time logs would retain interrupted or aborted work. Research adjudication would be reported separately from the effort required to prepare and use a narrative in practice. Meaningful reconstruction gains, tolerable workload, and error limits would be prespecified before testing.

Only a later study should test additional questioning. It could randomize usual follow-up against usual follow-up plus neutral questions about what happened next, what changed or remained unchanged, and what else changed. Necessary clinical follow-up would remain available in both groups; output representation would be identical. Contact opportunities and time would be matched or their differences explicitly treated as part of the intervention. The study would report assigned cases, contact attempts, reach, response, partial response, and nonresponse. Additional source-attributed information and workload would be evaluated per assigned case, with responder-only results supplementary. New reports and processing delays would be tracked without presuming a desirable direction.

The representation addresses processing and reconstruction. It cannot recover events that were never noticed or reported, and it creates no new information when source records are sparse. An audit might show that good routine processing already preserves the targeted relationships. Even when C improves reconstruction, additional preparation work or unsupported psychological conclusions could outweigh that gain. Such findings would argue against adoption or require redesign. A controlled reader experiment also does not establish effectiveness in routine workload conditions.

Active follow-up raises additional problems. Accounts may be selective, delayed, or shaped by hindsight. People who can be reached and are willing to discuss context may differ from nonresponders; observed response characteristics cannot exclude unmeasured selection. Retrospective timing should remain visibly approximate. Studies with prospectively collected clinical information may support richer assessment than routine spontaneous reports, but that advantage does not demonstrate routine feasibility. Expert perspectives on useful follow-up are valuable, while prospective information yield and burden remain empirical questions (). The initial setting is consequently a bounded starting point, not a representative sample of all medicines, symptoms, reporting channels, or patient groups. Findings would need replication where source availability, language, and processing arrangements differ.

Questioning can itself change what is reported. In a randomized study during a placebo run-in, a symptom checklist elicited more adverse-event reports than open questions (). This is evidence about ascertainment in a different setting, not a validation of the proposed questions or a determination of which reports were causally correct. Neutral wording and contact logs therefore cannot be assumed to eliminate questioning effects. More documented events could reflect greater ascertainment, altered reporting, or both.

Context must not become a shortcut for dismissing suspected reactions. Improvement after reassurance or a situation change does not exclude a medicinal-product contribution, and persistent symptoms require their own account. Legitimate evidence-based corrections remain possible, provided the original information, reasoning, and processing history are auditable. Neither reduced reporting volume nor unchanged seriousness distributions constitute a universal success criterion. Finally, shifts in causal ratings or signal measures require separate validation against an appropriate causal target; the facts reference proposed here cannot provide it. This Perspective’s literature assessment is narrative, and no prevalence estimate, implementation effect, or reduction in systematic causal error is claimed.

Source-attributed symptom and context sequences offer a specific documentation proposal that can be tested without introducing psychological diagnosis into PV intake. The immediate question is whether explicit representation helps readers reconstruct relevant information better than optimized routine narratives containing the same facts. A source audit and controlled comparison can test that limited claim. Adoption would additionally require acceptable workload and avoidance of unsupported dismissal; causal and signal benefits remain separate research questions.

psychology.title: Why do climate activists stay and why do they leave? Mixed-methods analyses of interview data point to collective efficacy and collective identity beliefs
psychology.abstract: Climate activist groups play a crucial role in driving policy change, yet they often struggle with small memberships and high attrition. To understand the psychology of what sustains membership in climate organizations, we interviewed activists. We compared those who stayed engaged (N = 18) to those who did not (N = 17) to find out whether the groups differed in (1) their reasons for staying engaged and (2) their obstacles to staying engaged. We report two kinds of qualitative analysis (one using bottom-up codes derived from the data and the other using top-down themes from the literature) and one quantitative analysis. We found that, across all three methods, staying engaged was related to various forms of collective efficacy, i.e., the belief that activist groups as a whole can make a difference, the belief that one's particular organization can make a difference, the belief that a particular change making strategy is effective, and the importance of celebrating wins. A second result, also quite consistent across methods, was that those who didn't stay engaged reported a lack of collective identity. This was expressed as weaker alignment with the organization's strategy, weaker community ties, greater interpersonal conflict, and a lack of racial, gender, and class sensitivity and inclusivity. These rich and nuanced analyses of interview data may provide insights to guide organizers to better engage their members.
psychology.text:
Global heating is accelerating (). Without a dramatic reduction in greenhouse gas emissions soon, we risk breaching the critical level of 2 °C between 2040 and 2060 (; ). In the face of widespread institutional inertia, it is critical for civil society, including grassroots climate activists, to impel policy to cut emissions and to prepare for climate impacts (). While grassroots organizations have mounted valiant efforts, their numbers are few and volunteer retention is challenging (; ). One way to better understand how to grow and retain membership in these groups is to examine the psychology of collective action.

Social psychology suggests that activist commitment is shaped by a combination of identity-based, moral, and social motivations (; ). These include: connection to nature, formative life experiences and a personal sense of mission (), connection to others, shared purpose, and the practices of self- and collective care (). Other research has focused on how activist resilience can be sustained through accommodating individual needs, building a sense of belonging (; ; ) and showing how a specific movement is effective (; ).

However, while dozens of such studies on collective action have been conducted over the past decade, a minority have specifically examined climate activists, whose social struggle has peculiar features (e.g., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). As an example, in-depth interview studies have shown that environmental values, such as non-consumerism, non-wastage, and lifestyle simplicity, as well as self-efficacy, awareness of the climate crisis, experiences in nature, role models, and education are strong motivators for sustained climate engagement (). Other qualitative research points to phases of the climate activist trajectory such as “epiphany” (a moment of moral or emotional awakening that motivates engagement), “immersion” (a period of intense involvement and identity integration), “crisis” (experiences of emotional strain, doubt, or burnout), and “resolution” (a reorientation that leads either to sustained engagement or withdrawal) (). However, because these studies rely primarily on bottom-up approaches by deriving findings solely from interview data, it is difficult to integrate their insights into the broader theoretical literature.

There are however some survey studies that adopt top-down frameworks drawn from existing theory; these have examined associations between climate activism and psychological factors such as social identification (e.g., ), moral obligation to act (e.g., ), and collective efficacy (e.g., ). But this approach also has a problem—it risks overlooking novel psychological dynamics that may emerge as motivators of collective climate action. Studies employing mixed-methods that try to integrate bottom-up and top-down designs remain rare (see, e.g., ).

Another weakness in the literature is that most studies of climate activism focus on currently active activists, overlooking those who disengage. A recent exception is , who compared active and retired Extinction Rebellion activists and identified barriers such as weak social integration, internal conflict, doubts about impact, burnout, and external stressors, alongside incentives including strong social ties, moral conviction, pragmatic perspectives on impact, and stress-management strategies. However, this study is limited by focusing on a single organization, when climate organizations differ widely.

To return to our original question of understanding how to grow and retain membership in climate activist organizations, we designed a mixed-methods study to examine who stays engaged and who disengages. Specifically, we focus on confirmed current and disengaged climate activists, collect data from them in a structured interview, and discover bottom-up psychological variables from the data while also applying top-down knowledge from the literature. We asked engaged and disengaged activists from several organizations:

(1) What are the most common reasons for staying engaged?

(2) What are the most common obstacles to staying engaged?

We did three kinds of analyses: qualitative bottom-up analysis, quantitative analysis and qualitative top-down analysis, in that order. For the first, we used an inductive, bottom-up coding approach in which codes were refined iteratively in response to patterns emerging from the interview data (; ), and we report the most commonly mentioned codes which are reasons for staying engaged and obstacles to staying engaged. Although this qualitative bottom-up analysis gives rich data, the large number of codes made it difficult to compare engaged and disengaged groups, and to contextualize the finding within the existing literature. In the second analysis we therefore grouped the codes into a smaller number of psychological factors from an earlier study () and used statistics in a quantitative analysis to test which psychological variables best related to being engaged and disengaged. In a third qualitative top-down analysis, we examined how engaged and disengaged activists differed with regard to four themes that we identified as particularly relevant to climate activism: (1) active hope and the social benefits of activism, (2) practicing organizing for transforming society, (3) the relative benefits of community-based vs. electoral organizing, and (4) individual and group wellbeing. These themes were selected as interpretive lenses based on the authors' long-standing experience with organizing and mobilizing on several justice issues, including climate justice and was also informed by relevant literature on climate activism and social movements. These four themes do not constitute an exhaustive account of the factors relevant to climate activism; rather, they represent a theoretically informed selection of codes that we considered particularly salient in contemporary climate activism.

Active hope and the social benefits of activism refers to the idea popularized by Joanna Macy and colleagues (e.g., ) that hope is something we do rather than simply feel (as opposed to passive, or “optimistic” hope). Active hope is about learning to act regardless of whether one expects to succeed, because acting is the right thing to do, because it teaches us the depths of our hearts, and the ties that bind us (see also ). Our experience that many climate activists explicitly hold these ideas, which sustain them in a struggle against near-impossible odds, is also supported by empirical evidence (; ; ).

Practicing organizing for transforming society refers to the idea that people engage in climate activism because it is a way to build community-organizing skills that go far beyond just cutting emissions. For example, the skills one learns in this space are essential for addressing a wide range of social struggles, such as energy and food democracy, worker rights, and fighting racism (; ). This linking of struggles has been quite explicit in, for example, the organizing strategy of the youth Sunrise Movement.

The relative benefit of community-based vs. electoral organizing refers to the observation that many climate activists favor a theory of change of taking local community action rather than merely expecting the electoral process to be successful.  showed that young activists combine community and electoral organizing and often discuss the trade-offs of working outside vs. inside “the system,” also see . Further, organizations such as Sunrise and the Climate Justice Alliance explicitly refer to the limitations of the elite-focused electoral strategy without mass movement pressure.

Individual and group wellbeing refers to the awareness that some activists have of moral burnout, overwork and the exhaustion and stress that come from volunteering in spaces where one is constantly exposed to the dread-inducing evidence of climate collapse as well as the obduracy of institutions and political structures. Interview-based evidence supports this awareness among activists (; ), and the training curricula of organizations such as Sunrise and Greenpeace include modules on preventing such activist burnout.

Thus, in what follows we do a qualitative bottom-up analysis to discover the codes that emerge from the interview data, a quantitative analysis to test statistically which factors differ between engaged and disengaged activists and a qualitative top-down analysis to examine the data through the lens of four central themes in climate activism. Our goal is both to integrate these findings with the existing theoretical literature and to identify patterns that can inform activists and organizers seeking to support sustained engagement and participation in climate movements.

Forty activists in California were recruited for this study, which reflects a medium-to-large sample size for qualitative studies (). Half of them were engaged activists and the other half were disengaged activists. Among the recruits, five were dropped from the study: three because they did not complete the interview, one because of lack of concentration during the study, and one because of data loss from technical issues with transcription. This resulted in a final sample size of N = 35 (N = 18 engaged and N = 17 disengaged). We focused on young adults (mean age = 24 years, minimum = 18, maximum = 33) because they have historically been strong agents of social and political change. California was selected as the study context because the research team was based there and had established connections with the organizations.

The group was mostly made up of women (68% women, 23% men, 6% non-binary, and 3% other responses) and was ethnically diverse (42% White, 31% Asian, 15% mixed, 9% Hispanic, 3% Black). Most participants identified as Democrats (71%), with the remainder selecting “Other” as their political affiliation (29%, e.g., “Independent,” “Socialist” or “no party affiliation”).

All participants engaged in activism within their organizations as unpaid volunteers.

We collaborated with three major climate activist organizations in California (Sunrise Movement, 350.org, and a University of California climate organization working on environmental advocacy). We distributed a link to a brief eligibility survey through announcements in virtual meetings and events, emails to members in the organizations, and snowball sampling (encouraging those who replied to the survey to pass it on to others).

To be eligible for the study, respondents had to be: 1) either currently active members of a climate organization, defined as having attended at least one meeting per month for the past 3 months (engaged activist), or former active members who had been disengaged for at least 3 months (disengaged activist), 2) proficient in English, and 3) aged 18–35 years old. If inclusion criteria were met, respondents were asked to report their age, gender, income, political orientation, and ethnicity. Eligible participants were then contacted to schedule an interview. Those who completed the interview were paid $30.

Each participant had a one-on-one semi-structured interview that was conducted by one of the authors via Zoom, between March and December 2022. Interviews lasted about 1 h (mean = 69.1 min, and SD = 6.16 min) and were audio and video recorded. Participants gave informed consent and all procedures followed a university-approved ethics protocol. The interviewer was trained to make the participant feel comfortable and to encourage them to speak freely. The interview script included questions about the participant's general beliefs about climate change and experiences with activism (see the  for full script). The main questions in the interview focused on participants' 1) reasons for staying engaged and 2) obstacles to staying engaged in their organizations. The interview script was identical for engaged and disengaged participants, except for the tense of the questions (e.g., “what keeps you involved with your organization?” for engaged participants and “what kept you involved with your organization when you were a member?” for disengaged participants).

Each interview was automatically transcribed using NVivo and subsequently reviewed and corrected by research assistants for accuracy. Two human coders then segmented the transcripts into distinct statements, each representing an independent paragraph conveying a single concept. The coders categorized each statement as either meaningful (i.e., containing information about reasons for or obstacles to staying engaged in activism) or not meaningful. In parallel, we developed a preliminary codebook comprising 11 psychological codes underlying pro-environmental behavior, drawing on the environmental psychology literature (; ) as well as suggestions from experienced California activists whom we surveyed prior to the interviews. The preliminary codebook was intended to guide the initial stages of coding and was subsequently expanded to incorporate new codes emerging from the interview data.

Four human coders were trained on the preliminary codebook and independently coded a subset of the interviews, assigning codes to each meaningful statement. The coders compared their coding and discussed discrepancies to clarify the application and interpretation of existing codes and to identify potential new codes. When coders encountered a potential new code that emerged in at least three interviews, it was added to the codebook through iterative discussion. This process allowed the codebook to be refined through repeated comparison and discussion among coders. All 11 preliminary codes were retained in the final codebook, alongside the additional codes identified through this inductive process. Coding discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus among the coders, and the codebook was subsequently “locked.” All 35 interviews were then coded according to the finalized codebook.

The finalized codebook yielded 46 codes for reasons for staying engaged (e.g., “concern for the natural world,” “sharing a theory of change with one's organization”) and 20 codes for obstacles to staying engaged (e.g., “lack of intersectionality,” “burnout or overwork”). We included only codes mentioned by at least three participants in the final analysis, resulting in a total of 61 codes. This three-participant threshold was used to focus the analysis on recurring patterns rather than idiosyncratic statements in this small interview sample. The full list of 61 codes, together with the frequency with which each code was mentioned, is shown in . For each interview, we assigned a “1” (present) or “0” (absent) for each code, separately for reasons for staying engaged and obstacles to staying engaged.

Bottom-up derived reasons for and obstacles against staying engaged.

We list all codes arising from the data, ordered by the percentage of all participants mentioning that code (%), and reporting the percentage of engaged and disengaged participants mentioning it. We only report codes mentioned by 3 or more participants.

We did not conduct a formal prospective assessment of thematic saturation. Rather, the coding framework was iteratively refined through coder discussion and comparison until the codebook was locked, with new codes retained when they emerged in at least three interviews (as a criterion used to determine which emergent codes were sufficiently recurrent to be incorporated into the codebook).

For both reasons for staying engaged and obstacles to staying engaged, we first calculated the percentage of engaged and disengaged participants who mentioned each of the 61 codes and extracted quotes from within each group for the three most frequent codes.

We transposed the 61 codes into nine psychological factors: emotional engagement, collective efficacy, self-efficacy, collective identity, personal identity, perceived behavioral control, social norm, attitude/worldviews, and theory of change, which we had identified in a previous study () (). While some codes are conceptually adjacent, we assigned them according to the factor definitions used in the referenced study, to avoid post-hoc double counting.  shows how we grouped the codes under these nine psychological factors. For each interview we assigned a “1” (present) or “0” (absent) for each psychological factor as follows: if the participant mentioned any of the codes grouped under that factor, we assigned “1,” otherwise, “0.” This binary coding avoided interpreting differences in the frequency of mentions as differences in psychological importance, as these may instead reflect participants' conversational style or the extent to which they elaborated on a topic.

Mapping of the bottom-up codes to 9 psychological factors.

For each of “reasons for staying engaged” and “obstacles to stay engaged,” we list all codes arising from the data, grouped by the 9 psychological factors (italics) and ordered by the percentage of participants mentioning that code (%). We only report codes mentioned by 3 or more participants.

Next, we assessed the reasons for staying engaged on which the engaged and disengaged activists differed. To answer this, we ran nine separate Fisher's exact tests with the dependent variable being whether participants were currently engaged or disengaged, and the independent variable being the percentage of mentions for each psychological factor, and using a Bonferroni-Holm multiple comparisons correction.

For obstacles to staying we took the same approach as above, but this time we ran seven rather than nine Fisher's exact tests, since two of the factors were not mentioned by participants as obstacles: theory of change and personal identity.

The data were analyzed using the R software ().

We looked at the overall differences between the two groups on the four themes we deemed central to climate activism today, each encompassing multiple emerging themes: 1) Active hope and the social benefits of activism, 2) Practicing organizing for transforming society, 3) The relative benefit of community-based vs. electoral organizing, 4) Individual and group wellbeing.

Several members of the research team, including the authors, have experience organizing within climate and social justice movements. This experience may have shaped recruitment, interview questions, coding, interpretation, and the selection of themes for the top-down analysis. To reduce the influence of individual assumptions, coding involved multiple coders (three of which had no experience in activism), a shared codebook, and discussion of discrepancies. We also acknowledge that the top-down analysis reflects a theoretically informed interpretation shaped by both relevant literature and the researchers' situated experience of activist organizing, rather than an exhaustive or objective account of climate activism.

The interviews were conducted in California between March and December 2022. This timing is relevant to the interpretation of participants' experiences, as the interviews took place in the period following the United States' reentry into the Paris Agreement in 2021, amid continued political contestation over climate policy and active opposition to climate action. We therefore interpret participants' experiences of engagement and disengagement within this particular political and historical context, rather than treating the broader political environment as a uniform or timeless backdrop.

In this section, we report the findings from the three analyses separately, with the interpretations grounded each analytical approach. Whenever quotes are presented, we use newly generated participant codes rather than the initials stored in the data sheet, to systematically distinguish participants while preserving their privacy and organizational affiliation.

The most mentioned reasons for staying engaged, each mentioned by over 70% of participants, were: sense of community (94% overall; 94% engaged, 94% disengaged), moral responsibility (83% overall; 78% engaged, 88% disengaged), and vision for the future (77% overall; 78% engaged, 76% disengaged) ().

The need for community is often expressed as a sense of belonging or kinship with other activists in the organization (; ; ; ; ). Community is also a central element of the well known Social Identity Model of Collective Action (SIMCA; ).

For many participants in our study, the social bonds they created with fellow activists were crucial in navigating the emotional and logistical challenges of activism. As one engaged participant explained, the support and solidarity within the activist community helped them cope with the high emotional demands of collective action:

“I think what really drives me out of it [the hardships of activism] is community, being able to talk with others, being able to work with others in this.” (eng_01)

Beyond building resilience, community is also a source of positive energy and emotional support. Another engaged participant emphasized the positive effect of being surrounded by people who share their values and vision:

“It feels good being a part of a community built on the same morals. It's almost like the other way of spiraling—instead of spiraling downward, it's spiraling up.” (eng_01)

The importance of community emerged also for disengaged participants. Some of them recalled how feeling part of a connected, supportive group had been a key factor in their past involvement. As one participant reflected, without those emotional and social ties, long-term engagement becomes difficult to sustain:

“It starts with providing a space for people to talk about things, talk about eco anxiety, their own experiences, building a connected community. I just think building community is by far the most important thing in grassroots organizations because we all have kind of the common fight, but there needs to be also something that kind of keeps us together socially, emotionally, and mentally.” (dis_03)

Moral responsibility refers to a strong moral commitment to protect people and other living beings affected by the climate crisis. This sense of duty has been identified in prior research as a motivating factor in climate activism, including within movements such as Fridays for Future (; ; ; ).

Among engaged activists, this moral duty translated into a deep sense of obligation to counterbalance the disproportionate impact of Western countries on all living beings, via land and labor exploitation:

“I mean, there's so many things that we have and we do that have negative impacts. I think we should all have a sense of personal responsibility. I think that's logical.” (eng_06)

For some, this sense of responsibility stemmed from their awareness of suffering happening within their own communities, which made inaction simply inconceivable:

“I would not find it bearable to take an honest look at the world around me, like my immediate community and see all of the pain and suffering and degradation and do nothing about it” (eng_09).

Others described their moral commitment due to their concern regarding climate impacts:

“For me, the stakes are too high. I can't just not do anything about it. Not doing anything about it is not an option for me.” (eng_14)

Disengaged participants also mentioned moral considerations as a central element of their past engagement. For some, the injustice of climate inaction, and particularly its disproportionate effects on future generations, was a key motivator:

“It's extremely unjust to marginalized communities, to pretend like climate change isn't happening right now just because it's not affecting us. And it's an injustice to our own generation and future generations. And everything we loved and nature and the environment. To not fight for it to be protected when it is very much at risk.” (dis_07)

Many participants were motivated to stay by their vision of a better future. The ability to imagine a positive transformation of the current status quo, such as a more sustainable relationship between humans and the rest of nature, has been shown to support engagement in collective action (, ; ).

One engaged participant expressed hope toward the growing resistance against fossil fuels:

“Sure. I mean, I think it's already been started. I'm just looking at what Extinction Rebellion has done, and students on campuses all over. I feel like that fight to really shut down fossil fuel infrastructure has already started.”

Another activist envisioned a broader transformation:

“Definitely a carbon tax, definitely valuing ecosystems, especially forests and things that draw down a lot of carbon value. You know, policies that either create tax incentives or force the agricultural sector to invest in carbon drawdown techniques and sustainable agriculture. Subsidizing clean energy and taking away all fossil fuel subsidies.” (eng_17)

Some found the vision of global systemic change too abstract, and instead focused on tangible, local improvements as the necessary start for greater transformations:

“I almost want to say that the big thought solutions are more thought exercises and not the small local actions that I really take part in. Not to echo the phrase—think globally, act locally—but that kind of is what it is like. This is the world I want to see on a big scale. So, what do I do in my community to make it better? That way, we can build up to that. What keeps me in activism is the stuff that I can be doing to my local community and the small victories and losses in my local organization.” (eng_04)

Even disengaged participants mentioned future visions related to community transformation as motivators of their past engagement. One participant described a hopeful vision of social and environmental justice, proposing ideas such as community welfare, shorter work weeks, sharing and repairing to reduce consumption, consistent with degrowth scholarship (; ):

“Communities where there are more parks so people can like, sit and relax, there's less car centric areas. There is great transportation, not just inside community, but also connecting communities, right? You know, there's a shorter workweek. I don't think we need 5 days. Yeah, I think there's better recycling, there's better education on recycling. What if there was like a service that didn't cost money that could take items from people's houses to other people's houses to make sure we're not putting things in landfill? Maybe if there was more places that you could fix things instead of having to just buy a new one?” (dis_08)

The most frequent obstacles to staying engaged were burnout or overwork (66% total, 78% engaged, 53% disengaged), competing responsibilities (66% total, 61% engaged, 71% disengaged), and prognostic frame misalignment (i.e., misalignment with an organization's mission; 34% total, 17% engaged, 53% disengaged) ().

Burnout refers to the physical and mental exhaustion of sustained overwork and/or a sense of moral injury (). Within the climate movement, the high stakes of societal and environmental preservation and deep emotional investment can easily turn into overwhelming fatigue, if they are not buffered by a sense of community, solidarity, and belonging ().

Several of our participants pointed out how burnout often arises when volunteer commitment is inconsistent, forcing highly dedicated people in the group to take on a disproportionate share of responsibilities. This unequal burden can create a vicious cycle where overwork leads to burnout, withdrawal, and emotional challenges for those who stay:

“Volunteers' capacity to help out and volunteer fluctuates. And because of that, it's hard to get consistent commitment. And when you don't have consistent commitment, people have to end up taking on a lot more themselves, who are really, really involved. And so that ends up burning them out.” (eng_08)

Another frequent source of burnout was the challenge of balancing activism with full-time work in a society that structurally prioritizes professional commitments over civic participation or volunteering. As one participant shared:

“I'm practically doing this like a part-time job outside of work, so it's difficult to balance life and volunteering and work. When work is already overbearing and stupid in the way that our society is structured, that makes it difficult, like burnout, the burnout makes it difficult.” (eng_10)

Burnout also appeared in contexts where activism took an extractive form, i.e., where the emotional and mental wellbeing of active members was overlooked, and a culture of relentless productivity prevailed:

“I think it is very easy to fall into traps of burnout. I guess extractive forms of activism itself [plays a role]. Finding oneself in that place of burnout is a very quick pathway to not wanting to be engaged.” (eng_11)

Multiple disengaged participants shared that the online shift during the COVID-19 pandemic made burnout more likely. During this time, the lack of boundaries in remote work, particularly Zoom meetings, contributed to a sense of overwhelm:

“I think I was honestly burnt out from doing it, especially because of the whole like, everything's on Zoom. I don't have any boundaries. I could do this literally all day and I would sometimes.” (dis_08)

Leadership roles were especially linked to burnout, as several disengaged participants described the high pressure of coordinating multiple groups, managing logistics, and maintaining momentum, often with little support:

“And also, I was a leader the whole time that I was in Sunrise. And I think that's also an extra added layer. From the time I started at 29 until about like a year ago, I was leading two teams. It was just a lot for me.” (dis_08)

The U.S. societal context in which the climate activists we interviewed operate is unforgiving, often demanding full-time work or study while simultaneously managing other responsibilities, such as caring for their family ().

Several engaged participants expressed that school and work commitments interfered with their ability to participate in activism. As one mentioned:

“The time commitment can sometimes be a lot—especially this year, which was my first year back to fully in-person school. I had gotten involved during virtual school, which had a lot more flexibility.” Another said: “Personally, I'd say school. Managing such a big responsibility—like getting a degree—while also needing to work to afford to live, that really gets in the way” (eng_07).

Others described how the pressure of everyone juggling major life responsibilities, and the lack of compensation for activist work (which can be a further challenge to those financially struggling), often led to people leaving, and others to take up their work:

“Having to balance the things you care about vs. unfortunately, the things that pay the bills. That's tough. We're all giving our time, and our volunteers are giving their time without being compensated, which is something many of us value” (eng_16).

One disengaged participant explained that their family became a priority when health issues arose, reducing their engagement in climate activism:

“The biggest reason I quit is because my dad got cancer. That was really stressful, and I just couldn't handle it—worrying about my family and my own health plus the climate stuff at the same time” (dis_10).

In addition to a lack of time, many reported that feeling exhausted after long days at work made activism feel unsustainable:

“I'm working full-time and barely have enough energy left to take care of my own basic needs—let alone do mutual aid work or activism” and “I got a job—a forty-hour-a-week job—and I just didn't have the time or the energy for it anymore.” (dis_09)

Prognostic frame alignment refers to the way that organizations frame or formulate their strategy for climate mitigation. For example, there is a tension between system-critical framings (“the problem is capitalism”) and those oriented around individual action. According to , there are three possible prognostic frames: a) reformist actions of working within the system to develop technological and legislative change; b) individual action that raises awareness but doesn't engage with politics; and c) systemic action which works against the system to end colonialism/capitalism. Disagreements with the solutions an organization proposes can be a significant obstacle to sustained involvement. Some engaged participants noted that different views on whether climate action should address electoral politics, or the degree to which climate justice should be central, can lead to internal tensions:

“One of the challenges is not seeing eye to eye with people—differences of opinion on politics. Yeah, how much social justice and environmental justice you want to include in our topics.” (eng_03)

Others expressed frustration with organizations whose leadership feels disconnected from their members, where leadership structures and goals are far from the day-to-day experiences of those doing the work:

“When big national organizations are not reflective of the people who are putting their blood, sweat, and tears into it, and ignore that—it's just heartbreaking to see.” (eng_04)

Among disengaged participants, some expressed disillusionment with the limited impact of certain campaigns that focused on narrow issues rather than systemic change:

“I feel like there are bigger fish to fry. That definitely made it hard for me to stay involved—like, for example, fighting against leaf blowers. That's such a specific issue. I mean, let's focus on corporations, you know what I mean?” (dis_17)

They became disheartened after engaging in electoral activism, feeling betrayed or let down by the politicians they supported after they gained power:

“When I first started working in political activism, I genuinely thought I could change the system. It's not that I don't believe in government—it's that politicians suck. For example, I did a lot of work for [local politician]... she claimed to care about our issues, but once she was elected, she didn't care about us anymore. I spent years helping her get elected, and none of the things she said turned out to be true.” (dis_17)

Engaged and disengaged participants expressed different views on electoral vs. community-based activism, which we discuss in the next section.

We next examined the differences in the reasons for staying engaged, between engaged and disengaged groups through the lens of the 9 existing psychological factors from a prior study (), after grouping our original codes into these factors. Descriptively, the largest difference was observed for collective efficacy, which was mentioned by 94% of engaged participants compared with 53% of disengaged participants, a difference of 42 percentage points (). Although this represented the largest between-group difference, the difference did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni–Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.065; OR = 13.9, 95% CI [1.49–705]). As illustrated in , our psychological factor of collective efficacy was in fact a construct made up of several codes: the efficacy of collective action in general, the efficacy of the specific organization, the efficacy of the group's particular change-making strategy (“prognostic frame alignment”) and the celebration of wins.

Collective identity showed the largest descriptive difference between groups, with 53% of disengaged participants vs. 22% of engaged participants mentioning this factor, a difference of 31 percentage points (). However, this difference was not statistically significant (adjusted p = 0.601; OR = 0.26, 95% CI [0.04–1.33]). Even so, this trend for collective identity appears informative and we accordingly examine it more carefully. Just as in the collective efficacy case above, the construct of collective identity was made up of several, more detailed codes: i.e., community, interpersonal conflict, and a lack of racial/gender/class sensitivity.

Here we looked at the overall differences between the two groups on the four themes we deemed central to climate activism today.

Recall that active hope refers to acting without necessarily expecting success because of forging the ties that bind, discovering one's courage, being virtuous and being involved in meaningful action. Many engaged activists mentioned that being surrounded by like-minded individuals helped them channel anxiety into action and provided a sense of belonging. One participant said,

“The community gives me a sense of purpose... it decreases the climate anxiety.” (eng_08)

Another noted

“I‘ve met some of my best friends through doing this work, and it's a unique friendship because we're all focused and driven by the same issue.” (eng_01)

The presence of others doing similar work also reinforced their constructive hope, even if maintaining a realistic sense of the complexity of the struggle: “I'm not hopeful that our effort will be successful. I'm hopeful that we will act, that we can get together and do as much as we can” (eng_17). Engaged participants often saw their activism as deeply rooted in personal values and meaning; one said

“operating off of a personal sense of justice, responsibility and finding meaning… it relates to me the way I see myself, my values and faith.” (eng_11)

They perceived local and concrete actions directly benefiting their communities as even more meaningful and hopeful compared to actions addressing issues on a larger scale:

‘I felt hopeless when I was thinking about things on a national level... I have refocused on a more local level, on college campuses—because that's a way that I can kind of overcome the hopelessness issue.” (eng_06)

Disengaged activists often described a complicated relationship with hope, perhaps indicating they were less familiar with the active hope concept. Many expressed having once felt optimistic and involved but gradually becoming disillusioned by systemic barriers and by the perceived inaction of others. Two people recalled the emotional toll of continuing despite the lack of a sense of progress toward concrete change:

“I lost hope and was still involved for over a year after that” and “I felt so helpless… I was still doing my part, but a part of me was like, I don't care anymore.” (dis_04)

Although some acknowledged the emotional weight of hopelessness, they tended to manage it through personal rather than collective coping strategies. One participant explained,

“I don't let [hopelessness] overpower me... I sit with it, I contemplate it, and then I kind of carry on.” (dis_03)

Another mentioned:

“When I start to feel it [hopelessness] creeping up, I go sit by the river or tend my garden.” (dis_09)

Even among those who still hoped that change could be possible, there was a deep skepticism about systemic obstacles, as one person said,

“I just feel like I'm a very hopeful person….But I'm also like realistic and realize that people's avarice gets in the way and greed of corporations is the biggest obstacle... it's probably not going to happen.” (dis_16)

Nevertheless, some disengaged activists still found meaning in their past efforts and in climate activism in general:

“It gave some meaning... maybe you're on the right side of history” (dis_05)

and in the emotional bond they once felt in the movement

“we all grieve, we grieve together and we fight together... the struggle is so real.” (dis_17)

In summary, these results are consistent with our prediction that engaged participants stayed involved through a sense of active hope, finding meaning in their activist community through their shared values, friendships and reciprocal support. On the other hand, disengaged participants felt more isolated and disillusioned, possibly due to their weaker connection to the collective, which led them to rely mostly on personal coping strategies to manage hopelessness.

Both engaged and disengaged activists acknowledged gaining useful skills that could be carried over to other activist spaces. However, some aspects of how they perceived this differed.

Engaged activists saw their climate organizing as a formative experience, both personally and politically. One participant mentioned how climate spaces shaped their view of leadership and community work:

“I think it forces me to be better at collaborating, better at problem solving and managing stress” (eng_02). Another explained, “Through climate action... I think the kind of learning that I've gotten has been very useful in thinking about just generally how we live in society and civic engagement.” (eng_11)

Several also described concrete ways in which activism opened up career paths related to climate mitigation, with one saying,

“That experience also got me [an] internship... working on climate for the mayor's office at the city of Sacramento.” (eng_11)

The intersectionality of climate and other struggles was central to their discourse, as another said,

“Once I recognized the intersectionality... it just taught me to learn about the interdisciplinary approaches to different issues.” (eng_18)

One perceived that her group focused on intersectional struggles beyond simple emission reduction:

“I think climate justice is [what keeps me motivated] because we focus on things other than just straight environmentalism like intersectionality between climate and racial justice, economic justice systems…”. (eng_02)

Thus, they described learning not just practical skills but also developing a long-term commitment to activism and a cross-sectional understanding of justice.

Disengaged activists presented their experience with climate organizing in more skills-based terms, often describing it as a temporary phase or as something that contributed to other parts of their lives. One gave an overview of the many transferable tools they gained,

“I think public speaking, writing with a clear message and clear intent. Being able to strategize and have a plan of action. Being able to work with other people and collaborate. Researching, in some words and using data to support.” (dis_01)

Many mentioned transferring what they learned to their job or other organizations:

“Just like the process of working with other people and delegating tasks I think has been helpful in the work that I do with other organizations…”

and

“It was just kind of a general organizing experience. And that's made me more confident with organizing within my union as well.” (dis_12)

Others described remaining engaged in climate-related work, in part because of what they had learned in the movement, but via other activist or educational spaces:

“Still feel like I'm involved, insofar as I think my labor organizing is oriented toward climate activism and so is my teaching. And so everything I'm kind of doing is kind of working toward that goal.” (dis_02)

Some mentioned being introduced to broader issues like climate justice, feminism, wealth inequality and other intersectional struggles by the climate movement, but others did not feel like these were central in their group predicament, which made them feel alienated:

“it [the climate organization] basically dodges the climate justice aspect altogether. In many regards, at least I felt that it does.” (dis_10)

One disengaged activist noted a lack of representativeness of various communities within the climate movement:

“It's really important to shed light on all the other different necessities of all the different communities and make sure that they're also included in the movement.” (dis_03)

In summary, as we predicted, engaged participants did perceive their climate organizing as a way to link to other struggles. On the other hand, disengaged activists also gained organizing skills but often described their involvement as temporary, and some felt alienated by a lack of focus on broader justice issues or insufficient inclusivity within their organization.

We expected that engaged activists would value community activism more than electoral routes. However, we found that engaged activists tended to express a greater, although sometimes conflicted, commitment to electoral goals as a necessary route to systemic change. They acknowledged the shortcomings of electoral systems, like short-termism, political corruption and limited representativeness; but most still advocated for political engagement to advance climate policy. One engaged activist said:

“Well, the irony is that I don't trust the current structures of government at all, but I know that we need a democratic government in order to make things work… So there needs to be a concerted political movement to get people who are progressive and want to do what's right into office.” (eng_04)

Many described change as multifaceted, including political change and community-level change happening in parallel:

“There's a political layer in which...people vote for politicians that act on climate… and then there's political action that can be taken outside of the scope of our democratic system.” (eng_05)

and

“I think you have to tackle this from every different angle... from the individual to the local city level and up to the international level.” (eng_08)

Others described the concrete work they were doing within political structures, as in:

“I'm part of the political team... I'm doing a lot of work like with our candidates that we're endorsing who are running... I did a lot of work with the Green New Deal.” (eng_12)

Many disengaged activists expressed deep skepticism about electoral activism, and considered community-centered, relational, and localized approaches more transformative. They stressed the importance of building resilient local networks, and supporting systems revolving around justice and meeting material needs. One disengaged participant described this as,

“I am a big fan of prefigurative politics... the world you‘re fighting for can't exist until you start building it in your own life and living by your values with your community.” (dis_09)

Another stated,

“I think my approach is like, forget the people at the top. Let's work on just building up a strong community.” (dis_10)

Another mentioned the importance of “bringing people to a good spot” allowing them to live and afford a healthy life, as a way to indirectly tackle climate change, i.e., transforming the oppressive system that affects everyday people just as much as the climate:

“working on community level, like increased tree canopies and make sure public transportation was a viable resource to get people to and from places and then like bike lanes…I think I've kind of disregarded the big climate change situation, I think more now about people and how can we get people to be at a good spot.” (dis_08)

A third rejected electoral approaches completely:

“I would say that the focus on electoralism... is more or less a waste of time.” (dis_13)

Others expressed concerns over prioritizing systemic-level climate action before addressing basic community wellbeing, as in:

“So I think what I would do to mitigate the climate crisis or to get rid of it would be getting more people to realize what's at stake for them and their children and the planet as a whole. But that conversation cannot be had with people who are also struggling to maintain their livelihoods. So by making it more convenient to just exist and to live and pay people like an actual wage, like I just think a lot of things would be better if we cared about people.” (dis_08)

This suggests that their focus on community and material needs may have shifted their activism away from the climate-specific context, reorienting it toward other more tangible, though still interrelated, issues.

In summary, engaged participants, even if cautious toward the electoral systems, still saw political engagement as an essential leverage to systemic change. Many engaged in multi-level action and were actively involved in both political campaigns or advocacy related to climate policy and community-level organizing. On the other hand, disengaged participants tended to reject electoral activism, and considered it ineffective or corrupt. They focused instead on building resilient, justice-oriented local communities that meet immediate material needs. For them, addressing climate began with supporting people's day-to-day wellbeing, rather than influencing top-down political solutions. Their quotes suggest that some of them might have disengaged from these climate organizations in order to focus on more tangible, social justice issues.

Engaged participants mentioned preserving wellbeing by setting personal boundaries, delegating responsibilities, and valuing rest. One engaged activist emphasized the importance of defining personal capacity: “I'm only one person... so defining my capacity has helped a lot” (eng_10). Some found empowerment in saying no and focusing their efforts. For example, one engaged participant reflected, “Not attending meetings, and not feeling sorry for it really helped” (eng_10), while another shared how her mentor taught her that “even just say[ing] no to something is self-care for me” (eng_14). These comments showed a conscious commitment to preserving mental energy and making organizing sustainable. Engaged activists talked about the efforts within their groups to address internal conflict and support constructive communication. One recalled how they raised concerns about a gender gap in leadership and felt listened to and validated:

“That allowed me to be able to say something and leadership... was like—Yeah, that actually is not a good thing. Let's do something about it.” (eng_14)

Another noted the importance of “clear boundaries and community agreements” to build a positive environment in her group. Generally, engaged activists framed their organizations as learning environments where both personal growth and community support were possible.

Disengaged activists also expressed setting boundaries as a fundamental strategy to preserve mental health. One person described their strategy as:

“Personally, I‘ve really been focusing on setting boundaries for myself, like, really understanding how much time I have available, how many responsibilities I can take on. So in order to prevent burnout, I really have to have a raw, honest conversation with myself.” (dis_03)

For them, speaking to other members about burnout and delegating overwhelming efforts was a key element. One disengaged activist mentioned:

“When I did experience burnout, it really helped me to just talk about it to the people who I was engaged with” (dis_03). Another said: “If I was too busy I'd let them know. And they would help take work off my plate and they were very understanding.” (dis_10)

When it came to conflict resolution, disengaged activists mentioned more unresolved interpersonal conflict, miscommunication and lack of proper facilitation and representativeness in taking decisions, which led some of them to exit their organization. One participant observed that

“there's not enough resource and attention on the interpersonal dynamics.” (dis_04)

Another shared that despite efforts to speak up,

“When I tried voicing that, I had a concern about it [the decision to support a local politician] I wasn't really given the opportunity to talk about it... there was this urgency of like, well, let's just vote... without really speaking it through.” (dis_04)

Some described witnessing dynamics where dissent was not welcomed and power was unevenly distributed. One recalled, “there wasn't that much feeling of an open discussion” and added that

“certain people have more power... there was this one person who disagreed... and she got shut down really quick.” (dis_05)

One further obstacle was seen in the disconnect between the national chapter of the larger organization, and the local chapters:

“they [the national chapter] would make decisions for hubs without talking to hubs… And there was a lot of miscommunication. There was a lot of disregarding people's [local activists'] very real lived experiences.” (dis_08)

and the divide between paid and unpaid activists in the organization created further tensions.

In summary, both engaged and disengaged participants recognized the importance of setting personal boundaries and prioritizing wellbeing, but differed in their experience of internal conflict within their activist groups. Engaged participants often mentioned supportive, communicative environments that valued personal capacity, rest, and collective care, and positive experiences of being heard and empowered by inclusive group norms. Disengaged participants encountered more frequent unresolved conflict, top-down decision-making, and a lack of inclusiveness, which made them feel disempowered and unacknowledged, and in some cases led to their departure from activist spaces.
