Summary of the results.

We interviewed engaged and disengaged climate activists from three organizations in California. We first did a qualitative analysis where we examined the 61 emerging codes, looking at the most frequent reasons for and obstacles to staying engaged in climate activism across all participants. Then we did a quantitative analysis where we mapped the emerging codes onto 9 psychological factors from the prior literature and used quantitative analysis to examine how reasons and obstacles differed between the engaged and disengaged groups. Finally, we compared the two groups on four key themes that we considered central to climate activism today: active hope, practicing organizing for transforming society, electoral vs. community-organizing and individual and group wellbeing.

For the qualitative analysis of codes across all participants, the main reasons to stay involved were community, moral responsibility, and a positive vision for the future, while the main obstacles were burnout or overwork, competing responsibilities, and a lack of alignment with the organization's strategy. For the quantitative analysis, collective efficacy (the belief in the group's power to create change) showed the largest descriptive difference between engaged and disengaged activists among the factors examined, while collective identity showed the largest descriptive difference in relation to obstacles to staying engaged. For the qualitative analysis of the four key themes we observed that engaged activists tended to experience more constructive hope, stronger collective support, and a sense of intersectionality and inclusivity in their groups. They were also more open to combining grassroots work with electoral politics and reported better practices for conflict resolution and collective care. Disengaged activists instead often shifted toward local, community-based organizing related to material needs and sometimes felt alienated after experiencing poor interpersonal dynamics and lack of inclusivity in the climate movement.

The most consistent finding across the analyses was the central role of collective efficacy and a sense of community in sustaining engagement. These themes emerged in the qualitative analysis of bottom-up codes, were reflected in the qualitative analysis of top-down themes, and, in the quantitative analysis, collective efficacy showed the largest observed difference between engaged and disengaged participants. People tend to stay in a given organization when they feel that their group is capable of making a difference and when they have a supportive community that shares their values and their vision for the future. This is in line with accounts of community building as a fundamental ingredient for sustained activism (; ; ; ). Given that our psychological factor of collective efficacy was in fact a construct made up of several codes, i.e., the efficacy of collective action in general, the efficacy of the specific organization, the efficacy of the group's particular change-making strategy (“prognostic frame alignment”) and the celebration of wins, these results point to different psychological facets of efficacy that organizers can focus on. For example, they could emphasize the importance of their particular change-making strategy, highlight past victories to inspire belief in collective power, celebrate current wins together and build efficient organizational structures with clear roles and even work distribution.

A second notable finding concerned collective identity, which emerged across all three analyses. It appeared in bottom-up codes as a lack of alignment with the organization's strategy, in the quantitative analysis as the largest observed obstacle-related difference between groups, and in the top-down themes through strong social ties and shared meaning among engaged activists, contrasted with alienation linked to poor interpersonal dynamics and lack of inclusivity among disengaged activists. The construct of collective identity was made up of several, more detailed codes: i.e., community, interpersonal conflict, and a lack of racial/gender/class sensitivity. Thus our study provides practical insight to organizers on how to boost these specific elements. For example, collective identity can be supported through group-care activities, conflict-resolution processes, and dedicated inclusion teams that can help bridge differences in class, gender, and age.

Apart from these overarching results, the qualitative analysis of top-down themes also pointed to two other elements that distinguished the engaged from the disengaged: “practicing organizing for transforming society” and views on the value of “community-based vs. electoral organizing.” On the first point, organizers might find ways to emphasize that the skills, thinking and experience of working within their particular organization have greater and wider relevance for transforming society—something that grows in relevance given that we not only have a climate crisis, but a climate, ecological and political crisis, with an authoritarian turn in many places. On the second point, we note that the disengaged expressed less confidence in the electoral route than the engaged and their quotes suggested that some of them might have disengaged from these climate organizations in order to focus on more tangible social justice issues. This is also something that organizers could be aware of—you might be more likely to retain people in your group if you emphasize the local transformational aspects of climate action focussed on people's material interest rather than system-level political change and moral aspirations (Young et al., in review).

Our findings suggest that disengagement from a particular climate organization should not necessarily be understood as disengagement from activism or collective action more broadly. Several participants classified as disengaged appeared instead to have redirected their energy toward other forms of political and civic engagement, including labor organizing, teaching, mutual aid, or other social justice-oriented local work. Organizational exit may therefore represent movement between forms of collective action rather than withdrawal from collective action itself. This distinction is theoretically important, as it suggests that what appears as disengagement at the organizational level may, in some cases, reflect a shift in the domain, strategy, or social justice focus of participants' activism rather than a decline in their broader commitment to social change.

Many of the above results confirm what was found by  in a group of current and retired Extinction Rebellion activists but our study expands those results by examining climate activists across multiple organizations and combining qualitative and quantitative methods, allowing for statistical comparison between engaged and disengaged participants.

Our study had limitations. First, because it was only focused on activists in three organizations in California in 2022, we cannot know how generalizable our results are. Second, our quantitative analyses should be taken cautiously for two main reasons. A cross-sectional design cannot show that collective efficacy or collective identity are causal to sustained engagement (that would require a longitudinal study with an appropriate experimental manipulation). Also our sample size may have hindered the power to detect group-differences for the psychological factors. Third, our study involved self-selection, in that we interviewed participants who decided to respond to our invitation, rather than selecting at random. Fourth, we had rather too few participants and rather too many codes to use a fully data-driven approach such as factor analysis, or multiple regression. Future studies with larger sample sizes might fruitfully use those approaches to discover other psychological factors than the top-down ones we applied here. Fifth, all participants in our sample were or had been unpaid volunteers within their organizations. Our findings therefore provide limited insight into activists whose organizing constitutes paid employment or who participate in movements with different models of activist labor. This is important because, although volunteer-based activism is usually the largest category of membership in mass organizations in the U.S., it should not be assumed to represent all activism more broadly, particularly across different national contexts (). Future research should examine engagement and disengagement across a broader range of organizational and labor arrangements, including movements in which activism is more closely integrated with paid work, community organizations, or other forms of collective labor. Lastly, our sample was restricted to participants aged 18–35. This age range limits our ability to examine how engagement and disengagement may unfold across longer life-course trajectories or how experiences accumulated over many years shape activists' participation. Future research should include a wider age range to better capture these longer-term dynamics.

This study pointed to the importance of collective efficacy for those who stay engaged. People may be more likely to stay when they feel that their group is capable of making a difference and when they have a supportive community that shares their values and their vision for the future. Active hope also featured more in those who stay engaged—suggesting they don't only feel that their group is capable of making a difference but that it is worthwhile to struggle even without expecting success but instead for developing one's own courage, skills and finding the ties that bind one to others. Conversely, the study pointed to a lack of collective identity for those who don't stay engaged. This was expressed as a lack of alignment with the organization's strategy, as weaknesses in community, more interpersonal conflict, and a lack of racial/gender/class sensitivity and also a lack of inclusivity in the climate movement. The insights from the rich and nuanced thematic analysis we undertook here, backed up by statistics, may be useful for guiding organizers to better engage their members, and likewise for the wider fields of environmental and climate psychology.

psychology.title: Assessors’ Perspectives on the Failure to Fail Underperforming Nursing Students: A Narrative Review
psychology.abstract: The aim of this narrative review is to explore reasons for the failure to fail of underperforming, nursing students, from the assessor perspective.When assessing student nurses on practice placements, assessors often have difficulty assigning a failing grade to students who fail to demonstrate competence in accordance with practice standards. Failure to fail is the act of passing nursing students on their clinical placement who do not display acceptable clinical performance. This issue can have considerable consequences for patient and staff safety, as well as legal implications for the workplace and the nursing profession.A mixed‐methods narrative review utilises thematic synthesis, following Thomas and Harden’s (2008) three‐stage approach of coding, development of descriptive themes and generation of analytical themes.A search of CINAHL, Emcare, Ovid and ProQuest—British Nursing Index and Google Scholar was conducted, and hand‐searching techniques were utilised. All data were sourced between November 2023 and January 2024. English‐language literature published since 2019, focusing on the assessment of underperforming students from the assessor’s perspective, was reviewed.Eleven papers were included in the review, nine of which were qualitative and two quantitative papers. Thematic synthesis was used to identify four main themes: educational assessment and feedback, student assessment, practical constraints and educational psychology.Failure to fail is an ongoing issue and was evidenced in the literature from a variety of high‐income countries. Assessors experienced various challenges in failing underperforming students. It is essential for assessors to have the support of practice educators and university faculties, to have protected time to complete assessments and associated documentation and to have access to further education and training.
psychology.text:
The purpose of pre‐registration nursing education is to prepare student nurses for future practice as registrants (Nursing and Midwifery Council [NMC] []). Clinical placements are a significant element of student nurse education (NMC []; Nyoni et al. []) for students to demonstrate professional values, knowledge, skills and attitude. This allows them to progress to the next stage of training and ultimately to become registered nurses (NMC []). The UK student nurse pre‐registration programme takes 3–4 years to complete, including 2300 practice hours (NMC []). Increasing the number of nurses, while also ensuring they have the correct skills, knowledge and attitudes is crucial to producing proficient nurses capable of providing safe and high‐quality care to patients (World Health Organisation [WHO] []).

In the UK, practice supervisors and assessors support and assess students in clinical placements (NMC []). Students’ assessments vary internationally, as do the titles and roles of those who assess students. There is consistency in that registered nurses supervise, support and assess students on clinical placements with some triangulation and input from clinical colleagues and university academics (Immonen et al. []). To ensure clarity, all personnel who evaluate students in practice are referred to as ‘assessors’ in this review.

The assessment of student nurses must be robust and evidence‐based, encompassing integrity (NMC []). As part of their professional code, nurses are expected to recognise and report unsafe care delivered by others, including students (Tanicala et al. []; NMC []). Assessors are crucial in identifying and managing underperforming students, and the possibility of students becoming registered nurses who lack the necessary clinical skills and attitude is of significant concern (Yepes‐Rios et al. []). It is vital that assessors receive adequate additional support, both from practice and partner universities to monitor student progress, ensure assessment meetings are effective and timely, and be capable of having difficult conversations with failing students when necessary (Maxwell et al. []).

Failure to fail is a term describing the practice of avoiding having to fail a student who does not demonstrate satisfactory clinical performance (Hughes et al. []). Hughes et al. [] reported that although 73.8% of assessors did not generally believe in giving students the benefit of the doubt, 23.5% of the participating assessors had done so, either sometimes or often. Passing tolerance decreased with the level of experience, with 12% passing underperforming first‐year students, 4.7% passing underperforming second‐year students and 1.3% passing underperforming final‐year students. Nearly half of participants recruited to Adkins and Aucoin [] quantitative study answered positively to questions that indicated a history of failure to fail. Natterøy et al. [] reported that few participants had formally escalated concerns, or failed students who were not achieving, but two participants stated that in retrospect, they should have failed underperforming students.

Failure to fail has been recognised within nursing education for over 2 decades and can have significant consequences for the student, clinical colleagues, patients, relatives, the healthcare trust and the NMC (Scholes and Albarran []). The reasons for failure to fail must therefore be understood by those involved in student nurse assessment to fully support and enable assessors to effectively fulfil their roles.

The aim of this narrative review is to explore reasons for the failure to fail of underperforming, nursing students, from the assessor perspective.

The design of this review is a mixed‐methods narrative review utilising a thematic analysis. A narrative review methodology was considered most appropriate for addressing the review aim, as it facilitated the synthesis of evidence from a diverse body of literature exploring factors influencing decisions to fail underperforming student nurses. Although systematic review methods informed the search, screening and appraisal processes, the review was primarily undertaken by a single reviewer, with supervisory oversight of selected decisions. Therefore, the review is presented as a narrative review rather than a systematic review, reflecting the pragmatic approach taken while maintaining methodological transparency.

The PEO framework (Bettany‐Saltikov []) was utilised for the purposes of this review to design the following research question:

While specific terms relating to barriers and enablers were not used, the exposure component was captured through search terms relating to assessment roles and assessment processes (e.g., assessor∗, mentor∗ and practice assessor), enabling identification of studies exploring factors that influence decisions to fail underperforming students.

The search method was discussed with information specialists ensuring that all relevant studies were included, and that databases and search terms were used effectively (Lefebvre []). The search terms used were as follows: (‘student nurses’ OR ‘nursing students’ OR ‘student nurse’ OR ‘nursing student’ OR ‘undergraduate nurse’ OR ‘pre‐registration’) AND (‘failure to fail’ OR fail∗ OR underperform∗ OR competenc∗ OR mentor∗ OR NMC OR ‘Nursing and Midwifery Council’ OR assess∗ OR ‘practice assessor’ OR ‘practice supervisor’). Subject headings and keywords were combined using Boolean operators AND/OR to allow for a more targeted search (EBSCO Connect []).

A search was conducted using the following databases: CINAHL, Emcare, Ovid and ProQuest—British Nursing Index. Using a combination of the databases aimed to enhance the comprehensiveness of the review (Bramer et al. []). An academic search engine was also used, which identified some grey literature. Citation chasing was carried out by reviewing the bibliography of references for each work (backward citation chasing) and searching Google Scholar (forward citation chasing) (Cooper et al. []). The search was performed between November 2023 and January 2024.

The inclusion and exclusion criteria can be seen in Table .

Inclusion and exclusion criteria.

The focus of the review being failure to fail in student nurses. The author did not wish to include literature concerning other healthcare students.

Various key words were included in the search to capture different terminology used to describe ‘student nurses’ and also capture the concept of assessment of those students, failure and underperformance.

The study selection and critical appraisal were conducted primarily by the author. To enhance methodological rigour and reduce potential bias, a sample of papers was independently reviewed by the author’s supervisor, and decisions were discussed throughout the review process. The study selection process is summarised in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Figure ).

Following the search of databases, 127 papers were selected by title. The removal of duplicates reduced the reference list to 100 titles. Of the 100 papers, 63 were eliminated following abstract screening, 37 articles underwent a full‐text evaluation, and 26 were rejected based on relevance to the topic and inclusion/exclusion criteria. The remaining 11 articles were appraised using the appropriate appraisal tools. Following appraisal, no studies were excluded, as the review aimed to provide a comprehensive synthesis of the available evidence. The quality of individual studies was considered when interpreting findings and drawing conclusions.

The qualitative appraisal tool (CASP []) and the Critical Appraisal of Cross‐Sectional Study appraisal tool were utilised (Centre for Evidence‐Based Management []). The final papers were reviewed and appraised. To mitigate risk of bias, a selection of papers was independently reviewed by the author’s supervisor. Critical appraisal indicated that the included studies were generally methodologically robust, although some methodological limitations and areas of uncertainty were identified. Full appraisal findings are presented in Tables  and .

Results of CASP appraisals for qualitative papers.

Results of critical appraisals of cross‐sectional studies.

A thematic synthesis was undertaken following the approach described by Thomas and Harden []. Findings from the included studies were coded, with data extracts identified through colour‐coded highlighting and assigned initial codes. Similar codes were grouped into descriptive themes representing recurring patterns across studies. A third stage of synthesis involved interpreting these themes to synthesise findings across the studies and explore their meaning in relation to the review.

From the 11 articles chosen for the review, nine were qualitative (Devlin and Duggan []; Rees et al. []; Christiansen et al. []; Rodger and Juckes []; Aase et al. []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []) and two were quantitative surveys (Hughes et al. []; Adkins and Aucoin []). Four of the papers were from Norway (Christiansen et al. []; Aase et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []); two from Australia (Hughes et al. []; Rees et al. []) and the UK (Devlin and Duggan []; Whaley et al. []); and one from Canada (Rodger and Juckes []), New Zealand (Borren et al. []) and the USA (Adkins and Aucoin []).

An analysis of the literature related to failure to fail identified four themes: educational assessment and feedback, student assessment, practical constraints and educational psychology.

Nine papers highlighted a struggle to understand the assessment process, documentation and defining competence (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []; Roger and Jukes []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []):

Despite unfamiliarity with formal suitability or competence assessment criteria, most assessors understood the concepts of competence, expectations and implications. However, differing views on competence led to subjectivity and variability in assessments (Christiansen et al. []; Borren et al. []):

Insufficient understanding of assessment processes was exacerbated by a lack of standardisation, recent changes to assessment standards in some countries and variation in assessment documentation across institutions, which further perplexed assessors supporting students from multiple universities (Borren et al. []; Whaley et al. []):

The practice educator was seen as a supportive role, facilitating the assessment process by acting as a liaison between the university and placement. This led to the early detection of students encountering difficulties and, consequently, reduced the risk of failure to fail (Devlin and Duggan []; Mathisen et al. []).

Despite educator and managerial support, some assessors felt overburdened due to too few nurses undertaking the role (Devlin and Duggan []), whereas the presence of a positive learning culture was considered crucial, involving all staff members in a collective responsibility for student progress, supervision and feedback (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []).

Assessors experienced self‐doubt and decision‐making difficulties, causing emotional stress and leading them to question their support of the student. The need for greater confidence in decision‐making when issuing a failing grade to an underperforming student was identified, along with the need for enhanced assessor education (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []; Roger and Jukes []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Borren et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []):

Assessors were divided on their self‐assessment of competence, but many reported that updates and specific education around the assessment of borderline students improved confidence, decreased feelings of self‐doubt and reduced failure to fail (Hughes et al. []; Roger and Jukes []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []). Those receiving support felt empowered, while others acknowledged the benefits and anticipated a reduction in failure to fail (Hughes et al. []). However, workload demands limited assessors’ ability to attend educational sessions (Roger and Jukes []).

Assessing competence or suitability was complex, as it encompasses clinical skills, knowledge, professional attitudes, communication, the capacity for compassion and empathy towards patients (Hughes et al. []; Christiansen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Psychosocial elements were considered more difficult to measure and define, but seen as important, even if they did not feature on the assessment criteria (Christiansen et al. []). Assessors were divided on failing a student solely due to their professional attitude (Hughes et al. []). Assessor intuition played a part, with some describing a sense or feeling when something was amiss, comparing it to clinical reasoning when caring for patients and adding an additional standard of quality; asking if they would like this student caring for their own loved ones (Christiansen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Assessors tolerated student mistakes if the student was reflective and accepting of feedback; however, unsafe student practices that compromised patient care were not tolerated (Rodger and Juckes []; Natterøy et al. []):

The importance of providing early support to assessors in managing underperforming students was recognised, as a lack of timely assistance, particularly in the absence of a second opinion prior to the midpoint assessment, contributed to reluctance or failure to fail (Mathisen et al. []). The appeals process was perceived as biased in favour of students, with reports of successful student appeals resulting in assessor decisions being overturned (Hughes et al. []).

Four studies highlighted the importance of formative assessments and dialogue between students and assessors (Hughes et al. []; Christiansen et al. []; Aase et al. []; Borren et al. []). Time constraints and limited communication diminished both the quantity of feedback and the quality of learning during formal assessments in clinical placements (Hughes et al. []; Christiansen et al. []; Aase et al. []):

While the Educational Assessment and Feedback theme centred on assessment processes, assessor competence and feedback practices, this theme highlighted the interpersonal, collaborative and organisational factors that influenced assessment decision‐making.

The interactions and relationships between students and their assessors play a crucial role in practice‐based learning (Davis et al. []; King et al. []). Collaboration and support between colleagues, nurse educators and university faculties were identified as important aspects, ‘another pair of eyes’ to ensure an unbiased and valid assessment, particularly for borderline students (Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []; Rodger and Juckes []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). In the absence of colleague support, assessors reported feeling isolated in carrying the weight of assessment responsibilities and expressed a need for greater collaboration with university lecturers (Christiansen et al. []).

While some assessors lacked awareness of the academic assessor or broader university role (Devlin and Duggan []; Whaley et al. []), many valued the support provided by the university, felt confident initiating contact and relied on it to inform their decision‐making (Hughes et al. []; Rodger and Juckes []; Natterøy et al. []). The value of the collaboration was dependant on individual tutors (Natterøy et al. []), with some reports of lack of support resulting in personal or psychological distress and feelings of isolation (Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []). Assessors expressed a need for stronger connections between practice colleagues and educational institutions, along with greater university visibility and involvement, to ensure adequate support (Whaley et al. []). Assessors valued the role of the practice educator, favouring familiar and readily accessible support over that provided by geographically dispersed academic tutors (Mathisen et al. []).

Power differential between students and assessors was acknowledged, highlighting the potential influence this imbalance can have on assessment dynamics and decision‐making (Rees et al. []; Borren et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Assessors recognised their power and influence in terms of student progression, with some expressing concern about wielding such power (Borren et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Although students were often perceived as powerless, some were observed to resist assessor authority by disregarding feedback, expressing disagreement, reacting inappropriately or openly challenging assessments (Rees et al. []; Natterøy et al. []):

Some students also exhibited challenging, manipulative or abusive behaviour. These behaviours intensified when students disclosed life circumstances such as visa requirements, care duties, prior nursing experience or financial concerns (Hughes et al. []; Rees et al. []; Rodger and Juckes []). Assessors felt concern for students and were interested in establishing the factors affecting their behaviour (Natterøy et al. []). A lack of insight was identified as a contributing factor in some students’ inability or reluctance to take responsibility, with blame occasionally redirected towards assessors through complaints or, in extreme cases, acts of aggression (Hughes et al. []; Rees et al. []; Rodger and Juckes []).

Workload pressures were a theme in six of the studied papers (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []; Aase et al. []; Borren et al. []; Whaley et al. []). While time constraints influenced feedback, learning opportunities and assessment processes, they were also identified as a broader organisational issue linked to workload pressures, competing clinical priorities and administrative demands. Participants described being overwhelmed in their work, with lack of time repeatedly cited as a barrier to effective supervision and assessment (Hughes et al. []; Christiansen et al. []; Whaley et al. []). Completing the subsequent documentation was seen as extra work, difficult to manage in addition to patient care and other registered nurse responsibilities, and was often completed at home during personal time (Devlin and Duggan []; Whaley et al. []):

Assessors raised concerns about the validity of assessments, as they felt they had not spent sufficient time directly observing their students (Aase et al. []; Borren et al. []):

UK‐based assessors reported feeling undervalued, with some expressing dismay that their previously earned mentoring qualifications had become obsolete under the NMC [] SSSA (Devlin and Duggan []; Whaley et al. []). The perceived lack of recognition from management, coupled with expectations to undertake additional responsibilities without remuneration, contributed to feelings of resentment (Devlin and Duggan []; Whaley et al. []). Although some assessors acknowledged these duties as inherent to their role as registered nurses, many considered them unjust, reinforcing negative perceptions of the assessor role:

The findings highlighted several psychological and emotional factors that influenced assessors’ decision‐making when evaluating underperforming students. For some assessors, supporting nursing students and observing their development evoked a tangible feeling of pride, reward and achievement (Hughes et al. []; Whaley et al. []). However, many reported role conflict between workload pressures and effective learner supervision and assessment (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []; Aase et al. []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Whaley et al. []). The emotional cost of assessment was also noted, with assessors reporting emotional distress for unsuccessful students, guilt over their investment and the weight of potentially ending a student’s career (Rodger and Juckes []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Developing personal connections with underperforming students was perceived as particularly challenging, given assessors’ awareness of students’ individual, familial and financial circumstances (Hughes et al. []; Rodger and Juckes []).

Adkins and Aucoin [] suggested that these emotional responses may contribute to failure‐to‐fail behaviours through face‐implicating factors, whereby assessors can be reluctant to deliver negative judgements because of concerns about their own self‐image, professional reputation, relationships with students or the emotional impact of failing them. They reported that many themes for failure to fail were synonymous with existing literature on face‐implicating factors, commonly known as the ‘MUM effect’, whereby individuals avoid delivering unwelcome messages because of concerns about damaging relationships, causing distress or being viewed negatively (Dibble []; Dibble and Sharkey []). The similarities between Adkins and Aucoin’s [] findings and the ‘MUM effect’ literature are outlined in Table .

Identified themes from Adkins and Aucoin [] and their comparison to the MUM effect in the literature.

Fear of an emotional reaction from the receiver

Fear of causing distress to the receiver

Assessors who had not previously engaged in failure to fail expressed stronger disagreement with face‐related concerns; reported being unaffected by pressures from colleagues, universities or students’ reactions; demonstrated greater confidence in their decisions; and did not interpret student failure as a reflection of their own competence or compassion (Rodger and Juckes []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Mathisen et al. []).

This review explored the factors that facilitate or hinder the failure of underperforming student nurses. Following comprehensive literature searches, the author justified the inclusion of studies from high‐income countries comparable to the UK, due to a lack of recent UK‐based publications. The findings suggest that assessor education and competence, student assessment practices, practical constraints and principles of educational psychology all influence the accuracy of student assessment. Consistent with the review findings, several themes identified in contemporary studies were also evident in earlier literature, suggesting that barriers associated with failing underperforming student nurses have remained persistent over time.

Three papers (Hughes et al. []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Natterøy et al. []) reported that some assessors admitted to passing incompetent students or giving them the benefit of the doubt‐findings consistent with prior research (Watson and Harris []; Duffy []; Gainsbury []; Hunt et al. []). This issue has persisted in British literature over the last 2 decades and is neither unique to the UK or the nursing profession (Scanlan et al. []; Hughes et al. []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Fisher et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Scarff et al. []). Irrespective of country, assessment framework or discipline, these reports have sustained concerns that some students who qualify are not fit to enter the profession (Natterøy et al. []). This can lead to costly, extended, supernumerary periods upon qualification, unsafe practice, increased clinical errors and subsequent removal from the nursing register.

Assessors faced significant barriers in evaluating students in relation to assessment criteria, terminology and expectations (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []; Roger and Jukes []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []). This was exacerbated by a lack of standardisation and national assessment tools and recent changes to assessment standards in some countries (Borren et al. []; Whaley et al. []).

To ensure robust and equitable evaluation, assessors are expected to demonstrate a strong understanding of required proficiencies and course outcomes (NMC []; NMC []). Practice‐based assessments should be transparent, rigorous and fair, serving two key purposes: formative assessment for ongoing feedback and learning, and summative assessment to determine overall competence (Price []).

In the UK, all practice assessors must complete some level of preparation to undertake the role, but the level and content of the training are at the discretion of the Approved Education Institutions (AEIs) and their practice partners, leading to variability and a lack of consistency (NMC []). Assessors are expected to maintain up‐to‐date knowledge and skills, and the NMC [] indicates that reflection on the assessor role as part of the revalidation process may be sufficient, as there is no formal requirement for mandatory updates.

This review highlights a clear need for enhanced training and support for assessors, citing persistent gaps in understanding the assessment process, navigating documentation and defining competence (Hughes et al. []; Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []; Roger and Jukes []; Adkins and Aucoin []; Borren et al. []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []). However, access to such support is often hindered by systemic pressures, including seasonal demand, reduced funding and workforce shortages (Merrifield []; HEE []; Devereux []).

The complexities of defining and assessing competence have been widely explored in the literature (Takase and Teraoka []; Fukada []; Christensen et al. []; Munangatire and McInerney []). Nursing competency as outlined by Takase and Teraoka [] encompasses three theories: behaviourism (demonstrating core skills), trait theory (attributes such as knowledge and critical thinking) and holism (a collection of elements, including knowledge, skills and values). The psychosocial elements, such as attitudes and behaviours, can be more challenging to assess, influenced by factors such as stress, coping strategies and motivation (Morrell‐Scott []). Their subjective and interpretive nature makes them difficult to quantify with the same precision as clinical skills or knowledge (Christiansen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Duffy [] highlights that competence issues often span cognitive, emotional and psychomotor domains, and that many failing students lack the insight necessary to accept feedback and implement change—frustrating mentors and limiting the effectiveness of supportive interventions. Given that reflection, critical thinking, self‐awareness and professional development are essential in nursing (NMC []), insight is crucial for identifying improvement areas, adapting to new practices and delivering high‐quality patient care.

The review highlighted assessors’ lack of time to complete assessments effectively (Hughes et al. []; Christiansen et al. []; Aase et al. []), a finding consistent with historical research (Watson and Harris []).

In addition to excessive workloads and time constraints, the additional burden of assessing students, particularly associated documentation, was perceived as challenging to manage (Devlin and Duggan []; Christiansen et al. []; Aase et al. []; Borren et al. []; Natterøy et al. []; Whaley et al. []). Supporting underperforming students further intensified this burden, leading to an overwhelming, increased workload for assessors due to additional meetings, feedback sessions, action planning and extensive assessment paperwork‐often completed without any extra time allocated (Duffy []; Scholes and Albarran []; Duffy []; Whaley et al. []). Ongoing nursing shortages further exacerbate these pressures by increasing clinical workload and reducing the time available for supervision and assessment. One strategy to address nursing workforce shortages and increase the future supply of registered nurses is to increase the recruitment of student nurses (NHS England []), as well as increase clinical placement capacity to accommodate them. However, this can inadvertently increase the supervisory load and dilute the quality of supervision and assessment (Williamson et al. []).

Failure to recognise the increased workload and emotional demands associated with the assessor role can exacerbate assessor anxiety (Pettit and Stephen []). This is particularly concerning given NHS staff surveys have highlighted high levels of work‐related stress and burnout (NHS England []). To mitigate this emotional burden and promote wellbeing, assessors require access to adequate training, structured support and restorative clinical supervision.

Workload pressures continue to undermine the quality of student learning, supervision and assessment (Grimwood []). The Safe Learning Environment Charter (SLEC) (NHS England []), developed in alignment with the NHS People Promise [], outlines key recommendations to promote supportive learning environments that enable learners to become competent, skilled and safe practitioners. Among these is the need for assessors to be allocated protected time for completing assessments, maintaining documentation and attending training on assessment standards, documentation practices and performance monitoring (NHS England []). There is also a clear need to safeguard and expand the role of practice educators, who may offer a cost‐effective solution by reducing supernumerary time, mitigating the consequences of poor practice and strengthening assessment processes to ensure the competence of newly qualified nurses.

The literature recognised the power imbalance between students–assessor relationships and the complexities in delivering student feedback (Rees et al. []; Borren et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Assessors were conscious of the power they exerted over students (Borren et al. []; Natterøy et al. []), but they also encountered students exerting their own power by opposing assessor authority or responding with challenging, manipulative or abusive behaviour, consistent with previous studies (Burgess et al. []; Duffy [], Hughes et al. []; Rees et al. []). Dweck and Yeager [] (pp. 484‐485) explore ‘mindset theory’ to explain variations in student responses to feedback; however, the feedback is delivered constructively. Learners who possess a good development attitude, emotional stability, responsibility and sociability are more motivated to actively seek and use feedback constructively. However, learners frequently underestimate their capacity to assume accountability for their own learning (King []). Negative assessments may result in shock, disbelief, rage, denial and blame from students, influenced by lack of insight, inaccurate self‐evaluation and past assessors incorrectly passing prior placements (King []; Duffy []; Hughes et al. []; Rees et al. []).

The literature extensively documents the emotional toll that assessors experience when they fail a student, with participants describing it as stressful, horrendous, traumatic and draining (Watson and Harris []; Duffy []; Duffy []; Hunt []; Rodger and Juckes []; Mathisen et al. []; Natterøy et al. []). Assessors rely heavily on their own emotional resilience to manage conflicting feelings (Hunt []). Assessors highlighted the need to mentally prepare oneself to ‘grasp that nettle’ when failing a student, identifying the need to be courageous, bold, assertive and undaunted in the face of opposition, noting that speaking up can feel dangerous or futile (Scholes and Albarran []; Hunt []).

Barriers to giving effective feedback included the fear of upsetting the student, student resistance, defensiveness and a lack of respect for assessors (Hesketh and Laidlaw []). Adkins and Aucoin [] examined face‐implicating factors, or the ‘Mum effect’, finding themes consistent with previous research on this topic (Dibble []; Dibble and Sharkey []). The MUM effect, known as ‘keeping mum’, describes the difficulty and hesitation of delivering unwelcome news. The ‘MUM effect’ is motivated by the messenger’s fear of being viewed in a negative way, being blamed and causing distress to the recipient, which can impede the efficient communication of bad news (Dibble []). Adkins and Aucoin [] concluded that participants who had not committed failure to fail were less affected by face‐implicating factors. Hunt [] identified the essential characteristics that robust and effective assessors need to possess, which include solidarity, tenacity, audacity, dependability and integrity. Assessors must confidently engage in difficult conversations and fail students when necessary (Duffy []). While selecting assessors with these specific characteristics may enhance assessment processes and reduce failure to fail (Hunt []), this could restrict the assessor pool, potentially impeding the students’ placement experience.

Consultation with an information specialist enhanced the search’s replicability and breadth, by clarifying key terms and suggesting suitable databases (Cooper et al. []). Despite this assistance, it is feasible that pertinent papers may not have been found. The terminology to describe student nurses and assessors differed geographically, and despite including several variations in the search, a relevant term may have been omitted. This review was undertaken by one researcher with supervisor guidance. The author acknowledges that a second reviewer would have improved accuracy, efficiency and reduced the risk of bias (Stoll et al. []).

Failure to fail remains a well‐researched and internationally recognised concept in nursing and healthcare despite variations in assessment methods. In the UK, NMC reforms (NMC []; NMC []) transformed the methods of mentorship in nursing education. Despite the scarcity of national research to assess the effectiveness of these standards and the impact on failure to fail, findings from Whaley, Hay and Knight [] align with existing international literature.

This review has identified the impact of inadequate assessor education, time constraints, motives for reluctance to provide feedback, and relationship and power dynamics.

The nursing profession must acknowledge the serious consequences of allowing incompetent students to graduate. Assessors who fail to fail neglect their duty of care to patients, students and the profession itself. Implementing recommendations from this review could enable regulatory bodies, educational institutions and placement providers to significantly reduce the barriers and better support assessors in making difficult, yet necessary decisions. Equipping assessors with the necessary knowledge, support and resources to be effective gatekeepers to the nursing profession is crucial for cultivating a high‐quality, future workforce. However, delivering high‐quality care also requires significant investment—a timeless principle Florence Nightingale affirmed:

The following recommendations are derived from the findings of this review and are supported, where appropriate, by relevant policy and published literature.•This review identified a lack of recent UK‐based research examining assessors’ experiences of failing underperforming student nurses. There is a need for more comprehensive national data to draw robust conclusions about the assessor experience in the UK. Enhanced data collection could inform targeted support strategies for educators, ultimately improving student supervision and learning environments (NHS England []).

This review identified a lack of recent UK‐based research examining assessors’ experiences of failing underperforming student nurses. There is a need for more comprehensive national data to draw robust conclusions about the assessor experience in the UK. Enhanced data collection could inform targeted support strategies for educators, ultimately improving student supervision and learning environments (NHS England []).

•Findings from this review highlighted persistent gaps in assessors’ understanding of assessment processes, documentation requirements and the interpretation of competence. These findings support the need for robust, standardised assessor preparation and regular updating opportunities. Assessors should be enabled to access ongoing education, including training in performance management, formative assessment and the delivery of constructive feedback, to enhance assessor confidence and assessment quality.

Findings from this review highlighted persistent gaps in assessors’ understanding of assessment processes, documentation requirements and the interpretation of competence. These findings support the need for robust, standardised assessor preparation and regular updating opportunities. Assessors should be enabled to access ongoing education, including training in performance management, formative assessment and the delivery of constructive feedback, to enhance assessor confidence and assessment quality.

•Consistent with findings that workload pressures and time constraints negatively impacted assessment practices, allocating protected time for assessors could alleviate workload pressures, reduce stress and burnout, and support the delivery of accurate, timely and defensible assessments. This may also help minimise student appeals and address the issue of failure to fail (NHS England []).•Additional support is needed for assessors, particularly when managing underperforming students. Strengthening and expanding the role of practice educators could offer a cost‐effective solution by improving assessment processes, reducing supernumerary time and preventing the long‐term costs of poor practice.

This may also help minimise student appeals and address the issue of failure to fail (NHS England []).
