psychology.title: Effects of Ergonomics Training Plus Structured Exercise Versus Ergonomics Training Alone on Musculoskeletal Pain, Disability, and Burnout in Schoolteachers: A Randomized Controlled Trial
psychology.abstract: Background/Objectives: Musculoskeletal disorders are common among teachers, but randomized evidence on adding exercise to ergonomics training is scarce. This trial compared ergonomics training plus structured exercise with ergonomics training alone. Methods: Eighty teachers with musculoskeletal pain lasting at least three months were stratified by school level and randomized 1:1. Both groups attended four ergonomics sessions and received weekly telephone calls; the ergonomics-plus-exercise group also performed a 12-week, largely self-directed program of stretching, strengthening, and core stabilization. Registered primary outcomes were the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Neck Disability Index (NDI), Maslach Burnout Inventory–Educators Survey, and Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire; pain intensity (VAS) was secondary. A blinded assessor collected outcomes at baseline and week 12. Results: All participants completed the trial. Group × time interactions favored ergonomics plus exercise for ODI (difference in change −6.80; 95% CI −9.22 to −4.38), NDI (−4.90; −7.53 to −2.27), emotional exhaustion (−2.63; −3.89 to −1.36), depersonalization, and personal accomplishment (Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.013), and for VAS (−1.18; −1.48 to −0.87). At least 30% improvement occurred in 80% versus 10% of participants for ODI and 90% versus 38% for NDI, but in 95% versus 93% for VAS. The number of symptomatic body regions decreased more with exercise (−0.67; −1.15 to −0.20); in unadjusted exploratory region-specific analyses, only the shoulder reached nominal significance, with baseline imbalance. Conclusions: Adding a structured exercise program to ergonomics training gave additional short-term improvements in disability and burnout. Mean differences were modest, outcomes and adherence were self-reported, and participants knew their allocation.
psychology.text:
Musculoskeletal disorders are a leading cause of disability worldwide [,], and teachers are among the occupational groups in which they are common. A meta-analysis of 44 studies covering nearly 16,000 teachers reported an overall prevalence of 68%, with the neck (47%), low back (47%), and shoulders (44%) most often affected []. This figure is of the same order as the roughly three in five workers who report musculoskeletal complaints in the European workforce as a whole [], and it approaches the 77% annual prevalence pooled across nurses []. Teachers therefore carry a burden close to that of occupations with heavy manual handling, although their work involves little lifting. Similarly high figures have been reported in studies of teachers from Africa, Latin America, and Türkiye [,,,].

The exposure profile of teaching explains this pattern. Teaching involves prolonged standing, sustained forward head posture while marking and preparing lessons, repeated arm elevation when writing on the board, and extended computer use []. These symptoms are associated with poorer quality of life [,]. They are more frequent in physical education teachers than in classroom teachers [] and are highly prevalent in special education teachers []. In one survey, nearly half of teachers reported absenteeism due to neck or shoulder pain or low back pain []. The burden is not only physical: musculoskeletal pain and burnout often occur together in schoolteachers, with workload related to exhaustion [], and physical activity appears to be related to burnout risk in teachers, although the relationship depends on the type and context of the activity [].

Ergonomics training is the most common preventive response. It is an educational intervention that teaches workers to recognize and reduce the physical risk factors in their own work: adjusting the workstation and its tools, adopting neutral postures, using safer techniques for recurrent tasks, and scheduling breaks. Unlike exercise therapy, manual therapy, or medication, it is directed at the exposure and not at the physical capacity of the worker or at the symptoms. Its effect on pain is small when results are pooled across occupations []. In teachers, an educational ergonomics program was followed by a lower prevalence of neck, shoulder, and back pain, but the evidence comes from an uncontrolled pre–post study [].

There are reasons to expect that exercise adds to ergonomics training. Much of the load in teaching cannot be removed by ergonomic adjustment, because standing, board work, and marking are inherent to the job. Exercise acts on the other side of the balance by increasing the strength, endurance, and mobility with which the remaining load is tolerated. Exercise is supported by systematic reviews for chronic neck pain [] and chronic low back pain [], and it probably lowers the risk of new neck pain episodes in working populations []. Teacher-specific trials are few. Adding deep cervical flexor training to conventional exercise reduced neck pain and disability in schoolteachers [], a three-week at-work exercise program added to an ergonomic brochure reduced low back and neck pain in nursery school teachers [], and workplace yoga improved pain in female teachers when compared with no intervention []. Part of the rationale therefore rests on trials in other occupations with largely static work, such as office workers [].

Whether exercise gives a benefit beyond ergonomics training itself is less clear. An integrative review suggested that combined ergonomic and physical activity interventions may reduce neck and hand or wrist pain in workers []. In randomized trials that used ergonomics training as the comparator, added exercise reduced pain more in tea workers [] and factory workers [] but not in construction workers []; a pilot trial in hemodialysis nurses found less discomfort after a combined program [], and in office workers, stretching combined with ergonomic modification was no better than either alone []. In teachers, the only trial of this kind lasted three weeks and did not assess burnout []. To our knowledge, no randomized trial in teachers has tested a longer exercise program against ergonomics training while assessing both physical outcomes and burnout.

This trial therefore asked whether adding a 12-week structured exercise program to ergonomics training improves low back and neck disability, burnout, musculoskeletal symptoms, and pain intensity in schoolteachers with musculoskeletal pain, compared with ergonomics training alone. We hypothesized that the combined program would produce greater improvements. An exploratory aim was to describe symptoms and burnout by school level.

This was a two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial with a 1:1 allocation ratio and blinded outcome assessment, reported in line with the CONSORT 2025 statement []. It was conducted in schools affiliated with the Tatvan District Directorate of National Education (Bitlis, Türkiye). The Üsküdar University Non-Interventional Research Ethics Committee approved the protocol (No. 61351342/020-2008; meeting of 25 February 2026), and the District Directorate granted permission to conduct the study. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki [], and all participants gave written informed consent. No payment or other incentive was offered for participation or completion.

The trial was registered prospectively at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07442383; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07442383 (accessed on 3 November 2026)). The record was submitted on 25 February 2026 and posted on 2 March 2026. The first participant was enrolled on 10 April 2026, and recruitment continued until early June 2026. Each participant was followed for 12 weeks, and the last week-12 assessment was made on 30 August 2026. Differences between the registration and this report are listed in .

Teachers working at preschool, primary, middle, and high school levels were invited to participate. Inclusion criteria were: age 30 to 60 years; at least five years of teaching experience; musculoskeletal pain lasting at least three months; pain intensity of at least 3 on a 0–10 Visual Analog Scale; and ability to attend the training and exercise program. Exclusion criteria were: a serious neurological or orthopedic disease; musculoskeletal surgery within the previous six months; and any medical or psychological condition that would prevent exercise.

Participants were recruited from 13 schools, with one to seven participants per school. Teachers of both groups worked in the same schools. To limit contamination, the ergonomics training and the exercise instruction were delivered individually, and teachers in the ergonomics-plus-exercise group were asked not to share the exercise program with colleagues.

The sample size was calculated a priori with G*Power 3.1 [] (F tests; ANOVA: repeated measures, within–between interaction). The inputs were an effect size f of 0.25, α of 0.05, power of 0.95, two groups, two measurements, a correlation of 0.5 between repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of 1, which gave a minimum total sample of 54. The effect size was the conventional medium value for the group × time interaction and was not derived from a specific outcome or from pilot data. The target was raised to 80 teachers to allow equal representation of the four school levels (20 per level, 10 per group) and to protect against attrition.

Randomization was stratified by school level. Before recruitment, a secretary who was independent of the research team prepared the allocation list for each stratum in Microsoft Excel: a computer-generated random number was assigned to each of the 20 sequence numbers of the stratum, the sequence numbers were sorted by this random number, and the first 10 were allocated to one group and the remaining 10 to the other. No blocks were used; the fixed 10:10 split within each stratum produced the balance. The list was kept by the secretary and was not accessible to the investigators. The physiotherapist who later delivered the interventions enrolled the participants and obtained consent, and a second physiotherapist performed the baseline assessment. Only then did the secretary disclose the assignment of that participant, in the order of enrollment within the stratum, face to face to the treating physiotherapist and the participant.

Participants and the treating physiotherapist were aware of the allocation. The assessing physiotherapist and the person who ran the statistical analysis were not. All questionnaires were administered as face-to-face interviews by the assessing physiotherapist, who read the items and recorded the answers, at baseline and at week 12. Because every outcome was reported by participants who knew their group, assessor blinding protects against biased recording but not against expectation or reporting bias.

Ergonomics training and telephone contact (both groups). All participants attended four face-to-face sessions at school in weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12. The sessions were delivered individually, lasted 30 to 45 min, and combined a short explanation with practical demonstration. They covered classroom workstation ergonomics, posture awareness, the ergonomics of daily teaching tasks, and break strategies (). Participants received a workstation checklist, a brochure, and a weekly self-monitoring form. The fourth session introduced a 2 to 3 min set of micro-exercises for use between lessons, which consisted of shortened versions of the phase 1 neck and trunk stretches. This set was taught in week 12, at the end of the intervention period, so the ergonomics-only group received no exercise prescription before the final assessment. All 80 participants attended all four sessions. The treating physiotherapist also telephoned every participant in both groups once a week to ask about their general condition and about any adverse event. Participants in both groups were asked not to start any other treatment for their musculoskeletal complaints during the trial.

Exercise program (ergonomics-plus-exercise group only). This group also followed a 12-week program performed three times a week, a frequency used in an earlier workplace stretching trial [], for a total of 36 sessions of about 45 min. The program had three 4-week phases (). Phase 1 consisted of stretching and postural awareness exercises. Phase 2 added scapular, isometric neck, and trunk extensor strengthening. Phase 3 added core stabilization, which improves pain and function in chronic non-specific low back pain []. The exercises of the earlier phases were continued in the later phases. Each session began with 2 to 3 min of light warm-up and ended with 1 to 2 min of diaphragmatic breathing.

Intensity was low to moderate. Stretches were held at the point of mild tension, isometric neck contractions were performed against light to moderate manual resistance, and strengthening and stabilization exercises used body weight only. Participants were instructed to work within a pain-free range and to stop any exercise that increased their pain. Progression was time-based: all participants moved to the next phase after four weeks, with the repetitions, sets, and holding times shown in . The program was standardized and was not tailored to individuals, and no exercise had to be modified or withdrawn for any participant.

The program was not supervised. The treating physiotherapist taught the exercises in one individual face-to-face session and gave each participant an illustrated written guide. Participants then performed the sessions on their own at school or at home. During later contacts, the physiotherapist occasionally checked technique and answered questions, but technique was not re-assessed on a fixed schedule. In the weekly telephone call, participants in this group were additionally asked how many of the three scheduled sessions they had completed. No exercise diary was kept, and session duration and the reasons for missed sessions were not systematically recorded. Adherence is therefore the self-reported completion of scheduled sessions.

Adverse events were defined as any new injury or any increase in pain that the participant attributed to the exercises or the training, and they were asked about in the weekly telephone calls in both groups. Compliance with the request to avoid other treatment, and leisure-time exercise outside the program, were not systematically recorded.

Outcomes were assessed at baseline (week 0) and after the intervention (week 12). Age, sex, school level, height, and weight were recorded at baseline.

Low back disability (registered primary outcome). The Turkish version of the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) was used []. It contains 10 items on pain and daily activities and is expressed as a percentage from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater disability.

Neck disability (registered primary outcome). The Turkish version of the Neck Disability Index (NDI) was used []. It contains 10 items and is expressed as a percentage from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater disability. Both indices were administered to all participants, because neck symptoms (73 of 80, 91.3%) and low back symptoms (70 of 80, 87.5%) were highly prevalent and most teachers had symptoms in several regions. Sensitivity analyses were restricted to participants with symptoms in the corresponding region at baseline.

Burnout (registered primary outcome). The Turkish adaptation of the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Educators Survey (MBI-ES) was used []. Its 22 items were rated from 1 to 5 and form three subscales: emotional exhaustion (9 items; range 9–45), depersonalization (5 items; range 5–25), and personal accomplishment (8 items; range 8–40). Higher emotional exhaustion and depersonalization scores and lower personal accomplishment scores indicate greater burnout.

Musculoskeletal symptoms (registered primary outcome). The Turkish version of the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ) [] records, for nine body regions, whether the participant had trouble (ache, pain, or discomfort) in the previous 12 months and in the previous 7 days, and whether the trouble had prevented normal activity (at home or away from home) in the previous 12 months. Symptoms in the previous 7 days were used to evaluate change, because this recall period was the same at both assessments and did not overlap the pre-intervention period at week 12. A symptom was classed as resolved when it was present in the previous 7 days at baseline and absent at week 12, and as new when it was absent at baseline and present at week 12. The activity-limitation item (“Have you at any time during the last 12 months been prevented from doing your normal work because of the trouble?”) was administered in the same form at both assessments, but its 12-month recall period at week 12 overlaps the pre-intervention period, so a change in this item cannot be attributed to the intervention. Responses to this item were therefore not used to evaluate the intervention and are not reported.

Pain intensity (secondary outcome). Participants rated their current pain in the region that they identified as most painful at baseline, on a 10 cm Visual Analog Scale (VAS) anchored at 0 (no pain) and 10 (unbearable pain). The same region was rated at week 12. Scores were recorded to the nearest whole number.

The original analyses were performed with SPSS version 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The additional analyses requested during peer review were performed on the same dataset with Python 3.13 (SciPy 1.18). All 80 randomized participants completed both assessments and were analyzed in the group to which they were allocated, so the intention-to-treat and complete-case populations are identical and no outcome data were imputed. Normality was assessed with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test together with skewness and kurtosis values. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation and categorical variables as n (%). Baseline characteristics are presented descriptively.

The registered primary outcomes were the ODI, the NDI, the three MBI-ES subscales, and the NMQ; the VAS was a secondary outcome. For each continuous outcome, the intervention effect was tested with the group × time interaction of a 2 × 2 mixed-design ANOVA, which with two time points is equivalent to comparing change scores between groups. Results are reported as the between-group difference in change with its 95% confidence interval, and partial eta squared (ηp2) with its 90% confidence interval []. To control the family-wise error rate across the registered primary outcomes, the Holm procedure was applied to one family of six tests: the five continuous primary outcomes and the questionnaire-wide NMQ analysis (the change in the number of symptomatic regions, described below). As sensitivity analyses, week-12 scores were compared between groups with adjustment for the baseline score (ANCOVA), and change scores were compared with the Mann–Whitney U test. Within-group changes (paired t-tests with Cohen’s dz) are given in  for completeness and were not used to judge the intervention effect.

The registration did not specify how the NMQ would be summarized. Within-group change in the 7-day prevalence of symptoms in each region was tested with the exact McNemar test. Three between-group comparisons were then made: the change in the number of body regions with symptoms (independent-samples t-test, confirmed with the Mann–Whitney U test), which gives one test for the questionnaire as a whole and was included in the Holm adjustment of the primary outcomes; the proportion of baseline symptoms that had resolved at week 12 in each region; and the week-12 prevalence in each region. Differences in proportions are reported with Newcombe 95% confidence intervals and Fisher’s exact test. The region-specific comparisons were not adjusted for multiplicity and are exploratory.

Two further sets of analyses were not prespecified and are exploratory. First, the proportions of participants whose VAS, ODI, and NDI scores improved by at least 30% from baseline, a threshold proposed for clinically important change [], were compared between groups; participants with a baseline score of zero were counted as non-responders. Second, school levels were compared with both groups pooled (one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests; Fisher–Freeman–Halton exact test for symptoms), and the group × school-level interaction on change scores was examined with two-way ANOVA. The significance level was p < 0.05.

A separate statistical analysis plan was not written; the analysis followed the ethics-approved protocol and the description above. The exercise guide and the ergonomics brochure are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Participant-level data are not shared because of ethical and privacy restrictions (see Data Availability Statement).

The following differences between the registry record and this report were identified. (1) The VAS was an outcome in the ethics-approved protocol, which predates the registration, but it was omitted from the registry entry by oversight. It is reported here as a secondary outcome. (2) The registry gave a time frame of 14 weeks for the outcomes; this was an entry error, and the final assessment was made at week 12, at the end of the program. (3) The registry described masking as double. The masked roles were the outcome assessor and the data analyst; participants and the treating physiotherapist were not masked. (4) The registry listed a pain score below 3 as an exclusion criterion and a psychological disorder that prevents exercise as a further exclusion criterion; these correspond to the inclusion threshold of at least 3 and to the exclusion of conditions preventing exercise in . (5) The registry described the NMQ recall periods as 12 months, four weeks, and the day of assessment, whereas the questionnaire used in the trial asked about the previous 12 months and the previous 7 days. (6) The registry described MBI-ES items as scored from 0 to 4, whereas items were scored from 1 to 5; this shifts the subscale ranges but not the differences between groups. (7) The registry gave 15 July 2026 as the primary completion date; the last week-12 assessment was made on 30 August 2026. (8) The registry named the four instruments as primary outcomes without ranking them or defining an analysis for the NMQ; the hierarchy and the multiplicity adjustment described in  were defined during the analysis and peer review. The registry record has since been updated to correct these entries.

A total of 143 teachers were assessed for eligibility, and 63 were excluded: 27 did not meet the inclusion criteria and 36 declined to participate. Eighty teachers were randomized, 40 to each group, and all completed the 12-week period and the final assessment (). Baseline characteristics are shown in . Shoulder symptoms in the previous 7 days were more frequent in the ergonomics-plus-exercise group (17 of 40) than in the ergonomics-only group (9 of 40); the other characteristics were similar.

The group × time interaction favored the ergonomics-plus-exercise group for all five continuous primary outcomes, and all remained significant after Holm adjustment across the six primary tests (, ). The between-group difference in change was −6.80 points for the ODI and −4.90 points for the NDI. For burnout, the differences were −2.63 points for emotional exhaustion, −0.88 for depersonalization, and +1.85 for personal accomplishment. Depersonalization showed the smallest effect (ηp2 = 0.08); it remained significant in the baseline-adjusted analysis but not in the Mann–Whitney comparison of change scores (p = 0.09; ). For the secondary outcome, the difference in change in VAS was −1.18 points. Baseline-adjusted analyses gave the same conclusions for all six outcomes ().

In the exploratory responder analysis, an improvement of at least 30% from baseline was reached by 80.0% of the ergonomics-plus-exercise group and 10.0% of the ergonomics-only group for the ODI, and by 90.0% and 37.5% for the NDI (). For the VAS, almost all participants in both groups reached this threshold (95.0% and 92.5%), and the groups did not differ.

When the analysis was restricted to participants who reported symptoms in the corresponding region in the previous 7 days at baseline, the differences in change were −6.92 points for the ODI (95% CI −9.31 to −4.52; n = 70) and −5.36 points for the NDI (−7.82 to −2.89; n = 73), close to those in the full sample.

At baseline, the neck and low back were the regions most often affected in the previous 7 days (, ). The mean number of regions with symptoms fell from 3.10 to 0.55 in the ergonomics-plus-exercise group and from 2.83 to 0.95 in the ergonomics-only group; the difference in change was −0.67 regions (95% CI −1.15 to −0.20; p = 0.006, Holm-adjusted p = 0.013; Mann–Whitney p = 0.008).

Within groups, the prevalence of neck, upper back, and low back symptoms decreased in both groups, and the prevalence of shoulder and hip or thigh symptoms decreased only in the ergonomics-plus-exercise group. In the unadjusted exploratory comparisons between groups, the proportion of baseline symptoms that had resolved was nominally higher with exercise only for the shoulder (16 of 17 versus 5 of 9; difference 38.6 percentage points, 95% CI 5.4 to 67.9; p = 0.034), a region in which the groups were unbalanced at baseline. Resolution did not differ significantly for the neck, upper back, low back, hip or thigh, or knee, and week-12 prevalence did not differ significantly in any region. New symptoms were rare ().

With both groups pooled, baseline emotional exhaustion and depersonalization were higher in middle and high school teachers than in preschool and primary school teachers, whereas baseline ODI, NDI, VAS, and personal accomplishment did not differ significantly by level (). Knee symptoms in the previous 7 days were more frequent in high school teachers (11 of 20) than at the other levels (1 to 5 of 20; exact p = 0.001). The group × school-level interaction on change scores was significant for emotional exhaustion (p < 0.001) and depersonalization (p = 0.045) and not for the other outcomes; the difference between groups in emotional exhaustion was largest among high school teachers. With 10 teachers per group at each level, these analyses have low power and no multiplicity adjustment.

According to the weekly self-reports, 33 of the 40 teachers in the ergonomics-plus-exercise group (82.5%) completed all 36 scheduled sessions, 4 (10.0%) missed two sessions, and 3 (7.5%) missed one session, corresponding to 99.2% of scheduled sessions. These figures were not verified independently. All participants attended the four ergonomics sessions. No adverse events were reported in either group.

In teachers with musculoskeletal pain, adding a 12-week structured exercise program to ergonomics training gave greater short-term improvements in low back and neck disability and in burnout than ergonomics training alone. The additional effect on pain intensity was statistically significant but small, and the questionnaire-wide reduction in symptomatic regions was greater with exercise, while in unadjusted exploratory region-specific analyses, only the shoulder comparison reached nominal significance, in the presence of baseline imbalance.

Statistical significance and clinical importance have to be separated. Proposed thresholds for a minimal important change in low back pain are 15 points on a 0–100 VAS, 10 points on the ODI, or an improvement of 30% from baseline []. The mean differences between groups, 1.18 VAS points (11.8 on a 0–100 scale) and 6.80 ODI points, were below the absolute thresholds, and the upper limits of their confidence intervals (1.48 VAS points and 9.22 ODI points) did not reach them. The average added benefit of the exercise package was therefore modest. This is expected with an active comparator: the ergonomics-only group itself improved by 1.9 VAS points and 6 to 8 points on the disability indices.

The responder analysis qualifies this picture. For pain, almost every participant in both groups improved by at least 30%, so exercise did not change the chance of a clinically relevant pain response. For disability, the proportion of responders was much higher with exercise, by 70 percentage points for the ODI and 53 for the NDI. This suggests that the main contribution of the exercise package was to function and not to pain. The responder analysis was not prespecified, the 30% threshold was developed for patients with low back pain, and some participants had low baseline scores, so a relative threshold can be reached with small absolute changes. These proportions should be read as supportive and exploratory.

The size of the added effect on pain is similar to that reported in the two earlier trials in teachers that used an active or minimal comparator. In schoolteachers with neck pain, adding deep cervical flexor training to conventional exercise for six weeks reduced pain by 2.0 points on a 0–10 scale compared with 0.9 points with conventional exercise alone, a difference of about 1.1 points []. In nursery school teachers, an extension-oriented exercise program added to an ergonomic brochure reduced low back pain by 1.7 points more than the brochure alone after two months []. The larger difference in the latter trial is consistent with its comparator, a brochure after which pain did not change, whereas our comparator was a four-session training after which pain fell by almost two points. Workplace yoga improved pain and disability in female teachers, but against no intervention []. Our result therefore agrees with the teacher literature and extends it to a 12-week program, a face-to-face ergonomics comparator, and burnout outcomes.

Trials with the same design in other occupations give a mixed picture. Exercise added to ergonomics training reduced pain more than ergonomics training alone in tea workers [] and factory workers []. In construction workers, the adjusted difference in pain was 0.34 points and not significant, and burnout did not improve more with exercise []. In office workers, stretching combined with ergonomic modification was no better than either alone []. The present difference of 1.18 points lies between these results. A plausible explanation is the load profile. Construction work involves heavy dynamic loading that an exercise program of this intensity may not offset, whereas the load in teaching is dominated by static postures and prolonged standing, for which stretching, postural endurance, and trunk stabilization are directly relevant.

The content of the program follows the exercise types with the best support. Motor control exercise reduces chronic neck pain in the short term [], core stabilization and related exercise improve pain and function in chronic low back pain [,], and exercise programs reduce pain and disability from work-related musculoskeletal disorders in manual workers []. A network meta-analysis found that three sessions a week and 12-week programs reduce low back pain, although sessions of 15 to 30 min and programs of 16 weeks or longer ranked highest []. The program was low in intensity, used no external load, and was unsupervised. Larger effects might be obtained with supervised or progressively loaded training, but at a higher cost and probably with lower adherence.

The two components of the program act at different points of the continuum from prevention to recovery. Ergonomics training is a preventive strategy: it addresses the occupational exposure by changing the workstation, the posture, and the organization of tasks, and its aim is to reduce the load that produces symptoms in the first place. Structured exercise is a rehabilitative strategy: it addresses the functional capacity of the worker who already has symptoms, by restoring mobility, strength, and endurance. The results reflect this division. The ergonomics-only group improved, which is consistent with a reduction in exposure, and the addition of exercise produced its largest additional effects on the disability indices, which measure function. A workplace program that combines the two therefore covers both the exposure and the capacity side of musculoskeletal health, whereas either alone leaves one side unaddressed.

The trial does not show that the combination is better than exercise alone, because it had no exercise-only arm. What it shows is that ergonomics training, which is the usual occupational response and was followed by clear improvement on its own, leaves room for further gains, mainly in function. The two components address different targets: the training reduces exposure, and the exercise raises the capacity to tolerate the exposure that remains. For school health services, the practical implication is that an ergonomics course alone may not be sufficient for teachers who already have symptoms. Whether exercise alone would achieve the same result, and whether the combination is cost-effective, cannot be answered with these data.

The intervention effect also has to be understood as the effect of a package. Both groups had the same four ergonomics sessions and the same weekly telephone calls, so the amount of contact was similar. The ergonomics-plus-exercise group additionally received an individual teaching session, an illustrated guide, questions about the exercises in the weekly call, and occasional checks of technique. The observed differences therefore combine the physiological effect of exercise with the effects of this instruction and monitoring and of the expectations of participants who knew that they were receiving the additional treatment. The design cannot separate these components.

Neck and low back symptoms in the previous 7 days were reported by 85% to 93% of participants at baseline, which is higher than the pooled prevalence in teachers [], because pain was an inclusion criterion. Symptoms decreased markedly in both groups. The formal comparison between groups supports a greater reduction in the number of symptomatic regions with exercise, by about two-thirds of a region on average. For individual regions, the evidence is weak: only the shoulder comparison reached nominal significance in unadjusted analyses, shoulder symptoms were twice as frequent in the exercise group at baseline, the confidence intervals are wide, and no adjustment was made for the number of regions tested. We therefore do not conclude that symptoms in any specific region resolve more often with exercise. Knee, elbow, wrist, and ankle symptoms were infrequent and did not change, which is plausible because the program contained no exercises for the extremities.

All three burnout subscales improved more in the ergonomics-plus-exercise group, although the program had no psychological component. Less disability may reduce the daily effort that teaching requires and thus lessen emotional exhaustion, in line with the co-occurrence of musculoskeletal pain and burnout in teachers []. Physical activity is often associated with lower burnout, particularly lower emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, in health care workers []; in teachers, higher physical activity was associated with lower burnout in a cross-sectional study [], and a prospective study found associations that varied with the intensity and domain of the activity [].

These findings need particular caution. Both groups were telephoned every week, so the frequency of contact with the physiotherapist does not explain the difference. Burnout is nevertheless the outcome most open to expectation in participants who knew their allocation, and the exercise group may have perceived more support because its calls concerned a program that it was carrying out. The effect on depersonalization was small and was not significant in the non-parametric sensitivity analysis. A trial with the same comparator in construction workers found no additional benefit for burnout []. Although the MBI-ES was a registered primary outcome, the program did not target the psychological or organizational determinants of burnout, and we therefore interpret the burnout results as exploratory. They are best regarded as a hypothesis to be tested in a trial with blinded participants or an attention-matched sham exercise comparator.

Middle and high school teachers started with higher emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, and the group × level interaction suggested a larger difference between groups in emotional exhaustion at the upper levels. Larger changes in those with higher baseline values may reflect regression to the mean, each cell contained 10 teachers, and several interactions were tested. These analyses do not establish that the effect of the program differs by school level. They raise two hypotheses for future trials: that teachers at upper school levels with high burnout may respond more, and that programs for high school teachers, who often reported knee symptoms, may need lower-limb exercises.

Strengths of the trial are prospective registration, stratified randomization with a concealed allocation list held by an independent person, an active comparator with the same schedule of sessions and weekly telephone calls, balanced representation of four school levels, complete follow-up and full attendance, and interviewer-administered outcomes collected by an assessor unaware of allocation.

The limitations bear directly on the interpretation. First, all outcomes were reported by participants who knew their allocation, and the exercise group may have expected and reported more improvement; assessor blinding does not remove this bias, and no objective measures such as range of motion, strength, or posture were collected. The estimates may therefore overstate the true effect. Second, although contact was similar in the two groups, the effect belongs to the whole exercise package (instruction, guide, and exercise-specific monitoring) and not to exercise as such. Third, adherence was self-reported in weekly calls made by the treating physiotherapist, without diaries or objective monitoring. The reported completion of 99.2% of sessions is unusually high for a self-directed program and probably overestimates the true dose through recall and social desirability; technique was checked only occasionally, so the quality and intensity of the exercise performed are uncertain. Fourth, outcomes were measured only at week 12, immediately after the program, so nothing can be said about durability. Fifth, the trial was conducted in a single district with volunteers, which limits generalizability; teachers of both groups worked in the same schools, and although instruction was individual and participants were asked not to share the program, contamination cannot be excluded and would bias the difference toward zero. Sixth, the registration did not rank the outcomes and omitted the VAS, the responder, regional NMQ, and school-level analyses were exploratory, and co-interventions and leisure-time exercise were not systematically recorded. Finally, the VAS referred to the most painful region and not to a fixed anatomical site, so it is a measure of each participant’s main complaint.

The program required one individual teaching session, an illustrated guide, no equipment, and a brief weekly call, and all participants completed the trial without reported adverse events. It is therefore feasible in schools and promising for the short-term management of disability in teachers with musculoskeletal symptoms. Higher adherence to workplace strength training has been associated with clinically relevant reductions in neck and shoulder pain [], and booster sessions and supervision may improve adherence to physiotherapy exercise [], so periodic contact is likely to be a necessary part of such a program. Recommendations for routine implementation should await replication in other regions, longer follow-up, objective outcomes and recorded adherence, a comparator that controls for expectation, and an evaluation of resources and cost-effectiveness.

In teachers with musculoskeletal pain, adding a 12-week structured exercise program to ergonomics training produced statistically significant additional short-term improvements in low back and neck disability, burnout, and pain intensity. The mean differences between groups were modest and, for pain and low back disability, below proposed thresholds for a minimal important change, although more participants reached a 30% improvement in disability. The number of symptomatic body regions decreased more with exercise, but differences for individual regions were not established. Because outcomes and adherence were self-reported, participants knew their allocation, and follow-up ended at week 12, the program should be regarded as a feasible strategy that supports further implementation studies rather than as an established recommendation; its routine use in school-based occupational health programs needs confirmation in trials with objective outcomes, verified adherence, control for expectation, longer follow-up, and cost evaluation.

psychology.title: A practical guide to self-organising maps in psychological research
psychology.abstract: Identifying shared and distinct profiles, whether of symptoms, personality traits, or cognitive abilities, is essential for understanding psychological phenomena, yet doing so requires navigating interrelated theoretical, conceptual, and technical complexities. First, most psychological phenomena typically exist along continuous spectra rather than discrete categories, complicating the characterisation of inherently heterogeneous constructs. Second, studying individual differences requires balancing population-level generalisation with person-level interpretability, which is critical for applied science and clinical practice. Third, psychological data often contain missing values, non-linear relationships, and high-dimensional patterns that violate standard statistical assumptions. Commonly used approaches for profile detection often fall short of these demands, producing oversimplified or difficult-to-interpret results that are hard to map back to the individual. In contrast, self-organising maps (SOMs) offer a powerful, visual, and intuitive solution that addresses these challenges. Despite growing interest, SOMs remain underutilised in psychology, likely due to a lack of accessible tutorials and clear guidelines tailored to the field. This tutorial introduces SOMs to psychologists without technical backgrounds, emphasising practical implementation. We provide evidence-based recommendations for key methodological decisions, accompanied by annotated R code. Using a dataset of depressive symptoms as an illustrative case, we present a complete workflow covering data preprocessing, map initialisation, parameter optimisation, and interpretation. We further discuss advanced SOM extensions relevant to psychological research and highlight key limitations of the method. By making SOMs accessible, this tutorial supports nuanced, person-centred analyses that preserve the complexity of psychological phenomena.The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03198-4.
psychology.text:
Researchers across psychological sciences, whether studying development (Nordahl et al., ; Vandewouw et al., ), mental health (Brucar et al., ; Feczko et al., ; Gao et al., ), or social, emotional, and cognitive processes (Azari et al., ; Santavirta et al., ), often seek to identify profiles of individuals who share similar characteristics. Ideally, such profiles should preserve the structure of psychological constructs (De Boeck et al., ; Haslam et al., ) and remain interpretable at the individual level (Woo et al., ). However, commonly used methods (e.g., factor analysis, standard clustering) often fall short of these goals by imposing categorical assumptions that are not grounded in real-world observation (Haslam et al., ; Lahey et al., ) or producing abstract components that cannot easily be mapped back to individuals (Hope et al., ; Mazziotta & Pareto, ; Watts et al., ).

To illustrate, in mental health research, current classification systems often fail to capture heterogeneity within psychiatric disorders and similarities across them (Dalgleish et al., ), prompting efforts to reclassify disorders using data-driven methods (Conway et al., ; Forbes et al., ; Gao et al., ). For example, exploratory factor analysis (EFA) has been used to group co-occurring symptoms into broader factors (e.g., physical, cognitive, and affective; Puhalla et al., ; Ringwald et al., ; van Loo et al., ). Alternatively, principal component analysis (PCA) has been applied to reduce symptoms into fewer components capturing as much variability in symptoms as possible (Forbes et al., ; Franklyn et al., ; Stout et al., ).

In practice, however, psychologists are often interested in how variables combine within individuals (Bennett et al., ). Whether hopelessness in depression co-occurs with meaninglessness and preserved energy, or with fatigue and anhedonia, may change our assessment of suicide risk (Klonsky et al., ; Tondo et al., ). This person-centred perspective fundamentally differs from variable-centred methods like EFA, which assume a common factor structure across individuals, and from variance-centred methods like PCA, which transform variables at the cost of interpretability. Additionally, psychological phenomena rarely manifest as purely separated clusters (Haslam et al., ). Therefore, forcing dimensional data into rigid categories can obscure gradual transitions between constructs and distort how psychological processes are represented (De Boeck et al., ). In turn, this may reinforce a false dichotomy between categories (e.g., “healthy” versus “disordered”), which may contribute to stigmatisation by implying that groups of people (e.g., those experiencing mental health difficulties) are fundamentally different, rather than part of the same continuum (Johnstone, ; Lahey et al., ). What is needed, then, is a participant-centred approach that reveals how variables combine within individuals, and how those combinations are structured across the data, without reducing people to simply being members of a single group.

One powerful such method is self-organising maps (SOMs). SOMs are an unsupervised machine learning method that creates a two-dimensional map where individuals with similar patterns of variables are placed close together, while those who differ are farther apart (Kohonen, ). SOMs retain the original variables (and thus their interpretability), allowing researchers to examine each individual profile directly. At the same time, the map reveals how these profiles are organised in relation to one another, capturing the broader landscape of the data (Fig. ). SOMs also capture non-linear patterns among variables (Yin, ), require fewer assumptions about data structure (Foody, ), and handle missing data more effectively than traditional approaches (Peeters & Dassargues, ). Together, these advantages make SOMs particularly valuable in psychology, where non-linear relationships and incomplete datasets are common (Failenschmid et al., ; Little, ), and where understanding heterogeneity within complex constructs is a central goal. To illustrate how SOMs differ from other methods, in the Supplementary Text, we apply four widely used methods (EFA, network analysis, PCA combined with k-means clustering, and latent profile analysis) to the same dataset used in this tutorial, enabling direct comparison. SOMs are already being used to explore constructs including personality (Weingärtner Junior et al., ), emotional and cognitive processes (Khosrowabadi et al., ), and mental health conditions (Fekihal & Yousif, ; Galkin et al., ; Kristensen et al., ; Leiva-Murillo et al., ; Tervonen et al., ; Zou, ). For example, SOMs were used in a large cohort of over 8,000 people to identify four distinct profiles of individuals who had attempted suicide, distinguished by different factors (mental health disorders, alcohol problems, impulsiveness, or childhood maltreatment), suggesting that suicide attempts may arise through different routes for different people (Leiva-Murillo et al., ). In another study, a map was created to organise individuals without depression by their psychological profiles (based on variables such as attitudes towards life, sense of control, and social connections; Galkin et al., ). Individuals with depression were then placed on this map, and were over-represented in a specific area. Because the map changes gradually, the researchers could trace a continuum of changing attitudes from this area to the area most resilient to depression.

In autism research, SOMs have helped reveal distinct anxiety profiles in children, which are linked to differences in depression and peer-related difficulties (Leachman et al., ). In adolescent mental health research, SOMs have identified reproducible profiles ranging from flourishing well-being to widespread difficulties, with intermediate profiles showing focal internalising or externalising patterns (Bennett et al., ). They have also been used in children to uncover profiles of school-related challenges that were not predicted by children's diagnoses, suggesting that children with the same diagnosis can differ in their cognitive profiles (Astle et al., ; Siugzdaite et al., ). SOMs have further been used to classify cognitive task performance following working memory training (Rennie et al., ).

Despite these promising applications, SOMs remain underused in psychology, likely because existing literature assumes strong mathematical knowledge. Although introductory pieces (Oliver et al., ; Thuneberg & Hotulainen, ) provide helpful overviews, they lack step-by-step practical guidance tailored to psychological science.

This paper bridges this gap by providing a theoretical introduction and hands-on tutorial, written in accessible language, specifically designed for psychological research. To support this, we include a step-by-step script using the kohonen package (v3.0.12; Wehrens & Kruisselbrink, ) in R (v4.4.1; R Core Team, ), with an illustrative example providing all the essential information for researchers to implement SOMs in their work. For the illustrative case, we focused on depressive symptoms since individuals can exhibit 1,030 different symptom combinations (Fried & Nesse, ), necessitating a better understanding of the profiles within this diverse population. We selected 301 participants from a previously published study (Trachtenberg et al., ) who scored above threshold on the seven-item depression scale of the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales–21 (Lovibond, ). The example covers all stages, including data pre-processing, SOM training, interpretation and further analysis, visualisation, and recommended approaches for assessing validity and reliability.

Figure  describes the structure and process of SOMs. A glossary summarising key terms (bolded at first mention) is included to support readers. At its core, SOM is a method for simplifying complex data while preserving the structure of relationships between similar observations. In other words, it reduces data with many variables into a two-dimensional map, called a grid (or feature map), where individuals with similar patterns are positioned close together. Each point on the grid is called a node, representing a group of similar observations (called data points). In psychology, data points are usually participants, each with a set of variables of interest (e.g., depressive symptoms; Fig. A). Each node is assigned a random set of weights, with a single number for each variable in the data (Fig. A and B, Randomised Initialisation). Each weight is expressed on the same scale as its variable, and together a node's weights form its profile.

Through an iterative process, the SOM adjusts the weights to match the data structure. At each step, a data point is presented (e.g., seven symptom scores of one participant) and compared with the weights of every node. The node with the most similar weights, called the best matching unit (BMU), is identified. The BMU and its neighbouring nodes then update their weights to become more like that data point, with each weight moving a small step towards the participant’s score on that variable. Nodes closer to the BMU typically undergo larger updates than those further away (Fig. B, Iterative Training). This process repeats over multiple cycles (called iterations or epochs). Because each participant pulls the surrounding region of the map towards their own profile, neighbouring nodes gradually come to hold similar profiles. Early in training, updates are larger, establishing the broad layout of the map. Later, they become smaller and more local, fine-tuning individual nodes (see  below). With each cycle, the map gradually organises itself so that similar data points end up near each other, creating a visual representation of the data’s underlying structure. By the end of training, each node's weights approximate the typical profile of the participants assigned to it, which is what researchers interpret.

Building a SOM involves three main steps (following data preprocessing), namely initialisation, optimisation, and interpretation (Fig. B). First, an initial map is set up with rough parameters. These are then fine-tuned by adjusting the grid size, shape, number of iterations, and other settings. These steps require careful decision-making to determine how detailed the final map should be, depending on the research questions and the dataset, allowing researchers to reveal either broader patterns or fine-grained heterogeneity. Once an optimal map is selected, the final stage is interpretation. While this can be accomplished through multiple approaches, this tutorial focuses on clustering similar nodes into distinct profiles. Below, we provide a step-by-step guide and introduce key terms for informed decision-making throughout the process. A flowchart summarising the guidelines is provided in Fig. .

Before generating the SOM, data should be prepared to ensure all variables are on the same scale. Variables with larger ranges can disproportionately influence the results. For example, if symptom severity is measured on a 0–3 scale, while intelligence quotient (IQ) is measured on a standard score scale, IQ could dominate the learning process due to its larger range. Common approaches, such as normalisation, where each variable is rescaled to range between 0 and 1, can address this.

Determining the grid size by choosing the number of nodes is one of the most critical decisions, directly affecting the SOM quality. The grid is typically two-dimensional (e.g., 10 × 10), with larger and more complicated datasets requiring larger maps. A common heuristic recommends that the number of nodes should be approximately five times the square root of the number of data points (Vesanto et al., ). For example, for 100 participants, the map would include approximately 50 (5 × √100) nodes (e.g., 7 × 7 grid). For smaller datasets, researchers suggest starting with a small grid (e.g., 5 × 5) and gradually increasing its size while monitoring the quality of the map (Riese et al., ).

The grid shape also affects the quality of the SOM. The most common shapes are rectangular and hexagonal (although other topologies exist; López-Rubio & Díaz Ramos, ). While rectangular grids may be more computationally efficient, hexagonal grids are often preferred because neighbouring nodes are arranged more evenly around this shape, producing smoother grids that better preserve the topology of the data (Kohonen, ; Villmann, ).

Regardless of the shape, asymmetrical grids (e.g., 9 × 11 rather than 10 × 10), tend to improve cluster separation (Kohonen, ; Ultsch & Herrmann, ; Wendel & Buttenfield, ). It is also recommended that the shorter dimension be at least half the length of the longer side (Kohonen, ). This “one-half rule” reduces uneven updates at grid borders, where nodes have fewer neighbours.

When constructing SOMs, several key parameters must be considered, as reviewed below.

The learning rate (alpha, ranging 0–1) controls how much the weights are adjusted during self-organisation. Higher values produce larger, faster updates, and lower values produce smaller, more gradual changes, affecting training speed and map stability. SOMs typically use a decreasing learning rate, starting high to allow large adjustments early in training when the structure is still forming, and then gradually declining for fine-tuning in later stages. The initial learning rate should be high enough to allow rapid adaptation, but not too high that it overshoots optimal weight values. The final learning rate should allow careful fine-tuning without disrupting the grid’s structure.

Many packages use an initial learning rate between 0.01 and 0.1 (Van Gassen et al., ; Wehrens & Kruisselbrink, ; Wittek et al., ). The kohonen package defaults to 0.05, which has been shown to be an efficient middle-ground that is neither overly liberal nor overly conservative (Arunachalam & Kumar, ; Tao et al., ; Wehrens & Buydens, ). Other packages, such as Python miniSOM (Vettigli, ), implement higher rates, although evidence comparing these defaults remains limited (Mersiovsky et al., ). Higher initial learning rates may be preferable for datasets with substantial proportions of missing values, especially when missingness is patterned rather than random (Khotimah et al., ), or for very large samples where faster training is required (Tao et al., ). Lower initial learning rates may be appropriate when finetuning is needed (Goodfellow et al., ). Another consideration is the decay algorithm used to reduce learning rate over time. The kohonen package applies a linear decrease in the learning rate to a default minimum of 0.01 (Wehrens & Kruisselbrink, ). Alternative decay functions are discussed elsewhere (Stefanovic & Kurasova, ).

As mentioned earlier, once the BMU is identified, surrounding nodes are also updated. The neighbourhood function determines the strength of these updates. The kohonen package supports Gaussian and bubble functions (Wehrens & Kruisselbrink, ), with the default Gaussian function applying stronger updates near the BMU and weaker updates to distant nodes. Gaussian function is generally suited for psychological data, but for large databases, alternatives may be considered (Clark et al., ; Natita et al., ; Ota et al., ; Stefanovic & Kurasova, ).

We also specify how far the influence of the BMU extends at each step, determined by the neighbourhood radius (sigma; Fig. B). Smaller values restrict updates to nodes near the BMU. Radii that are too small can reduce map quality by under-updating distant nodes, whereas overly large radii may reduce accuracy and increase error rates (Kolasa & Dlugosz, ). Default settings vary across packages (KratochvÌl et al., ; Vettigli, ; Wittek et al., ). The kohonen package uses the 67th percentile of the distances between nodes, which may be slightly large, but provides a reasonable starting point (Kolasa & Dlugosz, ). In practice, the “right” radius depends on the specific dataset and grid structure (Fukui & Numao, ), so trial-and-error should always be followed.

Like the learning rate, the neighbourhood radius decreases over time. A relatively low final radius (e.g., 0.5) is recommended to ensure only the closest nodes are updated in later stages (Bednar et al., ; Vesanto et al., ). It should be noted that some packages, including kohonen (Wehrens & Kruisselbrink, ), default to a final radius of 0, which may weaken local neighbourhood structure (Kohonen, ).

The number of iterations also affects SOM quality. Too few iterations may lead to insufficient learning, where nodes fail to adequately capture the data structure, whereas too many may make the map too specific to the data, potentially reducing its generalisability. Most packages use a default of 100 to 500 iterations (Vettigli, ; Vialaneix et al., ; Wehrens & Kruisselbrink, ), but optimal values depend on the dataset and are best determined through trial-and-error.

Selecting an optimal set of parameters is highly dependent on the data and, therefore, involves a trial-and-error process guided by theoretical and empirical considerations. During this process, the quality of the SOM should be monitored as parameters are adjusted until a final set is chosen. Many parameter combinations may work well, and no single solution is strictly correct. It should also be noted that when the data contain a strong underlying structure, different reasonable combinations often affect fine details (e.g., exact node boundaries) rather than main patterns (Cottrell et al., ). Nonetheless, choices should be justified to ensure appropriate parameters are selected. Below, we outline key quality metrics for this process, followed by practical suggestions for parameter optimisation.

Three complementary error measures guide optimisation. Quantisation error quantifies how well the grid matches the actual data, measuring the average distance between each data point and its BMU. Lower values indicate a better match (with zero representing a perfect fit). Since quantisation error is expressed in the original data units, which often lack standardised norms, it is often interpreted alongside explained variance, which is the proportion of variability in the data captured by the SOM (analogous to intuitive units like R2 in regression). While no standard benchmark exists, higher explained variance generally indicates better performance.

Low quantisation error does not necessarily indicate a well-organised map (Uriarte & Martín, ). Similar data points may still be assigned to distant nodes on the grid, even if each data point is near its BMU, a problem quantisation error cannot detect. The topographic error addresses this by measuring whether similar nodes are grouped together (Pölzlbauer, ). The topographic error estimates the proportion of data points for which the BMU and second-best-matching unit are not adjacent (Kohonen, ), with lower values indicating better topology.

Quantisation and topographic errors capture different aspects of SOM quality that can sometimes conflict. To solve this, Kaski and Lagus () proposed a combined measure, balancing accuracy (how well the grid represents the data) and organisation (how well relationships are preserved across the grid). Lower Kaski–Lagus error indicates higher SOM quality. The error metrics depend on the data, so there are no fixed thresholds for what constitutes “low” error. However, they are useful for comparing SOMs trained on the same dataset, and can guide the fine-tuning of the learning rate, neighbourhood function, and number of iterations required (Wendel & Buttenfield, ).

As noted, identifying an optimal SOM involves trial and error, where different maps are tested and compared (Kohonen, , ). The aim is to end up with a SOM with relatively low error, where data points are accurately represented on the grid and similar nodes are grouped together. This can be evaluated using the quality metrics alongside visually inspecting the maps.

We recommend beginning with the grid size and shape, as these strongly affect all other parameters (Gonzalez et al., ), and then adjusting the iterations, learning rate, and neighbourhood radius through a cyclical process (Fig. ). A fully worked example is included in the accompanying R code.

Choosing the optimal grid size depends primarily on the data, but standard error metrics are insufficient for this purpose. As the number of nodes increases, the average distance between data points and their BMU decreases mechanically, so quantisation error and explained variance cannot distinguish better-fitting maps from larger ones (de Bodt et al., ; Pölzlbauer, ). Similarly, topographic error is also limited for this purpose (Pölzlbauer, ). Instead, two visual diagnostics are recommended to guide grid size selection (Fig. A).

The first, the hit map, displays the number of data points assigned to each node. Ideally, data points should be relatively evenly spread. Many empty nodes may indicate that the grid is too large, while numerous highly concentrated nodes indicate it is too small or poorly shaped. The second diagnostic map, the unified distance matrix (U-matrix), shows how similar neighbouring nodes are, with lower values indicating greater similarity. When distinct profiles exist, they appear as small “islands” of similar nodes separated by higher-value boundary regions. Uniformly low values across the U-matrix indicate absence of distinct clusters or an undersized grid. Excessive gaps suggest that the grid is too large, making structure detection difficult. Together, these diagnostic maps guide optimisation of the grid size.

Once grid size is selected, the next step is assessing whether the SOM has trained for enough iterations by plotting the total change in node weights over time (Fig. B). A curve flattening near zero indicates the map has stabilised, and further iterations are unlikely to yield improvements. Next, error metrics can guide fine-tuning of the learning rate and neighbourhood radius. In our case, we tested a range of values and selected appropriate settings based on error metrics and map visualisations (Table ).
