Therefore, depression was harmonised to the least common denominator available across studies: a single binary baseline depression indicator. This indicator reflects clinically elevated depressive symptoms or a documented diagnosis and should not be interpreted uniformly as a confirmed diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Study-level depression burden was defined as the proportion of participants within each study who had a positive baseline depression indicator. This aggregate measure captures variation in sample composition and psychiatric burden across trials, even after propensity score weighting, and should not be interpreted as a causal contextual mechanism.

Treatment arms were categorised according to therapeutic focus and modality using a previously validated therapy coding framework (Hien et al., , ). Treatment conditions were grouped into the following classes: trauma-focused psychotherapy addressing PTSD (e.g. PE, CPT), SUD-focused psychotherapy (e.g. RP, CBT for alcohol or drug use); integrated psychotherapy explicitly targeting both PTSD and SUD (e.g. COPE [trauma-focused], Seeking Safety [non-trauma-focused]); pharmacotherapy targeting PTSD or substance use symptoms (e.g. sertraline, for PTSD; prazosin for PTSD-related nightmares; naltrexone for alcohol use disorder), and Treatment as Usual (TAU, defined as non-manualized care).

PTSD symptom severity was estimated as a latent construct using moderated nonlinear factor analysis (MNLFA) across item-level data from structured interviews (e.g. CAPS-5; Weathers, Blake, et al., ) and self-report measures (e.g. PCL-5; Weathers, Litz, et al., ). Moderated nonlinear factor analysis was used for analytic harmonisation (Bauer, ; Bauer & Hussong, ), which is used in integrative data analysis studies for scale score estimation that takes into account differences in item parameters (i.e. factor loadings, item intercepts) across measures and other key predictors of differential item functioning (DIF). Estimation of latent PTSD severity scale scores is based on 42 PTSD severity indicators across studies that had item-level PTSD data (i.e. 21 clinical interview symptoms and 21 self-report measure symptoms; Saavedra et al., ). Item parameters for the latent PTSD measure, including differential item functioning parameters by measure/reporter, are found in the Supplemental Materials in Hien et al. ().

Latent alcohol use severity scores and latent drug use severity scores were estimated separately (Hien et al., ; Saavedra et al., ). For alcohol use severity, a two-indicator latent severity variable was estimated using the number of days of alcohol use in the past 30 days and any past-30-day alcohol use to intoxication. For drug use severity, binary indicators of any past-30-day use of cocaine, heroin, opioids other than heroin, sedatives, other psychostimulants, and hallucinogens were used to estimate a six-indicator latent severity variable. The most common substance use measures across studies included the Timeline Follow-back (Sobell & Sobell, ) or Addiction Severity Index (McLellan et al., ). Full details on measurement modelling, MNLFA item parameters and measurement noninvariance tests are detailed in the Supplemental Materials in Hien et al. ().

The analytic approach proceeded in four steps. First, harmonised latent PTSD, alcohol use, and drug use outcomes were estimated using moderated nonlinear factor analysis. Second, propensity score weights were estimated to balance participant characteristics across treatment conditions within the pooled dataset. Third, multilevel growth models estimated treatment effects over time. Finally, individual-level and study-level depression were evaluated as moderators of treatment effects, with significant interactions probed at representative values of study-level depression burden.

Given that randomisation structures achieved within original RCTs are lost when merged, we estimated propensity scores to balance covariates in the harmonised dataset prior to outcome modelling using SAS Proc GLIMMIX. Covariates used for estimation of propensity scores included age, race/ethnicity, education, marital status, Veteran status, depression, any use of psychotropic medications, and baseline PTSD/alcohol/drug use severity. Treatment dosage was used as a post-assignment covariate (Rosenbaum, , ) given (a) self-selected dosage can be affected by treatment assignment and (b) dosage can affect PTSD and SUD outcomes (Morgan-López et al., ). Post-weighting baseline differences were all below standardised mean differences of |d| < .10 indicated adequate covariate balance for pre-treatment covariates (Hien et al., ).

A propensity score-weighted, three-level multilevel latent growth modelling structure was estimated in Mplus version 8 (Muthén & Muthén, –) that accounted for two forms of clustering: (a) repeated observations within participants and (b) participants within studies. At the between-person level, random intercepts and slopes were both specified; at the study level, only a random intercept was specified to account for (residual) variation in outcomes across studies, consistent with the optimal variance component structure from previous analyses of Project Harmony data (Blakey et al., ; Hien et al., ; Hill et al., ; Morgan-López et al., ). Primary predictors were intervention dummy variable indicators based on the treatment classification coding described in Hien et al. (, ) for each treatment class across studies: (a) trauma-focused (yes/no), (b) integrated (yes/no), (c) a trauma-focused by integrated interaction term, (d) PTSD medication (yes/no), (e) SUD behavioural (yes/no), (f) SUD medication (yes/no) and (g) placebo medication (yes/no); each of these codes were then crossed with two sets of depression indicators: individual-level depression (yes/no) and study-level depression (i.e. the proportion of patients with baseline comorbid depression in the study). Treatment class indicators, and the treatment-by-depression interaction terms predicted within-treatment changes (i.e. from pre- to post-treatment) and post-treatment changes (i.e. from post-treatment to 12-month follow-up) in outcome slopes for PTSD severity, alcohol use severity, and drug use severity. Missing data were addressed via multiple imputation for clustered data using the R package ‘mice’ (Van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, ) with 20 imputed datasets. Results were combined across the 20 datasets using Rubin’s () rules for combining results in multiple imputation.

Given previous analyses of Project Harmony reported on both intention-to-treat (Hien et al., ) and dosage-adjusted average treatment effect on the treated (Morgan-López et al., 2025) effects, the focal findings in the results will be on treatment by depression interactions. It is noted that no treatment by depression interactions were observed for individual-level depression, thus the results focus on interactions between treatment and variation in the proportions of patients with depression across studies. Probing of interactions was conducted by recentering the study-level depression burden measure to reflect ‘low’ (20% of participants with depression) and ‘high’ (80% of participants with depression) as shown in Aiken and West () and Bauer and Curran ().

Treatment by study-level depression interactions were observed for the combination of trauma-focused and integrated therapies. Participants in both low- and high-depression-burden trials exhibited improvement across conditions, providing no evidence that depression attenuates treatment response at the individual level. However, moderation analyses indicated that study-level depression burden altered these trajectories, with a significant trauma-focused by integrated by study-level depression interaction effect on changes in PTSD during treatment (b = 5.51, SE = 2.05, z = 2.68, p = .007, partial Cohen’s d = .08).

Based on simple interaction effects for studies with lower proportions of comorbid depression (20%; see (a)), the trauma-focused by integrated by in-treatment time interaction effect was significant (b = −2.17, SE = .77, z = −2.811, p = .005). Participants assigned to TAU showed significant decreases in PTSD severity during treatment (b = −.55, SE = .11, z = −4.70, p < .001) and no significant change from the end of treatment through 12-month follow-up (p = .97). Integrated non-trauma-focused treatments yielded less steep decreases in PTSD compared with TAU during treatment, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (b = .36, SE = .19, z = 1.86, p = .06), and no differences in change compared with TAU post-treatment (p = .28). Trauma-focused non-integrated treatments showed no differences in in-treatment changes in PTSD compared with TAU (p = .27) and a nonsignificant increase in PTSD severity relative to TAU post-treatment (b = .41, SE = .21, z = 1.90, p = .06). Trauma-focused/integrated treatments showed significant decreases in PTSD severity compared with TAU during treatment (p < .001) and no significant differences in post-treatment change compared with TAU (p = .55).

Simple interaction effects for studies with higher proportions of comorbid depression (80%; see (b)), the trauma-focused by integrated by in-treatment time interaction effect was also significant (b = 1.14, SE = .51, z = 2.21, p = .03) as was the corresponding post-treatment effect (b = .33, SE = .15, z = 2.28, p = .02). Participants assigned to TAU showed significant decreases in PTSD severity during (b = −.57, SE = .07, z = –7.39, p < .001), and post-treatment (b = −.15, SE = .03, z = −5.73, p < .001). Integrated non-trauma-focused treatments showed no differences in change compared to TAU (ps = .17 and .11). Trauma-focused non-integrated treatments showed steeper in-treatment decreases in PTSD compared to TAU (b = −.99, SE = .48, z = −2.06, p = .04) and further decreases compared to TAU (b = −.35, SE = .11, z = −3.14, p = .002). Trauma-focused/integrated treatments showed no differences in change compared to TAU.

Treatment by study-level depression interactions were observed for trauma-focused non-integrated therapies on both in-treatment (b = 1.61, SE = .61, z = 2.62, p = .01, partial Cohen’s d = .08) and post-treatment changes in alcohol use severity (b = −1.31, SE = .30, z = −4.29, p < .001, partial Cohen’s d = −.14). Simple interaction effects for studies with lower proportions of comorbid depression (20%; see (a)) showed that trauma-focused non-integrated therapies produced significantly steeper decreases in alcohol severity during treatment (b = −.90, SE = .31, z = −2.90, p = .004) but significant increases in alcohol severity post-treatment (b = .56, SE = .12, z = 4.55, p < .001). Simple interaction effects for studies with higher proportions of comorbid depression (80%; see (b)) showed significant decreases in alcohol severity during treatment for TAU (b = −.23, SE = .08, z = −2.76, p = .006) that did not differ for trauma-focused/non-integrated treatments (p = .88). Although no further decreases in alcohol severity were observed post-treatment for TAU (p = .82), trauma-focused/non-integrated treatments showed an estimated post-treatment decrease that did not reach statistical significance (b = −.19, SE = .10, z = −1.89, p = .06).

Treatment by study-level depression interactions were observed for trauma-focused non-integrated therapies on in-treatment changes in drug use severity (b = −.92, SE = .39, z = −2.38, p = .02). Simple interaction effects for studies with lower proportions of comorbid depression (20%; see (a)) showed that, while TAU showed significant decreases during treatment (b = −.56, SE = .07, z = −7.68, p < .001), trauma-focused non-integrated treatments showed significantly less steep decreases than TAU in drug use severity during treatment (b = .42, SE = .15, z = 2.69, p = .007); the differences between post-treatment decreases in drug use severity for trauma-focused non-integrated treatments and the post-treatment increases in drug use severity were non-significant (p = .12). Simple interaction effects for studies with higher proportions of comorbid depression (80%; see (b)), showed significant decreases in drug severity during treatment for TAU (b = −.54, SE = .06, z = −8.86, p < .001) and no further changes through post-treatment (p = .85). Trauma-focused non-integrated treatments did not differ significantly from TAU during the in-treatment (p = .38) nor post-treatment (p = .26) phases.

Propensity score weighting balanced treatment conditions, but variation in depression rates across studies cannot be interpreted as a causal influence of the study-level moderator. Thus, we examined study-level predictors to assess what may account for differences in depression rates across studies using multilevel logistic regression in Mplus 8 and the same set of predictors included in the propensity score weighting. Significant study-level predictors included sex (with higher study-level depression rates among samples with higher proportions of women; b = −1.11 [SE = .54], p = .02) and race (with higher study-level depression rates among samples with lower proportions of Black participants; b = −.96 [SE = .47], p = .02). The association with the proportion of Veterans did not reach statistical significance (b = .52 [SE = .37], p = .07). These findings suggest that study-level depression burden partly reflects differences in participant composition across trials rather than depression alone. Consequently, study-level depression burden should be interpreted as a composite marker of broader study characteristics and clinical complexity rather than a direct measure of contextual adversity.

This study examined whether baseline depression status moderates treatment response among patients with PTSD/SUD. Toward this end, we leveraged harmonised IPD from Project Harmony (Hien et al., ) from trials examining multiple treatment modalities. The primary and most clinically relevant finding of this study is that baseline depression status did not moderate treatment response at the individual level among individuals with co-occurring PTSD/SUD. Although the analyses did not detect individual-level moderation, this finding should not be interpreted as evidence that such effects do not exist. Participants with baseline depression showed meaningful improvement across treatment modalities, and we did not detect systematic differences in their symptom trajectories relative to participants who did not report baseline depression. Thus, within the detectable range of the present analyses, baseline depression was not associated with differential treatment response. Further, analyses were limited to presence/absence measures of depression, given the problem of having to harmonise depression data to the ‘least common denominator’. It is possible that, if dimensional measures of depression were used, particularly with adjustments for measurement variation (e.g. moderated nonlinear factor analysis of the BDI; see e.g. Saavedra et al., ) both study- and individual-level depression moderation effects could have emerged. However, as is the case with retrospective harmonisation across studies, we were limited to what was available among studies that were never structured to be harmonised with consistent measures of constructs.

The nonsignificant individual-level interactions must also be considered in relation to statistical power. The reliability-adjusted modelling approach reduced attenuation attributable to measurement error in the harmonised outcomes, but improved measurement precision does not overcome limited power to detect small interaction effects. Although the pooled individual patient dataset provided greater power than is typically available in individual trials, the analyses may still have been insufficiently powered to detect small individual-level moderation effects. Therefore, individual-level effects below the detectable range cannot be ruled out. One plausible explanation for the lack of statistically detectable individual-level moderation is that the interventions evaluated in this study engage transdiagnostic processes that are shared across PTSD, SUD, and depression (Blakey et al., ; Marlatt & Witkiewitz, ). Overlapping symptoms and maintenance processes include avoidance, behavioural withdrawal, negative cognitions, anhedonia, emotion dysregulation, and symptom-related functional impairment. Trauma-focused, integrated, and even some SUD-focused interventions target these mechanisms either explicitly or indirectly (Back et al., ; Foa et al., ; Marlatt & Donovan, ; Resick et al., ), such that depressive symptoms may improve as a downstream consequence of effective treatment for PTSD and/or substance use.

From this perspective, comorbid depression in PTSD/SUD populations may not represent a separate or competing treatment target, but rather part of an interconnected symptom network that is already addressed by extant evidence-based PTSD + SUD interventions. This interpretation is consistent with prior work showing that trauma-focused treatments often produce concurrent improvements in depressive symptoms and broader functioning (Paridaen et al., ). It is also consistent with the idea that depression status presence, while clearly associated with greater overall clinical burden, does not necessarily alter the fundamental capacity of individuals to benefit from treatment (Cuijpers et al., ).

Although the analyses did not detect moderation by the individual-level baseline depression indicator, study-level depression burden was associated with differences in selected treatment effects. These associations varied by outcome, treatment classification, and period of change. Because study-level depression burden was correlated with characteristics of the contributing samples, including demographic composition, it should be interpreted as an aggregate marker of trial composition and clinical complexity rather than as evidence that depression itself caused the observed differences.

Accordingly, the observed study-level effects should be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence of specific contextual mechanisms. The reported moderation patterns were concentrated in trauma-focused treatment classifications rather than SUD-focused treatments. In studies with lower depression burden, trauma-focused non-integrated therapies showed steeper during-treatment decreases in alcohol use severity but less steep during-treatment decreases in drug use severity relative to TAU; PTSD change during treatment did not differ from TAU, and the estimated post-treatment increase relative to TAU did not reach statistical significance. In studies with higher depression burden, trauma-focused non-integrated therapies showed steeper decreases in PTSD severity than TAU both during treatment and through follow-up, whereas their alcohol and drug use trajectories did not differ significantly from TAU during treatment; the estimated post-treatment decrease in alcohol use severity also did not reach statistical significance. These findings do not establish that any modality is preferable for an individual patient with depression. Rather, they identify treatment-by-study-context patterns that warrant replication and direct evaluation in comparative effectiveness and implementation research.

The timing of the observed associations also differed across outcomes. In high-depression-burden studies, trauma-focused non-integrated therapies were associated with greater PTSD improvement than TAU during treatment and from post-treatment through follow-up. For alcohol use severity, however, the same treatment classification did not differ from TAU during treatment, and its estimated post-treatment decrease did not reach statistical significance. In low-depression-burden studies, trauma-focused non-integrated therapies were associated with greater during-treatment improvement in alcohol use severity, followed by a relative increase after treatment. The significant trauma-focused by integrated interaction for during-treatment PTSD change also differed across levels of study-level depression burden, but the simple effects did not support broad claims that integrated trauma-focused or integrated non-trauma-focused treatment was consistently superior. These patterns suggest that the period over which outcomes are evaluated may matter, while mechanistic explanations concerning skill consolidation, exposure processes, or emotion regulation remain speculative and require direct testing.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the observed moderation effects were detected at the study level, not the individual level. Although we used PSW to balance individual-level depression status and other covariates across treatment types, unmeasured differences between studies (e.g. provider training, setting characteristics, intervention fidelity) may still confound the observed study-level effects. Second, depression was harmonised to the lowest common denominator available across studies because many contributing trials provided only a baseline diagnostic indicator rather than item-level symptom data. Consequently, we were unable to examine dimensional depression severity or specific depressive symptom domains, which may have been more sensitive for detecting individual-level moderation effects. This variability could obscure more nuanced individual-level depression effects, especially if certain depressive symptom dimensions (e.g. hopelessness, somatic symptoms) respond differently with treatment modality. Although this approach necessarily reduced measurement precision, the main advantage of the MIPD remains allowing inclusion of all contributing trials. Excluding studies that only contributed diagnostic information would have substantially reduced study representation, statistical power, and generalizability. We therefore considered this to be the most appropriate balance between measurement precision and comprehensive harmonisation. Nevertheless, accounting for measurement error does not resolve limitations in statistical power. Interaction effects generally require large samples to detect, and the present analyses may have been insufficiently powered to identify small individual-level moderation effects. Accordingly, the nonsignificant interactions indicate an absence of statistically detectable moderation and should not be interpreted as evidence that individual-level moderation effects do not exist. Third, the findings do not support causal inference. While we could not directly measure contextual factors related to depression (e.g. food security, housing security, discrimination), they may help explain differences in treatment outcomes observed across study samples. This possibility underscores the importance of attending not only to individual depression severity, but also to the characteristics of the settings and populations that interventions reach. Finally, although statistically significant, the observed interaction effect sizes were generally small, suggesting modest contextual moderation that should be interpreted alongside their clinical significance.

Future research could disaggregate depression into symptom dimensions to clarify which aspects of depression drive treatment differences across PTSD/SUD interventions. Examining other potential treatment mediators, such as emotional regulation capacity, therapeutic alliance, or treatment engagement, may help clarify how depression comorbidity shapes outcomes. Further, research should explore how site-level characteristics (e.g. veteran vs. civilian status, group vs. individual therapy delivery, hospital vs. community clinic vs. substance-use treatment settings) contribute to contextual effects. Finally, implementation strategies should consider both individual- and population-level comorbidity when selecting and adapting PTSD/SUD interventions, particularly in high-depression settings.

In conclusion, this large integrative analysis of PTSD/SUD treatment trials found no statistically detectable evidence that the individual-level baseline depression indicator moderated treatment response. Study-level depression burden, however, was associated with heterogeneity in selected treatment effects across outcomes, treatment classifications, and periods of change. Because this aggregate measure also reflected differences in trial composition, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence that depression exerted a causal contextual influence or that a particular treatment should be selected for an individual patient on the basis of depression status. Instead, they underscore the importance of distinguishing individual clinical characteristics from study-level sample composition when interpreting treatment effects. Future comparative effectiveness and implementation research should identify the characteristics captured by study-level depression burden and test whether they prospectively explain variation in treatment response.

psychology.title: Classroom Integration of AI-Simulated Patients and Automated Feedback in Doctoral Psychotherapy Training: Longitudinal Mixed Methods Study
psychology.abstract: Psychotherapy education increasingly emphasizes technology-assisted methods that extend deliberate practice beyond human supervision. AI has enabled automated skill assessment and patient simulations, yet few studies have examined how students experience such tools in real-world settings alongside established practice modalities.We aimed to evaluate students’ experiences with AI-augmented deliberate practice embedded in an existing psychotherapy course sequence. Secondary aims included identifying implementation barriers, ethical and pedagogical considerations, and factors influencing students’ acceptance of AI-assisted learning.Participants were 29 first-year clinical psychology doctoral students in a 2-quarter psychotherapy sequence at an American Psychological Association–accredited program. In the fall course, students completed weekly peer role-plays and could optionally submit transcripts to CARE for AI feedback to supplement peer feedback. In the winter course, students completed required weekly deliberate practice through Skillsetter video vignettes and could optionally practice with CARE’s voice-based AI-simulated patients, receiving AI and instructor feedback afterward. Surveys with Likert-type and free-response items were voluntary in the fall and required in the winter; 9 and 25 students completed them, respectively. Analyses included descriptive statistics, matched-pairs testing, and thematic analysis.In the fall course (n=9), where privacy concerns and survey nonresponse limited data on AI feedback, students rated peer feedback higher than AI feedback on being constructive and helpful (median 3, IQR 3-3 vs median 2, IQR 2-2; P=.02) and recognizing areas to improve (mean 5.22, SD 0.83 vs mean 4.33, SD 0.87; P=.046), citing transcription errors and a narrow focus on empathy while valuing AI’s alternative phrasing. In the winter course (n=25), Skillsetter was rated higher than CARE only for learning from mistakes (mean 4.52, SD 2.00 vs mean 3.20, SD 2.04; P=.03); immersion, spontaneous responding, communication beyond words, and alliance building did not differ significantly. Students valued CARE for interactive practice not possible with vignettes but reported undetected vocal pauses (20/25, 80%), insufficient realism (14/25, 56%), and limited emotional expression (13/25, 52%), and raised concerns about AI replacing peer support (22/25, 88%) and peer interaction (20/25, 80%). Asked about AI broadly, students expressed mixed views, citing concerns about supplanted relational dynamics, nonconsensual data use, and generative AI’s environmental impacts.Embedding AI-augmented deliberate practice into an existing course sequence was feasible, but students’ experiences favored established methods: they preferred human over AI feedback and described video vignettes as more realistic than voice-based AI interactions, while valuing AI-simulated patients for interactive practice other modalities could not provide. Implementation barriers included feedback quality, transcription accuracy, and instructor time required to supplement AI feedback. Perceptions of AI’s instructional utility appeared contingent on students’ trust in the technology, suggesting future deployments should weigh a sample’s attitudes toward AI and its value relative to existing training resources.
psychology.text:
Psychotherapy is a structured clinical intervention wherein trained professionals use established psychological methods, primarily through dialogue and relational engagement, to alleviate distress, reduce psychiatric symptoms, and promote psychological functioning and well-being [,]. Psychotherapy is a collaborative process in which the therapeutic alliance, defined as the emotional bond between the therapist and patient, as well as agreement on the goals of therapy and the tasks required to achieve the therapeutic goals [], is consistently associated with clinical improvement [].

Therapeutic communication skills cannot be fully developed through lectures or reading alone; instead, they are cultivated through experiential practice, structured feedback, and critical reflection. Accordingly, traditional psychotherapy training emphasizes didactic instruction (structured, instructor-led teaching methods, such as lectures, seminars, or presentations that convey foundational theories and practical guidelines) alongside supervised clinical practice, role-play, and reflective exercises. Collectively, these methods facilitate real-time interaction and iterative refinement of core therapeutic skills [].

Training psychotherapists, therefore, presents a distinctive pedagogical challenge: students must master not only theoretical and technical knowledge but also deeply interpersonal competencies, including empathic attunement, alliance building, and moment-to-moment responsiveness. A small yet steadily growing evidence base suggests that deliberate practice (DP) is an effective learning method that can outperform standard supervision and training []. Unlike didactic instruction, DP focuses on structured and intentional skill development through activities that include clearly defined goals, repeated practice, systematic opportunities for reflection, and real-time feedback from a supervisor or coach.

A common form of DP in graduate psychotherapy training contexts consists of a real-time session with a peer or clinical supervisor role-playing a simulated scenario and/or providing feedback following a rehearsal or therapy recording. Empirical evidence supports the effectiveness of DP in enhancing these skills. For example, learners who engaged in DP showed greater improvements in empathic expression compared to those who were trained using didactic methods alone []. Despite its potential benefits, the widespread implementation of DP in clinical psychology training programs is limited by the significant time and expertise required for 1-on-1, real-time supervision, and personalized feedback [].

Researchers have sought to enhance the accessibility and efficiency of psychotherapy training by developing technology-enabled platforms. Early efforts focused on structured tools for DP, such as video recording systems, which facilitate asynchronous supervision and reflective practice by enabling both students and instructors to review therapist-patient interactions outside of real-time sessions []. Similarly, video-response platforms such as Skillsetter (Theravue Inc) [] offer structured opportunities for practice by presenting short patient vignettes and requiring trainees to record therapeutic responses to those vignettes, which can later be reviewed for feedback by peers or supervisors. These innovations have expanded opportunities for repeated skill rehearsal, supplementing traditional classroom and supervisory contexts.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have further broadened this landscape, particularly through the development of AI-simulated patients that allow counselors to engage in practice dialogues within safe, controlled environments [,]. Parallel work has advanced AI feedback systems capable of automatically assessing microskills such as empathy, active listening, and motivational interviewing [-], while also generating alternative responses [,,] and explanatory rationales [,].

Within the emerging literature, AI-augmented psychotherapy training systems show both potential and methodological limitations. Recent experimental laboratory studies suggest that such simulations, when paired with feedback, may promote the acquisition of patient-centered counseling behaviors [,]. Avatar-based simulated patients can effectively support motivational interviewing practice, garnering high levels of usability and satisfaction among both student and professional counselors []. More recently, AI-simulated patients have been assigned within clinical education settings such as psychotherapy [,] and medical education []. However, even the most promising implementations fall short of assessing how trainees engage with AI over extended periods alongside traditional coursework, supervision, and peer practice. Consequently, questions remain about how trainees engage with AI tools when integrated into coursework as part of ongoing real-world classroom settings rather than deployed as standalone exercises.

Addressing the limitations of prior work, this study seeks to advance the understanding of how AI-augmented DP functions when directly embedded into psychotherapy training. As reviewed earlier, existing research on AI tools has primarily been restricted to controlled laboratory settings, short intervention windows, or isolated evaluations conducted outside of the classroom context. Such studies cannot fully address how AI interacts with real pedagogical structures, classroom dynamics, or established training methods such as peer role-play, supervised feedback, and video vignette exercises. Moreover, it remains unclear whether AI practice tools operate as meaningful complements to these traditional approaches, whether they inadvertently displace more valuable training modalities, or whether their integration reshapes learning in unanticipated ways.

To address these gaps, the present investigation examined students’ experiences with CARE, a voice-based, AI-augmented DP platform on which users speak in real time with AI-simulated patients, mirroring the pacing and unpredictability of an actual patient encounter rather than clicking through scripted prompts, when deployed across 2 academic quarters within a doctoral-level psychotherapy curriculum. CARE was integrated alongside existing training methods, including peer role-plays and the Skillsetter video-response platform, to enable structured comparison of AI-based approaches with established educational tools. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the feasibility and perceived value of implementing CARE in this classroom context. Secondarily, we explored implementation barriers, ethical and pedagogical considerations, and factors influencing students’ acceptance of and engagement with AI-assisted learning. Guided by these objectives, the study addressed 4 research questions (RQs):

RQ1: Comparative value—From the perspective of students, how do 2 bundled DP packages, an AI-augmented package (CARE: voice-based, multiturn practice with AI feedback) and an established video-based package (Skillsetter: single-turn vignette practice with instructor feedback), compare in perceived instructional value, and what distinct affordances do students attribute to each package as delivered?

RQ2: Usability and technical limitations—What factors about the AI-augmented package prototype (CARE) might enhance the pedagogical effectiveness of CARE within psychotherapy training?

RQ3: Course integration influence on acceptability—How are utility and acceptability influenced by how the AI-augmented package (CARE) is embedded into the psychotherapy classroom, including issues of onboarding, communication, and strategies to preserve instructor-student and peer-to-peer interaction within the deployment?

RQ4: Student beliefs about acceptance—(1) How do students perceive the legitimacy and acceptability of the AI-augmented package (CARE) in psychotherapy education, and (2) how has their exposure to AI in general influenced their views on its potential role in clinical training and practice?

Through its design, to our knowledge, the study provides one of the first longitudinal, classroom-based evaluations of an AI-augmented DP tool in psychotherapy education. By situating AI within authentic curricular structures rather than laboratory simulations, this work offers an ecologically valid assessment of both the pedagogical potential and the limitations of AI integration, thereby informing future directions for technology-mediated training in the mental health professions.

The protocol for this psychotherapy classroom deployment study was reviewed by Stanford University Institutional Review Board and was assessed as nonmedical exempt (protocol ID 72546). This research was conducted as part of normal educational practice in an introductory psychotherapy course in a clinical psychology PsyD program at the Palo Alto University–Stanford PsyD Consortium. AI-augmented practice components were added to standard weekly assignments. The study included mid-class and end-class surveys to assess students’ perceptions of AI feedback compared to peer feedback. Students received an information sheet explaining that while participation in course activities was expected as part of normal educational practice, they could opt out of having their data included in research analysis by emailing the protocol director. The instructor had no knowledge of which students opted out, ensuring no coercion or impact on grades. No compensation was provided as the AI-augmented assignments and surveys were integrated into normal course requirements.

To protect privacy and confidentiality, all data transmission was encrypted via HTTPS and stored on password-protected Amazon Web Services (AWS) servers accessible only to investigators listed on the protocol. Survey responses were linked to deidentified participant IDs through Qualtrics (Qualtrics International Inc). The research team committed that practice transcripts would not be publicly released or used to train autonomous AI therapy chatbots; we further describe in Data Privacy Protection in CARE’s System Architecture section how we honor that commitment within our data and AI processing pipelines. Audio recordings and transcripts would be stored for up to 3 years to allow for the completion of all scientific analyses by the authors before deletion. Only deidentified survey data, aggregated usage statistics, and feedback ratings could be presented at scientific meetings or published in journals. The AI feedback system underwent safety validations prior to deployment, including guard models to filter inappropriate content.

Participants were 29 first-year doctoral students enrolled in the abovementioned PsyD program. Of these participants, 4 students elected not to engage with CARE at any point during the study. The remaining 25 students participated in at least some component of the CARE activities and comprise the analytic sample reported here.

Students entered with heterogeneous training backgrounds: some held master’s degrees and had accumulated significant supervised clinical hours, whereas others entered with bachelor’s degrees supplemented by applied fieldwork or human services experience. This requirement for prior clinical experience differentiates PsyD training from many master’s mental health programs and some PhD programs, which often emphasize research over early clinical immersion.

Demographic data (eg, age, gender, and ethnicity) were not collected, which limits analysis of subgroup variation.

The study was embedded within a 2-quarter sequence forming part of the core first-year PsyD curriculum. This sequence is designed to provide foundational training in psychotherapy competencies, with a structured progression from introductory relational skills to more advanced therapeutic intervention. The study was conducted over 16 weeks, spanning 2 consecutive courses (September 2024 to March 2025).

The first course study emphasized pantheoretical elements of psychotherapy, including basic listening skills, therapeutic alliance formation, therapist verbal response models and intentions, and consideration of cultural and ethical factors. The second course quarter built upon these foundations by targeting pantheoretical competencies outlined by the American Psychological Association (APA) Division 29 Task Force on Psychotherapy Competence, such as alliance maintenance (task, goal, and bond), rupture repair, transference and countertransference, and termination processes.

In prior cohorts, the first course used weekly peer roleplays. Students alternated therapist and patient roles in 10-minute sessions, followed by mutual feedback and written self-reflections. Confidentiality agreements were required, and each student submitted recorded sessions that were periodically reviewed in small group meetings with instructors.

In the second course, prior cohorts engaged with Skillsetter’s video-based DP platform. Assignments required demonstration of specific therapeutic skills (eg, empathy, cultural humility, and alliance repair). Instructors or teaching assistants (TAs) provided feedback on a weekly basis, and the quarter culminated in a live roleplay with an instructor or TA portraying a patient, requiring integration of multiple therapeutic competencies. This established format of peer roleplay in the first course and Skillsetter video-based DP in the second course provided both relationally grounded and structured opportunities for iterative skill refinement.

Skillsetter is a web-based, video-based DP training platform designed to support practice in interpersonal and counseling skills []. It was developed to overcome logistical barriers commonly encountered in traditional psychotherapeutic training, such as the resource-intensive nature of instructor supervision and inconsistent feedback, by allowing learners to practice asynchronously, record responses to simulated prompts, and receive structured feedback. When using the platform, students submitted video-recorded responses to standardized patient vignettes performed by actors. Because feedback, rather than mere repetition, is central to DP, Skillsetter emphasizes scaffolded evaluation, either via instructor raters or automated scoring across domains.

The platform has achieved broad adoption across counseling, social work, and psychotherapy training programs, lending evidence of its acceptability and institutional integration. In the Learning Psychotherapy course series, feedback on Skillsetter practice was given by the course instructor and TAs. In applying it to this study, Skillsetter served as an established, scalable platform for implementing component-level practice (eg, empathy, reflections, and open questions) in a remote environment. This enabled learners to engage in deliberate rehearsal outside class hours while receiving targeted feedback.

Building on this structure, this study introduced CARE, an AI-powered simulation and feedback platform, to examine its potential role alongside traditional DP (). Our design maintained the integrity of the existing pedagogy while creating opportunities for systematic comparison.

In the first course pilot study in 2024, the instructional team prioritized interpersonal skill building and peer connection, continuing to rely on peer role-play as the primary experiential method. CARE was introduced as an optional feedback tool, allowing students to upload recorded peer sessions and receive automated feedback () on the use of 8 counseling skills (eg, empathy, validation, reflections, questions, suggestions, self-disclosure, session structure, and professionalism) derived from the helping skills and motivational interviewing models [,]. This integration provided an opportunity to explore the additive value of AI-generated feedback while preserving the emphasis on human relational practice in the early stages of training.

In the second course (CLIN 702), CARE was deployed more comprehensively in parallel with Skillsetter to enable structured comparison of 2 distinct DP modalities (). Students alternated between Skillsetter’s single-turn vignette responses and CARE’s multiturn, dynamic dialogues with AI-simulated patients. Both platforms were aligned with weekly curricular objectives, matched for duration and credit, and graded using consistent rubrics. This dual-modality design created an ecologically valid setting for evaluating the relative affordances and limitations of AI-augmented practice versus established methods.

Course 1 involved a different comparison (AI-augmented feedback and peer feedback on peer role-plays) and is described separately.

LLM: large language model.

TA: teaching assistant.

CARE’s scenario library included clinically challenging content, including alliance ruptures, mandated reporting, suicidal ideation and self-injury, and sexually inappropriate behavior toward clinicians. These topics were not introduced by the study. They are established components of the course curriculum, which addresses suicide risk and mandated reporting in week 7 and sexual attraction and boundary maintenance in week 8, and they reflect competencies specified by the APA Division 29 Task Force on Psychotherapy Competence []. Exposure to such material under supervision is a required element of doctoral clinical training, and these topics had been routinely taught in this course sequence with prior cohorts. CARE scenarios were mapped onto the existing weekly syllabus rather than developed independently, so students encountered simulated versions of material they were concurrently studying in class and practicing in Skillsetter.

Before deployment, each AI-simulated patient was reviewed by the TA and co-first author (EC), who had previously completed this course and held clinical training. Scenarios were additionally reviewed by the course instructor (JK), a licensed clinical psychologist and co-associate director of clinical training for the program, who confirmed their clinical appropriateness and alignment with the week’s learning objectives before they were released to students. Review criteria were clinical appropriateness, ethical soundness, and alignment with the week’s learning objectives. For scenarios involving trauma, self-harm, or suicidal ideation, review specifically assessed whether the AI-simulated patients supported rather than undermined the learning objective in the curriculum. Behavioral principles constraining each simulated patient were revised iteratively during this process. Nine of the 12 scenarios were adapted from existing Skillsetter transcripts already in curricular use; the remaining 3 were adapted from documented cases in the published literature [].

Faculty oversight operated through the courses’ existing structures rather than through study-specific monitoring. Students had established channels for raising concerns: in-class discussion, direct contact with the instructor or TA, and the program’s existing student support structures. As the instructor and TA reviewed Skillsetter submissions on the same weekly topics, distress surfacing in either modality could be identified and addressed through the same channels.

We did not review CARE session transcripts in real time, and no automated system flagged student distress during practice. Safeguards were therefore preventive rather than responsive: scenario prompts were constrained in advance, and guard models filtered inappropriate simulated-patient output before students encountered it. No students reported clinically inappropriate or harmful content from the simulated patients. However, because we did not systematically review sessions, we cannot confirm that none occurred. We address this further in the “Limitations” section.

CARE was developed as a web-based training platform designed to support novice counselors in practicing counseling skills within simulated environments powered by LLMs. The platform enables trainees to practice psychotherapy skills through roleplay conversations either with their peers or with AI patients and to receive automated feedback on their therapeutic responses, generated by an AI “mentor.” CARE builds on prior work in co-design with mental health experts to enhance the realism of AI-simulated patients [,,,] and on research advancing the fine-tuning of domain-specific LLMs to incorporate therapeutic knowledge capable of producing both evaluative feedback and alternative counselor responses [,,-].

From a technical standpoint, CARE was implemented as a web application with a Python Flask (Pallets) back end and a React (Meta) JavaScript front end, accessible to students through password-protected student accounts. In the first course, the CARE platform allowed students to upload an audio recording of a peer role-play conversation, which was automatically converted into a diarized transcript. The transcription process used the WhisperX system (open source) and the OpenAI API to help with LLM-assisted diarization between therapist and patient utterances. In the second course, students practiced a role-play conversation with AI-simulated patients. AI-simulated patients were powered by the GPT-4o Realtime API, with scenario-specific prompts defining patient background, conversational style, and behavioral principles []. The OpenAI Whisper model was also used to transcribe the audio dialogue into text-based utterances. This infrastructure enabled integration into classroom deployment studies, allowing systematic investigation of CARE as a pedagogical supplement to established DP methods.

Within the version of CARE deployed to the second course, practice was organized around a library of patient scenarios, each defined by a brief background vignette (eg, “Young adult with family issues: low mood and self-esteem”). These intentionally limited descriptions are designed to approximate authentic counseling encounters, in which the clinician must simultaneously build rapport, elicit patient context, and apply therapeutic skills (). For example, a novice peer counselor might initiate a practice session with an AI-simulated patient modeled as a 35-year-old veteran struggling to reconnect with his children amid legal and interpersonal challenges. The dialogue proceeds turn by turn, requiring the trainee to apply core counseling skills such as empathy, reflection, and problem exploration, while managing relational complexity as the conversation unfolds.

The platform provided students with AI-generated feedback on each of their utterances at the end of the session. CARE’s feedback implements an existing method for generating feedback that fine-tunes a Llama 2 13B (Meta) parameter model on an expert-annotated dataset covering psychotherapy-relevant skill assessment []. Feedback focuses on strengths, areas for improvement, feedback explanation, and a suggested alternative response that addresses any issues.

CARE’s system architecture was designed to protect the privacy of student audio recordings and voice data and ensure they were not used for training AI models. In places where OpenAI APIs were used, the data policy was set to opt out of using any input or output data for AI model training; the OpenAI data retention policy further states that only abuse monitoring logs are retained for a maximum of 30 days.

For the pipeline that transcribed student peer role-play audio (course 1), uploaded audio files were saved onto the private AWS EC2 instance; audio was transported to an ephemeral, serverless graphics processing unit (GPU) service that started the WhisperX transcription and diarization function; the transcript was given to a GPT-4o-assisted diarization pipeline to identify therapist and patient roles; finally, the therapist/patient messages were saved to a SQLite database on the AWS EC2 instance. In this way, long-term data are only retained on our private AWS EC2 instance and are governed by our maximum 3-year retention policy to support scientific analysis.

The pipeline to practice with voice-based AI-simulated patients (course 2) is fully handled by the gpt-realtime API with authentication to OpenAI handled through ephemeral client API keys issued by the server. The gpt-realtime API end point responds to audio events and uses the OpenAI Whisper API to transcribe the audio transcript. Our OpenAI data privacy policy restricts long-term data retention and training on data sent to the API.

The feedback generation pipeline relies on an ephemeral, serverless GPU service that loads the fine-tuned Llama 2 13B model weights and processes the utterances in the transcript. The generated feedback is saved into the SQLite database. Thus, transcript and feedback data are only retained on the private AWS EC2 instance and are governed by our maximum 3-year data retention policy to allow for scientific analyses.

The Learning Psychotherapy sequence spanned 2 quarters, 16 weeks total, and was structured to provide developmentally sequenced training in core psychotherapy competencies. The first course implementation spanned 6 weeks, whereas the second course implementation extended across 10 weeks. The study team began the first course in week 4 of the first course instead of week 1 to allow more time for finalizing implementation procedures.

The first course 2024 pilot, described in more detail in the following section, served as an initial, formative phase of the study, designed to explore the educational utility of AI-generated feedback with traditional peer feedback following role-play exercises. This phase was crucial in identifying themes that shaped the subsequent second course study, including the relative value of different feedback modalities (RQ1), early design limitations (RQ2), challenges of classroom integration (RQ3), and students’ broader attitudes about the role of AI in psychotherapy training and daily life (RQ4).

The first course provides a foundation for training beginning psychotherapists in the crucial elements of psychotherapy. Across weeks 1 to 7, instruction progressed via the gradual introduction of the core listening skills and verbal response modes, with particular attention in week 4 to how sexual, gender, and racial diversity can impact the therapeutic alliance. Weeks 8 to 9 introduced principles and strategies from motivational interviewing, with the course concluding in week 10 with a focus on ethics, professional boundaries, and therapist self-care.

Students engaged in 10-minute peer role-plays each week, alternating between therapist and patient roles, with assigned therapeutic skills tailored to that week’s topic. Recordings of these peer role-plays were uploaded to CARE, which generated automated feedback across 8 core counseling skill domains derived from the helping skills and motivational interviewing models. This process enabled the instructional team to evaluate student perceptions of AI-generated feedback as a supplement to traditional experiential exercises, while maintaining the central role of in-person peer practice in early clinical training.

The second course introduced students to the principles of DP, values-based care, and basic therapeutic skills. Instruction progressed from the concept of DP (week 1) to the therapeutic alliance, drawing on Bordin’s task-goal-bond framework (week 2) [], before moving to therapist self-disclosure, cultural humility, and the influence of power and identity within therapeutic relationships (weeks 3 and 4). The middle phase emphasized countertransference, resistance (week 5), alliance ruptures and repair (week 6), and clinical challenges such as mandated reporting and suicide risk (week 7). The sequence concluded with advanced relational concerns, including sexual attraction and boundary maintenance (week 8).

The course was designed to directly compare 2 distinct DP modalities: Skillsetter and CARE. This parallel design created a side-by-side comparison of vignette-based practice and conversational AI simulations, with both modalities aligned to weekly curricular goals and equivalent in duration, evaluation criteria, and grading weight.

To integrate CARE into the curriculum, the study team systematically mapped AI-simulated patients onto weekly course topics at week 4, enabling students to engage with simulated clinical encounters that corresponded directly with concepts under instruction. Students practiced with 12 AI-simulated patients across the quarter, 9 (75%) of which were adapted from Skillsetter transcripts and 3 (25%) adapted from documented examples of sexually inappropriate behaviors toward clinicians reported in prior empirical work [] (). CARE’s scenarios encompassed alliance ruptures, mandated reporting, and crisis management related to suicidal ideation and self-injury, thereby anchoring AI practice in clinically relevant challenges.

Prior to classroom deployment, CARE’s AI-simulated patients underwent an iterative review process conducted by the TA to ensure clinical appropriateness, ethical safeguards, and pedagogical alignment. Each AI-simulated patient was programmed to follow structured behavioral principles, with particular emphasis placed on scenarios involving emotionally sensitive content areas (eg, trauma and self-harm) to verify that AI-generated responses were trauma informed, ethically sound, and supportive of therapeutic learning objectives. Additional realism was introduced through varied voice models designed to convey emotional depth and natural conversational flow. Some identified limitations, including emotional flatness in voice-based responses, were addressed by adding principles to the voice-based AI-simulated patient’s prompt (eg, “Mention past attempts to please family that failed, with resigned sighs, and even breaths where the nose is runny as in crying”).

Students completed a midcourse survey in the first course, halfway through the introduction of CARE, and again at the end of the course. The 37-item questionnaire was specifically designed by the investigators for this study to gather insights into the challenges and obstacles students faced while using CARE, as well as their experiences with peer feedback and AI feedback on their peer roleplays. The full set of 37 items for the first course study is provided in  and .

To evaluate the comparative value of CARE and Skillsetter, students completed a 39-item investigator-designed survey at the end of week 16 in the second course. Items were adapted from national and professional surveys where possible [,]. Students rated their experiences across domains using 7-point Likert scales (1=strongly disagree to 7=strongly agree) and provided open-ended responses. Example items by domain are shown in . The full set of 39 items for the second course is provided in .

“The way I could use [CARE/Skillsetter] allowed me to make mistakes I could learn from.”

“After conversing with the patients in [CARE/Skillsetter], I feel more equipped to build and maintain a therapeutic alliance.”

“Receiving AI feedback shortly after completing CARE practice enhanced my learning experience.”

“I know when to ignore AI feedback when it is incorrect or does not make sense.”

“I found the self-reflections after a [CARE/Skillsetter] session valuable for understanding how to improve.”

“My concerns about CARE AI’s patients include: voices sound robotic; transcripts are inaccurate.”

“My concerns about CARE AI’s feedback include: wish it tracked progress over time.”

“Would you recommend CARE AI to next year’s PsyD cohort as a deliberate practice option?”

“Overall, would you say the increased use of AI in daily life makes you feel… (concerned vs. excited)?”

“Do you think AI in the classroom would lead to better or worse helping skills for therapists?”

RQ: research question.

Both surveys were investigator designed for this deployment, as no validated instrument exists for assessing student experiences with AI-augmented DP in psychotherapy training. Items were developed by the research team, which combined expertise in psychotherapy training and in AI systems for clinical education; the instructor and coinvestigators drew on prior experience teaching this course sequence to anticipate likely obstacles, including discomfort with recorded practice, concerns about data use, and skepticism about automated feedback on relational skills. Closed-ended response options for items on limitations and concerns were generated from these anticipated obstacles and from issues students raised during the first course. Items on general AI attitudes were adapted where possible from national and professional surveys [,]. The first-course survey served as a formative pilot, and its results informed revision of the second-course instrument.

No formal psychometric evaluation was conducted. Items were not subjected to cognitive interviewing, factor analysis, or reliability testing, and we report each item individually rather than computing scale scores. Quantitative findings should therefore be read as structured summaries of student reports rather than as validated measurements.

We conducted nonparametric paired hypothesis tests (2-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank) to evaluate students’ comparative perceptions of CARE versus the 2 traditional DP modalities: peer role-play feedback and Skillsetter (RQ1). Our investigation concerns different dimensions of student perceptions (eg, comfort in receiving feedback from AI vs peers and immersiveness of voice-based AI and video-based vignette practice) that we consider equally and independently rather than as surrogate indicators of an omnibus finding; therefore, each dimension defines an individual statistical hypothesis tested at an ⍺ of .05 level without correction [,]. There were no missing data to account for in these paired survey responses. Statistical testing was conducted using the SPSS package (version 29; IBM Corp). Descriptive statistics are reported for the remaining quantitative items, covering perceived limitations and design needs of CARE (RQ2), perceptions of course integration (RQ3), and attitudes toward AI (RQ4).

Open-ended survey responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke [,]. Coding was hybrid: codes were generated inductively from the response data, while the 4 research questions, which structured the survey instrument and therefore the domains in which students responded, oriented the analysis. Two authors (EC and RL) independently read the full response set for familiarization and independently coded all responses. They then met over 3 rounds to compare codes, discuss divergent readings, and develop shared interpretations of the data. Rather than resolving differences by adjudication or by calculating interrater reliability, we treated points of divergence as analytically generative, working through them in discussion until we arrived at interpretations both coders found defensible. This is consistent with the assumptions of reflexive thematic analysis, which positions researcher subjectivity as a resource rather than a source of bias to be controlled []. Candidate themes were then developed from the coded material, reviewed against the coded extracts and the full dataset, refined, and named.

Throughout the deployment, the TA and the co-first author kept informal written notes documenting classroom interactions, student questions raised during class, and technical problems reported in real time. Notes were written within 24 hours of each class session and were not systematically coded or analyzed as a data source. They served 2 limited purposes: to document implementation events that would otherwise go unrecorded (eg, the midquarter decision in course 2 to add supplemental TA feedback in response to student concerns) and to help the analytic team interpret survey responses that referenced specific classroom occurrences. We do not draw findings from the memos and do not treat them as qualitative data; where they inform the narrative, this is stated explicitly in the text.

We used a convergent design in which both strands were collected concurrently within the same surveys and analyzed separately, then integrated at the interpretation stage []. Integration proceeded by research question: for each RQ, we compared the direction and strength of the quantitative findings against the corresponding themes, noting points of convergence, divergence, and expansion. Convergence and divergence are reported explicitly in the “Results” section and revisited in the “Discussion” section.

Our team’s composition shaped both the deployment and its interpretation. The team includes computer scientists who developed CARE and its underlying models and clinicians who teach in the training program where the study took place. As developers, we had an investment in CARE functioning well. As instructors and program faculty, we held evaluative authority over the students whose experiences we report. Both students’ willingness to voice criticism and our readiness to hear it were conditioned by these relationships.

Several steps mitigated these risks. Research participation was decoupled from course participation; CARE was made optional in the first course as a supplement to peer feedback on students’ peer role-plays. In the second course, CARE was initially required; however, in the second week of the course, the instructional team made participation with CARE optional due to student concerns, and students could opt to complete weekly DP assignments using the Skillsetter video-based package only.

In coding and interpretation, the 2 coders included 1 coauthor without a role in developing CARE and 1 without. This positioning also bounds what the paper claims. We report students’ perceptions rather than an efficacy evaluation of CARE, and we treat students’ reluctance and ethical objections as findings in their own right rather than as barriers to be overcome.

This section outlines the findings from the 16-week deployment, structured to provide a clear progression of insights. We begin with the first course 2024 pilot study, which served as a preliminary investigation into students’ perceived value of AI feedback as a supplement to peer feedback. We then move to the more extensive second course study, which builds upon the first course to explore AI-simulated patients in greater depth. This ordering reflects the evolving nature of the research and the increasing complexity of the questions addressed.

The first course was a formative phase of the study in which we sought to understand students’ experiences of AI-generated feedback and traditional peer feedback following peer role-play exercises. Of the 29 enrolled students, 23 uploaded at least one peer role-play transcript to CARE and 22 received AI feedback on at least one transcript (). All findings reported below reflect survey respondents only. The survey was voluntary in this course, and 14 (48%) students completed it. The following results are based on 14 survey respondents, 5 of whom did not use CARE by choice or due to technical issues, leaving 9 students who reported on the experience of AI versus traditional peer feedback.

Course 1 completion rate assumes 6 chances to upload weekly peer role-plays to CARE×29 participating students; the rate is deflated because CARE use was optional and combines high-usage and no-usage students. Course 2 completion rate assumes 319 required assignments (11 required assignments×29 participating students); the rate is inflated because some students completed multiple sessions per week.

Quantitative comparisons from the first course pilot () show that students rated peer feedback significantly higher than AI feedback along 2 of the 3 dimensions. Specifically, peer partners’ feedback was rated as being more constructive and helpful to a great extent versus a moderate extent (median 3, IQR 3-3 vs median 2, IQR 2-2 on a 0‐4 scale; P=.02). Students’ peer partner feedback allowed them to better recognize areas to improve versus CARE with Likert ratings differing between moderately agree and slightly agree (median 5, IQR 5-6 vs median 4, IQR 4-5; P=.046). No statistically significant difference was found with regard to their comfort receiving feedback; the median student felt comfortable receiving feedback from peers and CARE’s AI system (median 6, IQR 6-6 vs median 6, IQR 5-6 on a 1‐6 scale). Nonetheless, peer partner feedback had higher mean and lower variance than CARE in terms of comfort (mean 5.88, SD 0.33 vs mean 5.44, SD 0.73), which indicates that a subset of students felt less comfortable with AI feedback.

P values are from Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing CARE and peer partner responses.

Rated on a 0-4 scale (0=not at all, 1=to a small extent, 2=to a moderate extent, 3=to a great extent, and 4=to a very great extent).

Rated on a 1-6 forced Likert scale (1=disagree strongly, 2=disagree moderately, 3=disagree slightly, 4=agree slightly, 5=agree moderately, and 6=agree strongly).

Qualitatively, students valued peer feedback for its ability to capture nonverbal cues and provide a patient-centered perspective. One student noted, “I think peer feedback considers the whole session, including tone, nonverbals, use of silence, etc, so it feels more relevant as a whole.”

Students identified both technical and substantive limitations in CARE’s design. Transcription errors, often linked to audio quality, sometimes undermined the utility of feedback: “There are occasional issues with the transcript... CARE is unable to identify or differentiate between patient and patient at times, resulting in occasionally inaccurate feedback.” Beyond technical issues, participants described the scope of feedback as narrow, with repeated emphasis on empathy and validation while overlooking other therapeutic strategies. As one noted, “Most of the feedback was suggesting that I empathize with and validate the patient, but there are many other techniques... which the AI doesn’t seem to recognize.” Others emphasized that responses were evaluated in isolation: “It feels like each response is being considered separate and apart from the rest, so it feels less relevant to the content overall.”

Despite these concerns, students highlighted the value of alternative phrasing and immediate suggestions. One remarked, “I like the alternative responses... it gives me ideas for how to better and more concisely word my responses.” Another added, “I appreciate how content-oriented AI is! I find the alternative responses extremely helpful as I can use certain phrases in future sessions.” While some described the system as “robotic” or “less personal,” others appreciated its consistency, contrasting it with the subjectivity of human feedback: “Human feedback might only apply for that individual client... I think AI gives broader and more objective feedback that applies to the situation instead of the person.”

The integration of CARE into the curriculum was shaped by instructional stance and student perceptions of the research team. In the first course, CARE was introduced under exploratory conditions, which encouraged discussion. Use of CARE’s role-play transcript feedback was optional, and its role was described as exploratory. Of the 29 students enrolled in the first course, 14 (48%) completed surveys about the integration of CARE into the course, and 9 (31%) provided comparative ratings about peer roleplay versus CARE.

When asked what prevented them from using CARE during the course, students most frequently cited concerns about privacy and data security, a preference for receiving feedback from a human rather than AI, uncertainty or lack of guidance on how to use the tool, and apprehension about the nature of the research being conducted by the research team (eg, “making a chatbot therapist”).

A key concern raised by students in the first course was the security and intended use of their video transcripts when uploaded to the CARE platform. To address these concerns, the study team provided detailed explanations during class and in the frequently asked questions (FAQs) document (). Students were informed that all video transcripts would be stored on a secure, password-protected cloud server. In rare cases where transcription errors occurred, a member of the research team would access the server to identify and troubleshoot the affected audio file. Aside from this limited quality control function, students were assured their audio files would not be used for any other purpose and would be deleted upon the completion of research analyses. Similarly, text transcripts were to be stored on a secure, password-protected server within CARE’s internal database. These transcripts were accessible only to the student and their selected peer partner. If students opted to use the “Review Feedback” tool, their transcripts were processed by CARE’s AI feedback model. Importantly, CARE’s model is entirely self-hosted and does not rely on commercial AI services (eg, ChatGPT), ensuring that student data are not used to train external proprietary models.

In addition to these measures, students were provided with a formal study information sheet outlining all data protections and ethical commitments associated with the project.

Building on the first course, the second course study shifted focus to the use of CARE’s voice-based AI-simulated patients for DP, comparing this to Skillsetter’s video-based practice. CARE enabled dynamic, back-and-forth dialogue with AI-simulated patients, whereas Skillsetter required a single, one-time response to a video prompt.

Students had already been introduced to the CARE platform in the prior term. The difference for the second course was that students could use CARE for DP, speaking with AI-simulated patients. Students could also receive AI feedback on the basic counseling skills used in their interactions with the AI-simulated patients. However, the focus was on the utility of the DP itself rather than the feedback.

As presented in , the only significant difference between modalities was learning from mistakes, which students rated higher for Skillsetter than CARE (mean 4.52, SD 2.00 vs mean 3.20, SD 2.04; P=.03; d=0.49). Descriptively, the remaining comparisons diverged in direction rather than favoring one modality overall: Skillsetter was rated slightly higher for immersion (mean 4.16, SD 1.97 vs mean 3.88, SD 2.05) and confidence responding spontaneously (mean 4.52, SD 2.10 vs mean 4.32, SD 1.82), whereas CARE was rated slightly higher for communication beyond words (mean 4.20, SD 1.96 vs mean 3.80, SD 2.02) and building a therapeutic alliance (mean 4.52, SD 1.85 vs mean 3.80, SD 2.26). These differences were small relative to the variability in responses (SDs ≈ 1.8‐2.3), and none approached significance. Qualitatively, students reported that CARE’s AI-simulated patients provided a “good opportunity to practice using the skills learned in class” and allowed for interactive dialogue, which is not possible with Skillsetter. One student noted they used the AI-simulated patients because “you don’t get to explore the back and forth with Skillsetter.”

P values come from Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing CARE and Skillsetter modalities.

Rated on a 1-7 scale (1=strongly disagree, 2=disagree, 3=somewhat disagree, 4=neither agree nor disagree, 5=somewhat agree, 6=agree, and 7=strongly agree).

While the second course did not include a peer role-play component, some students reflected on peer roleplay in the open-ended survey responses in course 2. CARE was also valued for simulating difficult scenarios that would be hard to practice with peers, such as dealing with an “angry client, silent client.” Despite these benefits, a strong preference for practicing with humans remained. Students felt that AI practice could not replicate the nuances of human interaction, with one stating, “Nothing replaces role plays.” There were also concerns that skills developed with the AI might not transfer to real therapy, with one student stating they had “learned how to orient towards receiving positive feedback from CARE rather than toward providing thoughtful and nuanced support for a human person.”

The most prevalent technical concern (20/25, 80% of respondents) was that the system does not detect vocal pauses, indicating a significant gap in the speech recognition capabilities. More than half of respondents (14/25, 56%) felt that the AI-simulated patients did not feel realistic, with a similar number (13/25, 52%) noting limited emotional expression in the voices. Transcript inaccuracy (10/25, 40%), robotic-sounding voices (9/25, 36%), lack of visual avatar representation (7/25, 28%), and voice recognition issues (6/25, 24%) were additional functionality concerns raised by participants.

Students expressed consistent concerns about the quality and personalization of AI feedback. The 3 top concerns received the same high level of response (17/25, 68%): students wished the AI-simulated patient could provide feedback from its perspective on how the student, as a therapist, made them feel. Students desired a system that tracked and referenced their progression over time. Many reported that the AI was providing unhelpful feedback. Nearly two-thirds (16/25, 64%) of respondents wished the feedback addressed the session as a whole. There was a desire for greater variety in evaluation criteria (15/25, 60%) and feedback that incorporates vocal elements rather than just written transcripts (13/25, 52%).

In response to students’ concerns about the limited utility of CARE’s feedback, the teaching team implemented a supplemental feedback process in which the TA provided individualized written feedback on students’ CARE transcripts. Each week, 3 to 5 students were randomly selected to receive this feedback, which was designed to enhance learning by integrating human insight with AI-generated suggestions. The TA provided weekly written feedback to each student who elected to use CARE, then emailed students individually to ask permission to post their feedback, identified by name, on the course Canvas (Instructure) page. Consenting students’ feedback was posted to a discussion thread so that all students could view it, contribute to the discussion, and potentially benefit from it. The decision to supplement CARE in this way was informed by feedback indicating that the AI’s responses alone were often perceived as insufficient for skill development. This feedback was obtained and documented in classroom memos by the TA.

One student reflected on the benefits of this hybrid model:

Additionally, I think everything involved with AI would have a better outcome when there is that human aspect. [TA] ended up providing additional feedback for us weekly for CARE. This combined the AI aspect with the human aspect, so it wasn’t only AI that we were interacting with. I feel like this maximized our learning. It would also have been interesting if we actually looked at some of the AI feedback and analyzed those using a forum, in addition to human feedback.
