I think doing so would again emphasize the aspect of human and AI [or AI-assisted human feedback], instead of just AI doing all the work. AI’s benefits wouldn’t come alive if there weren’t human input to modulate it.

This perspective underscores students’ desire for feedback that reflects both the analytical consistency of AI and the nuance of human clinical judgment.

The strongest concerns about CARE’s integration into the classroom centered around how AI might replace human elements of education (), with 22 (88%) of 25 respondents worried about AI replacing peer support and feedback, and 20 (80%) of 25 respondents concerned about AI replacing peer interaction. Many students (19/25, 76%) questioned whether they were simply user-testing a product rather than engaging in an educational experience. Students raised concerns about potential environmental impact (16/25, 64%), suggesting awareness of the computational resources required for AI systems, including potential environmental impacts.

Values indicate fields where more than half of the 25 respondents indicated concerns, with students able to select multiple concerns.

Data usage concerns were prominent, with 14 (56%) of 25 respondents worried about how their data are being used by the research team, and 12 (48%) of 25 respondents concerned about their data potentially being used to train AI therapists.

In addition to items about CARE, the second-course survey asked about AI in psychotherapy education and clinical practice generally. The responses below address this broader domain and should not be read as evaluations of CARE. Students articulated a range of perspectives, coalescing around three thematic domains: (1) openness to AI integration in training and administrative contexts, (2) boundary concerns regarding the application of AI in clinical care, and (3) broader ethical apprehensions related to AI’s societal impact.

Several students expressed cautious optimism about the integration of AI into psychotherapy, particularly in training contexts and administrative functions. For these individuals, AI was not viewed as a threat to the therapeutic profession, but rather as a supplemental tool that could enhance learning and reduce burdens associated with nonclinical tasks. As one student noted, “I do not personally hold the fear of AI replacing therapists, so the training and administrative help resonates with me.” Another student highlighted the relevance of technological adaptability in a rapidly evolving professional landscape:

As trainees in therapy, I truly see the importance of adapting to these changes and evolving with our society at large. Eventually, there will be other therapists who utilize AI, and we will be competing with those who know how to utilize it.

Administrative utility was a recurring subtheme, with several students noting the promise of AI in alleviating logistical tasks such as billing, insurance coordination, and website maintenance. One student proposed that “a better focus for AI in psychotherapy would be having an AI handle the billing, insurance, outreach, and website management that is non-billable time for therapists, rather than training.” Others concurred, suggesting that AI could support clinical infrastructure without compromising the therapeutic relationship.

Despite general receptivity to AI in administrative and educational settings, many students expressed strong reservations about potential clinical applications affecting direct patient care. A recurrent concern was that incorporating AI into training contexts might normalize its use in psychotherapy delivery, thereby facilitating a negative chain of future events. One student remarked, “Honestly, [I am] a bit more concerned, as I think while the benefits are there, it is a slippery slope.” Another reflected, “I still feel uncertain about... the possibility of AI eclipsing in-person therapy in the future.”

This apprehension was often anchored in the perceived irreplaceability of human relational dynamics. As one student articulated, “Nothing can replace in-person practice and human interaction. Beyond certain admin tasks, I do not think AI should be used in clinical practice.” Another student emphasized the importance of ethical containment: “It’s still important to be cautious with it, and it should never replace an actual human in any context other than training.” These sentiments underscore a shared appreciation for the therapeutic alliance and a desire to establish clear boundaries for emerging technologies.

A third thematic domain reflected broader ethical considerations about AI’s proliferation across societal and global systems. For some students, skepticism about AI in psychotherapy was rooted not solely in clinical concerns but also in a larger critique of AI’s sociopolitical implications. One student remarked, “It has increased my concerns about the increase of AI use throughout the world.” Another described their initial discomfort with the study’s AI component, stating, “As someone who has bigger-picture ethical concerns about AI, in relation to environment, jobs, and broader social/societal impact, I was initially pretty upset about having CARE be a required part of this course.”

Concerns about commercialization, technological determinism, and the disconnect between developers and end users were also prominent. One student stated, “The lack of awareness about therapy for those who are developing models frankly terrifies me,” while another wrote, “I feel very hesitant about the use of AI in any space in psychotherapy. To me, it feels like too slippery of a slope, and from history, it seems like things like this inevitably end up in the wrong hands, even if that is not the starting intention.” Reflecting these reservations, some students reported electing not to use the AI platform for training, citing “broader ethical concerns around AI and its rapid expansion.”

Together, these themes reflect a complex and multidimensional stance among emerging psychotherapists. While students acknowledged the potential utility of AI in specific educational and administrative contexts, they also articulated clear boundaries for its use in clinical care and raised critical ethical questions about its integration into psychotherapy and society more broadly.

This study examined how doctoral psychotherapy students experienced AI-augmented DP embedded across 2 required courses in a first-year psychotherapy sequence at an APA-accredited clinical psychology program. The 2 courses involved different configurations. The first course served as a formative pilot in which students completed weekly peer role-plays, and CARE was introduced only as an optional source of AI-generated feedback on the resulting role-play transcripts, supplementing the feedback students already received from their peer partners. The second course introduced AI-simulated patients as a practice modality and placed 2 bundled packages side by side, matched for weekly curricular objectives: CARE, comprising multiturn spoken dialogue with voice-based LLM-driven AI-simulated patients followed by automated feedback, and Skillsetter, comprising single-turn recorded responses to standardized video vignettes performed by actors, with instructor and TA feedback.

Three findings stand out across the sequence. First, uptake appeared to be governed less by platform performance than by students’ prior dispositions toward AI. In the first course pilot, 23 (79%) of 29 students uploaded at least one peer role-play transcript, but privacy concerns and a preference for human feedback were the reasons most frequently cited by those who did not, and comparable apprehension led the instructional team to adjust the second course’s initial requirement after the first week, so that students could elect to complete additional Skillsetter practice sessions instead of CARE. Second, students’ comparative ratings of the 2 second-course packages converged on most dimensions, with only learning from mistakes differing significantly in Skillsetter’s favor, while their open-ended responses expressed a clear and consistent preference for practicing with humans. Third, the concerns students raised were largely not instructional; the most frequently endorsed were that AI would displace peer support and peer interaction. Taken together, these findings suggest that the principal obstacles to embedding AI-augmented practice in this curriculum were relational and ethical rather than technical, although technical limitations were substantial and may have compounded them.

Students rated peer feedback significantly above CARE’s AI feedback on being constructive and helpful, and on recognizing areas to improve, attributing peers’ advantage to the capacity to integrate tone, nonverbal information, and a patient-centered stance. As CARE operated on transcripts, much of what students valued in peer feedback was information the system could not access, a constraint shared by LLM-based feedback systems relying on textual representations of therapy [,,]. The comparison may therefore have been less between human and machine judgment than between judgment informed by the full session and judgment informed by a degraded record of it.

Students’ explanations nonetheless resemble 2 documented patterns. Research on algorithm aversion finds that people lose confidence in algorithms more rapidly than in people after comparable errors [], which may help explain why transcription failures appeared to discredit CARE’s feedback more broadly than those specific errors would warrant. Longoni et al [] report that resistance to medical AI is associated with uniqueness neglect, the concern that automated systems cannot accommodate individual circumstances; our students described AI feedback as evaluating responses “separate and apart from the rest,” while peer feedback “considers the whole session.” We draw on these literatures interpretively because our design tested neither mechanism. Notably, 1 student inverted the framing entirely, valuing AI for giving “broader and more objective feedback that applies to the situation instead of the person,” a divergence cautioning against treating preference for human feedback as uniform.

Students’ ratings of the 2 packages appeared to converge on most dimensions. Skillsetter was rated significantly higher only for learning from mistakes, while immersion, confidence responding spontaneously, communication beyond words, and building a therapeutic alliance did not differ significantly, the latter 2 showing numerically higher means for CARE. Given wide variability and limited power, these patterns are best read as descriptive.

Students also reported concerns about realism, with 56% (14/25) indicating that the AI-simulated patients did not feel realistic, and 52% noting limited vocal expression. Simulation scholarship suggests one possible reading, having generally found fidelity to be largely independent of educational effectiveness, and proposed that functional task alignment may explain outcomes better than physical resemblance [], with work in mental health simulation reporting psychological fidelity as more critical to learning than physical fidelity []. Students may perhaps have experienced the simulated patients as unconvincing depictions of people, while still finding the task aligned with what the course asked them to rehearse.

A notable feature of the open-ended responses was that students introduced a comparison the survey did not ask about. The second-course items concerned CARE and Skillsetter only, and peer role-play was not a component of that course, yet several students referenced it unprompted, with 1 respondent stating that “nothing replaces role plays.” One interpretation is that live practice with a person functioned as an implicit reference point against which both packages were evaluated, although neither offered it. This would be broadly consistent with reports from other relational health professions, where trainees describe AI as acceptable in a supportive role but maintain that it cannot substitute for human-centered interaction and therapeutic communication [,]. Some students additionally expressed concern that practicing with AI might lead them to optimize for system-specific feedback rather than responsiveness to a person, an apprehension that appears to parallel deskilling concerns noted in health professions education []. Ratings and written responses thus seemed to diverge, with the latter suggesting a preference that the comparative items may not have been positioned to capture.

The concerns our students raised differ in kind from those documented among students in general higher education, where reservations about generative AI cluster around accuracy, academic integrity, and overreliance diminishing critical thinking []. These were largely absent from our data. No student framed CARE as a shortcut around effort or worried that using it would undermine their own learning. Their most endorsed concerns were that AI would replace peer support and feedback (22/25, 88%) and peer interaction (20/25, 80%), and nearly half worried their data might build an AI therapist that could replace them. The object of concern appears to have been not their academic conduct but their professional future.

This pattern resembles reports from other relational health professions more than from general education. A systematic review of nursing students and practicing nurses found consistent argument that AI should augment rather than replace human empathy and judgment, with fear of deskilling impeding adoption []; qualitative studies describe AI accepted as supportive but incapable of replacing therapeutic communication []. Jussupow et al [] offer a possible mechanism, reporting that threats to professional recognition and to professional capabilities predicted resistance among medical students and physicians, with students experiencing stronger identity threats than experienced clinicians. Students whose developing expertise is defined by relational work may appraise AI in that domain partly as a threat to the identity they are acquiring rather than solely as a tool of uncertain utility. If so, this resistance may call for different responses than those developed for general education. Guidance on academic integrity and appropriate reliance addresses concerns our students did not appear to hold; what they voiced was uncertainty about whether the relational core of their profession would be preserved. Such concerns seem more tractable through transparency about a system’s purposes, framing that positions AI as supplementing rather than substituting for human relationship, and protection of the peer and supervisory interactions students valued most. We note the limits of this comparison: we sampled 1 cohort in 1 program and rest the contrast on triangulation against published work rather than on data of our own.

Students’ design concerns appeared to center on feedback that did not attend to the session as a whole. Three were endorsed equally often (17/25, 68% each): that the simulated patient could not report how the student’s responses made it feel, that progress was not tracked over time, and that feedback was frequently unhelpful; 64% (n=16) wanted feedback addressing the whole session. Prior work suggests that pairing simulated practice with feedback is both desired [,] and associated with skill improvement [,]; sustained multiweek use may additionally surface a need for criteria matched to each week’s pedagogical goal rather than to a fixed set of listening microskills.

Across both courses, students seemed to prefer not better AI feedback but AI feedback accompanied by human feedback. Peer feedback was rated above AI feedback in the first course, and supplemental TA feedback on CARE transcripts appeared to be received positively in the second, with 1 student observing that “AI’s benefits wouldn’t come alive if there weren’t human input to modulate it.” Hybrid approaches have been examined in general and online education [,] and in mental health support [-]. As we did not measure skill, our findings cannot speak to whether hybrid feedback improves acquisition, but they may suggest that automated feedback alone was not readily accepted as a substitute in this setting.

Instructional stance played a critical role in shaping students’ engagement. Concerns about data security and transcript use were salient, leading the team to develop a detailed FAQ and formal information sheet to clarify protections. These lessons guided adjustments in the second course, where CARE was more fully embedded as a core pedagogical component. Incorporating CARE as a weekly course requirement corresponded to higher participation and normalization of its use. However, after the second week of the second course, CARE became optional due to students’ apprehension. They could choose to use CARE for DP or complete additional Skillsetter videos.

This phenomenon aligns with other recent course-based integrations of AI-simulated patients that vary in instructional requirements. Prior work has documented both optional and required approaches to AI-supported practice, with optional implementations associated with more limited uptake and required implementations designed to ensure broad exposure across learners [,]. Taken together, these approaches suggest that optional integration may limit reach, whereas required engagement may increase participation and normalize use. At the same time, the present findings indicate that when AI-based practice is required, sustained engagement may depend on parallel instructional investment, including responsiveness to student concerns and the provision of human feedback to contextualize and support AI-augmented learning.

In addressing acceptance of AI in psychotherapy education (RQ4), students articulated views that were neither uniformly negative nor organized around instructional considerations alone. Several expressed cautious openness, particularly toward training and administrative applications, with 1 proposing that AI might more appropriately handle billing and insurance coordination than training itself. This ambivalence appears broadly consistent with reports that health professions students often hold simultaneously positive and apprehensive attitudes toward AI [], and with findings in nursing that trainees accept AI as a supportive tool while resisting it in more central roles [,]. It also cautions against characterizing this cohort as uniformly resistant.

Where students did express reservations, these seemed to concentrate at the boundary between training and clinical care rather than within training itself. A recurrent concern was that normalizing AI in coursework might facilitate its later migration into practice, described by 1 student as “a slippery slope,” and such apprehension was typically anchored in the perceived irreplaceability of human relational processes widely regarded as foundational to psychotherapy [,,]. Notably, students drew this line at clinical care rather than at learning: their objection appeared to be less that AI cannot support skill development than that its presence in training might legitimize its presence elsewhere. This may distinguish their concerns from those documented in general higher education, where reservations more often center on integrity and overreliance affecting students’ own learning [].

A third set of concerns extended well beyond psychotherapy and was not anticipated in our design. Students raised commercialization and the perceived disconnect between developers and practitioners, with one writing that “the lack of awareness about therapy for those who are developing models frankly terrifies me.” Environmental impact was endorsed by 64% (n=16) of respondents, a theme that appears to have received limited attention in the psychotherapy training literature to date, and some students reported declining to use the platform partly on these grounds. A few spontaneously referenced the January 2025 Southern California wildfires; because this association was not systematically assessed, we note it only as possible context. Taken together, these responses may suggest that acceptance of a particular educational tool is partly conditioned by students’ appraisal of the broader industry producing it, a consideration that instructional design alone may be poorly positioned to address.

Several limitations should be noted. This study was conducted within a single graduate training program, and the experiences of this cohort may reflect the particular pedagogical environment, instructional style, or program culture in which CARE was introduced. The program’s highly selective nature, which admitted 30 students from 644 applicants during the 2024 to 2025 cycle (a 7.1% admit rate), may further limit generalizability to less clinically experienced graduate students. In addition, the sample consisted of first-year graduate students enrolled in a multiyear program characterized by intensive supervision, including regular review of recorded therapy sessions with experienced supervisors. This context likely shaped student perceptions of AI-assisted training and may limit generalizability to settings where trainees have fewer opportunities for expert feedback (eg, peer counselors or paraprofessionals with limited supervision access).

Beyond the characteristics of the program itself, participation varied within the cohort. The first-course survey was optional and completed by 14 (48%) of 29 students; the second-course survey was a required component of the coursework and completed by 25 (86%) of 29. Students who used CARE and completed the first-course survey may differ systematically from those who did not, particularly given the privacy and data security concerns reported by students who declined the tool, so the 9 students providing comparative ratings of AI and peer feedback are not representative of the cohort. The first course was also shorter, spanning 6 weeks rather than 10, and CARE was an optional supplement rather than an assigned activity. We report these findings as preliminary and include them to provide context for the second-course deployment. Throughout, we describe findings as those of survey respondents rather than of the cohort.

The CARE platform integrated existing technologies for voice-based AI-simulated patients and feedback generation that were best performing in December 2024. Technical issues may have reflected the specific version deployed rather than inherent limitations of AI-assisted training tools: voice-based practice interactions had issues with transcription accuracy, speech recognition, and limited emotional expression, while feedback was limited to skill-based content on patient-centered listening skills rather than scenario-specific guidance regarding therapeutic-alliance challenges.

Our safety procedures relied on the courses’ existing supervisory structures rather than on study-specific monitoring. This design has a defensible rationale: the topics were already part of the curriculum, taught by the same faculty, and practiced concurrently in an established platform, but it means we cannot report a systematic account of whether the AI-simulated patients generated inappropriate content or whether students experienced distress that went unvoiced. Deployments at larger scale, or in settings without an embedded clinical instructor, would require monitoring procedures we did not implement here: routine transcript review, automated flagging of high-risk content, or structured post-session check-ins.

A central constraint on interpretation is that CARE and Skillsetter differed simultaneously along several dimensions rather than a single manipulated variable. The 2 packages contrasted voice-based with video-based interaction, multiturn dialogue with single-turn response, and a research prototype with an established commercial platform. Because these attributes were bundled, the present design cannot isolate the educational contribution of any one of them, including AI per se, voice interaction, dialogic format, feedback source, or platform maturity. We therefore frame our findings as an evaluation of students’ perceptions of 2 bundled instructional packages as actually delivered in the classroom, rather than as a test of “AI versus traditional training.” The comparative ratings should be read as package-level judgments; disentangling the individual active ingredients will require factorial or component-controlled designs in future work.

All outcomes reported here are student self-report. We did not assess objective change in psychotherapy competence, skill acquisition, alliance-building ability, or clinical readiness, and we make no claims that CARE improved these. Perception items (eg, feeling “more equipped to build a therapeutic alliance”) index students’ subjective experience, not measured skill.

The findings and limitations of this study suggest several priorities for future research on AI-assisted psychotherapy training. Short-term work should focus on improving the technical functionality of AI platforms. Students in this study consistently identified transcription errors as well as AI-simulated patients with limited vocal expressiveness as barriers to engagement. Research is needed to evaluate whether improvements in speech recognition, naturalistic prosody, and affective responsiveness increase the realism and pedagogical value of AI-simulated patients.

Parallel efforts should advance feedback systems toward greater context awareness. Current utterance-level approaches offer timely guidance on specific communication skills, but models that process turns independently can produce feedback that is repetitive, contradictory, or disconnected from the broader therapeutic process. Prior work on automated feedback and performance assessment in psychotherapy and counseling has similarly noted that utterance-level or narrowly scoped feedback may be insufficient for supporting integration of relational and process-oriented skills across the flow of a session [,,]. Approaches that consider the entire session history and enforce global consistency during feedback generation could better support students in developing coherent, session-oriented improvements. Moreover, consistent with emerging evidence that human–AI collaborative feedback may enhance contextual understanding and learner trust [-], short-term research should further evaluate hybrid feedback models that combine AI-generated suggestions with human commentary, an approach that students in the present study viewed as particularly beneficial.

Beyond technical functionality, future studies should evaluate whether AI-assisted training translates into measurable improvements in clinical skill acquisition. Recent research on AI-supported counseling and psychotherapy training has highlighted the need to move beyond learner self-report toward objective indicators of competence, including supervisor ratings, behavioral coding of microskills, and structured performance assessments [,,]. Critically, such assessments should extend beyond generic skill-based evaluations (eg, patient-centered listening) to include scenario-specific rubrics aligned with the particular competencies being taught, whether therapeutic-alliance navigation, crisis intervention, or other course-specific learning objectives. Experimental designs that directly compare AI-only, human-only, and hybrid feedback approaches would clarify the specific pedagogical contributions of each modality and help determine whether AI-supported practice confers additive benefits beyond established training methods. Multisite studies are also essential to assess whether findings generalize across programs with differing curricula, instructional philosophies, and trainee populations, a limitation frequently noted in early evaluations of AI-based training tools [,].

At a broader level, long-term research should address how AI integration reshapes the pedagogy and culture of psychotherapy training. Questions include whether repeated practice with AI-simulated patients influences professional identity formation and sensitivity to relational nuance. Ethical considerations will remain central, particularly regarding transparency in data use, the potential displacement of human elements in training, and environmental sustainability. The salience of ecological concerns in this study, possibly amplified by the January 2025 Southern California wildfires, highlights the need for future work to consider how external sociocultural contexts intersect with classroom-based experiences of AI. Ultimately, research must examine whether AI can be a useful adjunct to psychotherapy training, enhancing current methods, or whether its widespread adoption risks altering the relational foundations of psychotherapy education.

These recommendations were informed by student feedback across both terms, as well as by the adjustments made between the first course pilot and the second course deployment.

Clear, proactive communication about data use, research protocols, and pedagogical aims is essential to building student trust. The second course implementation benefited from refinements to communication strategies developed in response to concerns raised during the first course pilot.

Combining AI feedback with human oversight may mitigate concerns about impersonality and enhance learning outcomes. The addition of supplemental TA feedback during the second course exemplified this adjustment and was positively received by students. Future research may benefit from systematically examining the impact of required AI integration on students’ perceptions of the teaching team, including measures of instructional alliance, trust, and perceived support, to assess whether and how AI-mediated feedback influences the relational dynamics of the learning environment.

Student reflections suggested that instructional framing influenced their engagement with CARE. In the first course, the tool was positioned as optional following student concerns and apprehension, and several students reported feeling more willing to try it under these conditions than when it was framed as required. In the second course, CARE was initially presented as a central, required component of the course, which corresponded with higher participation early in the term. However, after concerns were raised, the instructional team shifted to making it optional, where students could engage in additional Skillsetter practice instead of CARE. These observations suggest that how the AI tool is introduced and framed by instructors plays a role in shaping student engagement, and that providing choice in an assigned activity can foster greater willingness to engage with AI-assisted training.

The integration of CARE across 2 academic terms illustrates both the promise and challenges of AI-assisted psychotherapy training. The first course pilot surfaced key concerns regarding feedback quality, course integration, and data transparency, while the second course study demonstrated how iterative adjustments, such as clearer communication, hybrid feedback models, and shifts in instructional framing, enabled more effective implementation. At the same time, students expressed persistent preferences for human-based training and raised concerns about realism, data use, and broader societal implications, including environmental impact. Taken together, these findings suggest that at this stage of development, AI has the potential to serve as a valuable adjunct to psychotherapy education when framed as a supplement to human interaction, implemented transparently, and paired with human oversight.

Looking ahead, priorities for advancing this field can be organized across 3 levels. Short-term priorities involve addressing technical limitations and refining feedback mechanisms. Medium-term priorities focus on evaluating whether AI-assisted practice translates into measurable improvements in clinical performance, ideally through controlled, multisite studies that include objective learning outcomes. Long-term priorities include examining how AI integration reshapes the pedagogy and culture of psychotherapy training, professional identity formation, and ethical considerations such as data use, role displacement, and environmental sustainability.

The utility of AI-augmented psychotherapy training may differ across educational contexts. In this graduate program, students receive intensive supervision, including live or taped review of clinical encounters, which may shape how they perceive the added value of AI. In other settings, such as programs with more limited supervisory resources, AI tools may assume a more prominent role in supporting DP and providing structured feedback.

Thus, the pedagogical value of AI may not be uniform but instead contingent on the broader training environment, with its potential relevance varying according to the availability of human supervision and feedback.

By situating AI within authentic classroom contexts and iteratively adapting implementation based on student feedback, this study provides a strong foundation for future inquiry in psychotherapy pedagogy. Its contribution lies not only in documenting students’ perceptions of AI-assisted training but also in demonstrating how responsive piloting can inform best practices for responsibly integrating emerging technologies into psychotherapy education.

psychology.title: Disgust, Contagion Beliefs, and Contamination-Related Obsessive-Compulsive Symptoms in Hospital and Non-Hospital Workers
psychology.abstract: Background: Recent research highlights the role of disgust in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), particularly contamination-related OCD (C-OCD). Beyond elevated trait disgust, individuals with C-OCD often endorse strong beliefs about the spread of contamination through contact (contagion beliefs). Hospital workers (HWs) operate in environments where contamination is part of daily life and must manage genuine infection risks and their own disgust responses. Methods: To examine whether hospital work and medical training may confer resilience relevant to C-OCD, disgust and contagion beliefs (confirmatory outcomes), as well as OCD symptoms and situation-specific contamination concerns (exploratory outcomes), were assessed using self-report questionnaires in an online cross-sectional study. Participants included psychology students (N = 52), medical students (N = 69), non-medical HWs (N = 44), and medical HWs (N = 111). Results: We hypothesized that medical HWs would report the lowest levels of disgust and contagion beliefs, followed by medical students, non-medical HWs, and psychology students. This hypothesis was partially supported for trait disgust only. Contrary to expectations, HWs, regardless of medical background, reported the highest levels of contagion beliefs. Despite these elevated beliefs, HWs reported significantly lower contamination concerns than psychology students. Moreover, contagion beliefs were not associated with C-OCD symptoms among medical HWs, whereas this association was present in all other groups. Conclusions: Contagion beliefs may not be associated with C-OCD symptoms in the same way across contexts, particularly among individuals who regularly manage genuine contamination threats. Future research should investigate which factors may buffer HWs against the typically maladaptive association between contagion beliefs and C-OCD symptoms.
psychology.text:
Contamination-related obsessive-compulsive disorder (C-OCD) is frequently identified as the most prevalent obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) subtype (e.g., ref. []). Although well-established and empirically supported treatments are available (with exposure and response prevention (ERP) therapy considered the gold standard for treating OCD []), about 30% of individuals show little to no improvement []. Over the past two decades, research has identified disgust as a key factor in the development and maintenance of OCD [,], suggesting that it may play a crucial role in successful treatment (e.g., refs. [,,]). ERP operates, among other mechanisms, through expectancy violation, inhibitory learning, and habituation []. However, this is precisely where the difficulty in treating C-OCD appears to lie, because previous studies have shown that exposure-based interventions reduce disgust responses less strongly and more slowly than fear responses [,]. Several mechanisms may account for this specificity. The following four illustrate key possibilities (for a German review, see []).

Disgust associations often develop through evaluative conditioning, whereby stimuli acquire a stable negative valence that is less susceptible to change through expectancy violation or habituation (e.g., refs. [,]).

Expectancy violations are more difficult to experience in the context of disgust, as negative consequences (e.g., illness) tend to occur with a temporal delay and are not immediately verifiable (e.g., ref. []).

Disgust is frequently accompanied by attentional avoidance, which may limit key learning processes during exposure (e.g., ref. []).

Finally, specific cognitive biases such as the “laws of sympathetic magic,” particularly the “law of contagion,” play an important role. Individuals with C-OCD show pronounced beliefs about transfer, which contribute to an overestimation of a contamination risk [,] and thus reinforce avoidance and cleansing behaviors [].

While all the above discussed mechanisms presumably play an important role, this study will focus on aspects 2 and 4, the potential temporal delay of safety signals in disgust exposure as well as the impact of contagion beliefs on C-OCD symptomatology and its relation to disgust.

Contagion beliefs implicate that contamination persists and spreads through contact, even when no objective threat is present. This assumption is consistent with the law of contagion, which proposes that once two objects come into contact, properties of one object are believed to transfer to the other and to persist even after contact has ended (e.g., a clean shirt touching a contaminated surface is perceived as permanently contaminated; ref. []). In C-OCD, these beliefs maintain fear and avoidance and consequently may reduce the effectiveness of ERP, because patients continue to perceive contamination as persistent despite repeated exposure to objectively safe situations.

Taken together, these two mechanisms suggest a joint explanation for why ERP may be less effective in C-OCD: expectancy violations regarding disgust-based threats are difficult to experience because negative consequences (e.g., illness) often occur with a delay and cannot be immediately verified as absent, while contagion beliefs assume that contamination persists through contact even without objective threat—thereby maintaining fear and avoidance despite repeated safe exposure. Hospital settings offer a naturalistic model for examining whether repeated, long-term exposure to contamination-relevant cues—without the time limit typical of ERP protocols—can provide the kind of repeated, verifiable safety signal that classical exposure interventions struggle to deliver. Hospital workers are routinely confronted with cues related to illness, pathogens, and infection, giving them repeated opportunities to learn, over time, that contact with such cues does not often result in the feared consequences [].

Consistent with this model, healthcare workers and students consistently show lower disgust propensity (DP) than other populations [,,,], an effect that increases with professional experience [,,,] and age []. This pattern has been attributed to habituation [], self-selection effects [,,], or the development of coping strategies that offset frequent disgust-eliciting experiences []. At the same time, high disgust remains associated with emotional exhaustion and stronger intentions to quit among hospital workers [], and more than half of nursing students report disgust experiences at work severe enough to make them consider leaving the profession []. While this evidence indicates that DP decreases with sustained occupational exposure, it remains unknown whether the same pattern extends to contagion beliefs, situation-specific contamination concerns, and C-OCD symptoms, or how these constructs relate to one another across groups. This gap is also theoretically relevant: it is unclear whether elevated contagion beliefs in C-OCD reflect primary appraisal (how contagious a stimulus is judged to be) or secondary appraisal (how well one believes one can cope with that contagiousness; ref. []). Distinguishing contagion beliefs (primary appraisal) from contamination concerns (a combination of primary and secondary appraisal; ref. []) helps address this: lower contagion beliefs in hospital workers would indicate reduced primary appraisal, whereas unchanged contagion beliefs alongside reduced contamination concerns would instead point to more effective coping with perceived infection risk. The present study addresses this gap by comparing hospital workers with a medical background (i.e., involved in direct patient care) to three comparison groups—hospital workers without a medical background, medical students, and psychology students—on DP, contagion beliefs, contamination concerns, and C-OCD symptoms. If long-term hospital workers show lower contagion beliefs and contamination concerns than medical or psychology students, this would suggest that the repeated, real-world experience of not becoming infected constitutes a stronger safety signal than the time-limited exposure typical of ERP.

On this basis, our preregistered hypotheses (see ) were that hospital staff with a medical background would show (1) lower levels of DP and (2) lower levels of contagion beliefs than non-medical hospital staff, medical students, and psychology students. Medical hospital workers and psychology students were chosen as two groups differing strongly in their current and past exposure to potential pathogens as well as in patient contact and disease-related knowledge. Medical students and non-medical hospital workers were included to disentangle two aspects of this exposure: Medical students share medical knowledge and an interest in diseases, and typically have some patient contact through clinical training, but have less sustained pathogen exposure than medical staff. Non-medical hospital workers (e.g., administrative or technical staff) encounter potential pathogens in their everyday work environment, but have no direct patient contact and no medical training. Comparing these groups therefore allows us to test whether lower contagion beliefs and DP are related to occupational pathogen exposure, medical knowledge, or both. Based on the frequency of current and past patient contact and pathogen exposure, we expected the following order: medical hospital workers (most exposure), followed by non-medical hospital workers and medical students, and finally psychology students (least exposure).

As additional, non-preregistered variables, C-OCD symptomatology and contamination concerns were assessed to further characterize the relationship between psychopathology, contagion beliefs, disgust, and situational contamination concerns. Given that contagion beliefs, contamination concerns, and DP have all been linked to C-OCD symptomatology, the relationship between these constructs and C-OCD symptoms was additionally examined separately as an exploratory analysis.

The study, including the power analysis, was preregistered (AsPredicted #232,767; https://aspredicted.org/f9b4-v37c.pdf (preregistred on 10 June 2025)). In summary, the planned sample consisted of 32 participants in each comparison group (i.e., psychology students, medical students, and hospital workers without a medical background) and 96 hospital workers with a medical background. This sample size corresponds to a statistical power of 0.80 for detecting significant results with an effect size of d=0.5, which is approximately the effect size reported by Edgar et al. [].

Participation in the study was voluntary. Recruitment was conducted between 15 July and 15 October 2025; two reminders were sent in August and September to encourage participation. Convenience sampling was applied in accordance with the two-centre recruitment design: Medical students and hospital staff with a medical background were recruited at one centre (University Medicine Göttingen), while psychology students were recruited at another centre (University of Potsdam). Psychology students were able to obtain course credit for participation. The survey link was distributed via staff and student multipliers, internal communication channels, and student social media groups (e.g., WhatsApp). Owing to the open and untracked dissemination of the link and limited response activity, the number of individuals reached could not be determined; consequently, an exact response rate could not be calculated.

Participants were eligible if they (a) provided informed consent, (b) were medical or psychology students (currently enrolled, with no restriction regarding academic year) or hospital workers (HWs) with or without medical background, (c) were at least 18 years old, (d) reported no neurological disorder or addiction to psychoactive substances (except caffeine or nicotine), and (e) completed the study in a quiet environment or using headphones. Participants were excluded if they answered fewer than 70 % of the questions, reported an attention level of 50 % or lower, had a within-person standard deviation <0.5 across all DP items, had a longstring index more than 3 SD above the mean on the DP questionnaire, did not provide an answer about group assignment or did not complete the DP questionnaire. In total, 561 participants started the study by clicking on the study link, of whom 339 completed it. Of these, 319 answered at least 70% of the questions, and 289 reported an attention level above 50% while completing the questionnaires. Three participants were excluded because of a high longstring index on the DP questionnaire, and one because of a very small within-person standard deviation (<0.5) across the DP items. One further participant was excluded because the question on group assignment was not answered. Of the remaining 284 participants, 5 had not completed the DP questionnaire, and 3 could not be reliably assigned to a group: they selected “other” and specified their occupation as “biologist”, “infection biologist”, and “student”, and also reported not working in a hospital. The final sample comprised 276 participants: 111 HWs with medical background, 44 HWs without medical background, 69 medical students, and 52 psychology students.  shows the distribution of gender and age for all four groups. All group sizes exceeded the minimum sample size (N = 32 for control groups and N = 96 for the comparison group) determined by the power analysis.

DP was assessed using the German version of the Disgust Scale (FEE; Fragebogen zur Erfassung der Ekelempfindlichkeit; refs. [,]). This validated questionnaire consists of 37 items spanning 5 distinct disgust domains: death, body secretions, hygiene, spoilage, and oral rejection. The scale exhibits excellent internal consistency overall (original, α=0.9; this study, α=0.94), with domain-specific reliabilities ranging from α=0.69 for oral rejection (this study, α=0.77) to α=0.85 for death (this study, α=0.68).

Contamination concerns were assessed using the Multidimensional State Disgust Questionnaire (MSDQ, ref. []). The MSDQ is a situation-specific assessment tool, designed to measure the four dimensions of physical, moral, self disgust, and contamination concerns. For this study, only the contamination concern scale was investigated. The 4-factor structure of the 18-item MSDQ was confirmed via exploratory and confirmatory factorial analysis; the internal consistency of the 4-item-contamination concern scale was high, with α=0.84.

Contagion beliefs were assessed using the video-based Chain of Contagion Task (CCT; ref. [], originally developed by Tolin et al. []). The CCT measures perceived contamination across multiple degrees of separation. In the task, a neutral pencil is initially brought into contact with a disgust-eliciting stimulus and is then used to sequentially contaminate additional pencils, such that the first pencil contacts the second, the second contacts the third, and so forth, until the twelfth pencil in the original paradigm. For each pencil, participants rated perceived contamination. All ratings were provided on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 100 (very much). In contrast to the original version of the task, only nine pencils were used in the present study. This modification was based on prior findings from correlational analyses indicating negligible interindividual variability beyond the eighth pencil and no additional informational value beyond the tenth pencil [].

Obsessive-compulsive symptom severity was assessed using the Dimensional Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (DOCS; ref. []), a 20-item self-report measure that assesses overall OCD severity across four symptom dimensions: contamination, responsibility, unacceptable thoughts, and symmetry. Each dimension is evaluated across five severity parameters (time spent, avoidance, distress, functional interference, and resistance) using a 5-point scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely). The German version of the DOCS [] demonstrates excellent internal consistency (Cronbach’s α≥0.90) and good test–retest reliability (r≈0.80), as well as satisfactory construct validity and diagnostic accuracy; criterion validity is reported to be limited. In the present study, only the five items from the contamination dimension (C-DOCS) were assessed.

The study was conducted entirely online and in German. Participants were instructed to complete an online version of the CCT along with a series of questionnaires assessing relevant hygienic and psychological aspects: DP, contamination concerns, contagion beliefs, and C-OCD-symptom severity, as well as approximately ten additional items regarding participants’ professional experience in the hospital setting (e.g., “How long have you been working in the hospital?” and “How would you rate your own knowledge regarding hospital hygiene?”). Additionally, all participants were instructed to think of a disgusting situation within a hospital (or, if they did not remember one, outside a hospital) and afterwards answered the MSDQ. The complete flowchart, including all questionnaires and questions, is presented in . Mean of the total participation time was 25.6 min (SD=8.94). For group assignment, each participant indicated whether they were a psychology student, a medical student, a non-medical hospital worker, a medical hospital worker, or other. Participants who selected “other” and specified “student of dentistry” were assigned to the medical student group. All “other” responses were inspected individually; these participants were either assigned to the corresponding group or excluded from the sample (see above ).

For the dependent variables, mean scores of all 37 items of the FEE were calculated to assess DP; the aggregated score of the question about contamination level for each of the 9 successive pens within the CCT was used to assess contagion beliefs; the mean of the 4 items of the respective subscale of the MSDQ was calculated to estimate contamination concerns; and the mean score of the 5 items of the C-DOCS were computed to assess C-OCD symptom severity.

Visual inspection of Q-Q plots indicated moderate deviations from normality in the tails of the residual distributions for the contagion beliefs, contamination concerns, and C-DOCS models, likely reflecting floor-and-ceiling effects inherent to these bounded scales, along with a small number of correspondingly extreme observations; residuals of the FEE model showed close alignment with the theoretical normal distribution across most of the range. Given the sample size (N = 276, with group sizes exceeding 40), these deviations are unlikely to compromise the validity of the parameter estimates, as the central limit theorem supports approximately normal sampling distributions of the coefficient estimates regardless of residual non-normality. To guard against potential heteroscedasticity, all models were additionally estimated using heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (HC3; ref. []). Across all models, results were substantively unchanged compared to conventional OLS standard errors.

To compare the expression of the dependent variables across groups, separate linear models were computed for each dependent variable, with group as a predictor variable. In all models, HWs with medical background served as the reference category against which all other groups were compared, because this group was the main focus within the hypotheses. Also, due to previous findings indicating lower disgust for men [] and, to a lesser extent, older participants [], the models were always controlled for age and gender. The variable age was mean-centred prior to analysis by subtracting the sample mean (M=34.9), while the original unit (years) was retained. Mean-centring was applied to facilitate the interpretation of the intercept, which consequently represents the expected outcome at the mean age of the sample. Gender was included as a categorical predictor with three levels (male, female, non-binary), with male as the reference category. Two participants identified as non-binary; given this small subgroup size, the corresponding coefficient is not meaningfully interpretable in any model and is therefore not discussed in the main text. Thus, each linear model contained group (with the four levels of occupation), age and gender as predictor variables. Firstly, the models were computed in full and then post hoc pairwise comparisons were computed for a more detailed understanding of group comparisons.

Regarding the relationship between the dependent variables and C-OCD symptomatology, a linear model was computed with C-OCD symptoms as the dependent variable, along with contagion beliefs, group, and their interaction as predictor variables, controlling for contamination concerns and DP as covariates. Age and gender were included as additional covariates in the model. Given the conceptual overlap between contagion beliefs, contamination concerns, and DP, variance inflation factors (VIFs) were inspected to assess multicollinearity among predictors; all values for non-interaction terms were below 2 (GVIF1/(2·df)), indicating no problematic multicollinearity. All statistical analyses were conducted in R (version 4.4.3; ref. []) using the dplyr, effectsize, car, emmeans, sandwich, and lmtest packages [,,,,].

The results of the group comparisons for all dependent variables are presented in . The following paragraphs summarize these findings separately for each dependent variable. Effect sizes, standard error of the mean, as well as F-, t-, and p-values are reported for statistically significant comparisons. It should be noted that analyses concerning contagion beliefs and DP were preregistered, whereas analyses involving C-OCD symptoms and contamination concerns were not.

Mean DP measured with the FEE for all four groups can be seen in a. A linear regression with HC3-robust standard errors was conducted predicting DP from group membership, age, and gender (R2=0.17). As hypothesized, HWs with medical training reported significantly lower DP than psychology students (β=−0.33, SE=0.12, t=−2.75, p=0.006, d=−0.63) and HWs without medical training (β=−0.29, SE=0.09, t=−3.11, p=0.002, d=−0.56). However, no significant difference between medical students and HWs with medical training could be observed (p=0.41). Women reported significantly higher DP than men (β=0.35, SE=0.07, t=4.83, p<0.001), while age was not a significant predictor (β=−0.005, SE=0.003, t=−1.56, p=0.119). Exploratory Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons further revealed that medical students also reported significantly lower DP than psychology students (Δ=0.41, t=3.89, p<0.001, d=−0.78) and HWs without medical training (Δ=0.37, t=3.28, p=0.006, d=0.71). HWs without medical training and psychology students did not differ significantly (p=0.99).

A linear regression with HC3-robust standard errors was conducted predicting contagion beliefs from group membership, age, and gender (R2=0.05). Contrary to the hypotheses, HWs with medical training reported significantly higher contagion beliefs than psychology students (β=12.12, SE=4.97, t=2.44, p=0.015, d=0.53). Additionally, HWs with medical training also reported significantly higher contagion beliefs than medical students (β=14.64, SE=4.58, t=3.20, p=0.002, d=0.64), while HWs without medical training did not differ significantly from HWs with medical training (p=0.44). Age was a significant negative predictor (β=−0.37, SE=0.15, t=−2.56, p=0.011), while gender was not significant (p=0.68). Exploratory Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons revealed that medical students (Δ=17.84, t=3.49, p=0.003, d=−0.78) as well as psychology students (Δ=15.31, t=2.81, p=0.027, d=−0.67) reported significantly lower contagion beliefs than HWs without medical training. Medical students and psychology students did not differ from each other (p=0.936).

A linear regression with HC3-robust standard errors was conducted predicting contamination concerns from group membership, age, and gender (R2=0.15). HWs with medical training reported significantly lower contamination concerns than psychology students (β=−0.80, SE=0.23, t=−3.43, p<0.001, d=−0.75) and HWs without medical training (β=−0.43, SE=0.18, t=−2.31, p=0.021, d=−0.40). Age was a significant negative predictor (β=−0.016, SE=0.006, t=−2.53, p=0.012), while gender was not significant (p=0.203). Exploratory Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons further revealed that medical students also reported significantly lower contamination concerns than psychology students (Δ=−0.81, t=−3.91, p<0.001, d=−0.75). No further significant differences emerged between any other group pairs (all p≥0.098). The differences in contamination concerns is displayed in c.

A linear regression with HC3-robust standard errors was conducted predicting C-OCD-related contamination symptoms (C-DOCS) from group membership, age, and gender (R2=0.04). Group membership did not significantly predict C-DOCS scores, with none of the groups differing from HWs with medical training (all p≥0.53). Age was a significant negative predictor (β=−0.032, SE=0.015, t=−2.06, p=0.040), while gender did not predict the C-DOCS score significantly (p=0.305). Exploratory Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons confirmed the absence of group differences, with all pairwise contrasts being non-significant (all p≥0.887).

Given that the findings regarding contagion beliefs were contrary to the hypothesized direction, whereas the pattern for DP was consistent with the hypotheses and the exploratory findings for contamination concerns followed a similar direction as DP, differences in the influence of contagion beliefs on C-OCD symptoms between hospital workers and the other groups were examined. As indicated in the introduction, increased contagion beliefs alongside decreased contamination concerns suggest that, for hospital workers, heightened contagion beliefs are not necessarily problematic and should therefore not contribute to C-OCD symptomatology. Thus, while previous studies have shown an association between contagion beliefs and C-OCD symptoms [,], the analyses indicated that this relation might not be present in hospital workers. This rationale is based on the assumption that extensive knowledge of, and diverse experiences with, contaminating stimuli enhance hospital workers’ self-efficacy without altering their beliefs themselves.  shows the influence of DP, contagion beliefs, and contamination concerns on C-OCD symptoms across the four groups in separate colors. None of these analyses were preregistered and thus are all exploratory.

A model containing age, gender, group, contamination concerns, and FEE as covariates, along with the interaction between group and contagion beliefs, significantly improved fit over the corresponding main-effects model (Wald test: F(3,253)=3.05, p=0.029). Specifically, the interaction between contagion beliefs and group was significant when comparing HWs with medical background to psychology students (β=0.06, SE=0.02, t=2.60, p=0.010), indicating that the positive association between contagion beliefs and C-OCD symptoms was significantly weaker in HWs with a medical background compared to psychology students. A similar, non-significant trend was observed when comparing HWs with medical background to medical students (β=0.03, SE=0.02, t=1.65, p=0.101) and to HWs without medical training (β=0.03, SE=0.02, t=1.54, p=0.124). Grouping participants by medical background alone (medical vs. non-medical) confirmed this pattern, with a significant contagion beliefs × medical background interaction (Wald test: F(1,257)=6.01, p=0.015).

In sum, disgust propensity and contamination concerns were lower in the medically trained groups, whereas contagion beliefs were highest in HWs, and C-OCD symptoms did not differ between groups. The association between contagion beliefs and C-OCD symptoms was weaker in HWs with a medical background than in psychology students.

In an online study, we examined disgust propensity (DP), contagion beliefs, contamination concerns, and C-OCD symptoms in hospital workers (HWs) with and without a medical background, medical students, and psychology students. The key finding was a dissociation in medically trained HWs: contagion beliefs were elevated, whereas contamination concerns were low and the association between contagion beliefs and C-OCD symptoms was weaker than in psychology students.

Partially confirming Hypothesis 1, DP was lower for HWs with medical background than for psychology students and HWs without medical background. However, medical students did not differ from HWs with medical background. This is in line with previous studies [,], supporting the notion that DP acts as a robust predictor of career selection. The absence of a difference in DP between medical students and HWs with a medical background is also relevant to the treatment of C-OCD. Notably, HWs with a medical background had worked in hospital settings between 2 and 48 years (M = 19.6 years), suggesting that even prolonged occupational exposure to potentially disgust-evoking stimuli may not be associated with substantially lower DP. This interpretation is consistent with previous evidence indicating that disgust is relatively resistant to habituation through mere exposure [,]. One study of healthcare assistants in care homes [] found a reduction in disgust domains specific to the healthcare environment, with some evidence for generalization beyond it. This contrasts with the absence of a difference between HWs and medical students in the present study, and points to a need for further research on how DP changes over time in hospital work. Age has previously been negatively correlated with DP (e.g., ref. []), yet age was not a significant predictor of DP here, despite a larger sample than that of Ousey et al. []. Sample characteristics may also explain the diverging findings: Edgar et al. [] studied healthcare assistants, whereas the young comparison group here consisted exclusively of medical students and did not include, for example, nursing students. One possible explanation is that habituation to disgust, and the associated decline in trait disgust, occurs early in medical education and then remains relatively stable. Rozin [], for instance, found a rapid decline in disgust toward death and body-envelope violations within only a few months of medical school. Similarly, Adagide et al. [] found a decline in disgust across the years of nursing school. However, these studies were either short-term or cross-sectional. Longitudinal studies tracking medical students’ DP before, during, and after training would help clarify this trajectory.

A surprising result, contradictory to H2, was that HWs with a medical background showed higher contagion beliefs than psychology students, despite their lower DP. This effect was specific to HWs, since medical students did not show elevated contagion beliefs. One explanation is that contact precautions, used daily in hospitals to prevent cross-transmission of pathogens such as multi-drug-resistant bacteria, keep the contact transmission route salient for HWs. Because the result regarding contagion beliefs was surprising, additional exploratory analyses were conducted.

The exploratory results revealed that within HWs with a medical background, contagion beliefs were unrelated to C-OCD symptoms and contamination concerns were very low. This is notable because contagion beliefs have been identified as an important factor in the development and maintenance of C-OCD, and are targeted by several disgust-focused OCD treatments (e.g., ref. []). The present results suggest that professional experience in an environment where contamination is either constantly present or a frequent, actively managed risk may break the link between contagion beliefs and C-OCD symptoms. This points to a hypothesis for future intervention studies: contagion beliefs may not be inherently maladaptive; instead, it may be the appraisal of contamination and one’s perceived ability to cope with it that determines whether these beliefs become clinically relevant.

Returning to the four processes proposed to reduce the effectiveness of exposure therapy in C-OCD (see []), the present results speak to two of them. First, strong contagion beliefs, as measured via performance on the CCT [], were not necessarily associated with C-OCD symptoms among individuals with extensive experience and knowledge in managing pathogens. Second, regarding the absence of expectancy violation, HWs with many years of workplace experience did not differ in DP from medical students. Therefore, within this sample, long-term workplace exposure was not associated with lower disgust. Exposure therapy might therefore benefit more from directly targeting expectancies, for example, by focusing on promoting and increasing self-efficacy (e.g., “I will [not] be able to stand this amount of disgust”; see []), than from simply extending exposure time—though further studies are needed to confirm this.

One strength of this study is its comparatively large number of hospital workers, including both those with and without a medical background, exceeding the sample size estimated in the power analysis. Recruiting hospital staff is often difficult given their demanding schedules and limited time for research participation. However, participation was voluntary: of the 561 participants who started the study, only 319 finished it, and those with a particular interest in disgust, contamination, or related topics may have been more likely to complete it, introducing a possible self-selection bias. A further strength is the study’s interdisciplinary approach, which combines psychological and medical perspectives on contamination-related processes. This integration may help clarify how contamination-related beliefs and responses matter both for psychological symptoms and for infection prevention and control in healthcare settings. The findings on contamination concerns, and their relationship to profession and C-OCD symptoms, were exploratory. Because the pattern of results for contagion beliefs was completely reversed relative to the hypothesized direction, a new hypothesis was formulated before running the corresponding analyses, but without preregistration; replicating these results is therefore necessary to strengthen their impact. For contamination concerns, participants generated their own contamination-relevant situation. This likely produced more individually valid, idiosyncratic disgust responses, but at the cost of standardization and, potentially, reliability; replicating the study with standardized hospital situations could strengthen these results further. Groups also differed considerably in age, reflecting the natural age distribution within each group. The sample was over 70% female, which is broadly representative of the gender distribution within the professions studied; all analyses were controlled for age and gender to reduce bias from these demographic differences. The final analysis deviated slightly from the preregistered group classification. The preregistration specified that hospital staff with a medical background and patient contact would show lower disgust and contagion beliefs than the other groups. However, patient contact could not be operationalized unambiguously: current patient contact was assessed for participants currently working in a hospital, while previous patient contact was assessed for those who had worked in a hospital in the past. As a result, several participants reported currently working in a hospital without patient contact despite substantial previous patient contact. The final analysis therefore used four groups instead—hospital workers with a medical background, hospital workers without a medical background, medical students, and psychology students—deviating from the preregistration. As indicated above, the cross-sectional design does not allow conclusions about causality—longitudinal studies are necessary to track trajectories of disgust and contagion beliefs to better understand when and how they change throughout occupational experience. A final limitation concerns sample composition: the non-medical HW group included many members of the hygiene/infection prevention control department, who are specially trained to manage the transmission and contamination of pathogens, which may have influenced their contamination concerns and contagion beliefs. The medical HW group was also heterogeneous, comprising nurses and physicians from various disciplines exposed to different types and amounts of disgust-inducing stimuli. Further research on profession-specific differences in trait disgust and contamination beliefs could clarify whether and how occupational exposure to disgust-inducing stimuli acts as a resilience factor against C-OCD symptoms.

In a sample of N = 276 participants comprising psychology and medical students as well as hospital workers (HWs) with and without a medical background, disgust propensity (DP), contagion beliefs, contamination concerns, and C-OCD symptoms were assessed. In the preregistered analyses, DP was lower in medically trained groups than in psychology students and non-medical HWs, whereas contrary to our hypothesis, contagion beliefs were highest in HWs. Exploratory analyses further showed that contamination concerns were lower in medically trained participants and that, among medically trained HWs, contagion beliefs were not correlated with C-OCD symptoms. Because of the cross-sectional design, these differences cannot be attributed to medical training or hospital experience. Taken together, the findings suggest that the clinical relevance of contagion beliefs may depend less on the beliefs themselves than on their interpretation, perceived coping capacity, professional knowledge, and repeated real-world experience. This interpretation requires replication. Future research should use longitudinal designs, standardized contamination paradigms, and profession-specific analyses within the hospital context. Intervention studies could test whether strengthening perceived coping capacity and self-efficacy can refine exposure-based treatment for C-OCD.

psychology.title: “Surprised that men could Care?”: gendered professional identity and occupational well-being among male clinical psychologists in India: a qualitative study
psychology.abstract: Clinical psychology is a care-oriented profession in which empathy and emotional attunement are central to practice and are often culturally associated with femininity. This study explored gendered professional identity, emotional labour, therapeutic practice, and occupational well-being among male clinical psychologists in India.Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 14 male clinical psychologists registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India. Data were analysed using a six-phase thematic analysis approach.Five themes were developed: Pathways into Clinical Psychology; Systemic and Gendered Contexts; Negotiating Masculinity and Professional Identity; Learning and Professional Socialisation; and Sustaining Well-Being and Envisioning Change. Participants described navigating stereotypes associating care and emotional sensitivity with femininity, professional isolation, gendered client expectations, therapeutic boundary demands, financial pressures, and institutional constraints. Their accounts also reflected adaptive identity negotiation, professional learning, supportive relationships, reflective practice, and efforts to sustain occupational well-being.Gendered expectations and institutional conditions intersected in shaping participants’ professional identities and well-being. Gender-responsive supervision, peer-support networks, clearer professional structures, and greater institutional attention to clinician well-being may support more inclusive and sustainable professional environments.
psychology.text:
Psychology and psychotherapy have historically been perceived as care-oriented professions culturally associated with femininity, empathy, nurturance, and emotional expression (Cena et al., ). Male clinical psychologists working in such contexts may therefore experience tension between traditional masculine expectations and the emotional demands of therapeutic work. Traditional masculine expectations commonly position men as emotionally restrained, self-reliant, strong, and authoritative, while discouraging emotional openness and help-seeking (Del Castillo, ; Gillen, ). These expectations may be particularly relevant to emotional labour in psychotherapy. Hochschild,  conceptualised emotional labour as the management of emotion and emotional expression in accordance with occupational expectations. In psychotherapy, this may involve maintaining emotional presence, empathy, and professional composure while managing personal responses to clients’ distress, hostility, trauma narratives, or dependency. Male clinical psychologists may therefore need to negotiate social expectations of emotional restraint alongside professional expectations of emotional engagement and responsiveness.

The development of therapeutic competence, professional identity, and emotional responsiveness is shaped by professional training, supervision, and clinical experience. Trainees can learn how to handle boundaries, emotional intensity, ethical quandaries, and client vulnerability through reflective practice, supervision, mentorship, and clinical exposure. For male trainees and early-career professionals, these settings may also provide opportunities to integrate emotional responsiveness, reflective practice, and authentic therapeutic engagement into their developing professional identities. As a result, training settings may become significant sites where therapeutic identity, professional socialisation, and gendered expectations converge. Male trainees may be more visible due to their numerical minority status and have less access to mentors or peers of the same gender, yet little research has examined these experiences in clinical psychology training (Schweitzer et al., ).

Some evidence suggests that male therapists may be perceived as less warm or nurturing than female therapists, potentially influencing expectations in work involving children, trauma, or emotional vulnerability (Schweitzer et al., ). Research has also highlighted concerns related to emotional exhaustion, burnout, secondary trauma, and difficulties balancing personal and professional demands (Allwood and Geisler, ; Baum & Moyal, ; Felt, ). Traditional masculine expectations may discourage help-seeking and emotional openness, thereby increasing vulnerability to stress and burnout (Tay et al., ; Tran, ).

Client and therapist gender may become particularly salient in specific clinical contexts. Clients may associate female therapists with warmth, safety, and emotional understanding, resulting in a preference for female practitioners in some therapeutic settings (King, ; Schweitzer et al., ). In eating-disorder and body-image work, therapists reported fewer male than female clients and perceived gender-related differences in emotional openness, engagement with therapeutic tasks, and connection within therapy. Some male clients were also reported to seek male therapists, while therapists’ own gender appeared to influence their emotional responses and comfort when addressing aspects of eating-disorder treatment (Tragantzopoulou & Giannouli, ). Conversely, male clients may prefer male therapists because of shared gender experiences and perceived understanding of masculinity-related concerns (Holloway et al., ; Seidler and Wilson, ). Research on client–therapist gender matching has produced mixed findings. Bhati () found differences in alliance ratings across gender dyads but no evidence that gender matching was more important only during the initial stages of therapy, suggesting that gender alone is insufficient to explain therapeutic-alliance quality. Taken together, therapist and client gender may shape initial expectations and engagement for some clients but does not preclude the development of a strong therapeutic alliance.

The representation and availability of healthcare professionals also vary across professional cadres and geographical settings. A global analysis of 20 healthcare cadres, including psychologists, across 204 countries and territories found that women constituted 68.9% of the health workforce in 2023, although sex composition differed substantially across professions. Healthcare-worker density also varied considerably across regions, with high-income regions generally having the highest densities, while substantial workforce shortages persisted in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa (GBD 2023 Human Resources for Health Collaborators., ). These findings indicate that experiences of gendered representation and numerical minority status occur within broader geographical and structural differences in workforce availability.

These experiences are further complicated by the Indian sociocultural setting. Research within a working-class community in Mumbai demonstrated how masculinity and male authority were closely connected with economic provision, family responsibility, and social standing (George, ). More recently, a study of young urban Indian men found that stronger endorsement of masculine norms was associated with greater self-stigma and less favourable attitudes towards seeking mental health support (Joshi & Krishnan, ). Such sociocultural expectations may shape male clinical psychologists’ experiences of financial stability, professional reputation, social status, emotional expression, and responsibility as providers. Structural issues within the Indian mental health sector, including uncertain career opportunities, inconsistent professional pathways, variable access to supervision, and the demands of private practice, may further intensify these pressures (Agrawal, ; Sharan & Tripathi, ; Sodemba & Panwar, ).
