However, how gendered expectations intersect with financial insecurity, professional credibility, and the care-related demands of clinical psychology remains insufficiently understood. It is therefore important to examine occupational well-being not only in relation to therapeutic encounters but also within the institutional and sociocultural conditions in which clinical psychologists work.

Although previous studies provide valuable insights into therapist burnout, gender stereotypes, supervision, and therapeutic relationships, there remains limited qualitative research specifically examining the experiences of male clinical psychologists in India. Much of the available literature comes from Western contexts, and its transferability to India’s distinct professional, institutional, and sociocultural conditions remains questionable. Furthermore, existing research often focuses on challenges and deficits while paying less attention to resilience, coping strategies, identity negotiation, and professional growth.

Addressing this gap may inform gender-responsive training, reflective supervision, supportive workplaces, and more inclusive mental health systems. Accordingly, this study aimed to explore how male clinical psychologists in India experience and negotiate gendered professional identities, emotional labour, clinical practice, and occupational well-being.

A qualitative exploratory approach was adopted to address the following research question: How do male clinical psychologists in India experience and negotiate gendered expectations within their professional work and occupational well-being?

The study employed an exploratory qualitative design to examine how male clinical psychologists in India experienced and negotiated gendered expectations within their professional work and occupational well-being. The design was suitable for examining an under-researched area and enabled participants to describe their professional journeys, gendered experiences, and occupational well-being in their own words and in depth. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews guided by a researcher-developed, expert-reviewed interview guide. The semi-structured format enabled the researcher to maintain consistency across interviews while allowing participants to elaborate on their significant experiences. The research was conducted over a duration of 1.5 years from October 2024 to March 2026 through the Department of Clinical Psychology at Manipal College of Health Professions, Manipal. All interviews were conducted via a secure online platform, audio-recorded, and held without third parties present. Online interviews were conducted to reach a wider sample across various regions of India.

The study centred on the work experiences of Indian male clinical psychologists. Participants were eligible if they self-identified as men and held valid registration as clinical psychologists with the Rehabilitation Council of India. Participants were required to be currently practising as clinical psychologists in India.

Participants had to speak English and be able to use an internet-connected device to take part in an online interview. As the interviewer was fluent in English, English-speaking participants were included to ensure accuracy in data interpretation, transcription, and interviewing. In order to keep clinical psychologists as the professional group of interest, male psychiatric social workers and male psychiatrists were excluded.

Homogenous purposive sampling was used to recruit participants who could provide information rich accounts of working as male clinical psychologists in India. Purposive sampling was used to recruit members of a relatively homogeneous professional and gender group while allowing variation in geographical location, career stage, and employment setting. Recruitment flyers were also distributed through LinkedIn, Institutional networks, Alumni networks, and Direct professional contacts. Participants were contacted via phone and email.

Individuals who expressed interest were screened for eligibility and received a participant information sheet. Those who met the eligibility criteria and provided written informed consent were enroled. Fourteen participants were recruited, all of whom completed the interview. During data collection, preliminary familiarisation with the transcripts and field notes indicated recurring patterns as well as variation across participants’ accounts. Following the fourteenth interview, the dataset was considered sufficiently rich and diverse to address the study aim. Formal coding and theme development were undertaken subsequently. No participants withdrew from the study.

Participants ranged in age from 27 to 45 years (M = 32.50, SD = 5.02). Eleven reported an urban upbringing and three a rural upbringing. Seven participants were unmarried and seven were married; 11 belonged to nuclear families and three to joint families. Eleven identified as Hindu, two as Christian, and one as Muslim. Three participants reported practising online, while 11 reported practising primarily offline. All participants held an MPhil in Clinical Psychology, and two additionally held doctoral degrees. They worked across private practice, private clinics, hospitals, employee assistance programmes, academic institutions, and other mental health organisations, although employment was predominantly within the private sector ().

Demographic and Professional Characteristics of Participants (n = 14).

Note: A joint family refers to an extended family arrangement in which members from more than one generation or related nuclear family live together and share household responsibilities and resources. “Mode of practice” refers to participants’ primary mode of providing clinical services.

After the research proposal was approved by the Departmental Committee, approvals were sought from the Institutional Research Committee and the Institutional Ethics Committee, Kasturba Medical College, and Kasturba Hospital Institutional Ethics Committee- 2 (Student Research). The IEC approval number was 120/2025. The study was then registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI).

A researcher-developed sociodemographic form was used to document participants’ age, qualifications, years of clinical experience, geographical location, and employment setting. Following recruitment, before each interview, the researcher explained the interview process, addressed participants’ questions, and engaged in brief, informal conversation to facilitate rapport. Interviews were guided by a semi-structured comprising 11 principal open-ended questions with flexible follow-up prompts. The interview guide explored participants’ pathways into clinical psychology, professional experiences, interactions with clients and colleagues, occupational well-being, coping strategies, and perspectives on gender within their professional roles. Participants were invited to reflect on aspects of their work they considered significant. The interview guide was reviewed by a panel of five professionals with expertise in psychology, men’s mental health, and qualitative research. The guide was piloted with three individuals who met the study’s eligibility criteria. Based on their feedback, questions were rephrased, overlapping questions were combined, and additional prompts concerning well-being and professional support were included. Interviews were conducted by the principal investigator (clinical psychology trainee). Each interview was conducted once and lasted 50-60 minutes. Field notes were taken during and after each session. All sessions were recorded with consent, anonymised, and securely stored.

Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using an inductive reflexive thematic analysis, guided by Braun and Clarke’s six-phase approach and its subsequent methodological refinements (; Braun & Clarke,  (Braun & Clarke, 2006, 2021). This approach was selected because the study sought a contextually situated and interpretive understanding of how participants made sense of their gendered professional identities, clinical practice, and occupational well-being. Codes and themes were developed through the principal investigator’s active engagement with participants’ accounts rather than imposed through a predetermined theoretical framework. The analysis was recursive rather than strictly linear, with movement between the transcripts, coded extracts, developing themes, and complete dataset. Coding was conducted manually, and Microsoft Excel was used to organise coded extracts, analytical notes, and successive versions of the developing thematic structure.

During the first phase, the principal investigator read and reread each transcript to become familiar with the data and recorded initial observations and analytical notes. In the second phase, each transcript was coded line by line to identify features relevant to participants’ professional journeys, gendered experiences, clinical practice, and occupational well-being. Codes were organised separately for each participant and subsequently compared across interviews to identify recurring patterns, variations, and divergent accounts.

During the third phase, conceptually related codes were grouped into preliminary subthemes and broader candidate themes. In the fourth phase, the candidate themes were reviewed against the coded extracts and the complete dataset to assess their internal coherence, distinctiveness, boundaries, and relevance to the research question. Themes and subthemes were combined, separated, reorganised, renamed, or removed where necessary. During the fifth phase, the central organising concept and scope of each theme were clarified, and the final themes and subthemes were defined and named. In the sixth phase, representative quotations were selected, and the findings were developed into an analytical narrative connecting participants’ accounts with the research question and existing literature.

The principal investigator led the coding and theme development. Two members of the research team independently reviewed the developing coding framework, candidate themes, and selected data extracts. They acted as critical reviewers by questioning assumptions, considering alternative interpretations, and contributing to the refinement of the analysis. These discussions were not intended to calculate inter-rater reliability, establish coding consensus, or identify a single objectively correct interpretation. The research supervisor and co-investigators subsequently reviewed the developing thematic structure for conceptual coherence and relevance to the research question. The final themes were cross-referenced against the complete dataset to ensure that they represented recurring patterns as well as meaningful variations and divergent accounts. Reflexive journaling and an audit trail were maintained throughout the analytical process to document interpretive decisions and revisions to the thematic structure.

The first author, a female clinical psychology postgraduate trainee with training and certification in qualitative research methodologies, conducted the interviews. Prior to data collection, all participants were informed of the researcher's role and the study's goal; there was no prior relationship between the researcher and participants. The possible impact of the researcher's gender on interview dynamics was recognised at every stage as a female researcher questioning male participants regarding gendered professional experiences. Building rapport and asking insightful follow-up questions were made possible by familiarity with clinical psychology training and therapeutic culture, which also necessitated the deliberate bracketing of insider presumptions. Throughout data collection and analysis, the first author maintained a reflexive journal to document and critically examine assumptions, emotional responses, methodological decisions, and emerging interpretations concerning gender, clinical training, and professional identity. Members of the study team from academic, clinical, and experiential backgrounds contributed insider and outsider perspectives that enhanced understanding of the gendered, emotional, and cultural aspects of participants' experiences.

Several strategies were employed to enhance the credibility of the findings. Peer debriefing involved regular discussion of emerging interpretations with supervisors and research team members. Reflexive journaling documented ongoing analytical decisions and researcher positioning. An audit trail maintained a transparent record of methodological choices throughout the research process. Three participants took part in member reflection. Each received only their own interview transcript and was invited to comment on its accuracy; participants were not given access to other participants’ transcripts. Summaries of the preliminary themes were subsequently shared with these participants, who were invited to comment on their clarity, resonance, and completeness. Their feedback was treated as an additional source of interpretive reflection rather than as verification of a single correct account. The analysis attended to both recurring patterns and divergent accounts, helping preserve variation within the participant group rather than presenting their experiences as uniform.

The research was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) [Approval No. 120/2025] and officially registered with the Clinical trials Registry-India (CTRI) [CTRI No. 2025/06/106372]. Participants were provided with a participant information sheet detailing the purpose of the study, procedures involved, voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality measures, and their right to withdraw from the study at any time without penalty.

Before any data was collected, each participant provided written informed consent. To gather pertinent background data, participants also completed a sociodemographic data sheet. There was no payment for taking part. Only with participants' permission were interviews audio recorded, and they were conducted via a secure internet platform. Audio recordings were transcribed verbatim, and identifying information was removed from the transcripts.

All information was anonymised and securely stored in a password-protected system accessible only to the research team and the principal investigator. Data will be retained securely for three years following completion of the study, in accordance with institutional requirements, and subsequently destroyed.

Line-by-line coding generated an extensive initial set of codes, which was iteratively reviewed and consolidated during theme development. Nineteen subthemes were organised within five overarching themes: (1) Pathways into Clinical Psychology; (2) Systemic and Gendered Contexts; (3) Negotiating Masculinity and Professional Identity; (4) Learning and Professional Socialisation; and (5) Sustaining Well-Being and Envisioning Change. The themes and corresponding subthemes are presented in .

Themes and Corresponding Sub-themes.

This theme explores the processes through which participants developed an interest in psychology, made sense of it as a career option, and began to see themselves as belonging to the field, shaped by personal meaning and social influences during the initial stages of their academic lives. The theme comprises four sub-themes: Motivations and Personal Meaning, Decision-Making and Career Entry, Social Reactions to Career Choice, and Early Identity Development. Participants followed varied pathways into clinical psychology. Five described reaching a point at which their previous educational or occupational direction no longer felt meaningful, prompting them to consider an alternative career.

“I did my bachelor’s in hotel management. I was working as a chef, and I found the job quite monotonous...I felt it was very mechanical, and I realised it was probably the wrong career choice…So, my getting into clinical psychology was purely an accident. I chose it because some of my friends whom I got to know are in that batch. But then I think that was my destiny. I really started loving the subject. Since then, there is no turning back.” (P9)

P9’s account moved from describing clinical psychology as an “accident” to framing it as “destiny,” illustrating how an initially unplanned career transition was retrospectively incorporated into a meaningful professional identity.

Participants described clinical psychology as offering a sense of purpose and personal meaning that extended beyond conventional ideas of career advancement.

“I started my journey to the field of psychology in 2012.... My bachelor’s degree was in forensic science, and I had a forensic psychology subject...of course, it was more interesting, as some of you learned some things about yourself, which is very fascinating, and it allows you to make certain modifications in yourself. Improve your quality of life to strengthen relationships and make sense of the world around you. I think I was also going through a rough time during this, and I started using that in my life and personal relationships. And it kind of gave me a good feeling that I want to pursue this in my future slowly.” (P8)

The participant's account suggests that psychology became personally meaningful through its relevance to his own experiences. Developing greater self-understanding during a difficult period appeared to strengthen his motivation to pursue clinical psychology.

Eight participants described making a deliberate decision to pursue psychology after independently exploring the discipline through reading, educational guidance, or exposure to the field.

“I had heard of therapy and psychology. But at the time, I thought the main options were biology, math, and law. So, I prepared for medicine, but during that preparation, I came across this field. From there, I started to explore, started to learn, got a few books read up, and that’s when I realised that I think this is something that I want to do.” (P1)

Unlike participants who entered the profession by chance, P1 described an exploratory process through which psychology gradually became a deliberate educational choice.

Participants encountered varied responses from family members and peers, shaping whether their decision to pursue psychology was supported, questioned, or required justification.

“I told my family and teachers, I am going to continue to pursue psychology, and it is not something boys do, but girls will go for it. Mathematics and all were in the past. I don't remember somebody wholeheartedly saying, 'Wow, it's very good to go.'But then I pursued my UG and it all started to make sense for me and others as well.” (P5)

The participant’s experience reflects the influence of societal gender norms on career choices. While his decision to pursue psychology initially received limited support, greater exposure to the field appeared to foster increased acceptance over time.

Participants’ professional identities developed gradually across undergraduate education, postgraduate training, and independent clinical practice, during which the field became clearer and more personally meaningful for them, contributing to an emerging sense of professional identity. The transition from formal training to independent clinical practice was particularly important in developing a more embodied sense of professional identity, as P4 explained:

“Even though I completed my MPhil, there were many areas where I still had to learn. MPhil served as a runway for me; the flight actually takes off when you start seeing cases by yourself.” (P4)

This metaphor shows how participants saw direct clinical practice as the start of a more embodied and self-assured professional identity, whereas training was seen as a foundation.

In summary, the theme demonstrates that participants’ entry into clinical psychology involved not only developing a professional identity but also negotiating gendered expectations associated with choosing a care-oriented profession. As they progressed in their training and careers, participants described gradually reconciling their professional aspirations with societal perceptions of masculinity and establishing a sense of belonging within the profession.

This theme captures how gendered norms and institutional structures shaped participants’ professional visibility, sense of belonging, access to mentorship, and ability to navigate clinical psychology as a profession. This theme comprised three sub-themes: Social Perceptions, Stigma, and Gender Representation, Absence of Male Role Models, Institutional Barriers, Power, and Gatekeeping. Eleven participants described difficulties navigating institutional systems, including uncertainty about whom to approach, unclear decision-making authority, and limited access to formal support mechanisms. Participants understood these difficulties not simply as individual problems but as reflecting broader gaps in institutional governance, role clarity, and professional support.

“In our institution, they had a private restroom for women, but not for men. We’ll be using the restroom that patient has been using over there, too.” (P2)

For P2, the absence of comparable facilities for men represented an institutional assumption that the workforce and its needs were predominantly female.

This subtheme captures the subtle and often unspoken judgements encountered by male clinical psychologists across professional and social contexts. These experiences reflect underlying assumptions about gender norms within caregiving professions, where men’s presence is perceived as atypical, as one of the participants explained.

“But people don’t say it out loud anymore. But they clearly judge, and I pick it up, you know, when they say, "Oh," and then they say they won’t say, isn’t that a female-dominatedfield? Rather, why did you pick this field? And it’s not always inquisitiveness, it’s like 'oh this doesn’t do well or how silly of you.' There's a tone of judgement as well.” (P10)

P10 distinguished genuine curiosity from questions conveying implicit disapproval. Rather than being expressed explicitly, the judgement was communicated through tone, requiring him to interpret and navigate underlying gendered meanings that remained socially deniable.

Three participants contrasted clinical psychology with other healthcare professions, noting that men were perceived as having greater professional authority and more readily regarded as trustworthy. They felt that these perceptions did not consistently extend to clinical psychology, where being a man could instead prompt questions about their warmth, suitability for caregiving roles, and overall fit within the profession.

“There is a primary bias, which I think is a very significant bias in the medical field. Male doctors are more competent than female doctors. If you want to go to a surgeon, you go for a male surgeon, and it is proven by a study, to some extent, this is also true in psychology, although not very significant.” (P14)

P14's account illustrates how gendered assumptions differed across healthcare professions. While men were perceived as benefiting from greater authority and competence in medicine, he suggested that these perceived advantages were less evident in clinical psychology.

Being a numerical minority shaped participants’ professional positioning in contradictory ways, producing both heightened visibility and a sense of isolation. Six participants described being more easily noticed or remembered because there were relatively few men in their training or professional environments. Participants experienced this visibility in different ways: some viewed it as advantageous, while others found it uncomfortable or context dependent. At the same time, several participants described feeling isolated as a gender minority within a female-dominated profession, particularly when they had limited opportunities for informal interaction with other men in the field.

“Psychology does have a higher number of women than men, so I was sort of expecting that.… I was there to do a job and learn; that was the main focus. But yes, it is a little bit lonely, I guess. You don’t have that much male company, but that’s not the main concern.” (P11)

P11 acknowledged a degree of loneliness while deliberately minimising its professional importance. His account illustrates that numerical minority status was noticeable but did not necessarily undermine professional commitment or functioning.

This subtheme captures participants’ limited access to senior male clinical psychologists who could serve as mentors or professional role models. Ten participants reported limited exposure to men in senior, supervisory, or mentoring roles. Even when participants actively sought male mentors, opportunities were often limited.

“The man,like male mentorship, is not easily available. Even when I look for supervisors, I’ve almost always found a female supervisor. I possibly know, maybe a handful of two or three male supervisors.” (P10)

Participants generally valued the guidance received from women supervisors. However, some felt that access to a senior man might have helped them discuss gender-specific experiences, professional isolation, or the negotiation of masculinity within therapeutic work.

Six participants described difficulties navigating institutional authority and establishing professional credibility. They perceived psychiatrists as occupying a higher position within mental health hierarchies. At the same time, the roles of clinical psychologists, counsellors and psychiatric social workers were not always clearly differentiated by clients, colleagues, or institutions.

“Working in multi-specialist centres where you have to establish yourself, there you work in a psychiatry setting where you work with a psychiatrist, neurologist and all, where you need to establish yourself as a clinical psychologist, establish your footing. So that was something challenging always, still challenging.” (P14)

P14's account illustrates how perceived professional hierarchies required ongoing efforts to establish credibility within multidisciplinary teams. For some participants, these experiences occurred alongside the negotiation of their professional identity as male clinical psychologists.

Participants described ambiguity in how the roles and scopes of practice of psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors, and psychiatric social workers were understood within some workplaces and by members of the public. Participants occasionally had to reiterate the scope of clinical psychology and establish their credibility with clients, colleagues, and institutions due to this lack of clarity. Although these issues were not described as unique to men, participants experienced them within the broader context of being male clinical psychologists in a female-dominated profession.

“Uniform functionality is important.... If I am a clinical psychologist, what is my role description? If I am a social worker, what is my role description? If I am a psychiatric nurse, what is my role description? It should be very well clearly established till today; we will not see that being implemented.” (P6)

P6's account suggests that an inconsistent understanding of professional roles contributed to uncertainty about the scope of clinical psychology. While this issue was not described as unique to men, participants experienced it alongside broader efforts to establish their professional identity within a female-dominated field.

Participants also described institutional opacity, including uncertainty about who held decision-making authority and how to escalate concerns through formal channels. These accounts indicate that participants’ professional difficulties extended beyond gender representation to broader organisational concerns, including ambiguous hierarchies, limited role clarity, and inconsistent support structures.

“In a hospital setting, a medical officer will become the head of the department...When it comes to power dynamics, you may not be seen as an equal.” (P14)

P14's account illustrates how organisational power structures shaped participants' sense of professional standing, requiring them to negotiate their position within institutional hierarchies.

Taken together, being a man in clinical psychology produced a form of complex visibility. As members of a numerical minority, participants were sometimes more noticeable, memorable, or presumed to possess authority. However, the same minority position could also generate loneliness, restricted access to same-gender mentorship, and uncertainty about belonging within a feminised care profession. These gendered experiences operated alongside broader institutional problems, including professional hierarchy, role ambiguity, and limited formal support.

This theme captures how participants negotiated masculine norms while developing professional identities within a care-oriented profession. Gendered assumptions shaped how they were perceived as emotionally capable and professionally legitimate, while expectations of self-reliance, financial provision, constant availability, and emotional control affected their well-being. The theme comprises four sub-themes: Gendered Stereotypes and Professional Legitimacy; Client Gender Preferences and Bias; Emotional Labour, Vulnerability, and Burnout; and Breadwinner Pressures and Financial Insecurity.

“I get a lot of biased comments like this, ‘this is a course girls will take on!’ As a male psychologist, what do you actually do?” (P2)

P2's account suggests that repeated questioning positioned clinical psychology as an unusual or inappropriate career for men, requiring him to continually negotiate his masculinity while explaining and legitimising his career choice and professional identity. Through these interactions, he appeared to reaffirm the compatibility of caregiving work with his identity as a male clinical psychologist.

This subtheme captures how participants navigated gendered assumptions about their suitability and legitimacy within a predominantly female profession. Ten participants described encountering stereotypes that associated men with aggression, emotional restriction, or limited empathy, as one of the participants explained. These assumptions sometimes created a sense that participants had to demonstrate their warmth, emotional competence, and suitability for therapeutic work.

“The stereotypes always stigmatise us. I have heard comments such as, Being a man, you will not be able to serve in psychology. Men are very rough; they do not show emotion or understand the feelings of others, and their decisions are not based on emotion.” (P13)

Professional legitimacy was therefore relational rather than qualification-based alone: participants felt that competence had to be demonstrated against assumptions that therapeutic sensitivity was naturally feminine.

These assumptions sometimes created a sense that participants had to demonstrate their warmth, emotional competence, and suitability for therapeutic work. Rather than rejecting these expectations, some participants described responding by demonstrating empathy through their own therapeutic style and allowing their clinical practice to challenge prevailing assumptions over time.

“I also think there is this... concept or understanding that women are very empathetic... However, I also wanted to battle that belief by showing in my own way that, as a male psychologist, you can hold space as well, maybe not the same way, in your own way.” (P1)

His account suggests that negotiating masculinity involved demonstrating therapeutic competence through an authentic style of care rather than conforming to conventional expectations of either masculinity or caregiving.

This subtheme captures how clients’ gender preferences and assumptions influenced initial trust, expectations of therapeutic warmth, and participants’ experiences of clinical work. Some participants described clients expressing surprise when male therapists demonstrated sensitivity, patience, or empathy. Such reactions reflected an underlying expectation that caregiving qualities were more characteristic of women.

“There was this case I had to transfer, this guy actually never knew he was being assigned to a male therapist, and he was actually really good when we were having an interaction, and right next day, he actually asked the receptionist, can I actually get a change in therapist because I feel more comfortable when I am around women. I do not understand why, but then if the client is not okay, it is better that he goes; it is beyond my control.” (P4)

Caregiving traits such as care, trust, and empathy were commonly associated with women. At the same time, some noted a societal expectation that men are less likely to pursue clinical psychology as a career, which shapes how male professionals are perceived in the field.

“Even from new clients, boundaries are being crossed in a way off and not making it up in a professional way of going about the relationship, but maybe a little more personal in the way of calling the therapist a bro or bhai or by all those things might happen.” (P1)

This account highlights the importance of maintaining professional boundaries in therapeutic relationships. Participants described how informal forms of address and attempts to personalise the therapist-client relationship required ongoing boundary management.

This subtheme captures how the emotional and professional demands of clinical practice intersect with gendered expectations of availability, self-reliance, and emotional control within a female-dominated profession. Several unmarried participants felt that colleagues assumed they had fewer family responsibilities and were therefore continuously available for additional cases, holiday work, or weekend duties. Although a strong work ethic helped participants establish professional credibility, it sometimes came at the cost of work–life balance and reinforced expectations of continual availability. For some, declining additional work risked appearing insufficiently committed or resilient, reflecting masculine expectations that professional strain should be managed without complaint. Participants described how these cumulative demands contributed to emotional and physical exhaustion, making it increasingly difficult to sustain their professional practice.

“So, in the hospital, it is a different story. It is a very tiring work for, 1 ½ years, that even in M Phil also. It really affects my core because every time I am thinking about the cases and other things. Also, regarding burnout, you might know it's very high. The reason is that we talk about work-life balance, we talk about practitioners’ mental health but never practice. So even in the hospital, they’ll never talk about it. They give us more tasks.” (P7)

P7's account suggests that negotiating professional identity also involved negotiating expectations of resilience and availability. Enduring heavy workloads appeared to become part of demonstrating commitment, even when it came at the expense of personal well-being.

This subtheme captures the dual pressure of being expected to provide financially for one’s family while navigating low or irregular earnings and limited economic security within clinical psychology. Across the interviews, participants described a widely shared expectation that men should demonstrate financial and professional stability.

“In Indian culture, the male partner is often seen as someone who needs to be stable, can support the other partner, be a breadwinner and things like that. Moreover, you grow up listening to a lot of these things.” (P10)

Breadwinner pressure is not a single event, but a set of repeated social messages internalised across development. Financial stability consequently carried moral and relational significance beyond occupational success alone.

Uncertainty about income stability and long-term earning potential shaped participants’ confidence in sustaining a career in clinical psychology, as expressed by one of the participants,

“My family wanted me to have a steady income, so there was pressure to become financially independent. I decided that if I did not get a job, I would have to look in another city or take up a full-time assistant professor position because I could not afford to waste my initial years.” (P8)

P8's account suggests that career decisions were shaped by a perceived timeline linking age, marriage, and financial independence. Employment was experienced not only as a professional milestone but also as a means of fulfilling socially expected responsibilities associated with adult masculinity.

Broadly, this theme demonstrates how participants negotiated tensions between culturally dominant expectations of masculinity and the relational demands of therapeutic care. They encountered assumptions that men were less empathic or naturally suited to clinical work while simultaneously facing expectations of financial provision, emotional self-control, continual availability, and professional competence. Participants did not simply experience these expectations passively; they challenged them in various ways, integrated care into their masculine and professional identities, and developed confidence through experience. Nevertheless, these negotiations shaped their professional legitimacy, boundaries, financial security, and occupational well-being.

This theme examines how participants learned to become clinical psychologists through practical exposure, supervision, mentorship, reflection, and collaborative work. It also encompasses the social dynamics, interactions, and relationships between male and female colleagues that shape professional skills, values, and identity. This theme comprises four subthemes: Training Pathways and Educational Experiences; Supervision, Mentorship, and Feedback; Collegial Relationships and Gender Dynamics; and Reflective Learning and Skill Development. Participants consistently emphasised the importance of practical exposure, particularly conducting clinical interviews and applying theoretical knowledge in supervised clinical settings.

“During my initial training, I felt blank. We knew the models and micro skills, but when I began applying them, I wondered, ‘What do I actually do at this point?'” (P2)

P2’s account illustrates the gap participants experienced between knowing therapeutic concepts and developing the situated judgement required to apply them in practice.

This subtheme captures participants' experiences of entering MPhil training and transitioning into the role of trainee therapists. Six participants described entering MPhil training with a combination of enthusiasm and uncertainty. They were excited to begin clinical work but initially lacked clarity about how to translate theoretical learning into therapeutic practice.

“I am a reader, and in practice, it is very difficult. On the first day, my supervisor told me to take the case and come back for supervision. I asked, but I don’t know how to take a session. Moreover, he said you will know how to jump into the water, and you will know how to swim.” (P7)

P7's account reflects a shift from theoretical knowledge to experiential learning, in which clinical confidence was cultivated through practice and supervision rather than by prior certainty.

Regarding training, participants described actively engaging in their trainee roles and making sustained use of learning opportunities. They reported that this period contributed significantly to the expansion of their skills, understanding, and professional knowledge.

“Throughout my training, I was always observing sessions, sitting with trainee
psychiatrists, and learning through observation and discussions. I really enjoyed
those opportunities to learn.” (P9)

P9's account illustrates how participants actively sought learning opportunities beyond direct clinical responsibilities, reflecting an experiential approach to developing professional knowledge and skills.

This subtheme captures participants’ experiences of supervision, mentorship, and feedback during and after training. Supportive supervision fostered reflection, confidence, and professional development, while more critical or emotionally intense supervisory encounters could also generate distress, as one participant noted.

“Supervision is a space where you can bring up professional challenges, discuss and reflect on how your work is going, and identify room for improvement. That was a big deal because it gave me guidance and direction in breaking through.” (P10)

Supervision is seen as both an educational and relational space. Its value came not only from technical guidance but also from having a trusted senior professional with whom difficulties could be discussed without judgement.

In contrast, three participants described supervisory feedback as emotionally challenging, particularly when mistakes were discussed in ways they experienced as highly critical. These experiences appeared to influence their confidence and emotional responses during training, although participants generally regarded such feedback as a demanding but expected aspect of professional development. Reflecting on these experiences, they acknowledged both the challenges and the learning opportunities associated with supervision and its role in shaping their professional growth and occupational well-being.

“I also come out of the room sometimes crying, and others also come out of the room, sometimes crying; it is like everybody went through the same thing.” (P12)

Participants described emotionally challenging supervisory feedback as a demanding yet meaningful aspect of their professional learning and development.

This subtheme captures participants’ perceptions of gender dynamics within predominantly female training cohorts, including visibility, collegial relationships, feedback, and case allocation. Although participants generally perceived formal treatment as equal across genders, some described their minority status as both advantageous and challenging. Five participants described increased visibility as a potential advantage of being the only man or one of the few men in their training cohort. This was expressed as,

“During MPhil training, while we were doing evening inpatient rounds, if there were patients who were violent, aggressive, or abusive, there was an automatic understanding that the male trainees would be pushed forward because of safety concerns. Sometimes, supervisors would say, 'Let them stay back; you go in, interact, and collect the MSE.' It supposedly came from a good place, but I think it created unequal opportunities for the female colleagues.” (P1)

This account illustrates how gendered assumptions shaped the allocation of physically risky cases during training. Although framed as protecting female trainees, participants reflected that this practice redistributed both risk and learning opportunities, disadvantaging women colleagues' clinical exposure.

This subtheme captures how participants developed clinical competence through repeated practice, reflection on mistakes, feedback, and increasing self-awareness.

“I reflect on the mistakes I have made and what I can change to help the client feel comfortable. I try to maintain empathy while also thinking practically and logically.” (P13)

This account demonstrates an effort to use reflection on mistakes to improve therapeutic responsiveness and balance empathy with clinical judgement.

In essence, this theme demonstrates that professional socialisation occurred through formal training and everyday encounters with supervisors, peers, clients, and institutional expectations. Participants described moving from theoretical knowledge towards situated clinical judgement through practical exposure, feedback, and reflection. Supervision could provide relational safety, confidence, and professional direction, but it could also become a source of distress when corrective feedback was delivered without sufficient psychological safety. Training was additionally gendered: male trainees experienced heightened visibility and were sometimes assumed to be more capable of managing physically risky patients. These assumptions exposed men to risk while restricting women’s learning opportunities. Professional development was therefore shaped not only by formal curricula but also by supervisory relationships, institutional norms, and gendered expectations.

This theme captures the personal, relational, and professional resources that supported participants’ occupational well-being and continued engagement in clinical psychology. It also examines the meaning participants derived from therapeutic work and the systemic changes they considered necessary for a more sustainable professional future. The theme comprises four subthemes: Family, Peer, and Professional Support; Self-Care, Boundaries, and Sustainable Practice; Meaning, Fulfilment, and Professional Commitment; and Envisioning Systemic Change.

Participants highlighted the need for greater role clarity and public awareness to strengthen the professional identity of clinical psychology.

“People do not know about clinical psychology. Everybody has their own roles, but people do not know about them... It is defined, but we do not put it into practice because it is an emerging field... I think in the future it will be clear.” (P12)

This reflects participants' perception that improving awareness and the consistent implementation of professional roles are essential to the profession's future recognition and sustainability.

This sub-theme captures the emotional, social, and professional resources that participants drew upon to navigate the demands of clinical practice. It highlights the role of family, friends, peers, supervisors, mentors, and professional networks in fostering resilience, coping, and occupational well-being, while recognising the importance of maintaining boundaries between work and personal life.

“To become a good clinical psychologist, you need family support, especially financial support. Psychology is a long process, and to study at a good institute, you need support from your family.” (P12)

This account highlights the importance of family support in enabling participants to navigate the prolonged demands of clinical psychology training.

Professional support through supervisors, seniors, and peers is an important resource. Supportive relationships, collaboration, and a sense of collegiality fostered confidence and professional growth.

“My supervisor, seniors, and batchmates had zero jealousy or competitiveness. They did not let me fail they gave me opportunities to grow beyond them.” (P7)

This account highlights how supportive professional relationships fostered participants' confidence and development.

This sub-theme explores how participants maintained their occupational well-being through self-care practices, boundary management, and sustainable approaches to clinical work. It highlights the importance of balancing professional responsibilities with personal well-being to support continued engagement in the profession.

“Proper sleep, eating on time, and following a routine help me stay organised.
Because work disrupts that, I go for bike rides, travel, and eat my favourite food to
support my mental well-being.” (P13)

This account highlights how self-care was not only about leisure, but about restoring structure, physical health, and emotional regulation in response to the demands of clinical work.

Awareness of when to establish boundaries and the ability to maintain them within professional settings enabled participants to achieve balance between their work and personal lives.

“I keep my professional and personal life separate. At home, I am a husband and a
father, not a psychologist. Spending time with my family helps me feel grounded.”
(P9)

This account highlights how maintaining clear professional boundaries supported participants' work–life balance and personal well-being.

This subtheme captures the sense of meaning and personal satisfaction that therapists derive from clients' progress and the perceived effectiveness of their work. It captures the emotional rewards of therapeutic engagement, independent of career growth or recognition.

“When clients begin to feel they need therapy less often, I realise therapy has worked. That is the most rewarding aspect for me.” (P3)

This account highlights how witnessing clients' growing independence was experienced as a meaningful indicator of therapeutic success.

Follow-up sessions were described as particularly rewarding, as clients returned to share that therapy had been beneficial and as therapists observed meaningful changes in their functioning.

“The follow ups I mean I would have seen the case six months back and they have
gone through the therapies of what I had suggested them and they have come back to
me to get another assessment, so when I see the child he will be totally different from
when I saw him in the first session that is how it will be very nice for me and they
have worked it into and what I have said has also been done overtime there.” (P2)

This account highlights how observing positive client outcomes contributed to participants' sense of professional fulfilment.

This subtheme refers to participants' reflections on how the profession and training systems could become more inclusive and supportive for male clinical psychologists. This theme encompasses recommendations for improving professional training, supervision, workplace culture, mentorship, and public awareness, alongside advice for men considering a career in clinical psychology.

“Build your personal brand, upskill yourself, and stay dedicated. Keep asking questions and remember that failure is part of learning and growth.” (P7)

Participants emphasised the importance of proactively building visibility, continuously developing their skills, and embracing lifelong learning to establish a successful career in clinical psychology.

It highlights participants' perspectives on the structural, institutional, and societal changes needed to foster greater inclusion, reduce gender-based assumptions, and enhance the professional experiences and well-being of male clinical psychologists.

“We need more government opportunities and better pay. Clinical psychologists put
significant effort into their work, yet many in government jobs are underpaid despite
the rising cost of living.” (P4)

P4 viewed greater institutional recognition, fair remuneration, and improved employment opportunities as essential for strengthening the profession and supporting male clinical psychologists.

Overall, this theme illustrates how participants sustained their work as clinical psychologists through supportive personal and professional relationships, self-care, and clear professional boundaries. Their commitment to the profession was reinforced by the meaning and fulfilment derived from clients' progress. At the same time, they also highlighted the need for greater institutional support, recognition, and systemic changes to foster a more sustainable and inclusive future for male clinical psychologists.

The present study explored the work experiences of male clinical psychologists in India, demonstrating how gendered expectations, institutional contexts, and evolving professional identities shaped their occupational well-being. Despite entering the profession through diverse pathways, participants consistently negotiated societal assumptions about masculinity while establishing professional legitimacy within a predominantly female profession. Professional identity developed through training, clinical practice, and reflection, while supportive relationships, self-care, and meaningful therapeutic work sustained well-being. Collectively, these findings extend the limited literature by highlighting the interplay of gender, professional socialisation, and the Indian sociocultural context in shaping male clinical psychologists’ experiences.

Theme 1, Pathways into Clinical Psychology, emphasises that people entered the field in various ways, such as a lifelong interest, job dissatisfaction, or a gradual exploration of psychology. Participants frequently created significant narratives about their professional decisions in retrospect, indicating that admittance into the field was actively understood over time. This is consistent with Lancaster () and Wise (), who characterise meaningful work and a developing sense of professional identity as the driving forces for career moves into helping professions. Through reading, educational advice, and exposure to the topic, participants actively investigated psychology, indicating that career entry was frequently thoughtful and well-informed. Consistent with earlier research on retrospective career meaning-making, even those who initially characterised their decision as accidental later reconstructed it as significant through education, clinical experience, and personal development. Consistent with Bhola et al. (), Scaffidi and Wilson,  and Wise (), participants' professional identities evolved progressively rather than being formed upon qualification, through training and clinical experience. Gaining more clinical experience boosted self-assurance and a sense of community, and autonomous practice emerged as a crucial turning point where theoretical knowledge transformed into embodied professional competence. The study's main conclusion was that navigating gendered societal expectations was a necessary part of starting a profession. Due to gendered occupational norms within the Indian sociocultural setting, psychology was perceived as a profession better suited to women, which led to scepticism among classmates, professors, and family for several participants (Del Castillo, ; Johnson et al., ). These responses prompted participants to defend their decisions, even though they did not hinder career admission. This suggests that professional identity formation began before formal training, challenging gendered assumptions about care-oriented occupations.

Theme 2, Systemic and Gendered Contexts, focuses on how institutional structures and gendered expectations influenced participants' experiences. In line with earlier studies, participants had to negotiate their professional suitability amid subtle stigma and assumptions that psychology was better suited to women (Baker, ; Del Castillo, ; Himmerich, ). They faced increased exposure and isolation, exacerbated by their restricted access to senior male mentors, similar to that experienced by women in other predominantly female professions (Scaffidi and Wilson, ). Participants noted institutional issues that went beyond gender, such as ambiguous professional boundaries, hierarchical ties with psychiatry, and a lack of organisational support. These results imply that challenges in the workplace were not only gendered but also represented structural problems in mental health treatment. Within the Indian setting, where professional duties and career paths may be ambiguous, these structural circumstances appeared to exacerbate participants' efforts to build professional credibility and find their place in the profession.

Theme 3, Negotiating Masculinity and Professional Identity, highlights how participants developed identities as clinical psychologists while continuously navigating culturally dominant norms of masculinity. In line with earlier studies, participants encountered stereotypes depicting men as less sympathetic, less emotionally expressive, and less suited to caregiving roles; to establish professional legitimacy, they had to show warmth and therapeutic competence (Del Castillo, ; Wisch & Mahalik, ). Participants indicated that they incorporated caring behaviours into their professional identities rather than rejecting masculinity, suggesting that therapeutic work actively repaired masculinity. According to social constructionist viewpoints, masculinities are negotiated and changeable rather than fixed (Connell, ). Additionally, participants discussed how traditional standards of masculinity went beyond therapeutic practice. Expectations of emotional independence, unwavering availability, and financial provision influenced experiences of burnout, work-life balance, and career decision-making. This is consistent with broader research showing that adherence to masculine norms can negatively affect men's well-being and help-seeking (Mahalik et al., ; Seidler and Wilson, ). These results collectively imply that developing a professional identity required not just gaining clinical competence but also balancing the relational requirements of clinical psychology with culturally ingrained expectations of masculinity in the Indian sociocultural setting.

Theme 4, Learning and Professional Socialisation, highlights that being a clinical psychologist required more than just learning theory; it was a relational and experiential process moulded by mentorship, supervision, introspection, and regular clinical practice. In line with Bhola et al. (), Kaur et al. () and Wise (), participants viewed professional competence as evolving gradually through feedback, reflective learning, and practical experience rather than only formal training. A key element of professional development, supervision promotes self-assurance, introspective practice, and clinical judgement. However, participants also reported emotionally upsetting supervisory feedback, which is consistent with research highlighting the significance of psychologically safe supervisory relationships. This suggests that the way in which feedback is given may affect confidence, willingness to acknowledge uncertainty, and professional development (Scaffidi and Wilson, ). Participants also emphasised how gendered interactions during training influenced professional socialisation. Male trainees were occasionally thought to be more qualified to handle physically hostile patients, which is consistent with earlier studies on gendered expectancies in helping professions (Johnson et al., ; Lancaster, ). These presumptions redistributed both clinical risk and learning opportunities, even though they were frequently presented as guaranteeing safety. This shows how informal gender stereotypes continued to influence professional training beyond the official curriculum.

These findings have particular implications for younger psychologists and trainees, whose early learning environments may shape their subsequent professional identities and clinical practice. Training programmes should provide psychologically safe and gender-responsive supervision, equitable case allocation, access to mentors and peer networks, and structured opportunities to examine how gendered expectations influence emotional expression, authority, caregiving, and the management of clinical risk. In the present study, male trainees’ numerical minority status sometimes heightened their visibility and contributed to assumptions that they were more capable of managing physically aggressive clients. If such assumptions remain unexamined, they may influence trainees’ professional confidence, willingness to seek support, use of supervision, comfort with emotional vulnerability, and later preferences regarding clinical roles. Although Abou Chabake et al. () focused on students’ involvement in traumatic-stress research rather than clinical training, they similarly identified unequal access to mentorship and professional networks, limited autonomy and institutional recognition, financial barriers, and gender-related constraints such as those associated with parenthood. They recommended structured mentorship, peer-support networks, flexible timelines, equitable workload distribution, and meaningful opportunities for student participation. Such support may enable young psychologists to develop professional identities and practices that are reflective and responsive to gender without treating gender as determinative of clinical competence.

Theme 5, Sustaining Well-Being and Envisioning Change, highlights how a combination of professional boundaries, self-care routines, supporting relationships, and the significance of therapeutic work helped participants maintain their occupational well-being. In line with Bhola et al. (), participants emphasised the value of interpersonal ties in promoting resilience and ongoing professional progress, characterising professional development as an ongoing process supported by family, peers, supervisors, and mentors. The importance of family support also reflects the Indian sociocultural milieu, where family ties are often crucial in helping people navigate the demands of long-term schooling and employment (Sodemba & Panwar, ). Additionally, participants emphasised the importance of maintaining distinct boundaries between their personal and professional lives, suggesting that boundary management and self-care were essential for sustaining long-term involvement in clinical practice. Consistent with Kumaria and Bhola, , observing clients' development and therapeutic transformation emerged as the primary source of professional fulfilment, highlighting the significance of meaning and purpose in keeping practitioners going despite the pressures of their jobs. Participants emphasised that maintaining occupational well-being requires both individual resources and broader institutional commitment to supporting the profession. In addition to individual strategies, they promoted stronger mentorship, better professional recognition, equitable compensation, and more career opportunities.

This study has several limitations. It included a focused purposive sample of 14 participants; therefore, the findings should be understood as contextually situated accounts rather than as representative of all male clinical psychologists in India. Although participants represented varied professional contexts, the sample may not capture the diversity of experiences across India’s geographical regions, institutional settings, linguistic backgrounds, and career stages. Participants worked predominantly in private-sector settings, and the experiences of clinical psychologists working in public, community, rural, or non-governmental services may differ. Participation required proficiency in English and access to an internet-enabled device. This may have favoured more urban, technologically connected, or English-speaking professionals and excluded psychologists who preferred to discuss their experiences in other Indian languages. The findings also reflect participants’ retrospective accounts and the meanings they attributed to their experiences at the time of the interviews. These accounts may have been shaped by memory, self-presentation, and the interpersonal context of the interview. In addition, the interviewer’s position as a female postgraduate trainee in clinical psychology may have influenced what participants chose to disclose and how they framed their gendered professional experiences. Although reflexive journaling and research-team discussions were used to critically examine this influence, the researcher's positionality remained part of the co-construction of the findings.

The study intentionally focused on male clinical psychologists and therefore cannot establish how their experiences compare with those of women or gender-diverse clinical psychologists. It also does not capture how clients, supervisors, trainees, or other mental health professionals understand the gendered dynamics described by participants. Despite these limitations, the study provides insight into the gendered professional identities and occupational well-being of an underexplored group of mental health practitioners in India. The findings demonstrate how masculine norms, emotional labour, client expectations, institutional structures, and financial pressures intersect in shaping professional practice and well-being. They also illuminate participants’ complex visibility within a female-dominated care profession, where being a man could generate increased recognition and presumed authority in some contexts while producing scrutiny, isolation, or doubts about caregiving ability in others.

The findings suggest value in incorporating structured reflection on gender, masculinity, emotional labour, therapist identity, and practitioner well-being within clinical psychology training. Supervisory spaces may benefit from explicitly considering how gendered expectations shape client interactions, case allocation, professional boundaries, emotional expression, vulnerability, and professional confidence. Attention to psychological safety is also important when providing corrective feedback and when supporting trainees in discussing mistakes or emotional strain. Institutions and professional bodies could strengthen mentorship and peer-support networks, clarify professional roles and career pathways, promote manageable workloads, and improve access to practitioner-support services. Such measures should complement, rather than replace, individual self-care.

Future studies could include more geographically, linguistically, and institutionally diverse samples and examine variations across public and private settings and different career stages. Comparative research involving women and gender-diverse clinical psychologists could identify shared and gender-specific professional experiences. Research incorporating the perspectives of clients, supervisors, and other mental health professionals may provide a more relational understanding of therapist-gender expectations. Longitudinal studies could also examine how professional identity, coping, and occupational well-being change across training and later career development.

This study investigated the gendered professional identities and well-being experiences of male clinical psychologists in India. The results demonstrate how the intersections of masculinity, clinical training, therapeutic practice, client expectations, institutional frameworks, and wider societal norms influenced participants' career paths. In addition to identifying fulfilment in therapy relationships, client advancement, and meaningful contribution to the profession, participants expressed difficulties with underrepresentation, gendered stereotypes, emotional labour, financial demands, and workplace dynamics. Overall, the study shows that male clinical psychologists in India have a complicated role in a care-oriented field that is both visible and scrutinised. The results highlight the necessity of reflective supervision, peer support, gender-sensitive training, and more robust institutional frameworks to enhance practitioner wellbeing and create a more diverse clinical psychology environment in India.

psychology.title: Neurocognition of dance: Guidelines for using dance as model behavior and research subject in cognitive neuroscience
psychology.abstract: Dance and movement science bridges cognitive psychology, neuroscience, cultural studies, philosophical aesthetics, and the performing arts. The field has evolved significantly, examining physical, social, psychological, and neural aspects of dance and movement execution and perception, contributing to a deeper understanding of human cognition and of dance itself. As the field expands, shared guidelines that support methodological rigor, reproducibility, and cultural relevance are of paramount importance. This paper synthesizes current research and introduces a comprehensive seven-principle research design framework for using dance in cognitive neuroscience. Key elements include the operationalization of “dance” in empirical sciences, the definition of who is a dancer, measures of expertise, and the importance of a culturally sensitive, holistic, and interdisciplinary approach to its investigation in the laboratory and in ecologically valid settings. This framework benefits research in dance and movement aesthetics, as well as investigations in social cognition, affective neuroscience, computer science, and artificial intelligence.
psychology.text:
Empirical research using dance as a model behavior to study neurocognitive processes, and dancers as neurocognitive models of expertise, offers valuable insights into how the human brain processes, learns, and responds to non-verbal, expressive, full-body movement and social interactions. Dance practices support cognitive rehabilitation and recovery from dysfunction, sometimes with higher success rates than traditional rehabilitation regimes. Evidence from the past 20 years supports the relevance of studying dance in basic and applied research across psychology, neuroscience, education, and computer science. However, guidelines and best methodological practices still need to be established to ensure the rigor, quality, and validity of such research, particularly given the methodological heterogeneity that may contribute to variability in reported outcomes.

Although dance is a complex phenomenon, it can be operationalized and investigated with the same scientific rigor applied to other forms of human movement. In July 2022, we, the authors of this paper, hosted a symposium titled “Emerging Multi-disciplinary Perspectives and Cutting-Edge Advancement in Dance Neuroaesthetics” at the ESCAN (European Society for Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience) biennial meeting. We highlighted state-of-the-art methodologies, challenges and open questions, and proposed a comprehensive seven-principle research design framework for using dance in cognitive neuroscience as a model behavior to investigate human cognition, or as a subject of research in itself. This paper is the result of the interdisciplinary dialogue between the authors that followed from this meeting. See .

The manuscript offers a guide for operationalizing dance (Section ), defining and measuring dance expertise (Section ), maintaining ecological validity across laboratory and real-world settings (Section ), improving reproducibility and methodological standards (Section ), fostering interdisciplinary approaches (Section ), incorporating cross-cultural and individual difference perspectives (Section ), and designing translational research in health and wellbeing contexts (Section ). See .

Our methodological framework draws on empirical work, literature reviews, and meta-analyses demonstrating how dance provides:(i)a model behavior for investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying action- and emotion perception, and movement representation.,, Research has established how dance observation recruits visuomotor (simulation) processes depending on the observer’s expertise, and how observers decode expressive whole-body movement in terms of affective and intentional meaning. For a review, see Foster Vander Elst et al. (2023).(ii)a tool to study the interplay of brain networks affording aesthetic appreciation of movement,,, such as the visual, sensorimotor, and reward systems. Studies in empirical aesthetics have determined how movement features, expertise, and contextual framing contribute to subjective evaluations and aesthetic experience of dance. For a review, see Kirsch et al. (2016) and Orlandi & Candidi (2025).(iii)a neurocognitive model of expertise to study neuroplasticity and learning.,,, Comparisons between trained dancers and non-dancers have revealed training-related differences in brain structure and connectivity, providing a model for studying experience-dependent plasticity. For an overview, see Karpati et al. (2015).(iv)a valuable tool for rehabilitation and recovery from disease and dysfunction in clinical settings.,,, Dance movement therapy and other dance-based interventions have been shown to have positive effects on motor, cognitive, and mental health outcomes across neurological and psychiatric populations. For a review, see Millman et al. (2021).

A comprehensive discussion of this literature lies beyond the scope of this paper. Focusing instead on providing a methodological framework, this work contributes to improving theoretical precision, research questions, operationalization, and reproducibility in dance-based cognitive neuroscience and related fields.

Everyone recognizes dance, yet no two people’s notions of what dance is are exactly the same. The term “dance” refers to behaviors ranging from simple rhythmic groove movements performed to a regular beat, to codified dance styles that can be learned by anyone, to highly structured movement repertoires requiring years of athletic and artistic practice. In some cultures, dance is not even differentiated from other performing arts such as music, song, and percussion., See  for examples and key differences between dance styles in terms of neurocognitive predispositions involved and potentially modulated by dance. The nature of a dance, whether social or competitive, can also depend on the dancer’s mindset or intention. For example, an Argentine tango milonga may serve purely as a relaxed, social gathering focused on internal connection (e.g., dancers moving with eyes closed), or as a highly performative and competitive display influenced by external attention (e.g., dancers hunting the gaze of others).

Most dance styles contain expressive elements, but the extent and form of expressivity can vary widely. For instance, Bharatanatyam places strong emphasis on storytelling, with specific hand gestures, facial expressions, and eye movements, with clear meanings to the trained eye, choreographed into its structure. While Western ballet also has codified repertoires and expressive potential, recreational dancers may not engage with these narrative elements as deeply. Interestingly, both Bharatanatyam and ballet allow for complete improvisation, in which expressivity becomes more personal and may not follow a shared or recognizable code among practitioners.

The term ‘classical’ dance is used here to refer to historically codified dance styles and techniques such as Western classical ballet and Indian classical dance (e.g., Bharatanatyam). These styles are traditionally performed in formal theatrical settings, typically featuring conventional staging, a proscenium layout, and a clear separation between performers and audience. More broadly, borrowing from scholarship on classical music and the arts, classical refers to cultural practices that are formalized through theory and pedagogy, shaped by specific social and historical contexts, and maintained across generations through institutional teaching, expert transmission, and a recognized canon of exemplary works.

In empirical research, scientists deconstruct phenomena into “independent variables” to study how they contribute to specific outcomes ("dependent variables"). Depending on the neurocognitive mechanism under investigation and the research question, one dance style may be more appropriate than another. Using the following four neurocognitive mechanisms, an example is provided for how research questions can be organized. (These four are illustrative and do not represent the full range of neurocognitive processes associated with dance. For a more extensive mapping of processes, see Section ; ).(i)Action simulation and entrainment – enabling humans to follow and synchronize their body movements with external rhythms or movements of other agents.,,,(ii)Neural plasticity/motor skill learning – reflecting adaptive (brain and body) changes associated with training, rehearsal, and repeated performance.,,,(iii)Imitation – enabling socialization through the acquisition and enactment of shared movement practices (e.g., who dances, when, and how).,,(iv)Enculturation – influencing how dance is perceived, interpreted, and valued within culturally specific contexts.,,

Action simulation and entrainment – enabling humans to follow and synchronize their body movements with external rhythms or movements of other agents.,,,

Neural plasticity/motor skill learning – reflecting adaptive (brain and body) changes associated with training, rehearsal, and repeated performance.,,,

Imitation – enabling socialization through the acquisition and enactment of shared movement practices (e.g., who dances, when, and how).,,

Enculturation – influencing how dance is perceived, interpreted, and valued within culturally specific contexts.,,

These mechanisms emerge early in life, while their expression and refinement depend on neurodevelopmental maturation, exposure, motor learning, and practice.,,,,,,,,, The engagement of these four may vary considerably, for example, depending on whether participants within an experiment watch a performance of Western contemporary dance or Indian classical Bharatanatyam.(A)A Western contemporary dance performance, unfamiliar to anyone watching. Two dancers walk on stage, make eye contact with the audience, and grin manically while standing still, without music, external rhythm, or synchronized movements.,,, In this performance, non-linear narratives, improvisation, and immersion are core aesthetic features.,(B)An Indian classical Bharatanatyam performance, where a dancer moves to familiar, mostly rhythmic music and conveys popular mythological stories, especially to those familiar with the mythology of that culture. The aesthetic features here are codified hand and facial gestures (mudras), body postures, and full-body movements that “tell” a story, in addition to moments of synchronous movement.,
