The aesthetic features here are codified hand and facial gestures (mudras), body postures, and full-body movements that “tell” a story, in addition to moments of synchronous movement.,

These two dances also differ with regard to other dimensions among the 11 outlined in .  compares these two dance styles with a third with respect to these dimensions. Even within the same dance style, dimensions such as co-presence, social touch, and synchrony may vary across performances, possibly engaging different neurocognitive processes in performers and observers.

Conclusions drawn from studies using these performances would be problematic without a clear conceptualization of what is meant by “dance” in each context and of the neurocognitive process under investigation. From a neuroscience perspective, the two examples represent very different classes of behavior.

Define what is meant by “dance” in the context of your study. Classify dance behaviors according to the neurocognitive mechanisms needed to perform and perceive them (refer to ; ; see also  in section ). Justify the selection of a specific dance style or technique based on movement features, dance dimensions of interest (e.g., movement complexity, music and rhythm, proximity and social touch, intention, expression), research questions, and neurocognitive mechanisms of interest (e.g., entrainment, plasticity/expertise, imitation, enculturation). Avoid generalizing findings across dance styles, techniques, or cultures without acknowledging these differences and discussing their implications. Ambiguities in classification are often part of cross-cultural research and should be addressed transparently, with decisions justified and documented, for example, through footnotes or supplementary material (e.g., ritual movement practice operationalized as “dance” in research on rhythmic coordination).

Central to the question of what dance is, is who is considered a dancer. Expertise studies in cognitive neuroscience require operationalizing the level of skill. The Cambridge Dictionary defines expertise as “a high level of knowledge or skill”, but a precise and standardized quantification of what constitutes a “high level” remains elusive in cognitive neuroscience and psychology, particularly in sports and the performing arts.,

Formal dance training changes the body, brain structure, and function. It provides complex technical visuo-motor skills to perceive, reproduce, and deconstruct complex movement into its constituent movement chunks. Watching dance regularly also modulates visual, motor, and memory systems,,, contributing to what is summarized as “visual dance expertise”.

Depending on expertise level and professional status, dance training includes: academic technique training, expressive practice, improvisation, partnering work, group synchronization practices, repertoire practice, musical practice, stage rehearsals, live performances, teaching, and choreography. These activities refine somatosensory and motor processes, memory, attention, emotional processes, non-verbal communication, social cognition, and higher-order skills such as divergent thinking (see Section ).

A number of questionnaires have been proposed to measure expertise across these domains. An overview of standardized inventories is provided in . Most have only recently been made publicly available or are not yet published in peer-reviewed journals. They were primarily developed in Western dance contexts and do not yet capture all dimensions of dance engagement, especially informal or digitally mediated participation). Existing questionnaires should therefore be considered useful tools for characterizing dance expertise rather than definitive standards for all dance populations. Future research should develop and validate measures capable of capturing emerging forms of dance engagement and training, including those enabled by rapidly evolving digital and immersive There is not yet a unified measure that combines practice-oriented and achievement/skill-oriented measures of dance expertise. A recent genetically informative study of 6610 Swedish twins suggests that factors contributing to dance achievement may not fully overlap with those associated with engagement and practice levels, highlighting the importance of considering both dimensions when characterizing dance expertise.

The most common practice in published experiments involving dance “experts” has been to report years of dance practice. Under this measure, “expertise” broadly includes all time spent in dance-related activities. Therefore, what constitutes “an expert” varies greatly across studies, from 3 years to 18 years of practice. Such discrepancies complicate cross-study comparisons. In what follows, the daily training behaviors relevant to dance expertise measures are outlined.

In daily academic training, dancers learn technically complex and precise movements, often in coordination and synchronization with others, and usually to music. Training builds stamina, endurance, breathing control, and memory for long movement sequences. It enhances proprioception, interoception, and the integration of visual, motor, and auditory information, which support action anticipation, error detection, motor control, motor learning, interpersonal coordination, and memory.

Through live performances, dancers develop stage presence and the ability to captivate an audience through their expressivity., They refine non-verbal communication and learn to convey emotions and meaning through movement. A broader movement repertoire enhances the range and precision of bodily expressions, supporting emotion expression and recognition, emotion regulation, self-awareness, and multisensory sensitivity to audience feedback., Performance also requires memory recall, interpersonal coordination, multisensory integration, and management of attention across dancers, the stage environment, and the audience.

Rehearsals are crucial for refining choreography, movement execution, and expressive skills. Dancers combine physical and mental practice, alternating between reproducing movement sequences and mentally simulating them., Kinesthetic (or motor) imagery is a powerful training tool in dance and other physical disciplines, supporting multisensory integration and enhancing body awareness. Depending on dance style, dancers may engage in auditory imagery, involving mental representations of music and sounds, as well as interoceptive or somatic imagery, involving representations of internal bodily states.

Three additional behaviors warrant attention when defining expertise: teaching,,
choreography, and improvisation.
Teaching movement to others strengthens verbal and non-verbal communication and fosters social cognition, including empathy and theory of mind. These processes are supported by attentional focus and by the ability to create and structure motor chunks, both critical for effective knowledge transfer.,

Choreography demands advanced visuospatial and memory skills, higher-order functions such as creativity (convergent and divergent thinking), and decision-making. These cognitive abilities enable dancers to design pieces that are emotionally expressive and meaningful (e.g., dramaturgy), visually engaging, novel, and captivating.

Improvisation is an integral part of a dancer’s skillset., It emerges from kinesthetic experience, movement habits, physical constraints, training, and memory, while employing divergent thinking during decision-making. Although central to Western contemporary dance,, contact improvisation, breakdancing, and Iranian classical dance, it is relatively uncommon in codified or highly structured styles such as ballet and modern dance (e.g., Graham, Horton, and Cunningham), which emphasize mastery of set vocabulary and technique.,, Dance styles vary in the extent to which they incorporate improvisation, and future research may benefit from considering improvisational practice in assessment of dance expertise. Compared to daily training, improvisation involves quickly adapting to environmental changes (e.g., sounds, other dancers) and engages divergent thinking, decision-making, multisensory integration, and interpersonal coordination.

For instance, contact improvisation differs from Western classical ballet not only in its reliance on improvisation, but also in the sensory modalities it emphasizes. While contact improvisation prioritizes touch, body awareness, and kinesthetic connection between dancers, ballet depends more heavily on visual information. This example shows why the neurocognitive competences developed through different dance behaviors cannot be fully captured by measuring “years of training” alone.

Dance experts also differ in the extent to which different neurocognitive competences are developed, depending on their level of engagement and the style or technique they practice.  outlines a practice-oriented and aspirational mapping of dance behaviors and the neurocognitive processes that may be associated with them. The table is intended to guide participant characterization and hypothesis generation, rather than to represent an exhaustive taxonomy or definitive evidence of one-to-one relationships between dance behaviors and neurocognitive processes.Table 3Assessing dance expertise: Neurocognitive processes likely stimulated by the practice of specific dance behaviorsDANCE behaviorsAcademic daily trainingRehearsalsLive performanceTeachingChoreographyImprovisationNEUROCOGNITIVE PROCESSESPerception proprioceptionXXXX interoceptionXXXX action anticipation/error detectionXXXXXX entrainment/movement-music synchronizationXXXX multisensory integrationXXXXMotor functions motor control/coordinationXXXX motor learningX motor chunk creationXXX interpersonal coordinationXXXMemory memory encodingXXX memory recallXXXXXXImagery/mental training(visual, motor, somatosensory, auditory)XXXXXAttention joint action/joint attentionXXXX divided attentionXXXXEmotion emotion expressionXXXX emotion regulationX emotion recognitionX self-awarenessXXXX awareness of audience reactionsXXXCommunication/Language non-verbal communicationXXXXX verbal communicationXSocial cognition theory of mindXXX empathyXXXXXHigh-order functions convergent thinkingXX divergent thinkingXX decision makingXX

Assessing dance expertise: Neurocognitive processes likely stimulated by the practice of specific dance behaviors

Most formal dance education combines multiple techniques and somatic practices,,, making it difficult to identify dancers trained exclusively in one style. Consultation with a dance expert, such as a performer, teacher, or choreographer, is therefore strongly recommended when selecting participants across training backgrounds (see also Section ).

Age of onset refers to the age at which a skill is first acquired. Although no longitudinal studies have investigated the effect of long-term dance practice in children, short-term intervention studies suggest that dance can support the development of motor and executive functions, and social skills., Therefore, it is valuable to collect the age of dance training onset alongside existing expertise inventories (e.g., Gold-DSI), which capture duration and extent of training but not when training begins.

Differentiating between visuomotor and visual expertise in dance is important because visual experience alone can lead to covert movement simulation, and the left premotor cortex may be sensitive to multisensory integration. However, there is no clear consensus on how best to quantify visual expertise in dance observers. Most studies rely on the number of live performances attended annually,,, while other forms of exposure, such as films (e.g., Bollywood), online videos, and social media, are rarely considered. These digital experiences often involve simple, repetitive routines that differ from professional or live performances, and it remains unclear whether they constitute meaningful visual expertise. Similarly, the influence of viewing medium, such as smartphone vs. large display, on biological motion perception has yet to be systematically examined. A promising development is the inclusion of dedicated items assessing observational experience in recent psychometric instruments, such as in the Gold-DSI.

Dancers are not only trained in motor skills but also in artistic and emotional expressivity. Feelings, meanings, and narratives are conveyed through bodily movements. As a result, dancers may exhibit enhanced interoceptive accuracy or awareness. Moreover, expert dancers generally show superior physical fitness, lower body mass index (BMI), enhanced proprioceptive abilities, and greater body awareness than non-dancers.,,,, These characteristics are difficult to assess through self-report questionnaires alone, and the most appropriate measures of expertise may vary with the research question.

We propose defining dance expertise multidimensionally, considering activities such as daily training, live performance, rehearsal, teaching, choreography, and improvisation, that develop distinct neurocognitive competences (see ). We recommend differentiating visuomotor and visual expertise across dance styles, reporting age of onset, and using validated inventories such as the Gold-DSI as part of a multidimensional assessment of expertise, ideally complemented by physiological and other psychometric measures relevant to dance training. Collaborating with dance professionals is essential for accurate classification.

Most dance-related studies have been conducted in laboratory settings, with low ecological validity, where participants viewed dance videos or pictures, often in greyscale, with contextual elements blurred or removed.  provides an overview of research settings, methods, and stimuli employed in dance research with regard to (1) the setting in which dance is performed and/or experienced and (2) the quality and realism of stimuli used to represent it.

Movement degrades signal quality in neuroimaging. However, advances in mobile brain imaging make it possible to record neural activity and cognitive responses in ecological (performance) settings, including real-world full-body behaviors,,,, and dance—on stage, in nightclubs, and in social spaces.

Dynamic social interactions can be indexed by measuring interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), the similarity in brain activity between individuals over time.,,, However, most studies measure neural synchrony between individuals experiencing the same stimulus sequentially, rather than simultaneously, and studies involving large groups sharing the same physical space remain rare. One notable exception was Rai et al. (2025). An interdisciplinary team recorded mobile EEG from 23 audience members simultaneously in a theater. INS between spectators was highest in the delta frequency band and varied with the dancers’ movements and subjective ratings of expected audience engagement, as predicted by the choreographer and performer. Neural synchrony was highest during moments of direct interaction with the dancers (i.e., eye contact), and was significantly higher than during solo laboratory viewing of the same performance. These findings provide initial neuroscientific evidence that experiencing dance involves active communication between performers and spectators, and that artistic intentions can be “detected” as INS among audience members. Together with other studies,,, this illustrates the importance of co-presence for the full aesthetic experience, which is only possible in ecological settings.

While artifact rejection methods have been developed for cleaning movement-induced noise in EEG recordings, these have been evaluated primarily during walking or cycling, with limited testing for more complex, dance-like movements. There is, so far, no standard method for processing locomotive EEG data. It is therefore important to consider whether the type and range of movement involved in a choreography can be reliably measured using mobile brain imaging equipment. The mobile brain/body imaging approach combines physiological measurements, motion tracking, and data-driven EEG analyses to differentiate neural from non-neural activity. First studies have successfully implemented this approach, recording EEG in participants spontaneously moving to music.

Methods from vision science can also support the study of cognitive processes in ecologically valid dance research. Eye-tracking can monitor observers’ visual behavior in laboratory and real-world environments. Although still limited, available evidence suggests that dance expertise enhances visual processing speed, potentially enabling experts to anticipate movements and process choreographic material faster. Expert dancers exhibit faster saccades and more clustered fixations, particularly when music and dance are synchronized., Measuring audience gaze with mobile eye tracking, especially when combined with objective estimates of body kinematics, may provide novel insights into collective attention during live dance performances (Arthuis et al., 2024. Conference poster at https://osf.io/4v7j2) and assist with eye-gaze/head movement artifact removal.

Combining methodological approaches, research beyond traditional laboratory environments can offer a more comprehensive understanding of the neural and cognitive processes engaged during dance performance and observation. Novel methods for artifact removal also support research in countries where access to traditional laboratory infrastructure is limited. However, efforts to increase ecological validity entail practical challenges and costs (challenging particularly for researchers working in under-resourced contexts). Besides, participants experience fatigue from wearable devices or extended recording time. These constraints may represent important challenges still to be resolved.

Early studies using dance as a research tool investigated neurocognitive functions such as action perception, visual processing, visuo-motor integration, and motor learning. These studies often employed videos of short dance sequences and recruited dancers as movement experts.,,,, Stimuli were typically brief (e.g., 5–20 s) and often drawn from Western classical ballet due to its formalization and experimental controllability. To maintain control, dance stimuli were often deprived of contextual information, with dancers filmed against plain backgrounds or reduced to point-light displays via motion capture. The advantage of such well-controlled paradigms is the ability to investigate the contribution of carefully controlled variables including temporal features (e.g., velocity, acceleration, smoothness, or synchrony), or spatial features (e.g., body positioning, visual overlap, or two-body entanglement) to dance evaluation. Dance movement stimuli can be validated, either by comparing ratings from expert and non-expert dancers or by quantifying movement features. Algorithms based on deep neural networks, such as OpenPose and DensePose, can estimate body kinematics for statistical analyses.

Importantly, approaching dance purely as a set of reducible, quantifiable features risks overlooking the essence of the experience itself., Critical features are lost, including the performer’s physical presence and expressivity, set and lighting design, and the dynamic structure of choreography or narrative over time. Future research may address these limitations by leveraging technological advances in brain imaging and applying data-driven, multivariate time-series analyses to capture the multidimensional, embodied nature of dance as it is experienced in real-life settings.

Different research questions require different research settings. Traditional laboratory settings and ecologically valid, live, or social contexts each have specific advantages and limitations. When feasible, combining methods can provide converging evidence. Mobile brain/body imaging, including wearable EEG or fNIRS, allows neural responses to be collected in naturalistic settings. Combining qualitative dancers’ reports of movement intention with interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) and computer vision tools (e.g., OpenPose, DensePose) helps connect performer intention to observer perception without reducing dance to kinematic variables alone. Striking a balance between experimental control and ecological realism is key for meaningful generalization.

Amid growing scrutiny of research reliability, particularly in light of the replication crisis in psychology and neuroscience, dance research stands to benefit from adopting rigorous methodological and reporting standards.,,,, Given the variability described in sections , , and , detailed information on dance style choice, (1) participants’ characteristics (e.g., multidimensional assessment of dance expertise; ) and (2) stimulus characteristics (;  and ) is required to allow evaluation, comparability, and replicability. Besides, Open Science practices ensure transparency, reproducibility, and interdisciplinary impact. These include open-access publications or preprints, open datasets, shared stimulus sets, protocols, and analysis code.

Dance research poses distinct challenges for reproducibility because of the embodied character, stylistic diversity, and cultural specificity of dance itself, as discussed further in Section . Where feasible, sharing movement recordings or kinematic datasets in standardized formats can enable comparison and reanalysis. Because stimulus standardization is closely linked to ecological validity, shared stimuli should be supported by comprehensive metadata. Relevant descriptors include the number of dancers, movement vocabulary, or step names (where applicable; some dance techniques rely on formally defined vocabularies (e.g., classical ballet), while others do not), music and sound properties, costumes, lighting, stage design, and recording conditions. Visibility is also important: while open-access publications can increase access for academic and non-academic audiences, dissemination through press releases, podcasts, workshops, and public engagement initiatives raises the profile of this field. Besides, events that integrate scientific presentations with movement-based activities also foster dialogue between researchers, artists, and practitioners.

Provide transparent descriptions of stimuli and clear rationales for choosing specific dance styles. Specify participants’ inclusion criteria, favoring a multivariate assessment of dance expertise when engaging with professional or semi-professional dancers. Clearly justify research settings and design choices, especially in out-of-the-lab contexts. Conduct a priori power analyses, report effect sizes, and pre-register study protocols and analysis plans. Adopt open and reproducible workflows, sharing stimulus sets, data, and code where possible, to support replication, comparability, and alignment with broader Open Science standards.

Science aims to systematize the natural, social, and personal phenomena into measurable variables that can be studied with qualitative or quantitative methods. Because methods differ across disciplines, interdisciplinary teams are essential, also in dance research. Just as meaningful scientific insights into athletic performance require collaboration with athletes, dance research needs collaboration with dancers, performers, and choreographers. Dance expertise alone is not sufficient to design scientifically rigorous studies, but plays a critical role in “translating” what dance is to non-dancer scientists within the team, enriching both the creative and the scientific process., Jola (2020) proposed two complementary approaches: (1) embodied neuroscience, in which scientists embody the physical practice of their topic of investigation, and (2) experimental choreography, in which artists engage with science so that performances emphasize both artistic and scientific value.,

Collaboration with artists provides guidance in navigating the diversity of dance styles, techniques, and training domains discussed in Sections , , and . Dance experts contribute to the creation and selection of movement features, ranging from single steps to complex sequences. Their knowledge of semiotics and dramaturgy (semiotics = how bodily gestures, postures, and spatial dynamics convey meaning, emotion, and narrative; dramaturgy = the conceptual, structural, and interpretive development of a dance piece) offers valuable insight for studying non-verbal communication through movement and helps overcome technical limitations, since some dance movements may be difficult to record using video or motion tracking suits, or may not be physically feasible under experimental constraints., Finally, interdisciplinary teams benefit from establishing shared terminology and definitions (for example, two individuals may be differently classified as “interacting” depending on whether the framework comes from social cognition or choreographic theory).

Recent interdisciplinary projects combining dance, digital humanities, computer science, psychology, and neuroscience have contributed to cultural preservation, technological innovation, and artistic practice, besides scientific advancement. Using a combination of filmography and motion tracking methods, for example, the Motion Bank project (https://www.motionbank.org/), the Virtual Dance Museum (https://dancemuseum.cs.ucy.ac.cy) for Cypriot folk dances, and the Iranian classical dance documentation project,,,, have contributed to dance documentation, transmission, and preservation. A methodological framework developed to aid such endeavors in the future is the EMOKINE framework, an open-access motion capture analysis tool that extracts statistics from kinematic features of full-body movement and is compatible with multiple motion capture systems.

Expanding dance research into computer science and robotics has already borne fruit. AI-powered digital technologies, and avatar-based media feed into the emerging area of “choreorobotics”, which applies principles of choreography, movement analysis, and somatic practice to expressive robotic systems. Besides, the novel technologies can inform choreographers about how aesthetic responses vary when dance movements are performed by a human dancer, a humanoid avatar, or an artificial agent,,,, with results suggesting that, despite the seductive allure of the novel technologies, human dance remains the most aesthetically pleasing to the human brain. These developments also extend to dance production and educational contexts, where AI-based systems are increasingly explored as tools for creative collaboration (Jobin, G. (2024). CIE Gilles Jobin Studios44/MocapLab https://www.gillesjobin.com/en/), and classroom-based movement interventions.,,

Build interdisciplinary teams involving scientists, dance professionals, and experts from relevant artistic and technological fields as equal collaborators. Co-develop research questions, methods, and stimulus design, drawing on both scientific and artistic expertise. Where available, use validated tools (e.g., motion capture) and validated analysis software (e.g., EMOKINE), to support innovation in both the arts and sciences, and translate embodied knowledge into applications in education, society, and healthcare.

Cross-cultural empirical (neuro)aesthetics investigates the universality and distinctiveness of cognitive and neural processes underlying aesthetic experiences across cultures. Despite its ubiquitous presence across societies, dance remains a relatively neglected topic in this domain. In most cultures, dance occupies an important social role, while in others it is deeply embedded in religious, spiritual, or cultural practices. Cultures have developed unique dance traditions, each practiced for specific expressive reasons., Dance also fulfills multiple psychobiological functions and regulates social and emotional behaviors.,,

Dance is culturally and socially constructed, yet it relies on core neurocognitive mechanisms such as motor control, entrainment, simulation, and expression. The multicultural nature of dance styles makes it difficult to define truly universal perceptual, cognitive, and emotional processes associated with “dance”. This cultural complexity must be accounted for in study design. However, many current investigations are limited by a broadly Western-centric perspective. Recognizing these cultural differences is crucial to understanding dance as a multisensory, multicomponent practice rooted in social and cultural contexts.

In immigration psychology, enculturation refers to the neurodevelopmental process through which individuals adopt cultural norms, while acculturation occurs when exposure to a new culture after migration shapes behaviors and preferences., These processes influence cultural life, including dance, and are shaped by both conscious and unconscious experiences. Despite their relevance, few cross-cultural studies have directly investigated differences and universals in dance perception and practice.

Recent studies demonstrate that dance evaluation is shaped by prior exposure, cultural background, enculturation, acculturation, and dance training, influencing emotional recognition and aesthetic preferences. Cross-cultural studies suggest that participants may show ethnocentric biases, meaning that they may evaluate or interpret dance more favorably when it is culturally familiar, as shown by Darda and Cross (2022), who also found that this bias was reduced in dance experts. Related work involving Western, Indian, Japanese, and Iranian contexts further suggests that cultural background, enculturation, and acculturation can shape dance preferences and emotion recognition.,, Future research should consider that concepts such as dancing bodies, spatiality, movement quality, aesthetic values, communicative functions, and expertise criteria are often framed through specific cultural lenses and may not apply universally across dance traditions. Deconstructing these ethnocentric biases is essential to place dance forms across different cultures on an equal footing and promote a more inclusive and representative study of dance.

Learning from studies with non-Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) dance traditions and participants is critical for generalizing to and learning from other populations. For example, Western ballet is typically structured around syllabus-based training focused on technique,, whereas Iranian classical dance is more imitation-based, allowing expressive movement at earlier learning stages., Because dance training style influences aesthetic preferences and the perception of unfamiliar dance styles, exploring embodied concepts such as corporeality and spatiality within different dance contexts could enhance cross-cultural understanding. The complex nature of dance also calls for multidisciplinary and mixed-method approaches to fully capture its dynamic role in human culture.

Both cultural specificity and universal foundations of dance behaviors are important mechanisms to study. Mechanisms such as entrainment and simulation may be shared across humans, yet their manifestation is shaped by cultural context. Participants’ cultural background, prior exposure, and experiences of enculturation or acculturation can be assessed with questionnaires (e.g., the Enculturation and Acculturation Quiz; EAQ). Findings from one dance tradition cannot be generalized to all dance traditions.

The benefits of dance practice in the general population are noted across health-related scientific disciplines.,,,, Dance-based interventions draw on partnered (e.g., standard dance, Argentine tango), group (e.g., jazz dance, contemporary, hip-hop), and traditional dance forms (e.g., African dance Nogma). In neurological diseases, dance interventions have supported treatment adherence, mental health, psychosocial functioning, cognitive capacity, and motor skills. In Parkinson’s disease, meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have found that dance improves motor symptoms, functional mobility, cognition, and quality of life.,, Similar benefits have been reported in oncology and cardiac disease populations, where dance supports increased physical activity, mental health, and overall quality of life. Yet, recent reviews have also reported mixed, small, or contradictory effects in some populations and outcome measures.

Variability in intervention protocols, sample characteristics, and outcome measures continues to challenge the field. Heterogeneity in study designs, including differences in sample sizes, age groups, treatment frequencies, specification of treatment factors, and clinical populations—and importantly, of dance style—makes it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about efficacy. For example, Argentine tango has been associated with greater improvement in motor-related symptoms in individuals with Parkinson’s disease compared to other dance forms. Identifying what differentiates Argentine tango from styles such as Waltz for individuals with Parkinson’s disease may help tailor dance interventions to better target specific neurocognitive, emotional, or motor processes. In general, interventions often lack standardization and valid control groups, further complicating comparisons across studies. Consequently, distinguishing genuine null effects from limitations in the available evidence remains challenging.

A notable exception is dance movement therapy (DMT). DMT is a validated psychotherapeutic dance intervention package with clear therapeutic factors approved for clinical settings. DMT is grounded in the principle that physical movement can reflect emotional states, and that modifying these movement patterns can influence both psychological and social experiences. A recent scoping review of DMT and other Creative Arts Therapies (CATs) identified therapeutic factors at three levels. These include common psychotherapy factors such as the therapeutic alliance, emotional regulation, and the creation of a safe environment. They also include factors shared across CATs, such as artistic engagement, symbolic work, self-display, and re-enactment. DMT-specific factors include embodiment, understood as experiencing the body and increasing body awareness, expressing, and sharing emotions non-verbally through movement, using movement metaphors and bodily sensations for insight, and artistic agency. A meta-analysis about DMT showed that expressivity was the treatment factor most directly linked to reductions in symptoms of depression and anxiety., Relational processes, such as kinesthetic empathy, mirroring, movement dialogue, and synchrony, are also central to DMT. In clinical populations, DMT has been shown to reduce symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress. As a psychotherapeutic approach, DMT may offer benefits beyond general physical exercises, meditation, or other CATs, including enhanced proprioception and interoception, refined motor imagery, and improved emotional awareness, capacities also developed through professional dance training.

Dance-based (non-DMT) interventions can use DMT as a model for implementing structured methods and identifying factors that may contribute to positive health outcomes, optimizing dance style choice, treatment duration, frequency, and intensity of any intervention for a specific health outcome.

Standardized practices and methodological improvements are needed across domains of dance-based interventions for health. Priorities include larger sample sizes, rigorously designed RCTs with appropriate blinding, long-term follow-ups, development of disorder-specific protocols, specification of treatment factors, reporting of key intervention variables (e.g., frequency, duration, facilitator expertise), use of standardized outcome measures, and an operationalization statement about how key variables are hypothesized to modulate the neurocognitive process under investigation, ensuring also gender balance and representation of minoritized and Indigenous groups.

By strengthening the theoretical and methodological foundations of dance-based interventions, future studies can contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for healthcare and policy. We recognize that dance-based health research remains underfunded compared with other arts-based therapies, such as music and art therapies, and that high methodological standards can be challenging under limited resources. Yet, even partial alignment with these principles can move the field forward and strengthen its credibility, visibility, funding opportunities, and translational impact.

By examining what defines dance, how dance expertise can be measured, and how dance can be studied across laboratory and real-world contexts, this seven-principle framework promotes a systematic approach.

Emphasizing inclusivity, individual variation, cross-disciplinary collaborations, replicability, and visibility, the framework supports evidence that can deepen our understanding of dance’s impact on individuals and communities. Ultimately, it aims to bridge academic inquiry and societal application while fostering innovation across disciplines.

psychology.title: Feasibility of Mini Group Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT-G Mini) for Kenyan Adolescents
psychology.abstract: Background: Group interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT-G) has universal elements that appeal to non-Western cultural contexts, while offering flexibility for contextual adaptations, making it an intervention of choice for adolescent populations in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). We anticipate that a shorter four-session version, which we are calling IPT-G Mini, offered to adolescents and young people during the COVID-19 pandemic, would effectively mitigate psychological distress.Objective: The objective of this study was to test the feasibility of a short version of IPT-G among adolescents screened for depression and anxiety.Methods: IPT-G Mini was offered by lay health workers to 40 adolescents aged 10–19 years in Nairobi, Kenya, experiencing depressive, stress, and anxiety symptoms during the COVID-19 pandemic during June–September 2021. Primary outcomes were a reduction in depression and psychological distress on the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), Revised Children’s Anxiety and Depression, and Kessler Psychological Distress (K10) scales.Findings: The intervention was effective, with a significant reduction in psychological distress (K10) and depression (PHQ-9) scores at the end of the intervention (with p < 0.05), Cohen’s d = 0.49 (95% C.I. = 0.04–0.94) and d = 0.51 (95% C.I. = 0.06–0.96), respectively. Younger participants (10–14 years) had better outcomes than older ones on K10 and PHQ-9 assessments.Conclusions: IPT-G Mini must be tested in a more controlled setting with a larger and more diverse sample. It does appear to reduce distress and depressive symptoms, and further evaluation may be needed to refine the adapted version. Despite the challenges brought by the pandemic, the timely and effective intervention focused on interpersonal issues proved beneficial to participants. Addressing various problem areas helped provide perspective and support in dealing with multiple losses and socioeconomic hardships experienced by our young participants.
psychology.text:
Mental health disorders are highly prevalent in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [], and tailored mental health services are not only underdeveloped but also underfunded within the health system. The 2019 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) data for adolescents aged 10–24 years in Kenya showed the highest prevalence of mental disorders in depressive, anxiety, and conduct disorders []. Studies have also underscored the discrepancy between the demand and availability of mental health care for adolescents and youth populations throughout the world [, ]. Additionally, the COVID-19 pandemic further worsened the detrimental effects on children and adolescents due to lockdown, disrupted schooling, adversely impacted learning outcomes, and decreased opportunities for socialization and recreation [].

The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) as a key evidence-based intervention [, ] for task-shared and task-shifted mental health delivery in low-resource contexts. In this sense, it is the redistribution and delegation of activities and tasks among health workforce teams, where both fully trained and qualified health workers, alongside other nonspecialist or lay health workers with shorter training duration, work together to deliver mental health services []. The WHO’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) [] and its associated quality and service improvement guidelines promote the idea of quick assessment, management, and referral pipeline in primary and tertiary care. IPT is one of the recommended treatments within the WHO mhGAP.

Several studies have used IPT during the pandemic [–]. A case report by Hu et al. documented that four sessions of IPT delivered face to face to a patient diagnosed with depression, anxiety, and COVID-19 led to a reduction in his depression symptoms and anxiety. This was evidenced by a decrease in assessment scores using the Hamilton rating scale and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) to measure depression and anxiety levels after the therapy []. Another study by Swartz et al., in 2014, found that the concentrated focus on brief interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT-B) is highly beneficial for individuals dealing with various interpersonal issues. The framework of IPT-B compels patients (and therapists) to target the most urgent—and ideally resolvable—interpersonal problem as the core of the treatment. This approach offers a sense of direction and structure amid the turmoil []. Considering Kenyan adolescents, Kumar et al. developed a model for implementing IPT within the WHO’s mhGAP—a depression-care framework for pregnant adolescents. The authors enhanced the existing eight-session version in their model by incorporating additional implementation strategies such as stigma reduction, task-sharing, and peer engagement. Additionally, they tailored a shorter four-session version called IPT-G Mini to effectively address perinatal depression among this population [].

The protocol for this mini IPT was published a few years back [, ], and the publications highlighted the possible benefits of task-shifting in addressing mental health problems within low-resource settings in Kenya and demonstrated that delivery of IPT-G was acceptable and feasible by lay and nonspecialist health workers to adolescents receiving primary care services []. Mattos et al. concluded that implementing IPT-G in primary care is a complex process involving several steps. In the first step, successful training of health professionals is crucial; the subsequent steps are more complex and, therefore, require careful planning to maximize the success of an integrated treatment within primary care settings [, –].

This study was embedded under a UNICEF Measurement of Adolescent Mental Health at Population Level [], where we worked with Nairobi County and the Ministry of Health’s Division of Mental Health and Substance Use to test population-level measurement of key mental health tools such as PHQ-9 [], Revised Children’s Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS) [], and UNICEF Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) [] assessment for adolescent functioning [, ]. Participants who were screened with high depression and anxiety or found to have suicidal thoughts, intent, and actions were provided referrals to the county and national referral hospitals available in Nairobi. We also included high-risk participants, such as those who lost family members due to COVID-19, as they were expressing distress and need for help. The pandemic caused a lot of disruption in routine family activities, affecting the flow of income, food security, boredom due to lockdown, unusual conflicts following unmet needs within the families, anticipated grief in some instances arising from panic from the disturbing scenes on social media, and an increase in teenage pregnancy; hence, in this context, we decided to deploy IPT-G Mini, which is a four-session therapy model.

A survey on the mental health needs of adolescents aged 10–19 years was carried out from June to July 2021 in two primary care clinic sites (n = 250) where large informal settlement neighborhoods are based. This survey was a UNICEF’s Measurement of Mental Health among Adolescents at the Population Level (MMAP) initiative [] that was embedded within a larger study on mental health interventions for pregnant adolescents (INSPIRE) []. Participants who had a score of moderate to severe depression (PHQ-9 score of 15–27) or anxiety or had suicidal ideations were invited to participate in the intervention (n = 40). Participants above 18 years gave consent, while those below 18 years gave assent, followed by their parent or caregiver’s consent. The intervention was delivered in the primary healthcare clinic in Nairobi, which was accessible and closer to the participants’ homes.

We used the mental health needs of adolescents’ survey as baseline screening information to recruit participants for this rapid trial and follow-up that happened between August and October 2021. The baseline survey collected sociodemographic information, depression, anxiety, and social functioning. This assessment was conducted by lay health workers, also known as community health promoters (CHPs). They are not formally trained as healthcare professionals but belong to and possess both cultural and linguistic understanding of the community they serve, thus playing a crucial role in promoting and improving community health. The lay health workers were trained in identifying participants, assenting and consenting, conducting research with human subjects, and administering the measures used in the baseline survey item by item. A few participants were invited, and CHPs piloted the tools under the close supervision of the research team. Post-intervention (after delivery of four sessions) data were collected using a recently validated PHQ-9 scale by Tele et al., which established that the psychometric properties of both English and Swahili-adapted versions were comparable indications they were reliable and valid instruments for detecting major depressive disorders among adolescents []. Depression is a clinical diagnosis characterized by a prolonged, persistent state of low mood, while psychological distress, as assessed using Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10) [], is a broader domain encompassing a range of emotional and mental health symptoms that may not meet the criteria for a specific mental health disorder (see ).

Kariobangi Health Center is a level three facility managed by Nairobi City County Government. Level three health facilities include health centers, maternity, and subdistrict hospitals. The Health Center is situated in the northeastern part of Nairobi, Kenya, and serves a low-income resident population that largely depends on public health services offered at minimal or no cost to the residents. This area comprises both lower middle-class areas and slum-type regions known as Kariobangi North, with a population of 18,903 residents. The Health Center plays a vital role in the community’s well-being []. Similarly, Kangemi Health Center, the second study site, is a level three facility managed by Nairobi City County Government. The facility is located in a small valley on the outskirts of the city, and according to the 2019 census, Kangemi is home to 116,710 residents []. Therefore, this health facility serves a large informal settlement community, catering to their medical needs at minimal or no cost.

Community health volunteers, currently referred to as CHPs, recruited community members to participate in the mental health survey. The CHPs obtained consent from the participants and assent from minors and caregivers’ consent where it was required. The baseline data were collected through a survey administered by the CHPs. Participants identified as having moderate to severe depression were invited to attend a short therapy program. This therapy consisted of four sessions that were held once per week. The group sessions were facilitated by CHPs who had received training as facilitators of group Interpersonal psychotherapy. At the beginning of each session, the participants were assessed for psychological distress by the CHP facilitator. This screening was aimed at monitoring their progress and helping facilitators provide appropriate support throughout the therapy. Upon completion of the four sessions, the participants were screened again using the same tools used for baseline assessment. This intervention screening took place 1 month after the therapy had ended. The purpose of the screening was to evaluate the progress and any changes in the mental health status.

Ethical approval was obtained from the Kenyatta National Hospital/University of Nairobi Ethical Review Committee (No. P694/09/2018) and a research permit from the Kenya National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation (NACOSTI/P/19/77705/28063). Permission was also obtained from these study sites through the Nairobi County Directorate of Health (Approval no. CMO/NRB/OPR/VOL1/2019/04). This study was nested under M.K.’s work on Implementing mental health interventions for pregnant adolescents in primary care LMIC settings (INSPIRE) study. Participants were assigned unique identifiers to protect their identities; collected data were stored in password-protected computers, while consent and assent forms or any document containing identifying information were kept in lock-and-key cabinets only accessed by authorized study staff. Oral and written consent was obtained from participants, as well as informed assent, which was followed by seeking parental/caregiver consent for participants who were below 18 years.

M.K. developed an outline of the four-session intervention by utilizing qualitative evidence that delved into the mental well-being of peripartum adolescents, with a specific emphasis on four IPT problem areas during the formative phase; the researchers were able to gain a richer understanding [, ]. The interpersonal framework revealed crucial insights into adolescent depression, indicating its potential to guide the development of strategies to relieve their distress [, , ]. The implementation of this four-session IPT-G Mini was a collaborative effort. O.Y., a trainer in IPT-G with a background in clinical psychology, and V.N. a trainer in carrying out IPT assessments and program delivery in community settings, developed standard operating procedures. Training of CHPs and intervention delivery procedures were further developed with J.K. and S.M., who are clinical psychologists and county staff, and were undergoing training to become IPT field supervisors. They carefully reviewed the overall mental and physical health needs of recruited participants. M.K. and O.Y. conducted training for the CHPs on delivering the IPT-G Mini. We adhered to the mini IPT protocol that was recently published, which outlined the challenges faced by peripartum adolescents in Kenyan primary care settings while also exploring strategies to strike a balance in addressing issues of adaptation, fidelity, and modification of the intervention []. A rapid online workshop over 5 days virtually provided readiness for the intervention delivery. This was followed by a workshop on refinement of intervention implementation protocol based on training feedback from CHPs.

The aim was to create an engaging and therapeutic group process where participants felt at ease, and the group context accelerated social contact and the opportunity to learn. This efficacy trial provided IPT-G Mini for 40 participants experiencing significant distress, as identified through our survey.

The trained IPT facilitators delivered the intervention according to the IPT-G Mini protocol, receiving on-site supervision from IPT supervisors. Sessions were held weekly for four weeks, each lasting 90 minutes (see ).

The participants were grouped based on age: 10–14 years old formed one group, while 15–19 years old formed another group. This age-based grouping aimed at providing therapeutic approaches unique to each age group’s needs and developmental stages. Importantly, grouping participants by age was a deliberate design decision and not a post-hoc arrangement. Each therapy group underwent the intervention based on their respective age categories, ensuring a focused and personalized therapeutic experience. Additionally, we offered brief psycho-educational support to the caregivers of these participants, equipping them with valuable tools to enhance the support they provide to the adolescents at home.

Data were collected using tablets, with baseline information on the participants retrieved from a previous MMAP survey that identified them as high risk for psychological distress. In June and July 2021, CHPs conducted baseline data collection under the supervision of team members V.N. and A.T. The CHPs received 3 days of intensive training on assessment tools, ethical considerations when dealing with adolescents, and general guidelines for data protocols.

PHQ-9: This is a 9-item self-report scale consisting of 9 criteria used for diagnosis of depression in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-V) [, ]. This scale is derived from the primary care evaluation of mental disorders, an instrument developed to assist primary care clinicians in making diagnoses of the most common mental disorders []. This 9-item scale is among the tools included in the MMAP protocol for assessing symptoms of depression among adolescents. The tool was developed for screening and assessing the severity of depressive symptoms in both clinical and research contexts [].

K10: This 10-item scale was developed using sensitive items that identify psychological distress in the general population and measure the frequency with which symptoms are experienced within a month []. These symptoms include nervousness, sadness, tiredness, hopelessness, and worthlessness, with responses recorded on a 5-point Likert scale where 1 indicates “None of the time” and 5 indicates “All of the time.” High scores point to psychological distress, with research suggesting a cut-off point of 24 and above for psychological distress [].

RCADS: This tool follows the Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale [] with a few more items on general anxiety and major depression symptoms per the DSM-V criteria []. It was initially designed as a 47-item questionnaire for ages 8–18, but a shorter 25-item version was then developed [], which has since been validated and shortened to 22 items that demonstrated acceptable categorization for 10–14 and 15–19 year olds []. We are reporting on RCADS anxiety items here as the reliability of the anxiety subscale was the most robust.

Outcome measures were collected at four distinct time points: baseline, post-intervention (after four sessions), and 1-month post-intervention. The results are presented as means and standard deviations (means ± SD), along with effect sizes calculated using Cohen’s d. To assess group disparities, exploratory longitudinal regression analyses were conducted for each outcome. All analyses were conducted using SPSS v25.

Overall, participants were predominantly female (n = 26; 65%). The mean age was 15.2 years (SD = 2.9), with the majority (n = 24; 60%) aged between 15 and 19 years. A large proportion of the respondents (n = 31; 78%) resided with their parents. The majority (n = 22; 55%) were in primary school, 40% were in secondary school, and 5% were engaged in vocational and livelihood programs at the tertiary level. Most respondents (40%) reported an average monthly income between Kenyan shillings (Ksh.) 5,000 and 9,999 (50–100 USD per month). About 38% reported their average income to be Ksh. <5,000, and 23% had an average income of Ksh. 10,000 and above (100 USD per month and over that). Baseline characteristics of the trial population by age were comparable between age groups (see ).

Baseline characteristics segregated by ages.

Attendance for each session was tracked by CHPs, who counted the number of participants assessed using the K10 scale, which was administered during every session. In the initial session, 40 participants attended a group session; in the second session, 37 participants attended; in the third session, 38 participants attended; while in the final (fourth) session, 40 participants attended groups. In total, four groups were created, with each site having two groups. Following the intervention, there was a notable decrease in psychological distress (K10) and depression score (PHQ-9) with a medium effect size of Cohen’s d for psychological distress (d = 0.49; 95% C.I. = 0.04–0.94) and depression (d = 0.51; 95% C.I. = 0.06–0.96), respectively (see  for comparisons).

Intervention outcomes.

aRange 11–50 (Higher scores = Higher psychological distress); bRange 4.7–50.7 (Higher scores = Higher Anxiety); cRange 1–27 (Higher scores = Depression).

However, there was a nonsignificant increase in anxiety (on RCADS) that we noticed post-intervention. The percentage of respondents at heightened risk of psychological distress decreased from 40% at baseline to 30% at the end of the intervention and was found to be 31% at 1-month post-intervention. Similarly, the percentage of respondents with probable depression decreased from 40% at baseline to 30% at the end of the intervention and remained the same at 1-month post-intervention.

The analysis of group variances from the exploratory longitudinal regression analyses for each outcome (see ) indicated a significant decline in psychological distress (as measured by K10) and depression (as measured by PHQ-9) scores at the end of the intervention p < 0.05. Notably, younger participants aged 10–14 years exhibited more favorable outcomes compared to older adolescents on both psychological distress and depression.

Summary of mean group differences for outcome measures.

*p<0.05, **p<0.001, ***p<0.001; C.I.: Confidence Interval; Ref: Reference Category.

During the 1-month follow-up after the intervention, we found both clinically and statistically significant reductions in psychological distress (Cohen’s d = 0.49; 95% C.I. = 0.05–0.94), while depression scores showed a statistically nonsignificant decrease. However, the IPT team considered participant improvements to be clinically significant. We did, however, find an increase in RCADS anxiety scores.

To explore the turning point at which significant changes occurred in the outcome measures following the intervention sessions, we performed pre- and post-intervention analyses testing psychological distress from session 1 to 1 month after the intervention while controlling for age and gender (see ).

Effects of intervention per session.

β: Regression Coefficient; S.E.: Standard Error; C.I.: Confidence Interval; Ref: Reference Category.

The analysis revealed a consistent decrease in psychological distress with each session, showing a marked reduction specifically at the fourth session. This decrease in distress persisted even 1 month after the intervention’s completion. We therefore conclude that statistically significant changes were discernible after the completion of four sessions (see  and ).

IPT-G Mini effectively reduced the levels of psychological distress and depression among our young participants. These positive effects were sustained for up to 1-month post-intervention. However, a noteworthy increase in anxiety scores following the sessions prompts further investigation. We would also like to underscore that the intervention was delivered at the pandemic’s peak. As a result, communities were experiencing high levels of distress and uncertainty. There are a few explanations underpinning our findings. We suspect that mixing participants of somewhat different ages and varying severities of symptoms in groups may have led to the emergence of anxiety symptoms, particularly among those recovering from severe comorbid symptoms associated with grief and trauma. We also noted that at the start of the sessions, there was a rise in anxiety levels, and this could be attributed to various factors, such as the ongoing pandemic amplifying fears and worries among the adolescents, lack of basic needs such as food, insecurity, escalating poverty, and parental well-being, which were not all adequately addressed in our intervention, as this was a complex, evolving situation everywhere with lockdown and national economic stress. Additionally, after completing the four sessions, we also observed that triggers for anxiety were the termination of the session, as participants expressed their desire to extend their time together. Toward the end of the session, participants exhibited separation anxiety as they had begun to form an attachment with the group and facilitators. Fortunately, CHPs could follow up with participants, and the study team also provided information to caregivers for additional support during the pandemic. No adverse events were encountered during this trial.

Our participants were experiencing a range of challenges. The ongoing stress of the COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with unprocessed grief arising from abusive family dynamics, contributed to significant distress. Insights from prior focus group discussions with adolescents aged 10–14 and 15–19 years, as well as caregivers of children aged 10–14 years [, ], revealed poignant stories. Adolescent girls disclosed accounts of contemplating suicide in relation to their experience of unplanned pregnancy, sometimes due to coercive sex, and shared attempting unsuccessful abortion. These problems around adolescent sexual and reproductive health, rights, and safety are well-documented, and during the pandemic, the closure of schools for long periods contributed to significant distress for families, children, and adolescents with limited resources [].

Earlier studies [, –] have indicated that briefer therapeutic interventions are well-received and viable [, ]. Adini et al. determined that interpersonal psychotherapy-adolescent-suicide crisis intervention (IPT-A-SCI) is feasible and as effective as the standard therapy in alleviating suicidal tendencies, depression, and anxiety symptoms in children and adolescents [].

The utilization of lay health workers known as CHPs in the Kenyan context—some of whom are affiliated with healthcare facilities while others are embedded within community settings—presents a valuable transition from using the workforce in formal to informal care, bringing psychosocial interventions to communities and adolescents during times of need. Our study benefited from the seamless network of these health workers, as evidenced by the lack of dropouts among our participants.

In light of the pressing need for prompt interventions, we organized our study participants into groups based on ease of access to the facility from their homes. Group therapy sessions were conducted at their nearest primary care center. The therapy was well-received and provided relief by alleviating symptoms of depression, addressing suicidal ideations, grief, and loss feelings, and relieving pandemic-associated worries, isolation, and social disconnect through enhancing and leveraging group support in a safe environment.

The primary constraint of our study included limited sample size and the absence of a control group or comparison group. This was happening during the real-world constraints of the pandemic. Provision of timely support to selected adolescents with high need was an advantage despite these limitations; our implementation of IPT-G Mini proved to be safe, feasible, and highly acceptable to participants and our lay CHPs who delivered the intervention.

The study demonstrates the effectiveness of IPT-G Mini sessions in significantly reducing psychological distress among our young participants, with these positive effects lasting for up to a month after intervention. Nonetheless, the noted increase in anxiety scores warrants further examination. This increase may be linked to individuals with higher anxiety symptoms and may be a result of participants recovering from unaddressed severe comorbid psychopathologies such as trauma exposures, which were not specifically addressed during the intervention. It is important to acknowledge that the intervention coincided with the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, a time when communities were experiencing high levels of distress and uncertainty. Our findings suggest IPT-G Mini needs to be tested further in controlled conditions to examine its effectiveness for a general population of adults and adolescents.

psychology.title: Museum exhibition-space psychology of sequential organization and cinematic spatial cues: an exploratory mixed-model association analysis
psychology.abstract: This exploratory study examines whether perceived sequential organization and perceived cinematic spatial cues in ordered museum-exhibition images are statistically associated with perceived route clarity, narrative transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention. An image-based evaluation dataset included 397 returned responses and 314 valid respondents, yielding 918 valid participant-material observations after screening. Each respondent evaluated one high-, one medium-, and one low-level stimulus set, creating the repeated participant-material structure analyzed below. Participant-random-intercept linear mixed models were used for repeated participant-material evaluations; control-adjusted, stimulus-variance-component, and participant-clustered analyses were retained as sensitivity checks. Perceived sequential organization was associated with perceived route clarity (beta = 0.358, 95% CI [0.296, 0.421]), perceived cinematic spatial cues were associated with narrative transportation (beta = 0.320, 95% CI [0.257, 0.384]), and narrative transportation was associated with emotional engagement (beta = 0.374, 95% CI [0.311, 0.436]). Perceived route clarity (beta = 0.248, 95% CI [0.184, 0.312]) and emotional engagement (beta = 0.234, 95% CI [0.170, 0.298]) were both associated with visit intention. Participant-clustered bootstrap estimates further supported the statistical indirect association from cinematic spatial cues through narrative transportation to emotional engagement (indirect effect = 0.109, 95% CI [0.079, 0.144]). The findings provide preliminary evidence of statistical associations among perceived exhibition-space cues, subjective route clarity, transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention in image-based evaluations, without implying actual gallery movement or causal mediation.
psychology.text:
The functional identity of museum exhibition space is undergoing a profound shift—from “displaying objects” toward “organizing visitor experience.” Where traditional exhibition practice centered on the preservation and presentation of collections, contemporary museums increasingly emphasize how space itself can organize, guide, and shape the act of visiting (). Space, on this view, is no longer a neutral vessel holding artifacts, but a medium that actively engages perception, cognition, and emotion. Recent work reinforces the point: museums are not only sites of knowledge transmission but also settings where visitors find emotional fulfillment, construct meaning, and even experience psychological wellbeing (). Spatial sequence, sightline organization, rhythmic variation, concealment and revelation, the placement of key exhibits, and the overall emotional atmosphere together form the material and psychological ground on which visitor experience unfolds.

This shift resonates closely with a central concern of environmental psychology—the reciprocal relationship between people and the built environment, and particularly how built settings influence perception, cognition, emotion, and behavioral intention. The Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) framework offers a classic foundation here:environmental cues (S) are related to internal psychological states (O), which are associated with approach or avoidance responses (R) (). In the museum context, empirical studies have shown that architectural elements, lighting, sound, materials, and spatial organization can systematically shape visitors’ emotional experience (). Research on emotional responses to architectural imagery similarly indicates that people form stable emotional judgments from visualized spatial materials (), while work on smart art museums points to the role of environmental interaction design in regulating visitor emotion (). Taken together, this evidence supports a basic premise: the spatial features of a museum can be studied as measurable environmental-psychological variables.

Running parallel to the space–emotion pathway is a research tradition concerned with museum narrative and emotional connection. Studies of digital storytelling suggest that museum narratives can strengthen the emotional connection, historical empathy, and personal relevance that visitors feel toward objects, history, and cultural themes (). Work on museum digitalization further argues that narrative is not mere information transfer, but a means—through character, situation, theme, and emotional cues—of fostering a deeper dialogue between visitors and cultural heritage (). Research on exhibition narrative at a national museum likewise shows that narrative structure and modes of exhibition interaction markedly affect visitors’ learning experience and engagement (). Narrative, in short, is widely regarded as an important driver of emotional engagement in museums.

At the level of integration, however, a clear gap remains. Space, narrative, emotion, and movement have often been examined in separate strands: space-syntax and simulation studies address how layout, path, and accessibility shape visitor movement (), whereas online-review and machine-learning studies infer spatial preferences from indirect data (). Few studies have operationalized visitors’ perceptions of sequential organization and cinematic spatial cues in exhibition imagery as measurable variables and examined, within an exploratory association framework, their statistical associations with perceived route clarity, narrative transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention. In particular, cinematic spatial cues have remained largely within architectural and design discourse, with limited effort to test them as a questionnaire-based psychological construct.

Against this background, the present study analyses a questionnaire dataset based on existing museum exhibition and gallery images. It examines how perceived sequential organization and perceived cinematic spatial cues in these images are statistically associated with perceived route clarity, narrative transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention within an exploratory association framework. Here, perceived sequential organization refers to the perceived beginning-to-closure structure of the image sequence, while perceived cinematic spatial cues refer to framing, concealment-revelation, visual focus, spatial rhythm, and scene progression.

Because the design is image-based, the study measures perceived route clarity rather than actual movement behavior in galleries. It treats perceived sequential organization, perceived cinematic spatial cues, perceived route clarity, narrative transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention as self-reported perceptual, experiential, and intention variables associated with visitors’ evaluations of exhibition imagery. The high-, medium-, and low-level material groups were formed through a combined theory-driven coding procedure; therefore, the design does not establish fully independent manipulations of narrative and cinematic cues. In this article, perceived route clarity refers to the inferred clarity of route direction, starting-point recognition, and spatial focus; it is a perception derived from the image sequence rather than observed movement.

Accordingly, the study asks two linked questions: (1) whether perceived sequential organization is associated with perceived route clarity; and (2) whether perceived cinematic spatial cues are associated with narrative transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention through the specified statistical paths. These questions motivate the exploratory association analyses described in the next section.

summarizes the exploratory statistical-association map. The figure presents theory-informed associations among image-based perceptual appraisals, experiential responses, and visit intention; the questionnaire measures are not a direct test of the classical S–O–R model. The arrows indicate exploratory statistical associations based on image-based self-reports. H4 denotes the exploratory indirect association rather than an experimentally established causal mediation effect.

Environmental psychology offers a systematic framework for understanding how museum exhibition space relates to visitor experience. Within this framework, the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model describes how environmental stimuli (S) are related to internal psychological states (O), which in turn are associated with approach or avoidance responses (R) (). In a museum, layout, lighting, materials, sound, and visual organization constitute potential environmental cues. Applying this framework to virtual museum experiences, prior research has linked perceived exhibition-space quality with behavioral intention through psychological variables such as emotion and cognition (). This perspective supports examining exhibition-space features as perceived environmental cues and visitor responses as psychological variables, while keeping the direction and causal status of the relationships open to empirical testing. In the present study, the ordered image sets constitute the stimulus context, whereas questionnaire scores represent post-viewing perceptual appraisals, experiential responses, and visit intention. Because objective environmental stimuli and pleasure-arousal-dominance dimensions were not measured, the study draws on S–O–R reasoning only as a general perspective and does not test the classical S–O–R model.

A substantial body of work has confirmed that museum spatial atmosphere can systematically mobilize visitors’ emotional experience. A study of the Jewish Museum Berlin found that architectural elements, lighting, sound, materials, and spatial organization are not passive backdrops but actively organize, arouse, and regulate emotional responses (). Experiments using editable 360-degree VR panoramas went further, showing that a single spatial parameter such as ceiling height can be enough to elicit measurable emotional differences (). Research on the multimodal sensory perception of museum environments indicates that visual and haptic channels jointly participate in visitors’ construction of exhibition atmosphere (), while studies linking emotion to neural responses to architecture corroborate, at the physiological level, the stable connection between spatial features and emotional experience (). Together, these findings support a basic premise: visitors can form stable, measurable psychological responses from the visual features of exhibition space.

As extended reality (XR) has been adopted in the cultural-heritage field, a growing body of work has examined how emotionally oriented environmental design relates to visitor engagement. Reviews suggest that emotional design is becoming a key strategy for connecting spatial features with visitor experience (). Much of this work, however, relies on immersive technologies or on-site deployment and therefore provides less evidence about how visitors evaluate spatial features from static imagery alone. This distinction motivates the present study’s image-based focus on perceptual evaluations of exhibition-space cues.

How museum space organizes visitor movement has long been a central question in space-syntax research. Space-syntax theory holds that the topological structure of a built space itself embodies a “spatial logic” that largely governs how people move, pause, and encounter one another within it (). Building on this, wayfinding research points out that the visibility, accessibility, and sequentiality of a spatial configuration are decisive for whether visitors can orient themselves: clear sightlines, intuitive circulation, and hierarchical spatial transitions together form a spatial language that visitors can “read” (). Empirical work in open-plan exhibition settings has likewise confirmed that layout features systematically shape visitors’ spatial behavior (), and recent reconsiderations of the relationship between space syntax and design reaffirm the foundational role of spatial structure in organizing exploratory paths ().

In recent years, quantitative research on museum layout, path configuration, and accessibility has deepened. Studies using visibility-graph analysis and intelligent-agent simulation show that corridors and paths play a key role in organizing movement through exhibition space, which indicates that “movement” or a “sense of path” is a reasonable and measurable spatial variable (). Analyses of the relationship between layout and visitor paths in modern museums similarly show that spatial-layout types—such as sequential versus choice spaces—directly affect how circulation forms (), and space-syntax examinations of natural-science museums underscore the close link between spatial permeability and wayfinding ().

Most of this work, however, centers on actual movement in real space and pays less attention to the perceived route clarity that visitors may infer from exhibition imagery. When a sequence of exhibition images presents a clear beginning, development, focal point, and closure—that is, when it conveys a strong perceived sequential organization—viewers may form subjective judgments about the direction of the visit, the clarity of the route, and the location of key areas. Thus, a stronger perceived spatial-narrative structure is expected to be associated with greater perceived route clarity. The present study measures this perceptual judgment rather than actual visitor movement in a gallery (). Accordingly:

H1: Perceived sequential organization is positively associated with perceived route clarity.

In this study, “perceived cinematic spatial cues” denotes a perceptual construct informed by work at the intersection of architecture and film. In that literature, space is often understood as a sequence experienced “frame by frame”: concealment and revelation, sightline framing, visual focus, and spatial rhythm can direct attention and create a sense of scene and image (). These ideas provide a conceptual basis for examining whether viewers perceive cinematic qualities in exhibition-space imagery. The construct is therefore used here as a questionnaire-based psychological perception, rather than as a claim that the images reproduce film techniques or independently manipulate a distinct environmental feature. It comprises concealment–revelation, visual focus, spatial rhythm, and a sense of scene progression.

Narrative-transportation theory provides a theoretical basis for examining how perceived cinematic spatial cues may relate to visitors’ psychological experience.
