The theory defines transportation as an integrated state of attention, imagery, and affect—the experience of being immersed in a narrative world and temporarily leaving reality behind (). The transportation-imagery model further emphasizes the role of vivid mental imagery in transportation and its links with mental simulation, attitudes, and beliefs (). A meta-analysis across contexts likewise shows that transportation is systematically related to antecedent narrative features and to experiential and behavioral outcomes (). In the present study, the “narrative” does not refer to a verbal plot or to physically entering a narrative world. It refers to the perceived progression inferred from an ordered image set, including contextual framing, transition, concealment and revelation, visual focus, spatial rhythm, and closure. These features may help viewers infer continuity and scene progression, sustain attention, evoke mental imagery, and support affective involvement, making a narrative-transportation-related association plausible. Narrative transportation is treated as distinct from immersion, presence, visual absorption, spatial interest, and emotional engagement, although these experiences may be related. In this image-based study, transportation refers to attention, mental imagery, and affective involvement inferred from an ordered image sequence.

Evidence from immersive and digital-museum research provides contextual or indirect support for the psychological plausibility of this account, but it does not directly test the present static-image pathway. Research on digital storytelling in virtual-reality museums has linked multidimensional narrative transportation—including immersion, emotional arousal, and mental imagery—with visitor–object experience (). Studies of digital storytelling in VR exhibitions have also reported associations between narrative organization and visitors’ sense of presence and immersion (). Comparisons of immersive realities (VR, VR360, and MR) report differentiated patterns of presence, engagement, and motivation across media (), while experiments on immersive media, emotion, and memory indicate that immersion is related to emotional experience and memory performance (). In addition, work treating interactive storytelling as an exhibit in its own right highlights the immersive potential of narrative within museum space (). These findings are relevant as contextual evidence because they indicate that narrative organization, imagery, and affective involvement may matter in museum-related experience. However, they do not show that static images reproduce stereoscopic depth, embodied viewpoint, sensorimotor interaction, spatial presence, or active exploration. In the present study, these findings therefore serve as boundary evidence rather than direct validation of the association between perceived cinematic spatial cues and narrative transportation. Accordingly:

H2: Perceived cinematic spatial cues are positively associated with narrative transportation.

Narrative transportation has also been linked to emotional engagement. In the present study, emotional engagement is treated as a multidimensional self-reported response involving emotional connection, historical empathy, personal relevance, interest, being moved, and emotional resonance (). Studies of museum digital storytelling report that narrative and immersive experience are associated with emotional connection and empathy (). Within transportation theory, focused attention, mental imagery, and situational involvement are proposed as psychological conditions under which emotional responses may emerge (). From an embodied-cognition perspective, perception, movement, and spatial experience likewise provide contexts in which exhibition-related emotion can be formed (). Accordingly:

H3: Narrative transportation is positively associated with emotional engagement.

Beyond this direct link, transportation may statistically account for part of the association between cinematic spatial cues and emotional engagement. Because the dataset is cross-sectional and same-source, this hypothesis is framed as an indirect-association pattern rather than as evidence of a causal mechanism. This logic is consistent with the narrative features-transportation-experiential outcomes chain identified in the transportation-imagery model and its meta-analysis (; ). Accordingly:

H4: Narrative transportation statistically accounts for part of the association between perceived cinematic spatial cues and emotional engagement.

For the step from experience to behavioral intention, prior research has reported links between digital museum experience and on-site visit intention through psychological variables such as cultural identity and perceived value (). Research on virtual-museum experience quality has similarly identified associations with offline visit intention (). Studies of art-craft and cultural-heritage museums have reported relationships between visitors’ emotions, emotional engagement, satisfaction, and subsequent behavioral intentions (), while research on cultural-heritage tourists has linked emotional experience with behavioral intention through variables such as place attachment and satisfaction (). Work grounded in cognition–emotion–behavior theory also highlights the statistical relevance of emotion-related variables to recommendation intention in online museums (). Related mediation analyses in museum tourism () and studies of immersive exhibition experience () further suggest that experiential and emotional responses may be connected with visit or recommendation intention. Perceived route clarity may likewise be associated with willingness to continue a visit or attend in person: when visitors perceive the direction as clear and the route as well defined, a stronger intention to visit may be reported.

Perceived route clarity and emotional engagement may each show a distinct statistical association with visit intention, while also being correlated with one another. The present study therefore enters both variables into a single visit-intention model and estimates their associations with visit intention under mutual adjustment, rather than treating either path as an isolated causal effect. Accordingly:

H5: Perceived route clarity is positively associated with visit intention.

H6: Emotional engagement is positively associated with visit intention.

This was a formal online questionnaire study conducted in Chinese. Participants were recruited in mainland China through open online recruitment, primarily by forwarding a Wenjuanxing questionnaire link through the researchers’ social-network channels. The study used convenience sampling with voluntary participation. Eligibility required participants to be at least 18 years old, voluntarily consent to participate, be able to read the Chinese questionnaire, and view all museum-exhibition images in the questionnaire. No art or design background or specific museum-visiting experience was required. Data were collected from March 5 to June 5, 2026, and no monetary compensation was provided. This manuscript reports the formal questionnaire study and the theory-based stimulus-coding procedure used to organize the image materials.

The dataset contains 397 questionnaire records, corresponding to 1,191 raw participant-material observations because each respondent evaluated three stimulus groups. After questionnaire-level screening, 314 valid respondents were retained (), corresponding to 942 expected participant-material observations. After material-level attention and completeness screening, 918 valid material-level observations remained. The primary mixed models used 830–852 complete scale-score observations depending on the variables in each model, whereas the control-adjusted sensitivity models used 812–832 observations; the clustered bootstrap indirect-association models used 789–818 complete scale-score observations, and 743 rows were fully complete across all focal item-level measurement variables.

Respondent characteristics and data-quality screening (N = 314).

Before data collection, the study protocol specified the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Inclusion required age ≥ 18, voluntary participation, Chinese-reading ability, and complete viewing of all stimulus materials. Exclusion criteria were markedly short completion time, failed attention checks, repeated selection of the same response option (straightlining), incomplete viewing, severe missingness in key variables, and an overall response pattern judged to be random or of very low quality (random_low_quality). The last category involved 19 participants. Of 397 returned questionnaire records, 314 were retained as valid respondents (79.1%). The 83 excluded records comprised speeding (n = 21), random_low_quality (n = 19), attention-check failure (n = 18), straightlining (n = 14), incomplete viewing (n = 7), and excessive missingness (n = 4). The 314 valid respondents generated 942 expected participant-material observations; 918 remained after material-level screening.

The stimulus materials comprised eight candidate museum exhibition and gallery image sets selected from official online exhibition pages, virtual-tour screenshots, and open-licensed image sources. The candidate pool contained two high-sequential sets (H01 Louvre; H02 Vatican Museums), three medium-sequential sets (M03 Rijksmuseum; M01 Scottish National Gallery; M02 National Museum of China), two low-sequential/open-space sets (L02 National Gallery of Ireland; L01 The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Temple of Dendur)), and one object-heavy backup set (B01 American Museum of Natural History Northwest Coast Hall). Seven sets were retained for the formal questionnaire. The backup set was excluded because its emphasis on object display was less compatible with the required exhibition-space sequence, route continuity, and narrative progression.

Two authors, Ziqin Yuan and Chao Zhou, both of whom had training in art and design, independently coded all eight candidate stimulus sets. The coding used six prespecified theory-based indicators: clarity of starting point, sequential continuity, concealment-revelation, visual focus, spatial rhythm, and sense of closure. Each indicator was scored from 0 to 2, producing total coding scores from 0 to 12. Preliminary grouping was defined as low (0–4), medium (5–8), and high (9–12). During independent coding, each coder worked without viewing the other coder’s scores. For discrepant ratings, the coders reviewed the relevant image sequence and coding definitions item by item, discussed the discrepancy, and established a consensus coding result; if a discrepancy remained, Chao Zhou made the final adjudication under the coding rules. No formal inter-rater reliability coefficient, such as weighted Cohen’s kappa or an intraclass correlation coefficient, was calculated. The coding was used for theory-informed stimulus screening rather than as a primary outcome measure, so the final material classification is interpreted together with the participant-level manipulation checks. The procedure was not intended to claim that the image sets were equivalent in museum fame, topic, visual style, or photographic quality; these material differences are treated as limitations.

The final coding scores were as follows, in the indicator order listed above: H01 Louvre, 2/2/2/2/2/1, total 11 (high); H02 Vatican Museums, 2/2/2/2/1/1, total 10 (high); M03 Rijksmuseum, 1/2/1/2/1/1, total 8 (medium); M01 Scottish National Gallery, 1/1/1/1/1/2, total 7 (medium); M02 National Museum of China, 1/1/1/1/1/1, total 6 (medium); L02 National Gallery of Ireland, 1/1/0/1/0/1, total 4 (low); and L01 The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Temple of Dendur), 1/0/0/1/0/1, total 3 (low). The backup set B01 was excluded because it emphasized object display and had weaker spatial sequence, route continuity, and narrative progression than required for the present stimulus-screening purpose.

For article presentation,  uses non-repeating illustrative examples to clarify the spatial-cue categories, and  summarizes the stimulus-screening logic. Source and license metadata for the illustrative photographic panels are reported in .

Because the actual questionnaire stimulus materials include museum website images, virtual-tour screenshots, or open-licensed images, full-resolution stimuli are not redistributed publicly owing to copyright constraints. In the paper and in data sharing, only stimulus IDs, source URLs, license and author information, metadata, coding criteria, and anonymized questionnaire data are provided. The photographic examples shown in  are separate copyright-safe illustrative examples selected for publication display.

All focal constructs were measured using items presented after each six-image stimulus sequence. Each stimulus block contained 26 evaluation items: perceived sequential organization (PSN; 4 items), perceived cinematic spatial cues (CSC; 4 items), perceived route clarity (PMG item block; 4 items), arrative transportation (NT; 4 items; adapted from ; ), emotional engagement (EE; 4 items), visit intention (VI; 3 items), and three sensitivity covariates—topic interest, visual attractiveness, and familiarity—with one item each. All items used a 7-point Likert-type response scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. Construct scores were calculated as the arithmetic mean of the corresponding items. Higher scores indicated stronger perceived organization, spatial cues, route clarity, narrative transportation, emotional engagement, or visit intention, as applicable.

The measures were designed for the evaluation of ordered museum-exhibition images rather than for the assessment of physical movement in an actual gallery. Accordingly, perceived route clarity refers to respondents’ inferred judgments about the starting point, directional continuity, and spatial focus represented in the image sequence; it does not measure observed walking routes, dwell time, or on-site circulation. Visit intention refers to stated willingness to visit, revisit, recommend, or learn more about the represented exhibition or museum. The construct-to-item mapping and measurement sources are reported in .

Control variables comprised interest in the exhibition topic (topic interest), the visual attractiveness of the material (visual attractiveness), and familiarity with the museum or exhibition (familiarity). Topic interest, visual attractiveness, and familiarity were treated as post-viewing sensitivity covariates rather than primary controls because they may partly reflect respondents’ immediate reactions to the same stimulus materials; including them in the primary models could therefore over-adjust the focal spatial-cue associations. Their effects are reported separately in the control-adjusted sensitivity models ().

In the questionnaire procedure, each respondent evaluated three stimulus sets: one high-sequential, one medium-sequential, and one low-sequential set. Within each level, the available sets were H01/H02 for the high level, M01/M02/M03 for the medium level, and L01/L02 for the low level. These options generated 12 possible high-medium-low combinations, all of which were observed among the 314 respondents retained at the questionnaire level; their participant-level frequencies are reported in . Each respondent therefore received one material from each level. The three level blocks were presented in randomized order. Each selected set contained six images displayed in the fixed sequence predefined for that set. The evaluation items and attention-check items were presented in fixed order; item randomization was not used. The complete set of realized combinations and their frequencies is reported in . Respondent-level and material-level records were retained accordingly. The dataset included low-quality cases, mild item-level missingness, incomplete viewing records, and response-style heterogeneity, which were addressed through screening and sensitivity analysis. Before each image set, respondents were instructed to view the six images in order and to imagine moving through the space while doing so. This instruction operationalized image-guided imagined progression; it did not measure physical movement, observed routes, or dwell time in an actual exhibition space.

The analysis proceeded as follows. First, sample characteristics and data-quality exclusions were summarized. A post hoc sensitivity-oriented power interpretation followed Cohen’s effect-size guidance (). Second, participant-level manipulation checks compared the high, medium, and low material levels for PSN and CSC using participant-random-intercept mixed models because respondents evaluated repeated material sets. These checks evaluated whether participants perceived the intended graded distinction; because the material grouping was based on a combined theory-driven coding procedure, the results were not interpreted as evidence that the narrative and cinematic cues had been independently manipulated. Third, reliability and item-level measurement diagnostics were computed; the diagnostics included raw alpha, standardized alpha, PCA-based loading ranges, HTMT-style discrimination checks, and a Harman single-factor common-method diagnostic (; ; ). Fourth, the primary hypothesis tests used participant-random-intercept linear mixed models to account for repeated participant-material observations (; ; ; ; ). Fifth, control-adjusted, stimulus-variance-component, and participant-clustered models were used as sensitivity analyses. Statistical indirect associations were estimated using participant-clustered percentile bootstrap resampling with 5,000 resamples (; ; ). Analyses were conducted in Python 3.13 using pandas, scipy, statsmodels 0.14.5, and matplotlib; compact computed sensitivity, diagnostic, sample-screening, stimulus-coding, questionnaire-item, assignment, and manipulation-check outputs are reported in .

The repeated participant-material structure is important because each respondent evaluated multiple stimulus sets, so observations should not be treated as fully independent. The primary models included participant random intercepts. Stimulus variance components were not folded into the primary fixed-effect table because the seven-stimulus design makes stimulus-level variance sensitive to between-stimulus material differences; those estimates are instead summarized as a sensitivity diagnostic in .

For visit intention, perceived route clarity and emotional engagement were entered into a single primary model so that each path was estimated while adjusting for the other focal predictor. Topic interest, visual attractiveness, and familiarity were treated as sensitivity-analysis variables because they may themselves be affected by stimulus viewing. Therefore, control-adjusted coefficients are reported separately rather than being mixed into the primary hypothesis table.

The dataset contained 397 questionnaire records and 1,191 raw participant-material observations. After participant-level screening, 314 valid respondents remained (79.1% of returned records). The 83 excluded records comprised speeding (n = 21), random_low_quality (n = 19), attention-check failure (n = 18), straightlining (n = 14), incomplete viewing (n = 7), and excessive missingness (n = 4); the stage-by-stage sample flow is summarized in . These respondents generated 942 expected participant-material observations; 24 material-level observations were removed because of material-level attention or completeness screening, leaving 918 valid participant-material observations. The primary mixed models used 830–852 complete scale-score observations, the control-adjusted sensitivity models used 812–832 observations, the clustered bootstrap indirect-association models used 789–818 observations, and 743 all-item-complete rows were available for same-source measurement and common-method diagnostics.

The participant-level manipulation check showed the expected graded pattern, with mean scores increasing from low to medium to high materials (). For perceived sequential organization, mean scores were 3.87 (SD = 0.82; n = 297), 4.82 (SD = 0.82; n = 291), and 5.62 (SD = 0.77; n = 299) for the low, medium, and high groups, respectively; the participant-random-intercept mixed model yielded Wald chi-square(2) = 833.23, p < 0.001, participant ICC = 0.163. For perceived cinematic spatial cues, the corresponding means were 4.01 (SD = 0.81; n = 299), 4.98 (SD = 0.83; n = 296), and 5.75 (SD = 0.77; n = 290); the mixed model yielded Wald chi-square(2) = 801.07, p < 0.001, participant ICC = 0.132. Thus, participants reported progressively higher levels of both perceptions across the low, medium, and high material groups. Because the levels were formed through a combined theory-driven material-coding procedure, these checks support perceived differentiation among the material groups but do not establish that narrative and cinematic cues were independently manipulated.

Manipulation-check results across material levels.

Valid Ns vary slightly across variables because scale scores were computed only when all items of the corresponding scale were complete.

summarizes scale reliability and item-level measurement diagnostics; raw Cronbach alpha values ranged from 0.709 to 0.801 across the six scales. A Harman single-factor diagnostic was conducted using the item-level dataset. The first unrotated factor explained 23.35% of the total variance, below the commonly used 50% rule of thumb. This result indicates that a single dominant common factor was not apparent in the dataset, although Harman’s test is a low-sensitivity descriptive diagnostic and common method bias remains a design limitation because all focal variables were collected through the same questionnaire. Item-level HTMT-style ratios ranged from 0.155 to 0.649 (N = 743), below the commonly used 0.85 threshold (), supporting discriminant separation among the focal constructs as a descriptive diagnostic. Although perceived sequential organization and perceived cinematic spatial cues were the most strongly correlated pair (HTMT = 0.649), this value remained below conservative discrimination thresholds, supporting their empirical separability in this dataset. Nevertheless, because these two spatial-cue dimensions are conceptually adjacent, future work should test competing measurement models with larger and more balanced stimulus pools.

Reliability and measurement-model diagnostics.

Descriptive statistics and correlations are reported in  for the valid dataset. Construct means ranged from 4.31 to 4.91 on the 7-point scale, with standard deviations from 0.92 to 1.08. The correlations were positive and ranged from r = 0.093 to r = 0.508. Because observations were nested within respondents, the correlation matrix is interpreted descriptively; participant-level and model-based analyses were used for inferential claims.

Descriptive statistics and correlations in the valid dataset.

Values below the diagonal are Pearson correlations computed from valid participant-material rows. Diagonal values are raw Cronbach alpha coefficients rather than Fornell–Larcker square roots of AVE; inferential interpretation should rely on the mixed models and clustered sensitivity analyses.

reports the standardized main-path estimates from the primary participant-random-intercept mixed models. Control-adjusted, stimulus-variance-component, and participant-clustered sensitivity outputs are reported in  rather than combined with the primary fixed-effect table.

Linear mixed-model results (standardized fixed effects).

H5 and H6 were estimated jointly within a single visit-intention model. The primary models include participant random intercepts and do not include post-viewing control variables. Standard errors are reported to four decimals to reduce rounding discrepancies among beta, z, and confidence intervals. Across primary models, participant variance ranged from 0.015 to 0.027, residual variance ranged from 0.837 to 0.883, total ICC values ranged from 0.016 to 0.031, marginal R2 values ranged from 0.103 to 0.140, and conditional R2 values ranged from 0.118 to 0.163 (). Control-adjusted, stimulus-variance-component, and participant-clustered sensitivity estimates are reported in .

The primary mixed models supported all five main statistical paths. Perceived sequential organization was positively associated with perceived route clarity, beta = 0.358, SE = 0.0319, 95% CI [0.296, 0.421], N = 852, marginal R2 = 0.128, conditional R2 = 0.155, supporting H1. Perceived cinematic spatial cues were positively associated with narrative transportation, beta = 0.320, SE = 0.0325, 95% CI [0.257, 0.384], N = 843, marginal R2 = 0.103, conditional R2 = 0.118, supporting H2. Narrative transportation was positively associated with emotional engagement, beta = 0.374, SE = 0.0320, 95% CI [0.311, 0.436], N = 840, marginal R2 = 0.140, conditional R2 = 0.163, supporting H3. In the joint visit-intention model, perceived route clarity, beta = 0.248, SE = 0.0326, 95% CI [0.184, 0.312], and emotional engagement, beta = 0.234, SE = 0.0326, 95% CI [0.170, 0.298], were both positively associated with visit intention, supporting H5 and H6.

Sensitivity checks showed the same directional conclusions in control-adjusted LMMs, stimulus-variance-component LMMs, and participant-clustered regressions. Because the stimulus-variance-component specification shifts much of the variance into stimulus-level differences, those estimates are treated as diagnostic rather than as the primary fixed-effect table.

As exploratory analyses, two additional statistical indirect associations were positive: perceived sequential organization → perceived route clarity → visit intention (indirect effect = 0.086, 95% CI [0.059, 0.116]), and narrative transportation → emotional engagement → visit intention (indirect effect = 0.073, 95% CI [0.042, 0.106]). These estimates were not treated as additional confirmatory hypothesis tests.

Taken together, the primary mixed models supported H1-H3, H5, and H6. The clustered bootstrap analysis was consistent with H4 as a statistical indirect-association hypothesis: the indirect association from perceived cinematic spatial cues through narrative transportation to emotional engagement was 0.109, 95% CI [0.079, 0.144].  reports the primary participant-random-intercept LMM fixed effects, while  reports the clustered bootstrap indirect associations.

Participant-clustered bootstrap indirect associations (5,000 resamples).

Indirect effects were estimated with 5,000 participant-clustered bootstrap resamples. The b-paths are partial coefficients estimated with the independent variable included in the model, and therefore differ from the corresponding bivariate fixed effects in . For example, the emotional-engagement b-path on visit intention (0.202) is smaller than the corresponding  fixed effect (0.234) because narrative transportation is held constant in the statistical indirect-association model, so the two tables are consistent rather than conflicting.

The first theoretical contribution concerns the conceptual vocabulary for image-based exhibition-space perception. Existing environmental-psychology and museum-layout accounts have primarily emphasized configuration, visibility, accessibility, path organization, and spatial structure (; ; ; ; ; ; ). The present study adds a perceptual vocabulary—framing, concealment–revelation, visual focus, spatial rhythm, and scene progression—for describing how an ordered set of exhibition images may be experienced as organized and affectively engaging. This contribution is preliminary: perceived cinematic spatial cues are a questionnaire-based perceptual construct derived from architecture–film theory, not an independently manipulated or fully validated environmental feature. Its value lies in connecting architecture–film concepts with environmental-psychological accounts at the level of perceived spatial organization ().

The second contribution clarifies the boundary between image-based perceptual evaluation and classical environmental-psychology models. The ordered museum/gallery images constitute the stimulus context, while the questionnaire measures respondents’ perceptual appraisals, experiential responses, and visit intention. The study therefore does not directly test the classical S–O–R model, because objective environmental stimuli and the pleasure-arousal-dominance dimensions were not independently measured. This distinction prevents post-viewing questionnaire scores from being treated as if they were the environmental stimuli themselves. The cross-sectional, same-source design is consequently interpreted as an exploratory association design rather than as evidence of a temporal or causal S–O–R process.

The third contribution concerns the proposed interpretive ordering of spatial perception and narrative transportation. The results are consistent with a sequence in which viewers first infer continuity, focus, and progression from an ordered image set and may then report narrative-like involvement involving attention, mental imagery, and affect. This provides a theoretical rationale for examining the association between perceived cinematic spatial cues and narrative transportation, and for treating transportation as an experiential state potentially related to emotional engagement (; ; ; ). The ordering is theoretical rather than empirically demonstrated: because all focal variables were collected in the same cross-sectional questionnaire, the present estimates do not establish temporal precedence or causal mediation.

Finally, the study defines a form of museum narrative that differs from conventional narrative accounts centered on curatorial text, exhibit labels, interactive storytelling, or visitor accounts. Here, narrative refers to perceived progression across an ordered set of exhibition images—contextual framing, transition, concealment and revelation, visual focus, spatial rhythm, and closure. This image-derived narrative is therefore a claim about visual representation and psychological appraisal, not about a complete narrative world or embodied gallery experience. Static images do not provide stereoscopic depth, embodied viewpoint, sensorimotor interaction, spatial presence, active exploration, or actual circulation. The theoretical contribution is consequently bounded: the study offers a preliminary account of how exhibition space may be visually organized and perceived, while claims about physical navigation remain questions for on-site, behavioral, or interactive research (; ; ).

This study examined perceived sequential organization and perceived cinematic spatial cues as environmental-psychological variables and their statistical associations with perceived route clarity, narrative transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention. Because participants evaluated exhibition imagery rather than galleries in situ, the findings concern image-based perceptions and intended responses; they do not establish actual movement behavior, fully independent cue manipulations, or causal mechanisms in physical galleries.

First, the H1 estimate, beta = 0.358, indicates a positive statistical association between perceived sequential organization and perceived route clarity, without implying a claim about actual walking behavior. This pattern is compatible with the possibility that clearly staged entrance, transition, focus, and closure cues help viewers form subjective judgments about route clarity when evaluating exhibition imagery.

Second, the cinematic-cue pathway was consistent with the proposed statistical sequence: perceived cinematic spatial cues were positively associated with narrative transportation, beta = 0.320, and the clustered bootstrap analysis yielded an indirect association from cinematic cues through transportation to emotional engagement of 0.109, 95% CI [0.079, 0.144]. This pattern is compatible with a transportation-related account of emotional engagement, but it does not show that cinematic cues independently caused transportation or that transportation causally produced engagement.

Third, the downstream paths formed a coherent statistical model. Narrative transportation was positively associated with emotional engagement, beta = 0.374; perceived route clarity and emotional engagement were each positively associated with visit intention in the joint model, beta = 0.248 and beta = 0.234, respectively. These estimates distinguish the observed statistical paths and joint associations from evidence of a causal process.

Taken together, the findings indicate two statistically coherent patterns rather than a confirmed dual-path process. One exploratory indirect association ran from perceived sequential organization through perceived route clarity to visit intention, indirect effect = 0.086. A second exploratory indirect association ran from perceived cinematic spatial cues through narrative transportation and emotional engagement, with the cinematic-cue → transportation → emotional-engagement indirect association = 0.109 and the transportation → emotional-engagement → visit-intention indirect association = 0.073. These patterns provide an integrated interpretation of the results while remaining bounded by the image-based, cross-sectional design.

The findings point to several candidate designable spatial features as perceived through exhibition imagery. Sequential organization corresponds to perceivable starting points, transitions, focal nodes, and closure. Route clarity relates to entrance visibility, sightline continuity, directional cues, and spatial hierarchy. Cinematic spatial cues concern framing, visual focus, concealment–revelation, and spatial rhythm. These correspondences define possible links between designable spatial features and viewers’ perceptual responses, but they should be interpreted as exploratory perceptual associations rather than evidence that manipulating any single feature would change actual visitor movement, dwell time, or on-site behavior. The present study did not independently manipulate these features.

The findings suggest several provisional design implications. First, in perception-oriented exhibition planning and image-based evaluation, designers could attend to the structural organization of entrance, transition, focus, and closure so that visitors have clearer route judgments. This implication concerns perceived route clarity and should not be read as evidence that these features determine actual gallery movement.

Second, perceived cinematic spatial cues—such as concealment–revelation, framing, visual focus, and spatial rhythm—may offer a vocabulary for discussing how exhibition imagery organizes attention and emotional involvement. Because these cues were derived from a combined material-coding procedure and measured as perceptions, this implication is conceptual and design-oriented rather than evidence that any single cue independently produces a given response.

Third, the joint visit-intention model suggests that movement-related design may be considered not only in terms of traffic organization but also in relation to visitors’ perceived route clarity and emotional involvement. This implication concerns intended responses in image-based evaluation and should be tested with on-site behavioral measures before being generalized to actual visitation.

Several limitations warrant caution in interpreting the results.

First, and most importantly, the study measures perceived route clarity, not actual movement behavior. Image materials can reflect visitors’ subjective judgments of spatial guidance, but they are not equivalent to movement paths in a real gallery. Future work could combine on-site observation, indoor positioning, eye-tracking, or dwell-time data to test the correspondence between perceived route clarity and actual movement (; ). The viewing instruction asked respondents to imagine moving through the space. This may have strengthened route-clarity and narrative-transportation judgments, so future studies should compare alternative instructions and test whether the observed associations persist without an imagined-movement prompt.

Second, image stimuli cannot fully substitute for an on-site visit. The sense of scale, the multisensory atmosphere, and bodily presence in a real gallery are all difficult for two-dimensional images to reproduce. Future work could run A/B tests in real galleries or temporary exhibitions, or use immersive means such as VR for comparison, to test the ecological validity of these conclusions (; ; ).

Third, the stimulus materials came from different museums and differed in theme, visual style, cultural background, and exhibit appeal, which may confound the results. Although topic interest, visual attractiveness, and familiarity were controlled, material heterogeneity cannot be fully ruled out. Consistent with this concern, the stimulus-variance-component sensitivity models showed that stimulus-level differences accounted for a substantial portion of outcome variance, with conditional R2 values near 0.72 (see ). The observed associations may therefore partly reflect material-specific features, such as museum type, image quality, theme familiarity, or visual style, rather than only the intended sequential or cinematic spatial cues. This concern is reinforced by the combined coding procedure and the limited pool of seven retained stimulus sets, which do not fully separate cue-level perceptions from stimulus-specific heterogeneity. The findings should therefore be interpreted as evidence from an image-based perceived-evaluation design rather than as general evidence about all museum exhibition spaces. Future studies should use a larger and more systematically balanced stimulus pool to distinguish cue-related associations from stimulus-specific heterogeneity. Moreover, copyright constraints prevent some stimuli from being fully released, which may affect reproducibility; future work could prioritize open-licensed images or secure authorization through museum collaboration.

Fourth, the measurement framework is preliminary: several focal constructs were adapted or newly worded for image-based evaluation, and the three covariates were single items. Although construct–item mapping was used, confirmatory validation was beyond this study. Future work should test the measurement structure with larger and more balanced stimulus pools.

Finally, although cluster-robust standard errors, linear mixed models, and bootstrap indirect-effect estimates were used as robustness checks, the dataset remains cross-sectional and same-source. These procedures strengthen the stability of the reported estimates but do not establish temporal order or causal effects; the mixed-model, cluster-robust, and bootstrap results should therefore be interpreted as convergent statistical evidence rather than confirmation of a causal mechanism. The respondent sample was also relatively young and highly educated, which limits generalization to broader museum visitor populations. Future studies should include more age-diverse and education-diverse samples, especially among on-site visitors.

This exploratory study examined how perceived sequential organization and cinematic spatial cues in museum-exhibition images relate to visitor experience and behavioral intention using a repeated participant-material analysis pipeline. Using participant-by-material online image-evaluation data, the analysis drew on 314 valid respondents, 918 valid material-level observations, and 830–852 complete-case primary mixed-model observations, yielding mixed-model coefficients from 0.234 to 0.374 and participant-clustered bootstrap indirect associations from 0.073 to 0.109.

The contribution lies chiefly in two respects. First, the study provides a preliminary operationalization of cinematic spatial cues as a questionnaire construct in museum exhibition-space psychology. Second, it shows how repeated participant-material evaluations can be analyzed with mixed models, clustered sensitivity checks, and bootstrap indirect-association estimates while keeping causal claims appropriately limited.

In practical terms, the study suggests that perceived sequential structure and cinematic spatial cues may be relevant to visitors’ subjective route clarity, transportation, emotional engagement, and visit intention in image-based evaluations. These implications should be tested in future studies using authorized stimuli, on-site behavioral measures, or experimental manipulations.

psychology.title: Exploring the role of Human Factors and Ergonomics in supporting safe insulin dispensing in community pharmacy: a pilot webinar-based training intervention
psychology.abstract: Ensuring safe dispensing of insulin remains a patient safety priority in community pharmacy, with errors related to product similarity, task complexity and workload. Human Factors and Ergonomics (HF/E) principles and methods assist in examining these system-level issues but are underused in this setting.A pilot educational intervention of three 2-hour online interactive webinars was developed and delivered to pharmacy staff (n=27 to 32) in Northern Ireland. Topics covered included foundational HF/E concepts, such as the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework, Systems Thinking principles and human-centred design of standard operating procedures (SOPs). Participants applied SEIPS to a real-world insulin incident scenario to identify performance-influencing factors influencing outcomes. A simple ‘Quick Checker’ tool to support SOP development was co-designed.Participants identified multiple interacting system factors affecting safe insulin dispensing, including technology limitations, workflow complexity and product design. Post-session evaluation was uniformly positive: all respondents agreed the sessions were useful and improved their understanding of HF/E, and 78% (n=18/23) of those attending the session strongly agreed they could apply SEIPS in practice. Educational resources were packaged into an accessible bundle for further dissemination and the ‘Quick Checker’ guide for SOP development was produced.This pilot demonstrated the feasibility and value of embedding HF/E education in time-pressured community pharmacy to support safer insulin dispensing. Integrating HF/E concepts into pharmacy education and development would assist in developing more resilient medication safety systems.
psychology.text:
Medication incidents reported from Northern Ireland (NI) community pharmacies identified that the safe supply of insulin is a priority area for improvement. A thematic review of reported insulin incidents identified the most common incident types are wrong insulin type, device or strength. These are internationally recognised safety hazards; compounded by the vast array of insulin products, product packaging and naming similarity.

Addressing these risks requires more than individual vigilance; it requires a systems perspective that considers how tasks, technologies, environments, work organisation and people interact in daily practice and influence wanted and unwanted outcomes.

Human Factors and Ergonomics (HF/E) is a science focused on optimising human well-being (eg, patient safety and workforce welfare) and organisational performance (eg, productivity and efficiency). It evaluates and improves all aspects of human work and seeks to support team performance by making work conditions easier for people to do the right thing safely, effectively and efficiently. The World Health Organisation, professional bodies, royal colleges and regulators endorse integration of HF/E into all aspects of patient safety education and improvement.– However, this integration has been hampered by a lack of understanding of HF/E and a failure to recognise it as a design-based systems science and practice, summarised in Sujan and Pickup, 2026.

This quality education report describes an innovative webinar-based educational intervention introducing HF/E principles to community pharmacy staff, focused on insulin safety. The aim was to increase understanding of HF/E and its practical application to local work systems and to co-design a simple tool to support SOP redesign.

By raising awareness of basic HF/E approaches, it was anticipated that community pharmacy staff would:

Have an enhanced understanding of the insulin supply context and support system redesign to reduce risks to As-Low- As- Reasonably-Practicable.

Understand the importance of user-centred design of standard operating procedures (SOPs).

Consider applying HF/E principles to other medication/patient safety issues.

Recognise the need for team discussions to understand safety culture.

Be able to support development of an HF/E toolkit for local safety assessment and management.

Three interactive 2-hour evening webinars were delivered to accommodate pharmacy staff schedules. Two HF/E specialists led the sessions (PB and HV), co-designed with senior pharmacists from medication safety (AC), primary care and the professional leadership body - NI Pharmacy Forum.

Learning objectives were as follows:

Introduce foundational HF/E concepts.

Enable participants to apply the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework to analyse work systems.

Explore performance influencing factors impacting on insulin dispensing.

How to develop purposeful SOPs.

A summary of the webinar intervention is provided in .

Topics included introductions to HF/E, SEIPS, Walk-Through-Talk-Through analysis, Human-Centred Design of SOPs, Systems Thinking for complex care systems and Safety Culture.

Supporting resources were packaged as a reusable educational bundle accessible to all participants.

Between 27 and 32 community pharmacists and primary care pharmacy advisers attended the webinars via an open invitation to all registered pharmacists from the NI Pharmacy Forum.

The SEIPS framework informed a substantive element of the webinar series. SEIPS, an entry-level HF/E model, builds on Donabedian’s structure–process–outcome model of healthcare quality, where sociotechnical work systems influence processes and outcomes. It is a multi-functional problem-solving tool that can be applied by healthcare professionals and others.

Participants were introduced to a SEIPS Worksheet provided as a downloadable Word document. This two-page tool depicts six interacting work system elements (tasks, technology, physical environment, people, organisation and external factors) and two system outcomes—performance and well-being. The reverse page lists examples of Performance Influencing Factors for each element.

Participants used the SEIPS Worksheet to analyse a real-world insulin dispensing incident ().

As the scenario unfolded, participants identified interacting factors (), including prescription scanning challenges, expanding insulin ranges, space allocation, product design, workplace distractions and SOP usability, often reflecting ‘work as imagined’ rather than ‘work as done’.

Using SEIPS as a prompt, participants reflected on system-wide issues that inhibit system performance (eg, practice safety and productivity) and human well-being (eg, patient safety and workforce well-being) both in terms of insulin supply but also on wider work system safety. Chat discussions and verbal contributions generated qualitative data which was thematically analysed using a deductive approach using SEIPS headings as codes.

Participants completed post-webinar polls containing attitudinal statements rated using a 5-point Likert scale evaluating:

Perceived usefulness of the sessions.

Clarity, relevance of content.

Confidence in applying SEIPS in practice.

Free-text feedback and thematic analysis of discussion comments were used to capture perceived system issues.

Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of this quality improvement project, as it was based on retrospective analysis of routinely collected data.

This project was conducted as a quality improvement/service evaluation initiative and did not constitute research as defined by the NI Public Health Agency’s Health and Social Care Research and Development Division. Therefore, formal ethical approval and individual informed consent were not required.

Across three sessions, there were 32 participants. 73 poll responses were received (Webinar 1 n=32; Webinar 2 n=18; Webinar 3 n=23). The five-point Likert Scale: (1) Strongly agree, (2) Agree, (3) Neither agree nor disagree, (4) Disagree, (5) Strongly disagree.

100% found the webinars useful; 47%–74% strongly agreed.

95%–97% found content clear and easy to understand.

94%–100% judged the material to be interesting and relevant.

100% reported improved understanding of HF/E and SEIPS.

78% of final-session participants strongly agreed they could apply SEIPS in their own practice.

While it is acknowledged that improved understanding is self-reported, participants were asked to define HF/E at the beginning of the webinar. It was clear that initial understanding was poor. Towards the end of the series, it was apparent that discussions around HF/E had matured, supporting the claim of improved understanding.

Participants identified multiple system-level factors affecting insulin dispensing, grouped under SEIPS work system headings (see ). Examples noted included:

Relevant patient safety and HF/E resources, primarily from NHS Education for Scotland’s Human Factors Hub, were introduced during the webinars and packaged as a bundle for participants and wider dissemination.

To make it easier for teams to design effective SOPs and based on feedback from the participants, the HF/E specialists developed a ‘Quick Checker’ tool, adapted from the Chartered Institute of Ergonomics and Human Factors’ Guidance on Design of Effective Work Procedures.

The Quick Checker supports user-centred SOP design in community pharmacy, aiding local teams to assess and improve procedures for safe insulin dispensing ().

This pilot demonstrated that a virtual HF/E educational intervention can engage community pharmacy staff and enable participation for busy teams.

The sessions enhanced understanding of work systems and supported practical application of SEIPS to an insulin dispensing scenario.

Safe supply of medication in a community pharmacy setting is symptomatic of wider system issues affecting performance and well-being (). To address medication safety requires adopting a safety management system, that extends beyond examining incident reports to: safety culture, work procedures, staffing, product management risk assessment and SOP design; all achievable through a HF/E approach.

This analysis illustrated how multiple interacting factors affect performance and well-being of staff and service users. Many of these factors are familiar for those concerned with medication safety. For example, the influence of packaging designs on safety has long been recognised. In a prospective study of 35 UK community pharmacies, 7.6% of reported dispensing incidents were attributable to similar packaging and 16.8% related to similar drug names. Similarly, issues such as software design and alert fatigue are known to impact directly on safety. It is not the factors themselves that are of great interest, but the breadth and depth of factors identified. Many are acting at a distance from frontline activity and therefore often invisible to staff. However, the discussion-based approach used across these webinars allowed multiple system perspectives to be captured, painting a much broader picture of the dispensing process. This is important from an improvement perspective: on first consideration, a dispensing error may appear to be the ‘fault’ of the dispenser. This superficial level of analysis likely leads to an intervention based on retraining or punishment. A system analysis positions the problem as a systems outcome with multiple contributory factors. Understanding this supports the design of improvement activity aimed at the appropriate level within the system. Primary care has been slower than other parts of healthcare to adopt a systems based approach. A decade ago, there was almost no evidence of its application in primary care, and it remains limited. This report captures an innovative and practical approach to developing basic Human Factors skills in the pharmacy primary care workforce.

It also demonstrated the value of SEIPS for structured reflection and problem identification.

There is increasing recognition across healthcare of the value of integrating HF/E to enhance patient safety and workforce well-being.

In community pharmacy, a clear opportunity exists to further explore patient safety and support skill development in this area. This small-scale study represents a novel approach, and to our knowledge, the SEIPS framework has not yet been applied in community pharmacy settings to uncover system-wide issues of this nature.

Integrating this approach into pharmacy education and continuing professional development would assist to develop more resilient medication safety systems.

psychology.title: Motivational predictors and configurations associated with youths’ intention to share intangible cultural heritage knowledge on Douyin: a PLS-SEM and fsQCA study
psychology.abstract: Intangible cultural heritage (ICH) depends on the continued transmission of culturally embedded knowledge across generations, yet digital exposure does not necessarily translate into active knowledge sharing among young people. This study examines the motivational structure associated with young adults’ intention to share intangible cultural heritage knowledge (ICHK) on Douyin, a short-video platform in China. Drawing on the Motives, Values, and Preferences Inventory (MVPI), an exploratory qualitative pretest was first used to identify seven motivational domains that were contextually salient to Douyin-based ICHK sharing. Survey data from 400 eligible respondents aged 18–24 in Sichuan Province were subsequently analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). PLS-SEM was used to estimate the net associations between individual motives and sharing intention, whereas fsQCA was used to identify combinations of motivational conditions associated with high intention. The PLS-SEM results show that aesthetic, altruistic, commercial, affiliation, tradition, and recognition motives are positively associated with sharing intention, while hedonistic motive shows no significant independent net association. The fsQCA analysis identifies nine equifinal sufficient configurations in the baseline solution. Notably, hedonistic motive appears in seven configurations despite its nonsignificant PLS-SEM coefficient, illustrating the distinction between independent net relevance and configurational relevance. The findings suggest that digital heritage knowledge sharing is motivationally heterogeneous and context-dependent, with cultural, social, expressive, reputational, hedonic, and instrumental motives operating in different combinations. The study contributes to digital media psychology and cultural heritage communication by integrating a broad motivational taxonomy with complementary variable-centered and configurational perspectives.
psychology.text:
Intangible cultural heritage (ICH) depends on the continued transmission of culturally embedded knowledge, skills, practices, and meanings across generations (). More broadly, digital transformation research has demonstrated the growing role of digital technologies in enabling sustainable transformation across institutional contexts (). In the cultural domain, as traditional modes of transmission face pressures associated with social transformation and changing patterns of cultural participation, digital platforms have become increasingly important environments through which younger generations encounter and engage with heritage knowledge (; ). However, greater digital exposure does not necessarily translate into active participation. Young users may view, follow, or interact with heritage-related content without actively contributing to its circulation or explaining the knowledge embedded within it (). This distinction is consequential because the sustainability of ICH depends not only on access to cultural content but also on continued knowledge transmission and participation by younger generations (; ; ). Understanding what is associated with youths’ intention to actively share intangible cultural heritage knowledge (ICHK) is therefore important for explaining participation in contemporary digital heritage communication.

Existing research on social-media knowledge sharing has identified a wide range of motivational factors, including altruism, rewards, reputation, reciprocity, self-efficacy, enjoyment, and affiliation (; ; ; ; ; ; ). Much of this evidence, however, has been developed in relation to platforms such as Facebook, WeChat, Zhihu, and Wiki, where knowledge exchange is commonly embedded in text-oriented communication or relatively stable social relationships (; ; ; ; ). Douyin provides a different communicative environment. Its short-video format foregrounds audiovisual expression, while recommendation-based distribution can extend content visibility beyond existing interpersonal networks and make audience responses observable through views, likes, comments, shares, and follower growth (). These characteristics do not necessarily create new motives, but they may alter the opportunities through which existing motives are expressed, rewarded, and made behaviorally salient. Motivational relationships identified on conventional social-media platforms therefore cannot simply be assumed to operate in the same way when culturally embedded knowledge is shared through an algorithmically curated short-video environment (; ; ).

A second unresolved issue concerns the type of knowledge being shared. ICHK differs from generic online information because it is embedded in cultural practices, collective memory, historical continuity, and intergenerational transmission (). Its circulation may therefore involve familiar social-media motives such as enjoyment, recognition, affiliation, and economic reward while simultaneously invoking aesthetic appreciation, helping others understand cultural traditions, and a perceived commitment to cultural continuity. Previous studies have identified individual motivational factors associated with cultural-heritage knowledge sharing and digital engagement, including rewards, relational expectations, enjoyment of helping, reciprocity, edutainment, and environmental or experiential qualities (; ). Nevertheless, these factors remain relatively fragmented across different theoretical perspectives. Consequently, existing research provides limited insight into how a broader set of motivational dispositions can be organized within a common framework when the object of sharing is culturally embedded heritage knowledge.

A third issue concerns how motivational relevance is conceptualized. Most studies of knowledge-sharing intention adopt a variable-centered perspective and examine whether individual predictors have statistically significant average relationships with behavioral intention (). Such analyses are useful for estimating the independent association of a particular motive while accounting for other predictors, but they do not fully address whether different motives may complement or substitute for one another (). This issue is particularly relevant to digital heritage participation, where a young user may share ICHK because of cultural responsibility and altruistic concern, whereas another may arrive at similarly high sharing intention through aesthetic expression, social recognition, affiliation, or legitimate instrumental incentives. Recent configurational research has shown that the effectiveness of ICH communication on Douyin can be associated with different combinations of platform characteristics, content attributes, and user-engagement conditions (). However, the configurational structure of youths’ underlying motivations for actively sharing ICHK remains less clearly understood. It therefore remains necessary to distinguish between the independent net relevance of individual motives and their configurational relevance when they operate in conjunction with other motivations.

To address these issues, the present study adopts the Motives, Values, and Preferences Inventory (MVPI) as a broad motivational taxonomy and applies it contextually to youths’ ICHK-sharing intention on Douyin. Rather than assuming that all original MVPI dimensions are equally relevant across technological and cultural settings, an exploratory qualitative pretest was first used to assess which motivational domains were salient in this specific context. Seven dimensions—aesthetic, affiliation, altruistic, commercial, hedonistic, recognition, and tradition motives—were subsequently examined in the quantitative study. This context-sensitive use of the MVPI allows the study to investigate how broad motivational dispositions are expressed when culturally embedded knowledge is communicated through a visually oriented short-video platform, rather than merely transferring an established inventory to a new empirical setting.

The study then combines partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine two complementary aspects of motivational relevance. PLS-SEM is used to estimate the net associations between individual motivational predictors and youths’ intention to share ICHK, whereas fsQCA is used to identify combinations of motivational conditions associated with high sharing intention. The two approaches are therefore not treated as alternative tests expected to yield identical conclusions. Instead, their integration permits examination of whether a motive that is important on average is also recurrent within sufficient configurations and, conversely, whether a motive with limited independent net relevance may become salient when combined with other conditions. In this way, the study contributes to digital media psychology, social-media knowledge-sharing research, and cultural heritage communication by linking a broad motivational taxonomy with the cultural characteristics of ICHK, the communication environment of Douyin, and a configurational account of motivational heterogeneity.

Motivation stands as a pivotal determinant of human behavior, influencing an individual’s actions, choices, and achievements (). Scholars have formulated various theories to elucidate motivation, including the hierarchy of needs, achievement motivation, two-factor theory, goal-set theory, expectancy theory, attribution theory, and self-determination theory, aiming to understand the drivers of individuals’ pursuits and successes across diverse domains. Each theory offers a unique perspective on human motivation, unveiling intricate psychological mechanisms that influence individual behavior. Drawing from these theoretical frameworks, several assessment tools have been devised to discern key motivational dimensions along the intrinsic-extrinsic spectrum. The MVPI stands out for directly assessing individual motives (). Developed by , the MVPI integrates insights from eight decades of motivation, values, and interest research, encompassing 10 motives/preferences, including aesthetic motive, altruistic motive, commercial motive, hedonistic motive, power motive, recognition motive, scientific motive, security motive, affiliation motive, and tradition motive.  illustrates the definition of each motivation.

To achieve a comprehensive understanding of the theoretical underpinnings, empirical substantiation, and pragmatic application of MVPI across various domains, a thorough review of the extant literature was conducted. As shown in , most scholars directly use the original measurement dimensions of MVPI in their research, and the focus is mainly on the aspects of psychometric characteristics and validation (; ; ), individual differences and personality (; ; ), and organizational behavior and leadership (; ; ). The framework therefore offers a sufficiently broad motivational vocabulary for examining heterogeneous reasons for action, but it was not developed specifically for social-media knowledge sharing or cultural heritage communication.

This distinction is theoretically important. Applying the MVPI to ICHK sharing does not imply that all 10 original dimensions should necessarily exhibit equal behavioral relevance in every technological or knowledge context. The original taxonomy defines the available motivational domains; the empirical salience of those domains may vary according to the behavior under investigation. In the present study, the MVPI is therefore treated as a broad theoretical taxonomy rather than as a fixed 10-factor behavioral model that must be reproduced unchanged in every setting.

Knowledge-sharing research provides empirical support for several motivational domains that conceptually correspond to the broader MVPI taxonomy. Previous studies have identified altruistic helping, rewards, reputation, enjoyment, and affiliation as relevant to knowledge-sharing intention across online environments (; ; ; ; ; ). Other studies have also examined inhibiting considerations related to security or the perceived loss of knowledge power (; ). These findings suggest that knowledge sharing is motivationally heterogeneous rather than reducible to a single intrinsic or extrinsic incentive.

ICHK sharing introduces an additional layer of contextual specificity because the knowledge being communicated is culturally embedded. ICH consists not only of information but also of practices, meanings, skills, identities, and forms of collective memory that depend on continued social transmission (). Sharing such knowledge can therefore involve motivations associated with cultural appreciation, helping others understand heritage, moral commitment to cultural continuity, social connection, recognition as a cultural communicator, enjoyment of creative expression, and potential material rewards. Consequently, the behavioral relevance of a motivational domain depends not only on the general act of knowledge sharing but also on the cultural meaning attached to the knowledge being shared.

Platform context provides a second source of contextual differentiation. Research on digital heritage communication has shown that social media, livestreaming, short video, and algorithmically curated platforms structure heritage visibility, audience interaction, and content circulation in different ways (; ; ; ; ). On Douyin, audiovisual production creates opportunities for aesthetic expression; visible audience feedback provides opportunities for recognition; interaction around shared interests enables affiliation; and the creator economy provides potential instrumental or commercial incentives. These affordances should not be interpreted as generating the underlying motives themselves. Rather, they provide different conditions through which existing motives may be enacted and become behaviorally salient.

The theoretical relationship can therefore be expressed as a process of contextual motivational salience: broad motivational dispositions provide potential reasons for action, while the characteristics of the knowledge domain and communication environment shape which of these reasons become particularly relevant to a specific behavior. In the present context, the behavior is not generic social-media participation but the intentional sharing of culturally embedded knowledge through a visually oriented short-video platform.

Because several motives may coexist within the same sharing decision, conceptual differentiation is necessary before examining their empirical relationships. In this study, aesthetic motive refers to the value attached to self-expression, cultural form, and aesthetic experience; its defining concern is the expressive and sensory quality of the activity. Altruistic motive is other-oriented and concerns the perceived value of helping others acquire or understand knowledge. Affiliation motive concerns social connection, interaction, and belonging, whereas recognition motive concerns attention, approval, prestige, and favorable evaluation by others. The distinction between these two social motives is therefore relational connection versus evaluative status. Tradition motive is conceptually different from altruism and affiliation because it concerns adherence to moral, normative, and culturally established values rather than helping particular others or forming social relationships. In ICHK sharing, it is associated with a perceived obligation to contribute to the continuity of cultural knowledge. Commercial motive, by contrast, reflects instrumental interest in economic reward and value creation. Finally, hedonistic motive concerns enjoyment, pleasure, excitement, and fun arising from the sharing activity itself. These dimensions may correlate empirically, but they represent theoretically distinct valued outcomes and therefore need not produce identical relationships with sharing intention.

Before the formal survey, an exploratory qualitative pretest was conducted to assess which MVPI domains were contextually salient in accounts of Douyin-based ICHK sharing. The purpose of this procedure was not to redefine the original MVPI taxonomy but to determine which domains were sufficiently relevant to the focal behavior to warrant inclusion in the empirical model. Seven domains—aesthetic, affiliation, altruistic, commercial, hedonistic, recognition, and tradition motives—were retained. Scientific, power, and security motives were not spontaneously identified in participants’ open-ended accounts and were therefore treated as contextually non-salient for the present study rather than as universally irrelevant motivations. The participant characteristics, interview procedure, coding process, and retention criteria are reported in the Methodology section.

The aesthetic motive reflects a preference for artistic expression, cultural form, and visually appealing experiences (). Aesthetic considerations are particularly relevant to ICHK because many heritage practices are communicated through visible forms such as performance, craftsmanship, dress, ritual, movement, and material detail (). In digital storytelling, visual presentation can support cultural legibility and audience engagement, while aesthetic value has been associated with participation in cultural content on social media (; ; ). Douyin provides a communication environment in which such preferences can be enacted through short-form audiovisual production, including composition, editing, music, movement, and visual storytelling (). Its recommendation-based distribution can also expose visually presented heritage content beyond users’ immediate social networks (). These characteristics do not imply that the platform creates aesthetic motivation; rather, they provide an environment in which aesthetic expression may become particularly relevant to ICHK sharing. Young users who place greater value on aesthetic expression may therefore be more inclined to regard sharing ICHK on Douyin as a meaningful form of cultural and self-expression. Hence, the hypothesis posits:

H1. Aesthetic motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The altruistic motive refers to a preference for helping others and contributing to their welfare without requiring direct personal reward (; ). Altruism has been consistently associated with knowledge-sharing activities in online communities and social-media environments, where individuals may contribute information because they believe it will benefit other users (; ; ; ; ). This motivation has particular relevance to ICHK sharing because heritage knowledge may be understood as a cultural resource whose continuity depends partly on being explained, documented, and made accessible to others. Sharing information about a heritage practice can help audiences understand its techniques, meanings, histories, or cultural context and can contribute to broader public awareness. Douyin enables such knowledge to reach audiences beyond immediate interpersonal networks through accessible short-form content. For young users who value helping others understand cultural heritage, sharing ICHK may therefore constitute a form of prosocial knowledge contribution. Therefore, the following hypothesis is posited:

H2. Altruistic motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The hedonistic motive reflects the value individuals place on enjoyment, pleasure, excitement, and fun (). Enjoyment has been associated with technology use and online knowledge-sharing activities, particularly where participation itself provides an intrinsically rewarding experience (; ; ; ; ; ). Sharing ICHK through short video may involve creative activities such as selecting cultural material, developing a narrative, editing audiovisual content, combining music and imagery, and interacting with audiences. These processes can make cultural knowledge sharing an experiential and creative activity rather than a purely informational task (). Douyin’s short-form audiovisual environment therefore provides opportunities through which enjoyment and creative engagement may become relevant to the sharing process. Young users who derive greater pleasure from producing and communicating cultural content may consequently report stronger intentions to participate in ICHK sharing. Consequently, the subsequent hypothesis is proposed:

H3. Hedonistic motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The commercial motive reflects an orientation toward financial return, economic value, business opportunity, and material reward (). Prior knowledge-sharing research has shown that tangible rewards and economic incentives can be associated with individuals’ willingness to contribute knowledge in online environments (; ; ; ). The relevance of commercial motivation to ICHK sharing arises from the increasing integration of cultural content into digital creator economies. Short-video production can involve substantial time and creative effort, while successful cultural content may generate opportunities related to traffic incentives, cultural-product promotion, creator collaborations, or other forms of economic return (). In this context, economic motivation need not be interpreted as incompatible with cultural communication. Rather, material return can coexist with cultural, social, or expressive reasons for participation. Young users who place greater value on economic and instrumental outcomes may therefore show stronger intentions to contribute ICHK through Douyin. Hence, the following hypothesis is posited:

H4. Commercial motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The affiliation motive reflects a preference for interpersonal connection, frequent social interaction, and a sense of belonging (; ). Knowledge sharing can provide opportunities to establish or strengthen relationships with individuals who have common interests, and previous research has associated affiliation motivation with knowledge-sharing participation on social media (; ). ICHK provides a potential basis for interest-oriented social interaction because users who share concern for particular traditions, crafts, performances, communities, or cultural practices may interact around common cultural interests. On Douyin, comments, following, sharing, and creator–audience interaction can facilitate connections among users who may not have pre-existing offline relationships. Accordingly, the relevance of affiliation differs from that of recognition: affiliation concerns the formation and maintenance of social connection, whereas recognition concerns favorable evaluation and status. Young users who value social connection may therefore be more inclined to share ICHK when doing so provides opportunities to interact with culturally interested others. Therefore, the subsequent hypothesis is proposed:

H5. Affiliation motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The tradition motive reflects a preference for established values, normative standards, moral commitment, and continuity with culturally embedded ways of life (). In knowledge-sharing contexts, moral obligation can provide a reason for contributing information when individuals regard knowledge as a collective or public good (; ). This motive is especially relevant to ICHK because intangible heritage consists of living practices and knowledge whose continuity depends on repeated transmission, interpretation, and participation across generations (; ). Sharing ICHK may therefore be understood by some young users as more than an act of online content production; it can also represent a culturally or morally meaningful contribution to maintaining knowledge about inherited practices. This distinguishes tradition motive from altruism: altruism centers on benefiting others, whereas tradition centers on consistency with normative and cultural commitments. Consequently, this hypothesis is proposed:

H6. Tradition motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The recognition motive reflects a preference for attention, approval, acknowledgement, prestige, and favorable evaluation by others (; ). Recognition has been associated with online knowledge sharing because contributing visible or valued information can strengthen users’ perceived reputation and social standing (; ; ). Recognition may acquire particular relevance on short-video platforms because audience evaluation is highly visible. Views, likes, comments, follower growth, featured content, and other observable responses can provide users with signals of how their contributions are received. In the case of ICHK, sharing culturally informative content may also allow users to be perceived as knowledgeable or engaged cultural communicators (). These platform conditions do not establish that recognition necessarily causes sharing; rather, they provide observable opportunities through which recognition-oriented users may experience social acknowledgement. Young users who place greater value on such acknowledgement may therefore report stronger intentions to share ICHK. Hence, the following hypothesis is formulated:

H7. Recognition motive is positively associated with youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

This study employs a dual-methodological approach, integrating SEM and fsQCA, to comprehensively examine the factors influencing youths’ intention to share ICHK via Douyin.

SEM is a widely recognized statistical technique used to analyze linear causal relationships between variables and to quantitatively test theoretical frameworks (). In this study, SEM is utilized to validate the direct effects of various motivational factors on the intention to share ICHK via Douyin. These factors include aesthetic motive, affiliation motive, altruistic motive, commercial motive, hedonistic motive, recognition motive, and tradition motive. SEM provides a robust framework for confirming hypothesised relationships and quantitatively assessing their strength.
