However, SEM assumes data homogeneity and may not fully capture potential nonlinear or configurational interactions among variables ().

To complement the linear analysis provided by SEM, this study also applies fsQCA, a method grounded in complexity theory. Complexity theory posits that social phenomena are shaped by multiple interdependent factors that interact in nonlinear, asymmetric ways (). Unlike traditional regression-based methods, fsQCA allows the identification of numerous causal pathways and accounts for configurational interactions among variables (). The equifinality principle of complexity theory further supports the idea that different configurations of motives can lead to the same outcome (). Thus, by integrating SEM and fsQCA, this study provides a more holistic understanding of the motivational factors underlying ICHK sharing (see ). The SEM model provides a quantitative assessment of the direct effects of the identified motivational factors. The fsQCA model illustrates the configurational relationships and multiple causal pathways that influence the intention to share ICHK via Douyin. This dual-methodological approach allows for a comprehensive analysis that combines the strengths of both quantitative and configurational methods, providing a richer and more nuanced understanding of the complex motivational dynamics at play in ICHK sharing among youths.

Before the formal survey, an exploratory qualitative pretest was conducted to assess the contextual salience of the 10 motivational domains represented in the MVPI for Douyin-based ICHK sharing. The purpose of this pretest was not to redefine the original MVPI taxonomy but to determine which motivational domains were sufficiently relevant to the focal behavior to warrant inclusion in the subsequent quantitative model.

24 young participants aged 18–24 were recruited from the four study regions: Chengdu, Aba, Ganzi, and Liangshan. Six participants were recruited from each region, with three males and three females per region, resulting in an overall gender distribution of 12 males and 12 females. All participants met the eligibility criteria subsequently applied in the formal survey: they were aged 18–24, resided in one of the four study regions, had active experience using Douyin, and possessed basic awareness of ICH.

Individual face-to-face interviews were conducted, each lasting approximately 30–45 min. With participants’ consent, the interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The interview protocol followed a two-stage sequence. Participants were first asked open-ended questions about their experiences of Douyin, their understanding of ICH, and their reasons for being willing or unwilling to share ICHK. These open-ended questions were intentionally presented before any theory-informed prompts so that participants could articulate motivational considerations in their own terms. The second stage used probes corresponding to the MVPI domains to explore the relevance of motivational themes that might not have emerged spontaneously. The interview guide is provided in the .

Two researchers independently reviewed and coded the interview transcripts. Initial coding focused on statements indicating reasons, expected benefits, concerns, values, or anticipated outcomes associated with ICHK sharing. These codes were then compared with the 10 MVPI domains. Coding disagreements were discussed until agreement was reached. No numerical inclusion threshold was predetermined before the interviews; instead, the decision focused primarily on whether a motivational domain emerged spontaneously and recurrently in participants’ accounts. Each of the seven retained domains was spontaneously mentioned by at least two participants.

The pretest indicated recurrent contextual relevance for aesthetic, affiliation, altruistic, commercial, hedonistic, recognition, and tradition motives. By contrast, scientific, power, and security motives were not spontaneously identified in participants’ open-ended accounts. These three motives were therefore treated as contextually non-salient for the present focal behavior and were not included in the quantitative model. Their exclusion should not be interpreted as evidence that these motives are universally irrelevant to cultural heritage sharing; rather, the pretest indicated limited salience in this specific population, platform, and behavioral context.

The formal survey was administered online through Wenjuanxing between July 30 and October 30, 2023. Before accessing the questionnaire, respondents were informed of the research purpose, voluntary nature of participation, anonymity, confidentiality, and right to withdraw. Electronic informed consent was required before respondents could proceed. The study protocol was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of Universiti Sains Malaysia (Approval No. USM/JEPeM/PP/23040337) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Participants were required to satisfy four eligibility criteria. First, they had to be aged 18–24 years. Second, they had to reside in Chengdu, Aba, Ganzi, or Liangshan in Sichuan Province. Third, they had to qualify as active Douyin users. Active use was operationalized as participation in at least one of three forms of platform activity: contribution activities, such as liking, commenting, forwarding, following, or saving content; enhancement activities, such as editing videos, applying filters or transitions, adding music or subtitles; or creation activities, such as producing videos, livestreaming, or interacting with followers. Respondents who were not Douyin users or who reported only viewing videos were excluded. Fourth, respondents were required to demonstrate basic ICH awareness.

Basic ICH awareness was operationalized using a screening item assessing familiarity with ICH elements relevant to the study context. Respondents rated their familiarity on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (very good). A respondent was eligible to continue if a score of at least 3 was reported for at least one listed ICH element; respondents who did not meet this criterion were screened out. The formal questionnaire presented respondents with the official Chinese definition of ICH before this screening procedure.

Because no complete sampling frame was available and eligible participants were geographically dispersed, exponential non-discriminative snowball sampling was employed. Initial participants were recruited through multiple pre-existing WeChat networks, including university associations, volunteer networks, and cultural-interest groups, across the four regions. These participants subsequently referred other eligible respondents, allowing recruitment to expand across multiple referral networks rather than a single institutional source.

Equal regional quotas were used to ensure that each of the four study areas contributed a sufficient and analytically comparable number of observations and to reduce the possibility that recruitment would be dominated by a single, more accessible regional network. The target was 100 valid responses per region. These quotas were not population-proportional and were not intended to make the sample statistically representative of the youth populations of the four regions.

A total of 500 questionnaires were collected. After application of the eligibility and data-quality criteria, 400 valid cases were retained for analysis, corresponding to 100 respondents from each region. Cases were excluded if respondents fell outside the target age range, did not meet the active-Douyin-use criterion, did not satisfy the ICH-awareness screening criterion, resided outside the four study regions, or provided incomplete or inconsistent responses.

The final sample consisted of 400 participants (see ). Males accounted for 52.8% of the sample (n = 211) and females for 47.3% (n = 189). Most respondents were aged 18–21 years (83.8%, n = 335), whereas 16.3% (n = 65) were aged 22–24 years. Regarding education, 74.0% (n = 296) were in the college/university category, 15.5% (n = 62) were in secondary/high school, 9.8% (n = 39) were postgraduates, and 0.8% (n = 3) reported another educational status. By design, Chengdu, Aba, Ganzi, and Liangshan each contributed 100 respondents (25.0%). In terms of Douyin-use experience, 74 respondents (18.5%) were categorized as participating in contribution activities, 149 (37.3%) in enhancement activities, and 177 (44.3%) in creation activities.

Characteristics of the final sample (n = 400).

Measurement items for the eight constructs were adapted from previously validated scales (see ). Aesthetic motive was measured using three items adapted from , affiliation motive using four items from , altruistic motive using three items from , commercial motive using three items from , hedonistic motive using three items from , recognition motive using five items from , tradition motive using three items from , and intention to share ICHK on Douyin using three items from .

The items were contextually adapted so that the referent behavior consistently concerned sharing ICHK on Douyin. Adaptation focused on construct–item fit, relevance to Douyin-based ICHK sharing, clarity of wording, ambiguity, and equivalence between the English and Chinese versions. The underlying conceptual meaning of each construct was retained while the behavioral referent was made specific to the study context.

Content validation was conducted by four experts with academic expertise in communication, knowledge management, ICH/cultural heritage, psychology, social media, measurement, or bilingual questionnaire adaptation. The panel included professors and associate professors with empirical research experience related to youth behavior. Experts evaluated the correspondence between each item and its intended construct, relevance to Douyin-based ICHK sharing, contextual appropriateness, wording clarity, potential ambiguity, and bilingual consistency. Written item-level comments were collected and further discussed through face-to-face or online consultation where clarification was required.

Item relevance was evaluated on a four-point scale and summarized using the item-level content validity index (I-CVI) and the scale-level content validity index based on the average method (S-CVI/Ave). I-CVI values ranged from 0.75 to 1.00, and the S-CVI/Ave was 0.99. Items receiving relatively lower agreement were reconsidered through expert discussion and were revised or removed where necessary rather than being retained automatically.

Expert review resulted in several contextual and linguistic revisions. For example, the midpoint response label was revised from “neutral” to “neither agree nor disagree” to reduce ambiguity; the questionnaire introduction adopted the official Chinese definition of ICH for the formal Sichuan survey; and the age question was converted from an open response format into predefined screening categories. The Douyin-use item was also refined to distinguish passive viewing from contribution, enhancement, and creation activities. Items judged redundant or insufficiently aligned with the focal construct were reconsidered and removed where appropriate.

The instrument was initially developed in English and translated into Chinese. Two bilingual experts reviewed and refined the Chinese wording, after which two independent bilingual experts conducted back-translation into English. The original and back-translated versions were compared for semantic consistency, and discrepancies were discussed until agreement was reached. The final questionnaire was administered in Chinese.

Because predictor and outcome variables were collected from the same respondents using the same questionnaire, common method bias was assessed using two post hoc diagnostics. Harman’s single-factor test indicated that the first unrotated factor accounted for 32.68% of the total variance. In addition, full-collinearity VIF values ranged from 1.417 to 2.879, below the 3.3 criterion. Taken together, these diagnostics did not indicate substantial common method bias, although post hoc statistical tests cannot completely rule out common method variance.

PLS-SEM was conducted using WarpPLS 8.0. The method was selected because the study has an explanatory–predictive orientation and seeks to estimate the relative net associations of multiple motivational predictors with sharing intention, while also providing a variable-centered counterpart to the configurational analysis. The choice was therefore based primarily on the analytical objective rather than on sample-size limitations.

A two-stage assessment procedure was followed (). First, the measurement model was evaluated in terms of indicator reliability, internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability, convergent validity using average variance extracted (AVE), and discriminant validity using the heterotrait–monotrait ratio (HTMT), with values below 0.90 used as the criterion.

Second, the structural model was evaluated using collinearity diagnostics, the coefficient of determination (R2 and adjusted R2), path-specific effect sizes, predictive relevance (Q2), and the magnitude and statistical significance of the structural coefficients. Statistical inference was based on 5,000 bootstrap resamples, with bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence intervals. Out-of-sample predictive performance was additionally assessed using the PLSpredict procedure by comparing PLS-SEM prediction errors with those obtained from a linear-model benchmark.

The seven motivational conditions and the outcome were calibrated into fuzzy sets using the direct calibration method. Because no externally established substantive thresholds were available for these multi-item motivational constructs, sample-relative anchors were adopted. The 95th percentile was used to indicate full membership, the 50th percentile as the crossover point, and the 5th percentile as full non-membership (). The 95th and 5th percentiles were used rather than the sample maximum and minimum to reduce sensitivity to extreme observations, while the median provided a transparent sample-relative point of maximum membership ambiguity.

For the sufficiency analysis, the truth table was constructed using a frequency threshold of three cases, a raw-consistency threshold of 0.80, and a PRI-consistency threshold of 0.80. Truth-table rows meeting these criteria were retained for logical minimization.

The measurement model was evaluated in terms of indicator reliability, internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. As shown in , all indicator loadings exceeded 0.70 (), ranging from 0.719 to 0.911. Cronbach’s alpha values ranged from 0.700 to 0.839, and composite reliability values ranged from 0.834 to 0.886, indicating satisfactory internal consistency across the eight constructs. Average variance extracted (AVE) values ranged from 0.581 to 0.702 and therefore exceeded the recommended 0.50 criterion, supporting convergent validity.

Measurement model assessment.

CR,composite reliability; AVE,average variance extraction.

Discriminant validity was assessed using the heterotrait–monotrait ratio (HTMT; see ). All HTMT values were below the 0.90 criterion (). The highest value was 0.866 between altruistic motive and intention to share ICHK, indicating that the constructs remained empirically distinguishable despite their theoretical relatedness. The measurement model therefore demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity.

Heterotrait–monotrait ratios (HTMT) for discriminant validity.

All values are below the 0.90 criterion. AESM, aesthetic motive; AFFM, affiliation motive; ALTM, altruistic motive; COMM, commercial motive; HEDM, hedonistic motive; RECM, recognition motive; TRAM, tradition motive; INT, intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

Prior to interpreting the structural coefficients, collinearity was assessed. As shown in , the full-collinearity VIF values ranged from 1.417 to 2.879, remaining below the conservative threshold of 3.3 and indicating no substantial collinearity concerns. The seven motivational predictors jointly explained 65.3% of the variance in intention to share ICHK on Douyin (R2 = 0.653; adjusted R2 = 0.646). Stone–Geisser’s Q2 value for sharing intention was 0.680, indicating predictive relevance.

Path-specific effect sizes were 0.155 for aesthetic motive, 0.057 for affiliation motive, 0.173 for altruistic motive, 0.099 for commercial motive, 0.001 for hedonistic motive, 0.124 for recognition motive, and 0.069 for tradition motive. Using conventional benchmarks (), aesthetic and altruistic motives showed medium effect sizes; affiliation, commercial, recognition, and tradition motives showed small effect sizes; and the effect size of hedonistic motive was negligible.

Out-of-sample predictive performance was further assessed using the PLSpredict procedure (). All three indicators of sharing intention yielded positive Q2 predict values (0.318–0.524; see ). In addition, the PLS-SEM prediction errors were lower than those of the linear-model benchmark for all three indicators in terms of both RMSE and MAE. Specifically, PLS-SEM RMSE values ranged from 0.441 to 0.666, compared with 0.451 to 0.684 for the linear model. These results indicate high out-of-sample predictive performance according to the PLSpredict benchmark.

PLSpredict assessment of out-of-sample predictive performance.

Positive Q2predict values indicate predictive relevance for the holdout observations. Lower PLS-SEM RMSE and MAE values relative to the linear-model (LM) benchmark indicate superior out-of-sample predictive performance. RMSE = root mean squared error; MAE = mean absolute error; LM = linear model.

Statistical inference was based on 5,000 bootstrap resamples with bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence intervals (see ). Aesthetic motive was positively associated with sharing intention (β = 0.216, p < 0.001), as were altruistic motive (β = 0.264, p < 0.001), commercial motive (β = 0.161, p < 0.001), affiliation motive (β = 0.124, p < 0.001), tradition motive (β = 0.134, p = 0.003), and recognition motive (β = 0.177, p < 0.001). Hedonistic motive showed no significant net association with sharing intention (β = 0.001, p = 0.484). Accordingly, H1, H2, H4, H5, H6, and H7 were supported, whereas H3 was not supported.

Structural model results.

Bootstrap resamples = 5,000. AESM, aesthetic motive; AFFM, affiliation motive; ALTM, altruistic motive; COMM, commercial motive; HEDM, hedonistic motive; RECM, recognition motive; TRAM, tradition motive; INT, intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

Before the analysis, the seven motivational conditions and the outcome were calibrated into fuzzy-set membership scores. In the baseline specification, the 95th percentile was used as the threshold for full membership, the 50th percentile as the crossover point, and the 5th percentile as the threshold for full non-membership (). The actual calibration anchors for each condition and the outcome are reported in . The full-membership anchors ranged from 4.67 to 5.00, the crossover anchors from 3.67 to 4.00, and the full non-membership anchors from 3.00 to 3.33.

Calibration anchors for the fsQCA analysis.

AESM, aesthetic motive; AFFM, affiliation motive; ALTM, altruistic motive; COMM, commercial motive; HEDM, hedonistic motive; RECM, recognition motive; TRAM, tradition motive; INT, intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

Necessity analysis was then conducted to assess whether any individual condition or its negation was necessary for high sharing intention. A consistency threshold of 0.90 was used as the criterion for necessity (; ). As shown in , none of the individual motivational conditions reached this threshold for high sharing intention. Among the positive conditions, tradition motive showed the highest necessity consistency (0.82), followed by altruistic motive (0.80), aesthetic motive (0.79), commercial motive (0.79), hedonistic motive (0.79), affiliation motive (0.73), and recognition motive (0.74). These results indicate that no single motivational condition was individually necessary for high ICHK-sharing intention.

Necessity analysis for high and low ICHK-sharing intention.

‘∼’ represents the ‘negation’ of a logical operation. AESM, aesthetic motive; AFFM, affiliation motive; ALTM, altruistic motive; COMM, commercial motive; HEDM, hedonistic motive; RECM, recognition motive; TRAM, tradition motive; INT, intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

A truth table was constructed using a frequency threshold of three cases and a raw-consistency threshold of 0.80 (; ). PRI consistency was also considered using a threshold of 0.8 (). Truth-table rows meeting the predefined criteria were retained for logical minimization. The resulting intermediate solution identified nine sufficient configurations associated with high ICHK-sharing intention. The overall solution consistency was 0.96 and the solution coverage was 0.69, indicating that the identified configurations displayed a high degree of subset consistency with the high-intention outcome and jointly covered a substantial proportion of cases belonging to that outcome set.

The nine configurations are summarized in . Their individual consistencies ranged from 0.96 to 0.97, while raw coverage ranged from 0.35 to 0.50. Unique coverage values were relatively small, ranging from 0.00 to 0.03, reflecting substantial overlap among the sufficient configurations.

Sufficient configurations associated with high intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

“●” indicates the presence of a condition; “⊗” indicates the absence; Blank spaces indicate “do not care.” AESM, aesthetic motive; AFFM, affiliation motive; ALTM, altruistic motive; COMM, commercial motive; HEDM, hedonistic motive; RECM, recognition motive; TRAM, tradition motive; INT, intention to share ICHK on Douyin.

The identified configurations were:

C1: AFFM * ALTM * COMM * TRAM

C2: AESM * ~ AFFM * ALTM * HEDM * TRAM

C3: AESM * AFFM * COMM * HEDM * TRAM

C4: AESM * ALTM * COMM * RECM * TRAM

C5: AESM * AFFM * HEDM * RECM * TRAM

C6: AESM * ALTM * HEDM * RECM * TRAM

C7: AFFM * COMM * HEDM * RECM * TRAM

C8: ALTM * COMM * HEDM * RECM * TRAM

C9: AESM * AFFM * ALTM * COMM * HEDM * RECM.

Pattern 1: social–instrumental–tradition configurations

Configurations 1 and 3 share the simultaneous presence of affiliation, commercial, and tradition motives. These configurations suggest that social connection, instrumental return, and cultural or normative commitment can coexist within high sharing intention. In Configuration 3, aesthetic and hedonistic motives are additionally present, indicating a more expressive and enjoyment-oriented variant of the same broader motivational pattern.

Pattern 2: aesthetic–altruistic–tradition configurations

Configurations 2 and 4 share the presence of aesthetic, altruistic, and tradition motives, indicating a pattern in which cultural expression, helping others, and normative commitment jointly characterize high sharing intention. Configuration 2 additionally includes hedonistic motive and the absence of affiliation motive, whereas Configuration 4 combines this pattern with commercial and recognition motives. The contrast between the two configurations illustrates equifinality: similar levels of high intention can arise through different accompanying social and instrumental conditions.

Pattern 3: hedonistic–recognition configurations

Configurations 5–8 share the joint presence of hedonistic and recognition motives together with tradition motive, while Configuration 9 also contains hedonistic and recognition motives but treats tradition as a “do not care” condition. These solutions indicate that enjoyment and social recognition frequently occur as part of broader motivational combinations associated with high sharing intention, rather than functioning as independently sufficient motives.

Hedonistic motive appeared in seven of the nine sufficient configurations, despite having no significant net association in the PLS-SEM model. Tradition motive was present in eight of the nine sufficient configurations, making it the most recurrent condition in the baseline solution. However, its necessity consistency was only 0.82, below the 0.90 threshold, so it should not be interpreted as a necessary condition. Across the baseline solution, tradition motive appeared in eight configurations, hedonistic motive in seven, aesthetic, altruistic, commercial, and recognition motives in six each, and affiliation motive in five. The absence of affiliation motive appeared in Configuration 2. These frequencies should be interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence of isolated importance because fsQCA evaluates conditions conjuncturally.

Robustness checks were conducted using alternative calibration anchors (90th/50th/10th percentiles) and a stricter raw-consistency threshold of 0.85. The resulting solutions were substantively consistent with the baseline analysis, with only minor differences in individual configurations. The principal motivational patterns, as well as overall solution consistency and coverage, remained stable across specifications.

This study examined youths’ intention to share ICHK on Douyin from two complementary analytical perspectives. The PLS-SEM results indicate that aesthetic, altruistic, commercial, affiliation, tradition, and recognition motives are positively associated with sharing intention, whereas hedonistic motive shows no significant independent net association. The fsQCA results, in contrast, identify multiple motivational configurations associated with high sharing intention. Taken together, the findings indicate that motivational relevance cannot be reduced to whether a single motive has a statistically significant average association with the outcome; some motives also acquire relevance through the combinations in which they occur.

At the variable-centered level, the results suggest that ICHK sharing is associated with multiple forms of motivation rather than a single intrinsic–extrinsic distinction (; ; ; ; ). Aesthetic motive reflects the expressive and visual character of communicating cultural knowledge; altruistic motive reflects the perceived value of helping others understand heritage; affiliation and recognition capture different social outcomes of sharing; commercial motive reflects instrumental return; and tradition motive reflects normative and cultural commitment. The simultaneous significance of these motives is consistent with the culturally and socially embedded nature of ICHK sharing, where expressive, prosocial, relational, reputational, instrumental, and normative considerations may coexist within the same behavioral domain.

The nonsignificant PLS-SEM coefficient for hedonistic motive is especially informative. Hedonistic motive showed virtually no independent net association with sharing intention (β = 0.001, p = 0.484), despite prior research linking enjoyment to online participation and knowledge-sharing activities. This result suggests that enjoyment alone may not distinguish young users with stronger ICHK-sharing intention once the other motivational predictors are considered simultaneously. In the context of cultural heritage knowledge, sharing may involve responsibilities, meanings, and expected social outcomes that extend beyond enjoyment itself. However, this interpretation should not be taken to mean that hedonistic motivation is irrelevant, because the configurational results provide a different picture.

The fsQCA results clarify this distinction. Hedonistic motive appears in seven of the nine sufficient configurations, even though it is nonsignificant in the PLS-SEM model. This is the clearest illustration of the difference between independent net relevance and configurational relevance. Hedonistic motivation may contribute little as an isolated statistical predictor but become relevant when it co-occurs with recognition, tradition, aesthetic, affiliation, altruistic, or commercial motives. The finding therefore cautions against interpreting a nonsignificant net coefficient as evidence of theoretical irrelevance. A second cross-method pattern concerns tradition motive. Its PLS-SEM coefficient is positive but comparatively modest (β = 0.134, p = 0.003), whereas it appears in eight of the nine baseline fsQCA configurations. At the same time, its necessity consistency for high sharing intention is 0.82, below the 0.90 criterion. Tradition motive should therefore be interpreted as highly recurrent but not necessary. This distinction is theoretically important: a culturally or morally oriented commitment appears frequently within high-intention combinations, but high sharing intention can still occur through at least one configuration in which tradition is not required. Altruistic motive presents the reverse analytical pattern. It has the largest positive PLS-SEM coefficient (β = 0.264, p < 0.001), yet it appears in only six of the nine baseline configurations and does not satisfy the criterion for necessity. A relatively strong average association therefore does not imply that a motive must be present across all high-intention configurations. Similarly, affiliation motive is positively associated with intention in PLS-SEM (β = 0.124, p < 0.001), but Configuration 2 explicitly includes the absence of affiliation motive. This indicates that high sharing intention can emerge even under low affiliation when other motives compensate for its absence.

These cross-method differences support an equifinal interpretation of ICHK-sharing motivation. Young users need not arrive at high sharing intention through a uniform motivational profile. Some configurations combine social connection, instrumental return, and cultural commitment; others combine aesthetic expression, altruism, and tradition; still others repeatedly combine enjoyment and recognition with additional cultural, social, or instrumental conditions. The value of the dual-method design therefore lies not in requiring PLS-SEM and fsQCA to produce identical findings, but in showing how average net associations and conjunctural motivational patterns provide different forms of evidence about the same behavioral intention.

The study contributes theoretically in three related areas.

First, it contributes to motivation theory by showing that the behavioral salience of broad motivational dispositions is context-dependent. The MVPI provides a general taxonomy of valued outcomes, but the present findings suggest that their relevance to a specific behavior depends on the knowledge domain and communication context in which they are enacted. This is evident both in the qualitative pretest, which identified only seven contextually salient MVPI domains, and in the quantitative findings, where those motives displayed different forms of net and configurational relevance. The contribution is therefore not the creation of new motivational dimensions, but the demonstration that broad motivational dispositions require contextual interpretation when applied to culturally embedded digital practices.

Second, the study contributes to digital media psychology by conceptualizing platform characteristics as conditions for motivational enactment rather than as sources that create motivation. Douyin’s audiovisual format, visible audience feedback, interaction mechanisms, and creator-oriented economic environment provide different opportunities through which aesthetic, recognition, affiliation, commercial, and hedonistic motives may be expressed. Importantly, these platform characteristics were not modeled as mediators or moderators in the present study. The findings therefore do not establish that algorithmic distribution changes users’ underlying motives. Instead, they suggest that a platform environment can recontextualize the conditions under which existing motives become behaviorally salient.

Third, the study contributes to cultural heritage communication by showing that digital ICHK sharing involves motivational hybridity. Heritage communication is not explained solely by preservation-oriented or culturally normative motivations. Tradition and altruism coexist with aesthetic expression, social affiliation, recognition, enjoyment, and commercial considerations. The fsQCA results make this particularly visible because high sharing intention emerges through multiple combinations that mix culturally oriented and platform-oriented motives. This suggests that participation in digital heritage communication should not be conceptualized as a simple opposition between cultural commitment and contemporary platform incentives; the two can coexist within the same motivational configuration.

Methodologically, the integration of PLS-SEM and fsQCA further contributes by distinguishing independent net relevance from configurational relevance. A motive can have a strong net association without being necessary across configurations, as illustrated by altruistic motive, while another motive can have little independent net association but recur across multiple sufficient configurations, as illustrated by hedonistic motive. This distinction provides a more precise account of motivational heterogeneity than either analytical perspective would provide in isolation.

The findings suggest that interventions designed to support ICHK sharing should not rely on a single universal motivational appeal. The PLS-SEM results indicate that several motives are independently associated with sharing intention, while the fsQCA results show that high intention can emerge through different motivational combinations. Cultural authorities, ICH institutions, and platform practitioners should therefore consider differentiated intervention designs that align with distinct motivational profiles rather than assuming that all young users respond to the same incentive.

One intervention pathway can combine aesthetic, altruistic, and tradition-oriented appeals. Cultural institutions can provide short-video storytelling templates, visual-production guidance, concise heritage-information resources, and access to expert or inheritor consultation. Such support would allow young creators to present culturally accurate information while also making heritage content visually intelligible and useful to others. Campaigns organized around cultural explanation, intergenerational transmission, or “help others understand this tradition” can align aesthetic expression with prosocial and cultural-responsibility motives.

A second pathway can combine tradition, affiliation, and commercial motives. Institutions can establish creator communities, creator–inheritor co-production programmes, peer-review networks, workshops, micro-grants, or legitimate cultural-product and tourism partnerships. In this configuration, commercial incentives should be tied to culturally responsible production rather than traffic volume alone. Material support can therefore function alongside community participation and cultural commitment without requiring commercial motivation to displace heritage values.

A third pathway concerns the recurrent combination of hedonistic and recognition motives. Because hedonistic motive was nonsignificant as an independent net predictor but appeared repeatedly in the fsQCA configurations, entertainment-oriented design should not be treated as a sufficient strategy by itself. Instead, playful storytelling, creative challenges, audiovisual experimentation, or participatory formats can be combined with forms of culturally meaningful recognition. These might include expert-reviewed selections, thematic featuring, creator–inheritor co-credit, public exhibitions, or heritage-contributor recognition. Such mechanisms provide acknowledgement without reducing recognition solely to likes, follower counts, or traffic metrics.

The recurrence of tradition motive across most baseline configurations also suggests that culturally meaningful framing can function as a cross-cutting element in many interventions, although it should not be treated as universally necessary. Different motivational combinations remain viable, and a single intervention model is therefore unlikely to fit all young users.

For platform practitioners, the findings support the development of differentiated creator-support mechanisms, heritage-themed spaces, co-creation opportunities, contextual information prompts, and recognition systems for culturally responsible contributions. Because algorithmic recommendation mechanisms were not directly measured in this study, the findings do not justify specific claims about how ranking or recommendation systems should be altered. Future platform experiments could test whether changes in visibility, feedback, recognition, or monetization features modify actual heritage-sharing behavior.

Several limitations define the boundaries of the present findings. First, the study focuses on behavioral intention rather than observed sharing behavior. Intention provides an important proximal indicator of participation, but users who intend to share cultural knowledge may not ultimately do so. Future research could combine survey measures with behavioral indicators such as actual posting, forwarding, commenting, content production, or longitudinal creator activity.

Second, the motivational framework was contextually delimited on the basis of the qualitative pretest. Scientific, power, and security motives were not spontaneously salient among the 24 pretest participants and were therefore not included in the formal model. This decision improved alignment between the empirical model and the focal context but does not imply that these motives are irrelevant to ICHK sharing in other settings. Scientific motivation may become more salient in documentation or research-oriented heritage contexts, security concerns may matter where cultural or intellectual property is contested, and power-related motives may emerge where authority over cultural representation is more prominent. Cross-platform and cross-context studies are needed to examine these boundary conditions.

Third, the non-probability snowball sampling design limits population-level generalizability. Recruitment through university associations, volunteer networks, and cultural-interest groups may have overrepresented respondents who were more socially connected, digitally active, or culturally engaged than the broader youth population. Equal quotas ensured balanced representation of the four study regions within the analytical sample but did not correct referral-chain homophily or reproduce the underlying population distribution. Future studies should consider probability-based, stratified, or larger multi-site sampling designs.

Fourth, the study was limited to young people aged 18–24 and to Douyin users in four regions of Sichuan. The motivational patterns identified here may differ among older users, less digitally active populations, other cultural regions, or users of platforms with different affordance structures. Comparative studies across Douyin, WeChat, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, TikTok, Instagram, or other platforms could provide stronger evidence about which motivational patterns are platform-specific and which are more generalizable.

Finally, the present study integrates variable-centered and configurational analyses, but the model does not directly measure platform affordances, cultural identity, perceived authenticity, or other psychological mechanisms that might explain why specific motivational combinations become salient. Future research could extend the framework by incorporating these constructs as theoretically justified antecedents, moderators, or mediating mechanisms, provided that such extensions are tested with designs capable of supporting the corresponding interpretations.

This study examined the motivational structure associated with young people’s intention to share ICHK on Douyin by integrating PLS-SEM and fsQCA. The PLS-SEM results indicate that aesthetic, altruistic, commercial, affiliation, tradition, and recognition motives are positively associated with sharing intention, whereas hedonistic motive shows no significant independent net association. The fsQCA analysis provides a complementary perspective by identifying multiple equifinal configurations associated with high sharing intention. No single motivational condition was individually necessary for the outcome. Importantly, hedonistic motive appeared in seven of the nine baseline sufficient configurations despite its nonsignificant PLS-SEM coefficient, while tradition motive appeared in eight configurations without meeting the criterion for necessity. These findings illustrate that independent net relevance and configurational relevance are analytically distinct: a motive may contribute little as an isolated predictor yet remain salient when combined with other motivational conditions. Taken together, the findings support a context-sensitive and conjunctural understanding of motivation in digital heritage communication. Young people may arrive at similarly high ICHK-sharing intention through different combinations of cultural, social, expressive, reputational, hedonic, and instrumental motives. The study therefore extends research on social-media knowledge sharing by showing that motivational relevance depends not only on individual predictors but also on the combinations in which motives occur. These findings should be interpreted within the boundaries of the research design. The data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the outcome is behavioral intention rather than observed sharing behavior, and the snowball sampling procedure limits population-level generalizability. Accordingly, the reported relationships should be interpreted as statistical and set-theoretic associations rather than established causal effects. Future longitudinal, experimental, and behavioral studies could examine how these motivational patterns develop over time and whether specific platform conditions alter actual ICHK-sharing behavior.

psychology.title: Scaffolded acquisition of a robot self–world distinction in a layered architecture model of the developing self
psychology.abstract: How does the sense of self emerge in human development, and could an artificial system acquire a similar sense using algorithmic principles and given a suitable embodiment and experience? Here, we describe a machine learning framework, inspired by developmental psychology and neurobiology, that acquires a self–world distinction and minimal self-model. Unlike previous approaches, we introduce a gradual formulation, integrating correlation-based and predictive techniques within a layered architecture. Using a simulated humanoid, we show first how a self–world distinction can emerge through correlation-based self-supervision. This model uses dependencies between proprioception and vision to distinguish its own body from its surroundings during infant-like motor babbling. Next, we construct a model of how these sensory signals will evolve in time. This predictive capacity uses the self–world distinction acquired by the lower layer as input to neural ordinary differential equation models that learn continuous dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate scaffolding of the higher layer by the lower one, showing that predictive learning occurs more rapidly with the lower layer already in place. By integrating these mechanisms, our approach offers a framework for characterizing a minimal robotic self that can inform our understanding of the emergence of the sense of self in the human mind/brain.This article is part of the discussion meeting issue ‘From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self’.
psychology.text:
The self–world distinction is the separation of experience (perceptual and cognitive) as deriving from the self (‘me’) or from its counterpart, the world (‘not me’) []. For the human self, this distinction seems closely tied to the sense of ownership of the physical body and of signals emanating from inside body (or as relating to the body, for instance, when you observe yourself) and to the sense of agency—the experience of owning and originating actions and their consequences []. Following Piaget [], the distinction between self and world may also be seen as a prerequisite for a self–other distinction with respect to the social world [,], that is, the separation of the mental life of the self from that of other selves [,]. Although conceptually we can distinguish these different aspects of the sense of self, understanding how they stand with respect to each other and how each might emerge in both evolution and development remains mysterious. Here, we take a synthetic ‘understanding through building’ approach [] to begin to untangle these interdependencies.

As we will explore in this article, the self–world distinction is not all-or-nothing and can manifest in different ways. It can be non-conceptual, or anoetic, where the self is experienced as distinct but without any insight or self-awareness [,]. On the other hand, it can also be reflective, or noetic, where the self can be a subject of thought and judgement [,]. Finally, it can be autonoetic where the self can be conceived of and experienced as existing across time []. These three aspects can be present alongside each other. The anoetic aspects may contribute a feeling of the self as motivated, integrated and bounded, while the noetic aspects become more prominent during self-reflection and autonoetic when remembering the past or imagining the future.

In psychiatric conditions, different aspects of the self–world distinction can become disturbed, such as in asomatognosia where a part of the body is experienced as not belonging to the self, or in autoscopia where a visual hallucination of the self is projected into the outside world []. Likewise, altered states of consciousness, such as those induced by meditation or psychoactive drugs, can lead to a partial dissolution of the self–world boundary []. Experimental devices, such as the rubber hand illusion, and technologies, such as virtual reality and robotic telepresence, can also alter the experience of the self–world boundary, such that we might experience ownership of an artificial hand [] or have a feeling of the self as being outside the physical body [,]. This evidence points to the actively and continuously constructed nature of the experience of selfhood [].

In developmental terms, construction of a self–world distinction likely begins with the infant's own body and with the interoceptive, proprioceptive and somatosensory signals it generates []. For instance, basic visceral neural circuits, such as those underlying heartbeat, breathing and swallowing, emerge by the second trimester of pregnancy [] and could provide a backdrop of predictable internal sensory dynamics to which new kinds of signals can be associated as also belonging to the self [,]. Proprioceptive signals provide evidence to the developing brain of its own agency as they vary in correlation with internally generated motor signals [,,]. Somatosensory signals emanating from the skin—the body–world boundary—afford different experiences when the unborn baby touches innervated and non-innervated regions of her body []. This may provide the developing fetus with one of the earliest indications of her separate and bounded nature.

By the time we are born, human experience likely includes a distinction between self and world, albeit of an anoetic nature [,,]. This is indicated, for instance, by a touch on the cheek of a neonate which will trigger a rooting response except when the infant touches herself []. In the newborn, hearing and vision offer new means of learning about the self through reafference—observation of the sensory consequences of self-generated movements and sounds [,,]. For instance, when awake and alert, and in a supported position, a newborn may engage in arm and hand movements, a portion of which will fall within her visual field []. These movements, which appear exploratory but not goal-directed and are sometimes referred to as hand or motor ‘babbling’ [,], provide a new means of distinguishing the bodily self and its actions. By three months, exploratory movements are largely replaced by coordinated visually guided reaching that appears more intentional [] and, by around six months, by reach and grasp behaviours that are suitably adapted to context [,].

In this contribution, we are specifically concerned with the question of how reafference might contribute to the emergence of the self–world distinction. We take a synthetic approach [,] using machine learning and (simulated) robotic modelling to explore how visual reafference, as in the infant's observations of her own limb movements, might guide the emergence of a visual self–world distinction (VSWD). We have previously argued that a unified experience of self emerges from the activity of multiple self ‘subsystems’ in the mind/brain [,,]. Moreover, building on early proposals from Damasio [], Panksepp [,] and Northoff et al. [], we have also argued that this ‘self system’ is organized in the form of a layered architecture [,], whereby some core aspects of self—principally those related to anoetic senses of agency and ownership—are available in young infants (0–3 months of age), while other aspects emerge more gradually during childhood [,]. For instance, while the newborn is thought to live ‘in the moment’, by age two, the developing child will begin to distinguish past from future. However, this is still only the beginning of the emergence of a sense of the self in time. Full autonoetic experience, including the capacity to mentally ‘time travel’ into the past or future, may only arise alongside the acquisition of autobiographical memory capacities by age 4 or later [,,].

According to this view, postnatal experience, alongside brain maturation, is critical in assembling the human sense of self. Here, we propose and test, using a robot simulation of motor babbling, a layered architecture hypothesis for the acquisition of a VSWD during the first few months of infancy. Specifically, as illustrated in , we first model a learning layer, inspired by Hebbian principles, that uses the correlation between visual and proprioceptive signals to provide an initial decomposition of the visual world into self and non-self components. We then extend this model with a predictive learning layer that constructs a dynamical model of the relationship between proprioception and visual experience of the self and is able to predict how each could evolve in the near future. We show that by training the simpler correlation-learning layer first, and by providing its latent (internal) representation of self–world as input to the predictive layer, we are able to ‘scaffold’ [,] the capacity of the latter to learn effectively and quickly.

As further set out below, both learning systems are forms of deep neural network building on current approaches in machine learning. To be clear, we are not arguing that these are strongly analogous to specific brain processes since we are not modelling brain circuits directly or attempting to closely match the visual and proprioceptive systems of the infant. Nevertheless, we do consider that this work can be informative in understanding the organization and emergence of the self–world distinction in the human mind/brain and return to this topic in the discussion in relation to potential cortical and subcortical substrates for distinguishing self from non-self. We next describe our robot simulation environment and the design and testing of, first, the correlation learning model and, second, the full model with correlation-based and predictive learning layers.

We use a full-physics simulation of the Unitree G1 humanoid () using a faster than real-time GPU (graphics processing unit)-accelerated simulation, ManiSkill []. We select the G1 as it has a human-like morphology, including two legs, two arms and two three-fingered hands. The robot's 23 degrees of freedom allow it to make movements of the arms and legs that resemble those of humans, although it has no neck joints. The robot is equipped with a head-mounted monocular RGB-D (red, green, blue–depth) camera with segmentation, with 85.2∘×58∘×94∘ field of view. We use only the monocular two-dimensional RGB images for our study since infants’ eyes are poorly coordinated and stereo vision does not emerge until three to four months []. We place the robot on its back to resemble a human infant in a cot and add to the visible environment a collection of coloured boxes arranged in a rotating circle that resembles a baby ‘mobile’ (a patterned toy often suspended above a baby's cot that rotates to provide enriched visual experience).

To generate training data for our models, we implement motor babbling by sampling target hand positions using a three-dimensional Gaussian with an assigned variance per dimension. Targets are represented as the desired change in position, Δ(x,y,z), with respect to the robot base, for each of the end-effectors (both hands). When a new target is chosen, we actuate the robot using Manikskill's built-in PID (proportional, integral, and derivative) controller, which issues expected delta movements to the robot's joints. This is done per end-effector, i.e. each hand samples from its own Gaussian distribution of target positions and is appropriately actuated to move towards it. Once the target position is reached, a new one is selected. The simulation is configured to run at 100 Hz (physics time step). Every five simulation steps (i.e. at a frequency of 20 Hz), the control loop receives sensory data—proprioceptive data (positions, velocities and effort per joint) and camera frames specified as ‘rgb+depth+segmentation’ with a resolution of 128 ×  128—and issues control commands. The depth map is ignored, while the segmentation image, which provides object identities (ids) per pixel, is further processed to create a self-segmentation ground truth where all the ids related to the robot's links are given an id of 1. Additionally, for each processed frame, we compute a scalar per-pixel estimate of optic flow to provide a motion cue.

As will become clear in the following sections, our layered architecture learns to disentangle self and world in its internal representation via self-supervised learning, while also predicting the consequences of its actions. To assess the quality of the resulting latent spaces, and to guide optimization, we adopt decoders that reconstruct the input modalities, making explicit what information is captured by each latent. Ideally, the self latent should reconstruct the body, whereas the world latent should reconstruct the external object (the mobile). For visual reconstructions, we quantify performance using pixel-wise accuracy and soft Dice coefficient [] measures computed over a region of interest (ROI). Full definitions are provided in the supplementary material; here, we summarize the essential information. Given a decoded attention map, we retain the top-k attended pixels and compare them against the corresponding ground-truth segmentation. Pixel-wise accuracy is computed after hard-thresholding the reconstruction: we retain the top-k pixels, binarize them and compare the resulting mask to the ground-truth segmentation. By contrast, the soft Dice coefficient is computed on the continuous reconstructed values within the ROI, yielding a graded measure of overlap between prediction and ground truth without binarization. We will report pixel-wise accuracy when assessing the behaviour of the proposed architecture and illustrating basic qualitative trends as it has a simple and intuitive interpretation. The soft Dice coefficient is widely used in the development of image segmentation models as it provides a graded measure that can capture finer-grained overlap information; it is therefore useful for comparing between alternative training methods. We use it here when comparing different model variants in  and in the supplementary material.

The correlation-learning layer, illustrated in , is designed to differentiate between self and non-self, while also constructing a latent representation that can support higher-level components. We employ an encoder–decoder structure where the encoder is designed to separate self-related and world-related information into two distinct latent spaces. These representations enable the decoders to independently reconstruct both the agent (self) and its surrounding environment.

To reinforce the separation of self and world, the visual features contributing to the self-representation are passed through an information bottleneck, promoting a focus on self-related content. This can be understood as follows. Following the self pathway (black and red arrows in ), the latent representation associated with the self is used to reconstruct both proprioceptive and visual information. By contrast, the world-related pathway (grey arrows) is dedicated solely to reconstructing visual input. The demand for proprioceptive reconstruction in the self pathway acts as the bottleneck, effectively filtering for visual features that are specifically relevant to the self. Optimization proceeds in two stages. In stage 1 (104 iterations), we encourage the model to form a minimal sense of self by suppressing the world pathway. This forces the self pathway to learn an initial spatial mask, in the form of a 128 × 128 image filter with values in the range 0–1 per pixel, that will guide subsequent learning. In stage 2 (up to 105 iterations), we train all pathways jointly. The significance of this sequential training process will be further analysed in .

Overall, this network can be regarded as a correlation-learning mechanism because the encoder–decoder design compresses the inputs into a latent space that must capture statistical dependencies, including cross-modal correlations, in order to accurately reconstruct the information at the current time. As such, future observations are not required; the model operates solely on information available at the present time and does not perform any explicit prediction. The current model processes visual and proprioceptive data; however, the architecture is inherently modular and could be extended to integrate additional sensory signals, such as audition or touch.

We next explain the network architecture in more detail. As shown in , we adopt separate visual encoders and decoders for the self and the world to prevent information leakage between the two processing pathways. Each encoder/decoder is implemented as a convolutional neural network, while the decoder for proprioceptive information is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). We denote the visual input and its reconstruction by xv(t) and x^v(t), respectively, where both are 128×128×4 tensors of per-pixel RGB and optical-flow values. Similarly, we write the proprioceptive input and its reconstruction as s(t) and s^(t), respectively, where both are 46-dimensional vectors of joint positions and velocities. The self and world latent spaces are zs(t) and zw(t). Finally, we denote the visual self-, visual world- and proprioceptive encoders by Eϕv,sv,s, Eϕv,wv,w and Eϕp,sp,s, respectively, and the corresponding decoders as Dθv,sv,s, Dθv,wv,w and Dθp,sp,s. For notational convenience, we omit the lowercase parameter indices of the encoder and decoder architectures from now on and implicitly assume that each function is defined by its own set of parameters.

Under this notation, the latent spaces are defined as
(2.1)zs(t)=αEv,sxv(t)+(1−α)Ep,ss(t)(2.2)and zw(t)=Ev,wxv(t),
where α∈[0,1] balances the contributions of the visual and proprioceptive signals to the self latent and is randomly and uniformly sampled once per training sequence to promote robustness to changes in sensory-modality availability.

The proprioceptive reconstruction is s^(t)=Dp,s(zs(t)). For visual reconstruction, we combine the self and world decoders using a spatial attention mask m(t)∈[0,1]H×W (broadcast along channels):
(2.3)x^v(t)=m(t)⊙Dv,s(zs(t))+(1−m(t))⊙Dv,w(zw(t)),
where ⊙ denotes the element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication. The spatial attention mask m(t)∈[0,1]H×W is computed from the decoded self-visual prediction as
(2.4)m(t)=f(⟨Dv,s(zs(t))⟩ch−c),
i.e. we first take a channel-wise average ⟨⋅⟩ch to obtain a single H×W intensity map and then apply a shifted sigmoid f(⋅) (with shift c) to obtain values in [0,1]. The constant c controls the operating region of the sigmoid (in practice, any c∈[0,1] works well, and we set c=0 in all simulations). Finally, the term 1−m(t) is the element-wise complement of m(t) and weights the world-related reconstruction accordingly.

Optimization of the layer is performed through backpropagation by minimizing the cost function:
(2.5)Lcorr=‖xv(t)−x^v(t)‖1+||s(t)−s^(t)||22+β∑i=0T−1‖zs(ti)−zs(ti+1)‖22=Lv+Lp+β∑i=0T−1‖zs(ti)−zs(ti+1)‖22,
where ‖⋅‖1 and ‖⋅‖2 denote the mean absolute error and mean squared error, respectively, ti=t0+iΔt and β is a scaling factor of the temporal regularization term. This third factor in the loss function enforces temporal proximity across time in the latent space and preparing zs to be modelled as a dynamical system (). As noted above, there are two optimization stages. In stage 1, we set zw(t)≡0 to completely suppress the world pathway; we then remove this constraint in stage 2. We plot three self-accuracy curves corresponding to testing the trained system with different input configurations: proprioception only (p), vision only (v) and a combination of the two (p+v); we also plot one curve corresponding to reconstruction of the visual world. These metrics are computed by evaluating the model on a test set at logarithmically increasing intervals and using ground-truth segmentation provided by the simulator (). The plots show that, in stage 1, the self pathway learns a coarse segmentation of its own body against the environment, while the world pathway remains at chance level (since its output is suppressed). After the transition to stage 2, self accuracy exhibits a sharp jump and continues to improve, and the world pathway learns to focus on objects in the scene (the mobile), achieving strong final performance. A coherent sense of self should be resilient to the loss of a modality; this is demonstrated by the relatively small differences between the various self curves—all testing regimes perform well, though the small drop in the no-proprioception (v) condition visible at the end of training underlines the importance of proprioceptive input for an optimal self representation. We further notice that performance in the proprioception only (p) condition is comparable to the one attained in the combined (p+v) setting. The reason is that proprioception acts as an explicit information bottleneck used to induce a self–world distinction. Because the self latent is trained to reconstruct proprioceptive signals, the model learns a proprioception-centred representation and naturally relies on proprioceptive inputs whenever they are available. Visual input can still contribute, but it becomes most relevant when proprioception is weak or absent, where it provides robustness by allowing the self-state to be inferred from visual cues alone.

Finally,  provides qualitative examples of the capacity of the model to reconstruct the visual world and to decompose it into self and world components. As expected, the image reconstructed by the self decoder (dii) concentrates on the agent's body, whereas the world decoder highlights objects in the scene (diii), specifically, the mobile. Notably, the world representation exhibits lower luminance over the arms and hands, while retaining some information about the more static torso. This is consistent with the torso's limited motion and the fact that static, low-frequency information is easier to reconstruct, enabling the world pathway to represent some torso-related information despite primarily focusing on external objects. The masks (div and dv) partition the scene appropriately, and the three rightmost reconstructions (dvi–dviii) illustrate that all input configurations yield accurate results, with the combined (v+p) and proprioception-only (p) conditions performing best.

Beyond its role in generating a minimal VSWD, the correlation layer also supports the operation of the layer 1 predictive learning system. Specifically, its design encourages the emergence of a smoothly varying latent space that can be modelled as a dynamical system. After training, as described above, the weights in the correlation-learning layer are fixed. The predictive layer then builds on this system to provide a near-term forecast of what will happen next.

More specifically, the predictive layer is implemented as a neural ordinary differential equation (neural-ODE), i.e. an ordinary differential equation parametrized by a neural network. Rather than predicting the next system state directly, this network outputs the temporal derivative of the system state, and a numerical integrator is then used to obtain its evolution over time. The predictive layer thus allows us to evolve the latent state forward as a dynamical system driven by the planned action sequence. As a result, the model can imagine future latent states and, via the decoders, the corresponding future proprioceptive and visual observations. For comparison purposes, we also test a version in which the output of the model is provided as its own input in the next prediction step without a numerical integration procedure. This does not directly emulate a dynamical system but could generate similar outcomes. Optimization of this architecture proceeds with the encoder and decoder parameters kept frozen (unless otherwise specified in the experiments in). This design lets the correlation layer scaffold the predictive layer and is also computationally efficient as explored further below.

To train the predictive model, we drive it with a sequence of external control signals corresponding to the relative change in hand position required to move to the next target position (as specified by the motor babbling); the outputs of the model are generated through the proprioceptive and visual decoders of the correlation layer for predictions of up to 100 time steps in the future.

As illustrated in , the neural-ODE is defined over the self latent space zs(t) and is driven by an external control signal a(t), corresponding to the actions the robot intends to perform. The purpose of this layer is to forecast the future latent representation and associated proprioceptive states, given an initial condition zs(t0) and a sequence of actions a(t). For the current model, the sequence of actions is the sequence of target hand positions ().

Formally, letting z^s(t) denote the predicted latent state, the dynamics of the neural-ODE are defined as:
(2.6)dz^s(t)dt=h(z^s(t),a(t)|θpred)(2.7)z^s(t0)=zs(t0),
where h is a neural network—a standard MLP in our implementation—parametrized by θpred, and the caret superscript ⋅^ makes explicit the difference between the modelled and target latent states. The loss function used to train the predictive component is:
(2.8)Lpred=∑i=1T‖z^s(ti)−zs(ti)‖22+∑i=1T||s(ti)−Dp,s(z^s(ti))||22=Lz+Lp.
In , the first term aligns the latent trajectory predicted by the neural-ODE with the latent activities produced by the correlation layer, while the second term penalizes errors in reconstructing proprioception. During predictive training, we use the latent space consistency loss Lz in place of a visual reconstruction loss, thereby avoiding repeated and costly decoding passes. In all settings, unless otherwise stated, neural-ODE integration is performed using a second-order Runge–Kutta scheme with discretization step Δt=0.1. To assess the importance of using an explicit numerical integrator and a neural-ODE formulation, we also evaluate an autoregressive MLP baseline that predicts the latent state forward in time directly, without any integration method. Further details of variant models and their computational costs are provided in  and in the supplementary material.

In , we show how the mean squared error (MSE) of the proprioceptive prediction error (panel b) and the pixel-wise error rate (1–accuracy) (panel c) depend on the temporal horizon T () and on whether numerical integration is used. The reported metrics are averaged over 100 step-ahead predictions. Overall, the errors decrease as the model is trained to predict longer trajectories, and incorporating an integration scheme yields consistently better performance. These results highlight the importance of treating prediction as learning a dynamical process over extended horizons, rather than as a one-step forecasting problem.  shows how the same measures (MSE of the prediction error and pixel-wise error rate) vary as a function of prediction horizon for a neural-ODE model, with explicit integration, trained with T=50. As expected, error accumulates as the predictive layer rolls the latent state further into the future; nevertheless, pixel-level accuracy remains close to 90% even 100 steps ahead. In other words, despite the accumulation of error, the model is able to generate plausible future trajectories.

Our architecture and learning procedures are deliberately modular—the model combines heterogeneous adaptive components with complementary cost terms, and optimization is performed in multiple stages that reflect an overall layered structure ().

In an earlier paper, Wilson & Prescott [] defined scaffolding such that, given two processes, one with faster (earlier) dynamics, B, can serve as a scaffold for the organization of a slower (later) process, A, if the functional consequences of process B constrain A, such that some product of process A may be improved. These authors further suggested that scaffolding can occur without direct interaction between the two processes—all that is required is for process A to be measurably impacted by process B in a positive way.

In our architecture, we implement two forms of scaffolding motivated by our aim to understand the role of scaffolding in human development (as considered further in the Discussion). First, we pretrain the self pathway of the correlation layer (layer 0), while suppressing the world pathway, before simultaneously training both. This biases the model to find a way to reconstruct the visual scene using proprioceptive input rather than simply building a compressed representation of the scene. This is an example of scaffolding as the pretraining of the self pathway scaffolds learning in the world pathway even though they interact only directly (they share the same error signal and spatial mask). Second, we fix the encoders/decoders of the correlation layer prior to training the layer 1 predictive model. This stands as a more direct form of scaffolding as the self latent representation generated in layer 0 is provided as input to layer 1. Note that these two forms of scaffolding are similar in that both simplify the learning problem for the other part of the system. In the layer 0 case, this is by allowing the world pathway to focus on the non-self; in the layer 1 case, this is by providing as input a latent representation that is useful for learning how the self will evolve in time.

To test the utility of scaffolding, we next compare this standard architecture against variants in which scaffolding is removed or altered. From a machine learning perspective, it is also important to understand how scaffolding impacts on optimization. We therefore also test additional variants to better understand the behaviour of the scaffolded model as compared with end-to-end backpropagation through time (BPTT). End-to-end backpropagation is the standard approach for training deep neural networks as it enables gradients from the final objective to be propagated through all intermediate computations and, in recurrent settings, through time, thereby updating all parameters jointly to directly minimize loss. Although we expect BPTT to have high accuracy, one of the benefits of the standard architecture is that it may be computationally more efficient than other variants particularly those that update all parameters throughout training. We explore this further below and in the supplementary material.

Here, we explore five variants as defined below. For completeness, we also investigate a number of further variants in the supplementary material. All variants use numerical integration in the predictive layer and are trained with a time horizon of T = 50 until convergence. With the exception of variant (i), all variants also employ the self-pretraining phase.
(i)W/o layer 0 scaffolding. We remove the self-pretraining of the correlation layer and train all layer 0 pathways jointly from scratch. This directly tests the utility of the first form of scaffolding described above.(ii)Continuous training. We jointly optimize both layer 0 and layer 1 throughout the whole training process. This tests whether there is a benefit to training level 0 to convergence before training level 1, as compared to training both layers from the outset. In other words, this tests the utility of the second form of scaffolding described above.(iii)End-to-end BPTT. We jointly optimize both layers and allow prediction errors to flow through the entire architecture so that the correlation layer parameters (including encoders and decoders) are updated using gradients from both  and . We expect this variant to have good performance but to be computationally costly.(iv)W/o proprioception. The standard architecture but with both layers trained without proprioceptive input though still trying to predict future proprioceptive states (i.e. retaining the loss term Lp). This condition tests whether visual information by itself is sufficient to induce a self–world distinction (for instance, through temporal correlation of moving body parts) and predict future self-states.(v)End-to-end backpropagation through time without proprioception (BPTT, w/o p). We jointly optimize both layers using backpropagation, as in variant (iii), but driving the system without proprioceptive input as in variant (iv). This condition again tests whether visual input is sufficient to induce a self–world distinction but this time under end-to-end optimization using backpropagation.

W/o layer 0 scaffolding. We remove the self-pretraining of the correlation layer and train all layer 0 pathways jointly from scratch. This directly tests the utility of the first form of scaffolding described above.

Continuous training. We jointly optimize both layer 0 and layer 1 throughout the whole training process. This tests whether there is a benefit to training level 0 to convergence before training level 1, as compared to training both layers from the outset. In other words, this tests the utility of the second form of scaffolding described above.

End-to-end BPTT. We jointly optimize both layers and allow prediction errors to flow through the entire architecture so that the correlation layer parameters (including encoders and decoders) are updated using gradients from both  and . We expect this variant to have good performance but to be computationally costly.

W/o proprioception. The standard architecture but with both layers trained without proprioceptive input though still trying to predict future proprioceptive states (i.e. retaining the loss term Lp). This condition tests whether visual information by itself is sufficient to induce a self–world distinction (for instance, through temporal correlation of moving body parts) and predict future self-states.

End-to-end backpropagation through time without proprioception (BPTT, w/o p). We jointly optimize both layers using backpropagation, as in variant (iii), but driving the system without proprioceptive input as in variant (iv). This condition again tests whether visual input is sufficient to induce a self–world distinction but this time under end-to-end optimization using backpropagation.

We should point out that it is also possible to continue to optimize layer 0 during layer 1 training, rather than freezing the layer 0 weights in the second training phase. This could further test whether having a stationary level 0 is beneficial to training level 1 (as compared to variant (ii) where both layers are trained from the outset). In practice, however, since layer 0 is trained to convergence during the initial phase, the weights would not change further during training of layer 1. In other words, this version will have a similar outcome to the standard model (although this would not be the case if the training data were to change).

The soft Dice scores are much lower (panel d) and MSE scores much higher (panel e) for all tests.

BPTT, w/o p. This variant has the same available information as variant (iv), which fails dramatically, but achieves marginally better performance. Indeed, it does surprisingly well at predicting future proprioceptive states (panel e). Overall, however, it fails to provide a satisfactory VSWD as indicated by the poor self–world separation in the image reconstructions (panel a(v)) and low soft Dice scores (panel d).

Overall, we observe that the staged training approach of the standard model performs well in these comparisons. Compared to variant (i), which lacks pretraining, it develops a reliable VSWD. Performance is similar to variant (ii) that allows joint optimization of both layers throughout the training process, and even marginally better on vision-only reconstruction of future self-states. Removal of the proprioceptive input (variant (iv)) demonstrates that the performance of the model leverages these internal signals in order to distinguish self from world and predict how the self will evolve.

As anticipated, end-to-end BPTT is able to improve on the results obtained with the layered architecture; however, this comes at some cost. By keeping the layer 0 encoders and decoders frozen during layer 1 training, the layered model obtains substantial efficiency savings—reducing the number of multiply–accumulate operations by around 98% compared to end-to-end BPTT. Indeed, we see substantial savings even in the continuous training setting (see the supplementary material for further explanation and detailed estimates). This performance improvement is achieved through the separation of timescales as predicted by Wilson & Prescott [], with faster processes providing latent decompositions that scaffold acquisition of the slower predictive dynamics.

With regard to the origins of the self in body exploration in early infancy, the developmental psychologist Phillipe Rochat wrote:
Self-produced action causes the infant to have overlapping experiences through his other senses. […] This experience specifies the body as differentiated from other objects in the environment. When my hand crosses my visual field, for example, I perceive that it is my hand and not someone else's, because I see it and feel it proprioceptively moving at exactly the same time and by a commensurate amount [, p. 37].

Self-produced action causes the infant to have overlapping experiences through his other senses. […] This experience specifies the body as differentiated from other objects in the environment.
