When my hand crosses my visual field, for example, I perceive that it is my hand and not someone else's, because I see it and feel it proprioceptively moving at exactly the same time and by a commensurate amount [, p. 37].

In this contribution, we have investigated Rochat's proposal for the differentiation of self from world in infancy using a synthetic approach. Specifically, we have shown that a correlation-learning system can decompose the visual field of a simulated robot into self and non-self (). If proprioceptive signals are considered to already be part of the self because they originate from inside the body [], then this learning system extends the self—in relation to an anoetic sense of body ownership—to parts of the visual world.

We have further shown that this minimal self–world distinction can usefully scaffold learning of continuous dynamical system models (neural-ODEs) that predict the future evolution of both proprioceptive and visual self-states (). Here, we have learned to predict the sensory outcomes of randomly generated ‘babbling’ actions; however, this predictive capacity should also be extendable to provide control signals for intentional, goal-directed actions (see below). Our model therefore aligns with theoretical discussions in which a pre-reflective sense of agency is seen as arising from congruence between the predicted sensory signals arising from voluntary action and the flow of reafferent sensory signals [,].

We next discuss our findings in relation to wider research on: (i) the minimal self in robotics, (ii) machine learning for multi-modal perception, (iii) the neural substrates for the human self–world distinction and its emergence during development, (iv) the role of scaffolding in the development of the human cognitive architecture, and (v) the future extension of the model towards noetic and autonoetic aspects of self.

Within the broader field of synthetic science [], the current work can be regarded as following a cognitive neurorobotics methodology that uses robot experiments to explore potential mechanisms underlying embodied cognition [,]. Rather than attempting to capture the detailed behaviour of neural circuits, this approach focuses on exploring high-level algorithmic principles and on aligning system dynamics and behaviour with findings from neuroscience and psychology; as such, it complements computational neuroscience modelling and neurorobotics approaches at lower levels of analysis []. By taking inspiration from the trajectory of human cognitive development, our study also aligns with wider research in the field of developmental robotics []. Here, we briefly review some related work that has taken a similar approach to understanding the self–world distinction and sense of agency through robotics. (For wider discussions of robotic models of self, see [,,,].)

In a pioneering study of robot sense of self, Tani [] explored a layered architecture in which a recurrent network was trained to predict the sequence of perceptual outputs of an associative network controlling a vision-based mobile robot in a navigation task. Tani [] suggested that a form of self emerges in the dynamics of the predictive network when its predictions diverge from the outputs of the lower-level controller. Tani & White [] refined this proposal suggesting that a form of implicit self is already present when the robot correctly predicts its future sensory states (as in the definition of pre-reflective agency above), but that when this synchrony breaks down, and effort is required to refocus the system, the distinction between self and world is brought into consciousness. This proposal suggests one way in which the current architecture could be developed towards a noetic (reflective) sense of self, through monitoring of whether anoetic systems are achieving intended goals (see further discussion below).

An early study of robot self-recognition, by Michel et al. [], used the expected time delay between action initiation and observed arm movement to judge whether visual motion was self-generated. Saegusa et al. [] subsequently showed that correlation learning can be used to allow a motor babbling robot to visually recognise its own body parts. This was further demonstrated by Demirel et al. [] who used correlation-based learning of the relationship between robot arm velocities and tracked visual tags. Bechtle et al. [] trained a forward model to predict the visual consequences of a humanoid robot's own movements and used this to attenuate sensory signals arising from the robot's own body. These authors related the behaviour of their model system to a sense of agency and also argued that suppressing self-related visual signals could assist the robot in acquiring object permanence []. Lanillos et al. [] have developed various models of robot self-perception based on predictive learning frameworks. These included a visual self–other distinction, generated by using proprioceptive signals to predict visual input, which allowed a robot to recognize its own mirror reflection []. Our model builds on these previous approaches by including both correlational and predictive learning into one architecture. Specifically, our correlation layer maps heterogeneous inputs (vision and proprioception) into a compact, well-posed latent space upon which predictive learning systems can be defined that forecast self-related states. This extends previous cognitive neurorobotics models by showing how a layered model can emulate aspects of the developmental timeline for sense of agency seen in human infants (see further below).

The design of our model is also inspired by multi-modal state representation learning in robotics. For example, the proposed correlation layer is closely related to the variational autoencoder formulation of Meo & Lanillos []. This approach learns a joint latent from multiple sensors and enables cross-modal reconstruction under partial observability. Our architecture departs from this framework in three key ways. First, we explicitly factor the latent into a self component zs and a world component zw, which (together) support information preservation while yielding an interpretable separation between agent and environment. Second, we endow the latent space with continuous-time dynamics via a neural-ODE driven by intended actions. This provides accurate prediction of future self-states through multi-step forecasting in latent space. Third, the presence of an explicit world representation, and of the dynamical prior, leads us to different architectural choices and loss terms from multi-modal autoencoder baselines. This connects our work to a growing literature in computer vision that has employed dynamical models to create image/video latent spaces. This research includes combining foundational neural-ODEs with latent ODEs [,], constructing second-order/physics-informed latent models [,] and neurally inspired or continuous-time video generation models [,]. These approaches have collectively demonstrated improved long-horizon rollout and more temporally consistent prediction compared to earlier work.

Predicting the future consequences of an agent's actions is closely related to the idea of using forward models in model-based reinforcement learning [,]. In this context, our architecture provides a simple self-supervised route to a self–world decomposition, which could help to structure learned world models by separating controllable (agent-related) from exogenous (environment-related) factors. Although speculative, such a factorization has clear potential advantages, including more modular reuse of predictive components across tasks and improved generalization when the agent or the environment changes independently.

Panksepp [,] described a ‘primal self’ as arising from the convergence of emotional (evaluative), sensory and motor schemata with a body map and a core motivational arbitrator situated in subcortical regions of the brain. Key structures relevant to this include the periaqueductal grey (PAG), the hypothalamus and the medial reticular formation, all of which are important motivational and emotional structures [,], and the superior colliculus (SC) a critical site for multi-sensory convergence that is also involved in regulating head, eye and body movements [,]. All of these structures are appropriately connected to each other and to motor and sensory systems before birth and are operational in the human newborn. In addition, insular cortex, which is a key site for the convergence of exteroceptive and interoceptive signals, is likely to be involved in the early emergence of the self–world distinction and could encode an initial distinction between self and non-self based on interoception and self-touch [,]. Insular is the first cortical area to appear in the fetus and is considered to be both phylogenetically old and early maturing [,]. In , we highlight these structures, and particularly the SC and insular, as being potentially involved in a minimal, anoetic sense of self, and analogize them with layer 0 of our robot cognitive architecture (the correlation-learning layer). This proposal aligns with Rochat [] and Rochat & Striano's [] account of the emergence of a VSWD during early infancy that builds on a simpler non-visual distinction based on self-touch already present at birth. We next explore this neurodevelopmental proposal in more detail.

As shown in , the SC receives direct input from the retina alongside indirect input from auditory and somatosensory systems and a wide range of subcortical and cortical structures. SC is both a sensory and motor structure and is often studied in relation to orienting to salient stimuli and the control of spatial attention []. Indeed, the superficial layers of the SC are well-known as encoding a head-centred representation of the world that aligns visual, auditory and tactile inputs [,], while the deeper layers act to generate eye and head movements to fixate or track objects of interest []. The SC is also known to provide corollary discharge signals for eye movements that help to stabilize visual perception []. However, while less studied, the SC and equivalent midbrain structures in non-mammalian vertebrates (the tectum) also play a wider role in movement generation (i.e. beyond orienting), including in reaching [] and in whole body movement [,]. Interestingly, in primates, the deeper layers of the SC have been found to include cell populations that encode arm movements in gaze-related coordinates []. Other populations in SC, and the underlying PAG, show neural activity that correlates with shoulder, arm and trunk electromyography recordings during reaching [], i.e. putative proprioceptive signals. Importantly, the SC does much more than simply provide a topographic map of the visual world. For instance, it is also involved in determining the salience of any objects in view with regard to future action [,]; indeed, in young infants, it is the primary site for this []. SC intrinsic circuitry has been modelled as implementing forms of correlation-based learning (e.g. [,]). Thus, in principle, SC seems a plausible site in the neonate brain for the acquisition of a VSWD, similar to that generated by layer 0 of our model, that could provide the developing infant with the capacity to identify areas of her visual world as belonging to self or world.

Cortical systems involved in visual processing mature rapidly during the first few month as they come to dominate the subcortical visual system [,]. There is evidence of function in visual cortical areas at birth [], but the wider system is known to be incomplete and weakly integrated [,]. The brain expands in size during the first year, with cortical grey matter more than doubling, driven by the proliferation of intracortical synapses, myelination and increasing functional connectivity []. During this time, different cortical systems mature progressively, steered by experience [,] and beginning with sensorimotor and sensory areas, with a more gradual emergence of networks that process signals generated by these primary domains [,,]. This aligns with theoretical proposals that cortical functional organization can be described by a hierarchy of predictive models [].

From around three to four months of age, the infant brain gains the capacity to anticipate the future over short time frames, for instance, making prospective saccades towards the likely future position of a moving object or anticipating where an object might reappear that has become occluded (object permanence) [,]. As previously noted, predictively anticipating the sensory consequences of one's own movement is a key aspect of human agency [,,]. Of the various cortical systems likely to be involved in a predictive VSWD the inferior parietal lobe (IPL) may be especially critical. In human adults, this area has been found to (i) encode the goal of motor actions [], (ii) have topographic maps of the visual field and of the body [,], (iii) enable an allocentric body model that can be flexibly applied in representing the self or in reasoning about the actions of others [], (iv) encode self-related body information [], and (v) be active in studies that measure sense of agency [,]. As shown in , the IPL receives movement-related input from areas such as premotor cortex [], information about the visual scene via the dorsal visual stream [] and information about visually detected body parts from the extrastriate body area (EBA) []. It also reciprocally connects with the insular cortex [], which, as we have already noted, may be one of the first cortical structures to be involved in the experience of self. With regard to its early development, there is evidence of functional activity related to action recognition in associative regions of cortex, including in areas that will become the IPL, emerging from around four to seven months [,].

Interestingly, the IPL has strong two-way connections with SC. Direct projections from IPL to SC terminate in the intermediate and deep layers [,], while IPL receives an indirect, topographically organized projection from SC superficial layers via the lateral pulvinar []. Input signals arriving in the lateral intraparietal area, which lies in the intraparietal sulcus (adjacent to the IPL), are not thought to be solely oculomotor but to be concerned with visual processing more generally []. Signals from SC may also be relayed to IPL via pulvinar projections to extrastriatal areas including the EBA []. It therefore seems plausible that the construction of a predictive VSWD, resembling that in layer 1 of our model, could involve the IPL and that this could build on subcortical representations of the visual field. This is consistent with imaging studies of the rubber hand illusion [] that have implicated the SC as part of a broader system involved in bodily self-awareness in human adults.

A further important structure is the (hindbrain) cerebellum, which interacts with premotor cortex [] and the IPL [] via dysnaptic pathways involving the pontine nuclei and the thalamus. Its role in predicting sensory signals, including those related to self-movement, means that it is likely to be integral to the acquisition of a predictive VSWD []. The cerebellum also interacts reciprocally with the SC, again via the pontine nuclei [,]. The cerebellum has been modelled as an adaptive filter performing decorrelation [], as being involved in calibrating collicular maps [] and in sensory noise cancellation based on efference copy signals [] (itself a form of self–world distinction). Cerebellar and pontine development is protracted but spikes during the early postnatal months. Although it is unclear to what extent the cerebellum could be involved in self–world discrimination in the earliest phase of infancy, its rapid post-birth development and interactions with key midbrain and cortical systems suggest that it could play an increasing, and potentially integrative, role as development proceeds.

Our model implements two forms of staged learning both of which can be regarded as forms of scaffolding [].

At level 0, during training of the correlation-based layer, we first focus on the self pathway and suppress training of the world pathway. We do this to ensure that the model learns to use proprioceptive signals to predict visual self-movement. Developmentally, this could be considered to be a form of attention (overt or covert), which prioritizes some forms of signal over others. Interestingly, the visual system of neonates is known to have very limited depth of field such that objects beyond 30 cm are poorly discriminated []. In learning terms, this could have the benefit of allowing the infant to focus on proximal stimuli such as her own hand movements (also human faces), without being distracted by more distal stimuli. Infants are also known to spend time visually fixating their own hands [], an activity that has been noted in newborns [] and peaks before the onset of targeted reaching [], thus ‘self-structuring’ [] the visual signals provided to the developing brain.

Layer 1 scaffolding involves delaying training of the predicted layer until layer 0 training is completed and fixing the weights of the lower layer. This illustrates a broader principle that may apply elsewhere in human development, which is the capacity of representations acquired early on to scaffold learning in later maturing networks. In Wilson & Prescott [], we discuss this in relation to the examples of infant face processing and mammalian thermoregulation. For example, there is good evidence of an early-developing subcortical face detection system, in the SC, that scaffolds the emergence of cortically based face recognition capacity [,,]. We suggest that a similar form of scaffolding could be taking place in the emergence of the self–world distinction, again with the SC scaffolding learning in cortical structures such as IPL. Scaffolding is also likely to be important between cortical subsystems that form predictive hierarchies.

In the mammalian brain, there is significant postnatal development in the SC, particularly with respect to multi-sensory integration, regulated, at least in part, by top-down innervation from maturing cortical systems []. As noted above, representations in SC may also be modified and refined by developing SC-cerebellar circuitry. While we have focused in this discussion on scaffolding of the cortex by the sub-cortex, in Wilson & Prescott [] we also discuss scaffolding of subcortical systems, such as the SC, by the cortex, but over much longer, evolutionary timescales. In evolving from the pre-mammalian tectum, we can expect that the SC will have changed under evolutionary pressure to better support cortical function, for instance, in constructing representations of the sensory world that are well-suited to act in consort with more predictively oriented cortical modules. In our architecture, the third term in , which enforces a form of temporal continuity in the layer 0 latent space (see analyses in the supplementary material), could be a model of this kind of evolution-imposed constraint.

In our analysis of model variants, we showed that our layered architecture approach is up to 98% more efficient than a prevailing machine learning benchmark (end-to-end BPTT) while still effectively segmenting the visual world and predicting future self-states. There are substantial efficiency gains even with the continuous training variant (see the supplementary material). Brain development is known to be energetically costly, with the brain in childhood requiring a significantly larger share of energy resource than in adults []. Indeed, the metabolic cost of brain development is considered to be an explanatory factor in the slow and protracted nature of childhood growth in humans compared to other mammals []. As training of AI models consumes an increasing share of the world's resources, we may be able to learn from the layered architecture of the human brain how to build and train very large network models more efficiently.

We envisage extending our synthetic model to include further components and tiers with the goal of capturing wider aspects of the anoetic self and, beyond that, of the noetic and autonoetic self. Here, we briefly consider some paths forward.

As previously noted, hand and arm movements in early infancy are largely exploratory though they can be accompanied by reflexive grasping when an object touches the palm of the hand [,]. Intentional movements towards visual targets emerge from around age three months [] and goal-oriented reach and grasp behaviour from around five to seven months [,]. This development sequence has already inspired a number of developmental robotics approaches (e.g. [,]). We foresee extending the current model along the following lines.

In order to predict future self-states, layer 1 of our architecture acquires a model that is functionally similar to inverse kinematics; however, to construct this, we need targeted movement. We currently use an engineered PID controller to generate babbling movements that bring body parts into the visual field. A more biomimetic approach, based on studies of spontaneous movement in the fetus [], would involve generating pre-reaching movements using combinations of muscle/motor synergies similar to those generated in the brainstem and spinal cord [,]. Such synergy patterns could themselves form the target for layer 1 training in place of the direct proprioceptive states used in the current model (see [] for evidence that cortical systems select muscle synergies). Note that what we are proposing here can again be viewed as a form of scaffolding in which subcortical systems generate movement patterns and representations that are useful targets for cortical learning.

A further extension is to use our architecture to generate reaching behaviours towards visual targets as seen in three-month-old infants. To do this, we need to map reaching targets in visual coordinates to the (x, y, z) world coordinates used in our layer 1 model. This model can then be used to generate movement trajectories to target locations, for instance, to reach towards visually salient objects. It should be possible to acquire the required mapping either during motor babbling or by driving the layer 1 model with a distribution of sample actions and using the imagined visual consequences to generate end positions in head-centred visual space. This problem is relatively straightforward in our current robot model as there are no separate degrees of freedom for the head, and it would become trivial if we add the depth signal from the robot RGB-D camera. For a robot with a head/neck morphology more similar to humans, the spatial locations of target stimuli will need to be updated with respect to head movements (e.g. []). The extension to goal-directed reaching, as observed in five- to seven-month-old infants, will require the integration of sensorimotor control with motivation as discussed next.

A further step will be to integrate evaluative and motivational systems into our architecture to build towards a more complete model of sense of agency and of goal-directed behaviour. In Prescott & Jimenez-Rodriguez [], we analysed the mammalian brain architecture for motivation from a layered architecture perspective. This review identified several important subcortical substrates for motivated behaviour, including the medial reticular formation, the PAG, the hypothalamus and the basal ganglia. As noted above, these structures were also identified by Panksepp [] as being implicated in the construction of a primal (anoetic) self equipped with ‘a primitive sort of intentionality (an automatized action readiness) and primitive forms of psychic coherence (global affective states of the brain)’ [, p. 566]. Insular cortex is also considered to be a key forebrain structure for motivation, particularly in relation to homeostasis []. These structures likely contribute to the anoetic sense of agency, for instance, in relation to the experience of action authorship. Other cortical areas related to motivation are found in the medial and frontal cortical regions. These more slowly developing networks are usually associated with cognitive aspects of motivation, including representation of value, planning and monitoring, and are likely to be more involved in reflexive judgements about agency (see [] and noetic self below). We expect to extend our layered architecture in the direction of goal-directed behaviour by building on some of our earlier neurorobotic models of relevant brain structures, including reticular formation [], basal ganglia [,] and hypothalamus [].

We have focused here on the self–world distinction which is likely to be a pre-requisite for the self–other distinction [], where other is understood as a social other. Theories of the development of a self–other distinction typically begin with the hypothesis that the human brain uses self-representations as a model for understanding the actions and intentions of others [,]. Indeed, some of the brain structures in , such as premotor cortex and the IPL, are often found to be active in experimental settings that test for this kind of self–other mapping []. The possibility of using a robot self-model to distinguish self from a human or robot other, or to reason about the actions of a social other, has already been investigated in a number of studies [,,,]. The current model will lend itself naturally to adding a further decomposition of the world that distinguishes socially important cues such as facial expressions and body movements as a means to inferring intentions. We have reported some prior work in this direction [].

A layered systems view of self, which is also consistent with predictive processing approaches [] and with the hierarchical nature of human cortical development [], would conceive of the progression towards the noetic self as involving the addition of new processing layers. Research by Tani & White [] (reviewed above) suggests one possibility, which is the emergence of a noetic self through processes that monitor the anoetic self and respond to errors. For instance, when expectations about the reafferent sensory signals generated by self-movement are violated (see also []). Candidate structures in human cortex include the anterior cingulate, which has been proposed as playing a role in cognitive control of more automatic processes [] as part of a wider ‘salience’ network []. As additional processing layers are added, representations of self can be expected to be increasingly multi-modal, or amodal, to encode expectations (priors) over longer time spans and to be the subject of self-referential thought. In the human brain, this conceptual representation of self likely involves the default mode network (DMN) [] as discussed next.

The ability to reflect on the self as existing in time, the autonoetic self, is generally held to emerge more gradually in development and to follow other childhood milestones, such as language acquisition and autobiographical memory [,,]. From around age two, children show early signs of an awareness of a personal past and future, for instance, by reporting on past events and through appropriate use of the past tense of activity verbs. However, the capacity to fuse together autobiographical memories and self-concept using narrative-like structures is typically not in evidence until the pre-school years [,]. In the brain, this likely involves higher-order networks in the superior parietal lobe, the posterior cingulate cortex and the hippocampus. These structures form part of the DMN which is active during self-reflective thinking and mental time travel [,]. We expect to investigate these ideas by integrating our work on the self–world distinction with research on event memory systems where we have used cognitive robotics approaches to test models, inspired by the hippocampal system, that reconstruct the past and anticipate the future in embodied robotic settings [,].

We have argued that the human self–world distinction is acquired progressively and begins in an anoetic fashion (i.e. without self-awareness) with systems that learn to discriminate sensory signals emanating from (or generated by) the self, from those arising from the non-self. This distinction can guide attention, for example, towards the body for self-exploration, or away from it, to better understand the world. A basic distinction of this form can also support learning of more sophistical forms of self–world distinction, for instance, those that predict how the future will evolve. Here, we have demonstrated a layered control architecture for a simulated humanoid robot that implements these two forms of self–world distinction—one correlational, the other predictive—and have shown scaffolded (faster and better) learning of the predictive model if the correlation layer is already in place and provided as input.

We have framed this modelling approach in the context of human brain development and infant behaviour. Specifically, we have argued that early infancy might involve the acquisition of a non-predictive VSWD, analagous to our layer 0 network, largely in subcortical areas of the brain, and partly through the infant's observation of her own motor babbling. During the first year of life, and as the brain further develops, this could lead to the acquisition of a second form of VSWD, cortically based, predictive in nature and analogous to layer 1 in our model. This two-layered architecture, still essentially anoetic, demonstrates an important aspect of agency, specifically the ability to predict the future consequences of one's own actions. The analogy with our robotic model follows a cognitive neurorobotics methodology and is focused at the systems level rather than in terms of specific mechanisms. Nevertheless, we hope that this decomposition into pathways and layers, alongside the distinction between correlational and predictive learning systems, could prove helpful in understanding the emergence of the human self–world distinction, particularly with respect to the role of early-developing self subsystems in scaffolding later ones.

psychology.title: Development of a Knowledge Map for Managing Symptoms of Graft-Versus-Host Disease in Patients Undergoing Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation
psychology.abstract: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a critical complication affecting patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), with multifaceted symptoms requiring systematic management. Current clinical practices lack structured tools to guide nurses in addressing GVHD-related symptoms across diverse organ systems. This review aims to synthesize evidence on GVHD symptom management to construct a knowledge graph, enhancing nursing interventions and improving patient outcomes.Relevant authoritative books, guidelines, and expert consensuses such as the “Clinical Nursing Manual for Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation” and the “Chinese Expert Consensus on Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute GVHD After Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (2024 edition)” were referenced. Literature related to GVHD in HSCT was searched, with a time limit from 2014 to 2024. The knowledge graph was constructed using a combination of manual annotation and computer processing.A GVHD knowledge graph centered on symptom management for HSCT patients was constructed, encompassing 7 aspects of symptom management, including skin, oral cavity, liver, eyes, gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and bones and joints, as well as health knowledge related to nutrition and psychology.This knowledge graph provides a structured, evidence-based framework for GVHD symptom management, addressing gaps in standardized nursing protocols. By integrating multidisciplinary recommendations, it supports clinical decision-making, reduces practice variability, and prioritizes patient-centered care. Future studies should validate its impact on complication rates and quality of life in real-world settings. The tool’s adaptability allows updates as new evidence emerges, ensuring alignment with evolving guidelines. For nurses, this resource enhances competency in managing complex GVHD presentations, ultimately improving care delivery for HSCT recipients.
psychology.text:
Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has emerged as an advanced treatment for leukemia, lymphoma, and other malignant hematological and immunologic diseases, significantly extending patients’ survival rates.– Despite the remarkable achievements of HSCT in the treatment of hematological malignancies, patients still face a series of challenges post-transplantation. Among them, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a major complication following HSCT, posing a severe threat to patients’ quality of life and significantly reducing their survival rates post-transplantation. The occurrence of GVHD not only increases the physical and psychological burden on patients but also becomes a crucial barrier to successful transplantation.– Currently, health care professionals have made tremendous efforts in managing GVHD symptoms, yet numerous challenges remain. Nurses, as vital guides in the patient recovery process, often struggle to provide comprehensive and accurate symptom management due to the lack of systematic knowledge and structured, visual presentation methods. This not only affects patients’ comprehension ability but also reduces their treatment adherence, further exacerbating the impact of GVHD on their quality of life., Therefore, in light of the current status of GVHD symptom management, a novel knowledge representation and management approach is needed to improve nurses’ work efficiency and help patients better understand and manage their symptoms.

Knowledge graphs, as an emerging technology, enable rapid retrieval and intelligent reasoning of medical knowledge by structuring it., They not only allow patients to quickly grasp the relationships between knowledge and diseases but also help them master the key content of symptom management, thereby enhancing their self-management capabilities. A knowledge graph is a structured semantic knowledge base that uses graph structures to represent entities, concepts, and their relationships, enabling visualization, reasoning, and intelligent retrieval of knowledge. In nursing informatics, knowledge graphs help integrate fragmented clinical guidelines, nursing pathways, and patient data into a unified knowledge network, enhancing the systematicity and transparency of nursing decision-making. Unlike concept mapping, which is often used for teaching and brainstorming, knowledge graphs place greater emphasis on semantic relationships and logical reasoning between entities, support dynamic updates and cross-system integration, and are suitable for building intelligent nursing assistance systems. Currently, knowledge graphs have been widely applied in the management of patients with breast cancer, asthma, and other conditions, achieving remarkable results. However, there is still a lack of a comprehensive and systematic knowledge graph for GVHD symptom management in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation patients. Therefore, this study intends to adopt a top-down approach to construct a knowledge graph for GVHD symptom management in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation patients. This knowledge graph aims to provide nurses with an efficient and convenient health education tool, further enhancing their professional expertise in GVHD symptom management.

The evidence-based textual knowledge related to GVHD symptoms in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) was collected using the literature review method as the knowledge source for the knowledge base. The inclusion criteria for the literature were: (1) the study population was adult patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; (2) the research content involved the diagnosis, treatment, and management of GVHD in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. GVHD can be classified into acute GVHD and chronic GVHD based on the time of onset and clinical manifestations, and can involve rejection reactions in the skin, oral cavity, liver, eyes, gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and bones and joints; (3) the literature type was clinical practice guidelines, evidence summaries, or expert consensuses; (4) the language of the literature was Chinese or English; (5) the search period was from 2014 to 2024. The exclusion criteria were: (1) inability to obtain the full text; (2) guideline interpretation literature. The English search terms included: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation, stem cell transplantation, bone marrow transplantation, Graft vs Host Disease, Graft-versus-Host Disease, Guidelines, consensus, evidence summary, etc. The Chinese search terms included: hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, stem cell transplantation, cellular transplantation therapy, graft-versus-host disease, guidelines, expert consensus, evidence summary, etc. Eight Chinese and English databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, JBI Evidence-Based Nursing Database, CNKI, Wanfang Data, and SinoMed, as well as 5 association or guideline websites, including Guidelines International Network (GIN), National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), American Cancer Society (ACS), American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), and Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN), were searched. The retrieved bibliographic records were imported into EndNote X9 for deduplication. Two trained researchers screened the literature based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and in case of disagreement, a third researcher made the final decision after discussing the full text. A total of 1026 articles were collected in this study, with 988 duplicates or irrelevant articles removed, leaving 38 articles for initial screening. After further reading the full text and applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 22 articles were excluded, leaving a final inclusion of 16 articles.– The 16 articles were uniformly organized to establish the primary framework of the knowledge map, including skin, eye, gastrointestinal, liver, bone and joint, lung, and oral mucosa care, as well as nutrition and psychological support. After discussion within the research group, the secondary framework was formulated with reference to the “Clinical Nursing Manual for Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation.”

Knowledge extraction is one of the primary steps in constructing a GVHD knowledge graph for patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The process utilizes a BERT-CRF-BiLSTM model trained on medical corpora for entity-relationship extraction, supplemented and refined with AI techniques. The BERT-CRF-BiLSTM model combines the contextual understanding of BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers), the label constraint capability of CRF (conditional random fields), and the sequence modeling strength of BiLSTM (bidirectional long short-term memory). This hybrid approach is well-suited for high-precision recognition of medical terminology and their complex relationships. To ensure the accuracy and comprehensiveness of the extracted knowledge, a combination of manual and automated techniques was used based on established primary and secondary frameworks. Specific automated techniques included Named Entity Recognition (NER) for identifying key medical concepts, relation extraction for establishing connections between entities, and entity alignment for resolving inconsistencies across different knowledge sources. This process was complemented by manual curation and expert review to ensure accuracy and comprehensiveness. Following initial extraction, manual screening was conducted by 2 hematologists, 2 nursing masters, and 2 nurses with over 10 years of clinical experience, to ensure that the selected terms were both highly specialized and comprehensively reflective of all aspects of GVHD. The screening results were further subjected to expert consultation and internal team discussion, ultimately resulting in the identification of 410 high-quality terms closely related to GVHD.

Given the diversity and complexity of knowledge sources, extracted knowledge often contains duplications or even contradictions. Therefore, in the process of constructing the knowledge graph, the extracted knowledge needs to be cleaned and integrated to eliminate redundant information and ensure the quality of knowledge within the graph. During knowledge fusion, 2 nursing masters first identified and merged entities with duplication, inclusion, or being included relationships, such as “micronutrients” and “magnesium.” Subsequently, all merged entities were rigorously reviewed by senior nurses and doctors to ensure the accuracy and rationality of the merging results. Through this series of cleaning and integration operations, a high-quality entity set was ultimately obtained.

After completing knowledge extraction and fusion, the next step is to store the integrated knowledge in an appropriate format. Neo4j, as a high-performance graph database storage tool, can efficiently store and query complex relational data. Its suitability for health care knowledge graphs is well-documented, supporting intuitive modeling of clinical relationships and efficient path-based queries., In Neo4j, extracted entities and relationships are represented as nodes and edges, respectively, and connections between entities are constructed in the form of triples. This representation is not only intuitive and easy to understand but also facilitates subsequent knowledge querying and reasoning. In addition, Neo4j has the advantage of allowing data to be added and modified at any time, making it convenient for nurses to add new entities and relationships to the knowledge graph or revise and optimize existing ones to better align with clinical practice and research needs.Neo4j has been widely adopted for building knowledge graphs in health care, such as modeling clinical pathways, analyzing drug-drug interactions, and assessing disease risk. Its ability to intuitively represent complex relationships and support path-based queries and reasoning makes it particularly accessible for nursing professionals to understand and apply.

GVHD is a major complication of HSCT and one of the significant causes of patient mortality. GVHD is prone to occur when the recipient possesses allogeneic graft antigens different from those of the donor, stimulating a strong immune response in the recipient. GVHD can be classified into acute GVHD (occurring within 100 d post-transplant) and chronic GVHD (occurring after 100 d post-transplant) based on the time of onset and clinical manifestations. There are similarities between acute GVHD and chronic GVHD in terms of nutritional management, psychological care, and nursing measures for various organs. A knowledge graph is used to visualize the commonalities in symptom management between the 2. Figure  displays the content of acute and chronic GVHD symptom management in different organs and the relationships among related entities. Circles in the figure represent different entities, lines between circles indicate the connections between entities, and arrows point from hyponyms to hypernyms. In this context, arrows indicate an “is-a” or “belongs-to” relationship (hyponymy/hypernymy). For example, “diarrhea” is a hyponym (subordinate term) of “gastrointestinal symptoms,” which is its hypernym (superordinate term). This hierarchical structure helps users understand symptom classification and relationships. Centered on symptom management, the knowledge graph unfolds sequentially around the primary and secondary framework content.

The primary target organs affected by acute GVHD are the skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract. For chronic GVHD, the primary target organs include the skin, mouth, liver, eyes, gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and bone joints., Personalized guidance is provided based on the different symptoms affecting these organs. Gastrointestinal symptoms associated with acute GVHD are severe and have a significant impact on patient prognosis. Therefore, gastrointestinal management is particularly important, including care for diarrhea symptoms and fecal microbiota transplantation. Chronic GVHD onset is concealed, with a prolonged and persistent course. Thus, for high-risk patients with chronic GVHD, continuous self-monitoring and self-management are crucial factors in improving their quality of life (Figs. , ).

This study is dedicated to constructing a knowledge graph for GVHD symptom management in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation patients, aiming to systematically integrate and present relevant disease knowledge through scientific methods. First, we extensively collected and screened authoritative literature and clinical guidelines on GVHD symptom management to ensure the reliability and accuracy of the information sources. Second, we utilized the Bert-CRF-BiLSTM model trained on medical corpora for entity relationship extraction, complemented and refined this process with AI assistance, and established logical relationships among various knowledge points, resulting in a clear and hierarchical structure for the knowledge graph. In addition, we paid special attention to the intrinsic connections between acute and chronic GVHD, as well as the integration of symptom management across different organ systems, striving to comprehensively and systematically present all aspects of GVHD symptom management within the knowledge graph. This series of scientific and systematic construction processes can provide valuable references for medical staff and patients. Currently, knowledge graphs have been widely used in chronic patient self-management and nursing curriculum teaching, achieving significant results. Studies have shown that for diabetic patients, knowledge graphs can integrate information such as patients’ dietary habits and blood glucose levels, providing customized dietary plans and exercise recommendations, and helping patients improve their quality of life. This study constructs a GVHD patient symptom management knowledge graph, establishes the intrinsic connections between acute and chronic GVHD, systematically presents the symptom management systems for various organs such as skin care, gastrointestinal care, and bone health management, emphasizes the importance of preventing infection and real-time symptom monitoring while providing disease knowledge, enhances nursing skills, reduces the risk of complications, and improves patients’ quality of life. By structuring scattered guidelines into an interactive and navigable knowledge model, this knowledge graph makes evidence-based recommendations more accessible at the point of care. It supports interdisciplinary communication by providing a shared visual framework of symptom management priorities. Furthermore, the graph’s underlying structure can inform the design of health information technology systems, such as clinical decision support tools or patient education platforms, ensuring they are better aligned with nurses’ workflows and patients’ self-management needs.

The knowledge graph addresses the critical gap in GVHD symptom management by unifying fragmented guidelines into a cohesive framework. By integrating 7 organ-specific domains (eg, skin, gastrointestinal tract) with cross-cutting themes like nutrition and psychology, this tool enhances nurses’ ability to deliver holistic care. The application of the BERT-CRF-BiLSTM model ensures precise entity-relationship extraction, while Neo4j’s graph database enables dynamic updates, aligning with evolving clinical needs. This systematic approach contrasts with prior studies that focused on isolated symptoms or organs, thereby reducing the risk of oversight in patient care.

Although this study has currently only completed the construction of the knowledge graph and has not yet been widely applied in practical settings, based on the characteristics and content of the knowledge graph, its broad application prospects and practicality in future medical care can be foreseen. First, the visualization feature of the knowledge graph makes complex information intuitive and easy to understand. Health care professionals or patients can quickly grasp relevant GVHD knowledge through the intuitive graphical interface, thereby enhancing their ability to manage symptoms. Second, the intelligent integration capability of the knowledge graph enables personalized nursing recommendations tailored to individual patient differences. This data-driven precision nursing aids in early detection and timely intervention of GVHD symptoms, alleviating patient suffering and improving treatment outcomes. For example, Yun and Jing have pioneered the integration of structured knowledge into clinical nursing pathways, as documented in the Clinical Nursing Manual for Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation. Their work demonstrates a practical framework for translating guideline-based knowledge into actionable nursing workflows. This established precedent provides a crucial real-world foundation and a validated pathway for implementing the digitally interactive knowledge graph constructed in this study. The graph can be integrated with existing nursing systems or electronic health records to form a clinical decision support tool, thereby enabling systematic and personalized symptom management in real-world scenarios., When the knowledge graph is integrated with advanced technologies such as remote nursing monitoring systems and nursing assessment systems, its application prospects will become even broader. Patients and their families can access the knowledge graph through mobile devices at any time to understand the frequency of patient symptom monitoring and daily nursing precautions, and upload symptom monitoring data in real-time. This allows the nursing team to remotely monitor the patient’s status and promptly provide guidance or adjust the nursing plan. This convenient and continuous nursing service not only enhances the patient’s nursing experience but also ensures that patients receive professional and effective management at home. The construction of the knowledge graph for GVHD symptom management in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation patients will help improve patients’ self-management abilities and provide health care professionals with an advanced and efficient management approach, laying a solid foundation for the future intelligent medical care system.

The current study has several limitations. First, while the knowledge graph was rigorously constructed using evidence-based sources, its clinical efficacy remains theoretical; empirical validation through real-world implementation is needed to assess its impact on patient outcomes such as symptom control, complication rates, or quality of life. Second, entity extraction relied on an AI model (BERT-CRF-BiLSTM) trained on existing medical corpora, which may inadvertently overlook rare or emerging GVHD manifestations not well-represented in literature from 2014 to 2024. Third, the graph’s generalizability may be constrained by its primary reliance on Chinese and international consensus guidelines, necessitating further testing in diverse health care contexts (eg, resource-limited settings). Fourth, the focus on adult HSCT recipients excludes pediatric populations, whose GVHD pathophysiology and management differ significantly. Finally, while Neo4j enables real-time updates, sustaining the graph’s relevance requires continuous evidence integration—a process demanding dedicated resources and infrastructure that may challenge clinical adoption.

This study developed a structured, evidence-based knowledge graph to unify GVHD symptom management for HSCT patients, integrating 7 organ-specific domains (eg, skin, gastrointestinal tract) with cross-cutting themes like nutrition and psychology. By synthesizing multidisciplinary guidelines through AI-assisted entity extraction (BERT-CRF-BiLSTM) and graph database technology (Neo4j), the tool standardizes fragmented protocols into an updatable, actionable framework for nursing practice. It addresses critical gaps in existing care by enabling rapid visualization of symptom relationships, supporting personalized interventions, and reducing practice variability. Future work should validate the graph’s clinical utility through outcome studies, explore integration with telehealth platforms, and expand its applicability to pediatric populations. This innovation establishes a foundation for AI-enhanced precision nursing in HSCT survivorship care, with potential to improve patient self-management and long-term quality of life.

psychology.title: Effects of infertility on relationship quality and mental health outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review
psychology.abstract: Infertility is associated with significant psychosocial challenges, and relationship strain yet remains underprioritized in sub-Saharan African policy and research. We conducted a scoping review to examine the effects of infertility on relationship quality and mental health outcomes among people experiencing infertility in sub-Saharan Africa. We utilized the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. We searched databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, JSTOR, Scopus, Academic Search Complete, PsycINFO, and the Psychology and Behavioral Science Collection. Eligible articles focused on the effects of infertility on mental health and relationship quality in women, men, and couples experiencing infertility and were published between January 2000 and November 2025. We extracted data and conducted an iterative narrative synthesis. We included 70 articles: 36 quantitative, 5 mixed methods, and 29 qualitative. Four key themes emerged, which fit within the socio-ecological model: 1) infertility and relationship quality, 2) infertility and mental health, stigma and discrimination, 3) adaptive coping mechanisms, and 4) maladaptive coping mechanisms. Infertility was associated with anxiety, depression, and emotional distress. Studies revealed profound experiences of isolation and grief over unfulfilled reproductive goals, compounded by societal pressures. Diminished relationship quality was a common outcome among individuals with infertility, manifesting as intimate partner violence, verbal and emotional abuse, loss of intimacy, infidelity, and separation or divorce. Couples with infertility attempted multiple care pathways, including religious, biomedical, and traditional care. Lack of psychosocial support was common, and individuals often coped through substance and drug abuse, isolation, and active avoidance. Complexity of the relationship between infertility, mental health, and relationship quality, reinforces the need for urgent integrated individual and structural interventions that promote holistic fertility care and social support.
psychology.text:
Infertility refers to the inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of unprotected sexual intercourse. It is classified as either primary infertility (where couples have never conceived) or secondary infertility (where couples who have previously conceived are unable to do so) []. Global estimates suggest that about 186 million people are affected by infertility, with the majority living in low-income countries []. According to a review by Cox et al. 2022, one in six individuals worldwide suffered infertility at some point in their lives []. This translates to a lifetime prevalence of 17.5% and a period prevalence of 12.6% as of 2022 []. A pooled estimate of lifelong infertility in Africa is 13.1%, while the pooled estimate of period infertility (the percentage of individuals or couples that are infertile at a particular time) is 16.4% []. In the sub-Saharan African (SSA) region, the prevalence of infertility ranges from 14.3% in The Gambia [] to 21.2% in Ethiopia [] and from a high of 30% in Nigeria [] and 11.8% among women and 15.8% among men in Ghana []. While these estimates vary widely by study approach (hospital-based versus community-based) and were not drawn from nationally representative surveys, they offer crucial insights into the magnitude of infertility and the extent of data on the topic in SSA.

Compared to pregnancy, childbirth, and family planning, infertility remains underprioritized in sexual and reproductive health policy and programming despite its significant prevalence and varied consequences on people’s well-being []. Further, there is minimal attention to men, both in research and discussions around infertility []. Even so, the varying prevalences across settings emphasize the need for region-specific research and interventions that promote infertility-related policies for better access to infertility services and comprehensive support for people living with infertility [].

Causes of infertility vary widely, with several myths and misconceptions around the causes (e.g., past contraceptive use, “past promiscuity”, bewitchment/witchcraft, and divine punishment, past abortion), particularly reflecting the social meaning ascribed to childlessness [,].

Infertility is associated with various health, social, and economic challenges. Couples often experience stress, anxiety, and depression, which can strain their relationship and is often associated with physical abuse []. Socially, they may not attend child-related activities or events, leading to feelings of loneliness and isolation, often worsened by cultural stigma []. Individuals and couples who experience infertility frequently face shame, anxiety, despair, ostracism, and low self-esteem, which can have negative consequences [,,]. Infertility can lead to marital instability, resulting in separation and divorce [,]. Economically, infertility can impose significant financial burdens, often leading to catastrophic healthcare expenditures []. These costs may result in asset depletion, debt accumulation, and difficulty meeting essential needs [,]. The cost of infertility treatment, particularly assisted reproductive technology (ART), is often cited as a significant barrier to access, especially in low- and middle-income countries [,].

Notably, the high prevalence of infertility has not translated to increased availability and access to infertility treatment in Africa []. Access remains acutely limited, mainly due to the high cost of treatment, lack of appropriate infrastructure and skilled personnel, and the absence of public funding for medical services and medication []. A recent multiyear analysis showed that women who used fertility treatments had a lower risk of divorce up to 20 years after the marriage, whether the treatment succeeded or not []. The burden of seeking fertility treatment disproportionately falls on women whose social and cultural identity is defined by motherhood [].

Existing studies in sub-Saharan Africa have examined aspects of the psychosocial consequences of infertility; however, there are no reviews that synthesized the evidence on the relationship between infertility and both mental health and relationship quality among men, women, and couples experiencing infertility. The lack of extensive research and documentation on the effects of infertility inhibits its prioritization as a policy-relevant topic needing urgent interventions []. Recent scoping reviews in Africa have focused on the fear of infertility [], interventions addressing infertility-related gendered stigmatization [], and the psychosocial aspects of infertility []. One scoping review, concluded in 2022 and published in 2024, focused on the effects of infertility on mental health in Africa []. This review aimed to close this gap by examining the effects of infertility on both mental health and relationship quality among women and men (including couples) experiencing infertility (whether primary or secondary) and community members in SSA. The review findings are crucial for highlighting gaps in fertility care and guiding targeted interventions toward holistic infertility care as part of family planning services.

We situate this scoping review within Bronfenbrenner's socio-ecological model (SEM) [], which links individual, relational, community, and structural influences on social phenomena. The SEM is a useful framework for understanding how infertility affects relationship quality and mental health by situating individual experiences within layered social and environmental contexts []. The SEM organizes determinants and outcomes across five nested levels: (1) individual (e.g., personal psychological responses such as anxiety, grief, depression, and self-stigma); (2) interpersonal (e.g., impacts on marital communication, intimacy, and stability); (3) organizational/community (e.g., social stigma from extended family, religious institutions, or healthcare providers); (4) societal (e.g., pronatalist cultural norms and gender-role expectations, social pressures); and (5)] policy (e.g., lack of public funding and infrastructure for infertility care) []. This multi-level framework is especially relevant for SSA, where strong pronatalist cultures and structural barriers amplify the psychological burdens of infertility. This helps explain why the same condition can have different psychological and relational impacts across contexts, especially in settings where fertility is highly valued.

What is the extent of research conducted on infertility and its effects on mental health and relationship quality in SSA between 2000 and November 2025?

This review aimed to identify and synthesize the effects of infertility on mental health and relationship quality among individuals (women, men, and couples) experiencing infertility in SSA. Specifically;

To identify the scope and range of studies available on infertility, mental health, and relationship quality among individuals living with infertility in SSA

To map key findings from the studies on the effects of infertility on mental health and relationship quality among individuals living with infertility

To highlight gaps in the current evidence base in relation to settings, participants involved, study designs, and specific care and outcomes around infertility.

This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews [,]. We followed five steps: 1) defining the research question, 2) identifying articles, 3) selecting articles, 4) extracting data and compiling, and 5) summarizing and presenting the review findings in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) []. We registered the scoping review protocol in the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5AX6F).

We included all studies that addressed the relationship between infertility and mental health and/or relationship quality. We included primary quantitative studies of all designs: observational studies (cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort) and experimental designs (randomized controlled trials and quasi-randomized controlled trials). We also included primary qualitative studies using qualitative designs (e.g., ethnography, phenomenology, case study, grounded theory, and qualitative process evaluation). We included studies that used qualitative data collection methods (e.g., interviews, focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and observations) and analysis methods (e.g., thematic analysis, grounded theory, and framework analysis). We included mixed‐methods studies from which we could extract primary qualitative and primary quantitative findings.

We excluded any studies that were not primary quantitative or qualitative studies, including review studies (such as systematic, scoping and narrative reviews), commentaries or short communications, conference proceedings or workshop summaries, dissertations or theses, records for which full texts were unavailable, and studies or documents that do not include any aspect of infertility lived experiences around mental health and relationship quality among those living with primary or secondary infertility ().

The phenomenon of interest in this review was infertility (whether primary or secondary infertility) and its relationship or effects on mental health outcomes (i.e., the range of psychosocial challenges such as anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and suicidal Ideation). We focus on the relationship between infertility and marital relationships (i.e., divorce, separation, infidelity, sexual satisfaction, and forms of gender-based violence). We also explored the coping mechanisms associated with these mental health and relationship quality outcomes, both adaptive and maladaptive coping mechanisms. Finally, we also explored the supportive structures and systems available to individuals experiencing infertility.

We included studies that presented the perspectives of sexually active men and women (including couples) experiencing infertility, regardless of whether they had primary or secondary infertility. We also included studies that considered the perspectives of family members, in-laws, and community members.

We included studies conducted within countries in SSA. Study settings included formal and informal health care settings, communities (e.g., churches), and informal settings (e.g., traditional birth places, shrines).

The search strategy incorporated keywords, Boolean logical operators and their respective synonyms, truncations, adjacency searches and inverted commas. The search strategy followed three distinct stages. First, we conducted an electronic search of the MEDLINE/PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, JSTOR, Scopus, Academic Search Complete, PsycInfo, and Psychology and Behavioural Sciences Collection databases in June 2024 and updated it in November 2025. The following words made up the variants of search terms across the targeted databases: “Infertility OR childless* OR sterile OR impoten* OR infecundity OR “primary infertility” OR infertile OR “secondary infertility” OR “Assisted Reproduction” OR “In Vitro Fertilization” OR “Fertility Clinics” AND “Intimate partner violence” OR IPV OR “marital dissolution” OR divorce OR separation OR “domestic violence” OR “domestic abuse” OR anxiety OR depression OR stigma OR stress AND “sub-Saharan Africa” OR “East Africa” OR “Southern Africa” OR “West Africa” OR “Central Africa.” We searched each database using a specific search strategy, as detailed in . Second, we screened the reference lists of all eligible studies to identify additional eligible articles.

We used Rayyan software, an online tool that allows reviewers to independently screen several articles simultaneously. We uploaded search results to Rayyan for de-duplication and to manage the selection process. At least two review authors screened article titles and abstracts independently to determine eligibility according to the pre-agreed inclusion and exclusion criteria. For articles lacking an abstract, we reviewed the full text. At least two review authors independently conducted full-text screening and documented the reasons for exclusion. The review authors resolved disagreements through discussion or, when required, by involving a third review author. Where appropriate, we contacted the study authors for further information. Where the same study, using the same sample and methods, was presented in different reports, we collated these reports so that each study (rather than each report) was the unit of interest in our review. We included a PRISMA flow diagram to show our search results and the process of screening and selecting studies for inclusion.

Three independent reviewers (EO, MC, MA) extracted data from each article. We used a pre-designed data extraction template in Microsoft Excel to extract general study details (including study title, publication year, author, country, study type, study design, data collection tools, study objectives, setting, sample size, participants’ sex, age, religion, education, marital status, type of marriage, chronology of marriage, type of infertility, and duration of infertility (years)). We also extracted specific details covering infertility-related themes (such as psychosocial challenges/problems due to infertility (stress, forgetfulness, lack of sleep, loss of appetite, poor concentration, anxiety, depression, anger, low self-esteem, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation). We also extracted information on the effects of infertility on marital and family relationships (divorce, separation, infidelity, reduced sexual satisfaction, intimate partner violence, and verbal abuse, emotional abuse). We also included details on adaptive coping and maladaptive coping mechanisms, and support systems. We also gathered information on study limitations.

The data extraction tool was developed according to Pollock et al.’s guidance on best practices for data extraction, analysis, and presentation within scoping reviews []. We piloted the form across a sample of five studies. Based on the pilot results, we revised the data extraction form as needed.

We conducted an iterative narrative synthesis to analyze and integrate key findings from the review, as described by Popay et al. []. First, we inductively analyzed the qualitative data to identify emerging themes. Two authors independently coded the extracted qualitative data using NVivo 12 and a codebook that was developed and iteratively refined as the analysis progressed. The coded data were then organized into themes and subthemes. To integrate the qualitative and quantitative findings, the quantitative findings were mapped onto the existing themes and subthemes from the qualitative findings, and additional themes were created where the existing themes did not fit.

An assessment of methodological quality was not conducted, which is consistent with accepted scoping review methods [].

Our search strategy identified 3013 articles. After excluding 228 duplicates, we were left with 2,785 articles for the title and abstract screening. After this screening and eligibility assessment, we excluded 2,705 articles outside the scope of this review, leaving 80 articles for full-text screening. We excluded an additional 10 articles during full-text review for reporting the wrong outcome and included the remaining 70 articles in the scoping review ().

The highest proportion of the 70 articles included in this scoping review were published from Nigeria (35.7%) and Ghana (27.1%). Other countries represented included Ethiopia (8.6%), South Africa (4.3%), Malawi (4.3%), Zimbabwe (4.3%), Gambia (2.9%), and the remaining countries had 1.4% each (Zambia, Tanzania, Uganda, Senegal, Rwanda, Mali, and Kenya). Two multi-country studies were included: the first covered Tanzania and Ghana, while the second covered Cameroon, Gabon, Lesotho, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, at 1.4% each ().

Most of the articles were published between 2010 and 2019 (31.1%), followed by those from January 2020 to December 2024 (35.7%), with smaller fractions published between 2000 and 2009 (14.3%) and in 2025 (12.9%). Most articles published data focused on women (65.5%), with about one-quarter reporting data from both sexes (24.1%), and those focused exclusively on men accounted for just 10.3%.

Most articles used data collected within health facility settings (74.3%), with community settings at 18.6%, Medical colleges and Traditional Health Practitioners (THPs) at 1.4% each, and other contexts at 1.4%. Lastly, 2.9% of the studies included did not report the setting in which they were conducted. Slightly over half of the articles were quantitative studies (55.2%), followed by qualitative studies (39.7%) and mixed-method studies (5.2%).  presents a detailed description of the included articles.

Fifty-one studies reported on the relationship between infertility and relationship quality. Findings showed an association between infertility and poorer relationship quality that co-occurred with infidelity, separation and divorce, decreased sexual satisfaction, and physical and emotional abuse. Additional details on the findings from each study are presented in .

Four studies in Ghana reported on the relationship between infertility and reduced sexual satisfaction [38,39,42,45]. Infertility severely affected the sexual pleasure and lives of individuals and was associated with poor sexual relationships, sexual disengagement, and reduced sexual satisfaction, with some characterizing the sexual activity as “pointless”, “fruitless”, “unfulfilling” and “unenjoyable” [–]. Studies across SSA confirmed this notion, and specific examples in Ghana highlighted that 61.6% (77/112) of couples experiencing infertility had sex solely for reproduction, and 64.3% (72/112) experienced unfulfilling and unenjoyable sex []. Findings also emphasized the social meaning of infertility through the substantial pressure exerted on individuals living with infertility, ultimately affecting their sexual pleasure and satisfaction []. Other studies demonstrated the intimate link between infertility-related stress and controlling behavior (such as coercive sexual behavior), emotional strain (mainly from accusations of abortion and conflicts over communication), and erosion of intimacy and social functioning in marriage or relationships [,]. Qualitative studies also affirmed how this distressed marital environment contributed to reduced sexual interest due to its perceived futility []. One man recounted how, for six months, he had not engaged in sexual activity with his wife because it is a waste of energy: “Why do you continue to have fruitless sex with your wife” [].

Nine studies from Cameroon, Ghana, Malawi, Nigeria, Rwanda and Zimbabwe reported on the association between infertility and the occurrence of extramarital affairs or infidelity. Studies emphasized the association between infertility and infidelity, with one study in Rwanda asserting that more men experiencing infertility (16%; 41/254 versus 3%; 6/189) were engaged in extramarital relationships compared to women []. Findings from a multi-country analysis confirmed that married women experiencing infertility were two times more likely to engage in marital infidelity compared to married women with children []. Qualitative studies in Zimbabwe, Nigeria, and Rwanda described a pattern of extramarital affairs by both men and women whose partners were experiencing infertility, ostensibly to save their marriages [,,,]. These extramarital affairs bred doubt within the relationship, weakening trust and stability. One respondent in Zimbabwe lamented how infertile men engage in multiple extra-marital relationships, hoping to impregnate one woman along the way, and this practice exposes the couple to risks of sexually transmitted infections and HIV []. In some cases, the emergence of infidelity was due to pressure from in-laws, with a male respondent in Nigeria acknowledged that “the husband is often urged to take another wife” []. A study in Malawi reported that it was the husband pushing the wife to engage in an extramarital affair, by suggesting to “hire a man to impregnate her”, acknowledging his own inability to achieve a pregnancy []. Not all extramarital affairs ended well, and some women in Ghana narrated how they endured painful rituals as punishment after their secret extramarital affairs were discovered [,].

Fifteen studies highlighted how infertility intersects with various forms of violence, reshaping the lives of women and men far beyond their private spheres [,–]. Violence was perpetrated not only by husbands or partners but also by other family members [,]. A Gambian study found that women facing infertility were beaten by husbands and female in‑laws for supposedly not being “real women” because they could not conceive []. Quantitative studies from Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania and Zambia show that around 38%–64% of women experiencing infertility face violence [,–]. The most common forms were psychological and verbal abuse, though many women endured multiple, overlapping forms of violence, including physical assault, sexual violence, emotional aggression, and deprivation [,].

Qualitative findings revealed how infertility permeated women’s and men’s lives across social, professional, and intimate spheres []. Women living with infertility were subtly dismissed at the workplace, with assumptions that they lacked caregiving responsibilities, reinforcing the belief that womanhood is incomplete without motherhood, and this caused deep emotional hurt []. Women faced ridicule and degrading comments that intensified feelings of inadequacy and isolation []. Some women in The Gambia, Senegal, and Malawi recounted how people in the community called them “witches” and labeled them “barren” [,,], while other women lamented such demeaning remarks from their own husbands/partners, with one mentioning how her husband insulted her and called her names like “you dog, you are very stupid” []. Such verbal abuses strained relationships and escalated to intimate partner violence, with infertility becoming the fault line that exposed rigid gender expectations and pressures within families and communities []. Few studies also revealed how men experienced profound but often hidden suffering by enduring humiliation, public ridicule, and jokes questioning their masculinity. In Zimbabwe, men in these situations felt compelled to hide their distress, protect their partners, and silently carry shame and emotional pain [].

Twenty-three studies in this review showed that infertility was associated with increased marital tension and mistrust, and most men and families often blamed women whenever couples were childless []. Family members and in-laws exerted pressure on infertile couples, sometimes leading to separation and dissolution of marital unions, and several women and men living with infertility had multiple failed relationships and divorces []. Quantitative studies found that many women (e.g., Nigeria - 61.7%; 127/205) observed changes in their partner’s behaviour, relationship dynamics, and stability, and nearly half (Nigeria - 54.2%; 111/205) experienced increased marital discord []. Across contexts, infertility was associated with higher risks of relationship breakdown and divorce—for example, up to 95% (8319/8757) of childless women in Ethiopia experienced divorce within 20 years, with 85% (7444/8757) divorcing in the first five years—illustrating how infertility rapidly and severely undermines marital stability []. Men often resorted to secret arrangements and explored alternative childbearing plans to achieve pregnancy, as was the case in South Africa, where some men resorted to polygamy, leading to separation [,].

Qualitative studies described experiences of infertility in the context of relationship challenges, including conflict, instability, and marital breakdown. In Malawi, some men responded by seeking second marriages or turning to close female relatives—such as a wife’s sister—for informal surrogacy []. Across many African communities, the return of the bride price when a woman does not conceive further weakened marital bonds, effectively dissolving kinship ties and releasing both partners to pursue their reproductive goals independently [].
