A total of fifty-three studies highlighted the relationship between infertility and the occurrence of poor mental and psychological outcomes across multiple African contexts. Quantitative studies from Nigeria and Ethiopia reported high prevalence of depressive symptoms among individuals experiencing infertility (17–39% in Nigeria and 42.1% in Ethiopia), with varying levels of severity ranging from mild to severe depression [–]. Across studies, infertility was associated with emotional distress, anxiety, mood disturbances, and reduced psychological functioning, suggesting that mental health challenges are a pervasive consequence of infertility experiences. Evidence also indicates that psychological distress may intensify with prolonged infertility and repeated treatment failure [].

Findings from qualitative studies further elucidate the understanding of these experiences by showing that infertility-related distress is shaped by uncertainty, fear of the future, and perceived or actual social expectations []. The studies show that participants commonly described persistent worry, anxiety, sadness, and emotional exhaustion from persistent concerns about their fertility status and multiple unsuccessful attempts to find a resolution [,]. In some instances, infertility was associated with severe psychological outcomes, including suicidal ideation, particularly among men [].

We also identified the social dimensions of psychological distress associated with infertility. Feelings of loneliness, isolation, and social disconnection emerged across studies, with participants reporting withdrawal from family and peers due to stigma and societal pressure surrounding childbearing []. Social scrutiny, gossip, and expectations to conceive shortly after marriage further exacerbated anxiety, rumination, and sleep disturbances, while experiences of dehumanization often culminate in diminished self-worth and intensify emotional suffering [].

Furthermore, two studies reported that infertility-related distress affects daily functioning and cognitive well-being. Individuals experiencing infertility experience difficulties with concentration, persistent intrusive thoughts, and reduced ability to manage routine activities and self-care [,]. Feelings of desperation and helplessness were reported among those who had multiple attempts at medical investigations and unsuccessful fertility treatments [].

A more pertinent manifestation of societal reception to infertility was the presence of pervasive stigma (enacted) – represented by negative attitudes and behaviors directed towards persons experiencing infertility and was associated with social exclusion and public humiliation []. Studies across SSA presented accounts of how women and men with infertility were judged, mocked, gossiped about, labelled (e.g., witches or barren), and faced contemptuous ridicule from partners, family, and community members, and in all settings – workplace, religious, and family settings []. Infertility stigma was mainly driven and reinforced by various factors including limited biomedical understanding of infertility, societal framing of infertility as a curse [,], infertility as a personal failure to achieve parenthood [,], and blame of infertility being a result of past transgressions []. Some of these stigmatizing expressions emanated from comparisons of women experiencing infertility with their peers, neighbors, and in-laws, as narrated by a woman in Ghana who said, “I got married before a neighbor, but she gave birth almost immediately []. Everyone is talking about me because I have kept long [in giving birth” []. Qualitative studies also highlighted how men faced such demeaning experiences from close relatives and neighbors who keep their children away from people who are childless. One man in Ghana recalled how he was humiliated and insulted for sending a neighbor’s child to the shop, and the mother [of the child sent to the shop] told the man, “to impregnate your wife and have your own children whom you can send on errands” [].

Feelings of internalized stigma and self‑blame were also frequent among individuals experiencing infertility. Individuals often absorbed these societal beliefs that equated fertility with personal worth, and this contributed to social isolation and hopelessness among affected persons, intensifying feelings of guilt and avoidance of care, self-questioning, and sadness when comparing themselves to those with children []. Other women blamed God, and as one woman remarked in Ghana, “life is not fair; I sometimes feel God shouldn’t have created me” [].

This internal distress compounded experiences and manifestations of stigma and was associated with widespread social exclusion. Across studies in Ghana and Nigeria, individuals living with infertility were frequently marginalized within their communities, excluded from social gatherings, and denied participation in events centered around children. Quantitative findings consistently reinforced this pattern of social exclusion [,]. Beyond everyday social interactions, infertility also exposes individuals to cultural and ritual-based discrimination. Ethnographic accounts describe exclusionary burial practices for those who experienced infertility, signaling a stigma that extends beyond life. In some places, ritual purification practices have involved degrading and violent acts, such as stripping women naked and using thorns to scour their genitals—practices justified through cultural narratives linking infertility to moral transgression or impurity [].

Six studies from Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria reported on the various adaptive and maladaptive mechanisms that individuals living with infertility employ to cope with the experience of infertility and its social consequences (e.g., stigma, marital strain, uncertainty about the future). None of the studies in this review focused explicitly on any coping responses directed at mental health symptoms, but rather at the stressors generated by infertility — such as social pressure, repeated treatment failure, and fear of relationship dissolution.

There was a rich interplay between infertility and seeking spiritual, traditional, and biomedical interventions. Four studies in Zambia, Ghana, Ethiopia and Mozambique reported reliance on spiritual coping, and in some cases, positive religious coping was significantly associated with higher levels of somatization and anxiety, whereas negative religious coping was significant and positively correlated with age, duration of infertility and depression [,,,]. Individuals in these studies articulated beliefs in divine timing and the power of prayer, conveying hope grounded in their spirituality [,,].

Across multiple settings, studies show a strong reliance on traditional (herbal) and faith‑based healing before or alongside biomedical care. In Mali, 71% (37/52) of participants used both traditional “African medicine” and Western treatments, often concurrently []. Similar patterns appear in Nigeria-57% (237/415) and Zimbabwe-80% (249/311), where the majority of individuals first sought help from traditional or faith‑based healers before turning to biomedical options. Together, these studies highlight the widespread use of pluralistic health‑seeking practices in navigating infertility [,].

Regarding biomedical treatment approaches, a hospital-based study in Nigeria showed that a significant portion of the population used medical treatments (62%; 257/415), while surgical interventions were utilized by about (33%; 137/415) of individuals []. The financial burden of these treatments was evident, with many participants expressing that the cost was secondary to the value of having children, emphasizing the profound emotional and social implications of infertility []. There has been an increasing demand for infertility treatment in SSA, particularly the demand for assisted reproductive technologies (ART), yet access to quality ART remains acutely limited. In many countries, ART services are very costly and primarily delivered by the private sector [], except in Nigeria and South Africa []. Whittaker et al. (2023) observed that in SSA, Kenya had the fewest fertility clinics at 11, followed by Ghana at 18, South Africa at 40 and Nigeria with the highest number at 96, primarily set up to attend to international clients []. With the exceptions of Uganda and South Africa, where private insurance compensates ART treatments, and Tanzania, where the government provides partial coverage, other SSA governments barely prioritize ART in their policies. Tabong and Adogo (2013) reported that some women accepted their situation and resorted to pursue other things, including education, after waiting for several years to become pregnant in vain [].

Mashaah et al. reported a spectrum of coping strategies, including acceptance and not pursuing serious relationships, choosing to focus on enjoying life, and avoiding the stress and stigma of remarriage or being labeled barren []. This finding aligns with Behude et al., who report that individuals facing infertility may come to terms with the possibility of not having biological children []. This shift in mindset helps them reframe their situation, enabling a focus on moving forward, pursuing alternative routes to parenthood, or embracing a life without children []. In contrast, other individuals opt for commitment to family-building through child fostering and adoption [,]. Likewise, Musa et al. reported that more than half (59.2%) of the study participants considered adopting a child as a coping strategy in Nigeria [].

Anabila Adda et al., Behude et al., and Araya et al. reported spousal support as a key coping strategy, recognizing and valuing spouse’s persistent efforts despite repeated conflicts. These studies described situations where separation seemed possible, yet the couple chose to stay married, providing the emotional support needed to navigate relationship stress [,,]. Likewise, Musa et al. reported that involving partners and getting financial aid were coping strategies for most individuals in Nigeria []. The scoping review findings illustrated that the adaptive coping strategies were not mutually exclusive; they coexisted and complemented each other.

Individuals experiencing infertility resorted to isolation and avoidance to cope with infertility‑related stressors such as societal stigma and emotional distress. Across multiple settings (Ghana, Ethiopia, and Nigeria), individuals withdrew from social gatherings out of fear of judgment and painful inquiries about their fertility status [,,,]. Avoidance often manifests as physical isolation, with individuals preferring to stay home or lock themselves away []. Quantitative findings concurred that people with infertility issues had high scores of active-avoidant syndromes, which were associated with lower levels of quality of life [], and most of those engaging in escape-avoidance also exhibited mild depression [].

Denial and defensiveness frequently emerged as maladaptive coping strategies among individuals facing infertility []. Both males and females often lied about their fertility circumstances to avoid scrutiny and retain a sense of control over their personal narratives [] for instance, by arguing that they were still studying []. Others turned to substances, including alcohol, to escape their pain and frustration []. Such defensiveness functions as a protective response to infertility‑related stigma, allowing individuals to shield themselves from judgment and preserve social standing.

The review findings also capture some extreme suspicions, such as fear that childless individuals may steal other people's children [,]. Oti-Boadi and Asante (2017) found that negative religious coping was significantly correlated with age, duration of infertility, and elevated levels of somatization, depression, and anxiety []. The interplay of avoidance, denial, substance use, and negative religious coping underscores the need for supportive interventions that integrate care for psychological distress linked to infertility and the social stigma that fuels maladaptive responses.

There is an increasing number of studies in the last decade inquiring into the effects of infertility on mental health and relationship quality in SSA [,], yet this review identified several critical evidence gaps. This trend may reflect growing recognition of the burden of infertility; however, there remains a paucity of studies documenting interventions to mitigate its impact []. Studies in the review predominantly targeted women (66%; 38/58), perhaps highlighting the traditional focus on women around reproduction and infertility []. One-quarter of articles focused on both sexes (24%), and only 10% targeted men, implying that research on effects of infertility on mental health and relationship quality may be under-representing male perspectives and experiences, yet these are critical in designing interventions that fit the targeted populations.

Studies in this review affirmed the association of infertility with mental health experiences and relationship outcomes [,,,,]. More particularly, the review findings were consistent on the emotional distress infertility exerts on individuals, further exacerbating existing tensions within relationships, leading to communication breakdowns and, in severe cases, separation or divorce [,,]. Notably, there were few reports of the psychosocial support and therapy individuals and couples receive when seeking fertility-related services [,]. As such, these findings point to an essential programmatic gap in infertility management that integrates provision of proactive counselling and a range of psychosocial support services focused on improving communication and emotional resilience [,].

The review findings also suggested how societal stigma surrounding infertility is pervasive and manifests in different ways, including ostracization and discrimination from community activities, degrading insults, and abuse [,]. These expressions further triggered feelings of shame, blame, self-worthlessness, and actions including avoidance, isolation, social withdrawal, secrecy, and lying about their fertility situation []. Stigma drives women and men towards several forms of maladaptive coping mechanisms, sometimes harmful to their health and well-being. Support networks, such as peer-led groups that bring together individuals living with infertility (physically or virtually, like in WhatsApp groups), have been shown to offer safe spaces for sharing experiences and fostering connections []. Participants struggling with infertility shared their experiences in peer groups and emphasized the value and comfort derived from deep understanding and empathy when they shared experiences within the peer groups []. The empathetic connection helped individuals feel seen, understood, and less isolated in their struggles. Prior studies show that shared traumatic experiences foster deeper empathy and understanding, and that support from peers navigating similar journeys was particularly impactful.

However, more research and attention are required on interventions at the societal or community levels to mitigate infertility-related stigma, to enhance the lived experiences of individuals suffering from infertility, and to improve their physical and mental health [].

Review findings also showed the intersection between infertility and experiences of violence, abuse, and diminished human rights of individuals []. Studies reported a heightened risk of experiencing various forms of emotional and physical violence due to infertility. Studies have suggested that marital counselling is among the effective interventions for couples with a history of IPV or psychological trauma and living with infertility []. A systematic review of structural interventions for intimate partner violence suggested integrating IPV screening and counselling within infertility clinics could help enhance early detection of IPV, and mitigation, including timely referrals for specialized care, such as psychological support groups or law enforcement, when necessary [].

The findings showed that individuals with infertility relied on multiple therapy approaches, sometimes concurrently or sequentially, beginning with traditional and religious approaches, followed by professional medical care []. These healthcare-seeking patterns around infertility may partly reflect the conceptualization of infertility in many African societies as a non-medical issue that can be redressed using non-medical interventions [,,]. Nonetheless, it is also primarily associated with the inaccessibility of fertility care, both due to cost and the availability of these services in much of SSA [,]. There is substantial literature on the unavailability of fertility care and how it diminishes human rights and reproductive justice - the right and ability to access infertility treatment and services, especially for the economically marginalized in societies [].

The review findings suggest that health providers need to integrate a combination of resources when attending to patients seeking infertility treatments, including offering support towards spiritual, traditional, and biomedical care pathways that resonate with the personal beliefs and values of those faced with infertility. This holistic approach can enhance coping mechanisms, allowing individuals to feel more in control of their experiences and less stigmatized by societal pressures. Additionally, support systems, including healthcare providers and peer networks, are recommended as they play a crucial role in enhancing resilience and promoting mental well-being among people suffering from infertility.

Infertility can have wide-ranging implications for individuals and couples because it often affects emotional wellbeing, intimate relationships, social identity, and everyday functioning at the same time [,]. The effects may differ across contexts, but several common implications are consistently reported. The effects highlighted in this scoping review could also lead to broader outcomes: increased need for mental health and psychosocial support services or reduced healthcare-seeking due to fear, stigma or discrimination, and greater financial burden from expensive and prolonged treatment. It also affects family wellbeing, social participation, and life planning. Infertility should therefore be understood not only as a biomedical condition, but also as a social, psychological, and relationship issue with important implications for wellbeing and quality of life.

There is a critical gap in the development and testing of interventions that address the common relationship and mental health challenges associated with infertility in SSA []. Investment in such programs remains inadequate and contributes to poor outcomes related to infertility. In contrast, studies from high-income settings have reported several successful interventions that could be transferable and integrated into care systems within low- and middle-income settings with low resource inputs []. For instance, the Fertility Life Counselling Aid has shown great potential in addressing the psychological distress and stigma associated with infertility. The program follows a three-step process: (1) recognizing unhealthy thought patterns, (2) replacing them with healthier ones, and (3) practicing these positive thoughts and behaviors []. A context-specific counselling aid (adopted from FELICIA) could empower individuals dealing with infertility to develop healthier coping strategies and reduce stigma by fostering greater societal acceptance and understanding.

Talaei and colleagues confirmed that availing cognitive behavioral therapy to women living with infertility was associated with decreased depressive symptoms and psychological problems []. Other studies have confirmed the effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy on men []. Such interventions could optimize management of stress that is linked to infertility and potentially reduce the risk of relationship dissolution.

This scoping review has several limitations. First, the review was limited to studies published from the year 2000 onward. This may exclude valuable insights from earlier research that could provide a broader context for understanding the evolving dynamics of infertility and its impact on relationships and mental health in the region. However, we also believe this timeframe covers enough research to provide a detailed scope of the state of evidence on this topic. This decision was mainly influenced by the need to be focused, practical, and pragmatic, given the scope the researchers could manage with available resources and time.

Additionally, the review predominantly focused on studies written in English, which may inadvertently overlook significant findings from research published in other languages, particularly in a multilingual region like SSA. We nevertheless made every effort to obtain studies from the francophone and other parts of Africa that were published in English.

Because scoping reviews do not typically include critical appraisal of the methodological quality of included studies, we could not systematically assess the strength and quality of the available evidence. A future systematic review incorporating formal quality and risk-of-bias assessments would help further evaluate the robustness of the evidence identified in this review.

Lastly, the review emphasizes published articles and excludes grey literature such as dissertations and reports from non-governmental organizations. This omission may result in a narrower perspective on the impact of infertility on mental health and relationship quality, as grey literature often contains valuable data that can illuminate local experiences and interventions not captured in peer-reviewed journals.

This scoping review highlights several critical research gaps, with very few studies employing ethnographic approaches. Ethnographic research could offer deeper, longitudinal insights into individuals’ lived experiences and warrants further exploration. Notably, there is a scarcity of interventional studies aimed at addressing infertility and its effects on relationship quality and mental health. This lack of intervention-focused research limits the ability to identify effective support and care strategies. Additionally, geographic distribution of the existing literature suggests that many regions within SSA are underrepresented in research on the topic. These regions offer unique policies, health systems, and cultural contexts that shape experiences of infertility, and it is valuable to generate research and evidence from these settings. The review also notes the dearth of community-based quantitative studies, which are essential for understanding the broader societal implications of infertility. Addressing these gaps will be crucial for building the evidence base on infertility and its effects, potentially strengthening efforts to prioritize the topic in public policy discourses and increase investment towards greater access and affordability of fertility treatments in Sub-Saharan Africa.

The scoping review revealed that infertility was closely associated with mental health and relationship problems, especially because infertility is often overlooked in health policies, programs, and services in sub-Saharan Africa. Many studies reported that people experiencing infertility face stigma, discrimination, anxiety, and depression. Infertility also affects relationships, with studies describing experiences such as infidelity, emotional and physical violence, separation, and divorce. The stigma around infertility can lead to social isolation and unhealthy coping behaviors. However, most studies focused mainly on women, with limited attention given to men’s experiences. In addition, some countries and regions in SSA remain underrepresented in the existing evidence on infertility. The scoping review highlights several critical research gaps and the need for broader social interventions that improve access to fertility services, strengthen social support, and promote healthy coping strategies. Counselling services and community-based programs are also needed to reduce stigma and protect the mental well-being of individuals affected by infertility.

psychology.title: Potential Applications of Brain–Computer Interface Technology in the Rehabilitation of Patients with Anxiety Disorders: A Narrative Review
psychology.abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent mental disorders worldwide and can cause persistent impairment in emotional regulation, cognition, and social functioning. Pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, exercise, and non-invasive brain stimulation are widely used, yet their effectiveness may be constrained by dependence liability, interindividual variability, treatment engagement, incomplete response, and limited objective measures of treatment processes. Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) acquire, decode, and feed back neural signals—most commonly electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), or real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (rt-fMRI)—thereby converting anxiety-related brain activity into targets that can be monitored, trained, or used to trigger intervention. This narrative review examines the mechanistic rationale for BCI-assisted anxiety rehabilitation, technological approaches across levels of invasiveness, and integration with pharmacological, psychological, and exercise-based care. Current evidence indicates that EEG has been used for both anxiety-state recognition and neurofeedback; rt-fMRI enables targeted modulation of deep emotion-related networks and functional connectivity; and fNIRS offers promise for portable prefrontal monitoring and as an input signal for closed-loop systems. Invasive closed-loop systems can directly record from and stimulate local or deep circuits, but anxiety-related evidence is derived mainly from animal studies, patients undergoing intracranial monitoring, and neurological populations with comorbid anxiety, and therefore demonstrates technical feasibility rather than efficacy in primary anxiety disorders. Overall, BCIs are better positioned as potential adjuncts to established care than as replacements. The field remains limited by small, single-center studies, inadequate follow-up, heterogeneous acquisition and training protocols, and unresolved governance of neural data. Because this is a narrative review without a formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis, its conclusions should be regarded as exploratory. Multicenter randomized controlled trials, harmonized technical and reporting standards, cross-device external validation, and risk-proportionate ethical and regulatory frameworks are needed to determine whether BCIs can be translated from proof of concept into safe, effective, and implementable tools for anxiety rehabilitation.
psychology.text:
Mental ill-health is a major global public-health challenge. Anxiety disorders are the most common group of mental disorders; the World Health Organization estimates that 359 million people—approximately 4.4% of the global population—were living with an anxiety disorder in 2021. These disorders can impair family, social, educational, and occupational functioning and are associated with depression, substance-use disorders, and physical-health problems. Their socioeconomic impact is also substantial: depression and anxiety are estimated to account for 12 billion lost working days and approximately US$1 trillion in lost productivity each year. These burdens underscore the need for interventions that address not only symptom reduction but also functional recovery, relapse prevention, and sustained social participation.

Established interventions include pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, exercise, and physical neuromodulation. Benzodiazepines act rapidly, but prolonged or inappropriate use can cause psychological and physical dependence, withdrawal, and cognitive adverse effects., Psychological treatments such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are effective, yet dropout, documented in a 2015 meta-analysis, and treatment engagement, examined in a 2013 study, influence real-world outcomes. Exercise can reduce anxiety symptoms, although dose, adherence, and neurophysiological effects are often assessed without continuous objective measures., Non-pharmacological approaches such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation are promising, but the consistency and durability of their effects remain uncertain.,

Incomplete response is a further challenge. Even with guideline-endorsed first-line treatments—selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), and CBT—only 50% to 67% of patients show an adequate clinical response after the first treatment trial, and in a 9-year naturalistic follow-up 32.1% of cases showed only intermittent recovery and 8.6% a consistently chronic course. A 2018 meta-analysis found that remission rates after CBT vary substantially by diagnosis and by how remission is defined. In 2024, an international Delphi panel proposed operational criteria for treatment-resistant anxiety disorders—failure of at least two adequate trials of first-line pharmacotherapy and/or at least one adequately delivered course of first-line psychotherapy—and identified neuromodulation as one of the approaches to be tested in this population. A central challenge is therefore to identify anxiety-related neural states in real time and use that information to deliver individualized, adjustable interventions.

Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) provide a technical framework for this goal. A BCI records and analyzes neural activity and translates it into commands or feedback that can be interpreted by an external system, thereby establishing a direct information pathway between the brain and the environment., In anxiety-related applications, the purpose is not limited to device control: abnormal arousal, electrophysiological rhythms, or emotion-regulation network activity can be transformed into observable and trainable signals. Electroencephalography (EEG) neurofeedback has been proposed for anxiety disorders and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD),, and a low-cost wearable EEG system combined with motor-imagery training has produced preliminary symptom reductions in chronic PTSD., Nevertheless, the literature spans state recognition, neurofeedback, brain stimulation, and mindfulness training, with inconsistent conceptual boundaries and levels of evidence., This review therefore addresses three questions: (1) through which neural mechanisms might BCIs influence anxiety; (2) what are the respective roles of, and levels of evidence for, invasive, partially invasive, and non-invasive systems; and (3) how might BCIs complement pharmacological, psychological, and exercise-based rehabilitation? The overall conceptual framework for BCI-assisted anxiety rehabilitation is illustrated in .

We conducted a narrative review of research on BCI-assisted rehabilitation for anxiety disorders, organized around the three questions stated in the Introduction. The aim was to map mechanisms, technical approaches, and evidence gaps rather than to estimate the pooled effect of any single intervention. The review was therefore not prospectively registered as a systematic review. To make the search and selection process transparent and reproducible, we report the databases, search dates, database-specific search strategies, time window, eligibility criteria, selection procedure, author roles, and procedure for resolving disagreements, in line with recommendations for rigorous narrative reviews.,

PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and IEEE Xplore were searched, and the reference lists of included articles, systematic reviews, and highly cited reviews in the field were screened manually. The primary searches of all five databases were run between 12 and 18 June 2026 and covered records published from 1 January 2004 onward (the upper publication-date limit entered in the database filters was 30 June 2026). An incremental update search was completed on 9 October 2026 using the five primary search strategies (S1–S5), restricted to publications dated from 30 June to 9 October 2026, inclusive. Newly retrieved records were screened using the same eligibility criteria. The update-search date and publication-date window are reported in Supplementary Table S1. Searches were limited to English-language publications, with no restriction on study design. Supplementary Table S1 reports the common search interval; database-specific execution dates were not separately documented in Supplementary Table S1. Methodological references cited in the Methods and Discussion (for example, on bias and evidence synthesis) were identified separately and do not form part of the evidence base.Table 1Comparison of Brain–Computer Interfaces by Degree of InvasivenessBCI TypeSignal-Acquisition SiteImplementationMain StrengthsMain LimitationsFully invasiveIntracortical or deep brain structuresImplanted microelectrode arrays or deep electrodesHigh signal-to-noise ratio and spatiotemporal resolution; neuronal or local-field-potential recording; bidirectional read–write potentialSurgery; infection and tissue-response risks; maintenance and long-term stability; substantial ethical concernsPartially invasive/ minimally invasiveSubdural or epidural cortical surface, or cerebral vasculatureECoG arrays or endovascular stent-electrode systemsSignal quality generally superior to scalp EEG; less direct parenchymal injuryStill requires an invasive procedure; surgical or vascular risk; uncertain long-term stability; limited indicationsNon-invasiveScalp, body surface, or imaging environmentEEG, fNIRS, fMRI/rt-fMRISafe and repeatable; high acceptability; some systems are portable and suitable for monitoring and trainingModality-specific limits in signal-to-noise ratio, localization, or depth; artifacts; high cost and restricted setting for fMRINote: The table summarizes signal-acquisition sites, implementation, principal strengths, and principal limitations of each category.Abbreviations: BCI, brain–computer interface; ECoG, electrocorticography; EEG, electroencephalography; fNIRS, functional near-infrared spectroscopy; fMRI, functional magnetic resonance imaging; rt-fMRI, real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging.
