Second, the study relied on convenience and snowball sampling via social media, which may have introduced selection bias (e.g., over-representation of mothers with higher education, as 64.8% held a bachelor's degree), future studies should use stratified random sampling to capture a more diverse demographic profile. Third, the low Cronbach's alpha for the Child Function domain (0.590) and the questionable reliability for the Child Psychology domain (0.614) suggest that these subscales may benefit from item revision in future studies. Fourth, the child age range (2–6 years) included some children below the typical preschool age, but this reflects real-world heterogeneity. Fifth, the study did not include test-retest reliability, although this was previously established by Farsi et al. (). Sixth, clinical caries data were available only for a subset of participant (n = 150) and were not incorporated into this psychometric analysis, therefor, criterion-related validity against objective caries measures (e.g., dmft scores) was not evaluated. Finally, the two items that did not load (pronunciation difficulty and missed school) may require cultural adaptation or re-wording for Arabic-speaking populations.

The Arabic version of the Early Childhood Oral Health Impact Scale (A-ECOHIS) demonstrated a four-factor structure comprising Family Impact, Child Self-Image, Child Psychology, and Child Function and Symptoms in a large sample of Saudi mothers, using a rigorous split-sample approach with independent subsamples for exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. The total scale and the Child Self-Image subscale demonstrated good reliability, whereas the Family Impact subscale showed acceptable reliability. The Child Psychology subscale demonstrated questionable reliability, highlighting the need for further psychometric refinement of this domain.

The four-factor model demonstrated acceptable fit in confirmatory factor analysis, with adequate convergent and discriminant validity. The original 13-item A-ECOHIS remains a useful instrument for measuring OHRQoL in Arabic-speaking preschool children, with the caveat that users should be aware of its multidimensional structure and the need for further psychometric refinement, particularly for the Child Psychology factor and the two items not retained. Resulting in a provisional 11-item, four-factor model. This reduced structure should be considered preliminary rather than a newly validated version of the A-ECOHIS, as its psychometric properties and factor structure have not yet been confirmed in an independent sample. External validation using a newly recruited and independent sample is therefore warranted before the 11-item model can be considered a validated alternative to the original 13-item A-ECOHIS.

psychology.title: A pilot randomized controlled trial of a physical activity and positive affect intervention after metabolic and bariatric surgery
psychology.abstract: To test the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of a positive emotion-focused physical activity intervention for individuals with recent metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS).This pilot randomized controlled trial tested an intervention developed and refined following the ORBIT model. Patients with MBS in the past 6–12 months and less than 200 minutes/week of self-reported moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) were recruited and randomized to either mailed physical activity education plus a Fitbit or the GOALS intervention (10 weekly 30-minute phone sessions plus a Fitbit and written manual). Participants learned positive psychology tools to increase positive emotions associated with physical activity, and used behavioral strategies (e.g., goal-setting, self-monitoring) to increase physical activity. The primary outcomes were feasibility (percentage of intervention sessions completed) and acceptability (participant ratings of session ease and utility on 0–10 Likert scales). Other outcomes assessed at baseline, 10, and 24 weeks included accelerometer-measured physical activity, physical activity attitudes, and psychological, cardiometabolic and functional outcomes. We ran mixed effects regression models and calculated effect sizes.In 58 participants, the intervention was feasible (96% of sessions completed) and acceptable (ratings >8/10). Compared to the control group, GOALS increased MVPA (30 additional minutes/week at 24 weeks, Cohen’s d=0.5), attitudes related to physical activity (d’s=0.3–0.9), and MBS self-care (d=1.0); general psychological well-being did not differ between groups.The GOALS intervention has promise for physical activity promotion post-MBS and should be tested for efficacy in a fully powered trial.
psychology.text:
Obesity affects nearly 41% of adults () and is associated with comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer (; ). Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) effectively treats obesity (body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30kg/m2), resulting in significant weight loss and reduction in comorbidities (). However, at least 25% of patients struggle to achieve or maintain the expected weight loss after MBS (; ).

Physical activity improves weight loss, percent body fat, and lean mass retention after MBS (; ). Furthermore, physical activity post-MBS positively affects insulin sensitivity, glucose effectiveness, and cardiorespiratory fitness (; ). Despite its importance, most individuals who have MBS do not meet physical activity recommendations for US adults of at least 150 minutes/week moderate-intensity activity plus resistance training at least twice per week (; ; ). In fact, when it has been measured objectively with accelerometry, less than 10% of patients post-MBS meet these guidelines (; ). Existing post-MBS physical activity interventions have shown mixed success (). Factors such as required in-person attendance for exercise sessions can be burdensome and may not effectively prepare participants to maintain effects when the provided training sessions end (; ; ).

One’s emotional association with physical activity is a critical aspect of physical activity engagement and maintenance. Positive affect has been shown to predict physical activity goal setting and attainment and can be an important reinforcing factor in building a physical activity habit (; ). It is also associated with more weight loss post-MBS 12–15 years after surgery (). However, individuals who have MBS are likely to have more negative associations with physical activity due to commonly reported experiences such as past injuries, pain, weight stigma, and higher rates of psychiatric comorbidity (). Weight loss alone does not necessarily change psychological factors that contribute to a negative experience of exercise.

Positive psychology (PP) interventions teach simple skills designed to increase positive psychological well-being constructs such as gratitude, meaning, and self-confidence and are proven to increase well-being in general populations and those with medical or psychiatric illness (; ). When combined with behavioral strategies such as motivational interviewing, PP interventions have shown promise for increasing physical activity, although existing studies show mixed results and are mostly underpowered (; ; ). PP could be a novel approach to combat the common negative associations with physical activity post-MBS to help this population build and maintain a physical activity habit, via multiple mechanisms including increased positive affect, self-efficacy, motivation, and knowledge.

The Gaining Optimism After weight Loss Surgery (GOALS) program is a 10-week remotely delivered PP-based intervention to address psychological barriers associated with increasing physical activity following MBS (). It was developed following the ORBIT model of intervention development, starting with a qualitative study and then a proof-of-concept trial to align the intervention to relevant physical activity barriers in this population and to refine intervention content and study procedures (; ; ). This present study is a two-arm, single-blinded pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) of the GOALS intervention. The primary aims were to establish feasibility and acceptability of the intervention, and secondarily we examined preliminary efficacy of the intervention on physical activity and other outcomes. We hypothesized that the GOALS intervention would be feasible to deliver and acceptable to participants. We also expected that the GOALS intervention would be associated with larger changes in accelerometer-measured moderate to vigorous physical activity (MVPA) post intervention and at 24-week follow-up, and with changes in attitudes related to physical activity, psychological well-being, and physical health measures, compared to a physical activity education plus Fitbit control condition.

This is a pilot parallel RCT with 1:1 allocation. The study was approved by the Mass General Brigham IRB (#2021P001006) prior to initiation; all participants provided written informed consent. The study was prospectively registered and analysis plans were shared on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04868032). This article describes how we determined sample size and all data exclusions, manipulations, and measures that were included in the study. We follow the CONSORT guideline for reporting pilot and feasibility trials. Analysis code is available in the included supplement, data are not publicly available, and research materials (e.g., surveys) are available via references. Data were analyzed using Stata version 16.1 (College Station, TX).

Participants were adults with a history of MBS within 6–12 months of enrollment, less than 200 minutes/week self-reported MVPA on the International Physical Activity Questionnaire Short Form (IPAQ-SF), and a desire to increase their physical activity (). Patients were ineligible to participate if they had cognitive deficits (using a 6-item cognitive screen), an inability to be physically active, severe medical or psychiatric illness, participation in another program targeting physical activity, lack of a telephone, or inability to speak or read English ().

Potential participants who had either gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy surgery within the designated timeframe at a large urban hospital in the northeastern United States were identified through clinician referrals and systematic searches of the electronic health record. Study staff completed chart reviews of patients to identify potentially eligible candidates. Study invitation letters (physical or digital via patient portal) were sent to these patients, followed by recruitment calls to those who did not opt out via phone or email. Eligible and interested patients were mailed or emailed a copy of the consent form to review ahead of study enrollment.

summarizes study procedures. At the initial in-person study visit (Visit #1), the study coordinator obtained informed consent and collected baseline data. Trained nurses measured height, weight, and blood pressure, conducted the six-minute walk test (6MWT), and drew blood (). Participants self-reported their weight on their home scale the next day, or on a provided scale if they did not have one, to collect a consistently measured weight if participants completed follow-up remotely. At the end of the study visit, participants were given an ActiGraph GT3X-BT accelerometer and directed to wear the belt for 7 days (minimum accepted use was 4+ days with at least 10 hours of recorded data).

At Visit #2 (in-person or remote), participants returned their ActiGraph in person or by mail to be checked for sufficient wear time. If wear time did not meet guidelines, the participant was asked to wear it for another week. Once sufficient wear time was confirmed, the participant was randomized 1:1 using a random number generator in Stata to the GOALS intervention or the physical activity education control condition. Participants and study staff learned of the participant’s study condition contemporaneously after all baseline assessments were complete. Randomization assignments were created by the study principal investigator (PI) and were kept in an Excel spreadsheet that had each assignment blacked out concealing all assignments prior to randomization. Regardless of study condition, all participants were given a Fitbit Inspire 2 or 3 and physical activity educational materials. GOALS participants also received a study manual. Fitbits were set up with a study login so that the study team could access Fitbit data during their participation period.

After 10 weeks (or after completing the 10-week intervention for GOALS participants), participants completed an initial follow-up visit (Visit #3) either in-person or remotely. They wore the ActiGraph for seven days and completed questionnaires and physiological measures again. Next, at 24 weeks participants completed a final follow-up (Visit #4) either in person or remotely, again completing the same measures. Remote visits differed from in-person visits in that body weight was self-reported, the 6MWT was not completed, and blood was drawn at a local Quest Diagnostic Service Center location. Finally, participants randomized to the GOALS intervention completed an exit interview about their experience in the study. This was a single-blind study. While the primary research coordinator, interventionists, and participants were aware of their condition, a blinded research assistant collected all follow-up data.

The GOALS intervention consisted of 10 weekly 30-minute telephone sessions with an associated manual (see ). Each session included a PP and a physical activity goal-setting topic. The PP skills aimed to help participants increase positive emotions experienced during physical activity, and the goal-setting skills provided strategies for increasing activity. At the first session the interventionist introduced the participant to the program, explained rationale for the different intervention components, helped the participant identify their values and motivators for getting more active, and set an overall goal for the end of the GOALS program. The interventionist then introduced the topics in Session 1 and assigned them as homework. At each subsequent session the interventionist reviewed the prior week’s activities with the participant, collected acceptability ratings, and introduced the next session’s topics. Additionally, each week participants monitored their physical activity using the provided Fitbit and tracked positive emotions experienced during physical activity. Each week they set a physical activity goal; the participant self-selected activity goals based on their prior activity and discussion with the interventionist. These goals were reviewed the next week to determine if the participants met the goal they had set during the previous session and identify and troubleshoot any relevant barriers. A motivational interviewing approach was used for all intervention communication.

The intervention was delivered by a licensed clinical psychologist (study PI; EF) and trained clinical psychology doctoral students. Sessions were reviewed in weekly group supervision meetings and a selection of sessions completed by students were assessed for intervention fidelity by the study PI using fidelity scales developed for the study that measured adherence to assigned session topics.

Participants randomized to the physical activity educational control group were provided with a Fitbit and educational information regarding physical activity and the benefits of exercise but did not receive the weekly intervention phone calls or the treatment manual. The control condition materials were given to both groups at four different time points throughout the study: in person or by mail or email at Visit #2, and by mail or email at Weeks 3, 6, and 9. The information in the educational materials included publicly available infographics from the Centers for Disease Control and resources from the hospital system’s primary care offices. These materials discussed overcoming common barriers to being physically active and described some basic at-home strength exercises. The content was similar to what MBS patients at the study hospital receive through usual post-operative clinical care. This control condition was selected to approximate usual care while providing a low level of contact (mailings) throughout the intervention to encourage retention and included the Fitbit to ensure group differences were not due solely to Fitbit use.

The primary outcomes of the study were intervention feasibility and acceptability. Feasibility was measured as rate of GOALS phone session completion; we decided a priori that the intervention would be considered feasible if participants completed a mean of at least 7/10 sessions, as in prior studies (; , ). Acceptability was assessed via weekly ratings of each PP and goal-setting topic on ease (0–10 scale, 0 = very difficult, 10 = very easy) and utility (0–10 scale, 0 = not at all helpful, 10 = very helpful). As in prior studies, we determined that the intervention would be considered acceptable if ratings averaged at least 7/10 (; , ). Further context for feasibility and acceptability was collected through exit interviews with participants randomized to the GOALS condition. These were conducted after all other study procedures were complete.

We measured physical activity and associated attitudes in several ways. Our primary physical activity outcome was MVPA minutes/week. We assessed MVPA and steps/day using the ActiGraph GT3X-BT hip-worn accelerometer (ActiGraph LLC, Pensacola, FL) which is reliable, validated, and can discriminate between different levels of physical activity (). We assessed self-reported physical activity using the IPAQ-SF (). We objectively measured functional fitness via the 6MWT, as meters walked in 6 minutes (). We also assessed several aspects of physical activity attitudes: barriers to being active with the Barriers to Being Active Quiz (BBAQ), exercise identity with the Exercise Identity Scale (EIS), self-efficacy for exercise with the Self-Efficacy for Exercise Scale (SEE), and physical activity enjoyment with the Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES) (; ; ; ).

Obesity-related outcomes included MBS-self management (Bariatric Surgery Self-Management Questionnaire; BSSQ), BMI, internalized weight bias (Weight Bias Internalization Scale – Modified; WBIS-M), blood pressure, and hemoglobin A1c (; ). BMI was calculated using weights measured at study visits if the participant attended all visits in person (67% of participants). If they had at least one remote visit, their at-home weight was used for all BMI calculations for consistency. General psychological outcomes included positive affect (Positive and Negative Affect Scale positive subscale; PANAS), optimism (Life Orientation Test – Revised; LOT-R), self-efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), and anxiety and depression symptoms (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale anxiety and depression subscales; HADS-A and HADS-D) (; ; ; ).

Baseline sociodemographic characteristics and outcome measures were reported with descriptive statistics. For feasibility and acceptability, we used descriptive statistics and compared results to our a priori thresholds. Other outcomes were analyzed using repeated measures, mixed effects regression models with unstructured covariance matrices to allow for inclusion of participants with missing data. Because this pilot study was not powered to identify significant between-group differences in these analyses, we calculated effect sizes (modified Cohen’s d) using the difference in the change with time divided by the standard deviation of the change, estimated using the variance components of the mixed model. Tests to assess statistical significance used a two-tailed α level of 0.05.

Qualitative data in exit interviews were analyzed using a content analysis approach with Dedoose software (). Two coders (BH, JF) read all transcripts and drafted an initial codebook with input from the PI (EF) using inductive and deductive methods. Then the coders each independently coded each interview. The team met regularly with the PI to establish consistent code definitions and resolve discrepancies. We then extracted themes from the data.

This pilot study was powered to measure feasibility and acceptability. With 29 participants, there was 80% power to detect a difference between the expected proportion of participants completing at least 7.5/10 intervention sessions and the null hypothesis (true proportion of 50% or less) at the α = 0.05 level using a proportion test (power oneproportion). For acceptability, prior similar studies observed mean ease and utility ratings of 8.1 (SD = 1.9) (; , ). Assuming the same mean rating in this study, this study had 92% power to detect a mean acceptability rating ≥ 7/10 (power onemean).

Fifty-eight participants enrolled in the study between July 2022 and June 2024; data collection continued through January 2025. They were 44.5 years old on average; 88% were women, 60% were White, 26% were Black, and 19% were Hispanic or Latino. Most participants were employed (81%), and 55% had a four-year college degree or higher. Participants had an average BMI of 36.1, and at enrollment they had lost 55% of their excess body weight since starting the MBS process; they were 9.2 months post-MBS on average. At baseline, participants were engaging in 109.9 minutes/week MVPA as measured by the ActiGraph. See  for baseline information and  for a CONSORT participant flow diagram.

For intervention feasibility, participants completed an average of 9.6/10 intervention session (SD = 1.5). For acceptability ratings of session ease (0 = very difficult, 10 = very easy) and utility (0 = not helpful, 10 = very helpful) were averaged for the PP topics and goal-setting topics. PP topics were rated as 8.5/10 for ease (SD = 1.7) and 8.9/10 for utility (SD = 1.5). Goal-setting topics were rated as 8.6/10 for ease (SD = 1.6) and 9.0/10 for utility (SD = 1.4).

The impact of the GOALS intervention compared to the control on study outcomes was assessed next. All participants were included in analyses regardless of missing follow-up data. See  for detailed results. When comparing GOALS to the education plus Fitbit control condition, there was minimal difference in MVPA change between groups from baseline to post-intervention (d = 0.1) and a larger increase in MVPA in the GOALS condition at 24 weeks (30 additional minutes/week, d = 0.5; see ). Groups did not differ in change in overall physical activity (steps/day) at either timepoint (d’s = 0.1–0.2). For self-reported activity via the IPAQ, groups did not differ in change at post-intervention (d = 0.2), but the GOALS group showed a small-to-medium effect size larger increase at 24 weeks (d = 0.4). Physical function measured with the 6MWT improved with small effect size at 24-week follow-up (d = 0.3). The intervention showed small-to-medium effect size positive impacts on exercise identity and physical activity enjoyment (d’s = 0.1–0.3), and medium-to-large effects on self-efficacy for exercise and barriers to being active (d’s = 0.5–0.9).

The GOALS intervention showed mixed effects on obesity-related outcomes. MBS self-care improved significantly more with GOALS than the control condition at both timepoints with large effect sizes (d’s = 0.8–1.0). BMI reduced more in the GOALS group at both timepoints with small effect sizes (d’s = 0.3). Internalized weight bias reduced more with GOALS with a small effect size at 24 weeks (d = 0.3). There were also promising trends for improvements in A1c, diastolic blood pressure, and HDL and LDL cholesterol with small-to-medium effect sizes (d’s = 0.3–0.5), but not for systolic blood pressure (d’s = 0.1–0.2).

Contrary to our hypothesis, the intervention did not impact overall psychological well-being. Effects on positive affect, optimism, and symptoms of depression and anxiety were minimal (d’s = 0.1–0.3), and in some cases, in the opposite direction than expected (e.g., positive affect and depression worsened more in the GOALS condition at 24 weeks, d’s = 0.4). There were small-to-medium-effect size improvements in general self-efficacy (d’s = 0.3–0.4).

Exit interviews were completed with 17 participants. There were no significant differences between exit interview completers and non-completers in demographics or baseline MVPA. Participants were asked for feedback on the intervention to better understand its effect. When asked about barriers to physical activity, lack of motivation was the most frequently mentioned barrier prior to the intervention, while no one named this as a barrier at the time of the post-intervention interview. One participant described, “Once I started being mindful—to be positive… That’s the thing I remember to help motivate me to keep going… now it’s like every time I go on my walk… I appreciate kind of like the fresh air” [Black non-Hispanic woman, age 47]. Most participants found the accountability helpful: “Because there were accountability factors with the call-ins, and obviously also with the device. So there were accountability things where making my ‘maybe I should’ve’ into action” [White non-Hispanic woman, age 70]. Participants also described how the PP exercises affected their physical activity mindset: “Some of the gratitude pages… were very, very helpful. Thinking about things you’re grateful for as you’re running… to keep you motivated… I’m doing it for my family… my future… for feeling good, looking good” [Black non-Hispanic woman, age 50]. Another described, “By just reinforcing the positives, it made me feel like I was accomplishing a lot more on those walks than I was by just talking out of the negatives” [Black non-Hispanic woman, age 48].

The most common post-intervention barriers to activity identified in interviews were lack of time (35%) and new medical issues (23%). Some participants described how they used strategies they developed during the intervention to problem-solve these barriers: “It’s time, but… now that I sort of make that more of a priority over something else. Laundry can wait, and I can jump on the treadmill for 20 minutes. It’s okay. It’ll benefit me, and then I feel better after. And I’m like, “All right. Glad I did it” [White non-Hispanic woman, age 57].

This pilot RCT found that the GOALS intervention was feasible and acceptable to participants. Compared to a low-touch Fitbit plus physical activity education control condition, GOALS led to improvements in physical activity attitudes at post-intervention and 24-week follow-up, increased MVPA at 24-week follow-up, and increased MBS self-management.

Session completion rates were very high, with 96% of sessions completed, surpassing our a priori criteria of at least 70% of sessions completed for feasibility. This is higher than in similar trials in other populations (73% – 92%), potentially reflecting the high motivation for change during the post-MBS time-period (; , ). Our sample was also younger and likely healthier than those in other studies, potentially with fewer medical reasons for missing sessions. Acceptability ratings ranged from 8.5 to 9.0/10, also surpassing our a priori acceptability cutoff of 7/10. High acceptability was reflected in exit interviews which were overwhelmingly positive.

As shown in , there was a gradual trajectory of change in MVPA in both groups. Participants in the GOALS condition showed a modest increase in MVPA at post-intervention, and they further increased the minutes per week spent on MVPA at 24-week follow-up. This could be because PP skills require practice to be internalized and affect behavior (). Notably, the control condition, despite being provided with a Fitbit and sent educational materials throughout the intervention period, showed a steady decrease in MVPA over time, demonstrating a need for increased support. There were no differences between groups in overall physical activity, measured as steps per day, even though the intervention included weekly tracking of steps with the Fitbit. Effects seemed to be more limited to higher-intensity activity. As shown in , at 24 weeks, when the difference between groups was the largest, 36% of participants in the GOALS condition and only 16% in the control condition were meeting the 150 minutes/week MVPA national guideline (). There is still substantial need for physical activity support post-MBS, and simple interventions such as Fitbit provision combined with post-MBS usual care do not seem to be sufficient for this population.

Contrary to our hypothesis, there were not group differences in changes in general psychological well-being (e.g., depressive symptoms, positive affect). differs from our prior studies in other populations that showed large effect size improvements in positive affect and other outcomes (; , ). In this study we modified the PP intervention used previously, based on results of our qualitative study. This included focusing the PP exercises more on affective experience during physical activity rather than general well-being. While some exercises targeted general well-being (e.g., positive reappraisal part 1, gratitude for positive events), this was a substantial shift from prior interventions where PP is focused wholly on general well-being. Therefore, our more targeted approach may have more specifically affected its proximal targets such as self-efficacy for exercise, but not broader psychological well-being. There were also baseline differences between groups in positive affect, depression, and anxiety, with higher well-being in the GOALS condition. A potential intervention effect could be masked by regression to the mean, with the more distressed group improving more naturally over time, or a ceiling effect restricting improvement in the GOALS group. It is also possible that, because psychological well-being typically improves naturally post-MBS (reflected by significant increases over time in positive affect and reductions in depressive symptoms across groups), intervention effects were imperceptible.

Effects on cardiometabolic outcomes were mixed and generally in the expected direction. Given the nature of this pilot study these outcomes were exploratory, and significant effects were not expected. The most notable effect was on post-MBS self-care, where the GOALS condition led to statistically significantly larger improvements at both timepoints with large effect sizes. This measure assesses dietary behaviors, vitamin adherence, fluid intake, and physical activity. The same result was found when creating a total score excluding the physical activity subscale. Although the intervention only discussed physical activity, increasing motivation in one area of self-care may have broader effects. This type of “transfer effect” has been studied previously with some evidence for psychological factors such as exercise enjoyment promoting a larger transfer effect onto diet quality (; ).

Strengths of the present study include its randomized design with a clinically relevant control condition, use of blinded outcome assessors, inclusion of objective measures of physical activity and physical function, a diverse sample in terms of race/ethnicity and education level, and a theory-driven intervention developed in a stepwise approach following the ORBIT model. The study also has limitations. By design, the small sample size limits power to detect significant between-group effects as well as generalizability. Participants and interventionists were not blinded to study condition. We used an inconsistent body weight measurement due to a mix of in-person and remote visits (although measurement type was kept consistent within each participant). Ten of the 58 participants had missing ActiGraph data from at least one assessment; it is possible that they were not missing at random, although those with missing data did not differ from completers on baseline MVPA or demographics. Finally, we recruited from a single academic medical center and only 13% of contacted patients enrolled, with 73% either not interested or unreachable. This further limits generalizability, as the enrolled sample likely has more free time and higher health literacy compared to the general post-MBS population.

In summary, a positive emotion-focused physical activity intervention for adults post-MBS was feasible to deliver, acceptable by participants, and showed encouraging effects on MVPA, physical activity attitudes, and MBS self-care. Future studies should test the efficacy of this intervention on physical activity increase and maintenance, and to examine broader clinical outcomes in this vulnerable population. Future work is also needed to expand intervention reach to patients with lower health literacy, limited phone access, more severe psychiatric comorbidity, and to non-English speakers. If effective, this intervention could be incorporated into post-MBS clinical care and meet a common need for more physical activity support.

psychology.title: Integrating Functional Cognitive Rehabilitation With Activity-Based Stroke Telerehabilitation: Intervention Design and Development Study
psychology.abstract: Many stroke survivors experience chronic cognitive deficits that, together with motor impairments, negatively impact well-being and daily function. Critically, poststroke cognitive deficits can interfere with successful engagement in rehabilitation programs aimed at improving participation in home and community activities. To address this issue, we developed a new telehealth intervention that integrates brief, functional cognitive rehabilitation (COG) into an existing upper extremity-focused, activity-based occupational therapy (OT) telerehabilitation program.To describe the development and specification of a telehealth intervention (COG+OT) that integrates functional cognitive rehabilitation into activity-based stroke telerehabilitation.COG+OT was developed using a multi-disciplinary, theory-informed process guided by principles of functional cognitive rehabilitation. It is reported according to the Template for Intervention Description and Replication checklist for rehabilitation (TIDieR-Rehab). The intervention was developed by a team with expertise in stroke rehabilitation from the fields of OT, neuropsychology, clinical psychology, and speech-language pathology. Cognitive rehabilitation content was adapted from an evidence-based compensatory strategy program and condensed into a brief “primer” format. The COG component was iteratively integrated into an existing upper-extremity, activity-based OT telerehabilitation program to support engagement and transfer of strategies to real-world functional tasks. In this paper, we describe the intervention structure, content, delivery, and tailoring procedures.COG+OT is an 8-week, 13-session telehealth intervention delivered in three phases: (1) cognitive strategy training (“primer”; sessions 1-4), (2) review and guided application of strategies within OT activities (sessions 5‐10), and (3) integration of strategies to support generalization to everyday contexts (sessions 11-13). The intervention combines individualized, strategy-based cognitive rehabilitation with goal-oriented OT using a titrated approach. Patient-facing materials, structured session workflows, and therapist-guided metacognitive strategies support tailoring and real-world application.COG+OT is a theory-informed, user-centered intervention that provides a structured approach for integrating functional cognitive rehabilitation into stroke telerehabilitation. This work establishes a well-specified, replicable intervention model and supports future feasibility, effectiveness, and implementation studies.
psychology.text:
Poststroke cognitive deficits occur in up to 70% of stroke survivors, most commonly in the domains of memory, attention, and executive function []. These multifaceted cognitive deficits are consequential for stroke recovery, as they are associated with lower mood and quality of life, reduced participation in daily activities, and more protracted disability [,]. Cognitive rehabilitation interventions are effective at remediating cognitive dysfunction across many clinical conditions [], and growing evidence indicates that functional cognitive rehabilitation, defined as strategy-based training aimed at enhancing real-world cognitive functioning, is particularly useful for improving everyday functioning poststroke []. However, cognitive rehabilitation is underutilized in stroke care due to prioritization of physical over psychosocial and cognitive recovery [], limited access to cognitive rehabilitation services, lack of a well-defined replicable intervention model, and the burden of conventional multiweek treatment schedules. Furthermore, it is typically delivered as a stand-alone intervention, separate from other therapies in which cognitive strategies could be practiced and applied, creating a missed opportunity for integrated rehabilitation that enhances generalization of skills into daily life routines. With the increasing recognition of cognitive health as critical for functioning and quality of life, poststroke therapies combining physical and cognitive rehabilitation are an urgent need.

In prior work, we developed a telerehabilitation occupational therapy (OT) program that integrates upper-extremity task practice [] with metacognitive strategy training (ie, teaching individuals to plan, monitor, and evaluate their own performance) based on the Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance approach []. In a recent study in adult stroke survivors, we showed that this activity-based telerehabilitation OT program improved paretic upper extremity motor skills, activity performance, self-efficacy, and skill generalization []. However, because this program is cognitively demanding, with metacognition components (ie, the process of thinking about one’s own thinking and adjusting accordingly []) that require collaborative goal setting, self-reflection, error analysis, and problem solving, stroke survivors with cognitive deficits may struggle to fully engage and benefit. This challenge served as the motivation for integrating functional cognitive rehabilitation into this activity-based OT program.

This new intervention, called COG+OT, pairs a brief, functional cognitive rehabilitation “primer” (COG; this abbreviation specifically refers to the brief cognitive rehabilitation component of this intervention) with the previously developed activity-based OT program. The rationale for combining these approaches is based on evidence that compensatory cognitive strategies enhance the attention, metacognition, and goal management skills needed for therapy engagement [], and cognitive strategies generalize most effectively when practiced within meaningful everyday activities []. The cognitive rehabiliation intervention we adapted was based on compensatory cognitive training approaches that have demonstrated benefits for cognition, functional capacity, and quality of life in randomized controlled trials including individuals with acquired brain injury and other neuropsychiatric conditions []. Our central hypothesis is that delivering COG before and alongside OT may enhance cognitive readiness, thereby supporting engagement in activity-based OT and yielding greater gains in real-world activity performance and participation.

We recently completed a single-arm pilot feasibility trial of 8-week COG+OT with 20 adults with chronic stroke and upper extremity paresis. Initial pilot testing supported the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention, as reported previously []. Given these findings, the purpose of the current paper is to describe the COG+OT intervention to support transparency, replication, and future intervention evaluation. The primary objective of this manuscript is to detail the conceptualization, design, and specification of the COG+OT intervention using systematic reporting via the Template for Intervention Description and Replication checklist for rehabilitation trials (TIDieR-Rehab) [].

The intervention was developed and tested in a pilot feasibility trial that was approved by the Medical University of South Carolina Institutional Review Board (Pro00136303) and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06555302). All participants provided informed consent.

The intervention embeds functional cognitive rehabiliation into an existing 9-session stroke telerehabilitation program [] (OT) by using brief COG sessions as a “primer” to boost engagement in and benefit from OT (A). Compensatory cognitive training was selected based on theoretical models emphasizing that functional cognitive improvement is best achieved through metacognitive strategy training, habit learning, environmental scaffolding (ie, external supports that facilitate performance), and contextualized practice rather than isolated restorative exercises [,]. These models highlight mechanisms such as teaching compensatory strategies (ie, working around deficits and capitalizing on intact abilities), enhancing self-regulatory and metacognitive processes, and applying strategies in meaningful real-world contexts to promote transfer. These principles align closely with a person-centered, goal-oriented, activity-based OT program.

The existing OT program [] is cognitively demanding, combining (1) upper-extremity task practice within the context of individualized activity goals identified using the American Occupational Therapy Association (AOTA) Occupational Profile [] and the Patient-Specific Functional Scale [] and (2) metacognitive strategy training based on the Cognitive Orientation to Daily Occupational Performance approach [] (B). Therapists encourage participants to use the “Goal-Plan-Do-Check” global cognitive strategy as a framework to plan, perform, and evaluate task performance. These elements require cognitive flexibility, self-monitoring, problem-solving, and sustained attention. Thus, the COG “primer” was intentionally designed to bolster functional cognition so participants could more effectively engage in the OT program. Specifically, COG session content focuses on learning and applying attention, organization, memory, and problem-solving strategies to facilitate performance of real-world tasks. Examples include planning a modified approach to challenging daily tasks, eliminating distractions to improve attention during functional activities, using reminders to implement learned strategies while completing activities, and engaging in a structured reflection process to self-analyze performance during the OT sessions.

Unlike conventional cognitive rehabilitation programs delivered over multiple weeks, we condensed the content into a brief format that was delivered using a titrated model to reduce participant burden and facilitate integration of cognitive strategies directly into OT. This design aimed to optimize generalization by first introducing strategies, then applying them during functional activities. Titration occurred across three phases (A): (1) individualized cognitive strategy instruction (sessions 1-4), (2) brief review and application of strategies within activity-based OT (sessions 5-10), and (3) continued integration of strategies into OT to promote generalization and habit formation (sessions 11-13). Personalized homework assigned at each session supported skill generalization to home and community environments.

COG materials were adapted from the 8-week Motivationally Enhanced Compensatory Cognitive Training for Mild Cognitive Impairmentprogram (M Huckans, et al; Motivationally Enhanced Compensatory Cognitive Training for Mild Cognitive Impairment [ME-CCT for MCI]; unpublished treatment manual; 2013), an iteration of evidence-based Compensatory Cognitive Training and Cognitive Symptom Management and Rehabilitation Therapy (EW Twamley, et al; Cognitive Symptom Management and Rehabilitation Therapy [CogSMART] for Traumatic Brain Injury; unpublished treatment manual; 2010). Materials for ME-CCT/CogSMART are available on the CogSMART website [] and were adapted with permission for research use and acknowledgment of the original sources. These interventions emphasize compensatory cognitive strategies and habit learning and have been delivered via telehealth in prior research studies and clinical care settings [-]. Study team members (occupational therapists [PF, SG, JL, KR, MLW] and a neuropsychologist [SA]) reviewed the ME-CCT manual, selected stroke-relevant content, and condensed it into four 1-hour sessions (B). Intervention delivery was designed to be individualized in terms of time spent on each cognitive strategy (based on relevance), focus on improving vs optimizing skills (based on impairment level), and application to activities/settings (based on context and goals).

The intervention was developed by a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team with expertise in cognitive rehabilitation and stroke telerehabilitation, including a clinical neuropsychologist (SA), occupational therapists (PF, SG, JL, KR, MLW), a clinical psychologist (LMM), and a speech-language pathologist (DSB). The neuropsychologist led development of the COG component, including strategy selection and adaptation (SA in consultation with EWT), while the OT team led integration of cognitive strategies into the existing activity-based telerehabilitation program. The speech-language pathologist guided adaptation of patient-facing materials to accommodate individuals with mild-to-moderate aphasia.

The intervention development process resulted in COG+OT, an 8-week, 13-session telerehabilitation program delivered across three phases: (1) cognitive strategy training (sessions 1-4), (2) guided application of cognitive strategies within activity-based OT (sessions 5-10), and (3) continued integration and generalization of strategies during OT sessions (sessions 11-13; ). The completed TIDieR-Rehab checklist [] for the COG+OT intervention is reported in , and details are provided in the following sections.

COG+OT is designed to be delivered by licensed occupational therapists with training in stroke rehabilitation and telehealth. In this implementation, therapists were experienced in both domains and received structured training in the COG component and its integration with the OT program as well as ongoing supervision via weekly group case consultation with lead clinicians (SA, MLW).

COG+OT is designed for delivery via synchronous telehealth using a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)–compliant videoconferencing platform (in this study, doxy.me), enabling participation from home and community environments. This intervention uses participants’ real-world contexts by incorporating personally meaningful activities and readily available household spaces and materials into therapy sessions. Therapists ensure camera positioning to allow clear visibility of movements and task performance. Assistance and training with the videoconferencing technology is provided as needed. When appropriate, caregivers may assist with technology setup or safety monitoring. This home-based delivery model is intended to enhance ecological validity, accessibility, and generalization of cognitive and motor strategies to everyday activities.

The COG+OT intervention is intended for adults with subacute and chronic stroke experiencing upper-extremity motor impairment and co-occurring cognitive challenges who are able to participate in telehealth-based rehabilitation. The COG+OT model is intended to be broadly applicable to stroke survivors who would benefit from integrated cognitive and activity-based rehabilitation and is therefore applicable to individuals with mild-to-moderate cognitive deficits in various domains (eg, attention, memory, executive function). The intervention is also designed to accommodate individuals with mild-to-moderate aphasia through the use of adapted, “aphasia-friendly” materials [,] and multimodal communication supports (developed in consultation with the speech-language pathologist [DSB]). Consideration for safety (eg, fall risk) and the potential need for caregiver assistance are incorporated into intervention delivery.

At the pretreatment assessment visit, therapists complete an AOTA Occupational Profile [] via semistructured interview to identify participants’ occupational history, patterns of daily living, values, and participation priorities. Insights obtained through the occupational profile are used to inform individualized goal setting and intervention planning. As participants complete the 4 initial COG sessions, the occupational profile is used to guide collaborative conversations to help the therapist gain a deeper understanding of participants’ routines, habits, and roles in relation to their cognitive functioning.

At the pretreatment assessment visit, therapists administer the Patient Specific Functional Scale [] to identify each participant’s activity goals. Participants are asked to generate up to 5 meaningful activities that have been made difficult due to upper extremity motor impairment since having a stroke. Participants then rate their ability to perform each activity on a 0‐10 scale, with higher numbers indicating better self-perceived performance. Throughout the OT program, sessions focus on optimizing participant performance in the context of these goals. Therapists regularly reference and revisit the goals with the participant when identifying target activities for the treatment sessions. This scale is readministered at the posttreatment assessment to assess change in self-perceived performance of individualized activity goals.

Prior to beginning the phase-2 COG+OT sessions (at the end of session 4), the participant’s hemiparetic arm/hand impairment is measured using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Upper Extremity [], which is the gold-standard assessment of poststroke arm/hand motor impairment. In prior work, we modified this measure for use in telerehabilitation [], reducing it to 22 items that can be assessed virtually. Administration involves the therapist observing the participant’s performance of 22 movements (ie, moving the hemiparetic arm/hand through a series of postures), rating each on a 3-point scale (0=unable to perform, 1=partially performed, 2=near normal performance). Items are summed to a total score between 0-44 points, with lower scores indicating more severe motor impairment. Using a procedure described in detail previously [], the participant’s Fugl-Meyer item performance ratings are mapped onto an item hierarchy (ranging from easy to difficult) to indicate person-specific arm/hand movements that are optimally challenging targets for task practice therapy. This process, termed “keyform recovery mapping” (or “recovery ruler”) [], is an emerging evidence-based method that operationalizes how item difficulty and performance are used to select individualized treatment targets. To monitor progress and refine individualized movement targets, the Fugl-Meyer Assessment is readministered and mapped to the keyform at the intervention midpoint (end of session 7) and at the end of phase-2 COG+OT sessions (end of session 10). To evaluate change in motor function, it is administered again at the posttreatment assessment.

Therapists document session activities and participant progress using study-developed Session Tracking Notes in REDCap. The notes differ slightly in structure across the 3 intervention phases, but each session’s note contains the following content: (1) Subjective (participant report and direct quotes), (2) Objective Session Content (checklist of completed content, documentation of functional task practice activities, and notes on activity grading per therapist report), (3) Assessment (checklists capturing therapists’ ratings of participant response to the intervention and barriers to progress), and (4) Notes/Follow-Up Plan, including assigned home activity program (therapist narrative). The narrative portions of the Subjective, Assessment, and Plan sections reflect best-practice rehabilitation documentation procedures.

A manual was developed to guide therapists during COG sessions (sessions 1-4). The manual outlines session procedures and content to be covered, provides examples that could be shared with participants, and includes guidance for adjusting the complexity of information to support participant comprehension in the presence of cognitive and/or language impairment.

For each COG session, we created 1‐2-page patient-facing worksheets, written at an eighth-grade reading level, that can be screen-shared, mailed, and/or emailed to the participant to guide discussion. Each session’s worksheet contains (1) an introduction section that included descriptions of core concepts, definitions of key terms, and educational content followed by (2) a “Let’s Practice” section containing real-life examples, space for self-reflection, and discussion prompts focused on functional application of cognitive strategies. Participants (and/or caregivers when present) are encouraged to take notes and regularly reference the worksheets outside of sessions.

The intervention consists of 13 one-on-one telehealth sessions (45‐60 minutes each) over 8 weeks (A). The schedule is 2 sessions per week for the first 5 weeks, followed by 1 session per week for the final 3 weeks. The reduction in session frequency during the latter phase is intended to promote greater independence and encourage skill generalization and transfer to real-world activities. To accommodate participant scheduling challenges, we allow make-up sessions to be added to any intervention week and for sessions to extend into one additional week (9 weeks total), if needed. The approximate proportion of each session allocated to COG vs OT activities varies over the 3 phases of the intervention (described in the following sections).

Each COG session focuses on specific topics, listed in B. Although the COG content follows a structured sequence, it is intentionally flexible to allow therapists to individualize the emphasis based on participant needs (eg, relevance, interest). Similarly, the use of cognitive strategies to compensate for deficits vs optimize intact abilities is personalized based on cognitive impairment level and contextual demands. Using the patient-facing worksheets via screensharing, therapists first introduce the session topic and review the associated compensatory strategies. The therapist and participant then collaboratively identify which strategies are most relevant to the participant’s goals and cognitive challenges. Remaining session time focuses on practicing these strategies and discussing how they might be applied in daily activities. Personalized homework is assigned to reinforce real-world use of cognitive strategies and is reviewed with the therapist at the beginning of each following session. Throughout these sessions, therapists make note of strategies that emerge as most relevant or useful for each participant. Additional worksheets covering topics beyond the core sessions (eg, calendar use, additional memory strategies) are available and may be incorporated when relevant and if time permits. No new strategies are introduced after session 4.

Each session begins with a brief review of the participant’s use of learned cognitive strategies in their daily lives (10-15 minutes). The remainder of the session focuses on direct application of the strategies during OT activities. During the first COG+OT session (session 5), the telerehabilitation version of the Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Upper Extremity keyform (described in Intervention Materials) is completed, and the therapist and participant review item performance scores to identify optimally challenging hemiparetic upper extremity movements to target in therapy. Together with the participant’s goals from the Patient Specific Functional Scale and Occupational Profile, this information guides selection of meaningful in-home activities. Participants then practice these activities while being coached by the therapist using metacognitive strategy training and guided discovery based on the Cognitive Orientation to Daily Occupational Performance approach [] (B). Therapists use the “Goal-Plan-Do-Check” global cognitive strategy as a framework (ie, participants identify the task “goal,” verbalize the “plan” to achieve the goal, attempt to “do” the task, and then self-reflect to “check” their own overall performance) while encouraging the participant to apply relevant cognitive strategies to support task completion. See  for an example session.

Cognitive strategies are no longer explicitly reviewed during these sessions, but participants are encouraged to continue applying the strategies during OT functional task practice (using the same procedures as sessions 5‐10). For example, a participant who had identified self-talk as a helpful strategy in earlier sessions would be coached to verbalize task steps during OT functional task practice to enhance attention and performance (see ). Therapists reinforce effective cognitive strategy use during target activities and facilitate generalization of new cognitive and motor skills to home and community contexts.

Multiple procedures are implemented to support consistent delivery of the intervention. All therapists receive training in both the COG component from the study neuropsychologist (SA) and in the OT program from the lead occupational therapist (MLW). A treatment manual was developed to standardize procedures, and standardized session workflows are used to guide intervention delivery and promote consistency across therapists. Intervention session activities and participant progress are documented using Session Tracking Notes (described in Intervention Materials) within a secure data management platform (ie, REDCap). These data are used to track progress and guide subsequent sessions. Protocol deviations, barriers to progress, and adverse events are systematically recorded in REDCap and reviewed. If the planned content is not fully covered in the allotted time or when additional practice is needed, this is noted in REDCap and addressed in subsequent sessions to ensure each participant is exposed to all the core material.

We developed COG+OT, a theory-informed intervention that integrates brief, functional cognitive rehabilitation into activity-based stroke telerehabilitation. This work addresses the well-documented challenge in poststroke care of siloed services for cognitive vs motor rehabilitation and lack of a well-defined multidisciplinary intervention protocol, which limits opportunities to apply cognitive strategies to meaningful activities and contexts. By embedding cognitive strategy training within meaningful, goal-directed activities, COG+OT is intended to support both engagement in rehabilitation and transfer of skills to everyday life.

An innovative design feature is the titrated integration of cognitive and motor components across 3 phases. The initial “primer” phase introduces compensatory cognitive strategies in a structured but individualized format, allowing participants to develop awareness and understanding of their cognitive challenges and strategies for addressing them. This is followed by guided application of these strategies within activity-based OT sessions and then continued integration to promote skill generalization into daily activities to form routines and habits. This progression aligns with contemporary models of functional cognitive rehabilitation, which emphasize metacognitive strategy training, contextualized practice, and repeated application across settings to facilitate generalization to real-world activities [,].

The use of a brief cognitive “primer” is intended to reduce burden while retaining core elements of evidence-based compensatory approaches, including personalization and strategy use in everyday contexts. Crucially, the COG sessions make cognitive strategies explicit for participants, complementing the implicit use of these strategies within the therapists’ metacognition-based coaching. For example, therapists may introduce visual imagery during COG sessions as a strategy for planning and organization, then prompt participants to visualize each step of a task during OT sessions to support more accurate and efficient motor performance. Although the COG component draws from evidence-based materials (ie, ME-CCT/CogSMART), there are several other established cognitive rehabilitation programs that could have been considered. Approaches such as the Multicontext Approach, Goal Management Training, and other functional cognitive interventions [,,] also include theoretically grounded elements (eg, metacognitive strategy training, guided practice, contextualized transfer) that may further strengthen components of COG+OT. Future iterations of the intervention may therefore benefit from selectively integrating features from these programs, particularly those that support generalization. In addition, explicit incorporation of motivational interviewing techniques may further enhance engagement, goal alignment, and sustained strategy use in daily life.

COG+OT was designed for real-world implementation through its telehealth delivery and use of participants’ home environments to enhance ecological validity. Structured yet flexible materials support intervention fidelity while allowing for individualized tailoring. Additional features, including patient-facing worksheets, aphasia-friendly materials, and optional caregiver involvement increase inclusivity and make COG+OT amenable to implementation in a variety of settings (eg, outpatient clinics, community-based rehabilitation, hybrid telehealth models). Moreover, because compensatory cognitive strategies and metacognitive training are relevant across many neurologic and medical conditions, there is strong potential to adapt COG+OT for use in other populations (eg, individuals with traumatic brain injury, mild cognitive impairment, or other chronic conditions in which functional cognition supports daily participation) or clinical services (eg, speech therapy, physical therapy). Therefore, a key next step is to evaluate the feasibility, effectiveness, and implementation of COG+OT across diverse populations and settings. To support future dissemination, additional work is needed to develop standardized training and fidelity-monitoring procedures alongside evaluation of scalable delivery models and factors influencing real-world adoption.

Initial pilot testing supported the feasibility and acceptability of COG+OT telerehabilitation for stroke survivors, as reported previously []. The current manuscript extends that work by providing a detailed description of the intervention’s theoretical basis, structure, materials, and delivery procedures to support replication and ongoing research. Analyses are underway to examine preliminary effects on cognitive, psychosocial, and participation-related outcomes, while qualitative feedback from participants and therapists will inform continued refinement of the intervention. Although aphasia-friendly adaptations were incorporated into COG+OT, additional research including greater representation of people with aphasia will be needed to evaluate their appropriateness. Future studies will also examine the added value of integrating functional cognitive rehabilitation into activity-based telerehabilitation, informing the design of future randomized controlled efficacy trials.

This paper focused on the systematic specification of the COG+OT intervention, including its theoretical basis, structure, and delivery procedures. Overall, COG+OT provides a structured and adaptable model for integrating functional cognitive rehabilitation into stroke telerehabilitation. This development work lays the groundwork for future refinement, evaluation, and broader implementation of COG+OT as an evidence-based, manualized intervention.

psychology.title: Adapted Massed Exposure Therapy Enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (aMETEMP): A randomized, double-masked protocol adapted for Veterans Affairs healthcare system
psychology.abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) remains prevalent and disabling, especially among veterans, with a substantial proportion failing to achieve remission following first-line evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapies. 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is hypothesized to enhance psychotherapy outcomes through effects on fear extinction, cognitive flexibility, and emotional engagement, and is being studied as a promising augmentation strategy for PTSD psychotherapy. There is limited research combining MDMA with evidence-based PTSD treatment. MDMA-assisted psychotherapy trials to date have also been limited by lack of an active comparator and functional unmasking. We describe the methodology of an ongoing randomized, double-masked, pilot trial evaluating massed prolonged exposure (PE) therapy enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (aMETEMP), adapted for a U.S. Veterans Affairs outpatient setting. Up to 20 veterans with PTSD in the VA will receive a 6-8hr in-person MDMA dosing session (randomized dose 35 mg - 125 mg) integrated with a 3-week massed exposure protocol. The remaining visits are virtual and include PE sessions and sessions to prepare for and process the MDMA session (28-30hrs total over 11 visits), with the use of telehealth intended to improve access and ease patient burden. After treating the first 4 participants, who were fully informed of the trial design, we switched to using an incomplete disclosure strategy (not disclosing the number of treatment arms or specific possible doses) to further improve masking. Primary outcomes include PTSD severity using the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5, safety, feasibility, and masking success. Findings are intended to provide preliminary descriptive information regarding feasibility, safety/tolerability, masking integrity, and symptom-change signals for aMETEMP with incomplete disclosure in a large outpatient healthcare system.NCT06117306.
psychology.text:
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a chronic and debilitating psychiatric disorder, with estimated global lifetime rates of 3.9% in civilians , approximately 7% in U.S. veterans overall , and up to 20% in those exposed to combat . Left untreated, PTSD is associated with a cascade of challenges including increased psychiatric and medical comorbidities, interpersonal and occupational difficulties, suicide risk, and healthcare utilization , , , . While PTSD is considered a treatable condition, and trauma-focused psychotherapies recommended by clinical practice guidelines as first-line treatments are effective , , a substantial proportion of patients fail to achieve remission or discontinue treatment prematurely  and military populations demonstrate worse post-treatment PTSD remission rates compared to civilians . Therefore, novel augmentation strategies that can enhance first-line PTSD treatments are needed. Ideally, these treatment models would be accessible and implemented in large integrated health settings such as the Veterans Affairs (VA) healthcare system.

There is tremendous interest in the potential of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) to augment PTSD psychotherapy. Pharmacologically, MDMA promotes release, inhibits reuptake, and prolongs synaptic activity of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine, with the serotonergic effects believed to account for most of MDMA's subjective effects, while norepinephrine and dopamine effects are believed to account for most of MDMA's physiological effects , . The monoamine-releasing effects of MDMA lead to the release of downstream signaling molecules thought to be important for neuroplasticity, such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor, as well as hormones such as oxytocin and cortisol, that affect the emotional memory circuits relevant to PTSD and fear extinction . Extinction learning has been found to be better retained when enhanced with MDMA . Psychologically, MDMA has been reported to enhance feelings of trust and emotional openness and may increase capacity to engage with painful trauma-related material with greater emotional tolerance, all of which are important factors for facilitating trauma processing , . Further, preclinical research suggests MDMA may induce a 2-week “neuroplastic window” of heightened learning and emotional flexibility . Together, these findings provide a rationale for studying whether MDMA, when combined with psychotherapy, may enhance trauma-related processing while reducing avoidance and emotional overwhelm, especially during massed treatment in which therapy is completed over several weeks rather than several months.

While two Phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (MDMA-AT) have demonstrated large reductions in PTSD symptoms , , several limitations constrain interpretation and future clinical implementation. First, the lack of an active comparator and the presence of significant functional unmasking in these studies are major concerns, as 90% of all participants from the first Phase 3 trial correctly guessed treatment assignment , while 75% of participants in the control group and 94.2% of participants in the MDMA group in the second Phase 3 trial correctly guessed treatment assignment , , potentially inflating treatment effects . Functional unmasking, combined with high treatment expectancy in these studies  and across MDMA and psychedelic studies more broadly, raises concerns about the ability to make causal inferences. Second, while the ‘psychotherapy only’ control arm of the Phase 3 trials demonstrated a large effect size for PTSD symptom reduction and had been manualized and refined over more than two decades , the ‘inner-directed therapy’ modality  was built around the MDMA experience and lacked prior evidence as a standalone treatment for PTSD (without MDMA) and had not been directly compared to standard PTSD therapies. Furthermore, the Phase 3 protocols involved three day-long dosing sessions and twelve non-dosing therapy sessions, requiring extensive therapist time and limiting scalability and accessibility. Finally, while one Phase 2 trial involved veteran participants outside of the VA , participants in the Phase 3 studies were primarily non-veteran, White, non-Hispanic women with a history of developmental trauma. The ability to generalize these findings to the veteran population seeking care within the VA healthcare system remains unclear.

In addition to the limitations of the Phase 3 trials, there is still uncertainty surrounding the most efficacious dosage of MDMA based on the wide range of dosages tested in previous MDMA trials overall, in which doses of 25 mg - 40 mg were used for active placebo comparator conditions vs. doses of 50 mg - 180 mg for the active therapeutic dose . Using a range of possible MDMA doses as active comparators may therefore address the critical need for improved masking in MDMA trials and the need to explore different possible doses for efficacy. Three prior Phase 2 trials of MDMA-AT compared various doses of MDMA with the goal of improving masking; relative to the high level of correct guessing in the Phase 3 trials that included inactive placebo, accuracy was lower when different doses of MDMA were used , , . The correct guess rate for participants in these trials ranged from 46% to 73%. While there is no accepted threshold for a successfully masked trial in the field of psychopharmacology, it has been suggested that a correct guess rate below 70% would indicate an adequately masked trial, a threshold that these low-dose controlled MDMA trials approached . Rater masking also appeared to be potentially improved in these trials relative to the inactive placebo trials , suggesting that a truly double-masked MDMA study is possible through the use of low-dose controls.

Massed Exposure Therapy Enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (METEMP; ) is a novel model that integrates the ‘inner-directed therapy’ approach ,  and prolonged exposure (PE) on dosing day, but uses a single MDMA dose paired with two weeks of massed exposure therapy completed during an intensive outpatient program. METEMP leverages translational evidence supporting MDMA's role in facilitating fear extinction  and utilizes an established, broadly disseminated, first-line PTSD therapy, PE, delivered in a massed format to capitalize on the putative “neuroplastic window” following MDMA administration. Preliminary open-label data from METEMP support further study, while requiring confirmation in controlled trials .

The present protocol, aMETEMP, is a version of METEMP that has been adapted for implementation in an outpatient integrative health care setting. The psychotherapy and integration are delivered via telehealth through multiple sessions per week over three weeks (instead of daily sessions over two weeks) in order to increase feasibility within the broader VA healthcare system. aMETEMP is designed to build on evidence supporting outpatient massed PE  and telehealth for the delivery of PTSD treatment within the VA . aMETEMP has the potential to enhance efficiency, increase scalability and accessibility, reduce patient, provider, and system burden, and inform future research on whether and how MDMA-assisted therapy models could be evaluated within large healthcare systems, if supported by future evidence and regulatory decisions.

Importantly, our study design incorporates an incomplete disclosure strategy  in which participants are informed that they will receive a dose of MDMA anywhere between 35 mg and 125 mg. They are not told the specific number of arms in the trial or the specific dosages within this range that will be provided. This study design may inform future large-scale MDMA and psychedelic research by including active comparators, strategies to improve masking, and rigorous assessment of treatment expectation.

This study is a randomized, double-masked pilot trial evaluating aMETEMP in up to 20 veterans in a VA outpatient healthcare setting. After giving informed consent and being deemed eligible for participation, veterans meeting DSM-5 criteria for PTSD  are randomized to receive a dose of MDMA (between 35 mg and 125 mg) during a single MDMA session integrated with a 3-week massed PE protocol that includes sessions to prepare for and process the MDMA sessions, and 12 exposure sessions (see ). The primary aims are to evaluate feasibility, characterize safety/tolerability, assess masking integrity, and generate preliminary descriptive estimates of symptom change with assessments at baseline, post-treatment (1-3 weeks after the last PE session; primary endpoint), and 2- and 4-month follow-up. Randomization is conducted by the research pharmacy using concealed allocation procedures.

To mitigate attrition, we inform participants that they may be offered an open-label MDMA session and up to three additional integration sessions that would take place after their primary study treatment, depending on the dose to which they are initially randomized. At each participant's 2-month follow-up, they and their treatment providers are unmasked to the dose they were randomized to during treatment. This is done at the 2-month follow-up to ensure retention at the early pilot phase. Depending on the dose they previously received, they may be given the option to complete the additional sessions within 30 days of their 2-month follow-up.

In clinical trials, participants’ beliefs and expectations about the intervention being investigated can impact how well they respond to the intervention; people believing that they will improve tend to have better outcomes than those who believe they will not improve , , . While this phenomenon is not unique to MDMA-AT trials, the recent increase in media coverage promoting the effectiveness of psychedelic-assisted therapy makes assessing and controlling for treatment expectations especially important in these studies. Therefore, treatment expectancy is assessed using the Stanford Expectations of Treatment Scale (SETS; ) at three timepoints: baseline assessment, at the end of the MDMA preparation session, and at the start of the optional open-label MDMA session (if applicable).

The possibility of confounding effects related to treatment expectations is increased if participants believe they know the treatment condition they are assigned to; therefore, it is crucial to take steps to prevent functional unmasking to treatment condition. In this study, participants, therapists, project coordinators, research assistants, and assessors are all masked to MDMA dose received during treatment, and participants are also masked to the number of possible arms and the exact dosages that are possible within those arms. Participants and study staff are only unmasked at each participant's 2-month follow-up assessment (not including the CAPS-5 assessors, who remain masked at each timepoint). Masking checks of both the participants and the therapists are administered at the end of the MDMA session, the post-treatment assessment, and the 2-month follow-up assessment.

To optimize rigor, mitigate expectancy bias, and improve integrity of masking compared to placebo-only designs , the study uses an incomplete disclosure strategy described in Matvey and colleagues . Initially, 4 participants were informed of the specific MDMA doses that they could be randomized to; however, preliminary qualitative data revealed that participants' pre-existing beliefs about having a “profound psychedelic experience,” paired with knowledge of the potential treatment arms, were likely impacting their treatment expectations. Following the 4th participant's study completion, we shifted to using the incomplete disclosure strategy in an effort to better mitigate expectancy bias. Participants are now informed that they will receive a dose of MDMA that could be anywhere between 35 mg and 125 mg, but are not told the exact number of treatment arms nor the exact possible doses. This incomplete disclosure strategy decreases the amount of information about the study design provided to participants in order to decrease their ability to guess their assignment. This strategy also has the potential to reduce nocebo effects, as participants are all aware that they are receiving a dose of MDMA, rather than an “active” or “inactive” treatment, paired with a front-line evidence-based therapy for PTSD. In line with ethical standards for the use of incomplete disclosure, risks associated with each treatment arm are still disclosed during the informed consent process, and all participants undergo full debriefing at the 2-month follow-up. This includes disclosure of the study design and masking approach, and an opportunity to ask questions about their participation.

The actual MDMA dose each subject received will be compared to participant responses on the masking check questionnaire (see ) to assess masking integrity qualitatively. It will also be compared with provider guesses as to treatment dose received, although providers are not masked to the trial design and so are aware of the exact potential doses the participants could have received.

The masking checks were designed to collect information on participants' and providers’ beliefs about treatment without inadvertently reinforcing treatment expectations.
