Each masking check asks the participant/provider to make a guess about the dose received, their confidence in that guess on a 5-point Likert scale (“Not at all confident” to “Completely confident”), and their reasoning. The first masking check (see ) is administered at the end of the MDMA session and asks participants to guess what dose they received on a scale from 35 mg to 125mg. This same masking check is administered to participants at their post-treatment assessment. The final masking check is done at the 2-month follow-up assessment. Participants are informed of the actual doses they could have received; with this additional information, we ask them to make a final guess about the dose they received along with their confidence in that guess, allowing us to capture a binary correct/incorrect datapoint. This strategy allows us to capture qualitative and quantitative masking data from participants and providers while not revealing the actual dose possibilities until after the primary assessment endpoint, minimizing the impact of treatment expectancy on outcomes.

The study is being conducted under an FDA Investigational New Drug application. MDMA is a Schedule I investigational product and is not approved by FDA for the treatment of PTSD. The protocol was approved by the VA San Diego Healthcare System Institutional Review Board (#H230116; Initial Approval: 9/12/2023), VA Research and Development Committee, Research Advisory Panel of California (RAP-C), and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

The aMETEMP intervention consists of 12 massed PE sessions (see ; ) delivered over approximately three weeks, all offered in person or virtually, except for PE sessions 3-4 (the MDMA session), which are in person. The initial session (PE sessions 1 & 2 combined into one 3.5-h visit) focuses on psychoeducation and development of a hierarchy list of in vivo exposures. The next visit is a 1.5-h MDMA preparatory session the business day prior to MDMA administration, in which participants are oriented to the MDMA session, provided with psychoeducation about MDMA, and given the space to ask questions about the MDMA session day. This psychoeducation emphasizes the variability in MDMA response, distinguishes MDMA from classic psychedelics, and tries to minimize specific expectations about the experience given that the subjective effects of MDMA can be influenced by a variety of biological, psychological, and environmental factors . During this session, in addition to continuing to build therapeutic alliance and trust, the therapists provide guidance on what to expect during the MDMA session, and how to respond to the memories and feelings that could arise during treatment.

The business day after the preparation session is a 6-8 h in-person MDMA + PE session that includes alternating periods of inner-directed focus and interaction with the therapists. Consistent with the METEMP protocol, two guided imaginal exposures related to the pre-identified index trauma are completed during the MDMA session (PE sessions 3 & 4). The next day includes a 3-h session that consists of the integration session and PE session 5. The integration sessions are participant-led, unstructured periods where participants are invited to share their experiences from the MDMA session and any trauma-related insights that occurred during or since the MDMA session . The remaining treatment visits are PE sessions 6-12. Consistent with traditional PE, imaginal exposures are conducted within these sessions and recorded, and participants complete assigned homework, including listening to recordings and engaging in vivo exposure assignments between sessions. Subjective Units of Distress are collected throughout sessions. Following the 2-month follow-up assessment, participants may be offered an optional additional MDMA session with up to 3 additional integration sessions, depending on the dose they received in their randomized session. PE sessions are delivered by a primary therapist, who is joined by a co-therapist for the preparation, MDMA, and integration sessions.

The MDMA sessions are intended to support trauma processing and may yield trauma-related content that can be explored both within the session and in subsequent integration and PE sessions. MDMA sessions occur in a private room at the VA San Diego Healthcare System that has been specially designed for MDMA-assisted psychotherapy research . This space is equipped with comfortable seating and access to nearby medical support if needed. The participant's urine drug toxicology screen and blood alcohol level are collected and confirmed to be negative the morning of the session. Temperature, blood pressure, and pulse are assessed and confirmed to be within protocol-defined acceptable ranges before, during, and at the end of the MDMA session, in consultation with a study physician who is on call for intervention if needed. Administration of MDMA occurs in the morning (9 a.m.) and the participant is required to stay on site (approx. 6-8hrs) and have planned transportation home with a prearranged driver after the session. The participant is encouraged to alternate between inner-directed exploration of emotional, cognitive, and somatic experiences , , optionally facilitated by eyeshades and curated music, and engagement with the therapists, which includes two imaginal exposures and subsequent processing. During the integration session that follows the day after the MDMA session(s) but also in subsequent PE sessions, participants may share insights or feelings related to their MDMA experience.

Therapists are doctoral-level clinicians with PTSD treatment experience and training in PE and MDMA-AT. Training includes completion of MDMA-AT training through Resilient Pharmaceuticals and Sunstone Therapies, as applicable. Sessions are audio and video recorded and reviewed for fidelity, with supervision by expert massed PE clinicians and an expert MDMA therapist, producing independent adherence ratings.

Participants are assessed at baseline, post-treatment, and 2- and 4-months after treatment. The primary clinical outcome is clinician-rated PTSD severity using the CAPS-5 . Secondary clinical outcomes include self-reported PTSD symptoms (PCL-5; ), depression (PHQ-9; ), sleep (PSQI; ) and other psychosocial measures (see ). Safety assessments include suicidality using the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS; ) and adverse event monitoring. Measures of treatment expectancy, satisfaction, and masking integrity are collected, along with qualitative interviews for additional feedback. Self-report surveys are completed in-person on paper or through VA REDCap surveys, depending on visit type and participant preference. The sample size of up to 20 participants is intended to evaluate feasibility and acceptability, characterize safety/tolerability, assess masking integrity, and generate preliminary descriptive estimates to inform a future randomized controlled trial. This preliminary study is not powered to detect statistically significant effects or differences between MDMA groups, so only descriptive statistics will be reported for primary and secondary outcomes without tests of within-subjects or between-group differences. Missing data will be handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) analyses and/or multiple imputation prior to analysis. Preliminary efficacy will be derived primarily from descriptive statistics for within-person change in primary and secondary outcomes from baseline to post-treatment, as well as maintenance of change from post-treatment through 2- and 4-month follow-up. Effect sizes will be calculated based on growth curve estimated slopes and/or model-implied estimated means and standard deviations at each assessment, using standardized mean change for within-group change (i.e., pooled standard deviations and a repeated-measures correction). Exploratory growth-curve analyses may be used to estimate the magnitude and trajectory of symptom change over time; these analyses will be interpreted descriptively given the pilot sample size. Nonlinear (e.g., quadratic or piecewise) slope parameters will be tested if appropriate based on visual inspection of the data.

Main analyses for the primary outcome (change in PTSD symptom total severity score assessed by CAPS-5) will compare dose groups using the modified intent-to-treat (mITT) sample of veteran participants who completed the MDMA session and had at least one follow-up CAPS-5 assessment. Analysis will be conducted following the final 4-month assessment at the conclusion of the study. Reliable and clinically significant change will be calculated for each participant using the method described by Jacobson and Truax , which uses sample-specific dispersion parameters and is considered best practice in clinical psychology. Sensitivity analyses will be conducted using the sample of participants who completed treatment.

Main and sensitivity analyses for all exploratory secondary outcomes (see ) will use the same methods as the primary outcome. Additionally, moderation analyses will explore whether the presence of secondary traumatic stressors (as assessed by the Life Events Checklist for DSM-5 ) and/or adverse childhood experiences (as assessed by the Adverse Childhood Experiences  scale) moderate the degree of improvement in CAPS-5 PTSD severity scores during the study.

Veterans with PTSD continue to face high rates of non-remission and dropout from first-line therapies. While MDMA-AT holds promise, trials to date have been limited by functional unmasking, lack of active comparators, and protocols that are difficult to scale. aMETEMP is designed to address several of these limitations. We adapted the previously developed METEMP model into a practical outpatient protocol for the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) that combines a single MDMA dose with three weeks of telehealth or in-person delivered massed PE, a gold standard PTSD therapy. Given that 90–94% of participants in Phase 3 MDMA-AT trials correctly guessed treatment assignment, this protocol uses a range of MDMA doses plus an incomplete disclosure strategy to improve masking. This approach has already shown improved masking in prior dose-response MDMA-AT trials and may improve interpretability relative to designs using inert placebo, although causal conclusions will remain limited by the pilot sample size and study design.

Designed for real-world VHA implementation, aMETEMP sessions are primarily delivered via telehealth, reducing burden and increasing access. Our goal is to generate data that will inform future large scale clinical trials designed to address key concerns about MDMA-AT raised by the FDA  and VA ,  regarding masking, scalability, and using an evidence-based trauma-focused therapy approach. Notably, the protocol's use of a range of MDMA doses as active comparators, coupled with an incomplete disclosure strategy, represents a methodological advancement to address the persistent issue of functional unmasking across psychedelic research. This design aims to enhance the credibility of the masking process, as preliminary findings from prior studies suggest that masking is more effective when using lower doses of MDMA comparators rather than inert placebo , , , . Building on these findings, our protocol integrates comprehensive psychoeducation and an intentional incomplete disclosure approach to further minimize expectancy effects and better characterize treatment effects and expectancy-related influences in future research.

A potential critique of this approach is that lower doses of MDMA may still provide some therapeutic benefit for PTSD. This pilot may provide preliminary descriptive signals regarding symptom change, tolerability, subjective experience, and masking across different MDMA doses, inform optimal selections for both active and control conditions, assess subjective experiences related to treatment response and unmasking, and evaluate strategies to mitigate expectancy effects. Additionally, these data will help refine trial design elements important for regulatory and clinical acceptance, potentially informing the design of future trials evaluating MDMA as an augmentation strategy for evidence-based PTSD psychotherapy.

This pilot protocol has several limitations. The study is not powered to detect statistically significant within- or between-dose effects, and efficacy-related findings will be interpreted descriptively. The disclosure strategy was modified after the first four participants, which may affect expectancy and masking outcomes. Accordingly, masking and expectancy findings will be interpreted in light of potential differences between participants enrolled before and after this change. Although active-dose comparators and incomplete disclosure are intended to improve masking, functional unmasking and expectancy effects may still influence participant and clinician-reported outcomes. Finally, the sample is limited to veterans receiving care within one VA healthcare system, which may limit generalizability. Similarly, a limitation of this study and other MDMA trials is the set of exclusion criteria, which limit participation to only some veterans with PTSD, e.g., those who have not been suicidal in the past 6 months and who are able to safely taper off medications. Further studies should be designed to determine whether more relaxed exclusion criteria could be implemented safely, including research specifically investigating the interaction of MDMA with other psychiatric medications.

Given the use of incomplete disclosure as a masking strategy, we recognize the ethical imperative to prioritize participant autonomy and informed choice throughout the protocol. Due to the consciousness-altering effects of these substances, ensuring ethically appropriate informed consent is especially salient in research involving MDMA or other psychedelics, particularly when an IRB-approved incomplete disclosure strategy is used. To address this, the aMETEMP protocol emphasizes clear communication about the voluntary nature of all exposure-related activities and ensures that participants retain control over the pacing, intensity, and continuation of such interventions. Study therapists are trained to continually assess participants’ comfort and willingness to proceed, providing multiple opportunities to reaffirm consent before and during dosing sessions. By reinforcing participant agency in this manner, we aim to balance methodological rigor in masking with respect for the autonomy, rights, and well-being of our participants.

Overall, the aMETEMP model is designed with the unique needs of large health care systems like VA in mind, including feasibility and scaling, should FDA approve an MDMA-containing therapy for the treatment of PTSD in the future. The majority of participant visits are virtual, and the use of telehealth is a novel contribution that increases implementation feasibility of the protocol. Findings from this pilot may inform the design of future multi-site trials and, if supported by future evidence and regulatory decisions, implementation considerations.

psychology.title: Interpersonal Synchrony During a Client–Therapist Role‐Play Interaction: The Role of Modalities, Facets, and Relational Context
psychology.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony (IS), the temporal coordination between individuals during interaction, is a complex phenomenon that manifests across different modalities (e.g., behavioral and physiological) and coordination facets (e.g., strength and flexibility). In psychotherapy, IS is increasingly considered a potential embodied marker of the client–therapist relationship. However, little is known about how relational context shapes IS coordination patterns, or how they relate to perceived relationship quality. This study aimed to identify IS coordination patterns associated with two relational contexts (emotion‐focused vs. solution‐focused conversations) and to examine how these patterns relate to subjective perceptions of the client–therapist relationship. 168 psychology students (84 dyads) participated in two consecutive 13‐min client–therapist role‐play conversations with different goals: exploring emotions (emotion‐focused) and brainstorming solutions (solution‐focused). Windowed Cross‐Lagged Correlation was used to quantify IS from upper‐body movement (using Motion Energy Analysis), high‐frequency heart rate variability, and electrodermal activity (average and slope). For each modality, six IS facets were extracted, representing three facet families: strength, flexibility, and leading–following dynamics. IS was above chance level across all modalities and facets in both conditions (ds ≈0.26–1.09). Although the context manipulation was effective at a subjective level, no condition differences in IS were observed after correction for multiple testing. Analyses accounting for dyads' interaction history (i.e., sequence of conditions) revealed context‐dependent effects in two modalities: movement strength and EDASlope leading–following dominance. Both modalities were also related with the perceived emotional bond, but not with perceived collaboration, and these associations varied as a function of relational context. These findings suggest that contextual factors, including conversation goals and dyadic history shape coordination dynamics. Implications for modality and facet selection, and context manipulation in IS research are discussed.
psychology.text:
Interpersonal synchrony (IS), the moment‐to‐moment temporal coordination between individuals during social interaction, has received increasing attention across a range of research fields. Examples include developmental psychology (Birk et al. ; Feldman ), research on romantic partners (Coutinho et al. ; Timmons et al. ), joint action research (van der Wel et al. ), relational neuroscience (De Felice et al. ; Levy et al. ), teamwork (Mayo et al. ; Palumbo et al. ; Wiltshire et al. ), and psychotherapy (Kleinbub ; Nyman‐salonen and Kykyri ; Ramseyer and Tschacher ; Wiltshire et al. ). Despite the large body of work linking IS to prosocial and relational processes (for reviews, e.g., daSilva and Wood ; Hu et al. ), understanding its underlying mechanisms and its relation to perceived relationship quality remains challenging. One reason for this is that IS is inherently a multimodal and multifaceted emergent phenomenon (Kelso ; Nowak et al. ; Vial and Cornejo ). During social interactions, individuals coordinate across multiple bodily modalities (e.g., movement and physiology), and the way this coordination unfolds over time manifests in different forms or dynamic facets (e.g., interaction partners may move in and out of IS or alternate in leading and following roles). A further challenge lies in the context‐dependent nature of IS (Gordon et al. ; Gordon and Bartsch ; Scheidt et al. ). As an emergent phenomenon, IS patterns observed at any given moment are shaped by the context (e.g., goals and histories of the interaction partners), which constrains and organizes social interactions by defining what is required and what is possible in that moment (Juarrero ). The role of modalities, facets, and context in understanding IS, is particularly evident in psychotherapy research, where IS has been extensively studied as a potential marker of the perceived quality of the client–therapist relationship or working alliance (WA; Atzil‐slonim et al. ; Koole and Tschacher ; Wiltshire et al. ). The WA consists of an emotional bond component and a collaborative component involving agreement on treatment goals and tasks (Wampold and Flückiger ) and is consistently found to be a strong predictor of treatment outcomes (Flückiger et al. ; Horvath et al. ). WA has most commonly been assessed in relation to IS using the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI), or one of its validated short forms (e.g., Cohen et al. ; Reich et al. ; Tal et al. ; Bar‐Kalifa et al. ), although some studies have used alternative methods such as the Bern Post Session Report (BPSR) (e.g., Ramseyer and Tschacher , ). Despite being heavily studied, the observed relation between IS and WA remains inconsistent: Some studies report positive associations (Cohen et al. ; Ramseyer and Tschacher ), others negative (Reich et al. ), and some no relation at all (Ramseyer ). In the following subsections, we argue that accounting for modalities, facets, and context could help explain these inconsistencies in IS research.

Social interaction can be conceptualized as a dynamic complex system in which not only individuals interact but also multiple bodily modalities within and between individuals continuously interact and coordinate (Gelo and Salvatore ; Mayo and Gordon ). Movement IS, or the coordination of nonverbal behaviors between individuals, has been the most extensively studied modality, largely due to advances in motion‐tracking technologies, which enable accessible and noninvasive quantification of body movement from video recordings (Fujiwara and Yokomitsu ; Kleinbub and Ramseyer ; Ramseyer ). Despite many studies, the functional meaning of movement IS remains not fully understood. Early work on nonverbal mirroring and behavioral matching has linked movement IS to embodied rapport and social affiliation (Hove and Risen ; Vacharkulksemsuk and Fredrickson ). In psychotherapy research, IS of different body parts has been linked to different therapeutic outcomes: IS in upper‐body movements has been shown to predict session‐level therapeutic success and WA ratings (BPSR) in an outpatient sample primarily comprising patients with anxiety and affective disorders, whereas head movement IS predicted longer term treatment outcomes (Ramseyer and Tschacher ).

Similarly, physiological IS, or the temporal alignment of physiological processes between individuals, has received increasing attention in the study of natural social interactions due to advances in wearable technologies. Physiological IS is commonly conceptualized in terms of coordination of the autonomic nervous system (ANS), with a distinction between modalities reflecting sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activity and those reflecting parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity (Denk et al. ). The SNS is primarily associated with increased physiological arousal, whereas the PNS is more associated with regulation (Shaffer et al. ). In psychophysiological research, electrodermal activity (EDA) is a well‐established marker of SNS activity (Boucsein et al. ; Posada‐Quintero and Chon ), while high‐frequency heart rate variability (HF‐HRV) is commonly used as an index of PNS activity (Shaffer et al. ; Shaffer and Ginsberg ). Importantly, emerging evidence suggests that IS in these different branches of the ANS may relate differently to interpersonal processes. For example, a recent review found that IS in SNS‐related measures (including EDA) was generally positively associated with relationship outcomes, whereas IS in PNS‐related measures (including HF‐HRV) showed negative associations with such outcomes (Mayo et al. ).

Although multimodal approaches are essential for capturing the full spectrum of embodied relational processes underlying the working alliance (Nyman‐salonen and Kykyri ), and social interaction more broadly, psychotherapy research shows a fragmented body of findings (Kleinbub ). For example, EDA IS between client and therapist has been linked to the emotional bond component of the working alliance (WAI), but not to its collaborative component, in clients with test anxiety (Bar‐Kalifa et al. ). One multimodal study further suggested that the relationship between movement IS and the WA (WAI) may be moderated by heart rate IS in a depressed client (Tal et al. ). Another multimodal study suggested EDA IS and movement IS to reflect distinct processes during couple therapy (Kykyri et al. ). Although these findings suggest that different modalities may index distinct relational processes, in the absence of a unifying theoretical framework (Kleinbub ), it remains difficult to synthesize meaningful conclusions about what different IS modalities represent or how they relate to client–therapist relational processes, particularly since all existing studies are observational in nature (Atzil‐slonim et al. ; Wiltshire et al. ), which limits causal inference.

An additional layer of complexity arises from the fact that even within a single modality, multiple facets or patterns of coordination can be observed. Most of the above‐mentioned psychotherapy studies have operationalized IS focusing on synchrony strength, the overall degree to which interaction partners' signals are aligned across a given episode, often the duration of an entire therapy session. However, methodological developments, particularly the use of windowed cross‐lagged correlation (WCLC) and peak‐picking algorithms, suggest that IS comprises multiple facets of coordination dynamics that may reflect different underlying functions (Moulder et al. ; Schoenherr et al. ). As a result, other facets have begun to receive increasing attention. One such facet is flexibility, referring to the extent to which interaction partners move in and out of synchrony over time (Gordon et al. ). Another interesting facet concerns leading–following dynamics, which captures who leads and who follows at a given moment in the interaction.

Taken together, WCLC allows for the distinction between at least three families of IS facets, strength, flexibility, and leading–following dynamics (Moulder et al. ), each of which may serve different functional roles within an interaction. Within each of these facet families, different indices can be extracted depending on how the time‐series data are analyzed. For instance, peak‐detection algorithms can be applied to identify moments of maximal and stable coordination (Boker et al. ; Moulder et al. ). Accordingly, some studies report peak‐based indices (e.g., peak strength), whereas others rely on global indices, such as the average strength of IS across all time points (Atzil‐slonim et al. ). A similar distinction applies to flexibility, which can be quantified either as a global measure (e.g., variability in IS over the whole‐time window; Gordon et al. ), or in terms of variability during peak moments (Moulder et al. ). In contrast, research on leading–following dynamics has primarily focused on directional dominance, or who tends to lead the interaction overall. However, an additional largely unexplored facet is the degree of switching between leading and following roles (Moulder et al. ), which may be particularly relevant in contexts where adaptive flexibility plays a central role.

Another pivotal step in understanding the role IS serves in relationships is to conceptualize it as an emergent phenomenon that is shaped within a relational context (Nowak et al. ). Multiple theoretical contributions have highlighted the importance of context when studying IS (Gordon et al. ; Gordon and Bartsch ; Scheidt et al. ). From a complex systems perspective, Juarrero () conceptualizes context as a dynamic web of constraints, in which multiple factors such as goals, histories, and situational conditions interact to shape which actions and interactions are possible in each moment. Within this framework, relational goals (e.g., collaborating to solve a problem) can be understood as higher level, context‐dependent constraints that organize how individuals coordinate with one another. These constraints do not dictate specific behaviors, but rather shape the space of possible coordination patterns, allowing certain forms of IS to emerge while constraining others (Juarrero ). This perspective aligns with the idea that changing task demands (e.g., goals) can give rise to different configurations of coordination dynamics (daSilva and Wood ; Fusaroli et al. ; Gordon et al. ). In other words, different relational goals may push dyads into different coordination configurations (i.e., affecting different facets or modalities) depending on what the dyads want to achieve.

Few psychotherapy studies investigated how patterns of IS differ across therapeutic contexts. For instance, in clients with test anxiety, the association between EDA IS and treatment outcomes appears to depend on the therapeutic context. Higher EDA IS was associated with higher client wellbeing during imagery rescripting segments, but not during cognitive‐behavioral segments (Prinz et al. ). In a later multimodal study using the same treatment protocol, lower EDA IS has been associated with greater symptom improvement during cognitive interventions, but not during emotion‐focused interventions, whereas the relationship between movement IS and symptom change did not differ between intervention types (Uhl et al. ). A group couple therapy study found EDA IS in therapist–therapist dyads but not in client–client dyads, while respiration IS did not show this pattern (Coutinho et al. ), suggesting that IS patterns are structured by interactional roles. The role of context is further illustrated in experimental studies from other domains showing, for example, that physiological IS varies systematically between competitive and cooperative tasks (Chanel et al. ; Yarmolovsky and Geva ). Taken together, these findings suggest that IS is not a uniform process and varies as a function of context‐specific constraints. However, studies investigating the effects of context on multimodal IS and relationship quality are scarce. Furthermore, because psychotherapy studies are primarily observational, they are limited in their ability to draw causal inferences about the role of context in shaping coordination dynamics, which likely contributes to inconsistent findings regarding the relationship between WA and IS. It remains difficult to integrate findings from multiple IS modalities, facets, and contextual influences within a unified experimental and theoretical framework. To address this gap, we designed a novel client–therapist role‐play interaction task in which we measured multimodal IS and WA while we experimentally manipulated the relational context.

In this study, we aimed to create relational contexts that map onto the core components of the WA (Wampold and Flückiger ): an emotional component (i.e., the emotional bond between client and therapist) and a collaborative component (i.e., collaboration and agreement on therapeutic goals and tasks). Accordingly, we designed two relational contexts in which a “client” and “therapist” discussed the client's problem, with distinct goals: an emotion‐focused context (goal: exploring emotions) and a solution‐focused context (goal: brainstorming about solutions). Video and physiology were recorded throughout both interactions to compute movement, EDA and HF‐HRV as well as the IS facets strength, flexibility, and leading‐following dynamics. To ensure the effectiveness of our manipulation, we first tested if the emotion‐focused condition elicited higher emotion exploration‐related outcomes and the solution‐focused condition higher collaboration‐related outcomes, and that there were no significant differences in the control variables perceived stress, difficulty, and problem significance between conditions. In addition, we expected and tested if genuine IS would be elicited in both conditions, resulting in higher observed IS in comparison to pseudosynchrony.

Subsequently, the first aim of this study was to identify markers (i.e., modalities and facets) of IS in the two relational contexts. Our hypotheses were grounded in a theoretical account of IS as a mechanism for integrating the self with the other during social interaction (Gordon et al. ; Heggli et al. ; Hoehl et al. ; Hu et al. ; Mayo and Gordon ). Within this framework, IS is thought to function by blurring the boundaries between self and other, thereby reducing interpersonal variability. For example, greater integration may be beneficial in contexts requiring high alignment (e.g., empathically listening to someone's emotional experience), whereas greater segregation may be advantageous in contexts requiring flexibility (e.g., generating novel ideas during problem‐solving). Based on this perspective, we hypothesized:Hypothesis 1
The emotion‐focused context would involve a greater need for dyadic integration, reflected in higher strength of physiological IS.

The emotion‐focused context would involve a greater need for dyadic integration, reflected in higher strength of physiological IS.

This expectation aligns with prior work linking physiological IS to empathic processes (Marci et al. ). In contrast, we hypothesized:Hypothesis 2
The solution‐focused context would involve greater dyadic segregation, reflected in higher IS flexibility across modalities.

The solution‐focused context would involve greater dyadic segregation, reflected in higher IS flexibility across modalities.

Consistent with theoretical accounts suggesting that flexibility supports the incorporation of novel, self‐generated contributions in collaborative interactions (Gordon et al. ; Wood et al. ). Furthermore, we hypothesized:Hypothesis 3
The emotion‐focused condition would be characterized by more client‐leading dynamics.
Hypothesis 4
The solution‐focused condition would show more therapist‐leading dynamics.

The emotion‐focused condition would be characterized by more client‐leading dynamics.

The solution‐focused condition would show more therapist‐leading dynamics.

This prediction was informed by psychotherapy theory. Client‐centered and emotion‐focused psychotherapy approaches emphasize therapist nondirectiveness and position the client as the primary driver of the therapeutic interaction (Rogers ). In contrast, cognitive‐behavioral approaches are more structured and place the therapist in a more directive role within the interaction (Kazantzis and Dobson ). Additionally, as brainstorming may require more rapid shifts in coordination, we expected:Hypothesis 5
Greater switching between leading and following dynamics in the solution‐focused condition.

Greater switching between leading and following dynamics in the solution‐focused condition.

The second aim of this study was to explore the relation between different IS markers and the two components of the WA across relational contexts. Building on prior work showing that physiological IS is more strongly associated with the emotional bond component of the WA in imagery‐based treatment contexts (Bar‐Kalifa et al. ), and evidence linking physiological IS to empathy (Marci et al. ), we hypothesized:Hypothesis 6
Greater physiological IS strength would be more strongly associated with the emotional bond component of the WA in the emotion‐focused condition.

Greater physiological IS strength would be more strongly associated with the emotional bond component of the WA in the emotion‐focused condition.

Conversely, we hypothesized:Hypothesis 7
Higher flexibility across modalities would be more strongly associated with the collaborative component and goal‐oriented component of the WA in the solution‐focused condition.

Higher flexibility across modalities would be more strongly associated with the collaborative component and goal‐oriented component of the WA in the solution‐focused condition.

It is consistent with the idea that flexible coordination supports collaborative, task‐focused engagement. All hypotheses were preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CE48Y).

In addition to these theoretical aims, this study directly addresses current methodological challenges in the quantification of IS by comparing multiple modalities and facets, and calculating different quantification metrics, within a unified experimental framework. This allows for a systematic evaluation of how different IS indices converge or diverge across relational contexts, thereby informing the selection of appropriate methods for specific experimental designs and data characteristics of IS. Accordingly, we conclude with methodological recommendations regarding the selection of IS modalities and facets, as well as the experimental manipulation of relational context.

Participants (N = 168) were recruited from the psychology and pedagogical sciences bachelor's (44% first year, 16% second year, 18% third year) and master's programs (22%) of the Radboud University in the Netherlands. Participants were paired in dyads based on three criteria: No existing bond (i.e., being unacquainted), same gender, and same language preference (English or Dutch). Choosing same‐gender dyads is common practice to reduce gender‐related variability (see for example, Ramseyer and Tschacher ; Tschacher et al. ), as previous research has shown that IS can differ as a function of dyad gender composition (Li et al. ). There were 16 male dyads, 67 female dyads, and 1 nonbinary dyad in the final sample (Age: M = 22, SD = 4.5). Out of these, 36% had the conversations in Dutch. Participants were compensated with either a 15 euros voucher or 1.5 course credits. The recruitment and data collection took place at the Behavioral Sciences Institute of the Radboud University. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Radboud Faculty of Social Sciences (ECSW‐2023‐088). This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/ce48y/overview), and deviations are reported in the  (Table ).

The WAI (Hatcher and Gillaspy ) for client and therapist were used both as a manipulation check (for the context manipulation) and as the primary outcome measure of perceived relationship quality. The short (12‐item version) was adapted following recommendations by Falkenström et al. () to tailor it for repeated measures and specific interactions: We changed the verb tense of items from present to past (e.g., “I believe my therapist liked me”), and the Likert‐scale ranged from 0 “not at all” to 5 “completely”. The average scores of the goal and task subscales (8 items) and the average score of the bond subscale (4 items) were used as collaboration and emotional bond measures, respectively. The collaboration component reflects the perceived agreement on goals and tasks, whereas the emotional bond reflects the perceived trust, acceptance, and mutual confidence between the client and therapist. Internal consistencies in the present sample were good: WAI collaboration (therapist α = 0.88; client α = 0.89), WAI bond (therapist α = 0.76; client α = 0.87).

The Empathic Understanding subscale was used as context manipulation check in two versions: Myself‐toward‐the‐Other for the therapist and Other‐toward‐Self for the client (Barrett‐Lennard ). Both subscales measure perceived therapist empathy. Each version consists of 12 items and was scored on a 5‐point Likert scale (0 “not at all” to 5 “completely”). In line with the WAI above, the verb tense of items was changed from present to past (e.g., “My therapist usually sensed or realized what I was feeling”). Internal consistencies in the present sample were good (therapist α = 0.75; client α = 0.88).

The FIS‐Empathy item and the FIS‐Collaboration item were also used to assess the context manipulation (Santos et al. ). These two items measure client's perceptions of the therapist's ability to empathize and collaborate, respectively. Each item is rated on a 5‐point Likert scale, ranging from poor skill demonstration (e.g., empathy: “My therapist offered no sense that he/she actually understood my experience, or even distorted my experience”) to ideal skill demonstration (e.g., empathy: “My therapist offered appropriate reflections demonstrating that he/she was not only listening but also had an exceptional understanding of what I was/am experiencing”).

The HSM‐Exploration subscale was used to assess emotion‐focus, and the HSM‐Action subscale to assess solution‐focus (Hill and Kellems ). The Exploration subscale contains four items that measure whether the therapist helped the client explore their feelings and thoughts. We adapted this subscale to focus on feelings only, by removing references to ‘thinking’ from the questions: “My therapist asked questions to help me explore what I was feeling”. Items were rated on a 6‐point Likert scale (1 “strongly disagree” to 6 “strongly agree”) with the instruction to use the option “strongly disagree” only for therapist behavior that did not occur in the past interaction. The Action subscale contains five items (all reverse coded) that measure collaboration on changing a problem (e.g., “My therapist did not help me think about changes I could make in my life”). The average score of each subscale was calculated. Internal consistencies were good (HSM‐Exploration α = 0.83; HSM‐Action α = 0.87).

Perceived difficulty and stress were measured as a manipulation check for both participants using two self‐constructed items (“How stressed were you?” and “How difficult was this conversation?”). In addition, the client was asked how significant the problem they shared was (“How important to you was the problem you shared?”). All three items were rated on a 10‐point Likert scale (0 “not at all” to 10 “extremely”).

Participants were instructed to imagine themselves in a real therapy room during a first therapy session. From this point onward, we use the terms “client” and “therapist” to refer to the roles adopted by participants in the role‐play. Therapists were instructed to start the conversation by inviting the client to share the problem they wanted to discuss. Clients shared a different problem in each conversation. Both client and therapist received written instructions tailored per interaction to manipulate the conversational goal: Exploring emotions (emotion‐focused interaction) vs. brainstorming solutions (solution‐focused interaction):

Therapists were informed that the goal of the conversation was to help their clients explore their feelings and to empathize with them. We also instructed them not to attempt to fix their clients' problems. Therapists were asked to help their clients express their feelings regarding their problems, explore an emotionally charged moment they identified together, and try to validate their clients' feelings. Therapists also watched a 3‐min animated video explaining empathy. To ensure their engagement, clients also received instructions stating that the goal of the conversation was to explore their feelings, and they were given three emotion‐focused questions to self‐reflect on their problem as preparation.

Therapists were informed that the goal of the conversation was to help their clients brainstorm about concrete means to solve their problem. They were asked to help their clients reflect on how they handled their problem, identify a goal to achieve together, and brainstorm solutions to achieve that goal. Therapists also watched a 3‐min animated video explaining how to collaborate with a client to agree on goals and solutions together. Clients also received instructions stating that the goal of the interaction was to brainstorm about solutions to their problem with the therapist and they were given three solution‐focused questions to self‐reflect as preparation. Role‐play instructions and videos are available at the OSF repository (https://osf.io/5r9gv/overview).

Participants filled in their preferred language and availabilities while signing up to participate in the study. They were then contacted by phone and/or email to pair them into dyads and schedule a lab visit. They were asked to fill in several trait questionnaires (e.g., attachment style) before their visit, which are beyond the scope of the current paper. To prepare for their lab visit, they were asked to think of two real problems they would like to share in case they were assigned the client role. On the day of the experiment, participants were randomly assigned to play either the client or therapist role by drawing one of two concealed pieces of paper labeled “client” or “therapist”. Each participant remained in the assigned role throughout both interaction conditions. The study followed a within‐subject design with all dyads having two consecutive 13‐min interactions: one emotion‐focused and one solution‐focused. The order of the interactions was counterbalanced by alternating the order between successive dyads. The client's problems were randomly assigned to the two interactions. Participants were asked to sign a nondisclosure agreement stating they would not share the problems discussed with anyone to protect their privacy.

Participants were seated at a 45‐degree angle to one another for the video recording, and the physiological sensors were attached to them. They were both given the written role‐play instructions along with a laptop and a headset for the therapist to watch the video. After they finished, they were informed they would have 13 min for their first conversation and that they would hear a knock on the door when they had 1 min left as a sign to wrap up. The researcher monitored the conversation (without sound) from an adjacent experimenter room via the video recording. Participants were informed that the researcher could see them through the camera but could not listen to what they were saying to make sure they felt safe.

After the first interaction was over, participants were asked to complete all the self‐report questionnaires in Qualtrics using a laptop. After they finished, they were handed the role‐play instructions to prepare for the second interaction. Then, participants were reminded about the knock before beginning the second interaction. Afterwards, participants completed all the self‐report questionnaires again. A sliding room divider was always placed between participants when they were filling in questionnaires and while attaching the physiological sensors for privacy. The total duration of the study was 90 min.

The interactions were video recorded using a Logitech HD Pro Webcam recording via OBS Studio (OBS Project, n.d.) with a video‐codec of H264‐ MPEG‐4 AVC, 1920 × 1080, 30 fps. Electrocardiogram (ECG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) were recorded using Biopac MP‐160 with a 1000 Hz sampling rate. The ECG was acquired with a high pass filter of 0.05 Hz and a gain of 2000. Disposable ECG electrodes were attached according to an adapted Lead II configuration by placing the active leads on the lower left rib and right collarbone, and the reference lead on the left collarbone (Quigley et al. ). EDA was acquired with a low‐pass filter set at 10 Hz, and a gain of 5 μS/V. Two Ag‐AgCl electrodes with isotonic gel were placed on the medial phalanx of the index and middle finger of the nondominant hand and cables were taped to the participant's arm to minimize motion artifacts.

Movement was quantified using motion energy analysis (MEA; Ramseyer ). MEA works by calculating the changes in pixel values over time by comparing consecutive video frames for a Region of Interest (ROI). Assuming the only movement within the ROI is from the participant, the MEA outputs a coarse‐grained measure of moment‐to‐moment general movement magnitude. For each participant, the ROI covered the upper body from the chair's seating area to the arms, excluding the head, given that upper‐body IS has been found to predict session‐level WA ratings (Ramseyer and Tschacher ). The 45‐degree seating arrangement allowed unobstructed visibility of both participants' upper bodies while capturing both participants in the same frame. This seating arrangement is common in the majority of IS research (e.g., Ramseyer and Tschacher , ). The raw motion energy time series for clients and therapists were extracted and preprocessed using the rMEA package (Kleinbub and Ramseyer ). This entailed smoothing, using a moving average window of 0.5 s, rescaling using the Standard Deviation (SD), standardizing using z‐scores, and removing extreme outliers exceeding 10 SD in the data. The resulting z‐score standardized time series with 1 s resolution were used in subsequent analysis.

ECG preprocessing was conducted in Python using Jupyter Notebook (Project Jupyter, n.d.) and the NeuroKit2 library (Makowski et al. ). The ECG signal was first cleaned using NeuroKit2's automated filtering procedures. R‐peaks were then detected using a fully automated algorithm (Emrich et al. ), with fallback to an alternative method (Nabian et al. ) when detection failed. Heart period (HP; interbeat interval) time series were derived from successive R–R intervals. Following general recommendations for R‐R interval editing (Peltola ), artifact detection and correction were performed using a hybrid automated procedure combining median absolute deviation (MAD)‐based detection, percentage change thresholds (25%–35%), physiological plausibility bounds (0.35–1.6 s), and pattern‐based detection of abrupt swings and nonphysiological ramps. Additionally, R‐R intervals were visually inspected, and artifact selection was manually adjusted when artifacts were not adequately identified by the automated procedure. Isolated outliers were corrected with linear interpolation, and continuous outlier segments were corrected using local interpolation based on surrounding valid intervals. The number and percentage of corrected intervals were quantified for each recording. To ensure data quality, extended interpolated segments (> 3 s) were considered unreliable, and recordings with more than 5% of R‐R intervals corrected were excluded (n = 1). The corrected R‐R series was interpolated using cubic spline interpolation to obtain a uniformly sampled time series at 4 Hz (Quigley et al. ). HF‐HRV was calculated using a short‐time Fourier transform approach based on procedures described in Gates et al. (). Spectral estimates were computed using a 32 s sliding window with 1 s steps (128 samples per window). Within each window, power spectral density was estimated using Welch's method, combined with multitaper spectral estimation to stabilize spectral estimates. Power spectra across tapers were averaged to obtain a single spectrum per window. HF‐HRV was quantified as spectral power within the 0.12–0.40 Hz frequency band, reflecting vagally mediated heart rate variability associated with respiratory sinus arrhythmia (Pham et al. ). HF power values were log‐transformed prior to analysis, resulting in a time series of log HF‐HRV values sampled at 1 s resolution across each interaction.

EDA signals were also processed in Python using NeuroKit2. Raw signals were minimally filtered with a 1 s median filter, a 1 s moving average, and a 10 Hz fourth‐order Butterworth low‐pass filter to reduce noise. Artifacts were automatically identified using rule‐based thresholds (implausible amplitudes: outside 0.01–100 μS, abrupt step changes: > 0.3 μS within 30 ms, and excessive slopes: > 5 μS/s). Short artifact segments (≤ 3 s) were linearly interpolated, whereas longer segments were marked unreliable during manual screening. Three dyads were dropped in both conditions due to poor signal quality (> 5% of unreliable segments) in either the client or therapist recording, and one additional dyad was dropped only from the solution‐focused condition. Client and therapist signals were resampled to a shared 4 Hz time grid and segmented into time‐locked 5 s windows (1 s step size). Within each window, we extracted both Average and Slope EDA values. EDAAverage reflects the overall tonic level of sympathetic arousal, whereas EDASlope captures dynamic changes in the signal over time and may reflect spontaneous fluctuations in the tonic level or nonspecific skin conductance responses (Boucsein et al. ). Although prior work has primarily focused on EDASlope (Marci et al. ; Palmieri et al. ), this study examined both signals to explore potential differences in their sensitivity to contextual changes. Finally, both EDAAverage and EDASlope time series were z‐standardized resulting in two EDA time series at 1 s resolution.

Time‐locked cleaned therapist and client time series (movement, HF‐HRV, EDASlope, and EDAAverage, described above) were used for all IS computations. To assess whether observed IS exceeded chance levels, surrogate datasets were generated to serve as a control comparison (Moulder et al. ). The surrogate function from the nonlinearTseries package in R was used to apply a fast Fourier transform. This method constructs artificial time series that preserve each signal's power spectrum (i.e., its autocorrelation structure) while randomizing phase information (i.e., meaningful alignment between signals). This allows testing whether observed IS arises from autocorrelations (noise) or genuine interaction. For each dyad and condition, 100 surrogate time series were generated separately for client and therapist data. These surrogate datasets were then used to estimate pseudosynchrony by applying the same IS analysis procedure as used for the observed data (see below).

Windowed Cross‐Lagged Correlation (WCLC) was used to compute IS, where cross‐correlations are computed within overlapping sliding windows. A typical WCLC matrix is a time‐by‐lag matrix in which columns represent time lags and rows represent successive overlapping windows across the interaction. The number of rows/windows depends on the interaction duration, window size, and step size. Parameter choice impacts the sensitivity of IS detection, especially the window size as it determines the number of observations per segment (Behrens et al. ). Given inconsistencies in the literature (Atzil‐slonim et al. ), we adopted a combined theory‐informed and data‐driven approach (as preregistered) by first comparing the three most commonly used window sizes in the literature and then choosing the one that maximized the difference between observed and surrogate IS, irrespective of condition. For each modality, three window sizes were tested (movement: 10, 30, 60 s; HF‐HRV: 16, 32, 60 s; EDA: 15, 30, 60 s), with corresponding step sizes proportional (~1/3) to the window length (movement: 4, 10, 20 s; HF‐HRV: 5, 10, 20 s; EDA: 5, 10, 20 s). Within each window, cross‐correlations were computed across modality‐specific maximum lags (movement: 5; HF‐HRV: 7; EDA: 10 s), reflecting the different temporal dynamics of each signal. For example, HF‐HRV primarily reflects respiratory sinus arrhythmia, with a typical adult respiration cycle ranging from approximately 4–7 s (Fisher et al. ), while EDA responses typically reach their peak approximately 3–5 s after activation, with recovery periods lasting several additional seconds (Posada‐Quintero and Chon ).

For each dyad, WCLC matrices were computed separately for observed and surrogate time series using identical procedures. For parameter sweeping, we compared average observed IS with average surrogate IS (both computed using three window sizes per modality). For each dyad, IS was calculated by averaging correlation coefficients across all time windows separately for each lag. WCLC was computed for both observed and surrogate time series using the same method. For the surrogate data, IS values from 100 surrogate pairs were averaged to produce a single surrogate IS profile per dyad, window size, and lag. Next, two‐sided paired‐sample t‐tests were conducted comparing observed and surrogate IS for each window size using average absolute IS across lags. See Figure  for an example from the HF‐HRV analysis, with window sizes on the y‐axis, time lags on the x‐axis, and cells representing t‐statistics comparing observed and surrogate IS. Results from these t‐tests for all modalities indicated that all tested window sizes showed significantly higher observed IS compared to surrogate data (see  for detailed results). To maintain consistency across modalities, we selected the 60s window size for all following analyses. Each modality was assigned its modality‐specific maximum lag; therefore, all references to time lags below correspond to the maximum viable lag within that modality.

Using the selected parameters, WCLC matrices were computed per dyad and condition (for both observed and surrogate data) and Fisher z‐transformed. The WCLC matrices were used to extract the following six facets: (1) The mean of absolute Fisher z‐transformed cross‐correlations was used as a global strength measure reflecting the average correlation magnitude between client and therapist across all time lags (Ramseyer and Tschacher ). (2) The variance between all correlations was used as a global flexibility measure reflecting the total variability between client and therapist across all time lags (Gordon et al. ).

A peak‐picking function using a Loess‐smoothing algorithm was then employed on the raw WCLC matrices to identify the dominant lag within each time window, resulting in a vector with peak correlations and the time lags at which they occurred (Boker et al. ; Moulder et al. ). peak detection was applied to each windowed correlation after Loess‐smoothing across lags (span = 0.25) to reduce noise. The dominant peak was defined as the maximum absolute correlation, with a look‐ahead stopping parameter (Lsize = maximum lag) which determines how many successive search expansions of the lag window are allowed without finding a stronger peak before the search terminates. (3) The mean of absolute peak correlations was used as a peak strength measure reflecting the maximum strength of IS observed between client and therapist. (4) The SD of absolute peak correlations was used as a peak flexibility measure reflecting the amount of variation in peak correlations between client and therapist. (5) The average of the time lags of peak correlations was used to represent dominance in the leading‐following dynamics (positive = client leading, negative = therapist leading). (6) The SD of the time‐lags of peak correlations was used to represent switching in the leading‐following dynamics between the client and therapist (with higher values indicating higher switching).

All statistical analyses were conducted in R (version 4.4.1) using linear mixed‐effects models (package lme4). See  for packages version and reference lists. Dyad was treated as the primary sampling unit and included as a random intercept in all models. Condition was sum‐to‐zero coded and specified as a fixed factor (−1 = emotion‐focused, 1 = solution‐focused). When included, continuous predictors were centered. All models were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML). To control for multiple testing, p‐values for condition effects were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Model assumptions were checked using the check_model function from the performance package. Overall, diagnostics indicated that model assumptions were adequately met. As preregistered, model comparisons between base and interaction models (explained below) were conducted using likelihood ratio tests and information criteria (AIC). Gender, age, and therapists' experience (i.e., years of study) were checked as control variables and none of them improved model fit. All codes for preprocessing and analyses will be available on OSF repository (https://osf.io/5r9gv/overview).

To test the experimental manipulation of relational context, a series of linear mixed‐effects models examined the effect of condition (emotion‐focused vs. solution‐focused) on client‐ and therapist‐rated variables (Base model: Outcome ~ Condition + (1 | Dyad)). FDR corrections were applied to the analyses within each hypothesis family (emotion exploration‐related outcomes, collaboration‐related outcomes, and control variables). Emotion exploration‐related outcomes included: WAI‐Bond, BL‐Empathy, Affective empathy, and Cognitive empathy, all rated by client and therapist, as well as client‐rated FIS‐Empathy and HSM‐Emotion exploration. Collaboration‐related outcomes included: WAI‐Collaboration, rated by client and therapist, as well as client‐rated FIS‐Collaboration and HSM‐action. Control variables included perceived stress and difficulty (rated by client and therapist), as well as client rated significance of the problem.

To test whether observed synchrony exceeded chance levels, paired one‐sided t‐tests compared observed synchrony against surrogate synchrony for each modality across four synchrony facets (global strength, peak strength, global flexibility, and peak flexibility) within each condition. We did not compare facets indexing leading‐following dynamics to surrogate data, as these positional facets are interpreted only in the context of above‐chance global synchrony. FDR correction was applied separately for each modality and condition across the four synchrony facets (i.e., eight tests per modality).

To test whether synchrony facets and modalities differed between conditions (Hypotheses , , , , ), we conducted another set of linear mixed‐effects models with the different IS modalities and facets as outcome (Base model: IS ~ Condition + (1 | Dyad)). FDR correction was applied across facets per modality (i.e., correcting for six tests per modality). To check for potential order effects of the two conditions, we ran control analyses (interaction models) by adding sequence (A: emotion‐focused condition first; B: solution‐focused condition first), and the Condition × sequence interaction to the base models. The results reported below are from the base models (without sequence) unless stated otherwise, in cases where sequence affected the conclusions regarding condition effects.

To investigate whether the relations between IS and the experienced relationship quality depended on the relational context (Hypotheses  and  ), we ran a series of mixed‐effect models to see whether the different IS modalities and facets predicted the experienced WAI (bond and collaboration, separately for clients and therapists) differently per condition (WA ~ Condition * IS + (1 | Dyad)). FDR correction was applied within theoretically defined facet families (strength, flexibility, leading‐following), separately for each person (client, therapist) and WA component (bond, collaboration). Each correction was applied to eight tests per family (4 modalities × 2 facets per family). We report below the models that showed significant results after FDR correction. The full list of results (2 roles × 2 subscales × 4 IS modalities × 6 IS facets = 96 models) is available as .

Descriptive results are reported in Table  and results from the linear mixed‐effects models are reported in Table . As expected, the emotion‐focused condition was associated with significantly higher therapist self‐rated empathy in comparison to the solution‐focused condition (BL, Affective Empathy, and Cognitive Empathy). Therapist empathy, as rated by the client (BL, FIS), was also high in the emotion‐focused condition, but not significantly higher than in the solution‐focused condition. Client‐rated emotional exploration of their problem (HSM‐Exploration) also did not differ significantly between conditions after correcting for multiple testing. Finally, experienced WAI‐Bond was high and did not differ significantly between conditions for both therapists and clients.

In summary, pseudosynchrony results across modalities and facets showed above‐chance levels of IS in both conditions. Effect sizes were similar for global and peak strength facets but differed between strength and flexibility facets. Condition differences were observed only for movement strength facets and EDASlope dominance and were moderated by sequence.

To investigate whether the relations between IS and the experienced relationship quality depended on the relational context, we ran another series of mixed‐effect models to see whether the different IS modalities and facets predicted the experienced WAI differently per condition. In other words, we found no relations between IS and the collaborative component of the WAI.
