Competitive spirit refers to athletes' psychological tendency to pursue victory, defeat opponents, and achieve excellent results in competitive contexts, reflecting strong competitive motivation, goal orientation, and outcome awareness (). For track and field athletes, the long-term repetitive training process and highly competitive competition environment require sustained goal persistence and competition commitment. A higher level of competitive spirit may help athletes maintain focus, withstand pressure, and actively strive for advantages during training and competition, thereby being associated with better athletic performance. Based on this, self-management may further influence track and field athletes' athletic performance by enhancing competitive spirit.

H3: Competitive spirit plays a single mediating role between self-management and athletic performance (path ed).

From the perspective of a continuous psychological process, the influence of self-management on athletic performance may not be achieved through a single psychological variable, but through the sequential effects of psychological resilience and competitive spirit. Athletes with higher levels of self-management are generally better at planning training, monitoring their condition, and regulating stress. This helps improve their psychological resilience, enabling them to maintain stable adaptive capacity when facing training loads, competition pressure, and performance fluctuations (; ). Athletes with higher psychological resilience are more likely to perceive pressure and competition as challenges rather than threats, thereby further stimulating their competitive spirit and strengthening their motivation to pursue victory, persist in goals, and engage in active competition (; ).

The sequential effects of psychological resilience and competitive spirit further contribute to athletic performance. Psychological resilience helps athletes maintain emotional stability and focus under stressful conditions, while competitive spirit transforms this psychological adaptability into stronger training commitment and competition execution. Previous studies have indicated that psychological resilience is closely related to protective factors such as motivation, confidence, and concentration (), while competitive spirit reflects athletes' desire to pursue victory in competition (). Therefore, self-management may first enhance psychological resilience, then further improve competitive spirit, and ultimately promote athletes' athletic performance.

H4: Psychological resilience and competitive spirit play a chain mediating role between self-management and athletic performance (path bcd).

Based on the above theoretical analysis and literature review, this study constructs the research model shown in , aiming to explore the mechanism through which self-management influences track and field athletes' athletic performance and to examine the single and chain mediating roles of psychological resilience and competitive spirit.

A non-probability convenience sampling technique was used to recruit Chinese track and field athletes (). Recruitment was conducted across Shandong, Liaoning, Jiangsu, Henan, Hebei, Hunan, and Hubei Provinces, as well as through track and field clubs in other regions of China. Participants were recruited from high schools, sports colleges, track and field teams, and clubs, with teachers and coaches assisting in distributing the questionnaire through Wenjuanxing (Questionnaire Star), a widely used online survey platform in China. To be eligible for participation, individuals were required to be currently engaged in track and field training and to participate voluntarily in the study.

The first page of the questionnaire explained the purpose and procedures of the study, the principles of anonymity and confidentiality, and participants' right to withdraw at any time. Participants proceeded to the formal questionnaire only after providing informed consent.

After data collection, responses were screened for questionnaire completeness, response time, patterned responding, and duplicate submissions. A total of 847 questionnaires were collected. After excluding 75 invalid responses, 772 valid questionnaires were retained for the final analysis, yielding an effective response rate of 91.1%.

Among the valid samples, 679 participants were male (88.0%) and 93 were female (12.0%). In terms of educational level, 597 participants had a high school education (77.3%) and 175 had a university education (22.7%). Regarding athletic level, 94 participants were first-level athletes (12.2%), 240 were second-level athletes (31.1%), 180 were third-level athletes (23.3%), and 258 were non-ranked athletes (33.4%). In terms of sport event, 685 participants were sprinters (88.7%) and 87 were long-distance runners (11.3%). Regarding years of training, 283 participants had trained for 1–2 years (36.7%), 221 for 2–3 years (28.6%), 117 for 3–4 years (15.2%), 47 for 4–5 years (6.1%), 34 for 5–6 years (4.4%), and 70 for more than 6 years (9.0%). The specific demographic characteristics are shown in . Given the composition of the sample, the findings should be interpreted primarily in the context of a predominantly male and sprint-oriented group of Chinese track and field athletes. In this study, “non-ranked athletes” referred to participants who did not hold an official athletic-level classification at the time of the survey.

Demographic characteristics of participants.

This study used four established scales to assess self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance. Based on the theoretical foundations and dimensional structures of the original instruments, each scale was translated, back-translated, and contextually adapted for Chinese track and field athletes. To establish content validity and contextual appropriateness, three experts in sport psychology, physical education, and sport measurement and evaluation independently reviewed the items in terms of content representativeness, linguistic accuracy, clarity of expression, and contextual relevance. Item wording was revised according to the experts' feedback before the final questionnaire was administered. The content validation process was qualitative; therefore, no quantitative content validity index was calculated. Subsequently, the reliability and construct validity of the final instruments were evaluated using Cronbach's α, composite reliability (CR), average variance extracted (AVE), and confirmatory factor analysis.

All scales adopted a 5-point Likert scoring method, ranging from 1 = “strongly disagree” to 5 = “strongly agree,” with higher scores indicating higher levels of the corresponding variable. Meanwhile, this study used confirmatory factor analysis to examine the structural validity of the measurement model, and evaluated the internal consistency reliability and convergent validity of each scale using Cronbach's α, composite reliability, and average variance extracted. The details are as follows.

The Athletes Self-Management Questionnaire (ASMQ) developed by  was used. The scale includes four dimensions: physical management, interpersonal relationship management, training management, and mental management, with a total of 18 items. Cronbach's α = 0.895.

The Resilience Quotient Test (RQT) developed by  was used. The scale includes three dimensions: control, positivity, and sociality, with a total of 27 items. Cronbach's α = 0.931.

The Competitive Spirit Scale (CSS) developed by  was used. The scale includes three dimensions: fighting spirit, self-confidence, and desire to win, with a total of 18 items. Cronbach's α = 0.897.

The Athletic Performance Scale (APS) developed by , was used. The scale includes three dimensions: competition operation ability, competition confidence, and technical level ability, with a total of 14 items. Because the present study focused on athletes' perceived performance-related functioning rather than objective competition results, a self-report questionnaire was considered appropriate for assessing these multidimensional aspects of athletic performance. Cronbach's α = 0.887.

The measurement properties of the four instruments were further evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency reliability. As shown in , all four instruments demonstrated acceptable model fit and satisfactory reliability.

Reliability and model fit of the measurement instruments.

The criteria for model fit were χ2/df < 3, RMSEA < 0.06, and GFI, AGFI and NFI approaching or exceeding 0.90. Cronbach's α values above 0.70 indicated acceptable reliability. SM, Self-Management; PR, Psychological Resilience; CS, Competitive Spirit; AP, Athletic Performance

Multiple statistical methods were adopted to address the research objectives and test the hypothesized relationships among self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance. SPSS 31.0 was used for data screening, descriptive statistics, and correlation analysis, whereas AMOS 31.0 was used for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

First, to examine common method bias (CMB), a single-factor CFA was conducted using AMOS 31.0. All measurement items were loaded onto one latent factor to construct a single-factor model, thereby testing whether obvious common method bias existed in the measurement data.

Second, regarding the measurement model test, AMOS 31.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis on the latent variables of self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance, in order to examine the structural validity of the scales. At the same time, Cronbach's α coefficient, composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE) were used to examine the internal consistency reliability and convergent validity of each scale.

Finally, to directly address the research hypotheses, SEM was used to estimate the structural paths among self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance. AmosEstimandVB programming combined with the Bootstrap method with 5,000 repeated samples was then used to estimate bias-corrected confidence intervals for the direct, single mediating, and chain mediating effects. If the confidence interval did not include zero, the effect was considered statistically significant.

To reduce systematic errors that may arise from the same measurement source, this study adopted procedural control measures in the questionnaire design, including anonymous responses, random presentation of items, and interspersed arrangement of different constructs. At the statistical level, single-factor confirmatory factor analysis and comparison with the complete model were conducted for testing ().

The fit indices of the single-factor model were as follows: χ2 = 16,969.889, df = 2,845, χ2/df = 5.965, GFI = 0.491, AGFI = 0.463, CFI = 0.542, NFI = 0.497, TLI = 0.529, and RMSEA = 0.080. Compared with the complete multifactor model, χ2 = 3,434.622, df = 2,830, χ2/df = 1.214, GFI = 0.899, AGFI = 0.893, CFI = 0.980, NFI = 0.898, TLI = 0.980, and RMSEA = 0.017, the single-factor model showed substantially poorer fit. This indicates that serious common method bias is unlikely to pose a substantial threat to the validity of the research findings (). However, because all variables were collected at the same time point through self-report questionnaires, the possibility of residual common method bias still cannot be completely excluded. Therefore, appropriate caution should be exercised when interpreting the findings, and future research may combine self-report data with objective behavioral indicators or multisource data.

The overall measurement model demonstrated an acceptable fit to the data: χ2 = 3,434.622, df = 2,830, χ2/df = 1.214, GFI = 0.899, AGFI = 0.893, CFI = 0.980, NFI = 0.898, TLI = 0.980, and RMSEA = 0.017. These results supported the adequacy of the overall measurement model for subsequent structural model analysis (; ).

AMOS 31.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) on the four core latent variables, and squared multiple correlations (SMC), composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE) were calculated to examine the convergent validity of each latent variable.

The results in  show that all measurement items loaded significantly on their corresponding factors (p < 0.001), with standardized factor loadings exceeding 0.70. The CR values ranged from 0.853 to 0.921, and the AVE values ranged from 0.529 to 0.625, indicating satisfactory convergent validity. More specifically, for self-management, standardized factor loadings ranged from 0.712 to 0.812, with CR values ranging from 0.853 to 0.865 and AVE values ranging from 0.550 to 0.611 across its four dimensions. For athletic performance, standardized factor loadings ranged from 0.737 to 0.817, with CR values ranging from 0.869 to 0.878 and AVE values ranging from 0.573 to 0.625 across its three dimensions. These results confirmed adequate measurement quality of the focal predictor and outcome constructs before hypothesis testing. Psychological resilience and competitive spirit also met the recommended criteria for convergent validity ().

Confirmatory factor analysis results.

Prior to hypothesis testing, preliminary assumption checks were conducted for normality and multicollinearity. The skewness values ranged from −0.573 to −0.381, while the kurtosis values ranged from 0.396 to 1.029, indicating no substantial deviation from normality. The correlations among the study variables ranged from 0.426 to 0.523, with no excessively high correlations observed, suggesting no serious multicollinearity problem ().

Descriptive statistics and correlations among the study variables are presented in . Significant positive correlations were observed among self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance (p < 0.01). In addition, the square root of the AVE for each latent variable exceeded its correlations with the other constructs, supporting adequate discriminant validity (). Overall, the preliminary analyses indicated that the data were suitable for subsequent structural equation modeling and hypothesis testing.

For the direct effect path of H1, effect “a” was β = 0.234, SE = 0.096, 95% CI [0.035, 0.418], supporting H1. Based on data from 772 Chinese track and field athletes, this study examined the pathways through which self-management influences athletic performance. The results showed that self-management had a significant positive effect on athletic performance. Meanwhile, psychological resilience and competitive spirit each played a significant positive mediating role between self-management and athletic performance. In addition, psychological resilience and competitive spirit formed a significant positive chain mediating pathway.

Self-management was positively associated with athletic performance among Chinese track and field athletes, supporting H1. This finding is consistent with recent evidence showing that athletes with stronger self-management tend to report better performance-related outcomes. For example,  found that self-management was significantly associated with perceived performance among judo athletes, while  reported that physical, training, and mental management were significantly related to performance among university athletes. Similar findings have also been observed in team-sport athletes, where self-management was positively associated with athletic performance ().

The present finding extends this evidence to Chinese track and field athletes, a context in which effective self-regulation may be particularly important because athletes must continually manage training load, recovery, psychological state, and performance goals across prolonged training and competition cycles. This interpretation is also consistent with recent research on distance running showing that successful performance involves ongoing self-regulatory processes, including goal monitoring, adjustment, and adaptive goal revision during competition (). Accordingly, the present result suggests that self-management should be understood not merely as a routine training habit, but as a broader behavioral-regulatory resource associated with athletes' perceived performance.

Self-management was positively associated with psychological resilience, which in turn was positively associated with athletic performance, supporting H2. This pattern is consistent with recent sport research suggesting that stronger self-regulatory capacities are closely related to athletes' ability to adapt to stress and adversity. , for example, reported a positive association between self-management and resilience among paragliding athletes, while  showed that self-regulation training can strengthen athletes' resilience under stressful conditions. These findings are also consistent with the broader view of sporting resilience as a dynamic adaptive process shaped by athletes' cognitive, emotional, and behavioral regulation ().

The association between psychological resilience and athletic performance is likewise supported by recent evidence.  found that elite athletes with stronger resilience profiles tended to report more favorable performance-related outcomes, and a recent systematic review and meta-analysis further confirmed a robust positive relationship between resilience and athletic performance across different sport contexts (). Together, these studies suggest that resilience is not merely a protective resource for coping with adversity, but also an important psychological capacity associated with maintaining effective performance under demanding competitive conditions.

The present study extends this literature by integrating these two relationships within a single indirect pathway. Rather than treating resilience only as an independent correlate of athletic performance, the findings suggest that it may serve as an adaptive psychological resource linking athletes' self-management with their perceived performance. For track and field athletes, the continuous regulation of training, recovery, emotional responses, and competitive demands may contribute to stronger adaptive capacity, which may in turn support more stable performance-related functioning.

Self-management was positively associated with competitive spirit, which was subsequently associated with better athletic performance, supporting H3. This finding is broadly consistent with contemporary research highlighting the close interplay between self-regulatory functioning and competition-oriented motivation in sport.  showed that the need to compete is embedded within a broader achievement-oriented motivational system involving self-efficacy, grit, anxiety, and flow, while more recent studies have linked achievement-oriented motivational dispositions with athletes' self-management and sustained engagement in training (; ). Although competitive spirit is conceptually distinct from achievement-goal orientation, these findings collectively suggest that effective behavioral regulation and competitive striving are closely interconnected within the athletic context.

The association between competitive spirit and athletic performance is also consistent with recent evidence showing that achievement- and competition-oriented motivation is relevant to performance-related functioning.  reported that stronger achievement-goal orientation was associated with more favorable performance among adolescent basketball players, while , in a systematic review and meta-analysis, demonstrated that achievement-goal orientations are meaningfully related to sport performance across a range of competitive settings. Taken together, this literature supports the view that athletes who maintain clearer competitive goals and a stronger orientation toward achievement may be better able to sustain effort, commitment, and performance-directed behavior under demanding training and competition conditions.

The present study extends this line of research by positioning competitive spirit not merely as an independent motivational characteristic, but as a potential motivational pathway through which self-management is associated with athletic performance. For track and field athletes, the systematic regulation of training, recovery, physical condition, and psychological state may help preserve goal clarity and competitive commitment across prolonged and repetitive training cycles. In this sense, self-management may do more than organize athletes' behavior; it may also provide the regulatory foundation through which competitive motivation is maintained and translated into performance-related functioning. This interpretation broadens the role of self-management from a behavioral control process to a mechanism potentially linked with the development and maintenance of athletes' competitive striving.

Psychological resilience and competitive spirit sequentially mediated the association between self-management and athletic performance, supporting H4. This finding suggests that self-management may be linked to performance through a progressive process involving behavioral regulation, psychological adaptation, and competitive motivation. Effective management of training, recovery, physical condition, and psychological states may enhance athletes' sense of control and strengthen their capacity to cope with pressure, setbacks, and performance fluctuations. In turn, stronger psychological resilience may help athletes maintain goal focus, confidence, and competitive engagement under demanding conditions, thereby supporting stronger competitive striving. This interpretation is consistent with recent evidence linking self-management with resilience and with contemporary perspectives that conceptualize sporting resilience as a dynamic adaptive process involving cognitive, emotional, and behavioral regulation rather than a fixed personal trait (; ).

More importantly, the present study extends previous research by integrating psychological resilience and competitive spirit within a single sequential mechanism. Whereas resilience and competition-oriented motivation have often been examined separately in relation to athletic performance, the present findings suggest that adaptive psychological resources may provide an important foundation for sustaining competitive motivation in challenging sport environments. Recent research has similarly emphasized the relevance of resilience and achievement-oriented motivation to athletes' performance-related functioning (; ). Although competitive spirit is conceptually distinct from achievement-goal orientation, these findings collectively support the idea that athletes' behavioral self-regulation may be associated with performance through a sequence of strengthened adaptation and competitive striving. Thus, the contribution of the present study lies in showing how behavioral regulation, psychological adaptation, and competitive motivation may operate as an interconnected pathway associated with athletic performance.

Although this study constructed and tested a chain mediation model of the influence of self-management on track and field athletes' athletic performance, and revealed the mechanisms of psychological resilience and competitive spirit within this relationship, several limitations remain.

First, this study adopted a cross-sectional design, and all variables were measured at the same time point. Therefore, caution is needed when interpreting the temporal order and causal relationships among the variables. Although this study constructed the mediating pathways based on theoretical assumptions, the results are more appropriately understood as indirect associations in a statistical sense. Future research may adopt longitudinal tracking, cross-lagged models, or experimental intervention designs to further verify the findings of this study.

Second, data were collected using self-report questionnaires. Although common method bias was controlled and tested, the results may still be affected by subjective judgment, recall bias, and social desirability effects. Future research may combine multiple sources of data, such as competition results, coach evaluations, and training monitoring, to further improve the objectivity and ecological validity of measurement.

Third, the sample was substantially imbalanced by gender and event type, with a predominance of male athletes and sprinters. Given possible gender- and event-related differences in competitive orientation and performance-related psychological characteristics, this distribution may limit the generalizability of the findings to female athletes and to athletes in other track and field disciplines. In addition, 33.4% of the participants were non-ranked athletes, defined here as athletes without an official athletic-level classification. Because detailed competitive history was not separately assessed and athletic performance was measured using self-report rather than objective indicators such as competition times, personal bests, or official rankings, the findings for the non-ranked subgroup should be interpreted with caution. Future studies should recruit more balanced samples across gender and event categories and incorporate objective performance indicators and more detailed competition-history information.

Taking Chinese track and field athletes as the research participants, this study constructed and tested a mediation model of the influence of self-management on athletic performance based on self-regulation theory and relevant perspectives in sport psychology. The results showed that self-management had a significant positive effect on athletic performance; the higher the athletes' level of self-management, the better their athletic performance. Psychological resilience and competitive spirit each played a significant positive mediating role between self-management and athletic performance, and together they formed a significant positive chain mediating pathway. Self-management can not only directly promote athletic performance, but also improve athletic performance by enhancing psychological resilience and strengthening competitive spirit.

This study further indicates that the formation of track and field athletes' athletic performance does not depend only on physical fitness, technical skills, and sport-specific training, but is also jointly influenced by self-regulation ability, psychological adaptation ability, and competitive goal orientation. For track and field athletes, long-term, repetitive, and high-intensity training can easily lead to physical fatigue, psychological pressure, and performance fluctuations. If athletes lack good self-management ability, it is difficult for them to continuously maintain a stable training state and competition performance. Therefore, self-management should be regarded as an important psychological and behavioral foundation for improving athletic performance, rather than merely a part of athletes' daily life management or training discipline. At the same time, the mediating roles of psychological resilience and competitive spirit between self-management and athletic performance also indicate that the effect of self-management on athletic performance does not follow a single pathway, but is further realized through the sequential effects of psychological adaptation ability and competitive motivation.

At the practical level, the findings of this study suggest that coaches and sport team managers should incorporate the cultivation of self-management ability, psychological resilience, and competitive spirit into the daily training system of track and field athletes. Specifically, training plan management, phased goal setting, training log recording, recovery status monitoring, and post-competition feedback can be used to help athletes develop stable training habits and self-regulation ability. Meanwhile, pressure-situation simulation, review of failure experiences, and emotional regulation training can be used to improve athletes' psychological recovery ability when facing setbacks, injuries, competition losses, and performance fluctuations. In addition, when cultivating competitive spirit, coaches should avoid simply emphasizing competition results. Instead, they should guide athletes to establish positive, healthy, and stable competitive goals, enabling them to further transform self-management and psychological resilience into sustained training commitment, competition confidence, and competitive motivation.

psychology.title: Norms for a German version of the Phenomenological Control Scale: measuring the capacity for creating and controlling experience
psychology.abstract: The ability to create experiences which misrepresent reality and thereby meet strategic goals is a stable trait that varies substantially in the general population. The capacity for such phenomenological control can be measured by response to imaginative suggestions for a variety of experiences, e.g. hallucination in various modalities, amnesia, paralysis, or motor actions, which are experienced as involuntary. Here, we present norms for a German translation of the Phenomenological Control Scale [Lush et al. (The Phenomenological Control Scale: measuring the capacity for creating illusory nonvolition, hallucination, and delusion. Collabra: Psychology 2021;7:29542)]. Data were collected from a representative sample of native-German speakers (N = 299) using a single-session online screening procedure. We show that the translated scale is psychometrically sound, and in line with the results of the original scale in terms of mean scores, distribution, and internal consistency. All analyses, code, data, materials, and the full questionnaire script are made freely available. Other researchers in the field of psychology are welcome to access and encouraged to use the German norms for the Phenomenological Control Scale, e.g. to assess the degree to which trait phenomenological control may be involved in other psychological effects.
psychology.text:
The capacity to alter subjective experience in line with one’s beliefs and goals (phenomenological control; alternatively, “the ability to alter experience”; , ) can be measured by response to imaginative suggestions across multiple sensory and motor modalities. Although phenomenological control has historically been investigated primarily within the context of hypnosis research (), the hypnotic context (e.g. an induction procedure which aims to produce a special “state”) is not required for response to imaginative suggestion (; ). Because the use of phenomenological control is not limited to the particular social context of hypnosis, it may be used to fulfill particular needs or perceived social roles in a variety of situations. For example, to produce experiences in response to experimental demand characteristics (; ; ; ) or to mentally distance oneself from physical or emotional pain (). There is therefore a need for tools which can support research into individual differences in this trait capacity, e.g. to measure the degree to which psychological effects are differentially reported by those high or low in phenomenological control (e.g. , 2026).

The Phenomenological Control Scale (PCS), originally developed in English by , provides a standardized method for assessing this capacity. The PCS is an adaptation of the Sussex-Waterloo Scale of Hypnotisability, itself a modification of the Waterloo-Stanford Group Scale of Hypnotic Suggestibility, Form C (), and therefore ultimately derived from the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (). The PCS differs from the Sussex-Waterloo Scale of Hypnotisability in that all references to a hypnotic context have been removed (e.g. references to sleep and relaxation or a special state), and the scale is presented as a test of a capacity to generate particular experiences, rather than as a hypnotic induction procedure. The scale consists of 10 items involving suggestions across a range of domains, including amnesia, auditory, visual, gustatory, tactile, motor, and paralysis experiences. Participants rate their subjective responses on a scale from 0 to 5, yielding an average PCS score that reflects the extent to which individuals can generate the suggested experiences. Score distributions are approximately Gaussian and broadly comparable to those obtained from classic hypnotic suggestibility scales. While non-hypnotic imaginative suggestions historically have been shown to produce a slightly weaker response than “hypnotic” procedures (), PCS norms show higher scores than those for the hypnosis scale from which it is adapted driven by a shift of low scorers toward the mid-range. This shift may be attributable to the reframing of imaginative suggestion as a capacity or skill, which may reduce the impact of negative preconceptions associated with hypnosis (e.g. the myth that responding to suggestion implies that one is “suggestible,” or unusually socially compliant; ; ). The PCS inherits practical advantages offered by the Sussex-Waterloo Scale of Hypnotisability over the scales on which it is based, notably, substantially shorter administration time and modifications which allow online delivery (; ). The PCS can be administered online in around 30 min using common online questionnaire platforms (e.g. SocSci, RedCap, etc). Norms for a Japanese adaptation of the PCS (PCS-J; ) show similar properties to the original scale norms.

The present study aimed to develop and validate a German version of the PCS (PCS-GER) to facilitate future research on the effects of phenomenological control in native German-samples. Further, we aimed to verify the feasibility of online administration, following prior work demonstrating the suitability of recorded audio instructions for remote delivery (; ). To this end, the PCS script was presented via audio recordings in German, and the data was collected online to evaluate the psychometric properties of the PCS in a German-speaking sample.

A total of N = 357 participants were recruited online for the study. The preregistered sample size was 300 participants set as a minimum recruitment target to account for potential exclusions and to obtain robust information about the usability and psychometric performance of the scale (). In the end, 262 of the participants were recruited using the participant pool provider Prolific; the remaining 95 participants were recruited via the local study platform SONA of the University of Tübingen.

To assess response quality, we excluded participants who completed the survey in less time than was considered realistically necessary to listen to the instructions (n = 57). At the end of the survey, participants also indicated whether they had completed the items meaningfully and conscientiously. Two participants reported that they had not responded meaningfully, one of whom had already been excluded based on completion time. In total, 58 participants were excluded. These criteria were applied in addition to the preregistered exclusion criterion (https://osf.io/b7yfx), which excluded participants who did not complete all survey items.

The 299 participants (185 female, 112 male, and 2 diverse) included in the analysis ranged in age from 18 to 72 years (M = 31, SD = 12). Participants were compensated either with course credit or £3.75 for their participation. Participants provided informed consent prior to participation. The collected data were anonymous.

Participants completed this online study on their own computers; they were asked to do it in a quiet room with no distractions and to wear headphones for the whole duration of the study.

The stimulus material consisted of the PCS, translated from English into German using official guidelines for questionnaire translation (). The initial translation from the original script (English) into German was translated and checked by three independent bilingual translators (). Two of the translators were aware of the concepts the questionnaire intends to measure to best resemble the original instrument. Another naïve German speaker without a background in psychology or neuroscience was asked to read the translation and make small changes if necessary to reflect the nuances of the spoken German language. Finally, the text was back-translated by the researchers to ensure the accuracy of the translation and checked by a native English speaker (also part of the research team) to avoid misunderstanding and unclear wording. The translated materials can be found in the .

The script was then audio recorded by a male native German speaker. Within the study, the first part of the audio was presented via a YouTube video with a black screen and only the audio playing except for an image of three balls (red, green, and blue) being shown at the end (see “negative visual hallucination”). The rest of the text was presented via audio snippets. All audio files, images and the full text can be found on GitHub (; https://github.com/Schiwo/The-German-Phenomenological-Control-Scale). The data was collected online via SoSciSurvey (www.soscisurvey.de).

The translated scale consisted of the same 10 items as the original PCS in English. There are four ideomotor suggestions (i.e. suggestions for experience of involuntary movement): hand lowering (a suggested experience of a heavy object in the participant’s outstretched hand) and moving hands together (a suggested experience of a “magnetic” force pulling the participant’s outstretched hands together). There are two ideomotor items involving suggestions for an inability to move: arm rigidity (the arm is so rigid that it cannot be bent) and arm immobilization (the arm cannot be lifted from the participant’s lap). There is one post-session suggestion in which participants are told that they will press the space bar six times in a row but will not remember being told to do so. The remaining items are cognitive–perceptual suggestions: experience of a mosquito (tactile or auditory experience), music (hearing Happy Birthday played), negative visual hallucination (participants are shown a slide of three colored balls and told they can see only two), amnesia (participants are unable to remember anything from the session until that point), and taste (suggestions for experiences of sweet and sour tastes).

The “subjective” scale records experience (e.g. how much it felt like there was a magnetic force drawing the hands together) on a Likert scale (from 0–5). Responses were recorded by participants using their computer mouse, on a presented Likert rating scale.

Participants were recruited via Prolific or registered through the university SONA system. Upon accessing the study link, participants were asked to provide demographic information and were given the opportunity to provide informed consent before proceeding to the experiment.

A sound check was conducted at the beginning of the session to ensure that the audio volume was adequate and comfortable. Participants were then instructed to start the video when they felt ready. The video began with a brief imagination task designed to familiarize participants with the procedure, followed by the presentation of the imaginative suggestions.

After the audio stimuli had concluded, participants were asked to rate the strength of each of the 10 individual experiences using a 6-point Likert scale ranging from 0 to 5, with scale anchors translated from the PCS. The response scale was explained prior to each exercise. The median study duration was 16 min (minimum 15.5 min; maximum 65.4 min). At the end of the session, all participants were debriefed and informed about the purpose and nature of the study.

At the item level, the following analyses were conducted. We investigated the item distribution indicators compared with the originally published data set by , excluding the retest data. Indicators of internal consistency were calculated, including Cronbach’s Alpha and Cronbach’s Alpha if item deleted. 95% confidence intervals were estimated using a bootstrapping procedure with 5000 iterations. Finally, item-to-PCS score correlations were computed.

At the scale level, PCS-GER scores for each participant were calculated, as specified in the preregistration document, as the mean across all 10 scale items. Consistent with the original scale, two items were derived from pairs of subjective responses to separate suggestions. Item 4 (taste hallucination) was computed as the arithmetic mean of responses to suggestions involving experiences of sweet and sour taste, whereas Item 10 (post-hypnotic suggestion) was computed as the geometric mean of the reported urge to press the space bar and the reported amnesia following the suggestion to forget the previous instruction. In addition, the same distribution metrics as those used for the individual items (mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis) were calculated for the scale scores and compared with the original data (; retrieved from https://osf.io/4x25a).

Item score distribution indicators for the German validation sample (in this order: mean, standard deviation, item-drop Cronbach’s alpha with 95% CI, and corrected item-to-total correlation).

CIs were calculated using bootstrapping procedures. Corrected item-to-total correlation means correlating an item with the scale score excluding that specific item’s contribution.

The mean scale PCS-GER score was 1.8 (SD = 0.7), closely matching the mean score reported for the original PCS (M = 1.9, SD = 0.7). Across all ten items, Cronbach’s Alpha showed adequate internal consistency, α = 0.73, 95% CI [0.67, 0.77], comparable to the internal consistency for the original scale (α = 0.68, 95% CI [0.60, 0.74]). The PCS-GER score revealed a mean correlation with the ten individual items of R = 0.53 (original data: R = 0.51). A visual inspection of the density histograms at the item level for the two samples (see ) shows similar distributions for each item. Distribution parameters are shown in . A more detailed descriptive comparison between scale- and item-level statistics of the validation samples of the PCS-GER and the original PCS () can be found in the .

displays the PCS score distribution of the German version against the distribution of the original data and a theoretical normal distribution, showing a similar approximately normal distribution for each scale. Additionally, a two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was conducted to compare the distribution of PCS scores for the Original and German sample. The test revealed no statistically significant difference between the distributions, D = 0.090, P = .232, indicating that the largest absolute difference between the empirical cumulative distribution functions of the two samples was 9%. A comparison of the latent factor structure between the German and the original data can be found in the .

Here, we present the German version of the PCS (PCS-GER), designed to measure the trait ability to generate perceptual experiences in response to external suggestions. This version represents a direct translation of the original English PCS developed by  conducted in accordance with established guidelines for questionnaire translation (). To validate that the German version of the PCS captures the same construct as the original scale, a large sample was collected.

Distribution parameters were compared with those reported in the validation study of the original PCS (). The distribution of PCS scores obtained with the PCS-GER showed similar properties to the distribution observed in the original English-language PCS sample. Internal consistency was also comparable to that reported in the original study. Inspection of individual item distributions indicated that they reflected the expected variation in item difficulty and item score distributions. Finally, these distributions closely matched those observed in the validation sample of the original PCS.

The present findings are consistent with previous studies that administered measures of responsiveness to imaginative suggestions online. In particular, the distribution of PC scores closely matched that reported for the Japanese translation of the PCS () with comparable distribution parameters, indicating that comparable PC score distributions can be obtained across different language versions of the PCS. Notably, whereas the original PCS validation sample was assessed in the laboratory, both the present study and the Japanese validation study collected data online. This pattern is consistent with the observations of , who likewise reported that online administration of measures assessing responsiveness to imaginative suggestions yields outcomes comparable to those obtained with traditional in-person administration.

A limitation of the present study is that neither test–retest reliability nor construct validity was assessed, e.g. through within-subject comparisons with related constructs, such as hypnotizability (; ). Thus, although the current findings provide initial evidence for the instrument’s psychometric performance, they do not constitute a comprehensive psychometric validation of the PCS-GER. However, both the original PCS and the Japanese version demonstrated good test–retest reliability and convergent validity (; ). Because the PCS-GER retained the original items, response format, and underlying construct, there was no strong theoretical reason to expect substantial differences in temporal stability and construct validity. Nevertheless, translation and cultural adaptation may influence how individual items are interpreted. Future studies should therefore address this limitation by assessing test–retest reliability as well as convergent and discriminant validity in a German sample evaluated for phenomenological control ability.

In summary, the present findings demonstrate that the German translation, PCS-GER, exhibits psychometric properties highly comparable to those of the original English-language PCS. Accordingly, the PCS-GER represents an appropriate instrument for assessing trait phenomenological control in German-speaking populations.

psychology.title: Defending the narrative self
psychology.abstract: The idea that the self is narrative in form is widely expressed in both academic study and everyday speech. It has also been widely disparaged. Criticism from philosophers has been especially vociferous, arguing not only that narrative views do not represent the best conception of self, but that they are misleading and potentially dangerous. In this paper, I develop and defend an account of the narrative self that addresses these challenges. I begin by exploring the charges made against narrative views in more detail, uncovering three distinct but interrelated objections. Using lessons from constructivist theories of episodic memory and narrative accounts of the self in developmental psychology (especially that of Robyn Fivush), I describe a view according to which a particular form of self-narration constitutes us as mature human selves by conferring a range of cognitive, behavioural and experiential capacities that enable sophisticated forms of social engagement. On this view, the self is not constituted by a self-narrative so much as we constitute ourselves as human selves by becoming self-narrators who construct our narratives within the constraints of a social–cultural framework. I show how this account addresses each of the three objections outlined at the beginning.This article is part of the discussion meeting issue ‘From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self’.
psychology.text:
The idea that the self is somehow narrative in form—that you are your story—has been widely expressed in both academic study and everyday speech. It has also been widely disparaged. Criticism from philosophers has been especially vociferous, arguing not only that narrative views do not represent the best conception of self, but that they are misleading and potentially dangerous. Our lives are not stories, critics insist, and narrative views are therefore necessarily both epistemically and morally harmful.

As is the case for most disputes that evoke passionate argument on both sides, there is a certain amount of talking past one another in debates about the narrative self. This paper aims to resolve some of the talking past and to articulate a view of the narrative approach that avoids the standard objections. Although critics offer plausible and familiar examples of potential pitfalls of a narrative conception of self, these are based on the assumptions that a narrative account of self must see our lives as like works of literature, constructed according to similar principles, and that whatever story we tell about ourselves is, according to narrative views, the unassailable truth of who we are. But this need not be so. We can see our lives as narrative in form without modelling them on literary narratives, and they can be narratives while still being constrained by fact. In what follows, I use resources from constructivist theories of episodic memory and developmental psychology to articulate an alternative picture of the narrative self. According to this view, we constitute ourselves as mature human selves by becoming self-narrators who track our ongoing lives within the constraints of a social–cultural framework.

I begin () with a discussion of the relevant objections to the narrative self. Next, I discuss how constructivist theories of episodic memory () and narrative approaches in developmental psychology () support a view of the narrative self as a natural developmental outcome for mature enculturated humans rather than, as critics seem to suppose, an optional, self-consciously constructed story we tell about ourselves. I then return to the original objections to the narrative approach (), showing how this account addresses them.

A common line of criticism levelled at narrative approaches to self argues that narrative is a singularly inappropriate framework for understanding the self. Narratives, critics argue, are inherently situational and selective, and this means that no narrative of a human life can possibly represent it accurately. Self-narratives, which are often taken to constitute the self according to narrative views, are especially suspect. The events we include in our self-narratives and our sense of their significance, critics warn, are inevitably shaped by distorting motivations—self-interest making them self-aggrandizing, or coercive social pressures making them oppressive. Trying to fit our lives into a narrative structure, they worry, makes us misrepresent our histories. Peter Goldie, for instance, says that ‘the demands of narrativity … seem to drag us towards thinking of our past thoughts, feelings, and deliberations as more determinate than they in fact were, and as reflective of an agency of which at the time we seemed quite bereft’ []. Galen Strawson argues that narrative always involves revision and invention. Turning our lives into narratives, he says, overwrites what actually happened, replacing it with a fictional version. In self-narration, one therefore risks moving away from ‘accurate self-understanding’ and the ‘truth of one's being’ []. Self-narrative necessarily distorts the self, according to Peter Lamarque, because literature and life are inherently different kinds of endeavours. Novels are artefacts created for aesthetic purposes, with each event and word chosen to further those purposes. Lives, by contrast, are messy natural processes, filled with accident and contingency [].

The harms of mistaking one's self-narrative for the actual self are not just epistemic, critics emphasize. The self-deception and self-aggrandizement/deprecation associated with self-narrative also interfere with wellbeing and moral engagement. Our tendency to remember ourselves as better, smarter, kinder and braver than we were prevents us from recognizing and addressing character flaws. Alternatively, we might take up a pathologically negative narrative that prevents us from recognizing our own worth. As Galen Strawson puts it, narrative understandings of the self can ‘close down important avenues of thought, impoverish our grasp of ethical possibilities, needlessly and wrongly distress those who do not fit their model and are potentially destructive in psychotherapeutic contexts’ [, p. 429].

Many of the worries raised about narrative seem plausible, but to be clear on their implications we will need to think more carefully about what the objections really claim and what evidence is provided for them. On close inspection, there seem to be three main, interrelated but distinguishable objections levelled against the narrative self. One (seen in Lamarque's objections []) is a broad rejection of narrative as a vehicle for self-understanding or self-constitution based on the disconnect in form between narrative and human life. Selves are not stories, according to this objection, and presenting them as such necessarily distorts them. A second, somewhat more modest claim (of which Goldie's is an example []) is that self-narratives are subject to irresistible distorting influences. We are motivated to see ourselves in a good light or play down our faults, and our sense of self can be infiltrated by pernicious stereotypes. The claim here is not about the narrative form itself, but the inherent unreliability of self-narratives as examples of the form. The third claim (seen in Strawson []) is the practical upshot of the first two. It argues that it is a harmful mistake to think of oneself as living a story and that we would do well to break ourselves of this habit.

The forms of unreliability and distortion these critics describe are familiar and plausible enough, but the conclusion that they negate the possibility of an illuminating and valuable narrative conception of self rests on implicit assumptions about epistemology and about the role narrative plays in constituting the self. The next two sections provide the resources to challenge these assumptions and develop an alternative understanding of the narrative self.

In arguing that the form of narrative necessarily distorts the truth of the self, critics tend to point especially to three features: first, narrative is by its nature selective. In developing a life narrative, we include some elements of our personal histories and not others. Second, it is interpretive. Narrative does not provide an objective recapitulation of historical facts but puts a spin on what we remember. Third, narrative is reconstructive. We remember in ways that serve our narratives rather than as things really happened. Because of this, narratives will inherently omit parts of our histories that would cast us in a different light, fail to be objective and deviate from fact. This means, critics conclude, that they cannot help but misrepresent the truth of the self.

I concede that narrative, self-narrative included, is selective, interpretive and reconstructive, but I reject the conclusion that this necessarily falsifies the self or makes narrative understandings of self harmful or misleading. If self-narrative were to select, interpret and reconstruct in just the way an author does in crafting a literary work, the resulting presentation of the self would indeed be suspect. But there are other principles by which we can and do select, interpret and reconstruct information that are both illuminating and valuable. This section uses constructivist views of episodic memory to support this general claim. The next section will provide more details about how the lessons learned here apply specifically to self-narrative.

The most straightforward way in which narrative mechanisms might appear falsifying is in their reconstruction of the personal past that represents what happened in a way that demonstrably deviates from the facts. My memory that I made a brilliant comment in a faculty meeting or took a heroic action last week may fit nicely into my self-narrative, according to which I am brave and wise. If in fact it was my colleague who made the remark or my neighbour who undertook the heroic deed, however, my self-narrative seems simply false. If we understand ‘truth’ as faithful correspondence to historical fact, and falsity as the opposite of truth, this argument is sound. Whatever our epistemological commitments, however, the more important point here is that deviating from historical fact does not always make a narrative misleading or harmful. On the contrary, there is reason to think that some forms of memory reconstruction yield insights more valuable and illuminating than strict reproduction.

The fact that our memories of specific past events often get details wrong is not news to anyone. I may vividly remember stopping at that diner with the great pie on our last road trip, but misremember the colour of the rental car we were driving, or the song playing on the jukebox when we walked in. The frequency of these common kinds of mistakes is empirically well documented []. If deviation from a comprehensive and entirely faithful reproduction of an event in one's history in recalling the personal past is a problem as critics allege, it is one that applies more broadly and not just to narrative views. Some forms of misremembering are highly pathological, of course, and even trivial forms of mistaken memory can have ill effects in specific contexts (e.g. eyewitness testimony in court). A crucial lesson of recent memory research, however, is that common misremembering is not always problematic, but can be instead adaptive.

The idea that memory is reconstructive, and that this is not necessarily a bad thing, is not new. In 1932, Frederic Bartlett argued that the nature and ubiquity of common memory errors suggest that we must give up the idea ‘that memory is primarily or literally reduplicative, or reproductive. In a world of constantly changing environment, literal recall is extraordinarily unimportant … memory appears to be far more decisively an affair of construction rather than one of mere reproduction’ [, pp. 204–205]. Recent decades have yielded deeper understanding of the cognitive and neural processes by which memory reconstruction takes place []. A strong connection between episodic memory and imagination has been demonstrated both in clinical contexts (patients with deficits in episodic memory also show difficulty imagining future or counterfactual scenarios [,]) and in neuroimaging studies, which show significant overlap in the neural mechanisms involved in episodic memory and those involved in imagining future and counterfactual scenarios [,,,]. This has led to the suggestion that instead of a dedicated system for reproducing past experiences in episodic memory, we have a more general system for constructing representations of specific episodes or scenes [;, pp. 100–101]. This system can produce episodic memories, representations of past counterfactuals (episodes that might have occurred but did not), or imaginings of possible future episodes.

These findings support Bartlett's original assertion that memory errors in healthy people can be adaptive. Schacter and Addis [,,] argue that, in many cases, alterations of an experience in memory are not the result of random error. They occur instead because, during the process of reconstruction, the event remembered is interpreted, contextualized and updated in ways that are cognitively useful. Schacter [] concludes that the ‘seven sins’ of memory (transience, absent-mindedness, blocking, suggestibility, bias, persistence and misattribution) that are commonly found in healthy populations serve an adaptive purpose. These manipulations allow us to extract relevant information from past experiences and present it in a way that serves present needs efficiently. Bartlett suggested that the memory errors he observed ‘were based on the operation of a schema that serves to organize and interpret experiences’ for our use, and Schacter sees present findings as vindicating this insight [,].

De Brigard emphasizes that this adaptive function of memory reconstruction undermines standard philosophical assumptions about the epistemology of memory. In the provocatively titled ‘Is memory for remembering?’ [], he notes that it is often taken for granted in philosophy that an ideally functioning memory system should faithfully reproduce past experiences. Although it is acknowledged that we misremember all the time, this is taken to be an unwanted consequence of the imperfection of our memory systems. The findings of Schacter and Addis, De Brigard argues, show that, on the contrary, we are frequently better off with a representation of an episode that presents information that has been condensed and distilled from multiple relevantly similar past experiences than we would be with an accurate recreation of one specific experience. Perfect fidelity should not always be taken as the ideal.

If we accept this approach, the argument that reconstruction by itself makes self-narrative misleading is not compelling. The kind of reconstruction I have described here involves selection and interpretation, so these narrative elements are also vindicated in this context. The narrative form thus does not seem necessarily distorting. It remains possible, however, that reconstruction is a special problem in the context of self-narrative. The kind of reconstruction that takes place in episodic memory according to constructivist views occurs at the sub-personal level as the operation of an evolved episodic memory system that serves to provide effective information about how to navigate the natural environment. Self-narration, by contrast, is a higher-order, linguistically mediated form of reconstruction that provides information about the self. To assess the value of reconstruction in the narrative context, I turn to work in developmental psychology.

Narrative views of self have played an important role in developmental psychology []. These views hold that humans construct an internalized, evolving life story, a process that begins in the preschool years and continues throughout the life course. This self-narrative provides a sense of oneself as a continuing being and generates a suite of capacities that allow new kinds of engagement with the natural and social world. Understanding these views better provides insight into how and when selection, interpretation and reconstruction can make a self-narrative illuminating and valuable, and what principles must be followed for it to do so.

Although there are many narrative theorists, Robyn Fivush puts special emphasis on how the reconstructive resources of episodic memory are harnessed and developed to produce a self-narrative, and I will focus on her work here. Especially important for our purposes is a distinction Fivush draws between episodic memory and what she calls ‘autobiographical’ memory []. Tulving's [] definition of episodic memory includes two components. One is ‘the idea that the memory is specific to what, when, and where (i.e., that the memory is of a specific event that happened at a particular time and place in the past)’ [p. 562]. The other is a sense of ‘mental time travel’, a feeling that we are ‘revisiting’ the past. This involves autonoetic awareness of the episode remembered as part of one's personal history. Fivush believes it is a mistake to assume that these two features always occur together (see also []).

There is ample evidence, she argues, that ‘what, where, when’ representation can be present without autonoesis. Research on the question of whether nonhuman animals have episodic memory ‘clearly demonstrates … that animals can recall specific experiences that occurred in the past and can use these experiences to guide their current and future behavior’. Moreover, the ability to remember specific past experiences is also demonstrated in the first year of human life, before autonoetic awareness is present [, p. 562]. She therefore distinguishes ‘episodic memory’, the kind of ‘what, when, where’ memory found in young humans and nonhuman animals, from the ‘ability to represent oneself as an experiencer of events, as a continuous being with a past, present, and future that links specific episodic representations into a meaningful sequence of events that define a person and a life’, which she sees as ‘a uniquely human ability’ [, p. 563]. ‘Autobiographical memory’, as she defines it, is this ‘uniquely human form of memory that moves beyond recall of experienced events to integrate perspective, interpretation and evaluation across self, other and time to create a personal history’ [, p. 560].

This kind of autobiographical memory is an acquired form of memory, a ‘complex human skill’ that ‘continues to develop and evolve across the lifespan’ [, p. 560]. It is, moreover, a skill that requires intensive social scaffolding in its development. Children need to be taught how to structure their memories in complex narrative forms by ‘participating in socially and culturally organized reminiscing in which one's own memories of a past event can be compared to another's.’ These interactions provide children with ‘the skills for creating more coherent and connected narratives that lead to the construction of a personal timeline’, thereby developing autonoetic consciousness, or ‘the sense of a subjective self as an experiencer of events’ [, p. 565].

As carers rehearse the day's events with children, often at bedtime, they help them develop expressions of recalled events into rudimentary stories that connect these events to other events, to affect, to their consequences and to future plans. If the child says ‘strawberries’, for instance, suggesting a recollection of eating strawberries earlier, the carer might reply, ‘Yes, we had strawberries today, they were yummy weren't they?’, adding, perhaps ‘Where did we get the strawberries? That's right, we went to the store and got them and brought them home. We ate them while we watched your show. What happened when your brother came home? That's right, you wouldn't share so I took the strawberries away, didn't I? Your brother was sad, wasn't he? But then you said ‘sorry’ and made up. What do you think? Do you want strawberries on your birthday cake?’ When regularly exposed to this kind of reminiscence (and projection), children begin telling simple narratives on their own. These stories become increasingly complex over time, turning eventually into mature adult narratives. As self-narratives become more sophisticated and robust, so does the subjective sense of self, which constitutes both a sense of identity through time and the autonoetic awareness that characterizes autobiographical memory. ‘Whereas episodic memories are of a series of single past events’, Fivush says, ‘autobiographical memory links past events together into a personal history that relates self through past, present, and future, essentially forming a life narrative’ [, p. 560].

The representational structure and content of simple ‘what, when, where’ memory is altered by subsuming it into a narrative. Personal memory in adults is complex, often including not only easily demarcated, discrete events but also extended events (e.g. a vacation to Paris), repeated events (e.g. birthdays when I was growing up) and life periods (e.g. while I was at university) [,]. Fivush follows the changes in content and structure of personal memories in Nelson's [] recordings of 2-year-old Emily's bedtime conversations with her parents and pre-sleep monologues over a 15-month period. At the beginning, Emily recalls very specific events of short duration. Over time, she describes events spanning longer and longer durations. Eventually, she starts to embed descriptions of subroutines within her recollection of routines (e.g. eating breakfast as part of the routine of getting ready to go to preschool), includes more mention of her own thoughts and feelings, talks more about the thoughts and feelings of others and what they are likely to do, and connects these causally. Her recollections become increasingly narrative in form, more diachronically extended and hierarchically organized, developing ‘from a loose collection of memories that are not coherently organized in time to recollection of related memories organized along a timeline’ [, p. 279].

Autobiographical memory is not, as Fivush sees it, a separate system that replaces episodic memory, but rather an augmentation of it. She takes on board the basic constructivist picture of episodic memory as involving adaptive reconstruction that allows us to navigate the natural world efficiently (described in ), and argues that this purpose can be met without autonoetic awareness. Autobiographical memory, however, serves a different purpose, which does require autonoesis. ‘Whereas event memory serves the function of organizing our knowledge of the world, a predictive function’, she says, ‘autobiographical memory serves the function of organizing our knowledge about ourselves, a self-defining function’ [, p. 277]. It ‘goes beyond the episodic memory function of guiding current and future behaviour to serve social and emotional functions’ [, pp. 560–561]. For this reason and based on ‘findings that individual autobiographical memory is socially and culturally variable and dependent on specific social-cultural interactions’, she speculates that this form of memory developed in humans to serve primarily social and cultural purposes [, p. 574].

Although this gives autobiographical memory a different set of reconstructive principles from episodic memory (organizing, contextualizing and updating information about the self for purposes of social interaction as opposed to organizing, contextualizing and updating information about the natural world to navigate it more effectively), Fivush is explicit that these are not separate memory systems. The ‘same memories’, she says, can simultaneously allow us to anticipate and predict the world around us and help define how we think about ourselves’ [, p. 277]. If episodic memory condenses, interprets, contextualizes and updates information about the world gained from multiple experiences, autobiographical memory condenses, interprets, contextualizes and updates information about the self over time. In so doing, it adds a new dimension to our overall memorial structure, making reconstructive use of the fully narrative tools of social–cultural schemas in addition to the proto-narrative reconstructive tools of the episodic memory system.

The narrative organization found in autobiographical memory requires language. ‘Narratives are canonical linguistic forms that specify a sequence of actions and the links between them’, Fivush says. But autobiographical memory is not itself linguistic [, p. 565]. Like all memory, she continues, ‘autobiographical memory is composed of multiple sensory components that are stored and retrieved across multiple brain areas [,]. … Thus, the argument is that culturally defined narratives, linguistic forms that provide schemes and guidelines for understanding how human events occur [] help shape the way in which individuals come to recall their personal past’ [, p. 565]. Shared reminiscing adds new reconstructive tools to the episodic toolbox in the form of socio-cultural norms, causing us to remember in new ways. The complex form of memory this yields simultaneously expresses useful information about the natural world and about oneself in the social world, allowing us to predict and act effectively in each domain.

It is worth pointing out, though this is not something Fivush emphasizes, that social reminiscing does not just teach children how to organize specific memories, connecting them to one another, and to their social circumstances. It also conveys an abstract overall template for living a human life and encourages the child to internalize a sense of itself as a human among humans, living such a life. In social reminiscing, children are prompted not only to look backward and organize their understanding of what happened but also to consider what might have happened, to connect their understanding of the actual and counterfactual past to how things are for them now, and to use this understanding to anticipate and plan for the future. As the span of autobiographical memory expands, so does the span of past and future projection, and of overall narrative scope scaffolded by carers. Children are encouraged to look forward to when they will go to school like their elder siblings or get married and have children of their own. They are asked what they are going to be when they grow up. The specifics of these promptings vary in different social–cultural contexts. Across cultures, however, children are made aware of the standard cultural milestones and know roughly the shape their own life is expected to take [,]. As Addis et al. put it, we ‘possess an understanding of how, within our culture, the prototypical life should unfold in terms of the order and timing of significant life events’. This, they say, provides a ‘temporal ‘template’ that organizes past experiences and gives us a sense of what to anticipate in the future’ [, p. 800;,].

This does not mean that everyone will automatically meet every cultural milestone, nor that they will, or should, aspire to. Nonetheless, these milestones, met or missed, pursued or rejected, form a backdrop against which our day-to-day experience takes place. It is not just what happened in the past that influences our experience or actions, but when it happens. Setbacks when one is starting out in adult life, for instance, may have a different valance from those that occur towards its end. A medical complication or a windfall may similarly have different significance depending on when it occurs, in part because this affects the degree to which it interferes with or supports the expected unfolding of a life [,]. In addition to tracking and organizing the specific details of our lives and their relation to one another, self-narration also tracks progression along the life course. This tracking is also usually implicit, operating in the background. I know roughly where I am on my life course, whether I am just starting out or nearing the end, whether milestones like finding a mate, having children, building a career (or personally and culturally appropriate analogues) are probably in front of or behind me. This all makes a difference in how I see and move through the world.

In the typical case, the tracking of specific autobiographical facts and of whole life progress are deeply interconnected. Just how much the development of autobiographical memory alters our experience of self-in-time can be seen, however, by noting that the overall sense of oneself living a human life appears capable of surviving the loss of the capacity for autobiographical memory that gave rise to it. Addis and colleagues have found that individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD) appear, at least for a time, to retain perception of themselves as diachronically unified individuals leading a human life, despite severe deficits in autobiographical memory [,]. Studies on individuals with episodic amnesia also reveal that their attitudes towards their own pasts and futures, including temporal discounting and the ability to predict future regret, remain intact [,]. Those with severely compromised autobiographical memory often express distress at their inability to place and contextualize their experience. The experience of lack seems to presuppose retained awareness that they are living a life that is theirs to track, while lacking the wherewithal to do it.

The understanding of the narrative self I propose is thus a self that emerges from a more basic or ‘minimal’ self (e.g. []) when children are inducted into the practice of self-narrative within their cultural context, coming to track their progress along a broad expected life trajectory, both implicitly and explicitly, at many levels of specificity and awareness. This tracking gives rise to experiential, emotional and cognitive capacities, which in turn make it possible to engage in activities, abilities and forms of experience that characterize the mature human self. These include, for instance, developing and pursuing long-term goals and plans, considering the future consequences of acting on our desires, experiencing existential angst and committing to and fighting for our values. A self-narrative, on this view, is not a story I might or might not decide to spin about myself. It is a way of organizing experience that serves to constitute a mature human self, and its effects are profound and transformative.

described three interrelated objections commonly levelled against narrative approaches to the self. Having outlined the particular narrative view I wish to defend, I am now in a position to offer a quick account of how it can respond to each objection.

The first objection targets narrative form, arguing that self-narration is necessarily misleading (and probably harmful) because narrative is inherently selective, interpretive and reconstructive. The discussion of constructivist accounts of episodic memory in  gave us reason to reject the assumption that selection, interpretation and reconstruction automatically mislead. Memory reconstruction that summarizes and contextualizes information gained in the past, presenting it in a way that informs effective prediction and interaction with the environment is, to the contrary, illuminating and beneficial. Fivush's account of self-narrative as a means of organizing experience in a way that facilitates social coordination and engagement shows how selection, interpretation and reconstruction are similarly instructive and useful in the context of self-narration insofar as they succeed in presenting summarized and contextualized information about oneself that supports effective social interaction.

The second worry concerns biases that, according to critics, distort self-narratives. Even if a self-narrative could in principle be illuminating, this argument suggests, in practice it will not be because of these powerful motivations to narrate inaccurately. I do not deny that such biases exist, nor that they can and do sometimes mislead us. But this does not mean that they will inevitably do so, or even that they usually do. The examples of motivated self-misrepresentation provided are anecdotal, and we are given no information about their frequency. Moreover, it is not obvious that, even when they do occur, they make one's self-narrative deeply misleading. Just as many deviations from historical fact in episodic memory are trivial and harmless, so are many minor distortions in self-narrative. Moreover, the view I have described provides a criterion for identifying and potentially correcting significantly deviant self-narratives.

Once again, an analogy with episodic memory is useful. When memory is reconstructed in a way that is not suited to its purpose, it will lead to failures of prediction and ineffective interactions with the environment. If this happens only occasionally, it can provide important information that can be used to improve reconstructive success in the future. Reconstruction that persistently and pervasively leads to ineffective interactions with the environment, however, is pathological, and we have a principled way to identify it as such.
