To say that reconstructed memory is not necessarily misleading just because it deviates from faithful reproduction of historical fact is not to say that it is never misleading. The relevant point here, however, is that this is the exception rather than the rule. The existence of occasional pathology does not undermine the claim that reconstruction done well can be instructive and valuable, even if (indeed because) it deviates from faithful reproduction of a past event.

I suggest that the situation is much the same for self-narrative. In many cases, failure to faithfully reproduce past events in autobiographical memory will not be importantly misleading. If, for instance, I remember making a particular brilliant remark that I did not, but I make such remarks often and am widely known for my brilliance, the fact that I was wrong about this instance does not make my narrative fail to represent my nature, and will probably have few implications for social interaction. If, on the other hand, I consider myself generous because I have selectively included my few acts of largesse in my narrative, leaving out the vastly more numerous occasions on which I was withholding and stingy, the situation is different. Here, I will be operating with a sense of myself that will probably lead to false predictions about how I will be received by others and otherwise interfere with effective social interaction. In such cases, I will receive pushback from the social world in something like the way faulty episodic reconstruction leads to pushback from the natural environment. This might lead me to reconsider my self-narrative, adjusting and updating it. If this feedback does not have such an effect, however, and I persistently and pervasively select, interpret and reconstruct in ways that are deviant, my narrative will fail in its purpose of facilitating effective social interaction, and we will be able to identify it as pathological.

That this is so, is implied by the objection itself. The case that self-narrative is unreliable because it is subject to distorting biases is supported through examples. To do the intended work, the examples given must be clear and uncontroversial instances in which events are selected, interpreted or reconstructed in a way that results in a misleading or false self-narrative. Otherwise, they would fail as compelling examples of a falsifying narrative. If the faultiness of these acts of self-narration is evident in the examples, however, it will also be evident if we encounter such a case in vivo. We do meet people who we can recognize as unreliable self-narrators, impervious to feedback. And probably many, or even most, of us have biases or motivations that slightly distort our own sense of self. But the kind of systematic bias that fundamentally misrepresents who someone is in a way that constitutes or borders on delusion is relatively rare. The purpose of self-narrative, according to my view, is not to provide an entirely faithful version of one's history, or a completely unassailable representation of one's nature. It is to engage effectively in the social world. Small detectable distortions are compatible with this purpose, and pervasive and significant distortions, which are not, are recognizable as pathologies.

The third objection suggests that we would be better off if we were not self-narrators. It is difficult to answer this charge directly because it seems aimed at a narrative view according to which we decide to make our lives conform to some particular narrative archetype taken, perhaps, from myth, or literature, or film. This is very different from the view I have proposed, in which we acquire the capacity to constitute ourselves as mature human selves by learning to organize our experience narratively, tracking our ongoing lives in ways that allow us to make ourselves intelligible to others and to ourselves. In this picture, self-narration is not something we choose, but something that emerges as a developmental stage of humans in culture. Asking whether we should organize our experience in this way is somewhat like asking whether we should be episodic rememberers. Perhaps, because self-narration is an acquired capacity, there is a possibility for choice with respect to being self-narrators that is not present with respect to an evolved biological system like episodic memory. But the very ability to raise this question requires that we conceive ourselves as temporally extended beings who care about how our lives go and wonder about what kind of social organization will make them go best. To conceive and consider it, we need the kinds of cognitive tools bestowed by self-narration. Even if we could reject this form of self-narration, doing so would make us quite other kinds of beings than we are.

The standard objections raised against narrative conceptions of the self are aimed most directly at the view that we spin stories about who we are and what we are like, and that whatever story we spin is, by definition, the truth about us. I agree that such a view has serious difficulties, but it is not the only way to think of the narrative self, and I have offered an alternative. Beneath the specifics of these objections, however, there is an underlying thought that suggests a broader challenge that any narrative view does need to meet. At the most general level, the standard objections express a worry that if the self is narrative and narratives are stories we make up, there is no room for any self-narrative to be false or delusional, and it seems obvious that sometimes they are. I accept the claim that self-narratives can be, and sometimes are, misguided or delusional, but reject the assumption that seeing the self as a narrative construct makes this inevitable or even common. All that is required to avoid it is for there to be non-arbitrary constraints on identity-constituting self-narration. My disagreement with the critics is about what these constraints are and where they come from.

The standard objections imply that the only acceptable constraint is a strict and faithful correspondence to historical facts. This approach is implausible, suggesting that an accurate sense of self would have to be a comprehensive and uninterpreted representation of all the events in our history. Constructivist views of episodic memory provide a model of how successful construction can instead be constrained by success relative to a purpose, and Fivush's social-developmental view of autobiographical memory shows how this insight can be applied to self-narratives, which serve the purpose of allowing effective social engagement. We cannot make up just any story about ourselves and have it be true. But there are different ways a self-narrative can go wrong. Here are two: it can deviate from historical fact, or it can fail to be an accurate representation of what we are like as participants in the social world. I suggest that the constraints needed to avoid the second sort of failure are possibly more important. These come from the social world, and to meet them we need to be able to track our lives within basic social–cultural constraints. This is just what our self-narratives allow us to do, constituting us as mature human selves, even if we sometimes get things wrong.

psychology.title: The news we use: A systematic scoping review of fake news stimuli in psychological research
psychology.abstract: Research into fake news has surged in popularity, with over 3,000 publications on the topic each year since 2021. Definitions of what constitutes “fake news” vary across the field of psychology, where source, number, content, and presentation of stimuli may all be different yet still described as “fake news.” Thus, conclusions drawn from fake news research may only generalize to the particular definition or presentation of fake news used in a given study. Relatedly, stimuli may not be available or described clearly enough for reproducibility. To assess the scope of these potential issues, we conducted and reported a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) systematic scoping review of three databases including the last 11 years of psychology studies that used fake news stimuli. From the 881 included studies, we extracted and described the number, source, standardization, framing, and availability of fake news stimuli. Our findings suggest a large degree of stimuli variability, with high rates of example and full set availability. Most frequently, research stimuli were about politics and were framed as a social media post, and examples were given in-text. We also evaluated ratios of real to fake news stimuli, where an equal number of real and fake articles was the most frequent ratio. We recommend continued transparency, offering suggestions for open science practices following copyright law and considerations of generalizability regarding fake news in research.

psychology.title: Prevalence, Severity, and Functional Disability of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders Among Ophthalmologists in Saudi Arabia: A National Cross-Sectional Survey
psychology.abstract: Ophthalmology is a clinical and surgical specialty with high physical demands. Despite advancements in ophthalmic equipment, improper ergonomic practices contribute to work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), affecting practitioners’ performance and productivity.This study investigated the prevalence, severity, and functional disability of WMSDs among ophthalmologists in Saudi Arabia using the Total Disability Index (TDI) and examining associations between disability severity and task-related difficulty.A national cross-sectional survey included 280 ophthalmologists practicing in Saudi Arabia, recruited through institutional and professional channels and convenience-based dissemination. Data were collected from Jan–Apr 2025. Functional impairment was assessed using the validated 14-item TDI. Multivariable logistic regression modeled associations between TDI scores and task-related pain, adjusting for confounders.Among 280 ophthalmologists, 85.7% reported WMSDs symptoms, most commonly weekly. Mean TDI score was 8.0 ± 9.3. Most (90.0%) had minimal disability, 8.6% moderate, and 1.4% severe. None had crippling or bed-bound disability. The cervical (27.9%) and lumbar spine (25.7%) were most affected. Higher TDI scores independently predicted pain during clinic examinations (adjusted OR = 1.124; p < 0.001), laser procedures (OR = 1.064; p < 0.001), and surgery (OR = 1.065; p < 0.001).WMSDs are highly prevalent among ophthalmologists practicing in Saudi Arabia and are associated with measurable task-related difficulty. These findings support structured ergonomics education, exercise programs, and institution-level workplace modifications.
psychology.text:
Ophthalmology is a clinical and surgical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and treating eye diseases. Practice in this field frequently requires awkward and repetitive postures, prolonged static loading, and recurrent bending or twisting while maintaining fine motor control and sustained visual focus. These demands are common during routine daily tasks such as slit-lamp examinations and the use of diagnostic lenses, indirect ophthalmoscopes, loupes, and surgical microscopes. Collectively, these occupational exposures are strongly associated with an increased risk of work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), which have been reported in more than half of ophthalmologists across multiple studies.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines WMSDs as injuries to muscles, tendons, and joints resulting from work-related conditions and poses significant challenges across various professions, particularly in healthcare., In the US, WMSDs account for over $20 billion annually in workers’ compensation. Importantly, WMSDs may have significant occupational consequences, including reduced clinical and surgical workload, changes in working hours, and, in severe cases, early withdrawal from clinical practice.

The prevalence of WMSDs among ophthalmologists varies across different countries. In the United States, a survey found that 66% of ophthalmologists experienced work-related pain. Similarly, 62.4% of respondents in the United Kingdom reported back or neck pain. Additionally, Indian studies have consistently demonstrated a high prevalence of WMSDs among ophthalmologists, ranging from 74.77% to 75.3%,, while another Indian study found that 73% of oculoplastic surgeons reported work-related pain during surgery and 11.7% were forced to discontinue operating because of severe discomfort.

In Saudi Arabia, a study conducted at a tertiary eye institute found a 70% prevalence of self-reported neck and back pain among ophthalmologists and allied eye care professionals. Another study reported a 66.7% prevalence of WMSDs.

Despite the high prevalence of WMSDs among ophthalmologists, their functional impact remains less well characterized. This study addresses this gap by using the validated Total Disability Index (TDI) to quantify functional impairment using a unified disability score and to examine its association with difficulty performing key ophthalmic tasks. The TDI was chosen because it provides a quantitative assessment of functional disability, unlike other commonly used instruments that focus primarily on the presence and anatomical distribution of musculoskeletal symptoms.

A cross-sectional survey was conducted among ophthalmologists practicing in Saudi Arabia, including residents, fellows, registrars, specialists, and consultants across ophthalmology subspecialties. The survey targeted clinicians who routinely use ophthalmic instruments that pose ergonomic risks, including slit lamps, indirect ophthalmoscopes, loupes, and surgical microscopes. Data collection occurred between January and April 2025. Reporting followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for observational studies.

Ethical approval was obtained from three institutional review boards: Alfaisal University (IRB20299), Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital (DESH1153), and King Khalid Eye Specialist Hospital and Research Center (RD/26001/IRB/0169-25). Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study complies with the Declaration of Helsinki.

The study included ophthalmologists aged 25–74 years who were actively practicing in Saudi Arabia (consultants, fellows, specialists, registrars, and residents), regardless of nationality, and employed in either the government or private sectors. Exclusion criteria included incomplete surveys, individuals outside the specified age range, and those not actively practicing in Saudi Arabia.

The target population comprised ophthalmologists actively practicing in Saudi Arabia. The ophthalmologist population was estimated at 2697 based on statistics from the Saudi Ministry of Health. Sample size was calculated using an online sample size calculator, assuming a previously reported WMSDs prevalence of 72.5% from Tan et al, a US ophthalmology study that also used the TDI, with a 95% confidence level, and a 5% margin of error. This yielded a minimum required sample size of 276. A total of 303 responses were received; 280 responses met eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis after excluding incomplete surveys and responses from individuals not practicing in Saudi Arabia.

A mixed recruitment approach was used. The survey link was disseminated through official Email lists and professional channels affiliated with the Saudi Ophthalmology Society (SOS), King Khalid Eye Specialist Hospital and Research Center (KKESH-RC), and Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital (DESH). Additional recruitment was conducted through convenience-based dissemination, including outreach via X and WhatsApp, as well as direct contact with eye hospitals across Saudi Arabia. Before participation, respondents were informed of the study objectives, confidentiality and the intended use of the data.

The research instrument was a 31-item, self-administered, structured English-language questionnaire administered via Microsoft Forms (Appendix 1). The questionnaire was not formally pilot-tested; however, the validated 14-item TDI was used without modification, including its original items, response options, and scoring algorithm. The questionnaire comprised four domains: (1) participation and eligibility/consent; (2) demographics and practice characteristics; (3) working conditions and MSK; (4) disability assessment using the Total Disability Index (TDI).

WMSDs were defined as episodes of pain or discomfort. Participants were asked to report the frequency of pain episodes over the past year (ranging from daily to once every few months) and the specific clinical settings where discomfort occurred, such as during slit-lamp examinations, laser procedures, or surgery. The functional impact of pain on clinical tasks was assessed using a five-level scale ranging from “doesn’t affect” to “caused me to stop this activity”. It also measured the functional impact of this pain on clinical tasks and whether it necessitated changes in working hours. Additionally, Participants could optionally provide narrative comments.

Functional disability was assessed using the 14-item Total Disability Index (TDI), a statistically validated scale that quantifies the effects of neck, back, spinal, and global musculoskeletal pain on daily living and professional activities. It measured 14 distinct items: pain intensity, personal care, lifting, walking, sitting, standing, sleeping, social life, traveling, reading, headaches, concentration, work capacity, and driving.

The TDI is a composite instrument derived from a combination of the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and the Neck Disability Index (NDI). The TDI comprises nine items from the ODI and five from the NDI; each item was scored on a 6-point Likert scale that represents a range of disability levels, from 0 to 5, with 5 indicating the most severe disability. The score from each question is summed, and the maximum possible score is 70. This sum is then divided by the product of the number of answered questions multiplied by 5. The result is then multiplied by 100 to convert it into a percentage.

Afterwards, it was categorized based on TDI score percentage, ranging from minimal disability all the way to bed-bound disability. The TDI score (%) interpretation is as follows: minimal (0–20%), moderate (21–40%), severe (41–60%), crippling (61–80%), or bed-bound (81–100%) disability, consistent with published scoring conventions., Higher TDI scores were hypothesized to be associated with greater workload among ophthalmologists.

Independent Variable: Gender, age, job title, subspeciality, work sector, years of practice.

Dependent Variable: TDI score.

The statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS (version 29). Only complete eligible responses were included in the final analysis; no missing data were present in the analyzed variables, and no imputation was required. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics, presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for continuous variables and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. For the logistic regression analyses, the five-level task-related difficulty response was dichotomized for each clinical task into no difficulty (“doesn’t affect”) and any difficulty (all other response categories). Multivariable logistic regression models were then used to assess the association of TDI score, pain location, and pre-career musculoskeletal diagnosis with task-related difficulty during clinic examinations, laser procedures, and surgery. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated; p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Group comparisons of TDI scores across demographic and clinical subgroups were performed using an independent-samples Welch’s t-test for two-group comparisons and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for comparisons across more than two groups.

The study included 280 ophthalmologists. More than half were male (156, 55.7%), while females accounted for 124 (44.3%). The majority of participants were aged 25–34 years (154, 55.0%). The largest BMI category was normal weight, and the mean BMI was 25.8 ± 4.2 kg/m2. Nearly half were consultants (127, 45.4%), and 111 (39.6%) were residents. Most participants reported a single Ophthalmology surgical sub-specialty (222, 79.3%), while 46 (16.4%) practiced both surgical and medical Ophthalmology subspecialties (). Nearly half of the participants had 1–5 years of practice (121, 43.2%). Pre-career MSK diagnosis were uncommon, with 244 (87.1%) reporting no prior diagnosis ().

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) have been identified globally as a leading cause of absenteeism and productivity loss across diverse professions., Despite advanced ophthalmic equipment, poor ergonomic practices remain a major contributor to pain and disability.

This study aimed to investigate the prevalence, severity, and functional disability of WMSDs among ophthalmologists practicing in Saudi Arabia and to examine the relationship between disability severity and task-related difficulty across key ophthalmic activities.

Our study demonstrates a high prevalence of WMSDs in this population, with 85.7% of participants reporting symptoms within the past year. This prevalence exceeds most comparable international studies and is higher than previously reported local estimates.

Compared with the international literature, previous studies from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and India have reported WMSDs prevalence ranging from 52% to 75.3% among ophthalmologists.,,

Locally, a study conducted at a tertiary eye institute in Saudi Arabia reported a 70% prevalence of self-reported WMSDs among ophthalmologists and allied eye care professionals. Another Saudi study showed the prevalence of WMSDs was 66.7%.

In contrast to previous studies that relied on small, single-center samples and non-standardized, subjective measures, this study offers a national-level assessment of ophthalmologists across Saudi Arabia with broad representation of practice settings and training levels. It extends existing evidence by combining prevalence with functional disability within a comprehensive framework.

Our findings align with the landmark US study by Tan et al, which was the first to apply the TDI among ophthalmologists. Both studies demonstrated that the cohort remained within the minimal disability range overall. Tan et al reported a mean TDI score of 6.2 ± 7.3% out of 100% with only 5.0% (n=5) experiencing moderate disability and no participants in severe, crippling, or bed-bound categories. In contrast, our study demonstrated a higher mean TDI score of 8.0 ± 9.3% (range: 0–47.1%), with 90.0% experiencing minimal disability (0–20%), 8.6% moderate disability (21–40%), and 1.4% severe disability (41–60%), and no participants in crippling (61–80%), or bed-bound (81–100%) categories.

Notably, 10.0% of our cohort had moderate-to-severe disability, compared with 5.0% reported by Tan et al. Severe disability accounted for 1.4% of participants in our study, whereas no severe cases were reported in the Tan et al cohort. This difference is notable given that the cohort in Tan et al was older (mean age 50.0 ± 10.4 years) than ours (mean age 38.4 ± 11.6 years), suggesting that factors beyond age may contribute to the observed burden of occupational disability. Differences in ergonomic exposures, work patterns, and population characteristics may have influenced this variation, while reverse causation and generational or practice-pattern cohort effects may also partly explain the between-study differences.

Multivariable logistic regression, adjusting for pain location, Pre-career MSK diagnosis, age, gender, BMI, and daily working hours, demonstrated that higher TDI scores independently predicted increased odds of task-related difficulty: clinic examinations (adjusted OR = 1.124; p < 0.001), laser procedures (OR = 1.064; p < 0.001), and surgical procedures (OR = 1.065; p < 0.001).

Pain location was additionally significant for clinic examinations (OR = 1.168; p = 0.021). In contrast, neither previous MSK diagnosis nor daily working hours were statistically significant predictors in any of the three models. Several factors merit consideration when interpreting these null findings: (1) Limited subgroup power: the pre-career MSK diagnosis group (n=36, 12.9%) was relatively small, which may have constrained statistical power to detect clinically meaningful effects even if they exist; (2) Potential ceiling/floor effects: the lack of daily working hours association aligns with prior studies (Kitzmann et al, 2012) and may reflect that ergonomic quality—rather than volume of exposure—determines occupational impairment, though our cross-sectional design cannot definitively establish this mechanism; (3) Absence of evidence vs evidence of absence: the non-significance of these variables should not be interpreted as proof that pre-existing pathology or workload have no role, but rather that they were not independently significant in this particular cohort after adjustment for other factors. Overall, our findings suggest that functional disability and current pain severity—rather than workload volume or remote pre-career MSK history—are more robust predictors of acute task-related difficulty, a finding consistent with the functional impairment framework proposed by Kitzmann et al.

Female ophthalmologists reported significantly higher mean TDI scores than males (p = 0.001). This gender disparity is consistent with previous reports., Proposed mechanisms include greater physiological susceptibility to repetitive strain injuries, differences in upper-body muscle mass and endurance, and hormonal influences.

Interestingly, despite higher overall disability scores in females, female gender was independently associated with lower odds of reporting pain-related difficulty during laser procedures (OR = 0.333, p= 0.002). It may reflect differences in laser practice patterns, ergonomic adaptations, or unmeasured confounding factors; Therefore, this association should be interpreted cautiously and warrants further investigation.

BMI showed significant association (p = 0.022), with highest scores among obese participants (11.69 ± 12.15), compared to underweight (8.57 ± 8.33), normal weight (7.63 ± 8.70). Even modest obesity was associated with substantially elevated TDI scores, underscoring the potential value of weight management.

Exercise frequency was the only behavioral variable significantly associated with TDI scores (p = 0.045), with lower scores among more frequent exercisers. Scores declined progressively from 9.76 ± 10.25 among non-exercisers to 4.17 ± 5.19 among those exercising 5–6 days/week. However, the daily exercise group (n=5) showed unexpectedly high scores (10.57), which may reflect the effect of the small subgrouped sample or survivor bias or other unmeasured confounding factors. Eventually this inverse dose-response relationship between the TDI and the exercise provides strong evidence that physical activity is the most beneficial of the self-directed strategies used to reduce WMSDs. This is consistent with evidence from a randomized controlled trial by Shariat et al, where a structured exercise program significantly improved neck, shoulder, and lower back pain over time. Similarly, Al Taisan et al found a higher prevalence of WMSDs among ophthalmologists who didn’t engage in running, supporting a protective effect of regular aerobic exercise. The finding that 40.0% reported not exercising represents a substantial modifiable risk factor. Physical wellness programs could represent a high-impact, low-cost intervention strategy.

TDI was strongly associated with symptom burden. Participants reporting daily pain had highest TDI scores (16.15 ± 12.00), declining through weekly (9.29 ± 9.64), monthly (6.75 ± 7.28), and occasional pain (5.63 ± 6.85), while asymptomatic participants had lowest scores (2.64 ± 4.65; p < 0.001). This dose-response highlight the generalizability of the TDI validity.

Participants changing their working hours had substantially higher TDI scores (16.15 ± 13.00 vs 7.29 ± 8.60; p = 0.004), providing convergent validity linking self-reported disability with concrete behavioral consequences.

The impact Clinical provides additional insight into how WMSDs affect ophthalmic practice. While 48.1% reported no effect on examinations, this proportion declined to 36.0% for laser procedures and 35.2% for surgery, suggesting that physically demanding and precision-dependent tasks are more vulnerable to the effects of WMSDs a small subset reported discontinuing activities altogether, including laser procedures (2.1%), surgery (0.9%), and examinations (0.8%).

Consistent with this observation, 8.2% reported pain-necessitated changes in working hours. This finding aligns with previous reports demonstrating reductions in working hours of up to 10% and early retirement in 1–2% of affected clinicians due to WMSDs. Similarly, Rafique et al (2022) found that 35.5% of ophthalmologists experienced decreased productivity, while 23.36% modified their outpatient activities (p < 0.01).

Limitations include reliance on self-reported data, the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference, small cell counts in some subgroup analyses, the absence of objective ergonomic measurements, and potential selection bias. Because recruitment combined targeted institutional lists with open channels, including Twitter/X and WhatsApp, a formal response rate could not be calculated.

Future research should employ longitudinal designs, objective posture monitoring, and economic analyses. Clinically, routine TDI screening could identify at-risk practitioners. Interventions should target modifiable factors, particularly physical inactivity and obesity. Integration of occupational health education into training programs and institutional ergonomic support are essential for long-term workforce health.

WMSDs represent a significant occupational health burden among ophthalmologists in Saudi Arabia, with a high prevalence (85.7%) and predominant involvement of the cervical and lumbar spine. The mean TDI score was 8.0 ± 9.3, and higher TDI scores independently predicted greater pain-related difficulty during essential clinical activities, including clinic examinations, laser procedures, and surgery. In addition, 8.2% of participants reported modifying their working hours because of symptoms. Female sex and obesity emerged as significant risk factors, whereas regular exercise appeared protective. These findings support structured ergonomics education, workplace modifications, and physical wellness initiatives to reduce the occupational impact of WMSDs.

psychology.title: Effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted cognitive behavioral therapy on mental health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis protocol
psychology.abstract: Sexual and gender minority populations experience disproportionately high rates of mental disorders due, in large part, to their chronic exposure to stigma, discrimination, and minority stress. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established evidence-based psychotherapy; however, conventional CBT was primarily developed among predominantly cisgender, heterosexual individuals and not often addresses identity-specific stressors relevant to LGBTQ individuals. Emerging adaptations of LGBTQ-affirmative CBT integrate components that affirm sexual and gender minority identities and target minority stress. Although the number of investigations testing such interventions has increased, evidence remains fragmented across studies. To our knowledge, no systematic review has examined the efficacy of LGBTQ targeted CBT on improving mental health outcomes.This systematic review aims to synthesize empirical evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted CBT interventions in reducing mental health symptoms among sexual and gender minority adults.A comprehensive search will be conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus, supplemented by gray-literature searches. Eligible studies include RCTs conducted on adults aged 18–65 and evaluating LGBTQ targeted CBT compared with usual care, waitlist, or active controls. Outcomes include depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorder symptom changes at post-intervention and follow-up. Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, with risk of bias assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Where feasible, meta-analyses using random-effects models in R will estimate standardized mean differences or risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Overall efficacy and potential moderators, such as intervention delivery mode and duration, will be investigated.By consolidating the evidence base for LGBTQ targeted CBT, this review will clarify its efficacy, identify key intervention features associated with improved outcomes, and provide guidance for evidence-based mental health care for sexual and gender minority populations.This protocol has been pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: CRD420251173207).
psychology.text:
The lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) population encompasses a wide range of identities and experiences around the world. Despite this diversity, a consistent pattern emerges across cultural settings: sexual minority individuals often remain socially marginalized and invisible, facing numerous risk factors that threaten their physical and psychological well-being []. Research continues to show that compared to heterosexual individuals, gender and sexual minorities are disproportionately affected by mental health challenges, such as higher rates of depression, anxiety, and substance misuse [–].

A widely cited explanation for these disparities is the minority stress model [,], which argues that chronic exposure to stigma-related stressors, including discrimination, victimization, and harassment, contributes significantly to negative health outcomes. Expanding on this perspective, the psychological mediation framework [] emphasizes that persistent exposure to prejudice and social exclusion disrupts both internal processes (e.g., self-regulation, coping) and interpersonal relationships, ultimately increasing vulnerability to mental health disorders. Given that minority stress influences cognitive, emotional, and behavioral functioning [], it is closely linked to mental health difficulties as well as various health risk behaviors. Depression, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and substance use disorders represent some of the most prevalent and impairing mental health conditions among LGBTQ individuals and are strongly associated with minority stress exposure. With the ongoing disproportionate mental health burden faced by LGBTQ individuals, it is crucial to address these disparities by identifying and implementing effective, evidence-based interventions that can reduce their mental health symptoms and promote well-being.

Psychotherapy is well established as an effective treatment for a wide range of mental health problems. Among these approaches, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most empirically supported treatments and is suitable for addressing cognitive, affective, and behavioral minority stress processes []. However, traditional CBT protocols were largely developed and validated in cisgender, heterosexual samples and were not specifically designed to address minority stress processes or identity-specific challenges, such as stigma, concealment, or rejection, that are particularly salient for LGBTQ individuals [].

In response, researchers have developed LGBTQ-affirmative CBT adaptations that integrate strategies to target minority stress-related cognitive, affective, and behavioral mechanisms. For instance, a 10-session transdiagnostic CBT intervention targeting young sexual minority men produced small-to-moderate improvements in depression, anxiety, substance use, and suicidality, highlighting the potential of minority stress-focused CBT to address co-occurring mental health difficulties []. Another trial with gender-diverse sexual minority women found that affirmative CBT produced large reductions in depression and anxiety relative to a waitlist control []. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of LGBTQ-affirmative internet-based CBT, conducted among LGBTQ youth in the United States [] and sexual minority men in China [], found that the interventions reduced psychological distress and improved depression and anxiety symptoms, with stronger effects among participants exposed to higher levels of stigma.

Together, these findings indicate that CBT, when affirmatively adapted, might yield meaningful improvements in mental health outcomes for LGBTQ populations. These outcomes, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, OCD, and substance use disorders, are also among those with the most robust empirical support for CBT, making them theoretically and clinically appropriate targets for evaluating the effectiveness of LGBTQ adapted CBT interventions. Nonetheless, the evidence base remains scattered. Many trials involve small samples, brief follow-ups, and heterogeneous outcome measures that limit comparability across studies. This highlights the need for systematic synthesis to clarify the overall effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted CBT interventions.

Although the number of RCTs on LGBTQ-affirmative CBT has grown, few reviews have synthesized evidence from these trials across mental health outcomes. A recent systematic review [] examined evidence-based cognitive and/or behavioral interventions for LGBTQ populations, but it did not restrict inclusion to interventions explicitly grounded in CBT or evaluate trials that integrated both cognitive and behavioral components. A CBT-specific synthesis is therefore necessary to reduce conceptual heterogeneity, enable more accurate estimation of CBT-related outcomes, and clarify whether the theorized synergistic effects of jointly applied cognitive and behavioral components are empirically supported. In addition, Dunn et al. [] conducted a preliminary meta-analysis examining CBT for internalizing disorders among LGBTQ populations and reported promising effects. However, the review did not distinguish LGBTQ adapted CBT from standard CBT and included non-controlled trials, increasing the risk of bias. Consequently, it remains unclear whether LGBTQ-affirmative CBT, as a distinct intervention, demonstrates consistent efficacy across mental health domains. Furthermore, the above two studies did not include sexual health or substance use outcomes within the broader scope of mental health. The present review addresses these limitations by focusing specifically on RCTs of LGBTQ adapted CBT interventions and by including studies in which sexual health- or substance use-related interventions incorporate mental health outcomes alongside behavioral ones.

This systematic review will comprehensively identify and synthesize evidence from RCTs of LGBTQ targeted CBT for adults aged 18–65, encompassing mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and substance use disorders. By summarizing effect sizes and exploring moderators such as delivery mode and intervention duration, the review aims to provide a clearer, evidence-based foundation for responsive clinical practice and future research.

This systematic review will address the question: “What is the effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted CBT in improving mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and substance use disorders among sexual and gender minority populations?” The question was formulated using the adapted PICO framework. The review aims to synthesize empirical evidence on LGBTQ targeted CBT and to inform guidelines for clinicians in improving mental health care for sexual and gender minority populations.

This systematic review protocol was prepared in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines [] (). It has been pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD420251173207, registered on October 27, 2025). The document outlines the eligibility criteria, search strategy, data extraction process, and risk of bias assessment to promote transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor throughout the review.

Types of studies. We will include only RCTs that evaluate LGBTQ targeted CBT interventions. No restrictions will be placed on publication year, geographic location, or specific affirmative adaptations, such as integration of minority stress psychoeducation, identity-affirming cognitive restructuring, and stigma coping skills.

Types of participants. Eligible studies will include adults aged 18–65 years who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or with other sexual and gender minority identities.

Types of intervention. Interventions must explicitly target LGBTQ populations (i.e., include adaptations or modifications targeting LGBTQ populations) and be based on CBT principles. Eligible formats include in-person, videoconference, telephone, or live-chat modalities, delivered in any setting, including outpatient and inpatient facilities, charitable organizations, educational institutions, or any other community or home settings.

Types of comparators. Comparator conditions may include treatment as usual, waitlist, or active control interventions.

Types of outcomes. Eligible studies must assess mental health-related outcomes, including but not limited to depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD, or substance use disorders. Both immediate post-intervention and follow-up outcomes will be included.

The exclusion criteria include:

Studies focusing on children and adolescents (<18 years) or older adults (>65 years) will be excluded; studies with a mixed sample age range will be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Studies including participants who presented with current active suicidality or homicidality (excluding passive suicidality), psychotic symptoms, or significant cognitive impairment.

Studies involving participants who were undergoing two or more concurrent therapies during enrollment in the RCT.

Reviews, observational studies, case reports, abstracts, cohort studies, lab-based experimental studies, single-arm studies, and other types of research studies.

Non-CBT interventions.

Studies that only examined behavioral outcomes, such as HIV risk reduction, substance use frequencies, or sexual behaviors.

Studies with th incomplete data or insufficient information to determine intervention outcomes.

The use of concurrent psychotropic medication will not constitute an exclusion criterion. Information regarding medication status, such as the proportion of participants receiving medication, will be extracted and considered in sensitivity or subgroup analyses where feasible.

An initial search strategy for RCTs was developed and pilot-tested on Ovid MEDLINE on October 26, 2025, to evaluate keywords and indexing terms relevant to LGBTQ  targeted CBT interventions. Following this preliminary testing, and with input from a public health librarian, the finalized search strategy will be adapted for each database. The following electronic databases will be searched: PubMed, EMBASE (Ovid), PsycINFO (Ovid), the Cochrane Library, and Scopus. To capture additional relevant materials, we will search for trial registrations through the ClinicalTrials.gov database. We will conduct both forward and backward citation searching to identify additional eligible studies []. The search strategy will be implemented by one reviewer (K.N.). The preliminary search terms on Ovid MEDLINE are provided in . The finalized formal search will be conducted as planned on PubMed, EMBASE (Ovid), PsycINFO (Ovid), Cochrane Library, and Scopus.

Any amendments to the inclusion or exclusion criteria, databases, or search parameters will be documented and justified in the final manuscript, along with an assessment of their potential impact on the review findings.

All search results from the selected databases will be imported into Zotero 7.0.26 for reference organization. The reference list will then be uploaded to Covidence [] to facilitate title-abstract and full-text screening by the review team.

Two reviewers (J.D.C. and Y.Y.) will independently screen studies. First, titles and abstracts will be assessed against the predefined eligibility criteria. Subsequently, the same reviewers will evaluate the full texts of potentially eligible articles to determine final inclusion. All screening results will be cross-checked for consistency. Any disagreements between reviewers will be resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by consulting a third senior reviewer. When essential information is missing or unclear, the corresponding author of the study or the principal investigator llisted in the trial registration will be contacted for clarification. Cohen’s kappa statistic will be used to assess inter-rater agreement. A list of excluded studies and corresponding reasons for exclusion will be provided in the final review.

Two reviewers (J.D.C. and Y.Y.) will extract data independently from each included study using a standardized and pre-piloted data extraction form developed in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). The form will be pilot-tested on a small subset of eligible studies to ensure clarity and consistency. Disagreements between reviewers will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The inter-rater reliability for data extraction will be assessed using Cohen’s kappa statistic and will be reported.

The extraction form will include study-level and intervention-level variables, including study identification details (authors, publication year, journal, country, funding source, study registration), study characteristics (design, setting, sample size, aims, inclusion/exclusion criteria), participant characteristics (age, gender identity, sexual orientation, mental health condition, comorbidities, baseline severity, psychotropic medication use), intervention characteristics (the type of CBT intervention, duration, number and length of sessions, delivery modality, setting, therapist qualifications, theoretical adaptations), comparator details (type, duration, delivery), and outcomes assessed (depression, anxiety, PTSD, OCD, substance use disorders).

When relevant information is missing or unclear, study authors will be contacted for clarification.

The methodological quality of all included RCTs will be assessed independently by two reviewers (J.D.C. and Y.Y.) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool []. The assessment will evaluate five domains: (1) bias arising from the randomization process, (2) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (3) bias due to missing outcome data, (4) bias in measurement of the outcome, and (5) bias in selection of the reported result. Each domain will be rated as low risk, some concerns, or high risk of bias according to Cochrane guidelines. For completeness of outcome data (attrition bias), we will consider both the amount and balance of missing data. Consistent with Cochrane guidance,  > 20% overall attrition or >10% differential attrition will be judged as high risk. We will also note whether studies used intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, as appropriate handling of missing data lowers the risk of attrition bias.

Discrepancies between reviewers will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third senior reviewer. Following individual domain ratings, an overall risk of bias judgment will be assigned to each study using RoB 2’s algorithm. A summary of risk of bias for each domain and across studies will be presented both in tabular form and as visual figures (e.g., risk of bias summary plots) generated using RevMan 5.4 [] or the robvis package [] in R.

Data from included studies will first be summarized narratively, accompanied by descriptive tables detailing study characteristics (e.g., population/diagnosis, baseline severity, setting), intervention components (e.g., core CBT techniques, adjunct elements, delivery modality, cultural/theoretical adaptations), participant demographics, and outcomes (e.g., instrument and timepoint). When sufficient homogeneous data are available, a quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis) will be performed using the R statistical software (version 4.4.0; R Core Team, 2024). Sufficient homogeneous data will be defined as data from at least two studies with the same comparison and comparable outcomes, with I2 less than or equal to 50%, indicating low to moderate heterogeneity to compute an effect size.

For continuous outcomes in the meta-analysis, results will be pooled as standardized mean differences (SMDs; Cohen’s d) [] with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RRs) [] with 95% CIs will be computed. All pooled estimates will be calculated using a random-effects model [].

We will also employ the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation) framework to assess the strength of evidence []. GRADE rates the certainty of evidence for each critical outcome as high, moderate, low, or very low by considering domains such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. We may summarize judgments in a Summary of Findings table.

Heterogeneity across studies will be assessed using Cochran’s Q test (χ²) and the I² statistic, with thresholds of 25%, 50%, and 75% representing low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. When high heterogeneity (I² ≥ 75%) is detected [], potential sources will be explored through subgroup analyses and meta-regression, examining factors such as intervention modality (e.g., in-person vs. telehealth), target disorder, study location, and population subgroup (e.g., cisgender vs. mixed samples) when feasible.

To minimize potential publication bias, a comprehensive and systematic literature search will be undertaken. To further ensure the transparency and objectivity of the review, information regarding study funding sources and author conflicts of interest will be extracted and examined. When appropriate, potential publication bias will be evaluated using funnel plots [].

Sensitivity analyses will be performed by excluding studies with high risk of bias or small sample sizes to test the robustness of the pooled results. We will define “small sample” a priori as trials with fewer than 25 participants per arm, consistent with meta-epidemiological evidence that very small trials are more susceptible to small-study effects and may yield more favorable treatment estimates than larger trials [].

Despite growing recognition of minority stress as a key contributor to LGBTQ mental health disparities, evidence on the effectiveness of LGBTQ-affirmative CBT remains limited and mixed. Existing trials vary widely in intervention structure, adaptation methods, follow-up duration, and outcome measurement, leading to inconsistent findings regarding efficacy. This methodological diversity makes it difficult to identify the active components driving improvement.

The present systematic review will address these gaps by synthesizing RCTs of LGBTQ adapted CBT interventions for adults. By examining short- and long-term effects across mental health outcomes and evaluating moderators such as delivery mode and intervention duration, the review aims to clarify both the effectiveness and mechanisms of affirmative CBT. The findings will provide an evidence base to inform culturally responsive clinical practice and guide future development of LGBTQ inclusive mental health treatments.
