psychology.title: A Multistage Fine-Tuning and Empathy Alignment Approach for an Emotional Support Dialogue System: Development and Evaluation Study
psychology.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for text-based emotional support. However, general-purpose LLMs may not consistently recognize emotional cues, adapt supportive strategies to contexts, or generate responses aligned with psychologically informed communication. The limited availability of large-scale, structured Chinese counseling data further constrains the development of models for context-sensitive emotional support.We developed and evaluated YuanChat, a family of specialized LLMs for context-sensitive emotional support; assessed whether E-URIAL improved response quality; and compared YuanChat with base LLMs.We constructed 2 datasets from anonymized real-world counseling sessions: ECD-3 (104,897 counselor response turns) for fine-tuning and Dgold (9413 manually annotated counselor responses). Annotations covered emotional support conversation stages (exploration, comfort, and action), counseling techniques (clarification, support, and challenge), and empathic effects. We developed 2 YuanChat variants using GLM-4-9B-Chat and Huozi 3.5 as backbone models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then developed E-URIAL, an inference-time framework combining predicted emotion and support strategy labels with retrieved labeled exemplars. Given the dialogue history through the help seeker’s latest utterance, each model generated a counselor-style response. We compared YuanChat with GPT-4, ERNIE 4.0, CharacterGLM, GLM-4-9B-Chat, and Huozi 3.5. The evaluation comprised (1) automatic evaluation on in-domain and external datasets, assessing empathy identification and empathic expression; (2) evaluation of empathy-related situational reasoning using an expert-developed multiple-choice benchmark; (3) evaluation by clinical experts (n=8) of empathic attunement, support strategy appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence; and (4) a complementary evaluation by volunteer master’s students in clinical and counseling psychology (n=50) of response fluency, empathy, and perceived helpfulness.Fine-tuning increased YuanChat-Huozi3.5’s empathic expression score from 0.57 to 0.68; empathy identification score increased from 0.54 to 0.59. In expert evaluation, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 received a higher empathic attunement score than the base Huozi3.5 model (1.279 vs 0.327; mean difference 0.952, 95% CI 0.746‐1.152). Using professional counselor responses as the reference, the mean differences for YuanChat-Huozi3.5 were 0.148, 0.079, 0.039, and 0.002 in empathic attunement, supportive appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence, respectively. No statistically significant differences were detected between YuanChat-Huozi3.5 and the counselor references (all Holm-adjusted P≥.29). Higher scores were observed when E-URIAL was applied. When E-URIAL was applied with 3 retrieved exemplars, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 achieved an empathy identification score of 0.69 versus 0.59 without E-URIAL, an empathic expression score of 0.79 versus 0.68, and a perceived helpfulness score of 0.74 versus 0.61.The findings indicate that fine-tuning on real-world counseling data and annotating models with structured emotional support labels improved context-sensitive empathic responding in LLMs. Without updating model parameters, E-URIAL further improved empathy identification and empathic expression across multiple models. Together, these methods provide a scalable, theory-informed approach to enhancing the emotional support capabilities of LLMs.
psychology.text:
The global mental health crisis has created an extensive demand for accessible counseling services; however, access to professional counseling remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries [,]. Digital mental health technologies, particularly text-based empathic conversational agents, have emerged as potentially scalable approaches to narrowing the mental health service gap []. However, realizing the potential of these systems requires moving beyond generic expressions of comfort toward more context-sensitive and theoretically grounded emotional support [].

Although modern large language models (LLMs) show strong general-purpose language capabilities, their empathic responses often remain repetitive, insufficiently probing, and inadequately attuned to the user’s specific emotional context [-]. Training LLMs on high-quality counseling dialogues grounded in established psychological frameworks can help them recognize context-specific emotional cues and select more appropriate support strategies [].

Existing datasets, including EmpatheticDialogues and ESConv, have provided valuable benchmarks for developing and evaluating empathic dialogue systems [-]. However, their conversations were elicited from crowdworkers through recalled situations or role-play scenarios, rather than collected from naturally occurring interactions between help seekers and trained counselors (). Consequently, many existing datasets often lack ecological validity, offering a partial representation of the nuanced, multistage intervention strategies used by professional counselors, including those described in the helping skills framework []. This motivated the development of the Empathic Counseling Dialogue–3 (ECD-3) dataset, named for its 3 emotional support conversation stages: exploration, comfort, and action. On the basis of this, the research question (RQ) 1 was formulated:

RQ1: How does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a counseling-informed dataset affect the empathic performance of LLMs in emotional support dialogue?

For datasets involving translation, the primary target language is reported to avoid ambiguity.

LLM: large language model.

For LLMs’ empathic dialogue, fine-tuning matters because performance hinges on empathy language cues and strategy selection conditioned on the seeker’s affect []. To bridge this gap between general pretraining and specialized emotional support expertise, we used a fine-tuning strategy on the ECD-3 dataset. In particular, we used parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques, such as weight-decomposed low-rank adaptation (DoRA) and quantized DoRA (QDoRA), for efficiently adapting the models while preserving their foundational reasoning capabilities. However, SFT alone encodes emotional support patterns in model parameters, leaving adaptation constrained by the training distribution and without dynamic access to case-specific guidance at inference. We therefore introduced empathy untuned LLMs with restyled in-context alignment (E-URIAL), a retrieval-augmented in-context learning (ICL) framework for inference-time alignment method that retrieves contextually relevant strategies and demonstrations to complement SFT and improve emotional support performance [].

Conceptually, E-URIAL extends the untuned LLMs with restyled in-context alignment (URIAL) framework by incorporating theory-driven strategic constraints to guide empathic generation []. Drawing from psychological counseling literature, E-URIAL augments retrieved exemplars with multidimensional labels, including the emotional support conversation (ESC) stages, which conceptualize empathic support as a progression through exploration, comfort, and action, as well as specific counseling techniques and empathic language cues [,].

E-URIAL complements the parametric adaptation through a nonparametric mechanism. At inference time, it dynamically retrieves high-quality exemplars from the human-annotated subset and aligned with relevant support strategies. This hybrid approach combines the expertise encoded through fine-tuning with external, case-specific guidance, enabling more adaptive and context-sensitive emotional support responses without additional parameter updates. Thus, RQ2 was formulated:

RQ2: How does E-URIAL affect task-specific empathic performance?

This study aimed to systematically enhance LLMs’ empathic response generation to provide more professional mental support in daily contexts. To address this, we define the following 3 specific research objectives:

To construct a large-scale emotional support dataset (ECD-3) grounded in counseling knowledge and authentic counseling sessions;

To enhance the emotional support capacity of LLMs by internalizing specialized knowledge through fine-tuning on the ECD-3 corpus; and

To evaluate the effectiveness of E-URIAL, a retrieval-augmented framework, in providing dynamic strategic guidance for more adaptive and resonant mental support in everyday scenarios.

The primary contributions of this study can be organized into 3 dimensions:

Data contribution: We introduce ECD-3, a large-scale counseling-dialogue dataset from China consisting of 104,897 counselor-response turns. Furthermore, we built Dgold, a high-quality subset of 9413 counselor-response turns with multilayer labels, providing a structured annotation scheme informed by counseling theory. Model and evaluation contribution: We introduce YuanChat, a family of empathy-enhanced LLMs from China developed through fine-tuning on the ECD-3 dataset. Across automatic and human evaluations, we observe consistent improvements in human-rated empathy and support quality while maintaining strong linguistic fluency.

Methodological contribution: We introduce E-URIAL, a retrieval-augmented ICL framework designed to steer empathic generation. By predicting strategy labels and dynamically retrieving exemplars, E-URIAL provides the model with professionally grounded guidance during inference. Our experiments suggest that this approach can improve empathic performance, offering a scalable solution for adaptive digital empathy.

Empathy is generally defined as the ability to recognize and respond to others’ emotional experiences, and it is particularly important in mental health support [-]. Prior studies have often distinguished cognitive empathy (understanding others’ emotions) from affective empathy (sharing or mirroring emotions) []. Recent studies have evaluated whether LLM outputs are perceived as empathic and whether they adapt to context (eg, [,]). Although many models can produce fluent supportive responses, they often show limited accuracy and preference bias in turn-level support strategy selection, reducing their ability to adapt to users’ changing emotional needs [,]. This limitation is particularly consequential in support-oriented, multiturn interactions. Examples include daily ESCs, chronic disease care, and educational tutoring. In such scenarios, empathic quality directly affects user trust and satisfaction [-].

A key reason is that pretraining on large-scale internet text exposes models to emotional language but provides limited specialized support knowledge for a systematic understanding of empathy []. SFT can yield incremental gains; yet, progress is often constrained by limited ecological validity and coarse supervision signals [,]. In mental health settings, agents perceived as more empathic are associated with higher user trust, highlighting the need for models that can move beyond generic consolation toward context-aware mental support [-].

Recent studies have evaluated empathy in LLMs using standardized benchmarks or psychometric instruments, automatic text-based metrics, human ratings, and hybrid protocols that combine automatic and human assessment [,-]. As a benchmark study, EmoBench focuses on emotion understanding and response appropriateness under controlled scenarios, showing that models can approach human-level performance on some cognitive empathy tasks []. Human evaluation complements benchmarks by measuring perceived empathy. A previous study combined common automatic metrics (eg, Bilingual Evaluation Understudy [BLEU]-1 and BLEU-2 and embedding average cosine similarity) with human ratings and observed that models that incorporated an empathy recognition framework performed better on deep empathy tasks []. Despite these advances, current evaluation pipelines face 2 recurring limitations []. First, many schemes are weakly grounded in empathy support–related theories in annotation systems, leading to fragmented operationalizations, limited cross-model comparability, and reduced interpretability of evaluation outcomes []. Second, ecological validity is often limited because evaluation corpora and contexts cannot reflect authentic supportive interactions []. Such limitations motivate the need for theory-informed dataset construction and evaluation metrics aligned with professional constructs.

On the basis of prior literature (), methods for improving empathic behavior can be broadly grouped into parameter updating approaches and inference-time approaches, or a combination of both [,]. Parameter updating methods such as SFT adapt model behavior using task-specific data, while inference-time methods (eg, ICL) steer generation with demonstrations without updating parameters [].

SFT: supervised fine-tuning.

ECC: Emotion-Cause Conversation.

CoT: chain-of-thought.

ICL: in-context learning.

These methods improve empathic responses by training models on emotion-related corpora via SFT or preference-based optimization. Representative resources include EmpatheticDialogues and related emotion-annotated dialogue datasets. Strategy-oriented datasets such as ESConv offer finer supervision by annotating support strategies [,]. However, many existing corpora can exhibit limited realism for counseling-style interactions and sometimes lack explicit grounding in counseling theory. Domain-focused systems (eg, SoulChat) further suggest that adapting base models using mental support data can improve supportive response quality. Reinforcement learning from human feedback has been explored for empathy alignment, but it typically requires costly feedback and careful reward design [-].

These methods guide generation at inference time using prompts or exemplars. Prior studies have explored role prompts and reasoning-oriented prompting for empathic responding []. Role-based prompts ask LLMs to respond as a specific helper role (eg, a patient listener or counselor), which can increase supportive and empathic language when compared with neutral prompts. For reasoning-oriented prompting, chain-of-thought prompting further encourages models to first reflect on the user’s emotional state before generating a response, improving contextual appropriateness. Emotion-conditioned prompting injects explicit affective cues into the prompt to improve emotion consistency [], and a related study extended such prompting to spoken emotional understanding [].

The design of the prompts and the examples influences the effect of inference-time alignment methods. As a representative approach, the URIAL study suggested that base LLMs can achieve competitive alignment without parameter updates by combining a system prompt with 3 constant stylistic examples []. Subsequent studies have used URIAL as a baseline and examined adaptations of demonstration design and decoding settings. For example, in dynamic rewarding with prompt optimization, the study team used dynamic rewards to optimize alignment instructions without parameter updates [].

For the approach design and dataset construction, grounding in established empathy and counseling frameworks provides theoretically valid and interpretable labels, distinguishes affective understanding from strategic intervention, and captures how professional support unfolds across dialogue stages. This structure converts counseling expertise into explicit supervision for model training, retrieval, and evaluation []. Thus, we integrated stage-wise support strategy and counseling practice in empathic dialogue and proposed E-URIAL, a counseling theory–informed extension of URIAL. E-URIAL extends URIAL in 2 key aspects ().

Label-enriched exemplars: Each in-context exemplar is augmented with theory-informed labels, such as ESC-stage labels, counseling-technique labels [], and empathic language cues, together with emotion information, so that exemplars can explicitly guide beyond semantic similarity.

Dynamic retrieval of in-domain counselor exemplars: Unlike URIAL, which uses fixed generic demonstrations, E-URIAL dynamically retrieves contextually relevant counselor exemplars. Candidate exemplars are ranked by sentence bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (SBERT)–based semantic similarity and incorporated, together with the predicted labels and system instruction, into the final prompt.

We conceptualized emotional support response generation as 3 linked functions: recognizing the seeker’s state, selecting an appropriate support strategy, and realizing that strategy in language. Emotion- and context-related labels represent the seeker’s current state and support needs. ESC-stage labels locate the response within the broader support process, whereas counseling technique labels characterize the specific supportive techniques used in the response. We selected these variables because they correspond to the central task of this study: interpreting the seeker’s emotions and situation and generating a contextually appropriate supportive response.

At the process level, we adopted the ESC model, which builds on Hill’s helping skills theory and adapts helping strategies to everyday emotional support dialogue. The model organizes emotional support into exploration, comfort, and action. Exploration helps seekers articulate and clarify their situations, thoughts, and emotions. Comfort centers on empathy, understanding, and emotional support. Action helps seekers consider feasible ways to address their difficulties. These stages do not constitute a fixed sequence. Instead, the appropriate strategy depends on the seeker’s evolving needs and the dialogue context.

At the turn level, counseling techniques specify how a support strategy is enacted. We grouped these techniques into 3 categories []. Clarification techniques, such as asking for details, explaining concepts, and summarizing, help organize the seeker’s account and clarify the problem. Support techniques, including active listening, emotion reflection, and validation, communicate acceptance, understanding, and encouragement. Challenge techniques draw attention to discrepancies or potentially unhelpful patterns and invite the seeker to consider alternative interpretations or actions.

Together, the ESC stages and counseling techniques provide complementary process-level and turn-level structures for multilayer data annotation, SFT, and label-guided retrieval in E-URIAL. These constructs also informed the evaluation dimensions concerning state understanding, strategy appropriateness, empathy, and helpfulness.

Building on the abovementioned review, we developed an integrated framework informed by empathic methodologies. First, we constructed a dataset from real counseling dialogues with deidentification and multilayer annotation. Second, we fine-tuned 2 base models on this dataset to obtain empathy-enhanced generation models. Third, to test whether retrieval can effectively guide generation, we introduced E-URIAL, which dynamically retrieves in-domain counseling exemplars to steer empathic generation. Finally, we evaluated both fine-tuned and inference-time methods using an assessment protocol grounded in the key elements of real counseling, thereby combining automatic metrics with human ratings.  shows the overall study logic. The figure summarizes the main research logic from ECD-3 (our training data) dataset construction to supervised fine-tuning, E-URIAL–based retrieval-augmented in-context alignment, and evaluation. RQ1 encompasses dataset construction and supervised fine-tuning. RQ2 addresses E-URIAL–based retrieval-augmented alignment; manually annotated subset; and automatic evaluation metrics, which are empathy identification score, empathic expression score, and empathy ability calculation.

This study followed a structured approach, encompassing 3 main stages: dataset creation, model development, and evaluation. In the first stage, we developed the 2 datasets: ECD-3 dataset and Dgold dataset. ECD-3 contained 104,897 counselor-response turns. This dataset served as the foundation for the development of YuanChat models. Dgold contained 9413 manually annotated counselor-response turns. This dataset was divided at the counseling case level into nonoverlapping evaluation and retrieval subsets. The evaluation subset was used to assess model performance. The retrieval subset provided counseling exemplars for E-URIAL. This study was prepared in accordance with the TRIPOD+LLM (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis–Large Language Model) reporting guideline, and the completed checklist is provided in .

During model development, we separately fine-tuned GLM-4-9B-Chat and Huozi3.5 [,] on ECD-3, producing YuanChat-GLM4-9B and YuanChat-Huozi3.5. We also developed E-URIAL, an inference-time prompt enhancement framework that combined predicted emotion and support strategy labels with retrieved counselor exemplars. E-URIAL did not require additional training or parameter updates. To evaluate YuanChat’s performance, we conducted a comparative analysis with other generative AI models (eg, GPT-4 and CharacterGLM) and assessed its effectiveness through expert clinical assessments.

Model fine-tuning and analysis were performed using Python (Python Software Foundation) and Python-based machine learning frameworks and libraries. These included PyTorch (originally developed by Meta), DeepSpeed (originally developed by Microsoft), and Transformers, Datasets, and Accelerate (Hugging Face). The fine-tuning process leveraged high-performance computing resources to optimize model performance and efficiency. All local model training and inference were performed on a compute node equipped with 4 NVIDIA A100 80 GB graphics processing units (GPUs).

The data were obtained from real-world counseling sessions conducted by a Chinese psychological service provider between May 2022 and May 2023. The corpus comprised sessions involving 68 counselors and 4063 clients. Among these clients, 3778 participated in audio-recorded sessions, whereas 285 used text-based counseling (). The audio sessions lasted 30 to 90 minutes. We transcribed the audio recordings using Tencent Cloud’s automatic speech recognition API, which also performed speaker diarization. To accommodate the context window limits of foundation LLMs while preserving semantic coherence, we divided the dialogues into segments of no more than 1000 Chinese characters. We also removed nonsubstantive expressions, such as “En” and “Oo.” The processed dialogues were classified into 6 primary topics and an “Other” category, which included topics such as childhood trauma and cyberbullying (). This preprocessing yielded 188,409 counselor response turns for subsequent screening and annotation.

The original corpus was divided into 2 separate parts for processing, which were used to construct the Dgold manually annotated dataset and the ECD-3 model training dataset. First, we selected 200 counseling cases with high satisfaction ratings for manual annotation. These cases comprised 9778 counselor response turns. Second, the remaining 178,631 counselor response turns were used as the candidate pool for construction of the ECD-3 training dataset.

Annotation is a crucial stage in natural language processing studies that ensures the validity of psychological constructs []. We adopted a theory-driven annotation framework to map professional strategies to support empathic responses ().

ESC: emotional support conversation.

ESC stages: On the basis of helping skills theory, this model divided emotional support into 3 stages, namely, exploration, comfort, and action, to support interactions in everyday social contexts.

Counseling techniques: These were specific verbal interventions used for facilitating understanding and change. We annotated 3 core categories, namely, clarification, support, and challenge.

Empathy effect: To ensure the inclusion of only high-quality empathic dialogue samples, we assessed the perceived quality of the empathy conveyed.

We randomly recruited 8 data annotators from the authors’ university. All annotators were master’s students in psychological counseling and had at least 1 year of counseling practice experience. Before formal annotation, all annotators participated in a standardized training program that covered the annotation guidelines, representative examples, and live demonstrations. The training aligned their understanding and application of the psychological concepts underlying the annotation framework. All annotations were completed through a custom Streamlit platform.  presents an example of the annotation process.

We randomly selected 200 counseling cases. The annotators reviewed the dialogue context and labeled each counselor response in every selected case. For each assigned label, they also highlighted the relevant text spans in the response as evidence for the annotation, such as “That is truly unfortunate” and “This is indeed distressing.”

The initial annotation covered 9778 counselor responses to client utterances from 200 counseling cases. We excluded 19 cases comprising 365 responses because their labels were ambiguous or inconsistent, resulting in a final annotated dataset of 9413 counselor responses from 181 cases. We designated this manually annotated dataset as Dgold. At the case level, we partitioned Dgold into 2 subsets. The E-URIAL exemplar pool contained 7530 responses from 137 cases, whereas the held-out evaluation pool contained 1883 responses from 44 cases. None of the 44 evaluation cases appeared in either the ECD-3 training set or the E-URIAL exemplar pool, preventing case-level information leakage during model evaluation.

We assessed interrater reliability (IRR) using Cohen κ []. This coefficient is a chance-corrected measure suitable for categorical annotations, making it appropriate for our multidimensional annotation design []. Cohen κ was calculated for each annotator pair and averaged across pairs. The mean pairwise κ was 0.5857 for the ESC stages, 0.4219 for counseling techniques, and 0.5887 for empathy effect, indicating moderate agreement. We then reported the unweighted mean across dimensions as the overall IRR of 0.5321. The relatively low agreement on counseling techniques likely reflects the interpretive demands of fine-grained technique classification, a challenge also observed in prior psychotherapy annotation research [].

Manual annotation was resource intensive and could not feasibly cover the full corpus []. We therefore constructed the ECD-3 from the 178,631 counselor response turns. We applied a dual-model label consistency procedure in which a locally deployed empathy strategy model and GPT-4 independently predicted the ESC stage and counseling technique labels for each response. A response was retained only when the 2 models assigned the same label for both annotation dimensions. This procedure retained 104,897 responses and excluded 73,734 responses because of label disagreement. GLM-4 subsequently rewrote each of the 104,897 retained responses under the prespecified constraints described below. This one-to-one rewriting procedure produced the final ECD-3 training dataset of 104,897 counselor response turns. Specifically, the ECD-3 dataset construction involved the following 3 steps.

We implemented a dual-model verification mechanism to ensure label reliability. A previously developed empathy computing model () and GPT-4 independently predicted the ESC stage and counseling technique associated with each counselor response. We retained a response only when the 2 models assigned the same label for both annotation dimensions. This criterion retained 104,897 responses and excluded 73,734 responses because of model disagreement.

We used GLM-4 (Zhipu AI) to rewrite the 104,897 retained responses. We selected GLM-4 because of its Chinese-language generation capabilities and support for a context window of up to 128,000 tokens []. Using the dialogue context and the agreed labels from step 1, GLM-4 rewrote each counselor response under three constraints: (1) strengthen the correspondence between the response and its assigned ESC stage and counseling technique, (2) preserve the original meaning and coherence of the dialogue context, and (3) check and remove any residual direct or indirect identifiers from the dialogue. The source counseling records had been anonymized before they were made available to the research team. As an additional safeguard, the rewritten outputs underwent a postrewriting privacy review, and any remaining potentially identifying information was removed before inclusion in ECD-3. This process produced 1 rewritten response for each retained response. The resulting ECD-3 dataset contained 104,897 counselor responses.

To examine the quality of the ECD-3, we conducted an expert evaluation. We recruited 2 professionals with extensive experience in clinical psychology and psychological counseling through our professional networks. Using stratified random sampling, we selected 216 counselor response turns across 18 strata defined by 3 ESC stages and 6 dialogue topics, with 12 turns sampled from each stratum. The same-sex relationship topic was excluded because it contained too few eligible instances. Both experts independently evaluated all selected turns. Further details are provided in .

On the basis of a previous framework [], the evaluation was performed on a 5-point Likert scale across the following 3 crucial dimensions:

Contextual authenticity: whether the response mirrored a real-world counseling scenario;

Empathic appropriateness: whether the response aligned with professional empathy strategies and techniques; and

Semantic naturalness: linguistic fluency and conversational flow of the rewritten text.

The results () indicated that the sampled turns performed strongly on key dimensions. With a total score of ≥12 as the threshold for acceptance, the overall acceptance rate was 71.99%. IRR, assessed using Gwet AC2 [], was 0.69 for contextual authenticity, 0.66 for empathic appropriateness, 0.68 for semantic naturalness, and 0.77 for the total score.

The results suggested that the generated responses were both context consistent and linguistically natural. Although empathic appropriateness was comparatively low, it remained above the midpoint of 3. A majority of the samples met the ≥4 criterion.

We used ECD-3 exclusively for model fine-tuning. ECD-3 contained 104,897 counselor responses derived from real-world counseling sessions after label consistency filtering and constrained rewriting.

We evaluated the models using 2 test sources with distinct data provenance. The evaluation subset of Dgold provided an in-domain benchmark comprising manually annotated counselor responses from real-world sessions. SMILECHAT served as an external source benchmark. It is a publicly available Chinese text-based dataset containing 55,165 multiturn mental health support dialogues. The dataset was constructed using the SMILE method, which prompted ChatGPT to transform publicly available single-turn question-answer pairs from PsyQA into dialogues containing at least five turns. The original study used SMILECHAT to examine lexical, semantic, and topic diversity and to fine-tune ChatGLM2-6B for developing the mental health support chatbot MeChat [].

For the automatic evaluation, we randomly sampled 1000 counselor responses from the Dgold evaluation pool and 1000 response instances from SMILECHAT, resulting in a balanced test set of 2000 instances. For the counseling trainee evaluation, we subsequently selected a stratified random sample of 100 dialogue contexts, including 50 instances from Dgold and 50 from SMILECHAT. The clinical professional evaluation used the 70 real-world counseling contexts from Dgold.

We also constructed an independent Chinese-language situational reasoning benchmark (EAC benchmark) comprising 200 multiple-choice items to evaluate empathy reasoning in LLMs. Each item presented a social or emotional scenario and required the model to infer the thoughts, feelings, or intentions of a person in that scenario. Each item contained 4 to 5 response options and 1 intended answer. Guided by the empathic accuracy framework and research on cognitive empathy and perspective taking [-], the items were developed by 5 licensed psychological counselors with a mean of more than 5 years of professional experience. The experts independently reviewed each item for construct relevance, clarity, cultural appropriateness, and answer ambiguity and independently identified the intended answer. Items without unanimous agreement were revised or excluded. Only items receiving unanimous agreement from all 5 experts after revision were retained. Examples are provided in .

To comprehensively assess empathic performance, we compared our fine-tuned models against several baselines. For backbones, we selected 2 representative architectures for fine-tuning: GLM-4-9B-Chat and Huozi3.5 [,]. GLM-4-9B-Chat is a dense model optimized for long-context dialogue, following the GLM-4 family released by Zhipu AI and THUDM. Huozi3.5, released by HIT-SCIR, is a mixture-of-experts model further optimized based on HuoZi-3.0 and Chinese-Mixtral-8x7B.

For comparison models, we benchmarked against the following 3 strong proprietary models: GPT-4, CharacterGLM, and ERNIE 4.0. GPT-4 is the fourth generation of the GPT series []. It is trained on a very large and diverse text dataset and is well known for producing human-like responses. CharacterGLM was developed by Lingxin AI and Zhipu AI []. CharacterGLM is a derivative of ChatGLM optimized for “human-like” character interactions. ERNIE 4.0 is the fourth generation of Baidu’s ERNIE model []. ERNIE 4.0 worked well for complex, multiturn conversations and could adapt to different domains. All systems used the same prompt template. The specifications for all models are presented in .

To ensure compatibility with their distinct architectures, we use their respective native chat templates to concatenate multiturn dialogue histories. This alignment ensures that input formatting remains consistent with each model’s original training paradigm. We provide full template specifications in .

The target output Y was the empathic reply to the final seeker query, designed to provide effective empathic support consistent with our human evaluation criteria. All training files were stored in the JSON format.

We used a learning rate of 1×104, a per-device batch size of 4, and a maximum of 3000 training steps. The maximum input length was 2048 tokens, and the maximum output length was 2048 tokens. Training was conducted on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs (80 GB each).

We adopted parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to adapt the backbones under a fixed compute budget: DoRA for GLM-4-9B-Chat and QDoRA for Huozi3.5.

DoRA decomposes pretrained weights into magnitude and direction components and fine-tunes them separately, while maintaining the same inference overhead as LoRA []. In our empathy-related task, this approach also improved instruction following. QDoRA (4-bit NF4 quantization with DoRA-based directional adaptation) injected adapters only into the activated expert subnetworks under Top-2 gating, enabling effective fine-tuning under limited GPU memory.

In both methods, the backbone model weights were frozen, and only the adapter parameters were trained. To ensure comparability, we controlled the maximum steps, per-device batch size (4), context length (4096 tokens), optimizer (8-bit AdamW), and learning rate schedule (cosine decay with 200 warmup steps) consistent across experiments. We also used the same prompt template and tokenization scheme in all settings. Our objective was to evaluate whether ECD-3 and E-URIAL improved empathic performance across representative backbones and not to compare PEFT algorithms. All experiments were conducted on a cluster equipped with 4 NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs, using DeepSpeed ZeRO-2/3 for memory optimization and FlashAttention-2 to accelerate attention computation. The core adapter hyperparameters for each backbone model, including rank, scaling factor, dropout, and quantization settings, are summarized in .

E-URIAL is an inference-time prompt enhancement approach adapted from URIAL for emotional support tasks. It requires no additional training or parameter updates. We evaluated whether its structured contextual guidance could improve emotional support responses across multiple LLMs and provide further gains for the domain-fine-tuned YuanChat models. As shown in , for each input, E-URIAL first predicts emotion and empathy strategy labels and then retrieves the most semantically similar labeled counselor exemplars from the exemplar subset of Dgold. The predicted labels, retrieved exemplars, system instruction, and current dialogue context are integrated into a structured prompt that guides the target LLM in generating the final supportive response.

We specified the model’s role as an experienced psychological counselor who should respond professionally, empathically, honestly, and competently. The instruction also established safety boundaries prohibiting false, harmful, unethical, discriminatory, or otherwise socially irresponsible content and included a step-by-step reasoning instruction to promote structured and consistent responses.

For each input, we predicted 2 emotion labels for the help seeker: a dialogue-level emotion and a current-turn emotion. The dialogue-level emotion was inferred from the complete dialogue history up to the current turn and summarized the help seeker’s overall emotional state throughout the conversation. The current-turn emotion captured the immediate emotion expressed in the help seeker’s most recent utterance. We used a fixed YuanChat-Huozi3.5 checkpoint as the emotion-label predictor and applied a standardized prompt template to generate both labels: “Based on the dialogue history, the help seeker’s overall emotion is ...; in the current utterance, the help seeker’s emotion is ...” The predictions were mapped to Ekman’s 6 basic emotion categories: anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise. Cases that could not be reliably mapped to these categories were left unlabeled. To ensure comparability across response generation models, the emotion labels for each input were generated once and supplied unchanged to all evaluated models.

We represented empathy strategy at 2 levels: strategic intent and linguistic realization. Strategic intent defined the appropriate supportive action. It comprised the ESC stage (exploration, comfort, or action) and counseling techniques (clarification, support, or challenge). Linguistic realization defined how the strategy was expressed. Empathic language cues guided the model to produce emotionally responsive and contextually appropriate wording.

For each input, we used a locally deployed strategy prediction model to predict the ESC-stage and counseling technique labels. Its architecture, training procedure, and validation results are described in . After exemplar retrieval, we used a locally deployed empathic-language-cue tagging model to annotate the retrieved counselor exemplars. This specialized model used ChatGLM3-6B as its backbone and identified positive and negative empathy cues in each response. Its training procedure, validation results, and implementation settings are provided in . Both labeling models remained frozen throughout E-URIAL inference. Their outputs were used only for prompt construction and were not used to train or update the response generation models. Neither labeling model had access to the target response or the corresponding counselor reference response from the evaluation set.

We used SBERT to retrieve in-domain counselor exemplars from the retrieval subset of Dgold (n=7530 responses). For each test input, SBERT encoded the dialogue context up to and including the help seeker’s most recent utterance. It also encoded the corresponding seeker-side context of each candidate exemplar. We applied mean pooling to the token representations to obtain a fixed-length sentence embedding for each context. Candidate exemplars were ranked according to their cosine similarity to the current dialogue context. The highest-ranked exemplars were retrieved together with their counselor responses and annotation labels and incorporated into the structured prompt.

The retrieval subset contained 7530 counselor response turns. It was separated from the evaluation subset at the counseling case level; therefore, no dialogue context or counselor reference response from the evaluation set was eligible for retrieval. To examine the effect of exemplar quantity under the input length constraints of the evaluated LLMs, we tested prompts containing 1, 3, and 10 retrieved exemplars.

We combined the system instruction, current dialogue context, predicted emotion and strategy labels, and retrieved labeled exemplars into a structured prompt. The resulting prompt was provided to the target LLM to generate the final supportive response.

E-URIAL followed URIAL’s prefix prompt structure. The final prompt consisted sequentially of the system instruction, retrieved exemplars ranked by semantic similarity, and the current input. Each exemplar used standardized field markers to present the help seeker’s context, ESC stage, counseling technique, empathic language cues, and counselor response. The current input section contained the dialogue context up to the current turn and the predicted emotion, ESC stage, and counseling technique labels. The prompt ended with a response start marker, after which the target model generated the supportive response. After tokenization with the target model’s tokenizer, the maximum input length was set to 4096 tokens, and the maximum generation length was also set to 4096 tokens.

Building on prior research on emotional support dialogue, conventional metrics such as semantic similarity and general task performance do not adequately capture contextualized empathic expression. Existing studies therefore commonly evaluate models in terms of the appropriateness of empathic expression and their understanding of others’ emotions and perspectives. However, expert evaluations of professional appropriateness and safety remain limited [-]. Accordingly, our evaluation framework comprised 4 complementary components: response-level assessment of empathy identification and empathy expression, representing empathy strategy mechanism and empathy expression evaluation, respectively; assessment of empathy-related contextual understanding and reasoning; counseling trainee ratings of response quality; and clinical professional assessments of professional appropriateness and safety. As this study aimed to enhance emotional support capabilities rather than evaluate clinical effectiveness, symptom improvement and treatment outcomes were not included as evaluation variables.

Specifically, we used a 4-part evaluation framework to assess YuanChat and the comparison models. First, we conducted an automatic evaluation using test sets drawn from 2 different sources, Dgold and SMILECHAT, to examine response quality of model performance across data sources. Second, we used scenario-based multiple-choice questions developed by experts to conduct an Empathy Ability Calculation (EAC) evaluation, testing the models’ ability to infer others’ emotions, perspectives, and intentions []. Third, counseling trainees conducted a blinded evaluation of the fluency, empathy, and perceived helpfulness of the model-generated responses. Fourth, clinical counseling and psychotherapy experts used real-world counselor responses as a professional baseline, assessing the model-generated responses for professional appropriateness, safety, and adherence to professional boundaries. By integrating automatic metrics, ratings from graduate students in clinical and counseling psychology, and professional judgments from counseling experts, this framework identified the strengths and limitations of each model in terms of performance across data sources, emotional support quality, and professional safety.

We used 2 automatic evaluation metrics: the Empathy Identification Score (EIS) and the Empathic Expression Score (EES).

EIS quantified the expressed empathy mechanism in model-generated responses using the EPITOME framework []. EPITOME captures both affective and cognitive components of empathy and evaluates each response in relation to the corresponding help seeker’s input, thereby supporting context-sensitive assessment of expressed empathy and making it suitable for the present study.

EPITOME characterizes textual empathy through 3 communication mechanisms: emotional reactions, interpretations, and explorations. Emotional reactions capture expressions of warmth, compassion, or concern in response to the seeker’s experiences. Interpretations capture communicated understanding of those experiences. Explorations capture gentle and specific inquiries into feelings or experiences that the seeker has not explicitly stated. EPITOME uses a multitask biencoder architecture built on RoBERTa-base. The S-Encoder encodes the help seeker’s input, whereas the R-Encoder encodes the corresponding response. An attention mechanism integrates the 2 representations to identify empathic expression in the response. The released model includes 3 independently trained classifiers for emotional reactions (ER), interpretations (IP), and explorations (EX). Each classifier assigns the corresponding mechanism an expression level of 0, 1, or 2, representing no, weak, or strong expression, respectively.

We adapted the publicly released EPITOME model for Chinese mental health support dialogues and internally validated the resulting evaluator. On the test set drawn from Dgold, its accuracy and macro-F1-score were 0.8875 and 0.7457 for ER, 0.8599 and 0.7468 for IP, and 0.8850 and 0.7189 for EX. Details of its Chinese adaptation and training are reported in .

For each response, we summed the predicted expression levels for ER, IP, and EX and divided the result by the maximum possible total of 6, producing a normalized response-level EIS ranging from 0 to 1. We then calculated the EIS for each evaluated model by averaging its response-level scores across all responses. Higher EIS values indicated greater expression of the 3 empathy mechanisms.

As strategy alignment does not necessarily ensure that support is linguistically expressed in an emotionally validating and context-sensitive manner, EES was included to assess the realized empathic expression in each response. EES was treated as a supplementary proxy measure and was interpreted alongside the blinded ratings provided by counseling trainees and clinical professionals. EES assessed the extent to which a generated response conveyed contextually appropriate emotional understanding and supportive expression. Responses were evaluated using a prespecified rubric covering emotional recognition, perspective understanding, and supportive communication. For scalable automatic scoring, a separate LLM evaluator applied the same rubric to all responses. To assess scoring accuracy, the researchers randomly sampled 200 of the responses and manually checked the automated cue labels against the prespecified rubric. Following the cue-coding procedure detailed in , the evaluator identified the presence of prespecified positive empathy cues (P) and negative cues (N).

For the ith response, hi,j∈{0,1} denoted whether empathy cue J was present, with 1 indicating presence and 0 indicating absence. Cue presence was identified by the rubric-based automatic evaluator. As empathic wording may reflect stylistic imitation without understanding of another person’s internal state, EAC was included to assess empathy-related situational reasoning independently of response fluency and supportive language use. For a more comprehensive evaluation of YuanChat and E-URIAL, we subsequently conducted a human evaluation. We recruited 50 master’s students from the authors’ university. Participants were recruited through public notices posted on campus bulletin boards and social media. All participants joined voluntarily and received no compensation. Eligibility criteria required participants to be master’s students in clinical or counseling psychology and to have completed more than 50 hours of formal training in counseling skills. The participants comprised 27 women and 23 men, ranged in age from 23 to 25 years, and had a mean age of 24.8 (SD 0.49) years. Before participation, we obtained written informed consent and informed the participants that the data would be used for research purposes. All participants were required to read the evaluation instructions, operational definitions of each dimension, and scoring examples. No private or personally identifiable information was collected during the study.

We sent the evaluation forms to the participants by email. The evaluation set comprised responses generated by 7 models for 100 dialogue contexts randomly sampled from Dgold and SMILECHAT. We used a randomized balanced assignment design. Each evaluator assessed 10 dialogue contexts and rated the 7 anonymized model-generated responses for each context, resulting in 70 context-response pairs per evaluator. Each dialogue context was independently evaluated by 5 evaluators; therefore, each model-generated response received 5 independent ratings. To reduce order effects, the presentation order of the 7 responses within each context was randomized. Model identity and dataset source were concealed from the evaluators.

Evaluators rated each response on a 3-point scale (0=poor, 1=fair, and 2=good) across the following dimensions:

Fluency (Flu.) assessed grammatical correctness, coherence, readability, and naturalness. A score of 0 indicated errors that substantially impeded comprehension; 1 indicated an understandable response with minor errors or awkward wording; and 2 indicated a grammatically correct, coherent, and natural response.

Empathy (Emp.) assessed whether the response appropriately recognized and addressed the seeker’s emotions and perspective. A score of 0 indicated that the response ignored, misinterpreted, or responded inappropriately to the seeker’s emotional state; 1 indicated partial or generic emotional recognition; and 2 indicated accurate, sensitive, and contextually appropriate emotional understanding.

Perceived helpfulness (Help.) assessed the perceived usefulness of the response in providing emotional support. A score of 0 indicated an irrelevant, unhelpful, or potentially inappropriate response; 1 indicated a somewhat relevant but generic or limited response; and 2 indicated a relevant, constructive, and potentially helpful response. This dimension assessed perceived emotional support rather than symptom improvement, therapeutic efficacy, or clinical outcomes.

Interrater agreement was assessed using Fleiss κ. The coefficients were 0.69 for fluency, 0.77 for empathy, and 0.73 for perceived helpfulness.

To evaluate the effect of fine-tuning with ECD-3 on the models’ emotional support performance, we recruited 8 clinical professionals with direct experience in clinical and counseling psychotherapy through our professional networks and academic connections. The panel included 2 recent clinical counseling graduates who were working in hospital psychology outpatient clinics; 3 certified psychotherapists with at least 3 years of professional experience in clinical psychology; and 3 psychologists registered with the Clinical and Counseling Psychology Registration System of the Chinese Psychological Society, each with at least 5 years of experience in clinical psychological counseling and psychotherapy. All evaluators participated voluntarily and received no financial compensation.

We used 70 real counseling scenarios from Dgold. For each context, the evaluators were presented with responses generated by 6 high-performing models (CharacterGLM, GPT-4, GLM-4-9B-Chat, YuanChat-GLM4-9B, Huozi3.5, and YuanChat-Huozi3.5) and the original response of the counselor in the same counseling session, yielding 490 context-response pairs. All responses were anonymized.

We developed a dedicated web-based platform for the expert evaluation (). Evaluators first provided written informed consent and then accessed an evaluation manual within the platform. The manual described the evaluation procedure, the operational definitions of the 4 dimensions, and the criteria for assigning each score. After completing standardized training, evaluators reviewed each dialogue context and rated each response on a 3-point scale (0=poor, 1=fair, and 2=good). The 4 dimensions were defined as follows.

Empathic attunement assessed how accurately and sensitively the response recognized and addressed the seeker’s emotions, circumstances, and perspective. Appropriateness of the support strategy assessed whether the response applied an appropriate ESC strategy while remaining relevant, respectful, nonjudgmental, and suited to the help seeker’s needs and conversational context. Perceived helpfulness assessed the response’s potential to provide meaningful emotional support or an appropriate next step. Safety and adherence to professional boundaries assessed whether the response avoided potentially harmful content, unsupported diagnoses, and unwarranted treatment recommendations or assurances. It also considered appropriate acknowledgment of risk and referral when warranted. After rating all responses within a dialogue context, evaluators selected the response they judged best overall, considering all 4 dimensions.

The collection and secondary research use of the counseling records used to construct ECD-3 and Dgold were approved by the Ethics Committee of Huazhi Xinzhu Technology (approval HZXZ-IRB-202201017). Before receiving counseling services, each service user completed a written informed consent form that included an option to permit the use of their anonymized counseling records for research purposes. Only records from users who explicitly consented to such use were eligible for inclusion in ECD-3 and Dgold; records from users who did not provide consent were excluded. The data were anonymized before being provided to the research team, and no personally identifiable information was collected or received by the researchers.

The human evaluation procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Central China Normal University (approval CCNU-IRB-202403051). All evaluators provided written informed consent before participation. Participation was entirely voluntary and anonymous, and no compensation was provided for participation in this study. No personally identifiable information was included in the evaluation data analyzed in this study.

The fine-tuned Mixtral model achieved higher scores than its corresponding baseline on Dgold. It presented improvement in EIS (+0.05) and EES (+0.11), suggesting that task-specific fine-tuning aligned the model’s output with professional counseling standards.

On the out-of-domain SMILECHAT dataset, both fine-tuned models generally achieved higher scores than their corresponding base models. Compared with GLM-4-9B-Chat, YuanChat-GLM4-9B achieved higher EIS (0.53 vs 0.42), EES (0.67 vs 0.41), and empathy ratings (0.81 vs 0.72), while its fluency rating increased slightly and perceived helpfulness remained unchanged. YuanChat-Huozi3.5 also achieved higher scores than Huozi3.5 in EIS (0.59 vs 0.49), EES (0.61 vs 0.55), empathy (0.83 vs 0.74), and perceived helpfulness (0.67 vs 0.65), with no change in fluency. These results indicate that the performance gains associated with fine-tuning on ECD-3 extended to the external dataset, particularly for empathy-related measures. These findings suggest that the benefits of fine-tuning on ECD-3 generalized to a dataset differing in source and dialogue characteristics, primarily improving empathy-related performance without compromising fluency.

The fine-tuned variant achieved considerably higher scores than its base model across all empathy dimensions. Notably, EES (empathic language cues) increased from 0.38 to 0.60, and EAC (empathic reasoning) improved from 0.58 to 0.63. Human evaluators rated YuanChat-GLM4-9B higher in perceived empathy (Emp: 0.79 vs 0.61), validating that even smaller parameters (9B) could lead to substantial empathy gains when aligned with high-quality domain data.

These results addressed RQ1 by suggesting that fine-tuning on ECD-3 improved emotional support performance in both model families. Across Dgold and SMILECHAT, YuanChat-GLM4-9B and YuanChat-Huozi3.5 achieved higher EIS, EES, and human-rated empathy scores than their corresponding base models. The same pattern across the 2 datasets suggests that the improvements in empathy-related performance were not limited to the in-domain evaluation data.

The cross-model comparisons also distinguished linguistic fluency from empathic performance. GPT-4 achieved the highest fluency scores on both datasets (0.95 and 0.96), but its empathy ratings were lower than those of both fine-tuned models. YuanChat-GLM4-9B and YuanChat-Huozi3.5 also exceeded GPT-4 in EIS and EES, although CharacterGLM obtained the highest overall empathy-related scores. These results indicate that high linguistic fluency alone does not ensure strong empathic performance and that task-specific fine-tuning contributed to better performance on the evaluated empathy measures. As the models differed in architecture, parameter scale, and pretraining, the present comparisons do not isolate the effect of model size.
