Consistent with the evaluation framework, we used a combination of automated evaluation metrics and human assessment. To ensure evaluation efficiency while focusing on the core research objective, we selected empathy (Emp.) as the representative human metric.

Dynamic retrieval was the cornerstone (w/o retrieval). Replacing dynamic retrieval with static exemplars caused the most extreme performance drop across all metrics (eg, EES decreased by 0.11). This indicated that the effectiveness of ICL in emotional support tasks could be considerably influenced by the semantic alignment between the exemplars and the current query.

Explicit labels improved response generation. Removing emotion labels reduced automated evaluation performance (eg, EES decreased by 0.08) and weakened the model’s ability to track changes in the seeker’s emotional state. Removing ESC and counseling technique labels resulted in more generic expressions of comfort and reduced empathy ratings by 0.09. Qualitative analysis showed that these models frequently produced general responses such as “I’m sorry to hear that” instead of applying specific counseling techniques such as clarification or support. The results also supported the synergistic effect reported in previous research []: emotion labels represented the seeker’s emotional state, ESC and technique labels guided response strategy, and retrieved exemplars influenced response style.

To concretely illustrate the impact of dynamic retrieval, we analyzed a representative case from our test set. The removal of retrieval mechanisms resulted in a loss of strategic depth ().

E-URIAL: empathy untuned large language models with restyled in-context alignment.

Taken together, the ablation results indicated that dynamic retrieval was the most influential component. Emotion and strategy labels collectively served as indispensable guide rails that reduced empathy drift and superficial responding. These findings suggested that each component of E-URIAL contributes uniquely to empathic response quality and that the framework performs optimally when all 3 elements operate in concert.

While the E-URIAL framework enhanced empathic performance, a qualitative analysis of outlier cases suggested 2 primary failure modes. First, contextual contamination, or exemplar drift, explained the diminishing returns observed when k> 3. It occurred when retrieved exemplars, namely language stylistic anchors, introduced linguistic cues from mismatched life contexts (eg, using workplace terminology to address academic stress). Even if the predicted strategy labels were correct, these “leaked” cues could dilute the response’s relevance, suggesting that semantic precision in retrieval was more important than mere exemplar quantity. Second, strategic misalignment occurred when the model overrelied on problem-solving, where the model bypassed the [Comfort] stage and moved prematurely to [Action].

Experimental results suggested that the integration of strategic SFT (YuanChat) and dynamic inference-time alignment (E-URIAL) created a robust framework for professional emotional support.

YuanChat-Huozi3.5 achieved its strongest overall performance when combined with E-URIAL, suggesting that SFT and inference-time guidance played complementary roles. Fine-tuning on ECD-3 improved empathy-related performance relative to the backbone model. E-URIAL provided additional context-specific guidance through predicted emotion and strategy labels and dynamically retrieved counselor exemplars, without further parameter updates. The ablation results showed the largest performance decline when dynamically retrieved exemplars were replaced with static exemplars, indicating that contextually relevant demonstrations were an important contributor under the evaluated conditions. Together, these findings suggest that combining domain-specific parameter adaptation with retrieval-based guidance could improve the contextual appropriateness and strategic consistency of emotional support responses.

The performance gains of YuanChat-GLM4-9B over its GLM-4-9B-Chat backbone suggest that a relatively compact model can benefit from domain-specific, structured supervision. Fine-tuning on ECD-3 improved its empathy identification, empathic expression, and human-rated empathy across both evaluation datasets. These results indicate that parameter-efficient adaptation using counseling-informed data could enable relatively compact models to achieve competitive performance on empathy-related tasks.

Across the evaluated models and metrics, k=3 generally provided the strongest overall performance, whereas increasing the number of retrieved exemplars to k=10 yielded limited additional gains and, in several cases, lower scores. This pattern suggests diminishing returns as the number of exemplars increased under the evaluated conditions.

At k=3, a small set of highly ranked exemplars may have provided sufficient contextual and stylistic guidance for generating responses consistent with the predicted emotion and strategy labels. Increasing k to 10 may have introduced redundant or less relevant contextual information, thereby increasing prompt complexity and reducing the relative prominence of the current dialogue and its associated labels. Prompt length represents another possible explanation. As the model input was limited to 4096 tokens, longer prompts may have increased the likelihood of truncation or reduced the effective influence of relevant information.

This study makes 3 theoretical contributions. First, it conceptualizes machine empathy as the coordination of strategic intent and linguistic realization across changing dialogue contexts. Strategic intent concerns the selection of an appropriate emotional support stage and counseling technique, whereas linguistic realization concerns how that strategy is expressed through empathic language. This distinction connects counseling theory with computational response generation and provides an interpretable account of how LLMs can adapt their responses to users’ emotional and support needs.

Second, the findings clarify the role of explicit, theory-informed labels in empathic response generation. The ablation results showed that removing emotion or strategy labels reduced performance, suggesting that these labels help models identify the user’s emotional state, select an appropriate supportive action, and express that action in language. The results support the use of structured intermediate representations in domain-specific fine-tuning and inference-time guidance. They also suggest that structured domain knowledge can help smaller models achieve competitive performance, although the present experiments did not directly compare different levels of label granularity.

Third, the findings provide evidence about how dynamic retrieval contributes to inference-time alignment. Replacing dynamically retrieved exemplars with static exemplars produced the largest performance decline in the ablation study. Performance generally improved when the number of exemplars increased from 1 to 3 but did not improve consistently with 10 exemplars. These results indicate that contextually relevant demonstrations can improve strategy realization, while additional exemplars may introduce less relevant information. The effectiveness of retrieval-augmented ICL therefore depends on both exemplar relevance and exemplar quantity.

The YuanChat models and E-URIAL framework have several practical implications for emotional support systems. First, the performance of YuanChat-GLM4-9B suggests that relatively compact models can benefit from domain-specific fine-tuning and structured inference-time guidance. Second, the construction of ECD-3 provides a practical approach to converting real-world Chinese counseling dialogues into structured training data while incorporating counseling theory, label-consistency filtering, and privacy safeguards. This approach may inform the development of similar datasets in other languages and cultural contexts. Third, the distinction between strategic intent and linguistic realization may be applicable to other forms of supportive communication, including health care communication and personalized education. Further domain-specific validation would be required before applying the framework in these settings.

First, although the ECD-3 dataset provided high-quality counseling dialogues, its source from a single Chinese company could introduce sample homogeneity; therefore, the current findings are primarily grounded in Chinese emotional support settings. Future researchers should incorporate cross-cultural and multisource mental health data to enhance generalizability. Second, although differentiated PEFT methods and the auxiliary use of GPT-4 for label filtering were controlled for consistency, future studies would require the employment of cross-validation across diverse architectures and broader baseline models to further mitigate potential methodological biases. Third, the proposed framework was evaluated in emotional support contexts; its translation into formal clinical mental health settings would require meeting substantially more rigorous standards, including expert clinical oversight, systematic safety evaluation, risk management protocols, and validation through real-world clinical trials. Future work will therefore focus on strengthening the clinical applicability and real-world deployment. Fourth, acknowledging the inherent variability in LLM outputs for complex emotional tasks, we plan to implement multirun stability quantification using metrics such as text consistency coefficients to ensure relatively robust performance evaluations in professional psychological scenarios.

Finally, future work should address the potential confusion between empathy and sycophancy. Although both empathy and sycophancy may involve emotionally responsive language, they differ in function. Empathy is oriented toward long-term psychological well-being and, when necessary, challenges users’ maladaptive cognitions. Sycophancy is driven by users’ immediate satisfaction; it uncritically agrees with users and avoids conflict []. The evaluation framework in this study already contains implicit safeguards against sycophancy. For example, the challenge category of counseling techniques includes identifying contradictions in users’ narratives and questioning maladaptive beliefs, and the negative linguistic cues in the EES metric, such as fabricated conclusions and uncritical agreement, can penalize overly accommodating responses. However, this study did not include an explicit sycophancy detection metric. Future research should incorporate explicit detection mechanisms into the evaluation framework and use long-term satisfaction rather than immediate satisfaction to assess empathic quality.

This study highlighted 3 contributions that advanced emotional support systems. First, it helped narrow the gap between generic consolation and professionally grounded emotional support by training on the ECD-3 dataset, which provided a foundational resource for emotional support research and model development. Second, it optimized empathic alignment via the E-URIAL method, which operationalized composite strategy, strategic intent, and linguistic realization to improve stylistic coherence. Third, the findings suggest that structured, fine-grained strategy labels may help improve the emotional support performance of smaller models.

By embedding professional counseling techniques into AI-driven dialogue, our findings pave the way for scalable and strategy-aware digital interventions that can effectively complement traditional psychotherapy and expand the accessibility of preliminary mental health support. The findings also suggest the potential value of such systems for medical mental health settings, particularly in expanding access to scalable and context-sensitive supportive interactions. At the same time, their contribution to health care should be understood as clinically promising rather than clinically established, given the continued need for stronger external validation, standardized outcome assessment, and explicit safety governance.

Building on these findings, several directions remain for future exploration. One promising avenue is cross-cultural empathy adaptation, which would involve expanding the dataset and framework to incorporate diverse cultural and linguistic nuances, thereby enhancing generalizability and robustness. Another direction concerns stability and reliability quantification, focused on developing methods to measure and control output variability in emotionally sensitive interactions, with the aim of obtaining consistent emotional support quality across different runs. A third direction is multimodal emotional perception, which would extend the E-URIAL framework to integrate nonverbal cues such as voice and facial expressions, enabling a more comprehensive human-machine empathic interaction.

psychology.title: Types of statistical arguments in empirical research in psychology
psychology.abstract: Numerous solutions have been proposed to address the problem of statistical misuse and misunderstanding in research in psychology. This might have diverted attention from how or whether scientists are actually engaging in statistical reasoning by arguing about and with statistics within the context of the reasoning involved in empirical research in their written papers. In this paper, we studied statistical reasonings in psychological research papers. Specifically, we inductively coded arguments of 42 papers from seven highly cited psychology journals. With these data, we formed a partial, empirical typology with which we described different types of statistical arguments used in the literature. Papers, and their statistical arguments, in empirical psychology can be interpreted as possessing a ‘legal’ nature. Common arguments, such as statistical significance, are often used as a tacit and concise way of certifying that a claim, including conclusions, is empirically and statistically substantiated under the social standards of good research in our field. However, approval of research based on certifications may hinder the exposition and clarity of statistical arguments.
psychology.text:
How do researchers bridge the gap from formal statistical results to conclusions about their research questions? In what has been termed statistical reasoning, researchers ‘reason with statistical ideas and make sense of statistical information’ [, p. 1]. Attempts to understand this process have mostly focused on misuse and misunderstanding of statistics [], especially of statistical concepts strongly connected to inference []. However, we know surprisingly little about empirical researchers’ statistical reasoning aside from what we consider faulty or skewed. In this study, we attempt to learn more about how researchers employ statistical reasoning in empirical research.

In 1942, Joseph Berkson [] pointed out a problem with making inferences with certainty using null hypothesis significance testing (NHST). It is impossible to absolutely disprove the null hypothesis when testing merely indicates that the difference between two groups is unlikely to be derived from a population difference of zero. This implies that one must always address the possibility that chance brought about the results of an experiment. Furthermore, researchers neither know the probability of their result being a false positive after rejecting the null hypothesis [,] nor the probability of the null hypothesis itself []. This uncertainty, however, is not always addressed in empirical research [].

In addition to researchers, editors and reviewers also seem to expect significance (p < 0.05) to mean much more than what it really does []. This culture [,] of seeking significant results based on misinterpretations or false expectations seems to ensue in a high frequency of p-values below 0.05 [] and questionable research practices [] and has led to unsuccessful attempts to replicate initially considered robust findings in psychology []; sparkling reform movements that either sought to instaurate estimation instead of NHST [] or a Bayesian approach instead of a frequentist framework [] to improve empirical research. However, problems of expectation and interpretation are also found when people make estimations using confidence intervals (CIs) [] or when they test hypotheses with Bayes factors [,].

Although the work on identifying statistical reporting errors is prolific, less is known about what statistical thinking and, thus, reasoning look like [,,], let alone in written format. There is no descriptive account of how researchers make inferences and interpret statistical results by combining ideas about data and chance in their reports []. Statistics is a deductive, logical structure from which conclusions can be drawn []; therefore, when using it, researchers must present in-depth arguments that validate and contextualize the inferences that follow this structure. When drawing conclusions, they must understand how variation, uncertainty, sampling process, data collection, unobservable variables’ impact, measurement and bias interact when carrying out an analysis [,]. Considering how hard it is to formulate a valid statistical inference, we would expect that researchers deal with complex and challenging ideas and information, especially while writing their final report. Consequently, their paper should show such thought complexity, for researchers are making a sensible case for their conclusion by laying out the arguments for and/or against it.

Six years after Berkson's article [], Dorothy Sayers highlighted two shortcomings that hampered argumentative discussions and comprehension during their time. Firstly, Sayers [] criticized writers of her day for failing to define their terms when arguing. Above, we alluded to erroneous definitions of statistical concepts that can undermine the conclusions reached by researchers. Secondly, Sayers [] claimed that mathematics teaching was disjoint from logic, so students believed that they were unrelated. Chris Wild made a very similar remark about education a few decades ago. ‘We do not want to develop graduates who keep what they know about psychology … and what they know about statistics in separate mental compartments’ [, p. 170]. We do not know whether logic, psychology and statistics are segregated by ‘water-tight bulkheads’ [, p. 4] when learned nowadays. Nevertheless, by inspecting statistical reasonings through arguments in written articles, we should be able to observe how connected and disconnected these three are.

In this project, under the larger umbrella of reasoning, we consider arguing as offering a set of reasons for or against a conclusion []. We undertake a qualitative approach to identify the scope of statistical reasoning used in articles published in prominent psychology journals. Thus, we would like to describe the set and structure of reasons that psychologists give to support or undermine a scientific inference. For this aim, we intend to identify the different arguments researchers lay out with and about statistical information stemming from their results through inductive content analysis [] and the construction of an empirically grounded partial typology [,]. To this end, we have collected data on and about the statistical results of an article's first inferential claim, which should be in the sections of results and discussion []. We are making two assumptions throughout our work. First, we assume that authors write with intention, so we are not carving out what we think authors wanted, tried or subconsciously attempted to convey. Rather, we attempt to stay as close as possible to what the authors communicated in writing [,].

Our second assumption is that when someone argues in a research article, said argument can be identified by analysing the principled relationships between propositions, which are assertions or statements about something. Connecting words, like ‘despite’, ‘because’ and ‘for’, should aid us in identifying such principled relationships []. Our overall purpose is to provide a description of written statistical arguments indicated by data [], which should shed light on relevant aspects that could explain how people think and reason about and with statistics in the larger context of scientific reasoning when reporting empirical research.

The authors of this paper have a sceptical attitude towards the typical use of statistical inference in general and NHST in particular and have explicitly written about these concerns. Undoubtedly, this has coloured our interpretation of the outcomes of the present investigation and has influenced the approach that we have taken. Finally, the first author has some familiarity with theological literature, including a biblical study method, which has influenced the approach that we have taken.

For the present study, we followed a qualitative research design. On the qualitative research continuum, our study leaned more towards tightly rather than loosely structured research designs [,]. Decisions on research questions, sample characteristics and coding style were made before collecting data owing to time constraints, practicality and the nature of our investigation. Still, we remained flexible in altering our research design when necessary.

Accordingly, we analysed arguments’ premises (the reasons for) and conclusions through their syntactic composition [,,]. Subsequently, we inductively coded [] and aggregated these arguments according to patterns similarly to how it is done in conventional content analysis []. However, when we were gathering data, we chose to make a partial typology [,] based on an argumentation layout framework []. We did so because we believed a typology gave a better account of the written arguments in comparison to aggregating them by pattern similarity. You can view the process of our study in greater detail in .

We gathered data from English-written psychology papers that reported at least one quantitative analysis on empirical data. We have included meta-analysis and empirical studies that had at least one inferential statistical analysis. Descriptive articles that made such a claim were also included. We ruled out articles about statistical procedures dealing with mathematical facts, simulation or psychometric studies.

Our sample is from journals that have a high journal impact factor (JIF), H-index (H) and CiteScore (CS), which are metrics of journals’ influence that use citations for calculation. Thus, articles published in these journals are, on average, frequently read and referenced. The measurements for the JIF were gathered from [], for the H-index from [] and for the CS from []. In the SCImago Lab and Elsevier websites, we selected the subject area of ‘Psychology’ and the filter of ‘Journals’ for our search. Then, we did a quick inspection of the 50 psychology journals with the highest CS score up to the latest available measurement – 2023. We did the same for the 40 psychology journals with the highest H-index up to 2024. We selected journals based on their description, excluding those that published mostly review, theoretical and methodological articles. We also excluded journals in which psychology articles were published occasionally on a quick inspection of their latest volume. Finally, we also based our selection on comparing and selecting the highest JIF possible between journals. The six chosen journals are as follows:
—American Psychologist (JIF = 12.4; H = 283; CS = 18.5)—Journal of Applied Psychology (JIF = 9.4; H = 353; CS = 17.8)—Psychological Bulletin (JIF = 17.3; H = 379; CS = 33.6)—Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics (JIF = 16.3; H = 123; CS = 29.4)—Nature Human Behaviour (JIF = 22.3; H = 113; CS = 36.8)—Cognition (JIF = 2.8; H = 235; CS = 6.2)

Journal of Applied Psychology (JIF = 9.4; H = 353; CS = 17.8)

Psychological Bulletin (JIF = 17.3; H = 379; CS = 33.6)

Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics (JIF = 16.3; H = 123; CS = 29.4)

Nature Human Behaviour (JIF = 22.3; H = 113; CS = 36.8)

Cognition (JIF = 2.8; H = 235; CS = 6.2)

Cognition was chosen because the previously selected cognitive psychology journal published few empirical articles. Next, we selected seven papers published during 2025 from each journal. It was within our original plan to extend our sample beyond 42 papers if we had not reached saturation by then. Nevertheless, we consider that increasing our sample would not bring new or informative data [] that would change our interpretation at its core. We selected the journals’ issues published between April and June of 2025. A list of exclusions can be viewed in appendix A in the supplementary material, and our dataset can be found in our OSF repository, together with the preregistration of our study.

The first author read and collected data from each article. We identified (i) each article's first mentioned inferential claim. Then, we gathered (ii) its corresponding statistical result and also collected (iii) the ensuing discussion and/or conclusion. Here the units of analysis [] were the sentence(s) or paragraph(s) in which authors argued about how their result(s) supported or undermined a conclusion(s) about their main hypothesis. Accordingly, we did not only collect arguments using statistical results but also arguments about said statistical results. That is, premises that were used to support the inference made with a statistical result, for example ‘our results replicate previous findings’. Even so, we excluded propositions that were too far removed from a statistical result and its ensuing claim, like those more concerned with theory construction.

To support argument recognition, we used some elements of a theological method called arcing [,,]. The aim of this method is to provide a ‘list of possible logical relationships, with descriptive names’ [, p. 10] to aid text interpretation. For example, a keyword like ‘because’ signals that, frequently, following ‘because’ we find the argument that supports the statement before said keyword. This is a ground subordinate relationship, for the second clause functions as the ‘ground’ of the first one [,,]. Sometimes writers do not explicitly use connecting keywords between sentences. However, for instance, understanding that one distinct statement can function as the ‘ground’ of the previous proposition will help us to detect arguments that are not explicitly spelled out. Appendix B in the supplementary material presents some logical relationships employed in this method called arcing. In summary, we started off by looking at the syntax of sentences and paragraphs to examine potential logical relationships between clauses. Then, we looked for patterns or similarities between logical relationships to codify our data.

Our codification was inductive [,]. We cyclically collected and analysed units of analysis, creating codes that could be removed, confirmed or modified by new data input later. As we were grouping codes with similar arguments, we realized that we could create types of arguments based on a combination of attributes [,]. To construct this typological system, we used Toulmin's argumentation model []. Argumentation is ‘a communicative and interactional act complex aimed at resolving a difference of opinion with the addressee by putting forward a constellation of propositions the arguer can be held accountable for to make the standpoint at issue acceptable to a rational judge who judges reasonably’ [, p. 2102].

The gist of argumentation theory is to ‘provide adequate instruments for analysing, evaluating and producing argumentative discourse’ [, p. 2104]. We availed ourselves of one of these models because we considered that arguments in papers were presented to be judged by rational judges who were tasked with evaluating how cogent the reasons for a standpoint or conclusion were []. In fact, the model that we are using [] also showed examples with keywords that are similar to the ones used in arcing. Because of that similarity, it was simpler to organize our codes into types based on the model as we describe next.

We grouped our collected data in a typology based on three attributes: (i) result claims, (ii) presuppositions, and (iii) argumentation components. First, result claims were propositions that revolved around or referred to the statistical results of a study. In the majority of cases, these were conclusions. Said claims were further divided according to whether they were consonant or dissonant with authors’ expectations.

Expectations in the context of our research could be indicated through a hypothesis, a theoretical statement or a prediction (i.e. finding a large instead of a small effect size). Thus, a consonant result claim was defined as a statistical result that was consistent with or followed any sort of expectation, regardless of whether authors later qualified said consonant claim with a limitation. For instance, a result that is not generalizable to other populations but that supports the hypothesis is considered consonant. Such a claim, however, would be considered dissonant if it does not follow the expectation set by a hypothesis, regardless of whether authors later accepted and qualified it with a set of limitations. For example, authors may conclude that a treatment worked for a subgroup of women because the corresponding result was the only statistically significant one of their study, even when their expectation was that the psychotherapy would be effective for everyone. That would be a dissonant result claim even if authors later stated that a subgroup result should be taken with caution.

Secondly, analogous to our approach with consonant and dissonant result claims, we divided the attribute of presuppositions into two extremes: credible and contested. Pieces of text in the credible presuppositions category refer to authors stating that some presuppositions they had were, reasonably, upheld. Presuppositions here could be arguments for why the results answered the research question or arguments for why results had more credence because of some authority (i.e. a respected paper or expert) or an employed statistical technique. All of these have the purpose of arguing for why the results of a study should be considered as trustworthy. The category of contested presuppositions was for when authors considered that the alluded properties of a trustworthy study and its results could be called into question. Then we categorized texts arguing for or against these credited or contested presuppositions.

We were inspired by Stephen Toulmin's [] model of argumentation (see ) for the third attribute: argumentation component. We considered that there are usually three ways in which authors lay out their argumentation in papers: inferences, backings and rebuttals. This is different from the original model, which included six components.

To begin with, the first component of the original model is the data—from here on ground (i) to avoid confusion. The ground is the information or facts that function as the foundation upon which the arguer seeks to establish a proposition, that is a claim (ii), which is the second original component. The ground could take the form of what traditionally is known as the minor premise, while the claim would be the conclusion. Toulmin's [] example of a ground is ‘Harry was born in Bermuda’ to which the claim is ‘Harry is a British citizen’.

The third component, the warrant (iii), is the bridge that takes one from the ground to the claim. That is, it is a rule, principle or anything else that legitimizes the inference by showing that the ground has a bearing on the claim. It can take the form of what is usually known as the major premise: ‘if p, then q’. The warrant of Toulmin's example [] is ‘a man born in Bermuda will generally be a British citizen’. The rebuttal (iv) applies to those circumstances or conditions in which the warrant no longer works, while a qualifier (v) – ‘certainly’, ‘may’, ‘presumably’ etc. – indicates the strength of the warrant once the rebuttals have been weighed. One rebuttal that may refute our warrant is that ‘Harry has changed his nationality’ or that ‘both of his parents are extraterrestrials’ []. Therefore, because we do not have assurances about both of these rebuttals, we would have to add a qualifier like presumably to our claim: ‘so presumably he is a British person/citizen’.

Finally, there is the backing (vi) of the warrant, which sustains the soundness of the argument. Arguers back their warrants with other assurances like facts or theoretical considerations that grant them authority or currency in the subject under discussion. So, if Toulmin's [] warrant about Harry, ‘a man born in Bermuda will generally be a British citizen’, would be challenged, he could back this warrant by citing the specific statutes of the British Nationality Act. Of course, the backing here is about how Harry is seen in the eyes of the law. Not all backing can be done with the law. For instance, backing a warrant such as that a whale may be taken to be a mammal by means of a law would be nonsensical. Instead, such warrants are backed by a scientifically accepted taxonomy. Thus, there is a field-dependency [] when it comes to the needed backings to establish warrants.

Coming back to the three components we used in our research, we grouped those propositions in the backing (i) component, the meaning of which seemed to support the legitimacy of any principle that authors follow to move from a piece of information to a claim. The inference (ii) component refers to texts written in such a way that we could verify that the movement from ground to claim had been done []. An inference, thus, could contain three to four of Toulmin's components: ground, claim, warrant and, from time to time, backing. In our data, the inference had a claim that was usually explicit, a ground that was often explicit and a warrant that was never explicit. Authors commonly mentioned the backing instead of the claim. We can take another example from Toulmin [, pp. 101–102] to show what we mean by this:

Ground: Petersen is a Swede;

Backing: The proportion of Swedes who are Roman Catholic is less than 2%

Warrant: A Swede can be taken almost certainly not to be a Roman Catholic;

Claim: So, almost certainly, Petersen is not a Roman Catholic.

People could use an abridged version of this argument in daily life by saying that the proportion of Roman Catholic Swedes is less than 2% (this is the backing in Toulmin's model), so, almost certainly, Petersen is not Roman Catholic because he is Swedish (the conclusion). Rebuttal (iii), the third type of argumentation component, was for when authors acknowledged or argued about instances or conditions by which their result claims would no longer be valid. We stress that we used Toulmin's model as a guide to create our typology rather than a strict theoretical framework to be followed.

The final combination of the typological attributes that we described in our methods can be seen in . It shows the types of statistical arguments in empirical research in psychology that we have constructed with our data by combining such attributes. These types will further be described below, each accompanied by two example quotations. It is worth noting that after examining all the included papers, we scarcely found instances in which written argumentation resembled the complete, integrated layout of Toulmin's model for argumentation. As we will see, the components are rather fragmented and isolated, following the traditional format for articles in psychology [], which encourages segregating introduction, methods, results and discussion into different sections. In addition, we have included other quotations to each type of argument in appendix C in the supplementary material.

Theoretically conceivable combination of attributes.

Note: This is a partial typology because not all combinations of attributes (cells) were filled even though merger was theoretically conceivable.

The first type of backing that we distinguished in our data for consonant result claims was obtaining or having results that resembled those registered in the literature as a precedent. How and in what way was usually not very clear:P22: ‘This result aligns with existing literature on therapeutic interventions for …’P27: ‘Our findings focusing on Europe mirror somewhat those of Surkalim et al. (2022).’

P22: ‘This result aligns with existing literature on therapeutic interventions for …’

P27: ‘Our findings focusing on Europe mirror somewhat those of Surkalim et al. (2022).’

A second type of backing was when sensitivity results were used to support the main result's validity. In the legal setting, we could think about them as assurances that the results were not circumstantial owing to statistical artefacts:
P8: ‘Importantly, all relationships remained significant after controlling for previously examined moderators (leader benevolence and power distance orientation) and alternative positive and negative states’P36: ‘These results were supported by the analyses on pain unpleasantness ratings (see APPENDIX A: Supplementary material 3).’

P8: ‘Importantly, all relationships remained significant after controlling for previously examined moderators (leader benevolence and power distance orientation) and alternative positive and negative states’

P36: ‘These results were supported by the analyses on pain unpleasantness ratings (see APPENDIX A: Supplementary material 3).’

Thirdly, authors thought that preregistration, methodology, type of statistical analysis, design or any other characteristic of their study backed how they got their inference. These characteristics have some value for the research community to which authors appeal for assurances about their inferences. How valuable they are and why was not usually made explicit in the papers:
P1: ‘With this comprehensive multilevel, multivariate meta-analysis, we set out to shed light on the question …’P10: ‘In the first preregistered hypothesis it was predicted that the investigated conditions would … This hypothesis was confirmed…’

P1: ‘With this comprehensive multilevel, multivariate meta-analysis, we set out to shed light on the question …’

P10: ‘In the first preregistered hypothesis it was predicted that the investigated conditions would … This hypothesis was confirmed…’

Finally, authors further clarify or define their results in theoretical or methodological ways. After all, a reader might not be convinced without understanding what the author is talking about. Hence, these explanations function as rhetorical devices to give assurances to the reader that the result is coherent or does make sense in light of theoretical predictions, methodology or reasonableness in general:
P9: ‘There was very little difference in the risk associated with moderate or high-memory specificity, consistent with the theory (Williams et al., 2007) that mental illness only arises if …’P21: ‘These day-specific changes align with the structured design of B4DT, in which each day of the treatment is intended to target different psychological processes.’

P9: ‘There was very little difference in the risk associated with moderate or high-memory specificity, consistent with the theory (Williams et al., 2007) that mental illness only arises if …’

P21: ‘These day-specific changes align with the structured design of B4DT, in which each day of the treatment is intended to target different psychological processes.’

Alternatively, authors use a few ways of backing dissonant result claims, although this happens less frequently than the backing of consonant result claims. In three articles, researchers saw the need to provide assurances that what they found was relevant to their final claim despite some other features that indicated the opposite. For instance, when authors thought that a small effect size did not follow initial expectations, they gave assurances about their result by indicating that it was, for example, either statistically significant or clinically meaningful. In other words, authors emphasize a specific feature of the result. In , we called this type of argument despite small, the effect is important:
P11: ‘Although overall effect sizes were small-to-moderate, small effects are clinically meaningful when accumulating over time (Funder & Ozer, 2019).’P12: ‘Small but significant differences across levels of cognitive demand (p = .005) emerged for chronic studies’

P11: ‘Although overall effect sizes were small-to-moderate, small effects are clinically meaningful when accumulating over time (Funder & Ozer, 2019).’

P12: ‘Small but significant differences across levels of cognitive demand (p = .005) emerged for chronic studies’

In other instances, inferences were dissonant with their hypotheses, theories or expectations, so authors pointed out the existence of literature or alternative antecedents that could provide assurances:
P27: ‘Our findings for midlife in the United States contrast with those of historical declines and stability observed in … (Clark et al., 2015; Hawkley et al., 2019; Mund et al., 2020) but are similar to … (Buecker et al., 2021)’P34: ‘This finding is in line with other international studies on trust in scientists 5–7. Our study thus confirms, expands and strengthens previous work that refutes the narrative of a wide-ranging crisis of trust’

P27: ‘Our findings for midlife in the United States contrast with those of historical declines and stability observed in … (Clark et al., 2015; Hawkley et al., 2019; Mund et al., 2020) but are similar to … (Buecker et al., 2021)’

P34: ‘This finding is in line with other international studies on trust in scientists 5–7. Our study thus confirms, expands and strengthens previous work that refutes the narrative of a wide-ranging crisis of trust’

Authors also gave assurances to the choices they made in their research. Avoiding type III errors in  refers to when authors justified conducting an analysis or the overall study in a certain way to avoid ‘giving the right answer to the wrong problem’ [, p. 134]. Thus, they used the objective of their study as a justification for making certain choices:

Researchers made inferences to support claims in empirical research in multiple ways, logically, since the set of statistical techniques and approaches to take from is broad. There are, overall, two ways in which researchers argue for their final claim after making an inference. Reasonings that did not fall into these two groups were placed in the type labelled ‘other’ (see ). The first group encompasses researchers directly addressing their statistical information. This group consists of reasonings in which researchers wind up accepting the null hypothesis of no effect based on a null result (not necessarily through significance testing) or accepting the difference between a null result and another significant result as a significant difference:

Namely, researchers used the consistency of multiple analyses, results, experiments and/or studies to give support to a claim or conclusion. In this article, we have examined how researchers report their statistical reasoning in empirical research. We did so by inductively collecting qualitative data to create a partial typology of the types of statistical reasonings expressed in arguments within the larger context of scientific reasoning in papers. Our aim in examining 42 empirical studies in psychology was to explore rather than evaluate how researchers argue with and about statistics in the field.

We have distinguished different types of arguments in papers that share three distinct purposes: (i) give assurances about the legitimacy of inferences in the form of backings, (ii) make the movement from premises to claim in the form of inferences, and (iii) set constraints to claims in the form of rebuttals. These types of arguments could be applied in the context of consonant results, dissonant results or (credible or contested) presuppositions. In our results, we see two natures of statistical reasoning in empirical research. First, a sort of ‘legal’ nature of papers that may influence how arguments are presented. Second, the particularities that we see may be related to the nature of the reasoning itself.

To begin with, when discussing inferences, we distinguished four types of arguments or reasonings in which researchers directly addressed their statistical result in order to make a claim: accepting the null hypothesis, rejecting the null hypothesis, estimation and description. Authors mostly reported the backing of their final argument, which would be the result of the test with or without its attached label; for example, the test is significant (p < 0.05), or the effect size is small (d = 0.2, 95% CI [0.01–0.03]).

With this, authors would claim that something was higher, lower, small, moderate, larger, different, the same, existing or absent based on a statistical result. This is closely related to the final claim of the study suggesting, for example, that a relationship exists between variables. In such reasoning, we contend that the report of the statistical result functions as a sort of certification. It certifies that a claim is empirically and statistically substantiated. It seems that this certification is the reason that the statistical report is intertwined with claims that are very similar to the study's conclusion: this is higher, this is reduced, there is no effect etcetera. Consequently, even though the backing and claims are reported, the statistical warrant remains implicit.

That is, a warrant like ‘if the probability of the observed data from an experiment or data more extreme occurring given that the claim is false is less than the established significance threshold (e.g. p < 0.05), the data are inconsistent with the claim (e.g. hypothesis, theory, etc.) being false’ is assumed to be known by the reader. Similarly, the estimation warrant was usually/always/typically left unspoken: ‘the relative frequency of observations of an event is fairly close to the event's probability of occurrence as the number of experiments is fairly large’. If manifested, authors would explicitly state the warrant with their result in the argumentation; for example, that the probability of the observed or more extreme data if the null hypothesis were true is below the significance threshold. Or that their observations lead them to believe that their 95% CI may include the true effect size, given that they have the property that if the procedure were to be repeated an infinite amount of times, it would contain the parameter in 95% of these cases.

The fact that scientific writing typically leaves the warrant implicit makes us believe that papers reflect a sort of ‘legal-like’ documentation procedure in which claims are justified or legitimized on how consistent the statistical proof is with the, frequently fuzzy, expectations, standards or certifying norms of the field or its subfields. These standards and expectations can be seen in an article in the form of, for example, the terminology accepted by our scientific community to certify or decertify a claim or its validity. We say that they are fuzzy because they usually do not show a clear meaning in papers; and yet, authors use them frequently, like when they use significance or an effect size label to characterize a result.

These procedures beget tacit argumentation where both the communicator and receiver assume that both know the behind-the-scenes statistical argument. That is, if a paper says that a finding is significant, it is assumed that the author and reader know what the implications are for the underlying hypotheses and expectations without further exposition. As we have mentioned in our introduction, this assumption is not substantiated by research, for in papers, surveys and textbooks mis- and over-interpretation of statistical concepts is frequent. Furthermore, in our research, we have seen authors erroneously claiming that the null was supported on the basis of statistically non-significant results (e.g. see []). This implicitness also happens with CIs and effect sizes. We found several instances of researchers using CIs as a backdoor to significance testing by stressing that the interval does not include zero. While it can be good practice to report estimated effect sizes, it does not add additional information if the final claim is written solely based on significance testing. Some may argue that this suffices because the goal is only to certify the potential presence of an effect. Nevertheless, under that logic, the reporting of the CI and the effect size still remain superfluous to that goal because the claim has nothing to do with the estimation paradigm.

To us, this ‘legal’ nature of a paper becomes evident in the strict compliance with the schematic segregation of sections within articles. In our study, we inspected the results, discussion, limitations and conclusion sections, which encompass the division promoted by the APA format []. Following the structure of these four sections preserves a certain sensation of order for the price of unification. When argumentation is unified, it looks different:
P14: ‘Finally, one should also keep in mind that, despite decades of research, the efficacy of existing treatments is still limited. The NNTs [Numbers Needed to Treat] we found in this meta-analysis exemplify this: even for the most effective interventions, compared to inactive controls, at least three patients need to receive the treatment to generate one additional case of improvement. It should be noted that this effect may still be overestimated. For most mental health problems, we found lower point estimates when only low-risk-of-bias studies were considered and maybe there are unknown biases that this analysis did not control for. We also saw that, for many indications, wait-lists still dominate as the comparator. As mentioned in the introduction, wait-lists are often considered one of the weakest control groups, and they might inflate treatment effects (Furukawa et al., 2014; Mohr et al., 2009, 2014). In the future, more realistic comparisons are needed to ensure that psychological treatments pass a “severe test” (Harrer et al., 2023; Mayo, 2005).’

P14: ‘Finally, one should also keep in mind that, despite decades of research, the efficacy of existing treatments is still limited. The NNTs [Numbers Needed to Treat] we found in this meta-analysis exemplify this: even for the most effective interventions, compared to inactive controls, at least three patients need to receive the treatment to generate one additional case of improvement. It should be noted that this effect may still be overestimated. For most mental health problems, we found lower point estimates when only low-risk-of-bias studies were considered and maybe there are unknown biases that this analysis did not control for. We also saw that, for many indications, wait-lists still dominate as the comparator. As mentioned in the introduction, wait-lists are often considered one of the weakest control groups, and they might inflate treatment effects (Furukawa et al., 2014; Mohr et al., 2009, 2014). In the future, more realistic comparisons are needed to ensure that psychological treatments pass a “severe test” (Harrer et al., 2023; Mayo, 2005).’

Here, the authors are integrating several reasons in favour of two claims, the first one being that the efficacy of current treatments seems to be limited. They say this because (i) they find that an NNT of 3 is still large when compared to inactive controls; and (ii) these effects might be overestimated because (ii.1) lower point estimates were found for low-risk of bias studies, and (ii.2) there might be other unknown biases; moreover (iii) the use of wait-lists as a comparison group also raises concerns about overestimation; therefore, (iv) better studies are needed – which is the second claim they are looking to make. You could agree or disagree with these two statements, but to do so, you would have to deal with the reasons the authors are giving for them. Reasons that are based on results that, in turn, should be held up by presuppositions that you may want to examine, too. A zealous attitude towards abiding by the segregation of information in APA style could obscure this argumentation, making it difficult to assess the reasoning's validity. We also must acknowledge that this integration reflects an expertise on meta-analysis besides psychotherapeutic research, so similar arguments with and about statistics may require some proficiency in statistics that many may not (want to) possess.

We can make a similar analysis of an integrated argumentation using our typology (note that integrated does not necessarily equal valid). Take for instance the next paragraph: ‘Our multilevel, multivariate meta-analysis provides the most comprehensive and rigorous compilation and assessment of relevant studies to date. We found a small effect in the expected direction, which remained robust to outliers and potential publication bias. At the same time, we found substantial effect heterogeneity. Moreover, in line with other researchers, we cannot preclude that the effect is in fact spurious or could even go in the opposite direction (as indicated by the prediction interval).’ The authors begin with (i) two backings—study characteristics—and, thus, their results; that is, doing a multilevel, multivariate meta-analysis, and then, with such methodology, providing the most comprehensive and rigorous compilation … to date. Later, they make (ii) an inference when they say that they found a small effect in the expected direction.

Then, the authors (iii) back again their result—consistency of sensitivity analyses—when they state that the effect remained robust to outliers and potential publication bias. They write (iv) a first rebuttal later: at the same time, we found substantial effect heterogeneity. Next, the authors back—literature—their study's high heterogeneity (v) in their phrase in line with other researchers, we cannot preclude that the effect is in fact spurious. We coded the part of the whole paragraph as (vi) a credibility rebuttal since the authors argue that their results could be owing to heterogeneity. Also, we coded the whole paragraph as well as (vii) a suggestive consonant result claim.

Our aim in this study was not to create a model of how argumentation is in empirical research, but rather to make an exploration of reasonings in research. To do the former, a much larger project is needed to hone, change, remove and add types in search of constructing a typological model. For exploration, we consider that our preliminary typology is enough.

Since we have fragmented language by coding in our study, it may be that the arguments that we have presented seem more fragmented than what they really are. Nevertheless, one of the reasons why we have not made an analysis of more complex arguments was that we did not find enough to group them into types.

We have argued that a paper can be seen as a ‘legal-like’ document in which statistical argumentation is used to settle a claim dispute. Heavily adapting [, p. 7] the definition of argumentation, for us, statistical argumentation in empirical psychological papers is a written communicative act aimed at justifying knowledge or lack of it by putting forward a constellation of propositions and/or certifications the researcher can be held accountable for to make the alluded conclusions acceptable to the scientific community. While this is not detrimental per se, there might be so much focus on the social aspect of how papers should be written, what norms there are and what they should look like that it might cost space for reasoning and exposition (see also []). In the end, we can see the benefits of the social demands imposed by the scientific community that should improve the quality of the research output. Hence, the certifications of a paper that uses correlation could be the statistically significant result, mentioning that correlation is not causation as a limitation and having pre-registered the study as an assurance of the result. We would argue that although such certifications—since they follow standards of good research in our field—are useful, research needs reflection as it is more than a social endeavour.

It might be said that we are being too influenced by Toulmin's model of argumentation. After all, Toulmin got inspired by the legal setting and philosophy to develop his model. Since Toulmin developed it to create a layout to aid argument interpretation in real life, it could also be argued that the model fits the argumentation of statistical reasoning used in papers instead of the argumentation being accommodated into the model. We think that the layout has helped us to understand what was missing, for example the warrants, in our set of articles. It definitely is not the most up-to-date model [], but it gave us a needed footing to analyse our data. It also provided a structure of what a consistent line of reasoning from the ground to the claim might look like. Consistency that is seen in the empirical endeavour as it begins with the setting of a hypothesis, its testing or estimation and the ensuing conclusion. In psychology, we attempt to establish warrants that could guide us in claiming something out of some other piece of information; for instance, providing therapy to someone suffering from depression could cause remission of symptoms. Psychology is a science that seeks to establish rather than disprove relationships. In that sense, the fact that Toulmin's model does not describe argumentations disproving or challenging a claim should not affect our understanding of the type of reasoning in papers that, instead, ought to be consistent to establish a warrant.

There are other alternative explanations for why researchers take shortcuts in their written statistical reasonings that do not have to do with our idea of certification. To begin with, researchers may have the desire to be concise; ‘authors seeking publication and students completing assignments increase their chances of success when they write concisely’ [, p. 113]. It may also be the case that authors must be brief under journal norms. Three of the journals we examined (American Psychologist, Journal of Applied Psychology and Nature Human Behaviour) at the time of this writing have a word/page limit, two journals (Cognition and Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics) had recommendations about succinctness, while Psychological Bulletin was the only one that did not have an explicit statement about it. Finally, it may also be the case that researchers assume that their audience shares specialized knowledge with them. This assumption is bona fide, for researchers do write for quite specific, small audiences. Yet, it also derives from the idea that writing an article is mainly about telling or transmitting knowledge [,]. While assuming that the audience knows or already understands what one is talking about is slightly different than what we have deemed here as certification, they both may come from the same philosophical tradition underpinning scientific writing in psychology papers:
…readers are no longer cast in the role of people trying to understand or solve some problem. Rather they are presumed to be looking for additional bits of knowledge to fit in with their previous bits … The author must display competence to the audience, rather than persuade readers of the truth of an idea. If properly demonstrated by a-proper experiment, the hypothesis must be accepted by the audience. In an intellectual sense, the audience has little to say about the meaning of an experiment or even about the truth of a hypothesis. Its role, rather, is to judge the propriety of the experimental proof. [, pp. 274–275]

…readers are no longer cast in the role of people trying to understand or solve some problem. Rather they are presumed to be looking for additional bits of knowledge to fit in with their previous bits … The author must display competence to the audience, rather than persuade readers of the truth of an idea. If properly demonstrated by a-proper experiment, the hypothesis must be accepted by the audience. In an intellectual sense, the audience has little to say about the meaning of an experiment or even about the truth of a hypothesis. Its role, rather, is to judge the propriety of the experimental proof. [, pp. 274–275]

While statistics is a deductive, logical structure from which conclusions can be drawn [], we believe that in empirical research statistical reasoning takes the form of defeasible reasoning, for ‘… the premises taken by themselves may justify us in accepting the conclusion, but when additional information is added, that conclusion may no longer be justified’ [, p. 481]. Particularly, the presence of rebuttals shows this nature of applied statistics. Once we work with empirical data, there will always be a ‘but’ in our experiment. Something will not go according to plan, subpopulations will be left out, a type I or II error might occur, or a variable will not be taken into account. There will always be questions and challenges to claims hinging on collected data because new data could always change those claims. In psychology, it is even more important to recognize that because we are dealing with human behaviour, we will be guaranteed not to do it perfectly in every circumstance and context.

This brings about, first, the importance of attaching qualifiers of uncertainty to our claims. We need to deal with the fact that the idealized experiment does not exist, and, hence, full certainty cannot be part of empirical research. Even if multiple studies are conducted, there are still some beliefs that we as researchers depend on, yet they are beliefs nonetheless. For example, regularity in nature—whatever has happened in the past will happen in the future—in our research is an assumption with which researchers made inferences. However, ultimately, nothing really guarantees that what happened yesterday will happen again tomorrow, let alone in human behaviour.

Regarding this belief, it was not always clear to us how researchers claimed that there was consistency between their results and others besides being statistically significant or showing effect sizes being superior to a comparison group. Moreover, sometimes, consistency was claimed without any explicit warrant or backing. Hence, it may also be important to define, as a community, to what extent we expect consistency among multiple studies or results. For instance, should researchers expect all the experiments they conduct within a single study to be significant? If we, as a community, cannot adjudicate a final answer on this, then we should equip researchers with the thinking tools to adjudicate this themselves in their study. After all, thinking tools should be essential to deal with the inherent inconsistencies—rebuttals—of research. In our, as a community, idealized vision of science, things may be too consistent. This was evident when we saw that researchers were even using non-significant results to support the consistency of their hypotheses and research.

Statistical reasoning in empirical research in psychology is particularly/unavoidably subjective. Researchers apply a deductive structure of reasoning to a concrete, contextualized moment and from a particular point of view. Let us use an example to clarify this point []. To start off, let us say that I want to sit down, and I see a chair in the distance. When I get close to that chair, I see that it is weak, so I do not believe that it will hold me up and look for another chair.

We can connect from this point on the continuation of the example with what happens in research. In science, we get closer to a phenomenon, examine it and give reasons for students, researchers and practitioners to believe whether a theory, description or intervention will hold up or not. We build knowledge about the sturdiness of the chair by adducing reasons like its materials, usage and dimensions. In the end, we can claim that a chair is weak, yet when we sit on it, it turns out to be strong and remains firm despite what we said. Or claim that it is sturdy, only to fall over after sitting down because the chair is weak. The job of the scientist is to give reasons, with their inherent uncertainty, to believe in the sturdiness or weakness of the chair. Whether the chair holds up does not depend on the researcher's explanation, but the knowledge that it will do so does depend on how close that explanation, with its respective arguments, is to the truth about the chair's sturdiness []. For example, the first author will never forget how he fell at a conference because one of the legs of his plastic chair had bent owing to sunlight that had become stronger because it was passing through the thick glass of a window for hours—this happened to nobody else, for their plastic chairs were quite safe under different conditions. Therefore, with our explanations, we must get as close as possible to the truth, whatever that is, of the phenomenon, but in the end, there will always be uncertainty about whether the chair holds up or not. It might happen that some other variable, a different condition or any type of additional information was not taken into account by our explanation, and that we might have to change our knowledge and beliefs about the phenomenon.

This example is also relevant for explaining why, in our research, literature or sensitivity analyses could be used in multiple ways for different reasons. An author must write a valid argumentation, but there is not one way to do it. Statistics is so vast and complex that we cannot imagine an adequate use and approach to it that sloughs off reflection and rationality. Even in the group of papers that we have analysed, there was a smorgasbord of approaches, and in the effort to find patterns, we might have lost nuance in describing our results in the end. Namely, arguments may be more complex than what we are depicting here, not only outside of our sample, but within it as well. In addition, to balance the handling of all the papers, we gathered data related to the first inferential claim rather than collecting data from multiple results, which could have affected our analysis. This is merely a first step to finding out how researchers write arguments with and about statistics to, then, elucidate how their reasoning is.

In summary, we believe that argumentation in empirical research must be logical, clear and reasonable if we accept the role of the scientist as the one who gives reasons for belief. This also implies that when researchers see a weak chair, they denounce it. Therefore, a reasonable argument must be accompanied by uncertainty and transparency. Perhaps it might be time to question whether the way we write research in psychology conforms to these principles.

Our study's goals, design and analytical approach were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) []. We made the following deviations to our original preregistration:
—We originally planned to use only content analysis. In a later stage, we added the construction of a typology which employed elements from Toulmin's model, because we became aware of this and believed it to be very suitable in classifying researcher's arguments.—We replaced the journal Trends in Cognitive Sciences with Cognition, because the former publishes few empirical articles.—We initially planned to evaluate the validity of statistical arguments, but we changed our approach to a more neutral one, so as to remain scientifically dispassionate.

psychology.title: Temporal cortical gray matter volume relates to symptom improvement during cognitive behavioral therapy for depression
psychology.abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a first-line treatment for depression, yet treatment responses vary considerably. Understanding neurobiological factors associated with symptom improvement may help elucidate mechanisms underlying therapeutic change. This study investigated whether baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) is associated with reductions in depressive symptom severity during CBT. Therefore, n = 52 patients with unipolar affective disorders and at least mild depressive symptoms (according to BDI-II) and n = 42 healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and structural MRI at baseline; depressive symptom severity was reassessed after six months of outpatient CBT. Multiple regression analyses examined associations between pre-treatment cortical GMV and reductions in depressive symptoms under false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Additional models included anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma as predictors. Compared to controls, patients exhibited significantly higher depressive symptom severity at baseline and greater symptom reduction over time (all p < 0.001). Within patients, baseline GMV of the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) was significantly associated with symptom reduction (baseline–follow-up; β = 0.55, pFDR = 0.033). Right MTG volume accounted for additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical variables (ΔR² = 0.15). Group differences in GMV did not remain significant following FDR correction. These findings suggest that temporal gyrus GMV is associated with symptom improvement following CBT in unipolar depression, extending the focus beyond traditionally emphasized limbic regions. Preserved temporal morphology may support cognitive and emotional processes engaged during CBT, underscoring the relevance of temporal cortical structure for understanding the neurobiological correlates of psychotherapy response.
psychology.text:
Depressive disorders represent one of the leading causes of mental health-related burden worldwide [, ], with a global prevalence of approximately 6% []. Although depressive disorders can manifest in highly diverse phenotypes, they share common features such as a tendency toward relapse and impairments in emotional and cognitive functioning []. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based psychotherapy for depression, is widely recommended in clinical guidelines as a first-line psychological treatment, and produces enduring reductions in depressive symptoms []. However, treatment response to CBT remains heterogeneous: while many patients experience substantial improvement, a considerable proportion fail to achieve full remission []. Identifying factors associated with treatment response prior to therapy may improve patient–treatment matching and clinical outcomes, and investigating the neurobiological mechanisms underlying such variability may help inform more personalized psychotherapy approaches.

Neuroimaging research has consistently identified structural brain alterations in depression, particularly within cortico-limbic regions such as the hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex, which are implicated in emotional processing and regulation [–]. However, structural correlates of depression identified through case-control comparisons have proven to be subtle and inconsistent across studies. In their large meta-analysis (N > 10,000), Ho et al. [] reported cortical thinning in adults with major depressive disorder relative to controls, with effect sizes ranging from d = 0.10–0.14 []. Most recently, a multi-cohort investigation confirmed that reliable structural correlates of depression are restricted to a small set of regions, including the frontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and insula, while several classically implicated regions, including subcortical structures, showed no consistent association []. Together, these findings indicate that structural brain differences between depressed patients and healthy individuals are real but modest in magnitude, likely reflecting substantial between-subject heterogeneity within diagnostic categories. This heterogeneity motivates a shift in emphasis from case-control comparisons toward individual-differences approaches that examine how structural variation within patients relates to clinically meaningful outcomes, and, building on these findings, studies have increasingly examined neural factors associated with treatment response in depression. Both structural (e.g., []) and functional (e.g., []) imaging studies have reported brain correlates of psychotherapy outcome, particularly within neural networks implicated in emotion regulation, cognitive control, and self-referential processing [–]. Several studies have used functional MRI data to predict treatment response [–], while others have focused on structural measures, such as regional brain volume [], cortical surface metrics [], or structural connectivity []. However, findings across studies remain inconsistent, likely reflecting small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and diagnostic variability.

Research on the neural structural correlates of psychotherapy response has largely focused on subcortical and limbic regions, such as the amygdala, hippocampus, and anterior cingulate cortex, as well as prefrontal regions implicated in cognitive control and emotion regulation (e.g., [, ]). Comparatively less attention has been directed toward cortical structures that may also play an important role in psychotherapy-related change and may contribute to variability in treatment response. In particular, regions within the temporal and parietal cortex are involved in processes such as social cognition, autobiographical memory, and the integration of emotional and cognitive information [–]. These functions are frequently engaged during CBT and may therefore be relevant for understanding individual differences in therapeutic change.

A growing body of work indicates that depressive symptom improvement depends in part on a patient’s broader clinical context, including current perceived stress, stable trait anxiety, and exposure to early-life adversity [–]. Building on this literature, we assessed these variables and evaluated them as established predictors in the present study.

The present study aimed to identify cortical neurostructural baseline markers associated with CBT treatment outcome, expanding prior work that has largely emphasized subcortical circuitry. To this end, cortical gray matter volumes were examined as baseline correlates of subsequent reductions in depressive symptom severity over the course of six months of therapy in patients with unipolar depression (MDD). By examining structural brain correlates of symptom improvement, this study seeks to contribute to the growing field of precision psychiatry and to inform neurobiologically grounded approaches to individualized treatment strategies. We hypothesized that greater baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) would be associated with greater subsequent symptom reduction during CBT, reflecting the possibility that greater structural integrity may be associated with greater capacity to engage in cognitive and emotional processes relevant to CBT. We were particularly interested in examining cortical GMV across the brain to identify cortical regions associated with treatment response. Specifically, the study addressed (1) whether baseline cortical GMV is associated with individual differences in symptom reduction during CBT and (2) whether cortical structural measures provide incremental value beyond established clinical predictors, including perceived stress, trait anxiety, and childhood trauma exposure.

N = 94 participants, including n = 52 depressed patients (age: M = 28.31 years, SD = 8.30; gender: 36/16 [f/m]) and n = 42 matched healthy controls (HC; age: M = 27.45, SD = 7.59; gender: 28/14 [f/m]), were recruited at the Department of Psychology, University of Halle between October 2022 and November 2025 prior to the beginning of CBT (MDD). HC were included as a normative comparison group to characterize baseline differences associated with depression; however, they do not constitute an active control condition and therefore cannot isolate CBT-specific treatment effects. All participants underwent structural MRI, the German Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 disorders (SCID-5-CV) [], and completed clinical questionnaires, including the German Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) [], a 21-item retrospective self-report questionnaire that assesses presence of current depression symptoms, alongside the German Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) [], the trait-version of the German State Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-T) [], and the German Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) [, ]. All baseline MRI and clinical assessments were completed before initiating CBT.

Patients were required to meet full diagnostic criteria for a current depressive disorder according to the SCID-5-CV [], which served as the primary diagnostic assessment. HC were only included if they did not meet criteria for any disorder according to the SCID-5-CV. In addition, a BDI-II score >9, indicating at least mild depression according to the Center for Cognitive Therapy guidelines for patients with affective disorders [], was required for inclusion in the patient group and served as an exclusion criterion for HC at baseline. A medication load index for each patient was computed following the approach of Hassel []. Exclusion criteria for all participants were any history of neurological (e.g., concussion, stroke, tumor, neuroinflammatory disease) or medical conditions (e.g., cancer, chronic inflammatory or autoimmune disorders, cardiovascular disease), as well as current or past substance-use disorders.

All patients received standardized outpatient CBT delivered by licensed psychotherapists or therapists in training in the outpatient units of either the University of Halle-Wittenberg or the Halle Institute for Psychological Psychotherapy training. HC were recruited through public notices and newspaper announcements. Six months after initial recruitment, participants were invited to complete the follow-up assessment consisting of the BDI-II. The mean interval between baseline and follow-up assessment was M = 27.70 weeks (SD = 2.08). Information on the study sample, including psychiatric comorbidities, is presented in Table . All participants received financial compensation.
