Sociodemographic and clinical sample characteristics.

Groups included depressed patients (MDD) and healthy controls (HC); clinical diagnoses were assessed using the German Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 disorders []. Group differences in age, years of education, and assessment interval were assessed using Welch’s t-tests. All other continuous variables were compared between groups using analysis of covariance models adjusted for age and gender. Gender was compared using a χ2-test. Depressive symptom severity was measured with the German Beck Depression Inventory-II [] at baseline and at follow-up after cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). At baseline, trait anxiety was assessed using the German State-Trait Anxiety Inventory [], perceived stress using the German Perceived Stress Scale [], and childhood trauma experiences using the German Childhood Trauma Questionnaire []. Medication load index for each patient was computed following the approach of Hassel [].

All MR data were collected using a 3 T scanner (Magnetom Vida 3 T, Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) with a 64-channel head/neck coil. Whole-head T1-weighted anatomical images were collected with a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo (MP-RAGE) sequence, isotropic voxel size = 0.8 mm, repetition time = 2400 ms, echo time = 2.24 ms, inversion time=1030 ms, flip angle = 8°, acquisition matrix = 320 × 300 × 208, and GRAPPA with R = 2 and 32 reference lines, yielding an acquisition time of 6:38 min.

Structural MRI data were processed using the automated cortical reconstruction and volumetric segmentation pipeline implemented in FreeSurfer (version 5.3). Preprocessing was performed using the standard recon-all stream with default parameters, which includes intensity normalization, skull stripping, and cortical surface reconstruction. Cortical regions were parcellated according to the Desikan-Killiany atlas []. GMV of all 68 cortical regions (34 per hemisphere) was extracted and used for subsequent analyses. Segmentation quality was assessed through visual control, statistical outlier screening, and quantitative assessment of cortical surface reconstruction quality using the FreeSurfer Euler number, an established index of reconstruction quality from cortical surface topology [], with lower values indicating a greater number of topological defects.

All statistical analyses were conducted using R (v4.5.0) and RStudio (v2023.06.1). Standard statistical analyses were performed using the stats (v4.5.0) package. Elastic net models were estimated using the glmnet (v4.1.10) [] and caret (v7.0.1) [] packages. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05; all analyses were performed two-sided for exploratory reasons. For analyses of GMV data, resulting p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure at α < 0.05 due to multiple testing. Analyses were conducted in two sequential steps, the first including all participants, the second including only MDD patients.

First, to characterize baseline differences between MDD and HC, group comparisons of sociodemographic, clinical, cortical GMV, and MRI reconstruction quality data were performed using Welch’s t-tests and additional Mann-Whitney U tests for sociodemographic variables and Euler numbers due to the non-normal distribution as confirmed by group-wise Shapiro-Wilk tests, as well as linear models with group as the primary predictor (ANCOVA). Treatment-related change in depressive symptoms was assessed separately within the MDD group by comparing pre- and post-treatment BDI-II scores using a paired-samples t-test, given normality of pre–post differences (Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.898). In addition, a mixed-design group × time analysis of variance (ANOVA) was computed to examine main and interaction effects on depressive symptom severity across time.

Second, in MDD patients, associations between baseline clinical characteristics and cortical GMV with reductions in depressive symptom severity over the course of 6 months of CBT were examined. Therefore, multiple linear regression analyses were conducted using total and percentage reductions in BDI-II scores as outcome variables. Age, gender, and medication load index were included as covariates of no interest in all analyses. In all analyses involving cortical GMV measures, total intracranial volume (TIV) was additionally included as a covariate of no interest to account for individual differences in head size. All continuous variables were z-standardized prior to analysis.

Regional GMV for each of the 68 cortical regions was entered separately as the predictor of interest, yielding 68 individual regression models (one per cortical region). Model assumptions (residual normality, homoscedasticity, multicollinearity, and case influence) were assessed for all regression models; full details are reported in the . Sensitivity analyses, including the total FreeSurfer Euler number as an additional covariate in the primary regression models to assess MRI reconstruction quality, are reported in the .

In an exploratory analysis, BDI-II symptoms were further divided into cognitive and affective-somatic domains based on the proposed two-factor structure by Beck et al. []. A linear mixed-effects model was used to test whether the association between identified significant regions and symptom improvement differed between domains. Results are provided in the . To examine whether treatment response status (defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in BDI-II scores) moderated the association between cortical GMV and treatment response, an additional moderation analysis was conducted for identified significant predictors. Thus, a separate multiple linear regression model was estimated including interaction terms between regional GMV and response status. Additionally, patients who improved versus those whose symptoms worsened during treatment were compared (see ).

To evaluate whether cortical GMV explained additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical predictors, hierarchical multiple regression analyses were performed. In the first model step, baseline perceived stress, trait anxiety, and childhood trauma exposure were entered as predictors. In the second model step, regional cortical GMV was added. Incremental variance explained by cortical volume was quantified using the change in explained variance (ΔR²).

Finally, in an exploratory post hoc analysis, elastic-net regularized linear regression was used to examine out-of-sample predictive performance of both baseline clinical and neuroanatomical measures with respect to depressive symptom reduction. Total BDI-II reduction served as the outcome variable. Baseline childhood trauma, perceived stress, trait anxiety, gender, age, estimated total intracranial volume (TIV), and medication load were included as unpenalized covariates, while cortical GMV measures were entered as penalized predictors. Model training and evaluation were conducted using repeated nested five-fold cross-validation to reduce potential estimation bias, with hyperparameter tuning restricted to inner training folds. Predictive performance was quantified using cross-validated coefficients of determination (R²) and root mean squared error (RMSE).

Data from n = 52 MDD patients and n = 42 HC were analyzed in this study (see Table ). While the groups were comparable in terms of age, gender distribution, or years of education (Welch’s t-tests: p ≥ 0.439; Mann-Whitney U tests: p ≥ 0.433), ANCOVAs revealed significantly higher levels of trait anxiety and childhood trauma experiences in MDD compared with HC (p ≤ 0.002). Regarding FreeSurfer-derived baseline cortical volume measures, nominal group differences were observed in the left caudal middle frontal gyrus, right entorhinal cortex, right rostral anterior cingulate gyrus, and right inferior parietal gyrus (p ≤ 0.039, see Supplemental Table ). However, none of these differences remained significant after FDR-correction (pFDR ≥ 0.239). Regarding MRI reconstruction quality, no group differences were observed (p ≥ 0.178, see  and Supplemental Table ).

At baseline, BDI-II scores differed between MDD patients and HC, with patients showing higher symptom severity after adjustment for age and gender (F(1,89) = 205.71, p < 0.001). At follow-up, BDI-II scores remained higher in MDD patients than in HC after adjustment for age and gender (F(1,89) = 53.08, p < 0.001). Within the MDD group, BDI-II scores decreased significantly from pre- to post-treatment (mean change [SD] = 8.19 [11.28], t(51) = 5.24, p < 0.001), indicating a significant reduction in depressive symptom severity over the course of CBT. Individual changes in BDI-II scores from baseline to follow-up are presented in Fig. . The corresponding group × time ANOVA is reported in the .

Within the MDD group, baseline perceived stress and childhood trauma showed positive associations with baseline depressive symptom severity (both p < 0.0024; Intercorrelations among study variables are presented in Table ). *p < 0.0024, ** p <0.001.

Among cortical measures, baseline GMV of the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) was significantly associated with total BDI-II reduction after FDR correction (total reduction: β = 0.55, pFDR = 0.033; percentage reduction: β = 0.49, pFDR = 0.063; see Fig. ). Left MTG volume showed only a trend-level association (pFDR ≥ 0.196). No other cortical regions were significantly associated with symptom reduction (all pFDR ≥ 0.05).

Treatment response status (≥50% reduction in BDI-II scores) did not moderate the association between MTG volume and symptom change (p < 0.321), although the association was descriptively stronger among responders (n = 19, β = 0.64) than non-responders (n = 33, β = 0.34).

To examine whether cortical volume explained additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical predictors, hierarchical linear regression analyses were conducted, including trait anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma in the first model step. When right MTG volume was added in the second step, the increase in explained variance was moderate in magnitude but did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons (ΔR² = 0.15, pFDR = 0.066).

In an exploratory post hoc analysis, out-of-sample predictive performance of both baseline clinical and neuroanatomical measures was evaluated. The combined model demonstrated modest predictive performance (MR² = 0.04, 95% CI [0.00, 0.12]; MRMSE = 12.39, 95% CI [11.01, 13.98]). Overall, baseline cortical volume measures provided limited additional predictive value beyond established clinical and demographic variables in the out-of-sample prediction setting. Given the exploratory nature of these analyses, the modest predictive performance, and the sample size, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and require replication in independent samples.

In this study, we investigated whether baseline GMV is linked to reductions in depressive symptom severity following six months of outpatient CBT in patients with unipolar depression. Compared to HC, MDD patients exhibited heightened levels of clinically relevant symptoms, including depression and anxiety, as well as the risk factor of childhood maltreatment. A significant depressive symptom reduction over the course of CBT was observed. The findings suggest that pre-treatment GMV of the right MTG was associated with greater symptom improvement. Importantly, the association remained substantial after accounting for established clinical variables, including baseline depressive symptom severity, anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma, suggesting that right MTG morphology provides unique value for characterizing individual variability in psychotherapy response.

These findings extend prior research primarily focused on subcortical and limbic structures, such as the hippocampus and amygdala, by highlighting the potential relevance of the temporal cortex in psychotherapy outcomes. While the temporal lobe is classically associated with auditory and visual processing [, , ], the MTG is particularly implicated in the processing of complex cognitive, social, and emotional information, including semantic memory, empathy, emotion regulation, and the integration of contextual cues with emotional appraisal [, , –], processes often impaired in depression []. Functional and structural alterations in the MTG in MDD patients have been associated with deficits in these functions, alongside negative cognition and mood processing in MDD patients [, , ]. These functions are particularly relevant to CBT, which often requires patients to reinterpret social and emotional experiences, retrieve alternative cognitive frameworks, and flexibly integrate new perspectives into their thought patterns. Even though there were no group differences in MTG volume observed within this study, it may provide a neuroanatomical substrate that facilitates these processes, allowing patients to more effectively engage with cognitive restructuring and emotion regulation exercises.

Previous studies repeatedly exhibited GMV decreases in the MTG in depression (e.g., [, ]), which were accompanied by a progressive decrease over time, which was in turn attributed to disease progression []. McCurdy et al. [] showed that GMV reduction in the right MTG is associated with involvement in CBT []. In this context, greater preservation of temporal cortical structure may be relevant to individual differences in treatment-related improvement. One possibility is that preserved MTG morphology supports higher-order processes involved in identifying, contextualizing, and modifying maladaptive cognitions, including negative beliefs and automatic thoughts. The MTG may also contribute to the adaptive processing of self-referential and emotionally salient information during therapy through interactions with large-scale networks such as the default mode and salience networks []. These mechanisms provide a plausible framework for understanding why individual differences in right MTG volume might be associated with CBT-related symptom improvement.

However, our exploratory analysis of cognitive versus affective-somatic BDI-II symptoms did not provide evidence for a domain-specific association with MTG volume. Thus, while the potential involvement of temporal cortical morphology in cognitive processes relevant to CBT remains an interesting possibility, the present findings do not establish a specific relationship between MTG structure and improvement in negative cognitions or other cognitive symptoms. Future studies incorporating more specific measures of negative beliefs, automatic thoughts, and rumination, as well as functional and connectivity-based approaches, could more directly test this proposed mechanism. Taken together, the findings suggest that structural preservation of the right MTG may serve as a key neural factor contributing to individual differences in CBT responsiveness, which was not attributable to differences in MRI reconstruction quality, highlighting the importance of temporal cortical regions beyond the limbic system traditionally emphasized in depression research.

Also, the MTG has been implicated in different psychiatric disorders before, such as obsessive-compulsive disorder [], childhood maltreatment/PTSD [], social anxiety disorder [], and addiction disorders []. Another study highlighted its mediating role within the association between smartphone use and depressive symptoms in students []. The heterogeneity of treatment response also warrants consideration. In an exploratory comparison, patients whose symptoms worsened during treatment did not show consistent differences in demographic or clinical characteristics compared with those who improved, except for childhood maltreatment, a risk factor for treatment-resistant depression [, ], and, at trend-level, bilateral MTG volume. Larger samples will be needed to determine whether non-response or deterioration during CBT is associated with distinct neurobiological profiles.

The exploratory out-of-sample analysis provides a more cautious perspective on the potential utility of baseline cortical GMV. Although the combined model yielded modest out-of-sample performance, cortical volume measures provided limited additional predictive information beyond established clinical and demographic variables. This finding suggests that the association between baseline right MTG volume and subsequent symptom improvement should not be interpreted as evidence that MTG volume alone cannot allow accurate individual predictions. Rather, the finding may indicate that structural variation in the MTG captures individual differences relevant to symptom change.

We did not observe significant GMV differences between patients and HC at baseline after FDR correction. This is consistent with recent large-scale evidence indicating that structural cortical differences in depression are small in magnitude and inconsistent across samples [, ], particularly in outpatient populations with mild-to-moderate symptomatology, and suggests that reliable case-control structural effects typically require sample sizes considerably larger than those attainable in single-site clinical studies, including the present one. While other work has reported significant case-control differences [], such findings often derive from larger or pooled samples better powered to detect effects of this magnitude; the present null result is therefore more plausibly attributable to limited power than to a genuine absence of structural alteration in this cohort. Nevertheless, within-group variability in cortical morphology appears to meaningfully relate to treatment outcomes, underscoring the value of examining individual differences in brain structure as predictors of clinical change, rather than relying solely on case-control contrasts to establish their relevance.

This study has several notable strengths, including matched samples without meaningful GMV differences, an innovative research question, and a sophisticated design in the still underexplored field of neuroimaging in major depressive disorder. Together, these features provide novel insights into neurobiological factors associated with CBT response. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses accounting for FreeSurfer-derived Euler numbers yielded comparable results, increasing confidence that the observed association was not explained by differences in cortical surface reconstruction quality. If replicated, right MTG volume could serve as a promising biomarker to inform treatment selection by helping identify patients most likely to benefit from CBT. More broadly, the findings may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of individual differences in treatment response when considered alongside established clinical characteristics.

Several limitations should also be acknowledged. The sample size, while consistent with prior neuroimaging studies of psychotherapy, was modest and may limit generalizability. Structural MRI captures only brain morphology; future studies could incorporate functional and connectivity analyses to better elucidate the dynamic mechanisms underlying CBT-related improvement. Although a subset of participants exhibited worsening of depressive symptoms during CBT, the present sample was not sufficiently powered to characterize neurobiological differences between treatment responders and patients who fail to improve or deteriorate. Future studies with larger samples should specifically investigate these clinically important subgroups. Additionally, the absence of a patient control group (e.g., receiving alternative treatment or no intervention) limits the ability to draw conclusions about the specificity of the observed effects to CBT, as improvements may reflect more general treatment-related or time-related changes within MDD patients. Due to the comparably small sample size, replication in larger, independent cohorts is highly recommended. Finally, the observational design precludes causal inference; longitudinal imaging during therapy would strengthen causal interpretation.

In conclusion, this study provides preliminary evidence that pre-treatment GMV of the right MTG is associated with symptom improvement following CBT in unipolar depression. These findings highlight temporal cortical regions as potentially relevant for understanding individual variability in treatment response and underscore the value of integrating neurobiological measures with clinical measures. Future research in larger, independent cohorts, incorporating multimodal neuroimaging and longitudinal designs, is warranted to replicate and extend these findings and to explore their translational utility in personalized treatment planning.

psychology.title: Outcome indicators used in recovery college effectiveness studies: a scoping review
psychology.abstract: Recovery Colleges (RCs) are educational, recovery-oriented approaches in mental health. Differences in evaluation purposes and settings may lead to diverse outcome indicators, making it important to map their use and supporting measurement evidence. This scoping review aimed to identify the outcome indicators used in RC evaluations and clarify their measured constructs, patterns of use, and reporting of reliability and validity. Methods: The review followed JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance. PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL Ultimate, ERIC, and seven databases accessed through ProQuest were searched. English-language journal articles reporting quantitative RC evaluations, including quantitative components of mixed-methods studies, were eligible. Eligible data included questionnaire scores before and after RC participation and health service utilization indicators, such as hospital admissions and service contacts. Three reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts. Data were extracted collaboratively by two reviewers and independently checked by a third. Measured constructs were classified using inductive content analysis. Results: Of 336 records identified, 149 remained after deduplication and 22 articles were included. Thirty-nine measure and indicator entries were identified across three domains: intra-personal and psychological changes, behavioral and social changes, and system and environment. The Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS), including its short version (SWEMWBS), appeared in 11 articles (50.0%) and the Questionnaire about the Process of Recovery (QPR) in four (18.2%); 28 entries appeared in one article only. Fifteen articles (68.2%) cited previous psychometric information or identifiable validation literature, two (9.1%) explicitly reported within-study reliability estimates, and six (27.3%) reported neither specific psychometric evidence nor an identifiable validation citation. One article was not applicable to scale psychometrics. Conclusion: RC evaluations used diverse measures, while direct assessment of educational processes and outcomes was comparatively limited. This review mapped measurement choices rather than RC effects. The findings can inform co-produced decisions about outcome selection and study design, alongside further evaluation of existing instruments’ suitability for the intended RC populations. Involving learners and other stakeholders in these decisions can help align evaluation with research purposes and RCs’ educational philosophy while ensuring that participants’ individual goals are also assessed.
psychology.text:
Recovery Colleges (RCs) have evolved as an educational practice based on adult learning models to support the recovery of individuals experiencing mental health challenges (, ). A core feature of RCs is the emphasis on co-production, which integrates the experiential knowledge of individuals with lived experience and the expertise of professionals (, ). In addition to co-production, RCs emphasize educational rather than clinical approaches, strengths-based and self-directed learning, equality between learners and educators, social connectedness, and community orientation (). Notably, not only individuals with mental illness but also family members, supporters, and health and social care professionals can participate as “students.” In recent years, RCs have been positioned not merely as an individual recovery support intervention, but as open learning spaces within the community and a novel model of mental health practice (, ). Since the first RC opened in England in 2009, the model has expanded internationally, with RCs now operating across diverse mental health systems and cultural contexts (, ). This expansion has occurred alongside growing international recognition of recovery-oriented care in mental health policy and practice, emphasizing opportunities to lead meaningful lives beyond symptom reduction. RCs offer a practical educational approach consistent with this shift, supporting the development of knowledge, skills, and social connections ().

Research on RCs has steadily accumulated over the past decade. A 2020 literature review demonstrated the breadth of RC research, reporting that various outcomes have been investigated, including personal recovery, well-being, goal achievement, knowledge acquisition, self-management, stigma reduction, and service utilization (). A subsequent co-created scoping review synthesized approaches used to evaluate RCs and highlighted considerable variation in evaluation designs, methods, and outcomes (). Furthermore, a 2025 state-of-the-art review synthesized 64 RC evaluative studies published between 2013 and 2024 (). This review highlighted that while RC research has progressed from implementation studies to outcome evaluations, significant heterogeneity remains in study designs and evaluation methods. It concluded that consolidating evaluation studies and streamlining measurement tools are critical future challenges ().

Previous reviews have synthesized the development and evaluation of RCs, including their implementation, evaluation approaches, and reported outcomes (, , ). Building on these broader syntheses, the present review focuses specifically on the quantitative outcome measures and objective indicators used across RC effectiveness studies. Its contribution is to integrate, at the measure level, the constructs assessed, patterns of use, and reporting of reliability and validity. For instance, recent related studies have focused on specific aspects, such as a document analysis of RC course content in England () and a scoping review of outcome measures used in RC dementia courses (). The present review complements this work by providing a structured inventory across RC evaluation contexts, linking what has been measured with how it has been measured and what psychometric evidence has been reported.

This focused synthesis can support the accumulation of knowledge in RC research and help contextualize cross-study comparisons. In contrast to conventional symptom-focused approaches, RCs represent a multifaceted practice embodying values and principles such as well-being, personal recovery, empowerment, learning, co-production, and social participation (, , ). Given the educational foundations of RCs, evaluation should also consider whether current outcome measurement captures learning-related processes and changes, including knowledge acquisition, self-directed and collaborative learning (, ). This educational perspective also directs attention to learner agency, identity development, and the transfer of learning to everyday life, including how learners make choices, develop valued roles, and apply knowledge and skills beyond the classroom (). Moreover, because co-production is a core principle of RCs, consideration of meaningful outcomes should extend beyond researcher-defined indicators and incorporate the perspectives of people with lived experience and other RC stakeholders ().

Accordingly, clarifying what is evaluated as an outcome and what scales are used for measurement is a prerequisite for adequately understanding how RC outcomes have been evaluated. In addition, examining whether reliability and validity are reported for the measures used can provide information on the psychometric evidence supporting current measurement practices. However, agreement on which outcomes matter—what to measure—is distinct from selecting and evaluating instruments to assess them—how to measure. The former requires consideration of the priorities of learners and other stakeholders; the latter requires evidence that an instrument’s measurement properties are adequate for the intended population and purpose. Mapping psychometric reporting can identify the evidence described in RC evaluations and gaps requiring further investigation, but it does not itself establish instrument suitability or determine a core outcome set. Together with the constructs assessed and patterns of measure use, this mapping can inform measure selection and study design and, if a core outcome initiative is pursued, provide supporting information for stakeholder deliberation and subsequent instrument evaluation. Therefore, this scoping review aimed to identify the outcome indicators used in RC effectiveness studies and to synthesize their measured constructs, patterns of use, and reporting of reliability and validity. Specifically, the review addressed the following questions (1): What outcomes have been evaluated in RC effectiveness studies? (2) What measures and objective indicators have been used to assess these outcomes and how frequently? and (3) What evidence of reliability and validity has been reported for the measures used?

This scoping review aimed to identify and synthesize outcome measures and objective indicators used in quantitative evaluations of RCs, including the quantitative components of mixed-methods studies. The review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews () and reported following the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) (). The review mapped the constructs assessed, patterns of measure use, and reporting of reliability and validity. A review protocol was prepared but was not registered and is not publicly available.

A scoping approach was selected to map the range and conceptual coverage of measures across diverse evaluation designs, rather than estimate pooled intervention effects or rank instruments.

The initial searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and CINAHL Ultimate on March 8, 2026. To broaden coverage of education and social science literature, additional searches were conducted in ERIC and through the ProQuest platform on September 8, 2026. The ProQuest search was conducted simultaneously across seven databases: Coronavirus Research Database, Education Research Index, MEDLINE, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses A&I, PTSDpubs, Publicly Available Content Database, and Research Library.

All searches covered publications dated on or before March 8, 2026, with no lower publication-year limit. The additional searches retained this publication cutoff to align with the initial searches.

The search strategies combined terms related to RCs with terms related to outcomes, evaluation, and measurement. Strategies were adapted to the syntax requirements of each database or platform while maintaining equivalent search concepts. The complete search strategies, search dates, publication limits, and numbers of records retrieved are presented in . Language and publication-type eligibility criteria were applied during screening.

Studies were eligible if they directly evaluated RCs, including Recovery Education Centers and Discovery Colleges operating within the RC model, and reported quantitative data collected or analyzed to assess participant outcomes, perceived impacts, or the recovery-supporting environment and program provision. Quantitative studies and mixed-methods studies with quantitative evaluation components were eligible. Measures could include standardized instruments, study-specific questionnaires, individualized goal indicators, service-use data, and economic indicators. Cross-sectional evaluations were eligible when the quantitative data were used for these evaluative purposes. Studies conducted solely to develop or validate an instrument, without evaluating RC-related outcomes, were excluded. Qualitative-only studies, reviews, protocols, and descriptive reports without eligible quantitative evaluation data were also excluded.

Eligibility was restricted to original research and service evaluation articles published in English in academic journals and reporting methods and results. The English-language restriction reflected the review team’s language capabilities. Non-English publications, conference abstracts, dissertations, and grey literature, including local service evaluation reports published outside academic journals, were excluded.

Search results were managed in Google Sheets. Duplicate records within and across search sources were identified and removed by comparing DOIs; when a DOI was unavailable, titles were compared. Three reviewers (YS, AB, and MT) independently screened all titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. All articles retained for full-text assessment were subsequently evaluated independently by each of the three reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion among all three reviewers, with re-examination of the relevant articles until consensus was reached.

Two reviewers (YS and AB) jointly extracted data using a shared Google Sheets form, checking the source articles together. The form was piloted on seven randomly selected candidate articles before eligibility decisions were finalized. No changes to the form or recording rules were made after piloting. Following completion of data extraction, a third reviewer (MT) independently checked all extracted data against the source articles. Thus, extraction was conducted collaboratively by YS and AB, followed by independent verification by MT, rather than independent duplicate extraction.

The form included authors, publication year, country, title, DOI, relationship to RCs, whether the article reported an evaluation study, study design, participant characteristics and sample sizes, reported outcomes, measurement instrument names, measurement time points, whether measures were standardized or study-specific, and reported information on reliability and validity. Eligibility decisions and the reasons for these decisions were recorded in the same form.

Disagreements concerning data extraction were discussed by all three reviewers (YS, AB, and MT). Each reviewer’s rationale and the relevant passages in the source articles were examined until all three reviewers reached consensus; decisions were not determined by majority vote.

Information on reliability and validity was extracted as reported in the included articles, including the types of properties described and numerical estimates, such as Cronbach’s alpha and intraclass correlation coefficients. Information explicitly pertaining to short or modified versions was recorded for those versions. Cited instrument development and validation studies were not independently retrieved or assessed.

An integrated inventory was created by consolidating repeated occurrences of the same measure across included articles into a single entry. Full and short versions of the same instrument were grouped under one instrument entry. Where an article used only a subscale or a modified version, the specific content used was retained in the extraction notes. Alternate names were consolidated only when they were identified as referring to the same instrument, with version-specific information retained. Standardized instruments, study-specific measures, objective indicators, and cost-related indicators were included in the same inventory, with their types distinguished.

Study-specific questionnaires were consolidated only when they were identified as the same measure. Self-reported service use was distinguished from record-derived utilization. “Standardized” denoted a previously developed instrument, rather than a judgment that its measurement properties were adequate in the included evaluation. Separate entries could represent components of the same questionnaire and were therefore not necessarily independent instruments.

Frequency of use was calculated as the number of included articles reporting each measure. This analysis described patterns of measurement use in RC evaluations and identified commonly used and less frequently reported measures. Frequency was interpreted as an indication of use, rather than evidence of measurement quality or suitability. Grouping full and short versions for frequency analysis did not imply that their psychometric properties were equivalent.

Each article contributed at most one count to each inventory entry. Article-level counts were used rather than counts of participants or independent cohorts. Study characteristics and measurement contexts were summarized descriptively to aid interpretation of differences in measure use.

Outcome measures were categorized using inductive content analysis to identify conceptual patterns across the diverse measures used in RC evaluations (, ). This approach was selected because the review concerned the meaning and conceptual focus of measures, including study-specific and objective indicators, for which instrument names alone were insufficient. Inductive content analysis allowed categories to be developed from the extracted descriptions rather than imposed from an existing recovery framework.

Two reviewers (YS and AB) jointly examined the descriptions provided in the included articles, the constructs measured, and the subscales to identify the principal measurement focus of each measure. These conceptual descriptions formed the basis for coding and grouping measures according to similarities and differences. Categories were developed inductively and iteratively merged, split, or renamed as the analysis progressed.

A third reviewer (MT) reviewed the resulting classification. When this review identified differences in interpretation or category assignment, all three reviewers discussed the relevant descriptions, constructs, and subscales until consensus was reached. Measures spanning multiple domains were assigned to the single domain that best represented their principal measurement focus, based on their closest conceptual fit.

The analysis yielded three domains: (1) Intra-personal and psychological changes, (2) Behavioral and social changes, and (3) System and environment. These domains describe the conceptual focus of the measures and do not imply that every included study assessed change over time.

Psychometric reporting was summarized descriptively by measure. The summary distinguished between evaluations conducted within the included study sample and references to previous validation research, based on the descriptions in the included articles. Information not reported in an included article was recorded as “not reported.” This synthesis characterized the reporting of measurement properties rather than formally appraising their quality. Frequency of use, reported psychometric information, and measurement quality were treated as distinct considerations.

For article-level summaries, reporting was classified as previous psychometric information or identifiable validation citations, confirmed within-study reliability, within-study validity information, unclear provenance, no reported psychometric information, or not applicable to scale psychometrics. Statistical validity reporting and non-statistical face/content descriptions were distinguished. Categories could overlap, and percentages used all included articles as the denominator. Coefficients with unclear provenance were not counted as confirmed within-study estimates. A source citation alone was not treated as a validation citation.

Consistent with the mapping purpose of this scoping review, no formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies was conducted. Psychometric reporting was not treated as a formal evaluation of study quality or instrument quality.

As a result of the literature search, a total of 336 records were identified: 80 from PubMed, 40 from Web of Science, 76 from CINAHL Ultimate, 13 from ERIC, and 127 through the ProQuest platform. After merging these records and removing 187 duplicates, 149 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 122 were excluded, leaving 27 reports sought for retrieval. Three reports could not be retrieved. The remaining 24 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility, and two were excluded because they concerned instrument or fidelity development without evaluation of RC-related outcomes. Twenty-two articles were ultimately included in this review (; ).

Characteristics of included studies (n = 22).

RC, Recovery College; NHS, National Health Service; SWEMWBS, Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale; SIS, Social Inclusion Scale. Measurement time points are presented as reported in each study.

The included articles were published between 2015 and 2026 and reported research from the United Kingdom (n = 11), Canada (n = 6), Australia (n = 2), Switzerland (n = 1), Ireland (n = 1), and Slovakia (n = 1). Study populations included RC students, adults transitioning from homelessness, NHS staff, and RC stakeholders (–). Designs included pre–post and longitudinal evaluations, mixed-methods studies, service evaluations, and cost-benefit analyses (, –).

Sample sizes and the availability of outcome data varied substantially. Cartier et al. () included eight evaluation participants, seven of whom completed questionnaires, whereas Bourne et al. () included 463 RC students. Measurement schedules included cross-sectional assessments, immediate post-workshop assessments, and follow-up assessments over subsequent months. Service-use analyses also examined periods extending to 18 months before or after RC registration (, , , ). Further study characteristics are presented in .

Outcome measures and indicators used in quantitative RC evaluations, including the quantitative components of mixed-methods studies, were extracted. A total of 39 outcome measure and indicator entries were identified, including objective indicators such as health service utilization data derived from clinical or administrative records. These measures assessed personal recovery, well-being, empowerment, self-efficacy, symptoms, stigma, quality of life (QOL), social participation, learning outcomes, and satisfaction, as well as service utilization, economic outcomes, recovery-oriented environments, and recovery-supporting care.

The most frequently used scale was the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS), including its short version (SWEMWBS), which was used in 11 of the 22 articles (50.0%). The Questionnaire about the Process of Recovery (QPR), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7), and the Opening Minds Stigma Scale for Health Care Providers (OMS-HC/OMS-HCP) were each used in four articles (18.2%). The Empowerment Scale, reported as the Consumer Constructed Scale to Measure Empowerment (CCSME) or the Rogers Making Decisions Empowerment Scale, was used in four articles (18.2%), whereas health service utilization data derived from clinical or administrative records were used in four articles (18.2%) ().

Overview of extracted outcome measures.

Counts represent the number of included articles using each measure or indicator (22 articles overall); each article is counted once per row, irrespective of repeated assessments or subscales. Full and short versions are combined. Study-specific questionnaires are retained separately unless they are the same instrument. This table contains 39 inventory entries, not 39 independent standardized scales. Some indicator rows overlap with questionnaire rows: the self-reported service-use item in Ebrahim (2018) () is also part of its course-feedback questionnaire. Therefore, counts across rows should not be summed. “Standardized” identifies previously developed instruments and does not establish their measurement quality in RC settings. “Objective” identifies clinical/administrative or economic data; self-reported service use is shown separately. Demographics, contextual COVID-19 stress and qualitative data-collection methods are not counted as outcome instruments.

The contexts and measurement schedules in which these instruments were used varied. In UK studies, WEMWBS/SWEMWBS was used in evaluations of general RC provision, arts courses, and a Feldenkrais and vocal improvisation workshop (, , ). Wilson et al. () used SWEMWBS alongside the Social Inclusion Scale at baseline and at three- and six-month follow-up, whereas Cartier et al. () administered SWEMWBS before the workshop and at two-week follow-up. In Canadian online RC evaluations, GAD-7 and OMS-HC/OMS-HCP were used within repeated-measures designs incorporating baseline, post-intervention, and subsequent follow-up assessments (, –). QPR was used to assess personal recovery in populations including general RC students and adults transitioning from homelessness (, , , ). Cross-sectional evaluations also used measures for different purposes: Doroud et al. () used the Developing Recovery Enhancing Environments Measure (DREEM) and a modified Mind Australia satisfaction survey (MASS) to assess the recovery-supporting environment and program satisfaction in an Australian RC, while O’Brien et al. () used the Recovery Assessment Scale (RAS) and Recovery Knowledge Inventory (RKI) to assess personal recovery and recovery-related knowledge in an Irish recovery education evaluation. Service-use and economic evaluations incorporated clinical or administrative records and cost-related indicators (, , ).

Of the 39 inventory entries, 28 were used in only one article. Alongside previously developed instruments, studies used study-specific questionnaires and indicators assessing personal goal attainment, learning-objective achievement, personal resources, current emotions, and course experiences (, , , ). Burhouse et al. () used a pre/post self-rating questionnaire covering hope, recovery, knowledge/self-awareness, and self-management, together with the Manhattan Recovery Measure, which combined common questions with individualized questions.

Self-reported service-use indicators were distinguished from utilization data obtained from clinical or administrative records (, ). The inventory entries were not necessarily independent instruments: for example, the service-use item in Ebrahim et al. () also formed part of the course-feedback questionnaire. Full and short versions of the same instrument were counted together, whereas study-specific questionnaires were retained separately unless they were identified as the same instrument ().

The measured constructs were grouped into three major categories: (1) intra-personal and psychological changes, (2) behavioral and social changes, and (3) system and environment (). These categories contained 26, seven, and six inventory entries, respectively. The categories were defined according to the principal object of measurement, rather than the identity of the respondent or the data-collection method. Each inventory entry was assigned to one category according to its principal measured content. The term “changes” in the category labels denotes the outcome domain and does not imply that every included study assessed change over time.

Classification of outcome measures by measured constructs.

Each of the 39 inventory entries in  is assigned to one domain according to its principal measured content. Full and short forms are combined. For questionnaires covering several concepts, the assigned domain does not encompass every item. Program-appraisal questionnaires include individual-level benefits and goal attainment alongside course experience. Domain totals therefore describe inventory entries, not independent scales or numbers of studies. Classification does not indicate measurement quality. QOL, quality of life; RC, Recovery College. Within each major category, subcategories are ordered by the number of inventory entries, and specific constructs are grouped and ordered similarly within each subcategory. Ties retain their previous relative order.

continued — Definitions of categories and subcategories

Categories are defined by the principal object of measurement, rather than respondent identity or data-collection method. Each inventory entry is assigned to one category. “Changes” denotes an outcome domain and does not imply that every study assessed change over time.

(1) Intra-personal and psychological changes. Individuals’ internal experiences, knowledge, attitudes, perceived capacities, and mental health status, including personal recovery and psychological functioning.

① Recovery and its process: Personal recovery, understanding of recovery, and progress toward self-defined recovery goals.

② Empowerment and subjective control: Perceived agency, personal resources, self-worth, resilience, and capacity to manage one’s health and life.

③ Well-being and QOL: Mental well-being and perceived quality of life, including health-related quality of life.

④ Symptoms and emotional states: Mental health symptoms, associated clinical or functional difficulties, and current positive and negative emotional states. Measures of current emotions do not necessarily assess symptom severity.

⑤ Stigma-related attitudes and self-stigma: Stigmatizing beliefs and attitudes concerning mental illness, including internalized stigma and attitudes toward social distance, disclosure, or help-seeking.

⑥ Learning outcomes: Knowledge and skills addressed through RC education, including perceived achievement of learning objectives and reported use of tools introduced through learning.

(2) Behavioral and social changes. Participation in activities and social life, relationships and social circumstances, and patterns of health service use and their economic consequences. This includes reported experiences of social connection as well as participation and service-use indicators.

① Health service utilization and health economics: Contacts with health services, reported need for services, employment and income-related circumstances, and costs or economic consequences associated with service use and RC participation.

② Social connectedness: Participation in shared activities, relationships with others, social inclusion and acceptance, and experiences of loneliness or isolation.

(3) System and environment. Characteristics of RC provision and the surrounding recovery-supporting context, together with participants’ appraisals of the program and support received. The object of evaluation is the environment, provision, or support, even when individuals report the information.

① Program appraisal and experience: Participants’ evaluations of RC provision, including satisfaction, acceptability, helpfulness, enjoyment, and perceived program benefits.

② Recovery-oriented environment: The extent to which the learning or service environment is experienced as supporting recovery.

③ Recovery-supporting care: The extent to which staff support individuals’ personal recovery and recovery goals.

The categories are conceptually related rather than mutually exclusive at the item level. Stigma measures include interpersonal attitudes, clinical functioning measures may include social functioning, and program-appraisal questionnaires may include confidence, motivation, or goal attainment. Assignment follows the principal measured content; additional content is retained in the measure descriptions. Placement in the system and environment category does not imply direct measurement of organizational change, and individual-level placement does not exclude social influences.

This category encompasses individuals’ internal experiences, knowledge, attitudes, perceived capacities, and mental health status, including personal recovery and psychological functioning. It includes six subcategories:

This subcategory encompasses personal recovery, understanding of recovery, and progress toward self-defined recovery goals. Measures included the Recovery Assessment Scale (RAS) and QPR for personal recovery, the Recovery Knowledge Inventory (RKI) for recovery-related knowledge, CHOICE for psychological recovery and mental health, and the Personal Goal Questionnaire for individual goal attainment (, , , ). Burhouse et al. () used a pre/post self-rating questionnaire covering hope, recovery, knowledge/self-awareness, and self-management, together with the Manhattan Recovery Measure to track personal recovery. The latter included common questions and four individually designed questions; detailed scoring and the attribution of individual outcome results to the measures were not fully specified.

This subcategory encompasses perceived agency, personal resources, self-worth, resilience, and capacity to manage one’s health and life. Measures included the Empowerment Scale (CCSME/Rogers Making Decisions Empowerment Scale), Empower Flower, the single-item self-esteem scale, CD-RISC-10, MHSQ, PAM, and the Pearlin Mastery Scale (, , , , ).

This subcategory encompasses mental well-being and perceived quality of life, including health-related quality of life. Measures included WEMWBS/SWEMWBS and WHO-5 for well-being, and QoLi-20, SF-12, and EQ-5D-5L for quality of life. Study-specific assessments also addressed staff experiences and perceived impacts (, , , ).

This subcategory encompasses mental health symptoms, associated clinical or functional difficulties, and current positive and negative emotional states. GAD-7 assessed anxiety symptoms, HoNOS assessed clinical and social functioning, and the Feelings Chart assessed current emotional states (, , ). Measures of current emotions do not necessarily assess symptom severity.

This subcategory encompasses stigmatizing beliefs and attitudes concerning mental illness, including internalized stigma and attitudes toward social distance, disclosure, or help-seeking. OMS-HC/OMS-HCP assessed stigma-related attitudes, while the five-item application subscale of the Self-Stigma of Mental Illness Scale–Short Form (SSMIS-SF) assessed the application of self-stigmatizing beliefs (, , ).

This subcategory encompasses knowledge and skills addressed through RC education, including perceived achievement of learning objectives and reported use of tools introduced through learning. A study-specific questionnaire assessed mental health knowledge, use of intervention tools, and perceived learning benefits ().

This category encompasses participation in activities and social life, relationships and social circumstances, and patterns of health service use and their economic consequences. It includes reported experiences of social connection as well as participation and service-use indicators. Two subcategories were identified:

This subcategory encompasses contacts with health services, reported need for services, employment and income-related circumstances, and costs or economic consequences associated with service use and RC participation. Indicators included service-use data obtained from clinical or administrative records, self-reported service-use indicators, the Client Socio-Demographic and Service Receipt Inventory (CSSRI-EU), and cost-effectiveness or cost-benefit indicators. CSSRI-EU also captured employment and income-related information (, , , , , ).

This subcategory encompasses participation in shared activities, relationships with others, social inclusion and acceptance, and experiences of loneliness or isolation. Measures included the Arts Participation Measure, the Campaign to End Loneliness Scale, and the Social Inclusion Scale (, , ).

This category encompasses the characteristics of RC provision and the surrounding recovery-supporting context, together with participants’ appraisals of the program and support received. The object of evaluation is the environment, provision, or support, even when individuals report the information. Three subcategories were identified:

This subcategory encompasses participants’ evaluations of RC provision, including satisfaction, acceptability, helpfulness, enjoyment, and perceived program benefits. Measures included the modified Mind Australia satisfaction survey (MASS) and study-specific questionnaires addressing course experiences, perceived benefits, and acceptability (, , , ).

This subcategory concerns the extent to which the learning or service environment is experienced as supporting recovery. The Developing Recovery Enhancing Environments Measure (DREEM) assessed the recovery-enhancing environment ().

This subcategory concerns the extent to which staff support individuals’ personal recovery and recovery goals. INSPIRE assessed perceived staff support for personal recovery ().

The categories are conceptually related rather than mutually exclusive at the item level. For example, stigma measures include interpersonal attitudes, clinical functioning measures may include social functioning, and program-appraisal questionnaires may include confidence, motivation, or personal goal attainment. Assignment followed the principal measured content, while additional content was retained in the descriptions in . Placement in the system and environment category does not imply direct measurement of organizational change, and placement in an individual-level category does not exclude social influences on the measured construct.

An examination of reliability and validity reporting distinguished assessments conducted within the included studies from references to previously published psychometric information ().  covers 37 questionnaire and indicator entries; the two aggregate entries for record-derived service use and cost indicators were excluded from scale psychometrics. Of the 22 included articles, 15 (68.2%) cited previous psychometric information or identifiable validation literature for at least one extracted measure. Two articles (9.1%) explicitly reported reliability estimates calculated from their own study data (, ).

Reporting status of reliability and validity.

The 37 questionnaire/indicator entries follow  order; its two aggregate entries for record-derived service use and costs are excluded from scale psychometrics. “Not reported” means no identified reporting, not poor measurement quality. Prior information includes explicit psychometric descriptions and identifiable validation/evaluation citations; cited papers were not independently assessed. A generic instrument-source citation is insufficient. Current-sample reliability requires explicit attribution; unclear provenance is flagged. Non-statistical face/content-validity descriptions are distinguished from statistical testing. Evidence is version-specific and is not automatically transferable. Cited responsiveness and change-interpretation thresholds are contextual information, not new RC-specific validation. Internal consistency may not apply to single items, individualized goals or heterogeneous checklists. Article-level percentages use 22 articles with overlapping categories; Cronin (2023) () is not applicable to scale psychometrics. MCID, minimum clinically important difference; KMO, Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy; RMSEA, root mean square error of approximation; CFI, comparative fit index; TLI, Tucker–Lewis index.

Reference numbers in parentheses correspond to the manuscript reference list.

Rapisarda et al. () reported Cronbach’s α values of 0.87 for GAD-7, 0.81 for OMS-HC, 0.80 for SWEMWBS, and 0.77 for CCSME. O’Brien et al. () reported α = 0.93 for RAS and α = 0.75 for RKI. One additional article (4.5%) reported reliability coefficients without clearly identifying whether they were estimated in the current sample or obtained from previous research; these were retained as having unclear provenance rather than counted as confirmed within-study estimates ().

One article (4.5%) reported undertaking statistical assessments of validity within the study (). The authors stated that convergent and divergent validity testing had been conducted and reported communalities above 0.5 and a Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin value of 0.8, although the allocation of these statistics to individual scales was not fully specified. Two further articles (9.1%) included non-statistical descriptions concerning face or content validity: Stevens et al. () stated that face and content validity had been established for the Arts Participation Measure, while Ebrahim et al. () described participant feedback supporting the face validity of Empower Flower but explicitly noted that formal reliability and validity testing had not been undertaken.

Six articles (27.3%) provided neither identifiable reliability or validity evidence nor a specific validation citation for the extracted measures (, , , , , ). Burhouse et al. () cited the source of the Manhattan Recovery Measure but reported no specific reliability or validity evidence; this source citation was not classified as a validation citation. One article (4.5%), a record-based service-use and cost-benefit analysis, was classified separately as not applicable to scale psychometrics (). All percentages use the 22 included articles as the denominator. Reporting categories overlap because an article could report more than one type of information.

Outcome measures were used to evaluate psychological changes, such as personal recovery, well-being, empowerment, and stigma, before and after program participation (, , , ). Some studies incorporated subsequent follow-up assessments to examine outcomes beyond the immediate post-intervention period (, , ). Measures were also used to examine differences in individual patterns of change across several outcome dimensions ().

In addition, indicators were used to assess learning-objective achievement, personal goal attainment, and participation in social or creative activities (–, ). Burhouse et al. () used self-report measures to evaluate hope, recovery-related knowledge, self-management, and progress toward personal recovery goals within a quality-improvement project. Studies focusing on service use and economic outcomes examined contacts with health services, hospital admissions, employment-related outcomes, and potential cost savings associated with RC participation (, , , ).

Other measures were used to assess recovery-supporting environments, perceived staff support, satisfaction, and participants’ experiences of RC provision (, , , ). O’Brien et al. () used cross-sectional quantitative data to evaluate personal recovery and recovery-related knowledge in the context of recovery education. Thus, the purposes of measurement included both the assessment of participant outcomes and the evaluation of RC provision, and were not limited to longitudinal assessments of individual change.

In this study, an examination of the outcome measures used in RC evaluation studies identified 39 outcome measure and indicator entries across 22 articles. These measures were categorized into a multi-layered framework comprising intra-personal and psychological changes, behavioral and social changes, and system and environment. This breadth indicates that the included evaluations addressed more than symptom reduction, encompassing personal recovery, social participation, and the support environment itself (, ).

Particularly, the frequent use of measures assessing intra-personal changes, such as well-being, personal recovery, and empowerment, is consistent with the emphasis of RCs on individuals’ strengths and agency (). Notably, the repeated use of WEMWBS/SWEMWBS and QPR, in 11 and four articles, respectively, indicates sustained attention to well-being and personal recovery in current evaluation practice. However, frequency of use does not establish these as agreed core outcomes or demonstrate that the instruments are the most meaningful, responsive, or appropriate for RC participants.

Conversely, more than two-thirds of the extracted inventory entries (28 of 39) were used in only a single article, indicating diversity in outcome evaluation. This diversity may reflect the multifaceted and individualized nature of RC practice and legitimate differences in evaluation purposes, populations, and contexts. For example, evaluations involving adults transitioning from homelessness, NHS staff, or participants in creative workshops may reasonably require different outcomes (, , ). Diversity should therefore not automatically be interpreted as a problematic lack of uniformity. Nevertheless, disparate measures and measurement schedules can hinder comparison when studies address similar questions. Some commonality may support synthesis while retaining outcomes appropriate to particular participants and settings.

Furthermore, this study suggests that important concepts reflecting the unique ethos of RCs may not be adequately represented by the measures used. Although many measures addressed psychological outcomes, direct assessment of learning processes, learner experience, knowledge application, self-directed learning, educational engagement, and transfer into everyday life was comparatively limited. Co-production, learning, belonging, and social inclusion were not entirely absent: studies assessed learning-objective achievement, self-management, individualized goals, social inclusion, loneliness, and recovery-supporting environments (, , , , , ). However, these related assessments do not necessarily capture the full educational and relational contribution of RCs. This suggests a possible gap between intervention philosophy and evaluation focus. Future evaluations could also consider community-level outcomes, such as reciprocal links with local organizations and opportunities for inclusive participation, where these reflect stakeholder priorities. The question is whether selected measures capture what matters within RC philosophy and practice, rather than simply whether those outcomes are readily measurable.

Existing RC-specific instruments should also be considered. For example, the RECOLLECT Fidelity Measure addresses features including learning, co-production, tailoring provision to the student, and social connectedness (). Related RECOLLECT Checklists assess alignment with RC principles from student, peer-trainer, and manager perspectives (). These tools were not used in the included evaluations. Some included studies predated their development, and the timing of availability may have influenced uptake. However, the reasons for their non-use in the included evaluations remain unclear from the available evidence; awareness and alignment with evaluation aims are possible considerations. Their absence therefore does not establish limited use across RC research. The development study was excluded because it evaluated the instrument rather than RC-related outcomes. Whereas many included evaluations focused on individual outcomes, combining fidelity assessment with participant measures could help investigate whether and how adherence to RC principles relates to individual change, learning, and educational outcomes. Researchers and learners should jointly consider existing tools’ coverage, acceptability, and respondent burden when designing such evaluations (, ).

Additionally, the use of objective outcomes such as health service utilization data and economic indicators across multiple studies is noteworthy (, , ). These findings illustrate the value of considering service and institutional outcomes alongside subjective self-report measures. Their interpretation nevertheless requires attention to context: reduced service use alone does not demonstrate improved recovery. Future studies should adopt multifaceted evaluations combining subjective and objective measures where appropriate to their purposes, with educational processes and outcomes considered alongside psychological change.

Regarding psychometric reporting, 15 of the 22 articles cited previous psychometric information or identifiable validation literature, whereas only two explicitly reported reliability estimates calculated from their own data. Six provided neither specific psychometric evidence nor an identifiable validation citation. These findings indicate limitations in reporting, rather than poor measurement quality. Previous validation does not automatically establish suitability for a particular RC population, instrument version, or evaluation purpose. Future reports should distinguish prior evidence from analyses undertaken in the current sample and explain instrument selection. Internal consistency alone does not establish validity or responsiveness and is not applicable to every indicator, including single items and administrative data.

Therefore, future research should prioritize three directions. First, outcomes should be selected according to research purposes and target populations, and the reliability, validity, and responsiveness of existing instruments should be evaluated in the intended RC populations. For self-report scales, the COSMIN Study Design checklist can guide studies of measurement properties, including content validity and the ability to detect change (). Second, study designs should support the appropriate use of existing measures, with learners, people with lived experience, peer educators, families, educators, clinicians, researchers, and service planners involved in decisions about outcomes, measurement schedules, and feasibility (, ). Long-term follow-up could help examine sustained outcomes and the application of learning in everyday life (). Third, where existing evaluations insufficiently cover outcomes important to RC stakeholders, a co-produced core outcome set could be explored through qualitative work, a Delphi process, and consensus meetings (). Agreement on what to measure should be distinguished from validation of the instruments used to measure it, and shared outcomes should retain individualized goals and context-specific priorities. Adaptation or development of measures may be considered where important gaps remain. The present inventory can inform these decisions without prescribing a fixed measurement set.

A strength of this review is its systematic mapping of outcome measures and objective indicators, integrating their measured constructs, patterns of use, and reporting of reliability and validity. By making the coverage of existing evaluations more explicit, this mapping can help learners, researchers, and other stakeholders consider whether selected outcomes reflect RC principles and the changes that matter to participants. It provides a basis for co-produced decisions about outcome selection and evaluation design, including how existing measures can address educational, personal, and social priorities and where further assessment of their suitability is needed. In this way, the review can support evaluations that better reflect the educational and co-produced nature of RCs while retaining individualized goals and context-specific priorities.

This study has several limitations. First, this review mapped what researchers have chosen to measure in published quantitative RC evaluations; it did not synthesize intervention effects to determine what RCs actually achieve. Because eligibility required quantitative outcome measures or objective indicators, studies employing exclusively qualitative methods were excluded. Consequently, aspects central to RC philosophy and practice, such as co-production, learning processes, belonging, and relational changes, may not have been fully represented in the extracted inventory. The absence or limited representation of a domain in this review therefore does not demonstrate that RCs have no effect in that domain or that it is unimportant to participants. Studies conducted solely to develop or validate instruments were also excluded. The inventory should thus not be interpreted as a comprehensive catalogue of all available RC measures or all outcomes associated with RC participation.

Second, the diversity of outcome indicators is a substantive finding of this review rather than a limitation in itself. The limitation concerns the context in which patterns of measure use can be interpreted. Included studies differed in their populations, designs, countries, RC operational models, and measurement schedules. Consequently, aggregate frequencies combine measures used for different purposes and under different conditions, limiting direct comparison of measurement choices across studies. The review could describe these patterns but could not determine whether differences in measure use reflected appropriate adaptation to evaluation aims, practical constraints, or inconsistent selection. Frequencies indicate how often an instrument appeared in the included articles, not its importance to participants, responsiveness, or measurement quality. They also count articles rather than necessarily independent study populations. Assigning multi-concept instruments to a single principal domain further simplifies their content and may underrepresent educational or social concepts embedded within measures assigned to other domains.

Third, the synthesis of reliability and validity was based on reporting in the included articles rather than a systematic re-evaluation of the psychometric properties of the instruments themselves. Original validation studies were not independently appraised, and no formal critical appraisal of the included studies was undertaken. The review therefore describes the reporting of psychometric evidence and does not establish the comparative quality of the measures or support definitive recommendations about which instruments should be used.

Fourth, the selected databases and eligibility criteria may have limited coverage. PsycINFO and Scopus were not searched because institutional subscription access was unavailable. Restriction to English-language journal articles also excluded dissertations, non-journal local service reports, and other grey literature. Locally developed indicators and measures used in routine practice or non-English-language settings may therefore be underrepresented. In addition, three reports could not be retrieved. The distribution of measures should be interpreted as describing the included literature rather than the full range of RC evaluation practices.

This scoping review mapped 39 outcome measure and indicator entries across 22 RC evaluation articles, covering intra-personal and psychological changes, behavioral and social changes, and system and environment. Repeated use of WEMWBS/SWEMWBS and QPR reflected common measurement practices, while the diversity of indicators may reflect differing evaluation purposes and contexts. Direct assessment of educational processes and outcomes was comparatively limited in the included quantitative literature, but this describes what researchers measured rather than what RCs achieved. The mapping can inform co-produced decisions about outcome selection and study design, alongside further evaluation of existing instruments’ reliability, validity, and responsiveness in the intended RC populations. Involving learners and other stakeholders in these decisions can help align evaluation with RC principles and participant priorities while retaining individualized goals and context-specific outcomes.

psychology.title: Gendered affective representations in AI-assisted music videos: a qualitative multimethod study
psychology.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly visible in music-video production, influencing both production practices and the ways in which emotion, bodies, and gender are portrayed visually. This study examines gendered emotional representation in AI-assisted music videos.A qualitative multimethod design combined interpretive visual analysis of four purposively selected AI-assisted music videos with asynchronous written expert interviews involving six creative-industry professionals and four psychology experts (N = 10). The videos were analysed through an interpretive coding framework covering emotion, gender, body and face, power relations, AI aesthetics, and traces of bias.Across the cases, emotion was conveyed not only through facial expression but also through atmosphere, colour, movement, editing, and spatial transitions. The selected works sometimes reproduced familiar conventions, including heteronormative intimacy, militarised masculinity, and idealised female bodies, but also unsettled them through female anger and solidarity and mutable synthetic bodies. Ambiguity in a body’s appearance did not necessarily unsettle its gendered narrative role. Industry accounts described how prompting, selection, revision, and post-production shape representations, while general psychology-expert perspectives informed their interpretation.The findings position AI-assisted music videos as co-produced sites of synthetic visual culture in which established gendered conventions may be repeated, negotiated, or challenged. Neither expert group provided direct evidence about the production or reception of the selected videos. The findings underline the practical importance of representational review, consent, diversity, and transparent disclosure in AI-assisted cultural production.
psychology.text:
Artificial intelligence has moved from a specialist research field into everyday communication and cultural production. Its history is commonly traced from Turing’s question of machine intelligence () to the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, which helped establish AI as a distinct field (). Since the early 2020s, generative systems have expanded the capacity to produce text, images, sound, and moving images, bringing AI more directly into creative workflows.

Music and communication are among the fields in which the use of artificial intelligence has recently become more visible. Music videos have evolved beyond a means by which artists bring their songs to listeners; they have become a form of expression that combines visual and auditory aesthetics and directly represents the artist’s image and communication. The role and use of generative AI in these music videos are likewise increasing steadily. As in all works of visual culture, generative AI systems offer new experiences and possibilities to artists, creative teams, and audiences alike in music videos. These developments have opened up possibilities for individual creators as well as the wider sector. In visual culture, however, AI now does more than offer technical efficiencies or reduce production time and cost. It can also affect the way a work tells its story and frames gender, emotion, and the emotional basis of the narrative. The gains in speed, efficiency, and customisation therefore sit alongside continuing concerns about privacy, bias, fairness, and changes to human labour ().

Once understood mainly as visual accompaniments to songs and, particularly from the 1980s onward, as promotional devices for the popular-music industry, music videos now fulfil a much wider role. What matters centrally is what emerges from the relationship between image and sound. Lighting, bodies, movement, setting, imagery, and editing work as communicative resources; together with the song, they shape emotional codes and representations of gender.

Recurring arrangements of bodies, gazes, movement, costume, and space also assign gendered roles within music videos.
