Neither the persistence nor the removal of stereotypes describes the sample adequately. Heteronormative intimacy, militarised masculinity, and idealised femininity appear alongside female anger, solidarity, and changing synthetic bodies. Panopticom makes the tension particularly clear: an ambiguous bodily appearance can belong to a conventionally gendered story. The works can bring such contradictions into view without resolving them.

These readings connect research on generative AI to questions of gender and emotional representation in synthetic visual culture. Familiar representational patterns recur, but the videos can also make those patterns available for scrutiny. AI-assisted production consequently calls for attention to bias and gender conventions, while offering artists ways to experiment with identity, bodies, and emotional expression.

The theoretical contribution is an approach to AI-assisted music videos as synthetic environments in which emotional codes and gendered meanings are organised. This directs attention beyond technical novelty to the relations among movement, faces, bodies, and the cultural coding of emotion. The interpretive framework brings those relations into a shared discussion across affective science, visual culture, media and communication, gender research, and AI ethics.

The psychology experts helped us question the readings by drawing attention to context, idealisation, and uncertainty. Their general responses cannot establish what audiences make of the four videos. Read alongside the industry accounts, they contribute professional perspectives to the interpretation while keeping visible representation, production experience, and possible reception distinct.

For creative practice, the findings point to a need for review at each stage, from writing prompts and selecting images to publishing and circulating a video. Technical quality, cost, and speed are relevant, but so are the emotional meanings and gender representations being put into circulation. Attention to these choices, and to the responsibilities of those making them, can support more pluralistic and ethically considered production.

psychology.title: Evolutionary foundations of social identity
psychology.abstract: Social identity theory provides a rich description of how humans relate to various kinds of social groups, but no substantive account of why human psychology evolved to be so group-minded in the first place. We propose that the evolutionarily original form of social identity was one's moral identity as a cooperative group member. For ancient humans, survival depended on being an assimilated member of a cultural group, which, in turn, competed against other groups. In this context, humans evolved skills and motivations for engaging in the collective agency of a cultural group, especially the self-reflective capacity to adopt a social identity (i.e. to construe oneself as a member of a ‘we’) and the concomitant self-regulatory motivation to maintain a positive social identity (i.e. to strive for ‘I’, the individual, to meet the standards that ‘we’ uphold). In this evolutionary proposal, behavioural effects of group identity, inferences of common knowledge and moral emotions are all manifestations of the function of social identity as a self-regulatory system for maintaining one's good standing as a cooperative group member.This article is part of the discussion meeting issue ‘From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self’.
psychology.text:
Social identity, or self-conception as a member of a group, has long been a prominent focus of cultural discourse as well as social psychological research []. Beginning with social identity theory [], extensive research in social psychology has explored why individuals self-identify with groups, focusing on the proximate psychological level of explanation. This research has provided a rich description of the diverse proximate motivations that lead individuals to adopt a social identity, such as the needs for positive self-regard, distinctiveness, meaning and belonging [,]. However, classical accounts of social identity neglect the question of why individuals self-identify with groups on the evolutionary level of explanation, that is, why humans evolved to be so group-minded in the first place.

Modern humans construct complex social identities based on diverse features such as race, ethnicity, gender, nationality, occupation and social class. Although these features are significant aspects of modern life and have been the focus of much research, they were probably not core elements of social identity in its evolutionarily original form. As noted by Kinzler et al. [, p. 625], race and ethnicity were not informative for most of human history because ‘neighboring groups of humans in ancient times did not likely look different in terms of physiognomy or skin colour’. While gender played a role in intragroup divisions of labour, it was not informative for intergroup differentiation. Nationality, occupation and social class are modern constructs that do not map onto the small-scale hunter-gatherer lifeways that comprised most of human history [].

We propose that the evolutionarily original form of social identity was one's moral identity as a cooperative member of one's cultural group. If social identity is defined as self-conception as a member of a group [], then, in order to determine the evolutionarily prototypical social identity, one must determine the evolutionarily prototypical group with which it was important for individuals to identify. This group was the cultural group—the large-scale bands of mutually acquainted tribes united by common language, customs, artefacts and so on—which we hypothesize emerged around the onset of the Late Pleistocene (around 130 kya). The moral dimension is of unique importance, as individuals' identification with the values and norms of the group—both following them and enforcing them on others—is what sustains group coherence.

In the following sections, we expand on this hypothesis. First, we elaborate on our evolutionary claim that the cultural group was the evolutionarily prototypical group. We outline a natural history of human evolution up to the point at which cultural groups acquired their critical significance as evolutionary selection pressures. Next, we bolster our psychological claim that humans are psychologically disposed to form a moral identity by reviewing evidence of its early manifestations in children.

The natural starting point for discussing the evolution of uniquely human capacities, such as social identity, is the last common ancestor (LCA) of humans and other great apes. Extant great apes may serve as a model for the LCA because the capacities found in common across extant great ape species are more likely to have descended from a common ancestor than to have evolved independently multiple times in a short time frame []. Extant great apes exhibit diverse forms of instrumental rationality, such as planning for future goals, making causal and logical inferences, and self-monitoring uncertainty [].

Therefore, the LCA probably had a relatively sophisticated kind of individual agency. By individual agency, we mean self-regulation for individual goal pursuit by means of feedback control systems such as self-monitoring and self-control. However, humans diverged from other great apes in their ability to engage in not only individual agency but also shared agency. By shared agency, we again mean self-regulation for goal pursuit, but in this case, the goal being pursued is a joint goal shared by multiple individuals and the mechanisms of self-regulation include interpersonal feedback control systems (whereby individuals regulate each other's behaviours), not just intrapersonal feedback control systems (whereby an individual only regulates his or her own behaviour).

Effectively, humans combined their individual ‘I-level’ agencies into shared ‘we-level’ agencies capable of ‘we-level’ goal pursuit. Humans became able to think and act from the perspective of a ‘we’: what ‘we’ want to do, how ‘we’ plan to do it and how ‘we’ regulate ourselves and each other in the service of joint goals [,]. While great apes display some apparently group-based behaviours, such as group border patrols or grooming of familiar others, such behaviours lack the interpersonal feedback control systems characteristic of human shared agency, as great apes do not appear to normatively expect others to engage in such behaviours or enforce ‘punishment’ against those who do not engage in them. Moreover, although great apes display certain mentalistic and behavioural foundations that are indeed necessary for engaging in joint action (e.g. gaze following and considering others' perceptual states, both necessary steps towards establishing joint attention; [,]), they do not appear to coordinate their mental states and actions in pursuit of joint goals, as humans do from early ages (for a review, see []).

We propose that the human capacity for shared agency evolved in two steps: joint agency and collective agency. The first step, the evolution of joint agency, occurred approximately 2 million years ago as early humans began engaging in collaborative foraging, such as working in groups to hunt or scavenge large game that individuals could not secure alone []. The shift from an individualistic to a collaborative foraging strategy may have been prompted by ecological changes, such as variations in climate that led to the expansion of terrestrial monkeys who competed with early humans for individualistically foraged food sources [].

In game-theoretic terms, collaborative foraging aligns with the incentives of a stag hunt game. Rather than obtaining smaller pay-offs (hares) through individualistic action, actors are better off obtaining larger pay-offs (stags) through joint action. Great apes may be characterized as following a ‘hare-oriented’ strategy, with their reliance on individualistically gathered food sources such as leaves and fruits. While some chimpanzee groups hunt monkeys, they do so as a multitude of separate agents, each pursuing its own individual goal, not as a shared agent pursuing a shared goal. They do not intentionally communicate to initiate or coordinate group hunts (which are instead initiated via a ‘leader–follower’ dynamic in which individuals see that others are already pursuing a monkey and take advantage of this situation to try to catch it for themselves), nor do they intentionally share the spoils at the end [].

Humans, by contrast, may be characterized as following a ‘stag-oriented’ strategy, with their reliance on collaboratively obtained food sources. Over iterations of the stag hunt across early human history, individuals who were better at engaging in shared agency with others, i.e. at forming a functioning ‘we’ capable of coordinating on larger pay-offs, were advantaged and selected for [,]. Thus, collaborative foraging was a key catalyst in the evolution of early human joint agency.

During this first phase of human evolution, social identity, in the sense of self-conception as a group member, probably did not play a significant role. This is because individuals engaging in small-scale (i.e. dyadic or small-group) collaborative activities characteristic of early human joint agency knew their collaborative partners on a first-hand basis. Moreover, even if individuals identified to some degree with different ‘familial subdivisions’ within their tribe, all tribe members were still directly acquainted. Assessing whether others were members of one's in-group did not become an issue until the second phase of human evolution, when humans began assembling in larger bands in which one was not necessarily acquainted with every other in-group member []. We hypothesize that this second phase of human evolution overlapped with the onset of the Late Pleistocene (around 130 kya), given the genetic and archaeological evidence of increases in human population sizes during this period [,].

The impetus for this second phase of human evolution was none other than the success of the first phase. Increases in the number and size of groups, owing to the efficacy of the early human collaborative foraging strategy, entailed corresponding increases in the competition between groups over resources. This context of intergroup competition favoured groups whose members were more loyal, coordinated and capable of collective action—or, in agentic terms, groups that were better able to engage in collective agency and act as a collective ‘we’ []. To sustain collective agency, groups used group-level feedback control systems to regulate the behaviours of individual group members in the service of group-level goals. These group-level feedback control systems undoubtedly included things such as social norms, institutions, fictive kinships, narratives, worldviews and other social realities that are still operative in human groups today [,]. We propose that social identity was also one of the group-level feedback control systems sustaining collective agency.

Social identity was necessary for both group and individual functioning. Regarding group functioning, group members needed a way to recognize who belonged to the group, given that members of large bands were not all personally acquainted. Social identity markers, such as clothing, language and conformity to group norms, fulfilled this need. This, in turn, enabled groups to ensure that the spoils of collaboration accrued to norm-abiding group members (rather than to outsiders or norm violators, such as non-reciprocators), which was important for sustaining group cooperation in the long run []. Moreover, tangible markers of group identity were also necessary for group members to be able to rally together into large-scale coalitional alliances, e.g. for group defence against a common enemy [].

Regarding individual functioning, individual survival depended on being accepted by one's group. Indeed, this was especially true in the context of intergroup competition. As noted by Baumeister & Leary [, p. 499], there is a ‘severe competitive disadvantage of the lone individual confronting a group when both want the same resource. When other people are in groups, it is vital to belong to a group oneself’. Displays of social identity helped ensure one's continued acceptance by the group and one's survival. Thus, both group and individual selection pressures favoured the evolution of skills and motivations for maintaining a social identity.

These skills and motivations included the cognitive capacity to adopt a social identity in the first place—the self-reflective capacity to construe oneself as a member of a collective group, a collective ‘we’. Building on this capacity, humans also evolved the concomitant self-regulatory motivation to maintain a positive social identity. As a point of clarification, by positive social identity, we do not mean the positive differentiation of oneself in comparison to others (e.g. [,]) but rather one's positive fulfilment of group expectations. Because groups have normative expectations for how group members should think, act, dress and so on, group members are continually immersed in evaluative standards for what it means to be a ‘good’ group member. Accordingly, a motivational disposition to want to be a ‘good’ group member, i.e. to want to maintain a positive social identity, was selected for because it facilitated individuals' acceptance by the group.

To be clear, we are not suggesting that the evolved motivation to maintain a positive social identity is solely a matter of strategically wanting to maintain a positive reputation in the eyes of others. Instead, it is also a matter of genuinely wanting to fulfil one's own values in one's own eyes. This is because individuals are socialized intensely from early on to internalize their group's cultural worldview as their own; the way ‘we’ see the world becomes the way ‘I’ myself see the world []. Consequently, whenever one attends to any object of perception in the world, one's perception of that object is coloured by the epistemic-normative lens of one's cultural worldview []. This is also the case when the object of perception is one's own self. One perceives one's own self (the ‘me’) from the value-laden perspective of the group (the ‘we’). As this self-perception is inherently normative, involving an evaluation of whether one's own self is fulfilling the values and standards that it should be, we term it ‘moral identity’. Our usage of the term moral identity thus aligns with psychological and philosophical accounts that individuals seek to maintain a positive self-conception as someone whose behaviours are consistent with their values [].

We have proposed that moral identity evolved as a result of two steps in the evolution of human agency. First, humans diverged from the individualistic agency of other great apes in becoming able to form a joint ‘we’ for collaborative foraging. Later, humans expanded their sense of ‘we’ to encompass their cultural in-group as a whole, at which point moral identity—the self-reflective capacity to identify as a group member and the concomitant self-regulatory motivation to behave as a ‘good’ group member—evolved as the prototypical social identity.

Another point of clarification is worth mentioning. Our hypothesis that humans evolved capacities and motivations for sustaining collective agencies and moral identities does not mean that such adaptations emerge ‘innately’ in ontogeny as a direct outcome of gene expression. Humans, with their highly plastic brains and slow periods of maturation [], are exceptionally receptive to learning from the inputs of their species-typical niche. For humans, the species-typical niche is a cultural niche. As such, the specific forms of collective agency and moral identity that individuals develop depend on both their social learning of the inputs specific to their culture and the kinds of inputs offered by their culture, as determined by cultural evolution []. Neither of these processes (i.e. individual-level social learning or group-level cultural learning) is reducible to genetic bases alone. For example, on the scale of cultural evolution, adaptive cultural practices may propagate across groups simply owing to the fact that successful strategies attract imitators [], without the need for a specific genetic basis for a given strategy. In the next section, we review the developmental evidence for the psychological claim that humans are psychologically disposed to form a moral identity.

In ontogeny, as in evolution, moral identity emerges in two steps. Children first develop competencies for joint agency, which later scale up into competencies for collective agency. We review this shift in four key competencies relevant to moral identity: social self-regulation, prosociality, common ground and moral emotions ().
Table 1.Four key competencies relevant to moral identity.competencyjoint agencycollective agencysocial self-regulation:joint commitments→social normsprosociality:helping partners→in-group favouritismcommon ground:personal→culturalmoral emotion:personal guilt→collective guilt

Four key competencies relevant to moral identity.

The prototypical form of social self-regulation underlying joint agency is a joint commitment. Once you and I commit to an activity together, our commitment creates obligations for how we should act. We expect each other to play our respective roles in the activity, not to abandon the activity arbitrarily, and to respectfully ‘take leave’ when we want to exit the activity. By the age of 3 years, children understand joint commitments and their accompanying obligations. For instance, 3-year-olds are more likely to resist temptations to abandon an activity and are more likely to take leave when exiting an activity if they had made a commitment to do the activity with the partner than if they had not made a commitment [,]. Vasil & Tomasello [] found that simply framing an activity as something ‘we’ are doing together, as opposed to something ‘you’ and ‘I’ are doing in parallel but separately, increases 3-year-olds' leave-taking when exiting an activity.

When reacting to partners who fail to play their role in a joint commitment, 3-year-olds protest more if the partner intentionally defects from the activity than if the partner is simply ignorant about how the activity works [], and they also protest more if the partner abandons the activity abruptly than if the partner takes leave []. Altogether, these studies demonstrate how 3-year-olds already possess interpersonal and intrapersonal feedback control systems for engaging in joint commitments, such as protesting against uncooperative partners or delaying individual gratification for joint goals; see also [,].

Analogous to how joint agency is regulated by joint commitments, collective agency is regulated by social norms. A joint commitment refers to an agreement between social partners that ‘we’ (meaning the specific individuals in the immediate situation) agree to do something together in a certain way. A social norm also refers to an agreement between social partners, but one in which the sense of ‘we’ is scaled up to encompass not just the specific individuals in the immediate situation but rather all members of one's group, including members whom one may not even know. Essentially, a social norm exists when ‘we’ members of a group agree to do something together in a certain way. Children understand social norms by the age of 3 years, as evidenced by their willingness to not only follow norms but also enforce them and protest when others violate them [].

Importantly, children also understand that following group norms is an integral part of identifying with a group. In a study by Schmidt et al. [], 3-year-olds protested more against a violation of an in-group conventional norm if the violator was an in-group member as opposed to an out-group member, reflecting an understanding that the norms that ‘we’ endorse apply primarily to those who identify with the ‘we’ and not so much to outsiders. In a study by Li et al. [], which focused on children's own adherence to in-group norms, 3-year-olds were invited to identify with a university in-group (‘We are Duke!’) and then set up a tea party. The 3-year-olds conformed more to a model's choices of tea party items when the choices were framed as in-group norms (e.g. ‘For tea parties at Duke, we always use this kind of cup’) versus personal preferences (e.g. ‘For my tea party today, I feel like using this cup’). Altogether, children's early-emerging understanding, observance and enforcement of social norms reflect a deep psychological disposition to maintain a positive moral identity as someone who respects and fulfils the norms of the group.

Children as young as 2 years old perform prosocial acts, such as helping and sharing []. By the age of 3 years, children show heightened prosociality towards collaborative partners with whom they have formed a joint agency. In a study by Hamann et al. [], pairs of 3-year-olds retrieved rewards from a pulling apparatus through either individual or joint action. The 3-year-olds were more likely to equally share the obtained resources if their partner's help had been necessary for retrieving the resources, compared to if they had retrieved the resources individually. A follow-up study found that after 3-year-olds had already obtained their own reward in a collaborative activity, they were still willing to keep collaborating until their partner also obtained a reward []. Young children even cheat in games specifically to benefit collaborative partners or previous benefactors [,], revealing the force with which collaborative interactions impact children's prosocial motivations.

With age, children's prosocial tendencies appear to scale up from being directed towards specific collaborative partners to being directed towards in-group members in general. As strikingly demonstrated in the minimal group paradigm, in which individuals are assigned to groups that differ only along arbitrary features such as clothing colour, children from 4 to 5 years of age show diverse forms of in-group favouritism, such as greater in-group liking, helping, sharing and loyalty when keeping a secret, despite the arbitrariness of the in-group identity []. As proposed by Dunham [, p. 786], such in-group-favouring tendencies may reflect ‘an evolved system of coalitional reasoning’. In agentic terms, they may reflect an evolved system for engaging in collective agency with in-group members. In any case, they show that adopting a social identity leads children to behave prosocially towards others who share the same identity.

To collaborate effectively in a joint agency, partners need to have common ground—mutual knowledge about ‘what we both know that we both know’ [,]. By the age of 3 years, and increasingly throughout the later preschool years, children track how much common ground they share with a partner when discussing what to do and justifying their decisions [,], as well as when coordinating their decisions without explicit communication [,]. By the age of 3 years, children also understand that groups are constituted by mutual intentions—the common ground consensus among group members that ‘we’ all want each other to be part of the same group [,].

With increasing age, children come to realize that they share not only personal common ground with specific others based on shared direct experience, but also cultural common ground with in-group members in general based on shared cultural experiences []. Soley [] found that 5-year-olds expect greater common ground about music, an important form of culture, among members of the same group than among members of different groups. In another study, Soley & Aldan [] found that 5-year-olds expect greater common ground about music among individuals who speak the same language (an honest signal of group enculturation) than among individuals of the same gender (a non-coalitional identity). A third study by Karadağ & Soley [] found that 5-year-olds prefer to teach conventional norms to in-group members as opposed to out-group members.

Overall, cultural common ground is a necessary condition for effective collaboration at the level of large groups. It allows in-group members to coordinate with each other, even when personal common ground is sparse. By the age of 5 years, children understand that cultural common ground is tied to group identity and are motivated to help fellow in-group members acquire this cultural knowledge.

An important competency for engaging in joint agency is relationship repair. Joint activities do not always go according to plan, and sometimes one's own self is to blame. In such cases, it becomes incumbent upon oneself to try to make amends and repair the relationship. The prototypical moral emotion befitting this situation is guilt, which is operative by the age of 3 years. In a study by Vaish et al. [], 3-year-olds were led to believe that they had harmed another person's property. As a result, the 3-year-olds displayed signs of guilt, such as taking responsibility for the act and trying to make reparations. The fact that humans feel sincerely guilty about wrongdoing (at least some of the time) is evidence, in our view, that individuals genuinely internalize the viewpoint of their group (i.e. ‘how we see me’) and are not solely driven by strategic reputational concerns (i.e. ‘how others see me’).

By the age of 5 years, children display a particularly striking effect of social identity. As shown by Over et al. [], 5-year-olds feel collective guilt—guilt about transgressions that were committed not by oneself but by fellow in-group members. In their study, 5-year-olds displayed more nonverbal signs of guilt and were more willing to take reparative action following a transgression committed by an in-group member versus an out-group member. Thus, adopting a social identity as a member of a group can have such a profound effect on children that they even feel responsible for the actions of fellow group members.

Another phenomenon worth noting, although it does not directly map onto our proposed two-step sequence from joint to collective agency, is the use of justifications to preserve one's moral identity. We briefly review the developmental research on justifications, as they are an important part of how individuals construct moral identities and defend them in the eyes of themselves and others. Like guilt displays, justifications mitigate the negative impact of one's own failings. From 3 to 5 years of age, children progress in their reason-giving and justification abilities, and are eventually able to use sophisticated discourse strategies such as counter-arguments, indirect evidence and meta-talk [].

Kanngiesser et al. [] examined children's ability to justify their own transgressions by enticing them to break a promise and then asking them what happened. At the age of 3 years, children provided more relevant justifications if they had a prosocial reason for breaking the promise (e.g. they had been asked to help someone) than if they only had a selfish reason (e.g. they were playing with a toy), reflecting an early-emerging understanding that prosocial reasons are more acceptable than selfish ones. Children from 3 to 5 years of age also prioritize prosocial over selfish justifications when evaluating others' reasons for promise-breaking [].

Over ontogeny and into adulthood, individuals become more skilful at deploying justifications to protect their moral identity in the eyes of both themselves and others. While individuals desire, on the one hand, to be seen by both themselves and others as morally upright, they also desire, on the other hand, to reap the benefits of unethical acts. Self-serving justifications and rationalization techniques, e.g. moral disengagement (i.e. downplaying an unethical action as ‘not so bad’) or deliberate ignorance (i.e. choosing not to know about the consequences of one's actions), give individuals justificatory ‘wiggle room’ to act unethically while maintaining a positive moral identity [].

Our theory would benefit from empirical testing. For example, we have claimed that children's norm-following is not reducible to a desire for a positive reputation (i.e. ‘how others see me’) but also reflects a genuine internalization of the group's legitimate evaluative viewpoint (i.e. ‘how we see me’). Research has found that children act more prosocially when observed by others, reflecting reputational concerns [,]; however, more studies are needed to investigate how children act when unobserved, reflecting their internalized values. As one example, Engelmann et al. [] found that 5-year-olds sometimes do the right thing and share with a needy recipient, even if no one would know about their generous act. Moreover, we have claimed that competencies for collective agency are ‘scaled-up’ versions of earlier-emerging competencies for joint agency. This claim could be tested through longitudinal studies on the emergence of different competencies for joint and collective agency.

Several future directions of research could be built on the present proposal. For instance, what are additional competencies for collective agency beyond the four that we have discussed? What are the impacts of individual difference variables (e.g. temperament, executive function, cultural background) on children's competencies for collective agency and moral identity? Two variables whose effects on moral identity would be interesting to explore are autobiographical memory and theory of mind. Autobiographical memory, the ability to integrate multiple memories into an overarching self-conception [], seems to be necessary for sustaining a moral identity over time. Theory of mind, the ability to represent others' mental states, is closely associated with the ability to represent one's own mental states [], which, in turn, probably plays a pivotal role in the construction of the self-concept. Theory of mind also enables one to predict how others will react to one's own actions. An awareness that others are more likely to react predictably when one's own actions are predictable (e.g. in line with social norms), coupled with the fact that predictable information is metabolically preferable (i.e. less costly) to process than unpredictable information [], may lead individuals to have an intrinsic motivation to follow social norms and maintain a positive social identity. The metabolic bases of individuals' self-regulatory attempts to maintain their social identities would be interesting to explore in future research.

In conclusion, we propose that humans have an evolved psychological disposition, evident in young children, to adopt and maintain a positive moral identity as a cooperative group member. The skills and motivations to adopt and maintain a moral identity are part of the suite of psychological competencies that humans evolved for engaging in collective agency, building on evolutionarily and ontogenetically earlier capacities for engaging in joint agency. Our proposal may offer a novel evolutionary lens for interpreting the diverse and profound effects of social identity on human thinking and behaviour.

psychology.title: Interdisciplinary approach to the study of neighbourhood social cohesion and health: a new framework based on a scoping review
psychology.abstract: We aimed to synthesise empirical evidence on neighbourhood social cohesion (NSC) to construct an interdisciplinary schematic framework.An interdisciplinary scoping review was conducted to identify the factors and outcomes related to NSC drawn from journals in sociology, psychology, public health and urban planning.A search of empirical literature was administered using PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Scopus for English-language studies.We included all studies that examine the role of NSC as a predictor, mediator or outcome within populations residing in Western countries. Systematic reviews or measurement studies were excluded from this review.Study characteristics, factors, outcomes and the role of NSC (eg, predictor, mediator) were extracted from 202 studies. To build the schematic framework, we aggregated all factors and outcomes into broader categories previously established by other frameworks. Connections between any two categories were labelled by whether the authors used a longitudinal design and if they attempted to establish causal evidence using a mediation analysis.The scoping review identified that NSC functions as a social determinant embedded in environmental, structural and psychosocial processes that can operate throughout the life course, interact with demographic structures and contribute to health trajectories through a network of direct and indirect pathways. Childhood exposure to high NSC was associated with developing stronger social skills and prosocial behaviour into adulthood, while exposure to low NSC increased the risk of developing anxiety, depression and substance use during adolescence. Individual resilience and self-efficacy were found to be a linking psychological mechanism between NSC and mental health.Our framework identifies NSC as a dynamic determinant of health shaped by reciprocal interactions between individuals and their neighbourhood environments. Advancing this field will require research designs that can capture these feedback processes and inform interventions aimed at reducing neighbourhood health disparities.
psychology.text:
Neighbourhood social cohesion (NSC), defined as the existence of implicitly shared norms within residential public spaces by close and distant neighbours, has been linked to numerous health– and behavioural outcomes. The availability and proximity of residential public spaces can affect health through the effects of NSC.– NSC has been considered as a determinant of health-related outcomes across disciplines such as public health, sociology, psychology and urban planning; however, the mechanisms linking environmental, social and individual-level factors to NSC and its health effects remain understudied within an integrated framework.

Schematic frameworks have been used to synthesise and illustrate interactions between factors and outcomes producing an emergent effect across time and can serve as a steppingstone for future research designs. They are especially suitable for examining NSC because they provide an interpretive lens for understanding complex social reality.

The aim of this paper is to develop an interdisciplinary schematic framework of NSC. The framework specifically aims to include factors that have either been overlooked in existing frameworks or addressed only within single-discipline contexts. In addition, we document the level of methodological complexity, including whether a study attempted to establish causal evidence and considered temporal dynamics. To build this framework, we conducted an interdisciplinary scoping review guided by the following research questions:

Which factors and outcomes have been studied in relation to NSC?

What is the level of complexity of study design and modelling approach used?

The conceptualisation and framing of NSC has varied between disciplines. In sociology, researchers typically study social cohesion at the societal level, and conceptualise it as a matter of trust towards both individuals and institutions. Fenger created a macrolevel framework that showed how government policies and structural factors (eg, employment, ethnic density) shape cohesion and, in turn, influence outcomes such as crime, poverty, health and state policies. Studies at the intersection of sociology and social psychology have further examined how group composition and intergroup dynamics shape cohesion at the neighbourhood level, generally treating NSC as an outcome of social context rather than a determinant of it. Meer and Tolsma highlighted diversity as a potential challenge to NSC. They proposed that ethnic heterogeneity undermines NSC by intensifying resource competition and increasing anxiety over divergent norms.

Within urban and environmental planning, cohesion has been framed as a mechanism through which built and natural structures exert effects on individual well-being. Romagon and Jabot created a framework that showed how urban planning, housing and shared public spaces can foster interaction and strengthen ties. Both Clarke et al and Wan et al developed frameworks on green spaces showing that their safety, usability and capacity to foster social activity and resident participation enhance NSC.

Although NSC was originally conceptualised within sociology, public health has produced the largest body of quantitative research on the topic. Within this tradition, NSC is generally conceptualised as an umbrella term that encompasses constructs such as social capital, sense of community, sense of belonging or merely contacts with the neighbours. NSC is typically framed as a social determinant of health, functioning as an upstream factor that shapes individual health. Diez Roux and Mair created a framework that linked NSC to health by showing how structural inequality shapes neighbourhood environments, which then affect physical, mental and behavioural health outcomes. Schepers et al indicated that both physical (eg, walkability, green space) and social factors (eg, neighbour contact, crime) predict loneliness.

Additional factors related to NSC have been studied but have not been systematically integrated into a framework.

In some studies, the associations between NSC and health-related outcomes are modified by age, gender, ethnicity and other demographic characteristics. For instance, when faced with an incohesive neighbourhood environment, older adults report more feelings of loneliness compared with younger adults, women report poorer health outcomes and lower rates of physical activity compared with men, and ethnic minorities experience more isolation compared with ethnic natives.

Incohesive neighbourhoods experienced during childhood or adolescence are suggested to infringe on social-cognitive development. Growing up in neighbourhoods characterised by distrust, whether directly experienced or modelled by parental behaviour, has been associated with increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, indirect aggression and substance abuse. Further evidence points to a link between NSC and child abuse and neglect.

Residential mobility, defined by residents moving in or out of a neighbourhood, has been suggested to be a determinant and consequence of NSC. Changes in the ethnic composition of a neighbourhood can influence affluent natives to move to more ethnically homogeneous and potentially more prejudiced neighbourhoods, while deprived individuals are left in disadvantaged, ethnically heterogeneous neighbourhoods.

The main aim of this paper was to develop an interdisciplinary schematic framework on NSC. To accomplish this, we conducted an interdisciplinary scoping review. The proposed scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) Checklist and JBI methodology for scoping reviews (see ). The JBI methodology specifies the inclusion criteria for participants, concept and context.

A preliminary search of PROSPERO, JBI and Google Scholar was conducted and no current or ongoing reviews on NSC that matched our objectives were identified. An initial limited search of PubMed and Google Scholar was performed to identify discipline-specific language and keywords and develop a full search strategy (see search code in ). Studies published in English were included until June 2025. The databases searched include PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Scopus.

This review included only populations residing in Western countries (ie, North America, Europe and Australia) to minimise heterogeneity within the framework and due to practical limitations in resources and scope.

Although definitions of NSC vary, this review adopts a conceptually precise definition: NSC is defined as the existence of shared norms within residential public spaces (eg, parks, communal areas and shared building infrastructure). This definition is more circumscribed than earlier conceptualisations that converge NSC with constructs such as social capital that emphasise resilient or close social relationships, a distinction with substantial implications for how we interpret the included literature. First, NSC is a neighbourhood-level concept whereas social capital reflects an individual asset. Second, neighbourhoods are often characterised by social relations encompassing both familiar and unfamiliar residents. Consequently, we chose to conceptualise NSC as relying on generalised expectations of neighbours’ trustworthiness that can only be formed in neighbourhood public spaces rather than from enduring interpersonal ties.

For the purpose of this review, we included studies that had varying definitions of NSC and identified the number of studies that aligned, partially aligned or did not align with our definition. We searched all studies that examine the role of NSC as a predictor, mediator, moderator or outcome. We included an operationalisation of NSC that involves residents trusting, feeling attachment to, acting reciprocally with and sharing neighbourhood-specific values with their neighbours. Studies in which social capital or sense of community was the central concept but NSC was not separately operationalised were excluded.

We define a neighbourhood as an area of residence determined by physical proximity.

This scoping review considered all types of study designs. Systematic reviews and measurement studies were excluded from this review.

After duplicates were removed, titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers for assessment against the inclusion criteria (Owen Callahan and Odile Sauzet). The full text of selected studies was assessed in detail by three independent reviewers (Owen Callahan, Jan Kössendrup and Odile Sauzet). Any disagreements between the reviewers at any stage of the selection process were resolved through discussion.

The following items were extracted from quantitative studies: title, authors, journal, country, data source, date(s) of data collection, sample characteristics, operationalisation of NSC, study design, statistical analysis, factors, outcomes and the role of NSC (eg, predictor, mediator). Information on qualitative studies was reported narratively in the results. Lastly, five pooled analyses were conducted on NSC and common health outcomes to serve as additional quantitative information for readers (see ).

The studies were coded according to the role of NSC (predictor, mediator or outcome), the factors and outcomes studied, and the complexity of the study design (cross-sectional, longitudinal, mediation, moderation). Given the substantial heterogeneity of variables identified across the literature, conceptually related variables were consolidated into broader categories established in previous research. For instance, neighbourhood sidewalks, infrastructure and recreational facilities were subsumed under the single category of the built environment. These categories were then arranged temporally relative to NSC and further distinguished by whether the evidence originated from longitudinal studies and whether the authors attempted to establish causality using a mediation analysis. While aggregating variables improves the clarity and interpretability of the main framework, it also obscures variation among specific indicators. To preserve this, we developed two supplementary subframeworks that provide a more detailed representation of the individual variables examined in relation to NSC.

None.

A total of 3508 papers were initially collected from the comprehensive search, and 1781 papers were duplicates and removed. After reviewing titles and abstracts, 1388 papers were excluded. This left 402 papers for further consideration. An additional 201 papers were excluded after considering the full texts. The sample comprised 201 quantitative studies. An additional 11 qualitative studies were reviewed and only one was included in this review. The final sample comprised 202 studies. The complete list of publications is provided in the  including the numbering used to refer to articles in the sequel (see table of numbered studies in ). The +symbol indicates that more than five papers are cited for a particular finding. The study characteristics are listed in .

NSC, neighbourhood social cohesion.

Nine categories of aggregated variables are reported below listing the number of longitudinal designs, mediations, moderations and associations (see ). A schematic framework on NSC in  illustrates the dynamic interactions among these categories (see ).

As, association; BMI, body mass index; Lg, longitudinal; Me, mediation; Mo, moderation; NSC, neighbourhood social cohesion; PTSD, post-traumatic stress disorder.

The process of extraction and synthesis revealed that the relationships among NSC and its correlates could not be adequately represented as a single, unidirectional pathway proceeding from the societal level, through the neighbourhood level, to the individual level. Several included studies indicated that individual-level variables such as behaviour and mental health were not only shaped by NSC but in turn influenced neighbourhood-level conditions. Rather than a linear causal sequence, the synthesised evidence pointed to a system of feedback loops, in which effects propagate downward from structural and environmental conditions to individuals, and subsequently loop back upward as the aggregated behaviours and health states of individuals reshape the neighbourhood conditions from which they emerged.

We therefore depict this process as a recursive system, illustrated in . Structural inequalities shape neighbourhood-level factors, which in turn influence NSC. As individuals are affected by these conditions, their behaviours, health states and social participation aggregate to reshape neighbourhood-level factors. The neighbourhood level therefore appears twice in the framework; once as a determinant of individual outcomes and once as an emergent product.

The domestic environment emerged as a common outcome through which NSC and individual health jointly influenced household dynamics. Disruptions in life also played an important role shaping NSC, which we briefly discuss later in this section.

Green space (2, 13, 31, 32, 72 +), accessibility and walkability (19, 44, 45, 59, 137 +) and social infrastructure (13, 35, 160, 182, 192 +) were all associated with high NSC. In contrast, neighbourhood disorder (8, 27, 29, 42, 99+), noise annoyance (6, 13) and rodent sightings (49) were associated with low NSC. Active use of parks or recreational facilities was associated with higher levels of NSC and fewer depressive symptoms reported by residents (72). In addition, the relationship between the characteristics of the built environment and NSC varied by ethnicity and socioeconomic status (SES).

In the single qualitative study, participants in interviews on neighbourhood redevelopment highlighted that high-rise buildings provided fewer opportunities for neighbourly contact than the historic small houses with gardens they replaced. They also emphasised the importance of designing redevelopment projects with shared spaces that facilitate interactions between new and long-term residents (202).

Social support (35, 41, 55, 65, 114+), social control (1, 16, 115), social belonging (118), participation in social activities (62, 95, 113), neighbourhood safety (28, 29, 35, 96, 195+), collective efficacy (30, 166) and reporting crime (191) were positively associated with NSC. In contrast, discrimination (58, 67, 75, 97, 121+) was negatively associated with NSC, and the strength of this relationship varied by ethnicity and age. NSC also functioned as a predictor of social organisation through collective efficacy (166, 191), social control (115, 166) and externalising behaviours (83).

NSC was associated with depression (1, 5, 7, 17, 21+), stress (1, 11, 24, 26, 36+) and loneliness (31, 41, 65, 111, 130+). Studies also reported associations with post-traumatic stress disorder (55, 138), cognition (11, 63, 87, 152, 112), life satisfaction (73, 151), and happiness (40). For physical health outcomes, NSC was associated with cardiovascular health (27, 79, 109, 121, 140+), obesity and body mass index (33, 37, 44, 57, 199), sleep quality (38, 161, 190, 197), diabetes (70, 87, 175), human immunodeficiency viruses (173, 193) and further outcomes. For health-related behaviour, NSC was associated with physical activity (10, 12, 27, 28, 33+), smoking (18, 25, 92, 96, 136+), diet (45), substance use (23, 68, 102, 149) and sexual activity (122, 132, 139).

NSC was used to predict place attachment (192), child commuting (176, 179), partner abuse (125, 153), homicide rates (164), outgroup threat (151) and food accessibility (50, 107, 113).

26 studies assessed whether the association between NSC and health-related outcomes varied according to gender, age, ethnicity, SES or sexual orientation. Low NSC amplified the negative effects of neighbourhood disadvantage on physical health more strongly for African American men than for women (39), while for African American women, higher NSC was associated with lower levels of interleukin-6, compared with men (69). Its protective effects against stroke mortality were more evident in elderly white populations, not for their Black counterparts (48). Ethnicity also significantly moderated the effect of NSC and physical disorder on social isolation (74). In a unique finding, perceived NSC was negatively associated with loneliness, but this association was strongest among White respondents and significantly weaker among Black respondents (65). Women who lived in neighbourhoods with low NSC experienced greater psychological distress and higher body mass index than men (57). Furthermore, young girls in gentrifying neighbourhoods reported lower NSC and elevated internalising symptoms (88) compared with boys. The protective role of NSC varied by age: its benefits grew stronger for older children, who are more embedded in neighbourhood social environments compared with younger children (76), while elderly populations, especially those with functional limitations (46), reported higher levels of loneliness (65) and depression (67, 80) compared with middle-aged adults. In a study that used sexual orientation as a moderator, the mental health of gay men was most affected by NSC (84) compared with straight men. All demographics significantly moderated the association between NSC and diabetes (85).

NSC and physical activity acted as mediators between the built and natural environment and health (see ). NSC mediated the relationship between green space and both mental health (2, 13, 27, 31, 32) and physical activity (33). Additionally, NSC mediated the effects of noise pollution on reported mental health (6, 13) and the relationship between social infrastructure and overall well-being (35). Stress mediated the relationship between green space and mental health (33), and physical activity mediated the relationship between NSC and obesity (33), mental health (12) and cardiometabolic risk (27).

NSC mediated the relationship between ethnic heterogeneity and both psychological distress (9, 26), perceived disorder (34) and physical health (26), while perception of in-group size mediated the relationship between ethnic heterogeneity and NSC itself (14).

Psychological mechanisms such as resilience and self-efficacy emerged as mediators between NSC and mental health. Resilience was found to mediate the relationship between NSC and distress (36), while NSC mediated the pathway between self-efficacy and depression (30).

The lasting effects of NSC can extend throughout the life course (see ). Children exposed to high NSC were associated with empathy (97), cognitive functioning (112), participation in extracurricular activities (116) and a greater likelihood of living in a cohesive neighbourhood during adulthood (10). Children exposed to low levels of NSC were associated with increased anxiety (88, 147), violence (147), substance abuse (17, 23, 25), depression (147) and difficulties with their development of an ethnic identity (22) during adolescence. Stress and parental depression mediated the effect of NSC on adverse health outcomes in children (1, 17, 24). Longitudinal analyses further strengthened the evidence of associations between NSC and development. NSC mediated the association between childhood SES and adolescent depression (21) and adult physical activity (10). Higher NSC moderated the relationship between child attachment and developing strong social skills (60). Childhood NSC also predicted cognitive development and prosocial behaviour in adolescence (112, 147). In one reviewed study, high NSC increased the likelihood of adolescent substance abuse through the diffusion of peer substance use (23).

NSC moderated the effects of housing relocation (51), stressful life events (146), natural disasters (128) and the COVID-19 pandemic (78) on mental health and mediated the link between residential mobility and depression (3, 7).

The aim of this study was the development of an interdisciplinary schematic framework. To achieve this, we conducted a scoping review.

Studies in urban or environmental planning indicated that walkable neighbourhoods, green spaces and social infrastructure can improve NSC and subsequent health. In line with,– public neighbourhood spaces can provide safe and functional means to encourage social and healthy activities, but their condition must be maintained to avoid health outcomes associated with neighbourhood disorder.

Some aspects of social support have been suggested to be a fundamental component of NSC, but according to our review, other aspects are found to buffer the effects of loneliness associated with low NSC. These buffers may only be available to residents with high social capital, which may aggravate health inequalities.

Our results indicated how demographic factors shape NSC in two distinct ways: as attributes of individuals and as characteristics of the neighbourhood. At the individual level, the effect of NSC can differ depending on minority status, age, gender, SES and sexual orientation. Minorities can be more negatively affected by low NSC because they sometimes lack the social and economic support needed to mitigate the adverse effects of low NSC. Although we did find one study in which the majority group experienced worse health outcomes, we assert that this finding is more likely to be anomalous rather than a consistent effect across neighbourhoods. At the neighbourhood level, demographic composition is associated with NSC, a pattern consistent with findings in related reports. While several theories have been proposed to explain this relationship, additional research is needed to determine a causal link.

A unique contribution of our paper was synthesising the evidence relative to childhood development. We found that low NSC can increase parental stress by reducing available social support and increasing daily strain, which some studies link to higher risks of conflict or neglect within households. According to the papers in our review, childhood exposure to low NSC can lead to reduced supervision and fewer prosocial role models, which may give reason to why our results also indicated that childhood NSC is associated with poorer cognitive and social development, higher substance use, lower physical activity and difficulties in forming cultural identity. Together, these findings point to self-reinforcing feedback loops in which NSC affect the domestic environment and child development, which in turn reproduce inequalities across generations. Yet despite this evidence, few studies have tracked the developmental consequences of NSC from childhood into adolescence or adulthood using longitudinal designs, and none have examined these dynamics using simulation-based studies, which are well-suited for capturing intergenerational transmission. Moving closer towards identifying any causal path will depend on how well researchers can study how health inequalities associated with NSC arise over time.

The central theoretical contribution of this review is the reconceptualisation of NSC as a dynamic variable and mechanism. Neighbourhood environments and individuals mutually and continuously influence one another. Existing research has predominantly treated NSC as a static exposure, measured at a single point in time and regressed against health outcomes. Our framework challenges this framing by making explicit the recursive pathways through which NSC is simultaneously shaped by environmental, structural and demographic conditions and exerts effects on individual health trajectories across the life course. This distinction has direct methodological implications. If NSC operates as a dynamic, generative mechanism rather than a fixed determinant, then cross-sectional observational designs are structurally incapable of capturing the recursive processes our framework describes, which is not to say that these designs are irrelevant in NSC research. Establishing the directionality and temporal unfolding of these pathways will require longitudinal designs with repeated measurement, and ultimately, simulation-based approaches capable of modelling how NSC emerges from the aggregated interactions of heterogeneous individuals over time.

The interdisciplinary scope of this review is itself a contribution to this understanding. By synthesising evidence from public health, sociology, psychology and urban and environmental planning, we were able to identify mechanisms, such as the interplay between the built environment, demographic composition, psychological resilience and health, that are not visible within a single disciplinary tradition. The resulting framework makes these cross-domain mechanisms explicit and provides an integrated empirical foundation that can inform future theory development and research design.

This review has limitations. First, by excluding studies conducted outside the USA, Europe and Australia, we may have restricted the global scope of the framework. Future reviews should expand coverage to include evidence from other regions to understand how our findings may be context related. Second, although our review included many studies, it is possible that our search strategy missed relevant publications. This limitation is common in reviews, but we believe that the breadth of included studies was sufficient to provide a robust assessment of NSC. Third, our scoping review identified few urban and environmental planning studies compared with the other disciplines, and therefore it is possible that our framework left out built and natural neighbourhood factors. Finally, we identified only one study that explicitly examined the potential disadvantages of NSC for health (eg, spread of negative social norms of health behaviour), yet emerging literature suggests that the adverse consequences of NSC may be more widespread than recognised in our review.

This paper advances understanding of NSC as a dynamic, recursive mechanism linking neighbourhood environments to individual health trajectories across the life course. The framework makes explicit a set of feedback processes that observational study designs cannot adequately capture, pointing to a clear methodological agenda for future research: longitudinal and simulation-based designs that can model the temporal and emergent nature of NSC. By providing an integrated empirical foundation across disciplines, this review offers a resource for researchers, practitioners and policymakers working to understand and address the structural determinants of neighbourhood health inequality.

psychology.title: Bouldering-Psychotherapy for treating depression in adolescents (BooSt): study protocol for a randomized controlled trial
psychology.abstract: Currently, there are hardly any validated group therapy programs for depressed adolescents in Germany. A recent meta-analysis confirmed a moderate antidepressant effect of exercise in adolescents with depressive symptoms. In addition, four recent systematic reviews reported positive effects of exercise interventions on psychological well-being, mood, and quality of life in adolescents with depression or depressive symptoms. We developed a manualized behavioral-therapy-based group program involving Bouldering-Psychotherapy (BPT) for adolescents (BPT-J) based on the adult version of BPT, which has already demonstrated its efficacy. The aim of the study is to evaluate the efficacy of BPT-J.The study is designed as a randomized, controlled, prospective, longitudinal, single-blind trial with two arms (BPT-J intervention group [IG], waitlist-control group [CG]). The primary aim is to investigate the efficacy of the BPT-J group therapy for adolescents for treating depressiveness. Eligible participants are adolescents with subclinical and clinical depressive symptoms between 13 and 18 years of age. The adolescents in the CG are offered participation in an identical intervention after t1. The 10-week intervention is accompanied by four data collection points for all participants: participants and their legal guardians fill out online questionnaires at the start of therapy (t0), immediately after IG therapy (t1), after CG therapy (t2), and 12 months after finalizing the intervention (follow-up, t3). In addition, structured video interviews are conducted at t0 and t1.BooSt trial addresses the limited availability of evidence-based group interventions for adolescents with depressive symptoms in routine care. If efficacy is confirmed, BPT-J may represent a scalable, manualized, and potentially well-accepted treatment approach that could complement existing psychotherapeutic services for adolescents. Given the increasing demand and limited access to psychotherapy, the intervention may contribute to improving accessibility of mental health care. The group-based format may additionally support cost-effective implementation, reduce waiting times, facilitate peer support, and help reduce stigmatization associated with mental health treatment. Findings from the BooSt trial may further inform dissemination and implementation strategies in child and adolescent mental health care.ISRCTN, ISRCTN79659949, prospectively registered 19/02/2025, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN79659949, URL: https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN79659949.
psychology.text:
Recent data indicate that depression in adolescents in Germany has increased about 30% since 2018 and remains at an elevated level, particularly among girls. The prevalence of depression in adolescents is approximately 8% [–]. These national trends align with the World Health Organization’s assessment, which identifies depression as a leading contributor to disease burden and suicide in young people globally, underscoring its significance as a major public health concern in adolescence [].

Children and adolescents seemed to have particularly strong reactions to the stress associated with the COVID-19 pandemic [, ]. Data collected during the pandemic as part of a nationwide, population-based study showed increases in psychological stress and feelings of depression and anxiety [, ]. The global guidelines on depression recommend a staged treatment approach, ranging from psychosocial interventions to psychotherapy and pharmacological treatment, either alone or in combination []. In contrast to the effectiveness of medication in adults, the effectiveness of anti-depressant drugs in adolescents is limited []. Additionally, data show that only around one fifth of children and young people with signs of mental health problems have had contact with specialized care providers at least once []. Possible reasons for the infrequent utilization of specialist support by children and adolescents affected by mental health symptoms or their families lie in the psychotherapeutic care gap and the lack of knowledge in the population about the type, content, accessibility, or financing options of support services. At the same time, scientists agree that early professional action (i.e., selective or indicated prevention or treatment) can reduce the current and long-term burden of psychological symptoms in children and adolescents, particularly with regard to depressive illnesses, as reviews have shown [, ]. Delayed intervention, especially in the highly dynamic and vulnerable stage of puberty, often leads to significant deterioration and chronification of mental illness. The associated loss of important formative experiences often cannot be remedied [, ]. Furthermore, a recent review showed that selective prevention measures for at-risk groups are more effective in terms of efficacy and costs than universal prevention programs aimed at all children and young people []. Regarding a long-term burden, reviews have found a close connection between psychological symptoms in childhood or adolescence and mental illness in adulthood [, ].

Due to the sharp rise in demand for therapeutic services for children and adolescents, there are calls for an urgent expansion of group therapy in these age groups. With regard to efficacy, there is generally no difference between individual and group cognitive behavioral therapy approaches [], but group therapies have a number of advantages: They are more cost-effective, have reduced waiting times, and facilitate mutual support and feedback among participants. In addition, group processes may help counteract stigmatization [].

At present, few validated group-based therapy programs exist for adolescents with depression in German-speaking countries. The two best-known group programs for the treatment of depression, MICHI [] and “Coping with mood problems [Stimmungsprobleme bewältigen]” [], were examined in an outpatient setting in studies with n = 15 [] and n = 24 adolescents [], each without a control group.

Several recent systematic reviews have reported beneficial effects of exercise interventions on psychological well-being, mood, and quality of life in adolescents with depression or depressive symptoms [–]. In line with these findings, individual studies have shown that sports-based interventions may reduce depressive symptoms with moderate effect sizes and potential long-term benefits [, ]. In the follow-up measurements of a randomized controlled study by Helgadóttir et al. [], improvements in depressive symptoms were maintained for more than 12 months. Such improvements were found in particular for light and high-intensity training []. In addition, recent research findings indicate that the social component of sporting activities can be important in the treatment of depressive symptoms []. In the multimodal treatment of mental illnesses, regardless of age, exercise therapy makes a decisive contribution to activating and strengthening physical, psychological, and social resources; offers a variety of therapeutic approaches to the patient’s experience and behavior; and alleviates symptoms specific to the disorder []. As a positive side effect, it also counteracts the trend toward the deterioration of health behavior in adolescents identified in recent decades due to increased screen time and decreased exercise time []. Exercise is also recommended in the American and British guidelines for the treatment of mild depression in children and adolescents [, ].

As an answer to these challenges, we designed a psychotherapeutic group treatment for adolescents based on cognitive behavioral therapy that includes practical physical experiences on the bouldering wall.

Bouldering-Psychotherapy (BPT), which we developed, has already been shown to be efficacious for adults [–] and has the potential to effectively address both problem areas (psychotherapeutic care gap and lack of exercise) and to apply the associated recommendations in combination []. Additionally, it is designed to be applied both in early preclinical and clinical stages of depressive symptoms. Integrating bouldering into a psychotherapeutic setting offers several advantages. It may reduce stigmatization, promote physical activity and mindfulness, and create a complex range of interactions among participants and between individuals and the climbing wall. These situations can amplify diagnostically relevant behaviors and provide immediate, experiential material for therapeutic work. Novel and often unexpected functional coping strategies for situations previously perceived as difficult, shame-inducing, or frightening can be developed with therapeutic guidance and subsequently transferred to everyday life. Based on these considerations and in adaption of the Bouldering-Psychotherapy Manual for Adults (BPT), a manualized group intervention for adolescents (Bouldering-Psychotherapy for Adolescents [Jugendliche]; BPT-J) was developed. Following evidence of its efficacy in adults with depression and its non-inferiority to traditional cognitive behavioral group therapy, the present study aims to evaluate the efficacy of BPT-J in adolescents.

The aim of the present study is to investigate the efficacy of group-based Bouldering-Psychotherapy for adolescents (BPT-J) in Bavaria, Germany, with regard to the reduction of preclinical or clinical depressive symptoms. For this purpose, the BPT-J intervention group (IG) is compared with a waitlist-control group (CG) in a randomized-controlled, yet naturalistic design. The research hypotheses are as follows:

I.Patients in the IG improve significantly (p < .05) more than patients in the CG in terms of the severity of depression symptoms.II.This improvement is clinically relevant in terms of effect size (Cohen’s d ≥ 0.35 or η2 ≥ 0.035).III.The proportion of patients with clinically relevant improvement is higher in the IG than in the CG. A number needed to treat (NNT) of ≤ 5 is considered sufficient [].

Patients in the IG improve significantly (p < .05) more than patients in the CG in terms of the severity of depression symptoms.

This improvement is clinically relevant in terms of effect size (Cohen’s d ≥ 0.35 or η2 ≥ 0.035).

The proportion of patients with clinically relevant improvement is higher in the IG than in the CG. A number needed to treat (NNT) of ≤ 5 is considered sufficient [].

The effects on secondary outcomes (e.g., depression diagnosis (categorical), quality of life, self-efficacy, suicidality, comorbid psychological symptoms) will be investigated on an exploratory level.

The study is designed as a randomized, waitlist-controlled, multi-center, interventional, prospective, longitudinal, single-blind study with two arms (IG: BPT-J group; CG: waitlist-control group). After completing a two-stage screening process and submitting a declaration of informed consent (from the participant and their legal guardian), participants are being randomly assigned to either a 10-week group intervention (IG) or a CG (see Fig. ). For all participants, the trial is accompanied by four data collection points: All participants and their legal guardians are being asked to complete a series of online questionnaires at the start of IG therapy (t0), immediately after IG therapy (t1), after CG therapy (t2), and 12 months after t1 (follow-up, t3). In addition, structured video interviews are being conducted for categorical determination of the diagnosis of depression at t0 and t1. After the IG completes the BPT-J, the participants in the CG are being offered the opportunity to take part in an identical BPT-J. All participants who finish the 10-session BPT-J will be offered participation in an aftercare bouldering group.

Four centers with at least four therapy cycles each are planned in the project. Figure  depicts one example center with the therapy cycles and data collection points.

The study is being conducted with community-dwelling adolescents in four cities in Bavaria, Germany (Erlangen, Nuremberg, Bamberg, Regensburg). Adolescents can register online (www.boulderdichstark.de) for one of the cities. Therapy sessions are being delivered in cooperating bouldering gyms in each city for the IG and CG.

In order to increase external validity, only a few inclusion and exclusion criteria are being applied. Inclusion criteria are acute depressive symptoms in at least a relevant subclinical range, operationalized by the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) ≥ 6 [], informed consent to participate in the study (especially with regard to randomized allocation and data collection) from both the participants and their legal guardians, the ability and time to participate in the intervention, and access to digital devices for video interviews.

Exclusion criteria are an age over 18 or under 13 years at t0, weight in an age percentile below 10%, or a body mass index (BMI) ≥ 35, taking medication for psychiatric symptoms, or a change in psychopharmacology medication ≤ 6 weeks before start of intervention. Further exclusion criteria are a planned inpatient stay (beyond a short-term crisis intervention) during the intervention period, physical contraindications to bouldering as judged by a medical doctor (physical complaints or pregnancy), diagnosed psychotic disorder or diagnosed manic illness, dependence on alcohol or illegal substances, and self-injurious behavior that goes beyond superficial scratching within the last 6 months. Self-injurious behavior without the intention to kill oneself is explored in a structured screening interview with items from the German version of the SITBI-G (Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors Interview: German) [, ]. Individual outpatient psychotherapy is not a reason for exclusion.

For safety reasons, a step-by-step plan for dealing with suicidal thoughts and impulses is drawn up and confirmed by all participants during the screening. Interested individuals who are not willing or able to enter into such an agreement are not included. Instead, they receive a personalized consultation for suitable alternative offers.

Screening takes place in a two-stepped procedure (Fig. ): First, an online questionnaire is completed. If basic inclusion criteria such as age, weight, and depressive symptoms match, the remaining criteria are assessed in a structured screening interview. Subsequently, a definitive decision on study eligibility is made.

All adolescents interested in participating and their legal guardians are invited to attend one of the general information sessions held by the study staff in each wave via Zoom for all four centers. Relevant information on the intervention and an explanation of the conditions of participation (e.g., randomization procedure) are being provided there. All questions are answered in detail at the event or in a one-on-one meeting. Furthermore, all information sheets (for adolescents and their legal guardians) as well as the data protection form are available on the website (www.boulderdichstark.de). Adolescents who decide to participate are asked to complete a screening questionnaire and screening interview on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Written informed consent is obtained from the adolescents and at least one person with parental authority.

Not applicable. No biological specimens are being collected.

The study design incorporates a waitlist-control-group configuration, thereby enabling participants in the CG to participate in Bouldering-Psychotherapy as well. The implementation of a uniform intervention across all participants has been demonstrated to enhance adherence to the study protocol and mitigate the likelihood that the data will be missing at random. There is a high probability that the interventional BPT-J will also prove effective for adolescents because the BPT intervention has demonstrated effectiveness in adults. However, this study will be the first time that BPT-J has been tested in an adolescent population. A comparison with a waitlist-CG thus combines the advantages of ethical conduct (i.e., providing a potentially effective intervention to all participants) and of a first-trial intervention with treatment as usual (i.e., the freedom for all participants to attend whichever treatment is prescribed by their treating physician). Subsequent comparisons with other effective interventions might follow.

Participants are being randomized to one of two study arms.

BPT-J is a manualized, body-oriented psychotherapeutic intervention that integrates bouldering with cognitive behavioral therapeutic techniques and a humanistic, client-centered framework. Bouldering is climbing without a rope on climbing walls at a height that permits the climber to jump off. The intervention consists of 10 consecutive group sessions. Each session lasts two hours and takes place weekly in the afternoon at a local bouldering gym. Each group comprises six to ten participants, who are guided by a team of two therapists. In each team, at least one of the therapists is a clinical psychologist or psychotherapist and at least one has additional training as a climbing instructor. All therapists have intensive experience working with groups of youth, have their own climbing experience, and have undergone two days of training specifically for the study.
