Regular supervision is being conducted (two visits to the group per wave, three supervision meetings per wave).

The curriculum, which has already been demonstrated to be effective in treating depression in adults, has been adapted and expanded in several feasibility groups to meet the needs and realities of young people’s lives (for BPT for adults, see: www.bouldering-psychotherapy.com). In BPT-J, participants are regarded as experts of their own lived experiences, and the definition of therapeutic goals lies with the adolescents themselves. Therapists support the articulation, clarification, and pursuit of these goals. The therapeutic rationale assumes that bouldering functions as a medium of transfer and amplification, whereby psychosocial challenges from everyday life become visible and experientially accessible through bouldering problems on the wall. In the protected therapeutic setting, participants are encouraged to experiment directly with new coping strategies and solution patterns, which are subsequently reflected upon and transferred to everyday contexts. Therapeutic themes are not introduced verbally but emerge from participants’ automated coping strategies during the bouldering exercises, with therapeutic work focusing on the individual themes that arise during each exercise. As a reflective and transfer-supporting element, BPT-J incorporates the use of a “resource carabiner.” Each participant is provided with a personal carabiner to which brief written notes capturing insights, positive experiences, or perceived strengths can be attached throughout the intervention. The resource carabiner serves as a concrete memory aid to support self-reflection and the transfer of therapeutic experiences to everyday life.

All 10 manualized sessions contain a fixed schedule and consist of three main components: an opening phase (approximately 15 min), including check-in and optional therapeutic input; an active bouldering phase (approximately 80 min), which begins with different exercises on group cohesion and a warm-up followed by specific bouldering exercises (see Table ); and if any time remains, free bouldering, where all participants work on their individual “projects” with the support of the therapists. At the end of each session, there is a closing phase (approximately 25 min) for sharing experiences and for reflection and transfer. While the overall structure is identical across all sessions, therapists have flexibility in designing the opening and closing phases and the warm-up by drawing on a predefined pool of exercises. The bouldering phase is manualized, with exercises specified for each session. The opening and closing phases take place in a room that is separate from the bouldering gym (e.g., a yoga room) to ensure privacy and confidentiality.

Overview of the bouldering-psychotherapy sessions

During the intervention phase, the CG is not receiving any study-specific additional therapy but has access to standard psychotherapeutic and psychiatric treatment options. Participants assigned to the CG are being offered exactly the same treatment rationale as the IG (participation in a 10-week BPT-J program in a group setting) after the conclusion of measurement points t0 (Baseline, pre-intervention) and t1 (after 3 months, post-intervention for the IG). Besides the wait time of approximately 3 months, the CG’s treatment plan is equivalent to the IG’s.

For all participants who complete their respective BPT-J group, an additional aftercare bouldering group is being offered on a weekly basis for at least 3 months.

Participation in the study as well as in the therapy groups is voluntary. The first of only two criteria that would lead to discontinuation of the intervention for a given participant, despite their own wishes, would be (a) worsening of suicidality to the degree that the agreement for dealing with suicidal thoughts and impulses leads to the next level, for example, in-patient care. In this case, therapists will initiate immediate help. The second criterion is (b) worsening of self-harming behavior or behavior endangering others, including serious violations of safety rules.

Under certain circumstances, participants can be allowed to join a group that is starting later, especially if they are members of the CG.

The therapists for each BPT-J group are independently documenting for each session if there were relevant deviations from the curriculum, if certain elements could not be delivered, or if there had been any adverse events. Furthermore, participant-specific content documentation is being used. Every team is being visited during each 10-session round at least once by a member of the study headquarters and given face-to-face feedback and supervision. Additionally, three supervision meetings are being held with one member of the study headquarters experienced in BPT and one licenced psychiatrist for children and adolescents. Participation in three supervisions per 10 therapy sessions is mandatory for each center (two for each therapist). Each adolescent’s participation is being closely monitored and documented. Participants with complete t1 data will be provided one free bouldering gym entrance for the aftercare group.

While participating in the study, participants are permitted to take part in individual out-patient psychotherapy, to receive psychiatric medication if they had begun taking this medication more than 6 weeks before the study began, and to receive a change in the dose of an existing psychiatric medication. A prescription for a new anti-depressant treatment or in-patient stays are recorded and considered reasons for exclusion from the statistical analyses. However, such participants are allowed to remain in the group and attend the remaining sessions if possible.

During the intervention, we are providing insurance that covers liability in case of death or gained, permanent disability caused to the patient by their participation in the study. As there is mandatory health insurance in Germany, and every study site has excellent medical treatment facilities, aftercare for injuries is secured for every participant at no personal costs. To sustain therapeutic gains and encourage ongoing physical activity, an open aftercare group will be offered from when the intervention ends until the last follow-up assessment. Participation in this group is voluntary and will be documented and factored into the follow-up evaluation.

The primary outcome is the severity of depression (dimensional) as measured by self- and proxy ratings. Therefore, the self- and parental/legal guardian questionnaires on depression (SBB-DES and FBB-DES) from the DISYPS-III (Diagnostic System for Mental Disorders as specified in the ICD-10 and DSM-V for Children and Adolescents - III) [] are being used. The SBB-DES includes 29 items that capture the depressive symptom criteria as specified in the ICD-10 and DSM-5 and uses them to calculate a score. The response format ranges from 0 = not applicable at all to 3 = particularly applicable. The SBB-DES is designed for the age range of 11 to 18 years. Age-dependent norms are available for the SBB-DES, separately for boys and girls (stanine values). The FBB-DES assesses the depressive symptoms and the competencies of adolescents as proxy ratings (i.e., from the perspective of the parents/legal guardians). The FBB-DES items correspond to the SBB-DES items, including the response format. Corresponding age-differentiated norm values are available for the FBB-DES (stanine values). The SBB-DES and FBB-DES questionnaires are being administered at all four timepoints (t0 to t3; Fig. ). The change from baseline to t1 (immediately after the intervention phase for the IG) in both the CG and IG will be compared as the primary analysis.

The (categorical) clinical diagnosis of depression assessed by trained raters in a structured clinical interview at t0 and t1 using the ILF-INTERNAL of the DISYPS-III is being measured to complement the dimensional assessment of depression []. The diagnostic interview includes an exploration of the symptom criteria, functional impairment, and level of suffering. Clinical standards are specified in the DISYPS-III manual for the procedure of categorizing the diagnosis on a 4-point scale (0 = not present or age-appropriate; 1 = slightly pronounced, criterion not met; 2 = clearly pronounced, criterion met; 3 = very pronounced). The frequency of all 4 categories will be analysed at t0 and t1.

Adolescents’ health-related quality of life is being measured with the KIDSCREEN-10 [] at t0, t1, t2 and t3 as a self-assessment rating and a proxy rating (legal guardians). It considers the physical, mental, and social aspects of well-being. The questionnaire contains 10 items, answered on a 5-point Likert scale. An overall mean value will be calculated, varying from 1 to 5, with higher values indicating a higher health-related quality of life. The change from t0 to t1 will be analyzed.

Participants’ self-efficacy is being measured with the scale for general self-efficacy expectations (SWE) [] at t0, t1, t2 and t3 as a self-assessment. The questionnaire consists of 10 items, answered on a one-dimensional 4-point scale ranging from 1 (does not apply) to 4 (applies exactly). Subsequently, we will calculate a sum score that can range from 10 to 40, with higher values indicating greater self-efficacy [, ]. Numerous studies have demonstrated good psychometric parameters for the instrument; standardized values are available []. The change from t0 to t1 will be analyzed.

Suicidal behavior and suicidal thoughts are being recorded during the DISYPS interview at t0 and t1 and additionally assessed by self- and proxy ratings with two items (ranging from 0 to 3) from the DISYPS-III self- and peer-assessment questionnaires (SBB-DES and FBB-DES) at t0, t1, t2 and t3 []. The frequency of suicidality between t0 and t1 is compared.

Other psychological comorbid symptoms are being recorded by the parents/legal guardians with the SDQ questionnaire (Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, German version) at t0, t1, t2 and t3 [–]. The instrument is used to quantify emotional and behavioral problems. The parents/legal guardians are asked to rate different behaviors concerning the last 6 months as not applicable, partially applicable, or clearly applicable. The questionnaire comprises 25 items, which are divided into five scales: emotional problems, behavioral problems, hyperactivity, behavioral problems with peers, and prosocial behavior. The first four scales are summed to form the total problem score. The change from t0 to t1 in that score will be analyzed.

To enable subsequent cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses from a societal perspective the participants’ all-cause utilization of health and supportive care services along with travelling distances (components of direct costs) as well as the participant’s and their legal guardians’ loss of working hours (indirect costs) will be assessed at t0, t1, t2 and t3 based on the previously applied FIM-K []. The FIM-K represents an adaptation of the established FIMA [] to children and adolescents-specific cost components (e.g., parental accompaniment to inpatient treatment episodes, parental productivity). The eference period of assessment is set to the previous three month at each timepoint, to contextualize costs incurred during the 10-week intervention period appropriately. Reported health care utilization is subsequently monetized using Germany-specific unit costs [], which are updated to the most recent base year (most likely 2025) via source research and inflation if required. Intervention costs (hall rental, manual, training of therapist team, hourly rates for BPT-J therapist team) are based on the study documentation.

To reflect Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) gained after the intervention ends, health-related quality of life will be assessed with the EQ-5D-Y via the adolescents’ self-ratings at each timepoint (see Fig.  and the “Health-related quality of life” section). The EQ-5D-Y is the child- and adolescent-specific version of the EQ-5D-3 L [], which assesses problems in the five domains of mobility, independence, everyday activity, pain, and anxiety/depression with a 3-point scale (no problems, some problems, major problems). The individual answers can be converted into a person-specific health status (5³ = 125 possible statuses) for which a Germany-specific population-related tariff is available, enabling a transformation into QALYs [].

Proxys are asked to report any medication use (prescription and “over-the-counter” pharmaceuticals) including trade name, pharmaceutical central number, package size, dosage (per day/week/month), route of administration and start date. In addition, the structured video interview specifically assesses initiation of antidepressant medication within the past six weeks.

The use of psychotherapy during the past three months is assessed using the FIM-K (see above), including the differentiation between individual and group therapy and the number of sessions. In addition, during the structured video interview, adolescents report lifetime and current psychotherapy, including onset and whether therapy is individual or group-based.

Adverse events (AEs) such as injuries, accidents, mental health crises, or hospitalizations and their intensity (mild, moderate, severe) are being assessed during the intervention period and during the year following the intervention. The intensity of these events is assessed on the basis of the extent of the impact on the participants’ lives and the resulting need for treatment. Mild AEs are defined as any injuries or emotional crises that can be handled without external care and have no lasting consequences (e.g., bruises, emotional outbursts handled within the therapy). Moderate AEs are defined as any injuries or emotional crises that need ambulatory external care but are reversible within weeks (e.g., sprains, emotional crises leading to professional contact with an external psychotherapist/psychiatrist or other health care provider). Severe adverse events (SAEs) would be any injuries or emotional crises that require hospitalization and have (potentially) irreversible consequences (e.g., head injuries, severe suicidal ideation, suicide attempts). Mild AEs are recorded by the therapists during the sessions (before t1 in the IG, before t2 in the CG). Moderate and severe events are being assessed in the following ways: IG/CG: by the therapists during the intervention; by the legal guardians in the questionnaires at t1, t2 and t3.

Current engagement in sports activities respectively exercise and if so – which kind and how many hours per week are assessed at all time-points. At baseline additionally, the engagement in sports/exercise before the start of the study is investigated.

The enjoyment of sport is assessed by an adapted version of the Sports Enjoyment Scale for Adolescents (FEFS-J) which was specified for bouldering as sports activity. Two scales (“enjoyment” and “recovery”) with three items each are evaluated on a 4-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 4 (always) at t1 (IG)/t2 (CG) (see Fig. ).

Life-time prevalence, 12-months-prevalence and age of first consumption concerning the substances alcohol, tobacco/e-cigarettes/vapes and cannabis are assessed. Items used were evaluated before and have been incorporated in representative epidemiological studies [, ].

After completing a short digital initial screening form, which checks Part 1 of the inclusion and exclusion criteria (including depressive symptoms based on PHQ-9, age, height, and weight), participants are being automatically informed about whether they are suitable for detailed screening for study participation (see Fig. ). Thereafter, at least within one month, interested and potentially eligible individuals participate in a diagnostic video screening interview to assess the remaining inclusion and exclusion criteria (screening Part 2) before being informed about whether they can participate in the study. The screening interview is followed by the structured clinical interview (DISYPS-III) for baseline assessment (t0) concerning clinical diagnosis of depression (categorical expression). Subsequently, self- and proxy-rated questionnaires are completed at baseline (t0) by the participants and their legal guardians if they are deemed eligible and give consent.

After participants complete the screening and baseline assessment (t0), the randomization, allocation, and start of the intervention for the IG takes place. Thus, the treatment phase for the IG is between t0 and t1, and the treatment phase for the CG is between t1 and t2 (see Fig. ).

As soon as the participants of the IG complete the intervention, the depressive symptoms (categorical) are assessed again via video interview using the structured clinical interview (DISYPS-III) for all participants (IG and CG). Changes in participants’ current medication and/or eventually used parallel psychotherapeutic treatment are documented at t1. Furthermore, self- and proxy ratings made by participants and their legal guardians via questionnaires assessing the primary and secondary outcomes are collected at t1.

Questionnaires for assessing the primary and secondary outcomes by the participants and their legal guardians are also collected after the participants of the CG have completed their participation in the BPT-J (t2) and 12 months after each individual has completed their BPT-J participation (t3).

The primary outcome of the study is the group difference in the pre- vs. post-treatment within-subject difference in depressive symptoms. Correspondingly, the sample size was determined from a two-sided t-test of the scores change between the two groups, acknowledging that more complex methods will also be used in the statistical analysis of the results.

We expect the standard deviation of the outcome variable to be twice as large at t1 compared with the standard deviation before the intervention. Since a meta-analysis of the effectiveness of group-based behavioral therapy in adolescents [] showed only a small effect, we set the effect of the intervention of at least ¼ to ½ standard deviation of the difference in the outcome measured pre- vs. post-treatment. With this assumption and targeting a statistical power of at least 80% and a significance level of 5%, the study requires 97 to 127 participants per group, so between 194 and 250 in total.

In our experience, around 20% of those who apply to take part in a study do not meet the inclusion criteria. Thus, around 300 individuals have to be screened.

Participants are being recruited through a multi-faceted strategy aimed at maximizing sample representativeness. The initial outreach is targeting schools, parent associations, school psychologists, school district administrations, and community departments for youth and family services, with requests to broadly disseminate information about the study.

Additional recruitment efforts are including the distribution of informational materials (e.g., flyers, posters) in psychiatric clinics, psychotherapy practices, general practitioners and pediatric offices, pharmacies, and other psychological and social service institutions such as self-help groups and counseling centers as well as in bouldering gyms. Furthermore, psychotherapists, psychiatrists, and general practitioners in outpatient clinics, training outpatient centers, and private practices are being contacted and asked to share the study invitation with patients on their waiting lists.

To enhance visibility and accessibility, a dedicated project website was launched, and social media platforms (e.g., Instagram, TikTok) are utilized, including those affiliated with the University Hospital Erlangen and various local climbing gyms.

People interested in participating can use the screening links on the web page and directly begin enrolling in the study. Those agreeing to be contacted for the upcoming or a later cycle of the study are being contacted by e-mail. Before each wave, press releases are being issued and addressed to various local newspapers. For recruitment and informed consent, several public project information sessions are being organized online for each cycle. To reach a maximum number of adolescents, recruitment and therapy periods are scheduled for outside the Bavarian school holidays.

A stochastic minimization algorithm is being employed to reduce group imbalances. It includes the following stratification variables: age, sex, and severity of depressive symptoms []. More specifically, 1,000 random permutations of group allocations with equally sized groups are being generated for the new participants in each block.

The first permutation that minimizes the summed chi-squared statistics for group differences regarding age group (< 16 vs. ≥16), sex, and symptom severity (0–3) is selected. The resulting allocation is not predictable. The randomization algorithm is implemented in the statistical software environment R [].

We are assessing the pretest data before randomization. Every participant is given a pseudonym, which is sent to the statistician with only the information that is relevant for stratification. After gathering the pretest data for all participants for the respective wave, the statistician performs the randomization and provides an allocation list to the study center. All participants and their parents are then informed about when and where they should meet for the first session.

The blockwise randomization per study cycle and center is being carried out externally by the Institute for Medical Informatics, Biometry and Epidemiology (IMBE) of the Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg. The statistician transmits the group assignments back to the study center. After randomization, the participants are informed about their allocation (immediate group start: IG, delayed group start: CG) and are given detailed information about their group participation by the study staff.

All individuals who are collecting data, particularly the interviewers, are blinded to participants’ group assignments. At the beginning of each interview, participants are reminded that their allocation is confidential and that they must not tell the interviewer which group they are in. Due to the nature of the intervention, neither therapists nor participants can be blinded. However, the therapists do not know which participants have been allocated to the IG or CG except for those in the first (only IG) and last (only CG) intervention cycles.

Interviewers should not be unblinded until after the last interview. Any questions that arise about therapy are managed by the study center in direct contact with parents, participants, or therapists.

The main outcome data are being assessed via self-report questionnaires from the respective adolescent and by proxy ratings from their parents, as well as via clinical interviews. This approach allows for crosschecks regarding potential issues with reliability or validity. To test interrater reliability, 10% of all video interviews are being assessed by two differently paired raters. The quality of the data is being ensured by strict data monitoring at the study center across the entire study period. For an overview of the data collection instruments used, see the Outcomes section and Fig. .

All outcome data are being collected for all participants even if the respective participant discontinued the intervention (for the list of outcomes, see Fig. ).

To retain participants in the trial and promote their participation in the interviews and surveys, we implemented a number of incentives for participants: Participants from both groups are being given a voucher for a free session at their local bouldering gym (about 12 €) after completing t1 and another voucher after completing t3. Participants are only allowed to take part in one of the IG if they participated at all timepoints before their respective intervention. After the 10 weeks of the intervention, all participants with complete data are being offered participation in an aftercare bouldering group.

The interviewers have been thoroughly trained and are being supervised by the staff at the study center. Before each timepoint, all interviewers receive special training and practice under supervision. Weekly supervision sessions are held by members of the scientific staff. Data are recorded via proven online tools (RedCap) [] and exported on a regular basis. Allowed data ranges and data dropdown lists have been programmed into the software to reduce the likelihood of incorrect data entries. Every participant is given his or her own unique data identifier, which is included in RedCap and double-checked at the beginning of each interview. Questionnaires are programmed with personalized links and automatically sent by the RedCap software.

The data are being collected via interviews or online questionnaires. Additionally, therapists are collecting data on the intervention sessions (adherence, participation, and adverse events). Data collection is being conducted with the data-secure RedCap participant data collection system, which is hosted on the University Hospital Erlangen’s server. The interviews are being conducted with the Samedi software, certified by the National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Physicians (KBV – Kassenärztliche Bundesvereinigung).

Data handling is in accordance with European and German data protection laws, and the information sheet contains a data protection declaration. No personal data are being stored in the data collection system, except for participants’ e-mail address, for which consent has been given. Other sensitive data collected during the video interviews or in the questionnaires are being pseudonymized to guarantee the ability to match the data across the different measurement points and store that data in password-protected devices and programs. The names of the participants, their contact information, and the corresponding codes are being recorded in a separate, password-protected document. The key file for pseudonyms and participants’ data (names and addresses) is being stored securely on the University Hospital Erlangen’s server and is password-protected. Only members of the study team have access to this list. The informed consent sheets are being digitalized and stored in password-protected devices. The published material will not contain any identifying information.

Not applicable. No genetic or molecular data will be collected or analyzed.

The Primary Outcomes (severity of depression, self- and proxy assessment) will be expressed as a linear combination of 29 ordinal random variables (answers to the questionnaires) per participant, whereas particular distributions of those variables (i.e., responses to the questionnaire items) across the participants are not relevant in this study and the importance of all questionnaire items for the assessment of the severity of depression are equally weighted. Under the assumption that these underlying variables are independent and conditional on a participant (which we acknowledge is not completely true), we can take advantage of the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and treat the resulting average across the 29 responses as approximately normally distributed. The design of the study—with the outcome variable (and the explanatory variables) collected at baseline and then at three follow-up timepoints—leads to a hierarchical structure of the data with occasions (Level 1) nested within participants (Level 2 clusters). Therefore, the data will be analyzed with Linear Mixed Models (LMM). In the main (fixed effects) structure, the treatment effect will be represented by the interaction between the group and the occasion, possibly in presence of covariates. Since it is rather unlikely that the evolution of the outcomes will be linear in time, the occasions will be treated as a categorical variable. In the random part, intra-subject homogeneity will be addressed by including a subject-specific random intercept, and the conditional (on participants) dependence of the residuals across occasions will be reflected by the appropriate structure of the residual covariance matrix (e.g. 1st order autoregressive). In addition, a hybrid model will be formulated in which a random intercept (hierarchical) LMM formulation will be combined with a marginal formulation, with exponential structure of the residuals to reflect serial correlation of the outcomes that do not approach zero and that are collected at unequally spaced timepoints []. The main structures of the models will be modified and tested for potentially better fit by adding/removing covariates in a forward-backward non-automatic strategy. Likelihood Ratio Tests and/or Information Criteria (in case the candidate models are not nested) will be used. Model parameters will be estimated by maximization of the likelihood (MLE). Modeling will be performed in Stata (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). To test the hypotheses, p < .05 will be considered significant.

In addition to the testing of Hypothesis I, effect sizes will be calculated both for the group difference and for improvement during the therapy period. The secondary outcome variables (depression diagnosis (categorical), quality of life, self-efficacy, suicidality, comorbid psychological symptoms) will be tested in an exploratory fashion using Generalized Linear Models (GLM) and respectively LMM.

The clinical relevance of the change in symptoms in Hypothesis III will be tested analogously to Goletz et al. [] and Walter et al. [], on the basis of both external assessment and self-assessment using two criteria.

Criterion 1 was defined as dichotomized depressive symptoms based on age-normed stanine values. Stanine values ≥ 7, indicating above-average symptom severity relative to the normative sample, were classified as conspicuous, whereas stanine values < 7 were considered inconspicuous.Additionally, the RCI (Reliable Change Index) will be used to determine the course of symptom severity between t0 and t1. The RCI is calculated according to Jacobson et al. [] and based on Hanisch et al. [].

Criterion 1 was defined as dichotomized depressive symptoms based on age-normed stanine values. Stanine values ≥ 7, indicating above-average symptom severity relative to the normative sample, were classified as conspicuous, whereas stanine values < 7 were considered inconspicuous.

Additionally, the RCI (Reliable Change Index) will be used to determine the course of symptom severity between t0 and t1. The RCI is calculated according to Jacobson et al. [] and based on Hanisch et al. [].

Using the combination of both clinical relevance criteria, the participants will be classified into five groups after completion (see Table ), and relative frequencies will be determined. The proportion of adolescents with clinically relevant improvement in their depression scores (response) and the proportion of adolescents who improved into the normal range (remission) will be compared in the response analysis with the adolescents whose depression scores did not improve. For this purpose, a regression model for binomial outcome will be calculated with the variable response/remission as the dependent variable (DV) and the factors of influence discussed in the literature as independent variables (Hypothesis III). Additionally, the number needed to treat will be calculated.

There will be no interim analyses of depression scores. As a result of repeated tests of the same hypotheses, there is an increased risk of making incorrect conclusions about the efficacy and safety of an intervention []. For unintended adverse events, see {22}.

The cost-effectiveness of BPT-J will be assessed immediately after the intervention (main analyses), from the perspective of a healthcare payer (primary analyses), and from a societal perspective (secondary analyses). From the payer’s perspective, only direct costs borne by the statutory health insurance will be considered, whereas from the societal perspective, out-of-pocket payments, informal care, and indirect costs will also be accounted for. Costs will be modeled along a gamma distribution with a log-link in order to take appropriate account of the right-skewed distribution []. Here, depending on the proportion of participants with zero costs, either one-part gamma models or two-part gamma models will be applied []. The effect side is reflected by the primary clinical outcome (FBB-DES, SBB-DES) and within a sensitivity analysis by QALYs gained, assuming a zero-truncated Gaussian distribution for both parameters. For the primary ITT analysis, missing data immediately after the intervention will be imputed with multiple imputation. The analysis model is structured likewise as the main model for the primary outcome(s).

Subsequently, incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICER), which reflect the adjusted mean difference in total costs divided by the adjusted mean difference of effects (FBB-DES, SBB-DES, QALYs gained) will be calculated. To align the cost-effectiveness analysis with the analysis of clinical effectiveness, the same covariate structure will be applied. To address uncertainty around the point estimate of the ICER, 1,000 simultaneous bootstrap replications will be performed and will be translated into cost-effectiveness planes. In addition, cost-effectiveness acceptance curves (CEAC) will be created to determine the probability of cost-effectiveness for different willingness-to-pay thresholds [, ]. To check the robustness of the results, the cost-effectiveness analyses will be repeated in the per protocol sample.

Access to bouldering groups is being given only at the respective timepoint on the basis of the randomization. Therefore, no member of the CG can participate in the IG. Participants who are randomized into the IG but do not show up to the bouldering sessions are analyzed as members of the IG. “Dropout” can be included as a covariate if necessary.

As stated in the previous section {20a}, the data will be analyzed with LMM by maximization of the likelihood functions. In contrast to the somewhat old-fashioned ANOVA family, estimates from regression models—as long as they rely on the likelihood theory—are asymptotically consistent in the presence of missingness, assuming that the data are Missing At Random (MAR) []. This consistency is due to the property of the likelihood estimation called ignorability, which holds true if scientific interest is not directed toward the missingness mechanism and the parameter spaces of the outcomes (fixed effects and covariance parameters), and the missingness processes are disjoint [].

Pseudonymized data without personal information potentially identifying patients will be made publicly available via an open data repository after all analyses have been completed.

The trial coordination is being led by two psychologists, one a Professor of Psychotherapy Research and fully approved CBT-psychotherapist and the other a Professor of Medical Psychology and Sociology. Organization of the day-to-day running of the trial and data management is being coordinated by two M.Sc. Psychologists. Psychotherapists working on the trial are further supervised by a chief physician in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. An additional M.Sc. Psychologist is supporting the organization and overseeing data management.

The data monitoring committee (DMC) consists of one full professor of clinical psychology and psychotherapy for children and adolescents, one full professor from the institute of biometrics and epidemiology, and one senior physician in the clinic for psychiatry and psychotherapy. The DMC is completely independent from the sponsor and has no competing interests. The DMC is regularly informed about the progress of the study and consulted before all important milestones. In particular, the DMC monitors the occurrence of adverse events and decides whether the termination criteria have been met.

Adverse events (AEs) are categorized according to severity into mild, moderate, and severe adverse events. Severe adverse events (SAEs) require long-term care and include, for example, severe head injuries, spinal cord injuries, mental health crises leading to hospitalization, suicide attempts, and death. Moderately severe events require treatment but are temporary, such as injuries to bones in the extremities or torn/strained ligaments. Minor adverse events are temporary injuries that do not require treatment, such as abrasions or bruises. AEs are documented weekly by the therapists during the intervention periods. In addition, moderate and severe adverse events are assessed at all post-intervention timepoints in the proxy ratings of parents or legal guardians.

After each timepoint, the frequency of AEs in the IG and CG is compared and presented to the DMC. The final decision about the termination of the intervention lies with the DMC. In the case of moderate AEs, the intervention will be terminated if there are three more AEs in the IG than in the CG if the AEs are determined to be a direct result of the intervention.

Mild AEs will be recorded but will not result in the termination of the program. If an SAE occurs in the bouldering group and is determined to be a direct result of the intervention, the program will be terminated if the intervention is determined to be directly responsible for the SAE.

As in all physical activities, there is a risk of injury associated with participation in the BPT-J. In a study on sport climbing injuries, an average of 0.2 injuries per 1,000 h of climbing (which carries a higher risk of serious injury than bouldering) was found in a sample of approximately 2,000 climbers []. In our study, bouldering time is limited to a maximum of 10*2 hours per patient. Serious injuries are therefore not to be expected. In our previous studies, no SAEs occurred in more than 4,000 h of bouldering. All therapists are thoroughly trained by a bouldering instructor from the German Alpine Association, and special safety plans (no jumping, strict warm-up routine) are implemented.

Due to the low-risk nature of the intervention, no formal trial auditing has been established. Instead, attendance and therapy progress as well as AEs in the IG will be documented weekly by the therapists. This documentation will be cross-checked by the coordinating center. The overall conducting of the trial is being monitored through weekly meetings of the coordinating center to review the progress of the study, ensure adherence to the trial protocol, and address challenges. Data integrity, assessment, and documentation are being overseen by the DMC (see {21a}).

The external funder, the Bavarian State Ministry of Health, Care and Prevention, is continuously being informed about the progress of the study. If any important protocol modifications need to be made, we will inform the Ethics Committee, the funder, and the trial registry platform ISRCTN.

The research group intends to publish the data generated from this study in peer-reviewed journals. In addition, results will be communicated at international conferences, national conventions with the funders, the study’s webpage, and the press.

The study is designed as a naturalistic randomized waitlist-controlled trial with high external validity to provide evidence on the efficacy and clinical relevance of short-term BPT-J for the treatment of (subclinical) depression.

In recent years, numerous epidemiological studies have shown a growing psychological burden among children and adolescents. This trend intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic and could not be reversed even after restrictions had been lifted. For years, suicide has been the leading cause of death among adolescents between the ages of 10 and 24 [] in Western societies—surpassing traffic accidents, violence, and medical conditions. Many suicides are preceded by a mental disorder, most commonly depression.

In a recent study, 18.8% of adolescents in the 9th -12th grades reported regularly thinking about their own death, and 8.9% had already attempted suicide in the past []. The everyday lives of many adolescents have increasingly shifted into the digital sphere, and the average screen time among adolescents in Germany is 201 min per day []. Besides the often-discussed potential negative impacts on mental health, excessive screen time also reduces physical activity and thereby indirectly increases the risk of developing psychological disorders. Evidence from longitudinal observation suggests that replacing screen time with physical activity has mental health benefits for adolescents [].

At the same time, many countries, including Germany, currently face an inadequate psychiatric and psychotherapeutic care infrastructure, with waiting times for outpatient therapy of up to 12 months. Inpatient facilities are also experiencing capacity shortages and are often limited to acute crisis interventions. In research as well, psychotherapy for adolescents is not as well-established as research for adult patients: Compared with the vast number of psychotherapy studies conducted with adults (see recent meta-analyses), psychotherapy research with high scientific standards involving depressed adolescents is still scarce []. Moreover, studies have consistently found smaller effect sizes for psychotherapy in adolescents compared with adults [, ].

The approach presented in this paper—a sport-based group psychotherapy program—aims to address both the psychological and the physical components. As a cognitive behavioral group therapy, it translates effective therapeutic mechanisms such as emotional exposure, practicing alternative behaviors, and training social skills into the experiential context of bouldering. Physical activity shifts the attentional focus from external appearance (“How do I look?”) to internal experience (“How does this movement feel?”), allowing the body to be experienced as a source of self-efficacy.

The typical age-appropriate shyness and fear of discussing emotional problems in a group setting are mitigated by the action-oriented nature of Bouldering-Psychotherapy: Work focuses on what emerges in the moment. Dysfunctional strategies are addressed through brief one-on-one interventions on the wall rather than in front of the entire group.

At the same time, the practical consequences of adopting more functional strategies can be experienced immediately and can be physically anchored. Furthermore, Bouldering-Psychotherapy, as a group-based intervention, is economically efficient and suitable for providing treatment to a larger number of adolescents in the healthcare system. The well-established program for adult patients with depression [, ] was modified according to the needs and lived experiences of adolescents in three feasibility groups with adolescents.

The study is designed as a naturalistic randomized waitlist-controlled trial. Only clinically relevant exclusion criteria are applied, providing high external validity. With up to 250 adolescents, the sample size will be large enough to detect moderate effect sizes and is larger than in most adolescent outpatient trials [].

Suicidality is higher among adolescents with mental illness [] and is therefore being strictly monitored throughout the study. In the therapy sessions, therapists are following good clinical practice in monitoring suicide risk. In case of acute risks, suicide risk management plans have been established. Therapists are receiving regular supervision by psychotherapists and psychiatrics who specialize in adolescent psychotherapy. While the primary outcome is assessed via self-report and proxy ratings, the assessment of the categorial outcome, which serves as basis for the analysis of clinical relevance, is assessed by blinded raters.

As the analyses also have a strong focus on clinical relevance, the study is designed to be useful for clinicians as well as for researchers. Including participants who already show subclinical symptoms may give important insights into the efficacy of early interventions.

This study also comes with a handful of limitations:

Including participants with subclinical depression reduces the potential span of improvement, thereby leading to a reduction in the achievable effect size. This limitation might be a threat to detecting significance.

During and after the intervention, participants are free to start or continue other individual therapeutic treatments without any disadvantages. Already ongoing treatment plans are not changed by their participation in this study. Therefore, possible confounding effects due to simultaneous interventions cannot be ruled out. However, ongoing and new treatments as well as changes to treatment plans during the study are recorded in the video interviews, and such data will be taken into account in the analyses. For ethical reasons and to increase therapy adherence, all adolescents are being offered the same intervention at different timepoints. Thus, the main outcome is the comparison between the IG and CG at post-test. Follow-up analyses will provide data on the course of symptom severity and can no longer be seen as a controlled comparison.

This study is distinguished by its naturalistic design, resulting in high external validity, and a long follow-up period of 12 months. We are applying high research standards by having the interviews conducted by blinded interviewers and by meeting a possible selection bias with strict randomization of participants. To our knowledge, there are very few studies with out-patient adolescents with depression with a comparable quality and sample size.

Protocol version 1.0, 05/2026. The overall start date of the study was October 1st, 2024. Recruitment began on May 6th, 2025 and will continue until September 5th, 2026.

psychology.title: Paradoxical pain localization and mirror-image laparoscopic cholecystectomy in situs inversus totalis: a case report and literature review
psychology.abstract: Situs inversus totalis (SIT) is a rare congenital anomaly characterized by complete mirror-image transposition of the thoracic and abdominal organs. Although laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the standard treatment for symptomatic gallstone disease, reversed anatomy creates unique diagnostic and technical challenges for both surgeons and radiologists. An even less common phenomenon is paradoxical right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain despite a left-sided gallbladder, which may delay diagnosis by masking biliary disease behind an apparently normal pain pattern.A 48-year-old Persian woman presented with a 2-day history of progressively worsening RUQ pain. Physical examination demonstrated localized tenderness without generalized peritonitis. Routine electrocardiography unexpectedly revealed dextrocardia, prompting further radiologic investigation. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated multiple gallstones within a left-sided gallbladder, while contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed complete SIT. After comprehensive preoperative cardiologic and anesthetic assessment, laparoscopic cholecystectomy was successfully performed using a mirror-image operating room configuration and reversed trocar placement. Despite altered anatomical orientation and ergonomic challenges, the critical view of safety was achieved before clipping and division of the cystic duct and artery. Histopathological examination confirmed chronic calculous cholecystitis. Recovery was uneventful, and the patient remained symptom-free at 6-month follow-up.This case highlights that the principal challenge in SIT extends beyond mirror-image anatomy to include paradoxical symptom localization and altered operative ergonomics. Recognition of laterality disorders, comprehensive preoperative imaging, and meticulous ergonomic adaptation allow laparoscopic cholecystectomy to be performed safely while maintaining the same fundamental surgical principles applied to patients with normal anatomy.
psychology.text:
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is among the most commonly performed abdominal procedures worldwide and has become the standard treatment for symptomatic gallstone disease. Its safety relies on predictable anatomical relationships, accurate interpretation of clinical findings, and well-established ergonomic principles during dissection of Calot’s triangle. In patients with situs inversus totalis (SIT), however, these assumptions are fundamentally altered because the thoracic and abdominal organs are completely transposed into a mirror-image configuration.

SIT is a rare congenital laterality disorder with an estimated incidence ranging from 1 in 8000 to 1 in 25 000 live births[,]. Although the condition itself is usually asymptomatic, it presents significant diagnostic and technical challenges when common surgical diseases occur. Cholelithiasis is not more prevalent in patients with SIT than in the general population; nevertheless, diagnosis may be delayed because abdominal pain does not always correspond to the anatomical position of the affected organ[,].

One of the most intriguing manifestations of biliary disease in SIT is paradoxical pain localization. While inflammation of a left-sided gallbladder would be expected to produce left upper quadrant (LUQ) or epigastric pain, several published reports have described patients presenting with conventional right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain despite complete visceral transposition[,,]. The exact neurophysiological basis of this phenomenon remains uncertain. Proposed mechanisms include incomplete reversal of cortical functional lateralization, preserved organization of visceral afferent pathways, and complex central processing of visceral nociceptive signals during embryological development[,].

From a surgical perspective, laparoscopic cholecystectomy in SIT requires considerably more than simple mirror-image trocar placement. Surgeons must continuously adapt their visuospatial orientation, hand dominance, and instrument coordination while preserving the universal principles of safe biliary surgery, particularly achievement of the critical view of safety before division of any structures[,–]. Consequently, meticulous preoperative planning and ergonomic adaptation are essential for minimizing technical difficulty and avoiding biliary injury.

Although more than 100 laparoscopic cholecystectomies in patients with SIT have been reported, most publications focus primarily on the rarity of the anatomical anomaly rather than on its diagnostic implications or operative ergonomics[]. Furthermore, paradoxical RUQ pain remains an uncommon presentation that continues to pose a diagnostic challenge for emergency physicians and surgeons alike[,].

We report a patient with SIT who presented with classic RUQ pain despite having a left-sided gallbladder and underwent successful laparoscopic cholecystectomy using a mirror-image operative approach. In addition to describing the operative strategy, this report discusses the neuroanatomical basis for paradoxical pain localization, practical ergonomic modifications during minimally invasive surgery, and lessons derived from contemporary literature that may facilitate the management of similar patients. This case report adheres to the SCARE 2025 Criteria[].

A 48-year-old Persian woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressively worsening RUQ abdominal pain. The pain was dull, constant, and non-radiating, with no clear relationship to food intake. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, changes in bowel habits, or urinary symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no previous abdominal surgery, chronic medical illnesses, or regular medication use. There was no relevant family history of congenital anomalies, laterality disorders, or hepatobiliary disease.

On admission, the patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination demonstrated localized tenderness in the RUQ without guarding, rebound tenderness, or signs of generalized peritonitis. Murphy’s sign was considered equivocal because of the unexpected localization of pain. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations revealed no significant leukocytosis or biochemical evidence of biliary obstruction. Liver function tests were within normal limits except for a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase level (245 U/L). The white blood cell count was 4.0 × 103/μL with 37.7% neutrophils, and C-reactive protein measured 3.2 mg/L. Cardiac biomarkers were within normal limits.

Routine electrocardiography (ECG) unexpectedly revealed dextrocardia, prompting further evaluation for a possible laterality disorder. Chest radiography confirmed a right-sided cardiac apex and a right-sided gastric bubble, strongly suggesting SIT (Fig. ). (As this was the only original preoperative radiograph available, Figure  is presented to document the available imaging findings and should not be interpreted as demonstrating clinically significant colonic distension or as being directly related to the primary diagnosis.)

Subsequent abdominal ultrasonography (US) demonstrated multiple gallstones within a left-sided gallbladder, associated with mild wall thickening but without biliary duct dilatation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) confirmed complete SIT, demonstrating a left-sided liver and gallbladder with the stomach and spleen located in the RUQ (Fig. ). Figure  is intended to demonstrate the visceral laterality associated with SIT rather than the gallstones, which were identified on US.

Because congenital cardiovascular anomalies may coexist with SIT, a comprehensive preoperative assessment was performed before surgery[]. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated structurally normal cardiac anatomy, apart from dextrocardia, with preserved ventricular function. Following multidisciplinary evaluation by the cardiology and anesthesiology teams, the patient was considered an appropriate candidate for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. For perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis, ceftriaxone (1 g) and metronidazole (500 mg) were administered intravenously as single doses before the skin incision.

The operating room was arranged in a complete mirror-image configuration (Fig. ). The primary surgeon and camera assistant stood on the patient’s right side, whereas the first assistant stood on the left. Pneumoperitoneum was established using an open Hasson technique through a 10-mm infraumbilical trocar. Three additional trocars were inserted in a mirror-image fashion replicating the conventional laparoscopic cholecystectomy setup described for patients with normal anatomy[,].

Initial laparoscopic exploration confirmed complete mirror-image transposition of the abdominal viscera. The liver and gallbladder were located in the LUQ, whereas the stomach and spleen occupied the RUQ. Dense inflammatory adhesions surrounding the gallbladder were carefully dissected using a combination of blunt dissection and electrocautery. After meticulous exposure of Calot’s triangle, the cystic duct and cystic artery were clearly identified, and the critical view of safety was achieved before clipping and division of either structure, in accordance with established principles of safe cholecystectomy. The cystic duct and cystic artery were secured with laparoscopic clips before division. A drain was not placed at the end of the procedure (Fig. ).

The principal technical challenge arose from the reversed anatomical orientation rather than from any anatomical variation of the biliary tree. Continuous visuospatial adaptation was required throughout the dissection because the mirror-image anatomy altered instrument trajectories and surgeon ergonomics. For a right-handed surgeon, fine dissection frequently had to be performed using the nondominant hand while maintaining adequate countertraction with the dominant hand. Despite these ergonomic constraints, the procedure was completed entirely laparoscopically without intraoperative complications, bile duct injury, excessive bleeding, or conversion to open surgery[,].

The gallbladder was retrieved in a specimen bag through the epigastric port. A final laparoscopic inspection confirmed meticulous hemostasis and the absence of bile leakage. The patient recovered uneventfully, resumed oral intake on the first postoperative day, and was discharged home in good general condition.

Histopathological examination confirmed chronic calculous cholecystitis without dysplasia or malignancy. At 6-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic, with complete resolution of abdominal pain and no evidence of postoperative complications or recurrent biliary disease. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a left-sided gallbladder containing multiple gallstones.Day 0 – further evaluationContrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed situs inversus totalis with complete visceral laterality.Day 0 – surgical managementFollowing preoperative cardiology and anesthesia assessment, mirror-image laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed. The critical view of safety was obtained, and the gallbladder was removed without intraoperative complications.Postoperative day 1The patient had an uneventful postoperative recovery and was discharged according to routine postoperative care.6-month follow-upThe patient remained asymptomatic with no reported postoperative complications.

SIT is a rare congenital laterality disorder characterized by complete mirror-image transposition of the thoracic and abdominal viscera[]. Although the condition itself is usually asymptomatic, it substantially complicates the diagnosis and surgical management of otherwise common abdominal diseases. Cholelithiasis occurs with a frequency comparable to that of the general population; however, once biliary disease develops, clinicians are confronted with two major challenges: atypical symptom localization and unfamiliar operative orientation[,].

The distinctive contribution of this report lies in the combination of paradoxical pain localization, incidental recognition of the laterality disorder via dextrocardia, and detailed documentation of the ergonomic adaptations required during laparoscopic surgery. First, despite complete transposition of the abdominal organs, the patient presented with classic RUQ pain rather than the expected left-sided symptoms. Second, laparoscopic cholecystectomy was successfully completed using a mirror-image operative configuration without compromising the principles of safe biliary dissection. Together, these observations demonstrate that the principal challenge in SIT is not the abnormal anatomy itself but the cognitive assumptions derived from normal anatomical orientation.

One of the most intriguing aspects of this case is the paradoxical localization of pain. Classical anatomical teaching predicts that inflammation of a left-sided gallbladder should produce LUQ or epigastric pain. Nevertheless, several reports have documented patients with SIT presenting with conventional RUQ pain despite complete visceral transposition[,,]. Although uncommon, this phenomenon has considerable clinical importance because clinicians may prematurely exclude biliary pathology when symptom localization appears inconsistent with organ position.

The neurophysiological basis of paradoxical pain localization remains incompletely understood. One proposed mechanism is incomplete reversal of cortical functional lateralization during embryological development. Although the abdominal viscera undergo complete mirror-image transposition, cortical networks involved in visceral nociceptive processing may retain their usual functional organization, resulting in preservation of conventional pain perception[]. Another plausible explanation involves the complex organization of visceral afferent pathways. Unlike somatic sensory innervation, visceral afferent fibers follow intricate autonomic and spinal pathways that may not undergo complete mirror-image rearrangement in patients with SIT[]. While these hypotheses remain speculative, they provide biologically plausible explanations for the discordance observed in our patient and in previously published reports.

From a diagnostic standpoint, this case illustrates the importance of avoiding anchoring bias when evaluating abdominal pain. Reliance solely on the anatomical location of pain may delay diagnosis in patients with laterality disorders. In the present case, the unexpected finding of dextrocardia during routine ECG prompted further imaging, ultimately leading to the diagnosis of SIT before surgery. This observation emphasizes that unexpected findings such as dextrocardia or a right-sided gastric bubble on plain radiography should immediately prompt reassessment of visceral orientation rather than the exclusion of biliary disease[,].

Preoperative imaging plays a pivotal role for these patients. US remains the preferred first-line investigation for suspected gallstone disease, whereas contrast-enhanced CT provides a comprehensive assessment of visceral orientation and facilitates operative planning[,]. Additional imaging modalities, such as magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, may be useful when biliary anatomical variations or choledocholithiasis are suspected[].

The technical challenge of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in SIT extends well beyond mirror-image trocar placement. Reversed anatomy fundamentally alters visuospatial orientation, hand dominance, instrument trajectory, and surgeon ergonomics. Right-handed surgeons often experience greater technical difficulty because precise dissection within Calot’s triangle must be performed under unfamiliar ergonomic conditions[,,]. Consequently, successful surgery depends less on modification of the operative technique than on deliberate ergonomic adaptation while maintaining the universal principles of safe biliary surgery.

Emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation technologies may provide additional support during laparoscopic procedures involving complex or reversed anatomy. AI-based systems have recently been investigated for anatomical recognition and intraoperative identification of critical structures during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Although AI-assisted technology was not used in the present case, such systems may have potential value in supporting spatial orientation and anatomical recognition in patients with SIT. Further clinical evaluation is required to determine their feasibility and effectiveness in this setting[].

In the present case, a complete mirror-image operating room arrangement allowed comfortable instrument handling without altering the essential steps of laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Careful adhesiolysis, meticulous identification of the cystic duct and cystic artery, and strict achievement of the critical view of safety enabled the safe completion of the procedure without bile duct injury or conversion to open surgery. Our experience is consistent with the systematic review by Enciu et al, which demonstrated that favorable outcomes are primarily related to careful operative planning and adherence to standard surgical principles rather than any specific trocar configuration[].

To further contextualize the present case, we reviewed published cases of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in patients with SIT. Table  provides a concise comparison of the present patient with representative published cases, focusing on pain localization, diagnostic evaluation, and operative considerations.
