Because shyness and fear scores were strongly correlated, their simultaneous inclusion in the cluster analysis may have influenced the resulting cluster structure, which should be considered when interpreting these exploratory findings. Furthermore, data on the birth environment of stray cats, based on owner reports alone, may not be precise. In future research, it will be necessary to clarify the details of birth circumstances or conduct experiments on individuals whose births are known.

The results of our study indicate that despite exhibiting fear, certain cats engage in approach behaviors. This finding suggests that progressively increasing human interactions may facilitate the swift adjustment of cats to the presence of humans. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of individual fear levels and other personality traits in cats could enable shelters and owners to tailor their environments to better accommodate these specific traits. Consequently, this would enhance our overall understanding of cat personalities and lead to improved practices among cat owners and shelter workers, optimizing welfare and interaction strategies.

The Excel file contains three worksheets: S1, profiles of cats in Study 1 (n = 82); S2, profiles of male cats in Study 2 (n = 114); and S3, profiles of male cats born as strays in Study 3 (n = 114).

psychology.title: Surgeon Ergonomics of Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion Across Four Patient Positions: A Proof-of-Concept Simulation Study Using Motion Capture and Electromyography
psychology.abstract: Proof-of-concept simulation-based biomechanical pilot study.To compare surgeon posture and muscle activity across four lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) positions and rank them by overall ergonomic burden.Five right-handed spine surgeons (case volumes 15 to 500 or more) each simulated a single-level LLIF on a synthetic model in four positions, three using direct vision (lateral decubitus, prone seated, prone lateral) and one using a camera and monitor (prone camera). Whole-body motion capture and surface EMG were recorded simultaneously, analyzed by surgical phase, and summarized per surgeon.Neck-flexion intensity was greatest in lateral decubitus and lower in every prone position, with the same ranking in all five surgeons (exact Friedman p=3.0e-06, Kendall W=1.00). Arm elevation was highest in prone seated. Across four summaries of posture and muscle activity, prone camera was the most favorable position in every surgeon, while the others reordered by measure. All positions scored medium-to-high risk. No two-position comparison reached adjusted significance, as expected at this sample size.Patient position in LLIF does not appear to change patient outcome, but it changes what the operation costs the surgeon. Lateral decubitus loaded the neck in every surgeon regardless of case volume or preference, prone seated loaded the shoulder, and prone camera was most favorable overall. Surgeons can reduce their exposure through position and setup, and ergonomics offers an objective way to compare setups when patient outcomes cannot separate them. These are proof-of-concept findings in five surgeons and require confirmation in a larger sample.
psychology.text:
Lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) allows spinal access through a minimally invasive retroperitoneal transpsoas approach and has become a widely used option for lumbar interbody fusion.

 It was originally developed with the patient in lateral decubitus and the surgeon standing posterior to the patient, looking downward into a laterally placed surgical field.

 Single-position prone techniques were subsequently developed so that interbody work and posterior pedicle-screw fixation could be completed without repositioning the patient., Prone variants differ in how the surgeon visualizes the disc space and include direct visualization with the surgeon standing or seated, a prone position with the table tilted away from the surgeon, and a retractor-mounted camera shown on an elevated monitor, introduced to relieve the awkward posture of looking laterally into a prone wound.-

Each position differs in how the surgeon stands, looks, and reaches, so a choice that is neutral for the patient may not be neutral for the operator. Work-related musculoskeletal disorders are common among surgeons and contribute to pain, disability, and early departure from practice, and spine surgeons appear particularly at risk given the sustained non-neutral postures intrinsic to the work.- Reframing the comparison of LLIF positions around surgeon ergonomics therefore addresses a question that current clinical evidence leaves open.

A hazard that is not measured cannot be reduced in any deliberate way, and surgeon ergonomics has until recently been difficult to measure during an operation. Wearable inertial sensors now capture whole-body posture continuously and have been used to measure ergonomic risk in operating surgeons,

 and combined with surface electromyography (EMG) they quantify surgeon physical workload.

 In spine surgery, EMG has shown that manual pedicle-screw placement drives the neck, trapezius, and forearm muscles into overuse-injury ranges that power-assisted instrumentation reduces.

 Such capture spans the entire procedure, unlike observational instruments such as the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), which grade only a single posture., While display monitors and other ergonomic interventions have been studied in other specialties,- such research in spine surgery remains sparse and dominated by self-report.

 To our knowledge, no study has objectively measured and compared surgeon ergonomics across LLIF positions.

We therefore compared surgeon posture and muscle activity across four LLIF positions in a simulation model, using synchronized inertial motion capture and surface EMG. Our aims were to localize the dominant musculoskeletal load, to distinguish exposures modifiable through position and operating-room setup from those built into instrument handling, and to rank the positions by overall ergonomic burden so the comparison gives an answer that can be acted on. Raising the surgeon’s line of sight from the wound to an elevated monitor reduces operative neck flexion in other specialties,,, so we hypothesized that the monitor-based prone-camera setup would be most favorable overall and that lateral decubitus, which requires sustained downward vision into a laterally placed surgical field, would be the most neck-demanding. This is a proof-of-concept study. Five surgeons, all right-handed and male, cannot show how large these differences are in general. The aim was narrower, to find out whether motion capture and muscle recording can tell operative setups apart at all, and to raise questions a larger study can answer.

Five right-handed male spine surgeons with LLIF case volumes of approximately 15, 25, 200, 200, and greater than 500 each performed the operative motions of a single-level transpsoas LLIF on one synthetic spine simulation model in a surgical skills laboratory. Every surgeon approached the disc space from the same side in all four positions, so the relationship between hand dominance and approach side, which itself alters the ergonomics of a lateral approach, was held constant. The four positions were lateral decubitus (standing at the model side with direct downward vision into a laterally placed surgical field), prone seated (seated on a stool with direct vision), prone lateral (the table tilted approximately 45 degrees away from the surgeon, standing with direct vision), and prone camera (standing and viewing a retractor-mounted camera on an elevated monitor). Each surgeon completed all four positions sequentially within a single session, with a scrub technician simulating instrument passing, and the five surgeons were studied on separate days. Surgeon characteristics, including case volume and the position each uses most in practice, are given in . The positions are shown in . The surgeons differed in anthropometry and experience and the sample is small, so results are interpreted per surgeon rather than pooled. The order of the four positions was randomized for each surgeon, and the sequence each surgeon received is listed in
Supplementary Table S10. Randomizing within a surgeon is not the same as counterbalancing across the group, and two surgeons drew the same sequence. Predominant LLIF position in practice indicates the position each surgeon uses most in clinical practice; surgeons recorded as having no predominant position use the lateral and prone approaches in comparable proportions. Whole-body kinematics were recorded with a 17-sensor inertial motion-capture system (Xsens MVN Analyze, 23 segments) at 60 Hz, and surface electromyography at 2148 Hz from 16 channels (Delsys) through the motion-capture software EMG plug-in. Electrodes were placed bilaterally over the sternocleidomastoid, cervical (C4) paraspinal, upper trapezius, biceps brachii, triceps brachii, forearm flexor, forearm extensor, and lumbar paraspinal muscles following surface-EMG placement guidelines. All eight muscle pairs are reported in Supplementary Tables S4 and S6. Four pairs (C4 paraspinal, upper trapezius, lumbar paraspinal, and forearm extensor) were chosen in advance as the set that separates the positions carried in the main text and ‒. Kinematics were reconstructed after a standing neutral-pose calibration, and the EMG was exported with the same recording, so the two recordings share a single time base.

Each recording was divided into four sequential phases (exposure, dilation and retractor placement, discectomy, and trial and implant placement) using start and end times recorded with a stopwatch. Metrics were computed per phase and for the whole procedure. One lateral-decubitus motion recording ended before the trial and implant phase. The affected kinematic cells are reported as missing, and the corresponding EMG is complete.

Ergonomic joint angles were derived for the head and neck, the trunk, and bilateral upper-arm elevation, with segment angles for the elbow, wrist, and knee. For each joint, position, and phase we computed how far the joint typically sat from its neutral resting position, termed the intensity (the mean absolute deviation from neutral); the largest angle reached (the peak); the total postural dose, which combines how far the joint was displaced with how long it stayed there (the cumulative joint angle, the time integral of the absolute angle in degree minutes); and the share of time spent in each risk band.

Every frame of joint motion was graded Low, Medium, or High risk using published thresholds that define how far a joint may deviate from neutral before sustained work in that posture is no longer recommended. Neck-flexion and trunk-flexion limits follow ISO 11226:2000 (trunk inclination beyond 20 degrees time-limited and beyond 60 degrees not recommended; neck flexion beyond 25 degrees not recommended),

 upper-arm elevation limits follow EN 1005-4 (0 to 20 degrees acceptable, 20 to 60 degrees conditionally acceptable, beyond 60 degrees not recommended),

 and the wrist and standing-knee limits follow the RULA and REBA schemes., Risk was assigned per frame against the direction-specific boundaries listed in Supplementary Table S1 and weighted by sample duration. Boundaries not defined by a primary source, and channels for which no validated cutoff exists (cervical axial rotation, forearm rotation, trunk lateral bending, and all EMG channels), are flagged in Table S1 and shown without risk shading. The thresholds assume an upright, weight-bearing posture, so the knee bands are restricted to standing intervals. Robustness of the neck finding to the flexion threshold was examined at 20 to 40 degrees (Supplementary Table S2).

EMG signals were band-pass filtered from 20 to 450 Hz, notch filtered, and converted to a 100 ms root-mean-square envelope. A maximum voluntary contraction was not recorded, so amplitude was normalized to a per-surgeon session reference (the 99th-percentile RMS across that surgeon’s four recordings) and reported as percent of reference. For each muscle, position, and phase we computed the mean and peak amplitude; the level the muscle rarely relaxed below, which reflects sustained low-level loading that never lets the muscle rest, termed the static level (the 10th percentile of the amplitude distribution); the total muscular dose over the procedure (the cumulative EMG); and the rate at which the signal’s frequency content declined, which falls as a muscle fatigues and is independent of how forcefully it works (the median-frequency slope).

 Surface EMG has no validated amplitude risk threshold, so it was interpreted as a within-surgeon comparison across positions. Since sustained low-level activation rather than peak effort drives neck and shoulder overuse injury,, muscle demand was judged from the static level and fatigue slope rather than mean amplitude alone. We did not record a maximum voluntary contraction, meaning the hardest a muscle can pull, before the trials began. Muscle activity therefore has no absolute scale and cannot be compared between surgeons. Each muscle was instead scaled to that surgeon’s own busiest activity, taken as the 99th percentile of all four of their recordings. This is one number per surgeon and muscle, so it shifts all four positions by the same amount and cannot change which position ranks best. Scaling to the single highest reading instead left every ranking unchanged (Supplementary Table S11). We kept the 99th percentile because that single highest reading was on average 3.3 times larger, and 57 times larger in one channel, which points to a recording artifact rather than real effort. The fatigue measure depends on the frequency of the signal rather than its size, so it is unaffected by this choice.

Whole-body REBA and upper-limb RULA scores were derived for each surgeon and position., Joint-angle inputs (trunk, neck, upper arm, forearm, and wrist of the right operating side) were taken from the synchronized inertial recording at each frame, and categorical inputs (light hand-instrument load, fair coupling, sustained static muscle use, and supported or standing legs) were assigned from photographs. Scores were computed at every frame and summarized three ways, as the median (typical) posture, the worst (95th-percentile) posture, and, because a seven-point ordinal score summarized by its median discards most of the variation, the percent of procedure time spent at the highest action level. The wrist and forearm-rotation inputs derived from distal-hand tracking that exceeded physiological ranges (see Limitations), so the combined scores reflect the trunk, neck, and arm, plus a fixed hand score that is the same in every position. The unreliable wrist and forearm values were handled as follows. We deleted no frames, since that would break the shared timing with the EMG recording, and we replaced no values. These inputs simply reached the top score in every position for every surgeon, so they add the same amount everywhere and cannot favor one position over another. The combined scores therefore reflect the trunk, neck, and arm, with a fixed contribution from the hand. Wrist and forearm rotation are also reported on their own, without risk shading.

No formal sample-size calculation was performed. The sample was determined by feasibility, and the study is exploratory and hypothesis-generating. The primary endpoint family was pre-specified as head/neck-inclination intensity and percent High-risk time, dominant-arm elevation intensity, and trapezius median-frequency slope over the whole procedure. All other comparisons are exploratory. Across the four positions we used the exact Friedman test, which asks whether the five surgeons ranked the positions in a consistent order, with Kendall W as the effect size, a value from 0 (no agreement between surgeons) to 1 (all five produced an identical ranking). At five surgeons the exact two-sided pairwise p is bounded below by 0.0625, so no pairwise contrast can reach conventional significance, whereas the omnibus test can reach 3.0e-06 when all five share one ranking. Pairwise results are therefore summarized by how consistently the difference ran in the same direction across surgeons and by effect size. A Holm correction across the four primary endpoints leaves the same three endpoints separating the positions at the 0.05 level. Results are reported per surgeon rather than pooled. Analyses were performed in R 4.6. Five surgeons set a hard limit on what any test can show. When two positions are compared in five surgeons, the smallest p value the exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test can give is 0.0625, so no single pair of positions can reach 0.05 however large the difference. Across all 2,190 pairs the smallest adjusted value was 0.0625 and none reached 0.05. We therefore report pairs descriptively, with effect sizes and the number of surgeons who moved the same way, and we claim no difference between any two positions. Formal testing is limited to the Friedman test, which compares all four positions at once and can reach smaller p values.

To summarize which position imposed the least overall ergonomic burden, the four positions were ranked within each surgeon under four ways of summarizing the recordings. Posture was summarized as the mean joint angle and as the cumulative joint angle (the area under the absolute-angle curve), and muscle activity as the mean amplitude and as the cumulative EMG. Within each surgeon and phase the positions were ranked from 1 (lowest exposure) to 4 within each validated region (neck flexion, left and right arm elevation, trunk flexion) or muscle (left and right C4 paraspinal, trapezius, and lumbar paraspinal). Ranks were averaged across regions or muscles and then across surgeons, and a combined score was formed as the mean of the four method scores. The two summaries of the same measurement were strongly correlated, so the design weights posture and muscle activity equally, and reporting them separately tests whether the ranking depends on how each one is summarized. Agreement among surgeons was quantified with Kendall W and the Friedman test, reported descriptively because the asymptotic approximation is unreliable at five subjects. Distal-hand channels were excluded because they did not separate the positions and were unreliably tracked.

was prepared with artificial-intelligence assistance. Real photographs of the surgeons in each of the four study positions were converted into flat cartoon illustrations with an AI image-editing tool.  was not generated from scratch, and the illustrations are derived from and accurately represent the actual positions in the source photographs. ‒ are quantitative data figures produced in R from the study data without AI image tools. A generative artificial-intelligence large language model (Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic) was used to improve the language and readability of the manuscript. No generative artificial-intelligence tool was used to create, generate, or alter any research data, and the authors reviewed all content and figures and take full responsibility for their accuracy and integrity.

Twenty recordings were analyzed (five surgeons across four positions), ranging from approximately 4 to 12 minutes, with motion-capture and EMG streams synchronized on a common clock. One lateral-decubitus motion recording ended before the trial and implant phase, so its kinematic values for that phase are missing. The corresponding EMG is complete. Inertial tracking was reliable for the proximal joints but not for the distal hand, where wrist flexion and extension and forearm rotation exceeded physiological ranges and are interpreted with caution throughout. The distal-hand panels in ‒ are clipped to a physiological display range.

Neck flexion was greatest in lateral decubitus for every surgeon, with intensity ranging from 17.8 to 39.0 degrees across surgeons and 30.7 to 87.1 percent of the procedure in the High-risk band. Every prone position was lower in every surgeon, with intensity ranging 8.5 to 17.1 degrees in prone seated, 14.1 to 26.6 in prone lateral, and 10.1 to 18.2 in prone camera. All five surgeons ranked the positions identically for neck-flexion intensity (exact Friedman p=3.0e-06, Kendall W=1.00, the smallest exact p that is possible and therefore an index of perfect rank agreement rather than of effect size). Head torsion remained below 5 percent High in all positions (‒; Supplementary Table S3), and the lateral-decubitus ranking was preserved within every surgeon at flexion thresholds of 20 to 40 degrees (Supplementary Table S2).

Shoulder and arm elevation was highest in prone seated in every surgeon (left-arm intensity 29.3 to 62.2 degrees). Arm elevation was lowest in lateral decubitus, where the arms rest at the table side, and among the prone options the dominant right arm was lowest in prone camera in all five surgeons. Dominant right-arm elevation intensity, a pre-specified primary endpoint, differed across positions (exact Friedman p=0.001, Kendall W=0.81), as did non-dominant left-arm elevation (p<0.001, W=0.86). Sizes varied widely between surgeons, consistent with differing anthropometry and prior injury, which is why arm exposure is interpreted per surgeon. Trunk inclination remained modest in every position and did not separate them. It is reported by intensity rather than percent High-risk time, since a near-neutral trunk oscillating around the upright frequently crossed zero and would otherwise be marked too high (Supplementary Table S3).

Right trapezius amplitude was highest in lateral decubitus in most surgeons, broadly mirroring the neck-posture pattern, although the position with the lowest trapezius amplitude varied between surgeons. Cervical and lumbar paraspinals were active for more than 80 percent of the procedure in all positions. A steep median-frequency decline in the loaded limb was observed in prone seated in several surgeons, but the trapezius fatigue slope did not differ systematically across positions, so the fatigue findings are descriptive. Amplitude is normalized to each surgeon’s own session reference and is therefore compared within, not across, surgeons (‒; Supplementary Table S4). Scaling muscle activity to each surgeon’s single highest reading instead of the 99th percentile left every ranking of the positions unchanged (Supplementary Table S11).

Neck flexion and arm elevation were what separated the positions. Lateral decubitus held the neck in the High-risk band for the largest share of the procedure in every surgeon, and prone seated did so for arm elevation, whereas trunk flexion remained in the Low zone in every position (). Cumulative joint angle and cumulative EMG reproduced the same pattern for the neck and shoulder (Supplementary Tables S5 and S6). Distal-hand demand was high but did not separate the positions and could not be classified reliably. Knee flexion reached the High band only in prone seated, reflecting the seated posture rather than a true mechanical load, since the thresholds assume a standing stance and classify the flexed but stool-supported knee as High from its angle alone (Supplementary Table S3).

Of the four pre-specified whole-procedure primary endpoints, neck-flexion intensity differed across positions with an identical within-surgeon ranking in all five surgeons (exact Friedman p=3.0e-06, Kendall W=1.00). Neck percent High-risk time separated the positions less strongly (p=0.012, W=0.65), with lateral decubitus still the worst position in all five surgeons. Dominant right-arm elevation intensity differed across positions (p=0.001, W=0.81); and the trapezius median-frequency (fatigue) slope did not differ across positions (left p=0.67, W=0.10; right p=0.14, W=0.36), so the fatigue-slope interpretation is reported descriptively and as secondary. No comparison between two individual positions reached 0.05 after adjustment, which five surgeons cannot support, so these are reported as effect sizes rather than as significance tests.

Combined REBA and RULA scores were high in all four positions. Averaged across surgeons, the typical (median) REBA score ranged from 3.8 in prone camera to 4.8 in prone seated, and the typical RULA score from 5.2 in lateral decubitus to 5.8 in prone seated, all corresponding to the investigate-and-change action level. Summarized this way the combined scores separated the positions poorly and RULA ranked lateral decubitus most favorably, the reverse of the joint-specific result. Time-resolving the same per-frame scores recovered the position difference. The percent of procedure time spent at the highest RULA action level was lowest in prone camera (13.0 percent), intermediate in lateral decubitus (18.0) and prone lateral (19.9), and highest in prone seated (37.4), and the five surgeons agreed on this ordering more closely than on any single-posture summary (Kendall W=0.71 for percent time at the highest action level and 0.58 for the mean per-frame score, compared with 0.29 for the median). The time-resolved combined score therefore reproduced the joint-specific ranking, with prone camera most favorable and prone seated least, whereas the median posture did not (; Supplementary Table S9).Table 2.Whole-body REBA and upper-limb RULA scores by surgical positionPositionREBA medianREBA worstRULA medianRULA worstLateral decubitus4 (4 to 6)7 (5 to 8)5 (4 to 6)7 (6 to 7)Prone seated5 (4 to 6)7 (6 to 8)6 (5 to 6)7 (7 to 7)Prone lateral4 (3 to 5)6 (5 to 8)6 (4 to 6)7 (7 to 7)Prone camera4 (2 to 5)6 (5 to 6)6 (4 to 6)7 (6 to 7)Values are the cohort median (range across 5 surgeons). Scores were computed at every frame from the synchronized IMU (right operating side); the median is the typical posture and the worst is the 95th percentile of the per-frame score. Categorical inputs (light hand-instrument load, fair coupling, sustained static muscle use, and supported or standing legs) were assigned from photographs of the study positions; the load category was held constant across phases, and the wrist and forearm-rotation subscores were derived from distal-hand tracking that exceeded physiological ranges, so the combined score reflects the trunk, neck, and arm, plus a fixed hand score that is the same in every position. The thresholds assume a standing, weight-bearing posture. REBA risk: 1 negligible, 2 to 3 low, 4 to 7 medium, 8 to 10 high. RULA action: 1 to 2 acceptable, 3 to 4 investigate, 5 to 6 investigate and change soon, 7 change now. REBA, Rapid Entire Body Assessment; RULA, Rapid Upper Limb Assessment. n = 5.

Whole-body REBA and upper-limb RULA scores by surgical position

Values are the cohort median (range across 5 surgeons). Scores were computed at every frame from the synchronized IMU (right operating side); the median is the typical posture and the worst is the 95th percentile of the per-frame score. Categorical inputs (light hand-instrument load, fair coupling, sustained static muscle use, and supported or standing legs) were assigned from photographs of the study positions; the load category was held constant across phases, and the wrist and forearm-rotation subscores were derived from distal-hand tracking that exceeded physiological ranges, so the combined score reflects the trunk, neck, and arm, plus a fixed hand score that is the same in every position. The thresholds assume a standing, weight-bearing posture. REBA risk: 1 negligible, 2 to 3 low, 4 to 7 medium, 8 to 10 high. RULA action: 1 to 2 acceptable, 3 to 4 investigate, 5 to 6 investigate and change soon, 7 change now. REBA, Rapid Entire Body Assessment; RULA, Rapid Upper Limb Assessment. n = 5.

Ranking the four positions within each surgeon and averaging across surgeons gave a consistent answer across the different summaries (). Prone camera was the most favorable position under all four methods (mean rank 1.70 to 1.87 on the 1-to-4 scale) and under the combined score (1.78, Kendall W=0.74, Friedman p=0.011). It was each surgeon’s single best position under the combined score in all five surgeons and the worst position for no surgeon. The other three reordered depending on the measure. On posture, prone seated was the least favorable, reflecting its high arm and shoulder elevation, while lateral decubitus and prone lateral were intermediate and closely spaced. Averaging across regions makes lateral decubitus look better than it is, which held the neck in the most flexed posture of any position in every surgeon. On muscle activity, lateral decubitus was the least favorable by mean amplitude, whereas prone lateral was more clearly favored under cumulative EMG. Prone lateral was never the least favorable on average, although it was individually worst for one surgeon under two summaries. Ergonomic advantages and costs of each position

Positions are ordered from the most to the least favorable overall (). Entries summarize the study’s motion-capture and electromyography measures interpreted per surgeon; they describe surgeon ergonomics only and do not address patient outcomes, which the comparative literature reports as similar across positions, nor operative time and radiation, which differ by workflow and are lower for single-position than for two-position surgery. The modifiable levers are operating-room setup changes that do not alter the surgical approach. n = 5.

Across surgical phases (Supplementary Table S7), prone camera was the most favorable position under every summary during dilation, discectomy, and the whole procedure. The exceptions were the exposure phase, where prone lateral was most favorable under four of the five summaries, and the trial and implant phase, where prone camera ranked third under both muscle summaries. On the combined score, prone camera was most favorable in every phase except exposure, where prone lateral ranked first. The per-surgeon best positions are given in Supplementary Table S8. The exceptions to prone camera were few and individual, involving the surgeon with a prior shoulder and wrist injury, for whom lateral decubitus was most favorable on posture, and two surgeons for whom prone seated or prone lateral was most favorable on muscle activity.

All surgeons employ all positions in their practice. Measured strain did not follow what each surgeon prefers. Two of the five named a position they use most, and the other three use the lateral and prone approaches about equally (). For the surgeon who works mostly in lateral decubitus, that position gave the lowest arm elevation of their four recordings (16.0 degrees), and this is also the one surgeon with a prior right shoulder repair. The same position gave the highest neck flexion of anyone in the group (39.0 degrees), and prone camera was still their best position overall. For the surgeon who works mostly in prone lateral, that position was best on neither the neck nor the arm. Preference therefore followed the body part each surgeon seems to protect rather than total strain, and in neither case did the preferred position give the lowest overall burden.

The most consistent finding in this study was that the extra neck strain of lateral decubitus did not depend on the surgeon. Lateral decubitus was the most neck-demanding position for all five surgeons across a case-volume range from roughly 15 to more than 500 procedures, and regardless of which position each favors in practice. The surgeon who operates almost exclusively in lateral decubitus showed the same pattern as the surgeon who works predominantly prone lateral, and in fact recorded the highest lateral-decubitus neck flexion of the cohort, while the most experienced surgeon showed the lowest absolute neck angle but the same position ranking (). Familiarity therefore reduces the size of the cervical exposure without removing it. The comparison is also not affected by the usual effect of experience, since the outcome is joint angle and muscle activity rather than operative speed or accuracy. That the penalty persists despite high familiarity points to the geometry of the approach, a laterally placed surgical field viewed from above, rather than to a learning curve, and implies it is relieved by changing the line of sight rather than by accumulating cases.

Prone camera was the only position simultaneously low on the neck and on the shoulder, and that combination, rather than a neck advantage alone, is why it led the overall ranking. Prone seated held the neck in less flexion than prone camera in every surgeon but required the highest arm elevation of any position, while lateral decubitus traded low arm elevation for the most flexed neck. The neck still matters more than the others, as neck and cervical complaints are among the most common work-related musculoskeletal disorders in surgeons, second only to the low back,, and sustained neck flexion has been associated with neck pain in occupational studies.

 That prone camera kept cervical flexion low while carrying among the lowest sustained trapezius static loads is consistent with viewing an elevated monitor rather than looking down into the wound, and mirrors evidence from other specialties that raising the line of sight reduces operative neck flexion and reported pain.,,, A prior comparison in minimally invasive lumbar decompression found that a tubular-mounted digital camera lowered REBA scores relative to the operating microscope while shortening operative time.

 The evidence linking occupational neck flexion to neck pain is suggestive rather than definitive, so these findings are best read as reduced ergonomic risk exposure rather than demonstrated injury prevention, and the trade-off for prone camera was a modest increase in trunk flexion or forward reach in a subset of surgeons.

Comparing positions on ergonomics makes sense precisely because their patient-level outcomes are similar, with no clinically important difference in complications, radiographic correction, or patient-reported outcomes between single-position prone and lateral LLIF, and the differences that exist confined to workflow.- When the clinical result does not distinguish the options, the surgeon’s own exposure becomes a fair basis for choosing, and for the prone variants, which the clinical literature treats as a single entity, it is essentially the only axis that separates them. Measuring that exposure is what makes it possible to act on it, since a surgeon cannot correct a posture he has never quantified, and preference alone gave no way to tell which setup was costing the most. To our knowledge this is the first study to measure that axis across LLIF positions with synchronized motion capture and EMG resolved by surgical phase. Instrumented ergonomic assessment in spine surgery otherwise remains sparse and dominated by self-report,

 and existing prone reports emphasize patient and workflow outcomes. Each surgeon served as his own control, isolating position effects from between-surgeon anthropometric differences.

 The value of continuous capture is visible within the observational instruments themselves. Scored once as a typical posture, REBA and RULA looked similar across positions and RULA even inverted the ranking, but the same per-frame scores summarized by how long the surgeon spent at the highest action level separated the positions and agreed with the joint-specific result. What limits a single-posture instrument is therefore not only the instrument but the decision to summarize a procedure by one snapshot.

Among the remaining positions the ranking depended on which region carried the most weight, and that dependence was itself informative, since lateral decubitus and prone seated traded a extra neck strain against a shoulder penalty. Prone seated is a reminder that measurement, not intuition, is needed. A seated posture might be expected to spare the surgeon, yet it was the least favorable on posture, since the seated surgeon reaches up and over the prone surgical field and the neck is not the limiting region. It was therefore the least suitable default for a surgeon with a shoulder problem, illustrated by the surgeon with a prior right shoulder injury, in whom prone seated produced his highest arm-elevation dose and highest sustained trapezius load, including on the injured side. Averaging across regions partly hides this trade-off, leaving lateral decubitus mid-table on posture despite being worst for the neck in all five, so a surgeon whose weak point is the neck should place it lower than its averaged rank suggests, while prone lateral represents a balanced compromise (Supplementary Table S8).

The dominant musculoskeletal effort separates into a position-modifiable component, neck flexion and shoulder or arm elevation, and a built-in component, distal-hand demand, which was present in every position and is a feature of instrument handling rather than a target for position choice. The modifiable component can be reduced without changing surgical technique by attending to position and operating-room setup, including monitor and table height, arm and elbow support, and visualization aids. The neck-flexion penalty of lateral decubitus, for example, is partly correctable by raising the table and lifting the line of sight rather than by abandoning the approach.  summarizes the advantage, cost, and relevant setup lever for each position.,,

Higher muscle amplitude is not harmful by itself, and the data illustrate why. The highest trapezius amplitudes, for example in lateral decubitus, coincided with a positive median-frequency slope, that is, high activation without measurable fatigue.

 Positions were therefore compared by sustained static load and fatigue slope rather than by mean amplitude alone, and the trapezius amplitude that did track neck posture is reported as within-surgeon support for the kinematics.

Threshold choice does not drive the conclusions, which is a strength of the within-subject design. The results rest on the direction and ranking of within-surgeon differences rather than on the absolute risk classification, since EMG was normalized to each surgeon’s own reference and joint angles were compared across positions within the same surgeon.

This study has important limitations. It included five surgeons and is descriptive rather than powered, and all were right-handed men, so handedness- and sex-related variation is not represented. The operative steps were simulated on a synthetic model rather than performed on tissue, so tissue resistance, bleeding, true instrument forces, fluoroscopy, and operative cognitive load were absent. The single model geometry and absence of clinical monitor- and fluoroscopy-directed gaze may also change the absolute size of the lateral-decubitus extra neck strain, although an effect consistent across all five surgeons is unlikely to be reversed by these factors. EMG was normalized to a session reference rather than a maximum voluntary contraction and is compared only within surgeons, and one lateral-decubitus recording truncated before the trial and implant phase. Several displayed risk boundaries lack a validated primary source, and distal-hand tracking without finger sensors was unreliable, so wrist and forearm rotation are interpreted with caution, whereas the proximal joints underlying the comparison were within physiological range. The thresholds assume a standing posture, so the stool-supported knee in prone seated is classified as High risk from its angle alone. Finally, each surgeon completed the four simulations sequentially, so later runs may have built up fatigue. Position order was randomized for each surgeon, however, so a consistent position effect is unlikely to be a fatigue artifact. Three limitations deserve emphasis. First, five right-handed male surgeons cannot stand for surgeons in general, which is why we present this as a proof of concept. Second, a laboratory differs from an operating room in ways that affect posture and muscle work. There was no tissue to cut, no bleeding, no real force between instrument and tissue, no fluoroscopy and so no C-arm to work around and no lead apron, and none of the mental load of operating on a patient. The C-arm matters most, since it limits where the surgeon can stand and may change the line of sight in lateral decubitus, the position carrying our main finding, so it could widen or narrow the difference we measured. Third, the knee result in prone seated is a flaw in the scoring rather than a finding. The scores assume the surgeon stands on the leg, but here the leg rests on a stool, so a bent knee is marked high risk from its angle alone. That result should be ignored. We keep it only to show the scoring in full.

The capture also provides synchronized kinematics and muscle activity that can drive a musculoskeletal model, for example OpenSim with the OpenSense inertial pipeline and EMG-informed methods, to estimate the internal loads reaching the cervical spine and shoulder.- The next step is a powered clinical study with maximum voluntary contraction normalization, counterbalanced position order, and patient-level covariates, linking ergonomic exposure to symptom outcomes and evaluating table height, monitor placement, and arm support within the prone-camera workflow. Loupes may offer a simpler fix than changing position. Lateral decubitus strains the neck because the surgeon looks down into the surgical field. Prismatic loupes, which bend the light so the surgeon can see the same field while holding the head more upright, should ease that strain without changing the approach. In fifteen surgeons operating in a real operating room, these loupes lowered trapezius and neck muscle activity, forward head bending, and neck pain after surgery.


A review of orthopaedic surgery found loupes to be the most effective posture aid reported in spine surgery.


Against this, loupes and headlamps add weight to the head, which raises neck load.


Whether the gain outweighs the added weight has not been tested, and the method used here could test it, since loupes can be changed while position and surgeon stay the same.

Patient position during LLIF has a substantial effect on the surgeon’s physical exposure, and this effect varies between positions that produce similar patient outcomes in the literature. Lateral decubitus produced the highest neck flexion in every surgeon, prone seated produced the highest arm and shoulder elevation, and the prone-camera setup ranked most favorable overall in all five surgeons. The lateral-decubitus neck finding held across a wide range of case volumes and across surgeons whose usual practice differed, which suggests it reflects the geometry of viewing a laterally placed surgical field from above and can be addressed by raising the line of sight through a retractor-mounted camera and elevated monitor or by adjusting table height. Surgeon ergonomic exposure is therefore a reasonable additional consideration when choosing among these positions, particularly for surgeons with a known weak point. A prospective, adequately powered clinical study is the next step to further understand the ergonomic impact of these positions in LLIF procedures. These conclusions come from five surgeons in a simulation and are offered as a proof of concept, so they indicate what is measurable and worth testing rather than what is established.

Louie, Anthony Y. Jeong, Renzo A. Laynes, Mir Amaan Ali, Kento Yamanouchi, Kenneth T. Nguyen, Jean-Christophe Leveque, Venu M. Nemani, and Aiyush Bansal in Global Spine Journal.

psychology.title: Attitudes toward treating functional neurological disorders: psychological service provider perspectives
psychology.abstract: Functional neurological disorders (FND) are characterized by involuntary sensory, motor, and/or other seemingly neurological symptoms lacking expected medical explanation. Once diagnosed, patients often are referred to mental health providers for psychotherapy, which is effective in treating many FND symptom presentations either alone or as part of an integrative approach. Mental health providers may feel reluctant or unprepared to accept these referrals, however.We conducted a U.S.-based online survey of 286 practicing psychological service providers (psychologists, psychiatrists, counselors, social workers in private practice, neuropsychologists) to examine knowledge of, attitudes toward, and preparedness to treat FND.Findings revealed that most of our sample had limited exposure to FND in routine practice. Confidence in treating FND was modest, with neuropsychologists reporting more knowledge of and more confidence in treating FND than other psychologists/mental health providers. Greater perceived adequacy of psychotherapy training for, and more experience working with, FND each were associated with more positive FND attitudes, including greater confidence and enjoyment in treating FND and greater belief that symptoms would improve.This study is novel in its examination of knowledge and attitudes among psychological service providers, who are pivotal in furnishing effective treatment for FND patients but may not be well-versed in their needs. In contrast to existing studies of medical providers that revealed stigma as a major barrier to providing adequate care for FND, our findings suggest lack of knowledge and lack of access to FND patients may limit the ability to gain more training and expertise. Targeted training and consultation for mental health providers may improve confidence and motivation and expand the workforce capable of delivering effective treatment for FND.
psychology.text:
Functional neurological disorders (FND) are characterized by various symptoms including sensory, motor, and cognitive symptoms lacking expected medical explanation. In the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5th Edition (DSM-5-TR), FND is listed as Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder, with Conversion Disorder listed parenthetically (). There are two major or most common subtypes of FND (which are heterogeneous in presentation and can co-occur): Functional movement disorder (FMD) and functional/dissociative seizures (FDS). FMD consists of movement symptoms without distinctly identifiable neurological origin, and diagnosis requires a physical examination from a neurologist trained in movement disorders (). In addition to information from a neurologist’s examination, diagnosis of FDS (also known as psychogenic non-epileptic seizures) requires the presence of seizure-like behaviors without epileptic cortical activity during the FDS events based on video electroencephalogram (vEEG) (, ). Per a recent review, estimated FND incidence is 10-22/100,000 and estimated minimum prevalence is 80-140/100,000, with an estimated prevalence range of 50-1,600/100,000 (). Because FND symptoms outwardly mimic neurological ones, patients typically present for diagnosis and treatment in neurology clinics or are referred to neurologists from emergency departments (). Although prognosis for FND is generally unfavorable, younger age of onset and earlier diagnosis after symptom onset are associated with better outcomes (), and treatment can be promising as discussed below.

After an FND diagnosis is confirmed, the neurologist must communicate sensitively that the condition is FND () rather than the presumed counterpart neurological condition, and that psychological treatment is recommended – either on its own or as part of an interdisciplinary approach. The patient is then referred to mental health professionals for psychiatric care and psychotherapy. This is often counterintuitive, as the observed FND symptoms (e.g., seizures, tremors, paralysis) are not inherently associated with psychotherapy. Thus, even after addressing the major challenges of 1) diagnosing FND and 2) facilitating the patient’s acceptance of the diagnosis and willingness to seek psychological services, an equally serious challenge arises: determining and ensuring the availability of knowledgeable mental health providers willing and able to treat FND. As discussed below, there are a host of reasons why psychologists and other mental health providers may be reluctant to treat FND, including both a lack of knowledge and preconceived notions about these conditions.

Systematic examination of mental health provider perspectives is essential, because without understanding how to create an adequate mental health treatment pipeline, patients may return to their neurologist and/or otherwise remain in a cycle without proper treatment. To address this issue, we conducted a survey to investigate U.S.-based mental health providers’ knowledge of FND, services provided for FND, attitudes toward FND patients, and FND-related training experiences and attitudes.

The key impetus for assessing psychological service providers’ knowledge of and attitudes toward FND is that psychotherapy, either as a stand-alone treatment (especially for FDS) or in the context of interdisciplinary treatment modalities (e.g., including physical, occupational, and/or speech therapy for FMD), is essential for FND treatment [reviewed in () and ()]. Although treating comorbid conditions with psychiatric medication may improve quality of life and stress, there is no current medication to directly ameliorate FND symptoms (, ).

For FDS, which is the most common subtype of FND, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have pointed to significant improvement with psychotherapy, specifically cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and neurobehavioral therapy (NBT) (, ) see () and () for review and meta-analysis). For example, FDS-tailored CBT has improved FDS frequency and severity, quality of life, and comorbid psychological conditions (, , ). The large multi-site Cognitive Behavioural Therapy vs Standardised Medical Care for Adults with Dissociative Non‐Epileptic Seizures (CODES) trial found greater treatment effectiveness after a 12-month follow up when CBT was added to Standard Medical Treatment versus Standard Medical Treatment alone, with respect to period of time without seizures (albeit without differences in seizure frequency) and subjective quality of life indicators (e.g., less bothered by seizures, less impact of seizures on functioning) (–). Other psychotherapy approaches also have shown evidence of effectiveness, including Retraining and Control Therapy (ReACT) for pediatric FDS (), mindfulness-based therapy (), psychoeducation (), psychodynamic therapy (), interdisciplinary brief psychotherapeutic intervention (), and trauma-focused therapy, including based on pre-RCTs and a small RCT of prolonged exposure (–). Whereas for FDS, physical therapy and physiotherapy interventions typically would not be recommended unless there are additional motor or sensory symptoms, these latter treatments are part of a first-line approach for FMD (, ). For FMD, randomized feasibility and clinical trials demonstrate treatment efficacy with physiotherapy and a combination of CBT plus physiotherapy interventions [ (, , ); also reviewed in ()]. For example, in the Physio4FMD RCT, although there were not differences in the primary outcome of physical functioning, physiotherapy was associated with greater perceived or subjective control over motor symptoms (59% of patients working with a physiotherapy specialist reported improvement after 12 months versus 38% given treatment as usual), alongside improvement in subjective indicators of quality of life and functioning (, ).

Much of the research examining healthcare provider perspectives and experiences with FND has focused on physicians, primarily neurologists/epileptologists and psychiatrists [reviewed in () and ()]. While these studies provide invaluable insight as to the clinical challenges that arise when treating patients with FND, they often overlook the roles of most mental health care providers. Mental health provider perspectives are critical to include, because once neurological conditions are ruled out and FND is diagnosed, mental health providers are responsible for implementing intricate treatment plans involving psychotherapeutic intervention, which is the treatment of choice for FDS and integral to an interdisciplinary approach for FND. A small qualitative study underscored psychotherapists’ challenges working with FDS patients after they have undergone an often-lengthy and confusing diagnostic process; furthermore, therapists lack clear guidance from the field regarding how to meet the individual treatment needs of this heterogeneous patient group (). This is in contrast to the substantial efforts by the neurology community to train their providers in FND, and to provide guidance in working with this population. These prior findings provide an important foundation for the current study, which addresses perceptions with a larger range of providers.

Negative healthcare provider attitudes towards patients with FND (e.g., that patients are difficult or unpleasant to work with, both in general and compared with other patients) have been documented across specialties within medicine and, albeit to a lesser extent, psychology (–). Although the literature surrounding FND has changed over time, with neurologists and other specialties more knowledgeable about FND as a legitimate neuropsychiatric condition, many health care professionals still view FND as less legitimate than neurological conditions and often attribute symptoms to malingering, manipulation, attention seeking, or disability seeking (–). These attitudes are demonstrated based on implicit as well as explicit measures among a heterogeneous sample of healthcare providers (e.g., combining neurologists, psychiatrists, psychologists, and others) and are associated with lower likelihood of making appropriate referrals (). Thus, this stigma may have real consequences for who is willing to treat, or even gain knowledge about how to treat, FND.

Mental health professionals (e.g., psychologists, psychiatrists, mental health counselors, clinical social workers) who are trained to provide psychotherapy to treat emotional, behavioral, psychological, interpersonal, or other difficulties can be in a strong position to treat FND. Different modalities, therapeutic techniques, and specific tools that providers already may deploy in their day-to-day practice likely apply to FND. For example, in addition to developing a narrative of the patient’s history, treatments for FDS typically include psychoeducation, symptom monitoring with seizure logs, sensory grounding (e.g., to prevent the onset of an episode), emotion and/or trauma processing, cognitive restructuring, mindfulness, and other strategies for emotion regulation, self-care, and problem-solving (). Knowledge that psychotherapy can help alleviate FND symptoms across theoretical orientation and provider type () could pave the way for mental health providers who may not ordinarily treat FND to provide these services.

Neuropsychologists, who are trained as clinical psychologists while also receiving specialized training in brain-behavior relationships and the assessment of those relationships, play a unique role for FND patients. They often work closely with neurologists, including working in medical settings with epileptologists and movement disorder specialists, and therefore may be more likely than other types of psychologists and mental health providers to encounter individuals with FND and serve as a point of contact for psychoeducation and referrals. Additionally, patients of any kind reporting cognitive complaints would likely be referred to a neuropsychologist for testing. Given that the primary role of neuropsychologists is to provide assessment rather than ongoing psychological treatment including psychotherapy, FND patients referred to a neuropsychologist would likely need to be referred again to a mental health provider for therapy, perpetuating the cycle of multiple referrals and providers. To the extent that neuropsychologists have received training that allows them to provide therapy or otherwise feel equipped to address FND symptoms, and to the extent that their role (e.g., job responsibility allocation) builds in time for the provision of therapy, they could provide an additional and important avenue for patient care.

A large majority of patients are referred by neurologists to mental health providers in the community with the expectation that these providers understand FND and are equipped to effectively manage the care of these patients. These providers may not believe they have adequate training in FND to competently treat the complexity of this population. This may lead to patients re-presenting to neurology due to continued FND symptoms despite efforts to pursue mental health treatment. Thus, this can lead to helplessness and frustration for the neurologist and for the patient.

While mental health providers are typically trained in CBT, psychodynamic therapy, mindfulness, or other psychotherapeutic approaches that may be applicable to FND, their exposure to FND is often limited. Although psychodynamically-oriented training programs in the past may have discussed the concept of conversion symptoms and disorders, and training programs that emphasize a medical model may discuss diagnostic (DSM) criteria for somatic symptom disorders, a gap remains in bridging to current thinking about FND. To our knowledge, most clinical and counseling graduate programs and even clinical internships in the United States do not provide training experiences focused on FND, which can result in less enthusiasm for working with this population and/or psychologists viewing themselves as unprepared to work with this population.

Psychologists familiar with traditional diagnostic nomenclature and concepts could be expected to have knowledge of the Freudian notion of Conversion Disorder and of other mental health-related illness presentations [e.g., somatic symptoms associated with anxiety and depression; bodily symptoms in populations that express distress somatically ()]. They may not know to consider applying this knowledge when encountering or working with FND patients, especially if their training settings did not offer exposure to these patients. Even in a mental health context, neurological-seeming behaviors (e.g., seizures, tremors) are likely to be taken at face value and perceived as requiring neurological/medical intervention.

The current study is one of few that investigates mental health providers’ knowledge of, extent of training in, and comfort in providing treatment to patients with FND. We assessed this online in a national (primarily U.S.-based) sample through providers’ quantitative ratings and open-ended responses.

We anticipated that participants would report, first, limited knowledge of and experiences with FND and, second, mean ratings reflecting negative attitudes toward working with FND patients, including negative expectations, perceptions that FND patients are challenging to treat, a belief that FND symptoms are unlikely to improve, and minimal confidence in treating FND. Third, we expected that participants would report feeling minimally prepared based on their training to provide psychotherapy for FND and would report barriers to training, such as a lack of access to available training opportunities. Finally, we expected that more FND knowledge, experience, and perceived training preparedness would be associated with less negative and more positive attitudes toward working with FND.

Additionally, given the role of neuropsychologists in bridging neurology and psychology, we compared neuropsychologists with other (i.e., non-neuropsychologist) psychologists/mental health providers, and explored alternative possibilities that neuropsychologists would either report more positive attitudes toward FND than other mental health providers, given greater training and knowledge, or would report more negative attitudes, given working more closely with medical providers where there may be more stigma as documented previously ().

illustrates a framework for how the complex factors involved in FND as described above may come together to hinder the provision of psychological treatment for FND. For example, patients may not be referred to psychologists/other mental health providers, and if they are, providers may not feel they have the needed expertise, may believe that FND reflects an underlying medical condition requiring a different set of providers, and/or may have other perceptions or concerns that result in the turning down of referrals that do come to their practice.

The study aims and methodology were approved by the Institutional Review Board; below we follow STROBE sample reporting guidelines for cross-sectional observational studies (). Our focus was on providers with psychologically-based clinical training experiences who were in practice and providing mental health treatment or assessment.

Our recruitment strategy comprised emails, listserv announcements, and direct outreach aimed at mental health providers nationwide in a variety of settings (e.g., behavioral health hospitals, academic hospitals, outpatient clinics, private/group practice) and with different approaches and roles (e.g., trauma therapists, neuropsychologists, CBT practitioners). Recipients were asked to pass the information to other relevant individuals.

To encourage participation across the possible range of FND knowledge, recruitment materials included this statement, “Even if you have no knowledge about FNDs, you are invited to participate, as we are interested in learning about the scope of knowledge and understanding across a range of providers.” These methods captured psychologists and other kinds of mental health providers (e.g., counselors, clinical social workers) but also resulted in survey completion from those in adjacent fields outside of psychology/mental health.

Of the 473 respondents who initially began the survey, 134 did not meet inclusion criteria, namely having a clearly indicated psychology and/or psychotherapy background or practice, and were excluded prior to any analysis. They comprised 98 physical therapists, two occupational therapists, two psychometrists, three physicians (one epileptologist, two double- or multi-board certified in neurology and other specialties), two nurses, three unspecified “other,” seven trainees, and 17 who did not identify their provider type. Of the remaining 339 respondents, we excluded 53 who did not provide data through and beyond the FND definition. Our final sample of 286 participants included 177 neuropsychologists, 77 psychologists, 20 counselors, seven social workers in private practice, and five psychiatrists. For comparisons of neuropsychologists with other mental health practitioners providing care for FND, we combined the latter four groups (n = 109). We note that all of the participating counselors, social workers, and psychiatrists either worked in private/group practice or community mental health settings and/or were providing psychotherapy to FND patients in those or other settings. Although all psychologists/neuropsychologists were not necessarily providing psychotherapy to FND patients at the time of the survey, they offered therapy, assessment, or other related services and presumably received the theoretical and practical training relevant to testing our study aims.

The online survey comprised questions regarding participants’ demographics, professional background, and practice characteristics; their attitudes toward and knowledge of FND and its treatment; their desired and completed education and training for FND; and perceived barriers to that training. Items were adapted from previous similar studies that focused primarily on medical providers (e.g., neurologists/epileptologists) (, , –). Our goal was to maximize participation of full-time psychological service providers; we therefore followed prior similar studies [e.g ()] and minimized time burden by using single, face-valid items to assess FND knowledge, attitudes, and training.

Participants reported their profession (i.e., provider type), years in practice, practice setting, and geographic region, as well as age, gender, and racial/ethnic background.

An initial open-ended question assessed knowledge of FND as follows: “To your knowledge, what is a ‘functional neurological disorder’ (FND)? Also, to your knowledge, what are some examples? If you do not know, please say don’t know.”

First, we coded as “0” responses where participants made explicit mention of uncertainty or not knowing what FND is (e.g., “I don’t know” or “I’m not sure”), without providing any additional information. Second, for any attempt at a definition, we rated level of understanding as “1” = minimal/weak understanding, “2” = moderate or “so-so” understanding, or “3” = strong understanding. A trained undergraduate research assistant and a trained graduate student (co-author LH) each coded the definitions. Both individuals coded all responses. Percent agreement was 77%, with a weighted kappa of.760. For definitions on which there were disagreements, they were resolved via discussion and adjudication by a third reviewer (co-author NR). Analyses with these ratings used a final scale of 0 to 3, where 0 reflected responses of “I don’t know” without a definition or further information provided, and 1, 2, or 3 were the aforementioned codes (weak, moderate, strong) for any definition (or speculation) provided. Finally, concepts and terms that frequently emerged in participants’ definitions were coded (e.g., mention of conversion disorder, mention of FND as a disorder of exclusion), with a “1” assigned if present. Examples of definitions assigned different codes are included in the .

After participants provided their own definition, the survey presented the following brief FND definition on which participants could anchor their remaining survey responses: “Functional neurological disorders (FND), such as psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES), historically have been described as conversion disorders. They are symptoms that may appear neurological but do not have the expected medical/neurological basis. In PNES, for example, the person shows seizure-like symptoms yet does not have epilepsy or any brain-based signs of a seizure.”

Participants used a slider with percentages from 0 to 100 to indicate percentage of their patients with FND. Using checkboxes (multiple selections were allowed), participants indicated if they provided psychotherapy, psychological assessment, neuropsychological assessment, medication management, and/or other treatment to FND patients, as well as if they provided FND patients with referrals to other providers for psychotherapy or medication management. They also used checkboxes (again, with multiple selections allowed) to indicate the type of psychotherapy they provided for FND (e.g., cognitive-behavioral therapy, trauma-focused therapy), including an option for “other therapy.”

Attitudes toward FND were assessed with a series of items developed for this study based on themes and items adapted from previous studies as noted above. Participants were asked five questions on a Likert scale (1=strongly disagree to 5=strongly agree) regarding whether they found patients with FND to be 1) “more challenging to work with than other patients,” 2) “more enjoyable to work with than other patients; and whether they 3) “get concerned that FND patients’ symptoms are in fact neurological/medical,” 4) “feel that patients with FND should be working with a medical provider regarding their symptoms instead of a psychological services provider”; and 5) “have negative expectations about working with FND patients.” They also rated their confidence in treating FND patients on a 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident) scale and rated, “To what extent do you believe patients with FND can have symptom improvement?” on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much).

After asking participants to rate these items regarding attitudes toward FND, we provided an opportunity in an open-ended fashion: “Please indicate anything else you would like to mention regarding working with patients with FND.”

FND training perceptions, experiences, interest, and barriers were assessed. First, participants were asked to rate (1=little to no adequate training to 5=very well trained) whether they believed they had adequate training to provide psychotherapy, medication management, psychological assessment, or neuropsychological assessment, respectively, for patients with FND. Second, using checkboxes, participants were asked to indicate the types of FND training previously received (e.g., via graduate coursework, during a practicum rotation; multiple selections were allowed). Third, participants rated (1=not at all interested to 5=very interested) their interest in specific kinds of training for FND (e.g., professional conference presentations, private supervision/consultation). Fourth, participants rated (1=not at all interested to 5=very interested) in retrospect how interested they would have been in each of several FND training opportunities at the time of their educational training (e.g., graduate coursework, rotation on an epilepsy monitoring unit/in a movement disorders clinic). Finally, participants rated how much each of several items would be a barrier to obtaining education in FND at present (1=not a barrier at all to 5=a very large barrier) and were prompted to respond in an open-ended fashion to the item, “Please indicate any other barriers you envision to your obtaining education in functional neurological disorders now.”

After providing informed consent, participants completed a brief (designed to be completed in ~10 minutes) online survey administered via Qualtrics.com, a secure data collection platform. The survey was completed anonymously. Participants were given the option of providing their contact information at the end of the survey (linked separately) for entry into a drawing for one of two $50 gift cards. All procedures were approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board and participation was voluntary.

Data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics software (v29.0.2). Given the study aims, results are largely descriptive (i.e., summaries of quantitative and categorized open-ended responses), with bivariate Pearson product-moment (r) correlations used to test associations between attitudes toward FND patients and providers’ FND knowledge, training, and experience (with pairwise deletion of missing data). Spearman’s rho (ρ) correlations are also reported for reference, given the use of single-item measures. To compare background, experiences, and attitudes between psychologists/mental health providers and neuropsychologists, univariate analysis of variance (with partial eta squared as a measure of effect size) was used for continuous variables, and chi-square and post hoc pairwise tests of proportions (with z-values representing adjusted standardized residuals for the latter) were used for categorical variables. For these comparisons, family-wise corrections for multiple tests used the Holm’s sequential Bonferroni procedure, which has been used in neuropsychological research and is less conservative than the traditional Bonferroni procedure ().

Based on mean ratings, cost, time, and access to in-person training locations were the top three barriers to obtaining training about FND at present; however, these mean ratings were not particularly elevated (see ). Rather, the low volume of FND patients encountered was stated repeatedly in participants’ open-ended responses as a barrier to obtaining further training. Several participants also noted a lack of available supervisors for FND cases. Thus, the cost-benefit ratio may be a barrier to training for providers with a low number of FND patients, rather than a lack of FND interest or training opportunities per se.

Means, standard deviations, and intercorrelations among provider attitudes toward working with FND patients (seven single items) are presented in . Attitudes were related in the expected directions, with the two more disparate items (i.e., concern symptoms might be neurological/medical, and belief that a medical provider would be better than a psychological services provider) less consistently related to positive and negative (affective/emotion-related) attitudes. Providers on average endorsed the belief that symptoms can improve, which was the most strongly-endorsed attitude. Although they perceived working with FND patients as challenging, they did not report high negative expectations with respect to working with FND patients.

Participants who perceived that their prior training prepared them to provide psychotherapy to patients with FND reported that they were more confident and had fewer negative expectations in working with FND patients, found them more enjoyable and less challenging to work with, and held a greater sense that symptoms can improve. They also rated less concern that symptoms were actually neurological/medical (see ). Findings were similar but showed fewer significant associations with respect to perceived adequacy of training to provide psychological or neuropsychological assessment for FND.

After asking providers to rate items assessing their attitudes toward FND, we asked them to indicate anything else they would like to mention regarding working with patients with FND. Approximately half of the sample (n = 153 or 53.5%) responded to this item. Many of the responses echoed participants’ ratings, in terms of expressing a belief that symptoms can improve and that those with FND are both enjoyable and challenging to treat [also consistent with prior qualitative findings described in ()]. Comments underscored many of the systemic challenges facing those with FND and the consequences for mental health service providers, particularly those delivering psychotherapy and/or assessment. Many comments reflected a lack of awareness regarding established treatment protocols for FND, and, even with awareness of such protocols, there was a reported lack of guidance regarding how to access them easily and how to tailor them to a heterogeneous range of FND clients. Other providers in our sample expressed a lack of contact with FND patients, and a tone of ambivalence or neutrality was more salient across responses than one of criticality or negativity. Multiple comments reflected possibilities for addressing gaps that otherwise perpetuate unmet patient need, such as via neuropsychologists as noted below (see Discussion). These and other themes and examples are provided in the .

While many neuropsychologists provide psychotherapy or other forms of intervention in addition to offering testing and recommendations, we expected that FND knowledge and training experiences would differ between neuropsychologists and non-neuropsychologists (described here as psychologists/mental health providers). Age, years in practice, and gender distribution did not differ between neuropsychologists and non-neuropsychologists in our sample; there were some differences in practice setting, and more neuropsychologists were non-Hispanic White, and more psychologists/mental health providers were Hispanic/Latino (see ; ).
