Finally, with respect to attitudes toward treating FND (see ), neuropsychologists reported more confidence in working with FND than psychologists/mental health providers, yet greater negative expectations. With statistical correction for multiple comparisons, there were not significant group differences in how challenging FND patients were perceived, in the belief that symptoms could improve, or in the concern that symptoms were actually medical or that a medical (instead of psychological) service provider should treat FND.

Psychotherapeutic interventions are integral to FND treatment, yet psychologists and other mental healthcare providers may not have the training, nor awareness of the extent of unmet patient need, to be able and willing to support FND patients. This is especially relevant for patients with FDS, for whom psychotherapy is the primary treatment of choice. Guidelines for neurologists that include referring to clinicians for psychosocial or other intervention () may be challenging to implement without an adequate provider base, leaving well-intentioned neurologists at a loss.

The present survey study aimed to gain a better understanding of the perspectives and practices of psychologists, neuropsychologists, and other mental healthcare providers in the U.S. with respect to FND.

Findings yielded encouraging results, demonstrating that knowledge about FND is evolving. Definitions included but extended beyond conversion disorder and medically unexplained symptoms. Providers overall reported interest in gaining more knowledge about FND. They also reported a strong belief that FND symptoms can improve, as shown in both their quantitative and open-ended responses. Prior literature has often described providers’ stigmatizing beliefs and attitudes as a primary obstacle to successful FND healthcare experiences. However, there is also evidence, including the relatively low mean ratings and infrequent open-ended reports of such attitudes in our sample, that ideas about FND are changing (). Although some negative attitudes were expressed in participants’ open-ended comments, they focused largely on systemic issues rather than patient-specific ones. Open-ended comments also conveyed both empathy for patients’ experience and a level of optimism regarding the potential for FND symptoms to improve with psychological treatment.

These results are novel and do not merely echo prior research that reported negative provider perceptions of FND. Rather, they parallel themes of “frustration and hope” found in previous qualitative work (). In addition to a possible shift in attitude across the board as providers gain more awareness of FND (with greater guidelines for neurologists in addressing FND as noted above), our results may suggest that mental health care provider attitudes may be less negative than medical providers (). This is particularly encouraging, because when providers treating FND hold less stigmatizing attitudes and feel more engaged in their clinical services to FND patients, improved treatment outcomes are likely. Positive attitudes also are important, given that most psychologists have a choice as to whether to take on FDS patients or to serve as part of an interdisciplinary team to treat FMD patients (i.e., whereas those working in a neurology milieu may not have such a choice).

Our data revealed an absence of contact or interaction with FND patients among psychologists/mental health providers as potentially problematic, as it may self-perpetuate the cycle of less knowledge, greater reluctance, and fewer available providers. Findings revealed that a larger percentage of FND patients in one’s practice and greater perceived preparedness to provide psychotherapy to FND – and not simply extent of knowledge about FND – were associated with fewer negative expectations and more enjoyment working with FND patients. Knowledge may be a critical starting point, but does not necessarily translate into positive attitudes and a willingness to take on patients with FND in one’s practice. Instead, providers who begin with a greater inclination to work with this population may be able to better anticipate the value and benefit of working with them; reciprocally, actively working with FND patients may promote more positive views and attitudes. Providers can further enhance the therapeutic alliance by understanding illness perception in FND patients, acknowledging their perceived lower control over their disorder, and by providing psychoeducation regarding the biopsychosocial complexities of FND ().

Unexpectedly, lack of access to training per se was not reported as a barrier to gaining more knowledge about FND. Rather, the high ratio of cost (in terms of time and investment) to benefit was a notable barrier for providers who were only treating a small percentage of FND patients, or none at all. Even providers describing an interest in making such an investment noted that there was a lack of access to FND patients to further develop their treatment skills. In other words, whereas in certain medical settings (e.g., epilepsy monitoring units, movement disorders clinics) FND patients are present irrespective of the provider’s expertise and interest, paradoxically, psychologists may not regularly – or ever – encounter FND patients, and therefore it may require greater effort to learn how to provide treatment for this population most effectively.

Close to half of our sample reported conducting psychotherapy as the service provided to FND patients, either alone or with assessment. Consistent with prior literature suggesting CBT is the primary type of treatment for FND (FDS and, where applicable, FMD), the majority of participants in our sample offering psychotherapy reported using CBT with FND patients, over half with an additional treatment modality (e.g., mindfulness-based, psychodynamic). This finding is encouraging, given that current recommendations for enhanced CBT, in the form of neurobehavioral therapy (NBT), combines components from multiple theoretical orientations. Based on their open-ended responses, providers are clearly drawing on a range of approaches – from psychoeducation to music therapy to family therapy – to address and/or treat FND. Continuing to not only develop new treatment protocols (e.g., such as NBT), but also to disseminate established protocols more widely and systematically; to provide guidance on how best to tailor them to unique patient needs; and to convey how clinicians can leverage skills they already have to treat FND are crucial next steps for the field.

The neuropsychologists in our sample reported more knowledge of FND, greater perceived training preparedness, and greater confidence in working with FND than the non-neuropsychologists/mental health providers. At the same time, neuropsychologists reported more negative expectations than non-neuropsychologists about working with FND. As we initially speculated, it is possible that closer contact with neurologists and other medical providers is associated with greater confidence and perhaps also greater stigma in attitudes toward FND. The nature of assessment itself (e.g., specific measures administered, short-term interaction with the client) is typically more structured and standard than ongoing therapy, which may result in more preparedness and confidence even when working with a complex condition such as FND.

Neuropsychologists’ knowledge of FND may be particularly important in the early stages of the patient’s understanding of their diagnosis and of treatment options, at the time when they are initially (or subsequently) assessed. As participants noted in their open-ended responses, presenting recommendations during an assessment feedback session also is an opportunity to educate other family members/caregivers (for pediatric or adult patients) about FND. Furthermore, neuropsychologists (or anyone conducting assessments) who use a testing battery and intake questions specifically for FND can provide essential information that will guide the treatment provider. Using performance validity tests during neuropsychological evaluation can enhance standard battery results and guide treatment by distinguishing between subjective and objective cognitive complaints (). This further equips providers to select interventions (i.e., therapy modalities) that target specific psychological factors that may contribute to the cognitive performance results, allowing for opportunities for improvement in both domains. For example, patients found to have psychological trauma and PTSD symptomatology may be best treated with trauma-informed treatment. Collectively, although neuropsychologists may not be directly treating FND patients with these modalities, they can assist in guiding multidisciplinary treatment and goal setting due to having a distinct understanding of the patient’s cognitive profile, as reviewed in ()]. As functional cognitive disorder (FCD) becomes better known (, ), neuropsychologists may play an increasingly pivotal role in differential diagnosis.

Approximately 28% of the neuropsychologists in our sample were providing psychotherapy to FND patients. Multiple participants suggested that neuropsychologists could be more involved in therapy or interdisciplinary treatment for FND. We echo the role of neuropsychologists as an important bridge between neurologists, who are the providers encountering and diagnosing FND patients, and community mental health providers, who conduct therapy but would not routinely encounter FND. There is also an opportunity for neuropsychologists to enter the referral pipeline by providing more FND treatment, and even to spearheading interdisciplinary treatment clinics as noted below.

There are several notable limitations of this study, including sampling bias and potential lack of generalizability. We focused on knowledge, training, and attitudes of providers within the U.S., which may not reflect those of providers in other countries given likely healthcare system infrastructure and cultural differences. However, we cast a broad net by recruiting mental health providers across the U.S. and in a variety of practice environments to maximize representativeness with respect to practice characteristics. We also emphasized in our recruitment materials that providers did not need to be familiar with FND to take the survey. Consequently, many of our providers did not regularly encounter or work with patients with FND. We believe this reflects the general population of psychologists/mental health professionals, consistent with our initial speculation, although this cannot be confirmed based on the present design. At the same time, it is likely that we attracted clinicians for whom FND is more salient. Perhaps reflecting the salience of FND to certain sub-disciplines, we had a high proportion of neuropsychologists in our sample, but fewer than anticipated mental health providers/therapists, especially from disciplines such as counseling and clinical social work. Thus, in our subgroup comparisons we combined across the non-neuropsychology groups, as these specialties are similar overall in their focus on psychotherapy during training, rather than on assessment of neurocognitive functioning.

Further, 29% of participants overall (and 41% of neuropsychologists in our sample) reported having had an internship or fellowship with an epilepsy or movement disorders rotation, which may be higher than the general population of mental health/neuropsychologist practitioners. We did not assess whether participants had different training and practice experiences with subtypes of FND, such as FMD versus FDS. Given that treatment differs in important ways for these subtypes, it would be important in future studies to be more differentiated regarding how psychotherapists are delivering therapy in an individual context (more common for FDS) or integrating with multidisciplinary teams (e.g., therapies for movement, sensory, speech, and swallowing difficulties that are more likely to characterize FMD).

Another limitation of our study is the use of self-report, which is subject to social desirability bias even with anonymous questionnaires. This may be especially the case when assessing undesirable attitudes (e.g., negative perceptions of FND). Additionally, survey items were adapted from prior literature investigating FND-related attitudes, beliefs, and training among providers from other health care specialties (e.g., neurology, psychiatry, nursing, physical therapy), and those studies primarily used single items (, , –). While the current authors were guided by domain-related norms in terms of the approach and specific items they used (e.g., one study we used as a model consulted with the FDS task force of the International League Against Epilepsy [ILAE] when designing their questionnaire () survey items were not subjected to formal psychometric validation, potentially limiting reliability and replicability of the results.

There were also limitations with respect to specific items. For example, with respect to training attitudes, we asked, “How adequate was your training in preparing you to treat FND?” Ratings, therefore, may have reflected either FND-specific training (e.g., psychotherapy for FND), and/or perceptions of training in general (e.g., in psychotherapy), which respectively allowed participants to feel equipped (or not) to treat FND. Importantly, we do not have information on attitudes (e.g., confidence, enjoyment, negative expectations) in working with patients without FND. Consequently, comparisons of neuropsychologists and psychologists/mental health providers (e.g., greater confidence among neuropsychologists) may reflect general differences between these two groups, rather than FND-specific ones. Finally, the coding system used to categorize definitions of FND was developed for this study. Therefore, although it is face-valid, its reliability and generalizability are untested.

Our study is one of the few to focus on mental health care providers’ knowledge of and attitudes toward FND. We recruited clinicians nationally within the US and across practice settings, which allowed us to assess perceptions among clinicians on the potentially receiving end of FND referrals, versus solely those embedded in FND and/or medically/neurologically-focused clinics.

Our findings underscore the importance of collaboration among psychologists/mental health providers, neuropsychologists, neurologists, and other specialists to exchange knowledge and coordinate medical and mental health treatment (, ). There are already a small but growing number of FND clinics embedded in inpatient and outpatient settings, and these serve as important treatment models. Gilmour et al. () suggest creating an FND clinic that shares similarities with other complex care centers, and their paper provides an example of a clinic structure for patients with FMD. Barbey et al. () provides an overview of their first Swiss FND clinic (both inpatient and outpatient settings). They suggest an interdisciplinary approach to treatment with individualized treatment for each patient. Finkelstein et al. () provide guidelines for setting up an FND interdisciplinary clinic that offers multiple therapies to FND patients, which aims to reduce costs, save time, and increase consistency for patients. These clinics are not a “one size fits all” approach but rather allow for adaption to changing FND symptoms over time ().

Nevertheless, as establishing infrastructure for FND treatment is still in its infancy in many geographic areas, community mental health providers are needed for continued mental health treatment (especially for those with FDS, where stand-alone psychotherapy is recommended). To facilitate transition of care, based on our findings we suggest collaboration between the diagnosing neurologists or clinic and mental health providers, specifically targeting those providers (50-75% in our study) who are relatively interested in further FND training. This could involve a specified team leader (e.g., neurologist, neuropsychologist, psychiatrist, psychologist) who will facilitate these referrals to community mental health providers willing to accept FND patients into their practices and clinics. Ongoing collaboration with neurologists may assuage initial or downstream concerns held by mental health providers about the symptoms being medical, and would offer someone they can contact during a potential medical emergency.

Additionally, it would be beneficial for mental health providers to have access to an established network of providers who offer supervision and/or consultation to mental health providers treating FND. Clinicians interested in working with FND patients and/or providing consultation about FND can designate in marketing materials that they have expertise in this area (). Another option for providers is listing their practice as part of available resources (e.g., the “Expert Information and Resources” page of www.nonepilepticseizures.com [managed by co-author LM]).

As our participants’ FND definitions highlight, effective referrals to mental health providers would likely benefit from bridging the gaps in terminology and conceptualization among conversion disorders, dissociative disorders, and FND (). One consideration is that there may be a lack of knowledge regarding the terminology of FND added to the DSM-5 (i.e., Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder). Providers may feel better equipped to treat patients if the referral conveys that the patient has “somatic symptoms.” Providers also may be more familiar with the terminology of “conversion disorder,” as was the case for a number of participants in our sample. However, this term has been associated with stigma and/or psychoanalytic modalities, and therefore newly-trained clinicians – especially in cognitive-behavioral approaches – may need yet other language to understand the context of the patient’s symptom presentation.

A key step is helping clinicians recognize that they already possess a strong skillset that they can use to treat FND, because the integration of even a small number of FND patients into one’s clinical practice may result in a meaningful difference in treatment availability. Treatments that focus on enhancing emotional awareness and distress tolerance (e.g., dialectical behavior therapy) or re-interpreting physical sensations (e.g., CBT for anxiety) are already adapted for FND. This is consistent with the integration of different theoretical orientations and approaches in NBT, an evidence-based treatment for FDS. There is mounting evidence for the efficacy of prolonged exposure therapy for FDS; because this treatment is widely known and practiced (given high prevalence of trauma and PTSD), it may be a readily-available option to address FDS symptoms (). Additionally, group therapy with FND (embedded with other neurorehabilitation therapies) may be a promising intervention when it combines psychoeducation, aspects of CBT and emotion regulation, and a biopsychosocial framework to improve coping ().

Finally, providing training experiences to clinicians through practicum placements at sites that provide psychotherapy to FND patients, adding continuing education on FND to national and international conferences, and providing internship and fellowship training to mental health providers in centers that offer a multidisciplinary approach to treatment can prepare mental health providers, including neuropsychologists, to feel confident in providing psychological treatment to FND patients.

In sum, the psychological community is in a strong position to establish larger networks of mental health providers who can treat FND by providing education and training experiences at the graduate and post-graduate levels (e.g., coursework, practica, internships, fellowships). Psychologists/neuropsychologists in medical settings who provide assessment and/or treatment for FND can foster collaborations with other disciplines such as neurology and cultivate a community network of mental health providers able to recognize and meet the FND treatment need.

psychology.title: Orthogonal Factorial Designs for Trials of Therapist‐Delivered Interventions: Randomizing Intervention‐Therapist Combinations to Patients
psychology.abstract: It is recognized that treatment‐related clustering should be allowed for in the sample size and analyses of individually‐randomized parallel‐arm trials that evaluate therapist‐delivered interventions such as psychotherapy. Here, interventions are a treatment factor, but therapists are not. If the aim of a trial is to separate effects of therapists from those of interventions, we propose that interventions and therapists should be regarded as two potentially interacting treatment factors (one fixed and one random) with a factorial structure. We consider the specific design where each therapist delivers each intervention (crossed therapist‐intervention design), and the resulting therapist‐intervention combinations are randomized to patients. We adopt a classical Design of Experiments (DoE) approach to propose a family of orthogonal factorial designs and their associated data analyses, which allow for therapist learning and center too. We set out the associated data analyses using ANOVA and regression and report the results of a small simulation study conducted to explore the performance of the proposed randomization methods in estimating the intervention effect and its standard error, the between‐therapist variance and the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect. We conclude that more purposeful trial design has the potential to lead to better evidence on a range of complex interventions and outline areas for further methodological research.
psychology.text:
Kiesler [] defined psychotherapy as lying “somewhere in the therapist and his behavior” (p. 128). Their behavior is detailed in an intervention manual [], which sets out the behaviors which are regarded as mandatory, optional, and prohibited []. The primary focus of trials is generally on estimating the effects of the intervention (e.g., the therapy or procedure). However, disentangling the effect of the therapists from the effect of the interventions has long been considered a challenge in individually‐randomized, parallel‐arm trials [, ]. Walwyn et al. [] have set out 10 possible ways of designing a trial to separate the effects of the intervention and the therapist by including therapists as a factor when generating the randomization sequence. These possibilities depend on the design of the complex intervention (the “therapist‐intervention design” [] here), which describes the structural relationships between the components of the complex intervention, irrespective of the randomization. Five types of therapist‐intervention design were proposed by Walwyn et al. []. In the first, each therapist delivers all the interventions in a “crossed” design. Using this terminology, therapists are crossed with interventions, with every combination of each therapist and intervention being observed in the trial. Crossed designs have been suggested for psychotherapy trials where the aim is to control for enduring therapist traits [], such as gender and personality, and where therapist allegiances to specific interventions are not a concern []. Crossed surgeon‐intervention designs are the predominant design in surgical trials [], as each surgeon usually undertakes all the procedures under investigation. Crossed therapist‐intervention designs are commonly used in trials of psychotherapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and rehabilitation [].

It has long been recognized that variation in average patient outcomes between therapists is expected []. More recently, it has been accepted that, likewise, patient outcomes are clustered by therapists, leading to intra‐therapist correlation (for a review, see Walwyn and Roberts []). This consensus led to guidance on trial reporting []. There has been much discussion about whether [, , ] and when [, , , ] therapists should be included as a fixed or random factor in analyses. In the early medical statistics literature, it was recommended that therapists are typically included as a random factor [, , , , ] because there is often no interest in the outcomes of specific therapists in a trial. Instead, it is assumed that therapists are a random sample from a population of interest. Statistical models have been proposed (for a summary, see []). In all cases, the random effect of the therapist was allowed to vary by intervention, leading to use of the term “treatment‐related clustering.” For crossed designs, there was a consensus that a random coefficient model is appropriate, including a fixed effect for intervention, a random effect for therapist, an intervention‐by‐therapist random effect and a patient error [, ]. A method for calculating sample size was also proposed []. For psychotherapy, and a parallel literature on individually randomized group treatment (IRGT) trials, greater attention has been given to designs in which therapists are nested or partially nested in interventions (e.g., [, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]). This has left the literature on crossed therapist‐intervention designs relatively underdeveloped.

In the statistical literature, it has largely been assumed that interventions are randomized to patients in an individually randomized, parallel‐arm design (see [, ]). In this design, interventions are not randomized to therapists, and neither are therapists randomized to patients []. So, the intervention is regarded as a treatment factor, but the therapist is not. Here, we assume both the intervention and the therapist are treatment factors, with one combination of the levels of these two treatment factors (the “treatment”) randomized to each patient (see Example A in []). We acknowledge that, in many trials, there are other contextual factors affecting the complex intervention delivered to patients that cannot be randomized. Therapists deliver interventions to patients sequentially in categorical or continuous time (see [] for a review of the surgical literature on learning curves). While various measures of therapist learning are possible (e.g., number of previous patients seen and therapist caseload), the simplest is arguably time itself. Also, ongoing supervision and intervention policies can vary across centers. Centers may be recruiting centers, clinical services, or regions, but our focus is on the way in which therapists are grouped. Here, we suggest that time and center are accounted for in the randomization by including them as stratification (or “blocking”) factors (see Figure  for a summary of the complex intervention designs considered in this article).

There is a large body of statistical work on the Design of Experiments (DoE) and their data analysis that began with Fisher []. Perhaps apart from crossover designs, this has become separated from clinical trials, despite their common origins and its relevance. So, medical statisticians are largely unaware of developments in the DoE field and experts in the DoE are largely unaware of the problems encountered in clinical trials. Typically, in the DoE literature, treatment factors are all fixed. As such, adaptations are needed to include therapists as a random treatment factor. One general approach to DoE is that described in Bailey []. Instead of giving readers a menu of recognized designs, the approach gives them tools needed to develop experimental designs for the problem presented to them. Despite the flexibility of this approach, the first 10 chapters of the book are limited to so‐called “orthogonal” designs. These are, arguably, the theoretical ideal. From our perspective, their relative simplicity makes them a good place to start.

Using Bailey's [] approach, the aim of this article is to propose a family of increasingly complex, orthogonal factorial experimental designs, and their associated data analyses, for trials of therapist‐delivered interventions, incorporating therapist learning and center. We outline two motivating examples in Section . In Section  we introduce our (i) completely randomized, (ii) randomized block, and (iii) multicenter randomized block factorial designs, each illustrated with a theoretical example, inspired by the two motivating examples. In Section  we outline the resulting data analyses. Following Bailey [], we give the analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each design first. Recognizing that trialists are often more familiar with regression, the equivalent regression analysis is also given. We summarize a small simulation study and end with a discussion and some conclusions in Sections  and , respectively.

Barkham et al. [, ] reported the design and main results of PRaCTICED, a trial embedded in the Sheffield Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) service. The patients were recruited through general practices and there were four geographical districts in Sheffield, UK. For our purpose, however, this was a single center trial, because the therapists were grouped within one IAPT service. In total, 50 therapists were involved. One of two interventions (Counseling for Depression (CfD), Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)) was randomized to 510 patients with block randomization stratified by practice, using randomly varying blocks of size 2, 4 and 6. Therapists were non‐randomly allocated to patients, and interventions started when a therapist became available in continuous time. Interventions were delivered by different samples of therapists (counselors and therapists), so a nested therapist‐intervention design was used, reflecting routine practice. It is conceivable, however, that counselors could be trained to deliver both CfD and CBT, because some counselors use an eclectic approach in practice. The advantages of a crossed relative to a nested design are twofold. First, it allows separation of the therapist and intervention‐by‐therapist random effects []. Second, fewer patients are required as the increase in sample size due to an intervention‐by‐therapist random effect is countered by a decrease in sample size required from the therapist random effect [].

Shapiro et al. [, ] reported the design and results of the Second Sheffield Psychotherapy Project. This involved a single center in the sense that the five therapists were all embedded in the research team. Patients self‐referred or were referred by general practitioners or mental health services. By design, a combination of “duration” (8 or 16 weekly sessions), “method” (cognitive behavioral psychotherapy or psychodynamic‐interpersonal psychotherapy), and “therapist” (1 to 5) was randomized to patients in each of three ranges of depression severity (low, moderate, high). So, in this trial, there was one blocking factor (severity) and three treatment factors (duration, method, therapist), even if allocation of therapists to patients was described as an extra randomization (constrained by therapist availability, personal communication). The design was equally replicated; there were two replicates of each treatment combination in each block (level of Severity), with each therapist treating two patients with each level of severity in each of the four combinations of duration and method. Therefore, this trial provides an example of an orthogonal factorial design in practice.

First consider a trial conducted in a single center, where the interventions therapists deliver remain constant over time. Patients are the experimental units, and the treatments are all combinations of the levels of two treatment factors, I (Interventions) and T (Therapists), which have nI and nT levels, respectively. Assuming the nInT treatments are each replicated nR times, the total number of patients is N=nInTnR. We assume a continuous outcome is collected on patients at a single timepoint, so the observational units are also patients. Here, treatments are randomized to patients (see Figure  for a theoretical example).

Figure  is a two‐tiered example of the randomization diagrams introduced by Brien and Bailey [] (see also []). The two boxes represent two sets of factors (or “tiers”), the set of treatments and the set of experimental units, which in this case are the patients. Following the convention of [], the arrow representing the randomization is from treatments to units. The two lines from the left‐hand tier to the black dot indicate that it is the 32 combinations of Interventions and Therapists that are randomized to the patients. In practice, randomization would be achieved by (i) numbering rows of a table from 1,…, N, (ii) assigning each of the nInT treatments to nR rows in a “systematic design”, (iii) choosing a random permutation of {1,…,N} by obtaining a sequence of distinct random numbers, (iv) assigning the random numbers to rows in order, (v) reordering the rows in the systematic design by reordering the random numbers in ascending order, and (vi) renumbering the rows in natural order, giving a random order of treatments for the rows (now patients) as they are recruited into the trial. This is equivalent to permuted block randomization with a single block, equal in size to the total number of patients. It has been described as randomizing the labels given to units []. Importantly, it leads to equal replication, which has useful properties for the analysis [].

Next, we relax the assumption that the interventions therapists deliver remain constant over time. Interventions may commence when a therapist becomes available in continuous time or at the start of a “batch” in categorical time. Suppose patients are nested in blocks that are defined by time periods, creating the blocking factor B (Batches), and assigned to nR replications of the combinations of levels of treatment factors I and T in each block. Factors I, T and B have nI, nT and nB levels respectively, and the total number of patients is N=nInTnBnR. As the precise treatment delivered to a patient can vary according to their position in their therapist's learning curve, one might consider randomizing the time interventions commence, giving nInTnB treatments. However, as in most trials, it is not possible to randomize Batches to Patients, there are nInT treatments (combinations of I and T) here as before. Treatments are randomized to patients independently in each batch (see Figure ). Batches appears in the unit tier reflecting time being a blocking rather than a treatment factor in our design.

In Figure , there are 64 patients in each batch, giving two replications of 32 treatments in each batch and 10 replications overall. Each therapist has four patients in each batch, two for each intervention, so over five batches, each therapist treats 20 patients. As such, nI=2, nT=16, nB=5 and nR=2, and the total number of patients is nInTnBnR=320. The randomization would be done by (i) numbering rows in a table from 1,…,nInTnR in each batch, (ii) assigning each of the nInT treatments to nR rows in each batch in a systematic design, (iii) choosing an independent random permutation of {1,…,nInTnR} for each batch, and finally (iv) reordering and renumbering, as before, to give the random order of treatments for patients as they are recruited. This is equivalent to permuted block randomization with nB blocks of fixed size nInTnR. Note that there are not nBnR blocks of fixed size nInT. This becomes important in the analysis (see []).

Finally, we relax the assumption that the trial is conducted in a single center. Here, patients are nested in the combinations of levels of two blocking factors, centers (C) and Batches (B). Factors C and B have nC and nB levels, respectively, creating nCnB blocks. Often therapists will already have a centre, so in this design nT Therapists are nested in each of nC Centres; it is not possible to assign Therapists to Centers. Note that previously nT denoted the total number of therapists. Patients are assigned to nR replications of the combinations of the relevant levels of treatment factors I and T in each batch in each center, so the total number of patients is N=
nInTnCnBnR. As the precise treatment delivered to each patient also varies according to the center a therapist belongs to, one might consider randomizing a combination of centers and batches, giving nInCnBnT treatments. However, usually there will only be nInCnT treatments, as there are nCnT therapists, and each intervention occurs with every therapist. So, the number of centers contributes to the number of treatments. In each combination of Centers and Batches, treatments (combinations of I and T nested in C) are independently randomized to patients (see Figure ). As Therapists and Patients are nested in Centers, the double lines connecting Centers across tiers indicates that Centers is a factor that spans both tiers. Although this situation is common in clinical trials (see []), it was not faced in any of the relevant Brien–Bailey papers [, , , , , , ].

In Figure , there are 16 treatments and 160 patients in each of six centers, so 96 treatments and 960 patients overall. There are 32 patients and two replications of the 16 treatments in each of 30 center‐batch combinations, and two replications of the 96 treatments in each batch. Each of 48 therapists has four patients in each batch, two for each intervention. So, in total each therapist treats 20 patients. Hence, nI=2, nC=6,nB=5,nT=8 and nR=2, so N=960. The randomization would be done by (i) numbering rows in a table from 1,…,nInTnR in each combination of Centres and Batches, assigning nInT treatments to each of nR patients in a systematic design, (ii) choosing an independent random permutation of {1,…, nInTnR} for each centre‐batch combination and (iii) reordering and renumbering as before to give the random order of treatments for patients as they are recruited. This is like stratified permuted block randomization with nCnB blocks of size nInTnR, except that there is no overlap in the therapists from one center to the next. There are not nCnBnR blocks of fixed size nInT.

Figure  gives a concise way of describing the randomization. However, to understand the design sufficiently to determine the data analysis, we drew Hasse diagrams (see []) of the treatment and unit factors to make the relationships between the factors in the design even clearer. In contrast to [], we found that, where treatment factors contribute both fixed and random effects, it is helpful to draw separate Hasse diagrams for fixed and random factors, rather than for treatment and unit factors (see Supplementary File  for the Hasse diagrams for our proposed designs). Because Batches and Centers form part of the complex intervention design, interactions between treatment (Interventions and Therapists) and blocking (Batches and Centers) factors are plausible. We therefore included the random factors for all block‐treatment combinations in the relevant Hasse diagram. Next, we used the Hasse diagram for the random factors to identify the eigenspaces of the variance–covariance matrix Cov(Y) of patient outcomes. Our completely randomized factorial design is relatively straightforward, since it has an orthogonal block structure in the sense defined by Houtman and Speed []. Unusually, in our randomized block factorial design and our multicenter randomized block factorial design, we found that, although fixed factor I does not contribute a new variance parameter, it was necessary to include it in the Hasse diagrams of the random factors because it contributes a random effect, which is entirely dependent on other observed random effects. We call its contribution a “dependent random effect” (for details see Supplementary File ). As a result, the block structures in our randomized block and multicenter randomized block factorial designs are not orthogonal under the Houtman and Speed [] definition (for details see Supplementary File ).

The standard linear model for the outcome variable Yω on patient ω is a sum of several terms, one for each relevant factor. A factor with fixed effects contributes a (unknown in advance) constant for each of its levels. A factor with random effects contributes a random variable for each of its levels. All the random variables have zero mean and are mutually independent, and all the random variables defined by levels of the same factor have the same variance. For each design in Figure , the corresponding Hasse diagram in Supplementary File  was used to construct the first three columns in the ANOVA table shown in Table . These ANOVA tables are called skeleton analysis of variance tables in [] because they do not include the sums of squares and mean squares which are there after experimental data become available.

Skeleton analysis of variance (ANOVA).

Note:
I∧T is the factor of combinations of levels of factors I and T, I∧B is the factor of combinations of levels of factors I and B, T∧B is the factor of combinations of levels of factors T and B, I∧T∧B is the factor of combinations of levels of factors I, T and B, I∧C is the factor of combinations of levels of factors I and C, C∧B is the factor of combinations of levels of factors C and B, and I∧C∧B is the factor of combinations of levels of factors I, C and B. Note that the vector τ0 has the overall mean in every position, and then vector τI+τ0 has the relevant treatment mean in every position. Then τ02 and τI2 are the sums of squares of the entries in τ0 and τI respectively. The ξ are the eigenvalues of Cov(Y).

The eigenspaces of Cov(Y) are the “strata” in Table  (the first column). The subspaces of the strata are the “sources of variation” (given in the second column). The dimensions of these subspaces are the degrees of freedom (given in the third column). Degrees of freedom associated with the strata are given on the right‐hand side, and those relating to the sources of variation are given on the left‐hand side. Any residual degrees of freedom are calculated by subtraction from the relevant stratum total.

The appropriate stratum for fixed factor I is identified using a Hasse diagram that combines the fixed and random factors (see Supplementary File ). In the completely randomized factorial design, the appropriate stratum is that associated with factor I∧T, which represents combinations of levels of factors I (Interventions) and T (Therapists). As can be seen in Table , the I∧T stratum has a source of variation associated with the fixed factor I and a residual, the latter sometimes being referred to as the intervention‐by‐therapist interaction. In the randomized block factorial design, the relevant stratum for fixed factor I is the subspace associated with factor I. However, the fixed effect of I takes up the whole of this, so no part of the stratum can give a residual mean square whose value can be used to provide an unbiased estimator of the appropriate residual. Instead, a linear combination of random factors is indicated. This is the case for the multicenter randomized block factorial design as well, except that the linear combination of random factors indicated differs.

The final column of Table  gives the expected mean squares. Note that the vector τ0 has the overall mean in every position, and the vector τI+τ0 has the relevant treatment mean in every position. Then τ02 and τI2 are the sums of squares of the entries in τ0 and τI respectively. The ξ are the eigenvalues of Cov(Y) (see Supplementary File  for details). These make it clear which residual is appropriate for testing the fixed effect of I and what the appropriate F tests of the random effects are (for the latter, see Supplementary File ).

In a completely‐randomized factorial design, the appropriate residual for testing the fixed effect of I is the one whose expected mean square is ξI∧T. Importantly, it is not the residual whose expected mean square is ξE or 15ξI∧T+288ξE/303, both of which are smaller than ξI∧T. If the therapist variance σT2=0 then ξT=ξI∧T and so MST/RMSI∧T has an F‐distribution on 15 and 15 degrees of freedom in the running example, where MST is the observed mean square for T and RMSI∧T the observed residual mean square for I∧T. If the therapist variance in the intervention effect σI∧T2=0, then ξI∧T=ξE and so RMSI∧T/MSE has an F‐distribution on 15 and 288 degrees of freedom in the running example, where MSE is the observed mean square for Patients.

In a randomized block factorial design, the appropriate residual for testing the fixed effect of I is one whose expected mean square is a linear combination of eigenvalues of Cov(Y), ξI∧T+ξI∧B−ξI∧T∧B. Although the random structure is not an orthogonal block structure, the linear dependence on three other eigenvalues means that a linear combination of mean squares from the ANOVA can provide an unbiased estimator of the appropriate residual mean square. Satterthwaite [] proposed that if a sample variance is a linear combination of independent mean squares, its exact distribution can be approximated by a chi‐square distribution whose effective degrees of freedom are given by a specified formula involving the relevant mean squares and their degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom for the linear combination of mean squares estimating the appropriate residual can be approximated by 
(1)
dfI=MSI∧T+MSI∧B−MSI∧T∧B2MSI∧T2nI−1nT−1+MSI∧B2nI−1nB−1+MSI∧T∧B2nI−1nT−1nB−1

where MSI∧T, MSI∧B and MSI∧T∧B are the observed mean squares for factors I∧T, I∧B and I∧T∧B, respectively. This result can be used to provide an approximate F‐test for the effect of I.

A similar situation arises in a multicenter randomized block factorial design, where the appropriate residual for testing the fixed effect of I is one whose expected mean square is ξI∧C+ξI∧B−ξI∧C∧B. The degrees of freedom for the linear combination of mean squares estimating the appropriate residual can be approximated by 
(2)
dfI=MSI∧C+MSI∧B−MSI∧C∧B2MSI∧C2nI−1nC−1+MSI∧B2nI−1nB−1+MSI∧C∧B2nI−1nC−1nB−1

where MSI∧C, MSI∧B and MSI∧C∧B are the observed mean squares for factors I∧C, I∧B and I∧C∧B. This can also be used to provide an approximate F‐test for the fixed effect of I.

In clinical trials, the linear model is often written as a regression model (see e.g., [, , , ]).

Here, the regression model for a continuous outcome for patient i
(i=1,…,320) nested in therapist j
(j=1,…,16) can be given as the following random coefficient model, 
(3)
Yij=δ0+δ1Iij+u1j+v1jIij+eij

where the notation Yij means that patients and therapists are numbered from 1 to 320 and 1 to 16, respectively. In this model, Iij are indicator variables for the intervention assigned to patient i and therapist j. The Iij are not dummy (0, 1) variables. They are treatment contrasts with coefficients that sum to zero. For two equally‐replicated interventions, a single dummy variable may be replaced by an effect‐coded (−1, 1) one; −1 for the control and 1 for the experimental intervention. Here, δ0 is the overall mean outcome, δ1 is the difference between the mean of all outcomes for each intervention and δ0, u1j is a random effect around δ0 for the jth therapist, v1j is a random effect around δ1 for the jth therapist, and eij is the patient level error. Here, u1j∼N0,σu12,v1j∼N0,σv12 and eij∼N0,σe2 and u1j,v1jandeij are all mutually independent, so σu12 is the between‐therapist variance, σv12 is the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect and σe2 is the patient‐level variance. Note that in a linear mixed model normality of random effects is nearly always assumed; this is not so in ANOVA.

To generalize Model () to nI interventions, the contrast Iij is replaced by nI−1 orthogonal contrasts, I1ij,…,InI−1ij. Each of these contrasts has coefficients that sum to zero across all patients, and each pair of contrasts is such that the product of their coefficients sums to zero across all patients. For three interventions, the two contrasts may be one coded 1/2, 1/2, and −1 and one coded 1, −1, and 0 for interventions 1, 2, and 3. Here, δ0 remains the overall mean outcome, δ11 is the difference between δ0 and the mean of all outcomes for intervention 3, and δ21 is half the difference between the mean of all outcomes for interventions 1 and 2. The variance parameters are unchanged. Except multiplying the coefficients of either contrast by a constant, and/or relabelling the interventions, there is no other meaningful orthogonal option for three interventions. For more interventions, the set of orthogonal contrasts should match any plausible structure in the interventions.

Regardless of the number of interventions, it is possible to write the eigenvalues ξE, ξI∧T, ξT and ξ0 in the ANOVA in terms of the variance components σe2, σu12 and σv12 from the regression as follows, 
(4)
ξE=σe2


(5)

(6)

(7)
ξ0=0+nInRσu12+nRσv12+σe2

In this variance components model, there is a sum of random variables, each contributing a different variance, all of which are non‐negative, and which together give the variance–covariance matrix of the outcomes. This model can be generalized by defining the variance–covariance matrix directly, so that no variance is negative, but the correlation between outcomes can be. If so‐called “negative variance components” are allowed, the regression defined in () and the ANOVA (Table ) are identical.

Here, with nI=2, the regression model for a continuous outcome Yijk for patient i(i=1,…,320) nested in a combination of therapist j
(j=1,…,16) and batch k
(k=1,…,5) can be written as a cross‐classified or crossed random effects model as follows,

Yijk=δ0+δ1Iijk+u1j+u2k+u3jk+v1jIijk+v2kIijk+v3jkIijk+eijk

where the notation Yijk means that patients, therapists and batches are numbered from 1 to 320, 1 to 16, and 1 to 5, respectively. Here, Iijk is an indicator for the intervention assigned to patient i nested in therapist j and batch k. As before, the Iijk represent an orthogonal treatment contrast, coded 1 and −1 for levels 1 and 2 of factor I, so δ0 is the overall mean, δ1 is the mean intervention effect (defined as the difference between the mean of all outcomes for each intervention and δ0), u1j is a random effect around δ0 for the jth therapist, u2k is a random effect around δ0 for the kth batch, and u3jk is a random effect around δ0+u2k for the jth therapist. Also, v1j is a random effect around δ1 for the jth therapist, v2k is a random effect around δ1 for the kth batch, v3jk is a random effect around δ1+v2k for the jth therapist, and eijk is the patient level error. Here, u1j∼N0,σu12,u2k∼N0,σu22, u3jk∼N0,σu32, v1j∼N0,σv12, v2k∼N0,σv22, v3jk∼N0,σv32 and eijk∼N0,σe2 where u1j, u2k, u3jk, v1j, v2k
v3jk and eijk are all mutually independent. Thus, σu12 is the between‐therapist variance, σu22 is the between‐batch variance, σu32 is the between‐therapist‐by‐batch interaction, σv12 is the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, σv22 is the between‐batch variance in the intervention effect, σv32 is the therapist‐by‐batch‐by‐intervention interaction and σe2 is the patient‐level variance. Model (8) can be generalized to nI interventions in the same way as Model (3).

Here, with nI=2, the regression model for continuous outcome Yijkl for patient i(i=1,…,960) nested in a combination of therapist j
(j=1,…,8) and batch k
(k=1,…5), where j is nested in centre l
(l=1,…6) and k is crossed with centre l, can be written as a cross‐classified model as, 
(9)
Yijkl=δ0+δ1Iijkl+u1j+u2k+u3jk+u4l+u5kl+v1jIijkl+v2kIijkl+v3jkIijkl+v4lIijkl+v5klIijkl+eijkl

where the notation Yijkl means that patients, therapists, batches and centres are numbered from 1 to 960, 1 to 48, 1 to 5, and 1 to 6, respectively. Here, the Iijkl are indicators for the intervention assigned to patient i nested in therapist j, batch k and center l. The Iijkl again represent a treatment contrast, coded 1 and −1 for levels 1 and 2 of factor I. Hence, δ0 is the overall mean outcome, δ1 is the mean intervention effect (defined as the difference between the mean of all outcomes for each intervention and δ0), u1j is a random effect around δ0 for the jth therapist, u2k is a random effect around δ0 for the kth batch, u3jk is a random effect around δ0+u2k for the jth therapist, u4l is a random effect around δ0 for the lth center and u5kl is a random effect around δ0+u2k for the lth center. Additionally, v1j is a random effect around δ1 for the jth therapist, v2k is a random effect around δ1 for the kth batch, v3jk is a random effect around δ1+v2k for the jth therapist, v4l is a random effect around δ1 for the lth center, v5kl is a random effect around δ1+v2k for the lth center and eijkl is the patient level error. Thus, u1j∼N0,σu12, u2k∼N0,σu22, u3jk∼N0,σu32, u4l∼N0,σu42, u5kl∼N0,σu52, v1j∼N0,σv12,v2k∼N0,σv22, v3jk∼N0,σv32, v4l∼N0,σv42, v5kl∼N0,σv52 and eijkl∼N0,σe2 where u1j, u2k, u3jk, u4l, u5kl, v1j, v2k, v3jk, v4l, v5kl and eijkl are all mutually independent. Hence, σu12 is the between‐therapist variance, σu22 is the between‐batch variance, σu32 is the between‐therapist‐by‐batch interaction, σu42 is the between‐centre variance, σu52 is the between‐center‐by‐batch interaction,σv12 is the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, σv22 is the between‐batch variance in the intervention effect, σv32 is the therapist‐by‐batch‐by‐intervention interaction, σv42 is the between‐centre variance in the intervention effect, σv52 is the centre‐by‐batch‐by‐intervention interaction, and σe2 is the patient‐level variance. Model (9) can be generalized to nI interventions in the same way as Model (3).

The relationships between the eigenvalues from the ANOVA and the variance components from the regression are given in Supplementary File  for the randomized block and multicenter randomized block factorial designs.

The analysis can be done either via the aov command or the lmer command in R (Example output is given in Supplementary File  where factor I has two or three levels). The following code can be used to obtain the ANOVA for the completely randomized factorial design:


aov1 < − aov(y ∼ I + Error(T + I:T), contrasts =
 list(I = contr.sum), data = CrossedDataset1)
summary(aov1)
coefficients(aov1)
print(model.tables(aov1,"means"))

These commands give the ANOVA table, an F test for the fixed effect of I and estimates of ξT, ξI∧T and ξE. They give estimates of δ0 and δ1 from Model (). To get F tests for the random effects of factors T and I∧T, it is necessary to calculate the F statistics by hand using the estimates of ξT, ξI∧T and ξE to get the p value.

The following code gives the regression using residual maximum likelihood (REML):


reg1 < − lmer(y ∼ I+(1|T)+(1|I:T), contrasts = 
list(I = contr.sum), data = CrossedDataset1)
summary(reg1)
ls_means(reg1, which = “I”, pairwise = TRUE)
ranova(reg1)

The regression table, a t‐test for the fixed effect of I and estimates of σu12, σv12 and σe2 can be obtained, along with the least squares mean difference for the fixed effect of I and likelihood ratio tests for the random effects σu12 and σv12. This analysis constrains the correlation between σu12 and σv12 to be zero. The contrast specified also ensures the correlation between estimates of δ0 and δ1 is zero.

The ANOVA for the randomized block factorial design can be obtained using the following code:


aov2 <- aov(y∼I+Error(I*T*B), contrasts=list
(I=contr.sum), data=CrossedDataset2)

The fixed effect of I appears in the fixed and random parts of the model. If it is omitted from the random part, R allocates the fixed effect of I to either the I∧T or I∧B stratum, depending on whether I:T or I:B is included in the random part of the model first. An F test is given with the observed residual mean square relating to ξI∧T or ξI∧B not ξI∧T+ξI∧B−ξI∧T∧B. The observed residual variance for I can be calculated by hand using the estimates for ξI∧T,ξI∧BandξI∧T∧B. The approximate F statistic is MSI/MSI∧T+MSI∧B−MSI∧T∧B. Numerator degrees of freedom can be taken from the ANOVA table and denominator degrees of freedom from Equation (). This gives an approximate F test for the main effect of I. Approximate F tests for the random effects of T and B can be found using Supplementary File . Exact F tests for the random effects of I∧T, I∧B, T∧B, and I∧T∧B are straightforward, but also need to be done by hand.

The following code gives the regression for the randomized block factorial design:


reg2 < − lmer(y ∼ I+(1|T)+(1|B)+(1|T:B)+ 
(1|I:T)+(1|I:B)+(1|I:T:B), contrasts
 = list(I = contr.sum), data=CrossedDataset2)

Here, the approximate t‐test for the fixed effect of I using a Satterthwaite approximation for the degrees of freedom is given directly.

The ANOVA for a multicenter randomized block factorial design can be obtained using:


aov3 < − aov(y ∼ I + Error(B + I + C + T + I:B + C:B 
+ T:B + I:C + I:T + I:C:B + I:T:B), contrasts
 = list(I = contr.sum), data=CrossedDataset3)

The effect of I appears in the fixed and random parts of the model. If it is omitted from the random part, R allocates the fixed effect of I to either the I∧T, I∧C or I∧B stratum, depending on whether I:T, I:C or I:B is included in the random part of the model first. An F test is thus given with the observed residual mean square relating to ξI∧T, ξI∧B or ξI∧C not ξI∧C+ξI∧B−ξI∧C∧B. The appropriate residual variance for I can be calculated by hand using estimates for ξI∧C, ξI∧B and ξI∧C∧B. The approximate F statistic is MSI/MSI∧C+MSI∧B−MSI∧C∧B. Numerator degrees of freedom can be taken from the ANOVA table, denominator degrees of freedom come from Equation (). This gives an approximate F test for the main effect of I. Approximate F tests for the random effects of C, B, I∧C, T, and C∧B can be found using Supplementary File . Exact F tests for the random effects of I∧B, I∧T, I∧C∧B, T∧B and I∧T∧B are straightforward, but again need to be done by hand.

The following code gives the regression for the multicenter randomized block factorial design:


reg3 <+ lmer(y∼I+(1|T)+(1|B)+(1|T:B)+(1|C)
+(1|C:B)+(1|I:T)+(1|I:B)+(1|I:T:B)+(1|I:C)+
          (1|I:C:B), contrasts=
           list(I=contr.sum),
           data=CrossedDataset3)

Here, an approximate t‐test for the fixed effect of I using a Satterthwaite approximation for the degrees of freedom is again given directly.

A simulation study was conducted to explore the performance of the proposed randomization methods on the estimation of the intervention effect δ1 and its standard error, the between‐therapist variance σu12, and the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect σv12, from Models (), (), and () (see https://github.com/arpan52/Randomising‐IxT‐combinations‐to‐patients). Specifically, we compared the following five methods: (i) non‐randomly assign therapists to patients after randomizing interventions to patients; (ii) non‐randomly assign therapists to patients before randomizing interventions to patients; (iii) block the randomization of interventions to patients by therapists; (iv) randomize the combination of therapist and intervention to patients (our proposed method); and (v) randomize interventions to patients, then randomize therapists to patients, blocking the latter by the randomized intervention. We made four comparisons: (1) method (i) versus (ii); (2) method (ii) versus (iii); (3) method (iii) versus (iv); and 4) method (iv) versus (v). For each comparison, 10 000 simulated datasets were generated for each of the three illustrative examples taken from Figure . We generated the systematic design then fixed the true values of the fixed and random effects for each example as summarized in Table  below.

Data generating mechanism.

We varied the degree to which the non‐random assignment of therapists to patients was determined by matching patients to therapists based on a baseline characteristic of the patient that was predictive of patient outcome (for each therapist, the average value of this baseline covariate was assumed to follow a Normal distribution with mean δ2 and variance one (i.e.,[N(δ2,1]). For all five methods, in the systematic design (see Sections , , and ) δ2 was set to be either zero or 0.2. When δ2=0, the baseline covariate was excluded from the data generation process. These values were chosen because our preliminary simulations indicated that once δ2 is non‐zero, the magnitude of its expected value has minimal impact on the estimation of δ1 or the associated inference. We further varied the degree to which the non‐random assignment of therapists to patients was influenced by knowledge of the intervention assignment, again using a baseline characteristic of the patient that was predictive of patient outcome (for each therapist, the average value of this baseline covariate was assumed to follow a Normal distribution with mean δ3 and variance one (i.e., Nδ3,1). If therapists were assigned to patients before (or at the same time as) interventions were randomized to patients (i.e., methods (ii), (iii), and (iv)), δ3 was set to be zero (the baseline covariate was excluded from the data generation process), assuming that allocation of interventions to patients was perfectly concealed at the point where therapists were assigned to patients. Where therapists were assigned to patients after interventions were randomized to patients (i.e., methods (i) and (v)), δ3 was set to be either zero or 0.2 in the systematic design for similar reasons as for δ2.

Then we generated the randomized design. First, the randomization method for allocating therapists and interventions to patients in batches and centers was determined for each method i∈{1,…,5} and example j∈{1,2,3}, according to design Dij. Second, continuous patient outcomes were generated consistent with the example (i.e., with (), (), and () for example j=1,2,and3 respectively), using the specified model parameters (see Table ) in addition to δ2 and δ3. Third, the data were analyzed using regression using REML as specified in Section  (the lmer () function from the lmerTest package in R), omitting the effects of the patient covariates associated with δ2 and δ3. Fourth, the following quantities were extracted from the fitted model: the intervention effect δ^1, its standard error (SE(δ^1)), estimates of the variance components σu12 and σv12, whether either variance component was estimated to be zero (a boundary estimate), and indicators for false positives (Type I error) and false negatives (Type II error) in testing the null hypothesis that δ1=0 against the alternative hypothesis that δ1≠0 with a 5% significance level. Fifth, steps 1 to 4 were repeated for 10 000 replications, and the average of each estimated quantity was computed over all replications.

Note:
δ^1 is the fixed intervention effect, SE(δ^1) is the standard error of δ^1, σ^u12 is the between‐therapist variance, σ^v12 is the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, δ2 is the fixed coefficient of the baseline patient covariate associated with how therapists are allocated to patients and δ3 is the fixed coefficient of baseline patient covariate associated with how therapists are allocated to patients with knowledge of the randomized intervention. Boundary estimates are where σu12 or σv12 is estimated to be zero and a warning is given by the software. The model converged in every case.

The results of our simulation study are summarized in Table  below for Example 1 (the completely randomized factorial design). The results for Examples 2 and 3 can be found in Supplementary File . Allowing for Monte Carlo error, the intervention effect, δ1, was estimated without bias, regardless of the size of δ2 and δ3, across all five randomization methods. The between‐therapist variance, σu12, was estimated to be about 0.1 when δ2 and δ3 were both zero but increased substantially to near 1.0 when δ2=0.2 and therapists were non‐randomly allocated to patients (D11, D21 or D31), as expected. When therapists were randomized to patients (D41 or D51), the between‐therapist variance, σu12, was again estimated to be about 0.1, showing that randomizing therapists to patients aids unbiased estimation of the between‐therapist variance. Likewise, the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, σv12, was estimated to be near 0.15 when δ2 and δ3 were both zero. It increased substantially to about 1.0 when δ3=0.2 and therapists were non‐randomly allocated to patients after the intervention was allocated with knowledge of this randomized intervention (D11), as expected. When δ3=0 and therapists were non‐randomly allocated to patients before allocating the intervention, thus concealing the intervention (D21 or D31), we constrained the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, σv12, to be about 0.15. Yet, when δ3=0.2 and therapists were randomized to patients (D41orD51), σv12 was again estimated be about 0.15. This indicates that concealing the randomized intervention when allocating the therapist, or randomizing therapists to patients, facilitates the unbiased estimation of the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect. The consequences of increases in the estimated variance components can be seen in the estimated standard error of δ^1 and the Type II error.

The standard error of δ^1 was estimated to increase substantially where the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, σv12, was estimated to increase substantially (when δ3=0.2 for D11). This substantial increase in the standard error of δ^1 was associated with a similar substantial increase in the estimated Type II error rate, as expected. The standard error of δ^1 was estimated to increase modestly where δ2=0.2 across all five randomization methods, associated with a similar modest increase in the estimated Type II error rate. The estimated substantial increase in the between‐therapist variance, σu12, observed if therapists were non‐randomly assigned to patients (D11, D21 and D31), made little or no difference to the estimated standard error of δ^1 or the associated Type II error rate.

The Type I error rate was consistently estimated to be 0.05 (5%) regardless of the size of δ2 and δ3, across all five randomization methods, except where δ3=0.2 and the therapists were randomized to patients after interventions were randomized to patients (D51). Here, the Type I error increased when the covariate related to δ3 was included in generating the data after interventions were randomized to patients. This issue appeared in D51 but not D11. The reason is that the covariate related to δ3 created an imbalance in the types of patients assigned each intervention. Once intervention assignment was fixed, therapists were then randomly selected in a way that balanced this covariate in each level of I∧T. Because the interventions were already randomized, this balancing created an imbalance in the number of patients in each level of I∧T, and in turn across interventions with respect to the covariate. As this imbalance was not adjusted for in the analysis model, it sometimes falsely indicated that the intervention effect was statistically significant, even when this effect was only due to the covariate related to δ3. Moreover, the imbalance associated with this covariate became more pronounced with larger sample sizes, with greater inflation of the Type I error rate as the sample size increased.

We found that the variance components σu12 and σv12 were estimated to be zero in a large proportion of simulations giving boundary estimates. When σv12 is estimated to be zero, the analysis is equivalent to an analysis based on the assumption that σv12 is known to be zero []. Thus, the degrees of freedom available to test the null hypothesis that δ1=0 increased substantially.

The statistical literature to date has recognized the sample size and analysis implications of treatment‐related clustering due to therapists delivering interventions in individually‐randomized parallel‐arm trials. We have used and adapted the DoE approach described in Bailey [] to formally set out the statistical implications of considering therapists as a random treatment factor in a family of orthogonal factorial designs, and their associated data analyses. We refer to these randomization designs as “completely randomized,” “randomized block,” and “multicentre randomised block” factorial designs, respectively, to reflect the absence of any blocking (i.e., stratification) factors, the inclusion of categorical time (Batches) as a blocking factor and the further inclusion of Centers as a blocking factor. We have shown how a formal approach to designing trials of therapist‐delivered interventions leads to recommendations about how to randomize and analyze such trials. We have reported the results of a small simulation study, which back up the theory. Our simulations indicate the impact of (i) randomizing therapists to patients on estimation of the between‐therapist variance, (ii) concealing the intervention in assigning therapists to patients or randomizing therapists to patients on estimation of the between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, (iii) consequent impact on the standard error of the intervention effect and its Type II error, and (iv) the impact of separately randomizing interventions to patients then therapists to patients on its Type I error.

A challenge we have started to address is how to handle factors that would ideally be randomized but due to practical constraints cannot be. These were Batches and Centers here. It leads to designs in which the treatment structure is not fully representative of the complex intervention design. In this article, we have suggested blocking these factors to ensure that factors that affect the delivery of the intervention package are orthogonal to the treatment factors, enabling unbiased estimation of treatment effects and better estimation of interactions between the components of an intervention package. Further work is needed to inform decisions about which factors to include in both the randomization and the analysis, and which to include just in the analysis where there are too many to include all in the randomization. We have included all the block‐treatment interactions in the primary analysis. Further work is needed to better appreciate the importance of these interactions in routine data and in historical trials.

In our simulation study, blocking the randomization of interventions to patients by therapists made no discernible difference beyond the necessity to assign therapists to patients beforehand and therefore to conceal the intervention when allocating the therapist. This implies that some lack of balance in the data is unlikely to have much of an effect. However, randomizing therapist‐intervention combinations when compared to randomizing the intervention then therapist to patients separately had a clear effect on the Type I error. This implies that our proposed approach to randomization is preferable. If one of the secondary aims of the trial is to unbiasedly estimate the between‐therapist variance and between‐therapist variance in the intervention effect, we have shown that either randomization method is to be preferred. At a minimum, we suggest concealing the intervention when assigning therapists to patients to avoid inflating the Type II error and decreasing the power to detect the intervention effect. Further simulation work is needed to fully evaluate performance in a range of realistic scenarios.

Based on the statistical considerations, we would recommend randomizing therapists to patients (or at least concealing the intervention when assigning therapists to patients) but the barriers and enablers to making this feasible in practice need to be understood. The Second Sheffield Psychotherapy Project [] employed research therapists to deliver the interventions, which gave the researchers control over their randomization. Many more recent trials (including PRaCTICED []) use therapists embedded in routine clinical services, giving less control to the researchers. Building on [], work is planned to build (i) variation in therapist capacity to take on patients, (ii) there only being a subset of therapists in a center available to take on a patient at the point of randomization, and (iii) therapist turnover, into a more flexible randomization method. Moreover, the number of centers or batches may be limited in practice, questioning the assumption we have made that Batch and Centre contribute random effects. Further work is planned to apply an optimal design approach and to understand the sample size implications of the randomization designs that we have proposed here.

The randomization designs proposed here are specifically for the case where each therapist delivers each intervention (the crossed therapist‐intervention design []), there is a single therapist‐per‐patient and a single continuous outcome. Other therapist‐intervention designs lead to randomization designs with potentially different statistical and practical considerations. Planned and unplanned multiple therapist‐per‐patient designs are common, as are longitudinal outcomes and other outcome types. We did not consider the possibility of intervention contamination, nor the possibility of therapists taking on patients in continuous time. These are areas that require further work. Finally, we assumed that the therapists are a random sample from a population of interest. This may not be the case in practice. If a convenience sample of therapists is used, caution must be given when considering the generalizability of the trial results.

To our knowledge, this is the first time that a formal DoE approach has been taken to designing trials of therapist‐delivered interventions. This has led to a better understanding of the data analysis, which follows the design. Based on this, we would recommend that: (i) the primary data analysis should fully reflect the randomization, including blocking by time; (ii) Satterthwaite's [] method for calculating the degrees of freedom should be used routinely; (iii) treatment contrasts are orthogonal, estimating main effects and interactions; (iv) although many of the calculations can be done by hand, software is needed enabling ANOVA to be used more widely if there are ‘dependent’ random effects. It is possible that use of ANOVA for the data analysis of these trials would lead to fewer unintended consequences of boundary estimates on the degrees of freedom when testing the intervention effect. This needs further research.

More purposeful trial design has the potential to lead to better evidence on a range of complex interventions. We have focused here on psychotherapy, but the methods described are applicable to trials of physiotherapy, rehabilitation, surgery, and any complex intervention delivered by a person.

The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
