psychology.title: When college students perceive GAI feedback as credible: the role of perceived GAI feedback credibility in promoting deep learning through cognitive engagement
psychology.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has raised new questions from an educational psychology perspective. Why does GAI feedback promote meaningful learning for some college students but fail to produce similar learning benefits for others? To answer this question, this study develops a theoretical framework based on Information Processing Theory, Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Constructivist Learning Theory. This study examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ deep learning and explores the mediating role of cognitive engagement in this relationship. This study adopts a stratified simple sampling method and collects questionnaire data from 506 undergraduate students and uses structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed model. The results show that perceived GAI feedback credibility has positive relationships with both cognitive engagement and deep learning. In addition, cognitive engagement plays a significant mediating role between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning, suggesting that credible GAI feedback may support deep learning by encouraging college students to engage in cognitive processing and reflective thinking. This study extends research on learning psychology in GAI-supported learning environments by explaining how college students evaluate and process GAI feedback. The findings indicate that the influence of GAI feedback on learning does not simply result from the technology itself. Instead, college students’ judgments of feedback credibility and their following cognitive engagement play important roles in shaping deep learning processes.
psychology.text:
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has introduced a new feedback context in which college students increasingly interact with GAI, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao, during learning activities. From an educational psychology perspective, feedback is not simply external information provided to learners. Instead, the influence of feedback depends on how college students perceive, understand, and cognitively process information. Traditionally, feedback has mainly occurred through teacher-student interactions and has supported learning by helping learners identify knowledge gaps, regulate cognitive processes, and develop deeper understanding. However, with the emergence of large language model-based systems such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, college students increasingly need to evaluate feedback provided by non-human information sources (). Although GAI systems can generate immediate explanations, suggestions, and evaluations based on college students’ questions and learning contexts (), the psychological value of GAI feedback does not automatically come from the availability of technology. Instead, it depends on college students’ judgments about the credibility of GAI feedback information and their willingness to engage in cognitive processing ().

Based on this perspective, this study introduces the concept of perceived GAI feedback credibility, which refers to college students’ subjective evaluations of the reliability, accuracy, and dependability of GAI feedback during learning activities. It is important to clarify that perceived GAI feedback credibility does not represent the objective correctness of GAI feedback information. Instead, it reflects how college students understand and evaluate GAI feedback as a source of learning information. From the perspective of cognitive psychology, college students are not passive recipients of external information. Rather, they actively evaluate, understand, and integrate information based on their previous experiences, knowledge structures, and learning contexts (). Such evaluations influence whether college students are willing to invest cognitive resources to further examine, process, and use the provided GAI feedback. Therefore, examining perceived GAI feedback credibility does not aim to evaluate the effectiveness of GAI technology itself (). Instead, it aims to understand how college students make information judgments and regulate cognitive processing when they interact with new types of feedback sources ().

Although college students’ perceptions of GAI feedback credibility may influence their learning processes, an important question remains, how does the psychological evaluation of GAI feedback relate to college students’ cognitive activities during learning? Perceiving an information source as credible does not automatically lead to meaningful learning. Educational psychology research has consistently emphasized that learning depends on how college students actively attend to, process, and integrate information into their existing knowledge structures. Even when college students consider GAI feedback reliable, they may accept the provided information without further reflection, evaluation, or connection with their existing understanding (). In this situation, the potential value of GAI feedback may not be fully realized because meaningful learning requires college students to actively participate in cognitive activities. Therefore, the role of perceived GAI feedback credibility does not only concern whether college students accept GAI feedback information. More importantly, it concerns whether this psychological evaluation can encourage college students to engage in deeper cognitive processing of GAI feedback information.

Accordingly, cognitive engagement can serve as an important psychological mechanism for explaining how GAI feedback influences learning. Cognitive engagement refers to the extent to which college students actively invest mental effort and cognitive resources to process, evaluate, and understand information during learning. Unlike simple learning participation or behavioral engagement (), cognitive engagement focuses on how college students think about and process information (). In GAI-supported learning environments, when college students perceive GAI feedback as credible, they may become more willing to actively examine and process such feedback rather than simply consider it as the final answer. This psychological state encourages college students to evaluate the relevance and accuracy of GAI suggestions, compare them with their own understanding, and actively participate in the feedback processing process. Therefore, perceived GAI feedback credibility may promote college students’ active cognitive processing by increasing cognitive engagement (). Furthermore, cognitive engagement not only reflects how college students process and understand GAI feedback but also represents an important process through which information processing contributes to deep learning.

In traditional learning environments, deep learning is influenced by instructional design, teacher guidance, and college students’ learning strategies (). However, the involvement of GAI provides new possibilities for supporting learning development. GAI can provide immediate cognitive support, but whether such support can promote deep learning depends on whether college students actively process and evaluate GAI feedback rather than simply accept GAI outputs. If college students consider GAI as a substitute for their own thinking, GAI may lead to passive dependence and surface learning. In contrast, if college students use GAI as a tool to support their own thinking and learning activities, GAI feedback may promote deeper knowledge understanding and application (). Therefore, understanding how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences deep learning through cognitive engagement is important for explaining learning processes in the era of GAI.

Although research on the educational application of GAI has increased rapidly, existing studies still have several limitations. First, many studies () focus on whether college students use GAI, whether college students accept GAI, or how to increase GAI adoption intention. However, fewer studies examine how college students psychologically evaluate GAI information. Second, previous studies have mainly focused on the relationship between GAI use and learning outcomes, including academic achievement, higher-order thinking, and learning performance, while relatively less attention has been given to the psychological and cognitive processes through which GAI influences learning (; ). Although recent research has begun to examine learner-related factors and human-GAI interaction, how college students evaluate and cognitively process GAI feedback remains insufficiently understood (; ). Third, current research has not fully explained how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ active cognitive processing. Existing studies have shown that GAI can provide personalized support, immediate feedback, and cognitive assistance, which may facilitate students’ engagement and learning outcomes (; ). However, research on cognitive offloading suggests that reliance on external cognitive resources may also reduce individuals’ internal cognitive effort and alter information-processing strategies (). Therefore, it remains unclear whether perceiving GAI feedback as credible encourages deeper cognitive engagement or leads to reduced cognitive effort through reliance on GAI-generated information. Finally, recent studies further indicate that GAI-supported learning involves complex interactions among technological functions, college students’ cognition, and knowledge construction. Existing studies have examined the effects of GAI on learning outcomes (), the design of GAI-supported learning environments based on constructivist principles (), the importance of metacognitive abilities when college students interact with GAI systems (), and how human-GAI interaction influences learning processes (). These studies suggest that the educational value of GAI depends not only on the information provided by GAI systems but also on how college students evaluate, process, and actively engage with GAI information.

Based on self-reported questionnaire data from college students, this study develops a theoretical model including perceived GAI feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and deep learning to examine how college students’ evaluations of GAI feedback relate to their cognitive processing and learning experiences in GAI-supported learning environments. By examining the psychological pathway from perceived GAI feedback credibility to deep learning through cognitive engagement, this study provides further insight into how college students interpret GAI feedback and regulate their cognitive activities during learning. The findings provide some implications for explaining the psychological processes involved in college students’ interactions with GAI feedback.

This study integrates the Elaboration Likelihood Model, Information Processing Theory, and Constructivist Learning Theory as complementary theoretical perspectives to explain how perceived GAI feedback credibility relates to cognitive engagement and deep learning in GAI-supported learning environments. These theories share the assumption that learners actively participate in the learning process rather than simply receive external information. However, each theory emphasizes different aspects of this process. The Elaboration Likelihood Model explains how learners evaluate information sources and decide whether to engage in deeper information processing. Information Processing Theory explains how learners attend to, organize, and integrate external information through cognitive activities. Constructivist Learning Theory further explains how learners construct understanding by connecting new information with existing knowledge. Therefore, integrating these perspectives provides a more comprehensive explanation of how college students interact with GAI feedback than relying on any single theoretical perspective.

The Elaboration Likelihood Model proposed by  provides an important explanation for how college students’ evaluations of GAI feedback credibility may influence their willingness to engage with feedback information. The theory suggests that individuals process information through different levels of elaboration depending on their motivation, cognitive ability, and evaluation of the information source. When individuals perceive information as valuable and reliable, they are more likely to carefully examine and process the information through the central route. In contrast, when individuals have limited motivation or perceive information as less valuable, they may rely more on simple cues and invest fewer cognitive resources in information processing. In GAI-supported learning environments, GAI feedback represents a new type of information source that differs from traditional human feedback. Although GAI feedback can provide immediate explanations, suggestions, and evaluations, college students still need to judge whether such feedback is reliable and useful before further processing it. Therefore, the Elaboration Likelihood Model helps explain why perceived GAI feedback credibility may influence college students’ willingness to allocate cognitive resources and engage with GAI feedback.

However, the Elaboration Likelihood Model alone cannot fully explain how college students process GAI feedback after they evaluate its credibility. To explain this cognitive process, Information Processing Theory provides an additional perspective. Information Processing Theory explains how individuals receive, encode, store, and use external information.  proposed the multi store model of human memory, suggesting that information processing involves sensory memory, short term memory, and long term memory. From this perspective, external information cannot directly become meaningful knowledge. Instead, learners need to actively select, organize, and integrate information through cognitive activities.  further emphasized that meaningful learning depends on learners’ active cognitive processing rather than simple exposure to information. In the context of GAI-supported learning, GAI feedback functions as an external information input. Nevertheless, such feedback cannot directly produce learning experiences. College students need to evaluate, interpret, compare, and organize the information through their own cognitive activities. Therefore, Information Processing Theory helps explain why college students who perceive GAI feedback as credible may show greater cognitive engagement, as they may be more willing to invest mental effort in processing and understanding the provided feedback.

At the same time, Information Processing Theory mainly focuses on how individuals process information, but it does not fully explain how processed information develops into deeper understanding and knowledge construction. Constructivist Learning Theory provides an additional explanation for this aspect. Based on Piaget’s cognitive constructivism and Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, Constructivist Learning Theory emphasizes that learners actively construct knowledge through interaction with information, experiences, and external support.  argued that learners develop knowledge by adjusting their existing cognitive structures through assimilation and accommodation.  further emphasized that cognitive development occurs through social interaction and the use of cultural tools. From this perspective, GAI feedback serves as a learning resource that can support knowledge construction, but meaningful learning depends on whether college students actively interpret and integrate the information into their existing knowledge structures. Therefore, Constructivist Learning Theory explains why cognitive engagement with GAI feedback may contribute to deeper learning experiences characterized by meaningful understanding, knowledge connection, and knowledge application.

Together, these three theoretical perspectives provide an integrated explanation of the learning mechanism associated with GAI feedback. The Elaboration Likelihood Model explains the initial evaluation process through which college students determine whether GAI feedback deserves further attention and processing. Information Processing Theory explains how college students cognitively process and organize GAI feedback after they decide to engage with it. Constructivist Learning Theory explains how such cognitive activities contribute to the construction of understanding and deeper learning experiences. Importantly, these perspectives do not represent separate theoretical stages. Instead, they describe interconnected aspects of the same learning process in which information evaluation, cognitive processing, and knowledge construction continuously influence one another. The three theoretical perspectives adopted in this study should not be understood as independent explanations for individual variables. Instead, they provide overlapping and complementary explanations for the psychological processes underlying learners’ interactions with GAI-generated feedback. Specifically, ELM explains not only how learners form credibility judgments about GAI feedback but also how such judgments influence their willingness to engage in further cognitive processing. Information Processing Theory provides a broader explanation of how learners attend to, elaborate on, and integrate GAI feedback information, thereby explaining both cognitive engagement and the development of deeper understanding. Constructivist Learning Theory further emphasizes learners’ active role in constructing meaning, which is closely related to both cognitive engagement and deep learning approaches. Together, these three theoretical perspectives offer an integrated explanation of how learners evaluate, process, and construct knowledge when interacting with GAI feedback. Rather than representing separate theoretical stages, they jointly explain the interconnected psychological processes through which perceived GAI feedback credibility is associated with cognitive engagement and deep learning.

Based on the above theoretical perspectives, this study further develops an Information evaluation–Cognitive processing–Knowledge construction Framework to explain the psychological processes through which college students interact with GAI feedback in GAI-supported learning environments (). This framework suggests that GAI feedback does not directly lead to learning outcomes. Instead, it requires college students to actively participate in processes of information evaluation, cognitive processing, and knowledge construction. Specifically, when college students encounter GAI feedback, they first need to evaluate whether the information is credible and valuable, which influences whether they are willing to further attend to and process the feedback. Then, college students need to invest cognitive resources to understand, analyze, compare, and integrate the feedback information, allowing external information to connect with their existing knowledge structures. Finally, information that college students actively process can support deeper understanding and knowledge application.

Following this psychological mechanism, this study selects perceived GAI feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and deep learning as the core research constructs. First, the information evaluation process represents the starting point of college students’ interaction with GAI feedback. Therefore, it is necessary to examine how college students form credibility judgments about GAI feedback and how these judgments influence subsequent learning activities. Second, information evaluation itself does not automatically lead to learning development. College students still need to actively process the obtained information through cognitive activities. Therefore, cognitive engagement represents an important psychological process that connects information evaluation and learning experiences. Furthermore, the value of cognitive processing depends on whether college students can connect new information with existing knowledge and develop deeper understanding and application. Therefore, deep learning reflects an important learning experience associated with knowledge construction. Based on this theoretical logic, this study further examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility relates to deep learning and how cognitive engagement plays a role in this relationship.

Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, Cognitive Engagement, and Deep Learning represent three distinct but related concepts in GAI-supported learning environments. Although they are examined within the same learning context, they reflect different psychological and learning dimensions. Specifically, Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility refers to students’ evaluations of the reliability, accuracy, and usefulness of GAI-generated feedback. Cognitive Engagement represents the cognitive process through which students actively attend to, process, analyze, and reflect on GAI feedback during learning. Deep Learning refers to the learning outcomes associated with deeper understanding, knowledge integration, and meaningful application of knowledge. In this study, these constructs were measured through students’ self-reported perceptions and experiences. Therefore, the measures capture students’ reported cognitive engagement processes and perceived deep learning outcomes rather than directly observing cognitive processes or objectively assessing learning performance.

It is important to distinguish between trust and perceived credibility in GAI-supported learning environments. Although these two concepts are closely related, they refer to different levels of psychological judgment. Generally, trust is a broader psychological concept that refers to whether learners are willing to believe in and rely on an GAI system and its recommendations (). For example, when students believe that “ChatGPT is a reliable learning tool and I am willing to use it to support my learning,” they demonstrate trust in the GAI system as a whole. Trust concerns the overall relationship between learners and GAI, including whether learners are willing to consider GAI as a dependable source of support during learning. In contrast, perceived credibility refers to learners’ evaluations of specific information provided by GAI (). It focuses on whether learners consider a particular piece of GAI feedback to be accurate, reliable, and valuable for learning. For example, when students receive GAI-generated feedback, they may ask: “Is this feedback accurate?” “Is this explanation consistent with my understanding?” or “Can this suggestion help me improve my learning?” These judgments are directed toward specific feedback rather than the GAI system as a whole. Therefore, the main difference between trust and perceived credibility is that trust concerns whether learners believe in and rely on the GAI system, whereas perceived credibility concerns whether learners consider specific GAI-generated information worthy of acceptance and further processing. During learning, students may perceive a specific piece of GAI feedback as credible without developing general trust in the GAI system. For example, students may consider ChatGPT’s explanation of a particular concept accurate, while still remaining cautious about using GAI to solve all types of learning problems. Based on this distinction, this study focuses on Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility rather than general trust in GAI. The reason is that this study does not examine whether students are willing to rely on GAI systems in general. Instead, it focuses on how students evaluate the reliability and value of GAI-generated feedback and how such evaluations are related to their subsequent cognitive processing and learning experiences. Therefore, perceived GAI feedback credibility more directly reflects the psychological process examined in this study, namely how learners evaluate GAI feedback information before engaging with it during learning.

Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility refers to students’ subjective judgment regarding whether GAI-generated feedback is reliable, accurate, and trustworthy (). This construct focuses exclusively on learners’ perceptions of the feedback source and the information provided by GAI systems (). It captures whether students believe that GAI-generated feedback is credible enough to be considered and used during learning (). Importantly, perceived GAI feedback credibility does not indicate whether students actually engage with the feedback or whether their understanding of knowledge has changed. A student may perceive GAI feedback as highly credible but may not actively process the feedback or achieve deeper learning ().

Cognitive Engagement refers to the mental effort and cognitive activities that learners invest when processing learning information (). Unlike perceived GAI feedback credibility, which reflects learners’ evaluation of GAI-generated feedback, cognitive engagement reflects learners’ responses after receiving such feedback (). It describes the process through which students actively examine, analyze, interpret, and evaluate information provided by GAI systems. Therefore, cognitive engagement focuses on how students process feedback, rather than whether the feedback is considered credible or what learning outcomes are eventually achieved.

Deep Learning refers to the quality of learning outcomes that learners achieve after engaging in learning activities (). It reflects whether learners develop meaningful understanding, establish connections among concepts, integrate new knowledge into existing knowledge structures, and apply knowledge to new situations (). Unlike cognitive engagement, which occurs during the process of information processing, deep learning reflects the results produced by that process. In other words, cognitive engagement describes the effort and activities involved in learning, whereas deep learning describes the depth and quality of understanding developed through learning ().

The distinction among these three constructs can therefore be summarized as follows: perceived GAI feedback credibility answers “How do students evaluate GAI feedback?”; cognitive engagement answers “How do students process and interact with GAI feedback information?”; and deep learning answers “What level of understanding and knowledge development do students achieve after learning?” Accordingly, this study proposes that students’ perceptions of GAI feedback credibility may influence their cognitive engagement, which subsequently contributes to deep learning ().

Conceptual distinction among perceived GAI feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and deep learning.

Feedback represents an important mechanism that supports learning because it provides students with information about the differences between their current understanding and expected learning goals. Effective feedback can help students identify learning problems, adjust cognitive strategies, and reorganize knowledge structures (; ). However, feedback itself does not guarantee learning improvement. Previous research suggests that the educational value of feedback depends on whether students actively interpret, evaluate, and use feedback information during learning (; ). Therefore, students’ evaluation of feedback information represents an important condition influencing whether feedback can contribute to learning development. From the perspective of source credibility theory, individuals do not accept external information only based on the availability of information. Instead, they evaluate whether information sources possess sufficient reliability, expertise, and trustworthiness before deciding whether to accept and use the information (). Research on information credibility further indicates that perceived credibility influences individuals’ willingness to consider and apply external information (; ). In educational contexts, this suggests that students are more likely to use feedback as a learning resource when they perceive the feedback information as reliable and valuable.

The emergence of GAI has introduced a new information source into learning environments. Unlike traditional teacher feedback, GAI feedback requires students to evaluate information generated by technological systems that may provide useful explanations while also producing inaccurate or incomplete information (). Recent studies have shown that students’ acceptance and use of GAI feedback depend on their perceptions of usefulness, reliability, and trustworthiness of GAI systems and their feedback information (; ; ). Moreover, students’ judgments of GAI feedback are influenced by both the characteristics of feedback information and their perceptions of the GAI source (; ). These findings indicate that perceived GAI feedback credibility may determine whether students regard GAI feedback as meaningful learning information. Deep learning requires students to move beyond information reproduction and develop meaningful understanding, knowledge integration, and knowledge application (). Research on learning approaches further suggests that deep learning occurs when students actively connect new information with existing knowledge structures and construct coherent understanding (; ). Cognitive learning theories also emphasize that meaningful learning depends on learners’ ability to select, organize, and integrate relevant information into existing cognitive structures (). Therefore, the learning value of GAI feedback may depend on whether students perceive the information as credible enough to support such knowledge construction processes.

Recent research on digital learning environments also suggests that learning outcomes depend not only on the availability of technological resources but also on how students interact with and interpret information provided by digital tools (; ). Studies examining GAI-supported learning further indicate that GAI can influence students’ learning outcomes when students effectively evaluate and use GAI information during learning activities (; ; ; ; ). Therefore, perceived GAI feedback credibility may represent an important psychological factor that determines whether students treat GAI feedback as valuable information for developing deeper understanding. However, perceived GAI feedback credibility does not mean that students blindly accept GAI feedback. Excessive dependence on external information sources may reduce students’ own cognitive effort and lead to cognitive offloading (). Thus, perceived GAI feedback credibility reflects students’ evaluation of the learning value of GAI feedback rather than passive acceptance. When students perceive GAI feedback as credible, they may be more likely to use the information as a basis for reflection, knowledge integration, and understanding development, thereby supporting deep learning. Accordingly, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H1: Perceived GAI feedback credibility positively influences college students’ deep learning.

Cognitive engagement includes students’ attention, analysis, evaluation, and integration of information during learning (; ). Previous research in educational psychology indicates that university students do not allocate the same level of cognitive resources to all information. Instead, they evaluate the value and reliability of information before deciding whether to invest further mental effort (; ). Therefore, students’ evaluation of learning information may influence their willingness to engage in deeper cognitive processing. In learning environments, cognitive engagement depends not only on whether students receive information but also on whether they actively process and use the information. Previous studies suggest that feedback can support learning when students interpret, evaluate, and apply feedback information during learning activities (; ). From a cognitive learning perspective, meaningful learning requires students to select relevant information, organize new knowledge, and connect new information with existing knowledge structures (). Therefore, students’ judgments about the value and reliability of feedback information may influence their cognitive investment in processing feedback.

This relationship becomes especially important in GAI-supported learning environments because GAI feedback provides university students with a new type of learning information. Unlike traditional feedback sources, GAI feedback requires university students to evaluate whether the information has sufficient reliability and learning value before they use it. Existing studies indicate that university students’ acceptance and use of GAI feedback depend on their perceptions of usefulness, reliability, and trustworthiness (; ).  found that university students’ perceptions of usefulness and trustworthiness influence their attitudes toward GAI feedback.  also showed that university students evaluate feedback differently according to their perceptions of the feedback source. These findings suggest that perceived GAI feedback credibility may influence whether university students are willing to further process GAI feedback.

Based on previous research, perceived GAI feedback credibility may positively influence cognitive engagement because credibility can increase university students’ willingness to invest cognitive effort in processing information. When university students perceive GAI feedback as credible, they may consider the information meaningful and worthy of further examination. This perception may encourage them to compare GAI feedback with their existing knowledge, evaluate the suggestions provided by GAI feedback, and consider how the information can support their learning. These activities represent important features of cognitive engagement because they require active attention, analysis, and knowledge construction (). Research on credibility and information use also supports this relationship. Studies indicate that individuals are more likely to consider and apply information when they perceive the information source as reliable and valuable (; ). In educational contexts, students are more likely to treat feedback as a learning resource when they believe that the feedback provides meaningful support for improving their understanding (). Therefore, when university students perceive GAI feedback as credible, they may show stronger willingness to examine and interpret the information rather than simply ignore it.

However, perceived GAI feedback credibility does not always lead to active cognitive engagement. Highly credible information may sometimes function as a simple judgment cue, which encourages individuals to accept information without sufficient evaluation (). This issue deserves attention in GAI-supported learning environments because excessive dependence on GAI feedback may reduce university students’ own thinking effort and result in cognitive offloading (). Therefore, perceived GAI feedback credibility should not represent unconditional acceptance of GAI feedback. Instead, it reflects university students’ evaluation of whether GAI feedback provides reliable and meaningful information for learning. This study argues that perceived GAI feedback credibility promotes cognitive engagement when university students use GAI feedback as a learning resource rather than a replacement for their own thinking. Learning with GAI feedback requires university students to understand feedback information, compare it with existing knowledge, judge its relevance, and decide how to apply it. These processes require active cognitive effort rather than simple acceptance. Recent research on GAI-supported learning also suggests that the educational value of GAI depends on how university students evaluate and use GAI information during learning activities (; ; ). Studies on GAI learning outcomes further indicate that students’ interaction with and processing of GAI information influence their learning behaviors (; ; ; ).

In summary, previous studies indicate that students’ perceptions of information credibility influence their willingness to process and use learning information. In GAI-supported learning environments, perceived GAI feedback credibility may encourage university students to invest cognitive resources in examining, evaluating, and integrating GAI feedback. Although excessive trust may cause passive acceptance in some situations, learning feedback requires active processing to support meaningful learning. Therefore, perceived GAI feedback credibility may serve as an important psychological factor influencing university students’ cognitive engagement. Accordingly, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H2: Perceived GAI feedback credibility positively influences college students’ cognitive engagement.

proposed that cognitive engagement represents learners’ willingness to exert effort and employ advanced learning strategies when encountering learning tasks. Similarly,  argued that cognitively engaged learners are characterized by active meaning construction, strategic thinking, and continuous regulation of their own understanding.  further suggested that meaningful learning depends on students’ intention to understand concepts, connect ideas, and organize knowledge rather than simply reproduce information.  also emphasized that active and constructive cognitive activities are essential for meaningful learning. Therefore, cognitive engagement represents a critical psychological process through which external information is transformed into internal knowledge. Based on this understanding, previous educational research has consistently emphasized that cognitive engagement determines the quality of learning processes rather than merely the amount of learning activities. Early research on learning approaches demonstrated that learners differ fundamentally in how they process information.  found that some learners focus primarily on memorizing information and reproducing knowledge, whereas others actively search for meaning, establish connections among concepts, and relate new information to existing knowledge structures. This distinction is consistent with , who found that deep learning approaches involve active understanding, knowledge organization, and the integration of new information with existing knowledge structures. The latter learning approach, characterized by deeper cognitive involvement, leads to more meaningful and stable understanding. These findings suggest that learning outcomes are not determined only by exposure to information but also by the extent to which learners cognitively process and interpret that information.

Building on this perspective, subsequent studies have further examined how cognitive engagement contributes to effective learning outcomes.  found that students with higher cognitive engagement were more likely to use elaboration strategies, critical thinking, and self-regulated learning behaviors, which subsequently improved their academic achievement. Similarly,  highlighted that cognitive engagement is closely associated with self-regulated learning because engaged learners actively monitor their understanding, evaluate their learning progress, and adjust their strategies when necessary. These findings collectively indicate that cognitive engagement functions as a bridge between information exposure and meaningful learning outcomes. Without sufficient cognitive engagement, learners may obtain information but fail to integrate it into their existing knowledge systems.

This mechanism becomes particularly important in GAI-supported learning environments. Unlike traditional learning environments where information is mainly provided through textbooks or instructors, GAI introduces a new form of interactive information source that can generate explanations, suggestions, and feedback according to learners’ questions and needs (). However, the availability of GAI-generated information does not automatically guarantee effective learning. Since GAI outputs may contain inaccurate, incomplete, or contextually inappropriate information, learners need to actively evaluate, interpret, and integrate GAI content during interaction (). Therefore, cognitive engagement becomes an essential condition determining whether learners can benefit from GAI assistance. When students cognitively engage with GAI feedback information, they are more likely to compare GAI suggestions with their prior knowledge, identify potential limitations, and reconstruct their understanding through reflection and analysis.

Furthermore, cognitive engagement provides the psychological mechanism through which GAI-supported learning can develop into deep learning. Recent studies on GAI-supported learning have suggested that learning outcomes depend on how university students interact with, evaluate, and process GAI information rather than simply receiving information from GAI systems (; ; ). Deep learning emphasizes meaningful understanding, conceptual integration, critical reflection, and the ability to transfer knowledge to new contexts rather than simple information acquisition (). Achieving deep learning requires learners to actively process information by organizing new knowledge, connecting it with existing cognitive structures, and generating personal interpretations. Cognitive engagement directly supports these processes because cognitively engaged learners are more willing to invest mental effort in elaboration, reasoning, and knowledge construction (). In contrast, when learners interact with GAI systems without cognitive engagement, they may simply accept GAI-generated answers or rely on GAI to complete thinking tasks, which may result in superficial learning rather than deep understanding.

The importance of cognitive engagement is further highlighted by research on cognitive offloading.  argued that external cognitive tools can reduce mental effort by allowing individuals to rely on external information sources instead of internal cognitive processes. Although cognitive offloading can improve efficiency, excessive reliance on external tools may reduce opportunities for active thinking and knowledge development. In the context of GAI-supported learning, this suggests that GAI itself does not determine whether learning becomes deeper or more superficial. Instead, the outcome depends on whether learners actively engage with GAI information and use it as a cognitive support mechanism rather than a substitute for their own thinking. Thus, cognitive engagement represents the key psychological pathway through which GAI-supported interactions are transformed into meaningful learning experiences.

Taken together, previous research suggests that cognitive engagement plays an important role in supporting learning development by encouraging students to actively process learning information. In GAI-supported educational environments, students with higher cognitive engagement are more likely to devote mental effort to examining and processing GAI feedback information rather than passively accepting GAI outputs. Such active processing provides the necessary conditions for learners to make effective use of feedback during learning activities. Therefore, this study proposes that cognitive engagement positively influences college students’ deep learning.

H3: Cognitive engagement positively influences college students’ deep learning.

Perceived GAI feedback credibility may influence deep learning not only through a direct pathway but also through a cognitive processing pathway. In learning environments, students’ perceptions of information quality and reliability may shape how they allocate attention and cognitive resources during learning activities. Therefore, cognitive engagement may serve as an important psychological mechanism that explains how perceived GAI feedback credibility is transformed into deeper learning outcomes. Specifically, perceived GAI feedback credibility may first influence students’ willingness to process GAI feedback information, and this cognitive processing may subsequently promote knowledge construction and deep learning.

First, perceived GAI feedback credibility may influence students’ cognitive engagement by shaping their willingness to invest cognitive effort in processing feedback information. Previous research on information credibility suggests that individuals are more likely to consider and use information when they perceive the information source as reliable and valuable (; ; ). In educational settings, students are more likely to actively use feedback when they recognize its value and relevance for improving their learning (; ). This mechanism may also apply to GAI-supported learning environments. Recent studies have shown that students’ acceptance and use of GAI feedback are influenced by their perceptions of usefulness, reliability, and trustworthiness of GAI information (; ; ). When students perceive GAI feedback as credible, they may be more willing to examine, evaluate, and reflect on the feedback rather than ignore or dismiss it. Such willingness provides the basis for cognitive engagement.

Second, cognitive engagement may serve as the process through which students transform information processing activities into deep learning. Educational psychology research consistently indicates that cognitive engagement involves students’ active effort to analyze information, apply learning strategies, and regulate understanding during learning (; ). The ICAP framework further explains that meaningful learning occurs when students actively construct and integrate knowledge rather than simply receive information (). Similarly, studies on learning approaches show that deep learning requires students to connect new information with existing knowledge structures and develop meaningful understanding through active cognitive processing (; ; ). Therefore, cognitive engagement represents a necessary process through which learning information can contribute to deeper understanding.

Third, cognitive engagement may become particularly important in GAI-supported learning because GAI feedback requires students to actively interpret and evaluate information rather than simply accept the provided responses. Research on GAI in education suggests that the educational effects of GAI depend on how students interact with, evaluate, and apply GAI information during learning activities (; ; ). Recent reviews further indicate that GAI supports learning outcomes when students actively participate in information processing and knowledge construction (; ; ). Meanwhile, research on digital learning environments emphasizes that learning benefits from technology depend on learners’ cognitive activities during interaction with digital tools (). Therefore, perceived GAI feedback credibility may promote deep learning by encouraging students to engage cognitively with GAI feedback information. Without such engagement, credible GAI feedback may only result in information acceptance rather than meaningful learning. This perspective also addresses the potential risk of cognitive offloading, where excessive reliance on external information sources reduces individuals’ own cognitive effort ().

Taken together, perceived GAI feedback credibility may be associated with deep learning through both direct and indirect pathways. Directly, credible GAI feedback can provide meaningful and reliable information that supports students’ understanding and knowledge construction. Indirectly, perceived credibility may stimulate cognitive engagement, through which students actively analyze and integrate GAI feedback information into their learning processes. Therefore, cognitive engagement is proposed as an important mediating mechanism rather than the only pathway linking perceived GAI feedback credibility with deep learning. Based on this reasoning, the following hypothesis is proposed:

H4: Cognitive engagement mediates the positive relationship between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning.
