It is worth noting that the relationship between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning may not be explained only by cognitive engagement. Based on research in educational psychology and learning sciences, learners’ judgments about the credibility of external learning information may influence their learning approaches through different psychological processes. For example, perceiving GAI feedback as credible may increase students’ perceived usefulness of the feedback, making them more willing to use GAI feedback information as a learning resource for understanding and applying knowledge. In addition, credible feedback may strengthen students’ learning confidence and motivation, which may encourage them to adopt deeper learning approaches. Furthermore, students’ recognition of the value of GAI feedback may influence their self-regulated learning processes, such as adjusting learning goals, monitoring learning progress, and selecting appropriate learning strategies. These psychological processes may provide possible explanations for the direct relationship between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning.

However, this study selects cognitive engagement as the mediating mechanism based on the perspectives of Information Processing Theory and feedback research. Unlike simply receiving learning information, the use of GAI feedback requires learners to actively understand, evaluate, and integrate the provided information before it can become personal knowledge. Therefore, whether learners are willing to invest cognitive resources in processing feedback represents an important link between their evaluation of feedback and their learning approaches. When students perceive GAI feedback as credible, they may be more willing to examine the feedback content, evaluate the suggestions provided, and connect the information with their existing knowledge. These activities reflect the core characteristics of cognitive engagement. Therefore, this study does not assume that cognitive engagement is the only psychological pathway through which perceived GAI feedback credibility is associated with deep learning. Instead, cognitive engagement is considered one important theoretically supported mechanism. By examining the mediating role of cognitive engagement, this study aims to explain how learners’ judgments about the credibility of GAI feedback may be related to their active information processing and, subsequently, their deep learning approaches.

This study employed a multi-stage stratified sampling method to collect data, aiming to enhance sample representativeness and ensure the reliability of the empirical results. The participants were undergraduate students enrolled in full-time universities in Jinan City, Shandong Province, China. Jinan was selected as the research site for two main reasons. First, as the capital city of Shandong Province, Jinan hosts a diverse range of higher education institutions, including research-oriented universities, comprehensive universities, and application-oriented universities. The diversity of these institutions provides students with different educational backgrounds and levels of exposure to digital technologies, making the city an appropriate context for examining students’ experiences with generative artificial intelligence (GAI). Second, limiting the study to a single geographical area helps reduce the potential influence of regional differences in economic development, educational resources, and digital infrastructure, thereby improving the internal validity of the research model.

In the first stage of sampling, a university sampling framework was established based on university type, educational level, and student population size. Considering that institutional characteristics may influence students’ access to and use of digital technologies, universities were classified into three categories: research-oriented universities, general undergraduate universities, and application-oriented universities. A proportional sampling strategy was then adopted to select universities from different categories. Finally, 10 full-time undergraduate universities in Jinan were selected as the research sites, including 2 research-oriented universities, 6 general undergraduate universities, and 2 application-oriented universities. This distribution was designed based on the overall structure of higher education institutions and the relative proportion of undergraduate students in Jinan. Specifically, general undergraduate universities accounted for 60% of the selected institutions because they represent the largest proportion of undergraduate education providers and therefore reflect the characteristics of the majority of university students. Research-oriented universities accounted for 20% of the sample to capture students with relatively higher exposure to advanced digital technologies, while application-oriented universities also accounted for 20% to represent students from practice-oriented educational environments.

In the second stage of sampling, students within each university were further selected using stratified sampling based on academic year and gender. Each university was assigned approximately 70 questionnaires, resulting in a planned sample size of 700 questionnaires. To ensure balanced representation across learning stages, students from four undergraduate years were included with approximately equal proportions. Specifically, each university distributed 18 questionnaires to first-year students, 18 questionnaires to second-year students, 17 questionnaires to third-year students, and 17 questionnaires to fourth-year students.

The balanced distribution across academic years was designed based on the consideration that students at different stages of university education may have different learning experiences and patterns of GAI use. Compared with junior students, senior students generally possess richer disciplinary knowledge and are more likely to apply GAI tools in complex academic tasks, such as academic writing, professional problem-solving, and research-related activities. Therefore, a sample concentrated in a particular academic year might introduce bias into the findings. Maintaining a relatively equal distribution across academic years allows the study to better capture the general relationship between perceived GAI feedback credibility and students’ cognitive engagement.

Regarding gender distribution, the study controlled the proportion of male and female participants according to the approximate gender composition of undergraduate students in Jinan universities. Rather than relying entirely on convenience sampling, gender quotas were established during the questionnaire distribution process. For example, due to the relatively higher proportion of male students in research-oriented universities, approximately 38 male students and 32 female students were recruited from each research-oriented university. For general undergraduate universities, the distribution was adjusted according to institutional characteristics, with approximately 35 male and 35 female students recruited from each university. Application-oriented universities maintained a relatively balanced gender ratio. Overall, among the 700 planned questionnaires, approximately 360 were allocated to male students (51.4%) and 340 to female students (48.6%), ensuring that the final sample structure was close to the actual undergraduate student population.

In the third stage of data collection, questionnaires were distributed through university instructors, student organizations, and student communication groups. Each participating university appointed one or two student coordinators who were responsible for distributing questionnaires according to the sampling requirements provided by the research team. For example, each university was required to complete approximately 70 valid responses, including 18 first-year students, 18 s-year students, 17 third-year students, and 17 fourth-year students. The coordinators were also instructed to maintain gender balance during distribution to avoid excessive concentration of respondents from a particular gender or academic year. Before completing the questionnaire, all participants were informed of the academic purpose of the study and assured that their responses would be used only for research purposes, reducing potential social desirability bias.

A total of 700 questionnaires were distributed, and 550 responses were collected, resulting in a response rate of 78.57%. After data screening, several procedures were conducted to remove invalid responses. First, questionnaires completed within an unusually short period (e.g., less than 120 s for the entire questionnaire) were excluded. Second, responses showing clear patterns of careless answering, such as selecting the same option for all items, were removed. Third, questionnaires with substantial missing values in key variables were eliminated. Finally, attention-check items were used to identify respondents who did not carefully read the questions. After these screening procedures, 44 invalid responses were removed, leaving 506 valid questionnaires. The effective response rate was therefore 92.00%.

It is worth noting that the questionnaire also included several screening questions regarding participants’ GAI learning experience, including whether they had used GAI tools for learning purposes, the types of GAI tools they had used, the duration and frequency of GAI use, and the primary purposes of using GAI tools in learning activities. These questions were used to identify participants with actual experience of using GAI in learning contexts and to ensure that subsequent evaluations of GAI feedback information were based on real interaction experiences rather than hypothetical situations.

This study used SPSSAU and AMOS 23.0 for data analysis. During the pilot testing stage, SPSSAU conducted item analysis, reliability analysis, validity analysis, and Harman’s single-factor test, while AMOS 23.0 conducted confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with the pilot data. During the formal survey stage, SPSSAU conducted reliability analysis, validity analysis, and Harman’s single-factor test, while AMOS 23.0 conducted confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis with the formal survey data.

Importantly, this study employed Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed theoretical model and test the hypothesized relationships among the research constructs. SEM was selected because the model involves several latent variables, including Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, Cognitive Engagement, and Deep Learning. These constructs represent students’ psychological perceptions and learning processes, which cannot be directly measured by a single observable indicator. Instead, they need to be assessed through multiple measurement items. SEM is therefore suitable because it allows researchers to examine both the relationships between latent constructs and their measurement indicators and the relationships among different constructs within one analytical framework.

The use of SEM is particularly appropriate for this study for three reasons. First, the research aims to explore the process through which students’ perceptions of GAI feedback influence their learning behaviors. Specifically, students who perceive GAI feedback information as credible may be more willing to accept and use such feedback, which can further encourage their active involvement in learning tasks. This relationship involves psychological processes that cannot be fully captured by simple correlation analysis. SEM enables the simultaneous examination of multiple relationships, providing a clearer understanding of the proposed theoretical model.

Second, SEM helps address potential measurement errors in psychological research. Variables such as perceived credibility and cognitive engagement are abstract concepts that are usually measured through several questionnaire items. By separating the measurement model from the structural model, SEM allows researchers to first confirm whether the observed items accurately represent the intended constructs and then evaluate the relationships among these constructs. This approach improves the accuracy of the empirical analysis.

Following the two-step procedure of SEM analysis, this study first assessed the measurement model through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Reliability and validity tests were conducted to evaluate the quality of the measurement scales, including internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. After the measurement model was confirmed, the structural model was examined to test the proposed hypotheses. The significance of path coefficients was evaluated to determine whether Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility had a significant influence on Cognitive Engagement. Moreover, SEM is well suited to the context of GAI-supported learning because students’ responses to GAI feedback information depend not only on the technical performance of the system but also on their perceptions of its credibility and usefulness. Understanding how these perceptions shape students’ learning engagement requires an analytical method that can capture the interaction between technological perceptions and learning behaviors. SEM provides such an approach by linking students’ cognitive evaluations of GAI feedback with their subsequent engagement in learning activities.

The measurement instruments used in this study were newly developed based on a review of relevant theoretical and empirical literature. Although previous studies have examined related concepts, such as feedback perception, cognitive engagement, and deep learning, existing instruments were not directly applicable to the context of GAI feedback information in higher education. Therefore, rather than directly adapting existing scales, we developed the items by identifying the core dimensions of each construct from prior studies and tailoring the item wording to the specific context of students’ interactions with GAI feedback. The development process focused on maintaining consistency with the theoretical definitions of the constructs while ensuring that the items could accurately capture students’ perceptions and learning experiences in the GAI-supported learning environment.

Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility was measured as students’ subjective evaluations of whether feedback generated by GAI systems is accurate, relevant, reasonable, dependable, convincing, and capable of increasing their confidence in GAI-generated information. Drawing on previous research on information credibility and trust in intelligent systems, this study focuses on students’ judgments of the credibility-related characteristics of GAI feedback information rather than their intention to use GAI, perceived usefulness of feedback, or learning outcomes. Accordingly, the construct was operationalized through six dimensions of feedback credibility: accuracy, relevance, reasonableness, dependability, convincingness, and confidence ().

Measurement items, dimensions, and sources of perceived GAI feedback credibility.

The first item assessed accuracy, referring to whether students perceived the information provided by GAI feedback as correct. The second item measured relevance, indicating whether the feedback was related to students’ specific learning contexts. The third item captured reasonableness, focusing on whether the feedback was supported by logical reasoning. The fourth item assessed dependability, examining whether students considered GAI feedback a reliable source of information. The fifth item measured convincingness, referring to whether the explanations provided by GAI feedback were persuasive. The sixth item measured confidence, reflecting whether GAI feedback increased students’ confidence in the information provided by the system. All items were measured using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”). These items were developed and refined based on previous studies on information credibility, feedback quality, and trust in artificial intelligence systems to fit the context of GAI-supported learning. By distinguishing credibility from related concepts such as perceived usefulness, behavioral intention, cognitive engagement, and learning outcomes, this measurement captures students’ evaluations of whether GAI feedback information can be considered credible information.

The measurement items for Cognitive Engagement were developed based on previous studies examining students’ mental involvement during learning activities (). Specifically, this study draws primarily on the ICAP framework proposed by , which provides a theoretical basis for understanding differences in students’ levels of cognitive involvement during learning. In addition, items related to students’ mental effort and cognitive strategy use were developed based on the conceptualization of cognitive engagement proposed by , who examined how students invest cognitive resources during learning tasks. Based on these theoretical foundations, the items were adapted to the context of GAI-supported learning, focusing specifically on students’ mental effort and information processing when interacting with GAI feedback information.

Measurement items, dimensions, and sources of cognitive engagement.

The measurement items for Deep Learning were developed based on previous studies that conceptualize deep learning as a learning outcome (). Specifically, this study was informed by the deep learning framework proposed by , which distinguishes deep learning from surface learning. In addition, the development of the items considered the dimensions of deep learning identified in the Revised Two-Factor Study Process Questionnaire (R-SPQ-2F) developed by , including seeking meaning, relating concepts, and applying knowledge. Furthermore, the ideas proposed by  regarding deep learning were considered, particularly students’ ability to apply knowledge across different contexts. Based on these theoretical foundations, the measurement items were developed and adapted to the context of GAI-supported learning to assess students’ deep learning outcomes after interacting with GAI feedback information.

Measurement items, dimensions, and sources of deep learning.

Before the formal survey, this study conducted a pilot test with 100 respondents to evaluate the initial quality and applicability of the newly developed measurement scales. Because the scales were developed specifically to capture students’ perceptions and learning experiences related to GAI feedback information, the pilot test was necessary to examine whether the measurement items accurately reflected the theoretical meanings of the constructs and whether any items required further refinement. The pilot test included item analysis (), reliability analysis (), validity assessment (), and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) (). The results indicated that the measurement items showed satisfactory psychometric properties, and no substantial issues regarding item clarity, reliability, or construct representation were identified. Based on these findings, this study retained the measurement items and proceeded with the formal survey using a larger sample. The data collected from the formal survey were subsequently used for further validation of the measurement model through reliability analysis, EFA, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), convergent validity assessment, and discriminant validity assessment before testing the hypothesized relationships.

Based on the results of the pilot test, this study proceeded with the formal survey and collected data from a larger sample. The data used for the descriptive statistics reported in Section 3.5 and all subsequent analyses were obtained from the formal survey. Specifically, the formal survey data were used to further examine the measurement properties of the scales through reliability analysis, EFA, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), convergent validity assessment, and discriminant validity assessment. After establishing the adequacy of the measurement model, the structural model and hypothesized relationships were examined.

Descriptive statistics were first examined to assess the distributional characteristics of all measurement items. As shown in , all items were measured using a five-point Likert scale. The median value of all items was 4.000, indicating that students generally tended to agree with the statements regarding their perceptions and learning experiences related to GAI feedback information. The item means ranged from 3.438 to 3.866, with variances ranging from 0.972 to 1.523 and standard errors ranging from 0.044 to 0.055. These results indicate that students generally reported positive evaluations of GAI feedback information, while sufficient variability existed among participants’ responses.

Descriptive statistics of measurement items.

For Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, the six items (GFC1–GFC6) showed mean scores ranging from 3.556 to 3.692. Among these items, GFC1 (The information provided by GAI feedback is accurate) received the highest mean score (M = 3.692), followed by GFC5 (The explanations provided by GAI feedback are convincing) (M = 3.690) and GFC3 (The feedback provided by GAI offers reasonable support for its suggestions) (M = 3.589). GFC2 (The feedback provided by GAI is consistent with my actual learning situation) obtained a relatively lower mean score (M = 3.579). Overall, these findings suggest that students generally evaluated GAI feedback information positively in terms of accuracy, explanatory quality, and reliability. However, they were relatively more cautious about whether GAI feedback could fully correspond to their individual learning situations. The coefficients of variation for the six items ranged from 29.745 to 34.126%, indicating meaningful individual differences in students’ evaluations of GAI feedback credibility.

For Cognitive Engagement, the six items (CE1–CE6) demonstrated mean scores ranging from 3.438 to 3.652. CE3 (I examine the specific content and details of feedback generated by GAI) obtained the highest mean score (M = 3.652), suggesting that students tended to examine the specific information contained in GAI feedback information during learning activities. CE6 (I continue to use GAI feedback information to support my subsequent learning activities) showed the lowest mean score (M = 3.438), indicating that continuously relying on previously generated feedback to support later learning activities was relatively less common. Overall, these results suggest that students actively engaged with GAI feedback information by attending to and processing the information provided, although differences existed in the extent to which students maintained engagement with feedback over time. The coefficients of variation ranged from 32.297 to 34.707%, indicating adequate response variability across the cognitive engagement items.

For Deep Learning, the six items (DL1–DL6) showed the highest mean scores among the three constructs, ranging from 3.714 to 3.866. DL3 (GAI feedback helps me develop an overall framework of the learning content) received the highest mean score (M = 3.866), followed by DL6 (I can apply the knowledge gained from GAI feedback to other learning situations) (M = 3.761) and DL5 (GAI feedback helps me apply what I have learned to solve new problems) (M = 3.760). DL2 (GAI feedback helps me establish connections among different concepts in the learning content) obtained the lowest mean score (M = 3.714), although it remained above the midpoint of the scale. These findings indicate that students generally perceived GAI feedback information as helpful in supporting their understanding, knowledge organization, application, and transfer of learning. The coefficients of variation ranged from 25.942 to 28.029%, which were lower than those of the other two constructs, suggesting relatively greater consistency in students’ perceptions of the learning outcomes supported by GAI feedback.

The distributional characteristics of all measurement items were further examined. The skewness values ranged from −0.781 to −0.488, while the kurtosis values ranged from −0.658 to 0.164. These values indicate that none of the items showed substantial departures from normality, supporting the suitability of the data for subsequent analyses, including confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM). In addition, the interquartile ranges (IQRs) were mainly between 1 and 2, suggesting that participants’ responses showed sufficient dispersion rather than being concentrated around a single response category.

The final sample consisted of 506 undergraduate students from 10 full-time universities in Jinan City. Among them, 258 participants were male (51.0%) and 248 were female (49.0%). Regarding academic year, 127 students were first-year students (25.1%), 126 were second-year students (24.9%), 128 were third-year students (25.3%), and 125 were fourth-year students (24.7%). In terms of university type, 102 participants were from research-oriented universities (20.2%), 304 were from general undergraduate universities (60.1%), and 100 were from application-oriented universities (19.7%). Overall, the final sample demonstrated a relatively balanced distribution across university types, academic years, and gender groups, providing an appropriate foundation for subsequent structural equation modeling and hypothesis testing ().

Information of participants.

To ensure that participants had actual experience with GAI-supported learning, this study also collected information about participants’ GAI usage experience through the personal information section of the questionnaire before measuring the main constructs. All 506 participants reported that they had used GAI tools for learning activities, indicating that their evaluations of Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility were based on actual experiences with GAI systems rather than hypothetical situations.

Regarding the types of GAI tools used in learning activities, participants reported using various GAI platforms. Among them, ChatGPT was the most widely used tool, with 352 students (69.6%) reporting its use, followed by DeepSeek (318 students, 62.8%), Doubao (146 students, 28.9%), Gemini (96 students, 19.0%), and Claude (72 students, 14.2%). In addition, 58 students (11.5%) reported using other GAI tools. Since multiple choices were allowed for this question, the total percentage exceeds 100%.

Regarding the duration of GAI use, 86 students (17.0%) had used GAI tools for less than 3 months, 132 students (26.1%) for 3–6 months, 158 students (31.2%) for 6–12 months, and 130 students (25.7%) for more than 1 year. These results indicate that most participants had accumulated a certain level of experience with GAI-supported learning before participating in the survey.

Regarding the frequency of GAI use, 46 students (9.1%) reported using GAI tools less than once a month, 108 students (21.3%) several times a month, 176 students (34.8%) several times a week, 126 students (24.9%) almost every day, and 50 students (9.9%) multiple times per day. The results suggest that GAI tools had become a relatively common learning support resource among university students.

Regarding the main purposes of using GAI tools in learning activities, participants mainly reported using GAI for understanding course concepts (318 students, 62.8%), receiving explanations about learning materials (342 students, 67.6%), obtaining feedback on assignments or answers (356 students, 70.4%), improving written work or reports (284 students, 56.1%), solving learning problems (301 students, 59.5%), and summarizing course materials (236 students, 46.6%). Since multiple responses were allowed, the percentages do not add up to 100%.

Overall, participants demonstrated relatively rich experience with GAI use in university learning contexts, particularly in activities involving feedback provision, explanation of learning materials, and problem solving. Therefore, the measurement of Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility in this study was based on students’ actual experiences of interacting with GAI feedback information rather than evaluations of an imagined situation. Because some questions regarding GAI usage characteristics allowed multiple responses, the corresponding results are not presented in the sample characteristics table. To maintain consistency and clarity, the Sample Information table only reports basic demographic characteristics of participants, including gender, academic year, and university type. Detailed information regarding participants’ GAI usage experience is presented separately in the text.

To assess the internal consistency of the measurement instruments, Cronbach’s alpha coefficients and corrected item-total correlations (CITC) were examined. As presented in , all constructs demonstrated satisfactory reliability, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.70. Specifically, the Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility (GFC) scale, consisting of six items, achieved a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.893. The CITC values for the GFC items ranged from 0.691 to 0.758, indicating strong correlations between individual items and the overall construct. The Cognitive Engagement (CE) scale also exhibited excellent internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.898 and CITC values ranging from 0.698 to 0.763. The Deep Learning (DL) scale demonstrated good reliability, with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.840. The CITC values of the six DL items ranged from 0.592 to 0.653, suggesting that all items contributed adequately to the measurement of the construct. Overall, the reliability analysis indicated that all measurement scales possessed acceptable to excellent internal consistency.

Reliability analysis of the measurement scales.

An exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted to examine the construct validity of the measurement scales (). Prior to conducting the factor analysis, the suitability of the data was assessed using the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett’s test of sphericity. The results showed that the KMO value was 0.935, indicating excellent sampling adequacy. Bartlett’s test of sphericity was significant, χ2(153) = 4457.807, p < 0.001, suggesting that the correlation matrix was appropriate for factor analysis. The EFA results revealed a three-factor structure consistent with the theoretical framework of the study. Three factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted, explaining 62.553% of the total variance. Before rotation, the three factors accounted for 39.002%, 13.507%, and 10.043% of the variance, respectively. After rotation, the variance explained by the three factors was 21.976%, 21.747%, and 18.829%, respectively. All measurement items showed satisfactory factor loadings, ranging from 0.686 to 0.815, with no item exhibiting cross-loading problems. Specifically, the six Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility (GFC) items loaded strongly on Factor 2, with factor loadings ranging from 0.762 to 0.815. The six Cognitive Engagement (CE) items loaded on Factor 1, with loadings ranging from 0.719 to 0.808. The six Deep Learning (DL) items loaded on Factor 3, with loadings ranging from 0.686 to 0.721. All communalities exceeded 0.50 (range = 0.534–0.718), indicating that the extracted factors adequately explained the variance of each item.

Validity analysis of the measurement scales.

To assess the potential influence of common method bias (CMB), Harman’s single-factor test was conducted. All measurement items were entered into an unrotated exploratory factor analysis (EFA). The results indicated that three factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted, and the first factor accounted for 39.002% of the total variance, which was below the recommended threshold of 40%. Therefore, no substantial common method bias was identified, suggesting that CMB was unlikely to significantly affect the results of this study.

This study employed structural equation modeling (SEM) to analyze the data. The analysis consisted of two main steps. First, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to evaluate the reliability and validity of the measurement model. Second, the structural model was examined using SEM to investigate the hypothesized relationships among the constructs.

After assessing the reliability and validity of the measurement scales, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to examine whether the observed items appropriately represented the three latent constructs: Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility (GFC), Cognitive Engagement (CE), and Deep Learning (DL). The CFA was performed using maximum likelihood estimation based on the data from 506 undergraduate students ().

Confirmatory factor analysis.

***indicates statistical significance at p < 0.05.

The results indicated that the proposed three-factor measurement model showed an acceptable fit with the observed data. The chi-square value was 141.245 with 132 degrees of freedom, and the chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio (χ2/df) was 1.070, which was below the recommended value of 3. The model also achieved satisfactory values for other fit indices. Specifically, the goodness-of-fit index (GFI) was 0.971, the adjusted goodness-of-fit index (AGFI) was 0.962, the comparative fit index (CFI) was 0.998, the incremental fit index (IFI) was 0.998, the normed fit index (NFI) was 0.969, and the Tucker–Lewis index (TLI) was 0.998. In addition, the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) was 0.012, and the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) was 0.028, both meeting commonly accepted criteria. The 90% confidence interval of RMSEA ranged from 0.011 to 0.025, further indicating that the model estimation was within an acceptable range. These results suggest that the measurement model was consistent with the observed data.

The standardized factor loadings of all measurement items were examined to evaluate the relationship between the observed indicators and their corresponding latent constructs. For Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, the standardized loadings of GFC1–GFC6 ranged from 0.737 to 0.811. Specifically, GFC2 showed the highest loading (β = 0.811), followed by GFC1 (β = 0.788). For Cognitive Engagement, the standardized loadings of CE1–CE6 ranged from 0.741 to 0.815, with CE2 showing the highest loading (β = 0.815). For Deep Learning, the standardized loadings of DL1–DL6 ranged from 0.648 to 0.732, with DL5 showing the highest loading (β = 0.732). All factor loadings were statistically significant (p < 0.001), indicating that each item was significantly associated with its intended construct. The CR values of GFC, CE, and DL were 0.893, 0.898, and 0.840, respectively, indicating satisfactory internal consistency. The AVE values were 0.583, 0.596, and 0.467, respectively. Together with the significant factor loadings of all measurement items, these results indicate that the constructs demonstrated acceptable convergent validity.

In addition, the squared multiple correlation (SMC) values indicated that the measurement items explained a meaningful proportion of variance in their corresponding constructs. The SMC values ranged from 0.543 to 0.658 for GFC items, from 0.549 to 0.665 for CE items, and from 0.419 to 0.536 for DL items. These results suggest that the observed indicators provided adequate measurement information for their respective latent variables. Taken together, the CFA results indicate that the three-factor measurement model demonstrated acceptable model fit, reliability, and validity. The measurement model provided a suitable basis for further analysis of the relationships among Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, Cognitive Engagement, and Deep Learning.

Discriminant validity was assessed using the Fornell–Larcker criterion by comparing the square roots of the average variance extracted (AVE) values with the correlations among the constructs. As shown in , the square root of AVE for Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility (GFC) was 0.764, which was higher than its correlations with Cognitive Engagement (CE) (r = 0.388) and Deep Learning (DL) (r = 0.455). Similarly, the square root of AVE for CE was 0.772, exceeding its correlation with DL (r = 0.471). The square root of AVE for DL was 0.683, which was also higher than its correlations with the other constructs. These results indicate that the square roots of AVE for all constructs were greater than their corresponding inter-construct correlations, suggesting that GFC, CE, and DL have adequate discriminant validity and represent empirically distinct constructs.
