Discriminant validity was further assessed using the Heterotrait–Monotrait ratio (HTMT). As shown in , the HTMT values were 0.434 between GFC and CE, 0.527 between GFC and DL, and 0.543 between CE and DL. All HTMT values were below the recommended threshold of 0.85, indicating satisfactory discriminant validity among the three constructs. These results suggest that although Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, Cognitive Engagement, and Deep Learning were significantly related, they represented empirically distinct constructs.

HTMT (Heterotrait–Monotrait ratio) results.

After confirming the reliability and validity of the measurement model, structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted to examine the proposed relationships among perceived GAI feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and deep learning. The structural model was estimated using maximum likelihood estimation based on data from 506 undergraduate students. The results showed that the structural model demonstrated satisfactory fit with the empirical data. Specifically, χ2 = 141.245 with df = 132, resulting in a χ2/df ratio of 1.070. Other fit indices also indicated acceptable model fit, including GFI = 0.971, AGFI = 0.962, CFI = 0.998, IFI = 0.998, NFI = 0.969, and TLI = 0.998. The error indices were also within acceptable ranges (RMSEA = 0.012; SRMR = 0.028). These results indicate that the specified structural relationships were statistically consistent with the observed data. However, because the structural model included all possible paths among the three latent variables, the model was saturated, and the fit indices should not be interpreted as evidence supporting the superiority of the proposed causal ordering over alternative models. Therefore, the following analyses focus on examining the statistical associations among the constructs and the proposed indirect effect rather than establishing causal direction ().

Structural equation modeling analysis.

***indicates statistical significance at p < 0.05.

The standardized path coefficients were then examined to evaluate the hypothesized structural relationships (). As shown in , perceived GAI feedback credibility had a significant positive effect on deep learning (β = 0.356, p < 0.001). This finding indicates that students’ perceptions regarding the credibility of GAI feedback information directly contribute to their deep learning outcomes. Specifically, when students perceive GAI feedback as accurate, reliable, and useful, they are more likely to accept the feedback as meaningful learning information and incorporate it into their knowledge construction processes. From a cognitive learning perspective, credible feedback can reduce uncertainty regarding learning tasks, enhance students’ confidence in evaluating their own understanding, and encourage deeper processing strategies, such as reflection, elaboration, and knowledge integration. Therefore, the results provide empirical evidence that perceived GAI feedback credibility represents an important antecedent of deep learning in GAI-supported educational contexts. Thus, H1 was supported.

In addition, perceived GAI feedback credibility significantly predicted cognitive engagement (β = 0.428, p < 0.001), providing support for H2. Among all hypothesized structural paths, this relationship showed the strongest standardized coefficient, suggesting that students’ perceptions of GAI feedback credibility play a particularly important role in stimulating cognitive engagement. This result implies that students are more likely to invest cognitive effort when they trust the information generated by GAI systems. When GAI feedback is perceived as credible, students may be more willing to actively examine feedback content, compare it with their existing knowledge, identify knowledge gaps, and revise their understanding accordingly. Conversely, if students doubt the accuracy or reliability of GAI feedback, they may simply ignore the feedback or engage with it superficially. Therefore, perceived credibility functions as a psychological prerequisite that determines whether students actively process and utilize GAI feedback during learning.

Furthermore, cognitive engagement was found to significantly and positively influence deep learning (β = 0.394, p < 0.001), supporting H3. This result demonstrates that students’ active cognitive involvement is a key mechanism underlying deep learning development. Deep learning requires students not only to receive information but also to actively interpret, analyze, evaluate, and connect new knowledge with existing cognitive structures. The significant path from cognitive engagement to deep learning confirms that students who devote greater mental effort to learning activities are more likely to achieve higher levels of conceptual understanding and meaningful knowledge construction. This finding is consistent with cognitive learning theories, which emphasize that learning outcomes depend largely on the depth of learners’ information processing rather than merely on exposure to learning materials.

To further examine the mediating role of Cognitive Engagement in the relationship between Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility and Deep Learning, a bootstrap mediation analysis was conducted within the latent variable structural equation modeling framework using AMOS 31.0. The bootstrap procedure was performed with 2,000 resamples, and bias-corrected percentile confidence intervals were used to assess the statistical significance of the indirect effect. The results showed that the indirect effect of Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility on Deep Learning through Cognitive Engagement was statistically significant (β = 0.168, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.115, 0.232]). Since the 95% bootstrap confidence interval did not include zero, the mediating effect of Cognitive Engagement was supported. This result indicates that Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility was statistically associated with Deep Learning partly through its relationship with students’ Cognitive Engagement. Specifically, Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility was positively associated with Cognitive Engagement (β = 0.428, p < 0.001), and Cognitive Engagement was positively associated with Deep Learning (β = 0.394, p < 0.001). In addition, the direct effect of Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility on Deep Learning remained significant after Cognitive Engagement was included in the model (β = 0.356, p < 0.001). Therefore, Cognitive Engagement played a partial mediating role in the relationship between Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility and Deep Learning.

Furthermore, based on the latent variable SEM results, the total effect of Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility on Deep Learning was calculated as the sum of the direct effect (β = 0.356) and the indirect effect (β = 0.168), resulting in a total effect of β = 0.524. The indirect effect accounted for approximately 32.1% of the total effect. This finding suggests that Cognitive Engagement represents an important pathway through which students’ perceptions of GAI feedback credibility are statistically associated with their deep learning outcomes. This finding suggests that credible GAI feedback influences deep learning through two complementary mechanisms. First, students may directly benefit from high-quality and trustworthy feedback by improving their understanding and correcting misconceptions. Second, credible feedback increases students’ willingness to actively engage in cognitive processing, which further facilitates deeper learning.

The mediation result provides important insights into the psychological mechanism underlying GAI-supported learning. Although generative GAI systems can provide immediate feedback and learning guidance, the educational effectiveness of such feedback does not solely depend on the technological capability of the system. Instead, students’ perceptions of feedback credibility determine whether they actively engage with the provided information. When students trust GAI feedback, they are more likely to allocate cognitive resources toward analyzing and applying the feedback, thereby transforming GAI-generated information into meaningful learning experiences. Thus, the findings extend previous research on technology-enhanced learning by demonstrating that cognitive engagement serves as a critical psychological pathway linking GAI feedback perceptions to learning outcomes.

This study makes several theoretical contributions to research on generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in education by shifting attention from what GAI systems can provide to how learners understand and respond to GAI feedback information. Existing studies on GAI-supported education have mainly focused on technological functions, tool adoption, and the possible benefits of GAI applications. However, less attention has been given to the psychological processes through which learners evaluate GAI feedback information and engage with such feedback during learning activities. By introducing Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility as a key psychological construct, this study shows that students’ perceptions of GAI feedback credibility are positively associated with Cognitive Engagement and self-reported Deep Learning. These findings suggest that the educational value of GAI feedback is not simply determined by the ability of GAI systems to generate information, but is also related to whether learners consider such information credible and worthy of cognitive processing. Therefore, this study does not demonstrate that GAI itself directly produces better learning; rather, it explains how students form learning-related associations with GAI feedback information through psychological evaluation and cognitive engagement processes.

First, this study explores the theoretical understanding of GAI-supported learning from an educational psychology perspective by integrating the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), Information Processing Theory, and Constructivist Learning Theory to explain how learners interact with GAI feedback information. Previous research on educational GAI has mainly focused on technological functions, user acceptance, and the potential educational benefits of GAI applications. However, less attention has been given to the psychological processes through which learners evaluate GAI-generated information and transform such information into meaningful learning experiences. By introducing Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility as a key psychological construct, this study demonstrates that learners’ evaluations of GAI feedback credibility are positively associated with Cognitive Engagement and self-reported Deep Learning. These findings suggest that the educational value of GAI feedback does not arise simply from the system’s ability to generate information. Instead, learning-related outcomes depend partly on how learners evaluate, process, and utilize GAI-generated information. Therefore, this study supports the shared assumption of the three theoretical perspectives that external information does not automatically become knowledge; rather, learning requires learners’ active evaluation, cognitive processing, and meaning construction.

Second, this study extends the explanatory application of ELM and Information Processing Theory to GAI-supported learning environments. ELM proposes that individuals’ evaluations of information sources influence their willingness to further process information, while Information Processing Theory emphasizes that meaningful knowledge development requires active cognitive activities, including attention, interpretation, organization, and integration. Consistent with these theoretical perspectives, the findings show that Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility significantly predicts Cognitive Engagement, suggesting that learners’ judgments regarding the credibility of GAI feedback information are related to their subsequent cognitive involvement. Unlike traditional learning environments where information is mainly provided by teachers or human experts, GAI-supported environments introduce GAI systems as new sources of learning information. In this context, learners need to evaluate whether GAI feedback information is reliable and valuable before engaging with it. Thus, this study extends existing cognitive theories by demonstrating how information evaluation and cognitive processing operate in an GAI-mediated learning context.

Third, this study contributes to the application of Constructivist Learning Theory in GAI-supported learning environments. Constructivist perspectives emphasize that learning is not a passive process of receiving external information but an active process in which learners interpret, organize, and integrate new information based on existing knowledge structures. The findings indicate that Cognitive Engagement is positively associated with Deep Learning and partially mediates the relationship between Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility and Deep Learning. This result suggests that GAI feedback information does not directly create deeper learning by itself. Instead, its relationship with deeper learning experiences depends partly on whether learners actively engage with the information and construct meaning from it. Therefore, this study extends constructivist explanations of learning by highlighting the continuing importance of learner cognition in environments where knowledge-related information is increasingly generated by artificial intelligence.

Fourth, this study provides additional insights for research on cognitive engagement and feedback processes in GAI-supported learning environments. It should be noted that cognitive engagement theory and traditional feedback research were not the primary theoretical foundations used to develop the research model; rather, they provide additional perspectives for interpreting the empirical findings. The results show that learners’ responses to GAI feedback involve more than simple acceptance of information. Instead, they involve evaluating feedback credibility, investing cognitive effort, and actively processing GAI-generated information. Furthermore, unlike traditional feedback research that mainly examines feedback provided by teachers or human experts, GAI-supported learning introduces a new feedback source whose reliability requires learner evaluation. Therefore, this study provides further understanding of how feedback processes and learner cognition may operate when feedback is generated by artificial intelligence.

Fifth, this study expands feedback research by examining feedback credibility in the context of GAI-mediated learning. Traditional feedback research has mainly focused on feedback provided by teachers or human experts and has emphasized characteristics such as specificity, timing, and usefulness. However, GAI changes the source of feedback by introducing a new type of feedback provider that can generate immediate explanations, suggestions, and responses. In this context, learners need to evaluate not only the content of feedback but also the credibility of information provided by a GAI system. By identifying Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility as an important factor related to students’ responses to GAI feedback, this study extends feedback research beyond traditional human-to-human interactions and provides a theoretical perspective for understanding feedback processes in GAI-supported learning environments.

Finally, this study provides a new understanding of the learner’s role in GAI-supported learning. Previous discussions of educational technology have often emphasized the functions and capabilities of technological tools, while this study highlights the active role of learners in interpreting and processing GAI feedback information. The findings show that the relationship between GAI feedback and self-reported Deep Learning is not a simple relationship between technological input and learning experience. Instead, it involves learners’ psychological evaluation of feedback and their cognitive engagement with the provided information. This perspective positions GAI-supported learning as a process involving technological information, learner perception, and cognitive processing, rather than merely a process of receiving information from a technological system.

Overall, this study contributes to the theoretical understanding of GAI-supported learning by establishing a learner-centered perspective based on the relationship among Perceived GAI Feedback Credibility, Cognitive Engagement, and Deep Learning. Rather than viewing GAI feedback as an independent factor that automatically improves learning, this study demonstrates that learners’ perceptions and cognitive engagement are important aspects for understanding how GAI feedback information is associated with learning processes. This perspective provides a theoretical basis for further examining the interaction between GAI feedback information and learner cognition in educational contexts.

The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is changing the way students interact with learning information. Compared with traditional sources of feedback, GAI can provide immediate explanations, suggestions, and evaluations, creating a new learning situation in which information is no longer provided only by teachers or textbooks but also needs to be actively interpreted and processed by learners. Therefore, in GAI-supported learning environments, the key issue is not simply whether students have access to GAI tools, but how they develop meaningful psychological engagement with GAI feedback information. The practical implication of this study is that the value of GAI feedback as a learning resource depends not only on the information generated by the technology itself but also on how learners understand and process such information. Therefore, educational practices should pay greater attention to learners’ psychological activities during interactions with GAI feedback information rather than focusing only on technological functions.

First, this study suggests that educators should reconsider the abilities students need in the GAI era. Traditional learning environments often emphasize acquiring, memorizing, and applying knowledge, whereas GAI-supported environments require students to interact with explanations and feedback generated by intelligent systems. In this context, learning ability is reflected not only in obtaining information efficiently but also in understanding, analyzing, and using externally generated information appropriately. Educational practices can include reflective learning activities that encourage students to examine the relationship between GAI feedback and their learning goals and to explain how they interpret and use generated information. For example, students may be asked to identify how GAI feedback changes their understanding, which aspects require further consideration, and how the feedback can be incorporated into their own learning process. Such activities may help students treat GAI feedback as a resource for active learning rather than simply as received information.

Second, this study provides practical implications for applying feedback theories in GAI-supported learning contexts. Previous feedback research has mainly focused on feedback provided by human instructors and examined characteristics such as specificity, timing, and usefulness. However, GAI feedback introduces a new psychological issue: how learners understand and respond to information provided by a non-human source. In educational practice, teachers should therefore pay attention not only to whether GAI provides feedback but also to how students participate in the interpretation of such feedback. For instance, teachers can design learning tasks that require students to evaluate the relationship between GAI feedback and their own understanding, explain why they accept or modify certain suggestions, or develop their own ideas based on generated feedback. Such designs may transform feedback from a one-way information delivery process into an active cognitive activity involving learners.

Third, this study highlights the importance of cognitive engagement in GAI-supported learning and provides implications from a psychological process perspective. Learning does not occur simply because information is available; rather, it depends on whether learners actively process and organize information. Therefore, when designing GAI-assisted learning activities, educators should pay attention to whether students are genuinely involved in processing feedback rather than only completing tasks involving GAI. Specifically, learning activities can include opportunities for students to explain, compare, and reflect on GAI feedback information. Such designs may create conditions that encourage students to invest cognitive effort and participate in deeper learning processes.

Fourth, this study provides new insights into the role of teachers in GAI-supported learning environments. The development of GAI does not mean that teachers simply become managers of technology; instead, it highlights the continued importance of teachers as designers of learning experiences and supporters of students’ psychological processes. When GAI becomes part of learning activities, teachers need to pay attention to how students interpret feedback, engage in cognitive processing, and connect external information with their existing knowledge. Therefore, the focus of teachers’ guidance may shift from only delivering knowledge to creating learning environments that encourage explanation, reflection, and active participation.

Overall, the practical significance of this study lies in showing that the value of GAI-supported learning does not depend only on the ability of GAI to generate information, but also on how learners establish psychological connections with generated information. GAI changes the source of learning information, but learning processes still depend on learners’ understanding, processing, and active involvement. Therefore, the application of GAI in higher education should consider learners’ psychological processes and focus on supporting students’ meaningful engagement with GAI feedback information and deeper learning processes.

Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping the way information is accessed and processed in learning environments. However, a fundamental psychological question remains insufficiently understood: When students encounter GAI feedback information, what determines whether GAI functions as a tool that facilitates cognitive development or becomes a substitute that undermines autonomous thinking? By revealing the psychological pathway of perceived GAI feedback credibility–cognitive engagement–deep learning, the present study provides a new explanation for this question. The findings demonstrate that the educational value of GAI does not originate solely from its information-generating capability; rather, it depends on how learners psychologically evaluate GAI feedback and how such evaluations subsequently influence their cognitive processing. Therefore, this study suggests that future GAI-assisted learning practices should move beyond a focus on “technological effectiveness” toward “psychological effectiveness,” emphasizing the dynamic interplay among trust, engagement, and cognitive activity during human-AI interaction.

First, this study provides important implications for understanding the psychological relationship between students and GAI. Current discussions regarding educational GAI have primarily focused on a technological question: whether GAI can provide accurate, timely, and personalized feedback. However, the present findings indicate that the effectiveness of GAI feedback in promoting learning does not depend solely on the quality of the feedback itself, but also on whether students perceive GAI as a credible source of information. Perceived GAI feedback credibility reflects learners’ psychological evaluation of the value and reliability of GAI-generated information and serves as an important psychological bridge linking technological outputs to learning behaviors. Therefore, in future GAI-enhanced learning environments, educators should not simply encourage students to “trust GAI” or “avoid using GAI”; instead, they should help students develop a more sophisticated trust framework that enables them to evaluate the credibility of GAI feedback based on evidence and contextual relevance. Such calibrated trust can prevent two undesirable outcomes: excessive reliance on GAI suggestions that may lead to cognitive dependency, and insufficient trust that prevents students from benefiting from valuable GAI-based cognitive support.

Second, this study highlights cognitive engagement as a key psychological mechanism connecting GAI feedback experiences with deep learning outcomes. This finding is particularly important because it challenges the technology-deterministic assumption that providing students with more information through GAI will automatically result in improved learning. The results suggest that GAI feedback can facilitate deep learning only when it activates students’ active thinking, analysis, and reflection. From a cognitive psychological perspective, learning is not merely the accumulation of information input; rather, it involves learners’ active selection, processing, organization, and integration of information. Therefore, the primary goal of GAI-assisted learning design should not be to maximize GAI-generated outputs, but to maximize students’ cognitive activities during GAI interaction. For example, GAI systems can encourage deeper information processing by asking students to explain why they accept or reject GAI feedback, compare GAI suggestions with their own perspectives, or anticipate the potential consequences of adopting specific recommendations. In other words, effective GAI-supported learning environments should not enable students to “think less,” but should help them “think better.”

Third, this study provides psychological insights into addressing challenges related to students’ cognitive autonomy in the era of generative GAI. As GAI tools continue to reduce the costs of information searching and knowledge generation, a new educational concern has emerged: students may outsource cognitive tasks to GAI and consequently reduce their own mental effort. However, the present findings suggest that the positive role of GAI does not come from reducing cognitive effort, but from stimulating learners’ cognitive activities through meaningful feedback interaction. Therefore, future GAI-based educational practices should not focus primarily on restricting GAI use; instead, they should cultivate students’ psychological abilities to regulate their interaction with GAI. Specifically, students need to develop metacognitive monitoring abilities that allow them to recognize gaps in their own understanding, evaluate whether GAI feedback aligns with their learning goals, and make informed decisions about when to rely on GAI assistance and when to engage in independent reasoning. Through such psychological regulation, GAI can serve as a tool for expanding human cognitive capabilities rather than replacing human thinking.

Overall, this study advances an important psychological perspective: whether generative GAI promotes learning does not depend on how much information GAI can generate, but on how learners understand, evaluate, and utilize that information. By demonstrating the roles of perceived GAI feedback credibility and cognitive engagement in the development of deep learning, this study provides new insights into the psychological processes underlying human-AI collaborative learning. Future educational practices should therefore focus not only on enabling students to use GAI, but also on helping them establish a productive psychological relationship with GAI, one that promotes autonomous thinking, deep cognitive processing, and sustained intellectual development.

Although this study provides important insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying how perceived GAI feedback credibility promotes deep learning through cognitive engagement, several limitations should be acknowledged.

First, the present study employed a cross-sectional survey design, which limits the ability to draw definitive causal conclusions regarding the relationships among perceived GAI feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and deep learning. Although the hypothesized model was supported by structural equation modeling and mediation analyses, the findings primarily reflect associations among psychological constructs at a single point in time. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs, experimental approaches, or experience-sampling methods to further examine how students’ trust in GAI feedback develops over time and how changes in GAI-related perceptions influence learning processes.

Second, the sample consisted of undergraduate students from universities in a single Chinese city, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to students from different educational levels, cultural backgrounds, or institutional contexts. Future studies could extend this research by recruiting more diverse samples across different regions and countries, allowing researchers to examine whether cultural values, educational systems, and levels of GAI literacy influence the psychological mechanisms identified in this study.

Third, this study relied primarily on self-reported measures to assess students’ perceptions and learning experiences. Although self-report instruments are widely used in educational psychology research and demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity in the present study, they may not fully capture students’ actual cognitive behaviors during GAI-assisted learning. Future research could combine self-report data with behavioral indicators, such as GAI interaction logs, learning analytics, task performance measures, or think-aloud protocols, to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of students’ cognitive engagement processes.

Fourth, the measurement scales developed in this study should be further validated in future research. Because GAI-supported learning and GAI feedback information represent relatively emerging educational contexts, existing measurement instruments may not fully capture students’ perceptions and learning processes in this new environment. Therefore, this study operationalized the examined constructs through newly developed scales based on relevant theoretical literature. Before the formal survey, this study conducted a pilot study and performed reliability and validity analyses to examine the preliminary quality of the measures. The formal survey data were further used to assess the measurement model through EFA, CFA, and other validity tests. Nevertheless, these scales have not yet been extensively examined across independent samples, different educational contexts, or diverse GAI application scenarios. Future research should continue to test and refine these measures to further establish their applicability across broader contexts.

Finally, this study did not examine the potential role of GAI usage intensity in the proposed model. Although participants’ GAI usage experience, including usage frequency and duration, was collected through the questionnaire, these characteristics were not incorporated into the current analysis. The present study focused on how students perceive and process GAI feedback information after entering a GAI-supported learning context, rather than on how differences in GAI usage experience shape students’ interactions with GAI systems. However, students with different levels of GAI exposure may develop different levels of familiarity with GAI feedback information, which could influence their perceptions of feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and learning experiences. Future research could further investigate whether GAI usage intensity functions as a boundary condition by examining its role as a control variable or moderator in the relationship among perceived GAI feedback credibility, cognitive engagement, and deep learning.

neuroscience.title: Longitudinal characterization of a Leigh-like presentation associated with the MT-ND4 m.11470A>C variant
neuroscience.abstract: Leigh syndrome comprises genetically heterogeneous mitochondrial disorders, but interpretation of rare mitochondrial DNA variants is often limited by sparse longitudinal data. We report a male patient followed from childhood to age 16 with the MT-ND4 m.11470A>C (p. (Lys237Asn)) variant. Right-eye strabismus and optic atrophy appeared at age 3, followed by progressive limb weakness, gait instability, and dysarthria. At age 16, magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral lesions involving the basal ganglia, thalami, midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The patient subsequently developed respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. The variant was detected in saliva at a pipeline-reported heteroplasmy level of 51.8% and was not detected by Sanger sequencing in saliva from the mother or dizygotic twin brother. APOGEE 2 predicted a potential deleterious effect, the affected residue was conserved, and static structural visualization suggested altered local contacts. A targeted review identified previous associations of m.11470A>C with MELAS and a Leigh syndrome record in a pediatric cohort. This detailed longitudinal case adds clinical and neuroimaging resolution to the reported m.11470A>C spectrum and supports integrating disease trajectory, tissue source, heteroplasmy, and family data when interpreting rare mitochondrial DNA variants.
neuroscience.text:
Leigh syndrome is a progressive mitochondrial encephalopathy characterized by neurological deterioration and bilateral lesions of the basal ganglia, brainstem, or both. Its genetic basis spans mitochondrial and nuclear genomes, and the relationship between a specific variant and clinical presentation is often modified by heteroplasmy, tissue distribution, and genetic background (; ; ).

MT-ND4 encodes a membrane subunit of mitochondrial respiratory complex I. Variants in MT-ND4 have been associated with Leigh syndrome, Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes (MELAS), optic neuropathy, and other mitochondrial phenotypes (; ). The m.11470A > C substitution, which changes lysine 237 to asparagine, was reported in a Chinese MELAS cohort (). A later pediatric cohort also recorded the variant in one patient classified as having Leigh syndrome, but did not provide an individual longitudinal description ().

Here, we provide a 13-year clinical, neuroimaging, and genetic characterization of a patient with a Leigh-like presentation associated with m.11470A>C. We also place the case within a targeted review of reported MT-ND4 phenotypes and reassess the strength of the variant evidence using mitochondrial DNA-specific interpretation criteria.

A 16-year-old male was admitted with a 13-year history of right-eye strabismus, a 3-year history of limb weakness, and dyspnea for 1 week. After obtaining written informed consent from the patient and his legal guardian, we collected the patient’s clinical data, including physical examination, laboratory tests, and cranial MRI findings. This written informed consent form includes the publication of case text, test results, imaging data, sequencing images, and genetic/family information.

Saliva samples were obtained from the proband, his mother, and his dizygotic twin brother. Genomic DNA was extracted with the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). DNA concentration and purity were assessed with a Qubit 4.0 fluorometer and NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, United States).

Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed by a clinical laboratory. We received the final clinical sequencing report and did not have access to raw sequencing data. Whole-exome sequencing was performed with the Illumina DNA Prep with Exome 2.5 Enrichment kit on a NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States) using 150-bp paired-end reads. The clinical WES target comprised 20,858 nuclear genes, including nuclear genes associated with Leigh syndrome and mitochondrial encephalopathies (Specific gene list can be found in ). Mitochondrial reads were recovered from off-target WES data and processed with an in-house mitochondrial genome pipeline. The mitochondrial genome analysis included 37 mitochondrial genes. Candidate variants were evaluated by Sanger sequencing in the proband and tested relatives.

The missense variant was assessed with APOGEE 2, a mitochondria-specific ensemble predictor with scores ranging from 0 to 1. ND4 sequences from 12 species were aligned with ClustalW and visualized in Jalview to assess residue conservation.

Static structural visualization was performed in PyMOL version 2.5 (Schrödinger, New York, NY, United States) using the cryo-electron microscopy structure of human mitochondrial complex I (PDB 6ZR2). The Lys237Asn substitution was introduced with the mutagenesis tool, and local residue contacts were inspected by distance measurement. This analysis was treated as hypothesis-generating and not as functional validation.

Evidence was reassessed with the mitochondrial DNA-specific ACMG/AMP specifications proposed by . Evidence codes were applied only when the available data met the mitochondrial DNA-specific definitions. A negative Sanger result in a single maternal tissue was not considered sufficient to confirm a de novo event or to apply the PS2 criterion; therefore, the family findings were described as apparently de novo.

PubMed was searched on October 14, 2026 using the terms (MT-ND4 OR ND4 OR “NADH dehydrogenase subunit 4”) AND (Leigh OR MELAS OR encephalopathy OR optic neuropathy). The search returned 359 records. After removal of duplicates 359 records were screened by title and abstract. Titles and abstracts were screened by two authors (L.L. and H.L.), and disagreements were resolved by consensus. 150 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Studies were included if they reported human case reports or case series with an MT-ND4 point variant or a mitochondrial deletion involving MT-ND4 together with clinical phenotype data. Experimental studies without human phenotype data were excluded. Point variants and large deletions were summarized separately because a multigene deletion cannot support an MT-ND4-specific inference. A total of eight point variants from 16 articles and 2 large deletions from 2 articles were included.

This male patient had right-eye strabismus and optic atrophy documented at age 3. MRI performed at age 3 was reported to show bilateral basal ganglia signal abnormalities. However, due to the passage of time, the original imaging data was no longer available. Over the following decade, the patient developed left upper-limb weakness, gait instability, and dysarthria. At age 16, he was admitted with inspiratory dyspnea.

Neurological examination at age 16 showed dysarthria, restricted movement of the right eye, left eye exotropia, decreased visual acuity, ptosis, grade 4 muscle strength in all four limbs, and clumsy finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements. Serum lactate was 1.52 mmol/L. MRI showed bilateral signal abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalami, midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata (). The progressive neurological course and bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem lesions were considered consistent with a Leigh syndrome.

During hospitalization, respiratory failure required intubation and mechanical ventilation, which was initiated in SIMV + PSV mode with FiO2 40%, PEEP 5 cmH2O, and VT 8 mL/kg. Consciousness declined to stupor; the pupils were 2.0 mm bilaterally and remained reactive to light. In addition to supportive care, a mitochondrial cocktail was administered (Coenzyme Q10 300 mg/d, divided into three oral doses; levocarnitine 2 g/d, intravenous drip; idebenone 90 mg/d; Vitamin B1 300 mg/d; Vitamin B2 50 mg/d; and Vitamin B6 30 mg/d). Due to the patient’s articulation disorders and swallowing difficulties, a nasogastric tube was placed for enteral nutrition support.

Invasive mechanical ventilation lasted for 11 days. On the 8th day after admission, the patient’s consciousness changed from stupor to drowsiness, and the pupils recovered to 2.5 mm and reactive to light. His spontaneous breathing rhythm tended to be regular. Re-examination of arterial blood gas (at FiO2 30%) showed PaO2 88 mmHg, PaCO2 42 mmHg, and pH 7.40. On the 12th day, the endotracheal tube was successfully removed, followed by nasal high flow humidified oxygen therapy (FiO2 28%, flow rate 35 L/min), and then gradually transitioned to nasal cannula oxygen therapy (2 L/min), with blood oxygen saturation maintained at 95%–98%.

The patient’s clinical status gradually improved during hospitalization. However, because invasive mechanical ventilation, oxygen therapy, enteral nutrition, and the mitochondrial cocktail were administered concurrently, and because no objective efficacy endpoints were available, the contribution of the mitochondrial cocktail to this improvement cannot be determined. At the time of discharge, the patient’s consciousness was clear, the questions and answers were relevant, and the articulation disorder was reduced compared to before. The limb muscle strength improved to grade 4+/5. With the help of others, the patient was able to walk short distances. The finger nose test and rapid rotation movements improved compared to when admitted, but there was still mild ataxia in the left limb and blurred vision. Before discharge, a follow-up head MRI showed no significant progression of abnormal signals in the brainstem and basal ganglia, and blood lactate decreased to 0.98 mmol/L.

After discharge, the patient continued to receive coenzyme Q10, idebenone, and B vitamins, and was regularly followed up at the neurology clinic. At the three-month telephone and outpatient follow-up, the patient was able to walk independently at home (with slightly unstable gait), without the need for assisted ventilation. Oral feeding was good (nasogastric tube has been removed), and no respiratory failure or consciousness disorders have occurred again. Daily life self-care (Barthel index score 65), articulation disorders and limb weakness symptoms did not progressively worsen compared to discharge.

Collectively, according to the diagnostic criteria of Leigh syndrome spectrum (), the progressive neural processes and bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem lesions were consistent with the neuroimaging core criterion of the Leigh syndrome spectrum. However, the absence of biochemical or mitochondrial abnormality meant that the full diagnostic criteria for Leigh syndrome were not met. Confirmatory neuropathology was also not available. Consequently, the presentation of this patient was termed Leigh-like presentation.

The clinical WES target comprised 20,858 nuclear genes and spanned 37,837,472 bp. Target coverage was 99.72%, mean depth was 127.27×, and 97.97% of target bases were covered at ≥20×. The nuclear genes associated with Leigh syndrome and mitochondrial encephalopathies were included in this WES target set. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic nuclear variant concordant with the patient’s phenotype was identified within the laboratory’s established analytical scope and reporting thresholds. The clinical report listed two heterozygous variants in autosomal recessive genes as suspected pathogenic findings: DNAJB2 c.91C>T, p. His31Tyr, and GUSB c.1145G>A, p. Arg382His. Each variant was heterozygous in an autosomal recessive condition, neither was phenotype-concordant, and neither was validated in parents. They were therefore not considered explanatory.

Mitochondrial reads were recovered from off-target WES data and processed with an in-house mitochondrial genome pipeline. The mitochondrial genome analysis included 37 mitochondrial genes and spanned 16,569 bp. The mitochondrial reference genome was covered at 100%, with a mean depth of 15,848.91×, and 100% of sites were covered at ≥20×. The m.11470A>C variant, which remains classified as a VUS, was identified in the proband’s saliva. The heteroplasmy level was 51.8%, derived directly from the NGS read fraction, that is, the mutant allele frequency calculated from total reads covering the locus, rather than from Sanger chromatogram peak-height quantitation. The laboratory’s stated detection limit for heteroplasmic variants by this platform is approximately 25%, and the reported level of 51.8% exceeds this general threshold. However, site-specific read counts, including total depth, reference and mutant read numbers, strand bias, and NUMT filtering, were not available in the provided sequencing report. Therefore, the 51.8% value is treated as a pipeline-reported heteroplasmy level rather than an independently confirmed quantitative measure. No other mitochondrial DNA variant exceeding the laboratory’s reporting threshold was detected in the proband’s mitochondrial genome reads.

Sanger sequencing confirmed the heteroplasmic state in the proband, whereas the variant was not detected in saliva from the mother or dizygotic twin brother (). However, the mother was only tested by PCR-Sanger sequencing, with no NGS data available, and the Sanger detection limit for heteroplasmic variants is reported as ∼25% by the testing laboratory. Furthermore, maternal biological relationship was not confirmed by polymorphic marker analysis. Therefore, although the family findings are compatible with an apparently de novo event, low-level (particularly <25%) or tissue-restricted maternal heteroplasmy cannot be definitively excluded. The whole-exome sequencing data were also systematically interrogated for pathogenic variants in nuclear genes implicated in Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalopathies. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic nuclear gene variants were identified within the laboratory’s established analytical scope and standard reporting thresholds. Furthermore, no other mitochondrial DNA variants exceeding the laboratory’s reporting threshold were detected in the proband’s mitochondrial genome reads.

Consequently, the PS2 criterion (de novo, confirmed in parents) was not applied in the ACMG classification because a confirmed de novo event was not established. The variant therefore remains classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS), supported by PM2_Supporting (absent from population databases) and PP3_Supporting (APOGEE 2, a mitochondria-specific ensemble predictor, returned a deleterious score of 0.9). This classification is consistent with the original clinical laboratory report, which also classified the variant as VUS based on the same evidence codes.

APOGEE 2 returned a score of 0.9, and Lys237 was conserved across the 12 aligned species (). Static visualization placed residue 237 within a transmembrane helix and suggested altered local contacts after substitution of lysine by asparagine (). The model did not directly test proton translocation, complex I assembly, or respiratory-chain function.

Reassessment under mitochondrial DNA-specific ACMG/AMP criteria, applying only evidence codes that met the mitochondrial DNA-specific definitions, did not alter the original VUS classification. PM1 was not applied because the mitochondrial DNA specifications do not use this criterion; PP3 was retained only at supporting strength; and PP4 was not applied because the required biochemical evidence was unavailable. A de novo code was not applied because maternal testing was limited to saliva and Sanger sequencing. The variant was therefore treated conservatively as a variant of uncertain significance, while the repeated disease associations and the present phenotype were considered clinically informative.

The targeted review showed that individually reported MT-ND4 point variants span Leigh syndrome, MELAS, atypical MELAS, optic-neuropathy-plus, and late-onset encephalopathy phenotypes (). Large mitochondrial deletions involving MT-ND4 were analyzed separately and were not used to infer an MT-ND4-specific phenotype.

For m.11470A>C specifically, Zhao et al. reported the variant in a Chinese cohort ascertained for MELAS and MELAS/Leigh overlap (). A case report from 2021 showed a patient classified as Leigh syndrome who also had the m.11470A > C mutation, but did not provide personal longitudinal details (). Accordingly, the contribution of the present case is a detailed longitudinal characterization rather than a claim of the first Leigh syndrome association.

This report adds a 13-year clinical history, including detailed characterization of the acute presentation at age 16 and short-term follow-up, to the reported phenotypic spectrum of MT-ND4 m.11470A > C. The patient progressed from childhood ocular abnormalities and optic atrophy to limb weakness, gait instability, dysarthria, extensive bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem lesions, and respiratory failure requiring invasive ventilation. The clinical trajectory, neuroimaging, and genetic findings support a potential association with the Leigh phenotype, while the data do not independently establish molecular causality.

The main alternative phenotype to consider is MELAS, given that m.11470A>C was initially reported in a Chinese MELAS/MELAS–Leigh overlap cohort in a 36-year-old woman with stroke-like episodes and cortical lesions (). A later pediatric cohort reported m.11470A > C in one patient classified as having Leigh syndrome (). These findings suggest that m.11470A > C may be associated with more than one mitochondrial phenotype. MELAS is classically defined by mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes; clinically, it may manifest with stroke-like attacks, seizures, headache, and vomiting, and imaging typically shows cortical lesions, often asymmetric or migratory (; ). In contrast, our patient presented in childhood with strabismus, optic atrophy, symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions, and no stroke-like episodes. This pattern is more consistent with the Leigh syndrome spectrum than with classic MELAS. However, MT-ND4 variants can produce overlapping and age-dependent phenotypes, and transitions between Leigh syndrome and MELAS have been reported for other MT-ND variants (). Given that m.11470A>C has been reported in both MELAS and Leigh syndrome phenotypes, and that the present patient shows a Leigh-like presentation, we describe the phenotype at the presentation level rather than assigning the variant to a single diagnostic category.

Phenotypic variation is expected in mitochondrial disease because heteroplasmy and threshold effects differ across tissues and over time (; ; ; ). However, the 51.8% value in this patient was measured only in saliva at one time point. During follow-up, we considered additional non-invasive sampling, including urinary epithelial cells and buccal swabs, to assess tissue-related heteroplasmy variation. However, owing to financial constraints, the patient and his family declined further testing. Therefore, the tissue distribution of m.11470A > C remains uncharacterized, and the saliva-based heteroplasmy value should not be extrapolated to clinically affected tissues such as brain and muscle, nor can it explain the absence of symptoms in relatives in whom the variant was not detected. The family results therefore contribute descriptive context rather than direct evidence for a tissue threshold.

The computational findings provide supporting, hypothesis-generating evidence. APOGEE 2 and residue conservation indicate that the substitution is not readily dismissed as neutral, while the static model suggests a local structural change. The predicted transmembrane location of Lys237 adds a further structural consideration. This residue is a conserved charged component of the proton-translocation pathway within the ND4 subunit, where it participates in a network of ion pairs and water-mediated proton transfer (; ). Its protonation state regulates local conformational changes that propagate to the ND4–ND5 interface (). Substitution of this positively charged lysine with a neutral, polar asparagine is therefore expected to be energetically unfavorable within the hydrophobic environment of transmembrane helix 8, potentially disrupting the local helical geometry and the ion-pair network required for proton translocation. Furthermore, loss of the positive charge at this position may impair the conformational coupling between ND4 and ND5, affecting the stability or assembly of the distal membrane arm of complex I (). However, no functional evidence currently demonstrates that m.11470A > C impairs complex I activity, assembly, or proton translocation. The absence of muscle biochemical testing, multi-tissue heteroplasmy measurements, and functional assays limits the certainty of pathogenic classification, but it does not remove the clinical value of documenting the associated phenotype.

This case does not justify changing gene-panel composition because MT-ND4 is already an established mitochondrial disease gene. Its practical contribution is more specific: m.11470A>C should be interpreted across mitochondrial syndrome boundaries, with attention to disease trajectory, neuroimaging, tissue source, heteroplasmy, and family data. Further individually documented cases and functional studies will be needed to determine the variant’s molecular effect and penetrance.

This longitudinal case broadens the clinical characterization of the MT-ND4 m.11470A > C spectrum by describing a progressive Leigh-like presentation in a patient harboring the variant with extensive basal ganglia and brainstem involvement. The findings support a phenotype-level association and illustrate the need for evidence-calibrated interpretation of rare mitochondrial DNA variants. However, the variant remains a VUS and causality is not established.

neuroscience.title: An interpretable physics-informed graph neural network for forecasting longitudinal tau progression in Alzheimer’s disease
neuroscience.abstract: Forecasting the progression of tau pathology by modeling its spatiotemporal dynamics is critical for characterizing Alzheimer’s disease (AD), where tau is a key driver of disease progression. Tau is an important prognostic biomarker for AD and is a primary endpoint for many ongoing clinical therapeutic trials. Tau burden can be quantified in vivo using positron emission tomography (PET), while its propagation is hypothesized to follow the structural connectome derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), providing a framework for modeling network-driven tau spread. Deep learning approaches, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), enable data-driven learning of regional changes in tau burden by leveraging brain connectivity. However, purely data-driven models are prone to overfitting and may fail to capture biologically meaningful propagation patterns. To address this, we present here a physics-informed GNN framework for tau forecasting that incorporates prior models of tau propagation, specifically the Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (FKPP) equation and the epidemic spreading model (ESM), as regularization terms in the latent space of the network. Our analysis relies on PET and DTI data from N = 462N=462 amyloid-positive human subjects from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Our results demonstrate that physics-informed models improve model performance over the unregularized baseline across multiple evaluation metrics, with regularization in the latent space improving robustness compared to that in the feature space. The FKPP formulation achieves the best mean predictive performance, followed closely by ESM. We further implement post-hoc interpretability using Integrated Gradients to identify key regions and connections driving the model’s predictions. The interpretability analysis is consistent with the observed performance gains, indicating that physics-based regularization yields more localized attribution within biologically relevant regions. Overall, our findings demonstrate that integrating prior formulations of tau propagation with GNNs enhances predictive accuracy and interpretability, providing a promising framework for modeling network-driven spread of tau pathology.

neuroscience.title: Exploring the cost-effectiveness of blood biomarker tests to select patients with head injury and possible traumatic brain injury for CT brain scans in the UK setting
neuroscience.abstract: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) carries a risk of intracranial haemorrhage which may require observation, be prognostically significant, and in a small proportion of patients be life-threatening requiring urgent neurosurgical intervention. In the emergency department, a key component of the initial assessment is determining the need for a CT brain scan. An approach of providing CT scans to all patients is inefficient as more than 90% of CT scans performed for mTBI show no intracranial injury, and only 1%–2% result in neurosurgical intervention. However, delayed neurosurgery can result in avoidable deaths. Blood-based biomarker tests offer a potential solution by enabling improved risk stratification for CT imaging; however, their cost-effectiveness remains uncertain.To evaluate the potential cost-effectiveness of blood biomarker tests for triaging patients with mTBI for further neuroimaging.Decision-analytic health economic modelling using parameter inputs based on data from a Collaborative European Neurotrauma Effectiveness Research mTBI (CENTER-TBI) cohort, published literature and clinical input. The model is composed of a 6-month decision tree followed by a lifetime state-transition model estimating health outcomes and costs based on whether treatment was prompt or delayed due to the diagnostic accuracy of the testing strategy. In the base case, all biomarker tests were assumed to have ≥95% sensitivity with specificity ranging from 8% to 42%; these data are derived from data from CENTER-TBI.UK National Health Service.Patients with mTBI who have been identified as needing a CT brain scan using UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Guidelines.‘CT all’ versus provision of CT only when blood biomarker result is positive.Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained and costs valued at 2023/2024 prices.The base case model suggests that current biomarker tests generate less QALYs gained and incur higher costs compared with ‘CT all’ strategy. This is driven by the lower sensitivity of biomarkers, leading to more false negative cases, delayed treatment and QALY losses. This is coupled with the higher costs of treating false negative patients and in some patients incurring both the costs of biomarkers and CT scans. This finding is consistent across all scenarios.Current biomarker tests are not estimated to be cost-effective in this setting compared with a ‘CT all’ strategy. However, should future biomarker tests achieve both a very high sensitivity and high specificity they could become a cost-effective alternative to CT scans for all.NCT02210221.
neuroscience.text:
Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) patients, defined as those presenting with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores of 13–15 after head injury and clinical or radiological evidence of TBI, cost the UK approximately £15 billion annually. Worldwide, over 60 million people are estimated to sustain a TBI each year of which >85% are classified as mild, with a cost to the global economy exceeding US$400 billion. A clinically important proportion of patients with mTBI sustain intracranial haemorrhage, which may require hospital observation and/or further follow-up and, in a small subset of cases, may be life-threatening and require neurosurgical and/or neurocritical care intervention. Current practice is to perform a CT to detect such injuries, which comes with a cost and radiation burden as well as increasing the time spent in the emergency department (ED) by the patients. For head injury patients with a GCS 13–15, the CT scan will reveal intracranial injury in 2%–8% of patients depending on the imaging clinical decision rule used. Most patients with an intracranial injury identified on CT scan are admitted to hospital; however, only a quarter require active treatment, consequently resulting in a low therapeutic yield from imaging this population, apart from the value of observation and potentially in some settings a higher priority for follow-up.

The potential development of blood biomarker tests with high sensitivity has raised the possibility that referrals for CT scans in mTBI patients who are at lower risk of subsequent deterioration could be reduced without endangering many patients, thereby lessening the workload of the ED caused by a long waitlist of CT scans. There are a number of candidate biomarkers which are elevated after TBI and show promise in acting as a screening tool to change the pretest probability of an intracranial injury, potentially facilitating a reduction in radiation exposure while avoiding missing clinically important lesions. The most commonly studied blood biomarkers are proteomic and include those released from the astroglial cells (S100 calcium binding protein B (S100B) and glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP)); neurons (neuron-specific enolase (NSE), ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1)); axons (neurofilament light (NFL), neurofilament heavy) and dendrites (Tau). In particular S100B, and the combination of GFAP and UCH-L1, have gained regulatory approval in specific jurisdictions for this purpose and are integrated into some clinical guidelines. However, even a high sensitivity biomarker could miss clinically important intracranial lesions in mTBI that would be detected by CT testing. Uptake into clinical practice has been slow indicating a need for more evidence of safe and cost effective implementation as identified in the recent National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) head injury guideline evidence review. In the UK, the clinical and health economic benefits of using biomarkers for selecting patients for CT have not been validated; in particular in conjunction with NICE guidelines which have a higher specificity when compared with other TBI CT Clinical Decision Support Tools.

Current NICE guidelines recommend CT testing for all patients with suspected clinically significant intracranial injuries according to the clinical decision rule; a ‘CT all’ strategy, based on cost-effectiveness evidence indicating that benefits of detecting additional cases of intracranial injury outweigh the additional costs and potential radiation harms incurred by CT scans. We therefore aimed to evaluate the potential cost-effectiveness of highly sensitive blood biomarker tests for triaging patients with mTBI for neuroimaging.

We developed a de novo economic model using Microsoft Excel to explore the cost-effectiveness of diagnostic strategies in patients with mTBI who have been identified as needing a CT brain scan using UK NICE Guidelines. The interventions considered were ‘CT all’ (standard practice) and blood biomarkers that would be used initially with only patients with a positive biomarker receiving a CT scan. Cost-effectiveness was measured as the incremental cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gained by each strategy compared with the next most effective alternative on the efficiency frontier (ie, non-dominated or non-extendedly dominated alternative). The economic analysis was conducted from the perspective of National Health Service (NHS) and Personal Social Services over a 44-year (lifetime) horizon. Unit costs were valued at a 2023/2024 price year, including uplifting of older cost estimates using inflation indices, where necessary. All health outcomes and costs were discounted at a rate of 3.5% per annum as recommended by NICE.

The diagnostic pathways in the model were informed by current clinical practice as per the NICE guideline and evidence review as to how blood biomarkers could inform the decision to carry out a CT brain scan. The structure of the model is shown in . The model comprises a decision tree which models the first 6-month period using the estimated sensitivity and specificity for each test, followed by a long-term model estimating expected lifetime health outcomes and costs based on a patient’s underlying health condition which is dependent on whether treatment was prompt or delayed as a result of diagnostic accuracy of the testing strategy. Three underlying health conditions are considered for the patient with mTBI: intracranial lesions which require neurosurgery, intracranial lesions which do not require neurosurgery and no intracranial lesions.

The decision tree estimates test results based on the diagnostic accuracy of each testing strategy. Patients with positive test results (true (TPs) or false positives (FPs)) are referred for a CT brain scan to confirm the diagnosis, followed by appropriate prompt treatment for specific intracranial lesions or discharge if no intracranial lesions are found. Patients with negative test results (true negatives (TNs) or false negatives (FNs)) are not referred for any test and discharged immediately. Patients with FN results are assumed to return to the ED with late symptoms (eg, deterioration), eventually leading to correct diagnosis via CT scans and delayed treatment. Death within 6 months depends on (1) the underlying health condition, (2) whether prompt or delayed treatment was provided and (3) age-matched and sex-matched general population mortality in England. Patients alive at the end of first 6 months enter the long-term model which is composed of two mutually exclusive and exhaustive health states: alive and dead. The expected long-term survival of each patient group was modelled by applying a constant relative risk to the estimated age-matched and sex-matched general population mortality risk in England. The utility of patients was based on Glasgow Outcomes Score (GOS) (declining as a patient ages in accordance with Hernández Alava et al). Life expectancy and utility were combined to allow an estimate of the QALYs conditional on prompt or delayed treatment and on neurosurgical or non-neurosurgical lesion. The cycle length of the long-term model is 12 months, and half-cycle correction was employed in both short- and long-term models.

In the base case model, six groups of parameters are included: patient characteristics, disease prevalence, diagnostic accuracy, mortality risks (short-term and long-term), health-related quality of life and resource use and costs.

On model entry, patients are assumed to have a mean age of 52 years and with 34% being female, as reported by Whitehouse et al. This represents a subset of patients (n=1589) from the Collaborative European NeuroTrauma Effectiveness Research in Traumatic Brain Injury (CENTER-TBI, https://www.center-TBI.eu) core dataset (n=4509) selected for having sustained a mTBI and had blood biomarkers measured within 24 hours of injury. CENTER-TBI is a prospective observational longitudinal cohort study on patients of all severities of TBI, presenting between 19 December 2014 and 17 December 2017, conducted at 65 sites centres across 18 countries in Europe and Israel (RRID/SCR_017004, Core Data V.3.0, EC Grant 602150, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02210221). Institutional affiliations of CENTER-TBI collaborators are provided in the  titled ‘Collaborators’ Institutional List’.

The prevalence of lesions in the mTBI patients in the model was estimated from a prospective, multicentre cohort study of 4557 patients in the Netherlands by Foks et al. In the study, 3742 patients underwent CT scans, of whom 10.26% had an intracranial traumatic finding on CT and 1.97% had a potential neurosurgical lesion where neurosurgery and/or life-threatening deterioration could occur. In the model, 1.97% of patients are assumed to have lesions requiring neurosurgical treatment and 8.29% to have non-neurosurgical lesions (ie, 10.26%−1.97%).

Sensitivity and specificity were estimated from an analysis of the biomarker data from the CENTER-TBI core dataset. For this analysis, patients aged >16 years with GCS 13–15 who had up to 6 blood-based biomarkers measured within 24 hours of injury were selected (N=1889). These biomarkers are S100B, NSE, GFAP, TAU, UCH-L1 and NFL. S100B and NSE were measured with a clinical-use automated system, using an electrochemiluminescence 149 immunoassay kit (ECLIA) (Elecsys S100B and Elecsys NSE assays) run on the e602 module of Cobas 8000 modular 150 analyser (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) at the University of Pecs (Pecs, Hungary). GFAP, UCH-L1, NFL and t-tau were analysed with an ultrasensitive immunoassay using digital array technology (Single Molecule Arrays, SiMoA)-based Human Neurology 4-Plex B assay (N4PB) run on the SR-X benchtop assay platform (Quanterix, Lexington, Massachusetts, USA) at the University of Florida (Gainesville, Florida).

To explore the effect of variation in threshold on decision-making, we tested the blood biomarkers at different diagnostic thresholds. More specifically, we calculated specificity (with 95% CIs) at biomarker threshold that resulted in varying sensitivity for detecting any intracranial lesion or depressed skull fracture (≥90%, ≥95%, ≥99%; ). Where the exact sensitivity values could not be obtained the first available sensitivity value greater than the chosen value was used. The analyses were performed in R V.3.5.3. In the base case, all biomarker tests were assumed to have a sensitivity of ≥95% (with varying specificity ranging from 8% to 42%, as described in ), while the CT scan was assumed to have perfect sensitivity and specificity for neurosurgically important lesions. Scenario analyses explored alternative assumptions that all biomarker tests had sensitivities of ≥90% and ≥99%, with corresponding specificities presented in .

Biomarker concentrations are dynamic and change over time according to their half-life, meaning that diagnostic accuracy may also be time-dependent. Therefore, the diagnostic accuracies of blood biomarker tests were explored in the subgroup of patients whose biomarker samples were taken within 6 hours of ED arrival. This subgroup included 531 patients, of whom 205 (38.6%) were female, with a median age of 49 years (IQR: 31.5 to 65.0) and a median time of taking samples of 3.8 hours (IQR: 3.0 to 4.8). Three additional scenario analyses were conducted to explore the impact of this subgroup data at varying sensitivities of ≥90%, ≥95% and ≥99% () using the same rule as for the main dataset. As summarised in , the diagnostic accuracy and biomarkers thresholds differ in the subgroup analysis compared with those observed in the whole dataset.

Patients with neurosurgical lesions were assumed to have a 9.33% probability of death in the initial 6-month period with prompt treatment and increasing to 20.34% probability with delayed treatment. This was informed by the clinical expert input, based on halving the values reported by Grieve et al which reported values for ‘early’ transfer group and for ‘no or late’ transfer group. The mortality values reported by Grieve et al were not considered directly applicable to our model as the study included a higher risk group of patients with moderate and severe as well as mild TBI and all patients were treated in adult critical care units.

For the remaining groups in the short-term model (patients with non-neurosurgical lesions and those with no intracranial lesions) and for all patient groups in the long-term model, a relative risk of 1.83 was applied to the general population mortality risk in England, derived from the ONS life tables for England (2017–2019). The expected probability of death was estimated to be 0.30% (1.83* 0.0016, where 0.0016 represents the 6-month mortality risk of a 52-year-old patient in England). The relative risk of 1.83 was taken from McMillan et al, which is a prospective case control and record linkage study estimating the 15-year survival following mild head injury in adults. The study reported an annual mortality of adults admitted to hospital with mild head injury as being 2.45% per year (95% CI 2.32% to 2.58%) compared with the community control mortality of 1.33% per year (95% CI 1.23% to 1.44%), resulting in a relative risk of 1.83 (95% CI 1.66 to 2.00). As McMillan data were based on the 15-year follow-up, a scenario explored the impact of assuming that beyond this period, individuals return to the same mortality risk as the age-matched and sex-matched general population. Another scenario analysis tested the impact of assuming a relative risk of 1, equivalent to the general population mortality, in both short-term model (non-neurosurgical and no intracranial lesions) and long-term model (all groups).

The utilities for patients with intracranial lesions, with and without delayed treatment, were estimated as weighted averages based on the distributions of GOS categories from Holmes et al
 and the GOS category-specific utilities from Fuller et al (see ). Based on clinical expert input, it was recognised that the non-neurosurgical group in Holmes et al included some of the Foks et al neurosurgical cohort at risk of life-threatening deterioration but not amenable to neurosurgery, hence the same utility was assumed for patients with non-neurosurgical lesions regardless of treatment timing. For patients with no intracranial lesions, an initial utility value of 0.86 was assumed, which is the weighted utility of the modelled population (age=52 years and female proportion=34%) based on the general population utility in the UK reported by Hernández Alava et al. Subsequent utility values were age-adjusted and sex-adjusted using Hernández Alava et al. The ranking of average utility values with severity was preserved in the probabilistic sensitivity analysis, by sampling decrements from an anchor state. Thus, the average utility value for a non-neurosurgical lesion is always lower than for no lesion, the average utility associated with delayed treatment of a neurosurgical lesion is always lower than for prompt treatment of a neurosurgical lesion, and the average utility associated with prompt treatment of a neurosurgical lesion is always lower than for non-neurosurgical lesion ().
