GOS, Glasgow Outcome Scores; QALY, quality-adjusted life-year.

The economic model accounts for QALY losses associated with radiation-related cancer in patients receiving CT scans. For the modelled population, using estimates from Holmes et al, the estimated lifetime cancer risk is 0.01% (calculated as 0.0077 multiplied by age in years−1.076) and the corresponding QALY loss is 0.0026 (calculated as 0.0401 multiplied by age in years−1.675). The model incorporates QALY losses by multiplying the cancer risk by the associated QALY decrement, discounted over 10 years reflecting the delayed onset of radiation-induced cancer, in line with the assumptions applied in Pandor et al.

The short-term model includes the costs associated with diagnostic testing strategies (including the initial test and the confirmatory scans), the first and second ED visits, craniotomy and admission to critical care unit and hospital wards, where applicable. The cost of each biomarker test was £30, as provided by the manufacturers, and the costs of ED visits, craniotomy and hospital admissions were taken from NHS Reference Costs 2023/24. Unit cost of first ED visit was assumed to be £503 for patients receiving prompt treatment for neurosurgical or non-neurosurgical lesions (VB05Z—Emergency Medicine, Category 2 Investigation with Category 3 Treatment) and £269 for patients with no intracranial lesions or those receiving delayed treatment (VB08Z—Emergency Medicine, Category 2 Investigation with Category 1 Treatment). It was assumed that only patients with a delayed diagnosis would incur a second time ED visit. The second ED visit was assumed to cost £1180 for neurosurgical lesions (VB01Z—Emergency Medicine, Any Investigation with Category 5 Treatment) and £503 for non-neurosurgical lesions. We have assumed that the costs of CT scans for people with intracranial cranial lesions diagnosed as positive on their first ED visit in the ‘CT all’ arm are incorporated in the more expensive ED costs. This also applies to the confirmatory CT scans in the biomarker arm either at first ED attendance (TPs) or for those who have returned for a second ED visit after an FN diagnosis. Contrastingly, for patients who are diagnosed with no intracranial lesions on their initial ED visit, the costs of CT scans are added to the ‘CT all’ arm (TNs), but not to the biomarker arm (TNs or FNs).

Based on the clinical input and Foks et al, assumptions were made for the proportions of patients receiving prompt or delayed treatment for neurosurgical lesions who would require craniotomy and admission to critical care and hospital wards.  summaries the detailed calculations for the costs associated with hospital admissions and treatment. Overall, in the short term, patients with neurosurgical lesions receiving prompt treatment (TPs) are expected to incur resource use costs of £14 471 compared with £16 393 for those receiving delayed treatment (FNs).

Resource use costs by patient groups included in the short-term model

*One-off costs.

CC, complications and comordities; N/A, not applicable; NHS, National Health Service.

As for the calculations of utility values, the long-term costs were estimated as weighted averages, based on the distributions of GOS categories from Holmes et al and the GOS category-specific costs by Williams et al. Weighted costs are summarised in . Williams et al reported the costs separately for the first and subsequent years, and these costs were uplifted from 2017 to 2018 prices. Based on clinical advice, the same cost was assumed for patients with non-neurosurgical lesions, irrespective of treatment timing. Patients with no intracranial lesions were assumed to incur no long-term costs. For the lifetime costs of radiation-induced cancer, a one-off cost of £43 153 was applied in the model, taken from Pandor et al which included the costs of glioma treatment (£23 651) and palliative care (£3087). The costs were uplifted from 2003 to 2004 prices.

Estimates of mean life-years gained, QALYs and costs for the base case were estimated using both deterministic and probabilistic versions of the model. The incremental cost-effectiveness of biomarker tests versus ‘CT all’ was evaluated using fully incremental analysis. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis was conducted using Monte Carlo sampling across 1000 iterations to generate distributions of expected health outcomes and costs for each diagnostic strategy. Uncertainty around diagnostic accuracy was handled using distributions of sensitivity and specificity estimated via bootstrapping at specified sensitivity thresholds. A summary of the distributions applied to each model parameter is presented in . One-way sensitivity analyses (OWSA) were conducted by varying each parameter across its 95% CI where available, or within a 10% range of its base case value where uncertainty estimates were unavailable, while holding all other parameters constant. All model parameters were included in OWSA, with the exception of the sensitivity of the chosen biomarker test, the diagnostic accuracy of CT, model cycle length and discount rate which were not varied. Among the testing strategies, the OWSA compared the two strategies that generated the highest incremental net monetary benefit (INMB) in the base case analysis. Scenario analyses were also conducted to explore the impact of alternative assumptions: (1) assuming 90% and 99% sensitivities of biomarker tests, (2) stopping the relative risk of 1.83 at 15 years, (3) assuming a relative risk of 1 for non-neurosurgical and no intracranial lesions in the short-term model and for all groups in the long-term model, (4) the age and proportion of female based on the data from Marincowitz et al (58.2 years and 33% female) and (5) diagnostic accuracies of biomarker tests based on the data from the subgroup of patients whose biomarker samples were collected within 6 hours of ED arrival (assuming ≥90%, ≥95% and ≥99% sensitivities of biomarker tests).

The executable model was verified by one modeller. Model inputs were validated against their original data sources. Outputs were assessed by comparing point estimates with expected values and probabilistic results with deterministic values. Extreme value testing was also performed. Any discrepancies identified were systematically investigated and the model amended as required. Where appropriate, parts of the model were checked by a second modeller.

shows the deterministic base case results. Both deterministic and probabilistic results are similar, suggesting that all biomarker tests are dominated by ‘CT all’, which has the lowest costs and highest health benefits among all diagnostic strategies. This finding is consistent across all scenario analyses (). The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, as shown in , indicates that ‘CT all’ has a 100% probability of being cost-effective at the willingness-to-pay threshold of £30 000 per QALY gained, while all other biomarker tests have probabilities of zero; this conclusion held for all willingness-to-pay thresholds. The INMB of GFAP compared with ‘CT all’ was −£114 assuming a threshold of £30 000 per QALY gained; this means that if GFAP were used instead of ‘CT all’ the NHS would lose £114 per person having translated health losses into money and combining this with additional costs. The OWSA identified the total lifetime discounted QALYs for patients with neurosurgical lesions in the promptly treated group as the parameter with the greatest influence on the INMB. The relative impact of the ten most influential parameters is shown in the tornado diagram (), none of these made the use of GFAP cost-effective.

Base-case cost-effectiveness results

*Values differ only at eighth decimal place.

ICER, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio; LYG, life-years gained; NFL, neurofilament light; NSE, neuron-specific enolase; QALY, quality-adjusted life-year; UCHL1, ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1.

Our economic model suggests current biomarker strategies are expected to be more costly and to generate fewer QALYs than ‘CT all’ resulting in all biomarker tests being dominated in patients with mTBI who have been identified as needing a CT brain scan using UK NICE Guidelines. The reasons for this result are: (1) biomarker strategies have lower sensitivity than the ‘CT all’ resulting in more FNs with subsequent delayed treatment which are associated with higher short-term mortality risks and lower long-term utility, both of which produce fewer QALYs, (2) patients requiring a confirmatory CT scan (TP or FP) have both the costs of the biomarker test and the CT scan and (3) the costs of ED attendance increase for FNs who also have estimated longer lengths of hospital stay. However, future biomarkers could be cost-effective and we undertook threshold analyses to determine indicative diagnostic accuracies at which ‘CT all’ would have a cost per QALY of approximately £30 000 compared with the biomarkers. These diagnostic accuracies were 99% sensitivity with 43% specificity and 97% sensitivity with 80% specificity. At these values, the use of biomarkers may be seen as cost-effective under current NICE guidance and proposed changes to the NICE cost-effectiveness thresholds.

Our findings are different from recent published studies which show cost savings for biomarker strategies when compared with CT. Most of these are costing studies in the short term and do not include the costs (or outcomes) in the long term, which is a significant limitation. A recent cost-effectiveness analysis in the French healthcare setting suggested modest cost savings; however, the finding was based on different assumptions from our model. Differences in the previous analysis included (1) employing a much lower prevalence of neurosurgical lesions, (2) using higher sensitivity and specificity estimates of the biomarker strategies, (3) not incorporating a high short-term risk of mortality for those with neurosurgical lesions and (4) having more similar GOS profiles between early and delayed treatment of neurosurgical lesions.

Our decision-analytic modelling is based on robust estimates of the diagnostic accuracy of biomarker strategies derived from a large dataset (CENTER-TBI) and draws on clinical expertise to ensure that the model adequately reflects the complexities of the clinical problem while retaining transparency. The estimated model outcomes are based on the lifetime horizon. The CENTER-TBI cohort was used in this analysis as it is the largest available study with detailed CT metrics, biomarkers and outcomes in this population. Age and sex parameters were obtained from Whitehouse et al, which used a subset of the CENTER-TBI core dataset. This is the same dataset used to estimate the diagnostic accuracy of the biomarker tests in our analysis, thereby preserving internal validity. We note that the age and sex parameters used in the economic model were broadly representative of the CENTER-TBI core dataset, the CENTER-TBI registry data, and UK data reported by Marincowitz et al. We conducted a scenario analysis using the age and sex distributions reported by Marincowitz et al, which demonstrated minimal impact on the model results. The prevalence data used in the model were informed by Foks et al, which reported a lower CT positivity rate (10.2%) compared with Whitehouse et al (45.6%), CENTER-TBI core dataset (57.8%) and registry data (31.10%). This difference is explained by the CENTER-TBI core study having recruited higher rates of patients admitted after TBI after a positive scan (as those with a negative CT scan ready for ED discharge are more reluctant to enrol in studies requiring new blood tests). As our aim was to evaluate the cost impact of biomarkers based on the real-world CT positivity rates we therefore used data from Foks et al. To our knowledge, there is no evidence that variation in CT positivity affects the diagnostic accuracy of the biomarkers.

As with all diagnostic modelling studies, our analysis involves some simplifications. We assumed that all patients who tested negative on CT scan or biomarker would be discharged from the hospital. While it is likely that some patients who tested negative on CT scan will need admission (eg, due to intoxication, patients living alone, patients with other illnesses or injuries requiring inpatient care such as sepsis, pneumonia, stroke or patients that were FNs and would require treatment), we did not capture this additional detail in our model. In addition, all patients with FN results were assumed to reattend the ED incurring costs, with no deaths occurring before reattendance. Another limitation relates to uncertainties in the model inputs across patient groups. As the sensitivity and specificity estimates were applied to all lesions, the lesions requiring neurosurgical treatment were assumed to be detected (or missed) at the same rate as other non-neurosurgical lesions. Additionally, due to the limited data, the long-term mortality risk was assumed to be equivalent across all patient groups based on the clinical input. The availability of specific diagnostic accuracy or long-term mortality data for neurosurgical lesions would allow more accurate estimation of model outcomes. In the analysed study (CENTER-TBI), the median time of biomarker sampling was 11.8 hours (IQR 5.4 to 18.6 hours) which is notably higher than the median time to CT scan (2 hours (IQR 1.4 to 3.6 hours)). This does not accurately reflect the clinical scenario where the results of blood biomarkers are available to be used to decide whether a CT is needed. Blood biomarker levels after TBI are dynamic and are affected by the time after injury at which sampling occurs, hence diagnostic performance of biomarkers sampled prior to a CT scan may differ from those we have used from CENTER TBI. Restricting the analysis to patients in whom biomarkers were sampled before a CT would be optimal for informing CT decision making and consistent with manufacturers’ recommendations. However, the subgroup meeting this requirement comprised only 6.4% of the overall cohort, decreasing to 4.3% within 4 hours and 3.5% within 2 hours prior to CT. Using this subgroup would substantially reduce the sample size and increase the uncertainty in the estimated results hence the selection of the ‘sampled within 6 hours of ED arrival’ subgroup. In some cases, a second biomarker test may be required because biomarkers are not always in the detectable range immediately after brain injury. This assumption was not included in the model and incorporating it would increase the incremental costs of biomarkers and make the cost-effectiveness of tests less favourable. Perfect diagnostic accuracy of CT was assumed to reduce the model complexity in this exploratory analysis. Given that CT is included in both arms, any impact on cost-effectiveness is likely limited. Additionally, the value of biomarker tests is not solely confined to prediction of TBI visible on CT scans and may confirm additional prognostic value. Finally, the results produced assume a UK setting; these results may not be generalisable to other jurisdictions.

This model-based economic evaluation suggests that in patients who have been identified as needing a CT brain scan using UK NICE Guidelines using biomarkers to decide who does get a CT scan is expected to be more costly and less effective compared with the strategy of ‘CT all’ with indications in the clinical decisions rule—the current NICE Head Injury Guideline recommendation in the UK. However, biomarkers that have very high sensitivity and concurrently high specificity have been estimated to be cost-effective. Further research is needed to reduce the uncertainty around the long-term mortality risks for each underlying health condition.

neuroscience.title: OpenDrive: An Open-Source Microdrive for Large-Scale Neurophysiology
neuroscience.abstract: Neuropixels-NHP probes have ushered in a new era of high-density neurophysiology recording in large animal models. Here, we present OpenDrive, an open-source microdrive system designed specifically for acute insertion of Neuropixels-NHPs. OpenDrive combines a custom motorized microdrive, six-drive control console, and software platform. Compared with commercially available options, OpenDrive offers (1) low cost, (2) precise, accurate, and stable probe movement, (3) scalability to many-probe recording, and (4) open-source hardware designs and software. In our experiments, OpenDrive has already supported recordings from thousands of neurons across a variety of cortical and subcortical structures. By lowering technical barriers and enabling community-driven development with OpenDrive, we aim to accelerate Neuropixels recording in large animal models.

neuroscience.title: Editorial: Machine learning integration in computational neuroscience: enhancing neural data decoding and prediction
neuroscience.abstract: No abstract
neuroscience.text:
Integration of machine learning with computational neuroscience is a challenging effort because of the intrinsic challenges associated with complex dynamics, heterogeneous measurements, big data, and interactions across biological scales. Specifically, machine learning is built to make accurate predictions from large, clean datasets, while computational neuroscience needs models that are biologically plausible and relate to the brain function. Its data are scarce, noisy, multiscale and often lack ground truth, so high accuracy alone is not sufficient. As result, integration of machine learning with computational neuroscience requires representations that preserve relevant biological information, models that generate testable hypotheses, and validation that establish their reliability beyond individual datasets. The seven contributions to this Research Topic address key aspects of this challenge, spanning neural dynamics, neuromorphic learning, brain aging, neuroimaging, transcriptomics, and broader applications of pattern recognition and predictive modeling.

A central theme is the integration of learning algorithms with models of neural organization. Hall et al. introduce a framework combining Kuramoto-based synchronization, modeled energy constraints, and reinforcement learning to investigate transitions among cognitive states. Their approach connects adaptive input regulation with neural synchrony and compares simulated activity with EEG and fMRI benchmarks. Its contribution lies in treating cognition as a dynamic process shaped by both coordination and resource constraints. Nevertheless, simplified connectivity, indirect energy estimates, and the absence of demonstrated generalization across subjects identify important directions for further empirical development. The framework provides a platform for investigating hypotheses about cognitive regulation rather than a complete account of its biological mechanisms.

Complementing this system's level perspective, Krenzer and Bogdan investigate feedback-driven learning in spiking neural networks through reinforced liquid state machines. Using the Spiking Heidelberg Digits benchmark, they compare positive reinforcement with a strategy that also weakens synapses following incorrect predictions. Both approaches improve classification relative to the unsupervised baseline, although their overall performance does not differ significantly. These findings highlight how feedback can reshape internal representations and improve temporal pattern discrimination. They also suggest that the choice of feedback mechanism should reflect task requirements, including whether improvements across classes or correction of errors are the primary objective.

The relationship between informative representations and interpretable prediction is further developed by Hu et al. Their NEOBA framework combines multiple EEG oscillatory features with inter-oscillatory dependency coefficients obtained through sparse group lasso. Evaluated using a multinational dataset spanning ages 5–97 years, the model achieves a mean absolute error of 2.95 years, compared with 3.44 years when using oscillatory features alone. By examining age-related feature trajectories and model relevance, the study links prediction to interpretable electrophysiological variation. Its broader significance is the demonstration that relationships among features can contribute information beyond individual spectral descriptors, supporting further investigation of accessible EEG-based markers of brain development and aging.

In neuroimaging, Slimi et al. combine DenseNet121 and Xception to classify Alzheimer's disease-related MRI patterns. Their hybrid architecture reports 99.85% classification accuracy and evaluates robustness under several forms of image noise. The study illustrates the potential of combining complementary pre-trained representations to improve discrimination. Translating such performance into clinical utility, however, requires a further step: establishing reliability in independent populations, across acquisition settings, and under clinically realistic conditions. For future studies, subject-level separation and protection against data leakage should accompany performance reporting, while prospective evaluation should determine whether classification improves diagnostic decisions.

Extending the collection to molecular neuroscience, Yin et al. integrate transcriptomic datasets associated with equine encephalitis virus infection, traumatic brain injury, and organophosphorus nerve-agent exposure. Their machine learning workflow identifies shared and condition-specific gene associations, followed by functional interpretation through gene ontology and pathway analyses. This contribution demonstrates how integration across heterogeneous datasets can reveal candidate molecular relationships among distinct causes of neurological injury. The identified genes provide hypotheses for biomarker and therapeutic research; establishing causal involvement and neuroprotective value will require targeted biological validation.

Two additional contributions broaden the methodological scope. Balti et al. combine invariant moments, singular value decomposition, and modified principal component analysis for fingerprint recognition, evaluating performance across multiple databases. Although the application is outside neuroscience, it illustrates a relevant computational principle: carefully designed compact representations can support effective discrimination without relying exclusively on increasingly complex architectures. Whether these methods benefit neural datasets remains an open question requiring application-specific evaluation.

Similarly, Xie et al. develop an attention-weighted stacking framework for coal and gas outburst prediction, combining support vector machines, random forests, and k-nearest neighbors with an XGBoost meta-learner. This industrial application demonstrates the use of complementary learners in a complex prediction task. Its connection to computational neuroscience is methodological: combining models may help address heterogeneous information and competing predictive relationships. Transfer to neural data, however, cannot be assumed from performance in the original domain.

Taken together, these contributions support an editorial perspective in which successful integration depends on three priorities: informative representation, adaptive learning, and rigorous validation. Progress will require reproducible workflows, transparent evaluation, and explicit distinctions between predictive association and biological explanation. Multimodal and multiscale approaches offer opportunities to connect molecular alterations, electrophysiological dynamics, and structural imaging, provided that their integration is guided by clearly formulated scientific questions.

The next stage of machine learning in computational neuroscience should therefore focus on models that are accurate, interpretable, and experimentally useful. By connecting computational innovation with biological entities and principles, accompanied by empirical evidence, the field can advance toward a deeper understanding of neural function and more dependable tools for neurological disease assessment. We thank the contributing authors and reviewers for their efforts and hope this collection encourages further collaboration across neuroscience, engineering, and machine learning.

neuroscience.title: A 3D printable device for non-invasive longitudinal neuroimaging in adult zebrafish
neuroscience.abstract: Zebrafish are a powerful model for imaging studies of development and neurobiology. However, most studies have focused on developing zebrafish due to technical and biological challenges of imaging adult stages. These include increased tissue opacity and illumination depth limitations, and difficulty maintaining life support and anesthesia in a 2-4cm long fish. There are currently limited tools for intravital imaging of the adult zebrafish brain. The ability to image the brain in the same individual repeatedly without physical damage would facilitate the use of zebrafish to study aging and neurodegenerative disease. We designed and applied a 3D-printable device for non-invasive, repeatable multiphoton neural imaging of genetically non-pigmented adult zebrafish across multiple ages and sizes. Animals successfully recovered after multi-hour imaging sessions and can be imaged repeatedly over periods of weeks to months. We show the utility of this approach through imaging the dynamic cells of the neuroimmune system, as well as radial glial cells and oligodendrocytes. This technique could be widely used and beneficial for other cell-scale neuroimaging studies in adult fish.
neuroscience.text:
As we discover the expansive roles of microglia in the brain, there is increased interest in studying microglial biology during aging and disease progression in relevant animal models. Intravital imaging of dynamic behaviors of microglia is difficult in mammalian models and generally requires surgery or skull thinning. These procedures require a large skill and time investment and can alter the local environment of the brain (; ). Small thin skulled vertebrate teleost fish such as zebrafish and Danionella are an excellent alternative model for the study of longitudinal, dynamic neuroimmune biology. Microglia are difficult to image intravitally in mice and rapidly change transcriptional state and behavior in cell culture, so zebrafish serve as a strong bridge between the experimental flexibility of cells and the translational physiology of the mouse. In this work we describe a method to perform repeated imaging sessions on live adult zebrafish over periods of weeks to months with minimal physical and behavioral stress on the animal. Several animal health concerns limit the ability to serially image individual animals, including physical trauma from mounting and unmounting, hypoxia from inadequate oxygenation, and the possibility of neurological effects from repeated sedation. To avoid some of these complications we endeavored to design an open-source 3D printable device that allows for quick and reproducible positioning of a fish in an upright position with minimal handling and use of force. Our device’s design allows the fish’s head to remain accessible to a water dipping objective in an upright orientation and keeps the gills free from any obstruction. Intubation of fish has been previously demonstrated (; ; ; ) to allow sustained oxygenation, sedation, and long-term imaging. Thus, our design is compatible with intubation as well as circulation of additional water to provide adequate water temperature control (in the range of 26-29 °C) within the chamber. Additionally, the design needed to accommodate adult fish across age ranges and length scales to facilitate longitudinal imaging in a continuously growing animal. No currently published teleost imaging device was appropriate for our specific applications (see discussion below), so this novel design contributes a valuable, easily adopted, and adaptable tool for the zebrafish research community.

There have been a handful of published approaches for imaging juvenile and adult Danio species. While zebrafish are still the most prevalent model, Danionella are becoming popular due to their small size, optical accessibility, and diverse behaviors including vocalization (; ; ). Limited work has been done showing the ability to image other species, such as cave fish ().

Previous approaches have varied greatly in their mounting strategy, achieved depth, and goals for imaging. All approaches have used some form of intubation to provide for sedation and oxygenation. Some designs modified existing lab supplies to create a temporary mounting device (; ; ; ). A drawback of this approach is that the improvised nature of these devices can lead to a lack of reproducibility both between individual experiments and across different labs. However, this work beautifully demonstrated that multiphoton microscopy could be used to image brain regions of both adult zebrafish and Danionella.

In 2022, Castranova et al. created the first reproducible imaging chamber for studying wound healing in live adult zebrafish using an inverted microscope (). The study demonstrated that zebrafish could be imaged while under anesthesia for up to 20 hours while still being recoverable. While this device greatly increased reproducibility and professionalized intravital imaging in zebrafish, it provided no fixture for the fish. During imaging, the fish is immobilized using a sponge or stabilizing weights while in a side-lying position. While useful for a wide variety of applications, this approach is not easily compatible with upright mounting for neuroimaging.

subsequently demonstrated a reproducible imaging chamber for Danionella that is compatible with both upright and inverted imaging. Unlike previous examples, Lam did not rely on anesthesia to prevent movement and instead secured the fish in place by encasing it in low melting point agarose, though intubation is still used to provide oxygenation. Fish could be imaged up to 3 hours using this method. Conveniently, the smaller size of Danionella and their lack of a skull roof plate allows for high resolution neural imaging with just a standard confocal. We have found this chamber to be appropriate for imaging juvenile zebrafish.

Development of re-usable, reproducible chambers that maintain animal viability over long periods of time and repeated imaging sessions is the first step in increasing adoption of adult intravital imaging in fish species. Unfortunately, none of these strategies were highly suited to the needs of our research. Namely, we wanted a design that was non-invasive, allowed for highly reproducible upright positioning of adult zebrafish of varying sizes, and could maintain the health of the fish during both long-term imaging and serial imaging. We built upon these existing strategies to make an easy-to-use open-source 3D printable imaging chamber for adult zebrafish neural imaging at the cell-scale using multiphoton microscopy. It features a removable restraint chamber with a V shaped well to accommodate fish of varying ages and sizes, fine adjustment for intubation tube fit, temperature monitoring, and an overflow reservoir to prevent leaks. The device is easily adaptable to any upright microscope stage by pairing it with stage adaptors or modifying the chamber base footprint using CAD, and is designed to work with long working distance water-dipping objectives. Here we demonstrate its utility for upright non-invasive neuroimaging over hours to months.

To confirm the utility of our designed device (, , ) for long-term neuroimaging, we imaged cells of the neuroimmune system in the zebrafish telencephalon and optic tectum (). These areas are superficially positioned and accessible to imaging. We imaged transgenic zebrafish expressing a marker of the vasculature (kdrl:mCherry) along with a marker of phagocytic immune cells (mpeg1:eGFP) in a pigmentless Casper background. The inclusion of a secondary structural marker such as the vasculature is helpful to correctly identify the same regions over longitudinal imaging periods, especially since the zebrafish brain is capable of continuous neuroproliferation and growth throughout the fish’s lifespan (; ). However, autofluorescent or second-harmonic signal in the bone or other tissues may also be suitable for re-identifying regions across time (). Using two Bruker multiphoton microscopes setups, a Bruker Ultima and Ultima 2P+, we were able to image at depths of up to 500 μm using a Spectra Physics Insight ultrafast laser. Laser power measured at the imaging plane at generally used settings was 10-13mW. The depth we measured from the top of the skin to the start of brain tissue varied by age and brain region, ranging from as little as 25 μm in the telencephalon of a 3-month-old fish to 225 μm in the telencephalon of a 19-month old fish (). We found the optic tectum tends to remain closer to the skull and thus can be easier to image in older animals. We were able to visualize both the vasculature of the telencephalon and neuroimmune cells through the intact skin and skull of a 2.5 month old zebrafish (, , ). Mpeg1:eGFP positive neuroimmune cells ranged in morphology from small, rounded vessel-associated cells to larger and more ramified cells that could be close to vessels or in the parenchyma. The majority of mpeg1:eGFP+ neuroimmune cells that could be easily visualized were located more superficially, just below what we presume to be the meninges, generally within the first 25-50μms of brain tissue. However, brighter mpeg1:eGFP+ cells could be identified as deep as 200μm within the brain tissue. Since the mpeg1:eGFP line does not specifically label microglia, we focused on the larger and more ramified cells as being more consistent with morphology associated with microglia versus other brain phagocytes like border associated macrophages. We achieved sufficient resolution to be able to identify individual cells of interest to target for imaging at greater magnification (, , arrowheads). Cellular behavior was live imaged for 10-30 minutes for analysis (, , ).

In agreement with previous intravital imaging studies of microglia in mice (), we found that ramified mpeg1:eGFP positive cells are highly dynamic in their protrusive behaviors (, ). We recorded no significant translocation of the cell bodies of these cells during the imaging window. We also found that total cell area did not change dramatically but instead was balanced between cycles of protrusion and retraction. This was consistent between cells in the telencephalon () and the optic tectum () of the 2.5 month old zebrafish from . These results confirm that adequate resolution for the study of the cell biology and dynamic behavior of neuroimmune cells can be achieved with non-invasive 2-photon imaging.

Due to our interest in following changes in neuroimmune cell morphology over time and during disease progression, we wanted to confirm that we could reproducibly image the same brain region serially in the same individual. We tested if longitudinal imaging could be achieved non-invasively, without skin removal or skull thinning. We imaged a series of individual animals, including the same individual from  and , for multiple weeks in both the telencephalon and optic tectum (, ,). Animals were imaged for up to 2 hours each session. Rough estimates of imaging area were obtained through transmitted light visualization, then adjusted based on imaging of the vasculature and autofluorescence of the skull and meninges. The vasculature could be used successfully to identify specific regions and reliably re-identify them over weeks (, ). Local neuroimmune cells were more difficult to reliably re-identify than vascular structures, as morphology and location changed significantly over the scale of the intervals between imaging sessions.

To test the versatility of this imaging approach, we sought to image other glial populations. We were able to successfully image radial glial cells in gfap transgenic lines, which are widely distributed throughout the telencephalon of the adult as previously reported (; ) (, ). Radial glial cell bodies could be readily visualized with gfap:GFP and individual nuclei could be identified at imaging depths up to 160 μm using a gfap:H2A-mCherry line (, , ). Finally, we also imaged oligodendrocytes labeled by mbpa:GFP. We were able to make out cell bodies as well as extensions at a depth of 125 μm beneath the skin (, , , ).

Finally, we tested whether much older and larger animals were suitable for non-invasive intravital imaging. We were able to image animals as old as 22-months and obtain a similar degree of detail and ability to capture dynamic cellular behavior (, ,,). Larger animals sit higher in the standard V shaped chamber, and benefit from robust stabilization with dental wax. Alternatively, the larger restraint device can be used (). No skull thinning or tissue removal was performed to obtain these results. Imaging older fish does pose some additional challenges, as we observed the distance between the skull and the first layers of brain tissue becomes larger. There is also an increase in structures we suppose to be lipid pockets () which can have a distorting effect when imaging underlying structures. The best imaging outcomes can be obtained by using brightfield imaging to identify areas with minimal lipid pockets before imaging. We found that both the telencephalon and optic tectum remained accessible for imaging in these older animals. We were able to image a similar field of view for both brain areas in aged adult animals as in younger animals (, ). Specific sub-regions of the telencephalon were identified (, ) and selected for live imaging for periods of up to 30 minutes ( and ). Neuroimmune cells within the brains of the individual aged zebrafish we imaged displayed increased dynamic behavior and motility compared to that of the younger animals we imaged. We were able to observe examples of cell-cell interaction (, ) and retraction of cellular process (, ) during our imaging window. We also saw what may be examples of phagocytic behavior, where a process extends, forms a cup like structure, then retracts (, ). Unlike what we observed in younger fish, where little translocation of cell bodies was measured, tracked cells in these aged animals showed increased average velocity (). Cell velocities for both animals tracked were consistent with published reports of translocation speed of surveilling microglia. (; ; ) This demonstrates that changes in cell behavior across lifespan can be investigated using our method for non-invasive intravital imaging in zebrafish.

We have developed and tested a chamber intended for live intravital neuroimaging of adult zebrafish. Zebrafish are a cost-effective and efficient model organism to conduct longitudinal non-invasive imaging for the study of neuroimmune cell biology. We have demonstrated that it is possible to non-invasively image the superficial layers of two regions of the zebrafish brain, the telencephalon and optic tectum, longitudinally in individual zebrafish. We are particularly interested in non-invasive imaging to study the cell biology of the neuroimmune system, where creating wounds or environmental disturbances can complicate interpretation of imaging data. However, in cases where this is not a concern, improved imaging depth could likely be achieved through previously demonstrated techniques like scale removal or skull thinning (). We have shown that non-invasive imaging is suitable for imaging eGFP and mCherry expressing cells up to 200μm deep, however the use of brighter and more red-shifted fluorophores or 3-photon illumination could further improve depth of imaging. Additionally, photoconvertible fluorophores may be necessary to accurately identify individual cells in local populations longitudinally. We used protrusion/retraction measurements and cell tracking to demonstrate that this technique is suitable for the study of in vivo cellular dynamics. While drift and movement associated with respiration do occur during imaging, they can be limited through mounting strategy and corrected using freely available computational registration tools as described in . Further study is needed to compare the behavior and morphology of mpeg1:eGFP positive neuroimmune cells in superficial layers versus deeper layers. We have also demonstrated that this technique can be used for imaging other neuronal cell types, and the modular design of the restraint device means it could be easily modified and redesigned to accommodate different mounting orientations for imaging different structures. Ultimately we believe this device and these data strengthen and broaden the utility of the adult zebrafish model as a tool for neuroimaging and neurobiological study.

We designed a device to facilitate fast and reproducible mounting of adult zebrafish with minimal restraint. This device utilizes mostly off-the-shelf and3D printed components so it can be reproduced with limited skills and reasonable effort. The design features a removable restraint device (, , , ) which secures the fish in place via a V-shaped channel and a small well for low-melting point agarose. The use of the well confines the agarose to only the tail of the fish and allows the fish to be freed from the chamber with minimal effort. Importantly, this prevents low melting point agarose from contacting the fish’s gills. Dental wax (widely available from drugstores) must be affixed over top of the fish’s back for further stabilization (, )

The restraint device docks securely via magnets into the inner reservoir (, ). We have designed the reservoir to include a second overflow reservoir (), and two water outlet channels to prevent overflows. For unattended imaging, we recommend adding water overflow sensors (). The inner reservoir also features a dock for a temperature monitor probe (). The fish is intubated during the imaging period to allow for adequate oxygenation and delivery of anesthetic. To increase the ease of the intubation process, we have added a thumbscrew-adjustment on the intubation tubing support (, ) to change the position of the tubing quickly and accurately. This allows for fine adjustments of tube position to accommodate different lengths/ages of fish.

Two versions of the design are currently made available: the standard design with a smaller restraint chamber, and a multi-size design that can fit both the standard and large restraint devices. Though we have successfully used the standard design for all ages imaged in this paper, individuals regularly wanting to image large females may find the larger restraint device more useful. The docking brackets of the base have been updated in the multi-size design to accommodate both the large and small restraint devices, and allow for more flexibility in future restraint chamber designs (ie, to accommodate other positions).

This imaging device was designed in SolidWorks to fit an ASI stage insert and can easily be modified for other stages by changing the footprint or using a stage adaptor. Various methods and materials can be used to create the 3D printed parts for this device, however, crucial properties to consider include resolution, biocompatibility and porosity, which affects ease of cleaning and the ability to hold water. Photocured resin printers offer very good resolution without porosity, but most photopolymers retain some toxicity to living samples. We chose to have the parts printed by a 3D printing vendor (Midwest Prototyping) in glass-filled Nylon-12 using SLS (selective laser sintering) and vapor smoothing post-processing. Nylon-12 is a chemically inert thermoplastic that is ISO 10993 and USP Class VI compliant and the addition of glass particles to the Nylon-12 results in good part rigidity and reduced part warpage. The vapor smoothing process produces an even glossy finish and reduces water absorption. The device can be easily disinfected via soaking in 10% bleach without degradation of the material. A complete diagram of assembly steps can be found in , and additional assembly instructions are included online (https://morgridge.org/research/labs/fablab/designs/).

Adult zebrafish (Danio rerio) were kept in a 14/10 hr. light/dark cycle and fed Gemma Micro 500. Serially imaged fish were separated into distinguishable pairs in 1L tanks on a quarantine rack to allow for accurate re-identification of individual animals. Transgenic lines Tg(kdrl:mCherry, mpeg1:eGFP, also known as mpeg1.1)(; ), Tg(gfap:H2A-mCherry)(), Tg(gfap:GFP)(), Tg(mbpa:GFP)() were maintained in a pigmentless Casper roya9, nacrew1 double mutant (; ; ). We have found that nacrew1 mutants were also usable for intravital imaging, and the presence of iridophores does not prevent imaging. We confirmed that expression of any given promoter was maintained in the adult using expression information collected on ZFIN before attempting imaging. () Equal numbers of male and female animals were used. All animals in these studies were handled in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the care and use of laboratory animals, and the University of Wisconsin Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). These studies were approved by the University of Wisconsin IACUC (protocol L006536).

As previously noted, multiple strategies have been used for anesthetizing adult zebrafish for microscopy. The goals for sustained anesthesia for long term microscopy differ from those of general anesthesia for brief procedures. MS-222 (tricaine) has been widely adopted for use in zebrafish for anesthesia. However, there are no standardized guidelines for adult dosage based on age and/or weight in zebrafish. We found that for animals over 60 days of age and above 180mg, maintenance concentrations of tricaine in the range of 160mg/L to 170mg/L is effective and well-tolerated (). Tricaine is tolerated very well in embryonic, larval, and adult zebrafish. However, we and others have found that the metamorphic stages in juveniles (roughly ages 21-70 days) tolerate tricaine poorly and have an increased risk of death during periods of anesthesia regardless of length of exposure or concentration of MS-222 (). Therefore, we do not recommend imaging of fish in juvenile stages using MS-222 if it is vital that the fish be recovered. Alternative anesthetic strategies (such as combined use of isoflurane with tricaine) could also be considered (; ; ). Use of a chamber that allows full encasement in agarose in place of tricaine to restrain juveniles during imaging is also a viable strategy ().

A major drawback to the use of tricaine as an anesthetic for neural imaging is that it can increase respiration (and thus gill movement) (). This can result in increased jitter, drift, and imaging artifacts. At our current resolution, most jitter can be resolved computationally through widely available registration tools. However, in certain instances where it is crucial to have continuity of frame over time, paralytic agents such as pancuronium bromide or full encasement in low-melting point agarose could be considered. Both methods will likely affect the length of time the fish can be viably imaged, and the ability to recover the fish after imaging.

Tricaine anesthetic (Syncaine by Syndel) was prepared at a stock concentration of 10mg/mL and gradually adjusted to pH 7.0 with Tris buffer (pH 9.0). Tricaine is highly acidic when dissolved in water so the pH should be carefully controlled to ensure comfortable anesthesia. If tricaine is not dissolved correctly, it can have an appearance like oil droplets on the surface. This can happen if pH is brought up too quickly, or not properly dissolved. We recommend discarding the solution if this occurs and consider a lower stock concentration if continued problems occur. Water for initial induction is prepared in a 1L tank at a concentration of 180-200mg/L in fresh system water. The maintenance dose of tricaine is prepared in the main reservoir at a concentration range of 150-170mg/L. Fish were fasted for at least 15 hours prior to imaging to avoid regurgitation and prevent mortality. Adult fish were anesthetized by placement into the induction tank until loss of righting response was observed and the fish becomes unresponsive to a gentle tail pinch. After induction was achieved the fish remained deeply anesthetized for several minutes, during which mounting and intubation can be performed. If intubation is not achieved within ~3-5 minutes, the fish may begin to show signs of movement and will have to be re-induced. The goal is to maintain a very light anesthesia for maximum chance of routine survival. Body standard length has been previously reported as an indicator of anesthesia tolerance in embryonic and larval zebrafish (), but length becomes more variable in adults older than 90 days and is not reliable. We assessed anesthesia dosage per body weight and found animals weighing 180mg and above to be the most reliable for anesthesia at tricaine concentrations of 160-170mg/L (). Animals in the metamorphic (juvenile) state, where reliance on passive oxygen diffusion through the skin begins to wane in favor of active oxygen uptake via the gills, are more susceptible to tricaine overdose and exhibit unpredictable responses to tricaine (). The age of the tricaine stock is also very important. Tricaine made from powder nearing the end of its shelf-life and frozen tricaine stocks nearing their expiration date have resulted in less predictable outcomes in our hands.

All materials were prepared and at hand prior to initial induction of anesthesia in the fish, since the time between induction and intubation should only be brief (2-3 minutes). Prior to starting the imaging device was securely placed on the microscope stage, the peristaltic pump and tubing were attached to the device, and water was warmed to 28° C and circulating in the chamber.

Low melting point (LMP) agarose (2% in PBS, Sigma-Aldritch) is prepared in aliquots, melted at 75° C and maintained at 42° C in a heat block in preparation for mounting. The restraint device is prepared by wrapping parafilm around the agarose reservoir that will secure the tail (). After induction of anesthesia in the fish was confirmed (detailed in  section) the fish was removed from the induction tank by using a pair of soft tipped forceps to grip the tail fin and immediately placed into the groove of the restraint device (). The device was tilted from horizontal to vertical and softly tapped on the counter to allow the fish’s tail to slide back into the agarose reservoir (). If the tail was caught on top of the parafilm, soft-tipped forceps or a pipette tip were used to position the tail into the agarose reservoir. The fish should easily fall into an upright position due to the device shape, but upright positioning can be ensured by gently using soft-tipped forceps to adjust. Once the position was correct, LMP agarose is immediately added to the reservoir area of the restraint device while it is still held vertically (). Maintaining a mostly vertical position ensures that agarose was kept away from the gills. No agarose should be beyond the anal fin of the fish (, dotted line). The LMP agarose was allowed to solidify. An ice pack can be helpful to hasten this process as long as care is taken to ensure that the fish does not come in direct contact with the ice pack. Once the agarose is solidified, the chamber was immediately placed into the inner chamber containing water with Tricaine at the maintenance dosage. Dental wax was draped over the upper body of the fish and pinched onto the sides of the restraint device to further stabilize the fish for imaging (). The fish was carefully intubated by placing the 0.5mm ID, 1mm OD silicone tubing into the fish’s mouth. Water flow from the intubation tube was kept at ~6ml/min, corresponding to a pump rate of 26.5 rotations per minute with our specified pump and tubing. A more detailed protocol is available online at (https://morgridge.org/research/labs/fablab/designs/).

All imaging was performed with a Bruker Ultima or Ultima 2P+ equipped with a Spectra Physics Insight ultrafast laser and a Nikon CFI75 LWD 16X water-dipping objective. The period between frames for live imaging varied based on stack size but typically ranged from 30-45 seconds for a total of 10-20 minutes per movie. Fish were imaged for a maximum of 2 hours each imaging session. Temperature at the chamber was maintained between 27° C and 28° C and was consistently monitored via a temperature probe. The imaging plane was identified by focusing past the skin and skull (identified by autofluorescent signal and appearance of skin macrophages in Mpeg1 transgenics) and to the point where characteristic brain blood vessels and either sparse immune cells or other glial cells could be identified depending on the line. After imaging was completed, the intubation tubing was removed, and animals were recovered from the chamber by unwrapping the parafilm and using the end of a forceps or wooden applicator stick to dislodge the agarose from the restraint device. The fish are then easily slid out of the device into an individual tank containing fresh water for resuscitation. The agarose will generally fall off as soon as the fish resumes movement, though use of a transfer pipette to agitate the water around the fish’s tail can help this process. Fish were housed in as individuals or in distinguishable pairs and monitored for an hour after recovery. Fish were checked again 12 hours after imaging to ensure no unusual behavior or injuries were present. We have found that fish are quick to recover from light anesthesia, but if a fish does not begin to show signs of movement within a minute, a transfer pipette can be used to force water past the fish’s gills to increase oxygenation and speed recovery. All fish successfully recovered from imaging survived for over a year until they were euthanized according to normal stock maintenance practices in our animal protocol.

Z-stacks obtained from intravital imaging were corrected for drift using FIJI () plugins – primarily “Correct 3D Drift” () and “Linear Stack Alignment with SIFT Multichannel” (). Sometimes movement during imaging will result in the appearance of doubling of a structure (as seen in ). When this happens, manual adjustment of thresholding masks or discarding of the data for that frame may be necessary. Where appropriate, gamma adjustments were made in mpeg1:egfp images to aid in visualization of deep neuroimmune cells for publication purposes. Imaris was used for 3D visualization and to remove the skin and skull layers to avoid obscuring the brain signal with brighter external signal. Cell tracking was done using Manual Tracking plugin for Fiji.

neuroscience.title: Neuroimaging Patterns and Outcomes in Acute Ischemic Stroke With Infective Endocarditis According to the Causative Microorganism
neuroscience.abstract: Infective endocarditis (IE) is a major cause of embolic stroke and is often complicated by hemorrhagic transformation (HT) and poor outcomes. Its neurological manifestations may differ with the causative microorganism, but the comparative data remain scarce. We investigated the characteristics and outcomes of IE-related stroke.This retrospective study analyzed patients diagnosed with definite IE and acute ischemic stroke. Pathogen-related comparisons were conducted to examine clinical characteristics and outcomes across groups infected with Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS), streptococci, and enterococci. A multivariable analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of mortality and HT.The pathogen-related analysis was conducted in 140 of 170 patients with IE-related stroke: S. aureus (n=55), CoNS (n=18), streptococci (n=51), and enterococci (n=16). S. aureus demonstrated the highest rates of HT (61.8%, 50.0%, 29.4%, and 12.5% for S. aureus, CoNS, streptococci, and enterococci, respectively; p<0.001) and 3-month mortality (28.6%, 12.5%, 8.5%, and 6.7%, respectively; p=0.042). The multivariable analysis identified that relative to infection with streptococci, S. aureus (odds ratio [OR]=5.31, 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.42–24.03, p=0.012) and unidentified pathogens (OR=9.14, 95% CI=1.42–63.43, p=0.021) were independent predictors of mortality. Additionally, S. aureus (OR=4.41, 95% CI=1.78–11.61, p=0.001) was associated with increased risks of HT.S. aureus infection and unidentified pathogens were associated with increased mortality in IE-related stroke. S. aureus infection also demonstrated an elevated HT risk. These microorganism-specific findings will contribute to a better understanding of the pathophysiology underlying IE-related stroke complications.
neuroscience.text:
Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a serious cardiovascular infection associated with considerable morbidity and mortality despite improvements in diagnostic tools and treatment options. Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is the most common neurological complication of IE and is associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality. Patients with IE-related stroke have increased risks of recurrent embolic events and hemorrhagic transformation (HT). Additionally, intravenous thrombolysis in this population is associated with poor outcomes and a higher incidence of postthrombolytic intracerebral hemorrhage. This elevated hemorrhagic risk arises from unique pathophysiological mechanisms such as septic arteritis, mycotic aneurysm formation, and pyogenic vessel-wall destruction, which distinguish IE-related stroke from other embolic etiologies.

The main pathogens causing IE are staphylococci, streptococci, and enterococci, with Staphylococcus aureus emerging as the predominant causative microorganism in industrialized nations. Patients with S. aureus-related IE experience higher mortality rates than those with non-S. aureus-related IE, along with higher rates of embolic events and central nervous system (CNS) complications. In contrast, Streptococcus species are considered less-aggressive pathogens that are associated with lower mortality. The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying these microorganism-related differences remain incompletely understood.

A recent meta-analysis of cases of IE-related AIS found that S. aureus-related IE was associated with a higher risk of AIS. However, there have been few comparative studies examining pathogen-specific neuroimaging characteristics, HT patterns, and neurological outcomes after ischemic stroke. While current guidelines offer broad recommendations for addressing neurological complications in IE, they lack detailed guidance tailored to specific causative microorganisms. This absence of pathogen-specific guidance may hinder individualized risk assessments and therapeutic planning. This situation prompted the present study to examine brain lesion patterns, HT, and the clinical outcomes of IE-related stroke according to the causative microorganism. We hypothesized that different causative pathogens result in distinct neuroimaging and clinical characteristics due to their inherent pathophysiological mechanisms. Such an understanding would be particularly important in Asian populations, given their documented higher susceptibility to hemorrhagic stroke complications.

We conducted a retrospective observational study screening patients diagnosed with AIS and definite IE admitted to Asan Medical Center (Seoul, South Korea) between January 2012 and May 2024. The inclusion criteria were as follows: 1) diagnosis of AIS within 7 days after symptom onset, 2) age 18 years or older, and 3) definite IE according to the modified Duke criteria. Both native valve and prosthetic valve endocarditis cases were included. Patients who did not undergo brain MRI during hospitalization were excluded. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Asan Medical Center (2024-0710). The requirement to obtain informed consent from participants was waived due to the retrospective design of the study. This study was conducted and reported in accordance with the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

Patients were categorized based on microbiological findings and the research objectives. The pathogen-related analyses comparing clinical characteristics and outcomes considered the four-most-common microorganism groups: S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS), streptococci, and enterococci. The HT analyses examining overall risk factors and predictors included the entire cohort of patients with definite IE. The mortality analysis included all patients who had undergone 3-month follow-up assessments.

Baseline demographic characteristics, prior medical conditions, concurrent medications, and clinical characteristics were extracted from electronic medical records. Laboratory assessments performed at admission included the complete blood cell count, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), C-reactive protein, total protein, total bilirubin, prothrombin time—international normalized ratio, and activated partial thromboplastin time. All patients underwent blood culture sampling at the time of admission and before the initiation of antibiotic therapy. Antimicrobial therapy was administered according to the American Heart Association guidelines.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) was performed within 72 hours of admission in patients with suspected embolic stroke. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was performed in clinically stable patients to confirm the diagnosis when TTE findings were inconclusive and also to evaluate residual vegetation characteristics to further clarify the embolic risk. Left atrial dimensions and the left ventricular ejection fraction were measured using TTE. The affected valve and vegetation size (measured as the maximum diameter) was primarily determined by TEE, with TTE utilized when TEE could not be performed. The history of cardiac valve surgery and postoperative stroke events was reviewed. Data on acute reperfusion treatment were also collected and analyzed.

Each patient underwent brain MRI, which was performed using either a 1.5-T or 3.0-T scan depending on the scanner availability at the time of imaging. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), and contrast-enhanced MRA were performed in all patients. Additional sequences such as gradient-echo (GRE) imaging, susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), T2-weighted imaging, fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery (FLAIR) imaging, and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging were also performed in some patients.

The analysis of DWI lesions included the number, size, and territorial distribution of lesions, following previously established methodologies. Lesion size was measured as the maximum diameter of the largest lesion in axial DWI. Vascular territories were classified into left anterior circulation, right anterior circulation, and posterior circulation regions, with the number of affected territories determined by the lesion distribution. HT was identified using GRE imaging or SWI, and was defined as any hemorrhagic change observed from the initial presentation up to 1 month after the ischemic stroke onset.

Large-vessel occlusions were identified using MRA. The vascular assessment included extracranial arteries (proximal internal carotid and vertebral arteries V1–V3) and intracranial arteries (distal internal carotid, middle cerebral M1 and M2, anterior cerebral A1 and A2, posterior cerebral P1 and P2, basilar, and vertebral V4 segments). Additional neurological complications including mycotic aneurysms, meningitis, and cerebral abscesses were also evaluated.

Follow-up imaging including DWI, FLAIR imaging, GRE imaging, SWI, and time-of-flight MRA was performed between 2 and 5 days after admission, regardless of the clinical status. Additional MRI with DWI was performed in cases of neurological deterioration or at the discretion of the treating physician to detect new ischemic changes. Images were interpreted independently by two blinded investigators (K.S. and T.K.), with discrepancies resolved by a third investigator (B.J.K.).

Clinical outcomes included 3-month mortality, which was assessed through outpatient follow-up visits or structured telephone-based assessments conducted by a trained nurse. Imaging outcomes included HT, parenchymal hematoma (PH), and new ischemic lesions occurring within 1 month after stroke onset. HT was categorized as either hemorrhagic infarction, defined as petechial hemorrhage within the infarct without a mass effect, or PH, defined as dense hemorrhage within the brain parenchyma with a mass effect. New ischemic lesions were identified as hyperintense areas in follow-up DWI within 1 month after onset that were absent in initial imaging, regardless of the clinical symptoms. Follow-up DWI performed after cardiac surgery for IE was excluded from the new-lesion analysis due to the high risk of perioperative embolic events.

Clinical and neuroimaging characteristics were analyzed in patients with IE associated with S. aureus, CoNS, streptococci, and enterococci. Patient characteristics were also compared according to HT status and 3-month mortality. Continuous variables are presented as mean±standard deviation values, while categorical variables are expressed as numbers and percentages. Comparisons between two groups were performed using chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables and independent t-tests for continuous variables. Comparisons involving four groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance or the Kruskal–Wallis test for continuous variables, depending on the data distribution. Missing data were excluded from the analyses.

A multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of HT and mortality. Firth’s penalized logistic regression was used due to the small number of outcome events. Covariates in the mortality model included age, hemoglobin, BUN, the causative microorganism, and lesion size ≥15 mm. The HT model included male sex, the causative microorganism, and lesion size ≥15 mm. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software (version 27.0, IBM Corp.) and R software (version 4.4.1, https://cran.r-project.org/). A two-sided p value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Between January 2012 and May 2024 there were 11,319 patients with AIS admitted to our institution, of which 2,076 (18.3%) had a cardioembolic stroke etiology, and among whom 264 (12.7%) were initially suspected of having an IE-related stroke. Applying the exclusion criteria identified 94 patients: 39 (14.8%) did not meet the modified Duke criteria for definite IE, 26 (9.8%) developed stroke following cardiac valve surgery, 17 (6.4%) did not undergo appropriate brain imaging, and 12 (4.5%) were diagnosed with nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis. Consequently, 170 patients with definite IE and AIS were finally included in the study (). The age of this cohort was 62.6±16.4 years, and it included 79 (46.5%) males.

The microorganism-related comparative analysis examined the 140 patients infected with the four-most-common causative microorganisms: S. aureus (n=55, 39.3%), CoNS (n=18, 12.9%), streptococci (n=51, 36.4%), and enterococci (n=16, 11.4%). The remaining 30 patients had either other microorganisms (n=18) or no identified pathogen (n=12), and were excluded from the microorganism-related comparisons performed in this study. The microbiological spectrum of these less-common pathogens is detailed in  (in the online-only Data Supplement). There were no significant differences in demographic characteristics across the four groups. Echocardiographic findings—including infected valve location, vegetation size, and left ventricular ejection fraction—also did not differ significantly across the four groups. Underlying valvular disease was present in 67 (47.9%) patients, with prior valve surgery or procedure in 47 (33.6%) and prosthetic valves in 43 (30.7%). Immunocompromising conditions were identified in five (3.6%) patients: active chemotherapy in three, prior organ transplantation in one, and chronic immunosuppressant therapy in one. These factors did not differ significantly with the pathogen group ().

Significant differences in inflammatory markers and clinical parameters were observed between the pathogen groups. The body temperature was highest in patients with S. aureus infection (38.9°C±0.9°C), followed by those with CoNS (38.2°C±0.9°C), streptococci (38.3°C±0.8°C), and enterococci (38.3°C±0.7°C) infections (p=0.001). Similarly, C-reactive protein was markedly elevated in those with S. aureus infection (19.3±11.1 mg/L), followed by CoNS (9.3±5.4 mg/L), streptococci (9.0±6.7 mg/L), and enterococci (8.8±4.0 mg/L) infections (p<0.001). Hemoglobin levels were higher and platelet counts were lower in the S. aureus group than in both the streptococci and enterococci groups (both p=0.014).

The proportion of patients with multiple embolic lesions (≥10 lesions) was numerically highest in S. aureus infection (58.2%), followed by CoNS (55.6%), enterococci (37.5%), and streptococci (29.4%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance across the four microorganism groups (p=0.072). The number of affected vascular territories did not differ significantly with the pathogen group (p=0.153). Initial HT in admission imaging was most common in S. aureus infection (34.5%), followed by CoNS (22.2%), streptococci (10.0%), and enterococci (6.7%) infections (p=0.003) ().

The incidence of HT within 1 month differed significantly between the pathogen groups. The overall incidence was highest for S. aureus infection (61.8%), followed by CoNS (50.0%), streptococci (29.4%), and enterococci (12.5%) infections (p<0.001). The occurrence of new ischemic lesions in follow-up DWI did not significantly differ between the groups. Three-month follow-up data were available for 127 of the 140 patients included in the pathogen-related analysis (90.7%). Mortality rates also demonstrated significant differences: 28.6% in S. aureus, 12.5% in CoNS, 8.5% in streptococci, and 6.7% in enterococci infections (p=0.042) ().

The frequencies of other CNS complications did not differ significantly between the pathogen groups. Mycotic aneurysm was identified in three (5.5%), two (11.1%), five (9.8%), and two (12.5%) patients in the S. aureus, CoNS, streptococci, and enterococci groups, respectively, while brain abscess was identified in two (3.6%), zero (0%), two (3.9%), and zero (0%) patients, and meningitis was identified in five (9.1%), zero (0%), one (2.0%), and zero (0%) patients.

Three-month mortality occurred in 26 (16.9%) of the 154 patients with available follow-up data. Nonsurvivors were significantly older (71.7±13.4 years vs. 58.9±16.4 years, p< 0.001) and had higher prevalence rates of diabetes mellitus (42.3% vs. 20.3%, p=0.017) and chronic kidney disease (26.9% vs. 9.4%, p=0.021). Laboratory parameters demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers and renal dysfunction in the mortality group, including the white blood cell count (16.7±11.2×109/L vs. 12.3±4.7×109/L, p=0.002), BUN (39.3±25.5 mg/dL vs. 21.6±15.8 mg/dL, p<0.001), and C-reactive protein (16.6±10.9 mg/L vs. 11.0±8.2 mg/L, p=0.004). The distribution of causative microorganisms demonstrated a tendency that did not reach statistical significance (p=0.062). S. aureus infection accounted for 53.8% of mortality cases but only 27.3% of survivors. Notably, patients with unidentified pathogens also exhibited elevated mortality (11.5% vs. 4.7%). PH within 1 month was more common in nonsurvivors (26.9% vs. 9.4%, p=0.021) ().

In the multivariable analysis, infection with S. aureus (OR=5.31, 95% CI=1.42–24.03, p=0.012) and unidentified pathogens (OR=9.14, 95% CI=1.42–63.43, p=0.021) relative to streptococci infection were independently associated with 3-month mortality; older age, lower hemoglobin, and elevated BUN were also independent predictors ().

To identify predictors of HT, we analyzed the entire cohort of 170 patients with definite IE. HT developed within 1 month in 73 (42.9%) patients; these patients were more likely to be male (71.2% vs. 47.4%, p=0.002) and to present with neurological symptoms at stroke onset (83.6% vs. 53.6%, p<0.001). They also had larger ischemic lesions, with 76.7% exhibiting lesions ≥15 mm, compared with only 28.9% of those without HT (p<0.001). Laboratory findings showed higher C-reactive protein (14.5±10.6 mg/L vs. 10.7±7.6 mg/L, p=0.012) and hemoglobin (11.4±7.5 g/dL vs. 10.7±2.0 g/dL, p=0.042) in patients with HT. The distribution of causative microorganisms differed significantly between the groups (p=0.003), with S. aureus infection accounting for 46.6% of HT cases compared with 21.6% of non-HT cases. Additionally, the number of lesions was significantly higher in patients with HT than in those without HT (p=0.001) ( in the online-only Data Supplement).

The multivariable analysis showed that S. aureus infection compared with streptococci infection (OR=4.41, 95% CI=1.78–11.61, p=0.001), lesion size ≥15 mm (OR=7.63, 95% CI=3.69–16.61, p<0.001), and male sex (OR=2.42, 95% CI=1.14–5.24, p=0.021) were independently associated with HT ( in the online-only Data Supplement).

We additionally compared between methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (n=36) and methicillin-resistant S. aureus (n=19). There were no significant differences between these two groups in baseline characteristics ( in the online-only Data Supplement), imaging findings ( in the online-only Data Supplement), or clinical outcomes including 3-month mortality (29.0% vs. 27.8%, p=0.925) ( in the online-only Data Supplement).

This study has revealed significant microorganism-specific variations in IE-related AIS, with S. aureus infection exhibiting the most-severe phenotype. S. aureus infection had the highest burden of embolic lesions, the highest rates of HT both at presentation and within 1 month, and elevated 3-month mortality. These findings provide insights into the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms and have implications for clinical risk stratification and management strategies.

The observed differences reflect distinct virulence mechanisms inherent within each pathogen group. The higher mortality for S. aureus infection than for other pathogens further confirms its well-established high virulence, as evidenced by the highest levels of inflammatory markers and rates of HT observed across all the investigated pathogen groups. S. aureus secretes coagulase, which destabilizes cardiac vegetations to make them prone to fragmentation and thereby generating emboli. Staphylococci infection also increases platelet activation and aggregation, which correlates with the thrombocytopenia that we observed. These pathophysiological mechanisms are consistent with the numerically higher prevalence of multiple embolic lesions observed in S. aureus infection, although this difference did not reach statistical significance.

Intracranial hemorrhage is a common neurological complication in IE-related stroke, with primary causes being HT following ischemic stroke and ruptured mycotic aneurysms. The incidence rate of HT in our cohort exceeded those typically reported in general cardioembolic stroke populations, with this being particularly high in S. aureus infection. Histopathological studies have identified pyogenic arteritis caused by septic emboli as the main mechanism underlying hemorrhagic complications in IE-related stroke. Notably, the association between S. aureus infection and HT persisted even after adjustment for lesion size, suggesting that the increased hemorrhagic risk is not solely attributable to a larger infarct burden. Pathogen-specific vascular injury mechanisms such as septic arteritis and vessel-wall destruction caused by highly virulent microorganisms may additionally contribute to hemorrhagic complications. Given that the presence of intracranial hemorrhage is a recognized factor influencing the timing of cardiac surgery in IE, the elevated HT risk associated with S. aureus infection may warrant closer neuroimaging surveillance to guide surgical decision-making in this condition. This finding may be particularly relevant in Asian populations, who have demonstrated increased susceptibility to hemorrhagic complications following ischemic stroke relative to other racial groups.

Current treatment guidelines for IE recommend administering appropriate antimicrobials as a cornerstone intervention, which significantly reduces neurological complications such as ischemic stroke and hemorrhagic stroke. Our patients with unidentified causative pathogens had a substantially higher mortality risk, although this finding should be interpreted cautiously due to the relatively small number of cases and the wide CIs. The increased mortality may reflect delayed pathogen identification, prior antibiotic exposure, fastidious microorganisms, greater clinical severity, or poor targeting by empirical antimicrobial therapy. The selection of an initial empirical antimicrobial regimen in IE depends on various factors, including patient characteristics, prior antibiotic exposure, and the epidemiological context. Given the importance of applying individualized antimicrobial therapy, incorporating the neuroimaging characteristics associated with IE-related stroke that have been revealed by our study may provide valuable guidance when selecting an appropriate empirical regimen.

This study had several limitations that warrant consideration. The retrospective, single-center design may have introduced selection bias and reduced the generalizability of the findings to diverse populations with varying antimicrobial resistance profiles and surgical interventions. The relatively small samples in the CoNS and enterococcal groups may have reduced the statistical power in detecting subtle differences in neuroimaging patterns and clinical outcomes. The pathogen-related comparisons were primarily descriptive, and given the multiple comparisons performed across the four microorganism groups, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Therefore, the results should be interpreted with an emphasis on the magnitude and consistency of pathogen-related differences rather than on isolated p values from any single comparison. Additionally, heterogeneity in the MRI methodologies could have introduced bias in hemorrhage detection. However, a sensitivity analysis found no significant differences in lesion characteristics or hemorrhagic outcomes across imaging parameters ( in the online-only Data Supplement). Finally, 16 patients (9.4%) were lost to the 3-month follow-up; although these patients were older, no other significant differences were observed in other baseline, laboratory, microbiological, and imaging characteristics between the groups. Therefore, while potential attrition bias cannot be fully excluded, the proportion of patients lost to follow-up was relatively small ( in the online-only Data Supplement).
