Notwithstanding these limitations, our study utilized a prospective registry at one of the largest tertiary centers in South Korea to perform thorough analyses of a substantial cohort of IE-related stroke patients. Notably, a microorganism-related analysis of neurological outcomes in IE-related stroke populations was performed. Furthermore, our findings provide valuable data on the neurological outcomes of CoNS-associated IE, which is a field that has received little attention in the literature.

In conclusion, this study has revealed significant variations in the neurological complications of IE according to the causative pathogen. S. aureus infection, which carries a high risk of AIS, exhibited the most-severe neurological phenotype, characterized by an elevated risk of HT and increased mortality. A numerically higher prevalence of multiple embolic lesions was also observed in S. aureus infection, although this difference did not reach statistical significance. Patients with unidentified pathogens also had a substantially elevated mortality risk, underscoring the critical importance of applying appropriate antimicrobial therapies. These findings align with current guidelines that emphasize managing endocarditis with a multidisciplinary team and applying individualized treatment approaches. Furthermore, knowledge of the causative microorganisms may facilitate neurological risk stratification in IE-related ischemic stroke, particularly regarding the HT risk and the need for closer neuroimaging surveillance. The pathogen-specific neuroimaging phenotypes identified in this study may help to improve individualized management strategies in this high-risk population.

neuroscience.title: Diagnostic test accuracy of the TriAGe+ score for detecting stroke in adults presenting with vertigo or dizziness: a protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
neuroscience.abstract: Vertigo and dizziness are frequently encountered neurological presentations, accounting for approximately 2%–5% of emergency department visits. These symptoms may signal stroke, especially posterior circulation stroke, which is often underdiagnosed. The TriAGe+ score is a clinical risk stratification tool that guides emergency and acute care physicians and other competent healthcare professionals in distinguishing stroke from non-stroke causes of vertigo and dizziness using easily obtainable clinical variables. However, no previous systematic review or meta-analysis has evaluated its diagnostic accuracy to date. The aim of our systematic review and meta-analysis is to assess the diagnostic accuracy of the TriAGe+ score for detecting stroke among adults presenting with vertigo or dizziness, using neuroimaging as the reference standard.Our review will include cross-sectional and cohort diagnostic accuracy studies that assessed the TriAGe+ score in adults (≥18 years) against MRI-diffusion-weighted imaging, CT perfusion or non-contrast CT/blood-sensitive MRI (for haemorrhagic stroke). Searches will be conducted in databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection for published studies, without any language barrier or date restrictions. Two independent reviewers will screen the studies, extract data and assess risk of bias using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2, and any discrepancies between them will be resolved by a third reviewer. Pooled sensitivity and specificity will be estimated using appropriate statistical models. Certainty of evidence will be evaluated by the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach using the GRADEpro Guideline Development tool (GDT tool.This study involves the synthesis of data from previously published studies and does not require an ethics committee approval. No individual-level, identifiable patient data will be collected. The study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations at emergency medicine and neurology conferences in regional, national and international settings.CRD420251242124.
neuroscience.text:
Vertigo and dizziness are among the common neurological presentations to the emergency department (ED) amounting to approximately 2%–5% of ED visits,
 representing a significant clinical challenge due to the broad range of underlying causes. These symptoms span a spectrum from life-threatening posterior circulation stroke (PCS) at one extreme to benign conditions such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo at the other.
 Rapid and accurate identification of stroke is critically important, as missed diagnosis can lead to significant morbidity and even fatality. Despite this importance, only a minority, approximately 5% of patients with vertigo or dizziness, are ultimately diagnosed with stroke, due to the necessity of advanced and expensive imaging modalities such as diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) or CT-based perfusion studies for ischaemic stroke, or non-contrast CT/blood-sensitive MRI for haemorrhagic stroke, to establish a definitive diagnosis. Given the limited availability, cost and logistical constraints associated with advanced neuroimaging, there is a critical need for reliable bedside or point-of-care clinical tool that can facilitate early stroke detection and guide imaging prioritisation in patients presenting with vertigo or dizziness.

Existing bedside tools such as the HiNTS (Head-Impulse, Nystagmus, Test-of-Skew) exam require considerable expertise to perform and interpret correctly and have therefore seen limited uptake in routine emergency practice.– The ABCD2 (Age, Blood pressure, Clinical features, Duration of symptoms and Diabetes) score, originally developed to predict early stroke risk after transient ischaemic attack (TIA) using age, blood pressure, clinical features, duration and diabetes, has also been evaluated as a simple risk-stratification tool in patients with suspected posterior circulation events, but the sensitivity and specificity of HiNTS and ABCD2 scores are 97%–81% and 71%–62%. The limitations of these current approaches, coupled with the high stakes of missed diagnosis, underscore the urgent need for structured clinical decision tools that are both accurate and feasible for widespread use, especially in settings where access to specialist expertise and advanced neuroimaging is limited.

The TriAGe+ score is a clinical risk stratification tool designed to help emergency and acute care physicians distinguish stroke from non-stroke causes of vertigo and dizziness using easily obtainable clinical variables. The score incorporates eight clinical components, including symptom triggers, atrial fibrillation, sex, blood pressure, brainstem or cerebellar signs, focal neurological symptoms, dizziness characteristics and absence of prior vestibular disease, with a total score ranging from 0 to 17. Although several primary diagnostic accuracy studies have assessed this score, reported performance metrics vary widely across different populations, settings and reference standards. To date, no systematic review or meta-analysis has synthesised the evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy of TriAGe+ for this patient group, resulting in uncertainty regarding its clinical value.

This review will address this knowledge gap by synthesising evidence on this score against neuroimaging, for the diagnosis of stroke among adults presenting to the healthcare setting with vertigo or dizziness. By providing pooled estimates of diagnostic accuracy and exploring sources of heterogeneity, this review will inform clinicians and guideline developers about the potential role of TriAGe+ in triage pathways, imaging prioritisation and early stroke detection in acute vestibular presentations. The findings will also identify evidence gaps and guide future prospective validation studies and implementation research.

This review will be conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA) statement. The protocol has been prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; Registration ID: CRD420251242124).

Our review will follow the Population–Index test–Reference standard–Target condition (PIRT) framework, consistent with the Cochrane Handbook for DTA Reviews.

We will include cross-sectional and cohort diagnostic accuracy studies, including nested case control studies that have evaluated the performance of the TriAGe+ score for identifying stroke among adults presenting with dizziness or vertigo. We will include studies where all the participants have received the index test and reference standard. We will include studies that have extractable diagnostic accuracy data or that provide sufficient information from which a 2×2 contingency table (true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives) can be reliably derived. We will exclude case reports, case series, case–control studies, review articles (including systematic reviews), conference abstracts lacking full data and any studies in which diagnostic accuracy metrics cannot be extracted or reconstructed.

We will include studies on adults aged 18 years and older presenting to any healthcare setting (including ED and non-ED settings) with dizziness or vertigo, as the TriAGe+ score was developed and validated exclusively in adult populations. Vertigo will be defined as illusory self-motion (typically described as spinning), while dizziness will be defined as disturbed spatial orientation without vertigo. Studies enrolling mixed-age participants will be included only if data for adults with dizziness or vertigo can be clearly isolated.

No restrictions will be applied regarding clinical setting. However, to account for differences in care pathways and access to imaging, diagnostic accuracy estimates will be reported separately for ED and non-ED settings when such data are available.

The index test for this review is the TriAGe+ score, a clinical decision tool designed to identify stroke in adults presenting with dizziness or vertigo. TriAGe+ score was derived from a large ED cohort with MRI-confirmed outcomes and was reported to demonstrate higher discriminative accuracy than the ABCD2 score in its derivation study (area under the curve (AUC) 0.818 vs 0.726).
 It relies on accessible clinical variables that can be administered by non-specialists, which may enhance its practicality in routine care; however, this single-study estimate of superiority has not yet been externally validated across multiple populations, which is the gap this review and meta-analysis aims to address. Its strength over prior tools lies in its ability to discriminate stroke even in patients without focal weakness, a group in which ABCD2 performs poorly.
 The total score ranges from 0 to 17 and is based on eight clinical features: symptom triggers, atrial fibrillation, sex, blood pressure, brainstem or cerebellar signs, focal neurological symptoms, dizziness characteristics and the absence of prior vestibular disease. This review will evaluate the TriAGe+ score as originally developed and validated in the included primary studies. Variations in the operational definitions and assessment of individual score components (eg, atrial fibrillation, dizziness characteristics and neurological signs) will be extracted where reported and considered during quality assessment and interpretation of heterogeneity. We will include studies that evaluate the TriAGe+ score in any reporting format, whether presented as a continuous score, as grouped risk categories, as predefined cut-off points or as study-derived thresholds identified through post hoc analyses.

For the purposes of this review, we will accept three neuroimaging modalities as valid reference standards for confirming or excluding stroke:

MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (MRI-DWI).

CT perfusion imaging (CT perfusion).

Non-contrast CT or blood-sensitive MRI sequences for confirmation of haemorrhagic stroke.

MRI-DWI will be considered the preferred reference standard. Though both the modalities have established diagnostic accuracy for ischaemic stroke, MRI-DWI is considered more sensitive, particularly for identifying PCSs and small infarcts.
 Ischaemic stroke on MRI-DWI will be defined as a hyperintense lesion on DWI with corresponding hypointensity on the apparent diffusion coefficient map, consistent with an arterial vascular territory and not attributable to alternative causes such as chronic infarction, artefact or non-ischaemic T2 shine-through. CT perfusion imaging will also be accepted as a reference standard where MRI-DWI is not performed. Ischaemic stroke on CT perfusion will be defined as a perfusion abnormality within a recognised arterial vascular territory, characterised by reduced cerebral blood flow with corresponding perfusion delay parameters, with infarct core identified using established quantitative thresholds. Haemorrhagic stroke will be confirmed by the presence of acute intraparenchymal, intraventricular or subarachnoid haemorrhage identified on non-contrast CT, or by a corresponding acute haemorrhagic lesion on blood-sensitive MRI sequences. We will include those studies only if the choice of reference standard was independent of the TriAGe+ score or if diagnostic accuracy results are reported separately for each reference standard type.

To ensure reliable verification of stroke status, we will include only studies in which neuroimaging is performed within 72 hours of the initial TriAGe+ assessment and interpreted by radiologists.

The target condition for this review is stroke of any vascular territory, defined consistent with the original TriAGe+ derivation study as a new, sudden neurological deficit of vascular origin, confirmed by an accepted neuroimaging reference standard. We are particularly interested in PCSs, given their strong clinical overlap with presentations of dizziness and vertigo, and it is likely to be a sizeable proportion of all ischaemic strokes presenting with vertigo or dizziness.

We will include studies that assess stroke of any subtype, including ischaemic stroke (small-vessel, large-vessel or embolic infarction) and haemorrhagic stroke. We will exclude studies that focus on chronic infarction, non-ischaemic structural lesions or TIA without imaging confirmation. Studies reporting stroke as an outcome will be eligible. If a study reports disaggregated 2×2 data for ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke separately, these will also be eligible and considered in subgroup or sensitivity analyses where feasible.

This clinical pathway for patients with vertigo or dizziness presenting to healthcare settings provides a structured approach for the evaluation and management. Patients presenting with acute vertigo or dizziness undergo routine clinical assessment, during which the clinical variables required for calculation of the TriAGe+ score are obtained. The TriAGe+ score is then calculated to estimate the probability of stroke and guide decisions regarding neuroimaging. The exact clinical pathway may differ between studies, and this review evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of the TriAGe+ score as applied in the original studies rather than a specific management algorithm. For the current review, patients with high (scores 8–9) or very high (scores 10–17) TriAGe+ scores proceed to immediate neuroimaging. If no stroke is detected, admission and evaluation for peripheral vestibular causes are recommended; if stroke is confirmed, management is guided by the last-known-well time, with thrombolysis considered within 4.5 hours and mechanical thrombectomy considered when beyond the 4.5-hour window. Patients with low (scores 0–4) or intermediate (scores 5–7) TriAGe+ scores may be safely discharged from the ED with appropriate follow-up ().

We will undertake a comprehensive search of both published and unpublished literature to identify all diagnostic accuracy studies evaluating the TriAGe+ score for the detection of stroke in adults presenting with dizziness or vertigo. We will search the electronic bibliographic databases of MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection for published studies. We will search the ClinicalTrials.gov registry and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) to identify ongoing trials. In addition, we will conduct backward citation searching and forward citation tracking of all included studies. We will contact experts in the field to seek information on ongoing or unpublished data. Additional grey literature searches will include Open Grey and abstract books from major emergency medicine and neurology conferences.

Electronic searches were conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus and Web of Science from database inception to the date of the final search. Search results were exported into reference management software for deduplication prior to screening. The searches will be updated immediately before the final analysis to ensure inclusion of the most recent evidence.

A search strategy was developed in accordance with the PRESS 2015 guideline statement and was peer-reviewed. No restrictions were applied on language, publication date, geographical region or participant characteristics. We have used a combination of controlled vocabulary terms (eg, MeSH, Emtree) and free-text keywords related to dizziness, vertigo, acute vestibular presentations, the TriAGe+ index test, stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic) and diagnostic accuracy metrics. Boolean operators, truncation and proximity operators were applied as appropriate to capture variations in terminology and indexing across databases. The complete search strategy is provided as .

To identify additional relevant studies, manual searching will include screening the reference lists of all included studies and relevant review articles. Citation tracking will be performed using Scopus and Web of Science. Conference abstracts, grey literature sources, and trial registries (eg, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP) will also be searched where appropriate to minimise publication bias.

All information sources, including final, reproducible search strategies for all included electronic databases, search dates, and the number of records retrieved from each source, will be reported in the final review article as .

The database search outputs will be exported in RIS or XML format and stored in a secure repository. Search results will be imported into the review management platform Covidence. Original, unmodified search files will be retained to document the search history. Duplicate records will be removed using automated algorithms within Covidence. Potential duplicates flagged by the system will be verified manually. A log of removed duplicates will be retained. Title/abstract and full-text screening will be conducted within Covidence using independent, duplicate reviews. The system will produce a timestamped audit trail documenting reviewer decisions, conflicts, and exclusion reasons, which will be recorded in the PRISMA flow diagram. A standardised and piloted form will be used for data extraction. Two reviewers will extract data independently, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer at every stage. Extracted data will be stored in structured digital formats within the review platform and a secure data repository. Risk of bias assessments (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2, QUADAS 2) will be completed using a dedicated tool specific to the review question. All review materials, including search strategies, extracted data, analytic files, and drafts, will be stored on a secure cloud platform. Automated backups will be performed regularly. Cleaned datasets used for meta-analysis will be maintained separately with corresponding analytic code in R software or Stata.
 Code and outputs will be archived to enable full reproducibility of results. All decisions, protocol deviations, correspondence with authors, and data clarifications will be documented in a review log. Automated activity logs from screening and extraction software will serve as the audit trail. On completion, the final dataset, analytic code, search strategies and supplementary materials will be archived in a secure cloud repository and, where appropriate, deposited in a public repository (OSF/Zenodo). Records will be retained in accordance with mentoring team and funder policies.

Two independent reviewers will screen the titles and abstracts of all retrieved records. Each reviewer will classify studies as include, exclude or may be based on the predefined eligibility criteria. Disagreements will be resolved by a third reviewer. Studies marked as include or may be will proceed to full-text screening. The same two independent reviewers will assess the full text of potentially eligible articles. Reasons for exclusion at this stage will be recorded and any disagreements will be resolved by consulting a third reviewer. A PRISMA flow diagram will document the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included at each stage.

Standardised data-extraction forms will be developed specifically for this review to ensure consistent and comprehensive capture of relevant information. Prior to full implementation, the forms will be piloted on a sample of eligible reports. The pilot will assess clarity, completeness and usability of the form items. Based on reviewer feedback, the forms will be revised to refine data definitions, instructions and response fields. The final version of the data-extraction form will be applied uniformly across all reports.

Each reviewer will extract the complete set of predefined variables without access to the other reviewer’s entries. On completion of independent extraction, the two datasets will be compared for discrepancies. Differences will be resolved by consensus. All changes and rationale for decisions will be documented. Periodic quality checks of completed extraction forms will be conducted to ensure adherence to procedures and consistency in interpretation across reviewers.

If essential data (eg, outcome values, methodological details, subgroup results) are missing, unclear or inconsistently reported, study investigators or corresponding authors will be contacted for clarification. A standardised request template will be used to ensure consistent communication. Up to two follow-up attempts will be made at intervals of approximately 2 weeks if no response is received. All communication with investigators will be logged, including the date of contact, the specific information requested and any responses or supplementary materials received. All information derived from investigator correspondence will be clearly flagged in the final dataset.

The data items that will be collected from the eligible articles are as follows:

Study identification and characteristics: name of the first author, corresponding author and his/her email address, year of publication and country in which the study was conducted and funding details.

Study design and methods: study design (prospective, retrospective, cross-sectional), sampling method (consecutive, random, convenience), hospital setting (ED or non-ED) will be noted.

Details of the study participants: total number of participants screened, enrolled and the reasons for exclusion and analysed.

Index test details (TriAGe+ score), including how the score was administered and scored (continuous score, risk category, predefined cut-off, or post hoc threshold); who performed the TriAGe+ assessment, including examiner specialty, professional background and training; operational definitions of individual score components (eg, atrial fibrillation, including history-based vs examination/ECG-based ascertainment, and paroxysmal vs persistent); the definition of dizziness characteristics used by the study and details of nystagmus assessment (eg, bedside examination, Frenzel goggles, videonystagmography), where reported, will be collected.

Reference standard details will include the neuroimaging modality, timing of neuroimaging relative to symptom onset and to the index test, repeat imaging where performed, final diagnostic confirmation, the image interpreter’s qualifications/competence and details regarding blinding. We acknowledge that early diffusion-weighted MRI may be falsely negative in posterior circulation ischaemic stroke, particularly when performed soon after symptom onset; this limitation does not apply to the identification of haemorrhagic stroke, which is reliably detected on non-contrast CT from the time of onset. These timing and repeat-imaging details will therefore be considered during assessment of methodological quality and interpretation of findings, particularly for ischaemic stroke.

Diagnostic accuracy data: From each study true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives using either DW MRI, CT perfusion imaging or non-contrast CT/blood-sensitive MRI will be recorded. Where available, data relating specifically to PCS will be extracted separately as a prespecified subgroup and included in sensitivity and subgroup analyses.

The data extraction form to be used in this review is provided in .

Primary outcomes: Pooled sensitivity and specificity of the TriAGe+ score or the summary ROC curve (if the cut offs are highly variable across the studies) for detecting stroke against the reference standard (MRI-DWI, CT perfusion or non-contrast CT/blood-sensitive MRI for haemorrhagic stroke). Secondary outcomes: Pooled sensitivity and specificity of the TriAGe+ score for detecting PCS where such data are available. Additional diagnostic performance measures like positive and negative likelihood ratio (LR+ and LR−), diagnostic OR, AUC, positive and negative predictive value (PPV and NPV) will be estimated.

For each article included in this study, data required to construct a 2X2 contingency table (true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives) will be extracted to calculate the sensitivity, specificity, PPVs and NPVs of the index test. If they are not mentioned in the study, either they will be derived from the tables and figures; or the authors contacted for the data. From the above data obtained, the pooled sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPVs of the index test will be calculated using R or Stata software.
 All the eligible articles will be treated similarly. Studies using MRI-DWI and CT perfusion, or non-contrast CT/blood-sensitive MRI will be pooled, with separate analyses performed for each reference standard where possible.

The QUADAS-2 will be used to assess the risk of bias for each study included for data extraction of this review. Risk of bias will be assessed across the four QUADAS-2 domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard and flow and timing.

The document will record each variable after carefully going through the article. This will be done in duplicate by two reviewers, and any disparity will be sorted by the arbitrator. To assess the risk of bias, the QUADAS 2 guidance document for this study has been prepared to record bias and applicability of each domain and included as .

We will consider the results of TriAGe+ score as the index test and compare them with the reference standard. The analyses will be conducted in R software, using R packages ‘meta’, for univariate random effect DTA model, ‘lme4’ for bivariate random effects model and ‘HSROC’ for hierarchical summary receiver-operating characteristics parameters. We will estimate pooled sensitivity, pooled specificity and diagnostic OR using bivariate random effect model. If the threshold values are highly varying across the studies, we will construct summary ROC curve using HSROC model. We will perform predefined subgroup analyses using a bivariate random-effects model. Subgroups were based on (1) study setting (ED vs non-ED) and (2) reference standard (DW MRI only vs DW MRI±CT perfusion imaging vs non-contrast CT/blood-sensitive MRI for haemorrhagic stroke). Heterogeneity will be assessed by visual inspection of coupled forest plots of sensitivity and specificity, examination of the ROC space, and estimation of the between-study variance (tau-squared) from the random effects model. For studies reporting a single diagnostic threshold, the presence of a threshold effect will be evaluated using the Spearman correlation between the logit-transformed sensitivity and the logit-transformed false-positive rate within the bivariate random-effects model. For studies reporting multiple thresholds, threshold variation will be modelled directly using a random effects multiple-threshold model; therefore, a separate assessment of the threshold effect using the Spearman correlation will not be performed. Potential sources of heterogeneity will be further explored through predefined subgroup analyses and meta-regression, where sufficient studies are available.

We will not assess publication bias as it will be difficult and not routinely recommended, but note that selective reporting, if any, will be noted for assessment of bias.

The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) method will be employed to systematically evaluate the body of evidence. The quality of evidence will be independently evaluated by two researchers across the following dimensions:

Risk of bias (QUADAS-2): We will downgrade the certainty of evidence by one or two levels depending on the number (percentage) of included studies considered to have a high or unclear risk of bias for one or more of the QUADAS‐2 domains.

Indirectness: We will downgrade the certainty of evidence for indirectness if there are important differences between the participants in the studies and the population stated in the review question, with respect to either prior testing, spectrum of disease or comorbidities, or study settings. We may also downgrade if there are important differences between the characteristics of the index test(s) and/or the expertise of the people applying the test(s) in the studies compared with the characteristics of the test(s) and/or users in real‐world settings. Evidence may also be downgraded in case of comparative questions if the index test were not directly compared in each of the studies included in the test comparison (ie, indirect comparisons).

Inconsistency: We would downgrade for unexplained inconsistency in sensitivity and specificity estimates. We will not downgrade if the inconsistency can be explained, for instance, due to differences in setting, population or index test execution.

Imprecision: We will analyse the width of the 95% CIs of the summary estimates of sensitivity and specificity and assess imprecision.

We will use GRADEpro GDT software to create a Summary of Findings table that presents the key results, summarises the supporting evidence for each outcome, and reports the overall certainty of the evidence.

There will not be any patient or public involvement at any stage of this study, as this will be a review of available published or unpublished data.

This protocol outlines a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy that will evaluate the performance of the TriAGe+ score in identifying stroke among adults presenting to a healthcare setting with vertigo or dizziness. These symptoms are frequently encountered in emergency settings and considered diagnostically complex, particularly because PCS can closely mimic benign vestibular disorders. The TriAGe+ score incorporates easily obtainable clinical variables and is designed to be applied by non-specialists, which makes it particularly useful in settings with limited access to neurological expertise or advanced neuroimaging facilities. However, existing studies with TriAGe+ score have used different study designs, variable thresholds for cut-off scores and different reference standards, leading to uncertainty regarding its clinical utility. A structured synthesis of available evidence is therefore necessary to understand the performance characteristics and clinical utility of TriAGe+ score in healthcare settings. This review will therefore evaluate whether the TriAGe+ score demonstrates adequate sensitivity and specificity to support its clinical utility as an initial screening tool.

The strengths of this protocol include the use of prespecified eligibility criteria based on the PIRT framework, comprehensive literature searches and adherence to PRISMA-DTA and Cochrane DTA methodological guidance resources. Despite these strengths, several challenges are anticipated in synthesising existing evidence. Heterogeneity across primary studies is expected due to variations in participant selection, clinical settings, application of the TriAGe+ score, including variability in thresholds used TriAGe+ score. In addition, reference standards are likely to vary, with some studies relying exclusively on diffusion-weighted MRI while others incorporate CT-based imaging. These sources of heterogeneity will be explored using predefined subgroup and sensitivity analyses, where data permit.

We also anticipate methodological limitations that are inherent to diagnostic accuracy studies. Differential verification may occur if neuroimaging is preferentially performed in patients with higher clinical suspicion, potentially influencing estimates of test performance and introducing selection bias. Incomplete reporting of diagnostic accuracy data and variability in the timing between index testing and reference standard assessment may affect the precision of pooled estimates. These issues will be addressed through assessment of study-level limitations by the predesigned QUADAS-2 guidance document and transparent reporting of risk-of-bias.

The findings from the review will provide the most comprehensive synthesis to date of the diagnostic accuracy of the TriAGe+ score in adults presenting with vertigo or dizziness. By generating pooled estimates and identifying sources of heterogeneity, the review will help clarify the potential role of TriAGe+ in healthcare settings and inform clinical decision-making regarding prioritisation for neuroimaging. The findings will also highlight gaps in the current evidence base and inform priorities for future prospective validation studies using standardised thresholds and consistent reference standards.

This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesises data from previously published studies and does not require research ethics committee approval as it does not involve collection of any new or individual patient-level identifiable data. The study findings will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed journal, and through presentations at regional, national and international emergency medicine and neurology conferences.

neuroscience.title: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis Unmasking Molecularly High-Risk but Clinically Indolent Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: A Case Report
neuroscience.abstract: We report a patient who presented with acute-onset diplopia and fatigable ptosis, subsequently diagnosed with Myasthenia Gravis based on elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Neuroimaging and chest imaging were unremarkable, excluding structural causes and thymoma.During evaluation, persistent lymphocytosis prompted further hematologic workup, which confirmed early-stage Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia with trisomy 12 and a TP53 mutation. The patient received pyridostigmine and a tapering course of corticosteroids, resulting in rapid clinical improvement and complete resolution of ocular symptoms. The leukemia remained asymptomatic and was managed conservatively with a watchful waiting approach. The clinical course was favorable with sustained remission of myasthenia gravis off therapy and stable hematologic parameters on follow-up.This case highlights the diagnostic interplay between autoimmune and lymphoproliferative disorders and underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing such overlapping clinical entities.
neuroscience.text:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a mature B cell lymphoproliferative neoplasm characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity ranging from indolent disease requiring long-term observation to progressive disease necessitating targeted therapy.

 Contemporary prognostication integrates clinical staging with molecular and cytogenetic features including TP53 aberrations, immunoglobulin heavy chain variable region (IGHV) mutational status, and recurrent chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 12, which refine risk stratification but do not independently define treatment initiation. Current management decisions remain primarily guided by established International Workshop on Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (iwCLL) criteria based on clinical disease activity rather than molecular risk alone.

Beyond its malignant phenotype, CLL is increasingly recognized as a disorder of immune dysregulation characterized by impaired B cell receptor signaling, T cell dysfunction, and loss of immune tolerance. This immune derangement contributes not only to infectious susceptibility but also to autoimmune complications, most commonly autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia. In contrast, non-hematologic autoimmune manifestations are uncommon and less well characterized.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an antibody-mediated neuromuscular junction disorder typically associated with acetylcholine receptor antibodies and represents a rare autoimmune association in patients with CLL. Reported cases are limited, and the underlying mechanism is thought to reflect generalized immune dysregulation rather than direct leukemic transformation. Importantly, MG presenting prior to or contemporaneously with the diagnosis of CLL remains exceptionally rare, and its clinical implications in patients with biologically high-risk disease are not well defined.

We report the case of a 76-year-old woman who presented with ocular MG, subsequently found to have asymptomatic CLL with a monotypic CD5-positive B cell population and a high-risk molecular profile including TP53 mutation, trisomy 12, and mutated IGHV status.

 This case highlights an unusual autoimmune presentation leading to the diagnosis of otherwise clinically silent CLL and underscores the critical dissociation between adverse molecular features and absence of treatment indications under current iwCLL criteria. This case report was prepared in accordance with the CARE (CAse REport) guidelines,

 and the completed CARE checklist is provided as a supplemental file.

A 76-year-old Caucasian woman with a medical history significant for systemic hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, osteoarthritis status post bilateral total knee arthroplasty, vitamin B12 deficiency, and carpal tunnel syndrome presented for evaluation of progressive lymphocytosis found during workup for new ocular myasthenia gravis (MG). In July 2024, she developed intermittent diplopia and blurry vision, initially raising concerns about cerebrovascular disease. Initial neurological evaluation included magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and computed tomography (CT) angiography of the head and neck, both of which were negative for acute cerebrovascular pathology, structural lesions, or large-vessel disease. Symptoms were limited to ocular complaints, and she denied bulbar, limb, sensory, or generalized weakness. She also reported a penicillin allergy. Family history is notable for a mother with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ischemic heart disease, and a father with lung cancer. She was a lifelong non-smoker, drank alcohol socially, denied recreational drug use, and remained active and independent in daily activities. Subsequent serologic testing revealed markedly elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies (binding antibody 8.07 nmol/L [reference range 0.0–0.4 nmol/L]; blocking antibody 43% [reference range 0–26%]), confirming ocular myasthenia gravis.  summarizes the principal differential diagnoses considered during evaluation of the patient’s diplopia, along with the rationale for their exclusion. A contrast-enhanced chest CT showed no evidence of thymoma or a mediastinal mass. Dedicated thymic imaging (e.g., MRI) can occasionally provide additional assessment of subtle thymic pathology beyond contrast-enhanced CT, a minor limitation of diagnostic workup rather than evidence of an inadequate evaluation. Differential Diagnosis

During this diagnostic period, routine laboratory testing in August 2024 incidentally demonstrated leukocytosis (WBC 12.72 ×109/L) with absolute lymphocytosis (ALC 6.11 ×109/L), which progressed on repeat testing in October 2024 (WBC 15.26 ×109/L; ALC 10.38 ×109/L).  shows the evolution of leukocytosis and absolute lymphocytosis over time. Hemoglobin (12.4 g/dL) and platelet count (219 ×109/L) remained preserved. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood identified a CD5-positive, CD19-positive, dim CD20-positive, CD23-positive, CD43-positive, FMC7-negative, CD10-negative monotypic B-cell population, phenotypically consistent with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, with an absolute monoclonal B-cell count of 5.5 K/µL. This clonal B-cell lymphocytosis persisted on serial testing over several months, supporting a diagnosis of CLL rather than MBL. No blast population was identified. Advanced molecular and cytogenetic profiling revealed a biologically complex disease. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detected trisomy 12, and next-generation sequencing identified a pathogenic TP53 mutation (p.A159V). Immunoglobulin heavy chain variable region (IGHV) analysis demonstrated a mutated IGHV (IGHV3-15*07) genotype. This constellation of findings defined a molecularly high-risk CLL phenotype despite clinically indolent presentation. At the time of the hematology consultation, the patient was asymptomatic hematologically. She denied constitutional “B symptoms,” including fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, or recurrent infections. There was no bleeding tendency, lymphadenopathy, abdominal discomfort, or symptoms suggestive of organomegaly. Physical examination was unremarkable, and imaging showed no thoracic or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. She remained physically active and socially engaged, reporting recent travel and sustained functional independence. Based on the absence of lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, the patient’s CLL was classified as Rai Stage 0 (Binet stage A) at diagnosis.

Given the absence of clinical symptoms, preserved hematologic parameters, and no end-organ involvement, the team adopted a strategy of active surveillance (“watchful waiting”) in accordance with contemporary CLL management guidelines. The patient was counseled that asymptomatic disease does not require treatment and would be managed with close clinical and laboratory monitoring, with therapy reserved for symptomatic progression or steroid-refractory autoimmune disease. In the absence of clinical evidence of lymphadenopathy or disease progression, routine surveillance imaging was deferred. Age-appropriate cancer screening and routine vaccinations were recommended, and she was confirmed to be up to date with her 2025 influenza vaccination.

At follow-up in January 2026, she remained clinically stable and asymptomatic, off pyridostigmine without recurrence of myasthenic symptoms, with stable blood counts and only mild normocytic anemia. Adherence and tolerability were assessed by patient interview and clinical review at each follow-up visit. She took prednisone and pyridostigmine as prescribed and tolerated both without adverse effects. No disease-related complications, infections, or autoimmune sequelae were observed. The patient and her significant other demonstrated understanding of the management plan, with follow-up laboratory testing planned in three months and clinic reassessment in six months; earlier evaluation was advised if new symptoms developed.  presents a chronological summary of the patient’s clinical course, and  provides therapeutic interventions and clinical outcomes.Table 3.Chronological Clinical TimelineDateDomainClinical EventKey Findings1-Jul-24NeurologySymptom onsetDiplopia and blurry vision1-Jul-24ImagingMRI + CTANormal15-Jul-24OphthalmologyAChR testingPositive antibodiesLate July 2024TreatmentTherapy startedPyridostigmine + Prednisone6-Aug-24HematologyInitial labsLymphocytosis14-Aug-24ImagingCT chestNo thymoma25-Oct-24HematologyFlow cytometryCLL diagnosed11-Nov-24MolecularNGS/FISHTP53 mutation, Trisomy 1216-Apr-25NeurologyFollow-upSymptoms resolved5-Jan-26LabsCBCStable9-Jan-26ClinicalFinal follow-upOff meds, stableTable 4.Summary of Management, Therapeutic Response, and Follow-upComponentInterventionDose & DurationResponseNotes/TimelineSymptomatic therapy (OMG)Pyridostigmine (Mestinon)Started July 2024: 60 mg TID → reduced to 60 mg BID (Oct 2024) → discontinued Jan 2026Immediate improvement in diplopiaMild urinary frequency; Chronological Clinical Timeline

Summary of Management, Therapeutic Response, and Follow-up

The patient shared that the sudden onset of double vision was frightening and that she initially feared a stroke. She was relieved when treatment restored her vision to normal. Although the diagnosis of leukemia was unexpected, she felt reassured after learning that it did not require treatment at this stage, and she is comfortable with regular monitoring.

CLL is the most common adult leukemia in Western countries and is well recognized for its tendency to cause autoimmune complications, most commonly autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

 Its association with myasthenia gravis (MG), a neuromuscular junction disorder mediated by acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies, remains poorly understood and infrequently reported.

 This case is notable because of the incidental diagnosis of CLL during workup for ocular MG, and a high-risk genetic profile with asymptomatic clinical presentation.

MG itself is an uncommon disorder, with an estimated prevalence on the order of 1 in 5000 - 10,000 individuals, and roughly 15-20% of patients present with a purely ocular phenotype, as seen in this patient, which may remain localized or progress to generalized disease. Most MG arises independently of hematologic malignancy; its occurrence in the setting of CLL, as in the present case, has been described only sporadically in the literature, most notably in a case report describing MG as an unusual non-hematologic autoimmune manifestation of CLL, underscoring how infrequently the combination is documented and reinforcing the educational value of reporting additional cases such as this one.

Immune dysregulation in CLL creates a biological environment that can lead to autoimmune disease. CLL cells suppress normal immune surveillance while promoting polyclonal B-cell activation, leading to loss of self-tolerance.

 Autoimmune complications occur in approximately 10 to 25% of CLL patients.

 The mechanism by which CLL triggers AChR antibody-mediated disease is not fully established. One proposed explanation is that the dysregulated B-cell clone directly contributes to autoantibody production, or both conditions share a common predisposition toward aberrant immune activation.

 Proposed mechanisms linking CLL to AChR antibody-mediated disease include CLL-driven abnormal antigen presentation, activation of autoreactive T-helper cells, impaired B cell tolerance, and polyreactive or aberrant antibody responses arising within the altered immune microenvironment.

 These mechanisms remain hypothetical in this particular patient, and a direct pathogenic link between the CLL clone and anti-AChR autoantibody production cannot be demonstrated. In this patient, chest CT excluded thymoma, making CLL-associated immune dysregulation the most plausible underlying contributor to her ocular MG.

Molecular and cytogenetic profiling revealed a biologically complex picture. Trisomy 12, identified on FISH analysis, occurs in approximately 20% of CLL cases and is associated with atypical morphological and immunophenotypic features and an intermediate prognosis.

 TP53 mutation at codon p.A159V was also identified on next-generation sequencing.TP53 aberrations are among the strongest adverse molecular prognostic markers in CLL. TP53 mutations represent the highest-risk molecular category in CLL, leading to resistance to conventional chemotherapy and poor outcomes with alkylator-based regimens.

 TP53 mutations can occur independently of 17p deletion, as in this case, and carry the same adverse prognostic significance.

 Additionally, a mutated IGHV genotype (IGHV3-15) is associated with slower disease progression and better long-term outcomes than unmutated IGHV.

 The coexistence of a TP53 mutation with mutated IGHV represents a molecularly discordant profile, reinforcing the need for comprehensive genomic characterization.

The longitudinal absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) decline observed between November 2024 and October 2025 coincided with corticosteroid therapy (prednisone initiated at 20 mg/day and subsequently tapered), which is a well-recognized cause of lymphocyte redistribution; therefore, it represents an important confounder of the observed ALC kinetics, and the apparent stabilization should not be interpreted as independent evidence of biologically indolent disease. Rather, the decision to continue observation was anchored primarily in the patient’s persistent absence of constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, progressive cytopenias, or other clinical indications for CLL-directed therapy. Despite these high-risk molecular features, initiating treatment was not indicated. Both the iwCLL and NCCN guidelines recommend guiding treatment decisions by clinical criteria rather than molecular risk alone, reserving therapy for patients who develop symptomatic lymphadenopathy, progressive cytopenias, constitutional B symptoms, or rapidly rising lymphocyte counts.

 The phase III CLL12 trial further clarified that early treatment in asymptomatic CLL, even with targeted agents such as ibrutinib, delayed progression to symptomatic disease but did not demonstrate an overall survival advantage sufficient to replace the established watch-and-wait strategy for asymptomatic early-stage CLL.

 This patient met none of these criteria. When treatment eventually becomes necessary, keep the TP53 mutation in mind. If treatment becomes indicated, a TP53 aberration would favor modern targeted therapy (BTK inhibitors or BCL2 antagonists) over conventional chemoimmunotherapy, given the well-documented resistance of TP53-mutant disease to fludarabine-based regimens.

This case carries several practical lessons. CLL should be considered as a potential underlying cause in patients presenting with autoimmune conditions, particularly when routine labs reveal unexplained lymphocytosis.

 Comprehensive molecular testing at diagnosis is essential, as the molecular profile determines the appropriate treatment class. Finally, clinical decision-making in CLL must remain anchored in symptom-based criteria. As targeted therapies continue to improve outcomes in high-risk CLL, this case highlights the importance of multidisciplinary evaluation, thorough genomic workup, and close surveillance in managing these patients.

The strengths of this report include serologic confirmation of myasthenia gravis with exclusion of thymoma, comprehensive immunophenotypic, cytogenetic, and molecular characterization of the leukemic clone, and approximately 18 months of documented follow-up. This case report has several limitations. First, the variant allele frequency of the TP53 mutation was not available, limiting assessment of clonal burden. Second, the observed decline in absolute lymphocyte count coincided with corticosteroid therapy, a recognized confounder of lymphocyte kinetics, limiting the ability to attribute the trend to disease biology alone. Third, as with any single case report, causal inference regarding the relationship between CLL and Myasthenia Gravis cannot be established, and the observed association may reflect shared predisposition rather than a direct mechanistic link. Fourth, this report describes a single patient evaluated at a single center, limiting generalizability. And finally, follow-up extends to January 2026, which, while reassuring, remains relatively short for drawing conclusions about the long-term natural history of TP53-mutated CLL.

This case highlights a rare but clinically meaningful coexistence of Myasthenia Gravis and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia, illustrating how autoimmune and lymphoproliferative processes can intersect in subtle ways. The patient’s presentation with isolated ocular symptoms supported by positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies and unremarkable imaging pointed toward ocular myasthenia gravis, while persistent lymphocytosis led to the diagnosis of early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Recognizing this overlap was important as it allowed for focused treatment of myasthenia gravis without initiating unnecessary therapy for an otherwise indolent leukemia. The patient responded well to pyridostigmine and a carefully tapered course of corticosteroids, achieving sustained remission while the leukemia remained stable under observation. This case underscores the importance of a thoughtful multidisciplinary approach and close follow-up in managing patients with overlapping autoimmune and hematologic conditions.
