neuroscience.title: Engineering a low cytotoxicity recombinant rabies virus neurotracer via N-gene recoding
neuroscience.abstract: Viral-vector-based tracers have proven invaluable for mapping neural circuits. Rabies virus (RV)-based retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracers have been widely used for depicting the input neural circuit of targeted neuronal populations. However, the cytotoxicity of the RV tracer limits its application. Here, we employed the synthetic attenuated virus engineering technology to recode the N gene of the RV SAD-B19 strain by codon pair deoptimization to generate attenuated RV tracers. The characteristics of the recoded RV tracers were tested both in vitro and in vivo. The full-length recoded N gene abolished viral rescue, whereas the partial recoded N gene supported successful viral recovery. Compared to its parent, the recoded RV trans-monosynaptic tracer exhibited lower cytotoxicity and labeled more input neurons. It can also robustly express proteins to visualize the neuronal morphology and manipulate the neural circuit activity. Collectively, our work generated a new retrograde trans-monosynaptic tool, which complements existing neural circuit tracers.Viral vectors play an important role across multiple fields in biomedicine. In the neuroscience community, rabies virus (RV)-based retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracers have been widely used to map the input neural circuits of targeted neuronal populations. However, the inherent cytotoxicity of RV-based tracers limits their broader application. In this study, we utilized synthetic attenuated virus engineering technology to recode the RV N gene, generating an attenuated neurotracer that will significantly benefit future neuroscience research.
neuroscience.text:
The rabies virus (RV)-based trans-monosynaptic tool has been widely used in the neuroscience community (). RV possesses five genes, which encode the N, P, M, G, and L proteins, respectively (, ). To achieve cell-type-specific monosynaptic retrograde tracing, a multi-component engineering system has been developed (). First, the glycoprotein (G) gene is removed from the RV genome to restrict autonomous transmission (RV-delG). Next, a chimeric EnvA glycoprotein is generated by fusing the cytoplasmic domain of the RV G protein with the extracellular portion of the envelope protein (EnvA) from the avian sarcoma leukosis virus subtype A. This chimeric protein is then stably expressed in a packaging cell line to package the RV-delG genome, yielding pseudotyped viral particles (EnvA-RV-delG). Concurrently, two separate adeno-associated virus (AAV) helpers are designed for Cre-dependent delivery, with one expressing the G protein and the other co-expressing the EnvA receptor TVA along with a fluorescent reporter (AAV-G and AAV-TVA-Reporter). Consequently, the pseudotyped EnvA-RV-delG can exclusively gain entry into specific starter neurons that have been successfully transduced by the AAV-TVA-Reporter. Within these starter neurons where EnvA-RV-delG, AAV-G, and the AAV-TVA-Reporter co-exist, the expressed G protein trans-complements the RV-delG. This allows the assembly of infectious RV-delG particles that are uniquely capable of trans-monosynaptic spreading retrogradely to label upstream input networks ().

The first generation of RV trans-monosynaptic tracer was engineered based on the vaccine strain SAD-B19 (, ), but its cytotoxicity has limited its applications. To address the issue, several strategies have been adopted to develop less-toxic or nontoxic tracers. Previous studies have demonstrated that different RV strains exhibit varying degrees of pathogenicity, neuroinvasiveness, and immunogenicity (). Accordingly, Reardon TR et al. developed a first-generation system based on the challenge virus standard CVS-N2c strain of RV, which exhibited lower toxicity and enhanced spreading efficiency compared to the SAD-B19-based tracer (). Nevertheless, cytotoxicity remains a concern for both SAD-B19 and CVS-N2c-based tracers, necessitating further optimization. Therefore, protein proteolysis technology (PPT) has been used to generate non-toxic SiR tracers by adding a destabilization domain (PEST) to the C terminus of the nucleoprotein (N) of the RV SAD-B19 and CVS-N2c strains (, ). Additionally, an alternative strategy involving the deletion of the L and G genes of RV has been used to construct a non-toxic tracer (). Collectively, although the PPT and gene deletion strategies significantly reduce viral toxicity, they also severely compromise trans-monosynaptic spreading efficiency. Ideally, an optimal tracer for mapping neural connectivity should feature both low cytotoxicity and high trans-monosynaptic efficiency. Therefore, the engineering of a new RV-based retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracer capable of simultaneously mitigating cellular toxicity and enhancing transfer efficacy holds substantial value for the dissection of neural circuits.

Here, we leveraged the synthetic attenuated virus engineering (SAVE) approach (, ) to recode the N gene of RV, exploring whether this strategy could effectively mitigate its cytotoxicity and enhance its trans-monosynaptic efficiency. Our results demonstrate that this recoding strategy successfully reduces RV-induced cytotoxicity. Importantly, our work confirms that SAVE technology represents an efficient and accessible platform for optimizing RV-based tools for the neuroscience community.

The role of the N protein is to package the RV genome and form a complex with the P protein, which is important for viral replication (). Although degradation of the N protein can seriously reduce the trans-monosynaptic efficiency of RV, it can also significantly reduce its cytotoxicity (, ), which indicates that the N protein is a potential target for reducing RV’s cytotoxicity. Thus, we attempted to use SAVE technology to reduce RV’s cytotoxicity by recoding the N gene of RV ().

First, we recoded the full-length N gene to NDDD using a deoptimized codon pair based on mouse codon pair score (CPS, ) and found that NDDD cannot be rescued. The codon pair bias (CPB) value of NDDD was −0.5243 (). Second, we attempted to partially recode the N gene by separately dividing the N gene into three equally long segments and constructed six chimeric RVs, named WDD, DWD, DDW, WWD, DWW, and WDW (). Their CPB values ranged from −0.1498 to −0.3423 (). The order of their CPB values is NWDW, NDWW, NWWD, NDDW, NWDD, and NDWD (). Among them, only DWW and WWD were successfully recovered ().

Characteristics of wild-type and recoded N genes

Next, we compared DWW and WWD () to determine which variant exhibited lower cytotoxicity. B7GG cells were infected with G-coated WWW, DWW, and WWD at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1. The supernatants were collected at 1, 2, and 3 dpi, and the viral titer of each sample was tested. We found that WWW had the highest viral production ability among them, and DWW had a higher ability than WWD (). Regarding viral transcription kinetics, temporal profiling revealed distinct regulatory dynamics for the N, P, and mNeonGreen genes among the three viruses, rather than a uniform increase over time (). At 1 dpi, the wild-type WWW exhibited the highest mRNA levels across all genes, whereas the recoded variants (DWW and WWD) showed significantly lower transcript accumulation. By 2 dpi, mRNA levels rose across all groups, with DWW displaying a more pronounced upregulation than WWD. Remarkably, by 3 dpi, the transcription patterns shifted dramatically as WWD transcription remained restricted at a lower level, whereas mRNA expression in the DWW group increased sharply, eventually surpassing that of the wild-type WWW (). Consequently, we focused on WWD for subsequent experiments. Then, we examined whether the low efficiency of RNA replication is a result of the reduction of the protein expression level caused by the recoded NWWD and found that the expression levels of N, P, and mNeonGreen in WWD are lower than in WWW at 1 dpi (). Meanwhile, the expression levels of these proteins increased over time in WWD (). Together, these results indicate that WWD is a good candidate for preparing an attenuated tracer.

To confirm whether WWD has lower cytotoxicity than WWW in vivo, we first performed a time course analysis of the number of mNeonGreen-positive neurons after injecting equal doses of G-coated WWD and WWW into the brains of mice. These two viruses were separately injected into the M1 region of the brain of C57BL/6J mice, and brain slices were prepared at 1, 2, 3, and 4 weeks post-infection (wpi). We observed that the fluorescence intensity of mNeonGreen increased over time in WWD and WWW (), and the number of fluorescent neurons increased over time in the WWD group, from 1 to 2 wpi, and then reduced from 2 to 4 wpi (). Meanwhile, the number of fluorescent neurons was reduced over time in the WWW group, from 1 to 4 wpi (). These results indicate that the recoded RV WWD has lower cytotoxicity than its parent WWW in vivo.

Next, to determine the physiological effects of WWD and WWW on neurons in vivo, transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) of the brain tissue infected by these viruses and PBS at 1 wpi was performed. Significant alterations in gene expression were observed following WWW injection, with a total of 2,184 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) compared to the PBS control. Among them, 1,452 DEGs were exclusive to the WWW group, whereas 149 DEGs were exclusive to the WWD group (). Compared to the PBS control, WWW infection resulted in the upregulation of 1,908 RNA transcripts and the downregulation of 276 transcripts. Meanwhile, WWD infection led to the upregulation of 700 transcripts and the downregulation of 181 transcripts (; ). In addition, we observed significant upregulation of immune-related transcripts following WWW injection, whereas following WWD injection, these transcripts showed markedly reduced or no significant changes in the expression levels. Consequently, to validate these findings, we selected 12 immunologically relevant genes for validation via RT-qPCR. The results show high concordance with the sequencing data (; ). For these 12 genes (Mmp8, Tarm1, Tnfrsf14, Cfb, Pdcd1lg2, Trem1, Lilrb4a, Tlr8, Ccr1, Il18rap, Cd177, and Spib), the transcriptomic fold changes ranged from 0.19 to 0.56, whereas the corresponding RT-qPCR fold changes ranged from 0.05 to 0.34. A heatmap comparison of the overall transcript levels of the WWW- and WWD-infected groups relative to the PBS control () indicated that the transcript levels of the WWD group were more similar to the PBS control, suggesting fewer transcriptional changes.

To assess the functional implications of the DEGs, we conducted gene ontology (GO) analysis. The majority (5,305) of the enriched GO terms in the WWD group overlapped with those in the WWW group, with only 64 terms unique to WWD infection (). These unique terms showed no specific correlation with immunity or neuronal function (). All DEGs from both the WWW and WWD groups were classified into three categories: biological processes (BPs), cellular components, and molecular functions (MFs). The GO categories enriched in WWD compared to WWW were significantly reduced (). Filtering the top 20 GO categories enriched in the WWW group based on the FDR values revealed that these categories were predominantly related to the immune response. Both the number of significantly changed genes and their significance were reduced in the WWD group ().

To further delineate the specific BPs driven by each virus, we scrutinized the functional profiles of their enriched GO terms. Intriguingly, the top common pathways enriched in both the WWW and WWD groups were predominantly centered around early cell-intrinsic defense mechanisms, including positive regulation of response to biotic stimulus, positive regulation of innate immune response, defense response to virus, and response to interferon-beta (). However, a stark functional divergence emerged when investigating the top-tier GO categories distinct to each group. Following WWW infection, the host transcriptional landscape shifted drastically toward robust leukocyte-mediated immunity and adaptive immune mobilization, characterized by the prominent enrichment of lymphocyte differentiation, T/B cell activation, and leukocyte cell-cell adhesion. Conversely, WWD infection failed to provoke this cascading inflammatory response; instead, its top enriched categories were completely reoriented toward homeostatic cellular and structural events, such as phosphatidic acid metabolic process, triglyceride biosynthetic process, and anatomical structure morphogenesis. Taken together, these transcriptomic data demonstrate that WWW induces a much stronger, broader, and potentially detrimental host response in the injected brain region, characterized by extensive differential gene expression and the intense activation of adaptive immune and leukocyte-related pathways. In contrast, WWD triggers a substantially milder transcriptional profile that shifts closer to the PBS control, featuring fewer DEGs and attenuated pathway enrichment. These findings strongly support the conclusion that WWD exhibits profoundly reduced immunogenicity and less host transcriptional disruption, underscoring its significantly lower cytotoxicity for in vivo neural circuit tracing.

Given that WWW and WWD exhibit distinct infection kinetics (), we additionally performed bulk RNA-seq on WWD-infected tissues at 2 wpi to investigate whether prolonged tissue responses would alter the overall interpretation. Compared with WWW at 1 wpi, WWD at 2 wpi exhibited fewer DEGs and fewer significantly enriched GO categories. Moreover, KEGG pathways related to host immunity and antiviral responses showed reduced enrichment in WWD relative to WWW, characterized by both fewer contributing DEGs and lower enrichment significance (). Collectively, these results indicate that WWD does not trigger heightened tissue-level immune or antiviral transcriptional activation even at this later time point. Instead, the overall diminished engagement of immune- and antiviral-related pathways further supports the conclusion that WWD induces less host transcriptional disruption than WWW.

Based on the above results, we know that WWD is attenuated. To verify whether neurons infected with WWD are physiologically normal, whole-cell recording and optogenetic assays were performed. We first injected G-coated WWD and WWW into the M1 region of the brain of C57BL/6J mice () and then conducted whole-cell recordings of the brain slices at 2 wpi. We found that no significant differences were measured in the membrane properties (the Rs, resting membrane potential [RMP], AP threshold, AP amplitude, and rheobase) between the neurons infected with WWD and the non-infected controls after 2 wpi (). In contrast, it was hard to perform the membrane seal test in the neurons that were infected with WWW at 2 wpi. The success rate of membrane sealing was 0 out of 10 neurons, 10 out of 10 neurons, and 6 out of 6 neurons in WWW, WWD, and control groups, respectively. These data indicate that WWD did not produce detectable changes in the membrane properties of the neurons, whereas WWW seriously affected the function of the infected neurons. Next, we determined whether the attenuated WWD could be used to express channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) to manipulate neural activity. G-coated WWD-ChR2-mNeonGreen was injected into the M1 region of the brain of C57BL/6J mice (), and the signals were recorded at 2 wpi. We found that photo-illumination at a 473 nm wavelength could elicit action potentials (APs) in neurons infected by the virus in acute brain slices for up to 2 weeks after infection (). These results indicate that WWD can deliver functional proteins to the neurons to manipulate neural activity through the optogenetic method.

High trans-monosynaptic spreading efficiency is required for an ideal tracer to map the neural circuit. Therefore, it was necessary to measure and compare the trans-monosynaptic ability of WWD and WWW. Based on the results of their neuronal cytotoxicity and physiological activities, we hypothesized that WWD has higher trans-monosynaptic efficiency than WWW due to two reasons: (i) WWD is less toxic and has lower immunogenicity, thus causing a delayed clearance; (ii) prolonging the time period of virus propagation is beneficial to produce more virus and extend the trans-monosynaptic time. We injected a mixture of two helper AAVs into the ventral hippocampal CA1 (vCA1) region of the brain of Thy1-cre mice (): one expressing G protein for the virus package and the other expressing TVA for EnvA-coated RV entry. Two weeks later, the EnvA-coated WWD and WWW were separately injected into the same region (). The primary neurons were defined as a co-expression of mNeonGreen from RV and mCherry from the helper virus. The input neurons were defined as an expression of mNeonGreen from RV. Then, the brain slices were prepared at 2 wpi, and the number of primary and input neurons in the brain was counted. The total number of primary neurons in the WWD group is more than the ones in the WWW group (), which might indicate that the WWW has higher cytotoxicity than WWD. At the same time point, the total number of input neurons in the WWD group is more than the ones in the WWW group (). In addition, the number of neurons in each input region in the WWD group is also more than the ones in the WWW group. Here, we randomly selected five input regions, piriform cortex (PIR), entorhinal cortex (ENT), diagonal band nucleus (NDB), medial septal nucleus (MS), and reuniens thalamic nucleus (RE), as the representative input regions to compare the tracing ability of WWD and WWW (). These results demonstrate that the attenuated RV WWD facilitates an expanded temporal window for neural circuit tracing, thereby enabling the labeling of more inputs compared with its parent WWW.

Depicting the morphology of neurons in the neural circuit is helpful to elucidate their working mechanisms and discover their new functions (, , ). To confirm whether WWD can express sufficient fluorescent protein to display neuronal morphology, G-coated WWD was injected into the mouse brain (G-coated WWD in M1), and the neuronal morphologies of the neurons in the injection site for the G-coated WWD were visualized after 2 weeks of infection by RV (). The mNeonGreen-positive neurons in M1 had clear cell body and fiber morphology (). At higher magnification (), the morphological details of the fluorescent neurons, such as dendritic spines and other fine processes, were clearly visualized. These results indicate that the recoded RV WWD can express robust fluorescent proteins to display the neuronal morphology.

An ideal neural circuit tracer has the following five key features: (i) is sufficiently attenuated in neurons in vivo to extend the temporal window for use in the functional analysis of the neural circuit; (ii) has high trans-monosynaptic efficiency for mapping more input or output neural circuits; (iii) expresses fluorescent proteins to visualize the neuronal morphology of the neurons in the neural circuit, and functional proteins to manipulate the neural circuit activity; (iv) has a convenient protocol for production in cell lines; (v) has an easy operation protocol for injection in animal models.

The trans-monosynaptic retrograde tracer RV is a powerful technique to identify the connectivity of neural circuits since its introduction in 2007 (, ). To improve an ideal RV tracer, many teams have made great efforts to achieve these goals (, ). To reduce RV’s cytotoxicity, the main strategies include (i) deletion of viral proteins by directly deleting the RV gene or degrading the protein encoded by the gene (). These measures significantly reduce the cytotoxicity of RV, which provides excellent tools for long-term labeling and imaging of neural circuits. However, optimizing the experimental conditions to enhance their spreading efficiency and protein expression ability is also needed; (ii) development of a first-generation system based on a challenge strain of RV (CVS-N2c), which shows lower toxicity and higher spreading efficiency than the vaccine strain (SAD-B19) (). However, Lee et al. applied the SiR strategy to the CVS-N2c strain to further reduce its cytotoxicity (). To enhance RV’s spreading efficiency, several efforts focus on the G protein of RV: (i) engineering chimeric G proteins by combining the cytoplasmic domain of G from SAD B19 strain and the extracellular domain of G from other RV strains (); (ii) improving the expression level of G by codon-optimizing methods () or codon pair recoding (); and (iii) developing a single-AAV helper to co-express G, TVA, and fluorescent proteins (, ). To improve the production efficiency of RV, Sumser et al. engineered a cell line expressing EnvA and TVA, thereby significantly boosting viral titers (). Collectively, these works have promoted the development of RV tracers. Nonetheless, there are still many issues that need to be addressed. Any improvement of RV tracer as proposed above is a welcome addition for the field.

Therefore, we made an attempt to use a synthetic biology method, named SAVE, to reduce RV’s cytotoxicity. In this study, we selected the N gene of RV vaccine strain SAD-B19 as a model and successfully used SAVE technology to reduce its cytotoxicity compared to its parent virus. In addition, it can be efficiently and easily produced in cells in vitro, such as B7GG and BHK-EnvA cells, and easily used for injection in vivo, like the first-generation RV system (, ). The nucleotide sequences of each recoded N gene are different from its parent, while their amino acid sequences are the same. Among these recoded viruses, only WWD and DWW were successfully rescued, albeit with lower efficiency than the WWW. The precise mechanisms underlying this phenomenon have yet to be fully elucidated. However, several factors may be involved. Synonymous mutations can modulate RNA secondary structure, stability, and the molecular interactions between various RNAs and proteins (). Furthermore, ribosomes exhibit differential compatibility toward various synonymous aminoacyl-tRNA pairs as they traverse the mRNA during elongation (, ). Ribosomal stalling often stems from high rare-codon frequencies. The entry of low-abundance aminoacyl-tRNAs into the A-site is diffusion-limited, thereby becoming the rate-limiting step of the elongation cycle (). Consequently, codon pair deoptimization (CPD) resulted in a lower expression level of NWWD compared to NWWW (), consistent with previous studies showing that CPD effectively reduces viral protein synthesis (, ). In our study, the frequencies of CpG and UpA were increased from 34 to 74 and from 67 to 86, respectively, between NWWW and NWWD (). Since CpG and UpA dinucleotides are typically underrepresented in RNA virus genomes to evade innate immune sensors, their increased frequency often triggers enhanced host immune responses that restrict viral replication (). Previous studies have shown that the increased frequencies of CpG and UpA dinucleotides may result in increased host immune responses that restrict the virus (). Therefore, the WWD was expected to undergo stronger host immune recognition. Paradoxically, however, transcriptomic analysis of brain tissues infected with WWD, WWW, or PBS revealed that WWD infection leads to a significant reduction in immune response activation and overall transcriptional disruption compared to WWW (; ). Therefore, the growth curves of these two viruses show that the replication efficiency of WWD is slower than WWW (), which results in lower cytotoxicity of WWD than WWW ().

Interestingly, viruses incorporating the recoded N gene region (451–900 bp) were non-viable. While the precise mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain to be fully elucidated, several potential factors may be involved. First, the RNA sequence within this specific region may harbor essential functional motifs. For instance, the conserved distribution of rare synonymous codons in the virus capsid is strategically utilized to facilitate translational pauses, which are critical for ensuring accurate polypeptide folding (). Consequently, large-scale alterations in codon composition within the central region of the RV N gene might disrupt these strategic pause sites, potentially leading to the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Second, excessive ribosomal stalling could trigger the premature dissociation of the translational complex from the mRNA, yielding truncated polypeptides that are rapidly degraded. Regardless of the specific underlying mechanisms, our strategy for generating attenuated neural circuit tracers has been proven successful and effective.

In addition, the WWD exhibits distinct functional characteristics compared to existing RV tracers regarding cytotoxicity, heterologous gene expression, and trans-synaptic spreading efficiency. In terms of cytotoxicity, non-toxic RV tracers, such as SiRV (including SiR-B19 and SiR-N2c) and gene deletion RV (), facilitate long-term in vivo trans-synaptic labeling of input neural circuits. In contrast, WWD retains a degree of cytotoxicity, resulting in a trans-synaptic labeling window of approximately 2–3 weeks relative to its parental strain. Regarding spreading efficiency, non-toxic RV tracers typically exhibit reduced performance relative to the wild-type virus when compared at the same post-infection intervals (, , ). This limitation may stem from a disruption of the homeostatic balance between the viral life cycle and cellular defense mechanisms caused by the total deletion of essential viral genes, even when these genes are complemented in vivo by helper viruses. Notably, WWD demonstrates enhanced spreading efficiency relative to the wild-type strain under our experimental conditions. Regarding heterologous gene expression, non-toxic RV tracers usually necessitate the expression of recombinases to amplify signaling via recombinase-dependent fluorescent reporters in transgenic mice or via helper viruses (). In contrast, WWD appears capable of driving robust fluorescent protein expression, which may better facilitate the visualization of detailed neural morphology.

Reducing viral replication kinetics is a strategy for mitigating cytotoxicity. However, this approach represents a double-edged sword for neural circuit tracing. If viral titers are suppressed excessively, the virus may fail to produce a sufficient threshold of progeny within primary infected neurons, thereby compromising its capacity for trans-synaptic neural circuit mapping. Crucially, such an attenuation strategy remains effective only if the virus maintains a replication level that satisfies the minimum quorum required for successful trans-synaptic tracing. In this study, although the growth curve of the recoded WWD was visibly restricted compared to that of the wild-type WWW (), our in vivo animal experiments demonstrated its robust tracing efficacy (). Remarkably, the number of labeled upstream neurons in the WWD group even exceeded that observed in the wild-type WWW group under identical experimental conditions (). These findings underscore that despite its reduced replication kinetics and lower viral titers, WWD meets the requirements for neural circuit tracing.

Previous work has shown that the brain should be collected after 1 week of infection or less with the first generation of RV SAD-B19 tracer (, ); in our work, we prolonged the infection time to 2 weeks after infection with WWD. Thus, WWD was given a long time period for the animal experiments. At the same time, the WWD RV labeled more inputs than the parental virus (), and WWD also expresses a robust fluorescent protein to visualize the morphology of neurons (). Collectively, we confirmed the advantages of SAVE technology to reduce the cytotoxicity of RV tracer, which will greatly benefit further neuroscience research. In addition, we have reason to believe that using SAVE technology to recode other RV genes can further reduce RV cytotoxicity, which might also be used for attenuating other RV strains and other viral tracers.

B7GG cells were used to generate G-coated RV (). BHK-EnvA cells were used to generate EnvA-coated RV (). TVA800 cells were used to determine the titer of the EnvA-coated RV (). BHK21 cells (ATCC CCL-10) were used to test the titer of the G-coated RV. All cells were grown in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum. B7GG, BHK-EnvA, and TVA800 cells were kindly provided by Prof. Edward M. Callaway (Salk Institute for Biological Studies, La Jolla, CA, USA).

Eight-week-old C57BL/6 mice were used to assess the cytotoxicity of various recombinant RVs. Eight-week-old Thy1-Cre mice [Jackson Laboratory, strain name: FVB/N-Tg(Thy1-cre)1Vln/J, stock number: 006143] were mated with C57BL/6J mice. Both male and female adult mice were used to analyze the retrograde trans-monosynaptic efficiency of the RVs. All mice were housed in a normal light/dark cycle for all experiments.

Previous studies have shown that codon pair deoptimization can result in the attenuation of the virus (, , ). Therefore, the N gene of rabies virus vaccine strain SAD-B19 was recoded using the codon pair deoptimization strategy (; ). First, we calculated the CPS of each of the 3,721 codon pairs in the mouse genome () based on a previously described method (). Ultimately, the recoded gene had the same amino acid sequence as its original version. Then, the recoded gene underwent chemical de novo synthesis (Sangon Biotech, Shanghai, China).

To construct various recombinant RVs, the green fluorescent protein gene mNeonGreen was inserted into the rabies virus vector pSADdeltaG-F3(2) to generate the reporter vector RV-mNeonGreen(WWW), then all recoded viral genes were separately inserted into the RV-mNeonGreen(WWW) to yield the plasmids RV-NDDD, RV-NDWW, RV-NWDW, RV-NWWD, RV-NDDW, RV-NDWD, RV-NWDD, and RV-NWWD-ChR2-mNeonGreen (WWD-ChR2-mNeonGreen). All plasmids were sequenced (Sangon Biotech, Shanghai, China). All primers used for constructing these RV plasmids are provided in .

Various RVs were prepared using the method described above (, ). Briefly, B7GG cells were transfected with a combination of each of the various expression vectors (6 μg for each RV plasmid of WWW, DDD, DWW, WDW, WWD, DDW, DWD, WDD, and WWD-ChR2-mNeonGreen) and helper vectors (3 μg for pSAD-B19N, 3 μg for pSAD-B19P, 1.2 μg for pSAD-B19L, and 1.5 μg for pSAD-B19G). The virus was collected and propagated by re-infecting the B7GG cells several times. Then, the virus was filtered, purified, and concentrated. In addition, the EnvA-enveloped rabies virus was prepared by infecting BHK-EnvA cells using G-coated RVs. Then, the BHK21 and TVA800 cells were used to determine the titers of the G- and EnvA-coated RVs, respectively (, ).

To assist in the trans-monosynaptic spread of RV, two helpers (AAV-EF1α-DIO-RVG-WPRE-bGHpA and AAV-EF1α-DIO-mCherry-F2A-TVA-WPRE-bGHpA) were produced. In addition, to generate antibodies against RV-N and RV-P, two AAVs (AAV-EF1α-RVN-WPRE-bGHpA and AAV-EF1α-RVP-WPRE-bGHpA) were also prepared. The expression cassettes of RV-G, mCherry-2A-TVA, RV-N, and RV-P were separately inserted into the AAV2 core vector (addgene 20298#) to construct the core plasmids of these four AAVs. Then, these AAVs were separately packaged with the AAV9 capsid using the method described previously (). Briefly, the HEK293T cells were co-transfected with the plasmids of AAV helper AAV-RC9 and each of these four AAV core plasmids. After 3 days, the culture media and the cell pellets were collected, respectively. Then, the cell pellets were lysed in lysis buffer and digested with 50 U/mL of benzonase (Sigma) with the addition of 150 mM of NaCl at 37°C for 1 h, and then clarified using centrifugation at 2,500g for 15 min. The virus from the media and the supernatant of the treated cell lysates were then concentrated with PEG precipitation and resuspended in lysis buffer for downstream purification using an iodixanol density gradient. The rAAV titer was described as the vector genome (vg) per milliliter (vg/mL). The virus titers were determined with a quantitative PCR (qPCR) assay using the iQ SYBR Green Supermix kit (Bio-Rad). All primers used for constructing these AAV plasmids and qPCR are provided in .

To analyze the cytotoxicity of the WWW and WWD RVs, these two RVG-coated viruses (150 nL, 6.33 × 106 fluorescent forming units [FFU]/mL for WWD; 6.16 × 106 FFU/mL for WWW) were injected into the M1 region (AP: −0.98 mm, ML: +1.5 mm, DV: −1.50 mm). Then, the mice brains were collected after injection at 1, 2, 3, and 4 weeks, and the brains were sectioned into 40 µm slices. All brain sections were imaged using the Olympus VS 120 slide scanning system, and representative images for each mouse at the indicated times were taken using the Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope. To fully compare the cytotoxicity of these two RVs, the number of all mNeonGreen-positive neurons in each slice was counted.

In addition, whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed. For the brain slice recordings, 500 nL of WWW (6.13 × 106 FFU/mL) or WWD (6.21 × 106 FFU/mL) was injected into the M1 region (AP: −0.98 mm, ML: +1.5 mm, DV: −1.50 mm) of the brains of eight-week-old C57BL/6J mice. After 2 weeks, the mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane, and the brains were quickly extracted and placed into ice-cold oxygenated solution containing the following: 2.5 mM of KCl, 0.5 mM of CaCl2, 7.2 mM of MgCl2, 25 mM of NaHCO3, 1.1 mM of NaH2PO4, 25 mM of D-glucose, 11 mM of sodium ascorbate, 3 mM of sodium pyruvate, and 97 mM of choline chloride saturated with 95% O2 and 5% CO2. Coronal sections of 300 μm were acquired using a vibratome (Leica, VT1000S) at 0°C–4°C. The slices were incubated for 30 min at 34°C with oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) consisting of 118 mM of NaCl, 2.5 mM of KCl, 2 mM of CaCl2, 2 mM of MgCl2, 26 mM of NaHCO3, 0.9 mM of NaH2PO4, and 11 mM of D-glucose, and then left to recover for 30 min at room temperature. After incubation, the slices were transferred to a recording chamber and superfused with oxygenated ACSF at 2 mL/min for recording.

Visually identified neurons expressing mNeonGreen and nearby non-expressing neurons were recorded with borosilicate glass pipettes with a tip resistance of 2–6 MΩ (Sutter Instrument Co., P-1000) and filled with an intracellular solution consisting of 140 mM of K-gluconate, 5 mM of KCl, 2.5 mM of MgCl2, 10 mM of HEPES, 4 mM of Mg-ATP, 0.4 mM of Na-GTP, 10 mM of Na-phosphocreatine, and 0.6 mM of EGTA (pH of 7.2; osmolarity of 290 mOsm). The signals were amplified with a MultiClamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices, USA) and digitized at 10 kHz with a DigiData 1440A (Molecular Devices, USA). The data were analyzed using Clampfit 10.3 software and Origin 9.0.

The membrane properties of each recorded neuron were evaluated in the voltage- and current-clamp modes. The access resistance (Rs) and membrane resistance (Rm) were calculated from a membrane seal test conducted in voltage-clamp mode. The RMP, AP threshold, and rheobase were measured in current-clamp mode. In order to evaluate the AP threshold, the AP amplitude, and the minimal current necessary to induce firing (rheobase), a current ramp was delivered in the current-clamp mode.

To assess the trans-monosynaptic efficiency of the WWW and WWD RVs, two AAV helpers (AAV-EF1α-DIO-RVG-WPRE-bGHpA, 1.83 × 1012 vg/mL; AAV-EF1α-DIO-mCherry-F2A-TVA-WPRE-bGHpA, 2.20 × 1012 vg/mL) were mixed (1:1; total volume of 80 nL) and injected into the vCA1 (AP: −3.16 mm, ML: +2.95 mm, DV: −4.10 mm) of the brain of Thy-1 cre mice. Then, 150 nL of EnvA-coated RVs (WWD, 2.50 × 107 FFU/mL; WWW, 1 × 108 FFU/mL, diluted to 2.50 × 107 FFU/mL) were separately injected into the same region after 2 weeks. All brain sections were imaged using the Olympus VS 120 slide scanning system. Then, all fluorescent positive neurons (starter cells and input cells) were counted.

To prepare the brain slices, 500 nL of RVG-coated WWD-ChR2-mNeonGreen RV (2.30 × 107 FFU/mL) was injected into the M1 region (AP: −0.98 mm, ML: +1.5 mm, and DV: −1.50 mm) of the brains of C57BL/6J mice. After 2 weeks, the mice were anesthetized with pentobarbital sodium (i.p., 90 mg/kg) and subjected to cardiac perfusion with ice-cold dissection buffer saturated with 95% O2 and 5% CO2 and containing 234 mM of sucrose, 11 mM of glucose, 24 mM of NaHCO3, 2.5 mM of KCl, 1.25 mM of NaH2PO4, 0.5 mM of CaCl2, and 2 mM of MgSO4. The brain was subsequently removed and slowly sliced with a vibratome (VT 1200S; Leica Inc.). Coronal brain slices (250 µm) from the M1 region containing the injection sites were recovered at 37°C for 60 min in a chamber filled with oxygenated ACSF containing 126 mM of NaCl, 26 mM of NaHCO3, 2.5 mM of KCl, 1.25 mM of NaH2PO4, 2 mM of CaCl2, 2 mM of MgCl2, and 10 mM of glucose, equilibrated with 95% O2 and 5% CO2. One hour later, the holding chamber with the slices was placed at room temperature, and the slices were ready for the patch-clamp recordings.

To perform the patch-clamp recordings, the slices were transferred to a recording chamber, and carbogen-saturated ACSF was perfused constantly at a flow rate of 2–3 mL/min at room temperature. The whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were obtained with a MultiClamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices), a Digidata 1440A analog-to-digital converter (Molecular Devices), and pClamp 10.4 software (Molecular Devices). The voltage traces were sampled at 10 kHz and filtered at 2 kHz. The mNeonGreen-positive neurons in the M1 were identified and recorded. For the whole-cell recording of the light-evoked APs, pipettes were filled with a solution containing 135 mM of K-gluconate, 5 mM of KCl, 0.5 mM of CaCl2, 10 mM of HEPES, 2 mM of Mg-ATP, 0.1 mM of GTP, 5 mM of EGTA, and 300 mM of mOsm (pH adjusted to 7.3 with KOH). Blue light (473 nm) was delivered through a 200 μm diameter optic fiber, which was positioned at the slice surface over the recorded neurons. To test the efficacy of the ChR2 expression, we ran a 5 Hz photostimulation protocol on the neurons held at their resting membrane potential. The spike probability was defined as the number of photostimulation-evoked spikes divided by the number of light stimuli.

First, antibodies against the N and P proteins were separately prepared using intramuscularly immunized BALB/c mice, as described in a previous study (). Briefly, the BALB/c mice were immunized twice at a 2-week interval using intramuscular injections of AAV-EF1α-RVN-WPRE-bGHpA (3.0 × 1010 vg) and AAV-EF1α-RVP-WPRE-bGHpA (2.0 × 1010 vg), respectively. Two weeks later, the sera were collected to detect the N and P proteins.

Secondly, the expression levels of the N and P proteins of the WWW and WWD RVs were analyzed using western blot following a previously described method (). Briefly, the two G-coated RVs (MOI = 1 for each virus) were separately used to infect B7GG cells. Then, the cells were collected at 1, 2, and 3 dpi, and the cell lysates were separately analyzed on a 12% SDS-PAGE and electro-transferred to PVDF Immobilon-P membranes (Millipore). The antibodies of RV-N (1:5,000 dilution), RV-P (1:5,000 dilution), mNeonGreen (1:5,000 dilution, ChromoTek no. 32F6), beta-actin (1:5,000 dilution, Proteintech no. 66009-1-lg), and HRP Goat against rabbit (1:5,000 dilution, Abcam, no. ab205718) were used for targeted protein analysis. The signals were detected using the ECL western blotting reagent.

B7GG cells were separately infected by G-coated WWW and WWD RVs at an MOI of 1, and the culture supernatants were collected at 1, 2, 3, and 4 dpi. Then, the viral titers of these samples were determined. Briefly, a series of 1:10 dilutions of each virus (100 μL) were added into individual wells of 12-well plates containing sub-confluent BHK-21 cells and incubated under 5% CO2 at 37°C for 2 days. Then, the numbers of the mNeonGreen-positive cells were counted to calculate the titer of each viral sample.

For transcriptome sequencing, 150 nL of G-coated RVs (2.10 × 107 FFU/mL for WWD; 2.00 × 107 FFU/mL for WWW) were injected into the M1 region (AP: −0.98 mm, ML: +1.5 mm, DV: −1.50 mm) of the brain of C57BL/6J mice. The brain tissues in the M1 region were collected at 1 wpi. The total RNA of the dissected brain tissue was extracted and purified to prepare the RNA library and carry out transcriptome sequencing, which was performed by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). To determine the differentially expressed genes, the adjusted P-value was set to less than 0.05, and the |log2(FoldChange)| value was greater than 1.

To quantify the RNA copies of the RV-N, RV-P, and mNeonGreen genes in the B7GG cells infected with the G-coated WWW and WWD RVs, respectively. These two viruses (MOI = 1 for each virus) were used separately to infect the B7GG cells, and the cells were collected at 1, 2, and 3 dpi. The RNA was extracted from these cells using Trizol RNA reagent (Takara). To quantify the RNA copies of the RNA-seq-determined genes in the mice brains infected with the G-coated WWW and WWD RVs, RNA of the dissected brain tissue was prepared. Then, 1 μg of RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using HiScript III reverse transcriptase (Vazyme) and oligo(dT) primer. Specific primers () were used for qPCR using the SYBR Green Master Mix (Vazyme) on the Applied Biosystems QuantStudio 1 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher). GAPDH was used as an internal control.

neuroscience.title: WHITE-Net: White matter HyperIntensities Tissue Extraction using deep learning network
neuroscience.abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are a hallmark of cerebral small vessel disease, a highly prevalent condition in aging, making their accurate detection in large-scale magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies critically important. Currently available semi-automated and automated segmentation methods are frequently limited by sensitivity to variations in imaging conditions and computational constraints, restricting their applicability across diverse acquisition settings. We present WHITE-Net, a deep learning-based framework for automated WMH segmentation built on a 3D ResUNet architecture and trained on multisite MRI data encompassing substantial variability in scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, spatial resolution, and image characteristics. Evaluated across three independent datasets—BrainLaus, ADNI, and WMH Challenge, WHITE-Net achieves high segmentation accuracy and ranks among the top-performing methods across datasets, enabling a comprehensive assessment of generalizability in varied imaging environments. WHITE-Net maintains stable performance in a wide spectrum of lesion loads and demonstrates a favorable balance between precision and recall, effectively limiting false positive detections—a common limitation of existing approaches. Beyond accuracy, WHITE-Net requires no parameter tuning and offers fast inference times, making it well suited for deployment in large-scale neuroimaging studies. The obtained results highlight the value of training on diverse multisite data for improving generalizability and position WHITE-Net as a reliable, scalable tool for automated WMH segmentation in computational anatomy research.
neuroscience.text:
White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are areas of abnormal signal intensity on diagnostic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) protocols sensitive to tissue water content, such as fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Their etiology varies depending on the clinical context: WMHs of presumed vascular origin are strongly associated with cardiovascular risk factors and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (; ; ; ; ; ), while in migraine (; ), and multiple sclerosis (; ; ), the underlying processes are inflammatory or partially unknown; and in leukodystrophies they reflect hereditary or acquired disorders of myelin maintenance. WMHs of vascular origin are strongly associated with aging and represent a common incidental finding in the general population, with prevalence rising beyond the age of 60 years. They are a hallmark feature of cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD), which is a major contributor to vascular cognitive impairment (; ), and dementia (; ).

The importance of automated, accurate detection of WMHs complementary to the neuroradiological diagnostic expertise is well recognized in both clinical and research context. The sheer volume of data acquired in large-scale MRI studies precludes manual lesion delineation, making automated WMH segmentation indispensable. Despite its well-known limitations in terms of time investment and inter-rater variability (; ), manual lesion annotation remains the gold standard in neuroimaging. Currently available automated WMH segmentation algorithms span a broad spectrum from intensity-based approaches (; ) to machine learning () and deep learning methods (; ).

Intensity-based methods rely on predefined or automatically determined thresholds to identify WMH based on voxel intensity and morphology. While straightforward, these approaches are often limited by their sensitivity to noise and imaging protocols variability. Machine learning approaches overcome this by training classifiers on intensity and spatial features, better capturing lesion variability, although generalizability across heterogeneous datasets remains a challenge. Deep learning models, in particular convolutional neural networks (CNNs), automatically extract complex features from imaging data, improving WMH segmentation performance, but require large training datasets and considerable computational resources (). Despite their strong performance, CNN-based methods are frequently affected by variability in scanner hardware, image acquisition protocols, and image quality, which can limit their robustness and generalizability in multisite settings ().

Existing WMH segmentation methods offer clear advantages in accuracy and time efficiency relative to manual annotation. However, most algorithms are trained on data comprising well-defined conditions in clinical populations, such as multiple sclerosis (; ), stroke, or neurodegeneration (; ; ), which reduces their generalizability to epidemiological MRI datasets. The emergence of large-scale studies in the community-dwelling population incorporating brain MRI, such as the UK Biobank () targeting 100,000 acquisitions, highlights the pressing need for accurate and automated WMH segmentation tools. Robust and reliable segmentation across cohorts characterized by a wide age range, image quality variability, and a spectrum of aging-associated pathologies is essential to ensure the validity of computational anatomy studies at scale.

Current evaluations of WMH segmentation methods predominantly rely on global overlap metrics such as the Dice coefficient, which may obscure important differences in segmentation behavior (). In particular, methods achieving similar Dice scores can exhibit markedly different error profiles with respect to false positive detections and missed lesions (). A more comprehensive evaluation framework encompassing lesion-level metrics and analysis across varying lesion loads and imaging conditions is, therefore, necessary to more fully characterize method performance.

Against this background, we present WHITE-Net (White matter HyperIntensities Tissue Extraction Network), a fast, user-friendly, and generalizable deep learning algorithm for WMH segmentation based on a 3D ResUNet architecture. Unlike many existing approaches, WHITE-Net is trained on multisite MRI datasets encompassing substantial variability in scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, spatial resolution, and image characteristics, with the aim of improving robustness to domain shifts and enhancing generalizability across heterogeneous datasets. Performance is evaluated across multiple independent datasets and benchmarked against established methods using both global and lesion-level metrics. Beyond overall accuracy, we systematically assess robustness across distribution shifts; performance stratified by lesion load, lesion size, and scanner characteristics; and differences in segmentation error profiles across methods.

Taken together, the results demonstrate that WHITE-Net achieves accurate and robust WMH segmentation across heterogeneous imaging datasets, with strong generalizability across varying lesion loads, scanner types, and acquisition protocols. It maintains a favorable balance between precision and recall, effectively limiting false positive detections. These characteristics make WHITE-Net particularly well suited for large-scale epidemiological neuroimaging studies, where robustness to imaging variability and reliable lesion detection is essential.

We used three MRI datasets with distinct demographic characteristics, imaging protocols, and clinico-epidemiological profiles: BrainLaus, the WMH Segmentation Challenge, and the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). The BrainLaus cohort consists of community-dwelling individuals, whereas ADNI and the WMH Challenge datasets include older participants with neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular pathologies. Together, these datasets provide substantial variability in scanner hardware and acquisition protocols, enabling evaluation of model robustness and generalization.

Throughout the manuscript, unless explicitly stated otherwise, the terms in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) refer specifically to the relationship between the evaluation datasets and the training distribution of WHITE-Net. These labels should not be interpreted as universal properties of the datasets or as describing the training distribution of the other comparison methods, whose models were trained on different datasets or, in the case of methods such as BIANCA, trained specifically in the present study. For pretrained comparison methods, their own original training datasets and corresponding distributional coverage are described in .

The BrainLaus dataset originates from the CoLaus|PsycoLaus cohort, a population-based study investigating associations between cardiovascular risk factors and mental health (; ). A subset of 163 participants was selected based on image quality and Fazekas score distribution (mean age: 59.65 years; range: 19.78–92.83; 56.6% female). The dataset was split into training (n = 81) and testing (n = 82) sets.

The WMH Segmentation Challenge dataset () includes individuals with neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular conditions acquired under heterogeneous imaging protocols. The training set comprises 60 scans acquired on 3 MRI scanners (3T Philips Achieva, 3T Siemens TrioTim, and 3T GE Signa HDx), while the test set includes 110 individuals acquired on 5 scanners, including 3T Philips Achieva, 3T Siemens TrioTim, 3T GE Signa HDx, 3T Philips Ingenuity, and 1.5T GE Signa HDxt.

The Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) is a multicenter longitudinal study aimed at developing imaging biomarkers (; ). It includes cognitively normal individuals (NC), patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer’s disease, providing a broad spectrum of neurodegenerative phenotypes. Here, a subset of 115 scans with available FLAIR MRI was selected () for the training set including heterogeneous acquisitions from multiple 3T scanners (Siemens, GE, and Philips), while the test set contains 32 scans acquired on previously unseen scanners, allowing evaluation of cross-scanner generalization.

MRI data were acquired on a 3T whole-body system (Magnetom Prisma - Siemens, Erlangen Germany), using a 64-channel radiofrequency receive head coil and a body coil for transmission. FLAIR acquisition parameters are provided in .

Table summarizing MRI sequence parameters across all included datasets (BrainLaus, ADNI, WMH Challenge), detailing scanner- and site-specific acquisition settings, along with the distribution of MRIs used for training and testing, including sample sizes (n) per group.

Slices are reported with orientation: t = axial (transversal), s = sagittal.

MRI data were acquired across five scanners from different vendors and field strengths. Acquisition parameters and scanner details are summarized in  (; ).

ADNI MRI data were acquired across multiple sites using harmonized protocols on 3T scanners from Siemens, GE, and Philips (). Detailed acquisition parameters are provided in .

All MRI data were preprocessed using SPM12-based (www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) CAT12 toolbox () in MATLAB R2021 (MathWorks, Sherborn, MA, USA). Images were denoised using a spatial adaptive non-local means filter () and corrected for intensity non-uniformity using bias field correction.

In BrainLaus, quality control was performed based on visual inspection for motion artifacts (). A motion score ranging from 1 (minimal motion) to 4 (severe motion) with 0.5 increments was assigned, and only scans with a score below 2.5 were retained.

In BrainLaus, WMH severity was additionally assessed using the Fazekas scale (), evaluating periventricular (PVWM) and deep white matter (DWM) lesions (0–3 each), resulting in a combined score ranging from 0 to 6. Participants were selected to ensure balanced representation across Fazekas scores.

All images underwent skull stripping using SPM12s unified segmentation, followed by min–max intensity normalization. Data were resampled and zero padded to a fixed size of 192 × 176 × 160
 voxels. If resampling was required, corresponding WMH segmentation outputs were transformed back to original space for analysis.

Manual WMH annotation was performed on FLAIR images using the MINC-tool Display software. Lesions were manually delineated slice-by-slice by trained raters (C.C. and A.B.), with simultaneous visualization in all three orthogonal planes to ensure spatial consistency. Prior to independent annotation, both raters underwent a training on approximately 20 datasets to harmonize lesion definition criteria. Raters were blinded to Fazekas scores during segmentation to avoid bias. Participants were selected based on image quality to span the full spectrum of WMH burden (Fazekas 0–6), ensuring representation of both small and large lesions and approximately balanced sampling across Fazekas levels. Selection was not based on age or sex. Demographic characteristics across Fazekas levels are reported in Supplementary Table S1. Segmentation followed standard criteria for WMH identification on FLAIR images, comprising hyperintense regions within the white matter while excluding non-pathological signal changes and anatomically ambiguous regions. Specifically, lesions in subcortical gray matter and the brainstem were not annotated, and thin periventricular hyperintense rims (one voxel in thickness) were excluded to avoid lesion overestimation. All segmentations were subsequently reviewed and validated by an experienced neurologist (F.C.), ensuring anatomical accuracy and consistency across participants.

WMH annotations were generated by four expert raters per scan (). Final binary masks were obtained by thresholding the consensus annotations, with voxels reaching at least 50% rater agreement labeled as WMH.

WMH annotation was carried out by a trained radiology resident using ITK-SNAP () and following standardized guidelines, excluding non-pathological signal changes and anatomically ambiguous regions to ensure consistency across subjects ().

To improve model robustness and generalization across heterogeneous MRI acquisitions, we applied on-the-fly data augmentation during training using the TorchIO framework (). The augmentation combined spatial transformations and intensity-based perturbations to simulate realistic variability of MRI data (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Spatial augmentations included random right–left flipping, affine transformations, and elastic deformations, enabling the model to learn invariance to anatomical orientation, scaling, and non-linear deformations. Acquisition-related variability was simulated through random anisotropy to mimic differences in voxel spatial resolution, and through motion, ghosting, and spike artifacts that reproduce common MRI acquisition imperfections.

Intensity-based augmentations included bias field simulation to account for coil inhomogeneity and gamma transformations that model contrast variability. Rician noise was additionally introduced to realistically emulate MRI magnitude noise, implemented by adding Gaussian noise to both real and imaginary signal components of the signal and calculating the resulting magnitude data.

To further increase data diversity, each training sample is replicated four times, generating one original and three augmented versions per subject. Augmentations were applied probabilistically, ensuring a wide range of transformations while preserving anatomical plausibility, and were disabled during validation.

The proposed architecture is a ResUNet (), variant of the standard Unet () that integrates residual learning to enhance image segmentation performance. The model takes FLAIR images as inputs and is trained to produce binary WMH masks.

The architecture comprises an encoder and a decoder path (Supplementary Fig. S3). The encoder progressively reduces spatial information while increasing feature dimensionality through a series of convolutions layers, with Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activations and max-pooling. Within each block, a residual skip connection adds the block input directly to its output, mitigating the “vanishing gradient” problem and improving the network’s ability to learn complex features representations.

The decoder reconstructs feature and spatial resolution information through deconvolutions and concatenation with high-resolution features from the corresponding encoder levels via skip connections. Dropout layers are incorporated to prevent overfitting. The encoder begins with 16 kernels, doubling at each downsampling step. The decoder mirrors this pattern in reverse, reducing the kernel count as spatial resolution is restored.

The network is implemented in Python3 using the PyTorch framework (). The model is trained on one NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU with 16 GB RAM. The optimization process is performed with an Adam optimizer, batch size = 2, learning rate = 1e−4 for 300 epochs. The 20% of the training set, randomly selected, is used as the validation set. The model weights are saved each time the validation metric increases. Early stopping is used if the validation loss did not decrease for 20 epochs. The model is optimized using a variant of the Dice loss () as follows:

LP−DSC(ytrue, ypred)=1−2ytrue · ypred+ϵytrueγ+ypredγ+ϵ
(1)

with γ = 2. The power γ increases the sensitivity to difference in prediction. It amplifies the differences, therefore, the loss largely penalizes misclassification.

During inference, an adaptive thresholding strategy is applied to refine the final lesion segmentation from the predicted probability map. First, an initial binary mask is obtained using a fixed threshold (0.5) to estimate lesion load, defined as the number of voxels above this threshold. Cases are categorized based on lesion load as low (<300 voxels), medium (300–5000 voxels), or high (>5000 voxels), which determines the adaptive decision threshold (0.8, 0.7, and 0.5, respectively) to account for variability in disease burden. Connected component analysis is then performed, and only components with at least five voxels whose mean probability exceeds the adaptive threshold are retained in the final segmentation mask.

The Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) is used to evaluate the spatial overlap between the manually annotated WMHs and the generated WMH mask using the following equation.

DSC=2TP2TP+FP+FN,
(2)

where TP, FP, and FN denote the number of true positive, false positive, and false negative voxels, respectively. If both the prediction and the ground truth are empty, DSC is set to 1.

The absolute volume difference (AVD) between manual WMH segmentation and algorithm output is defined as

AVD=|Vtrue − Vpred |Vtrue.
(3)

If the manual segmentation contains no lesions, the AVD is set to 0 if the predicted mask is empty and 1 if the reverse is true.

The 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) measures the boundary discrepancy between the manual and automated segmentations.

HD95(Strue, Spred)=P95(D(Strue, Spred)         ∪D(Spred, Strue)),
(4)

where D(Strue, Spred) denotes the set of shortest Euclidean distances from each boundary voxel in Strue to the closest voxel in Spred, and vice versa. Hausdorff distance is defined only if the manual segmentation and the predicted mask contain lesions.

For each subject, ground-truth and predicted WMH masks were decomposed into individual lesion clusters using connected-component analysis (26-connectivity). Candidate correspondences between ground-truth and predicted lesions were quantified using the intersection-over-union (IoU), and an optimal one-to-one assignment between ground-truth and predicted lesions was obtained using the Hungarian algorithm (linear assignment problem), maximizing the total IoU across matched pairs. Assigned pairs with IoU ≥0.1
 were classified as true positives (TP). Assigned pairs below this threshold, along with any unmatched ground-truth and predicted lesions, were classified as false negatives (FN) and false positives (FP), respectively. Note that because matching is enforced as one-to-one, a predicted lesion spatially overlapping multiple ground-truth lesions (or vice versa) is matched to only one counterpart, with the remaining lesion(s) counted as FN or FP.

WMH volume was calculated by multiplying the number of voxels in the manually segmented WMH mask by the voxel volume derived from the NIfTI image header, yielding total WMH volume in mm3. For analyses involving total WMH volume, values were transformed as log10(WMH volume+1) to reduce skewness and accommodate scans with zero WMH volume.

Lesion-wise recall evaluates the proportion of ground-truth lesions correctly detected, that is, matched to a predicted lesion according to the procedure described in .

Recall=TPTP+FN.
(5)

Lesion-wise precision evaluates the proportion of predicted lesions that correspond to a true lesion.

Precision=TPTP+FP.
(6)

The lesion-wise F1-score is defined as the harmonic mean of lesion-wise recall and precision.

F1=2 · Precision · RecallPrecision+Recall=2TP2TP+FP+FN.
(7)

Note that this expression is mathematically identical to the Dice coefficient (): the two metrics differ only in the level at which TP, FP, and FN are defined: voxel-wise for DSC, lesion-wise () for F1.

WHITE-Net was compared with a range of publicly available WMH segmentation tools and frameworks, encompassing three methodological categories: (i) classical or probabilistic approaches that do not require supervised training on the target dataset, (ii) generic machine-learning frameworks that require training on the target dataset, and (iii) pretrained WMH-specific models developed and trained on independent datasets. In this third category, performance reflects both the underlying segmentation architecture and the characteristics of the data and training procedure used by the original developers.

Classical and probabilistic methods. The following methods were applied using their publicly available implementations and recommended settings, without retraining on the present datasets:LPA: Lesion Prediction Algorithm () from the lesion segmentation toolbox (LST) for SPM12. LPA is a supervised machine-learning approach based on logistic regression and was originally developed for the detection of white matter lesions in FLAIR images.LGA: Lesion Growth Algorithm () from the lesion segmentation toolbox (LST) for SPM12. LGA uses a probabilistic model and region-growing procedure to identify WMH based on FLAIR and T1-weighted images.CAT12 (): The Computational Anatomy Toolbox based on SPM12. Its WMH detection procedure uses tissue probability maps and image intensity information to identify voxels and clusters compatible with WMH.SamSeg (; ): A parametric Bayesian whole-brain and lesion segmentation method, implemented within the FreeSurfer framework. SamSeg estimates anatomical structures and lesion classes using probabilistic models and does not require training on the target dataset.

LPA: Lesion Prediction Algorithm () from the lesion segmentation toolbox (LST) for SPM12. LPA is a supervised machine-learning approach based on logistic regression and was originally developed for the detection of white matter lesions in FLAIR images.

LGA: Lesion Growth Algorithm () from the lesion segmentation toolbox (LST) for SPM12. LGA uses a probabilistic model and region-growing procedure to identify WMH based on FLAIR and T1-weighted images.

CAT12 (): The Computational Anatomy Toolbox based on SPM12. Its WMH detection procedure uses tissue probability maps and image intensity information to identify voxels and clusters compatible with WMH.

SamSeg (; ): A parametric Bayesian whole-brain and lesion segmentation method, implemented within the FreeSurfer framework. SamSeg estimates anatomical structures and lesion classes using probabilistic models and does not require training on the target dataset.

Generic machine-learning framework.
BIANCA (): The Brain Intensity AbNormality Classification Algorithm, implemented in FSL. BIANCA uses a k-nearest-neighbor classifier and, therefore, requires training examples from the target dataset. In the present study, BIANCA was trained using the same training set as WHITE-Net and was evaluated using two input configurations: FLAIR only (BIANCA1) and FLAIR together with T1-weighted images (BIANCA2). Following systematic evaluation, a probability threshold of 0.1 was selected for BIANCA.

BIANCA (): The Brain Intensity AbNormality Classification Algorithm, implemented in FSL. BIANCA uses a k-nearest-neighbor classifier and, therefore, requires training examples from the target dataset. In the present study, BIANCA was trained using the same training set as WHITE-Net and was evaluated using two input configurations: FLAIR only (BIANCA1) and FLAIR together with T1-weighted images (BIANCA2). Following systematic evaluation, a probability threshold of 0.1 was selected for BIANCA.

Pretrained WMH-specific deep-learning models. The following methods were evaluated using pretrained models released by their respective authors. None of these models was retrained or fine-tuned on the BrainLaus, ADNI, or WMH Challenge datasets used in the present study.
PGS (): The PGS model, originally developed for the 2017 MICCAI WMH Segmentation Challenge (). PGS is an ensemble of U-Net models with multi-scale highlighting of foreground regions. The model was trained on the 60-subject training set of the WMH Segmentation Challenge (presented in ), which comprised paired T1-weighted and FLAIR MRI acquired at three institutions using five scanners. The remaining 110 subjects formed the WMH Challenge test set and were not available for model training (). The publicly released pretrained model was used directly in the present study.MARS-WMH1
(MD-GRU) (; ): This model is one of two pretrained deep-learning pipelines released as part of MARS-WMH. The model was trained by the MARS-WMH authors on a heterogeneous dataset comprising 304 subjects from three cohorts: ADNI (n = 244), RUNDMC (n = 38), and VASCAMY (n = 22). The model was trained using multimodal MRI data including FLAIR and T1-weighted images. The training data were selected to cover a broad range of WMH volumes and MRI hardware, including different scanner models and acquisition protocols. WMH reference masks were generated semi-automatically and subsequently manually corrected by an expert rater according to STRIVE criteria; lacunes were excluded. This pretrained MARS-WMH model is based on a multi-dimensional gated recurrent unit (MD-GRU) architecture. The pretrained model was applied without retraining or fine-tuning.MARS-WMH2
(nnU-Net) (; ): The nnU-Net-based model from MARS-WMH. Importantly, this model was trained within the MARS-WMH framework using the same heterogeneous training dataset and reference annotations as the MARS-WMH1 model. The publicly released MARS-WMH2 model was applied without retraining or fine-tuning.segcsvd (): A convolutional neural network-based WMH segmentation method developed for heterogeneous clinical cohorts. The model was developed using 947 3T FLAIR scans from seven studies, encompassing heterogeneous patient populations, imaging parameters, and WMH burden. The training data included cohorts with Alzheimer’s disease, vascular cognitive impairment, aphasia, sleep apnea, carotid stenosis, and healthy controls. The method uses FLAIR together with anatomical information derived from SynthSeg () in a two-stage segmentation pipeline. The publicly released model was applied without retraining or fine-tuning on the present datasets.SYSU-MEDIA2 (): A U-Net-like fully convolutional neural network using an ensemble of three networks trained with different initializations and data augmentation. The publicly available implementation was successfully executed on our data but failed to produce meaningful WMH segmentation outputs on BrainLaus and was, therefore, excluded from the quantitative comparisons.

The remaining 110 subjects formed the WMH Challenge test set and were not available for model training (). The publicly released pretrained model was used directly in the present study.

The model was trained by the MARS-WMH authors on a heterogeneous dataset comprising 304 subjects from three cohorts: ADNI (n = 244), RUNDMC (n = 38), and VASCAMY (n = 22). The model was trained using multimodal MRI data including FLAIR and T1-weighted images. This pretrained MARS-WMH model is based on a multi-dimensional gated recurrent unit (MD-GRU) architecture. The pretrained model was applied without retraining or fine-tuning.

MARS-WMH2
(nnU-Net) (; ): The nnU-Net-based model from MARS-WMH. Importantly, this model was trained within the MARS-WMH framework using the same heterogeneous training dataset and reference annotations as the MARS-WMH1 model. The publicly released MARS-WMH2 model was applied without retraining or fine-tuning.

segcsvd (): A convolutional neural network-based WMH segmentation method developed for heterogeneous clinical cohorts. The model was developed using 947 3T FLAIR scans from seven studies, encompassing heterogeneous patient populations, imaging parameters, and WMH burden. The training data included cohorts with Alzheimer’s disease, vascular cognitive impairment, aphasia, sleep apnea, carotid stenosis, and healthy controls. The method uses FLAIR together with anatomical information derived from SynthSeg () in a two-stage segmentation pipeline. The publicly released model was applied without retraining or fine-tuning on the present datasets.
