Fresh faecal samples were collected from participants after a 12‐h fast, placed in ice packs, transported to the laboratory within 2 h and immediately stored at −80°C until 16S rDNA amplicon sequencing. A total of 200 mg of each faecal sample was utilised.

Total genomic DNA was isolated from individual faecal specimens following the manufacturer's protocol of the QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen). The V3–V4 hypervariable region of the bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA gene was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 95°C for 3 min; 30 cycles of 98°C for 20 s, 58°C for 15 s and 72°C for 40 s and a final extension at 72°C for 5 min. Amplification was performed using barcoded primers 341F (5′‐CCTACGGGRSGCAGCAG‐3′) and 806R (5′‐GGACTACVVGGGTATCTAATC‐3′). Each 25 μL PCR reaction contained 12.5 μL of KFX HiFi 2× PCR Master Mix, 1 μL of each primer (10 μM), 50 ng of template DNA and nuclease‐free water to volume. Negative controls consisting of empty sterile storage tubes were processed identically during DNA extraction and amplification; no detectable amplification was observed in these controls. PCR amplicons were separated on 2% agarose gels, extracted and purified using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen Biosciences) according to the manufacturer's instructions. DNA concentration was quantified using Qubit® 2.0 (Invitrogen). Equimolar amounts of amplicons were pooled and subjected to paired‐end sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq platform (Illumina, Inc.).

Primer sequences were trimmed from the raw reads using cutadapt within QIIME2 (v2022.2). The DADA2 plugin in QIIME2 was subsequently employed to perform quality filtering, denoising, merging of paired‐end reads and removal of chimaeric sequences, resulting in a table of amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). Taxonomy was assigned to representative ASV sequences by comparing them with the SILVA database (v138). Downstream analyses were conducted based on the resulting species‐level abundance table (Realbio Genomics Institute). Intergroup comparisons were performed using the rank‐sum test (R language wilcox.test function). Biomarker screening and functional prediction were conducted using the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) tool (LDA > 2 as the threshold), and Phylogenetic Investigation of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States, version 2 software, respectively. For visualisation, LDA scores were assigned positive or negative signs according to the group in which the taxa were enriched.

High‐resolution T1‐weighted and resting‐state blood oxygenation level‐dependent images were acquired on a 3.0 T Siemens Trio MRI scanner (Siemens Healthcare). T1‐weighted anatomical images were collected using a magnetization‐prepared rapid gradient‐echo sequence (repetition time [TR] = 2530 ms, echo time [TE] = 3.65 ms, inversion time = 1100 ms, flip angle = 7°, 224 slices, 1.0 mm isotropic resolution). All images were visually inspected by an experienced radiologist to exclude gross abnormalities. Resting‐state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were acquired using a gradient‐echo echo‐planar imaging sequence (TR = 2000 ms, TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 77°, field of view = 220 × 220 mm2, slice thickness = 3 mm, voxel size = 2.973 × 2.973 × 3.0 mm3). During the 8‐min scan, participants kept their eyes open and fixated on a central crosshair.

MRI data were preprocessed using PhiPipe (v1.0) on the INCloud platform, integrating FreeSurfer (v6.0.0), AFNI (v17.2.07), FSL (v6.0.0), ANTs (v2.2.0) and Convert3D (v1.0). Structural image quality was evaluated using CAT12, which provided an image quality rating (IQR‐CAT12) based on resolution, bias and noise. Participants with IQR‐CAT12 < 0.8 (below grade B) were excluded. Structural measures were extracted using FreeSurfer's recon‐all, including volumes of nine subcortical structures and cortical volume, surface area and thickness for 34 regions defined by the Desikan–Killiany atlas. Resting‐state fMRI preprocessing included discarding the first five volumes, motion correction with mean frame‐wise displacement (FD) estimation, boundary‐based registration to structural images, motion censoring and interpolation of volumes with FD > 0.5 mm, nuisance regression (white matter and ventricular signals and Friston's 24‐parameter motion model), temporal band‐pass filtering (0.01–0.1 Hz) and grand mean scaling to 10 000. Motion censoring, nuisance regression and filtering were performed using AFNI's 3dTproject.

Associations between gut microbiota features and neuroimaging measures were examined using partial correlation analyses within the SAD group, with age and body mass index (BMI) included as covariates. Statistical analysis employed the two‐tailed Student's t‐test or Mann–Whitney U rank‐sum test to compare differences in continuous variables between groups; categorical variables were analysed using the chi‐squared test or Fisher's exact test (results expressed as frequencies [%]), with the specific method determined by the data type. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

We included 48 participants (17 HCs and 31 with SAD) with both MRI and faecal samples in the analyses. There was no significant between‐group difference in sex or BMI. However, the mean age of the SAD group was significantly higher than that of the HC group, and subsequent analyses controlled for this variable. Scores on all core scales assessing social anxiety were significantly higher in the SAD group than in the HC group, including SASC total score, DSRS‐C score, FNE total score and SCARED total score. SCARED subscale scores differed significantly in social phobia, school phobia, somatic/panic and generalised anxiety. Only the separation anxiety subscale showed a non‐significant difference between groups. Results indicate that, compared with HCs, the SAD group exhibited significantly more severe social anxiety symptoms, broader anxiety‐related emotional problems (particularly social phobia, generalised anxiety and school phobia), higher levels of depressive symptoms and a more intense fear of negative evaluation. These findings collectively suggest the presence of emotional dysfunction within this cohort (see table ).

We further analysed microbial differences between the HCs and adolescents with SAD. LEfSe analysis revealed multiple predominantly differentially abundant taxa between the two groups (LDA score > 2). Taxa enriched in the SAD group included Roseburia, Parasutterella and Clostridium sensu stricto 1. Taxa enriched in the HC group included Prevotella, Collinsella and Saccharimonadales (figure ). Following age‐matching, 21 adolescents with SAD and 17 HCs were included, and the biological trends revealed by the microbiome analysis were consistent with those in the original report. The predominant enriched taxa in the SAD group included Parasutterella and Clostridium sensu stricto 1; in the HC group, the predominant enriched taxa were Collinsella and Ruminococcus gauvreauii (figure ). Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed a distinct separation trend in microbial composition between groups, indicating overall structural differences (figure ). Heatmaps further illustrated the relative abundance distribution of horizontally differentiated taxa at the genus level (figure ). LEfSe analysis based on the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes database revealed pathways significantly differing between groups. Pathways enriched in the SAD group included the photosynthesis_antenna proteins, inositol phosphate metabolism and chloroalkane and chloroalkene degradation. Pathways enriched in the HC group comprised the Vibrio cholerae pathogenic cycle and retinol metabolism (figure ).

A group comparison between adolescents with SAD and HCs revealed nominally significant differences in multiple brain morphometric and functional indices after controlling for age, as illustrated in figure . In terms of brain structure, we observed nominally significant volumetric alterations in several regions, including the left caudal anterior cingulate and left caudal middle frontal cortices, as well as the right entorhinal cortex (figure ). Cortical thickness was notably different in the right rostral anterior cingulate and right posterior cingulate, whereas the left paracentral cortex showed a reduction in thickness (figure ). Surface area differences were prominent in the left caudal middle frontal and right precentral regions, among others (figure ). Functionally, nominally significant differences in ALFF were identified in the right pars opercularis and right pars triangularis (figure ). ReHo was altered in temporal and limbic areas such as the bilateral parahippocampal gyri, left middle temporal and left fusiform cortices, with one parietal region (right inferior parietal) showing decreased ReHo (figure ). Fractional ALFF (fALFF) differences were localised to the bilateral pars opercularis (figure ).

Within the SAD group, partial correlation analyses adjusted for age and BMI revealed several nominally significant associations between differential gut microbial genera and MRI‐derived brain measures (figure ). Specifically, right rostral anterior cingulate thickness showed a negative association with Roseburia; right entorhinal volume and left caudal middle frontal volume showed positive associations with Clostridium sensu stricto 1; left paracentral thickness showed negative associations with Prevotella, Roseburia and Parasutterella; right pars opercularis ALFF showed a negative association with Collinsella; right parahippocampal ReHo showed a positive association with Prevotella; left lingual ReHo showed a positive association with Desulfovibrio and left fusiform ReHo showed a negative association with Roseburia. These findings indicate that, among adolescents with SAD, inter‐individual variation in gut microbial features covaries with inter‐individual variation in both structural and functional brain measures, particularly in regions implicated in emotion regulation, fear‐related memory processing and self‐referential or perceptual integration.

In this exploratory analysis, we conducted internal validation by constructing univariate logistic regression models using these individual features—differential gut microbiota genera and MRI‐based brain region metrics—on the same sample cohort. This validation was performed after adjusting for age and BMI. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis for gut microbiota genera (figure ) revealed that Clostridium sensu stricto 1 achieved the highest classification accuracy (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.852), followed by Parasutterella (AUC = 0.846) and Roseburia (AUC = 0.827), indicating the potential of specific microbial taxa as non‐invasive biomarkers for SAD. For MRI‐based biomarkers (figure ), right parahippocampal ReHo showed the highest discriminative ability (AUC = 0.871), closely followed by left lingual ReHo (AUC = 0.867) and right rostral anterior cingulate thickness (AUC = 0.863). Other notable structural and functional brain measures included right entorhinal volume (AUC = 0.852) and right pars opercularis ALFF (AUC = 0.850). These findings suggest that both gut microbiota composition and brain structural/functional alterations hold promise as complementary diagnostic tools for SAD.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate adolescent SAD within the microbiota–gut–brain axis framework by integrating 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and multimodal MRI. Four main findings emerged. First, adolescents with SAD showed altered gut microbial composition and predicted functional pathways, together with more severe anxiety‐ and depression‐related symptoms. Second, they exhibited widespread structural and functional brain alterations in regions implicated in emotion regulation, self‐referential processing and fear‐related circuitry. Third, specific gut microbial genera were associated with brain measures in these regions, suggesting the presence of microbiome‐brain coupling in adolescent SAD. Fourth, both microbiota‐derived and MRI‐derived features showed promising discriminatory performance in distinguishing adolescents with SAD from HCs.

Among the differential taxa, Roseburia, Parasutterella and Clostridium sensu stricto 1 were enriched in the SAD group. Roseburia is a known major producer of short‐chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, which exerts anti‐inflammatory effects, maintains intestinal barrier integrity and regulates neurofunction.,  However, reports on its abundance variation in psychiatric disorders are inconsistent, with both elevated and reduced levels documented in depression.,  These findings suggest that the association between Roseburia and psychopathology may depend on the developmental stage, diagnostic context, symptom profile and methodological characteristics of the study. The increased Roseburia in this study may reflect a compensatory butyrate‐linked response to stress‐related immune or neuroendocrine dysregulation. Recent Mendelian randomisation studies further support the idea that microbiota‐psychiatric associations are symptom‐ and pathway‐specific rather than uniform across disorders., ,  Another study showed that Parasutterella was enriched in HCs. Such inconsistencies may stem from differences in study populations (adolescents vs. adults), geography, diet or analytical methodologies, suggesting SAD‐associated dysbiosis may exhibit high contextual specificity rather than a single universal pattern.,  Research indicates that under conditions of anxiety, depression and other emotional disorders, as well as during periods of stress, the abundance of Prevotella within the gut is significantly reduced, consistent with our findings. The diminished functions of this microorganism—including its anti‐inflammatory properties, role in maintaining the intestinal barrier, support for serotonin synthesis and buffering of stress responses—collectively constitute the gut microbiological basis for the onset and progression of SAD in adolescents. In addition, functional prediction analysis indicated enrichment of retinol/vitamin A metabolism in HCs, which may reflect a gut environment more supportive of neurodevelopmental and immunoregulatory processes.

The neuroimaging findings involved brain regions broadly consistent with the neural circuitry implicated in SAD. The ACC is critically involved in conflict monitoring and emotional regulation. Dysfunction in this region has been directly linked to exaggerated monitoring of social threat and impaired internal regulation in individuals with SAD,,  where it acts as a key hub mediating emotional regulation deficits. Alterations in the parahippocampal gyrus and medial temporal lobe structures, including the fusiform gyrus, may affect the retrieval of fear‐related memories. This is in line with the clinical observation that individuals with SAD tend to repeatedly recall past negative social experiences, which together form the neurobiological basis of persistent avoidance behaviour in social contexts. Dysregulation in the caudal middle frontal gyrus (in terms of volume and surface area) and the opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus, as reflected by altered ALFF/fALFF, may impair the ability of individuals with SAD to suppress task‐irrelevant anxious thoughts during social interactions. Finally, the posterior cingulate cortex is involved in self‐referential processing and somatosensory integration. Structural alterations in these regions may contribute to excessive self‐focused attention and heightened sensitivity to bodily sensations (e.g., blushing and trembling) commonly reported by individuals with SAD.

An important contribution of this study is the identification of associations between gut microbial features and multimodal brain measures in adolescents with SAD. These findings are biologically plausible given that gut microbiota may influence brain development and function through metabolic, immune, neuroendocrine and vagal pathways.,  At the same time, these associations should not be interpreted as uniquely specific to SAD. Rather, they may represent altered or developmentally accentuated microbiome‐brain relationships in a disorder‐relevant context. The observed microbial and imaging features should therefore be considered preliminary candidate markers requiring replication and external validation.

Several limitations should be noted. First, the sample size was relatively small, and the cross‐sectional design precludes causal inference. Second, the age difference between groups is important because adolescence is a period of ongoing maturation in both the gut microbiome and frontolimbic brain systems; thus, developmental effects may have influenced both microbial and neuroimaging findings. Third, detailed dietary characteristics were not systematically assessed. Although faecal samples were collected after a 12‐h fast, unmeasured habitual diet, probiotic or prebiotic exposure and appetite‐related factors may still have confounded the microbiome results.

These findings support a more systemic view of adolescent SAD, suggesting that it may be understood not only as a disorder of brain function but also in relation to peripheral biological processes operating through the microbiota–gut–brain axis. They also suggest that combining microbiome profiling with targeted neuroimaging measures may improve the biological characterisation of SAD and inform future multimodal assessment strategies. More broadly, the results provide a rationale for longitudinal and mechanistic studies examining whether microbiome‐related alterations contribute to symptom progression and whether microbiome‐targeted interventions may have adjunctive value in adolescent SAD.

In summary, this study provides evidence of altered microbiota–gut–brain axis functioning in adolescents with SAD. We identified disorder‐related gut microbial features, multimodal brain abnormalities and associations between microbial variation and brain measures. These findings support a more integrative model of SAD pathophysiology and provide a foundation for future work on microbiome‐informed biomarkers and interventions.

neuroscience.title: MicroRNAs in Intracranial Aneurysm: From Vascular Cell Dysfunction to Candidate Non-Invasive Biomarkers of Formation and Rupture
neuroscience.abstract: Intracranial aneurysms (IAs) are pathological dilatations of the cerebral arterial wall that affect 2–5% of the population and may rupture, causing subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) with a mortality rate approaching 40%. Despite advances in neuroimaging, a reliable circulating biomarker capable of detecting IAs or accurately predicting rupture risk remains lacking. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), small non-coding RNAs regulating gene expression at the post-transcriptional level, have emerged as promising, minimally invasive biomarkers due to their stability in body fluids, and involvement in pathways fundamental to vascular homeostasis. This review evaluates current evidence on circulating and tissue-derived miRNAs implicated in IA formation and rupture. Numerous studies demonstrate differential expression of specific miRNAs in patients with unruptured (UIA) and ruptured aneurysms (RIA), as well as in relation to aneurysm morphology, multiplicity, and individual vascular risk factors. Low miR-21 expression appears to promote vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) apoptosis and weaken arterial wall integrity, suggesting a potential role in rupture susceptibility, although the reported direction of change is not consistent across studies. Conversely, miR-29a contributes to extracellular matrix remodeling and VSMC apoptosis, with elevated circulating levels correlating with IA presence and, in some studies, rupture. Several miRNAs, including miR-143, miR-200a-3p, miR-16, miR-26a, miR-448-3p, and miR-1246, exhibit expression patterns associated with aneurysm progression, inflammation, and vascular remodeling. Exosomal miR-152-3p and circulating miR-126 demonstrate particularly strong diagnostic potential, independently predicting rupture risk or postoperative complications. Collectively, the available evidence supports the biological plausibility of miRNAs as candidate biomarkers of IA detection and rupture risk. Their translation is, however, constrained by pronounced inter-study heterogeneity in biological compartment, normalization strategy and preanalytical handling, by the scarcity of independent replication, and by the fact that none of these molecules is specific to intracranial aneurysm, being equally dysregulated in aortic aneurysm or atherosclerosis. On present evidence, miRNAs in IA are best regarded as etiopathogenetically informative rather than as validated diagnostic tests, and large-scale, multi-centre studies with standardized methodology and prospective validation remain necessary.
neuroscience.text:
An intracranial aneurysm (IA) is a pathological, permanent dilatation of the cerebral arterial wall, most commonly located within the circle of Willis. It affects approximately 2–5% of the general population. The formation of an intracranial aneurysm results from a complex interplay of hemodynamic, inflammatory, degenerative, and molecular processes, leading to endothelial cell injury, extracellular matrix degradation, loss of internal elastic lamina integrity, and weakening of the arterial smooth muscle layer., The consequence of these pathological alterations may be aneurysmal rupture, resulting in subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH), which carries a mortality rate of 40%, making IA one of the most serious cerebrovascular diseases.,

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short, non-coding RNA molecules that regulate gene expression at the post-transcriptional level. They influence key cellular processes such as proliferation, apoptosis, inflammation, and vascular wall remodelling. Over the past decade, numerous studies have demonstrated that miRNAs can be detected in various body fluids, making them attractive candidates for early, minimally invasive biomarkers of vascular diseases, including intracranial aneurysms., Altered expression profiles of specific miRNAs have been implicated both in the pathomechanisms and in the evaluation of rupture risk.,

To date, however, no circulating biomarker with sufficient sensitivity and specificity has been identified that could enable the detection of intracranial aneurysms or accurately predict their risk of rupture beyond imaging methods. This gap remains clinically significant, as decisions regarding invasive treatment (endovascular or neurosurgical) carry procedural risks and, in some cases, might be avoided if a reliable tool for rupture risk assessment were available.

Our group has investigated candidate biomarkers of intracranial aneurysm across successive levels of biological regulation. Early work identified compartment-specific inflammatory signatures in the cerebrospinal fluid, showing that the ratio of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to serum IL-8 is elevated in patients with unruptured aneurysm (UIA) and that the IL-6 quotient discriminates such patients from controls with a broader panel of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines subsequently found to be altered in the cerebrospinal fluid of this population. Parallel studies addressed the signalling pathways underlying this response, demonstrating activation of the canonical NF-κB pathway together with the GRO-α/CXCR2 axis in UIA patients, and linking NF-κB activation to increased plasma 20S proteasome activity. More recently, the analysis was extended from protein to transcript level, with elevated TGFB1 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) associated with aneurysm formation and TGFB3 expression implicated in rupture. This was complemented by a review from our group examining the mechanistic evidence linking TGF-β signalling, vascular cell dysfunction and macrophage-driven wall remodelling to aneurysm formation and rupture. These findings consistently point to chronic, locally amplified inflammation and extracellular matrix remodelling as central to aneurysm pathobiology, precisely the processes that miRNAs regulate post-transcriptionally.

Building on this line of investigation, the present review synthesises current evidence on the role of microRNAs in intracranial aneurysm: from their canonical functions in vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cell biology, through their dysregulation in the aneurysmal wall, to their behaviour in the circulation, and appraises whether the available data support their use as non-invasive indicators of aneurysm presence and rupture risk.

This article is a critical narrative review. Systematic review methodology was not applied, and the search is reported to allow readers to reproduce it rather than to claim exhaustive retrieval of the literature. In total, the reference list comprises 100 publications. A structured PubMed search combining aneurysm-related terms (Block A: “intracranial aneurysm”, “cerebral aneurysm”, “brain aneurysm”, “unruptured/ruptured intracranial aneurysm”, “subarachnoid hemorrhage/haemorrhage”) with microRNA-related terms (Block B: “microRNA”, “microRNAs”, “miRNA”, “miRNAs”, “miR-”), restricted to the Title/Abstract fields and filtered to 2003–2025 and English/Polish language, retrieved 243 records. All 243 records were screened by title and abstract, from which 32 aneurysm-and-miRNA-specific studies were identified as directly relevant and included. (Supplementary data: Table S1 and Figure S1).

The remaining references provide conceptual and clinical background (the criteria of an ideal diagnostic biomarker, and the clinical and pathological background of intracranial aneurysm), n=41, and publications by our own group (identified by an author-specific PubMed search, n = 7). The latter two topics were not amenable to a structured keyword search, since generic biomarker-science and aneurysm-pathophysiology terms return an unfiltered fraction of the biomedical literature that database screening could not narrow to the topic-specific literature actually needed; these references were therefore selected as established background and conceptual literature, consistent with standard practice for background sections of a narrative review.

During the revision process, 20 further references were identified and added in response to Reviewer comments: 15 concern the canonical, tissue-independent molecular function of the candidate miRNAs, and 5 concern methodological and reporting-standard literature.

An ideal diagnostic biomarker should fulfill a comprehensive set of analytical, clinical, and practical criteria to ensure reliability, clinical relevance, and feasibility for routine implementation. From an analytical perspective, it must demonstrate high sensitivity and specificity to enable accurate discrimination between diseased and non-diseased individuals while minimizing false-positive and false-negative results.,, Ideally, an effective biomarker should be detectable early in the disease course. A key advantage of an ideal marker is that it can be assessed in readily available biological material collected in the least invasive manner (eg, blood, urine, other body fluids). Equally important are the clinical applicability and validation of the biomarker, supported by standardised reference intervals and validated cut-off values that enable clinical decision-making. From a practical perspective, a valuable biomarker should be readily available, affordable, and easy to measure, facilitating its integration with current diagnostic procedures. Crucially, it must also provide clinical utility and should demonstrate generalisability and population validity., Finally, an optimal biomarker should display biological stability,,
.

MicroRNAs are small non-coding RNA molecules, typically 18–22 nucleotides in length. They play a crucial role in post-transcriptional gene regulation by binding to the 3′ or 5′ untranslated regions (UTRs) of target messenger RNAs (mRNAs), thereby suppressing their translation. This interaction results in either translational repression or degradation of the target transcript. miRNAs are transcribed in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II or III as long primary precursors known as pri-miRNAs. These transcripts are then processed by the RNase III enzyme Drosha to generate hairpin-shaped intermediates, termed pre-miRNAs. The pre-miRNAs are exported to the cytoplasm via Exportin-5, where they undergo further cleavage by the RNase III enzyme Dicer, producing a short RNA duplex. One strand of this duplex is incorporated into an Argonaute (Ago) protein to form the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC). The mature miRNA then guides the Ago–miRNA complex to complementary sequences within the target mRNA.

Through this mechanism, miRNAs modulate mRNA stability and translational efficiency, influencing a wide range of cellular processes including differentiation, proliferation, migration, and apoptosis (). Dysregulation of miRNA expression has been implicated in numerous pathological conditions, and specific miRNAs can be linked to distinct tissues and disease states, underscoring their potential as highly specific biomarkers. The number of individual miRNAs in humans is substantial and comparable to the number of transcription factors or RNA-binding proteins. Many of them are expressed in a tissue- or developmentally specific manner, thereby contributing significantly to cell type–specific protein expression profiles. Recent studies have demonstrated that human miRNAs are highly conserved and may regulate the expression of approximately 30% of all genes in the human genome, highlighting their pivotal role in the regulation of complex cellular functions.

Moreover, the detection of miRNAs in various body fluids has emphasized their potential to provide valuable insights into both physiological and pathophysiological processes, reflecting dynamic alterations in gene expression patterns. Circulating miRNAs exhibit remarkable stability across a wide range of biological specimens, including whole blood, plasma, serum, and other body fluids. However, one limitation of circulating miRNAs is that many are released passively from apoptotic or necrotic cells, which may reduce their ability to accurately reflect ongoing biological processes within the vasculature. In contrast, some miRNAs are selectively packaged and transported via exosomes secreted into the peripheral circulation by various cell types, including endothelial and smooth muscle cells. Exosomal miRNAs are increasingly regarded as more specific and biologically relevant biomarkers than freely circulating miRNAs. Enclosed within lipid bilayer vesicles, they are protected from RNase-mediated degradation and from adverse environmental conditions such as temperature fluctuations, pH changes, and repeated freeze–thaw cycles.

Alterations in the expression profiles of miRNAs may occur at early stages of various diseases, making them potential indicators of early molecular dysregulation. Dysregulated miRNA expression can impair cellular and biological functions, thereby contributing to disease progression, including vascular pathologies. It has been well established that miRNAs play a pivotal role in maintaining vascular integrity and homeostasis. For instance, deficiency of Dicer, a key enzyme in miRNA biogenesis in smooth muscle cells, results in abnormal vascular formation, while aberrant miRNA expression has been observed in injured vascular walls.

It is currently known that approximately 70% of human miRNAs are present in the brain. This, in turn, makes miRNAs an excellent target for research on central nervous system disorders. In vitro experimental studies have demonstrated that miRNAs play a crucial role in gene expression and endothelial cell function. Accumulating evidence indicates that miRNAs are critical mediators in the pathogenesis of vascular diseases by regulating vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cell functions through mechanisms such as proliferation, migration, apoptosis, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix protein synthesis., These processes collectively contribute to the formation and growth of intracranial aneurysms and may influence their subsequent rupture. Changes in circulating and especially exosomal miRNA expression profiles can reflect ongoing pathophysiological states. Several studies have demonstrated that miRNA levels differ between healthy individuals and patients with unruptured intracranial aneurysms, as well as between those with ruptured and unruptured aneurysms, and across varying disease severities.,, Given their stability in biological fluids and disease-specific expression patterns, miRNAs are being increasingly investigated as promising non-invasive biomarkers for early detection and rupture risk assessment of intracranial aneurysms.,,

Before considering the individual miRNAs implicated in IA, it is useful to recall that none of them is a disease-specific molecule. Each was first characterised in another biological context and exerts a canonical, tissue-independent function that is retained in the vasculature. miR-21 is a mechanosensitive, pro-survival miRNA acting largely through the PTEN/AKT axis;, miR-143, co-transcribed with miR-145, is a master switch of the contractile vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) phenotype;, miR-29a is a principal negative regulator of extracellular matrix synthesis;, the miR-200 family governs endothelial barrier integrity through ZEB1/ZEB2 and claudin-5; and miR-16 is best characterised as a regulator of apoptosis acting on BCL2, while also being one of the most frequently used endogenous reference genes in circulating-miRNA studies,,, including studies in which it is simultaneously proposed as a candidate biomarker of aneurysm presence., Recognising these canonical roles clarifies why the same molecules recur across unrelated vascular and non-vascular diseases, and provides the mechanistic framework within which their behaviour in aneurysmal tissue and in the circulation should be interpreted. Abbreviations: ACE, angiotensin-converting enzyme; AKT, protein kinase B; ARE, antioxidant response element; AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; BCL2, B-cell lymphoma 2; CCL2/CCL5, C-C motif chemokine ligand 2/5; CCND1, cyclin D1; CI, confidence interval; CLDN5, claudin-5; COL1A1/COL3A1, collagen type I/III alpha 1 chain; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; EC, endothelial cell; ECM, extracellular matrix; ELK1, ETS transcription factor ELK1; ELN, elastin; FBN1, fibrillin 1; GSK3B/GSK-3β, glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta; IA, intracranial aneurysm; KLF4/KLF5, Krüppel-like factor 4/5; MCL1, myeloid cell leukemia 1; MCP-1, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1; MEF2C, myocyte enhancer factor 2C; MMP2, matrix metalloproteinase 2; mTOR, mechanistic target of rapamycin; NF-κB, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells; NIHSS, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale; Nrf2, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2; PDCD4, programmed cell death protein 4; PI3K, phosphoinositide 3-kinase; PIK3R2, phosphoinositide-3-kinase regulatory subunit 2; PP2A, protein phosphatase 2A; PPP2CB, protein phosphatase 2 catalytic subunit beta; PRKAR1A, protein kinase cAMP-dependent type 1 regulatory subunit alpha; PSD-93, postsynaptic density protein 93 (DLG2); PTEN, phosphatase and tensin homolog; qRT-PCR, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction; RIA, ruptured intracranial aneurysm; SPRED1, sprouty-related EVH1 domain containing 1; SPRY1, sprouty homolog 1; SRF, serum response factor; TGFBR1/2, transforming growth factor beta receptor 1/2; TGF-β, transforming growth factor beta; TP53, tumour protein p53; UIA, unruptured intracranial aneurysm; VCAM-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule 1; VEGF/VEGF-A, vascular endothelial growth factor A; VSMC(s), vascular smooth-muscle cell(s); WFNS, World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies; YY1, Yin Yang 1; ZEB1/ZEB2, zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1/2.

Emerging evidence indicates that miR-21 plays a protective role in maintaining vascular wall integrity, and its markedly reduced expression has been proposed as a potential molecular indicator of increased rupture risk in intracranial aneurysms. Nearly thirty target genes have been experimentally validated, and predicted to be linked to miR-21 mediated regulation during cerebrovascular remodelling. These include key determinants of vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) function, such as vascular endothelial growth factor C (VEGFC), phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN), B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2), and programmed cell death protein 4 (PDCD4). miR-21 has been shown to modulate VSMC phenotype and contractility, in part through the regulation of tropomyosin. Downregulation of miR-21 leads to PTEN upregulation, consequently suppressing AKT phosphorylation and activity, a central node of prosurvival and proproliferative signaling, that contributes to limiting aneurysm progression and adaptive vascular remodeling. Concurrently, increased PDCD4 expression promotes VSMC apoptosis, while reduced Bcl-2 levels associated with low miR-21 further enhance apoptotic susceptibility.

Collectively, these molecular alterations suggest that insufficient miR-21 expression disrupts vascular homeostasis by favoring pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative pathways, ultimately weakening the vascular wall and increasing the likelihood of intracranial aneurysm rupture. Evidence on the direction of miR-21 dysregulation is, however, not uniform. An independent cohort found miR-21 to be significantly increased in both whole blood and aneurysm tissue relative to healthy controls, with no difference between ruptured and unruptured cases, and within one serum study microarray and quantitative RT-PCR yielded opposite directions in the same patients.

The miR-29 family is widely expressed in vascular tissues and plays a critical role in maintaining arterial wall integrity. Among its members, miR-29a has been implicated in the regulation of genes encoding extracellular matrix (ECM) components, including collagen I, collagen III, fibrin-1, and elastin-1, which are essential for vascular elasticity and tensile strength., Reduced miR-29a expression has been associated with excessive collagen deposition and diminished vascular elasticity, thereby contributing to aneurysm formation and progression.

In the study by Ansari et al, a significant increase in circulating miR-29 expression was observed in patients with ruptured aneurysms, accompanied by a marked reduction of its expression in the cerebrospinal fluid in these patients compared with controls. This apparent tissue-specific regulation may reflect compartmentalized miRNA dynamics, where circulating miR-29a elevation represents systemic vascular stress, while its depletion in CSF mirrors local depletion associated with aneurysmal wall degeneration. Moreover, the authors reported high diagnostic performance for CSF miR-29a, with an AUC of 0.95 and 100% specificity. Boga et al reported overexpression of miR-29a in tissue samples from patients with cerebral aneurysms compared with those undergoing surgery for other vascular pathologies. Importantly, expression levels did not differ between ruptured and unruptured aneurysms or according to aneurysm location. Other clinical studies have also demonstrated increased miR-29a expression in the peripheral blood of patients with aneurysms compared with control individuals., Wang et al reported that elevated miR-29a levels were not significantly associated with age, sex, aneurysm size, or location, but were significantly correlated with aneurysm rupture. Based on these findings, they suggested that miR-29a may play a role in IA development. Similarly, Liao et al reported increased miR-29a expression in plasma exosomes from patients with aneurysms compared with healthy controls. No significant differences were observed between ruptured and unruptured aneurysms, and miR-29a levels were not associated with sex, diabetes, alcohol consumption, or smoking. They further proposed that miR-29a may serve as an independent, noninvasive biomarker for IA development.

Experimental and clinical studies have highlighted a multifaceted role of miR-29a in the pathophysiology of IA., In vitro models, it has been shown that miR-29a overexpression promotes apoptosis of human brain vascular smooth muscle cells (HBVSMCs) through mitochondrial pathways by targeting the anti-apoptotic protein myeloid cell leukemia 1 (MCL-1). Similarly, in vivo studies using IA models confirmed that miR-29a overexpression enhances the expression of pro-apoptotic genes, such as caspase-3, −8, and −9, as well as cytochrome c, thereby promoting vascular cell apoptosis and weakening of the arterial wall.

Given its dual involvement in ECM remodeling and vascular smooth muscle cell apoptosis, miR-29a represents a promising biomarker candidate for evaluating rupture risk in intracranial aneurysms, with particularly strong diagnostic potential.

Current evidence identifies miR-143, miR-200, and miR-16 as biologically relevant contributors to IA pathology, each showing distinct expression patterns related to aneurysm development, rupture risk, multiplicity, and patient-specific risk factors. Feng et al reported that circulating miR-143/145 expression was significantly reduced in IA patients compared with healthy controls, suggesting that downregulation of this cluster may facilitate IA initiation and progression. Consistently, decreased miR-143 expression has also been observed in other IA studies, where this reduction is thought to influence the phenotypic modulation of vascular smooth muscle cells., In contrast, Al-Jehani et al reported significantly higher expression levels of miR-143, miR-200, and miR-16 in patients with IA than in the control group. Moreover, miR-143 expression levels were nearly two-fold higher in patients with ruptured aneurysms compared with those with unruptured IAs (p < 0.05), indicating a potential association with rupture related vascular remodeling. Conversely, miR-200 and miR-16 showed slightly higher expression in patients with unruptured aneurysms. Notably, previous studies have reported selective upregulation of miR-200a-3p in patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage, suggesting its potential involvement in rupture susceptibility. In a recent study, Ansari et al demonstrated a marked elevation of miR-200a-3p expression in blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples from patients with aSAH, achieving high diagnostic performance (AUC > 0.8). miR-200a-3p also differentiated ruptured from unruptured aneurysms (AUC 0.855), indicating its association with molecular processes involved in vascular wall destabilization. miR-200 family plays a key role in regulating endothelial cell function, vascular permeability, and angiogenic signaling. Overexpression of miR-200a-3p may promote increased endothelial permeability and disruption of vascular barrier integrity, which may contribute to mechanisms underlying aneurysm rupture.

Differences in expression have also been reported with respect to aneurysm multiplicity. All three miRNAs (miR-143, miR-200, and miR-16) displayed higher expression in patients with single aneurysms than in those with multiple lesions. The most prominent change was observed for miR-200, which was almost twice as highly expressed in single-aneurysm cases. These findings raise the possibility that distinct miRNA-dependent regulatory pathways may underlie the development of multiple aneurysms within an individual. Sex-specific differences have also been documented. Expression levels of all assessed miRNAs were higher in male patients compared with females, with miR-143 showing nearly double the expression in men. In addition, levels of miR-143 and miR-16 were almost three-fold higher in patients without a history of stroke, suggesting potential interactions between miRNA expression and cerebrovascular comorbidity. Traditional vascular risk factors appear to further modulate circulating miRNA levels. Hypertensive patients exhibited nearly two-fold increased expression of all three miRNAs, with a particularly marked rise in miR-16. Patients with diabetes mellitus and active smokers also demonstrated elevated expression across all miRNAs (miR-143, miR-200, and miR-16).

Collectively, these data demonstrate that miR-143, miR-200, and miR-16 exhibit distinct and clinically relevant expression profiles in intracranial aneurysm patients. Variability associated with rupture status, aneurysm multiplicity, sex, and vascular risk factors underscores their potential diagnostic and prognostic utility. As circulating biomarkers, these miRNAs may support improved phenotyping of IA and contribute to future stratification strategies aimed at assessing rupture risk and understanding aneurysm biology.

miR-26a, a highly conserved microRNA, plays a crucial role in regulating vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and apoptosis and has been implicated in various vascular pathologies. Boga et al reported elevated miR-26a expression in aneurysm tissue compared with controls, irrespective of aneurysm location, with no significant difference between ruptured and unruptured aneurysms, suggesting that miR-26a overexpression may contribute to the development of IA. In contrast, Liu et al observed lower miR-26a expression in IA tissue relative to normal superficial temporal artery samples. The precise role of miR-26a in IA pathogenesis therefore warrants further investigation, and the existing findings should be interpreted as preliminary.

miR-448-3p is overexpressed in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) within atherosclerotic plaques, where it promotes VSMC proliferation and migration by targeting and suppressing MEF2C. Boga et al reported increased miR-448-3p expression in aneurysm tissue compared with controls, independent of aneurysm location, with no difference observed between ruptured and unruptured aneurysms. These findings suggest that miR-448-3p overexpression may contribute to the pathogenesis of intracranial aneurysm development.

According to bioinformatic analyses, miR-1246 targets key regulatory molecules including TP53, GSK, and YY1, implicating its involvement in cellular stress responses, immune activation, and atherosclerosis-related signaling cascades. A growing body of evidence underscores the role of chronic inflammation as a pivotal determinant of IA development. In this context, findings by Jiang et al highlight the functional relevance of miR-1246, as its elevated expression in patients with IA suggests the presence of a systemic inflammatory signaling component. Bott et al showed that miR-1246 serves as a central driver enhancing inflammatory activation in mesenchymal stem and stromal cells. This is particularly important given that miR-1246 modulates PRKAR1A and PPP2CB, thereby influencing NF-κB pathway activation and enhancing the secretion of pro-inflammatory chemokines CCL2 and CCL5, which further amplify vascular inflammation. Moreover, recent reports indicate a significant role of miR-1246 in M2 macrophage polarization through NF-κB-dependent mechanisms, which is especially relevant considering that imbalance among macrophage subtypes contributes to vascular wall instability and increases the risk of aneurysm rupture.

Distinct miRNA signatures are emerging as critical molecular regulators underlying the initiation and progression of intracranial aneurysms. In the study by Jiang et al, a profound and multidirectional dysregulation of the miRNA was demonstrated, reflecting the complexity of the vascular response, with particular emphasis on the coordinated suppression of clusters such as miR-1/miR-133a, miR-143/miR-145, miR-23b/miR-24-1, and miR-29b-2/miR-29c. These clusters are tightly linked to endothelial dysfunction, impaired phenotypic modulation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), pathologically enhanced extracellular matrix remodeling, and activation of inflammatory pathways, processes that are central to IA pathogenesis.,

Aneurysm blebs (aneurysms with daughter sacs) as well as multilobulated or daughter outpouchings have previously been identified as factors significantly increasing the risk of rupture.,, Tsukahara et al reported an annual overall rupture rate of 3.42%, which rose to 28.3% per year in aneurysms presenting with blebs. Jin et al propose that aneurysm initiation, enlargement, and eventual rupture may be driven by distinct molecular mechanisms, a concept reflected in the heterogeneous miRNA expression profiles they observed. In their analysis of 86 miRNAs, the authors demonstrated substantial variability in expression across different aneurysm morphologies. Elevated levels of miR-21, miR-22, miR-720, and miR-3665 were found both in patients with solitary aneurysms and in those with sister aneurysms, suggesting a potential contribution to the maintenance of pathological vascular wall homeostasis. Conversely, miR-3679-5p was upregulated in patients with daughter aneurysms as well as in those with RIA, indicating a possible association with more structurally complex morphologies.

A distinct pattern was observed for miR-1471, miR-3945, miR-4253, miR-4314, and miR-574-5p, whose reduced expression appeared in both solitary aneurysms and RIA. Jin et al in a separate study demonstrated that fibrinogen is one of the molecular targets of miR-139-5p, and that the expression of miR-139-5p is markedly suppressed in intracranial aneurysm tissue compared with normal vascular samples. The authors underscore that this subset of miRNAs may play a fundamental regulatory role in the early stages of aneurysm formation and in the molecular processes governing further progression. Accordingly, Jin et al identify patients with daughter aneurysms as a high-risk group, characterized by a widespread upregulation of nearly all assessed miRNAs, including those involved in the regulation of vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) function, endothelial signaling, and growth-factor related pathways. This phenomenon may reflect intensified pathological vascular remodeling accompanied by enhanced activation of compensatory mechanisms. Mechanistically, miR-106b, miR-22, and miR-498 modulate the activity of vascular endothelial growth factor receptors, whereas miR-671 positively regulates VSMC proliferation. Moreover, miR-574 contributes to VSMC proliferation and vascular morphogenesis via EDN1, and miR-21 is known to induce apoptosis through extracellular signaling cues. miR-720, hsa-miR-365, and hsa-miR-936 also demonstrated significant regulatory functions.,, Altogether, Jin et al identified 8291 predicted target genes associated with the 86 examined miRNAs, illustrating an extensive, multidirectional post-transcriptional regulatory network encompassing pathways essential to aneurysm formation, progression, and the potential for rupture. The observations of Jin et al, align with evidence indicating that elevated miR-21 levels are associated with active vascular wall remodeling through modulation of VSMC proliferation and survival, while alterations in miR-22 and miR-574 expression reflect the regulation of inflammatory activity, VSMC phenotypic switching, and extracellular matrix dynamics.,

Subsequent studies indicate that the expression of selected miRNAs in patients with intracranial aneurysms is independent of aneurysm morphology, location, or size. Zheng et al demonstrated that, in patients with RIA, plasma expression of miR-23b-3p, miR-590-5p, miR-20b-5p, miR-142-3p, and miR-29b-3p was significantly downregulated compared with neurologically healthy individuals, regardless of aneurysm location, type, or size. In this study, 32 potential target genes of these miRNAs were identified, including TGM2, EREG, EDN1, and COL4A1, with extracellular matrix development and the TGF-β signaling pathway emerging as the most enriched biological processes. In the context of previous literature, miR-29b and miR-23b-3p have been reported to be differentially expressed in intracranial aneurysm tissue compared with normal vascular tissue. MiR-20b-5p may influence actin cytoskeleton biogenesis, while miR-23b modulates inflammatory responses. Reduced expression of miR-590-5p promotes angiotensin II–induced endothelial apoptosis. Although no direct association between miR-142-3p and RIA has been reported, animal studies suggest a role for miR-142-3p in regulating macrophages in inflammatory diseases and in controlling TGF-β–dependent smooth muscle cell contractile phenotype via inhibition of migration. Furthermore, Zheng et al demonstrated that the plasma expression profile of these miRNAs may serve as an independent predictor of aneurysm progression.

Exosomes are nanoscale (40–160 nm), double-membrane vesicles that mediate intercellular communication by transferring proteins, lipids, DNA, and RNAs, including miRNAs and lncRNAs, to recipient cells, thereby modulating cellular function and contributing to disease progression. Recent evidence highlights the role of CSF-derived exosomal miRNAs in intracranial aneurysms. In particular, Li et al demonstrated that cerebrospinal fluid exosomal miR-152-3p is markedly downregulated in unruptured aneurysms and represents a robust predictor of RIA. Mechanistically, miR-152-3p modulates HVSMC proliferation and migration via PTEN-dependent signaling, implicating it in vascular smooth muscle cell dysfunction. Importantly, both CSF exosomal miR-152-3p levels and aneurysm size independently predicted progression to RIA. These findings position CSF exosomal miR-152-3p as a dual-purpose biomarker, linking mechanistic insight into vascular smooth muscle cell dysregulation with clinically relevant prediction of aneurysm rupture risk.

Mature miR-126 is essential for endothelial homeostasis, angiogenesis, and the regulation of inflammatory signaling. Owing to these functions, it has gained attention as a circulating biomarker in vascular disorders, including intracranial aneurysms (IA). Mathioudakis et al reported elevated circulating miR-126 levels in patients with unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIA) compared with healthy controls, and also higher levels in ruptured aneurysms (RIA), suggesting an association between increased miR-126 expression and aneurysm instability. Wu et al confirmed higher circulating miR-126 expression in patients with UIA compared with healthy controls and, in patients with aSAH, measured plasma levels at four time points after the event (days 1, 3, 7 and 14). Expression rose substantially from day 1 to day 7 and decreased moderately thereafter, peaking on day 7. Diagnostic performance against healthy controls was consistent across all comparisons (AUC 0.75 for UIA, and 0.75, 0.82, 0.87 and 0.79 on days 1, 3, 7 and 14, respectively), supporting the potential of miR-126 as a non-invasive marker of high-risk aneurysms and of the early post-rupture vascular response. Similarly, Yang et al found significantly elevated miR-126 expression levels in IA patients, with excellent diagnostic performance (AUC 0.966). Increased expression correlated with larger aneurysm size and independently predicted rupture risk (AUC 0.827).

In contrast, Luo et al observed decreased miR-126 expression in IA patients; however, the biomarker retained high diagnostic performance (AUC 0.945). Moreover, miR-126 expression correlated positively with elevated TNF-α and IL-6, suggesting inflammation-related modulation. Postoperatively, higher miR-126 levels predicted cerebral vasospasm (AUC 0.859), and logistic regression identified elevated miR-126 expression, hypertension, higher Hunt–Hess scale, and prior bleeding as independent risk factors.

Despite variability in reported expression patterns, circulating miR-126 shows promising diagnostic and prognostic performance across IA phenotypes. Its associations with endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, aneurysm morphology, rupture status, and postoperative complications highlight its promise as a clinically relevant, non-invasive biomarker supporting risk stratification in intracranial aneurysm management.

When the available evidence is assessed against the criteria for an ideal diagnostic biomarker outlined above (), several systematic limitations become apparent. Although a number of miRNAs recur across studies of IA, the published data are marked by pronounced inconsistency, with the same molecule frequently reported to change in opposite directions between cohorts. This heterogeneity constrains the reproducibility of candidate signatures and currently limits their translation into clinical practice.

A first consideration concerns the biological material itself. The present review deliberately includes studies performed on aneurysmal tissue alongside those analysing circulating compartments (). Tissue studies do not constitute biomarker evidence in the diagnostic sense, since the aneurysm wall is accessible only during surgery; their value lies in establishing biological plausibility and in nominating candidates for subsequent validation in an accessible compartment. Importantly, however, concordance between the vessel wall and the circulation cannot be assumed. Plasma miR-143 and miR-145 are reduced in patients with IA and both are likewise downregulated in ruptured aneurysm domes, yet a peripheral-blood study reported the opposite direction for the same cluster. Circulating levels therefore reflect not only release from the lesion, which constitutes a negligible fraction of total body cell mass, but also a systemic response of blood and endothelial cells throughout the vasculature.

The most conspicuous discrepancies concern the direction of dysregulation. This is evident even at the level of whole tissue profiles: genome-wide screening of aneurysm walls identified a mixed pattern, with 72 miRNAs upregulated and 85 downregulated relative to control arteries, whereas other tissue studies reported an almost uniformly downward shift, 18 of 18 validated miRNAs downregulated in one series and 67 of 70 in another, while a third found the opposite, with miR-26a, miR-29a and miR-448-3p all upregulated. The authors of the genome-wide screen themselves noted this divergence. miR-29a shows a further, compartment-dependent inconsistency, being upregulated in whole blood but simultaneously downregulated in the CSF of the same ruptured patients; and although increased miR-29a has been linked to rupture in one cohort, no association with rupture status was detected in aneurysm tissue in another. Serum miR-126 has likewise been reported in both directions.,

Several methodological factors plausibly account for these divergences. First, the compartment is not interchangeable: miRNA content differs between tissue, whole blood, plasma, serum, CSF and their exosomal fractions. The choice of control tissue is equally variable, with studies using the superficial temporal artery,, the middle meningeal artery or the intercostal artery as the comparator, a difference that has itself been proposed as a source of discordance between tissue studies.

Second, there is no consensus reference for normalization. Studies have variously used U6,, the haemolysis-sensitive miR-16,, or an exogenous spike-in such as cel-miR-39,, while one report applied a ΔCt method without naming its reference gene. Because U6 is a small nuclear RNA rather than a miRNA, and miR-16 is abundant in erythrocytes, both are vulnerable to compartment-specific artefacts in plasma or serum. The problem is compounded by inconsistency in which molecules are treated as stable references: miR-16 serves as the internal control in two studies,, yet is itself a candidate biomarker in others,, and one study normalized to a panel of five endogenous miRNAs including miR-126-3p and miR-21-5p, both proposed as biomarkers elsewhere in this literature (). A molecule assumed to be invariant in one study is thus the analyte of interest in another, which alone can generate opposite apparent directions of change.

Third, preanalytical and temporal variables differ widely, and their impact is measurable rather than hypothetical: whole-blood miR-21 and miR-92 remained stable at room temperature for up to 18 hours but fell significantly by 24 hours, and both declined by 14 days after surgical treatment. Sampling windows are correspondingly incomparable, ranging from within three days of rupture to a fixed fifth day after subarachnoid hemorrhage, to samples obtained at least two years after the hemorrhage in patients whose ruptured aneurysm had already been occluded.

Furthermore, differences may occur depending on the platforms used. In a study using two methods in the same patients, microarray screening showed an increase in serum miR-21 in two subgroups, whereas quantitative RT-PCR on an expanded set of the same cohort showed the opposite. When a single study can yield opposite directions for one miRNA depending on the platform, discordance between independent studies using different platforms, normalizers and cohorts is unsurprising.

Finally, the quantitative basis for biomarker claims is uneven. Formal diagnostic-performance metrics were not reported in a substantial proportion of studies (); where high accuracy was reported, it was generally derived from small, single-centre cohorts without independent validation,,, conditions under which area-under-the-curve estimates are prone to optimistic bias. The scale of the reproducibility problem is illustrated by the minority of studies that attempted formal replication: in one two-stage design with blinded assessors, only four of fourteen candidates identified by microarray remained significant on RT-qPCR in independent cohorts, and in another, two of five candidates failed to replicate. Taken together, the absence of standardized compartments, normalization strategies, preanalytical protocols and reporting standards, compounded by the scarcity of independent replication, represents the principal barrier to establishing circulating miRNAs as reliable clinical biomarkers of IA presence or rupture.

As noted above, none of the candidate miRNAs is specific to intracranial aneurysm (), and the consequences of this for biomarker interpretation deserve explicit consideration. miR-29a is a well-characterised regulator of extracellular-matrix turnover in aortic dilation and aneurysm, and genome-wide profiling of aneurysmal tissue places it within a functional node shared with aortic dissection; the miR-143/145 cluster is downregulated in atherosclerosis and after vascular injury as a consequence of its generic role in smooth-muscle-cell phenotypic modulation;, and miR-26a and miR-448-3p have both been examined in abdominal aortic aneurysm and atherosclerotic plaque. A signal that tracks any process of arterial-wall remodelling cannot, in isolation, distinguish an intracranial aneurysm from another vascular condition.

This has a direct and under-appreciated consequence for reported diagnostic accuracy. In most studies the comparison group comprised healthy volunteers, and several explicitly excluded individuals with hypertension, diabetes or other cardiovascular disease.,, The high discriminatory values so obtained therefore reflect separation from unusually healthy controls rather than from the population encountered in clinical practice, in whom the same miRNAs are perturbed for reasons unrelated to the aneurysm. Areas under the curve above 0.9,, should be interpreted in that light, and the single study using a diseased comparator group, enrolling patients with hydrocephalus, remains an exception. Multimarker panels, exosomal miRNAs with a defined cell of origin, and measurement in cerebrospinal fluid, may improve specificity; on present evidence, however, miRNAs in intracranial aneurysm are best regarded as etiopathogenetically informative rather than as validated diagnostic tests.

The studies reviewed here rely overwhelmingly on RT-qPCR with relative quantification, typically preceded by candidate selection from microarray or next-generation sequencing (). This near-exclusive dependence on a single amplification-based platform is itself a source of the variability described above. Several limitations are, however, addressable with existing technology. Locked-nucleic-acid chemistry improves discrimination between family members differing by a single nucleotide, pertinent for the miR-29 and miR-143/145 families. Droplet digital PCR provides absolute quantification without a standard curve and greater tolerance of inhibitors, and is well suited to the low-abundance miRNAs typical of plasma and CSF. Amplification-free multiplexed platforms reduce amplification bias, whereas small-RNA sequencing permits unbiased, genome-wide discovery at the cost of expense and analytical complexity. Beyond the platform, the field would benefit from adherence to established reporting frameworks, the MIQE guidelines for qPCR, and the STARD criteria for diagnostic-accuracy studies, together with routine exogenous spike-in normalization, prospectively defined compartments, and independent external validation.

In summary, numerous recent studies have demonstrated distinct miRNA expression patterns in the circulation (peripheral blood, plasma, CSF), tissues, and exosomes of patients with unruptured and ruptured intracranial aneurysms. Several miRNAs (miR-21, miR-29a, miR-143, miR-200a-3p, miR-16, miR-26a, miR-448-3p, miR-1246, miR-152-3p, and miR-126) have emerged as candidate biomarkers reflecting different aspects of aneurysm biology, including apoptosis, vascular remodeling, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation, with some showing potential relevance for rupture risk assessment.

The available evidence supports the biological plausibility of miRNAs as non-invasive biomarkers for intracranial aneurysm detection and rupture risk stratification. However, when considered against the stringent criteria of an ideal diagnostic marker, the current data remain preliminary. As detailed above, methodological heterogeneity, the absence of standardized normalization and reporting, limited sample sizes and the lack of independent replication together limit their immediate clinical applicability. Therefore, large-scale, multicenter studies with standardized methodologies and prospective validation across diverse populations are essential before selected miRNA signatures can be reliably integrated into routine clinical practice.

neuroscience.title: Arginine vasopressin deficiency in children—a practical guide to etiological diagnosis and long-term surveillance
neuroscience.abstract: Arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) is an uncommon but clinically important cause of the polyuria–polydipsia syndrome. Establishing the diagnosis extends beyond confirming hypotonic polyuria and requires differentiation from primary polydipsia and arginine vasopressin resistance, together with identification of the underlying etiology. Unlike adults, children and adolescents with AVP-D frequently present with the earliest manifestation of an evolving neoplastic, infiltrative, inflammatory, congenital, autoimmune, or genetic disorder, making longitudinal clinical, endocrine, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) surveillance integral to the diagnostic process. Using three illustrative clinical cases, this review presents a practical approach to the evaluation of AVP-D, integrating clinical assessment, biochemical investigation, dedicated hypothalamic–pituitary MRI, and risk-adapted longitudinal surveillance. We discuss the strengths and limitations of the water deprivation test, the emerging role of copeptin-based diagnostics, and current evidence supporting arginine-, urea-, and glucagon-stimulated copeptin testing. Emphasis is placed on the longitudinal interpretation of MRI, consensus recommendations for PST, and the concept that idiopathic AVP-D should be regarded as a provisional diagnosis requiring continued etiological reassessment. Emerging biomarkers, including neurophysin I and oxytocin, may further refine the assessment of hypothalamic–neurohypophyseal dysfunction but remain investigational in children. Ultimately, AVP-D should be viewed not as the end of the diagnostic process but as its beginning, with clinical assessment, neuroimaging, endocrine evaluation, and structured surveillance integrated to achieve the earliest possible etiological diagnosis.
neuroscience.text:
Arginine vasopressin deficiency, previously termed central diabetes insipidus (), is an uncommon but clinically important childhood disorder caused by impaired arginine vasopressin (AVP) secretion, resulting in hypotonic polyuria and compensatory polydipsia. It belongs to the polyuria–polydipsia syndrome, which also includes AVP resistance (AVP-R), previously termed nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and primary polydipsia (PP). Although clinically similar, these disorders differ substantially in pathophysiology, prognosis, and treatment, making accurate differentiation essential (). The terms AVP-D and AVP-R were introduced to better reflect the underlying pathophysiology and reduce confusion with diabetes mellitus. Such confusion has contributed to inappropriate inpatient management, delayed desmopressin administration, and preventable adverse outcomes ().

The diagnostic challenge in childhood extends beyond confirming AVP-D. Unlike adults, children may present with the earliest manifestation of an evolving neoplastic, infiltrative, inflammatory, congenital, autoimmune, or genetic disorder. Diagnosis therefore requires integration of clinical history, biochemical evaluation, MRI, endocrine assessment, and longitudinal surveillance ().

Patti et al () highlighted an important clinical pitfall: apparent improvement in polyuria or reduced desmopressin requirements may reflect evolving anterior pituitary failure, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, hypothalamic dysfunction, or progression of the underlying disease rather than recovery of AVP secretion. The consensus guidelines subsequently provided a structured, risk-based framework for children and young people with idiopathic PST, AVP-D, or both, incorporating MRI, pituitary assessment, serum β-hCG and α-fetoprotein (AFP), ophthalmological evaluation, and systematic investigation for occult LCH ().

Recent advances include copeptin-based diagnostics, stimulation tests using arginine, urea, or glucagon, and increasingly dynamic interpretation of MRI findings (). However, most evidence derives from adults, and pediatric data remain insufficient to support direct application of adult diagnostic thresholds. Emerging tests should therefore complement, rather than replace, clinical assessment, MRI, endocrine evaluation, and surveillance.

This review presents a practical approach to children and adolescents with suspected AVP-D, integrating confirmation of hypotonic polyuria and AVP-D, etiological investigation, neuroimaging, and risk-adapted follow-up to facilitate early recognition of the underlying disorder.

At 7 years and 10 months of age, a previously healthy girl born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery developed polyuria (measured urine output, 60 mL/kg/24 hours) and polydipsia. After exclusion of other causes of hypotonic polyuria, including glycosuria by urinalysis, AVP-D was diagnosed, and desmopressin was initiated. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) performed 4 months later demonstrated pituitary stalk thickening (PST) of approximately 6 mm with loss of the posterior pituitary hyperintensity (PPHI). Eight months later, PST had progressed to approximately 8 mm, with mild anterior pituitary enlargement.

At 9 years and 3 months, impaired linear growth prompted endocrine reassessment. Growth hormone deficiency (GHD) was confirmed by insulin tolerance and arginine stimulation tests, and central adrenal insufficiency was identified; central hypothyroidism developed subsequently. The combination of AVP-D, progressive PST, anterior pituitary enlargement, and evolving multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies raised strong suspicion for neurohypophyseal germinoma. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) α-fetoprotein (AFP) and β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) remained negative, and CSF cytology showed no malignant cells.

Continued stalk enlargement led to endoscopic transsphenoidal biopsy at 10 years and 2 months. Histopathology confirmed a localized, nonsecreting neurohypophyseal germinoma. Chemotherapy followed by whole-ventricular radiotherapy and a tumor-bed boost produced a marked radiological response (). At the most recent follow-up, at 17 years of age, she remained free of recurrence with preserved gonadotropic function.

A 16-year-old male was referred for recurrent polyuria and polydipsia with progressive hypothalamic–pituitary dysfunction. Symptoms had first appeared at 7 years, when a water deprivation test was reportedly normal and no diagnosis was established. Nine years later, recurrence was accompanied by hypernatremia, AVP-D, central hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypertransaminasemia. Desmopressin normalized urine output and serum sodium.

MRI demonstrated an enhancing midline hypothalamic lesion, initially with normal pituitary stalk and anterior pituitary morphology. Serum and CSF tumor markers remained negative, and stereotactic biopsy was nondiagnostic. One year later, MRI showed progression of the hypothalamic lesion with infundibular enlargement and homogeneous enhancement (). The combination of AVP-D, progressive hypothalamic–infundibular disease, and multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies suggested an infiltrative disorder.

Systemic evaluation revealed cholestatic liver disease, hepatic steatosis, splenomegaly, hepatic and renal abnormalities, and diffuse cystic interstitial lung disease. Lung and bone marrow biopsies confirmed multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). Treatment according to the LCH-III protocol achieved remission, although AVP-D persisted and anterior pituitary dysfunction progressed. More than 7 years later, rectal involvement confirmed recurrent LCH, and treatment according to the LCH-IV protocol was initiated ().

A 12-year-old male was referred after a 9-month history of polyuria and polydipsia. He had obesity but normal linear growth and no relevant medical history. Evaluation confirmed marked hypotonic polyuria, with urine output of 166 mL/kg/day. During supervised water deprivation, urine remained dilute despite plasma osmolality exceeding 300 mOsm/kg and a 3.5% reduction in body weight. Urine osmolality increased from 140 to 500 mOsm/kg after intranasal desmopressin, confirming AVP-D. Within a research protocol, arginine-stimulated copeptin testing showed undetectable basal and persistently low stimulated concentrations, providing additional evidence of AVP-D.

Anterior pituitary evaluation and ophthalmological examination were unremarkable. Serum and CSF AFP and β-hCG, CSF cytology, brain and spinal MRI, and whole-body MRI incorporating short tau inversion recovery sequences were negative for neoplastic or infiltrative disease. MRI demonstrated homogeneous PST of 4.5 mm with absent PPHI ().

MRI after 3 months showed slight reduction in stalk thickness, followed by stability. With no identifiable etiology, he was provisionally classified as having idiopathic AVP-D with mild PST. Because follow-up remains limited, definitive etiological classification is not yet possible, and structured endocrine and MRI surveillance continues.

The evaluation of suspected AVP-D begins with objective confirmation of true hypotonic polyuria rather than proceeding immediately to water deprivation or copeptin-based testing (). Reported urinary frequency should not be assumed to represent polyuria; whenever feasible, urine output should be measured to distinguish true high-volume polyuria from urinary frequency (pollakiuria) with normal total urine volume. In children older than 2 years and adolescents, polyuria is generally defined as urine output exceeding 40 to 50 mL/kg/day, although age-adjusted thresholds are required in infants and younger children (150 mL/Kg/die in the newborns and 100 to 110 mL/Kg/die up to 2 years of age) (). Hypotonic polyuria is characterized by excessive urine output with inappropriately dilute urine, typically with urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg or urine specific gravity <1.005 ().

Secondary causes should first be excluded, including diabetes mellitus, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, chronic kidney disease, diuretic therapy, sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor use, and other causes of osmotic diuresis. Initial evaluation should include urinalysis, including assessment for glycosuria and urine specific gravity, together with plasma glucose, electrolytes, calcium, potassium, urea, creatinine, plasma osmolality, and urine osmolality (, ).

Plasma sodium is informative but rarely diagnostic alone. Hypernatremia (plasmatic sodium >145 mmol/L) or high-normal sodium supports AVP-D or AVP-R, whereas low or low-normal values favor PP. However, many patients with AVP-D maintain normal sodium through intact thirst and adequate water intake, while hyponatremia is not universal in PP. Partial AVP-D diagnosis is challenging, and it could be suspected when urine osmolality is 300 to 500 mOsm/kg and plasmatic sodium >143 mmol/L. Plasma sodium must therefore be interpreted alongside the clinical and biochemical findings ().

Clinical history provides important diagnostic clues. Abrupt-onset polyuria, marked nocturia, excessive nocturnal drinking, preference for cold water, or a history of hypothalamic–pituitary disease, neurosurgery, head trauma, or infiltrative disorders increase the likelihood of AVP-D. Impaired growth, pubertal abnormalities, headache, visual disturbance, fatigue, or excessive daytime somnolence should prompt evaluation for an underlying hypothalamic–pituitary disorder (, , ).

The causes of AVP-D differ substantially between children and adults (). Whereas postsurgical and traumatic etiologies predominate in adults, childhood AVP-D is more often associated with neoplastic, infiltrative, inflammatory, autoimmune, congenital, vascular, or genetic disorders (, , , , ). Idiopathic AVP-D remains a provisional diagnosis, as children initially classified as idiopathic may later be diagnosed with germinoma, LCH, exceptionally hypophysitis, or another systemic disorder, sometimes years after presentation (, , , ).

Etiology of arginine vasopressin deficiency in children

In children, idiopathic AVP-D or idiopathic PST should be regarded as provisional. Longitudinal endocrine, clinical, visual, and imaging reassessment is mandatory.

Abbreviations: AVP-D, arginine vasopressin deficiency; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; hCG, human chorionic gonadotropin; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; NPII, neurophysin II; PST, pituitary stalk thickening.

Age at onset provides an important etiological clue. In our previous cohort, children with familial AVP-D and LCH presented earlier than those with intracranial tumors, whereas idiopathic cases showed an intermediate age distribution (). No intracranial tumors were identified before 5 years of age, and no familial forms presented after 7 years. Thus, AVP-D presenting in infancy or early childhood should prompt evaluation for congenital and genetic causes, whereas onset in late childhood or adolescence should heighten suspicion for germinoma or another intracranial neoplasm. Age also helps guide family counseling and the intensity and duration of surveillance.
