Among children with AVP-D and unexplained PST, neoplastic disorders, including LCH, germinoma, and craniopharyngioma, are more common than inflammatory or autoimmune diseases (, ). Adult diagnostic priorities, such as routine investigation for neurosarcoidosis or IgG4-related disease, should therefore not be directly extrapolated to pediatric practice ().

Germinoma is a major diagnostic consideration because it may initially present as isolated AVP-D. Serum and CSF tumor markers are commonly negative, while MRI abnormalities can be subtle and evolve gradually (, , ). Isolated AVP-D should therefore not be considered reassuring when progressive hypothalamic–pituitary abnormalities are present. Case 1 illustrates this principle: histological confirmation of a nonsecreting germinoma was achieved more than 2 years after AVP-D onset despite persistently negative serum and CSF tumor markers.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis may also present as isolated AVP-D before bone, skin, lung, lymph node, or other systemic manifestations emerge (, , , , , ). Continued surveillance for occult systemic disease is therefore required even when the initial evaluation is unrevealing.

Hypophysitis and infundibulo-neurohypophysitis are important differential diagnoses of AVP-D associated with PST but are less common in children than in adults (, ). No single clinical, biochemical, or radiological feature reliably distinguishes inflammatory disease from germinoma or another infiltrative disorder. Homogeneous pituitary stalk enhancement and anterior pituitary enlargement may suggest hypophysitis, but these findings are nonspecific and occur in neurohypophyseal germinoma and, rarely, LCH. Hypophysitis should therefore remain a diagnosis of exclusion based on integration of clinical findings, endocrine evolution, MRI, and longitudinal follow-up. Histopathological confirmation should be reserved for selected patients with progressive disease or persistent diagnostic uncertainty (, , , , , , ).

Autoimmune mechanisms may contribute to a subset of apparently idiopathic cases. Antirabphilin-3A antibodies have been reported as promising biomarkers of lymphocytic infundibulo-neurohypophysitis, but pediatric validation remains limited and routine testing cannot yet be recommended ().

Genetic AVP-D should be considered in patients with early-onset disease, a positive family history, isolated AVP-D without PST, or otherwise unexplained disease (). Mutations in the AVP-neurophysin II gene are the most common cause of autosomal dominant familial AVP-D and typically lead to progressive degeneration of AVP-producing neurons (, , ). Wolfram syndrome should be suspected when AVP-D is associated with diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, hearing impairment, urinary tract abnormalities, or neurodegenerative features (). Congenital midline defects, including septo-optic dysplasia and holoprosencephaly, usually present in infancy and are frequently associated with multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (, , ).

Delayed etiological diagnosis is a strong argument against prematurely labeling a child as having idiopathic AVP-D. In a pediatric cohort of intracranial germinoma, more than half of patients experienced diagnostic delay, sometimes exceeding 6 years despite repeated medical evaluations (). These findings reinforce the concept that AVP-D may be the earliest manifestation of an evolving hypothalamic–pituitary disorder and support prolonged endocrine and MRI surveillance.

Once true hypotonic polyuria has been documented and AVP-independent causes have been excluded, the next objective is to establish whether the patient has AVP-D rather than PP or AVP-R. In clinically unequivocal presentations, the combination of plasma sodium and osmolality with inappropriately dilute urine may establish the diagnosis; otherwise, water deprivation with desmopressin administration or, where available, copeptin-based testing may be required. Once AVP-D is confirmed or strongly suspected, etiological investigation should proceed promptly and include MRI of the hypothalamic–pituitary region, assessment of anterior pituitary function, and targeted investigation for underlying neoplastic, infiltrative, inflammatory, congenital, or genetic disease.

Anterior pituitary function should be assessed at baseline in children with confirmed AVP-D when an acquired hypothalamic–pituitary disorder is possible and particularly in those with PST or other MRI abnormalities, impaired growth, pubertal disturbance, symptoms suggestive of cortisol or thyroid deficiency, or visual abnormalities. Assessment should include growth and IGF-1, free T4, and Thyroid-stimulating hormone, morning cortisol with stimulation testing when indicated, and gonadotropins and sex steroids according to age and pubertal stage. Importantly, anterior pituitary dysfunction may evolve or partially recover over time. In our previous prospective cohort, GHD generally emerged early, whereas thyroid and adrenal deficiencies could develop years after AVP-D onset; conversely, partial recovery of pituitary function was documented in a substantial proportion of patients and was related to the severity of pituitary stalk involvement (). Accordingly, evolving or recovering pituitary function should be interpreted longitudinally together with MRI findings and clinical evolution.

Second-line investigations are reserved for patients with persistent diagnostic uncertainty or progressive clinical, endocrine, or radiological abnormalities. These include CSF β-hCG and AFP, CSF cytology, and whole-body imaging to identify occult LCH or other biopsy-accessible lesions (, ). In selected high-risk patients, whole-body MRI incorporating short tau inversion recovery sequences may detect clinically silent skeletal or extraskeletal disease and identify safer extracranial biopsy sites than the pituitary stalk. Pituitary stalk biopsy remains the definitive diagnostic procedure when noninvasive investigations fail to establish an etiology but should be reserved for carefully selected high-risk patients because of the risk of permanent hypothalamic–pituitary injury (, , , ). Current practice favors a multidisciplinary stepwise approach in which biopsy is considered only after comprehensive endocrine, neuroradiological, oncological, and systemic evaluation, including CSF tumor markers and, when appropriate, whole-body imaging ().

Case 1 illustrates this strategy. Despite progressive PST, evolving multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies, and increasing radiological suspicion of germinoma, serum and CSF β-hCG and AFP remained negative. Histological confirmation was achieved only after transsphenoidal biopsy, demonstrating that negative tumor markers do not exclude a nonsecreting germinoma.

Although etiological investigations proceed in parallel, confirmation of AVP-D, especially the partial forms, may require assessment with water deprivation and desmopressin administration or copeptin-based testing when the clinical and biochemical findings are not diagnostic.

Once AVP-D is suspected, the next objective is to distinguish it from PP and AVP-R. For decades, the water deprivation test has been the cornerstone of this differential diagnosis. During controlled dehydration, patients with complete AVP-D fail to concentrate urine but respond to desmopressin, whereas patients with AVP-R remain unable to concentrate urine despite desmopressin and those with PP recover urinary concentrating ability (, , , ).

Despite its enduring value, the water deprivation test is labor-intensive, requires prolonged supervision, is often poorly tolerated, and performs less well in partial AVP-D and chronic PP. In PP, chronic overhydration reduces the renal medullary concentrating gradient, whereas residual AVP secretion in partial AVP-D may still permit partial urine concentration. Consequently, these disorders overlap considerably, with diagnostic accuracies of only 70% to 77% in partial forms (). These limitations have stimulated the development of copeptin-based diagnostic strategies.

Copeptin, the C-terminal portion of the AVP precursor peptide, is secreted in equimolar amounts with AVP but is considerably more stable ex vivo, allowing reliable laboratory measurement (, ). In adults, basal copeptin concentrations >21.4 pmol/L reliably identify AVP-R, whereas differentiation between AVP-D and PP generally requires stimulation testing (, , , ). Hypertonic saline–stimulated copeptin has been considered the adult reference standard, while arginine-, urea-, and glucagon-stimulated protocols have emerged as potentially simpler alternatives (, , ).

The principal conventional and copeptin-based diagnostic approaches, their proposed thresholds, and the strength of pediatric evidence are summarized in . Pediatric evidence remains limited to relatively small observational studies evaluating basal and stimulated copeptin concentrations () (). Although these studies support the feasibility of copeptin measurement, they do not yet establish robust pediatric diagnostic thresholds. Accordingly, copeptin should currently be regarded as an adjunct, not a replacement, for careful clinical assessment, conventional biochemical evaluation, MRI, and longitudinal surveillance.

Diagnostic tools in polyuria–polydipsia syndrome

Most copeptin, urea, glucagon, oxytocin, and neurophysin I data derive from adult studies. Pediatric use requires caution and should be integrated with clinical and MRI findings.

Abbreviations: AVP, arginine vasopressin; AVP-D, arginine vasopressin deficiency; AVP-R, arginine vasopressin resistance; IV, intravenous; MDMA, 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine; PP, primary polydipsia.

The role of copeptin in the diagnosis of AVP-D in pediatric age

None of the proposed copeptin cutoffs have yet been universally validated in pediatric populations and should not replace careful clinical, biochemical, and MRI assessment.

Abbreviations: AVP-D, arginine vasopressin deficiency; F, female; GHD, growth hormone deficiency; GHRH, growth hormone releasing hormone; LCH, Langerhans cell histiocytosis; M, male; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PPS, polyuria–polydipsia syndrome; PST, pituitary stalk thickening; WDT, water deprivation test.

Neither prolonged water deprivation nor copeptin testing is required in every patient. Following hypothalamic–pituitary surgery, the combination of abrupt hypotonic polyuria, hypernatremia, elevated plasma osmolality, and inappropriately dilute urine is usually sufficient to establish AVP-D and initiate desmopressin without additional testing. Likewise, prolonged water deprivation may be impractical or unsafe in infants and very young children, in whom diagnosis should rely on integration of the clinical presentation, biochemical findings, and MRI.

Importantly, no basal copeptin threshold can currently be recommended to distinguish AVP-D from PP in children. Basal concentrations overlap between these disorders, and the threshold >21.4 pmol/L is primarily useful for identifying AVP-R and is derived predominantly from adult data. In infants and very young children, basal or early-morning copeptin obtained after physiological overnight dehydration may provide supportive information when formal water deprivation is impractical, but should not currently be interpreted using a stand-alone pediatric diagnostic cutoff. In the postoperative setting, particularly after hypothalamic–pituitary surgery, rapidly available copeptin measurements may also provide complementary information on AVP secretory capacity and the evolution of transient, triphasic, or permanent AVP-D. Serial measurements may be especially informative during the postoperative triphasic response, although this application requires prospective pediatric validation and should complement, rather than replace, close monitoring of urine output, plasma sodium and osmolality, and urine concentration.

A practical integration of diagnostic confirmation, etiological investigation, and longitudinal surveillance is summarized in .

Case 3 illustrates this evolving diagnostic approach. AVP-D was supported by both the conventional water deprivation test and arginine-stimulated copeptin testing before MRI demonstrated mild PST. Although arginine-stimulated copeptin remains investigational in children, this case illustrates how conventional and emerging diagnostic tools may be integrated in specialized centers.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and hypothalamic–pituitary region is essential in all children with confirmed or strongly suspected AVP-D because it underpins etiological diagnosis, risk stratification, and surveillance. Magnetic resonance imaging should be interpreted as a dynamic component of the diagnostic process, integrated with clinical findings, endocrine evolution, and serial imaging.

The consensus guideline recommends MRI in all children presenting with AVP-D, PST, or both (). Thin-slice sagittal and coronal T1-weighted sequences should be complemented by high-resolution heavily T2-weighted imaging to optimize pituitary stalk visualization (, ). A pituitary stalk diameter ≥4 mm at the optic chiasm or ≥3 mm at its pituitary insertion is considered abnormal. These thresholds, however, should be regarded as guidance rather than absolute criteria. Based on our experience and long-term follow-up, the entire pituitary stalk should be assessed, including focal or segmental thickening, contour, symmetry, enhancement, and interval evolution. These features may be more informative than maximal diameter alone, and a pituitary stalk below the proposed cutoffs may still be abnormal in the appropriate clinical, endocrine, and radiological context ().

Pituitary stalk measurements should also be interpreted according to the MRI sequence used. Current thresholds were established using contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging. High-resolution heavily T2-weighted sequences such as T2-Driven equilibrium (DRIVE) provide highly reproducible delineation of pituitary stalk morphology without gadolinium; however, absolute measurements obtained with T2-DRIVE are not directly interchangeable with those obtained using contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging. Serial comparisons should therefore preferably use the same acquisition technique ().

Magnetic resonance imaging interpretation extends beyond pituitary stalk measurement. Loss of PPHI supports AVP-D but lacks specificity, as PPHI may be absent in healthy individuals and in PP, whereas some patients with early AVP-D retain a visible PPHI (, , , , , ). Posterior pituitary hyperintensity should therefore be interpreted together with pituitary stalk morphology, anterior pituitary appearance, and the clinical context.

Among MRI abnormalities, PST has the greatest diagnostic and prognostic significance but remains nonspecific. It may occur in germinoma, LCH, hypophysitis, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and other infiltrative disorders. More importantly, PST is dynamic: it may regress, remain stable, or progress. Progressive enlargement raises concern for an evolving neoplastic or infiltrative process, whereas apparently stable PST is not necessarily reassuring early in follow-up, as germinoma and other infiltrative disorders may evolve slowly despite initially unchanged imaging ().

Anterior pituitary morphology provides additional prognostic information. Anterior pituitary enlargement associated with PST and loss of PPHI should raise strong suspicion for neurohypophyseal germinoma or, less commonly, hypophysitis, although similar appearances have rarely been reported in LCH (, , , ). Conversely, progressive anterior pituitary involution suggests chronic hypothalamic–pituitary injury and an increasing risk of anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. Magnetic resonance imaging should therefore always be interpreted together with endocrine evolution, as progressive hormone deficiencies increase the likelihood of an evolving hypothalamic–pituitary disorder even when radiological changes remain subtle.

The mismatch pattern, defined as discordance between pituitary stalk dimensions measured on heavily T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted sequences, has been associated with reduced anterior pituitary size and a higher prevalence of anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies, particularly GHD (). Its appearance was followed by stabilization of pituitary stalk morphology, suggesting that it may reflect evolution toward a chronic, relatively stable fibrotic or postinflammatory lesion rather than active progressive disease. Although not etiologically specific, the mismatch pattern may therefore provide useful prognostic information and contribute to longitudinal risk stratification.

The use of gadolinium should be individualized according to the diagnostic question. Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging is particularly valuable at baseline when a structural, neoplastic, infiltrative, or inflammatory lesion is suspected and during follow-up when new or progressive abnormalities require further characterization. High-resolution heavily T2-weighted sequences such as T2-DRIVE are particularly useful for anatomical assessment of pituitary stalk size and morphology without gadolinium administration. In our previous study, T2-DRIVE provided highly reproducible pituitary stalk measurements and greater interobserver reliability than conventional pre- and postcontrast T1-weighted imaging, while adding <3 minutes to the examination (). It also improved visualization of subtle or residual stalk structures and, in selected patients without an evident sellar or suprasellar mass, provided anatomical information comparable to postcontrast imaging.

These findings support the use of T2-DRIVE for repeated assessment of pituitary stalk morphology during longitudinal surveillance, particularly in clinically and radiologically stable children. This is relevant because cumulative exposure to gadolinium-based contrast agents has raised concerns regarding intracranial gadolinium deposition, particularly in the dentate nucleus and globus pallidus, although its long-term clinical significance remains uncertain (). Accordingly, judicious use of gadolinium is appropriate during prolonged pediatric surveillance. T2-DRIVE should not, however, be considered a universal substitute for contrast-enhanced MRI. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted imaging remains important when enhancement characteristics are required to characterize suspected neoplastic, infiltrative, or inflammatory disease or to investigate radiological progression. The 2 techniques should therefore be regarded as complementary, with surveillance protocols adapted to clinical and radiological risk.

The clinical cases illustrate the value of serial MRI. In case 1, progressive PST and anterior pituitary enlargement preceded histological confirmation of germinoma by more than 2 years despite persistently negative serum and CSF tumor markers. In case 3, mild PST partially regressed and then remained stable, emphasizing that MRI findings should be interpreted longitudinally and alongside endocrine evolution rather than determining management in isolation.

Magnetic resonance imaging surveillance should be individualized according to estimated disease risk (). Risk stratification should integrate imaging findings, endocrine evolution, age, and the likelihood of specific etiologies. Progressive PST, anterior pituitary enlargement, hypothalamic involvement, the mismatch pattern, or evolving anterior pituitary dysfunction warrant closer imaging, repeated tumor marker assessment, systematic evaluation for occult LCH, and multidisciplinary review.

MRI findings and prognostic implications in children with AVP-D

MRI findings should be interpreted longitudinally and in conjunction with endocrine, visual, and clinical data.

Abbreviations: AVP-D, arginine vasopressin deficiency; GHD, growth hormone deficiency; LCH, Langerhans cell histiocytosis; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PPHI, posterior pituitary hyperintensity; PST, pituitary stalk thickening.

Magnetic resonance imaging may also provide insight into disease pathophysiology. In selected patients with AVP-D, absent PPHI, and no PST or other structural abnormalities, contrast-enhanced perfusion MRI, based on temporal changes in posterior pituitary enhancement following intravenous gadolinium administration, has demonstrated reduced posterior pituitary blood flow consistent with dysfunction of the inferior hypophyseal arterial circulation (). This technique remains investigational and is not part of routine AVP-D evaluation or surveillance.

Long-term surveillance is integral to the diagnostic pathway. Because apparently idiopathic AVP-D may represent the earliest manifestation of an evolving hypothalamic–pituitary disorder, follow-up should be active, structured, and individualized according to disease risk. New clinical, endocrine, or radiological findings may ultimately establish the underlying diagnosis.

The consensus guideline recommends surveillance for all children and young people with idiopathic PST, AVP-D, or both, including periodic clinical and endocrine assessment, ophthalmological evaluation when indicated, and serial MRI (). In clinically stable patients, reassessment is recommended every 3 months during the first 6 months, every 6 months for the subsequent 2 to 3 years, and annually thereafter, with intervals adapted to clinical, endocrine, and radiological evolution (, ). Although surveillance intervals may be progressively extended in clinically stable, low-risk patients, discontinuation of routine MRI after several years of persistently normal imaging should not be equated with discharge from follow-up. In selected patients with isolated AVP-D, no PST or other structural abnormality, stable anterior pituitary function, and no visual or systemic warning signs, MRI surveillance may eventually be discontinued according to the consensus framework; however, periodic clinical and endocrine reassessment should continue throughout childhood because late disease evolution has been documented.

Long-term studies support this approach. Di Iorgi et al () showed that systematic surveillance improved etiological classification, with some patients diagnosed years later with LCH or, more rarely, Hodgkin lymphoma. The same study demonstrated that anterior pituitary function is dynamic: hormone deficiencies may emerge years after AVP-D onset, whereas partial recovery of previously impaired axes may also occur. Accordingly, anterior pituitary function should be reassessed according to growth, pubertal progression, clinical symptoms, and MRI evolution, and promptly whenever new clinical or radiological abnormalities emerge (). In selected high-risk patients, whole-body MRI incorporating short tau inversion recovery sequences may identify clinically silent lesions and safer extracranial biopsy targets. When feasible, tissue diagnosis should preferentially be obtained from extracranial lesions rather than the pituitary stalk.

Risk stratification should integrate age, MRI findings, endocrine evolution, and the results of the initial etiological evaluation rather than pituitary stalk size alone. Progressive PST, anterior pituitary enlargement, hypothalamic involvement, the mismatch pattern, visual abnormalities, or evolving anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies warrant closer neuroradiological and endocrine follow-up, repeated serum and CSF tumor marker assessment, systematic investigation for occult LCH, and multidisciplinary reassessment ().

Risk-based diagnostic work-up and follow-up in children with AVP-D, PST, or both

This table adapts the consensus recommendations of Cerbone et al () and the long-term outcome data of Di Iorgi et al (). Surveillance intensity should be individualized according to age, symptoms, stalk size, endocrine evolution, visual findings, and local expertise.

Abbreviations: AFP, α-fetoprotein; AVP-D, arginine vasopressin deficiency; β-hCG, β-human chorionic gonadotropin; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; FDG-PET, fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography; LCH, Langerhans cell histiocytosis; MDT, multidisciplinary team; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PST, pituitary stalk thickening; STIR, short tau inversion recovery.

The clinical cases illustrate how surveillance guides management. In case 1, progressive MRI abnormalities and evolving anterior pituitary deficiencies ultimately led to histological confirmation of germinoma despite persistently negative serum and CSF tumor markers. In case 3, mild PST with negative first- and second-line investigations was managed with structured surveillance rather than immediate pituitary stalk biopsy.

Children and adolescents treated for suprasellar or hypothalamic tumors represent an additional high-risk group. The high prevalence of postoperative hypothalamic–pituitary insufficiency, including permanent AVP-D and cortisol deficiency, supports multidisciplinary perioperative planning, careful postoperative monitoring of fluid balance and electrolytes, and lifelong endocrine follow-up when hypothalamic–pituitary structures have been affected (, ).

Surveillance extends beyond imaging and endocrine testing. Education should begin at diagnosis and continue throughout follow-up. Patients and families should promptly report persistent headache, visual disturbance, impaired growth, pubertal abnormalities, excessive daytime somnolence, bone or back pain, limping, persistent or unexplained cough, progressive dyspnea, skin lesions, or other features suggestive of systemic disease. Recognition of these warning symptoms may facilitate earlier diagnosis of evolving neoplastic, infiltrative, inflammatory, autoimmune, congenital, or genetic disorders.

Long-term care should also address broader unmet needs. An international multidisciplinary consensus identified diagnostic delays, variable access to specialist care, and insufficient patient and family education across the patient journey (). These observations support structured multidisciplinary follow-up and coordinated transition from pediatric to adult endocrine care.

Although AVP-D has traditionally been considered a disorder of water homeostasis, structural lesions of the hypothalamic–posterior pituitary axis may also impair oxytocin secretion. AVP and oxytocin are synthesized by closely related magnocellular neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and transported along their axons through the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary; lesions affecting this system may therefore disrupt both neuropeptide pathways (). Adult studies suggest that some patients with AVP-D may have concomitant oxytocin deficiency, with possible effects on social behavior, emotional processing, anxiety, and quality of life, although these observations have not been validated in children ().

Direct oxytocin measurement is challenging because circulating concentrations are low, secretion is pulsatile, and assay performance is variable. Neurophysin I is generated from the same precursor as oxytocin and is coreleased with it in equimolar amounts but is analytically more stable. It may therefore serve as a surrogate marker of endogenous oxytocin secretion, conceptually analogous to copeptin as a surrogate for AVP (). Recent adult experimental studies demonstrate a close relationship between stimulated neurophysin I and oxytocin responses. However, neither oxytocin nor neurophysin I measurement currently has a role in routine pediatric practice, and prospective pediatric validation is required. Future pediatric studies should determine whether assessment of oxytocin or neurophysin I can improve characterization of hypothalamic–neurohypophyseal dysfunction beyond disturbances of water homeostasis.

Arginine vasopressin deficiency in children and adolescents should be regarded as a dynamic hypothalamic–pituitary disorder rather than a static defect of water homeostasis. Idiopathic AVP-D remains a provisional diagnosis because it may be the earliest manifestation of an evolving condition. Structured clinical, endocrine, and neuroradiological surveillance is therefore integral to diagnosis.

Magnetic resonance imaging remains central to etiological assessment and risk stratification. Interpretation should integrate pituitary stalk morphology, PPHI, anterior pituitary abnormalities, endocrine evolution, and interval radiological changes rather than rely on isolated findings. Education of patients and families is equally important because early recognition of new symptoms may prompt timely reassessment.

The clinical cases illustrate how longitudinal evaluation may establish the diagnosis when the initial work-up is inconclusive. Copeptin-based testing, newer stimulation protocols, and biomarkers such as neurophysin I may refine future diagnostic strategies but remain investigational in children. Ultimately, AVP-D should be viewed not as the end of the diagnostic process but as its beginning.

neuroscience.title: Corneal nerve status as a biomarker for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases: a narrative review
neuroscience.abstract: Corneal nerve status has gained prominence as a potential adjunctive biomarker for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases, as corneal small-fibre abnormalities can be detected in peripheral neuropathy and may precede conventional manifestations in certain conditions. Advances in in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) allow non-invasive, cellular-level assessments of corneal nerve alterations in real-time. Corneal nerve metrics have been associated with disease progression and severity. This review explores the role of corneal nerve status in the evaluation and monitoring of neurodegenerative and neurological diseases or conditions, including diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), Parkinson’s disease (PD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia, multiple sclerosis (MS), schizophrenia, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), migraine, tauopathies, and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP). The strength and maturity of evidence vary substantially between conditions. DPN has the most established evidence base, with replicated cross-sectional and longitudinal studies showing reductions in corneal nerve fibre density, branch density and length, and evidence that corneal nerve loss may precede conventional manifestations of neuropathy. In MS, longitudinal studies demonstrate progressive corneal nerve loss associated with worsening disability. In PD, the extent of corneal nerve fibre loss correlates with severity of motor deterioration, cognitive impairment and development of autonomic dysfunction, although proposed applications in prodromal detection, disease phenotyping, and prognostication remain largely dependent on small, single-centre studies. Studies in MCI and dementia suggest potential diagnostic and prognostic utility, including comparisons with neuroimaging, but are largely derived from overlapping single-centre cohorts. Evidence in CIDP, migraine, ALS, and schizophrenia remains limited or conflicting, while evidence in tauopathies is predominantly pre-clinical. Overall, current literature supports corneal nerve parameters primarily as promising adjunctive rather than established diagnostic, prognostic, treatment-response biomarkers. Direct evidence that IVCM provides incremental diagnostic or prognostic value over established biomarkers remains limited. Furthermore, heterogeneity in confocal platforms, image acquisition, image sampling, and analytical methods must be considered in the interpretation across studies. Standardised acquisition and analysis protocols, prospective multicentre longitudinal studies, appropriate adjustment for confounders, and direct comparison with established biomarkers are necessary before broader clinical translation.
neuroscience.text:
The cornea is a transparent, avascular tissue in the eye that plays a crucial role in vision and has dense innervation and the ability to reflect peripheral nerve changes []. Recent research has suggested the potential value of corneal nerve architecture as a biomarker for various neurodegenerative and neurological diseases. The nerves observed in in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) typically consist of peripheral C and Aδ sensory neurons originating from the trigeminal ganglion []. Corneal neurons have shorter axons and exist in a slightly different tissue environment at their peripheral terminals. However, they seem similarly susceptible to metabolic and toxic insults, making them a promising non-invasive biomarker for detecting sensory peripheral neuropathy [].

Advancements in automated analysis techniques have improved the accuracy and efficiency of IVCM assessments. Fully automated IVCM analysis, such as the ACCMetrics software developed by Dabbah et al., has been instrumental in these findings. Moreover, automated analysis enables rapid image analysis, facilitating scalability for large cohort studies and longitudinal assessments [].

Emerging evidence has supported the use of corneal nerve fibre parameters as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases, including but not limited to diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). Quantitative changes in corneal nerve metrics, evaluated by IVCM, have been associated with disease progression and severity. This review synthesises current research findings and evaluates corneal nerve status as a potential biomarker for various neurodegenerative and neurological diseases. Through a comprehensive analysis of the literature, we aim to underscore the role of corneal nerve fibre assessments in advancing our understanding of neurodegenerative and neurological diseases and potentially improving clinical practice.

This article is a narrative review. To provide an overview of the role of corneal nerve status as a diagnostic and monitoring marker for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases, an electronic literature search of the PubMed database was performed. The PubMed search initially focused on articles published from 2015 to June 2025. Relevant earlier publications and newer papers encountered during revision were also included.

We employed a combination of keywords and medical subject headings (MeSH) to capture a broad yet focused range of relevant studies. The search terms included but were not limited to “corneal nerves” AND “diabetic peripheral neuropathy”, “peripheral neuropathy”, “corneal nerves” AND “neurodegenerative diseases”, “corneal confocal microscopy” AND “Parkinson’s disease”, “corneal nerve fibre” AND “dementia” OR “Alzheimer’s disease”, “corneal neuropathy” AND “multiple sclerosis”, “in vivo confocal microscopy” AND “schizophrenia” OR “amyotrophic lateral sclerosis”, “in vivo confocal microscopy” AND “motor neuron disease”, “corneal sensitivity” AND “migraine”, “tauopathies” AND “corneal nerves”, “chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy” AND “corneal nerves”.

The authors included only articles published in English with full texts available, and restricted the date range to the most recent 10 years (2015–2025) to ensure the inclusion of current and relevant research. The authors also manually reviewed the bibliographies of the selected articles to identify additional pertinent studies that might not have appeared in the initial database search. Both observational and interventional studies that provided qualitative or quantitative data on corneal nerve changes in these conditions were identified. Large language models were used for language editing only; all scientific content was reviewed and verified by the authors.

Consistent with the narrative design of this review, articles were selected by the authors on the basis of relevance to each disease section rather than through a formal screening protocol. No PRISMA framework, duplicate independent screening or standardised risk-of-bias instrument was applied. Studies were instead appraised qualitatively, with attention to study design, sample size, the availability of longitudinal follow-up and whether findings had been replicated by independent groups. These appraisals are presented at the end of each disease section, are compared across conditions in the section comparing the strength of evidence across diseases, and the limitations of this approach are acknowledged under Limitations and Future Directions.

DPN is the most frequent long-term complication of diabetes [], characterised by damage to the peripheral nerves, leading to neuropathic pain, loss of sensation, and in severe cases, limb amputation. The diagnosis and monitoring of DPN pose significant challenges due to the insidious onset and slow progression of the disease []. Recently, IVCM has emerged as a promising non-invasive technique to detect early signs of DPN by examining corneal nerve status. This technique offers unique advantages in the early detection and monitoring of DPN progression and severity [].

The mechanisms underlying corneal nerve changes in DPN are largely driven by hyperglycaemia-induced metabolic and vascular disturbances. Chronic hyperglycaemia leads to the accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and inflammation, causing neuronal damage and loss []. Metabolically, excess glucose shunted through the polyol pathway leads to the accumulation of harmful by-products such as sorbitol and fructose, increasing osmotic and oxidative stress. Additionally, microvascular dysfunction reduces blood supply to nerves, exacerbating ischaemia and nerve degeneration []. Inflammatory mediators further worsen neurodegeneration []. While both diabetic corneal neuropathy (DCN) and DPN share these mechanisms, IVCM provides an imaging modality to directly visualise small-fibre nerve changes in the cornea, which are often the earliest detectable signs of neuropathy, making DCN a valuable adjunctive biomarker for DPN.

On IVCM evaluation, corneal sub-basal nerves appear as well-defined, densely anastomosed, thin and linear structures with homogeneous reflectivity and Y-shaped or H-shaped branches []. IVCM presentations in DPN are characterised by decreased Corneal Nerve Fibre Density (CNFD), Corneal Nerve Fibre Length (CNFL), tortuous nerves, and nerve beading ().

In the early stages of DPN, IVCM can detect subclinical corneal nerve alterations before traditional diagnostics become abnormal: patients with diabetes show reduced CNFD, corneal nerve branch density (CNBD), and CNFL compared to healthy controls, with these deficits preceding both clinical symptoms and nerve conduction changes in DPN [, –]. In a longitudinal rat model of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, animals fed a high-fat diet exhibited significant early reductions in CNFL and corneal sensitivity, even before alterations in intraepidermal nerve fibre density or thermal nociception, thereby corroborating IVCM’s superior sensitivity for detecting subclinical DPN []. Among IVCM parameters, reduced CNFL, particularly within the inferior whorl region, has emerged as the most sensitive early marker of diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy, often preceding overt symptoms by years and outperforming conventional nerve conduction studies in subclinical detection [].

Corneal nerve parameters are reliable and reproducible biomarkers for detecting and staging DPN. Quantitative corneal nerve parameters, including CNFL, CNFD, and CNBD, are significantly reduced in patients with DPN compared to those without [, ]. A meta-analysis that included 13 studies and 1680 participants concluded that corneal nerve parameters were significantly reduced in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM), especially when the DM status was complicated with DPN, implying that corneal nerve morphology assessment is useful for the detection and evaluation of early nerve damage in patients with DM []. CNFL has demonstrated good reproducibility as a potential biomarker of early DPN []. This was corroborated by a longitudinal assessment study examining 396 participants across three groups, which found CNFL was significantly lower in the DPN group versus diabetics without neuropathy (14.0 ± 6.4 mm/mm2 vs. 19.1 ± 5.8 mm/mm2, P < 0.001) [].

Conventional DPN diagnostics, such as nerve conduction studies, demonstrate limited sensitivity for detecting small-fibre pathology. Skin biopsy, the current gold standard for diagnosing small fibre neuropathy, is invasive and hence less appealing as a diagnostic and screening tool []. In contrast, IVCM provides direct visualisation of small unmyelinated C-fibres and Aδ-fibres, which are the first neural structures affected by hyperglycaemia-induced metabolic toxicity. Corneal nerve parameters demonstrate substantial diagnostic utility, with Ahmed et al. reporting area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.88 for CNFL and 0.84 for CNFD for distinguishing participants with diabetes with versus without DPN []. Ferdousi et al. also reported a CNFD AUC of 0.81 []. Moreover, CNFD had a higher diagnostic AUC than intraepidermal nerve fibre density in the same cohort (0.81 versus 0.73) [].

Corneal nerve metrics also provide predictive value for DPN development. A CNFL threshold of <14.9 mm/mm2 predicted diabetic peripheral neuropathy development with a sensitivity of 0.82 and a specificity of 0.69 []. Furthermore, CNFL provided prognostic information up to 6 years before DPN diagnosis, with an optimal cut-off of 14.1 mm/mm2, yielding a sensitivity of 67% and specificity of 71% []. A sustained abnormal CNFL for at least 50% of a 2-year observation period demonstrated superior predictive capacity for incident DPN (AUC: 0.763, p < 0.0001) compared to single measurements, emphasising the value of serial monitoring [].

Corneal nerve parameters correlate closely with DPN severity, providing both functional and structural assessments of disease progression. Functionally, corneal sensitivity decreases significantly with advancing DPN, showing strong correlations with clinical neuropathy scores (r = 0.441, P < 0.001) and quantitative sensory thresholds, including cold, vibration, and warm sensation [, ]. Structurally, CNFD, CNBD, and CNFL progressively decline with increasing DPN severity, as assessed by neuropathy scores and nerve conduction studies (P < 0.001), enabling stratification of patients across mild, moderate, and severe neuropathy stages [, ]. CNFD correlated inversely with the Total Neuropathy Score (ρ = −0.783, P < 0.01) []. Separately, cross-sectional evidence suggests that CCM can detect small-fibre abnormalities at earlier clinical stages of diabetic neuropathy than skin-biopsy-derived intraepidermal nerve fibre assessment, while providing a rapid, non-invasive examination [].

These corneal metrics show significant negative correlations with neuropathic symptom severity scores and pain intensity, with CNFD, CNBD, and CNFL all declining with increasing pain severity on visual analogue scale ratings [].

The progressive corneal nerve changes enable identification of patients at risk for serious DPN complications. CNFD demonstrates high specificity for early-stage small fibre neuropathy (84%), DPN diagnosis (75%), and individuals at risk for foot ulceration (72%), serving as an objective marker for complication stratification []. Furthermore, patients developing diabetic neuroosteoarthropathy show significantly reduced corneal nerve metrics compared to non-diabetic controls, and corneal nerve changes correlate with neuropathic pain severity [, ]. Thus, IVCM assessment of corneal nerve status enables risk stratification across the spectrum of DPN severity and complications, guiding the optimal timing of therapeutic interventions.

Recent advances have harnessed artificial intelligence (AI) to automate and enhance IVCM analysis for DPN detection, addressing limitations of manual quantification, including inter-observer variability and time-intensive processing.

Deep learning algorithms have significantly improved diagnostic performance. A convolutional neural network (CNN)-based algorithm employing data augmentation enabled rapid quantification of multiple nerve parameters, including fibre length, branch points, tail points, nerve segments, and fractal dimensions, without manual intervention. This approach achieved an AUC of 0.83, specificity of 0.87, and sensitivity of 0.68 for DPN diagnosis, outperforming the ACCMetrics tool []. Another CNN trained on IVCM images achieved 96% accuracy in separating healthy controls from diabetics with neuropathy, without the need for manual nerve tracing or parameter extraction []. Advanced ResNet-50 models incorporating Grad-CAM (gradient-weighted class activation mapping) visualisation achieved sensitivity of 0.91, specificity of 0.93, and AUC of 0.95 in patients with Type 1 DM (T1DM), Type 2 DM (T2DM), and prediabetes using IVCM images of the sub-basal nerve plexus, without requiring prior manual quantification of corneal nerve parameters []. In a cross-sectional study of 369 participants, including healthy controls and people with T1DM, T2DM or prediabetes, a CNN classifier was developed to process single corneal images for DPN severity stratification, achieving F1-scores of 0.91 for healthy controls, 0.88 for participants without peripheral neuropathy, and 0.91 for participants with peripheral neuropathy [].

U2Net-based segmentation tools outperformed ACCMetrics in consistency with manual annotation and achieved an AUC of 0.75 for DPN diagnosis, further improving the reliability of automated nerve quantification [].

Transformer-based models represent recent advances. A Swin transformer network outperformed traditional CNNs with an AUC of 0.94 for DPN diagnosis, highlighting the potential of transformer architectures for rapid, accurate screening [], while Vision Transformer models achieved an AUC of 0.99, sensitivity of 98%, and specificity of 92% for DPN diagnosis from IVCM images without manual segmentation []. Hybrid approaches combining deep learning with an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system for DPN diagnosis achieved an AUC of 0.95 with 92% sensitivity and 80% specificity, demonstrating the potential for rapid, automated, and accurate diagnosis [].

A recent deep learning model extracted features directly from corneal images and, when combined with HbA1c, achieved an AUC of 0.94 for predicting diabetic foot risk []. Integration with serum creatinine produced an AUC of 0.93 for identifying high-risk patients with diabetic foot (). Notably, quantitative nerve parameters did not enhance performance compared with raw images, indicating that deep learning can capture diagnostically relevant features without manual extraction. This approach provides a novel screening methodology for diabetic foot risk categories.

Despite the preponderance of data supporting the diagnostic value of using corneal nerve status, not all studies corroborate its reliability as a DPN biomarker. A recent meta-analysis found that standard corneal nerve parameters (CNFL, CNFD and CNBD) do not significantly differ between patients with painful and painless DPN, indicating that these metrics cannot distinguish between pain subtypes and are therefore limited as pain-specific biomarkers in DPN []. Furthermore, a lack of association was found between corneal nerve density and clinical measures of DPN, including neuropathy symptoms and disability scores, nerve conduction studies, and quantitative sensory tests []. These results underscore the need for cautious interpretation of IVCM findings and highlight the importance of developing more accurate quantitative tools and multimodal diagnostic approaches for DPN assessment.

The evidence base in DPN is the strongest of any condition considered in this review. It comprises large cross-sectional cohorts, prospective longitudinal studies with follow-up of two to 6 years, and meta-analytic synthesis. The core findings - reduction of CNFD, CNBD and CNFL in diabetes, and the predictive value of CNFL for incident DPN, have been reproduced by independent groups in different countries. Several caveats nonetheless apply. Most diagnostic accuracy estimates derive from single-centre cohorts analysed with a common software pipeline, few studies report blinded assessment or pre-specified diagnostic thresholds, and the artificial intelligence studies in particular are susceptible to optimistic performance estimates where external validation datasets were not used. Findings relating to the detection and progression of DPN may therefore be regarded as robust, whereas the pain-specific and artificial intelligence-based applications remain exploratory.

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder primarily characterised by motor symptoms such as tremors, bradykinesia, and rigidity. However, non-motor symptoms, including hyposmia, sleep disorders, and autonomic dysfunction, are increasingly recognised as significant contributors to the disease burden and often precede other motor manifestations []. Emerging data indicate that both dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic pathology underlie these non-motor features, with the alpha-synuclein pathology starting in the gastrointestinal autonomic plexus and spreading along the neuronal pathways []. There is also accumulating evidence demonstrating early α-synuclein deposition and small-fibre degeneration within the skin, autonomic nervous system, and enteric plexus [, ]. Given that corneal nerves are predominantly small, unmyelinated sensory fibres, analogous to those affected in cutaneous and autonomic neuropathy, corneal nerve involvement in PD is biologically plausible. This provides a mechanistic rationale for evaluating corneal nerve alterations as an adjunctive biomarker of peripheral small-fibre neurodegeneration in PD. To support this, recent studies have suggested that corneal nerve fibre alterations could serve as a novel biomarker for diagnosing and monitoring PD.

Multiple studies have demonstrated that corneal nerve fibre loss is present in early and even prodromal PD, preceding overt motor symptoms. In a clinical cross-sectional study including 26 patients with newly diagnosed PD and 22 control subjects, these patients presented with significantly reduced CNFD and CNFL as compared to controls. Skin biopsies showed similar epidermal nerve densities between groups, indicating that IVCM is more sensitive for detecting early small fibre neuropathy in PD. The authors thus concluded that corneal nerve metrics provided evidence of pre-clinical peripheral neuropathy in newly diagnosed PD patients, aiding in the early diagnosis and management of PD [].

The deterioration of corneal nerve metrics shows a consistent pattern across the disease spectrum, from healthy individuals to prodromal and manifest PD. A cross-sectional study demonstrated that CNFD and CNFL values declined progressively from healthy controls through prodromal PD to manifest PD, supporting their application as early screening markers for PD [].

In a systematic review of IVCM and its applications in PD assessment, Che and Yang comprehensively analysed findings from multiple IVCM studies and consistently identified significantly reduced CNFD in PD patients relative to healthy controls []. Notably, the magnitude of corneal nerve fibre loss showed progressive worsening with advancing disease severity. The authors concluded that IVCM might serve as a supplementary tool for assessing PD progression. Through highlighting the sensitivity of IVCM in detecting early nerve fibre alterations, they proposed its use as a diagnostic tool for PD-related neuropathy.

Research has demonstrated a link between corneal nerve fibre loss and cognitive impairment in patients with PD. A study by Che et al. demonstrated that patients with PD exhibited significant corneal nerve fibre loss compared to controls, with CNFD positively correlating with cognitive performance as assessed by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, indicating that corneal nerve fibre loss is associated with the severity of cognitive dysfunction [].

Another study observed a marked reduction in corneal sub-basal nerve plexus density in PD patients compared to healthy controls, and this reduction was significantly correlated with cognitive impairment as measured by the Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination-Revised score []. This was the first study to directly demonstrate an association between corneal nerve loss and cognitive dysfunction in PD, supporting the involvement of the peripheral nervous system in what was previously considered a purely central nervous system disorder.

Autonomic dysfunction is a common non-motor symptom in PD, often complicating the clinical picture. Identifying autonomic involvement early, especially before overt symptoms arise, is crucial for guiding tailored interventions.

Evidence shows that IVCM can distinguish PD patients with autonomic involvement from those without. Corneal nerve parameters, including CNFD, CNBD, CNFL, and the CNBD/CNFD ratio, were all significantly lower in PD patients exhibiting autonomic dysfunction compared to those without. These findings suggest that IVCM offers a non-invasive method for stratifying PD patients based on autonomic nervous system involvement [].

In support of this, another study demonstrated that CNFD was reduced in PD compared to controls, while CNBD and CNFL were closely correlated with both autonomic symptoms and parasympathetic dysfunction. These findings reinforce the utility of IVCM in identifying autonomic involvement in PD, as the technique’s parameters were not influenced by disease duration or levodopa dose, but rather by the presence of autonomic symptoms. This supports a pathophysiological link between small fibre degeneration and impaired autonomic regulation in PD [].

CNFD has shown promise as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression in PD. Lim et al. conducted a prospective study evaluating the association between baseline CNFD and motor decline over 12 months in PD []. Using the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale as an outcome measure, they found that patients in the lowest quartile of CNFD at baseline experienced a significantly greater worsening in motor scores compared to those in the highest quartile. These findings suggest that reduced CNFD predicts faster motor deterioration, underscoring its potential utility in identifying PD patients at risk for more rapid functional decline.

Recent investigations have demonstrated significant correlations between corneal nerve parameters and the severity of motor symptoms in PD. Notably, lower CNFD and CNFL were correlated with higher motor symptom scores, indicating that as motor impairment becomes more severe, corneal nerve loss increases [].

Additionally, IVCM has demonstrated potential in phenotyping motor subtypes within PD. Che et al. reported that patients with the postural instability and gait disturbance subtype exhibited greater corneal nerve fibre loss than those with the tremor-dominant (TD) subtype []. Logistic regression analysis revealed that higher CNFD and CNFL were significantly associated with the TD phenotype (OR = 1.265 and OR = 1.706, respectively). Furthermore, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated excellent discrimination between tremor-dominant and PIGD subtypes using combined corneal nerve metrics (AUC = 0.832), indicating IVCM’s broader applicability in PD phenotyping beyond autonomic classification.

Consistent with these findings, Che and Yang also demonstrated that decreased CNFD correlated with more pronounced motor symptoms, reinforcing the role of corneal nerve status as a marker of disease progression in PD [].

Multiple system atrophy (MSA) and PD share several clinical features, making differential diagnosis challenging. Niu et al. explored the use of IVCM in distinguishing MSA from PD. Results showed that both CNFD and CNFL were significantly lower in MSA patients compared to PD patients. In the combined MSA + PD group, CNFD was negatively correlated with the Orthostatic Grading Scale. In the MSA group alone, CNFD was significantly negatively correlated with both unified multiple system atrophy rating scale (UMSARS) I and II, and regression analysis confirmed that both CNFD and CNFL were inversely associated with MSA severity, demonstrating a statistically significant relationship between corneal nerve fibre loss and disease severity. ROC analysis showed that the algorithm utilising CNFL achieved an AUC of 0.72 with 73.3% sensitivity and 73.0% specificity for distinguishing MSA from PD after adjusting for age, gender, and disease duration. The algorithm combining CNFD, CNBD, and CNFL produced a similar AUC of 0.72. Although the overall discriminatory power was modest, the greater corneal nerve fibre loss in MSA indicates that IVCM can detect a quantitatively distinct pattern of peripheral denervation. When integrated with clinical and paraclinical evaluations, IVCM may provide a useful non-invasive biomarker to aid differential diagnosis in cases where MSA and PD present with overlapping features [].

Moreover, Lim et al. found significantly lower CNFD, CNBD and CNFL in both PD and MSA than in healthy controls []. These comparisons with controls do not establish a direct difference between MSA and PD.

The PD literature consists predominantly of small to moderate cross-sectional and case-control studies, with a single prospective study of motor progression over 12 months. The reduction of CNFD and CNFL in PD relative to controls has been reproduced by several independent groups and may be considered reasonably established. In contrast, the applications of greatest clinical interest - detection in the prodromal phase, motor subtype phenotyping, prediction of motor progression, and discrimination of MSA from PD - each rest on one or two single-centre studies, show only modest discriminatory performance, and have not been validated in multicentre cohorts. These findings should therefore be interpreted as promising but in the preliminary stage.

Dementia and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent a continuum of neurodegenerative disorders characterised by progressive cognitive and functional decline, with the most common subtype being Alzheimer’s disease (AD). MCI represents a stage at which cognitive decline exceeds normal ageing but does not yet meet the criteria to diagnose dementia []. MCI may be a precursor to dementia, and brain changes underlying AD occur at least 20 years prior to the onset of symptoms, providing an optimal window for early diagnosis and effective interventions []. Early diagnosis and intervention have emerged as one of the key components of the national dementia strategy in certain European countries []. Currently, well-established biomarkers for dementia due to AD are visualisation of beta-amyloid (Aβ) and tau deposition in cerebrospinal fluid studies and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or radionuclide imaging to assess the degree of atrophy, hypometabolism, or hypoperfusion []. IVCM is now gaining prominence in the context of neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia.

The medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA) scoring has been a well-established biomarker for dementia due to its ease of application in clinical practice [], together with its ability to differentiate between AD and healthy controls and predict the progression of MCI to AD []. However, its diagnostic relevance to MCI is still indeterminate and conflicting [].

In recent times, several studies have shown that there is an association between corneal nerve measures and cognitive impairment. In a comparison between IVCM and the widely used MTA scoring, the diagnostic accuracy of corneal nerve measures was reported to be non-inferior to MTA scoring for dementia, and higher than MTA scoring in MCI, with a higher sensitivity (81% versus 70%) and specificity (81% versus 75%) []. Between IVCM and brain volumetry, IVCM also had a higher diagnostic capability in identifying MCI compared to brain volumetry within the studied cohort [].

In a study conducted by Ponirakis et al. that focused on the predictive value of IVCM parameters versus brain volumetry for progression from MCI to dementia, MCI patients who progressed to dementia had both significantly lower IVCM parameters, including CNFD, CNBD, CNFL, and lower hippocampal volume compared to those who did not []. IVCM parameters were significantly associated with cognitive function and functional independence in both MCI and dementia in a similar study [].

Additionally, further evidence from Gundogan et al. showed significantly lower CNFL, CNFD, and CNBD in AD patients compared to healthy controls. Corneal sensitivity, the clinical functionality of corneal nerve metrics, was also significantly lower in AD patients compared to healthy controls, in conjunction with the aforementioned IVCM parameters [].

Existing studies provide preliminary evidence that IVCM parameters may represent a non-invasive biomarker of neurodegeneration and could potentially complement established cognitive and neuroimaging assessments. However, available evidence remains largely derived from single-centre cohorts with substantial overlap in investigators, limiting independent validation and generalisability of the reported diagnostic and prognostic performance.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, particularly affecting young women []. It commonly involves the optic nerves, brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord. Axonal loss occurs early in the disease course and is a major determinant of progressive neurological disability, highlighting the need for biomarkers that facilitate early diagnosis and treatment [].

MRI is an important imaging endpoint in MS clinical trials and is used to assess disease activity and progression []. Retinal nerve fibre layer thickness measured by optical coherence tomography has also been investigated as a marker of neuroaxonal damage [], although its correlation with clinical disability remains limited. IVCM may provide an additional means of quantifying corneal axonal loss and assessing disease severity.

In a study of 26 patients with MS and 23 healthy controls, total corneal nerve fibre density was reduced in MS [80]. In a separate study, CNFD, CNBD and CNFL were reduced in MS, and CNFD was inversely associated with the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) and Multiple Sclerosis Severity Score (MSSS) []. In another study comparing clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting MS, secondary progressive MS, and healthy controls, CNFD, CNFL, and corneal nerve fractal dimension (CNFrD) were significantly reduced across MS disease courses [].

Among IVCM parameters, CNBD showed the highest discriminative performance between healthy controls and patients with relapsing-remitting MS, while CNFD showed the highest discriminative performance between healthy controls and secondary progressive MS [].

Serial IVCM may detect changes associated with disability progression. In a 2-year prospective cohort of patients with relapsing-remitting MS, corneal nerve fibre area (CNFA) and corneal nerve fibre width (CNFW) decreased significantly as expanded disability status scale increased. Changes in CNFD and CNFL also correlated with changes in expanded disability status scale and multiple sclerosis severity score [].

Similarly, Petropoulos et al. followed patients with relapsing-remitting MS, secondary progressive MS, and healthy controls over 2 years. CNFD, CNBD, and CNFL decreased significantly in relapsing-remitting MS, while CNFD and CNBD decreased significantly in secondary progressive MS [].

These findings suggest that corneal nerve abnormalities are detectable across MS disease courses and may change with disability progression, supporting further evaluation of IVCM as a complementary imaging biomarker.

The MS literature includes two prospective cohort studies and several cross-sectional studies, giving it one of the stronger evidence bases for IVCM after DPN. Longitudinal studies demonstrate progressive corneal nerve loss over 2 years in association with worsening disability, suggesting that IVCM may reflect dynamic neuroaxonal change.

However, the longitudinal cohorts remain relatively small with limited follow-up. Whether IVCM provides additional information beyond MRI or retinal nerve fibre layer assessment by optical coherence tomography has not been formally established. Its diagnostic, prognostic, and disease-monitoring roles therefore remain investigational, and larger prospective multicentre studies comparing IVCM with established MS biomarkers are required before routine clinical use.

Schizophrenia is a chronic, debilitating psychiatric condition characterised by positive, negative and cognitive symptoms most commonly attributable to genetic susceptibility and environmental influences []. While no objective diagnostic markers are available at present, well-accepted diagnostic criteria in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, are commonly used []. This reliance on clinical assessment may limit diagnostic accuracy. Changes in ocular physiology, including corneal nerve alterations, are therefore being investigated as potential biomarkers [].

In a cross-sectional study involving 62 subjects, there were significant reductions in CNFD, CNFL, CNBD and the CNBD:CNFD ratio in patients with schizophrenia compared with healthy controls []. The ratio is CNBD:CNFD MRI brain volumetry also showed a significant decrease in cingulate gyrus volume in schizophrenia patients. The area under the ROC curve for distinguishing schizophrenia from healthy controls was 88% for CNFL, 84% for CNBD, 79% for CNFD and 73% for cingulate gyrus volume.

Neither IVCM parameters nor cingulate gyrus volume correlated with symptom severity or cognitive dysfunction []. Structural MRI findings may also be confounded by treatment-related factors such as antipsychotic-associated brain volume changes [], and have limited correlations with clinical outcomes other than cognitive impairment [], with no established diagnostic or prognostic role in psychosis []. Although IVCM showed greater discriminative accuracy than cingulate gyrus volumetry in a single study, further validation is required before its diagnostic utility can be established.

The evidence synthesised in this review regarding schizophrenia is confined to a single cross-sectional study of 62 participants. Although the reported discriminative performance was high, possible confounding factors including dry eye, antipsychotic exposure and metabolic syndrome were not formally assessed or adjusted for. Current limited evidence should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence of diagnostic utility.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting upper and lower motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness, bulbar dysfunction and, in advanced disease, respiratory failure []. Diagnosis remains largely clinical and is supported by electrodiagnostic findings, due to clinical heterogeneity and the lack of reliable objective biomarkers []. CSF, biochemical and neurophysiological tests may support diagnosis, but none are sufficiently robust to serve as the primary outcome measure in clinical trials []. Although traditionally considered a motor disease, ALS is increasingly recognised to involve subclinical C-fibre sensory dysfunction [], providing a rationale for IVCM assessment of corneal nerve degeneration.

In a cross-sectional study of ALS patients and healthy controls [] conducted to assess corneal nerve parameters and dendritic cell densities, CNFL was significantly lower, while corneal dendritic cell densities were significantly higher in patients with ALS than in controls. In addition, inferior whorl corneal length was significantly associated with disease severity and progression in ALS. Patients with bulbar involvement also showed significantly lower inferior whorl corneal length and higher inferior whorl dendritic cell density compared to patients without bulbar involvement. In a study of a similar design, there was a significant reduction in total corneal nerve length (CNL) and an increase in nerve tortuosity in ALS patients compared to healthy controls. Importantly, there was a significant correlation between CNL and the ALS functional rating scale bulbar subscore as well as the ALS severity score bulbar subscore [], which are commonly used clinical measures to quantify the degree of bulbar dysfunction through assessments of speech and swallowing. Use CNL for total corneal nerve length and for the bulbar-score correlations. In contrast, Turhan et al. found significantly higher corneal dendritic cell density in ALS patients than healthy controls, but no significant differences in CNFD, CNFL or CNBD [].

Overall, the three small cross-sectional studies in this review demonstrate discordant results: two reported corneal nerve loss, while one found no difference in IVCM parameters apart from dendritic cell density. No longitudinal data are available, and no study has examined whether IVCM parameters can predict functional decline. The evidence is therefore best described as conflicting and preliminary.

Migraine is a common, chronic neurological disorder characterised by recurrent disabling attacks of headache, and continues to be one of the world’s leading causes of disability [] and poor quality of life. The aetiology of migraine is not well understood at present, but is believed to be due to a constellation of genetic, environmental, and neurological factors. Currently, the diagnosis of migraine is largely clinical, and is based on a comprehensive history and clinical examination []. The lack of objective biomarkers, together with the clinical heterogeneity of migraine, poses significant challenges to the development of effective and individualised management. The cornea receives its sensory supply from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. The close association between the trigeminal nerve and the pathogenesis of migraine underscores the potential value of corneal nerve neuropathic changes as objective biomarkers for migraine diagnosis, disease progression, and treatment response [].

Corneal nerve alterations have been reported in migraine, with Kinard et al. finding significantly lower CNFD in patients with chronic migraine than in healthy controls []. This is further corroborated by a study by Guldiken et al. who also demonstrated a significant decrease in CNFD, CNBD, and CNFL in patients with migraine compared to healthy controls, regardless of variables such as number of headache days or the presence of dry eyes. There was no significant difference in IVCM parameters for various migraine durations, number of headache days over the recent three months or pain intensity []. The significant corneal neuropathic changes reported in the above studies are consistent with the trigeminovascular hypothesis [] in the pathogenesis of migraines, and suggest that corneal nerve parameters merit further evaluation as candidate biomarkers in migraine.

Two cross-sectional studies form the basis of this section. Both report reductions in corneal nerve parameters relative to controls, but neither demonstrated a consistent relationship with headache frequency, migraine duration or pain intensity. Dry eye disease, which is more prevalent among patients with migraine and independently reduces corneal nerve metrics, was not consistently accounted for. Current evidence therefore supports an association between migraine and corneal nerve alterations rather than an established biomarker role.

Tauopathies are chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterised by abnormal tau deposition in the central nervous system []. Tau aggregates form neuropathological inclusions within neurons, causing neuronal death []. Clinical manifestations include movement, cognitive and behavioural disorders with substantial heterogeneity []. Diagnosis is confirmed by neuropathological assessment at autopsy, except in inherited autosomal dominant tauopathies or clinically defined syndromes such as progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) [].

As substantial neuronal damage often precedes overt symptoms and approximately one-third of disease-modifying therapies in development target tau aggregation or synthesis [], early detection of tauopathies is increasingly important []. Peripheral tissues may provide accessible biomarkers. Skin has emerged as a minimally invasive marker of neurodegeneration because of its bidirectional interaction with the central nervous system through the skin-brain axis []. Vacchi et al. demonstrated tau immunoreactivity along somatosensory and autonomic cutaneous nerve fibres in patients with degenerative tauopathies []. Given the similar embryological origins of skin and corneal fibres, corneal nerve degeneration has also been investigated in tauopathies.

Experimental studies have demonstrated corneal nerve abnormalities in tauopathy models. In an animal study comparing mouse models of tauopathy (P301L) and wild type [], CNFL and CNFD were significantly decreased compared with wild-type mice, while corneal regeneration after injury was significantly impaired []. In another murine model, mice overexpressing human non-mutated tau showed significantly decreased stromal corneal nerve occupancy at 4 months, with no change in sub-basal plexus nerve occupancy compared with wild-type mice. Htau mice experienced corneal nerve degeneration before any memory deficit or learning impairment was apparent [].

Evidence supporting IVCM as a biomarker for tauopathies remains predominantly pre-clinical. Experimental studies demonstrate corneal nerve degeneration and impaired regeneration, with some abnormalities preceding neurological deficits, suggesting potential sensitivity to early tau-associated neurodegeneration. However, human evidence remains extremely limited. Although corneal nerve abnormalities have been reported in small cohorts including patients with PSP [], there is insufficient evidence that these changes are specific to tau pathology or correlate directly with tau burden. Longitudinal human studies incorporating tau-PET, CSF or plasma phosphorylated tau are needed to determine whether IVCM can distinguish tauopathies from other neurodegenerative disorders and detect pre-clinical disease.

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) is a chronic, progressive immune-mediated neuropathy affecting peripheral nerves and nerve roots. The disease course is generally slow and progressive, but approximately one-third of patients with CIDP may experience a relapsing-remitting course []. CIDP can manifest as different clinical forms. The classical presentation is characterised by both proximal and distal symmetrical weakness with sensory loss predominantly affecting proprioception and vibration sense [].

Diagnosis and treatment of CIDP remain challenging because reliable disease biomarkers are lacking, limiting patient stratification and individualised treatment. Although disease activity can be assessed using established severity scores, objective measures remain limited []. Early axonal loss has been associated with clinical outcomes and shown to predict long-term disability and muscle strength [, ]. Given this association, corneal nerve assessment may provide an objective measure of axonal loss in CIDP ().

In a prospective cohort of 17 patients, IVCM was used to assess corneal nerve degeneration and immune cell infiltration over 18 months []. Baseline total cell infiltrates >30/mm2 demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for predicting clinical progression over 18 months. However, total cell infiltrates did not change subsequently in either progressive or stable CIDP, raising uncertainty about their ability to monitor treatment response. Corneal parameters also did not correlate with disease duration or severity.

Among the studies included in this review, the evidence in CIDP consists of a single prospective cohort of 17 patients. A limited sample size renders the reported sensitivity and specificity of 100% for predicting clinical progression statistically fragile. The absence of correlations between corneal parameters and disease duration or severity is difficult to reconcile with a straightforward biomarker interpretation. Replication in substantially larger cohorts is required before clinical inference can be drawn.

The quantity and quality of evidence supporting corneal nerve status as a biomarker vary substantially across the conditions reviewed. Amongst all conditions reviewed, DPN has the broadest and most independently replicated evidence base. Multiple independent groups have reported concordant findings in large cohorts. Prospective longitudinal follow-up extends up to 6 years and predictive thresholds for incident neuropathy have been proposed and tested. MS is also supported by two prospective cohorts with 2-year follow-up, which demonstrate that corneal nerve loss parallels disability progression. However, the longitudinal evidence base remains relatively small and includes overlapping investigators, limiting the extent of fully independent replication. In PD, the core cross-sectional observation of corneal nerve loss is well replicated, but evaluation of clinically important applications such as prognostication and phenotyping still largely rests on single-centre studies. Evidence in dementia and MCI mostly originates from one research group, with only one independent Alzheimer’s disease cohort, although findings are internally consistent. CIDP, migraine, ALS, schizophrenia and tauopathies are each supported by one to three small studies, with conflicting results in ALS and predominantly pre-clinical data in tauopathies; the evidence in these conditions should be regarded as exploratory.

summarises the evidence according to the number and design of included publications, the largest study sample, availability and duration of longitudinal follow-up, and evidence of independent replication or multicentre validation.

Comparison of the evidence base for corneal nerve status as a biomarker across neurodegenerative and neurological conditions.

Abbreviations: AUC, area under the curve; CNBD, corneal nerve branch density; CNFD, corneal nerve fibre density; CNFL, corneal nerve fibre length; IVCM, in vivo confocal microscopy; DPN, diabetic peripheral neuropathy; MS, multiple sclerosis; PD, Parkinson’s disease; MCI, mild cognitive impairment; CIDP, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy; ALS, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

summarises the maturity of the evidence base according to publication number and study design, number and independence of participant cohorts, largest sample size, availability of longitudinal follow-up, and independent or multicentre replication. A formal evidence grade was not assigned because this narrative review did not apply a validated risk-of-bias or evidence-certainty framework. Publication number should not be interpreted as equivalent to the number of independent patient populations.

Independent cohort was defined as a distinct participant population. Publications reporting follow-up, extension, secondary analyses or clearly overlapping recruitment programmes were grouped as a single cohort family. Pooled multicentre studies were evaluated according to their contributing cohort sources where these could be identified.
