Reviews and meta-analyses were included in publication counts but were not counted as independent cohorts. Pre-clinical studies were considered separately from human cohorts. Where participant-level overlap could not be determined confidently from the published reports, the minimum number of clearly distinguishable independent cohorts (≥n) is reported.

A related and largely unanswered question is whether IVCM parameters provide incremental value over existing biomarkers. Direct comparisons are available in only a small number of contexts. In DPN, CNFD had a higher AUC than intraepidermal nerve fibre density obtained by skin biopsy within the same cohort (0.81 versus 0.73) [], and IVCM detects abnormality earlier than nerve conduction studies []. In MCI, IVCM parameters showed higher diagnostic AUCs than medial temporal lobe atrophy scoring and brain volumetry within the studied cohorts, whereas performance in dementia was broadly comparable; one MCI cohort also reported higher apparent prognostic accuracy for progression to dementia than brain volumetry [–]. In schizophrenia, the single available study reported a higher AUC for CNFL than for cingulate gyrus volume on magnetic resonance imaging within the same cohort, although neither measure correlated with symptom severity []. In MS, corneal nerve measures and retinal nerve fibre layer thickness have been compared using ROC analyses in the same cohort [], but incremental clinical value over established imaging remains unproven; and in PD no comparison has been made with dopamine transporter imaging or with skin biopsy for phosphorylated α-synuclein. In CIDP, a single 17-patient cohort reported 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for baseline corneal immune-cell infiltration greater than 30/mm2, compared with 80% sensitivity and 88% specificity for nerve ultrasound, but this has not been externally validated []. Demonstrating incremental value over existing modalities, rather than simply a difference from healthy controls, is the principal evidential gap facing the field.

shows an overview of direct comparisons between IVCM and existing biomarkers across diseases.

Direct comparisons between IVCM and existing biomarkers across diseases.

Abbreviations: AUC, area under the curve; BUS, bochum ultrasound score; CCM, corneal confocal microscopy; CIDP, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy; CNFD, corneal nerve fibre density; DPN, diabetic peripheral neuropathy; IENFD, intraepidermal nerve fibre density; IVCM, in vivo confocal microscopy; MCI, mild cognitive impairment; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; MS, multiple sclerosis; OCT, optical coherence tomography; PD, Parkinson’s disease.

This article is a narrative rather than a systematic review. Studies were identified through a single database and were selected on the basis of relevance rather than by duplicate independent screening; no formal risk-of-bias instrument was applied; and the appraisals of evidence strength presented at the end of each disease section represent the qualitative judgement of the authors. Publication bias is likely to favour positive findings, particularly in the smaller literatures such as schizophrenia, migraine and CIDP where few studies exist. In addition, several disease areas are dominated by a small number of research groups, so that apparent consistency of findings may in part reflect shared methodology rather than biological reproducibility.

A further limitation lies in the current evidence base for tauopathies, where current data are predominantly derived from animal models, with very limited human evidence. Although pre-clinical models provide valuable insight into the mechanisms of tau-related neurodegeneration, they may not fully reflect the complexity of human disease. Human data presently available are limited, and the clinical relevance of corneal nerve findings in tauopathies therefore largely remains unestablished. This limitation should be borne in mind when interpreting the section on tauopathies.

Ageing, ocular surface inflammation, dry eye disease, DM without neurological involvement, contact lens wear and prior ocular surgery may confound corneal nerve measurements. Ageing is associated with reduced corneal nerve fibre density and length [], while ocular surface inflammation and dry eye disease alter corneal nerve morphology. Neuropathic corneal pain, which may be confused with dry eye disease, is associated with corneal microneuromas that could be mistaken for disease-related neurodegeneration [].

DM may alter corneal nerve parameters before neuropathy is clinically apparent. In 37 individuals with impaired glucose tolerance compared with 20 healthy controls, CNFD, CNBD and CNFL were all significantly reduced, and 40.5% had CNFD below a neuropathy-consistent threshold despite no clinical diabetes or peripheral neuropathy []. Diabetic corneal neuropathy also correlates with diabetic peripheral neuropathy severity [] and independently predicts diabetic foot risk, with corneal changes preceding clinical foot complications [, ]. Keratorefractive surgery [, ], cataract surgery [] and orthokeratology contact lens wear may also induce corneal denervation and alter the normal architecture of the sub-basal nerve plexus [].

Methodological heterogeneity across studies may affect the comparability and reproducibility of corneal nerve measurements. Different confocal microscopy platforms, such as the Nidek ConfoScan 4 and the Tandem Scanning confocal microscope, differ in resolution, field of view, and image acquisition characteristics, and have been shown to yield subbasal nerve density estimates that differ by two-to three-fold for the same tissue []. Laser scanning platforms, such as the Heidelberg Retina Tomograph II, provide high-resolution imaging of the corneal subbasal nerve plexus and may detect smaller-calibre nerve fibres []. Acquisition protocols also contribute to variability between studies. The number of images sampled per cornea affects measurement accuracy, with as many as eight non-overlapping central images required to bring nerve branch density estimates within 30% of the true mean [], while the precise location of images sampled within the central cornea can independently produce significant differences in nerve parameter values, reflecting the heterogeneous, whorl-centred distribution of the subbasal nerve plexus []. In addition, manual and automated (or semi-automated) analysis software packages, such as CCMetrics and ACCMetrics, do not produce equivalent results. Automated analysis has been shown to systematically underestimate corneal nerve fibre length relative to manual tracing, despite preserving good reproducibility [], and automated analysis has shown a non-significant tendency to underestimate corneal nerve measurements relative to manual tracing following refractive surgery-induced corneal reinnervation, attributed to thin, short regenerating fibres being more readily missed by automated software [].

Future research should prioritise the development of consensus-based, standardised protocols for image acquisition, sampling, parameter definition, and analysis. Moreover, studies should also report the confocal platform, image acquisition protocol, and analysis software used, adopt a fixed and consistent image-selection strategy, and, where possible, validate findings using more than one analysis method, so that results can be compared reliably across the field. Larger prospective multicentre cohorts with longitudinal follow-up should subsequently apply these standardised methods to establish robust normative reference ranges, validate diagnostic and prognostic thresholds, and assess the value of IVCM parameters over existing biomarkers. Further refinement of IVCM image acquisition may additionally improve the precision and representativeness of corneal nerve measurements. Integration of validated automated or artificial intelligence-based analysis may facilitate reproducible assessment across centres. As corneal nerve imaging becomes more widely applied as a biomarker for neurodegenerative and neurological disease, future studies should screen for and document ocular and systemic factors, such as ageing, ocular surface inflammation, dry eye disease, DM without neurological involvement, contact lens wear, and prior ocular surgery and either exclude affected individuals or statistically adjust for these variables, so that observed corneal nerve changes can be attributed to the disease under investigation.

Collectively, these developments will be critical for establishing corneal nerve status not only as a diagnostic adjunct, but also as a reliable and generalisable adjunctive biomarker in future studies of neurodegenerative and neurological diseases.

IVCM has emerged as a promising non-invasive approach for evaluating corneal nerve alterations across a broad spectrum of neurodegenerative and neurological diseases. Based on the available literature, reductions in corneal nerve fibre density, length, and branching have been associated with disease presence, severity, progression, and, in selected conditions, future clinical deterioration. However, the strength of this evidence is highly disease-dependent. The most robust support currently exists in diabetic peripheral neuropathy and multiple sclerosis, where findings have been reproduced across independent cohorts and supported by longitudinal data. In Parkinson’s disease and dementia, corneal nerve alterations are consistently reported and show potential diagnostic and prognostic value, although several clinically important applications remain dependent on small, single-centre cohorts and require external validation. Evidence in ALS, migraine, schizophrenia, CIDP, and tauopathies remains comparatively limited, conflicting, or predominantly pre-clinical and should therefore be considered exploratory.

Although IVCM shows promise as a non-invasive biomarker, future large-scale, multicentre longitudinal studies using standardised imaging and analysis protocols, with appropriate adjustment for confounders are needed. Advances in wide-field imaging, automation, and artificial intelligence may further improve reproducibility and scalability [], supporting the potential integration of IVCM into the diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of neurological diseases.

neuroscience.title: Implantable sensors in modern healthcare: advances, clinical applications, and future directions
neuroscience.abstract: Implantable sensors are emerging as powerful tools for continuous, real-time monitoring of physiological and biochemical parameters, thus facilitating improved disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and personalized healthcare. Recent advances in microelectronics, materials science, and wireless technologies have accelerated the development of miniaturized implantable devices with enhanced sensitivity, biocompatibility, and long-term operational stability. This review outlines the fundamental principles and major categories of implantable sensors, including biochemical, electrophysiological, pressure, and temperature sensing systems. Particular attention is given to material selection, biointerface engineering, wireless communication, data processing, and integration with biological environments. Current applications in chronic disease management, cardiovascular monitoring, neuroengineering, and precision medicine are highlighted alongside key challenges related to biofouling, immune responses, power supply, device reliability, and data security. Ethical, regulatory, and clinical translation considerations are also examined. Finally, emerging trends in smart materials, self-powered platforms, and intelligent implantable systems are discussed, emphasizing their potential to advance next-generation healthcare technologies.
neuroscience.text:
Implantable sensors allow early detection of complications, such as infection, loosening of the implant and other adverse events related to the implanted devices and surrounding tissues. Such complications may result in implant failure and require secondary surgical intervention, thus increasing the risks to the patient. Early detection allows for timely intervention and better clinical outcomes. Conventional monitoring of implants typically depends on imaging and laboratory-based evaluations, but these methods are usually not continuous and do not necessarily provide direct information of local physiological changes. These limitations have resulted in the development of in vivo sensing technologies that can monitor continuously.

Certain biological or physiological alterations can be sensed by implantable sensors and changed into electric signals or other measurable outputs. In implantable systems, sensing elements are combined with signal-processing, power, and communication components in compact, biocompatible devices designed to operate in the body.  shows the general architecture of implantable sensor systems with emphasis on the main sensing components, device structure and electronic element integration.  illustrates the general sensing workflow.  illustrates the implanted sensor and its external unit. The structure of the sensor is shown in , and the wireless power and data transmission routes for remote monitoring and data acquisition are shown in .

These sensors can be incorporated into “smart implants” that have diagnostic and therapeutic functions to support multifunctional biomedical applications. However, malfunction or failure of the sensing component can compromise the monitoring capability of the implantable system and reliable operation of the sensor remains critical. Thus, the development of implantable sensors calls for careful consideration of sensing performance, biocompatibility, stability, power requirements and data transmission. Recent advances in miniaturization, materials science, and low power electronics have made it possible to develop implantable sensors to monitor a broad spectrum of physiological and biochemical parameters within the human body including glucose, metabolites, inflammatory biomarkers, pressure, temperature, and electrophysiological signals. In certain applications, these systems can offer localized measurements with high temporal resolution and continuous tracking that is difficult to achieve with conventional periodic assessments. Thus, implantable sensing has received growing interest in the fields of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, epilepsy, inflammatory disorders, and cancer.

Notwithstanding these advances, several technical and clinical challenges remain that hinder broad acceptance of implantable sensors. Among these are sensor calibration and long-term stability, power consumption, heat generation, biofouling and biological responses, wireless communication, data security, and regulatory requirements. Furthermore, the reliable analytical performance during long-term implantation is still challenging because of the complex and dynamic biological environment that the sensors are exposed to.

The review provides an integrated assessment of implantable sensors and the challenges impacting their adoption and clinical translation. Unlike past reviews which have mostly concentrated on specific sensor types, materials or individual technologies, the current review encompasses sensing mechanisms, material selection, biological integration, power management, wireless communication, clinical applications, regulatory issues, and clinical translation. We pay particular attention to the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches, and to the trade-offs that determine their applicability to particular uses. Furthermore, quantitative performance indicators and clinically evaluated case studies are discussed to correlate sensor characteristics to practical healthcare applications and to provide a more critical perspective on their current clinical potential and remaining limitations.

Relevant papers on implantable sensors and their use in healthcare were identified by a systematic literature review. Investigations were conducted with Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed and ScienceDirect. The search strategy comprised combinations of the keywords “implantable sensor”, “implantable biosensor”, “in vivo sensor”, “implantable device”, “wireless implantable sensor”, “implantable monitoring”, “biocompatible materials”, “wireless communication”, “RFID”, “Bluetooth Low Energy”, “clinical applications”, and “implantable healthcare.” The keywords were combined using Boolean operators AND and OR. The probe largely focused on works published from 2015 to 2026. We also reviewed prior work that demonstrated substantial groundwork, developed sensing techniques, or pioneering developments in implantable sensor technology. Publications were included if they dealt with sensor design, sensing mechanisms, materials, miniaturization, biological integration, wireless communication, data processing, applications in health care, clinical assessment, regulatory factors, or issues regarding long-term implantation. Review articles and original research papers provided both a broad context and specific technological or clinical data. Publications that reported solely on wearable or non-implantable sensors, irrelevant biomedical devices or topics that were outside the scope of implantable sensing were excluded. The literature identified was appraised against the aims of the review and classified under the major themes discussed in the following sections.

Implantable sensors can be classified based on implantation approach, communication and power strategy, and sensor type. Implantation approaches include subcutaneous (intrasubcutaneous, intramuscular), endovascular (intra-arterial, venous), and deep tissue (intracranial, intrathecal) placements. Common communication and energy methods rely on wireless radio-frequency transmission and energy harvesting. While categories overlap, sensors are usually selected based on performance metrics and target application. Sensors can also be grouped by the type of transduction principles. Biophysical sensors detect physical properties such as motion, pressure, and temperature using resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoresistive, or piezoelectric transduction; they are simple and robust but sensitive to environmental noise, often corrected via algorithms. Electrical sensors record bioelectrical activity from neural, cardiac, or muscular cells (e.g., ECG, EEG, EMG, bioimpedance) and remain a fabrication “gold standard”. Biochemical sensors measure specific biomarkers (pH, CO2, metabolites, electrolytes, hormones) with high sensitivity and specificity but require complex processing, face slower reaction kinetics, and often consume more power.

Implantable biochemical sensors have true sensor functionality (that is, the ability to convert a single parameter signal into a single data signal) and allow continual monitoring of key biomarkers of physiology or pathology, often supplying critical information that is different from enzymatic or affinity-type biochemical reactions, which limits their viability and operability due to factors such as sensor surface drift, loss of the biological recognition element, and biological fouling of what is available from external measurements. Implantable biochemical sensors are often state-of-the-art and represent cutting-edge capability. For example, implantable glucose monitors are FDA-cleared, while systems for measuring lactate, CO2, pH, etc., are still in the research stage, demonstrating a variety of engineering opportunities and challenges.

Biochemical sensors have advantages of generally high specificity and excellent sensitivity compared to other sensor types, but these gains typically come at the cost of reduced longevity and increased complexity. Almost all implantable biochemical sensors rely on electrochemical or optical detection of enzymatic or affinity-type biochemical reactions, which limits their viability and operability due to factors such as sensor surface drift, loss of the biological recognition element, and biological fouling. Enzymatic or affinity-type biochemical reactions limit the viability and operability of these sensors due to factors such as sensor surface drift, loss of the biological recognition element, and biological fouling. That said, and because of the body's strong grasp on homeostasis, most parameters of primary interest (like glucose, lactate, CO2, etc.) are present at concentrations orders of magnitude greater than those of their interferences.

shows the working principles of implantable biochemical sensors and representative sensing configurations.  shows antibody-based biochemical sensing through target-induced FRET changes for continuous cortisol monitoring using functionalized fiber-optic sensors.  shows an illustration of an implantable aptamer-based electrochemical sensor for interleukin-6 (IL-6) along with images of the sensor setup, and depictions of the sensor's target recognition, signal generation and analytical performance evaluation. These approaches allow detection of clinically relevant analytes by different recognition and transduction mechanisms.

Perhaps the most mature and widely used example of an implantable biochemical sensor is the electrochemical glucose sensor, which works by a potentiometric mechanism. A planar electrode is coated with an ion-selective membrane, and the potential is measured against a stable reference electrode. The magnitude of the potential, which is generally changed by polarization at an auxiliary electrode is correlated to the concentration of the selected ion. Continuous monitoring of blood CO2 concentration via an extracorporeal catheter and a commercially available CO2 monitor is critical as an indicator of respiratory failure. The quantitative performance of implanted sensing was evaluated by compiling common performance indicators for selected classes of biomarkers, e.g. glucose, lactate, dopamine, and inflammation (). The reported metrics are dependent on the sensing principle and target analyte but may include sensitivity, accuracy, detection limit, signal quality, response characteristics and measurement stability. When directly reported by the relevant reference methods, corresponding quantitative data obtained from conventional monitoring methodologies were included. These results provide a quantitative basis for comparing the analytical and monitoring capabilities of implanted sensors with conventional methodologies. However, as the presented values were obtained using different sensor architectures, reference methodologies, experimental settings and validation protocols, they should be interpreted as indicative values and not as direct head-to-head comparisons. This contrast also highlights one of the key features of implanted platforms, namely the ability to obtain repeated or continuous data in vivo, compared to traditional techniques which often provide discrete measurements requiring external sample or laboratory analysis.

Abbreviations: SNR, signal-to-noise ratio; LOD, limit of detection; MARD, mean absolute relative difference; CGM, continuous glucose monitoring; CV, coefficient of variation.

Numerous medical conditions can lead to damaged tissues and organs, which in turn can induce a vast number of electrochemical signals constantly in the human body, indicative of their biological or pathological states. Biological and physiological signals measured by electronic devices have led to the development of many types of sensors, many of which are now commercially available. In general, those sensors can be classified into three types based on their anatomy and operation status: biosensors for ex vivo operation, robust health condition monitoring (HCM) sensors for wearable operation, and implantable biosensors for in vivo operation.

Ex vivo biosensors are mainly used to test biological samples like blood, urine, saliva, or other specimens that are not inside the body. They usually give measurements at specific times. Wearable sensors, in contrast, are designed for non-invasive or minimally invasive monitoring at the body surface and can continuously record physiological and biochemical parameters. However, measurements obtained from wearable platforms may be affected by motion artifacts, environmental conditions, biofluid availability, and the distance between the sensing interface and the target biological environment. Implantable biosensors are usually miniaturized and must operate wirelessly to detect chronic environmental parameters and telemeter and remotely record the measured signals in a healthy and less invasive way. By positioning the sensing element within the body or directly adjacent to the target tissue, implantable biosensors can provide localized and potentially continuous measurements of biochemical and physiological changes. Depending on the application, these systems can monitor glucose, lactate, neurotransmitters, inflammatory biomarkers, pH, pressure, temperature, and electrophysiological activity.

The implantable sensing platform generally integrates the sensing element with signal-transduction, signal-processing, power-management, and wireless communication components within a compact device. Wireless telemetry is particularly important because direct physical connections to an implanted device can increase the risk of infection and restrict long-term use. Wireless power transfer and energy-harvesting strategies have therefore been investigated to reduce dependence on conventional batteries and enable smaller, longer-lasting implantable systems.

In addition to analytical performance, implantable biosensors must maintain stable operation within complex and continuously changing biological environments. Adsorption of proteins and cells at the sensor interface can produce biofouling, while inflammatory and foreign-body responses can alter the local tissue environment and affect sensor performance over time. Consequently, successful implantable biosensor design requires a balance among sensitivity, selectivity, response time, long-term stability, biocompatibility, miniaturization, power consumption, and reliable wireless communication. These requirements represent important differences between implantable, wearable, and ex vivo sensing platforms and are central to the translation of implantable biosensors from laboratory prototypes to clinically useful monitoring systems.

Several medical conditions, including congestive heart failure, hydrocephalus, glaucoma, and other disorders associated with abnormal pressure, require reliable assessment of internal pressure over time. Implantable pressure sensors provide a means of obtaining measurements directly from the relevant anatomical site, which can be particularly valuable when pressure varies substantially with posture, activity, or disease progression. A typical system combines a pressure-sensitive transducer with signal-conditioning electronics, power management, and wireless telemetry for transferring measurements to an external receiver. Depending on the application, piezoresistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, and resonant transduction mechanisms can be employed. The choice of sensor architecture depends strongly on the implantation site and the required pressure range and resolution. In addition to accurate pressure conversion, chronic systems must maintain stable performance despite temperature fluctuations, mechanical deformation, encapsulation effects, and changes in the surrounding tissue. Sensor drift is particularly important because even small baseline changes can lead to clinically meaningful errors during long-term monitoring. Therefore, calibration stability and compensation strategies are important considerations in chronic pressure-sensing systems.

Intracranial pressure monitoring is an important application in hydrocephalus and other neurological disorders. Continuous or repeated pressure measurements can provide information about pressure fluctuations and treatment response that may not be captured by isolated clinical assessments. Similarly, implantable intraocular pressure sensors are being developed for glaucoma monitoring, where repeated measurements could provide a more comprehensive representation of pressure variations than measurements obtained during periodic clinical visits. Cardiovascular applications provide another important example, particularly pulmonary artery pressure monitoring in patients with heart failure, where remotely obtained pressure data can support longitudinal disease management.

Despite their clinical potential, chronic pressure sensors must balance measurement accuracy with miniaturization, biocompatibility, mechanical robustness, power requirements, and reliable data transmission. Encapsulation and packaging are particularly important because they protect the electronic components from body fluids while allowing the pressure-sensitive element to respond accurately to the target pressure. Thus, the development of implantable pressure sensors is not solely a transducer-design problem but requires coordinated optimization of the sensing element, packaging, implantation interface, power strategy, and telemetry system.

Finally, recent efforts to advance chronic implantable pressure sensors to meet additional challenges associated with their tissues of implantation are detailed, including long-term material stability, mechanical adaptability, and cloud-integrated data handling for patient-specific analysis.

An important biophysical parameter in biological sensing applications to examine metabolic processes, biochemical reactions, and pathological alterations of tissues is temperature monitoring. Body temperature changes are often associated with tissue injury, necessitating the application of temperature sensors for targeted monitoring of tissues such as skeletal muscle and heart in medical applications. Accurate signal processing and calibration are essential in implantable wireless temperature sensors. A wireless, passive temperature sensor system based on acoustic metamaterial structure has been proposed, featuring a low-profile size and millikelvin (mK) resolution for in vivo applications. Transduction is based on the plasmonic resonance property of the structure when interfaced with the biological environment. The structure is optimized and analyzed, and preliminary in vitro tests with fabricated prototypes demonstrate sensor functionality.

A segment of the metallization is removed to achieve peak sensitivity, which can serve as a reference point in implanted sensors to correct for drift in the operational environment. Future research is focused on refining the structural design to optimize both sensitivity and quality factor. Continuous monitoring of such parameters is expected to further uncover unknown physiological responses to illnesses, pharmaceutical treatments, and mitigation strategies. There is a growing demand for medical monitoring implants that can enable intervention at the cellular level, requiring a new generation of implantable temperature sensors. Wireless sensors in smart orthopedic implants already provide near real-time information on in vivo load, position, and tissue healing. A novel injectable animal temperature chip with a flexible antenna, embedded in plastic resin, has been developed to monitor temperature bio-signals in small animals, with a compact form factor of 12 mm × 11 mm. Such transdermal wireless temperature monitoring systems are well suited for preclinical animal experiments, as well as monitoring fever, core brain temperature, and pyrogenic drug testing.

Importantly, performance demonstrated in small-animal models should not be directly equated with readiness for human implantation. The injectable temperature chip described above primarily demonstrates the feasibility of wireless temperature monitoring in small animals. Translation to human implantable devices requires further evaluation of long-term biocompatibility, tissue response, encapsulation stability, signal drift, power consumption, wireless communication, sterilization, and mechanical durability. Differences in anatomy, implantation depth, tissue properties, and physiological conditions between rodents and humans may also influence sensor performance. Therefore, animal studies provide an important step for demonstrating sensing feasibility and initial biological compatibility, but further engineering validation, human-relevant preclinical studies, and clinical evaluation are required before clinical deployment.

Medical devices and sensing technologies are critical to physical and mental well-being, which is central to healthcare. Integrated circuits are frequently utilized as biomedical sensors for detecting physiological parameters, tracking health conditions, and controlling biological functions, such as electrical stimulation. Implantable devices are systems that are designed to be inserted into the body for extended periods of time, from days to years, to allow for ongoing surveillance and regulation of biological processes. When tissue biopsy or surgical removal is unsafe or impractical, they provide a minimally invasive alternative, enabling long-term observation of disease progression.

Implantable sensors are used to monitor key physiological parameters including temperature, electrocardiogram, blood pressure, pH, and glucose level which are vital to managing chronic diseases. The growing demand for continuous and remote healthcare monitoring has boosted the development of biocompatible wireless implantable systems that communicate with external receivers. Such systems generally use small sensors, wireless transmission components and small antennas to transmit physiological data. They can sense several biophysical and biochemical markers such as pressure, electrical activity, oxygen concentration, and ion concentrations.

The choice of material is critical to the performance and longevity of implantable sensors. The appropriate materials should be biocompatible, mechanically flexible and resistant to corrosion in physiological environments, while maintaining stable signal transduction. Common sensing technologies include thermistors for temperature monitoring, capacitive humidity sensors based on polymer dielectric layers, and electrochemical sensors such as conductometric, potentiometric, and amperometric sensors used to detect ions, metabolites, and gases. Many implantable sensors remain uncommercialized despite promising experimental results due to challenges including material degradation, signal drift, and integration limitations. The growing burden of chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disorders and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has amplified the demand for continuous digital health monitoring technologies. Wearable devices enable temporary external monitoring while implantable sensors allow long-term real-time physiological tracking, which is necessary for diseases that require uninterrupted monitoring such as cardiac arrhythmia, sleep apnea, and glucose management in diabetic patients. Recent developments are turning implantable devices into smart systems that employ multiple types of sensors, onboard signal processing, and machine learning algorithms to examine physiological data and identify problems. Wireless communication technologies have been improved, especially in the frequency range of 1 to 8 GHz, which also support high data transmission, low power consumption and miniaturization of devices for long-term biomedical applications.

Wearable and implantable sensors offer complementary approaches to physiological monitoring, as shown in . Wearable sensors allow for the non-invasive monitoring of physiological parameters and body functions at various body sites (). Conversely, implantable sensors make it possible to perform local sensing inside tissues and organs. For example, a wireless thermal sensor that can be implanted allows for continuous measurement of microvascular blood flow in tissue flaps and organ grafts. The system consists of a thermal sensing probe with wireless electronics for data transmission, and biodegradable fixation barbs that help hold the probe to the tissue (). These approaches show the complementary roles of wearable and implantable technologies for continuous health monitoring.

Nevertheless, the design of implantable systems poses significant engineering challenges. They include biocompatibility, stable long-term function, low power operation, miniaturization and robust encapsulation. Furthermore, the inclusion of energy harvesting techniques, including thermoelectric, piezoelectric, or biofuel cell-based approaches, offers promising pathways for battery-free operation, thus decreasing the physical footprint and the requirement for surgical battery replacement. Illustrative of these principles, modern implantable devices are typically built from the following core components: sensor modules for acquisition of physiological or biochemical signals (e.g. pressure, glucose, ECG). Signal conditioning analogue front-end circuitry. Control and signal processing with microcontrollers or ASICs. Real time data transfer wireless transceivers. Power modules battery, inductor coil or harvesting units. Biocompatible encapsulation layers (e.g. parylene-C, PDMS or silk fibroin). Each of these subsystems involves different design trade-offs regarding power consumption, size, response time and mechanical compatibility with tissue.

With the expansion of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), implantable sensors are expected to assume an increasingly prominent role in closed-loop systems, where sensor data can automatically initiate therapeutic interventions such as drug delivery, stimulation, or feedback-controlled actuation.

There has been constant discussion and innovation because of the problems of the materials used in implantable devices and the need for long term biocompatibility. In this regard, considerable attention has been paid to biosensors and high-capacity MEMS devices possessing biodegradable capabilities. Biodegradable implants may offer temporary functionality and slow in situ regeneration of biosensor components after degradation, in line with emerging paradigms in sustainable medical technology. Materials such as metals, metal oxides and insulating dielectrics need significant chemical or structural modification to improve their biocompatibility and degradability.In vivo, the implantable biodegradable sensors should be responsive to biological parameters including temperature, pH and enzymatic activity. On the transponder side of implantable devices, there exists a range of biomedical sensors for individual monitoring applications like pressure, strain, and acceleration, particularly in wearables and chronic disease management. Special emphasis is given to polymers including polyurethanes, polylactide, polyacrylate and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), which have tunable mechanical properties, chemical inertness and compatibility with human tissues. Fibrotic encapsulation is a major problem for long-term implants because protective membranes can develop around the device, causing it to become functionally isolated.  summarizes reported quantitative data for commonly used encapsulation materials since encapsulation stability is a significant determinant in long-term implant performance.

To overcome this, organically modified nanoparticles have been used to transform hydrophobic polylactide into hydrophilic, biocompatible platforms for long-term biosignal acquisition. Recent advances include biodegradable platforms based on FDGA that allow for rapid diagnostic screening, a simplified device architecture, and reduced medical costs, especially in resource-limited settings. Biodegradable electronics have been employed in passive sensors, disposable telemetry units and semiconductor devices integrated with biocompatible matrices. We have also developed a hybrid materials approach enabling the fabrication of multilayered biodegradable devices with robust electronic performance. These innovations pave the way for the next generation of bioresorbable biorobots and actuators, enhancing applications in disease diagnosis, real-time monitoring, and minimally invasive therapeutic systems.

Conducting polymers exhibit a unique combination of electrical conductivity, mechanical flexibility, and biocompatibility, making them highly attractive for implantable electrodes and chronic biosensing applications. Conducting polymers are organic semiconductors, which can be integrated with soft packaging materials through low-cost, scalable fabrication methods, which is especially beneficial for implantable devices. A remarkable example is the use of silk, a biodegradable material, as a substrate, passivation layer or packaging element. Embedding conducting polymers in silk matrices has resulted in fully organic, flexible and conformal biosensors. For neurotechnology platforms, implantable devices have been fabricated using a silk-based screen-printing technique that allows dual functionality as recording sites and supporting layers.

The first conducting polymers discovered, such as polyaniline, polypyrrole and PEDOT:PSS have drawn interest due to their tunable electronic properties and low elastic modulus which are more compatible with the mechanical properties of biological tissues than inorganic materials. This compliance greatly improves the stability of the tissue–device interface and reduces inflammation during chronic implantation. Conducting polymers can be chemically doped or electrochemically modified to enhance biodegradability and biocompatibility, and thus their relevance in bioelectronic and neuromodulation applications. These polymers can be directly electropolymerized on flexible substrates and thus enable the fabrication of organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) and photoacoustic imaging components with integrated sensing functionalities. The addition of conjugated polyelectrolytes has extended the use of such materials to biosensing, thin film transistor arrays and label free detection platforms for biomolecules including DNA, proteins and cytokines. Their chemical versatility allows for fine-tuning of the surface properties of the electrodes to induce pK shifts and superior proton coupled electron transfer behavior-critical for pH sensing and selective detection of biomolecules.

To summaries, conducting polymers provide a versatile platform for the development of next generation implantable bioelectronics where mechanical compliance, signal transduction and functional adaptability are integrated in one material system.

Metallic materials are key to transforming implantable sensors, actuators and closed loop therapeutic systems from passive signal mapping to active electromechanical transduction. Biocompatible metals, alloys and metal oxides (e.g. iridium oxide, titanium oxide) are used because these materials show high electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness and fabrication compatibility, and are essential in microdevices for biomedical applications. Metals like platinum, gold, titanium, and stainless steel are ideal for chronic implants, particularly in neuroprosthetics, musculoskeletal monitoring, and cardiac sensing applications, due to their biocompatibility and chemical stability. Additionally, resorbable metals such as magnesium and zinc alloys have been increasingly used in temporary implantable sensors and biodegradable scaffolds because of their controlled corrosion profiles and decreased long-term toxicity. Microfabrication techniques such as photolithography, thin film deposition and etching are regularly used to incorporate metallic layers in microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and flexible substrates. These methods allow a precise patterning of electrode arrays, interconnects and sensor platforms which then can be embedded into stretchable polymeric scaffolds by soft lithography for hybrid integration. Metal actuators exhibit mechanically responsive behaviors via modulation of thermal, electrochemical or surface tension effects.

For instance: vanadium dioxide (VO2) undergoes a thermally induced phase transition (α to β) and can be used in temperature-responsive devices. Bistable actuators are designed in the form of resistively heated copper–titanium alloy bow structures to enable specific mechanical movement with electrical stimuli. Nickel beams controlled by electrocapillary effects use changes in surface tension to generate curvature changes when voltage is applied. Shape memory alloys (SMAs) have unique ratcheting and hysteresis properties allowing programmable mechanical locking, which is ideal for implantable microgrippers, self-deploying stents and drug-release triggers. Besides their structural roles, metals have functional roles in thermal management, signal transduction and electrochemical sensing, contributing to integrated closed-loop systems for real-time physiological monitoring and feedback-based therapy. Metallic materials provide unmatched electrical, mechanical, and fabrication versatility and form the backbone of many implantable medical devices. Their ever-evolving biocompatibility, mechanosensitivity, and smart actuation capability continue to open up new frontiers for minimally invasive, autonomous, and multifunctional biomedical implants. In general, the three material classes represent complementary approaches to designing implantable sensors. Mechanical compliance and conformability are preferred when biocompatible polymers are used, electrical functionality must be combined with soft interfaces when conductive polymers are utilized, and high conductivity and structural robustness are required when metallic materials are implemented. The choice among them therefore depends on the particular balance between mechanical requirements, electrical performance, long-term stability and compatibility with the biological environment.

Generally, the form factor of all active implantable systems is constrained by the miniaturized components employed inside and the targeted sensing region of the system. Therefore, a large part of the design workflow needed for the development of new devices has to deal with the customization of the external envelope of active implantable systems, prior to the selection of internal components such as sensors or telemetry front ends. In such cases, evidence of the possible arrangement of off-the-shelf components within a predefined envelope can demonstrate the potential functionality of each internal element and guide the selection process. Monitoring devices are generally composed of at least one sensing unit and a wireless communication module, contained within ceramic or biocompatible metal housings, sealed with epoxy or similar materials to avoid corrosion and fluid ingress. Fluid compatible materials of choice are biocompatible metals such as titanium, stainless steel and cobalt–chromium alloys because they are versatile in fabrication, mechanically stable, inexpensive and available in many forms. Ceramic materials are lightweight, resistant to corrosion, and strong, but are brittle, and expensive to machine, limiting their wider use. The packaging of the sensor systems is often tailored to particular clinical requirements, with the goal of minimizing the device volume while keeping the desired dynamic range of measurement. For multi-sensor platforms or integrated monitoring solutions, standardized data formats are needed to allow for supervisory control, inter-device compatibility and multi-modal analysis. Interface standards such as USB can be useful for data recovery and software integration, but can also increase the development cost and require more complex hardware testing. A good compromise would be to restrict the interfaces to a simple data port, and use specific software for efficient access and processing of relevant data.

Power supply remains a fundamental challenge in the development of implantable medical devices, where continuous operation, miniaturization, biocompatibility, and safety must be simultaneously addressed. Implantable systems typically rely on three main categories of power sources: batteries, inductive power transfer, and biophysical/biofuel-based energy harvesting. Batteries remain widely used because they provide a relatively high and predictable energy supply; however, their achievable energy density, lifetime, and form factor depend strongly on battery chemistry, architecture, and packaging. Thin-film batteries offer improved integration and mechanical flexibility, but they still require additional encapsulation, which can increase device footprint and potentially affect thermal dissipation.

Inductive power transfer offers a promising alternative to battery-based power sources. Reported wireless power transfer efficiencies vary substantially with the transfer mechanism and system configuration. Inductive coupling has achieved efficiencies approaching 95% in some reported systems, although the actual efficiency depends on coupling distance, alignment, implant location, operating frequency, coil geometry, and tissue-related constraints.

This technique is used in various commercially available devices; however, research is underway to increase the efficiency of implanted power converters and optimize them for lower power operation, thereby increasing device longevity and safety. A third category of energy sources is based on bio-physical and bio-fuel-based systems which harvest energy from metabolic heat or biochemical reactions such as glucose oxidation in blood. Such systems are naturally compatible with human physiology and attractive for long-term operation without any external intervention. However, their low power output usually necessitates larger collection or conversion structures, making implantation and miniaturization more difficult. shows the three main power delivery methods, batteries, inductive transfer, and energy harvesting, and their integration into modern implantable devices. Thermal management is essential in all power delivery schemes to preserve tissue viability and sensor performance. The biocompatibility requires that the local temperature remain below 42 °C even at peak operation. Thus, transducers and power components should be placed as close as possible to the sensing or actuation site. This design can reduce the thermal load, decrease the power needed for transmission, and avoid excessive heat build-up. Moreover, power and heat routing need to be co-optimized, as larger and more complex devices are more challenging in terms of thermal dissipation and increase surgical complexity.

In general, implantable sensors use three main power management strategies: battery-based power, wireless power transfer, and energy harvesting. Batteries offer a predictable, continuous power supply but are restricted by lifetime, size and encapsulation needs. Wireless power transfer can reduce dependence on implanted batteries and enable prolonged operations, though its performance is dependent on variables such as alignment, implant depth, tissue properties and thermal constraints. Energy harvesting has the potential for battery-free operation by using physiological or environmental energy, but the output is typically limited and variable.  depicts the main strategies, which include battery-based power, wireless power transfer and energy harvesting, each providing different options for satisfying the energy needs of implantable medical devices.  summarizes these approaches by comparing their representative characteristics, advantages, limitations and applications, highlighting the trade-offs that influence power-strategy selection for implantable sensors.

Most implantable biosensors measure chemical or biochemical quantities and require telemetry to transmit their measurements. The telemetry system must transmit information without disturbing the healthy operation of the implanted device and without endangering the health of the patient. Most telemetry systems are analog, in which the analog output of the biomedical sensor becomes the input for the transmitter. Most transmitters use RF signals between around 315 Hz and 2.4 GHz. The RF field produced by the RF antenna induces an RF voltage in the receiving coil, which subsequently generates the voltage across the demodulator and low-pass filter electronics. This method is suitable for subcutaneous input, for example, for measuring biomedical parameters in blood vessels by using chemical sensors. Wireless data transmission is an essential part of implantable biosensors that allows the physiological signals to be communicated to external devices for remote monitoring purposes.  presents different methods: radio frequency transmission with signal processing and Wi-Fi based data transfer (), wireless and batteryless blood-flow monitoring for prosthetic heart-valve function and data transmission to a smartphone (), and wireless endovascular neural interface (ENI) for neural stimulation (). These solutions enable remote sensor data access and reduce the need for wired connections.

An opto-electronic pulse oximeter capable of simultaneously measuring blood oxygen saturation and temperature was developed. A coherent laser beam was transmitted through the skin and received in a photodiode, from which the optical path length could be extracted. Using the light source as a modulator or transmitter, cardiac parameters, such as heart beats and blood flow, could be determined at arbitrary depths in the skin. The light transmission system is expected to be widely utilized in future wearable or implantable systems.

Most implantable biosensors need telemetry to transmit the measurements. Nevertheless, systems requiring telemetry are often simpler from an implementation perspective. The telemetry system must transmit information without disturbing the healthy operation of the implanted device. The combined TTL logic output from several measuring chips can be encoded at 500 Hz with split-tone modulation before external transmission. The speed of approach can be improved, for example, by re-modulating the transmitted pulse stream, locking the external clock to the telemetry modulation frequency.

Biological systems possess very efficient sensing and regulatory systems for maintaining physiological homeostasis. These natural systems have inspired the development of implantable and wearable sensors for continuous tracking of physiological parameters across multiple scales of the human body. The successful implementation of such devices requires smooth integration with biological tissues, which includes physical, chemical and biological interactions at micro- and nanoscale. Recent advances in nanotechnology and microelectronics have led to the development of highly sensitive sensing platforms based on silicon, graphene and nanoparticle-enabled materials. Such technologies allow for a wide range of sensing modalities including electrochemical, piezoelectric, optical, and nanomechanical sensors that are capable of detecting biomarkers with remarkable sensitivity, sometimes approaching single-molecule resolution.

Long-term operation in physiological environments remains challenging because implantable sensors are susceptible to biofouling, signal drift, material degradation, foreign-body responses, and fibrous tissue encapsulation, which can compromise sensing accuracy and device performance. Biofouling can hinder analyte transport to the sensing surface, while foreign-body responses may lead to inflammation and fibrous encapsulation that further impair sensor function. Developing stable interfaces between nanoscale sensors, engineered actuators, and biological tissues therefore remains an important challenge. Advances in biointerface engineering, including antifouling coatings, biocompatible materials, and strategies to reduce fibrotic encapsulation, are essential for improving device stability, tissue integration, and long-term functionality.

Implantable biosensors are highly valuable scientific tools in advancing basic neuroscience research and clinical applications. These neurotechnologies provide direct readouts of neurological signals and neurochemical processes. Their value to basic and applied research within these fields is maximized as performance capacities are extended over months and years, across multiple studies and/or clinical evaluations. While these tools have improved over the last several decades in terms of both their sensor performance capacity and surgical insertion paradigms, there are still critical biological challenges that drastically reduce the performance capabilities of all existing and new designs. The breaching of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) to insert devices triggers a cascade of biochemical pathways, resulting in a complex series of molecular and cellular responses to implanted devices. Each sensor interrogates the brain with a unique electrical and chemical readout that is dependent on the tissue microenvironment and properties of the device.

Changes to the tissue microenvironment surrounding the device occur because of insertion injuries, and a foreign body response can dramatically impact electrochemical and electrophysiological signal sensitivity and stability over time. This phenomenon is especially relevant to the developing markets in implantable devices for the central nervous system (CNS), where robust, stable, active interfacing with tissue over years, and even lifelong, is necessary.

As these devices continue to interface with the brain and record target signals, none of the sensors evaluated are “immune” to the biological response that occurs because of the brain–device interface. Findings from several studies show that insertion injuries and a foreign body response impact signal quality across all implanted CNS sensors to varying degrees. A significant number of recent studies have focused on understanding how and why the newly created brain–device interface changes over space and time, and why this variability impacts sensors across a wide size range. Understanding the underlying biological processes behind the brain tissue response at the cellular and molecular levels has led to various intervention strategies aimed at improving device signal sensitivity and longevity.

The long-term implantation of sensors is challenged by the foreign body response. Tissue injury and glial scar formation can reduce electrode sensitivity and signal stability over time for neural implants. Previous studies have reported a loss of sensitivity of about 50% within 1 month after implantation in rodents. However, this should not be taken as a general limitation of modern implantable sensors, but is based on previous work. Several strategies to mitigate the foreign body response have been investigated in recent studies including modifications to electrode materials or surface treatments, device flexibility, and management of inflammation and glial scar formation. The potential of flexible and biodegradable implants has also been explored to reduce glial scar formation and improve the implant interaction with surrounding tissue. Although these strategies may be useful in maintaining sensor performance during long-term implantation, long-term stability of performance remains a challenge.

Long-term biological stability remains a challenge for implantable sensors. Proteins and other biomolecules may adsorb onto the sensor surface after implantation, causing biofouling that might change mass transfer, obstruct active sensing sites, and lower signal stability. Immune cell infiltration and the development of fibrotic tissue surrounding the implanted device are examples of the inflammatory and foreign-body reaction that might result from tissue damage. Tissue encapsulation can gradually alter sensitivity and response time by increasing the diffusion distance between the sensor and the target analyte. The place of implantation, the device's geometry, the surface characteristics, mechanical mismatch, and the length of implantation all affect how much of an impact these effects have. To overcome these constraints, research has been done on antifouling surface coatings, surface modification, flexible and mechanically compliant materials, and methods to regulate inflammatory and glial responses. However, during the duration of the planned implantation, improvements in biocompatibility should be balanced with mechanical stability and sensing performance. Thus, variations in sensor performance, tissue response, encapsulation, and functional stability with extended implantation should be considered in addition to the lack of acute toxicity when evaluating long-term biocompatibility.

Wireless communication and data processing are of utmost importance in the development of implantable sensor systems to allow continuous tracking of physiological parameters for cardiac disease, diabetes, and neurological disorders. Although tremendous improvements have been achieved in the miniaturization of devices, biocompatibility, and long-term stability, reliable wireless data transmission is still challenging due to signal attenuation in biological tissues, power limitations, and thermal safety issues. High-frequency communication systems offer greater transmission ranges and higher data rates but may increase the risk of tissue heating. In contrast, low-frequency approaches generally provide better biocompatibility but suffer from limited transmission performance.

Furthermore, implantable devices will require efficient data processing, storage and security mechanisms to enable long term monitoring and retrospective analysis. However, the implementation of advanced on-chip analytics and large-scale data management systems is still hindered by the limitations in memory capacity, energy availability, computational resources and interoperability. Security and privacy issues provide additional incentives for the need of developing robust cryptographic and authentication frameworks. Beyond these technical challenges, the long-term success of implantable sensors depends on the biocompatibility and bioresorbability of the materials used. Major obstacles include chronic inflammatory responses, foreign body reactions and tissue remodeling, thus prompting continued research into biodegradable materials, optimized implant geometries and advanced biointerfaces that can enhance device integration and long-term clinical performance.

Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) are two of the most promising wireless communication technologies used in implantable sensor systems because of their low power requirements and their compatibility with biomedical applications. RFID technology offers wireless power transfer and data communication without a large power supply onboard, which is an attractive choice for miniaturized implantable devices. Passive RFID systems can also provide sensing, identification and biotelemetry functions with reduced device size and maintenance requirements. Recent advances have demonstrated RFID-based implantable temperature sensors, energy-harvesting platforms and low-power wake-up circuits that boost operational efficiency and prolong the device lifetime. RFID is even more promising for long-term implantable monitoring applications due to the ability to combine different sensing modalities and communication protocols. Another important wireless communication strategy for implantable and wearable healthcare systems is Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). BLE is optimized for low power operation, allowing reliable short-range communication with very low energy consumption, thereby enabling devices to operate over long periods of time with small batteries. BLE is also well suited to continuous physiological monitoring with communication rates of 40–100 transmissions per second and energy requirements as low as 0.01 mJ per transaction. Although its communication range is typically about 30–40 m, it is sufficient for most personal and home health care applications. Moreover, BLE is an important enabling technology for Internet of Things (IoT)-based healthcare systems, allowing remote patient monitoring, smart medical devices, and emerging applications, such as the integration of machine learning, localization technologies and increased cybersecurity features.

summarizes the respective benefits and drawbacks of RFID and BLE, which offer complementary wireless communication methods for implantable healthcare equipment. While BLE offers more flexibility for frequent data transfer and standardized connectivity with external devices, RFID is best suited for passive or battery-free systems. The particular needs of the implant, such as power availability, communication requirements, device size, implantation settings, and monitoring strategy, will determine which of these technologies is best.

The implantable sensor systems require efficient data storage and processing for ongoing monitoring, retrospective analysis and intelligent clinical decision making. However, implantable devices are limited to severe memory, energy consumption, computational power, and long-term storage of physiological data. To overcome these challenges, modern implantable platforms are increasingly using hybrid architectures that combine onboard memory with external storage and cloud-based resources. Phase-change memory (PCM) is one of the emerging storage technologies that has attracted considerable attention, owing to its non-volatility, low energy consumption, scalability and long-term data retention that makes it especially suitable for miniaturized implantable electronics. These advances allow for secure data logging, real-time signal acquisition, and integration into closed-loop health care systems. Real-time data processing is also important to convert raw physiological signals into clinically relevant information. Typical processing pipelines include signal denoising, calibration, feature extraction, and anomaly detection, e.g., via wavelet-based filtering, compressed sensing, sensor fusion, and machine-learning algorithms.

Some implantable devices incorporate limited on-chip processing capabilities, while external wearable or cloud-connected platforms often handle computationally intensive tasks. Such systems enable real-time classification, event detection, and adaptive therapeutic responses, thereby supporting personalized medicine and next-generation smart healthcare applications.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can further enhance implantable sensing by enabling automated signal interpretation, event detection, prediction, and adaptive responses. However, the computational requirements of conventional deep-learning models can be difficult to accommodate within highly miniaturized implants. TinyML provides a potential approach by deploying compact machine-learning models directly on resource-constrained embedded hardware. Techniques such as model quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, and hardware-aware model design can reduce memory requirements and computational complexity, making on-device inference more feasible under strict energy constraints. In implantable systems, these methods need to achieve a balance between how accurate the model is, how much memory it uses, how much processing power it needs, how long it takes to make a decision, and how much energy it uses. Excessive computational activity can increase power demand and may also contribute to undesirable heat generation, making energy-efficient inference particularly important for long-term implantation.

Edge processing can complement TinyML by moving selected analytical functions closer to the sensor rather than continuously transferring raw physiological data to a remote server. This approach can reduce wireless data transmission, lower latency, and improve operation when continuous external connectivity is unavailable. On-device or near-device processing may also reduce the transmission of raw physiological data, although appropriate cybersecurity and data-protection measures remain necessary. For implantable neural interfaces, on-device machine-learning and neuromorphic approaches have been investigated as a means of processing neural activity locally while reducing the need for power-intensive telemetry. However, available power, memory, processing capability, and thermal constraints limit the complexity of algorithms that can be directly implemented within an implant.

Importantly, high classification accuracy obtained from laboratory datasets or retrospective analyses should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical readiness. AI/ML models intended for implantable healthcare applications require validation using sufficiently representative patient populations and clinically relevant data, with assessment of robustness, generalizability, false-positive and false-negative rates, and performance across different physiological and pathological conditions. External and prospective clinical validation are particularly important because models trained on limited or highly controlled datasets may perform differently when exposed to real-world patient variability. Thus, future implantable sensing platforms will require a coordinated approach in which sensing hardware, energy-efficient computation, wireless communication, data security, and clinically validated AI/ML models are designed as an integrated system rather than as independent components.

In 2017, the U.S. FDA approved the first fully implantable programmable intravascular drug delivery system, a significant milestone in the clinical translation of implantable biomedical technologies. Building on decades of progress in chronically implanted devices, this achievement further accelerated the development of MEMS-based implantable systems capable of continuous surveillance, controlled drug delivery and closed-loop therapeutic intervention. Integration of sensing, actuation, wireless communication and data processing functions within modern implantable platforms is increasing, enabling more personalized management of chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disorders and neurological conditions. Recent developments in nanomaterials, CMOS compatible electronics and miniaturized system architectures have further extended the capabilities of implantable devices towards bioelectronic medicine, neural prosthetics and organ-specific monitoring systems. In combination with cloud computing and machine learning these technologies provide opportunities for real time physiological monitoring and predictive healthcare. However, challenges related to long-term biocompatibility, patient privacy, regulatory approval, scalability, accessibility, and device reliability remain significant barriers to widespread clinical adoption. As illustrated in , implantable sensors have diverse applications in chronic disease monitoring, postoperative monitoring, and fitness tracking. Chronic disease monitoring involves the long-term assessment of physiological signals, infusion rates, and biochemical markers, whereas postoperative monitoring focuses on mechanical strain, pressure, inflammatory markers, and temperature to assess recovery and detect potential complications. Fitness tracking focuses on activity, heart rate, and skin and tissue properties. The collected physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical data can be transmitted to external devices for processing, storage, and assessment, supporting clinical monitoring, postoperative recovery, and health and fitness management.

Remote health monitoring covers a wide variety of technologies. It is generally defined as systems for detecting health events that use telecommunications for data acquisition, transmission, and analysis. These systems vary from simple devices such as glucose meters to measure blood sugar to very advanced systems that allow real-time continuous tracking with the help of wearable sensors or implantable biochips. In terms of precision and signal fidelity, implantable sensor systems have a clear advantage, as they near speech artefacts, but the signals recorded with sensors implanted within the heart could have much lower distortion and a higher signal-to-noise ratio. This insight has spurred cross-disciplinary innovation in invasive sensing platforms for critical organs, notably the heart, lungs and brain. Most commercial systems for cardiac monitoring use external electrodes, but their performance is often degraded by motion artefacts and poor electrical coupling to the myocardium. In contrast, implantable cardiac monitors, e.g., quasi-endocardial sensing units, can provide better monitoring closer to the source of the cardiac signal. In particular, the combination of electrocardiography (ECG) and impedance cardiography (ICG) in implantable systems allows the continuous recording of heart rate (HR), ECG waveform and cardiac output (CO), all of them vital indicators in heart failure, arrhythmias and ischemic events. A more sophisticated approach is to implant a bipolar ring electrode around a branch of the coronary sinus vein (CS) surgically. This arrangement enables the reliable recording of cardiac bioelectric signals and mechanical activity. These systems, which incorporate wireless telemetry and closed-loop feedback, can enhance real-time clinical intervention or patient self-management. As chronic diseases like heart disease, diabetes and hypertension increase, the use of implantable monitoring devices is expected to grow, offering new opportunities for customized, real-time and predictive healthcare.

Orthopaedic surgeries are commonly applied for treating musculoskeletal defects caused by trauma, degenerative diseases or tumor resection, including surgeries with fixation implants. The implants are generally designed as passive, biostable structures to provide mechanical support during bone healing. Implant failure remains a major concern despite low complication rates. Progressive loosening over time is the most common reason for implant failure. Failure of the implant can lead to a cascade of biomechanical problems such as stress shielding, atrophic bone resorption and finally the detachment of the interface between the implant and the material. This progression not only compromises the structural integrity of the bone-implant system, but can also lead to revision surgeries, increasing the risk of infection, surgical complications, and patient morbidity. For example, hip implants can break from the uneven sharing of load between the femoral stem and the surrounding bone. In such cases retrieval of deeply embedded bone cement is extremely difficult and may even be anatomically inaccessible. Early detection of implant instability is crucial, to allow timely clinical intervention and to avoid catastrophic failures. Traditionally, monitoring has been based on radiographic imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI) and laboratory testing.

Although imaging provides anatomical and positional information, it requires specialised equipment, repeated exposure to radiation and imposes logistical burdens on patients and health care systems. Laboratory tests (e.g., CRP, ESR) are similarly general inflammatory markers, but lack spatial specificity to the implant site and are often limited in resolution. These diagnostic tools' overall limitations highlight the need for ongoing in vivo sensing technologies. This need has resulted in the creation of implantable sensor systems, often incorporated into so-called smart implants. The next generation devices combine therapeutic function with intrinsic diagnostic capabilities allowing real-time monitoring of mechanical strain, inflammation, pH shifts, or biochemical markers in the peri-implant environment. Smart implants have huge potential especially in the area of regenerative scaffolds, complex orthopaedic reconstructions and fetal surgery, where conventional monitoring techniques are inadequate. Besides clinical utility, smart implants decrease the need for subjective patient-reported outcomes and enhance postoperative rehabilitation by continuously monitoring the performance of the implant. Such a capability could revolutionize paradigms of post-surgical care from reactive interventions to predictive and preventive strategies for long-term implant success and patient safety.

Although wearable technologies currently dominate sports and fitness monitoring, implantable sensors could provide complementary capabilities when physiological or biomechanical parameters cannot be reliably measured from the body surface. Therefore, the main significance of implantable sensors in sports and fitness applications is in the possibility to provide direct in vivo measurements of physiological and biomechanical parameters during physical activity, rather than replacing conventional wearable fitness devices. Implantable sensors placed within or near specific tissues can offer continuous measurements with less susceptibility to some external motion artifacts and environmental influences. Parameters of interest are cardiac electrical activity, tissue temperature, pressure, mechanical strain, force, and displacement.

Implantable electrophysiological sensors may be useful for monitoring cardiac and neuromuscular responses to physical activity. By being close to the biological source, they can provide high-quality physiological signals that can be used to complement external measurements when motion, electrode displacements, or muscle interference affect surface recordings. Similarly, implantable pressure and strain sensors integrated with orthopedic implants can provide information about mechanical loading, implant stability, and tissue response during movement and rehabilitation. In vivo implantable sensors have been studied for the measurement of joint loads, forces, strains, and other biomechanical parameters while performing activities like walking, which provide quantitative information that cannot be directly obtained from conventional external monitoring.

Also, implantable temperature and biochemical sensors could create opportunities for monitoring physiological changes associated with physical activity. Local tissue temperature can provide information on metabolic activity, inflammation, or abnormal tissue responses. Implantable biochemical sensors could be used to monitor analytes such as glucose, lactate, electrolytes, or other metabolites. Nonetheless, most implantable biochemical sensors for exercise-related applications are still at the experimental or preclinical stage compared to implantable glucose monitoring. Further validation of long-term stability, response time, calibration, biofouling resistance, and safety in repeated physical activity will be required to translate them into sports and fitness applications. Thus, a key distinction between wearable and implantable approaches is the intended monitoring objective. Wearable sensors are advantageous for non-invasive measurement of motion, heart rate, oxygen saturation, skin temperature, and other external physiological signals and are appropriate for routine fitness tracking. Implantable sensors are more invasive and require surgical placement but can provide access to internal physiological or biomechanical parameters that are difficult to measure externally.
