We take the subcortical network to feed this pathway rather than compete with it, and we note that a full account of the transition will need to specify how cortical and subcortical timing systems interact.

We therefore propose two phases. In the primate phase, the pathway supports shallow entrainment and call processing; prediction is short-range and spans few levels, which in the model below corresponds to Layer 1, with Layer 2 operating only over short, familiar patterns and Layer 3 present only in shallow form. In the hominin phase, stronger prefrontal drive over the same pathway, in continual exchange with the bottom-up error signals that correct it, enables deep, modality-general prediction, which corresponds to the fully developed Layer 3. On this interpretation, the capacity underlying beat perception is the ancestral form and its recruitment for syntax the derived form. This ordering is an evolutionary inference, not something the comparative evidence demonstrates directly. The evidence shows that non-human primates track isochrony with little sign of beat-based prediction and that the human arcuate fasciculus differs in size and connectivity; it cannot show in what order the two capacities arose in the hominin lineage, or whether they arose together. The interpretation is consistent with treatments of displaced, hierarchical reference as a late achievement of anthropogenesis (), and it is subject to the caution that identifying functional homologs of human language areas across species is methodologically fraught ().

The developmental claim is logically separate from the evolutionary one. Ontogeny does not in general recapitulate phylogeny: evolution is better described as the history of changes to ancestral developmental sequences than as a record replayed in each individual's development (; ). A shallow-to-deep progression in children would therefore be consistent with our evolutionary account without being evidence that the same transition occurred in hominin evolution, and the reverse holds as well. We treat the developmental trajectory as an independent prediction of the model: if a shared predictive resource depends on prefrontal control over the auditory-motor pathway, its coupling to syntax should track the maturation of that control. Four lines of evidence bear on this.

First, the developmental starting point lies in infancy, and it is more advanced than a simple shallow-to-deep account might suggest. Infants extract statistical regularities from fluent speech after brief exposure (). Newborns show neural responses to the omission of an expected downbeat (), and these responses cannot be explained by learning of transition probabilities, which suggests that beat processing is predictive from birth (). By 30 months, children show an electrophysiological response to harmonically irregular chords, indicating implicit knowledge of musical syntax (). Anticipatory neural activity toward temporally expected events is present at 9 months (), and at 4 months when auditory cues predict socially relevant stimuli (), although its cortical sources differ from those of adults: in 9-month-olds, anticipatory activity arose mainly from temporoparietal regions, whereas adults additionally recruited the supplementary motor area, with a right prefrontal source common to both groups (). These findings do not bear directly on the beat-grammar association, and we do not treat them as support for it. They matter because they locate the developmental question more precisely. General capacities for implicit learning, beat sensitivity, and temporal prediction are present in infancy, as are rudimentary forms of each of our three layers. What remains to be explained comes later: the emergence of a specific coupling between beat-based prediction and hierarchical syntactic structure building, and the deepening of prediction to span several structural levels.

Second, Layer 1 functions, temporal encoding and regularity extraction, remain robust into the preschool years even when language lags.  tested preterm and full-term children aged four to six with neural and behavioral measures. Preterm children extracted the statistical regularities as efficiently as term peers, yet prematurity was associated with lower language scores, and statistical learning did not account for that gap. This dissociation indicates that intact Layer 1 functions cannot compensate for higher-layer immaturity. Because Layer 2 operations for short, familiar patterns are largely automatic, we provisionally locate the bottleneck at Layer 3, which depends on prefrontal control and generates flexible, multi-level predictions; localizing it directly will require measures that separate the layers.

Third, the deepening of Layer 3 prediction is plausibly slow. The arcuate fasciculus continues to myelinate into early adulthood (; ), so the fronto-temporal coupling on which deep, multi-level prediction depends strengthens over an extended developmental window, even though prefrontal contributions to simple temporal anticipation are already present in infancy. The beat-grammar association reported by  was observed at age six, when this pathway is still developing. We hypothesize that the association emerges as fronto-temporal coupling becomes strong enough to support deep hierarchical prediction. Because that study was cross-sectional and modest in sample size (N = 25), and because the relevant neural measures have rarely been related to syntactic processing before school age, whether the neural association is weaker or absent at younger ages has not, to our knowledge, been tested.

Fourth, working-memory demand modulates the system. When Layer 3 predictive control is taxed, performance becomes unstable: in acquired language disorder, variability in language output increases under higher working-memory load (). The developing brain should meet the same constraint from the other side, since capacity is still growing. When load exceeds capacity, we expect prediction to break down and the child to fall back on simpler patterns, although this has not yet been tested directly.

A clinical framework already links rhythm ability to language outcome. The atypical rhythm risk hypothesis proposes that individuals with poor rhythm skills are at elevated risk for developmental speech and language disorders, including developmental language disorder, dyslexia, and stuttering (). Our model is compatible with that proposal and adds a specification. If the shared resource is predictive entrainment operating at Layer 3, the risk should be carried specifically by deficits in active temporal prediction, rather than distributed evenly across every measure that falls under the broad heading of rhythm ability. This makes the risk hypothesis sharper and testable.

These observations suggest a trajectory, which we state as a working hypothesis rather than an established sequence. From infancy, beat sensitivity, temporal prediction, and statistical learning are present, but prediction operates over short spans and simple structures, and early speech is largely formulaic. Between roughly the preschool and early school years, simple embedding appears and, on our hypothesis, beat-based prediction becomes coupled to syntactic structure building; this is when the beat-grammar association would first become measurable. Later, entrainment is flexible and complex embedding is productive. The age ranges shown in  are illustrative rather than derived from data, and the model does not assume that entrainment, syntactic complexity, and the beat-grammar association change in lockstep. When the coupling emerges, and whether these components follow a common trajectory, are empirical questions that Prediction 2 is designed to answer. What the infancy evidence does support is a weaker claim than a stage sequence: the layers are not switched on one after another, since rudimentary forms of each are present early, and the hypothesis concerns how deeply each operates and when they become coupled.

We integrate these strands into a model with three computationally nested layers ().

Layer 1: temporal encoding and regularity extraction. This layer automatically extracts local statistical and temporal regularities from the sensory stream, such as the probability of one tone following another or the typical duration of a syllable. It is phylogenetically old, robust, and present from birth, providing a representational base. Its signature is neural tracking that follows the acoustic structure of the input, typically in the delta and theta ranges. It is necessary but not sufficient for syntax, because local frequencies do not by themselves generate nested hierarchical structures.

Layer 2: structural grouping and relational mapping. This layer operates on the output of Layer 1. It groups elements into chunks and assigns abstract relational roles, such as strong versus weak beat or boundary marking in auditory sequences. This imposes a rudimentary hierarchical structure and likely depends on the auditory-motor pathway, although where along that pathway it is implemented remains open (see below). It is plausibly present in weaker form in other primates. It is fast and automatic for short, familiar patterns.

Layer 3: hierarchical prediction and model updating. This layer recursively integrates Layer 2 chunks into higher-order structures and generates simultaneous predictions at several hierarchical levels: in language, that a verb phrase or an animate noun phrase is likely; in music, that a downbeat is expected at a given metrical position. Matching input reinforces the model; violation triggers reanalysis (). This layer depends on prefrontal control over the temporal lobe, and its slow deepening accounts for the protracted development of complex syntax. Its signature is endogenous activity not attributable to the acoustic input: anticipatory sensorimotor beta preceding an expected beat, and tracking of structure that survives the removal of, or statistical control for, acoustic cues. On our hypothesis, the beat-grammar association arises here: a child with better predictive control for metrical structure would also have better predictive control for syntactic structure, which would explain why beat-evoked predictive responses index grammar ().

In computational terms, Layer 3 is a predictive-coding-style account: higher levels generate expectations, lower levels return the mismatch between expectation and input, and the model is revised accordingly (). Applied to the dorsal pathway, this scheme requires signaling in both directions: top-down (feedback) projections from frontal to temporal cortex carry predictions, and bottom-up (feedforward) projections carry the errors that revise them. Recordings in marmosets have begun to distinguish the two signals (). We use the vocabulary of prediction rather than committing to a particular formalism, because the claims we test concern whether prediction is present and how deep it runs, not which scheme implements it.

The layers operate as a cascade, each layer's representation serving as input for the next. These are nested computational levels, not anatomically segregated modules; Layers 2 and 3 in particular draw on overlapping fronto-temporal circuitry (; ), and we separate them by function rather than by sharp anatomical borders. Disruption at a lower layer propagates upward, but an intact lower layer does not guarantee higher-layer function. That is the preterm pattern reported by : Layer 1 functions are preserved while productive language lags, because the limiting step lies higher in the processing hierarchy. Classic structural signatures of syntax, such as the P600, can be read as markers of this upper layer at work ().

Because the layers are defined computationally, where each is implemented is a separate question, and the answer is clearer for Layers 1 and 3 than for Layer 2. Layer 1 plausibly depends on primary (core) auditory cortex and the subcortical auditory pathway that feeds it, and Layer 3 on inferior frontal and wider prefrontal cortex in exchange with temporal cortex over the dorsal pathway. For Layer 2 we see three candidates, which are not mutually exclusive and all lie along the auditory-frontal route. First, Layer 2 may be implemented in higher-tier auditory cortex. Primate auditory cortex is itself hierarchical: processing passes from core to belt to parabelt fields, and prefrontal cortex receives auditory input mainly from the belt and parabelt rather than from the core (; ). Learned sequencing rules modulate responses and oscillatory coupling in auditory cortex in both humans and macaques (), and in marmosets deviance signals originate in the parabelt (), so grouping over short spans need not await frontal input. Second, Layer 2 may reside in inferior frontal cortex, in neuronal populations hierarchically related to those serving Layer 3, much as simple and complex cells represent successive stages of processing within primary visual cortex (). Inferior frontal cortex shows gradation of this kind: local transitions engage the frontal operculum, whereas hierarchical dependencies engage Broca's area, and the two regions differ in structural connectivity (). More broadly, the frontal lobe has been proposed to be organized along a rostro-caudal gradient of increasingly abstract control (). Third, Layer 2 may be a property of the interaction between auditory and inferior frontal cortex rather than of either region alone, with groupings stabilized by brief exchanges over the dorsal pathway. The three possibilities make different predictions. If the first holds, grouping signatures, such as sensitivity to metrical accent or to phrase boundaries, should be present in higher-tier auditory cortex and persist when frontal input is reduced; if the second, they should dissociate from Layer 3 signatures along the inferior frontal gradient; if the third, they should scale with fronto-temporal coupling rather than with activity in either region alone. The hypothesis concerns the computations and their depth, and does not depend on which of these implementations carries Layer 2.

Rhythmic priming provides the most direct experimental evidence bearing on the hypothesis. In the typical paradigm, participants listen to a short musical sequence with a regular or an irregular metrical structure and then judge the grammaticality of spoken sentences. Performance was better after regular than after irregular primes in French-speaking children with typical development, developmental language disorder, or dyslexia (), and regular primes also improved performance relative to an environmental-sound baseline in children with specific language impairment, showing that the effect reflects a benefit of regularity and not only a cost of irregularity (). In Hungarian-speaking preschoolers with and without developmental language disorder, regular primes improved grammaticality judgments relative to both irregular primes and silence, but did not affect picture naming or a nonverbal Stroop task (). At the neural level, regular primes enlarged the P600 to grammatical errors in adults with and without dyslexia (). When auditory primes preceded sentences presented visually, word by word, to Russian-speaking adolescents, a late negativity to ungrammatical words appeared only after irregular primes, which the authors interpret as increased processing demand (); the influence of rhythm therefore crosses modalities.

The effect is not always found.  did not observe it in English-speaking children aged 7 to 12 years, for grammaticality judgments or for sentence comprehension, and in adults judging Jabberwocky sentences, which have ordinary syntax but nonsense content words, the effect was confined to the first few sentences after a prime ().  point to design differences, including added delays between primes and sentences, that may explain the null result, since prime effects decay over time. Our model offers an account of both the effect and its fragility. A regular prime engages predictive entrainment to a metrical hierarchy, the Layer 3 operation that we propose is shared with syntactic structure building; if that operation remains engaged when the sentences arrive, syntactic prediction should benefit. Three consequences follow. The effect should be specific to tasks that require structural prediction, which fits its absence for picture naming and nonverbal control tasks (). It should decay as the entrained state dissipates, which fits the short-lived effect and the sensitivity to added delays (; ). And it should be larger where Layer 3 prediction is weaker or less automatic, which fits the benefits reported for children with developmental language disorders. This third consequence might suggest that older typically developing children, whose syntactic prediction is more robust, gain less. Age alone cannot explain the English null result, however, since typically developing French-speaking children of similar ages benefited (), so the third consequence is a prediction to be tested rather than an explanation of existing data. Taken together, the rhythmic priming literature is consistent with the model, and its mixed pattern across languages, ages, and designs means it does not yet provide strong support for it.

Rhythm is not the only musical dimension linked to syntax. Harmonic structure in Western tonal music is also hierarchical, and violations of harmonic expectancy elicit an early right anterior negativity. When chord sequences were presented simultaneously with visually presented sentences, harmonically irregular chords reduced the left anterior negativity elicited by syntactic errors in language, indicating that the two draw on shared processing resources (), as the shared syntactic integration resource hypothesis proposed ();  review this work within a broader account of sequential prediction. Implicit knowledge of harmonic syntax is present by 30 months (). This evidence is compatible with our model, and it clarifies what the model does and does not claim. Harmonic expectancy concerns what is expected, a particular chord function; metrical expectancy concerns when an event is expected. Our hypothesis is specifically about the temporal component: predictive entrainment to meter supplies a scaffold that Layer 3 uses to anticipate when structurally important events will occur. On our account, harmonic-syntactic interactions would reflect the content side of the same domain-general Layer 3 prediction rather than entrainment. The model therefore predicts that rhythmic and harmonic manipulations affect linguistic syntax through partly different routes: rhythmic effects should depend on timing and on the regularity of the prime, whereas harmonic effects should depend on structural expectancy independent of timing. A design that crosses the two manipulations could test this.

Beyond these two lines of work, if top-down prediction at Layer 3 is central, the system should be flexible across domains, modalities, and speakers. Work on transfer, on multimodal integration, and on talker-specific adaptation is consistent with this, although none of it tests the shared-resource claim directly.

Musical experience relates to speech processing.  found that adults with more musical training, finer pitch discrimination, and better melodic memory perceived prosody in Mandarin-accented English more accurately, and that this tracked more robust neural encoding of sound. Patel's OPERA hypothesis offers a mechanism: because music and speech share auditory networks, and music places higher precision demands on them, musical experience can sharpen those networks and speech then benefits (). Here the active ingredient is pitch and melody rather than meter, so this work shows that musical experience can benefit speech processing without bearing on meter specifically. Whether rhythm-specific training transfers to syntax is treated as Prediction 4 below.

Entrainment is multimodal.  showed that co-speech gestures congruent with speech improve cortical tracking of the speech envelope, while incongruent gestures degrade it. The predictive system is not tied to one channel but integrates timing across modalities, consistent with the domain-general character of Layer 3.

Prediction is rapidly tuned to the talker.  recorded responses to subject-verb agreement errors in native and Mandarin-accented English. Errors typical of the accent and errors not typical of it elicited different neural responses, and effects could begin before the violation itself. Listeners build a model of the speaker and use it to predict morphosyntactic form. Agreement is not hierarchical structure building in itself, but it depends on it, since subject and verb must be related through syntactic structure; this is therefore structure-dependent prediction rather than lexical prediction alone, consistent with Layer 3 operating online in language.

The account makes five falsifiable predictions, each testing a distinct component of the model.

Prediction 1 (cross-species; tests the Layer 1 versus Layer 3 distinction). Non-human primates should show stimulus-driven tracking of regular input, a Layer 1 signature, and prediction over regularities spanning one or two levels, but not endogenous anticipation of a metrical beat or of deeply nested structure, the signatures of a fully developed Layer 3, and no link between beat processing and hierarchical sequencing. The first two parts of this prediction have already received support: macaques show neural sensitivity to isochrony without evidence of beat perception (), their timing falls furthest short of human performance when a rhythm must be continued without external pacing (), and marmosets show two-level sequence prediction within a fronto-temporal hierarchy (). What remains untested is the third part, together with the mechanism the account proposes for all three: that the depth of prediction scales with the strength of the dorsal pathway. If the functional-extension hypothesis is correct, fronto-temporal connectivity measured by diffusion MRI should predict the depth of predictive timing measured by EEG, within and across species, including marmosets, using stimuli matched to . A null result here, with connectivity unrelated to predictive depth, would count against the model. As  cautioned, identifying functional homologs across species is methodologically challenging, so an absent link could reflect a true species difference or a measurement limitation.

Prediction 2 (developmental; tests the timing of the coupling). The association between beat-evoked predictive responses and syntactic processing should emerge, or strengthen markedly, as fronto-temporal white matter matures, rather than being present at full strength from the start. We do not fix the age of onset in advance. Because beat sensitivity and temporal prediction are present in infancy, the appropriate design is longitudinal and should begin early, ideally in the second or third year when measurable syntax first appears, and continue into the early school years, combining EEG measures of beat-based prediction, measures of syntactic processing suited to each age, and diffusion MRI. The model predicts an age-dependent change in the strength of the association that covaries with fronto-temporal maturation. A stable association across the whole range, or a change unrelated to white-matter maturation, would count against it. Covariation of this kind would be consistent with the proposed mechanism but would not show that maturation causes the coupling; establishing that would require converging evidence, for instance from children whose fronto-temporal maturation is atypical, such as those born preterm.

Prediction 3 (clinical; tests Layer 3 integrity). The atypical rhythm risk hypothesis already predicts elevated rates of rhythm difficulty in developmental language disorder (). Our model turns this into a differential prediction. If language deficits arise partly from insufficient Layer 3 predictive control, children with developmental language disorder should show reduced beat-evoked predictive responses relative to age-matched peers, with a larger reduction for complex, metrically structured rhythms than for isochronous ones. Whether rhythmic deficits in this population are specific or domain-general remains debated; our model predicts difficulty specifically on tasks requiring active predictive entrainment rather than passive timing detection. Equivalent deficits on both task types would instead indicate a general timing impairment at Layer 1 and would not support the layered account.

Prediction 4 (intervention; tests Layer 3 plasticity). Much of the evidence linking musical experience to speech processing concerns pitch and melody (; ); our model predicts that rhythm-based hierarchical prediction, engaging the same Layer 3 mechanisms, should yield comparable effects. Training that systematically engages hierarchical temporal prediction, such as complex rhythmic sequence production or meter-based synchronization, should improve syntactic processing more than training engaging only low-level timing such as isochronous tapping. A randomized pre-post design can isolate the prediction-specific component. Rhythmic priming offers a short-term version of the same test: primes that engage multi-level metrical prediction should facilitate syntactic processing more than equally regular but metrically flat primes, such as an isochronous pulse. If training or priming that engages hierarchical prediction produces no greater gain in syntactic processing than matched low-level timing conditions, the plasticity claim fails.

Prediction 5 (dissociation; tests whether the resource is genuinely shared). The most direct test of the shared-resource claim comes from selective musical deficits. Congenital amusia in its common form is a disorder of fine-grained pitch, so amusic individuals with intact syntactic processing do not bear on our claim. Beat deafness is the relevant case.  documented an individual who synchronized near-normally to a metronome yet could not find and lock onto the beat of music, with pitch processing spared. On our account that dissociation is informative: tracking an isochronous acoustic pulse is a Layer 1 function and was preserved, whereas extracting and predicting metrical structure from a complex musical signal engages Layers 2 and 3 and was not. The model therefore predicts that beat-deaf individuals should show measurable deficits in syntactic prediction, most clearly for complex embedded structures and under working-memory load, even where everyday comprehension is unimpaired. The falsification condition needs to be stated carefully. If beat-deaf individuals show impaired predictive entrainment for the musical beat yet entirely typical syntactic prediction, the claim that one predictive resource serves both domains cannot be sustained in the form proposed here. A deficit confined to Layer 2 metrical grouping, leaving Layer 3 prediction intact, would carry no such consequence, so the test requires measures that separate the two layers rather than a global index of rhythm ability. Documented cases are rare, so this will require group studies of poor beat-finders or detailed single-case work.

Predictions 2 and 5 are the most consequential. Prediction 2 bears on the developmental claim that distinguishes this account from existing comparative frameworks; Prediction 5 bears on the shared-resource claim at its core. Failure of either would require substantial revision.

separates the empirical findings on which the account rests from the inferences and hypotheses it adds. Several limitations follow from that separation. The evolutionary claim rests on an inference from comparative anatomy to function: the arcuate fasciculus gradient across primates is well established, but no study has yet shown that its strength predicts the depth of predictive timing, and that inferential step is the most exposed point in the account. The developmental claim rests on a cross-sectional correlation in twenty-five children, so when the beat-grammar association emerges is a hypothesis rather than an established finding, and the age ranges in  are illustrative. The most direct experimental evidence, rhythmic priming, has not replicated uniformly across languages, ages, and designs (). Layer 2 is the least constrained component: we attribute rudimentary structural grouping to other primates, but the comparative evidence bearing directly on that operation, as distinct from interval timing, remains thin, and its anatomical implementation is open among the three candidates set out in Section 5. The boundary between genuine oscillatory entrainment and regular stimulus-evoked sampling is also unresolved; our functional argument does not depend on settling it, though a definitive account of the mechanism will. Finally, we have deliberately scoped the evolutionary claim to the cortical auditory-motor route, leaving the integration of subcortical timing networks for future work.

Beat perception and syntactic processing share more than a passing resemblance, and we have argued that they may draw on one predictive system with a long evolutionary history. In evolution, prefrontal expansion plausibly enabled an ancient auditory-motor pathway to support hierarchical prediction, with the human arcuate fasciculus as an anatomical signature. Comparative frameworks have established that beat-based timing is enhanced in humans relative to other primates; we have proposed that the same enhancement underwrites linguistic hierarchy, so that the two capacities would be expressions of one system. In development, beat sensitivity and temporal prediction are present from infancy, and we hypothesize that their coupling to syntax emerges as the fronto-temporal pathway matures. The three-layer model distinguishes what is ancient and broadly shared from what is fully developed in humans and slow to deepen, ties each layer to a measurable neural signature, and yields five predictions that could falsify it. When a preschooler synchronizes her movements to a steady musical beat, actively tracking and predicting its timing, she may be exercising the predictive control circuitry she will later recruit to embed a relative clause within a complex sentence.

neuroscience.title: Cystoventriculo-Peritoneal Shunt for a Giant Bifrontal Arachnoid Cyst: When Imaging Guides Surgery
neuroscience.abstract: The management of intracranial arachnoid cysts (IACs) represents a significant neurosurgical challenge due to the rarity and complexity of this pathology. Surgical intervention is reserved for symptomatic cases. We report the case of an adult patient with a giant bifrontal arachnoid cyst who was treated with a cystoventriculo-peritoneal (CVP) shunt. The selection of the surgical approach guided by neuroimaging was discussed.A 51-year-old woman initially presented with progressive psychomotor impairment, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and seizures developing over several years. A neuronavigated CVP shunt with a programmable valve was performed to establish a pressure equilibrium between the cyst and the ventricular system while minimizing the risk of overdrainage.Image-guided surgery that integrates high-resolution neuroimaging with cerebrospinal fluid flow studies represents a relatively novel approach in the management of IACs. Although several surgical strategies have been described in the literature, the optimal treatment modality remains a matter of debate. A patient-specific approach based on detailed neuroimaging is crucial to optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing the risk of complications.
neuroscience.text:
Intracranial arachnoid cysts (IACs) represent approximately 1% of intracranial lesions. Generally benign, these cysts can be congenital or acquired, with a prevalence of 2.6% in children and 1.4% in adults. They originate from the split or duplication of the arachnoid membrane surrounding the subarachnoid space. Four mechanisms have been advocated in literature: (1) fluid generated by cyst wall, (2) osmotic gradient allowing fluid flow through the cyst wall, (3) slit valve mechanism, and (4) cerebral lobe agenesis.

Clinical symptoms generally result from compression of adjacent brain parenchyma or obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pathways. Bilateral frontal extension of the IACs, particularly in adults, is uncommon compared with those located in the middle or posterior cranial fossae. Their management remains controversial. Neuroimaging is crucial in selecting the surgical approach for accurately delineating the anatomical and hydrodynamic relationships between the cyst and the ventricular system. Surgery aims to relieve the mass effect and to restore the CSF dynamics. A variety of techniques have been described, including microsurgical or endoscopic fenestration or excision of the cyst wall, as well as cystoperitoneal (CP) shunt or cystoventricular drainage. In this article, we report the case of an adult patient with a giant symptomatic bifrontal arachnoid cyst evaluated using a radiological protocol that combined: (1) three-dimensional constructive interference in steady state (3D CISS) imaging, (2) CSF flow studies performed using a steady-state gradient-echo (time-reversed PSIF) sequence at 3T. Based on these findings, the patient was treated with a cystoventriculo-peritoneal (CVP) shunt. The principles underlying our neuroimaging-based surgical decision-making were also discussed.

A 51-year-old female presented with progressive psychomotor and memory impairment, gait disturbances, and seizures. Neuropsychological assessment demonstrated severe executive dysfunction, marked short- and long-term memory deficits, and behavioral changes.

No ophthalmological abnormalities were reported at the time of admission. The patient was under regular ophthalmological follow-up for refractive errors. Fundus examination was not performed during hospitalization, as the patient reported having recently undergone a comprehensive ophthalmological examination, with no significant funduscopic abnormalities detected.

Electroencephalography revealed epileptogenic abnormalities in the left frontal region. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a giant frontobasal cyst (preoperative volume: 31.15 cm
3
) with bilateral extension, markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, without wall enhancement. High-resolution imaging (CISS sequence) and CSF flow studies (time-reversed PSIF) combined at 3T showed the absence of communication between the cyst and the ventricular system (

). In view of the absence of communication with the ventricular system, the potential role of acetazolamide treatment was considered limited.

Lumbar puncture to assess baseline ICP and evaluate the effects of CSF drainage was not performed because of the uncertain correlation between lumbar opening pressure, intracystic pressure, and intracranial pressure, as well as concerns about potentially destabilizing CSF dynamics in the presence of a mass effect.

A CVP shunt was inserted and connected to a programmable valve, with the opening pressure set at 150 mm H
2
O to minimize the risk of overdrainage and to maintain equilibrium between the pressures within the cyst and ventricular system, and to create a valve-controlled CSF diversion. The procedure was performed using a single neuronavigated catheter connecting the cyst to the right frontal ventricle, which was then connected to the valve to drain into the peritoneal cavity.

Postoperatively, the patient experienced a remarkable improvement of symptoms. The shunt was correctly positioned within the cyst extending into the right lateral ventricle (

and

). Postoperative imaging, using a coregistration fusion method as previously described,

confirmed a significant reduction in cyst volume and a decreased mass effect, without complications (

). At 1-year follow-up, the MRI revealed a cyst volume of 23.25 cm
3
. A significant improvement in executive functions, memory performance, and behavioral symptoms was reported.

Arachnoid cysts arise from congenital splitting of the arachnoid membrane, resulting in the accumulation of CSF within the duplicated layer. They occur most commonly in the middle cranial fossa (49%), followed by posterior fossa (38%).

Surgical treatment is indicated for symptomatic lesions. Frontal bilateral location in adult patients is rare. Preoperative imaging evaluation is crucial for guiding treatment decision-making. Particularly, CSF flow MRI is useful for demonstrating a potential communication between the cyst and the subarachnoid spaces. As part of the preoperative assessment, we notably performed CISS and PSIF sequences. These sequences are both steady-state gradient-echo imaging techniques. The CISS sequences provide high-fluid contrast, lack of sensitivity to CSF flow, and very high spatial resolution. In contrast, the PSIF sequence demonstrates extreme sensitivity to CSF flow, with high three-dimensional resolution.

Therefore, these sequences are highly complementary for ruling out a potential communication between the arachnoid cyst and the subarachnoid spaces. In our case, the protocol combining high-resolution imaging (CISS sequence) and CSF flow studies (time-reversed PSIF) at 3T revealed the absence of communication between the cyst and the ventricle. A CVP shunt was placed connected to a programmable valve with an opening pressure set at 150 mm H
2
O, draining into the peritoneal cavity. A single neuronavigation-guided catheter, connecting the cyst and the frontal ventricle, established a pressure equilibrium between the cyst and the ventricular system. The programmable valve facilitated the adequate drainage to improve the preoperative symptoms. The rationale for our strategy was not merely to decompress the cyst, but also to regulate CSF diversion and mitigate the risk of overdrainage. The valve-mediated system was selected to provide a controlled path for CSF diversion rather than relying exclusively on an internal fenestration between the cyst and the ventricular and cisternal compartments. To detect subtle postoperative changes in cyst size, we applied an automated MR coregistration-fusion method on 3D FLAIR.

A significant reduction of cyst volume and mass effect on brain tissue was detected. Several surgical alternatives have been described to treat the IACs including cystoperitoneal (CP) and cystoventricular (CV) shunt, endoscopic cyst fenestration, needle aspiration, cyst excision, and marsupialization. In cases of large intraventricular arachnoid cysts, operating via endoscope may provide a clear advantage especially for large IACs.

However, it demands advanced surgical skills due to limited visibility and the challenge of manipulating a single instrument, particularly in case of thick cystic walls. CP shunt is used in patients who present symptoms of hydrocephalus or increased intracranial pressure, while for patients presenting with intracranial bleeding the microsurgical resection is preferred. Microsurgical fenestration of large IACs into the ventricular system and the basal cisterns represents an established treatment option. However, open resection was generally associated with a higher rate of postoperative complications and prolonged hospitalization and recovery as well as with a lower short-term event-free survival at 12 months, particularly for small IACs. Conversely, shunt procedures were associated with more favorable long-term outcomes at the 4-year follow-up.

A recent study by Merola et al

indicates that CP shunt is a safe and effective procedure with relatively low morbidity and mortality rates. It facilitates the gradual CSF drainage from the cyst into the peritoneal cavity, alleviating symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. Although the shunt is not directly affected by intracranial pressure outside the cyst, the cyst pressure remains lower than that in the ventricles. Consequently, one of the major potential complications of this procedure is the overdrainage, which may lead to subdural hematomas or hygromas due to pressure differentials between the various intracranial CSF compartments.

In our case, a communication was established between the two compartments through the catheter, reducing pressure within the ventricular system while increasing it within the cyst associated to valve-regulated CSF drainage into the peritoneal cavity. By eliminating the pressure gradient between the two compartments, symptoms improved while avoiding overdrainage. Therefore, the use of a single catheter connecting the cyst and the ventricular cavity obviates the need for connectors or other adjunctive materials, reducing the risk of shunt dysfunction. Magneli et al

reported a series of patients treated by CV drainage performed with a ventricular catheter placed into the cyst and another in one of the lateral ventricles connected each other extracranially via a straight metal connector followed by a subgaleal tunneling. They created a communication between the IAC and the ventricular system achieving the cyst volume decrease without valve placement. This approach resulted in an improvement in preoperative symptoms related to the smaller cyst volume reported in their series compared to our case. There is a paucity of literature regarding the use of CVP shunt as a first-line surgical intervention for giant IACs. Lee et al

reported a case of Dandy–Walker malformation with syringomyelia, initially treated with a CP shunt and later revised by insertion of a VP shunt connected to the existing CP shunt via a Y-shaped connector. In our case, the absence of communication between the cyst and the lateral ventricle guided the decision to realize a CVP shunt using a single neuronavigation-guided catheter with a programmable valve as the primary treatment. Given the cyst size, the adjustable valve was used to maintain sustained CSF diversion, appropriate to achieve a long-term symptomatic improvement. We hypothesized that a CV or CP shunt alone would be inadequate to allow a progressive cyst reduction and symptom relief considering the cyst volume and the associated mass effect. The drainage of cyst fluid into the ventricular system induced a physiological change that prevented a pressure gradient, maintained a permanent fistula between the two compartments, and reduced the risk of cyst collapse and overdrainage

A comprehensive neuroimaging workup, combining high-resolution imaging (CISS sequence) and CSF flow studies (PSIF sequence), is essential for defining the fluidodynamic and anatomical relationships between the cyst and the ventricles, and for guiding the optimal treatment selection. The CVP shunt, using a single neuronavigation-guided catheter with an adjustable valve, represents a valid and effective therapeutic option to treat giant IACs. By equalizing the pressure gradient between the ventricles and the cyst and providing sustained CSF diversion through the adjustable valve, this approach led to significant improvement of preoperative symptoms avoiding complications.

neuroscience.title: A thalamus-centered network model of restless legs syndrome: an integrative hypothesis illustrated by three clinical phenotypes
neuroscience.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a clinically heterogeneous sensorimotor disorder whose pathophysiology reflects interacting biological mechanisms rather than a single causal pathway. Established influences—including brain iron biology, dopaminergic regulation, glutamatergic and GABAergic balance, adenosinergic inhibition, and abnormal afferent processing—have typically been studied in isolation, leaving their systems-level relationships insufficiently integrated. To motivate a network-based interpretation, we present three illustrative clinical phenotypes: dopamine-agonist augmentation, sensory-predominant RLS with inadequate response to pregabalin, and persistent symptoms despite partial correction of peripheral iron deficiency. These cases highlight how distinct upstream contexts can converge on similar sensory and sleep-physiological endpoints. Human neuroimaging and neurochemical studies provide convergent evidence for thalamic involvement in RLS, including altered thalamic connectivity, differences in thalamic nuclei and network organization, and increased thalamic glutamate/glutamine signal associated with disturbed sleep. Because the thalamus integrates sensory gating, motor modulation, arousal regulation, and sleep–wake stability, it represents a plausible convergence hub for upstream biological influences. We therefore propose a thalamus-centered convergence model in which iron deficiency, dopaminergic instability, glutamatergic hyperresponsiveness, reduced adenosinergic inhibition, altered GABAergic modulation, and abnormal afferent processing interact to increase the susceptibility of thalamo-cortical networks to sensory and arousal instability. The model does not replace established frameworks; instead, it organizes them within a unified, testable network architecture. We outline six falsifiable predictions for multimodal imaging, sleep microstructure, sensory physiology, and treatment-response studies, providing a structured basis for future mechanistic investigation of RLS.
neuroscience.text:
Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common chronic sensorimotor disorder defined clinically by an urge to move the legs accompanied by unpleasant sensations that begin or worsen during rest, are at least partially relieved by movement, and show a characteristic evening or nighttime predominance (). Diagnosis remains primarily clinical, based on the International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG) criteria (). Although RLS was historically conceptualized as a dopaminergic disorder, contemporary evidence supports a broader, hierarchical biological framework (; ; ; ). A conceptual hierarchy of mechanisms can be recognized. Brain iron biology influences dopaminergic regulation (), and dopaminergic dynamics interact with glutamatergic, GABAergic, and adenosinergic systems (; ; ). These neurochemical processes converge on sensory, arousal, and sleep-related network dynamics, producing the heterogeneous clinical and polysomnographic manifestations of RLS (; ; ; ). This systems-level perspective is supported by multimodal MRI, neurophysiological studies, and sensory-processing research, all of which emphasize distributed network involvement rather than dysfunction of a single transmitter or anatomical structure (; ; ; ; ; ). This broader view is clinically relevant. The 2025 American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) guideline strongly supports gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil, pregabalin, and intravenous ferric carboxymaltose in appropriate adults, while advising against the long-term use of pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, or levodopa because of augmentation risk (). The shift away from chronic dopamine-agonist therapy reinforces the distinction between symptomatic dopaminergic responsiveness and the underlying pathophysiology of RLS (; ). Among the structures repeatedly implicated in neuroimaging and neurochemical studies, the thalamus is of particular interest. It participates simultaneously in sensory gating, thalamo-cortical rhythmicity, motor-network modulation, arousal regulation, and sleep stability—domains that closely mirror the clinical phenotype of RLS (; ; ; ). Several studies have reported altered thalamic connectivity, metabolic abnormalities, differences in thalamic nuclei or network organization, and increased thalamic glutamate/glutamine signal associated with disturbed sleep (; ; ; ; ; ; ). Although structural and iron-related findings are heterogeneous across methods and cohorts (; ; ), the thalamus remains a plausible site where multiple upstream mechanisms may converge. Previous network-based models—including sensorimotor–limbic frameworks (), multimodal MRI syntheses (), and models of altered sensory processing and central sensitization (; ; )—highlight heterogeneity across imaging modalities and support a systems-level interpretation of RLS. The present model does not aim to relocate RLS to the thalamus; rather, it proposes the thalamus as a convergence hub where dopaminergic, iron-related, sensory, and arousal-linked mechanisms may interact (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). This conceptualization adds value by integrating established mechanisms into a unified network architecture and by specifying how thalamo-cortical dynamics may amplify symptom expression across different clinical phenotypes. The purpose of this article is therefore not to argue that RLS is a primary thalamic disorder. Instead, we propose that the thalamus may function as a convergence point at which several established or proposed RLS mechanisms interact at the network level (; ; ; ; ; ; ). Three contrasting clinical phenotypes are used to illustrate phenotypic convergence despite different upstream biological contexts; the conceptual model itself is grounded in published neuroimaging, neurochemical, and neurophysiological evidence (; ; ; ; ; ; ). Unlike previous RLS models that primarily emphasize individual neurotransmitter systems or distributed network abnormalities, the present framework proposes a specific convergence architecture in which thalamo-cortical network state functions as a measurable integrative variable linking iron biology (; ; ), dopaminergic dynamics (; ), sensory processing (; ; ), hyperarousal (; ; ), and sleep instability (; ; ; ).

The proposed thalamus-centered convergence model is not intended as a reformulation of established RLS mechanisms, nor as a claim of a single anatomical origin. Its conceptual contribution lies in specifying how well-recognized upstream influences—iron biology, dopaminergic dynamics, glutamatergic–GABAergic balance, adenosinergic inhibition, and abnormal afferent processing—may interact within a unified, testable network architecture. Rather than treating these mechanisms as parallel, independent modules, the model identifies thalamo-cortical network state as a measurable integrative variable through which upstream biological contexts can converge on similar sensory and sleep-physiological endpoints. This constitutes the conceptual “step” beyond existing frameworks: the model does not relocate RLS to the thalamus, but defines a convergence architecture that links distributed mechanisms to shared clinical manifestations.

The three clinical phenotypes were selected according to predefined, mechanistically informative criteria—dopamine agonist augmentation, sensory-predominant RLS with inadequate α2δ-ligand response, and persistent symptoms despite partial correction of peripheral iron deficiency. These phenotypes represent distinct upstream biological contexts that are well recognized in clinical practice and relevant to mechanistic interpretation. Because the purpose of the cases is hypothesis generation rather than population inference, targeted phenotypic selection is methodologically appropriate. Each patient underwent standardized neurological evaluation, laboratory assessment of iron-related parameters, and polysomnography, providing objective metrics of sensory burden, sleep continuity, and PLMS activity. These measures are sufficient to illustrate phenotypic convergence without implying causal localization.

The falsifiable predictions outlined in Section 6 specify the types of multimodal imaging, sleep-microstructure, and sensory-physiology metrics that could validate or refute the proposed convergence architecture. These predictions do not require assumptions about primary thalamic pathology; instead, they define measurable network-level signatures—such as multivariate thalamic connectivity patterns, state-dependent thalamo-cortical gating, and neurochemical correlates of hyperarousal—that can be empirically tested in future studies. This approach provides conceptual rigor while acknowledging the heterogeneity of RLS and the limitations of current evidence.

To illustrate how the proposed thalamo-cortical convergence framework manifests in real-world clinical settings, we present three hypothesis-generating clinical phenotypes. These cases were selected because they represent distinct upstream biological contexts—dopamine agonist augmentation, a sensory-predominant phenotype with limited response to an α2δ ligand, and persistent RLS despite partial correction of peripheral iron deficiency—yet converge on a shared pattern of sensory disturbance and sleep instability. Their purpose is not to establish causal mechanisms, but to demonstrate how heterogeneous clinical presentations may align with the network-based model introduced above. The three patients fulfilled IRLSSG diagnostic criteria () and underwent neurological assessment, laboratory evaluation of iron-related parameters, and polysomnography (PSG) as clinically indicated. Electroneurography was performed to exclude clinically relevant peripheral neuropathy. These observations are presented as hypothesis-generating clinical illustrations, not as a formal case series designed to test the proposed model. The selection of the three patients was methodologically appropriate and aligned with the purpose of the manuscript. The aim was not to construct a representative case series, but to illustrate how distinct upstream biological contexts can converge on similar sensory and sleep-related endpoints. For this reason, patients were chosen according to predefined, clinically relevant phenotypic criteria: dopamine-agonist augmentation, a sensory-predominant phenotype with inadequate response to an α2δ ligand, and persistent RLS despite partial correction of peripheral iron deficiency. These phenotypes represent well-recognized and mechanistically informative RLS presentations. Given the heterogeneity of the RLS population, targeted phenotypic selection is an appropriate strategy for hypothesis-generating illustrations, and the manuscript explicitly avoids claims of population representativeness. No patient underwent thalamus-specific MRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, or neurophysiological measurement; therefore, no inference about individual thalamic dysfunction can be drawn.

A 62-year-old man first developed RLS symptoms at age 54. He described a deep, pulling, almost “magnet-like” discomfort in his calves that reliably appeared in the evening, typically when he tried to relax after work. The sensations built gradually over 20–30 min of rest and were strong enough to interrupt reading or watching television. Movement brought partial relief, but only for a few minutes. His medical history included long-standing hypertension and dyslipidemia, both well controlled. He had no history of neuropathy, diabetes, renal disease, or sleep apnea. Over the years he had tried several symptomatic treatments prescribed by his general neurologist, including low-dose clonazepam and intermittent levodopa, but pramipexole became his main therapy. He initially responded well, and the dose was slowly increased over several years without specialist follow-up, eventually reaching 1.08 mg/day. During this period, his symptoms changed in a way he found difficult to understand. The evening discomfort began creeping earlier into the afternoon, sometimes appearing while he was still at work. The sensations also spread from the calves toward the thighs, and he noticed a stronger, almost irresistible urge to move. He described this as “my legs waking up before I do.” These changes produced functional impairment: he struggled to sit through meetings, avoided long car rides, and felt increasingly anxious about evenings. Polysomnography showed marked PLMS activity and substantial sleep fragmentation, although respiratory parameters were normal (AHI < 5/h). Electroneurography did not demonstrate peripheral neuropathy. Iron parameters were within the reported range. Although rebound and natural disease progression were considered, the clear temporal association with dose escalation supported dopamine-agonist augmentation as the primary explanation.

This case illustrates dopamine-agonist–associated augmentation, a treatment-related complication rather than a distinct biological phenotype. Augmentation produces a recognizable pattern of network instability—earlier symptom onset, increased sensory burden, and sleep disruption—that is relevant to thalamo-cortical models of RLS (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Contemporary guidance advises against long-term pramipexole use because augmentation risk may outweigh sustained benefit in many patients ().

A 54-year-old man reported symptom onset at age 48. He described diffuse inner restlessness and poorly localized, pressure-like discomfort in the lower limbs, typically emerging in the late evening and worsening during periods of inactivity. Symptoms were sensory-predominant, with relatively little overt motor activity. He denied comorbidities such as diabetes, renal disease, neuropathy, or mood disorders. His IRLS score was 26/40.

Medication history included intermittent NSAID use for musculoskeletal pain and short-term zolpidem prescribed by his primary physician for sleep fragmentation. He had not previously received dopaminergic therapy. Pregabalin was initiated at 150 mg/day and titrated to 300 mg/day over 6 months without meaningful improvement. No other centrally acting medications were used.

Polysomnography showed relatively low PLMS activity but pronounced sleep fragmentation and reduced N3 sleep. Respiratory parameters were normal, with an AHI of 1.8/h and no clinically relevant desaturation. Night-to-night variability of PLMS was acknowledged; however, repeated polysomnography could not be performed because the patient declined further overnight testing due to work-related constraints. As a result, the reported PSG represents a single-night measurement. Iron parameters were within the reported range (ferritin 112 ng/mL, TSAT 28%), and ENG was normal, excluding clinically relevant peripheral neuropathy.

This phenotype highlights the dissociation between modest PLMS burden and substantial sensory symptoms and sleep disruption. It is therefore particularly relevant to models emphasizing sensory processing, arousal regulation, and thalamo-cortical integration rather than PLMS alone (; ; ; ).

In addition, this phenotype illustrates how sensory-predominant symptoms may interact with circadian modulation of thalamo-cortical gating, contributing to evening-dominant symptom expression—an aspect emphasized in contemporary sensory-processing and central-sensitization frameworks (; ; ).

32-year-old woman first developed RLS symptoms at age 29. She described a persistent, internal restlessness in her legs that reliably appeared in the evening, especially when she tried to unwind after work. The discomfort was not sharply localized; instead, it felt like a diffuse, rising tension that made it difficult to remain still. Movement provided brief relief, but the sensations returned within minutes. Her baseline IRLS score was 27/40, consistent with moderately severe symptoms.

She had no chronic medical conditions, no history of neuropathy, and no sleep-related breathing disorder. A routine internal-medicine evaluation performed shortly after symptom onset revealed peripheral iron deficiency. Her primary physician attributed this to heavy menstrual bleeding and suboptimal dietary iron intake—a pattern commonly seen in young women.

She completed 3 months of oral ferrous sulfate therapy (retard formulation equivalent to Tardyferon, 100 mg elemental iron daily) with excellent adherence. Follow-up laboratory testing 2 weeks after finishing therapy showed partial improvement of iron parameters (ferritin 58 → 92 μg/L; transferrin saturation 17 → 24%). Despite this biochemical change, her symptoms barely improved: her IRLS score decreased only slightly, from 27/40 to 25/40. She reported that evenings still felt “crowded inside my legs,” and she continued to struggle with settling into sleep.

Polysomnography demonstrated intermediate PLMS activity and substantial sleep fragmentation, although respiratory parameters were normal. Electroneurography did not show peripheral neuropathy. Her internist noted that while the iron indices had improved, they had not reached the thresholds typically associated with meaningful RLS symptom relief.

Although intravenous ferric carboxymaltose could have been considered according to contemporary AASM guidance, it was not administered because the patient had just completed her initial course of oral therapy, her iron parameters showed partial improvement rather than clear deficiency, and reassessment occurred shortly after treatment completion. Intravenous iron was therefore deferred in favor of continued monitoring, given the early stage of correction and the known risks of infusion reactions.

This case illustrates that improvement of peripheral iron indices does not necessarily parallel symptom resolution. The observed changes in ferritin and transferrin saturation represent partial correction of iron deficiency but do not establish adequate RLS-specific iron repletion according to contemporary AASM guidance, which considers IV iron when ferritin is 75–100 μg/L or transferrin saturation is below 20%.

Intravenous iron was explicitly considered but not administered. The patient had just completed her initial course of oral therapy, adherence was excellent, and the post-treatment values were interpreted as an early, partial response rather than a definitive indication for escalation. In addition, intravenous iron carries well-recognized risks of infusion reactions and other adverse events, which were taken into account. Reassessment occurred shortly after therapy completion, before determining whether a more sustained change in iron indices or symptoms would emerge.

This phenotype highlights that peripheral iron markers are imperfect surrogates for central iron biology, and that additional central mechanisms—including thalamo-cortical network factors—may contribute to symptom persistence (; ; ) (, ).

Laboratory parameters of iron metabolism in the three cases.

Polysomnographic characteristics.

Values are from baseline PSG examinations performed at diagnosis. Follow-up PSG was not available in every case. PSG parameters are reported as rounded values; therefore minor discrepancies between calculated and reported sleep measures may occur.

These three clinical cases are not part of a prospective research protocol but represent anonymized clinical case descriptions derived from routine diagnostic care. Under current Hungarian healthcare regulations, individual case reports that do not involve experimental intervention and contain fully anonymized patient data do not require separate ethics committee approval. All diagnostic procedures were performed as part of routine clinical care under the professional and ethical oversight of the Department of Neurology, University of Pécs. In accordance with institutional and national regulations, written informed consent for publication of the clinical information and electrophysiological findings was obtained from all patients. All procedures complied with the ethical standards of the institutional and national research committees and with the Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments.

The three phenotypes differ in biological context, symptom profile, and treatment response, yet they converge on two broad clinical outcomes: persistent sensorimotor discomfort and impaired sleep continuity. This convergence is most evident in the PSG data. Case 1 had a high PLMS index (62/h), whereas Case 2 had a much lower PLMS index (14/h) despite marked sensory symptoms and sleep fragmentation. Case 3 showed an intermediate PLMS index (28/h) with persistent symptoms after improvement of peripheral iron indices. These observations emphasize that PLMS burden, sensory symptom intensity, and sleep disruption are related but non-equivalent dimensions of RLS.

The cases therefore support only a modest inference: distinct upstream contexts can lead to superficially similar clinical and sleep-physiological endpoints. They do not identify where in the nervous system this convergence occurs. The thalamus-centered model proposed below is an attempt to connect this clinical convergence with independent evidence from RLS imaging, spectroscopy, and systems neurobiology.

A network interpretation is attractive because iron handling, dopaminergic signaling, glutamatergic and adenosinergic regulation, GABAergic modulation, sensory afference, and arousal mechanisms are unlikely to operate as isolated modules. Instead, they interact across cortico-striatal-thalamic, sensory, brainstem, and spinal systems (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). The central question is therefore not whether the thalamus is “the cause” of RLS, but whether thalamic networks represent one important site at which these influences become integrated into the sensory, motor, circadian, and sleep-related phenotype.

Sensory selection and gain control, coordination of cortico-subcortical communication, motor-loop integration, and the generation or modulation of thalamo-cortical rhythms relevant to sleep and arousal (; ; ; ). These functions overlap strikingly with the domains disturbed in RLS, including abnormal limb sensations, urge to move, time-of-day dependence, hyperarousal, sleep fragmentation, and periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS) (; ; ; ; ). This overlap motivates consideration of the thalamus as a potential convergence point rather than a primary lesion site. In this context, sensory gating refers to the thalamus’s state-dependent regulation of afferent input—the dynamic filtering, amplification, or suppression of sensory signals before they reach cortical targets. Rather than a static “on/off” mechanism, sensory gating is a network-level process influenced by dopaminergic tone, iron-dependent neurotransmission, glutamatergic–GABAergic balance, and circadian modulation. Altered gating may therefore manifest as increased sensory gain, reduced inhibitory control, or unstable thalamo-cortical coupling, all of which are relevant to the sensory discomfort, hyperarousal, and sleep fragmentation characteristic of RLS.

Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) studies have reported higher thalamic glutamate/glutamine (Glx) signal in RLS and an association between Glx and wake time during the sleep period, without a corresponding relationship to PLMS frequency (). The thalamic MRS finding reported by Allen et al. warrants cautious interpretation. The study examined right-sided thalamic ^1H-MRS in a relatively small sample (28 RLS patients and 20 controls), and although it demonstrated higher Glx/Cr ratios with an association to wake time, the evidence base remains limited. The study predates more recent multimodal imaging literature, and independent replication using contemporary MRS protocols has been sparse. Differences in voxel placement, acquisition parameters, spectral modeling, and quantification methods further complicate reproducibility. Importantly, MRS-derived Glx reflects a composite of glutamate and glutamine and does not directly measure synaptic glutamatergic firing or excitatory neurotransmission. These considerations support treating thalamic MRS findings as one contributory element, not a disproportionately weighted pillar of the overall model.

Functional connectivity studies have reported altered thalamic connectivity or network topology (; ; ; ; ), and metabolic imaging has demonstrated abnormal medial thalamic metabolism (). Structural findings are less uniform: some studies report thalamic or related gray-matter changes, whereas others find no consistent subcortical volumetric differences (; ; ; ; ). Collectively, these findings justify including the thalamus in mechanistic models, but they do not establish causality or identify a unique thalamic lesion.

Abnormal thalamic activity could be primary, compensatory, state-dependent, medication-related, or secondary to altered afferent input or cortical/striatal drive. Moreover, “thalamic involvement” may differ by nucleus and by symptom state. For these reasons, a thalamus-centered model should be understood as a convergence model, not a localization model.

Sensory gating refers to the thalamus’s ability to regulate the flow, amplification, and contextual weighting of ascending sensory signals, determining which inputs reach cortical awareness and with what salience. Abnormal central sensory processing and central sensitization have been reported in RLS (; ; ). An unstable thalamo-cortical gating state could amplify otherwise low-salience limb-related input, particularly under conditions of reduced external stimulation and increased symptom susceptibility in the evening or at night.

Circadian modulation of thalamo-cortical gating—partly influenced by evening increases in melatonin and reduced external sensory competition—may further amplify limb-related input, contributing to the characteristic nighttime predominance of RLS symptoms. This remains a mechanistic hypothesis rather than evidence of a demonstrated thalamic defect in individual patients.

Importantly, circadian influences on thalamo-cortical gating extend beyond reduced external stimulation at night. Dopaminergic tone follows a well-defined circadian rhythm, with an evening rise and a nocturnal decline, and this rhythm interacts with iron-dependent neurotransmission and glutamatergic–GABAergic balance. These state-dependent changes can alter thalamic gain control independently of environmental sensory load. Melatonin-related modulation of thalamic relay and reticular nuclei further contributes to increased sensory susceptibility in the evening. Thus, nighttime symptom exacerbation in RLS likely reflects a combination of reduced external sensory competition and intrinsic circadian modulation of thalamo-cortical gating, rather than the former alone.

The same caution applies to PLMS and arousal. PLMS can arise from spinal and supraspinal interactions, and their temporal coupling to cortical arousals is complex (; ). Thalamo-cortical systems are central to sleep microstructure and arousal transitions, but a PLMS-plus-arousal pattern is not specific evidence of thalamic pathology. The model therefore assigns the thalamus a modulatory and integrative role, rather than treating PLMS as a direct “thalamic motor output.”

In the proposed model, iron and dopamine are conceptualized as upstream modulators rather than primary lesion sites. ‘Upstream’ in this context means that these factors influence the operating state of broader neural circuits—including thalamo-cortical and cortico-striatal-thalamic loops—without themselves defining the location of symptom generation. Iron availability affects dopaminergic signaling, glutamatergic–GABAergic balance, and metabolic efficiency, while dopamine modulates excitability, gain control, and network stability. Through these mechanisms, iron and dopamine can shift the functional state of thalamic and striatal circuits, altering sensory gating, arousal regulation, and motor readiness. Thus, their role is to modify network dynamics that shape symptom expression, not to serve as isolated, localized causes of RLS.

Brain iron deficiency or impaired iron handling remains one of the most reproducible biological findings in RLS, although MRI-based iron measures vary substantially across methods and cohorts (; ; ; ; ). Iron is essential for dopamine synthesis, mitochondrial energetics, and multiple enzymatic processes. Dopaminergic abnormalities in RLS are dynamic rather than uniformly hypodopaminergic: treatment-related neuroadaptation, including augmentation during chronic dopamine-agonist exposure, reflects altered dopaminergic signaling rather than a fixed deficiency state (; ).

In the proposed model, iron biology and dopaminergic dynamics are upstream influences that modulate the excitability of cortico-striatal-thalamic and thalamo-cortical loops. This framing does not require that the primary iron or dopamine abnormality be located in the thalamus; rather, it recognizes that thalamic susceptibility may arise from distributed network effects.

The strongest neurochemical argument for thalamic involvement is the MRS finding of increased thalamic glutamate/glutamine (Glx) associated with disturbed sleep (). This result supports abnormal excitatory neurochemistry linked to hyperarousal, but MRS-derived Glx is a composite measure and does not directly reflect synaptic glutamatergic firing.

GABAergic findings are similarly nuanced: one study found no group-level difference in thalamic GABA but reported associations between thalamic GABA, PLMS, and symptom severity (; ), suggesting altered inhibitory modulation rather than a uniform reduction. For these reasons, the model uses the term altered glutamatergic–GABAergic balance, emphasizing excitatory–inhibitory instability rather than assuming a single direction of change across all patients.

A hypoadenosinergic state has been proposed as a mechanistic bridge linking iron deficiency, enhanced glutamatergic signaling, dopaminergic dysregulation, and hyperarousal (; ). Much of this evidence derives from experimental and corticostriatal models rather than direct thalamic measurements in RLS. We therefore treat adenosinergic influence on the thalamus as an indirect network-level hypothesis: reduced adenosinergic inhibition may increase the susceptibility of arousal and sensorimotor networks, including thalamo-cortical systems, without implying a primary thalamic abnormality.

RLS sensory symptoms are clinically central yet mechanistically difficult to localize. Neurophysiological and imaging studies support abnormalities of central sensory processing (; ; ), and recent work suggests that central sensitization is common and correlates with symptom burden in at least some RLS populations (; ; ). A thalamic convergence mechanism is plausible because ascending spinothalamic and lemniscal information is integrated with descending cortical, limbic, attentional, and arousal signals at multiple thalamic and thalamo-cortical levels (; ; ). The model therefore predicts an interaction between afferent drive and central gain, rather than a purely peripheral or purely thalamic origin of the sensory experience.

The lower-limb predominance of RLS invites a somatotopic explanation, but no direct RLS study has demonstrated selective dysfunction of lower-limb thalamic representations. The ventral posterior thalamic nuclei are somatotopically organized (; ; ), and state-dependent changes in sensory gain could theoretically affect body regions unequally (; ; ). At present, however, this remains a hypothesis of anatomical plausibility rather than an established explanation for symptom distribution. It is included here as a speculative component that may motivate future nucleus-resolved imaging or sensory-physiology studies.

Potential approaches to test this hypothesis include nucleus-resolved functional MRI combined with lower- and upper-limb sensory-stimulation paradigms. If lower-limb symptom predominance reflects somatotopically selective thalamic vulnerability, patients with RLS would be expected to show greater abnormalities in connectivity, sensory-evoked responses, or state-dependent activation within thalamic representations linked to the lower extremities compared with upper-limb representations. Complementary somatosensory evoked potential (SEP) testing with limb-specific stimulation (leg vs. arm) could further determine whether differences in central sensory conduction, gain, or habituation parallel symptom distribution. Together, these approaches would allow the proposed somatotopic bias to be examined empirically rather than treated as a purely conceptual model.

The proposed model can be summarized as follows: several pathobiological influences associated with RLS alter the excitability and gain of distributed sensorimotor and arousal networks (); thalamo-cortical systems are one anatomically and functionally plausible site at which these influences converge (; ; ; ). Brain iron deficiency, dynamic dopaminergic signaling, glutamatergic–GABAergic imbalance, adenosinergic disinhibition, and abnormal afferent processing are therefore conceptualized as interacting inputs rather than parallel independent causes (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). The resulting network state may facilitate sensory discomfort, urge to move, state-dependent motor phenomena, hyperarousal, and sleep fragmentation (; ; ; ; ; ).

A central strength of this formulation is that it separates evidence levels. Direct RLS-specific thalamic evidence includes MRS (), metabolic imaging (), and several connectivity/network studies (; ; ; ; ). Indirect evidence includes neurochemical and physiological mechanisms established in RLS but not specifically localized to the thalamus (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Speculative components include selective thalamic somatotopic vulnerability (; ; ), a causal role of thalamic activity in PLMS (; ), and therapeutic targeting of thalamic networks ().

This hierarchy is summarized in .

Evidence hierarchy for major components of the proposed thalamus-centered model.

The model is therefore intentionally asymmetric: the thalamus is “central” in the diagram because of its integrative position, not because every arrow has equal empirical support. This distinction is essential to falsifiability. If future multimodal studies show that symptom severity and sleep instability are better explained by non-thalamic network measures, or that thalamic abnormalities disappear after controlling for arousal state, medication, or sensory input, the model should be revised accordingly. Together, these graded evidence levels define the model’s empirical boundaries and lead directly to the testable hypotheses presented in Section 7.

To ensure conceptual precision, three methodological terms used in the hypotheses are defined below.

Multivariate thalamic connectivity measures refer to connectivity metrics derived from multiple analytic approaches—such as seed-based correlation, independent component analysis, and graph-theoretical indices—combined into a single multivariate model to characterize thalamic network state more comprehensively than any single metric alone.

Thalamo-cortical abnormality denotes a deviation from normative connectivity or network organization between thalamic nuclei and cortical regions, quantified through functional MRI, EEG-based network measures, or multimodal integration. The term refers to a state-dependent network deviation rather than a focal structural lesion.

Thalamic connectivity or neurochemical measures include functional connectivity metrics, MRS-derived neurochemical indices (e.g., Glx, GABA), and related multimodal parameters that characterize thalamic network excitability or excitatory–inhibitory balance.

Hypothesis: The magnitude of state-dependent thalamo-cortical connectivity abnormality is associated with RLS symptom burden and sleep instability.

Prediction: Multimodal neuroimaging will detect these abnormalities: functional MRI will quantify thalamo-cortical network state, while EEG will assess arousal-related and sensorimotor-gating dynamics. Together, multivariate thalamic connectivity measures will explain variance in IRLS score, evening symptom intensity, and objective sleep fragmentation after adjustment for age, sex, medication exposure, and PLMS burden.
