Hypothesis: Higher thalamic Glx is more closely related to hyperarousal and sleep instability than to the motor expression of PLMS.

Prediction: Thalamic Glx measured by MRS will correlate more strongly with wake after sleep onset, microarousal burden, spindle/CAP abnormalities, and sleep efficiency than with PLMS index. This extends the dissociation suggested by the original thalamic MRS study ().

Hypothesis: Thalamic sensory-gating and connectivity abnormalities are state-dependent and become more pronounced during the symptomatic evening/night period.

Prediction: Within the same untreated or stably treated patient, evening imaging or sensory-evoked paradigms will show greater thalamic or thalamo-cortical abnormality than morning measurements, and the within-person change will track the change in symptom intensity. This prediction is more directly testable than inferring circadian dopamine tone from symptoms alone.

Hypothesis: RLS symptom intensity reflects an interaction between sensory afferent processing and central thalamic gain rather than either factor alone.

Prediction: A model combining quantitative sensory or evoked-potential measures with thalamic fMRI/MRS metrics will explain clinical severity better than peripheral/sensory or thalamic measures considered separately. Experimental modulation of afferent input should alter thalamic responses in proportion to symptom change.

Hypothesis: If thalamo-cortical instability contributes to RLS-related sleep fragmentation, sleep microstructure should contain measurable signatures beyond conventional PLMS indices.

Prediction: Sleep spindle density, spindle spectral characteristics, cyclic alternating pattern (CAP), and microarousal measures will correlate with thalamic connectivity or neurochemical measures and will mediate part of the association between RLS severity and subjective sleep disturbance.

Hypothesis: If thalamic network dysfunction is a convergence phenomenon rather than a treatment-specific mechanism, successful therapies acting through different upstream pathways should share at least partial normalization of thalamic or thalamo-cortical biomarkers.

Prediction: In prospective studies, improvement after iron therapy, α2δ-ligand treatment, or other effective interventions will be associated with normalization of selected thalamic connectivity, MRS, or sleep-microstructure markers. Neuromodulation may be explored as a mechanistic probe, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend thalamic stimulation as an RLS treatment; the isolated report of improvement after thalamic DBS in essential-tremor patients should be regarded as hypothesis-generating only ().

The proposed thalamus-centered convergence model has several important limitations that define both its scope and its testability.

First, the three clinical phenotypes are illustrative rather than evidentiary. They lack thalamus-specific MRI, spectroscopy, or neurophysiological measurements and therefore cannot provide direct support for thalamic involvement. Their purpose is limited to demonstrating how distinct upstream biological contexts may converge on similar sensory and sleep-related outcomes.

Second, most published thalamic findings in RLS are cross-sectional and associative. Medication exposure, symptom state, sleep deprivation, comorbidities, and methodological differences may all influence connectivity, metabolic, or neurochemical measures, contributing to variability across studies (; ; ). Consequently, current evidence supports thalamic involvement but does not establish causality.

Third, structural and brain-iron findings remain heterogeneous. Contemporary multimodal MRI syntheses emphasize methodological variability and partial replication rather than a single reproducible anatomical signature. Findings may differ according to acquisition parameters, image analysis strategies, cohort composition, and disease phenotype.

Fourth, the term “thalamus” encompasses a highly heterogeneous collection of nuclei and circuits with distinct sensory, motor, cognitive, and arousal-related functions. Future investigations should therefore move beyond whole-thalamus analyses and incorporate nucleus-resolved connectivity, spectroscopy, quantitative susceptibility mapping, and state-dependent assessments.

Fifth, several components of the model remain indirect or speculative. The proposed role of adenosinergic mechanisms is supported primarily by broader RLS neurobiology rather than direct thalamic evidence. Likewise, lower-limb thalamic somatotopy and the contribution of thalamic networks to PLMS remain anatomically and physiologically plausible hypotheses that require targeted investigation.

Most importantly, the model does not assume that the thalamus is the sole or dominant convergence site in RLS. Cortico-striatal circuits, brainstem arousal systems, spinal mechanisms, and distributed sensory networks may contribute equally or even more strongly in specific patient subgroups. The value of the present framework therefore rests not on the centrality of the thalamus itself, but on whether its predictions can explain clinically meaningful variance beyond competing network models.

The model should ultimately be judged by its empirical performance: if thalamic network measures improve the explanation of symptom severity, sleep instability, phenotypic heterogeneity, or treatment response, the framework will gain support; if not, alternative convergence architectures should be favored.

RLS is best understood as a multilevel sensorimotor and sleep-related network disorder in which iron biology, dopaminergic dynamics, excitatory–inhibitory balance, adenosinergic regulation, sensory processing, and arousal interact (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). The thalamus represents a plausible convergence hub because it occupies a strategic position at the intersection of sensory gating, motor-loop modulation, thalamo-cortical rhythmicity, and sleep–wake regulation, and because direct RLS studies have identified thalamic neurochemical, metabolic, and connectivity abnormalities (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ).

The proposed thalamus-centered model does not suggest that the thalamus is the primary generator of RLS or that all patients share a single thalamic lesion. Its purpose is narrower: to outline how diverse upstream mechanisms may converge on thalamo-cortical network state in a subset of patients or symptom states, thereby linking sensory discomfort, hyperarousal, urge to move, and sleep fragmentation. The three clinical phenotypes illustrate why such convergence is clinically conceivable but do not constitute evidence for it.

The value of the model will depend on prospective falsification. Nucleus-resolved multimodal imaging, repeated morning–evening measurements, MRS combined with detailed PSG microstructure, sensory-challenge paradigms, and treatment-response studies can determine whether thalamic network markers explain clinically meaningful variance beyond PLMS and beyond competing non-thalamic models (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). If supported, this framework could help shift RLS research from single-transmitter explanations toward mechanism-based network phenotyping. Importantly, the model is not intended to prioritize the thalamus over other candidate convergence hubs, but to provide a testable framework whose explanatory and predictive value can be empirically compared with competing cortico-striatal, brainstem, or spinal network models (; ; ; ; ; ; ).

neuroscience.title: Clinical Characteristics and Interpretive Challenges of CSF Varicella-Zoster Virus Detection by Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing: A Retrospective Case Series
neuroscience.abstract: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) may cause heterogeneous central nervous system (CNS) manifestations, often without a typical herpes zoster rash. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) enables broad pathogen detection in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), but VZV reads may be difficult to interpret when additional microorganisms are detected or confirmatory testing is incomplete. This study described the clinical characteristics and interpretive challenges of patients with suspected CNS infection in whom VZV was detected in CSF by mNGS.This retrospective descriptive case series included patients evaluated at The Second Qilu Hospital of Shandong University from January 2019 to December 2024. Among 278 patients with suspected CNS infection who underwent CSF mNGS, 23 met the prespecified operational inclusion criteria. Clinical, CSF, neuroimaging, microbiological, treatment, and short-term outcome data were reviewed. Detected microorganisms were interpreted through integrated clinical assessment rather than sequencing findings alone. No comparison group was included.VZV reads meeting the inclusion criteria were detected in 23 of 278 patients (8.3%). The median age was 44 years, and 15 patients (65.2%) were male. Clinical syndromes spanned encephalitis, meningitis, meningoencephalitis, encephalomyelitis, and myelitis. A herpes zoster-associated rash was present in 10 patients (43.5%). All patients had CSF leukocytosis with lymphocytic predominance, and 21 (91.3%) had elevated CSF protein. VZV-specific polymerase chain reaction was not performed. Qualitative CSF anti-VZV IgM and IgG testing was performed in six patients, of whom two had positive IgM results. Additional microorganisms were co-detected in six patients, including Epstein–Barr virus, low-abundance herpes simplex virus type 1, and Listeria monocytogenes. The median Karnofsky Performance Status score at discharge was 90 (interquartile range, 90–100), with three patients (13.0%) scoring below 90.VZV detection by CSF mNGS occurred across heterogeneous neurological presentations, sometimes alongside additional microorganisms. VZV reads alone cannot establish pathogen causality, and their clinical significance requires integrated assessment of the neurological syndrome, CSF findings, neuroimaging, conventional microbiological investigations, immune status, co-detected microorganisms, and clinical course. The findings are descriptive and do not establish the diagnostic accuracy of mNGS.
neuroscience.text:
Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a neurotropic double-stranded DNA virus that establishes lifelong latency in cranial nerve ganglia, dorsal root ganglia, and autonomic ganglia after primary infection. Reactivation of latent VZV may cause herpes zoster and a broad spectrum of neurological complications, including meningitis, encephalitis, myelitis, vasculopathy, and cranial neuropathies.

The clinical presentation of VZV-related central nervous system (CNS) disease is heterogeneous. Patients may present with headache, fever, nausea, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures, focal neurological deficits, behavioral or cognitive disturbances, cranial nerve involvement, or acute myelopathy. These manifestations overlap with those of other viral or bacterial infections, autoimmune encephalitis, inflammatory disorders, and cerebrovascular disease. Moreover, a characteristic herpes zoster rash may be absent. In previous clinical series, cutaneous lesions were documented in fewer than half of patients with VZV CNS involvement, demonstrating that the absence of rash does not exclude VZV-related neurological disease., Consequently, early etiological attribution may be particularly difficult in patients with atypical neurological presentations or without concurrent cutaneous manifestations.

The diagnostic evaluation of suspected VZV CNS infection requires integration of the clinical syndrome, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammatory findings, neuroimaging, and microbiological evidence. VZV-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and assessment of intrathecal anti-VZV antibody production are commonly used diagnostic approaches. However, their relative diagnostic yield may vary according to the neurological syndrome, disease stage, timing of lumbar puncture, and prior antiviral treatment. For example, detection of intrathecal anti-VZV IgG may provide greater diagnostic sensitivity than CSF VZV DNA in patients with VZV vasculopathy. Therefore, negative results from a single microbiological assay may not be sufficient to exclude VZV-related CNS involvement, and laboratory findings should be interpreted in the appropriate clinical context. Timely etiological assessment is clinically important because delayed recognition of VZV-related CNS involvement may postpone antiviral treatment, whereas overinterpretation of nonspecific or co-detected microbial reads may lead to unnecessary or inappropriate antimicrobial therapy.

Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) enables broad, hypothesis-independent detection of microbial nucleic acids and has increasingly been incorporated into the diagnostic evaluation of patients with suspected meningitis, encephalitis, or myelitis. Prospective and large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated that CSF mNGS can identify pathogens missed by conventional investigations and provide clinically relevant microbiological information in diagnostically challenging CNS infections. Nevertheless, mNGS should be regarded as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, conventional microbiological testing. Detection of VZV reads in CSF does not independently establish that VZV is the causative pathogen. Interpretation may be complicated by low read counts, latent or bystander viral DNA, environmental or reagent contamination, incomplete confirmatory testing, and the concurrent detection of other microorganisms. In particular, Epstein–Barr virus and VZV have previously been identified together in patients with CNS infection, indicating that herpesvirus co-detection may represent clinically relevant coinfection in selected patients but may also require cautious interpretation.

Previous studies have described the clinical characteristics and microbiological findings of patients with VZV-related neurological disease detected by CSF mNGS., However, the clinical significance of VZV reads may remain uncertain at the individual-patient level, particularly when confirmatory virological testing is incomplete, additional microorganisms are simultaneously detected, or competing etiologies cannot be excluded.

In this retrospective case series, we analyzed 23 patients with suspected CNS infection in whom VZV was detected in CSF by mNGS. We aimed to characterize their clinical manifestations, CSF and neuroimaging findings, microbial co-detections, treatment, and short-term outcomes, with particular attention to the interpretive challenges of VZV detection and patient-level pathogen attribution. This study was designed as a descriptive case series rather than a diagnostic accuracy study, and the presence of VZV reads was not considered sufficient by itself to establish causality.

This retrospective descriptive case series was conducted at The Second Qilu Hospital of Shandong University and included patients evaluated between January 2019 and December 2024. During the study period, 321 patients with suspected central nervous system (CNS) infection were evaluated, of whom 278 underwent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) according to the clinical judgment of the treating physicians. CSF mNGS was mainly performed in patients with atypical, severe, progressive, or unexplained clinical presentations, or when broad pathogen detection was considered clinically necessary. Patients were not selected for mNGS solely because routine polymerase chain reaction (PCR) screening was negative. Patients in whom varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reads were reported in CSF by mNGS were subsequently screened for eligibility.

Patients were included if they met all of the following criteria:

acute or subacute onset, with a disease duration of <2 months;

clinical features suggestive of CNS infection, including meningitis (eg, headache or meningeal signs), encephalitis (eg, altered consciousness, seizures, or behavioral or cognitive changes), or myelitis (eg, acute myelopathy);

at least one supportive laboratory, neuroimaging, or electrophysiological finding, including a body temperature ≥38.0 °C during the disease course, a CSF white blood cell count >5 × 106/L, lymphocytic predominance in the CSF differential cell count, inflammatory abnormalities on CNS magnetic resonance imaging, or abnormal electroencephalographic findings; and

Detection of VZV reads in CSF by mNGS with a species-specific read number (SSRN) ≥3. This threshold was used as an operational criterion for selecting VZV detections for retrospective clinical review and was not considered a validated diagnostic cutoff or sufficient evidence by itself to establish VZV as the causative pathogen.

Patients with insufficient clinical data or an alternative noninfectious diagnosis that fully explained the clinical presentation were excluded.

Among the 278 patients who underwent CSF mNGS, 23 had laboratory-reported VZV detections meeting the SSRN ≥3 criterion. All 23 patients fulfilled the study eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis. No patients meeting the laboratory reporting threshold were excluded on the basis of the clinical eligibility criteria.

The presenting neurological syndromes were retrospectively classified by the study team through review of the medical records, based on documented clinical manifestations, CSF findings, and available neuroimaging results. Patients were categorized as having meningitis, encephalitis, meningoencephalitis, myelitis, or encephalomyelitis according to the overall pattern of neurological involvement. These classifications described the clinical syndromes and did not, by themselves, establish VZV as the causative pathogen.

All patients were identified through retrospective review of hospital records. Clinical and laboratory data were obtained from routine clinical documentation, and no additional samples were prospectively collected for research purposes.

The study population was selected from patients who underwent CSF mNGS for suspected CNS infection, rather than from an unselected population undergoing routine VZV screening. Eligibility required a compatible acute or subacute neurological presentation, supportive clinical or laboratory findings, and VZV detection meeting the operational inclusion threshold. Therefore, the included patients represented a clinically selected case series requiring subsequent assessment of the etiological relevance of VZV detection.

Clinical data were extracted from the electronic medical record system. The collected variables included demographic characteristics, clinical manifestations, comorbidities, and immunosuppressive conditions.

Laboratory and auxiliary examination data included blood tests, inflammatory markers, routine and biochemical CSF parameters, neuroimaging findings, electroencephalographic findings, and available conventional microbiological investigations. The interval from symptom onset to lumbar puncture and mNGS testing was recorded. The timing of mNGS result reporting and the initiation of antiviral therapy were also reviewed from the medical records. None of the included patients had received antiviral therapy before hospital admission, and CSF samples for mNGS were collected before antiviral treatment was initiated at our hospital.

VZV-specific PCR was not routinely performed during the study period and was not performed in the included cohort. Qualitative CSF anti-VZV IgM and IgG antibody testing was performed in a subset of patients during routine clinical care. Paired serum–CSF antibody measurements and antibody index calculations were not available; therefore, intrathecal anti-VZV antibody production could not be assessed. Accordingly, this study was not designed to compare the diagnostic performance of mNGS with that of VZV PCR or CSF anti-VZV antibody testing.

Treatment regimens, length of hospital stay, and clinical outcomes were also collected. Short-term functional outcomes were evaluated using the Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) score at hospital discharge, which was available for all 23 patients. Routine and biochemical CSF results were available for all included patients. C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and magnetic resonance imaging results were available for 18, 16, and 20 patients, respectively. For the remaining patients, the corresponding test results could not be retrieved from the medical records. Descriptive summaries were based on available data, and denominators were specified for variables with incomplete records. All data were recorded and managed using standardized data collection forms.

CSF samples (1.5–3 mL) were collected under sterile conditions according to standard clinical protocols. All CSF samples used for mNGS were obtained during the initial diagnostic lumbar puncture after hospital admission and before the initiation of antiviral therapy at our hospital.

A 300 μL aliquot of each CSF sample was used for DNA extraction with the TIANMicrobe Pathogen Microorganism DNA Extraction Kit (NG550-01; TIANGEN BIOTECH, Beijing, China). Library preparation included DNA fragmentation, end repair, adapter ligation, and PCR amplification. Sequencing was performed on the BGISEQ-50/MGISEQ-2000 platform (BGI-Tianjin, Tianjin, China).

Raw sequencing data were processed by removing low-quality reads and filtering out human-derived sequences using the Burrows–Wheeler Aligner. The remaining reads were aligned to the BGI Pathogen Metagenomics Database for microbial identification.

For this retrospective descriptive case series, a VZV species-specific read number (SSRN) ≥3 was used as the operational criterion for case inclusion, based on the VZV reporting and interpretation threshold in the available laboratory reports. This criterion applied specifically to VZV case selection and did not represent a universal reporting threshold for other microorganisms. Additional microorganisms with fewer than three reads could also be reported as supplementary findings.

The VZV read threshold was not regarded as a validated cutoff for establishing VZV as the causative pathogen. All reported microbial detections were interpreted in conjunction with the clinical presentation and available conventional microbiological findings.

Interpretation of mNGS findings was based on integrated clinical assessment rather than sequencing results alone. For each detected microorganism, its potential clinical relevance was evaluated according to:

consistency between the detected microorganism and the clinical syndrome;

its recognized pathogenic potential for CNS infection;

the relative abundance of sequencing reads;

supporting laboratory, neuroimaging, or electrophysiological findings;

the overall clinical evolution and therapeutic context, interpreted cautiously because treatment response is nonspecific and may be influenced by concomitant therapies; and

consideration of autoimmune or other inflammatory etiologies when the clinical presentation was atypical.

In cases with multiple microorganisms detected by mNGS, all co-detected organisms were reviewed in relation to the clinical presentation, read abundance, CSF inflammatory profile, neuroimaging findings, conventional microbiological results, immune status, and clinical course. Low-abundance microbial detections without compatible clinical or laboratory evidence were interpreted cautiously and were not automatically considered causative pathogens.

Viral detections with known potential for latency or nonspecific reactivation, such as Epstein–Barr virus, were interpreted cautiously. Such detections were neither automatically considered causative nor automatically dismissed as clinically irrelevant; instead, their possible significance was assessed according to compatible clinical and laboratory evidence.

The detection of VZV reads in CSF by mNGS was not considered sufficient by itself to establish causality. For each patient, the clinical relevance of VZV detection was assessed by integrating the neurological syndrome, CSF findings, neuroimaging features, presence or absence of a zoster rash, results of other infectious investigations, co-detected microorganisms, exclusion of more plausible alternative diagnoses, immune status, and the overall clinical course. Noninfectious mimics, including autoimmune encephalitis, were considered when clinically indicated and when relevant testing was available.

For descriptive purposes, the clinical relevance of VZV detection was further categorized at the individual-patient level as clinically probable VZV-associated CNS involvement, clinically possible VZV-associated CNS involvement, VZV detection of uncertain clinical significance, or an alternative primary etiology with concurrent VZV detection.

Two investigators with clinical experience in CNS infections independently reviewed the medical records of all 23 patients and assigned attribution categories based on an integrated assessment of the available clinical and microbiological evidence, with particular attention to supporting findings and competing etiologies. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. If consensus could not be reached, a third senior investigator was designated to adjudicate the case.

These categories represented retrospective clinical interpretations rather than independently validated etiological diagnoses. VZV read counts alone were not used to determine the attribution category.

Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs), and categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages. Because this study was designed as a descriptive retrospective case series, no inferential statistical analyses were performed. Statistical summaries were generated using R version 4.4.1.

Among the 278 patients with suspected central nervous system (CNS) infection who underwent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) during the study period, 23 had varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reads meeting the prespecified operational inclusion criteria, corresponding to a detection proportion of 8.3% among mNGS-tested patients.
