The median age was 44 years (interquartile range [IQR], 32.0–59.5; range, 18–78 years). Based on retrospective review of the clinical records, the presenting neurological syndromes were classified as encephalitis in 15 patients, meningitis in 4, meningoencephalitis in 1, encephalomyelitis in 2, and myelitis in 1. Twelve patients had comorbid conditions, including coronary heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. Two patients were receiving immunosuppressive therapy for myasthenia gravis and kidney transplantation, respectively. The median length of hospital stay was 24 days (IQR, 15.5–28.5).

The most common symptom was headache (95.7%, 22/23), followed by nausea (78.3%, 18/23), fever defined as a body temperature ≥38.0 °C (65.2%, 15/23), and vomiting (56.5%, 13/23). Additional neurological manifestations included movement disorders (21.7%, 5/23), sensory abnormalities (17.4%, 4/23), psychiatric or behavioral disturbances (13.0%, 3/23), impaired consciousness (13.0%, 3/23), and cranial nerve involvement (13.0%, 3/23). No seizures were documented in this cohort. A rash compatible with herpes zoster was present in 10 patients (43.5%), whereas meningeal irritation signs were observed in 5 patients (21.7%).

Peripheral blood testing showed elevated white blood cell counts in 7 patients (30.4%) and increased neutrophil percentages in 16 (69.6%). C-reactive protein was elevated in 4 of 18 tested patients (22.2%), and procalcitonin was elevated in 8 of 16 tested patients (50.0%). Abnormal liver function tests were observed in 12 patients (52.2%). The median interval from symptom onset to lumbar puncture was 7 days (IQR, 5.5–9.0).

None of the patients had received antiviral therapy before hospital admission. Lumbar puncture and CSF sampling were performed during the initial diagnostic evaluation and before the initiation of antiviral therapy at our hospital. Elevated CSF opening pressure was observed in 12 patients (52.2%). All 23 patients had CSF leukocytosis with lymphocytic predominance. Elevated CSF protein and lactate levels were observed in 21 patients (91.3%) and 17 patients (73.9%), respectively, whereas decreased CSF glucose levels were observed in 11 patients (47.8%). Available conventional microbiological investigations, including Gram staining, India ink staining, acid-fast staining, and cryptococcal antigen testing, were negative in all patients with available results. VZV-specific polymerase chain reaction was not performed in this cohort. Qualitative CSF anti-VZV IgM and IgG testing was available for six patients, of whom two had positive CSF anti-VZV IgM results. Brain and/or spinal magnetic resonance imaging results were available for 20 patients, of whom 4 (20.0%) had newly developed abnormalities potentially related to the presenting neurological syndrome.

Additional microorganisms were co-detected by mNGS in 6 patients and are described in detail in CSF mNGS Findings and Microbial Co-Detections.

All patients received individualized management based on their clinical presentation and the judgment of the treating physicians, including antiviral treatment with acyclovir. Acyclovir was initiated after CSF sampling for mNGS at our hospital. Thus, mNGS was incorporated into the initial diagnostic workup before antiviral treatment was initiated; however, because treatment decisions were made in conjunction with evolving clinical and laboratory information, the independent contribution of the mNGS results to treatment decisions could not be quantified.

Selected patients also received short-term adjunctive glucocorticoid therapy to reduce inflammatory responses, cerebral edema, or inflammation-related neurological injury. The maximum regimen used was dexamethasone 10 mg once daily, followed by rapid tapering according to the patient’s clinical condition. Given the retrospective design and concomitant therapies, the independent therapeutic effects of antiviral and immunomodulatory treatments could not be distinguished.

At hospital discharge, the median Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) score was 90 (IQR, 90.0–100.0), and 3 patients (13.0%) had a KPS score below 90. Discharge KPS scores were available for all 23 patients.

As described in the Methods section, a prespecified operational threshold of a VZV species-specific read number (SSRN) ≥3 was used for case inclusion. This threshold was applied specifically to VZV case selection and did not exclude the reporting of additional microorganisms with lower read counts. Among the 23 included patients, the median number of VZV sequence reads was 442 (range, 5–30,080) (). Because raw mNGS read counts may be influenced by sample processing, sequencing depth, host nucleic acid background, and other technical factors, these values were not interpreted as direct quantitative measures of viral load.

VZV was co-detected with additional microorganisms by mNGS in 6 patients (26.1%). Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) was detected in 5 patients, with read counts of 2, 3, 28, 38, and 2743, respectively. One of these patients also had herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) detected at a low read count of 2. In another patient, 50 reads corresponding to Listeria monocytogenes were detected. Detailed microbiological findings for all patients are provided in Supplementary Table S1.

The potential clinical relevance of these co-detections was assessed using the pathogen attribution framework described in the Methods section. EBV co-detection was interpreted cautiously because EBV may persist latently, undergo reactivation, or be detected incidentally in CSF. The low-abundance HSV-1 detection was considered of uncertain clinical significance because no compatible clinical or laboratory evidence supported HSV-1 as a causative pathogen. In the patient with Listeria monocytogenes detection, the severe CSF inflammatory profile and immunosuppressive background supported Listeria monocytogenes as the probable primary pathogen. Concurrent VZV detection was interpreted as possible co-detection or potential co-involvement in view of the recent history of herpes zoster and positive CSF anti-VZV IgM.

Following retrospective patient-level pathogen attribution assessment, 22 patients were classified as having clinically probable VZV-associated CNS involvement, while one patient was classified as having an alternative primary etiology with concurrent VZV detection. No patients were assigned to the clinically possible or uncertain-significance categories. The patient with an alternative primary etiology had concurrent detection of Listeria monocytogenes, which was considered the more likely primary pathogen based on the clinical and microbiological findings. Individual attribution categories are presented in Supplementary Table S1.

To illustrate the clinical heterogeneity and interpretive complexity of VZV detection by CSF mNGS in patients with suspected CNS infection, three representative cases are presented.

A 61-year-old man presented with a 20-day history of left-sided facial pain and diplopia, followed by progressive right-sided limb weakness over 2 days. His illness began with pain involving the left eye and forehead, accompanied by a vesicular rash compatible with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Although the local symptoms partially improved after initial treatment, he subsequently developed focal neurological deficits.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed acute infarctions involving the left thalamus, cerebral peduncle, and medial temporal lobe. Neurological examination demonstrated anisocoria, a dilated left pupil with an impaired light reflex, restricted ocular movements, reduced muscle strength in the right upper and lower limbs, and a positive right Babinski sign. Follow-up MRI showed progression of the ischemic lesions involving the left cerebral peduncle, thalamus, basal ganglia, and temporo-occipital regions, together with abnormalities of the optic nerve and extraocular muscles ( and ).

Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 190 mmH2O, a CSF white blood cell count of 26 × 106/L, a lactate level of 2.6 mmol/L, and a protein level of 426 mg/L. Available conventional CSF microbiological investigations were negative. CSF mNGS detected 46 VZV reads, together with 38 Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) reads and 2 herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) reads.

The EBV co-detection was regarded as potentially relevant but was interpreted cautiously because of the possibility of latent persistence or incidental detection. The low-abundance HSV-1 finding was considered of uncertain clinical significance because it was not supported by compatible clinical or laboratory evidence. In the context of recent herpes zoster ophthalmicus, multiple cranial neuropathies, inflammatory CSF findings, and progressive multifocal cerebral infarctions, the overall presentation was considered clinically compatible with probable VZV-associated CNS involvement, including possible VZV vasculopathy.

The patient received intravenous acyclovir and supportive treatment. His neurological deficits gradually improved, with recovery of limb strength, and he was discharged in a stable condition.

A 61-year-old woman presented with acute behavioral abnormalities and urinary incontinence. She had a 22-year history of myasthenia gravis treated with corticosteroids and azathioprine, as well as coronary artery disease and hyperglycemia. She had also experienced herpes zoster approximately 1 month before admission.

On admission, the patient was febrile and somnolent, with impaired mental status and peripheral leukocytosis. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed newly developed lesions involving the right basal ganglia and frontal lobe ( and ). CSF analysis demonstrated marked inflammation, with a white blood cell count of 598 × 106/L, a protein level of 2489 mg/L, and a lactate level of 9.7 mmol/L.

CSF mNGS detected 50 reads of Listeria monocytogenes and 113 reads of VZV. CSF anti-VZV IgM was also positive. Given the patient’s immunosuppressive background, severe CSF inflammatory profile, and detection of L. monocytogenes, this organism was considered the probable primary pathogen. Concurrent VZV detection was regarded as potentially clinically relevant but was interpreted as possible co-detection or co-involvement rather than definitive evidence of VZV as the primary cause, particularly in view of the recent herpes zoster and positive CSF anti-VZV IgM result.

The patient received intravenous ampicillin and acyclovir. Her level of consciousness and neurological symptoms gradually improved. Follow-up MRI showed partial resolution of the lesions, and repeat CSF examination demonstrated improvement in inflammatory parameters. She was discharged with substantial clinical recovery.

A 71-year-old woman presented with a recent episode of herpes zoster, followed by fever, dizziness, vomiting, and progressive left-sided limb weakness. Her neurological condition subsequently deteriorated, with impaired consciousness and severe motor deficits.

Neurological examination showed complete paralysis of the left upper and lower limbs and moderate weakness of the right limbs. Pain sensation was reduced below the C4 level on the right side, producing a Brown-Séquard–like clinical pattern. CSF analysis demonstrated marked inflammatory abnormalities, including a white blood cell count of 406 × 106/L, a protein level of 4581 mg/L, and a lactate level of 3.5 mmol/L. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging revealed multifocal abnormalities involving the cerebellum, brainstem, and cervical spinal cord ( and ).

CSF mNGS detected 4777 VZV reads. Serum and/or CSF testing for aquaporin-4 (AQP4), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) antibodies was negative, providing no supportive evidence for common antibody-associated demyelinating or autoimmune astrocytopathic disorders. In the context of recent herpes zoster, marked CSF inflammation, multifocal brain and spinal cord abnormalities, and VZV detection in CSF, the overall presentation was considered clinically compatible with probable VZV-associated encephalomyelitis.

The patient received antiviral therapy, corticosteroids, and supportive treatment. Her level of consciousness improved during hospitalization; however, severe left-sided motor deficits persisted. She was discharged in a stable condition and transferred for further rehabilitation.

Central nervous system infections remain diagnostically challenging because their manifestations often overlap across infectious, inflammatory, autoimmune, and vascular etiologies. In this retrospective case series, we described 23 patients with suspected CNS infection in whom VZV was detected in CSF by mNGS among 278 mNGS-tested patients, corresponding to a detection proportion of 8.3%. These patients showed heterogeneous clinical phenotypes, rash was absent in more than half of the cohort, inflammatory CSF abnormalities were common, and additional microorganisms were co-detected in approximately one quarter of patients. This study provides a clinically detailed description of cases with VZV detected in CSF by mNGS and the interpretive challenges encountered in routine practice, particularly in patients with atypical presentations or mixed microbial detections. However, it should be regarded as a descriptive retrospective case series and was not designed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of mNGS or establish mNGS read counts as quantitative markers of viral burden.

VZV is an important cause of adult encephalitis after HSV-1. Following primary infection, VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia and may reactivate later in life, particularly with aging or immunosuppression, causing herpes zoster and neurological complications such as meningitis, encephalitis, myelitis, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, and vasculopathy-related stroke syndromes., Although VZV-related CNS complications are more commonly described in older or immunocompromised individuals, they may also occur in younger or apparently immunocompetent patients., In our cohort, 13 patients (56.5%) were younger than 50 years, and only two had identifiable immunosuppressive conditions. Rash was absent in 56.5% of patients, consistent with reports that VZV-associated CNS involvement may occur without rash or that rash may not coincide temporally with neurological symptoms., CSF leukocytosis and elevated protein levels are common but nonspecific and may complicate differentiation from bacterial, tuberculous, autoimmune, or other inflammatory CNS disorders. VZV-associated vasculopathy may additionally produce ischemic or hemorrhagic lesions, further increasing diagnostic complexity.,

Conventional diagnostic methods for VZV CNS infection mainly include CSF PCR and assessment of intrathecal anti-VZV antibody production. Their diagnostic yield may vary with the timing and phenotype of infection, and the two approaches may therefore be complementary. In VZV vasculopathy, for example, CSF anti-VZV IgG may remain detectable when VZV DNA is no longer identified. PCR may be affected by the timing of CSF collection, low viral nucleic acid abundance, and prior antiviral exposure, whereas antibody testing may be influenced by sampling time and uncertainties in interpreting CSF and serum results., In the present cohort, VZV-specific PCR was not performed, and qualitative CSF anti-VZV IgM and IgG testing was available in only six patients, with two showing IgM positivity. Because paired serum–CSF testing and antibody index measurements were unavailable, intrathecal anti-VZV antibody production could not be established, further limiting etiological certainty. Although CSF samples used for mNGS were obtained before antiviral therapy was initiated at our hospital, mNGS findings still required careful interpretation rather than being regarded as standalone evidence of causality.

mNGS provides a hypothesis-free approach for detecting microbial nucleic acids in CSF and may identify unexpected or multiple pathogens in a single specimen. Prospective and large-scale studies have shown that CSF mNGS can provide complementary diagnostic information in meningitis and encephalitis, while also emphasizing the need to integrate sequencing results with conventional microbiological investigations and clinical evidence. However, because this cohort was assembled on the basis of VZV detection and no comparison group was included, the present study cannot assess sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic accuracy, background detection rates, or superiority over conventional testing. The SSRN threshold of ≥3 was used solely as an operational inclusion criterion specific to VZV and should not be regarded as a validated diagnostic cutoff. Raw VZV read counts alone, whether low or high, cannot establish active CNS infection or pathogen causality and do not exclude an alternative infectious, autoimmune, or inflammatory disorder. Interpretation should therefore integrate the neurological syndrome, CSF inflammatory pattern, neuroimaging, immune status, conventional microbiological data, alternative diagnoses, and clinical course. In ambiguous cases, targeted testing for autoimmune encephalitis or demyelinating disorders may also be appropriate. Clinical improvement after treatment should likewise be interpreted cautiously because antiviral agents, corticosteroids, and other therapies may have been administered concurrently.

Among the 23 included patients, 22 were classified as having clinically probable VZV-associated CNS involvement, whereas one was classified as having an alternative primary etiology with concurrent VZV detection. The predominance of clinically probable cases should be interpreted in the context of the clinically selected study population, which included patients with compatible neurological presentations and VZV detection meeting the operational inclusion criterion. Importantly, these attribution categories reflect integrated retrospective clinical judgments rather than independently confirmed virological diagnoses, and the observed distribution should not be generalized to all patients with VZV reads detected by CSF mNGS.

Microbial co-detection represented a major interpretive challenge. EBV reads were detected together with VZV reads in five patients. Although EBV can cause CNS disease and has been reported together with VZV and other pathogens, EBV DNA in CSF may also reflect latency, reactivation, or incidental detection and is frequently found with other microorganisms., Detection of more than one herpesvirus in CSF has also been documented using mNGS; Ramachandran et al reported varicella vaccine virus meningitis in which both varicella vaccine virus and human herpesvirus 7 DNA were detected in CSF. These findings support the plausibility of herpesvirus co-detection but do not prove dual pathogenic involvement. The low-abundance HSV-1 finding in one patient was considered of uncertain significance because it lacked compatible clinical or laboratory support. The patient with concurrent Listeria monocytogenes and VZV detection further illustrates patient-level pathogen attribution. Her immunosuppressive background, severe CSF inflammatory profile, and detection of Listeria monocytogenes supported Listeria as the probable primary pathogen, whereas recent herpes zoster and positive CSF anti-VZV IgM raised the possibility of concurrent VZV involvement without establishing it. Therefore, co-detection should not automatically be equated with confirmed coinfection.

Previous studies have described the clinical characteristics and microbiological findings of patients with suspected or clinically diagnosed VZV-related CNS disease. Zhu et al evaluated 31 patients with varicella and neurological symptoms using CSF mNGS alongside VZV-specific PCR and CSF IgM testing, with VZV reads identified by mNGS in 16 patients. Tang et al described 28 patients with VZV detected in CSF by mNGS and assessed follow-up outcomes, while excluding cases of encephalitis attributed to multiple-pathogen infections. More recently, Ci et al reported 108 non-immunocompromised patients with VZV detected by CSF mNGS using a sequence-read threshold greater than three and evaluated functional outcomes at three months. Herpes zoster was reported in 47.2% of their patients, compared with 43.5% in our cohort.

These studies demonstrate that heterogeneous clinical manifestations and the absence of a typical rash have already been well documented. Compared with these reports, our smaller series focuses more specifically on the uncertainty of pathogen attribution in routine clinical practice, particularly when additional microorganisms are detected or an alternative primary etiology is plausible. Nevertheless, differences in patient selection, microbiological confirmation, and follow-up preclude direct comparisons of diagnostic performance or clinical outcomes across these cohorts.

From a clinical-management perspective, patients with compatible CNS syndromes may warrant timely consideration of intravenous acyclovir, including those without a typical rash. However, the present retrospective study cannot establish whether mNGS results independently initiated, accelerated, or changed antiviral treatment decisions. Sequencing findings should inform rather than replace integrated antimicrobial decision-making. In patients with immunosuppression, marked CSF inflammation, or detection of a credible bacterial pathogen, antibacterial treatment should not be delayed or discontinued solely because VZV reads are present. The Listeria monocytogenes case illustrates the importance of prioritizing the organism most consistent with the overall clinical and microbiological evidence when multiple microorganisms are detected.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this was a single-center retrospective case series with a limited sample size and possible selection bias because CSF mNGS was performed according to physician judgment rather than as universal screening. Second, no mNGS-negative or control group was included; therefore, diagnostic performance, background detection rates, and comparative diagnostic yield could not be evaluated. Third, VZV-specific PCR, CSF anti-VZV antibody testing, and autoimmune encephalitis-related antibody testing were not systematically performed, limiting pathogen attribution and differential diagnosis. In particular, the absence of paired serum–CSF antibody testing prevented confirmation of intrathecal anti-VZV antibody production. Fourth, the SSRN threshold was an operational inclusion criterion rather than a validated diagnostic cutoff. The number of samples with VZV reads below this threshold could not be determined from the available retrospective records. Finally, raw mNGS read counts may be affected by contamination, latent viral detection, low-abundance organisms, sequencing-depth differences, host nucleic acid background, and other technical variability; therefore, they should not be interpreted as validated quantitative markers of viral burden or outcome predictors. As this retrospective study relied on clinical mNGS reports, detailed sequencing-run metadata and batch-specific quality-control results were not available to the investigators for independent verification, limiting the assessment of assay-level analytical performance. Treatment and short-term outcomes were assessed descriptively, and improvement could not be attributed solely to antiviral therapy because corticosteroids and other interventions were sometimes administered concurrently. Furthermore, outcomes were evaluated at discharge, limiting conclusions regarding long-term neurological sequelae.

In this retrospective case series, patients with suspected CNS infection in whom VZV was detected in CSF by mNGS showed heterogeneous neurological presentations and clinically important diagnostic complexity, particularly in the absence of a typical herpes zoster rash or when additional microorganisms were detected. CSF mNGS may provide useful adjunctive microbiological information; however, VZV reads should not be interpreted as standalone evidence of causality. Their clinical relevance requires integrated assessment of the neurological syndrome, CSF inflammatory findings, neuroimaging, conventional microbiological investigations, immune status, co-detected microorganisms, alternative diagnoses, and the overall clinical course. Future prospective studies incorporating systematic VZV PCR, assessment of intrathecal anti-VZV antibody production, standardized mNGS interpretation criteria, appropriate comparison groups, and longer follow-up are needed to clarify the clinical significance of VZV detection in CSF.

neuroscience.title: Cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages in primary central nervous system vasculitis: a potential radiologic marker
neuroscience.abstract: Primary central nervous system vasculitis (PCNSV) is a rare inflammatory vasculopathy with diverse clinical and radiological manifestations that often delay diagnosis. Although abnormalities on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and contrast-enhanced imaging, are increasingly recognized, a characteristic imaging pattern that may facilitate diagnosis has not yet been described. We aimed to evaluate cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages (CTH) as a potential imaging marker of PCNSV.We conducted a retrospective observational study at a tertiary neuroscience referral center in India. The discovery cohort included 51 patients with biopsy-proven PCNSV and 44 hypertensive microangiopathy controls who underwent MRI between 2018 and 2024. The imaging findings were independently reviewed for CTH and associated enhancement patterns. The reproducibility of this imaging pattern was subsequently assessed in an independent replication cohort of 55 patients with digital subtraction angiography (DSA)-proven PCNSV, evaluated between 2018 and 2026.CTH were identified in 35/51 (68.6%) biopsy-proven PCNSV patients compared with 9/44 (20.4%) hypertensive controls (p<0.001). In the biopsy-proven discovery cohort, CTH demonstrated a sensitivity of 68.6% (95% confidence interval [CI], 54.1–80.9%) and specificity of 79.5% (95% CI, 64.7–90.2%) for distinguishing PCNSV from hypertensive microangiopathy and remained associated with PCNSV after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 12.52, 95% CI 3.46–56.94). This association persisted in exploratory age-restricted sensitivity analyses. Associated punctate or linear contrast enhancement was present in 33/35 (94.3%) CTH-positive biopsy-proven patients and was not observed in hypertensive controls with available contrast-enhanced MRI (0/4). In the independent DSA-proven replication cohort, CTH were observed in 41/55 (74.5%) patients, of whom 23/39 (58.9%) demonstrated associated cerebellar tonsillar enhancement on contrast-enhanced MRI. Interobserver agreement for CTH detection was high in the combined discovery cohort (Cohen’s κ = 0.94) and the DSA-proven replication cohort (κ = 0.91). CTH frequently occurred in the absence of clinical ataxia or diffuse brainstem involvement.CTH represent a frequent and reproducible imaging finding in both biopsy-proven and DSA-proven PCNSV. The presence of CTH, particularly when accompanied by punctate or linear enhancement, may improve the radiological suspicion of PCNSV and help distinguish inflammatory microangiopathy from hypertensive small-vessel disease.
neuroscience.text:
Primary central nervous system vasculitis (PCNSV), also known as primary angiitis of the central nervous system (CNS), is a rare inflammatory disorder that affects the blood vessels of the brain, spinal cord, and leptomeninges. The disease presents with diverse neurological manifestations (headache, cognitive dysfunction, seizures, encephalopathy, and focal neurological deficits), examination and imaging findings, in the absence of a diagnostic serological or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) test, often resulting in substantial diagnostic delay ().

The diagnosis of PCNSV remains challenging in contemporary clinical practice. Current diagnostic criteria proposed by Calabrese and Mallek rely on either histopathological confirmation from a brain biopsy or characteristic angiographic abnormalities on digital subtraction angiography (DSA) after exclusion of secondary causes of CNS vasculitis (). However, both modalities have recognized limitations. Brain biopsy, although considered the diagnostic gold standard, has limited sensitivity due to the patchy and segmental nature of vascular inflammation. Conversely, angiographic abnormalities may lack specificity and can overlap with several mimics, including reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and other non-inflammatory vasculopathies (). A systematic review of published PCNSV cases demonstrated poor concordance between angiographic and histopathological findings, highlighting the limitations of existing diagnostic modalities and the need for more reliable imaging biomarkers in PCNSV ().

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities are present in the vast majority of patients with PCNSV; however, they are highly variable and nonspecific. Reported findings include multifocal infarcts, white matter hyperintensities, gadolinium-enhancing lesions, leptomeningeal enhancement, and intracranial hemorrhages (). Historically, hemorrhagic manifestations were considered uncommon in PCNSV. However, recent studies using susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) have demonstrated that cerebral microhemorrhages and macrohemorrhages are frequent manifestations of the disease, likely reflecting underlying inflammatory microangiopathy (). Despite these observations, no characteristic anatomical distribution of hemorrhages has been systematically described.

In our clinical practice, we observed a recurrent predilection for cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages (CTH) on SWI imaging in patients with PCNSV. Preliminary observations suggested that CTH were highly prevalent in both biopsy-proven and DSA-proven PCNSV, while being uncommon in hypertensive microangiopathy, an important radiological differential diagnosis. Many of these lesions also demonstrated punctate or linear contrast enhancement, suggesting active inflammatory vascular injury.

We therefore hypothesized that CTH may represent a characteristic imaging marker of PCNSV. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the prevalence and diagnostic performance of CTH in patients with biopsy-proven PCNSV compared with hypertensive microangiopathy controls. The secondary objective was to assess the reproducibility of this imaging pattern in an independent replication cohort of patients with DSA-proven PCNSV.

We conducted a retrospective observational study at a tertiary neuroscience referral center in India, comprising two independent PCNSV cohorts: a biopsy-proven discovery cohort and a DSA-proven replication cohort.

For the discovery cohort, consecutive patients with histopathologically confirmed PCNSV who underwent brain MRI with SWI between January 2018 and December 2024 were retrospectively identified from institutional neurology, neuropathology, and neuroradiology databases. Their MRI scans were independently reviewed for the presence of CTH, and the findings were compared with those of patients with hypertensive microangiopathy, including atherosclerotic ischemic stroke, vascular cognitive impairment, and hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, who underwent MRI during the same period.

An independent cohort of patients with DSA-proven PCNSV who underwent brain MRI between January 2018 and January 2026 was evaluated to assess the reproducibility of the CTH imaging pattern observed in the discovery cohort. No separate comparator group was included in this replication cohort.

The diagnosis of PCNSV was established after a multidisciplinary evaluation incorporating clinical, neuroimaging, angiographic, and histopathological findings, with the exclusion of secondary causes of CNS vasculitis and other vasculopathies. Histopathological diagnosis was based on the demonstration of transmural vascular inflammation on meningo-cortical biopsy specimens. DSA-proven PCNSV was diagnosed in patients with characteristic angiographic abnormalities in an appropriate clinical context after exclusion of infectious, systemic autoimmune, neoplastic, and reversible vasoconstrictive disorders.

All imaging datasets were anonymized and reviewed in a diagnosis-masked manner. Each MRI and DSA study was independently evaluated by two of three senior neuroradiologists (AG, LJ, and SBG). The reviewers were blinded to the final diagnostic category, histopathological subtype, and clinical outcome at the time of imaging review. Discrepancies between the two initial readers were resolved by joint review and consensus among all three neuroradiologists.

Demographic, clinical, laboratory, CSF, neuroimaging, angiographic, and histopathological details were extracted from medical records using a predefined structured proforma.

Secondary causes of CNS vasculitis were excluded through detailed clinical evaluation, laboratory investigations, CSF analysis, and neuroimaging, where appropriate. Laboratory evaluation included testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B and C, antinuclear antibody (ANA), extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibodies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), venereal disease research laboratory test (VDRL), beta-2 glycoprotein antibody, anticardiolipin antibody, lupus anticoagulant, and Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-B51.

MRI examinations were performed using either a 3T Philips Ingenia scanner (Philips Healthcare, Best, The Netherlands) or a 1.5T GE Optima MR450w scanner (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA). The imaging protocols included three-dimensional fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or susceptibility-weighted angiography (SWAN), T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging, and post-contrast T1-weighted imaging. Detailed MRI acquisition parameters for both scanners are provided in .

Magnetic resonance imaging acquisition parameters for the 3T Philips Ingenia and 1.5T GE Optima MR450w scanners.

*Diffusion-weighted imaging was acquired using b-values of 0 and 1000 s/mm² on both scanners. Diffusion gradients were applied in three orthogonal directions to generate isotropic (trace) images and apparent diffusion coefficient maps.

^Postcontrast images were acquired following intravenous administration of gadobenate dimeglumine or gadoterate meglumine at a standard dose of 0.1 mmol/kg.

MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; 3D, three-dimensional; FLAIR, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; SWI, susceptibility-weighted imaging; SWAN, susceptibility-weighted angiography; PROPELLER, periodically rotated overlapping parallel lines with enhanced reconstruction; TR, repetition time; TE, echo time; TI, inversion time; FOV, field of view.

CTH were defined as globular, punctate, or linear foci of susceptibility blooming within the cerebellar tonsillar parenchyma on SWI. The presence of at least one such focus was sufficient to classify a patient as CTH-positive, irrespective of lesion size. Susceptibility foci outside the cerebellar tonsils were not considered CTH. When postcontrast T1-weighted images were available, associated punctate or linear enhancement of CTH was documented. The presence of associated supratentorial and infratentorial lesions, brainstem microhemorrhages, and contrast-enhancement patterns was also recorded.

DSA examinations were evaluated for vascular abnormalities involving the arterial and venous phases. Arterial abnormalities assessed included segmental narrowing or occlusion, irregular vessel contours, alternating stenosis and dilatation producing a beaded appearance, and aneurysmal changes. Venous-phase assessment focused on dilatation and tortuosity of small veins, abnormal contrast pooling or staining, and prominence of transmedullary veins with irregular outlines, collectively suggestive of a pseudophlebitic pattern. Angiographic abnormalities in either phase were considered evidence of vascular involvement.

Brain biopsy specimens were examined by experienced neuropathologists (MCS and VS) for evidence of vasculitis involving meningeal and cortical vessels. Biopsies were classified as targeted when tissue was obtained from radiologically abnormal regions or as blind frontal pole biopsies when sampling was performed without a specific imaging-defined target. Histopathological confirmation of PCNSV required transmural inflammatory infiltration of small- or medium-sized meningo-cortical vessels, with an overall pathological assessment consistent with vasculitis. Confirmed cases were further categorized according to the predominant histopathological pattern as granulomatous, lymphocytic, or necrotizing vasculitis.

Continuous variables were expressed as median with interquartile range (IQR), while categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages. Group comparisons were performed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables and the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, as appropriate. For the biopsy-proven PCNSV discovery cohort, the diagnostic performance of CTH for distinguishing PCNSV from hypertensive cerebral microangiopathy was evaluated by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, and univariable odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the independent association between CTH and biopsy-proven PCNSV after adjustment for age and sex, with results reported as adjusted ORs and 95% CIs. Exploratory sensitivity analyses restricted to overlapping age ranges (40–60 and 35–65 years) were performed using the same regression approach to assess the robustness of this association. Interobserver agreement for CTH detection was assessed using Cohen’s kappa (κ), with 95% CIs calculated using an asymptotic normal approximation. A two-sided p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.5.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

The study was approved by the Institute Ethics Committee of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (Ethics Approval No. IEC-507/05-06-2020, RP-19/2020). The research was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the Institute Ethics Committee and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The requirement for informed consent was waived owing to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of de-identified data.

Fifty-one patients with biopsy-proven PCNSV and 44 patients with hypertensive microangiopathy fulfilled the study criteria. Among patients with biopsy-proven PCNSV, 45 (88.2%) underwent MRI on a 3T scanner and 6 (11.8%) on a 1.5T scanner; the corresponding numbers in the hypertensive microangiopathy group were 39 (88.6%) and 5 (11.4%), respectively. Baseline demographic and imaging characteristics are summarized in . All patients in both groups demonstrated supratentorial and infratentorial abnormalities on T2/FLAIR and SWI sequences.

Clinical and imaging characteristics of biopsy-proven PCNSV and hypertensive microangiopathy cohorts.

# Contrast-enhanced MRI was not performed in 1 patient.

^ Contrast-enhanced MRI was performed in 4 patients.

*p<0.05 is statistically significant.

PCNSV, Primary central nervous system vasculitis; IQR, Interquartile range; SWI, Susceptibility-weighted imaging; FLAIR, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; CTH, Cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages.

CTH were identified in 35/51 patients with biopsy-proven PCNSV compared with 9/44 patients with hypertensive microangiopathy (68.6% vs 20.4%; p<0.001). Among CTH-positive patients with PCNSV, 33/35 (94.3%) demonstrated punctate or linear contrast enhancement. No enhancement was observed in the hypertensive microangiopathy group, in whom contrast-enhanced MRI was available (0/4 patients; p<0.001).

Interobserver agreement for CTH detection was high in the biopsy-proven PCNSV cohort (Cohen’s κ = 0.91; 95% CI, 0.79–1.00; agreement, 49/51 [96.1%]) and in the overall discovery cohort, including hypertensive controls (κ = 0.94; 95% CI, 0.87–1.00; agreement, 92/95 [96.8%]).

Brainstem microhemorrhages showed a different distribution between groups. Midbrain involvement was observed in 15/51 PCNSV patients and 21/44 hypertensive controls (29.4% vs 47.7%; p=0.067). Pontine involvement was significantly less frequent in PCNSV than in hypertensive microangiopathy (20/51, 39.2% vs 38/44, 86.4%; p<0.001). Medullary involvement was comparable between groups (15/51, 29.4% vs 11/44, 25.0%; p=0.631).

Among patients with hypertensive microangiopathy with CTH, all 9/9 (100%) demonstrated concomitant pontine microhemorrhages, while 6/9 (66.7%) and 5/9 (55.6%) also had associated midbrain and medullary microhemorrhages, respectively. No patient in either group demonstrated sulcal siderosis.

Among patients with PCNSV, 23 (45.1%) had granulomatous vasculitis, 27 (52.9%) had lymphocytic vasculitis, and 1 (2.0%) had necrotizing vasculitis. CTH morphology and distribution did not differ appreciably between granulomatous and lymphocytic vasculitis subtypes.

Representative MRI findings from the biopsy-proven PCNSV cohort are shown in  and , and those from the hypertensive microangiopathy cohort are shown in .

Diagnostic performance of CTH in the biopsy-proven discovery cohort is summarized in . CTH demonstrated a sensitivity of 68.6% (95% CI, 54.1–80.9%) and specificity of 79.5% (95% CI, 64.7–90.2%) for distinguishing biopsy-proven PCNSV from hypertensive microangiopathy. On univariable logistic regression, CTH was associated with increased odds of PCNSV (OR 8.51, 95% CI 3.44–22.86). This association remained significant after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR 12.52, 95% CI 3.46–56.94). In exploratory sensitivity analysis restricted to patients aged 40–60 years, CTH remained significantly more frequent in PCNSV than in hypertensive microangiopathy (70.6% vs 23.8%; p=0.008), with the association persisting after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR 9.40, 95% CI 2.14–53.75; p=0.005). Similar findings were observed in a broader age-restricted analysis (35–65 years). Both sensitivity analyses are presented in .

Diagnostic performance of cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages (CTH) in biopsy-proven primary CNS vasculitis versus hypertensive microangiopathy controls.

*p<0.05 is statistically significant.

CI, Confidence interval; CTH, Cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages; OR, Odds Ratio.

An independent cohort of 55 patients with DSA-proven PCNSV was evaluated to assess the reproducibility of the imaging findings observed in the biopsy-proven cohort. Of these, 52 (94.5%) underwent MRI on a 3T scanner and 3 (5.5%) on a 1.5T scanner. Clinical and imaging characteristics are summarized in . All patients revealed supratentorial and infratentorial abnormalities on T2/FLAIR and SWI sequences.

Clinical and imaging characteristics of the DSA-proven PCNSV replication cohort.

^11 patients did not undergo CSF analysis.

*Contrast-enhanced MRI was not performed in 2 patients.

DSA, Digital Subtraction Angiography; PCNSV, Primary central nervous system vasculitis; IQR, Interquartile range; SWI, Susceptibility-weighted imaging; FLAIR, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; CTH, Cerebellar tonsillar hemorrhages.

CTH were identified in 41/55 (74.5%) patients. Corresponding cerebellar tonsillar enhancement was observed in 23/39 (58.9%) CTH-positive patients. Interobserver agreement for CTH detection in the DSA-proven cohort was high (Cohen’s κ = 0.91; 95% CI, 0.79–1.00; agreement, 53/55 [96.4%]). Brainstem involvement was observed in the midbrain, pons, and medulla in 14/55 (25.4%), 18/55 (32.7%), and 11/55 (20%) patients, respectively. No patient demonstrated sulcal siderosis.

Importantly, CTH were frequently identified in the absence of clinical ataxia or diffuse brainstem microhemorrhages. Representative imaging findings from the DSA-proven cohort are shown in .

In this study, we identified CTH as a frequent imaging finding in PCNSV across both biopsy-proven and DSA-proven cohorts. In the biopsy-proven discovery cohort, CTH demonstrated moderate sensitivity and good specificity for distinguishing PCNSV from hypertensive microangiopathy and remained independently associated with PCNSV after adjustment for age and sex. CTH were also frequently associated with punctate or linear contrast enhancement. High interobserver agreement across both cohorts further supported the reliability of CTH detection. Together, these findings suggest that CTH may represent a useful radiological marker of PCNSV and expand the evolving spectrum of hemorrhagic manifestations recognized in this disorder.

PCNSV remains a diagnostically challenging and heterogeneous inflammatory vasculopathy, with highly variable clinical and radiological manifestations. Large cohort studies from the Mayo Clinic and the French COVAC cohort have emphasized the marked clinical and radiological heterogeneity of PCNSV, with MRI abnormalities ranging from multifocal infarcts and white matter lesions to leptomeningeal enhancement and intracranial hemorrhage (, ).

Recent Asian cohorts have increasingly highlighted the importance of hemorrhagic manifestations and SWI in PCNSV. In an Indian cohort of 82 angiography- and/or biopsy-confirmed PCNSV patients, microhemorrhages and macrohemorrhages were seen in all patients and were more frequently encountered than previously reported in Western cohorts (). Similarly, a subsequent biopsy-based SWI study involving 56 histopathologically confirmed cases demonstrated hemorrhages on SWI in 96.4% of patients and dot-linear enhancement in 87%, further highlighting the hemorrhagic manifestations of inflammatory vascular injury in PCNSV (). In parallel, a Chinese SWI-based study demonstrated that cerebral microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis, and venous abnormalities were significantly more common in autoimmune CNS vasculitis than in multiple sclerosis, further supporting the utility of susceptibility imaging in detecting inflammatory vascular injury ().

However, although prior studies described the prevalence and distribution of hemorrhagic lesions, none systematically identified a characteristic anatomical predilection involving the cerebellar tonsils. The present study extends these observations by demonstrating that CTH constitute a reproducible and anatomically distinctive infratentorial imaging pattern across both biopsy-confirmed and DSA-confirmed diseases. The cerebellar tonsils have a complex vascular anatomy, with arterial supply from branches of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, particularly its tonsillomedullary and telovelotonsillar segments (, ). Although this vascular organization may provide a potential substrate for inflammatory vascular injury, its role in the apparent tonsillar predilection remains uncertain. Histopathological studies in PCNSV have demonstrated transmural inflammatory infiltration affecting small- and medium-sized vessels, with associated vascular wall injury, thrombosis, and necrosis (). In our cohort, most CTH demonstrated associated punctate or linear enhancement, suggesting active blood-brain-barrier disruption and ongoing inflammatory vascular injury rather than chronic hemosiderin deposition alone. Furthermore, cortical microhemorrhages, diffuse infratentorial susceptibility abnormalities, and venous phase abnormalities on DSA frequently coexisted in the same patients. Prior studies have demonstrated venous phase abnormalities in >90% patients who underwent DSA, predominantly in the form of pseudophlebitic venous patterns (, ). Collectively, these observations suggest that inflammatory vascular injury, potentially involving both arterial and venous vessels, may contribute to the hemorrhagic manifestations of PCNSV.

An important finding of the present study was the distinction between CTH in PCNSV and the hemorrhagic patterns encountered in hypertensive microangiopathy. In the hypertensive cohort, cerebellar tonsillar involvement was uncommon and, when present, was associated with extensive pontine and diffuse brainstem hemorrhages, a pattern typical of chronic hypertensive arteriopathy. In contrast, patients with PCNSV frequently demonstrated selective or disproportionate tonsillar involvement, often with associated punctate enhancement and without the diffuse pontomedullary pattern usually encountered in hypertensive disease. This distinction is clinically relevant because hypertensive microangiopathy remains one of the most important radiological differentials in patients presenting with multiple cerebral hemorrhages on SWI ().

The diagnosis of PCNSV remains challenging because of the limited diagnostic accuracy of angiography and the invasive nature of brain biopsy (, , ). Prior studies have demonstrated substantial discordance between angiographic and histopathological findings, and a recent systematic review reported that disagreement between the two modalities was more than five times more likely than concordance (, , ). Similarly, DSA altered clinical management in only a minority of patients with suspected CNS vasculitis, highlighting the limitations of angiography in isolation (). Against this background, recognition of CTH on SWI, particularly when accompanied by punctate enhancement and cortical microhemorrhages, may improve radiological suspicion for PCNSV and assist in selecting patients for targeted biopsy or further angiographic evaluation. The moderate sensitivity observed in our biopsy-proven cohort likely reflects the heterogeneous pathological and radiological spectrum of PCNSV, with CTH representing one manifestation of inflammatory vascular injury rather than a universal imaging feature. Conversely, its relatively high specificity for distinguishing PCNSV from hypertensive microangiopathy suggests that, when present in an appropriate clinical and radiological context, CTH may increase diagnostic confidence, although its absence should not exclude the diagnosis. The reproducibility of this imaging pattern in an independent DSA-proven cohort further supports its potential clinical utility. However, prospective validation is required before CTH can influence decisions regarding deferral of brain biopsy.

Our study has several limitations. First, this was a retrospective single-center study and is therefore subject to referral and selection bias. However, the inclusion of both biopsy-proven and independent DSA-proven cohorts, along with a hypertensive microangiopathy comparator group, strengthens the internal validity of the observed imaging pattern. Second, MRI acquisition protocols and scanner strengths were not completely uniform across the study period. Nevertheless, the consistent identification of CTH across different MRI platforms may also suggest that the imaging finding is robust and reproducible in routine clinical practice. Third, the comparator group was restricted to hypertensive microangiopathy, and the specificity of CTH against other important mimics of PCNSV, including reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and systemic vasculitides with CNS involvement, remains to be established. Fourth, the PCNSV and hypertensive comparator groups were not age-matched, with median ages of 34 and 60 years, respectively. Although CTH remained independently associated with PCNSV after adjustment for age and sex, residual confounding from other unmeasured differences between the groups cannot be completely excluded. Fifth, contrast-enhanced MRI was available in only four hypertensive controls; therefore, the apparent absence of associated tonsillar enhancement in this group should be considered preliminary and cannot be generalized to hypertensive microangiopathy. Sixth, the cerebellar tonsillar lesions themselves were not histologically sampled. The inflammatory basis of CTH, therefore, remains inferential. Seventh, the DSA-proven replication cohort rests on a reference standard of limited specificity and lacked a control arm; consequently, it confirms the reproducibility of CTH rather than its diagnostic accuracy. Finally, larger multicenter prospective studies will be needed to confirm the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of CTH across diverse PCNSV populations and MRI platforms.

In conclusion, CTH represent a frequent, reproducible, and potentially useful imaging marker of PCNSV. Recognition of this distinctive SWI pattern, particularly when accompanied by punctate or linear contrast enhancement, may improve radiological suspicion for PCNSV and help distinguish inflammatory microangiopathy from hypertensive small-vessel disease. However, prospective multicenter validation is required before CTH can be incorporated into routine diagnostic algorithms.

neuroscience.title: Prolong Life with Nine Turn-Method versus CBT-I for Sleep-Onset Chronic Insomnia: A Randomized Controlled Trial Protocol Integrating fMRI and PSG
neuroscience.abstract: Sleep-onset chronic insomnia is one of the most common sleep disorders in clinical practice and carries a substantial multidimensional burden, including somatic symptoms, emotional distress, and impaired quality of life. Although Prolong Life with Nine Turn-Method has long been used to promote sleep, its specific efficacy for this subtype lacks adequate empirical support.To assess the long-term efficacy and safety of PLWNT in sleep-onset chronic insomnia and to investigate, via multimodal techniques, its modulatory effects on cerebral cortical networks.This prospective, single-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trial will enroll 128 patients with ICSD-3-diagnosed sleep-onset chronic insomnia, randomized 1:1 to a 12-week PLWNT or CBT-I intervention in a superiority design. The primary endpoint is the baseline-to-week-12 change in PSQI total score. Secondary measures include validated scales (ISI, PSAS, HADS, PSS, HAS, MEQ, MFI-20, GSRS, SF-36), sleep diary, actigraphy, blood biomarkers, gut microbiota, PSG, and resting-state fMRI. Exploratory mechanistic endpoints include (1) EEG-derived spectral power and wPLI within the DMN, SN, and CEN during wakefulness, sleep-onset latency, and sleep stages (N1–N3, REM), and (2) resting-state fMRI connectivity of the same networks. Clinical assessments occur at baseline (week 0), week 6, week 12 (end of intervention), and weeks 16, 20, 24, and 36 after randomization (7 time points); laboratory and imaging measures are obtained at baseline and week 12 only. Primary analysis will use generalized estimating equations on LOCF-imputed data, with multiple imputation as a sensitivity analysis.This randomized controlled trial directly compares PLWNT with CBT-I for sleep-onset chronic insomnia, integrating clinical outcome measures with neuroimaging-based mechanistic insights. The findings could position PLWNT as a non-drug therapeutic option backed by objective imaging data.
neuroscience.text:
Insomnia stands as one of the most widespread sleep disorders. It frequently triggers daytime fatigue, poor concentration, emotional distress, and a marked drop in quality of life., It affects about 16.2% of people globally, yet the impact is even more pronounced in China. In 2020, Chinese studies reported symptom rates of 30.9%; a later survey involving 8970 individuals put that figure at 46.8%. Among the various types, sleep-onset insomnia is particularly common. In the US, 14.5% of adults reported trouble falling asleep in 2020. Under strict diagnostic criteria, chronic cases affect up to 14% of the population, a figure that continues to rise. Characterized by a 30-minute sleep latency occurring at least three times weekly for over three months, this condition does far more than just impair daily function. It also carries a higher likelihood of leading to nocturnal enuresis, depression, and Alzheimer’s disease compared with other insomnia subtypes., Meanwhile, the cardiovascular hazards of this subtype are particularly pronounced. The data reveal a stark link to physical health: an objective sleep latency exceeding 14 minutes triples the risk of hypertension, while a latency over 17 minutes raises that risk fourfold. Therefore, targeting sleep latency may not only improve sleep quality per se but could also mitigate sleep-related health risks, thereby potentially enhancing overall quality of life.

Several pharmacological agents have demonstrated targeted efficacy in mitigating sleep-onset difficulties among patients with chronic insomnia. Benzodiazepines and non-benzodiazepine sedative-hypnotics offer rapid relief for initiating sleep in the short term; however, their extended use is frequently complicated by the emergence of drug dependence, physiological tolerance, withdrawal phenomena, and next-day residual sedation. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I), widely acknowledged as a frontline non-pharmacological intervention, carries no intrinsic medication-related side effects and enjoys substantial empirical support. Nevertheless, its real-world dissemination remains severely constrained by a combination of factors, including a shortage of qualified therapists, limited accessibility across diverse healthcare settings, and suboptimal patient adherence, rendering it particularly difficult to implement at the primary care level.,

The neurobiological model of sleep-onset chronic insomnia centers on sustained central hyperarousal that disrupts cortical, cognitive, and physiological functions., Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies have increasingly pointed to default mode network (DMN) dysfunction as a key feature. Resting-state fMRI reveals that patients with prolonged sleep latency exhibit sustained hyperconnectivity among DMN hubs and fail to disengage this network activity. This persistent activation sustains self-referential thinking, which in turn delays sleep onset. The salience network (SN) fails to properly modulate DMN overactivity, while the central executive network (CEN) shows inconsistent connectivity. Collectively, this destabilizes the balance across these systems. Structural MRI reveals cortical thinning in the anterior cingulate cortex and altered covariance between sensory and motor regions. Electrophysiologically, patients display elevated beta power and blunted alpha decline during the wake–sleep transition, pointing to impaired switching from arousal to sleep., These patients also remain hypervigilant across all sleep stages, suggesting that prolonged sleep latency may reflect a persistent vigilance-regulatory disorder. Together, these observations suggest that effective treatment should aim to reduce DMN hyperexcitability and restore dynamic homeostasis across the DMN, SN, and CEN.

Prolong Life with Nine Turn-Method (PLWNT) integrates eight abdominal massage techniques with upper-torso rotation and has long been used for insomnia. Our earlier work showed that PLWNT improves sleep quality in chronic fatigue and extends to sleep latency, duration, disruption, and daytime impairment., A randomized fMRI trial reported that PLWNT increased ALFF in the right superior frontal gyrus and left median cingulate gyrus, decreased ALFF in occipital and temporal regions, and enhanced functional connectivity between the median cingulate gyrus and middle temporal gyrus, with changes correlating with clinical improvement. In chronic insomnia, a multicenter protocol has been registered to compare PLWNT with CBT on sleep quality and hyperarousal.

Sleep-onset chronic insomnia involves central hyperarousal and disrupted DMN–SN–CEN dynamics; CBT-I reliably improves subjective sleep-onset latency, with moderate effect sizes that attenuate over time, whereas objective PSG-defined sleep latency changes are inconsistently detected. Although PLWNT improves sleep quality in chronic fatigue and modulates activity and connectivity in regions overlapping with the DMN and SN,, the sleep-onset subtype remains unexamined. Furthermore, no single PLWNT trial has integrated PSG-derived EEG source analysis with resting-state fMRI to assess dynamic interactions across the DMN, SN, and CEN. Previous work has also never compared PLWNT with CBT-I using PSG-defined sleep-onset latency as a prespecified objective endpoint. The present trial therefore examines PLWNT in sleep-onset chronic insomnia, with baseline-to-week-12 change in PSQI total score as the primary endpoint and PSG-defined and diary-defined sleep-onset latency as secondary endpoints. Mechanistically, the study combines sLORETA-based EEG source analysis (spectral power and wPLI at sleep onset and across sleep stages) with resting-state fMRI connectivity to characterize state- and stage-dependent oscillatory dynamics and static network coupling within the DMN, SN, and CEN, in a trial comparing qigong with CBT-I.

This trial pursues two main objectives. The first is to assess whether PLWNT and CBT-I differ in their sustained clinical benefit for patients with sleep-onset chronic insomnia. The second is to determine whether PLWNT exerts its effects by modulating the excitability and interactive dynamics among the DMN, SN, and CEN. This is a superiority trial. The confirmatory hypothesis is that PLWNT is superior to CBT-I in improving sleep quality, operationalized as a greater reduction in PSQI total score from baseline to week 12. The primary outcome will be analysed with a one-sided test at α = 0.025, with a superiority margin of Δ = 0 (ie, statistical superiority); no equivalence or non-inferiority margin is specified. Mechanistic outcomes will be analysed using the prespecified statistical models described in Statistical Analysis Plan and reported as exploratory findings.

The design of the present trial adheres to the SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) guidelines and follows the reporting framework set forth by the CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) statement.

This trial will recruit participants at Shanghai Municipal Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine. This is a single-center, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial with blinded outcome assessment. Participants will be assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the PLWNT group or the CBT-I control group. The intervention period runs from week 0 to week 12 after randomization. Week 12 is defined as the end of the intervention. Assessment time points are at weeks 0, 6, 12, 16, 20, 24, and 36 after randomization. This yields a total of 7 assessment time points across a study duration of 36 weeks.

All participants will provide written informed consent before enrollment. The study will be conducted in compliance with relevant data protection regulations and the ethical standards set forth in the Declaration of Helsinki.  illustrates the study flowchart, and  summarizes the key protocol elements and assessment time point.
