Participants will be eligible for enrollment if they meet all of the following criteria: (1) a diagnosis of chronic insomnia that conforms to the International Classification of Sleep Disorders, third edition (ICSD-3) criteria; (2) age between 18 and 65 years, inclusive, and right-handedness; (3) a Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) total score greater than 7 and an Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score of 8 or above; (4) a primary complaint of difficulty initiating sleep, defined as a sleep-onset latency of 30 minutes or longer, occurring at least three times per week, with a disease duration of 3 months or more; and (5) willingness to participate voluntarily in the trial and provide written informed consent. Detailed information regarding concomitant medication use—including drug names, therapeutic classes, dosages, and weekly frequency—will be systematically documented at baseline. To minimize confounding, participants will be required to be either medication-free or on a stable dose of any concurrent medication for at least three months prior to enrollment. During the 12-week intervention period, concomitant medication will be re-recorded at each assessment visit; newly initiated hypnotic or psychotropic medication will be documented. Medication data collected after week 12 will be recorded for descriptive purposes only.

Exclusion criteria are as follows: (1) other sleep disorders, including obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy, or restless legs syndrome; (2) a known history of central nervous system disorders, such as dementia, epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease, cognitive impairment, Parkinson’s disease, major depressive disorder, or anxiety disorders; (3) acute exacerbation of any condition that could affect sleep, including diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, chronic nephritis, or chronic pain; (4) pregnancy or intention to become pregnant during the trial; (5) previous experience with either PLWNT or CBT-I; (6) rotating shift work; or (7) concurrent participation in another interventional trial.

Reasons for premature withdrawal from the study include the following: (1) a participant’s decision to leave the study of their own accord; (2) withdrawal of the informed consent documentation previously signed; or (3) inability to maintain contact with the participant for follow-up assessments (ie, loss to follow-up).

Individual withdrawal from the study may occur under either of the following circumstances: (1) the participant exhibits emotional instability or other adverse reactions during the intervention or assessment periods that compromise their ability to adhere to clinical procedures, polysomnographic recordings, or other protocol-required evaluations; or (2) the participant develops a new medical condition that necessitates external treatment beyond the scope of this trial.

The criteria below define exclusion from the per-protocol set only; they do not apply to the full analysis set (FAS) or the primary intention-to-treat analysis. Data from enrolled participants will be excluded from the per-protocol set if either of the following applies: (1) they demonstrate non-adherence to the assigned intervention that does not improve despite investigator-led corrective efforts; or (2) they fail to complete the prescribed treatment sessions in accordance with the training standards and quality control measures specified in the protocol. Participants meeting these criteria will remain in the FAS and will be included in the primary analysis according to the intention-to-treat principle.

To ensure enrollment of the target sample size (n = 128) within the planned recruitment period, participants will be identified and recruited through multiple approaches, including targeted advertisements via WeChat, QQ, the hospital’s official WeChat public account, and hospital posters. A secure screening database will be maintained to track recruitment progress weekly and optimize enrollment efficiency. Interested individuals will then be invited to an introductory session for initial screening using standardized scales (including the PSQI and ISI) in conjunction with a semi-structured clinical interview. Those with a PSQI score exceeding the pre-specified cutoff will proceed to the second screening step, which employs overnight polysomnography to objectively confirm a sleep-onset latency of ≥ 30 minutes. Following completion of all screening procedures and baseline assessments, eligible participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the CBT-I or PLWNT group.

The PLWNT protocol and its operational standards are derived from the nationally recognized textbook Tuina Exercise (Fine Series of Traditional Chinese Medicine for General Higher Education) and are delivered via a standardized 30-minute instructional video. The PLWNT protocol consists of nine sequential movements, described as follows.

In Movement 1, participants overlap the index, middle, and ring fingers of both hands, with the right hand beneath the left, place them over the epigastric region (below the xiphoid process), and massage in a clockwise circular motion for 21 repetitions. In Movement 2, using the same overlapping finger position, they stroke downward from the epigastrium (below the xiphoid process) along the midline to the pubic symphysis for 21 repetitions. In Movement 3, they stroke upward from the pubic symphysis to the epigastrium (below the xiphoid process) with a bilateral separating motion for 21 repetitions. In Movement 4, participants overlap the three fingers of both hands, with the right hand beneath the left, and push straight downward from the epigastrium (below the xiphoid process) to the pubic symphysis for 21 repetitions. In Movement 5, the left hand hangs relaxed while the right hand is centered on the navel and massages the abdomen clockwise for 21 repetitions. In Movement 6, the right hand hangs relaxed while the left hand is centered on the navel and massages the abdomen counterclockwise for 21 repetitions. In Movement 7, the left hand is placed against the anterior superior iliac spine, with the thumb pointing forward and the four fingers pointing backward in an open “tiger’s mouth” position, applying firm pressure; simultaneously, the middle three fingers of the right hand push from beneath the left breast straight down to the inguinal groove for 21 repetitions. In Movement 8, the right hand is placed against the anterior superior iliac spine, with the thumb pointing forward and the four fingers pointing backward in an open “tiger’s mouth” position, applying firm pressure; simultaneously, the middle three fingers of the left hand push from beneath the right breast straight down to the inguinal groove for 21 repetitions. Movement 9 serves as the concluding phase: after completing Movements 1 through 8 as one full cycle, participants sit with legs crossed, place each hand on the knee of the same side, and rotate the upper torso clockwise 21 times, followed by 21 counterclockwise rotations. Throughout all movements, pressure is applied evenly and gently, without abrupt or forceful manipulation.

The intervention spans 12 weeks, with one 60-minute supervised session and six home sessions per week. Each supervised session comprises a 10-minute warm-up, 20 minutes of posture correction and individualized guidance, and 30 minutes of complete PLWNT practice. On the remaining six days, participants practice at home for 30 minutes daily using the standardized instructional video, following the same sequence: Movements 1–8 as one cycle, then Movement 9 with clockwise and counterclockwise torso rotations of 21 repetitions each, at a slow and relaxed pace without breath-holding. Each home session is recorded on a weekly practice record card documenting date, duration, and movements completed, and cards are returned to the designated card manager at the end of each week.

The CBT-I protocol is developed in accordance with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia: Session-by-Session Guide and the intervention framework described by Yu and colleagues. All sessions are delivered by licensed psychotherapists with extensive experience in behavioral sleep medicine. The intervention comprises five core components.

First, sleep hygiene education: participants and their family members receive a structured educational booklet on sleep hygiene principles and are asked to review the material to reinforce their understanding of sleep-promoting behaviors. Second, stimulus control therapy: patients are advised to limit wakeful time spent in bed or the bedroom, thereby strengthening the association between the sleep environment and sleep onset. Third, sleep restriction therapy: an individualized sleep window is prescribed based on each participant’s baseline sleep patterns, with the goal of aligning time in bed with actual total sleep time, thereby consolidating sleep and improving efficiency. Fourth, relaxation training: progressive muscle relaxation and breathing techniques are introduced and practiced under guidance at the appropriate stage of the course to reduce somatic tension and pre-sleep arousal. Fifth, cognitive therapy: through regular structured sessions, therapists work collaboratively with patients to identify and correct maladaptive beliefs and misconceptions about sleep.

The intervention lasts 12 weeks, with one 60-minute supervised session per week. On the remaining six days, participants implement and consolidate that week’s content through home practice: reviewing psychoeducational materials (eg, the 3P model, sleep hygiene), applying stimulus control and the prescribed sleep window, practicing the relaxation techniques introduced in class before bedtime, and reviewing cognitive therapy worksheets. The complete CBT-I protocol and home-practice guidelines are provided in Supplemental Table 1.

The primary endpoint is the baseline-to-week-12 change in the Chinese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) total score., The PSQI is a widely used self-report instrument. It comprises 19 self-rated items and 5 items rated by bed partners or roommates. The scale captures seven clinically relevant dimensions. These dimensions are subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of hypnotic medication, and daytime dysfunction. Together, these dimensions provide a comprehensive assessment of overall sleep status in individuals with insomnia. A negative change score indicates improvement.

Secondary endpoints cover a range of patient-reported, physiological, and biological measures, each assessed using validated Chinese versions of the respective instruments. These include the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), the Pre-Sleep Arousal Scale (PSAS), the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), the Perceived Stress Scale-10 (PSS-10), the Hyperarousal Scale (HAS), the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire-5 (MEQ-5), the 20-item Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI-20), the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS), and the MOS 36-Item Short-Form Health Survey (SF-36). Additionally, a daily sleep diary will be used to capture subjective sleep parameters.

Beyond these self-report measures, several objective and biological assessments will also be performed. These include wrist actigraphy, overnight PSG, resting-state fMRI, venous blood sampling, and gut microbiome analysis. Detailed descriptions of these secondary outcome measures are provided in the supplementary Materials. This includes the scales, sleep diary, actigraphy, gut microbiome, and other biological assessments within the section titled “Supplemental 1” in the supplementary Material.

Overnight polysomnography will be performed in the sleep monitoring laboratory at Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (Natus Medical Incorporated, San Carlos, CA, USA). Recordings are scheduled from 22:00 to 07:00. The sleep environment is maintained at 22–25 °C and complete darkness. Relative humidity is kept between 35% and 45%. The PSG montage includes 19 EEG channels placed according to the international 10–20 system (Fp1, Fp2, F7, F8, F3, F4, T7, T8, C3, C4, P7, P8, P3, P4, O1, O2, Fz, Cz, Pz). Additional channels include electrooculography, submental electromyography, electrocardiography, thoracic and abdominal respiratory inductance plethysmography, nasal airflow, and snoring signals. Data are collected at a sampling rate of 512 Hz. Impedance is kept below 10 kΩ, and a 50 Hz notch filter is applied. Sleep stages will be scored by two independent registered polysomnographic technologists according to the AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events (version 3), blinded to group allocation and assessment time point; disagreements will be resolved by a third senior scorer.

For each participant and each sleep stage of interest (N1, N2, N3, REM), we will extract a contiguous 5-minute segment of artifact-free EEG. If a given stage contains less than 5 minutes of artifact-free data, we will use all available artifact-free epochs from that stage. We will record the actual duration analyzed. This same segment will be used for source reconstruction, spectral power, and wPLI computation. Consequently, all stage-specific EEG measures are derived from an identical data segment. Stage-specific analyses will include participants with at least 2 minutes of artifact-free data in that stage. The number of included participants and the analyzed duration will be reported separately for each stage. Missing data for each sleep stage will be reported independently. No imputation will be performed for stage-specific EEG measures.

Offline preprocessing is carried out using MATLAB R2024b. This follows several sequential steps. First, the data are downsampled to 256 Hz and bandpass filtered at 0.4–80 Hz to remove artifacts and line noise. Next, bad channels are identified and interpolated. Finally, independent component analysis (ICA) is applied for artifact rejection. Cortical source activity is then reconstructed from the selected segment. This uses standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA) with the MNI152 template and a three-layer concentric sphere head model. The source space is restricted to cortical gray matter. sLORETA incorporates weighting factors for spatial resolution and signal-to-noise ratio in the inverse solution to improve localization accuracy. This method has been validated in multiple EEG studies.

Regional sources are defined according to Brodmann areas (BA), with 43 regions of interest (ROIs) delineated across the cortical surface., Among these, the default mode network includes 10 BA partitions, the salience network includes 4, and the central executive network includes 5 (a full breakdown is available in Supplemental Table 2). For each participant, neural activity within each ROI is extracted by averaging the sLORETA current density time series across all voxels within a 19 mm radius sphere centered on each target BA. Spectral power and functional connectivity will be computed in predefined frequency bands. These bands are delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), sigma (12–15 Hz), beta (15–30 Hz), and gamma (30–80 Hz). These band definitions are fixed a priori. They will be applied identically to all participants and sleep stages.

Functional connectivity between ROIs is quantified using the weighted phase lag index (wPLI), which improves upon the conventional phase lag index by weighting each phase-angle difference according to its distance from the real axis, thereby reducing the influence of zero-lag interactions. The wPLI is formally defined as the ratio of the expected value of the absolute imaginary component of the cross-spectrum to the expected absolute imaginary component. This metric has been shown to outperform other connectivity measures when applied to source-reconstructed network data. These other measures include directed transfer function, partial directed coherence, Pearson correlation, and amplitude envelope correlation., EEG epochs containing residual artifact after ICA, or with more than 20% of channels interpolated, will be excluded. The number of valid epochs and the proportion of excluded epochs will be reported separately for each sleep stage and each participant. A comprehensive illustration of the source analysis workflow and the cortical ROIs is provided in .

Structural and functional MRI data will be acquired using a 3.0 Tesla GE Discovery MR750 scanner. Before scanning, participants will sit quietly for 15 minutes to stabilize their emotional state, and will then be instructed to keep their eyes closed, remain awake without falling asleep, and avoid systematic thinking or mental arithmetic; they will be told that the scan lasts approximately 15 minutes and that they may signal discomfort by raising a leg. During scanning, participants lie supine with limbs uncrossed, maintain a natural posture, keep the body relaxed, and minimize movement. Foam padding is used to restrict head motion, and earplugs are provided to reduce scanner noise. Eyes-closed rest is specified because it reliably enhances posterior alpha activity relative to eyes-open rest, providing a more stable baseline for subsequent EEG–fMRI comparison.

Functional MRI data are obtained using a T2*-weighted gradient-echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence covering from the vertex to the foramen magnum. Acquisition parameters are as follows: repetition time (TR) = 2000 ms, echo time (TE) = 30 ms, slice thickness = 4 mm, field of view (FOV) = 240 × 240 mm, acquisition matrix = 64 × 64, flip angle = 90°, and 39 axial slices per volume. High-resolution anatomical T1-weighted images are acquired using a three-dimensional fast spoiled gradient-recalled echo sequence with the following parameters: slice thickness = 1 mm, TR = 8.2 ms, TE = 3.2 ms, FOV = 256 × 256 mm, flip angle = 12°, and matrix size = 256 × 256, yielding 136 axial slices per participant.

Preprocessing of functional images will be performed in SPM12 (Wellcome Centre for Human Neuroimaging, London, UK) running under MATLAB R2024b. The first 10 volumes of each functional run will be discarded to allow for T1 equilibration and scanner stabilization. The remaining volumes will then undergo slice-timing correction, motion realignment, co-registration to each individual’s anatomical image, segmentation of gray matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid, spatial normalization to the Montreal Neurological Institute space, and spatial smoothing with a 6 mm isotropic Gaussian kernel.

Head motion will be quantified as framewise displacement (FD). Volumes with FD > 0.5 mm will be flagged, and participants with more than 20% of volumes exceeding this threshold, or with maximum FD > 3 mm, will be excluded from fMRI analyses; the number of excluded participants and reasons will be reported.

Based on the acquired structural and functional imaging data, core regions of interest (ROIs) will be defined for the default mode network (DMN), salience network (SN), and central executive network (CEN). After preprocessing, independent component analysis (ICA) will be applied for two purposes: (i) to identify and remove residual motion-related or physiological noise components from the preprocessed BOLD data; and (ii) to define data-driven network components corresponding to the DMN, SN, and CEN, which will be used to cross-check the a priori ROI definitions. The primary connectivity analysis will use the a priori ROI-based estimates; ICA-derived components will serve as a secondary, data-driven validation of network identification and will not replace ROI-based estimates.

Nuisance regression will include 24 motion parameters (6 rigid-body parameters plus their first-order temporal derivatives and squared terms), white matter and cerebrospinal fluid signals (top 5 principal components each, extracted from eroded masks), and global signal regression. Flagged volumes will be censored, and censored frames will be interpolated linearly before connectivity estimation.

To characterize functional connectivity patterns, Pearson correlation coefficients are computed between the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) time series extracted from each pair of ROIs. These analyses allow us to assess both within-network nodal connectivity strength and inter-network functional connectivity across the three large-scale cortical networks, thereby quantifying connectivity changes in patients with chronic insomnia before and after the intervention.

Additional endpoints include the documentation and reporting of adverse events, as well as the assessment of participants’ adherence to and experiential feedback on the prescribed exercise regimen. Adverse events will be actively solicited at each supervised session and each assessment using a structured checklist, in addition to spontaneous reporting. Events will be recorded in the case report form with onset, duration, severity, relationship to the intervention, and outcome; serious adverse events will be reported to the ethics committee within 24 hours.

Sample size was estimated for a one-sided superiority test comparing two independent means, with a superiority margin of Δ = 0 (statistical superiority). Parameter estimates were drawn from previously published literature., The expected post-treatment PSQI total score was set at 8.45 for the PLWNT arm and 9.92 for the CBT-I arm, with a shared standard deviation of 2.65. Because the primary endpoint is the baseline-to-week-12 change in PSQI total score, and baseline PSQI scores are expected to be comparable between arms after randomization, the between-group difference in post-treatment scores (1.47 points) was used as the assumed between-group difference in change scores. With a one-sided α = 0.025 and β = 0.20 (80% power), the computation indicated that 51 participants per group would be needed to detect this difference. After factoring in a projected 20% attrition rate, the final recruitment target was set at 64 participants per group, for a total of 128 randomized participants. No equivalence or non-inferiority margin was specified; the calculation was based on detecting superiority of PLWNT over CBT-I in PSQI total score with Δ = 0.

To minimize variability in instructional style, PLWNT will be delivered by three dedicated certified coaches, and CBT-I will be delivered by three dedicated licensed psychotherapists, both following uniform treatment manuals. Intervention fidelity will be monitored in both arms. For the PLWNT group, therapist fidelity is ensured through strict adherence to the standardized 30-minute instructional video and uniform verbal cues. For the CBT-I group, therapists will follow the session-by-session guide. Patient-level fidelity will also be assessed: for PLWNT, coaches will conduct 20-minute posture correction and individualized guidance during every weekly supervised session to ensure movements are performed correctly (eg, correct hand positions and repetition counts); for CBT-I, therapists will review patients’ completed worksheets and cognitive therapy handouts to confirm their understanding and application of the taught strategies.

Adherence will be monitored by the designated coach or therapist through weekly online contact and a participant-completed weekly practice record card documenting the date, duration, and content of each home session. Cards will be returned to the designated card manager at the end of each week; adherence rates will be calculated from these records and reported by arm.

A multi-component strategy will support retention and compliance. After each weekly session, participants will receive reinforcement regarding the anticipated sleep-related benefits of continued engagement. Those who return for all follow-up visits will receive complimentary topical pain-relief patches and health ointments. These incentives are modest, non-coercive, and identical across arms; they support retention rather than influence outcomes, are not contingent on clinical response, and are consistent with local ethics committee guidance for non-commercial trials. The scheme follows the principle of participant priority: incentives reflect the time, travel, and practice burden borne by participants rather than expected clinical benefit, and are provided equally to both arms irrespective of response.

Because this is an open-label trial, several measures are specified to minimize performance and reporting bias. Home practice differs in nature between arms (PLWNT: six 30-minute home sessions plus one 60-minute supervised session per week; CBT-I: one 60-minute supervised session per week plus home application of learned strategies). To quantify rather than assume equivalence, practice records (weekly cards for PLWNT and worksheets for CBT-I) will document session frequency, duration, and completion for both arms, and total weekly practice time and the number of supervised sessions attended will be reported descriptively by arm; the number and duration of all study-related contacts will also be recorded for comparison. Because self-reported sleep outcomes are vulnerable to expectancy effects, participants will be informed at enrollment that the trial compares two active non-pharmacological interventions of unknown relative efficacy, without stating a hypothesized superior arm. Self-report scales will be self-administered under standardized instructions without assessor prompting.

Participants will be assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the PLWNT group or the CBT-I group using a block randomization procedure. The randomization sequence will be generated by a researcher who is not involved in participant recruitment or outcome assessment. To ensure allocation concealment, the sequence will be sealed in sequentially numbered, opaque envelopes. These envelopes will remain unopened until a participant has completed all screening procedures and provided written informed consent; at that point, the envelope bearing the participant’s unique identification number will be opened to reveal the group assignment.

This trial is designed as a parallel-group, open-label randomized controlled trial. Both participants and intervention providers will be aware of the assigned treatments. The statisticians responsible for data analysis will be blinded. They will remain unaware of group allocation until the final database is locked. Outcome assessors will handle scale administration, PSG scoring, and imaging data handling. These assessors will also be blinded to group allocation and will not be involved in delivering either intervention. Participants will not have direct contact with outcome assessors. Self-report scales will be completed independently. PSG and imaging data will be transferred to assessors under coded participant identifiers. These identifiers will contain no group information. Blinding integrity will be checked by asking assessors to guess allocation at week 12. The proportion of correct guesses will be reported.

The full analysis set (FAS) will include all randomized participants who have at least one post-randomization assessment of the primary outcome. This definition operationalizes the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle as described in ICH E9, which specifies that the FAS comprises all randomized participants with the fewest and most reasonable exclusions., Missing data for both primary and secondary outcomes will be handled using the last observation carried forward (LOCF) method (Statistical Analysis Methods). Baseline comparability analyses will use observed data without imputation. The per-protocol set will comprise participants who complete the 12-week intervention with adequate adherence (Sensitivity Analysis Plan) and no major protocol deviations.

All analyses will be conducted in SPSS version 26.0 under the intention-to-treat principle. The primary endpoint will be tested as a superiority hypothesis at a one-sided α = 0.025, with a superiority margin of Δ = 0.

Missing data. Missing post-baseline values for primary and secondary outcomes will be imputed using LOCF, with all primary and secondary analyses performed on the LOCF-imputed datasets. LOCF assumes no post-dropout change from the last observed value; robustness to this assumption will be assessed through the multiple imputation sensitivity analyses in Sensitivity Analysis Plan.

Continuous variables meeting normality and homogeneity of variance will be expressed as mean ± SD and compared using independent-samples t-tests (between groups) or paired-samples t-tests (within groups). Non-normally distributed variables will be presented as median (P25, P75) and compared using the Mann–Whitney U-test. Categorical variables will be summarized as frequencies or percentages and compared using the chi-square or Mann–Whitney U-test, as appropriate.

The primary endpoint is confirmatory; all other analyses are supportive. For repeatedly measured outcomes, generalized estimating equations (GEE) will be used, with treatment group, time, treatment-by-time interaction, age, sex, BMI, and education as covariates, an exchangeable working correlation structure specified a priori, and an independent structure as fallback if the model fails to converge. GEE was chosen because it handles missing data under ITT without requiring complete cases, does not assume sphericity, and gives population-average estimates consistent with the superiority framework. The primary between-group comparison will be tested one-sided at α = 0.025 with Δ = 0; superiority of PLWNT will be declared if the one-sided p-value is below 0.025. Secondary endpoints will be tested two-sided at α = 0.05 with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction (q = 0.05) applied within two prespecified families for all repeated measures across follow-up visits.

To evaluate the robustness of the primary and secondary findings, a series of sensitivity analyses will be conducted following established practices:,
(1)Adherence-stratified analysis. Participants will be classified as high adherence (attending at least 8 of 12 supervised sessions and completing at least 70% of home practice) or low adherence. The primary outcome (baseline-to-week-12 change in PSQI total score) will be re-analyzed within the high-adherence subgroup and the full analysis set to assess whether the direction and magnitude of the between-group difference remain consistent. This analysis is exploratory and does not alter the primary superiority inference.(2)Per-protocol analysis. The primary outcome will be re-evaluated in the per-protocol set and compared with the full analysis set. Agreement will be interpreted as robustness of the between-group difference estimate.(3)Multiple imputation sensitivity analysis. To assess whether LOCF-based conclusions depend on the no-change assumption, primary and secondary outcomes will be re-analyzed using MI under a missing-at-random assumption. For each outcome, the imputation model will include the baseline value, age, sex, treatment group, and all post-baseline assessments of that outcome; 20 imputed datasets will be generated separately by treatment arm, and estimates will be combined using Rubin’s rules. LOCF- and MI-based estimates will be compared in direction, magnitude, and precision; for secondary outcomes, the number of participants contributing observed data at each time point will also be reported. Any divergence will be reported and discussed.

Data will be managed through dual entry: two independent researchers will transcribe the original paper case report forms into a single electronic database. Any discrepancies or queries during entry will be logged on a query resolution form and referred to the principal investigators for clarification. After trial completion, the final dataset will be reviewed and exported for statistical analysis. The Institutional Review Board of Shanghai Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital will oversee the study, monitoring conduct for compliance with the approved protocol and applicable regulatory standards. The board will also review study progress, verify data objectivity and integrity, and examine adverse event documentation in the case report forms. Patients and the public were not involved in setting the research question, selecting outcome measures, or designing recruitment and implementation strategies. During the trial, participants’ experiential feedback on the PLWNT regimen and study procedures will be collected through the adherence and experience assessment; results will not be disseminated directly to participants unless requested.

The trial protocol, the informed consent form, and all study materials involving direct participant contact must be submitted to the Ethics Committee of the Shanghai Municipal Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine for review and written approval before any study procedures begin. The principal investigator is responsible for submitting an annual progress report to the committee throughout the trial period. In the event of early termination or study completion, the board must be notified in writing. Any proposed changes to the protocol or study procedures should be reported promptly and may not take effect without prior written authorization, except when such changes are necessary to eliminate an immediate and apparent risk to participants. Should an urgent modification be required, the review board will be notified without delay.

Prior to enrollment, all participants were provided with a detailed Participant Information Statement that explained the study objectives, intervention protocols, potential risks and benefits, data handling procedures, and their right to withdraw at any time without consequences. All participants provided written informed consent by signing the approved consent form. A copy of the signed form was retained by the research team, and another copy was given to the participant.

This study examines a traditional Chinese training practice by directly comparing PLWNT with CBT-I in patients with sleep-onset chronic insomnia. The trial incorporates both resting-state fMRI and PSG-based source-localized EEG within a single protocol. Beyond evaluating the clinical efficacy and long-term sustainability of PLWNT in this population, the study includes polysomnographic and neuroimaging assessments to explore underlying neural mechanisms. Using a superiority design, we seek to determine whether PLWNT outperforms CBT-I in improving sleep quality. We also draw on multimodal mechanistic evidence to clarify the pathway through which each intervention may exert its effects. If the superiority hypothesis is confirmed, the results will help expand evidence-based non-pharmacological options for insomnia care and promote standardized integration of traditional Chinese exercise practices into clinical guidelines.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is widely recognized as a first-line non-pharmacological intervention for chronic insomnia. Meta-analytic evidence indicates that CBT-I yields a moderate effect size (Hedges’ g = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.50–0.78) for improving sleep-onset latency. These benefits persist for up to 12 months post-treatment, with effect sizes of 0.38, 0.29, and 0.40 at 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups, respectively. Additional analyses have reported a mean reduction of 19.03 minutes (95% CI: 14.12–23.93) in subjective sleep-onset latency following CBT-I, with internet-delivered versions showing comparable efficacy (mean reduction of 16.8 minutes).

However, two critical issues regarding the efficacy profile warrant particular attention. First, the aforementioned improvements are derived almost exclusively from subjective measures—namely, patient sleep diaries. By contrast, objective polysomnographic (PSG) assessments generally fail to detect significant reductions in sleep-onset latency following CBT-I. Second, longitudinal follow-up studies have indicated that the sleep-promoting effects of CBT-I tend to attenuate progressively over time. A meta-analysis demonstrated a marked decline in effect sizes beyond 12 months post-treatment. These limitations highlight the need for alternative, low-cost, community-accessible interventions, such as traditional Chinese exercise modalities.

PLWNT is a classic qigong exercise originally taught by Fang Kai, a Qing Dynasty health preservation expert. Its design centers on achieving health benefits through specific abdominal massage and rotational movements, guided by the principle of “movement within stillness”. All nine forms can be performed in a seated position, making the technique easy to administer. The core maneuvers involve pushing and rubbing along the Ren Meridian (from the navel to the pubic bone) with three fingers, as well as circular kneading around the navel in both clockwise and counterclockwise directions. No complex limb coordination, rhythmic breathing, or active mental guidance is required. This aligns with the original description of PLWNT as “gentle movements, no special training needed, simple and easy to perform”.

The EEG and fMRI metrics used here are exploratory and not interchangeable. Each one indexes a distinct aspect of cortical activity and supports a separate inference. Although these techniques rely on different physiological signals, fMRI measures BOLD responses linked to neurovascular coupling, whereas EEG records postsynaptic potentials. Both yield quantifiable indices of network activity. A direct linear relationship between the two has been reported.

Spectral power is derived from sLORETA current density within predefined frequency bands. It quantifies the magnitude of oscillatory activity in cortical regions of interest. Furthermore, it is sensitive to changes in the amplitude of synchronized neuronal activity. Researchers have used band-specific power to characterize arousal-related alterations in insomnia, including elevated beta power and blunted alpha decline during the wake–sleep transition. Oscillations in distinct frequency bands reflect different neural processes. Delta (0.5–4 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) support sleep homeostasis and slow-wave activity during NREM sleep. Sigma (12–15 Hz) tracks thalamocortical rhythms underlying sleep spindles. Beta (13–30 Hz) and gamma (30–80 Hz) are tied to cortical arousal and active cognition. In this trial, spectral power is used to test whether PLWNT alters the amplitude of state- and stage-dependent cortical oscillations during sleep onset and across sleep stages.

The weighted phase lag index (wPLI) quantifies the consistency of phase relationships between regions of interest. It down-weights zero-lag interactions to reduce the influence of volume conduction. It is mathematically and conceptually distinct from spectral power. Power concerns the amplitude of activity within a region, whereas wPLI concerns the consistency of timing between regions. wPLI has been shown to perform well on source-reconstructed network data relative to other connectivity measures. We use it here to test whether PLWNT alters phase synchronization among DMN, SN, and CEN regions. Resting-state fMRI functional connectivity is estimated as the Pearson correlation of BOLD time series between regions of interest. It quantifies the temporal covariance of spontaneous activity and indexes static, stage-averaged network coupling., This fMRI measure differs from both spectral power and wPLI in the physiological signal it captures, specifically neurovascular coupling rather than postsynaptic potentials. It also differs in the timescale over which coupling is estimated. fMRI connectivity is used here to test whether PLWNT alters the baseline architecture of DMN–SN–CEN coupling.

These three metrics index distinct aspects of cortical activity and are analyzed separately. Spectral power indexes the amplitude of oscillatory activity within regions of interest. wPLI indexes the consistency of phase relationships between regions. fMRI connectivity indexes the temporal covariance of spontaneous BOLD activity between regions. Each addresses a separate exploratory question. We ask whether PLWNT is associated with changes in cortical oscillatory amplitude, in inter-regional phase synchronization, and in static network coupling, respectively. Concordance across metrics, defined a priori as agreement in the direction and standardized magnitude of change, will be reported descriptively and interpreted as consistent with a broader reorganization of network activity. Discordance will be reported as indicating that changes are limited to specific timescales or specific aspects of network activity.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, fMRI and PSG-EEG data were acquired separately rather than simultaneously. This precludes the assessment of temporal synchrony or cross-modal coupling between the two modalities during the sleep-onset period. Second, 19-channel EEG source localization is spatially limited. A standard head model was used. However, the low electrode density confines analyses to cortical network–level interactions and precludes the reliable assessment of subcortical structures. sLORETA offers acceptable localization for macroscopic cortical activity with a reduced montage, but it remains subject to greater spatial ambiguity than higher-density setups such as 64- or 128-channel EEG. The limited channel count also hinders robust examination of hemispheric differences. Third, intervention intensity differed between groups, including the number of supervised sessions and the duration of home-based practice. These differences could not be perfectly matched. Attendance management and standardized quality control procedures were applied across both arms to minimize potential bias, but residual differences in practice burden and participant contact cannot be excluded. Fourth, the open-label design means that participants and intervention providers were aware of group assignment. Self-reported sleep outcomes are particularly vulnerable to expectation effects. Outcome assessment was blinded and statistical analysis was performed by blinded statisticians, but expectancy-related bias on subjective endpoints cannot be fully ruled out. Fifth, excluding participants with major depressive or anxiety disorders improves internal validity but limits generalizability. Anxiety and depression are highly prevalent comorbidities in everyday insomnia populations. Therefore, the present findings apply most directly to patients without severe psychiatric comorbidity and may not extend to the broader insomnia population. Comorbidity itself is associated with altered DMN–SN–CEN dynamics and hyperarousal, so the neurological findings may differ in comorbid patients. These patients often receive antipsychotic medication or psychotherapy concurrently. CBT-I delivery and PLWNT feasibility may also differ in this group. Future trials should enroll comorbid patients, stratify by comorbidity status, and prespecify subgroup analyses. Sixth, fMRI and PSG assessments were restricted to baseline and week 12, which was the end of the intervention. There was no follow-up measurement at weeks 16–36 owing to the difficulty of conducting these procedures within the trial. As a result, we cannot determine whether the observed neural changes persist over time or which mechanisms sustain long-term effects. Seventh, mediation analyses were not prespecified in the protocol. Any mediation analysis conducted after trial completion will be reported as exploratory and hypothesis-generating and will not be used to support confirmatory mechanistic inferences. Future research should extend the intervention and follow-up period, incorporate fMRI and PSG assessments at follow-up time points, include participants with comorbid anxiety or depression, and prespecify mediation models. This will better characterize the sustained neurophysiological effects and mechanisms of action.

The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Shanghai Municipal Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine (reference no. 2026SHL-KY-71-02). It was also registered with the International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry (ITMCTR2026001653) on July 6, 2026. All participants will provide written informed consent prior to enrollment. The trial is conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the SPIRIT guidelines. Results will be published in a peer-reviewed journal following CONSORT reporting standards. This protocol describes a superiority randomized controlled trial comparing PLWNT with CBT-I in patients with sleep-onset chronic insomnia. The baseline-to-week-12 change in PSQI total score serves as the primary endpoint, with follow-up extending to week 36 after randomization. The trial is designed to determine whether the two interventions differ in clinical benefit. It also aims to explore whether PLWNT is associated with changes in cortical oscillatory amplitude, inter-regional phase synchronization, and static DMN–SN–CEN coupling. These mechanistic explorations will use resting-state fMRI and PSG-derived EEG source analysis. If the anticipated clinical and mechanistic contributions are confirmed, the results would inform the evidence base for non-pharmacological insomnia care. They would also support the integration of traditional Chinese exercise practices into clinical guidelines. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentation, and the trial registry. De-identified data and analysis code will be made available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request after trial completion.

neuroscience.title: "Pipe-Laying": A novel fusion of 3D MRI and health records for the early detection and diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease using deep learning
neuroscience.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a prevalent form of dementia that impacts brain cells. Although its likelihood increases with age, there is no transitional period between its stages. In order to enhance diagnostic precision, physicians rely on clinical judgments derived from interpreting health data, considering demographics, clinical history, and laboratory results to detect AD at an early stage. While patient cognitive tests and demographic information are primarily presented in text, brain scan images are presented in graphic formats. Researchers typically use different classifiers for each data format and then merge the classifier outcomes to maximize classification accuracy and utilize all patient-related data for the final decision. However, this approach leads to low performance, diminishing predictive abilities and model effectiveness. We propose an innovative approach that combines diverse textual health records (HR) with three-dimensional structural magnetic resonance imaging (3D sMRI) to achieve a similar objective in computer-aided diagnosis, utilizing a novel deep learning technique. Health records, encompassing demographic features like age, gender, apolipoprotein gene, and mini-mental state examination score, are fused with 3D sMRI, enabling a graphic-based deep learning strategy for early AD detection. The fusion of data is accomplished by representing textual information as graphic pipes and integrating them into 3D sMRI, a method referred to as the “pipe-laying” method. This unified approach enables simultaneous processing of textual health records and 3D sMRI data within a single convolutional framework. Experimental results from over 4000 sMRI scans of 780 patients in the AD Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset demonstrate that the pipe-laying method enhances recognition accuracy rates for Early Mild Cognitive Impairment (EMCI) and Late Mild Cognitive Impairment (LMCI) patients, accurately classifying all AD patients. In a 4-class AD diagnosis scenario, encompassing AD, LMCI, EMCI, Cognitively Normal (CN) accuracy improved from 86.87% when only 3D images were used to 90.00% when 3D sMRI and patient health records were included. Thus, the positive impact of combining 3D sMRI with HR on 4-class AD diagnosis was established.
neuroscience.text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, leading to cognitive confusion. The disease advances gradually, resulting in the deterioration of brain cells, impacting memory and cognitive functions, and disrupting daily activities. According to data from the World Health Organization, around 55 million individuals suffer from dementia, with AD constituting 60–70% of these instances. As the elderly population continues to grow, the number of diagnosed patients is projected to escalate to 97 million in the foreseeable future. Developed nations currently observe a 13% prevalence of AD among people aged over 65, and this rate is on the rise []. Since AD is a type of dementia with a surreptitious onset in the form of episodic memory loss, its early-stage diagnosis poses challenges. Although no definitive cure for AD exists, treatment methods have shown the potential to slow down or even halt disease progression []. Given that cognitive impairments become noticeable in later stages, rendering effective treatment challenging, early diagnosis becomes crucial to apply interventions that can decelerate or even stop the disease's advancement.

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is the stage between the anticipated age-related decline in memory and cognitive function and the more profound deterioration characteristic of dementia. MCI serves as the intermediary stage and might escalate into dementia as cognitive decline becomes more severe. However, it remains unclear whether the symptoms observed at this stage lead to AD. Investigations centered on sMRI images of patients in this stage have revealed various physical changes in the brain structure []. Noteworthy transformations encompass the shrinkage of the hippocampus, pivotal for learning and memory, increased ventricular space, and decreased glucose utilization in certain brain regions. Late and early stages of MCI were established to enhance the comprehension of how MCI impacts Alzheimer's disease. Early Mild Cognitive Impairment (EMCI) exhibits distinct traits like amyloid buildup, disruptions in functional networks, and variations in brain volume. The ADNI findings indicate that individuals with Late Mild Cognitive Impairment (LMCI) and EMCI face a greater risk of developing dementia linked to Alzheimer's disease. Contrasted with LMCI patients, those with EMCI demonstrate more heterogeneous characteristics and are more prone to show negative indicators of AD pathology. At the EMCI stage, baseline cognitive function and APOE4 positive status associated with poor cognitive and functional outcomes. In the LMCI phase, the risk of AD escalates with episodic memory impairment [].

Various learning methods have been developed in this area because of the importance of the early and accurate diagnosis of AD. In addition to imaging modalities, several other factors may be linked to the early diagnosis of AD [, ]. Age, gender, education level, speech pattern, retinal abnormalities, postural kinematic analysis, cerebrospinal biomarkers, neuropsychological measures, and the values of certain genes are essential factors for disease identification []. In addition, different cognitive and reliable clinical test scores [], such as the mini-mental state examination, Montreal cognitive assessment, clinical dementia staging score, grey auditory verbal learning test, everyday cognition test, Alzheimer’s disease rating scale, and logical memory test, are required to diagnose AD. After the neurological examination, blood tests, and mental tests, brain imaging should be performed; and in some cases, electroencephalography (EEG), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) lumbar puncture, and psychiatric consultation may be required []. Using this information together with learning methods will make diagnosis faster and more precise [].

The majority of deep learning studies have employed neuroimaging techniques, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) []. However, studies utilizing alternative diagnostic data are scarce, and the majority of proposed methods have been designed for use with 2D images. Textual and numerical measurement data, aside from images, are integrated into deep learning approaches for diseases that require early diagnosis. The incorporation of demographic, genetic, and cognitive score data into the diagnostic process contributes to a more precise identification of diseases [, ].

The diagnostic process for cognitive diseases entails the evaluation of a diverse set of data. Simultaneous and integrated analyses of these data are crucial for early diagnosis. Machine learning- and deep learning-based applications have incorporated data fusion methods to achieve this objective. Data fusion involves extracting relevant information from a combination of diverse data originating from various sources. This approach amalgamates multiple data sources to facilitate comprehensive analysis. Data fusion studies involve merging data of the same type into different formats and integrating distinct data types into different formats [].

The data fusion methods suggested in the literature for the diagnosis of AD and MCI stages are primarily focused on combining different images, such as MRI and PET []. Analyzing contextual data such as age, gender, education level, genetics, and cognitive test scores also holds significant importance in the early disease diagnosis.

A key contribution of this study is the development of a fusion-based “pipe-laying” method that enables simultaneous processing of textual health records and 3D sMRI data within a single CNN framework. Unlike traditional multimodal approaches that process each data type independently and later merge their outputs [], the proposed fusion-based “pipe-laying” method enables simultaneous processing of textual and graphical data within a single convolutional framework. By embedding patient health record information into the 3D sMRI volume as structured graphical representations, the CNN can jointly learn spatial and semantic correlations between clinical attributes and brain morphology during training. This integrated learning process allows the model to automatically exploit cross-modal dependencies—for instance, how demographic or cognitive features influence specific neuroanatomical patterns—without requiring explicit feature-level alignment or late fusion mechanisms. Consequently, the proposed approach not only unifies the learning pipeline but also enhances the network’s ability to capture subtle interrelations between text-based clinical features and image-based biomarkers, leading to more robust and biologically meaningful diagnostic predictions. This unified approach not only allows the model to exploit cross-modal relationships between clinical attributes and brain structures but also significantly reduces time complexity by training and inferring through one network instead of two, and lowers space complexity by sharing parameters within a single model. As a result, the proposed method achieves higher diagnostic accuracy with reduced computational and memory requirements compared to traditional separate-model approaches.

Given the crucial significance of early AD diagnosis, this study proposes a 3D convolutional deep learning (CNN) model to classify cognitively normal, early mild cognitive impairment, late mild cognitive impairment, and AD stages in a multi-class classification. Corresponding medical systems work on either 3D- or 2D-imaging. Therefore, the whole methodological flow is repeated for inputs in these different dimensions. This combined approach was named “3D sMRI with Health Records” (3DMRIwHR) for 3D images and “2D sMRI with Health Records” (2DMRIwHR) for 2D images.

The key contributions of this study are outlined as follows.

The development of a fusion-based “pipe-laying” method that enables simultaneous processing of textual health records and 3D sMRI data within a single CNN framework.

Utilizing 3D CNN while preserving the image's spatial information.

The 3DMRIwHR fusion method for combining neuroimages and textual data results in reduced algorithm space and time complexities.

Make use of information between layers for early detection of AD using 3D sMRI processing

Comparative analysis of classification performance between the 3D and 2D CNN models.

Enhanced early and late MCI diagnosis through the inclusion of HR for both 3D and 2D sMRI classification.

For the early diagnosis of AD, different methods, such as data diversification or model development, are preferred for the multi-classification of its stages. Demographic information, cognitive scores, genetic and neuroimaging data are commonly utilized in data diversification studies. These data are evaluated either as individual features or integrated with the image data.

In a study published in 2018 that focused on separate evaluations of various data, it was observed that the addition of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score to MRI improved accuracy in the classification of healthy controls, MCI, and AD groups using different machine learning methods []. Another study conducted in the same year combined MRI, positron emission tomography (PET), Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and Electrocochleography Testing (ECogT) standard neuropsychological test scores to classify stages such as AD, EMCI, LMCI, and cognitively normal (CN) [].

Data fusion has found application in various neuroimaging studies, with some combining diverse image types while only a minority integrates demographic information with images. An example involves the combination of MRI and PET using a zero-masking strategy, aiming to extract complementary information from distinct data modalities []. Additionally, Punjabi et al.[] demonstrated the fusion of MRI and amyloid PET, two widely used imaging modalities. Preprocessing steps for the scans encompassed MRI bias field signal correction, affine recording, and skull stripping. Initially, the methods were individually compared through the utilization of a 3D CNN. In the fusion approach, both imaging datasets underwent parallel processing in separate branches, with features combined in the latter portion of the network through fully connected (FC) layers.

In 2021, a method based on embedded feature selection and fusion using multi-modal neuroimaging was proposed for AD diagnosis. By combining MRI, PET, and Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Factor biomarkers, promising outcomes were obtained for the classification of Healthy Control, MCI, and AD []. It has been suggested that the performance of the method for multiple classifications of AD can be improved using multi-modal data. In this regard, various modalities have been developed that combine MRI, PET, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers, and genetic features. It has been observed that more effective results were achieved regarding the multi-modal data scored with the linear discriminant analysis method [].

In addition to multi-class studies, another study was conducted wherein different types of data were integrated into the image, aiming to ascertain the transition from the MCI stage to AD. Through the fusion of different data formats, Pelka et al.[] employed a long short-term memory-based recurrent neural network (RNN) model for image classification. This data fusion study implies that superior outcomes can be achieved by integrating socio-demographic and medical data for disease diagnosis. Pelka et al. introduced a branding approach wherein socio-demographic and genetic data were encoded using markers on 2D MRI to attain a more advanced image representation and reduce computational load. By employing the ADNI Phase I and Heinz Nixdorf Recall study databases, the study generated five distinct markers denoting age, gender, education, marital status, and ApoE ԑ4 gene values. The outcomes of the study, wherein branded and unbranded images from each marker group underwent separate classification processes, underscored the general impact of branded data on specificity, F1-score, and accuracy performance metrics for both the Heinz Nixdorf Recall and ADNI Phase I databases.

Payan and Montana [] proposed a two-step approach for feature extraction in a 3D CNN for the classification of sMRI scans. They built a 3D CNN in which the convolutional layers were pretrained using a sparse autoencoder, and directly used 3D sMRI as input data. However, pretraining with the autoencoder was not fine-tuned; therefore, it was suggested that the performance would have been improved by fine-tuning. The model achieved higher accuracy than those of previous studies for multiple classifications. Similarly, a deeply supervised and adaptable 3D CNN (DSA-3D CNN) built on a 3D convolutional autoencoder (3D-CAE) was proposed to capture variations in anatomical sMRI brain scans based on a previous study []. As a threshold, the 3D-CAE was pretrained using the CAD-Dementia dataset. The proposed model can learn general and transferable features in different regions. The Hierarchical Attention-based Deep Neural Network (HadNet) architecture was suggested for the classification of MRI images that were normalized and skull-stripped [].

It was concluded that this architecture achieved superior results in terms of sensitivity and specificity. In another study, demographic information and clinical brain activity test scores were marked on MRI images as landmarks for multi-classification. The preprocessed images and landmarks were trained in the CNN model as two separate inputs. During training, the positions of the landmarks were controlled, and the training of landmarks and images was conducted separately. Joint learning was implemented during training. The main deficiency is that landmark detection and landmark-based classification processes are independent []. The brain images with the landmark skull in the study included colored data on disease classification. Thus, landmarks should be learned independently from CNN in unsupervised learning. In a previous study in which binary and multi-classifications were made, four classes were used: AD, EMCI, LMCI, and CN []. In this study, 75 samples from each class label were used in the experiments.

It has been revealed that CNN models outperform machine learning methods in the domain of medical image classification. Due to their revolutionary capabilities in capturing multi-region features, CNN are widely used in the medical field to identify different types of diseases using different medical imaging as input data []. While a majority of data is in 2D format, like chest X-rays or bone X-rays, and is well-suited for 2D CNNs. Advanced medical imaging (3D) produced by sophisticated equipment can be exceptionally well-identified through the utilization of 3D CNNs. Unlike 2D CNNs, 3D CNNs incorporate cross-layer contexts that are not easily discernible through visual inspection. A pivotal distinction between 2D and 3D CNNs lies in the fact that 3D CNNs can retain the spatial information inherent in images. Volumetric CNNs employ 3D filters and generate a 3D volume output by processing the input through a sequence of convolutional layers, including activation, pooling, dropout, and FC layers. Consequently, volumetric CNNs function on the voxels of 3D images while preserving their spatial attributes.

L. Liu et al.[] introduced the Multi-Modal Mixing Transformer (3MT), an innovative hybrid deep learning architecture explicitly engineered to address the prevalent and critical challenge of incomplete multi-modality data within AD classification. Previous research addressing this missing-modality problem often relied on discarding samples with missing modalities, a common workaround that leads to considerable data under-utilization. The 3MT framework utilizes a CNN component to efficiently extract local and global features from 3D sMRI data. These features are integrated with various non-imaging inputs, including up to 12 clinical data types (such as demographics, cognitive test results, and genetic information), which are handled as tabular data. The model employs Transformer encoders, specifically a novel Cascaded Modality Transformers (CMTs) architecture, leveraging cross-attention mechanisms to iteratively aggregate and refine multi-modal information in a latent space. A critical innovation, the Modality Dropout mechanism, is proposed to explicitly simulate various missing data scenarios during training. This design enhances the model’s robustness against missing features and allows the network to generate consistent predictions by effectively utilizing all available data. The primary challenge of this study lies in the fact that applying Transformers directly to large-scale 3D medical imaging data is computationally expensive. Moreover, multi-modal information is fused within a latent space through separate deep learning components,(CMT). In contrast, our proposed approach eliminates the need for an additional deep learning component for the fusion process, thereby substantially reducing computational overhead. Although this study integrates multi-modal data—including both neuroimaging and clinical features—its predictive framework remains limited to binary classification tasks, specifically distinguishing between AD and CN subjects, as well as between progressive MCI (pMCI) and stable MCI (sMCI) groups. In contrast, our proposed model adopts a more comprehensive four-class classification scheme encompassing CN, EMCI, LMCI and AD, thereby enabling a more detailed and clinically meaningful representation of the continuum of Alzheimer’s disease progression.

Y. Liu et al.[] introduced a novel deep learning framework aimed at enhancing the classification accuracy of early Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) by addressing the challenges inherent in fusing heterogeneous multimodal data. Their work leverages sMRI, which provides morphological insights into brain morphology, and resting-state Magnetoencephalography (rsMEG), which elucidates functional aspects of the brain. To overcome the difficulties in effectively integrating these disparate feature types, the researchers proposed an innovative CNN-Transformer framework. This architecture utilizes the InterFusion strategy, anchored by the novel Spatial-Channel Cross-Attention Fusion (SCCAF) module. The SCCAF module is designed to dynamically aggregate complementary features, capturing global feature correlations efficiently via cross-modal attention mechanisms. Evaluated on the BioFIND dataset, the InterFusion approach achieved a classification accuracy of 0.827, significantly surpassing the accuracy of unimodal methods (rsMEG only at 0.710 and sMRI only at 0.749). The study is noted as the first to employ deep learning techniques to combine sMRI and rsMEG for disease diagnosis, thereby highlighting the significant potential of integrating structural and functional data in neuroscience diagnostics. Methodologically, the framework is constrained by its reliance solely on two neuroimaging modalities (sMRI and rsMEG), and the authors explicitly acknowledge the limitation that integrating non-imaging data is required to achieve a more comprehensive multi-modal approach. The experimental design is limited to a binary classification between CN and MCI subjects, which constrains the model’s capacity to capture finer distinctions at the early stage of the disease. In contrast, our proposed framework refines this approach by further subdividing the MCI group into EMCI and LMCI stages, thereby providing a more granular and clinically meaningful representation of Alzheimer’s disease progression.

Al-Atroshi et al.[] introduced an innovative continuous learning (CL) framework for automated early-stage Alzheimer’s detection by integrating sMRI and electroencephalography(EEG) based spike neural signals. This system directly addresses the critical challenge of catastrophic forgetting inherent in continually expanding clinical datasets. To mitigate this, the model utilizes Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and memory replay mechanisms, allowing it to learn from new, incremental data while preserving crucial prior knowledge. The continuous learning framework employs a multimodal fusion strategy, specifically using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) like ResNet to extract MRI spatial features and a Recurrent Neural Network (LSTM) to analyze EEG temporal dynamics. The researchers tested three integration strategies—early, mid-, and late fusion—and found that the mid-fusion approach delivered the highest overall performance. Specifically, mid-fusion achieved 86% accuracy, 84% sensitivity, and 88% specificity for AD identification. The proposed continuous learning multimodal fusion strategy thus validates the potential for developing scalable and real-time diagnostic solutions that are adaptable to the incremental nature and heterogeneity of clinical data in early-stage AD diagnosis and patient management. The core methodological challenge of this study resides in the fact that the optimal mid-fusion strategy, despite yielding superior performance, necessitates high computational complexity and considerable resource requirements due to the underlying parallel processing streams. Furthermore, the framework is intrinsically constrained by its focus on integrating only two neuroimaging modalities: MRI and EEG. This limitation is explicitly recognized by the authors, who concede that extending the model’s application range requires the future incorporation of other data types, including genetic or behavioral ones. In addition, their experimental design is restricted to a binary classification (normal vs. abnormal), whereas our proposed framework extends this task to a four-class classification setting, allowing for a more granular differentiation among disease stages.

In contrast to conventional multimodal approaches that process each data type separately, the proposed fusion-based “pipe-laying” method enables joint processing of textual and 3D sMRI data within a single CNN. By embedding clinical and demographic features directly into MRI volumes, the model learns spatial and semantic relationships between health records and brain structures simultaneously. This integrated framework enhances the discovery of cross-modal correlations and improves the robustness and biological relevance of Alzheimer’s disease predictions, while supporting a comprehensive multi-class classification scheme encompassing CN, EMCI, LMCI and AD for a more detailed and clinically meaningful characterization of disease progression.

The data employed in this study were derived from the ADNI dataset. Initiated in October 2004 under the guidance of Dr. Michael W. Weiner, the ADNI dataset comprises clinical, biochemical, and genetic biomarkers, along with neuroimaging modalities such as MRI and PET. These resources can be used for early diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of AD. The study encompassed the initial six years of the ADNI project, denoted as ADNI 1. Subsequent phases include ADNI GO (2009–2011), ADNI 2 (2011–2016), and the ongoing ADNI 3 (2016 to the present). Throughout these stages, image protocols were refined, new participants were incorporated, and diverse data types were integrated into the project [].

Human Ethics Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative: “All ADNI data are shared without embargo through the LONI Image and Data Archive (IDA), a secure research data repository. Interested scientists may obtain access to ADNI imaging, clinical, genomic, and biomarker data for the purposes of scientific investigation, teaching, or planning clinical research studies. Access is contingent on adherence to the ADNI Data Use Agreement and the publications’ policies outlined in the documents listed below. Note: documents are subject to updates by ADNI.” More information is available at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/data-samples/access-data/.

In this study, a cohort of 780 participants was examined, comprising 178 AD patients, 176 patients with EMCI, 161 patients with LMCI, and 265 CN patients. The 3D sMRI scans were acquired in T1-weighted format, with an in-plane spatial size of 1.25 × 1.25 mm² and a thickness of 1.2 mm in 3D MPRAGE format. In addition to neuroimaging data, the study encompassed demographics, cognitive metrics, and genetic information of the participants. Patient health records, encompassing demographic factors like age and gender, ApoE-ε4 genetic data, and MMSE cognitive measure data were fused with 3D sMRI data. Consequently, a 3D CNN model based on 3DMRIwHR images was deployed to classify the four distinct cognitive states associated with dementia: normal cognition, early mild cognitive impairment, late mild cognitive impairment, and AD.  provides details about the participant count and health records information for each group. The majority of participants were over 65 years old, with MMSE scores exceeding 19, and a greater prevalence of negative ApoE-ε4 values compared to positive ones.

The mean age was calculated as approximately 75.04 years, with a median of 75.2 years, indicating that the dataset primarily represents an elderly population. The age range spanned from 55.6 to 94.4 years, suggesting a broad distribution while exhibiting a concentration toward the upper age spectrum. The standard deviation(STD) of approximately 7.32 reflects that the age distribution does not exhibit excessive dispersion around the mean, yet still demonstrates a degree of variability among individuals. The observed standard deviation values (~6–8) further suggest that the age groups maintain relatively similar distributions.

Taking computational efficiency into consideration, the initial step involved preprocessing the images through the utilization of FMRIB Software Library v6.0.5.2 []. The 3D sMRI data, initially registered using FMRIB’s Linear Image Registration Tool module, underwent bias field correction using the FLIRT module. This procedure eliminated the density gradient that could impact the segmentation algorithm. MRI measurements pertaining to the skull, skin, fat, muscle, neck, and eyeballs were deemed insignificant for disease identification. A Brain Extraction Tool (BET) module was applied to remove non-brain tissues, including the skull. Subsequently, intensity normalization was executed to rectify density variations potentially arising due to differing image sizes. The final preprocessing stage involved resizing the 3D images from 176 × 240 × 256–50 × 30 × 20, a resolution validated in []. The adoption of larger image sizes would result in heightened computational complexity, rendering them unfeasible for implementation on conventional computers.

To compare the impact of fusing health records with MRI scans for multi-class image classification, both 2D and 3D image data fusion methodologies were employed. From the preprocessed and unresized 3D images, 2D slices were extracted after skull-stripping. The extracted slices were automatically rotated in the sagittal plane to enhance marker visibility. In the final phase of 2D MRI preprocessing, these slices were saved in PNG format with 256 × 256 pixels.

Within the ADNI dataset, subjects with health records encompassing age, gender, ApoE-ε4, and MMSE are limited and are imbalanced across AD, LMCI, EMCI, and CN categories.

In the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, a specialist physician conducts a range of examinations after reviewing the patient's medical history. These examinations encompass neuropsychological, neurophysiological, genetic, laboratory, neuroimaging, and nuclear medicine tests. Disease diagnosis isn't solely reliant on neuroimaging; it also involves the analysis of diverse data types. Healthcare professionals face restricted opportunities to effectively utilize these varied data forms. Despite the growing body of research on this subject, MRI remains the preferred approach. In this study, we introduced a method named 3DMRIwHR, which facilitates the assessment of neuroimaging data by combining demographic, genetic, and cognitive test score outcomes. When selecting test results represented by 3D-HR markers, factors that heightened the risk of AD symptoms were considered.

3D sMRI contains additional information between layers, a feature not present in 2D sMRI. However, extracting this information through visual inspection of 3D sMRI images is not trivial. Machine learning techniques, however, can effectively harness this information. To underscore the interdimensional impact of the 3D method, a fusion procedure was applied to 2D slices derived from 3D images within the proposed deep learning model. This approach, utilizing the same data, is designated as 2DMRIwHR.

The approach used in the study encompassed the fusion of text-based information with sMRI scans through the utilization of 3D volumetric pipe-shaped markers. In marker design, preference was given to half and full rectangular prism shapes in black or white, with each color symbolizing specific attributes. These textual attributes included age, gender, ApoE-ԑ4 gene value, and MMSE score ranges.

The pipelying method, as shown in , integrates health records (HR) in text format with 3D MRI images to create fused 3D representations. Some key aspects of the pipelying method are as follows:

All categories of a given text feature should maintain the same proportions on the representative 3D volumetric pipe-shaped markers. Additionally, color coding (black and white markers) is used to ensure that different categories have uniformly sized 3D markers.

The 3D representations of different text features should be proportional to each other to prevent any single feature from having a disproportionately greater influence. In our representation, each feature is visualized as a bar with a length corresponding to the 3D cube covering the MRI scan.

The graphical encoding of health-record vaiables and 3D MRI images should not interfere with or overlap each other. To achieve this, the corners of the 3D cube representations are utilized.

illustrates the attribute values associated with these colored volumetric pipes. The characteristics of the markers utilized in the fusion of 2D images, along with their corresponding value ranges and arrangement on the image, were applied similarly to the 3DMRIwHR method, with no changes except for spatial criteria. Upon extracting the 2D images as detailed in the data preprocessing section, they were combined with 2D markers that represented textual information. This methodology was labeled as 2DMRIwHR. Following this technique’s application, training was done on the proposed 2D model without including any additional image enhancements.

In this study, four distinct health records — age, gender, MMSE, and ApoE-ԑ4 gene data — were utilized to construct 3D-HR pipes. Each of the 3D pipes created using the 3DMRIwHR method had a height of eight pixels, a width of 20 pixels, and a depth of 256 pixels.

The processing involved 3D images in NIfTI format, with dimensions of 176 × 240 × 256, carried out in the axial plane, spanning from pixel points (2, 10) to (10,49). Gaps of size (5 × 4) were deliberately left between the pipe markers to ensure that volumetric markers did not generate any erroneous correlations. 3D-HR pipes were located in the corners of the 3D sMRI scans for the purpose of data fusion. The corner's selection was such that it didn't impede the 3D brain image.
