In the case of the 2DMRIwHR method, 2D planar markers, with dimensions of eight pixels in height and 20 pixels in width, were employed. The positioning process on the image closely resembled that of the 3DMRIwHR method.

To visualize the Nifti scans, the 3D axial preprocessed and 3DMRIwHR images were transformed into PNG files, as shown in . The 3D-HR pipes representing age, gender, ApoE-ԑ4, and MMSE scores on the image were placed in a specific sequence and order, consistent with the corner placement and dimensional specifications established in the methodology. This spatial arrangement enables the transformation of textual health records into graphical pipe representations.

Consistent with this fusion methodology and the coding scheme illustrated in , the participant data corresponding to the visualized image in  were evaluated. The assessment revealed that the participant falls within the 66–75 age range, is female, possesses a negative value, and exhibits an MMSE score within the 0–9 interval.

2D MRI images were extracted from the 3D sMRI images by means of slicing. After the slicing phase, the 2D images in Nifti format were combined with health records using 2D encoding. The markers employed in the 2D images denoted the same values as those in the 3D-HR pipes. While the alignment of marker images remained consistent, due to the 2D and planar nature of the images, the 2D markers were depicted as rectangles, measuring eight pixels in height and 20 pixels in width.

The preprocessed dataset, prior to any augmentation, consisted of 4,000 MRI images, with 1,000 images for each diagnostic category (AD, CN, EMCI, and LMCI). The images of each class were partitioned at an 80:20 ratio before any augmentation, yielding 800 training and 200 test images per class. Data augmentation was applied on the fly, exclusively during model training and only to the training data. No augmentation was applied to the test data, and augmented images were not stored as additional samples in the dataset. The number of samples per class is presented in .

CNNs are a specific type of neural network designed for processing data organized in matrix form. Convolutional networks have proven effective in real-world applications, yielding satisfactory outcomes not only with large datasets but also when adeptly modeled for smaller datasets. In the realm of image processing studies [, , ], the architecture of CNN best fits the concept of learning regional patterns by transforming pixel data into matrices. Given that dementia impacts specific brain regions, we employed 2D and 3D CNN architectures to classify the four classes, namely CN, EMCI, LMCI, and AD.

The proposed model comprises three 3D convolutional layers and three 3D max pools. Following these layers, a dropout layer was introduced, succeeded by a flattened layer. At the model's last layer, there existed an FC layer employing a softmax activation function. The 3D convolutional layers were all equipped with 3 × 3 × 3 kernels and 1 × 1 × 1 stride values, featuring 64 filters in the initial two convolutional layers and 128 filters in the final layer. The pooling layer kernels were all of size 3 × 3 × 3, with stride values set at 2 × 2 × 2. The number of training parameters was 1,710,660, whereas the number of non-trainable parameters was 0. For optimization during parameter training, the adaptive moment-estimation (ADAM) optimization algorithm was utilized with a learning rate of 0.001.

Since the rectified linear unit (RELU) is currently the most commonly applied function [], it was used as the activation function in the three convolutional layers. A dropout value of 0.5 was selected to mitigate the risk of overfitting. Following the softmax activation function in the final FC layer, a 4-class disease classification was executed. The architectural layout of the 3D CNN model can be observed in .

In the 2D CNN model, there were three 2D convolutional layers accompanied by three 2D max pools. These were followed by a dropout layer, succeeded by a flattened layer. The model's conclusion included an FC layer employing a softmax activation function. The 2D convolutional layers all consisted of 3 × 3 kernels with 1 × 1 stride values, with 64 filters present in the initial two convolutional layers and 128 in the last convolutional layer. The pooling layer kernels were all 3 × 3 in size, with stride values set at 2 × 2. The number of training parameters was 16,889,284, whereas the number of non-trainable parameters was 0. An optimization algorithm, specifically “ADAM” was utilized with a learning rate of 0.001 during parameter training.

As for the activation function, RELU was utilized for the three convolutional layers due to its widespread application []. A dropout value of 0.5 was selected to counteract overfitting. The classification of the four dementia groups was carried out based on the softmax activation function in the final FC layer.

In this study, we evaluated the performance of the proposed “pipe-laying” method using a set selection of critical performance metrics. In the context of diagnosis, it is vital to minimize both false negatives (missed diagnoses) and false positives (incorrect diagnoses). While minimizing false negatives is particularly important to ensure timely intervention and potentially slow disease progression, minimizing false positives is also important. False positives can lead to unnecessary anxiety, further invasive or expensive testing, and potential misdiagnosis, placing an undue burden on patients and the healthcare system. Our evaluation focused on assessing the effectiveness of the method in a 4-class AD diagnosis scenario, encompassing the other three class labels.

Therefore, the metrics were specifically chosen due to their relevance in evaluating the performance of classification models, especially in medical diagnosis where both sensitivity/recall (correctly identifying patients with the disease) and precision (correctly identifying patients among those predicted to have the disease) are crucial. These metrics offer a nuanced understanding of a model’s ability to correctly identify individuals with the disease while minimizing both false positives and false negatives.

In the context of diagnosis, where early intervention can be crucial, recall takes on particular significance. A high recall value indicates that the model is effectively identifying a large proportion of actual cases with the disease, thus minimizing the risk of missed diagnoses (false negatives). While maximizing recall is essential, precision also plays a vital role. High precision ensures that the model’s positive predictions (diagnoses of the disease) are mostly correct, reducing the number of false positives. False positives can lead to unnecessary anxiety, further testing, and potential misdiagnosis. The F1-score, being the harmonic mean of precision and recall, provides a balanced measure that considers both aspects. We aimed to optimize the F1-score to achieve a model that is both sensitive (high recall) and specific (high precision) in its diagnostic capabilities.

In our study, the main aim is to enhance the procedure using fused textual data, especially in 3D, while interpreting the difference between 3D and 2D inputs. To that end, the experimental design includes all these comparisons, as illustrated in . In detail, mark A represents the within-case comparisons for both the 3D and 2D MRIs with fused textual data. Specifically, within the 3D case, it involves comparing the performance of the 3D-MRI model (test1) versus the 3D-MRI with fused textual data (3DMRIwHR) model (test2) to evaluate the added value of the textual information (HR: Health Records). Similarly, within the 2D case, it compares the performance of the 2D-MRI model (test3) versus the 2D-MRI with fused textual data (2DMRIwHR) model (test4). Moving on, mark B is the cross-modal comparison between the optimal 3D and 2D models that include the fused textual data. This comparison specifically evaluates the performance difference between the 3DMRIwHR model (test2) and the 2DMRIwHR model (test4), aiming to determine whether the 3D imaging data, when augmented with textual information, yields a significant improvement over the 2D augmented data. Finally, mark C denotes the overall comparative analysis without fused textual data, which encompasses the results from 3D-MRI model (test1) and 2D-MRI model (test3). All these comprehensive comparisons allows for a holistic assessment of the overall impact of both the dimensionality (3D vs. 2D) and the fused textual data (wHR vs. no HR) on the final model performance, thereby achieving the main aim of the study.

To illustrate the effect of health records on recognition rates, the comparison was made between 2D MR vs. 2DMRIwHR, and 3D MR vs. 3DMRIwHR (shown in  mark A) utilizing 2D CNN and 3D CNN deep-learning techniques respectively. The 2D and 3D classification methods were implemented using the Keras 2.8.0 library in Python 3.9, built on TensorFlow-gpu 2.8.0. The execution occurred on a PC equipped with an NVIDIA RTX2060 GPU running the Windows operating system. In the network, the Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM) optimizer was employed, starting with an initial learning rate of 0.001. A dropout rate of 0.5 was set to mitigate overfitting. For 3D classification, the batch size was set to 64, while the 2D classification employed a batch size of 128.

The image count for each class was divided into two sets using a 0.8 training and 0.2 testing ratio, as described in the Data Augmentation section and reported in . Data augmentation was subsequently applied to the training set only, during training, and did not alter the number of stored images. During the classification phase, only images belonging to the class with the lowest image count were utilized to accurately assess the impact of the pipe-laying process. This approach ensured balanced representation among classes.

The main aim is to enhance the procedure using fused textual data, especially in 3D, while interpreting the difference between 3D and 2D inputs. To that end, the experimental design includes all these perspectives, as illustrated in  (mark A and marks B&C, respectively).

Different studies in the literature are presented in . As expected, binary classification results show higher accuracy compared to multi-class approaches. Additionally, early detection phases of Alzheimer's disease have not been extensively studied, except in the work of Liu et al.[]. They examined Alzheimer's using four classes, similar to this study; however, their accuracy rates were very low.

AD: Alzheimer’s Disease,CN: Cognitively Normal, c-MCI: Convertible Mild Cognitive Impairment, EMCI: Early Mild Cognitive Impairment, LMCI: Late Mild Cognitive Impairment, pMCI: Progressive Mild Cognitive Impairment, sMCI: Stable Mild Cognitive Impairment

Although various studies on Alzheimer's diagnosis exist, researchers have used their own datasets, making direct accuracy comparisons between publications unreliable. To ensure consistency and integrity in this research, the ADNI dataset was used, and similar datasets were applied to both 2D and 3D studies. The results are reported accordingly.

Upon examining the , it is observed that although the study by Payan and Montana [], as well as Hosseini et al.[, ], achieved a comparable accuracy value, their work was limited to a three-class classification task. In contrast, our study focuses on a four-class disease classification, making the problem more complex and clinically relevant. Additionally, the model used by Hosseini et al.[] exhibits high computational and algorithmic complexity, which may limit its practical applicability.

Similarly, the study by Liu et al.[] incorporated a multiclass classification approach; however, their use of ResNet50, which is primarily optimized for 2D image processing, presents a limitation. ResNet50 does not adequately capture the full 3D spatial information inherent in MRI scans. In contrast, our proposed 3D CNN model directly processes MRI images while preserving their spatial features, allowing for a more comprehensive analysis.

Folego et al.[] also conducted a multiclass classification study, but their model demonstrated a significantly lower accuracy. This can be attributed to their fully automated approach, which lacked essential preprocessing steps, and their limited dataset size, which may have constrained model generalization.

The work presented by Pei et al.[] is a unimodal approach based on structural sMRI data. This methodology utilized pseudo-3D (P3D) blocks to decouple 3D convolutions, aiming to increase processing efficiency, while integrating expanded Global Context (GC) blocks to capture the long-range dependency mechanism. Crucially, however, their method constrained the classification task solely to binary distinctions, such as AD/CN and MCI/CN.

The study presented by George et al.[] introduced an efficient 3D CNN framework specifically designed for Alzheimer’s disease classification utilizing unimodal 3D sMRI data. This approach focused on preserving volumetric information that is frequently neglected in 2D analyses. Central to their architecture was the integration of coupled spatial and channel attention mechanisms, intended to enhance model performance by dynamically selecting the most relevant features within the input volume. The methodology was evaluated across multiple tasks, including several binary classification scenarios (AD vs. CN, MCI vs. CN, and AD vs. MCI) and a three-class multi-classification (AD vs. MCI vs. CN). Although the implementation of the attention modules improved performance across all tested classification types, the overall accuracy achieved for the three-class task was 79%. Notably, the authors acknowledged the resulting accuracy as “not optimal” for AD classification, indicating that the system would require substantial testing before being applied to real-life clinical problems.

The research conducted by Abbasian and Hammond [] introduced a tailored 3D-CNN architecture focusing on the critical binary task of differentiating EMCI from CN. This unimodal methodology utilized exclusively structural sMRI data, analyzing the entirety of the patient's 3D volumetric scans. A key endeavor of their work was the pursuit of model explainability through the deployment of GRAD-CAM heatmaps, which were used to visually track discriminative regions influencing the predictions. Nevertheless, the architecture encountered inherent limitations during training due to the relatively small dataset (446 subjects). This scarcity led the authors to note challenges associated with potential overfitting. Consequently, this tendency toward overfitting restricted the model's transparency objective, resulting in instances where the GRAD-CAM heatmap generation occasionally failed due to issues like vanishing gradients.

On the other hand, Helaly et al.[] reported a notably high accuracy of 95%. One contributing factor to this exceptional performance is their extensive dataset, consisting of approximately 48,000 samples, which enhances model robustness.

Considering these studies, our proposed model demonstrates a lower computational and space complexity and effectively achieves an accuracy level comparable to high-performance studies. This is attributed to the efficiency and simultaneous processing of textual health records and 3D sMRI data within a single CNN framework, which optimizes feature extraction and classification in a structured manner.

The 3D CNN method using only MRI achieved an accuracy of 86.87%, while the inclusion of health records (3DMRIwHR) improved accuracy by 3.13% for multi-class classification of preprocessed medical images involving AD, LMCI, EMCI, and CN categories. Similarly, the 2D CNN method without health records achieved an accuracy of 81.50%, which increased to 87.00% when health records were integrated. Given the improved performance of both 2D and 3D CNN models with health records, it can be inferred that combining health records with MRI data leads to superior outcomes. Furthermore, it was observed that the 3D CNN model with health records outperformed the 2D CNN model with health records due to its ability to leverage spatial information between the 2D layers of MRI. As depicted in  and , the training and test accuracies provide evidence that the proposed models function effectively without overfitting.

Evidently, the 3D CNN model surpassed the 2D CNN model in classifying both pre- and post-method datasets. The utilization of information across layers in 3D sMRI scans, as opposed to 2D images, grants the 3D CNN model a greater classification advantage. The difference in accuracy rates before and after applying the method was less pronounced in 3D classification compared to 2D classification, mainly due to the richer features present in 3D images. Notably, the additional features introduced alongside health records exhibited a more substantial impact on the classification accuracy of pre- and post-method 2D images, despite their lower overall feature count.

The confusion matrix illustrates the performance of the proposed 3D classifier in distinguishing various class labels when the 3DMRIwHR method is not utilized, as depicted in . Without the application of the 3DMRIwHR method, 691 out of 800 images were accurately predicted, while 109 were predicted incorrectly. In the post-method classification, 720 out of 800 images were correctly predicted, and 80 were inaccurately predicted. By ranking disease stages by severity as AD, LMCI, EMCI, and CN, the error matrix revealed that the detection capability improved with the 3DMRIwHR method as the disease progressed to more severe stages.

The confusion matrix shows the effectiveness of the proposed 2D classifier in categorizing different class labels when the 2DMRIwHR method is both applied and not applied, as shown in . In cases where the 2DMRIwHR method was not used, 645 of the 800 images were accurately predicted, while 155 were incorrectly predicted. Following the post-method classification, 698 out of 800 images were correctly predicted, and 102 were predicted inaccurately. Similar to the 3D classifier, a pattern emerged in the confusion matrix for the 2D classifier, indicating improved detection ability with the 2DMRIwHR method as the disease severity escalated.

Comparing results before and after the application of the 3DMRIwHR method in the order of class levels CN, EMCI, LMCI, and AD revealed an increase in the predictive capability of the proposed model with rising disease levels. Notably, the 3D CNN model accurately identified all images in the AD class, regardless of the presence of this method. The highest estimation for the healthy class (CN) was achieved when the 3DMRIwHR method was applied, utilizing a single MMSE 3D-HR marker. Within the EMCI class, the highest estimation occurred in the classification following the 3DMRIwHR method, wherein all markers were applied collectively. The proposed method notably heightened predictive accuracy for the early MCI level, which signifies the disease's initial stage and aligns with the study's goal of early diagnosis.

Regarding the LMCI class, the method's application using a single age 3D-HR marker resulted in the highest predictive accuracy. The decreased classification accuracy observed when combining images with ApoE ε4 3D-PI markers, compared to the rate without the method, can be attributed to the dataset's composition: 285 participants exhibited positive values, while 495 displayed negative values.

The evaluation of the model encompassed the analysis of accuracy, loss, confusion metrics, F1 score, recall, and precision parameters.  presents the performance metrics of the model after 100 learning epochs.

The precision column displays values signifying the actual criteria for accurately classified images among all samples categorized as positive. Without utilizing this method, the precision criterion for correctly classifying patients with AD was 0.97. With the implementation of this method, this ratio improved to 1.00. Notably, precision values exhibit a progressive increase in accordance with the proposed method as patient groups are arranged from worse to better.

The second column presents the sensitivity (recall) scale, which signifies the model's capability to detect positive samples. For the patients with EMCI, the sensitivity rate elevated from 0.74 to 0.90. Application of the 3DMRIwHR method led to increased sensitivity rates in diagnosing patient groups but decreased rates in the healthy group.

The F1 score, a harmonic mean of precision and sensitivity values, was chosen to avoid incorrect model selection in unbalanced datasets. Given the study's use of balanced datasets, the F1 score closely mirrored the precision values in the research outcomes. Noticeably, these values escalated for all classes, with no imbalance between precision and sensitivity. While F1 scores did not decrease for cases before and after applying the method, enhancements were evident in the AD, LMCI, and CN classes.

For the 2D CNN performance metrics,  details precision, sensitivity, and F1 scores for each class in scenarios with and without the proposed method. Prior to employing the 2DMRIwHR method, the precision criterion for AH images was 0.78, which increased to 0.86 with the method. The sensitivity also grew by 0.10 for patients with EMCI. F1 scoring values witnessed elevation for all classes and there was no imbalance between the precision and sensitivity values. In post-method classification, all metrics in the model exhibited improvement, barring the sensitivity value for the CN class.

Separate processes were conducted on both 2D and 3D images to assess the impact of the data fusion method across dimensions. Based on performance metrics, classification outcomes for 3D-HR data were consistently superior to those achieved without 3D-HR data in both models. Moreover, our study affirmed that a 3D CNN outperformed a 2D CNN in MRI classification accuracy. Similarly, akin to the 3D fusion method, patient health records were incorporated with 2D MRI images. However, extracting meaningful information from 3D sMRI visually is a nontrivial task. It has been evidenced that deep learning techniques applied to 3D sMRI, leveraging inter-layer information, yielded enhanced recognition results compared to other techniques employing 2D sMRI.

The 3DMRIwHR and 2DMRIwHR classification models demonstrate critical clinical utility, particularly in the multi-class classification of early-stage cognitive decline. Overall model accuracy substantially improved across both architectures, with the 3D CNN rising from 86.87% to 90.00%, and the 2D CNN increasing from 81.50% to 87.00%. A defining factor of this enhancement is the impressive surge in EMCI recall (sensitivity), a metric paramount for early intervention. This heightened sensitivity, evidenced by gains of +0.16 and +0.10 respectively, directly minimizes the occurrence of false negatives, thereby optimizing the likelihood of timely clinical management.

The observed change in CN class metrics reflects a strategic prioritization: CN recall slightly declined in both models. This reduction in CN recall raises the potential for the model to inadvertently classify genuinely healthy individuals into EMCI patient category, which increases the false positive risk within the diagnostic output. Higher EMCI recall means more early cases are detected (fewer missed patients). The model now identifies substantially more true EMCI patients — a valuable improvement for early detection — though at the cost of labeling a few additional borderline cases as EMCI. A slight decrease in precision is acceptable when patients are subsequently followed up with confirmatory tests.

Crucially, however, this trade-off is counterbalanced by a marked increase in CN precision. For instance, CN precision surged from 0.82 to 0.95 in the 3D CNN, and from 0.80 to 0.93 in the 2D CNN. Such high precision substantially reinforces the reliability of all classifications labeled as CN. Clinically, in the setting of neurodegenerative diseases with constrained treatment options, the strategic decision to prioritize the maximization of early detection (indicated by high EMCI recall, which effectively mitigates false negative errors) is generally favored over the marginal increase in the potential false positive risk. This assessment is further supported by the F1 score, the balanced harmonic mean of precision and recall, which improved across all classes, including CN. For the CN class, the F1 Score increased by +0.02 and +0.03 for the 3D and 2D fusion models, respectively

This data fusion study encompasses several factors contributing to its uniqueness, such as preprocessing and 3D-HR encoding, simultaneous utilization of neuroimages and health records, and harnessing the 3D CNN architecture to achieve elevated accuracy through learning regional patterns, distinguishing it from prior studies. To highlight the impact of the fusion method, results both with and without the fusion method are presented. We trained markers as features, transforming them into features during the preprocessing stage, thereby avoiding separate training and reducing computational time.

One limitation of this study is that the proposed framework was trained and validated solely on the ADNI dataset, which predominantly represents a U.S.-based cohort. Although ADNI provides high-quality and standardized imaging data, it may not fully capture the demographic, ethnic, and socioeconomic diversity observed in real-world populations. Another limitation concerns the restricted set of clinical variables used in the model. Only four features (age, gender, ApoE-ε4 status, and MMSE) were included, while other potentially informative biomarkers—such as CSF proteins, blood-based measures, cognitive scores, and medication history—were not incorporated.

Additionally, this study did not include a benchmarking analysis with alternative fusion strategies (e.g., late-fusion, attention-based models, or multimodal transformers). This limitation is an important consideration when evaluating the broader clinical relevance of the findings.

Computer-aided systems have the potential to aid doctors in achieving faster and more precise diagnoses during the early stages of AD. To achieve this goal, data beyond patient images is employed within the diagnostic process. Consequently, the types of data utilized can be diverse. CAD systems can experience enhancements when incorporating various data types. In our study, alongside image data, demographic information like age, gender, MMSE, and ApoE-ε4 was integrated.

In this study, classification was performed using a CNN architecture based on fused sMRI data, with textual health records coded as image markers to detect AD. Data fusion was performed on the preprocessed MRI by transforming participant attributes such as demographic features like age, gender, ApoE-ε4 gene information, and MMSE cognitive scores into image markers. In multi-class classification, accuracy values were obtained for the 2D and 3D CNN. The test results demonstrated that fusing health records increased the recognition rates for Alzheimer's diagnosis.

Our study revealed that different types of data can be used to detect AD. Adding health records to MRI scans increases the AD diagnosis recognition rates. The accuracy of 3DMRIwHR is better than that of 2DMRIwHR because the 3D image architecture exploits the spatial information between 2D slices in sMRI. However, the 2D CNN classification method produces a better accuracy than the 2D LSTM-based RNN because of its pattern detection approach. The 3DMRIwHR method achieved a high recognition accuracy with multi-class dementia evolution. Thus, practitioners can gain better insights by observing the early phases of dementia diagnosis based on multiple features.

Reducing examination time and facilitating diagnoses through CAD systems can expedite the dementia diagnosis process for healthcare professionals. Our study demonstrates that diverse data formats can be combined to achieve enhanced accuracy rates while maintaining lower computational complexity. This empowers doctors and specialists to diagnose dementia by utilizing all available patient-related data.

In conclusion, our study proposes that the 3D data fusion approach can serve not only for classification but also for predicting convertible MCI. In conclusion, our study proposes that the 3D data fusion approach can serve not only for classification but also for predicting convertible MCI.

Future research should incorporate datasets collected from a broader and more diverse range of clinical centers, including independent and multi-center cohorts, to enhance the generalizability and robustness of CAD systems. Additionally, integrating a greater variety of clinical biomarkers—such as blood test results, genetic markers, CSF protein levels, extended cognitive assessments, neurophysiological data (e.g., EEG), and medication history—alongside MRI images could further improve system performance and provide a more comprehensive view of disease progression. The use of different deep learning approaches, including hybrid models and transformer-based architectures, is recommended to facilitate comparative analyses with existing methods and to explore more effective feature representation strategies. Furthermore, the performance of various data fusion techniques should be systematically evaluated to determine which integration methods yield the most reliable and clinically meaningful results. In particular, future work will focus on benchmarking the proposed “pipe-laying” fusion approach against alternative strategies such as late-fusion, attention-based, and transformer-based multimodal frameworks to provide a broader understanding of fusion performance. Collectively, these directions are expected to improve the interpretability and applicability of the proposed framework across heterogeneous, real-world clinical populations.

neuroscience.title: Apolipoprotein E genotype, PET and MRI biomarkers, and vascular risk: A multi‐modal investigation of memory performance in US POINTER
neuroscience.abstract:
The apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is a key genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the etiology of impairment in non‐carriers is less understood.We used regression and mediation models to test the cross‐sectional relationships among APOE genotype, positron emission tomography amyloid and tau, vascular risk factors, and episodic memory within the US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk ancillary imaging dataset of non‐demented older adults.In our cohort (N = 880), APOE ε4 carriers showed higher global amyloid, higher meta‐temporal tau, smaller hippocampal volume, poorer memory, and a stronger relationship between amyloid and tau standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR; ∆β = 0.22, p < 0.001). Tau predicted memory (p < 0.01) and partially mediated the APOE–memory association. In a stratified analysis, higher Framingham Heart Study risk score (FHS; p = 0.022) and not tau SUVR (p = 0.1) were associated with memory among APOE ε4 non‐carriers, whereas tau SUVR (p = 0.048) but not FHS risk score (p = 0.55) was associated with memory amongst APOE ε4 carriers.Drivers of cognitive performance appear to be specific to APOE ε4 carrier status, emphasizing the need to identify alternative, or contributing, disease mechanisms among non‐carriers.
The US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk (U.S. POINTER) cohort is composed of older adults at elevated risk of cognitive decline and cardiovascular disease burden.Further multimodal neuroimaging data was collected through the POINTER Imaging ancillary study.At baseline evaluation, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 genotype was significantly associated with amyloid and tau pathology, hippocampal atrophy, and poor episodic memory performance.
APOE ε4 genotype stratification analysis showed significant associations of Framingham cardiovascular risk score and smoking status with memory in non‐carriers only.Etiological pathways of dementia may differ in contributive strength to cognitive deterioration within this at‐risk cohort.
neuroscience.text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the predominant etiology of cognitive impairment and dementia and one of the leading contributors to global mortality and disability., , ,  The amyloid cascade hypothesis, which positions amyloid beta (Aβ) deposition as the critical upstream initiator of tau pathology and neurodegeneration, has historically defined AD research, providing the mechanistic basis for recent anti‐amyloid immunotherapies., , ,  Of note, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is widely recognized as the strongest genetic risk factor for late‐onset AD (LOAD) in some populations,,  as its isoform‐specific effects span Aβ aggregation and clearance, neuroinflammation, and lipid homeostasis., ,

APOE ε4 non‐carriers, however, constitute ≈ 75% of the general population and account for an estimated 33% to 50% of clinically diagnosed AD dementia cases, depending on ancestry and study cohort. Transcriptomic analyses indicate that AD pathogenesis in non‐carriers may also engage immunological and cardiovascular pathological pathways in addition to the amyloid‐driven pathology, a pattern further supported by genome‐wide association studies identifying immune and vascular susceptibility loci beyond the APOE region.,  Therefore, the extent to which biological mechanisms may drive cognitive decline in non‐carriers, especially in the preclinical stages of AD, remains incompletely understood.

Additionally, some degree of vascular comorbidity is the second most common pathology among patients with AD, with extensive neuropathological evidence implicating additive or synergistic contributions of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk burden to cognitive loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)‐based measures of white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), infarcts, and cerebral microbleeds generally display brain changes conferred by cerebrovascular processes, with WMHs as a specific, well‐supported marker of small vessel disease., , ,  These biomarkers are often associated with vascular risk factors, such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia, that may additively contribute to both CVD and dementia risk. However, the role of the APOE ε4 genotype within this framework has been less studied., , , , , , ,

To examine the impact of the APOE ε4 genotype on a more representative population, we assessed cross‐sectional differences by APOE ε4 genotype from participants of the US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk (US POINTER) randomized clinical trial. This study enrolled a diverse cohort of unimpaired older adults at elevated risk for cognitive decline due to family history, limited weekly physical activity, and elevated cardiometabolic risk, with multimodal neuroimaging and vascular data. Our goal was to evaluate (1) whether the APOE ε4 genotype is more likely to be associated with a “canonical AD” phenotype of reduced episodic memory performance, hippocampal atrophy, and elevated amyloid and tau positron emission tomography (PET); (2) whether the relationships among these measures differ by APOE genotype, and if so; (3) do vascular factors also differ in their association with cognition by APOE genotype.

Our study draws from participants of the POINTER Imaging study, an ancillary study of the US POINTER clinical trial. The parent trial evaluated whether two multidomain lifestyle interventions produce differential outcomes in cognitive trajectories over a 2‐year period.,  Participants were 60 to 79 years of age, led a sedentary lifestyle, followed a suboptimal diet, and carried an elevated risk for future cognitive decline based on these cumulative factors, with additional well‐recognized risk markers including CVD, a family history of memory impairment, and ethnoracial background. Participants were also free of meaningful cognitive impairment, which was operationalized as a modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (mTICS) score > 32, a global Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score of ≤ 0.5, and a CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR‐SB) score of ≥ 1.,

To reduce bias across demographic subgroups, mTICS scores were adjusted to account for age, education, and race/ethnicity, specifically +3 points for participants from minoritized ethnoracial backgrounds with a maximum adjustment of +5 points. Adjusted scores were capped at 50. Other criteria excluded individuals with significant neurological, psychiatric, or peripheral organ system diseases; recent or active alcohol/substance abuse; regular use of medications that may alter cognition; and assisted living or nursing home status. Under exceptional circumstances, such as an unreliable study partner, central review could approve enrollment of such individuals whose CDR‐SB score was ≥ 1. Further eligibility criteria have been delineated in a separate study.

Enrollment into the US POINTER trial and POINTER Imaging study opened in May 2019 and August 2020, respectively, with both trials completing recruitment in March 2023. Beginning August 2020, every newly randomized US POINTER participant without contraindications to MRI or PET imaging was invited to enroll in the POINTER Imaging study. Data used in preparation for this article were obtained from the US POINTER database on November 19, 2025. The POINTER Imaging study was composed of 1052 participants. Of these individuals, 172 were missing complete exposure or outcome data at the time of baseline evaluation, resulting in 880 individuals for our analysis.

All demographic information, including age, sex, ethnoracial group, and years of education, was obtained by self‐report. Physical measures, such as body mass index (BMI) and blood pressure, were measured by standard protocols. Standardized questionnaires were used to self‐report past medical history, while laboratory values, including hemoglobin A1c and cholesterol, were assessed from specimens that were collected after 10‐hour fasting.
APOE genotyping was performed for subsequent participant classification into APOE ε4 non‐carriers or APOE ε4 carriers with at least one ε4 allele. Of our total sample, 20 participants were APOE ε2/ε4 carriers. Because US POINTER aimed to reflect the diversity of the general population, we included these individuals in our analyses and classified them as APOE ε4 carriers.

Baseline cognition was assessed with the POINTER‐modified Neuropsychological Test Battery (PmNTB). This comprised the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test, Story Recall, and Visual Paired Associates for the episodic memory composite score; Number Span, Verbal Fluency, and Trail‐Making Test for the executive function composite score; and Trail‐Making Test, Part A and Digit Symbol Substitution Test for the processing speed composite score. Each sub‐score from these individual tests was converted to z scores using means and standard deviations derived from the full set of US POINTER baseline values. These z scores were then averaged to create the composite scores for episodic memory, executive function, and processing speed, with further scoring details previously reported in the parent study. For the purposes of our study, we used episodic memory performance to better evaluate aging trajectories that were susceptible to AD onset. We used the CDR‐SB score rather than global CDR because of its greater sensitivity to subtle cognitive changes.

By design, the US POINTER cohort is at higher risk for CVD. Prevalent CVD was defined by participant self‐report of any of the following: myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, congestive heart failure, uncontrolled arrhythmia, uncontrolled angina, cardiac surgery (stent placement, angioplasty, bypass, or valve replacement), or thromboembolic events (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or transient ischemic attack). Overall risk was indexed using the Framingham Heart Study (FHS) CVD risk score, an established estimator of the 10‐year probability of a major cardiovascular event, in which higher scores reflect greater risk. The FHS risk score is computed from age, sex, systolic blood pressure, current antihypertensive medication use, BMI, current smoking status, and history of diabetes. This score was calculated for our POINTER Imaging sample using available data, including participants who self‐reported prevalent CVD. Thus, our analysis focuses on the FHS risk score measure to operationalize prospective CVD risk.

T1‐weighted structural MRI was acquired on Siemens 3T platforms (Tim Trio, Magnetom, Verio, Skyra, or Prisma Fit) using a three‐dimensional magnetization rapid gradient echo (3D MPRAGE) sequence harmonized to the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) 3 protocol (repetition time [TR] = 2300 ms, echo time [TE] = min full echo, voxel size = 1 mm isotropic, and field of view = 256 mm). Cortical and subcortical parcellation was performed with FreeSurfer v7.1. Our hippocampal segmentation method uses a standard atlas‐based diffeomorphic approach with the minor modification of label refinement. We further modified this approach to include the European Alzheimer's Disease Consortium–ADNI harmonized hippocampal masks to assure standardization across cohorts. Hippocampal volume was then residualized by total cranial volume (TCV) to adjust for head size differences. Fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery images were also acquired (resolution = 1 × 1 × 1.2 mm, [TR] = 4800 ms, [TE] = 300 to 450 ms, inversion time = 1550 to 1800 ms, echo train length = 100 to 250 ms) and used with T1 MPRAGE to produce segmented WMH volumes, according to established protocol. All WMH volumes were residualized by TCV, although WMH volumes were natural logarithm transformed prior to residualization to normalize variance.

Aβ PET was acquired with [18F]florbetaben (FBB) and tau PET with [18F]MK6240. Image acquisition was performed on GE Discovery MI or ST, Siemens Biograph mCT 40 or Vision, or Phillips Gemini TF scanners. Participants received ≈ 8 mCi of FBB or 5 mCi of MK6240, with imaging performed from 90 to 110 minutes post‐injection across four 5‐minute frames. Pre‐processing followed the ADNI‐derived multisite harmonization pipeline used by the POINTER Imaging core analysis labs.,  Fully pre‐processed images were retrieved from the Laboratory of Neuro Imaging (LONI) and intensity‐normalized using the whole cerebellum (FBB) or inferior cerebellar gray matter (MK6240) as the reference region. Tracer‐specific regions of interest (ROIs) were sampled from FreeSurfer parcellations of each participant's native‐space T1 MRI. Global cortical FBB, meta‐temporal MK6240, and entorhinal cortex MK6240 standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) were computed by published methods., ,  The meta‐temporal ROI was used as the primary tau biomarker region in our analyses due to its established efficacy in capturing transitions between Braak stages. Full acquisition parameters and processing details have been previously reported.

We characterized all demographic, biomarker, and cognitive outcomes by APOE genotype using standard descriptive statistics of analysis of variance and Pearson chi‐squared test for the full dataset. All analyses were performed using the R statistical package version 4.5.0. Multivariate linear regression was used to assess associations among APOE genotype, global FBB amyloid, meta‐temporal and entorhinal cortex tau MK‐6240, hippocampal volume, WMH, peripheral vascular risk factors, and cognitive domain scores. Interaction terms were tested for APOE ε4 genotype x amyloid and APOE ε4 genotype x FHS risk score. We implemented parametric and non‐parametric mediation analysis using linear regression to predict episodic memory at baseline evaluation using the R mediation package 4.5.1. This package implements previously established methods and recommendations., , ,  In addition to the estimation of causal mediation effects, the software also allows researchers to conduct sensitivity analysis for certain parametric models. All analyses were adjusted for potential confounding variables of age, sex, education, ethnoracial group, and CDR‐SB. We tested for multicollinearity in models including FHS risk score and covariates of age and sex using variance inflation factors, which remained ≤ 2.

Our cohort consisted of 880 cognitively unimpaired older adults with a mean age of 68.4 ± 5.2 years, of whom 539 were female (61%), 250 (28.4%) were APOE ε4 genotype carriers, and 258 (29%) were amyloid positive. Subject characteristics for the whole group and stratified by APOE ε4 genotype are shown in Table . Univariate analysis found that APOE ε4 carrier participants had significantly higher global FBB amyloid (p < 0.001) and meta‐temporal tau MK6240 (p = 0.008), as well as poorer episodic memory performance (p = 0.019), than APOE ε4 non‐carrier participants. APOE ε4 genotype was not associated with participant age, sex, education, FHS risk score, CDR‐SB, or ethnoracial group. Mean raw hippocampal volumes and raw WMH volumes were smaller among APOE ε4 carriers, although these differences did not reach significance.

We further investigated whether the APOE ε4 genotype was associated with amyloid, meta‐temporal tau, hippocampal volume, and WMH in the full cohort (Table ). In linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, education, race/ethnicity, and CDR‐SB, we found that APOE ε4 genotype remained significantly associated with three biomarkers at baseline evaluation: greater amyloid (β = 0.10, 95% confidence interval [CI: 0.08, 0.12], p < 0.001) and meta‐temporal tau (β = 0.04, 95% CI [0.02, 0.06], p < 0.001) and smaller hippocampal volume (β = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.32, −0.04], p = 0.010). We also note that participants who self‐identified as Black had significantly lower overall amyloid (β = −0.05, 95% CI [−0.08, −0.02], p = 0.003) and tau burden (β = −0.04, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.01], p = 0.018), but significantly smaller hippocampal volumes (β = −0.28, 95% CI [−0.47, −0.09], p = 0.004). APOE ε4 genotype was not significantly associated with WMH.

We next tested whether there was an APOE ε4 genotype x amyloid interaction in predicting meta‐temporal tau using a linear regression model. We found a significant interaction (β = 0.223, 95% CI [0.103, 0.343], p < 0.001; Table ), with both amyloid and tau quantified as continuous values with mean‐centered amyloid SUVR values. Greater amyloid burden was associated with greater tau among APOE ε4 carrier participants (β = 0.42, 95% CI [0.34, 0.51], p < 0.001). In contrast, greater amyloid burden was associated with less pronounced meta‐temporal tau in APOE ε4 non‐carrier participants (β = 0.20, 95% CI [0.11, 0.29], p < 0.001). These associations were significantly different when comparing APOE ε4 carrier to the APOE ε4 non‐carrier group (∆β = 0.22, p < 0.001; Figure ) using a Wald t test comparison.

We then looked at the independent baseline association of each biomarker with cognitive performance for the entire group (Table ). In individual linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, education, race/ethnicity, CDR‐SB, and APOE ε4 genotype, only meta‐temporal tau was significantly associated with worse episodic memory (β = −0.56, 95% CI [−0.94, −0.19], p = 0.003). Amyloid burden, hippocampal volume, and WMH were not significant predictors of memory performance at baseline. We also looked at the associations between (1) WMH and executive function (p = 0.521) and (2) WMH and processing speed (p = 0.113) based on evidence showing stronger effects of vascular contributions on these cognitive domains.,  Neither of these relationships were significant. APOE ε4 genotype remained significantly associated with worse episodic memory across all models (all p < 0.01).

Because meta‐temporal tau was the sole significant biomarker predictor of memory performance, we examined whether it accounted for the cross‐sectional association between APOE genotype and episodic memory using path‐analytic mediation with bootstrapped confidence intervals (k = 500 resamples). APOE genotype was associated with greater tau burden (β = 0.038, 95% CI [0.016, 0.061], p < 0.001), which in turn was associated with worse episodic memory (β = −0.563, 95% CI [−0.938, −0.189], p = 0.003). The indirect effect of APOE genotype on memory through tau was β = −0.201 (bootstrapped 95% CI [−0.048, −0.004]), consistent with partial mediation accounting for 10.8% of the total effect (Figure ). The direct effect of APOE genotype on memory remained significant after adjustment for tau (β = −0.180, 95% CI [−0.318, −0.053], p < 0.001) but was slightly attenuated relative to the total effect (β = −0.201, 95% CI [−0.339, −0.071], p < 0.001).

In a parallel analysis, substituting meta‐temporal tau for entorhinal tau, a brain region important to memory and one of the earliest regions affected by tauopathy in AD, the indirect effect accounted for 19% of the total effect (indirect β = −0.038, bootstrapped 95% CI [−0.073, −0.011]; Figure ). The direct effect remained significant (β = −0.162, 95% CI [−0.297, −0.026], p = 0.032) relative to the total effect (β = −0.200, 95% CI [−0.332, −0.058], p = 0.004), again with most of the association unaccounted by the tau pathway. To confirm that these effects were consistent in a preclinical AD stage, we reran mediation analyses in the amyloid‐positive subset of our cohort (Figure  in supporting information), and the results were essentially unchanged.

Previously, Harrison et al. demonstrated that vascular risk was related to brain structure, but not to amyloid or tau, and contributed to memory independently of AD pathology in the POINTER Imaging baseline study. We subsequently examined whether the APOE ε4 genotype modified the relationship between vascular risk and episodic memory. In linear regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, education, race/ethnicity, CDR‐SB, and APOE ε4 gene dosage (none, heterozygote, homozygote), FHS risk score was significantly associated with episodic memory performance (β = −0.006, 95% CI [−0.010, −0.001], p = 0.020; Table  in supporting information). The effect of APOE ε4 gene dosage on episodic memory also remained significant for both heterozygotes (β = −0.133, 95% CI [−0.263, −0.002], p = 0.046) and homozygotes (β = −0.397, 95% CI [−0.735, −0.059], p = 0.022). Conversely, in separate models, FHS risk score was not associated with executive function or processing speed when treated as independent variables using the same predictors. The APOE ε4 gene dosage x FHS risk score interaction was not significant when predicting episodic memory in a separate model adjusting for covariates (p = 0.1).

We performed an exploratory stratified analysis by APOE ε4 carrier status identical to those previously reported by Harrison et al. (Table  in supporting information). FHS risk score (β = −0.006, 95% CI [−0.011, −0.001], p = 0.022) was significantly associated with episodic memory performance among APOE ε4 non‐carriers, but not APOE ε4 carriers, whereas meta‐temporal tau SUVR (β = −0.656, 95% CI [−1.306, −0.006], p = 0.048), but not FHS risk score, was significantly associated with episodic memory among APOE ε4 carriers. We also sought to examine whether component vascular risk factors of the FHS score might explain cognitive variance among non‐carriers. In genotype‐stratified models adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, CDR‐SB, and amyloid and tau PET, we observed that smoking history (β = −0.152, 95% CI [−0.271, −0.032], p = 0.013) was the only component variable significantly associated with worse memory performance in individual linear regressions for non‐carriers (Table  in supporting information). These stratified estimates describe associations within APOE ε4 non‐carriers and do not constitute evidence that associations significantly differ by genotype.

The well‐established association between APOE ε4 genotype and LOAD risk has been substantiated by isoform‐specific studies of APOE–Aβ interactions.,  Yet the classical amyloid cascade, even when amplified by APOE,,  may not fully account for dementia risk in APOE ε4 non‐carriers., ,  Here, we determined the effects of APOE ε4 genotype on the associations among neuroimaging biomarkers, vascular risk, and cognition in the POINTER Imaging study, a cohort selected for increased risk of CVD and cognitive decline. Across the full cohort, we confirmed significant associations of APOE ε4 genotype with higher amyloid, higher tau, smaller hippocampal volume, and poorer episodic memory performance, consistent with prior evidence that APOE ε4–related genetic susceptibility is biologically expressed even in preclinical and prodromal stages. Because amyloid is thought to facilitate tau aggregation and spreading in traditional AD pathophysiology,,  we extended this framework by showing that APOE ε4 genotype carrier status moderates the baseline cross‐sectional association between amyloid and tau. This suggests that amyloid‐positive APOE ε4 carriers in this cohort had a more advanced expression of the canonical AD trajectory than non‐carriers,, ,  likely facilitated by tau expression. The smaller amyloid–tau associations first observed in the parent study by Harrison et al. and interpreted as indicating overall less AD pathology may therefore reflect pathological heterogeneity as a cause of reduced episodic memory performance (either additively or independently), because among APOE ε4 carriers, the AD canonical pathway appears strong.

Our mediation analyses demonstrated that meta‐temporal and entorhinal tau partially accounted for the APOE genotype–memory association by 10.8% and 19%, respectively. The stronger entorhinal effect is consistent with evidence that the entorhinal cortex is an early site of tau accumulation closely tied to memory outcomes. These significant effects were sustained for amyloid‐positive participants (n = 258), concurrent with the biological definition of AD.,  Together, these findings support tau burden as a potential marker linking APOE ε4 carrier status to lower memory performance, plausibly through APOE‐related exacerbation of Aβ‐triggered neurotoxicity and tau hyperphosphorylation, confirming our hypothesized AD canonical pathway for APOE ε4 carriers., ,  The direct effect of APOE genotype on memory, however, persisted after tau adjustment, indicating that this AD pathway does not fully account for memory. It remains uncertain how distinct APOE isoforms regulate neurotoxic gain or loss of function, including cell death, synaptic failure, or cerebrovascular dysfunction, in downstream neurodegeneration,, ,  or even their relationships with amyloid and tau.

Among our selected biomarkers (hippocampal and WMH volumes, amyloid and tau PET SUVR), only meta‐temporal tau burden significantly predicted memory performance. This aligns with growing recognition of tau PET as a more robust indicator of cognitive decline. The absence of significant associations of amyloid, hippocampal volume, or WMH with memory likely reflects the preclinical phase of this cohort. Unlike tau pathology, amyloid burden alone may not fully explain AD severity as an upstream process, while neuronal injury leading to measurable atrophy may be too subtle to capture earlier disease‐related change., ,

Because POINTER was selectively enriched for CVD, we sought to determine whether the composite FHS score and component risk factors were associated with cognition. Vascular processes are thought to contribute to cognitive impairment and dementia,, ,  and our prior work showed that FHS risk score was associated with episodic memory. Like Harrison et al., FHS risk scores remained significantly associated with episodic memory when added to the model containing amyloid and tau PET measures (Table ). Episodic memory scores were also significantly worse in both APOE ε4 homozygotes and heterozygotes. Given conflicting evidence on interactive associations between FHS risk and amyloid burden on tau accumulation and cognitive outcomes,,  we tested an APOE ε4 gene dosage x FHS risk score interaction on episodic memory, which was not significant. Due to the pleiotropic nature of APOE ε4 and its sustained effect in all our models, we performed exploratory analyses stratified by APOE ε4 genotype. Here, we evaluated possible differences among identical predictors of episodic memory performance within carriers and non‐carriers separately (Table ). We also examined independent associations of FHS risk score components with episodic memory within carriers and non‐carriers using the same models (Table ). Although we show FHS risk score significantly predicted memory in APOE ε4 non‐carriers, we interpret this cautiously due to a lack of a significant interactive effect. Vascular‐metabolic injury arguably occupies an important etiological role, but the parallel pathways of cognitive aging through amyloid and vascular pathology may not necessarily be independent due to intrinsic genetic risk alone. Rather, APOE ε4 heterogeneity may shift toward amyloidosis as a more dominant pathological contributor to cognitive performance in carriers. Conversely, cognitive decline for the APOE ε4 non‐carriers may manifest through a broader set of non‐amyloid or mixed pathologies, but these remain more difficult to detect, particularly in non‐impaired individuals., , , , , ,

The absence of significant associations between vascular risk factors and episodic memory among APOE ε4 carriers certainly does not exclude cerebrovascular disease in this group. Instead, APOE ε4–associated vascular injury may operate through mechanisms not captured by the vascular markers examined here. For example, APOE ε4 carriers show accelerated blood–brain barrier breakdown in the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe, both regions central to episodic memory, which can be detected in cognitively normal individuals and predicts subsequent cognitive decline independently of amyloid and tau status. This has been mechanistically linked to an APOE ε4–driven cyclophilin A‐MMP9 cascade in pericytes that degrade proteins, alongside reductions in cerebral blood flow and glucose uptake reported in non‐demented carriers.,  Crucially, this pathway is not captured by FHS risk score, smoking status, or MRI WMH measures. Other MRI measures may be better suited to detect preclinical vascular contributions to memory in APOE ε4 carriers and should be investigated in future baseline and longitudinal settings. Similarly, FHS risk score has been associated with cognitive impairment even after adjusting for PET measures of AD and MRI measures of vascular brain injury, likely reflecting systemic processes such as inflammation or toxic angiogenesis.,  How these downstream effects interact is not yet clear, as there is no current standard for demonstrating the additive effects of cerebrovascular disease and AD pathology.

These findings may have implications for the design and interpretation of future dementia prevention trials. The parent US POINTER trial reported that the structured‐intervention benefit on global cognition was consistent across APOE ε4 carriers and non‐carriers. Similarly, the Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) found no significant interaction between APOE ε4 genotype and intervention arm on its neuropsychological composite, although point estimates within APOE ε4 carriers were nominally larger. We note, however, that a longitudinal, multimodal intervention study for dementia in Japan did find a significant benefit of intervention on cognition for APOE ε4 carriers (p = 0.035), whose participants, unlike those of POINTER and FINGER, were already diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment. Therefore, multidomain interventions may operate through different biological mechanisms across APOE ε4 groups and disease stages. Further longitudinal biomarker modeling of our POINTER imaging cohort should be conducted to evaluate whether the strength of pathological pathways differs by APOE ε4 carrier status, particularly if vascular or cardiometabolic mechanisms are relevant among non‐carriers. This may better elucidate the comprehensive impact of hybrid lifestyle intervention programs.

Several strengths support our findings. US POINTER is currently one of the largest ethnoracially diverse cohorts of cognitively unimpaired older adults at risk for cognitive decline, recruited through community engagement at geographically distinct sites. The POINTER Imaging study further provides harmonized multimodal phenotyping, including PET, MRI, and vascular measures, with APOE genotyping. Studying this group at a pre‐symptomatic stage reduces the risk that the associations between biomarkers and cognitive outcomes are confounded by overt impairment, addressing the need to understand early disease indicators for the general population.

Inclusion of participants from different ethnoracial backgrounds also identified unique findings worthy of further research. For example, participants who self‐identified as Black/African American had lower amyloid and tau burden, and yet smaller hippocampal volume, higher FHS risk score, and overall worse memory, despite no significant difference in APOE ε4 prevalence compared to other ethnoracial groups, indicating the potential influence of mixed pathologies as previously reported. This should be interpreted in the context of broader social determinants of health, as previous studies suggest that AD and related dementias disparities may reflect compounded consequences of socioeconomic disadvantages, including neighborhood deprivation, chronic disease, and reduced medical access. This further speaks to the need for larger, more nuanced study cohorts representative of the US aging population in health care and research.

Our study is not without limitations. First, our cross‐sectional analyses cannot establish temporal ordering among neuroimaging biomarkers, vascular risk, and memory. Second, US POINTER participants were pre‐selected for elevated CVD risk and within a compressed range of cognitive function, which may introduce bias, attenuate our observed associations, and limit generalizability to lower risk older adults. Finally, the main study aims focused on WMH volume as the measure of vascular brain injury. Diffusion tensor imaging measures of fractional anisotropy or free water, both known to be associated with vascular brain injury in non‐impaired cohorts,,  might further elucidate subtle differences related to vascular risk factors.

As the field explores risk and protective factors that can identify disease earlier within at‐risk populations, understanding the biological substrate of APOE ε4 genotype–specific effects will offer a more robust translation of AD heterogeneity into clinically meaningful prevention and intervention strategies.

neuroscience.title: Mirror Movements in a Child With a TUBB‐Related Tubulinopathy: Expanding the Phenotypic Spectrum
neuroscience.abstract: Congenital mirror movements (CMM) are involuntary contralateral movements that mirror intentional unilateral actions and are most commonly associated with pathogenic variants in genes such as DCC, NTN1, and RAD51. Tubulinopathies, caused by mutations in tubulin‐encoding genes, are recognized contributors to abnormal motor pathway development; however, mirror movements have rarely been reported in association with TUBB‐related disorders. We report a 6‐year‐old girl with normal development and bilateral mirror movements of the upper limbs who carries a de novo heterozygous TUBB variant, NM_178014.4:c.155A > G; p.(Asn52Ser), classified as likely pathogenic. Neuroimaging revealed corpus callosum dysgenesis, basal ganglia abnormalities, and brainstem hypoplasia, consistent with a tubulinopathy. This case expands the phenotypic spectrum of TUBB‐related tubulinopathies and supports the role of tubulin dysfunction in corticospinal tract development and interhemispheric motor control.
neuroscience.text:
Mirror movements (MM) are involuntary symmetrical movements on one side of the body that mirror voluntary movements on the opposite side []. These movements result from disruptions in the function of the corticospinal tract and the communication between the brain hemispheres. While physiological MM may occur transiently during early childhood, persistent MM are considered pathological and can be congenital []. The affected individuals struggle to perform purely unimanual movements and find it challenging to carry out tasks that require independent use of both hands, such as opening a jar, holding a cup while it is being filled with water, or playing a musical instrument []. Congenital mirror movements (CMM) disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Most individuals with CMM caused by pathogenic variants in the main CMM‐associated genes—DCC, NTN1, and RAD51—inherit the variant from a parent who may or may not exhibit symptoms [].

Tubulinopathies are caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding α‐tubulin (TUBA1A), β‐tubulin (TUBB2A, TUBB2B, TUBB3, TUBB4A, and TUBB), and γ‐tubulin (TUBG1) []. Tubulin is a microtubule component, playing a vital role in cell morphogenesis and chromosomal segregation []. These are essential for the development and maintenance of neurons including neuronal proliferation, migration, and the trafficking of cortical biosynthetic cargo within developing axons and dendrites []. Patients suffering from tubulinopathies often experience basal ganglia dysplasia, corpus callosum hypoplasia or dysplasia, cerebellar hypoplasia or dysplasia, and dysplasia of the cerebral cortex []. MM have been only rarely described in association with TUBB‐related tubulinopathies. Their occurrence in this context represents an emerging area of research, highlighting the potential role of tubulin dysfunction in abnormal neurodevelopment and motor pathway organization. We report a 6‐year‐old girl with bilateral MM associated with a de novo heterozygous TUBB variant, NM_178014.4:c.155A > G; p.(Asn52Ser). The variability in clinical presentations in our patient with TUBB mutations suggests that MM may be a symptom of broader neurodevelopmental issues, reflecting the complexity of tubulinopathies. Understanding these mutations can enhance prenatal counseling and management strategies for families at risk of tubulinopathies.

A 6‐year‐old left‐hand–dominant female was referred to the pediatric neurology clinic for evaluation of persistent bilateral MM involving the upper limbs. The abnormal movements were first noticed by her mother at approximately 3 years of age and were characterized by involuntary, symmetric movements of the contralateral hand during voluntary unimanual activities. There was no history of other abnormal involuntary movements, seizures, weakness, or loss of motor skills. Over time, the pattern of MM remained stable without progression. At the time of presentation, the child was functioning well in daily activities. She was attending first grade and demonstrated preserved fine motor abilities, including a good pincer grasp, appropriate handwriting for age, and independent feeding. The MM did not significantly interfere with school performance or activities of daily living.

She was born via full‐term normal spontaneous vaginal delivery following an uncomplicated pregnancy. There was no history of perinatal distress or neonatal intensive care unit admission. Growth and nutrition were appropriate for age, and vaccinations were up to date. Developmental milestones were largely age appropriate, except for speech delay. The speech delay was attributed to conductive hearing impairment secondary to recurrent middle ear effusion, which subsequently improved according to parental report. She slept approximately 10 h per night and followed a regular family diet. There was no history of parental consanguinity. The patient had six siblings (four males and two females), all of whom were healthy with normal neurodevelopment. No family history of similar movement disorders, other neurological conditions, or known genetic diseases was reported. The family pedigree and segregation analysis are presented in Figure . On clinical examination, the patient appeared well and nondysmorphic. She was alert, interactive, and able to answer simple questions appropriately. No abnormal movements were observed at rest. Neurological examination revealed intact cranial nerve function, with pupils equal and reactive to light and normal extraocular movements. Facial sensation and symmetry were preserved. Muscle bulk, tone, and strength were normal in all extremities, with power graded 5/5 and deep tendon reflexes graded +2 symmetrically. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Gait was normal, and coordination testing, including finger‐to‐nose and heel‐to‐shin maneuvers, was intact. During purposeful voluntary movements of one hand, mild but sustained involuntary mirroring movements were consistently observed in the contralateral hand and were graded as 2/4 on the Woods and Teuber Scale [] (Supporting Video ). No other involuntary movements were observed.

Genetic testing was undertaken as part of the diagnostic evaluation. Chromosomal microarray analysis was normal. Whole‐exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant in TUBB NM_178014.4:c.155A > G; p.(Asn52Ser). This variant has previously been reported in ClinVar. Although pathogenic variants in TUBB are known to cause autosomal dominant tubulinopathies, the variant was initially classified as a variant of uncertain significance by the diagnostic laboratory. Parental segregation testing demonstrated that the variant was absent in both parents, supporting a de novo occurrence. Following multidisciplinary genotype–phenotype correlation with the diagnostic laboratory and clinical geneticist, the variant was reclassified as likely pathogenic in accordance with the ACMG criteria PS2, PM2, PP2, and PP4.

Brain MRI demonstrated hypoplasia and abnormal configuration of the pons with mild atrophy of the brainstem and superior cerebellar peduncles. Partial dysgenesis and thinning of the corpus callosum were present. The basal ganglia showed asymmetric configuration with malrotated caudate heads protruding into the lateral ventricles. Additional asymmetry was noted in the insular cortex and Sylvian fissures, which appeared shallow on the left side (Figure A–C). No classical malformations of cortical development such as polymicrogyria or heterotopia were identified. Right periventricular parieto‐occipital white‐matter cystic changes and gliosis were observed, likely reflecting a remote prenatal or postnatal insult. Magnetic resonance angiography and venography were unremarkable apart from a fetal origin of the right posterior cerebral artery.

The differential diagnosis initially included isolated familial CMM related to DCC, RAD51, or NTN1 variants; MM secondary to callosal dysgenesis; and motor overflow associated with developmental coordination disorder. Acquired causes such as perinatal stroke, structural corticospinal tract lesions, or epileptic phenomena were considered unlikely given normal strength, absence of seizures, and a stable clinical course. The combination of callosal and brainstem abnormalities on MRI raised suspicion for an underlying tubulinopathy, subsequently supported by the TUBB variant.

Based on the clinical presentation, neuroimaging findings, and genetic results, a diagnosis of CMM associated with TUBB‐related tubulinopathies was established. The imaging abnormalities align with known disruptions of neuronal migration and corticospinal tract development described in tubulin disorders.

The patient has remained clinically stable with preserved fine motor abilities and no progression of symptoms. No pharmacological treatment was initiated. The management plan includes follow‐up in the pediatric neurology clinic every 6 months with monitoring of motor development and surveillance for additional features associated with tubulinopathies.

CMM are most commonly associated with pathogenic variants in the main CMM‐associated genes, DCC, NTN1, and RAD51, which play a key role in axonal guidance and midline crossing of corticospinal fibers [, ]. MM are not a well‐recognized feature of TUBB-related tubulinopathies, although they have occasionally been reported in association with other tubulin genes. A recent study described CMM in an 11‐year‐old girl and affected family members carrying a heterozygous TUBB2B mutation, in whom diffusion tensor imaging demonstrated reduced corticospinal tract decussation, a mechanism similar to that observed in classical genetic causes of CMM []. These findings suggest that tubulinopathies can disrupt axonal guidance and interhemispheric motor control, identifying tubulin genes as an additional developmental mechanism underlying MM.

Another report described a child with severe CMM associated with a pathogenic TUBB3 variant. The patient exhibited mild psychomotor delay, ocular abnormalities, and significant difficulties with both bimanual and unimanual motor tasks. Neurological examination revealed a mild cerebellar syndrome with dysmetria, ataxia, and intention tremor. Marked bilateral MM of the upper limbs were a prominent clinical feature []. Another case described a 6‐year‐old boy with TUBB3‐associated tubulinopathy who presented with developmental delay, acquired microcephaly, intractable seizures, and involuntary MM of the upper limbs. Whole‐exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant in Exon 4 of TUBB3. This case further supports the association between TUBB3 variants and abnormal motor‐control manifestations [].

Tubulinopathies are a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding α‐, β‐, and γ‐tubulin isoforms. These disorders are characterized by abnormalities of neuronal proliferation, migration, and axonal pathfinding, resulting in a wide spectrum of brain malformations. Common neuroimaging findings include basal ganglia dysplasia, corpus callosum hypoplasia or dysgenesis, brainstem abnormalities, and cerebellar involvement []. A study described two families with heterozygous TUBB3 pathogenic variants reported mild motor and language delay, cerebellar signs, and MM in affected individuals. Neuroimaging demonstrated hypoplastic corpus callosum, asymmetric ventriculomegaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, and frontal dysgyria []. The similar findings observed in our patient, such as corpus callosum thinning, abnormal basal ganglia configuration, and brainstem hypoplasia, further confirm the association of tubulinopathies with MM.

A cohort study of nine individuals from five families with CMM identified pathogenic variants in several CMM‐associated genes, including DCC, TUBB3, TUBB, TUBA1A, and POMGNT1. Affected patients exhibited corpus callosum abnormalities, dysgyria, cerebellar and basal ganglia malformations, and ventricular asymmetry on neuroimaging. These findings demonstrate that CMM are frequently associated with structural brain abnormalities []. Another notable feature of this case is the absence of developmental delay or intellectual disability, which contrasts with many previously reported tubulinopathies that present with severe neurodevelopmental impairment []. The stable course of MM without progression and the absence of seizures or spasticity distinguish this case from other tubulinopathies that frequently involve epilepsy or motor deterioration []. This suggests that MM may represent an isolated or early manifestation in patients. Overall, this case expands the phenotypic spectrum of TUBB‐related tubulinopathies by identifying MM as a clinical feature.

To contextualize the present case within the existing literature, all previously reported cases of CMM associated with tubulinopathy gene variants are summarized in Supporting Table . Collectively, these reports demonstrate an expanding association between MM and variants in several tubulin genes, including TUBB, TUBB2B, TUBB3, and TUBA1A, and support the role of tubulin dysfunction in abnormal corticospinal tract development and motor pathway organization.

This case demonstrates that CMM can be a clinical manifestation of TUBB‐related tubulinopathy. The association of MM with structural abnormalities of the corpus callosum, basal ganglia, and brainstem supports a shared pathogenic mechanism involving disrupted axonal guidance and corticospinal tract organization. Our findings expand the phenotypic spectrum associated with TUBB variants and highlight the importance of considering tubulinopathies in the genetic evaluation of patients with CMM, even in the absence of significant neurodevelopmental impairment.

No funding was received for this research.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient’s legal guardian for publication of this case report and any accompanying images.

The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
