neuroscience.title: Interactions Between Cancer and the Nervous System: a Review of Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer Neuroscience
neuroscience.abstract: The emerging field of cancer neuroscience investigates how neural activity shapes tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic response. Recent research aims to define the bidirectional communication between neurons, glial cells, and tumor cells, and to clarify how neural signals influence the tumor microenvironment (TME).Neuronal activity promotes glioma growth via paracrine mediators such as neuroligin-3 (NLGN3), BDNF, TSP-1 and IGF-1, activating PI3K–mTOR signaling and supporting tumor proliferation. Cancer cells also exploit glutamatergic synapses, with AMPA and NMDA receptor activity driving survival and invasion, suggesting opportunities for repurposing antiseizure drugs such as perampanel. Ionic signaling through K⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels further facilitate tumor–neuron coupling. Beyond gliomas, sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs, as well as chronic stress–induced HPA axis activation, modulate angiogenesis, immune evasion, and metastasis.Neural regulation of cancer encompasses neurotrophic signaling, neurotransmitter pathways, ion channel activity, and stress-mediated neuroendocrine responses, collectively shaping tumor biology and revealing novel therapeutic targets.
neuroscience.text:
The neural microenvironment is increasingly recognized as a critical regulator of tumor biology, yet it remains underexplored compared with vascular and immune contributions. Neural elements—including neurons, glia, and peripheral nerves—can influence tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance through direct synaptic integration, paracrine signaling, and systemic neuroendocrine pathways. Histological studies consistently demonstrate that the presence of neuronal markers or perineural invasion correlates with poor prognosis across multiple malignancies, underscoring the prognostic significance of tumor–nerve interactions [–].

In gliomas, functional incorporation of tumor cells into cortical and subcortical circuits has been demonstrated through bona fide synapses, whereby glutamatergic transmission via AMPA and NMDA receptors enhances tumor proliferation and invasion [–]. Activity-dependent release of neuronal factors such as neuroligin-3 (NLGN3) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) further accelerates glioma growth through PI3K–mTOR and related signaling pathways, establishing a feed-forward loop of neural excitation and tumor expansion [–]. Beyond gliomas, diverse systemic cancers exploit neurotransmitters, neuropeptides, and axonogenesis to remodel the tumor microenvironment (TME), while reciprocal signals from cancer cells promote neuritogenesis and local innervation, reinforcing a cycle of tumor–nerve co-dependence [–].

Mechanistically, tumor–neuron interactions extend beyond synaptic communication. Ionic fluxes, particularly through K⁺ and Ca²⁺ channels, as well as alterations in gap junction and myelin plasticity pathways, contribute to the establishment of electrical and paracrine coupling between neoplastic and neural cells [–]. These pathways not only facilitate proliferation and invasion but also reshape immune surveillance by modulating immune cell infiltration and function within the TME [–]. Importantly, the nervous system’s systemic outputs also modulate cancer biology. Activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system (SNS) during chronic stress leads to sustained release of glucocorticoids and catecholamines [, ]. These stress mediators enhance angiogenesis, promote epithelial–mesenchymal transition, foster immune evasion, and confer resistance to apoptosis and DNA damage, collectively accelerating tumor progression [, ].

This review aims to summarize the current knowledge of neuron–cancer interactions, with particular emphasis on bidirectional signaling between tumor and neural elements. It will also examine mechanisms of neuronal input into tumor growth, how tumor cells reciprocally drive neural remodeling, and the systemic impact of neurologically driven stress on cancer progression, an area of great emerging interest in cancer. By integrating evidence across molecular, cellular, and physiological levels, this overview highlights convergent pathways that could be leveraged for therapeutic intervention (Fig. ).

The interaction between neurons and cancer has received increasing attention due to significant discoveries related to the role of neuronal circuits in cancer growth and invasion [, ]. Neuronal activity has been associated with progression of both high-grade glioma (HGG) and low-grade glioma (LGG). In addition, optic nerve activity has been associated with the initiation, growth, and maintenance of optic pathway LGG []. Studies in genetically engineered mouse models of neurofibromatosis type 1, which develop optic pathway glioma at 9 weeks, showed that animals kept in darkness prior to tumor development did not develop optic pathway gliomas and that optogenetic stimulation of retinal ganglion cell axonal activity induced tumor growth []. Studies in mouse models have also shown that olfactory neuronal activity is related to HGG growth via an activity dependent release of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) []. Another key interaction between neurons and cancer cells is between axons and oligodendroglial precursor cells (OPCs) in which neuronal activity has been shown to promote OPC proliferation and change myelin development and plasticity [].

Additionally, neuronal activity over a distance can be associated with tumorigenesis. For instance, neuronal activity, particularly from callosal projection neurons remote from glioblastoma, has been shown in mouse models to drive tumor progression and activity-dependent infiltration through bi-directional synaptic signaling, with Semaphorin 4 F (Sema4F) emerging as a key regulator of this neuron–tumor interaction which can also remodeling synapses near the tumors towards network hyperactivity [].

Other mechanisms by which cancer cells interact with the nervous system include hijacking myelin plasticity and using neurotransmitters (particularly norepinephrine and glutamate) and paracrine signaling to promote tumor progression, growth, and metastasis, cell membrane depolarization, and changes in electrical currents and cell contact mechanisms [].

Most studies of neuron–cancer interactions have focused on brain tumors and the central nervous system; however, emerging evidence also supports diverse roles for such interactions in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) in promoting tumor growth and invasion in particular, related to its role immune regulation and response to tissue damage []; such interactions may vary by cancer type, as evidenced by studies in models of breast cancer, gastric cancer, melanoma, and colon cancer [–]. The following sections will review some of the proposed mechanisms of neuron–cancer interaction and its translational potential.

Conventional neurobiology has largely highlighted the direct neuron to neuron physical connections in the form of the highly specialized synaptic junctions which form the basis of neuron-neuron communications mediated by electrochemical signaling. However, it is well known that synapses can form between neurons and OPCs in regulating oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin formation although the function of these synapses remains incompletely understood. The finding by Bergles et al. that neurons in the hippocampus form synapses with OPCs and generate a rapid signaling pathway that is mediated by excitatory, glutamatergic synapses, changed the view that neurons could form synapses only with each other []. Further, glutamatergic neurons form functional synapses with both neuronal stem cells and oligodendrocyte precursors in the developing and mature brain to drive circuit-specific responses [, ]. OPCs may respond to such activity by proliferating or differentiating, which are key characteristics in regulating oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin formation [].

Venkatesh et al. demonstrated the presence of synaptic structures in glioblastoma samples with electron microscopy and proved synaptic interaction in glioma samples by identifying green fluorescent protein on the post-synaptic side of synaptic structures []. They also noted that neuroligin-3 (NLGN3) is important to the formation of neuron-glioma synapses and showed that synaptic communication occurs through alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid (AMPA) receptors. The presence of direct communication channels with ultrastructural features of synapses, between neurons and glioma cells reported by Venkataramani et al., which also demonstrated glutamate receptor-mediated post-synaptic currents, added support to the concept that these are functional synapses of neurons to glioma cells similar to those between neurons []. The role of AMPA receptors and glutamate in eliciting a neuronal response in glioma samples was also described by other investigators including the role of paracrine or autocrine AMPA receptor signaling in promoting growth of both LGG and HGG regardless of differences in their baseline molecular characteristics [, , ]. Additionally, calcium signaling mediated by AMPA receptors has been shown to regulate the growth and motility of glioblastoma cells by activating the serine/threonine kinase protein kinase B through oncogenic signaling cascades and cytoskeletal remodeling [, , ]. Blocking AMPA receptors has been reported to increase the effectiveness of conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy in not only glioma cells but also certain other cancers including lung carcinoma, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and medulloblastoma cells [].

The role of glutamate in glioma growth is of particular interest, given that glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS. Glutamate dysregulation helps induce seizures, which are common in patients with gliomas with up to 15–25% of patients with HGG having drug-resistant epilepsy which is a favorable prognostic factor in glioblastoma patients [, ].

Changes in ion currents and membrane polarization independent of synapses may also have a role in tumorigenesis. Glioma cells also exhibit prolonged, activity-dependent currents that are distinct from classical synaptic responses and instead reflecting coupling to population-level neuronal activity. This suggests that glioma cells integrate into neural circuits not only through synaptic inputs but also through gap-junction coupling and via broader network-driven signaling mechanisms []. Similarly, membrane depolarization of glioma cells induced by neuronal activity has been shown to promote proliferation in glioma xenografts []. Studies in mouse models of glioma have also shown depolarization spreading across cortical hemispheres, whereas studies in humans have demonstrated circuit dysregulation within infiltrative regions remote from the primary tumor [, ]. In this context, it has become clear that while neurons form synapses with only a subset of glioma cells and that these tumor cells are connected through existing or new tumor microtubules to entire networks of glioma cells and can propagate calcium currents across such networks facilitating tumor cell survival and growth [, ].

Changes in the nervous system may also influence other mechanisms that promote a microenvironment that supports tumor growth, including the tripartite interactions between the nervous system, the tumor cells and local immune system. Neuron-cancer cell circuits can modulate immune cell behavior and trigger immunosuppression by several mechanisms including recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and promoting T-cell exhaustion. For instance, nociceptors have been reported to use G protein–coupled receptors to integrate signals from immune cell–derived sensitizing factors and directly participate in immunosurveillance []. Sensory and vagal nerves detect molecular signals within the tumor immune microenvironment and relay them through central circuits involving the insular cortex, amygdala, hypothalamus, and brainstem nuclei, via norepinephrine (NE) and acetylcholine (Ach)-mediated signals, ultimately modulating the immune microenvironment via sympathetic (NE) and parasympathetic (ACh) outputs. In parallel, the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis activation by the PVN can regulate immune responses through glucocorticoid and catecholamine release, establishing bidirectional neuro-immune-cancer circuits that shape tumor progression [].

In the setting of peripheral nerves, CGRP signaling from trigeminal and sensory nerves appears to shape tumor immunity across multiple cancers [, ]. In oral and oropharyngeal cancers, increased αCGRP+ innervation and RAMP1 expression correlate with poor prognosis, while genetic or pharmacologic blockade enhances CD4+, CD8+, and NK cell responses and reduces tumor growth []. In melanoma, CGRP–RAMP1 drives CD8 + T cell exhaustion, with higher RAMP1 + T cell frequency linked to worse survival []. Mechanistically, CGRP promotes cancer cell autophagy under nutrient stress and disrupts dendritic cell development in medullary thyroid cancer, though it can enhance Th1/Tc1 differentiation via RAMP3 in infection models, indicating context-dependent effects []. In addition, in gastric cancer, nociceptive nerve expansion driven by NGF and CGRP+ peptidergic signaling establishes functional cancer–neuron circuits, where sensory neuron activation enhances calcium influx in tumor cells to promote growth and metastasis; conversely, neuronal ablation or CGRP inhibition suppresses tumor progression and improves survival in several cancers [, ]. More recently, perineural invasion and cancer-induced nerve injury have been shown promote resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy in multiple cancers by driving IL-6– and type I interferon–mediated inflammation that skews the tumor microenvironment toward immune suppression, a process reversible through neuronal or cytokine pathway targeting [].

Paracrine signaling represents a critical mechanism through which neuronal activity can shape cancer biology, particularly in gliomas. Several secreted factors, including neuroligin-3 (NLGN3), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and insulin-like growth factor 1, have been implicated in glioma progression [, ]. NLGN3, a synaptic adhesion molecule, induces transcriptional programs in both LGG [] and HGG [] that regulate pathways associated with synaptogenesis, tumor microtubes, potassium channel activity, axon guidance, and expression of thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1), a synaptogenic factor []. NLGN3 shedding was also noted to promote the proliferation of each major subtype of HGG []. BDNF and glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78) were also identified as secreted proteins that promoted glioma cell proliferation in an activity-dependent manner and to increase the number of neuron–glioma synapses and contribute to a pro-tumorigenic environment [].

Similar to the CNS, neurotrophin-like nerve growth factor and BDNF promote axonogenesis in the PNS in cervical, breast, and prostate cancers [, , ]. Studies in breast cancer have shown that tumor growth and neoangiogenesis may be facilitated by the tumor innervation through CGRP or nerve growth factor secretion [, ]. Sensory neuron–derived CGRP also has a role in modulating antitumor immunity, and targeting CGRP along with receptor activity modifying protein 1 (RAMP1) restores B-cell function and enhances anti–programmed cell death protein 1 therapy [].

Parasympathetic nerve signaling has also been shown to have a role in tumorigenesis by disrupting muscarinic receptors in prostate cancer [], gastric cancer [], and hepatocellular carcinoma []. Sympathetic signaling involving alpha and beta adrenergic receptors also has a role in antitumor immunity [].

GABA, well known for its role as a neurotransmitter, is interestingly also secreted by B cells and serves a pro-tumorigenic role by driving monocytes into immunosuppressive macrophage phenotype which suppresses effector CD8 + T cell activity as seen in in mouse models of colon adenocarcinoma []. Similarly, serotonin could also be considered a paracrine agent, as platelets have been found to secrete serotonin into pancreatic and colorectal tumors’ microenvironments, and the depletion of serotonin has been shown to decrease these tumors’ growth and improve their response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 therapy []. While a direct role for peripheral nerve-secreted GABA or serotonin in tumor progression remains to be demonstrated, the hijacking of neurotransmitter function to serve cancer cell growth and immunosuppression of the TME highlights another paradigm for cancer-mediated modification of normal physiology.

Myelin, an important part of CNS regulation, provides metabolic support to axons and increases the velocity of the action potential conduction []. OPCs can lead to myelin changes, likely due to the neuronal activity–induced axon–OPC synapses that lead to OPCs’ differentiation into myelinating oligodendrocytes. Neuronal activity leads to myelination, and studies in mouse models have shown that decreasing neuronal activity results in decreased OPC differentiation and reduced myelination [].

Myelin development is an important aspect of glioma formation. In children, there are similarities between chronological and topographical patterns of myelin development and glioma formation; for instance, windows of intense myelination in specific regions of the developing human cerebrum overlap with peak susceptibility to pediatric high grade gliomas []. In adults, the regions that are associated with tumor development exhibit ongoing oligodendroglial and myelin plasticity []. Some myelination changes can be regulated by neuronal activity, but other changes occur independent of neuronal function [–]. OPCs also form an intricate relationship with macrophages in the margins of gliomas and appear to collaborate to establish a stem cell–like niche, fostering therapeutic resistance and recurrence [].

Neuronal processes establishing synapses and neurotransmitter release when they contact tumor cells could represent an inadvertent but pro-tumorigenic hijacking of a normal neurophysiologic process in the setting of cancer. However, cancer cells can have reciprocal effects on neurons and influence both the CNS and PNS through pathological mechanisms that promote tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, and treatment resistance. These complex interactions can also lead to various neurological symptoms []. Cancer cells have been reported to enhance their sensory and adrenergic innervation by triggering neurogenesis, the process by which new neuronal pathways are created, which in turn supports tumor growth, angiogenesis, immune evasion, and eventually disease progression [, , ]. Notably, in addition to influencing local nerve endings and axonal contacts, cancer stem cells in colorectal and gastric cancers have been shown to give rise to neurons, which can lead to tumor progression [].

As described above, neuronal activity can drive glioma growth and progression in preclinical studies []. Gliomas themselves can increase neuronal activity, leading to glutamate release and seizures, as initially described by Campbell et al. []. Venkatesh et al. proposed that gliomas can increase neuronal activity, which could help promote tumor growth and neuronal hyperexcitability, resulting in symptoms such as seizures due to glutamate release []. In a mouse model of adult glioma, early microglial infiltration was correlated with seizure onset, which suggests that microglia can play a role in neuronal excitability [].

Bidirectional glioblastoma and neuronal crosstalk has been demonstrated to influence tumor progression in preclinical studies; however, this remains to be validated in clinical settings including whether its effect on tumor biology can potentially influence patient outcome []. Tumor cells have been shown to secrete TSP1, whose pharmacological inhibition decreased glioblastoma cell proliferation; additionally, tumor cell networks connected by microtubules supported by neuron-tumor cell symbiosis can enable widely invasive tumors [].

Preclinical studies in adult glioma models showed that gliomas can induce neuronal hyperexcitability and seizures through the non-synaptic secretion of glutamate [, ] and the secretion of synaptogenic factors [] and by reducing inhibitory interneurons in the glioma microenvironment []. In isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutant gliomas, the high levels of the secreted onco-metabolite, D-2-hydroxyglutarate, in the tumor microenvironment has been shown to induce neuronal hyperexcitability through mTOR activation which is associated with epileptogenesis [].

Sleep disturbances were seen in a mouse model of non-metastatic breast cancer with the abnormal activity of hypothalamic neurons causing sleep cycle and metabolic dysfunction in addition to seizures. Dual hypocretin/orexin antagonists reversed the abnormal activity, suggesting that cancer can have modulatory effects on multiple nervous system pathways []. Given that orexin neuropeptides have essential roles for maintaining wakefulness and are therapeutic targets for sleep disorders, dual orexin receptor antagonists such as suvorexant, which have shown clinical efficacy for insomnia [], may be important in the management of sleep disturbances in cancer patients.

The effects of cancer on both the CNS and PNS strengthen neuron–cancer interactions, ultimately contributing to cancer growth and its associated symptoms. Perineural invasion has long been recognized as a pathway through which pancreatic, head and neck, and prostate cancers invade the PNS, leading to disease progression and poor prognosis []. Invasion of peripheral nerve fibers by cancer cells, described in pathology as perineural invasion, can cause chronic pain syndromes due to cancer and inflammatory cell infiltration, nerve compression, and peripheral nerve remodeling. Abnormal pain signaling and increased neuronal excitability can lead to severe pain in cancer patients [, ].

Understanding the mechanisms by which the nervous system is hijacked to support tumor growth and induce treatment resistance in various cancers has raised the possibilities of new therapeutic options that are based on modulation of the pathological neuron-cancer axis in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. Early clinical investigations of cancer neuroscience–based approaches are under way but have been limited to use of existing neuromodulatory drugs predominantly from the antiseizure and psychiatric repertoire of medications. The finding that seizures are a positive prognostic factor in glioblastoma patients [] have raised the question whether anticonvulsants could also have antitumor effects and modulate tumor biology, which in turn is opening new areas of clinical investigation.

The use of AMPA receptor antagonists has gained significant interest given the substantial role of glutamate in glioblastoma growth. A phase 2 clinical trial of talampanel did not show significant activity in patients with recurrent glioma, whose median progression-free survival duration was 5.9 weeks []. However, perampanel has been shown to have antitumor activity by mediating apoptosis and having a synergistic effect with temozolomide in glioblastoma cell lines []. In these studies, perampanel did not show antitumor activity in gliomas with high protein expression of SERPINE1 [], although additional studies are needed to see if this could be a therapeutic target for increasing the potential anti-tumor activity of perampanel.

Preclinical studies have shown that using meclofenamate to target gap junction–mediated Ca2 + transients can decrease glioma growth and invasion [, ]. In patient-derived xenograft models, gabapentin reduced glioma growth by mediating TSP1 signaling, which resulted in glioma-induced synaptogenesis []. Retrospective studies have noted increased survival of patients with glioblastoma who were treated with gabapentin and suggest that reduced serum TSP-1 levels may serve as a biomarker for this effect []. Gabapentin also inhibits glutamate release and interferes with the activation of NMDA receptors. However, such results need to be prospectively validated in a multivariate setting in future studies to determine their independent value. An ongoing trial (NCT05664464) is examining the role of addition of glutamate inhibitors including gabapentin in patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma undergoing standard therapy [].

Drugs that target the RAMP1–CGRP axis may restore T-cell effector function and improve immunotherapy response and thus are of interest for role in cancer treatment. In this context, studies testing the ability of agents such as rimegepant (a CGRP receptor antagonist), aprepitant (a neurokinin 1 receptor antagonist), atenolol, and suzetrigine (a Nav1.8 inhibitor) to modulate neuro-immune interactions in mouse models are ongoing to assess the potential of such agents including those investigating the use of CGRP or substance P inhibitors [, ].

Another potential area of investigation is whether the use of intracranial stimulation can modulate tumor growth. Current approaches for such neuromodulation include deep brain stimulation, responsive neurostimulation, and vagal nerve stimulation that are currently in clinical use. Although cases of gliomas developing in patients who underwent deep brain stimulation have been reported, these anecdotal reports are not supported by larger studies to confirm an increase in brain tumor incidence after the use of epilepsy treatment devices [, ]. The use of tumor-treating fields has been shown to extend survival in patients with glioblastoma in combination with temozolomide []; the potential mechanisms of action include the direct effect of the electrical fields and an immune-mediated response []. However, its role in glioma biology related to the cancer-neuron interaction a role for tumor-treating fields in cancer neuroscience has not yet been established.

Additional research to improve our understanding of cancer–neuron interactions, as well as these interactions’ relationships with the immune system, will be crucial for the development of cancer management and treatment strategies [, , ].

Depending on its duration, stress has different effects on the human body. Unlike acute stress, chronic stress may contribute to exhaustion or mood disorders such as anxiety or depression [, ]. Patients with diagnosis of cancer, including glioblastoma, experience chronic stress due to their diagnosis, the aggressive treatments needed to control disease and extend survival, and overall poor prognosis of many malignancies [, ]. In patients with HGG, those with depression have a worse prognosis than those without depression []. In LGG patients, Arja et al. found that those with preoperative depression had shorter progression-free survival than patients without preoperative depression, a phenomenon not observed among HGG patients; however, the study had a small sample size and the patients’ histories of therapeutic interventions and psychological treatments were unknown []. These studies open the question of the potential contribution of chronic stress in influencing the prognosis of patients with gliomas and other cancers but remain to be studied in well controlled prospective studies although these trials can be challenging due to the variables involved.

In the past three decades, several preclinical and clinical studies investigated the mechanisms underlying the link between cancer and chronic stress []. The two main neuroendocrine systems known to be activated by chronic stress are the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system (SNS) [, ]. Under chronic stress, the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone, triggering the pituitary gland to secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone, which stimulates the adrenal gland to secrete stress hormones such as cortisol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine. The SNS, which is part of the autonomic nervous system, can stimulate the adrenal medulla or neurons to secrete dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine []. These three stress-related hormones are key regulators of the chronic stress environment [, ]. Under chronic stress, the HPA axis and SNS are generally stimulated to secrete stress-related hormones such as glucocorticoids and adrenocorticotropic hormone as well as stress-related neurotransmitters such as dopamine, epinephrine and norepinephrine [, ]. Several studies have demonstrated that these regulators can be blocked by specific receptor inhibitors [, ]. Such inhibitors include beta blockers, which are competitive catecholamine antagonists. Although beta blockers had potent effects against glioma cell proliferation, migration, and survival in preclinical studies [, ], they failed to improve progression-free survival in clinical trials [].

Evidence indicates a bidirectional relationship between mood disorders and chronic stress [], and several studies have shown that chronic stress can induce mood disorders in mice []. However, there is no definitive evidence showing that chronic stress is a cause or outcome of tumor development and progression. A 10-year population-based study by Benros et al. indicated that patients experience emotional disturbances after being diagnosed with cancer [], but other studies indicated that depression and anxiety occur before cancer diagnosis and thus may be early symptoms of the tumor itself []. In their study of 530 brain tumor patients, Keschner et al. found that 78% of patients had psychiatric symptoms; in 18% of these patients, these symptoms were the first clinical indication of the tumor []. The correlative studies mentioned earlier support the need for additional well-controlled translational and clinical studies to determine the contribution of chronic stress to glioma progression in order to overcome the limitations of the current evidence [, , ].

Ongoing clinical trials are investigating the degree to which psychological stress is correlate with the progression of newly diagnosed oligodendroglioma (NCT05536986) and newly diagnosed astrocytoma (NCT05532969). Another clinical trial proposes to investigate the degree to which psychological stress is correlated with disease progression in glioblastoma patients (NCT05515133).

Preclinical studies have shown that sympathetic nervous system activation under stress can promote breast cancer metastasis by engaging β-adrenergic signaling, which enhances macrophage infiltration and induces a pro-metastatic gene program in the primary tumor. While the primary tumor growth remains unaffected, this neural pathway was shown to drive metastatis to lymph nodes and lungs, which could be reversed by β-blockade or macrophage suppression, highlighting stress-mediated neuroimmune interactions as therapeutic targets in metastasis []. Similar association between chronic stress and various cancers mediated of neurotransmitters and neuropeptides have been reported in preclinical studies but remain to be validated in human cancer []. Anecdotal studies in LGG patients has suggested that post-traumatic stress disorder, identified after the diagnosis of the tumor, is associated with poorer survival upon multivariate analysis []. In patients with newly diagnosed gliomas, the role of psychological stress in affecting prognostic or therapeutic factors remains unclear. Additional studies into the mediators of the complex interactions between the autonomic and peripheral nervous systems and various cancers and their association with stress are needed to provide more actionable insights in this field. Parallelly, trials to determine whether chronic stress can be modulated by exercise (NCT05431348) or the positive support and involvement of the patient’s caregiver (NCT02129335) are ongoing. The successful completion of these trials will shed further light into the role of chronic stress in these malignancies.

The neural microenvironment is now recognized as a fundamental regulator of tumor biology, shaping initiation, progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Evidence across malignancies demonstrates that neuronal activity, neurotransmitters, and neuropeptides directly support tumor proliferation and invasion through synaptic and paracrine mechanisms, while reciprocal tumor-derived signals drive axonogenesis, myelin remodeling, and network hyperexcitability. In gliomas, bona fide synapses mediated by glutamatergic signaling and neuroligin-3 establish tumor–circuit integration, whereas oligodendrocyte precursor cell interactions and myelin plasticity further support stemness and recurrence. Beyond the CNS, peripheral sensory and sympathetic nerves modulate tumor growth and immunity through CGRP, norepinephrine, and other mediators, with perineural invasion and nerve injury linked to immune suppression and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Stress-activated HPA and sympathetic pathways exacerbate these processes by fostering angiogenesis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and immunosuppression. Together, these findings establish neuron–cancer crosstalk as a bidirectional, system-wide axis of tumor progression with profound clinical implications. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including neuromodulatory drugs, synaptic and paracrine signaling inhibitors, CGRP and adrenergic blockade, and electrical modulation, highlight the translational promise of targeting neural mechanisms. Future research will need to clarify context-dependent effects across cancer types, dissect neuro-immune interactions, and evaluate how chronic stress and psychological factors integrate into the cancer–neural axis, with the ultimate aim of transforming these insights into novel, mechanism-based interventions.

neuroscience.title: Interpersonal physiological synchrony in piano ensemble performance: an interdisciplinary study of music psychology and psychophysiology
neuroscience.abstract: Whether autonomic nervous system (ANS)-level physiological synchrony exists between ensemble performers, and whether such coupling predicts the quality of collaborative musical performance, has not been directly examined.Thirty professional piano duos (N = 60) performed four pieces corresponding to a four-quadrant emotional design—high arousal/positive valence (HA/PV), high arousal/negative valence (HA/NV), low arousal/positive valence (LA/PV), and low arousal/negative valence (LA/NV)—based on the valence–arousal circumplex model, in a within-participants repeated-measures design. Heart rate (HR) and electrodermal activity (EDA) were recorded continuously; dyadic synchrony indices were computed via cross-correlation functions (CCF) with cross-pair surrogate permutation control. Multilevel linear models examined whether synchrony predicted expert-rated expressiveness, ensemble cohesion, and overall quality.Both HR-CCF and EDA-CCF significantly exceeded surrogate baselines across all conditions, with peak synchrony under HA/PV. Negative-valence conditions significantly suppressed rated expressiveness, and HR-CCF uniquely predicted ensemble cohesion, whereas EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness. Neither collaboration duration nor trait empathy reached significance, and no systematic unidirectional leader-follower structure was identified.These findings provide the first objective physiological evidence for ANS-level interpersonal physiological synchrony between co-performing musicians and offer partial support for functional differentiation between HR and EDA synchrony channels.
neuroscience.text:
Interpersonal physiological synchrony—the temporal co-variation of autonomic nervous system (ANS) activation patterns between two interacting individuals—is considered a fundamental biological substrate of social bonding and collaborative behavior (; ; ; ). Across diverse social contexts ranging from mother-infant interaction to psychotherapeutic dialogue, research has consistently demonstrated that peripheral physiological indicators—including heart rate, electrodermal activity, and respiration—can exhibit significant temporal coupling between interaction partners that exceeds chance levels (; ), and that the degree of such coupling is associated with interaction quality, group cohesion, and task performance (; ; ; ; ). Notably,  provided direct evidence that physiological and behavioral synchrony constitute independent predictors of group cohesion, with distinct contributions to collaborative outcomes—suggesting that interpersonal physiological coupling carries social information that cannot be fully captured through behavioral observation alone ().

Musical ensemble performance offers an ecologically valid context for investigating interpersonal synchrony (). Ensemble performers must simultaneously achieve precise motor-level temporal coordination and reach a shared understanding of emotional content ()—a dual demand that renders ensemble playing an ideal paradigm for examining how physiological, behavioral, and emotional synchrony jointly serve high-quality group performance. Substantial evidence for physiological synchrony has been established at the audience level: ,  documented significant synchronization of heart rate, skin conductance, and respiration among concert audience members, with synchrony levels correlating with listening experience and emotional engagement;  further confirmed that peripheral physiological synchrony among audiences at live classical music concerts significantly exceeded random baselines and that musical structural features modulated this synchrony. Evidence is markedly more limited, however, when the focus shifts to active performers.  employed dual-brain neuroimaging and found that interbrain synchrony between piano duo performers has endogenous cognitive origins that cannot be attributed entirely to shared sensorimotor input;  similarly demonstrated, using wireless EEG hyperscanning, that cross-individual neural oscillatory coupling at the neural level is associated with behavioral synchrony accuracy between performers (). These findings collectively establish the existence of cross-individual neural coordination in ensemble playing, yet remain confined to the level of the central nervous system. Whether the autonomic nervous system—a channel more directly reflective of emotional arousal and regulation—exhibits genuine cross-individual synchrony between co-performing musicians has not been directly examined.

It was precisely against this backdrop that , in a review of collaborative musical creativity, explicitly identified the question of whether emotional transmission between ensemble performers exists as unconfirmed (). This gap is not a minor oversight; it speaks directly to the core mechanisms of ensemble coordination. Emotional co-regulation is considered a prerequisite for the emergence of group flow in ensemble performance, and group flow states are associated with higher levels of musical performance quality (; ) yet without objective physiological evidence for emotional synchrony between performers, this theoretical chain remains speculative. Furthermore,  reported an intriguing finding in their audience study: more emotionally invested listeners exhibited a negative association between their physiological synchrony and a structural listening factor, whereas sound-color focus and structural listening were associated with higher synchrony levels. This result suggests that “physiological synchrony” and “convergence in the intensity of emotional experience” may not be equivalent—the former more likely reflecting a shared attentional alignment rather than concordant subjective emotional states. Whether this distinction holds in the context of active performance, and whether the two physiological channels (HR and EDA) possess differential predictive validity for distinct dimensions of performance quality, constitute the central empirical questions addressed in the present study.

The present study adopts  two-dimensional circumplex model of affect, representing emotional states along valence (positive/negative) and arousal (high/low) dimensions, and employs a four-quadrant emotional condition design to enable the decoupled examination of the independent effects of valence and arousal. High-arousal, positive-valence states are associated with approach motivation and an outward, jointly directed attentional orientation, which should facilitate the dynamic co-variation of performers' autonomic activation; synchrony was therefore expected to be strongest under the HA/PV condition. Preliminary evidence from  suggests that HR synchrony correlates with reductions in negative affect while skin conductance synchrony correlates with increases in positive affect, implying that distinct peripheral physiological channels may exhibit differential sensitivity to the two-dimensional structure of emotion. At the level of channel function, EDA is a purely sympathetic index that tracks the co-variation of emotional intensity (), whereas HR integrates both sympathetic and parasympathetic regulation and is more sensitive to the moment-to-moment coordination of rhythmic and dynamic control (; ); these distinct physiological properties motivate the tentative, channel-specific predictions formalized below. This functional mapping (EDA → expressiveness, HR → ensemble cohesion) is, however, conceptually distinct from the affect-dimension correspondence reported by , and is therefore advanced as an exploratory rather than a strong confirmatory hypothesis. Whether these relationships generalize to an active dyadic performance context remains to be established.

Trait empathy, as an individual difference variable, has received sustained attention in research on interpersonal coordination.  demonstrated that higher empathic perspective-taking capacity is associated with stronger adaptive following behavior in improvised musical collaboration, with high-empathy individuals exhibiting more precise coordination in ad hoc pairings.  originally distinguished two levels of affective attunement in ensemble playing—sympathetic attunement, which supports the coordination of a cohesive performance, and empathetic attunement—with the latter considered more closely linked to the emergence of group flow and high-level performance (see also ). However, the moderating role of trait empathy on physiological synchrony has been inconsistent in the existing literature:  found that physiological synchrony intensity could not be reliably predicted by trait empathy scores in an empathic self-disclosure context, suggesting that this relationship may be constrained by collaborative context and interaction history. Specifically, long-term collaborators who have internalized a shared coordinative schema for their partner's musical interpretation may exhibit a reduced marginal contribution of trait empathy; by contrast, ad hoc partners may rely more heavily on real-time empathic perception to achieve coordination. This boundary condition has not been directly tested at the level of physiological synchrony.

Based on the theoretical background and identified gaps outlined above, the present study employed a professional piano duo paradigm with dual-channel physiological measurement of HR and EDA, combined with cross-pair random permutation surrogate control and multilevel linear modeling, to systematically test the following four hypotheses: H1 (confirmatory), the degree of HR and EDA time-series synchrony between co-performers differs significantly from a random-pairing baseline, with strongest synchrony anticipated under the HA/PV condition for the reasons outlined above; H2 (confirmatory for the overall synchrony-quality association, exploratory for the channel-specific pattern), physiological synchrony indices (HR-CCF and EDA-CCF) are positively associated with blind expert ratings of performance quality, with possible channel-specific predictive relationships between HR-CCF and ensemble cohesion and between EDA-CCF and expressiveness; H3 (exploratory), temporal lag analysis will test whether a systematic unidirectional leader-follower dynamic characterizes emotional co-regulation between co-performers. To render this hypothesis falsifiable, such a dynamic is defined a priori by two joint criteria: (a) within-duo consistency in the direction of physiological precedence across emotional conditions—that is, the same performer's physiological activation leads (peak lags of consistent sign) in most or all conditions—and (b) a duo-level mean peak lag that departs significantly from zero. Evidence meeting both criteria would support systematic unidirectional precedence, whereas its absence would indicate a bidirectional, near-simultaneous mode of coupling; H4 (exploratory), IRI trait empathy scores are positively associated with HR and EDA synchrony indices, with higher-empathy pairs expected to exhibit greater physiological synchrony, though this effect may vary as a function of pair collaboration duration. Of these, H1 and H2 constituted the primary, confirmatory tests, whereas H3 and H4 were treated as exploratory, because the present 30-dyad design was powered primarily to detect synchrony and its association with performance quality rather than higher-order interaction or directional effects. Regarding H3, although bidirectional, mutually adaptive coupling is the more common observation in free-running joint action (), asymmetric leader-follower patterns have been reported under explicit role-assignment paradigms (). Because the present paradigm assigns no explicit performance roles, H3 concerns temporal precedence between the two recorded performers rather than of role-based musical leadership, with the operational details specified in Section 2.8.7. Regarding H4, this prediction is necessarily tentative, because the IRI indexes a stable dispositional trait whereas physiological synchrony is a dynamic, minutes-scale state; a state-level measure such as the Perceived Emotional Synchrony Scale may therefore be more proximally related to in-performance synchrony.

Participants were recruited as established piano duos through conservatory announcements and targeted social media outreach. Inclusion criteria were: current enrollment in or graduation from a professional music conservatory, a minimum of 6 months of regular piano duo collaboration experience with their current duo partner, no history of cardiovascular disease, and no use of medications known to affect heart rate or ANS function (including beta-blockers and anxiolytics) within the preceding 3 months. Only piano four-hand or double-piano duo combinations were included; all other (non-piano or mixed-instrument) ensembles were thereby excluded by definition. Singing-involving combinations are noted specifically because the respiratory patterns associated with singing would systematically confound heart rate variability (HRV) measurement.

Sample size was determined through a priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1 (). Assuming a multilevel linear modeling framework with a medium effect size (f
2 = 0.25), α = 0.05, and power = 0.80, a target sample of 30 dyadic pairs (N = 60) was established; this a priori calculation relied on a single-level approximation, and statistical power for the multilevel models—particularly for Level-2 moderators—is considered further in the Limitations (Section 4.5). Demographic information collected included age, collaboration duration, and total years of music training. Ensemble format (four-hand vs. double piano) and collaboration duration were entered as stratified control variables in all subsequent statistical models. Ensemble format was controlled because four-hand performance places both pianists at a single shared instrument, introducing greater physical proximity and potential mechanical coupling (e.g., through the shared bench and soundboard) than the double-piano configuration, in which the two performers play separate instruments; the present sample comprised 17 four-hand and 13 double-piano pairs. All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Jimei University (Approval Number: JMU-IRB-2024-096) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. A within-participants repeated-measures design was employed, with each pair performing under all four emotional conditions; emotional condition served as the within-pair factor, and pair identity as the random effects unit.

Four piano duo pieces were selected to correspond to the four quadrants of  circumplex model of affect along the valence-arousal space: high arousal/positive valence (HA/PV), high arousal/negative valence (HA/NV), low arousal/positive valence (LA/PV), and low arousal/negative valence (LA/NV). The four-condition design was intended to manipulate valence and arousal as orthogonal dimensions to enable decoupled examination of their independent effects on physiological synchrony, thereby avoiding the methodological confound that arises when only diagonal conditions are selected.

Prior to the main experiment, a pilot calibration study was conducted to establish the affective ratings of candidate pieces. Twenty music students rated candidate pieces using the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS; ). One-way ANOVAs were conducted separately for valence and arousal dimensions to verify that the four pieces differed significantly on both dimensions, with pairwise significance confirmed via Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons. The four pieces finally selected were, respectively: the galop “Le bal” from Bizet's Jeux d'enfants (Op. 22, No. 12; HA/PV); Brahms's Hungarian Dance No. 5 in F-sharp minor (WoO 1; HA/NV); the “Berceuse” from Fauré's Dolly Suite (Op. 56, No. 1; LA/PV); and a piano four-hands arrangement of Satie's Gymnopédie No. 1 (LA/NV). The first three belong to the standard original piano four-hands/duo repertoire, whereas the Satie was performed in a four-hands arrangement of the original solo work. All four were excerpted or adapted to a comparable duration (approximately 2–3 min each) and lay within the technical command of conservatory-trained performers; we note, however, that technical demands were not formally equated across pieces and tended to co-vary with the arousal dimension, as the high-arousal pieces were faster and more technically demanding than the low-arousal pieces (a constraint addressed in Section 4.5).

At least 2 weeks before the experiment, participants received scores for all four pieces and were asked to practice them independently. On the day of the experiment, a 10-min warm-up session was conducted, after which the experimenter confirmed technical proficiency before recording commenced. Piece presentation order was counterbalanced across pairs using a 4 × 4 Latin square design to control for order and fatigue effects (). A 2-min rest interval was provided between consecutive pieces, during which participants completed immediate affect ratings and allowed physiological states to return to baseline.

Heart rate and HRV: As outlined in the Introduction, peripheral ANS indices more directly reflect emotional arousal and regulation; HR and EDA were therefore selected, and they additionally remain robust to the substantial head and body movements that would render EEG unusable during piano performance while affording greater ecological validity and wearability (). Cardiac signals were recorded using a Polar H10 chest strap (Polar Electro, Finland) at a sampling rate of 130 Hz. Prior validation studies have confirmed that the Polar H10 shows high agreement with gold-standard ECG equipment under both resting and exercise conditions (), and its chest electrode configuration yields substantially lower data loss rates in high-movement scenarios than optical pulse wristband devices, making it particularly suitable for piano performance contexts. Raw R–R interval data were processed in Kubios HRV Premium software () using automated artifact detection supplemented by manual inspection by a trained research assistant. Heart rate (HR, in bpm) was extracted as the primary analytical index. Given the well-documented impact of continuous limb movement during piano playing on HRV measurement accuracy (), HRV-derived indices such as RMSSD and HF power (0.15–0.40 Hz) were not included in the primary analyses.

Electrodermal activity (EDA): Skin conductance signals were recorded using a Shimmer3 GSR+ sensor (Shimmer Research, Dublin, Ireland), at a sampling rate of 64 Hz, with Ag/AgCl electrodes attached to the volar surface of the index and middle fingers of the non-dominant hand. This device has been shown to provide superior data quality and stability under movement conditions (). Raw EDA signals were decomposed into phasic (SCR; reflecting phasic sympathetic activation) and tonic (SCL; reflecting baseline arousal level) components using Ledalab software (). Given the continuous movement of the non-dominant hand during piano performance, the raw EDA signal was visually inspected, and rapid deflections exceeding 10 μS/s in amplitude rate were identified as motion artifacts and excluded; these segments were then replaced via linear interpolation (maximum interpolation window: 2 s). Both the artifact-rejection threshold and the interpolation procedure followed standard publication recommendations for electrodermal data quality control (). The proportion of artifact-affected data in the present sample was below 5% across all recordings, a level that does not materially affect the primary analyses.

Inter-device temporal synchronization: An external trigger signal (combined auditory and LED flash) was transmitted simultaneously to all devices at the onset of each recording. Timestamp errors were controlled to within 50 ms, and data alignment was performed in MATLAB R2023a.

Prior to the experiment, participants completed the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; ), assessing four dimensions of trait empathy—perspective taking, empathic concern, fantasy, and personal distress—which served as the moderator variable. The Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; ) was administered once before and once after the performance task to characterize the overall affective impact of the session and to verify that it did not induce systematic negative affect; unlike the trial-level SAM ratings, the PANAS provided a session-level index of global affective state. The PANAS yields separate Positive Affect (PA) and Negative Affect (NA) scores, each comprising 10 items rated from 1 (very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely), with subscale totals ranging from 10 to 50.

Within a 2-min rest interval following each piece, participants completed 9-point pictorial ratings on the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM; ) for immediate valence and arousal, which also served as the emotional condition manipulation check. To ensure consistent understanding of SAM dimensions across participants, standardized training was administered prior to the experiment. The valence dimension was operationally defined as the degree of emotional pleasantness experienced during performance (ranging from extremely unpleasant to extremely pleasant); the arousal dimension was defined as the level of physiological and psychological activation during performance (ranging from extremely calm/relaxed to extremely excited/activated). Training included a standardized presentation of the SAM pictorial scale, music-specific examples, and practice ratings on two to three non-experimental pieces to confirm understanding. The experimenter individually confirmed each participant's understanding before the experiment commenced, repeating training as necessary until accurate comprehension was achieved.

It should be noted that SAM ratings were completed within 2 min following each piece and thus represent retrospective assessments; real-time moment-to-moment emotional dynamics during performance could not be captured, and recall biases and emotional smoothing effects may have influenced rating accuracy. This design limitation is addressed in the limitations section (Section 4.5).

A 7-point Likert item (“At this moment, I feel that my emotional state is very similar to my partner's”) was appended to the SAM rating form, and participants completed a researcher-developed Perceived Emotional Synchrony Scale (PESS; 5 items rated on a 7-point scale, total score range 5–35) following completion of all performances to assess subjective experience of emotional concordance with their partner throughout the collaborative session. Participants also completed an approximately 5-min open-ended interview describing the most salient affective experiences during performance; interview data were archived as background material and were not incorporated into formal statistical analyses.

High-quality audio recordings (44.1 kHz, stereo) were made throughout each performance using professional recording equipment. Recordings were evaluated blind by three professional musicians with a minimum of 10 years of performance or teaching experience; raters were uninformed of participant identities and emotional conditions. A standardized training session was held prior to rating, in which operational definitions for each dimension were clarified and example audio recordings were used to calibrate rating standards. The three evaluated dimensions were expressiveness (clarity and emotional impact of emotional communication), ensemble cohesion (fluency and responsiveness of mutual coordination), and overall quality (comprehensive professional-level musical performance), each rated on a 10-point scale. The expressiveness dimension directly reflects the effectiveness of emotional communication and is theoretically linked to subjective perceptions of emotional synchrony; the ensemble cohesion dimension reflects the quality of collaborative coordination and constitutes the primary target of H2.

Interrater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC; two-way mixed-effects model, consistency type, 95% confidence interval), with ICC > 0.75 considered indicative of good reliability (). The mean score across the three raters served as the final performance quality score.

Upon arrival, participants rested for 10 min to minimize the influence of external stressors before donning the Polar H10 chest strap and Shimmer3 GSR+ sensor. Demographic information was collected, and participants completed the IRI and the pre-task PANAS. Immediately before the performance task, participants completed a 5-min quiet adaptation period to allow signal stabilization and quality inspection; this period was not retained or analyzed as a dedicated resting-state physiological baseline. A 2-min rest period was provided after each piece, during which SAM ratings and immediate synchrony perception items were completed, with the remaining time used for physiological recovery. Upon completion of all four pieces, participants completed the post-task PANAS, the Perceived Emotional Synchrony Scale, and the open-ended interview. The total session duration was approximately 110–120 min.

Physiological coupling between performers' ANS signals (cross-correlation of HR and EDA time series) was adopted as the objective physiological proxy for emotional synchrony and, together with the self-report Perceived Emotional Synchrony Scale, constituted a multimodal measurement system for emotional synchrony.

Dyadic physiological synchrony indices were calculated using the cross-correlation function (CCF). For each piece, HR and EDA time series were segmented into consecutive 30-s windows. Within each window, the cross-correlation between the two performers' homologous signals was computed over lags from −5 to +5 s, and the maximum positive coefficient within this lag range was taken as that window's synchrony value; the lag at which this maximum occurred (the peak lag) was retained for the directionality analysis (Section 2.8.7). These window-level maxima were Fisher Z-transformed and averaged across all 30-s windows of a piece to yield the synchrony index for that condition (; ). The ±5-s lag range was chosen because autonomic responses (HR and EDA) evolve over a scale of seconds, so this window is wide enough to capture plausible physiological lead-lag between performers reacting to shared musical and emotional events, yet narrow enough to avoid spurious associations arising from unrelated slow trends ().

The number of valid analysis windows per piece depended on actual performance duration: a 2-min piece yielded approximately 4 windows and a 3-min piece approximately 6 windows, with a mean of approximately 4.8 windows per condition (SD = 0.6). The limited number of windows per piece may affect the stability of CCF mean estimates; this limitation is addressed in Section 4.5.

A two-level nested structure was employed: trial level (Level 1, N = 120) nested within pair level (Level 2, N = 30). Physiological synchrony indices (HR-CCF, EDA-CCF), SAM valence and arousal ratings, and performance quality scores were entered as Level 1 trial-level variables, whereas IRI trait empathy scores, collaboration duration, and ensemble format were entered as Level 2 pair-level variables. All MLM analyses were based on this two-level nested structure. Ensemble format was coded as a binary variable (four-hand = 0, double piano = 1), and collaboration duration as a continuous variable (unit: months). Statistical power and sensitivity. The a priori sample size was determined using a single-level regression power formula in G*Power (f
2 = 0.25, α = 0.05, power = 0.80) and did not incorporate the hierarchical structure of the multilevel models, whose power is jointly governed by the intraclass correlation and the number of observations per cluster. A sensitivity analysis was therefore conducted to characterize the effects detectable at the pair level (N = 30). With α = 0.05 and power = 0.80, the smallest detectable pair-level correlation was approximately |r| = 0.49, and the smallest detectable Level-2 (IRI × synchrony) interaction corresponded to f
2 ≈ 0.28. Level-2 moderation tests (H4) should accordingly be regarded as having limited sensitivity to small and moderate effects, and the corresponding null results are interpreted in this light in Section 4.5.

Cross-pair random permutation surrogate control was employed: surrogate baselines were generated by randomly pairing each performer with a performer from a different duo who had played the same piece (i.e., within the same emotional condition), repeated over 1,000 permutations to generate a null distribution. Because surrogate pairs were matched on the musical stimulus and emotional condition, the surrogate baseline preserves any synchrony attributable to shared musical structure, tempo, or task demands while removing genuine interpersonal coupling. Paired-samples t-tests were used to compare true-pair and surrogate synchrony indices. Cross-pair random permutation eliminates all interpersonal coordination information by disrupting the pair structure; the surrogate baseline therefore reflects the coupling attributable to the shared musical context alone, with genuine interpersonal coordination removed. The large effect-size difference between true-pair synchrony and this baseline is methodologically expected and should not be interpreted as anomalous data, but rather as an inherent property of this control approach ().

Multilevel linear models were used to examine the predictive effects of physiological synchrony indices on each performance quality dimension, with the trial level (Level 1) nested within the pair level (Level 2) and pair ID entered as a random intercept. Level 1 fixed effects included HR-CCF, EDA-CCF, and emotional condition (a four-level nominal variable with HA/PV as the reference category); Level 2 covariates included dyadic mean IRI, collaboration duration, and ensemble format. To test for interaction effects between emotional condition and synchrony indices, nested model comparisons were conducted: a base model (Model A) containing main effects of emotional condition and synchrony indices, and an extended model (Model B) adding emotional condition × synchrony index interaction terms. The incremental contribution of interaction terms was evaluated using marginal R2 change (ΔR2) and likelihood ratio tests (χ2); an interaction was considered substantively meaningful when χ2 was significant (p < 0.05) and ΔR2 ≥ 0.02 ().

Pearson correlations were computed between each IRI subscale and synchrony indices. Product terms (IRI × synchrony index) were added within the MLM framework to test whether trait empathy moderated the synchrony → performance quality pathway. The same nested model comparison logic was applied: a base model (Model C) containing synchrony index and dyadic mean IRI main effects, and an extended model (Model D) adding the IRI × synchrony index interaction term. The same criteria were applied (p < 0.05 and ΔR2 ≥ 0.02).

One-way repeated-measures ANOVAs were conducted separately for valence and arousal dimensions to examine differences in SAM ratings across the four emotional conditions, with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons used to confirm pairwise significance across all conditions. If any pair's SAM ratings failed to differentiate the four conditions, that pair's data would be reported separately in a sensitivity analysis and excluded from the primary analysis.

To examine the independent contributions of valence and arousal to physiological synchrony, parallel MLMs were constructed within the Level 1 framework using post-performance SAM valence and arousal ratings as time-varying continuous predictors, and the significance of the valence × arousal interaction term was tested.

CCF coefficients were computed at lags from −5 s to +5 s (step size = 0.5 s) to identify systematic directional biases in the lag corresponding to the maximum cross-correlation, thereby exploring leader-follower dynamics in emotional co-regulation. To operationalize the a priori criteria for H3, two complementary indices were derived from the trial-level peak lags. First, within-duo directional consistency was assessed by classifying each trial's peak lag as P1-leading (negative sign), P2-leading (positive sign), or simultaneous (zero), and quantifying, for each duo, whether the same performer led across the four emotional conditions. Second, for each duo a mean peak lag was computed and tested against zero. A systematic unidirectional leader-follower structure was operationally defined as the conjunction of (a) a clear majority of duos showing consistent directional sign across conditions and (b) duo-level mean peak lags departing significantly from zero; failure to meet either criterion was taken to indicate bidirectional, near-simultaneous coupling. P1 and P2 were administrative identifiers assigned for sensor labeling and data management, not experimentally defined musical roles. Consequently, a test of whether the overall proportion of P1-led vs. P2-led trials departs from chance carries limited interpretive value: because the P1/P2 labels are arbitrary, a null result is expected by construction, and a significant imbalance would most plausibly indicate confounding between the label and some systematic factor rather than a meaningful leadership asymmetry. This proportion test is therefore reported as a descriptive check only, and the primary evaluation of H3 rests on the within-duo consistency and mean-lag criteria defined above. Within each duo, the division of parts (and, for double-piano pairs, of instruments) followed the pair's established rehearsal arrangement, was neither assigned nor manipulated by the researcher, and was held constant throughout the experiment; part allocation was therefore not recorded as a separate experimental variable. Because part allocation was neither manipulated nor recorded, the data do not permit a post hoc re-analysis of directionality by musical role (primo/secondo or melody/accompaniment); this constraint is revisited in Section 4.5. Accordingly, peak-lag directionality was interpreted only as the physiological temporal precedence between the two labeled performers, not as evidence of role-based (primo/secondo or melody/accompaniment) leadership. A non-zero peak lag does not necessarily reflect interpersonal influence: both performers may respond to shared musical events with differing latencies, and the location of the maximum is sensitive to filtering and smoothing parameters. All analyses were conducted in R 4.3.0; the significance threshold was set at α = 0.05, and effect sizes (Cohen's d and η2) were reported throughout.

Manipulation checks confirmed significant differences in SAM ratings across emotional conditions for both the valence dimension [F(3, 87) = 275.2, p < 0.001] and the arousal dimension [F(3, 87) = 316.8, p < 0.001], with all pairwise comparisons significant after Bonferroni correction (all p < 0.001), indicating successful manipulation of the four-quadrant emotional conditions (see ). Interrater reliability for all three performance quality dimensions met the criterion for good reliability (Expressiveness ICC = 0.874; Ensemble Cohesion ICC = 0.894; Overall Quality ICC = 0.863); mean ratings across the three raters were used as the final performance quality scores in all subsequent analyses.

H1 (confirmatory) predicted that HR and EDA synchrony between co-performers would significantly exceed a random-pairing baseline, with the strongest synchrony under the HA/PV condition. As shown in , at the trial level (N = 120 performances), true-pair HR-CCF (M = 0.353, SD = 0.112) significantly exceeded the surrogate random-pairing baseline (M = 0.131, SD = 0.071) [t(119) = 17.94, p < 0.001, d = 1.64]. EDA-CCF similarly exceeded the baseline [true-pair M = 0.327, SD = 0.120 vs. surrogate M = 0.096, SD = 0.057; t(119) = 16.96, p < 0.001, d = 1.55]. At the pair level (N = 30 pairs), paired-samples t-tests (df = 29) confirmed that synchrony in both channels significantly exceeded the surrogate baseline (all p < 0.001). H1 was supported.

As shown in  and , synchrony strength differed significantly across the four emotional conditions [HR-CCF: F(3, 87) = 10.04, p < 0.001; EDA-CCF: F(3, 87) = 19.81, p < 0.001]. Peak HR-CCF (M = 0.411) and EDA-CCF (M = 0.408) were observed under the HA/PV condition, whereas the lowest values were observed under LA/NV [HR-CCF M = 0.272; EDA-CCF M = 0.251]. Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons showed that, for HR-CCF, synchrony under HA/PV, LA/PV, and HA/NV each significantly exceeded LA/NV (p < 0.001, p = 0.002, and p = 0.021, respectively). For EDA-CCF, both HA/PV and LA/PV significantly exceeded HA/NV and LA/NV (all p < 0.001), whereas HA/PV vs. LA/PV and HA/NV vs. LA/NV did not differ. True-pair synchrony significantly exceeded surrogate baselines across all four conditions (all p < 0.001; see ).

To examine whether the physiological synchrony indices corresponded to performers' subjective sense of emotional concordance, the PESS was scored for each performer (P1: M = 21.10, SD = 2.99, Mdn = 21.00, range 15.00–28.00; P2: M = 20.77, SD = 2.42, Mdn = 21.00, range 16.00–26.00) and averaged to a dyadic mean (M = 20.93, SD = 1.89, Mdn = 21.00, range 17.50–24.50). At the pair level (N = 30), the dyadic-mean PESS was not significantly correlated with either HR-CCF (r = −0.073, p = 0.701, 95% CI [−0.422, 0.295]) or EDA-CCF (r = −0.019, p = 0.922, 95% CI [−0.376, 0.344]). Although the pair-level sample (N = 30) yields wide confidence intervals, both point estimates were close to zero, providing no evidence that stronger physiological coupling was accompanied by a stronger subjective sense of emotional synchrony; the CCF-based indices and self-reported emotional concordance thus appear to capture distinct, non-overlapping facets of the shared performance experience (see Section 4.2).

H2 predicted that physiological synchrony would be positively associated with expert-rated performance quality (confirmatory for the overall synchrony-quality association), with possible channel-specific links between HR-CCF and ensemble cohesion and between EDA-CCF and expressiveness (exploratory). MLM results are presented in . HR-CCF significantly predicted ensemble cohesion (β = 0.230, t = 2.21, p = 0.027), whereas EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness (β = 0.057, t = 0.52, p = 0.605); H2 was partially supported (HR-CCF → ensemble cohesion supported; EDA-CCF → expressiveness not significant; see ). Neither HR-CCF for expressiveness (β = −0.033, p = 0.749) nor EDA-CCF for ensemble cohesion (β = 0.057, p = 0.616) reached statistical significance, indicating a differential predictive pattern between the two physiological channels and distinct performance quality dimensions.
