With HA/PV as the reference condition, the HA/NV condition significantly suppressed expressiveness (β = −0.815, t = −2.89, p = 0.004), as did the LA/NV condition (β = −0.789, t = −2.52, p = 0.012); the LA/PV condition did not significantly affect expressiveness (β = −0.214, p = 0.384). For ensemble cohesion, none of the three emotional conditions differed significantly from the HA/PV reference group (HA/NV: β = 0.162, p = 0.570; LA/PV: β = 0.041, p = 0.868; LA/NV: β = −0.260, p = 0.415). These results suggest that emotional condition has a pronounced influence on expressiveness—negative-valence conditions, regardless of arousal level, suppressed the clarity of emotional communication—while its influence on ensemble cohesion was comparatively limited.

Collaboration duration did not significantly predict any of the three performance quality dimensions (expressiveness: β = 0.139, p = 0.154; ensemble cohesion: β = −0.003, p = 0.977; overall quality: β = −0.133, p = 0.234). Similarly, dyadic mean IRI did not significantly predict any dimension (expressiveness: β = −0.100, p = 0.249; ensemble cohesion: β = −0.032, p = 0.742; overall quality: β = +0.058, p = 0.564). Marginal R2 values ranged from 0.047 to 0.166, and conditional R2 values ranged from 0.101 to 0.166.

Nested model comparisons indicated that adding emotional condition × synchrony index interaction terms (Model B) to the base model (Model A, containing main effects of emotional condition and synchrony indices) did not produce substantive improvements in model fit for any of the three performance dimensions: expressiveness ΔR2 = 0.056, χ2(6) = 8.40, p = 0.210; ensemble cohesion ΔR2 = 0.028, χ2(6) = 3.82, p = 0.701; overall quality ΔR2 = 0.038, χ2(6) = 4.73, p = 0.579. Although the ΔR2 for expressiveness (0.056) exceeded the 0.02 substantive threshold, the χ2 test did not reach significance, indicating that the incremental contribution of the interaction terms was not statistically reliable. Overall, emotional condition did not systematically moderate the synchrony → performance quality pathway, and the predictive effect of HR-CCF on ensemble cohesion was relatively stable across conditions.

Parallel MLMs were constructed using post-performance SAM valence and arousal ratings as Level 1 time-varying continuous predictors to examine their explanatory role in the synchrony-performance quality relationship.

In the expressiveness model, SAM valence significantly predicted expressiveness (β = 0.241, t = 2.27, p = 0.024), whereas arousal did not (β = 0.030, p = 0.736). After controlling for SAM continuous predictors, neither HR-CCF nor EDA-CCF significantly predicted expressiveness (HR-CCF: β = 0.027, p = 0.777; EDA-CCF: β = 0.147, p = 0.158; marginal R2 = 0.124).

In the ensemble cohesion model, the positive predictive effect of HR-CCF on ensemble cohesion remained significant after controlling for SAM continuous predictors (β = 0.256, t = 2.68, p = 0.007), whereas neither valence (β = 0.052, p = 0.576) nor arousal (β = 0.114, p = 0.203) reached significance (marginal R2 = 0.102).

H3 (exploratory) examined whether temporal lag analysis would reveal a unidirectional leader-follower dynamic, whereby changes in one performer's physiological activation systematically preceded those of the other. As shown in , analyses of the peak lag distribution across the 120 trial-level observations revealed an overall mean lag of 0.046 s (SD = 2.99 s), highly concentrated around zero. Performer 1 (P1) led physiologically in 61 trials (51%) and Performer 2 (P2) led in 57 trials (48%), with zero lag observed in 2 trials; the proportions did not differ significantly [χ2(1) = 0.13, p = 0.715]. Within each condition, mean lags were +0.283 s (HA/PV; P2 leading marginally), −0.750 s (HA/NV; P1 leading marginally), −0.267 s (LA/PV), and +0.917 s (LA/NV), but none of the within-condition P1/P2 leadership proportions differed significantly (all p > 0.30). The two a priori criteria for a systematic unidirectional structure (Section 2.8.7) were then evaluated. For criterion (a), only 5 of the 30 duos (16.7%) showed a consistent direction of physiological precedence across all four conditions (2 consistently P2-leading, 3 consistently P1-leading), whereas the remaining 25 duos (83.3%) reversed the sign of their peak lag across conditions. For criterion (b), a one-sample t-test on the duo-level mean peak lags (M = 0.046 s, SD = 1.597) did not differ significantly from zero, t(29) = 0.157, p = 0.876, 95% CI [−0.526, 0.617]. Neither criterion was met: the large majority of duos failed to maintain a consistent leading-following direction across conditions, and the duo-level mean lag was statistically indistinguishable from zero. Because both criteria failed, these results indicate that co-performers do not exhibit a systematic unidirectional physiological leadership structure, but rather a bidirectional, near-simultaneous pattern of coupling that persisted across all four emotional conditions. These results, however, must be interpreted with caution given the relatively homogeneous collaborative experience within the sample; it remains possible that a unidirectional leadership structure may emerge under conditions involving greater role differentiation, more contrasting levels of musical expertise, or pairs with shorter or longer collaborative histories. H3 was not supported under the present conditions.

H4 (exploratory) tested whether IRI trait empathy was positively associated with HR and EDA synchrony, with higher-empathy pairs expected to show greater synchrony. Pearson correlations revealed no significant associations between any of the four IRI subscales and either HR-CCF or EDA-CCF [Perspective Taking: r(HR) = −0.146, p = 0.440, r(EDA) = −0.061, p = 0.750; Empathic Concern: r(HR) = 0.104, p = 0.584, r(EDA) = 0.072, p = 0.706; Fantasy: r(HR) = −0.121, p = 0.526, r(EDA) = −0.217, p = 0.250; Personal Distress: r(HR) = 0.059, p = 0.757, r(EDA) = 0.125, p = 0.511]. When dyadic mean IRI was entered into the MLM framework, it did not significantly predict any performance quality dimension (expressiveness: β = −0.100, p = 0.249; ensemble cohesion: β = −0.032, p = 0.742; overall quality: β = 0.058, p = 0.564; see ). Nested model comparisons showed that adding the IRI × synchrony index interaction terms did not yield substantive improvements in model fit (all ΔR2 <0.02, all likelihood ratio test p > 0.25), indicating that trait empathy did not significantly moderate the synchrony → performance quality pathway. H4 was not supported in the present study; however, these null findings should be interpreted cautiously in light of the restricted variability in IRI scores across the sample (grand mean SD = 1.27), which may have limited statistical power to detect potential moderation effects.

In brief, the four hypotheses fared as follows. H1 was supported: HR and EDA synchrony significantly exceeded the condition-matched surrogate baseline across all conditions, peaking under HA/PV. H2 was only partially supported: HR-CCF predicted ensemble cohesion, whereas the predicted EDA-CCF → expressiveness link was not significant. H3 (exploratory) was not supported: no systematic unidirectional leader–follower structure was detected. H4 (exploratory) was not supported: trait empathy neither correlated with synchrony nor moderated its link to performance quality, although this null is inconclusive given the limited power (Section 4.5).

The present study provided, for the first time in a professional piano duo context, direct evidence for interpersonal physiological synchrony at the level of the autonomic nervous system between co-performing musicians, and showed that one synchrony channel was selectively associated with one dimension of expert-rated performance quality: HR-CCF significantly predicted ensemble cohesion, whereas EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness, so the synchrony → performance-quality link received only partial support. These findings speak directly to the core question identified by  in his review of collaborative musical creativity—by providing objective evidence of ANS-level physiological synchrony, while remaining agnostic about the direction of any emotional transfer.

Across all four emotional conditions, true-pair HR-CCF and EDA-CCF significantly exceeded the surrogate random-pairing baseline with large effect sizes, indicating that the observed cross-individual physiological coupling did not arise merely from the shared musical stimulus and experimental context, but rather reflected genuine ANS co-regulation between performers. Several lower-level processes could in principle inflate cross-individual physiological coupling, including a shared tempo, similar gross body movements, common respiratory entrainment, exposure to the same acoustic and emotional content of an identical score, and a shared physical environment. The present design addresses the most important of these through the structure of the surrogate baseline: because surrogate pairs were formed from performers of different duos who played the very same piece (condition-matched permutation; Section 2.8.2), the surrogate distribution already embodies whatever coupling is attributable to the shared musical structure, tempo, and task. The observation that true-pair synchrony substantially exceeded this condition-matched baseline therefore indicates that the excess coupling cannot be explained by the shared score alone, but reflects coordination specific to the two individuals actually performing together. This does not isolate the source of any shared emotional state—music-driven vs. partner-driven—nor does it establish directional transmission; rather, it demonstrates that genuine interpersonal coupling exists over and above the common stimulus. This conclusion is directionally consistent with the findings of  in a percussion ensemble context—a study that similarly employed cross-pair random pairing as a baseline control and demonstrated that IBI synchrony possessed independent predictive validity beyond behavioral coordination. A key distinction is that physiological synchrony in the present study occurred in a free-performance context unconstrained by an external metronome, and performers were not instructed to synchronize their behavior. The observed ANS coupling therefore reflects a relatively endogenous origin, converging at a cross-level analysis with the argument advanced by  regarding “endogenous interbrain synchrony” in piano duo performers.

The differential effects of the four emotional conditions on synchrony strength provide further corroboration. Peak HR-CCF and EDA-CCF were observed under the HA/PV condition, whereas both reached their nadir under LA/NV. Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons further revealed that valence independently modulated EDA-CCF. This is partially consistent with findings reported by  in a concert audience study, where SCR synchrony was associated with increases in positive affect and HR synchrony with decreases in negative affect—suggesting channel-specific correspondences between distinct ANS channels and emotional dimensions. In the active performance context of the present study, the concurrent peak of both channels under HA/PV may reflect the facilitative effect of high-arousal, positive-valence states on performers‘ outward attentional orientation: when the musical emotional framework is highly congruent with performers' own affective states, their ANS activations may more readily co-vary dynamically.

In terms of channel-specific predictive patterns, HR-CCF significantly predicted ensemble cohesion, while EDA-CCF did not significantly predict expressiveness. This predictive pattern is directionally consistent with H2, but received only partial empirical support; the complete dual-channel functional dissociation (i.e., HR-CCF independently predicting ensemble cohesion and EDA-CCF independently predicting expressiveness) awaits verification in larger-sample studies. As specified in the Introduction, the channel-specific mapping was advanced as an exploratory rather than a confirmatory prediction. In the present data only one of the two predicted links was supported (HR-CCF → ensemble cohesion), while EDA-CCF did not predict expressiveness; the dual-channel dissociation should therefore be regarded as a tentative hypothesis for future, adequately powered tests rather than an established effect.

The effects of emotional condition on the expressiveness dimension warrant separate consideration. MLM results showed that, relative to the HA/PV reference condition, the HA/NV condition produced the strongest suppressive effect on expressiveness, followed by the LA/NV condition, while the LA/PV condition did not reach significance. This pattern reveals the central role of the valence dimension in the clarity of emotional communication: under negative-valence conditions—regardless of arousal level—the clarity and affective impact of performers' emotional communication were significantly lower than under the high-arousal positive-valence condition, whereas reducing arousal while maintaining positive valence (LA/PV) did not produce equivalent suppression. This corresponds, at the behavioral level, to the independent contributions of valence and arousal posited in  two-dimensional model: arousal primarily drives physiological synchrony strength, whereas valence more directly influences the overt quality of emotional expression. The dissociation of these two effects provides methodological support for the necessity of the four-quadrant design adopted in the present study—if only diagonal conditions had been selected, the independent effects of valence and arousal could not have been disentangled.

The systematic review and meta-analysis by  demonstrated that sympathetic synchrony is positively associated with task performance, whereas the direction of the association for parasympathetic synchrony is more complex, reflecting distinct contribution pathways of the two channel types to group performance. In the present study, EDA as a purely sympathetic index captures the co-variation of performers‘ emotional intensity dynamics, corresponding to the “clarity and affective impact of emotional communication” perceivable by raters; HR synchrony integrates bidirectional sympathetic and parasympathetic regulatory information, more sensitively reflecting real-time coordination between performers in rhythmic control and dynamic balance, and thereby associating with “the fluency and responsiveness of mutual coordination”—i.e., ensemble cohesion. The non-significant prediction of expressiveness by EDA-CCF may partly reflect insufficient statistical power due to sample size constraints, but may also reflect a more substantive mechanistic issue: under negative-valence conditions, the decline in the clarity of emotional communication is primarily driven by performers' subjective experience of the emotional character of the piece (with SAM valence ratings significantly predicting expressiveness) rather than by the degree of sympathetic synchrony.

These results prompt a reconsideration of a counterintuitive finding reported by : emotional listening—that is, deep immersion in the affective experience of music—was found to reduce physiological synchrony among audience members, whereas structural listening and tonal focus promoted synchrony. The proposed explanation is that extreme emotional immersion draws individuals into highly private experiential states, thereby decoupling them from collective synchrony rhythms. The present study's channel-specific results are logically consistent with this account: pairs exhibiting stronger physiological synchrony were not those with the most intense emotional experiences, but rather those whose attention was more jointly directed toward the musical output itself during performance. Direct support for this interpretation comes from the present data: performers‘ subjective sense of emotional synchrony (PESS) was uncorrelated with either physiological synchrony index (both ns; Section 3.2.1). In other words, the pairs whose autonomic activity co-varied most strongly were not those who felt most emotionally in tune with one another.  identifies this external attentional focus as a key condition for the emergence of group flow, which in turn co-occurs with elevated HR correlations. In sum, the present findings support the theoretical position that physiological synchrony in collaborative performance more closely reflects the joint alignment of performers' attentional and ANS states than the convergence of their subjective emotional investment—two phenomena that are conceptually distinct and empirically separable ().

None of the four IRI subscales showed significant correlations with HR-CCF or EDA-CCF, and nested model comparisons confirmed that model fit did not improve substantively upon addition of IRI interaction terms; H4 was not supported in the present sample, though this null finding carries theoretical value in its own right and should not be dismissed as a simple power issue. A first consideration is conceptual rather than statistical: the IRI indexes a stable, dispositional form of empathy, whereas physiological synchrony is a dynamic state unfolding over minutes. A strong trait-state coupling is therefore not guaranteed a priori, and the absence of one is consistent with this measurement mismatch. Notably, even the more state-proximal measure of perceived emotional synchrony (PESS) was uncorrelated with the physiological indices (Section 3.2.1), reinforcing the view that dispositional empathy is unlikely to map directly onto minute-scale autonomic coupling during performance. A plausible interpretation is that all participants in the present study had a minimum of 6 months of regular collaborative experience; long-term joint rehearsal may have led both partners to develop a highly internalized coordinative schema for each other's musical interpretive tendencies, such that the marginal contribution of trait empathy was substantially reduced by this skill-based, automatized coordination mechanism. This contrasts meaningfully with the findings of , who demonstrated that empathic perspective-taking promoted coordination accuracy in ad hoc pairings of unfamiliar performers—suggesting a clear boundary condition for the moderating role of trait empathy: it may be operative only when partners lack an established coordinative schema.  similarly reported that trait empathy did not consistently predict physiological synchrony in an empathic self-disclosure context, further indicating that the relationship between empathic disposition and ANS coupling is inherently context-dependent.

Notably, collaboration duration did not significantly predict any of the three performance quality dimensions in the present sample. This result may reflect the limited variance in collaboration duration within the sample, with insufficient between-pair variability in collaboration history to produce detectable differences in performance quality. This does not imply that collaborative experience is theoretically irrelevant to performance quality; rather, it suggests that the range of the present sample constrained the effective examination of this variable's effect. Variability in dyadic mean IRI was similarly restricted, with limited between-pair variability after aggregation at the pair level. The moderating effects of both individual difference variables warrant examination in studies employing broader sampling ranges.

The near-equal physiological leadership proportions between the two performers, the lack of within-duo directional consistency across conditions, and the high concentration of peak lags around zero collectively indicate that no persistent unidirectional physiological leadership structure exists between piano duo performers with established collaborative experience; H3 was not supported under the present conditions. It is possible, however, that directional asymmetries may emerge in dyads with greater differences in musical expertise or under conditions of more explicit role assignment.  did record role-related asymmetric heartbeat synchrony patterns in a dyadic alternating tapping task, but their study employed an explicit role-assignment paradigm—a fundamentally different context from the intrinsic, mutually adaptive coordination observed in the present study.  similarly observed bidirectional rather than unidirectional synchrony in free-play percussion ensembles, interpreting this as indicative of mutual adaptation among group members. In the present study, peak lags converging toward zero most likely reflect that familiar collaborators hold nearly identical anticipatory representations of phrase trajectories and emotional turning points, such that the two performers' ANS responses occur virtually simultaneously rather than sequentially along a stimulus-response chain. This contrasts sharply with the asymmetric leadership structures commonly observed in mother-infant synchrony research, suggesting that highly mature adult collaborative relationships may correspond to a relatively symmetric mode of emotional co-regulation—a hypothesis worthy of systematic examination in future research through comparison of pairs at varying levels of collaborative maturity.

Two further considerations help explain why a systematic leader-follower structure was unlikely to emerge here. First, the physiological signals under study evolve on a relatively slow time scale. Leading-following relationships in ensemble performance have frequently been detected at the level of discrete, rapidly unfolding events such as note onsets (), and also in body sway, which fluctuates more slowly than note onsets yet still faster than emotional states (). Heart rate, and the emotional states it partly indexes, change more gradually still than either of these signals. Any directional precedence in emotional co-regulation would therefore be expected to surface only intermittently—at isolated phrase transitions or emotional turning points—rather than as a stable, piece-wide asymmetry detectable in averaged peak lags. Second, leading and following in ensemble playing carry a strong social dimension; emotional precedence, in particular, may depend more on interpersonal and personality dynamics within a duo than on the musical division of labor. Consistent with this, and as noted above, part allocation was not an experimentally defined variable in the present study (Section 2.8.7), so the present null directionality finding should not be read as evidence about melody-vs.-accompaniment leadership specifically, but only about the absence of a fixed physiological precedence between the two performers. Peak-lag estimates are, moreover, sensitive to filtering and smoothing choices and need not reflect interpersonal influence, since both performers may respond with different latencies to shared musical events; the directionality results should be read with this in mind.

The primary theoretical contributions of the present study operate at three levels. First, it provides the first empirically rigorous demonstration, with strict surrogate control, of ANS-level physiological synchrony in collaborative piano performance, addressing the core gap identified by  regarding the unconfirmed existence of emotional transmission in ensemble playing. Second, it extends the endogenous interbrain synchrony framework of  to the level of the autonomic nervous system, and reveals functional specificity between HR and EDA channels in predicting distinct performance quality dimensions, providing finer-grained empirical evidence for understanding the mechanisms of physiological synchrony. Third, building on the synchrony → group performance pathway established by , it represents the first inclusion of emotional conditions as moderating variables in a musical performance context, while the null results illuminate the substitutive role of skill-driven automatized coordination mechanisms in displacing trait empathy's moderating contribution.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. As demonstrated by , HRV indices show substantially reduced measurement accuracy in dynamic interactive states compared to resting conditions; given that hand and arm movements in piano performance far exceed those in conversational settings, the HRV-related results of the present study should be interpreted with caution and should not be overgeneralized; future studies may address this limitation by including dedicated resting-state baseline recordings matched in duration to the performance segments. Before the performance task, participants completed a 5-min quiet adaptation period after sensor attachment to allow signal stabilization and quality inspection; however, this period was not retained or analyzed as a dedicated resting-state physiological baseline. Accordingly, the present study did not include an independent resting-state EDA baseline against which performance-related EDA artifacts or responses could be systematically compared, and the reported sub-5% artifact rate should be interpreted in that light; future studies should record dedicated resting baselines before and after performance to quantify movement-related effects on signal quality. A further measurement limitation concerns the EDA montage: because Ag/AgCl electrodes were placed on the volar pads of the index and middle fingers of one hand that nonetheless contributes to playing, the sensors may have affected tactile feedback or comfort to some degree. Participant comfort was not systematically assessed, and future studies should either quantify any such interference or adopt alternative electrode sites (e.g., the medial phalanges or the foot) less likely to interfere with performance. The sample was also restricted to current conservatory students, limiting the ecological validity of the conclusions; the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference regarding the direction of the synchrony-performance quality relationship, and whether synchrony is an antecedent, concomitant, or consequence of high-quality performance requires clarification through longitudinal or experimentally controlled designs. Future research may profitably combine the ANS indices of the present study with EEG hyperscanning (following the paradigm of ) to simultaneously obtain neural and autonomic synchrony maps within the same performance context; systematic comparison of pairs at varying levels of collaborative maturity may also be used to test the theoretical hypothesis of “collaborative maturity and the symmetrization of physiological synchrony directionality”; and the introduction of improvised vs. score-reading performance conditions would help further disentangle endogenous emotional coordination from shared sensorimotor contributions in ensemble synchrony. Systematic test-retest reliability assessment of the SAM was not conducted prior to the experiment; future studies should complete scale temporal stability verification before the main data collection.

SAM ratings were completed retrospectively following each piece, and performers' recall of their in-performance emotional states may have been affected by memory decay and emotional smoothing effects, thereby failing to fully capture the moment-to-moment emotional dynamics during performance. Future studies may consider incorporating continuous in-performance valence-arousal rating devices (e.g., a continuous dial rating system) to track performers' real-time affective states at higher temporal resolution and align these with the physiological synchrony time series on a moment-by-moment basis.

Regarding statistical power, the sensitivity analysis reported in Section 2.8.1 indicates that the pair-level design (N = 30) was sensitive only to relatively large Level-2 effects. The empathy-synchrony correlations and IRI × synchrony interactions observed here fell well below these detectable thresholds; the null results for H4, together with the null PESS-synchrony correlations, are therefore most appropriately interpreted as inconclusive with respect to small or moderate effects rather than as evidence of their absence.

The four pieces were matched on emotional target but not on technical difficulty; because tempo, textural density, and motor load of real piano-duet repertoire tend to co-vary with arousal, the high-arousal pieces were also faster and more technically demanding. Condition effects on synchrony and on rated quality should therefore be interpreted as the combined product of emotional arousal, musical structure, and performance load, rather than as effects of emotional arousal in isolation.

Given the 2–3 min duration of each piece, the 30-s sliding window yielded an average of only 4–6 valid CCF estimation windows per piece; the limited number of windows may affect the precision of trial-level synchrony index estimates, and future studies should consider using longer performance excerpts or shorter sliding windows to improve the stability of CCF estimates.

Finally, partners practiced the pieces individually and performed each only once after a brief warm-up, without a dedicated joint-rehearsal phase; the limited opportunity to co-develop an expressive interpretation may have constrained, in particular, the expressiveness ratings, and future designs could incorporate a joint-rehearsal stage to examine its effect on both performance quality and physiological coupling.

The present study provides direct empirical evidence that interpersonal physiological synchrony at the autonomic nervous system level occurs between co-performing professional pianists, with HR-CCF and EDA-CCF indices significantly exceeding cross-pair surrogate baselines with large effect sizes across all four emotional conditions. Synchrony strength was highest under the high-arousal, positive-valence condition and was independently modulated by both valence and arousal. Negative-valence conditions selectively suppressed expressiveness scores regardless of arousal level, while HR-CCF independently predicted ensemble cohesion; the corresponding EDA-CCF-expressiveness association did not reach significance, and the hypothesized complete dual-channel functional dissociation received only partial support. Trait empathy and collaboration duration did not significantly predict synchrony or performance quality within the present sample, and no consistent leader-follower directionality was identified. These directional and empathy-related questions were addressed as exploratory analyses; given the limited pair-level sample, their null results are best regarded as inconclusive rather than as evidence against the existence of such effects. These findings address a previously unverified question regarding whether interpersonal physiological synchrony reflecting shared emotional states arises in ensemble performance and offer partial physiological evidence for the functional differentiation of HR and EDA synchrony channels in ensemble emotional coordination.

neuroscience.title: The clinical, radiological, and genetic features of Pantothenate Kinase-Associated Neurodegeneration and Mitochondrial membrane Protein-Associated Neurodegeneration in Neurodegeneration with Brain Iron Accumulation: a case series
neuroscience.abstract: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) represents a group of rare, genetically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorders characterized by excessive iron deposition in the basal ganglia, especially globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Among its subtypes, pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration (MPAN) are among the most common NBIA subtypes. Reporting these cases is significant due to the rarity of NBIA, the diversity of its genetic etiologies, and the characteristic imaging patterns that aid early diagnosis. This series highlights the clinical and molecular spectrums of NBIA in an Indian cohort, emphasizing the diagnostic importance of integrating neuroimaging and genetic testing.Four children diagnosed with NBIA at a tertiary care hospital in South India were evaluated. Two unrelated children, a 4-year-old girl and a 6-year-old girl, from India, presented with early-onset dystonia, global developmental delay, and progressive motor disability. Brain MRI revealed the classic “eye-of-the-tiger” sign in the globus pallidus, and genetic testing identified pathogenic variants in the PANK2 gene, confirming PKAN. The remaining two children were a 16-year-old boy and a 16-year-old girl, first cousins from a consanguineous Muslim family in South India, developed gait disturbances and dysarthria in mid-childhood. MRI showed hyperintense streaking of the globus pallidus, and molecular analysis detected a likely pathogenic variant in the C19orf12 gene, confirming MPAN. All four children exhibited progressive motor decline, with supportive management focusing on physiotherapy, symptomatic control, and genetic counseling.This case series underscores the clinical and genetic heterogeneity of NBIA and the diagnostic value of characteristic MRI findings coupled with targeted genetic testing. Recognition of specific imaging patterns, such as the “eye-of-the-tiger” sign and hyperintense streaking of the globus pallidus, can guide clinicians toward accurate molecular diagnosis. Reporting such cases from diverse populations expands the understanding of NBIA’s phenotypic spectrum and reinforces the need for multidisciplinary evaluation, early diagnosis, and family-based genetic counseling to optimize patient care and inform future therapeutic strategies.
neuroscience.text:
Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) comprises a heterogeneous group of inherited progressive disorders characterized by pathological iron deposition in specific brain regions, particularly globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata. These regions are highly metabolically active and vulnerable to oxidative stress, making them particularly susceptible to iron-mediated neurotoxicity. The excess iron promotes oxidative damage, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration, contributing to the progressive extrapyramidal symptoms typical of NBIA [].

Clinically, NBIA is marked by progressive dystonia, rigidity, parkinsonism, dysarthria, spasticity, and cognitive decline. The disease course varies widely, from early-onset rapidly progressive forms to slowly progressive adult-onset variants []. MRI plays a crucial role in early recognition, revealing characteristic T2 hypointensity of the basal ganglia due to iron accumulation, sometimes accompanied by specific patterns such as the “eye-of-the-tiger” sign in PKAN or hyperintense streaking in MPAN [].

All forms of NBIA are classified as ultra-rare disorders, with an estimated prevalence of less than 1 per 1,000,000 individuals []. Over 15 causative genes have been identified, encompassing pathways related to iron metabolism, mitochondrial function, lipid remodeling, coenzyme A biosynthesis, and autophagy []. The major subtypes include pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN; PANK2 gene), phospholipase A2-associated neurodegeneration (PLAN; PLA2G6 gene), mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration (MPAN; C19orf12 gene), and beta-propeller protein-associated neurodegeneration (BPAN; WDR45 gene) []. Most NBIA subtypes follow an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance, whereas a few exhibit autosomal dominant inheritance (such as FTH1-associated neuroferritinopathy) or an X-linked pattern, as seen in BPAN.

Although NBIA disorders are individually rare, they collectively represent an important cause of childhood-onset neuroregression. Their recognition is particularly crucial in resource-limited settings, such as India, where access to advanced molecular diagnostics is still emerging. Recent availability of next-generation sequencing (NGS) panels and whole-exome sequencing (WES) has significantly improved the diagnostic yield and enabled early genetic confirmation, facilitating genetic counseling and identification of potentially treatable subtypes.

We present four children from South India with genetically confirmed NBIA—two unrelated cases of PKAN and two cousins with MPAN. These cases highlight the clinical heterogeneity, characteristic MRI findings, and diagnostic value of exome sequencing in a tertiary pediatric setting.

A 4-year-old girl, the first child of non-consanguineous parents from the Jain community in North India (but was in Bengaluru at the time of the diagnosis) was born at term following an uneventful pregnancy and perinatal period. Early development was delayed, with both motor and language milestones affected. Although her language gradually improved to the use of meaningful words and short phrases, her motor development remained significantly delayed, and she achieved assisted ambulation by 2 years of age. At 3 years of age, she developed progressive abnormal posturing and dystonic movements involving the limbs, followed by rapid loss of previously acquired motor abilities and functional regression. Over the ensuing months, her condition deteriorated rapidly, with increasingly frequent episodes of severe generalized dystonia. She presented to our center at 4 years of age in dystonic crisis, with marked generalized dystonia, persistent opisthotonus, and severe bruxism. Despite the severity of her motor impairment, there did not seem to be significant cognitive decline. She was managed with supportive care, including physiotherapy and medical therapy with baclofen and trihexyphenidyl; however, her neurological status continued to worsen. She experienced relentless clinical progression and died approximately six months after the initial presentation to our hospital a disease course consistent with the rapidly progressive classical phenotype of pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN). The family went back to their hometown in North India, and this information was communicated electronically.

Evaluation for autoimmune encephalitis, Wilson’s disease, and neurometabolic disorders was negative.

Her brain MRI revealed T2-weighted hypointensity in bilateral globus pallidus, and gradient echo (GRE) sequences confirmed marked hypointensity consistent with iron deposition as shown in Fig. A.

WES detected a homozygous single base insertion in exon 1 of the PANK2 gene (NM_153638.4: c.545_546insA; p.(Arg183Glufs*47)), confirming the diagnosis of PKAN. This frameshift variant is predicted to cause premature protein truncation. The variant is registered in ClinVar (VCV001878518) as pathogenic, concordantly classified by four independent submitters, and has been previously reported as a recurrent PANK2 pathogenic allele in Indian patients with early-onset classic PKAN, including as a founder mutation in the Agrawal community. Based on ACMG criteria—PVS1 (null variant in a gene with an established loss-of-function disease mechanism), PM2 (rare in population databases; gnomAD South Asian allele frequency 0.0145%), PS4 (significantly increased prevalence in affected individuals relative to controls, supported by prior cohort data), and PP3 (multiple lines of computational evidence supporting a deleterious effect)—the variant was classified as pathogenic.

A 6-year-old girl, second child of consanguineous parents, from a village in the state of Andhra Pradesh, South India, presented with frequent falls and gait unsteadiness since age three. She also had a history of global developmental delay and gradually developed feeding difficulty, dysarthria, and constipation. On examination, she exhibited dystonic hand posturing, forefoot adduction, and spasticity. She underwent evaluation for secondary and treatable causes of her developmental delay. Biochemical investigations revealed primary hypothyroidism, for which thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine was commenced. She was also started on antidystonic medication and physiotherapy. Her ophthalmological examination was normal and showed no KF ring.

This child was symptomatically better after starting baclofen and trihexyphenidyl and may be following a slowly progressive atypical course. This needs to be monitored carefully since there may be periods of crisis and deterioration.

Susceptibility-weighted angiography (SWAN) sequence of the brain MRI in Case 2 demonstrating hypointensities in the basal ganglia with central hyperintensity giving the characteristic “ eye-of-the-tiger” sign as depicted in Fig. B.

WES revealed a homozygous two base-pair deletion in exon 3 of the PANK2 gene (NM_153638.4: c.1176_1177del; p.(Gly393_Val394insTer)) that results in a frameshift and premature truncation of the protein downstream to codon 393, confirming PKAN. The variant was classified as pathogenic based on ACMG criteria (PVS1, PM2, PP4).

A sixteen-year-old girl, from South India, presented with a history of frequent falls since four years of age and progressive worsening of gait difficulty. Her parents also reported reduced speech clarity and slowness of speech beginning at fourteen years of age. She was the child of consanguineous parents, with an uneventful perinatal period and normal early developmental milestones. On examination, she had dystonic posturing of both hands, with extension at the proximal interphalangeal joints and flexion at the distal interphalangeal joints. She also exhibited reduced facial expressions, resembling the mask-like facies seen in Parkinson’s disease. Visual impairment was noted, and she required corrective spectacles. Fundus examination demonstrated bilateral partial optic atrophy, while slit-lamp examination showed no Kayser–Fleischer rings. MRI demonstrated hyperintense streaking of the globus pallidus along the medial medullary lamina (Fig. A). This finding, which is similar to the “eye-of-the-tiger sign”, was initially diagnosed as PKAN, and a trial of pantothenate was given. WES identified a homozygous missense variant in C19orf12 gene, which is the gene for MPAN, (NM_001031726.3): c.139G>A, p.(Gly47Ser), that results in the amino acid substitution of Serine for Glycine at codon 47, classified as likely pathogenic (ACMG: PM2, PP3, PP4, PM3). Once the diagnosis of MPAN was established, the pantothenate tablets were stopped. She initially responded well to Baclofen and Syndopa, but continued to slowly worsen. She gradually also developed neuropsychiatric manifestations and emotional lability, consistent with MPAN.

A 16-year-old boy, a cousin of patient 3, from a village in South India, presented with a history of frequent falls, toe walking, and slurred speech since seven years of age, all of which have progressively worsened over time. He currently needs support to walk and is gradually becoming non-ambulant. Examination revealed spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar response. MRI brain showed hyperintense streaking of globus pallidus, cerebellar, and cortical atrophy as shown in Fig. B and C. He was initially diagnosed to have neurological Wilson’s disease because of the MRI findings and indeterminate laboratory reports. Serum ceruloplasmin was 0.206 g/L (reference range: 0.20–0.40 g/L), at the lower limit of normal. Baseline 24-hour urinary copper excretion was mildly elevated at 155.21 µg/24 h. Following a D-penicillamine challenge, 24-hour urinary copper excretion was 310 µg/24 h, which was not diagnostic of Wilson disease. Slit-lamp examination did not reveal Kayser–Fleischer rings. Brain MRI did not demonstrate the characteristic "eye-of-the-tiger" sign of pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), although subtle hypointense signal changes within the globus pallidus, suggestive of mineral deposition, were noted. Given the borderline biochemical findings and the absence of definitive neuroimaging features of PKAN, Wilson disease was initially considered, and treatment with zinc and D-penicillamine was commenced.

Later, genetic testing revealed the same homozygous C19orf12 gene, c.139G>A (p.Gly47Ser) variant, confirming MPAN in the child. After the diagnosis of MPAN was made, zinc and penicillamine were stopped. The addition of the two drugs did not ameliorate or slow down the symptoms. His vision also has been progressively worsening, his ophthalmic findings showed bilateral optic nerve atrophy. KF ring was negative.

Both children were initially misdiagnosed with disorders that clinically mimic NBIA. The provisional diagnosis was guided primarily by clinical judgment given the challenges in obtaining the recommended diagnostic investigations. Key barriers included the requirement for hospital admission, the need for sedation to perform MRI, and the associated financial constraints. Although the cost of genetic testing has reduced substantially in recent years, it continued to pose a significant limitation, contributing to the delay in establishing a definitive diagnosis.

NBIA encompasses a spectrum of genetically and clinically diverse disorders unified by the hallmark feature of pathological iron deposition in the basal ganglia. The mechanism of iron accumulation is multifactorial, often secondary to defects in mitochondrial metabolism, lipid remodeling, and autophagy. Excess iron contributes to oxidative stress, impaired cellular homeostasis, and neuronal death, leading to progressive motor and cognitive decline [].

In PKAN, mutations in PANK2 impair pantothenate kinase, the first enzyme in coenzyme A biosynthesis, resulting in accumulation of cysteine derivatives that chelate iron and produce free radicals []. Classical PKAN typically presents before six years of age with rapid progression, dystonia, and the characteristic “eye-of-the-tiger” MRI appearance, which may be absent in early stages. Our identified frameshift PANK2 variants predict loss of function and are consistent with severe early-onset disease, correlating with previous reports.

MPAN, caused by C19orf12 mutations, is the third most common NBIA subtype. The gene product localizes to the outer mitochondrial membrane and endoplasmic reticulum, implicating defects in mitochondrial lipid metabolism []. Clinically, MPAN overlaps with PKAN but is distinguished by spasticity, optic atrophy, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. The cousins described here demonstrate both intrafamilial variability and the hyperintense streaking MRI pattern, supporting the diagnosis of MPAN.

Literature highlights genotype–phenotype correlations: truncating PANK2 mutations result in earlier onset and severe dystonia, while missense mutations yield milder or atypical presentations []. Our patient 2, though harboring a truncating variant has a relatively stable clinical course. In MPAN, clinical variability can occur even among individuals with identical genotypes, suggesting modifying factors. Table  presents a comparative summary of the key clinical, genetic, and radiological features distinguishing PKAN and MPAN.

In India, published NBIA literature remains limited to isolated reports, and the true burden may be under-recognized due to restricted access to next-generation sequencing. This series demonstrates the feasibility of exome sequencing in diagnosing ultra-rare neurodegenerative conditions in tertiary care. Early molecular diagnosis enables precise classification, carrier testing, and prenatal counseling, in addition to facilitating inclusion in evolving therapeutic trials.

While no curative treatment exists, several emerging disease-modifying strategies are under study. Iron chelation with deferiprone provides biochemical improvement but limited clinical benefit []. Research trials are underway at various stages evaluating therapeutic strategies for PKAN, including the brain-penetrant PanK activator PZ-2891 (pantazine), agents designed to restore coenzyme A biosynthesis, such as pantethine and fosmetpantotenate (RE-024), and pantothenate kinase inhibitors (PANKi) [, ]. The development of disease-modifying treatment strategies for MPAN remains in its early stages. Promising preclinical models have provided valuable insights into the function of the C19orf12 protein and its crucial role in maintaining mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum-associated membrane integrity [].

Supportive multidisciplinary management—physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy, nutritional optimization, and symptomatic control of dystonia—remains the mainstay. Symptomatic treatments included baclofen, trihexyphenidyl, and levodopa, administered in different combinations according to individual clinical features. Establishing regional NBIA registries can enhance awareness, promote early detection, and support national research collaborations.

The strength of this study lies in its focus on two very rare genetic conditions, with longitudinal follow-up of affected children. By documenting progression over time and comparing the 2 groups, the study effectively highlights the important contrasts. Although the subtypes appear radiologically similar, their genetic and clinical presentation differ notably and this comparison brings out those subtle yet significant differences.

The main limitation of this series is the small sample size. A larger cohort would strengthen the findings and provide more data.

Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) encompasses a group of ultra-rare neurodegenerative disorders characterized by basal ganglia iron deposition arising from diverse genetic causes. Among these, PKAN and MPAN represent the major subtypes, each with distinct genetic, clinical, and radiological features. Our four cases illustrate the marked clinical and genetic heterogeneity within the NBIA spectrum. Accurate molecular diagnosis enables appropriate genetic counseling and facilitates access to emerging targeted therapies. Broader genomic testing and integrated multidisciplinary care remain essential to improving outcomes for affected children.

neuroscience.title: Functional impairment statistically mediates the association between hyperarousal neuropsychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline: a prospective cohort study
neuroscience.abstract: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are prevalent in older adults and are associated with cognitive decline. This study investigated the association between hyperarousal NPS (HNPS) and cognitive progression, focusing on the mediating role of functional impairment and its link to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology.Using data from 1,657 non-demented participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we evaluated the Hyperarousal Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire (HNPI-Q, comprising agitation, anxiety, and irritability), the Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), APOE ε4 status, Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13 (ADAS13) scores, regional brain volumes, and amyloid-β (Aβ) positron emission tomography (PET) Centiloid values. Analyses included Cox and linear regression, mediation analysis, and nomogram development.HNPS predicted 5-year cognitive decline (HR = 1.14, p = 2.7 × 10–4), an association attenuated after adjusting for FAQ. HNPI-Q scores were longitudinally associated with functional and cognitive decline. Mediation analyses indicated that functional impairment statistically mediated the association between HNPS and cognition. Notably, the rate of functional decline was strongly correlated with the rate of Aβ accumulation, a coupling that was also evident in participants who progressed to cognitive deterioration. Predictive models based on HNPI-Q and FAQ showed excellent discrimination (AUC: 0.838 and 0.845) and calibration.HNPS was associated with cognitive decline, an association that was statistically mediated by functional impairment, which itself co-varies with Aβ pathology. The HNPI-Q stratified the 5-year risk of cognitive deterioration in this cohort, and whether intervening on these symptoms or on functional decline alters the clinical course remains to be further investigated.
neuroscience.text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) accounts for 60%–90% of dementia cases, with a high prevalence and limited treatment options, imposing a heavy burden on families and society (; ). Given the pathological progression of Alzheimer’s disease from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and eventually to dementia (), it is crucial to identify those individuals in the CN or MCI groups who are most likely to experience rapid progression. This identification is essential for the development of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) aimed at delaying disease onset and mitigating its impact. Although traditional diagnostic approaches, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing (), positron emission tomography (PET) (), and plasma biomarkers (), have shown effectiveness in early screening, their clinical application is constrained by their invasive nature, high cost, and time-consuming procedures. Consequently, the identification of noninvasive and readily implementable biomarkers is of paramount importance. These biomarkers will facilitate the initial screening of high-risk outpatients and increase the recruitment rate of clinical trial participants. Additionally, the use of noninvasive markers can significantly reduce clinical research-associated costs and increase overall trial efficiency.

Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) encompass a range of psychiatric and behavioral manifestations, such as apathy, depression, and psychosis, which are prevalent throughout the entire course of AD (). Up to 50% of patients with MCI and up to 97% of those with early AD exhibit at least one NPS (), and the presence of the NPS serves as a prognostic indicator for disease progression (; ). However, the specific symptoms or symptom clusters that directly contribute to cognitive decline remain poorly understood. Current approaches often rely on empirical syndrome classifications (), which can be limited by subjective assessment and may lack precision. Although advanced methods such as latent class analysis have been used to identify NPS patterns (), their results are frequently difficult to interpret and translate into clinical practice. Furthermore, most studies have focused on patients with MCI and AD, while the potential of the NPS in predicting cognitive decline among cognitively normal populations has rarely been investigated. Finally, although the NPS is practical for predicting cognitive decline, its exact neurobiological mechanisms and clinical development trajectories still need to be further clarified to guide targeted therapeutic strategies.

Functional decline constitutes a critical diagnostic feature of dementia. Patients with both MCI and AD exhibit diminished instrumental activities of daily living, which serve as robust predictors for the progression from MCI to AD (; ). NPS have been shown to predict functional impairment both in non-AD adults () and in AD patients (; ), and severe functional decline is often accompanied by persistent and severe NPS (). Beyond its clinical significance, functional decline may also reflect and interact with the core neuropathological processes of AD. Growing evidence links impairment in daily activities to biomarkers of AD pathology, including amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition and neurodegeneration (; ). However, the specific NPS profiles that contribute to functional decline remain poorly defined. Moreover, the complex interrelationships among NPS, functional decline, and cognitive deterioration have not been fully elucidated. Importantly, whether functional decline progresses in parallel with the underlying AD pathophysiology remains unknown. Clarifying these pathways would advance our understanding of how NPS influence cognitive trajectories and could provide a theoretical foundation for mechanism-based interventions aimed at preserving cognitive function by targeting daily functioning.

Therefore, this study aims to: (1) identify and define the hyperarousal neuropsychiatric symptoms (HNPS) that best predict 5-year cognitive decline in CN and MCI individuals; (2) examine the interrelationships among HNPS, functional impairment, and cognitive performance; (3) explore the longitudinal association of functional decline with amyloid-β accumulation; and (4) develop and validate a clinical prediction model based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), cognitive scores, and the HNPS/FAQ to stratify risk in non-demented older adults.

The data for this study were sourced from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) repository, which is accessible at http://adni.loni.usc.edu. Since its launch in 2003, this project has been dedicated to studying the progression of Alzheimer’s disease through the integration of clinical, genetic and neuroimaging biomarkers. The study protocol adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional review boards of all involved sites, with written informed consent provided by all subjects. For current updates, researchers are directed to http://www.adni-info.org.

The study sample included individuals diagnosed as CN or with MCI according to the ADNI criteria (), all of whom had recorded Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire (NPI-Q) results at baseline. Participants with insufficient data on demographic characteristics, genetics, or functional and cognitive assessments were excluded. The ADNI conducts biannual follow-up assessments for participants. To monitor longitudinal changes in functional and cognitive abilities effectively, we excluded those who did not have any follow-up data within 5 years. The final analytical cohort consisted of 1,657 subjects, among whom 718 were classified as having a CN at baseline and 939 were diagnosed with MCI. The detailed participant selection and operational procedures are illustrated in the flowchart ().

The assessment of the NPS was conducted via the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) or its abbreviated form, the NPI-Q. The NPI is a comprehensive tool specifically designed to evaluate the presence, frequency, and severity of 12 aspects of symptoms, including delusions, hallucinations, agitation, depression, anxiety, euphoria, apathy, disinhibition, irritability, aberrant motor behavior, and changes in sleep or appetite. In contrast, the NPI-Q is a simplified derivative tool that records the severity of symptoms, on a 3-point scale ranging from mild to severe for scoring. The total score of this scale ranges from 0 to 36, with higher scores indicating greater severity of neuropsychiatric disorders. To harmonize the NPS data, we used the available NPI-Q to assess NPI items throughout all phases of the ADNI.

The Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ) was employed to assess performance across 10 daily living activities, including tasks such as writing checks, independent shopping, and preparing balanced meals. Each participant’s performance in these activities was rated on an ordinal scale from 0 (normal) to 3 (dependent). The total FAQ score was calculated by summing the scores of all the items, ranging from 0 to 30. A higher score indicates a greater degree of functional impairment.

Global cognitive status was assessed via the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale Cognitive Subscale 13 (ADAS13), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating Scale Sum of Boxes (CDRSB), and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Four composite measures were employed to evaluate specific domains of cognitive function: Memory (MEM), Language (LAN), Executive Function (EXF), and Visuospatial Ability (VSP). All participants completed these assessments at both the baseline visit and the follow-up. Owing to the loss of more than 50% of the follow-up data in this study, the MoCA and VSP were excluded from the longitudinal cognitive analysis. Notably, higher scores on the CDRSB and ADAS13 indicate poorer cognitive performance, whereas lower scores on the MoCA, MMSE, MEM, EF, LAN, and VSP reflect more severe cognitive impairment.

The MRI volumetric measurements were extracted from T1-weighted images obtained via a 1.5 Tesla scanner. All volume segmentation and quantitative analyses were performed using the FreeSurfer v4.3 software package, which is publicly available. The technical details of the complete processing pipeline are provided online at http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/fswiki/FreeSurferMethodsCitation. For image analysis, we employed the standardized volumes of the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, medial temporal lobe, and fusiform gyrus, and corrected the total cranial volume via the proportional method ().

Amyloid-β PET data were obtained from the ADNI Laboratory of Neuroimaging (LONI) database, as previously described (). Global cortical Aβ burden was quantified using the standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) with the whole cerebellum as the reference region. For participants across ADNI-2 and ADNI-3 cohorts, SUVR values were converted to the Centiloid scale to harmonize data acquired with different tracers (florbetapir or florbetaben). Longitudinal Aβ PET measurements were available at baseline and at follow-up visits (years 1–5), and the Centiloid value was used as a continuous measure of Aβ load in all analyses.

Cognitive status at each visit was assigned according to the ADNI criteria (adni.loni.usc.edu). CN participants had no significant impairment in cognition or in activities of daily living, an MMSE score of 24–30 and a CDR of 0. MCI was defined as a memory complaint, objective memory impairment on the Wechsler Memory Scale Logical Memory II with education-adjusted cut-offs, a CDR of 0.5, preserved activities of daily living and no dementia. AD was diagnosed according to the NINCDS-ADRDA criteria for probable AD. The primary outcome was cognitive decline over the 5-year follow-up, defined as progression from a baseline CN diagnosis to MCI or AD, or from a baseline MCI diagnosis to AD, at any follow-up visit. The remaining cognitive measures (ADAS13, MMSE, MoCA, MEM, EXF, LAN and VSP) were analyzed as separate, secondary outcomes and were not combined to define the primary outcome.

Because the ADNI diagnostic criteria incorporate the CDR, and because a diagnosis of dementia requires functional impairment, progression defined by these criteria overlaps conceptually with the FAQ, which is examined here as a potential mediator. We therefore performed a pre-specified analysis using a function-independent cognitive outcome. Cognitive deterioration was defined as an increase of at least 5 points on the ADAS13 between the baseline assessment and the last available follow-up assessment within 5 years (). This threshold corresponds to approximately one standard deviation of the baseline-to-follow-up change observed among participants who remained cognitively stable (SD = 5.25), that is, a magnitude beyond the range of normal fluctuation (). The time to the event was defined as the first visit at which the threshold was met and remained met until the end of follow-up, and participants who never reached the threshold were censored at their last assessment.

For univariate analysis, the Shapiro–Wilk test was used to evaluate the normality of continuous variables. Continuous variables that conformed to a normal distribution are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) and were analyzed via the Student’s t-test. Conversely, nonnormally distributed continuous variables are expressed as medians and interquartile ranges and were analyzed via the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages and were analyzed via the χ2 test.

To identify risk factors for cognitive decline within a 5-year period, we employed a time-dependent multivariate Cox proportional hazards model. Model 1 was unadjusted. Model 2 was adjusted for age, gender, education, APOE ε4 status, baseline ADAS13 and the baseline volumes of the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, medial temporal lobe and fusiform gyrus. Model 3 included the same covariates together with the baseline FAQ score. The NPI-Q symptoms (agitation, anxiety, and irritability) that were statistically significant in Model 2 formed the Hyperarousal Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire (HNPI-Q), which was subsequently subjected to further Cox regression analysis. Although delusions, hallucinations, and appetite changes were statistically significant, they were not included in the subsequent analysis because of the limited number of positive cases. The optimal cut-off values for the NPI-Q and HNPI-Q were determined using the maximum selected rank statistics method (), and then applied to categorize the continuous variables into high-risk and low-risk groups. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were plotted to describe the risk of cognitive progression on the basis of the optimal cut-off values, and were formally compared via the log-rank test. Additionally, a risk table was provided to indicate the number of patients at risk over time.

Multiple linear regression models were employed to examine cross-sectional associations at baseline, specifically between HNPI-Q scores and FAQ, between HNPI-Q scores and cognitive test results, and between FAQ and Aβ Centiloid. To model longitudinal trajectories, linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual annual rates of change for FAQ, cognitive performance, and Aβ burden. Subsequently, multiple linear regression analyses were applied to assess the longitudinal associations of baseline HNPI-Q scores with subsequent changes in FAQ and cognition, as well as the association between the rate of functional decline and the rate of Aβ accumulation. To test whether the strength of an association differed between the cognitive stability and the cognitive deterioration group, a multiplicative interaction term between the exposure and group status was added to each model, and the resulting P for interaction is reported. Group-specific estimates are presented for descriptive purposes.

Mediation analyses were conducted within the counterfactual framework, and are reported as the average causal mediation effect (ACME, that is, the indirect effect), the average direct effect (ADE) and the total effect. Both the mediator and the outcome were modeled with linear regression, no exposure-mediator interaction was included, and the ACME therefore equals the product of the exposure-mediator (a) and mediator-outcome (b) coefficients. All models were adjusted for age, gender, education, APOE ε4 status and the volumes of the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, medial temporal lobe and fusiform gyrus; these are the same covariates used in the cognition models. The proportion mediated (ACME divided by the total effect) is reported only when the direct and indirect effects have the same sign and the ACME is statistically significant; otherwise it is reported as not defined, because the ratio is then unstable or uninterpretable. Ninety-five per cent confidence intervals for every estimate, including the proportion mediated, were obtained from 5,000 bootstrap resamples of participants. Because ACME estimates depend on the sequential-ignorability assumption (no unmeasured confounding of the exposure-mediator, exposure-outcome or mediator-outcome relationships, and no reverse causation), we report the E-value for each ACME, that is, the minimum strength of association that an unmeasured mediator-outcome confounder would need to have with both the mediator and the outcome to shift the indirect effect to the null. If this assumption is violated the indirect effect would be biased away from the null and the proportion mediated would be correspondingly overstated, so the mediation results are interpreted as statistical associations rather than as established causal pathways. The analyses were repeated separately in participants who were CN and MCI at baseline. A directed acyclic graph summarizing the hypothesized relations among confounders, HNPI-Q, the FAQ, cognitive outcomes and AD pathology, together with the assumptions underlying the mediation models, is provided in .

By integrating all statistically significant independent predictors from the aforementioned two multivariate Cox regression models, we constructed prognostic nomograms. The discriminatory ability of the two models was quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC); the two AUCs were compared with the DeLong test for correlated curves. The calibration of the model was assessed using calibration curves generated through 1000 bootstrap resampling iterations. The closer the deviation is to the diagonal, the higher the predictive accuracy. The clinical utility of the nomograms was evaluated through decision curve analysis (DCA), which computes the net benefit at stratified probability thresholds and compares it with the default strategies of universal treatment or nonintervention.

Statistical significance was defined as a two-tailed p-value of less than 0.05. All data analyses were performed with SPSS 26 and R 4.3.1, while GraphPad Prism 10 was used for figure creation. Exact p-values are reported throughout. Values are given to three decimal places, or in scientific notation when below 0.001; p-values below 1 × 10–10 are reported as p < 1 × 10–10, because the asymptotic tests used here do not provide meaningful resolution at smaller magnitudes and because the corresponding effect sizes are described in full in the accompanying tables.

This study included 1,657 participants, among whom 718 were from the CN cohort and 939 from the MCI cohort. The median age was 73.00 years (interquartile range (IQR), 68.20–77.90), and 771 participants (46.53%) were female. The median years of education was 16 years (IQR, 14–18 years), and 690 participants (41.64%) carried the APOE ε4 allele. The median follow-up period was 3 years (IQR, 2–4 years), during which 418 participants (25.23%) experienced cognitive decline. Compared with the CN group, the MCI group had fewer female participants, lower educational attainment, and a higher rate of APOE ε4 allele carriage. Additionally, NPS, cognitive impairments, and functional impairments were more prevalent in the MCI group than in the CN group, and the MCI group also showed more pronounced regional brain atrophy. While the median follow-up duration for the MCI group was shorter than that for the CN group, the proportion of individuals with cognitive decline was approximately three times greater in the MCI group ().

Baseline demographic characteristics of participants included.

ADAS13, Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13; APOE ε4, Apolipoprotein ε4; CDRSB, Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes; CN, Cognitively normal; EXF, Executive function; FAQ, Functional Activities Questionnaire; LAN, Language; MCI, Mild cognitive impairment; Med Temp, Medial temporal; MEM, Memory; MMSE, Mini-Mental State Examination; MoCA, Montreal Cognitive Assessment; NPI-Q, Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire; VSP, Visuospatial.

A total of 44.2% of the participants presented at least one neuropsychiatric symptom, with these symptoms being significantly more prevalent in individuals with MCI (59.7%) compared to CN controls (23.8%). The most common neuropsychiatric symptoms included irritability (18.2%), depression (16.6%), sleep disturbances (15.4%), anxiety (11.0%), agitation (10.7%), and apathy (10.0%). The MCI group exhibited a greater prevalence of all individual neuropsychiatric symptoms compared to the CN group ( and ).

The results of the bivariate (Model 1) and multivariable Cox regression (Model 2) analyses, adjusted for baseline age, gender, education, APOE ε4, ADAS13 scores, and the volumes of the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, medial temporal lobe, and fusiform gyrus, indicated that the NPI-Q was predictive of cognitive progression within 5 years (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.14, p < 1 × 10–10; HR = 1.05, p = 0.006). The Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed a significant difference in the cumulative proportion of individuals with cognitive stability between the high NPI-Q group (≥4) and the low NPI-Q group (<4) (p < 1 × 10–10). More than 50% of individuals with high NPI-Q levels (≥4) progressed from CN to MCI or converted from MCI to AD, whereas the risk of cognitive deterioration in the low NPI-Q group was reduced by half (, ). The predictive capability of NPI-Q became statistically insignificant in Model 3, which controlled for additional FAQ (HR = 1.00, p = 0.951) ().

We subsequently analyzed the individual symptoms within the NPI-Q using Cox regression models. After adjusting for relevant covariates, the results from Model 2 indicated that delusions, hallucinations, agitation, anxiety, irritability, and appetite changes could independently predict cognitive deterioration. However, after controlling for FAQ, the predictive power diminished. Since agitation, anxiety, and irritability are hyperarousal symptoms characterized by over-reactivity, we combined their scores to create the HNPI-Q for further analysis. The results of the Cox regression and Kaplan–Meier survival curve analyses for HNPI-Q were similar to those for NPI-Q, with an even more pronounced prediction of cognitive decline (Model 1, HR = 1.30, P < 1 × 10–10; Model 2, HR = 1.14, p = 2.7 × 10–4; Model 3, HR = 1.07, p = 0.059) (, ,  and ).

The Cox proportional hazards models of NPI-Q score.

Model 1: Bivariate Cox regression; Model 2: multivariable Cox regression, adjusted for baseline age, gender, education, APOE ε4, ADAS13, and the volumes of the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, medial temporal lobe, and fusiform gyrus; Model 3: multivariable Cox regression, adjusted for variables in model 2 and FAQ. ADAS13, Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13; FAQ, Functional Activities Questionnaire; HNPI-Q, Hyperarousal Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire; HR, hazard ratio. Bold values indicate statistically significant associations (P < 0.05).

Because the ADNI diagnostic criteria and the FAQ share a functional component, all Cox models were repeated using a function-independent cognitive outcome (ADAS13 deterioration, defined as an increase of at least 5 points; ). In the overall cohort (n = 1,633; 500 events), HNPI-Q predicted ADAS13 deterioration in Model 2 (; HR = 1.11, 95% CI 1.04–1.19, p = 0.002), and the association was attenuated after further adjustment for FAQ (; Model 3: HR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.98–1.13, p = 0.170), whereas FAQ itself was associated with the outcome (HR = 1.07, 95% CI 1.04–1.09, p = 1.4 × 10–8). The same pattern was observed in the MCI stratum (, ; Model 2: HR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.01–1.16, p = 0.025; Model 3: HR = 1.03, 95% CI 0.96–1.11, p = 0.366). In the CN stratum, HNPI-Q was not associated with ADAS13 deterioration (, ; Model 2: HR = 0.93, 95% CI 0.64–1.34, p = 0.682). Estimates were slightly larger in a sensitivity analysis that did not adjust for baseline ADAS13 (overall Model 2: HR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.23), indicating that the primary model is conservative with respect to the association of interest.

Building on prior findings that the FAQ diminishes the predictive capacity of the HNPI-Q for cognitive deterioration, this study investigated the relationships between HNPI-Q, its individual symptoms, and FAQ. Adjustments were made for baseline age, gender, education, APOE ε4, ADAS13 scores, and the volumes of the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, medial temporal lobe, and fusiform gyrus. Linear regression analysis detected a positive linear correlation between HNPI-Q scores (as well as individual symptoms such as agitation, anxiety, and irritability) and FAQ scores, indicating that higher HNPI-Q scores were associated with more severe functional impairment. This association was stronger in the cognitive deterioration group than in the cognitive stability group for agitation (β = 2.008 vs 1.325, P for interaction = 0.006), anxiety (β = 2.306 vs. 1.280, P for interaction = 6.1 × 10–4) and the composite HNPI-Q score (β = 1.064 vs. 0.842, P for interaction = 0.016), whereas no such difference was detected for irritability (P for interaction = 0.327); equivalent NPI-Q scores in the cognitive deterioration group therefore signified greater functional impairment ( and ).

Linear regression analysis demonstrated a negative relationship between baseline HNPI-Q scores and cognitive performance across the overall cohort, after adjusting for age, gender, education, APOE ε4, and volumetric measures. Higher HNPI-Q scores correlated with higher ADAS13 scores (β = 0.825, 95% CI 0.569–1.082, p = 3.4 × 10–10), as well as with lower MMSE scores (β = −0.125, p = 4.8 × 10–4), MoCA scores (β = −0.314, p = 2.4 × 10–4), MEM (β = −0.065, p = 8.9 × 10–9), EXF (β = −0.049, p = 3.7 × 10–5), LAN (β = −0.057, p = 1.8 × 10–6), and VSP (β = −0.023, p = 0.029). After further adjustment for FAQ, these associations were largely attenuated, and only the association with LAN remained statistically significant in the overall cohort (β = −0.030, p = 0.020). Formal tests for interaction between HNPI-Q and cognitive progression status provided no evidence that any of these cross-sectional associations differed between the cognitive deterioration and the cognitive stability groups (P for interaction > 0.16 for all outcomes) ( and ).

Linear regression analysis indicated a positive longitudinal relationship between baseline HNPI-Q scores (as well as individual symptoms) and functional decline, after controlling for baseline covariates. Specifically, baseline HNPI-Q scores were positively correlated with the annual rate of change in FAQ scores (β = 0.389, 95% CI 0.304–0.474, P < 1 × 10–10), suggesting that more pronounced neuropsychiatric symptoms were associated with greater declines in daily functional activities. Formal tests for interaction indicated that this longitudinal association was stronger in the cognitive deterioration group for anxiety (β = 0.813 vs 0.331, P for interaction = 7.3 × 10–4), irritability (β = 0.514 vs. 0.369, P for interaction = 0.037) and the composite HNPI-Q score (β = 0.349 vs. 0.258, P for interaction = 0.012), but not for agitation (P for interaction = 0.339) ( and ).

Associations between HNPI-Q and cognitive change were also identified. Baseline HNPI-Q scores were positively associated with the annual rate of change in ADAS13 scores (β = 0.390, p = 1.7 × 10−7) and negatively associated with the annual rate of change in MMSE scores (β = −0.094, p = 1.4 × 10–4) and MEM (β = −0.016, p = 0.037); no association was observed for EXF (β = −0.005, p = 0.385) or LAN (β = −0.009, p = 0.101). Following adjustment for changes in FAQ, the associations with ADAS13, MEM, EXF and LAN were no longer statistically significant, whereas the coefficient for MMSE reversed in sign (β = 0.056, p = 0.006), an inconsistent-mediation pattern that precludes a simple interpretation of the direct and indirect effects. Formal tests for interaction between HNPI-Q and cognitive progression status were non-significant for every outcome (P for interaction > 0.10), indicating that these longitudinal associations did not differ between the cognitive deterioration and the cognitive stability groups ( and ).

The cross-sectional analyses examined whether baseline FAQ statistically mediated the association between baseline HNPI-Q and baseline cognitive performance ( and ).
