As discussed above, this requires brain–sound mappings to generalize beyond the data used to estimate them [,,,,,,,], generated sounds to preserve the stimulus relationships relevant to the neural hypothesis without introducing confounding artifacts [,,,], and iterative experiments to remain reliable under practical constraints such as measurement noise, limited trial budgets, participant fatigue, and state-dependent variability [,,,,]. Most importantly, it remains to be established whether repeated brain-guided generation and testing yield more reproducible or diagnostically informative scientific inferences than matched predefined or non-neural alternatives. Until these requirements are met, brain-guided generative auditory neuroscience should be regarded as a prospective research framework supported by a specific auditory proof of principle and independently demonstrated methodological capabilities, rather than as an already validated integrated system.

Brain-guided generation can expand the space of auditory hypotheses, but it cannot adjudicate which of those hypotheses should ultimately be accepted as scientific explanations. Neural evidence can help formulate candidate hypotheses that would be difficult to derive from acoustic analysis alone, and generative systems can translate those hypotheses into sounds that can be tested experimentally. Yet neither a generated stimulus nor the response it is designed to elicit provides an autonomous verdict on what that result means. Determining whether a candidate explanation should be retained, revised, or rejected remains a human scientific responsibility, requiring investigators to judge the result in relation to competing explanations, experimental constraints, and the broader empirical context. Brain-guided generation should therefore be understood as a means of expanding and sharpening the hypotheses that can be brought into experiment, not as an autonomous process for deciding their scientific validity.

A second boundary concerns how the structures discovered through brain-guided generation should be interpreted. A generated stimulus space is not equivalent to the full space of auditory representations, because every discovery is constrained by the neural measurements, stimulus representations, and generative systems used to explore it. If a generator cannot produce a particular sound or variation, this does not imply that the auditory system does not encode that structure; it may simply indicate that the current generative space does not provide access to it. Conversely, an effective direction or feature combination within a generative representation should not be interpreted as a direct readout of how the brain organizes sounds. The discovered relationship may overlap with an underlying auditory organization within the range of stimuli that have been explored, while still providing only a partial description of the computations that generate the neural response. A correspondence that is useful for predicting or manipulating responses therefore does not necessarily reveal the complete structure of auditory representation. Determining its broader significance requires testing whether the inferred organization remains stable across alternative stimulus realizations, representations, and generative approaches. The goal of brain-guided discovery is therefore not to recover a definitive map of auditory space, but to identify experimentally useful structures whose relationship to human auditory organization can be progressively clarified through further testing.

Finally, recursive brain–sound inference requires a criterion for when continued exploration is no longer expected to substantially change the scientific inference. The endpoint of an adaptive loop should not be defined by reaching a maximal neural response or by exhausting the available stimulus space, because neither condition indicates that the underlying auditory organization has been resolved []. Instead, recursion should provide a principled way to reduce uncertainty about the relationship being investigated: additional generations can progressively refine candidate stimulus relationships, boundaries, or explanatory distinctions, while new human measurements can evaluate whether these inferred structures remain supported or whether alternative interpretations remain plausible [,]. This principle parallels stopping criteria in adaptive experimental design, where sampling is terminated not when optimization is complete but when additional observations provide limited expected information gain []. In brain-guided auditory experiments, once a candidate organization remains stable across independently generated stimuli, participants, or measurement conditions, the goal should shift from further adaptive exploration to confirmatory testing. The endpoint of brain-guided discovery is therefore not a sound that can no longer be improved, but a stimulus–brain relationship whose interpretation no longer depends on continued searching.

Beyond these epistemic and methodological boundaries, increasingly adaptive and individualized brain-guided experiments introduce additional requirements for reproducibility, model transparency, and responsible data management. A reproducible pipeline should document the complete process from neural preprocessing and target definition to auditory representation, brain–sound mapping, generative constraints, adaptive stimulus selection, and stopping criteria. Relevant implementation details include model architectures and versions, pretrained checkpoints where available, training-data provenance, key hyperparameters, random seeds, software dependencies, and stimulus-generation settings. Code, configurations, and stimulus metadata should be shared where feasible and consistent with participant consent, data-protection requirements, and model licensing []. When closed or proprietary models prevent full disclosure, these limitations should be stated explicitly, and the robustness of the findings should be assessed across available model versions or alternative generators. Such transparency is important because a result that depends strongly on one particular model or generation pipeline may not reflect a stable property of auditory representation.

Individualized neural models also raise privacy concerns because neural recordings and derived representations may contain or permit inferences about participant-specific characteristics []. Their collection, storage, reuse, and sharing should therefore be governed by informed consent, data minimization, appropriate access controls, and secure data management. A further methodological risk is adaptive overfitting: because each new stimulus is selected in response to previous neural measurements, chance fluctuations may be repeatedly reinforced and mistaken for meaningful brain–sound structure. This risk is related to the broader problem of circular analysis, in which selecting and evaluating effects using non-independent data can produce misleading conclusions []. Discovery and confirmation should therefore be separated through held-out stimuli, independent measurement sessions or participants where appropriate, and prespecified confirmatory outcomes. Shuffled or mismatched neural-guidance controls and stability checks across random seeds, model configurations, and generative pipelines can further help determine whether an inferred relationship reflects reproducible neural organization rather than measurement noise or model-specific idiosyncrasies. These safeguards are essential for establishing the credibility of increasingly adaptive and personalized auditory experiments.

Building on existing demonstrations of brain-guided sound construction and validation, the framework developed here extends the scientific use of brain-guided auditory generation in several connected directions. It organizes the scientific scope of the approach around six classes of auditory question for which relevant stimulus structure is not fully specified in advance, and develops recursive brain–sound inference as a way for new human measurements to refine the brain–sound relationship and guide subsequent experimental interventions. The framework also treats the added value of brain guidance as an empirical question, to be assessed against appropriately matched predefined or non-neural alternatives. These elements position brain-guided generative auditory neuroscience as a question-driven and iterative experimental strategy in which neural evidence helps shape the construction, testing, and progressive refinement of auditory experiments.

The strength of this approach will ultimately depend on whether brain guidance produces scientific evidence that cannot be obtained as effectively from predefined, non-neural, or otherwise matched alternatives. Brain-derived relationships can motivate candidate stimulus structures, and generative systems can instantiate them as experimental probes, but neither the generated stimuli nor the computational procedures that produce them determine their scientific meaning; interpretation remains tied to human experimentation, comparison, and inference. The central opportunity is therefore not to replace conventional auditory experimentation, but to add a complementary route in which neural evidence helps define the next experiment itself. If that route can reveal reproducible relationships that survive independent testing and remain informative beyond the particular models and generators through which they were discovered, brain-guided generation could become a powerful means of turning observations of auditory brain responses into progressively more targeted questions about human auditory organization.

neuroscience.title: Frequency-specific cortical swallowing-network responses following neuroengineering-guided individualized multichannel tDCS
neuroscience.abstract: Neuromodulatory interventions for dysphagia are increasingly explored as adjunctive rehabilitation strategies, yet their efficacy may be limited by non-individualized stimulation protocols and insufficient consideration of network-specific brain dynamics. Advances in neuroengineering now enable individualized targeting based on functional neuroimaging and computational modeling, offering the potential for precision neuromodulation of swallowing-related brain networks.We investigated whether individualized multichannel transcranial direct current stimulation (mc-tDCS), optimized using magnetoencephalography (MEG)-derived target localization, MRI-based finite-element head modeling, and a distributed constrained maximum intensity (D-CMI) optimization framework, modulates the cortical swallowing network. In a randomized sham-controlled crossover design, eight healthy adults underwent three stimulation conditions: low-intensity mc-tDCS (1.5 mA), high-intensity mc-tDCS (4.0 mA), and sham stimulation. Swallowing-related cortical activity was assessed before and after stimulation using MEG source reconstruction of event-related desynchronization during uncued voluntary swallowing and a visually cued swallowing task requiring precise timing. A repeated-measures Dose × Task × Time model tested the hypothesized interaction separately in five frequency bands, with Holm correction across bands.No Dose × Task × Time interaction was significant after Holm correction across the five frequency bands (all adjusted p ≥ 0.274). Within-condition pre–post analyses identified alpha- and beta-band changes after 1.5-mA stimulation during challenged swallowing and a low-gamma change after 4.0-mA stimulation during uncued swallowing. Challenged-task timing accuracy increased over time, without significant Dose or Dose × Time effects.This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating individualized MEG-based targeting, subject-specific head modeling, and optimized multichannel stimulation. The hypothesized Dose × Task × Time interaction was not significant. Exploratory within-condition pre–post differences were observed in alpha, beta, and low-gamma activity, but do not establish stimulation-specific effects. Larger controlled studies are needed to evaluate the physiological effects of this individualized approach.The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12984-026-02214-0.
neuroscience.text:
Swallowing is a complex sensorimotor function governed by a distributed network comprising cortical, subcortical, and brainstem structures [, ]. Disruption of this network results in dysphagia, a frequent and clinically significant complication of neurological disease, particularly after stroke, and a major contributor to morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs due to complications such as aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition [, ]. Despite its high prevalence and clinical impact, effective therapeutic options for dysphagia remain limited, highlighting the need for novel, mechanism-based treatment strategies. In this context, non-invasive brain stimulation has emerged as a promising approach to modulate dysfunctional brain networks and support neurorehabilitation [, , ].

Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a widely used non-invasive neuromodulation technique that can facilitate synaptic plasticity and motor learning processes [–]. In the domain of swallowing, early studies demonstrated that anodal tDCS increases excitability of cortical swallowing representations []. Subsequent work showed that tDCS induces bilateral, frequency-specific modulation of swallowing-related cortical activity, accompanied by behavioral improvements during a swallowing task requiring precise timing in response to visual cues []. These neurophysiological effects translate into clinically relevant outcomes, as demonstrated in randomized controlled trials in dysphagic stroke patients, where repeated tDCS enhanced functional recovery compared to sham stimulation []. Meta-analyses support an overall beneficial effect of tDCS on swallowing function but consistently report substantial heterogeneity in stimulation protocols and effect sizes, underscoring the need for more individualized and mechanistically informed approaches [, ].

A key limitation of conventional tDCS in this context is its reliance on standard bipolar montages, which may be suboptimal for modulating distributed sensorimotor networks. Bipolar stimulation produces relatively diffuse electric fields, potentially leading to co-stimulation of non-target regions and reduced focality at the intended cortical site []. Moreover, conventional approaches typically neglect interindividual variability in anatomy, functional organization, and tissue conductivities, all of which critically shape the spatial distribution and orientation of induced electric fields [–]. These limitations are particularly relevant for complex functions such as swallowing, where cortical representations are distributed, dynamically organized, and subject to substantial inter- and intra-individual variability. More broadly, a central unresolved challenge in neurotherapeutics is how to define stimulation “dose” at the level of brain networks rather than in terms of applied current intensity alone. Emerging evidence suggests that neuromodulatory effects depend on interactions among electric field properties, target orientation, and the ongoing functional state of the network [–], , –]. However, current clinical protocols rarely systematically incorporate these factors, which may contribute to treatment effect variability and limited reproducibility.

To address these limitations, multichannel tDCS (mc-tDCS) approaches have been developed that enable individualized, model-based optimization of current distribution. Distributed constrained maximum intensity (D-CMI) optimization allows the generation of subject-specific electrode configurations that maximize electric field intensity along a predefined target orientation while distributing currents across multiple electrodes to improve tolerability and focality []. Proof-of-principle work has demonstrated that this approach can outperform conventional bipolar stimulation in modulating cortical targets, resulting in enhanced source-level effects []. Building on these advances, the present proof-of-concept study investigated whether a neuroengineering-guided approach integrating MEG-based target localization, subject-specific finite-element head modeling, and D-CMI optimized multichannel stimulation can modulate the cortical swallowing network. We hypothesized that individualized mc-tDCS would induce measurable frequency-specific changes in swallowing-related cortical activity and tested whether these changes showed a Dose × Task × Time interaction. Because the two tasks differed in several features, we interpreted any task-specific pattern at the experimental task-condition level rather than as a single isolated physiological state.

We investigated the effects of individually optimized multichannel tDCS (mc-tDCS) at different stimulation intensities on cortical swallowing activity in healthy adults in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover design. Eight participants (mean age: 29.6 ± 7.9 years; 4 females) were included. None had a history of neurological, psychiatric, or otolaryngological disorders or were taking medication affecting the central nervous system. The local ethics committee approved the study protocol, and all participants provided written informed consent.

The study was divided into two parts: targeting and stimulation (see Fig.  for workflow). First, we recorded a 15-minute uncued voluntary swallowing MEG measurement in each participant. Using MEG source analysis, we reconstructed an individual right-hemispheric cortical stimulation target within the broader swallowing network. The temporal analysis window encompassed the swallowing event around peak submental EMG activity and did not permit phase-specific attribution. After reconstructing this target individually for each subject, we optimized a personalized mc-tDCS montage using each subject’s segmented anatomical MRI, digitized head shape, and a coregistered electrode cap, along with the previously established D-CMI algorithm.

In the stimulation phase, participants completed three randomized, sham-controlled crossover sessions: individually optimized anodal mc-tDCS at 1.5 mA, anodal mc-tDCS at 4 mA, and sham stimulation, with observed inter-session intervals of 8–77 days (median 35 days). Swallowing-associated cortical network activity was recorded with MEG before and after mc-tDCS during uncued voluntary swallowing and a visually cued challenged task requiring swallowing within a 150-ms target interval []. The experimental factor Task therefore contrasted two task conditions that differed simultaneously in external cueing, temporal precision, performance monitoring, immediate feedback, and attentional demand; it was not intended to isolate any one of these dimensions. The after-effects for each tDCS condition were statistically analyzed and compared. The study was designed as a mechanistic proof-of-concept investigation.

We used a 275-channel MEG system (Omega 275, CTF Systems Inc.) to identify cortical activity during swallowing. Participants were positioned upright, facing a screen approximately 80 cm in front of them, and instructed to keep their eyes open during the MEG session. To facilitate swallowing, still water was continuously infused at a slow rate of 8–12 ml/minute into the mouth via a plastic tube. Magnetic-field data were acquired at 600 Hz and online low-pass filtered at 150 Hz.

Submental sEMG was recorded synchronously at 600 Hz using a bipolar pair of Ag/AgCl skin electrodes, with one electrode over the left and one over the right submental muscle group, and a separate ground electrode over the clavicle. Signals were recorded using a DSQ 2017E bipolar EOG/EMG amplifier (CTF Systems Inc., Canada; nominal gain 1) and high-pass filtered at 0.1 Hz. For the exploratory peripheral endpoints, manually identified swallow onset and offset defined the interval used to calculate swallow duration, peak-to-peak amplitude, and RMS amplitude. Amplitudes were baseline-corrected using the 1-s interval preceding swallow onset and converted to microvolts. Events that could not be reliably delineated because of substantial artifacts were excluded during visual review. No additional filtering, automated artifact rejection, rectification, smoothing, or normalization was applied. Because these non-normalized amplitudes depend on electrode placement and individual tissue properties, they were interpreted only as exploratory within-subject measures. Stimulus and sEMG events were synchronized with the MEG acquisition [, –].

For MEG target reconstruction, we recorded voluntary uncued swallowing for 15 min. To assess intervention effects, the uncued task was repeated and followed by a previously developed challenged swallowing task requiring precisely timed swallow initiation in response to visual cues (10 min; approximately 40 trials) [, ]. The task order was fixed across visits and was not counterbalanced. After stimulation, uncued swallowing therefore occupied approximately 5–20 min and challenged swallowing approximately 20–30 min after the end of mc-tDCS. A trial, including one with multiple detected swallow onsets, was classified as on time if the first identifiable onset occurred within the 150-ms target interval. Trials without an identifiable swallow onset were treated as missing. Participants received immediate feedback indicating “too early,” “on time,” or “too late.” Visual stimuli and feedback were delivered using Presentation software (NeuroBehavioral Systems, Inc., USA).

MEG data were analyzed using an established pipeline designed for our swallowing tasks and implemented in custom MATLAB scripts within the FieldTrip toolbox (http://www.ru.nl/fcdonders/fieldtrip) [, –]. This process included frequency filtering across the theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), low gamma (30–60 Hz), and high gamma (60–80 Hz) bands. For individualized targeting, the 15-minute uncued swallowing recording was reconstructed separately with an LCMV beamformer on a 3-mm grid. The resulting functional source estimate, together with the participant’s individual anatomical MRI, was transferred to the modeling team for FEM/D-CMI montage optimization. This targeting-specific 3-mm reconstruction was independent of the regular pre/post MEG analyses reported here, which were computed on a 10-mm source grid. For the regular analyses, an LCMV beamformer was applied to estimate swallow-related event-related desynchronization (ERD) []. ERD was calculated in a time window of − 0.4 to + 0.6 s relative to peak sEMG swallowing activity, using a 1-s post-swallow baseline. The targeting reconstruction informed individualized montage optimization; separately, the 10-mm volumetric source maps were used for the group-level statistical analyses. The primary outcome measure was the change in source-level swallowing-related ERD within the predefined cortical swallowing network. Modulation effects were examined across stimulation intensities and task states. Frequency-band–specific and spatially resolved effects were treated as exploratory [, –].

For pre–post comparisons of intervention effects, each subject’s volumetric source estimates were spatially normalized to a template MNI brain (T1, Montreal Neurological Institute, Canada) using SPM8 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm). Grand averages of normalized and realigned source activation maps were calculated for all time points, conditions, and frequency bands. The region of interest (ROI) comprised cortical regions known to be involved in swallowing (Supplementary Table ) [, , ]. Cluster-based nonparametric randomization implemented in FieldTrip was used to identify source locations that were modulated in separate within-condition pre–post comparisons (p < 0.05), controlling for multiple spatial comparisons within the predefined ROI []. To test the hypothesized interaction directly, ROI-mean ERD values were entered into a repeated-measures model with factors Dose (1.5 mA, 4.0 mA, sham), Task (challenged, uncued), and Time (pre, post), separately for theta, alpha, beta, low-gamma, and high-gamma bands. The primary term was Dose × Task × Time; Greenhouse–Geisser-adjusted p values were used when available and Holm correction was applied across the five bands. The separate cluster-based pre–post findings were treated as exploratory descriptive results and not as formal evidence of state- or intensity-dependence. As an exploratory crossover sensitivity check, the ROI-mean pre–post change in the three reported frequency-band/task combinations was modeled with participant, current dose, and session period. The joint Period tests were Holm-adjusted across these three checks.

Structural MRI data acquired from a MAGNETOM Prisma 3.0 T Scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) provided realistic head models for the mc-tDCS optimization procedure [, ]. In brief, gadolinium markers were placed at the nasion, left, and right external auditory canal openings (ear canal fiducials) for landmark-based co-registration purposes. Imaging included T1-weighted Imaging: High-resolution (1 mm³) anatomical scans using a fast gradient-echo sequence for scalp, gray, and white matter segmentation; T2-weighted Imaging: Segmentation of the compact and spongy layers of the skull. Diffusion-weighted Imaging: Acquiring for white matter anisotropy modeling with diffusion sensitivity values (b = 0 and 1000 s/mm²) in 20 directions, uniformly distributed on a sphere.

To compute individually optimized mc-tDCS montages for stimulation of the cortical swallowing target, dipole location and orientation at the individual right-hemispheric activation peak within the swallowing network were taken from the MEG source estimates. Skull-conductivity-calibrated realistic head models were generated from each participant’s MRI, as previously published [, ]. In brief, a compartment head model for each subject, representing the tissues scalp, skull compacta, skull spongiosa, cerebrospinal fluid, gray matter, and white matter, was generated. Geometry-adapted hexahedral finite element method (FEM) modeling [] of the segmented head model was carried out using SimBio-VGRID.1 (a generic environment for bio-numerical simulations www.simbio.de), and different tissue conductivities were modelled.

The 39 possible electrode positions of the mc-tDCS cap (Starstim-8 cap, Neuroelectrics, Barcelona, Spain) corresponding to the international 10/20 EEG system were digitized with each individual’s headshape and anatomical landmarks (nasion, left, and right external auditory canal openings, as was coregistered during MRI and MEG) using a Polhemus device (FASTRAK, Polhemus Incorporated, Colchester, VT). For each subject, the locations of the digitized sensors were registered on the head model and MEG source estimate using landmark-based co-registration.

Using Helmholtz reciprocity, the individualized FEM forward models were also used for D-CMI mc-tDCS optimization as described by Wagner et al. [] and Khan et al. [] to maximize field intensity along the target-orientation, the so-called target directionality. This approach was chosen to enable stimulation with high target directionality while adhering to established safety constraints. The optimization ensured:

High directionality at the target site.High parallelity of the electric field to the target dipole orientation.Reduction of side effects and skin-level sensations by current distribution over multiple stimulation electrodes.

High directionality at the target site.

High parallelity of the electric field to the target dipole orientation.

Reduction of side effects and skin-level sensations by current distribution over multiple stimulation electrodes.

Established safety constraints were imposed on the model: individual electrode current < 2 mA and total injected current ≤ 4 mA. Optimization was implemented using the CVX toolbox [] (CVX, MATLAB) and following Khan et al. [], we used regularization to add convexity to the optimization term and to distribute the currents across multiple electrodes. The output of the optimization algorithm for each individual included the recommended electrode montage, the number and positions of the cathodal and anodal electrodes on the EEG cap, and the stimulation intensity (mA) for each active electrode.

To deliver stimulation, we used a Starstim-8 tDCS system (Neuroelectrics, Barcelona, Spain) with Ag/AgCl gel electrodes (Starstim NG Pistim). Each participant underwent three stimulation sessions in a randomized order. Before the first stimulation session, the investigator delivering mc-tDCS used MATLAB to generate the complete randomized sequence of the three conditions for each participant and knew the assigned condition before each session. Participants and the MEG technician conducting the recordings were not informed of the assignment. MEG with voluntary swallowing and a challenged swallowing task was performed before the interventions and after each intervention. Post-stimulation MEG recordings started 5 min after mc-tDCS to allow some time for repositioning in the MEG chamber. Stimulation conditions included: Low-Intensity anodal mc-tDCS (1.5 mA) and High-Intensity anodal mc-tDCS (4.0 mA) with the individually optimized electrode montages and stimulation parameters, and sham mc-tDCS with the same electrode montage as used in the low intensity condition. The current was gradually increased over 30 s, held at the target stimulation intensity for 9 min, and then gradually decreased. In the sham condition, the current was ramped up and down for 30 s to mimic a sensory effect (tingling) at the beginning of stimulation. Still, no current was sustained for the remaining 9 min []. We applied 1.5 mA based on prior evidence of physiological effects in swallowing-related networks, and 4.0 mA to explore intensity-dependent modulation within the device’s safety limits [, , , ]. During each mc-tDCS session, participants were instructed to suck on a lemon-flavored lollipop to activate sensory afferents and increase spontaneous swallowing rates. This concurrent sensory activation is intended to enhance the efficacy of tDCS by explicitly engaging the targeted swallowing network.

After completion of each post-stimulation MEG recording, participants selected one of three response options – high-intensity, low-intensity, or sham – to indicate which stimulation condition they believed they had received; no unsure or don’t-know option was available. Blinding success was summarized using the percentage of correct identifications for each applied condition and agreement between perceived and applied conditions using Cohen’s κ.

Behavioral data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics 28.0 (IBM Corp., USA). Descriptive statistics were used to characterize participants. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs with factors intervention type and time were used to ensure comparability of MEG task performance (head movement, swallow count) and to evaluate exploratory changes in submental EMG measures and timing accuracy (percentage of trials classified as ‘on time’) during the challenged task. The hit rate was considered a measure of performance on the experimental timing task, not a validated measure of swallowing function. Mauchly’s test was used to determine the sphericity assumption, and the Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied in case of violation. If ANOVA identified significant main effects or interactions, post-hoc contrasts were constructed and compared across conditions using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Effect sizes for the challenged-task hit-rate model were quantified as partial eta squared (ηp²) for Dose, Time, and Dose × Time.

All participants completed all three stimulation sessions without dropouts. Stimulation was well tolerated, and no adverse events were reported during or after any of the mc-tDCS interventions. MEG task performance data are summarized in Table . Head movement and the number of analyzed swallowing events remained stable across baseline and post-intervention measurements, with no significant differences between conditions (all ANOVAs, p > 0.05), confirming comparable measurement conditions. For challenged-task hit rate, the repeated-measures analysis showed a significant main effect of Time (F(1,7) = 47.67, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.872). The Dose main effect did not reach significance after Greenhouse–Geisser correction (F(2,14) = 3.57, p = 0.061, ηp² = 0.338), and the Dose × Time interaction was not significant (F(2,14) = 1.23, p = 0.319, ηp² = 0.150). These results support a general improvement across repeated task assessments but not a confirmed dose-specific behavioral effect. Submental EMG measures did not change during uncued swallowing. During challenged swallowing, a significant intervention type × time interaction was observed for EMG peak-to-peak amplitude. Post-hoc comparisons indicated increased peak-to-peak amplitude following low-intensity mc-tDCS compared to sham, which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (p = 0.036). RMS amplitude showed a similar pattern, reaching trend-level significance after correction. These behavioral and peripheral physiological measures primarily served as feasibility and control indices and were not considered as primary outcome measures of the study. No stimulation-related discomfort beyond transient tingling was reported.

Blinding assessment revealed fair agreement between perceived and applied stimulation conditions (Cohen’s κ = 0.375, p = 0.009). Correct identification was highest for high-intensity mc-tDCS (75%); low-intensity mc-tDCS and sham were each correctly identified in 50% of sessions.

Uncued swallowing elicited the expected activation pattern of the cortical swallowing network, with prominent ERD in pericentral sensorimotor regions. This activity was most pronounced in the beta frequency range, which was therefore selected for individual target definition in the right hemisphere. Figure  illustrates the swallowing-related beta-band ERD for each participant, along with the corresponding target dipole derived from MEG source reconstruction and the individually D-CMI-optimized multichannel tDCS electrode montage.

At baseline, swallowing elicited ERD across the theta to high-gamma frequency bands, with alpha- and beta-band oscillatory changes most pronounced across participants. Cortical activation was localized bilaterally in pericentral cortex, encompassing primary and secondary sensorimotor areas, with predominantly right-hemispheric involvement. In grand averages of baseline measurements, absolute peak ERD was most frequently observed in the beta band and was primarily localized in Brodmann areas 4 and 6 in the right hemisphere (Supplementary Table ).

No Dose × Task × Time interaction survived Holm correction across the five frequency bands: theta, F(2,14) = 0.51, Greenhouse–Geisser-adjusted p = 0.527, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000; alpha, F(2,14) = 0.72, p = 0.431, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000; beta, F(2,14) = 3.92, p = 0.055, Holm-adjusted p = 0.274; low gamma, F(2,14) = 0.56, p = 0.499, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000; and high gamma, F(2,14) = 0.21, p = 0.677, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000. The within-condition analyses below therefore characterize the observed responses but cannot by themselves establish differential effects between doses or tasks.

In an exploratory sensitivity analysis of the three band–task combinations with reported within-condition responses, the participant- and dose-adjusted period term was not significant for challenged alpha [F(2,12) = 0.51, Holm-adjusted p = 0.615], challenged beta [F(2,12) = 1.46, p = 0.545], or uncued low gamma [F(2,12) = 1.97, p = 0.545].

In the separate within-condition analysis of the challenged swallowing task, low-intensity mc-tDCS was associated with a pre–post reduction in source-level ERD in the alpha band (p = 0.025) and beta band (p = 0.048). High-intensity mc-tDCS did not show significant pre–post changes in these bands (all p > 0.05). No significant pre–post ERD changes were observed in the gamma or theta bands for either active intensity or sham.

In the separate within-condition analysis of uncued swallowing, high-intensity mc-tDCS was associated with a pre–post change in low-gamma ERD (p < 0.001). Low-intensity mc-tDCS did not show significant pre–post ERD changes in any frequency band.

The spatial distribution of the pre–post changes was examined using cluster-based nonparametric statistics within the predefined swallowing-network ROI. During challenged swallowing, clusters associated with the low-intensity pre–post comparison were located primarily within bilateral sensorimotor and premotor cortical regions, including precentral and postcentral gyri and medial frontal areas; additional clusters were observed in parietal regions encompassed by the ROI. During uncued swallowing, clusters associated with the high-intensity pre–post comparison were located predominantly within sensorimotor cortical areas, with additional frontal and parietal involvement. Grand averages and cluster maps are presented in Fig.  and Supplementary Figures –. These maps show that the observed within-condition responses were spatially expressed within the predefined swallowing network.

This proof-of-concept study implemented a neuroengineering-guided approach integrating MEG-based target localization, subject-specific MRI-based finite-element modeling, and D-CMI-optimized multichannel stimulation. The hypothesized Dose × Task × Time interaction was not significant after Holm correction. Exploratory within-condition analyses identified alpha- and beta-band pre–post differences during challenged swallowing after 1.5-mA stimulation and a low-gamma difference during uncued swallowing after 4.0-mA stimulation. These observations describe changes within individual conditions; they do not establish stimulation-specific effects or differential responses across doses and tasks. The integrated workflow provides a methodological basis for further controlled investigation.

The separate within-condition patterns warrant cautious interpretation in relation to the processes engaged by each task. Alpha- and beta-band oscillatory activity within the swallowing network has previously been associated with sensorimotor integration, cortical resource allocation, and task-dependent control processes [, , , –]. Challenged swallowing additionally involved visual cue processing, precise timing, performance monitoring, and immediate feedback. These associations provide physiological context but do not establish which processes underlie the present exploratory pre–post differences. Although the cluster analyses controlled for multiple spatial comparisons within the predefined ROI [], the separate within-condition comparisons do not establish stimulation-specific modulation or differential responses across doses and tasks. Because uncued swallowing always preceded challenged swallowing, task condition was also confounded with elapsed post-stimulation time and measurement order. Order and timing were identical across stimulation conditions, and pharyngeal corticobulbar after-effects have been reported for up to 60 min after a different tDCS protocol []; however, this does not resolve the task–time confounding in the present study. Whether individualized mc-tDCS interacts with ongoing network activity, as suggested by previous work in other settings [], remains a question for future studies with counterbalanced task order and independently manipulated task components.

An important methodological aspect of the present study is the use of individualized, optimized multichannel stimulation based on a D-CMI approach [, , ]. Although swallowing is mediated by a distributed cortical network [–], targeting was deliberately based on a focal cortical site defined by its individual location and dominant dipole orientation derived from MEG source reconstruction. A key advantage of the D-CMI framework is its ability to enable high directional electric field strength along the target orientation while respecting safety and tolerability constraints [, ]. In contrast to maximum-intensity (MI) optimization, which can achieve maximal directionality at the cost of increased peripheral stimulation [, ], D-CMI incorporates regularization and side constraints that distribute current across multiple electrodes, thereby enabling near-maximal effective directionality with reduced skin sensations [, ]. The present study implemented this individualized targeting strategy for a focal cortical site within the distributed swallowing network. Future work should systematically compare optimization strategies along the intensity–focality continuum to delineate their physiological and practical trade-offs [].

Previous studies indicate that the physiological effects of tDCS do not necessarily increase monotonically with applied current intensity [, , –, , ]. Proposed mechanisms include homeostatic regulation, recruitment of inhibitory processes, and intensity-dependent changes in neuronal polarization; electric-field distribution, sensory effects, and expectancy may also influence responses. The present study did not establish differential effects across doses and tasks and therefore cannot determine whether these mechanisms contributed to the observed within-condition pre–post differences. The findings should consequently not be interpreted as evidence for a nonlinear dose–response or greater efficacy of 1.5-mA stimulation. Further dose-ranging studies incorporating measures of target engagement, sensation, and expectancy are needed to distinguish these possibilities.

The two task conditions provide a controlled experimental contrast but not a selective manipulation of a single network-state dimension. In addition, high-intensity stimulation was correctly identified in 75% of sessions. Cutaneous sensations, expectancy, attention, or arousal may therefore have influenced post-stimulation MEG activity. In particular, attentional interference during the more demanding challenged task or non-specific arousal during uncued swallowing are plausible alternative interpretations of the low-gamma pattern. However, the present data provide no direct evidence that these factors account for the observed cortical changes. Because trial-wise sensation and expectancy measures were not available for covariate analysis, non-specific and neuromodulatory contributions cannot be separated conclusively. Future studies should use improved active controls, collect graded sensation and expectancy ratings, and prespecify analyses that incorporate these variables.

Cortical pre–post changes were observed without a confirmed dose-specific change in behavioral task performance. Challenged-task hit rate improved over time across conditions, with a large Time effect (ηp² = 0.872), whereas the Dose effect and Dose × Time interaction were not significant. This pattern is compatible with repeated-task practice or familiarization and does not provide evidence of a stimulation-specific behavioral benefit. Whether the exploratory cortical pre–post differences have functional relevance remains unresolved. The challenged-task hit rate indexes performance on a laboratory timing task and is not a validated clinical measure of swallowing function. The submental EMG amplitude finding should be interpreted as exploratory. Future patient studies should combine neurophysiological target-engagement measures with clinically meaningful endpoints such as instrumental swallowing-safety and efficiency measures, validated dysphagia scales, nutritional or respiratory outcomes, and patient-reported function.

Although the present study was conducted in healthy participants and was not designed to assess clinical efficacy, the individualized workflow may have important implications for dysphagia rehabilitation. Post-stroke dysphagia is increasingly understood as a network disorder characterized by lesion-induced disruption and adaptive reorganization of cortical swallowing control [, , , , ]. Recovery depends on the recruitment and reweighting of residual network components, with substantial interindividual variability related to lesion location, structural connectivity, and compensatory mechanisms [–]. This variability may partly explain the heterogeneous results reported in clinical tDCS studies and meta-analyses [, , , ]. Individualized multichannel stimulation offers a potential strategy to address this variability by enabling targeted modulation of patient-specific network configurations. The present MEG/FEM/D-CMI workflow provides an experimental platform for examining how individualized targeting, electric-field orientation, stimulation intensity, and ongoing network activity jointly shape neurophysiological responses.

A potential translational pathway would involve several stages. Researchers could first examine target engagement and response reliability in a larger healthy cohort with stronger blinding and appropriate active comparators, including conventional bipolar or non-individualized multichannel stimulation. If target engagement proves reproducible, subsequent patient studies could assess feasibility, tolerability, and clinical effectiveness. Given the resource requirements of the full MEG/FEM/D-CMI pipeline, future work could additionally investigate whether targets derived from structural MRI combined with atlas-based priors or from task fMRI provide a sufficiently close approximation to MEG-informed targeting for broader clinical use. Prospective comparison of simplified and fully individualized workflows would be important before clinical implementation.

Several limitations should be considered. First, the sample size was small and limited to healthy young adults, restricting generalizability, precision, and power to detect interactions. Second, only acute after-effects of a single stimulation session were assessed, and it remains unclear whether repeated individualized stimulation induces cumulative or long-lasting plastic changes. Third, no conventional bipolar or non-individualized comparator was included, so effects cannot be attributed specifically to individualized targeting. Fourth, blinding was only partially preserved at 4.0 mA, and sensation, expectancy, attention, and arousal were not quantified for statistical adjustment []. Fifth, the task contrast combined cueing, timing, feedback, attentional, and motor differences and cannot isolate a single physiological state. The fixed task order confounded task condition with elapsed post-stimulation time and measurement order. No evidence of a period effect was detected in the targeted sensitivity analysis; given the sample size, residual period or carryover effects cannot be ruled out. Sixth, behavioral measures were exploratory and did not include validated clinical swallowing outcomes. Finally, the resource-intensive MEG/FEM/D-CMI pipeline and focus on a single cortical target limit immediate clinical scalability. These constraints reinforce the hypothesis-generating nature of the descriptive pre–post findings.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating functional neuroimaging, computational head modeling, and optimized electric-field targeting and reports exploratory frequency-specific pre–post differences within the cortical swallowing network. The formal interaction analysis did not confirm differential effects across doses and tasks; the within-condition findings therefore remain hypothesis-generating and do not establish stimulation-specific modulation. These findings support targeted replication in larger cohorts with strengthened blinding, active comparator conditions, behavioral effect estimates, and clinically meaningful outcomes.

neuroscience.title: From Silver Stains to Deep Learning: Neurohistological Analysis and Digital Mapping of the Brain of Domestic and Laboratory Animals in Veterinary Neuroscience
neuroscience.abstract: For over a century, scientists have studied the brain by cutting it into thin slices, staining them, and examining them under the microscope. These methods were first developed and refined mainly on human, mouse, and rat brains. Today, computers and artificial intelligence can analyze thousands of microscope images automatically, measure brain cells with greater precision, and combine this information with brain scans and genetic data into detailed digital maps. However, the brains of domestic animals, such as dogs, cats, horses, cattle, pigs, and sheep, differ markedly in size, shape, and internal organization, and tools designed for mice or humans often perform poorly on them. In this review, we trace how brain tissue analysis has evolved, from early staining techniques to modern computer-based methods, and identify what is still missing for domestic animals: shared image collections, dedicated brain atlases, and methods able to handle their diversity.
neuroscience.text:
Histological analysis has been central to neuroanatomy since the first microscopic observations of neural tissue by Hooke, Malpighi, and van Leeuwenhoek [,,]. In the nineteenth century, selective staining methods, above all Golgi’s reazione nera as used by Ramón y Cajal, led to the formulation of the neuron doctrine [,,].

Since then, the histological analysis of the brain has moved from descriptive microscopy to quantitative and increasingly automated analysis. Stereology made it possible to estimate three-dimensional parameters without bias from two-dimensional brain sections [,]. Digital microscopy turned brain sections into computable images [], and machine learning and deep learning now extract relevant features directly from these images [,]. More recently, three-dimensional imaging and spatial transcriptomics have begun to combine histology with magnetic resonance imaging, synchrotron tomography, and gene expression data in multimodal brain maps [,].

However, these advances have been developed and validated almost exclusively on human, mouse, and rat brains [,,].

Although mammalian brains share a common basic organization, humans, laboratory mice and rats, and domestic animals differ markedly in brain size, cortical architecture, regional proportions, and functional specialization [,]. The human brain has a large, highly folded neocortex with extensive association areas. Mice and rats have relatively small, largely lissencephalic brains, with prominent olfactory structures and specialized sensory regions, including the whisker-related barrel cortex in the primary somatosensory cortex []. Domestic mammals exhibit substantial variation in brain size, cortical folding, and sensory specialization. In the primary visual cortex of ungulates, the prominence and definition of layer IV vary across species and may differ from the more clearly delineated granular layer found in primates []. The organization and functional contribution of corticospinal pathways also differ among mammalian species, reflecting interspecific variation in descending motor control [].

Consequently, findings obtained in humans, mice, or rats cannot be applied directly to veterinary species. Differences in brain size, cellular organization, and regional anatomy can affect the interpretation of histological findings, the use of immunohistochemical markers, and the performance of image-analysis algorithms trained on human, mouse, or rat data. Likewise, anatomical landmarks and registration procedures developed for one species may not identify the corresponding structures in another.

In addition, brain tissue from many veterinary species is scarce and of heterogeneous origin [], and standardized brain atlases, annotated datasets, and analytical pipelines are lacking []. Methods developed in humans, mice, and rats therefore need to be adapted and validated before they can be used in veterinary neuroscience. At the same time, the anatomical diversity of these brains offers a natural test of whether methods developed in a few reference species apply to mammals in general [].

These gaps are also clinically relevant, because many common neurological diseases of domestic animals are diagnosed and characterized on the basis of brain lesions [,]. In dogs and cats, these include meningoencephalitis of unknown origin, intracranial tumors, cerebrovascular disease, and age-related changes such as canine cognitive dysfunction [,,,,]. In other domestic animals, infectious, metabolic, nutritional, and toxic encephalopathies also require clinical signs to be interpreted together with neuroanatomical and neuropathological findings [,]. In all these conditions, histology and immunohistochemistry of the brain remain essential to characterize lesions and to interpret MRI findings (). Comparative brain mapping is clinically useful for three reasons. First, species-specific brain atlases are needed to localize lesions on MRI and histological sections and to distinguish them from normal variation, such as age-related brain atrophy, which differs among dogs with different skull conformations (). Second, comparison with human, mouse, and rat brains shows which diagnostic markers, imaging criteria, and analytical tools can be transferred to domestic animals and which require species-specific validation. Third, several spontaneous brain diseases of domestic animals, such as canine gliomas and canine cognitive dysfunction, resemble human disorders, so comparative brain mapping can support both veterinary diagnosis and translational research within a One Health perspective [,].

Several reviews have described the evolution of methods for studying the human brain, including neuromorphometry [], tract tracing [], architectonic mapping from Brodmann to modern multimodal approaches [,], human brain atlases [], and deep learning in medical image analysis [,]. These reviews, however, focus on the human brain or on single methods, and, to our knowledge, none has examined the evolution of neurohistological analysis of the brain, from classical to computational methods, from the perspective of species of veterinary interest. We focus on the brain because most of the methods discussed here, such as cytoarchitectonic analysis, stereotaxic and digital atlases, and multimodal brain mapping, were developed for the brain, and because differences between species, particularly in cortical organization and folding, are most marked there. In addition, many common neurological diseases of domestic animals that require histological characterization mainly affect the brain. The spinal cord and peripheral nervous system, although clinically important, have distinct anatomical features, methods, and diagnostic problems and deserve separate treatment.

The aims of this review are: (i) to describe how neurohistological methods for studying the brain have evolved, from classical staining to quantitative, computational, and multimodal approaches, and how they have been applied to species of veterinary interest; (ii) to identify the main factors that limit the use of methods developed in humans, mice, and rats in these species; and (iii) to outline the resources needed for future research, such as species-specific brain atlases, shared datasets, and validated analytical methods. We also emphasize that anatomical differences between species reflect real biological variation and should be preserved and studied, rather than removed during data analysis.

This narrative review addresses the following research question: How have neurohistological methods for studying the brain evolved in species of veterinary interest, and what are the current challenges and opportunities in applying quantitative, machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal approaches to the brains of species of veterinary interest?

In this review, the term computational brain mapping refers to the creation of digital maps of the brain of an individual animal or of a species. These maps are built from anatomical data, such as histological sections, magnetic resonance images, or molecular data, and each brain structure is assigned a defined position within a common three-dimensional coordinate system. This allows brain structures to be measured quantitatively and compared across individuals and species [,,].

For the purposes of this review, species of veterinary interest are the domestic animals for which brain studies were retrieved, namely the dog (Canis lupus familiaris), cat (Felis catus), horse (Equus caballus), cattle (Bos taurus), pig (Sus scrofa domesticus), sheep (Ovis aries), goat (Capra hircus), and llama (Lama glama). Studies on humans, non-human primates (Macaca mulatta, Pan troglodytes), and common laboratory animals, namely mice (Mus musculus), rats (Rattus norvegicus), Syrian hamsters (Mesocricetus auratus), and rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus), were included only when they introduced a brain research method later applied to domestic animals or served as a direct comparator []. Aquatic, exotic, and wild species were not included. The species included in each study are listed in . The review was restricted to the brain; studies focusing on the spinal cord or peripheral nervous system were not included.

The literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection. Google Scholar was used additionally, in a targeted and non-systematic way, to identify historical works, monographs, and book chapters not indexed in bibliographic databases; because these searches were not systematic, the number of Google Scholar results was not recorded. Database searches covered publications from January 1990 to June 2026, and the last search was performed on 15 June 2026. The search strategy combined three groups of terms with the Boolean operator AND: (i) terms related to the brain and to neurohistological and morphometric analysis (e.g., brain, cerebral cortex, cytoarchitecture, Nissl, Golgi, immunohistochemistry, stereology, morphometry); (ii) terms related to digital and computational methods and brain mapping (e.g., digital histology, whole-slide imaging, image analysis, machine learning, deep learning, segmentation, brain atlas, magnetic resonance imaging); and (iii) terms related to species of veterinary interest (e.g., dog, cat, horse, cattle, sheep, goat, pig). Within each group, synonyms were combined with the operator OR. The complete search strings used for each database are reported in . Peer-reviewed articles, books, and book chapters were eligible if they were published in English or had an English abstract (with the exception of foundational historical works; see below), and if they concerned the brain and addressed one of the following: neurohistological techniques applied to brain tissue; stereology or morphometry of the brain; computer-assisted or digital histology of brain sections; machine learning or deep learning applied to histological or neuroimaging data of the brain; or brain atlas development or multimodal brain mapping.

In each case, the work had to concern the brain of species of veterinary interest within a comparative framework, or describe a brain research method subsequently applied to these species. Primary research articles, reviews, and methodological papers were all considered. As the only exception to the language criterion, and given the historical scope of the review, foundational contributions (e.g., original descriptions of neurohistological staining methods) were included regardless of publication date and language ().

Studies were excluded if they concerned exclusively humans or laboratory mice and rats and lacked methodological or comparative relevance to the brains of species of veterinary interest. Conference abstracts and the grey literature were also excluded, with the exception of publicly accessible online brain repositories, namely the Comparative Mammalian Brain Collection (brainmuseum.org), BrainMaps.org, the Scalable Brain Atlas, the Digital Brain Bank, and braincatalogue.org, which were consulted directly and are described in  and .

Three authors (A.P., J.-M.G., and T.G.) independently screened the records retrieved from the database searches against the eligibility criteria described in , first by title and abstract and, when necessary, by full text. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and the final selection was agreed upon by consensus among the three authors. Backward citation tracking was performed by screening the reference lists of the included articles and of previous reviews; forward citation tracking was not performed systematically. As this is a narrative rather than a systematic review, the number of records retrieved, screened, and excluded at each stage of the selection process was not systematically recorded.

Because abstract and keyword indexing in bibliographic databases is incomplete for publications prior to 1990, historical sources could not be reliably retrieved through database searches. Foundational works published before this date were therefore identified through Google Scholar, reference monographs, and the reference lists of the included studies, and were included when they introduced a technique, concept, or reference atlas subsequently adopted in brain research (e.g., the original descriptions of the Golgi, Nissl, and myelin staining methods), irrespective of language or study design.

This review has several limitations.

First, its broad temporal and taxonomic scope required selective coverage; relevant contributions published in languages other than English, or available only as the grey literature, may not have been fully captured despite the search and selection strategy described in  and .

Second, the heterogeneity of species, study designs, and brain research methods precluded formal quantitative synthesis, so the integration of evidence necessarily involves an element of interpretive judgment.

Third, given the rapid pace of development in machine learning and computational neuroanatomy, some very recent contributions may not be represented.

Fourth, the scarcity of openly accessible brain datasets from species of veterinary interest () prevented systematic benchmarking of methods across species, and the resulting methodological comparisons are therefore necessarily qualitative.

Fifth, as this is a narrative review, the number of records retrieved and screened at each stage of the selection process was not systematically recorded (), which limits the reproducibility of the selection.

Finally, annotation biases and the anthropocentric assumptions embedded in many existing analytical frameworks may influence the interpretation of brain data from species of veterinary interest in ways that are difficult to fully account for within the current evidence base; addressing this issue in depth lies beyond the scope of the present review, whose aim is to describe the current status of brain research in species of veterinary interest.

An early precursor of systematic comparative neuroanatomy was Félix Vicq d’Azyr, whose standardized sectioning, species comparisons, and iconography of cerebral structures anticipated principles of quantitative neuroanatomy []. Selective staining techniques then made it possible to visualize specific components of neural tissue ( and ). Golgi’s reazione nera, which impregnates a small, apparently random subset of neurons in their entirety (as shown in the barrel cortex of the mouse, Mus musculus) [], provided unprecedented insight into neuronal morphology and contributed to the neuron doctrine formulated by Ramón y Cajal on the nervous system of humans and other vertebrates [,,,].

Nissl staining, which labels the rough endoplasmic reticulum of neurons and the nuclei of glial and endothelial cells, became the basis for the study of cortical lamination, cell density, and cytoarchitecture, and for comparative cortical parcellation, established by Brodmann in the human brain and in many other mammalian species [,].

Myelin stains, developed by Weigert on human brain tissue and later combined with a Nissl counterstain by Klüver and Barrera in the rhesus monkey (Macaca mulatta) and humans, and silver methods such as the Bielschowsky impregnation, applied to rat and human brain tissue, revealed fiber systems, white matter architecture, and neurofibrils [,,]. Nissl and myelin preparations remain the primary substrate for automated segmentation, cytoarchitectural analysis, and atlases, including in ungulates (e.g., the horse), non-human primates, and humans [,,].

From the 1940s onward, histochemistry and immunohistochemistry added a neurochemical dimension to the same sections, allowing the identification of enzymes, neurotransmitters, and cell populations that conventional stains could not distinguish [,,,,]. Cholinesterase histochemistry, first described in rat tissues, introduced the principle of translating the enzymatic identity of cells into tissue maps, a precursor of marker-based segmentation [], and immunohistochemistry enabled the mapping of neurotransmitter systems, neuronal subpopulations, and glial phenotypes, initially mostly in the rat brain [,,,]. In veterinary species, however, antibodies developed for human, mouse, or rat tissues show variable specificity and require careful validation [] (for a review, see []).

Connectivity was first studied with the silver impregnation of degenerating axons developed by Nauta and Gygax in the rat brain [,,,]. From the 1970s, this approach was replaced by tracers actively transported along axons and injected in vivo, as in the mouse, rat, and cat [,,], and by carbocyanine dyes applicable to fixed post-mortem tissue, as in the rat spinal cord []. Tract tracing has been applied to sheep, dogs, cats, and rabbits [,,,,,], but in vivo injections are rarely justifiable in these species, which makes post-mortem methods particularly relevant for material from necropsies. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and tractography now allow the non-invasive reconstruction of putative white matter pathways, including in ex vivo brains of large animals such as the sheep, although they do not resolve individual axons or synaptic connections [,].

At the macroscopic level, white matter tracts can also be studied by anatomical dissection. In fiber dissection (Klingler’s technique []), formalin-fixed brains are usually frozen and thawed before the white matter fibers are separated by blunt dissection, revealing the course and relationships of the major tracts in three dimensions. This method has been used to describe the major white matter tracts in the horse, cat, and dog [] and in the pig [], and the association fasciculi in cattle, pigs, and rabbits []. Although its resolution is limited to macroscopic fiber bundles, dissection provides a direct anatomical reference for the interpretation of tractography.

Because histological analysis is inherently two-dimensional, three-dimensional structures were first reconstructed from serial sections, as in the albino rat, and later with registration approaches applied to rat, cat, and human brain data [,,]. Tissue-clearing methods such as CLARITY [] and iDISCO [], developed mainly on the mouse brain [] and combined with light-sheet or two-photon microscopy, now allow volumetric imaging of entire brain regions or whole small brains [,], complementing electron microscopy-based connectomics of the mouse visual cortex []. Their application to the large brains of cattle and horses requires substantial adaptation of protocols, but is expected to increase the availability of atlases and datasets for comparative analysis. The main methodological transitions are summarized in , and the principles, advantages, disadvantages, and species of application of each method in .

Summary of the main historical and methodological transitions in neurohistological analysis of the brain relevant to veterinary neuroanatomy. For each phase, the table reports the historical phase or transition, the main methodological innovation, its relevance to the study of the brain in veterinary species, the primary limitations, the section of this review in which it is discussed, and the key references. Transitions are presented in broad chronological sequence, from early optical microscopy to contemporary multimodal computational brain mapping.

Main neurohistological, tract-tracing, and imaging methods discussed in this review. For each method, the table summarizes its principle, main advantages and disadvantages, the species in which it has been applied (examples cited in the text), and the key references.

Macroscopic morphometry measures the size and shape of the whole brain and of its main subdivisions, such as the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, grey and white matter, and ventricles, on gross specimens, serial slices, or magnetic resonance images. Volumes can be estimated without bias with the Cavalieri principle, which combines systematic sampling of slices with point counting on their cut surfaces [,]. This approach has been applied, for example, to the brain of the sheep [], to the cerebral hemispheres, grey and white matter, and lateral ventricles of sheep and goats [], and to the brain, cerebral hemispheres, and cerebellum of New Zealand rabbits []. Combined with magnetic resonance imaging, it has also been used to describe age-dependent changes in albino rats [].

At the microscopic level, design-based stereology provides unbiased estimates of cell number, density, and volume through systematic random sampling [,,,]. The optical fractionator and the disector were first applied to the human and rat hippocampus [,,,]. Haug [] showed that apparent age-related neuronal loss in the human cerebral cortex often reflected tissue shrinkage due to fixation, underlining the need to account for tissue processing when comparing quantitative data. Because stereology is labour-intensive, particularly in large brains (), computational imaging methods were progressively adopted.

The digitization of microscopy was gradual, from the first computer-assisted microscopes and early digital morphology [,,] to scanning microscopes [], CCD cameras [,], and machine vision [,], and was followed by semi-automated measurement, morphometry, and statistical analysis [,]. The computer-microscope of Glaser and Van der Loos [], which reduced the reconstruction of Golgi-stained rabbit cortical neurons from hours to minutes, marked the passage from analog observation to computer-based measurement. Early algorithmic morphometry relied on handcrafted descriptors that increased objectivity but transferred poorly across staining protocols and species [,], a limitation particularly evident in comparative neuroanatomy [,,,].

Machine learning and deep learning, applied in supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and weakly supervised settings [], shifted image analysis from rule-based quantification to learning features directly from images. Convolutional neural networks, U-Net-based segmentation models, and transformer architectures are now the main tools for the segmentation and classification of histological images [,,,,,,]; their contributions and limitations, including the limited biological interpretability of learned features [,,], are summarized in , and strategies for veterinary datasets are discussed in .

Early computer-assisted histology focused on the quantification of Nissl-stained sections: the Grey Level Index, introduced by Schleicher, Zilles, and Wree in the rat brain, measures the proportion of each sampling field occupied by Nissl-stained cell bodies; it reflects cell packing density and supported the detection of cortical boundaries, but it depends on staining and image acquisition and is not an unbiased cell count []. This approach was complemented by receptor architectonics, which added a neurochemical dimension to cortical parcellation in the human and rat brain [,,].

Similar approaches have been used to estimate neuronal and neuropil parameters across cortical areas in humans, great apes, and Old World monkeys [,], but rarely in large-brained species such as the horse and artiodactyls [,]. In parallel, cell segmentation algorithms were developed for confocal images of human tissues and Caenorhabditis elegans embryos [] and for brightfield images of mouse brain sections [], including methods for resolving clustered neurons in Nissl-stained sections of the bovine cerebellum [].

Machine learning and deep learning methods were then developed specifically for cell recognition and segmentation in human pathology [,,] and in neuroanatomy, for example on macaque cortical sections and cultured mouse and rat neurons [,], shifting histological analysis toward high-throughput automated processes in human histopathology []; this approach has also been extended to disease classification from human neuroimaging data [,]. In veterinary histopathology, deep learning is also increasingly applied beyond the nervous system and across species, for example to the automated diagnosis of seven canine skin tumor types on hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images [], the histological classification of canine and feline lymphoma [], and the classification of canine testicular tumors [].

These developments are often discussed within the frameworks of computational pathology [] and computational neuroanatomy [,], and overlap with computational neuroscience, the broader field of mathematical analysis and modelling of neural systems []. In this review, we use the term computational histology for the application of digital image analysis, machine learning, and deep learning to digitized histological data. In veterinary neuroscience, the open CISCA framework for cell segmentation in whole-slide images and the CytoDArk0 dataset of annotated Nissl-stained brain sections from several mammalian species, including mouse, chimpanzee, macaque, and cattle (Bos taurus), represent early steps toward addressing annotation scarcity [].

Applied in veterinary neuroanatomy, these methods have revealed patterns of cortical organization related to motor adaptation, evolutionary divergence, and functional specialization. In the horse, the laminar organization of the motor cortex differs markedly from that of primates, limiting the transfer of canonical neocortical models to distant lineages [], while in the sheep the integration of cytoarchitectural, neurochemical, and DWI data improved the interpretation of species-specific features [,]. Comparisons across ungulates and primates, and across domestic dog lineages, have revealed structural differences potentially related to evolutionary history, ecological adaptation, or functional specialization [,].

Statistical modeling has further extended the analysis of digitized tissue, for example to sexual dimorphism in the bovine cerebellum [], hemispheric asymmetry in the area 44 homolog of the chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) [], the effect of estrogens on the aging brain of the dog [], and the motor cortex of the domestic pig and the wild boar [] (see also ).

Together, these studies show that digital histology supports both automated cell detection and quantitative statistical analysis in developmental, evolutionary, comparative, and pathological contexts, providing a foundation for addressing the challenges discussed below. The methodological evolution from classical neurohistology to computational analysis is summarized in .

Brain atlases have evolved from static reference maps to digital systems that integrate several imaging modalities and biological data. Classical atlases were based on histological sections, gross dissection, documentation of gyri and sulci, and expert cytoarchitectural parcellation, as in the cytoarchitectural map of the sheep cortex and the stereotaxic atlas of the beagle brain [,]. These atlases organized information mainly around morphological and cytoarchitectural reference spaces and could integrate different datasets less easily than modern digital platforms [].

Modern brain maps combine several spatial scales and data types, including histology, MRI, connectivity, gene expression, and cellular data, within a common three-dimensional reference space, as in the Allen Mouse Brain Common Coordinate Framework [].

This integration can reveal relationships between cytoarchitecture, molecular organization, and gene expression that no single method can show, as demonstrated in the human brain [].

A key step was the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (Mus musculus), which mapped genome-wide gene expression onto a standard anatomical reference [,].

The Allen Human Brain Transcriptome Atlas extended this approach to the human brain [], and the Human Connectome Project provided a multimodal framework for mapping human brain structure, function, and connectivity [,].

In small brains, automated whole-brain histological imaging and quantification are now possible, as shown by high-throughput 3D histopathology pipelines in mice []. Surface-based cortical atlases have also been built for non-human primates, such as the rhesus monkey (Macaca mulatta) [].

These surface-based atlases provide standard spatial frameworks for comparing cortical areas and neuroimaging data across individuals and species.

In other species, atlases often rely on a single method; for example, the Catlas is an MRI-based three-dimensional cortical atlas of the domestic cat [].

Spatial transcriptomics, connectomics, and high-throughput imaging have extended brain atlases beyond morphology, mainly in mouse and human tissues [,,], and describe the brain as a multiscale system in which cell identity, gene expression, connectivity, and topology interact, as shown by connectomic studies in the mouse and by the reconstruction of rat neocortical microcircuits [,,].

Although deep learning has shown potential for disease classification and data integration in human neuroimaging [,,,], comparable resources are still limited in veterinary neuroscience. Species-specific resources do exist, but their scope and methods vary widely. Examples include stereotaxic and neuroimaging atlases of the dog [,], MRI-based anatomical references for the horse [,], an MRI-based atlas of the pig brain [], and ongoing work toward standard sheep brain atlases []. MRI-based descriptions of normal brain anatomy are also available for the cat [] and, among laboratory species, for the rabbit at 3 T [].

A few multispecies repositories are available—the Comparative Mammalian Brain Collection (brainmuseum.org) [], BrainMaps.org [], the Scalable Brain Atlas [], the Digital Brain Bank [], and the Animal Brain Collection []—which cover many mammalian species and, in the last case, other vertebrates. Domestic and large mammals, with their distinct evolutionary histories, sensory specializations, and spontaneous diseases, are therefore an undervalued source of comparative neuroanatomical data [,,,,]. Available atlases and reference studies in species of veterinary interest are listed in  and summarized in .

Neurohistological analysis and comparative brain mapping contribute to veterinary neurological diagnosis by providing information on tissue organization, lesion distribution, cellular pathology, and species-specific anatomical variation. Neurological examination and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are fundamental to the investigation of brain disorders, but imaging findings do not always establish the cause of disease.
