Histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular analyses complement this information; integrating them with clinical findings and neuroanatomical localization is essential for interpreting brain lesions [,].

Histological examination, using hematoxylin and eosin staining and immunohistochemistry where indicated, enables the characterization of tissue damage and cellular responses and, together with clinical and MRI findings, supports the distinction between inflammatory, degenerative, and vascular processes [,,,]. Wolff et al. [] conducted a multicenter retrospective study of 121 dogs: 77 had histologically confirmed brain disease, while 44 had a clinical diagnosis of idiopathic epilepsy. Overall, MRI detected the presence of a brain lesion with a sensitivity of 94.4% and a specificity of 95.5%. However, sensitivity for classifying cerebrovascular disease was 38.9% when images were interpreted without access to clinical data. This estimate was based on six dogs and had a wide 95% confidence interval (16.1–67.0%); it should therefore be interpreted cautiously and understood as referring to the classification of the cerebrovascular disease category in this study population.

Necrotizing meningoencephalitis, necrotizing leukoencephalitis, and granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis are commonly grouped under the term meningoencephalitis of unknown origin (MUO). A presumptive diagnosis is based on neurological examination, MRI, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and the exclusion of infectious causes. Definitive subtype classification, however, requires histopathological examination, generally performed post mortem or, less frequently, on an ante-mortem biopsy [,,,]. The limited availability of ante-mortem histopathological confirmation also affects treatment decisions. Available reviews primarily describe immunosuppressive treatments, but they draw on heterogeneous studies and do not establish a clearly superior treatment protocol [,]. Histopathological examination allows the disease subtype to be defined, but its value in guiding treatment selection and predicting outcomes remains unclear. In vascular lesions, histopathology likewise enables the characterization of ischemic damage and hemorrhage; its contribution nevertheless depends on lesion location, disease stage, sampling, and tissue preservation.

Comparative brain mapping can help distinguish physiological aging from pathological changes, particularly in companion animals with progressive behavioral or cognitive decline. Borràs et al. [] compared the brains of 20 aged dogs and 10 young dogs, documenting age-related changes in the meninges, choroid plexuses, blood vessels, neurons, and glial cells. These included lipofuscin accumulation, polyglucosan bodies, cerebrovascular amyloid deposition, and ubiquitin-positive structures; some of these changes may contribute to canine cognitive dysfunction.

On MRI, age-associated changes include iron-related hypointensities in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra [] (), as well as cerebral atrophy. Pugliese et al. [] assessed cerebral atrophy using a semiquantitative rating scale in 98 dogs representing 27 breeds and identified differences associated with skull shape. Youssef et al. [] reviewed age-related neuropathological changes in domestic and laboratory animals; comparative studies of aging and naturally occurring diseases in veterinary species [,,] further demonstrate the value of species-specific reference data. Atrophy, iron accumulation, or amyloid deposition should therefore not automatically be interpreted as evidence of a specific neurological disease, but should instead be evaluated in relation to age, clinical findings, and, when available, pathological confirmation.

MRI provides noninvasive information on brain morphology, whereas histology enables the examination of cellular and microstructural features that cannot be resolved by conventional MRI. In a study of 19 Beagle dogs aged 8 months to 16 years, Kimotsuki et al. [] observed a correlation between age and lateral ventricular space volume, as well as age-associated hypointensities in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra on T2-weighted images. In the single 16-year-old Beagle that underwent post-mortem examination, Perls’ staining revealed iron accumulation in areas corresponding to the MRI hypointensities. The same animal also had a hyperintense area in the periventricular white matter, which the authors interpreted as a possible perivascular alteration, although this finding was not specifically verified histologically. Advanced MRI approaches, including measurements of the apparent diffusion coefficient and magnetization transfer ratio, as well as magnetic resonance spectroscopy, can provide complementary information on tissue composition. However, the correspondence between these parameters and specific histopathological processes requires further validation, ideally through studies correlating MRI with post-mortem histology, supported by the atlases and registration systems described in  and .

Immunohistochemistry and molecular analyses can document cellular and molecular alterations that are not detectable by conventional MRI. In their study of canine cognitive dysfunction, Schütt et al. [] examined the prefrontal cortex of 15 aged dogs with normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, or cognitive dysfunction, comparing it with that of two young dogs. They detected diffuse cortical amyloid-β deposits and accumulation of the peptide in vessel walls. Amyloid-β pathology correlated with age but not with the severity of cognitive impairment; no neurofibrillary tau pathology was found, and proinflammatory cytokine levels were generally low, with no significant associations with cognitive status. Extending these analyses to other naturally occurring diseases requires species-specific validation of the antibodies and markers used ().

Digital histology and artificial intelligence could standardize lesion quantification and reduce observer-related variability, for example when measuring neuronal density, inflammatory cell burden, gliosis, and tissue loss. Open resources such as CISCA and CytoDArk0 [] provide a methodological basis for automated cell segmentation in Nissl-stained brain sections. However, their diagnostic or prognostic value in veterinary patients has not yet been demonstrated; evaluating this value will require disease-specific datasets, validated annotations, and testing across institutions and acquisition protocols. Cell segmentation, cell-type classification, density estimation, and unbiased estimation of total cell number are distinct tasks; the last requires design-based stereological sampling, and all of them require validation against histological ground truth by experts.

Overall, the established clinical applications of neurohistology include the characterization of brain lesions, the interpretation of abnormalities observed on imaging, and the study of brain aging. Automated multimodal diagnosis and prognostic assessment remain promising but have not yet been validated.

As noted in the Introduction, most large research infrastructures, standard brain atlases, curated image repositories, and machine learning pipelines have been developed for humans, non-human primates, and mice, where large standardized datasets allowed robust methods to be built [,,]. Veterinary neuroscience is therefore underrepresented in large computational and neuroinformatic initiatives.

Digital pathology has developed rapidly over the past decade [,,], and high-throughput whole-brain histological pipelines have already been applied to the mouse brain []. Their implications for veterinary neurological diagnosis are discussed in .

A major obstacle is the large anatomical variability among mammalian brains.

Differences in cortical layers, white matter architecture, and regional proportions make it difficult to transfer processing pipelines developed for human, mouse, or rat brains [,].

This variation can reduce both the accuracy and the biological interpretability of computational methods applied to species with very different brain organization [,]. Model performance should therefore be reported separately for internal test sets, independent laboratories, and new species, and differences in staining and scanners, fixation, annotation uncertainty, and phylogenetic differences in brain organization should be treated as distinct sources of error.

Comparative analyses are also limited by differences in tissue preparation, image acquisition, processing, and annotation. Existing resources are spread across institutions, produced with different methods, and often lack standard metadata and compatible annotations []. Experience in neuroinformatics shows that poorly organized data and metadata make data sharing, reuse, and automated processing much more difficult [].

Many veterinary species still lack standard stereotaxic coordinates and whole-brain atlases. Published atlases and volumetric studies rarely cover the whole brain and use different acquisition protocols, which makes it difficult to compare data between institutions and species (). The available evidence for each species, including brain regions, methods, sample types, main findings, and limitations, is summarized in , which also distinguishes methods directly applied to veterinary species from those whose application is still potential.

Some historical comparative collections are difficult to use in current computational workflows because their digitization, annotation, metadata, and access differ. The Comparative Mammalian Brain Collection (formerly neurosciencelibrary.org, now brainmuseum.org), for example, offers extensive histological material from many mammalian species [], but its digital coverage, annotation, and metadata vary widely between specimens. Other repositories focus on a single type of data (e.g., braincatalogue.org), which limits the integration of histological, MRI, molecular, and connectivity data. These limitations reduce the reproducibility and scalability of comparative research. Direct evidence from studies in veterinary species is summarized in , and  compares the main methods, their advantages and limitations, and their applications in veterinary species, to help choose the most suitable method for a given question.

Direct evidence from neurohistological, morphometric, imaging, and neuropathological studies in veterinary species. For each study, the table reports the species, the brain region investigated, the method, the sample type, the objective, the main findings, the limitations, and the reference. Only studies in which the method was applied to the species indicated are included; approaches whose application to veterinary species remains potential are discussed in the text and in . Abbreviations: DTI, diffusion tensor imaging; GME, granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; NME, necrotizing meningoencephalitis; V1, primary visual cortex.

Comparative overview of neurohistological, imaging, and computational methods for neuroanatomical analysis in veterinary species. For each method, the table reports the type of information provided, the main advantage, the key limitation, and the current veterinary application, to support the selection of the most appropriate method for a given neuroanatomical or diagnostic question. In the last column, “Direct” indicates a documented application in veterinary species; “Limited” a documented application subject to specific practical or technical constraints; and “Potential” an application not yet adequately validated in the veterinary context considered. A method may have been applied directly in one species or context while remaining potential in another. Abbreviations: MRI, magnetic resonance imaging.

Artificial intelligence offers important opportunities to address these limitations. Automated segmentation, morphometry, and multimodal registration can reduce manual work and allow the analysis of large image collections [,,]. These tools could speed up cytoarchitectural mapping in large-brained species, such as cattle and horses, for which manual analysis is very time-consuming. Self-supervised learning, weak supervision, and transfer learning may partly overcome the lack of annotations and improve performance across datasets [,].

Future progress will depend on three complementary directions: AI-assisted tissue analysis, multimodal integration of imaging and molecular data, and explicitly comparative frameworks across species.

A priority is the development of multimodal atlases that combine cytoarchitecture, MRI, connectivity, and molecular data in shared or linked coordinate systems [,,].

This will require open data infrastructures, common metadata standards, shared annotation protocols, and reference frameworks across species. For veterinary neuroscience, the challenge is not simply to reuse tools developed for humans or laboratory animals, but to develop methods that allow standardized quantitative comparison while preserving differences between species, because subtle structural differences may reflect real evolutionary divergence rather than technical variation to be removed during image registration or model training.

This review shows that the analysis of the brain has developed through cumulative rather than substitutive methodological advances. Gross anatomical dissection and classical preparations, such as Nissl and Golgi staining, remain the material on which macroscopic and microscopic morphometry, stereology, digital histology, and deep learning now operate, and each step has added a new level of information, from brain volume and white matter organization to cell morphology, neurochemistry, connectivity, and quantitative cytoarchitecture. In domestic animals, however, direct evidence is still limited to a few species, mainly the dog, horse, sheep, cattle, pig, and cat, and to selected brain regions, while most computational tools and multimodal atlases developed in humans and laboratory animals remain potential rather than validated applications.

Three main implications follow. First, reference brain atlases and quantitative normative data for each domestic species are a priority for veterinary neurology and neuropathology, because the interpretation of brain lesions depends on them. Second, methods developed in humans, mice, and rats should be validated on the brains of domestic animals before use, and their outputs should remain interpretable in anatomical terms. Third, the open sharing of brains and digital data from domestic animals, including animals examined at necropsy, would allow current analytical frameworks to be tested across the brains of different species.

neuroscience.title: Modern management of third nerve palsy: neuroimaging triage and surgical rehabilitation
neuroscience.abstract: Third nerve palsy (TNP) is a complex neuro-ophthalmic condition that requires rapid differentiation between benign microvascular ischemia and life-threatening or otherwise serious causes, including aneurysmal, neoplastic, inflammatory, infectious, demyelinating, traumatic, and cavernous sinus pathologies. Given the high prevalence of diabetes, understanding both pupil-involving and pupil-sparing presentations is critical. Current literature often fragments TNP management across isolated medical specialties. Rather than presenting an evidence-based consensus guideline, this paper provides an expert narrative synthesis proposing a bipartite clinical framework. This framework sequences acute neuro-ophthalmic triage (Weeks 1–12) and chronic ophthalmic rehabilitation (>6 months) to coordinate immediate etiological workup with subsequent surgical and rehabilitative planning. TNP manifestations vary based on the dual anatomy of the third nerve. Compressive lesions typically paralyze superficial pupillomotor fibers, whereas ischemic insults preserve them. Because pupillary status alone cannot definitively rule out emergencies, acute care triage requires neuroimaging tailored to the clinical context. Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) and Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) serve as primary modalities when an aneurysm is suspected; contrast-enhanced MRI is preferred when brainstem, cavernous sinus, orbital, inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic pathology is suspected; and CT is used first in acute trauma. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is reserved for specific cases to detect microaneurysms smaller than 3 mm when initial imaging is inconclusive. Chronic or unresolving cases are managed through sequentially planned interventions, where strabismus alignment is typically prioritized before ptosis repair. Ultimately, this review proposes an evidence-informed, phase-based framework designed to support the timely identification of potentially fatal etiologies and guide individualized functional and esthetic rehabilitation. Multidisciplinary collaboration, utilizing prospective registries, is essential to address current data gaps and enhance long-term rehabilitative success in patients with TNP.
neuroscience.text:
The oculomotor nerve (CN III) comprises outer parasympathetic fibers that regulate the pupil and accommodation, and inner somatic fibers that innervate the levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) and four extraocular muscles (). While complete paralysis of CN III yields a highly recognizable “down and out” positioning of the globe with pronounced ptosis (, ), overlapping etiologies heavily complicate third nerve palsy (TNP) diagnosis. Clinicians are frequently forced to rapidly differentiate between benign microvascular events and life-threatening compressive lesions (). Because the diverse manifestations of this condition can obscure clinical decision-making during critical care windows, historical textbook descriptions often lead to disjointed diagnostic and rehabilitative steps across isolated medical specialties (, ).

The clinical presentation diverges significantly depending on whether the underlying etiology is a compressive lesion (e.g., posterior communicating artery (PComA) aneurysms, trauma, or uncal herniation) or an ischemic lesion (most commonly secondary to diabetes mellitus or hypertension) (, ). Despite classical clinical distinctions, relying solely on pupillary status is insufficient to safely rule out life-threatening emergencies (, ). Painful TNP with pupil sparing in diabetic patients often indicates a microvascular ischemic event, but failure of the palsy to resolve or worsening pain necessitates urgent re-evaluation (). Rapid clinical evaluation and urgent neuroimaging tailored to the clinical context are paramount to identify aneurysmal and other serious causes, including vascular malformations such as carotid-cavernous fistulas (CCFs), as well as central ischemic, neoplastic, inflammatory, infectious, demyelinating, and traumatic lesions ().

Recent literature has been instrumental in determining clinical outcomes for specific neurosurgical and diagnostic profiles (, , ). However, because these highly specialized studies focus narrowly on isolated therapeutic or diagnostic questions, the resulting data remains heavily fragmented across the distinct silos of the neurology, neurosurgery, and ophthalmology literature. To resolve these clinical ambiguities and bridge the gap between disciplines, our expert narrative synthesis translates existing evidence into a cohesive, timeline-driven treatment framework. Rather than presenting new primary clinical data, this bipartite roadmap structures historically isolated evidence into two operational phases:

Phase 1 (Weeks 1–12): Details immediate diagnostic triage (Days 1–7) to safely evaluate acute manifestations and identify aneurysmal and other serious causative pathology, followed by a conservative observation window for patients in whom a presumed microvascular palsy is supported.

Phase 2 (> 6 Months): Critically assesses advanced, muscle-specific surgical advancements (such as sophisticated transposition and ptosis correction methods) alongside non-surgical neurorehabilitation interventions for attaining functional and esthetic alignment in persistent deficits.

A comprehensive narrative review of the PubMed and MEDLINE databases was conducted for literature published up until July 2026. The primary objective was to synthesize current diagnostic and surgical evidence to construct a multidisciplinary, timeline-driven clinical pathway for unilateral TNP. The search approach was specifically designed to capture contemporary diagnostic and surgical breakthroughs, prioritizing literature published within the last 15 years to ensure the proposed clinical pathways reflect modern management paradigms. However, select foundational publications from the early 2000s were retained specifically to provide necessary context for established strabismus and ptosis techniques.

The core search strategy utilized combinations of the following terms: “third nerve palsy,” “diabetic third nerve,” “oculomotor nerve palsy,” “isolated oculomotor nerve palsy,” “oculomotor nerve paralysis,” “oculomotor nerve palsy treatment,” “isolated third nerve,” and “isolated third nerve palsy.” These terms were iteratively combined with specific concept terms representing phase-specific interventions (e.g., “CTA,” “MRA,” “muscle transposition,” “Botulinum Toxin”) to retrieve literature relevant to each distinct phase of care.

Inclusion criteria were restricted to articles in English that focused on adult or pediatric populations and provided actionable data on neuroimaging techniques or surgical results. While adult cases are predominantly driven by microvascular or aneurysmal etiologies (), pediatric TNP literature highlights different primary etiologies (congenital, traumatic, or inflammatory) and prioritizes amblyopia risk management (). To ensure the statistical reliability of reported surgical and rehabilitative outcomes, studies with fewer than five patients were generally omitted from our review. However, targeted exceptions were made for high-impact case reports detailing rare, life-threatening neurovascular presentations that directly informed emergency triage protocols.

Study selection and critical appraisal were expert-driven, prioritizing high-impact publications, clinical guidelines, and studies that directly addressed protocols or outcomes related to the stated objectives. Because this manuscript is designed as a narrative review synthesizing current diagnostic and surgical evidence, rather than a formal systematic review or meta-analysis—a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) flowchart for paper stratification is not methodologically applicable.

CN III can suffer damage anywhere along its five distinct neuroanatomical segments: the midbrain nucleus, midbrain fascicles, subarachnoid space, cavernous sinus, and orbit (, ). The clinical features are tightly bound to the precise site of injury and the nature of the lesion, as outlined in .

Anatomical localization, clinical presentation, and triage of TNP.

Distinguishing between adult and pediatric populations is vital when evaluating the underlying etiology of a TNP, as their clinical profiles dictate divergent diagnostic approaches. While adult presentations are overwhelmingly dominated by microvascular ischemia or compressive lesions, pediatric cases are distinctly different. In children, congenital anomalies, birth trauma, closed head injuries, and post-viral inflammatory conditions represent the most common etiologies, whereas aneurysmal compression or diabetic microvascular ischemia is exceedingly rare (, ). The diagnostic algorithm for pediatric patients shifts away from acute vascular screening and instead prioritizes broad-spectrum neuroimaging, specifically favoring MRI to minimize the risk of ionizing radiation exposure while ruling out structural, neoplastic, or inflammatory causes (, ).

The structural organization of the third nerve explains the crucial clinical distinction between pupil-involving and pupil-sparing palsies (). The small, unmyelinated parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run superficially along the outer dorsomedial aspect of the nerve sheath (). The blood supply to these fibers is sourced from the adjacent pial network (). Extrinsic mechanical forces—such as an expanding PComA aneurysm, trauma, or uncal herniation—directly compress these outer fibers first, leading to an unresponsive, dilated pupil and loss of accommodation (, ).

Conversely, the inner somatic trunk is supplied by the microvascular network of the vasa nervorum. Microvascular diseases, such as diabetes mellitus and hypertension provoke deep ischemic necrosis within the central core of the nerve (). This inner core damage spares the outer parasympathetic fibers, leaving pupillary function intact and reactive to light (). In adult patients over the age of 50, an isolated, pupil-sparing TNP is most often secondary to diabetes mellitus or hypertension (, , ).

Patients with TNP typically report acute binocular diplopia due to eccentric image placement on the extrafoveal retina (). Paradoxically, severe ptosis often hides this symptom by acting as a natural occluder. Ocular pain is an important warning feature (, ). Severe, sudden-onset, progressive, or atypical headache or orbital pain should lower the threshold for urgent neuroimaging, particularly when accompanied by pupillary involvement, neurological deficits, proptosis, chemosis, or other atypical features. However, pain may also occur in microvascular ocular motor nerve palsy and should not be used as an isolated etiological discriminator (, ). When compressive or traumatic injuries disrupt the endoneurial sheath, misdirected axonal regrowth can lead to aberrant regeneration (). This causes lid-gaze dyskinesis (the pseudo-Graefe sign, where the upper lid retracts during adduction) or pupil-gaze dyskinesis, resulting in paradoxical pupillary constriction during convergence or downward gaze (, , ).

While Phase 1 covers the first 12 weeks, clinical urgency is dictated by etiological suspicion. We categorize the first 7 days as “Immediate Emergency Triage,” requiring rapid exclusion of life-threatening compressive (aneurysmal), inflammatory or infectious (e.g., GCA), neoplastic, or traumatic etiologies (). The subsequent period (Weeks 2–12) functions as “Recovery Monitoring” for patients in whom no causative abnormality has been identified and the presentation is consistent with microvascular palsy, whether neuroimaging was negative or was appropriately deferred in a classic presentation (, ). Patients who do not meet these criteria are not observed; they proceed to specialist review and further targeted evaluation.  summarizes this pathway, a general acute diagnostic triage and management pathway for adult third nerve palsy that includes aneurysmal and nonaneurysmal causes.

The acute management window requires prioritizing this rapid diagnostic triage over surgical corrections to identify life-threatening neurovascular and other serious conditions (). When a patient presents with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and mydriasis, immediate neuroimaging is required to rule out compressive lesions, which can be fatal (, ). As shown in , pupil-sparing patients under 50 years, or with progressive pain or an incomplete palsy, also go directly to urgent neuroimaging, and the imaging result then determines management as described in Step 3.

The initial clinical assessment focuses on defining the extent of the oculomotor deficit. Clinicians must perform cover testing across all nine diagnostic positions of gaze to quantify the strabismus, which typically manifests as a classic exotropia and hypotropia (). This assessment determines whether the palsy is complete or partial; atypical, incomplete presentations can indicate an evolving compressive lesion and warrant a lower threshold for urgent neuroimaging. Simultaneously, the upper eyelid should be examined to assess whether the ptosis fully obscures the visual axis (). For suspected microvascular cases, it is essential to immediately record systemic blood pressure and order baseline laboratory evaluations, including a complete blood count (CBC), hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), C-reactive protein (CRP), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (, ). Giant cell arteritis (GCA) should be considered in older patients with compatible systemic symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, visual symptoms, or ischemic features (, ). Although isolated third nerve palsy is an uncommon manifestation, its recognition is important because delayed diagnosis may result in irreversible visual loss and other ischemic complications (, ). Depending on the presentation, neuroimaging should be considered concurrently to exclude aneurysmal and other structural causes (, ).

Advanced imaging must be selected based on pupillary status, pain characteristics, completeness of the presentation, age, vascular risk factors, progression of the deficit, associated neurological or orbital signs, and any traumatic, inflammatory, or infectious context (, ), as summarized in the triage algorithm (). Practical decision-making for selecting the appropriate modality depends heavily on the suspected etiology and specific clinical subtype. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) serves as the standard for direct cranial nerve and soft-tissue evaluation (, ). T1, T2, and Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) sequences are indispensable for detecting brainstem infarctions, demyelination, or neoplasms (, ). High-resolution MRI with contrast, specifically targeting the brain, orbits, and cavernous sinus, is strongly recommended when the patient presents with multiple cranial neuropathies or orbital signs (e.g., chemosis, proptosis) indicating a cavernous sinus or orbital apex syndrome (). MRI is the preferred frontline modality for pediatric TNP to limit radiation exposure, and for recurrent TNP to rule out slow-growing tumors or chronic inflammatory processes (, ). At the subarachnoid level, time-of-flight Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) provides specialized, non-invasive vascular mapping (, , ).

Conversely, non-contrast brain CT is the immediate choice in emergency settings to rapidly rule out acute subarachnoid hemorrhage or uncal herniation, and it is the initial imaging of choice for traumatic TNP to assess for orbital or skull base fractures (, ). Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) features high spatial resolution and offers up to 90% sensitivity for detecting cranial aneurysms 3 mm or larger (, ). CTA is often preferred over MRA for rapid emergency vascular screening and is the ideal alternative for individuals with claustrophobia or metallic implants (, ).

The clinical context influences the urgency, modality, and anatomical areas of interest for neuroimaging. In acute trauma, urgent CT of the head, orbits, and skull base is indicated to rule out fractures and intracranial injury, with CT angiography or MRI added as guided by the suspected injury pattern (e.g., suspected vascular injury, cavernous sinus involvement, or brainstem injury) (, ). If an inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic process is suspected, particularly in the presence of cranial neuropathies, fever or systemic inflammatory symptoms, immunosuppression, meningism, or orbital signs suggesting cavernous sinus involvement, urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain, orbits, and cavernous sinus is recommended, with anatomical coverage guided by the suspected site of pathology (, ).

Catheter-based Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is reserved for highly specific cases, acting as the definitive diagnostic standard for detecting tiny microaneurysms smaller than 3 mm or low-flow dural-cavernous fistulas (, , ). Because it carries an inherent risk of stroke and is highly invasive, DSA is typically reserved for cases when initial non-invasive CTA or MRA is negative, but the patient presents with a painful, pupil-involving TNP, or an atypical partial (incomplete) TNP, where the clinical suspicion for a microaneurysm remains high (, ).

For pupil-sparing presentations, contemporary imaging thresholds must be strictly applied. Historically, pupil-sparing patients 50 years of age or older with vascular risk factors were managed solely with laboratory evaluation and observation (, ). However, because aneurysms can occasionally present without initial pupillary involvement, some contemporary clinical paradigms suggest considering urgent high-resolution imaging (such as MRI or MRA) even in this older demographic to rule out structural compression, though this aggressive screening approach remains actively debated in routine clinical practice (, , ). If initial imaging is deferred in favor of observation—typically for patients presenting with an isolated, complete, painless, and pupil-sparing TNP who fit the classic microvascular demographic—clinicians must adhere to an explicit threshold for emergency re-evaluation. Urgent neuroimaging is triggered if the pupil becomes involved at the 7–10 day reevaluation, if pain worsens, if motor symptoms fail to improve within 4 to 6 weeks, or if atypical features (e.g., aberrant regeneration) develop (, , ).

After urgent neuroimaging, management follows : urgent neurovascular treatment, including endovascular coiling or microsurgical clipping as appropriate, if a causative aneurysm is confirmed (, , ); etiology-specific management if another causative abnormality is identified, such as a stroke pathway for midbrain infarction or other central ischemia, neuro-oncology for neoplasm, neuro-immunology for demyelinating or inflammatory disease, infectious disease management for infection, and the relevant trauma, cavernous sinus, or orbital specialty (, , ); and specialist review with further targeted evaluation, including DSA if suspicion of a microaneurysm remains, when the presentation is atypical (, , , ).

For patients who reach observation, If no causative abnormality is identified and the presentation is consistent with microvascular palsy, whether neuroimaging was negative or was appropriately deferred in a classic presentation, management shifts toward medical stabilization. Microvascular ischemic palsies follow a self-limiting course, and most cases resolve spontaneously within 6 to 12 weeks (). However, recent meta-analyses demonstrate that isolated ischemic oculomotor nerve palsies are not entirely benign; patients with an ischemic TNP face up to an eightfold increased risk of subsequent stroke within the first year following the palsy (). Acute care during this observation window must center on internal medicine optimization—specifically stringent glycemic control and blood pressure regulation—paired with symptomatic diplopia relief to mitigate long-term systemic vascular risks (, , ).

Surgical management is generally deferred until the clinical presentation has remained stable and unresolved for at least 6 months, allowing for the possibility of spontaneous microvascular recovery (). While a systematic strategy in which strabismus correction precedes ptosis repair is typically recommended—since vertical extraocular muscle adjustments can significantly alter the resting position of the upper eyelid—this sequencing requires careful clinical nuance (). Important exceptions to this timeline exist. For instance, severe corneal exposure may necessitate earlier, temporizing eyelid intervention, while in pediatric populations, immediate visual axis obstruction poses a profound amblyopia risk that supersedes standard surgical timelines and demands urgent ptosis correction (, , ). Patient age, cosmetic concerns, and the psychosocial burden of the palsy must also be weighed heavily when timing these sequential interventions. Current literature indicates that while achieving a functional field of single binocular vision in the primary gaze is a realistic goal, complete restoration of physiological motility is rarely attainable (, ). A 2024 prospective analysis confirmed that tailored extraocular muscle transpositions successfully collapse complex strabismus patterns and improve primary position alignment even in profound CN III deficits, provided patient selection is rigorous (). Tailored muscle transposition procedures for partial palsies generally report alignment success rates between 60 and 80%, though definitive outcomes vary greatly depending on the extent of native muscle preservation and follow-up duration, and must be interpreted cautiously due to the retrospective and heterogeneous nature of the supporting literature (, , ). Conversely, severe complete palsies requiring supramaximal resections or mechanical globe fixation carry higher risks of consecutive deviations, often requiring intensive, long-term monitoring (, ). Across all major surgical approaches, the risk of residual peripheral diplopia and exposure keratopathy must be thoroughly discussed with patients preoperatively. The frequent need for subsequent reoperations—with reported revision rates often exceeding 30% specifically within heterogeneous cohorts managing complete palsies, traumatic etiologies, or those requiring complex supramaximal resections—highlights the necessity of establishing realistic rehabilitative expectations (, , ).

Before proceeding to permanent surgery, several temporary strategies can assist with vision rehabilitation. Initially, alternate occlusion therapy (patching) the dominant eye or using frosted lenses mitigates intractable diplopia. This is the standard of care to prevent amblyopia development, particularly in pediatric populations, provided all refractive errors are simultaneously corrected (, ). Additionally, temporary Fresnel prisms or ground-in prisms are integrated into prescription glasses to realign small horizontal or vertical deviations. This helps patients achieve binocular fusion in the primary gaze position once the ptotic lid begins to elevate (, ). For active deviation management, injecting botulinum toxin directly into the functional, unopposed lateral rectus muscle induces temporary paralysis. This safely treats exotropia and counters horizontal drift, positioning the eyes in the primary position while awaiting spontaneous nerve regeneration during the late observation period ().

Conservative management differs significantly between adult and pediatric cohorts. In adult patients, conservative measures such as unilateral patching, Bangerter foils, or Fresnel prisms are utilized primarily for the symptomatic relief of intractable diplopia while awaiting spontaneous recovery (, ). Conversely, in pediatric patients—particularly those within the critical period of visual development under the age of eight—the overarching clinical priority is the rapid prevention of stimulus deprivation amblyopia (, ). If a pediatric ptosis completely obstructs the visual axis, or if severe strabismus disrupts binocular fusion, clinicians cannot simply observe the patient. They must urgently initiate aggressive amblyopia therapy, which typically requires cycloplegic refraction and rigorous patching regimens, independent of the timeline for eventual surgical rehabilitation ().

When muscle deficits persist past 6 months, strabismus surgery is prioritized to center the globe in the primary position. Restoring full physiological motility is rarely achievable; the primary goal is maximizing the field of single binocular vision (). The surgical pathways are dictated by the severity of the palsy ().

In cases of complete TNP affecting all four extraocular muscles, standard muscle adjustments are typically insufficient and surgical goals are limited to achieving alignment in primary gaze. For severe exotropia requiring extensive correction, the lateral rectus can be fully disinserted from the globe and anchored directly to the lateral orbital wall to prevent outward drifting (). Alternatively, a supramaximal recession-resection may be employed, where a maximal lateral rectus recession is paired with a large medial rectus resection. To correct associated vertical misalignment in this scenario, the resected medial rectus tendon can be shifted upward (supraplacement) or downward (infraplacement) (, ). When no active muscle force remains, the eye must be mechanically anchored in place through globe fixation techniques. One established method involves transposing the superior oblique tendon to the medial rectus insertion site to act as a nasal tether (, ). Alternatively, the globe can be anchored directly to the medial orbital periosteum using non-absorbable sutures passed near the anterior lacrimal crest (, ). While these fixation methods effectively center the eye in the primary gaze, they result in a permanently “frozen globe” with no residual natural mobility, which can sometimes be cosmetically undesirable.

Conversely, for incomplete TNP, surgical plans must be highly tailored to target only the specific paretic muscles identified during testing. Isolated medial rectus involvement is addressed by combining a medial rectus resection with an antagonist lateral rectus recession (, , ). If the patient presents with superior division palsy, characterized by isolated deficits in superior rectus and LPS function causing impaired elevation, Knapp’s procedure is indicated (, , ). In this technique, the full tendons of the medial and lateral recti are transposed directly to the superior rectus insertion site (, , ). Crucially, this is only performed if a Forced Duction Test (FDT) confirms there is no mechanical restriction of the inferior rectus. If inferior rectus restriction is present, a 5–6 mm recession of the inferior rectus must be performed first, ensuring careful dissection of the lower lid retractors to prevent postoperative eyelid malposition (, , ). For inferior division palsy, multi-muscle strategies are recommended to achieve primary position alignment. This is addressed by transposing the superior rectus tendon to the medial rectus insertion area and the lateral rectus to the inferior rectus insertion site, combined with a superior oblique tenotomy (, ). This transposition produces sufficient active force to stabilize the globe and counteracts the intorsion caused by the unopposed action.

Ptosis surgery is primarily performed to prevent amblyopia progression and clear the visual axis. Ptosis repair should generally be prioritized after strabismus surgery is complete, as vertical extraocular muscle adjustments can significantly alter the resting position of the upper eyelid. The subsequent surgical approach for eyelid restoration is then dictated by the patient’s residual levator muscle function (). For severe ptosis presentations featuring poor native levator muscle function (excursion measurement less than 4 mm), a frontalis sling is the preferred method. In this procedure, a sling material connects the upper tarsal plate directly to the frontalis muscle of the forehead, allowing the patient to open the eye by elevating their brow (, ). In contrast, a levator advancement is utilized when the patient retains fair-to-good levator function (excursion measurement 5 mm or greater). Here, the surgeon shortens and tightens the levator aponeurosis by advancing it onto the anterior surface of the tarsus, directly enhancing the muscle’s native lifting capacity (, ). Regardless of the approach, surgeons must carefully balance the risk of undercorrection (permanent eyelid retraction) against overcorrection. Overcorrection can lead to exposure keratopathy if the patient cannot close the eyelid completely (). Due to these intrinsic complexities, subsequent revision operations are frequently required to optimize the final functional outcome.  summarizes the key diagnostic and therapeutic evidence underpinning this framework.

Summary of representative key evidence underpinning the clinical framework.

The management of TNP remains one of the most challenging paradigms in neuro-ophthalmology and requires a dual approach that transitions from acute neuro-ophthalmic triage to structured, chronic visual rehabilitation. Quickly and accurately differentiating pupil-sparing microvascular conditions from pupil-involving compressive etiologies remains a vital clinical skill, although pupillary status alone cannot exclude a serious cause (, ). While traditional clinical markers generate initial suspicion, neuroimaging tailored to the clinical context is central to identifying aneurysmal and other serious structural causes (, ): CTA or MRA for suspected aneurysm, CT of the head, orbits, and skull base in acute trauma, and contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain, orbits, and cavernous sinus for suspected inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, demyelinating, brainstem, cavernous sinus, or orbital pathology. DSA remains the reference standard for small aneurysms (, ). In the proposed pathway (), management after imaging depends on whether a causative aneurysm is confirmed and, if not, on other imaging findings and the clinical context, rather than on aneurysm exclusion alone. Observation is reserved for patients with typical features and no causative abnormality, whereas atypical or pupil-involving presentations with unrevealing imaging warrant specialist review and further targeted evaluation, including consideration of DSA if suspicion of a microaneurysm remains (, , , ). Because ischemic oculomotor palsies are not entirely benign (), observation should be paired with vascular risk-factor control.

Once urgent structural and other serious causes have been excluded or treated, long-term rehabilitation should follow a systematic, timeline-based sequence to re-establish functional binocularity and appearance. Spontaneous recovery is common in ischemic cases within the first 12 weeks. For persistent deficits lasting past 6 months, carefully staged surgeries—where strabismus correction (ranging from standard recession-resection to multi-muscle transpositions and globe fixation) typically precedes ptosis repair—support individualized functional and esthetic outcomes while aiming to safeguard corneal health.

As a narrative review designed to bridge the gap between acute neuro-ophthalmic triage and chronic ophthalmic rehabilitation, our methodology has inherent limitations. The expert-driven selection of literature introduces the potential for selection bias, and the exclusion of studies with fewer than five patients—while intended to ensure the statistical reliability of surgical outcomes—may omit highly specific case reports detailing rare neurovascular presentations. Furthermore, because this study does not adhere to systematic review protocols (e.g., PRISMA guidelines), a formal meta-analysis of surgical outcomes was not performed. The proposed framework has not been prospectively validated or endorsed by a guideline body; therefore, it is intended as an evidence-informed synthesis rather than a definitive standard of care.

Although there have been substantial therapeutic advancements, the existing clinical literature still exhibits considerable gaps. Future research should focus on establishing prospective registries and multicenter observational cohorts with standardized outcome measures to systematically compare the long-term functional and esthetic outcomes of various advanced muscle transposition protocols. There is a pressing need to establish reliable predictive clinical models that can pinpoint patients with microvascular or partial TNP who are most likely to fail conservative therapy and monitoring. This would allow clinicians to streamline care and tailor surgical preparation timelines. Moving from fragmented specialty care toward a unified, bipartite roadmap may help shift TNP management from a period of diagnostic uncertainty to a more structured continuum of care. By sequencing acute neurovascular triage and chronic strabismus correction, this framework provides a structured approach that may facilitate timely management without sacrificing long-term visual rehabilitation.

This narrative review presents an evidence-informed, phase-based framework for evaluating and managing third nerve palsy. Early evaluation and appropriately directed neuroimaging are essential to identify aneurysmal and other potentially serious causes requiring urgent treatment. Following stabilization and etiological management, ophthalmic rehabilitation should be individualized according to the extent of spontaneous recovery, residual ocular misalignment, ptosis, diplopia, and patient priorities. While this framework integrates available evidence and clinical expertise, prospective studies are needed to evaluate its effect on diagnostic timeliness, visual function, quality of life, and clinical outcomes.

neuroscience.title: The MIND Diet and Physical Activity in Cognitive Ageing: From Mechanisms to Multidomain Trials
neuroscience.abstract: Preserving cognitive function against the effects of ageing and neurodegenerative disease is the goal of lifestyle-based approaches to brain health. This review examines the evidence for the Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet, for physical activity covering aerobic, resistance, and mind–body exercise modalities, and for the multidomain programmes in which both are embedded. For each, we consider the mechanistic rationale, the biomarker, neuroimaging, and the observational and interventional evidence. Overall, a substantial body of evidence links both exposures to better cognitive performance; however, uncertainties remain regarding optimal intervention dose, duration, target populations, and whether MIND diet and exercise exert independent or synergistic effects. We further propose that the discordance between cohort and trial findings may reflect baseline neurodegenerative risk, with benefit being hardest to detect in low-risk populations over short follow-up. Few trials have tested the MIND dietary pattern change alongside structured exercise, and none has isolated the contribution of either within a multidomain programme. More strategically designed trials, with clinical endpoints and single domain comparators, are needed to answer these questions.
neuroscience.text:
Population ageing has driven a rise in neurodegenerative disorders. An estimated 57.4 million individuals worldwide were living with dementia, a figure projected to reach 152.8 million by 2050 [], with a staggering global societal cost of dementia estimated to be US$1.3 trillion in 2019, with approximately 50% attributable to informal caregiving [,]. In the absence of curative pharmacotherapies, the attention has shifted toward prevention and early intervention. The 2024 Lancet Commission on Dementia Prevention estimated that up to 45% of dementia cases may be attributable to modifiable risk factors. Several of these include hypertension, obesity, physical inactivity, diabetes, high LDL, etc. []. These factors are modified directly by diet and exercise, placing lifestyle intervention among the few prevention strategies available at population scale.

This review focuses on two accessible and scalable lifestyle strategies: the Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet and physical activity. The rationale for considering them together rests on more than their independent efficacy. A substantial body of mechanistic evidence indicates that diet and exercise converge on the same core neurobiological substrates such as cerebrovascular and endothelial function, neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, and neurotrophic signalling, and it is believed that their combined application may exert complementary effects on synaptic plasticity and cognition []. They are also the two components common to every major multidomain prevention trial conducted to date, yet they are more often reviewed in isolation than together, and the question of whether their combination confers synergistic benefit beyond either alone remains largely unknown. Prospective cohorts report substantial protective associations for MIND diet adherence [,], while the largest randomised trial of the diet was null []; multidomain interventions have produced clear cognitive benefit in some populations and none in others, sometimes within the same trial network and under closely comparable protocols [,,,,]. This discordance is usually attributed to methodological heterogeneity. An additional hypothesis is that baseline cognitive and neurodegenerative risk may modify the observable benefits of lifestyle intervention, with effects potentially less detectable in low-risk populations due to limited cognitive decline during follow-up, and in those with advanced neuropathology due to reduced capacity for modification. However, this proposed relationship remains speculative and requires prospective validation. Accordingly, this narrative review synthesises mechanistic, biomarker, observational and interventional evidence for the MIND diet and physical activity independently, before examining how these two lifestyle cornerstones are incorporated within multidomain intervention strategies, and considers the implications of the evidence for clinical translation.

A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus from database inception to August 2026. Search terms included “MIND diet,” “Mediterranean diet,” “physical activity,” “exercise,” “aerobic exercise,” “resistance training,” “cognition,” “cognitive decline,” “mild cognitive impairment,” and “dementia,” combined using Boolean operators. Eligible publications included observational studies, randomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses examining dietary patterns and/or physical activity in relation to cognitive outcomes. Relevant mechanistic, biomarker, and neuroimaging studies were also considered. English-language publications were selected through title, abstract, and full-text screening based on their relevance to the review objectives. Evidence was synthesised qualitatively across mechanistic, observational, and interventional domains.

The MIND diet was introduced in 2015 by Morris et al. as a hybrid of the Mediterranean and Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diets, specifically designed to target the neuropathological processes underlying cognitive decline and dementia []. It comprises 15 dietary components classified into 10 “brain healthy” food groups to be encouraged, and five food groups to be limited. Each component is scored 0, 0.5 or 1 according to intake frequency, giving a total of 0 to 15; the half-point tier captures partial adherence and accounts for the non-integer scores reported through the cohort literature []. Two scoring features merit comment. First, the wine component awards a full point only for intake of one glass daily, with abstention and two or more glasses both scoring zero. Its inclusion is now difficult to justify, and several adaptations have removed or substituted it []. Importantly, this scoring criterion should not be interpreted as a recommendation to initiate wine consumption for cognitive protection. Second, absolute scores are not strictly comparable across studies, given differing dietary instruments, serving size conversions, inconsistently reported scoring decisions [], and culturally adapted components [].

The cognitive benefits of the MIND diet have been attributed to multi-targeted neurobiological action. Experimental evidence suggests that these constituent bioactive compounds such as antioxidant vitamins (E, C), carotenoids, polyphenols, flavonoids, B vitamins (B6, B9, B12), omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), dietary fibre, and phylloquinone are proposed to act in concert across four principal mechanistic axes: amyloid proteostasis, neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, vascular integrity, and synaptic plasticity []. However, much of this mechanistic evidence is derived from animal models or individual nutrients, and direct evidence demonstrating equivalent effects from the complete MIND dietary pattern in humans remains limited. The key bioactive compounds and their proposed mechanistic pathways across individual MIND diet components are summarised in .

In experimental models, dietary antioxidants [], B vitamins [], polyphenols, and PUFAs [] have been shown to inhibit the formation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) oligomers and fibres. Oleocanthal, the key phenolic compound of extra virgin olive oil (EVOO), enhanced Aβ clearance by increasing the activity of Aβ transport proteins at the blood–brain barrier (BBB) [,]. In rodent studies, omega-3 PUFAs (DHA and EPA) from fish promote efficiency of the glymphatic system enhancing interstitial Aβ clearance via an Aquaporin-4 (AQP4)-dependent pathway [], although the exact clinical relevance of this mechanism in humans remains uncertain. Simultaneously, exogenous antioxidants with a focus on vitamin E from nuts and whole grains may exert anti-inflammatory effects and modulate oxidative stress through cellular signalling pathways and endogenous antioxidant defences, thereby reducing the oxidative damage induced by β amyloid, that would otherwise induce cytotoxicity [].

Chronic neuroinflammation is an established driver of neurodegeneration []. Omega-3 fatty acids suppress pro-inflammatory cytokine production by inhibiting nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) activation, which is a key transcription factor involved in the expression of genes encoding proteins involved in inflammation, and generating specialised pro-resolving mediators (resolvins, protectins) [], while dietary polyphenols commonly found in many of the plants produce similarly block-NF-κB-dependent inflammatory gene expression []. The MIND diet’s broad antioxidant provision, encompassing vitamins E and C, and carotenoids from leafy greens and nuts, limits the generation of lipid peroxidation products, which have been implicated in amyloid β misfolding and synaptic dysfunction []. Meanwhile, MUFAs abundant in olive oil appear to have anti-inflammatory effects that may attenuate the chronic inflammation of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, which are implicated in dementia risk []. Adherence to the MIND diet has been associated with lower odds of hippocampal sclerosis and with attenuated inflammation cognition relationships [,].

Individual components of the MIND diet synergistically promote vascular health through improvements in lipid profile, glucose metabolism, and anthropometric indices. Adherence to a Mediterranean diet lowers oxidised low-density lipoprotein, which is a promoter of oxidative stress-associated neurodegenerative disorders [], improves glucose control [], and promotes weight loss []. These cardiometabolic improvements optimise vascular cerebral health by preserving endothelial function, reducing oxidative stress and atherosclerotic burden, and limiting disruption of the blood–brain barrier []. Improved cerebral blood flow in turn attenuates neurotoxic accumulation, minimising neuronal dysfunction. In addition, it improves amyloid-β clearance at the blood–brain barrier, preventing hyperphosphorylation of tau, which leads to neurofibrillary tangle formation [].

Anthocyanins and other flavonoids, which are particularly abundant in berries, upregulate BDNF expression in experimental models, promoting synaptic plasticity and adult hippocampal neurogenesis [,]. This axis is of particular relevance to integration developed in , since BDNF-mediated plasticity is also a principal pathway through which aerobic exercise is thought to act.

Individual MIND diet components: Key bioactives and mechanistic pathways A.

Abbreviations: dAGE = dietary advanced glycation end product; BDNF = brain-derived neurotrophic factor; DHA = docosahexaenoic acid; EPA = eicosapentaenoic acid; MUFA = monounsaturated fatty acid; PUFA = polyunsaturated fatty acid; and SCFA = short-chain fatty acid. A The mechanistic pathways summarised are largely derived from experimental and nutrient-level evidence and should not be interpreted as established effects of the complete MIND dietary pattern.

Biomarker, neuroimaging, and neuropathological studies provide growing biological support for the neuroprotective potential of the MIND diet, although the strength of evidence varies across pathological domains. At the amyloid neuropathological level, in the Rush Memory and Aging Project [], MIND diet adherence was associated with lower global AD pathology and reduced β-amyloid burden on postmortem examination, with each one-point increase in MIND score corresponding to an amyloid-related pathological burden approximately equivalent to 4.25 fewer years of age. In contrast, MIND diet adherence was not significantly associated with p-tau tangle burden, suggesting that its neuropathological associations may be more closely related to amyloid-related pathways than to tau pathology. This pattern is also consistent with the mechanistic evidence discussed in , in which several components of the MIND diet have been implicated in Aβ formation, clearance, and proteostasis.

This amyloid signal is also supported by biomarker and neuroimaging studies. In the ALBION study, higher MIND adherence was associated with lower odds of pathological CSF Aβ42 concentrations in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged adults []. Similar findings have been reported with Mediterranean-style dietary patterns, which form the dietary foundation of the MIND diet. Higher Mediterranean or MIND diet adherence has been associated with lower cerebral amyloid deposition on 11C-PiB PET [], while longitudinal studies suggest that lower adherence may be accompanied by greater accumulation of amyloids and faster cerebral hypometabolism over time [,]. Collectively, these findings provide convergent evidence across postmortem tissue, CSF biomarkers, and PET imaging that greater adherence to MIND or closely related Mediterranean dietary patterns may be associated with a lower amyloid burden.

Evidence for the preservation of brain tissue structure is less consistent. Observational MRI studies have generally suggested that healthier dietary adherence may be associated with greater preservation of total brain or hippocampal volume, although associations with cortical thickness, grey matter volume, and other structural measures have not been uniformly demonstrated [,,]. These findings suggest that the potential biological effects of dietary adherence may extend beyond amyloid metabolism to broader structural pathways. However, the interventional evidence remains considerably less convincing. The neuroimaging sub-study of a landmark RCT–Trial of the MIND Diet for Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Older Persons showed no significant between-group differences in white matter hyperintensity volume, hippocampal volume, or total grey and white matter volumes over three years between the MIND diet and the caloric restrictive control group []. Interpretation is limited by the small imaging subsample, and using an active control diet that also incorporated caloric restriction and dietary improvement, which may have reduced the biological contrast between groups.

Taken together, the biomarker literature provides a consistent support for an association between MIND or similar Mediterranean-style dietary adherence and lower amyloid burden, with more tentative evidence for favourable effects on structural brain change. However, these associations do not establish causality or demonstrate that dietary intervention directly modifies amyloid production or clearance in humans, particularly as randomised biomarker and neuroimaging evidence is still limited. Nevertheless, these findings provide a biological rationale for the MIND diet as a neuroprotective strategy, while underscoring the need for adequately powered, long-duration trials with integrated biomarker and radiological endpoints to confirm the magnitude and durability of these effects.

Building upon this mechanistic and biomarker foundation, observational and interventional studies have examined whether adherence to the MIND diet translates into meaningful reductions in cognitive decline and dementia risk across diverse adult populations.

The seminal evidence was established [] in the Memory and Ageing Project (MAP), in which 960 Chicago older adults without dementia were followed over 10 years. MIND diet adherence was associated with slower cognitive decline, with participants in the highest adherence tertile estimated to be cognitively 7.5 years younger than those in the lowest. Benefit was also observed with moderate adherence, and associations persisted after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors, suggesting that the relationship may not be explained solely by cardiovascular risk reduction. In a separate analysis of 923 participants from the same MAP cohort, Morris et al. [] found that higher MIND diet adherence was associated with lower incidence of Alzheimer’s disease over a mean follow-up of 4.5 years, and the observation persisted after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors and other potential confounding factors.

However, the strength of this association has not been uniformed across all cognitively unimpaired populations. In the Nurses’ Health Study, a large prospective cohort of 16,058 American women aged ≥70 years, long-term MIND diet adherence was associated with better verbal memory but not with global cognitive decline over six years []. Likewise, the DO-HEALTH study found no significant association between baseline MIND adherence and cognitive decline over three years in 2028 generally healthy community-dwelling older adults across five European countries []. The same pattern was seen in the Framingham Heart Study (FHS) cohort, where higher MIND adherence was associated cross-sectionally with better global cognition and larger total brain volume, but not with cognitive decline over a mean 6.6 years of follow-up []. What these three cohorts share is comparatively low baseline vulnerability. All were free of dementia and largely free of clinically significant cardiovascular disease at entry, and significantly younger at baseline than the MAP participants. In relatively healthy populations with low short-term risk of decline, fewer cognitive events and smaller changes over follow-up may reduce the ability to detect an effect. This supports the possibility that the benefits of MIND adherence are most readily observable in populations with sufficient underlying neurodegenerative or vascular risk for cognitive trajectories to diverge measurably over time.

Additionally, sub-analysis of the Nurses’ Health study [] also further demonstrated that excluding the unhealthy components, namely butter and margarine, as well as pastries and sweets, attenuated its protective association with verbal memory, underscoring that the diet’s cognitive benefits are dependent not only on adequate intake of its 10 brain healthy food groups, but also on adherence to the restriction of its five unhealthy components, which together define the diet’s full neuroprotective profile.

Longer-term cohort evidence provides additional support for MIND diet efficacy. In the Australian PATH Through Life cohort study of 1220 cognitively unimpaired adults with mean age 62 years, higher MIND adherence was associated with substantially lower 12-year odds of incident cognitive impairment, with each one-point increase in MIND score associated with a 19% reduction in odds []. Importantly, cognitive impairment was adjudicated using neuropsychological testing, MMSE performance, and functional assessment rather than defined solely by changes in a composite cognitive score. This suggests that the association may extend beyond test score differences to clinically meaningful transitions from normal cognition to MCI or even dementia.

The potential applicability of the MIND framework beyond Western dietary settings has also been explored. In the China Health and Nutrition Survey of 4066 Chinese individuals with mean age of 62.2 years, a culturally adapted 12-component MIND diet scoring foods was developed to reflect local dietary habits. The adaption excluded olive oil, butter and margarine, and cheese, which were rarely consumed in this population, while replacing wine with tea, given their shared polyphenol-rich composition. Despite these modifications, higher adherence remained associated with better global cognitive function, with every three-point increase in score corresponding to an effect size approximately equivalent to one year of younger cognitive age over a median study follow-up of 3 years []. These findings suggest that the neuroprotective framework of the MIND diet retains its cognitive relevance across widely divergent dietary contexts and cultural populations, provided its core mechanistic principles are preserved even when specific food items are substituted.

Evidence from a recent landmark RCT, however, is more equivocal. The largest randomised trial to date on the MIND diet is the Trial of the MIND Diet for Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Older Persons, which enrolled cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of dementia, BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2, and a suboptimal diet defined by a baseline MIND score of ≤8, randomising them to either a MIND diet with mild caloric restriction or an active control diet with equivalent caloric restriction. Global cognition over three years improved in both groups, with no statistically significant between-group difference (SMD 0.035, 95% CI −0.022–0.092) []. Interpretation is complicated by the control intervention. Both groups received caloric restrictions and lost weight. By trial completion, mean MIND diet scores had increased to approximately 11.0 in the intervention group and 8.5 in the control group, where the control group also exceeded the median score associated with cognitive protection in the middle adherence tertile of the original MAP cohort. The between-group dietary contrast was therefore narrower than intended, making this a comparison between greater and lesser degrees of dietary improvement, rather than between a MIND diet and an unchanged habitual diet. Without an untreated comparator, the improvement seen in both groups also cannot be attributed specifically to diet, since weight loss and repeated cognitive testing remain plausible contributors too.

Higher MIND diet scores have generally been associated with better cognitive outcomes, but no threshold for benefit can be identified. The absolute scores at which associations appear vary widely. In MAP, both moderate and higher adherences were associated with lower Alzheimer disease risk, with median scores of 7.5 and 9.5 respectively, compared with 6 in the lowest tertile. In the PATH Through Life cohort, each one-point increase in MIND score was associated with lower odds of incident cognitive impairment, while the highest adherence group had a mean score of only 7.8. By contrast, in the culturally adapted Chinese cohort, favourable cognitive associations were observed at substantially lower absolute scores, with a median score of 4.5 out of 12 and a mean of 5.5 in the highest tertile. Taken together, these findings suggest that greater adherence generally produces favourable results, but no single score can be considered an efficacy threshold. Differences in dietary assessment, scoring adaptations, population, follow-up, and outcome definitions further limit direct comparisons across studies. MIND scores should therefore be interpreted within the context of each study.

Overall, the current evidence is supportive of an association between greater MIND diet adherence and more favourable cognitive outcomes, particularly over longer follow-up and in populations with sufficient underlying risk for cognitive decline to become detectable. The strongest support comes from prospective cohorts, where higher adherence has been associated with slower cognitive decline and lower incidence of cognitive impairment. However, findings are less consistent in healthier, lower-risk populations, and randomised evidence remains limited. Further long-duration randomised trials with clearer dietary separation between intervention and control groups are needed to determine the magnitude of any cognitive benefit. The key observational and interventional studies examining the association between MIND diet adherence and cognitive outcomes are summarised in .

Physical inactivity is among the modifiable risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission. The literature conventionally divides physical activity into three common modalities: aerobic exercise (sustained cardiovascular loading), resistance training (progressive mechanical loading of skeletal muscle), and mind–body exercise (coordinated movement integrated with sustained attentional focus). Though each modality converges on several shared mechanistic pathways, each additionally recruits pathways distinct to themselves.

Physical activity confers neuroprotection through several partially overlapping mechanisms that complement the dietary pathways described above in . Amongst these, a foundational contribution is the modification of cardiometabolic risk. Exercise exerts favourable effects on blood pressure, lipid profile, insulin sensitivity, and body weight, each of which independently accelerates cognitive decline when dysregulated []. Building on this systemic foundation, physical activity enhances cerebrovascular function, increasing cerebral blood flow in various regions of the brain, increases production of endothelial nitric oxide synthase and supports blood–brain barrier integrity, allowing for more efficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the brain [].

Beyond these vascular effects, physical activity exerts direct neurobiological actions on brain tissue. It potentially promotes hippocampal neurogenesis and strengthens synaptic connectivity chiefly through upregulation of BDNF, mediating synaptic efficacy and neuronal connectivity, and using dependent plasticity []. In parallel, experimental studies suggest that physical activity also facilitates glymphatic clearance of neurotoxic solutes. including amyloid-β [], and reduces its neuronal accumulation via upregulation of the degrading enzyme neprilysin []. In addition, a separate pathway operates through neurotransmission, increasing the release of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin across key cognitive regions, supporting attentional control, memory, and mood regulation [].

Superimposed on these shared pathways, each exercise modality also contributes to a mechanistically distinct stimulus. Aerobic exercise is defined by sustained cardiovascular loading, driving three linked processes: improved cardiorespiratory fitness, augmented cerebral blood flow, and BDNF upregulation, with the last being directly linked to hippocampal neurogenesis and vascular neuroprotection []. Resistance training operates instead through insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) signalling. Resistance exercise stimulates peripheral IGF-1 secretion from liver and skeletal muscle, where circulating IGF-1 then crosses the blood–brain barrier to promote neuronal differentiation, synaptic plasticity, and angiogenesis [], while also attenuating brain tissue loss and upregulating BDNF and vascular endothelial growth factor in support of neuronal survival and cerebrovascular integrity, as well as resistance to age-related neurodegeneration []. A complementary mechanism is the muscle–brain axis, in which myokines secreted by contracting skeletal muscle enter the circulation, cross the blood–brain barrier, modulate neuroinflammation, and promote hippocampal neurogenesis []. As the modality most reliably shown to build muscle mass and counteract sarcopenia [], resistance training is uniquely positioned within this axis. Mind–body exercise integrates slow purposeful movement, balance, and mindful attention, deriving its benefit from the simultaneous integration of coordinated movement and sustained attentional focus rather than from cardiovascular loading or progressive resistance. Choreographed sequential movements demand skill-based learning and memorisation, activating the cingulate cortex, hippocampus, frontal lobe, and sensorimotor cortex, regions that are directly implicated in memory consolidation and executive control [], while its meditative and relaxation components confer psychological wellbeing, reducing anxiety and depression [], both of which are independently recognised as modifiable risk factors for cognitive decline. The proposed neurobiological mechanisms linking different physical activity modalities to cognitive outcomes are summarised in .

However, translating these mechanistic pathways into consistent clinical biomarker evidence has proven more difficult. Although animal models robustly demonstrate exercise-induced reductions in both Aβ accumulation and tau hyperphosphorylation [], observational and interventional human studies [,] examining the effects of exercise on Aβ and tau biomarkers have yielded inconsistent findings. Interpretation is limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous physical activity measurement, and biomarker endpoints that were rarely prespecified as primary outcomes. Yet, these mixed biomarker results do not necessarily negate a neuroprotective effect, but rather reflect the contribution of parallel mechanistic pathways that collectively drive cognitive protection independently of measurable amyloid or tau modification such as vascular mechanisms.

At the structural level, evidence is more encouraging []. A large neuroimaging study of 10,125 individuals [] found that moderate to vigorous physical activity was associated with greater volumes of total grey matter, the hippocampus, frontal cortex, parietal lobe, and occipital lobe, while longitudinal cohort evidence [] suggests that these structural benefits accumulate across the lifespan. Individual interventional studies have also shown that aerobic exercise can structurally reverse age-related brain atrophy. One of the landmark studies by Erickson et al. demonstrated that one year of aerobic training increased the anterior hippocampal volume by approximately 2%, effectively adding 1 to 2 years of hippocampal volume to older adults who would otherwise have experienced continued age-related decline []. However, a later meta-analysis [] on 14 interventional studies (n = 737) showed that aerobic exercises had no significant effect on the total hippocampal volume, though a sub-analysis of nine studies (n = 501) patients showed that there was a small positive effect on the left hippocampal volume. Beyond the hippocampus, aerobic exercise has also been found to increase grey and white matter volume in the frontal lobes over 6 months, with these structural benefits appearing most pronounced in older age groups []. This is also further supported by a large cross-sectional study of the UK Biobank (n = 16,725) [] where it showed that greater physical activity, as determined over a 7 day accelerometer measurement, had an association with total brain volume, grey matter, white matter, and total hippocampal volume, while being inversely associated with white matter hyperintensity volume.

Meanwhile, progressive resistance training has also been shown to attenuate hippocampal atrophy in older adults, protect white matter integrity, increase grey matter cortical thickness, and produce functional changes in the frontal lobe, all of which correspond to the executive function and memory domains improved by resistance training in a systematic review of interventional and cross-sectional studies [].
