However, translating these associations into trial evidence across mixed exercise modalities has proven more difficult. A 2021 systematic review [] of 19 RCTs using various types of exercise modalities found the neuroimaging findings to be mixed and highly heterogeneous, with no consistent protective effect on grey matter volume detectable across trials. However, these null RCT findings must be interpreted with caution, as the included trials were all short-term (≤12 months) and underpowered given that neuroimaging was not a primary outcome, and a subset examined neurological conditions unrelated to neurodegeneration, all of which substantially limit the reliability of the negative conclusion. Adequately powered, long-duration trials with amyloid and tau biomarkers, and neuroimaging as prespecified primary endpoints, are therefore needed before definitive conclusions can be drawn.

Physical activity is among the most frequently recommended interventions in clinical practice, yet among the least precisely prescribed. Where the MIND diet offers clinicians a discrete 15-item list, exercise recommendations are often reduced to generic encouragement, obscuring the fact that modality, intensity, and frequency each carry distinct neurobiological consequences. Meaningful appraisal therefore requires that the modalities and their prescription parameters be cross-examined with the evidence.

Across modalities, exercise interventions have generally demonstrated cognitive benefit, even as their relationships with biomarkers, neuroimaging, and neuropathological measures remain inconsistent. A systematic review and meta-analysis of nine studies reported that aerobic exercise produces significant improvements in memory and executive function []. Meta-analytic data from Landrigan et al. [] and Coelho Junior et al. [] collectively demonstrate that resistance training produces significant improvements in global cognitive function, executive function, and memory across both cognitively healthy older adults and those with mild cognitive impairment, with pooled effect sizes in the moderate range. Meta-analytic evidence across 45 studies involving 4602 cognitively intact and mildly cognitively impaired participants [] indicates that mind–body exercise produces a moderate effect on visuospatial construction and small but statistically significant effects on verbal memory, processing speed, working memory, and executive function, with MCI populations consistently deriving greater cognitive benefit than cognitively healthy older adults in the visuospatial construction and executive function domains. A complementary network meta-analysis of 58 RCTs [] further identified mind–body exercise as the most efficacious modality for improvement of overall cognitive function, especially in domains of executive function and working memory among cognitively unimpaired older adults, outperforming aerobic exercise and resistance exercises on these specific domains.

However, what is not so clear about this body of evidence presented so far is the prescription of exercise required to achieve cognitive improvement. Exercise prescription is conventionally specified through the FITT framework: frequency, intensity, time, and type [].

Current international guidance provides a reference standard for the time and frequency components of prescription. Both the World Health Organization [] and the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee [] recommend that older adults undertake at least 150 to 300 min of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, together with muscle-strengthening activity of at least moderate intensity on two or more days per week, and, for those with reduced mobility, multicomponent activity emphasising balance and functional training on three or more days per week. Unfortunately, there is no harmonised intensity metric spanning across all three modalities. While such a metric would simplify prescription, these modalities act through substantively different mechanisms, and a common intensity scale would confer an appearance of comparability that the biology does not support.

Aerobic exercise intensity can be quantified as a relative to maximum heart rate (%MHR). No specific aerobic modality has shown to be superior for cognitive outcomes due to the lack of evidence. Hence, the guiding principle is to achieve a sufficient cardiovascular stimulus, typically expressed as a target percentage of the maximum heart rate, while allowing individuals to self-select the activity most compatible with their preferences, fitness levels, and comorbidities, a patient-centred approach that will likely optimise long-term adherence.

Evidence supports moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, performed at 50–70% MHR, as the best-evidenced and most universally applicable prescription for cognitive protection in older adults. Studies exploring the dose–response relationship between exercise intensity and cognitive outcomes revealed that moderate-intensity protocols have the most robust and consistent evidence base, while high-intensity aerobic exercise (70–85% MHR) has produced heterogeneous results across trials, and low-intensity aerobic exercise has demonstrated mixed and less convincing cognitive efficacy []. This picture is not unchallenged. In EXERT, the largest trial to test it directly, 18 months of aerobic training at 70–80% heart rate reserve, did not outperform low-intensity stretching and balance work in adults with amenestic mild cognitive impairment []. Neither group declined cognitively over 12 months, and 12-month hippocampal volume loss was low in both at 0.51% []. Both arms were active, and this bears on the relative value of intensity rather than on whether exercise confers benefit at all. From a practical standpoint, moderate-intensity exercise represents the most clinically pragmatic threshold for this population where many older adults present with sedentary lifestyles, multiple comorbidities, and reduced exercise tolerance, rendering high-intensity protocols poorly tolerated and poorly adhered to, while low-intensity activity may fall below the stimulus required to drive meaningful neurobiological adaptation. Importantly, exercise intensity should not be evaluated purely through the lens of cognitive outcomes in isolation. The broader cardiometabolic benefits of sustained moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, including improvements in blood pressure, lipid profiles, insulin sensitivity, and cardiovascular fitness, have been linked to lower dementia risk [], and represent an important co-primary goal of any exercise prescription. Volume, unlike intensity, can be placed on a common scale. Within aerobic exercise, the metabolic equivalent of task minutes per week (METs-min/week) standardises dosing by multiplying intensity by duration across the weekly training load. Based on a Bayesian model-based network meta-analysis of 44 RCTs [] involving 4793 older adults, the estimated minimum exercise dose associated with a clinically meaningful improvement in global cognition was 724 METs-min per week, which was slightly above the WHO-recommended lower bound of 600 METs-min per week. Cognitive benefits increased markedly, up to approximately 1200 METs-min per week, beyond which additional volume yielded diminishing returns.

For resistance exercises, like aerobic exercise, current evidence does not support the superiority of any specific resistance modality either, which have all demonstrated broadly comparable efficacy for cognitive outcomes []. Rather than prescribing a specific apparatus, the guiding principle is progressive overload, which involves systematically increasing resistance over time to sustain an adequate neuromuscular and neurotrophic stimulus. This principle should guide prescription regardless of modality, and individuals should be encouraged to self-select the format most compatible with their physical capacity, joint health, and personal preference.

Regarding specific prescription parameters, intensity can be seen as a percentage of one repetition maximum (%1RM). NSCA guidelines [] recommend 2–3 sets of 1–2 multi-joint exercises per major muscle group, achieving intensities of 70–85% of one repetition maximum (1RM), 2–3 times per week. Current evidence suggests that resistance exercise performed at approximately 60–80% of 1RM may confer cognitive benefits, with comparable effects observed across moderate and higher intensities within this range []. However, the optimal intensity remains uncertain given the heterogeneity across studies, allowing for individualisation according to physical capacity and tolerance. Similarly, programmes of at least 16 weeks in duration, with a minimum frequency of two sessions per week, represent the threshold most consistently associated with cognitive benefits in the literature [], although these parameters should not be regarded as definitive minimum thresholds. These findings broadly align with WHO recommendations for twice-weekly moderate- or greater-intensity muscle-strengthening activity in older adults, whose cognitive protective rationale is now substantially reinforced by the mechanistic and clinical evidence reviewed here.

Unfortunately, when it comes to mind–body exercise, no equivalent consensus metric exists. Perhaps this is better explained by the fact that its cognitive stimulus derives from skill-based learning and sustained attentional demand rather than from cardiovascular or mechanical loading. Among the exercise subtypes, Tai Chi, Yoga, and Qigong demonstrate meaningfully greater effects [] on visuospatial construction compared to meditation alone, a distinction likely attributable to the fact that these modalities impose considerable spatial processing demands through proprioceptive engagement and goal-directed upper body movements that activate the parietal lobe, whereas meditation is a stationary behaviour that does not generate equivalent neuromotor stimulation. Despite the absence of any harmonised intensity metric or clear guidance on optimal modality, mind–body exercise has a clear clinical utility. Its low impact and accessible nature make it particularly well suited for individuals with limited exercise tolerance, physical frailty, high fall risk, or substantial comorbidities, groups for whom conventional aerobic or resistance training may be impractical or contraindicated. It should therefore be positioned not as a substitute, but as a complementary component within a comprehensive, multimodal exercise strategy for cognitive preservation.

Although MIND dietary modification and physical activity each have substantial independent evidence supporting their role in cognitive outcomes and converge on similar core neurobiological substrates, direct evidence evaluating their synergistic effects remains limited. Studies examining diet and exercise together as a two-component intervention are few and highly heterogenous [] with respect to study population and intervention design, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions regarding their combined efficacy. Evidence specifically evaluating the MIND diet together with structured physical activity and their interaction effects is further limited [,,,]. The two RCTs [,] examined specific exercise modalities and selected populations, including Baduanjin exercise and obese postmenopausal women, limiting the generalisability of their findings. Meanwhile, retrospective single-cohort studies [,] have not demonstrated consistent evidence of synergistic cognitive benefits from combining MIND diet adherence with physical activity. However, the limited number of studies and their methodological constraints preclude definitive conclusions regarding potential synergistic effects.

Cognitive impairment is a multifactorial condition, and the Lancet Commission has identified numerous modifiable risk factors spanning vascular, metabolic, behavioural, and psychosocial domains, suggesting that effective prevention is unlikely to depend on the modification of any two factors alone. Hence, it is also clinically relevant to examine MIND or MIND-aligned dietary modification and physical activity as foundational components within the broader multidomain interventions trials that provide an important evidence base for understanding how these two lifestyle cornerstones contribute to cognitive preservation.

The first major proof of concept for this approach was provided by the Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) trial []. FINGER randomised 1260 adults aged 60–77 years with elevated dementia risk to a two-year multidomain intervention comprising dietary modification, aerobic and resistance exercise, cognitive training, and vascular risk monitoring, compared with standard health advice. The dietary intervention was based on the Finnish Nutrition Recommendations [] rather than the MIND diet itself. Nevertheless, there is substantial conceptual and compositional overlap between the two approaches, including an emphasis on vegetables, fruits and berries, whole grains, fish, and unsaturated fats, together with restriction of saturated fats, excess sugar, and other nutritionally adverse foods. FINGER therefore provides an important proof of concept that dietary modification broadly consistent with MIND-aligned principles, together with structured physical activity, can be successfully embedded within a comprehensive dementia-prevention programme. Over two years, the intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvement in the neuropsychological test battery composite score than controls, which was equivalent to 25% higher in the interventional group than in control group. In addition, the intervention’s adherence rate across all four intervention components was high, with 72% of participants completing all four domains, thus reinforcing the real-world feasibility of intensive multidomain lifestyle intervention.

This model subsequently formed the basis of the Worldwide FINGERS (WW-FINGERS) network and was extended more directly to the MIND diet in the US Study to Protect Brain Health Through Lifestyle Intervention to Reduce Risk (US POINTER) []. US POINTER is particularly relevant to the present review because the structured intervention explicitly incorporated the MIND diet alongside aerobic, resistance, and flexibility exercise, cognitive engagement, and health coaching. Among 2111 cognitively unimpaired older adults at increased risk of cognitive decline, global cognitive performance improved in both study groups over two years, but improved significantly faster in those receiving the structured multidomain intervention. The effect was greater among participants with lower baseline cognitive performance, while mean team-meeting attendance remained high at 91% in the structured intervention group.

More recently, LatAm-FINGERS extended this framework across 11 Latin American countries, demonstrating that the multidomain model could be adapted successfully across markedly different cultural, socioeconomic, and dietary settings []. Among 1065 older adults with elevated dementia risk and suboptimal cognition, the structured lifestyle intervention which included regular MIND diet intervention counselling and a highly structured exercise programme involving aerobic, resistance, coordination and balance training produced a significantly greater improvement in global cognition over two years than the flexible comparator. In addition, unlike the earlier trials, exercise components were prescribed explicitly with four supervised sessions weekly, comprising 35 min of aerobic exercise, and twice-weekly 15 min resistance training and twice-weekly 15 min coordination and balance training, at 55–65% of maximum heart rate progressing to 70–80% after six months—a transferable FITT specification. Additionally, feasibility was also assessed prospectively as a co-primary outcome using RE-AIM measures, an approach well suited to complex behavioural interventions where delivery is as uncertain as efficacy []. The mean session attendance and the two-year retention rate were high, with a lower dropout rate in the systematic lifestyle intervention arm (15.2% vs. 20.2%).

It is, however, also important to note that the broader multidomain literature has not been uniformly positive. Earlier trials such as preDIVA [] and MAPT [], as well as subsequent WW-FINGERS studies including J-MINT [] and AgeWell.de [], did not demonstrate significant cognitive benefit in their primary analyses. However, these studies should not be considered directly equivalent to tests of the intervention strategy discussed here. None incorporated the MIND diet specifically, and there were substantial methodological differences in the nature and intensity of dietary counselling, exercise delivery, degree of supervision, study population, and comparator conditions. Their neutral findings therefore highlight the considerable heterogeneity inherent within multidomain intervention research rather than providing direct evidence against the combination of MIND dietary principles and structured physical activity.

Taken together, the most informative positive multidomain trials suggest an evolving continuum of evidence: FINGER established the initial proof of concept using a dietary pattern that substantially overlaps with MIND principles with physical activity as cornerstones; US POINTER subsequently demonstrated cognitive benefit in a structured intervention explicitly incorporating the MIND diet; and LatAm-FINGERS showed that the overall framework can be successfully adapted across diverse populations. However, the magnitude of benefit is generally modest and improvements in cognitive test scores do not necessarily establish reductions in dementia incidence. Importantly, these trials included additional components such as cognitive training and vascular risk management, making it impossible to isolate the individual or synergistic contributions of the MIND diet and physical activity. Rather, they support conceptualising dietary modification and physical activity as two complementary crucial lifestyle modifications within a broader, multifactorial strategy for cognitive improvement. The key multidomain intervention trials examining cognitive outcomes, including their intervention components and principal findings, are summarised in .

Across cohorts and trials, the relationship between baseline risk and observed benefit appears nonlinear rather than simply graded. At the low-risk end of the spectrum, intervention effects may be difficult to detect because cognitive decline and event rates are modest over the duration of follow-up, resulting in floor effects and limited statistical power. Conversely, at the high-risk end, where more established neuropathological changes may already be present, the potential for modification may also be attenuated. This raises the possibility that lifestyle interventions of the MIND diet and physical activity confer the greatest benefit among individuals at an intermediate stage of risk, those who are cognitively vulnerable but have not yet developed substantial irreversible pathology. However, a nonlinear relationship has not been formally established, and differences in intervention intensity, adherence, follow-up duration, comparator conditions, and cognitive outcome measures may also explain the variation across studies. Further prospective studies are needed to determine whether baseline risk modifies intervention efficacy and to identify populations most likely to benefit.

A practical strength of the MIND diet is its tiered adherence model. Even moderate adherence is associated with meaningful risk reduction, making it a realistic, prescribable framework for a broad patient population. Its emphasis on accessible whole foods aligns with existing nutritional guidelines and avoids the limitations of supplement-mediated nutrient delivery. For physical activity, the different modalities benefit cognition through partially distinct mechanisms, which support multimodality rather than single-modality prescription, although modality-specific trials remain heterogeneous in intensity, duration, and outcome measurement. Multidomain interventions that simultaneously target MIND dietary quality, physical activity, cognitive training, and vascular risk management currently carry the most replicable trial evidence. FINGER, US POINTER, and LatAm-FINGERS each demonstrated statistically significant improvements in composite cognitive scores among at-risk older adults, and each delivered its intervention in a structured, facilitated format with good adherence rather than as generic behavioural advice. Although these findings provide encouraging evidence, they are derived from a limited number of trials and do not establish the independent contributions of individual intervention components. Adherence appears to matter a great deal. The trials reporting benefit are generally those with high session attendance under supervision, which raises the possibility that simple advice may yield little benefit in clinical practice, and that patients may instead need referral to a structured programme designed to support adherence. Nevertheless, structured programmes require additional resources and supervision, while potential exercise-related adverse events should be considered, particularly in frail or multimorbid older adults.

An important clinical context for these findings is the expanding but substantially constrained availability of anti-amyloid therapies (AATs). The approvals of lecanemab and donanemab are genuine advances, demonstrating modest slowing of cognitive decline in early Alzheimer’s disease. However, eligibility requires confirmed amyloid pathology via PET or cerebrospinal fluid testing, is restricted to MCI or mild dementia, and carries a high annual drug cost. Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities also occur in 20–30% of participants across trials [], necessitating serial MRI and specialist oversight. Although AAT primarily targets patients with mild cognitive impairment to early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, lifestyle interventions have broader applicability across populations at risk of cognitive decline in general. Rather than viewing lifestyle interventions and AATs as competing strategies, a complementary paradigm is emerging in which multidomain lifestyle modification serves as a relatively accessible, low-risk foundation for cognitive preservation, addressing multiple pathological pathways simultaneously while remaining especially relevant for individuals in whom AAT is clinically unsuitable or practically or economically inaccessible.

Several limitations temper these conclusions. First, most of the MIND diet evidence is observational, and such studies are open to healthy user bias, residual socioeconomic confounding, and reverse causation, since prodromal neurodegeneration can alter food preference and physical activity years before diagnosis. Exposure measurement is a further limitation throughout: MIND scores and physical activity are largely self-reported and subject to misclassification, and cognitive outcomes are captured with instruments that are not interchangeable across studies. RCT evidence on the MIND diet alone remains sparse, and the one landmark trial was negative. Second, the physical activity literature is uneven across levels of evidence. Biomarker and structural imaging findings are heterogeneous and often derive from trials in which these were secondary endpoints, whereas the interventional evidence for cognitive outcomes is somewhat more consistent, though still variable in modality, intensity, and how outcomes were measured. Third, most of the evidence presented here used cognitive test performance as an outcome rather than a clinical disease state such as dementia. Improvement in cognitive scores may not translate into reduced risk of MCI or dementia, which is the outcome that matters most to patients and clinicians.

Priority future research directions should include, firstly, the minimum duration of interventions. Adequately powered, long-duration MIND diet trials are needed to establish how long adherence must be sustained before a cognitive effect emerges, ideally with plasma AD biomarkers and structural imaging as prespecified endpoints rather than secondary ones. The second is dosing. Head-to-head exercise trials are needed to determine the minimum prescription that yields cognitive benefit, since current guidance specifies frequency and duration but not the threshold at which benefit begins. The third is attribution. Mechanistic and factorial studies are needed to separate the individual contributions of diet and exercise from any synergy between them, which no trial to date has been designed to do. The fourth is delivery. Implementation research is needed to develop scalable, culturally adaptable models across diverse populations, while also understanding the cost-effectiveness of such structured interventions.

The MIND diet and physical activity represent two promising, modifiable lifestyle strategies for cognitive preservation and dementia risk reduction, supported by a growing body of evidence. Their mechanisms of action are potentially complementary, with experimental evidence suggesting that the MIND diet constituents may influence amyloid metabolism, neuroinflammation, and vascular health, while physical activity may support cerebrovascular function, neuroplasticity, and glymphatic clearance. However, the extent to which these mechanisms mediate cognitive benefits in humans remains uncertain. The convergence of mechanistic, biomarker, observational, and emerging trial data provides a supporting rationale for shifting from siloed lifestyle recommendations toward an integrated, multimodal strategy that combines MIND dietary optimisation with tailored exercise prescription. This approach is accessible, safe, and broadly applicable, and generally well tolerated when supervised, addressing not only cognitive trajectories but overall health and function across the lifespan, and offering an essential and equitable counterpart to pharmacological disease modification in the evolving dementia-prevention landscape.

neuroscience.title: Basolateral Amygdala Input to the Claustrum: Topology, Excitatory Synapse Properties and Cellular Targets
neuroscience.abstract:
What are the main findings?
Basolateral amygdala (BLA) input to the claustrum (CLA) is mostly excitatory and generates small synaptic responses compared to BLA input to neurons in the nearby insula or to cortical inputs to the CLA.While BLA axons preferentially overlap with CLA shell neurons more than CLA core neurons, and with dorsal CLA neurons projecting to the motor cortex more than CLA core neurons projecting to the retrosplenial cortex, functional innervation is uniform across all these regions.

What are the implications of the main findings?
The BLA is functionally coupled to the CLA and likely provides an excitatory bias instead of being a direct driver of CLA neuron firing.There is only a loose correlation between macroscopic anatomy and physiological function for BLA inputs to the CLA.
Although the claustrum (CLA) has been increasingly implicated in salience and attentional processing, its relationship with the basolateral amygdala (BLA)—a key structure for emotional valence—remains poorly defined. Here, we used viral tracing, optogenetics, and brain slice electrophysiology to characterize the spatial organization and function of BLA–CLA circuitry. We found a clear anatomical compartmentalization of axonal projections between the BLA and CLA within the ring-like outer shell of the CLA, with little axonal labeling in the CLA core. Given this anatomical segregation, it was surprising that optogenetic photostimulation of BLA axons produced comparable excitatory responses in neurons in both the CLA core and shell. Pharmacological experiments indicated that BLA axons make monosynaptic contact with both shell and core neurons, with the latter likely doing so via their distal dendrites that extend into the shell. When CLA neurons were stratified according to their projection targets, BLA axons overlapped more with CLA neurons projecting to the motor cortex than those projecting to the retrosplenial cortex. However, synaptic responses to BLA input were similar in CLA neurons projecting to both cortical targets. Our results provide the first functional characterization of a BLA input pathway that potentially carries valence-related signals to the CLA. Because the excitatory synaptic responses produced in CLA neurons by BLA input were small and subthreshold for action potential generation, our results also argue that the BLA input contributes to a broader convergence of excitatory inputs instead of being a primary driver of CLA activity.
neuroscience.text:
The claustrum (CLA) has long fascinated neuroscientists because of its extensive connectivity with almost the entire cerebral cortex and with other brain regions [,,]. Early work suggested that the CLA could be involved in multisensory integration []. However, since the landmark proposal by Crick and Koch that the CLA may serve as the seat of consciousness [,], most efforts have focused on the role of the CLA in cognition [,,,,,,,,]. For example, behavioral analyses have implicated the CLA in salience detection [,], attention [,,], impulsivity [,], learning and memory [,,,,], anxiety [], and sleep [,,,]. CLA function is highly specific and context-dependent: inhibiting the CLA selectively impairs performance when distractors are present or when associations are being learned but not during simple recall or undistracted performance [,]. Together, these findings suggest that the CLA helps select and prioritize information relevant for cognitive behavior.

The circuit mechanisms underlying the contributions of the CLA to cognitive function are poorly understood []. One major question is how limbic salience signals [] are integrated into CLA circuits. Subcortical inputs to the CLA are relatively sparse but arise from key limbic structures—such as the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) and basolateral amygdala (BLA)—that are central to emotional valence and motivational salience [,,,,]. This has given rise to the influential hypothesis that the CLA acts as an attention coordinator, integrating salience-related signals from regions such as the BLA and MD to guide cortical processing [,]. However, studies of the functions of pathways between subcortical structures to the CLA are scarce and are completely lacking for the BLA-to-CLA circuit.

Here, we combine viral tracing, optogenetics, and brain slice electrophysiology to define how BLA inputs engage claustral microcircuits and projection-defined subnetworks. We found that BLA inputs to the CLA are largely excitatory, but the resulting synaptic responses are small in amplitude and variable. Further, although we observed that BLA–CLA connectivity is anatomically biased toward the ring-like shell surrounding the PV-rich CLA core, excitatory BLA inputs are received by neurons present in both the shell and the core. We further demonstrate substantial anatomical overlap between BLA axons and CLA neurons projecting to both the motor cortex (M1) and the retrosplenial cortex (RSC), with similar functional BLA connectivity for both types of projection neuron. These results provide the first functional characterization of the BLA–CLA pathway and reveal a dissociation between structural topology and synaptic drive: anatomical imaging of input fiber density does not straightforwardly predict functional connectivity, particularly at the level of microcircuitry. Our results support a model in which BLA inputs do not act as the primary driver of CLA activity and instead provide a sparse, projection-biased salience signal that interacts with other cortical and subcortical inputs to shape how the CLA routes information to distinct cortical targets.

A total of 37 C56/BL6J wild-type male mice were used for the experiments (9 for anatomical tracing, 28 for electrophysiology). We employed only male mice to avoid potential complications due to estrous cycle variations in females. Mice used for tracing experiments were 2–3 months old at the time of virus injection, while mice used for the electrophysiological experiments were 1-2 months old at time of virus injection and 2–3 months old at the time of brain slice experiments. All animal procedures were performed according to the guidelines of the NTU Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol A18095, approved on 14 March 2019).

To inject viruses into the brain, mice were deeply anesthetized using isoflurane and placed in a stereotaxic frame equipped with a heating pad. Animal condition was monitored via respiration and body temperature throughout surgery. For pre-surgery analgesic relief, buprenorphine and lidocaine were injected subcutaneously above the back and at the incision site, respectively. A skin incision was made, followed by a craniotomy and dura removal above the target coordinates. Precise viral injections were made using glass pipettes with tip diameters of 30–50 μm and a pressure injector (UltraMicroPump3 and SMARTouch Controller; World Precision Instruments, Sarasota, FL, USA). Both the glass pipettes and Hamilton syringes (5 μL model with RN Compression Fitting; Reno, NV, USA) were first filled with mineral oil before front filling with virus solutions. Viruses were injected at 1–2 nL/s into each target region. The coordinates used were as follows: RSC (ML: 0.5, AP: −2.5, DV: 0.8, angle: 8°), M1 (ML: −1.8, AP: 1.7, DV: −0.8), BLA (ML: −3, AP: −1.55, DV: −4.6), CLA (ML: −2.7, AP: 1.3, DV: −2.9). These coordinates are defined based on the following conventions of medial–lateral (ML) and anterior–posterior (AP), with depth based on dura (DV) while the angle represents the deflection from midline, with pipette tip pointing toward the center where applicable. After completing the injections, pressure was allowed to equilibrate for 5 min before retraction of the glass pipette, followed by incision suturing and recovery on a warming pad. Mice were monitored and supplied with an analgesic (Meloxicam) and an antibiotic (Baytril) in their drinking water for 1 week post-surgery.

To determine bidirectional neuroanatomical connectivity between CLA and BLA, an AAV cocktail was injected into the BLA. The cocktail contained equal parts of AAVretro-hSyn1-EGFP-iCre (the Viral Vector Facility of the Neuroscience Center Zurich; 100 nL; 10 × 1012 vg/mL) and AAV5-hsyn-ChrimsonR-tDT (University of North Carolina [UNC] vector core; 150 nL; 10 × 1012 vg/mL), which were used to label inputs to and outputs from the BLA, respectively.

To investigate BLA innervation of projection-specific CLA neurons, AAVs were injected into 2–3 different locations per animal. BLA output fibers were anterogradely labeled via injection of AAV5-hsyn-ChromsonR-tDt (UNC vector core) into the BLA, while projection-specific CLA neurons were retrogradely labeled via injection of AAVs (AAVretro-hSyn-EGFP-iCre or AAVretro-hSyn-EBFP-iCre; VVF-ZNZ) into M1 and/or RSC separately.

For the expression of opsins (ChrimsonR/ChETA) in BLA axons and presynaptic terminals, 150–250 nL of virus was injected into the BLA, using either AAV5/2-Syn-ChrimsonR-tdTomato (UNC Vector Core) or AAV5/2-Syn-ChETA-EGFP (made in-house). pAAV.hSynap.ChETA(E123T/H134R)-eYFP.WPRE.hGH was a gift from Karl Deisseroth (Addgene plasmid #100049; http://n2t.net/addgene:100049 (accessed on 15 August 2026; RRID:Addgene_100049). Fluorescent proteins (EGFP or mCherry) were paired with opsins labeled with contrasting fluorophores (ChrimsonR-tDT or ChETA-GFP) to aid post hoc identification of CLA somata and BLA fiber locations. Surgical procedures were identical to those described in .

For both anatomical and physiological experiments, the injection sites in each mouse were inspected to confirm that viruses were injected into the correct target regions. Animals in which fluorescence was not localized to the target regions were excluded from analysis. In our anatomical experiments, 5 of the 9 injections were made into the anterior BLA, and these resulted in the dense labeling of BLA axons in the CLA shell and dysgranular insula (DI) []. The remaining 4 mice did not have sufficient BLA axonal labeling within the CLA to be useful. For our physiological experiments, 25 out of 28 mice yielded slices with CLA neurons that exhibited synaptic responses in response to BLA photostimulation. Two of the remaining mice had weak expression of opsins in BLA fibers within the CLA and yielded no measurable light-evoked synaptic responses (4–5 cells examined). The third mouse was excluded because of poor brain slice quality, which prevented reliable recordings.

To allow adequate time for expression of fluorophores in anatomical experiments, animals were perfused and sacrificed 2–4 weeks post-surgery. Transcardial perfusion was performed using saline, followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Dissected brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight, followed by 30% sucrose solution in PBS for 2 days, or until the brains sank. Brain sections (60 µm thickness) were first washed, blocked, and then stained with primary antibodies—rabbit-anti-PV (1:1000, Swant: PV-28, RRID:AB_2315235), chicken-anti-GFP (1:1000, Abcam:AB_13970, RRID:AB_300798), and rat-anti-mCherry monoclonal antibody (16D7; 1:1000, from Thermo Fisher Scientific, RRID:AB_2536611)—overnight at room temperature (RT, 24 °C) or for 2 days at 4 °C. These sections were then washed and treated with secondary antibodies (1:1000, Alexa Fluor 488, Alexa Fluor 568, and Alexa Fluor 647; RRID:AB_142924, RRID:AB_2534121, RRID:AB_2536101) at RT for 2–3 h. Stained sections were also counterstained with DAPI to visualize cell nuclei.

Images were acquired with a Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner (Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany). To reduce out-of-focus blur, stained sections were imaged at different focal depths (using z-stack) in Extended Depth of Focus mode, which combines in-focus images from each z-plane to reconstruct a 2D projection. Tiled images were subsequently flat-field corrected and stitched using the WholeBrain program created by Daniel Fürth []. All images were processed using custom R scripts in RStudio (Version 2025.09.2 Build 418, Posit Software, PBC) and ImageJ macros (ImageJ version 1.54p / Fiji version 2.16.1) to rotate slices, crop CLA/AI regions, and separately process individual fluorescent channels. Locations of neuronal somata were quantified using processes adapted from the QUINT workflow []. Retrogradely labeled somata were segmented using Pixel classification in ilastik [], followed by watershedding, particle exclusion (size: 60–infinity, circularity: 0.3–1), and binarization using ImageJ base functions. Anterograde-labeled axons were first extracted using a Hessian filter (FeatureJ version 2.0.0; https://imagescience.org/meijering/software/featurej/ (accessed on 15 August 2026); “largest eigenvalue of Hessian tensor” and “smoothing scale” factor set to 159), which enhanced the features of curvilinear fibers, followed by inversion and background subtraction (sliding paraboloid, 50-pixel radius = 33 µm) to enhance image contrast. PV-labeled sections were smoothed using a Gaussian Blur filter (sigma = 50) to homogenize fluorescence intensities to ease the identification of CLA and AI layers. The processed fluorescence channels were subsequently merged and quantified together.

To quantify soma and fiber fluorescence across the CLA and AI layers, line profile measurements were made using ImageJ and subsequently organized and plotted using custom R scripts. Using the PV channel as a reference, for all AP sections, a line profile (200 µm in width) was drawn in ImageJ that spanned from the anterior commissure to the pia and crossed the CLA core (). A region of interest (ROI) was generated for each channel, and the profile plot was used to quantify the density of fluorescence across the ROI. Results from the profile plot were subsequently exported and further analyzed in R.

To aid cross-animal and cross-section comparisons, raw fluorescence values were smoothed to generate an average profile for each fluorescence channel. These average profiles were subsequently aligned across animals, relative to the anterior commissure, by using the first peak of PV labeling to identify the CLA core. AI layers were also identified based on the enrichment of PV expression in layers 2/3 and 5, while the lack of PV expression was used to identify the remaining layers. Due to a lack of markers for the CLA shell, the first fluorescence minimum following the peak fluorescence of the PV core was identified as the transition point between the CLA and the AI (also referred to as the CLA shell). Measurements from each channel were subsequently normalized for fluorescence intensity and compiled across animals based on the position of the AP. To ease interpretation, an average fit line was generated for each channel using local polynomial regression (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing, LOESS) to emphasize fluorescence differences across the CLA and AI layers. Statistical comparisons were performed using custom R scripts.

Acute brain slices were prepared 2–4 weeks after virus injection to allow sufficient time for opsin expression. Mice were anesthetized with isofluorane and perfused with ice-cold artificial cerebrospinal spinal fluid (ACSF) prior to euthanasia via decapitation. ACSF comprised the following: 126 mM NaCl, 24 mM NaHCO3, 1 mM NaH2PO4, 2.5 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl2, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM glucose, and 0.4 mM ascorbic acid; 290–305 mOsm; pH 7.4; and gassed with 95% O2/5% CO2. Perfusion was done to clear blood vessels near the CLA. Brains were isolated and transferred into the cutting solution within 45 s to preserve slice viability. The cutting solution comprised the following: 250 mM sucrose, 26 mM NaHCO3, 10 mM glucose, 4 mM MgCl2, 3 mM myo-inositol, 2.5 mM KCl, 2 mM sodium pyruvate, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, 0.5 mM ascorbic acid, 0.1 mM CaCl2, and 1 mM kynurenic acid; 350–360 mOsm; pH of 7.4; and gassed with 95% O2/5% CO2. Coronal brain slices (250 µm) were cut using a Leica VT 1000S vibratome; slices designated for patching were incubated at 34 °C in ACSF for 30 min to recover from cutting, while slices containing the virus injection site were immediately fixed in PFA for subsequent histological examination. Slices designated for patching were subsequently transferred to ACSF at RT and allowed to equilibrate for 20 min prior to recording.

Whole-cell patch clamp recordings were performed using techniques described in detail in Graf et al. []. In brief, recording electrodes (3.5–8.5 MΩ tip resistance) were pulled from borosilicate glass and filled with K-gluconate-based internal solution containing the following: 130 mM K-gluconate, 10 mM KOH, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM HEPES, 4 mM Na2ATP, 0.4 mM Na3GTP, 5 mM EGTA, 5 mM Na2 phosphocreatinin, 0.2% neurobiotin, and/or Alexa 594 (285–295 mOsm, pH 7.4). Brain slices were submerged in a recording chamber that was continuously perfused with oxygenated ACSF at room temperature. The recording pipettes were positioned visually using a combination of the differential interference contrast and fluorescence channels of a two-photon microscope (Olympus FV-1000, Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan; 950 nm excitation wavelength). Recordings were excluded from analysis if the electrode access resistance was greater than 30 MΩ, or if the holding current was larger than 100 pA. Electrophysiological data were acquired at 50 kHz and filtered at 10 kHz using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA) and a Digidata 1440 interface (Molecular Devices).

Patched neurons were electrophysiologically identified by recording their responses to 1 s long current pulses that increased in amplitude at 20 pA increments. From these responses, 21 intrinsic electrical properties were extracted [] by using code adapted from the Claustrum Classifier: https://github.com/adityanairneuro/claustrum (accessed on 15 August 2026). These properties were extracted from voltage responses to 3 different current intensities: action potential (AP) threshold current (Ct), a current twice as large as Ct (Ct*2), and the current level where the maximum number of APs was evoked (Cmax). A brief description of these properties follows. The resting membrane potential and membrane resistance are characteristic passive membrane properties. Most other properties were calculated based on either the AP responses evoked by Ct*2 or by Cmax. The coefficient of variance (CV) is commonly used as a measure of firing variability; the larger CV, the more irregular AP firing is. CV was calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation of interspike intervals (ISIs) divided by the mean ISI. Since doublet spiking was observed in a large portion of neurons—a typical feature of CLA projection neurons []—two additional CV values were calculated, CV-1 and CV-2, which excluded the first action potential and the first two APs, respectively. The amplitude ratio of the first AP over the second AP, the second AP over the third AP, and the first AP/last AP were also taken to represent the AP amplitude adaptation that are often observed in CLA neuron responses to prolonged depolarization []. Extracted properties were compiled and analyzed using custom R scripts and used to identify neurons, either as projection neurons (PN1–5) or interneurons (PV, SST, and VIP) [].

BLA fibers expressing ChrimsonR or ChETA were photostimulated with light (denoted as hν in figures) from a mercury arc lamp delivered to the specimen via a GFP filter cube (470–495 nm excitation; 505 nm dichroic mirror) or a 436/514/604 nm dichroic mirror, which delivered light at 473–515 nm and 550–607 nm. The former provided 45 mW of light at 500 nm (to activate ChETA), while the latter provided a similar amount of light power at 590 nm (to activate ChrimsonR). The entire specimen field (0.24 mm2 area) was illuminated with light flashes, whose duration (4 ms) was controlled by an electronic shutter (Uniblitz).

Whole-cell patch clamp recordings were used to detect light-evoked postsynaptic currents under voltage-clamp conditions. These responses were averaged across 25 trials, with a 5 s interval between each trial to allow time for any short-term synaptic plasticity evoked by a prior light flash to subside. Reported voltages are not corrected for liquid–liquid junction potentials. Current responses were pre-processed using Clampfit software (Version 11.4.3, part of the pCLAMP 11 Software Suite, Molecular Devices; RRID:SCR_011323): traces were filtered using a low-pass (500 Hz) Gaussian filter and were baseline-adjusted by subtracting the mean current measured 50 ms before the light flash. All further analysis was done using custom scripts written in R. Light-induced synaptic currents were analyzed between 5 and 25 ms post-stimulation. To exclude spontaneous synaptic currents and noisy responses, individual responses were first automatically detected using two criteria: (1) peak time was later than the mean time of current onset and less than the sum of mean current decay time plus mean current peak time; and (2) response amplitude was greater than 5 pA. Each response was then visually inspected to confirm that it exhibited time-locked behavior and a normal waveform. Response percentage was calculated as the number of trials with synaptic responses that met these criteria, divided by the total number of trials. The 5–25 ms time window is sufficiently wide to detect delayed synaptic events associated with jitter in presynaptic photostimulation.

In a subset of experiments, light-evoked synaptic potential responses were also recorded under current-clamp conditions. Synaptic potentials were recorded in response to trains of light flashes (2 s duration, each flash 4 ms in duration) during widefield photo -stimulation at 5 Hz and 10 Hz. Synaptic potentials were averaged across at least 10 trials with 4 s intervals between trials.

A subset of cells exhibiting synaptic responses to BLA photostimulation were further tested for monosynaptic inputs [,]. In these experiments, tetrodotoxin (TTX; 1 µM), a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker, was used to prevent action potentials evoked by photostimulation. This was followed by treatment with saline containing both TTX and 4-aminopyridine (4AP; 100 µM) [,] for at least 10 min. A subset of TTX+4AP experiments were performed under increased extracellular Ca2+ conditions (4 mM instead of the usual 2 mM), to increase EPSC amplitude and improve the likelihood of detecting the small responses typically observed in TTX+4AP conditions.

To visualize the location of patched cells via their neurobiotin labeling, as well as the PV and fluorescent proteins used to determine the location of the CLA and its BLA inputs, brain slices were fixed in PFA overnight at 4 °C and then processed via standard immunohistochemical processing. In short, slices were rinsed with PBS, blocked, and then permeabilized in PBS with 0.25% Triton X-100 and 5% goat-serum for an hour, followed by incubation in primary antibodies for 48 h at 4 °C (rabbit-anti-PV, 1:800, Swant: PV-28, RRID:AB_2315235; chicken-anti-GFP, 1:1000, Abcam: ab13970, RRID:AB_300798; rat-anti-mCherry, 1:1000, Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat# M11217, RRID:AB_2536611; and fluorophore-conjugated streptavidin, 1:1000, Alexa Fluor 405, or Alexa Fluor 647, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Slices were washed again and incubated in secondary antibodies for 2–3 h at room temperature (1:1000, Alexa Fluor 488, Alexa Fluor 568, or Alexa Fluor 647; RRID:AB_142924, RRID: AB_2534121, RRID: AB_2866492, Thermo Fisher Scientific), followed by a final wash, and mounted onto slides with an anti-fading agent (PVA, 10981, Sigma Aldrich). Images were acquired on a confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM 800, Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany) using a 10x objective.

The locations of patched cells were first identified and labeled on post hoc stained images via Zeiss software (Zen Blue 3.2). Correlation of electrophysiological responses with neuron locations was done using a combination of live slice images and post hoc staining images. A custom ImageJ macro script was developed to further process the images for unbiased identification of the claustrum core and quantification of the location of patched cells. In brief, images from all channels were background-subtracted (Rolling Ball, 25 pixels (= 16.5 μm) radius, sliding paraboloid) and filtered (Gaussian Blur, 4 µm sigma). Each fluorescence channel was then binarized using different auto-thresholding methods. For retrogradely labeled CLA cells, Otsu was used [], while thresholding of BLA fibers and PV staining was done with Yen []. The claustrum core was identified by enrichment of PV staining, and an ellipse was fitted to the shape of the CLA core. Our thresholding method was reliable in most cases and only minor adjustments had to be made in a subset of slices where PV cell enrichment did not form a complete ellipse. In these cases, the BLA enrichment zone was referenced to ensure that the size of the PV ellipse was accurate. ROIs for the CLA core and patched cell locations were added, quantified, and exported. Further analysis using the location information extracted from ImageJ was done using custom R scripts. In summary, assignment of the CLA border was made purely based on PV and BLA fiber enrichment and was independent of physiological responses or locations of patched cells.

Because multiple neurons were often examined in the same animal, comparisons of most electrophysiological properties were performed using linear mixed-effects models (lme4, lmerTest [,]) with animal as a random intercept; comparisons of binary outcomes (e.g., response probability) instead used generalized linear mixed-effects models with a binomial link. Pairwise contrasts, 95% confidence intervals, and Cohen’s d effect sizes were obtained using emmeans and effectsize functions [], following established recommendations for nested neuroscientific data []. Where too few mice were available to estimate a random-effects variance, results are reported descriptively instead. p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons within each panel of properties using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure [].

We first examined the anatomical organization of connections between the BLA and the CLA. The lack of an external capsule has led to inconsistent structural definitions of CLA boundaries in rodents. We employed the most widely used criterion for labeling the CLA core: post hoc parvalbumin (PV) immunohistochemistry [,,,]. This allowed us to visualize the PV-rich CLA core as an oval region (A), as well as the strongly labeled PV interneurons in layers 5b and 2/3 of the nearby agranular insular cortex (AI; A).

To map the topography of BLA–CLA connectivity, we injected a mixture of retrograde and anterograde AAVs into the BLA (B,C) and imaged the spatial distribution of the fluorophores expressed by these viruses in coronal sections that included the CLA (rectangle in B). The retrograde virus (AAVretro-hsyn-Cre-2A-EGFP) produced a cytoplasmic GFP label in CLA neurons projecting to the BLA (toBLA; D,E and ), while the anterograde virus (AAV5-hsyn-ChrimsonR-TdT) labeled CLA-projecting BLA axons with membrane-bound tdTomato (BLAFibers; D,E and ).

We observed a relative absence of both EGFP (toBLA, green) and tdTomato (BLAFibers, red) within the CLA core (white dashed line; E). Instead, both fluorophores were enriched in the region immediately surrounding the core, forming a ring-like structure (D,E). This distinctive positioning is consistent with a location within the claustrum shell (CLA shell) [,,,,]. For inter-animal comparison and objective delineation of the CLA, we masked retrogradely labeled CLA somata (toBLA, green) and anterogradely labeled BLA axonal fibers (BLAFibers, red) and sampled fluorescence from the anterior commissure to the pia across the CLA center (). Raw density profiles were smoothed to generate average spatial profiles (F, bold lines). Profiles were centered on the first peak of PV staining (CLA core) from the anterior commissure; subsequent peaks were assigned to AI L5b and L2/3 (F). Lacking a molecular marker for the CLA shell, we defined the first trough of PV staining as the boundary between the CLA and AI (shell/L6a).

Retrograde tracing revealed an unexpected paucity of anatomical connectivity between the PV-rich CLA core and the BLA (D, toBLA). Most toBLA neurons resided in upper AI layers, with only sparse labeling near the CLA core (E). EGFP fluorescence was bright in upper-layer AI somata and neurites, whereas the neurites of CLA core neurons were weakly labeled. To focus on cell body locations, we segmented only toBLA somata. The fluorescence of masked toBLA somata was quantified from the anterior commissure to the pia, across the CLA core (, green), and smoothed to obtain average fluorescence spatial profiles (F, toBLA). These analyses revealed a small number of toBLA neurons near the CLA shell/AI L6a but few neurons within the CLA core (F). This paucity of toBLA neurons in the CLA core was consistent along the rostral–caudal axis in all mice, as reflected by low toBLA densities at the first PV peak (CLA core; , vertical line). A thin halo of toBLA neurons surrounded the CLA core along the entire rostral–caudal axis, appearing as narrow density peaks flanking the core that decreased with distance, in parallel with the shrinking CLA core (, background peaks). Our results indicate that BLA-projecting neurons largely avoid the PV-rich CLA core and preferentially occupy its border. This positioning of toBLA neurons suggests topological heterogeneity of neurons within the CLA complex according to their projection targets. In addition, many BLA-projecting neurons were located in L5a and L2/3 of the AI (E, toBLA; ), suggesting that AI-to-BLA connectivity could be greater than CLA-to-BLA connectivity.

CLA-based retrograde transsynaptic labeling indicates that BLA neurons project to the CLA [,], but it is unknown whether BLA axons innervate the entire CLA or only specific subregions. To resolve the structural organization of BLA inputs, we examined the distribution of anterogradely labeled BLA axons within the CLA (BLAFibers). BLAFibers largely avoided the CLA core and, instead, densely innervated the surrounding CLA shell (E, BLAFibers). To quantify BLAFibers across animals, we masked axonal fluorescence and sampled fiber density across the CLA (red in ), then generated smoothed average plots from raw measurements (F, BLAFibers). BLAFibers density was highest in the CLA shell and decreased toward AI L5b (F). The ring-like innervation pattern—two flanking density peaks that scaled with CLA size—was consistent along the rostral–caudal axis in all mice (). These observations indicate that BLA input preferentially innervates the CLA shell, though our functional analyses described next also surprisingly reveal a substantial BLA input to the CLA core.

Although the BLA-to-CLA pathway features prominently in hypotheses of CLA function [], the functional properties of this pathway are unknown. Therefore, we next combined electrophysiology and optogenetics to determine the function of BLA-to-CLA projections. Further, because our tracing data indicated a topological bias for BLA axons within the CLA shell rather than the CLA core, we compared BLA synaptic input to neurons within the CLA core versus neurons within the CLA shell.

To define the function of BLA-to-CLA projections, we combined optogenetic activation of BLA inputs with whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of synaptic responses of CLA neurons. The red-shifted opsin, ChrimsonR, was expressed in BLA neurons using an anterograde AAV, allowing selective photostimulation of BLA inputs when light was delivered to the CLA (A, right). Synaptic connectivity between the BLA and the CLA was then assessed in coronal brain slices by measuring postsynaptic responses evoked in CLA neurons in response to widefield (0.24 mm2 area) photostimulation of BLA axons within the CLA (A, inset). Recordings were obtained from a total of 89 projection neurons and 11 interneurons, as determined from their intrinsic electrical properties []. Neurons in both the CLA core and shell were examined. In some cases, both CLA core and shell neurons were patched simultaneously to allow direct comparison of BLA input properties (B). Patched neurons were also filled with neurobiotin, which diffused from the recording pipette into their cytoplasm. This allowed us to examine neuronal structure (B) and to determine the precise location of neurons (C) relative to the PV-defined CLA core (D) and to the distribution of ChrimsonR-expressing BLA axons (E,F).

To measure the synaptic responses of CLA neurons (n = 100 from 14 mice) to BLA axon photostimulation, we recorded light-evoked postsynaptic currents at two different membrane potentials, −70 mV and −40 mV. At each holding potential, responses were recorded over 25 trials (A,B; blue traces) and an average response was computed after excluding traces where no synaptic currents were evoked (A,B; red traces). Holding at −70 mV maximized the amplitude of excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs), which were inward at this potential and had a reversal potential near 0 mV. Holding at −70 mV also minimized the amplitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs), which had a reversal potential near −70 mV under our experimental conditions. Thus, responses observed at −70 mV were primarily EPSCs (A). In contrast, holding at a Vh of −40 mV increased the electrochemical driving force on chloride ions to reveal outward IPSCs (B), while reducing the driving force on EPSCs to yield smaller inward EPSCs (A). Thus, comparing responses measured at these two potentials allowed us to classify the inputs evoked by photostimulating BLA axons as excitatory, inhibitory, or mixed. To avoid spontaneous synaptic currents, only responses that were time-locked to the light flashes (between 5 and 25 ms after flash) were considered to be responses to BLA axon photostimulation. (Note that ChrimsonR has relatively slow activation kinetics that yield a latency of ~8 ms for evoking action potentials [].) Light-evoked responses in CLA neurons were mostly excitatory (A,D), with a small percentage of inhibitory responses (B,D) and one case of dual EPSC and IPSC responses (C,D).

Despite widespread expression of ChrimsonR in the BLA (e.g., C), widefield photostimulation of BLA axons evoked postsynaptic responses in only half of the 100 CLA neurons examined (D, top). This suggests that only a subset of CLA neurons receive BLA input. Both projection neurons and interneurons received excitatory synaptic input from the BLA (D, bottom), and there were no significant differences in the EPSCs produced by BLA photostimulation in the two types of postsynaptic neurons (). Although slice preparation inevitably severs some axons, widefield photostimulation is capable of evoking synaptic responses even from short axonal segments within the slice [,]; for this reason, most synaptic inputs present in vivo should be available for photostimulation, even if their axons were cut. Therefore, our observation of postsynaptic responses in only a fraction of CLA neurons is consistent with BLA axons targeting only a subset of CLA neurons.

We next characterized the properties of excitatory synaptic transmission between the BLA and the CLA (A). Within individual CLA neurons (n = 61 from 13 mice), light-evoked EPSCs were highly variable in amplitude (B,C). To obtain a reliable assessment of these responses in CLA neurons, BLA axons were photostimulated repeatedly; short-term synaptic plasticity was minimized by separating light flashes with relatively long inter-stimulus intervals (5 s) and this strategy was successful because we observed no systematic changes in EPSC amplitudes across the trials.

EPSC amplitudes fluctuated substantially from trial to trial (B, blue traces) and spanned a broad range (C, blue bars). Across all experiments, the mean amplitude of EPSCs was 18.4 pA (at −70 mV holding potential); this corresponds to a synaptic conductance of 0.26 nS and is several times smaller than the minimal current required to evoked APs in CLA projection neurons and interneurons []. To determine whether these EPSCs could evoke APs, in a subset of experiments we turned off the voltage clamp to record excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) evoked by BLA photostimulation (see Figure 6A,B below). Photostimulation indeed evoked only subthreshold EPSPs that had a mean amplitude of 0.95 ± 0.26 mV (n = 16 cells from four mice). This indicates that the small amplitude and low conductance of the EPSCs evoked by BLA axon photostimulation renders them insufficient to generate APs in postsynaptic CLA neurons, even under conditions where many of these axons are being photostimulated.

Synaptic variability was quantified by the coefficient of variation (CV) of EPSCs, which was calculated as the standard deviation of EPSC amplitudes divided by the mean EPSC amplitude. Only trials with measurable EPSCs were used to compute the mean EPSC amplitude (B, red line) and CV. The mean CV of CLA neuron EPSCs was 0.71 ± 0.25, indicating highly variable synaptic transmission. This is at, or slightly above, the high end of CV values calculated for other central excitatory synapses, which range from 0.2 to 0.7 [,]. Very similar results were obtained when using a different opsin, ChETA, to photostimulate BLA axons ().

In some trials, photostimulation of BLA axons produced no detectable EPSCs (flat traces in B), indicating synaptic failures (black bar in C). To quantify synaptic reliability for each neuron, we measured failure probability which was defined as the fraction of trials without an EPSC. The mean failure probability at BLA-to-CLA synapses was 0.45 ± 0.29, indicating that even CLA neurons responding to BLA axon photostimulation produced EPSCs only about half the time. A similar result was observed when photostimulating BLA axons with ChETA () Thus, BLA inputs to CLA neurons are small, variable, and unreliable at both single-cell and population levels.

Our observation that the high EPSC failure rate was present whether photostimulating BLA axons with either ChrimsonR or ChETA suggests that the apparent unreliability of BLA–CLA synapses is not a consequence of inefficient photostimulation. To further consider this possibility, we also recorded EPSCs in neurons within the neighboring AI (C,F) while using ChrimsonR to photostimulate the BLA axons that densely innervate the AI (E,F) []. In contrast to CLA neurons, L5b neurons displayed larger, more consistent, and more reliable EPSCs (n = 6/8 responding neurons from seven mice). In the recordings from a L5b neuron shown in E, median EPSC amplitude was 91.6 pA, which was higher than the median amplitude of 36.2 pA for the CLA neuron responses shown in B. Even though the amplitudes of EPSCs in L5b neurons were larger, EPSC amplitudes still spanned a wide range (F). Across all experiments, mean EPSC amplitude in L5b neurons was significantly (p.adj < 0.01) larger than in CLA neurons (G). Calculation of the effect size yielded a Cohen’s d value of 1.70, indicating a large difference between EPSCs in the CLA and L5b. Thus, BLA input onto L5b AI neurons is relatively strong in comparison to CLA neurons. Importantly, there were no failures: EPSCs were observed in response to every photostimulus applied to the BLA axons. At the population level, both the CV (H; Cohen’s d = 0.85, p.adj = 0.0022) and failure probability (I; Cohen’s d = 1.10, p.adj = 0.00016) of CLA EPSCs were significantly higher than those recorded in L5b. The robustness of light-evoked EPSCs in L5b neurons confirms that our experimental conditions were adequate to photostimulate BLA axons within L5b. Thus, the weakness and unreliability observed when photostimulating BLA inputs to the CLA appear to be genuine features of this circuit.

Because polysynaptic pathways typically exhibit longer latencies than monosynaptic connections [,], we also measured the latency for EPSC onset. BLA-evoked EPSCs in the CLA showed a broad latency range, with a mean of 9.3 ± 1.6 ms. On average, the latency of EPSCs recorded in L5b neurons (8.2 ± 1.3 ms) was shorter than for CLA neurons (J; Cohen’s d = 0.61, p.adj = 0.027). Accounting for the time required for ChrimsonR photostimulation to evoke action potentials (~8 ms) [], the latencies of L5b neuron EPSCs are consistent with monosynaptic transmission. The broader range of EPSC latencies for CLA neurons raises the possibility that CLA responses may comprise a mix of both monosynaptic and polysynaptic components. We will address this issue in depth in .

Given that the CLA is organized into core and shell domains, with the CLA shell apparently preferentially innervated by BLA fibers (), we next asked whether this topography could explain our observation that only a subset of CLA neurons receive BLA input (C). We used two criteria to divide the CLA into core and shell compartments: regions of dense BLA fiber projections were used to define the shell (E), while post hoc PV immunocytochemistry was used to delineate the PV-rich core (D). Neurobiotin filling (C) was used to identify the positions of CLA neurons relative to the core boundary (F) and thereby define whether these neurons were in the core or shell.

We recorded from neurons in the CLA core (n = 68 from 14 mice) and shell (n = 53 from 15 mice) to compare their responses to BLA axon photostimulation. Such photostimulation evoked EPSCs in neurons in both locations (A,B). The spatial distribution of core and shell neurons that responded to photostimulation of BLA axons (C, filled symbols) revealed that these cells were intermingled with neurons that did not respond (C, open symbols). Quantitatively, the fraction of cells exhibiting light-evoked EPSCs was below 60% in both the core and shell regions (D) and was not significantly different (odds ratio = 0.68, p.adj = 0.35). Thus, despite a clear anatomical difference in BLA axon density that we observed between the CLA core and shell ( and ), the fraction of CLA neurons located in these two compartments that responded to BLA axon photostimulation were not different (C). To determine whether this relatively low connection probability was specific to the CLA, we also compared the fraction of L5b cells within the AI that exhibited EPSCs. The response probability of these neurons was not significantly different (D; p.adj = 0.27) when compared to either CLA core neurons (odds ratio = 0.28) or to CLA shell neurons (odds ratio = 0.23).

Despite BLA connection probability being similar for neurons in the CLA core and shell, we next asked whether EPSC properties differed between the two regions. In fact, EPSCs were remarkably similar in both regions, with effect sizes for differences between all properties being negligible to small (n = 31 core cells from 12 mice and 30 shell cells from 10 mice). Mean EPSC amplitudes did not differ between core and shell neurons, indicating comparable synaptic strength in both regions (E; Cohen’s d = −0.06, p.adj = 0.95). Trial-to-trial variability in EPSC amplitude was prominent in both regions (A,B) and yielded nearly identical CV values for core and shell EPSCs (F; Cohen’s d = 0.19, p.adj = 0.82). Mean failure probabilities also were similar in both regions (Cohen’s d = 0.01, p.adj = 0.97) and spanned similar ranges (SDs of 0.28 and 0.31), indicating equivalent synaptic reliability (G). Finally, EPSC onset latencies were comparable between core and shell neurons (H; Cohen’s d = −0.07, p.adj = 0.95). All these results are consistent with CLA core and shell neurons having similar underlying circuit architecture.

We next asked whether the BLA-to-CLA circuit exhibits short-term synaptic plasticity in the core or shell neurons by measuring EPSPs evoked by photostimulation of BLA axons. Such stimuli evoked only subthreshold EPSPs in both CLA core neurons (A, top; n = 6 from four mice) and shell neurons (A, bottom; n = 10 from three mice). EPSP amplitude was similar between core and shell neurons (B), consistent with our measurements of EPSCs in these neurons (E). We examined short-term plasticity by measuring the amplitude of EPSPs evoked by repetitive photostimulation of BLA axons. EPSPs measured during 5 Hz photostimulation (C) were constant in amplitude over the duration of 2 s long trains (E,G). This was the case in both core and shell neurons (C,E,G) and indicates minimal synaptic plasticity at this rate of synaptic activity. During 10 Hz photostimulation, there was pronounced temporal summation of individual EPSPs (D) but a net depression of EPSP amplitude over the course of 2 s (D,F). The amount of synaptic depression was not significantly different between the claustral core and shell neurons (G; Cohen’s d = 0.58, p.adj = 0.70).

In summary, basal synaptic transmission between presynaptic BLA axons and postsynaptic CLA neurons does not differ between the CLA core and shell. Further, synaptic depression is evident at 10 Hz and this form of activity-dependent synaptic plasticity also does not differ between core and shell neurons.

The presence of functional BLA synapses in the CLA core, despite the low axon density there, raises the question of whether BLA inputs directly terminate onto CLA core neurons. We next addressed this question by asking whether BLA inputs to CLA neurons are monosynaptic. For this purpose, we used a pharmacological strategy developed by Petreanu et al. [] that is based on treatment with tetrodotoxin (TTX) and 4-aminopyridine (4AP) [,,]. TTX blocks voltage-gated sodium channels [], abolishing action potential propagation in BLA axons and thereby eliminating all postsynaptic responses. Subsequent addition of 4AP, a blocker of voltage-gated potassium channels, promotes local calcium spikes at axon terminals [] and can restore transmitter release from directly photostimulated terminals []. Thus, EPSCs observed in the presence of both drugs (TTX+4AP) should reflect direct, monosynaptic connections because action potentials in intermediate neurons of any polysynaptic circuit would still be blocked.

For neurons in both the CLA core (A) and the shell (B), light-evoked EPSCs were sequentially recorded in control conditions, in the presence of TTX and then in the presence of TTX+4AP. As expected, EPSCs observed in control conditions (A,B—top traces) were abolished by TTX (A,B—middle traces). In TTX+4AP conditions, five out of 12 CLA core neurons exhibited EPSCs (A—lower traces and pie chart). This demonstrates the existence of direct monosynaptic connections between the BLA and neurons within the CLA core, despite the low density of BLA fibers in the core. Similarly, one out of seven neurons in the CLA shell exhibited EPSCs in the presence of TTX+4AP (B—lower traces and pie chart), indicating the existence of direct monosynaptic BLA-to-CLA shell neuron connections. Thus, at least a subset of the excitatory connections from the BLA to the CLA core and the CLA shell are clearly monosynaptic, although other inputs may include polysynaptic components.

CLA neurons projecting to specific cortical targets are partially segregated into zones and inputs from related cortical areas preferentially innervate the same zones [,,,,,]. For example, CLA neurons projecting to M1 and RSC occupy distinct, minimally overlapping territories: the former reside within the dorsal CLA (dCLA), while the latter are within the CLA itself []. In addition, some inputs to the CLA selectively enrich the CLA shell but not the PV-rich CLA core (see  and , as well as references [,,]). These findings have led to the idea that different CLA zones form partially segregated input–output modules [,].

We determined whether such cellular topology reflects CLA functional organization by examining BLA inputs onto CLA neurons projecting to M1 or to RSC. The clear topographical segregation of M1-projecting and RSC-projecting CLA neurons [] makes these projection-defined cell populations useful for determining whether functional input to the CLA parallels cellular zoning. We first revisit the anatomical relationship between CLA neurons projecting to M1 or RSC and then will consider BLA innervation of each projection neuron subpopulation.

To label CLA neurons that project to M1 or to RSC, retrograde AAVs expressing different fluorophores were injected into each of these areas (A). Neurons projecting to M1 (toM1) and neurons projecting to RSC (toRSC) were present in clearly distinct CLA zones (B), as previously reported []. PV immunohistochemistry again was used to identify the CLA core as a landmark (PV in C) and revealed that toM1 neurons clustered in the dCLA, dorsal to the CLA core (C). In contrast, toRSC neurons clustered within the CLA core (C). These relationships were quantified via masked spatial profiles (D and ).

Given the ill-defined boundaries between CLA subregions, we measured fluorescence intensities across the full dorsal–ventral extent of the dCLA and CLA (C and ). Raw fluorescence values were smoothed to yield average density traces (D). The first PV peak was defined as CLA core and the subsequent trough in PV fluorescence as the transition between the CLA shell and dCLA (D, PV). Comparing the distributions of M1-projecting and RSC-projecting neurons along this axis, toRSC somata were clearly confined to the CLA core, as indicated by the near-complete overlap between peaks of toRSC and PV labeling (D, PV and toRSC). In contrast, toM1 neurons clustered in the dCLA, approximately 500 µm dorsal to the PV-rich CLA core (D). These results provide quantitative support for the conclusion that M1-projecting and RSC-projecting CLA neurons occupy distinct, projection-based zones within the CLA complex. This zone-specific localization was consistent along the rostral–caudal axis (): toM1 neurons clustered in dCLA and rarely appeared in CLA (), whereas toRSC neurons occupied CLA core and were rarely observed in dCLA (). Thus, M1- and RSC-projecting CLA neurons form largely non-overlapping topological subpopulations throughout the entire claustrum complex.

To compare the BLA input received by these two populations of CLA projection neurons, BLA axons again were labeled with an anterograde AAV expressing red-tagged ChrimsonR that was injected into the BLA. The red-labeled BLA axons (BLAFibers) were enriched in the region surrounding—albeit minimally within—the central region of the CLA core (B,C), consistent with the results shown in E and D. BLA axon density was quantified across the dorsal–ventral CLA axis (C and , BLAFibers). A comparison of the distributions of toM1 and toRSC somata with that of BLAFibers revealed an inverse relationship between the density of toRSC somata and BLAFibers (D). This suggests that toRSC neurons in the CLA core might receive little BLA input. Conversely, BLAFibers density was relatively high near the toM1 peak (D), suggesting that BLA input onto toM1 neurons could be substantial.

These anatomical relationships were consistent along the rostral–caudal axis: BLAFibers maintained peak densities flanking the CLA core and remained sparse within it (). BLAFibers distribution was consistently the inverse of that of toRSC somata (), again suggesting minimal BLA input to many toRSC neurons. In contrast, BLAFibers overlapped more strongly with toM1 somata in rostral sections (, top row), consistent with stronger BLA input to toM1 neurons rostrally. In intermediate and caudal sections, BLAFibers appeared reduced near the toM1 peak (, middle and bottom rows), suggesting weaker BLA innervation of toM1 neurons posteriorly. This may partly reflect limitations of profile averaging, where weaker BLAFibers signals in intermediate/caudal sections could cause a slight misalignment of peaks.

To more accurately compare BLA innervation of M1-projecting and RSC-projecting CLA neurons, we measured the fluorescence of BLAFibers in 50 µm × 100 µm areas centered on the peaks of toM1 or toRSC soma density. Mean BLAFibers fluorescence intensity within these regions was compared across sections and animals (E). This comparison was based on samples from two mice (14 sections total); because the unit of biological replication for this analysis is the animal, rather than the individual section, this result should be interpreted with some caution. However, for both mice, BLAFibers fluorescence was consistently higher in the location of toM1 neurons than the location of toRSC neurons in the same section and was also consistent across the rostral–caudal axis (), indicating stronger anatomical overlap between BLA axons and M1-projecting CLA neurons. Together, our tracing data suggest that BLA input varies systematically with projection target and CLA topology and that BLA innervation may be heavier for M1-projecting than for RSC-projecting CLA neurons.

We next determined whether these anatomical differences in BLA axons reflect differences in BLA synaptic input by measuring CLA projection neuron responses to BLA axon photostimulation. ChrimsonR was again expressed in BLA neurons using an anterograde AAV to enable photostimulation of BLA axon terminals (A,B—left column).
