CLA neurons projecting to M1 (A) or to RSC (B) were retrogradely labeled, allowing visually targeted whole-cell recordings from projection-defined neurons (A,B—left). By recording synaptic currents in labeled neurons during photo -stimulation of BLA axons (A,B—right), we were able to directly compare BLA synaptic input onto CLA neurons projecting to M1 (n = 27 from seven mice) versus those projecting to RSC (n = 39 from six mice).

Photostimulation of BLA axons evoked primarily excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in both M1-projecting and RSC-projecting claustral neurons (C,D). In a small number of experiments, BLA photostimulation also evoked IPSCs in toM1 neurons (one out of 24) and in toRSC neurons (two out of 30), indicating that BLA inputs on both types of projection neuron are predominantly excitatory. The presence of robust inward EPSCs following BLA photostimulation indicates that BLA inputs can excite both M1-projecting and RSC-projecting CLA neurons.

To determine whether BLA input probability differed between M1-projecting and RSC-projecting CLA neurons, EPSC responses (excluding failures) were averaged to generate a mean EPSC trace for each individual neuron (red lines in C,D). These average responses were then used to compare EPSC properties between the two projection-defined neuron populations. The spatial distribution of CLA neurons that did or did not produce EPSCs in response to BLA photostimulation are shown in A. In contrast to expectations based on the anatomical observations described above (), light-evoked EPSCs were observed in both RSC-projecting neurons within the CLA core and in M1-projecting neurons in the dCLA (A). Within each zone, responding neurons did not form obvious finer-scale clusters and, instead, were scattered across the dCLA for toM1 and across the CLA core for toRSC (A). We quantified EPSC response probability for each neuron type. Of the 27 toM1 neurons examined, nine produced EPSCs in response to BLA axon photostimulation (B). In comparison, 18 out of 39 toRSC neurons were responsive (B), although this difference was not statistically significant (odds ratio = 0.57, p.adj = 0.41). The fact that both projection neuron populations had a relatively low response probability further suggests that BLA axons innervate only a subset of each neuronal population.

Finally, we asked whether the properties of BLA synaptic input differed between toM1 (n = 9 from six mice) and toRSC (n = 18 from five mice) projection neurons. We first compared EPSC failure probability and found that BLA axon photostimulation produced EPSCs in fewer than half of trials for both types of projection neuron (C). Failure probabilities were statistically indistinguishable between CLA neurons projecting to M1 and those projecting to RSC (Cohen’s d = 0.43, p.adj = 0.62). However, toRSC neurons exhibited a broader range of failure probabilities, including 4 neurons that had highly reliable responses (failure probability < 0.10 in C). This hints at the existence of a subpopulation of toRSC neurons with particularly reliable BLA synapses.

While mean EPSC amplitude appeared different between toRSC and toM1 neurons (D), with a moderate/large effect size (Cohen’s d = −0.90), there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups (p.adj = 0.62). EPSC amplitudes in toRSC neurons did span a wider range, suggesting greater heterogeneity in connection strength onto toRSC neurons relative to toM1 neurons (D). The mean CVs for EPSCs did not differ significantly (Cohen’s d = 0.66, p.adj = 0.62; between toM1 and toRSC neurons, indicating similar trial-to-trial variability of BLA transmission in both populations (E). Finally, EPSC onset latencies were comparable (F; Cohen’s d = 0.79, p.adj = 0.62) for the two projection neuron types, consistent with similar underlying BLA input circuits for both populations.

In summary, our analyses demonstrate that BLA inputs to both M1-projecting and RSC-projecting CLA neurons are predominantly excitatory. Despite a higher BLA fiber density near M1-projecting neurons, the overall transmission properties of both synapses are similar. Thus, even though BLA fiber density is anatomically quite different for these two projection neuron populations, the functional input they receive is comparable.

Our results define how BLA inputs are anatomically organized within the CLA and how they functionally engage distinct subpopulations of claustral neurons. We found that BLA innervation of the CLA is shaped in a ring-like structure within the shell and surrounds the PV-rich core. Functionally, BLA input provides small and variable excitatory input onto a subset of neurons distributed across both the CLA core and shell. We further demonstrate that, despite greater anatomical overlap between BLA fibers and M1-projecting CLA neurons, BLA excitation is similar for RSC-projecting neurons, revealing a second dissociation between axon density and functional drive. These findings suggest a model in which BLA input contributes a weak, sparse, and relatively uniform excitatory bias to CLA activity. We note that our experiments were conducted exclusively in male mice. Because sex differences have been reported for amygdala connectivity [] and in CLA neuron function [] in mice, it remains to be determined whether the anatomical and functional organization of the BLA–CLA pathway described here is the same in females.

The borders and cellular organization of the claustrum have been debated for decades. Accumulating genetic and anatomical data increasingly support the idea that the CLA is subdivided into at least two zones: the PV-rich core and a surrounding shell [,,,]. Our viral tracing reveals an unexpected topological specificity in BLA–CLA connectivity that strongly reinforces this view: we found that both BLA-projecting CLA neurons and BLA axons are enriched in the shell region and sparse in the CLA core.

Our key to clarifying this organization relied on the use of a tracing strategy that was BLA-focused. This contrasts with earlier lower-resolution studies that employed viral tracing methods based on CLA-focused strategies and inferred bidirectional connectivity between the BLA and the CLA core [,]. In the CLA-to-BLA direction, labeling of apparently “core-specific” CLA neurons suggested that core neurons project to BLA. This conclusion appears to be incorrect and probably arose because there was no attempt to identify the spatial relationship between the neurons that project to the BLA and the CLA core; we have sidestepped this problem by simultaneously labeling the core via PV staining while retrogradely labeling BLA-projecting neurons of the CLA. In the BLA-to-CLA direction, previous transsynaptic labeling from the CLA core similarly suggested BLA inputs to only core neurons. While we have also detected functional connectivity between the BLA and core neurons, this probably results from BLA axons present in the CLA shell innervating the distal dendrites of core neurons. These axons in the CLA shell also provide similar input to neurons whose cell bodies reside within the shell. Thus, BLA inputs in the shell contact neurons that have cell bodies located in both the shell and the core.

Our finding of bidirectional BLA–CLA connectivity that is anatomically confined to the shell provides a further indication that the CLA has a shell region distinct from the core in both its input and output connectivity (although this distinction is less apparent in synaptic function). Importantly, this topological segregation is not unique to BLA–CLA circuitry. Other studies have reported that the orbitofrontal and auditory cortices also preferentially innervate the shell, whereas the visual and anterior cingulate cortices target the core []. Interneuron distributions also differ between core and shell, with distinct core enrichment of PV versus VIP/SST subtypes [,]. Together with our data, these findings argue that the CLA is partitioned into at least two partially segregated modules—core and shell—with distinct combinations of inputs, outputs, and local circuitry.

Our current anatomical findings, along with previous studies [,,], suggest a direct BLA-to-CLA pathway that could serve as a conduit to deliver valence-related and emotion-related information to the CLA. However, the function of this pathway had not been examined previously. We have provided the first functional characterization of this connection by combining optogenetic activation of BLA axons with whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of postsynaptic responses in CLA neurons. We found that light-evoked responses in CLA neurons were predominantly excitatory but were observed in only half of CLA cells. This suggests that BLA inputs selectively engage a subpopulation of CLA neurons. Moreover, the EPSCs produced in CLA neurons by BLA axon photostimulation were of relatively small amplitude, highly variable, and unreliable, even under conditions that were optimized for excitation (−70 mV holding potential in CLA neurons and wide-field photostimulation of many BLA axons). EPSPs evoked by photostimulating this pathway were similarly small in amplitude and well below the threshold for evoking APs.

EPSCs evoked in CLA neurons by BLA inputs were much smaller in amplitude (~5–55 pA) compared to those in neighboring AI L5b neurons (~15–100 pA). In contrast, photo- stimulation of ACC inputs can evoke EPSCs in the nA range in CLA projection neurons (and in interneurons) []. The coefficients of variation and failure probabilities of the EPSCs of CLA neurons were higher than those reported for many central synapses [,], implying that BLA input provides a noisy and inconsistent excitatory drive to individual CLA neurons and to the population as a whole.

To minimize confounds from short-term synaptic plasticity, we used a long inter-stimulus interval (5 s); only at much shorter inter-stimulus intervals (100 ms) is such plasticity evident (). EPSC amplitudes appeared to vary randomly across trials, without systematic time-dependent trends, arguing against activity-dependent plasticity as the main source of variability. Because EPSC responses depend on effective opsin activation in presynaptic BLA axons, it remained formally possible that some failures reflected insufficient excitation of BLA axons. To exclude methodological explanations for these results, for example related to opsin expression or light delivery conditions, we performed parallel recordings from layer 5b neurons in the AI. This cortical structure receives dense BLA input []. In these cells, BLA-evoked EPSCs were larger, less variable, and far more reliable than in CLA neurons, confirming that our optogenetic stimulation robustly activated BLA axons. In addition, similar results were observed in the CLA when a second opsin, ChETA, was used to photostimulate BLA axons (). Thus, the weak and noisy nature of BLA-to-CLA EPSCs appears to reflect a genuine property of synaptic transmission in this pathway.

Such properties imply that BLA inputs alone are insufficient to drive spiking in CLA neurons, a conclusion directly supported by our observations of small, subthreshold EPSPs produced in response to BLA axon photostimulation (). Instead, we hypothesize that BLA input acts as a regulatory or “gating” signal that is excitatory yet must converge with other excitatory inputs to reach action potential firing threshold. In contrast, CLA inputs from some cortical regions appear to be much stronger and more reliable [,,,]. Taken together, our results suggest that BLA inputs are not a primary driver of CLA activity but instead must be integrated along with other inputs to drive AP firing in CLA neurons.

Such weak and variable excitatory inputs can still serve an important function. Even background synaptic “noise” can enhance sensitivity to other subthreshold signals, increase spike probability in a non-linear fashion, and support gain modulation [,,,,,]. Because the BLA is classically associated with valence and salience processing, we speculate that BLA input could, in principle, contribute subthreshold depolarizations that increase the likelihood that coincident cortical input drives CLA spiking. Our results therefore favor a model in which BLA projections provide a sparse, stochastic salience signal that influences—rather than determines—CLA activity. Further, the local inhibitory circuitry of the CLA is wired to ignore weak excitatory input—such as that from the BLA—until this input is paired with additional strong excitatory input []. In vivo recordings of CLA neuron activity will be needed to test such ideas.

Our results also revealed a functional heterogeneity of BLA input to CLA neurons, with only a subset of CLA neurons receiving BLA-driven EPSCs. We asked whether this functional heterogeneity could be explained by the striking anatomical enrichment of BLA axons in the CLA shell. Surprisingly, BLA functional connectivity was remarkably uniform across both the core and the shell: input probability, EPSC strength, variability, failure rate, and latency all were similar in both regions.

This dissociation between fiber density and synaptic drive indicates that macroscopic axon topology does not straightforwardly define which CLA projection neurons are functionally innervated by the BLA. Most strikingly, we observed clear BLA-evoked EPSCs in core neurons despite a low innervation of BLA fibers in the periphery of the core and its near absence in the center of the CLA core. This is complementary to the recent observation that input to the CLA from the anterior cingulate cortex, which is anatomically restricted to the CLA core [,], also excites both projection neurons and interneurons in the CLA shell []. Such structure–function mismatches suggest that the anatomical impression of sparse core innervation does not necessarily translate to synaptic function. Such observations also raise broader questions about other “shell-specific” inputs reported anatomically, such as from orbitofrontal or auditory cortex []. Systematic functional studies of other shell-biased inputs will be needed to determine whether BLA input to the CLA represents a special case or whether topology serves purposes beyond simple input segregation (e.g., controlling where on the dendritic tree inputs arrive, or which local circuits they preferentially recruit).

It is also possible that the dense BLA innervation of the CLA shell could preferentially target interneurons. Although interneurons represent only ~10% of neurons in the CLA [], VIP and SST interneurons preferentially occupy the shell [,]. Thus, it is plausible that BLA axons in the shell target specific interneuron classes, such that the apparent core–shell difference in fiber density reflects differences in inhibitory microcircuit engagement rather than direct excitation of projection neurons. Future experiments will be needed to address this possibility.

When examining circuit function, it is always valuable to distinguish monosynaptic and polysynaptic connections. For this purpose, we used TTX+4AP treatment [,,]. The fact that EPSCs were detected in some (six out of 19) CLA neurons treated with TTX+4AP unequivocally demonstrated that some BLA–CLA connections are monosynaptic. This is consistent with previous transsynaptic tracing experiments demonstrating the existence of direct, monosynaptic BLA–CLA connections []. However, for technical reasons, it was difficult to conclude that polysynaptic BLA-to-CLA connections were responsible for the remaining 13 out of 19 experiments where EPSCs were not observed in TTX+4AP conditions. Poor signal-to-noise, particularly for the small, variable EPSCs we often observed when photostimulating BLA inputs, may make it difficult to detect the smaller EPSCs observed in TTX+4AP conditions ( and ). Another possibility is that some BLA–CLA synapses are “silent” at resting potentials—containing NMDA but few or no AMPA receptors—such that they would not be detected under our recording conditions but could be recruited during coincident depolarization []. Alternatively, it is possible that BLA input converges on a relatively small set of CLA projection neurons, which then make local, polysynaptic excitatory circuits []. Our results provide some indirect support for this possibility by revealing that the latency for EPSCs recorded in CLA neurons was more variable, and significantly longer on average, than for EPSCs in the AI (J). These results would be expected if the CLA responses were a mix of monosynaptic and polysynaptic responses while the AI responses were monosynaptic.

One possible explanation for the striking mismatch between our histological and functional data is that the dendrites of CLA core neurons extend into the shell, potentially allowing shell-restricted BLA axons to synapse onto distal dendrites of core neurons. Filling CLA core neurons with neurobiotin revealed that they can extend dendrites radially into the CLA shell (B). Given the shell-focused BLA fiber distribution (D), this morphology suggests that BLA inputs innervate mainly distal dendrites of CLA core neurons. This could also explain the presence of monosynaptic BLA connections onto CLA core neurons despite the near absence of BLA fibers within the core. Future work that directly maps the distribution of BLA terminals on CLA neurons will be required to determine the precise location of synapses on CLA core neurons [].

Several alternative mechanisms could also contribute. First, fiber fluorescence may not reflect synaptic terminal density: for example, regions with few labeled axons could still produce strong synaptic responses via high-probability synapses. Second, the location of the dendrites of CLA neurons and the plane of slicing may bias detection of BLA input, preventing our measurements from equally sampling synaptic connectivity across a neuron’s full dendritic arbor. Distinguishing these possibilities will likely require direct visualization of BLA synaptic terminals combined with more systematic dendritic sampling.

In contrast to projection neurons of the CLA core, the dendrites of CLA shell neurons were largely confined to the shell and avoided the core. Shell neurons also received less input from local PV interneurons, which were enriched in the core []. Such asymmetries suggest an information hierarchy, in which core neurons integrate inputs that terminate in both the core and the shell while shell neurons are restricted to shell-targeting inputs. Similar dendritic “cross-boundary” sampling has been proposed in other distributed cortical and subcortical systems [,]. In the superior colliculus (SC), superficial layer neurons only receive visual information, while deep layer neurons stretch their dendrites into the superficial layers to receive visual information for integration with other sensory modalities [,]. CLA core neurons may function in a similar manner, with such differences in input/dendritic organization potentially critical for integrating multiple input streams within the compact structure of the CLA.

We also examined how BLA inputs are distributed across two topologically and functionally distinct output channels of the CLA: M1-projecting (toM1) and RSC-projecting (toRSC) neurons. These projection neuron populations occupy largely non-overlapping territories within the dCLA and CLA core, respectively, and participate in different large-scale networks [,].

Our anterograde tracing showed that BLA axons preferentially overlapped with neurons within the toM1 zone in the dCLA, while BLA axon density was low for neurons within the toRSC-rich CLA core. This arrangement suggested that BLA inputs might influence the M1-related CLA network more strongly than the RSC-related network. This complements prior anatomical work on projection-specific CLA zones and suggests that different CLA output modules are differentially tuned to limbic drive. These anatomical observations also fit within a broader picture of CLA submodules associated with different cortical systems, including a dorsal module linked to motor networks (dCLA-to-M1), a CLA core linked to retrosplenial networks (CLA-to-RSC), and a dorsal endopiriform (DEn) region potentially linked to entorhinal–limbic circuits [,]. Our BLA tracing suggests that BLA input might be especially prominent in circuits associated with motor and limbic outputs, although we did not examine the function of inputs to the DEn.

Although our anatomical results suggested more BLA innervation of CLA neurons projecting to M1 than to those projecting to the RSC, in fact we observed very similar functional connectivity for both projection neuron types. This dissociation between axon density and functional connectivity again highlights the limitations of inferring synaptic influence from macroscopic anatomy alone. Labeling methods that do not directly label synapses are likely to show both synaptic terminations and passing fibers; thus, the dense BLA signal over toM1 neurons may include axons that do not make synaptic contacts with those neurons or make only weak excitatory contacts. Similar to our observations with CLA core neurons, RSC-projecting neurons in the CLA core may extend dendrites into BLA-rich shell areas, whereas some M1-projecting neurons may reside in regions with many passing axons but few synapses. More generally, the complex dendritic and axonal topology of CLA neurons allows functional circuits to cut across gross anatomical boundaries.

Taken together, our results argue that the BLA-to-CLA pathway is anatomically selective but functionally weak and unreliable. BLA axons preferentially innervate the CLA shell, yet form comparable excitatory synapses with both core and shell neurons. Within projection-defined CLA neuron populations, while anatomical overlap suggests stronger BLA influence on M1-projecting neurons, functional connectivity with the BLA was similar for both projection neuron populations. These structure–function mismatches underscore that macroscopic anatomical maps—while essential—are not sufficient to predict how salience-related and valence-related information flows through CLA circuits.

Based on these findings, we propose that the BLA provides an excitatory input to the CLA that is subthreshold and noisy but capable of interacting with stronger cortical inputs. In this framework, the CLA receives BLA-encoded signals and integrates them with incoming signals to influence distributed cortical networks, including retrosplenial and motor systems. Future work should leverage these insights to determine how BLA–CLA circuitry works in vivo to shape behavior, particularly in contexts that require the integration of emotional salience with spatial, memory, or motor signals.

neuroscience.title: Methylphenidate-associated brain structural changes and neuroimaging predictors of treatment response in youth with ADHD: a systematic review
neuroscience.abstract: Methylphenidate (MPH) is a psychostimulant widely prescribed to children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Although its clinical efficacy is well established, its lasting effects on the developing brain remain unclear.This systematic review aimed to examine associations between long-term MPH treatment and brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD using structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), distinguishing longitudinal treatment-effect studies from cross-sectional medication-history comparisons and baseline neuroimaging predictors of treatment response.A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE and Embase databases. Studies were included if they investigated structural brain changes (gray matter volume, white matter integrity and cortical thickness) after at least four weeks of MPH treatment in children with ADHD. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed using the NIH quality assessment tool.Eight studies met the inclusion criteria: three longitudinal studies using repeated MRI to assess within-subject treatment effects, two cross-sectional comparisons based on medication history, and three studies using baseline neuroimaging to predict subsequent treatment response. Greater putamen volume was associated with medication status ad volume with better treatment response in the cross-sectional and predictive analyses, while cortical effects were less consistent and mainly age-dependent in frontal areas. White matter findings were subtle and inconsistent across studies, and cortical thickness evidence—limited to one study—suggests short-term, possibly transient effects in children.MPH treatment is associated l with age-dependent differences in brain structure in children and adolescents with ADHD; however, the limited number of included studies varied substantially in design, (cross-sectional and predictive studies alongside longitudinal treatment-effect studies), methodology, and reported outcomes, making firm causal conclusions difficult. Future research should prioritize larger, standardized, long-term longitudinal studies that account for developmental factors.
neuroscience.text:
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most commonly diagnosed neurobehavioral condition in childhood population-prevalence of 5.3% (). The DSM-5 classifies attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) into three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined presentation (). ADHD is therefore considered a heterogeneous disorder and is associated with a substantial financial burden, increased family stress, and adverse academic outcomes (). Symptoms typically emerge in early childhood and include inattention, difficulty sustaining concentration, challenges in completing tasks, and forgetfulness or frequently losing items (). Not only is it a prevalent condition, but increasingly greater numbers of children and young adolescents are exposed to pharmacological treatments, many of whom likely do not even meet the criteria for ADHD (). In addition, it is estimated that between more than 60% of children diagnosed with ADHD are affected by one or more comorbid conditions, including oppositional defiant disorder, anxiety and mood disorders, sleep disorders, autistic spectrum disorder, tic disorders, and learning disabilities (; ). ADHD is thought to involve alterations in catecholaminergic neurotransmission, particularly affecting dopamine transporters (; ), which may result in reduced dopamine availability in the synaptic cleft (). Methylphenidate (MPH), the most commonly prescribed treatment for ADHD, inhibits the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, thereby increasing their synaptic availability, primarily in the prefrontal cortex (). It has been shown to effectively reduce symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity in up to 80% of affected children and its short-term safety is well-documented; however, its long-term effects remain insufficiently understood.

This gap is particularly concerning given the heightened neuroplasticity of the developing brain, which may render it more vulnerable to pharmacological interference with neurotransmitter systems. Existing evidence, largely derived from studies in healthy male animals, suggests that while stimulant exposure in adults induces only transient neuroadaptive changes, exposure during juvenile stages may result in more persistent or even permanent alterations, a phenomenon described as ‘neurochemical imprinting’ (). Despite these findings, research in humans on the long-term impact of MPH in children is scarce, prompting increasing concern regarding potential adverse developmental consequences. Accordingly, major regulatory and research bodies have underscored the urgent need for comprehensive investigations into its long-term safety profile in pediatric populations including the US Food and Drug Administration (), the National Institutes of Health () and the European Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (), and carefully evaluate both its beneficial and potential adverse effects on the brain.

To examine these effects in children with ADHD, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is frequently used (; ). Systematic reviews are considered to provide the highest levels of evidence in scientific research, as they synthesize findings across multiple studies. Their strength lies in their comprehensive, transparent, and reproducible methodology, which enhances the reliability and precision of their conclusions. In addition, systematic reviews play a key role in informing clinical guidelines and evidence-based practice (), as they summarize all relevant studies, making the available evidence more accessible (). This systematic review aimed to compare studies investigating the long-term effects of MPH treatment on structural brain development in children with ADHD. The primary outcomes included gray matter volume, white matter integrity—measured by fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD)—and cortical thickness. We focus specifically on structural MRI to assess more stable, anatomy-based brain changes associated with MPH treatment, as functional MRI captures more transient, state-dependent neural activity that is less directly comparable across studies.

This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines, which are widely recognized as international standards for systematic review methodology (). PRISMA enhances the transparency of the search and selection process and ensures that the results are reproducible ().

The search was conducted until 1 September 2025 using two databases, MEDLINE and EMBASE, which increased the likelihood of identifying relevant studies compared to relying on a single database. From 1 September 2025 until April 2026, databases were checked on additional papers. The search terms used in MEDLINE were attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity AND methylphenidate AND magnetic resonance imaging AND brain. The terms used in EMBASE were ‘attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity’/exp. AND ‘methylphenidate’/exp. AND ‘magnetic resonance imaging’/exp. AND ‘brain’/exp. (see details in Supplement 1). No language restriction was performed.

The selection of potential relevant studies was performed by DS. Titles and abstracts were screened to identify studies with potential relevance. Duplicates, letters, comments, editorials, conference abstracts, other diseases, reviews, studies involving only adults (≥18 years of age) or healthy volunteers, and animal studies were not considered as relevant and were excluded. In case of doubt, the article was checked by SB, a clinical epidemiologist with 20 years of experience in radiology.

All articles that met the inclusion criteria were further analyzed using a standardized case record form This part of the data extraction was performed by DS and double checked by SB.

A subset of items was used to evaluate the characteristics of the study design: 1) study type; 2) study design; 3) setting initiation institute (department, institution, and country of the first author); 4) period of recruitment; 5) kind of group division; 6) study approval mentioned; 7) source of funding; and 8) whether there was a role of the funders in the study.

For the purpose of comparing the included studies, patient characteristics were systematically analyzed according to the following items: 1) whether a consecutive or random sample of individuals was enrolled; 2) whether inclusion/exclusion criteria were specified; 3) number of individuals included in the study; 4) number of individuals included in the analysis; 5) age; 6) sex and/or gender; 7) intelligence quotient; 8) right-handedness; 9) comorbid conditions; 10) treatment naivety; 11) ADHD presentation; and 12) whether the history of head trauma was included.

Given the variability in the administration of MPH across studies, this review also included medication characteristics: 1) Duration of MPH treatment and 2) dose of MPH. This review included only MPH studies to ensure comparability, as MPH (a dopamine reuptake inhibitor) differs fundamentally from other stimulants like amphetamines, which act mainly as dopamine releasers.

To gain insight into the effects of MPH on brain structure as assessed using MRI, the following items were used: 1) type of MRI; 2) MRI strength; 3) number of channels in the head coil; 4) MRI parameters; 5) type of analysis; 6) number of follow-up assessments; 7) total follow-up time; 8) report of dropouts; and 9) sufficient description of follow-up procedure.

This part of the data extraction was also performed by DS and double checked by SB and LR.

The outcomes extracted were 1) gray matter volume, 2) white matter integrity (FA, fractional anisotropy; MD, mean diffusivity) and 3) cortical thickness.

This part of the data extraction was also performed by DS and double checked by SB and LR.

The National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool for case series () was used to evaluate the methodological quality of the included studies. This assessment considered multiple aspects, including the patient population, outcome measures, follow-up procedures, and statistical methods.

To minimize selection bias, the following data were collected:

Q1: Was the study question or objective clearly stated.

Q2: Was the study population clearly and fully described, including the case definition?

Q3: Were the cases consecutive?;

Q4: Were the subjects comparable?

Q5: Was the intervention described clearly?;

Q6: Were the outcome measures clearly defined, valid, reliable, and consistently implemented across all study participants?

Q7: Was the follow-up duration adequate?;

Q8: Were the statistical methods well described?

Q9: Were the results well described?

The answer options for the abovementioned questions (Q1-Q9) were ‘yes’, ‘no’, or ‘cannot determine/not applicable/not reported’. To evaluate the overall quality, an additional rating was assigned, categorized as ‘good’, ‘fair’, or ‘poor’. Overall quality was ‘good’ if 7–9 questions were answered with ‘yes’, ‘fair’ if 4–6 questions were answered with ‘yes’, and ‘poor’ if less than 4 questions were answered with ‘yes’.

For the consistency, National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool of controlled intervention studies () was used to evaluate the methodological quality of the randomized controlled trials (RCT). This assessment considered all aspects of RCT including randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, attrition (follow-up), or confounding,

The following data were collected:

Q1. Was the study described as randomized, a randomized trial, a randomized clinical trial, or an RCT?

Q2. Was the method of randomization adequate (i.e., use of randomly generated assignment)?

Q3. Was the treatment allocation concealed (so that assignments could not be predicted)?

Q4. Were study participants and providers blinded to treatment group assignment?

Q5. Were the people assessing the outcomes blinded to the participants' group assignments?

Q6. Were the groups similar at baseline on important characteristics that could affect outcomes (e.g., demographics, risk factors, co-morbid conditions)?

Q7. Was the overall drop-out rate from the study at endpoint 20% or lower of the number allocated to treatment?

Q8. Was the differential drop-out rate (between treatment groups) at endpoint 15 percentage points or lower?

Q9. Was there high adherence to the intervention protocols for each treatment group?

Q10. Were other interventions avoided or similar in the groups (e.g., similar background treatments)?

Q11. Were outcomes assessed using valid and reliable measures, implemented consistently across all study participants?

Q12. Did the authors report that the sample size was sufficiently large to be able to detect a difference in the main outcome between groups with at least 80% power?

Q13. Were outcomes reported or subgroups analyzed prespecified (i.e., identified before analyses were conducted)?

Q14. Were all randomized participants analyzed in the group to which they were originally assigned, i.e., did they use an intention-to-treat analysis?

The answer options for the abovementioned questions (Q1-Q14) were ‘yes’, ‘no’, or ‘cannot determine/not applicable/not reported’. To evaluate the overall quality, an additional rating was assigned, categorized as ‘good’, ‘fair’, or ‘poor’. Overall quality was ‘good’ if 10–14 questions were answered with ‘yes’, ‘fair’ if 6–9 questions were answered with ‘yes’, and ‘poor’ if less than 6 questions were answered with ‘yes’.

Following our search strategy, 507 articles were identified (see Supplement 1). After screening titles and abstracts, 27 articles were considered potentially relevant. The full texts of these studies were then evaluated against the inclusion criteria described above: minimum of 10 children (< 18 years) with ADHD included, at least 4-week treatment with MPH, and evaluation of the outcomes of interest. This process resulted in inclusion of eight studies (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ), see . No additional papers were found between September 2025 and April 2026. No additional papers were found after checking reference lists and forward citation of the included papers.

Most studies used 3.0 Tesla scanners, indicating generally high-resolution imaging quality. Only one study  used a 1.5 Tesla scanner, which may result in lower signal-to-noise ratio and reduced sensitivity compared to 3.0 T systems.  included two follow-up assessments, whereas all other studies had only one follow-up assessment. There was considerable variation in the total follow-up duration across the studies, ranging from 8 weeks to nearly 5 years. Almost all studies reported drop-outs (DO), except for the studies by  and . Still, all studies sufficiently described the follow-up procedures.

We observed substantial heterogeneity in acquisition parameters, including TR/TE, FOV, voxel size, and number of slices. Some studies provided detailed acquisition settings (e.g., ), while others reported incomplete information, with several parameters listed as not reported. This lack of standardization may affect the comparability of findings across studies. Additionally, voxel resolution and slice coverage varied considerably, which can influence the sensitivity to detect structural differences, particularly in small brain regions. Similarly, flip angle was inconsistently reported, and when provided, differed across studies.

The two sMRI studies (; ) indicated GM volume differences associated with MPH: ) compared medication groups cross-sectionally, while  examined cumulative MPH exposurelongitudinally.  reported increased GM volumes in subcortical regions, particularly the putamen, insula, and cerebellum, in medicated children. In frontal cortical regions, findings were mixed, with increased volumes in the middle frontal and precentral gyri compared to typically developing children, but reduced middle frontal gyrus volume compared to never-medicated children.  reported that higher cumulative MPH exposure was associated with increased gray matter volumes across multiple frontal regions, including the superior, middle, orbitofrontal, and precentral cortices, whereas no subcortical effects were observed. These effects were observed only in children who initiated treatment before age 12, with no significant associations in those who started later.

Across four studies examining white matter structures in children with ADHD (; ; ), the assessed outcomes included FA, with only  and  reporting both measures (FA and MD) within the same study.

Evidence related to FA was heterogeneous.  reported decreased FA in specific regions depending on genetic variation, including the right postcentral gyrus in C allele carriers and the right middle frontal cortex in T allele carriers. In contrast, in the RCT by  no significant FA effects in ROI analyses were found, although voxel-based analyses revealed significant time-by-medication-by-age interactions, with greater FA increases in left-hemisphere association tracts and the corpus callosum in MPH-treated boys; these effects were not observed in placebo-treated boys or adults.  found no significant differences in FA or MD using TBSS between medicated ADHD patients, drug-naïve patients, and healthy controls. However, an alternative tract-based analysis (GTS) revealed that medicated patients had lower MD than both groups in key white matter tracts, including the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, and corpus callosum, while no FA differences were observed, whereas  found no MD effects.

Only one study examined cortical thickness.  investigated regional cortical thickness changes after 16 weeks of MPH treatment in an RCT and found age-dependent, region-specific effects, with increased thickness (or reduced cortical thinning) in the right medial cortex ROI of the three ROIs (left frontal cortex, right medial cortex and right posterior cortex) in children receiving MPH compared with placebo. In contrast, both MPH- and placebo-treated adults showed cortical thinning across regions. Overall, these findings suggest that MPH-related effects on cortical thickness are age-dependent and primarily observable in children.

In a separate analysis focusing on treatment response,  reported that good responders showed increased gray matter volume in the putamen and reduced volume in the bilateral precuneus compared to poor responders. Using DTI,  found lower FA in the left anterior thalamic radiation in good responders compared to poor responders.

Quality assessment of RCT.

Q1. Was the study described as randomized, a randomized trial, a randomized clinical trial, or an RCT?

Q2. Was the method of randomization adequate (i.e., use of randomly generated assignment)?

Q3. Was the treatment allocation concealed (so that assignments could not be predicted)?

Q4. Were study participants and providers blinded to treatment group assignment?

Q5. Were the people assessing the outcomes blinded to the participants' group assignments?

Q6. Were the groups similar at baseline on important characteristics that could affect outcomes (e.g., demographics, risk factors, co-morbid conditions)?

Q7. Was the overall drop-out rate from the study at endpoint 20% or lower of the number allocated to treatment?

Q8. Was the differential drop-out rate (between treatment groups) at endpoint 15 percentage points or lower?

Q9. Was there high adherence to the intervention protocols for each treatment group?

Q10. Were other interventions avoided or similar in the groups (e.g., similar background treatments)?

Q11. Were outcomes assessed using valid and reliable measures, implemented consistently across all study participants?

Q12. Did the authors report that the sample size was sufficiently large to be able to detect a difference in the main outcome between groups with at least 80% power?

Q13. Were outcomes reported or subgroups analyzed prespecified (i.e., identified before analyses were conducted)?

Q14. Were all randomized participants analyzed in the group to which they were originally assigned, i.e., did they use an intention-to-treat analysis?

Overall quality: ‘good’ if 10–14 questions were answered with ‘yes’, ‘fair’ if 6–9 questions were answered with ‘yes’ and ‘poor’ if less than 6 questions were answered with ‘yes’.

Overall, the methodological quality of the included case studies was high ().

Only the study of  was rated as fair quality due to several unmet or unreported criteria. No studies were classified as poor quality, indicating a generally robust evidence base. Across studies, several domains were consistently well addressed. All studies clearly stated their research objectives (Q1) and described their study populations (Q2). In addition, outcome measures (Q6), follow-up duration (Q7), statistical methods (Q8), and reporting of results (Q9) were almost uniformly adequate, suggesting strong methodological rigor in study execution and reporting. Therefore, overall, the methodology quality can be considered as good, except for the inconsistencies in reporting - particularly regarding intervention details (Q5) and group comparability (Q4) and represent important limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings.

The methodological quality of the included RCTs are presented in . Data of 1 RCT are actually presented in 3 papers (; ; ).

MPH treatment characteristics varied widely across studies, with durations ranging from weeks to years (up to 5 years maximum) and dosage often inconsistently or incompletely reported, limiting comparability. The eight included studies also differed substantially in design and in the level of causal inference they support: three used repeated MRI to assess within-subject structural change associated with treatment , , and ; two were cross-sectional comparisons based on medication history  and ; and three used baseline neuroimaging to predict subsequent treatment response or clinical outcome rather than to assess MPH-induced structural change , , and . These design differences, discussed separately below, mean that most of the included evidence is observational or cross-sectional rather than randomized, which limits causal inference; most studies were nonethelessrated as good methodological quality on the NIH tool (Table 6, and see Section 5.5 for its limitations). Overall, the evidence suggests that MPH- use is associated with both cortical and subcortical brain differences, with more consistent findings in subcortical structures (e.g., the putamen) and more variable findings in the (frontal) cortex. Findings on white matter appear subtle and inconsistent, while findings on cortical thickness are limited to a single study. Age-dependent effects were reported across all outcome measures, although this evidence was based on a limited number of independent studies.

Across the three structural MRI studies (; ; ), subcortical effects—particularly in the putamen—were reported in two studies (; ), with increased putamen volume associated with both greater treatment exposure and better treatment response. Consistent with this,  identified the basal ganglia as the most robust site of ADHD-related structural differences and found that both increasing age and stimulant medication were independently associated with more normalized (i.e., increased) basal ganglia volumes. In contrast, cortical findings were more heterogeneous:  reported that higher cumulative MPH exposure was associated with increased gray matter volume in multiple frontal regions in children who initiated treatment before age 12 only and not thereafter, whereas  reported the opposite pattern, with reduced frontal GM volume observed in medicated children. Neurodevelopmental studies show that brain regions mature at different rates, with particularly prolonged development of the frontal cortex—among the last regions to fully mature—alongside continued structural changes in the striatum throughout childhood and adolescence. This extended developmental trajectory may confer greater sensitivity of these fronto-striatal circuits to treatment effects during earlier stages of development (). Taken together, the findings suggest that MPH-related brain changes involve both cortical and subcortical regions, with more consistent effects in subcortical structures such as the putamen and more variable, age-dependent effects in frontal cortical areas.

We found no strong, converging pattern across the three diffusion MRI studies, with one study reporting decreased FA (), one increased FA (), and two showing no significant effects in children (; ). Although the corpus callosum and fronto-association tracts were implicated, effects varied in direction, suggesting methodological and sample-related influences rather than a robust pattern. Interpretation is somewhat clearer when considering MD alongside FA, as increased FA and decreased MD both indicate improved white matter microstructure. In this context,  in the RCT reported increased FA in left-hemisphere association tracts in MPH-treated children (but not adults or placebo groups), while  found reduced MD in major tracts, together suggesting a potential positive effect of MPH on white matter organization. This finding is broadly consistent with prior evidence showing increased white matter volume in stimulant-medicated children (), as well as an association between greater cumulative stimulant exposure and lower MD in the orbitofrontal–striatal pathway (). , like  and  below, is cited here as supporting evidence rather than as an included study, as it examined stimulant treatment history broadly rather than MPH specifically, consistent with this review's a priori restriction to MPH studies for comparability (). It also aligns with animal studies reporting increases in FA in adolescent, but not adult, rats following stimulant exposure (), potentially linked to enhanced expression of axon-related genes induced by early MPH treatment (). Overall, the combined evidence tentatively suggests that early MPH treatment may enhance white matter maturation and microstructural organization in children with ADHD, with effects appearing more pronounced during developmental periods than in adulthood.

Only one study, a RCT (ePOD-MPH; ) examined cortical thickness and found that MPH increased cortical thickness in the right medial cortex ROI in children after four months, an effect not observed in the placebo group, nor adults. This is in line with , who reported similar effects of stimulant treatment (not specifically MPH) in the same ROI and additional regions, suggesting that stimulants may modulate typical cortical thinning trajectories. However, a four-year follow-up of the ePOD-MPH RCT by  found no association between stimulant use and cortical thickness in this ROI, indicating that these effects may be transient.  and  were not among the eight studies appraised in this review, as both examined broader stimulant medication use rather than MPH specifically, consistent with this review's a priori restriction to MPH studies for comparability (). In addition, no cortical thickness effects were observed in adults after four months, unlike in children ). Overall, these findings suggest that MPH-related cortical effects are age-dependent and possibly short-lived.

Two MRI studies (; ) examined long-term MPH response and found that treatment efficacy is associated with distributed differences across both gray and white matter systems. Good responders showed increased gray matter volume in subcortical regions, including the putamen, insula, and cerebellum, along with reduced precuneus volume (), and also exhibited lower FA in the left anterior thalamic radiation (). Together, these findings suggest that MPH response is linked to a specific pattern of neurodevelopmental organization involving both subcortical structure and fronto-parietal white matter pathways, rather than isolated regional abnormalities. This supports a network-level view of treatment response, where individual differences in brain organization may help explain variability in clinical outcome.

The evidence base of this systematic review is limited by substantial heterogeneity in study design, sample characteristics, and MPH treatment protocols, which reduces comparability and limits generalizability. Additional constraints include reliance on a single RCT, (reported in three publications), exclusion of comorbid conditions, and inclusion of mixed age groups, all of which further restrict clinical interpretation. Despite these limitations, most studies were rated as good methodological quality on the NIH quality assessment tools for case series and RCTs, although incomplete reporting of interventions and occasional group imbalances may introduce bias. However, the NIH tool does not assess randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, attrition, or confounding, and therefore does not fully capture risk of bias for either the randomized trial reports or the observational studies included here; a formal re-appraisal using RoB 2 for the randomized trial reports and ROBINS-I (or the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) for the observational studies is warranted before the strength of this evidence base can be considered fully established. Furthermore, three of the eight included studies—, , and —are not independent but are three reports derived from the same ePOD-MPH randomized controlled trial, sharing a 2011–2015 recruitment window and an overlapping sample of approximately 50 boys. As a result, the effective number of independent datasets underlying this review is therefore closer to five or six than eight, and this should be borne in mind when interpreting the strength of the evidence base. Two authors of this review (LR, ZvdP) are co-authors of these three studies (see Declaration of Competing Interest). Another limitation is that this review was not prospectively registered (e.g., in PROSPERO), no formal a priori protocol was developed, and that only two databases (MEDLINE and EMBASE) were searched which may have resulted in missed studies. However, comprehensive search strategies and routine screening of reference lists and forward citations of included studies may have reduced this risk. We therefore consider the potential impact on the overall findings to be limited. Title/abstract screening was performed by a single reviewer (DS), with adjudication by a second reviewer (SB) only in cases of uncertainty; no formal inter-rater agreement statistics were calculated. Two included studies,  and , have mean sample ages of 17.6 (SD 10.1) and 17.59 (SD 8.00) years respectively, indicating that a proportion of participants were young adults or transitional-age youth rather than children; indicating a child-versus-adult contrast rather than a developmental gradient within childhood. Overall, while methodological rigor is relatively strong, on several dimensions, the risk-of-bias limitations, design heterogeneity, and reporting gaps described above should be considered when interpreting the findings. A key strength of this review is its focus on MPH only, excluding other stimulants with different pharmacological mechanisms, thereby improving comparability across studies. This is important because MPH primarily acts as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor, whereas amphetamine derivatives also promote dopamine release, reflecting distinct pharmacological profiles () and have been associated with neurotoxic effects in preclinical studies ().

Future research should prioritize larger, well-powered longitudinal and meta-analytic studies to better characterize the developmental effects of MPH on brain structure. Clinical relevance would be enhanced by including children with comorbidities and by standardizing key methodological factors such as MRI protocols, treatment duration, and dosage reporting. In addition, this review highlights the importance of accounting for moderating factors such as age and developmental stage to better explain variability in treatment effects and response. Finally, longer follow-up periods—beyond five years—are needed to better reflect real-world MPH exposure, as many children remain on treatment for extended durations. The longest prospective follow-up to date, the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD (MTA), extending up to eight years, showed that initial between-group differences diminish over time, suggesting that early behavioral benefits are not maintained at long-term follow-up (). However, it remains unclear whether similar trajectories apply to brain structural outcomes, as the here reviewed neuroimaging follow-up studies were limited to approximately five years, warranting further investigation.

Overall, MPH treatment is associated with increased gray matter in subcortical regions, particularly the putamen, with more variable effects in frontal cortex. White matter findings are inconsistent, and may modestly enhance white matter microstructural organization in children with ADHD. Evidence on cortical thickness is limited and suggests short-term, possibly non-persistent effects. Across all outcomes, age appeared to be a key moderating factor. Future studies should use larger, standardized, longitudinal designs that better capture developmental effects of treatment.
