neuroscience.title: Neurological Masquerades of Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma: A Case Mimicking Motor Neurone Disease
neuroscience.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and typically presents with lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, or extranodal disease. Neurological presentations are uncommon and may mimic primary neurological disorders, which creates significant diagnostic challenges.A 67-year-old woman presented with progressive lower back pain, paraesthesia affecting all four limbs that left her bed-bound, faecal incontinence, dysphagia, weight loss, and evolving neurological deficits, including left-sided facial weakness and asymmetric tetraparesis predominantly affecting the left side. Initial neuroimaging demonstrated no acute intracranial pathology and no evidence of spinal cord compression. Electromyography (EMG) revealed widespread active and chronic denervation, which suggested an anterior horn cell disorder or motor neurone disease (MND). However, the presence of sensory symptoms, constitutional features, and progressive clinical deterioration prompted further investigation. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified cervical and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy confirmed DLBCL. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis did not demonstrate definitive evidence of central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. After six cycles of polatuzumab vedotin, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisolone (Pola-R-CHP), the patient achieved complete metabolic remission and showed substantial improvement in her neurological symptoms.This case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis in patients presenting with atypical neurological syndromes. DLBCL may rarely present with neurological features that mimic MND. Although a definitive paraneoplastic neurological syndrome (PNS) could not be established, a possible paraneoplastic neurological process was considered. Recognition of systemic red-flag features, such as weight loss and lymphadenopathy, was pivotal in reaching the correct diagnosis.
neuroscience.text:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), accounting for approximately 30-40% of cases worldwide []. It is an aggressive lymphoid malignancy characterised by the proliferation of mature B lymphocytes and predominantly affects older adults. Clinical presentation is heterogeneous and commonly includes rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, and extranodal involvement. Despite its aggressive nature, DLBCL is potentially curable with modern immunochemotherapy regimens []. Neurological manifestations of lymphoma may occur through several mechanisms, including direct infiltration of the central or peripheral nervous system, leptomeningeal disease, neurolymphomatosis, vascular complications, metabolic disturbances, infections, treatment-related toxicity, or immune-mediated paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (PNS). Such presentations may mimic primary neurological disorders and can cause significant diagnostic uncertainty, which may delay diagnosis and treatment [].

Paraneoplastic neurological syndromes are rare immune-mediated disorders that occur as remote effects of malignancy and are not caused by direct tumour invasion or metastasis. The 2021 PNS-Care criteria introduced a structured diagnostic framework that incorporates neurological phenotype, neuronal antibody status, the presence of associated cancer, and duration of follow-up, which allows classification as definite, probable, or possible PNS []. We describe an unusual case of DLBCL presenting with clinical and electrophysiological findings suggestive of an anterior horn cell disorder or motor neurone disease (MND). This represents a rare example of electromyography (EMG)-confirmed widespread denervation mimicking MND in a patient who was subsequently diagnosed with DLBCL and experienced neurological recovery following lymphoma-directed treatment. This case report highlights the importance of reconsidering an initial diagnosis when atypical neurological features and systemic red-flag symptoms are present.

A 67-year-old woman presented with a three-week history of severe lower back pain radiating to both lower limbs. She had no prior history of neurological disease, neuromuscular disorders, or autoimmune illness. The pain was associated with paraesthesia affecting all four limbs, progressive weakness, faecal incontinence, dysphagia, and unintentional weight loss, which eventually left her bedbound. Four months before admission, she had sustained a back injury that was managed conservatively for presumed musculoskeletal pain. Prior to symptom onset, the patient had been independent in all activities of daily living and had no significant mobility limitations.

Neurological examination demonstrated asymmetric weakness affecting all four limbs, predominantly on the left side, along with left lower motor neurone-pattern facial weakness. Muscle strength was graded according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale []. Shoulder abduction and adduction were preserved bilaterally (5/5). Elbow flexion and extension were reduced to 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Hip flexion was 4/5 on the left and 5/5 on the right, while knee extension was 5/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Bilateral toe dorsiflexion was reduced to 4/5. Deep tendon reflexes were generally diminished. Bilateral ankle clonus was present, while plantar responses remained flexor bilaterally. No other cranial nerve abnormalities were documented.

Given concerns regarding spinal cord pathology, CT imaging of the head and MRI of the spine were performed. CT imaging demonstrated no acute intracranial abnormality (Figure ). MRI of the spine demonstrated multiple minor degenerative disc bulges but no evidence of spinal cord compression, cauda equina syndrome, or other structural abnormalities that could adequately explain the patient’s symptoms (Figure ).

As symptoms progressed, a brain MRI was performed, revealing chronic small-vessel ischaemic changes without evidence of acute infarction, demyelination, an intracranial mass lesion, or abnormal enhancement (Figure ).

The neurosurgical team concluded that the spinal imaging findings were incidental and recommended conservative management. Pain was initially managed with oral morphine but subsequently required escalation to oxycodone, along with continuous subcutaneous midazolam, due to worsening symptoms. Formal neurophysiological assessment was subsequently performed on the recommendation of the neurology team.

Electromyography Findings

Neurophysiological studies demonstrated preserved sensory conduction velocities and normal sensory responses (Figure ). Motor responses involving the median, ulnar, tibial, and common peroneal nerves were significantly attenuated (Figure ). EMG demonstrated widespread active and chronic denervation affecting the cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral, and bulbar segments. The neurophysiology report concluded: “This electrodiagnostic study shows significant electrophysiological evidence of widespread active and chronic denervation involving multiple spinal segments, including the cervical, lumbosacral, thoracic, and craniobulbar regions. These findings are suggestive of an underlying anterior horn cell disorder or motor neurone disease.”

Based on these findings, riluzole 50 mg twice daily was commenced. Despite the electrophysiological findings, the neurology team identified several atypical features that were inconsistent with classical MND, including sensory symptoms affecting all four limbs, bowel dysfunction, constitutional symptoms, and rapid functional decline. Consequently, alternative diagnoses continued to be explored.

During admission, cervical lymphadenopathy was identified on clinical examination. Given the patient's unexplained weight loss and progressive functional decline, contrast-enhanced CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed. This revealed extensive retroperitoneal and inguinal lymphadenopathy, raising suspicion of an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder (Figure ).

An ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy was subsequently performed, confirming a diagnosis of DLBCL.

Lymph node biopsy report

Histopathological examination demonstrated sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with numerous mitotic and apoptotic figures. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for CD20, CD79a, PAX5, BCL2, BCL6, MUM1, and c-MYC, while CD3, CD10, and cyclin D1 were negative. The Ki-67 proliferative index exceeded 90%. These findings were diagnostic of DLBCL of non-germinal centre B-cell (non-GCB) phenotype.

Cerebrospinal fluid study

A lumbar puncture was performed to evaluate for central nervous system (CNS) involvement and exclude infectious causes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated clear, colourless fluid with a white cell count of 19 cells/mm³ and a lymphocytic predominance (80%). Gram stain showed no organisms, and CSF culture demonstrated no growth. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for parechovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, enterovirus, adenovirus, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus was negative. Cytological examination was essentially acellular and showed no evidence of malignant cells. Overall, there was no definitive evidence of CNS lymphoma or CNS infection.

The case was reviewed at a multidisciplinary haematology meeting. Given the absence of a structural neurological explanation, the atypical neurological presentation, and the diagnosis of DLBCL, a possible paraneoplastic neurological process was considered. However, a definitive diagnosis of PNS could not be established because specific neuronal antibody testing was not performed and the available evidence did not fulfil contemporary PNS-Care criteria for definite PNS.

The patient underwent six cycles of polatuzumab vedotin, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisolone (Pola-R-CHP). Following treatment, significant clinical improvement was observed. Appetite improved, pain decreased substantially, and neurological function also improved substantially. The patient is now able to mobilise with a walking stick and perform activities of daily living independently. Although residual weakness remained, the patient regained a considerably greater degree of independence than at diagnosis. End-of-treatment PET imaging demonstrated complete metabolic remission. The patient remains under regular haematology follow-up. The sequence of events from the patient's initial presentation through treatment and final clinical outcome is outlined in Table .

Chronological summary of the patient's presentation, diagnostic workup, treatment, and clinical outcome

CT: computed tomography; MRI: magnetic resonance imaging; EMG: electromyography; MND: motor neurone disease; CT CAP: computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis; DLBCL: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; MDT: multidisciplinary team; Pola-R-CHP: polatuzumab vedotin, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisolone; PET: positron emission tomography

This case report illustrates the diagnostic complexity that may arise when DLBCL presents predominantly with neurological manifestations. DLBCL is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity and most commonly presents with lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, or extranodal disease [,]. Neurological symptoms are relatively uncommon as initial presenting features and may obscure the underlying diagnosis. The differential diagnosis initially included spinal cord compression, cerebrovascular disease, MND, neurolymphomatosis, inflammatory neuropathy, CNS lymphoma, and paraneoplastic neurological syndromes. Structural causes were effectively excluded through neuroimaging, while electrophysiological findings guided further investigation towards an anterior horn cell disorder.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the most common form of MND, is characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurones, producing weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, and reflex abnormalities. Although the EMG findings in our patient were highly suggestive of MND, the overall clinical picture was atypical. Prominent sensory symptoms, bowel dysfunction, constitutional symptoms, and rapid progression are not characteristic features of classical ALS and should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses [,]. The identification of widespread lymphadenopathy ultimately led to a tissue diagnosis of DLBCL and substantially changed the management approach. This underscores the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with presumed MND, particularly when systemic red flags are present.

Neurological complications associated with lymphoma may occur through multiple mechanisms, including direct tumour infiltration, leptomeningeal disease, neurolymphomatosis, vascular injury, metabolic abnormalities, and paraneoplastic autoimmune phenomena []. Neurolymphomatosis was considered in this case because it may present with painful neuropathy, weakness, and multifocal neurological deficits. However, MRI did not demonstrate overt nerve infiltration, and CSF analysis showed no malignant cells. Nevertheless, neurolymphomatosis cannot be completely excluded because MRI and CSF cytology lack sensitivity, and neither dedicated FDG-PET assessment of peripheral nerves nor nerve biopsy was performed [,,].

CSF examination demonstrated mild lymphocytic pleocytosis but no microbiological evidence of infection or cytological evidence of lymphoma. Negative CSF cytology alone does not completely exclude CNS lymphoma, as its sensitivity remains limited, particularly in early disease [,]. A paraneoplastic neurological mechanism was also considered. According to the updated PNS-Care criteria, diagnosis relies upon the integration of the neurological phenotype, neuronal antibody status, associated malignancy, and clinical follow-up []. In this patient, neuronal antibody testing was unavailable, and therefore the available evidence was insufficient to establish a diagnosis of definite or probable PNS according to contemporary diagnostic criteria.

In addition to neurolymphomatosis, the differential diagnosis included a broader lymphoma-associated immune-mediated neurological syndrome. Features supporting this consideration included asymmetric tetraparesis, lower motor neurone facial weakness, sensory disturbance, bowel dysfunction, bilateral ankle clonus, widespread active denervation on electromyography, and mild CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, the available findings were insufficient to establish a diagnosis of paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis or another definite paraneoplastic neurological syndrome according to PNS-Care criteria. Furthermore, incomplete neuronal antibody testing, the absence of pathological confirmation, unremarkable conventional neuroimaging, and the inability to definitively exclude neurolymphomatosis all limit diagnostic certainty. Therefore, any lymphoma-associated immune-mediated neurological mechanism remains speculative.

Nonetheless, several observations support a possible association between the neurological syndrome and the underlying lymphoma. There was no convincing structural explanation for the neurological deficits; symptoms developed in temporal association with newly diagnosed lymphoma, and substantial neurological recovery occurred following successful lymphoma-directed treatment. Clinically, the patient progressed from being bedbound at presentation to mobilising with a walking stick and independently performing activities of daily living following completion of therapy. Although detailed follow-up neurological examination findings, including formal strength grading, reflex assessment, and sensory evaluation, were unavailable, the marked functional recovery would be unusual in classical ALS and supports a relationship between the neurological syndrome and the underlying malignancy [].

This case report reinforces the importance of revisiting initial diagnostic assumptions when clinical findings fail to fit a typical disease pattern. Recognition of sensory disturbance, bowel dysfunction, constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and rapid clinical deterioration ultimately led to the diagnosis of a potentially curable haematological malignancy.

Limitations

This report has several limitations. Comprehensive paraneoplastic antibody testing was not performed, which prevented definitive classification according to PNS-Care criteria. Delayed CSF processing limited further immunophenotypic analysis, and neurolymphomatosis could not be definitively excluded because dedicated peripheral nerve imaging and nerve biopsy were not undertaken. Baseline PET-CT imaging was unavailable, restricting assessment of the pre-treatment metabolic disease burden. In addition, representative histopathological images from the diagnostic lymph node biopsy could not be retrieved despite repeated attempts. However, the diagnosis of DLBCL was confirmed by formal histopathological and immunohistochemical assessment. Therefore, while the marked neurological improvement following lymphoma-directed therapy supports a lymphoma-associated neurological process, the precise underlying pathophysiological mechanism remains uncertain.

This case report underscores the diagnostic challenges posed by atypical presentations of DLBCL, particularly when neurological manifestations mimic primary neuromuscular or neurodegenerative disorders. The patient’s presentation initially suggested an anterior horn cell disorder or MND, supported by electrophysiological findings of widespread denervation. However, the presence of sensory symptoms, bowel dysfunction, constitutional features, and progressive systemic decline prompted further investigation, ultimately revealing an underlying aggressive lymphoma. This report highlights the need to investigate for underlying malignancy when systemic red-flag features, particularly unexplained weight loss and lymphadenopathy, are present in patients with presumed MND.

Although a definitive diagnosis of PNS could not be established, a possible paraneoplastic neurological process was considered after alternative explanations had been investigated. However, the available evidence did not fulfil contemporary PNS-Care criteria for definite or probable PNS, and the precise mechanism underlying the neurological presentation remains uncertain. This report also highlights that electrophysiological findings suggestive of an anterior horn cell disorder or MND should be interpreted within the broader clinical context, as lymphoma-associated neurological syndromes may produce misleading EMG findings and mimic primary neurodegenerative disease. Furthermore, multidisciplinary collaboration involving neurology, neurosurgery, radiology, pathology, and haematology was essential to challenge the initial diagnostic impression, facilitate further investigation, and ultimately establish the correct diagnosis. The report emphasises the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis, recognising systemic red-flag features, and reconsidering initial diagnostic assumptions when clinical findings are atypical. Successful treatment of the lymphoma resulted in complete metabolic remission and significant neurological improvement, highlighting the importance of timely tissue diagnosis in patients with unexplained neurological syndromes.

neuroscience.title: Neurobiology of Treatment-Emergent Mania Associated with Antidepressant: A Narrative Review Update
neuroscience.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a complex and debilitating condition in which antidepressant-associated treatment-emergent mania (TEM) poses a significant clinical challenge. This narrative review synthesizes current insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this phenomenon, aiming to update the understanding in the field.Clinical guidelines often caution against antidepressant monotherapy due to the risks of mood destabilization and switching, particularly in BD type I. A review of specific antidepressant classes reveals that tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) carry a high risk of TEM, which has been linked to disruptions in cholinergic-adrenergic balance and heightened noradrenergic activity. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), while less implicated than TCAs, are also associated with TEM, involving serotonin neurotransmission and potential interactions with muscarinic and histaminergic receptors. Furthermore, evidence suggests that even atypical antidepressants with non-monoaminergic profiles can induce manic switches, highlighting the vulnerability of some individuals and the influence of genetic predispositions. In addition, the effects of antidepressants associated with TEM can also be influenced by factors related to hepatic metabolism, as well as alterations in mitochondrial activity and immunoinflammatory processes, which can modulate the response to treatment and vulnerability to mood dysregulation.Antidepressants are one possible precipitant of TEM, but the phenomenon is better understood as a vulnerability-dependent outcome rather than a universal consequence of antidepressant exposure. Current evidence suggests that TEM may arise from neurobiological perturbations that are partially distinct across antidepressant classes and interact with individual susceptibility factors. These findings point to a broader network-level dysregulation of mood that extends beyond isolated neurotransmitter systems. These observations reinforce the importance of personalized treatment strategies that prioritize mood stabilization, careful patient selection, and close clinical monitoring when antidepressants are used in bipolar depression.
neuroscience.text:
Bipolar disorder (BD) is a debilitating condition characterized by a complex clinical landscape and significant cognitive and functional impairments that affect the quality of life of both patients and their families [, ]. Its symptomatology encompasses a spectrum of pathological mood swings, including euthymia, depression, mixed episodes, and the hallmark occurrence of mania and/or hypomania []. Mania is defined as a distinct period of at least one week of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, and risky behaviors [, ]. In contrast, hypomania presents as a less severe manifestation lasting at least four consecutive days; while it shares similar symptoms with mania, it typically does not require hospitalization or cause severe functional impairment, though it still involves significant behavioral changes that contrast sharply with the profound sadness and anhedonia characteristic of depressive episodes [].

The term “switch mania,” a hallmark phenomenon of BD, refers to the abrupt transition from a depressive or euthymic state to a manic episode []. This rapid shift in mood and behavior can be disruptive and challenging for individuals with BD, as well as for their families and healthcare providers []. Switch mania is characterized by a sudden onset of elevated mood, increased energy, impulsiveness, and decreased need for sleep, among other symptoms typical of manic episodes []. Triggers for the manic switch in individuals with BD can vary widely and are often individual-specific.

It is well described in the literature that some antidepressant medications, commonly prescribed for the treatment of depressive symptoms in BD, have been associated with the risk of triggering manic episodes or accelerating cycling between mood states, a phenomenon reported as treatment-emergent mania (TEM). Studies show that TEM occurs in 36–38% of patients exposed to antidepressants [, ], with the majority of cases occurring during antidepressant monotherapy []. This underscores the delicate balance required when treating BD with pharmacotherapy []. This phenomenon supports the theory that the mania switch may be linked to alterations in neurotransmission systems, particularly given that most antidepressants function by inhibiting serotonin reuptake []. Other changes in medication, including starting or stopping mood stabilizer drugs without proper supervision, can also destabilize mood and lead to a manic switch [].

Managing TEM in individuals with BD often requires a comprehensive treatment approach that may include mood stabilizers, antipsychotic medications, psychotherapy, and lifestyle modifications. Early detection of prodromal symptoms and close monitoring by mental health professionals are essential for preventing or minimizing the impact of switch mania episodes []. By deepening their understanding of the neurobiological underpinnings of TEM, researchers and clinicians can develop more precise and efficient interventions to help individuals with BD effectively manage their symptoms and enhance their quality of life. Therefore, this literature review aims to synthesize current insights into TEM, with a primary focus on the underlying neurobiological mechanisms. The present study is a narrative review of scientific articles published in peer-reviewed journals between 2014 and 2026. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed using the following terms: (“mania“[MeSH]) AND (“antidepressive agents“[MeSH]); (manic switch[Title/Abstract]); (“antidepressive agents“[MeSH]); (“treatment-emergent mania/hypomania“[MeSH]). Only articles published in English were included. After the removal of duplicates and the exclusion of narrative and/or systematic reviews, as well as studies deemed irrelevant to the scope of this review, a total of 25 studies were selected for inclusion (a summary of the included studies is presented in Table  and ). Additionally, other relevant articles were consulted to support the background and discussion of the findings.

The clinical management of BD remains a substantial challenge, requiring multimodal interventions and reflecting high rates of therapeutic non-adherence []. First-line long-term treatment primarily involves mood stabilizers such as lithium and anticonvulsants (e.g., valproate and lamotrigine), as well as atypical antipsychotics (e.g., quetiapine, aripiprazole, and cariprazine), which are recommended for both acute and maintenance therapy [, ]. Depressive symptoms — which are more prevalent than manic, hypomanic, or mixed episodes — often include persistent sadness, anhedonia, changes in sleep and appetite, psychomotor disturbances, and suicidal ideation [, , ]. Although these episodes share clinical features with major depressive disorder (MDD), their treatment differs significantly [].

Clinical guidelines recommend lithium and lamotrigine as first-line treatments for acute bipolar depression, with quetiapine, lamotrigine, and lurasidone preferred as monotherapies []. Antidepressants may be used in combination with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics, particularly for BD type II; however, they are not recommended as monotherapy for long-term treatment [, ]. In addition to their limited efficacy, antidepressants have been associated with an increased risk of mood destabilization, affective switching, number of manic episodes, hospitalizations, and accelerated mood cycling [, –]. These risks are particularly elevated in individuals with BD type I, females, those with a history of severe suicide attempts, concomitant mental illness, and individuals with frequent prior manic episodes [, , –]. The neurobiological mechanisms underlying antidepressant-induced manic switching are not yet fully understood. Therefore, a clear understanding of how each class of antidepressants influences the risk of manic switching is clinically useful.

The association between tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) and manic switching in BD is well-established [, , ], although some controversy remains []. A preclinical study demonstrated that imipramine could induce mania-like behavior in rats pretreated with ouabain (OUA) []. In this model, the OUA administration led to a mania-like state by the 7th day, followed by a depressive-like state by the 14th day. Notably, imipramine administration triggered mania-like behavior on the 14th-day post-OUA injection, mimicking a switch from depression to mania. At the molecular level, imipramine exacerbated OUA-induced oxidative damage in the rat brain, suggesting a potential synergistic interaction between imipramine and OUA [].

In clinical settings, a cohort study of patients with bipolar depression (n = 1,242) found that 4.8% experienced a TEM within four weeks of treatment, including those receiving TCAs such as imipramine []. Compared to non-tricyclic antidepressants, TCAs — such as imipramine, amitriptyline, clomipramine, and dosulepine — were associated with more than double the risk of induced TEM in patients with bipolar depression [–], as well as individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder []. The neurobiological mechanisms underlying this phenomenon are thought to involve disruptions in neurotransmitter balance (Fig. ). Evidence for neuroimaging, neuropharmacological intervention, and genetic association studies suggests that increased cholinergic activity contributes to depressive symptoms, while elevated catecholaminergic activity (dopamine and norepinephrine) is associated with mania [, ]. The heightened risk associated with TCAs has been hypothesized to be caused by their anticholinergic properties (via muscarinic receptor blockade), which may disrupt the cholinergic-adrenergic balance in limbic pathways [, , ]. Additionally, TCAs strongly inhibit norepinephrine reuptake via the norepinephrine transporter (NET), thereby increasing synaptic norepinephrine levels []. This excess noradrenergic activity may destabilize monoaminergic balance and contribute to the risk of a manic switch. Moreover, dopaminergic effects of elevated norepinephrine (via crosstalk) may further exacerbate this risk [].

Recent evidence suggests that hepatic metabolism may also modulate the risk of TEM. Joas and colleagues (2023) investigated the relationship between CYP2C19-predicted metabolism and antidepressant use, including TCAs, in BD. The authors evaluated two single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), rs4244285 and rs12248560, of the CYP2C19 enzyme. Regarding TCAs (such as amitriptyline 75 mg and clomipramine 100 mg), poor metabolizer phenotypes were associated with a higher risk of TEM (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.46). Furthermore, patients with an ultrarapid metabolizer phenotype had a higher risk of early treatment non-persistence (HR = 2.54). CYP2C19 metabolizes amitriptyline and clomipramine into their respective active metabolites, nortriptyline and desmethylclomipramine []. Slower metabolism of CYP2C19, with consequent higher drug exposure, may thus be a critical risk factor for TEM.

Although less common than with TCAs, TEM has also been associated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) therapy [, , ]. A case series by Amerio et al. [] reported that a 56-year-old woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder developed a manic episode after eight months of treatment with sertraline (200 mg/day). In another case, a 32-year-old man treated with citalopram (60 mg/day) developed a manic episode after three months. A multicenter study of bipolar patients (n = 1,720) found that a history of SSRI-induced switching, particularly fluoxetine, sertraline, and paroxetine, was associated with a higher risk of TEM []. Çiray et al. [] reported that fluvoxamine treatment carried the highest risk of TEM (reporting odds ratio (OR): 13.957). Furthermore, a retrospective cohort study of 21,012 adults with depression (2006–2013) found that SSRI therapy was associated with an increased incidence of mania or BD, at a rate of 13.2 cases per 1,000 person-years [].

In general, all SSRIs primarily inhibit serotonin reuptake in presynaptic neurons, thereby increasing the availability of serotonin (5-HT) to bind to postsynaptic receptors. Evidence suggests that 5-HT neurotransmission is involved in the pathophysiology of both depressive and manic episodes (typically decreased during depression and increased during mania) as well as in the mechanism of action of mood stabilizers [, ]. Some studies have also indicated that hypomanic and manic episodes are influenced not only by 5-HT levels but also by the modulation of specific 5-HT receptors, such as 5-HT1A, 5-HT1D, and 5-HT2 [, ]. However, the concomitant dysfunction of multiple monoaminergic systems is likely to further increase the risk of manic switch [, ].

A pharmacodynamic study suggested that one mechanism by which SSRIs may trigger mania involves their interaction with muscarinic (M1) and histamine (H1) receptors [] (Fig. ). Çiray et al. [] reported that the inhibitory constant values for M1 and H1 receptors were inversely correlated with the risk of SSRI-induced TEM, accounting for 98% of the observed variance. Interestingly, serotonergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic receptors did not significantly influence this risk []. Nevertheless, the mechanisms through which the muscarinic and histaminergic systems modulate mood are complex and remain incompletely understood.

Regarding SSRIs such as sertraline, the previously cited study by Joas and colleagues identified an association between TEM and slow CYP2C19 metabolism (HR = 1.33, 95% CI 1.05–1.69) []. This result suggests a genetically mediated dose-response relationship, in which reduced CYP2C19 enzymatic activity leads to increased systemic drug exposure, which in turn raises the probability of TEM. These findings indicate that, in many cases, TEM is a pharmacokinetic phenomenon and differs significantly between sexes []. Since neurotransmitter regulation in BD is inherently unstable, the increase in monoamine availability within the synaptic cleft is only tolerated if maintained within physiological limits [, ]. From this perspective, it is hypothesized that in patients with CYP2C19 deficiency, the actual drug exposure in brain tissue is substantially higher than the prescribed dose []. This overexposure may overwhelm the central nervous system’s compensatory mechanisms, triggering TEM.

While the potential for TEM with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) is well-documented, our search found few or no studies specifically addressing these classes between 2014 and 2026. One study reported TEM associated with SNRI use, with 33.5% of participants having a history of manic switching []. In this genome-wide association study, Nuñez et al. found that polygenic scores — used to estimate how an individual’s genetic profile predicts disease risk — can also forecast antidepressant response in MDD. Notably, this genetically predicted response was associated with an increased risk of TEM in BD, particularly in BD type I []. These findings suggest that individuals with BD type I may have both a higher clinical and genomic susceptibility to TEM.

Regarding atypical antidepressants, a case report documented a TEM associated with agomelatine []. A 31-year-old female patient with unipolar depression developed manic symptoms after two months of treatment with agomelatine (25 mg/day). The clinical presentation included increased self-confidence, pressured speech, episodic irritability, irregular eating patterns, and a reduction in sleep duration to four hours per night. Additionally, the patient exhibited compulsive cleaning and excessive spending behaviors. The symptoms were resolved following discontinuation of agomelatine. Agomelatine has a unique pharmacological profile, acting as a selective melatonin (MT1/MT2) receptor agonist and a 5-HT2C receptor antagonist, with no significant affinity for monoamine transporters (SERT, NET, DAT) or GABAergic receptors []. This case highlights that even antidepressants with non-monoaminergic mechanisms may trigger manic switches in vulnerable individuals.

Multimodal antidepressants have also been investigated in bipolar depression. In one study, three of 29 participants receiving vortioxetine in combination with lurasidone developed a manic switch []. Vortioxetine is a multimodal serotonergic agent that acts as a 5-HT1A receptor agonist, a 5-HT1B partial agonist, and antagonist at 5-HT3, 5-HT7, and 5-HT1D receptors, in addition to inhibiting SERT []. Beyond its primary serotonergic effects, evidence suggests downstream modulation of additional neurotransmitter systems, including norepinephrine, dopamine, acetylcholine, histamine, glutamate, and GABA [–]. Collectively, these findings highlight the need for further controlled studies to clarify the safety and risk of manic switching associated with vortioxetine as an adjunctive treatment for bipolar depression.

Different antidepressants may influence mitochondrial bioenergetics in distinct ways. According to Gardea-Resendez et al. [], antidepressants associated with increased mitochondrial activity (Mito+), such as bupropion, nortriptyline, paroxetine, and venlafaxine, were associated with a higher frequency of TEM compared with antidepressants associated with reduced mitochondrial activity (Mito−), such as amitriptyline and escitalopram. The authors observed that exposure to Mito+ antidepressants was associated with an approximately twofold higher rate of TEM (24.7% vs. 13.5%; OR = 2.21). Although the exact mechanisms remain uncertain, the findings suggest that alterations in electron transport chain activity and oxidative phosphorylation may contribute to vulnerability to mania in patients with BD. When considered alongside the findings of Joas et al. [] regarding enzymatic metabolism, these results reinforce the hypothesis that pharmacokinetic and bioenergetic factors may differentially influence antidepressant response in individuals with BD.

In addition to pharmacogenetic and bioenergetic factors, recent evidence suggests that immunological mechanisms may also contribute to vulnerability to TEM associated with antidepressants. According to Koc et al. [], pediatric patients with BD who developed TEM exhibited higher seroprevalence and higher titers of anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO-abs) compared to patients without a history of TEM. TPO-abs positivity was associated with a significantly increased risk of antidepressant-related TEM (OR = 3.67), independently of clinical and demographic factors. These findings reinforce the hypothesis that inflammatory and autoimmune processes may participate in the pathophysiology of antidepressant-induced TEM [, ]. The authors further suggest that markers of thyroid autoimmunity may help identify young BD patients at increased risk for ATEM.

It is important to acknowledge that some studies have reported a weak or non-significant association between antidepressant use and TEM [–]. However, in at least one of these investigations, concomitant treatments, such as mood stabilizers, were not evaluated, limiting extrapolation of the findings to antidepressant monotherapy in BD []. Jefsen et al. [] also suggest that TEM may be a natural course of the disorder. They identified that the peak number of manic episodes occurred approximately three months before the start of antidepressant treatment, and the number of depressive episodes peaked at the beginning of antidepressant prescription. The authors propose that the observed association between antidepressant use and TEM may reflect time-varying confounding by indication rather than a true causal relationship between antidepressant exposure and manic switching. In addition, esketamine administered in combination with a mood stabilizer has been suggested as a potential option for the treatment of bipolar depression, although the current evidence remains preliminary and requires further confirmation in larger, controlled studies []. Taken together, while emerging data suggest that the risk of TEM may not be uniformly elevated across all antidepressant strategies, the potential for mood destabilization should always be carefully considered when prescribing antidepressants for individuals with BD.

This concern is mirrored in the context of unipolar depression. Although the focus of this study was antidepressant-induced mania switching, antidepressant-associated hypomania represents a significant clinical challenge in this population, with incidence rates varying considerably, with reported rates ranging from 0.3% to 22.4%, depending on factors such as drug class and duration of clinical follow-up []. Antidepressant-associated hypomania manifests with greater prevalence in females, young patients, and those with a positive family history of bipolar disorder. Regarding pharmacotherapy, it is observed that broad-spectrum antidepressants—particularly TCAs and certain MAOIs—present a significantly higher risk of inducing hypomania when compared to more selective agents, such as SSRIs [].

When to consider an antidepressant in BD: Antidepressants may be considered in selected patients with bipolar depression, particularly when depressive symptoms persist despite adequate mood stabilization. Current clinical guidelines support their cautious use as adjunctive therapy combined with mood stabilizers or atypical antipsychotics, especially in BD type II and in patients without a recent history of manic or mixed episodes [, , ]. Antidepressants with lower switch liability, such as SSRIs, are generally preferred over TCAs, which consistently show higher rates of TEM [, ]. Careful patient selection, gradual dose titration, and close monitoring during the first weeks of treatment are essential.

When not to consider an antidepressant in BD: Antidepressants should generally be avoided as monotherapy in BD, particularly in BD type I, due to the increased risk of mood destabilization and TEM [, , , ]. Their use may also be inappropriate in patients with a history of antidepressant-induced TEM, rapid cycling, mixed features, frequent manic episodes, severe suicidal behavior, or comorbid psychiatric conditions associated with increased switching vulnerability [, , , ]. TCAs and antidepressants with broader monoaminergic or activating profiles should be prescribed with particular caution because of their stronger association with manic switching [–]. Emerging evidence further suggests that pharmacogenetic susceptibility, mitochondrial bioenergetic alterations, and autoimmune markers may increase the likelihood of TEM in vulnerable individuals [, , ].

We acknowledge some limitations in this review. As it is a narrative review, rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis, which may increase the risk of selection bias. The included studies are heterogeneous in terms of design, population characteristics, diagnostic criteria, exposure to antidepressants, and definitions of TEM, which limits direct comparisons between studies. Furthermore, several conclusions derive from observational studies, case reports, or preclinical models, which restrict causal inference. Finally, some classes of antidepressants remain poorly explored in the recent literature, particularly MAOIs and SSRIs.

The findings strengthen the argument that safe and effective treatment of bipolar depression requires a mechanistically informed, individualized approach that prioritizes mood stabilization and vigilant monitoring over antidepressant-centric strategies. Future research should therefore move beyond class-based risk generalizations and focus on: (i) identifying robust predictors of switching (genetic markers, clinical phenotypes, and biological signatures), (ii) clarifying how antidepressant-related perturbations propagate across cholinergic, adrenergic, serotonergic, and receptor-interaction networks to produce state transitions, and (iii) developing precision-treatment frameworks that can prospectively match patients to the lowest-risk interventions while preserving antidepressant efficacy where appropriate. Advancing this agenda is essential not only to reduce iatrogenic harm, but also to leverage antidepressant-induced switching as a window into the core neurobiology of mood instability—ultimately enabling more targeted, preventive, and personalized therapeutics for BD.

Although antidepressants may contribute to mood destabilization in susceptible individuals, TEM is not a universal consequence of antidepressant exposure. The evidence reviewed here suggests that TEM is better conceptualized as a vulnerability-dependent phenomenon arising from interactions between antidepressant-related neurobiological effects and individual susceptibility factors, including BD subtype, prior illness course, pharmacogenetic variability, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and immunoinflammatory status. Tricyclic antidepressants remain the agents most consistently associated with switching risk, whereas SSRIs and atypical antidepressants may also precipitate TEM under specific neurobiological conditions. Collectively, these findings support a more nuanced and mechanistically informed understanding of antidepressant-associated TEM and reinforce the importance of individualized treatment strategies that prioritize mood stabilization, careful patient selection, and close clinical monitoring in the management of bipolar depression.
