neuroscience.title: Spinal Cord‐Computer Interface for Motor Recovery After Spinal Cord Injury: Conceptual Framework, Mechanisms, and Clinical Translation
neuroscience.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) remains a clinically challenging condition characterized by profound functional deficits. For decades, traditional therapeutic strategies prioritizing structural repair, including axonal regeneration and biological scaffolds, have largely failed to yield significant functional recovery. This stagnation has catalyzed a paradigm shift driven by the convergence of neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and bioelectronic engineering, leading to the emergence of the spinal cord‐computer interface (SCCI). Unlike brain‐computer interfaces that typically bypass the body to control external devices, SCCI functions as an input‐based neural engineering technology designed to directly engage dormant yet anatomically intact neural circuits situated below the lesion. By delivering precise, programmable spatiotemporal epidural electrical stimulation, SCCI reactivates specific spinal motor circuitry to enable the restoration of voluntary motor control in previously paralyzed limbs. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of SCCI by tracing its conceptual evolution from early gate control theory to modern neuromodulation paradigms. We dissect the underlying physiological mechanisms and integrate global research findings to highlight how rapid technological advancements and clinical breakthroughs are reshaping the landscape of motor rehabilitation, ultimately offering a viable therapeutic pathway for patients worldwide.
neuroscience.text:
Spinal cord injury (SCI) represents a formidable global health challenge that imposes immense physical and psychological suffering on patients while placing a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems worldwide. This condition is not merely a localized trauma but a systemic disruption of central nervous system (CNS) function, effectively severing the critical communication pathways between the brain and the peripheral body []. Current epidemiological data underscore the gravity of this issue: the global prevalence of SCI has exceeded 20 million cases []. Furthermore, incidence rates continue to climb, driven by the high prevalence of traffic accidents, an increasing frequency of falls among the elderly, and sports‐related injuries []. Prognosis remains persistently poor for patients with severe SCI, particularly those classified as ASIA Grade A []. These patients face not only lifelong paralysis and a loss of independence but also a spectrum of debilitating secondary complications. These conditions, which include pressure ulcers, neuropathic pain, autonomic dysreflexia, and cardiovascular instability, severely compromise their quality of life [].

Understanding the limitations of current therapeutic modalities requires a clear elucidation of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying SCI. It is widely accepted that this pathological process proceeds in two distinct phases []. The first phase, designated as primary injury, refers to the immediate structural destruction caused by the initial mechanical trauma, which includes compression, laceration, or contusion []. This phase involves acute axonal shearing, vascular rupture, and disruption of neuronal membranes. These events collectively precipitate rapid neuronal necrosis within the lesion epicenter. Following this, the second phase, or secondary injury, ensues. This phase encompasses a cascade of sustained biological responses triggered by the primary event, which progressively expands the extent of tissue damage []. The hallmarks of secondary injury include local ischemia, edema, and excitotoxicity, alongside an intense inflammatory response characterized by the infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages. A defining feature of secondary injury is the formation of the glial scar. While this scar serves a protective role by containing the spread of inflammation, it simultaneously establishes a formidable physical and chemical barrier that impedes neural tissue regeneration. Specifically, reactive astrocytes within the scar tissue overexpress chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans. These molecules actively inhibit the extension of axonal growth cones and thereby prevent the spontaneous reconnection of damaged neural pathways [].

The historical trajectory of SCI management has been characterized by efforts to mitigate tissue damage or repair structural integrity, yet these conventional approaches have reached substantial efficacy plateaus, with prominent limitations across four core intervention domains []. First, in terms of pharmacological interventions, high‐dose glucocorticoids may alleviate edema and inflammation to a certain extent, but they fail to promote functional regeneration of damaged neural pathways []. Second, spinal decompression combined with internal fixation is crucial for stabilizing the spinal column and preventing persistent mechanical compression of residual neural tissue; however, this approach similarly fails to achieve functional repair []. Third, rehabilitation therapies play an indispensable role in maintaining muscle mass, joint mobility, and cardiopulmonary fitness, but rehabilitation alone cannot reliably restore voluntary motor control when descending motor commands remain interrupted []. Fourth, tissue engineering strategies, including transplantation of neural or mesenchymal stem cells and implantation of biomaterial scaffolds, have demonstrated potential in preclinical studies, but their clinical translation is still hindered by low cell survival in the hostile injury microenvironment, potential tumorigenic risks associated with stem cell transplantation, and the difficulty of guiding axonal regeneration toward functional synaptic integration [, , ]. Consequently, the path toward clinically meaningful structural repair remains obstructed by substantial biological and translational barriers.

Given the research bottlenecks encountered by structural regeneration and repair strategies, attention has shifted toward the specific pathological characteristics of SCI. Specifically, the neural circuits located below the level of injury largely remain structurally intact. These circuits encompass motor neuron pools that innervate muscle tissues, as well as central pattern generators (CPGs), which are complex spinal circuitry capable of generating rhythmic motor outputs [, ]. Crucially, the fundamental impediment in paralysis is not the functional impairment of spinal motor circuits or the muscle tissue itself. Rather, it is the obstruction of descending signal transmission from the brain. In fact, the functional capacity of spinal circuits to execute movement and the contractile ability of muscles remain preserved [].

Consequently, we use the spinal cord‐computer interface (SCCI) as a higher‐level spinal interface framework rather than as a simple replacement term for EES or SCS. Broadly defined, SCCI encompasses technologies that establish direct information exchange between the spinal cord and external devices, including both input‐oriented systems that deliver programmable stimulation to preserved spinal circuits and output‐oriented systems that record and decode spinal signals. In the narrower focus of this review, SCCI refers to an input‐based spinal neuroengineering framework for motor recovery, in which programmable spatiotemporal spinal stimulation is integrated with computational control, feedback sensing, rehabilitation training, and biological execution through preserved spinal sensorimotor circuits.

This conceptual distinction is important because modern motor‐restorative spinal neurotechnology is no longer adequately described by conventional analgesic SCS or by EES alone. With rapid advances in brain‐computer interfaces, artificial intelligence, wearable sensing, robotics, and implantable bioelectronics, the field is moving toward a multidisciplinary architecture that includes stimulation encoding, state recognition, closed‐loop adjustment, supraspinal intention decoding, and potentially spinal signal decoding. Therefore, the value of SCCI is not terminological novelty alone, but the establishment of a unifying framework that links electrical input, computational control, neural sensing, and biological motor execution within a single translational roadmap. This review first delineates the conceptual evolution of SCCI, then dissects its system architecture, mechanistic hypotheses, and clinical evidence, and finally discusses its distinctions from BCI, traditional SCS, and FES, as well as future directions for closed‐loop, multimodal, and bio‐hybrid translation.

The development of the SCCI rests upon a foundation established by over half a century of neurophysiological research and clinical practice in electrical stimulation (Figure ). Initially, efforts to effectively inhibit abnormal nociceptive inputs led to the formulation of the gate control theory. This theory provided the theoretical framework for the systematic application of SCS in pain management. However, the incidental clinical observation that electrical stimulation could evoke contractions in paralyzed limbs precipitated a fundamental paradigm shift. Consequently, the objective of neuromodulation transitioned from suppression to activation and functional reconstruction. Accordingly, this section outlines the mechanistic basis of the gate control theory and SCS, traces the conceptual emergence of spinal neuromodulation for motor control, and formally defines SCCI within this specific context.

In 1965, Melzack and Wall formulated the gate control theory of pain. This theory posits that the transmission of nociceptive signals within the spinal dorsal horn operates not as a direct relay to the brain but as a process modulated by the interaction between large‐diameter non‐nociceptive afferent fibers and small‐diameter nociceptive afferent fibers []. Specifically, the authors proposed that the activation of large‐diameter Aβ fibers excites inhibitory interneurons. This excitation subsequently closes the physiological gate to nociceptive signals transmitted by small‐diameter C‐fibers [].

This seminal theory provided the theoretical rationale for the inception of SCS. In 1967, Shealy et al. pioneered the implantation of the first dorsal column stimulator for the treatment of intractable pain []. Over the ensuing decades, SCS has predominantly utilized tonic, low‐frequency electrical pulses to manage neuropathic pain. Mechanistically, this approach recruits Aβ fibers to drive GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory interneurons within the spinal dorsal horn. This activation effectively suppresses the aberrant neural signaling associated with chronic pain states [].

From a mechanistic perspective (Figure ), the electrical field generated by SCS preferentially recruits large‐diameter Aβ fibers within the dorsal columns and the dorsal root entry zone []. This stimulation modulates afferent discharge at the level of the dorsal root ganglion (DRG). Upon entering laminae I‐V of the dorsal horn (Figure ), the collaterals of these fibers excite inhibitory interneurons to enhance GABAergic and glycinergic transmission. This process establishes both presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition [, , ].

Specifically, as detailed in the synaptic microenvironment (Figure ), SCS reduces the release of excitatory amino acids such as glutamate and aspartate from primary afferent terminals while increasing spinal GABA availability, an effect that can be reversed by dorsal horn GABA(B) receptor antagonism [, ]. Beyond classical “gate” inhibition, SCS has been shown to alter broader neurochemical signaling, exemplified by serotonergic and peptidergic mediators like 5‐HT and Substance P, and may influence transporter/ion‐channel dynamics and plasticity states that bias dorsal horn circuitry toward sustained inhibitory control (LTD‐like). Collectively, these segmental actions reduce ascending nociceptive traffic and constrain the maintenance of hyperexcitable dorsal horn states associated with central sensitization [].

Concurrently, SCS remodels the local neurochemical environment by influencing neurotransmitter systems and membrane excitability, promoting circuitry states that oppose sensitization‐related synaptic strengthening [].

Beyond segmental gating, SCS enhances endogenous analgesia through supraspinal engagement of descending inhibitory systems, including the periaqueductal gray‐rostral ventromedial medulla axis and the locus coeruleus noradrenergic pathway []. By suppressing persistent discharges associated with central sensitization and maladaptive affective pain processing, these mechanisms help explain clinical benefits of SCS across multiple chronic pain phenotypes [, ].

Finally, regarding the broader physiological milieu, accumulating evidence indicates that SCS can regulate neuroinflammation by reshaping neuroimmune signaling, notably through the reduction of pro‐inflammatory mediators such as IL‐1β and IL‐6 in preclinical paradigms, while simultaneously biasing the cytokine milieu toward anti‐inflammatory programs including IL‐10, thereby supporting neuro‐glial homeostasis (Figure ) [, ]. Moreover, SCS may improve microcirculation and ischemic perfusion by modulating sympathetic tone and vascular reactivity, a mechanistic basis often discussed in the context of ischemic pain components observed in refractory angina and related vascular pain syndromes (Figure ) [, , ].

During the 1970s and 1980s, while employing SCS to treat pain or spasticity, researchers incidentally observed that electrical stimulation could induce involuntary muscle contractions and even generate rhythmic, locomotor‐like movements in paralyzed limbs [, ]. Concurrently, basic research conducted on decerebrate cats confirmed the existence of autonomous CPGs within the lumbosacral spinal cord. These studies demonstrated that when spinal circuitry isolated from the brain was subjected to tonic electrical or chemical stimulation, they could generate coordinated locomotor patterns [, , ]. These findings revealed that the spinal cord is not merely a passive conduit for signal transmission but a sophisticated processing center responsible for regulating motor function.

The complementary findings from these clinical and preclinical studies collectively catalyzed the formation of spinal neuromodulation technology. Epidural electrical stimulation (EES) fundamentally alters the excitability state of spinal circuits. Following SCI, spinal neurons enter a hyperpolarized, dormant state due to the loss of descending monoaminergic drive from the brainstem, and EES compensates for this deficit via electrical modulation []. Mechanistically, the technology targets large‐diameter proprioceptive afferent fibers (types Ia and Ib) within the dorsal roots. By elevating the resting membrane potential of motor neurons and interneurons closer to their action potential firing threshold, EES effectively facilitates the spinal circuits. In this primed state, even weak residual sensory inputs or descending drive signals become sufficient to trigger robust motor outputs [].

Grounded in the theoretical framework of early spinal conduction models, the iterative evolution of multi‐site electrode arrays and the successful development of implantable pulse generators (IPGs) capable of independent multi‐channel modulation laid the critical hardware foundation [, , ]. These milestones formally inaugurated the era of SCCI‐related exploration for precise motor control. Importantly, the term SCCI has not been used uniformly across the literature. One route focuses on output‐type spinal cord‐computer interfaces, in which spinal signals are recorded and decoded to control external effectors; for example, Oliveira et al. demonstrated a direct spinal cord‐computer interface for paralysed hand control, but that system did not rely on EES‐based neuromodulation as defined in the present review []. In addition, invasive animal studies have shown that electrophysiological signals recorded directly from spinal descending, lateral, or dorsal tracts can be decoded to reconstruct forelimb force or hindlimb kinematics, indicating that future spinal interfaces may also include a spinal‐signal output or decoding dimension [, ]. The other route, which is the focus of this review, uses EES and related spinal neuromodulation to input programmable signals into preserved spinal circuits for motor recovery. Taken together, these developments indicate that SCCI should be understood as a bidirectional spinal interface framework with both readout and stimulation capacities, whereas conventional SCS and EES describe only individual therapeutic components within this broader architecture.

The need for this framework becomes particularly clear as spinal neuromodulation is increasingly integrated with BCIs, artificial intelligence, wearable sensing, rehabilitation robotics, and closed‐loop control [, , , , , , ]. Classical SCS for pain management prioritizes binary activation status and relatively static frequency or amplitude parameters. In contrast, neuromodulation for complex motor functions requires the precise regulation of spinal circuit states and behavioral phases. This represents a transition from generalized stimulation toward interpretable, optimizable, and transferable neural coding [, ]. Such a transition cannot be fully captured by SCS or EES alone because it involves not only where and how electrical pulses are delivered, but also how computational systems encode stimulation, interpret feedback, and coordinate biological motor execution.

This technological evolution manifests in three critical dimensions. First, electrode configuration and functionality must achieve motor control through anatomical adaptation and selective recruitment. Motor reconstruction requires precise spatial selectivity that targets specific lumbosacral segments and neural pathways. Therefore, electrodes must evolve from generic dorsal column devices into high‐density, scalable, and flexible arrays. These designs conform to spinal anatomy and allow for modulation that mimics physiological functional compartmentalization [, ]. Second, pulse‐generator output must depart from traditional constant‐drive mechanisms. The generation of actions such as walking, standing, or sitting relies on temporality and synergy; therefore, stimulation outputs must be synchronized with gait phases, motor intentions, and postural adjustments. Spatially, they must coordinate coding across multiple electrode sites to create reproducible spatiotemporal patterns rather than simple, fixed‐frequency tonic stimulation [, ]. Third, the integration of feedback signals is essential for adaptive optimization. Since the goal of motor modulation is stable and generalizable functional execution, systems must integrate multimodal feedback, including electromyography, inertial measurement units, plantar pressure, and kinematic metrics. Under closed‐loop control, stimulation parameters undergo dynamic adjustments in response to patient status, fatigue levels, training stages, and environmental changes [, , ].

Based on these transformative advancements, spinal neuromodulation has evolved from a singular therapeutic intervention into a complex neuroengineering system. This system comprises implantable hardware, external sensing, computational algorithms, and biological mechanisms that induce immediate spinal circuit responses and long‐term plasticity. To describe this complex architecture more precisely and to standardize its use in the context of motor recovery, we refine and extend the concept of the spinal cord‐computer interface, abbreviated as SCCI, rather than claiming that the term itself is entirely new. In this review, SCCI is not used merely as an output device for decoding spinal signals, nor is it used as a synonym for EES. Instead, we define SCCI as a spinal neuroengineering interface that inputs programmable spatiotemporal signals into residual neural circuits below the injury level, with the future potential to incorporate spinal signal recording and decoding as part of a bidirectional read‐write architecture. By delivering these programmable signals via electrode arrays, SCCI activates and reorganizes spinal circuitry to restore coordinated voluntary limb movement [, , ].

SCCI represents a paradigm shift toward active functional restoration. Unlike conventional spinal cord stimulation designed primarily for analgesia, SCCI is specifically engineered to interact dynamically with the dormant lumbosacral locomotor circuitry. By delivering precise, biomimetic electrical signals, it aims to re‐engage spinal circuitry that remains anatomically intact but functionally silent below the injury level, as shown in Figure . This section provides a comprehensive analysis of the SCCI framework, dissecting its architecture defined by the synergistic integration of bioelectronic hardware and adaptive control algorithms, exploring the mechanistic hypotheses that drive motor recovery, and evaluating the clinical efficacy that positions this technology as a cornerstone of modern neurorehabilitation.

The architectural composition of SCCI is defined by the synergistic integration of bioelectronic hardware and an intelligent software ecosystem. The hardware infrastructure encompasses the surgically implanted electrode array, the IPG, and an external controller responsible for parameter configuration []. Interfacing with these components, the software ecosystem serves as the computational core, orchestrating personalized spinal models, stimulation coding, state recognition, and adaptive closed‐loop strategies [, ]. Functionally, the hardware acts as the executive vehicle for electrical signal delivery and output. It determines whether stimulation can affect the target neural structures reliably and precisely [, ]. Conversely, the software system assumes the role of control and orchestration. It defines the stimulation coding, timing sequences, and contact combinations [, ]. By unifying the scheduling and dynamic adjustment of hardware outputs, the software transforms raw hardware capabilities into modulation protocols that spinal circuits can effectively utilize [, ].

In terms of hardware, SCCI shares morphological similarities with the pulse generators, epidural leads, and paddle electrodes of traditional SCS [, ]. However, the context of motor reconstruction imposes more stringent requirements regarding electrode conformability, resistance to migration, long‐term impedance stability [], and spatial selectivity [].

The first critical component is the electrode. Traditional SCS systems were originally designed for pain management. These systems rely on cylindrical percutaneous leads or paddle electrodes implanted in the epidural space. Such devices possess a relatively rigid texture with a Young's modulus in the megapascal range. This creates a severe mechanical mismatch with the soft spinal tissue, which has a Young's modulus of approximately 200 kPa [, ]. This disparity often precipitates spinal tissue compression and chronic stimulation‐induced injury. Furthermore, it promotes the formation of a fibrotic capsule around the electrode. This encapsulation acts as an electrical insulator that increases impedance and subsequently degrades therapeutic efficacy over time [, ]. Consequently, material and structural evolution has shifted from rigidity to compliance. Emerging designs include flexible thin‐film electrodes, conductive polymer/hydrogel interfaces, and high‐density arrays []. These innovations aim to mitigate inflammatory responses and enhance spatial resolution []. Simultaneously, the combination of high‐density arrays with precise spatial modulation enables the targeted recruitment of specific motor neurons and fibers [, ]. This provides the fundamental hardware basis for fine‐grained synergistic motor patterns.

The material requirements of SCCI are also influenced by the biological responses associated with chronic implantation. Mechanical mismatch, foreign body reactions, fibrotic encapsulation, and long‐term changes in impedance may reduce stimulation selectivity and energy efficiency. Therefore, flexible thin‐film electrodes, soft bioelectronic interfaces, coatings with low impedance, and conformal arrays with high channel density should be regarded not only as material improvements, but also as essential components for achieving stable long term interaction with the spinal cord [, , , , , , , , , , , , ].

The second component is the IPG. In SCS for pain, the core function of the generator focuses on long‐term analgesic stability and safety adaptation. In contrast, SCCI requires IPGs to satisfy not only long‐term implantable reliability but also the demands of complex stimulation paradigms. These include independent or grouped multi‐channel control, temporal sequencing, and rapid switching of frequency and pulse width, as well as onboard sensing/telemetry to support closed‐loop feedback–driven, real‐time parameter adaptation [, ]. The device must also balance power consumption, battery life, thermal safety, and output consistency []. Since motor reconstruction frequently involves rapid mode switching and complex orchestration, the output resolution, channel management capability, and parameter consistency of the IPG directly influence the long‐term viability of individualized therapies []. Furthermore, the integrated system formed by the IPG and leads must incorporate mechanisms for electromagnetic interference resistance, fault protection, and safety amplitude limiting. These features reduce risks associated with abnormal discharges, false triggering, or over‐stimulation [, , ]. Moreover, implantable closed‐loop platforms and high‐channel‐count wireless neuromodulation systems provide important engineering precedents for future SCCI devices that combine stimulation, sensing, telemetry, and power‐efficient control [, , ].

The third component is the external controller. This terminal serves as the critical interface bridging clinical parameterization, patient daily use, and algorithmic updates. It typically handles functions such as program downloading and switching, safety‐range intensity adjustments, rapid configuration during training scenarios, and data logging [, ]. It facilitates the transition of SCCI from laboratory settings to generalized multi‐scenario applications []. In motor reconstruction applications, the efficiency of human‐machine interaction significantly impacts system generalizability and patient compliance. This includes the ability to rapidly select gait phase programs or switch between situational modes like sitting, standing, and walking [].

More importantly, the integrated computational framework in SCCI transcends the simple provision of parameter options; it constitutes the core of temporal motor regulation. It executes the personalized anatomical‐functional mapping that determines which contacts correspond to synergies such as hip flexion, knee extension, or ankle dorsiflexion [, , ]. It also defines stimulation coding and timing strategies, such as when to stimulate within a gait cycle, the duration of stimulation, and the pulse waveform []. Additionally, it supports online parameter adjustment logic based on training progress and varying scenarios [, ]. Thus, the technological efficacy of SCCI is often embodied in the neuromodulation capability of its software coding. This capability is defined by the use of optimizable coding strategies and reproducible parameter management to schedule the output of the electrodes and IPG.

The ability of SCCI to induce immediate voluntary movement relies on the synergistic coordination between stimulation protocols and intrinsic neural circuits. The prevailing hypothesis posits that epidural stimulation functions through dorsal spinal neuromodulation. Specifically, EES does not directly activate α‐motor neurons. Instead, it preferentially recruits large‐diameter proprioceptive afferent fibers (such as types I and II) within the dorsal roots (Figure ) [, ]. Through spinal interneuronal circuits, these sensory inputs are transformed into motor outputs, forming a multi‐level sensorimotor loop capable of activation and enhancement []. Essentially, this mechanism leverages sensory input signals to reactivate motor circuits []. To implement this mechanism, SCCI systems employ spatiotemporal neuromodulation. This coding strategy precisely synchronizes stimulation pulses with the gait cycle. By applying targeted stimulation to specific spinal segments, such as stimulating the L2 segment during the swing phase and the S1 segment during the stance phase, the system mimics the natural propagation patterns of descending activation signals from the brain []. Such rhythmic stimulation signals reactivate dormant CPGs located in the lumbosacral enlargement, restoring them to an excitable state and thereby re‐enabling the output of coordinated locomotor rhythms [, , ].

Foundational studies on spatiotemporal neuromodulation and afferent‐mediated spinal circuit recruitment have demonstrated that phase‐specific stimulation can engage muscle synergies and correct gait or balance deficits after SCI. These studies are therefore cited at the first mechanistic discussion of spatiotemporal recruitment rather than being introduced only in later comparative sections [, ].

Beyond generating autonomous rhythms, the elevated excitability of CPGs serves a pivotal role in restoring voluntary control by enhancing the transmission efficiency of residual descending pathways []. Even in patients diagnosed with clinically complete spinal cord injury, a paucity of descending fibers often remains anatomically intact. However, the supraspinal drive carried by these fibers is typically too faint to breach the activation threshold of spinal motor circuits [, ]. This context underpins the “sub‐threshold intention enhancement” hypothesis []. By modulating spinal circuitry to a state of heightened physiological receptivity, SCCI effectively lowers the activation barrier. Consequently, weak, sub‐threshold motor intentions originating from the brain are amplified into robust commands capable of eliciting effective muscle contractions [, ]. This unmasking process enables the translation of faint neural signals into distinct, intention‐controlled actions such as walking or standing [].

Crucially, this mechanism implies that the therapeutic efficacy of SCCI is not autonomous but is intrinsically coupled with the physiological context. This dependence specifically encompasses the structural integrity of residual pathways, the fidelity of peripheral sensory inputs, and the intensity of rehabilitation training. This interplay elucidates the significant heterogeneity observed in patient outcomes and explains why efficacy varies across the clinical population [, , ].

Despite these mechanistic insights, the CPG‐centric model retains significant uncertainties. The precise cellular composition, quantity, and synaptic interaction modalities of the neurons constituting human CPGs remain elusive, constituting a fundamental gap in current anatomical and functional understanding []. This uncertainty has direct implications for the theoretical foundation and clinical implementation of SCCI. First, if the human locomotor CPG cannot yet be defined at a precise cellular level, stimulation targets cannot be selected solely according to a fixed cell‐type map. Second, inter‐individual differences in residual descending fibers, propriospinal connectivity, segmental excitability, and sensory feedback may strongly influence whether a given stimulation pattern can recruit functional locomotor output. Third, the lack of human cell‐level validation limits the ability to define universal stimulation parameters or predictive biomarkers. Therefore, SCCI should be understood as a functional systems‐level framework that modulates preserved sensorimotor networks, rather than as a technology whose efficacy depends on complete identification of every CPG constituent neuron. Given this complexity, future research is increasingly exploring complementary strategies, including more precise electrophysiological mapping, closed‐loop sensing, computational modeling, and alternative approaches that directly target motor neuron pools when circuit‐level recruitment is insufficient [].

Extending the scope of immediate motor induction, the chronic application of SCCI and SCCI‐relevant spinal stimulation can promote neural circuit remodeling, although the strength and type of evidence differ substantially between preclinical and clinical contexts [, , , ]. In particular, Courtine and colleagues characterized a population of spinal neurons recruited during stimulation‐enabled walking recovery in rodent models, providing important mechanistic evidence that activity‐dependent remodeling of defined spinal circuits can contribute to functional recovery after paralysis []. However, these rodent data should not be interpreted as direct proof that identical cellular mechanisms operate in humans. In clinical studies, evidence for plasticity is generally inferred from functional carry‐over, stimulation‐off retention, changes in voluntary control, electromyographic patterns, or improvements after intensive training, rather than from direct cellular or molecular measurements. Accordingly, this section distinguishes mechanistic evidence derived from rodent models from indirect translational evidence in human cohorts.

As illustrated in Figure , at the neural circuit level, SCCI‐relevant stimulation may recruit spinal propriospinal interneurons to drive intersegmental reorganization. This process can integrate previously isolated spinal segments into synergistic functional units, thereby enabling smoother multi‐joint motor control []. It should be noted that most molecular evidence currently comes from stimulated sublesional segments, peri‐lesional tissue, or rodent SCI models. Whether comparable molecular effects are induced at the supra‐lesional level in humans remains unresolved and should be examined in future studies. The direction of lesion‐spanning reorganization should also be interpreted cautiously. Rather than representing a single unidirectional pathway, the available evidence supports a potentially bidirectional process involving descending residual or sprouting pathways, ascending sensory/propriospinal signaling, and local intersegmental remodeling across spared spinal networks. Crucially, evidence indicates that electrical modulation can induce structural plasticity, marked by the upregulation of regeneration‐associated genes such as growth‐associated protein 43 (GAP‐43) []. This structural plasticity may facilitate the formation or strengthening of functional connections across or around the lesion site. In clinical observations, stimulation‐assisted training has been associated with partial carry‐over or retention of functional gains after stimulation is turned off, although this phenomenon remains variable and requires more systematic validation in human cohorts [, , , , ].

Accordingly, the chronic‐effect model proposed here should be interpreted as a translational hypothesis rather than a fully validated human mechanism. Future human studies should combine longitudinal neurophysiology, imaging, stimulation‐off testing, and standardized functional assessments to determine whether the molecular signatures and circuit reorganization observed in animals correspond to durable, clinically meaningful recovery in patients with SCI.

The fundamental advantage of SCCI lies in its capacity for programmable spatiotemporal modulation. This capability advances electrical stimulation beyond traditional tonic output and shifts the therapeutic logic toward precise neuromodulation interventions synchronized with specific motor tasks [, , , ]. Typically, SCCI utilizes epidural electrode arrays with multiple contacts covering the lumbosacral enlargement and relies on individualized contact selection to engage defined spinal segments and muscle synergies [, , ]. Through an external controller, the system initiates preset or personalized stimulation protocols that align distinct contact configurations with specific phases of the gait cycle. Consequently, bursts of short pulses can be delivered during critical intervals, including the swing and stance phases, to selectively induce and amplify the synergy among hip, knee, and ankle muscle groups [, ]. In contrast to tonic stimulation operating at a constant frequency, this strategy mimics the temporal organization of physiological motor control by relying on coding patterns that are contingent upon gait phases and specific to muscle groups. As a result, stimulation is transformed from a simple excitatory input into a structured interface signal capable of facilitating rhythmic, continuous, and task‐oriented motor performance [, , ].

Early clinical studies using lumbosacral spinal cord stimulation or epidural electrical stimulation provided the essential foundation for this therapeutic paradigm. These studies demonstrated that electrical neuromodulation can raise the excitability of dormant spinal circuits below the lesion and enable voluntary movement, standing, assisted stepping, or overground walking in selected individuals with severe SCI [, , , , ]. Their significance lies not only in the functional improvements observed, but also in the conceptual demonstration that anatomically preserved sublesional circuits can be re‐engaged when appropriate neuromodulatory input is provided. However, many of these pioneering studies mainly relied on open‐loop, manually optimized, or task‐associated stimulation paradigms. Therefore, they should be interpreted as SCCI‐relevant clinical precursors rather than strict SCCI evidence. This distinction is important because SCCI, as defined in this review, is not simply equivalent to conventional SCS or EES. Instead, it represents an input‐based neuroengineering interface that integrates epidural spinal neuromodulation with programmable spatiotemporal coding, individualized parameter optimization, digital computation, sensor‐driven adaptation, brain‐derived intention decoding, robotic rehabilitation, or closed‐loop control.

Under this stricter conceptual framework, the current clinical evidence for core SCCI remains limited but highly informative. Representative studies have advanced from feasibility‐oriented case reports toward more systematic explorations centered on personalized programming, contact‐specific functional mapping, task‐dependent stimulation, and multimodal rehabilitation paradigms [, , , , ]. In these studies, stimulation is no longer delivered as a static background input; rather, it is organized as a task‐specific and digitally adjustable signal designed to recruit defined spinal segments and muscle synergies according to the intended behavior. Researchers typically establish a “contact‐muscle‐function” mapping after implantation to identify which electrode contacts and stimulation parameters preferentially recruit specific muscles, joints, or functional outputs [, , , , ]. This mapping process provides the basis for constructing individualized stimulation programs. During rehabilitation, these programs are repeatedly refined according to motor performance, residual capacity, fatigue, task demands, and training progression. This allows the same subject to invoke distinct stimulation modes for different tasks, such as standing, stepping, overground walking, stair climbing, or other activity‐specific behaviors [, , ]. Across the studies summarized in Table , the reported therapeutic effects can be broadly categorized into several interrelated functional domains. The first is the restoration or enhancement of standing and weight‐bearing capability. This includes improved recruitment of anti‐gravity muscle groups, enhanced postural stability, and the ability to maintain upright posture for extended periods with assistance []. The second is the improvement of stepping and walking ability. Patients may demonstrate the capacity to perform treadmill stepping or overground walking while stimulation is active, and some individuals can achieve walking with the support of walkers, orthoses, body‐weight support systems, or robotic assistance. These improvements are often accompanied by measurable changes in walking speed, walking distance, step length, symmetry, and endurance [, ]. The third is the refinement of motor control quality. Muscle activation can transition from isolated or poorly coordinated contractions toward more organized synergistic sequences, gait rhythms may become more stable, and patients may perceive a stronger link between motor intention and motor execution [, ]. These outcomes are typically quantified using clinical and physiological assessment tools, including the 10‐meter walk test, the 6‐minute walk test, key muscle strength scores, gait parameters, and surface electromyography synergy patterns. Together, these measures provide an objective framework for evaluating the functional efficacy of SCCI‐mediated motor restoration [, ].

Nevertheless, the clinical response to SCCI remains highly individualized. Observed variations in efficacy indicate that SCCI is not a universal solution suitable for all patients with SCI. Rather, it is a personalized neuromodulation system whose clinical effect depends on the alignment between stimulation coding, residual neural connectivity, injury characteristics, musculoskeletal condition, and rehabilitation strategy []. Patients differ substantially in neurological level of injury, injury completeness, AIS grade, time since injury, residual descending connectivity, baseline motor function, spasticity, pain, endurance, and prior rehabilitation history. These factors may influence whether stimulation can successfully recruit functional spinal circuits and whether repeated training can consolidate stimulation‐enabled motor outputs into more stable functional gains. Therefore, patient stratification and individualized parameter optimization are essential for interpreting clinical outcomes and improving therapeutic reproducibility.

In this section, foundational concepts such as spatiotemporal stimulation, afferent recruitment, gait‐phase coding, and feedback control are supported by the core references introduced in earlier mechanistic and architectural sections. Therefore, the additional studies cited below are used specifically to summarize emerging clinical configurations, including non‐invasive stimulation, robotic/exoskeleton‐assisted rehabilitation, real‐time triggering, and closed‐loop control, rather than to re‐establish the basic mechanism of SCCI [, , , , ].

It is also worth emphasizing that SCCI is increasingly developing toward combinatorial therapeutic paradigms. Recovery of walking ability depends not only on the modifiability of spinal circuits but also on musculoskeletal integrity, joint mobility, cardiopulmonary endurance, balance control, spasticity, pain, and motor learning efficiency. Consequently, recent clinical studies have integrated spinal neuromodulation with activity‐based therapy, robotic‐assisted body‐weight‐supported treadmill training, and other rehabilitation protocols [, ]. This forms a continuous therapeutic pathway in which stimulation provides accessible neural output, while repeated task‐specific training consolidates, refines, and strengthens functional performance. In this context, SCCI should not be viewed merely as an assistive stimulation tool, but as a neuromodulatory platform that creates a permissive physiological state for rehabilitation‐driven plasticity.

Furthermore, SCCI exhibits natural complementarity with exoskeletons and assistive robotic systems during the training phase. Spinal stimulation provides neural drive and synergistic muscle recruitment, whereas robotic systems provide safe weight support, repetitive task practice, controlled gait trajectories, and adjustable training dosage. Recent studies and ongoing clinical protocols have therefore explored the combination of transcutaneous or epidural spinal stimulation with overground robotic exoskeletons, including real‐time triggered stimulation‐exoskeleton coupling and prospective exoskeleton‐assisted training designs [, , ]. Frontier directions further involve combining SCCI with brain‐computer interfaces or “digital bridge” strategies, aiming to restore biological motor execution driven by supraspinal motor intentions [, , ]. In addition, the incorporation of gait phase sensing, electromyography, inertial measurement units, or kinematic feedback within a closed‐loop framework may allow stimulation to become more stable in dynamic environments and better aligned with real‐time individual physiological states [, ]. Therefore, the future development of SCCI is likely to move from isolated stimulation toward multimodal neurorehabilitation systems integrating neural modulation, digital control, sensor feedback, intention decoding, and task‐specific training.

Despite these encouraging advances, the current clinical evidence base for SCCI‐mediated lower‐limb motor restoration remains preliminary and insufficiently standardized. Most available studies are single‐patient reports, proof‐of‐concept demonstrations, or small case series rather than prospective multicenter clinical trials [, , , ]. Intervention protocols vary markedly in electrode design, implantation location, stimulation frequency, pulse width, amplitude, contact configuration, mapping strategy, training dose, and the extent of integration with external sensors, robotic devices, or brain‐derived control signals. Outcome reporting is also heterogeneous. Some studies emphasize voluntary movement or isolated joint control, whereas others focus on standing ability, treadmill stepping, overground walking, walking distance, walking speed, gait symmetry, muscle strength, electromyographic activation, or stimulation‐off functional retention. As a result, although individual studies have reported impressive functional achievements, the available evidence cannot yet be directly pooled or compared using a conventional meta‐analysis framework. Given this methodological heterogeneity, a structured evidence‐mapping approach is more appropriate than conventional pooled meta‐analysis. To complement the study‐level data summarized in Table  and Figure  integrates the chronological maturation of SCCI‐related clinical platforms with the completeness of reporting across clinically relevant domains.

This synthesis indicates that technological sophistication has advanced more rapidly than clinical standardization, with the most persistent deficiencies involving long‐term follow‐up, stimulation‐off assessment, autonomous functional performance, and safety reporting. Another important unresolved issue is the lack of unified standards for defining responders, durability, and safety. In some studies, a responder refers to a patient who can generate voluntary movement during active stimulation [, ]. In others, response is defined by improved standing, assisted stepping, longer walking distance, reduced external assistance, better gait quality, or retention of function after stimulation is turned off [, , ]. Similarly, although repeated training combined with spinal stimulation may induce activity‐dependent plasticity and allow partial retention of function without active stimulation, follow‐up duration, stimulation‐off testing, home‐use evaluation, and long‐term safety reporting remain inconsistent [, , ]. Device‐related complications, lead migration, infection, stimulation discomfort, autonomic effects, hardware reliability, and revision procedures also need to be reported more systematically []. These limitations are particularly important because SCCI is an implantable and training‐intensive intervention that requires rigorous clinical validation before broader translation.

Overall, current SCCI clinical studies have demonstrated that neuromodulation schemes centered on spatiotemporal coding can yield quantifiable improvements in standing, stepping, walking, and motor control quality [, , , , , , ]. However, the field remains in an exploratory stage, characterized by rapid technological innovation but limited clinical standardization. Current evidence therefore favors a structured clinical evidence mapping approach rather than conventional pooled meta‐analysis [, , , , , ]. Such an approach can better distinguish strict SCCI from SCCI‐relevant precursor studies, clarify the maturity of different interface paradigms, and identify how patient characteristics, stimulation strategies, control architectures, and rehabilitation protocols may influence functional outcomes. Future advancements should prioritize high‐resolution programming, sustained interface stability, efficient personalized mapping, standardized reporting of stimulation parameters, harmonized functional endpoints, systematic safety monitoring, and long‐term follow‐up [, , ]. In addition, the synergistic integration of SCCI with robotic exoskeletons, BCI, and non‐invasive closed‐loop spinal stimulation will be essential for enhancing the stability, generalizability, and clinical applicability of therapeutic outcomes [, , , , , , , ].

SCCI represents a distinct therapeutic paradigm that differs significantly from BCIs [], traditional SCS [], and FES []. Although these technologies share partial similarities in hardware components, they rely on fundamentally divergent physiological principles and target distinct neural circuits. Elucidating these distinctions is critical for understanding the unique capacity of SCCI to reconstruct physiological motor function, as shown in Figure .

A fundamental conceptual distinction exists between the SCCI and the BCI. Although both technologies aim to restore independence in paralyzed patients, they operate on the nervous system in diametrically opposite functional directions. Traditional motor BCIs are inherently output‐based technologies []. Their core function involves signal extraction. This process entails recording neural signals from the motor cortex, decoding the user's motor intention, and transmitting this information to external effectors to control devices such as robotic arms, computer cursors, powered exoskeletons, or wheelchair systems [, , ]. The operational pathway can be summarized as decoding‐to‐output followed by external execution. BCIs have undeniably revolutionized communication and assistive device control in patients with profound motor deficits, including invasive intracortical decoders, ECoG‐based speech neuroprostheses, and non‐invasive BCI control systems [, , ]. However, many BCI applications are designed primarily to control external effectors rather than to directly reactivate spinal sensorimotor circuits. This distinction should not be interpreted as a limitation of all BCI‐based rehabilitation. In particular, long‐term BMI‐based gait training has been shown to induce partial neurological recovery in patients with paraplegia []. Thus, the conceptual contrast emphasized here is not that BCI lacks therapeutic potential, but that conventional output‐oriented BCI usually executes motor commands through external devices, whereas SCCI inputs structured signals into spinal circuits to recruit biological limb execution.

In sharp contrast, SCCI is defined as an input‐based neuromodulation technology. Rather than extracting signals from the brain, it inputs control signals into the spinal cord. This technology views the spinal circuits below the lesion not as severed cables but as anatomically intact biological processors that are temporarily idle due to the loss of descending drive [, ]. By delivering encoded electrical commands to lumbosacral circuits, SCCI reactivates the patient's own neuromuscular system [, ]. Its operational pathway follows a sequence of command input, in vivo modulation, and biological execution. This distinction holds significant clinical implications. SCCI preserves and repairs the biological substrates of motor function, maintaining muscle mass, bone density, and peripheral nerve health. Thus, it achieves a holistic restoration of physiological function rather than mere functional substitution.

However, these two technologies are not mutually exclusive. Instead, they resemble two halves of a severed loop. Current frontier research in neural engineering, often termed digital bridge technology or the brain‐spine interface (BSI), focuses on their integration [, ]. In this closed‐loop architecture, the BCI decodes motor intention and wirelessly transmits commands to the SCCI, which subsequently drives the body's own tissues to execute movements. In essence, the BCI acts as the trigger mechanism while the SCCI is responsible for motor execution. Their synergistic action seamlessly bridges the injury site to realize thought‐driven physiological gait recovery.

Although SCCI systems share distinct hardware similarities with traditional SCS devices used for analgesia, manifested by the utilization of comparable pulse generators and electrode lead configurations, their physiological objectives and underlying mechanisms diverge fundamentally []. As a standard therapy employed for decades, traditional SCS operates on the principle of neural inhibition based on the gate control theory of pain []. Electrodes are typically implanted in the thoracic or cervical epidural space, delivering continuous stimulation to the dorsal column fibers at conventional frequencies of 40‐60 Hz or high frequencies up to 10 kHz [, ]. The explicit goal of SCS is to recruit inhibitory interneurons, effectively gating the transmission of nociceptive signals to the brain and masking pain by inducing paresthesia [, ].

In contrast, while SCCI utilizes the same electrical energy, it aims to achieve neural activation and circuit reconstruction rather than sensory inhibition [, ]. As discussed in Section , SCCI electrodes are positioned over the lumbosacral enlargement and employ spatiotemporal neuromodulation to reproduce phase‐dependent motor recruitment patterns [, , ]. Rather than masking somatosensation, this approach triggers synergistic muscle contractions by amplifying proprioceptive feedback from group Ia and II afferent fibers and engaging spinal sensorimotor circuitry [, , ]. Consequently, while traditional SCS aims to block pathological pain‐related signals, SCCI is dedicated to reactivating dormant physiological signals that support motor function. Ideally, these two technologies represent the repurposing of related implantable hardware to transition from neural suppression to functional signal amplification [, ].

Finally, it is imperative to distinguish SCCI from FES, a technique employed for decades to activate paralyzed limbs [, , ]. FES systems induce muscle contraction by directly stimulating peripheral nerves or muscle bellies []. While effective for muscle strengthening, this peripheral targeting strategy faces intrinsic physiological limitations. Electrical stimulation of peripheral nerves recruits motor units in an order diametrically opposed to physiological states, characterized by the preferential activation of large‐diameter, fatigue‐prone fibers in violation of the body's inherent recruitment laws []. This reverse recruitment pattern leads to rapid muscle fatigue and results in robotic, mechanical movements that are difficult to sustain during complex functional activities such as walking [].

In contrast, SCCI circumvents these limitations by targeting central spinal circuits and engaging afferent‐mediated trans‐synaptic recruitment, as discussed in Section  [, , ]. Rather than directly stimulating muscles or peripheral axons, SCCI recruits motor outputs through spinal interneuronal networks and motoneuron pools [, ]. This mechanism is more compatible with Henneman's size principle, preferentially recruiting fatigue‐resistant motor units before larger fatigue‐prone units to generate smoother and more gradable force output []. Furthermore, the spinal cord retains endogenous muscle synergies, defined as neural maps capable of coordinating synchronous movements across multiple muscle groups [, , , ]. Leveraging this property, SCCI requires only structured spinal input to trigger complex multi‐joint cascades, such as synergistic flexion of the hip, knee, and ankle required for locomotion [, ]. Conversely, FES relies on sophisticated external controllers to artificially orchestrate the activation of individual muscles []. In summary, by harnessing the body's latent neural control mechanisms, SCCI achieves motor recovery that is more energy‐efficient, fatigue‐resistant, and natural than techniques relying on direct muscle stimulation [, ] (Table ).

Synthesizing the previously delineated bioelectronic hardware and an intelligent software ecosystem architecture, it becomes evident that the paramount challenge for SCCI has shifted from optimizing isolated components to achieving holistic systemic integration. Advancing SCCI will require continuous, coordinated refinement that hinges on the synergy between the long‐term biological stability of implanted hardware and the adaptivity of stimulation algorithms. The central scientific question, therefore, is whether these integrated systems can deliver reproducible and scalable clinical outcomes within the highly heterogeneous and individualized spinal environment. Accordingly, this section systematically analyzes the critical bottlenecks and future trajectories across three pillars: materials and device engineering (hardware), algorithmic closed‐loop strategies (software), and the roadmap for clinical translation.

As discussed in Section , the main hardware limitation of SCCI arises from the pronounced biomechanical mismatch between rigid implantable devices and soft spinal tissues [, , , ]. Current clinical electrode arrays, which are largely derived from analgesic SCS systems, have relatively high structural stiffness compared with the viscoelastic properties and low Young's modulus of the spinal cord and dura mater. During normal spinal movement, this mismatch may generate chronic compressive and shear stress at the interface between the tissue and the device, leading to persistent foreign body responses, fibrotic encapsulation, and long‐term changes in impedance [, , , ]. Consequently, engineering optimization focuses on the following dimensions:

Electrodes and Interface Materials: Hardware evolution is intrinsically linked to advancements in soft electronics. Incorporating composite interfaces, such as conductive polymers (e.g., PEDOT:PSS) or hydrogels, enhances charge injection capacity and minimizes interfacial impedance while maintaining mechanical compliance [, ]. The ultimate goal is to mitigate fibrosis, reduce long‐term threshold drift, and ensure reproducible stimulation. Furthermore, high‐density arrays can achieve stable, spatiotemporally selective modulation only if they maintain long‐term conformal contact with the spinal surface under low‐impedance conditions [, ].

Lead Fatigue and Stress Management: In the dynamic biomechanical environment of the spine, micromotion loads tend to accumulate at the transition zones between leads and connectors [, ]. Focusing solely on electrode flexibility while neglecting fatigue resistance and stress relief designs in the leads can result in long‐term fractures, contact failures, or impedance spikes, leading to fluctuating efficacy and increased maintenance burdens [, ].

Systemic Constraints on IPGs: As discussed in Section , SCCI requires IPGs capable of orchestrating complex spatiotemporal stimulation sequences, including multi‐channel independent control, rapid parameter switching, stable output consistency, sensing, telemetry, and power‐efficient closed‐loop control [, , , , ]. However, complex paradigms imply higher energy consumption and stricter thermal safety limits. Without stable, low interfacial impedance achieved through material optimization, IPGs may be forced into a vicious cycle in which high impedance necessitates higher output energy, thereby inflating power consumption and compromising battery longevity []. Thus, material optimization is the physical prerequisite for effective IPG power management.

Wireless Integration and MRI Compatibility: Future fully implantable systems must integrate wireless power and data transfer with miniaturized pulse generation to reduce infection risks associated with percutaneous leads and to support long‐term home‐based use []. Simultaneously, achieving MRI‐conditional compatibility is essential to enable longitudinal imaging follow‐ups and postoperative assessment [, ]. This necessitates complex optimization among wireless link stability, electromagnetic safety, thermal limits, device shielding, and image compatibility.

In summary, the trajectory of hardware development prioritizes precision and biocompatibility over mere stimulation intensity. The field is advancing toward flexible, integrated platforms characterized by attenuated inflammatory responses, minimal chronic threshold drift, high energy efficiency, and superior spatial selectivity to ensure long‐term stability.

Beyond bioelectronic hardware, a more formidable bottleneck for SCCI lies in the precise regulation of its high‐dimensional parameter configuration. The tunable dimensions, spanning electrode contact combinations, segmental mapping, frequency, pulse width, amplitude, phase timing, and multi‐channel synergy, collectively form a nearly infinite combinatorial parameter space [, ]. Traditional clinical calibration still depends largely on clinicians’ heuristic, iterative adjustments, which increases the time required for programming and introduces substantial variability across operators []. Furthermore, the significant heterogeneity among patients, characterized by anatomical variations, residual white matter ratios, and pathological circuit remodeling, necessitates a higher degree of technological sophistication for personalized stimulation coding [, ]. Strategies to address these challenges are categorized into three key dimensions:

Individualized Model‐driven Coding: The core strategy to transcend blind trial‐and‐error is the development of high‐fidelity, individualized in silico spinal models. By reconstructing anatomical structures from imaging data, feasible parameter ranges can be narrowed down in a virtual environment, allowing for the search of optimal stimulation codes under safety constraints. This represents a fundamental paradigm shift from heuristic clinical trial‐and‐error to predictive strategies governed by computational modeling [, ].

Learning Algorithms and Safe Exploration: The integration of machine learning, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian optimization enables closed‐loop self‐calibration using kinematics, electromyography, and postural states as feedback [, ]. These algorithms promise to rapidly screen personalized protocols and adaptively update them over months of rehabilitation in response to neuroplastic change [, ]. However, the critical challenge lies in balancing interpretability with safe exploration, requiring algorithms to operate within strict constraints on amplitude, energy, and risk prediction to prevent over‐stimulation, aberrant recruitment, or the induction of spasticity.

Engineering for Closed‐loop Modulation: Current SCCI systems predominantly operate on preset programs triggered by posture or behavior, effectively functioning as open‐loop or state‐dependent modalities. To enable true bidirectional interaction, critical engineering hurdles must be overcome, including stimulation artifact suppression, signal demixing, and low‐latency edge computing [, , , ]. Realizing this bidirectional capability is the prerequisite for restoring complex, adaptive motor behaviors, exemplified by maintaining balance on uneven terrain or modulating muscle force to prevent fatigue, thereby enabling artificial motor control to approximate the dynamic response characteristics of a healthy nervous system [, ]. Although ECAP‐controlled closed‐loop SCS studies in chronic pain populations do not constitute direct evidence for SCCI‐mediated motor recovery, they provide useful engineering experience for sensing‐stimulation co‐design, stability monitoring, and adaptive control architecture [].

Bringing SCCI from the lab to the clinic is inseparable from tightening who qualifies and how treatment is administered. A rigorous redefinition of inclusion criteria and protocol design is essential to maximize benefit while ensuring safety and reproducibility. The high heterogeneity within the SCI population, particularly the individual variability in residual white matter tracts, serves as a decisive determinant of neuromodulation efficacy, posing significant challenges for clinical trial design [, ]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to establish standardized biomarkers based on advanced neuroimaging or electrophysiological mapping. These tools are essential for predicting therapeutic feasibility and enabling scientific patient stratification [].

Furthermore, the surgical invasiveness associated with laminectomy for paddle lead implantation remains a major barrier to widespread adoption [, ]. This has catalyzed a surge in minimally invasive technologies, with percutaneous leads and non‐invasive transcutaneous stimulation emerging as focal points of research [, , ]. However, current minimally invasive approaches often necessitate a compromise, sacrificing spatial specificity of neuromodulation for the sake of surgical accessibility and reduced morbidity.

Looking forward, the trajectory of SCCI research is converging with regenerative medicine. Emerging bio‐hybrid therapies integrate electrical neuromodulation with biological interventions such as stem cell transplantation and pro‐regenerative pharmacotherapy, offering a theoretically promising solution to the limitations of purely physical stimulation [, ]. In this paradigm, the role of SCCI transcends that of a mere prosthetic substitute for motor function; it evolves into a critical catalyst for neurorehabilitation, guiding and reinforcing the formation of functional synaptic connections by regenerating axons through precise electrical activity [, ]. Ultimately, the goal is to transition SCCI from a manually operated tool to an intelligent, autonomous neuroprosthesis. Such a system would achieve seamless integration with the patients' physiological architecture, restoring more natural gait dynamics and volitional control, rather than merely reproducing movement.

Given the inherent limitations of monotherapy, the most promising trajectory for clinical translation lies in synergistic integration involving the combination of SCCI with supraspinal decoding via BCIs, external biomechanical assistance provided by exoskeletons, biological repair strategies, and emerging spinal‐signal decoding approaches. The ultimate objective is to advance functional reconstruction from merely evokable movement toward volitional, generalizable, and durable motor control [].

In a broader future vision, SCCI may evolve from a stimulation‐only interface into a bidirectional spinal read‐write platform. In this architecture, invasive spinal electrodes would not only deliver patterned stimulation to recruit sublesional circuits but may also record spinal electrophysiological activity to decode residual motor commands, sensory states, or locomotor phase information [, ]. Such a read‐write spinal interface would further distinguish SCCI from conventional SCS/EES, because it would combine spinal sensing, computational decoding, adaptive stimulation, and rehabilitation‐driven plasticity within the same therapeutic ecosystem.

Although BCIs can decode motor intent from the motor cortex, conventional output‐oriented BCI systems often bypass the sub‐lesional anatomy to drive external effectors. This statement should be interpreted with caution, because BCI‐based rehabilitation paradigms, especially those paired with gait training or FES, can induce neuroplastic changes and partial functional recovery [, , ]. In contrast, SCCI provides the necessary excitatory bias to activate dormant spinal circuitry directly []. Notably, the integration of both BCI and SCCI will compensate for their respective limitations, establishing a Brain‐Spine Digital Bridge architecture where the interface decodes cortical intent in real time and translates it into spatiotemporal stimulation codes delivered by the SCCI []. This mechanism effectively bypasses the lesion site by mapping the intention to walk directly onto executable commands of the lumbosacral circuitry, thereby restoring brain‐driven biological gait []. This combination is particularly crucial for patients with preserved intent but insufficient descending drive because it enhances volitional control and reduces reliance on pre‐programmed artificial modes [, ].

A further evolution in neuro‐mechanical synergistic control involves the integration of exoskeletons to form the brain‐spinal cord‐exoskeleton linkage system, as illustrated in Figure . Here, the exoskeleton serves as a mechanical compensator and safety buffer by providing necessary joint torque and postural stability when SCCI‐induced biological torque is insufficient, fatigue accumulates, or terrain becomes complex. Reciprocally, exoskeleton sensors, including joint angle encoders, plantar pressure monitors, and inertial measurement units, provide high‐fidelity state feedback for SCCI closed‐loop control. This realizes a comprehensive synergy integrating intent decoding, neuromodulation, mechanical assistance, and feedback correction [, ]. Fundamentally, this strategy establishes a dynamic allocation mechanism between neural execution and mechatronic execution. This approach ensures patients achieve high‐repetition gait training even in early severe stages while progressively transferring control authority from the exoskeleton back to the biological system as neural function improves [].

Regarding bio‐hybrid repair strategies, neuromodulation alone may fail to bridge the information gap for patients with severe structural disruption. The convergence of SCCI and regenerative medicine thus represents a dual mechanism driving structural reconstruction combined with functional remodeling. Although stem cell transplantation, biomaterial scaffolds, and pro‐regenerative pharmacotherapies aim to ameliorate the lesion microenvironment and promote axonal or synaptic regeneration, nascent connections often remain functionally silent [, ]. In this context, SCCI serves as a catalyst for rehabilitation by providing controlled spinal excitability and task‐dependent spatiotemporal input to amplify meaningful sensorimotor coupling. This approach leverages activity‐dependent plasticity to guide the functional integration of nascent pathways and enhance the efficiency and stability of regenerated connections []. Fundamentally, regenerative strategies establish the necessary structural bridge, while SCCI governs the functional signaling parameters and drives neural traffic to offer the greatest potential for sustainable long‐term recovery [].

Concerning systemic integration challenges, the core goal of combined applications extends beyond the simple superposition of devices to the embedding of SCCI into a cross‐hierarchical synergistic system. Within this framework, the supraspinal center provides intent while the spinal cord executes biological action and plasticity, external devices ensure safety and dosage, and repair strategies improve the structural foundation. Consequently, the key challenges shift to the level of systems engineering involving the millisecond‐level synchronization of multi‐source signals, cross‐device failsafe mechanisms, standardization of training dosages, and the design of clinical trials for complex combinatorial therapies [].

The SCCI is an emerging closed‐loop neuroprosthetic system specifically designed to restore motor function after SCI. It offers a pragmatic therapeutic approach that complements, rather than replaces, biological repair strategies such as tissue engineering. SCCI has arisen from the convergence of rapid advances in artificial intelligence, the steady evolution of BCI technology, and the pressing need for more effective motor recovery solutions for SCI patients.

Unlike traditional SCS for pain management or the early experimental use of EES, SCCI is a more sophisticated approach with distinct objectives and methods focused on motor restoration. It features real‐time closed‐loop control and finely programmable spatiotemporal stimulation patterns, effectively serving as an “artificial bridge” across damaged neural pathways. Structurally, SCCI combines implantable bioelectronic hardware with an intelligent computational core that generates programmable stimulation commands. Functionally, it amplifies residual descending signals and recruits latent CPG circuits in the spinal cord, converting sub‐threshold neural activity into robust, volitional movement. This strategy not only provides immediate functional improvements but also promotes activity‐dependent neuroplasticity, laying the groundwork for long‐term recovery.

Future advancements in SCCI will likely be defined by the convergence of multiple therapeutic modalities. Beyond its synergistic combination with regenerative therapies such as stem cells or biomaterial scaffolds to unite functional neuromodulation with anatomical repair, SCCI can be integrated with BCI. This integration establishes a digital bridge connecting the brain and the spinal cord, translating motor intent into spinal stimulation patterns organized by precise spatial and temporal coordinates. Concurrently, exoskeletons and assistive robotic systems can provide stability during the initial phases of treatment, ensure safe weight support, and facilitate intensive task practice. Furthermore, data derived from their sensors enhance the adaptive capabilities of the control system. However, realizing this vision requires addressing critical challenges. These include maintaining the stability of the interface between the electrode and tissue over extended periods and developing robust sensing mechanisms capable of mitigating artifacts within feedback loops. Additionally, there is a need for artificial intelligence algorithms that generalize effectively across diverse injury profiles, as well as the miniaturization of fully implantable systems for power and telemetry. Successfully addressing these barriers could transition SCCI into a scalable clinical solution capable of delivering durable and broadly applicable motor recovery.

neuroscience.title: ABA and stomatal biology: from transcriptional and biosynthesis to multicellular coordination across cell types
neuroscience.abstract: Abscisic acid (ABA) was first identified in plants over 6 decades ago and is now recognized as one of the central phytohormones in plants, regulating growth, development, and physiological adaptation to environmental changes. In this Centennial Update, we use two influential ABA-related articles published in Plant Physiology in the early 2000s and discuss complementary advances in stress-responsive transcription and ABA biosynthetic regulation. We extend the Update from ABA-relevant gene discovery to recent advances in multicellular coordination of stomatal control. Growing evidence supports the view that ABA-regulated stomatal movement and gas exchange are coordinated across multiple cell types, including guard cells, mesophyll cells, bundle sheath cells, and vascular tissues in roots and leaves. We also highlight emerging tools to dissect this ABA-mediated multicellular network by using emerging technologies in single-cell and spatial omics, plant optogenetics, and artificial intelligence. These advances will shape ABA research from single cell models toward multicellular collaborative networks for understanding plant-environment interactions. Together, this article links the history of ABA research with emerging single-cell resolution datasets and artificial intelligence–assisted computational approaches, proposing a framework for moving ABA biology from well-established guard cell signaling models toward a broader understanding of multicellular ABA coordination.
neuroscience.text:
Abscisic acid (ABA) is one of the central phytohormones, coupling developmental programs with responses to environmental change in plants. ABA-mediated metabolic and signaling pathways are important for a broad range of plant biological processes, including seed dormancy, germination, flowering, ion and solute transport, and epigenetic regulation, as well as biotic and abiotic stress adaptation (; ; ). Mechanistically, many key elements of ABA biosynthesis, catabolism, transport, perception, and downstream signaling have been identified through biochemical, genetic, molecular, and physiological approaches. These discoveries have provided a framework for engineering ABA signaling pathways to improve plant stress resilience, particularly under water-scarcity conditions in which ABA regulates transpirational water loss, water-use efficiency, and survival. Many aspects have been extensively discussed in recent reviews (; ; ; ). Therefore, this Update does not aim to comprehensively cover all facets of plant ABA biology. Instead, it focuses on ABA regulated stomatal behavior and gas exchange, particularly highlighting how ABA biosynthesis, transport, and signaling are coordinated across multiple cell types, while guard cells remain the major effectors of stomatal movement.

We first revisit the history of plant ABA research in the context of two influential Plant Physiology articles— and —by discussing how later work extended these foundations from transcriptional and metabolic regulation to multicellular coordination of ABA signaling. Among these processes, guard cells serve as a central signaling hub in plants for ABA-mediated stomatal movement and gas exchange—a process that enables carbon dioxide (CO2) uptake for photosynthesis and release of oxygen (O2) and water (H2O) via transpiration (; ). Guard cells, typically paired kidney shape cells surrounding stomatal pore in eudicots, adjust stomatal pore size and have provided a core framework for understanding ABA signaling (). However, stomatal function is also shaped by other leaf and vascular cell types, which influence guard cells by regulating leaf water supply (), photosynthesis-derived metabolic signals (; ), and root-to-shoot long-distance hydraulic, hormonal, and peptide signals (; ). Consequently, stomatal regulation provides an exceptional example to understand how ABA can regulate physiological responses beyond a single cell type. We propose that single-cell and spatial omics, plant optogenetics, and artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted analysis will empower the research to dissect how ABA's mode of action is organized across multiple cell types. These toolkits may be adapted to investigate broader ABA-mediated physiological and stress-responsive processes across tissues and organs in plants.

ABA was first isolated from plants over 6 decades ago, as DL-abscisin II, initially described as a substance accelerating cotton leaf abscission ().
