Plant Physiology became an early venue of ABA research in 1966, with one of the first studies published showing that DL-abscisin II inhibits the germination of excised embryos from two Ash species, Fraxinus ornus and F. americana. Such inhibitory effect could be antagonized by another phytohormone, gibberellin acid (). Abscisin II (or dormin) was also found to stimulate flowering development in short-day plant species, such as Chenopodium rubrum and Pharbitis nil () and reduce transpiration in excised leaves of wheat (Triticum aestivum) and barley (Hordeum vulgare) (). This compound was formally renamed as abscisic acid, to reconcile the parallel names abscisin II and dormin (). By the early 2000s, major advances had been made in understanding ABA biology in plants, including ABA-mediated ion transport in guard cells, signaling crosstalk (), transcriptional responses (), and the identification of core ABA biosynthetic enzymes (). However, less was known about how such biosynthesis was regulated by developmental and environmental cues, and how ABA-mediated transcriptional networks were conserved or diversified beyond Arabidopsis thaliana.

Plant Physiology has been the major venue for plant ABA research, with >1,500 ABA-related articles published (Web of Science 2026). Within this broader history, we revisit two influential Plant Physiology articles that provide complementary perspectives on ABA-responsive transcription () and ABA biosynthesis and regulation (). These studies built on substantial earlier advances in ABA and stress biology. For instance,  had investigated global expression profiles in Arabidopsis to probe shared and stress-specific transcriptional response to cold, salt, and osmotic stress, while  integrated early genetic and biochemical evidence into a conceptual framework for ABA signaling.  extended this transcriptomic framework to rice (Oryza sativa) and included ABA as a separated treatment, alongside cold, drought, and high salinity. Using a microarray comprising ∼1,700 complementary DNAs with RNA gel-blot analyses, the authors reported >70 stress-inducible genes, including >50 novel candidates not previously described in rice. Intriguingly, more than half identified rice orthologous genes had been reported in Arabidopsis, suggesting that Arabidopsis and rice may share conserved ABA regulatory mechanism for plant abiotic stress adaptation. Notably, 15 rice genes induced by all 4 treatments underscored shared core ABA-responsive components across stress contexts ().

Among these ABA-responsive genes identified by  were ABA-biosynthetic genes (e.g. OsZEP/ABA1 and OsSDR/ABA2), providing a natural link to a conceptual updated by  on regulation of ABA biosynthesis.  synthesized emerging evidence that ABA production is developmentally and environmentally regulated, including seed maturation, germination, and plant responses to abiotic stress. They highlighted major biosynthetic enzymes functionally characterized in Arabidopsis, including key ABA-biosynthetic marker genes—NCEDs (). These enzymes form the canonical ZEP-dependent ABA biosynthetic pathway. More recent studies identified an alternative ZEP-independent ABA synthetic pathway, involving unresolved isomerization, hydroxylation and epoxidation steps () (). However, evidence for this ZEP-independent pathway as a major abiotic stress-regulated ABA source remains limited (). ABA homeostasis has also extended by the identification of oxidative catabolism through cytochrome P450 superfamily members such as CYP707As (; ), and ABA conjugated pathway through ABA UDP-glucosyltransferases (; ) (). A central insight from  is that ABA biosynthesis can be feedback regulated: exogenous ABA and/or stress-triggered endogenous ABA can induce transcription of ABA biosynthetic genes, reinforcing ABA accumulation under stress (). A prominent example are NCEDs, encoding a rate-limiting enzyme for catalyzing stress-induced ABA synthesis (). In Arabidopsis, NCED3 is strongly induced by ABA and abiotic stresses such as salt, drought, and osmotic stress (; ). Together, these features make NCED3 a widely used reporter gene for ABA and stress-responsive ABA biosynthesis (). In the recent two decades, NCED expression has been repeatedly leveraged to dissect how ABA biosynthesis is modulated by diverse biotic and abiotic stresses and how this regulation contributes to stress adaptation (; ; ). Meanwhile, major advances further established the molecular framework for ABA dependent signaling, particularly in stomatal regulation, including identification of SLAC1 (; ), reconstitution of core ABA signaling modules (; ), and identification of ABA transporters (; ). These discoveries form the basis of many of the stomatal regulation and intercellular signaling mechanisms discussed subsequently.

ABA is a core regulator of guard cell function, stomatal development, and water loss across diverse environmental contexts, promoting stomatal closure under elevated CO2 (), low humidity (), and soil water deficiency (), while also controlling the extent of stomatal opening under light () and high temperature () and negatively regulating stomatal density (). Compared with bulk-tissue ABA-responsive studies (), Arabidopsis guard cell protoplast transcriptomics enabled cell type–specific advances, identifying >1,300 guard cell–enriched transcripts () to define ion transport, calcium (Ca2+) signaling, and water movement during ABA-mediated stomatal closure in Arabidopsis, as summarized in  and .

Briefly, ABA in guard cells can be synthesized locally or taken up from the apoplast through the plasma membrane ABA importer ABCG40 (; ) (). ABA then promotes stomatal closure through interconnected Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent pathways (). ABA-bound PYR/PYL/RCAR forms a protein complex with clade A PP2C proteins (e.g. ABI1 and ABI2), releasing OST1 from PP2C-mediated inhibition (; ; ; ; ). Then, OST1 amplified ABA signaling through activation of interconnected reactive oxygen species (ROS)-Ca2+ branches. It stimulates NADPH-dependent ROS production in guard cell apoplast via activating RbohD and RbohF (; ). ROS, particularly hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), can enter guard cells through OST1-dependent activation of plasma membrane aquaporin PIP2;1 (; ). Apoplastic H2O2 also triggers cytosolic Ca2+ signaling (). This ABA-dependent ROS-Ca2+ branch can suppress plasma membrane proton (H+)-ATPase (AHA) activity by promoting their dephosphorylation and reducing H+ extrusion (; ). In addition, vacuolar H+-ATPase (VHA)–dependent vacuolar acidification also contributes to ABA-induced stomatal closure in guard cells () and may be coupled with ABA-dependent Ca2+ signaling, as observed in bundle sheath cells (). Together, these processes favor cytosolic alkalinization and reduce the hyperpolarizing effect of AHA-mediated H+ pumping on plasma membrane potential (Em) (; ).

In parallel, OST1 directly phosphorylates and activates SLAC1 (; ) and ALMT12 () via phosphorylation, promoting guard cell anion efflux. ABA-induced Ca2+ signaling further reinforces anion release through Ca2+-dependent protein kinases (CPKs) and/or calcineurin B-like protein (CBL) paired with CBL-CIPK (CBL-interacting protein kinase), which phosphorylates and activate SLAC1 and SLAH3 (; ; ). In addition, CPK, such as CPK13, can inhibit potassium (K+) uptake through voltage-gated inward-rectifying K+ channels (KAT1) (), restricting K+ accumulation. ABA also activates anion release from vacuoles from ALMT4 (), reducing osmolyte storage in guard cells. Together, AHA inhibition, anion efflux, suppressed K+ uptake, and vacuolar solute release depolarize the Em in guard cells. This Em depolarization activates guard cell outward-rectifying K+ channels (GORK), promoting K+ efflux (; ) (). The combined loss of K+ and anions reduces guard cell osmotic content and turgor pressures, driving water efflux from both the cytosol and vacuole. This vacuolar water release may involve TIP2;1, and its contribution requires further investigation (; ). Although the plasma membrane ion efflux during ABA-mediated stomatal closure is relatively well characterized, this process must be coordinated with ion and water release across the vacuolar membrane. However, this part of mechanisms that integrate these two membrane systems remain elusive ().

In this process, GORK is primarily activated by membrane depolarization during ABA-induced closure (). Although direct GORK activation by Ca2+-dependent CBL1/9-CIPK5 modules was demonstrated in Xenopus laevis oocytes, rather than in guard cells, genetic evidence linked this module primarily with jasmonate- and wounding-induced stomatal closure (). Additionally, the regulation of SLAC1 appears context dependent: beyond OST1/CPK/CBL-CIPK-mediated SLAC1 activation, extracellular malate transported via ALMT12 may also activate SLAC1; however, whether this ALMT12-drived malate signal is integrated in ABA-mediated guard cell signaling remains unclear (; ; ) ().

Beyond controlling ion transporter and channel activity, ABA can alter transport capacity by regulating membrane protein abundance and localization through vesicular trafficking (; ). In guard cells, ABA facilitates selective endocytosis of KAT1, while the SNARE family protein SYP121 promotes its recycling to the plasma membrane, thereby influencing K+ uptake and stomatal opening (; ). SNARE-dependent mechanisms also regulate plasma membrane H+-ATPases. ABA enhances SYP132-dependent endocytic trafficking of AHA1 from the plasma membrane toward endomembrane compartments (). In addition, ABA increases plasma-membrane-associated vesicle-associated membrane protein 711 (VAMP711) and promotes its interaction with AHA1/2, then suppressing H+-ATPase activity (). As ABA-regulated transporter trafficking has been mostly studied in guard cells and well-reviewed elsewhere (; ), we only discuss it briefly before turning to ABA-mediated stomatal regulation across multiple cell types.

This guard cell–centered framework is also supported in monocots. Cell-type transcriptome profiling from barley and wheat identified guard cell-specific and guard cell-complex (guard cells plus subsidiary cells) enriched transcripts, reinforcing the core roles of ABA signaling in guard cells for stomatal regulation (; ). However, ABA-modulated stomatal control is not solely a guard cell-autonomous process. It is coordinated with broader water and carbon regulation across multiple cell types, including root-to-shoot signaling, bundle sheath cells, and mesophyll cells (; ; ). Collectively, we propose that ABA-mediated stomatal responses operate within a multicellular signaling network in plants.

Roots perceive soil water status and adjust shoot transpiration through long-distance root-to-shoot signaling (). Under drought, sulfate (SO42−) acts as an early root-to-shoot chemical signal transported through the xylem, promoting guard cell–autonomous ABA biosynthesis and stomatal closure (; ). In guard cells, SO42− induces NCED3 expression and is assimilated into cysteine through the plastid cysteine synthase complex; then, cysteine supports MCSU/ABA3-dependent AAO3 activation and local ABA biosynthesis (; ; , ). In addition, root-derived CLAVATA3/ESR-RELATED 25 (CLE25) peptides move through the vascular tissue from roots to shoots, where they are perceived by receptor-like kinases BARELY ANY MERISTEM 1 (BAM1) and BAM3 to promote NCED3 expression, stimulating ABA biosynthesis, stomatal closure, and enhanced water use efficiency in Arabidopsis (). By contrast, locally produced CLE5 dodecapeptide (CLE5p) can promote drought-induced stomatal closure without inducing ABA biosynthesis ().

Within this CLE25-NCED3 pathway, vascular NCED expression provides a useful transcriptional reporter of leaf ABA biosynthesis (; ), consistent with the evidence that drought-induced ABA biosynthesis occurs mainly in vascular parenchyma cells and other vein-associated tissues, rather than uniformly across the leaf (). ABA can also move from root to shoot to regulate stomatal aperture via ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter ABCG25, but its role in drought-induced stomatal closure is likely limited in Arabidopsis (). In some circumstances, local ABA biosynthesis can reduce dependence on long-distance ABA transport. For instance, soil-drying closing stomata in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) cv. Rheinlands Ruhm does not require root ABA production (), while drought-induced ABA accumulation in soybean (Glycine max) roots relies more on local NCED-dependent ABA synthesis, rather than on shoot-to-root ABA import (). Together, these findings indicate that stress-induced ABA accumulation can involve local biosynthesis, long-distance signaling, and ABA transport.

At the leaf scale, ABA coordinates both water transport and water loss by regulating leaf hydraulic conductance (Kleaf) and stomatal conductance (gs). Kleaf reflects water flow through the leaf from the xylem toward the evaporative sites (e.g. stomata), whereas gs determines water vapor diffusion from leaf airspaces to the atmosphere through stomatal pores. As such, Kleaf and gs are tightly coupled, linking xylem water supply with transpirational water loss via stomatal pores in response to environment (e.g. blue light) and endogenous signals (e.g. ABA) (; ; ). In this process, blue light is perceived by phototropins, which activate AHA in both bundle sheath cells and guard cells. In bundle sheath cells, activation of AHA2 drives H+ extrusion, increases cytosolic pH (pHcyt), and acidifies the surrounding apoplast/xylem sap; this is associated with enhanced Kleaf thereby facilitating radial water movement from the xylem toward the leaf airspace (, ). Concurrently, blue-light activation of AHA1 and AHA2 promote stomatal opening and increases gs (; ) (). By contrast, ABA inhibits AHA2-depedent acidification of the apoplast, increases apoplastic pH (pHapo), and promotes vacuolar H+ sequestration by VHA, such as VHA-a2 and VHA-a3, and consequently the reduced Kleaf (), which may partially involve pH-dependent regulation of aquaporins (). In guard cells, ABA similarly inhibits AHA1/2, promotes vacuolar H+ pumping, contributing to cytosolic alkalinization, stomatal closure and reduced gs (; ; ). Consistent with this model, impairment of ABA signaling in bundle sheath cells results in greater Kleaf and gs (), underscoring that ABA-mediated stomatal regulation is not restricted to guard cells but also depends on hydraulic and signaling inputs from surrounding leaf tissues ().

Additionally, it was shown that neither low (1 mM) nor high (11 mM) K+ supplement through the leaf petiole altered xylem sap pH in Arabidopsis. However, alkalinizing xylem sap by vanadate required high K+ supplementation (), suggesting that optimal xylem K+ homeostasis may facilitate xylem sap alkalinization mediated by AHA inactivation. Other studies found that bundle sheath cells maintained a more hyperpolarized Em () and accumulated higher K+, compared with other cell types, such as mesophyll cells (), a process potentially linked to AHA2 activity in bundle sheath cells (). Given that ABA stimulates K+ efflux to the guard cell apoplast during stomatal closure (), it remains unclear whether ABA-induced AHA2 inactivation and membrane depolarization also alters K+ flux across bundle sheath cells to the xylem, potentially facilitating xylem sap alkalinization ().

An early study demonstrated that guard cell protoplasts maintain higher ABA concentrations than mesophyll protoplasts in Vicia faba (). In Arabidopsis, vascular tissues and guard cells are established sites for ABA biosynthesis, whereas the extent to which mesophyll cells contribute to ABA biosynthesis remains less clear (; ; ). However, ABA signaling in mesophyll cells also contributes to stomatal regulation (; ).  used a mesophyll-specific promoter to drive expression of a dominant mutant ABI1 allele (abi1-1) in Arabidopsis, generating FBPase::abi1-1/MCabi (). In MCabi plants, foliar ABA application failed to strongly induce NCED3, confirming impaired ABA signaling in mesophyll cells (). Under control conditions, these lines displayed >25% higher gs and ∼10% greater photosynthesis (CO2 assimilation, AN) than wildtype plants, despite similar Rubisco carboxylation capacity (; ) and also showed higher Kleaf (). Although ABA reduced Kleaf, gs and photosynthesis in both genotypes, MCabi consistently maintained higher values under ABA treatment (; ) (). Similarly, two plasma membrane ABC transporters, ABCG17 and ABCG18, have been associated with ABA import into Arabidopsis mesophyll cells. Artificial microRNA knockdown of both genes reduced ABA uptake into mesophyll cells of mir17,18 lines, increasing ABA accumulation in guard cells and reducing stomatal pore opening under nonstress conditions. Under drought, both ABCG17 and ABCG18 were downregulated, potentially reducing ABA import into mesophyll cells and promoting guard cell ABA accumulation and stomatal closure (). Taken together, these studies highlight an important role for ABA accumulation and sensing in mesophyll cells in controlling stomatal behavior.

Mesophyll photosynthetic metabolism also influences stomatal behavior. In intact leaves, stomata of Tradescantia pallida and Pisum sativum responded rapidly to short-term changes in environmental light and CO2; however, these responses were significantly reduced in isolated epidermal peels and recovered when the epidermis was placed in contact with mesophyll layers. This provided early evidence that mesophyll-derived signals contribute to stomatal regulation to light and CO2 (). Consistently, in Commelina communis, stomata in leaf segment opened rapidly under red light; however, this opening response became much weaker in isolated epidermal strips and was reinstated when the epidermis was placed on mesophyll tissue. Furthermore, inhibition of photosynthesis by DCMU greatly suppressed red light–induced stomatal opening. Together, these findings support a stronger contribution of mesophyll photosynthesis to stomatal opening under red light (). A multispecies meta-analysis further linked photosynthesis-derived sugars—such as sucrose, glucose, and fructose—to stomatal regulation (). A recent report showed that red light–driven mesophyll photosynthesis increases apoplastic sugars in Arabidopsis and V. faba with sucrose reaching 1 to 2 mM concentrations (). Extracellular sucrose promoted AHA1 phosphorylation and inhibited SLAC1-mediated anion currents in guard cells, thereby proposed to facilitate stomatal opening under red light (; ) (). However, the pathway by which photosynthesis-derived sugars are exported from mesophyll cells into the apoplast remains unresolved () (), and it is not clear yet whether and how ABA modulates apoplastic sucrose availability/signaling (e.g. MCabi line). Because ABA influences phloem sugar loading and unloading (; ), it may also alter leaf apoplastic sucrose availability. Thereby, we present the possible link that impaired ABA sensing in MCabi plants may increase photosynthetic carbon assimilation and potentially apoplastic sucrose. Such increased sucrose availability could in turn promote AHA1-associated H+ extrusion and suppress SLAC1-mediated anion efflux in guard cells, thereby contributing to greater stomatal opening and higher gs as observed in MCabi plants (; ; ) (). This proposed mesophyll-ABA linked guard cell–sucrose pathway remains to be tested.

Intriguingly, this multicellular complexity of ABA signaling extends even further: responses are also heterogeneous within nominally uniform cell types. For instance, Arabidopsis spongy mesophyll protoplasts displayed a higher membrane osmotic water permeability (Pf) than palisade mesophyll protoplasts (∼20 µm s−1 in spongy mesophyll protoplasts vs. ∼13 µm s−1 in palisade mesophyll protoplasts). ABA reduced the Pf of spongy mesophyll protoplasts by up to 60%, whereas the Pf of palisade mesophyll protoplasts was largely unaffected even at high ABA concentrations up to 50 µM (). , therefore, proposed that higher basal Pf in spongy mesophyll cells may allow them to more directly regulate water movement from the apoplast toward the sites of evaporation during transpiration; while their greater ABA sensitivity may enable more rapid restriction of leaf water flux during stress (). Similarly, abaxial (lower surface) stomata are more responsive to light than adaxial (upper surface) stomata in Arabidopsis, linked with differential abundance of K+ channels on each surface (). Such comparable surface-dependent differences in stomatal behaviors have been also reported in other species, including a greater ozone (O3)-induced reduction in gs on the adaxial surface in 3 poplar (Populus deltoides × P. nigra) genotypes and stronger ABA response of abaxial stomata in C. communis and V. faba (; ). Taken together, we propose that stomatal regulation is coordinated by multicellular ABA signaling across guard cells, bundle sheath cells and mesophyll cells, which can be better understood in a surface-specific context as part of cellular heterogeneity.

Cell type–specific transcriptomic approaches (e.g. guard cell protoplasts [; ; ; ] and intact guard cells []) have been instrumental in dissecting ABA-mediated signaling pathways in guard cells underlying stomatal regulation and gas exchange. Recently,  demonstrated that the distinct light responsiveness in Arabidopsis guard cells of adaxial and abaxial stomata arises, at least in part, from differences in relative abundance of two inward rectifying K+ channels: KAT1 and AKT1. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of guard cell protoplasts isolated separately from the two leaf surfaces showed that both genes are expressed in guard cells, but KAT1 is enriched by >2-fold in abaxial guard cells, whereas AKT1 is more abundant on the adaxial guard cells. However, these processes are systemically coordinated across multiple leaf cell types, rather than by guard cells alone. Consequently, transcriptomic analyses that focused on a single isolated cell type cannot readily resolve multicellular organization, cell-cell interactions, or the spatial separation between ABA biosynthesis and ABA-responsive elements within intact tissue.

Recent advances in scRNA-seq, especially when integrated with spatial transcriptomics approaches, now allow reconstruction of plant cell atlases and provide a framework for examining how hormone-regulated responses are distributed across different cell types simultaneously (; ; ). A compelling ABA-relevant example is provided by a recent rice root study of soil compaction (), a condition in which soil becomes more densely packed and mechanically resistant (). In this study, a reference rice root atlas of >79,000 scRNA-seq profiles was generated to compare transcriptomic responses between compacted and noncompacted soil conditions, revealing that ABA biosynthesis genes (e.g. OsAAO1, OsNCEDs, OsZEP/ABA1) were upregulated predominantly in phloem-associated inner vascular tissues; whereas ABA-responsive genes, including pathogenesis-related genes (OsPR10s), dehydrin Rab16C (OsRAB16C), and abscisic stress-ripening protein 5 (OsASR5), were enriched mainly in outer root layers, especially exodermis. In parallel, compacted soil also induced cell wall–related genes in exodermis, including xylanase-inhibitor genes, xyloglucan endotransglucosylase 22 (OsXTH22) and xylan 3-O-Arabinosyltransferase 7 (OsXAT7). Functional analysis of ABA-biosynthetic rice mutants further showed that ABA biosynthesis is induced in inner root layers and required for compaction-induced lignin and suberin deposition, barrier formation, and reduced radial water loss in outer root layers (). Thus, it revealed that that scRNA-seq, spatial validation, and genetics together separated the cellular domain of ABA production from the domains of ABA-responsive transcription and downstream adaptive barrier formation ().

Notably, this study also illustrates how spatial omics methods can complement scRNA-seq analysis. In the initial scRNA-seq analysis, transcriptomic profiles were clustered according to transcriptomic similarity, and provisional cell identities were assigned using previously validated marker genes (). Because many clusters still lacked confident annotation,  validated more than 40 cell-type markers using multiplexed fluorescence in situ hybridization to refine the cell-type assignments. More broadly, this example aligns with growing evidence that spatial information can guide interpretation of scRNA-seq datasets, particularly because unsupervised scRNA-seq pipelines often focus on dominant sources of variation and may fail to resolve spatially distinct cell types when differential transcriptional profiles are limited (; ).

The same issue is likely relevant to leaf dorsiventrality and stomatal regulation (; ). Arabidopsis stomatal regulation is likely coordinated unequally across the two leaf surfaces, with spongy mesophyll cells and abaxial guard cells contributing differently from palisade mesophyll cells and adaxial guard cells, then dissociation-based scRNA-seq alone may be insufficient to resolve the relevant mesophyll or epidermal cell types ().  generated an early single-cell atlas of young developing Arabidopsis leaves and 14 differential cell populations; however, within the mesophyll cluster, spongy mesophyll-associated marker gene, trans-acting siRNA 3 (TAS3) (), and palisade mesophyll-associated marker gene, axial regulator YABBY 1 (YAB1) (), did not define clearly separated unsupervised clusters. Likewise, In mature Arabidopsis leaves,  showed that scRNA-seq alone could not distinguished upper versus lower epidermal cells or spongy versus palisade mesophyll cells, but integration of spatial transcriptomes resolved these subtypes. Together, these studies suggest that resolving multicellular ABA coordination in leaves will probably leverage not only scRNA-seq, but also spatially resolved or spatially supervised single-cell approaches ().

Beyond simply cataloging cell-type transcriptomics, integrated spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics could help resolve whether cellular domains of ABA biosynthesis, accumulation, perception, and downstream responses are spatially coincident or separated across leaf cell types (; ). In the context of stomatal regulation, combining these spatial omics could reveal how these cell type–specific processes are coordinated to regulate stomatal behavior, gas exchange, and water movement. However, spatial metabolomics alone is unlikely to directly resolve ion flux, and candidate ABA-regulated transport modules identified through spatial omics will still require physiological and functional validation. Therefore, plant optogenetics provides a complementary toolkit for dissecting such processes, as discussed below ().

ABA-mediated ion transport is a central downstream effector for guard cell osmotic adjustment and volume change for stomatal movement, representing best-defined outputs of ABA perception and signaling in guard cells (see reviews by  and  and references therein). These processes have been extensively dissected by electrophysiology since the early 1980s (; ), when microelectrodes were first applied to V. faba to examine the effect of ABA on Em, showing that ABA depolarizes the Em and providing early evidence that ABA modulates transmembrane ion fluxes in guard cells (). More recently, electrophysiology combined with plant optogenetics has further expanded our capability to interrogate ion fluxes and guard cell signaling with causal precision (; ).

Optogenetics uses genetically encoded photoreceptors to manipulate and define biological processes (). In plants, these tools include not only microbial rhodopsins, such as channelrhodopsins (CHRs), but also other engineered light-activated ion channels. Higher plants possess complex ion transport network but lack natural light-gated ion channels. These light-responsive ion channels can be exploited to selectively manipulate specific ion fluxes, examine downstream signaling consequences and define physiological outputs (; ). For instance, guard cell-specific manipulation of synthetic chimeric blue light-induced K+ channel (BLINK1) accelerated stomatal kinetics, improved water use efficiency, and enhanced Arabidopsis growth (). This strategy is highly relevant to ABA-triggered ion flux and signaling, because ABA, like many other signals, such as ROS (), CO2 (), and pathogen-associated molecular patterns (), can trigger increase in cytosolic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]cyt) in guard cells and promote stomatal closure (; ). How guard cells decode different Ca2+ signatures remained elusive until  used a Chlamydomonas reinhardtii Ca2+-permeable CHR-2 variant (ChR2D156H/ChR2-XXM) to impose defined [Ca2+]cyt signatures in N. tabacum guard cells. A single 0.1-s blue-light pulse triggered a unitary [Ca2+]cyt spike and amplified endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release and activation of S-type anion channels to promote stomatal closure. The stomatal closure scaled with [Ca2+]cyt transient number (∼10% stomatal closure after 1 pulse to nearly complete closure after 12 pulses), while higher pulse frequency accelerated stomatal closing speed (). Minimal effect on control plants suggests that ChR2-XXM can selectively manipulate Ca2+-dependent stomatal responses with limited interference from endogenous light signaling (; ).

The broader use of ChR2-XXM is illustrated by recent applications in Arabidopsis roots.  employed the ChR2-XXM to repeatedly execute [Ca2+]cyt oscillations, showing that the ChR2-XXM-mediated Ca2+ signaling was sufficient to trigger apoplastic ROS bursts, linked to auxin-associated root responses and mechanical navigation during soil growth (). Consistently,  used it to define [Ca2+]cyt inputs that modulated auxin-induced Em depolarization, transcriptional responses, and root growth. Similar approaches may be employed to ABA signaling by imposing defined [Ca2+]cyt inputs in ABA-signaling mutants to test whether Ca2+ can bypass specific signaling defects and separate components acting upstream or downstream of Ca2+ signals. This could help determine how ABA-dependent Ca2+ signals are perceived into ion transport and stomatal responses across different cell types.

Moreover, other types of light-regulated ion channels have also been adapted in plants. These include anion CHR GtACR1 from Guillardia theta, which is permeable to chloride and nitrate (Cl−/NO3−) (), and kalium CHR 2 (HcKCR2) from Hyphochytrium catenoides, which drives H+ import and alters pHcyt (). ABA-mediated stomatal regulation involves a complex, interconnected ion transport network, including K+, Cl−, NO3−, malate2−, H+, and Ca2+ (; ) (). Therefore, optogenetics provides a modular toolkit to interrogate major ABA-relevant ion fluxes without activating the entire ABA pathway at once (). In principle, such tools could be optimized to isolate individual ABA-regulated ion transport processes through bypassing upstream ABA perception or counteracting specific ABA-triggered events without disrupting other branches. For example, ABA is known to induce fast cytosolic alkalization in guard cells, followed by an increase in [Ca2+]cyt to close stomata (; ). In this scenario, HcKCR2 may be used as a light-gated tool to acidify pHcyt (), possibly attenuating ABA-induced cytosolic alkalinization in guard cells and enabling to test which types of ABA-regulated ion-transport events require this pHcyt shift (). Similar strategies could be also extended to test ABA-induced pHcyt shift in mesophyll cells and bundle sheath cells to determine whether pHcyt-dependent K+ efflux, anion transport, or [Ca2+]cyt transients operate upstream, downstream, or in parallel with ABA-triggered pHcyt regulation in comparison with guard cells.

Finally, ABA signaling is often interconnected with other signal elements, including pH, nitric oxide, ROS, and Ca2+, to shape physiological responses (, ; ; ; ). Multiple CHRs that respond to different light wavelengths (e.g. GtACR1 and ChR2-XXM) () can be combined and activated sequentially or simultaneously to separate and manipulate ABA-associated signaling modules, defining their individual and synergistic effect ().

In summary, spatial/single-cell omics and optogenetics could be complementary approaches to advance ABA research in different cell types in plants. Spatial and single-cell omics can identify ABA-regulated candidates, metabolites, and transport modules across guard cells, bundle sheath cells, and mesophyll cells, and optogenetics can test their physiological contribution by selectively manipulating defined ion fluxes or signaling events. Also, optogenetic manipulation of ion fluxes may generate controlled or defined signaling states that are then profiled by spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, or scRNA-seq, enabling the discovery of novel cell type–specific ABA-mediated response and intracellular signaling pathways.

Guard cells are among the most studied plant cell types and have also been extensively investigated with several mathematical modeling approaches to address complex guard cell signaling networks (), stomatal CO2 sensing mechanisms (; ; ; ; ), and ion transport dynamics (; ; ; ). For instance, by combining computational modeling of OnGuard3 platform with genetic perturbation,  predicted that KAT1 supports stomatal opening effectively, helping to explain differential light responses between adaxial and abaxial stomata. Similarly,  used GuardIon model to interpretate how GtACR1-mediated anion efflux and Em-depolarization activated GORK-like K+ efflux, interacts with H+-ATPase-mediated H+ pumping, and ultimately changes osmotic turgor in guard cells to close stomata in N. tabacum. However, these models mostly focus on guard cells (; ; ), highlighting the need to extend modeling frameworks to ion transport and signal in/outputs across interacting cell types, such as mesophyll cells and bundle sheath cells.

AI-assisted approaches, such as AlphaFold 3 modeling (), are beginning to turbo charge ABA-signaling research. ABA-mediated stomatal closure is not restricted to seed plants, but also occurs across diverse fern species, including Ceratopteris richardii (), Polystichum proliferum, Nephrolepis exaltata (), Athyrium filix-femina, and Dryopteris carthusiana (). Analysis of ABA signaling homologues suggests ABA-responsive stomatal regulation occurs at least in some early vascular land plants (; ). Early structural and biochemical analysis established that Arabidopsis PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors can function in dimeric or monomeric forms with distinct ABA sensitives, with monomeric receptors showing higher ABA-binding affinity than dimeric forms. Mutagenesis, generating PYR1H60P, further identified H60 as a key residue determine receptor's oligomeric state (). This principle was later extended across plant species using AI-assisted structural analysis. More recently,  investigated the structural evolution of the PYR/PYL/RCAR ABA receptors, including CsPYL1 and MpPYL1 respectively from an angiosperm (Citrus sinensis) and a liverwort (Marchantia polymorpha). CsPYL1 functions as an ABA-dependent dimeric receptor with lower ABA sensitivity (half-maximal inhibitory concentration, half-maximal inhibitory concentration = 230 nM), which is proposed to contribute to signaling at higher ABA levels during acute drought. In contrast, MpPYL1 is monomeric with high ABA sensitivity (half-maximal inhibitory concentration = ∼70 nM), and proposed to sense and decode mild stress-induced ABA concentration and signaling (; ). AlphaFold-based prediction identified a 5-residue signature that contributes to the receptors’ oligomeric state and ABA sensitivity. Reciprocal amino acid residue substitutions generated CsPYL1Mp (CsPYL1I91L/V112L/V192L/L195C/K199S) and MpPYL1Cs (MpPYL1L91I/L111V/L191V/C194L/S198K), respectively converting CsPYL1Mp toward MpPYL1-like monomeric, high ABA sensitivity and MpPYL1Cs toward CsPYL1-like dimeric, low affinity (). This provides an example of AI-assisted ABA receptors engineering, although whether such engineered receptors improve plant stress adaptation remains to be demonstrated.

Moreover, spatial and single-cell omics are expected to generate large, high-dimensional datasets that capture cell type–specific transcriptional, metabolic, and spatial responses, AI-assisted analysis can support the interpretation of these datasets by resolving cellular heterogeneity, identifying stress- and hormone-mediated modules, and prioritizing candidate genes, metabolites, and cell states associated with signaling outputs (; ; ). For example,  integrated meta-analysis and unsupervised machine learning algorithm to analyze multitranscriptomics in Arabidopsis across multiple stress, tissue, and time points. This study identified a core set of stress-related gene families involved in ethylene response, such as Expansins (EXP), Ethylene response factor (ERF), WRKY, Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), supporting ethylene as a central regulatory component of broad abiotic-stress transcriptional responses (). Similar strategies could be adapted to analyze ABA-mediated signaling at single-cell resolution ().

AI-assisted analysis may also complement optogenetics by converting complex perturbation-induced responses into quantitative, interpretable features, as demonstrated previously in mammals (; ). For instance, a recent study by  combined optogenetics and AI-driven analysis to provide an efficiency diagnose of extensive behavior evaluation of mice (Mus musculus) with Parkinson's disease. Although direct integrative studies of optogenetics and AI remains limited in plants,  provides a relevant precedent by using time-resolved root electrochemical sensing data to train a machine learning model that predicts ion-uptake behavior. This approach could be extended to ion transporter mutants to predict how altered transport mechanisms affect the overall ion uptake (e.g. NO3−) (), and demonstrates how AI can extract ion transport features from complex physiological outputs to guide the discovery of new ion transport regulatory mechanisms.

Taken together, AI-assisted approaches can accelerate ABA research by linking structural modeling, spatial/single-cell omics and optogenetics perturbation to identify, prioritize, and interpret ABA-responsive modules across multiple cell types and convert complex signaling and physiological outputs into multicellular ABA regulations ().

Over 6 decades after ABA was first discovered, major progress has clarified how this phytohormone regulates development, growth, stress responses and environmental adaptation. Here, we focused on recent progress in ABA-mediated stomatal movement and gas exchange, emphasizing its coordination across multiple cell types, rather than guard cells alone. We discussed how spatial/single-cell omics, optogenetics, and AI-assisted analysis could advance ABA research by resolving its cell type signaling events and complex networks. Recent evidence shows that coordinated stomatal and mesophyll functions can buffer CO2 diffusion under high temperature and high vapor pressure deficit, stabilizing chloroplast CO2 availability and supporting photosynthetic performance (). Thus, resolving how ABA coordinates stomatal, mesophyll, and vascular functions is not only important for understanding how plants sustain photosynthesis with minimizing water loss under hot and dry climates, but also a key challenge for future crop resilience and agricultural productivity.

Importantly, this conceptual framework could be extended to other ABA-mediated physiological processes in which cell identities and spatial and dynamic signaling are important. For example, temporal single-cell atlases of Arabidopsis seed development and germination by  may be leveraged to examine how ABA-associated regulators, transport process, and metabolic states control cell-specific germination programs. Similarly, machine learning–driven analysis of ABA-related defense experimental data predicts how ABA concentration, plant age, and pathogen lifestyle as major factors determine disease-resistance outcomes (). Spatial omics in developing leaves may also help link ABA-regulated different cell states with stomatal development (). Together, these studies illustrate how cell-resolution datasets, optogenetic intervention, and AI-assisted modeling can expand ABA research from stomatal control to broader developmental and stress-adaptive signaling networks in the future.

neuroscience.title: Editorial: Emerging talents in human neuroscience: psychophysiology and cognitive neuroscience 2025
neuroscience.abstract: No abstract
neuroscience.text:
This Research Topic highlights studies led by emerging researchers, including undergraduate and graduate students and researchers within the first years of their academic careers, showcasing the originality and scientific rigor of the next generation of scientists in psychophysiology and cognitive neuroscience. The works presented here cover the human lifespan and, although addressing diverse research questions, they can be organized around three complementary perspectives: the adaptive construction of bodily experience, the identification of neural markers of developmental and cognitive vulnerability, and the development of innovative approaches for modulating brain function, cognition, and emotional wellbeing.

The first perspective concerns the adaptive construction of bodily experience across the lifespan and under different physiological and clinical conditions. Bodily self-representation is increasingly conceptualized as a dynamic process grounded in the integration of multisensory bodily signals and their interaction with internal models of the body (; ; ). Building on psychophysical and computational approaches previously employed to investigate body representation and multisensory processing (; ), Martinelli et al. examined how the sense of body ownership changes with aging () by using a continuous life-span approach, from adolescence to old age. They showed that older age is associated with greater reliance on visual information, possibly compensating for the gradual decline in proprioceptive precision and helping to maintain a coherent representation of the body. In parallel, Gentili et al. provide a systematic mapping of the last 15 years of research on anorexia nervosa, reporting a crucial shift from studies focused primarily on perceived body image and aesthetic evaluation to more complex paradigms examining multisensory integration and the implicit body schema. This shift reflects a broader reconceptualization of anorexia nervosa as involving not only disturbances in the conscious evaluation of body appearance, but also alterations in the multisensory processes underlying bodily self-representation and supporting the development of interventions that directly target body representations through innovative technology-assisted approaches (; ). Complementing these perspectives, Bartolini et al. provide a mini-review of interceptive skills in visually impaired children, integrating evidence from both pediatric and adult populations. By examining how visual information contributes to the multisensory processes supporting goal-directed interactions between the body and the environment, their work reports how the absence of early visual input may constrain the development of motor coordination and social interaction. They further emphasize the need for more ecologically valid, multisensory, and longitudinal research, while discussing the potential of emerging technologies, such as virtual reality, to support accessible, engaging, and individualized rehabilitative interventions. Together, these studies show the dynamic and multisensory nature of bodily experience, demonstrating how body representation continuously adapts across development, aging, and clinical conditions.

The second perspective focuses on the identification of neural markers of developmental and cognitive vulnerability. Petri et al. provide a narrative review showing the complementary role of oscillatory and aperiodic EEG activity in characterizing early brain development, building on methodological advances that allow these spectral components to be parameterized separately (). By discussing methodological advances, developmental changes, and alterations associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, they emphasize the potential of spectral EEG analyses to advance both basic and clinical neuroscience. Extending this biomarker perspective to adulthood, Bi et al. explored the relationship between hippocampal subfield atrophy and working memory deficits in middle-aged and older cancer patients. Their results revealed reduced volumes in specific hippocampal subfields, particularly CA3 and CA4, while volumes of the hippocampal head and molecular layer were positively associated with working memory performance in cancer patients, in line with evidence that distinct hippocampal subregions are differentially vulnerable across disease and aging (). Finally, Li et al. demonstrated that auricular acupressure and massage can enhance cognitive functions in night shift nursing staff. Changes in P300 parameters, a well-established electrophysiological index associated with attentional and memory-related processes (), provided objective evidence supporting the cognitive effects of the intervention. These findings point to a non-invasive and cost-effective approach to counter the cognitive impact of shift work. Across these contributions, neurophysiological and neuroanatomical markers emerge as increasingly important for understanding cognitive functioning across the lifespan and for guiding future clinical applications.

The third perspective concerns the development of original strategies for modulating brain function, cognition, and emotional wellbeing. Pic Roca et al. present a novel protocol to modulate delta oscillations during general anesthesia using closed-loop auditory stimulation, building on evidence that phase-targeted auditory stimulation can enhance slow oscillatory activity (). This technique aims to stabilize the state of unconsciousness without increasing pharmacological doses, opening the possibility of safer and more personalized anesthesia. Yamamoto et al. complement this approach by showing that physiological responses to stimulation do not always translate into behavioral changes. They investigated the effects of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) on response inhibition, in the context of the well-established role of the locus coeruleus-noradrenergic system in regulating cognitive performance (). Although stimulation increased levels of salivary alpha-amylase (a marker of noradrenergic activity), no improvement in response inhibition, assessed with a stop-signal task, was observed after stimulation. This suggests that noradrenaline modulation via taVNS, at least under the protocol used, may not be sufficient to enhance inhibitory control in simple tasks. Finally, Moezzi et al. offer a perspective on visual art therapy, pointing to its potential to reduce stress and anxiety by modulating activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Their review stresses the need to use objective physiological measures (such as heart rate variability and cortisol levels) to validate the efficacy of art-based therapies in treating emotional pain, consistent with previous evidence that even a single art-making session can be associated with reductions in salivary cortisol (). Overall, these studies show both the promise and the complexity of modulating brain function through new interventions, and suggest that neuromodulation and complementary therapies should be evaluated through behavioral and objective physiological measures together, paving the way toward more effective and personalized clinical applications.

The contributions gathered in Emerging talents in Human Neuroscience: Psychophysiology and Cognitive Neuroscience 2025 illustrate the range of contemporary psychophysiology and cognitive neuroscience. The three complementary perspectives represented in this collection span the adaptive construction of bodily experience, the identification of neural markers of developmental and cognitive vulnerability, and the development of novel approaches for modulating brain function, cognition, and emotional wellbeing. Across these perspectives, behavioral, neurophysiological, neuroimaging, and computational approaches provide converging tools for addressing questions across basic and translational neuroscience. Collectively, these studies offer a glimpse into the future directions of psychophysiology and cognitive neuroscience, while also highlighting both the creativity and innovation of the next generation of scientists and the increasingly interdisciplinary field, integrating experimental rigor with clinical relevance to better understand brain function across diverse populations and contexts.

neuroscience.title: Effectiveness of Pain Neuroscience Education and Therapeutic Exercise in Adults with Musculoskeletal Pain: A Randomized Controlled Experimental Pilot Study
neuroscience.abstract:
What are the main findings?
Adding a structured pain neuroscience education (PNE) programme to therapeutic exercise was not associated, in this pilot sample, with a statistically significant additional reduction in pain intensity or increase in muscle strength beyond exercise alone in adults with chronic musculoskeletal pain.PNE combined with exercise produced significantly greater reductions in kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs than exercise alone, with good adherence and no adverse events.

What are the implications of the main findings?
In real-world rehabilitation settings, the added value of PNE combined with exercise may lie mainly in psychological outcomes rather than in pain intensity or strength gains.A larger, adequately powered multicentre randomized trial is warranted to confirm whether PNE provides clinically relevant benefits when added to structured therapeutic exercise.
Background/Objectives: Chronic musculoskeletal pain is a common public health problem with substantial functional and socioeconomic impact. Pain neuroscience education (PNE) has been proposed as a complementary strategy to therapeutic exercise; however, the available evidence shows considerable methodological variability and a limited number of studies evaluating its added effect in real-world clinical settings. This study evaluated the effect of incorporating a structured PNE programme into a therapeutic exercise protocol on pain intensity, kinesiophobia, and muscle strength in patients with musculoskeletal pain. Methods: A randomized controlled pilot trial was conducted in patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain. Participants were assigned to an experimental group (exercise + PNE) or a control group (exercise only). Participants were adults with chronic musculoskeletal pain of at least three months’ duration, predominantly women, with pain located mainly in the lumbar region, followed by the neck, shoulder, and knee. The intervention lasted 8 weeks, and pain, kinesiophobia, and muscle strength were assessed before and after the intervention. Outcome comparisons were performed using intra- and intergroup non-parametric statistical analyses, with the significance level set at p < 0.05. Results: No significant between-group differences were observed in pain intensity. The group receiving PNE showed greater improvements in kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs. Both groups significantly improved muscle strength, with no differences between them. Mean attendance at the PNE sessions was 88.3%; 31 of the 38 randomized participants (81.6%) were included in the final analysis, and no adverse events were observed. Conclusions: No statistically significant additional effect of PNE was detected on pain intensity or muscle strength in this pilot sample, although it was associated with greater reductions in kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs. Larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.
neuroscience.text:
Chronic pain constitutes a major public health problem. Recent studies estimate that approximately 25.9% of the Spanish adult population presents chronic pain, with a higher prevalence among women and middle-aged individuals []. Among the different clinical presentations, low back and neck pain are consistently reported as being among the most prevalent and disabling forms of chronic musculoskeletal pain, followed by shoulder- and knee-related pain [,]. This condition is associated with a reduction in the quality of life of those who suffer from it, constituting one of the main causes of disability, work absenteeism, and healthcare resource use [,]. Moreover, a considerable number of patients show no clear correlation between tissue damage and the pain experience, maintain their pain despite interventions targeting anatomical structures, and develop fear, avoidance, and dysfunctional beliefs [].

However, clinical practice continues to be dominated by a structural interpretation of pain, in which the intensity of symptoms is directly linked to the magnitude of observable tissue damage []. Although this approach can be useful in acute processes, it presents limitations when applied to persistent pain conditions, in which the correlation between structural findings and pain intensity tends to be weak or non-existent [,]. This fact suggests the involvement of mechanisms related to central pain processing []. For this reason, chronic musculoskeletal pain should not be addressed solely from a tissue-based perspective, but rather requires strategies that modulate physical and social factors [].

In recent decades, the understanding of pain has evolved from biomedical models focused exclusively on tissue damage toward biopsychosocial models that recognize pain as a complex, multifactorial experience []. These models consider the influence of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral factors on pain perception and maintenance, highlighting variables such as beliefs about pain, fear of movement, and avoidance behaviors [,]. At the neurophysiological level, these changes are related to a plastic reorganization of the central nervous system, which may affect not only pain processing but also motor control and muscle strength [,,]. In this context, the perception of threat associated with pain has been identified as a key element that can condition patient participation in physical activities and therapeutic interventions [], which has driven the development of treatment strategies aimed at modifying pain interpretation, among which pain neuroscience education (PNE) stands out []. This intervention is based on the structured delivery of knowledge about pain mechanisms, including aspects related to its physiology, the basic mechanisms involved in its perception, and the basic principles for its management in the clinical setting []. Through this educational process, PNE aims to promote changes in pain-related beliefs and facilitate patient participation in active treatment programs aimed at functional recovery []. Recent research notes that the educational component achieves its full value when combined with therapeutic exercise, since while PNE acts on beliefs and the cognitive interpretation of pain, exercise offers a pathway for progressive exposure to movement []. In fact, the available evidence shows that PNE applied in isolation achieves limited and poorly sustained effects over time [], compared with the greater long-term improvements in pain observed when it is combined with therapeutic exercise [].

Despite growing interest in PNE as part of the management of persistent musculoskeletal pain, the available evidence presents important limitations that make it difficult to establish firm conclusions about its clinical application. Recent systematic reviews have noted considerable heterogeneity in the content, duration, and format of educational interventions, as well as in their integration within therapeutic programs, which limits comparison between studies and generalization of results [,,]. Moreover, many studies have analyzed PNE as an isolated intervention or as part of poorly standardized multimodal programs, and the number of studies specifically evaluating its added effect when combined with structured therapeutic exercise programs applied in real clinical settings remains limited [].

The main objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of incorporating a structured PNE program into a therapeutic exercise protocol, compared with therapeutic exercise alone, on pain intensity in patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain. As secondary objectives, the study aimed to estimate the effect of this intervention on kinesiophobia, fear-avoidance beliefs, and muscle strength, as well as to assess the feasibility (recruitment, adherence to exercise and PNE sessions, dropout rate, and safety) of the study protocol with a view to informing a future larger-scale trial.

This is a randomized pilot clinical trial with a convenience sample. It was conducted following the guidelines of the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT 2025 Statement) [].

Following the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) model, the target population (P) consisted of adult patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain, the intervention (I) was the addition of PNE to a therapeutic exercise program, the comparator (C) was therapeutic exercise alone, and the outcome variables (O) were pain intensity, kinesiophobia, and muscle strength.

All individuals who were part of the therapeutic exercise working groups in a functional rehabilitation center were invited to participate, forming a sample selected through convenience sampling. During the recruitment phase, participants were provided with detailed information about the research project, including the assessment measures, type of intervention, duration, selection criteria, and study objectives, and were invited to participate.

Participants who met the inclusion criteria defined in the corresponding section were selected. Prior to the start of the study, informed consent was obtained, in which the nature of their participation, as well as the benefits and risks of the intervention, were explained. Personal, health, and demographic data were then collected through an interview in order to verify that participants met the selection criteria.

After recruitment, participants were randomly assigned to the intervention or control group through a simple randomization sequence with a 1:1 ratio using the randomizer.org application. Allocation was performed by a researcher once the baseline assessment had been completed. The random allocation sequence was generated using the randomizer.org web-based application by a member of the research team who was not involved in outcome assessment. The same researcher was responsible for enrolling participants and for performing the allocation, which was carried out only after the baseline assessment had been completed for each participant, thereby concealing group assignment from participants and outcome assessors until that point. Randomization was simple (1:1), without stratification or blocking by sex, age, or any other baseline variable. Given the relatively small sample size, this non-stratified procedure may have contributed to the sex imbalance observed between groups after randomization (see ).

Inclusion criteria: Being over 18 years of age, presenting chronic musculoskeletal pain (>3 months) regardless of its location, and signing the informed consent form to participate in the study. Both men and women were eligible for participation, with no upper age limit; the age of the participants finally included in the analysis ranged approximately between 41 and 59 years, based on the interquartile ranges reported by group in . Eligibility was confirmed for each participant through the structured baseline interview described in , which systematically collected sociodemographic and clinical information to verify compliance with the inclusion criteria and the absence of any exclusion criterion before enrolment.

Exclusion criteria: Presenting a psychiatric or psychological condition that hinders the execution or understanding of the intervention, both of the exercise program and the educational talks; presenting neurological diseases of a degenerative nature or affecting the central nervous system; having recently undergone surgery; or being pregnant.

Assessments were carried out at the Studio Pilates center (Pontevedra, Spain) by three physiotherapists external to the research team who were blinded to participant allocation; assessors were not informed of group assignment at either assessment time point and had no involvement in the delivery of the exercise or PNE sessions, which minimized the risk of unblinding. However, blinding effectiveness (e.g., by asking assessors to guess group allocation) was not formally tested, which is acknowledged as a limitation. Variables were recorded at two time points: before the start of the intervention and after it (week 9).

Sociodemographic and clinical variables: age, sex, weight, height, and pain location were collected for each participant.

Outcomes of interest: three scales validated in Spanish were used—the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) [] to assess the maximum pain experienced in the last 7 days; the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK-11) [] and the Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire (FABQ) [] to assess kinesiophobia and cognitive aspects linked to pain.

Muscle strength: four representative movement patterns were assessed—a knee-dominant exercise (squat), a hip-dominant exercise (deadlift), an upper-body push exercise (bench press), and an upper-body pull exercise (bench-supported row). Dynamic muscle strength was assessed using a linear velocity transducer (Vitruve, Speed4Lifts S.L., Madrid, Spain), which made it possible to quantify the movement velocity of the load during the execution of exercises with an Olympic barbell. A load equivalent to 70% of the one-repetition maximum (1RM) was used for all exercises [,,], except for the deadlift, for which a load of 80% of 1RM was used [], since the available literature on reference velocity values for this exercise is mainly described for this intensity. Each participant performed three attempts per exercise, with a five-minute recovery period between them, ensuring a safe and reproducible assessment while minimizing fatigue. For each participant and exercise, 1RM was not measured directly through a single maximal-effort repetition; instead, it was estimated indirectly from the individual load-velocity relationship recorded with the linear velocity transducer, following the procedures described in the load-velocity profiling literature [,,]. The kilogram values reported in the Results therefore correspond to the absolute external load (barbell load) lifted at the prescribed percentage of each participant’s estimated 1RM, rather than to a directly measured maximal load. Of the three attempts performed per exercise, the repetition showing the highest mean propulsive velocity for the corresponding load was retained for analysis, in accordance with standard velocity-based training procedures.

Once the assessments had been carried out and participants had been randomly assigned to the experimental and control groups, the intervention phase began, lasting 8 weeks. Both groups followed the same physical exercise program with the same dosage (see ). However, the experimental group also received a PNE intervention (see ), while the control group carried out only the therapeutic exercise program.

Participation in this study involved minimal risks associated with therapeutic exercise, such as transient muscle soreness or fatigue, and, in the case of PNE, a possible initial increase in attention to pain when new concepts were introduced [,]. To minimize these risks, all exercise sessions were supervised by qualified physiotherapists, who adjusted the intensity and progression of the exercise to the individual characteristics of each participant. The protocol allowed for the possibility of modifying or discontinuing the activity in the event of discomfort or any clinical incident, as well as referral to the participant’s usual healthcare professional in the event of significant worsening of pain or functional status. Discontinuing participation would not have entailed any detriment to participants’ usual care.

The experimental group received four PNE sessions, at a frequency of one session every two weeks. This dose (four sessions, one every two weeks, over the 8-week intervention period) was chosen a priori based on feasibility considerations for delivery in a routine clinical setting and on prior PNE protocols using a similarly limited number of sessions; a fortnightly interval was selected to allow participants time to reflect on and apply the concepts covered before the next session, while minimizing additional burden on participants who were concurrently attending exercise sessions. We acknowledge, however, that the optimal dose, session duration, and delivery format of PNE have not been firmly established, and that this relatively low-intensity format may have limited the magnitude of the effects observed, particularly on pain (see  and dose–response evidence []). PNE was delivered by one of the researchers, who was unaware of the results of the groups’ baseline assessments (blinded to assessment). The educational intervention was based on PNE principles, aimed at facilitating the reconceptualization of pain through an accessible explanation of the neurophysiological mechanisms involved. The sessions were delivered as theoretical classes in an online format, through videos uploaded to the YouTube platform, in which the currently known neurophysiological mechanisms of pain were explained using simple language. During the sessions, examples were provided and, with the support of graphic material and in an accessible way, the functioning of the excitatory and inhibitory pain mechanisms was explained, from their reception in the periphery to their modulation by the central nervous system. At the end of each session, a brief questionnaire was administered to verify attendance and understanding of the content covered. The videos were pre-recorded and were intended to be viewed independently by each participant at home, at their own pace; approximate session duration ranged between 10 and 15 min. Completion of each session was verified through the brief questionnaire administered immediately afterward, which participants completed and returned to the research team; this questionnaire served both to confirm that the video had been viewed and to check basic understanding of the key concepts presented, and was used as the basis for calculating adherence to the educational component.

Likewise, both groups received 50 min therapeutic exercise classes, with a usual frequency at the center of 1 to 3 sessions per week, aimed at improving strength, muscle coordination, aerobic capacity, and flexibility. The interventions were delivered in group format, with a maximum of four participants per session. These sessions took place at the Studio Pilates center (Pontevedra, Spain) and were delivered by the physiotherapists working there. The intervention consisted of a structured therapeutic exercise program, focused mainly on strength training. This was carried out using free weights, including dumbbells, weightlifting bars, and other similar equipment. In addition, the program included an aerobic exercise component. The frequency, intensity, duration, and progression of training were individualized according to the characteristics and abilities of each participant. The weekly frequency (1 to 3 sessions) was determined individually by the treating physiotherapist according to each participant’s usual availability and clinical status, following the center’s standard practice, and was applied identically to both study groups; as reported in , the number of exercise sessions completed did not differ significantly between groups, supporting a comparable overall exercise exposure despite the individualized weekly frequency. Adherence to the exercise program is reported in  relative to the number of sessions completed during the 8-week intervention period.

This project was carried out following the ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects established in the Declaration of Helsinki, also ensuring strict compliance with the confidentiality of personal data and results obtained during the study, in accordance with current national regulations.

Participation was entirely voluntary and had no negative impact on the usual care received at the center or on the physiotherapy services provided to those individuals who decided not to participate or to withdraw from the study at any time.

The project was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Physiotherapy of the University of Vigo under code number 205-2025-04 (28 November 2025). The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT07788781). Participant recruitment began on 16 February 2026; the intervention started on 9 March 2026; it was completed on 10 May 2026, and the study was finalized on 5 June 2026. The trial was registered retrospectively on ClinicalTrials.gov on 19 August 2026, after the completion of data collection. This delay resulted from an unintentional oversight in completing the public registration before participant enrolment, for which the authors apologize; the study protocol, including the randomized design, intervention and comparator groups, objectives, and main outcome measures, had nonetheless been finalized and approved by the Research Ethics Committee before recruitment began. The outcomes presented in this manuscript correspond to those specified in the registered protocol.

A descriptive analysis of the sample and the main study variables was carried out, stratified by allocation group. Quantitative variables were expressed as median and interquartile range (P25–P75), and qualitative variables as absolute and relative frequencies (n, %).

The normality of the variables was assessed using Q-Q plots and the Shapiro–Wilk test. Since several variables did not follow a normal distribution, non-parametric tests were used throughout the analysis.

Baseline comparability between groups was analyzed using the Mann–Whitney U test for quantitative variables and Pearson’s chi-square test for qualitative variables, with the p-value for the latter reported using Fisher’s exact test. To limit the impact of baseline values within each group, change scores (pre-post difference) were analyzed.

Within-group analysis was performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Effect size was calculated using Rosenthal’s r coefficient (r = |Z|/√N), with N considered as the number of observations. Effects were interpreted as r < 0.3, small; 0.3 ≤ r < 0.5, moderate; and r ≥ 0.5, large. No formal correction for multiple comparisons was applied across the multiple outcomes, subscales, and within- and between-group tests performed in this exploratory pilot study; this increases the risk of Type I error for the secondary and exploratory analyses, and is acknowledged as a limitation in .

The analysis was performed as a complete-case analysis, including only participants who completed the baseline and post-intervention assessments and who had data available for the study variables at both assessment time points. To minimize missing data, periodic reminders were carried out, and the reason for dropout was recorded whenever possible. Losses to follow-up were recorded and described in the CONSORT flow diagram () [,]. An intention-to-treat analysis was not performed because no post-intervention data were available for the seven participants who did not initiate or complete the assigned intervention after randomization (four in the experimental group and three in the control group; ); no baseline-carried-forward or imputed values were substituted for these missing post-intervention data. We acknowledge that this complete-case approach may introduce attrition bias, particularly given the small sample size, and that the characteristics of the excluded participants were not formally compared with those of participants included in the final analysis; this is discussed further as a limitation in .

As this was a pilot study, no a priori sample size calculation was performed. The sample size was determined based on feasibility considerations and participant availability during the recruitment period. Consistent with the objectives of pilot randomized trials, the study was designed to assess the feasibility of the protocol and to generate preliminary estimates of effect sizes to inform the planning of future definitive trials. Therefore, the study was not powered to detect statistically significant between-group differences, and findings should be interpreted as exploratory. Consequently, non-significant results may reflect insufficient statistical power rather than a true absence of effect. The results obtained are intended to inform sample size calculations and the design of future adequately powered randomized controlled trials. The statistical significance level (α) was set at 0.05 (p < 0.05). Statistical analyses and graphs were performed using the IBM SPSS Statistics software package for Windows, version 29 (Armonk, NY, USA: IBM Corporation).

Additionally, to complement the interpretation of statistical significance, a reduction of at least 2 points on the NPRS scale was considered clinically relevant [,]. This threshold was used to assess whether the magnitude of the observed change in pain intensity could be considered clinically relevant, regardless of its statistical significance. Participants meeting this threshold were classified as responders and the remaining participants as non-responders. Because responder status is a dichotomous variable, it was reported as the number and percentage of responders in each group and compared between groups using Fisher’s exact test (two-sided), which is appropriate given the small sample size and the expected cell counts below five. Point estimates for between-group differences are reported together with exact p-values and effect sizes (); 95% confidence intervals for the main between-group comparisons were not calculated in the original analysis plan and are noted as a limitation in , to be incorporated in future, adequately powered trials.

A total of 49 individuals were assessed for inclusion in the study, of whom 11 were excluded for not providing informed consent. The remaining 38 were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the experimental group (n = 19) or the control group (n = 19). In the experimental group, two participants never started the assigned intervention and two others discontinued it after they stopped attending the center, leaving 15 participants for the final analysis. In the control group, three participants did not start the assigned intervention, and 16 participants completed the study and were analyzed. No losses to follow-up or adverse effects were recorded. The final sample analyzed comprised 31 participants ().

Baseline sociodemographic and clinical characteristics are presented in . The groups were comparable at baseline in age, body mass index (BMI), and pain location (predominantly lumbar in both), with no statistically significant differences. In contrast, significant differences were found in sex (the experimental group consisted entirely of women, versus an even distribution in the control group), weight, and height.

In the experimental group (), pain intensity (measured with the NPRS) decreased significantly by the end of the intervention, while no significant changes were observed in the control group. In the between-group comparison (), the difference in the magnitude of change did not reach statistical significance, nor did the proportion of responders with a reduction of ≥2 points on the NPRS (experimental group: 7/15, 46.7%; control group: 3/16, 18.8%; Fisher’s exact test, p = 0.135).

The experimental group showed a significant reduction in kinesiophobia, with significant decreases in its activity avoidance and harm subscales (). No significant changes were recorded in the control group for any of these measures. The between-group comparison () showed statistically significant differences in favor of the experimental group in the total score and in both subscales, activity avoidance and harm.

In the experimental group, fear-avoidance beliefs related to physical activity (FABQ-PA) decreased significantly, with the total FABQ score at the borderline of significance (p = 0.050); the work subscale did not change (). The control group showed no significant changes in any of the FABQ scores. In the between-group comparison, significant differences were found in favor of the experimental group in the total score, with no significant differences in the physical activity or work subscales ().

Both groups showed a statistically significant increase in load across the four exercises assessed (). No significant between-group differences were found in the change in any of the strength variables ().

The number of exercise sessions completed () was similar in both groups (median of 8 sessions), with no significant differences. In the experimental group, adherence to the educational intervention was high; the median number of PNE talks attended was 4 (3–4), with a mean attendance of 88.3%. Of the 15 participants in the experimental group, nine (60.0%) completed all four sessions, five (33.3%) attended three, and one (6.7%) attended two. Because the weekly exercise frequency was individualized (1 to 3 sessions/week) rather than fixed, a single scheduled-session target was not defined for the cohort as a whole; taking the minimum expected frequency of one session per week over the 8-week intervention as a reference (i.e., a nominal minimum of 8 sessions), the median number of sessions completed (8 in both groups) corresponds to at least full adherence to this minimum reference frequency, without differences between groups. Adherence to the prescribed exercise volume (sets, repetitions, and load progression) within each session was not separately quantified and is acknowledged as a limitation in .

The main objective of this pilot study was to explore the effect on pain intensity in patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain of adding a structured PNE program to a therapeutic exercise protocol, compared with exercise alone. The results showed no statistically significant differences between groups in the primary variable (pain intensity). However, for the secondary variables (kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs), between-group differences were observed, with greater reductions in some measures in the group that received PNE. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the pilot nature of the study, the small sample size, and the baseline differences between groups. Regarding muscle strength, both groups improved significantly, with no differences between them. In addition, mean attendance at the PNE sessions was 88.3%; the number of exercise sessions completed was similar in both groups; 31 of the 38 randomized participants (81.6%) were included in the final analysis; and no adverse events were observed.
