As no feasibility criteria were prospectively established, these data are reported descriptively rather than as evidence that feasibility was formally demonstrated. Throughout this Discussion, we focus primarily on the between-group comparisons, which are the relevant test of a randomized trial’s efficacy; within-group pre-post changes are described only as supporting information and should not, on their own, be taken as evidence of a differential effect between the experimental and control conditions.

The final sample consisted of 31 participants with predominantly lumbar chronic musculoskeletal pain, recruited by convenience at a single center. The participants included were mostly women with low back pain, a distribution that partially reflects the current epidemiology of chronic pain in Spain [], so the characteristics of the sample are broadly consistent with profiles commonly observed in clinical practice. Nonetheless, participants were included regardless of pain location, and the resulting sample combined individuals with low back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain. Although this heterogeneity can be viewed as reflecting the diversity of presentations seen in routine clinical practice (see ), it also means that different pain mechanisms, degrees of kinesiophobia, and responses to exercise or to PNE may have coexisted within the same analysis, which could have diluted condition-specific effects and reduced the ability of this pilot study to detect treatment-related differences; this should be considered an additional source of heterogeneity alongside the baseline imbalance in sex described below.

However, the groups were not entirely homogeneous at baseline: although they were comparable in age, BMI, and pain location, they differed significantly in sex (the experimental group was composed entirely of women, whereas in the control group women accounted for only half of the sample). Significant differences were also found in weight and height, which may be attributable to the higher proportion of men in the control group. This imbalance should be taken into account when interpreting the results, particularly those related to strength, since the control group started from higher baseline loads. Analysis of change scores partially mitigates this bias, although it does not eliminate it completely. Because sex may influence not only physical performance but also pain-related and psychological responses, this imbalance may have confounded not only the strength results but also, to some extent, the psychological outcomes (kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs), and should be borne in mind when interpreting all between-group comparisons in this study, not only those related to strength. Beyond the analysis of change scores, we did not perform additional sensitivity analyses (e.g., adjusting for sex, weight, or height) to further examine the robustness of the between-group findings to this imbalance; this represents an additional limitation, and such adjusted or stratified analyses should be considered in future, larger trials. Accordingly, the present findings should be interpreted with caution, without attributing the observed between-group differences exclusively to the effect of the intervention.

The absence of significant between-group differences in pain intensity differs from what has been described in the literature. Some meta-analyses [,] have found that adding PNE to an exercise program reduces pain in the short term to a greater extent than exercise alone, although with moderate effect sizes and low-quality evidence due to high heterogeneity between studies. In the present study, by contrast, the reduction in pain did not differ between groups, with no statistically significant additional effect of PNE detected in this pilot sample. Moreover, the magnitude of change did not reach the threshold considered clinically relevant (a 2-point or 30% reduction on the NPRS) [,], and, although the proportion of responders was numerically higher in the experimental group (46.7% vs. 18.8%), this difference was not statistically significant (Fisher’s exact test, p = 0.135).

Several factors could explain this discrepancy: (1) the pilot nature of the study, which was not statistically powered to detect differences in this variable; (2) the low baseline pain intensity (median of 3–4 points on the NPRS), which leaves little room for improvement; (3) the use of a structured, progressive, and supervised exercise program as a comparator, which by itself may have promoted exposure to movement and pain reduction in both groups; (4) the dose and format of the educational intervention, possibly less intensive than that of studies with positive results, in line with the available dose–response analyses []; (5) the baseline imbalance in sex, weight, and height between groups (), which may have added variability that further limited the ability of this small sample to detect a between-group difference in pain; and (6) the heterogeneous pain locations included in the sample, since different musculoskeletal pain presentations may respond differently to PNE and to exercise, potentially diluting an average effect that could be more apparent in a more homogeneous population (). In addition, the categorical NPRS-responder analysis (Fisher’s exact test; see ) was likely underpowered in this pilot sample, given the small number of participants in each group; this further limits our ability to draw firm conclusions about the absence of a differential responder rate between groups. Taken together, these factors indicate that the absence of a statistically significant between-group difference in pain intensity should not be interpreted as evidence that PNE has no effect on pain; rather, with this sample size, the study cannot rule out a clinically meaningful effect, and the finding is best described as no statistically significant additional effect being detected in this pilot sample.

The addition of PNE to the exercise program appears to result in a significantly greater reduction in kinesiophobia than exercise alone, with a moderate effect size on the total TSK-11 score and on both of its subscales, activity avoidance and harm. In contrast, the control group did not show significant changes in any of these scores.

The fact that the added effect was also observed on the harm subscale may be consistent with the content of the intervention, since the central message of PNE—that pain does not necessarily equate to tissue injury—is directly aimed at the beliefs that underlie fear of movement. This pattern of results is consistent with previous findings by Cuenca-Martínez et al. [] and Medina-Viedma et al. [], who concluded that PNE reduces kinesiophobia in patients with chronic low back pain. In addition, Kim et al. [], in their randomized controlled trial in women with chronic low back pain who received PNE added to exercise versus exercise alone, likewise found a significantly greater reduction in kinesiophobia in the group that combined both interventions. Taken together, these findings support the idea that the educational component, by reducing the perceived threat associated with movement, enhances the effect of exercise on fear of movement beyond what exposure to effort achieves on its own [,]. Nonetheless, as with the other secondary outcomes, this finding should be interpreted with caution given the baseline imbalance between groups, the small sample size, the absence of correction for multiple comparisons, and the lack of long-term follow-up; the observed reduction in kinesiophobia is therefore best regarded as a preliminary finding warranting confirmation in a larger, adequately powered trial rather than firm evidence of a clinically established added benefit of PNE.

For fear-avoidance beliefs, the between-group comparison showed a significant difference in favor of the experimental group in the overall FABQ score. However, when the subscales were analyzed separately, this difference did not reach statistical significance for either physical-activity-related or work-related beliefs. In the within-group comparison, the experimental group significantly reduced physical-activity-related beliefs and showed a decrease at the borderline of significance in the overall score, whereas the control group did not change on any of the scores.

The fact that the between-group difference appears in the overall score but not in each subscale separately suggests that PNE may have a small additional effect on fear-avoidance beliefs, which would be more detectable in the combined measure than in its individual components, where the small sample size limits the ability to detect differences. In addition, both groups followed a structured exercise program which, in itself, constitutes a form of gradual exposure to movement and reduces fear of activity, which may have attenuated the between-group difference on this subscale. In fact, exercise alone has been shown to be capable of reducing fear of movement in people with chronic pain of spinal origin, especially those with chronic low back pain []. As for work-related beliefs, most participants started from low or null scores, leaving little room for further reduction, which could explain the absence of change. These results are in line with studies in which adding PNE to exercise improved fear-avoidance beliefs beyond exercise alone []. Given the small sample size, the multiple secondary analyses performed, and the borderline p-value obtained for the total FABQ score, these findings on fear-avoidance beliefs should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive, and require confirmation in an adequately powered trial.

Baseline comparability between groups for these variables was limited; the control group started from significantly higher loads, related to the initial imbalance in sex and, consequently, in weight and height. It should also be clarified that the term ‘muscle strength’ used throughout this manuscript refers to the external load lifted at a given percentage of an indirectly estimated 1RM (a performance-based measure of dynamic lifting capacity under the specific conditions of this protocol), rather than to a directly measured maximal voluntary contraction or an isometric strength value; this distinction, detailed in , should be considered when comparing our results with studies using other strength assessment methods.

Both groups showed a significant increase in the load moved across the four exercises assessed, with no significant differences between them. This result is consistent with the study design, since both groups followed the same strength exercise program, so the improvement in load reflects the adaptation to training common to both conditions. In this regard, a systematic review [] has shown that posterior-chain strength training produces greater improvements in muscle strength, pain, and disability than general exercise in patients with chronic low back pain.

PNE, in contrast, being a cognitive intervention aimed at beliefs about pain, does not constitute an additional training stimulus capable of increasing strength on its own. In fact, despite the experimental group showing a greater reduction in kinesiophobia, this was not translated into greater strength gains, which supports the idea that strength increases depended on training load rather than on changes in fear of movement. The literature specifically evaluating the added effect of PNE on strength is scarce. One exception is the study by Kim et al. [], which found a greater improvement in strength in the group that added PNE to exercise, although it was assessed as isometric contraction time of the trunk musculature, which differs from the load applied in this study, limiting direct comparison.

It is notable that the greatest increase occurred in the deadlift and that the squat started from low loads, both exercises that involve a direct load on the spine and that frequently generate apprehension in people with low back pain. In patients with chronic low back pain, the degree of perceived threat regarding a specific task predicts more protective movement behavior []. Although the present study did not assess fear specific to performing each exercise, only general kinesiophobia via the TSK-11, the progression of loads in both groups could reflect, in addition to training adaptation, greater confidence in loading the spine as exposure to exercise progressed.

As a secondary objective, the feasibility of the protocol was assessed given the pilot nature of the study. No feasibility criteria for recruitment, adherence, retention, or dropout had been prospectively defined; therefore, rather than concluding that feasibility was formally demonstrated, we report the observed recruitment, adherence, and retention data below, which may help to inform the design of a larger trial. Adherence to the educational component was high, despite being delivered online. Adherence to the exercise program was similar in both groups, indicating that the addition of PNE did not compromise participation in exercise. Adverse events were monitored throughout the study by the supervising physiotherapists and through participant report during sessions and follow-up contacts; no adverse events were observed during the study period. Given the limited sample size and monitoring methods, we consider it more appropriate to state that no adverse events were observed than to conclude that the intervention has been demonstrated to be safe.

Regarding recruitment, of the 49 individuals assessed, 38 were randomized, and 31 were analyzed, with a dropout rate of close to 18%, mainly attributable to participants who never started the assigned intervention and with no losses during follow-up.

Nevertheless, these results should be interpreted with caution, since participants were recruited at a single physiotherapy center where exercise-based management was already routinely implemented, which makes it difficult to generalize the findings; this setting likely selected participants with relatively favorable attitudes toward exercise and lower baseline fear-avoidance beliefs than might be expected in broader clinical populations less familiar with structured exercise programs. Even so, as this is a pilot study, these findings provide a basis for designing a larger study, with more participants from multiple centers, that can confirm or refute the observed effects.

This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the relatively small sample size, inherent to its pilot nature, together with convenience sampling and the absence of a formal a priori sample size calculation, may have reduced the study’s ability to detect statistically significant between-group differences. Therefore, non-significant results should be interpreted with caution, as they may reflect insufficient statistical power rather than a true lack of intervention effect. Accordingly, the findings should be regarded as preliminary and exploratory, serving mainly to provide feasibility data and effect size estimates for the planning of future adequately powered randomized controlled trials.

Second, the groups were not entirely comparable at baseline, with significant differences in sex, weight, and height, which may have influenced both the estimation of the intervention effect and the interpretation of the results, especially for the strength variables. Although the use of change scores partially mitigates this problem by adjusting each outcome to each participant’s baseline status, it does not allow it to be ruled out entirely, so the results relating to muscle strength should be interpreted with caution.

Furthermore, participants were already users of the physiotherapy center (where therapeutic exercise is routinely used), so they had some prior familiarity with exercise and basic prior notions about its role in pain management. This may have resulted in relatively low baseline values for kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs, reducing the margin for improvement attributable to PNE and limiting the generalizability of the results to people unfamiliar with therapeutic exercise.

The sample also included participants with musculoskeletal pain in different locations, which makes direct comparison difficult with studies focused on a single anatomical region, as is common in the available PNE literature. However, this heterogeneity could be viewed as a strength if it is assumed that, in chronic pain, the pain experience depends more on central mechanisms than on the peripheral location of damage [,]; combining different locations could better reflect the applicability of PNE in routine clinical practice, where patients rarely present a single, homogeneous pain pattern. At the same time, as noted in , this heterogeneity should also be regarded as a limitation, since combining several pain presentations in a small sample may have diluted condition-specific effects on kinesiophobia, pain, and strength, and reduced the study’s ability to detect treatment-related differences; both interpretations should be kept in mind when generalizing these findings.

In addition to the above: (1) the online format of the PNE sessions, which may have influenced the degree of adherence; (2) the absence of medium- or long-term follow-up, which makes it impossible to know whether the effects are maintained over time; (3) both the duration of the intervention and the dose and format of the educational component may have been insufficient to achieve greater results, particularly on pain, in line with the available dose–response analyses []; (4) the analysis was performed on a complete-case basis, without an intention-to-treat analysis, which may have introduced attrition bias given that seven randomized participants (four in the experimental and three in the control group) did not initiate or complete the intervention and could not be compared with those included in the final analysis; (5) no correction for multiple comparisons was applied across the numerous outcomes, subscales, and statistical tests performed, so some statistically significant findings, particularly among the secondary and exploratory analyses, may represent Type I errors; and (6) 95% confidence intervals were not calculated for the main between-group effects, which would have provided additional information on the magnitude and precision of the observed differences beyond statistical significance alone.

The results of this study open up several avenues for research. The main one would be to conduct a larger, multicenter randomized controlled trial with a sample size calculated in advance, to confirm the observed effects. It would also be advisable to include medium- and long-term follow-up to determine whether the effects are maintained over time.

It would also be of interest to study participants with varying degrees of familiarity with exercise, as well as to balance the composition of the groups, in order to improve the representativeness and comparability of the results.

Finally, future research could examine the optimal dose and format of PNE and incorporate other relevant clinical variables, such as disability and quality of life, to provide a more complete picture of the possible added benefit of PNE. It would also be of interest to compare participants receiving PNE with those receiving other cognitive therapies or therapies focused on improving individual resilience.

In this study, the addition of a PNE program to a therapeutic exercise program was not associated with a statistically significant additional effect on pain intensity or muscle strength in this pilot sample, but it was associated with a greater reduction in kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance beliefs than exercise alone. Taken together, these findings suggest that, in this sample, the added benefit of PNE was concentrated in psychological factors related to pain rather than in pain intensity or muscle strength. It should also be emphasized that although the experimental group showed a statistically significant within-group reduction in pain, this change did not reach the predefined threshold for clinical relevance, underscoring that the observed effects on pain, in either group, were of limited clinical magnitude. Because this is a pilot study, with a small sample size and the limitations noted above, the results should be interpreted with caution and require confirmation in larger trials. The observed adherence (mean attendance of 88.3% at the PNE sessions and a similar number of exercise sessions in both groups), retention (31 of 38 randomized participants analyzed), and the absence of observed adverse events may help to inform the design of a larger, adequately powered trial.

neuroscience.title: The perioperative sensory–cognitive interface: multimodal neuroimaging of hierarchical network reconfiguration in perioperative neurocognitive disorders
neuroscience.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) are commonly attributed to neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular stress, anesthetic neurophysiology, and pre-existing brain vulnerability. These mechanisms identify important insults but do not fully explain how they become disturbances of attention, perception, memory, executive control, and fluctuating awareness. We examine whether changes at the sensory–cognitive interface help explain these symptoms, focusing on postoperative delirium (POD) and early recovery within the broader PND classification. The interface comprises distributed, bidirectional operations that transform sensory evidence into context-sensitive representations through thalamocortical routing, integration, attention, and association systems. The framework makes three testable predictions: sensory function should add explanatory value beyond frailty and brain burden; perioperative effects should vary across hierarchical levels and time rather than reflect uniform suppression; and within-person recovery trajectories should explain outcome better than isolated scans. Anesthetic state-transition studies show that primary sensory responses can persist while feedback, thalamic broadcasting, and distributed integration are disrupted, but whether these changes cause PND remains unproven. Direct perioperative MRI and EEG studies identify pre-existing dysconnectivity, altered sensory and association-network organization, abnormal slow-wave and auditory-feedback dynamics, and incomplete postoperative recovery; nevertheless, findings are heterogeneous and sensory-specific tasks remain uncommon. These observations are compatible with established vulnerability–perturbation models and suggest that symptoms may depend on which networks recover and when. Structural–functional connectivity (SC–FC) coupling is one candidate measurement, not an established biomarker or a requirement of the framework. Longitudinal studies integrating sensory phenotyping, domain-specific cognition, delirium surveillance, MRI, EEG, physiology, and molecular markers should test whether this framework adds reproducible value beyond vascular injury, diffuse arousal failure, and latent neurodegeneration.
neuroscience.text:
The 2018 consensus nomenclature placed pre-existing neurocognitive disorder, postoperative delirium (POD), delayed neurocognitive recovery within 30 days, and postoperative neurocognitive disorder up to 12 months under the umbrella of perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) (). This framework was designed to align perioperative research with contemporary neurocognitive classification, not to imply that the included syndromes share a single mechanism. POD is an acute, fluctuating disorder of attention and awareness; delayed neurocognitive recovery and postoperative neurocognitive disorder require objective decline on neuropsychological testing, contextualized by subjective concern and functional impact. Emergence agitation, residual sedation, sickness behavior, and transient psychomotor slowing may overlap clinically but should not be used interchangeably.  separates these phenotypes, time windows, ascertainment requirements, and major mimics.

Terminology and clinical phenotypes relevant to perioperative cognitive research.

Phenotypes are separated by timing, defining features, and method of ascertainment. They should not be pooled without an explicit rationale.

Early international cohort studies established that older patients can show measurable cognitive decline after both cardiac and non-cardiac surgery and that a vulnerable subgroup has persistent impairment (; ; ). A recent meta-analysis of older adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery estimated that postoperative cognitive dysfunction was most common during the first postoperative weeks and declined markedly over subsequent months, while also documenting pronounced methodological heterogeneity (). POD is itself associated with worse functional recovery and a higher long-term risk of cognitive decline or dementia, although residual confounding and reverse causation remain important because delirium may expose pre-existing neurodegenerative vulnerability rather than independently cause all subsequent decline (; ; ). Contemporary clinical guidance therefore treats PND as a family of interacting phenotypes embedded in patient vulnerability, procedural stress, and recovery context rather than as a unitary “anesthetic toxicity” syndrome (; ; ).

Most mechanistic accounts begin with plausible upstream perturbations: systemic and central inflammation, blood–brain barrier disruption, endothelial and microvascular dysfunction, cerebral hypoperfusion, oxidative stress, neurotransmitter imbalance, disturbed sleep, pain, and drug effects (; ). How these processes disrupt communication between brain regions, leading to impaired attention and perception, remains incompletely understood.

We use the term sensory–cognitive interface for that architecture. It is not a new anatomical organ, a diagnostic label, or a replacement for inflammatory and vascular mechanisms. It is an operational systems-level construct encompassing the distributed processes that encode sensory evidence, regulate its gain, integrate information across modalities and time, compare input with prior expectations, assign salience, select information for attention, and make representations available to memory, executive control, and conscious report. The interface is intrinsically bidirectional: cognition is constrained by afferent information, while prior knowledge, goals, and internal state shape early sensory processing through feedback.

To prevent this construct from becoming an omnibus label, we impose an operational boundary. A finding supports the interface account only when it links at least two of three measurable domains: sensory evidence fidelity (including exteroception, interoception, and nociception), hierarchical routing or contextualization, and domain-specific cognitive or behavioral expression. A global change in arousal, inflammation, or connectivity without sensory-to-cognitive specificity is compatible with several competing models and is not sufficient evidence for this framework.

We review anesthesia-state, aging, and direct perioperative studies, distinguishing what each can establish. The principal question is whether impaired use of sensory evidence helps explain attention and perceptual disturbance in POD beyond global arousal failure. We also consider how far this explanation extends to later cognitive outcomes, without assuming a shared mechanism. We define the interface through links among sensory evidence fidelity, hierarchical routing or contextualization, and domain-specific cognitive expression. We then compare the evidence categories, including null findings and studies reporting changes in opposite directions. This comparison informs falsifiable longitudinal predictions based on sensory phenotyping and recovery trajectories, with SC–FC coupling as one candidate measurement. Throughout, we distinguish observations from anesthetized volunteers or experimental animals from direct patient evidence, and established findings from testable hypotheses.

This is a critical narrative Review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. During revision on 21 September 2026, five targeted search modules were executed in PubMed and Europe PMC, covering POD with sensory processing/EEG, POD with MRI/networks, human intracranial anesthetic evidence, ketamine/esketamine in older surgical patients, and EEG-guided anesthetic depth. Exact search strings, date limits, database return counts, and narrative selection principles are provided in the . We prioritized peer-reviewed human evidence, longitudinal perioperative cohorts, studies with validated cognitive or delirium ascertainment, major randomized trials, and foundational work needed to define the proposed architecture. Animal studies were retained only when they addressed a mechanistic step that is difficult to interrogate in humans. Publications were selected for conceptual relevance and evidential diversity, including null and directionally discordant findings; the search was not used to estimate pooled prevalence or effect size. The perioperative evidence map prioritizes original human perioperative MRI or EEG studies with defined clinical outcomes and measurement timing; nonsurgical anesthesia experiments, animal studies, reviews, protocols, and purely behavioral trials were not classified as direct perioperative imaging evidence. Related publications do not necessarily represent independent cohorts. Selection was narrative and question-driven; not all returned records underwent eligibility screening.

We group the evidence into four categories according to its relevance to the proposed mechanism; the categories do not rank study quality. Direct perioperative evidence comprises measurements obtained before, during, or after surgery and linked to delirium or cognitive outcomes. Perturbational evidence comprises human anesthesia studies that identify reversible changes in sensory, thalamic, electrophysiological, or large-scale network organization but do not establish PND mechanisms. Vulnerability evidence derives mainly from aging, sensory loss, cerebrovascular disease, and cognitive-reserve research. Mechanistic bridge evidence includes cellular or animal work connecting surgical inflammation and physiological stress to brain dysfunction. These categories are complementary but not interchangeable. We did not register a protocol, conduct dual independent screening, calculate pooled imaging effects, or perform formal study-level risk-of-bias scoring. Consequently, completeness cannot be assumed and mechanistic claims are weighted qualitatively according to design, temporality, replication, sample size, phenotype quality, and control of motion, physiology, medication, and attrition. The model should be evaluated against direct evidence, competing explanations, and the specificity of its prospective predictions.

Operational levels of the sensory–cognitive interface and candidate measurements.

The interface is a bidirectional hierarchy, not a single network. Each level supports distinct, testable operations. Directions are network-, region-, method-, and time-specific.

Classical models already rejected a strict separation between sensory and associative cortex.  described cognition as distributed processing across transmodal, heteromodal, and modality-specific zones rather than a serial progression through isolated centers. Contemporary connectomics has made this architecture measurable. The principal cortical gradient places visual and somatomotor regions at one extreme and default-mode, temporoparietal, and medial prefrontal regions at the other, with attention and control networks occupying intermediate positions (). Convergent analyses of anatomical connectivity, microstructure, laminar differentiation, and functional connectivity support a stepwise transition from highly differentiated sensory systems to integrative transmodal cortex, while also showing that structural and functional hierarchies are related but not identical (; ; ).

Primary sensory regions have short temporal receptive windows, dense local circuitry, and relatively direct thalamic drive. Transmodal regions integrate information over longer timescales and larger spatial contexts, support counterfactual and internally generated representations, and depend more strongly on distributed recurrent interactions (; ). A patient can therefore retain cortical responses to sound or touch yet fail to integrate them with place, time, goals, and memory.

The thalamus is central to this architecture but should not be reduced to a passive relay. First-order and higher-order nuclei participate in transthalamic corticocortical communication, regulate cortical synchrony, and route information according to behavioral state (). The core–matrix distinction provides one useful, if simplified, organizing principle. Core cells project relatively focally to middle cortical layers and support modality-specific signaling, whereas matrix cells have more diffuse projections to superficial layers and are positioned to coordinate distributed cortical activity (). Modern anatomical and functional data show gradients rather than a strict binary division, yet the distinction remains helpful when interpreting why anesthesia might preserve some sensory relay while disrupting broad transmodal coordination (; ). Human intracranial recordings provide complementary evidence: propofol reduced thalamocortical alpha/low-beta coherence in 10 patients undergoing deep-brain stimulation (), while recordings in 11 epilepsy patients identified distinct sensory and cognitive cortical alpha networks linked to thalamic projections by tractography in matched healthy surrogates (). Neither study directly identified core and matrix cell types, and these specialized cohorts do not establish the mechanism of POD.

Thalamic function is inseparable from ascending arousal and neuromodulatory systems. Cholinergic and monoaminergic pathways contribute to arousal and cortical state during wakefulness, sleep, and anesthesia (). The sensory–cognitive interface therefore depends on both network topology and physiological operating state: the same anatomical connections can support different information flow under different neuromodulatory regimes.

Perception is normally multisensory. Superior temporal, posterior parietal, insular, and frontal regions integrate visual, auditory, somatosensory, vestibular, proprioceptive, interoceptive, and nociceptive evidence. Integration is most beneficial when cues are temporally and spatially congruent and individually uncertain; incongruent or excessive signals instead generate conflict and attentional load (; ). The postoperative environment is rich in such conflicts: an unfamiliar room, reduced vision without spectacles, muffled speech without hearing aids, pain and visceral signals, intermittent alarms, nocturnal illumination, and disrupted proprioceptive input during immobility. These factors are not sufficient causes of PND, but they can raise the computational demand on an already perturbed system.

Interoception deserves particular emphasis. The insula, anterior cingulate, brainstem, and somatosensory systems integrate the physiological state of the body with affective salience and action. Pain, dyspnea, nausea, inflammation, and autonomic instability can therefore dominate limited attentional resources and alter the weighting of external sensory evidence (). In delirium, misperceptions and hallucinations may reflect not simply abnormal external sensing but an unstable balance between external evidence, internal bodily signals, and prior beliefs.

Predictive-processing accounts propose that cortical hierarchies continuously compare top-down predictions with bottom-up signals, transmitting residual prediction error while adjusting the precision—or reliability—assigned to each source (; ; ; ). Although no single predictive-coding formulation is universally accepted, its concepts are clinically productive. Sensory impairment lowers the precision of afferent evidence; unfamiliar environments increase uncertainty; pain and inflammation amplify salient internal signals; and anesthesia alters feedback and recurrent interactions. If the system assigns too little precision to reliable input, or too much precision to noisy internal predictions, perception may become unstable and context-inappropriate.

Conscious access also requires information to influence distributed systems beyond the region in which it was initially encoded. Global-workspace and related recurrent-processing theories differ in detail, but they agree that local sensory activation is not equivalent to flexible report, memory access, and goal-directed use (; ). The interface construct therefore separates three events that are often conflated: encoding of a stimulus, integration and selection of its meaning, and broadcast or access to systems that support sustained cognition.

Canonical resting-state networks offer a coarse but useful vocabulary. Dorsal attention systems support goal-directed selection; ventral attention and salience systems detect behaviorally relevant change and reorient processing; frontoparietal control systems maintain task rules and coordinate flexible behavior; default-mode systems integrate memory, semantic context, and internally generated models; and hippocampal–medial temporal circuits bind experience across time. The salience network, particularly anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate, has been proposed to coordinate switching between internally and externally oriented states (; ). Large-scale parcellations consistently identify these systems, although boundaries and labels vary (; ).

The interface is not synonymous with the “triple-network model,” nor does every cognitive symptom map one-to-one onto a network. Rather, the networks describe interacting operations. Sustained attention may fail because sensory evidence is weak, salience assignment is unstable, control systems cannot maintain a task set, or internally generated activity intrudes. Episodic memory may fail because encoding was impoverished, hippocampal binding was disrupted, or later retrieval could not access distributed representations. This process-level view argues for domain-specific cognitive phenotyping and against treating a global screening score as a complete neural phenotype.

White-matter pathways constrain which regions can communicate efficiently, yet functional interactions also depend on polysynaptic routes, common inputs, dynamics, and state. SC–FC coupling quantifies the correspondence between structural connectivity and functional connectivity, but there is no single canonical measure. Coupling can be estimated regionally, edge-wise, within networks, across subjects, or using graph-signal approaches that decompose functional activity into components aligned with or decoupled from the structural connectome (; ). Primary sensory cortex tends to be more tightly coupled to direct structural scaffolding, whereas transmodal cortex exhibits greater functional decoupling, consistent with flexible integration across diverse inputs ().

This spatial heterogeneity is central to our argument. High coupling is not universally beneficial. Tight coupling may support efficient sensory transmission, while an appropriate degree of transmodal decoupling may enable flexible cognition. We hypothesize that excessive decoupling could reflect noisy dynamics, whereas excessive coupling could reflect loss of flexibility. Developmental and aging studies show that coupling changes across the lifespan and relates to cognition, heritable factors, and disease burden (; ; ; ; ). We therefore hypothesize that perioperative vulnerability involves abnormal regional patterns and recovery trajectories of SC–FC coupling along the sensory-to-transmodal hierarchy, which a single global coupling value may not capture. Clinically, a patient might hear and recognize a familiar speaker yet fail to integrate the conversation into the hospital context, or recall isolated events without their temporal sequence. These examples illustrate impaired contextual integration; whether they reflect excessive SC–FC decoupling in POD remains untested.

With aging, resting-state systems become less segregated: within-network connectivity often declines while between-network interactions become less distinct, and lower segregation relates to poorer memory and executive performance beyond chronological age (; ). Task activations also become less selective, a phenomenon described as neural dedifferentiation (). Changes in functional gradients suggest that the separation between unimodal and transmodal organization can contract with age, potentially reducing the system’s repertoire of distinct network states ().

Not all broader recruitment is pathological. The HAROLD and compensation-related utilization of neural circuits hypotheses describe increased bilateral or additional recruitment that may maintain performance in older adults (; ). Preoperative hyperconnectivity may indicate successful compensation, inefficient over-recruitment, or reduced network specificity. Therefore, the direction of a connectivity difference cannot be interpreted without performance, longitudinal change, and network context.

Cognitive reserve further modifies clinical expression. Reserve is not a single imaging measure but a property inferred when individuals sustain function despite age- or disease-related burden (). Education and cognitively stimulating experience are imperfect proxies; network efficiency, flexible recruitment, brain maintenance, and sensory health may be closer mediators.

Hearing and visual impairment are among the most reproducible clinical vulnerability factors for delirium. Longitudinal population studies also associate hearing loss with accelerated cognitive decline and incident dementia, although social isolation, shared vascular pathology, reverse causation, and measurement bias contribute to the association (; ; ; ). From an interface perspective, sensory loss is not merely a covariate. Degraded input demands greater attentional effort and reliance on predictions, potentially altering long-term network organization.

Aging can increase behavioral benefit from congruent multisensory cues, especially when unisensory signals are weak, yet can also widen temporal binding windows and impair suppression of irrelevant or incongruent information (; ; ; ). This combination—greater dependence on multisensory redundancy but poorer selection under conflict—may be advantageous in a stable environment and fragile in an unfamiliar postoperative setting.

White-matter hyperintensities, lacunes, microinfarcts, and reduced tract integrity can weaken long-range communication and lower the threshold at which physiological stress produces disconnection. Classic delirium models describe a balance between baseline vulnerability and precipitating insult: a highly vulnerable patient may develop delirium after a modest stressor, whereas a resilient patient requires a larger insult (). Meta-analytic risk-factor work supports this multidimensional interaction, although effect estimates vary by setting and ascertainment ().

Structural burden need not produce a focal deficit before surgery. Redundant routes and functional compensation can preserve behavior until anesthesia, inflammation, hypotension, or sleep deprivation reduces the operating margin. This distinction matters for interpreting diffusion MRI. Lower fractional anisotropy or reduced global efficiency is not evidence that surgery caused white-matter injury when measured only preoperatively; rather, it may index latent disconnection risk. Conversely, new diffusion lesions after surgery may represent direct injury with consequences distinct from reversible network reconfiguration (; ).

Healthy aging studies show that SC–FC coupling varies with cognitive performance and small-vessel burden, but the field remains methodologically diverse (; ). A plausible perioperative vulnerability phenotype would combine: preserved or impaired structural capacity; baseline functional segregation; regional coupling along the cortical hierarchy; sensory function; and cognitive reserve.

The studies reviewed here have not validated SC–FC coupling as a perioperative biomarker for POD or postoperative neurocognitive disorder. It remains of mechanistic interest because structural networks change relatively slowly over days, while functional networks can reorganize rapidly; whether this difference helps explain perioperative cognitive changes requires testing.

Across drugs, anesthetic unconsciousness is better described as a reconfiguration of communication than as uniform cortical suppression (; ; ). Local sensory responses, spontaneous activity, and even some forms of implicit processing may persist, while long-range integration, feedback signaling, complexity, and flexible responsiveness decline. This state literature illuminates candidate operations within the sensory–cognitive interface, but it cannot by itself establish that the same changes cause postoperative disorders. Healthy volunteers typically recover completely, anesthetic concentrations differ from clinical practice, surgery and inflammation are absent, and measures obtained during unresponsiveness may reflect a physiological state rather than injury.  contrasts agent- and exposure-specific neural patterns, evidential context, limitations, and testable perioperative implications.

Anesthetic agents and perioperative exposures: network evidence, limitations, and testable implications.

State-transition and clinical evidence are distinguished. No exposure has a universally beneficial connectivity direction. Directions are network-, region-, method-, and time-specific.

Propofol studies provide some of the clearest evidence for hierarchical disconnection. Resting-state fMRI demonstrates breakdown of both within-network and between-network connectivity during loss of consciousness, with prominent effects in frontoparietal, default-mode, and thalamocortical systems (; ). Graph analyses suggest reduced integration and altered community structure rather than a simple global reduction in correlation (; ). Thalamic and association-cortical changes are substantial, yet primary sensory regions may retain stimulus-evoked responses. The critical deficit is therefore plausibly the capacity of sensory information to propagate, interact with contextual feedback, and influence distributed cognitive systems.

Recent work refines this account at two levels. Functional-gradient mapping indicates that propofol changes thalamocortical organization in a manner that preferentially weakens transmodal aspects of core–matrix architecture (). Intracortical recordings show that propofol-mediated loss of consciousness disrupts predictive routing: top-down alpha–beta interactions and bottom-up gamma-related signaling become uncoupled, impairing reciprocal communication across cortical hierarchy (). These studies support the interface model’s distinction between sensory registration and cognitive access, but their direct relevance to postoperative recovery remains untested.

Electrophysiologically, propofol produces dose-dependent frontal alpha activity, slow oscillations, altered phase–amplitude relationships, and eventually burst suppression. Loss and return of behavioral responsiveness do not correspond to a single universal EEG threshold (). Measures of perturbational complexity and spontaneous signal diversity often fall during unconscious states, consistent with a reduced repertoire of differentiated responses (; ).

Sevoflurane studies similarly show altered default-mode, ventral attention, frontal, and thalamic connectivity (). Simultaneous fMRI–EEG work found that moderate sevoflurane anesthesia reduced frontal and thalamic network integrity while primary sensory systems were comparatively preserved until deeper suppression (). Comparable dissociations between preserved early encoding and impaired higher-order processing have been reported in auditory paradigms under propofol () and in human intracranial recordings with the same drug (). These findings align with a hierarchy in which late, recurrent, and integrative operations are more state-sensitive than initial encoding.

BOLD connectivity is sensitive to vascular physiology as well as neural activity (); this complicates interpreting cross-agent differences. Cross-agent comparisons therefore require end-tidal or plasma concentration, physiological recording, harmonized arousal endpoints, and ideally concurrent EEG.

Dexmedetomidine, an α2-adrenergic agonist, produces a state with some sleep-like behavioral and electrophysiological features, including arousability at lighter levels. Yet it is not equivalent to physiological sleep. Network-topological studies show substantial reconfiguration, and direct comparisons with propofol identify distinct EEG dynamics despite similar behavioral unresponsiveness (; ). More recent work has further characterized the sleep-like but pharmacologically specific organization of dexmedetomidine sedation ().

Clinically, dexmedetomidine has been associated with lower delirium incidence in selected trials and meta-analyses, particularly when used for postoperative sedation, but effects are context-dependent and accompanied by bradycardia and hypotension. A large randomized trial reported reduced POD after low-dose postoperative dexmedetomidine in older intensive-care patients (), whereas other perioperative regimens and comparator contexts have produced less consistent findings. Network preservation is a plausible mediator, but direct mediation evidence remains sparse; reduced opioid exposure, improved sleep, lighter sedation, and different hemodynamics are competing explanations.

Ketamine illustrates why unconsciousness cannot be treated as a single network state. At anesthetic or subanesthetic concentrations, ketamine can produce dissociation, vivid internally generated experience, and altered sensory integration rather than uniformly reduced cortical complexity. Functional-connectivity studies show drug-specific changes in thalamocortical, frontoparietal, and sensory systems (), while cross-drug studies demonstrate that different anesthetics can disrupt frontal–parietal communication through distinct neurophysiological configurations (). Thus, the interface model predicts agent-specific trajectories rather than a universal “connectivity suppression” pathway.

Clinical trials have not established ketamine as a reliable strategy for preventing delirium or postoperative cognitive decline. The PODCAST trial did not show that a single intraoperative ketamine dose prevented postoperative delirium and documented psychotomimetic adverse effects (). Conversely, a trial of subanesthetic S-ketamine during hip or knee arthroplasty under neuraxial anesthesia reported less POD (8.1% versus 20.4%) but more hallucinations, dizziness, and nightmares (). Potential benefit and psychotomimetic harm should therefore be interpreted in relation to formulation, regimen, and clinical context. In older patients, baseline cognition, frailty, and coadministered sedatives warrant attention; these trials do not establish an age-by-treatment interaction.

Processed EEG indices, including BIS, summarize complex, age-dependent signals in a single number calculated by a proprietary algorithm. The raw EEG is needed to assess spectra, suppression, complexity, and connectivity independently (; ; ). Mechanistic trials must therefore retain raw waveforms and document acquisition settings and artifacts so that analyses can be reproduced. Trials of EEG-guided anesthesia have yielded inconsistent delirium results. Earlier studies suggested that bispectral or depth-guided management could reduce anesthetic exposure and postoperative delirium or cognitive dysfunction (; ). ENGAGES found that EEG-guided anesthetic administration reduced exposure and burst suppression but did not significantly reduce delirium (). In contrast, the BALANCED delirium substudy found less POD with a BIS target of 50 than 35 (19% versus 28%; odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.38–0.88) (). Differences in protocols, achieved depth separation, patient risk, delirium ascertainment, cointerventions, and the biological meaning of the monitored index complicate comparison.

The more defensible interpretation is that EEG reveals neural susceptibility, not merely delivered dose. Excessive slow-wave activity or burst suppression at modest concentrations may identify a brain with reduced reserve; prolonged suppression may also be a modifiable exposure. Contemporary cohort studies link intraoperative spectral features, connectivity, and suppression patterns to POD, but predictive performance and causal direction vary (; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Future trials should therefore test explicit EEG phenotypes and network mediators rather than assuming that reducing a proprietary index alone restores cognition.

Anesthesia-state studies suggest which processes may be affected, but the causes of persistent PND remain uncertain. The next question is whether brain networks recover normally after anesthesia. This requires direct measurement during recovery, because emergence may not retrace induction. We propose testing whether postoperative stressors disrupt network recovery even after wakefulness returns.

Tissue injury activates innate immune pathways and releases cytokines, damage-associated molecular patterns, and acute-phase mediators. Experimental models show that interleukin-1β, tumor necrosis factor, and microglial responses can impair hippocampal plasticity and memory after surgery (; ; ). More recent mechanistic work describes coordinated peripheral and central immune responses rather than a simple passive “spillover” of inflammation into the brain (). Human studies associate perioperative inflammatory markers with delirium or cognitive decline, but effect sizes are variable and temporality, comorbidity, infection, and surgical magnitude complicate causal interpretation ().

Blood–brain barrier and endothelial dysfunction offer a route by which systemic stress can alter neural homeostasis (). Yet neuroinflammation is not a complete phenotype-level explanation. Cytokines can alter neuromodulation, synaptic gain, glial metabolic support, and neurovascular coupling across many circuits. The interface model specifies a systems-level consequence: inflammatory signaling may reduce the precision and stability of long-range communication, amplify interoceptive salience, and impede the re-segregation of attention and association networks. This is plausible but requires simultaneous inflammatory and network measurements to establish mediation.

Hypotension, hypoxemia, anemia, hypocapnia or hypercapnia, embolic events, and impaired autoregulation can threaten a brain with limited vascular reserve. Observational studies associate intraoperative hypotension with adverse organ outcomes, but definitions and causal estimates vary (). Individualized blood-pressure management has reduced organ dysfunction in some trials (), yet evidence specifically linking such strategies to PND remains inconsistent (). A universal pressure threshold ignores baseline hypertension, cerebrovascular disease, collateral capacity, anesthetic agent, and the duration and pattern of exposure.

Perfusion also affects measurement. BOLD connectivity is sensitive to carbon dioxide and cerebrovascular reactivity (). Arterial spin labeling provides perfusion information (). Combining it with physiological measurements may help assess how much of a BOLD change is attributable to vascular factors. New diffusion-restricted lesions or infarcts should be analyzed separately from functional dysconnectivity because direct tissue injury and state-dependent network failure may coexist but imply different interventions.

Acute pain captures attention, disrupts sleep, enhances threat monitoring, and changes salience, default-mode, and control-network connectivity. Chronic-pain imaging demonstrates that individual pain experience depends on distributed networks rather than nociceptive pathways alone (). In older adults, undertreated pain and high opioid exposure can both contribute to delirium; the clinically relevant target is adequate, opioid-sparing analgesia without excessive sedation. Population studies also associate pain with cognitive burden, but directionality is complex ().

The interface account treats pain as high-precision internal evidence that competes with external orientation and goal-directed processing. Opioids provide analgesia but can also depress arousal (). Regional analgesia, non-opioid adjuncts, and patient-specific titration may therefore support cognition through several routes. Direct imaging studies that demonstrate network mediation are still uncommon, so analgesic strategy should not be ranked solely on theoretical connectivity effects.

Sleep disturbance is common before and after surgery and is associated with delirium and poorer cognitive recovery (). Sleep loss changes slow-wave activity, synaptic homeostasis, attention, and default-mode/control-network interactions. Pain, ward interruptions, nocturnal light, medications, and circadian phase shifts compound one another. The relationship is bidirectional: prodromal delirium disrupts sleep, while disrupted sleep may increase vulnerability.

Environmental sensory conditions are mechanistically relevant but easily oversimplified. Removing spectacles or hearing aids reduces reliable input; alarms and frequent care produce overload; isolation and immobility reduce orienting cues; masks and unfamiliar voices impair speech and face integration. The goal is not maximal stimulation. It is a stable, interpretable, circadian-appropriate sensory environment with adequate vision and hearing, clear communication, mobility, sleep protection, and orientation. Multicomponent programs such as the Hospital Elder Life Program reduce delirium by addressing several vulnerabilities simultaneously (; ; ). Their efficacy supports systems-level prevention, although it cannot isolate a specific sensory–cognitive mechanism.

Postoperative increases in neurofilament light, tau, and other neural-injury markers are reported in subsets of patients and may correlate with cognitive outcomes (; ; ). These markers should not be treated as interchangeable with network dysfunction. A patient may show substantial but reversible functional reconfiguration without measurable axonal injury, while focal or diffuse injury may occur without a particular cognitive syndrome. Moreover, concentrations depend on baseline neurodegeneration, renal function, blood volume, timing, assay, and procedure.

The strongest test is longitudinal mediation with temporally ordered measurements, not cross-sectional correlation between one biomarker and one network metric.

Residual drug effects and physiological factors influence emergence and can complicate cognitive assessment (). Imaging is rarely feasible in this interval, so assessment relies particularly on EEG, behavioral responsiveness, and the drugs administered. Emergence-related disturbances may involve some of the same network processes as POD. A diagnosis of delirium, however, requires the characteristic disturbances of attention and awareness and a fluctuating course, assessed with immediate recovery factors taken into account.

POD develops over hours to days and fluctuates. Hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed motor presentations can reflect different clinical manifestations of a common syndrome, but may also have partially distinct physiological contributors. Hypoactive delirium is particularly likely to be missed without repeated structured assessment (). Imaging biomarkers should be linked to temporally proximate delirium status and severity; a scan obtained after resolution addresses vulnerability or recovery, not necessarily the neural state of active delirium.

Delirium is a network-level disorder in contemporary models, involving arousal, attention, sensory interpretation, and integration of internal and external context (). Its association with later cognitive decline is robust at the population level, but three causal structures remain plausible and may coexist: delirium contributes to injury or accelerates decline; delirium is a marker of an insult that independently causes decline; and delirium reveals pre-existing pathology. Preoperative imaging and cognition are therefore indispensable.

Objective postoperative cognitive decline requires a baseline and an appropriate statistical definition. Single screening tools are insufficient to characterize domain-specific change, and repeated testing introduces practice effects. Reliable-change or normative approaches should include non-surgical controls when feasible, or at minimum account for age, education, test–retest effects, and baseline performance. The 30-day and 12-month nomenclature boundaries are clinically useful but do not imply abrupt mechanistic transitions ().

Memory, attention, processing speed, and executive control may have different neural mediators. A global composite improves statistical power but can obscure meaningful dissociations. The interface model predicts, for example, that impaired early sensory fidelity and attention can secondarily reduce memory encoding, whereas persistent hippocampal or default-mode dysfunction may impair memory despite recovered sensory processing. Imaging should therefore be related to both domain composites and functional outcomes rather than to a single binary PND label.

Many older surgical patients have mild cognitive impairment, frailty, sleep disorders, depression, or subclinical neurodegeneration before surgery. Preoperative screening is not merely risk stratification; it defines the denominator for postoperative change. Alzheimer-type cortical atrophy has been linked to delirium risk in some imaging cohorts (), and apolipoprotein E genotype may modify cognitive trajectories after surgery (), but findings are not uniform. Biomarker-positive neurodegeneration could influence network reserve, inflammation, and recovery without making surgery the primary cause of long-term decline.

The perioperative imaging literature is expanding but remains fragmented. Studies differ in surgery, age, urgency, anesthetic exposure, delirium assessment, cognitive definition, imaging time, preprocessing, and statistical scale. Sample sizes are often modest, postoperative attrition is informative rather than random, and many findings lack external replication.  maps representative human MRI and EEG publications, explicitly noting that several reports reuse the same cohorts and therefore do not constitute independent replications. Several recurrent observations nevertheless support a vulnerability-plus-reconfiguration framework more strongly than a focal-lesion model.
