Conventional structural MRI can quantify global and regional atrophy, hippocampal volume, cortical thickness, white-matter hyperintensity burden, and overt lesions. Findings are mixed. In 146 dementia-free adults aged at least 70 years undergoing elective surgery, presurgical white-matter hyperintensity, total brain, and hippocampal volumes were not significantly associated with delirium incidence or severity (). By contrast, a cardiac-surgery cohort linked white-matter hyperintensities to postoperative delirium (), and an Alzheimer-related cortical-thickness signature was associated with delirium severity, although not unequivocally with incidence, in another older elective-surgery cohort ().

These results are not simply contradictory. Global lesion volume may be insensitive to strategically located or network-disconnecting pathology; associations may differ between cardiac and non-cardiac procedures; and excluding dementia narrows the range of structural burden. Structural MRI is likely most informative when topology, location, and connectivity consequences are considered. In patients undergoing surgical aortic valve replacement, infarct-related structural disconnection—not merely lesion volume—was greater among those with delirium, implicating frontal and temporal pathways despite clinically “silent” infarcts ().

Structural measures are therefore best interpreted as reserve and injury context. A normal-appearing T1-weighted scan does not rule out microstructural, physiological, or functional vulnerability, while extensive atrophy or white-matter disease does not determine outcome (, ).

Diffusion MRI provides some of the strongest evidence that vulnerability precedes surgery. In the Successful Aging after Elective Surgery cohort, presurgical diffusion abnormalities in 136 dementia-free older adults were associated with delirium incidence and severity. Associations involved interhemispheric, cingulo-limbic, thalamic, basal-forebrain, cerebellar, and association pathways; several remained after adjustment for baseline cognition (). This distributed pattern is consistent with reduced reserve across arousal, relay, memory, and integration systems rather than one critical tract.

Longitudinal data from 113 participants in the same program showed that delirium occurrence and severity were associated with one-year diffusion changes in periventricular, frontal, and temporal white matter, which also related to cognitive change (). The design cannot determine whether delirium itself drove microstructural change, marked a shared insult, or identified brains already on a neurodegenerative trajectory. Nevertheless, it demonstrates why preoperative-only or postoperative-only imaging is inadequate for causal claims.

Diffusion measures have important limitations. Fractional anisotropy is sensitive but nonspecific; crossing fibers, extracellular water, edema, and scanner differences complicate interpretation. Tractography produces plausible streamlines, not direct axonal counts, and inter-algorithm variability can be substantial (). Perioperative studies should include robust distortion and motion correction, model free water where justified, quantify new diffusion lesions separately, and report tractography choices transparently. Network analyses should test prespecified pathways and whole-connectome topology while controlling multiplicity.

Several preoperative resting-state studies identify functional phenotypes associated with subsequent POD. In 57 patients with femoral-neck fracture, multivariate structural and resting-state features differentiated those who later developed delirium, suggesting that vulnerability was present before the operation (). In 120 adults older than 65 years undergoing major elective non-intracranial surgery, 31 developed POD. They showed lower preoperative within-network connectivity in salience–ventral attention, cognitive-control, and default-mode systems; visual and salience–ventral attention features contributed to a support-vector classifier with 68% reported accuracy (). This result is mechanistically informative but insufficient for individual clinical prediction without external validation. The coexistence of visual and higher-order network differences is directly relevant to a sensory–cognitive hierarchy.

Other cohorts show preoperative hyperconnectivity. In the BioCog study, 283 older patients underwent preoperative fMRI and 46 developed POD. Orbitofrontal, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampal networks were hyperconnected before surgery in patients who later developed delirium; among those returning for imaging 3–5 months later, selected connectivities decreased (). Hyperconnectivity may represent compensation for latent dysfunction, loss of network specificity, dopaminergic dysregulation, or a selection effect. The observation cautions against a universal “low connectivity equals risk” rule.

Resting-state prediction of delayed neurocognitive recovery has likewise highlighted interactions between association and visual systems. In a 74-patient cohort, delayed recovery at 7–14 days was associated with higher preoperative middle-cingulate activity and lower connectivity between middle cingulate and calcarine cortex (). Analyses of the same-sized cohort reported lower default-mode connectivity with visual-processing regions and high internal machine-learning performance (; ). These models require independent, multisite validation: small test sets, feature selection, imbalance, and repeated use of a single cohort can inflate apparent accuracy. Their mechanistic value is stronger than their current readiness for individual clinical prediction.

Imaging during active delirium is difficult and therefore rare. In patients with femoral-neck fracture, serial resting-state fMRI revealed altered default-mode interactions, reduced normal opposition between default-mode and task-positive regions, and abnormal subcortical–striatal–cortical connectivity during delirium (). The small number scanned during active episodes limits generalization, and motion or medication effects remain concerns, but the findings support disrupted reciprocity among internally oriented, control, salience, and subcortical systems.

Recovery studies provide a longer temporal view. In a multicenter cohort, stringent motion control left 246 participants with preoperative and three-month fMRI; 38 had developed POD. Connectivity strength increased after surgery in the overall cohort but decreased after POD, and decreasing connectivity was associated with worsening Trail Making Test performance (). In cardiac surgery, small longitudinal studies have reported changes in resting connectivity and task-related posterior-cingulate centrality at approximately six weeks (; ). APOE4-related differences were not uniformly detectable in cognition or network trajectories, underlining the need for adequately powered interaction analyses ().

A 2025 longitudinal cardiac-surgery study further suggested that global left-frontal connectivity moderated the relationship between postoperative inflammation and cognitive performance (). Its small sample makes the result hypothesis-generating, but the design exemplifies a more mechanistic question: not merely whether inflammation and cognition correlate, but whether network reserve changes their relationship. A 2026 BioCog analysis of 214 patients implicated pre- and postoperative connectivity of dopaminergic midbrain subnetworks in three-month cognitive dysfunction, extending the framework beyond canonical cortical networks ().

Resting-state fMRI is feasible and broad, but it cannot identify whether an abnormal edge reflects sensory encoding, salience detection, working-memory maintenance, or unrelated spontaneous state. Task paradigms can provide process specificity. N-back studies after cardiac surgery have identified altered posterior-cingulate centrality and local coherence as memory load increases (). However, complex tasks selectively exclude frail or cognitively impaired patients and conflate performance with neural activation.

Short, adaptive sensory tasks may be more suitable. Auditory oddball, speech-in-noise, audiovisual congruence, somatosensory prediction-error, or attention-reorienting paradigms can separate early encoding from later mismatch, feedback, and access. A longitudinal study in patients with frontal glioma linked gray-matter volume and resting-state visual-network connectivity to POD (). These measurements did not constitute diffusion-based SC–FC coupling. The specialized neurosurgical population and potential tumor-related reorganization limit generalization, but the study demonstrates that sensory networks can be interrogated directly rather than treated as passive comparators.

EEG measures neural dynamics at the timescale of information flow and can be repeated when MRI is unsafe or impractical. Increased delta or slow-wave activity and reduced functional connectivity are common during delirium, but frontal slowing also occurs after surgery in patients without delirium. In a multimodal cohort of 70 patients, delirium emerged when slow-wave activity extended from frontal to posterior regions alongside connectivity breakdown; connectivity changes related to inflammation and delirium severity (). Preoperative alpha features also differed, suggesting baseline susceptibility.

Evoked responses can test the sensory–cognitive interface more directly. Of 131 patients with EEG data, 110 contributed postoperative data (19 with POD), and 102 had paired recordings. POD was associated with smaller mismatch negativity and reduced model-estimated feedback from left superior temporal to primary auditory cortex; feedback strength related inversely to delirium severity, with exploratory, uncorrected associations with inflammation (). This supports impaired top-down sensory prediction in delirium, although model-derived connectivity does not demonstrate a causal mechanism. Replication, medication adjustment, and clarification of whether changes precede or follow delirium onset are still needed. Analyses should record hearing thresholds, stimulus audibility, and hearing-aid use, and account for opioid dose and timing, other sedatives, pain, and arousal when interpreting postoperative auditory responses.

Intraoperative EEG studies examine spectral power, connectivity, complexity, suppression, and age-adjusted signatures. These measures have been associated with delirium risk or suppression susceptibility, although they are not interchangeable biomarkers (; ; ). More consistent reporting would help comparison across studies. Proprietary indices should be accompanied by raw waveforms, with spectra provided as complementary derived data. Reports should describe electrode density, montage, and artifact handling, and include preoperative or postoperative awake baselines where possible.

Arterial spin labeling can quantify cerebral perfusion without contrast and may help interpret BOLD changes, but signal-to-noise and transit-time effects complicate quantification (). fNIRS offers portable cortical oxygenation and hemodynamic measurement, although limited depth and systemic contamination constrain inference (). These methods are best used to test explicit physiological mediators rather than as unvalidated substitutes for neural connectivity.

Structural MRI and diffusion characterize reserve and injury; BOLD and perfusion describe spatial organization and vascular context; EEG tests temporal routing and arousal; blood biomarkers index inflammation or neural injury; and cognition defines behavioral expression.

SC–FC coupling measures how closely functional coordination corresponds to anatomical connections. It may help relate baseline reserve to changes in network organization across perioperative states, although its value in this setting remains unvalidated. The sensory–cognitive account can also be tested using EEG, sensory tasks, and network measures without an SC–FC coupling analysis.

Regional SC–FC coupling is often estimated by correlating the structural weights incident on a region with the corresponding functional-connectivity edges, after prespecifying how absent edges, distance, weight transformation, and sign will be handled (; ). Edge-wise, network-level, graph-signal, and subject-level approaches address different questions and cannot be used interchangeably. Perioperative studies also need to distinguish between-person differences at a single time point from within-person changes in coupling. Only the latter directly describe reconfiguration, and even these changes may reflect altered hemodynamics unless physiological or electrophysiological findings support a neural interpretation. Vascular effects on BOLD connectivity are therefore relevant to the interpretation of SC–FC coupling (). ASL can provide perfusion measurements (), but cannot establish neural causation on its own; we propose physiological recording and EEG as complementary checks.  outlines the analysis from paired structural and functional connectomes to a spatial coupling profile and longitudinal clinical testing.  summarizes the information provided by each complementary modality and its limitations.

Multimodal measures, inferential value, and principal confounds.

Directions are network-, region-, method-, and time-specific.

Because structure–function relationships vary along the cortical hierarchy, whole-brain average coupling can conceal opposite regional effects (; ). A rigorous perioperative analysis should prespecify at least three scales:
Unimodal coupling, where relatively tight alignment may support reliable sensory transmission;Intermediate network coupling, including salience, attention, and control systems that coordinate flexible routing;Transmodal coupling or decoupling, where an appropriate degree of functional freedom may support contextual integration.

Unimodal coupling, where relatively tight alignment may support reliable sensory transmission;

Intermediate network coupling, including salience, attention, and control systems that coordinate flexible routing;

Transmodal coupling or decoupling, where an appropriate degree of functional freedom may support contextual integration.

Time-resolved coupling approaches may capture transient configurations, but their reliability and sensitivity to windowing require careful validation (). The expected direction must be stated for each region and time point. “Normalization” should mean movement toward a well-defined, age-appropriate reference profile associated with better function—not simply an increase.

Gradient analysis reduces complex connectivity into continuous axes of organization () and is well suited to testing whether perioperative perturbation compresses the separation between sensory and transmodal systems.

Dynamic functional connectivity offers complementary information about the repertoire and dwell time of network states. Yet dynamic analyses can create apparently meaningful states from sampling noise, motion, or arousal variation; strong null models and test–retest reliability are essential ().

Convergent findings across diffusion MRI, fMRI, and EEG strengthen a network interpretation when they are anatomically and temporally aligned.

Even when findings from different modalities agree, causal interpretation requires within-person changes measured in temporal order, appropriate controls, and explicit assumptions about confounding. An intervention that changes the proposed network mediator would provide stronger support.

Drawing on established accounts of vulnerability, perturbation, and recovery, we describe four proposed stages and three possible recovery trajectories (). The stages remain hypothetical; they have not been observed as a sequence in POD.

The model proposes that established vulnerabilities—including aging, sensory impairment, vascular disease, neurodegeneration, and frailty ()—reduce the fidelity and flexibility of the sensory–cognitive hierarchy. These features need not cause daily-life impairment because stable environments and compensatory strategies support function.

Anesthetic drugs reduce arousal and reconfigure thalamocortical, feedback, and transmodal interactions (; ). Surgery adds inflammation, hemodynamic stress, pain, embolic or direct injury risk, and metabolic disturbance. Sensory aids may be removed and environmental uncertainty increases. We hypothesize that these disturbances reduce the reliability of bottom-up sensory information and disrupt precision weighting. They may also increase the salience of internal bodily signals and restrict access to distributed cognitive processing.

Eye opening or command following indicates behavioral emergence, but brain networks may still differ from their preoperative state. Inflammation, sleep loss, residual drug effects, pain, and ambiguous sensory input continue to affect this period. Network recovery therefore needs to be considered beyond the first signs of awakening.

Unstable or regionally abnormal reconfiguration may contribute to the fluctuating disturbances of attention and contextual integration seen in POD. Persistent disruption, direct injury, or unmasked neurodegeneration may contribute to later cognitive disorders, which need not follow the same course as POD. The clinical presentation depends on the processes affected as well as the overall magnitude of network change.

Resilient recovery is characterized by transient, exposure-appropriate disconnection followed by rapid restoration of network differentiation, feedback, and domain-specific cognition. Compensated recovery shows abnormal baseline or early postoperative connectivity, possibly including hyperconnectivity, but recruits alternative pathways sufficiently to restore behavior; it may consume reserve and predict vulnerability to later stress. Failed or maladaptive recovery shows persistent reduction of state repertoire, inappropriate coupling along the hierarchy, loss of feedback, or disintegration across sensory, salience, and control systems, accompanied by delirium or cognitive decline.  depicts these as explicitly conceptual trajectories rather than observed patient-level curves.

gives a study design for each prediction and specifies findings that would argue against it. These tests need reliable measurements, sufficient variation in exposure, and adequate statistical power. A negative result for one candidate measure would challenge that measure without necessarily invalidating the wider framework:
1 Interaction prediction: baseline sensory function and network reserve should modify the association between perioperative exposure and cognitive outcome. Failure to detect the prespecified interaction in a sufficiently powered study would weaken this prediction. Additive effects would still be compatible with broader vulnerability models.2 Hierarchy prediction: transmodal and feedback interactions should show greater state sensitivity, while persistent symptoms during POD should involve impaired reintegration across sensory, salience–attention, and association levels rather than isolated global suppression.3 Trajectory prediction: within-person recovery slopes should explain delirium burden and domain-specific cognitive change better than a single preoperative or postoperative scan.4 Optional coupling prediction: spatially resolved SC–FC deviation from an age-appropriate hierarchy should predict recovery more accurately than global structural or functional metrics alone.5 Phenotype prediction: attention and perceptual instability should relate more strongly to thalamic, salience, and feedback measures; memory decline should additionally depend on hippocampal–default-mode and encoding-related changes.6 Mediation prediction: an intervention that reduces POD or cognitive decline through the proposed mechanism should measurably alter the predicted network trajectory, and mediation should remain after exposure and baseline vulnerability are modeled.7 Specificity prediction: network changes attributable only to residual drug level, motion, or vascular BOLD effects should not persist after those factors are addressed or reproduce in EEG and behavior.

1 Interaction prediction: baseline sensory function and network reserve should modify the association between perioperative exposure and cognitive outcome. Failure to detect the prespecified interaction in a sufficiently powered study would weaken this prediction. Additive effects would still be compatible with broader vulnerability models.

2 Hierarchy prediction: transmodal and feedback interactions should show greater state sensitivity, while persistent symptoms during POD should involve impaired reintegration across sensory, salience–attention, and association levels rather than isolated global suppression.

3 Trajectory prediction: within-person recovery slopes should explain delirium burden and domain-specific cognitive change better than a single preoperative or postoperative scan.

4 Optional coupling prediction: spatially resolved SC–FC deviation from an age-appropriate hierarchy should predict recovery more accurately than global structural or functional metrics alone.

5 Phenotype prediction: attention and perceptual instability should relate more strongly to thalamic, salience, and feedback measures; memory decline should additionally depend on hippocampal–default-mode and encoding-related changes.

6 Mediation prediction: an intervention that reduces POD or cognitive decline through the proposed mechanism should measurably alter the predicted network trajectory, and mediation should remain after exposure and baseline vulnerability are modeled.

7 Specificity prediction: network changes attributable only to residual drug level, motion, or vascular BOLD effects should not persist after those factors are addressed or reproduce in EEG and behavior.

Falsifiable predictions and study designs for the proposed model.

A useful model must specify what result would weaken it, not only what result would appear supportive. A negative result can weaken a prediction only if the study has reliable measurements, appropriate timing, sufficient exposure contrast, and adequate statistical precision. Statistical nonsignificance alone is insufficient.

Failure of SC–FC coupling to add out-of-sample value beyond age, cognition, frailty, sensory status, and conventional MRI would refute its proposed biomarker utility even if the broader interface concept remains viable. Likewise, if sensory measures do not modify network–outcome relationships, the model should be narrowed to a more general hierarchy-of-integration account.

The framework should not be mistaken for a recommendation to obtain clinical fMRI in routine perioperative care. The studies reviewed here have not established a network metric with adequate validation and clinical utility for diagnosing or predicting PND in individual patients. Its immediate value is to organize proven and low-risk clinical practices, identify potentially modifiable exposures, and improve the design of mechanistic trials.

Validated delirium-risk assessment, baseline cognitive and functional screening, repeated postoperative delirium surveillance, medication review, adequate analgesia, avoidance of unnecessary deep sedation, early mobility, hydration, sleep support, and timely return of glasses and hearing aids are justified by clinical evidence and consensus recommendations rather than by imaging theory alone (; ). Multicomponent prevention is more consistent with the multifactorial nature of delirium than any single drug or monitor.

The sensory component is practical. Clinicians should document hearing and vision, ensure aids are labeled and available, communicate face-to-face with adequate lighting, reduce avoidable noise at night, provide clear orientation cues, and avoid both deprivation and overload. These actions have favorable risk–benefit profiles even before their neural mediators are established. They should be personalized: a familiar voice may orient one patient, while repeated stimulation may distress another. HELP combines sensory aids, orientation, sleep, and mobility measures (). Within the proposed model, these components could support input fidelity, contextual updating, and arousal and attention. This remains a mechanistic hypothesis, because clinical benefit from the bundle does not establish mediation through a specific neural pathway.

Randomized comparisons do not support a universal claim that regional or neuraxial anesthesia prevents delirium better than general anesthesia. RAGA found no significant reduction in delirium with regional anesthesia without sedation compared with general anesthesia for hip-fracture surgery (). REGAIN likewise found no superiority of spinal over general anesthesia for major functional outcomes and did not establish a broad delirium advantage (). These trials address clinical strategies, not identical drug-free contrasts; sedation, conversion, surgical context, pain, and postoperative care still matter.

Several interventions are mechanistically attractive: age-adjusted EEG guidance; avoidance of prolonged suppression; individualized blood-pressure management; dexmedetomidine in selected contexts; opioid-sparing analgesia; perioperative sleep and circadian protocols; cognitive or sensory prehabilitation; and post-anesthetic network-targeted stimulation. Trials of cognitive prehabilitation remain promising but heterogeneous (), and combined pharmacological regimens such as dexmedetomidine plus acetaminophen require confirmation across procedures and populations (). No intervention should be described as restoring SC–FC coupling until that mediator has been measured prospectively.

converts the research agenda into a longitudinal core-versus-enhanced acquisition framework spanning baseline, anesthetic exposure, early recovery, the delirium-risk window, and longer-term cognition.

A definitive study should enroll a sufficiently large, representative cohort before major surgery, retain patients with common vulnerability rather than excluding them, and include a non-surgical or minimally exposed comparator when feasible. Imaging and behavioral measurements should be anchored to mechanistically meaningful phases:
Baseline, sufficiently before premedication to measure reserve, sensory function, cognition, sleep, pain, frailty, mood, and vascular burden;Intraoperative, with raw EEG, anesthetic concentrations, analgesia, blood pressure, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature, and major events;Early recovery, using bedside EEG and structured delirium assessment when MRI is often infeasible;Early postoperative imaging, after documenting residual sedative and physiological state;Intermediate recovery at approximately 1–3 months, when delayed recovery and postoperative neurocognitive disorder can be distinguished;Longer follow-up at 6–12 months for persistent function, quality of life, and neurodegenerative trajectories.

Baseline, sufficiently before premedication to measure reserve, sensory function, cognition, sleep, pain, frailty, mood, and vascular burden;

Intraoperative, with raw EEG, anesthetic concentrations, analgesia, blood pressure, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature, and major events;

Early recovery, using bedside EEG and structured delirium assessment when MRI is often infeasible;

Early postoperative imaging, after documenting residual sedative and physiological state;

Intermediate recovery at approximately 1–3 months, when delayed recovery and postoperative neurocognitive disorder can be distinguished;

Longer follow-up at 6–12 months for persistent function, quality of life, and neurodegenerative trajectories.

Repeated measurements before surgery in a subset would quantify test–retest reliability and ordinary temporal variation.

The clinical battery should combine daily delirium assessment with attention, processing speed, executive control, working memory, and episodic-memory measures. Alternate forms and reliable-change methods should address practice effects.

Sensory phenotyping should include hearing thresholds or speech-in-noise performance, visual acuity and contrast where practical, aid use, pain, interoceptive symptoms, vestibular or proprioceptive problems when relevant, and an audit of the postoperative sensory environment. These variables should be tested as effect modifiers, not only adjusted away as nuisance covariates.

A pragmatic MRI core comprises T1-weighted anatomy, FLAIR, diffusion MRI, resting-state fMRI, and arterial spin labeling where feasible. Susceptibility-sensitive and diffusion-weighted sequences can detect microbleeds and acute lesions. A short auditory or multisensory task can probe encoding and feedback, while simultaneous or closely paired EEG links oscillatory routing to macroscale topology. Blood sampling should target prespecified inflammatory and neuronal-injury pathways at aligned times.

Consensus neuroimaging reporting recommendations should guide acquisition and analysis (). fMRIPrep or an equivalently transparent pipeline can improve reproducibility but does not remove the need to justify denoising choices (). Scanner and site effects require prospective calibration, phantoms, traveling subjects where feasible, and harmonization that preserves biological variation ().

Primary endpoints should be few, reliable, and mechanistically ordered. A strong set might include: preoperative segregation across sensory, salience–attention, control, and default-mode systems; thalamocortical gradient geometry; early postoperative EEG feedback or complexity; and the slope of recovery toward an age-appropriate reference. Secondary analyses can examine regional SC–FC coupling, dynamic states, network control, and agent-specific signatures.

Longitudinal mixed-effects or latent-growth models should estimate within-person trajectories. Causal diagrams should be specified before covariate selection because adjusting for post-exposure mediators can create bias. Site, scanner, surgery, and anesthetic strategy require hierarchical modeling rather than simple pooling.

Prediction is a separate objective. Imaging models should be compared with a strong clinical baseline, use nested cross-validation, report calibration and decision-curve utility, and undergo temporal and external validation. Large neuroimaging samples show that small studies can overestimate brain–behavior associations ().

The highest-value trials will randomize a modifiable strategy and measure the proposed neural mediator. Factorial or adaptive designs can separate components, while mediation analysis can test whether improved outcome occurs through the predicted network path.

An anesthetic-strategy trial should not rely on nominal technique labels. It should quantify actual drug concentrations, EEG state, nociceptive and hemodynamic exposure, emergence dynamics, and postoperative care.

If patients at higher POD risk are less able to tolerate MRI or testing, analyzing only complete cases can introduce selection bias. Protocols should predefine abbreviated bedside assessments, portable EEG or fNIRS, proxy functional outcomes, reasons for missingness, and inverse-probability or joint modeling where appropriate. Scan-completion flow diagrams should compare included and excluded participants by baseline risk and delirium severity. For participants unable to undergo MRI, brief bedside tests of attention and orientation, validated delirium assessment, and portable EEG or fNIRS may allow continued longitudinal follow-up. fNIRS measures superficial cortical hemodynamics and can be affected by systemic physiology (), so it can supplement but cannot replace whole-brain MRI.

Older adults with sensory impairment, limited education, multiple languages, frailty, or baseline cognitive impairment should not be systematically excluded. Accessible task instructions, sensory correction, culturally appropriate tests, and capacity/consent procedures are scientific necessities, not only ethical accommodations.

provides a minimum reporting and quality-control checklist for perioperative connectomics.

Minimum reporting and quality-control checklist for perioperative connectomics.

The checklist is intended for protocols, preregistration, reporting, and peer review. ALFF, amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations; APOE4, apolipoprotein E ε4 allele; ASL, arterial spin labeling; BBB, blood–brain barrier; BIS, Bispectral Index; BOLD, blood oxygen level-dependent; BP, blood pressure; CBF, cerebral blood flow; CNS, central nervous system; CO2, carbon dioxide; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; DAG, directed acyclic graph; DAN, dorsal attention network; DCM, dynamic causal modeling; dMRI, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging; DMN, default-mode network; DNR, delayed neurocognitive recovery; DTI, diffusion tensor imaging; DWI, diffusion-weighted imaging; EEG, electroencephalography; FA, fractional anisotropy; FC, functional connectivity; FDR, false discovery rate; FLAIR, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; fMRI, functional magnetic resonance imaging; fNIRS, functional near-infrared spectroscopy; HbO, oxygenated hemoglobin; HbR, deoxygenated hemoglobin; MD, mean diffusivity; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; NCD, neurocognitive disorder; NfL, neurofilament light; O2, oxygen; OR, operating room; PMID, PubMed identifier; PND, perioperative neurocognitive disorder; POCD, postoperative cognitive dysfunction (legacy, source-defined term); POD, postoperative delirium; QC, quality control; rs-fMRI, resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging; SC–FC, structural–functional connectivity; SNc, substantia nigra pars compacta; SNR, signal-to-noise ratio; T1, longitudinal relaxation time (T1-weighted sequence); TMT-B, Trail Making Test Part B; VAN, ventral attention network; VTA, ventral tegmental area; WMH, white-matter hyperintensity.

BALANCED, Balanced Anaesthesia Study; BioCog, Biomarker Development for Postoperative Cognitive Impairment in the Elderly; ENGAGES, Electroencephalography Guidance of Anesthesia to Alleviate Geriatric Syndromes; IPOD-B3, Interventions for Postoperative Delirium: Biomarker-3; RAGA, regional anesthesia versus general anesthesia trial; REGAIN, Regional versus General Anesthesia for Promoting Independence after Hip Fracture; SAGES, Successful Aging after Elective Surgery.

Head motion can generate distance-dependent connectivity artifacts and correlate with age, cognition, pain, and delirium (; ). Frame censoring, motion models, component-based noise correction, and sensitivity analyses are mandatory, but aggressive denoising can also remove neural signal. Studies should report retained frames, group differences in motion, exclusion thresholds, and whether findings survive matched-motion analyses.

Respiration, carbon dioxide, heart rate, blood pressure, and vascular reactivity affect BOLD signals and can differ systematically after surgery. Physiological recording should be integrated whenever possible. Global-signal regression, scrubbing, and filter choices should be reported because they alter correlation structure and anticorrelations (). Awake eyes-open or eyes-closed state, drowsiness, residual sedatives, caffeine, analgesics, and time of day should also be documented.

Network results depend on parcellation and connectivity-estimation choices (). A primary atlas should be prespecified and key effects tested in at least one alternative parcellation. Reliability should be quantified for the actual scan duration and population. Thousands of edge-wise tests invite selective reporting; network-level hypotheses, permutation testing, false-discovery control, and replication are preferable to unstructured lists of regional findings.

SC–FC analyses require additional transparency: diffusion model and tractography algorithm; streamline weighting; handling of absent edges; transform applied to structural values; functional-connectivity measure; regional versus edge-wise coupling; and treatment of Euclidean distance. Different methods answer different questions. Results should never be summarized as “structure and function became uncoupled” without specifying scale, region, direction, and reference.

Vascular physiology can influence BOLD connectivity (). We recommend multimodal EEG–fMRI, perfusion measures, physiological covariates, and agent-specific controls to assess the contribution of vascular effects. Postoperative scans should record all centrally active medications and their timing. A correlation acquired during active delirium cannot be assumed to represent the same mechanism as a preoperative predictor or a three-month residual change.

Preregistration should distinguish confirmatory from exploratory endpoints. Acquisition parameters, preprocessing code, quality-control criteria, parcellations, and statistical models should be shared where consent and governance permit. Site-stratified results and uncertainty intervals matter more than a single pooled p value.

The framework proposes explanations for why early sensory responses can be preserved despite impaired cognitive access, why both unimodal and association systems are involved in perioperative studies, and why recovery topology and rate may be more informative than the magnitude of acute suppression. Its specific hypotheses distinguish early sensory encoding from the subsequent use of that information in context, and test whether sensory reserve modifies POD-related network change. Vulnerability, disconnection, and failed recovery are established concepts. Whether these additional measurements improve the explanation of POD remains unproven.

Global slowing, whole-brain connectivity loss, or elevated cytokines alone do not uniquely support a sensory–cognitive account. The model earns explanatory value only if sensory measures and hierarchical network metrics add reproducible information beyond age, frailty, baseline cognition, conventional MRI burden, achieved anesthetic exposure, and perioperative physiology. Competing accounts include strategic vascular injury, diffuse neuroimmune or neuromodulatory failure without privileged sensory involvement, residual drug effect, and latent neurodegeneration unmasked by surgery. These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and may define biologically distinct subgroups. A useful future analysis should therefore compare models rather than enter all candidate variables into one undifferentiated predictor set.

Direct sensory-specific perioperative evidence is still narrow: the most compelling observations come from auditory prediction-error EEG and a small number of visual-network studies (; ), whereas much of the proposed hierarchy is extrapolated from anesthesia, consciousness, aging, or non-surgical neuroscience. Perioperative cohorts are generally modest, phenotype definitions and imaging time points vary, active-delirium MRI is rare, postoperative attrition is informative, and repeated analyses of the same cohorts can create an impression of replication. Functional-connectivity direction is inconsistent across studies, and BOLD findings remain vulnerable to motion, arousal, medication, carbon dioxide, and neurovascular effects. Anesthesia-state evidence often derives from younger volunteers and controlled exposures that do not reproduce the older surgical brain. Animal models clarify immune pathways but cannot reproduce the human cognitive phenotype.

This critical narrative synthesis was not protocol-registered and did not use duplicate screening, formal risk-of-bias scoring, or meta-analysis. Selection and interpretive bias therefore remain possible despite deliberate inclusion of null and discordant findings. These hypotheses need prospective testing to distinguish the proposed mechanisms. The review does not validate an imaging biomarker or support routine clinical fMRI.

POD is unlikely to arise from a single region, molecule, or anesthetic exposure. The sensory–cognitive interface offers a proposed systems-level account of how afferent information is relayed, integrated, weighted, and used in context to support attention, memory, and executive control.

Direct human studies demonstrate preoperative dysconnectivity, altered sensory and association-network organization, abnormal slow-wave and feedback dynamics, and incomplete recovery after POD (; ; ; ), but they do not establish one causal pathway. Support for the framework requires replicated, out-of-sample evidence that sensory phenotypes, hierarchical metrics, and within-person trajectories add value beyond conventional vulnerability and competing mechanisms. It also requires evidence that an intervention changes both the predicted mediator and cognition. Otherwise, the framework should be narrowed. Extension to delayed neurocognitive recovery or postoperative neurocognitive disorder requires separate outcome-specific evidence.

neuroscience.title: Compositional Brain Age Profiles Reveal Disease-Related Neuroimaging Patterns Beyond the Brain Age Gap
neuroscience.abstract: Brain age models estimate how old a person’s brain appears from magnetic resonance imaging, but the usual output is a single number that cannot indicate which imaging patterns produced the estimate. We developed a method that uses thousands of measurements from several brain imaging modalities and organizes them into multiple learned patterns of brain ageing. For each participant, the method produces both an estimated brain age and an individualized profile describing the combination of imaging patterns underlying the estimate. In 37,894 UK Biobank participants, the model predicted age accurately and produced stable imaging pattern organization. Importantly, people with almost identical overall brain age differences could still have very different composition profiles. These profiles also helped to distinguish between selected neurological disease groups even after participants were matched by age and overall brain age difference. The results suggest that brain ageing may be better understood not only by asking how much a brain differs from its expected age but also by examining the combination of imaging patterns associated with this difference.
neuroscience.text:
Biological age measures aim to characterize variation in ageing that is not captured by chronological age alone. In neuroimaging, brain age models operationalize this concept by predicting the chronological age from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived measurements and comparing the predicted age with the observed age [,]. The resulting brain age gap (BAG) is typically interpreted as the extent to which an individual’s brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age [,]. Larger positive BAG values, reflecting accelerated brain ageing, have been associated with neurological and psychiatric disorders, cognitive decline, and adverse health outcomes [,,]. These associations have established the BAG as an increasingly used marker for studying age-related brain health and disease vulnerability [,].

Although the BAG provides a concise summary of brain age deviation, it does not retain the compositional information encoded in the underlying high-dimensional imaging features. A single BAG value cannot reflect whether similar brain age deviations reflect comparable or distinct underlying neuroimaging patterns. This distinction is important because brain ageing is expressed through heterogeneous patterns across cortical, subcortical, white matter, functional connectivity, and global MRI phenotypes, which may contribute differently to the same overall brain age deviation [,].

Recent multimodal brain age studies have shown that structural, diffusion, and functional MRI provide complementary information for characterizing brain ageing and can support modality-specific or integrated brain age estimates [,,,]. Regional and explainable brain age approaches have further localized age-related deviations and identified anatomical features contributing to individual predictions [,,]. In parallel, data-driven studies have identified multiple structural and functional ageing patterns and assigned individuals scores along distinct ageing-related dimensions [,,]. Together, these studies indicate that brain ageing is multidimensional and can be characterized across modalities, regions, and distributed ageing patterns.

Nevertheless, existing multimodal, regional, and dimensional approaches typically characterize this heterogeneity through modality- or region-specific estimates, post hoc explanations of scalar predictions, or separate ageing dimensions. Less explored is whether multiple imaging patterns can be jointly learned within a unified brain age model and expressed as participant-specific contributions that together form an interpretable composition of the predicted brain age.

Here, we developed a semantic-guided mixture-of-experts framework for individualized brain age composition profiling using multimodal imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs). The framework uses semantic information associated with the IDPs to organize heterogeneous imaging phenotypes across multiple specialized experts, encouraging specialized experts to capture distinct ageing-related imaging patterns. The expert-specific representations are then integrated to estimate the brain age and jointly form an individualized brain age composition profile that characterizes their relative contributions to the prediction.

We analyzed multimodal IDPs from UK Biobank MRI data. Cohort construction and analysis roles are summarized in A. IDPs were generated by the standardized UK Biobank image processing pipeline, including modality-specific preprocessing, registration, anatomical alignment, segmentation, and phenotype extraction []. They covered structural MRI, diffusion MRI, resting-state and task-based functional MRI, susceptibility-weighted imaging, and T2-FLAIR imaging. Each IDP was accompanied by metadata describing its anatomical and imaging context. Whole-brain or hemispheric summary measures were designated as global IDPs; the remaining regional and distributed measures were designated as local IDPs.

The model development reference cohort included participants with no qualifying records for prespecified neurological or psychiatric conditions at or before MRI or during the available follow-up. Exclusions were based on ICD-10 definitions and UK Biobank disease records and covered dementia; cerebrovascular disease; epilepsy; migraine and other headache syndromes; and selected inflammatory, degenerative, and demyelinating neurological disorders, as well as substance-related, psychotic, and mood disorders. Other diseases did not preclude eligibility. The exclusion criteria and ICD-10 code ranges are listed in  (). The reference cohort was randomly divided into training, validation, and test sets, whereas participants with prevalent or incident qualifying diagnoses were reserved for clinical evaluation.

Disease timing was assigned separately for each disease using the first qualifying record relative to MRI (B). Prevalent disease was recorded at or before MRI. Near-term incident disease was first recorded >0 to ≤2 years after MRI; late incident disease was first recorded >2 years after MRI. Future-any incident disease combined both incident categories within the available follow-up. Participants without a qualifying record were not cases for that disease. Because participants could have multiple diseases, the same participant could be assigned to different temporal categories for different diseases. Follow-up ended at the earliest point among death, recorded loss to follow-up, or administrative censoring.

Participants were excluded if more than 20% of their IDPs were missing. Preprocessing parameters were estimated from the brain age training set only and applied unchanged to the validation, test, and clinical evaluation cohorts. For each IDP, missing values were temporarily imputed with the median of that IDP calculated from the training set. The temporarily imputed training data were then used to estimate feature-wise means and standard deviations for z-score standardization. After standardization, originally missing entries were reset to zero, while their missing status was retained as a separate binary indicator.

The framework used multimodal IDPs to predict brain age while retaining expert-specific representations for each participant (). Each participant-specific IDP representation combined an encoded measurement with a metadata-derived semantic embedding of that IDP. Global IDPs were processed by an always-active global expert, whereas local IDPs were sparsely assigned to local experts according to metadata-guided routing. The resulting global and local expert representations formed a participant-specific composition profile, which was used by the prediction head to estimate brain age.

For a given participant, xi denotes the standardized value of IDP i, and δi denotes its missingness indicator, with δi=1 for missing values and δi=0 for observed values. A shared value encoder mapped (xi, δi) to a value embedding eival. The metadata describing each IDP were encoded using a frozen BioLORD [] encoder to obtain a pretrained semantic embedding eimeta. A trainable metadata encoder used a shared backbone and separate projections to produce e˜imeta for value fusion and ri for expert routing. The fusion embedding matched the dimension of the value embedding, allowing element-wise addition:(1)zi=eival+e˜imeta

The resulting IDP embedding combined participant-specific measurements with semantic information shared across participants. The metadata encoder was trained jointly with the brain age model, while the BioLORD embeddings remained fixed.

Before brain age training, the pretrained BioLORD metadata embeddings of local IDPs were clustered using k-means to initialize the IDP-to-expert assignments. We denote the number of local routed experts by K. The K clusters defined the initial assignments to the corresponding local experts. This initialization provided a semantic starting point for routing, grouping related imaging phenotypes while allowing their assignments to be refined during model optimization. Global IDPs were excluded from clustering and processed by the global expert.

During brain age training, the router mapped the metadata-derived representation ri of each local IDP i to routing scores over the K routed experts,(2)si=R(ri),si∈RK,
