with αik=0 for experts not selected for IDP i.

The set of IDPs assigned to routed expert k was therefore(5)Ik={i∣k∈Ti}.

For a given participant, each routed expert aggregated the corresponding IDP representations and generated a scalar expert-specific representation,(6)hk=Ek[Agg{αikzi:i∈Ik}],k=1,…,K.Here, zi is the IDP embedding defined above, Agg(·) denotes aggregation over the routed IDPs, and Ek(·) denotes the transformation of local expert k, which produces the scalar output hk. The original missingness mask was applied during aggregation so that missing IDP measurements did not contribute to the corresponding expert representation. Because an IDP could be routed to more than one expert, the resulting expert-specific IDP subsets could partially overlap.

Let G denote the set of global IDPs defined above. For a given participant, the scalar global representation was obtained as(7)hg=Eg[Agg{zi:i∈G}].Here, Agg(·) denotes aggregation over the global IDPs, and Eg(·) denotes the global expert transformation producing the scalar output hg. The global representation was concatenated with the K local expert-specific representations to form the brain age composition profile,(8)p=hg,h1,…,hK,p∈RK+1.With K=10 local experts and one global expert, the profile contained 11 scalar components.

The composition profile p was passed to a multilayer perceptron (MLP) prediction head to estimate the brain age, expressed in years:(9)y^=MLP(p)

On the original age scale, the age prediction objective was the mean squared error between the predicted brain age and chronological age,(10)Lage=1N∑n=1Ny^n−yn2.Here, N denotes the number of training participants. For participant n, y^n is the predicted brain age and yn is the chronological age at MRI, both expressed in years. The IDP encoder, routed experts, metadata-conditioned router, global expert, and prediction head were optimized jointly during brain age training.

Brain age prediction performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), expressed in years. The number of local experts was selected by grid search over K=6–12. We selected K=10 because it achieved the lowest validation MAE, and we fixed this configuration before evaluation on the test set. Models were trained using three random seeds (2026, 42, and 3407), with identical cohort splits across seeds. The test set was used for final brain age prediction evaluation, and the held-out clinical evaluation cohort was used for downstream disease analyses. Neither was used for brain age model selection.

The raw BAG was the difference between the predicted brain age and chronological age, both expressed in years:(11)BAGnraw=y^n−yn.

The raw BAG can retain a systematic age dependence arising from prediction bias. We regressed it on chronological age in the training reference cohort Ctrain. The fitted intercept γ^0,train and slope γ^1,train were used to remove the linear age trend: (12)BAGncorrected=BAGnraw−γ^0,train+γ^1,trainyn.

The corrected BAG remains in years and measures the deviation from the training cohort’s fitted age-specific expectation.

We then standardized the corrected BAG by its training-reference standard deviation (SD):(13)BAGnstandardized=BAGncorrectedSDBAG,train.Here, SDBAG,train is the SD of the corrected BAG in the training reference cohort. The standardized BAG is dimensionless; a value of +1 indicates a positive deviation of one training reference SD. All subsequent analyses used this standardized scale.

The correction parameters and residual SD were estimated separately for each model seed using the training reference cohort only. They were applied unchanged to the validation, test, and clinical evaluation cohorts.

Expert organization was characterized by the number and phenotype composition of assigned IDPs. Agreement between expert assignments across model seeds was quantified using the adjusted Rand index (ARI) and normalized mutual information (NMI).

Associations between the standardized BAG and each expert representation were summarized using the coefficient of determination (R2). Participants were sorted by standardized BAG and grouped into non-overlapping adjacent pairs. For each pair, we calculated the absolute standardized BAG difference and the Euclidean distance between the complete 11-dimensional composition profiles. Spearman’s correlation assessed the association between these two quantities.

A separate linear regression compared cases with reference-cohort participants for each disease and temporal phase. Disease status was coded as Dn=1 for cases and Dn=0 for reference participants:(14)BAGnstandardized=β0+β1Dn+βcov⊤cn+εn.The covariate vector cn contained MRI age yn, sex, and imaging center; εn denotes the residual. The fitted coefficient β^1 quantifies the adjusted mean case–reference difference in training-residual SD units. Positive coefficients indicate a higher standardized BAG in cases than in reference-cohort participants.

Association models were fitted separately for each brain age model seed. Disease coefficient P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Consistent significance required an FDR-adjusted P<0.05 in all three seeds. Effect estimates were summarized across seeds.

For each disease contrast, participants meeting exactly one of the two target disease definitions were included. Other diagnoses did not preclude inclusion.

All classifiers used L2-regularized logistic regression. The baseline included the MRI age, standardized BAG, sex, and imaging center. For each representation in , a separate augmented classifier was fitted by adding the representation to the baseline covariates. These representations included PCA-11, PCA-22, Bottleneck-11, Random-MoE-11, the complete 11-dimensional composition profile p, and Profile + PCA-11. Within each contrast, AUCs were evaluated using the same participants and repeated five-fold outer cross-validation splits. For each classifier, the inverse regularization strength C was selected by inner cross-validation within each outer training fold. All classifiers used the same candidate set, C∈{10−3,10−2,10−1,1,10,100}, and selection procedure.

Control representations were constructed using the training reference cohort and frozen before clinical evaluation. PCA-11 and PCA-22 comprised the first 11 and 22 principal components of the IDP data, respectively, and served as unsupervised dimensionality reduction controls. Bottleneck-11 used an 11-dimensional age-supervised representation learned without expert decomposition. Random-MoE-11 retained the expert architecture, routing constraints, age prediction objective, and training budget of the proposed model but randomized the organization of IDPs across experts. The proposed representation comprised the complete 11-dimensional global and local expert profile. Profile + PCA-11 concatenated this profile with PCA-11, yielding 22 features. Classifier-specific preprocessing and regularization selection were performed within the corresponding training folds.

A matched sensitivity analysis further assessed whether the profile retained discriminative information among participants with similar standardized BAGs. Participants were matched one-to-one by MRI age and standardized BAG within sex and imaging center strata. Only the baseline and baseline-plus-profile classifiers were evaluated. All other procedures followed the preceding section, with each matched pair kept in the same validation fold.

Within this matched analysis, matched-pair bootstrap resampling provided 95% confidence intervals for profile-versus-baseline AUC differences separately for each brain age model seed. Identical resamples were used for both classifiers. Evidence was classified as robust when the interval lay above zero in all three seeds. A positive mean gain with an interval including zero in at least one seed was classified as indicative.

Of 38,544 participants with MRI, 37,894 passed IDP quality control and 650 were excluded ( and ). The reference cohort comprised 24,004 participants and was divided into training (n=17,341), validation (n=3062), and test (n=3601) sets. The clinical evaluation cohort included 13,890 participants with prevalent or incident qualifying diagnoses. These participants were reserved for downstream disease analyses. The mean age was similar across the three reference cohort splits (63.8–63.9 years) and was 64.3 years in the clinical evaluation cohort. Women comprised approximately 51% of each reference cohort split and 57.2% of the clinical evaluation cohort.

Brain age prediction performance was similar across the three random seeds. Validation MAE ranged from 2.682 to 2.732 years, and test MAE ranged from 2.784 to 2.811 years. Across the three seeds, the test root mean squared error (RMSE) ranged from 3.497 to 3.547 years, and R2 ranged from 0.783 to 0.789 on the same 3601 reference test participants. These estimates describe prediction within the UK Biobank reference cohort. A single-center training and unseen-center evaluation analysis is reported in .

The global expert processed 26 whole-brain or hemispheric IDPs, and ten local routed experts processed the remaining 3604 IDPs (A,B). Structural groups differed in their emphasis on cortical area and volume, cortical thickness, regional volume and intensity, and cortical grey–white contrast. Several also distinguished between left- and right-hemisphere measurements. White matter groups mainly contained tract microstructure measures, while functional groups included connectivity and node amplitude phenotypes. Local group sizes ranged from 70 to 1539 IDPs; the largest group was dominated by resting-state functional connectivity. The resulting groups therefore differed in both measurement type and size.

Expert assignments were highly stable across the three model seeds with identical participants and semantic initialization (C). The pairwise ARI ranged from 0.993 to 0.996, and the NMI ranged from 0.970 to 0.979.

Associations with the standardized BAG varied in strength across the expert representations (D). The expert-wise R2 ranged from 0.1% to 31.5%, with an R2 of 17.6% for the global representation. In this analysis, the standardized BAG accounted for only part of the variation in each expert representation.

Participants with nearly identical standardized BAGs nevertheless had different composition profiles (E,F). Sorting participants by standardized BAG yielded 8745 non-overlapping adjacent pairs with a median absolute BAG difference of 0.00017 SD. Their complete profiles had a median Euclidean distance of 4.25 (interquartile range, 3.58–5.00). Within these BAG-matched pairs, no association was detected between the profile distance and the residual difference in the standardized BAG (Spearman’s ρ=0.003, p=0.790). F shows two representative high-distance pairs with distinct global and local expert output patterns. These examples illustrate the variation across expert outputs at a similar level of overall brain age deviation.

The standardized BAG was higher in several prevalent neurological and psychiatric disease groups than in the reference cohort (). The mean adjusted differences across the three model seeds were largest for multiple sclerosis (1.218 training-residual SD units). Other prominent differences were observed for other demyelinating disease (0.773), schizophrenia/psychosis (0.733), and bipolar disorder (0.636). These four associations were FDR-significant in all three seeds. Smaller positive differences were observed for stroke (0.337), epilepsy (0.260), and depressive disorder (0.122), which were also FDR-significant in all seeds. Prevalent migraine showed a small adjusted difference (0.010 SD units) that was not FDR-significant in any seed.

Positive associations were also observed for diagnoses recorded after MRI (future-any incident). The mean adjusted differences across seeds were 0.852 SD units for dementia, 0.678 for Parkinson’s disease, 0.375 for stroke, and 0.359 for substance use disorder. All four associations were FDR-significant in all three seeds. The Parkinson’s disease estimate warrants caution because the group included only 47 cases.

Phase-specific analyses showed positive associations for stroke and substance use disorder in both the near-term and late incident groups (C). For stroke, the mean adjusted differences were 0.355 and 0.382 SD units in the near-term and late incident groups, respectively. The corresponding estimates for substance use disorder were 0.323 and 0.379 SD units. All four associations were FDR-significant in all three seeds. Late incident dementia also showed a positive association (0.886 SD units; 77 cases), being FDR-significant in all three seeds. These phase-specific estimates describe differences between separate case groups and the reference cohort. Other disease-by-phase comparisons were non-significant.

Adding the composition profile increased the AUC in all four disease contrasts relative to the baseline containing the standardized BAG and demographic covariates (). The largest gain occurred for future-any dementia versus stroke, where the AUC increased from 0.613 to 0.673 (+0.060). For prevalent multiple sclerosis versus migraine, the AUC increased from 0.709 to 0.759 (+0.050). Smaller gains were observed for prevalent multiple sclerosis versus epilepsy (+0.035) and epilepsy versus migraine (+0.018). These comparisons support additional disease-discriminative information in the profile beyond the baseline covariates.

The profile had higher AUCs than all three 11-dimensional controls in every contrast. Its advantage over PCA-11 ranged from 0.010 to 0.020, while Bottleneck-11 remained close to the baseline performance. The profile also had higher AUCs than PCA-22 in three contrasts. In future-any dementia versus stroke, however, PCA-22 achieved a slightly higher AUC than the profile (0.676 versus 0.673). Thus, the profile’s advantage over alternative representations varied across disease contrasts, despite its consistently higher point estimates than the equal-dimensional controls.

PCA-11 captured the dominant variation in the imaging features without age supervision, whereas the composition profile was learned through the brain age prediction objective. Combining PCA-11 with the composition profile yielded the highest AUC across all four disease contrasts, with values ranging from 0.669 to 0.787. Compared with the profile alone, the combined representation increased the AUC by 0.018–0.042. It also outperformed PCA-22, which matched the combined representation in dimensionality, by 0.024–0.062. These results indicate that the improvement was not explained by increased dimensionality alone and that the two representations captured partly non-overlapping information relevant to disease discrimination.

We next assessed whether the profile gains persisted when the disease groups were restricted to participants with a similar MRI age and standardized BAG. After matching, the maximum absolute standardized mean difference in these variables was 0.036 across the four contrasts and three seeds (D). The baseline AUCs ranged from 0.497 to 0.506, indicating little discrimination from the balanced scalar covariates.

Adding the profile increased the mean AUC in all four matched contrasts ( and A,B). The largest gain occurred for prevalent multiple sclerosis versus migraine, with the AUC increasing from 0.501 to 0.665 (+0.163). For prevalent epilepsy versus migraine, the AUC increased from 0.500 to 0.590 (+0.090). Positive gains were also observed for multiple sclerosis versus epilepsy (+0.104) and future-any dementia versus stroke (+0.099). These results supported the retained disease-discriminative information among participants with similar overall brain age deviations.

Matched-pair bootstrap analyses assessed support for these gains across model seeds (C). Multiple sclerosis versus migraine and epilepsy versus migraine met the robustness criterion, with 95% intervals above zero in all three seeds. Multiple sclerosis versus epilepsy and future-any dementia versus stroke were classified as indicative, with intervals including zero in at least one seed. The latter contrasts contained only 47–53 matched pairs per seed and had less consistent bootstrap support. Because seed-specific matching retained different participant sets, the variation could reflect both model initialization and sample selection.

The complete matched disease pair matrices showed that added discrimination was selective (). Other contrasts had positive, near-zero, or negative mean gains, and some could not be estimated. The four highlighted comparisons therefore illustrated retained profile information in selected disease contrasts, while the broader results bounded its applicability across diseases.

This study showed that brain age composition profiles captured disease-related imaging differences beyond the standardized BAG. The semantic-guided mixture-of-experts model produced both an age estimate and a profile of its global and local expert outputs. Participants with a similar standardized BAG could have different profiles, and adding the profile improved discrimination in the four disease contrasts. The profile thus provides additional information about the imaging patterns associated with an overall brain age estimate.

The standardized BAG provides a single measure of the deviation between the predicted brain age and chronological age after age bias correction. Its broad disease associations were consistent with earlier brain age studies [,,]. However, a single BAG value does not specify which imaging characteristics underlie the deviation. Previous studies have addressed this heterogeneity through modality-specific and subsystem-level age estimates [,], as well as regional estimates and neuroanatomical ageing dimensions [,]. Our framework extends this approach by learning global and local expert outputs jointly within an age prediction model. Retaining these outputs makes it possible to compare imaging patterns among participants with similar overall brain age deviations.

The control comparisons suggest that adding more dimensions alone does not explain the profile’s gains (). The profile had higher AUC point estimates than PCA-11, Bottleneck-11, and Random-MoE-11 in all four contrasts, although each representation contained 11 features. These controls assessed different aspects of the representation: general imaging variation, age prediction without expert decomposition, and expert grouping without semantic guidance. Metadata on modality, anatomy, and phenotype guided the proposed expert grouping, which was stable across model seeds. The results support the value of this organization under the tested conditions. The profile was not uniformly superior: PCA-22 slightly exceeded it for dementia versus stroke. The reported AUC rankings also do not establish statistically significant differences between representations.

Combining the profile with PCA-11 improved discrimination further. PCA captures the dominant variation in the imaging features without using age labels, whereas the profile is learned through age prediction. Neither representation was trained using disease labels. Their combination achieved the highest AUC in all four contrasts and exceeded PCA-22, which had the same total dimensionality. This pattern suggests that the profile and PCA retain complementary information relevant to disease discrimination. The different learning objectives help to explain this complementarity but do not imply that PCA captures only information unrelated to age.

The matched analysis strengthened the evidence for profile information beyond the standardized BAG (). The profile gains persisted when the disease groups had a similar MRI age and standardized BAG, showing that useful imaging differences remained after these variables were balanced. Bootstrap support varied across contrasts, and the broader disease pair analyses showed that the gains were selective. These findings support disease-related imaging differences but do not establish distinct biological ageing mechanisms. The tasks evaluated discrimination between disease groups, so the results cannot establish screening performance or prospective individual risk prediction. Clinical interpretation therefore requires caution, consistent with broader assessments of brain age biomarkers [,].

Several limitations constrain the findings. The evaluation was internal to UK Biobank participants aged 44–83 years, without independent validation in other populations. Recorded diagnoses may miss subclinical disease, and diagnosis dates may differ from biological onset. Comparisons across diagnostic phases therefore do not describe within-person ageing trajectories. Small matched groups and differences in participant selection across seeds limit precision. The profiles also depend on the predefined IDPs, and their relationships with cognitive decline, functional outcomes, and longitudinal brain changes were not directly evaluated.

This study developed a semantic-guided mixture-of-experts framework for individualized brain age composition profiling from multimodal IDPs. In addition to brain age estimation and the standardized BAG, the framework retained a participant-specific representation of the global and expert-specific imaging patterns underlying each prediction. Whereas the standardized BAG summarizes the overall magnitude of brain age deviation, the composition profile captures heterogeneity in the imaging configuration associated with the deviation. These profiles improved disease discrimination beyond the MRI age, standardized BAG, sex, and imaging center in the four highlighted contrasts, with the gains persisting after BAG matching. These findings support brain age composition profiling as a complementary representation for investigating neuroimaging heterogeneity beyond the scalar BAG.

neuroscience.title: Clinical Spectrum, Outcomes, and Factors Associated With Encephalopathy in Children With Influenza‐Associated Neurological Complications: A Retrospective Cohort Study
neuroscience.abstract: This study aims to characterize the clinical spectrum, outcomes, and factors associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy in hospitalized children with influenza‐associated neurological complications.This retrospective cohort study included children younger than 18 years who were hospitalized with laboratory‐confirmed influenza at a tertiary university hospital between 2018 and 2023. We reviewed demographic, clinical, laboratory, neuroimaging, electroencephalographic, cerebrospinal fluid, treatment, and outcome data. Patients with and without encephalopathy were compared, and multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy.Among 3040 hospitalized children with laboratory‐confirmed influenza, 115 (3.8%) developed influenza‐associated neurological complications. The median age was 32 months (interquartile range [IQR], 19–58 months), and 67 (58.3%) were male. Influenza A accounted for 80.0% of infections. Seizures were the presenting neurological manifestation in all patients, with generalized tonic–clonic seizures occurring in 101 (87.8%). Encephalopathy and encephalitis were identified in 15 (13.0%) and 11 (9.6%) patients, respectively. Two patients (1.7%) were diagnosed with acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE). Most children recovered without permanent neurological deficits; however, one patient developed persistent neurological sequelae and two died during hospitalization. In multivariable analysis, focal seizures (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 16.98; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.42–84.27; p = 0.001) and higher lymphocyte counts (aOR, 1.53 per 1000 cells/mm3 increase; 95% CI, 1.11–2.12; p = 0.009) were independently associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy.Seizures predominantly characterized influenza‐associated neurological complications in hospitalized children and generally had favorable short‐term outcomes. However, influenza‐associated encephalopathy was associated with substantially greater clinical severity, including prolonged hospitalization, more frequent pediatric intensive care unit admission, and poorer in‐hospital outcomes. Recognition of focal seizures may help identify children who warrant closer assessment for concurrent encephalopathy and timely neurological evaluation.
neuroscience.text:
Influenza is a major cause of acute respiratory disease during the colder months and remains an important cause of hospitalization among children worldwide. Beyond respiratory illness, influenza virus infection has been associated with a broad spectrum of neurological complications, including Guillain–Barré syndrome, transverse myelitis, encephalitis, and seizures [, ]. Among these, seizures—particularly febrile seizures in young children—represent the most frequently reported neurological manifestation [, ].

Although influenza‐associated neurological complications are uncommon, they may result in significant morbidity, intensive care admission, permanent neurological sequelae, or death. Early recognition of these complications is therefore essential for timely diagnosis, appropriate management, and improved clinical outcomes.

In Türkiye, influenza activity typically extends from October through May, with a single annual epidemic peak. However, data describing the clinical spectrum, frequency, and outcomes of influenza‐associated neurological complications in hospitalized children remain limited. We therefore aimed to evaluate the prevalence, clinical characteristics, outcomes, and factors associated with neurological complications among hospitalized pediatric patients with laboratory‐confirmed influenza.

This retrospective observational study was conducted at Necmettin Erbakan University Faculty of Medicine Hospital, a tertiary referral center in Konya, Türkiye. The study included children aged 1 month to 18 years who were hospitalized with laboratory‐confirmed influenza between October 2018 and May 2023 and presented with neurological manifestations during the course of their illness.

We identified potential cases through the hospital information system using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD‐10) diagnostic codes for influenza (J09–J11), encephalitis and related inflammatory disorders of the central nervous system (G02, G04, and G05), and convulsions (R56 series). We then reviewed medical records individually to confirm eligibility.

We extracted demographic characteristics, underlying medical conditions, clinical manifestations, laboratory findings, neuroimaging and electroencephalographic findings, treatment modalities, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, length of hospital stay, and clinical outcomes retrospectively from electronic medical records using a standardized data collection form.

Neurological diagnoses were established after review by a pediatric neurologist based on clinical presentation and available laboratory, neuroimaging, and electrophysiological findings.

We confirmed influenza infection with rapid influenza antigen testing or reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT‐PCR). We performed RT‐PCR testing in patients with negative rapid antigen test results when clinical suspicion of influenza remained high.

Neurological complications included seizures, encephalitis, encephalopathy, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE), status epilepticus, movement disorders, and other clinically significant neurological manifestations occurring during laboratory‐confirmed influenza infection.

The treating pediatric neurology team diagnosed encephalitis based on the final clinical diagnosis from neurological examination, supported by laboratory, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), neuroimaging, and electroencephalographic findings when available.

Demographic and clinical data extracted from electronic medical records included age, sex, admission ward or intensive care unit status, underlying medical conditions, neurological and non‐neurological manifestations, influenza vaccination history, influenza virus subtype, antiviral and supportive treatments, length of hospital stay, laboratory findings, and clinical outcomes.

Available neuroimaging studies (cranial computed tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging) were independently reviewed by an experienced neuroradiologist. We also recorded electroencephalographic and CSF findings when available.

We defined neurological complications as clinically significant neurological disorders occurring during laboratory‐confirmed influenza infection. These included seizures, encephalitis, encephalopathy, ADEM, ANE, status epilepticus, movement disorders, and other neurologic manifestations documented by the treating pediatric neurology team.

Seizures were classified as occurring in children with pre‐existing epilepsy or as new‐onset seizures. New‐onset seizures were further categorized according to clinical presentation, including febrile seizures, recurrent seizures, and status epilepticus. Status epilepticus was defined as continuous seizure activity lasting longer than 5 min for generalized seizures or longer than 10 min for focal seizures [].

Acute encephalopathy was defined as altered mental status or behavioral change lasting longer than 24 h in the absence of an alternative explanation [].

ANE was recorded according to the treating pediatric neurology team's final diagnosis and available neuroimaging. For radiological assessment, bilateral symmetric thalamic involvement was considered a defining feature of typical ANE, whereas additional basal ganglia, brainstem, or white matter involvement was considered supportive but not diagnostic in isolation [, ].

Encephalitis was diagnosed according to the final clinical diagnosis established by the pediatric neurology team based on neurological examination, CSF analysis, neuroimaging, electroencephalography, and other supportive investigations when available.

We performed statistical analyses using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, United States).

Continuous variables were summarized as median (interquartile range [IQR]) or mean ± standard deviation, depending on data distribution, whereas categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages.

We compared groups using the chi‐square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, as appropriate.

We restricted candidate predictors a priori to demographic, baseline clinical, and laboratory variables available at or near presentation and considered clinically plausible predictors of encephalopathy. We did not consider diagnostic procedures, length of hospital stay, PICU admission, or in‐hospital mortality as candidate predictors because they occurred after, or as a consequence of, encephalopathy. Owing to the limited number of encephalopathy events, the multivariable logistic regression model was restricted to focal seizure and lymphocyte count to reduce overfitting. Unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. We considered a two‐sided p value < 0.05 statistically significant.

During the study period, 3040 children were hospitalized with laboratory‐confirmed influenza infection. Among these, 115 patients (3.8%) developed influenza‐associated neurological complications and met the study inclusion criteria. The median age was 32 months (IQR, 19–58 months), and 67 patients (58.3%) were male. Influenza A was identified in 92 patients (80.0%), whereas influenza B was detected in 23 (20.0%). Thirteen children (11.3%) had at least one underlying medical condition, most commonly epilepsy or cerebral palsy. We administered oseltamivir to 106 patients (92.2%).

Table  summarizes the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the study cohort. Two patients (1.7%) died during hospitalization, while one patient (0.9%) experienced persistent neurological sequelae at discharge.

Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of children with influenza‐associated neurological complications (n = 115).

Note: Underlying medical conditions included epilepsy (n = 4), cerebral palsy (n = 3), asthma (n = 2), isolated neutropenia (n = 1), retinoblastoma (n = 1), aplastic anemia (n = 1), Sjögren–Larsson syndrome (n = 1), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (n = 1), thalassemia minor (n = 1), and spina bifida (n = 1). Some patients had more than one underlying medical condition.

Abbreviations: IQR, interquartile range; PICU, pediatric intensive care unit.

Fever duration was available for 103 patients.

Seizures were the presenting neurological manifestation in all patients. Generalized tonic–clonic seizures were the predominant seizure type, occurring in 101 patients (87.8%), whereas focal seizures and atonic seizures were observed in 10 (8.7%) and four (3.5%) patients, respectively. Status epilepticus developed in five patients (4.3%). Influenza‐associated encephalopathy was diagnosed in 15 patients (13.0%), and influenza encephalitis in 11 (9.6%). Two patients fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for acute ADEM. Two patients were diagnosed with acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE).

We performed lumbar puncture in 16 patients (13.9%), electroencephalography (EEG) in 32 (27.8%), and brain neuroimaging in 31 (27.0%). We evaluated routine laboratory parameters as potential factors associated with encephalopathy. Among these, we selected lymphocyte count for inclusion in the multivariable model based on the univariable results and its clinical relevance.

Neurological complications requiring PICU admission occurred in five patients and included refractory status epilepticus, ADEM, ANE, and diffuse cerebral edema. At hospital discharge, 112 patients (97.4%) had recovered without persistent neurological deficits. One patient (0.9%) had residual neurological sequelae, and two patients (1.7%) died during hospitalization. Table  presents the spectrum of neurological manifestations, diagnostic investigations, and clinical outcomes.

Clinical spectrum, diagnostic investigations, and outcomes of children with influenza‐associated neurological complications (n = 115).

Note: Diagnostic categories reflect the original clinical diagnoses recorded in the retrospective cohort. MRI phenotypes are being reassessed in light of potential overlap with ALERD/AESD‐spectrum and HHE‐spectrum encephalopathy; no diagnostic reclassification or change in counts was made without confirmatory clinical–radiological information.

Abbreviations: ADEM, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis; ANE, acute necrotizing encephalopathy; CT, computed tomography; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PICU, pediatric intensive care unit.

Brain neuroimaging was performed in 31 patients (27.0%). Figure  illustrates heterogeneous patterns of influenza‐associated neurological injury. Panels 1–2 show encephalopathy in a child with pre‐existing leukoencephalopathy. Panels 3–4 and 7–8, originally categorized as ADEM, show bilateral white matter abnormalities for which an acute encephalopathy with restricted diffusion (ALERD/AESD‐spectrum) phenotype is an important differential diagnosis; the available descriptions do not establish diffusion restriction, its timing, or a biphasic clinical course. Panels 5–6 demonstrate chronic sequelae following a clinically recorded ANE episode. Panels 9–10 show unilateral frontoparietal cortical/subcortical diffusion restriction associated with focal seizures; peri‐ictal injury and the hemiconvulsion–hemiplegia–epilepsy (HHE) spectrum should be considered, although prolonged hemiconvulsions, acute hemiplegia, and subsequent epilepsy have not been established from the available records. Panels 11–12 show bilateral symmetric deep gray matter abnormalities in a patient recorded as having ANE, but the predominance of basal ganglia involvement and the degree of thalamic involvement warrant reassessment before radiological confirmation of typical ANE.

To identify factors associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy, we stratified patients by the presence or absence of encephalopathy and compared demographic characteristics, clinical manifestations, laboratory findings, diagnostic investigations, and clinical outcomes. Table  presents the results of the comparative analyses.

Comparison of demographic characteristics, clinical features, laboratory findings, diagnostic investigations, and outcomes between patients with and without influenza‐associated encephalopathy.

Abbreviations: CT, computed tomography; IQR, interquartile range; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; PICU, pediatric intensive care unit.

Patients with influenza‐associated encephalopathy had a significantly longer hospital stay than those without encephalopathy (median, 5 vs. 1 day; p < 0.001). Focal seizures were markedly more frequent in the encephalopathy group (40.0% vs. 4.0%; p < 0.001). Neuroimaging, electroencephalography, and lumbar puncture were performed significantly more frequently in patients with encephalopathy than in those without encephalopathy (all p ≤ 0.001). In addition, PICU admission and in‐hospital mortality occurred more frequently among patients with encephalopathy (both p = 0.016). We observed no significant differences in age, sex, influenza subtype, underlying medical conditions, or status epilepticus.

The complete‐case multivariable analysis included 105 patients; findings are summarized in Table .

Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses of factors associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy.

Note: The lymphocyte analyses included 105 patients with complete data; lymphocyte count was modeled per 1000 cells/mm3 increase. Given the small number of encephalopathy events, the adjusted model should be considered exploratory rather than confirmatory.

Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; OR, odds ratio.

Focal seizures were associated with encephalopathy (adjusted OR, 16.98; 95% CI, 3.42–84.27; p = 0.001), as was lymphocyte count (adjusted OR, 1.53 per 1000 cells/mm3; 95% CI, 1.11–2.12; p = 0.009). Given the limited number of encephalopathy events and wide CIs, these estimates are exploratory rather than predictive or causal.

In this retrospective single‐center study, we comprehensively evaluated the clinical spectrum, diagnostic findings, and outcomes of influenza‐associated neurological complications in 115 hospitalized children over five consecutive influenza seasons. Seizures, predominantly generalized tonic–clonic seizures, represented the most common neurological manifestation, whereas encephalopathy and encephalitis occurred in 13.0% and 9.6% of patients, respectively. Although the vast majority of children recovered without permanent neurological deficits, patients with encephalopathy experienced a substantially more severe clinical course, characterized by longer hospitalization, more frequent neurodiagnostic investigations, higher rates of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission, and increased in‐hospital mortality. Focal seizures and higher lymphocyte counts were also independently associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy.

Neurological complications are among the most important extrapulmonary manifestations of influenza in childhood, with seizures consistently representing the predominant clinical presentation. Pozailov et al. reported seizures as the most common neurological manifestation (58.7%) among children hospitalized with influenza A or B, while febrile seizures accounted for 13% of neurological presentations []. Similarly, Kwong et al. observed febrile seizures in approximately one‐fifth of pediatric influenza hospitalizations []. Consistent with these reports, seizures constituted the presenting neurological manifestation in all children included in our cohort, with generalized tonic–clonic seizures accounting for nearly 90% of cases. These findings reinforce previous evidence that influenza‐associated neurological involvement most commonly presents with seizure disorders during the early phase of infection.

Encephalopathy and encephalitis represented the most clinically significant neurological complications in our cohort. Previous studies have reported neurological complication rates ranging from 1.7% to 15% among hospitalized children with influenza [, , , , , ]. Although comparisons between studies are complicated by differences in case definitions and study populations, the frequency of encephalopathy observed in our series falls within the upper range of previously published data. More importantly, our comparative analyses demonstrated that children who developed encephalopathy had significantly longer hospital stays, required neuroimaging and other diagnostic investigations more frequently, and experienced higher rates of intensive care admission and in‐hospital mortality than children without encephalopathy. These findings emphasize that influenza‐associated encephalopathy, although relatively uncommon, remains one of the most clinically important neurological complications of pediatric influenza.

A principal finding of this study was the identification of focal seizures as an independent factor associated with influenza‐associated encephalopathy. Focal seizures were nearly 10 times more frequent among children with encephalopathy than among those without encephalopathy and remained independently associated with encephalopathy after multivariable adjustment. Although seizures are well recognized as the most common neurological manifestation of influenza, previous studies have largely focused on their overall frequency rather than on seizure semiology as a potential indicator of severe neurological involvement. Our findings suggest that focal seizure activity should prompt clinicians to consider underlying encephalopathy and pursue timely neurological evaluation, including neuroimaging and electroencephalographic assessment when clinically indicated. In addition, higher lymphocyte counts remained independently associated with encephalopathy. Although the biological significance of this finding remains uncertain, it may reflect a more pronounced systemic immune response accompanying severe neurological involvement and warrants further investigation in larger prospective studies.

Most children in our cohort had no documented underlying medical condition before influenza infection, consistent with previous reports indicating that severe neurological complications may also occur in previously healthy children []. Nevertheless, approximately one in nine patients had pre‐existing comorbidities, most commonly epilepsy and cerebral palsy. Although underlying medical conditions were not independently associated with encephalopathy in our analysis, children with chronic neurological disorders remain an important high‐risk population because they frequently require hospitalization and may experience more complicated clinical courses following influenza infection, as also shown by Newland et al., in whom underlying neurologic/neuromuscular disease and age 6 months–4 years were independent risk factors for influenza‐related neurologic complications []. These findings support current recommendations to monitor children with neurological comorbidities during seasonal influenza outbreaks closely.

Influenza A accounted for most infections in our cohort, whereas influenza B represented one‐fifth of all cases. This distribution is comparable to previous studies reporting that influenza A causes most cases of influenza‐associated neurological disease. In contrast, influenza B generally contributes a smaller proportion of cases [,  ]. Only three children were infected with the H1N1 subtype, preventing meaningful comparisons according to viral subtype. Consistent with previous observations by Wada et al. [], children infected with influenza B tended to be older than those infected with influenza A, although this difference was not statistically significant. These findings likely reflect annual variations in circulating influenza strains and regional epidemiological patterns rather than intrinsic differences in neurovirulence between influenza virus types.

Seasonal influenza vaccination had not been administered to any child in our cohort. Previous pediatric studies from Türkiye [ ] reported similar observations, where vaccination coverage among otherwise healthy children remains limited. Although direct evidence demonstrating protection against influenza‐associated neurological complications remains limited, previous epidemiological observations from Japan suggest that widespread influenza vaccination may reduce mortality related to influenza‐associated encephalopathy and encephalitis []. Consequently, increasing childhood influenza vaccination coverage, particularly among children with chronic neurological or other high‐risk medical conditions, may help reduce the burden of severe influenza‐related complications.

Finally, neurological manifestations developed early in the course of influenza infection in our patients, occurring a median of 1 day after fever onset. This observation is consistent with previous reports demonstrating that neurological symptoms usually emerge within the first 48 h of illness [, ]. Recognition of this narrow temporal window is clinically important because it emphasizes the need for careful neurological assessment in children presenting with influenza and new‐onset seizures or altered mental status shortly after the onset of fever. Early recognition may facilitate timely diagnostic evaluation and appropriate supportive management, particularly in patients at risk of developing encephalopathy.

Neurological injury associated with influenza is thought to result predominantly from an exaggerated host inflammatory response rather than direct viral invasion of the central nervous system. In our cohort, we performed CSF examination in 16 patients, which revealed only mild pleocytosis with elevated protein concentrations in four cases. These findings are consistent with previous studies reporting that CSF abnormalities are often absent or nonspecific in children with influenza‐associated neurological complications [, ,  ]. The relatively low frequency of CSF pleocytosis supports the hypothesis that immune‐mediated mechanisms, rather than direct viral neuroinvasion, play a central role in the pathogenesis of influenza‐associated encephalopathy and encephalitis []. Although this study did not evaluate viral RNA in CSF, previous investigations have shown that influenza viral RNA is rarely detected in CSF, further supporting an indirect mechanism of neurological injury [].

The precise biological pathways responsible for influenza‐associated neurological complications remain incompletely understood. Experimental and clinical studies suggest that genetically susceptible individuals may develop excessive pro‐inflammatory cytokine production following influenza infection, leading to blood–brain barrier disruption, endothelial dysfunction, and secondary neuronal injury []. Subsequent neuroinflammation and activation of immune‐mediated pathways may contribute to cerebral edema, altered consciousness, seizures, and encephalopathy. While several potential biomarkers—including platelet‐derived growth factor (PDGF), neopterin, and neutrophil elastase—have been proposed as indicators of neurological involvement [], none has yet demonstrated sufficient diagnostic accuracy or clinical applicability for routine use. Identifying reliable biomarkers that can predict neurological deterioration therefore remains an important priority for future research.

Neuroimaging is valuable for characterizing influenza‐associated neurological injury, but phenotype classification requires integration of imaging distribution, DWI/ADC findings, the timing of imaging, seizure course, and neurological examination. A recent meta‐analysis of infection‐triggered encephalopathy syndromes distinguished AESD (including ALERD‐spectrum presentations), HHE, and ANE on combined clinical and radiological grounds; it emphasized subcortical white matter diffusion restriction in AESD, often unilateral diffusion abnormalities in HHE, and symmetric thalamic lesions as a central ANE criterion []. Against this framework, the relatively symmetric white matter abnormalities originally labeled ADEM in our figure (Panels 3–4 and 7–8) merit consideration of ALERD/AESD‐spectrum encephalopathy, but a diagnosis cannot be assigned without the relevant DWI/ADC sequences, imaging chronology, and seizure evolution. Similarly, unilateral cortical/subcortical restricted diffusion (Panels 9–10) could reflect peri‐ictal change or an HHE‐spectrum injury; the required clinical evolution to hemiplegia and/or epilepsy was not sufficiently documented to establish HHE. The acute deep gray matter findings labeled ANE (Panels 11–12) appear to involve the basal ganglia prominently; because symmetric thalamic lesions are integral to a typical ANE diagnosis, we consider this classification provisional pending a targeted review of the original MRI sequences and clinical record. The follow‐up atrophy in Panels 5–6 is nonspecific and cannot independently verify the acute ANE phenotype. Accordingly, these MRI patterns are presented as descriptive examples rather than definitive subtype assignments, and no cohort frequencies have been reclassified on the basis of the figure descriptions alone.

Management of influenza‐associated neurological complications remains largely supportive because no standardized treatment strategy exists. Early antiviral therapy with oseltamivir is currently recommended for hospitalized children with suspected influenza‐associated neurological disease despite the limited high‐quality evidence supporting its neurological benefit []. In our cohort, more than 90% of patients received oseltamivir, reflecting current clinical practice. Encouragingly, almost all children recovered without permanent neurological disability, with only one patient experiencing persistent neurological sequelae and two patients dying during hospitalization. Compared with previous reports describing higher rates of severe neurological sequelae and mortality [,  ], the overall prognosis in our cohort was relatively favorable. Notably, two patients in our cohort were diagnosed with acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE), a severe influenza‐associated encephalopathy phenotype associated with substantial neurological morbidity and mortality [, ,  ].

The present study has several strengths, including a relatively large single‐center pediatric series from Türkiye and systematic characterization of clinical, laboratory, and short‐term outcome data. However, its retrospective design may have introduced incomplete clinical documentation and selection bias, and tertiary‐center referral may limit generalizability. Advanced virological and immunological assessments were not routine. Furthermore, DWI/ADC sequences, imaging timing, serial MRI, and clinical details needed to discriminate ALERD/AESD, HHE, ADEM, and typical ANE could not be verified systematically from the material available for this revision; thus, diagnostic subtype assignments in the illustrative figure remain provisional. Finally, only 15 encephalopathy events were recorded, making the two‐variable logistic model vulnerable to overfitting and imprecision despite its restricted size. The regression analysis should be interpreted as exploratory and requires independent validation.

Overall, our findings demonstrate that influenza‐associated neurological complications encompass a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from uncomplicated seizures to severe encephalopathy requiring intensive care support. Although the prognosis was generally favorable, encephalopathy was associated with substantially greater clinical severity and worse short‐term outcomes. Recognition of focal seizures may help identify children who warrant closer assessment for concurrent encephalopathy and prompt neurological evaluation. Larger prospective multicenter studies integrating clinical, neuroimaging, immunological, and molecular biomarkers are needed to improve risk stratification and optimize the management of influenza‐associated neurological complications in children.

Seizures predominantly characterized influenza‐associated neurological complications in hospitalized children and generally had favorable short‐term outcomes. However, encephalopathy represented the most severe neurological manifestation and was associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased intensive care requirements, and poorer in‐hospital outcomes. Recognition of focal seizures may help identify children who warrant closer assessment for concurrent encephalopathy and timely neurological evaluation. Prospective multicenter studies are warranted to validate these exploratory findings.

neuroscience.title: Syndrome-oriented CNS infectious complications after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and CAR T-cell therapy, part 1—viral encephalitis, meningitis, and myelitis: recommendations from the Practice Harmonization & Guidelines Committee of the EBMT
neuroscience.abstract: Viral encephalitis, meningitis, and myelitis are rare but life-threatening complications after autologous or allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HSCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, associated with 30–60% mortality and frequent neurological sequelae. The absence of harmonised definitions and diagnostic criteria contributes to delayed diagnosis, underreporting, and substantial heterogeneity across centres. This EBMT Practice Harmonization and Guidelines Committee expert consensus provides practical recommendations for the definition, diagnosis, treatment, response assessment, and prevention of viral encephalitis/meningitis and viral myelitis, developed through systematic literature review and multidisciplinary expert consensus following EBMT methodology. We propose standardised diagnostic categories for proven and probable viral encephalitis/meningitis and myelitis, alongside a unified diagnostic algorithm integrating clinical assessment, neuroimaging, electroencephalography, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and targeted virological testing. We highlight key neurotropic viruses for inclusion in initial cerebrospinal fluid multiplex PCR panels, including human herpesvirus 6, herpes simplex virus 1/2, varicella zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, adenovirus, polyomaviruses BK/JC, and selected community-acquired respiratory viruses, such as EV71, and recommend prompt, risk-based empirical antiviral therapy in suspected cases. These recommendations aim to standardise clinical practice, facilitate multicenter research, and improve outcomes. However, many rely on limited observational evidence or expert opinion, underscoring the need for prospective studies.
neuroscience.text:
Viral encephalitis, meningitis, and myelitis represent a rare but potentially devastating complication after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy. While the global incidence of viral encephalitis in the general population is approximately 5–10 per 100,000 persons per year,, ,  its incidence and case-fatality rates are markedly higher in immunocompromised patients., ,  Profound and prolonged T-cell dysfunction, disruption of the blood–brain barrier, and intensive immunosuppressive therapy predispose to viral invasion of the central nervous system (CNS).,  More than 100 viruses can cause viral encephalitis/meningitis or myelitis, but this document focuses on those most commonly reported in cell therapy recipients.

To date, standardised definitions, diagnostic algorithms, and management strategies for viral encephalitis/meningitis and myelitis in these immunocompromised populations remain lacking, contributing in part to under-recognition, delayed diagnosis, and reporting heterogeneity across studies. Initiated by EBMT Infectious Diseases Working Party (IDWP) and Practice Harmonization and Guidelines Committee (PH&G), the document provides a holistic, syndrome-oriented approach to viral CNS infections after autologous or allogeneic HSCT and CAR T-cell therapy, encompassing encephalitis, meningitis, and myelitis. It harmonises definitions, diagnosis, treatment principles, and response evaluation. Encephalitis and meningitis are addressed together because they are closely related and may coexist as meningoencephalitis. Evidence derives predominantly from allogeneic HSCT recipients; extrapolation to autologous HSCT and CAR T cells requires the consideration of the different types of immunosuppression given to these patient groups. Given its rarity and limited evidence, viral myelitis is addressed separately, covering recognition, differential diagnosis, diagnostic evaluation, and management.

A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed to identify relevant studies published between January 1, 2000, and September 2025. The strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms related to viral CNS infections, including “viral encephalitis,” “viral meningitis,” “meningoencephalitis,” “viral myelitis,” “encephalomyelitis,” and “central nervous system infection,” with transplantation-related terms: “Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation,” “Bone Marrow Transplantation,” “Transplantation, Autologous,” “Transplantation, Allogeneic,” “stem cell transplant⁎,” “bone marrow transplant⁎,” “hematopoietic cell transplant⁎,” “HSCT,” “BMT,” “CAR-T⁎,” and “transplant recipient⁎.” Additional targeted searches combined CNS-related terms with specific viral pathogens, including herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, Epstein–Barr virus, adenovirus, enterovirus, JC and BK polyomaviruses, community-acquired respiratory viruses, and arboviruses. Searches were limited to human studies published in English. Given the rarity of these complications, case reports and small case series were eligible. Reference lists of relevant publications and guidelines were manually reviewed to identify additional studies.

Definitions were aligned with the International Encephalitis Consortium criteria and refined for allogeneic HSCT and CAR T-cell populations.

This harmonization project includes two companion manuscripts (Part 1 of a syndrome-oriented series on CNS infectious complications following HSCT and CAR T-cell therapy, focusing on viral etiologies, and Part 2 will address bacterial, fungal, and parasitic CNS infections) that were developed as a single project following the expert-based methodology of the EBMT PH&G Committee, as previously described by Yakoub-Agha et al. The intended use is for specialists in the field managing these types of patients with the aim of supporting clinical decisions.

A multidisciplinary panel of hematology (n = 4), infectious diseases (n = 3), microbiology (n = 1), pediatric specialists (n = 4), and members of the EBMT PH&G Committee (n = 4) was convened. Committee members were selected and invited based on their clinical and scientific expertise in the field and the involvement in dedicated IDWP subcommittees, with consideration given to geographic diversity and representation of complementary specialties and competencies. Before the workshop, predefined clinical questions were formulated, and a structured literature review of the published registry analyses, cohort studies, case series, and systematic reviews were conducted. Designated panel members reviewed and summarised the evidence relevant to each question and circulated it to the group. Panel members discussed the evidence and proposed recommendations during a two-day EBMT workshop. Panel members presented and discussed available evidence and preliminary recommendations in plenary sessions. Given the scarcity and heterogeneity of the available evidence in the targeted patients’ population, particularly the absence of randomised trials or comparative observational studies for most diagnostic and therapeutic interventions, and the frequent need to extrapolate from other populations, we elected not to formally grade the evidence or the strength of recommendations. Instead, the supporting evidence and its limitations were described narratively. Recommendations based predominantly on indirect evidence, good clinical practice, or multidisciplinary expert consensus were explicitly formulated, and their wording was adjusted to reflect the associated uncertainty. Consensus was reached through iterative discussion and review of the relevant literature, with disagreements addressed and recommendations revised until all panel members were in agreement. The final recommendations were unanimously approved by the panel before internal review and validation in accordance with the EBMT PH&G Committee process in 2025.

Overall, viral encephalitis incidence after allogeneic HSCT ranges from 0.5% to 1.5%., , ,  Most common viruses include Human herpes virus-6 (HHV-6), human herpes simplex virus types 1–2 (HSV I-II), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), adenovirus, JC polyomavirus, Enterovirus 71 (EV71)., , , , ,  Of note, in allogeneic HSCT and CAR T-cell recipients, viral encephalitis most commonly results from reactivation of latent viruses under profound immunosuppression. Overall incidence and main characteristics of viral encephalitis in allogeneic HSCT recipients by virus type are summarised in . All viral encephalitis, except for HHV-6, are rare to very rare. Information on viral myelitis is even more limited., ,  Viral encephalitis in CAR T-cell recipients is also very rarely reported and limited to case series,,  even with systematic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation. However, it has been increasingly recognised, particularly due to HHV-6 and JC polyomavirus in the setting of delayed immune reconstitution., , , , ,  HHV-6 reactivation or detection has been reported during ex vivo T-cell activation and expansion for manufacturing of CAR T cells. HHV-6B is the leading cause of viral encephalitis after allogeneic HSCT, accounting for 70–80% of reported cases., ,  The EBMT IDWP analysis estimated an overall incidence of 0.45%, with higher rates in cord-blood (2.14%), unrelated donor (0.68%), and haploidentical (0.51%) transplants than in matched sibling donor transplants (0.06%). Key risk factors include cord blood, mismatched or haploidentical grafts, T-cell depletion, younger age, and high HHV-6 viremia., , , , , ,  Symptoms typically appear around 20–40 days after transplantation and include confusion, seizures, and amnesia.

CMV is a rare cause of viral encephalitis after allogeneic HSCT but carries a high mortality (up to 70%). Most of the data come from the pre-letermovir era, and letermovir prophylaxis has decreased all forms of CMV disease.,  While CMV viral encephalitis MRI commonly shows periventricular enhancement or ependymal involvement, these abnormalities may be absent in a significant percentage of patients.

HSV I-II encephalitis usually presents early in the post-transplantation period, particularly in the absence of prophylaxis,  or in cases of acyclovir-resistant HSV infection.

VZV CNS infection typically manifests later in patients with chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and prolonged corticosteroid exposure, presenting with vasculitis or ischemic lesions., ,  VZV viral encephalitis MRI may show encephalitic changes, but may also appear normal.

EBV encephalitis or EBV encephalomyelitis may occur with or without post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD). It generally presents months after transplantation, often in rituximab-naïve or heavily immunosuppressed patients., , ,

Only a few cases of adenovirus encephalitis have been reported in pediatric or cord-blood transplant recipients early after transplantation. Disseminated disease often coexists, and prognosis remains poor.,

JC virus–associated PML typically occurs late in recipients with chronic GVHD, rituximab exposure, or profound T-cell lymphopenia.,  In an EBMT series of 23 PML cases, classified following American Academy of Neurology criteria, the median onset was 14 months after transplantation, with 78% mortality despite treatment. BK virus encephalitis has only been reported in isolated allogeneic HSCT cases.

Non-herpesvirus viral encephalitis after allogeneic-HSCT is limited to isolated reports. Community-acquired respiratory viruses (CARVs), including influenza, RSV, and EV, have been detected in CSF, often in patients with hypogammaglobulinemia. EV accounted for 1.4% of viral encephalitis cases, with median onset at day +121 and 33.3% 6-month mortality. SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with encephalitis-like syndromes, though CSF detection and direct CNS involvement remain unproven. Parvovirus B19 and Coxsackie viruses (particularly CoxB3) caused 3.3% and 1.4% of viral encephalitis cases, respectively, with late onset and high mortality for Coxsackie.,  HHV-7 has been linked to fatal viral encephalitis in two cases. Flaviviruses, including WNV, JEV, ZIKV, TBEV, and Tuscany virus, are potential but anecdotal causes in this setting.

Isolated viral meningitis, defined as meningeal inflammation without parenchymal brain involvement, is rarely reported in allogeneic HSCT or CAR T-cell recipients and has not been independently quantified in published series., ,  Instead, most viral CNS infections appear to occur along a continuum of meningoencephalitis, with encephalopathic features dominating the clinical presentation and CSF abnormalities often being subtle or absent.,  Non-polio enteroviruses, including echoviruses and coxsackieviruses; HSV-2; and, in children, human parechovirus are well-recognised causes of meningitis in the general population, whereas EV71 more commonly causes rhombencephalitis. In immunocompromised patients, herpesviruses such as HHV-6 and HSV-1 are more typically present with encephalitic features. Syndromic CSF PCR panels may also detect viral pathogens in patients without overt encephalitis, particularly during the early stages of infection or in milder cases. Although many cases resolve with supportive care, antiviral treatment, usually with i. v. acyclovir, should be given for HSV-2 or VZV meningitis.

The following harmonised definitions were established to enable uniform case classification, reporting, and outcome assessment of viral encephalitis/myelitis in recipients of allogeneic HSCT or CAR T-cell therapy. Each definition is structured to allow grading of diagnostic certainty (proven, probable) and to incorporate objective parameters for assessing treatment response, thereby supporting either diagnostic, clinical management, or research comparability.

Encephalitis is defined as inflammation of the brain parenchyma associated with neurological dysfunction. viral encephalitis refers here to direct viral infection of the CNS, whereas post-infectious or immune-mediated encephalitis constitutes a distinct entity. Clinical manifestations may include altered mental status, cognitive or behavioural changes, seizures, and focal or multifocal neurological deficits, with or without fever, and an acute, subacute, or chronic course. Encephalopathy may present similarly but lacks confirmed brain inflammation and may result from metabolic, toxic, drug-related, infectious, or other causes. Although encephalopathy may prompt investigation for viral encephalitis, it is a presenting neurological syndrome rather than diagnostic evidence of encephalitis. In profoundly immunosuppressed patients, however, attenuated inflammatory responses may result in absent CSF pleocytosis or characteristic neuroimaging abnormalities despite genuine CNS infection. Viral meningeal involvement is frequently closely linked to encephalitis, both clinically and diagnostically, and both may coexist as meningoencephalitis. CSF examination, neuroimaging and virological testing commonly form part of the same diagnostic assessment.

To harmonise diagnostic certainty across EBMT centres, cases are categorised as proven or probable viral encephalitis and proven viral meningitis based on clinical and virological evidence, as summarised in . Clinicians often rely on surrogate indicators such as CSF inflammation or parenchymal changes on neuroimaging to infer viral encephalitis/meningitis. Nevertheless, viral encephalitis/meningitis may still be present even without marked CSF pleocytosis or identifiable abnormalities on imaging studies; therefore, if these parameters are absent, they do not conclusively exclude proven or probable viral encephalitis. Compatible neurological syndrome refers to symptoms due to acute or subacute temporal relationship between neurological symptom onset and the suspected viral infection, reasonable exclusion of alternative causes, and supportive objective evidence of CNS involvement, such as inflammatory CSF abnormalities, compatible neuroimaging findings, or relevant EEG abnormalities.

Detection of viral nucleic acid in CSF should not be interpreted as causal in isolation. Classification requires temporal and biological coherence with the neurological syndrome, reasonable exclusion of alternative diagnoses, and supporting evidence of CNS involvement. In profoundly immunosuppressed patients, the absence of CSF pleocytosis or characteristic neuroimaging abnormalities does not necessarily exclude viral encephalitis. For HHV-6, CMV and EBV, incidental detection, systemic reactivation, blood contamination, and, for HHV-6, chromosomal integration should be considered.

Meningeal inflammation is defined as the presence of at least one of the following: (a) abnormal CSF analysis with pleocytosis (>5 white cells/μLin adults or above age-related norms in children) (b) meningeal enhancement compatible with meningitis on contrast-enhanced brain CT or MRI (if lumbar puncture was not performed recently, as lumbar puncture can cause a non-specific meningeal enhancement). In severely immunocompromised patients (e.g., profound neutropenia <100 cells/mm3), the signs of inflammation (pleocytosis or imaging findings) can be attenuated. Case-by-case discussion is needed when a patient with suspected meningitis and identification of the plausible pathogen in the non-bloody CSF presents with a complete absence of meningeal inflammation.

In the absence of direct viral identification in CSF, NGS, or culture, such cases cannot be reliably attributed to a viral etiology and are therefore classified as meningitis of unknown etiology.

The possibility of a traumatic lumbar puncture and contamination by peripheral blood should be assessed based on the CSF appearance and the red blood cell (RBC) count. When interpreting RBC/white blood cell (WBC) ratios (in cases where there are large numbers of RBC in the CSF, such as with a traumatic lumbar puncture), the following formula may allow correction of the WBC count: True CSF WBC = actual CSF WBC - (WBC in blood x RBC in CSF)/RBC in blood. Notably, rules for adjusting leukocytes in blood-contaminated CSF have not been well validated.

In probable cases, causality should be attributed to the identified virus only when temporal, clinical, and radiologic correlations are consistent, and alternative etiologies (drug toxicity, GVHD, transplant-associated microangiopathy or ICANS) have been carefully evaluated and judged to be unlikely.

In CAR T-cell recipients, the possible diagnosis and management of ICANS should be prioritised when timing and phenotype are typical, particularly with previous CRS, without delaying indicated infectious evaluation or empirical antivirals. Given its low yield in typical ICANS, reserve lumbar puncture for atypical timing/evolution, infectious features, suggestive MRI/EEG or virology, or poor clinical response to treatment.

The initial assessment should include a detailed clinical history covering the type and timing of HCT or CAR-T-cell therapy, donor and recipient viral serostatus when informative and available, immune status, GVHD, current and previous immunosuppressive and antiviral treatment, and recent or previous episodes of viral DNAemia or systemic viral disease. Medication and vaccination history, recent infections or infectious contacts, travel and mosquito, tick or other relevant vector exposures should also be reviewed. Physical examination should include a comprehensive neurological assessment and evaluation for extra-neurological findings that may suggest a specific viral etiology, including skin or mucosal lesions, respiratory manifestations, retinitis or other end-organ involvement. Serostatus and blood DNAemia may support risk assessment but cannot independently confirm or exclude viral CNS infection.

Viral targets vary by platform: BioFire FilmArray ME includes HSV-1/2, VZV, CMV, HHV-6, enterovirus and parechovirus; QIAstat-Dx includes the same targets except CMV; and Allplex additionally covers EBV, HHV-7, adenovirus, mumps and parvovirus B19. Positive HHV-6, CMV or EBV results require dedicated quantitative CSF and blood PCR; eHHV6 should be excluded when appropriate. Negative panels require targeted testing for omitted pathogens, including JCV/BKV, and enterovirus typing when myelitis is suspected.

Blood PCR complements evidence of replication but cannot confirm or exclude CNS disease: positivity may reflect unrelated reactivation, whereas negativity does not exclude CNS-confined infection. Interpretation depends on viruses, timing, specimens, and assay; serum, plasma, and whole-blood loads are neither interchangeable nor comparable across laboratories. Integrate results with clinical, MRI, and CSF findings. Serial testing should use identical specimens and assays; persistently high HHV-6 DNA warrants evaluation for endogenous HHV-6.

Arboviruses should be investigated when suggested by travel or residence, season, local circulation, and mosquito, tick, or other vector exposure. Testing should be geographically directed and may include West Nile virus, tick-borne encephalitis virus and other regionally relevant arboviruses. Because viremia may be transient and PCR sensitivity in blood or CSF may be limited at neurological presentation, virus-specific IgM testing in serum and CSF, supplemented by paired or confirmatory serology when appropriate, should be considered. Serological findings require cautious interpretation because immune responses may be delayed or absent in HCT and CAR-T recipients and cross-reactivity may occur among flaviviruses.

The management of viral encephalitis/meningitis after allogeneic HSCT relies on rapid initiation of empirical or targeted antiviral therapy, reduction of immunosuppression when feasible, and appropriate neurological supportive care and virological monitoring. Because mortality and long-term neurological sequelae risk are high,, , ,  particularly for HHV-6, HSV/VZV and CMV encephalitis, early empiric treatment is justified when clinical and radiologic findings are compatible and virological results are pending. Finally, adoptive transfer of virus-specific T cells (VST) shows promise but remains limited to specialised centres. Several reviews and guidelines have addressed initial workup and empirical therapy in suspected viral encephalitis., , ,  Empirical antiviral treatment should be selected according to the relative pre-test probability of HHV-6/CMV versus HSV/VZV as summarised in . Foscarnet is preferred when HHV-6 is more likely, particularly during the early post-allogeneic HSCT period in profoundly immunosuppressed patients receiving reliably administered acyclovir prophylaxis, or when acyclovir-resistant HSV is suspected. An alternative option for acyclovir-resistant HSV is an helicase-primase inhibitor currently available on compassionate use in Europe. Intravenous acyclovir is preferred when sensitive HSV/VZV is more likely, particularly after antiviral prophylaxis has been discontinued, interrupted, or inadequately administered, and during later post-transplant periods when HHV-6 encephalitis is less frequent.
