Treatment of viral encephalitis in allogeneic HSCT recipients should be guided by viral etiology, CNS penetration, and patient-specific immune status.  outlines key antiviral agents used in the targeted treatment of CNS viral infections, highlighting their dosing, viral spectrum, CNS penetration, available human pharmacokinetic data, and recommended therapy duration. Therapy should be initiated promptly, adjusted for renal function, and continued for at least three weeks or until virological clearance in blood and/or CSF is documented.

HHV-6 and CMV encephalitis are treated with intravenous foscarnet or ganciclovir; combination therapy may be considered in severe or refractory cases, though with higher toxicity risk., ,  Maribavir and letermovir are not recommended due to poor CNS penetration. CMV-specific T-cell therapy may be considered when available.

HSV-1/2 and VZV are managed with intravenous acyclovir. In VZV vasculopathy, corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day) for 5–7 days may be added. In suspected acyclovir resistance, foscarnet or a new helicase-primase inhibitor (pritelivir or amenamivir) can be considered as compassionate use.

EBV encephalitis and CNS-PTLD are distinct entities that cannot be differentiated by CSF EBV DNA alone; CNS-PTLD requires integrated imaging, CSF, staging, and, when feasible, histopathological assessment. Non-PTLD EBV encephalitis has no proven pathogen-directed therapy; management is supportive, with cautious immunosuppression reduction, while antivirals lack demonstrated efficacy and EBV-specific VSTs remain investigational. CNS-PTLD is treated with rituximab, alone or combined with chemotherapy, VST, or radiotherapy. In a pilot study, tabelecleucel induced a high response rate of 78% and demonstrated promising survival (70.6% and 54.9% at one and 2 years after VST therapy, respectively) among patients with refractory EBV + CNS PTLD. Corticosteroids may help in immune-mediated cases. Antivirals are generally ineffective.,

Adenovirus encephalitis has no established CNS-directed therapy. Reduction of immunosuppression and immune recovery should be pursued whenever feasible. Cidofovir or adenovirus VSTs (if available) may be considered off-label, particularly in disseminated disease or concurrent significant DNAemia, but evidence for CNS efficacy is anecdotal and its use requires careful renal monitoring. Brincidofovir is a potential future option with a better CNS profile.

No antiviral treatment of established efficacy is available for JC polyomavirus-associated PML or BK polyomavirus encephalitis. Management should prioritise immune reconstitution. Cidofovir and mirtazapine lack demonstrated efficacy and should not be recommended as routine therapy. Checkpoint inhibitors and polyomavirus VSTs remain investigational and should be restricted to clinical trials or expert-center programs.,

For other viruses, supportive care is key. Ribavirin or neuraminidase inhibitors (e.g., oseltamivir) may be considered in specific cases (e.g., RSV, influenza). Immunoglobulins may help in EV71-related encephalitis.

Response assessment should be conducted by a multidisciplinary team (hematology, cell therapy, infectious diseases, neurology, neuroradiology specialists) and documented either at the end of the planned treatment course or upon clinical deterioration. Importantly, the timing and approach to response evaluation may vary depending on the viral etiology and the type of therapy administered. For instance, in HHV-6 encephalitis, early follow-up (within 2–3 weeks after antiviral therapy onset) with brain MRI and/or assessment of CSF or plasma viral load kinetics may provide valuable insights into therapeutic efficacy. In contrast, JC virus-related PML typically follows a subacute course, where radiological changes may lag behind clinical progression, and treatment relies primarily on immune reconstitution. In such cases, response assessment may require longer follow-up intervals (e.g., 4–8 weeks). Treatment response in viral encephalitis/meningitis is summarised in . Response can be evaluated across clinical, virological, and radiological domains. While optimal management relies on integrating all three, in patients with persistent neurological sequelae, virological clearance and radiological stabilisation or improvement may serve as more objective indicators of treatment response. Repeating CSF PCR and MRI at 2–8 weeks or at the end of planned therapy should be considered to assess virological and radiological response and guide decisions on treatment changes or discontinuation in cases with persistent or progressive neurological symptoms. The two CR definition categories represent alternative, not cumulative, pathways. Complete clinical recovery without sequelae requires no ancillary confirmation, whereas in patients with stable residual neurological deficits, resolution of active infection should be supported by radiological and/or virological resolution.

Repeat lumbar puncture is not recommended after complete clinical resolution (except for CMV and HSV). It may be considered, when safe, in patients with persistent neurological deficits if CSF findings are expected to guide treatment discontinuation or modification because of suspected treatment failure or antiviral resistance.

The presence or absence of neurological sequelae should be reported separately from the overall response assessment since there are no associations between the length of therapy and the probability of experiencing improvement of neurological sequelae.

In patients with persistent but stable or improving neurological manifestations, repeat lumbar puncture may be considered, when safe, to distinguish ongoing CNS infection from residual sequelae and to support treatment discontinuation when criteria for complete response with sequelae are otherwise fulfilled.

Outcomes of viral encephalitis/meningitis following allogeneic HSCT or CAR T-cell therapy remain poor, with high mortality. The prognosis varies considerably by viral etiology, timing of onset, immune reconstitution status, and promptness of diagnosis and therapy.

Across published cohorts, the overall case-fatality rate for viral encephalitis after allogeneic HSCT ranges between 30% and 60%.,  In the IDWP study of 97 HHV-6 patients, 30-day mortality was 27%, and overall survival at 6 months was 62%, with deaths primarily due to neurological progression or concurrent infections. In another multicenter study including 32 cases of post-transplant viral encephalitis mortality reached 53% despite antiviral therapy, emphasising the poor prognosis associated with delayed diagnosis or disseminated infection. Mortality in CMV or adenovirus encephalitis is similarly high (40–70%), while HSV and VZV encephalitis, if treated promptly, have lower mortality rates (<20%)., ,  In CAR T-cell recipients, mortality and long-term neurocognitive outcomes appear comparable when a viral etiology is confirmed., , , , ,

Reported conditions associated with adverse outcomes include: allogeneic-HSCT related factors, such as non-myeloablative conditioning, use of cord-blood or haploidentical grafts, reflecting delayed immune reconstitution,,  ongoing severe GVHD or high-dose corticosteroid use and/or profound lymphopenia; and viral encephalitis and treatment related factors, such as non-HSV viral encephalitis, multifocal MRI involvement or brainstem/ventricular extension, high CSF or plasma viral load at diagnosis, and/or delayed initiation of antiviral therapy (>1.5 days after onset).

A recent study developed the GTM (abbreviation for a model composed of three risk factors: GCS score <9 [2.5 points], severe thrombocytopenia [platelet count<20,000 per μL; 1 point], and lesions >3 lobes on MRI [2.5 points]) score to predict outcomes in allogeneic HSCT recipients with viral encephalitis, based on three variables: patients in the low-risk group (0–1 points) had an overall mortality of 11%, whereas those in the high-risk group (2.5–6 points) showed a 6-month mortality of 80%. This unvalidated score may inform future risk-stratification research but should not guide routine management.

Long-term follow-up studies are scarce. Among viral encephalitis survivors, persistent neurological deficits occur in 30–40% of cases. The most frequent sequelae include chronic neurocognitive impairment, anterograde amnesia, concentration deficits, emotional lability, executive dysfunction, epilepsy, and psychiatric symptoms consistent with limbic or temporal lobe injury. HHV-6–associated limbic encephalitis commonly results in selective hippocampal damage, detectable on MRI as atrophy or gliosis. Patients with delayed antiviral therapy, prolonged viremia, or extensive bilateral MRI lesions are at the highest risk for irreversible cognitive decline. In contrast, early antiviral initiation, particularly within 48 h of symptom onset, correlates with significantly improved neurological recovery. Rehabilitation interventions usually implemented after head trauma injury might be effective for viral encephalitis patients. Neuropsychological rehabilitation and seizure prophylaxis are recommended components of post-recovery care.

MRI follow-up at 3-months and 12-months after treatment typically shows hippocampal atrophy or leukoencephalomalacia in cases of HHV-6 and CMV viral encephalitis, correlating with cognitive outcomes. Despite these sequelae, early recognition and structured multidisciplinary management have progressively improved functional recovery and quality of life in recent years.

Preventive strategies focus on viral reactivation surveillance, antiviral prophylaxis where indicated, and optimising immune reconstitution after viral encephalitis.

HSV and VZV secondary prophylaxis with acyclovir or valacyclovir should be considered for at least 6–12 months after resolution of viral encephalitis, provided that the patient is no longer receiving immunosuppression and has no active GVHD. Discontinuation of prophylaxis should also consider evidence of immune reconstitution, such as rising CD4+ T-cell counts, recovery of immunoglobulin levels, documented vaccine responses, and complete resolution of GVHD-related signs or symptoms.

Based on expert opinion, CMV DNA PCR-based monitoring and prevention, with secondary letermovir prophylaxis, could be considered in high-risk patients after CMV viral encephalitis resolution for at least 3 months and/or until CMV-specific T-cell restoration. Regular plasma CMV DNA monitoring is required, and breakthrough or increasing DNAemia should prompt active anti-CMV treatment and, whenever feasible, resistance testing, particularly for UL56 mutations. However, information on letermovir's penetration into the CNS is very limited. If letermovir is not available, consider other antiviral alternatives. Letermovir does not protect against HSV, VZV, HHV-6, or adenovirus and thus should not be relied upon as broad CNS prophylaxis.

HHV-6 secondary prophylaxis is not recommended, as routine antivirals do not prevent reactivation, and viremia monitoring has not consistently predicted encephalitis.

For EBV, consider extending PCR monitoring of EBV DNAemia after EBV viral encephalitis resolution. Patients at high risk for EBV-PTLD after allogeneic HSCT should be closely monitored for symptoms or signs attributable to PTLD or other end-organ EBV disease. No recommendations exist for secondary pharmacological prevention of EBV infection.

Secondary prophylaxis is not recommended for adenovirus, BK, and JC viruses.

CARVs should be prevented through annual influenza, COVID-19, and possibly RSV vaccination, whereas respiratory isolation measures should be implemented, in particular during outbreaks.

Finally, restoring antiviral T-cell immunity by reducing or withdrawing immunosuppression and/or adoptive VST therapy likely remains the most effective long-term preventive measure, particularly for patients with prolonged lymphopenia or recurrent viral reactivation, and should be explored in prospective clinical trials.

Viral myelitis represents a rare but recognised manifestation of neurotropic viral infections in allogeneic HSCT recipients and, more rarely, after CAR T-cell therapy. Although considerably less frequent than viral encephalitis,, ,  it warrants specific diagnostic and therapeutic consideration due to its distinct anatomical involvement, clinical presentation, and outcome profile. Evidence on viral myelitis after HSCT and CAR T-cell-cell therapy is limited to isolated reports and small series; therefore, we provide a focused clinical overview.

Myelitis may arise from either infectious or non-infectious mechanisms. The differential diagnosis should include autoimmune or immune-mediated demyelinating disorders,, ,  such as multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis; compressive spinal lesions; spinal epidural infection; vascular myelopathy; relapse or malignant involvement of the spinal cord or leptomeninges; nutritional deficiencies; drug-related neurotoxicity; and other transplant-related complications, including chronic GVHD-associated CNS inflammation.

Viral myelitis is defined as inflammation of the spinal cord resulting from direct or immune-mediated viral injury. Infectious etiologies include HHV-6, CMV, VZV, human parvovirus B19 (B19V), and, in isolated reports, adenovirus, HSV and enteroviruses., , ,  Myelitis might be classified as proven/probable (see ) based on the pattern, e.g., by clinical presentation, neuroimaging, and other diagnostic findings. These patterns may include, among others, transverse myelitis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM), myeloradiculitis, and acute flaccid myelitis (AFM).

The overall incidence of viral myelitis after allogeneic HSCT is very low, and published data are limited to small case series. HHV-6 accounts for most reported cases, typically occurring within the first 60 days after transplantation and frequently in cord-blood or haploidentical recipients., ,  VZV, CMV, and Parvovirus B19 are less frequent but well-documented etiologic agents., ,

Myelitis can be associated with a wide range of clinical symptoms, including gait disturbances, weakness, sensory deficit, and impaired bladder and bowel control. Pruritus, pain, or numbness have been identified as important clinical symptoms in a retrospective analysis of 19 allogeneic HSCT recipients with HHV-6 myelitis. The course can be acute or subacute, and relapsing cases have been described in association with autoimmune or GVHD-related inflammation.

Diagnosis relies on spinal MRI and CSF analysis. MRI typically demonstrates T2-weighted hyperintensity within the cervical or thoracic cord; longitudinally extensive lesions involving ≥3 vertebral segments (LETM) are frequent in HHV-6 or CMV infection., ,  CSF studies should include cell count, protein, glucose, however, normal CSF parameters do not exclude disease. Molecular testing by multiplex PCR or NGS panels, such as the FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel (FAMEP), should be considered.,  Although rapid, this panel omits EBV, adenovirus, JC/BK polyomaviruses, and parvovirus B19; therefore, a negative result does not exclude viral myelitis. Targeted PCR or CSF mNGS should be considered in unresolved cases. Qualitative HHV-6 or CMV results require interpretation alongside clinical findings, spinal MRI, quantitative viral load, and blood testing.

Empirical antiviral therapy as suggested for viral encephalitis is reasonable when MRI and clinical findings suggest viral infection, pending confirmation. Treatment should target the underlying etiology according to existing guidelines. HHV-6, CMV, and VZV should follow the same antiviral and dosing principles as for viral encephalitis. VZV myelitis may require corticosteroids if vasculitis is suspected. Parvovirus B19 myelitis may respond to high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin.

No specific prophylaxis against viral myelitis is established, although we suggest following the same recommendations as for viral encephalitis. Vaccination remains essential: a recent study found that poliomyelitis vaccination initiated during the first year after allograft is immunogenic. Therefore, it should be performed in every HSCT recipient.

Reported outcomes of viral myelitis vary. HHV-6 myelitis generally has a favourable prognosis with early antiviral therapy, although residual sensory or sphincter dysfunction can persist., ,

When viral encephalitis/meningitis or myelitis is suspected, the initial diagnostic investigation should include CSF PCR for HSV 1-2, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV6, adenovirus, and JC virus. The likelihood that encephalitis-meningitis/myelitis is caused by a virus should be classified according to probable/proven category. Empirical antiviral therapy with acyclovir or foscarnet should be started immediately in patients with strong clinical and MRI suspicion of viral encephalitis/meningitis or myelitis. The choice of first line empiric antiviral drug should be based on the pre-test probability of HHV6, HSV, VZV or CMV.

The viral encephalitis/meningitis or myelitis treatment response should be evaluated at 2–8 weeks after therapy onset using standardised EBMT categories (Complete response, partial response, stable disease, or progression). Supportive care measures in probable/proven viral encephalitis/meningitis or myelitis should include reduction of immunosuppression whenever feasible, while carefully balancing the risk of GVHD.

neuroscience.title: 5-Fluorouracil-induced severe hyperlactatemic encephalopathy during chemotherapy for advanced colorectal cancer: Case reports and literature review
neuroscience.abstract: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a key drug in the treatment of advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). Although 5-FU is generally well tolerated, a small subset of patients may experience life-threatening neurotoxicity. Among these complications, 5-FU-induced encephalopathy accompanied by severe hyperlactatemia is a particularly serious metabolic emergency. Impaired drug clearance, especially due to underlying renal insufficiency, may substantially increase this risk. In the present study, the cases of three patients with advanced CRC who developed acute, severe impairment of consciousness 48 h after receiving 5-FU-based chemotherapy were retrospectively reviewed. Clinical presentations ranged from aphasia and confusion to deep coma. All patients exhibited marked hyperlactatemia, with peak blood lactate levels of 18.0, 18.19 and 15.56 mmol/l for Cases 1, 2 and 3, respectively. A total of two patients had marked baseline renal impairment (one with chronic kidney disease, the other with end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis). Neuroimaging (CT/CT perfusion/CT angiography/MRI) excluded acute cerebrovascular events in all cases. Chemotherapy was immediately discontinued and intensive supportive care was initiated. For the patient with anuric renal failure, early continuous venovenous hemofiltration was initiated. All three patients achieved complete neurological recovery and normalization of metabolic parameters. Notably, the hemodialysis-dependent patient subsequently underwent successful 5-FU rechallenge using a 50% dose reduction combined with prophylactic post-chemotherapy hemodialysis, without recurrence of neurotoxicity. 5-FU-induced severe hyperlactatemic encephalopathy is a potentially fatal oncological emergency. Underlying renal impairment may lead to the accumulation of toxic metabolites. For patients presenting with extreme hyperlactatemia (>10 mmol/l) and profound impairment of consciousness, early initiation of continuous renal replacement therapy may be an effective strategy to resolve neurological dysfunction. In patients with end-stage renal disease requiring subsequent fluoropyrimidine therapy, substantial dose reduction combined with prophylactic hemodialysis may offer a feasible rechallenge approach. Furthermore, clinicians must consider genetic mutations related to hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Evaluation of these organ-vulnerability genes before chemotherapy warrants further clinical investigation to prevent severe toxicity.
neuroscience.text:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most prevalent and lethal malignancies worldwide. Recent real-world epidemiological studies have shown that, although the overall incidence rate in the elderly population has decreased due to the wider use of screening, the incidence and related mortality of early-onset CRC (age, <50 years) are significantly increasing, and long-term survival remains a major challenge (). In this context, 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)-based regimens continue to serve as the backbone of both adjuvant and palliative chemotherapy for this disease (,). While 5-FU is generally well tolerated, with myelosuppression, mucositis and gastrointestinal toxicity being the most common adverse effects, a small proportion of patients may develop acute, life-threatening neurotoxicity, a condition termed fluorouracil-induced encephalopathy (FIE). Large-scale real-world pharmacovigilance data indicate that such marked metabolic encephalopathy can trigger severe brain edema and elevated intracranial pressure, potentially resulting in an irreversible deep coma or even brain herniation. FIE typically manifests as the sudden onset of confusion, lethargy, speech disturbance or altered muscle tone. Its clinical presentation is highly nonspecific, often mimicking acute cerebrovascular events or other metabolic encephalopathies, which poses substantial challenges for early recognition (). Pharmacovigilance data suggest that the intensive care unit admission rate for FIE can reach 57%, with a mortality rate of ~17% ().

Pathophysiologically, >80% of administered 5-FU is catabolized by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD, encoded by the DPYD gene) in the liver (). While FIE is occasionally complicated by hyperammonemia, metabolic encephalopathy accompanied by severe type B lactic acidosis is considered a more serious condition (). The underlying mechanism is thought to involve inhibition of mitochondrial aconitase by 5-FU metabolites (particularly fluoroacetate), which disrupts the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and forces a metabolic shift toward anaerobic glycolysis, resulting in excessive lactate production ().

Emerging evidence suggests that the risk of this metabolic crisis may reflect impairment of both pathways of drug clearance: Reduced DPD enzymatic activity [due to DPYD polymorphisms such as DPYD*2A (c.1905+1G>A)] impairs hepatic catabolism of the parent drug, while coexisting renal insufficiency compromises the excretion of downstream water-soluble toxic metabolites such as fluoro-beta-alanine (FBAL) (). However, clinical experience in managing the most severe presentations-patients with blood lactate exceeding 15 mmol/l and profound coma-remains limited, and the role of early continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in this context has not been well characterized.

The present study reported three cases of 5-FU-induced severe hyperlactatemic encephalopathy (peak lactate 15.56-18.19 mmol/l), including two patients with significant baseline renal impairment, all of whom achieved complete neurological recovery. The clinical features, the role of CRRT in acute management and a successful rechallenge strategy in a hemodialysis-dependent patient were discussed to provide information on the early identification and treatment of this rare but potentially fatal complication.

The clinical timeline, serial blood lactate levels and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores () of all three patients treated at Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital (Hangzhou, China) are summarized in .

In April 2026, a 75-year-old man was admitted for palliative chemotherapy for rectal cancer with liver metastases. The patient's baseline renal function indicated CKD, with a serum creatinine of 201 µmol/l (normal range, 57-111 µmol/l). A genetic test report from October 2020 indicated that the patient's tumor was wild-type for KRAS, NRAS and BRAF. In addition, the patient's DPYD genotype was wild-type [rs3918290 (C/C)]. However, ~48 h after receiving the 5-FU, leucovorin and irinotecan (FOLFIRI) plus cetuximab regimen (standard dose of 2,400 mg/m²), the patient suddenly developed nausea and vomiting, followed by rapid neurological deterioration, manifesting as ataxia, limb tremors, aphasia and lethargy. The patient became comatose (GCS score of 6), underwent emergency endotracheal intubation and was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) in April 2026. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe lactic acidosis: Blood lactate was 11.92 mmol/l (normal range, 0.5-2.2 mmol/l) at 56 h post-chemotherapy, which subsequently rose to a peak of 18.0 mmol/l at 60 h, with a pH of 7.378 and a base excess of -8.3 mmol/l (normal range, -2 to +3 mmol/l). Head CT and CT perfusion (CTP) imaging showed no acute hemorrhage or extensive ischemia (). A diagnosis of 5-FU-induced metabolic encephalopathy was established. Following immediate drug discontinuation and aggressive fluid resuscitation, the metabolic disturbances resolved rapidly. Repeat arterial blood gas analysis the next day showed that lactate had decreased to 2.8 mmol/l. The patient was successfully extubated and transferred back to the general ward. Following the completion of radiotherapy in May 2026, the patient has been under regular outpatient follow-up at our institution. The surveillance protocol includes monthly evaluations of serum tumor markers and imaging assessments every three months; to date, there has been no evidence of tumor progression.

A 66-year-old woman with widely metastatic colon cancer had uremia and had received regular hemodialysis for 14 years. The modified folinic acid, fluorouracil and oxaliplatin (mFOLFOX6) chemotherapy regimen (standard dose of 2,400 mg/m²) was administered during the interdialytic period. At ~48 h after chemotherapy administration, the patient suddenly became deeply comatose (GCS score of 3) with flaccid paralysis of all four limbs [muscle strength grade 0()] and was transferred to the ICU in March 2026. Laboratory tests revealed severe decompensated metabolic acidosis: pH 7.181 (normal range, 7.35-7.45), peak blood lactate 18.19 mmol/l and HCO3- 11.1 mmol/l (normal range, 18-23 mmol/l). Emergency head CTP imaging and plain head CT () ruled out intracranial hemorrhage and large-vessel lesions. Additionally, a bedside ambulatory electroencephalogram (AEEG) showed moderate-to-marked abnormalities, characterized by a lack of background alpha waves and continuous, diffuse moderate-to-high amplitude polymorphic theta (4-7 Hz) and delta (2-3 Hz) waves, consistent with severe metabolic encephalopathy () (). Considering that the anuric renal failure drastically exacerbated the accumulation of metabolites, the ICU initiated CRRT at 60 h (12 h after coma onset) using a continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) modality. Within 3 h after starting CRRT (at 63 h), the patient's level of consciousness improved markedly, with the GCS score rising rapidly from 3 to 12. Following discussion with the patient's family and obtaining informed consent, CRRT was temporarily paused due to financial constraints. The medical team closely monitored the patient's clinical status. Blood lactate levels remained stable between 65 and 117 h (ranging from 1.3 to 4.1 mmol/l). By 123 h, the GCS score reached 15 (fully awake), and the patient was transferred out of the ICU in a stable condition.

Notably, ~1 month after the patient's initial encephalopathy crisis (April 2026), the patient required further chemotherapy due to tumor progression. The medical team planned a cautious rechallenge strategy. In April 2026, the patient received mFOLFOX6 at a 50% dose reduction. Simultaneously, in collaboration with the nephrology department, early prophylactic post-chemotherapy hemodialysis was scheduled. Under strict clinical monitoring, the patient remained fully conscious (GCS score maintained at 15) throughout the chemotherapy process, without any recurrence of neurological abnormalities. A follow-up arterial blood gas analysis on the day after chemotherapy showed that the blood lactate level was within the normal range (1.94 mmol/l), with a pH of 7.31. Laboratory and clinical data confirmed that this strategy of substantial dose reduction combined with prophylactic dialysis successfully prevented the re-accumulation of toxic metabolites. The patient ultimately completed chemotherapy without complications and was discharged safely. In June 2026, the patient developed multiple pelvic metastases, which were confirmed by biopsy as originating from the primary CRC. The patient was subsequently lost to follow-up at our hospital and is currently receiving palliative care at a local institution.

A 74-year-old woman with a history of cerebral infarction was admitted with rectal cancer and abdominopelvic metastases following surgery in January 2026. After receiving a reduced-dose FOLFIRI regimen (2,000 mg/m², ~80% of the standard dose) combined with bevacizumab, the patient suffered sudden loss of consciousness and increased systemic muscle tone 48 h post-chemotherapy in January 2026. Blood gas analysis showed a markedly elevated lactate level of 15.56 mmol/l. Emergency head CTP () demonstrated no significant perfusion deficits. Furthermore, MRI/diffusion-weighted imaging and plain head CT () were also performed, which definitively excluded acute cerebral ischemia. In addition, bedside AEEG revealed the disappearance of background alpha waves, which were replaced by diffuse medium-to-high-amplitude polymorphic theta and delta waves occurring in prolonged runs, providing definitive electrophysiological evidence for severe toxic-metabolic encephalopathy () (). After chemotherapy was discontinued and continuous intravenous hydration was administered to promote metabolism, the patient's consciousness fully recovered within 24 h. A repeat arterial blood gas analysis showed a lactate level of 2.6 mmol/l and a pH of 7.446, with the acid-base imbalance corrected. During the latest outpatient follow-up in July 2026, the patient was undergoing antineoplastic treatment with a regimen consisting of irinotecan, raltitrexed and bevacizumab.

A retrospective review of the patient's medical records revealed that a pharmacogenomic panel conducted in December 2025 (prior to chemotherapy) showed wild-type genotypes for common DPYD variants [including rs3918290 (CC)]. Despite the absence of pathogenic DPYD mutations and the preemptive 20% dose reduction in the chemotherapy regimen, the patient still developed a life-threatening hyperlactatemic encephalopathy crisis. This underscores the rapid onset and unpredictability of 5-FU neurotoxicity in susceptible elderly patients. However, the same report revealed high-risk variants in other genes: ERCC1 [rs11615 (A/G)] and GSTP1 [rs1695 (A/A)] (). These genetic variants are associated with increased nephrotoxicity and severe overall drug toxicity. This suggests that the patient's organs were highly vulnerable to chemotherapy before treatment.

The most striking feature of this case series is the severe hyperlactatemia that suddenly emerged 48 h after 5-FU chemotherapy. In previous reports, peak lactate levels in 5-FU-related lactic acidosis generally range from 5-10 mmol/l (,). However, the lactate peaks in the patients of the present study reached 15.56-18.19 mmol/l and were accompanied by severely impaired neurological function. According to current biochemical models, degradation products of 5-FU (particularly FBAL) have potential mitochondrial toxicity and can inhibit key enzymes of the TCA cycle (). The anaerobic conversion of intracellular pyruvate to lactate and the depletion of energy substrates in the central nervous system () may together underlie the sudden deep coma and diffuse brain electrophysiological abnormalities (such as the slow-wave presentation on the AEEG of Case 3) observed in the present cases.

Given the critical clinical importance of rapid lactate monitoring, emerging diagnostic technologies, such as near-infrared fluorescent nanoprobes for highly sensitive L-lactate detection in CRC, may offer valuable translational potential in the future ().

The terminal toxic metabolites of 5-FU, including FBAL and its downstream product fluoroacetate, depend on renal excretion (). Of the three patients in this series, two had significant baseline renal impairment: Case 1 had chronic kidney disease with a serum creatinine of 201 µmol/l, and Case 2 had end-stage renal disease requiring maintenance hemodialysis. In both patients, the DPYD genotype was wild-type and DPD activity was therefore predicted to be normal. This suggests that renal impairment alone may be an important independent risk factor: When renal excretion is impaired, normal hepatic catabolism appears insufficient to prevent accumulation of water-soluble metabolites, which is consistent with the delayed hyperlactatemic episodes occurring 48-72 h after administration that were observed in Cases 1 and 2, and with previous reports of 5-FU encephalopathy in patients with end-stage renal disease (,) ().

Genetic factors beyond DPYD may also modulate individual susceptibility. Case 3 carried variants in ERCC1 (rs11615) and GSTP1 (rs1695) in addition to a wild-type DPYD genotype, and developed severe encephalopathy despite a 20% preemptive dose reduction. ERCC1 participates in nucleotide excision repair, and GSTP1 participates in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species; reduced activity of either may increase the susceptibility of renal tubular cells to cytotoxic stress. These variants may therefore have contributed to the acute kidney injury observed after chemotherapy, which may in turn have impaired metabolite clearance (). It should be emphasized that this association is observational, is based on a single patient and requires validation in larger cohorts before any causal role can be assigned.

Prevention in such patients should not rely on DPYD genotyping alone. International guidelines recommend pretreatment screening for DPYD variants such as DPYD*2A before fluoropyrimidine-based therapy (), and genotype-guided dose adjustment reduces the risk of severe toxicity. Because dosing based on body surface area does not capture interindividual variability in drug exposure, therapeutic drug monitoring of the 5-FU area under the curve may provide an additional safeguard, although it was not available during the crises described here ().

Regarding the therapeutic role of extracorporeal clearance in acute 5-FU encephalopathy, the following should be considered. For mild to moderate 5-FU encephalopathy, drug discontinuation and intensive hydration are usually effective (). In patients with renal insufficiency, severe lactic acidosis (>10 mmol/l) and oliguria or anuria, however, fluid resuscitation alone is unlikely to provide adequate clearance and carries a substantial risk of volume overload. In such life-threatening presentations (Case 2: pH 7.18, GCS 3), early initiation of CRRT appeared to be beneficial through two mechanisms.

First, CRRT provides direct extracorporeal clearance of the parent drug and its neurotoxic metabolites. 5-FU is a small molecule (130 Da) with high water solubility and low plasma protein binding (~10%), and FBAL and fluoroacetate also have low molecular weights. These properties make them amenable to blood purification, and previous pharmacokinetic work indicates that hemodialysis efficiently removes circulating 5-FU and FBAL.

Second, CRRT corrects the acid-base and energy disturbances. Lactate is a small molecule (~90 Da) and is removed across the extracorporeal circuit, while bicarbonate-containing replacement fluid corrects the extracellular acidosis. In Case 2, lactate fell and the GCS score improved within a short period after CVVH was started. This temporal association is consistent with a causal contribution of extracorporeal clearance, although causality cannot be established from a single case.

Regarding prophylactic renal replacement therapy before rechallenge, blood purification also has a preventive role. In patients with end-stage renal disease who require further fluoropyrimidine therapy, initiating hemodialysis soon after chemotherapy, combined with a substantial dose reduction, may prevent metabolite accumulation. Case 2 illustrates this approach: The 5-FU dose was reduced by 50% and prophylactic hemodialysis was scheduled after each cycle; no neurological toxicity recurred ().

In terms of differential diagnosis of hyperammonemic encephalopathy, the following may be considered. Among the central nervous system toxicities induced by 5-FU, hyperammonemic encephalopathy is the most commonly reported subtype in previous literature (). From a pathophysiological perspective, hyperammonemia and hyperlactatemia share a common mechanism of metabolic blockade: Toxic intermediate metabolites of 5-FU (particularly fluoroacetate) can strongly inhibit aconitase, a key enzyme in the mitochondrial TCA cycle, leading to a marked reduction in the production of intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Because the urea cycle in the liver (the process of converting ammonia to urea) is highly ATP-dependent, energy depletion inevitably leads to disruption of the urea cycle, subsequently triggering abnormally elevated blood ammonia (). Concurrently, the blockade of the TCA cycle forces cellular metabolism to shift towards anaerobic glycolysis, causing a massive conversion of pyruvate to lactate.

However, the clinical phenotype of the cases in this series is more consistent with an encephalopathy crisis driven primarily by severe lactic acidosis. Typical patients with 5-FU-induced hyperammonemia mostly exhibit mild to moderate elevations in plasma lactate (usually <8-10 mmol/l) and rarely present with profound decompensated acidemia (pH <7.2) (). By contrast, the patients of the present study (especially those with underlying end-stage renal disease or CKD) experienced markedly impaired excretion of toxic metabolites, causing a nearly complete blockade of mitochondrial function in target organs (particularly the energy-demanding central nervous system). To maintain basic survival, central neurons were forced to rely entirely on anaerobic metabolism, thereby producing a degree of hyperlactataemia rarely reported in this setting (peak blood lactate levels as high as 15.56-18.19 mmol/l).

This marked acidic shift in the intracellular and extracellular microenvironment not only directly interferes with normal neurotransmitter transmission and ion channel function () but is also a direct biochemical cause of sudden aphasia, ataxia and even a deep coma with a GCS of 3. Therefore, although the possibility of concurrent hyperammonemia during the disease course in the patients of the present study cannot be entirely ruled out, the severe hyperlactatemia and its resulting fatal acid-base imbalance are clearly the principal mechanisms underlying the clinical phenotype and prognosis of the crises in this series.

For patients with CRC who have experienced severe 5-FU encephalopathy but still require further treatment, the following options of subsequent antineoplastic treatment should be considered. In terms of emergency antidotal therapy and dose-reduced rechallenge, in patients who develop early, life-threatening 5-FU toxicity within 96 h of administration, the Food and Drug Administration-approved antidote uridine triacetate should be administered as early as possible, since it competitively inhibits incorporation of toxic metabolites into RNA and reduces mortality in fulminant fluoropyrimidine toxicity (). When the original regimen cannot be replaced and neurological recovery is complete, rechallenge with a substantially reduced dose is feasible: A French national survey of 5-FU encephalopathy supports dose reduction rather than permanent withdrawal (), and Case 2 shows that a 50% dose reduction combined with prophylactic post-chemotherapy hemodialysis allowed the patient with uremia to complete further cycles safely.

In terms of switching to regimens with alternative metabolic pathways, in patients with confirmed pathogenic DPYD variants, or in those who remain intolerant to 5-FU despite dose reduction, re-exposure to fluoropyrimidines should be avoided and a regimen that does not depend on DPD metabolism should be selected. Raltitrexed, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor, has antitumor activity comparable to 5-FU in CRC and bypasses the DPD pathway entirely, making it an appropriate intravenous alternative (). Trifluridine/tipiracil (TAS-102) is also not degraded by DPD and provides an additional oral option for such patients ().

Several limitations of the present study warrant consideration. First, this is a retrospective case series of only three patients without a control group, so the observations cannot establish the efficacy of any specific intervention. Second, 5-FU therapeutic drug monitoring was not available during the acute crises; systemic accumulation of toxic metabolites therefore remains an inference rather than a demonstrated mechanism, and the pathogenic role of renal impairment, although biologically plausible and supported by the clinical courses, cannot be proven from these data. Third, the proposed association between non-DPYD variants (ERCC1 rs11615 and GSTP1 rs1695) and organ vulnerability is strictly observational; mechanistic validation in larger cohorts is required before a causal relationship can be considered. Finally, the strategy of dose reduction combined with prophylactic hemodialysis is described in only one patient and should not be considered established practice.

In conclusion, 5-FU-induced severe hyperlactatemic encephalopathy is a challenging oncological emergency. Underlying renal insufficiency may be an important risk factor for the accumulation of toxic metabolites. For patients presenting with significantly elevated blood lactate (>10 mmol/l) combined with severe impairment of consciousness, early identification, immediate drug discontinuation and prompt intervention with CRRT are effective strategies for improving clinical outcomes. Furthermore, clinicians must look beyond standard DPYD screening. Attention should also be paid to genetic mutations associated with severe hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity (such as ERCC1 and GSTP1). Evaluation of these ‘organ-vulnerability’ genes warrants further validation in larger cohorts, especially for elderly patients, to prevent acute organ failure and subsequent severe metabolic decompensation.

neuroscience.title: Clinical characteristics and treatment strategies of ovarian teratomas associated with anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis based on a case series
neuroscience.abstract: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis is a potentially life-threatening yet reversible complication associated with ovarian teratoma. This study aims to systematically analyze the clinical features of anti-NMDAR encephalitis related to ovarian teratoma, with the goal of enhancing our understanding of the disease.A retrospective analysis was performed on 17 patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis associated with ovarian teratomas, who were admitted to Xuanwu Hospital, Capital Medical University, from August 2015 to August 2025. A systematic analysis was performed on their complete clinical data, including demographic characteristics, prodromal symptoms, typical neurological and psychiatric manifestations, cerebrospinal fluid and neuroimaging findings, anti-NMDAR antibody in cerebrospinal fluid, pathological features of the ovarian teratomas, comprehensive treatment strategies and follow-up outcomes.In this study, the age of the included patients was 25 years (21, 29). The time from symptom onset to diagnosis was 16 days (10.5, 27). The time from hospital admission to diagnosis was 4 days (2.5, 7). Two patients had a history of teratomas and methotrexate treatment. 15 patients (15/17, 88%) were directly admitted to the intensive care unit, while only 2 (2/17, 12%) were treated in general wards. The patients predominantly presented with multiple neurological abnormalities without clinical signs of teratoma compression. All patients received immunotherapy and tumor resection, and all patients achieved clinical improvement. At 3 months after surgery, mRS ≤ 2 was achieved in patients (4/17, 24%), mRS 3–4 in 5 paitents (5/17, 29%), and mRS 5 in 8 patients (8/17, 47%). Although all patients met the pre-defined criterion of clinical improvement in at least one neurological symptom, functional recovery remained limited.A history of teratoma and methotrexate treatment may be associated with a higher risk of teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis; however, this observation was based on only two patients and warrants further investigation. The disease is characterized by acute onset and rapid progression, and clinical improvement can be achieved through multidisciplinary collaboration combined with prompt immunotherapy and tumor resection.
neuroscience.text:
Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis is an inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system characterized by IgG antibodies directed against the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor (NMDAR) (). It can produce a constellation of symptoms resembling infectious encephalitis, and some patients may present exclusively with neurological and psychiatric manifestations (). Among patients diagnosed with anti-NMDAR encephalitis (NMDAR-E), an underlying neoplasm is identified in approximately 25–40% of cases, and around 90% of the associated tumors are ovarian teratomas (). More than 80% of patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis achieve recovery (); however, a small proportion may be left with sequelae such as neurological dysfunction, with an associated mortality rate of approximately 7% (). Several studies have characterized anti-NMDAR encephalitis in the setting of ovarian teratoma (, ). He et al. found that brain MRI and electroencephalography lacked specificity for the diagnosis of the disease, whereas detection of anti-NMDAR antibodies in cerebrospinal fluid was crucial for diagnosis ().

Chefdeville et al. analyzed the immunopathological features of 27 ovarian teratomas associated with anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Their results showed that the neuroglial tissue of three NMDAR-E-associated mature teratomas exhibited histopathological characteristics of central nervous system neuroglial tumors. NMDAR-E-associated teratomas also differed from sporadic ovarian teratomas by consistent and prominent infiltration of the nervous tissue component by immune cells (). These findings provide important experience for diagnosing and treating the disease. However, because of its rarity, most studies focus on single cases, and systematic analyses remain lacking. In addition, patients often initially present with psychiatric or neurological symptoms and are referred to psychiatric or neurological departments, so the interval from tumor detection to definitive surgical intervention tends to be prolonged even when a teratoma is present. This delay may cause patients to miss the optimal window for treatment. Therefore, there is an urgent need to analyze the clinical characteristics and treatment strategies, which could improve patient prognosis.

In this study, 17 cases of ovarian teratomas associated with anti-NMDAR encephalitis were retrieved and analyzed to improve clinicians’ understanding of the disease and facilitate early diagnosis and treatment.

This retrospective study was based on clinical data from 17 patients diagnosed with anti-NMDAR encephalitis coexisting with ovarian teratoma, all of whom were admitted to Xuanwu Hospital, Capital Medical University between August 2015 and August 2025. Clinicopathologic characteristics were systematically retrieved from archived medical records. The patients met the diagnostic criteria of anti-NMDAR encephalitis (, ) and ovarian teratomas. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) positive anti-NMDAR antibody in cerebrospinal fluid; (2) rapid onset (within 3 months) with one or more of the following: abnormal behavior or mental state; cognitive impairment; speech disorders; epileptic seizure; involuntary movement or movement disorders; decreased level of consciousness; central ventilation disorder or autonomic nervous dysfunction; (3) ovarian teratoma was confirmed by postoperative pathology. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) exclusion of other causes of encephalitis; (2) lack of clinicopathologic data. All anti-NMDAR antibody tests were performed using cell-based immunofluorescence assays (CBA).

We collected demographic information, laboratory test results, ultrasound and imaging findings, and postoperative pathological data from the included patients. Among these findings, abnormal cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) results were defined as the presence of specific parenchymal-related abnormalities, including medial temporal lobe or hippocampal involvement (e.g., FLAIR hyperintensity or atrophy), cortical or subcortical FLAIR hyperintensities, leptomeningeal enhancement, white-matter lesions, and ventriculomegaly. Isolated age-related changes were not classified as abnormal. Abnormal electroencephalography (EEG) results were defined as any reported abnormality, including diffuse or multifocal slow-wave activity, delta waves or extreme delta brushes, focal slowing, epileptiform discharges, and electrographic seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure, white blood cell count, and protein levels were interpreted based on institutional reference ranges (opening pressure: 80–180 mmH₂O; white blood cell count: 0–5 × 106/L; protein: 15–45 mg/dL). Detailed findings for each patient are presented in . The modified Rankin Scale (mRS) was employed to comprehensively evaluate patients’ neurological status at admission and throughout postoperative follow-up. As a widely recognized instrument, the mRS assesses functional independence and the degree of disability in individuals recovering from stroke or other neurological impairments (). In our study, clinical improvement was defined as documented resolution or notable reduction in at least one of the major neurological symptoms listed in the diagnostic criteria. Besides, an mRS score ≤2 indicated a favorable prognosis, a score of 3–4 signified moderate neurological disability, and a score of 5 represented severe neurological disability.

Examinations of the patients.

US, Ultrasound.

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 29.0. Quantitative data are expressed as median with interquartile range, while categorical data are presented as number (%).

The basic clinical information of the 17 patients is shown in . All patients were young females, with ages ranging from 16 to 40 years (median, 25 years; IQR, 21–29 years), including two patients under 18 years of age. Six patients had a history of delivery. The time from symptom onset to diagnosis ranged from 5 to 34 days (median, 16 days; IQR, 10.5–27 days), and the time from hospital admission to diagnosis ranged from 1 to 25 days (median, 4 days; IQR, 2.5–7 days). Review of the medical history revealed that one patient (Case 5) had undergone right ovarian teratoma excision 5 years before disease onset and had surgery for ectopic pregnancy 3 years prior to onset. One patient (Case 6) was found to have a left ovarian teratoma on pelvic ultrasound 1 month before disease onset. One patient (Case 8) had undergone surgery for ectopic pregnancy 1 year before disease onset. Another patient (Case 16) gave birth to twins, one of whom was diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy, while the other was a gene carrier. Both patients with a prior history of teratoma (Cases 5 and 6) self-reported previous methotrexate treatment for ectopic pregnancy; however, detailed regimens, doses, and treatment timelines were not retrievable from the medical records.

The general information and clinical characteristics of the patients.

Among the 17 patients, 13 (13/17, 76%) had an acute onset and 4 (4/17, 24%) had a subacute onset. Prodromal symptoms, including headache, fever, or both, were present in 12 patients (12/17, 71%), while the remaining 5 patients had no prodromal symptoms. The initial symptoms mainly included psychiatric or behavioral abnormalities, cognitive impairment, and diplopia. Specifically, 12 patients (12/17, 71%) presented with psychiatric or behavioral abnormalities as the initial symptom, 3 patients (3/17, 18%) presented with cognitive impairment as the first symptom, and 2 patients (2/17, 12%) presented with diplopia as the first symptom. The most common clinical manifestations were psychiatric or behavioral abnormalities (16/17, 94%) and involuntary movements (15/17, 88%), followed by seizures (13/17, 76%) and impaired consciousness (13/17, 76%), cognitive impairment (8/17, 47%) and central hypoventilation (8/17, 47%). None of the patients exhibited clinical signs related to teratoma compression, such as abdominal pain or distension, at the time of admission. The details are shown in .

Pelvic examination findings are presented in . Sixteen patients underwent pelvic evaluation via ultrasound (transvaginal ultrasound for married patients, transabdominal ultrasound for unmarried patients). Ultrasound detected ovarian teratoma in 11 patients. In 4 patients, teratoma was not identified on ultrasound but was detected on subsequent CT and/or MRI. One patient (Case 5) had imaging findings suggestive of ovarian cyst/cystadenoma on ultrasound, CT and MRI; however, the final pathological diagnosis was teratoma.

Cranial MRI findings were abnormal in 10 patients (10/17, 59%) and showed no abnormality in 7 patients (7/17, 41%). The abnormalities mainly involved the medial temporal lobes or hippocampi, cerebral white matter, leptomeninges, or the ventricular system, as detailed per patient in . Electroencephalography (EEG) showed abnormalities in 12 patients (12/17, 71%). The most common abnormality was diffuse or multifocal slow-wave activity (7/17, 41%), followed by delta waves or delta brushes (4/17, 24%); one patient exhibited status epilepticus on EEG (1/17, 6%). The specific EEG findings for each patient are detailed in .

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) detection showed positive anti-NMDA receptor antibodies and elevated white blood cell counts in all 17 patients. All pressure readings were obtained in the lateral decubitus position. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands were positive in 10 patients (). Elevated CSF pressure was observed in 10 patients, and increased CSF protein was found in 4 patients. The median CSF pressure was 200 mmH₂O (IQR: 150, 245), the median CSF white blood cell count was 32 × 106/L (IQR: 17.5, 66.5), and the median CSF protein level was 31 mg/dL (IQR: 20.1, 45.5) (; ).

Serological tests revealed elevated CA125 levels in 4 of the 17 patients, while CA125 was normal in the remaining patients.

All patients received first-line immunotherapy, including corticosteroids (17/17, 100%), intravenous immunoglobulin (16/17, 94%), and plasma exchange (14/17, 82%). Second-line immunotherapy was administered as rituximab alone in 9 patients, cyclophosphamide alone in 1 patient, and rituximab combined with cyclophosphamide in 1 patient. Long-term immunosuppression included mycophenolate mofetil (11 patients) and azathioprine (1 patient). One patient with refractory severe anti-NMDAR encephalitis also received bortezomib, and another patient with severe anti-NMDAR encephalitis complicated by super-refractory status epilepticus received additional tocilizumab. Fifteen patients (15/17, 88%) were admitted to the intensive care unit, whereas 2 (2/17, 12%) were treated in general wards. During hospitalization, 14 patients (14/17, 82%) required mechanical ventilation during hospitalization.

All procedures were completed laparoscopically with no conversions to open surgery, and no perioperative complications related to the operations were observed. Operative time ranged from 27 to 112 min, with a median of 35 min. Except for 2 cases that lasted over 1 h, all others were completed within 1 h. Fifteen patients underwent surgery during the acute phase, with a median interval from disease onset to surgery of 39 days (range 17–51 days). Two patients underwent surgery during the recovery phase, at 46 days and 143 days after onset, respectively. Among the 17 patients, 1 had bilateral ovarian teratomas and underwent bilateral ovarian teratoma resection. Ten patients had right-sided ovarian teratomas: 6 underwent right ovarian teratoma resection and 4 underwent right salpingo-oophorectomy. Four patients had left-sided ovarian teratomas: 1 underwent left ovarian teratoma resection and 3 underwent left salpingo-oophorectomy. Two patients required two surgical interventions during the acute phase: one first underwent right salpingo-oophorectomy for a right teratoma, followed by left ovarian teratoma resection for a left teratoma; the other underwent left ovarian teratoma resection twice for left-sided teratomas (). Postoperative pathology revealed immature teratoma with focal brain and neural tube tissue in 2 patients. The remaining 15 patients were diagnosed with mature cystic teratoma, among whom 10 showed brain/neural tissue on microscopic examination ().

The treatment and prognosis of the patients.

IVIG, intravenous immunoglobulin.

During treatment, the most common complications were bacterial pneumonia (15/17, 88%), electrolyte disturbances (11/17, 65%), anemia (11/17, 65%), and abnormal liver function (10/17, 59%). Other complications included respiratory failure (7/17, 41%), urinary tract infection (7/17, 41%), gastrointestinal bleeding (7/17, 41%), stress ulcer (2/17, 12%), pseudomembranous colitis (2/17, 12%), and deep vein thrombosis (5/17, 29%). Notably, 1 patient developed super-refractory status epilepticus, 3 had severe anti-NMDAR encephalitis, and 4 exhibited paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity syndrome.

We also assessed the prognosis of all patients at 1 and 3 months after surgery. At admission, the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score was 3 in 1 patient and 5 in the other 16. After neurological treatment, the mRS score improved to 1 in 2 patients, while the remaining 15 still had an mRS score of 5. At 1 month after surgery, 3 patients (3/17, 18%) had a favorable outcome, 5 (5/17, 29%) had moderate neurological disability, and the remaining 9 (9/17, 53%) still had severe neurological disability. At 3 months after surgery, 4 patients (4/17, 24%) had a favorable outcome, 5 (5/17, 29%) had moderate neurological disability, and 8 (8/17, 47%) remained with severe neurological disability. Based on the pre-defined criteria described in Methods, all 17 patients achieved clinical improvement after completing immunotherapy and surgical treatment, including the two patients who required a second operation (Cases 8 and 15). No recurrence, death, or loss to follow-up occurred during the follow-up period (; ).

Case 5 had undergone laparoscopic right ovarian teratoma resection 5 years before disease onset. Three years before onset, laparoscopic surgery for a right tubal ectopic pregnancy revealed no abnormalities in the right ovary. After disease onset, both ultrasound and CT indicated a right ovarian cyst, while MRI suggested a right ovarian cystadenoma. At admission, the mRS score was 3. Following medical treatment, the patient showed notable improvement, with the mRS score decreasing to 1. Therefore, surgery was performed during the recovery phase, 46 days after symptom onset. Intraoperatively, a 5 × 7 cm teratoma was identified in the right ovary, and a right salpingo-oophorectomy was carried out. Pathological examination confirmed a mature ovarian teratoma, with no brain or neural tissue detected.

Case 8 had undergone left salpingectomy for ectopic pregnancy 1 year before disease onset, with no notable abnormalities observed in either ovary during that surgery. After the onset of symptoms, ultrasounds indicated an ovarian cyst or a teratoma, and MRI suggested a teratoma. Therefore, surgery was performed on day 51 after onset. Intraoperatively, a 3 × 3 cm teratoma was found in the right ovary, whereas the left ovary appeared normal. A right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Postoperative pathology revealed a mature cystic teratoma containing mature brain tissue. After surgery, the patient’s symptoms persisted without improvement, and the titer of anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid remained 1:320 (strongly positive). Subsequent ultrasound and CT identified a teratoma in the left ovary. Therefore, a second laparoscopic surgery was performed 158 days after the first procedure. During this surgery, a 4 × 5 cm teratoma was found in the left ovary, and a left ovarian cystectomy was performed. Pathology also showed a mature cystic teratoma with abundant mature neural tissue.

Case 15 had a history of smoking and alcohol use, and high-risk sexual behavior, and her brother had a history of Japanese encephalitis and epilepsy. The first surgery was performed 40 days after disease onset. Intraoperatively, a 2 × 4 cm teratoma was found in the left ovary, and left ovarian cystectomy was performed. Pathology indicated a mature cystic teratoma without microscopic evidence of brain or neural tissue. Postoperatively, the patient showed no improvement, and anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid remained strongly positive. Subsequent ultrasound and MRI both suggested persistence of a left ovarian teratoma, prompting a second surgery 36 days later. During the second surgery, a 3 × 3 cm teratoma was found in the left ovary, and a left ovarian cystectomy was performed. The pathological findings were consistent with the previous result: a mature cystic teratoma without brain or neural tissue.

Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is the most common autoimmune encephalitis (), and it was first reported in 2007 (). Advances in medicine have revealed that the presence of teratomas in female patients is a notable contributor to anti-NMDAR encephalitis. This teratoma-associated form of encephalitis presents with a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, including psychiatric symptoms, seizures, cognitive decline, language disturbances, movement disorders, and other neurological deficits. If not diagnosed and treated promptly, the condition can lead to severe neurological sequelae or even prove fatal. Nevertheless, given the rarity of the disease, the existing literature is largely limited to individual case reports, which poses challenges in identifying common patterns across cases. Consequently, expanding the sample size to systematically investigate the shared characteristics of this condition is essential for deepening our understanding of the disease.

In our study, all 17 patients were young females with acute or subacute onset, most commonly acute. More than 70% presented with prodromal symptoms, including fever and/or headache. Among the 10 patients with headache, 7 had elevated CSF opening pressure, suggesting that headache may partly reflect intracranial hypertension in these patients. Psychiatric and behavioral abnormalities were the most common initial symptoms. The most prevalent clinical manifestations included psychiatric and behavioral disturbances, involuntary movements, seizures, and impaired consciousness (). In addition to the presence of positive anti-NMDAR antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), our study also identified abnormalities, notably the presence of specific oligoclonal bands in the CSF of the majority of patients, which was consistent with previous research findings (). However, due to the rarity of the condition, screening for anti-NMDAR antibodies in patients with ovarian teratoma is not indicated currently (). Previous studies have shown that cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) in patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis often lack specific manifestations. In this study, cranial MRI revealed abnormal signals in more than half of the patients. EEG recordings from seven patients revealed diffuse or multifocal slow-wave activity, whereas the characteristic EEG patterns typically associated with anti-NMDAR encephalitis—such as extreme delta brush or delta waves—were observed in only four cases. Although these ancillary findings were generally non-specific, they still played an important role in differentiating this condition from other neurological disorders and provided valuable supportive evidence for the diagnosis. Despite updates to diagnostic and treatment guidelines for autoimmune encephalitis issued by obstetrics, gynecology, and neurology departments in 2022, the interval from symptom onset to diagnosis in teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis often remains prolonged. This delay is largely attributable to the younger age at onset, the nonspecific nature of clinical manifestations, and the absence of distinctive findings on auxiliary examinations (). In this study, the time from onset to diagnosis in 17 patients ranged from 5 to 34 days, with an average exceeding 2 weeks. Therefore, the possibility of this disease should be considered in patients suspected of having viral encephalitis or psychiatric disorders, especially young female patients. Clinicians should promptly test for anti-NMDAR antibodies in cerebrospinal fluid and conduct differential diagnosis as early as possible to avoid delayed management.

Approximately 80% of patients could recover if timely treatment is provided, and early diagnosis and intervention are important prognostic factors (, ). Current studies recommend transvaginal ultrasound as the first-line screening tool. When ultrasound fails to detect a suspected teratoma, more sensitive modalities such as CT or MRI should be considered (, ). In our study, Case 8 underwent three ultrasound examinations during hospitalization. The first two suggested a possible right ovarian cyst, while the third raised suspicion of a teratoma, which was later confirmed by MRI. Ultrasound findings are highly operator- and experience-dependent, suggesting that repeated imaging evaluations and a combination of modalities may enhance teratoma detection. Although pelvic MRI is generally considered superior to CT, pelvic CT remains a viable alternative in some cases due to its shorter scanning time and better tolerance in certain patients.

The primary treatments for teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis include immunotherapy and tumor resection (). Immunotherapy encompasses first-line therapy (corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange), second-line therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide), long-term maintenance therapy (mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine), escalation therapy (tocilizumab), and adjunctive therapy (methotrexate and bortezomib) (, ). These immunotherapies work by suppressing antibody production, thereby reducing the pathogenic impact of antibodies on neuronal receptors (). All patients experiencing a first episode of anti-NMDAR encephalitis should receive first-line immunotherapy. If no improvement is observed after using two or more first-line therapies, second-line immunotherapy should be initiated promptly to improve patient outcomes (). For patients who show little improvement after intensive first-line therapy or following second-line therapy, long-term maintenance immunotherapy may be considered. Escalation or adjunctive immunotherapy should be reserved for severe, refractory cases of encephalitis ().

Early tumor resection has been shown to obviously improve outcomes in patients with teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis (, ), whereas delayed resection is linked to a poorer prognosis (). Therefore, it is widely accepted that systemic and neurological complications should not be regarded as absolute contraindications to surgery, even in patients with elevated anesthetic and surgical risks (). All patients in our study underwent surgical intervention. Our findings underscore the need for a multidisciplinary approach involving neurology, intensive care, gynecology, and anesthesiology in the management of these patients. A comprehensive preoperative evaluation is crucial for developing a coordinated treatment strategy, establishing perioperative protocols, and preparing for potential emergencies. Surgery should be scheduled at an appropriate time after standardized systemic therapy. Intraoperatively, efforts should focus on minimizing operative duration while maintaining close monitoring of vital signs. In this study, two patients underwent surgery during the recovery phase, supporting the notion that surgical intervention at this stage is safe and feasible for those who respond well to immunotherapy ().

Interestingly, in our study, two patients (Case 8 and Case 15) underwent two surgical procedures during their disease course. Case 8 initially underwent right salpingo-oophorectomy for a right ovarian teratoma; however, neither the disease course nor anti-NMDAR antibody showed improvement. Postoperative imaging revealed a left ovarian teratoma, prompting a second surgery for left-sided lesion resection. Case 15 required two left ovarian teratoma resections due to recurrent disease on the same side. In both cases, the lesions identified during the second operation were not detected during the initial surgical exploration. These findings suggest that although ipsilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may lower the risk of residual or recurrent microscopic disease on the same side, it does not eliminate the possibility of residual or newly developed lesions in the contralateral ovary. Therefore, during surgery, both ovaries should be systematically and thoroughly examined, with special attention paid to small or deeply embedded tumors. In cases where postoperative recovery is suboptimal, prompt pelvic imaging is recommended to rule out residual disease or newly developed lesions.

Additionally, this study identified two patients (Cases 5 and 6) with a prior history of teratoma who subsequently developed anti-NMDAR encephalitis triggered by a teratoma in the same ovary, indicating that a history of teratoma does not necessarily confer immunological safety. For patients wishing to preserve fertility, ultrasound surveillance every 6–12 months post-surgery is recommended. In contrast, for those without fertility intentions or with recurrent disease, ipsilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may be considered to lower the risk of encephalitis recurrence. Of note, both patients self-reported previous methotrexate treatment for ectopic pregnancy. However, detailed methotrexate administration timelines and cumulative doses were unavailable for two cases, as this information relied on patient self-reports and was documented only as part of their past medical history. Although the number of cases is small and lateral differences exist, the potential impact of ectopic pregnancy and methotrexate on the ovarian microenvironment and immune homeostasis warrants further investigation. Case 10 exhibited markedly elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure, reaching up to 357 mmH₂O, in the absence of prodromal symptoms such as fever or headache. This suggests that the lack of early warning signs does not necessarily correspond to a milder disease course. Furthermore, despite symptomatic improvement following treatment, the patient’s modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score remained at 5, indicating that elevated initial CSF pressure may serve as a potential predictor of poor prognosis in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

Patients with teratoma-associated NMDAR encephalitis generally have a favorable prognosis (). However, the mortality rate of severe anti-NMDAR encephalitis was about 6% (). In the present study, only three patients showed good outcomes at 1 month postoperatively, and nearly half still exhibited severe neurological impairment at 3 months post-surgery. This indicates that although the long-term prognosis of teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis is favorable, the functional recovery period is prolonged. Compared with previously reported cohorts (, , ), our patients demonstrated higher disease severity, as reflected by higher ICU admission (88% vs. 52.4–58.6%). The lower proportion of favorable outcomes at 3 months (24%) in oue study likely reflects the short follow-up duration and potential referral bias inherent to our tertiary center, rather than treatment failure. Recovery in anti-NMDAR encephalitis is known to be protracted, and longer follow-up is warranted (). Therefore, it is essential to fully communicate the expected rehabilitation timeline with patients’ families in clinical practice, adhere to long-term follow-up and rehabilitation interventions, and avoid premature discontinuation of treatment.

Comparison of our cohort with published studies on ovarian teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

This study has several limitations. First, because testing was performed by commercial laboratories, some results were qualitative, and cross-institutional titer comparisons were not feasible; Second, this was a retrospective record review with attendant missing data and a relatively short follow-up duration (3 months). Third, this was a single-center study with a small sample size, no control group, and potential referral bias from our tertiary neurological referral center, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to the broader population of teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis. In addition, diagnostic tools and therapeutic protocols changed over the 10-year enrollment period. Furthermore, because headache features were not consistently documented in the retrospective records, we could not fully determine whether headache persisted into the encephalitic phase or its relationship with lumbar puncture timing and treatment response. Future multi-center prospective cohort studies with standardized long-term follow-up (≥24 months) and collaborative registry networks across tertiary and general gynecological centers are warranted to better characterize the recovery trajectory and enhance the generalizability of findings.

In summary, we first emphasized that timely pelvic imaging should be performed to rule out residual or newly developed lesions when postoperative recovery is unsatisfactory, as this may improve patient prognosis. Additionally, patients with a history of teratoma and prior methotrexate treatment may be at increased risk for teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Although all patients showed improvement in at least one neurological symptom, only 24% achieved a favorable functional outcome (mRS ≤ 2) at 3 months, indicating a protracted recovery. Therefore, anti-NMDAR encephalitis associated with teratoma is characterized by acute onset and rapid progression, and clinical improvement can be achieved through multidisciplinary collaboration combined with prompt immunotherapy and tumor resection.

neuroscience.title: Case Report: Cerebral air embolism following fluid–air exchange during pars plana vitrectomy: a rare but severe complication
neuroscience.abstract: Cerebral air embolism (CAE) is a rare but potentially life-threatening neurological emergency, typically caused by the inadvertent entry of exogenous air into the venous circulation and subsequent migration to the cerebral vasculature. It presents with abrupt onset and a prognosis that heavily depends on early recognition and prompt intervention. We report a case of CAE that occurred during pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) involving intraoperative fluid–air exchange. The patient experienced sudden ocular pain intraoperatively, followed shortly post-operatively by acute neurological symptoms including altered consciousness, ataxia, and slurred speech. Brain MRI using a standard stroke protocol, including DWI with b values of 0 and 1,000 s/mm2 and ADC maps, revealed multiple acute infarcts in the bilateral frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, thalamus, and corpus callosum. DWI demonstrated widespread hyperintensity with corresponding ADC reduction. Although no definite intravascular air artifacts were detected, the combination of intraoperative pressure fluctuations, a hypercoagulable state, and elevated levels of D-dimer and cardiac troponin I strongly supported the diagnosis of CAE with possible concomitant microembolism-induced ischemia. The patient received prompt multidisciplinary intensive care and exhibited marked neurological recovery with favorable prognosis. This case highlights the need for high clinical suspicion of CAE during procedures involving air infusion, abrupt pressure changes, or vascular injury risk. Emergent neuroimaging and multidisciplinary management are critical to minimizing neurological sequelae and ensuring patient safety.
neuroscience.text:
Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) is a widely used surgical technique for the treatment of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, and macular pathologies. It is favored for its minimally invasive nature and rapid post-operative recovery (). However, despite continuous advancements in surgical techniques and instrumentation, intraoperative and post-operative complications such as choroidal hemorrhage, recurrent retinal detachment, and intraocular pressure dysregulation can still occur (; ). Expulsive suprachoroidal hemorrhage (ESCH) remains a rare but catastrophic event, characterized by abrupt onset and rapid progression, which can result in irreversible ocular damage or even loss of the globe if not managed promptly (). Importantly, recent studies have drawn attention to an even rarer but potentially fatal complication during intraocular surgeries—air embolism. In particular, when procedures involve sudden posterior segment pressure shifts, inadvertent venous injury, or infusion line mishandling, there is a theoretical risk of air entering the venous system and reaching the central nervous system (CNS), leading to acute neurological events such as cerebral infarction, seizures, or altered consciousness (; ). Ocular venous air embolism (OVAE) is a proposed mechanism, wherein the dislodgment of infusion cannulas during PPV may result in gas entering the suprachoroidal space, subsequently tearing vortex veins and allowing air to enter the systemic circulation (). The risk is further elevated in cases involving trauma, tumor excision (e.g., choroidal melanoma), or significant vascular exposure (). OVAE often presents insidiously, with sudden respiratory or cardiovascular collapse being the initial manifestation, followed in some cases by CNS complications.

In this study, we present a case of a 61-year-old woman who developed ESCH during vitrectomy for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, followed shortly by acute neurological deterioration. Imaging confirmed multiple acute cerebral infarctions. Based on intraoperative events, radiological findings, and review of the literature, we suspect intraoperative gas embolism or microembolism as the likely etiology. The patient made a favorable recovery with timely recognition and multidisciplinary intervention. This case underscores the need for heightened vigilance regarding systemic complications beyond the ocular field during intraocular surgeries, and provides valuable insight into the clinical recognition and management of intraoperative air embolism.
