A 61-year-old woman was admitted to the Department of Ophthalmology on April 7, 2025, with a 7-day history of decreased vision and visual shadowing in her right eye. Her past medical history was notable only for cataract surgery in the right eye (phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation in 2020), with good post-operative recovery. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, stroke, arrhythmia, thrombotic diseases, smoking, alcohol use, or hereditary disorders. On admission, physical examination revealed no light perception in the right eye and a visual acuity of 0.6 in the left eye. The anterior segment of the right eye was unremarkable, with normal intraocular pressure. Fundus examination revealed a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) extending to the macular region, with a horseshoe tear located at the 5 o'clock position. Optical coherence tomography (OCT), scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), and B-scan ultrasonography confirmed the diagnosis. PPV combined with laser photocoagulation and perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) injection was planned. On April 8, under local anesthesia, the patient underwent standard three-port PPV with subretinal fluid drainage. After injection of heavy liquid, the retina was successfully reattached. During preparation for silicone oil tamponade, the patient suddenly complained of severe ocular pain accompanied by profuse sweating and a near-death sensation. Pulse oximetry revealed a transient drop in oxygen saturation to 88%. A dome-shaped choroidal elevation was observed intraoperatively, raising suspicion for ESCH. The procedure was immediately halted, retaining only 3 mL of PFCL in the vitreous cavity. The sclerotomies were closed, and intravenous hemostatic agents (hemocoagulase and tranexamic acid) were administered. Estimated intraoperative blood loss was 2 mL, limited to the posterior segment without anterior chamber involvement or globe rupture. Approximately 1 h post-operatively, the patient developed sudden onset of altered mental status, slurred speech, and gait instability, rapidly progressing to inability to ambulate independently, raising suspicion for a CNS event. Emergent brain MRI was performed on a 1.5-T scanner using a standardized stroke protocol, including axial T1WI, T2WI, FLAIR, DWI with b values of 0 and 1,000 s/mm2, corresponding ADC maps. Section thickness was 4 mm with a 1 mm interslice gap, and no contrast agent was administered. DWI revealed multiple hyperintense lesions in the bilateral frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, as well as the right thalamus and corpus callosum, with corresponding hypointensity on ADC maps, consistent with acute infarcts. FLAIR showed corresponding hyperintensity at representative levels (). No definite intracranial air was identified within the veins, venules, capillaries, or other intracranial compartments on the available MRI sequences or on CT angiography. Cranio-cervical CTA showed no large-vessel occlusion or stenosis, and pulmonary CTA showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism (). All MRI and CTA images were acquired using a standardized stroke protocol and were reviewed by a radiologist with experience in neuroimaging. Laboratory tests showed elevated D-dimer (932 μg/L) and cardiac troponin I (cTnI, 2.981 ng/mL). Arterial blood gas analysis revealed mild hypoxemia (PO2: 72 mmHg). Electrocardiogram and echocardiography showed no signs of myocardial ischemia. Given the intraoperative hemodynamic stress, abnormal venous return, and suspected orbital hypertension due to hemorrhage, a diagnosis of cerebral air embolism (CAE) or microembolic cerebral infarction was strongly suspected. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was initiated (April 9, 19:30–22:50), followed by ICU admission for management including intracranial pressure reduction, neuroprotection, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, cardioprotection, and supportive care. The patient's neurological status improved progressively; by day 10, she was ambulatory and had fully recovered her speech and cognition. On post-operative day 11, under general anesthesia, she underwent successful completion surgery with PFCL removal and silicone oil tamponade. No further complications occurred. At discharge, her right eye visual acuity improved to hand motion. At 6-month follow-up, she remained neurologically stable with a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 0 and a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 1. Follow-up OCT demonstrated a well-attached retina.

The novelty of this case lies in the rare occurrence of cerebral air embolism during pars plana vitrectomy complicated by expulsive suprachoroidal hemorrhage, and in the characteristic pattern of multiple small subcortical infarcts without large-vessel occlusion. This combination has rarely been reported and highlights the need to consider systemic embolic complications during intraocular surgery, even when intravascular air is not directly visualized on imaging.  summarizes the key features of previously reported cases of ocular venous air embolism and choroidal hemorrhage during vitrectomy, alongside the present case. Unlike prior reports that focused primarily on ocular outcomes, the present case is notable for the development of multiple acute cerebral infarcts following an intraoperative pressure event, underscoring the need for systemic vigilance during intraocular surgery.

Comparison of the present case with previously reported cases of OVAE or CAE during vitrectomy.

An important differential or compounding mechanism in this case is paradoxical arterial embolism through a right-to-left shunt. The bilateral, multi-territory “shower” pattern of infarcts on DWI is not fully explained by a purely venous-to-pulmonary route, and raises the possibility that venous gas bubbles bypassed the pulmonary capillary filter through a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or another right-to-left shunt, or through transpulmonary passage when the pulmonary clearance capacity was exceeded (; ). In the context of pars plana vitrectomy, even a small volume of venous air entering the systemic circulation could reach the cerebral microvasculature through such a shunt, producing scattered ischemic lesions. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) with bubble-contrast study, or transcranial Doppler (TCD) with agitated saline, is the preferred approach to detect a right-to-left shunt, and its early use should be considered in similar cases. In the present patient, however, TEE and TCD were not performed during the acute event, so a right-to-left shunt could not be confirmed or excluded, this is acknowledged as a limitation.

Air embolism can enter the systemic circulation through various mechanisms. CAE is a rare but life-threatening neurological emergency characterized by sudden onset and rapid progression. Its prognosis is highly dependent on the extent of vascular involvement and the timeliness of medical intervention (). Cerebral air embolism most commonly occurs after cardiothoracic or interventional procedures. Once CAE occurs, interruption of cerebral perfusion leads to ischemic injury, typically manifesting as altered consciousness, seizures, or coma (). Imaging findings are often non-specific, especially as small gas bubbles may be rapidly resorbed and fail to appear on CT scans, making clinical suspicion and contextual judgment essential for diagnosis. PPV involves the intraocular infusion of exogenous gas or fluids—such as air, perfluorocarbon liquids (PFCL), and silicone oil—to maintain intraocular structure and retinal positioning. Under circumstances of infusion line malfunction, abrupt posterior segment pressure fluctuations, or rupture of choroidal vessels, the risk of air embolism, though rare, cannot be entirely excluded (). In the present case, the patient developed acute CNS symptoms—including confusion, gait instability, and slurred speech—within 1 h post-operatively. Brain MRI revealed multiple acute infarcts involving the bilateral frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, thalamus, and corpus callosum, primarily in a subcortical distribution. The temporal proximity to surgery, combined with the intraoperative occurrence of ESCH, elevated D-dimer levels, and a marked rise in cardiac troponin I (cTnI) in the absence of myocardial ischemia, strongly support the clinical suspicion of CAE or microembolism-related cerebral infarction. Intraoperative ESCH causes abrupt IOP elevation, which may promote retrobulbar venous congestion and allow small gas bubbles to enter the ocular venous system and reach the intracranial venous circulation. The proposed mechanism is dislodgement or slippage of the infusion cannula, causing suprachoroidal pressurized-air infusion, which tears the vortex veins and allows air entrainment into the valveless ocular venous system (). The anatomical route of OVAE is well-described: air enters the vortex veins, drains into the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, and then passes through the cavernous sinus into the jugular vein and right atrium (). Because these veins are valveless, air can travel along pressure gradients in a retrograde or antegrade fashion, reaching the intracranial venous system and, in the presence of a right-to-left shunt, the systemic arterial circulation (). This pathway explains why the infarcts in this patient were multifocal and bilateral rather than confined to a single vascular territory. Once within cerebral venous microcirculation—particularly in subcortical regions—these microbubbles, though minimal in volume, may disrupt local hemodynamics and provoke vasoreactive ischemia. Importantly, such gas bubbles are often rapidly absorbed by plasma and may be radiologically “invisible,” making DWI the most sensitive modality to detect resultant ischemic injury. In this case, the absence of visible intracranial air on imaging does not preclude the diagnosis of air embolism. An additional mechanism that may contribute to cerebral air embolism is paradoxical air embolism. In the presence of a right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale or pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, venous gas bubbles can bypass the pulmonary capillary filter and enter the systemic arterial circulation, potentially causing cerebral or coronary ischemia. Paradoxical air embolism may also occur through transpulmonary passage of gas when the pulmonary clearance capacity is exceeded. In the context of pars plana vitrectomy, even a small volume of venous air entering the systemic circulation could reach the cerebral microvasculature through such a shunt, producing scattered ischemic lesions. This mechanism is particularly relevant in patients with undiagnosed intracardiac shunts, and it may explain the pattern of multiple small infarcts observed in our patient. A recent case report and literature review on retrograde venous cerebral air embolism infarcts provides further insight into the radiological and clinical features of this condition (). Even minimal air emboli may result in disseminated subcortical ischemic lesions via microvascular obstruction or reactive vasospasm. The pattern of multiple small infarcts in this patient can be explained by the behavior of small gas bubbles in the cerebral microcirculation. When microbubbles enter the cerebral vasculature, they are distributed diffusely across subcortical and cortical microvascular beds rather than occluding a single large vessel. These bubbles can obstruct capillaries and venules, trigger local vasospasm, activate platelets and the coagulation cascade, and induce endothelial injury, collectively producing scattered ischemic lesions. In addition, the hypercoagulable state suggested by elevated D-dimer and cardiac troponin I levels in this case may have further promoted microthrombus formation and amplified the ischemic burden. This mechanism is consistent with the small, multiple, bilateral, and subcortical distribution of infarcts observed in our patient, and also explains why no large-vessel occlusion was identified on CTA. Therefore, in intraocular surgeries complicated by significant IOP changes or infusion abnormalities—especially when followed by acute neurological deterioration—CAE should be considered a high-priority differential diagnosis, even in the absence of radiologically detected gas. Prompt recognition and multidisciplinary intervention are crucial to minimizing neurological sequelae.

In addition to the possible contribution of air embolism, a hypercoagulable state induced by intraoperative physiological stress may have also played a role in this case. PPV is often the second ocular procedure in elderly patients, and intraoperative factors such as psychological stress, nociceptive stimulation, and abrupt IOP elevation can activate the sympathetic nervous system. This, in turn, may lead to vasoconstriction, platelet activation, and increased procoagulant activity. Post-operative local inflammation can further exacerbate coagulation factor elevation. Although non-specific, the markedly elevated levels of D-dimer and cTnI observed in this case suggest systemic inflammatory responses and endothelial dysfunction—both of which are recognized risk factors for microvascular occlusion (). Therefore, the cerebral infarction observed in this patient was likely the result of a multifactorial process, including retrobulbar hypertension induced by ESCH, residual microbubbles in the infusion system, and intraoperative stress-mediated microthrombus formation. This complex pathophysiological cascade highlights the need to look beyond the local surgical field when considering complications following intraocular procedures, and instead to anticipate and mitigate potential systemic embolic risks. The management pathway in this case also provides a useful reference for similar clinical scenarios. In any patient presenting with acute neurological symptoms shortly after ophthalmic surgery, prompt initiation of neuroimaging is essential. DWI should be prioritized to detect scattered subcortical infarcts or venous outflow obstruction. Concurrent laboratory assessments—including D-dimer, cTnI, electrocardiogram (ECG), and echocardiography—are recommended to evaluate for possible cardiogenic or thrombotic causes. If the clinical context, intraoperative events, and imaging findings suggest air or microembolic mechanisms, early admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) should be considered for comprehensive management. This includes neuroprotection, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, and intracranial pressure control. In this case, timely multidisciplinary intervention enabled the patient to achieve full recovery of ambulation and speech by post-operative day 10. Final follow-up showed stable retinal attachment on OCT, with a NIHSS score of 0 and a mRS score of 1—strongly supporting the clinical value of coordinated cross-specialty care.

In patients with acute neurological deterioration shortly after intraocular surgery, urgent neuroimaging should follow a standardized acute stroke imaging algorithm. The first-line MRI protocol should include diffusion-weighted imaging with b values of 0 and 1,000 s/mm2 and corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient maps, which are most sensitive for acute ischemic lesions. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery and T2-weighted imaging help assess lesion extent and exclude other structural causes. Susceptibility-weighted imaging or T2*-weighted gradient-echo imaging should be included to detect intracranial air or hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance angiography is recommended to exclude large-vessel occlusion and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. If MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable, non-contrast head CT may be used for initial triage, although it is less sensitive for acute ischemia and may miss small gas bubbles. When cerebral air embolism is suspected, the absence of visible intravascular air does not exclude the diagnosis, and diffusion-weighted imaging should be performed or repeated promptly. In parallel, laboratory tests including D-dimer, cardiac troponin I, arterial blood gas analysis, electrocardiography, and echocardiography should be obtained. This algorithm facilitates early recognition of cerebral air embolism or microembolic infarction and supports timely multidisciplinary intervention.

When CAE is suspected or confirmed, immediate systemic intervention is essential (). The first-line clinical measure is the administration of 100% high-flow oxygen, which facilitates the diffusion of nitrogen out of the air bubbles, accelerates bubble resorption, and improves tissue oxygenation. In patients with significant neurological involvement, early initiation of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is recommended. HBOT increases the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood and reduces bubble volume, thereby mitigating cerebral ischemia and secondary edema. When initiated within 6 h of symptom onset, HBOT has been shown to significantly improve neurological outcomes. In parallel, it is crucial to maintain stable hemodynamics through appropriate fluid resuscitation while avoiding hypotension, in order to preserve adequate cerebral perfusion. Based on individual risk assessment, antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy may be considered to prevent or treat microthrombus formation. A supine position is generally preferred to minimize intracranial pressure. In patients with radiological evidence of cerebral infarction, neuroprotective strategies—including osmotic agents for intracranial pressure reduction, glucose and temperature control—should be promptly implemented. In this case, the patient received timely HBOT and supportive care under the coordination of a multidisciplinary team. Prompt recognition and early initiation of oxygen therapy and antithrombotic treatment resulted in full neurological recovery. This underscores the critical importance of early diagnosis and rapid, targeted intervention in the effective management of CAE.

An important practical determinant of outcome in iatrogenic CAE is timely access to HBOT. In real-world settings, the availability of a hyperbaric chamber, rather than the clinical indication itself, often dictates whether treatment can be delivered within the therapeutic window. Current evidence-based recommendations support early HBOT for patients with significant neurological involvement, with the greatest benefit when treatment is initiated within 6 h of symptom onset (). However, this evidence is derived primarily from observational studies, case series, and expert consensus rather than randomized controlled trials (; ). As illustrated by Thomas et al., patients may require transfer to alternative facilities, including outpatient hyperbaric centers, when immediate access is not available at the treating hospital (). This logistical reality underscores the need for early identification of HBOT-capable centers and proactive coordination of transfer when CAE is suspected.

The management of thrombotic cerebrovascular disease offers instructive parallels, but also important distinctions. Air emboli are compressible and largely resorb, so mechanical thrombectomy devices designed for solid clot do not directly apply to CAE. However, the stroke code model of rapid multidisciplinary triage and standardized imaging-to-treatment intervals provides a useful structural comparator for organizing the acute response to suspected CAE. A closer anatomical parallel may be cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), in which the proposed air route in this case terminates. In CVST, anticoagulation is first-line therapy, while endovascular thrombectomy is reserved for patients' refractory to or ineligible for anticoagulation (). This paradigm supports the use of anticoagulation, rather than mechanical intervention, as the appropriate initial strategy in this patient, in whom the proposed mechanism involves venous-to-cavernous sinus air transmission with secondary microvascular ischemia.

The true incidence of ocular venous air embolism and cerebral air embolism during ophthalmic procedures is likely underestimated. Only 13 cases of OVAE have been reported in the literature, yet 69% of these were fatal, suggesting that fatal cases are more likely to be published while non-fatal or aborted events remain unreported (). A survey of vitreoretinal surgeons found that only 20% were aware of OVAE as a potential complication, and many cannula displacements are likely stopped before cardiovascular collapse occurs and therefore never reported (). Similar patterns of underreporting have been recognized in other embolization contexts. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of middle meningeal artery embolization explicitly noted “variability in adverse event reporting” and “insufficient documentation of rare complications” across the included studies (). While this observation comes from a different embolization procedure, it illustrates a cross-cutting methodological problem: rare but clinically important adverse events are systematically under-captured in retrospective cohorts and single-center series. By analogy, CAE following pars plana vitrectomy is likely underrecognized and underreported, and the absence of large case series should not be interpreted as evidence of negligible risk.

This case has several limitations. First, it is a single-case report, and the findings cannot be generalized to a broader population. Second, the intraoperative pressure event was reconstructed retrospectively from surgical records and clinical observations, rather than measured prospectively, which limits the precision of the proposed mechanism. Third, transesophageal echocardiography and transcranial Doppler were not performed during the acute event, so a right-to-left shunt or paradoxical embolism could not be confirmed or excluded. Fourth, the diagnosis of cerebral air embolism was inferential rather than radiographically confirmed, because no definite intravascular air artifacts were detected on the available MRI sequences or on CT angiography. An alternative explanation, namely stress-related microthrombosis in the setting of a hypercoagulable state, cannot be entirely excluded. These limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings.

In conclusion, although PPV is considered a routine ophthalmic procedure, the potential risk of air embolism and secondary cerebral infarction should not be overlooked, especially in the presence of intraoperative hemorrhage, fluid infusion, or structural disruption. Moving forward, clinical practice must place greater emphasis on pre-operative risk assessment, careful intraoperative gas and fluid management, maintenance of wound integrity, and rapid recognition of post-operative neurological abnormalities. This case highlights the need to shift the clinical mindset from ensuring “intraocular safety” alone to safeguarding “systemic safety” as a whole. The rare and complex progression observed in this patient not only reveals the true risk of uncommon complications associated with PPV but also provides valuable insights for the timely diagnosis and stratified management of post-operative neurological events.

neuroscience.title: Mapping the Oral–Nutrition–Brain Axis in Aging: A Scoping Review of Evidence Linking Oral Health, Nutrition, and Cognitive Outcomes
neuroscience.abstract: Background: Oral health, nutrition, and neurocognitive health are increasingly recognized as components of healthy aging; however, their multidimensional relationships and plausible biological connections relevant to Alzheimer’s disease and related dementia (AD/ADRD) risk remain incompletely characterized. Objective: To systematically map evidence linking oral conditions and function, nutrition-related factors and biomarkers, and neurocognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥65 years, and conceptualize an integrative Oral–Nutrition–Brain Axis (ONBA). Methods: This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance. Five electronic databases were searched for studies published from 2010 through June 2025. Evidence was harmonized across oral and functional indicators, nutritional/metabolic/inflammatory biomarkers, and neurological and cognitive outcomes. Results: Of 3415 records identified, 1988 unique records were screened, and 120 studies met eligibility criteria. Evidence was predominantly observational and geographically concentrated in East Asia. Periodontal inflammation, compromised dentition, impaired functional occlusion and masticatory performance were consistently associated with nutritional vulnerability, poorer cognitive performance, cognitive decline, and adverse AD/ADRD outcomes. Co-occurring nutritional and systemic markers included low body weight, hypoalbuminemia, low serum vitamin B12 and folate, hyperhomocysteinemia, and elevated inflammatory biomarkers. Mapped findings aligned across three proposed conceptual frameworks: inflammatory–microbial, nutritional–metabolic, and sensorimotor deafferentation axes. Studies incorporating neuroimaging biomarkers or integrating all three ONBA domains simultaneously remained limited. Conclusions: Oral health and functional dentition may represent key modifiable proxies associated with nutritional and neurocognitive vulnerability in older adults. Longitudinal studies incorporating harmonized oral, nutritional, inflammatory, and neurological phenotypes are needed to clarify temporal sequence, evaluate potential explanatory relationships, and inform multi-domain risk assessment for healthy cognitive aging.
neuroscience.text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) recognizes oral health as an integral component of overall health and well-being and describes healthy aging as maintaining the functional ability supporting well-being in older age. At the biological level, aging reflects the progressive accumulation of molecular and cellular changes that can reduce physical and cognitive capacity and increase disease vulnerability []. These trajectories are further influenced by nutritional vulnerability (susceptibility to inadequate nutritional intake or status due to biological, functional, or social factors) and malnutrition, compromising physical function, resilience, and cognitive health [,,,]. Importantly, these aging processes are neither linear nor uniform, varying substantially across individuals and diverse racial and ethnic population groups [,,,,,,,].

Oral diseases (ODs) and Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) affect nearly 4 billion and 50 million people worldwide, respectively, posing profound public health, social and economic burdens [,,,,,,,]. Neuropathological changes associated with AD/ADRD can begin up to 30 years before dementia symptoms emerge, highlighting the critical need for early detection and modifiable risk identification [,,]. Epidemiological evidence increasingly links oral-systemic health and cognitive trajectories [,,,,]. On one hand, cognitive decline and natural tooth loss increase susceptibility to ODs due to diminished self-care abilities and neglected oral hygiene [,]. On the other hand, chronic oral pathologies are increasingly recognized as potentially modifiable risk factor driving the onset and progression to potentially modifiable factors associated with AD/ADRD vulnerability [,,,,,].

Despite this growing recognition, standard neurodegenerative frameworks rely heavily on traditional neurological markers, often omitting upstream oral, nutritional, and one-carbon metabolic indicators (e.g., vitamin B12, folate, homocysteine) []. While population-based studies link tooth loss and periodontitis with cognitive decline, limited evidence explains how oral conditions interact with indirect, low-cost peripheral markers (such as B-vitamin deficiencies, hyperhomocysteinemia, and systemic inflammatory mediators) to influence cognitive outcomes []. Impaired dentition and reduced masticatory efficiency directly restrict dietary quality and nutrient intake, making nutritional status a key potential mediator connecting oral breakdown to systemic metabolic and neurocognitive vulnerability [,]. The Health and Aging Brain Study–Health Disparities (HABS-HD) provides an important interdisciplinary framework for investigating cognitive aging across diverse populations through integrated clinical, biomarker, and health disparity characterization [,,]. Motivated by this multidimensional approach, the present scoping review addresses a critical gap: the links connecting oral health conditions (e.g., orofacial pain, jaw dysfunction, functional dentition, chewing ability) and nutritional biomarkers to cognitive decline remain underexplored and unharmonized within a single conceptual framework [,,,].

To systematically map this evidence, we proposed an a priori conceptual framework (the Oral–Nutrition–Brain Axis [ONBA]) encompassing three hypothesized, interconnected biological pathways:The Inflammatory-Microbial Axis: Suggests that chronic periodontal infections and polymicrobial dysbiosis elevate circulating pro-inflammatory cascades and neuroinflammatory responses [,].The Nutritional-Metabolic Axis: Posits that structural oral alterations (tooth loss and impaired occlusal function) lead to dietary shifts toward soft, less nutrient-dense foods, potentially predisposing individuals to low body weight, reduced serum albumin, B-vitamin deficiencies, and elevated plasma homocysteine (a marker linked to microvascular injury and hippocampal vulnerability) [,].The Sensorimotor Deafferentation Axis: Proposes that loss of functional dentition and occlusal contacts reduced trigeminal sensory feedback during mastication, which may attenuate regional cerebral blood flow to cognitive centers like the hippocampus [,,].

The Inflammatory-Microbial Axis: Suggests that chronic periodontal infections and polymicrobial dysbiosis elevate circulating pro-inflammatory cascades and neuroinflammatory responses [,].

The Nutritional-Metabolic Axis: Posits that structural oral alterations (tooth loss and impaired occlusal function) lead to dietary shifts toward soft, less nutrient-dense foods, potentially predisposing individuals to low body weight, reduced serum albumin, B-vitamin deficiencies, and elevated plasma homocysteine (a marker linked to microvascular injury and hippocampal vulnerability) [,].

The Sensorimotor Deafferentation Axis: Proposes that loss of functional dentition and occlusal contacts reduced trigeminal sensory feedback during mastication, which may attenuate regional cerebral blood flow to cognitive centers like the hippocampus [,,].

By moving beyond traditional central neurological markers alone, this scoping review (ScR) aims to systematically map, synthesize, and identify evidence gaps regarding how oral health factors, nutritional biomarkers, and cognitive outcomes interact in older adults (≥65 years). By integrating evidence across these three intersecting domains into a unified ONBA framework, this review seeks to identify critical evidence gaps and generate a conceptual model to guide future longitudinal studies, harmonized risk modeling, and multi-domain preventive research in healthy cognitive aging [,,].

This scoping review (ScR) was conducted following the updated Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological guidance for scoping reviews [,]. Reporting was executed in strict compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines () [,]. The review was conducted according to an a priori prospective protocol detailing the core objectives, research questions, Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) eligibility criteria, search strategy (), and data extraction plan, which was publicly registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository (https://www.cos.io).

In alignment with JBI scoping review methodology, eligibility was structured around the Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework ():

Population (P): Older adults aged 65 years and older. Studies evaluating mixed-age cohorts were eligible only if data for participants aged ≥65 years were disaggregated or analyzed separately.

Concept (C): Research examining the multidimensional relationships across at least two of the three core domains defining the Oral–Nutritional–Brain axis (ONBA). Requiring multi-domain interaction was essential to capture across-domain interconnectedness rather than isolated single-domain outcomes:Oral Health, Functional Indicators, or Proxies (Block 1—Primary Exposures): Quantitative and qualitative metrics of anatomical dentition status (natural teeth count, edentulism, DMFT index [Decay, Missing, Filling Theet]), functional masticatory performance (maximal bite force, chewing efficiency, functional masticatory units or functional occlusal pairs [FMUs]), prosthetic rehabilitation status (type, quality, and occlusal restoration of removable or fixed prostheses), and periodontal or local inflammatory burden (Probing Pocket Depth [PPD], Clinical Attachment Loss [CAL], Bleeding on Probing [BOP], Periodontal Inflamed Surface Area [PISA], oral dysbiosis/pathogens).Nutritional, Metabolic, and Inflammatory-Related Biomarkers (Block 2—Systemic Mediators): Laboratory and metabolic intermediates acting as potential mediators or moderators, including B-complex vitamins (vitamin B12, folate), plasma homocysteine, serum albumin, CRP, pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α), or nutritional risk indices (Body Mass Index [BMI], Mini-Nutritional Assessment [MNA], Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index [GNRI]) [,].Neurological and Cognitive Outcomes (Block 3—Target Endpoints): Objective indicators of cognitive vulnerability and AD/ADRD pathology, including standardized screening tools (MMSE [Minimal Mental State Examination], MoCA [Montreal Cognitive Assessment]), domain-specific neuropsychological assessments (memory, executive function, attention), clinical diagnoses of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), all-cause dementia, or AD/ADRD, and neuroimaging/pathological markers (grey matter volume, hippocampal atrophy, PET amyloid/tau deposition).

Oral Health, Functional Indicators, or Proxies (Block 1—Primary Exposures): Quantitative and qualitative metrics of anatomical dentition status (natural teeth count, edentulism, DMFT index [Decay, Missing, Filling Theet]), functional masticatory performance (maximal bite force, chewing efficiency, functional masticatory units or functional occlusal pairs [FMUs]), prosthetic rehabilitation status (type, quality, and occlusal restoration of removable or fixed prostheses), and periodontal or local inflammatory burden (Probing Pocket Depth [PPD], Clinical Attachment Loss [CAL], Bleeding on Probing [BOP], Periodontal Inflamed Surface Area [PISA], oral dysbiosis/pathogens).

Nutritional, Metabolic, and Inflammatory-Related Biomarkers (Block 2—Systemic Mediators): Laboratory and metabolic intermediates acting as potential mediators or moderators, including B-complex vitamins (vitamin B12, folate), plasma homocysteine, serum albumin, CRP, pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α), or nutritional risk indices (Body Mass Index [BMI], Mini-Nutritional Assessment [MNA], Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index [GNRI]) [,].

Neurological and Cognitive Outcomes (Block 3—Target Endpoints): Objective indicators of cognitive vulnerability and AD/ADRD pathology, including standardized screening tools (MMSE [Minimal Mental State Examination], MoCA [Montreal Cognitive Assessment]), domain-specific neuropsychological assessments (memory, executive function, attention), clinical diagnoses of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), all-cause dementia, or AD/ADRD, and neuroimaging/pathological markers (grey matter volume, hippocampal atrophy, PET amyloid/tau deposition).

Context (C): Any epidemiological or clinical setting, encompassing community-dwelling populations, nursing homes/long term facilities, memory clinics, and population-based longitudinal studies or national administrative databases.

Studies were excluded if they failed to include participants aged ≥65 years or lacked subgroup reporting for this age demographic; evaluated only a single ONBA domain without examining interdomain links; were narrative reviews, commentary pieces, letters to the editor, editorials, or conference abstracts lacking full peer-reviewed text; utilized animal or in vitro model systems; or were published prior to 2010 or in languages other than English. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were screened for reference tracking but excluded from primary mapping extraction to avoid duplicate participant representation.

A comprehensive systematic literature search was developed and executed by an expert health sciences librarian on 17 June 2025. The search was performed across five major electronic databases: MEDLINE ALL (Ovid); Embase (Embase.com); Web of Science Core Collection; Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Cochrane Library, Wiley); Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Cochrane Library, Wiley). The search strategy covered studies published between 1 January 2010 and 30 June 2025 (capturing all indexed pre-prints and ahead-of-print records through the execution month). Language was restricted to English, which was recognized a priori as a potential language bias limitation.

Following PRESS (Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies) principles, search strings combined Controlled Vocabulary (MeSH in MEDLINE, Emtree in Embase) and free-text keywords covering three primary blocks:Block 1: “oral health”, “tooth loss”, “functional dentition”, “masticatory performance”, “occlusal force”, “chewing efficiency”, “periodontitis”, “periodontal disease”, “oral frailty”, and “orofacial pain”.Block 2: “vitamin B12”, “folate”, “homocysteine”, “albumin”, “C-RP”, “interleukin-6”, “TNF-α”, “malnutrition”, and “nutritional status”.Block 3: “dementia”, “Alzheimer disease”, “mild cognitive impairment”, “cognitive decline”, “MMSE”, “MoCA”, “neuroimaging”, and “brain atrophy”.

Block 1: “oral health”, “tooth loss”, “functional dentition”, “masticatory performance”, “occlusal force”, “chewing efficiency”, “periodontitis”, “periodontal disease”, “oral frailty”, and “orofacial pain”.

Block 2: “vitamin B12”, “folate”, “homocysteine”, “albumin”, “C-RP”, “interleukin-6”, “TNF-α”, “malnutrition”, and “nutritional status”.

Block 3: “dementia”, “Alzheimer disease”, “mild cognitive impairment”, “cognitive decline”, “MMSE”, “MoCA”, “neuroimaging”, and “brain atrophy”.

The full search strategies for each database are available in . Reference list screening of key reviews and forward citation tracking of included studies were additionally performed to ensure literature saturation.

All retrieved citations were exported to EndNote (Version 2025) for reference management and automated duplication removal. De-duplicated records were uploaded to Covidence for independent screening. Pilot testing was conducted on 20 citations to establish high inter-reviewer agreement (Cohen’s k > 0.85). Study selection followed an iterative, two-stage process:Title and Abstract Screening: Two independent reviewers (HN, SD) screened all titles and abstracts against the PCC criteria.Full-Text Evaluation: Potentially eligible studies underwent full-text retrieval and independent evaluation by the same two reviewers.

Title and Abstract Screening: Two independent reviewers (HN, SD) screened all titles and abstracts against the PCC criteria.

Full-Text Evaluation: Potentially eligible studies underwent full-text retrieval and independent evaluation by the same two reviewers.

Disagreements at either stage were resolved via consensus or arbitration by senior reviewers (RK, SC). Excluded full-text studies were documented with specific reasons (). In accordance with updated JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR standards, formal critical appraisal or risk of bias scoring was not performed, as the primary objective of this scoping review was to map the evidence landscape and gaps rather than evaluate intervention efficacy or generate a single pooled effect size [,].

Data extraction was structured using a pre-developed, standardized data charting form created in Microsoft Excel. The standardized charting form was developed to maintain data quality through double-checking and independent validation, ensuring accuracy and completeness (). The extraction form was piloted by the review team on three representative studies prior to implementation. Data extraction was performed in duplicate (HN, SD) to minimize extraction errors, with consensus verification by a third reviewer (SC). For each included study (n = 120), six primary parameters were charted:Study Metadata: Lead author, publication year, title, journal, country of origin, and specific cohort identifier (e.g., SONIC, Fujiwara-kyo, Hiyasama, CLHLS, HABS-HD) [,,,,,,,].Study Design and Methodology: Sampling methodology, study design (cross-sectional, longitudinal cohort, case–control, systematic review, trial), sample size, follow-up duration, and statistical modeling approach.Participants Characteristics: Age criteria, mean age, setting (community-dwelling, nursing home/long-term care, memory clinic), and cognitive baseline status.Oral Health Indicators (Harmonized): Quantitative natural tooth count, edentulism, DMFT index, masticatory performance (bite force, chewing efficiency, FMUs), prosthetic status (denture quality and wear), and periodontal metrics (PPD, CAL, BOP, PISA, bacterial loads).Nutritional and Inflammatory Biomarkers: Biochemical assays (B12, folate, homocysteine, CRP, IL-6, TNF-α, albumin) and anthropometric indices (BMI, MNA).Cognitive and Neurological Outcomes: Screening scores (MMSE, MoCA), clinical diagnostic categories (MCI, AD, ADRD), domain-specific cognitive metrics, and neuroimaging markers.

Study Metadata: Lead author, publication year, title, journal, country of origin, and specific cohort identifier (e.g., SONIC, Fujiwara-kyo, Hiyasama, CLHLS, HABS-HD) [,,,,,,,].

Study Design and Methodology: Sampling methodology, study design (cross-sectional, longitudinal cohort, case–control, systematic review, trial), sample size, follow-up duration, and statistical modeling approach.

Participants Characteristics: Age criteria, mean age, setting (community-dwelling, nursing home/long-term care, memory clinic), and cognitive baseline status.

Oral Health Indicators (Harmonized): Quantitative natural tooth count, edentulism, DMFT index, masticatory performance (bite force, chewing efficiency, FMUs), prosthetic status (denture quality and wear), and periodontal metrics (PPD, CAL, BOP, PISA, bacterial loads).

Nutritional and Inflammatory Biomarkers: Biochemical assays (B12, folate, homocysteine, CRP, IL-6, TNF-α, albumin) and anthropometric indices (BMI, MNA).

Cognitive and Neurological Outcomes: Screening scores (MMSE, MoCA), clinical diagnostic categories (MCI, AD, ADRD), domain-specific cognitive metrics, and neuroimaging markers.

In accordance with Peters et al. [,], extracted data were analyzed using descriptive statistics (frequency counts, percentages, and geographical distributions) and qualitative conceptual synthesis. Data synthesis was organized around the three predefined biological domains of the ONBA. Findings are visually presented through structured mapping tables, geographic breakdowns, and a conceptual framework diagram illustrating potential associations, candidate mediating pathways, and evidence gaps in linking oral health and nutritional biomarkers to AD/ADRD risk.

The initial search database yielded 3415 records across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane databases. Following automated and manual de-duplication, 1988 unique records underwent title and abstract screening. Full-text evaluation of eligible manuscripts identified 120 studies published between 2010 and June 2025 that met all PCC eligibility criteria for inclusion in this ScR (; see PRISMA ).

Research examining oral health, nutrition, and cognitive aging has increased globally, with a distinct concentration of observational studies across East Asia and Western nations. The included literature was predominantly observational (94.2%), comprising 52% cross-sectional studies and 38.3% prospective or retrospective cohort studies [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Case–control studies represented 4.2% [,,,,], systematic reviews/meta-analyses represented 3.3% [,,,,,,,,,], and original interventional trials/prosthetic rehabilitation studies represented 1.7% [,,,].

Japan contributed the largest body of evidence (35.8%) [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,], followed by the US (9.2%) [,,,,,,,], China (7.5%) [,,,,,,,,,], South Korea (6.7%) [,,,,,,,,], Taiwan (3.3%) [,,,], and Finland (3.3%) [,,,,]. Additional evidence originated from Brazil, Italy, the Netherlands, Australia, India, Sweden, Singapore, and Turkey [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,].

Studies predominantly evaluated community-dwelling older adults (81.7%) [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,], with additional subset from long-term care and nursing home populations (11.7%) and memory-clinic outpatients (6.6%) [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Cognitive vulnerability was primarily assessed using global screening tools (MMSE, MoCA; 55.8%) [,,,,], clinical diagnostic classification (MCI, AD, ADRD; 71.7%) [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,], domain-specific neuropsychological batteries (26.7%), and neuroimaging/fluid biomarkers (10.8%) [,,,,] ().

The mapped literature evaluated oral health across four harmonized functional and pathological categories (dentition status, functional and masticatory performance, prosthetic rehabilitation, and periodontal and inflammatory status), consistently reporting that adverse oral health metrics are associated with cognitive impairment.

Dentition Status: Natural tooth count was the most frequently investigated oral exposure. Across prospective cohorts, maintaining ≥20 natural teeth was consistently associated with a reduced risk of cognitive decline [,,,,,,,,,,]. Conversely, tooth loss (<10 teeth) and complete edentulism exhibited a dose–response relationship with accelerated cognitive decline and incident dementia [,,,,,,,]. In institutionalized and nursing home settings, complete edentulism correlated with clinical dementia severity [,,,,,,,,]. Studies employing a Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth (DMFT) index further confirmed that cumulative, untreated dental caries burden differentiates cognitively impaired from cognitively intact cohorts [,,].

Functional and Masticatory Performance: Beyond static tooth count, objective measures of masticatory physiology revealed notable associations with cognitive performance. Reduced maximal occlusal force, fewer FMUs, and impaired chewing efficiency (objectively measured via two-color wax or color-changing gum mixing tests) were independently associated with lower MMSE/MoCA scores and heightened MCI prevalence [,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Patients with diagnosed AD exhibited prolonged masticatory cycle times, reduced chewing velocity, and impaired grinding capacity compared to age-matched controls [,,,,].

Prosthetic Rehabilitation: Prosthetic status functioned as a key modifiable buffer. Across the longitudinal cohort, complete or partial denture wear was associated with attenuated cognitive risk related to tooth loss [,,,,,]. Effective prosthetic restoration improved chewing performance and bite force, which in turn correlated with stabilized cognitive trajectories and preserved regional gray matter volume on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [,,]. However, the quality and functional fit of the prosthesis were critical: ill-fitting dentures or un-rehabilitated edentulism yielded cognitive trajectories comparable to severe untreated tooth loss [].

Periodontal and Local Inflammatory Status. While tooth loss reflects cumulative lifetime disease, measures of active periodontitis (including PPD, CAL, BOP, and PISA) capture ongoing biological exposure. High periodontal inflammatory burden and elevated systemic/salivary loads of periodontal pathogens (Porphyromonas gingivalis, Fusobacterium nucleatum) were significantly associated with lower cognitive scores, faster 6-month cognitive decline, and increased incident MCI/AD [] ().

A major subset of included studies (40.8%) evaluated laboratory, somatic, and metabolic biomarkers alongside oral health, identifying potential biological intermediates linking oral breakdown to neurocognitive vulnerability [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,].

Nutritional and Somatic Vulnerability: Impaired mastication and severe tooth loss were consistently linked to markers of undernutrition and nutritional vulnerability (low BMI, unintentional weight loss, reduced nutritional status, and lower serum albumin) [,,,,,,]. Longitudinal path analyses supported nutritional status and reduced dietary intake (e.g., fruit, vegetable, and fibrous avoidance) as potential partial mediators linking tooth loss and incident cognitive decline [].

Micronutrient and One-Carbon Metabolism (B12, Folate, Homocysteine): Studies evaluating micronutrient-related pathways reported that masticatory dysfunction alters dietary patterns, compromising the intake and absorption of essential B-complex vitamins [,,,,,]. Deficiencies in serum B12 and folate were frequently co-observed with elevated plasma homocysteine concentrations [,]. Elevated homocysteine, in turn, correlated directly with executive dysfunction, memory impairment, and microvascular white matter burden, providing additional evidence for potential metabolic pathways contributing to cognitive vulnerability [,,] ().

Systemic Inflammatory Cascades: Active periodontal disease and high PISA scores were significantly correlated with elevated circulating inflammatory biomarkers, specifically CRP, IL-6, and Interleukin-1beta [,,,,,]. Studies incorporating multivariable path modeling suggested that systemic inflammation may act as a candidate mediator linking local oral infection and cognitive decline [,,] ().

Neurological and cognitive outcomes represented the brain-health component of the ONBA literature ranged from global cognitive screening and preclinical memory impairment to clinically diagnosed MCI, dementia, and AD [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. MMSE and MoCA were the most frequently used cognitive measures, with poorer dentition, masticatory dysfunction, and periodontal disease generally associated with lower cognitive performance or greater cognitive decline [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Additional studies identified associations with specific memory deficits and interactions with APOE ε4 susceptibility [,,]. A smaller body of neuroimaging evidence extended these findings to structural and pathological neurological markers, linking adverse oral health with differences in brain volume and AD-vulnerable regions on MRI, as well as greater tau deposition on PET [,,,] ().

When synthesized across the 120-study matrix, the literature provides a conceptual framework mapping three hypothesized biological pathways linking oral health to AD/ADRD risk:The Inflammatory-Microbial Axis: Suggests that chronic periodontitis maintains persistent low-grade systemic inflammatory signaling while permitting oral pathogens (P. gingivalis) and virulence factors (gingipains) to cross the BBB, potentially driving microglial priming, neuroinflammation, and amyloid/tau deposition [,,,] ().The Nutritional-Metabolic Axis: Posits that functional tooth loss is associated with dietary shifts toward soft, nutrient-depleted foods, contributing to B-vitamin (B12/Folate) insufficiency and impairing one-carbon methylation. The resulting hyperhomocysteinemia is hypothesized to exacerbate vascular endothelial dysfunction, microvascular brain injury, and hippocampal vulnerability [,,,,,,,] ().The Sensorimotor Deafferentation Axis: Proposes that loss of posterior occlusal contacts and periodontal mechanoreceptors deprives the central nervous system of vital trigeminal sensory feedback during mastication. Neuroimaging studies suggest that reduced masticatory stimulation correlates with decreased regional cerebral blood flow to the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, representing a candidate pathway for accelerated structural brain atrophy independent of inflammatory or nutritional factors [,,,,,,,,,] (). These interconnected life-course pathways and their conceptual integration with established AD/ADRD biomarker frameworks are illustrated in .

The Inflammatory-Microbial Axis: Suggests that chronic periodontitis maintains persistent low-grade systemic inflammatory signaling while permitting oral pathogens (P. gingivalis) and virulence factors (gingipains) to cross the BBB, potentially driving microglial priming, neuroinflammation, and amyloid/tau deposition [,,,] ().

The Nutritional-Metabolic Axis: Posits that functional tooth loss is associated with dietary shifts toward soft, nutrient-depleted foods, contributing to B-vitamin (B12/Folate) insufficiency and impairing one-carbon methylation. The resulting hyperhomocysteinemia is hypothesized to exacerbate vascular endothelial dysfunction, microvascular brain injury, and hippocampal vulnerability [,,,,,,,] ().

The Sensorimotor Deafferentation Axis: Proposes that loss of posterior occlusal contacts and periodontal mechanoreceptors deprives the central nervous system of vital trigeminal sensory feedback during mastication. Neuroimaging studies suggest that reduced masticatory stimulation correlates with decreased regional cerebral blood flow to the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, representing a candidate pathway for accelerated structural brain atrophy independent of inflammatory or nutritional factors [,,,,,,,,,] (). These interconnected life-course pathways and their conceptual integration with established AD/ADRD biomarker frameworks are illustrated in .

Synthesis of the mapped literature indicates that tooth loss serves as a static, cumulative biomarker of historical biological aging and structural oral health disparities [,,,,,]; whereas periodontitis represents an active, ongoing biological exposure driving systemic inflammation [,,,,,,]. The co-occurrence of severe tooth loss, periodontitis, B-vitamin deficiency, and hyperhomocysteinemia forms a high-risk oral-vascular-inflammatory cluster associated with accelerated cognitive decline and AD/ADRD vulnerability.

However, several critical evidence gaps emerged across the mapped landscape:-Geographic Concentration: Over 65% of included studies originated from East Asia (predominantly Japan, China, South Korea, and Taiwan), limiting the direct generalizability of specific masticatory and dietary thresholds to Western populations or diverse health disparity cohorts.-Scarcity of Multi-Domain Integration: Less than 12% of included studies evaluated all three ONBA domains (oral, nutritional, and neurocognitive) simultaneously within a single analytical framework.-Limited Biomarker and Neuroimaging Coverage: Only 10.8% of studies incorporated objective neuroimaging (MRI volume, white matter hyperintensities) of fluid/PET biomarkers (Aβ, tau), with most relying on global cognitive screening tools (MMSE, MoCA).-Rarity of Interventional Trials: Only 2 of the 120 studies (1.7%) evaluated clinical interventions (e.g., prosthetic restoration or combined dietary advice), highlighting a critical lack of interventional evidence to determine whether restoring oral function influences cognitive trajectories.

Geographic Concentration: Over 65% of included studies originated from East Asia (predominantly Japan, China, South Korea, and Taiwan), limiting the direct generalizability of specific masticatory and dietary thresholds to Western populations or diverse health disparity cohorts.

Scarcity of Multi-Domain Integration: Less than 12% of included studies evaluated all three ONBA domains (oral, nutritional, and neurocognitive) simultaneously within a single analytical framework.

Limited Biomarker and Neuroimaging Coverage: Only 10.8% of studies incorporated objective neuroimaging (MRI volume, white matter hyperintensities) of fluid/PET biomarkers (Aβ, tau), with most relying on global cognitive screening tools (MMSE, MoCA).

Rarity of Interventional Trials: Only 2 of the 120 studies (1.7%) evaluated clinical interventions (e.g., prosthetic restoration or combined dietary advice), highlighting a critical lack of interventional evidence to determine whether restoring oral function influences cognitive trajectories.

This ScR mapped 120 studies published between 2010 and 2025, systematically mapping the multidimensional relationship across oral health, nutrition-related biomarkers, and cognitive outcomes in older adults (≥65 years). By operationalizing a structured PCC framework, our synthesis indicates that poor oral health (severe tooth loss, loss of functional occlusion, impaired mastication, and active periodontitis) is consistently associated with cognitive vulnerability, accelerated cognitive decline, and increased risk of AD/ADRD.

Rather than viewing dental conditions in isolation, the mapped literature supports an integrative Oral-Nutritional-Neurodegenerative framework operating across three distinct biological pathways:The Inflammatory-Microbial Axis: Suggests that active periodontitis maintains persistent systemic inflammatory signaling (elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) and permits periopathogens (Porphyromonas gingivalis) and their virulence factors to compromise BBB integrity, potentially fueling microglial priming and neuroinflammation [,,,,,,,].The Nutritional-Metabolic Axis: Posits that reduced functional dentition and occlusal loss are associated with dietary shifts toward soft, processed foods, predisposing individuals to subclinical malnutrition, low serum albumin, and B-vitamin (B12 and folate) depletion [,,,,]. This metabolic impairment elevates circulating plasma homocysteine, an established marker linked to vascular brain injury and hippocampal vulnerability [,,,,].The Sensorimotor Deafferentation Axis: Proposes that loss of posterior occlusal contacts and periodontal mechanoreceptors deprives the central nervous system of vital trigeminal sensory feedback during mastication, which is hypothesized to correlate with reduced regional cerebral blood flow and structural volume changes in memory centers [,,,,,,,,,].

The Inflammatory-Microbial Axis: Suggests that active periodontitis maintains persistent systemic inflammatory signaling (elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) and permits periopathogens (Porphyromonas gingivalis) and their virulence factors to compromise BBB integrity, potentially fueling microglial priming and neuroinflammation [,,,,,,,].

The Nutritional-Metabolic Axis: Posits that reduced functional dentition and occlusal loss are associated with dietary shifts toward soft, processed foods, predisposing individuals to subclinical malnutrition, low serum albumin, and B-vitamin (B12 and folate) depletion [,,,,]. This metabolic impairment elevates circulating plasma homocysteine, an established marker linked to vascular brain injury and hippocampal vulnerability [,,,,].

The Sensorimotor Deafferentation Axis: Proposes that loss of posterior occlusal contacts and periodontal mechanoreceptors deprives the central nervous system of vital trigeminal sensory feedback during mastication, which is hypothesized to correlate with reduced regional cerebral blood flow and structural volume changes in memory centers [,,,,,,,,,].

A key objective of this ScR was to evaluate how evidence aligns across different study designs. While marked variations in sample sizes and regional populations exist, converging patterns emerged across epidemiological methodologies, highlighting consistent associations while exposing design-specific analytical limits.

Longitudinal studies provided the strongest evidence regarding temporal sequences linking poor oral health and neurocognitive decline [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Well-characterized cohorts (the Hisayama Study, AGES, and Ohasama Study in Japan, CLHLS in China, ELSA in the UK, and Health ABC in the US) consistently reported a dose–response relationship between tooth loss and incident dementia or cognitive decline [,,,,,,,]. Cohorts evaluating functional parameters confirmed that reduced bite force and objective chewing disability at baseline independently predict 3- to 10-year cognitive decline []. Furthermore, longitudinal path analyses supported dietary quality, body weight, and nutrient intake as potential partial mediators linking baseline tooth loss to subsequent cognitive trajectories [,,,,,,,,].

Cross-sectional studies across community-dwelling individuals, nursing home residents, and clinical outpatients showed high concordance regarding functional capacity and cognitive impairment severity [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Across diverse settings, individuals with MCI and diagnosed AD displayed significantly lower natural tooth counts, reduced FMUs, weaker bite force, and prolonged chewing cycles compared to cognitively intact controls [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Cross-sectional biomarker studies consistently identified significant correlations between active periodontal disease (elevated PISA/PDD) and systemic inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6), as well as between masticatory dysfunction and B-vitamin/homocysteine dysregulation [,,,,,,,,,]. Case–control studies differentiated clinical AD cohorts from non-demented controls based on oral disease burden and periodontal microbial profiles (e.g., P. Gingivalis antibody titers) [,,,,,,].

Interventional trials and prosthetic rehabilitation studies provided preliminary observational insights: restoring functional occlusion via complete or partial dentures improved maximal bite force, increased chewing efficiency, and was associated with altered regional cerebral blood flow or cortical activity on neuroimaging [,,,,]. However, these studies noted that while prosthetic rehabilitation attenuates cognitive decline risk, functional masticatory performance in rehabilitated edentulous older people rarely reaches the baseline performance of natural, fully dentate individuals [,,,,,,,,].

Synthesis of the 120 included studies indicates that tooth loss and active periodontitis represent distinct clinical exposures within neurodegenerative risk models. When periodontitis and elevated homocysteine co-occur, they form a high-risk oral–vascular–inflammatory risk cluster [,,,,,,]. Inflamed periodontal tissues disrupt chewing efficiency, predisposing individuals to B-vitamin (B12/Folate) deficiency and impaired one-carbon methylation [,,,,,,,]. The resulting hyperhomocysteinemia is hypothesized to induce endovascular injury, while circulating cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) exacerbate BBB permeability [,,,,,,,]. Concurrently, reduced masticatory movement decreases trigeminal afferent input to the brainstem and hippocampus, potentially attenuating regional perfusion [,,,,,,].

While the mapped evidence remains predominantly observational, these findings support potential translational hypotheses for geriatric clinical frameworks, encouraging a transition from siloed dental and medical care toward integrated oral–nutritional–cognitive models. Comprehensive geriatric research protocols should evaluate whether incorporating low-cost oral functional metrics (e.g., self-reported chewing difficulty, simple bite force assays, or FMU counts) alongside nutritional panels (serum albumin, B12, folate, homocysteine) provides accessible risk proxies for early cognitive vulnerability screening. Preserving natural functional dentition (≥20 teeth) and maintaining periodontal therapy represent key target areas for mid-to-late-life preventive strategies [,,,,,,]. For edentulous or partially dentate older adults, future studies should evaluate whether timely prosthetic rehabilitation combined with targeted B-vitamin supplementation can mitigate nutritional and sensorimotor drivers of cognitive decline.

International healthcare structures demonstrate marked contrasts in late-life oral healthcare provision.

Japan, for instance, combines high life expectancy with universal health coverage and longstanding national initiatives, such as the “8020 Campaign” (promoting retention of at least 20 natural teeth at age 80) []. In contrast, access to dental care among older adults in the United States remains fragmented, as traditional Medicare excludes routine preventive and restorative dental care, creating significant financial barriers that disproportionately affect socioeconomically disadvantaged and health disparity populations (such as those evaluated in HABS-HD) [,,,,,,].

Several methodological limitations inherent to scoping reviews and the underlying literature base must be acknowledged:Language Restriction: Restricting eligibility to English-language publications may have introduced language bias, particularly given that over half of the included evidence originated from West Asia.Observational Predominance: The heavy reliance on cross-sectional (52.5%) and observational cohort (38.3%) studies restricts causal inference and temporal interpretation.Absence of Critical Appraisal: In accordance with JBI scoping review standards, formal risk of bias scoring was not performed, preventing the distinction between stronger and weaker evidence within mapped associations.Non-Unique Sample Tallying: Cumulative sample sizes across included studies should not be interpreted as unique individual participants, as large longitudinal cohorts (e.g., Hiyasame, CLHLS, Fujiwara-kyo) contributed multiple publications across different follow-up waves.Exposure and Outcome Heterogeneity: Marked heterogeneity in definitions of tooth loss, periodontal disease (ranging from single-item self-reports to full-mouth PISA examinations), masticatory performance, and cognitive metrics (ranging from MMSE screening to neuroimaging/PET markers) limits direct comparability or meta-analytic pooling.A Priori Framework Categorization: The three-axis ONBA framework was defined a priori and may have influenced the categorization and qualitative synthesis of evidence.Domain Multiplicity Threshold: The requirement for studies to evaluate at least two ONBA domains may have excluded relevant single-domain studies while restricting the ability to quantify fully integrated three-domain evidence.Conceptual Mediation vs. Causal Testing: Several proposed mediating pathways were inferred conceptually from cross-sectional correlations rather than directly confirmed using formal causal mediation models or longitudinal path analyses. Reverse causation (e.g., early cognitive decline leading to oral hygiene neglect) and residual confounding (from socioeconomic status, lifelong dental access, and health literacy) remain possible.

Language Restriction: Restricting eligibility to English-language publications may have introduced language bias, particularly given that over half of the included evidence originated from West Asia.

Observational Predominance: The heavy reliance on cross-sectional (52.5%) and observational cohort (38.3%) studies restricts causal inference and temporal interpretation.

Absence of Critical Appraisal: In accordance with JBI scoping review standards, formal risk of bias scoring was not performed, preventing the distinction between stronger and weaker evidence within mapped associations.

Non-Unique Sample Tallying: Cumulative sample sizes across included studies should not be interpreted as unique individual participants, as large longitudinal cohorts (e.g., Hiyasame, CLHLS, Fujiwara-kyo) contributed multiple publications across different follow-up waves.

Exposure and Outcome Heterogeneity: Marked heterogeneity in definitions of tooth loss, periodontal disease (ranging from single-item self-reports to full-mouth PISA examinations), masticatory performance, and cognitive metrics (ranging from MMSE screening to neuroimaging/PET markers) limits direct comparability or meta-analytic pooling.

A Priori Framework Categorization: The three-axis ONBA framework was defined a priori and may have influenced the categorization and qualitative synthesis of evidence.

Domain Multiplicity Threshold: The requirement for studies to evaluate at least two ONBA domains may have excluded relevant single-domain studies while restricting the ability to quantify fully integrated three-domain evidence.

Conceptual Mediation vs. Causal Testing: Several proposed mediating pathways were inferred conceptually from cross-sectional correlations rather than directly confirmed using formal causal mediation models or longitudinal path analyses. Reverse causation (e.g., early cognitive decline leading to oral hygiene neglect) and residual confounding (from socioeconomic status, lifelong dental access, and health literacy) remain possible.

Future research should move beyond isolated oral, nutritional, inflammatory, and cognitive measurements toward longitudinal, multi-domain studies capable of evaluating temporal and bidirectional relationships. Future cohorts should harmonize standardized measures of dentition, periodontal inflammation (PISA), masticatory performance (FMUs, bite force), dietary intake, nutritional status, one-carbon biomarkers (B12, folate, homocysteine), inflammatory cytokines, global cognition, and neuroimaging. Analytical models must incorporate frailty, socioeconomic status, social isolation, depression, healthcare access, and caregiver support as potential confounders and effect modifiers.

Furthermore, research should leverage multi-ethnic cohorts (such as HABS-HD) to validate whether ONBA associations persist across diverse racial and ethnic groups. Advanced causal inference methods, including Mendelian randomization and structural equation modeling, should be applied to disentangle directional pathways. Finally, well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether combined periodontal care, high-quality prosthetic rehabilitation, and targeted nutritional supplementation can favorably modify cognitive trajectories and mitigate AD/ADRD risk in vulnerable older populations.

This scoping review indicates consistent associations connecting oral diseases, loss of functional dentition, and masticatory breakdown to neurocognitive vulnerability and AD/ADRD risk. Rather than establishing direct causality, the mapped literature supports a plausible conceptual framework operating across three interconnected pathways: the inflammatory-microbial, nutritional-metabolic, and sensorimotor deafferentation axes. While these biological mechanisms represent plausible conduits linking oral breakdown to neurodegeneration, their relative individual contributions and exact temporal directionality remain to be fully clarified. These conclusions must be interpreted in light of key evidence gaps identified across the mapped landscape, including the heavy predominance of observational and cross-sectional study designs (94.2%), significant geographical concentration in West Asia (>56%), marked heterogeneity in oral and cognitive outcome definitions, and a scarcity of studies evaluating all three ONBA domains simultaneously. Ultimately, determining whether preserving oral health, adequate nutritional status, and masticatory capacity contributes to healthy cognitive aging represents a critical interdisciplinary priority for preserving functional independence and quality of life in older adults.

neuroscience.title: Editorial: Molecular neuroscience: current and future challenges
neuroscience.abstract: No abstract
neuroscience.text:
Molecular neuroscience has undergone a remarkable transformation over recent decades. The challenge is no longer simply to identify the neurotransmitters and associated molecular mechanisms that enable neuronal communication. In recent years, our focus has shifted toward understanding how molecular processes interact across spatial and temporal scales to shape cellular function, synaptic connectivity, neural circuits and whole organism behavior. Today, molecular neuroscience has advanced significantly, thanks in large part to new technologies like CRISPR gene editing, molecular and pharmacological probes, spatiotemporal gene expression control, optogenetics, induced pluripotent stem cell technology, advanced microscopy and single-cell RNA sequencing. These tools have enabled scientists to investigate differences in the molecular machinery of neurons and glia in unprecedented detail. However, understanding how these differences contribute to distinct cellular functions and network behaviors in health and disease states remains a daunting task. The Research Topic Molecular Neuroscience: Current and Future Challenges brings together studies that highlight recent advancements in Molecular Neuroscience, ranging from fundamental mechanisms of neuronal and synaptic function to cutting edge studies of neurodevelopmental/neurodegenerative disorders and newly-emerging therapeutic strategies.

A recurring theme across the collection is the importance of understanding molecular mechanisms in a given cellular and functional context. For example, Chojnacka et al. investigated auditory hypersensitivity in fragile X syndrome (FXS), demonstrating delayed structural maturation of inner hair cell ribbon synapses in Fmr1 knockout mice. Although mature synapses lacked major ultrastructural abnormalities, altered postnatal synaptic development provided a potential link between loss of FMRP and the auditory abnormalities associated with FXS. At another level of synaptic organization, Gobbo et al. examined the relationship between neuronal activation and synaptic plasticity during hippocampal memory formation. Using molecular reporters of neuronal activation and postsynaptic potentiation, they demonstrated that the relative weight and spatial distribution of potentiated dendritic spines in hippocampal CA1 neurons differ between memory encoding and retrieval. Together, these studies illustrate how molecular changes at individual synapses can potentially influence sensory processing and higher-order functions such as memory.

The importance of ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors is similarly evident. Deng et al. reviewed the contribution of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels to intracellular calcium dysregulation and neuronal hyperexcitability in epilepsy. The diversity of TRP channel subtypes and their interactions with intracellular calcium, oxidative stress and other signaling pathways illustrates both the therapeutic opportunities and complexities associated with targeting neuronal ion channels in disease states. Wiessler et al. investigated autoimmune neurological disease caused by autoantibodies directed against inhibitory glycine receptors (GlyRs), key regulators of synaptic inhibition in the spinal cord and brainstem. Their findings indicated considerable patient-specific heterogeneity in GlyR subunit autoantibody recognition, with some antibodies recognizing epitopes in multiple subunits (α1-3 and β), complicating the identification of a universal neutralizing epitope. This work highlights an important challenge for precision medicine: even when a molecular target is known, individual differences in the mechanisms affecting that target may necessitate personalized therapeutic approaches.

The collection also emphasizes that molecular function cannot necessarily be inferred from gene or protein expression alone. Pronina et al. examined tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expressed in neurons of the hypothalamic supraoptic nucleus (SN). Despite detecting TH expression, their findings indicate that the TH protein in the SN does not exhibit the expected enzymatic activity required for L-DOPA synthesis, potentially because of potential differences in the N-terminal regulatory region. This study provides a useful reminder that the functional significance of a molecular phenotype requires investigation beyond simple transcript or protein analysis.

Gene regulation and cellular stress responses provide another level of complexity. For example, the alternative use of microexons, short exonic sequences of 3–30 nucleotides that undergo alternative splicing, has been implicated in several neurodevelopmental disorders. Mehnert et al. investigated microexon-associated junction usage in Parkinson's disease (PD) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 using deep RNA-sequencing of human postmortem brain tissue. Although no disease-associated events survived correction for multiple testing, substantially more microexons were detectable in human brain tissue than in corresponding cellular models. These findings emphasize both the subtlety of post-transcriptional regulation and the limitations inherent in extrapolating from simplified cellular systems to the complexity of human brain tissue. Huang et al. reviewed the role of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), a central component of the neuronal integrated stress response (ISR). They highlighted the context-dependent nature of ATF4 signaling, which can support neuronal homeostasis under some circumstances while contributing to neuroinflammation, ferroptosis and neuronal dysfunction when chronically dysregulated. Consequently, therapeutic intervention may require modulation of the timing and magnitude of stress signaling rather than simple pathway inhibition.

The importance of interactions beyond neurons themselves is particularly apparent in Parkinson's disease. Kroker Kimber and Tremblay reviewed communication between the gut microbiome and microglia, highlighting evidence that microbial dysbiosis may influence systemic inflammation, microglial activation and α-synuclein pathology. Probiotic interventions represent an intriguing approach to modifying this gut-brain communication, although direct evidence for modulation of human brain microglia remains limited. Tumpa et al. extended this perspective by considering interactions between peripheral and central innate and adaptive immunity in Parkinson's disease. Together, these contributions illustrate an increasingly important concept in molecular neuroscience: brain disorders cannot always be understood by studying the brain in isolation.

This broader “‘systems”' perspective is also evident in two contributions examining neurological dysfunction from translational viewpoints. Wen et al. reviewed the multifactorial molecular basis of age-related hearing loss (ARHL), also known as or presbycusis, encompassing oxidative stress, inflammation, altered autophagy, cellular senescence, genetic susceptibility and environmental influences. Emerging approaches including gene therapy, regenerative strategies, targeted drug delivery and biomarker-based early intervention—which illustrate the potential for mechanistic discoveries to generate new therapeutic opportunities, while also emphasizing the substantial challenges of clinical translation. Yan et al. similarly integrated molecular pathophysiology with neuroimaging in a review of sepsis-associated encephalopathy, linking blood-brain barrier disruption, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter imbalance and neuronal and glial injury with measurable imaging phenotypes. Such approaches provide an important bridge between molecular mechanisms and clinically accessible biomarkers.

Taken together, the contributions to this Research Topic illustrate both the extraordinary progress and the continuing challenges of molecular neuroscience. Increasingly powerful experimental approaches allow investigation from gene regulation and protein function through individual synapses, neural circuits and interactions between the nervous, immune and peripheral systems. However, greater resolution has also revealed additional biological heterogeneity and complexity.
