Future progress will depend not only on identifying new molecular mechanisms, but on determining when, where and in which cells these mechanisms operate, how they interact across body organs and systems, and how faithfully our cellular or animal models represent human disease. Ultimately, meeting these challenges will be essential if advances in molecular neuroscience are to be translated into meaningful biomarkers, precision interventions and effective therapies for disorders of the central and peripheral nervous system.

neuroscience.title: White Matter Hyperintensities Modify CYP2C19 Effect on Stroke Progression in Small Vessel Occlusion
neuroscience.abstract:
The association between CYP2C19 loss‐of‐function (LOF) alleles and early neurological deterioration (END) in acute small vessel occlusion (SVO) patients receiving dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) remains inconsistent. We hypothesized that white matter hyperintensities (WMH) burden act as a key moderator and investigated whether this modulates the association between CYP2C19 LOF and END.We conducted a retrospective study of SVO patients receiving DAPT. CYP2C19 genotypes were classified as LOF carriers or non‐carriers. The primary endpoint was END; secondary and safety endpoints included severe END, 90‐day mRS 0–2, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), bleeding, and mortality. Multivariable regression and interaction analyzes assessed associations between CYP2C19, WMH, and clinical outcomes.A total of 247 patients (median age 67.0 years; 28.7% female; 60.7% CYP2C19 LOF carriers), 54 (21.9%) experienced END. Multivariable analysis identified infarct diameter (aOR 1.26, 95% CI 1.13–1.39, p < 0.001) and total cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) burden (aOR 2.02, 95% CI 1.37–2.98, p < 0.001) as independent predictors. A significant multiplicative interaction was observed between CYP2C19 LOF and severe WMH on END risk (aOR 9.34, 95% CI 2.06–48.10, p = 0.005). Stratified analysis showed CYP2C19 LOF significantly increased END risk specifically in patients with severe WMH (aOR 3.44, 95% CI 1.12–10.55, p = 0.030), but not mild WMH. Predicted probability curves suggested a Fazekas score threshold of approximately 2.70. Secondary and safety outcomes were infrequent.
CYP2C19 LOF alleles increase END risk in SVO patients specifically with severe WMH. These findings highlight the value of integrating genetic and neuroimaging markers for risk stratification and personalized antiplatelet therapy.
neuroscience.text:
Small vessel occlusion (SVO) accounts for approximately 25% of all ischemic strokes []. Although SVO typically presents with mild initial deficits, early neurological deterioration (END) occurs in 16.9%–30.0% of patients and frequently leads to poor long‐term outcomes []. Despite guideline‐recommended dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) [], END still occurs in a subset of patients, and targeted prevention remains challenging. The mechanisms of END are multifactorial, with thrombus extension driven by platelet activation as a key contributor [].

Previous studies have identified multiple risk factors for END in SVO, including infarct location and size, baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, and capsular warning syndrome (CWS) [, , , , ]. Clopidogrel resistance is an important driver of this residual risk. As a prodrug, clopidogrel requires hepatic CYP2C19 metabolism to produce its active metabolite. Loss‐of‐function (LOF) alleles, predominantly CYP2C19*2 and *3, are prevalent in approximately 60% of East Asian populations, reducing active metabolite generation and platelet inhibition []. Although LOF carriers face an approximately doubled risk of END [, ], CYP2C19 genotype alone explains only 10%–12% of clinical response variability, suggesting that other physiological or genetic factors interact with LOF alleles to modulate antiplatelet efficacy [].

White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are the neuroimaging hallmark of chronic cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), reflecting cumulative microvascular damage and endothelial dysfunction [, ]. Because WMH and SVO share underlying small‐vessel pathology [], a severe WMH burden reflects reduced baseline cerebrovascular reserve []. When acute SVO occurs, such pre‐existing vascular compromise leaves the tissue highly vulnerable to perfusion failure, contributing to an increased risk of END [, ].

We hypothesized that CYP2C19 LOF carrier status and severe WMH burden interact to increase the risk of END, as insufficient platelet inhibition may lead to critical perfusion failure in an already compromised microvascular bed. Whether WMH burden modifies the effect of CYP2C19 LOF on END remains unexplored. Therefore, this retrospective cohort study investigated this gene‐imaging interaction in SVO patients receiving DAPT, aiming to provide a basis for more precise risk stratification and personalized antiplatelet strategies.

This single‐center, retrospective observational study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Geriatric Hospital (approval No. 2023‐030). The requirement for informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the analysis. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Between January 2023 and December 2025, 1208 acute ischemic stroke patients were admitted to the Department of Neurology, Beijing Geriatric Hospital. Inclusion criteria were: (1) admission within 48 h of onset; (2) age ≥ 18 years; (3) MRI‐confirmed diagnosis of SVO; (4) availability of complete brain MRI data for CSVD burden assessment; (5) treatment with aspirin plus clopidogrel; and (6) availability of CYP2C19 genotyping. Exclusion criteria included: (1) other determined stroke etiologies; (2) contraindications to DAPT (active bleeding, severe hepatic or renal impairment, platelet count < 100 × 109/L); (3) pre‐stroke modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score > 2; (4) received intravenous thrombolysis or endovascular therapy; and (5) lack of baseline data. Finally, 247 patients were eligible for the analysis (Figure ). Follow‐up mRS assessment at 90 days was completed in 240 patients (97.2%).

Stroke subtypes were classified according to the Trial of Org 10,172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) criteria []. For the SVO subtype, we adopted a modified definition based on previously established criteria: a single acute infarct within the territory of a penetrating artery, with a maximum axial diameter of < 20 mm on DWI, located in the subcortical area or brainstem, and without evidence of > 50% stenosis in the parent artery or a cardioembolic source [].

Clinical data were extracted from standardized medical records. Baseline characteristics included demographics, vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, stroke history, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, smoking, and alcohol use), and admission blood pressure. Neurological status was assessed using the NIHSS at admission and monitored daily, with additional evaluation performed upon suspected clinical deterioration. Functional outcome was assessed at 90 days post‐stroke using the mRS score. Laboratory tests included fasting plasma glucose, hemoglobin A1c, total cholesterol, triglycerides, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and platelet count. All patients were managed in the stroke unit according to institutional protocols for secondary stroke prevention, including standardized anti‐hypertensive and statin therapies.

Brain MRI was performed using a 3.0 T scanner (Ingenia 3.0 T, Philips, The Netherlands). The imaging protocol included diffusion‐weighted MRI (DWI), T1‐weighted, T2‐weighted, fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and susceptibility‐weighted imaging (SWI) sequences. CSVD markers were defined according to the Standards for Reporting Vascular Changes on Neuroimaging (STRIVE) consensus []. All images were evaluated by two experienced neuroradiologists blinded to the clinical data, with a third senior neuroradiologist adjudicating any discordant findings.

WMH was evaluated on FLAIR sequences using the Fazekas scale [, ], which independently scores periventricular (PVWMH) and deep (DWMH) WMH. The total Fazekas score (range 0–6) was calculated as the sum of PVWMH and DWMH scores. To categorize overall burden, patients were stratified into mild (0–2) and severe (3–6) WMH groups [, ]. The total CSVD burden score (range 0–4) was determined based on the method proposed by Klarenbeek et al. [], assigning one point for each of the following: (1) presence of ≥ 1 lacune; (2) extensive WMH (DWMH Fazekas score ≥ 2 or PVWMH Fazekas score = 3); (3) presence of ≥ 1 cerebral microbleed on SWI; and (4) moderate‐to‐severe basal ganglia enlarged perivascular spaces (score ≥ 2). Acute infarcts were characterized by location as strategic (involving the internal capsule, pons, or corona radiata) or non‐strategic [, ], because these strategic regions are rich in corticospinal tract fibers and prone to END.

CYP2C19 genotypes (*2, *3, and *17) were determined using the GMEX point‐of‐care genotyping system (Chongqing Jingyin Bioscience Co. Ltd.), a platform validated for identifying polymorphisms from buccal swabs and utilized in the CHANCE‐2 trial. Based on the genotype, patients were classified into LOF carriers and non‐carriers. LOF carriers were defined as individuals carrying at least one LOF allele (*2 or *3), including genotypes such as *2/*2, *3/*3, *2/*3, *1/*2, *1/*3, *2/*17, and *3/*17. Non‐carriers were defined as individuals without LOF alleles, including normal metabolizer (*1/*1) and rapid/ultrarapid metabolizer (*1/*17 or *17/*17).

Clinical outcomes were assessed through a combination of electronic medical records review and systematic telephone follow‐up. The primary endpoint was END, defined as an increase of ≥ 2 points in total NIHSS score or ≥ 1 point in motor items within 72 h of admission [, ]. Secondary endpoints included severe END (NIHSS increase ≥ 4 points within 7 days) [] and favorable functional outcome (mRS 0–2 at 90 days). Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), any bleeding event, and all‐cause mortality during the 90‐day follow‐up period. sICH was defined by the European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study (ECASS) III criteria as any intracranial hemorrhage on follow‐up imaging (CT or MRI) accompanied by neurological deterioration (≥ 4 points on the NIHSS) []. Any bleeding event was defined as a bleeding episode requiring clinical intervention or treatment modification. All outcomes were independently adjudicated by two senior neurologists blinded to the clinical and genetic data.

Continuous variables were presented as mean ± SD or median (IQR) and were compared using Student's t‐test or Mann–Whitney U‐test. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies (percentages) and compared by chi‐square or Fisher's exact test. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess association of WMH burden and CYP2C19 genotypes with END. Three models were fitted: Model 1 (unadjusted); Model 2 (adjusted for age, sex, baseline NIHSS); Model 3 (further adjusted for fasting blood glucose, admission systolic blood pressure [SBP], smoking, alcohol use, infarct location, and infarct diameter). Multiplicative interaction was tested by including a cross‐product term (Wald test) and confirmed by likelihood ratio test (LRT). Additive interaction was assessed using relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI), attributable proportion (AP), and synergy index (SI) as described by Andersson et al. []. Stratified analyzes examined the association between CYP2C19 LOF carrier status and END across WMH severity subgroups. All analyzes were conducted using SPSS (version 26.0) and R (version 4.5.3). A two‐tailed p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Baseline characteristics of the 247 patients are summarized in Table . The cohort had a median age of 67 (IQR 61–73) years, with 28.7% (n = 71) being female. CYP2C19 LOF carriers accounted for 60.7% (n = 150) of the population. During the hospital stay, END occurred in 54 (21.9%) patients, of whom 50 (92.6%) underwent treatment escalation (tirofiban or ticagrelor substituted for clopidogrel per institutional protocol).

In univariate analysis, patients with END had significantly higher admission NIHSS scores (median 2.9 vs. 2.0; p < 0.001), larger infarct diameters (median 10.1 vs. 7.0 mm; p < 0.001), and higher CSVD total burden scores (median 1.8 vs. 1.3; p = 0.005). Infarct location was significantly associated with END (p = 0.020), with a higher prevalence of strategic lesions in the END group (75.9% vs. 58.5%). While the proportions of severe WMH and CYP2C19 LOF carriers were numerically higher in the END group (57.4% vs. 50.3% and 66.7% vs. 59.1%, respectively), these differences did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.353 and p = 0.312). Admission SBP was higher in the END group than in the non‐END group (161.3 ± 20.9 vs. 156.0 ± 19.6 mmHg), but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.090). No significant differences were observed between the two groups in age, sex, vascular risk factors, or laboratory parameters.

Multivariable logistic regression (Table ) showed that, after adjustment for age, sex, SBP, NIHSS, smoking, alcohol, FPG, infarct location, and diameter, infarct diameter emerged as an independent predictor of END (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.26, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.13–1.39, p < 0.001). Conversely, severe WMH (aOR 1.72, 95% CI 0.80–3.70, p = 0.167) and CYP2C19 LOF carrier status (aOR 1.22, 95% CI 0.59–2.54, p = 0.591) were not significantly associated with END. In sensitivity analysis using CSVD total score instead of severe WMH (Table ), a higher CSVD total score was independently associated with END (aOR 2.02, 95% CI 1.37–2.98, p < 0.001), while the association between infarct diameter and END remained consistent.

Multivariable logistic regression analysis of factors associated with END.

Note: Bold values indicate statistical significance (p < 0.05).

Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; END, early neurological deterioration; FPG, fasting plasma glucose; LOF, loss‐of‐function; NIHSS, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale; OR, odds ratio; SBP, systolic blood pressure; WMH, white matter hyperintensities.

We evaluated the multiplicative interaction between CYP2C19 LOF carrier status and severe WMH on the risk of END (Table ). In the fully adjusted model (Model 3), the interaction term was significant (aOR 9.34, 95% CI 2.06–48.10, interaction p = 0.005), indicating that the association between LOF status and END is modified by WMH severity. This result was robust upon LRT (interaction p = 0.0034). For additive interaction, the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) was 1.65 (95% CI 0.57–2.72) and the attributable proportion (AP) was 1.15 (95% CI 0.50–1.80). The synergy index (SI) was not computed as the individual main effects of both LOF and severe WMH showed protective trends (OR < 1) in our model. Despite wide 95% CIs for the interaction terms—likely reflecting the limited number of END events—the direction and statistical significance of the interaction remained consistent across all adjustment models.

Multivariable logistic regression models for the multiplicative interaction between LOF and WMH on END.

Note: Model 1: Unadjusted model including LOF carrier, WMH, and their interaction term. Model 2 (Adjusted): Adjusted for age, sex, and baseline NIHSS score. Model 3 (Fully Adjusted): Adjusted for age, sex, baseline NIHSS score, fasting blood glucose, admission SBP, smoking status, alcohol use, infarct location, and infarct diameter. Interaction p were derived from the Wald test; likelihood ratio test results are reported in the text.

Abbreviations: END, early neurological deterioration; LOF, loss‐of‐function; WMH, white matter hyperintensities.

To further characterize this interaction, we performed stratified analysis by WMH burden (Figure ). The association between CYP2C19 LOF carrier status and END differed by WMH severity: among patients with mild WMH, LOF status was not significantly associated with END (aOR 0.37, 95% CI 0.12–1.10, p = 0.074), whereas among those with severe WMH, LOF status was significantly associated with an increased risk of END (aOR 3.44, 95% CI 1.12–10.55, p = 0.030).

When analyzing the Fazekas score as a continuous variable, the interaction term (LOF × Fazekas) was not significant (aOR 1.45, 95% CI 0.87–2.43, p = 0.156). However, predicted probability curves (Figure ) intersected at a Fazekas score of approximately 2.70; beyond this point, the predicted risk of END among LOF carriers shifted from lower to higher relative to non‐carriers. This intersection, combined with the significant multiplicative interaction observed with the binary WMH classification (Fazekas ≥ 3), suggests a potential threshold effect of WMH burden on the clinical impact of CYP2C19 LOF variants.

Secondary and safety outcomes are summarized in Table . Severe END occurred in 6.7% (10/150) of LOF carriers and 5.2% (5/97) in non‐carriers. At 90 days, a favorable functional outcome (mRS 0–2) was achieved by 95.2% (140/147) of LOF carriers and 97.8% (91/93) of non‐carriers. Safety events were infrequent: sICH occurred in only 3 patients (1.2%; 1 LOF carrier and 2 non‐carriers), and any bleeding event was reported in 1 (0.7%) LOF carrier. No mortality was recorded during the 90‐day follow‐up. Formal statistical comparisons were not conducted due to the low frequency of these clinical events.

Primary and secondary outcomes.

Abbreviations: END, early neurological deterioration; LOF, loss‐of‐function; mRS, modified Rankin Scale; sICH, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.

Percentages were calculated among patients who completed the 90‐day follow‐up (147 LOF carriers and 93 non‐carriers). Due to the low event counts, no formal statistical comparisons were performed.

In this retrospective cohort of 247 patients with SVO, the incidence of END was 21.9%. Larger infarct diameter and higher CSVD total burden independently predicted END. We identified a significant multiplicative interaction between CYP2C19 LOF alleles and severe WMH burden on END risk. While LOF status alone did not independently predict END, it increased the risk over threefold in patients with severe WMH but not in those with mild WMH. These findings suggest that the clinical expression of clopidogrel resistance may depend on the degree of pre‐existing microvascular damage. This novel gene‐imaging interaction may guide targeted early intensified antiplatelet therapy in high‐risk LOF carriers.

The underlying mechanism likely involves a “two‐hit” model of END in SVO. Severe WMH reflects chronic microvascular damage, endothelial dysfunction, and blood–brain barrier disruption [, ], with impaired hemodynamic regulation [], which together lead to exhausted microcirculatory reserve, impaired autoregulation, and compromised collateral flow [, , , ]. Zerna et al. found that WMH burden increased short‐term disability risk mainly when intracranial stenosis or occlusion was present, supporting WMH as an effect modifier []. In this vulnerable state, suboptimal platelet inhibition due to CYP2C19 LOF may act as a second hit, such that even minor thrombus propagation could precipitate END []. Conversely, mild WMH retains sufficient reserve to buffer this effect, which may explain why the genetic risk is only observed beyond a certain threshold.

Our observed LOF carrier frequency (60.7%) aligns with East Asian demographics [, ]. Prior meta‐analyzes linking LOF alleles to poor outcomes (RR 1.63) often included heterogeneous populations such as large artery atherosclerosis and cardioembolic strokes, where thrombotic burden predominates; however, this association was less consistent in SVO []. In our homogeneous SVO cohort with uniform DAPT, the lack of independent predictive value for LOF status suggests that the clinical impact of clopidogrel resistance may depend on stroke subtype and underlying pathophysiology.

WMH burden significantly modified the effect of CYP2C19 LOF status, with LOF‐associated risk mainly in severe WMH (Fazekas ≥ 3). This threshold pattern is consistent with prior studies: Ryu et al. found that only the highest WMH quintile predicted 3‐month outcomes in SVO [], and Guo et al. linked severe leukoaraiosis to increased END risk after thrombectomy []. Although the continuous Fazekas score × LOF interaction was not significant, the probability curves cross at a Fazekas score of approximately 2.70, suggesting a threshold effect; however, this cutoff should be interpreted cautiously given the limited sample at the score extremes.

The CSVD total burden score remained a robust predictor of END, likely because it integrates a broader range of small vessel pathology—lacunes, microbleeds, and enlarged perivascular spaces—beyond WMH alone []; these lesion types may contribute to END via distinct mechanisms.

Regarding infarct morphology, larger infarct diameter was independently associated with END (aOR 1.26 per 1 mm increase), consistent with Huang et al. [], who reported a sharp rise in END risk at diameter > 15 mm. Infarcts > 15 mm are more characteristic of branch atheromatous disease (BAD) than classic lipohyalinotic SVO, explaining their higher susceptibility to progression []. While our SVO criteria (lesion diameter < 20 mm) align with established standards, this threshold may introduce pathophysiological heterogeneity. Future studies using high‐resolution vessel wall imaging are needed to refine this definition. Additionally, previous studies have identified CWS as a strong predictor of END (aOR 7.00) []. However, CWS was not systematically recorded in our retrospective cohort, and internal capsule involvement was comparable between groups (7.4% vs. 6.7%). Because CWS is a clinical syndrome rather than an imaging finding, these data cannot exclude it as a potential unmeasured confounder.

Finally, 90‐day functional recovery was generally favorable, consistent with previous DAPT trials in SVO []. sICH was rare, and no moderate or severe bleeding events occurred. Given the limited sample size and the treatment heterogeneity, we did not perform formal statistical comparisons for safety endpoints. Nonetheless, the absence of excess bleeding in patients receiving intensified therapy suggests that genotype‐guided antiplatelet adjustment is safe even with severe WMH burden, consistent with the INSPIRES trial, where WMH severity did not modify bleeding risk [].

The present study has several limitations. First, its retrospective, single‐center design within a Chinese population and relatively small sample size may limit generalizability and statistical power; thus, our findings require validation in larger, multicenter prospective cohorts. Second, non‐standardized treatment escalation and the low frequency of bleeding events did not allow for a direct comparison across strategies. Although the low bleeding rate suggests that individualized therapy for LOF carriers is well tolerated, these findings should be interpreted with caution given the small sample and treatment heterogeneity. Third, we used the visual Fazekas scale rather than volumetric quantification. While volumetric analysis is more precise, the Fazekas scale is highly correlated with quantitative measures and is more feasible for daily clinical routine. Fourth, our SVO criteria (lesion diameter < 20 mm) likely included patients with BAD. While this reflects real‐world clinical heterogeneity, future studies incorporating high‐resolution vessel wall imaging are needed to better distinguish these pathological entities. Fifth, our study focused solely on major CYP2C19 genotypes (*2, *3, and *17) without screening for other variants (e.g., P2Y12 and GPIIIa) or performing platelet function testing, potentially failing to capture gene–gene interactions and the full pharmacodynamic response to clopidogrel []. Sixth, because of the retrospective design, clinical fluctuations typical of CWS were not systematically recorded, representing a potential unmeasured confounder. Additionally, infarct location was simplified into strategic versus non‐strategic categories to avoid model overfitting, which may have prevented more detailed analyzes of specific subregions. Finally, we could not include all potential confounders in our multivariable models, and residual or unmeasured confounding may remain and could partly explain the observed associations. Furthermore, excluding patients unable to complete MRI may have introduced selection bias toward less severe cases, potentially underestimating total event rates.

In conclusion, the impact of CYP2C19 LOF alleles on END in acute SVO patients was significantly modulated by WMH burden. CYP2C19 status was associated with END specifically in patients with severe WMH, suggesting that structural brain vulnerability amplifies the clinical consequences of suboptimal platelet inhibition. These findings underscore that genotype should not be interpreted in isolation and that integrating genetic testing with neuroimaging assessment may refine risk stratification for personalized antiplatelet therapy. Future studies are needed to validate this gene–imaging interaction and explore whether alternative P2Y12 inhibitors provide superior clinical benefits in this high‐risk subgroup.

neuroscience.title: A Homozygous Missense Variant in DCLK2 as a Potential Modifier of Disease Severity in PDHA1-Associated Primary Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex Deficiency
neuroscience.abstract: Introduction: Primary pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD) is a genetically heterogeneous mitochondrial disorder with marked clinical variability. PDHA1 is the most common cause of PDCD, but additional genetic factors may contribute to disease severity. Methods: A consanguineous family with two affected male siblings with clinical features of PDCD underwent clinical and genetic investigation. Whole-exome sequencing (WES), X-chromosome analysis, genome-wide autozygosity mapping, and segregation analysis were performed. Clinical, biochemical, neuroimaging, ophthalmological, and longitudinal medical records were reviewed. In silico analyses were performed for the identified variants. Results: Both siblings presented with neonatal lactic acidosis and severe neurological disease, including Leigh brain abnormalities, followed by progressive neuromuscular and multisystem manifestations. WES identified a novel hemizygous PDHA1 missense variant (c.754C>G; p.Leu252Val; rs1555934383), consistent with X-linked inheritance and providing the primary genetic explanation for PDCD. Autozygosity mapping identified a shared identical-by-descent interval on chromosome 4, within which a novel homozygous DCLK2 missense variant (c.101G>A; p.Ser34Asn) was identified. The variant was present in both affected siblings and segregated within the family. Despite sharing both variants, the siblings showed marked differences in disease severity. The younger sibling developed severe neurological and respiratory complications and died in childhood following a surgical procedure, whereas the older sibling survived into late adolescence but developed substantial neurological, metabolic, respiratory, and ophthalmological complications, including profound visual impairment and bilateral optic atrophy. Conclusions: The PDHA1 variant represents the primary genetic cause of PDCD, while the co-segregating homozygous DCLK2 variant is a candidate modifier of disease severity. Its localization within the shared IBD interval and biological relevance to neuronal stress responses support this hypothesis and suggest that DCLK2 may contribute to the phenotypic variability and severity of PDHA1-associated disease.
neuroscience.text:
Primary pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous mitochondrial disorder caused by impaired pyruvate oxidation and consequent reduction in cellular energy production [,]. The pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 component is an α2β2 heterotetramer composed of two E1α and two E1β subunits, with the E1α subunit encoded by PDHA1 []. X-linked PDHA1-related E1α deficiency (PDHAD; OMIM 312170) is the molecular form identified in the present family [,].

The major genetic forms of PDCD include E1α deficiency (PDHAD; OMIM 312170), caused by X-linked PDHA1 variants; E2 deficiency (PDHDD; OMIM 245348), caused by DLAT variants; E3-binding protein deficiency (PDHXD; OMIM 245349), caused by PDHX variants; E1β deficiency (PDHBD; OMIM 614111), caused by biallelic PDHB variants; and pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase deficiency (PDHPD; OMIM 608782), caused by PDP1 variants [,]. Clinical manifestations are predominantly neurological and may include congenital microcephaly, epilepsy, ataxia, hypotonia, developmental delay, and structural brain abnormalities such as Leigh syndrome and/or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. Principal metabolic abnormalities include lactic acidemia, increased plasma pyruvate, and metabolic acidosis [,].

In general, primary PDCD is diagnosed at a mean age of approximately 4 years, with a median age of around 1.5 years [,]. However, the disorder may be recognized prenatally when routine ultrasonography demonstrates abnormalities such as microcephaly, cerebellar hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly, paraventricular pseudocysts, delayed gyration, and/or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. Fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may provide additional evidence, including cerebral volume loss and periventricular T2-weighted hyperintensity [,]. Newborns may present with fetal growth restriction, microcephaly, structural or functional abnormalities of the brain, and lactic acidosis [,]. Less commonly, PDCD may present later in childhood with episodic limb paralysis or alternating hemiplegia [], paroxysmal dystonia or dyskinesia [,,], or intermittent ataxia [].

Developmental delay and axial hypotonia represent the most frequent neurological manifestations of PDCD. Other neurological features include ataxia, spasticity, epilepsy, and appendicular hypertonia [], peripheral neuropathy [], and episodes of dystonia triggered by stress, fever, or exercise [,]. Rare presentations include exercise-induced dyskinesia and episodic limb paralysis or hemiplegia []. Characteristic facial features may include a thin upper lip, long philtrum, and low-set ears [,]. Ophthalmological manifestations are uncommon and include optic atrophy, nystagmus, strabismus, ptosis [], and ophthalmoplegia [,]. Growth abnormalities include intrauterine growth restriction and primary or acquired microcephaly, whereas shortening of the long bones is reported less frequently. Musculoskeletal abnormalities may include acquired hip dysplasia. Psychiatric manifestations, including auditory hallucinations and delusional thoughts, have also been described, particularly among mildly affected individuals during adolescence or early adulthood [].

Common brain MRI abnormalities include cerebral atrophy, asymmetric ventriculomegaly, and dysgenesis or agenesis of the corpus callosum [,]. T2-weighted hyperintensities may also occur, most frequently involving the basal ganglia and, to a lesser extent, the brainstem and cerebellum []. Additional reported findings include periventricular cysts and/or intraventricular septations []. Hyporotation of the hippocampus is an uncommon MRI finding that has also been described in individuals with PDCD [,].

The principal laboratory abnormalities in PDCD are elevated blood lactate and pyruvate concentrations, generally with a lactate-to-pyruvate ratio within the normal range of approximately 10–20. Plasma pyruvate concentrations may exceed 0.2 mmol/L []. Lactate and pyruvate elevations may be intermittent and do not necessarily reflect disease severity, as pyruvate measurements can be affected by inappropriate sample collection and handling. Increased plasma proline and alanine concentrations have also been reported. Although the proline-to-leucine and alanine-to-leucine ratios may be sensitive indicators of primary PDCD, they are not specific to the disorder []. Increased lactate and pyruvate concentrations may also be detected in plasma, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) activity may be markedly reduced in cultured lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and/or skeletal muscle, although enzyme activity can differ between tissues within the same individual []. Newborn screening for PDCD is not yet widely available. In a pilot study using dried blood spots, screening based on a proline-to-leucine ratio > 3 and/or an alanine-to-leucine ratio > 4 identified three neonates with PDCD and two additional neonates with other mitochondrial disorders. The screening approach had a positive predictive value of 2.8% and a sensitivity of 80% [].

Among the genes associated with primary PDCD, PDHA1 is the most frequently implicated, accounting for approximately 76–85% of cases. The PDHA1 gene encodes the E1-alpha subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and is inherited in an X-linked manner. Pathogenic PDHA1 variants are associated with a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from neonatal lactic acidosis and Leigh syndrome [,,] to later-onset manifestations such as myopathy and ataxia [,]. Female heterozygotes may also exhibit substantial and asymmetric brain MRI abnormalities, including ventriculomegaly and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum [,]. Although a ketogenic diet may improve the clinical course in some individuals, treatment response is variable, and prolonged survival has been reported in selected patients [,].

Doublecortin-like kinase 2 (DCLK2) encodes a serine/threonine protein kinase enriched in the brain, with established roles in neuronal development, survival, and cytoskeletal regulation. Increasing evidence also implicates DCLK2 in neuronal responses to injury, particularly under ischemic and metabolic stress. Experimental studies of chronic cerebral ischemia and oxygen-glucose deprivation have demonstrated altered DCLK2 expression in hippocampal neurons, while modulation of DCLK2 expression influences neuronal survival [,,]. Mechanistic studies further implicate DCLK2 in neuronal inflammatory and cell-death pathways, including phosphorylation-dependent regulation of EHF and downstream activation of caspase- and GSDME-related pathways [,,]. These pathways regulate neuronal survival and injury responses and may therefore be relevant to the severe neurological and visual manifestations observed in the present family, particularly the extensive visual pathway involvement in the affected individual.

In addition, the RNA-binding protein CPEB4 regulates neuronal gene expression and has an important role in cellular responses to metabolic and ischemic stress. Under ischemic conditions, CPEB4 increases DCLK2 mRNA stability and expression, linking CPEB4-mediated post-transcriptional regulation to DCLK2-dependent neuronal stress responses [,,,]. Although these findings do not establish a role for DCLK2 in PDCD, they provide a biological rationale for considering DCLK2 as a potential modifier of neurological disease severity, particularly in a disorder characterized by neuronal vulnerability to impaired energy metabolism.

The marked clinical heterogeneity of PDCD suggests that additional genetic factors may influence disease expression, particularly in consanguineous families. Analysis of shared autozygous or identity-by-descent (IBD) regions can facilitate the identification of rare variants that may contribute to phenotypic severity beyond the primary disease-causing variant.

The present study aimed to characterize the clinical and molecular features of two affected siblings from a consanguineous family with PDCD, identify the underlying genetic cause, and investigate rare variants within shared IBD regions as potential contributors to the observed phenotype. In particular, we identified a homozygous DCLK2 variant within the shared IBD interval and evaluated its potential contribution to the severe neurological and visual manifestations observed in the family.

Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Kuwait Ministry of Health Research Ethics Committee (Ethics ID: 62/2013). The study was conducted with the participation of members of the affected family, and written informed consent was obtained from the adult participants for the review of medical records and genetic investigations. Blood samples were collected from the two affected individuals and their unaffected parents.

The affected siblings and their family members were initially evaluated at Al-Jahra Hospital by pediatricians based on their clinical presentation and relevant medical history. The family was subsequently referred to the Human Genetics Unit, Faculty of Medicine, Kuwait University, for specialist clinical and genetic evaluation and diagnostic confirmation. The affected siblings underwent detailed clinical assessment and molecular investigation, and the diagnosis was established through integration of the clinical, biochemical, radiological, and genetic findings.

Clinical information was obtained through direct clinical assessment and review of medical records, hospital admissions, and outpatient follow-up records. Clinical, biochemical, neurological, ophthalmological, and radiological findings were systematically reviewed to document the age at onset, longitudinal progression, and severity of manifestations in the two affected siblings. Relevant laboratory results, microbiological findings, ventilatory requirements, major interventions, and available brain neuroimaging findings were compiled from the medical records. The clinical and laboratory domains assessed are summarized in , while the principal demographic and birth characteristics of the affected siblings are presented in .

Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral whole blood using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). DNA concentration was determined by ultraviolet spectrophotometry using a NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific/NanoDrop Technologies, Wilmington, DE, USA).

Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed for the two affected male siblings, KU-50.IV-2 and KU-50.IV-5 (A). Exonic regions were enriched using SureSelect Human All Exon v6 hybridization-capture reagents (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The enriched libraries were sequenced on a HiSeq 2500 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). Variant call format (VCF) files generated from the exome sequencing pipeline were subsequently used for downstream variant screening and linkage/autozygosity analyses.

Autozygosity mapping was performed using the exome sequencing data, as previously described []. Homozygous regions shared between the affected siblings were identified to assess genomic regions that could contain candidate variants associated with the phenotype. AgileMultiIdeogram software (version 3) was used to visualize the identified homozygous intervals across the autosomal chromosomes and to facilitate assessment of shared regions between the affected individuals []. The analysis was based on the human genome reference assembly GRCh38 (UCSC Genome Browser).

The identified shared homozygous intervals were subsequently examined for candidate variants. Particular attention was given to variants located within regions shared by both affected siblings and compatible with the inheritance pattern observed in the family. The chromosome 4 identical-by-descent (IBD) interval identified through this analysis was subsequently evaluated by multipoint linkage analysis using the AgileVCFMapper software (version 3).

Candidate variants identified by exome sequencing were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and segregation analysis was performed in the two affected siblings (KU-50.IV-2 and KU-50.IV-5) and their parents (KU-50.III-1 and KU-50.III-2). Primers were designed using Primer3 software (https://primer3.org/; accessed 1 October 2025). Exonic sequences used for primer design were obtained from the UCSC Genome Browser (http://genome.ucsc.edu/; accessed 1 November 2025). For the PDHA1 variant in exon 6 (c.754C>G; p.Leu252Val; rs1555934383), the forward primer was 5′-ACCCAAAGCTCGGTTTTAGA-3′ and the reverse primer was 5′-CCATTCCATCCACCTGGTAA-3′. The DCLK2 variant identified in exon 1 (c.101G>A; p.Ser34Asn) was similarly confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The forward primer was 5′-TGCGGACACTTTTAGCTGAG-3′, and the reverse primer was 5′-CGGGTGAGCTCTATGAGGAG-3′. Sequencing reactions and subsequent analysis were performed as previously described [,]. The identified variants were evaluated in the available family members to determine their segregation with the disease phenotype and to establish their respective inheritance patterns.

In silico analyses were performed to assess the predicted functional and pathogenic effects of the identified PDHA1 and DCLK2 missense variants. Prediction scores were obtained from dbNSFP version 4.1a [], which provides aggregated annotations from multiple computational tools for nonsynonymous single-nucleotide variants.

The PDHA1 c.754C>G (p.Leu252Val) variant was evaluated using M-CAP, FATHMM, MetaLR, MutationTaster, MutPred, and REVEL. M-CAP was used to estimate the likelihood that the missense variant is pathogenic [], whereas FATHMM incorporates sequence conservation and hidden Markov models to predict the functional consequences of amino acid substitutions []. MetaLR integrates multiple annotation features using a logistic regression framework []. MutationTaster incorporates information relating to evolutionary conservation, protein features, and potential effects on splicing and other molecular processes []. MutPred was used to estimate the probability of pathogenicity and potential molecular consequences of the amino acid substitution []. REVEL, an ensemble predictor developed for the assessment of rare missense variants, was also included [].

The DCLK2 c.101G>A (p.Ser34Asn) variant was evaluated using GenoCanyon, the likelihood ratio test (LRT), PolyPhen-2 (HDIV model), MetaSVM, and FATHMM-MKL (coding) [,,,]. GenoCanyon was used to assess the functional potential of genomic positions based on evolutionary conservation and genomic features []. LRT evaluates evolutionary constraint by comparing conserved and neutral models []. PolyPhen-2 was used to predict the potential structural and functional impact of the amino acid substitution []. MetaSVM and FATHMM-MKL integrate multiple sequence- and genomic-level features to estimate the likelihood of deleterious effects [].

Brain and orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed without intravenous contrast at 18 years of age at Al-Jahra Hospital, Kuwait. MRI was acquired on a 1.5-Tesla system (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA). MRI was acquired on a 1.5-Tesla system (GE Healthcare, USA). The imaging protocol included axial T1-weighted, T2-weighted, T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) with fat suppression, T1-weighted and T2-weighted fat-suppressed sequences, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping, and susceptibility-weighted angiography (SWAN). Coronal and sagittal T2-weighted and T2-weighted fat-suppressed sequences were also obtained, together with coronal short-tau inversion recovery (STIR) and sagittal oblique T2-weighted fat-suppressed sequences targeted to the orbits. Three-dimensional axial time-of-flight (TOF) spoiled gradient-echo (SPGR) fat-suppressed magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) was additionally performed.

The study included two affected male siblings from the KU-50 family, KU-50.IV-2 and KU-50.IV-5, born to consanguineous parents of Bedouin ancestry from the Arabian Peninsula. Their clinical presentation was consistent with primary pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD), characterized by early-onset metabolic disturbances, neurological involvement, developmental impairment, and recurrent episodes of clinical deterioration. Their demographic and birth characteristics are summarized in .

KU-50.IV-2 presented with infantile generalized tonic–clonic seizures, which subsequently resolved after approximately one year, followed by recurrent episodes of ataxia and dysarthria, particularly during intercurrent illness. KU-50.IV-5 had no reported seizures but developed recurrent episodes of hypotonia, tremors, dysarthria, and abnormal eye movements from early childhood. Both siblings experienced recurrent neurological or metabolic decompensations, generally associated with intercurrent illness. The detailed neurological and early metabolic course is presented in .

Both siblings also developed persistent metabolic abnormalities and significant systemic complications (). Chronic or intermittent lactic acidosis was documented in both patients, with recurrent episodes of metabolic decompensation. The systemic complications differed between the siblings: KU-50.IV-2 developed severe obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and sensorineural hearing loss, whereas KU-50.IV-5 had a predominantly respiratory course characterized by recurrent respiratory failure and prolonged ventilatory dependence. The medical records confirmed that muscle biopsy and fibroblast PDH enzyme studies had been performed for patient KU-50.IV-2 overseas, with the reported findings consistent with PDH deficiency. The chronological clinical course and major disease milestones of both affected siblings are provided in the , including the timing of neurological, metabolic, respiratory, and systemic complications.

This study investigated a consanguineous family from the Arabian Peninsula. The KU-50 family comprised two affected male siblings (KU-50.IV-2, aged 18, and KU-50.IV-5, aged seven) and three unaffected siblings (see A). The affected individuals were born to first-cousin parents, which is consistent with the consanguineous pedigree. Genetic analysis revealed a hemizygous PDHA1 missense variant (c.754C>G; p.Leu252Val) in both affected males, which is consistent with X-linked PDHA1-related pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD). Segregation analysis also supported the observed inheritance pattern. Genome-wide autozygosity analysis was then performed to identify regions of shared homozygosity between the affected siblings. This analysis identified a shared region on chromosome 4, which was then evaluated using linkage and variant analyses (B,C). The detailed characterization of the shared homozygous region and the DCLK2 variant identified within this interval is presented in ,  and , respectively.

Both siblings required repeated hospital admissions because of metabolic decompensation, respiratory deterioration, and infections. KU-50.IV-2 experienced multiple respiratory and metabolic crises requiring PICU care and intermittent non-invasive or invasive ventilatory support. His treatment included sodium bicarbonate, mitochondrial-directed therapy, BiPAP support, and antiepileptic medication (). The chronological clinical course and major disease milestones of KU-50.IV-2 and KU-50.IV-5 are summarized in , respectively.

KU-50.IV-5 had a more severe respiratory course, with recurrent infections, hypercapnic respiratory failure, prolonged invasive ventilation, and tracheostomy. Infectious complications included MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with repeated positive cultures associated with the tracheostomy. He subsequently developed tracheostomy obstruction with granuloma formation and died at 7 years of age from acute respiratory failure secondary to tracheostomy obstruction (). Additional laboratory, neuroimaging, neurological, and ophthalmological findings are provided in , including detailed investigation results for both affected siblings. A detailed summary of hospitalizations, respiratory complications, infections, intensive care interventions, and treatment received by both siblings is provided in .

Neuroimaging demonstrated central nervous system abnormalities in KU-50.IV-2. Brain MRI showed basal ganglia signal abnormalities compatible with Leigh changes, together with multifocal cortical and subcortical abnormalities involving the bilateral anterior frontal lobes, particularly the parafalcine regions, caudate heads, left insular cortex, and bilateral parieto-occipital/visual cortices (). The affected regions showed high signal intensity on FLAIR and STIR sequences and corresponding low signal intensity on T1-weighted images. No diffusion restriction was observed on ADC maps, and susceptibility-weighted imaging showed no evidence of hemorrhage, microbleeding, or calcification (). The posterior cortical abnormalities demonstrated chronic signal changes, including features suggestive of cortical laminar necrosis. Marked reduction in the volume of both optic nerves and the optic chiasma was also noted, with preserved intrinsic signal intensity (). The imaging findings are summarized in .

An ophthalmological assessment of KU-50.IV-2 revealed severe bilateral visual impairment. Un-aided visual acuity was counting fingers at a distance of 50 cm in both eyes. There was poor fixation and a large-angle left exotropia of approximately 50 prism diopters. The anterior segments were normal, as were the ocular media. Fundoscopy revealed bilateral optic disc pallor, which was consistent with optic atrophy. The macula appeared clinically normal.

Spectral-domain macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) was limited by poor fixation and large-angle exotropia, as well as limited cooperation (signal strength 6/10 and automated foveal centration not achieved). In the right eye, central subfield thickness was within normal limits (265 µm); however, most of the parafoveal and perifoveal sectors fell below the first percentile of the normative database. This was indicative of reduced cube volume (8.5 mm3) and average cube thickness (236 µm), indicating thinning of the macula in the para- and perifoveal regions. Thickness analysis could not be computed for the left eye. On qualitative review, the horizontal B-scan of the left eye through the fovea showed a preserved foveal contour without obvious thinning (). Optic nerve head OCT was not available.

Neuroimaging revealed involvement of both the anterior and posterior visual pathways. Non-contrast MRI of the brain and orbits showed a reduced volume in both the optic nerves and the optic chiasm, with a preserved intrinsic signal intensity. This is consistent with optic atrophy (see ). Additionally, cortical and subcortical signal abnormalities involving the parietal and occipital regions, without diffusion restriction, were suggestive of chronic cortical injury ().

Taken together, the clinical, OCT and MRI findings were consistent with cerebral (cortical) visual impairment with concomitant bilateral optic atrophy, indicating combined involvement of the anterior and posterior visual pathways (see ).

Since both affected individuals were male and had a phenotype strongly suggestive of primary PDCD, whole-exome sequencing was performed in KU-50.IV-2 and KU-50.IV-5. Genome-wide autozygosity analysis identified several homozygous intervals. KU-50.IV-2 carried individual homozygous intervals on chromosomes 1 and 7.

Importantly, both affected siblings shared a subtle region of homozygosity on chromosome 4 that was barely discernible on the initial genome-wide analysis (B). Subsequent multipoint linkage analysis resolved this region more clearly and defined a shared interval of approximately 6 Mb on chromosome 4 (chr4:148,334,756–154,560,476) (C).

Interrogation of the shared interval using the exome data identified a homozygous missense variant in DCLK2, c.101G>A (p.Ser34Asn). The variant lies within the shared IBD region at chr4:150,078,445–150,257,438. It was not associated with an rs identifier in the NCBI dbSNP database at the time of analysis. The two affected siblings were homozygous for the variant.

The clinical phenotype and the occurrence of disease in two male siblings prompted additional examination of the X chromosome. Screening of the exome data for hemizygous variants identified a missense variant in exon 6 of PDHA1, c.754C>G (p.Leu252Val; rs1555934383), located at chrX:19,343,893–19,361,707. The PDHA1 variant is consistent with the established X-linked inheritance pattern of primary PDCD and provides a molecular explanation for the core disease phenotype. Sanger sequencing confirmed the presence of the variant in both affected siblings (), who were hemizygous for the change. The identification of the PDHA1 variant alongside the homozygous DCLK2 variant provided the basis for examining whether the chromosome 4 variant could contribute to the clinical variability observed in the family.

Segregation analysis confirmed that both variants were present in the family in patterns consistent with their respective modes of inheritance ( and ). The two affected siblings carried the hemizygous PDHA1 (c.754C>G; p.Leu252Val) variant () and were homozygous for the DCLK2 (c.101G>A; p.Ser34Asn) variant (). The mother, KU-50.III-2, was heterozygous for both variants. The father, KU-50.III-1, carried the wild-type PDHA1 allele and was heterozygous for the DCLK2 variant. The segregation pattern therefore supports maternal transmission of the X-linked PDHA1 variant and autosomal recessive inheritance of the DCLK2 variant from both parents. These findings establish the co-occurrence of the two variants in the affected siblings. The PDHA1 variant provides the primary molecular explanation for the X-linked PDCD phenotype, whereas the homozygous DCLK2 variant represents an additional inherited genetic finding located within the shared IBD interval.

Multiple computational predictors were used to assess the potential functional effects of the PDHA1 c.754C>G (p.Leu252Val) and DCLK2 c.101G>A (p.Ser34Asn) variants. For PDHA1, most predictors supported a deleterious effect, including FATHMM, MutationTaster, MetaLR, and MutPred, whereas M-CAP and REVEL provided weaker or borderline predictions. For DCLK2, GenoCanyon, the likelihood ratio test, PolyPhen-2, and FATHMM-MKL supported a potential damaging effect, while MetaSVM predicted a more tolerant effect. Overall, the computational findings provided supportive evidence for a potential functional effect of both variants. Detailed prediction scores and interpretations are provided in .

The identified PDHA1 and DCLK2 variants were evaluated according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) sequence-variant interpretation framework. The assessment incorporated the available population, computational, segregation, phenotype, and functional evidence. The evidence supporting the classification of each variant is summarized in  and .

The PDHA1 c.754C>G (p.Leu252Val) variant was identified in a hemizygous state in both affected male siblings and was absent from the unaffected father. The variant segregated with the disease phenotype through the mother, who was heterozygous for the variant. Multiple computational predictors supported a deleterious effect, although predictions were not completely concordant. In addition, the clinical phenotype of the two affected individuals was highly consistent with PDHA1-associated primary PDCD.

Taken together, the available genetic, clinical, computational and tissue-based evidence supports the pathogenic interpretation of the PDHA1 c.754C>G (p.Leu252Val) variant. The individual ACMG/AMP evidence criteria applied to this variant are presented in .

The DCLK2 c.101G>A (p.Ser34Asn) variant was identified in a homozygous state in both affected siblings and in a heterozygous state in each parent. The variant lies within the shared chromosome 4 identical-by-descent interval identified by genome-wide autozygosity and subsequent linkage analysis. Several computational tools predicted a potentially deleterious effect, although the results were heterogeneous, with some predictors supporting a damaging effect and others indicating tolerance.

The DCLK2 variant has not previously been established as a cause of PDCD, and no functional assay was performed to directly demonstrate an effect of the p.Ser34Asn substitution on DCLK2 protein function. Therefore, despite its homozygous segregation, localization within the shared IBD interval, and supportive computational evidence, the available data are insufficient to establish pathogenicity under the ACMG/AMP framework. The variant is consequently best reported as a variant of uncertain significance, while its potential contribution to disease severity is considered as a hypothesis requiring functional validation.

The ACMG/AMP assessment therefore supports a substantially stronger level of evidence for the PDHA1 variant than for the DCLK2 variant. The PDHA1 variant provides the established molecular basis for the primary PDCD phenotype, whereas the DCLK2 variant represents an additional homozygous genetic finding that may contribute to phenotypic severity. The latter interpretation remains provisional in the absence of direct functional evidence. The genetic findings, clinical presentation of the two affected siblings, and the proposed interpretation of the combined PDHA1 and DCLK2 variants are summarized in .

Primary pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD) is a genetically heterogeneous mitochondrial disorder with a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from neonatal lactic acidosis and Leigh syndrome to later-onset neurological, neuromuscular, and multisystem manifestations. Pathogenic variants have been identified in several genes encoding structural or regulatory components of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, including PDHA1, PDHB, PDHX, DLAT, DLD, PDP1, and PDK3, with PDHA1 accounting for approximately 76–85% of reported cases. In the present family, both affected male siblings carried the same hemizygous PDHA1 missense variant (c.754C>G; p.Leu252Val), inherited from their heterozygous mother, consistent with the established X-linked pattern of PDHA1-associated PDCD [,,]. The clinical phenotype of both individuals, including neonatal lactic acidosis, neurological involvement, and Leigh brain abnormalities, was also consistent with PDHA1-related PDCD.

The genetic investigation was particularly informative because the family structure and clinical presentation initially pointed towards a straightforward X-linked disorder. Both affected individuals were male siblings, and the identification of a hemizygous PDHA1 variant provided a convincing explanation for the primary disease. However, genome-wide autozygosity mapping revealed an additional shared homozygous region on chromosome 4. Autozygosity mapping is a well-established approach for identifying shared identical-by-descent (IBD) regions in consanguineous families and has been successfully used to identify autosomal recessive disease loci [,,,,]. In this family, the shared chromosome 4 interval prompted further examination of the exome data and led to the identification of a homozygous DCLK2 missense variant. This finding illustrates the value of considering additional genomic variation when the clinical course within a consanguineous family is more severe or variable than might be expected from a single established disease-causing variant.

Although the two affected brothers carried the same PDHA1 and DCLK2 variants, a direct comparison of their clinical phenotypes is limited by their different ages and disease courses. This is particularly true given that the younger brother died at the age of seven. The older sibling, KU-50.IV-2, experienced recurrent lactic acidosis and neurological episodes, including ataxia and dysarthria, together with basal ganglia abnormalities on neuroimaging characteristic of Leigh syndrome. He survived into late adolescence but developed significant multisystem complications, including morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, respiratory insufficiency, and sensorineural hearing loss. In contrast, KU-50.IV-5 developed severe neurological and respiratory disease at a younger age, with hypotonia, tremors, dysarthria, recurrent encephalopathic episodes, progressive respiratory failure, and prolonged ventilatory dependence. His clinical course ultimately resulted in death following complications associated with tracheostomy. The differences in age at onset, neurological progression, respiratory involvement and overall outcome emphasize the variation in clinical presentation and disease progression among individuals with closely related PDHA1 defects.

The neuroimaging findings in KU-50.IV-2 demonstrated basal ganglia abnormalities with multifocal cortical and subcortical involvement extending to the bilateral frontal, insular, and parieto-occipital regions. The relatively symmetric distribution and absence of diffusion restriction are compatible with a chronic metabolic or mitochondrial encephalopathic process, with superimposed chronic ischemic-type changes.

The visual phenotype of KU-50.IV-2 was severe, affecting both the anterior and posterior visual pathways. Bilateral optic disc pallor, together with reduced optic nerve and chiasmal volume on MRI scans, indicates established optic atrophy. Meanwhile, bilateral parietal-occipital signal abnormalities suggest a concomitant cerebral (cortical) component. Optic atrophy has been reported in PDCD [], which is consistent with the recognised vulnerability of retinal ganglion cells and their axons to impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism [,,,].

However, combined anterior and posterior visual pathway involvement of this severity is uncommon. It is not possible to determine from the available data whether the optic atrophy represents a primary mitochondrial optic neuropathy, retrograde transsynaptic degeneration secondary to cortical injury, or both. The large-angle left exotropia is most likely sensory, reflecting profound early visual loss and impaired binocular fusion. A contribution from mitochondrial extraocular myopathy cannot be excluded, although restriction of ocular motility was not documented. The severity and extent of visual pathway involvement may suggest the influence of additional genetic factors on the expression of this phenotype. In this context, the homozygous DCLK2 p.Ser34Asn variant may contribute to the neurological and visual phenotype, consistent with a potential modifier role.

Both affected siblings were homozygous for the novel DCLK2 missense variant c.101G>A (p.Ser34Asn), which lies within the shared chromosome 4 IBD interval. The variant was inherited from heterozygous parents and was present in both affected individuals, supporting its segregation within the family. Although the available evidence is insufficient to establish DCLK2 c.101G>A (p.Ser34Asn) as a primary disease-causing variant, its localization within the shared IBD region, homozygous state in both affected siblings, and potential biological relevance make it a plausible candidate modifier of the PDHA1-associated phenotype. In an individual already affected by mitochondrial energy failure, increased susceptibility to stress-induced neuronal injury could potentially contribute to a more severe neurological phenotype.

The biological functions of DCLK2 provide a compelling rationale for investigating its potential contribution to the neurological phenotype observed in this family. DCLK2 is a neuronal microtubule-associated protein that contains N-terminal doublecortin domains, which are involved in microtubule binding, as well as a C-terminal serine/threonine kinase domain. This links cytoskeletal organization to intracellular signaling. Experimental studies have implicated DCLK2 and related doublecortin-like kinases in dendritic development, axonal growth, neuronal survival, and regenerative responses following neuronal injury. Studies of retinal ganglion cells, in particular, have demonstrated that DCLK2 overexpression promotes growth cone reformation and axonal regeneration following optic nerve injury, thereby highlighting its importance for neuronal integrity and visual pathways [,].

The potential modifying role of DCLK2 is biologically plausible given its involvement in neuronal stress responses. Experimental studies of chronic cerebral ischemia and oxygen-glucose deprivation have shown that altered DCLK2 expression influences neuronal injury and survival [,,]. This is particularly relevant in PDHA1 deficiency, where impaired energy metabolism places neurons under metabolic stress.

DCLK2 has also been implicated in stress-associated inflammatory and cell-death pathways through EHF-dependent signaling and caspase-associated neuronal pyroptosis [,,], with the CPEB4-DCLK2-EHF pathway further linked to neuronal injury responses [,,,]. Although these findings do not establish a direct interaction between DCLK2 and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, they provide a plausible framework whereby altered DCLK2 function could modify neuronal vulnerability to metabolic stress. This may be particularly relevant to the severe neurological and visual phenotype observed in the present family.

In the present family, the coexistence of the homozygous DCLK2 p.Ser34Asn variant and an established, disease-associated PDHA1 variant suggests that altered DCLK2-dependent neuronal processes may modify the neurological and visual manifestations of primary pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency.

On this basis, we propose that the homozygous DCLK2 p.Ser34Asn variant may act as a genetic modifier rather than as the primary cause of PDCD. The hemizygous PDHA1 variant establishes the underlying X-linked metabolic disorder, while the additional biallelic DCLK2 variant may contribute to the severity or spectrum of neurological and visual manifestations. Therefore, we propose DCLK2 as a candidate modifier gene rather than an independent cause of the primary disorder. This hypothesis must be tested through variant-specific functional studies examining kinase activity, microtubule interactions, neuronal stress responses, and relevant visual system functions.

The findings also illustrate the value of comprehensive genomic analysis in consanguineous families, where multilocus variation may coexist with the primary disease-causing variant. In the present family, the combination of exome sequencing, autozygosity mapping, and segregation analysis identified both the hemizygous PDHA1 variant and the homozygous DCLK2 variant within a shared IBD interval. This approach may be particularly informative when the clinical phenotype is unusually severe or incompletely explained by a single pathogenic variant.

Taken together, the findings support a proposed two-hit model in which the primary PDHA1 defect is accompanied by the homozygous DCLK2 p.Ser34Asn variant, which may contribute to phenotypic severity. Functional studies will be required to determine whether and how this DCLK2 variant modifies neuronal responses to impaired energy metabolism.

neuroscience.title: EEG and hedonic responses to sonic-seasoning soundscapes: a dataset
neuroscience.abstract: This dataset comprises electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings from 30 adult participants exposed to two contrasting designed soundscapes — a natural, sustainability-conveying “organic jungle” soundscape and a contrasting “deconstruct” soundscape — together with their liking ratings of each soundscape and basic demographic information. The data extend the largely behavioral “sonic-seasoning” literature, which has shown that sound and music systematically shape the sensory and affective evaluation of consumer experiences, by adding a complementary neurophysiological measurement angle. EEG was acquired with a 14-channel consumer-grade EMOTIV EPOC X headset (128 Hz) on a web-based experiment platform that logged synchronized event markers. For each participant the dataset provides: a resting calibration recording (eyes-open and eyes-closed); the EEG recorded during a brief (∼17 s) isolated exposure to each of the two soundscapes; the corresponding liking ratings; the soundscape stimulus audio files; and demographic responses. EEG data are released as recorded, with the manufacturer's per-channel contact-quality and signal-quality indices retained, so that re-users can apply any preprocessing or analytic pipeline. These data are of value to researchers in sonic seasoning and multisensory marketing, affective and consumer neuroscience, and to those developing or benchmarking methods for consumer-grade EEG. The included liking ratings provide a behavioral anchor relating the neural data to the affective character of the soundscapes.
