These data add a neurophysiological (EEG) measurement angle to the predominantly behavioral (self-report based) sonic-seasoning literature, enabling researchers to examine brain responses to designed soundscapes alongside the explicit liking judgments those soundscapes elicit.

For each participant, the dataset pairs EEG recorded during brief soundscape exposure with a liking rating and a resting baseline. This supports analyzes that link spectral and topographic EEG measures to affective evaluation, and that normalize each participant's data to their own resting state.

Because EEG is released as recorded, re-users can apply and compare their own preprocessing, artifact-rejection, and analysis pipelines; and because the manufacturer's per-channel contact-quality and EEG-quality indices are released alongside the recordings, they can assess data quality objectively per channel and per participant.

The two 17-second soundscape clips used here are provided alongside the EEG, so re-users can align the neural data to the exact stimuli; the full stimulus set and its development are described in the associated research article [6].

The dataset is a compact, well-documented corpus for teaching, benchmarking, and methodological development with consumer-grade (14-channel) EEG, including resting baselines suitable for alpha-reactivity (Berger-effect) validity checks.

Sound shapes how we perceive and evaluate consumer experiences, particularly food and drink — an area of multisensory research often called sonic seasoning []. Music and ambient sound modulate the perception of taste and flavor and, importantly, the affective experience and liking of products. A sound's emotional tone often shapes these evaluations more strongly than narrow correspondences between acoustic features and tastes (e.g., higher pitch sounding “sweeter”) [].

A growing strand of this work uses deliberately designed soundscapes to communicate higher-order product and brand values. Prior work by the present team has shown that soundscapes engineered around targeted psychoacoustic features reliably evoke specific abstract associations (e.g., “sustainability”), establishing that crafted soundscapes are affectively potent [, , , , ]. How such soundscapes are reflected in neurophysiological measures remains underexplored: research to date has been almost entirely behavioral and self-report based.

This dataset [] supports that complementary angle. Participants heard two contrasting soundscapes — “organic jungle” and “deconstruct” — while EEG was recorded, and rated their liking of each. EEG offers candidate neural correlates of affect and arousal, such as frontal alpha asymmetry [] and alpha/beta-band power [], relatable to liking. Consumer-grade EMOTIV systems related to the EPOC X, such as the original EPOC and the EPOC Flex have been evaluated for research-quality EEG [,].

The dataset contains data from 30 adult participants, collected between 28 August and 1 December 2025, and is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS).

EEG channels follow the international 10–20 system: AF3, F7, F3, FC5, T7, P7, O1, O2, P8, T8, FC6, F4, F8, AF4 (14 channels, 128 Hz). The EEG is released as recorded—subject only to the EPOC X built-in hardware bandpass—with no additional software filtering, re-referencing, normalization, or artifact correction. Alongside the 14 EEG channels, each recording carries the manufacturer's continuously logged quality signals, all sampled at 128 Hz and listed with their units in each `channels.tsv': per-channel contact quality (`CQ_<electrode>', ordinal 0–4), overall contact quality (`CQ_Overall', percent), contact quality of the CMS and DRL reference electrodes (`CQ_CMS', `CQ_DRL', ordinal 0–4), per-channel EEG quality (`EQ_<electrode>', ordinal 0–4), the overall EEG-quality index (`EQ_Overall', percent), and the achieved-to-nominal sampling-rate ratio (`EQ_SampleRate'). Each file therefore contains 47 signals. Across the 30 released sessions contact quality was uniformly high (`CQ_Overall' M = 100.0, SD = 0.2, range 99.2–100.0), with no channel falling below the acceptable contact level in any session, whereas the EEG-quality index was more variable (`EQ_Overall' M = 62.0, SD = 18.4, range 22.1–90.4). Re-users are encouraged to apply their own thresholds to the per-channel indices rather than rely on a single summary. To read these files, use an EDF reader that parses the EMOTIV header correctly (for example `pyedflib' in Python, or EEGLAB's BIOSIG importer); a channel that loads as all zeros indicates a reader that has misparsed the header, not a defect in the data.

Each participant (sub-NN) has an eeg/ folder containing four files:FileContentssub-NN_task-soundscape_eeg.edfThe continuous EEG recording, comprising theresting calibration (eyes-open, eyes-closed) andthe two ∼17-s soundscape exposures (jungle,deconstruct), with the EEG and qualitychannels.sub-NN_task-soundscape_events.tsvOnsets, durations, and labels marking eachsegment (eyes-open, eyes-closed, jungle,deconstruct) within that participant's recording.sub-NN_task-soundscape_channels.tsvChannel names, types, units, sampling frequency, and a description of each quality channel.sub-NN_task-soundscape_eeg.jsonAcquisition metadata (sampling rate, reference,device, etc.).

At the repository root, a single `participants.tsv' is the aggregate participant-level table: one row per `sub-NN',holding each participant's demographics (age, sex, handedness), the brief baseline-state items (current stress, sleep duration, and recent exercise, alcohol, and caffeine), and the two soundscape liking ratings. The accompanying participants.json documents every column, giving the verbatim wording of each questionnaire item and the full set of response options, including the scale anchors for the stress and liking ratings and the seven fixed categories of the sleep item. Because rows are keyed by the same `sub-NN' identifier used in the folders, re-users can filter or select subjects directly. (`.tsv' files are tab-separated tables and open like a CSV in any spreadsheet or analysis tool.) The two soundscape audio clips are in `stimuli/' together with a per-file acoustic characterization.

A `derivatives/eeglab/' folder provides an optional convenience layer for EEGLAB/MATLAB users: the two soundscape conditions pre-split into EEGLAB-native `.set' files (one per condition per participant), with a short analysis script and documentation. The files at the repository root are the canonical data; users of other software (e.g., MNE-Python) can work directly from the EEG and `events.tsv'.

The eyes-open and eyes-closed segments are resting baselines and are not length-matched counterparts to the 17-s soundscape exposures. Each was 20 s by design, but advanced on a participant's voluntary “continue” press rather than a hard timer, so the marker spans segment onset to that press and recorded durations vary: eyes-open 23.9–202.1 s (M = 32.1) and eyes-closed 26.3–63.4 s (M = 32.5). The press times were not logged. The full segments are released unmodified, and how to trim or average them is left to the user. If a length-matched comparison with the soundscape exposures is wanted, the first 17 s of each segment falls within the fixed instructed window for all participants and precedes any post-task advance interval.

(descriptive) shows the group-mean scalp topography of relative band power (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) during the ∼17 s exposures to the jungle and deconstruct soundscapes, illustrating the spatial character and analytic tractability of the data across the full spectrum.

Thirty adults participated (19 male, 11 female; age M = 30.1 years, SD = 5.3, range 22–40; 28 right-handed, 2 left-handed). Participants were recruited from a pre-screened participant pool and enrolled through the EMOTIV experiment platform under its standard participant-account requirements. The study was designed at Universidad San Francisco de Quito under the ethical approval reported below, and participants received compensation for their time. Eligibility required adult age and the ability to complete a web-based session with audio; auditory acuity was not formally assessed, but a sound check confirmed that audio was audible to the participant before each soundscape was played (see Apparatus and EEG acquisition). Thirty participants were enrolled and all thirty are included in the released dataset; no participants and no channels were excluded. A brief baseline questionnaire additionally recorded each participant's current stress level, hours of sleep the previous night, and any vigorous exercise, alcohol, or caffeine consumption in the preceding hour (available per participant in `participants.tsv'), with the verbatim wording and response options of every item documented in participants.json). All participants gave informed consent at the start of the session (see Ethics Statement).

EEG was recorded with a 14-channel EMOTIV EPOC X headset (saline felt sensors) at AF3, F7, F3, FC5, T7, P7, O1, O2, P8, T8, FC6, F4, F8, AF4, referenced using the device's built-in Common Mode Sense / Driven Right Leg (CMS/DRL) scheme, at 128 Hz. The device applies a built-in hardware bandpass, and per-channel contact- and EEG-quality indices were logged continuously. Stimuli were presented, and synchronized event markers logged, through a web-based experiment platform. Before each soundscape was played, a sound check confirmed that audio was audible to the participant.

Two soundscapes were used: an “organic jungle” soundscape (sustainability-congruent) and a “deconstruct” soundscape (sustainability-contrasting), both drawn from the validated soundscape set described in the associated research article [], where their development and full characterization are reported. The “deconstruct” soundscape is a royalty-free stock instrumental track used here without modification. The “organic jungle” soundscape was produced by overlaying recorded jungle/nature-soundscape elements onto a base instrumental track from the same set. The underlying instrumental tracks derive from a validated music-stimulus database []. The clips are of comparable duration (16.9 s and 17.2 s) and were presented without normalization or condition-specific gain. They differ in level and in timbre: integrated loudness (EBU R128) is −12.74 LUFS for jungle and −18.17 LUFS for deconstruct, a difference of 5.43 LU, while peak levels differ by about 2 dB (−1.37 vs −3.33 dBFS); the deconstruct clip is correspondingly sparser and more dynamic (crest factor 17.2 vs 15.9 dB) and brighter (mean spectral centroid 2525 Hz vs 1485 Hz), whereas the jungle clip is denser, more sustained and darker. A per-file acoustic characterization is released with the stimuli (`stimuli/stimuli_acoustic_characterization.tsv').

1.Consent and a brief baseline questionnaire (demographics and current-state items).2.Resting calibration: eyes-open followed by eyes-closed (∼20 s each by design; see the note on recorded durations below).3.Soundscape exposure and liking: a brief isolated (∼17 s) presentation of the jungle soundscape and then of the deconstruct soundscape, each followed by a liking rating. All participants completed the four conditions in the same fixed order — eyes-open, eyes-closed, jungle, deconstruct — with no counterbalancing of the two soundscapes. These soundscape-exposure data were recorded within a single longer session of approximately 35 min that also collected other measures (reported elsewhere): the resting calibration occurred near the beginning of the session and the soundscape exposures and liking ratings near the end, after the intervening tasks. Only the calibration, soundscape exposures, liking ratings, demographics, and stimulus files are described and released here.4.Debriefing.

All participants completed the four conditions in the same fixed order — eyes-open, eyes-closed, jungle, deconstruct — with no counterbalancing of the two soundscapes. These soundscape-exposure data were recorded within a single longer session of approximately 35 min that also collected other measures (reported elsewhere): the resting calibration occurred near the beginning of the session and the soundscape exposures and liking ratings near the end, after the intervening tasks. Only the calibration, soundscape exposures, liking ratings, demographics, and stimulus files are described and released here.

Debriefing.

Descriptively, mean liking ratings were 5.13 (SD = 1.17) for the jungle soundscape and 3.93 (SD = 1.51) for the deconstruct soundscape (N = 30).

These data were acquired with a consumer-grade, 14-channel EEG system with a single sequential reference; this offers accessibility and ecological validity but provides lower spatial resolution than high-density research-grade montages, and high-frequency (beta/gamma) measures may carry muscle (EMG) contamination that re-users may wish to address. As collection took place in an applied web-based context rather than a shielded laboratory, environmental and movement artifacts may be present; the continuously logged per-channel contact- and EEG-quality signals are provided to help re-users screen for these. All participants received the conditions in the same fixed order (eyes-open, eyes-closed, jungle, deconstruct), and the two soundscapes were not counterbalanced; order and time-on-task are therefore confounded with soundscape identity, and any comparison between the two exposures should be interpreted with that in mind. The soundscape exposures also occurred near the end of a longer session, so they were not the first material participants encountered. The sample comprises 30 young adults (age range 22–40), a sample size in line with comparable within-subjects EEG studies; generalization to other age groups should nonetheless be made with care. The released portion is focused on the soundscape-exposure paradigm.

This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of Universidad San Francisco de Quito (Comité de Ética de Investigación en Seres Humanos, “CEISH-USFQ”; approval document Oficio N° 078–2022-CA-P22–053M-CEISH-USFQ). Informed consent was obtained from all participants at the start of each session. neuroscience.title: DANCE: Step‐by‐Step Protocol for Automated Quantification of Drosophila Aggression and Courtship
neuroscience.abstract:
Aggression and courtship are widely studied social behaviors in Drosophila melanogaster, but their accurate quantification remains a practical obstacle. Manual scoring of these behaviors is time consuming, prone to inter‐observer variability, and difficult to scale, while existing automated tools often require expensive hardware or specialized skills. This article provides step‐by‐step protocols for implementing DANCE (Drosophila Aggression and Courtship Evaluator), a low‐cost platform that combines supervised machine learning classifiers with recording hardware built from repurposed medicine blister packs, acrylic sheets, and consumer smartphones. The protocols describe how to construct the aggression and courtship arenas, acquire standardized videos using a smartphone over a tablet backlight, and process recordings through an automated pipeline that tracks individual flies in FlyTracker and scores behavior using six pretrained JAABA classifiers, one for aggressive lunges and five for the stages of male courtship. Additional protocols describe how to train new classifiers, validate classifier performance against manual annotation, and add an optogenetic stimulation module. Each protocol specifies the required materials, software versions, parameter settings, and expected outputs, so that a user with no prior experience in automated behavioral analysis can generate per‐dyad behavioral measurements suitable for statistical comparison. All classifiers, analysis scripts, and worked examples are available at https://github.com/agrawallab/DANCE. The platform was originally described and validated by Yadav et al. neuroscience.text:
Aggression and courtship in Drosophila melanogaster have been used for decades to study the genetic and neural basis of social behavior. Progress in this area depends on measuring these behaviors reliably, but quantification remains a bottleneck. Manually scoring aggressive lunges and courtship behaviors such as wing extension and copulation is time consuming, prone to inter‐observer variability, and difficult to scale to the number of animals that a genetic screen requires. This article describes how to set up and run DANCE, a low‐cost platform that automates the scoring of Drosophila aggression and courtship and can be assembled and operated by a single laboratory without specialized engineering or programming support.

Existing automated tools for Drosophila social behavior fall broadly into two groups, each with practical limitations. Rule‐based tools such as CADABRA (Dankert et al., ) and MateBook (Ribeiro et al., ) apply fixed definitions of each behavior. These definitions do not adapt well to differences between individuals, genotypes, or recording setups, and they can miss or misclassify behavioral events that manual ground‐truth scoring would capture (Simon and Heberlein, ). Classifiers built on supervised machine learning using JAABA (Kabra et al., ) are more adaptable, but they are often not shared publicly, and the pipelines that use them frequently depend on custom‐machined arenas or machine‐vision cameras that are costly to obtain (Chowdhury et al., ; Leng et al., ). As a result, automated behavioral scoring has remained inaccessible to many resource‐constrained laboratories.

DANCE was developed to address these limitations. The hardware is built from inexpensive, widely available materials and a consumer smartphone, and the analysis uses freely available classifiers that quantify aggressive lunges and five distinct courtship behaviors. The platform and its validation against existing methods are described in full in the original research article (Yadav et al., ). The present article provides the procedures needed to build the platform and apply it to new experiments.

The protocols follow the experimental workflow. Basic Protocol , together with Support Protocols , , and , covers construction of the aggression arena, fly husbandry, food and arena preparation, and standardized video acquisition. Basic Protocol  covers the construction of the courtship arena. Basic Protocol  describes the complete analysis pipeline, supported by Support Protocol  for fly tracking in FlyTracker and Support Protocol  for behavioral scoring with pretrained JAABA classifiers. Alternate Protocols  and  describe how to train and validate new classifiers, and Alternate Protocol  describes how to add an optogenetic stimulation module.

This protocol describes the step‐by‐step assembly of the DANCE recording platform for aggression assays. The hardware uses repurposed transparent medicine blister packs, mounted on acrylic base plates over an apple‐juice agar food surface, as behavioral arenas. Arena walls and ceilings are coated with Sigmacote to prevent wall‐climbing. Complete Support Protocol  (fly preparation) 6 days in advance, Support Protocol  (food preparation and arena coating) the day before recording, and Support Protocol  (video acquisition setup) before loading flies. A video demonstration of DANCE aggression hardware assembly and recording is available as Figure 6—video 2 of Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig6video2), and it is recommended that first‐time users view this before beginning assembly. An overview of the DANCE hardware components and recording setup is shown in Figure . Arena assembly for one 8‐well session takes ∼5 min.

NOTE: Prepare food plates and coat blister‐pack arenas with Sigmacote at least 12‐16 hr before beginning this protocol. See Support Protocol  for food preparation and arena coating instructions.

Select transparent medicine blister packs with circular wells to serve as behavioral arenas. The standard arena for aggression recording measures 13 mm diameter × 5.5 mm height. Alternative dimensions of 17 mm × 4 mm or 21 mm × 8 mm may be used for fly strains for which a different interaction density is required.

Verify that the arena walls and ceilings have been coated with Sigmacote and allowed to dry overnight (see Support Protocol , steps 11‐16). Confirm coating effectiveness by introducing a single fly into one coated well for 1‐2 min before the experiment: a properly coated arena will keep the fly on the food surface without wall‐climbing. Discard arenas in which wall‐climbing is observed.

CAUTION: All Sigmacote applications must be performed in a fume hood. Sigmacote (SL2) contains chlorotrimethylsilane in a heptane/xylene carrier and is flammable and a respiratory irritant. See Support Protocol  for full coating procedure.

Take the apple‐juice agar food plate prepared in advance, cut it to the appropriate size using a razor blade, and place on a flat surface with the food surface facing upward.

Secure the food plate using paper tape and 1‐mm acrylic side spacers.

Similarly, secure the loading base plate containing the medicine blister pack arenas using paper tape and acrylic spacers to ensure proper alignment and stability.

Load flies into the assembled arenas (loading base plate with medicine blister pack arenas) using a mouth aspirator. Transfer exactly two males from the same housing condition into each well through the 2‐mm loading hole, one at a time; confirm that the first male has entered the well before loading the second. Keep the loading hole covered by sliding the loading plate over the adjacent chamber between transfers.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Do not anesthetize males before loading—transfer males directly from their housing vials into the arena by mouth aspirator, without CO2 exposure. Anesthesia on the day of the assay will suppress aggression and render the recording unusable.

Some males should have been individually housed (experimental group) and others group housed (control group) for 6 days before this step (see Support Protocol , steps 5a and 5b). Do not load flies that appear lethargic or damaged.

Confirm that both males are inside the well, and seal the loading hole with a strip of paper tape, pressing firmly.

Apply a strip of paper tape along one end of the food plate.

This tape protects the food surface from damage when the blister‐pack arenas are slid into position during assembly.

Align the 2‐mm acrylic loading base plate with the flies in medicine blister pack arenas over the food plate. Join the two components with paper tape along the edges, ensuring that the food surface is level and aligned evenly with the loading base plate with medicine blister pack arenas.

Slide the coated blister‐pack arenas with flies over the food plate from the paper‐tape end, guiding the wells to align with the food surface. Slide slowly to avoid displacing the food.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Always slide the arenas from the paper‐tape end. The tape at the leading edge prevents the blister pack from catching and tearing the food surface during assembly.

Once the arenas are in position over the food plate, seal all edges with paper tape to prevent fly escape. Press tape firmly along all seams including between adjacent wells.

Verify that all wells are correctly positioned over the food surface by looking through the transparent blister‐pack ceiling. The food surface should be visible at the bottom of each well.

Allow flies to acclimatize in the sealed arena for 5 min. Place the loaded arena on the backlight setup (step 14) immediately after sealing. Keep the backlight on during acclimatization. Do not begin recording until the full acclimatization period has elapsed.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Acclimatization in the sealed arena is required before recording for the reliability of behavioral output. The 5‐min acclimatization period is not counted as part of the 20‐min recording window.

Place the assembled arena on an electronic tablet or smartphone displaying a white screen light application at full brightness. This serves as the backlight illumination source.

Place a transparent acrylic sheet with 4‐mm spacers on top of the backlight device. Place the arena on top of this sheet.

The 4‐mm air gap allows heat dissipation and prevents the arenas from overheating.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Never place arenas directly on the tablet or smartphone screen. The 4‐mm spacer is essential for preventing heat buildup, which suppresses behavioral output.

Position the smartphone camera directly above the arena in a fixed, vertical orientation. Configure recording parameters and begin recording as described in Support Protocol . Record for 20 min for aggression assays.

Hardware assembly (excluding overnight drying steps completed the day before) takes ∼5 min for an eight‐well session. Fly loading takes ∼3 min for eight wells. Acclimatization takes 5 min. Recording takes 20 min. Total time from assembly start to end of recording: ∼45 min. With practice, fly loading and assembly time decreases substantially from the estimates above. For higher throughput, multiple 8‐well arenas can be placed under separate smartphone cameras simultaneously, with two to four cameras running in parallel in a single session.

Do not use heat to dry arenas.• Re‐coat arenas with Sigmacote after every three to five uses or when wall‐climbing is observed.• Ensure all gaps are sealed before loading. Any unsealed gap will result in fly escape.

This protocol describes the rearing, collection, and housing conditions required for male Drosophila melanogaster used in DANCE aggression and courtship assays, and the preparation of female flies for courtship assays. Complete this protocol in advance of all behavioral experiments. Males must be collected and housed 6 days before the planned assay date. Steps 1‐9 apply to both aggression and courtship assays; steps 10a‐13a and 10b‐11b apply to courtship assays only.

Rear all fly stocks at 25°C, 65% relative humidity, under a 12‐hr/12‐hr light/dark cycle. Zeitgeber time zero (ZT0) is defined as the onset of the light phase. Record ZT0 for the incubator and use it as the reference for all assay scheduling in steps 7‐9.

Maintain Canton‐S stocks on standard Drosophila food. Transfer stocks to fresh food vials every 2‐3 weeks to avoid overcrowding. Do not use stocks that have been reared at nonstandard temperatures or under constant light.

On the day of collection (6 days before the planned assay), identify vials containing newly eclosed flies. Newly eclosed males are recognizable by their pale, unhardened cuticle, which darkens within several hours after eclosion. Collect males within 24 hr of eclosion.

Collecting males outside the 24‐hr post‐eclosion window introduces age heterogeneity within a cohort. Because male aggression levels increase with age and then plateau, even a 12‐hr difference in collection time can increase variance within groups.

Anesthetize flies briefly on a CO2 pad. Using a paintbrush or feather, sex‐sort flies under a stereomicroscope, transferring males to a holding vial with standard food.

For group‐housed (GH) control males: Transfer groups of 20 male flies to standard group‐housing vials (90 mm × 25 mm) containing standard food. Cap the vial and label with date of collection and genotype. House at 25°C, 65% relative humidity, 12‐hr/12‐hr light/dark cycle.

For single‐housed (SH) experimental males: Transfer 1 male fly each to individual housing vials (70 mm × 10 mm) containing standard food. Cap and label each vial. House under the same conditions as GH controls.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Flies should be divided into two groups, with some group housed and some singly housed. Single housing for 6 days substantially elevates male aggression relative to group housing. This is the standard pre‐assay condition used to produce robust, quantifiable aggression in Canton‐S males. Do not reduce isolation to <4 days, and do not extend isolation beyond 8 days before the assay.

House GH and SH vials in the same incubator to ensure identical temperature, humidity, and light cycle across conditions.

On the morning of the assay (Day 7), transfer vials from the incubator to the behavioral room at least 30 min before loading flies into arenas.

Perform aggression assays during ZT0‐ZT2.5 (the first 2.5 hr of the light phase). Record the clock time at the start of each assay session and verify it falls within the correct ZT window.

Drosophila male aggression is strongly gated by circadian time. Assays performed outside this window will produce reduced behavioral output and increased inter‐dyad variability.

Perform courtship assays during ZT0‐ZT3 or ZT9‐ZT12. Use the same ZT window consistently within an experiment. Do not mix morning and evening sessions with the same dataset.

Two methods of preparing female flies for experimentation are described below. Select the appropriate method based on the experimental design: mated females are used for standard courtship assays, whereas decapitated virgin females are used when assessing male courtship behavior independent of female behavioral feedback.

On the same day as male collection (Day 1), collect newly eclosed virgin female flies. Anesthetize briefly on a CO2 pad and transfer females to group‐housing vials (∼20 females per vial).

To confirm virginity: Virgin females eclose with a whitish, expanded abdomen and meconium (dark material visible through the abdominal wall). Collect females within 6 hr of eclosion to ensure virginity.

Add 10 Canton‐S males to each female housing vial (∼20 females per vial) on the day of female collection to allow mating. House mixed vials at 25°C for 4‐6 days.

On Day 6 after collection (24 hr before the assay), transfer individual mated females from GH vials to individual holding vials containing standard food. On the morning of the assay (Day 7), load females directly into the arena by mouth aspirator without CO2 anesthesia (see Basic Protocol , step 11).

Collect virgin female flies 2‐4 days before the planned assay. House females in small groups without males at 25°C.

On the morning of the assay, confirm that females are 2‐4 days old. Anesthetize females on a CO2 pad. Under a stereomicroscope, hold the female body using a paintbrush to prevent movement and use fine microdissecting scissors to remove the head of each female with a single clean snip at the neck. Proceed immediately to arena loading. Decapitated females remain behaviorally active for ∼1 hr and must be loaded within this window. During loading, confirm that each decapitated female is mobile and responsive and occasionally grooms herself. Discard females that show no movement after decapitation.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Decapitation must be performed immediately before the assay, not in advance. Decapitate females in batches and load them into arenas in sequence. For experimental comparisons, each dyad must use a female that has not been used in any other dyad in the same experiment, as the dyad is the independent unit of replication. Reuse of a decapitated female across multiple arenas is permitted only when generating classifier training or validation data, where the goal is diverse annotated behavioral bouts rather than statistically independent replicates.

Collection and housing setup on Day 1 takes ∼1‐2 hr. No active work is required on Days 2‐5. On the morning of the assay (Day 7), allow 30 min for vial transfer and room acclimatization before loading. Preparation of mated females requires 5‐10 min, and preparation of decapitated virgin females requires <30 sec per female.

Both procedures must be completed on the day before behavioral recordings, as food plates require 8‐12 hr of drying and Sigmacote‐coated arenas require overnight drying. Measure 300 ml of commercial apple juice into a 500‐ml heat‐resistant beaker. Weigh out 9 g agar and add to the apple juice. Stir briefly to distribute the agar.

Heat the mixture in a microwave oven or on a hot plate, stirring intermittently with a steel spatula, until the agar is fully dissolved and the mixture reaches a rolling boil. Monitor closely to prevent boiling over.

Agar dissolves slowly and requires sustained heating. Continue until no visible agar granules remain. Incomplete dissolution produces uneven food texture.

In a separate container, measure 100 ml apple juice and weigh out 10 g sucrose. Stir until completely dissolved. Heat for ∼2 min if dissolution is slow.

Final composition: 2.25% (w/v) agar in commercial apple juice with 2.5% (w/v) sucrose (total volume: 400 ml).

Allow both solutions to cool briefly (2‐3 min) until no longer boiling. Pour the sucrose solution into the hot agar mixture. Stir thoroughly to achieve a uniform consistency.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Do not allow the combined mixture to cool below ∼50°C before pouring. If the agar sets prematurely, reheat gently once only. Repeated reheating reduces food quality.

Place acrylic food plates on a level surface. Pour the combined apple juice/agar mixture in a uniform layer across the food plate surface, aiming for a consistent thickness of ∼2‐3 mm.

Immediately remove any trapped air bubbles from the surface by drawing a steel spatula gently across the surface in one smooth motion.

CAUTION: Air bubbles create uneven surface texture that interferes with fly movement and affects behavioral output. Remove all bubbles before the agar begins to set.

Allow the food to solidify at room temperature for 5‐10 min, and then cover the surface loosely with cheesecloth.

Allow the covered food plate to dry at 25°C and 55%‐60% relative humidity for 8‐12 hr (overnight). At ambient humidity above 60% relative humidity, extend drying time to up to 16 hr. The surface is ready when it appears matte and nonreflective under direct light. A shiny surface indicates excess moisture; discard and re‐prepare.

After drying, carefully remove the food plate from the tray using a razor blade. Cut excess food from the edges to produce a clean, uniform surface.

Store prepared food plates at 4°C covered with cling film for up to 3 days. Allow refrigerated plates to equilibrate to room temperature for at least 30 min before use. Do not use plates where condensation has formed on the surface.

Active preparation time: ∼25 min. Overnight drying: 8‐12 hr.

CAUTION: Sigmacote (SL2) contains chlorotrimethylsilane in a heptane/xylene carrier. It is flammable and is a respiratory irritant. All coating steps must be performed in a fume hood. Keep away from open flames. Consult the Safety Data Sheet before use.

Bring Sigmacote and cotton swabs to a fume hood. Do not perform coating outside a fume hood.

Before use, gently squeeze the cotton tip of each swab to loosen the fibers. Compact cotton tips do not absorb adequate Sigmacote and will produce uneven coating.

Dip the loosened cotton tip into the Sigmacote bottle. Remove the swab and allow excess to drain briefly.

Apply Sigmacote to the inner walls and ceiling of each blister‐pack arena well using the saturated cotton swab. Coat in a circular motion to ensure complete coverage of all inner surfaces including the ceiling and upper walls.

Verify coverage by holding each coated arena up to a light source and rotating it. Uncoated patches appear as areas with different optical texture.

Allow coated arenas to air‐dry overnight at room temperature (minimum 8 hr). Do not use arenas before they are fully dry.

Sigmacote older than 12 months may have reduced coating efficacy. If wall‐climbing is observed despite fresh coating, replace the Sigmacote stock.

Coating 8‐12 arenas takes ∼10‐15 min. Overnight drying (8‐12 hr) is required before use.

Place the electronic tablet or smartphone on a flat, stable surface. Launch the white screen light application and set the display to a full‐screen white image. Adjust screen brightness to maximum or until the arena background appears uniformly bright when viewed from above.

Place the transparent acrylic sheet on top of the backlight device, supported by four 4‐mm spacers positioned at the corners. This creates a 4‐mm air gap between the screen and the acrylic sheet.

IMPORTANT NOTE: The 4‐mm air gap is not optional. Screen surfaces generate heat during extended use, and direct contact between the screen and the arena base raises arena temperature and suppresses behavioral output. Verify that the spacers are in place before placing arenas.

Place the assembled DANCE arena on top of the acrylic sheet, centered over the backlight display.

Mount the smartphone camera directly above the arena on a tripod or fixed stand. Position the camera so that the lens axis is perpendicular to the arena surface (pointing straight down). Adjust height so that all arenas are visible within the camera frame.

Disable autofocus before recording. For Android smartphones, navigate to Pro or Manual mode in the camera application, and then tap and hold on the arena surface in the viewfinder to lock focus. Confirm that the focus lock indicator appears and does not change when flies move. For iPhone, tap and hold on the arena surface in the viewfinder until the AE/AF Lock banner appears. Autofocus is now locked and will remain so for the duration of the recording.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Autofocus must be disabled. Changes in focus during recording produce video artifacts that interfere with FlyTracker background subtraction and will corrupt tracking for all frames after the focus shift.

Set the following recording parameters in the camera application:

• Resolution: 1080p (1920 × 1080 pixels);• Frame rate: 30 fps;• Format: H.264 (.mp4);• White balance: set to a fixed value (Daylight or equivalent; do not use Auto white balance);• ISO: Set to the lowest available value that produces a well‐lit arena image (typically ISO 100 to 200).

• Resolution: 1080p (1920 × 1080 pixels);

• Frame rate: 30 fps;

• Format: H.264 (.mp4);

• White balance: set to a fixed value (Daylight or equivalent; do not use Auto white balance);

• ISO: Set to the lowest available value that produces a well‐lit arena image (typically ISO 100 to 200).

Specific menu paths for these settings vary across Android smartphone models. Consult the manufacturer's manual for the recording device in use.

Before loading flies, record a 10‐sec test clip of the empty arena. Review the clip and confirm that (a) the arena is fully in frame; (b) the food surface is visible through the well ceiling; (c) the image is in focus across all wells; and (d) there is no flickering due to backlight refresh rate.

If flickering is visible in the test clip, adjust screen brightness or reduce the screen refresh rate to 60 Hz if the device permits.

Place the recording smartphone in airplane mode before beginning each recording session, to prevent incoming calls, notifications, or background processes from interrupting the recording. On the backlight device, disable auto‐lock or screen timeout to prevent the display from dimming during the session.

Record for 20 min for aggression assays and 15 min for courtship assays. Begin timing from the end of the acclimatization period (Basic Protocol , step 13, or Basic Protocol , step 13).

Initial setup of the backlight, acrylic spacer, and camera mount takes ∼10 min per session. Parameter configuration and test recording take 5 min. Recording takes 20 min (aggression) or 15 min (courtship). Total setup and recording time: 35‐40 min.

This protocol describes assembly of the DANCE hardware for courtship recording. The courtship arena uses the same blister‐pack and acrylic base‐plate components as the aggression setup (Basic Protocol ), with the addition of thin slits cut into the top of each well to accommodate a separator comb made from repurposed X‐ray film. The separator divides each well into two compartments, allowing male and female flies to be loaded separately before the courtship session begins. Complete Support Protocol  (fly preparation) in advance and Support Protocol  (video acquisition setup) before loading flies. A video demonstration of DANCE courtship hardware assembly and recording is available as Figure 6—video 4 in Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig6video4), and viewing this before beginning assembly is recommended for first‐time users.

Select transparent medicine blister packs with the appropriate well dimensions. The standard courtship arena measures 11 mm diameter × 4.5 mm height. Alternative sizes of 13 mm × 5.5 mm or 17 mm × 4 mm can be substituted, though larger arenas may show modestly reduced encounter rates (Yadav et al., ).

Select blister strips containing multiple wells in a row (5 wells per strip is standard). Using a sharp razor blade, cut a single thin slit through the top surface of each well, running across the well diameter. The slit should be narrow enough to hold the separator comb firmly while allowing the comb to be lifted cleanly at the start of recording.

CAUTION: Cut with controlled, gentle pressure. Excessive force will widen the slit or crack the blister material. A slit that is too wide will not hold the separator comb in position during fly loading.

Cut separator combs from a sheet of repurposed X‐ray film. Before cutting, draw the comb shape on a sheet of white paper: each tooth should be as wide as the inner diameter of the circular arena well (11 mm for the standard courtship arena) and tall enough to reach the loading base plate when inserted through the slit. The number of teeth should match the number of wells in the blister‐pack strip. Use this paper drawing as a stencil by placing it on top of the X‐ray film and cutting along the outline with scissors. Each tooth must span the full inner diameter of the well so that neither fly can pass into the other compartment before the comb is lifted. Store the paper stencil for reuse across sessions to ensure consistent tooth width.

After cutting, apply a strip of transparent tape across the top bar of the comb to create a gripping surface. The tape should be applied to the top bar only and must not extend onto the teeth, which need to sit flush against the loading base plate when the comb is inserted.

The transparent tape handle makes it easier to grip and lift the comb cleanly at the start of recording without disturbing the flies or widening the slits. Lift the comb by holding the taped section between two fingers and pulling straight upward in a single smooth motion.

Courtship arenas modified with separator slits are reusable for ∼10‐15 sessions. When slits begin to widen and the separator comb no longer holds position, replace the blister‐pack strip.

Insert the separator comb through the slits from above, with one tooth entering each well. The comb tooth should divide each well into two equal compartments, one for the male and one for the female.

Verify that each comb tooth reaches the loading base plate at the bottom of the well. A tooth that does not reach the bottom will not effectively separate the flies after loading.

Align the acrylic base plate (with two loading holes per well) under the blister‐pack strip so that each loading hole falls under one compartment of the corresponding well. Join the blister‐pack strip and base plate with paper tape along the long edges, using 1‐mm acrylic side spacers to keep the assembly aligned and stable.

Seal both short ends of the assembly with paper tape to eliminate any gaps that could allow fly escape.

Place the assembled arena on a flat surface for fly loading.

Using a mouth aspirator, load one male fly into the male‐side loading hole of each well. Confirm that the male has entered the well before sealing the loading hole with paper tape. Designate one side of every arena consistently as the male side and label the assembly before loading.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Do not anesthetize males before loading—transfer males directly from their housing vials into the arena by mouth aspirator, without CO2 exposure. Anesthesia on the day of the assay will suppress courtship and render the recording unusable.

Some males should have been individually housed (experimental group) and some group housed (control group) for 6 days before this step (see Support Protocol , steps 5a and 5b). Do not load flies that appear lethargic or damaged.

Using a separate, clean aspirator tip, load one female fly into the female‐side loading hole of each well. If using mated females, use females prepared in advance (Support Protocol , option A: steps 10a‐13a). If using decapitated virgin females, load within 1 hr of decapitation (Support Protocol , option B: steps 10b and 11b). Seal the female‐side loading hole with transparent tape.

Place the loaded arena on the backlight setup, using a transparent acrylic sheet with 4‐mm spacers between the screen and the arena base.

Follow Basic Protocol , step 13, and allow flies to acclimatize in their respective compartments for 5 min with the separator comb in place. Keep the backlight on during acclimatization.

Position the smartphone camera above the arena in a fixed, vertical orientation on a tripod or mount. Configure recording parameters as described in Support Protocol . Record for 15 min.

After the 5‐min acclimatization period, gently lift the separator comb straight upward through the slits. Begin video recording immediately after comb removal. This moment defines the start of the courtship observation window.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Lift the separator comb vertically. Lateral movement widens the slits and will require the arena to be discarded. If the comb is difficult to remove, do not force it. Discard the arena and use a fresh one.

Separator combs and blister‐pack slits can be prepared in advance of the experimental session and stored for reuse across sessions. Assembly and sealing of one 5‐well strip takes ∼3 min. Loading males and females takes ∼3 min per strip. Acclimatization takes 5 min. Recording takes 15 min. Total per session for a single strip: ∼25 min. With practice, loading time decreases substantially from the estimates above. For higher throughput, multiple strips can be placed under separate smartphone cameras simultaneously, with two to four cameras running in parallel in a single session.

• Modified blister‐pack arenas are reusable for ∼10‐15 courtship sessions before slits widen.

This protocol describes the complete computational workflow for quantifying Drosophila aggression and courtship behaviors using the DANCE analysis pipeline. The pipeline proceeds in four stages: (1) video organization and chamber segmentation; (2) fly tracking using FlyTracker (Support Protocol ); (3) behavioral classification using pretrained JAABA classifiers (Support Protocol ); and (4) quantification of behavioral metrics using DANCE analysis scripts. The output is a set of .csv files containing per‐dyad behavioral indices suitable for statistical analysis. All DANCE analysis scripts are available at https://github.com/agrawallab/DANCE. Create a master project directory. Inside it, create a subfolder named with the recording date in DDMMYYYY format (e.g., 07052026). Place all raw video files (.mp4) from a single recording session into this date folder.

Verify that all videos meet the following specifications before proceeding: .mp4 format, H.264 encoding, 1080p resolution, 30‐fps frame rate. Open one video in a media player and confirm that fly bodies are visible against the backlit background with high contrast. If contrast is insufficient, re‐record using corrected lighting settings (Support Protocol , steps 1‐4).

Copy the organize.py script into the directory containing the raw video files from a single recording session. Open organize.py in Visual Studio Code and execute it by clicking the Run (Play) button. The script automatically creates a separate folder for each recording and organizes the corresponding files into their respective directories, thereby establishing a standardized folder structure for downstream processing. Successful completion of the process is indicated by the message “Organization complete.” displayed in the terminal.

Open Auto_Cropper.py in Visual Studio Code by double‐clicking the file. Click the Play button to run the script.

The terminal will prompt: “What is the path of the master video folder?” Copy and paste the full path of the date folder and press Enter.

The terminal will prompt again: “How many chambers are there per video?” Enter the number of chambers in the arena and press Enter.

The script segments each video and writes all cropped chamber videos into a single output folder. This structure allows one calibration file to be applied to every video from the session during tracking (see Support Protocol ).

Before proceeding, open the preview image saved alongside the output and confirm that every chamber has been correctly identified. If any chamber is missed or a spurious circle appears, adjust the circle detection parameters (minRadius, maxRadius, and param2) in Auto_Cropper.py to match the pixel size of the chambers in your recordings, and rerun segmentation. These parameters are specific to the camera and arena configuration in use and are not universal defaults.

When segmentation is complete, the terminal will display the message: “Cropped videos for X circles have been saved.” This confirms successful segmentation.

Ensure that the master video folder contains the necessary input video files before running the script. The output folder will be structured as required for FlyTracker. If any error occurs, verify that the correct folder path and number of chambers were provided.

Track all segmented chamber videos using FlyTracker. Follow Support Protocol  in full. Confirm that each segmented chamber folder contains a [videoname]_JAABA/ subfolder with trx.mat and a perframe folder before proceeding.

Generate behavioral score files using the pretrained DANCE classifiers. Follow Support Protocol  in full. For aggression experiments, load the Lunge_oneframe_classifer.jab classifier only. For courtship experiments, load all five courtship classifiers. Confirm that score files (e.g., scores_Lunge.mat) are present in each _JAABA/ folder before proceeding.

Perform steps 12a‐14a for aggression experiments only.

Open Lunge_Analyzer_indiC.py in Visual Studio Code. Click the Play button to run the script.

The terminal will prompt: “What is the complete path of the parent folder containing all videos and JAABA folders?” Enter the full path of the date folder and press Enter.

The script will process all lunge score files and generate a compiled .csv output file in the parent directory. Because the lunge classifier is a single‐frame classifier, each detected lunge is a discrete event rather than a bout with a measurable duration. The output contains one row per chamber, reporting the lunge frame numbers for each fly and the total lunge count for the dyad across the 20‐min session. Verify that the number of rows matches the number of dyads recorded.

Perform steps 12b and 13b for courtship experiments only.

Open courtship_bout_num_extractor.py in Visual Studio Code (or, if videos were not segmented into individual chamber folders, use courtship_bout_num_extractor_unsegmented.py). Click the Play button to run the script.

The terminal will prompt: “What is the complete path of the parent folder containing both video and JAABA folders?” Enter the full path of the date folder and press Enter. The script will rename and organize score files into a centralized score_files/ folder, and compile behavioral data from all five courtship classifiers into per‐classifier .csv files. Proceed to step 15.

Male identity assignment in the courtship output is based on the assumption that the fly with the higher wing extension count is the male. If the experimental design uses male‐male pairs, verify identity assignments manually.

Confirm that the following output files are present. Aggression: one compiled .csv file with lunge counts per dyad. Courtship: one compiled .csv file per classifier (wing extension, circling, following, attempted copulation, copulation), each containing behavioral indices per dyad. If the genotype or manipulation under study may reduce wing extension, also verify identity assignments manually on a subset of videos before analyzing a new experiment type.

Each courtship output .csv contains one row per recorded dyad and three columns: Fly 1 output, Fly 2 output, and assigned male identity. Male identity is derived from the wing extension assumption described above and is the value recommended for downstream analyses. The aggression output is structured differently (see step 14a).

Video organization and directory setup: ∼5 min. Chamber segmentation: ∼2‐5 min for eight videos. FlyTracker tracking for eight dyads: ∼10‐15 min (see Support Protocol ). JAABA classification for eight dyads with a single classifier: ∼5‐10 min; with all five courtship classifiers: ∼20‐30 min (see Support Protocol ). Running Lunge_Analyzer_indiC.py or courtship_bout_num_extractor.py: <1 min. Total time from organized raw videos to analyzed .csv output: ∼25‐60 min depending on experiment type.

This protocol describes how to track fly movements in segmented DANCE videos using FlyTracker, a freely available MATLAB‐based software that tracks the pose and maintains the individual identity of each fly across video frames (Eyjolfsdottir et al., ). Complete this protocol after video segmentation (Basic Protocol , steps 4‐9). The output is a trx.mat tracking file and a per‐frame features folder inside a JAABA‐compatible directory, which are required inputs for Support Protocol . Representative FlyTracker calibration, tracking, and identity swap correction outputs are shown in Figure . Tracking one batch of eight videos takes ∼25‐35 min.

NOTE: Both FlyTracker and JAABA must be added to the MATLAB path before beginning. In MATLAB, navigate to Home, then Set Path, then Add with Subfolders. Select the FlyTracker root folder, click Save. Repeat for the JAABA root folder. This step is required only once per MATLAB installation.

Download FlyTracker from https://github.com/kristinbranson/FlyTracker. Follow the installation instructions in the repository README. Confirm installation by typing tracker in the MATLAB command window. The FlyTracker GUI should open.

Download JAABA from https://github.com/kristinbranson/JAABA. Do not use the SourceForge distribution, which lacks functions required for courtship classifier feature computation. Follow installation instructions. Confirm by typing JAABAPlot in the MATLAB command window.

Add both FlyTracker and JAABA to the MATLAB path with subfolders as described in the Materials note above. Save the path.

In the MATLAB command window, type tracker and press Enter. The FlyTracker GUI will open.

Click Video Folder. In the dialog box, navigate to and select the folder containing all cropped arena videos from the recording session, produced by Auto_Cropper.py (Basic Protocol ). Click Select Folder.

For batch processing, all cropped arena videos from the same recording session are stored in a single folder by Auto_Cropper.py. FlyTracker applies one calibration file to every video in that folder. This is valid provided that arena size, camera position, and recording conditions are identical across the session, which is the case for videos segmented from a single recording.

Click Calibrate. A dialog box titled Loading Calibrator will appear, followed by a frame from the video with red boundary markers overlaid on the arena.

Click and drag the red markers to align precisely with the left and right inner edges of the circular arena boundary.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Inaccurate marker placement will cause FlyTracker to miscalculate the spatial scale of the video and will invalidate all downstream distance and velocity measurements. Align markers carefully, as this calibration will be applied to all videos in the folder.

In the right panel under Resolution, locate the Length of the ruler (mm) field. Enter 13 for the standard 13‐mm diameter aggression arena. Enter the appropriate diameter if using an alternative arena size (17 mm or 21 mm; see Basic Protocol , step 1), or 11 mm for the standard courtship arena and alternative arena size (13 mm or 17 mm; see Basic Protocol , step 1).

Click Continue. A progress dialog titled Computing background image will appear. MATLAB will display frame numbers in the command window as it processes the video. For a 20‐min video at 30 fps, 36,000 frames will be processed. Wait until the Background panel displays the Bg Mean, Bg Variance, and Sample Image.

Under Experimental Setup, enter 1 in the # Chambers field for individual segmented chamber videos (typically 1 arena per video). For multichamber recordings, enter the correct number.

Click Detect. A progress dialog will appear, and detected arena boundaries will be displayed as blue circles. If arena detection fails or produces incorrect boundaries, click the dropdown menu under Automatically Detect Chambers and select Manually Set Chambers. Adjust the arena boundary by clicking and dragging.

Verify that the # Flies Per Chamber field shows 2. If the software detects a different number, manually set it to 2.

Click Continue.

Adjust the Foreground Threshold slider until the fly body, legs, and wings are consistently highlighted in the preview window. Start with the default value and adjust in increments of 5.

Adjust the Body Threshold slider until the body outline of each fly is cleanly segmented from wings and legs. The color indicators in the corner of the calibration window show which pixels are classified as body versus wing.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Over‐thresholding will merge the two fly bodies into a single detected object. Under‐thresholding will fragment one fly into multiple objects. If either condition persists despite adjustment, recheck video contrast (Support Protocol ) before proceeding.

Click Finish. A dialog box titled Finalizing Calibration will appear.

Enter the number of CPU cores to use for parallel processing. Reserve two or three cores for operating system processes when selecting this value. Using all available cores risks freezing the computer. Click OK.

Ensure that the Save JAABA Folders checkbox is selected. Click TRACK. FlyTracker will automatically apply the calibration settings to all videos within the selected folder and process them in batch mode. Do not close MATLAB or interact with the GUI during tracking.

After tracking is successfully completed, navigate to the video folder and confirm that the following output files and folders are present in each video folder: [videoname]_JAABA/ (the JAABA‐compatible experiment directory); [videoname]_JAABA/trx.mat (the tracking data file); and [videoname]_JAABA/perframe/ (the per‐frame features folder containing .mat files for each computed feature).

If the perframe folder is absent or empty, tracking did not complete successfully. Check the MATLAB command window for error messages. The most common cause is an incorrect number of flies per arena (step 12). Correct the value and rerun from step 10.

Using a single calibration file for all the cropped arena videos substantially reduces analysis time while maintaining consistent tracking parameters across all arena videos from the session. This approach is recommended whenever arena geometry and recording conditions remain unchanged throughout the recording session.

Repeat steps 4‐19 for each folder in the dataset.

Alternatively, if arena positions, lighting conditions, or recording geometry vary between videos, proceed to steps 21‐23 to calibrate each arena video independently.

The video segmentation script can be configured to save each cropped arena video into a separate folder.

Open FlyTracker and select the folder containing a single arena video. Perform calibration, chamber detection, parameter tuning, and tracking as described above.

Repeat the calibration procedure for every arena video in the dataset.

This approach is substantially more time consuming than batch processing with a shared calibration file and should be used only when necessary. One‐to‐one calibration may improve tracking accuracy when experimental conditions vary between arenas or recording sessions.

After tracking all videos, inspect each result for identity swaps. In the FlyTracker GUI, click Visualizer and load the tracking output folder.

Step through the video using the frame slider. Identity swaps appear as an abrupt crossing of the two fly trajectories. Note the frame numbers where swaps occur.

Use the built‐in correction tool to manually correct identity swaps at the swap frame. Save the corrected tracking data.

A small number of identity swaps are expected during tracking, particularly when flies overlap or come into close contact. Potential identity swaps are automatically flagged by the FlyTracker Visualizer and should be manually inspected. Inspect every video as described in steps 24‐26, rather than only the flagged frames. Although a small number of identity swaps may occur, particularly during occlusions, the overall identity switch rate is typically low and does not substantially affect behavioral quantification.

Re‐save the corrected tracking data. The trx.mat file will be overwritten with the corrected version.

Installing FlyTracker and JAABA and adding them to the MATLAB path is a one‐time setup requiring ∼30 min. For a standard aggression experiment with eight dyads, tracking takes ∼10‐15 min total across all eight videos. Identity swap verification and correction for eight videos takes ∼15‐20 min. Total time for this protocol with a standard eight‐dyad dataset: ∼25‐35 min.

Under the Experiments section, click Batch. Navigate to the folder containing JAABA_paths.txt. Double‐click to open the .txt file.

Alternatively, under the Experiments section, click Add. Navigate to the folder containing a tracked video. Double‐click to open it, then double‐click on the [videoname]_JAABA subfolder to select it. Click Done.

IMPORTANT NOTE: You must select the _JAABA subfolder specifically, not the parent video folder. JAABA requires the directory that contains the trx.mat file and perframe/ folder. Selecting the wrong level will cause JAABA to fail to load experiment data.

Manual addition of experiments using the Add option is considerably more time consuming and less efficient than batch processing, as each experiment folder must be selected individually. Therefore, batch processing is recommended whenever multiple experiments (large number of recordings) are to be analyzed.

Repeat step 5 for each additional tracked video. Verify that all experiments appear in the Experiments panel.

Under the Classifiers section, click Add. Navigate to the folder where the DANCE .jab classifier files are stored.

For aggression experiments: Select Lunge_oneframe_classifer.jab and click Open.

For courtship experiments: Navigate to the directory containing the classifier files, select WingExt.jab, Circling.jab, Following.jab, Attempted_Copulation.jab, and Copulation.jab simultaneously (using multi‐select), and click Open. All selected classifiers will be loaded into JAABA in a single step.

For a standard aggression recording, load only Lunge_oneframe_classifer.jab. Loading all six classifiers for an aggression recording will produce empty score files for the courtship behaviors and will extend processing time unnecessarily.

Click Classify. JAABA will begin processing all loaded experiments against all loaded classifiers. Do not close MATLAB or interact with the JAABA window during classification.

Wait until the status display shows Ready for all experiments.

Verify that classification completed successfully. Navigate in the file system to the [videoname]_JAABA/ folder for one processed video. Confirm that score files are present: scores_Lunge.mat (aggression experiments); scores_WingExt.mat, scores_Circling.mat, scores_Following.mat, scores_Attempted_Copulation.mat, and scores_Copulation.mat (courtship experiments).

If score files are absent after classification completes, the most common cause is a mismatch between the frame rate of the videos used to train the classifier and the frame rate of the new videos. Verify that all videos were recorded at 30 fps (Support Protocol , step 6).

Repeat the classification process (steps 2‐11) for any additional recording sessions not yet processed.

After classification is complete across all sessions, see Basic Protocol  for automated quantification of aggressive lunges (steps 12a‐14a) and courtship behaviors (steps 12b and 13b).

For a standard eight‐dyad aggression experiment (eight videos, lunge classifier only), classification takes ∼5‐10 min. For a courtship experiment (eight videos, five courtship classifiers), classification takes ∼20‐30 min.

This protocol describes how to train a new JAABA classifier for a behavior not covered by the existing DANCE classifiers, or to retrain an existing classifier on videos recorded under experimental conditions that differ substantially from those used to generate the original training set, for example a different arena geometry, a different fly strain with an unusual body size, or a novel behavior of interest. Use this protocol when pretrained classifiers produce systematically low or inconsistent scores despite correct FlyTracker tracking and JAABA setup. Complete Support Protocol  on all videos intended for training and testing before beginning.

NOTE: Training a JAABA classifier is an iterative process requiring multiple rounds of annotation and retraining. Allow at least 2‐3 days for an initial classifier. Do not train a classifier on fewer than five independent videos.

Before beginning annotation, write a precise operational definition of the target behavior specifying: (a) the postural or kinematic features that characterize the behavior; (b) the minimum duration constituting a true bout in frames; and (c) criteria for distinguishing the behavior from closely related behaviors. All annotators must use the same written definition. Inconsistent annotation is the most common cause of poor classifier performance.

Divide tracked videos into two groups before any annotation begins: a training set (∼70% of videos) and a test set (remaining 30%). The test set must not be used during training. Do not open test videos in JAABA until the classifier is trained; they are annotated separately as ground truth in Alternate Protocol . Record the assignment of each video to train or test set before opening any video in JAABA.

IMPORTANT NOTE: If a test video is examined and annotated before training is complete, it is contaminated and cannot be used for unbiased validation. Discard contaminated test videos and designate new ones from the training pool.

In the MATLAB command window, type StartJAABA and press Enter.

A dialog box named “JAABA Open” will appear. Under the JAABA Open window, click New. In the New dialog box, under Target Type, select eyrun_flies from the drop‐down menu. Enter a descriptive name for the behavior to be classified (e.g., wing_flick) in the Behavior Name field. Specify the Movie File Name (e.g., movie.mp4) and Tracking Data File Name (trx.mat). JAABA will automatically generate the corresponding Output Score File Name (e.g., scores_wing_flick.mat). Leave the Advanced parameters at their default settings, and click Done to create the new classifier project.

Under the Experiments section, click Add. Navigate to and select the _JAABA subfolder of the first training video. Make sure that the folder contains movie.mp4, the perframes folder, and the trx.mat file, and then click Done. Repeat for each remaining training video. Do not add any test set videos at this stage.

The video and trajectory display will load in the JAABA window.

Once they are loaded, navigate through the video using the frame slider. When a behavioral bout matching the written definition from step 1 is identified, mark the corresponding frames by clicking on the “Behavior” label at the top right corner (red box). Mark frames that clearly do not contain the behavior by clicking on None (blue box).

IMPORTANT NOTE: JAABA requires both positive examples (labeled as Behavior) and negative examples (labeled as None) to train a classifier. Actively label clear non‐bout frames, especially those that superficially resemble the target behavior. If only positive bouts are labeled, JAABA treats all other frames as ambiguous, which reduces classifier specificity. Ensure that the Behavior and the None labels are roughly balanced to avoid prediction bias.

After annotating a few bouts and non‐bouts, the classifier can be trained by clicking on the “Train” button at the bottom right. The status bar will indicate that the training is running.

When you click on “Train” for the first time, it will ask you to select features for training. Once you click OK, a window for “Select Features” will pop up. Choose the per‐frame categories you want to include using All or None in the Select column. Set the Amount to normal, enter a positive integer for Window Size, and click Done to continue.

In the frame window, you will be able to see the predictions of the classifier based on the labeling you had done before “Train.” Darker colors indicate low confidence, while brighter colors indicate high confidence. However, some frames will not be labeled for prediction, for which you can click on the “Predict” at the bottom.

Review the predictions and identify false positives (frames labeled as behavior that are not genuine bouts) and label them as None in JAABA. Identify false negatives (genuine bouts that the classifier missed) and label them as Behavior.

Once you have finished correcting the labels, click Train again to retrain the classifier. You can compare the updated predictions with the previous results by selecting “Old” from the drop‐down menu at the bottom of the automatic predictions timeline.

The predictions can be made better, if needed, by using the Post‐processing option from the Classifier dropdown.

To quickly measure the classifier's accuracy and precision, go to the Classifier tab and select Cross‐validate. You will get a table showing all the errors made by the classifier based on the manual labels and the predictions.

Repeat steps 11‐14 until classifier performance on the training videos appears stable across iterations, meaning that three consecutive additions produce no improvement in precision and recall.

When classifier performance on training videos is satisfactory, click File, then Save Classifier. Save as a .jab file with a descriptive filename that includes the behavior name and date (e.g., wing_flick_07052026.jab).

Proceed to Alternate Protocol  to validate the saved classifier on the held‐out test set before using it for experimental data.

Setting up the JAABA project and completing initial annotation of three to five training videos takes ∼5‐7 hr. Each subsequent refinement round takes 1‐2 hr. A full training run for a lunge‐type single‐frame classifier typically requires 4‐5 days. These estimates are approximate and depend on annotator experience and computing resources. Duration‐based behaviors may require 5‐7 days due to large training frame requirements.
