In the MATLAB command window, type StartJAABA and press Enter.

A dialog box named “JAABA Open” will appear. Under the JAABA Open window, click Open in Ground Truthing Mode, and it will ask for the .jab file (developed classifier); click on the relevant classifier .jab file. Once loaded, go to File and click on the Change Experiment list and add all the test set videos.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Manual annotation must be completed before the classifier is run on any test video. Examining classifier predictions before completing manual annotation introduces observer bias and invalidates the validation. Do not run the classifier on, or view its predictions for, any test video until manual annotation of all test videos is finished (step 5). Predictions are generated in step 6.

Select the first test video from the Experiments panel. Navigate through the video using the frame slider.

Identify behavioral bouts matching the written behavioral definition (see Alternate Protocol , step 1). For each genuine bout, select the corresponding frames and click on Behavior. For frames that clearly do not contain the behavior, click on None. Annotate each test video completely before moving to the next.

If two annotators are available, annotate at least 20% of test videos independently and compare results using a non‐parametric test before proceeding. If inter‐annotator agreement is low (Cohen's kappa <0.6), revisit the behavioral definition in Alternate Protocol , step 1.

Repeat step 4 for all test videos. Save the JAABA project after completing each video.

After annotating all test videos manually, load the classifier .jab file: under the Classifiers section, click Add and select the .jab file. Click Classify. Wait until all experiments show Ready status.

Verify that score files (scores_[behaviorname].mat) are present in the _JAABA/ folder for each test video before proceeding.

Run the extractLabels script on the JAABA project file containing manual ground‐truth annotations. This script reads the .jab file and exports manually labeled bout boundaries to a test.csv file. Input: test.jab; output: test.csv.

Run the individual_video_manual_labels script on the test.csv output from step 8. This script calculates per‐video bout counts and produces individual bout files for each video and a summary file video_path_counts.csv listing total bout counts per video.

Run the Sheetnames_maker script, providing the list of video names from video_path_counts.csv as input. This script generates an empty Excel workbook, test_Workbook.xlsx, with one sheet per test video and a standard header row. Output: test_Workbook.xlsx.

Organize manual output and JAABA classifier output into separate subfolders. Run manual_JAABA_mateBook_to_workbook to compile all outputs into the test_Workbook.xlsx. Input: folder containing manual output, JAABA output, and the test_Workbook.xlsx file; output: populated test_Workbook.xlsx.

Run the Classification_metrices_table script on the completed test_Workbook.xlsx. This script compares predicted and ground‐truth bouts using the following criteria: a predicted bout is scored as a true positive (TP) if it overlaps with a ground‐truth bout by at least one frame (∼33 ms at 30 fps). Predicted bouts with no overlap are scored as false positives (FP). Ground‐truth bouts with no overlapping prediction are scored as false negatives (FN). Output: precision, recall, and F
1 score for each test video, and the same metrics calculated across all test videos combined. Precision is calculated as TP divided by (TP plus FP). Recall is calculated as TP divided by (TP plus FN). F
1 score is calculated as 2 multiplied by (Precision multiplied by Recall), divided by (Precision plus Recall).

Additionally, run the behavior_index_matebook_table script on the completed test_Workbook.xlsx. This script calculates a per‐video behavior index across different platforms, for a direct comparison between behavior indices derived from ground‐truth annotations and those predicted by the JAABA classifier. The behavioral index for courtship classifiers is calculated as the proportion of total frames classified as the behavior: behavioral index equals total frames classified as behavior divided by total frames in the recording.

To calculate performance metrics for a single‐frame classifier such as the lunge classifier, use the Overlap_analyzer script from the GitHub repository. The input file is an Excel sheet containing the manually annotated frames and the JAABA‐predicted frames; the output is the per‐video TP, FP, and FN counts.

Evaluate classifier performance against the reference values from the DANCE eLife validation study (Table ).

Classifier Performance on the Held‐out Test Set in the eLife Validation Study

Copulation is operationally defined as mounting lasting ≥45 sec, making it a temporally discrete and visually unambiguous event. This behavioral clarity accounts for the near‐perfect bout‐level classification performance. Frame‐level performance metrics, which are marginally lower across all classifiers including copulation (precision 98.17%, recall 95.55%, F
1 96.85%), are reported in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 of Yadav et al. ().

For a newly trained custom classifier, an F
1 score of ≥0.70 on the held‐out test set is the minimum acceptable performance before using the classifier for experimental data. An F
1 score <0.70 indicates that the classifier is undertrained or trained on insufficiently diverse data, or the behavioral definition requires revision. The 0.70 threshold is a general guide; the acceptable score depends on the experimental question, so also check classifier predictions against the video to confirm that the interactions relevant to the question have been captured.

If the F
1 score is below the acceptance threshold, return to Alternate Protocol , step 11, and add further training examples. A high FP rate indicates that the classifier is too liberal and requires more negative examples. A high FN rate indicates that the classifier is missing true bouts and requires more positive examples from the behavioral intensity range in which misses occur.

Once the classifier meets the acceptance threshold, record the test set performance metrics in the experimental lab notebook alongside the classifier .jab filename, training date, number of training videos, and number of labeled frames.

Manual annotation of 15 test videos takes ∼8‐10 hr. Running the analysis scripts takes <30 min. The full workflow from annotation start to generating final performance metrics takes approximately one full working day.

This protocol describes the integration of a green‐light optogenetics module with the DANCE recording hardware for circuit‐level dissection of aggression behavior. Two printed circuit boards, each carrying five green LEDs, are positioned diagonally ∼8 cm from the DANCE arena and controlled by an Arduino microcontroller. Illumination silences neurons expressing the anion channelrhodopsin GtACR1 during the 20‐min aggression recording window. The protocol assumes that DANCE aggression hardware has been assembled (Basic Protocol ), flies have been loaded and are acclimatized (Basic Protocol , steps 6‐13), and video acquisition has been configured (Support Protocol ). An annotated schematic and photograph of the complete optogenetics recording setup are shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 of Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig7s1).

NOTE: This protocol uses UAS‐GtACR1, which drives expression of a green‐light‐activated anion channelrhodopsin (Govorunova et al., ; Mohammad et al., ). GtACR1 is an inhibitory channelrhodopsin that silences neuronal activity upon green light illumination. GtACR1‐mediated silencing in these experiments was achieved without dietary supplementation with all‐trans retinal (Schnaitmann et al., ).

Worked example genotype from Yadav et al. (): Cross TH‐GAL4 virgin females (Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center, BDSC no. 51982) with UAS‐GtACR1 males (BDSC no. 92983; originally a gift from Gaurav Das, National Centre for Cell Science, Pune, India). Collect male progeny of the genotype TH‐GAL4/+; UAS‐GtACR1/+ for behavioral assays. Use parental control lines (TH‐GAL4/+ and UAS‐GtACR1/+ males) in the same session.

The white tablet backlight used for video recording contains spectral power within the GtACR1 excitation range and is not spectrally inert with respect to the opsin. Screen brightness was set to the minimum level that still permitted reliable tracking, and the same setting was used for the experimental genotype and both parental controls within a session. Under these conditions, no substantial change in aggression attributable to the backlight was observed.

Optogenetic silencing of dopaminergic neurons using TH‐GAL4 > UAS‐GtACR1 produced a significant increase in isolation‐induced aggressive lunges across arena sizes of 13 mm, 17 mm, and 21 mm diameter, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 of Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig7s3). Increasing arena size tends to reduce lunge frequency, though the differences were not statistically significant. Representative recordings showing the resulting increase in aggression upon dopaminergic neuron silencing are available as Figure 7—video 2 of Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig7video2).

Solder five green LEDs onto each of the two printed circuit boards, maintaining a spacing of ∼1 cm between adjacent LED positions. This creates the two LED strips that will illuminate the DANCE arena from the side.

Mount each of the two LED strips (five LEDs per strip) in its LED stand, positioned diagonally ∼8 cm from the behavioral chamber. Confirm that all wells of the arena fall within the combined illumination field of the two strips before proceeding.

Orient LEDs such that the light path crosses the arena plane as uniformly as possible. Uneven illumination will produce variable silencing efficiency across wells.

Connect the LED array to the Arduino microcontroller via the LED driver or current‐control module. Connect the Arduino to a computer via USB.

Upload Arduino control code to the microcontroller. The code should configure LED onset and duration to match the 20‐min recording window. Arduino code for DANCE optogenetics is available at https://github.com/agrawallab/DANCE.

Before placing flies in arenas, power up the LED array and confirm the drive parameters. Connect a multimeter in series with one LED strip, set to a DC current range of 200 mA, and confirm a current draw of ∼88 mA per strip at a supply voltage of 4.9 V. Record the measured voltage and current in the experiment log.

IMPORTANT NOTE: These drive parameters correspond to the hardware used to generate the silencing results reported in Yadav et al. (). Do not increase drive current without first validating behavioral and locomotor effects on the specific genotype in use. Verify voltage and current before every experiment.

Power off the LEDs. Assemble the DANCE arena with flies as described in Basic Protocol , steps 3‐13. Allow 5 min of acclimatization.

Place the arena on the backlight tablet. Position the smartphone camera above the arena for video recording. Configure recording parameters as described in Support Protocol .

Begin video recording (Support Protocol , step 9).

Immediately after starting the recording, activate the Arduino‐controlled LEDs to begin optogenetic stimulation. LED illumination and video recording should be simultaneous from the start of the 20‐min window.

Confirm that the LED illumination does not produce visible glare or overexposure artifacts in the recording. Review the first 30 sec of footage through the smartphone viewfinder. If the LED light source appears as a bright reflection in the arena ceiling, reposition the LED array to angle the illumination more obliquely.

Record for 20 min. At the end of the session, stop recording and power off the LEDs.

Initial LED soldering and PCB assembly is a one‐time setup process taking ∼20‐30 min. Verification of supply voltage and per‐strip current takes 5 min per session. Arena setup and fly loading take ∼5 min (see Basic Protocol ). Acclimatization takes 5 min. Recording takes 20 min. Total session time after initial setup: ∼60 min.

Dissolve 0.5 ml of Alcojet detergent (Alconox, cat. no. 1401‐1) in distilled water to 1000 ml to produce a 0.05% (w/v) solution. Submerge used blister‐pack arenas in the solution and wash gently. Do not scrub. Rinse thoroughly with distilled water at least three times to remove all detergent residue. Allow arenas to air‐dry completely at room temperature before recoating with Sigmacote. Avoid heat drying.

Prepare the day before use; plates require 8‐12 hr of drying at 25°C, 55%‐60% relative humidity, before use.

Part A: Combine 300 ml of commercial apple juice (no added sugars or preservatives) and 9 g agar (HiMedia, cat. no. GRM026) in a heat‐resistant beaker. Heat in a microwave or on a hot plate, stirring intermittently with a steel spatula, until the agar is fully dissolved and the mixture reaches a rolling boil.

Part B: Dissolve 10 g of sucrose (HiMedia, cat. no. GRM601) in 100 ml of commercial apple juice (no added sugars or preservatives) at room temperature.

Add Part B to the hot Part A mixture and stir thoroughly to combine.

Pouring and drying: Allow the mixture to cool to ∼50°C before pouring onto acrylic food plates on a level surface. Allow to solidify for 10‐15 min. Cover loosely with cheesecloth and allow to dry at 25°C and 55%‐60% relative humidity for 8‐12 hr before use. At ambient humidity >60% relative humidity, extend drying time to up to 16 hr.

Storage: Store prepared food plates covered with cling film for up to 3 days at 4°C. Allow refrigerated plates to equilibrate to room temperature for at least 30 min before use. Do not use plates if condensation has formed on the surface.

Final composition: 2.25% (w/v) agar in commercial apple juice with 2.5% (w/v) sucrose; total volume: 400 ml, sufficient for 16 standard 2‐mm acrylic food plates.

Sigmacote (Sigma‐Aldrich, cat. no. SL2) is used directly from the bottle without dilution. Apply to arena walls and ceilings using cotton swabs. Allow coated arenas to dry overnight (minimum 8 hr) at room temperature before use.

CAUTION: Sigmacote contains chlorotrimethylsilane in a heptane/xylene carrier. It is flammable and a respiratory irritant. All applications must be performed in a fume hood. Store at room temperature away from heat sources.

DANCE was benchmarked against CADABRA (Dankert et al., ) and MateBook (Ribeiro et al., ) in Yadav et al. (), using manual ground‐truth annotation as the reference, and matched or exceeded the corresponding rule‐based method on precision, recall, and F
1 across both the aggression and courtship classifiers, at a fraction of the hardware cost of conventional machine‐vision setups. Readers seeking the full benchmarking data are directed to that study.

The duration of pre‐assay single housing is the most important biological variable affecting aggression levels in male Drosophila and must be controlled precisely. In the eLife validation study (Yadav et al., ), Canton‐S males were collected within 24 hr of eclosion and housed individually (1 male per vial, 70 mm × 10 mm) for exactly 6 days prior to the aggression assay. Single‐housed (SH) males show substantially elevated lunge frequencies relative to group‐housed (GH) males across the full range of aggression levels. Reducing isolation to fewer than 4 days will markedly reduce aggression and push most dyads into the low‐aggressive category. Extending isolation beyond 8 days does not reliably increase aggression further and may introduce variability due to age‐related changes in behavior. For courtship experiments, males were also individually housed for 6 days. All assays were performed at 25°C and 65% relative humidity.

Aggression in Drosophila is strongly gated by circadian time. Aggression assays must be performed during ZT0‐ZT2.5 (the first 2.5 hr of the light phase), which corresponds to the morning activity peak. Courtship assays should be performed during ZT0‐ZT3 or ZT9‐ZT12. Performing assays outside these windows will reduce behavioral output and increase inter‐dyad variability. Record the clock time at which each assay was started and verify that it falls within the appropriate ZT window before including the resulting data in analysis.

The moisture content of the apple‐juice agar food plate at the time of assay directly affects fly locomotion and behavior. Excess surface moisture causes increased grooming, reduced locomotion, and suppressed aggression. Food plates should be dried at 25°C and 55%‐60% relative humidity for 8‐12 hr before use. At high ambient humidity (>60% relative humidity), drying may require up to 16 hr. The surface should appear matte and non‐reflective. A shiny surface indicates excess moisture; discard the plate.

Incomplete Sigmacote coating causes flies to climb arena walls and ceiling, which disrupts inter‐fly interactions and produces artifactually low behavioral scores. Before each experiment, visually inspect coated arenas under bright light to confirm uniform coating. Verify effectiveness by placing a single fly in a coated well for 1‐2 min before loading experimental flies. A correctly coated arena will keep the fly on the food surface. Re‐coat arenas where wall‐climbing is observed. Sigmacote coating must be performed in a fume hood. DANCE applies Sigmacote to both the walls and the ceiling in place of the Fluon wall coating used in conventional multiwell chambers (Dierick, ; Dankert et al., ), because Fluon dries to an opaque film that would obscure the ceiling through which recording is made.

The accuracy of all downstream behavioral quantification depends on correct FlyTracker calibration. The ruler length must match the actual arena diameter used (13 mm for the standard aggression arena; 11 mm for the standard courtship arena). Incorrect ruler length will cause all distance‐ and velocity‐based features to be systematically miscalculated, producing incorrect JAABA classification even when tracking appears visually accurate. After calibration, inspect the background model. The Bg Mean image should show a clean, uniformly lit background with no fly‐shaped artifacts. If fly shapes are visible in the background model, recalibrate using a video segment where both flies are moving throughout.

JAABA outputs a per‐frame probability score for each behavior. Do not modify classifier score thresholds unless generating a custom classifier (Alternate Protocol ). For the lunge classifier, output is reported as total lunge count per 20‐min session, not as a behavioral index. These calculations are performed automatically by the DANCE analysis scripts. For courtship classifiers, the behavioral index is calculated as the proportion of total recording frames classified as the behavior, using the courtship_bout_num_extractor.py script (see Basic Protocol , steps 12b and 13b).

Silencing efficiency depends on reproducing the LED drive conditions and geometry specified in Alternate Protocol : a 4.9‐V supply delivering ∼88 mA per strip of five high‐power green LEDs (520‐540 nm, peak emission 530 nm; Lumileds L128‐GRN1003500000), with each of the two strips positioned diagonally ∼8 cm from the behavioral chamber. Verify voltage and per‐strip current before each experiment using a multimeter connected in series with the strip. Changes to drive current, LED count, or working distance alter the delivered illumination and may produce inconsistent silencing.

The lunge classifier was trained and validated on wild‐type Canton‐S, wild‐type Berlin, and a GAL4 driver line outcrossed into the Berlin background. The five courtship classifiers were trained predominantly on wild‐type Canton‐S flies. JAABA per‐frame features combine tracked body and wing geometry with kinematic measures such as velocity, angular position, and distance to the other fly or the arena wall, so classifier performance is expected to hold across genotypes with comparable movement dynamics and body proportions to these training backgrounds, and to degrade for genotypes with pronounced differences in either, for example other Drosophila species, mutants with substantial wing or leg defects, or flies subjected to manipulations that markedly alter locomotor activity. Users working with such a genotype, or with different recording conditions or arena geometry, should validate the distributed classifiers on their own background using Alternate Protocol  before generating experimental data. Where the resulting F
1 score falls below 0.70, the acceptance threshold already specified for newly trained classifiers, retrain on the new background using Alternate Protocol .

The unit of replication in all DANCE experiments is the dyad (pair of flies), not the individual fly. Report n as the number of dyads per condition. Behavioral indices and lunge counts are typically non‐normally distributed and should be compared using non‐parametric tests (Kruskal‐Wallis ANOVA with Dunn's post‐hoc test for multiple comparisons, or Mann‐Whitney U test for pairwise comparisons). Statistical analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 8 in the eLife validation study.

Common problems encountered during this protocol, their likely causes, and recommended solutions are listed in Table .

Troubleshooting Guide for the DANCE Protocol

Users should expect to observe higher lunge counts in SH males compared to GH males. This is demonstrated for wild‐type Canton‐S males in Yadav et al. (; Fig. 7N and O). If lunge counts fall systematically below the expected range in comparably isolated wild‐type males, check isolation duration, assay timing, food plate moisture, and arena coating before concluding that an experimental manipulation reduced aggression. Representative visualization and quantification of lunge events from a single DANCE aggression recording are shown in Figure . Representative aggression and courtship behaviors recorded using DANCE hardware are shown in Figure 7—video 1 of Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig7video1).

Users should expect to observe higher courtship indices in SH males than in GH males for wing extension, attempted copulation, and circling. Following does not consistently differ between housing conditions. These patterns are demonstrated for wild‐type Canton‐S males paired with decapitated virgin females in Yadav et al. (; Figs. 7D, F, H, and J). Decapitated virgin females were also used in classifier training and validation to enrich rare behaviors such as attempted copulation and circling (Figs. 3‐5 of Yadav et al., ). Results obtained with decapitated virgin females and with mated females should not be pooled. If courtship indices fall systematically below the expected range in comparably housed wild‐type males, check isolation duration, assay timing, female preparation, and arena coating before concluding that an experimental manipulation reduced courtship. Representative visualization and quantification of courtship behaviors from a single DANCE courtship recording are shown in Figure . The 15‐min recording window captures the occurrence and latency of copulation but not its duration to completion; studies requiring copulation duration should extend the recording until copulation has ended. Representative courtship behaviors recorded using DANCE hardware are shown in Figure 7—video 1 of Yadav et al. (; https://elifesciences.org/articles/105465/figures#fig7video1).

Exclude a video from analysis if any of the following conditions are present: (a) one or both flies are not visible for >10% of the recording duration; (b) more than five uncorrectable identity swaps are present in the FlyTracker tracking output; (c) one fly died or became immobile during recording; or (d) the arena seal failed and one fly escaped. Record all exclusions in the experimental log with reason. Do not exclude videos based on low behavioral output alone.

The following schedule describes the recommended timeline for a standard 8‐dyad aggression experiment from arena preparation through final data output.

Day 1: Collect males within 24 hr of eclosion and house individually (Support Protocol ).

Day 6: Prepare and coat arenas with Sigmacote (Support Protocol , Part B). Allow to dry overnight at room temperature. This step cannot be compressed. The coating requires a minimum of 8 hr to cure, and coated arenas cannot be used the same day they are prepared. Prepare apple‐juice agar food plates (Support Protocol , Part A) and allow to dry at 25°C and 55%‐60% relative humidity for 8‐12 hr. Prepare the backlight tablet by opening the white‐screen light application. Verify smartphone recording settings (Support Protocol ).

Day 7, morning (ZT0‐ZT2.5): Assemble DANCE hardware (Basic Protocol , ∼5 min for 8 wells). Load flies by mouth aspirator (∼3 min for 8 wells; see Basic Protocol ). Allow 5 min of acclimatization per arena. Record 20‐min aggression videos. Total morning experimental time: ∼90 min.

Day 7, late morning: Transfer videos from smartphone to computer. Organize into a date folder. Run Auto_Cropper.py (∼5 min). Run FlyTracker tracking on all eight segmented videos (∼15 min). Inspect and correct identity swaps in FlyTracker Visualizer (∼20 min). Run JAABA lunge classification (∼10 min). Run Lunge_Analyzer_indiC.py (<1 min). Total computational time: ∼50 min.

Total elapsed time from start of hardware assembly to analyzed .csv output: ∼3 hr for a standard 8‐dyad aggression experiment. For courtship experiments, substitute the 15‐min recording window and add an additional ∼20 min for JAABA classification with all five courtship classifiers.

neuroscience.title: Clinical management of CADASIL in Europe: bridging evidence gaps and harmonizing care – a consensus review
neuroscience.abstract: •Care for CADASIL patients remains fragmented and poorly harmonized across Europe.•Cognitive and psychiatric symptoms in CADASIL lack effective treatment options.•Antithrombotic and thrombolytic therapy in CADASIL lack disease-specific evidence.•No standardized European guidelines exist for CADASIL surveillance.•Expanding access, standardizing care, and patient engagement are key priorities.
neuroscience.text:
Cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) is a major contributor to stroke, long-term disability, and cognitive decline worldwide []. Among monogenic forms of cSVD, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL), caused by cysteine-altering variants in the NOTCH3 gene, is the most common. Although the minimum prevalence of clinically recognized CADASIL is estimated at approximately 4 cases per 100,000 individuals [, , , ], population-based studies indicate that pathogenic NOTCH3 variants occur in approximately 1:300 individuals worldwide [], suggesting a broader disease spectrum and considerable underdiagnosis in routine clinical practice [, , ]. Clinically, classical CADASIL is characterized by recurrent subcortical ischemic events, progressive cognitive decline, and ultimately vascular dementia. Migraine with aura and neuropsychiatric symptoms, particularly mood disorders, are also frequent. Neuroimaging abnormalities, notably white matter hyperintensities, often precede the clinical symptoms by several years to decades [].

Despite advances in genetic and radiological characterization, clinical management of CADASIL remains poorly harmonized across Europe for several reasons. One major challange is the highly variable and difficult to predict disease trajectory: although the position of the pathogenic NOTCH3 variant within the 34 epidermal growth factor–like repeat (EGFr) domains has emerged as an important prognostic factor, individual outcome prediction remains imprecise [] as other modifiers also play a role such as conventional cardiovascular risk factor burden and also still unknown modifiers [,].

Currently there are no disease modifying treatments for CADASIL and pharmacological treatment strategies are largely extrapolated from sporadic cSVD rather than grounded in disease-specific evidence [,], resulting in scientific statements [] and consensus recommendations [] rather than formal guidelines for CADASIL based on clinical trial-based evidence.

Beyond these knowledge gaps, important disparities persist between European countries in disease awareness, access to specialized and multidisciplinary care, and availability of research infrastructure. Together, these factors sustain a landscape of fragmented, expert-dependent clinical practice. The European Academy of Neurology (EAN) has highlighted the need for a strategic, patient-centered research agenda to address these challenges in rare neurological diseases, including CADASIL [,].

This review provides an overview of current clinical management practices for patients with CADASIL across Europe, identifies key gaps in evidence and care delivery and outlines priorities for developing more harmonized, patient-centered, and evidence-based approaches.

Understanding the geographic distribution of pathogenic NOTCH3 variants is clinically relevant for European physicians. Since variant position within the 34 EGFr-domains is the strongest determinant of disease severity [,], the local prevalence of high-, moderate-, and low-risk variants directly shapes the expected disease burden across different European centres []. Depending on the predominance of specific NOTCH3 variants within and between countries, disease severity may vary substantially according to these genetic-geographical differences. The most commonly reported variants in European CADASIL populations include the high-risk variants p.Arg90Cys, p.Arg141Cys, p.Arg169Cys, p.Arg182Cys, p.Arg207Cys and p.Arg1006Cys, though their relative frequencies differ considerably by region []. Northern European populations, including the UK [,], France [,], and the Netherlands [,], have many NOTCH3 variants in common, with a predominance of high-risk variants. The most striking European example of a NOTCH3 variant with a founder effect has been reported in Finland, where a single variant accounts for nearly 70% of cases []. Region-specific clustering has similarly been hypothesised in central and northeastern Italy [,]. By contrast, Portugal, the Netherlands, and Slovakia display exceptional mutational heterogeneity, with numerous distinct variants, suggesting multiple independent mutational events [,].

The organization of care for CADASIL patients in Europe is characterized by heterogeneity in standards of care across countries. In many European countries, CADASIL patients are managed through a combination of local neurology services and academic expert centers, often embedded in services with expertise in cerebral SVD, rare neurological disorders, or rare genetic disorders. Referral pathways typically involve initial evaluation by general neurologists or stroke physicians, followed by referral to specialized centers for genetic confirmation, advanced neuroimaging, and multidisciplinary management [].

A European Stroke Organization (ESO) scientific seminar in 2025 highlighted the need for dedicated small vessel disease clinics that integrate vascular risk factor management, cognitive assessment, neuropsychiatric care, and patient education, a model particularly applicable to CADASIL and other monogenic SVDs []. Several NEUROVASC partner centres already operate dedicated CADASIL or monogenic SVD clinics embedding these components, representing existing hubs of expertise that could serve as models for broader implementation across Europe [].

The European Reference Network facilitates a European infrastructure for coordinating CADASIL care across Europe. Since 2022, CADASIL has been included within the NEUROVASC working group, currently comprising full members from Italy, the Netherlands, France, and Germany, with developing partners in Spain, Norway, and Czech Republic. The network facilitates virtual case discussions through the Clinical Patient Management System (CPMS), a secure web-based platform enabling clinicians to share diagnostically challenging cases, share neuroimaging, and obtain expert opinions from multiple centers across Europe [].

To further harmonize the diagnostic process, VASCERN experts have developed and published a CADASIL patient pathway () [], providing a standardized referral and diagnostic framework applicable across different European healthcare systems.

The diagnostic work-up of CADASIL is ideally conducted within a multidisciplinary centre specialised in rare cerebrovascular diseases. CADASIL should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with a relatively high load of white matter hyperintensities (WMH) on T2-weighted MR images, with or without other imaging markers of SVD. Suggestive family history and a characteristic clinical presentation should also arise the suspicion of CADASIL. However, given the broad phenotypic spectrum of NOTCH3-SVD, disease expression can be highly variable even within families, and diagnostic delays remain common, particularly in patients with atypical presentations or late-onset disease.

Brain MRI is a prerequisite for determining the NOTCH3-SVD stage, for which Fazekas score and lacune count are needed. This staging system was developed and validated in an international cohort of patients with CADASIL, and ranges from premanifest with normal brain MRI (stage 0) to severe disability with high MRI lesion burden (stage 4A) []. ()

MR-imaging should preferably include T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and FLAIR sequences, which allow for the detection of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), lacunes, and brain atrophy, while susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or T2-weighted gradient-recalled echo sequences are used to assess the presence of cerebral microbleeds (CMB) []. A comprehensive MRI evaluation should ideally also include diffusion-weighted imaging for identifying recent infarcts.

Beyond symmetrical high WMH lesion burden, the topographical distribution of lesions can be informative as patients with CADASIL relatively frequently show involvement of the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules, although in many patients WMH in these locations are absent. CADASIL can therefore be difficult to distinguish from sporadic small vessel disease especially in older patients () [].

To address the need for cross-cohort comparisons in CADASIL, the CADA-MRIT (CADASIL MRI Inventory Tool) was recently developed and validated across French, German, and Taiwanese cohorts []. Such standardized tools may facilitate harmonized imaging recommendations across centers and enable more robust longitudinal assessment and multicenter research collaboration.

Genetic confirmation through identification of a pathogenic NOTCH3 variant remains the gold standard for the diagnosis of CADASIL. Across Europe, genetic testing strategies differ substantially, reflecting variations in laboratory infrastructure, and reimbursement policies []. In some countries, targeted sequencing of NOTCH3 exons encoding EGFr domains is still routinely performed, whereas other centers increasingly rely on gene panels for monogenic small vessel diseases or for broader neurological disorders.

Regardless of the sequencing approach, complete coverage of all exons encoding the 34 EGFr domains is recommended to avoid missing pathogenic variants. Whole-exome sequencing may be used in selected cases with atypical phenotypes or negative targeted testing []. The above testing strategy applies to symptomatic individuals presenting with a clinical and neuroimaging picture suggestive of CADASIL. For at-risk family members of a known index case, directed sequencing targeting the familial variant is sufficient for predictive DNA testing.

Regardless of the method used, interpretation of genetic results poses additional challenges, particularly in the case of variants of uncertain significance such as most non-cysteinealtering variants [, , , ]. Skin biopsy showing vessel wall granular osmiophilic material (GOM) on electron microscopy and positive NOTCH3 immunostaining provides supportive diagnostic evidence.

Long-term follow-up of patients with CADASIL aims to monitor disease progression, manage complications, and provide anticipatory guidance. No standard European surveillance guidelines for CADASIL exist, and most follow-up protocols are based on expert opinion rather than prospective data.

The management of presymptomatic NOTCH3-positive individuals presents one of the most debated aspects of CADASIL care. In current practice, surveillance strategies vary markedly, reflecting the absence of disease-modifying therapies and limited evidence for the benefits of early monitoring and primary stroke prevention. Some centers offer regular neurological evaluations and MRI surveillance, whereas others adopt a more conservative approach, focusing on vascular risk factor control and patient education.

Psychological support and counseling are particularly important in this population, given the emotional burden associated with a presymptomatic genetic diagnosis and uncertainty regarding disease onset and progression. Integrating psychologists into multidisciplinary teams at CADASIL reference centers could help standardize access to psychological care.

Symptomatic patients are generally followed within specialized neurology or cerebrovascular clinics, often at referral centers with expertise in CADASIL. Follow-up typically focuses on secondary stroke prevention, management of cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms, migraine control, and functional status assessment, as well as psychological support, if available. The frequency of clinical evaluations depends on NOTCH3-SVD stage, the severity and type of symptoms and the needs of patients and their caregivers, ranging from low-frequency follow-up in stable patients to more frequent evaluations in those with rapid progression or significant disability.

There are no randomized controlled trials or disease-specific guidelines for antithrombotic therapy in CADASIL. Current practice is largely extrapolated from sporadic small vessel disease, [,] but it varies considerably across centres. Antiplatelet agents are commonly prescribed after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack in CADASIL, although this is not evidence-based [,]. In Japan, for instance, nearly 74% of CADASIL patients receive antiplatelet therapy []. Dual antiplatelet therapy is usually avoided due to the hypothesized increased risk of intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly in patients with cerebral microbleeds [,].

Anticoagulation is not routinely recommended in CADASIL and is typically restricted to patients with clear alternative indications, such as atrial fibrillation, after careful individual risk–benefit assessment [,]. In selected patients with high CHA2DS2-VASc scores and high microbleed count, left atrial appendage closure may be considered as an alternative to long-term anticoagulation [].

Intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator represents standard care for eligible patients with acute ischemic stroke in the general population []. However, its application in CADASIL remains controversial due to the disease’s unique pathophysiology and theoretical hemorrhagic risks []. Published experience with thrombolysis in CADASIL remains extremely limited, consisting primarily of case reports and small case series that preclude robust conclusions about safety or efficacy [, , ]. Significant questions about thrombolytic efficacy in CADASIL-related strokes have been raised, as CADASIL-related strokes are almost exclusively a consequence of intrinsic small vessel arteriopathy rather than large vessel occlusion or cardioembolism []. Furthermore, in the general stroke population, the presence of >10 cerebral microbleeds increases post-thrombolysys intracerebral hemorrhage risk approximately 12-fold compared to patients with ≤10 microbleeds, [] while the presence of WMH independentely doubles the risk of post-thrombolysis hemorrhage []. This raises particular concern in the CADASIL population in which both imaging findings are prevalent. Consequently, this supports a cautious and individualized approach to decision-making regarding thrombolysis in CADASIL. However, in cases of large-vessel occlusion related to a coexisting cardioembolic or atherothrombotic disease, decisions regarding reperfusion therapy should be made on an individual basis, taking into account the burden of underlying small vessel disease markers, especially cerebral microbleeds, as well as any prior intracerebral hemorrhage. In this setting, mechanical thrombectomy, with or without intravenous thrombolysis, may reasonably be considered on an individual basis in a CADASIL patient with large vessel stroke, given its established efficacy in large vessel occlusion stroke in the general population.

The management of cerebrovascular risk factors represents a cornerstone of clinical care in CADASIL, as it has been shown that a high cardiovascular risk factor burden is associated with more severe disease [,,].

Hypertension and smoking have been found to be strongly associated with worse outcomes in CADASIL, including incident stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, dementia, and cerebral microhemorrhages [,,, , ]. Strict blood pressure monitoring is therefore advised to all patients with CADASIL, and the importance of smoking cessation should be strongly emphasized[]. In contrast, the role of lipid management in CADASIL remains uncertain. No clear association between hyperlipidemia and clinical outcomes has been established, and a small study of short-term atorvastatin treatment showed no significant improvement in hemodynamic parameters in CADASIL patients []. To date, there is no compelling evidence for or against the prescription of statins for secondary prevention following a stroke. However, we do not yet know whether this treatment offers any real benefit to patients, nor what LDL cholesterol targets should be recommended [].

When considering preventive therapies, it remains unclear whether patients with a confirmed diagnosis of CADASIL who have never had a stroke or transient ischemic attack should routinely receive antiplatelet therapy, statins, and/or antihypertensive drugs.

Routine prescription of antiplatelet for primary prevention is not recommended, given the lack of proven efficacy and the potential bleeding risk associated with small vessel disease [,]. Similarly, there is no evidence supporting the routine use of statins in this setting. Statins and antihypertensive drugs should instead be prescribed according to standard indications, such as dyslipidemia or hypertension, in line with general cardiovascular prevention guidelines [,]. Counseling on smoking cessation is beneficial to reduce the risk of incident stroke [].

However, individual clinical and neuroimaging circumstances may justify a different management strategy. In selected patients with a higher NOTCH3-SVD stage [], preventive treatment may be considered on a case-by-case basis, after weighing the potential benefit against the bleeding risk, including microbleed burden and prior intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), and after shared decision-making with the patient.

Migraine with aura is a common and often early manifestation of CADASIL, occurring in up to 50% of patients, a prevalence five times higher than in the general population [,,]. Based on limited evidence, triptans and ergot derivatives are considered to be safe and effective []. Nonetheless, conventional analgesics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are preferred over vasoconstrictors by some, reflecting ongoing debate about theoretical risks []. NEUROVASC recommendations are to use triptans as a second or third-choice option, despite the absence of contraindications []. In this context, lasmiditan, a selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist, has been proposed as a theoretically safer alternative for acute migraine treatment in patients with vascular comorbidities. However, no data exist in CADASIL patients, and there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend it over other treatments.

Prophylactic options for CADASIL remain poorly supported by evidence. A meta-analysis found most common choices equivocal in efficacy, with propranolol potentially deleterious; acetazolamide and sodium valproate were considered physiologically plausible []. Acetazolamide showed some benefit in a small case series and demonstrated improved cerebral hemodynamics after 24 weeks []. Amitriptyline is used empirically but should be avoided with caution in cognitively impaired patients given its anticholinergic profile. Other suggested options include sodium valproate, lamotrigine, topiramate, verapamil, and flunarizine [].

The advent of novel migraine therapies has introduced specific concerns regarding cerebrovascular safety in CADASIL. No robust data exist on the benefit of CGRP (Calcitonin gene-related peptide) modulators in CADASIL and their use in CADASIL remains controversial due to theoretical safety concerns. CGRP serves as a vasodilatory safeguard during cerebral and cardiac ischemia, and blocking this system could potentially worsen ischemic events in patients with underlying small vessel disease []. A 2020 expert opinion cautioned against treating CADASIL patients with CGRP-blocking drugs until relevant safety data and long-term follow-up results become available []. However, recent case reports challenge this cautious stance, showing significant reduction in attack frequency and pain intensity, with improvement in quality of life and no adverse effects in two cases []. Non-pharmacological and adjunctive options, including onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine, peripheral nerve blocks, acupuncture, and wearable neuromodulation devices, have not been specifically evaluated in CADASIL-related migraine; however, given their generally favorable safety profile, they may represent reasonable therapeutic options to consider on an individual basis, extrapolating from their use in the general migraine population [].

Cognitive impairment is typically characterized by a progressive decline in executive functions, including attention, processing speed, planning, and mental flexibility, reflecting the predominant involvement of subcortical-frontal networks []. Memory complaints are also common, although they are often secondary to deficits in attention and retrieval []. Alongside cognitive decline, a wide range of psychiatric symptoms may emerge, most commonly including depression [,,,], along with anxiety symptoms and apathy, which is often associated with functional decline, and increased caregiver burden [,,]. Management of depression generally follows conventional pharmacotherapy, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors []. However, treatment response sometimes remains incomplete, and symptoms refractory [,,]. Beyond mood disturbances, pharmacologic interventions for cognitive symptoms remain limited. A randomized controlled trial of donepezil in CADASIL showed at 90 days follow up no benefit on global cognition but did demonstrate improvement in some executive function subscores [].

Beyond the classical triad of migraine with aura, ischemic stroke, and progressive cognitive decline, CADASIL encompasses a spectrum of less common manifestations that carry specific diagnostic and management implications despite the absence of disease-specific evidence.

Acute encephalopathy. Acute confusional episodes with reduced arousal, should initially be approached as a medical and neurological emergency, with exclusion of infection/meningoencephalitis, metabolic or toxic causes, acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, and nonconvulsive status epilepticus. In a large British national cohort of 340 symptomatic CADASIL patients, encephalopathy occurred in 10.3% and complete recovery within three months was observed in 96% of episodes, supporting a typically self-limited natural history []. No CADASIL-specific acute therapy has been established, and supportive management is generally appropriate.

Seizures and epilepsy. Epilepsy is uncommon in CADASIL. In a cohort of 446 patients, seizures were reported in 8.6% []. Management follows standard epilepsy practice, with antiseizure medication selected according to seizure type and attention to interactions and comorbid mood or cognitive symptoms.

Intracerebral hemorrhage and hemorrhage-risk states. Acute ICH prevalence in CADASIL varies considerably between European and Asian cohorts [,]. In predominantly European series, symptomatic ICH has generally been reported in the range of 0.5–2%, whereas East Asian cohortsreport substantially higher rates [,]. The reasons for this difference remain unclear. Genetic background, environmental factors, or a combination of both may contribute. ICH should be managed according to standard ICH protocols, as CADASIL-specific evidence is limited. With respect to secondary prevention, anticoagulant exposure is associated with a significantly higher risk of ICH, whereas this does not seem to be the case for antiplatelet exposure [].

Movement-disorder phenotypes. Vascular parkinsonism and, less commonly, atypical parkinsonian or chorea/dystonia phenotypes have been described, generally attributed to cumulative subcortical small vessel disease burden; response to levodopa is often limited in reported cases, so management typically emphasizes rehabilitation, gait and balance therapy, with cautious use of medication where appropriate [, , ].

In the absence of disease-modifying therapies, the management of CADASIL relies heavily on informed and proactive patient involvement. Recognizing this need, the VASCERN, through its NEUROVASC working group, has tried to translate expert consensus into practical, patient-oriented recommendations, aimed at supporting both clinicians and patients in everyday disease management. Practical “Do’s and Don’ts” for CADASIL have been published, providing accessible guidance on lifestyle modifications, and symptom management [].

The clinical management of CADASIL remains largely supportive and is constrained by the absence of disease-specific therapies and limited high-quality evidence.

Future priorities should include the development of multicenter registries and harmonized care pathways to enable longitudinal follow-up, facilitate research, and support the identification of biomarkers for disease progression and treatment response. International collaboration is critical for conducting adequately powered clinical trials and advancing targeted research into disease mechanisms and potential therapies.

Looking ahead, closing these gaps will require not only advances in disease-modifying therapies and harmonized care pathways, but also a greater integration of the patient perspective. Patient-reported outcomes are increasingly recognized as essential endpoints in rare disease research, and their incorporation into future CADASIL clinical trials will be critical to capture the full impact of the disease on daily functioning and quality of life [].

In summary, coordinated efforts to expand access, standardize care, and integrate patient engagement are essential for improving CADASIL patient care. International collaborations have resulted in important advances, including a validated MRI tool [], improved genetic risk stratification [], and a disease severity staging system [], enabling uniform data collection across centers worldwide. By fostering coordinated international efforts, we can leverage the statistical power, genetic diversity, and clinical insights needed to advance precision medicine for patients with CADASIL.
