Beyond disrupting proximal signaling, sustained sympathetic activity reinforces CD8⁺ T-cell dysfunction through both cell-intrinsic metabolic reprogramming and indirect remodeling of the inflammatory and stromal compartments within the TME. Prolonged β2-AR signaling suppresses the effector metabolic transition from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis by limiting glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) expression and membrane translocation, thereby promoting bioenergetic exhaustion in the nutrient-deprived TME [, ]. In parallel, elevated NE acts on TME-resident stromal and myeloid cells to elicit interleukin-6 (IL-6) release, which engages Janus kinase–signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (JAK–STAT3) signaling in neighboring T cells and, together with persistent suboptimal TCR stimulation, drives upregulation of co-inhibitory receptors PD-1 and T cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain containing-3 (TIM-3) and impedes central memory T cell formation via T-bet modulation [, , ].

Chronic stress states common in cancer patients may involve increased activity of the locus coeruleus and other brainstem catecholaminergic nuclei, potentially elevating circulating NE and reinforcing a systemic immunosuppressive loop [, ]. The systemic nature of this signal is illustrated by ambient-temperature experiments in mice: animals housed at standard conditions (22 °C, constituting mild cold stress) showed accelerated tumor growth, increased recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and regulatory T cells (Tregs), and reduced CD8⁺ T cell infiltration compared with mice housed at thermoneutrality (30 °C), where sympathetically driven immune suppression was abolished [, ]. These findings are consistent with a contribution from systemic sympathetic output, rather than establishing an exclusively local intratumoral nerve mechanism.

Based on these systemic mechanisms, pharmacological blockade of adrenergic signaling has emerged as a tractable immune-sensitization strategy. In murine melanoma models, the non-selective β-blocker propranolol reverses T cell exhaustion, enhances cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) infiltration, and synergizes with anti-PD-1 ICIs [, ]; the dual-receptor (β1-AR + β2-AR) action of propranolol is consistent with the emerging understanding that both subtypes contribute to CD8⁺ T cell suppression through partially distinct mechanisms [, , ].

These preclinical findings are supported by retrospective clinical evidence. A cohort study demonstrated that concomitant β-blocker use during ICI therapy was associated with significantly improved overall survival in patients with advanced melanoma []. In broader patient populations, including non-small cell lung cancer and other solid tumors, large multicenter retrospective analyses have reported heterogeneous effects, underscoring that the survival benefit of concurrent β-blockade may be highly dependent on the tumor type and the specific immunological context []. These data collectively support the initiation of prospective randomized trials of adrenergic blockade as an ICI sensitizer (Table ).

In contrast to sympathetic adrenergic signaling, vagal/cholinergic pathways modulate CD8⁺ T cell responses primarily through indirect mechanisms involving myeloid intermediaries [, ]. In the classical cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, ACh engages α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α7nAChRs) on macrophages and other myeloid cells [, ]. α7nAChR activation recruits Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) and activates STAT3, thereby suppressing macrophage activation and the release of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and other pro-inflammatory cytokines []. Because persistent inflammatory signaling can contribute to CD8⁺ T cell dysfunction within the TME, this myeloid anti-inflammatory program may indirectly reduce exhaustion pressure on infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells; however, direct tumor-specific evidence for this link remains limited. Against criteria i–iv, this is an indirect neuroimmune regulatory circuit: a CD8⁺ T cell-intrinsic inhibitory cascade and pharmacological ICI sensitization remain unestablished.

In the classical splenic neuroimmune relay, norepinephrine released from sympathetic splenic nerve terminals activates β2-ARs expressed by choline acetyltransferase-positive (ChAT⁺) memory CD4⁺ T cells, thereby promoting ACh release [, ]. This architecture provides a model of multicellular cholinergic immunoregulation rather than direct vagal receptor signaling in CD8⁺ T cells. However, whether this ChAT⁺ T cell relay operates within the TME and influences antitumor CD8⁺ T cell responses remain to be established. Direct norepinephrine–β2-AR signaling in splenic myeloid cells has also been proposed as an alternative pathway in some experimental settings []. These upstream neuroimmune relays warrant further investigation as potential targets in cancer immunotherapy (Fig. ).

The vagus nerve exhibits a complex, context-dependent role in tumor immunity [, ]. Vagal activity does not itself engage a unique immune receptor; rather, it alters local cholinergic output, and the biological effect is determined by the ACh receptor subtype and responding cell. In some settings, the myeloid α7nAChR pathway described above may constrain chronic inflammation and thereby indirectly reduce exhaustion pressure on CD8⁺ T cells [, ]. In gastric cancer, however, ACh released by vagal/enteric nerves and gastric tuft cells activates the M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor on epithelial and stem-like cells. M3 receptor signaling promotes Wnt-dependent stem-cell expansion and establishes an ACh–nerve growth factor (NGF)–tropomyosin receptor kinase (Trk)–Yes-associated protein (YAP) feed-forward circuit that increases tumor innervation and tumorigenesis [, ]. These tumor-cell-intrinsic muscarinic effects are mechanistically distinct from α7nAChR-mediated myeloid immunoregulation. Thus, the consequences of cholinergic signaling depend on receptor subtype, cellular compartment, and tumor context and should not be interpreted as a uniform direct effect on CD8⁺ T cells.

Non-invasive transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is being explored as a bioelectronic intervention in oncology. Preclinical studies show that VNS promotes the activation of tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells, as evidenced by upregulation of IFN-γ and CD137 []. These downstream changes do not establish direct vagal receptor-mediated signaling in CD8⁺ T cells. However, this local immune activation proved insufficient to suppress tumor growth in certain models, highlighting the complexity of translating neuro-immune modulation into durable anti-tumor efficacy []. VNS may also attenuate the pro-tumorigenic senescence-associated secretory phenotype [], although further investigation is required to determine whether it can potentiate immune checkpoint blockade (Table ).

Sensory nerve fibers, particularly transient receptor potential vanilloid 1-positive (TRPV1⁺) nociceptors, innervate peripheral tissues including tumors and tumor-draining lymph nodes [, ]. Tumor-derived neurotrophic factors and pro-inflammatory cytokines activate sensory afferent terminals, triggering local release of CGRP and SP, which act predominantly through local paracrine signaling; the tumor studies discussed below chiefly establish effects on intratumoral T cells [, ]. (Fig. )

CGRP and SP exert distinct, context-dependent effects through both direct and indirect mechanisms. At the CD8⁺ T cell-intrinsic level, CGRP engages the CLR/RAMP1 complex on CD8⁺ T cells to activate Gαs-cAMP-PKA signaling (Table ), which suppresses T-bet, downregulates CD25, and reduces IFN-γ and granzyme B synthesis, promoting an exhausted phenotype in tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells []. The CGRP–CLR/RAMP1 pathway supports criteria i–iii; transfer of RAMP1-deficient CD8⁺ T cells provides direct functional evidence, whereas pharmacological ICI sensitization (iv) remains unestablished in this study []. SP, in contrast, signals through the neurokinin-1 receptor (NK1R) to augment antigen-elicited IFN-γ production and to induce dendritic cell (DC)-derived interleukin-12 (IL-12), indirectly promoting type 1 cytotoxic responses [, ](Table ); however, SP also stimulates tumor cell proliferation and angiogenesis via NK1R on malignant cells, complicating its therapeutic exploitation []. SP–NK1R signaling, which can support antigen-elicited and DC-mediated responses, does not meet the same inhibitory-checkpoint definition.

In heavily innervated malignancies such as melanoma and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), the abundance of CGRP⁺ sensory fibers correlates with local immunosuppression [, ]. Genetic deletion of TRPV1⁺ sensory neurons or pharmacological blockade of the CGRP receptor with RAMP1 antagonists abrogates sensory-derived suppressive signals, reverses CD8⁺ T cell exhaustion, and prolongs survival in preclinical models []. However, sensory-neuron deletion and receptor-specific blockade are mechanistically distinct: denervation alters multiple neural, vascular, and tissue compartments and therefore cannot by itself establish a CD8⁺ T cell-intrinsic mechanism. Transfer experiments with RAMP1-deficient CD8⁺ T cells support a direct component, while systemic receptor blockade can also affect other compartments []. Because RAMP1 antagonists are already approved for migraine by United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), drug repurposing is feasible and provides a near-term avenue for evaluating sensory blockade as an ICI sensitizer in tumor types with documented CGRP⁺ innervation (Table ).

While the nervous system executes rapid and often spatially restricted control, the endocrine system imposes sustained, long-range regulation of CD8⁺ T cell fate across the circulation, lymphoid organs, and tumor microenvironment. Hormones released through the HPA axis, metabolic tissues, and gonadal axes reach CD8⁺ T cells directly and also remodel stromal and myeloid compartments that determine T cell priming, trafficking, bioenergetic fitness, and exhaustion.

Endocrine regulation is organized here around three principles that parallel the neural framework. First, context-dependent receptor signaling allows the same hormone to support homeostasis under physiological conditions yet promote dysfunction during chronic stress, obesity, or malignancy. Second, concentration, duration, and tissue-specific hormone metabolism determine whether endocrine inputs are stimulatory or suppressive. Third, sex, metabolic state, and circadian phase reshape both ligand availability and receptor responsiveness, creating clinically relevant heterogeneity in immunotherapy outcomes. The following sections examine these principles across glucocorticoid, metabolic-hormone, and sex-steroid pathways.

Glucocorticoids (GCs), primarily cortisol in humans, are the terminal systemic effectors of the HPA axis. Physiological concentrations maintain T cell homeostasis, but chronic stress or malignancy drives supraphysiological GC accumulation that imposes systemic immunosuppression [, ]. GCs signal through the intracellular GR; upon ligand binding, GR translocates to the nucleus and represses AP-1 and NF-κB transactivation, abrogating transcription of effector cytokines and cytolytic molecules, inhibiting the interleukin-2/interleukin-2 receptor α (IL-2/IL-2Rα) autocrine loop, and arresting clonal expansion (Table ) []. Concurrent GLUT1 downregulation and pro-apoptotic B-cell lymphoma 2-interacting mediator of cell death (BIM) upregulation impose metabolic and survival constraints on activated CD8⁺ T cells []. In the TME, endogenous GC–GR signaling also promotes a broad dysfunction-associated program and supports T cell factor 1 (TCF1) expression in precursor-like CD8⁺ T cells []. Such cells should not be equated with the terminally exhausted compartment: TCF1⁺PD-1⁺ cells with low or absent TIM-3 expression represent a progenitor or early exhausted state that retains self-renewal and proliferative capacity and remains responsive to ICI, whereas loss of TCF1 together with increased TIM-3 expression accompanies progression toward terminal exhaustion [, ]. GR has support for inhibitory signaling and tumor exploitation (ii–iii), while local ligand amplification and enzyme blockade provide context-specific evidence for i and iv (section “”). These intratumoral differentiation and effector effects are distinct from DC-mediated immune initiation and physiological blood–tissue trafficking described in section “”; receptor or ligand amplification (i) and reversal with ICI benefit (iv) must be assessed in the specific models tested.

The systemic immunosuppressive reach of the HPA axis extends beyond direct cytokine repression in tumor-infiltrating T cells. It is well documented in human physiology that cortisol controls circadian redistribution of T cell subsets between blood, bone marrow, and secondary lymphoid organs. In healthy adults, infusion of hydrocortisone at concentrations mimicking the morning cortisol surge reduces circulating naive CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell counts by approximately 40%, an effect mediated by cortisol-induced upregulation of CXCR4 and consequent homing to the bone marrow []. Catecholamines, acting on β-adrenoceptors, produce a counter-rhythmic daytime mobilization of terminally differentiated effector CD8⁺ T cells from the marginal pool []. These two systemic hormones therefore impose opposing daily rhythms on the trafficking and tissue distribution of the very T cell subsets that mediate anti-tumor immunity, providing physiological plausibility for temporal variation in immune-cell distribution, but not demonstrating that these rhythms improve tumor infiltration, cytotoxic function or ICI efficacy at a particular infusion time (section “”).

Stress-induced glucocorticoids can also impair immune initiation indirectly: GC-inducible TSC22 domain family member 3 (TSC22D3) in dendritic cells suppresses type I interferon responses and subsequent T cell activation, and DC-specific Tsc22d3 deletion restores therapy-induced tumor control in stressed mice []. The clinical correlates require separate interpretation: baseline corticosteroid use is associated with poorer PD-1/ PD-L1 blockade outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but this does not establish equivalent effects of all steroid indications or schedules [].

Chronic HPA dysregulation in cancer patients is rarely studied as a stand-alone immunological variable, despite its high prevalence. Cancer-related fatigue, sleep disruption, and comorbid depression or anxiety are each associated with flattened diurnal cortisol slopes and elevated evening cortisol, and patients exhibiting these phenotypes show measurably worse ICI response rates [, ]. These observations reframe baseline cortisol rhythm from a confounder to a modifiable systemic variable that may identify patients most likely to benefit from neuro-endocrine targeting, including the selective GR modulator relacorilant (NCT04373265) and the GR antagonist mifepristone in HER2-negative breast cancer (NCT03225547) (Fig. ; Table ) [].

Insulin operates as the principal anabolic cue for activated CD8⁺ T cells, engaging the insulin receptor (IR) to drive an insulin receptor substrate (IRS)–phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)–protein kinase B (Akt)–mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) cascade that upregulates GLUT1, sustains aerobic glycolysis, and supports clonal expansion (Table ) [, ]. The consequences are context-dependent. In the nutrient-depleted pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) TME, nutrient limitation and lipid-associated mitochondrial dysfunction can constrain CD8⁺ T-cell metabolic fitness [, ]. Conversely, systemic hyperinsulinemia secondary to insulin resistance acts on PDAC cells to upregulate PD-L1, providing an alternative endocrine route to immune evasion [].

Adipose tissue exerts systemic immunomodulation via adipokines that report whole-body energy status. Leptin signals through leptin receptor (Ob-R)–JAK–STAT3 and can support CD8⁺ T-cell activation and metabolism, including in experimental settings using engineered intratumoral delivery [, ]; adiponectin has context-dependent metabolic and immunomodulatory effects that are less directly established in tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells (Table ). Obesity disrupts this equilibrium: chronic hyperleptinemia drives sustained STAT3 activation in tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells, producing metabolic dysfunction, attenuated IFN-γ, and PD-1 upregulation [, ]. Paradoxically, the resulting high PD-1 baseline can render obese patients more responsive to PD-1 blockade, accounting for the so-called obesity paradox in cancer immunotherapy [].

A parallel lipid-driven mechanism converges on ferroptotic cell death. In lipid-enriched TMEs, CD36 upregulation on tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells drive unsaturated fatty acid uptake; the resulting lipid peroxide accumulation impairs cytolytic cytokine secretion and triggers ferroptosis (Table ) [, ]. CD36 blockade or ferroptosis inhibition restores effector function and enhances PD-1 blockade efficacy []. These metabolic pathways are not uniformly inhibitory checkpoints: physiological insulin/adipokine support differs from tumor-associated leptin or lipid dysfunction, and metabolic interventions do not automatically satisfy criteria i–iv.

Metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), supporting the metabolic fitness of memory CD8⁺ T cells []. It synergizes with PD-1 blockade by mitigating tumor hypoxia and rescuing tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells from apoptosis (Table ) [, ]. Dietary interventions affect tumor cells and antitumor immunity in a context-dependent manner. In preclinical models, a fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) enhanced chemotherapy through reduced tumor heme oxygenase-1 and CD8⁺ T cell-dependent effects [], and improved responses to anti-PD-L1 plus an OX40 (CD134) agonist []. Short-term starvation enhanced anti-PD-1 activity in lung cancer models through reduced insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and tumor-cell IGF-1 receptor (IGF-1R) signaling, with CD8⁺ T cells required for benefit []; however, cyclic FMD did not improve anti-PD-1/anti-CTLA-4-mediated tumor control in tested melanoma and lung cancer models []. Clinical immune changes do not establish enhanced PD-1 blockade efficacy or isolate dietary contributions during concurrent treatment [–]. In hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, fasting sensitized tumors to endocrine therapy through tumor-cell GR signaling, with the principal mechanistic evidence derived from immunodeficient xenografts []. Because T cell GR signaling can promote CD8⁺ dysfunction [], the net immune effect of fasting-induced glucocorticoids during checkpoint blockade remains unresolved. Separately, sustained dietary restriction supported CD8⁺ effector function through T cell ketone-body oxidation, a mechanism that should not be generalized to cyclic FMD (Fig. ) [].

Clinical data demonstrate significant sex-based disparities in cancer incidence and immunotherapy responsiveness [, ]. Males generally exhibit higher susceptibility and poorer prognoses, whereas females mount a more resilient basal immune response. Sex steroid hormones contribute to this dimorphism, but sex chromosome complement and X-linked gene dosage also shape immunity. For example, the X-inactivation escape lysine demethylase 6 A gene (Kdm6a) contributes to sex-biased CD8⁺ T cell exhaustion in preclinical glioblastoma (GBM) studies []. Acquired Y-chromosome loss in cancer and T cells is a separate chromosome-associated mechanism [], rather than a proxy for constitutional XX/XY differences. Here, we focus on the hormonal component [].

In several extracranial tumor settings, androgens exert suppressive effects on adaptive immunity via the androgen receptor (AR), although the direction and magnitude of these effects are tissue-context dependent. AR signaling regulates CD8⁺ T cell differentiation in a context-dependent manner. Yang et al. [] reported impaired stem cell-like properties and increased exhaustion-associated differentiation, whereas Kwon et al. [] demonstrated direct AR-mediated transactivation of the T cell factor 7 gene (Tcf7) and accumulation of TCF1⁺ progenitor exhausted cells with limited effector activity. Importantly, the latter retained precursor capacity, indicating that TCF1 expression and progenitor differentiation potential should not be equated with effective antitumor function []. Beyond TCF1-associated differentiation, AR-induced ubiquitin-specific peptidase 18 (USP18) expression inhibits transforming growth factor beta-activated kinase 1 (TAK1)–NF-κB signaling and suppresses T cell activity []. More recently, early growth response 4 (EGR4) was identified as a direct downstream transcriptional effector of AR contributing to CD8⁺ T cell dysfunction in HNSCC []. (Fig. ; Table ). Beyond direct T cell-intrinsic effects, AR signaling also shapes the tumor immune microenvironment: AR signaling restricts CD8⁺ T cell infiltration by repressing the IFN-γ–driven CXCL9/CXCL10/CXCL11 program in prostate cancer cells, and promotes alternatively activated M2-like macrophage polarization, creating a cold TME [–].

Estrogen receptor signaling exerts complex, context-dependent immunomodulatory effects. In preclinical models, estrogen receptor β (ERβ) acts directly in CD8⁺ T cells: TCR activation induces ERβ phosphorylation, which amplifies proximal TCR signaling through a non-genomic mechanism and supports antitumor effector function []. In tumor cells, estrogen receptor α (ERα) signaling regulates PD-L1 in a context-dependent, bidirectional manner, with reports of both upregulation and downregulation across tumor settings and regulatory layers [, , ]. (Fig. ; Table ). In murine melanoma, ERα signaling in macrophages promotes an immunosuppressive polarization state that indirectly contributes to CD8⁺ T cell dysfunction and exhaustion [].

In hormone receptor-positive breast cancer models, progesterone receptor (PR) signaling in tumor cells downregulates antigen processing and presentation machinery and surface major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I), thereby reducing susceptibility to CD8⁺ T cell-mediated killing []. Preclinical studies suggest that pharmacological PR antagonism may restore MHC-I expression and improve immunosurveillance, though clinical validation remains pending []. Within the four-criterion framework, AR is a candidate inhibitory node with preclinical reversal and ICI evidence, whereas ERβ is supportive and the ERα/PR mechanisms described here are largely indirect; shared steroid-receptor identity does not imply equivalent checkpoint status. Specifically, AR-mediated inhibitory signaling (ii) and reversal with ICI benefit (iv) are supported in selected preclinical tumor models; evidence for amplification and tumor exploitation (i and iii) is context-dependent [, , ]. ERβ-mediated support and tumor/myeloid ERα or PR effects are evaluated separately rather than assigned all four criteria.

AR antagonists such as enzalutamide can improve CD8⁺ T cell effector function in selected preclinical models, providing a rationale for combining AR blockade with immune checkpoint inhibition [, , ]. However, three phase III trials testing the combination of AR blockade and ICI in prostate cancer have yielded uniformly negative results. KEYNOTE-641 (enzalutamide plus pembrolizumab vs. enzalutamide plus placebo in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [mCRPC]) [] and KEYNOTE-991 (enzalutamide plus androgen deprivation therapy [ADT] plus pembrolizumab vs. enzalutamide plus ADT plus placebo in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer [mHSPC]) [] both failed to meet their dual primary endpoints of overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), with KEYNOTE-991 notably showing numerically inferior rPFS in the pembrolizumab arm (hazard ratio (HR) 1.20; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.96–1.49). A parallel trial, IMbassador250 (atezolizumab plus enzalutamide vs. enzalutamide in mCRPC), similarly showed no overall survival benefit (stratified HR 1.12; 95% CI, 0.91–1.37 []).

Several factors likely account for these failures, each carrying implications for the broader neuro-endocrine immune checkpoint paradigm. First, prostate cancer is a prototypically immunologically cold malignancy, characterized by low tumor mutational burden, sparse baseline CD8⁺ T cell infiltration, and low PD-L1 expression relative to melanoma or non-small cell lung cancer []. AR blockade may transiently enhance tumor immunogenicity, as preclinical data demonstrate increased T cell infiltration following androgen deprivation [], but this effect appears insufficient in most patients to cross the threshold required for productive ICI engagement. Second, all three trials enrolled unselected patient populations without prospective biomarker stratification. Notably, exploratory analyses from IMbassador250 revealed that patients with high PD-L1 expression in tumor-infiltrating immune cells, elevated CD8⁺ T cell signatures, and phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) loss derived progression-free survival benefit from the addition of PD-L1 blockade, suggesting potential biomarker-defined sensitivity to combined AR and PD-L1 blockade []. Third, the timing and duration of AR blockade relative to ICI may be critical: androgen deprivation-induced immune activation is transient, and prolonged AR blockade can itself drive GR upregulation as a resistance mechanism [], potentially replacing one neuro-endocrine immune checkpoint with another.

These failures should not be interpreted as evidence against the AR-immune axis per se, but rather as a demonstration that targeting a single neuro-endocrine checkpoint in an immunologically unfavorable context is insufficient. They motivate a pivot in two directions: toward AR-expressing malignancies with higher baseline immunogenicity, such as urothelial carcinoma (NCT05327647), and toward multi-target strategies that combine AR blockade with disruption of additional neuro-endocrine axes (e.g., GR modulation) [, ] and prospective biomarker selection (Table ). ERα antagonists and selective ERβ agonists are being investigated to mitigate estrogen-mediated immunosuppression; preclinical data in melanoma and breast cancer show reduced M2 macrophage polarization and enhanced ICI efficacy [, ]. PR-dependent MHC-I downregulation contributes to immune evasion, suggesting PR antagonism as a potential intervention []. This distinction between T cell-intrinsic mechanisms, tumor-cell effects and clinical translation is also emphasized in recent synthesis of the AR–immune literature [].

Recent evidence in GBM further illustrates this context dependence and reveals crosstalk between the gonadal and HPA axes. In immunocompetent male mice, surgical castration or pharmacological AR inhibition unexpectedly accelerated intracranial tumor growth, whereas castration delayed the growth of the same GBM cells implanted subcutaneously []. Mechanistically, androgen loss enhanced microglial inflammasome activation and IL-1β/TNF-α-driven neuroinflammation, leading to HPA-axis hyperactivation and increased circulating glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid signaling through GR-expressing myeloid cells subsequently promoted an immunosuppressive microenvironment and systemic T-cell dysfunction, accompanied by a shift of intratumoral CD8⁺ T cells toward terminal exhaustion []. This brain-specific androgen–HPA–immune circuit cautions that androgen deprivation cannot be assumed to enhance antitumor immunity across anatomical sites. Collectively, sex steroid receptor signaling shapes CD8⁺ T cell immunity in a cell-, tissue-, and treatment-dependent manner, underscoring the need for biomarker- and tumor-site-guided integration of hormone-directed therapies with ICIs.

The preceding sections examined neural and endocrine mechanisms as distinct, systemically distributed regulatory systems. In the intact organism, however, these pathways converge anatomically within the tumor microenvironment and physiologically through shared stress-response and circadian circuits.

Local neuro-immune integration within the TME presupposes that nerve fibers and neuro-secretory structures are physically present at sufficient density. Tumors do not passively rely on pre-existing innervation; they actively engineer their own neural infrastructure through tumor-derived factors that recruit and reprogram peripheral nerve fibers, establishing the anatomical substrate on which downstream suppressive mechanisms operate.

Sympathetic axonogenesis is driven primarily by tumor-secreted NGF and related neurotrophins, which promote ingrowth of sympathetic nerve fibers and elevate intratumoral NE concentrations, reinforcing a localized immunosuppressive milieu [, ]. Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles can also reprogram neuronal identity: Amit et al. demonstrated that p53 loss in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma reduces exosomal miR-34a and promotes sensory-to-adrenergic reprogramming. Independently, sensory neuron-derived CGRP can promote CD8⁺ T-cell exhaustion in melanoma and HNSCC [, , ]. The density of CGRP⁺ sensory fibers correlates with local immunosuppression in heavily innervated malignancies such as melanoma and HNSCC [, ]. The molecular identity of these infiltrating neurons was long obscured because neuronal cell bodies reside in distant ganglia and are absent from standard tumor sequencing datasets. Thiel and colleagues addressed this gap using Trace-n-Seq, a retrograde axonal tracing method coupled with single-cell transcriptomics, characterizing more than 4,000 PDAC- and healthy-pancreas-innervating sympathetic and sensory neurons []. The data revealed neuronal cell-states that are distinct to PDAC, pancreatitis, and melanoma metastases, providing direct molecular evidence that the peripheral nervous system is itself reshaped by malignancy rather than simply colonized by it. This single-neuron framework reinforces the case for viewing tumor-innervating nerves as an actively rewired cellular compartment of the TME with its own pharmacologically tractable cell-state vulnerabilities.

Within this remodeled neural scaffold, CD8⁺ T cells encounter multiple categories of local suppressive signal operating on overlapping spatial and temporal scales. Structural neuro-immune checkpoints depend on physical proximity between nerve elements and CD8⁺ T cells to establish locally constrained immunosuppressive niches that are invisible to systemic neurotransmitter measurements. Tumor-activated Schwann cells polarize tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells toward an exhausted phenotype through prostaglandin E release and the upregulation of PD-1 and CD73 on adjacent T cells []. In prostate cancer, autonomic nerve signaling regulates tumor and stromal compartments; during progression to neuroendocrine differentiation, lineage plasticity and MHC-I downregulation add a tumor-intrinsic layer of immune evasion [, , ]. A second proximity-dependent mechanism operates through restricted neurotransmitter delivery: Globig et al. [] showed that β1-AR⁺ terminally exhausted CD8⁺ T cells cluster around intratumoral sympathetic nerve fibers in a β1-AR-dependent manner, exposing them to local norepinephrine concentrations that systemic measurements do not capture.

Beyond these structural niches, the TME accumulates a parallel paracrine network of neuropeptides and atypical transmitters released by neurons, neuroendocrine cells, and malignant cells alike. VIP engages vasoactive intestinal peptide receptors 1 and 2 (VPAC1/2) to suppress CD8⁺ T cell effector cytokine production and to skew dendritic cells toward a tolerogenic phenotype that favors Treg induction []. NPY acts on the Y1 receptor to attenuate T cell effector function and migration []. (Fig. )

Several of these mediators are also secreted by malignant cells themselves: tumor-derived γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) limits CD8⁺ T cell infiltration [], and locally enriched serotonin engages 5-hydroxytryptamine 1 A (5-HT1A) receptors on lung cancer cells to drive autophagy–phosphorylated STAT3 (pSTAT3) signaling and upregulate PD-L1 []. Because neuronal and tumor-derived sources converge on overlapping receptors and downstream programs, paracrine signaling in the TME is best treated as a single integrated network rather than as discrete neural and tumoral compartments.

A distinct layer of local immunosuppression operates through local enzymatic amplification of glucocorticoid activity, which mechanistically bridges the neural and endocrine arms of TME suppression. In adrenocortical carcinoma, autonomous cortisol hypersecretion directly mediates CD8⁺ T cell exclusion [, ]. In melanoma, tumor-associated 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1) regenerates active glucocorticoids from inactive metabolites, converting cortisone to cortisol in humans and 11-dehydrocorticosterone to corticosterone in mice [, ]. In renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the 11β-HSD1-encoding gene HSD11B1 is predominantly expressed in tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells, and inhibitor studies support improved antigen presentation and responses to anti-PD-1 []. Enforced 11β-HSD1 expression in melanoma limits PD-1 blockade efficacy in a CD8⁺ T cell-dependent manner, whereas inhibition improves immune responses and anti-PD-1 activity in melanoma and renal cancer models through mechanisms that include myeloid regulation [, ]. These studies identify local glucocorticoid regeneration as an intervention point; however, HSD11B1 is also expressed in non-tumor tissues, and systemic inhibition should not be assumed to spare systemic steroid metabolism or HPA feedback [, , , ]. Therapeutic evaluation should distinguish modulation of intratumoral glucocorticoid activity from the effects of systemic drug exposure.

The same principle of spatially selective intervention informs efforts to disrupt the neural scaffold itself. In preclinical PDAC models, sympathetic denervation with 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) reduced tumor growth and induced inflammatory remodeling of the TME, with increased immune-cell infiltration and enhanced sensitivity to checkpoint blockade []. Still, safety and clinical translatability of these experimental neurotoxin-based approaches remain incompletely characterized. In PDAC models, nab-paclitaxel reduced intratumoral nerve density, particularly affecting sensory neurons, while combination with sympathetic denervation further reduced tumor growth []. These findings support further evaluation of nerve-targeting combinations. Taken together, the convergence of neural, paracrine, and glucocorticoid suppressive mechanisms within a shared anatomical niche argues for combination strategies that simultaneously target multiple nodes of this integrated network rather than any single effector pathway.

Chronic stress simultaneously activates the SNS and HPA axis, subjecting CD8⁺ T cells to convergent immunosuppressive pressure from catecholamines and glucocorticoids [, , ]. These two arms share a transcriptional target architecture, supporting convergent suppression; supra-additive synergy has not been established by these shared targets alone. At the transcription factor level, both the β-adrenergic receptor (β-AR)–cAMP–PKA cascade and the ligand-bound GR converge on NF-κB and AP-1, the two principal activators of effector gene transcription in CD8⁺ T cells. PKA phosphorylates the NF-κB inhibitor alpha (IκBα) and attenuates AP-1 via cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB)/CREM-mediated promoter competition [, ], while GR directly tethers to both NF-κB and AP-1 through protein-protein transrepression []. These shared targets provide a basis for complementary restraint of effector cytokine and cytolytic gene expression.

Beyond this transcriptional convergence, the two pathways impose complementary but non-redundant metabolic constraints. β2-AR signaling suppresses GLUT1 membrane translocation at the post-translational level [], whereas GR-mediated transactivation represses GLUT1 gene transcription and simultaneously upregulates the pro-apoptotic factor BIM [], creating a bioenergetic environment in which CD8⁺ T cells can neither fuel glycolysis nor resist apoptotic stress. The β1-AR–cAMP–CREM axis in terminally exhausted T cells [] and the GR–glucocorticoid-induced leucine zipper (GILZ)/BIM axis further occupy distinct downstream effector programs, suggesting that adrenergic and glucocorticoid signals coordinate the progressive trajectory from progenitor exhaustion to terminal dysfunction at separable epigenetic nodes.

Steroid-receptor crosstalk adds another layer: AR, GR and PR recognize partially overlapping response elements, but receptor-specific chromatin and co-regulatory contexts determine transcriptional output [, ]. In prostate cancer cells, GR can bypass AR blockade; this tumor-cell mechanism should not be assumed to operate identically in CD8⁺ T cells []. Some synthetic progestins also activate GR, with ligand-dependent potency rather than universal high affinity of PR ligands for GR []. Direct AR/GR/PR cross-regulation in tumor-specific CD8⁺ T cells remains incompletely defined. GR-mediated interference with PR signaling is therefore a context-dependent possibility, not an established brake on PR signaling in tumor-specific CD8⁺ T cells; overlapping ligand or DNA recognition alone does not establish antagonism.

Clinical associations with stress-axis activity remain indirect evidence of convergence. In the prospective STRESS-LUNG cohort, pretreatment emotional distress was associated with a lower ICI response rate in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer []. Baseline corticosteroid use predicts poor outcomes with PD-1 blockade in non-small cell lung cancer [], while some studies suggest a beneficial association between concomitant β-blocker use and ICI outcomes, but findings are heterogeneous and do not establish a causal benefit []. These separate associations do not demonstrate combined SNS–HPA causality or clinical synergy.

The dual GR/AR blockade strategy (enzalutamide plus relacorilant) tested in a phase I mCRPC trial (NCT03674814 []) represents the first clinical attempt to target two neuro-endocrine checkpoints simultaneously, although it addresses GR-AR rather than GR-β-AR convergence. A direct test of the stress amplification loop—combining a β-blocker with a GR modulator alongside ICI—has not yet been reported in a completed trial. Such a study, stratified by baseline cortisol and catecholamine levels, would constitute a definitive evaluation of whether dual disruption of the stress axis can overcome neuro-endocrine-driven ICI resistance, and would also serve as a proof-of-concept for the broader “multi-checkpoint” strategy implied by the four-criterion framework.

Sex steroids modify the systemic stress axis at central as well as peripheral sites. In gonadectomized male rats, hypothalamic ERα activation increased stress-induced adrenocorticotropic hormone/corticosterone release, whereas ERβ activation, including by the dihydrotestosterone (DHT) metabolite 5α-androstane-3β,17β-diol (3β-diol), reduced it []. These physiological findings do not establish a universal female-HPA/male-SNS pattern or sex-specific VNS benefit in cancer. Hormonal state and experimental context therefore matter when interpreting stress-associated immunity; the brain-specific androgen-loss–HPA circuit described in section “” provides a tumor example []. A second modifier is the gut. The evidence summarized here defines receptor-specific HPA modulation more directly than a general sex-steroid mechanism for SNS reactivity; SNS effects remain dependent on physiological state, tissue and experimental context.

The enteric relay also links autonomic output with systemic endocrine signals. Chronic SNS/HPA activation alters gut microbial composition and intestinal permeability [], potentially reducing the availability of microbiome-derived metabolites that support CD8⁺ T cell function. These include butyrate, which epigenetically lowers PD-1 expression through histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition [], and Lactobacillus-derived tryptophan metabolites, which promote CD8⁺ T cell IFN-γ responses and ICI sensitization through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling []. Together, these findings suggest a link between stress-related microbial changes and CD8⁺ T cell regulation, extending the systemic perspective beyond the conventional neuro-endocrine axes.

The circadian system can modulate anti-tumor immunity, but the relevant mechanisms are compartment- and context-specific []. In preclinical models, Brain and muscle ARNT-like 1 (BMAL1)-dependent programs in dendritic cells regulate CD80-mediated T-cell priming [], whereas endothelial BMAL1 controls rhythmic intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) expression and leukocyte entry into tumors []; rhythmic accumulation of PD-L1⁺ myeloid-derived suppressor cells may also alter the efficacy of anti-PD-L1 therapy []. These findings establish biological plausibility for temporal variation in tumor immunity, but they do not define a universal treatment window, and circadian phases in nocturnal mice cannot be directly mapped onto human clock time.

Neuro-endocrine rhythms should likewise not be interpreted as producing uniform activation or suppression of cytotoxic T cells. In healthy human physiology, the morning cortisol rise induces CXCR4-dependent redistribution of naive T cells from the blood toward the bone marrow, whereas catecholamines transiently mobilize differentiated effector CD8⁺ T cells into the circulation []. Redistribution in peripheral blood is not equivalent to functional activation or tumor infiltration, and transient, compartment-specific redistribution can coexist with the suppressive effects of sustained glucocorticoid and β-adrenergic signaling. Neither redistribution nor biological plausibility alone establishes an optimal ICI infusion time. Melatonin may modulate myeloid polarization in preclinical tumor models []. Although broader reviews have proposed additional immunomodulatory effects, generalization across tumors remains uncertain []. Melatonin may also influence tryptophan metabolism and augment vaccine-associated CD8⁺ T-cell responses when combined with indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) inhibition []. These observations do not establish an optimal time for ICI administration.

Clinical evidence for chrono-immunotherapy remains heterogeneous and does not establish a causal benefit of a particular ICI infusion time. A meta-analysis of retrospective studies associated earlier ICI infusion with longer overall and progression-free survival, but heterogeneous time cutoffs and potential scheduling, survivor, and cycle-number biases limit causal interpretation []. In a bias-aware analysis of pembrolizumab-treated participants from the SWOG Cancer Research Network trial S1404, infusion time was not associated with recurrence-free or overall survival []. The i-TIMES pooled patient-level analysis of eight lung-cancer trials reported non-inferior overall survival with later versus earlier administration during the first two ICI cycles; infusion time itself was not randomized, and the findings were reported in a conference abstract []. In the exploratory A-BRAVE analysis, infusion time was not associated with outcomes overall; however, a higher proportion of morning infusions was associated with better outcomes in immune-hot tumors and worse outcomes in immune-cold tumors. This conference-abstract subgroup analysis is hypothesis-generating; A-BRAVE did not randomize infusion time []. Taken together, current evidence does not support a universal ICI infusion schedule or timing recommendations based on tumor immune phenotype. Prospective trials should randomize infusion time and account for chronotype, internal circadian phase, and tumor immune context using standardized timing definitions.

This review has examined how the nervous and endocrine systems coordinately regulate CD8⁺ T cell anti-tumor immunity at the whole-organism level. The sympathetic nervous system, acting through both β1-AR and β2-AR, suppresses proximal TCR signaling, drives metabolic reprogramming, and promotes terminal exhaustion. Sensory nociceptors release CGRP to create spatially defined immunosuppressive niches, while vagal/cholinergic pathways indirectly modulate CD8⁺ T cell fate through myeloid intermediaries. On the endocrine axis, glucocorticoids impose transcriptional repression and metabolic constraints; metabolic hormones (insulin, leptin, adiponectin) regulate bioenergetic fitness; and sex steroids differentially program T cell exhaustion trajectories. Importantly, these neural and endocrine pathways do not operate in isolation: circadian oscillations temporally gate immune responsiveness, stress amplification loops create convergent SNS-HPA immunosuppression, and gut-relayed microbial signaling serves as a systemic relay.

Therapeutically, the four criteria distinguish candidate inhibitory checkpoints from broader neuro-endocrine regulators; evidence must be interpreted by responding cell, anatomical site and stage of the T cell response. Repurposing β-blockers, hormone deprivation therapies, and metabolic interventions provides translational strategies to mitigate CD8⁺ T cell exhaustion and potentiate ICI efficacy. However, mechanistic support is predominantly preclinical, and prospective clinical validation remains limited. The failure of KEYNOTE-641 and KEYNOTE-991 underscores the importance of biomarker-guided patient selection.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. The evidence reviewed here is predominantly derived from murine models and requires validation in human tumor immunity. Neuro-endocrine effects vary with cellular, tissue, and treatment context, limiting universal therapeutic strategies, while interactions among these axes remain insufficiently characterized. Our coverage also reflects the uneven depth of mechanistic evidence: thyroid hormones, growth hormone, prolactin, and vitamin D receptor signaling influence T cell biology but were not examined in depth, as the available CD8⁺ T cell-specific mechanistic evidence does not yet warrant their integration into the neuro-endocrine immune checkpoint framework.

Future studies should leverage spatial multi-omics platforms (e.g., multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization [MERFISH] and CosMx) combined with neural tracing technologies to map neuro-immune interactions at single-cell resolution. Systemic metabolic profiling integrated with circadian sampling can capture the temporal dynamics of neuro-endocrine immune regulation in patients. Prospective, biomarker-stratified clinical trials are needed to establish whether β-blockers, GR modulators, or chrono-immunotherapy can improve ICI outcomes. Bioelectronic medicine (e.g., VNS) offers non-pharmacological modalities for modulating neuro-immune circuits. The integration of neuroscience, endocrinology, and immunology will be essential to unlock the full potential of cancer immunotherapy.

neuroscience.title: Validity of stroke diagnoses in a long-term cohort across shifting diagnostic eras, Adult Health Study, 1958–2015
neuroscience.abstract: The validity of stroke diagnoses recorded in cohorts followed over decades amid changing clinical practice remains to be characterized.We examined stroke and non-stroke cerebrovascular disease (CVD) diagnoses recorded during biennial health examinations of the Adult Health Study cohort of atomic bomb survivors from 1958 to 2015. All diagnoses were adjudicated by expert chart review using predefined criteria. We evaluated the validity of the recorded diagnoses using the positive predictive value (PPV) for expert-verified stroke, overall and by calendar period and diagnostic subcategory. Stroke subcategories included ischemic stroke (IS), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and “unspecified stroke”; non-stroke subcategories included TIA and “other CVD.”A total of 1615 cerebrovascular diagnoses (1124 strokes and 491 non-strokes) were screened among 11,752 participants. Expert review confirmed 728 of the stroke diagnoses and 152 of the non-stroke diagnoses as probable stroke. The introduction of neuroimaging around 1980 was followed by an increase in subtype-specific diagnoses (IS/ICH/SAH) and a decrease in nonspecific coding (unspecified stroke and other CVD). Stroke subcategories had moderate to high PPVs (0.61–0.85) overall, but they varied across periods due to evolving neuroimaging technology. A significant proportion of non-stroke diagnoses were verified as stroke, especially within the “other CVD” subcategory during the pre-imaging era (up to 0.48).The validity of stroke diagnoses varied as clinical practices changed. Our findings support the use of stroke diagnoses recorded in multi-decade cohorts, while emphasizing the importance of expert adjudication to improve precision and sensitivity.
neuroscience.text:
Long-term cohort studies play a critical role in reducing the worldwide burden of stroke  by providing information on stroke incidence, temporal trends, and associated risk factors , , , . Unlike contemporary stroke registries, stroke events in population cohorts are often captured through health examinations, interviews, or questionnaires , , . These diagnoses are not necessarily made by expert neurologists or according to consistent diagnostic criteria, such as the WHO MONICA Project criteria . Furthermore, over decades of follow-up, diagnostic accuracy changes with shifting clinical practice, such as altering diagnostic criteria , International Classification of Diseases (ICD) revisions , and the introduction of computed tomography (CT) ,  and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) . Diagnostic inaccuracy arising from these sources can create false trends or bias risk estimation, especially when exposure or its effect varies over time . Despite these concerns, the validity of stroke diagnoses recorded in cohorts over decades amid clinical advancements has rarely been reported.

The Adult Health Study (AHS) cohort of atomic bomb survivors at the Radiation Effects Research Foundation (RERF) provides an opportunity to investigate this longitudinal validity. Since its establishment in 1958, the AHS has accumulated a repository of diagnoses through biennial clinical examinations. This study evaluated the validity of stroke diagnoses recorded between 1958 and 2015 and their changes across eras, including the advent of modern neuroimaging.

This validation study was conducted as part of a study examining the association between radiation exposure and stroke incidence among atomic bomb survivors in Hiroshima and Nagasaki between 1958 and 2015, motivated by the concern about potential misclassification during these shifting eras. The study was approved by the RERF ethics committee (Research Protocol 1–21). All participants agreed to the use of their health examination data for research at RERF and provided written informed consent obtained at each visit for specific examination items since 2000. Because this study was retrospective, informed consent specific to the present analysis was waived.

Since 1958, AHS participants have undergone biennial health examinations, with high participation rates (approximately 70–80%) maintained until recent years , . Cohort details are described elsewhere , . For this study, participants from the original in-city cohort (n = 14,996) and a 1977-expansion cohort (n = 2436) were eligible if they had known radiation dose estimates (n = 15,186). After exclusion of participants with one or fewer visits (n = 3322) and with a prevalent stroke record (n = 111) or hematologic disease (n = 1, per the parent study criterion) at baseline, 11,752 participants (7363 females) remained for stroke screening (Supplementary Figure S1).

During each examination, physicians and medical personnel obtained medical histories (including interim diagnoses, symptoms, hospitalizations, surgical and radiological procedures, and medication use) and performed physical examinations, chest radiography, electrocardiography, and routine laboratory tests. These tests evolved in parallel with contemporaneous clinical standards. Until 2010 in Hiroshima and 2020 in Nagasaki, medical personnel conducted health examinations for participants unable to visit clinics by visiting their homes, nursing homes, or hospitals. These outside examinations included detailed history-taking from participants, their families, and facility staff, as well as routine laboratory tests, but did not include electrocardiography or chest radiography. They accounted for approximately 6% of the health examinations conducted among the 11,752 eligible participants during the study period. The diagnoses assigned by the attending physician(s) were documented in the medical chart and stored as ICD codes, following an independent review by a supervising physician. Further details can be found on the RERF websites .

We screened first-ever stroke diagnoses recorded between 1958 and 2015 using ICD codes spanning the 7th through 10th revisions. According to the code, we classified the diagnoses as ischemic stroke (IS, or cerebral infarction), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or unspecified stroke (acute stroke without specified subtype or sequelae of stroke). To assess whether stroke cases had been missed among non-stroke cerebrovascular diagnoses, we also screened these diagnoses, divided into two subcategories: TIA and “other CVD” (e.g., cerebral atherosclerosis and unspecified hemiplegia). The ICD code mappings are provided in Supplementary Table S1. When diagnoses from multiple categories were assigned to the same event (n = 41), we assigned the most specific category according to a prespecified hierarchy: specific subtypes (IS/ICH/SAH), unspecified stroke, TIA, and other CVD, in descending order. When two or more subtypes were diagnosed (n = 6), we assigned the primary diagnosis as SAH first, then IS, and lastly ICH, based on typical clinical progression, such as vasospasm following SAH or hemorrhagic transformation following IS.

A board-certified stroke neurologist (TN) with more than 20 years of clinical experience reviewed the medical charts of all screened diagnoses. During the review, we abstracted information on diagnostic neuroimaging, including CT, MRI, or angiography. For SAH cases, we considered cerebrospinal fluid examination as part of diagnostic neuroimaging.

An expert stroke diagnosis was made when the clinical presentation and ancillary information were consistent with an acute cerebrovascular event. To this end, we prepared separate sets of criteria for SAH and non-SAH stroke. Non-SAH stroke was primarily adjudicated according to the WHO MONICA Project criteria (acute onset of focal neurological signs lasting ≥24 h) . Because detailed neurological findings at the time of onset were not consistently documented in our health examination records, we supplemented the adjudication criteria with information on interim medical care, including hospitalizations, specific treatments, diagnostic tests, and surgical interventions (Supplementary Table S2). SAH was adjudicated based on a characteristic clinical presentation and documented interventions to capture its life-threatening nature. (Supplementary Table S3). We classified adjudicated stroke cases as definite, probable, or possible. Definite or probable stroke served as the reference standard. For equivocal cases, a second board-certified stroke neurologist (KI) was consulted, and the final diagnosis was determined through discussion.

We evaluated the validity of stroke diagnoses by calculating positive predictive value (PPV) using expert-verified stroke as the reference standard. Similarly, we evaluated the yield of stroke cases from non-stroke cerebrovascular diagnoses by calculating the PPV for expert-verified stroke within these categories.

We assessed inter-rater reliability in 105 non-SAH and 21 SAH cases, randomly sampled from Hiroshima. These cases were independently reviewed by the second neurologist (KI), unaware of the initial assessment. Similarly, we assessed intra-rater reliability in 40 non-SAH and 10 SAH cases from Nagasaki that were re-reviewed by the same neurologist (TN) ≥6 months after the initial review. Sampling was stratified by diagnostic and review periods.

All analyses were conducted using Python 3.13.5. Confidence intervals (CI) for PPVs were calculated using the Wilson score method in the statsmodels library. Inter- and intra-rater agreements were summarized using agreement proportion and Cohen's kappa statistics using the scikit-learn library. Cohen's kappa values were interpreted according to the McHugh criteria .

Of the 11,752 eligible participants, we identified 1124 stroke diagnoses (56% women, 690 IS, 101 ICH, 47 SAH, and 286 unspecified stroke) and 491 non-stroke diagnoses (59% women, 169 TIA and 322 other CVD). Of these diagnoses, 1397 were from the original cohort, and 218 were from the 1977 expansion cohort. The mean age at the time of diagnosis was 72 years (range, 35–100) for stroke and 71 years (range, 30–100) for non-stroke. By ICD revision, 189, 291, 694, and 441 diagnoses were coded using the 7th (1958–1968), 8th (1969–1978), 9th (1979–1997), and 10th (1998–2015) revisions, respectively.

Overall, neuroimaging was documented in 449 (40%) of stroke and 40 (8%) of non-stroke cases. Imaging was rarely documented before 1980, except for SAH, in which imaging included cerebrospinal fluid tests (). After that, the availability increased sharply for stroke diagnoses, and more gradually for non-stroke diagnoses. Over time, subtype-specific diagnoses (IS/ICH/SAH) increased, and nonspecific diagnoses (unspecified stroke and other CVD) decreased ( and ). This shift paralleled the availability of neuroimaging, most notably for other CVD categories, which dropped after neuroimaging became widely available.

Of a total of 1615 cases screened (1124 stroke diagnoses and 491 non-stroke cerebrovascular diagnoses), the expert chart review adjudicated 880 as stroke events (728 from stroke and 152 from non-stroke diagnoses), including 711 classified as definite and 169 as probable. Additionally, 95 cases were classified as possible stroke ().

The PPV of stroke diagnoses was moderate overall (0.65 [95% CI, 0.62–0.68]) and ranged from moderate to high across diagnostic categories: 0.61 (95% CI, 0.57–0.65) for IS; 0.85 (95% CI, 0.77–0.91) for ICH; 0.79 (95% CI, 0.65–0.88) for SAH; and 0.64 (95% CI, 0.59–0.70) for unspecified stroke. PPVs within each category varied by calendar period (). The PPV of ICH was initially high and continued to increase after 1980. The PPV of SAH was initially moderate and rose steeply in the 1970s. The PPV of IS was moderate throughout, dipping slightly before 1970 and during the 1990s. The PPV of unspecified stroke was consistently moderate.

The stroke case yield from non-stroke diagnoses (PPV for expert-verified stroke) was low overall: 0.23 (95% CI, 0.17–0.30) for TIA and 0.35 (95% CI, 0.30–0.40) for other CVD. Across the study periods, the yield from TIA was consistently low. In contrast, the yield from other CVD diagnoses was initially moderate (48%) but decreased progressively, particularly after the widespread availability of neuroimaging ().

Similar trends were observed across ICD revisions (Supplementary Figure S2). Expanding the analysis to “possible” cases increased PPV, reflecting the broader case definition (). On the other hand, restricting to “definite” cases, which were verified using criteria less dependent on imaging availability, attenuated the increase in PPV during the imaging era. Nevertheless, the PPVs largely remained in the moderate range.

Inter-rater agreement was perfect (100% agreement) for SAH and strong for non-SAH stroke (91% agreement; Cohen's κ of 0.81 [95% CI, 0.69–0.91]) with no significant disproportionality between false-positive and false-negative classifications (Supplementary Table S4). Similarly, intra-rater agreement was perfect (100% agreement) for SAH and almost perfect for non-SAH stroke (98% agreement; Cohen's κ = 0.95; 95% CI, 0.84–1.00).

Among the 322 initial stroke diagnoses where stroke was ruled out by the expert review (i.e., verified as less than possible), alternative diagnoses were assigned to 260 cases. These diagnoses varied by ICD revision and subtype (Supplementary Figure S3). In earlier periods, the most frequent alternative diagnoses were nonspecific symptoms, such as dizziness and transient loss of consciousness, or central nervous system diseases other than stroke. In later periods, more false-positive diagnoses were attributable to asymptomatic conditions, particularly among cases coded as IS.

This study validated stroke diagnoses recorded in a cohort followed for 57 years, during which neuroimaging technology significantly transformed clinical practice. To ensure consistent validation of the diagnoses recorded across these different eras, we applied uniform diagnostic criteria through a thorough review by an expert. Inter- and intra-rater agreement further supports the robustness of the validation. Our findings demonstrate that although the PPV of recorded stroke diagnoses remained moderate to high overall, the validity was tied to the diagnostic eras in which the event was recorded.

As expected, the introduction of modern neuroimaging greatly impacted the diagnoses recorded in the cohort. It triggered an increase in subtype-specific diagnosis (IS/ICH/SAH) and a decrease in nonspecific diagnosis (unspecified stroke and other CVD). This shift likely reflects improved subtype differentiation facilitated by neuroimaging , . Improved subclassification inherently implies greater accuracy of overall stroke diagnosis, which is likely responsible for the simultaneous increase in the PPV of hemorrhagic stroke. The benefit of neuroimaging is most evidenced around 1980 when neuroimaging availability concurred with a drop in the number of “other CVD” diagnoses and in the proportion of stroke cases retrieved from this category. This decline indicates that substantial stroke cases were misclassified as ambiguous CVD diagnoses due to the diagnostic challenges of the pre-imaging era.

In contrast to the underdiagnosed or underspecified stroke events that characterized the pre-imaging era, neuroimaging has paradoxically introduced a unique form of false-positive misclassification. This is evident in the increase of asymptomatic false-positive diagnoses in the imaging era, particularly in the IS category. This type of misclassification can occur when incidental MRI findings, such as white matter lesions or silent infarcts, are mistakenly interpreted as strokes  and poses a contemporary challenge for population studies .

Our findings provide several insights into the use of historical stroke outcomes in long-term cohorts. The consistently moderate to high validity of recorded stroke diagnoses coded as stroke suggests that they can be used in analyses. However, it is important to note that the accuracy could be enhanced through additional verification. Conversely, underdiagnosed stroke cases within non-stroke categories, particularly in the other CVD category in the pre-imaging era (when nearly half of the recorded cases were verified as stroke), emphasize the importance of a case identification strategy that combines broad screening with expert review to maximize sensitivity. Finally, although we could not validate subtype-specific diagnoses, the rapid increase in subtype-specific diagnoses after the introduction of modern neuroimaging suggests that including subtype-specific diagnoses in analyses is acceptable, provided that the analyses are restricted to the modern imaging era.

This study has several limitations. First, detailed acute-phase information, such as neurological and neuroimaging findings, was not always available in our health examination records. Due to this insufficiency, our adjudication may be conservative. Additionally, the lack of detailed neuroimaging findings precluded us from the validation of subtype-specific diagnoses. Second, we screened potential false-negative cases only within the CVD diagnoses to avoid an overly extensive chart review. This restriction may have missed some false-negative cases. Finally, the AHS cohort is a specific survivor population, which was affected by the changing stroke incidence in Japan, particularly during the early study period, and its high-participation, biennial follow-up may have facilitated the ascertainment of stroke events. Therefore, the observed validity may not be directly generalizable to other populations or cohorts with less intensive follow-up.
