neuroscience.title: Potential Mechanisms of Chlorogenic Acid in Cognitive Impairment: A Comprehensive Review
neuroscience.abstract: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a clinical syndrome primarily affecting cognitive functions such as learning, memory, perception, and problem-solving. Its causes are heterogeneous, including neurological, psychiatric, metabolic, vascular, toxicological, and age-related factors. Currently, no specific and effective pharmacological therapies are available for CI in clinical practice. As one of the most abundant dietary polyphenols, chlorogenic acid (CGA) displays diverse biological effects and has recently garnered growing interest within cognitive neuroscience. This review summarizes the mechanisms by which CGA ameliorates cognitive impairment, encompassing neuroprotection, modulation of the gut–brain axis, inhibition of neuroinflammation, inhibition of oxidative stress, promotion of autophagy, inhibition of apoptosis, and suppression of amyloid-β (Aβ) formation. The signaling pathways implicated include activation of the PKC, Nrf2/PPAR and Nrf2/ARE pathways, as well as inhibition of the TLR4/NF-κB, mTOR/TFEB, p38 MAPK, and JNK/c-Jun pathways. This article provides an overview of current advancements in CGA, addressing its chemical attributes, dietary origins, drug metabolism, and the mechanistic basis for its efficacy in neurodegenerative diseases.
neuroscience.text:
Cognitive impairment (CI) constitutes a clinical syndrome that chiefly impacts higher-order cognitive functions, such as learning, memory, perception, and reasoning []. It constitutes a complex syndrome with a broad spectrum of manifestations, ranging in severity from mild cognitive decline to dementia []. Studies have identified cognitive decline as one of the most common age-related health issues among older adults [], with its prevalence increasing with advancing age and lower educational attainment [], Among adults aged 60 and older, the estimated prevalence of mild cognitive impairment ranges from 6.7% to 25.2% []. The consequences of CI include reduced physical activity, physical disability [], loss of social engagement [], an elevated risk of developing dementia [] and increased healthcare expenditures []. The currently recognized pathogenic mechanisms encompass impaired neuroprotective mechanisms [], alterations in gut microbiota homeostasis and their metabolites [], chronic neuroinflammation [], oxidative stress and autophagic dysregulation [,] and direct neurotoxicity induced by amyloid-β (Aβ) plaque deposition [,]. However, no effective pharmacological treatment is currently available for mild cognitive impairment [] or for vascular cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID) []. And for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), available therapies (e.g., Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, and anti-amyloid antibodies) offer only limited symptomatic or disease-modifying benefit [], making the prevention and treatment of CI a prominent research priority [].

Previous studies have demonstrated that moderate intake of dietary polyphenols can ameliorate cognitive impairment []. Chlorogenic acid (CGA) ranks as the most abundant polyphenol found in human dietary intake, with daily intake reaching the milligram-to-gram level []. Over the past few years, CGA has been acknowledged for its ability to protect neurons and boost cognitive function, and animal studies have demonstrated its efficacy in treating cognitive impairment []. Its therapeutic potential is garnering increasing attention in the field of cognitive research. This review synthesizes the literature from the past thirty-five years concerning CGA in the treatment of cognitive impairment, and focus on age-related CI in older adults, which spans the continuum from normal age-related cognitive decline to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) dementia, providing an updated and comprehensive evaluation to inform future clinical investigations of CGA for neurodegenerative diseases.

We searched the PubMed database from 1 November 1992 to 2 July 2026 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ (accessed on 13 August 2026)). The search terms combined the subject terms and free words, including chlorogenic acid, 5-caffeoylquinic acid, as well as cognitive impairment, cognitive decline, etc. The final search date was 13 August 2026. After removing duplicates and screening 249,900 records, 107 studies ultimately met the inclusion criteria. We included original in vivo, in vitro and randomized controlled trials, requiring chlorogenic acid as the main intervention and reporting cognitive-related outcomes; exclude preprints, conference abstracts, case reports, duplicate literature, and retractions. We extracted species/cells, models, doses, administration routes, treatment courses, controls, outcomes and mechanisms. Since this study was a narrative review, no formal bias risk assessment tool was used; instead, the quality of evidence was narratively evaluated based on elements such as study design, sample size, randomization/blinding, model validity, dose correlation, objectivity of cognitive results, and directness of evidence. Liver and intestinal studies were included in the main review because they are related to the gut–brain axis; studies not involving cognitive results were identified separately by cell type and clearly labeled as indirect evidence. The research results were narratively synthesized by mechanism. We used narrative synthesis and summarized the findings by mechanism.

Chlorogenic acid (CGA), or 5-caffeoylquinic acid (5-CQA), is a naturally derived phenolic acid. As a phenolic acid bearing an ortho-hydroxyl group, CGA is formed through the esterification of caffeic acid and quinic acid [,]. In the Traditional Chinese Medicine Systems Pharmacology (TCMSP) database, this substance is registered under the molecular identifier MOL001955. CGA appears as a white to pale yellow-beige powder with a density of 1.7 ± 0.1 g/cm3. Its molecular formula is C16H18O9, with a molecular weight of 354.31 g/mol and a melting point of approximately 205–209 °C. CGA is soluble in water, with a solubility of 40 mg/mL at 25 °C. The molecular structure of CGA is shown in .

Chlorogenic acid cannot be synthesized de novo by animals or humans and must therefore be obtained from dietary sources. CGA is widely distributed in food plants, including sweet potato [], potato [], Asian pear [], apple [], and coffee []. Additionally, CGA is abundantly present in numerous traditional Chinese medicines, including Lonicera japonica (Jinyinhua) [], Chrysanthemum morifolium (Juhua) [], Phellodendron amurense (Huangbo) [], Cichorium intybus root (Jujuigen) [], Bretschneidera sinensis (Bolaishu) [], Foeniculum vulgare (Huixiang) [], Eucommia ulmoides (Duzhong) [], Schisandra chinensis (Wuweizi) [], Acanthopanax senticosus (Ciwujia) [], Aralia nudicaulis L. [], and Sanghuangporus baumii (Pilát) []. The CGA content varies among these sources ().

No adverse events were reported in the randomized clinical trials included in a systematic review and meta-analysis of CGA supplementation []. These data suggest that CGA is generally well tolerated in humans, although the evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous []. Kitts and Wijewickreme further confirmed that mice exposed to dietary chlorogenic acid (0.2%, 2000 ppm) for 10 weeks exhibited no toxic reactions, with no effects on body, liver, or intestinal weights [].

CGA has low oral bioavailability. In rats, gastric administration of 2.25 μmol CGA yielded only 0.12 μmol/L intact CGA in the portal vein and 0.04 μmol/L in the abdominal aorta at 5 min []. In situ intestinal perfusion showed that net CGA absorption was 8% of the perfused flux, intact CGA was not detected in plasma or bile, and biliary excretion was <0.4%, suggesting limited enterohepatic recirculation []. Upon entering the large intestine, CGA is hydrolyzed by the microbial community [,]. Most CGA reaches the colon, where microbial esterases hydrolyze it to caffeic acid and quinic acid [,]. Human faecal extract converted 8 μg of 21 μg CGA to caffeic acid within 2 h [], and E. coli hydrolyzed about 80% of CGA within 1 h []. CGA undergoes reduction, methylation, sulfation, and glucuronidation [] to yield 11 key metabolites, with the principal products being dihydrocaffeic acid, dihydroferulic acid, and 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl) propionic acid []. Furthermore, the absorption and excretion of CGA can be inhibited through interactions with Streptococcus salivarius and other microbial components []. Although CGA and its metabolites can be detected in the brain or cerebrospinal fluid after administration, their blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability is generally low, and the transport mechanisms—rather than simple passive diffusion—remain to be fully elucidated. This limited but measurable brain exposure may nonetheless contribute to the neurotrophic and neuroprotective effects observed in preclinical models []. More importantly, the structural similarity of CGA to certain phenolic acids suggests that it may undergo trans-endothelial transport via monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) or members of the organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) family []. These properties confer upon CGA substantial therapeutic potential for central nervous system disorders ().

Chlorogenic acid (CGA) exerts neuroprotective effects through multiple synergistic mechanisms, thereby ameliorating cognitive impairment. These mechanisms operate at several levels by maintaining neuronal survival, regulating neurotransmitter systems, modulating the immune microenvironment and improving energy metabolism. First, CGA treatment effectively preserves the number of surviving neurons in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampal CA1, and CA3 regions [] and prevents the depletion of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in these areas []. The stabilization of BDNF contributes to the maintenance of long-term potentiation of synaptic transmission, thereby promoting neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and learning and memory capacity. In this context, CGA also regulates synapse-associated proteins: on one hand, it upregulates synapsin I expression in fetal mice raphe nucleus neurons, promoting serotonin (5-HT) release and consequently enhancing synaptic plasticity [,]; on the other hand, against neurotoxic proteins, CGA can inhibit the interaction between oxidized dopamine and α-synuclein (α-syn) in vitro, thereby preventing the aberrant aggregation of α-syn and mitigating the risk of dopaminergic neuronal death [].

Second, CGA acts on multiple neurotransmitter systems. In the dopaminergic system, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) is the rate-limiting enzyme of dopamine biosynthesis []. CGA enhances TH expression and protects dopaminergic neurons [], suggesting that CGA may promote TH-mediated dopamine biosynthesisand consequently regulating neural activities related to memory, emotion, and cognition [,]. In the cholinergic system, CGA ameliorates trimethyltin chloride (TMT)-induced acetylcholine disturbances [], thereby elevating synaptic acetylcholine levels and promoting neural plasticity and network connectivity []. Furthermore, CGA regulates intracellular calcium homeostasis, alleviating the abnormal intracellular Ca2+ elevation induced by glutamate overstimulation and counteracting excitotoxic injury. This protective effect is closely associated with the PKC signaling pathway () [].

Finally, CGA provides systemic support for neuroprotection by regulating the immune microenvironment and energy metabolism. In terms of immune regulation, the expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-4, IL-13) is enhanced by CGA, whereas the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-2) is suppressed [,], thereby attenuating neuroinflammation. Of particular importance, CGA also improves systemic energy metabolism: indirect evidence from an in vitro HepG2 study, although not in a cognitive or neuronal model, indicates that it upregulates the activity of glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) cycle, and the mitochondrial respiratory chain, promoting ATP synthase expression []. This finding supports, but does not directly prove, a neuronal mechanism of CGA. This metabolic modulation is also reflected in substrate profiles, with decreased plasma concentrations of glycolytic intermediates such as D-mannose and fructose-6-phosphate, alongside elevated phosphocholine levels, indicating active membrane phospholipid metabolism and an overall improvement in the energy supply efficiency of neural cells [].

The “gut–microbiota–brain axis” is a two-way communication network linking the gut and the brain. Its regulatory mechanisms encompass multiple dimensions, including signaling by microbial metabolites (e.g., short-chain fatty acids [SCFAs]), preservation of intestinal barrier integrity, and cascade regulation of central neuroinflammatory responses. SCFAs not only modulate synaptic plasticity and neurotransmitter levels but also influence neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative processes []. Within this axis, the dynamic balance of the gut microbiota, particularly the increase and decrease in beneficial bacteria that produce SCFAs (such as those in the Clostridiales family) and opportunistic pathogens (such as Helicobacter), exerts significant regulatory effects on cognitive function by influencing the systemic inflammatory state [,].

Emerging evidence suggests that CGA, administered via oral gavage, may improve gut microecology from both microbiota structural and metabolic dimensions, and may thereby exert cognitive protective effects through the gut-brain axis. Regarding microbiota structure, whether CGA intervention specifically increases the abundance of beneficial Lachnospiraceae remains to be directly demonstrated; however, Lachnospiraceae, including Lachnospira eligens, have been implicated in epileptogenesis []. In addition, it suppresses the proliferation of the pathogenic Helicobacter, and effectively reduces the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio, thereby restoring gut microbial homeostasis []. And this structural optimization directly alleviates colon inflammation, thereby contributing to the restoration of the colonic immune microenvironment []. In the general literature on microbiota metabolism, CGA has been reported to significantly elevates fecal levels of acetate, propionate, and butyrate (SCFAs) in mice []. These SCFAs not only contribute to the remodeling of gut microbial equilibrium and the maintenance of barrier integrity but also activate intestinal stem cells and promote epithelial regeneration [,,], providing a sustained driving force for intestinal barrier repair. Another indirect evidence shows that CGA also regulates the tryptophan metabolic pathway through gut microbiota modulation [], effectively inhibiting the accumulation of the harmful metabolite kynurenine in the mouse hippocampus [], thereby averting its associated neurotoxicity, excitotoxicity, and neuroinflammatory responses. Furthermore, CGA can ameliorate hippocampus-dependent spatial memory-related immune profiles through the Nrf2/PPAR signaling pathway [] ().

Neuroinflammation refers to a series of immune responses mediated by neuroimmune cells within the central nervous system, playing a crucial role in the development of cognitive dysfunction. The polarization state of microglia is considered the core link in regulating the inflammatory process. Under pathological conditions, resting microglia become activated and polarize into pro-inflammatory (M1) and anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotypes. M1 microglia secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines capable of damaging neuronal cells, whereas M2 microglia suppress inflammation and exert neuroprotective effects. Therefore, shifting microglia towards the M2 phenotype has been recognized as a critical therapeutic strategy for neuroinflammatory conditions. Studies have shown that CGA can inhibit BV-2 microglial polarization toward the M1 phenotype in vitro and promote M2 polarization, thereby attenuating neuroinflammation and ameliorating cognitive dysfunction [].

However, the regulatory network of neuroinflammation extends far beyond intrinsic phenotypic switching of microglia. During the inflammatory cascade, activated microglia release various chemokines that recruit peripheral immune cells (e.g., neutrophils) into the central nervous system []. Further research has demonstrated that human neutrophil elastase (HNE), released by neutrophils, acts as a key inflammatory protease [,] that may indirectly contribute to microglia, promote pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and damage neuronal and synaptic function, thereby exacerbating cognitive impairment. Consequently, inhibiting HNE activity represents another potential intervention target. Notably, CGA has been confirmed to effectively inhibit HNE activity [].

In terms of inflammatory signal transduction, the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway is a recognized key inflammatory cascade. Activation of this pathway releases large quantities of inflammatory cytokines, disrupts blood–brain barrier and cerebral white matter integrity, and eventually leads to cognitive impairment []. CGA-enriched coffee can downregulate the TLR4/NF-κB pathway, attenuating trimethyltin chloride (TMT)-induced neuroinflammation [], and inhibiting the excessive activation of astrocytes and microglia. Additionally, SRC, an upstream activator of NF-κB, also participates in inflammatory signal transduction and is closely associated with cognitive deficits [,,]. CGA in chokeberry and bilberry fruit extracts may have been demonstrated to exert a potent inhibitory effect on Src activity in prior research []. (). However, this remains to be demonstrated using isolated CGA in neuronal or cognitive models. It is noteworthy that the neuroinflammatory attenuation by CGA may involve broader systemic immune regulation, as it can significantly affect pathways related to immune diseases (ko05322) and the immune system (ko04610) [].

Oxidative stress drives neuronal vulnerability and disrupts the basal metabolic homeostasis essential for neuronal survival, thereby accelerating the pathological process of neurodegenerative diseases and ultimately leading to progressive cognitive decline []. CGA, by virtue of its distinctive phenolic hydroxyl structure, possesses multi-layered antioxidant capabilities and has been demonstrated to effectively mitigate oxidative damage across various pathological models [].

In terms of direct free radical scavenging, the phenolic hydroxyl groups in the CGA molecule can rapidly react with free radicals, donating hydrogen atoms to neutralize hydroxyl radicals and superoxide anions, thereby suppressing their activity []. CGA can also form protein-polyphenol complexes through hydrogen bonding, thickening the interfacial layer and limiting free radical diffusion, thus enhancing the antioxidant capacity of proteins []. Moreover, CGA exhibits DPPH radical scavenging activity [], and can both scavenge oxidizing radicals and repair pre-formed oxidizing radical adducts of purine nucleotides through fast electron transfer []. In peroxynitrite-related pathological processes, CGA has also been reported to possess scavenging capacity, potentially conferring protective effects in immature brain ischemia models [,].

At the level of oxidative enzyme activity regulation, CGA can downregulate the expression of NADPH oxidase (NOX) and dual oxidase 2 (DUOX2), inhibiting mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production []. Simultaneously, CGA can bind non-covalently to the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor site of xanthine oxidase, interfering with the electron transfer process and thereby inhibiting the xanthine oxidation reaction [,].

Regarding the endogenous antioxidant system, existing studies indicate that CGA can upregulate the expression of copper/zinc superoxide dismutase (SOD1) and manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), reverse the decline in superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) activities caused by cerebral ischemia or glutamate exposure, and increase the levels of malondialdehyde (MDA), the terminal product of lipid peroxidation [,,,]. Additionally, CGA also modulates the expression of thioredoxin, further participating in the ROS clearance process [].

At the signaling pathway level, CGA can activate the Nrf2/ARE signaling pathway, promoting Nrf2 nuclear translocation and increasing the expression of its downstream targets heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), thereby protecting against isoflurane (ISO)-induced cognitive impairment [] ().

Furthermore, CGA can display indirect antioxidant effects via the regulation of metal ions. It can reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ [], and inhibit Fe2+ autoxidation [].

Autophagy is a cellular mechanism wherein lysosomes are employed to break down and recycle damaged organelles and macromolecules. Its functional homeostasis is critical for maintaining the normal physiological activities of neurons. Dysregulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway has been identified as an important pathological mechanism of cognitive dysfunction. In this pathway, p62/SQSTM1, as a multifunctional scaffold protein, mediates the targeted delivery of ubiquitinated protein aggregates to autophagosomes by binding microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3). The accumulation of p62 is commonly regarded as a direct marker of blocked autophagic flux []. Furthermore, pathological changes such as amyloid-β (Aβ25–35) deposition and hyperphosphorylation and aggregation of Tau protein can both induce autophagy and, conversely, be exacerbated by impaired autophagic clearance.

The activity of the autophagy-lysosome pathway is finely modulated by multiple signaling molecules. Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase predominantly localized to the lysosomal membrane, is a key negative regulator of autophagy initiation. Transcription factor EB (TFEB), as the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, is phosphorylated by mTORC1 at multiple serine residues, including Ser211. Phosphorylation at Ser211 promotes TFEB association with 14-3-3 proteins and its retention in the cytoplasm []. Inhibition of mTORC1 results in TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, thereby activating the autophagy-lysosome pathway. Cathepsin D, the most abundant aspartyl protease in lysosomes, is activated only under acidic conditions and is responsible for degrading intracellular misfolded or aggregated proteins, playing a core role in the terminal degradation phase of the autophagy-lysosome pathway [].

Targeting the aforementioned regulatory network, the study by Lijuan Gao et al. revealed the neuroprotective mechanism of CGA. They found that CGA treatment restored autophagic flux homeostasis in the brains of APP/PS1 Alzheimer’s disease model mice by inhibiting the mTOR/TFEB signaling pathway [], thereby ameliorating cognitive impairment. Specifically, CGA significantly inhibited the excessive autophagosome formation induced by Aβ25–35 in SH-SY5Y cells, enhanced lysosomal acidification and degradative activity, and upregulated cathepsin D protein expression [,]. In terms of autophagic flux dynamics, the LC3-II/I ratio reflects the steady-state abundance of autophagosomes rather than flux per se. CGA treatment decreased the LC3-II/I ratio and lowered p62 protein levels, and this was accompanied by increased mCherry+GFP− puncta, enhanced lysosomal function, and CQ-sensitive protection, suggesting effective clearance of accumulated autophagosomes and restoration of impaired autophagic flux [].

Notably, transcriptional dysregulation of autophagy-related genes (ATG101, ATG13, ULK1, SQSTM1/p62, and ATG5) can lead to defective autophagosome formation, impaired lysosomal degradation, and interrupted mitophagy. Among these, autophagosome formation depends on the ATG5 protein, whose reduced expression inhibits autophagy. Mitophagy is primarily mediated by PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), which tags damaged mitochondria for selective clearance, while mitofusin 2 (MFN2) maintains mitochondrial network integrity by mediating outer mitochondrial membrane fusion. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK, encoded by the PRKAA1 gene), as a cellular energy sensor, can initiate autophagy by inhibiting mTOR activity. The research by Apoorv Sharma et al. further elucidated the mechanism of CGA at the gene expression level: CGA reduced PINK1 expression, thereby alleviating Aβ1–42-induced mitophagy, and upregulated MFN2 to restore mitochondrial fusion. At the autophagy pathway level, following CGA treatment, PRKAA1 (AMPK) mRNA levels were elevated, MTOR mRNA levels were decreased, and the transcriptional expression of ATG101, ATG13, ULK1, and SQSTM1 (p62) was increased, while ATG5 levels exhibited a declining trend [] ().

CGA can ameliorate cognitive function by inhibiting neuronal apoptosis, and its protective effects have been validated in both oxidative stress and excitotoxicity models. At the mechanistic level, CGA primarily targets members of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family: it can inhibit the aberrant phosphorylation of c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and p38 MAPK induced by hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), thereby blocking the initiation of apoptotic signaling []. More importantly, CGA exhibits bidirectional regulatory characteristics—while blocking death signals, it can also, as suggested by indirect evidence, dose-dependently reverse the downregulation of ERK1/2 and Akt protein expression, thereby reactivating cell survival signaling []. The combined actions of these two pathways ultimately reverse key events in the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway, including upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2, downregulation of the pro-apoptotic protein Bad, and inhibition of cytochrome c release into the cytoplasm [,]. Ultimately, these changes preserve pro-caspase-3 and suppress its cleavage into active caspase-3, thereby diminishing neuronal nuclear condensation and DNA fragmentation [] ().

In in vivo studies, Yu Xi et al. found that oral CGA administration can reverse neuronal damage in the mouse hippocampal CA1 region and dentate gyrus (DG) via the JNK/c-Jun pathway, specifically manifesting as reduced eosinophilic cytoplasm, inhibited nuclear pyknosis and karyolysis, and abundant Nissl substance in surviving neurons []. Notably, aberrant activation of the JNK/c-Jun pathway is strongly linked to heightened neuronal apoptosis and is regarded as one of the key pathological causes of neurodegenerative diseases [], providing an important theoretical basis for the intervention value of CGA ().

Amyloid-β (Aβ) is produced through sequential proteolytic processing of amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β-secretase (primarily β-site APP cleaving enzyme 1, BACE1) and γ-secretase. Under physiological conditions, the synthesis and removal of Aβ exist in dynamic equilibrium; however, when brain extracellular Aβ levels become abnormally elevated, they significantly inhibit hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP), thereby constituting one of the key initiating factors of memory impairment []. These excessively accumulated Aβ monomers have a high propensity for self-assembly, forming soluble oligomers—the most neurotoxic species—which further reassemble into protofibrils and ultimately deposit as insoluble amyloid plaques []. More importantly, excessive Aβ accumulation not only directly induces synaptic toxicity and neurotoxicity but also drives tau phosphorylation and aggregation, promoting the generation of neurofibrillary tangles, eventually leading to cognitive impairment [].

Targeting the aforementioned pathological cascade, multiple in vivo studies in recent years have revealed the multi-faceted intervention potential of coffee polyphenols, isolated 5-CQA, and solanesol-CGA nanomicelle formulations in anti-Alzheimer’s therapy. Current evidence indicates that these agents can act on both the downstream stages of Aβ aggregation and its clearance pathways. Specifically, evidence obtained with coffee polyphenols has shown that these polyphenols can directly degrade pre-formed Aβ protofibrils and promote their disaggregation []. Evidence obtained with isolated 5-CQA has shown that this compound modulates brain Aβ clearance mechanisms, significantly reducing Aβ deposition and plaque burden in APP/PS2 transgenic mouse models, while effectively improving cognitive behavior and attenuating neuronal loss []. In addition, Chenchen Wang et al. further employed nano-delivery technology to construct CI@SPK nanomicelles based on solanesol and CGA; this solanesol-CGA nanomicelle formulation not only reduced Aβ plaque burden in APP/PS1 mice but also significantly inhibited neuroinflammatory responses, thereby synergistically ameliorating learning and memory deficits []. The evidence from in vivo and in vitro studies on these mechanisms has been systematically summarized in .

Although in vitro and in vivo experimental evidence is encouraging, clinical evidence that chlorogenic acid (CGA) improves cognitive function remains limited. Among the human randomized controlled trials (RCTs) relevant to CGA and cognition from which specific trial details could be extracted, the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by Saitou et al. is the most directly informative []. This trial assigned 38 healthy participants to either a CGA-added beverage group or a placebo group for 16 weeks, and cognitive function was assessed using the Japanese version of CNS Vital Signs (Cognitrax) []. The CGA group showed significantly greater increases in Cognitrax domain scores for motor speed, psychomotor speed, and executive function than the placebo group, together with improved shifting attention test scores; blood analyses also showed increased levels of apolipoprotein A1 and transthyretin, which are considered candidate biomarkers of early cognitive decline []. However, this trial has clear limitations: a small sample size; healthy participants rather than patients with diagnosed cognitive impairment or dementia; a short intervention period of only 16 weeks; and use of a CGA-added beverage rather than a purified CGA supplement, making generalization to other formulations and populations difficult []. More importantly, the trial did not report the absolute daily CGA dose, did not measure circulating CGA or its metabolite concentrations, and did not assess brain exposure []. Therefore, even though cognitive-related endpoints improved, the dose–response relationship between intake, circulating exposure, and central exposure cannot be determined.

Apart from the above trial, human CGA RCTs with extractable sample sizes, formulations, doses, and cognitive endpoints remain scarce; no studies were identified that directly compared CGA concentrations used in cell experiments with achievable human circulating or brain exposure. The currently extractable preclinical evidence is mainly from animal dosing studies. For example, in a gerbil model of transient forebrain ischemia, pretreatment with 30 mg/kg CGA attenuated cognitive impairment and exerted neuroprotective effects []; in a zebrafish model of hyperglycemia combined with chronic stress, 50, 100, or 200 mg/kg CGA modulated antioxidant defense and improved indices related to brain homeostasis []; and in scopolamine-induced memory-deficit mice, co-administration of CGA with cilomilast reversed cognitive deficits and reduced amyloid beta accumulation and neuroinflammatory markers []. The doses used in these animal studies cannot be directly converted to the human exposure that was not reported in the RCT, and bridging data among cellular concentrations, human circulating concentrations, and brain tissue concentrations are lacking.

In addition, formulation differences (purified supplements versus coffee or food matrices) have rarely been compared in the available evidence, and the only RCT from which details could be extracted used a CGA-added beverage, further limiting extrapolation []. Doses used in experimental studies are generally much higher than those achievable through habitual dietary intake; therefore, it remains unclear whether the preclinical effects are relevant to habitual dietary consumption [,,]. Safety data for long-term high-dose supplementation also remain scarce.

Therefore, these limitations should be carefully considered when interpreting the current evidence. Future studies should include larger and more diverse populations, clearly report CGA dose, formulation, and intervention duration, directly measure circulating metabolites and brain exposure, establish quantitative comparisons between preclinical concentrations/doses and human achievable exposure, and systematically evaluate the safety of long-term high-dose supplementation [].

This review summarizes the potential mechanisms by which CGA may ameliorate cognitive impairment. At present, the evidence supporting these mechanisms is predominantly preclinical. Preclinical studies suggest that CGA may exert protective effects via multiple pathways, including neuroprotection, modulation of gut microbiota composition and metabolites, suppression of neuroinflammation, reduction of oxidative stress injury, regulation of autophagy and apoptosis, and inhibition of Aβ formation. The implicated signaling pathways include the JNK/c-Jun, TLR4/NF-κB, Nrf2/PPAR, Nrf2/ARE, and mTOR/TFEB pathways, among others. Although the proposed mechanisms of action of CGA are broad, encompassing diverse pathways and targets, clinical research on CGA in patients with cognitive impairment remains limited. There is also a lack of comprehensive studies on the safety, toxicity, teratogenicity, and carcinogenicity of CGA. Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying certain pathways still require further investigation. Additional preclinical and clinical studies are needed to determine whether CGA is therapeutically effective in patients with cognitive impairment.

neuroscience.title: Toward Robust and Reliable Muscle Synergy Analysis: A Methodological Survey of Synergy Extraction
neuroscience.abstract: Muscle synergy analysis has been widely applied in neuroscience, biomechanics, rehabilitation, and robotics. However, the reliability of muscle synergy extraction remains a critical issue, as results are highly sensitive to variations in experimental design, surface electromyography preprocessing, factorization algorithms, and the determination of the number of synergies. This narrative methodological review examines the key factors that influence the robustness and reliability of muscle synergies within the framework of limb neuromechanical controllers across anatomical regions and task contexts. By analyzing the current state of research in this field, we first summarize the conceptual and methodological foundations of muscle synergy analysis and then critically examine the factors that influence its robustness and reliability. This review provides practical recommendations to enhance methodological rigor, including greater methodological harmonization and transparent reporting of experimental protocols, the use of musculoskeletal simulation to evaluate muscle selection strategies, and the refinement of synergy extraction techniques. These insights aim to improve the reliability and robustness of muscle synergy analysis and promote its application in robotics, human–machine interfacing, and computational motor control.
neuroscience.text:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) is widely used in control applications because it provides a noninvasive, wearable, high-temporal-resolution means of capturing neuromuscular intent, enabling proportional and intuitive interfaces for limb assistive technologies []. In recent decades, sEMG has been increasingly applied in rehabilitation and clinical settings, including post-stroke and spinal cord injury therapy, orthopedic and neuromuscular disorder treatment, myoelectric prostheses, and robotic exoskeletons []. These human–machine interfaces (HMIs) and exoskeleton systems can support motor rehabilitation, improve functional independence, and augment human capabilities across clinical, industrial, and daily-life contexts.

Nevertheless, sEMG-based control faces several well-known challenges, including high-dimensional and redundant multimuscle signals; low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) caused by cross-talk and motion artifacts; pronounced nonstationarity and inter-/intra-session drift driven by electrode shift, skin impedance changes, and fatigue; and strong subject- and task-dependence that complicate cross-user and cross-task generalization []. As the number of controlled degrees of freedom (DOFs) increases and tasks become more diverse, control pipelines must process larger numbers of channels while adapting to time-varying signal characteristics, thereby increasing computational burden and reducing generalizability. Among these challenges, achieving robust and reliable musculoskeletal control under complex, disturbance-rich conditions with pronounced interindividual variability remains a primary bottleneck.

Given that simultaneous multi-DOF control using sEMG depends on the identification of complex intermuscular interactions, a principled way to mitigate these difficulties is to leverage muscle synergies. Muscle synergies are commonly described as low-dimensional modules that capture coordinated muscle-activation patterns and provide an interpretable representation of neuromuscular control []. The synergy framework addresses a fundamental problem in motor control: how the central nervous system (CNS) manages the massive redundancy of the musculoskeletal system. Rather than commanding individual muscles independently, the CNS has been hypothesized to activate groups of muscles as functional and coordinated modules [,,,,,]. In the commonly used matrix formulation, the preprocessed sEMG data X ∈ ℝ(m×N), where m denotes the number of recorded muscles and N denotes the number of sampled time points, is approximated asX ≈ WC + e(1)

Here, W ∈ ℝ(m×k) contains time-invariant muscle-weighting vectors, whereas C ∈ ℝ(k×N) contains time-varying activation coefficients; k is the number of extracted synergies and e denotes the reconstruction residual. Alternative formulations explicitly encode temporal structure, e.g., time-varying or spatiotemporal synergies that allow the patterns (or temporal kernels) to evolve over time, thus extending the basic factorization. By reducing dimensionality without discarding physiologically meaningful structure, synergies reduce the control burden while preserving task flexibility, improve noise tolerance, stabilize estimation across sessions, lower the number of learnable parameters, and facilitate real-time control. Embedding this modular representation within synergy-based neuromuscular controllers constrains estimation and control within a biologically plausible subspace.

Recent studies have increasingly integrated such synergy representations into neuromuscular controllers and musculoskeletal models, demonstrating their potential to reproduce coordinated muscle activation patterns in both simulated and experimental limb motor tasks. For example, Ruckert et al. employed time-varying synergies to accomplish sagittal-plane reaching in an open-loop scheme []. Chen et al. introduced a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework with memory and attention while constraining the policy to a predefined set of synergies derived from simulation, thus improving learning under imperfect observations but reducing physiological interpretability []. Han et al. addressed the challenge of learning human-like motor skills in embodied musculoskeletal models arising from high-dimensional and redundant muscle actuation []. Liu et al. proposed BioSynGrasp, a bio-inspired reinforcement learning framework to address the challenges of high-dimensional, coupled, and nonlinear control in anthropomorphic musculoskeletal robots during dexterous manipulation []. From an engineering perspective, instability in synergy structure can undermine the development of robust and reusable controllers for prosthetic and robotic applications. Although several studies have examined sources of inconsistency, important issues remain unresolved. These advances underscore the promise of synergy-informed neuromuscular control methods. However, they also show that synergy extraction is sensitive to methodological choices, raising concerns about robustness, consistency, and reliability.

Beyond proof-of-concept control, the broader literature in neuroscience, bio-inspired machine control, and engineering applications also demonstrates substantial promise for synergy-based intelligent systems. Notably, multiple studies report task dependence of synergies [,,]. When performing the same or similar biomechanical tasks, the number and structure of muscle synergies identified across repeated movements would be expected to show reasonable consistency. However, large variability exists within and across studies for a given task, even for healthy individuals []. For tasks like postural control [], gait [,,], and upper-extremity movement [] in healthy individuals, a low-dimensional representation consisting of approximately 4–6 synergies has been consistently identified [,]. However, the exact number and structure of synergies remain dependent on the task, population, anatomical region, recording set, and analytical pipeline. In addition, previous studies have shown substantial variability in the number of extracted muscle synergies in healthy individuals during walking, ranging from 2 to 6 [,,]. Lencioni et al. [] reported that, among 12 healthy subjects, 58% exhibited four muscle synergies and 42% exhibited three, while a similar distribution was observed in 17 persons with multiple sclerosis. Goudriaan et al. [] did not directly determine the number of synergies but assessed motor-control complexity using the variance accounted for by one synergy (VAF). Moreover, variability in muscle synergies was observed during upper-extremity reaching tasks. The reliability and repeatability of muscle synergies in healthy individuals are essential in evaluating patients’ functional performance after rehabilitation []. In patient populations, the number of muscle synergies is typically in the range of 2 to 5 []. Thus, it is important to note that these muscle synergies might not be pathological. This overlap makes it difficult to distinguish disease-related changes from methodological variation when comparing healthy and clinical populations []. Therefore, synergy number alone may be insufficient for identifying functional impairment in clinical populations. Moreover, the robustness of synergy estimates during genuinely multi-DOF limb movements has been discussed far less thoroughly [].

Despite growing interest, a persistent and critical challenge remains unresolved: the lack of methodological consistency and limited reliability across studies. Muscle synergies are typically extracted from sEMG signals by applying different factorization techniques. However, multiple methodological factors can influence the resulting synergy structure. In practice, synergy analyses vary widely in experimental design, acquisition protocols, electrode placement, and preprocessing (e.g., filtering and normalization) [,,,,], as well as in decomposition algorithms and criteria for determining the number of synergies [,]. Comprehensive sEMG coverage is often infeasible, particularly for deep or small muscles, due to electrode and anatomical constraints; combined with heterogeneous setups and pipelines, this yields poor reproducibility and limits cross-study comparability []. Outcomes may be sensitive to methodological choices at every stage; variation in any step can alter the inferred synergy structure and complicate cross-study comparison. Physiologically, this complicates discrimination between true neural adaptations and methodological artifacts when comparing populations or tasks [,,]. Pinpointing the most influential factors and quantifying how sensitive synergy estimates are to them is critical for reproducibility and for establishing muscle synergies as a dependable instrument in motor control.

In response to these issues, this review examines the methodological landscape of muscle synergy extraction within the framework of limb neuromechanical controllers. Whereas prior surveys by Turpin et al. [] and Cheung et al. [] synthesize broad evidence on muscle synergies, our focus is deliberately narrower: we identify and critically assess the specific methodological factors that determine the reliability and robustness of muscle-synergy analysis. Specifically, we analyze how choices across five dimensions shape decomposition outcomes: (1) experimental/acquisition design; (2) sEMG preprocessing and normalization; (3) factorization models and regularization, including time-varying and spatiotemporal variants; (4) model-order selection and stability; and (5) cross-trial/session/subject alignment and strategies for handling nonstationarity. We evaluate their impact on quantitative metrics (e.g., VAF and estimated module number) and qualitative properties. We conclude with recommendations that distinguish minimum reporting requirements from context-dependent analytical choices, with the aim of improving methodological consistency and physiological interpretability in muscle synergy analysis. Ultimately, clarifying how methodological choices influence synergy reliability can help bridge the gap between muscle-synergy analysis and its practical application in limb neuromechanical control, clinical rehabilitation, and engineering applications. Such methodological improvements may support the development of a more reproducible, interpretable, and broadly applicable synergy-based framework in related fields.

To ensure terminological consistency throughout this review, the terms robustness, reliability, repeatability, reproducibility, stability, and similarity are distinguished according to their experimental context and intended interpretation, as shown in . Robustness refers to the extent to which extracted synergy results remain consistent under reasonable methodological variations. Reliability refers to the consistency of repeated measurements and is generally evaluated using repeated-measures assessments. Repeatability describes consistency under essentially identical experimental and analytical conditions, whereas reproducibility refers to the ability to obtain comparable results when relevant conditions differ, such as across sessions, laboratories, acquisition systems, or analytical settings. Stability refers primarily to the consistency of an extracted solution across repeated algorithmic runs, resampling, different initializations, or parameter variations, whereas similarity describes the quantitative resemblance between extracted synergy structures, as assessed by measures such as vector correlation, cosine similarity, or spatial similarity. Physiological validity refers to the extent to which the extracted mathematical modules reflect genuine neural control strategies, rather than patterns introduced by the decomposition algorithm or data-processing procedures.

These terms were retained when explicitly used in the original studies reviewed in this manuscript. However, their operational definitions, quantitative criteria, and thresholds vary across studies. Accordingly, reported evaluation metrics, cutoff values, and analytical procedures should be interpreted within the methodological context of each study. Rigorous statistical reporting, including 95% confidence intervals, specification of the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) model where applicable, and effect sizes (e.g., Cohen’s d), is recommended to support quantitative interpretation. Nevertheless, universally accepted absolute thresholds are not currently available across all muscle synergy extraction methods. Therefore, study-specific thresholds, equivalence bounds, and decision criteria should be predefined and clearly reported according to the analytical approach, study design, and biomechanical characteristics of the task.

The execution of human voluntary movements requires coordinated interactions between the nervous and musculoskeletal systems [,], as shown in . Neural processing encompasses several stages at different levels of the nervous system (i.e., cortical and spinal) and the resultant synaptic inputs are transmitted to spinal motor neuron pools []. Then, the spinal motor neurons are recruited to activate the corresponding muscles to produce coordinated motions. One major challenge is how the CNS deals with this highly redundant and nonlinear system, which includes numerous degrees of freedom and motor units, to generate flexible and adaptive movements []. A long-standing hypothesis in motor control is that the CNS handles the high dimensionality of muscle activations with a hierarchical architecture composed of discrete basic motor modules []. From the perspective of motor control of complex systems, a hierarchical decomposition with modules, or building blocks, is employed as the most effective strategy to perform tasks []. Over the past century, several primitive hypotheses have been proposed about the modular organization underlying movement generation, i.e., the half-center model [], neuromotor synergies [], and unit burst generators []. More importantly, some studies have demonstrated that the output of a module can be characterized as a force field generated by discrete groups of coordinately activated muscles, commonly described as muscle modules or synergies [,]. These basic organizational principles can be used to interpret the rhythmic behaviors generated at the spinal cord level.

Building upon these early theoretical foundations, researchers have increasingly turned to animal models to explore the modular basis of motor control. Studies in animal models, including turtles [], frogs [,], rats, and cats [], have provided substantial evidence. With different approaches such as micro-stimulation of the spinal cord [], N-methyl-D-aspartate iontophoresis [], and examination of natural behaviors in intact and deafferented animals, evidence supports the concept that modular organizations can generate motor behaviors. In other words, these behaviors were generated by simultaneously recruiting and coordinating sets of muscles, thus supporting the hypothesis of modular organizations in motor control. The CNS may utilize the modular organization shown in  to generate motor commands. By doing so, it can substantially reduce computational load and help to address the redundancy inherent in motor control [,,]. Evidence has also emerged suggesting that similar organizational principles may contribute to the generation of voluntary movement in humans. A previous study suggested that muscle synergies were structured in the brainstem or spinal cord []. Furthermore, the organization of muscle synergies develops and adapts progressively across different developmental stages, from early childhood to adulthood.

Muscle synergy analysis infers control strategies from the variability and coordination of multi-muscle sEMG recorded during movement. A typical pipeline comprises (i) acquiring sEMG from multiple muscles during one or more behaviors; (ii) preprocessing to attenuate environmental noise, baseline drift, and electrode or skin motion artifacts [,,]; (iii) factorizing the processed sEMG to estimate the synergy structure W and activation coefficients C; (iv) selecting an appropriate number of synergies; and (v) evaluating the extracted synergies and their downstream performance []. Each step can affect robustness and reliability—through experimental design, the number and selection of muscles [,], preprocessing choices [], factorization techniques [,], and model-order criteria, among others. Next, this review analyzes these methodological dimensions within that pipeline, as shown in , and the key methodological factors affecting synergy extraction are summarized in .

The concept of muscle synergies has been formalized through various mathematical frameworks aimed at decomposing complex EMG signals into lower-dimensional representations of motor control. Depending on how temporal and spatial structures are represented, synergy models are typically grouped into three primary types that characterize coordination at different levels: spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dimensions []. The first category comprises synergies identified as fixed vectors, which are often referred to as synchronous synergies (i.e., time-invariant, or spatial muscle synergies). The synchronous synergies are built from synergistic groups of muscles activated with a fixed time course []. In contrast, the temporal synergy model assumes that activations of the synergies are sequenced similarly across movement cycles or tasks, and the weightings can vary in time. It represents invariant muscle activation waveforms across muscles and conditions [,]. Another proposed formulation is spatiotemporal muscle synergy, in which synergy vectors are both shifted in amplitude and scaled in time [,]. Collectively, these formulations provide complementary perspectives on how the CNS may organize muscle activations.

A major source of inconsistency across studies is that synergy estimates depend strongly on the chosen model class: the inferred number and structure of synergies, their stability, and cross-study comparability can all change with spatial vs. temporal vs. spatiotemporal assumptions. Spatial modules are often hypothesized to reflect spinal/corticospinal primitives, whereas time-varying patterns may relate to higher-level cortical–cerebellar coordination. Consequently, careful model selection and transparent reporting of assumptions are essential for interpretable, comparable synergy analysis.

The acquisition of high-quality EMG data is the foundation for reliable synergy extraction. Experimental design decisions, including the number of muscles recorded, electrode configuration, task protocol, and inter-individual variability, strongly influence both the signal quality and the stability of subsequent factorization [,]. For upper-limb studies, EMG signals are typically recorded from multiple muscles spanning the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints to capture inter-joint coordination. However, anatomical constraints, sensor placement limitations, and task-specific variability often prevent comprehensive muscle coverage. For instance, deep or small muscles (e.g., iliopsoas) are difficult to measure using surface electrodes but may still contribute substantially to motor coordination [].

Currently, no standardized guideline defines how many or which muscles should be included in EMG recordings for synergy analysis []. In practice, upper-limb studies typically record between 8 and 19 muscles [,,], while gait and lower-limb analyses typically include 8–16 muscles [,]. Muscle selection often represents a balance between anatomical coverage, task relevance, and signal quality. To ensure comparability across studies, it is critical to document muscle selection, electrode placement, and other relevant acquisition parameters. Other factors affecting EMG acquisition include (1) electrode placement and inter-electrode distance, which determine selectivity and cross-talk sensitivity; (2) task design, such as movement direction, load, or speed, influencing activation timing; (3) participant-related factors, including muscle morphology, skin impedance, fatigue, and learning effects; (4) instrumentation parameters, such as sampling frequency, filtering (20–450 Hz), and differential amplification to improve SNR.

Given the complexity of the musculoskeletal system, which comprises more than 600 muscles [,], it is not feasible to record the activation of all muscles contributing to complex upper-limb tasks. Therefore, EMG acquisition should aim for representative rather than complete muscle coverage, ensuring that the recorded muscle set sufficiently captures the functional synergies relevant to the task. Clear reporting of experimental configurations, electrode placement, and participant-specific adjustments is essential for reproducibility and facilitating cross-study comparisons.

sEMG provides physiological information on muscle activation that can be combined with computational methods to investigate neuromuscular coordination []. The characteristics of sEMG signals, especially the amplitude, temporal and frequency features, might be affected by the skin condition, electrode placement, movement artifacts, and other noise sources that are inherent and inevitable. For example, cross-talk among sEMG channels would be mistakenly treated as synergistic activity and influence muscle synergy structure [,,]. In addition, environmental and processing factors might affect the estimation of linear envelopes during sEMG measurement. Hence, a high-quality signal is an important foundation for sEMG applications []. To ensure the quality of the signal, the acquisition procedures and recommendations proposed by the Surface Electromyography for the Non-Invasive Assessment of Muscles project (SENIAM) were generally followed [,]. The objective of sEMG preprocessing is to acquire an accurate description of muscle activation for factorization across various tasks.

To ensure high-quality signals for muscle synergy extraction, sEMG preprocessing must reliably separate physiological muscle activation from environmental noise and movement artifacts. Following standard SENIAM recommendations, the processing pipeline typically follows a strict sequential structure:(1)Raw-EMG Filtering: Raw signals are first processed using a band-pass filter to attenuate motion artifacts and high-frequency noise. High-pass (HP) cutoffs typically range from 5 to 20 Hz [] (sometimes up to 50 Hz [,,] in the presence of severe artifacts), with low-pass (LP) cutoffs set at approximately 400–500 Hz. If low-frequency drift persists, baseline correction is performed prior to further processing; in cases of severe artifacts, channel rejection or segment masking is preferred over overly aggressive filtering.(2)Rectification: The filtered raw signal is then subjected to full-wave rectification.(3)Envelope Generation: A separate LP filter is subsequently applied to the rectified signal to extract the linear envelope. Cutoff frequencies at this stage typically range from 2 to 15 Hz [,,,,]. Because the reviewed literature does not support a single setting, this specific cutoff must be explicitly tailored to the task dynamics and analytical objectives, balancing necessary temporal resolution with noise suppression [,].(4)Temporal Normalization: To facilitate comparison across trials, sessions, and subjects, the envelope profiles are often aligned to specific kinematic events and time-normalized (e.g., to 100% of a movement cycle).(5)Amplitude Normalization: This final step is required to mitigate inter-subject and inter-session variability. Common scaling options include the maximum amplitude of the signal itself (SELF) [,,,], maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) [,], median trial maximums [], or unit variance scaling [,,]. Unit variance normalization is frequently preferred as it prevents high-variance muscles from dominating the decomposition, yielding more stable synergy patterns [,]. However, because comparative studies show varying results and no universal standard exists, the normalization method remains highly context-dependent [].
