Preprocessing choices at every stage can alter the spectral and temporal characteristics of the data and thereby influence synergy weights, activation profiles, and the estimated number of synergies. Transparent reporting of the full processing sequence and its consistent application are essential for reproducible synergy extraction [].

Common dimensionality-reduction methods for extracting muscle synergies from preprocessed sEMG include independent component analysis (ICA), nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) [], principal component analysis (PCA) [], and factor analysis (FA) []. Depending on the assumptions and implementation of each method, these matrix factorization approaches construct lower-dimensional representations of muscle activation patterns according to different statistical or optimization objectives [].

For instance, PCA constrains the columns of W to be orthonormal and the rows of C to be orthogonal to each other. The PCA orthogonal assumption permits negative values in the synergy subspace []. PCA identifies orthogonal components that sequentially maximize the variance explained in the data []. Unlike PCA, ICA assumes that muscle synergies represent independent sources of information []. ICA is designed to extract statistically independent components, typically by first whitening the data to remove second-order correlations and then rotating the whitened data to maximize statistical independence or non-Gaussianity among the extracted components. Thus, whitening alone does not establish independence but provides a preprocessing step for subsequent independent-component estimation.

Similarly to PCA, FA employs eigenvalue decomposition to obtain eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [] and seeks the smallest set of synergies to explain the common variance of a set of muscles. It is noteworthy that the number of degrees of freedom can affect the number of basis vectors in the muscle synergy model when assessed using FA. NMF is a machine-learning method that decomposes a high-dimensional nonnegative matrix into two nonnegative matrices []. A distinctive feature of NMF is its non-negativity constraint, which is compatible with the nonnegative nature of muscle activation amplitudes and facilitates an additive representation of muscle coordination patterns. Because the NMF optimization problem is non-convex, factor initialization can affect convergence and the resulting solution. Traditional implementations often use random nonnegative initializations, and different initializations may converge to different local optima. Accordingly, multiple runs with different initializations are commonly performed, and candidate solutions should be evaluated using predefined reconstruction-error, stability, or combined criteria. Singular value decomposition (SVD)-based initialization and sparse NMF constraints may improve convergence behavior or promote sparsity, depending on the analytical objective []. In addition to conventional NMF, alternative optimization and factorization approaches have been explored, including improved optimization strategies [], multivariate curve resolution–alternating least squares (MCR-ALS) [], and mixed matrix factorization (MMF) [].

Beyond conventional linear matrix decomposition methods, several advanced models and computational frameworks have been developed to address specific limitations of muscle synergy analysis. These approaches should not be considered universally superior to linear methods. Their suitability depends on the balance between identifiability, physiological plausibility, and interpretability, robustness to noise and methodological perturbations, and computational burden.

Probabilistic and Bayesian frameworks incorporate an explicit noise model and can quantify uncertainty in model parameters and, in some formulations, in the number of synergies. This feature may improve the interpretation of uncertain or noisy data and provide a principled basis for model comparison. However, the identifiability of the extracted synergies depends strongly on the assumed likelihood, prior distributions, model constraints, and available data quantity. Posterior inference and model comparison may also require substantially greater computational resources than conventional NMF.

Tensor-based decomposition extends matrix factorization to multidimensional data arrays and can preserve task-, trial-, and subject-specific structures that may be lost when the data are collapsed into a two-dimensional matrix []. This may better preserve the representation of spatiotemporal and cross-condition relationships. However, tensor methods require careful alignment of data dimensions and appropriate selection of tensor rank. Their identifiability and robustness depend on uniqueness conditions, preprocessing quality, missing-data structure, and imposed constraints. The additional data modes and parameters also increase computational complexity.

Nonlinear and deep latent-variable models, including autoencoder-based approaches, can represent nonlinear relationships in EMG data that may not be adequately captured by linear decomposition methods []. They may improve reconstruction or prediction under particular datasets and noise conditions, but high reconstruction performance should not be equated with physiological validity. Their robustness to distribution shifts, changes in initialization, and experimental perturbations remains data-dependent. These models generally require more training data and computational resources, and their latent variables may be difficult to identify uniquely or interpret physiologically.

Time-varying synergy models explicitly represent temporal changes in muscle coordination and are therefore particularly relevant to dynamic motor behaviors, although this additional flexibility increases model complexity [,]. By allowing synergy weights or activation profiles to evolve over time, these models can describe changes in muscle coordination that are not represented by time-invariant linear models. The additional temporal parameters may also increase computational burden. Because time-varying synergy weights and activation coefficients may be partially confounded, their identifiability requires appropriate constraints, regularization, or independent validation. Without such safeguards, the increased flexibility may reduce solution stability and increase the risk of overfitting.

Overall, these methods represent high-dimensional EMG signals using lower-dimensional or structured latent components, but their differing assumptions and optimization objectives necessitate evaluation across multiple dimensions, including reconstruction quality, stability, physiological plausibility, interpretability, robustness to noise and methodological perturbation, and computational cost. Importantly, a rigorous quantitative comparison across these methods would require them to be evaluated on the same dataset using identical or standardized preprocessing procedures, experimental conditions, parameter settings, and evaluation criteria. Otherwise, differences in data characteristics, signal quality, channel number, task design, preprocessing, and implementation may confound direct comparisons.

Moreover, there is currently no universally accepted set of quantitative criteria or fixed thresholds for evaluating identifiability, robustness, computational burden, physiological interpretability, and intended use across all methods. Therefore, these dimensions should be considered collectively rather than treated as absolute criteria or used to establish a fixed ranking among NMF, PCA, ICA, FA, MCR-ALS, nonlinear models, and deep-learning-based approaches. Method selection should instead be guided by specific research objectives, such as dimensionality reduction, source separation, physiological interpretation, real-time implementation, or predictive performance.

VAF is a common metric used to evaluate how well a muscle synergy model reconstructs the original EMG signals. VAF is commonly assessed at two levels: Total VAF and Local VAF. Total VAF, which evaluates the overall reconstruction accuracy across all recorded muscles and time points, is calculated according to a previous study [] as(2)Total VAF=1−∑i=1m∑j=1Nei,j2∑i=1m∑j=1NXi,j2×100%

The local VAF was calculated separately for each muscle based on Hug et al. []:(3)Local VAFm=1−∑j=1Nem,j2∑j=1NXm,j2×100%

Here, Xi,j denotes the original EMG value of the i-th muscle at the j-th sampled time point, whereas ei,j denotes the corresponding reconstruction residual. The index i = 1,…, m refers to the recorded muscles, where m is the total number of muscles, and j = 1,…,N refers to the sampled time points, where N is the total number of sampled time points. em,j denotes the m-th muscle at the j-th sampled time point reconstruction residual, Xm,j denotes the original EMG value of the m-th muscle at the j-th sampled time point. Total VAF evaluates the global mathematical performance of the synergy model across the entire dataset. However, a high Total VAF can sometimes mask poorly reconstructed individual muscles. Therefore, Local VAF may be evaluated concurrently to ensure no functionally critical muscle is discarded. The number of synergies is determined by sequentially increasing the model order and selecting the smallest number of synergies for which the Total VAF and all Local VAF values satisfy the predefined acceptance criteria. The optimal model order can then be defined as the smallest number of synergies for which the predefined global and local reconstruction criteria are satisfied.

High VAF values indicate that the synergy model provides an accurate reconstruction of the recorded EMG signals. Conversely, low VAF values indicate substantial unexplained variability in EMG data. Under this assumption, the number of muscle synergies is commonly determined using several VAF-based approaches, including the fixed threshold method [], best linear fit method [], knee point method [], and the “elbow” method []. In a fixed-threshold approach, the selected number is the smallest number of synergies that reaches a pre-specified total VAF criterion. Torres-Oviedo et al. [] proposed a fixed threshold method using a VAF threshold of 90% to determine the number of muscle synergies for extraction. The threshold should be reported explicitly because values used across studies differ. Cheung et al. [] presented the best linear fit method, which progressively increases the number of synergies and fits the residual portion of the VAF curve until the mean squared error (MSE) falls below the predefined criterion. The point at which the VAF curve plateaus to a straight line is then selected as the number of muscle synergies. The knee point method is assessed by computing the changes in the slope or curvature of every three adjacent points in the VAF-versus-number-of-synergies curve. The number of muscle synergies is identified at the point beyond which the incremental improvement in VAF becomes relatively small [,]. Finally, Tresch et al. [] suggested selecting the point at which the change in the slope of the curve was greatest. Such an “elbow” was interpreted as the point separating “structured” and noise-dependent variability. It can be used to define the minimum number of synergies that capture the task-related features. Besides the VAF metric, other criteria have also been proposed to determine the number of synergies. The reported VAF cutoff thresholds commonly range from 80% to 95% [,]. Accordingly, the appropriate threshold should be interpreted in relation to the task, dataset, noise level, population, and validation objective. Inconsistent thresholds make cross-study comparisons difficult, and synergy-number estimates should therefore be reported together with the chosen criterion and appropriate sensitivity analyses [].

Furthermore, interpretation of these thresholds requires a clear distinction between reconstruction quality, solution stability, and physiological validity. VAF quantifies reconstruction quality by measuring how well the extracted matrices reproduce the original EMG signal. Although a VAF exceeding 90% is often considered evidence of satisfactory decomposition, it does not establish that the extracted modules represent a physiologically correct solution. The residual EMG not explained by the model may contain functionally relevant, task-specific neural information rather than noise alone. Thus, a high VAF supports the mathematical adequacy of approximation but cannot, by itself, demonstrate that the extracted modules reflect genuine neural drives. The selected number of synergies should therefore also be evaluated for solution stability by examining consistency across repeated algorithmic initializations and supported by evidence of physiological validity, such as the ability to predict biomechanical outputs.

In general, these criteria aim to determine the number of synergy vectors required to represent the structural variability within a dataset [,]. Additionally, criteria based on the linear fit of the coefficient of determination (R2) and other criteria, such as Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Minimum Description Length (MDL) or Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), have also been proposed to determine the number of synergies [,,]. In practice, models with different numbers of synergies are fitted separately, and the model yielding the lowest criterion value is selected. AIC balances reconstruction goodness-of-fit against model complexity by imposing a penalty proportional to the number of estimated parameters. MDL selects the model that minimizes the total description length of both the model and the residual data; therefore, an additional synergy is retained only when the improvement in data description exceeds the extra complexity it introduces. BIC uses a similar likelihood–complexity trade-off but applies a stronger penalty that increases with sample size []. However, their estimates depend on the assumed noise distribution, the definition of the effective sample size, and the parameter-counting scheme. This issue is particularly relevant for EMG data, in which temporal autocorrelation means that successive samples may not be statistically independent []. To address the time-series autocorrelation inherent in continuous physiological signals, the effective sample size (Neff) must be adjusted rather than using the raw number of time points (N). For LP-filtered EMG data, Neff can be statistically estimated using the lag-1 temporal autocorrelation coefficient (ρ) via the approximation Neff≈N 1−ρ1+ρ. This mandatory adjustment ensures the correct statistical mechanics are applied to the penalty terms in AIC and BIC, preventing the over-penalization of model complexity. Consequently, using the total number of sampled time points may overestimate the effective sample size and affect model-order selection []. Accordingly, the effective sample size should account for temporal dependence and may be estimated from the autocorrelation structure.

Importantly, these model-order criteria are not restricted to conventional NMF-based analysis and may also be incorporated, with appropriate formulation, into more advanced probabilistic or Bayesian frameworks. In such approaches, uncertainty in model parameters and, in some cases, model order can be represented explicitly, although identifiability may remain dependent on prior assumptions, model constraints, and data quantity. However, the number of muscle synergies may be overestimated in the presence of signal noise []. Although these methods provide quantitative approaches for estimating synergy number, no universally accepted standard currently exists, and even apparently appropriate criteria may produce different results across studies [].

This narrative review employed a structured literature search to identify and synthesize evidence on methodological factors influencing the robustness, reliability, and interpretability of muscle-synergy extraction within limb neuromechanical controllers. Relevant literature published from January 2000 to July 2026 was identified through PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The search strategy combined terms related to muscle-synergy analysis and methodological evaluation: (“muscle synergy” OR “muscle synergies”) AND (“muscle coordination” OR “motor control” OR “motor primitive” OR “motor module” OR “electromyography” OR “sEMG”) AND (“methodology” OR “robustness” OR “reliability” OR “repeatability” OR “reproducibility” OR “factorization”). For ScienceDirect, the search string was adapted to comply with the database limit on Boolean connectors: (“muscle synergy” OR “muscle synergies”) AND (“electromyography” OR “sEMG” OR “motor control”) AND (“methodology” OR “reliability” OR “factorization”). The search syntax was adapted as necessary for each database. Reference lists of relevant original studies, methodological reviews, and key theoretical articles were also manually screened to identify additional publications.

Because this review was designed as a narrative rather than a systematic review, the literature search aimed to identify representative studies addressing major methodological approaches and key technical issues relevant to muscle synergy analysis. Studies were considered eligible if they met the following criteria: (1) they were full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles or conference papers published in English and provided sufficient methodological and results information; (2) they investigated muscle synergy extraction or analytical factors directly relevant to synergy estimation, including EMG acquisition and processing, matrix factorization algorithms, determination of the number of synergies, and experimental conditions; (3) they provided methodological information related to experimental design, EMG acquisition, preprocessing, factorization, model-order determination, robustness, reliability, or validation; and (4) they introduced, applied, or evaluated an approach of methodological relevance to muscle synergy analysis. Studies were excluded if they were not directly related to muscle synergy analysis, provided insufficient methodological information, or were available only as abstracts or non-peer-reviewed reports.

The electronic searches identified 513 records from PubMed, 890 from ScienceDirect, and 12,200 from Google Scholar. From the Google Scholar search results, the first 400 records ranked by relevance were retained for further screening. Records retrieved from the three databases were then combined, and additional studies were identified through manual screening of the reference lists of eligible articles and relevant reviews. After duplicate removal, the titles and abstracts of the remaining records were screened to identify studies explicitly relevant to muscle synergy methodology. Full-text articles were subsequently assessed according to the predefined eligibility criteria, and the most relevant studies were included in the review. This review was designed as a narrative review, with the literature search aimed at identifying representative studies addressing the major methodological approaches and key technical issues in muscle synergy analysis. Although the initial retrieval counts were retained and the above screening procedures were performed, a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-style screening log was not prospectively maintained. The studies included in this review were selected on the basis of their relevance and their ability to provide representative methodological evidence across the major domains addressed.

According to the reviewed studies, the robustness of muscle synergy structure appears to be context-dependent. Several studies reported relatively preserved synergy organization across controlled changes in biomechanical or sensorimotor conditions, as shown in . Torres-Oviedo et al. [] identified five functional synergies that remained robust across multiple postural conditions in a feline model, whereas Roh et al. [] reported relatively consistent synergy composition across spatial, load, and arm-position protocols in healthy participants. Gentner et al. [] found that synergy structure was preserved during visuomotor adaptation. Together, these findings support a degree of robustness under controlled experimental conditions. However, their direct comparability is limited by substantial differences in species, task type, and experimental design, and therefore they do not establish that muscle synergy structure is invariant across motor behaviors.

Other studies highlight important limits to this apparent robustness. Augenstein et al. [] showed that insufficient sampling of reaching directions altered the extracted synergy composition, indicating that the apparent validity of synergy structure depends partly on the breadth of the task space sampled. Geng et al. [] found modest adjustments in forearm synergy composition across changes in force level and arm position, whereas Munoz-Martel et al. [] reported recruitment of an additional complementary synergy under unstable balance conditions. These findings are not necessarily contradictory to the studies reporting preserved synergy structure; rather, they indicate that synergy organization may remain relatively stable under moderate variations in task conditions but may change when task demands, perturbation magnitude, or task-space coverage are altered more substantially. Accordingly, robustness should be interpreted relative to the range of experimental conditions actually tested rather than treated as an intrinsic and universal property of the extracted modules.

Subject- and environment-related variability represent additional sources of heterogeneity. Scano et al. [] reported that a reduced set of muscle modules remained similar and repeatable across subjects and sessions despite substantial variability in upper-limb movements. Zhao et al. [] evaluated intra-subject and inter-individual variability by comparing cosine similarity values with a data-driven random similarity reference. The random similarity was calculated as the mean similarity of paired synergy vectors pooled across all subjects and repetitions. Similarities were considered higher than the random reference when the statistical comparison was significant at p < 0.05. Therefore, the random matching level was not a fixed universal threshold, but rather an empirical reference derived from the specific dataset analyzed.

Evidence for repeatability is more heterogeneous and appears to depend strongly on the specific synergy outcome and acquisition procedure. Taborri et al. [] reported that synergy number was not repeatable within or between subjects and identified intrinsic sEMG variability and electrode repositioning as important sources of variation. Pale et al. [] similarly found lower spatial similarity between sessions than within sessions and showed that electrode repositioning altered synergy similarity. In contrast, other studies reported high repeatability of synergy vectors and activation coefficients under controlled conditions [,], while Shuman et al. [] found that synergy complexity and structure were repeatable across days when EMG signals were averaged over multiple gait cycles in both healthy participants and individuals with cerebral palsy. These apparently divergent findings may therefore arise partly because different studies evaluated different properties of synergy solutions, such as synergy number, spatial vectors, and temporal coefficients, and used different populations, acquisition procedures, and averaging strategies.

Overall, the reviewed evidence supports a context-dependent interpretation of muscle synergy robustness and repeatability. Synergy composition can remain relatively stable under controlled or moderately varying conditions, but this stability becomes less consistent when task sampling is insufficient or when subject-, session-, and acquisition-related variability increases. Evidence appears more consistent for the repeatability of synergy vectors and temporal activation patterns under standardized or averaged recording conditions than for the repeatability of synergy number or cross-session similarity. Importantly, the reviewed studies differ substantially in population, task design, acquisition protocol, and validation metric; therefore, apparent agreement or disagreement across studies should not be interpreted without considering these methodological differences. The available evidence supports conditional stability of extracted synergies, rather than universal invariance across tasks, populations, and recording conditions.

EMG acquisition for muscle synergy analysis involves an inherent trade-off between comprehensive anatomical coverage and experimental feasibility. sEMG has been widely used in clinical, robotic, and sports applications [], but signal quality and interpretability can be affected by experimental constraints, inter-individual variability, testing duration, and the number and configuration of recording channels [], including electrode spacing and inter-subject differences in muscle activation []. Because the human musculoskeletal system contains more than 600 skeletal muscles [,], recording all muscles involved in a motor task is generally impractical, and no universal standard currently defines either the number or identity of muscles that should be recorded []. Previous upper-limb studies have typically recorded approximately 8–19 muscles [,,], whereas gait studies have commonly included 8–16 lower-limb muscles [,], with relatively few studies able to sample all task-relevant muscles []. This limitation is particularly important for small or deep muscles that are inaccessible to surface electrodes []. Musculoskeletal simulations further suggest that unrecorded muscles may still contribute substantially to task-specific control; for example, Neptune et al. [] identified an iliopsoas-related module contributing to leg advancement, while additional modeling work indicated that omitted muscles may participate in balance and non-sagittal-plane control []. Thus, incomplete muscle sampling may limit the physiological interpretation of extracted synergies [], and both the number and identity of recorded muscles should be considered when interpreting synergy outcomes [,].

As shown in , comparative studies provide convergent evidence that reducing or altering the recorded muscle set does not necessarily eliminate the dominant synergy structure but may affect specific analytical outcomes. Steele et al. [] found that synergy similarity remained above 0.80 when more than 10 muscles were retained, although reducing the muscle set increased the risk of VAF overestimation. Similarly, Saito et al. [] showed that inclusion of deeper lower-limb muscles preserved three of four major synergy structures while altering one. Brambilla et al. [] further reported that a 32-muscle configuration required one additional synergy compared with a 12-muscle configuration to achieve comparable reconstruction performance, despite core synergy similarity remaining above 0.97. Taken together, these findings indicate that reduced muscle sets may preserve dominant modules while still modifying reconstruction quality, estimated synergy number, or task-specific muscle contributions. Importantly, the magnitude of these effects differed across tasks and muscle configurations, so numerical findings from individual studies should not be interpreted as universal minimum muscle requirements.

The suitability of a reduced muscle set also depends on the intended analytical objective and the method used for muscle selection. Chen et al. [] proposed the determination of optimal muscle synergies from estimated muscle activations (DOMSn-EMAs) framework to achieve more reliable and physiologically meaningful muscle synergies. It combines high-fidelity musculoskeletal modeling with a modified computed muscle control algorithm to generate high-density estimated muscle activations, then applies sparse NMF to extract synergy patterns and uses a composite reliability index to select the optimal number of synergies. In myoelectric control, Camardella et al. [] evaluated all possible combinations of 15 candidate muscles. The analysis identified an eight-muscle global optimal set and a six-muscle subject-specific set, corresponding to reductions of seven and nine muscles from the 15-muscle candidate pool, respectively. The reduced sets produced synergy similarity values ranging from 0.74 to 0.78, while their force-estimation performance was not significantly different from that of the full set. Guez et al. [] compared variance-based PCA with model-based recursive feature elimination for muscle selection. They found that recursive feature elimination (RFE)-chosen muscles exhibited strong correlation with subjects’ synergy structures, whereas PCA tended to favor muscles with high variability rather than those representative of synergies, underscoring the critical role of physiological information in effective channel selection.

Musculoskeletal and humanoid optimization studies provide complementary but more indirect evidence. Genetic-algorithm and convex-hull approaches have shown that redundancy can be reduced while preserving task performance in musculoskeletal or robotic systems [,,]. However, these findings do not directly establish the optimal number of muscles required for experimental human sEMG-based synergy analysis. Overall, the available evidence therefore supports task-relevant and anatomically representative muscle selection rather than a fixed universal number of channels. Reduced muscle sets may be appropriate in some contexts, but their validity should be evaluated against the intended outcome, including reconstruction quality, synergy similarity, model order, and task-specific muscle representation. Musculoskeletal modeling may provide complementary information for muscles that cannot be directly recorded but should not be regarded as direct evidence defining an optimal experimental muscle set.

Across the reviewed methodological studies, EMG preprocessing consistently influenced synergy-related outcomes, although the magnitude and direction of these effects varied according to the preprocessing procedure and the specific outcome evaluated. Studies focusing on filtering generally indicate that cutoff frequency can alter reconstruction metrics, muscle contributions, and the estimated number of synergies, although the effects are not quantitatively consistent across datasets. As shown in , regarding the effect of different EMG preprocessing techniques, Shuman et al. [] demonstrated that Total VAF was particularly sensitive to LP filtering, unit-variance normalization, and noise level, whereas synergy weights and activation profiles were less affected; consequently, these preprocessing choices could also influence the estimated number of synergies. Kieliba et al. [] likewise showed that changing the LP cutoff altered individual muscle contributions and tended to affect the estimated number of synergies. However, the exact change in synergy number was not consistently reported across these studies. Taken together, these findings support sensitivity of synergy extraction to filtering, but they do not establish a uniform cutoff-dependent effect or a universally optimal filter setting.

Normalization appears to represent another important source of variability, and recent comparative evidence suggests that its influence may be as large as, or in some datasets greater than, that of moderate changes in filter cutoff. Banks et al. [] found that trial-by-trial unit-magnitude normalization produced marked differences in synergy-vector variability, whereas neural-command variability was less sensitive to normalization and output normalization had relatively little influence. In a larger evaluation involving 135 participants and 225 combinations of preprocessing and factorization procedures, Zhao et al. [] reported that normalization strategy had a greater influence on extracted synergy structure than LP cutoff frequency. Ortega-Auriol et al. [] further showed that different amplitude-normalization strategies produced a difference of approximately one synergy under the tested conditions, and unit-variance normalization failed to satisfy the prespecified VAF criterion. These findings provide convergent evidence that normalization can materially influence synergy structure and model order, but the effect remains dependent on the normalization method and analytical outcome.

Evidence for other preprocessing and data-organization strategies is less uniform. Ghislieri et al. [] reported that extracting principal activations as a preprocessing step improved the robustness and interpretability of synergies during walking. By contrast, Oliveira et al. [] found relatively similar motor modules when comparing different EMG data structures, including single-trial, averaged, and concatenated data, suggesting a comparatively limited effect of data organization in their locomotor dataset. Colamarino et al. [] further identified a 10 Hz LP filter combined with non-normalized EMG as a favorable configuration for the Box and Block Test, with three synergies sufficient to characterize the task. However, such task-specific optimization should not be interpreted as evidence for a universally optimal preprocessing pipeline, because the evaluated tasks, populations, and outcome criteria differed across studies.

Overall, the available evidence indicates that preprocessing is an important source of methodological variability in muscle synergy analysis, but its effects are outcome- and context-dependent rather than uniform. Filtering, normalization, and data organization may differentially affect reconstruction metrics, synergy number, synergy structure, and trial-to-trial variability. Among the reviewed studies, normalization shows relatively consistent evidence of influencing synergy-related outcomes, whereas the effects of filtering and data organization are more heterogeneous and task-dependent. Therefore, preprocessing parameters should be selected according to the task and analytical objective, applied consistently within a study, and reported in sufficient detail to support reproducibility and cross-study comparison.

Comparative studies of conventional factorization methods do not identify a single algorithm that consistently performs best across all datasets, tasks, and evaluation criteria. As shown in , considering how matrix-factorization techniques affect muscle synergies, Tresch et al. [], Ebied et al. [] and Rabbi et al. [] compared several commonly used methods, including NMF, PCA, ICA, FA, and second-order blind identification (SOBI). Collectively, these studies showed that algorithm performance depends strongly on data characteristics, such as channel number, sparsity, noise level, component correlation, and task dynamics. NMF often performed favorably, particularly when its non-negativity assumption was compatible with the data and the number of synergies was smaller than the number of recorded channels. However, low-amplitude or highly correlated synergies remained difficult to identify, and some alternative methods performed poorly under limited-channel conditions. These findings therefore support NMF as a practical and widely applicable method, but not as a universally superior approach.

A second body of evidence indicates that the performance of NMF can be substantially affected by initialization, biomechanical constraints, and inter-individual variability, thereby motivating the development of modified factorization strategies. Soomro et al. [] showed that sparse initialization improved reconstruction compared with random and SVD initialization under the tested conditions, whereas Ma et al. [] reported improved repeatability and intra-subject consistency using MCR-ALS. Burkholder et al. [] and Steele et al. [] further demonstrated that biomechanical and task constraints, particularly correlated synergy activations, can reduce the accuracy with which factorization algorithms recover the underlying synergies. Other extensions have targeted different methodological limitations: Scano et al. [] introduced mixed matrix factorization to jointly analyze muscle and kinematic variables, Delis et al. [] developed an NMF-based approach to improve the categorization of spatial and temporal modules, and Shourijeh et al. [] reported greater cross-subject consistency using concatenated NMF. Taken together, these studies suggest that algorithmic modifications can improve specific properties such as repeatability, multimodal integration, or cross-subject consistency, but the observed advantages are linked to the particular limitation each method was designed to address and should not be interpreted as evidence of universal superiority.

Nonlinear and autoencoder-based approaches extend synergy analysis beyond the assumptions of conventional linear decomposition, particularly when nonlinear interactions or inhibitory contributions are of interest. Studies using unsupervised or constrained autoencoders [,,] showed that nonlinear latent representations can capture agonist–antagonist relationships or negative components that are not explicitly represented by standard nonnegative factorization. However, comparative evidence remains mixed. Zhao et al. [] found that although autoencoders outperformed some linear approaches, NMF and ICA achieved higher reconstruction and classification accuracy in their tested datasets. Similarly, Buongiorno et al. [,] reported that autoencoder-based methods improved task-oriented joint-moment prediction or motor-intention decoding, but these gains were not always accompanied by superior EMG reconstruction. Thus, nonlinear models may provide advantages for particular functional objectives but improved predictive performance does not necessarily imply better reconstruction or greater physiological interpretability.

Application-oriented studies further illustrate that advanced methods may be advantageous under specific clinical, multimodal, or noise-related conditions. Lee et al. [] applied autoencoder-based synergy analysis to distinguish spatial and temporal abnormalities during curved walking in individuals with stroke, whereas Russo et al. [] used mixed matrix factorization to jointly represent EMG and unconstrained kinematic data. Rusta et al. [] reported strong reconstruction performance and noise robustness for a deep-reinforcement-learning-based dynamic neuro-fuzzy system (DRL-DNF) in 24 manual wheelchair users. However, these results were obtained in specific populations and task settings and therefore require independent cross-dataset validation before broader conclusions can be drawn. Their contribution is better interpreted as demonstrating application-specific potential rather than establishing a new general-purpose standard for synergy extraction.

Recent studies also emphasize that reconstruction accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating synergy algorithms. Berger et al. [] incorporated force reconstruction into the factorization objective and showed that force-constrained NMF could outperform standard NMF in force-related tasks and under different noise conditions. Pan et al. [] used network analysis to characterize relationships among primitive synergies across simple and complex upper-limb tasks, extending evaluation beyond vector similarity alone. Brambilla et al. [], in a comparison of 16 autoencoder architectures, demonstrated a clear trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and physiological interpretability: architectures with the best reconstruction did not necessarily produce the most physiologically plausible synergies. Collectively, these findings show that algorithm evaluation should consider multiple dimensions, including reconstruction fidelity, task relevance, robustness, and physiological interpretability, rather than relying on a single performance metric.

Overall, the available evidence supports a context-dependent approach to algorithm selection. Conventional methods such as NMF remain widely used and interpretable, but their performance is sensitive to initialization, noise, channel configuration, signal correlation, and task structure. Modified, mixed, nonlinear, and autoencoder-based methods may improve specific outcomes, including repeatability, multimodal integration, task prediction, or robustness, but these advantages are not consistently observed across datasets or validation criteria.

Experimental studies investigating muscle synergies in synergy methodology.

ReLU: Rectified Linear Unit; tanh: Hyperbolic Tangent; RMSE: Root Mean Square Error; fICA, Fast Independent Component Analysis; sNM3F: Sample-Based Non-Negative Matrix Tri-Factorization; pICA, Probabilistic ICA. FCNMF: Force-Constrained Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. SMMA: Self-modeling Mixture Analysis. CNMF: Concatenated Non-negative Matrix Factorization.

Although VAF remains the most widely used reconstruction-based criterion for determining the number of synergies, the reviewed evidence does not support a single universal threshold. The absence of a consistent and objective criterion remains a major methodological challenge in muscle synergy analysis [] and VAF thresholds vary substantially across studies []. A threshold such as VAF > 90% has frequently been adopted to ensure adequate reconstruction and has also been used to characterize population-level distributions of synergy number []. However, high explained variance does not necessarily indicate that all task-relevant information has been captured. Barradas et al. [] showed that residual EMG components remaining after 90% of the variance had been explained could still contain movement-related information, while other studies have similarly suggested that residual components may reflect additional synergy-related structure []. Thus, VAF should be interpreted as a measure of reconstruction performance rather than as direct evidence that the selected model order fully represents the underlying motor-control organization.

The reliability of VAF-based model-order selection is further constrained by its sensitivity to inter-individual variability, preprocessing, noise, and task-space sampling. Kim et al. [] showed that applying a single VAF threshold across individuals could lead to inconsistent estimates of synergy number, motivating the use of additional statistical procedures such as intra-class measures, between-level correlation analysis, and clustering. Task sampling is another important source of variation: Augenstein et al. [] found that reducing the number of reaching directions altered VAF-based results and the validity of the extracted synergies. In addition, functional organization in task space should be considered when evaluating the adequacy of a synergy solution []. Collectively, these studies indicate that a fixed VAF threshold alone cannot distinguish methodological variation from biologically meaningful differences and should therefore be complemented by additional criteria or sensitivity analyses.

Alternative model-order criteria have been proposed to reduce reliance on arbitrary VAF cutoffs, but their advantages are also context-dependent. Ballarini et al. [] developed the method of choosing the optimal number of muscle synergies (ChoOSyn) and reported performance comparable to VAF-based approaches in simulated data, together with improved classification performance and error-related measures in the evaluated real datasets. Ranaldi et al. [] proposed an AIC-based approach that showed good model-order identification under the tested conditions, whereas MDL has been reported to perform better when the channel-to-synergy ratio is relatively high []. These approaches provide more explicit consideration of model complexity than fixed reconstruction thresholds, but their relative performance depends on data structure, channel configuration, noise assumptions, and the statistical formulation used. Therefore, current evidence supports their use as complementary model-selection tools rather than as universally superior replacements for VAF.

Task demands themselves may also change the number of synergies required to represent motor behavior, as shown in . Herzog et al. [], using an R2 knee-point criterion with bootstrap analysis in 36 healthy men, found that more synergies were required following adaptation to a force field than at baseline, indicating that model order can change with altered control demands. Kuska et al. [] similarly showed in a two-dimensional musculoskeletal simulation that models containing more synergies tolerated greater simulated knee-extensor weakness. However, this simulation provides indirect evidence concerning the functional consequences of model complexity and does not establish that a larger synergy number is universally associated with greater physiological robustness. Together, these findings suggest that the number of synergies may reflect both task demands and the model-selection procedure used to determine it.

Data organization and population characteristics introduce further heterogeneity. Zhao et al. [] showed in 15 healthy participants that concatenated, averaged, and other trial-processing approaches produced different estimates of synergy number during multidirectional reaching; the concatenated approach yielded the greatest number of synergies and the averaged approach the fewest, leading the authors to recommend at least five trials and four reaching directions under their experimental conditions. Population-related effects may be less evident in total synergy number than in synergy organization. Saito et al. [] found only a small, non-significant difference in median total synergy number between preschool and school-aged children, despite observing two additional synergy clusters in the older group. Similarly, Kian-Bostanabad et al. [] identified six synergies during six-direction maximum voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) but only two during maximum voluntary isometric extension (MVIE) in 14 healthy men using a five-criterion model-order rule. These findings indicate that task type, data organization, and population characteristics can influence different aspects of synergy organization, and that the total number of synergies alone may not capture all biologically or methodologically relevant differences.

Overall, VAF remains useful for reconstruction-based assessment, but no universal threshold is supported across populations, tasks, and preprocessing conditions. Alternative methods such as ChoOSyn, AIC, and MDL may reduce reliance on fixed VAF cutoffs, yet their performance also depends on dataset and model assumptions. Moreover, task demands, trial organization, and population characteristics can alter either the estimated number of synergies or the organization of the extracted modules. Accordingly, the estimated number of synergies should be reported together with the model-selection criterion, relevant preprocessing and data-organization procedures, and, where feasible, complementary stability and sensitivity analyses to enhance the interpretability and comparability of findings across studies.

Muscle synergy analysis has been increasingly applied in motor control, clinical, rehabilitation, and engineering research. However, heterogeneity in EMG acquisition, preprocessing, factorization, model-order determination, and validation continues to limit cross-study comparability and reproducibility. Based on the methodological and experimental evidence summarized in , ,  and , we propose several evidence-informed recommendations covering three major stages of the muscle synergy analysis pipeline: (1) data acquisition and preprocessing, (2) synergy extraction and model selection, and (3) validation and application-oriented approaches.

As summarized in , the strength of evidence varies across methodological factors. Available evidence indicates that muscle selection, filtering and normalization, trial organization, and task design can influence extracted muscle synergies. In contrast, universal recommendations for model-order thresholds, information-theoretic criteria, reduced muscle sets, and advanced factorization methods remain limited or strongly context-dependent. Therefore, these recommendations emphasize transparent reporting, methodological consistency, complementary model-evaluation criteria, and task-specific validation.

(1) Data acquisition and preprocessing: Reliable muscle synergy analysis depends on the quality and consistency of EMG acquisition and preprocessing. Muscle selection should reflect task biomechanics, anatomical coverage, and the study objective. Reduced or data-driven muscle sets may reduce recording dimensionality, but their suitability should be validated for the specific task and population because reducing the number of recorded muscles can affect VAF, synergy number, and task-specific muscle contributions. Filtering, normalization, trial organization, electrode placement, and other acquisition parameters should also be clearly reported and consistently applied. Rather than imposing a universal protocol, minimum reporting standards are recommended to improve transparency and cross-study comparison. The availability of open raw and processed EMG datasets, together with clearly defined evaluation metrics and processing procedures, may further enhance reproducibility and facilitate methodological comparisons.

(2) Synergy extraction and model selection: Factorization algorithms, initialization strategies, and model-order criteria should be selected according to the research objective and dataset characteristics. No single factorization method has been shown to be optimal across all conditions, because performance can vary with signal structure, channel number, noise level, component correlation, and task characteristics. Initialization procedures should therefore be reported and repeated, or alternative initializations may be considered when solution stability is important. Advanced factorization frameworks, including probabilistic/Bayesian, tensor-based, nonlinear, and deep latent-variable approaches, may offer advantages for representing uncertainty, multidimensional structure, or nonlinear neuromuscular relationships. However, these advantages remain context-dependent and should be evaluated in terms of interpretability, robustness, and computational cost. Model order should likewise not be determined solely using a fixed VAF or R2 threshold. Complementary criteria and sensitivity analyses should be considered where appropriate, and the statistical assumptions underlying information-theoretic criteria should be clearly reported.

(3) Validation and application-oriented approaches: Extracted muscle synergies should not be evaluated solely on the basis of reconstruction performance. Reliability and repeatability should be assessed when synergy stability is an important outcome, with particular attention to electrode placement and between-session acquisition consistency. Because synergy organization can also vary with task type and experimental constraints, the extracted modules should be interpreted within the specific task context in which they were obtained. Their functional relevance may be further examined by comparing synergy-related outputs with force, kinetic/kinematic measures, musculoskeletal-model predictions, or other task-relevant physiological observations. For muscles that can be experimentally measured, agreement between simulation-derived activation patterns and recorded EMG signals can provide additional support for the physiological plausibility of model-based estimates. Musculoskeletal simulation can also extend synergy analysis to small and deep muscles that are difficult to assess using conventional surface EMG, thereby providing a more comprehensive representation of neuromuscular coordination. However, such agreement provides only indirect and complementary evidence for physiological plausibility and does not independently demonstrate that the extracted modules represent genuine neural control primitives. In particular, for muscles that cannot be directly measured, it remains difficult to experimentally verify the accuracy of their estimated activations and their contributions to specific synergy modules.

Muscle synergy theory has been widely applied in neuroscience, robotics, sports science, and rehabilitation to investigate motor control and coordination strategies and to characterize functional impairments associated with pathological conditions. However, substantial methodological variability across studies remains a major challenge for interpreting and comparing reported synergy outcomes. This review highlights key methodological factors affecting the robustness and reliability of muscle synergy analysis, including experimental design, EMG preprocessing, synergy extraction approaches, model-order selection, and validation strategies.

The findings of this review suggest that improving the robustness and reliability of muscle synergy analysis may improve interpretation and broader application. Methodological criteria and emerging approaches should therefore be further refined and validated across different tasks, populations, and analytical settings. For example, experimental protocols may include multiple degrees of freedom and sufficiently diverse tasks to capture representative muscle activation patterns and characterize the relevant synergy subspace. In addition, open-source musculoskeletal modeling platforms such as OpenSim [] may provide a useful complementary tool for sensitivity analysis, evaluation of muscle-selection strategies, and assessment of biomechanical plausibility. However, musculoskeletal simulation provides only indirect and complementary support for the physiological plausibility of the extracted modules and cannot independently demonstrate that these modules correspond to genuine neural control primitives. Although simulation can extend synergy analysis to experimentally inaccessible muscles, its results should be interpreted together with experimental EMG and other physiological evidence when inferring the underlying neuromuscular control mechanisms. Overall, improved methodological rigor and transparent reporting may enhance the reproducibility, interpretability, and broader application of muscle synergy analysis across neuroscience, rehabilitation, and robotics.

neuroscience.title: Neurocognition of dance: Guidelines for using dance as model behavior and research subject in cognitive neuroscience
neuroscience.abstract: Dance and movement science bridges cognitive psychology, neuroscience, cultural studies, philosophical aesthetics, and the performing arts. The field has evolved significantly, examining physical, social, psychological, and neural aspects of dance and movement execution and perception, contributing to a deeper understanding of human cognition and of dance itself. As the field expands, shared guidelines that support methodological rigor, reproducibility, and cultural relevance are of paramount importance. This paper synthesizes current research and introduces a comprehensive seven-principle research design framework for using dance in cognitive neuroscience. Key elements include the operationalization of “dance” in empirical sciences, the definition of who is a dancer, measures of expertise, and the importance of a culturally sensitive, holistic, and interdisciplinary approach to its investigation in the laboratory and in ecologically valid settings. This framework benefits research in dance and movement aesthetics, as well as investigations in social cognition, affective neuroscience, computer science, and artificial intelligence.
neuroscience.text:
Empirical research using dance as a model behavior to study neurocognitive processes, and dancers as neurocognitive models of expertise, offers valuable insights into how the human brain processes, learns, and responds to non-verbal, expressive, full-body movement and social interactions. Dance practices support cognitive rehabilitation and recovery from dysfunction, sometimes with higher success rates than traditional rehabilitation regimes. Evidence from the past 20 years supports the relevance of studying dance in basic and applied research across psychology, neuroscience, education, and computer science. However, guidelines and best methodological practices still need to be established to ensure the rigor, quality, and validity of such research, particularly given the methodological heterogeneity that may contribute to variability in reported outcomes.

Although dance is a complex phenomenon, it can be operationalized and investigated with the same scientific rigor applied to other forms of human movement. In July 2022, we, the authors of this paper, hosted a symposium titled “Emerging Multi-disciplinary Perspectives and Cutting-Edge Advancement in Dance Neuroaesthetics” at the ESCAN (European Society for Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience) biennial meeting. We highlighted state-of-the-art methodologies, challenges and open questions, and proposed a comprehensive seven-principle research design framework for using dance in cognitive neuroscience as a model behavior to investigate human cognition, or as a subject of research in itself. This paper is the result of the interdisciplinary dialogue between the authors that followed from this meeting. See .

The manuscript offers a guide for operationalizing dance (Section ), defining and measuring dance expertise (Section ), maintaining ecological validity across laboratory and real-world settings (Section ), improving reproducibility and methodological standards (Section ), fostering interdisciplinary approaches (Section ), incorporating cross-cultural and individual difference perspectives (Section ), and designing translational research in health and wellbeing contexts (Section ). See .

Our methodological framework draws on empirical work, literature reviews, and meta-analyses demonstrating how dance provides:(i)a model behavior for investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying action- and emotion perception, and movement representation.,, Research has established how dance observation recruits visuomotor (simulation) processes depending on the observer’s expertise, and how observers decode expressive whole-body movement in terms of affective and intentional meaning. For a review, see Foster Vander Elst et al. (2023).(ii)a tool to study the interplay of brain networks affording aesthetic appreciation of movement,,, such as the visual, sensorimotor, and reward systems. Studies in empirical aesthetics have determined how movement features, expertise, and contextual framing contribute to subjective evaluations and aesthetic experience of dance. For a review, see Kirsch et al. (2016) and Orlandi & Candidi (2025).(iii)a neurocognitive model of expertise to study neuroplasticity and learning.,,, Comparisons between trained dancers and non-dancers have revealed training-related differences in brain structure and connectivity, providing a model for studying experience-dependent plasticity. For an overview, see Karpati et al. (2015).(iv)a valuable tool for rehabilitation and recovery from disease and dysfunction in clinical settings.,,, Dance movement therapy and other dance-based interventions have been shown to have positive effects on motor, cognitive, and mental health outcomes across neurological and psychiatric populations. For a review, see Millman et al. (2021).

A comprehensive discussion of this literature lies beyond the scope of this paper. Focusing instead on providing a methodological framework, this work contributes to improving theoretical precision, research questions, operationalization, and reproducibility in dance-based cognitive neuroscience and related fields.

Everyone recognizes dance, yet no two people’s notions of what dance is are exactly the same. The term “dance” refers to behaviors ranging from simple rhythmic groove movements performed to a regular beat, to codified dance styles that can be learned by anyone, to highly structured movement repertoires requiring years of athletic and artistic practice. In some cultures, dance is not even differentiated from other performing arts such as music, song, and percussion., See  for examples and key differences between dance styles in terms of neurocognitive predispositions involved and potentially modulated by dance. More broadly, borrowing from scholarship on classical music and the arts, classical refers to cultural practices that are formalized through theory and pedagogy, shaped by specific social and historical contexts, and maintained across generations through institutional teaching, expert transmission, and a recognized canon of exemplary works.

The nature of a dance, whether social or competitive, can also depend on the dancer’s mindset or intention. For example, an Argentine tango milonga may serve purely as a relaxed, social gathering focused on internal connection (e.g., dancers moving with eyes closed), or as a highly performative and competitive display influenced by external attention (e.g., dancers hunting the gaze of others).

Most dance styles contain expressive elements, but the extent and form of expressivity can vary widely. For instance, Bharatanatyam places strong emphasis on storytelling, with specific hand gestures, facial expressions, and eye movements, with clear meanings to the trained eye, choreographed into its structure. While Western ballet also has codified repertoires and expressive potential, recreational dancers may not engage with these narrative elements as deeply. Interestingly, both Bharatanatyam and ballet allow for complete improvisation, in which expressivity becomes more personal and may not follow a shared or recognizable code among practitioners.

The term ‘classical’ dance is used here to refer to historically codified dance styles and techniques such as Western classical ballet and Indian classical dance (e.g., Bharatanatyam). These styles are traditionally performed in formal theatrical settings, typically featuring conventional staging, a proscenium layout, and a clear separation between performers and audience. More broadly, borrowing from scholarship on classical music and the arts, classical refers to cultural practices that are formalized through theory and pedagogy, shaped by specific social and historical contexts, and maintained across generations through institutional teaching, expert transmission, and a recognized canon of exemplary works.

In empirical research, scientists deconstruct phenomena into “independent variables” to study how they contribute to specific outcomes ("dependent variables"). Depending on the neurocognitive mechanism under investigation and the research question, one dance style may be more appropriate than another. Using the following four neurocognitive mechanisms, an example is provided for how research questions can be organized. (These four are illustrative and do not represent the full range of neurocognitive processes associated with dance. For a more extensive mapping of processes, see Section ; ).(i)Action simulation and entrainment – enabling humans to follow and synchronize their body movements with external rhythms or movements of other agents.,,,(ii)Neural plasticity/motor skill learning – reflecting adaptive (brain and body) changes associated with training, rehearsal, and repeated performance.,,,(iii)Imitation – enabling socialization through the acquisition and enactment of shared movement practices (e.g., who dances, when, and how).,,(iv)Enculturation – influencing how dance is perceived, interpreted, and valued within culturally specific contexts.,,

Action simulation and entrainment – enabling humans to follow and synchronize their body movements with external rhythms or movements of other agents.,,,

Neural plasticity/motor skill learning – reflecting adaptive (brain and body) changes associated with training, rehearsal, and repeated performance.,,,

Imitation – enabling socialization through the acquisition and enactment of shared movement practices (e.g., who dances, when, and how).,,

Enculturation – influencing how dance is perceived, interpreted, and valued within culturally specific contexts.,,

These mechanisms emerge early in life, while their expression and refinement depend on neurodevelopmental maturation, exposure, motor learning, and practice.,,,,,,,,, The engagement of these four may vary considerably, for example, depending on whether participants within an experiment watch a performance of Western contemporary dance or Indian classical Bharatanatyam.(A)A Western contemporary dance performance, unfamiliar to anyone watching. Two dancers walk on stage, make eye contact with the audience, and grin manically while standing still, without music, external rhythm, or synchronized movements.,,, In this performance, non-linear narratives, improvisation, and immersion are core aesthetic features.,(B)An Indian classical Bharatanatyam performance, where a dancer moves to familiar, mostly rhythmic music and conveys popular mythological stories, especially to those familiar with the mythology of that culture. The aesthetic features here are codified hand and facial gestures (mudras), body postures, and full-body movements that “tell” a story, in addition to moments of synchronous movement.,

Two dancers walk on stage, make eye contact with the audience, and grin manically while standing still, without music, external rhythm, or synchronized movements.,,, In this performance, non-linear narratives, improvisation, and immersion are core aesthetic features.,

An Indian classical Bharatanatyam performance, where a dancer moves to familiar, mostly rhythmic music and conveys popular mythological stories, especially to those familiar with the mythology of that culture. The aesthetic features here are codified hand and facial gestures (mudras), body postures, and full-body movements that “tell” a story, in addition to moments of synchronous movement.,

These two dances also differ with regard to other dimensions among the 11 outlined in .  compares these two dance styles with a third with respect to these dimensions. Even within the same dance style, dimensions such as co-presence, social touch, and synchrony may vary across performances, possibly engaging different neurocognitive processes in performers and observers.

Conclusions drawn from studies using these performances would be problematic without a clear conceptualization of what is meant by “dance” in each context and of the neurocognitive process under investigation. From a neuroscience perspective, the two examples represent very different classes of behavior.

Define what is meant by “dance” in the context of your study. Classify dance behaviors according to the neurocognitive mechanisms needed to perform and perceive them (refer to ; ; see also  in section ). Justify the selection of a specific dance style or technique based on movement features, dance dimensions of interest (e.g., movement complexity, music and rhythm, proximity and social touch, intention, expression), research questions, and neurocognitive mechanisms of interest (e.g., entrainment, plasticity/expertise, imitation, enculturation). Avoid generalizing findings across dance styles, techniques, or cultures without acknowledging these differences and discussing their implications. Ambiguities in classification are often part of cross-cultural research and should be addressed transparently, with decisions justified and documented, for example, through footnotes or supplementary material (e.g., ritual movement practice operationalized as “dance” in research on rhythmic coordination).

Central to the question of what dance is, is who is considered a dancer. Expertise studies in cognitive neuroscience require operationalizing the level of skill. The Cambridge Dictionary defines expertise as “a high level of knowledge or skill”, but a precise and standardized quantification of what constitutes a “high level” remains elusive in cognitive neuroscience and psychology, particularly in sports and the performing arts.,

Formal dance training changes the body, brain structure, and function. It provides complex technical visuo-motor skills to perceive, reproduce, and deconstruct complex movement into its constituent movement chunks. Watching dance regularly also modulates visual, motor, and memory systems,,, contributing to what is summarized as “visual dance expertise”.

Depending on expertise level and professional status, dance training includes: academic technique training, expressive practice, improvisation, partnering work, group synchronization practices, repertoire practice, musical practice, stage rehearsals, live performances, teaching, and choreography. These activities refine somatosensory and motor processes, memory, attention, emotional processes, non-verbal communication, social cognition, and higher-order skills such as divergent thinking (see Section ).

A number of questionnaires have been proposed to measure expertise across these domains. An overview of standardized inventories is provided in . Most have only recently been made publicly available or are not yet published in peer-reviewed journals. They were primarily developed in Western dance contexts and do not yet capture all dimensions of dance engagement, especially informal or digitally mediated participation). Existing questionnaires should therefore be considered useful tools for characterizing dance expertise rather than definitive standards for all dance populations. Future research should develop and validate measures capable of capturing emerging forms of dance engagement and training, including those enabled by rapidly evolving digital and immersive There is not yet a unified measure that combines practice-oriented and achievement/skill-oriented measures of dance expertise. A recent genetically informative study of 6610 Swedish twins suggests that factors contributing to dance achievement may not fully overlap with those associated with engagement and practice levels, highlighting the importance of considering both dimensions when characterizing dance expertise.

The most common practice in published experiments involving dance “experts” has been to report years of dance practice. Under this measure, “expertise” broadly includes all time spent in dance-related activities. Therefore, what constitutes “an expert” varies greatly across studies, from 3 years to 18 years of practice. Such discrepancies complicate cross-study comparisons. In what follows, the daily training behaviors relevant to dance expertise measures are outlined.

In daily academic training, dancers learn technically complex and precise movements, often in coordination and synchronization with others, and usually to music. Training builds stamina, endurance, breathing control, and memory for long movement sequences. It enhances proprioception, interoception, and the integration of visual, motor, and auditory information, which support action anticipation, error detection, motor control, motor learning, interpersonal coordination, and memory.

Through live performances, dancers develop stage presence and the ability to captivate an audience through their expressivity., They refine non-verbal communication and learn to convey emotions and meaning through movement. A broader movement repertoire enhances the range and precision of bodily expressions, supporting emotion expression and recognition, emotion regulation, self-awareness, and multisensory sensitivity to audience feedback., Performance also requires memory recall, interpersonal coordination, multisensory integration, and management of attention across dancers, the stage environment, and the audience.

Rehearsals are crucial for refining choreography, movement execution, and expressive skills. Dancers combine physical and mental practice, alternating between reproducing movement sequences and mentally simulating them., Kinesthetic (or motor) imagery is a powerful training tool in dance and other physical disciplines, supporting multisensory integration and enhancing body awareness. Depending on dance style, dancers may engage in auditory imagery, involving mental representations of music and sounds, as well as interoceptive or somatic imagery, involving representations of internal bodily states.

Three additional behaviors warrant attention when defining expertise: teaching,,
choreography, and improvisation.
Teaching movement to others strengthens verbal and non-verbal communication and fosters social cognition, including empathy and theory of mind. These processes are supported by attentional focus and by the ability to create and structure motor chunks, both critical for effective knowledge transfer.,

Choreography demands advanced visuospatial and memory skills, higher-order functions such as creativity (convergent and divergent thinking), and decision-making. These cognitive abilities enable dancers to design pieces that are emotionally expressive and meaningful (e.g., dramaturgy), visually engaging, novel, and captivating.

Improvisation is an integral part of a dancer’s skillset., It emerges from kinesthetic experience, movement habits, physical constraints, training, and memory, while employing divergent thinking during decision-making. Although central to Western contemporary dance,, contact improvisation, breakdancing, and Iranian classical dance, it is relatively uncommon in codified or highly structured styles such as ballet and modern dance (e.g., Graham, Horton, and Cunningham), which emphasize mastery of set vocabulary and technique.,, Dance styles vary in the extent to which they incorporate improvisation, and future research may benefit from considering improvisational practice in assessment of dance expertise. Compared to daily training, improvisation involves quickly adapting to environmental changes (e.g., sounds, other dancers) and engages divergent thinking, decision-making, multisensory integration, and interpersonal coordination.

For instance, contact improvisation differs from Western classical ballet not only in its reliance on improvisation, but also in the sensory modalities it emphasizes. While contact improvisation prioritizes touch, body awareness, and kinesthetic connection between dancers, ballet depends more heavily on visual information. This example shows why the neurocognitive competences developed through different dance behaviors cannot be fully captured by measuring “years of training” alone.

Dance experts also differ in the extent to which different neurocognitive competences are developed, depending on their level of engagement and the style or technique they practice.  outlines a practice-oriented and aspirational mapping of dance behaviors and the neurocognitive processes that may be associated with them.
