Assessing dance expertise: Neurocognitive processes likely stimulated by the practice of specific dance behaviors

Most formal dance education combines multiple techniques and somatic practices,,, making it difficult to identify dancers trained exclusively in one style. Consultation with a dance expert, such as a performer, teacher, or choreographer, is therefore strongly recommended when selecting participants across training backgrounds (see also Section ).

Age of onset refers to the age at which a skill is first acquired. Although no longitudinal studies have investigated the effect of long-term dance practice in children, short-term intervention studies suggest that dance can support the development of motor and executive functions, and social skills., Therefore, it is valuable to collect the age of dance training onset alongside existing expertise inventories (e.g., Gold-DSI), which capture duration and extent of training but not when training begins.

Differentiating between visuomotor and visual expertise in dance is important because visual experience alone can lead to covert movement simulation, and the left premotor cortex may be sensitive to multisensory integration. However, there is no clear consensus on how best to quantify visual expertise in dance observers. Most studies rely on the number of live performances attended annually,,, while other forms of exposure, such as films (e.g., Bollywood), online videos, and social media, are rarely considered. These digital experiences often involve simple, repetitive routines that differ from professional or live performances, and it remains unclear whether they constitute meaningful visual expertise. Similarly, the influence of viewing medium, such as smartphone vs. large display, on biological motion perception has yet to be systematically examined. A promising development is the inclusion of dedicated items assessing observational experience in recent psychometric instruments, such as in the Gold-DSI.

Dancers are not only trained in motor skills but also in artistic and emotional expressivity. Feelings, meanings, and narratives are conveyed through bodily movements. As a result, dancers may exhibit enhanced interoceptive accuracy or awareness. Moreover, expert dancers generally show superior physical fitness, lower body mass index (BMI), enhanced proprioceptive abilities, and greater body awareness than non-dancers.,,,, These characteristics are difficult to assess through self-report questionnaires alone, and the most appropriate measures of expertise may vary with the research question.

We propose defining dance expertise multidimensionally, considering activities such as daily training, live performance, rehearsal, teaching, choreography, and improvisation, that develop distinct neurocognitive competences (see ). We recommend differentiating visuomotor and visual expertise across dance styles, reporting age of onset, and using validated inventories such as the Gold-DSI as part of a multidimensional assessment of expertise, ideally complemented by physiological and other psychometric measures relevant to dance training. Collaborating with dance professionals is essential for accurate classification.

Most dance-related studies have been conducted in laboratory settings, with low ecological validity, where participants viewed dance videos or pictures, often in greyscale, with contextual elements blurred or removed.  provides an overview of research settings, methods, and stimuli employed in dance research with regard to (1) the setting in which dance is performed and/or experienced and (2) the quality and realism of stimuli used to represent it.

Movement degrades signal quality in neuroimaging. However, advances in mobile brain imaging make it possible to record neural activity and cognitive responses in ecological (performance) settings, including real-world full-body behaviors,,,, and dance—on stage, in nightclubs, and in social spaces.

Dynamic social interactions can be indexed by measuring interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), the similarity in brain activity between individuals over time.,,, However, most studies measure neural synchrony between individuals experiencing the same stimulus sequentially, rather than simultaneously, and studies involving large groups sharing the same physical space remain rare. One notable exception was Rai et al. (2025). An interdisciplinary team recorded mobile EEG from 23 audience members simultaneously in a theater. INS between spectators was highest in the delta frequency band and varied with the dancers’ movements and subjective ratings of expected audience engagement, as predicted by the choreographer and performer. Neural synchrony was highest during moments of direct interaction with the dancers (i.e., eye contact), and was significantly higher than during solo laboratory viewing of the same performance. These findings provide initial neuroscientific evidence that experiencing dance involves active communication between performers and spectators, and that artistic intentions can be “detected” as INS among audience members. Together with other studies,,, this illustrates the importance of co-presence for the full aesthetic experience, which is only possible in ecological settings.

While artifact rejection methods have been developed for cleaning movement-induced noise in EEG recordings, these have been evaluated primarily during walking or cycling, with limited testing for more complex, dance-like movements. There is, so far, no standard method for processing locomotive EEG data. It is therefore important to consider whether the type and range of movement involved in a choreography can be reliably measured using mobile brain imaging equipment. The mobile brain/body imaging approach combines physiological measurements, motion tracking, and data-driven EEG analyses to differentiate neural from non-neural activity. First studies have successfully implemented this approach, recording EEG in participants spontaneously moving to music.

Methods from vision science can also support the study of cognitive processes in ecologically valid dance research. Eye-tracking can monitor observers’ visual behavior in laboratory and real-world environments. Although still limited, available evidence suggests that dance expertise enhances visual processing speed, potentially enabling experts to anticipate movements and process choreographic material faster. Expert dancers exhibit faster saccades and more clustered fixations, particularly when music and dance are synchronized., Measuring audience gaze with mobile eye tracking, especially when combined with objective estimates of body kinematics, may provide novel insights into collective attention during live dance performances (Arthuis et al., 2024. Conference poster at https://osf.io/4v7j2) and assist with eye-gaze/head movement artifact removal.

Combining methodological approaches, research beyond traditional laboratory environments can offer a more comprehensive understanding of the neural and cognitive processes engaged during dance performance and observation. Novel methods for artifact removal also support research in countries where access to traditional laboratory infrastructure is limited. However, efforts to increase ecological validity entail practical challenges and costs (challenging particularly for researchers working in under-resourced contexts). Besides, participants experience fatigue from wearable devices or extended recording time. These constraints may represent important challenges still to be resolved.

Early studies using dance as a research tool investigated neurocognitive functions such as action perception, visual processing, visuo-motor integration, and motor learning. These studies often employed videos of short dance sequences and recruited dancers as movement experts.,,,, Stimuli were typically brief (e.g., 5–20 s) and often drawn from Western classical ballet due to its formalization and experimental controllability. To maintain control, dance stimuli were often deprived of contextual information, with dancers filmed against plain backgrounds or reduced to point-light displays via motion capture. The advantage of such well-controlled paradigms is the ability to investigate the contribution of carefully controlled variables including temporal features (e.g., velocity, acceleration, smoothness, or synchrony), or spatial features (e.g., body positioning, visual overlap, or two-body entanglement) to dance evaluation. Dance movement stimuli can be validated, either by comparing ratings from expert and non-expert dancers or by quantifying movement features. Algorithms based on deep neural networks, such as OpenPose and DensePose, can estimate body kinematics for statistical analyses.

Importantly, approaching dance purely as a set of reducible, quantifiable features risks overlooking the essence of the experience itself., Critical features are lost, including the performer’s physical presence and expressivity, set and lighting design, and the dynamic structure of choreography or narrative over time. Future research may address these limitations by leveraging technological advances in brain imaging and applying data-driven, multivariate time-series analyses to capture the multidimensional, embodied nature of dance as it is experienced in real-life settings.

Different research questions require different research settings. Traditional laboratory settings and ecologically valid, live, or social contexts each have specific advantages and limitations. When feasible, combining methods can provide converging evidence. Mobile brain/body imaging, including wearable EEG or fNIRS, allows neural responses to be collected in naturalistic settings. Combining qualitative dancers’ reports of movement intention with interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) and computer vision tools (e.g., OpenPose, DensePose) helps connect performer intention to observer perception without reducing dance to kinematic variables alone. Striking a balance between experimental control and ecological realism is key for meaningful generalization.

Amid growing scrutiny of research reliability, particularly in light of the replication crisis in psychology and neuroscience, dance research stands to benefit from adopting rigorous methodological and reporting standards.,,,, Given the variability described in sections , , and , detailed information on dance style choice, (1) participants’ characteristics (e.g., multidimensional assessment of dance expertise; ) and (2) stimulus characteristics (;  and ) is required to allow evaluation, comparability, and replicability. Besides, Open Science practices ensure transparency, reproducibility, and interdisciplinary impact. These include open-access publications or preprints, open datasets, shared stimulus sets, protocols, and analysis code.

Dance research poses distinct challenges for reproducibility because of the embodied character, stylistic diversity, and cultural specificity of dance itself, as discussed further in Section . Where feasible, sharing movement recordings or kinematic datasets in standardized formats can enable comparison and reanalysis. Because stimulus standardization is closely linked to ecological validity, shared stimuli should be supported by comprehensive metadata. Relevant descriptors include the number of dancers, movement vocabulary, or step names (where applicable; some dance techniques rely on formally defined vocabularies (e.g., classical ballet), while others do not), music and sound properties, costumes, lighting, stage design, and recording conditions. Visibility is also important: while open-access publications can increase access for academic and non-academic audiences, dissemination through press releases, podcasts, workshops, and public engagement initiatives raises the profile of this field. Besides, events that integrate scientific presentations with movement-based activities also foster dialogue between researchers, artists, and practitioners.

Provide transparent descriptions of stimuli and clear rationales for choosing specific dance styles. Specify participants’ inclusion criteria, favoring a multivariate assessment of dance expertise when engaging with professional or semi-professional dancers. Clearly justify research settings and design choices, especially in out-of-the-lab contexts. Conduct a priori power analyses, report effect sizes, and pre-register study protocols and analysis plans. Adopt open and reproducible workflows, sharing stimulus sets, data, and code where possible, to support replication, comparability, and alignment with broader Open Science standards.

Science aims to systematize the natural, social, and personal phenomena into measurable variables that can be studied with qualitative or quantitative methods. Because methods differ across disciplines, interdisciplinary teams are essential, also in dance research. Just as meaningful scientific insights into athletic performance require collaboration with athletes, dance research needs collaboration with dancers, performers, and choreographers. Dance expertise alone is not sufficient to design scientifically rigorous studies, but plays a critical role in “translating” what dance is to non-dancer scientists within the team, enriching both the creative and the scientific process., Jola (2020) proposed two complementary approaches: (1) embodied neuroscience, in which scientists embody the physical practice of their topic of investigation, and (2) experimental choreography, in which artists engage with science so that performances emphasize both artistic and scientific value.,

Collaboration with artists provides guidance in navigating the diversity of dance styles, techniques, and training domains discussed in Sections , , and . Dance experts contribute to the creation and selection of movement features, ranging from single steps to complex sequences. Their knowledge of semiotics and dramaturgy (semiotics = how bodily gestures, postures, and spatial dynamics convey meaning, emotion, and narrative; dramaturgy = the conceptual, structural, and interpretive development of a dance piece) offers valuable insight for studying non-verbal communication through movement and helps overcome technical limitations, since some dance movements may be difficult to record using video or motion tracking suits, or may not be physically feasible under experimental constraints., Finally, interdisciplinary teams benefit from establishing shared terminology and definitions (for example, two individuals may be differently classified as “interacting” depending on whether the framework comes from social cognition or choreographic theory).

Recent interdisciplinary projects combining dance, digital humanities, computer science, psychology, and neuroscience have contributed to cultural preservation, technological innovation, and artistic practice, besides scientific advancement. Using a combination of filmography and motion tracking methods, for example, the Motion Bank project (https://www.motionbank.org/), the Virtual Dance Museum (https://dancemuseum.cs.ucy.ac.cy) for Cypriot folk dances, and the Iranian classical dance documentation project,,,, have contributed to dance documentation, transmission, and preservation. A methodological framework developed to aid such endeavors in the future is the EMOKINE framework, an open-access motion capture analysis tool that extracts statistics from kinematic features of full-body movement and is compatible with multiple motion capture systems.

Expanding dance research into computer science and robotics has already borne fruit. AI-powered digital technologies, and avatar-based media feed into the emerging area of “choreorobotics”, which applies principles of choreography, movement analysis, and somatic practice to expressive robotic systems. Besides, the novel technologies can inform choreographers about how aesthetic responses vary when dance movements are performed by a human dancer, a humanoid avatar, or an artificial agent,,,, with results suggesting that, despite the seductive allure of the novel technologies, human dance remains the most aesthetically pleasing to the human brain. These developments also extend to dance production and educational contexts, where AI-based systems are increasingly explored as tools for creative collaboration (Jobin, G. (2024). CIE Gilles Jobin Studios44/MocapLab https://www.gillesjobin.com/en/), and classroom-based movement interventions.,,

Build interdisciplinary teams involving scientists, dance professionals, and experts from relevant artistic and technological fields as equal collaborators. Co-develop research questions, methods, and stimulus design, drawing on both scientific and artistic expertise. Where available, use validated tools (e.g., motion capture) and validated analysis software (e.g., EMOKINE), to support innovation in both the arts and sciences, and translate embodied knowledge into applications in education, society, and healthcare.

Cross-cultural empirical (neuro)aesthetics investigates the universality and distinctiveness of cognitive and neural processes underlying aesthetic experiences across cultures. Despite its ubiquitous presence across societies, dance remains a relatively neglected topic in this domain. In most cultures, dance occupies an important social role, while in others it is deeply embedded in religious, spiritual, or cultural practices. Cultures have developed unique dance traditions, each practiced for specific expressive reasons., Dance also fulfills multiple psychobiological functions and regulates social and emotional behaviors.,,

Dance is culturally and socially constructed, yet it relies on core neurocognitive mechanisms such as motor control, entrainment, simulation, and expression. The multicultural nature of dance styles makes it difficult to define truly universal perceptual, cognitive, and emotional processes associated with “dance”. This cultural complexity must be accounted for in study design. However, many current investigations are limited by a broadly Western-centric perspective. Recognizing these cultural differences is crucial to understanding dance as a multisensory, multicomponent practice rooted in social and cultural contexts.

In immigration psychology, enculturation refers to the neurodevelopmental process through which individuals adopt cultural norms, while acculturation occurs when exposure to a new culture after migration shapes behaviors and preferences., These processes influence cultural life, including dance, and are shaped by both conscious and unconscious experiences. Despite their relevance, few cross-cultural studies have directly investigated differences and universals in dance perception and practice.

Recent studies demonstrate that dance evaluation is shaped by prior exposure, cultural background, enculturation, acculturation, and dance training, influencing emotional recognition and aesthetic preferences. Cross-cultural studies suggest that participants may show ethnocentric biases, meaning that they may evaluate or interpret dance more favorably when it is culturally familiar, as shown by Darda and Cross (2022), who also found that this bias was reduced in dance experts. Related work involving Western, Indian, Japanese, and Iranian contexts further suggests that cultural background, enculturation, and acculturation can shape dance preferences and emotion recognition.,, Future research should consider that concepts such as dancing bodies, spatiality, movement quality, aesthetic values, communicative functions, and expertise criteria are often framed through specific cultural lenses and may not apply universally across dance traditions. Deconstructing these ethnocentric biases is essential to place dance forms across different cultures on an equal footing and promote a more inclusive and representative study of dance.

Learning from studies with non-Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) dance traditions and participants is critical for generalizing to and learning from other populations. For example, Western ballet is typically structured around syllabus-based training focused on technique,, whereas Iranian classical dance is more imitation-based, allowing expressive movement at earlier learning stages., Because dance training style influences aesthetic preferences and the perception of unfamiliar dance styles, exploring embodied concepts such as corporeality and spatiality within different dance contexts could enhance cross-cultural understanding. The complex nature of dance also calls for multidisciplinary and mixed-method approaches to fully capture its dynamic role in human culture.

Both cultural specificity and universal foundations of dance behaviors are important mechanisms to study. Mechanisms such as entrainment and simulation may be shared across humans, yet their manifestation is shaped by cultural context. Participants’ cultural background, prior exposure, and experiences of enculturation or acculturation can be assessed with questionnaires (e.g., the Enculturation and Acculturation Quiz; EAQ). Findings from one dance tradition cannot be generalized to all dance traditions.

The benefits of dance practice in the general population are noted across health-related scientific disciplines.,,,, Dance-based interventions draw on partnered (e.g., standard dance, Argentine tango), group (e.g., jazz dance, contemporary, hip-hop), and traditional dance forms (e.g., African dance Nogma). In neurological diseases, dance interventions have supported treatment adherence, mental health, psychosocial functioning, cognitive capacity, and motor skills. In Parkinson’s disease, meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have found that dance improves motor symptoms, functional mobility, cognition, and quality of life.,, Similar benefits have been reported in oncology and cardiac disease populations, where dance supports increased physical activity, mental health, and overall quality of life. Yet, recent reviews have also reported mixed, small, or contradictory effects in some populations and outcome measures.

Variability in intervention protocols, sample characteristics, and outcome measures continues to challenge the field. Heterogeneity in study designs, including differences in sample sizes, age groups, treatment frequencies, specification of treatment factors, and clinical populations—and importantly, of dance style—makes it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about efficacy. For example, Argentine tango has been associated with greater improvement in motor-related symptoms in individuals with Parkinson’s disease compared to other dance forms. Identifying what differentiates Argentine tango from styles such as Waltz for individuals with Parkinson’s disease may help tailor dance interventions to better target specific neurocognitive, emotional, or motor processes. In general, interventions often lack standardization and valid control groups, further complicating comparisons across studies. Consequently, distinguishing genuine null effects from limitations in the available evidence remains challenging.

A notable exception is dance movement therapy (DMT). DMT is a validated psychotherapeutic dance intervention package with clear therapeutic factors approved for clinical settings. DMT is grounded in the principle that physical movement can reflect emotional states, and that modifying these movement patterns can influence both psychological and social experiences. A recent scoping review of DMT and other Creative Arts Therapies (CATs) identified therapeutic factors at three levels. These include common psychotherapy factors such as the therapeutic alliance, emotional regulation, and the creation of a safe environment. They also include factors shared across CATs, such as artistic engagement, symbolic work, self-display, and re-enactment. DMT-specific factors include embodiment, understood as experiencing the body and increasing body awareness, expressing, and sharing emotions non-verbally through movement, using movement metaphors and bodily sensations for insight, and artistic agency. A meta-analysis about DMT showed that expressivity was the treatment factor most directly linked to reductions in symptoms of depression and anxiety., Relational processes, such as kinesthetic empathy, mirroring, movement dialogue, and synchrony, are also central to DMT. In clinical populations, DMT has been shown to reduce symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress. As a psychotherapeutic approach, DMT may offer benefits beyond general physical exercises, meditation, or other CATs, including enhanced proprioception and interoception, refined motor imagery, and improved emotional awareness, capacities also developed through professional dance training.

Dance-based (non-DMT) interventions can use DMT as a model for implementing structured methods and identifying factors that may contribute to positive health outcomes, optimizing dance style choice, treatment duration, frequency, and intensity of any intervention for a specific health outcome.

Standardized practices and methodological improvements are needed across domains of dance-based interventions for health. Priorities include larger sample sizes, rigorously designed RCTs with appropriate blinding, long-term follow-ups, development of disorder-specific protocols, specification of treatment factors, reporting of key intervention variables (e.g., frequency, duration, facilitator expertise), use of standardized outcome measures, and an operationalization statement about how key variables are hypothesized to modulate the neurocognitive process under investigation, ensuring also gender balance and representation of minoritized and Indigenous groups.

By strengthening the theoretical and methodological foundations of dance-based interventions, future studies can contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for healthcare and policy. We recognize that dance-based health research remains underfunded compared with other arts-based therapies, such as music and art therapies, and that high methodological standards can be challenging under limited resources. Yet, even partial alignment with these principles can move the field forward and strengthen its credibility, visibility, funding opportunities, and translational impact.

By examining what defines dance, how dance expertise can be measured, and how dance can be studied across laboratory and real-world contexts, this seven-principle framework promotes a systematic approach.

Emphasizing inclusivity, individual variation, cross-disciplinary collaborations, replicability, and visibility, the framework supports evidence that can deepen our understanding of dance’s impact on individuals and communities. Ultimately, it aims to bridge academic inquiry and societal application while fostering innovation across disciplines.

neuroscience.title: Prognostic value of plasma brain‐derived phosphorylated Tau
neuroscience.abstract: Plasma brain‐derived phosphorylated Tau217 (BD‐pTau217) may provide a more Alzheimer's disease (AD) ‐specific plasma tau measure than total pTau217, but its prognostic value is unclear.We compared baseline plasma NULISAseq biomarkers for amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) progression (positivity: Centiloid ≥ 24.1; n = 175) and clinical progression to mild cognitive impairment or AD dementia (n = 508) in cognitively unimpaired Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants using Cox models and time‐dependent areas under the curve (tdAUCs).Over a median clinical follow‐up of 6 years (interquartile range [IQR], 3.0–7.3), BD‐pTau217 and total pTau217 had similar discrimination (full‐follow‐up AUC = 0.66 each; high‐versus‐low hazard ratios [HRs]; 95% confidence interval [CIs]: 2.8 [1.89–4.06] and 2.9 [1.96–4.35], respectively). Among initially amyloid‐negative participants, BD‐pTau217 better predicted progression to amyloid PET positivity at 2.5 years (tdAUC 0.82 vs. 0.69; HR = 10.54 [95% CI 2.3–48.1], p = 0.00015) and 4 years (tdAUC 0.77 vs. 0.64; HR = 7.03 [95% CI 1.9–25.6], p = 0.00055) compared to total pTau217.BD‐pTau217 better predicted near‐term progression to amyloid PET positivity than total pTau217, but showed no advantage for clinical progression, supporting its potential value as an early marker of AD pathological change.
neuroscience.text:
The ability to estimate the presence of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology through blood‐based measures represents a major advancement in both AD research and, increasingly, clinical care. In symptomatic individuals, elevated levels of phosphorylated Tau217 (pTau217) in the blood strongly suggest that the presenting symptomatology is attributable to AD, as a strong indicator of neuritic amyloid plaque pathology. Conversely, low levels indicate that AD pathology is unlikely to be present at a clinically significant level, and that the observed cognitive deficits may be better explained by an alternative cause.

It is consistently reported that the positive predictive value (PPV) of pTau217 is lower than its negative predictive value (NPV). This difference is partly attributable to lower disease prevalence in certain tested populations (e.g., cognitively unimpaired) but also partially reflects that elevated pTau217 levels can be occasionally observed due to other reasons, such as chronic kidney disease (CKD) or other medical conditions. In these instances, only more severe cases are likely to elevate pTau217 sufficiently to shift an individual into a different classification group. It has been shown that in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), p‐tau levels, including pTau217, are increased in the blood,  but not cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). This points to a potentially specific peripheral expression of p‐tau, localized, for example, to striated muscle tissue in ALS but also introduces uncertainty regarding other possible sources of circulating p‐tau if such tests are widely adopted in unselected, heterogeneous primary and secondary care populations.

Therefore, to mitigate potential peripheral contributions, whose frequency and impact remain uncertain, the use of brain‐derived phosphorylated Tau217 (BD‐pTau217) immunoassays is essential. Tau expressed in the periphery includes a 254‐amino acid insert encoded by exon 4a, commonly referred to as “big tau.” Because the sandwich immunoassay design of most pTau217 tests targets epitopes that span regions flanking exon 4a, these assays are not able to distinguish between peripheral pTau217 (if present) and pTau217 released from the central nervous system (CNS) in response to AD pathology. A BD‐pTau217 immunoassay can be designed using the same capture antibody targeting phosphorylated threonine 217, but with a detector antibody raised against the junction created when exon 4a is absent. In this configuration, the assay selectively recognizes CNS‐type tau and excludes “big tau” isoforms containing the exon 4a insert. To demonstrate this, Janelidze and colleagues compared different plasma pTau217 assay designs in ALS patients and found increases in total pTau217, but not BD‐pTau217. Therefore, with a more specific assay design, enhanced diagnostic performance of BD‐pTau217 for AD pathology has been reported , ,  including comparisons with post‐mortem neuropathology. In AD, cross‐sectional studies suggest that BD‐pTau217 offers modest diagnostic advantages over total plasma pTau217 for identifying cerebral AD pathology.

However, to date, there has not been an evaluation of the prognostic performance of BD‐pTau217 (and other BD‐pTau assays) compared to total pTau. In this study, we sought to address this knowledge gap by assessing the ability of plasma BD‐pTau217 to predict amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) and clinical progression in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort.

Data were obtained from the ADNI cohort. Participants with available plasma NULISAseq CNS 120 panel biomarker measurements were included. Diagnostic classification at baseline followed ADNI criteria for CU, MCI, or AD dementia. Demographic characteristics including age, sex, education, and average amyloid PET Centiloid (CL) values are shown in Table . For longitudinal analyses, participants were required to have baseline NULISAseq measurement and longitudinal amyloid PET or clinical diagnostic follow‐up. Prognostic analyses focused on baseline CU participants: amyloid PET progression analyses were restricted to CU participants without amyloid PET positivity at baseline, whereas clinical progression analyses followed CU participants for progression to MCI or AD dementia. All analyses were performed with publicly available de‐identified data from ADNI1/GO/2/3 participants (Figure ).

Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the plasma NULISAseq cohort

Note: Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of ADNI participants with plasma NULISAseq measurements, overall and by baseline diagnosis group. P‐values reflect overall group comparisons across CU, MCI, and AD dementia using ANOVA for continuous variables and chi‐square test for sex. Values are mean ± SD unless otherwise indicated.

Abbreviations: AD dementia, Alzheimer's disease dementia; ADNI, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative; ANOVA, analysis of variance; CL, Centiloid; CU, cognitively unimpaired; MCI, mild cognitive impairment; PET, positron emission tomography; SD, standard deviation.

Amyloid PET data ([18F]‐florbetapir PET scans) from baseline and follow‐up were preprocessed with an in‐house PET unified pipeline (PUP) , ,  using corresponding baseline T1‐weighted structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans for anatomical labeling in individual space with FreeSurfer v7 (http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/). Briefly, for semi‐quantitative Aβ burden, mean cortical standard uptake value ratios (mcSUVRs) were extracted and averaged across the set of FreeSurfer‐defined cortical regions of interest including frontal, parietal, temporal, and precuneus.,  We converted the mcSUVRs calculated with a cerebellar reference region to CL values.

Amyloid PET positivity (A+) was defined using a primary threshold of CL ≥ 24.1, selected a priori because it discriminates neuropathologically confirmed none or sparse versus moderate to frequent plaques in autopsy‐confirmed cases. For cross‐sectional analyses, amyloid PET status was determined with the closest visit associated with the NULISAseq measurement and for longitudinal assessments, follow‐up scans were used to assess progression from amyloid‐negative (A−) to A+. In sensitivity analyses, alternative literature‐supported thresholds for A+ were additionally evaluated (Centiloid ≥ 18 and ≥ 37)., ,  These analyses were performed to assess robustness of biomarker performance across commonly used definitions of A+.

Plasma biomarkers were measured at Michael T. Zuendel Biomarker Laboratory at Banner Sun Health Research Institute on an ARGO HT platform (Alamar Biosciences) using the NULISAseqTM CNS Disease Panel., ,  We used the NULISA Protein Quantification (NPQ) values on the log2 scale with intra‐and‐inter plate normalization. The highly multiplexed panel measures neurodegenerative disease‐related biomarkers in plasma or CSF with ultra‐broad dynamic range that can quantify extremely low concentrations of biomarkers like pTau217 in the attomolar range along with highly concentrated proteins from the same 250 µl sample.

Brain‐derived and total versions of phosphorylated tau biomarkers were evaluated, with BD‐pTau217 designated as the primary biomarker of interest based on prior evidence of strong diagnostic performance. The primary comparison focused on BD‐pTau217 versus total pTau217. BD‐pTau181 was included as an additional brain‐derived phosphorylated tau comparator in the primary amyloid progression table, while other pTau species, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and pTau/Aβ ratios were evaluated in secondary sensitivity analyses. Given that NULISAseq NPQ values are reported on a log2 scale, pTau/Aβ42 and Aβ40/Aβ42 measures were calculated by subtracting the denominator NPQ from the numerator NPQ. These measures represent log2 NPQ‐derived relative ratio scores and should not be interpreted as absolute concentration ratios.

Longitudinal outcomes included amyloid PET progression and clinical diagnostic progression. For amyloid progression analyses, baseline was defined as the earliest available amyloid PET assessment with a matched baseline plasma NULISAseq measurement. Analyses were restricted to CU participants who were A− at baseline, as defined in Section , and who had longitudinal amyloid PET follow‐up. Participants were followed to progression to A+ status or censored at their last available PET visit if they remained A−. Time‐to‐event was calculated from the baseline A− PET visit to the first A+ PET visit or last follow‐up. For sensitivity analyses, amyloid progression was also evaluated using alternative thresholds of CL ≥ 18 and CL ≥ 37., ,  Baseline biomarker measurements were matched to the baseline amyloid PET assessment using the closest available plasma sample within a 365‐day window. The broader baseline A− cohort with longitudinal amyloid PET and plasma biomarker data comprised 330 participants across diagnostic groups. The primary amyloid progression analysis was restricted a priori to 175 participants who were cognitively unimpaired and amyloid‐negative at baseline and had longitudinal florbetapir PET follow‐up. These restrictions reflected the study questions and availability of the required longitudinal outcomes rather than selection based on plasma biomarker values. Sensitivity cohorts included 166 participants at CL ≥ 18 and 185 at CL ≥ 37.

For clinical progression analyses, baseline was defined as the plasma NULISAseq collection date. Analyses included participants who were CU at plasma sampling, had no recorded MCI or AD dementia diagnosis on or before plasma collection, and had at least one subsequent diagnostic assessment. Participants were followed from plasma collection until the first qualifying progression event or were censored at their last available diagnostic assessment. Clinical progression was evaluated as progression from CU to MCI or AD dementia and, separately, from CU to MCI. Two participants with conflicting CU and MCI diagnoses recorded on the same date were excluded. Time‐to‐event was defined as the time interval between baseline plasma biomarker collection and the first recorded diagnosis of MCI or AD dementia, or censoring at the last available diagnostic assessment. Of the 1,427 ADNI participants with plasma NULISAseq measurements and an available baseline clinical diagnosis, 529 were cognitively unimpaired at baseline. Clinical progression analyses included 508 of these participants with longitudinal diagnostic follow‐up.

Longitudinal prognostic performance of the plasma biomarkers was assessed using complementary time‐to‐event and discrimination approaches. Cox proportional hazards (CPH) models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for amyloid and clinical progression associated with baseline biomarker levels. For binary comparisons, biomarker groups were defined using Youden index‐derived cutoffs estimated from receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. These cutoffs were used to define “high” and “low” biomarker groups for Kaplan–Meier (KM), log‐rank, and Cox model comparisons. For each biomarker and Centiloid threshold, a single Youden cutoff was estimated using conversion status over the full available follow‐up and was then applied unchanged in the 2.5‐ and 4‐year horizon‐restricted Cox and log‐rank analyses.

KM curves were used to visualize risk separation between biomarker‐defined high and low groups over time. For amyloid progression analyses, Cox models, log‐rank tests, C‐indices, and tdAUCs were evaluated at prespecified 2.5‐ and 4‐year horizons by censoring follow‐up at each horizon. For clinical progression analyses, Cox models, log‐rank tests, C‐indices, and full‐follow‐up AUCs were evaluated across the full available follow‐up, while tdAUCs were calculated at 2.5 and 4 years to summarize short‐term discrimination. Analyses focused on relative discrimination and ranking performance rather than absolute risk prediction.

We compared BD and total pTau biomarkers using paired analyses where applicable. Statistical significance was evaluated using two‐sided tests. In secondary adjusted Cox models, continuous biomarker values were standardized. Clinical progression models were adjusted for age, sex, education, and apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 copy number; amyloid PET progression models were adjusted for age, sex, and APOE ε4 copy number to evaluate whether associations were independent of these demographic and genetic risk factors. Analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.3) using the survival, riskRegression, timeROC, and pROC packages.

We included 1,427 participants with plasma NULISAseq biomarker measurements with a mean age 73.0 (SD ±7.3 years). Baseline age, sex distribution, education, and amyloid PET CL values differed across diagnostic groups (all p < 0.001; Table ). AD participants were older on average and had higher amyloid PET CL values than CU and MCI participants, while the CU group had a higher proportion of women. Prognostic analyses focused on baseline CU participants, including CU participants with longitudinal clinical follow‐up for clinical progression analyses and CU participants who were A− at baseline with longitudinal amyloid PET follow‐up for amyloid PET progression analyses.

Among CU participants with available baseline amyloid PET, 186 were A− and 76 were A+ at the primary CL ≥ 24.1 threshold. Baseline plasma BD‐pTau217 levels were higher in CU A+ than CU A− participants (median 11.9 [interquartile range {IQR} 11.6–12.3] vs. 11.0 [10.7–11.2] NPQ), as were total pTau217 levels (median 11.8 [11.3–12.1] vs. 10.6 [10.3–11.0] NPQ). For longitudinal amyloid progression analyses, 175 baseline CU A− participants with longitudinal amyloid PET follow‐up were included. At the primary amyloid positivity threshold (CL ≥ 24.1), BD‐pTau217 showed the strongest prognostic performance, whereas total pTau217 and BD‐pTau181 showed weaker and non‐significant associations (Table ). BD‐pTau217 showed the highest time‐dependent discrimination across follow‐up, with prespecified 2.5‐ and 4‐year estimates reported in Table  and the broader tdAUC trajectory is shown in Figure . This pattern was also apparent in the KM analyses, in which BD‐pTau217 showed clearer risk separation than total pTau217 over follow‐up (Figure ). At this primary threshold, most ratio measures and alternative pTau species, including BD‐pTau231 and pTau231‐based measures, showed weaker or non‐significant associations, supporting BD‐pTau217 as the strongest overall predictor.

Prognostic performance of plasma biomarkers for amyloid PET progression (A− to A+) in baseline cognitively unimpaired participants at the primary amyloid positivity threshold (Centiloid ≥ 24.1)

Note: Discrimination is summarized using tdAUC at prespecified 2.5‐ and 4‐year horizons. HRs and C‐indices were derived from Cox proportional hazards models comparing high versus low biomarker groups within each follow‐up horizon. Log‐rank p‐values compare KM curves for the same high versus low biomarker groups. High versus low biomarker groups were defined using Youden index cutoffs derived from overall amyloid progression status across the full follow‐up period.

Abbreviations: BD‐pTau, brain‐derived phosphorylated Tau; CI, confidence interval; HR, hazard ratio; KM, Kaplan–Meier; PET, positron emission tomography; pTau, phosphorylated Tau; tdAUC, time‐dependent area under the curve.

At 2.5 years (N = 175; converters = 12), elevated baseline BD‐pTau217 was strongly associated with amyloid PET progression (HR 10.54, 95% CI 2.3–48.1; log‐rank p = 0.00015; tdAUC 0.82). In contrast, total pTau217 and BD‐pTau181 were not significantly associated with progression and showed substantially lower discrimination. At 4 years (converters = 13), BD‐pTau217 remained the strongest predictor (HR 7.03, 95% CI 1.9–25.6; log‐rank p = 0.00055; tdAUC 0.77), while total pTau217 and BD‐pTau181 again demonstrated weak and non‐significant associations (Table ). These results suggest that prognostic performance at the primary threshold was strongest for BD‐pTau217 rather than reflecting a uniform signal across pTau measures.

Across sensitivity analyses, biomarker performance varied according to the amyloid positivity threshold used (Tables ). At the lower threshold (CL ≥ 18), discrimination was generally weaker and less consistent across single biomarkers, although selected pTau/Aβ42 ratio measures, including BD‐pTau217/Aβ42 and pTau217/Aβ42, showed stronger associations with amyloid progression compared with their corresponding single‐marker measures.

At the higher threshold (CL ≥ 37), several biomarkers and ratio measures demonstrated improved prognostic performance, including total pTau217, BD‐pTau181, BD‐pTau231, and corresponding pTau/Aβ42 ratio measures, consistent with increasing signal at more advanced stages of amyloid burden. Notably, at both CL ≥ 18 and CL ≥ 37, estimates at the 2.5‐ and 4‐year horizons were identical (although the corresponding tdAUCs varied slightly) because all amyloid conversion events observed within the 4‐year horizon occurred within the first 2.5 years (e.g., CL ≥ 18: 14 events by 2.5 years and 4 years; CL ≥ 37: 13 events by 2.5 years and 4 years), whereas at the primary threshold (CL ≥ 24.1), additional events occurring after 2.5 years resulted in differing estimates between time horizons. Overall, BD‐pTau217 demonstrated the highest observed time‐dependent discrimination at the primary CL ≥ 24.1 threshold.

In secondary adjusted Cox models, baseline BD‐pTau217 remained associated with amyloid PET progression after adjustment for age, sex, and APOE ε4 copy number at both 2.5 years (HR 1.43 per SD, 95% CI 1.07–1.92; p = 0.0155) and 4 years (HR 1.39 per SD, 95% CI 1.03–1.86; p = 0.029). Total pTau217 was not significantly associated with amyloid PET progression at 2.5 years (HR 1.37 per SD, 95% CI 0.92–2.04; p = 0.12) or 4 years (HR 1.28 per SD, 95% CI 0.85–1.93; p = 0.23).

Among the 508 baseline CU participants included, 106 progressed to MCI or AD dementia during a median follow‐up of 6.0 years (IQR 3.0–7.3). When restricting progression to MCI only, 101 participants progressed and 407 had no recorded MCI event. Five participants progressed directly to AD dementia without an intervening recorded MCI diagnosis.

Participants with high total pTau217 levels had a 2.9‐fold increased risk of progression compared with those in the low group (HR 2.9, 95% CI 1.96–4.35; log‐rank p < 0.001), with progression observed in 32.4% of the high group versus 12.8% of the low group. BD‐pTau217 showed comparable risk estimates (HR 2.8, 95% CI 1.89–4.06; high group 35.8% vs. low group 14.6% progressed). Similar risk estimates were observed for BD‐pTau181 (HR 2.7, 95% CI 1.81–4.05). Full‐follow‐up AUCs were similar across markers (0.65–0.66), and concordance indices ranged from 0.62 to 0.63. Time‐dependent discrimination at 2.5 and 4 years was also modest and overlapped across markers (tdAUCs approximately 0.59–0.63) (Table , Figure ). KM analyses showed separation for both BD‐pTau217 and total pTau217, but overall differences between markers were smaller than for amyloid PET progression (Figure ).

Prognostic performance of plasma pTau biomarkers for clinical progression from cognitively unimpaired to MCI or AD dementia

Note: The tdAUCs summarize discrimination at prespecified 2.5‐ and 4‐year horizons. Full‐follow‐up AUC summarizes continuous biomarker discrimination for overall clinical progression status across available follow‐up. HRs, log‐rank p‐values, and C‐indices are derived from full‐follow‐up Cox and KM analyses comparing high versus low biomarker groups. High versus low groups were defined using Youden index cutoffs derived from overall clinical progression status. CU→MCI and CU→MCI/AD yielded similar tdAUC estimates at the 2.5‐ and 4‐year horizons because nearly all early clinical progression events captured by these horizons were transitions from CU to MCI.

Abbreviations: AD, Alzheimer's disease; AUC, area under the curve; BD‐pTau217, brain‐derived phosphorylated Tau217; CU, cognitively unimpaired; KM, Kaplan–Meier; MCI, mild cognitive impairment; MCI, mild cognitive impairment; pTau, phosphorylated Tau; tdAUC, time‐dependent area under the curve.

Results were similar when we restricted progression to MCI alone, where high total pTau217 was associated with a 2.95‐fold increased risk of progression (95% CI 1.96–4.43), with progression rates of 31% in the high group versus 12.1% in the low group. BD‐pTau217 again had comparable performance (HR 2.7, 95% CI 1.85–4.04; progression rates 33.8% versus 14.0% in high and low groups, respectively), again with overlapping discrimination metrics across biomarkers (Table ). Across models, discrimination for clinical progression was modest but consistent.

In secondary adjusted Cox models, for clinical progression to MCI or dementia (N = 508; 106 events) after adjustment for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 copy number, baseline BD‐pTau217 remained associated with progression (HR 1.39 per SD, 95% CI 1.18–1.64; p < 0.001; C‐index, 0.683), as did total pTau217 (HR 1.39 per SD, 95% CI 1.16–1.67; p < 0.001; C‐index, 0.684). Results were similar for progression restricted to MCI (N = 508; 101 events).

In this study, we evaluated the prognostic performance of brain‐derived and total plasma pTau biomarkers for amyloid PET and clinical progression in cognitively unimpaired ADNI participants with plasma NULISAseq measurements. We found that BD‐pTau217 demonstrated stronger prognostic value for amyloid PET progression, particularly at the primary A+ threshold of CL ≥ 24.1. At this threshold, BD‐pTau217 was the only primary marker to show strong and statistically significant prediction at both 2.5‐and 4‐year progression, whereas total pTau217 and BD‐pTau181 showed weaker and non‐significant associations. Sensitivity analyses across CL ≥ 18 and CL ≥ 37 further suggested that biomarker performance varies by amyloid threshold, with broader pTau and pTau/Aβ42 ratio signals emerging most clearly with alternative thresholds.

In contrast to findings for amyloid PET progression, differences between brain‐derived and total plasma pTau measures for prediction of clinical progression were modest, with both assay designs showing similar discrimination for progression from cognitively unimpaired status to MCI or dementia. Exploratory analyses further indicated that incorporation of plasma Aβ42 into biomarker ratios did not materially improve prediction beyond pTau217 alone for clinical outcomes. These findings suggest that while plasma pTau217 measures are associated with future clinical change, improvements in biological specificity achieved through brain‐derived measurements appear to have greater relevance for predicting underlying pathological progression than for short‐term clinical transitions.

Prior studies of plasma pTau biomarkers have largely focused on cross‐sectional discrimination of amyloid and tau pathology, consistently demonstrating better performance of plasma pTau217 to discriminate between the presence or absence of amyloid plaques and the diagnosis of AD compared with blood biomarkers., , ,  Recent work has additionally suggested that selectively measuring brain‐derived fractions of plasma pTau may improve diagnostic performance., , ,  Our results extend these observations by demonstrating that BD‐pTau217 provides stronger prognostic information for future amyloid accumulation than total plasma pTau217, particularly at the clinically relevant CL ≥ 24.1 threshold. Although brain‐derived and total pTau217 capture overlapping biological signal, the stronger and more consistent discrimination observed for BD‐pTau217 suggests that isolating brain‐origin tau species may enhance sensitivity to active amyloid‐related neurobiological change by reducing non‐specific signal from the periphery.

In analyses focused on amyloid PET progression, the relative performance of biomarkers depended on the amyloid positivity threshold used. At the primary CL ≥ 24.1 threshold, a neuropathologically validated cutoff in autopsy confirmed cases, BD‐pTau217 clearly outperformed total pTau217 and BD‐pTau181, which showed weak and non‐significant associations with progression. At the lower CL ≥ 18 threshold, single‐marker discrimination was weaker and less consistent, while selected pTau/Aβ42 ratio measures, , including BD‐pTau217/Aβ42 and pTau217/Aβ42, showed stronger associations than their corresponding single‐marker measures.,  This supports the notion that Aβ peptides in plasma may play an important role in the earliest phase of cerebral amyloid accumulation, despite challenges in robustness. At the higher CL ≥ 37 threshold, a broader set of biomarkers became informative, including total pTau217, BD‐pTau181, BD‐pTau231, and several pTau/Aβ42 ratio measures. This threshold‐dependent pattern suggests that different plasma biomarker combinations may be informative at different stages of amyloid accumulation, while BD‐pTau217 remains the most robust single‐marker predictor at the primary clinically relevant threshold.

Across clinical endpoints, discrimination for progression from CU to MCI or MCI/AD was modest and largely overlapping across biomarkers. BD‐pTau217, total pTau217, and BD‐pTau181 showed similar risk estimates and concordance values (HRs, C‐indices, and tdAUC), indicating that brain‐derived measurements did not clearly improve prediction of clinical progression. In contrast to amyloid PET progression, where BD‐pTau217 showed more pronounced advantage at the primary amyloid threshold, differences between brain‐derived and total pTau measures were small for clinical outcomes. The weaker separation for clinical outcomes is consistent with clinical progression being influenced by multiple factors beyond amyloid and plasma tau burden, including downstream neurodegeneration, vascular factors, comorbid pathology, and individual resilience. Furthermore, because incident MCI is etiologically heterogeneous and some events may not reflect AD as the primary cause, this endpoint definition may have attenuated the differences between an AD‐specific biomarker such as BD‐pTau217 and total pTau217.

The stronger prognostic performance observed for amyloid PET progression compared with clinical progression likely reflects the closer biological relationship between plasma pTau biomarkers and underlying AD pathology than with downstream clinical symptoms, as our group has recently shown comparing BD p‐tau217 against neuropathology. Cognitive decline results from a combination of amyloid and tau pathology but also neurodegeneration, vascular factors, comorbid pathology (e.g., TDP‐43), and individual resilience, making clinical progression inherently more heterogeneous and difficult to predict. In contrast, progression from A− to A+ status more directly reflects ongoing AD pathological processes, which plasma pTau biomarkers are thought to capture. These findings suggest that plasma pTau measurements, particularly BD‐pTau217, may be valuable for identifying cognitively unimpaired, A− individuals at elevated risk of near‐term amyloid progression, including those who may be candidates for primary prevention trials aimed at preventing progression of AD pathology.

Several considerations should be noted for the interpretation of these findings. First, plasma biomarkers were measured using the NULISAseq research platform, which provides highly sensitive, multiplexed relative quantification but differs from emerging in‐vitro diagnostic platforms intended for routine clinical use. Therefore, the absolute performance metrics in this study may not directly translate to the clinical assays, underscoring the need to further validate across independent cohorts and assay platforms., ,  Second, clinical progression endpoints are influenced by multiple pathological and non‐pathological factors beyond amyloid and tau, which likely contributes to the moderate discrimination observed for the clinical outcomes. Third, the number of amyloid progression events was limited, particularly in horizon‐specific and threshold‐specific analyses, which may reduce the precision of some estimates. Lastly, we note that this was a single‐cohort, hypothesis generating analysis in a highly selected research sample. ADNI is a predominantly White and highly educated cohort (mean education, 16.2 years overall and 16.7 years among CU participants), detailed medical comorbidity burden was not included into the present models. Temporal alignment of the plasma measures and longitudinal PET or clinical follow‐up further restricted the analytic subset. More importantly, external validation in larger population‐based and clinically heterogeneous cohorts with greater racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, educational, and comorbidity diverse datasets will be necessary to determine biomarker performance across populations, assay platforms, and follow‐up intervals.

To summarize, plasma BD‐pTau217 has shown an added advantage in cross‐sectional prediction of AD pathology,, , ,  however, in this study, we demonstrated that BD‐pTau217 showed the highest observed time‐dependent discrimination at the primary CL ≥ 24.1 threshold for amyloid PET progression among cognitively unimpaired participants. At the primary ≥ 24.1 CL threshold, BD‐pTau217 clearly outperformed both pTau217 and BD‐pTau181, whereas differences between brain‐derived and total tau measures were smaller for predicting clinical progression. Sensitivity analyses indicated that biomarker performance varied across amyloid positivity thresholds, with selected pTau/Aβ42 ratio measures and additional pTau species becoming more informative at alternative cut points. Collectively, these preliminary findings support the use of BD‐pTau217 for risk stratification in prevention trials targeting the earliest detectable stages of Alzheimer's disease. Future studies should evaluate its performance in more diverse populations, over longer follow‐up periods, and across multiple assay platforms to facilitate clinical implementation.

neuroscience.title: Neuroimaging of Anxiety in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Integrating Structural, Functional, Molecular, and Network Perspectives—A Narrative Review
neuroscience.abstract: This narrative review summarizes neuroimaging evidence on the neurobiological correlates of anxiety symptoms in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) across the Alzheimer’s disease continuum. A literature search was conducted in PubMed from 1 January 2015 to 30 June 2026. Structural magnetic resonance imaging studies link anxiety to atrophy in medial temporal and prefrontal–limbic regions, with white matter disruption in the cingulum bundle and uncinate fasciculus. Functional magnetic resonance imaging shows altered interactions among the default mode network, salience network, and central executive network. Molecular imaging points to limbic glucose hypometabolism, amyloid deposition, and neuroinflammation. Emerging vascular and peripheral biomarker data further implicate blood–brain barrier disruption and gut–brain axis alterations. Most of the literature is cross-sectional and relies on heterogeneous anxiety assessments. Findings are further complicated by symptom overlap with depression and other neuropsychiatric manifestations, and anxiety-specific imaging studies in MCI are relatively scarce. Direct evidence specific to anxiety in MCI remains limited; some findings discussed here are derived from studies of Alzheimer’s disease dementia or general neuropsychiatric symptoms and should be interpreted accordingly. Longitudinal multimodal designs, standardized anxiety-specific instruments, and integrative models linking symptom dimensions to imaging and fluid biomarkers are needed to disentangle whether anxiety in MCI represents an early marker of neurodegeneration, a disease-course modifier, or both.
neuroscience.text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of disability and dependency among older adults and an escalating global public health challenge. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) marks the transitional stage between normal aging and dementia, offering a critical window for identifying individuals at high risk of developing AD and for implementing early interventions., MCI was defined according to the Petersen and NIA-AA criteria: objective evidence of cognitive impairment, largely preserved functional independence, and absence of dementia. MCI is clinically heterogeneous and not all individuals progress to AD dementia., Identifying neuropsychiatric features that characterize a higher-risk subgroup could refine prognostic precision beyond cognitive testing alone. Anxiety is one such feature. It may emerge early in the disease process and intersect with stress-related, inflammatory, vascular, and neurodegenerative pathways. Anxiety symptoms are prevalent in MCI and may be associated with higher conversion rates to AD dementia. Longitudinal data further suggest that anxiety may be associated with accelerated cognitive decline in cognitively normal older adults, independent of depression, baseline test performance, and other confounders. Greater baseline anxiety corresponds to faster subsequent deterioration. It remains unknown whether anxiety heralds incipient neurodegeneration, actively drives cognitive decline via stress pathway activation, blunted neuroplasticity, inflammation, sleep disturbance, and vascular compromise, or both. These processes likely interact bidirectionally, with their relative contributions shifting across the AD spectrum. In this review, anxiety is conceptualized according to the DSM-5 framework as excessive fear and worry accompanied by related behavioral and physiological disturbances. Operationally, we focused on anxiety symptoms quantified by validated rating scales (eg, the anxiety item of the Neuropsychiatric Inventory, HAM-A, GAI, STAI) or ascertained through clinical interview, including anxiety dimensions embedded within broader neuropsychiatric symptom (NPS) or mild behavioral impairment (MBI) frameworks, rather than restricting the review to formal DSM-5 anxiety disorder diagnoses.

Several reviews have examined neuropsychiatric symptoms in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) or mapped symptom-general neural correlates across the AD continuum., However, these works have typically treated anxiety as one item within a broad neuropsychiatric symptom (NPS) burden, focused on the dementia stage, or addressed single imaging modalities. The present review differs in three respects. First, it focuses specifically on anxiety in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) as a discrete phenotypic target rather than as a component of general NPS. Second, it integrates findings across structural, functional, molecular, and network-level imaging, together with emerging peripheral fluid biomarker data, to provide a multimodal synthesis. Third, it explicitly distinguishes direct evidence from anxiety-specific MCI studies from indirect evidence derived from AD dementia or general NPS populations, and frames the findings within a triple-network model to identify candidate targets for risk stratification and intervention.

This review integrates recent neuroimaging findings to better understand which individuals with comorbid MCI and anxiety face the highest risk of progression and to inform mechanism-based therapeutic development. We emphasize that neuropsychological assessment remains central to diagnosing MCI and evaluating anxiety in routine practice. Neuroimaging complements clinical assessment as a tool for elucidating mechanisms and identifying targets for novel interventions.

Accordingly, this review addresses the following questions: (1) What structural, functional, and molecular imaging alterations are associated with anxiety symptoms in MCI? (2) Can these regional findings be integrated into a coherent large-scale network model? (3) To what extent does current evidence support anxiety as an early marker of neurodegeneration, a modifier of disease course, or both? (4) What are the implications of this evidence for risk stratification, biomarker development, and mechanism-based interventions? Our objective is to synthesize the available neuroimaging evidence on these questions, delineate the boundary between direct and indirect evidence, and identify priorities for future research.

In this review, a narrative review methodology was used. The primary database searched was PubMed, from 1 January 2015 to 30 June 2026; the search was last executed on 10 October 2026. The search combined three concept blocks using the AND operator: (1) population (“mild cognitive impairment”, “MCI”, “Alzheimer*” “dementia”, “cognitive decline”, “cognitive impairment”, “mild behavioral impairment”); (2) symptom (“anxiety”, “anxiety symptoms”, “anxious”, “neuropsychiatric symptoms”, “mild behavioral impairment”, “behavioral symptoms”, “mood symptoms”); and (3) imaging (“neuroimaging”, “magnetic resonance”, “MRI”, “diffusion tensor”, “fMRI”, “functional connectivity”, “positron emission”, “PET”, “amyloid”, “tau”, “neuroinflammation”, “brain network*” “white matter”, “atrophy”, “biomarker*” “glucose metabolism”, “default mode”), all restricted to title/abstract fields. Consistent with the narrative review approach, formal systematic review procedures—such as multi-database searching, PRISMA-based study selection, and quantitative risk-of-bias assessment—were not applied. Reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews were also traced to identify additional studies.

Studies were eligible if they met the following criteria: (1) study populations comprising cognitively normal older adults, patients with MCI, or individuals across the AD continuum; (2) anxiety symptoms assessed via scales or clinical interviews, or anxiety dimensions included within neuropsychiatric symptom (NPS) or mild behavioral impairment (MBI) frameworks; (3) use of structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging, functional MRI (fMRI), positron emission tomography (PET), or multimodal imaging techniques; and (4) reporting of relationships between anxiety symptoms and brain structure, function, molecular pathology, functional connectivity, or disease progression. Records were excluded for the following pre-specified reasons: (a) ineligible publication type (editorials, case reports, study protocols, non-English publications, or intervention studies without observational imaging–symptom analyses); (b) animal or other preclinical studies; (c) review articles, which were retained for background and citation tracking but not as primary evidence; (d) ineligible study populations (eg, Parkinson’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, or other non-AD-spectrum conditions); (e) anxiety not examined as a study variable; and (f) no in vivo neuroimaging data. In addition, a small number of studies that did not meet all of the above criteria but provided directly relevant mechanistic, interventional, biomarker-disclosure, or clinical-outcome evidence were retained and are explicitly classified as indirect evidence in . The overall workflow of this review, from research question to evidence synthesis, is illustrated in .

Characteristics of the 44 Studies Constituting the Evidence Base and Six Background References Cited in This Review

The PubMed search yielded 4654 records. After title and abstract screening, 4614 records were excluded: ineligible publication type (n = 317), animal or preclinical studies (n = 729), review articles (n = 1185), ineligible population (n = 421), anxiety not examined as a study variable (n = 1590), and no in vivo neuroimaging data (n = 372). The remaining 40 records were included for the evidence synthesis, and 4 additional records were identified through citation tracking, yielding an evidence base of 44 studies. Six further references were cited as background: 3 records retained from the screened pool that did not meet the inclusion criteria, and 3 methodological references cited for diagnostic frameworks, yielding a total of 50 references cited in this review (). Titles and abstracts were screened by the first author (C.H.), and all included records were verified by the corresponding author (Z.G). The characteristics of the 44 studies constituting the evidence base, together with the six background references, are summarized in .

The limbic system and its prefrontal regulatory circuits form the anatomical substrate for anxiety-related structural alterations, predominantly regional gray matter volume reductions. Longitudinal MRI studies suggest that individuals with amnestic MCI and clinically significant anxiety symptoms exhibit faster annual atrophy of the entorhinal cortex than those without anxiety. Anxiety symptoms independently predict conversion to AD dementia after controlling for depressive symptoms and baseline memory impairment. Cross-sectional studies have further reported associations between greater anxiety severity and reduced volume or cortical thickness in the entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus. These structural associations may reflect the combined impact of stress-related hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis dysregulation, neuroinflammatory processes, and altered neuroplasticity on regions that are especially vulnerable in early AD. The evidence comes almost exclusively from cross-sectional studies, precluding inferences about temporal precedence. Anxiety may precede regional atrophy as an independent risk factor, arise as an early consequence of incipient neurodegeneration, or both. The existing evidence cannot distinguish between these possibilities.

At the hippocampal subfield level, high-resolution MRI has localized anxiety-related volume reductions to specific hippocampal subfields. Karim et al demonstrated that elevated worry severity was associated with smaller bilateral subiculum volume, whereas more adaptive cognitive reappraisal corresponded to larger subiculum and cornu ammonis 1 volumes after adjusting for demographic factors, illness burden, and neuroticism. Because the subiculum and cornu ammonis 1 are preferentially affected in the earliest stages of the AD continuum, these findings imply that emotion regulation capacity may modify hippocampal resilience. Whether these subfield changes predict anxiety persistence or cognitive decline in MCI needs prospective validation.

Beyond the classical medial temporal lobe structures, the mesolimbic–cortical dopamine pathway exhibits selective vulnerability across the MCI-to-AD continuum. Combined structural MRI and F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET (FDG-PET) analyses showed marked gray matter loss in dopamine pathway projection regions—including the ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex, and medial temporal lobe—across the MCI-to-AD progression spectrum. These structural changes were associated with overall NPS burden, though anxiety-specific effects were not isolated. Large-sample cortical morphometric studies further link anxiety with a distinct temporo-parietal morphological signature during the transition from normal cognition to AD. Individual neuropsychiatric symptoms appear to have relatively specific structural correlates.

Anxiety-related brain structural changes appear to show stage dependency. In patients with MCI, higher depression/anxiety scores are associated with increased cortical thickness in the banks of the left superior temporal sulcus. In AD dementia, the relationship inverts: greater symptom burden coincides with cortical thinning. This pattern is consistent with residual compensatory reorganization during the prodromal stage, although prospective data are required to confirm this interpretation. Frontotemporal atrophy is significantly associated with anxiety symptoms even in older adults without dementia (odds ratio = 2.15), suggesting that frontotemporal morphological change contributes to emotional dysregulation before dementia onset.

In MCI, anxiety-related white matter microstructural disruption (reduced fractional anisotropy) involve fiber pathways that support default mode network (DMN) connectivity and prefrontal–limbic communication. These pathways show reduced structural integrity alongside elevated cerebrovascular burden. Greater white matter hyperintensity burden was associated with clinical anxiety symptoms, and both cerebrovascular markers and anxiety independently predicted MCI. Connectome-based predictive modeling has localized anxiety-related white matter disruption to the cingulum bundle and uncinate fasciculus, together with reduced DMN functional connectivity. These structural and functional connectome changes may form a substrate for cognitive vulnerability in MCI.

Peripheral gut–brain axis findings align with central mechanisms. Hung et al demonstrated that, in amyloid-positive amnestic MCI, reduced fecal Ruminococcus was associated with greater affective symptom severity, an association partially mediated by left cingulate white matter disruption. This suggests that gut dysbiosis may contribute to anxiety-related white matter damage through neuroinflammatory pathways, although anxiety-specific validation is still needed.

Similarly, Sun et al used dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI with Patlak kinetic modeling to quantify blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability in amnestic and non-amnestic MCI. Compared with healthy controls, patients with MCI exhibited significantly elevated volume transfer constants in the hippocampus and frontotemporal regions, indicating increased BBB permeability. The amnestic MCI subgroup showed the most pronounced leakage. The amnestic MCI group also scored higher than both the non-amnestic MCI and control groups on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale and the Hamilton Depression Scale. Plasma phosphorylated tau 181 (p-tau181), intercellular adhesion molecule-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, and neurofilament light chain were likewise elevated. These findings suggest that BBB disruption may be a vascular event in MCI. Co-occurring neuroinflammatory and axonal injury markers may jointly contribute to the emergence of anxiety symptoms. Combining dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI-derived BBB permeability with plasma biomarkers thus provides a noninvasive way to probe the cerebrovascular–neuropsychiatric axis in MCI. Because anxiety and depression were assessed concurrently and the study was not designed to isolate anxiety-specific effects, these findings are best regarded as preliminary evidence of a vascular–inflammatory–affective axis rather than proof of an anxiety-specific BBB phenotype in MCI.

Abnormal DMN functional connectivity may be a key network feature of MCI with anxiety. Resting-state fMRI studies have demonstrated altered posterior cingulate cortex connectivity within the DMN in patients with MCI, with a pattern that partly overlaps with (but is generally less extensive than) that observed in AD dementia. Whether these alterations vary with NPS status remains to be clarified. To date, direct evidence linking DMN abnormalities specifically to anxiety in MCI remains limited. It is plausible that anxiety symptoms interact with the functional balance between the DMN and the salience network (SN), although this has not been demonstrated directly.

Frontal–limbic circuit dysfunction has been implicated in anxiety and other NPS across the dementia spectrum. In patients with MCI, reduced spontaneous activity (decreased amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation) involve the right insula, left orbitofrontal cortex, and bilateral superior frontal gyrus, regions that support cognitive and affective processing. Peripheral inflammatory markers moderate the relationship between these changes and cognitive performance. Cross-diagnostic studies of emotion regulation, though conducted outside AD populations, show that high vigilance styles involve diminished anterior cingulate activation during threat processing. This pattern offers a putative mechanistic framework for anxiety vulnerability.

The triple-network model helps integrate the findings described in Intrinsic Functional Connectivity Alterations, emphasizing dynamic interactions between the DMN, SN, and central executive network (CEN). The SN (anchored in the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex) orchestrates dynamic switching between internally oriented DMN processes and externally directed executive control. In MCI with anxiety, impaired salience detection or aberrant SN-driven switching predisposes patients to persistent threat monitoring, excessive self-referential processing, and inefficient cognitive control. Future work should characterize dynamic connectivity and network-switching mechanisms rather than relying solely on static within-network connectivity measures.

Task-based fMRI studies focusing on MCI are lacking. Indirect evidence from emotional processing and cognitive control paradigms in geriatric anxiety and across the AD continuum points to enhanced limbic reactivity with insufficient prefrontal regulation, consistent with an imbalance between enhanced threat processing and diminished cognitive control. However, whether this pattern holds specifically in MCI with anxiety requires empirical validation. Consistent with these findings, cross-diagnostic symptom dimension analyses have identified anxiety in MCI as a discrete dimension, separable from the affective clustering observed in AD and dementia with Lewy bodies, which supports stage-specific neurobiological underpinnings.

Factor-analytic work in a large multicenter Japanese cohort supports this view. Kanemoto et al performed exploratory factor analysis of the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) in AD, dementia with Lewy bodies, and MCI, combined with structural MRI and 123I-N-isopropyl-p-iodoamphetamine single-photon emission computed tomography. In the MCI group, anxiety formed as an independent factor separate from psychosis, agitation, and apathy, instead of clustering with depression within a broad affective disturbance syndrome. Higher anxiety factor scores were associated with greater dementia severity (Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes) in the MCI group. This factor structure suggests that anxiety in MCI has its own symptomatic and neural signature, distinct from the depression–anxiety clustering observed in later dementia stages. These dimensional findings emphasize the value of treating anxiety as a discrete phenotypic target in neuroimaging and biomarker studies of MCI.

FDG-PET studies prospectively suggest synergistic interactions between anxiety and neurodegeneration. In the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, 1363 cognitively unimpaired older adults were enrolled at baseline. The co-occurrence of regional glucose hypometabolism (FDG-PET+) and clinically significant anxiety (Beck Anxiety Inventory ≥10) was associated with a 7.21-fold higher risk of incident MCI relative to normal metabolism and no anxiety (hazard ratio [HR] = 7.21, 95% confidence interval: 3.54–14.7). The corresponding estimate for depression combined with hypometabolism was lower (HR = 3.66, 95% confidence interval: 1.75–7.65), although the confidence intervals overlapped. Among individuals without neurodegenerative evidence (FDG-PET−), anxiety alone did not elevate MCI risk.
