Increasing evidence suggests that these aggregates propagate through interconnected neuronal networks in a prion-like manner, facilitating disease progression across anatomically connected brain regions.

Optogenetics has emerged as a powerful platform for investigating how protein aggregates influence neuronal circuit function. Selective optical stimulation of vulnerable neuronal populations has demonstrated that pathological protein accumulation initially alters neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission before causing irreversible structural degeneration. In transgenic Alzheimer's disease models, optogenetic activation of hippocampal engram cells restored memory retrieval despite persistent amyloid deposition, indicating that early cognitive impairment may result primarily from circuit dysfunction rather than complete neuronal loss (). Likewise, gamma-frequency (40 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of cortical and hippocampal interneurons has significantly reduced amyloid burden by enhancing microglial phagocytosis and improving glymphatic clearance of extracellular protein aggregates (). These findings have fundamentally altered conventional concepts of amyloid pathology by demonstrating that neuronal activity itself influences protein aggregation dynamics and innate immune responses.

In synucleinopathies, optogenetic interrogation of dopaminergic circuits has revealed that α-synuclein accumulation disrupts basal ganglia network synchronization and alters neuronal firing patterns long before degeneration of substantia nigra neurons becomes extensive. Similar observations have been reported in Huntington's disease, where mutant huntingtin selectively impairs corticostriatal connectivity and disrupts neuronal oscillations underlying voluntary movement. Collectively, these studies suggest that abnormal protein aggregation should be viewed not merely as a static histopathological feature but as a dynamic regulator of neural circuit dysfunction that may remain therapeutically reversible during early disease stages ().

Synaptic dysfunction is increasingly recognized as one of the earliest and most important pathological mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration. Long before widespread neuronal death becomes apparent, abnormalities in neurotransmitter release, dendritic spine morphology, receptor trafficking, and synaptic plasticity progressively compromise neuronal communication, ultimately disrupting higher-order cognitive and motor functions (, , ). Consequently, synaptic failure has emerged as a stronger predictor of clinical disease severity than the absolute extent of neuronal loss in several neurodegenerative disorders.

Optogenetics has transformed understanding of synaptic pathology by enabling selective stimulation of defined neuronal pathways while simultaneously recording electrophysiological responses at downstream synapses. Such pathway-specific interrogation has revealed that amyloid-β oligomers preferentially impair long-term potentiation (LTP), facilitate long-term depression (LTD), and reduce dendritic spine density within hippocampal circuits responsible for learning and memory. Importantly, optogenetic restoration of physiological neuronal activity partially rescues synaptic plasticity and improves cognitive performance in several experimental Alzheimer's disease models, highlighting synaptic dysfunction as a potentially reversible therapeutic target ().

Similarly, optogenetic studies have demonstrated that dopaminergic depletion in Parkinson's disease profoundly alters corticostriatal synaptic transmission by disrupting the balance between direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways. Selective activation of direct-pathway medium spiny neurons restores physiological motor output, whereas stimulation of indirect-pathway neurons exaggerates motor impairment, thereby providing definitive evidence supporting classical basal ganglia circuit models (). In Huntington's disease, optical interrogation has revealed early impairment of corticostriatal glutamatergic transmission before overt neuronal degeneration, suggesting that dysfunctional synaptic communication precedes structural pathology.

Recent integration of optogenetics with super-resolution microscopy, genetically encoded calcium indicators, glutamate sensors, and single-synapse imaging has enabled direct visualization of activity-dependent receptor trafficking, neurotransmitter release, and dendritic spine remodeling. These multimodal approaches have demonstrated that synaptic dysfunction reflects complex interactions among neurons, astrocytes, and microglia rather than isolated neuronal abnormalities alone, emphasizing the importance of multicellular circuit interactions in neurodegenerative disease progression ().

Neuroinflammation has emerged as a central driver of neurodegenerative disease progression rather than merely a secondary response to neuronal injury. Chronic activation of microglia and astrocytes promotes sustained production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, complement proteins, and chemokines that progressively disrupt synaptic function, impair neuronal metabolism, and accelerate neuronal degeneration (, ). Although acute inflammatory responses may initially facilitate tissue repair and protein clearance, persistent neuroinflammation establishes a self-perpetuating cycle of neuronal injury and immune activation that contributes significantly to disease progression.

Optogenetics has provided unprecedented opportunities to investigate bidirectional communication between neurons and glial cells during neuroinflammation. Selective activation of neuronal circuits has demonstrated that neuronal firing patterns directly regulate microglial morphology, motility, and phagocytic activity through activity-dependent release of neurotransmitters, ATP, and chemokines. Conversely, optical manipulation of astrocytic calcium signaling has revealed that astrocytes actively modulate neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, and neurovascular coupling through gliotransmitter release rather than functioning solely as passive structural support cells ().

One of the most influential discoveries in recent years has been the demonstration that optogenetically induced gamma oscillations significantly modify innate immune responses in Alzheimer's disease. Gamma-frequency stimulation activates parvalbumin-positive interneurons, resulting in enhanced microglial recruitment, increased phagocytosis of amyloid plaques, reduced neuroinflammatory cytokine production, and improved cognitive function. These findings have established a direct mechanistic link between neuronal oscillatory activity and immune regulation within the central nervous system, providing a novel therapeutic paradigm in which modulation of neural circuit activity indirectly influences neuroimmune function ().

Furthermore, optogenetic interrogation of hypothalamic and brainstem inflammatory circuits has demonstrated that neuronal activity regulates systemic immune responses through autonomic pathways, illustrating the extensive integration between the nervous and immune systems. Combined with single-cell transcriptomics and spatial transcriptomic technologies, optogenetics now enables precise characterization of disease-associated microglial and astrocytic phenotypes within anatomically defined neural circuits. These multidisciplinary approaches are rapidly transforming understanding of neuroinflammation from a generalized pathological process into a circuit-specific and cell-specific mechanism that contributes directly to neurodegenerative disease progression ().

Mitochondria are indispensable organelles that regulate cellular energy metabolism, calcium homeostasis, redox signaling, biosynthetic pathways, and programmed cell death. Given the exceptionally high metabolic demands of neurons, maintenance of mitochondrial integrity is essential for sustaining synaptic transmission, axonal transport, and neuronal survival. Consequently, mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a central pathogenic mechanism shared by virtually all major neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (, ). Accumulating evidence indicates that mitochondrial abnormalities occur during the earliest stages of disease progression, preceding extensive neuronal loss and contributing directly to synaptic impairment, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and activation of multiple cell death pathways.

Healthy neurons rely on a dynamic mitochondrial network maintained through coordinated processes of mitochondrial biogenesis, fusion, fission, intracellular transport, and selective autophagic degradation (mitophagy). Disruption of these quality-control mechanisms results in defective oxidative phosphorylation, impaired ATP production, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, calcium dysregulation, and reduced metabolic flexibility. In Alzheimer's disease, amyloid-β and hyperphosphorylated tau interfere with mitochondrial respiratory complexes, impair mitochondrial trafficking along axons, and inhibit mitophagy, thereby compromising neuronal bioenergetics and accelerating synaptic degeneration (). Similarly, mutations in genes such as PINK1, Parkin, DJ-1, and LRRK2 disrupt mitochondrial quality-control pathways in Parkinson's disease, leading to accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria within dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra and increasing their susceptibility to degeneration ().

Optogenetics has provided unprecedented opportunities to investigate the causal relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal circuit activity. Unlike conventional biochemical analyses, which primarily assess mitochondrial abnormalities in isolated tissues or cultured cells, optogenetic approaches enable selective modulation of disease-relevant neuronal populations while simultaneously monitoring mitochondrial function in intact neural circuits. Optical activation of genetically defined neurons combined with genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors for ATP, calcium, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ROS has revealed that neuronal firing rapidly influences mitochondrial dynamics and metabolic activity. These studies demonstrate that mitochondrial function is not static but is continuously regulated by neuronal activity, synaptic demand, and intracellular calcium signaling ().

Recent advances have further expanded the application of optogenetics through the development of optogenetic control of mitochondrial function, commonly referred to as mito-optogenetics. In these systems, light-sensitive proteins are selectively targeted to mitochondrial membranes, allowing investigators to manipulate mitochondrial membrane potential, proton gradients, calcium uptake, or reactive oxygen species production with high spatial and temporal precision. Such approaches have enabled direct investigation of how transient mitochondrial depolarization influences neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, and metabolic adaptation without the confounding off-target effects associated with pharmacological mitochondrial inhibitors (). Furthermore, optogenetic regulation of mitochondrial dynamics has demonstrated that restoration of physiological mitochondrial function can improve neuronal survival and partially rescue synaptic deficits in experimental neurodegenerative disease models.

Another major contribution of optogenetics has been elucidating the relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal network activity. Hyperactive neuronal circuits impose substantial energetic demands that increase ATP consumption and calcium influx, thereby exacerbating mitochondrial stress and ROS production. Conversely, prolonged neuronal hypoactivity reduces mitochondrial biogenesis and impairs metabolic adaptability. Optogenetic manipulation of hippocampal and cortical circuits has demonstrated that restoring physiological patterns of neuronal activity normalizes mitochondrial calcium handling, improves respiratory efficiency, and enhances neuronal resilience against metabolic stress. These observations suggest that neuronal activity itself is an important determinant of mitochondrial health and that circuit-level interventions may indirectly improve mitochondrial function during neurodegeneration ().

Mitochondrial dysfunction also interacts closely with neuroinflammation and protein aggregation, creating a self-amplifying pathogenic cycle. Damaged mitochondria release mitochondrial DNA, cytochrome c, cardiolipin, and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that activate innate immune signaling and inflammasome pathways. Concurrently, impaired ATP synthesis and excessive ROS production promote protein misfolding, synaptic dysfunction, and activation of apoptotic and ferroptotic pathways. Optogenetic studies have shown that modulation of neuronal firing patterns can influence these interconnected processes by improving mitochondrial quality control, reducing metabolic stress, and preserving neuronal circuit integrity. Consequently, mitochondrial dysfunction is now recognized not only as a metabolic abnormality but also as a critical regulator of neuronal communication and disease progression.

Oxidative stress is a fundamental pathological mechanism underlying the initiation and progression of numerous neurodegenerative disorders. It results from an imbalance between the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) and the capacity of endogenous antioxidant defense systems to neutralize these reactive molecules. Owing to their exceptionally high oxygen consumption, abundant polyunsaturated fatty acids, relatively low antioxidant capacity, and dependence on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, neurons are particularly susceptible to oxidative damage. Persistent oxidative stress disrupts cellular homeostasis by damaging lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, and organelles, ultimately leading to synaptic dysfunction, impaired neuronal communication, mitochondrial failure, and progressive neurodegeneration (, ).

The principal intracellular sources of ROS include the mitochondrial electron transport chain, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidases (NOXs), xanthine oxidase, uncoupled nitric oxide synthase (NOS), and activated microglia. Under physiological conditions, low concentrations of ROS serve as essential signaling molecules regulating neuronal differentiation, synaptic plasticity, calcium homeostasis, and gene expression. However, excessive ROS production overwhelms antioxidant defense systems, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), glutathione (GSH), thioredoxin, and peroxiredoxins, resulting in oxidative damage to critical cellular components (). Oxidative stress therefore represents not merely a consequence of neurodegeneration but also a major driving force that amplifies disease progression through multiple interconnected molecular pathways.

Substantial evidence indicates that oxidative stress is an early pathological event in Alzheimer's disease. Soluble amyloid-β oligomers promote excessive ROS production by impairing mitochondrial respiration, activating NOX enzymes, and disturbing intracellular calcium homeostasis. Simultaneously, hyperphosphorylated tau further aggravates oxidative injury by disrupting axonal transport of mitochondria and reducing neuronal bioenergetic efficiency. The resulting oxidative damage promotes lipid peroxidation, protein carbonylation, DNA oxidation, and impairment of synaptic signaling, ultimately contributing to cognitive decline and neuronal loss (). Similarly, degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease is strongly associated with oxidative metabolism of dopamine, mitochondrial complex I dysfunction, iron accumulation, and neuroinflammatory activation, all of which synergistically increase ROS generation and accelerate neuronal degeneration ().

Optogenetics has significantly advanced understanding of the relationship between neuronal activity and oxidative stress by enabling precise manipulation of disease-relevant neural circuits while simultaneously monitoring intracellular redox dynamics. Conventional biochemical approaches generally measure oxidative damage at the tissue level and therefore fail to capture the rapid temporal changes occurring within individual neurons or specific neural circuits. In contrast, optogenetic stimulation combined with genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors for hydrogen peroxide, glutathione, and redox-sensitive green fluorescent protein (roGFP) enables real-time visualization of oxidative responses in living neurons during physiological and pathological activity (). These approaches have demonstrated that neuronal activity directly influences intracellular redox homeostasis through dynamic regulation of mitochondrial respiration, calcium signaling, and metabolic demand.

Recent advances in photo-oxidative neuromodulation have further expanded the application of optogenetics to redox biology. Selective optical manipulation of neuronal firing patterns has revealed that physiological neuronal activity promotes activation of endogenous antioxidant signaling pathways, particularly the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, which regulates transcription of numerous cytoprotective genes including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL), and superoxide dismutase (SOD). Conversely, prolonged hyperexcitability markedly increases mitochondrial ROS generation, suppresses antioxidant defenses, and sensitizes neurons to oxidative injury (). These findings indicate that neuronal activity exerts bidirectional effects on redox homeostasis depending upon its intensity and duration.

Optogenetic investigations have also highlighted the close interplay between oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Excessive ROS generated during neuronal hyperactivity activate microglia and astrocytes through redox-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB, leading to sustained production of inflammatory cytokines including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). These inflammatory mediators further enhance oxidative damage by stimulating NOX activity and impairing mitochondrial function, thereby establishing a vicious cycle that progressively exacerbates neuronal injury (). Optogenetic modulation of cortical and hippocampal circuits has demonstrated that restoration of physiological neuronal activity attenuates oxidative stress while simultaneously reducing neuroinflammatory responses, emphasizing the intimate relationship between neuronal excitability and cellular redox balance.

Another important contribution of optogenetics has been the investigation of oxidative stress during synaptic dysfunction. Reactive oxygen species profoundly influence neurotransmitter release, receptor trafficking, dendritic spine morphology, and synaptic plasticity. Moderate ROS concentrations participate in long-term potentiation (LTP) and memory formation, whereas excessive ROS disrupt glutamatergic transmission, inhibit N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor signaling, and facilitate long-term depression (LTD). Using pathway-specific optical stimulation, investigators have demonstrated that oxidative stress selectively impairs hippocampal and cortical synaptic plasticity before overt neuronal degeneration becomes apparent, suggesting that redox imbalance represents one of the earliest functional abnormalities during neurodegenerative disease progression ().

Emerging optogenetic technologies are increasingly integrated with advanced metabolomics, redox imaging, mitochondrial biosensors, and artificial intelligence-assisted image analysis to characterize oxidative dynamics at single-cell resolution. Such multidisciplinary approaches permit simultaneous monitoring of neuronal activity, mitochondrial metabolism, calcium signaling, and ROS production within intact neural circuits, thereby providing comprehensive insight into the molecular events linking neuronal activity to oxidative injury. Furthermore, development of photoactivatable antioxidant systems and optogenetic regulation of intracellular signaling pathways may offer novel opportunities to selectively enhance endogenous neuroprotective mechanisms while minimizing systemic side effects.

Progressive neuronal loss is the pathological hallmark of neurodegenerative disorders and results from activation of multiple regulated cell death pathways rather than passive degeneration. Recent evidence indicates that apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis interact closely with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and protein aggregation to drive neuronal death. Optogenetics has become an invaluable tool for dissecting these mechanisms by enabling precise modulation of neuronal activity and monitoring downstream molecular responses within disease-relevant neural circuits. Unlike conventional biochemical approaches, optogenetics establishes causal relationships between neuronal excitability and activation of specific cell death pathways, thereby providing important mechanistic insights into disease progression (, ).

Apoptosis is the best-characterized programmed cell death pathway involved in neurodegeneration and is primarily mediated through intrinsic mitochondrial and extrinsic death receptor pathways. Cellular stress caused by oxidative damage, DNA injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium overload, and protein aggregation activates pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax and Bak, resulting in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and release of cytochrome c. Subsequent activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3 initiates irreversible degradation of intracellular proteins, DNA fragmentation, and neuronal death ().

Optogenetic investigations have demonstrated that abnormal neuronal activity directly influences apoptotic signaling. Sustained neuronal hyperexcitability increases intracellular calcium influx and mitochondrial depolarization, thereby activating Bax-dependent apoptosis. Conversely, restoration of physiological neuronal firing through selective optogenetic neuromodulation suppresses caspase activation, preserves mitochondrial integrity, and improves neuronal survival in experimental models of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and cerebral ischemia (). These findings indicate that apoptosis is closely linked to neural circuit dysfunction and may be partially reversible during early stages of neurodegeneration.

Ferroptosis is a recently recognized iron-dependent form of regulated cell death characterized by excessive lipid peroxidation and catastrophic membrane damage. Unlike apoptosis, ferroptosis is independent of caspase activation and is initiated by intracellular iron accumulation, glutathione depletion, impaired glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPX4) activity, and overwhelming oxidative stress. Because the brain contains abundant iron and highly oxidizable membrane lipids, neurons are particularly susceptible to ferroptotic injury (). Growing evidence implicates ferroptosis in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Optogenetic modulation of neuronal activity has revealed that excessive neuronal firing increases mitochondrial ROS production and lipid oxidation, thereby sensitizing neurons to ferroptotic death. Conversely, normalization of neuronal activity reduces oxidative stress, preserves GPX4 activity, and limits lipid peroxidation. Integration of optogenetics with genetically encoded redox sensors has enabled real-time visualization of oxidative events preceding ferroptosis, providing valuable insights into how neuronal metabolism and circuit activity regulate iron-dependent neurodegeneration ().

Pyroptosis is a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death mediated by inflammasome activation and gasdermin-dependent membrane pore formation. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome promotes cleavage of pro-caspase-1, resulting in maturation of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18), cleavage of gasdermin D, membrane rupture, and release of pro-inflammatory mediators. Persistent inflammasome activation contributes significantly to chronic neuroinflammation and progressive neuronal damage in Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (, ). Optogenetic studies have revealed that neuronal activity influences inflammasome signaling through regulation of mitochondrial ROS production, ATP release, calcium homeostasis, and neuron–microglia communication. Gamma-frequency optogenetic stimulation has been shown to reduce inflammatory activation, suppress NLRP3 signaling, enhance microglial phagocytosis, and decrease amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease models (). These observations demonstrate that modulation of neuronal circuits can indirectly regulate innate immune responses and attenuate pyroptotic cell death.

Necroptosis is a caspase-independent regulated necrotic pathway mediated by receptor-interacting protein kinases RIPK1 and RIPK3 together with mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL). Following activation, phosphorylated MLKL oligomerizes within the plasma membrane, causing membrane rupture, cellular swelling, and release of intracellular damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), thereby amplifying neuroinflammatory responses (). Increasing evidence suggests that necroptosis contributes to neuronal degeneration following ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis and several chronic neurodegenerative disorders. Optogenetic manipulation has demonstrated that prolonged neuronal hyperactivity promotes activation of RIPK signaling pathways through mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium overload, and oxidative stress, whereas restoration of physiological circuit activity reduces necroptotic signaling and preserves neuronal viability. These findings further support the concept that regulated necrosis is closely linked to neural circuit dysfunction and may represent a promising therapeutic target.

Optogenetics has emerged as a powerful experimental platform for establishing causal relationships between neuronal activity, circuit dysfunction, and behavioural outcomes; however, its current applications in neurodegenerative disorders should primarily be considered as mechanistic research tools rather than clinically validated therapeutic approaches (, , ). Most studies in AD, PD, HD, ALS, MS and stroke have been performed in genetically modified rodent models, where cell-type-specific opsin expression and precise optical stimulation enable detailed investigation of disease-associated neural circuits (, , ). These studies have provided important insights into memory engrams, basal ganglia dysfunction, synaptic plasticity, neuroimmune regulation and activity-dependent circuit recovery (, –). However, functional improvements observed in preclinical models cannot be directly interpreted as clinical efficacy because human neurodegenerative disorders involve complex genetic backgrounds, heterogeneous progression patterns, extensive neuronal loss and multifactorial pathological mechanisms that are not completely reproduced in experimental models (, , ).

In AD models, optogenetic activation of hippocampal engram cells and gamma-frequency stimulation have improved memory-associated behaviours and modulated amyloid-related processes; however, their durability, safety and therapeutic relevance in humans remain uncertain (, ). Similarly, although optogenetic manipulation of dopaminergic and basal ganglia circuits has advanced understanding of PD pathophysiology and validated circuit-based therapeutic concepts, clinical translation requires overcoming challenges related to targeted gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune compatibility and deep-brain optical access (, , ). Comparable limitations exist across other neurodegenerative disorders, where optogenetics has primarily contributed to mechanistic understanding and target identification rather than demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in patients (, ). Therefore, current evidence supports optogenetics as a transformative neuroscience tool for dissecting disease mechanisms and evaluating circuit-based interventions, whereas its role as a clinical neuromodulation strategy remains investigational. Future translation will require large-animal validation, long-term biosafety assessment, optimized delivery systems, clinically compatible optical interfaces, regulatory evaluation and carefully designed human studies to determine whether experimental circuit modulation can be converted into safe and effective therapies (, , ).

Neurodegenerative disorders, including AD, PD, HD, ALS, MS and stroke-related neurodegeneration, are characterized by progressive neuronal loss, synaptic dysfunction, impaired neural connectivity, and chronic neuroinflammation. Although current therapies primarily provide symptomatic relief, they fail to halt disease progression or restore damaged neural circuits. Optogenetics has emerged as a transformative approach for investigating these disorders by enabling cell type-specific activation or inhibition of genetically defined neuronal populations with millisecond temporal precision and high spatial resolution. Unlike pharmacological or electrical stimulation, optogenetics permits precise dissection of disease-associated neural circuits, revealing that early abnormalities in network activity, synaptic plasticity, and excitatory–inhibitory balance often precede overt neurodegeneration (, ). Experimental studies have demonstrated that optogenetic modulation of hippocampal, basal ganglia, corticostriatal, corticospinal, and sensorimotor circuits can restore physiological neuronal activity, improve cognitive and motor functions, enhance neuroplasticity, promote remyelination, and facilitate functional recovery. Furthermore, integration of optogenetics with advanced imaging, electrophysiology, artificial intelligence, and regenerative therapies is accelerating the development of circuit-based precision neurotherapeutics. The following sections summarize recent advances in applying optogenetics to major neurodegenerative disorders and highlight its potential for both mechanistic investigations and targeted therapeutic interventions.

Optogenetics has emerged as a transformative approach for elucidating the circuit-level mechanisms underlying AD by enabling precise temporal and spatial control of genetically defined neuronal populations. Unlike pharmacological or electrical stimulation, optogenetics allows selective modulation of specific neuronal circuits, facilitating detailed investigation of how network dysfunction contributes to cognitive decline, synaptic failure, and disease progression. Studies in transgenic AD models have demonstrated that optogenetic manipulation can restore impaired neuronal communication, improve cognitive performance, and clarify the relationship between neuronal activity and pathological protein accumulation (, ).

The hippocampus is among the earliest brain regions affected in AD, exhibiting synaptic loss, impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), neuronal degeneration, and disrupted information processing. Optogenetic activation of excitatory neurons within the dentate gyrus (DG), CA3, and CA1 subfields has demonstrated that cognitive deficits frequently result from dysfunctional circuit activity rather than irreversible neuronal loss. Reactivation of hippocampal memory engram cells restores contextual and spatial memory retrieval in AD mouse models, indicating that memory traces remain stored but become inaccessible because of impaired network connectivity (). Furthermore, optogenetic regulation of parvalbumin-positive and somatostatin-positive interneurons has revealed that restoration of the excitatory–inhibitory balance improves synaptic plasticity, neuronal synchronization, and memory encoding (, ). These findings identify hippocampal circuitry as a major therapeutic target for reversing cognitive dysfunction.

Gamma oscillations (30–80 Hz) are essential for neuronal synchrony underlying learning, attention, and memory but are markedly disrupted in AD. Optogenetic stimulation of parvalbumin-positive interneurons at approximately 40 Hz entrains gamma oscillations, restores hippocampal-cortical synchrony, and improves cognitive performance. Importantly, 40-Hz gamma entrainment reduces amyloid-β deposition by promoting microglial activation and enhancing phagocytic clearance of amyloid plaques. Gamma stimulation also suppresses neuroinflammation, preserves synaptic integrity, and improves neuronal network function (, ). These findings demonstrate that gamma oscillations regulate both neuronal communication and immune-mediated clearance of pathological proteins, highlighting neuronal rhythm modulation as a promising therapeutic strategy.

Optogenetics has substantially improved understanding of how neuronal activity regulates amyloid-β and tau pathology. Experimental manipulation of neuronal firing demonstrates that sustained neuronal hyperactivity accelerates amyloid precursor protein processing, increasing amyloid-β production and extracellular plaque formation. Likewise, aberrant neuronal activity facilitates trans-synaptic propagation of hyperphosphorylated tau, accelerating disease spread across anatomically connected neural networks (, ). Conversely, normalization of network activity through optogenetic modulation decreases pathological protein accumulation, attenuates synaptic dysfunction, and limits neurodegeneration. These studies support the concept that AD progression is strongly influenced by activity-dependent mechanisms and that modulation of dysfunctional circuits may slow disease progression alongside reducing pathological protein burden.

One of the most compelling findings from optogenetic studies is that memory deficits in AD may reflect impaired retrieval rather than complete erasure of stored information. Selective optical reactivation of hippocampal memory engram cells successfully restores contextual and spatial memories in transgenic AD mice despite persistent amyloid pathology (). Repeated optogenetic stimulation further enhances LTP, strengthens hippocampal-prefrontal cortical connectivity, improves synaptic efficacy, and enhances cognitive performance (). These observations suggest that restoring circuit function may complement disease-modifying therapies by recovering cognitive abilities even in the presence of ongoing neuropathology. Collectively, optogenetic investigations have established AD as a disorder of dysfunctional neural networks and demonstrate that precise circuit modulation can simultaneously improve memory, restore synaptic function, and reduce pathological processes, supporting the development of next-generation circuit-based therapeutic interventions.

Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc), resulting in dopamine depletion within the striatum and disruption of basal ganglia circuitry. Clinically, PD manifests as bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, postural instability, and progressive cognitive impairment. Although pharmacological therapies and deep-brain stimulation (DBS) provide symptomatic relief, they do not fully restore physiological circuit function or prevent disease progression. Optogenetics has transformed PD research by enabling cell-type-specific manipulation of neuronal populations, allowing precise dissection of motor circuit dysfunction and identification of therapeutic targets beyond conventional electrical stimulation (, ).

The basal ganglia regulate voluntary movement through the coordinated activity of the direct and indirect pathways. Dopamine depletion disrupts this balance by reducing activity in dopamine D1 receptor-expressing direct pathway spiny projection neurons (dSPNs) while enhancing activity in dopamine D2 receptor-expressing indirect pathway neurons (iSPNs), leading to excessive inhibitory output from the globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra pars reticulata. Optogenetic studies have demonstrated that selective activation of dSPNs rapidly improves locomotion, whereas stimulation of iSPNs induces Parkinsonian motor deficits in healthy animals. Conversely, inhibition of the indirect pathway alleviates akinesia and rigidity, confirming that pathway-specific imbalance underlies PD motor symptoms (, ). These findings have fundamentally reshaped the understanding of basal ganglia physiology and established circuit-specific neuromodulation as a promising therapeutic strategy.

Selective optogenetic manipulation of dopaminergic neurons in the SNpc and ventral tegmental area has provided direct evidence for the causal relationship between dopamine signaling and motor control. Optical stimulation of surviving dopaminergic neurons enhances dopamine release in the striatum, improves motor coordination, and partially restores normal movement in experimental PD models (). Beyond motor regulation, optogenetics has revealed the functional heterogeneity of dopaminergic neurons, demonstrating that distinct neuronal populations differentially regulate movement initiation, reward processing, motivation, and motor learning. Moreover, optogenetic approaches have been widely used to evaluate stem cell-derived dopaminergic neuron transplantation by assessing functional integration of grafted neurons into host motor circuits, thereby facilitating the development of regenerative therapies ().

Optogenetic modulation has shown significant potential for restoring motor function by re-establishing physiological neuronal activity within impaired motor circuits. Stimulation of motor cortical projections, corticostriatal pathways, and surviving nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons enhances locomotor performance, improves gait, and reduces bradykinesia in animal models of PD. In addition to immediate motor improvement, repeated optogenetic stimulation promotes activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, strengthens corticostriatal connectivity, and facilitates functional reorganization of motor networks (). These findings suggest that circuit-specific neuromodulation may produce sustained therapeutic benefits by enhancing adaptive neuroplasticity rather than merely compensating for dopamine deficiency.

Deep-brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus interna remains an established treatment for advanced PD; however, its mechanisms of action have remained incompletely understood because electrical stimulation activates both neuronal cell bodies and passing axons indiscriminately. Optogenetics has helped clarify these mechanisms by selectively stimulating or inhibiting individual neuronal populations within DBS-targeted circuits. Experimental studies indicate that therapeutic benefits primarily arise from modulation of specific afferent cortical axons and downstream basal ganglia networks rather than simple suppression of STN neuronal activity (). These discoveries have informed the refinement of DBS parameters, improved understanding of stimulation-induced network dynamics, and supported the development of next-generation closed-loop neuromodulation systems capable of delivering adaptive, circuit-specific stimulation with reduced adverse effects. Collectively, optogenetic investigations have substantially advanced knowledge of PD pathophysiology by linking basal ganglia circuit dysfunction with motor impairment and identifying precise neuronal targets for more effective neuromodulatory therapies.

Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by expanded CAG repeats in the HTT gene, leading to the production of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. Progressive degeneration of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) within the striatum disrupts corticostriatal communication, resulting in chorea, dystonia, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbances. Optogenetics has become an indispensable tool for elucidating HD pathophysiology by enabling selective modulation of defined neuronal populations and revealing how dysfunction within corticostriatal circuits contributes to motor and cognitive impairment (, ).

The corticostriatal pathway, which connects glutamatergic neurons of the motor cortex with striatal MSNs, plays a central role in voluntary movement and motor learning. In HD, mutant huntingtin disrupts excitatory synaptic transmission, impairs long-term potentiation (LTP), enhances long-term depression (LTD), and alters the balance between the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways. Optogenetic stimulation of cortical afferents has demonstrated that early synaptic dysfunction precedes overt neuronal degeneration, indicating that circuit abnormalities are among the earliest pathological events in HD (). Furthermore, pathway-specific activation has shown that selective restoration of corticostriatal activity improves synaptic transmission, neuronal excitability, and activity-dependent plasticity. Optogenetic interrogation has also identified abnormalities in cortical interneurons and thalamostriatal projections, revealing that HD involves widespread network dysfunction extending beyond the striatum. These findings provide important mechanistic insights into disease progression and identify corticostriatal connectivity as a promising therapeutic target.

Motor impairment in HD results from progressive disruption of basal ganglia output caused by degeneration of striatal MSNs and impaired communication between cortical and subcortical motor networks. Optogenetic studies have demonstrated that selective activation of surviving corticostriatal projections or direct pathway neurons improves locomotor activity, movement initiation, and motor coordination in transgenic HD models, whereas inhibition of hyperactive indirect pathway circuits reduces abnormal involuntary movements (). Repeated optogenetic stimulation further enhances synaptic plasticity, promotes functional reorganization of motor circuits, and partially restores balanced neuronal activity within the basal ganglia. Beyond motor control, optogenetic investigations have revealed that dysfunction of corticostriatal networks also contributes to impaired procedural learning, executive dysfunction, and behavioral abnormalities observed in HD. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that circuit dysfunction precedes extensive neuronal loss and suggest that early circuit-specific neuromodulation may delay functional decline. Consequently, optogenetics provides a valuable experimental platform for evaluating disease-modifying interventions, including gene-editing strategies, RNA-targeted therapies, neuroprotective agents, and cell replacement approaches aimed at preserving corticostriatal integrity and improving motor function.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, resulting in muscle weakness, spasticity, paralysis, and ultimately respiratory failure. Although the precise mechanisms underlying ALS remain incompletely understood, accumulating evidence indicates that neuronal hyperexcitability, glutamate excitotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and impaired synaptic connectivity contribute to disease initiation and progression. Optogenetics has provided unprecedented opportunities to investigate these mechanisms by enabling selective manipulation of motor neurons and associated neural circuits with high temporal precision, thereby facilitating the identification of early pathological changes and potential therapeutic targets (, ).

Degeneration of corticospinal and spinal motor neurons is the pathological hallmark of ALS. Optogenetic approaches have been extensively employed to examine how altered neuronal activity influences motor neuron survival and neuromuscular function. Selective optical stimulation of corticospinal neurons and spinal motor neurons has demonstrated that excessive neuronal firing accelerates excitotoxic injury, whereas controlled modulation of neuronal activity improves synaptic stability and preserves neuromuscular junction integrity in experimental models (). Optogenetics has also enabled precise functional assessment of surviving motor neurons during disease progression, revealing that synaptic dysfunction and impaired motor circuit connectivity precede overt neuronal loss. Furthermore, combining optogenetics with calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings has clarified how abnormalities in intracellular calcium homeostasis contribute to progressive motor neuron degeneration. These findings indicate that activity-dependent mechanisms play a pivotal role in ALS pathogenesis and highlight neuronal excitability as a promising therapeutic target.

Cortical hyperexcitability is increasingly recognized as an early biomarker of ALS, often preceding clinical symptoms and widespread neurodegeneration. Increased excitability of motor cortical neurons enhances glutamatergic transmission, promoting excitotoxic damage to spinal motor neurons and accelerating disease progression. Optogenetic studies have demonstrated that selective modulation of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons restores the excitatory–inhibitory balance within the motor cortex, thereby reducing pathological network activity (). Experimental manipulation of corticospinal circuits has further shown that normalization of cortical activity improves motor output, preserves downstream spinal connectivity, and delays functional deterioration in preclinical models. In addition, optogenetic interrogation of astrocyte–neuron and microglia–neuron interactions has revealed that non-neuronal cells significantly influence cortical excitability through the release of inflammatory mediators and altered glutamate homeostasis. These observations emphasize that ALS is a network disorder involving reciprocal dysfunction among neurons and glial cells rather than isolated motor neuron degeneration. Consequently, optogenetics serves as a powerful platform for evaluating circuit-based interventions, gene therapies, and neuroprotective strategies aimed at reducing hyperexcitability, preserving motor neuron function, and slowing disease progression.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system characterized by inflammatory demyelination, axonal degeneration, gliosis, and progressive neurological disability. Loss of myelin disrupts saltatory conduction, impairs neuronal communication, and ultimately leads to motor, sensory, visual, and cognitive dysfunction. Although current immunomodulatory therapies reduce inflammatory relapses, they have limited efficacy in promoting remyelination and restoring neural circuit function. Optogenetics has emerged as a valuable experimental approach for investigating activity-dependent mechanisms that regulate myelin repair, oligodendrocyte function, and functional recovery by enabling precise control of neuronal activity within affected circuits (, ).

Optogenetic studies have demonstrated that neuronal activity plays a fundamental role in maintaining myelin integrity and regulating neuron–glia communication. In experimental demyelination models, selective stimulation of cortical and corticospinal neurons enhances activity-dependent signaling to oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), while altered neuronal firing contributes to axonal dysfunction and impaired signal transmission. Optical manipulation of specific neural circuits has shown that reduced neuronal activity exacerbates conduction deficits and synaptic dysfunction, whereas physiological stimulation partially restores neuronal connectivity by improving axonal conduction and synaptic transmission (). Furthermore, optogenetic approaches have enabled detailed investigation of interactions between neurons, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglia, revealing that inflammatory mediators and disrupted electrical activity jointly influence the progression of demyelination. These findings demonstrate that neuronal activity is an important regulator of both disease progression and circuit dysfunction in MS.

Remyelination is a critical regenerative process that restores axonal conduction and protects neurons from irreversible degeneration. Optogenetic studies have shown that activity-dependent stimulation promotes OPC proliferation, migration, differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes, and subsequent myelin formation around damaged axons. Enhanced neuronal firing increases the release of neurotransmitters and trophic factors that stimulate myelin repair and improve structural and functional recovery (). In addition, optogenetic activation of motor and sensory pathways accelerates restoration of conduction velocity, strengthens synaptic plasticity, and improves behavioral performance in experimental models of demyelination. These observations indicate that neural activity serves as a physiological signal coordinating communication between neurons and oligodendrocytes during myelin regeneration. Consequently, optogenetics provides a powerful platform for evaluating remyelinating therapies, stem cell-based interventions, biomaterial-assisted regeneration, and neuromodulatory strategies aimed at enhancing endogenous repair mechanisms (). Collectively, these studies establish that neuronal activity not only regulates myelin maintenance but also facilitates functional recovery following demyelinating injury, supporting the development of activity-dependent therapeutic approaches for progressive MS.

Stroke and traumatic brain injury (TBI) are major causes of long-term neurological disability, resulting from acute neuronal loss, disruption of neural circuits, neuroinflammation, and impaired synaptic connectivity. Although spontaneous recovery occurs to some extent through neuroplasticity, functional restoration is often incomplete because of limited regeneration of damaged neural networks. Optogenetics has become an important experimental tool for investigating post-injury circuit reorganization by enabling precise modulation of defined neuronal populations with high temporal and spatial resolution. This approach has significantly improved understanding of the mechanisms underlying cortical plasticity and has identified novel strategies for enhancing functional recovery after brain injury (, ).

Recovery following stroke or TBI depends largely on the capacity of surviving neuronal networks to undergo structural and functional reorganization. Optogenetic stimulation of neurons within the peri-infarct cortex, motor cortex, and corticospinal pathways has demonstrated that activity-dependent neuronal activation enhances synaptic plasticity, promotes dendritic spine remodeling, strengthens long-term potentiation (LTP), and facilitates the formation of new functional connections (). Furthermore, selective modulation of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons restores the excitatory–inhibitory balance disrupted after injury, thereby improving cortical network synchronization and information processing. Optogenetic studies have also shown that coordinated activation of corticocortical and corticothalamic circuits enhances axonal sprouting and compensatory network reorganization, indicating that targeted circuit modulation can accelerate endogenous neuroplastic mechanisms. These findings establish cortical plasticity as a key determinant of neurological recovery and identify neuronal activity as a major driver of post-injury circuit remodeling.

Beyond elucidating mechanisms of neural repair, optogenetics has demonstrated considerable potential for promoting functional recovery after stroke and TBI. Optical stimulation of motor cortical neurons, corticospinal projections, and sensorimotor pathways improves motor coordination, gait, forelimb function, and skilled motor performance in experimental models. Repeated stimulation further enhances activity-dependent neurogenesis, angiogenesis, synaptogenesis, and axonal regeneration, contributing to sustained improvements in neurological function (, ). In addition, optogenetic modulation reduces maladaptive network hyperexcitability, limits secondary neuronal damage, and improves functional connectivity between ipsilateral and contralateral cortical regions. When combined with stem cell transplantation, biomaterial scaffolds, rehabilitation, or pharmacological interventions, optogenetics provides a powerful platform for evaluating synergistic regenerative strategies and optimizing therapeutic timing. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that targeted modulation of neural circuits can enhance neuroplasticity, accelerate functional recovery, and improve behavioral outcomes following cerebral ischemia or traumatic brain injury. Although current applications remain largely preclinical, advances in optogenetic technologies and neuromodulation continue to provide valuable insights for developing next-generation precision therapies aimed at restoring neural circuit function after neurological injury.

Reported benefits of optogenetic manipulation should be interpreted according to the outcome measured and its relationship to underlying disease pathology. Symptomatic circuit modulation refers to improvements in motor, cognitive, or other functional endpoints during or shortly after stimulation without demonstrating altered disease progression. Functional compensation denotes recruitment or reorganization of surviving circuits that improves performance despite persisting pathology. Neuroprotection requires evidence that an intervention preserves vulnerable neurons, axons, synapses, or myelin relative to appropriate disease controls. Disease modification demands a stronger longitudinal demonstration that the intervention alters the trajectory of the pathological process or sustained clinical-relevant decline, rather than only producing transient functional improvement. These categories are not interchangeable, and a positive behavioural endpoint alone cannot establish neuroprotection or disease modification (, , ).

Across disease models, reactivation of memory engram cells in Alzheimer's disease supports functional retrieval despite persistent amyloid pathology (), whereas gamma-frequency entrainment has been associated with changes in amyloid-related and microglial endpoints in particular experimental models (, ). In Parkinson's disease, pathway-specific basal ganglia stimulation primarily demonstrates acute motor circuit modulation (, ); graft interrogation establishes functional integration rather than durable disease reversal (). Evidence discussed for Huntington's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis predominantly informs circuit dysfunction or excitability and does not independently establish modification of disease progression (, ). Activity-dependent oligodendrogenesis provides mechanistic support for adaptive myelination, but this should not be equated with clinical remyelination in multiple sclerosis (). Likewise, improvements after experimental post-stroke stimulation require separation from spontaneous recovery and general rehabilitation effects. Future studies should include stimulation-off follow-up, blinded functional endpoints, neuropathological measures, appropriate disease controls, and longitudinal assessment to determine the durability and biological meaning of reported improvements.

Recent advances in molecular engineering, neurotechnology and computational neuroscience have expanded the experimental capabilities of optogenetics beyond conventional circuit manipulation. Integration with closed-loop control systems, wireless photonic devices, artificial intelligence, brain computer interfaces, nanotechnology and regenerative approaches has introduced new strategies for improving spatiotemporal precision and understanding complex neural circuit dynamics. However, the translational maturity of these emerging technologies varies considerably, with most approaches remaining at experimental or preclinical stages. Although these platforms provide promising opportunities for future precision neuromodulation, their clinical implementation requires further validation regarding long-term safety, biological compatibility, delivery efficiency and regulatory feasibility. The current evidence status, demonstrated applications, and major translational challenges associated with emerging optogenetic technologies are summarized in . The emerging therapeutic platforms integrating optogenetics with advanced neurotechnologies are illustrated in , while the following sections discuss recent developments in closed-loop optogenetics, wireless neuromodulation, artificial intelligence-assisted optogenetics, brain computer interfaces, nanotechnology-enabled light delivery and combination approaches involving stem cells and gene editing.

Current evidence status and translational challenges of emerging optogenetic technologies.

Conventional optogenetic stimulation generally operates in an open-loop manner, delivering predefined light patterns irrespective of ongoing neuronal activity. In contrast, closed-loop optogenetics combines real-time neural recording with automated optical stimulation, allowing continuous monitoring of brain activity and immediate adjustment of stimulation parameters. Electrophysiological recordings, calcium imaging or electroencephalography (EEG) signals are processed to detect abnormal neuronal activity, which subsequently triggers precisely timed optogenetic intervention. In experimental models of epilepsy, Parkinson's disease and essential tremor, closed-loop approaches have been investigated for detecting and modulating pathological activity. Relative to continuous stimulation, feedback-guided protocols may reduce unnecessary stimulation and energy use, although consistent reductions in adverse effects and improvements in therapeutic outcomes have not been established. Integration with machine learning could support prediction of disease-associated activity and adaptive adjustment of stimulation parameters (, ); however, reproducibility, safety and clinical benefits require further validation.

One of the principal obstacles to clinical optogenetics is the dependence on tethered optical fibers, which restrict natural movement and increase surgical complexity. Advances in wireless neuromodulation have enabled the development of implantable, miniaturized, battery-free optoelectronic devices capable of delivering light to deep-brain structures while allowing unrestricted behavior. Flexible micro-LEDs, wireless photonic implants and bioresorbable electronic devices offer approaches to spatially controlled stimulation, although tissue responses depend on device design, implementation conditions and duration. Energy harvesting through radiofrequency, near-field communication, ultrasound or photovoltaic systems can reduce reliance on onboard batteries, but sustained operation and chronic implementation remain device-dependent challenges. Wireless systems have demonstrated reliable control of motor behavior, reward circuits and spinal cord activity in freely moving animal models. Their miniaturization, biocompatibility and reduced surgical burden enhance experimental flexibility and may improve future translational feasibility (, –); however, long-term stability, energy supply, tissue responses and safety remain important challenges.

Artificial intelligence is being explored alongside optogenetics for experimental design, neural decoding and stimulation-parameter selection. Machine learning algorithms can analyze large-scale electrophysiological, calcium imaging and behavioral datasets to identify complex neuronal activity patterns that are difficult to detect using conventional analytical methods (). AI-assisted systems may enable data-driven adjustment of stimulation frequency, pulse duration, intensity and timing under experimentally validated conditions. Deep-learning approaches may facilitate analysis of complex neural patterns, identification of candidate dysfunctional circuits and optimization of stimulation strategies; however, clinical implementation requires validated datasets, interpretability and robust biological testing. In selected experimental closed-loop platforms, computational algorithms can update stimulation parameters in response to measured neural dynamics, supporting investigation of adaptive neuromodulation approches (). Integration of AI with optogenetics could improve stimulation precision in experimental settings; however, its application in complex neurological disorders such as epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease requires further validation in diverse biological systems and clinically relevant models (, ).

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) establish communication between neural circuits and external devices and have been investigated for assisting motor, sensory and cognitive functions after neurological injury (, ). In experimental settings, combining optogenetics with BCIs offers the possibility of genetically targeted stimulation that conventional electrical interfaces generally cannot provide. Optogenetic BCIs can simultaneously record neuronal activity and deliver targeted optical stimulation, creating bidirectional communication between damaged neural circuits and assistive devices (). Experimental studies have examined neural decoding sensorimotor responses in models of spinal cord injury and stroke; these findings do not yet establish clinical efficacy of optogenetic BCTs. Integration with robotic prostheses, neuroprosthetic limbs and wearable rehabilitation systems may further enhance functional recovery by promoting activity-dependent cortical plasticity. Further advances in neural recording and adaptive decoding may facilitate evaluation of optogenetic BCIs, but clinical translation will require independent evidence of safety, reliability and functional benefit (, ).

Limited light penetration remains a major barrier to optogenetic therapy, particularly for deep-brain structures. Nanotechnology is being investigated as an alternative means of localized light generation, potentially reducing dependence on implanted optical fibers. Upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) convert deeply penetrating near-infrared (NIR) light into visible wavelengths capable of activating microbial opsins (). Quantum dots, plasmonic nanoparticles and biodegradable nanophotonic materials are also under investigation for localized optical effects, although their photothermal profiles and tissue safety require material-specific assessment (). Nanomaterials may provide multifunctional experimental platforms that combine imaging, drug delivery and optical stimulation, but proposed theranostic applications remain investigational. Targeted nanoparticle delivery is being studies to improve localization; whether this reduces off-target effects or produces therapeutic benefit in deep-brain disorder remains uncertain. Accordingly, nanotechnology-enabled light delivery should presently be regarded as a preclinical research strategy rather than an established minimally invasive treatment (, ).

Combining optogenetics with regenerative medicine represents one of the most promising strategies for restoring neural circuit function following neurodegeneration or injury. Stem cell-derived neurons genetically engineered to express light-sensitive opsins enable precise evaluation of graft survival, neuronal maturation, synaptic integration, and functional connectivity after transplantation (). Optogenetic stimulation enhances activity-dependent maturation of transplanted neural stem cells, promotes synaptogenesis, and facilitates incorporation into host neural networks. Simultaneously, gene-editing technologies such as CRISPR/Cas systems allow targeted correction of disease-causing mutations while optogenetics provides functional validation of restored neuronal activity (). Viral vectors including adeno-associated virus (AAV) and lentivirus remain the primary platforms for delivering opsin genes to transplanted or endogenous neurons, although efforts continue to improve targeting specificity and long-term safety (, ).

The combination of optogenetics with stem cell therapy has demonstrated encouraging results in experimental models of Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury, retinal degeneration and stroke, where transplanted neurons establish functional synaptic connections and improve behavioral outcomes. Combining regenerative medicine, gene therapy, biomaterials and adaptive optogenetic neuromodulation may offer routes for investigating circuit repair, but durable functional restoration and personalized clinical treatment have not yet been demonstrated (, ).

An important distinction is whether a technology has demonstrated optical control in living animals, therapeutic benefit in a disease model, or reproducible safety and efficacy in humans. These represent separate evidence thresholds. Red-shifted opsins have experimentally useful spectral properties, but longer excitation wavelengths do not eliminate scattering, absorption, dose constraints, or the requirement for spatially controlled illumination (, , ). Implantable and wireless micro-LED systems enable untethered stimulation in animal models, although chronic thermal, mechanical, power-delivery, and tissue-response constraints remain relevant for human use (). Closed-loop optogenetic control has been demonstrated experimentally, whereas clinically reliable disease biomarkers, algorithms, and integrated delivery systems are still needed (). Nanoparticle-mediated near-infrared stimulation has in vivo proof-of-concept evidence, but biodistribution, clearance, photothermal dose, repeated administration, and long-term toxicology remain unresolved (, ).

Evidence from optogenetic vision-restoration research illustrates that limited human translation is possible in a specific accessible sensory system (); this should not be extrapolated to deep-brain treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. For intracranial applications, an integrated platform would require reproducible cell-targeted vector delivery, dose-controlled and stable opsin expression, immune monitoring, illumination of anatomically defined targets, chronic device compatibility, demonstrable functional benefit, and an acceptable risk–benefit profile under relevant regulatory oversight. Accordingly, the technologies in  are classified by their demonstrated experimental status rather than by presumed proximity to clinical approval (, , ).

Despite remarkable advances in optogenetics over the past two decades, several technical, biological and translational challenges continue to limit its widespread clinical application. These include inadequate light penetration into deep-brain structures, long-term safety of opsin expression, immune responses to viral vectors and implanted devices and the need for more efficient photosensitive proteins. Advances in molecular engineering, biomaterials, artificial intelligence (AI) and bioelectronics may help address selected limitations, but their contribution to clinical translation remains to be determined. The major challenges, enabling technologies and future roadmap toward clinical translation are summarized in , highlighting research priorities that would need to be addressed before safe and effective clinical optogenetic interventions could be considered for neurological and neurodegenerative disorders.

Efficient light delivery to deep-brain regions remains one of the principal challenges in optogenetics. Visible light undergoes significant absorption and scattering within neural tissue, limiting effective stimulation depth and often necessitating invasive implantation of optical fibers. Although fiber-optic systems provide precise spatial targeting, chronic implantation may induce tissue damage, gliosis, inflammation and mechanical instability. Emerging technologies aim to overcome these limitations through minimally invasive approaches. Wireless micro-light-emitting diodes (micro-LEDs), flexible optoelectronic implants, UCNPs and NIR-responsive nanomaterials being investigated to improve access to deeper tissue, although their invasiveness and safety depends on the specific platform (, ). In addition, advanced waveguides, holographic light shaping and multiphoton stimulation improve spatial precision and permit simultaneous modulation of multiple neuronal populations. Further development may improve the technical feasibility of deep-brain optogenetic interventions, but long-term safety and clinical utility require dedicated evaluation (, , , ).

Stable and controlled expression of microbial opsins is essential for chronic neuromodulation. Most current optogenetic systems rely on adeno-associated viral (AAV) or lentiviral vectors to deliver opsin genes; however, long-term expression may vary because of promoter activity, vector tropism, epigenetic regulation and transgene silencing (, ). Excessive opsin expression can alter membrane properties, affect neuronal physiology and increase the risk of cytotoxicity. Future strategies focus on improving vector engineering, developing cell type-specific promoters and incorporating inducible gene-expression systems that permit reversible regulation of opsin levels. Advances in genome editing, particularly CRISPR/Cas-based targeted gene insertion, may further improve expression stability while reducing insertional risks. Whether these approaches improve long-term expression control, efficacy or safety in clinically relevant settings remains to be established (, –).

Immune reactions against viral vectors, microbial opsins, or implanted optical devices remain important barriers to clinical translation. Viral gene delivery can activate innate and adaptive immune pathways, leading to neuroinflammation, reduced transgene expression, and decreased therapeutic efficacy. Likewise, chronic implantation of optical fibers or electronic devices may provoke foreign-body responses characterized by microglial activation, astrocytic gliosis, and fibrotic encapsulation. Current research seeks to improve the biocompatibility of viral vectors and implantable materials while minimizing immunogenicity. Engineered AAV capsids, biodegradable polymers, flexible bioelectronic devices, and transient immunosuppressive strategies have shown promise in reducing inflammatory responses. A better understanding of neuron–glia interactions and host immune mechanisms will be critical for ensuring the long-term safety of optogenetic interventions in humans (, ).

The development of next-generation opsins is expanding the versatility and therapeutic potential of optogenetics. First-generation opsins often require high-intensity blue light and exhibit relatively slow kinetics or limited ion selectivity. Protein engineering has produced novel opsins with improved light sensitivity, faster activation and deactivation kinetics, enhanced ion conductance and shifted excitation spectra. Red-shifted opsins, including ChrimsonR and related variants, enable deeper tissue stimulation because red light penetrates biological tissues more effectively than blue light (, ). Anion-conducting channelrhodopsins and improved inhibitory pumps provide more efficient neuronal silencing, while bistable opsins permit prolonged modulation using brief light pulses (). Continued molecular optimization may support multiplexed control of neuronal populations and improve compatibility with emerging light-delivery systems; reduce phototoxicity and safety must be verified for each opsin and stimulation protocol (, ).

The proposed direction for optogenetic research is the integration of genetic targeting, real-time neural recording, computational modeling and adaptive stimulation. Unlike conventional electrical stimulation, optogenetics enables selective modulation of genetically defined neuronal populations while preserving neighboring circuits. Integration with closed-loop control systems, AI-based neural decoding, calcium imaging, electrophysiology and multimodal neuroimaging may permit activity-dependent adjustment of stimulation parameters in appropriately validated experimental platforms. Whether such adaptive approaches improve therapeutic efficacy or reduce adverse effects remain uncertain. Combining optogenetics with pharmacological interventions, electrical stimulation, rehabilitation or regenerative medicine also warrants investigation, although synergistic clinical benefits have not been established. These approaches provide a research framework for evaluating individualized circuit-based interventions rather than evidence of an imminent transition to precision medicine ().

Future research may benefit from combining neuroscience, molecular biology, bioengineering, nanotechnology, AI and regenerative medicine. Improved gene-delivery vectors, wireless optoelectronic devices, NIR-responsive nanomaterials and opsin engineering could address selected technical constraints, although no individual advance is likely to resolve all translational barriers. Stem cell transplantation, CRISPR-mediated gene editing and brain-computer interfaces may also support experimental investigation of circuit repair, but comprehensive functional restoration remains unproven. Clinical translation will require rigorous evaluation of long-term safety, durable gene expression, immune compatibility and ethical considerations associated with genetic manipulation. Standardization of stimulation protocols, optimization of patient selection and well-designed clinical trials will be essential for establishing therapeutic efficacy across neurological disorders. At present, optogenetics remains primarily an experimental platform for causal circuit investigation, with selected applications advancing toward translational evaluation. Its eventual role in clinical diagnosis, neuromodulation, or regenerative therapy will depend on reproducible evidence of patient benefit, acceptable risk, and regulatory feasibility, rather than technological capability alone.

Optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by enabling precise, reversible and cell-specific manipulation of neuronal activity with exceptional temporal and spatial resolution. By integrating microbial opsins, genetic engineering, optical technologies and systems neuroscience, it has shifted the study of brain function from descriptive observation to causal analysis of neural circuits. Throughout this review, we have highlighted how optogenetics has advanced understanding of neural circuit organization, synaptic plasticity, learning and memory, neurodevelopment, sensory processing, sleep regulation and the molecular mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative disorders. Importantly, optogenetic studies have demonstrated that circuit dysfunction often precedes irreversible neuronal loss, redefining neurodegenerative diseases as disorders of disrupted neural network activity rather than solely progressive neuronal degeneration. Precise modulation of disease relevant circuits has provided critical insights into protein aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress and regulated cell death, while demonstrating functional improvements in preclinical models of AD, PD, HD, ALS, MS and stroke. However, these findings primarily represent proof-of-concept evidence for circuit modulation rather than confirmed therapeutic efficacy in human patients. Thus, the current role of optogenetics remains predominantly focused on elucidating disease mechanisms, identifying therapeutic targets, and evaluating circuit-based interventions rather than serving as an established clinical treatment strategy. Despite remarkable progress, several challenges continue to limit clinical translation, including safe and efficient gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune responses, limited light penetration into deep-brain regions, device biocompatibility and regulatory considerations. Advances in red-shifted and near-infrared responsive opsins, wireless photonic implants, minimally invasive optical devices, nonviral gene delivery systems and nanotechnology may facilitate improved spatial targeting, reduced invasiveness and enhanced therapeutic feasibility; however, their clinical effectiveness requires further validation through long-term safety studies and human investigations. Furthermore, integration of optogenetics with single cell and spatial omics, genetically encoded biosensors, artificial intelligence, closed-loop neuromodulation, brain-computer interfaces and gene editing technologies may offer promising opportunities for comprehensive characterization and modulation of disease specific neural circuits, although most of these approaches remain at experimental or preclinical stages. In conclusion, optogenetics has evolved from an experimental neuroscience tool into a powerful platform for precision circuit analysis and an emerging, yet still investigational, approach for future neuromodulation strategies. Continued technological innovation and multidisciplinary validation may support future clinical assessment; however, practical implementation will depend on overcoming biological, engineering and regulatory barriers and demonstrating meaningful patient outcomes. Accordingly, potential diagnostic or therapeutic applications in neurodegenerative disorders should be regarded as research objectives rather than anticipated clinical achievements.

neuroscience.title: A neural circuit mediating altitude control in Drosophila
neuroscience.abstract: Flight is a remarkably efficient mode of locomotion that is largely responsible for the extraordinary evolutionary radiations of birds, bats, pterosaurs, and insects. Whereas walking animals need only control locomotion on a two-dimensional surface, flight requires active altitude regulation, a process by which the brain transforms self-motion cues into motor patterns that regulate lift. Using an integrative approach combining optogenetics, high-speed videography, two-photon imaging, robotics, and connectomics, we identified a single pair of descending neurons in Drosophila that controls altitude. To search for candidate cells, we performed an optogenetic screen of sparse driver lines targeting descending neurons that project to the flight neuropil of the ventral nerve cord, and identified one bilaterally paired neuron, DNa10, whose activation elicits changes in wing kinematics consistent with descent. A replay of the kinematics on a dynamically scaled robot confirmed that the wing motion elicited by DNa10 activation generates a reduction in upward force. Optogenetic activation of this neuron causes free-flying animals to descend, whereas ablation or silencing of the cell in tethered flies elicits fictive ascent. Functional imaging reveals that DNa10 is activated by downward visual motion and inhibited by upward motion. These results are consistent with a connectomic analysis showing that DNa10 receives monosynaptic input from large-field visual interneurons sensitive to vertical body motion and provides direct output to three wing motor neurons that regulate the lift.
