Collectively, these results identify core components of a circuit for altitude control that links the detection of visual motion to the alteration of aerodynamic forces.
neuroscience.text:
Insects were the first animals to evolve active flight, an adaptation responsible for their remarkable species diversity and ecological success. Although altitude regulation is a requisite feature of flight, the neuromechanical systems animals use to control vertical motion remain poorly understood. Unlike aircraft, which measure elevation directly via altimeters or GPS, animals must infer height from sensory cues such as optic flow–. Experimental studies on honeybee flight control, and computational models of flying gulls suggest that these animals determine their flight height primary from the pattern of optic flow beneath them. Hummingbirds, in contrast, appear to rely on wide-field optic flow, not just ventral visual motion, to stabilize altitude–. Likewise, Drosophila modulate their lift vector in response to wide-field optic flow in tethered preparations,, while free-flight studies have identified three distinct reflexes flies use to regulate altitude: nearby edge fixation, ventral collision avoidance, and a wide-field optomotor response,–. This well-characterized behavioral repertoire, together with flies’ robust and agile flight and their genetic accessibility, makes Drosophila a tractable system for identifying the neural circuits that implement altitude control.

Using vision to detect changes in altitude requires neural circuits that can continuously relay sensory information from the brain to the motor centers governing locomotor muscles. In Drosophila and other arthropods, this communication is mediated by a sparse population of ~650 bilateral descending neurons (DNs), representing the only direct pathway from the brain to leg and wing motor circuits in the ventral nerve cord (VNC),. Prior work leveraging a large collection of split-GAL4 driver lines targeting DNs has identified specific cells classes as initiators and regulators of a diverse set of behaviors, including walking–, grooming,, courtship–, predator evasion, takeoff, steering–, thrust, collision avoidance, and landing. To identify cells controlling altitude, we conducted a systematic activation screen of sparsely expressing DN driver lines in tethered flies while tracking their wing kinematics using 3D high-speed videography. From this screen and subsequent experiments, we characterized a simple yet elegant sensorimotor circuit for altitude control that transforms optic flow into motor commands for modulating aerodynamic forces.

We identified 24 split-GAL4 candidate driver lines that were sufficiently sparse to target morphologically distinct pairs or populations of DNs projecting directly to the flight neuropil within the VNC,. We optogenetically activated each line with CsChrimson in tethered animals flying under closed-loop conditions—an experimental protocol in which flies actively minimize the yaw velocity of a panoramic display by adjusting their left and right wing amplitudes,. Because even subtle adjustments in wing motion can result in large changes in flight trajectories, we captured the kinematics of flies with three high-speed cameras operating at 15,000 frames per second (). We then reconstructed the pose of the flapping fly wings to determine the three Tait-Bryan angles for stroke position (ϕ), stroke deviation (θ), and wing pitch (η), as well as an additional kinematic parameter that captures chord-wise camber (ξ) (, ). In seven of the driver lines we screened, optogenetic activation resulted in a reproducible rise in stroke amplitude expected of cells responsible for increasing lift or thrust during flight (), two of which (DNg02, DNa15) have been described by prior studies. DNg02 comprises a large population of morphologically similar cells thought to regulate flight speed and steering,. DNa15 is a single bilateral pair of neurons that, together with DNb01, appears to function as a command neuron for the rapid flight maneuvers called body saccades that are characteristic of Drosophila and other dipteran species. For 15 of the lines, optogenetic activation yielded no substantive changes in wing kinematics (, , ). Activation of just two lines (SS01070, SS02384)—both of which target DNa10 neurons—resulted in a reduction in stroke amplitude consistent with descent (, ). Because SS02384 targeted two DNs (DNa10 and DNa04), we tested a separate line that is selective for only DNa04 (SS55587) and observed no change in wing kinematics with optogenetic activation (). As a further verification, we identified an additional driver line targeting DNa10 (SS66183) that was not part of our initial screen and confirmed that optogenetic activation induced a decrease in wingstroke amplitude (, ).

To test whether changes in wing kinematics elicited by DNa10 generate a reduction in flight force consistent with descent, we replayed the wing kinematics recorded during optogenetic activation on a dynamically scaled robotic model of a flapping wing equipped with a sensor for measuring force and torque (). Compared to the baseline pattern, the wing kinematics elicited by activation generated a decrease in the magnitude of the stroke-averaged flight force, as well as a slight forward tilt in its orientation (, , ), results consistent with the hypothesis that DNa10 controls descent.

Prior behavioral research in many species suggests that optic flow provides the primary means by which an animal could sense changes in altitude during flight; whereas downward optic flow indicates ascent, upward optic flow signals descent,–,–. Thus, if DNa10 is part of an altitude stabilization circuit, we would expect that downward optic flow would activate this neuron, given that its optogenetic activation elicits a decrease in stroke amplitude. To evaluate this prediction, we presented tethered, flying flies with wide-field visual motion while recording from DNa10 expressing GCaMP7f using a 2-photon microscope (–). The activity of both the left and right DNa10 cells increased at the onset of flight and were synchronously active throughout each trial (). To characterize the influence of optic flow on the neuron, we created a shuffled panel of translational visual patterns: progressive, regressive, and downward optic flow; rotational patterns simulating yaw, pitch, and roll; and looming stimuli indicating an approaching threat. Whereas all the visual stimuli we presented elicited the expected compensatory changes in wing kinematics (), DNa10 was only activated by the three stimuli that induced bilateral decreases in stroke amplitude (progressive optic flow, pitch down rotational motion, and downward translation) during flight (). Of these three patterns, full-field downward motion—the optic flow that would be experienced during upward movement of the fly—evoked the largest excitation of DNa10 (). The neuron’s response to progressive (front-to-back) motion and simulated nose-up pitch might be explained by the fact that these two patterns include a large patch of downward optic flow in the center of the visual field. To test this hypothesis, we systematically varied the azimuthal extent of the patch of downward optic flow. Both the activity of DNa10 and the flies’ behavioral responses increased with the width of the stimulus (–, ). Furthermore, adding patches of upward motion in the stimulus periphery—as would be present in the optic flow field during nose-up body pitch—greatly reduced the response of DNa10 to downward motion in the frontal visual field (, ). Collectively, these results suggest that DNa10 receives input from one or more visual interneurons that serve as matched filters for panoramic downward optic flow, the visual stimulus resulting from upward movement of the fly. We also recorded from the DNa10 cells during quiescence (i.e. when the flies were not flying), but measured no response to downward motion or any other pattern of optic flow we presented ().

The selectivity of DNa10 for downward optic flow could explain how a fly that drifts upward would elicit a compensatory decrease in stroke amplitude to reduce the vertical component of its aerodynamic force. However, flying at a constant altitude requires a mechanism by which upward optic flow also elicits a compensatory increase in the vertical force created by the wings. Such functionality might arise via a dedicated antagonistic interneuron that transforms downward body motion into increased lift. However, given that activity of DNa10 is tonically elevated during flight (), DNa10 itself might provide the necessary bidirectional functionality provided it is inhibited by upward optic flow. To test this possibility, we recorded from DNa10 in flying flies while presenting them with a 9-fold range of vertical optic flow speeds ranging from −112.5 to +112.5 degrees s−1 (, ). The resulting tuning curve indicates that upward optic flow does indeed decrease the activity of DNa10, although the cell’s response to upward visual motion is modest compared to that generated by downward stimuli (). However, this response asymmetry might simply reflect the compressed dynamic range of GCaMP when reporting decreases in neural activity. Testing this conjecture directly would require whole-cell patch recordings, which are challenging in this flight preparation due to the anterior position of the DNa10 cell body. Nevertheless, these results are consistent with the hypothesis that DNa10 might be sufficient to regulate altitude in both directions without the need for a dedicated antagonistic pathway.

To test if DNa10 is necessary for the decreases in wingstroke amplitude induced by visual motion, we presented downward optic flow to flies whose DNa10 cells were ablated via expression of the pre-apoptotic genes reaper and hid (). DNa10-ablated flies responded to downward visual motion with a 52% smaller change in wingstroke amplitude compared to empty-vector controls [95% CI: 30.6, 75.1] (), as well as a 18% higher baseline wingstroke amplitude (red arrow, ) [95% CI: 5.5, 29.5]. This baseline shift in the absence of visual motion is consistent with a role of DNa10 in the continuous regulation of altitude during flight, although potential developmental effects induced by cell ablation complicate such interpretations. As an alternative approach that allows temporal control and avoids developmental confounds, we expressed the inhibitory anion-conducting channelrhodopsin variant GtACR1 in DNa10 cells (). When subjected to the activation light, flies expressing GtACR1 increased wingstroke amplitude (, ) (p = 1.163 x 10−2). In contrast, empty-vector controls exhibited only a brief change in wing kinematics at stimulus onset, presumably a behavioral response to the rapid increase in light intensity. Combined with our functional imaging results (), these ablation and silencing experiments suggest that DNa10 is tonically active during flight and plays a role in continually adjusting stroke amplitude in response to vertical optic flow.

To test the role of DNa10 under more naturalistic free-flight conditions, we optogenetically activated the cells in flies that were flying freely within a large wind tunnel (). Flies expressing CsChrimson in DNa10 received either a 630 nm light pulse or no light pulse (sham flash control) when they entered a specified trigger volume within the tunnel (). Light pulses elicited a controlled descent of 6.7 cm [95% CI: 6.1, 7.3] () compared to both sham and empty-vector controls. All controls exhibited a slow, steady increase in altitude of 9.2 cm [95% CI: 8.0, 10.4], likely a reaction to changes in visual features as they progressed down the tunnel (, ). Although we attempted complimentary experiments using GtACR1 to test whether optogenetic silencing of DNa10 increases altitude in free-flying flies, the results were uninterpretable. Because the free flight arena does not allow for focusing the LED on the head capsule, the 525 nm light pulses required to activate GtACR1 elicited strong upward flight responses even in empty vector controls, due to the high light intensity throughout the tunnel.

We used the female adult fly brain (FAFB) connectome to identify putative upstream neurons underlying the visual responses observed during our functional imaging experiments. Compared to all other individual visual projection cells, the lobula plate tangential neurons LPT-27 and LPT-49 provide the 1st- and 2nd-highest number of synaptic inputs to DNa10, and are predicted to be excitatory according to a machine learning classifier, (). Based on their presynaptic inputs, a prior study proposed that both LPT-27 and LPT-49 serve as matched filters for downward motion. To test this prediction, we functionally imaged LPT-27 and LPT-49 neurons in tethered, flying flies presented with a panel of visual stimuli and found that both neurons were most sensitive to downward motion during flight and quiescence (, ; ). Whereas LPT-49 was not modulated by the speed of translational motion, the neuron’s activity increased with the azimuthal extent of the downward motion stimulus (), comparable to our results for DNa10 (–). The results support a plausible role for these two LPT cells in mediating the visual response observed in DNa10. In addition, DNa10 is also directly downstream of a population of visual interneurons (LPLC4) and another descending neuron (DNp07) that elicit leg extension in response to an approaching object,, suggesting that DNa10 might also function to decrease lift during landing sequences, in addition to its role in continuously regulating altitude.

Using a genetic approach, we verified that DNa10 is cholinergic and thus excitatory (). Based on its connectivity in the VNC, DNa10 makes monosynaptic connections with motor neurons of the b3, i1, and i2 muscles (,), which have been shown to comprise a motor module for decreasing wingstroke amplitude,,. Two of these steering muscles (i2 and b3) are tonically active during flight, and thus are well suited for regulating altitude and other flight behaviors that require continuous adjustment—in contrast to the phasic muscles that actuate brief, fast maneuvers such as flight saccades. In addition to these monosynaptic connections, DNa10 also provides additional input to the b3, i1, and i2 motor neurons via an indirect, bi-synaptic pathway involving a population of 9 interneurons (IN12A059).

The neuron receiving the second highest number of output synapses from DNa10 is IN13A013, a class of putative GABAergic interneurons that synapse onto 3 motor neurons of dorso-ventral indirect flight muscles (IFMs) (DVMn1a-c, DVMn3a,b, and DVMn2a,b). The IFMs are large stretch-activated muscles whose cyclic contraction cause deformations of the thorax that drive the wings back and forth. This inhibition of the IFMs is consistent with the role of DNa10 in regulating altitude, as changes in stroke amplitude during flight must be balanced by adjustments in the total mechanical power required to flap the wings,. Altogether, our connectomic analysis supports a circuit model in which DNa10 receives information from visual interneurons that serve as matched filters for vertical body motion and regulates motor neurons that actuate changes in altitude ().

Prior work on insect flight suggest three principle mechanisms for altitude control: edge tracking, expansion avoidance, and wide-field stabilization, likely involving complementary neural circuits. In this study, we identified a single pair of descending neurons that integrates measurements of vertical optic flow and alters wing kinematics to decrease lift in a compensatory fashion. Although the DNa10 circuit we propose could not easily explain edge tracking behavior, as it relies on interneurons that pool optic flow over a large region of the visual field, our findings strongly support its role in regulating the wide-field vertical stabilization response. Using vertical optic flow to measure changes in altitude has been reported in other animals such as bees, hummingbirds, and gulls–, and employed in robotic aerial vehicles to enable more streamlined flight controllers–. This vision-based strategy is a simple solution for altitude regulation within a highly maneuverable and rapid flight system.

Although altitude regulation may involve descending neurons antagonistic to DNa10, the candidates identified in our screen that increase stroke amplitude (DNg02, DNa15, DNg03, and DNg17) are unlikely direct counterparts to DNa10. Prior work suggest that DNg02 and DNa15 function in steering and thrust control, rather than altitude regulation–, and an analysis using the FAFB connectome suggests that DNg03 and DNg17 do not receive direct input from visual interneurons. Although one neuron from our screen (DNb03) is downstream of Nod5, a pair of neurons predicted to be sensitive to upward motion, its activation did not elicit any detectable changes in wing kinematics (). It is likely, however, that other relevant neurons were simply not captured in the restricted set of sparse driver lines that we tested. Nevertheless, our results suggest that DNa10 might be sufficient to regulate altitude in both directions. According to this hypothesis, DNa10 operates at an elevated level during flight, with increases and decreases in activity generated from downward and upward optic flow, respectively. This scenario is akin to pushing the accelerator pedal of a car to speed up and releasing it to slow down. While this strategy might seem counterintuitive, it is worth noting that unlike steering—which is mediated by a bilaterally symmetric system of sensors, circuits, and actuators duplicated on the left and right sides—altitude control is regulated by a neuromuscular system that is not mirror-symmetric about the dorsoventral axis. A scheme by which a single set of bilaterally active muscles regulates both ascent and descent via increases and decreases in activity makes sense within this context. The decrease in activity of DNa10 observed in response to upward optic flow could be inherited from the upstream LPT-49 and LPT-27 neurons, which themselves show a small decrease to upward visual motion (). Downstream, DNa10 regulates changes in altitude through its direct and indirect connections to a set of three steering motor neurons b3, i1, and i2 that function collectively to decrease stroke amplitude and thus diminish the upward force generated during each wingbeat. Because of the tonic activity patterns of i2 and b3, decreases in DNa10 activity evoked by upward optic flow would elicit an increase in lift via the reduced activity of the same motor neurons. While such a scenario might represent the most parsimonious model at present, it remains quite possible that the actual circuit is much more complex.

In addition to visually-guided altitude stabilization, flies must also actively change altitude when they take off, requiring that they tolerate vertical optic flow without engaging in a compensatory reflex that would interfere with voluntary action. How nervous systems accommodate voluntary actions while compensatory reflexes are running in the background is a general and largely unresolved question in neurobiology, but may involve the use of efference copy signals to reduce the gain of reafferent feedback during active maneuvers,. One candidate for this role is the PLP213 neuron, which makes strong inhibitory connections that could silence DNa10 to facilitate active changes in altitude.

By uncovering the neuromechanical implementation of an altitude regulator that transforms sensory input into motor commands for modulating aerodynamic force, our findings provide insight into an essential function of active flight. We hope this work provides a tractable entry point for extending the recent advances in our understanding of the circuits responsible for azimuthal navigation in insects to flight control in all three dimensions.
