All experiments were conducted on 2-5 day-old female Drosophila melanogaster raised in a temperature and humidity-controlled incubator. For optogenetic experiments, flies were raised in darkness and fed media enriched with 0.2 mM all trans-Retinal (ATR) until eclosion, then switched to a 0.4 mM ATR diet. For experiments involving tethered flight, flies were first anesthetized on a cold plate and fixed to a tungsten pin with UV-curable glue after removing their front legs with fine scissors. For the optogenetic activation screen, split-GAL4 driver lines were obtained from Bloomington Drosophila Stock center or Janelia Research Campus. For optogenetic activation experiments, these split-GAL4 drivers were crossed with 20XUAS-CsChrimson-mVenus. The SS01070 split-GAL4 driver was crossed to w+;UAS-GCaMP7f;UAS-tdTomato for functional imaging experiments, to 20XUAS-GtACR1-EYFP for optogenetic silencing experiments, and to UAS-rpr, hid for ablation experiments. For free flight optogenetic experiments, the flies were crossed with 20XUAS-CsChrimson-mVenus on attp2 in a Berlin wild-type background which carries a copy of the wild-type White gene, as described previously (obtained from Janelia Research Campus). For functional imaging from LPT-27 and LPT-49, the SS02087 and SS02075 split-GAL4 driver lines were crossed to w+; UAS-GCaMP7f;UAS-tdTomato.

Sample size (N) indicates the number of individuals tested whereas (n) in , ,  indicate the number of wingbeats and in ,  the number of trajectories. Variance was estimated by bootstrapping the 95% confidence intervals of individual means (, ; , , , , , ; , , , ; ; ; ; ; , ). In , we calculated z-scores on a per fly basis according to (x - μ)/σ, where μ is the mean and σ is the standard deviation. The regression in  was performed using the scipy package for orthogonal distance regression, and the regression in  was performed using the scipy stats package for linregress. The 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals of the mean regression slope (m), and coefficient of determination (r2) reported in the text were generated from regressions determined on each fly.

To test the difference in means between two sample distributions, we performed two-sided permutation tests. For each test, we randomly shuffled the pooled observations, reassigned a label creating two groups of the original sizes, and recorded the absolute difference in group means. This process was then repeated for M = 1,000,000 random permutations. We then calculated the p value as (b + 1)/(M + 1), where b is the number of permutations with an absolute difference in means greater than or equal to the observed absolute difference. The smallest attainable p value is therefore 1/(M+1) = 1 x 10−6. In , mean changes to L+R WSA were compared during the light-on activation period for each group’s means. Our reported p values are the pairwise permuted p scores adjusted with the Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons using the multipletests package from statsmodels. In , we compared the mean change in ΔF/F during the visual stimulus period for each group’s means. In , we compared the difference in baseline L+R WSA (defined as the 2 second period before downward motion presentation) and the change in L+R WSA during presentation of downward motion for each group’s means. In , we compared the change in L+R WSA during the light-on period for each group’s means. In , , we compared the changes in altitude 1 second after the stimulus onset for all trajectories in each group. The reported p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using a Holm-Bonferroni correction.

For the optogenetic activation screen, tethered flies performed a closed-loop stripe fixation task in a panoramic 360° LED array (128 pixels diameter x 40 pixels high). We used a composite gel filter inserted over the LEDs (1X Roscolux #59 Indigo, 2X #39 Skelton Exotic Sangria, 2X #4390 Cyan) to shift the emission away from the sensitivity of CsChrimson channels. Left and right wing amplitudes were recorded using kinefly operating a Point Grey USB 3.0 camera recording at 30 Hz. In between continuous flight bouts of at least 10 s, we delivered 0.5 s, 658 nm light pulses via a focused 0.5 mW mm−2 laser aimed at the fly’s head. This stimulus was triggered 0.25s after the start of the 1.1s high speed video recording. We recorded ~5 flies per line, ~8 trials per fly, resulting in ~8,000 wingbeats per line. For the tethered optogenetic activation experiment in , flies received a 0.68 s long pulse from a 617 nm LED (M617F2, Thorlabs) (0.218 mW mm−2) focused to a 0.55 mm spot on the back of the fly’s head. Flies received 10 stimulations every 15 s during periods of closed-loop presentation of a starfield pattern. Trials in which the fly stopped flying during high-speed video recordings were excluded.

The high-speed video recordings and 3D pose estimation pipeline have been described previously. Briefly, three orthogonal cameras (Photron SA5) with a 0.5x telecentric lens (Edmund Optics, Platinum TL) recorded 1.1 s videos at 15,000 Hz with a 1/30,000 shutter speed and 256x256 pixel resolution. Cameras were calibrated using the direct linear transform (DLT) method and illuminated by collimated infrared (850 nm) backlights (M850LP1 LED and SM2P collimation lens, Thor Labs). We then used the FlyNet package, comprised of a convolutional neural network and particle swarm optimization, to estimate the pose vector of each wing. Each wing pose vector was run through an extended Kalman filter to smooth motion and remove outliers. The wing pose vectors were then represented by three Tait-Bryan angles that describe the orientation of the wing with respect to the stroke plane reference frame, defined by the first three principle components of the wing root translation vector. The stroke position, ϕ, is defined as the angle between the projection of the wingtip on the x-y plane and the y-axis (dorsal side is positive); the deviation angle, θ, is the angle between the wingtip and the x-y plane (above the stroke plane is positive). The wing pitch angle, η, is defined as the angle between the z axis and the leading edge of the wing (counterclockwise rotation is positive). Finally, ξ divides the total chord-wise wing deformation equally among the three flexure lines (counterclockwise rotation about the flexure lines is positive). The kinematic angles were then parsed into separate wingbeats and fit using Legendre polynomials (ϕ = 16 polynomials, θ = 20, η = 24 and ξ = 20) for wingbeat comparison across different frequencies.

To visualize the morphology of DNa10 cells, we dissected the intact nervous systems (brain and VNC) of 3-to-6-day-old adult females resulting from the crosses of the split-GAL4 driver line SS01070 and SS66183 with a 20XUAS-CsChrimson-mVenus responder line. The entire nervous systems (brain and VNC) were dissected in 1xPBS and fixed for 25 minutes in 4% paraformaldehyde diluted in 1x PBS at room temperature. We washed the samples twice for 15 minutes in 1 PBS and four times for 15 minutes in 0.3% PBS-T (1x PBS with 0.3% Triton-X). Samples were blocked in 7.5% normal goat serum diluted in 0.3% PBS-T for 1 hour at room temperature or overnight at 4°C. Samples were then transferred to a blocking solution containing primary antibodies (mouse nc82 at 1:30, chicken anti-GFP at 1:1000) for 4 hours at room temperature followed by 3 days at 4°C. We washed samples four times in 0.3%PBS-T and transferred them to the secondary antibodies (Cy5 goat anti-mouse at 1:300 and Alexa Fluor 488 goat anti-chicken at 1:1000) diluted in blocking solution, for 4 hours at room temperature followed by 3 days at 4°C. Stained samples were washed four times in 0.3% PBS-T and mounted on slides using Vectashield Plus (VectorLabs). We scanned the preparations using a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope using a 40X water objective, at 1.2uM intervals and 1024x1024 pixel resolution. To genetically evaluate the DNa10 neurotransmitter predictions from the connectome,, we generated three reporter lines for the transmitters acetylcholine, GABA, and glutamate. Each line included neurotransmitter-specific protein traps containing T2A-LexA::QFAD Trojan exons inserted into a MiMIC transposon for either ChAT, GAD1, or vGLUT. Each of the three neurotransmitter-LexA lines was combined with nuclear-targeted tdTomato under LexAop control (to label nuclei of all neurons of a given neurotransmitter) and GCaMP8m under UAS control (to label DNa10). Staining protocol for neurotransmitter experiments included rabbit anti-DsRED 1:1500 primary, anti-rabbit Cy3 1:1500 secondary antibody.

As previously described, we measured aerodynamic force and moments using a dynamically scaled robotic model of a flapping Drosophila wing immersed in a 2.4 x 1 x 1.2 m acrylic tank filled with mineral oil. The robot was equipped with one stepper motor (IMS M-2231-3) to control ϕ, two servo motors (HiTec D951TW) to control θ and η, and three micro-servo motors (HiTec HS-7115TH) to specify ξ. All the motors were controlled by a Teensy 3.2 microcontroller. The 25 cm long wing was constructed of acrylic panels with a 6 DOF force-torque sensor (ATI Nano 17) at the base of the wing, which we sampled at 200 Hz. The size of the wing, viscosity of the oil, and angular velocity of motion were chosen to match the Reynolds number of real fly wing during hovering flight (~100). We chose a background wing motion pattern from the activation screen and played it repeatedly for 7 cycles on the robotic wing, but only the 4, 5, and 6 wingbeats were analyzed to ensure that we had achieved steady-state conditions with respect to wake interactions. Gravity forces on the wing were measured in subsequent experiments by replaying wing motion at 0.2X the normal speed, which we then subtracted from the 1X speed experiments to isolate aerodynamic forces and torques.

As previously described, we tethered flies to custom-build stages and imaged them using a 2-photon microscope (ThorLabs) equipped with a galvanometric scan-mirrors and CFI apochromatic near-IR water immersion objective (Nikon, 40x mag., 0.8 N.A., 3.5 mm W.D.). DNa10, LPT-49, or LPT-27 cells expressing GCaMP7f and tdTomato were imaged with 128x64 resolution at 13.1 Hz (DNa10, LPT-49) or 128x32 resolution at 25.4 Hz (LPT-27). For DNa10 recordings, cells were imaged at either of two depths: a relatively anterior plane to distinguish the left and right descending branches or a more posterior plane that provided greater neurite volume and allowed decreased laser power. To correct for motion in the x-y plane, each image frame was registered using a cross-correlation between the tdTomato image and the trial-averaged image. Regions of interest (ROIs) were automatically detected by choosing the pixels with greatest variance over the trial, at a threshold determined by cell volume (single ROI: top 8% pixels for DNa10, 5% for LPT-49; multi-ROI: 4% for DNa10 descending branch and bilateral LPT-27, and 2% for unilateral LPT-27 recordings). Due to the wide, anterior FOV required for LPT-27 recordings, we typically could only visualize one of the two bilateral cells. For recordings in which both left and right cells were present, activity across the two cells were averaged. For all experiments, GCaMP7f florescence was normalized to tdTomato fluorescence to correct for movement artifacts in the z plane. We define change in fluorescence: ΔF/F = (Ft-Fmin)/Fmin, where Ft = (FROI−FB). FROI is the ROI fluorescence per frame, FB is the background fluorescence in each frame (defined as the 10% dimmest pixels within the FOV across the whole trial), and Fmin is the mean of the lowest 10% of ROI fluorescence over each trial. Neural activity was recorded while flies flew in a visual arena of filtered green LED 96x32 pixel arrays covering 216° azimuth and ~72° elevation. The display was lined with a composite gel filter to shift the emitted photons away from the sensitivity of the green channel PMT (one sheet of Roscolux #59 Indigo, two sheets of #39 Skelton Exotic Sangria, and two sheets of #4390 Cyan). After an initial period of closed-loop flight, flies were presented with 3 seconds of starfield visual motion, interspersed with post-epochs of static pattern presentation (2 s for the experiments in , 5 s for the experiments in –, and 7 s for experiments in –). The looming stimulus simulated a 0.15 m diameter disk approaching the fly at 1.5 m s−1 from 1.5 m away. The peripheral reversal stimuli included downward translational motion of 144° azimuthal width in the center of the visual field, and upward motion of 36° azimuthal width in the left and right periphery. All downward motion was presented at 112.5° s−1, unless noted, as in the experiments in , . Each stimulus was presented four times in a shuffled order for every trial. Stimulus presentations were excluded from the mean traces if a flight stop was detected in the period from 0.5 s before to 1 s after pattern motion.

Tethered flies flew in visual closed-loop within a 360° LED arena displaying a starfield pattern fitted with a neutral density filter (Rosco, 12%). Wingstroke amplitudes were recorded using kinefly. For ablation experiments, flies received 4 presentations of 3 s full-field downward motion interspersed with 1 s periods of a static pattern. For optogenetic silencing, flies received a 1 s, 530 nm light pulse (1.021 mW mm−2) confined to 0.9 mm spot on the back of the fly’s head through a 10x microscope objective (Nikon). Flies received 10 pulses at 20 s intervals. If a flight stop was detected in the interval of 1 s before to 1 s after the light stimulus, that stimulation was excluded from the mean calculation. Pattern presentations were excluded from the mean traces if a flight stop was detected in the period from 0.5 s before to 1 s after pattern motion.

The optogenetic activation wind tunnel apparatus is described previously. Briefly, the 1 x 0.5 x 0.5 m wind tunnel was illuminated by blue and white LEDs (STN-BBLU-B6A-08C1M-24V, Super Bright LEDs Inc), and the walls lined with diffusing film (Spye Smoke, Spyeglass). The tunnel airflow was generated by computer fans and controlled by Arduino microcontrollers (Mega, 2560). For visual contrast, a grid of IR transmissible films was placed on the floor to create a checkerboard pattern. The tunnel was also equipped with IR LEDs (PN: 7031, Waveform Lighting) for 3D fly tracking, and 2 arrays of red LEDs (Triple Bright RGB LEDs, SparkFun Electronics) for optogenetic stimulation. The fly trajectories were captured by 12 cameras (acA720, Basler) recording at 100 Hz and tracked using the Braid software. The real-time 3D position of the fly was used to determine whether a fly entered a pre-defined trigger-zone in the apparatus, in which a light pulse would either be randomly triggered (light-on condition) or not (no-light condition for a sham control), which is important for recording the natural flight behavior of the experimental genotype in the absence of a light pulse. The light-on stimulus consisted of a 675 ms, 42 μW mm2 light pulse, with a 5 s refractory period before another stimulation event could occur. To be incorporated our analysis, the data stream associated with each trigger event must have included a continuous tracking sequence from least 200 ms before the stimulus to 1 s afterwards, and the fly’s horizontal or vertical speed must not have exceeded 2 m s−1, which is a unnaturally high value for flies in a wind tunnel. At the start of each recording session, 15 flies were placed in the tunnel, but their identities could not be tracked over the 16-hour recording sessions. For the data plotted in ,  a maximum of 30 individuals contributed to each experimental and control group.

We identified the DNa10 cells in the FAFB and MANC connectome (783 production for FAFB, version 1.2.1 for MANC). We traced individual cells upstream of DNa10 in the brain with at least 2 synapses onto DNa10, then filtered the data using the super class tag ‘visual projection.’ Inputs were classified as ipsilateral or contralateral to the left or right DNa10 cell, and their weights were averaged across left and right sides. If an input cell type contained a population of cells, the input weight was averaged over all input cells of that type independently on the ipsilateral and contralateral sides. We employed similar criteria and analysis to find the top outputs of DNa10 in the VNC. Outputs with at least 2 synapses were classified as ipsilateral or contralateral to the left or right DNa10 cell, and their weights were averaged independently on the two sides. If an output cell type contained a population of cells, the output weight was averaged over all output cells of that type independently on the ipsilateral and contralateral sides.

neuroscience.title: A benchmarking framework for organoid computing
neuroscience.abstract: Organoid computing leverages functional neural networks of lab-grown neural organoids to recapitulate key aspects of human brain information processing, holding promising potential in brain-inspired computing, brain-computer interfaces, neuroscience, and medicine. However, its broad application remains constrained due to technical limitations including biological variability, interface instability, stochastic performance, and limited reproducibility. Here, we present a benchmarking framework that systematically quantifies the key performance determinants of organoid computing. We operationally define ‘benchmark-ready’ organoid substrates using optional criteria encompassing viability, cellular identity, structural integrity, functional maturation, and baseline networks, supported by multimodal phenotyping. We further establish qualification metrics for organoid-machine interface and intrinsic neural and network function, including physical coupling, spatial coverage, temporal stability, spontaneous activity, and network-level organization. Finally, we introduce a hierarchical evaluation framework for stimulation-evoked computation combined with information encoding criteria, standardized scoring, and statistical reporting. We believe that the benchmarking framework may provide an adaptable foundation for standardized, reproducible and comparable evaluation of organoid computing technologies, thereby facilitating the broad adoption and application of organoid intelligence.
neuroscience.text:
Human neural organoids, three-dimensional lab-cultured neural tissues derived from human stem cells, can recapitulate key structural, cellular, and functional features of the developing human nervous system , , , , , , . Various neural organoid models, including cerebral, cortical, midbrain, and spinal cord organoids, have been established as powerful human-relevant platforms for studying neurodevelopment, neurological disorders, drug discovery, toxicity screening, and regenerative medicine , , , , , , , , , . Unlike conventional two-dimensional neuronal cultures, neural organoids such as cortical organoids self-organize into complex architectures containing diverse neural cell types and progressively develop spontaneous electrical activity, synaptic connectivity, oscillatory dynamics, and functional neural networks that resemble aspects of the developing human brain , , , , , , , , , . These features have enabled disease modeling, including patient-derived cerebral organoids that recapitulate primary microcephaly-associated premature neuronal differentiation and progenitor depletion , , , , , as well as brain organoids derived from patients diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease that reproduce amyloid-β deposition, tau hyperphosphorylation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and progressive neurodegeneration , , , , , , , . Beyond disease modeling, these functional neural networks of these organoids provide a unique platform to investigate how living neural circuits encode, process, and adapt to information, opening new directions at the interface of neuroscience, artificial intelligence (AI), and engineering.

This potential has attracted growing interest in harnessing living neural networks as biological substrates for organoid computing, which refers here to the use of neural organoids for information processing and computational input-output tasks. Building on this foundation, organoid intelligence (OI) represents a broader paradigm that encompasses organoid-based computing as well as learning, memory, adaptation, and related applications across AI and medicine , , , , , , , , . By integrating lab-grown living neural tissues with bioelectronic interfaces, organoid computing enables external information to be encoded into neural stimulation, transformed by biological neural networks, and decoded into measurable outputs. Early demonstrations have established the feasibility of this concept through diverse biohybrid computing systems. Our Brainoware platform showed that human brain organoids interfaced with microelectrode arrays (MEA) exhibited reservoir-computing properties and performed computing tasks such as speech recognition and nonlinear equation prediction . Another study has demonstrated adaptive learning in cortical neurons embodied in a simulated Pong environment through real-time closed-loop biohybrid computing with continuous interaction between living neural networks of 2D cultured neurons and external systems . Moreover, goal-directed learning has been implemented using mouse cortical organoids through reinforcement-based training . Together, these studies suggest that neural tissue cultures can perform increasingly sophisticated forms of information processing, learning, and adaptation, positioning organoid computing as an emerging frontier in unconventional computing.

Despite this rapid progress, organoid computing remains in its early stages, and comparisons across studies remain challenging . Variations of organoid morphology, maturation, cellular composition, and cellular organization may affect the function of organoid neural networks , , , , , further substantially influencing computing performance. In parallel, engineering factors including organoid-device coupling, neural recording quality, neural stimulation protocols, feature extraction and decoding strategies may vary considerably for biocomputing tasks across laboratories , , , . Consequently, differences in reported computing performance often reflect a combination of biological, hardware, and analytical factors rather than intrinsic computational capability , . At present, widely accepted criteria are largely missing for determining whether an organoid is biologically qualified for computing, whether an organoid-device interface is sufficiently stable, whether spontaneous neural activity is adequate for information processing, or whether stimulus-evoked responses truly support reliable computation. The absence of standardized evaluation methods limits reproducibility, hinders comparison across platforms, and slows the development and translation of organoid intelligence. Establishing a benchmarking framework would enable rigorous qualification of organoid computing systems, facilitate objective comparison across studies, accelerate technology optimization, and promote broader adoption of organoid intelligence in neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and precision medicine.

Here, we present an initial benchmarking framework for organoid computing systems (). We first establish biological qualification criteria for identifying neural organoids suitable as organoid substrates. We then evaluate the organoid–device interface with respect to physical coupling, spatial coverage, and integration stability. Next, we assess electrophysiological readiness based on spontaneous neural activity and network organization, followed by systematic evaluation of stimulation-evoked responsiveness, pattern discrimination, and downstream decodability. Finally, we demonstrate how these hierarchical benchmarks support representative organoid computing tasks through structured scoring, platform-specific qualification criteria, and standardized reporting guidelines. By separating biological readiness, interface quality, intrinsic neural function, and task-level computation, this framework provides a practical foundation for improving the reproducible, comparable, and standardized evaluation of organoid computing technologies and supports the continued development and broad application of organoid intelligence.

Taking the organoid reservoir computing for an example, organoid computing can be framed as an input-reservoir-output system (). A brain organoid can receive encoded information inputs through an MEA chip, process the information using its living neural networks, and send out decoded information as computational outputs. In this configuration, computational performance depends on multiple coupled factors, including the biological quality of the organoid, the organoid network function, the stability of the organoid-machine interface, and its ability to generate stimulus-dependent responses. We therefore established a hierarchical benchmark framework covering four domains: biological characterization, organoid–machine interface, functional neural network, and stimulation-evoked computation. Biological characterization evaluates morphological integrity, viability, and neuronal maturation; the organoid-machine interface quantifies physical coupling, spatial coverage, and temporal stability on the MEA; resting-state activity assesses spontaneous neural firing and network function; and stimulation-evoked computation examines responsiveness, pattern separability, and decodability under external inputs. Each domain was further translated into defined qualification metrics and scoring rules to support reproducible assessment (). Through this progressive evaluation, an organoid-MEA system can be considered computation-ready only when it is biologically qualified, electrically active, stably interfaced, and capable of input-dependent information processing, providing a practical framework for downstream applications in biohybrid intelligence, brain-machine interfaces, and translational medicine.

Organoid computing relies on living three-dimensional functional neural network substrates for information processing. In particular, organoid morphology, cell viability, neural lineage development, cellular organization, and three-dimensional neurite architecture can all affect network excitability, electrode coupling, spontaneous firing patterns, and stimulation-evoked responses. To minimize variability caused by basic biological failure, we first established a biological qualification gate, which is an optional step for potential accessing functional neural networks of the neural organoid. This gate included four entry criteria: intact morphology, high viability, confirmed neural lineage, and organized three-dimensional neural structure (a). Organoids that failed these criteria were considered unsuitable for downstream benchmarking.

To assess these biological qualification criteria, we characterized cortical organoids as an example using bright-field imaging, section immunostaining, live/dead staining, and whole-mount staining. Bright-field imaging showed progressive organoid development across neural induction, neural progenitor expansion, early neuronal differentiation, and long-term maturation stages. During this process, organoids maintained a compact spheroid morphology without obvious collapse or fragmentation, supporting the morphology requirement for downstream coupling (b). Live/dead staining showed strong live-cell signals with limited dead-cell signals, indicating high viability before functional assessment (c, ). Immunofluorescence staining further confirmed neural lineage progression, with early proliferative neural progenitor populations, emerging neurons, and neuronal connectivity observed during maturation (d). Whole-organoid staining showed neuronal and astrocytic organization within a three-dimensional spheroid architecture, supporting the formation of a network-like neural structure suitable for electrophysiological interrogation (e). These benchmark assays validated representative cultures from the same workflow, while independent unstained organoids were used for downstream MEA experiments. Together, by confirming intact morphology, high cell viability, neural differentiation, and organized three-dimensional neural architecture, this qualification step ensured that subsequent differences in MEA coupling, resting-state activity, and stimulation-evoked computing responses were more likely to reflect functional interface and network properties rather than inadequate organoid development.

The organoid-machine interface provides the structural and functional access point for bidirectional communication between living neural tissue and external hardware , . In organoidcomputing, interface quality directly affects signal recording, stimulation delivery, channel accessibility, and the stability of input-output responses. Here, we used the organoid-MEA interface as a representative example and established an image-derived benchmark that quantified three key interface domains: physical coupling, spatial coverage, and temporal stability (a). Features including morphology score, maximum neurite length, neurite count, body-covered electrode ratio, total electrode coverage ratio, and their temporal changes from day 3 to day 12 after MEA attachment were extracted from bright-field images and converted into domain-level scores according to predefined rules (). Representative examples showed distinct interface phenotypes between well-coupled and weakly coupled preparations (b). Well-coupled interfaces exhibited more evident contact with the electrode array, detectable neurite extension, and greater neurite-mediated expansion over time, whereas weakly coupled interfaces showed limited neurite outgrowth and minimal interface development.

Feature-level comparisons further supported this distinction while highlighting the need for multi-feature integration (c–e). Well-coupled interfaces generally showed higher morphology scores, greater neurite counts, and larger increases in maximum neurite length and overall coverage. In contrast, body-covered area alone was less discriminative, and increased neurite count in weakly coupled samples could reflect delayed neurite emergence rather than stable early coupling. After scaling and integration, well-coupled preparations shifted toward higher physical coupling, spatial coverage, and temporal stability scores, with the clearest separation in temporal stability (f). The overall interface benchmark score separated most well-coupled preparations from weakly coupled preparations using the predefined cutoff (e.g., 50) (g). Together, these results show that high-quality organoid-MEA interfaces require stable attachment, neurite-mediated electrode access, and sustained interface development over time. This benchmark provides a structural gate for downstream electrophysiological and computing-related analysis.

Resting-state neural function refers to the spontaneous electrophysiological activity and coordinated network dynamics generated by organoids. This baseline state reflects whether the living network has sufficient excitability, active recording channels, burst organization, and synchrony to indicate functional organoid neural networks, and further supporting reliable input-output responses. We therefore evaluated resting-state organoid function using spontaneous MEA recordings and established an electrophysiology-derived benchmark with two domains: neural activity and network function (a). Mean firing rate, number of active electrodes, and burst frequency were used to quantify basal neural activity, whereas synchrony index, the number of electrodes participating in bursts, and network burst frequency were used to assess coordinated population-level dynamics. Representative recordings showed clear differences between qualified and unqualified organoids (b). Qualified organoids exhibited sustained spontaneous firing across multiple electrodes and recurrent network bursts, whereas unqualified organoids showed sparse firing, limited electrode recruitment, weak burst organization, or poorly coordinated activity ().

Feature-level analysis quantified these recording phenotypes across the two resting-state domains (c and d). In the neural activity domain, qualified organoids showed higher mean firing rates, more active electrodes, and increased burst frequency, indicating stronger and more spatially distributed spontaneous activity. In the network function domain, qualified organoids exhibited broader electrode participation during bursts, higher network burst rates, and stronger synchrony, reflecting more organized population-level dynamics. To enable unified comparison across features with different units and dynamic ranges, these measurements were converted into scaled scores for neural activity and network function and then integrated into an overall resting-state benchmark score (e and f). Qualified organoids scored higher in both domains and exceeded the predefined cutoff (e.g., 50), whereas unqualified organoids remained below the cutoff because of insufficient spontaneous activity, weak network organization, or both. Together, these results show that resting-state computing readiness requires sufficient basal excitability, active channel recruitment, burst organization, and population synchrony. This benchmark assesses the baseline functional state of organoids and identifies preparations with coordinated spontaneous activity suitable for downstream stimulation and computing-related analysis.

Stimulation-response function represents the core operational layer of organoid-based computing, because it determines whether external inputs can be converted into measurable and input-dependent neural output states. In this context, computing capacity depends on whether the organoid network can reliably respond to stimulation, generate distinguishable responses to different input patterns, and support decoding of these response states. We therefore used electrical stimulation-evoked activity as a representative input-output assay and established a stimulation-response benchmark with three domains: responsiveness, pattern separability, and decodability (a). Responsiveness assessed whether stimulation induced detectable and reliable activity changes; pattern separability evaluated whether different input patterns produced distinguishable neural response states; and decodability tested whether these response states could be classified above chance-level controls (). Representative repeated-stimulation recordings showed that qualified organoids generated time-locked firing increases across multiple electrodes, whereas the unqualified condition, represented here by CNQX-treated organoids (10 μM, 20 min), showed weak and inconsistent evoked responses (b). Patterned-stimulation analysis further demonstrated that responses to different input patterns formed partially separated clusters under the healthy control condition, while CNQX treatment largely reduced this separation and increased overlap between response states (c). These representative results indicate that stimulation-response qualification depends not only on the presence of evoked firing, but also on the ability of the organoid network to generate input-dependent response structures supported by glutamatergic synaptic transmission.

Feature-level analysis then quantified these stimulation-evoked phenotypes across the three benchmark domains (d–f, ). In this module, the unqualified condition was generated by CNQX treatment, which pharmacologically disrupted synaptic/network activity and served as a negative-control condition for impaired stimulation-response function. Compared with this CNQX-treated condition, qualified organoids showed stronger evoked response strength, broader responsive-electrode recruitment, and higher response reliability, supporting enhanced responsiveness. They also exhibited higher separation ratios and larger between-pattern distances, indicating stronger pattern-dependent state separation. Decoding analysis further showed higher classification accuracy in qualified organoids relative to the CNQX-treated condition and shuffle-label controls, supporting improved machine-decodable information in the evoked responses. To enable unified comparison across heterogeneous response features, these measurements were converted into scaled scores for responsiveness, pattern separability, and decodability (g). Integration of the three domain scores generated an overall stimulation-response benchmark score, with qualified organoids exceeding the predefined cutoff (e.g., 50) and CNQX-treated unqualified samples remaining below this threshold (h). Together, these results indicate that stimulation-based computing requires linked input-output properties: reliable, evoked responsiveness, input-dependent state separation, and machine-decodable response information. CNQX-induced disruption reduced all three properties, supporting that this benchmark captures network-dependent stimulation-response function. This stimulation-response benchmark serves as the final qualification layer for identifying organoid-MEA preparations capable of input-dependent and decodable neural output.

Reproducibility in organoid computing was evaluated using a staged quality-control workflow. This design was used because variability can arise at several coupled levels, including organoid generation, organoid-MEA interface formation, spontaneous network activity, stimulation-evoked responses, and downstream decoding . Therefore, the primary experimental unit was defined as an independent organoid-MEA preparation, whereas electrodes and stimulation trials were treated as nested repeated measurements within each preparation. Batch information, preparation number, recording duration, and stimulation trial number were reported for each benchmark module .

Biological qualification served as the entry-level QC step. Candidate organoids were evaluated primarily based on morphology, viability, and preservation of organized neural tissues before being used for MEA-based benchmarking. Operationally, acceptable organoids were required to maintain an intact three-dimensional structure with continuous and organized peripheral neural tissue, without obvious structural collapse, fragmentation, or extensive necrotic regions. These morphological features were evaluated together with viability assessment and neural-marker staining. Unlike the subsequent quantitatively scored modules, biological qualification was treated as an operational entry-level QC gate. Although viability and marker-positive areas were quantified, universal pass thresholds were not imposed because these measures vary with organoid protocol, developmental stage, and imaging/analysis conditions; qualification therefore relied on combined evidence of morphology, viability, lineage specification, and 3D neural organization. Because biological variability can arise from cell-line status, passage history, differentiation batch, organoid size, maturation state, and stress burden, biological QC should be performed across at least three independent differentiation batches, with multiple candidate organoids inspected within each batch . As an operational QC screen, evaluating approximately 5-6 candidate organoids per batch, or 15-18 organoids in total, provides a practical minimum for identifying obvious batch failure, within-batch outliers, and organoids unsuitable for downstream interface or electrophysiological assessment , .

The organoid-MEA interface benchmark was used to determine whether biologically qualified organoids established sufficient physical and electrical coupling with the recording platform. This module assessed physical contact or coverage, active electrode recruitment, and longitudinal interface stability. The interface benchmark included 12 independent organoid-MEA preparations from three differentiation batches, which was treated as a minimum reproducibility screen for interface usability. A larger number of preparations, approximately 15-18 across at least three batches, would be preferable when the goal is to establish stable reference ranges or compare interface designs .

The resting-state neural function benchmark required a larger sample size because spontaneous firing, burst organization, active electrode recruitment, and network synchrony are expected to vary substantially across organoids even after biological and interface QC . This module included 24 independent organoid-MEA preparations from three differentiation batches, with 5-min spontaneous recordings per preparation. Resting-state qualification was based on predefined features, including firing activity, active electrode fraction, burst or network-burst organization, and synchrony or connectivity measures. Preparations with insufficient spontaneous activity or limited electrode recruitment were not considered suitable for downstream input-output computation, because weak baseline activity would make stimulus-evoked classification difficult to distinguish from noise, artifacts, or decoder-dependent effects .

The stimulation-response benchmark evaluated whether organoid networks generated reproducible, artifact-excluded responses to defined input patterns . This module included 10 independent organoid-MEA preparations from three differentiation batches, with 30 stimulation trials per preparation. Because this layer is closest to the final computational claim and is most sensitive to trial-level noise, stimulus artifact, feature-window selection, and classifier instability, conclusions were based on multiple criteria rather than accuracy alone . These criteria included effective response rate, response reliability across trials, pattern separability, decoding performance above label-shuffled controls, and loss or weakening of the response after pharmacological perturbation . For future fully powered benchmarking, 15-18 preparations across at least three batches and at least 30 valid trials per class per organoid would provide a more conservative design for evaluating across-preparation and across-batch reproducibility.

All benchmark features were converted into scaled scores using predefined scoring rules and fixed reference ranges rather than batch-specific min-max normalization. This avoided artificially stretching weak experimental batches across the full score range and allowed scores to remain comparable across preparations, batches, and experiments. A predefined threshold (e.g., 50) was used as the minimum pass criterion for the interface, resting-state, and stimulation-response modules. The scoring structure was hierarchical, with each upstream tier serving as a prerequisite for downstream evaluation. This design reflects an operational dependency: inadequate biological quality can compromise MEA interfacing, poor interfacing can limit reliable electrophysiological recording, and insufficient spontaneous or evoked activity can constrain downstream computation. Accordingly, the framework was intended as a sequential qualification workflow. Importantly, the long-term stability of benchmark scores is expected to be highly system dependent rather than governed by a universal time scale. Factors including the differentiation protocol, maturation stage, culture and perfusion conditions, organoid size, recording/interface configuration, and whether the preparation is maintained under continuous or intermittent computational stimulation may all influence how biological state and functional performance evolve over time; therefore, benchmark validity over weeks or months should be established longitudinally for each experimental platform rather than assumed from a single measurement.

After completing the benchmark qualification workflow, we next examined whether benchmark-qualified organoid-MEA preparations could support a representative organoid computing task. For this validation experiment, the selected organoid-MEA preparations all passed biological qualification and exceeded the predefined pass threshold (e.g.,50) in the organoid-MEA interface, resting-state, and stimulation-response modules (). These benchmark results indicate that the validation organoids had already achieved stable electrode coupling, robust spontaneous network activity, and reliable stimulation responsiveness before being used for downstream computation. We then implemented an R/L input-pattern classification task, in which two spatial electrical stimulation patterns were delivered as inputs and the resulting spatiotemporal firing responses were decoded by a trained readout layer to predict the input class (a and b). Representative electrode-by-time response maps showed distinct evoked activity patterns for Pattern L and Pattern R (c), while trial-averaged firing profiles further confirmed stimulation-locked yet separable response dynamics across the two input conditions (). Classification of the evoked-response features yielded high performance, with 100% accuracy for R-pattern trials and 96% accuracy for L-pattern trials in the representative validation dataset (d). PCA of trial-wise response features also showed separation between L- and R-evoked response states (e), supporting that the two input patterns engaged distinguishable network dynamics rather than producing identical global activation. At the group level, organoid-based decoding accuracy was markedly higher than the MEA-only and shuffle controls and was comparable to the digital reservoir computing reference (f). These results indicate that the benchmark can identify computation-ready organoid-MEA preparations, and that preparations passing the predefined criteria can perform a downstream input-pattern classification task. This supports the use of the framework as a practical benchmark for organoid computing.

After completing the classification based on spatial stimulation patterns, we further examined whether organoid neural networks could process temporally structured inputs. To this end, we designed a simplified three-vowel recognition task using uw, iy, and ah as input classes. Each vowel segment was first divided into three consecutive time frames, and the power features from 12 frequency bands were extracted within each frame, forming a 3 × 12 time-frequency power matrix. These power features were then normalized, binarized, and mapped onto stimulation sequences delivered through different MEA channels and time windows (a). After receiving these sequential inputs, the evoked neural activity of the organoid network was used to decode vowel identity. The results showed that the organoid group achieved substantially higher classification accuracy than the MEA-only, shuffled-label, and TTX-treated control groups (1 μM, 20 min), suggesting that the decoding performance primarily arose from activity-dependent responses of the organoid network to temporally structured inputs, rather than from the electrodes themselves, random label associations, or non-biological signals (b and c).

Because this task relied on electrical stimulation and subsequent decoding of evoked neural responses, stimulation artifacts represented a critical potential confounder. These artifacts can arise from direct coupling between stimulation and recording channels, current spread through the culture medium or tissue, electrode polarization, and amplifier recovery. In our recordings, the artifacts appeared as stimulation-locked, high-amplitude transient deflections with channel-dependent shapes and durations, including narrow sharp peaks, wider biphasic responses, and occasionally repeated post-stimulation components (). Because these artifact signals can be much larger than biological spikes and may distort spike detection and firing-rate estimation within the early post-stimulation window, artifact removal was essential for evaluating organoid-based computation (). We therefore characterized and removed stimulation artifacts in the vowel-recognition task. Specifically, stimulation-locked waveforms were first inspected from the raw traces to estimate the duration and morphology of the artifact for each channel. A conservative artifact window was then defined, and samples within this window were blanked for each stimulation pulse. Spike detection and feature extraction were performed only outside the artifact window (). Because artifact morphology varied across channels and stimulation conditions, the optimal blanking strategy was determined from the raw signals rather than applying a fixed universal window. Control analyses further confirmed the importance of artifact removal. When stimulation artifacts were retained, high decoding performance could be observed not only in organoid recordings but also in MEA-only and TTX-treated controls, suggesting that the model could directly learn the stimulation artifact as an input signature. After artifact removal, the organoid group retained substantial decoding performance, whereas MEA-only, shuffled, and TTX controls dropped close to chance level (). These results support that the sequential vowel-recognition task primarily depended on genuine organoid neural responses.

We present a benchmarking framework to systematically quantify the key performance determinants of organoid computing systems. By integrating multimodal phenotyping and electrophysiological assessment, this framework defines benchmark-ready organoid substrates according to a set of biological and functional criteria, including structural integrity, cell viability, cellular identity, neural maturation, and baseline network activity. Beyond biological qualification, we established a series of quantitative metrics to evaluate the organoid-machine interface and intrinsic neural dynamics, covering physical coupling, spatial coverage, temporal stability, spontaneous neural activity, network-level organization, and neural synchronization. We further extended this framework to stimulation-induced computation by introducing a hierarchical assessment strategy that evaluates evoked responsiveness, input-dependent discrimination, and downstream decodability under external stimulation. Combined with standardized scoring rules, information-encoding criteria, negative-control analyses, and statistical reporting considerations, this framework provides a structured basis for evaluating whether an organoid-MEA preparation is suitable for reproducible computation-related assays. We anticipate that this benchmarking strategy will help improve the comparability, interpretability, and reproducibility of organoid computing studies and support the broader development of organoid intelligence as an experimental and translational technology.

Although this study focuses on organoid-MEA-based computing, the proposed benchmark can be adapted to other electrically responsive biological systems, including engineered neural tissues, cardiac tissues, neuromuscular constructs, and dissociated cell networks. The framework is also compatible with different input-output configurations, such as electrical input-electrical output, optical input-electrical output, electrical input-optical output, or fully optical interfaces. While we used an MEA-based reservoir computing task as a proof-of-concept, other biohybrid computing architectures may require additional metrics for temporal integration, adaptation, memory, learning stability, or closed-loop performance. Future extensions could incorporate long-term plasticity, learning- and memory-related network dynamics, and disease-specific phenotypes. Validation in patient-derived and neurological disease organoids may further support applications in drug screening, precision medicine, and personalized therapy. This perspective also aligns with substrate-independent approaches to reservoir characterization, while incorporating biological and interface-specific constraints unique to living systems . Several limitations should also be noted. A limitation of planar MEAs is that they mainly sample activity near the organoid surface and may not fully capture internal 3D network activity. Future studies could extend the framework to 3D bioelectronic interfaces, such as mesh or pin-array electrodes. External parameters, including MEA design, electrode density, stimulation waveform, recording bandwidth, spike-detection settings, and recording conditions, can affect benchmark scores. Intrinsic biological variables, including organoid protocol, developmental stage, cellular composition, size, attachment quality, and culture-condition changes after MEA integration, may also influence functional readouts. In particular, increasing tissue thickness and associated diffusion limitations or reduced internal viability may contribute to progressive changes or decay in electrophysiological activity during long-term, multi-week recordings. Therefore, the current feature weights and pass thresholds should be further validated across larger multi-batch, multi-platform, and multi-laboratory datasets. This will allow the framework to develop into a more general benchmark for organoid and biohybrid computing systems.

Human stem cell culture. The H9 hESC (human embryonic stem cell) line was obtained from the WiCell Institute. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the WiCell Institute and the Indiana University Biosafety Committee. ESCs were cultured on 6-well plates coated with growth factor-reduced (GFR) Matrigel (Corning). Cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2, and the medium (mTeSR Plus, Stemcell Technologies) was changed every 2 days. ESCs were passaged using ReLeSR (Stemcell Technologies) when they reached 70-80% confluence.

Generation of cortical organoids. Cortical organoids were generated using our previously established protocol, which was adapted from published methods. In brief, embryoid bodies (EBs) were initiated by seeding 9000 stem cells into each well of ultra-low attachment 96-well plates. From Day 0, cells were cultured in mTeSR Plus medium (STEMCELL Technologies) supplemented with 10 μM SB431542 (Stemgent), 1 μM Dorsomorphin (R&D Systems), and 10 μM Y-27632 (SelleckChem), with Y-27632 included only for the first 24 h. On Day 3, the developing structures were switched to cortical organoid maintenance medium consisting of Neurobasal medium (Life Technologies) with GlutaMAX, 1% Gem21 NeuroPlex, 1% N2 NeuroPlex (both from Gemini Bio-Products), 1% non-essential amino acids (NEAA), and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (P/S), supplemented with 10 μM SB431542 and 1 μM Dorsomorphin. The EBs were maintained individually in ultra-low attachment 96-well plates for the first 5 days. On Day 5, the developing EBs were transferred to ultra-low attachment 6-well plates and maintained on an orbital shaker at 90 rpm in the same cortical organoid maintenance medium. On Day 9, cultures were switched to cortical organoid maintenance medium supplemented with 20 ng/mL FGF2 (Life Technologies) for 7 days. This was followed by an additional 7 days in cortical organoid maintenance medium supplemented with both 20 ng/mL FGF2 and 20 ng/mL EGF (PeproTech). Subsequently, organoids were cultured in cortical organoid maintenance medium supplemented with 10 ng/mL each of BDNF, GDNF, and NT-3 (PeproTech), together with 200 μM L-ascorbic acid and 100 μM db-cAMP (Sigma-Aldrich) to support neural maturation. After 7 days, organoids were maintained in cortical organoid maintenance medium without additional supplements.

Live/dead staining. Organoids were gently washed with 1× DPBS (Gibco) three times to remove residual culture medium. Samples were then incubated with LIVE/DEAD™ Viability/Cytotoxicity Kit reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific, L3224) prepared in DPBS at final concentrations of 2 μM calcein AM and 4 μM ethidium homodimer-1 (EthD-1) for 45 min at room temperature in the dark. Following incubation, organoids were immediately imaged using a fluorescence microscope. Live cells were identified by green calcein fluorescence, whereas dead cells were identified by red EthD-1 fluorescence.

IF Staining. Organoids were rinsed three times with 1× PBS (Gibco), fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Thermo Scientific) at 4 °C, and subsequently transferred to 30% sucrose for an additional overnight incubation at 4 °C. The fixed tissues were then snap-frozen in O.C.T. (Fisher Scientific) using cryomolds (Sakura Finetek) on dry ice. Cryosections of 30 μm thickness were prepared using a Leica cryostat and mounted onto charged slides. For antigen retrieval, sections were incubated in citrate buffer at 96 °C for 20 min, followed by washing and blocking for 1 h in PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% normal donkey serum. Primary antibodies were applied overnight at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. After washing with PBS, sections were incubated with secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, and slides were mounted using ProLong Gold Antifade medium (Invitrogen).

Biological quantification of cortical organoids. Biological benchmark features were quantified from brightfield and fluorescence images using Fiji/ImageJ (NIH). For each organoid, a region of interest was first defined by segmentation of the organoid boundary, and feature extraction was subsequently performed within the same region across image modalities. Structural integrity was evaluated from brightfield images using morphology-based descriptors that capture shape regularity, compactness, and edge irregularity. Viability was evaluated from live/dead staining images by quantifying live-positive and dead-positive signals within the organoid region. Neural maturation was evaluated from immunofluorescence images by quantifying the relative positive areas of neural and astrocytic marker signals. Detailed feature definitions and mathematical formulas are described in the Supplementary Information.

Attachment to Axion MEA. Axion MEA plates were first disinfected with alcohol, cleaned overnight with 1% Tergazyme, and subsequently coated with 0.1% polyethylenimine (PEI) on the electrode area for more than 3 h or overnight. After four washes with sterile DI water and air drying, the electrode area was further treated with a freshly prepared surface-coating solution consisting of 10 μg/mL laminin and 10 μg/mL fibronectin in COM6 medium for 1 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2. The coating solution was then aspirated and mixed with fresh COM6 medium to prepare the rehydration medium (COM-LF). Organoids were transferred onto the center of the electrode area using a cut wide-bore pipette tip, and the medium volume was adjusted so that the top of the organoid was slightly exposed to air. The plates were then incubated for 1 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2 to facilitate initial attachment. Next, a sterilized 3D-printed scaffold was carefully positioned around each organoid. After a brief 2-min drying step, 200 μL of COM-LF was slowly added dropwise within the scaffold, followed by an additional 200 μL of COM-LF to each well. The MEA plates were then returned to the incubator and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2, with minimal disturbance during the first week. On days 3 and 6 after plating, 400 μL of BrainPhys medium was added to each well without removing the existing medium. From day 8 onward, partial medium changes were performed by replacing 200 μL of medium with fresh medium every 2 days, and the scaffold was removed once stable attachment had been established.

Longitudinal bright-field imaging and interface scoring. Following organoid attachment to the MEA, bright-field images were acquired on days 3 and 12 using an inverted microscope. These longitudinal images were used as the basis for interface assessment. Specifically, interface quality was evaluated across three dimensions: physical coupling, spatial coverage, and temporal stability. Physical coupling was quantified using morphology score, neurite outgrowth grade, and neurite length; spatial coverage was quantified using organoid coverage ratio and overall electrode coverage ratio; and temporal stability was quantified based on the changes in overall electrode coverage ratio, neurite length, and neurite outgrowth grade between day 3 and day 12. Detailed definitions of each metric, as well as the corresponding calculation and scoring procedures, are provided in the Supplementary Information. To obtain the dimension-level scores and the overall interface score, these image-derived metrics were integrated using a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)-based additive value model.

Neural activity measurements. Neural activity recordings were performed using the Axion BioSystems Maestro MEA system with AxIS Navigator 3.2 and the Neural Module. Organoids were cultured on 6-well Axion MEA plates and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2 during recording. Spontaneous neural activity was recorded 2-4 h after medium change. Continuous voltage signals were acquired at a sampling rate of 12.5 kHz. Spike detection was performed in AxIS Navigator using an adaptive threshold of 5.5 × standard deviation of the background noise. Burst detection was performed using an inter-spike interval (ISI) threshold, with a minimum of 5 spikes per burst and a maximum ISI of 100 ms. For each well, spontaneous activity was first surveyed to identify electrodes exhibiting neural firing, and electrodes with detectable activity were subsequently used for downstream analyses of neural activity, network function, and stimulation-evoked responses.

Resting-state neural activity analysis. Spontaneous neural activity was analyzed using the Axion BioSystems AxIS Navigator 3.2 neural analysis pipeline. After spike detection and burst detection, spike, burst, network burst, and synchrony metrics were calculated using the Neural Statistics Compiler, which outputs well-level Advanced Metrics files for downstream analysis. For the resting-state benchmark, six core features were extracted: mean firing rate, number of active electrodes, and burst frequency for the neural activity domain; and synchrony index, number of electrodes participating in bursts, and network burst frequency for the network function domain. Spike files (.spk) exported from AxIS Navigator were additionally used for visualization and quality control in MATLAB, including raster plot generation and inspection of electrode-level spike timing.

Electrical stimulation. Electrical stimulation was delivered to cortical organoids using the Axion Maestro MEA platform and AxIS Navigator software (Axion BioSystems). For the stimulation-response benchmark, stimulation electrodes were defined by predefined stimulation configurations. Depending on the assay, stimulation was delivered either across the predefined electrode set or through spatially distributed electrode subsets. For the downstream task-validation experiments, stimulation electrodes were selected from sites showing robust spontaneous spiking while maintaining spatial separation across the organoid-covered MEA region. Guided by our preliminary optimization and informed by previously reported organoid reservoir-computing paradigms, we applied charge-balanced biphasic voltage pulses with amplitudes of 500 mV and pulse widths of 500 μs; for pulse-train paradigms, the inter-pulse interval was set to 50 ms. Three stimulation paradigms were used, including single stimulation, spatial stimulation, and sequential stimulation. In the single-stimulation paradigm, isolated pulses were delivered through one selected electrode to probe basic evoked responsiveness. In the spatial-stimulation paradigm, distinct subsets of electrodes were activated to encode different spatial input patterns. In the sequential-stimulation paradigm, temporally ordered pulses were delivered across multiple electrodes to encode sequence information. Detailed waveform settings, electrode assignments, and task-specific encoding schemes for different tasks are provided in the Supplementary Information.

Readout function. We decoded the evoked neural activity using our previously established readout framework. Spike trains recorded from selected electrodes were binned within predefined time windows to construct an electrode-by-time response matrix, where each entry represented the spike count for a given electrode within a given time bin. The response matrix was flattened into a one-dimensional vector x, which served as the reservoir state and was used as input to a downstream logistic-regression readout. For binary classification tasks, the readout used a sigmoid function, y=σ(Wx+b), where W is the learned weight vector and b is the bias term. For the three-class vowel-classification task, a multinomial logistic-regression readout with a softmax output was used. Model training was implemented using the scikit-learn library in Python, and performance was evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation within each recording preparation. For the L/R pattern-classification task, each organoid-MEA preparation was analyzed independently using a preparation-specific readout, with 50 trials per stimulation pattern, and five independent organoid-MEA preparations were evaluated. For the vowel-classification task, acoustic stimuli were selected from the Hillenbrand vowel dataset . Each of the three vowel classes contained 45 distinct acoustic tokens, yielding 135 unique tokens in total; identical acoustic tokens were not repeated across trials. Thus, held-out test samples represented previously unseen acoustic exemplars within the tested vowel classes.

Weighted scoring model. Benchmark scores were calculated using a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)-based additive value model. Raw feature values were first normalized to utility scores between 0 and 1, with score direction unified such that higher values always indicated better performance. Dimension-specific scores were obtained by weighted aggregation of the normalized feature scores, and the overall benchmark score was calculated as the weighted sum of all dimension scores. All weights were defined a priori and kept fixed across samples.

Statistics. All analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8. Comparisons between two groups were made using Student's t-test. Statistical significance was indicated as follows: p < 0.05 (*), p < 0.01 (**), and p < 0.001 (***).

neuroscience.title: Development and validation of a risk stratification model for mild cognitive impairment among older adults with possible sarcopenia integrating traditional Chinese medicine constitution: a multicenter cross-sectional study
neuroscience.abstract: Possible sarcopenia is associated with cognitive impairment among older adults, while mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represents an important window for early identification. Existing MCI assessment approaches may depend on neuroimaging, genetic testing, or biochemical biomarkers, limiting their use in large-scale screening. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) constitution may provide accessible information on individual physiological and functional characteristics, but it has rarely been incorporated into MCI risk stratification.To develop and validate a machine learning-based risk stratification model integrating TCM constitution and conventional health-related indicators for MCI among older adults with possible sarcopenia.This multicenter cross-sectional study included 3,310 older adults with possible sarcopenia from ten tertiary hospitals in China and an independent single-institution external validation sample of 314 participants. The concurrent outcome was screening-defined probable MCI based on a prespecified Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) criterion. After a stratified 7:3 training–internal-validation split, data-dependent preprocessing parameters and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) feature selection were estimated using the training data only. Multilayer perceptron (MLP), gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, and AdaBoost models were fitted using prespecified settings and evaluated using discrimination, classification, calibration, and decision-curve measures. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used only to describe contributions to model output.Seven features were retained: educational attainment, sex, smartphone usage, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score, qi-deficiency constitution, and damp-heat constitution. The MLP showed the highest internal discrimination, with an AUC of 0.853 (95% CI: 0.827–0.878); its AUC was 0.799 (95% CI: 0.773–0.823) in the external sample. The internal and external Brier scores were 0.168 and 0.151, calibration intercepts were −0.07 and 0.18, and calibration slopes were 0.80 and 1.07, respectively. SHAP analysis ranked feature contributions to model output and was not interpreted causally.This cross-sectional screening framework integrated TCM constitution with conventional indicators to stratify the probability of current screening-defined probable MCI among older adults with possible sarcopenia. The single-institution external evaluation supports only limited transportability; prospective multicenter evaluation and, where needed, recalibration are required before clinical implementation.
neuroscience.text:
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is recognized as an important intermediate stage between normal cognitive aging and dementia, although its clinical course is heterogeneous (). Sociodemographic characteristics have been associated with incident MCI across several cohorts of older Chinese adults, highlighting the relevance of accessible population-level cognitive-status stratification (). The American Academy of Neurology guideline reported that 14.4%–55.6% of individuals with MCI reverted to normal cognition during follow-up, while noting that some remained at increased risk of subsequent cognitive decline (). Non-pharmacological management commonly includes physical exercise and cognitive training, and combined physical–cognitive interventions have been evaluated in older adults with MCI (). The Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) also demonstrated cognitive benefits from an integrated program of nutritional guidance, physical activity, cognitive training, and vascular risk monitoring (). Pharmacological disease-modification strategies remain an active area of investigation (). Together, these findings support the importance of accessible approaches for identifying older adults who are more likely to have concurrent cognitive impairment.

Existing approaches for MCI-related stratification can be broadly classified into five categories: (1) demographic-only models; (2) cognition-based models incorporating cognitive test scores with or without subjective memory complaints or demographic data; (3) health variable models utilizing self-reported or objectively measured health status; (4) genetic-information models incorporating APOE, PICALM, and other Alzheimer's disease-associated genes (BIN1, CR1, ABCA7, MS4A6A, MS4A4E, CD33), either alone or in combination with non-genetic variables; and (5) multivariable models integrating demographic, health, and lifestyle measures ().

However, some MCI stratification approaches incorporate information such as MRI-derived brain measures and genetic characteristics, as illustrated by large population cohorts including the Rotterdam Study (). Research frameworks for the biological characterization of Alzheimer disease also emphasize cerebrospinal-fluid and imaging biomarkers (). Although such measures are scientifically informative, their equipment, procedural, and technical requirements may limit their use in large-scale community screening. In addition, models developed in one population may not transfer directly to populations with different demographic, cultural, and health characteristics. Existing MCI risk-stratification models have rarely incorporated TCM constitution as an accessible population-level phenotype.

Previous studies have reported cross-sectional associations between TCM constitutional characteristics and cognitive status. Deng et al. found that yang-deficiency constitution, phlegm-dampness constitution, and blood-stasis constitution, together with elevated homocysteine, were associated with MCI status (). Wang et al. described the development of the nine-category TCM constitution framework and its application to the study of individual physiological and psychological characteristics (). More recent research has also reported associations between TCM constitution, mental health, and sleep quality (). This evidence supports further evaluation of TCM constitutional assessment as an accessible individualized health indicator for cognitive risk stratification, without establishing a causal relationship with MCI.

A longitudinal study reported an MCI incidence of 24.2% among participants with sarcopenia (), supporting an epidemiological association between the two conditions. Proposed pathways linking sarcopenia with cognitive impairment include chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and altered muscle–brain signaling (). These mechanisms remain biologically plausible explanations rather than causal pathways established by the present cross-sectional study.

Our model is designed to identify this priority screening population by integrating multiple dimensions of assessment, including clinical evaluations (such as sleep quality and depression symptom scores) and social determinants (such as educational attainment and digital device usage). Furthermore, it incorporates TCM constitutional characteristics as an individualized and accessible health indicator based on previous evidence.

The research highlights are reflected in three key aspects: (1) identifying older adults with possible sarcopenia as a priority group for MCI screening; (2) quantifying individual cognitive vulnerability through the lens of TCM constitutional theory; and (3) evaluating model transportability through multicenter data and independent external validation.

This multicenter cross-sectional study enrolled 3,310 older adults (mean age 70.6 ± 7.7 years) meeting possible sarcopenia criteria per the AWGS 2019 diagnostic thresholds (grip strength <28 kg for males, <18 kg for females) (). Participants were recruited from ten tertiary hospitals specialized in geriatric care and integrative medicine between January 2021 and December 2023. Each participant underwent a single study assessment; therefore, the variables and cognitive outcome represent approximately concurrent measurements rather than a longitudinal sequence. Participating institutions included academic medical centers located across China (complete list provided in ). The study protocol received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board at Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine Affiliated Hospital (No. 2021KL-055) in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Assessments included grip strength measured with a Xiangshan® mechanical hand dynamometer, MoCA screening (, ), and TCM constitution assessment using Wang Qi's Body Constitution Classification Questionnaire ().

This study employed the Xiangshan® mechanical handgrip dynamometer to measure grip strength, with participants maintaining a seated position and elbow joint flexion of 90°. The maximum value from three consecutive trials of the dominant hand was recorded. According to the AWGS 2019 criteria, possible sarcopenia is identified by decreased muscle strength (grip strength <28 kg for males and <18 kg for females), with or without impaired physical performance (time to complete five chair stands >12 s or 6-meter walking speed <1 m/s). Because eligibility in this study was based on decreased muscle strength, participants meeting the sex-specific grip-strength thresholds were classified as having possible sarcopenia.

Cognitive function was assessed with the Chinese Changsha version of the MoCA, version 7.1 (July 2010), with a score range of 0–30 (, ). In accordance with the instrument instructions, one point was added for participants with no more than 6 years of formal education, up to a maximum total score of 30. The operational cutoff was normal cognition at scores ≥26 and screening-defined probable MCI at scores from 18 to <26 (equivalent to integer scores of 18–25); scores <18 were excluded from the analytic cohort because the low score could reflect more severe cognitive impairment that could not be classified as probable MCI using this screening rule. Two source records had a recorded score of 25.5; because these values were below 26, they were included in the screening-defined probable-MCI group. The outcome was therefore a MoCA-based screening classification and not a clinical diagnosis of MCI.

Inclusion criteria encompassed community-dwelling adults ≥60 years meeting the AWGS 2019 criteria for possible sarcopenia and able to complete the standardized assessments. Exclusion criteria included: (1) a MoCA score <18; (2) neurological or psychiatric disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or Parkinson's disease); (3) sensory impairments that prevented completion of the standardized assessments; and (4) severe systemic comorbidities, including severe liver or kidney dysfunction and malignancy. All participants provided informed consent.

The original concatenated source file contained 14,520 records. A numeric MoCA total score was available for 13,773 records (94.9%); 747 records (5.1%) lacked a usable MoCA total score. Among records with a usable MoCA score, 2,649 (19.2%) scored <18 and were excluded according to the study rule, 5,856 (42.5%) scored 18 to <26 (including the two records with a recorded score of 25.5) and were classified as screening-defined probable MCI, and 5,268 (38.2%) scored ≥26 and were classified as normal cognition. These counts sum to all 13,773 records with a usable MoCA score. The sequential screening counts were 14,520 → 14,421 → 6,823 → 6,613 → 6,574 → 6,535 → 4,523 → 3,310. The corresponding exclusions were 99, 7,598, 210, 39, 39, 2,012 (225 without a usable MoCA score and 1,787 with a MoCA score <18), and 1,213. The 225 residual records without a usable MoCA score occurred after the preceding screening steps and therefore differ from the 747 missing-MoCA records in the original source file. Variable-level missingness and the complete flow are provided in . After these possible-sarcopenia eligibility, data-quality, outcome, and complete candidate-predictor requirements were applied, 3,310 participants remained in the analytic cohort.

A total of 3,310 participants were included in the analytic cohort: 1,013 (30.6%) in the normal-cognition group and 2,297 (69.4%) in the screening-defined probable MCI group. A standardized case-report form collected 23 variables across sociodemographic, clinical, and TCM constitutional domains. Basic indicators were sex, educational level, living alone, history of drug and food allergies, smoking history, alcohol consumption history, smartphone usage, computer usage, age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body mass index (BMI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) total score, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score, and Mini-Nutritional Assessment Short Form (MNA-SF) total score.
