TCM indicators were qi-deficiency constitution, qi-stagnation constitution, yang-deficiency constitution, yin-deficiency constitution, blood-stasis constitution, damp-heat constitution, phlegm-dampness constitution, and balanced constitution, based on Wang Qi's constitution framework ().

Trained study personnel administered Wang Qi's standardized Constitution in Chinese Medicine Questionnaire (CCMQ) using standardized instructions. Each item was scored on a five-point scale. For each of the nine constitution dimensions, the transformed score was calculated as [(raw score − number of items)/(number of items × 4)] × 100. A biased constitution was considered positive at a transformed score ≥40, a score of 30–39 indicated a tendency, and a score <30 was considered negative. Balanced constitution was defined by a balanced-constitution score ≥60 and scores <30 for all eight biased constitutions. When more than one biased constitution was positive, the constitution with the highest transformed score was assigned as the principal constitution. When no biased constitution was positive but more than one showed a tendency, the highest tendency score was used. Special-diathesis constitution was treated as one of the eight biased constitutions, remained eligible as the principal category, and was used as the reference category for the eight indicator variables representing the nine-level principal-constitution variable. Thus, constitution indicators were mutually exclusive for an individual participant. The questionnaire is reproduced in . Because qi-deficiency constitution and damp-heat constitution were uncommon in some data subsets, their prevalence and selection stability were examined separately and interpreted cautiously.

Univariate analyses were first conducted, with categorical variables presented as frequencies (percentages) and compared between groups using Pearson's chi-square test; continuity correction was applied to 2-by-2 contingency tables. Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Variables following a normal distribution were analyzed using the independent-samples t-test, while non-normally distributed variables were evaluated using the Mann–Whitney U test.

The analytic dataset was first divided into a training set (70%) and a locked internal validation set (30%) using stratified random sampling by screening-defined probable MCI status (random seed 42). All data-dependent preprocessing was confined to the training data. Binary indicators were encoded as 0/1; multi-category variables were one-hot encoded with the first category omitted; and continuous variables were standardized using means and standard deviations estimated in the training data. The same fitted encoders and scaling parameters were then applied without refitting to the internal and external validation data. The modeling extract used complete candidate-predictor records after prespecified data-quality screening; no model-based imputation was applied. The complete-case approach and source-data outcome accounting are described in the ; model performance should therefore be interpreted for participants with complete candidate-predictor data.

LASSO regression was performed exclusively within the training data to identify a parsimonious feature set. The candidate penalty sequence comprised 200 logarithmically spaced values from 10−4 to 1, with a maximum of 10,000 iterations. The penalty parameter was selected by stratified 10-fold cross-validation within the training set using the one-standard-error rule; the selected value was λ = 0.026. The selected features were then supplied to six machine-learning classification models: MLP (), GBDT (), support vector machine (SVM) (), K-nearest neighbors (KNN) (), logistic regression (), and AdaBoost (). Ten-fold cross-validation was restricted to training-set resampling and stability assessment; the mean validation-fold ROC AUC was not treated as an independent performance validation, and an optimism-corrected AUC was not separately estimated. The available workflow did not provide a fully nested estimate in which every preprocessing and feature-selection step was re-estimated within every cross-validation fold. Each final model was fitted to the full training set using prespecified settings and evaluated once in the locked internal validation set. No oversampling, undersampling, class weighting, or other class-imbalance correction was applied; stratification was used to preserve outcome proportions. The primary MLP used one hidden layer with 100 units, rectified linear-unit activation, the Adam optimizer, an initial learning rate of 0.001, L2 penalty parameter 0.0001, automatic batch size, a maximum of 1,000 iterations, no early stopping, and random seed 42. Exact fixed settings for the five comparator algorithms are listed in ; no grid or randomized hyperparameter search was used for the reported six-model comparison.

Discrimination and threshold-based classification were summarized by ROC AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score (). Paired bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals for differences between the MLP AUC and each comparator AUC. Calibration was summarized by the Brier score, calibration intercept, and calibration slope in both internal and external validation (). DCA quantified potential net benefit across a range of threshold probabilities (); no threshold was designated as a recommended clinical cutoff. SHAP values described the direction and magnitude of feature contributions to the fitted model output and were not interpreted as causal effects or independent etiological associations (, ).

External validation was performed in an independent sample of 314 participants (245 with screening-defined probable MCI and 69 with normal cognition) from a single institution, Henan University of Chinese Medicine, collected under the same protocol and not used in preprocessing, feature selection, training-set resampling, or model fitting. Mean grip strength in the external cohort was 15.83 ± 6.98 kg. Cohort characteristics are compared in –. Because the external data came from one institution and were relatively small, this evaluation was interpreted as limited external validation rather than proof of generalizability across regions or health-care systems. Sensitivity analyses forced age into the predictor set, excluded smartphone usage, repeated the workflow across five random seeds, and compared a conventional model without TCM constitution indicators with an extended model containing those indicators. Core machine-learning analyses were conducted using Python 3.8.10 with pandas 2.0.3, NumPy 1.24.4, scikit-learn 1.3.2, matplotlib 3.7.5, and SHAP 0.44.1; ancillary analyses used R 3.6.3. Statistical significance was set at P <0.05. Reporting was revised with reference to TRIPOD+AI (); this reporting guideline was used to improve transparency and was not treated as evidence that the model had been prospectively or comprehensively validated.

A total of 3,310 older adults with possible sarcopenia were included, of whom 2,297 (69.38%) met the MoCA-based definition of screening-defined probable MCI and 1,013 (30.62%) were classified as having normal cognition. Among the 23 analyzed features, statistically significant between-group differences (P <0.05) were observed for sex, educational level, history of drug and food allergies, smartphone usage, computer usage, PSQI score, PHQ-9 score, balanced constitution, and damp-heat constitution (P = 0.011). The high proportion with probable MCI reflects the selected tertiary-hospital sample of older adults with possible sarcopenia and should not be interpreted as population prevalence.

summarizes the characteristics of the study participants.

Characteristics of the study participants.

The reported LASSO analysis retained seven features from the initial 23 variables for cross-sectional probable-MCI stratification: educational attainment, smartphone usage, sex, damp-heat constitution, qi-deficiency constitution, PSQI score, and PHQ-9 score (). The selected penalty was the largest value within one standard error of the minimum training-fold cross-validated binomial deviance, with λ = 0.026. Age was not retained in the reported feature set; this does not imply that age is unimportant for cognitive health. In the sensitivity model that forced age into the predictor set, the internal-validation AUC increased from 0.853 to 0.877 (+0.024), while the Brier score changed from 0.168 to 0.166, the calibration intercept from −0.07 to −0.152, and the calibration slope from 0.80 to 0.808. Excluding smartphone usage produced an internal-validation AUC of 0.843, a decrease of 0.010, and did not change the remaining retained feature set. In the training set, Spearman correlations between age and educational attainment, smartphone usage, sex, PSQI, PHQ-9, qi-deficiency constitution, and damp-heat constitution were ρ = −0.005, −0.206, 0.050, 0.046, 0.086, 0.053, and 0.034, respectively. These correlations were weak, with the largest absolute value observed for smartphone usage. These data-specific changes suggest that smartphone usage contributed additional cross-sectional classification information, whereas age improved discrimination when forced into the model, but they do not establish a causal or biological hierarchy among the variables.

ROC curves were constructed to evaluate the six cross-sectional probable-MCI risk-stratification models in the internal and external validation samples (). Each model used the seven features retained through training-set LASSO. In internal validation, the MLP showed the highest discrimination, with an AUC of 0.853 [95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.827–0.878] (). The comparator AUCs were 0.807 for GBDT, 0.807 for SVM, 0.796 for KNN, 0.740 for logistic regression, and 0.749 for AdaBoost. Paired bootstrap differences favored MLP: 0.046 (95% CI: 0.02–0.07) vs. GBDT, 0.046 (0.02–0.07) vs. SVM, 0.057 (0.03–0.08) vs. KNN, 0.113 (0.08–0.14) vs. logistic regression, and 0.104 (0.07–0.13) vs. AdaBoost. The MLP achieved an accuracy of 0.791, sensitivity of 0.819, specificity of 0.729, and F1-score of 0.845. Its mean training-set 10-fold cross-validation ROC AUC was 0.874, with a standard deviation of 0.024 and a fold-level range of 0.839–0.908; this value is reported as a training-set resampling/stability estimate and not as a separate validation result or an optimism-corrected estimate. Across five random seeds, the internal-validation AUC ranged from 0.847 to 0.861, with a mean of 0.856 and standard deviation of 0.006, indicating limited variation in discrimination across seeds.

Performance of the machine-learning models in internal validation.

In a sensitivity analysis using an alternative screening definition, participants with MoCA scores of 18–21 were classified as screening-defined probable MCI and those with scores ≥22 as cognitively normal, while the prespecified exclusion of scores <18 was retained. This definition classified 1,364 participants as probable MCI. Using the same stratified 70:30 split, the MLP achieved an internal-validation AUC of 0.804 (95% CI: 0.772–0.834), accuracy of 0.758, sensitivity of 0.780, specificity of 0.692, and F1-score of 0.719. The Brier score was 0.222, with a calibration intercept of −0.277 and a calibration slope of 0.552. Discrimination remained acceptable, although calibration was less favorable than under the primary outcome definition.

In the pre-specified incremental-value analysis, the conventional MLP model without TCM constitution indicators had an AUC of 0.685, accuracy of 0.640, sensitivity of 0.748, specificity of 0.522, and F1-score of 0.686. The extended MLP model had an AUC of 0.853, accuracy of 0.791, sensitivity of 0.819, specificity of 0.729, and F1-score of 0.845. Both models used the same locked internal split, outcome observations, preprocessing framework, and MLP architecture. The paired difference in AUC was 0.166 (95% CI: 0.135–0.196), calculated from paired unrounded predictions and therefore not necessarily equal to subtraction of the displayed AUCs rounded to three decimals. The Brier scores were approximately 0.176 for the conventional model and 0.168 for the extended model; the paired difference was −0.008 (95% CI: −0.013 to −0.003), favoring the extended model. The conventional model had an internal calibration intercept of approximately 0.00 and slope of 1.17, compared with −0.07 and 0.80 for the extended model. DCA was evaluated over prespecified threshold probabilities from 0.30 to 0.70. The net benefits for the conventional and extended models were 0.56 and 0.58 at 0.30 (difference 0.02), 0.48 and 0.53 at 0.40 (difference 0.05), 0.37 and 0.48 at 0.50 (difference 0.11), 0.27 and 0.39 at 0.60 (difference 0.12), and 0.14 and 0.25 at 0.70 (difference 0.11). The corresponding treat-all net benefits were 0.563, 0.490, 0.388, 0.235, and −0.020, respectively; treat-none net benefit was 0 at every threshold. Model net-benefit values are reported to two decimal places and treat-all values to three decimal places. These DCA results are interpreted as potential net benefit, not as recommended clinical cutoffs. Because this comparison used the same internal sample and the external incremental-value analysis was not performed, it supports a cohort-specific incremental contribution rather than established clinical utility.

In the independent single-institution external validation sample (n = 314; 245 with screening-defined probable MCI and 69 with normal cognition), the MLP AUC was 0.799 (95% CI: 0.773–0.823), lower than the internal validation AUC of 0.853. The internal Brier score, calibration intercept, and calibration slope were 0.168, −0.07, and 0.80, respectively; the corresponding external values were 0.151, 0.18, and 1.07. The external intercept indicates modest overall underestimation of the observed outcome probability, while the slope suggests comparatively mild underfitting. Differences in sample size, probable-MCI proportion, single-institution recruitment, education, and predictor/constitution distributions may have contributed to the lower external discrimination. Additional performance measures and cohort characteristics are presented in –.

presents calibration and clinical-utility analyses. Calibration curves for five models (GBDT, SVM, KNN, logistic regression, and MLP) are shown in ; AdaBoost is not included in this panel. In DCA (), both the conventional and extended models showed potential net benefit relative to treat-all and treat-none strategies over parts of the prespecified threshold range. The extended model had higher net benefit than the conventional model at each reported threshold: 0.58 vs. 0.56 at 0.30, 0.53 vs. 0.48 at 0.40, 0.48 vs. 0.37 at 0.50, 0.39 vs. 0.27 at 0.60, and 0.25 vs. 0.14 at 0.70. The corresponding differences were 0.02, 0.05, 0.11, 0.12, and 0.11. These results describe potential net benefit across threshold probabilities and do not define a recommended clinical cutoff. Model selection therefore considered DCA together with calibration, discrimination, and model complexity rather than relying on AUC alone.

Clinical impact curves (CIC; ) were generated for a hypothetical sample of 1,000 older adults. The x-axis represents probability thresholds, and the left and right y-axes show the numbers classified as high probability and the observed probable-MCI cases among those classified as high probability. The convergence seen around 0.7 is descriptive only. It does not establish 0.7 as a clinical cutoff; any operational threshold would require a prespecified referral action, explicit weighting of false positives and false negatives, and prospective validation in the intended screening setting.

SHAP analysis ranked contributions to the fitted MLP output as follows: educational attainment > sex > PHQ-9 score > PSQI score > smartphone usage > qi-deficiency constitution > damp-heat constitution ().  shows how feature values shifted the model-assigned probability of screening-defined probable MCI in this dataset. These SHAP values explain the fitted model's output; they do not establish causal effects, independent risk factors, or effects of intervention.

This cross-sectional study identified sex, educational attainment, smartphone usage, sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and TCM constitution categories as features contributing to stratification of current screening-defined probable MCI among older adults with possible sarcopenia. The findings describe concurrent associations and model-output contributions, not predictors of future incident MCI. The proportion classified as having probable MCI was higher among women than among men [75.5% [993/1,316] vs. 65.4% [1,304/1,994]; P <0.001], consistent with population-based evidence from older Chinese adults showing a higher age-standardized prevalence of MCI among women (). Hormonal and reproductive mechanisms have been proposed in the broader literature (, ), but they were not measured here and cannot explain the present cross-sectional association.

The overall probable-MCI proportion of 69.4% is higher than population-based estimates and should not be generalized to community prevalence. Recruitment from tertiary hospitals and restriction to older adults with possible sarcopenia enriched the sample for physical vulnerability and may also have increased the proportion with low MoCA scores. In addition, the outcome was defined by a screening rule rather than adjudicated clinical diagnosis. These design features likely contributed to the high observed proportion.

Low educational attainment was retained as an important feature in the risk-stratification model. Prior evidence supports an association between education and cognitive function, often interpreted through the concept of cognitive reserve. Within the present cross-sectional sample, lower educational attainment was associated with concurrent screening-defined probable-MCI status, but the study design does not establish that education or muscle–brain axis dysfunction caused the observed difference.

Participants who used smartphones or computers were less likely to be classified as having probable MCI in the univariate comparisons, and smartphone usage was retained by LASSO regression. Excluding smartphone usage reduced internal AUC from 0.853 to 0.843 (0.010, or 1.0 percentage point), while the remaining retained feature set did not change. This indicates that smartphone usage carried additional cross-sectional classification information in this dataset. It does not demonstrate that digital device use prevents cognitive impairment: better current cognitive or functional status may enable device use, and access and socioeconomic factors may confound the association. A nationwide cross-sectional study likewise reported associations between multidimensional internet use and cognitive performance (). Smartphone usage should therefore be viewed as a concurrent screening feature rather than a modifiable causal factor.

Higher PSQI and PHQ-9 scores contributed to a higher model-assigned probability of concurrent screening-defined probable MCI. Previous cross-sectional research has reported associations of sleep disorders and fatigue with poorer cognitive function among older adults (). Longitudinal research has also linked depression with subsequent dementia risk (), while a meta-analysis identified overlapping structural brain alterations in cognitive impairment and depression (). These studies provide context but do not establish the direction or mechanisms of the relationships observed in the present cross-sectional sample.

Qi-deficiency constitution and damp-heat constitution were retained in the MLP and contributed to its model-assigned probability according to SHAP. Within the TCM constitution framework, these categories are intended to capture individualized functional and physiological patterns that may co-occur with differences in sleep, mood, nutrition, or physical functioning relevant to cognitive screening. This provides a conceptual rationale for evaluating them as accessible screening features, not evidence of a biological mechanism or causal effect. Previous cross-sectional studies have reported associations involving other TCM constitution categories and cognitive scores (, ). In the 500-resample training-set stability analysis, damp-heat constitution was selected in 493 resamples (98.6%), whereas qi-deficiency constitution was selected in 169 (33.8%). Thus, damp-heat constitution showed high selection stability, while the qi-deficiency result was less stable and requires confirmation in larger independent cohorts. The conventional-vs.-extended comparison suggested improved internal discrimination and Brier score after adding TCM constitution, but incremental value was not tested in the external sample. The findings therefore support a cohort-specific contribution that requires independent replication; they do not establish causal effects or intervention targets.

From a public-health perspective, TCM constitution may be evaluated as an accessible feature in individualized screening pathways and may inform the design of future preventive studies. Prior research has explored exercise, herbal, and acupuncture interventions in cognitive frailty, experimental Alzheimer disease, or MCI (–). These studies represent future intervention opportunities only; the present study neither tested an intervention nor established a TCM intervention strategy.

The MLP was retained as the primary research model because it showed the highest internal AUC and statistically higher paired AUCs than the five comparators. Nevertheless, selection of a model for implementation cannot rely on AUC alone. Its internal calibration slope of 0.80, threshold-dependent DCA findings, computational complexity, and the feasibility of collecting its inputs must be weighed against simpler alternatives. If future prospective evaluation shows comparable calibration and net benefit for a simpler model, that model may be preferable for routine use.

The decrease in MLP AUC from 0.853 internally to 0.799 externally is compatible with transportability loss. Potential contributors include the smaller external sample, a different probable-MCI proportion, recruitment from one institution, and differences in education, clinical characteristics, smartphone use, and constitution distributions. The external calibration intercept of 0.18 also suggests modest underestimation of outcome probability. Recalibration may therefore be needed before application in another setting, but no recalibration was performed or claimed in this study. With only 314 participants from one institution, the external analysis supports limited validation in a related setting and does not demonstrate generalizability across regions or health-care systems.

Recent longitudinal studies illustrate the temporal distinction that the present design cannot address. Long et al. used repeated CHARLS waves to predict a subsequent depression outcome and evaluated the model in CLHLS (); Chalmers et al. used baseline data to model 10-year incident dementia in the Sydney Memory and Ageing Study (). In contrast, the present variables and MoCA status were assessed concurrently. Its contribution is therefore an integrative cross-sectional screening framework, not a model of incident MCI or future cognitive decline.

This study has several limitations. First, its cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and cannot estimate incident MCI or future cognitive decline. Second, the outcome was screening-defined probable MCI based on the operational MoCA rule rather than a clinical diagnosis; participants scoring below 18 were excluded, and outcome misclassification remains possible. No clinician-adjudicated reference standard was available, so sensitivity and specificity of the study cutoff against a clinical diagnosis could not be estimated. Although the Changsha MoCA version has been validated as a cognitive-screening instrument in another Chinese clinical population (), the present 18-to-below-26 grouping, including the two source records with a score of 25.5, and exclusion of scores below 18 were operational study rules and were not separately validated in older adults with possible sarcopenia. An alternative screening definition using 18–21 vs. ≥22 was examined and yielded an AUC of 0.804, but its calibration was less favorable than that of the primary definition; education-stratified thresholds were not evaluated. Third, tertiary-hospital recruitment and restriction to possible sarcopenia likely enriched the sample and contributed to the high probable-MCI proportion, limiting applicability to community populations. Fourth, the external cohort contained only 314 participants from one institution. It therefore provides limited external validation and cannot establish transportability across regions, cultures, or health-care systems. Fifth, the external calibration intercept indicates that local recalibration may be required, but recalibration was not performed. Sixth, self-reported sleep, depressive symptoms, and digital-device use may be affected by reporting bias and reverse causation. Seventh, variable-level missingness is summarized in , but the complete-case analysis may still introduce selection bias if missingness was related to outcome or predictors. Eighth, the 500-resample selection frequencies for qi-deficiency constitution and damp-heat constitution, the age correlations with retained variables, and the fold-level dispersion of the training-set 10-fold resampling AUC are reported; however, the entire preprocessing and feature-selection pipeline was not evaluated in a fully nested cross-validation design, and an optimism-corrected AUC was not separately estimated. Finally, APOE genotype, laboratory biomarkers, and other potentially informative variables were unavailable. The framework should be evaluated as one component of a multi-step screening pathway followed by standardized cognitive assessment, not as a standalone diagnostic tool.

This study developed an interpretable cross-sectional machine-learning framework for stratifying the probability of current screening-defined probable MCI among older adults with possible sarcopenia. In the prespecified internal conventional-vs.-extended comparison, including TCM constitution indicators was associated with higher discrimination and lower Brier error; its incremental value requires external confirmation. The single-institution external evaluation supports only limited transportability. Prospective multicenter studies should evaluate calibration, operational thresholds, and clinical consequences before the framework is considered for use in a multi-step screening pathway.

neuroscience.title: Contextualizing biological heterogeneity in brain structural normativity assessments across the aging continuum with the nearest neighbor normativity framework
neuroscience.abstract: Despite established consensus about the individuality of brain physiology and structural changes, current neuroimaging biomarker paradigms heavily rely on population averages. Here, we define normativity not as a single reference point but as a landscape of permissible configurations arising from diverse physiological manifestations.We introduce the Nearest Neighbor Normativity (N3) framework, designed to parse the natural heterogeneity in brain structural measurements into a diversity-aware biomarker of brain structural decline. Through repeated comparisons within different demographic subgroups, N3 contextualizes an individual’s measurements from several viewpoints along the aging continuum. Relying on local density estimation, it accommodates multiple, shared normative configurations within and across age groups. We use T1-weighted MRI data from 29,883 individuals for training and 7,013 individuals for validation, and benchmark our framework against Brain Age models and Normative Modeling. We evaluate each biomarker’s ability to detect neurodegenerative diseases, using them as representative models of atypical brain structural decline.In group-level analyses, the N3 biomarker shows the largest effect sizes in the detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia. Similarly, the N3 biomarker achieves the highest predictive performance in the classification of neurodegenerative diseases on a single subject level. Notably, the N3 estimates remain stable across age and robust to compositional changes in the reference sample. Finally, correlation analyses indicate that it captures distinct and complementary aspects of brain structural variation compared to existing approaches.Our findings underscore that rethinking normativity assessments to explicitly accommodate natural inter-individual variability can advance our collective efforts toward truly personalized patient care.

neuroscience.title: Delayed Cerebral Ischemia as Progressive Neurovascular Unit Failure: A Hypothesis-Generating Perspective
neuroscience.abstract: Despite decades of investigation, delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) remains the principal cause of secondary neurological injury following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Successive paradigms including angiographic vasospasm, early brain injury, neuroinflammation, blood–brain barrier disruption, cortical spreading depolarization, microvascular dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic failure have each explained important aspects of disease biology. However, these mechanisms have largely evolved as parallel explanations rather than components of an integrated model, leaving the dissociation between vasospasm and DCI, delayed onset, interpatient heterogeneity, and limited efficacy of vasospasm-directed therapies incompletely explained. This perspective proposes, as a hypothesis, progressive neurovascular unit (NVU) failure as a conceptual framework for DCI after aSAH. We integrate experimental, translational, and clinical evidence spanning vascular biology, neuroimmunology, cerebrovascular physiology, electrophysiology, metabolism, biomarker research, and therapeutic trials to develop a hypothesis-generating framework. The established mechanisms of DCI may represent interacting manifestations of progressive disruption of coordinated signaling among endothelial, vascular smooth muscle, pericyte, astrocytic, microglial, and neuronal compartments of the neurovascular unit. Within this framework, early brain injury may initiate NVU dysfunction, which is amplified by interacting vascular, barrier, inflammatory, electrophysiological, and metabolic disturbances, culminating in neuronal metabolic failure and tissue injury. Vasospasm is therefore positioned as one contributor to this process rather than a sufficient explanation for DCI. This framework offers a possible basis for interpreting clinical heterogeneity and therapeutic discordance while generating testable predictions for multimodal biomarker development, biological phenotyping, and mechanism-informed therapeutic strategies. The framework does not introduce new mechanisms; rather, it proposes a testable distinction between compensated NVU dysfunction and NVU failure, frames compartment-specific non-additive interactions as an empirical question, and organizes biomarkers by the NVU compartment they reflect. These proposals remain to be validated.
neuroscience.text:
For several decades, delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) was viewed primarily as a consequence of angiographic vasospasm. Delayed narrowing of the large cerebral arteries was considered the principal cause of cerebral hypoperfusion, infarction, and subsequent neurological deterioration, making vasospasm the primary therapeutic target [,].

This paradigm was challenged by the CONSCIOUS-1 trial, which demonstrated that clazosentan significantly reduced angiographic vasospasm without improving functional outcome []. Subsequent reviews confirmed that therapies targeting vasospasm alone did not consistently improve disability or mortality, whereas reductions in delayed cerebral infarction were more closely associated with neurological recovery [,]. These findings suggested that vasospasm is an important manifestation of secondary injury but not its sole determinant.

Attention shifted to the earliest phase after hemorrhage. Sehba, Pluta, and Zhang introduced the concept of early brain injury (EBI), describing the immediate pathological response to aneurysm rupture during the first 72 h, characterized by transient global ischemia, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysregulation, apoptosis, and blood–brain barrier disruption []. Rather than resolving after the acute phase, these disturbances initiate processes that predispose the brain to delayed neurological deterioration.

At the same time, growing evidence also demonstrates disturbances across microcirculatory regulation, metabolic homeostasis, neuroimmune signaling, and cerebrovascular control, indicating that delayed injury reflects dysfunction of an integrated neurovascular network rather than isolated pathological processes [,]. Although each mechanism is supported by substantial evidence, they have largely been studied independently. The field has therefore progressed from a single-mechanism explanation to multiple validated contributors, but how these processes interact to produce delayed cerebral ischemia remains incompletely understood.

If DCI resulted predominantly from a single pathological mechanism, its clinical manifestations would be expected to follow predictable relationships with that mechanism. Instead, several consistent clinical observations challenge this assumption and suggest that delayed neurological deterioration arises from progressive disruption of an integrated neurovascular system.

The clearest example is the dissociation between angiographic vasospasm and clinical outcome. Although approximately 70% of patients develop angiographic vasospasm, only about 30% develop clinical DCI [,]. Similarly, the CONSCIOUS trials demonstrated that reducing vasospasm did not improve functional recovery [,]. Conversely, delayed cerebral infarction may occur without significant angiographic vasospasm or in territories unrelated to arterial narrowing [,]. Together, these findings indicate that large-vessel vasospasm contributes to DCI but cannot independently explain its development.

Additional observations support this conclusion. Endovascular rescue therapies frequently restore arterial caliber without consistently improving neurological outcome, whereas nimodipine improves outcome despite having relatively little effect on angiographic vasospasm [,]. Furthermore, cerebral microdialysis detects metabolic crisis before perfusion abnormalities become evident on imaging, while microvascular dysfunction may persist despite angiographically normal proximal vessels [,]. These findings suggest that tissue-level dysfunction and impaired neurovascular regulation may evolve independently of large-vessel abnormalities.

Marked interpatient variability provides further evidence against a single-mechanism model. Patients with similar hemorrhage severity often demonstrate markedly different autoregulatory capacity, metabolic responses, and neurological outcomes. Measures such as the pressure reactivity index and lactate-to-pyruvate ratio independently predict progression to DCI-related infarction, while DCI-related deterioration may remain clinically undetected in poor-grade patients [,]. Therefore, these observations suggest the value of a conceptual framework that integrates, rather than replaces, the recognized mechanisms of DCI.

Recognition that delayed cerebral ischemia is multifactorial represents important progress, but it does not, by itself, constitute a disease model. Current evidence supports the contribution of vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation, cortical spreading depolarizations, blood–brain barrier disruption, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired autoregulation to secondary brain injury after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage [,,,,]. However, identifying multiple contributing mechanisms does not by itself specify how they interact, which processes initiate disease, or how they collectively produce delayed neurological deterioration. Existing multifactorial accounts already recognize that these mechanisms interact and may act synergistically [,]; the framework proposed here does not claim otherwise but attempts to organize these interactions around the NVU and to state them in testable form.

An effective disease model should identify the biological system undergoing progressive dysfunction, distinguish initiating events from downstream consequences, and explain how interacting mechanisms amplify injury over time. Rather than viewing established mechanisms as parallel or competing processes, a systems-based framework should explain how they converge to produce the clinical syndrome of DCI [,].

The central challenge is therefore no longer determining whether these mechanisms contribute to DCI, as the evidence indicates that they do [,,,,]. Instead, the unresolved question is how these validated processes are integrated into a common biological framework that explains the temporal evolution, clinical heterogeneity, and therapeutic response of delayed cerebral ischemia. Addressing this question provides the rationale for proposing progressive neurovascular unit failure as the hypothesis-generating framework explored in this review.

The purpose of this perspective is to propose, as a hypothesis, a systems-based framework in which progressive neurovascular unit (NVU) failure serves as an organizing concept for delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.

The neurovascular unit is the functional biological system responsible for maintaining cerebral homeostasis through continuous reciprocal communication among vascular, glial, immune, and neuronal compartments. Through this coordinated network, the NVU regulates cerebral perfusion, blood–brain barrier integrity, metabolic homeostasis, immune signaling, and neuronal function. Early brain injury is thought to initiate disruption of this network, which may produce progressive neurovascular dysfunction that is subsequently amplified through microcirculatory impairment, blood–brain barrier disruption, neuroinflammatory signaling, and metabolic dysregulation [,,,,].

Accordingly, we define neurovascular unit failure as the progressive loss of coordinated communication among the vascular, glial, immune, and neuronal compartments, resulting in the inability to maintain cerebral perfusion, metabolic homeostasis, and blood–brain barrier integrity.

The central hypothesis of this review is that progressive neurovascular unit failure may represent a key underlying process in delayed cerebral ischemia, offering a systems-based framework that may help explain how established mechanisms of secondary brain injury converge to produce the clinical syndrome. On this view, DCI may be better understood as a disorder of neurovascular communication than of large arteries alone; how this framework differs from earlier multifactorial reviews is set out at the end of . The proposed conceptual framework is shown in .

The neurovascular unit (NVU) is a multicellular partnership between neurons, astrocytes, endothelial cells, pericytes, smooth muscle cells, basement membrane, and immune cells. Emergent communication between these components maintains perfusion, barrier integrity, and metabolic balance. Neurovascular coupling, the best-studied function, was once described as a simple relay in which neurons signal astrocytes, and astrocytes signal vessels. That view has not held up. Coupling is now understood as a distributed, multidirectional process across capillaries, penetrating arterioles, and pial arteries. The mediators engage these vessels in a coordinated sequence of initiation, modulation, transmission, retrograde propagation, and implementation []. This sequence is carried out by the network’s connectivity, not a singular cell.

This connectivity goes beyond a classic anatomical unit. NVUs are variable along the arteriole–capillary–venule axis and across the brain, and neighboring segments coordinate with one another. For instance, in retrograde vasodilation, a signal that begins in capillaries can travel upstream to adjust the arterioles’ tone several branches away []. Thus, the functional unit can be defined as the communication pathway connecting segments, not the vessel segment itself.

The core functions of the NVU arise from the collective networking of the comprising cells, not from any one cell acting alone. The integrity of the BBB relies on the combined contribution of endothelial tight junctions, pericyte control of transcytosis, and astrocytic maintenance of the basement membrane. The loss of any of these factors compromises the strength of another []. Autoregulation is driven by smooth muscle myogenic responses, with astrocytes and pericytes modulating capillary tone to fine-tune local blood flow []. Neurovascular coupling requires that the signal be initiated by neurons, relayed by astrocytes, and retrogradely propagated by the endothelium to upstream arterioles []. The coordinated action of barrier function, autoregulation, and coupling results in perfusion. Disruption of any of these components can limit flow, despite normal appearance of vessels. The output combination of barrier, flow, perfusion, and metabolic supply results in homeostasis.

Clinically, repairing a single component may not be sufficient to restore perfusion, barrier integrity, or metabolic supply, since no single element alone causes the problem. Reopening a constricted artery may improve conduit flow, but capillary-level regulation or barrier function is not necessarily restored, as these depend on communication pathways that the intervention does not reach [,]. In this context, delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) can be viewed as consistent with a failure of coordinated output rather than with injury to a single structural component.

The progressive loss of coordinated communication among the vascular, glial, immune, and neuronal compartments, when it exceeds the network’s adaptability, can be termed NVU failure. The use of the term failure is intentional, since related terms describe narrower or earlier stages of the same process. Dysfunction implies impairment that can be compensated for by regulatory reserves, preserving the overall output. Injury implies structural damage to a specific cellular component without denoting that system-level performance has been lost. Disruption describes an isolated abnormality confined to a single pathway or interface. In contrast, failure denotes the point at which compensatory mechanisms are exhausted and coordinated neurovascular communication is unable to maintain the integrated system composed of perfusion, barrier integrity, and metabolic homeostasis. This is a threshold, not a severity gradient, and different compartments may cross it at different times, as the evidence below illustrates. Operationally, dysfunction is a weakened response that recovers, whereas failure is a response that stays absent or inverted, for example, when spreading depolarization causes prolonged hypoperfusion instead of hyperemia in vulnerable tissue, or when sustained neuronal activity constricts vessels in mice [,]. Possible markers in patients include prolonged spreading ischemia on electrocorticography with flow monitoring and falling glucose with a rising lactate-to-glucose ratio on microdialysis [,]. Thresholds for these measures have been proposed for predicting DCI, but to our knowledge, none has been validated as marking the transition from dysfunction to failure []. The value of this distinction lies in its potential to identify when impaired NVU function exceeds the capacity for compensation, rather than simply reflecting more severe dysfunction. Although candidate physiological and metabolic markers may help characterize this transition, prospective studies are needed to establish operational criteria for distinguishing failure from potentially reversible dysfunction. Until such criteria are validated, the distinction between compensated dysfunction and failure should be regarded as a conceptual proposal rather than an established category.

Different NVU functions seem to fail at different times. Three studies in male C57BL/6 mice, all using filament-perforation SAH, show this [,,]. Within 3 to 4 h, pial and parenchymal arterioles no longer dilated to CO2, but neurovascular coupling (in vivo and in slices) and astrocyte endfoot calcium signaling were intact []. At 24 h, CO2 reactivity was still lost, and sustained stimulation caused parenchymal arterioles to constrict in vivo (forepaw stimulation) and in slices (electrical field stimulation), while the flow response to brief stimulation was preserved []. At one month, CO2 reactivity had recovered in parenchymal arterioles, but the response to brief stimulation was lost, and the response to sustained stimulation was reduced, though not significantly different from sham []. CO2 reactivity reflects chemoregulation of vascular tone and is distinct from pressure autoregulation, so these findings should not be taken as evidence about autoregulatory capacity. These time points come from separate groups of animals, since coupling cannot be followed in the same animal, and no similar course has been shown in patients, to our knowledge. This pattern fits different NVU functions failing at different times, not everything failing at once.

A similar phenomenon can be observed in coagulation. Cerebral microthrombi form within minutes of hemorrhage in rodent models, an early response proposed to be compensatory for the vessel injury, though this remains speculative. Reported timelines vary: some studies describe resolution within 48 h, while others report near-baseline levels by day 1, with burden peaking between days 2–5. A second, more variable wave later in the first two weeks has increasingly been attributed to platelet-leukocyte interactions and neutrophil extracellular traps, and was associated with infarction in human autopsy series and experimental studies []. This shift, from an early hemostatic response to a later, immune-driven pathology, reflects a threshold event within a compartment rather than a uniform collapse. This suggests functional dissociation may precede structural injury.

A critical way to evaluate this framework is to determine whether considering NVU failure as the initiating event, rather than as secondary to vasospasm, modifies evidence-supported predictions. A primary-NVU model would be expected to show three things: vasospasm-targeted therapy should improve outcome inconsistently across trials, endpoints, and populations, NVU-level disturbances should appear hours to days before DCI, and a network architecture should naturally generate the heterogeneity that single-mechanism models cannot explain.

The framework predicts that risk will not simply add up. Existing multifactorial models, in which several processes together produce a perfusion-metabolism mismatch, may also accommodate synergistic interactions, so non-additivity by itself does not distinguish the two views. The NVU framework is more specific about where such interactions should arise: if the effects were independent, DCI risk would rise gradually with each added abnormality []. A network running out of compensation instead implies a sharper rise when abnormalities in two compartments occur together in the same territory. This can be tested as an interaction in prospective monitoring studies. Additive risk, or vasospasm severity alone explaining DCI, would weaken the framework. This prediction provides a way to distinguish the proposed framework from purely additive models by testing whether interactions between established mechanisms contribute to deterioration beyond their individual effects. Whether such interactions occur and meaningfully influence DCI risk remains to be established.

One informative observation is the limited benefit of vasospasm-directed therapy. Suppressing vasospasm has not reliably improved outcomes. In CONSCIOUS-2 (clipping), clazosentan at 5 mg/h produced only a nonsignificant 17% relative-risk reduction (21% vs. 25%, p = 0.10), while poor Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE) outcome was actually slightly higher with treatment (29% vs. 25%) []. In CONSCIOUS-3 (coiling), the 15 mg/h dose did reduce the composite endpoint (27% to 15%; OR 0.474, 95% CI 0.275–0.818, p = 0.007), yet poor GOSE outcome again remained slightly more common (28% vs. 24%), and mortality was unchanged []. In contrast, two Japanese phase III trials of clazosentan at 10 mg/h reported benefit after both clipping and coiling, whereas REACT at 15 mg/h did not reduce clinical deterioration due to DCI [,]. Clazosentan benefit, therefore, varies by trial, endpoint, and population rather than being absent. Hemorrhage burden may help explain the gap between composite-endpoint benefit and functional outcome; a thick, diffuse clot predicts a far higher morbidity (36.1% vs. 14.7%) and poorer outcomes (32.7% vs. 16.2%) []. A pooled meta-analysis found that clazosentan reduced vasospasm-related infarcts and vasospasm incidence but did not significantly improve functional outcome or mortality []. One possible explanation is that clazosentan has minimal effect on concurrent microcirculatory dysfunction, including microthromboembolism, endothelial injury, and cortical spreading ischemia; this remains speculative []. Vasospasm and DCI co-occur only 30–80% of the time, and TCD carries its own well-known sensitivity and specificity limits [].

If the wrong layer is being targeted by therapy, network disturbance should show up before DCI, and several studies report it. Microdialysis shows falling glucose and rising lactate-to-glucose ratio up to about two to three days before CT-confirmed infarction, with glutamate rising only later []. Serum and CSF vascular injury markers rise within the first day, and inflammasome proteins increase from day 1 [,]. In mice, coupling fails by 24 h, and to our knowledge, the corresponding timing in patients is unknown []. Electrophysiology follows the same logic: cortical spreading depolarization (CSD) triggers opposite vascular responses depending on network state. CSDs occur in 72–80% of aSAH patients, independent of radiographic vasospasm; healthy tissue shows hyperperfusion, and compromised tissue prolonged hypoperfusion [,]. In one cohort, CSD count was more closely associated with DCI than angiographic vasospasm or perfusion CT (OR 2.064, AUC 0.836). In a small cortical-electrode series (n = 18), CSD had a positive predictive value of 86% and a negative predictive value of 100%, compared with a TCD positive predictive value of 57% in a meta-analysis []. These signals are reported before clinical DCI, making them candidates for biomarker-guided intervention.

Patients with similar hemorrhage severity often diverge clinically in ways single mechanism models cannot explain. A network model predicts why: if the endothelial, microvascular, neuroimmune, and electrophysiological compartments need not fail at identical timing or severity, then the compartment that dominates should vary across patients, even with matched hemorrhage burden. This is examined in , where unresolved disagreement over whether pericytes drive or follow microvascular constriction is addressed as a candidate case of compartment-specific divergence rather than treated as a single, settled mechanism. Moreover, this logic is not unique to DCI, as we can notice a persistent NVU dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease where ongoing NVU abnormalities are seen after initial insult rather than any single pathway causing the chronic inflammation and progressive injury [].

These findings, combined, suggest that the operative mechanism runs alongside large-vessel narrowing, appears before DCI’s clinical signature, and is only partially addressed by vasospasm-directed therapy. They do not prove that NVU failure is the main cause. Vasospasm may be one contributor within a failing network.

The first moments after aneurysm ruptures are thought to shape much of what follows. The rapid extravasation of arterial blood into the subarachnoid space results in an abrupt rise in intracranial pressure (ICP) [,]. This is followed by a fall in cerebral perfusion pressure and a transient period of global cerebral ischemia. This is not a focal injury but a shock to the network: all components of the neurovascular unit are simultaneously deprived of substrate, while its structural integrity is challenged by mechanical distortion. This insult is soon followed by oxidative stress, as ischemia-reperfusion and the earliest blood breakdown products generate reactive oxygen species that damage the lipids, proteins, and DNA of the endothelium, glia, and neurons [,,]. Mitochondria are at the heart of both energy provision and oxidative stress, are injured early, and become self-perpetuating amplifiers of stress rather than passive casualties. Damaged mitochondria produce more reactive oxygen species, which further compromise mitochondrial function and extend cellular injury long after the hemodynamic event has resolved []. In the first hour, mechanical shear from the hemorrhage itself disrupts capillary architecture and astrocytic-endothelial contact [,].

Despite the severity of this early insult, these events alone may be insufficient to explain the development of delayed cerebral ischemia. Trials of vasospasm-directed therapy, long believed to target the dominant late mechanism, have not consistently improved functional outcome, highlighting a disconnection between local vascular narrowing and the clinical syndrome it was thought to explain [,,]. This discrepancy suggests that EBI alone may not be sufficient to cause DCI, but may prime a network whose capacity for coordinated regulation is already impaired. We propose that this predisposes to progressive neurovascular unit failure rather than a fixed downstream event []; this remains a hypothesis supported mainly by experimental and observational data. This raises the next question: what sustains and propagates this initial network destabilization?

We propose that sustained exposure is a key contributing mechanism. Once in the subarachnoid space, hemoglobin, liberated iron, thrombin, and activated complement are not cleared instantaneously but remain in contact with the endothelial–glial interface for days, leading to persistent oxidative and proteolytic stress rather than a single toxic exposure [,,,]. Iron-catalyzed radical generation, thrombin-mediated receptor signaling on vascular cells, and complement-driven immune priming are mechanistically distinct but functionally converge on the same target: the degradation of the tight junctions and signaling architecture that allow the BBB to function as a regulated interface rather than a passive barrier [,,]. This is consistent with BBB permeability increasing progressively over the early post-hemorrhage period rather than appearing and resolving as a single event; the interface is continually stressed, not struck once [,]. Clinically, this persistent toxicity may help explain why interventions aimed at any single blood-derived mediator have shown limited translational success: targeting iron, or thrombin, or complement individually addresses one input into a network-level problem rather than the problem itself [,]. The unresolved question is how this sustained, multi-input stress is organized into the specific, reproducible sequence of dysfunction that culminates in DCI.

We propose that this progression from sustained network stress to delayed cerebral ischemia follows a hierarchical order. EBI is the inciting event, a synchronous shock involving ischemia, pressure elevation, oxidative and mitochondrial injury, and mechanical trauma [,,]. This shock is propagated by a primary network disturbance: endothelial dysfunction and microvascular dysregulation, clinically manifested as impaired autoregulation, microthrombosis, and loss of neurovascular coupling, independent of large-vessel narrowing [,,]. This disturbance is then compounded by BBB disruption, neuroimmune activation, and ongoing oxidative stress, which maintain and extend microvascular compromise, rather than being separate complications [,,,]. The final common pathway is progressive neuronal metabolic failure: neurons lacking dependable vascular and glial support lose the ability to maintain oxidative phosphorylation and ionic gradients, which clinically presents as delayed neurological decline, diagnosed as DCI [,]. This model does not replace vasospasm, inflammation, or cortical spreading depolarization, which are all real and clinically relevant processes [,,]. What the framework proposes to change is their explanatory status, not as competing causes of DCI but as possible manifestations of a single underlying process: progressive failure of neurovascular communication initiated by EBI and sustained by ongoing blood-derived toxicity. Importantly, this hierarchy is inferred from studies of individual components, many in experimental models and examined at different time points; it has not been demonstrated as a continuous causal sequence in patients.

Endothelial dysfunction after aSAH is not a localized injury. It is the disruption of a signaling relay that the rest of the NVU relies on. In health, the endothelium transduces capillary-level potassium changes into hyperpolarization by retrogradely conducting vasomotor signals. The hyperpolarization propagates through gap junctions to control tone in arterioles several branch points upstream []. This relay function explains why endothelial injury produces effects that outlast and outrun the injured segment itself.

Several distinct insults occur at the onset of disruption, compounding over the first hour to the first day. These include loss of nitric-oxide-mediated signaling, degradation of the glycocalyx, and oxidative injury to the endothelial cells themselves [,]. These converge on vasomotor conduction and barrier integrity. Instead of each compartment getting injured on its own, evidence suggests that a single upstream failure propagates across them.

Since the endothelium serves as both a barrier and a signaling relay, it is reasonable to expect the two to fail together, with damage spreading beyond the segment that initially made contact with blood. The same retrograde pathway that normally carries a healthy signal upstream does not distinguish a healthy signal from a failing one [].

Loss of coordinated control over vessel diameter at the capillary and arteriolar level defines microvascular dysregulation. In normal conditions, this control depends on continuous signaling among pericytes, smooth muscle, and the endothelium. At the arteriolar level, smooth muscle contributes independently of the capillary-bed pericyte debate: after SAH, smooth muscle cells undergo phenotypic transformation and migration, which we propose may add to calcium-driven constriction [].

The mechanism behind the breakdown of capillary-level control remains actively disputed, and the debate itself is revealing. Three lines of evidence directly conflict: one argues that pericyte calcium dysregulation drives sustained constriction; another links capillary narrowing to pericyte apoptosis rather than active contraction; and a third reports reduced capillary perfusion despite stable pericyte density and diameter, implying a passive deficit downstream of arteriolar constriction instead of a pericyte-mediated process [,,]. This review does not attempt to reconcile these differences; in a system with overlapping failure modes, different groups will naturally obtain discordant findings depending on the time points or compartments they sample, and the interpretations may be compatible with progressive NVU failure.

What is not contested is that microvascular constriction and microthrombosis occur in close temporal and spatial proximity, with microthrombi forming within minutes and aligning with arteriolar constriction; whether one causes the other or both share a trigger remains unclear []. This matters because the process may operate largely independently of the timeline of angiographic vasospasm, which is why microcirculatory dysfunction has been proposed as a more direct correlate of tissue perfusion than large-vessel narrowing [,]. Whether rescuing a single compartment is sufficient remains unknown; no study has directly compared pericyte-targeted and arteriole-targeted interventions in the same aSAH model.

BBB failure seems to amplify ongoing disturbances rather than initiate them. It converts localized dysfunction into a whole-brain problem by allowing unregulated exchange between blood and parenchyma. Its timing is consistent with this amplifying role. Substantial disruption appears early in the injury course. Tight-junction proteins are degraded at the same early time point at which oxidative stress affects endothelial and pericyte compartments []. Mechanistically, barrier failure appears to follow the same inflammatory signaling cascade triggered by injury to the endothelium and glycocalyx. Endothelial and astrocytic pathways converge on a shared degradative process despite having distinct upstream triggers [,].

Once the barrier is compromised, its failure feeds back onto affected compartments through two routes. Chemically, albumin extravasation disrupts astrocytic potassium buffering. This produces neuronal hyperexcitability and creates a direct link between vascular failure and neuronal signaling. Mechanically, albumin efflux raises interstitial oncotic pressure. This drives vasogenic edema on top of existing cytotoxic edema. The resulting tissue pressure may further compress the microvasculature, acting as a physical amplifier to the biochemical one []. Together, these processes appear to increase metabolic demand precisely when supply is least able to meet it.

Neuroimmune signaling seems to act as a second amplifying mechanism. In contrast to the barrier-related processes, it appears to rely on a two-way loop between astrocytes and microglia rather than on direct chemical escalation. The interaction seems to build over the first few days after the hemorrhage, supported by ongoing cross-talk between the two cell types.

Damage-associated molecular patterns released from injured or lysed cells bind receptors on both microglia and astrocytes at roughly similar times. Microglia often respond first, within minutes. Their early activity tends to influence astrocytes before producing any direct neuronal effects. One such example is HMGB1: it increases aquaporin-4 expression in astrocytes, but only when microglia provide IL-1β, suggesting a relay, not two independent responses to the same signal. Once activated, astrocytes signal back to microglia, increasing MMP-9 expression, contributing to barrier changes. A complement-based loop runs alongside the cytokine cycle. Microglia-derived C1q shifts astrocytes toward a more neurotoxic phenotype. Those astrocytes then produce C3, which acts on microglia via the C3–C3aR pathway, thereby increasing activation. The structure mirrors the cytokine loop but uses a different signaling axis. This complement activity also extends into the vascular compartment. Elevated CSF C3a has been linked to delayed ischemic deficits through activation of coagulation pathways, connecting neuroimmune amplification to microthrombosis and perfusion disturbances [].

These reciprocal loops reinforce one another. Each cycle increases the next round of glial activation and further weakens the barrier that would otherwise limit the spread of injury. This pattern is not limited to rodent models. Markers of vascular injury and inflammasome activation increase in serum and CSF starting on day 1 after hemorrhage, and an association with clinical course has been reported in four cohorts from three countries (UK, Germany, and Spain), although samples are small and biomarker panels and outcome measures differ [,,,]. In a retrospective 82-patient cohort, CSF IL-6 was associated with DCI-related infarction but not with angiographic vasospasm []. The lack of correlation suggests that at least part of the neuroimmune response may progress independently of large-vessel narrowing rather than merely tracking it.

The disturbances described above point to neuronal energy failure; to our knowledge, no single study has followed the entire progression from network disruption to metabolic collapse. At its core, this endpoint reflects neurons losing the ability to maintain their ion gradients when the damaged network can no longer meet the energetic demand. Human cerebral microdialysis shows this clearly: extracellular glucose falls, and the lactate-to-glucose ratio rises more than 2 days before CT can detect an infarction []. Glutamate increases later, marking the shift from a supply–demand imbalance toward more severe energy failure.

This transition is not only biochemical. It also has an electrophysiological component. Cortical spreading depolarization (CSD), a self-propagating wave of near-complete neuronal depolarization, is common in patients with aSAH. In healthy tissue, CSD produces a brief hyperperfusion response. In tissue where neurovascular coupling is already compromised, it produces spreading ischemia instead, a prolonged hypoperfusion that worsens injury []. The wave drives constriction through potassium-mediated smooth muscle depolarization and simultaneously suppresses nitric oxide production, removing the vasodilatory signal that would normally counterbalance it []. Whether CSD ends up protective or harmful depends on how intact the surrounding network was beforehand. The same ionic collapse also releases glutamate, initiating the excitotoxic cascade.

The excitotoxic pathway itself is well described. Glutamate activates NMDA receptors, leading to calcium overload and downstream lethal signaling. Selective GluN2B antagonism reduces neurological deficits following experimental hemorrhage and lessens the severity of vasospasm, suggesting that glutamatergic signaling may influence vascular responses []. Even this pathway, often treated as the final step, remains connected to the broader network.

A second cohort supports the clinical relevance of metabolic failure. In 49 SAH patients monitored with cerebral microdialysis, investigators recorded 113 minor and 42 major lactate-to-pyruvate ratio events over a median of six days. Intervention restored metabolic balance in most cases, and DCI-related infarction occurred in only 10 percent of patients, with just two infarcts appearing in monitored regions []. The sequence differs from Tholance et al., but the conclusion is similar: metabolic derangement is common, detectable, and potentially modifiable before infarction is established [].

Neuronal death beyond this point takes several forms. Ferroptosis is particularly well studied in this setting. In murine models, it affects endothelial cells and microglia as well as neurons, and inhibiting it preserves tight junctions []. Different cell populations follow distinct routes depending on timing and upstream stressors, but the endpoint remains the same: the loss of ionic gradient maintenance.

These processes may form a single trajectory, although this has not been shown as a continuous sequence in patients. Endothelial and microvascular disturbances are proposed to initiate the failure, with barrier breakdown, spreading depolarization, and neuroimmune signaling amplifying it. Neuronal energy failure is where these processes converge. Each part of the sequence describes a different cell population caught within the same deteriorating network.
