The previous section explored the mechanistic basis through which progressive NVU failure may culminate in delayed cerebral ischemia. So, this section will focus on determining if this framework can actually translate clinically, particularly the observations that have challenged traditional disease models.

This framework offers one possible interpretation of a central clinical challenges in DCI: the dissociation between angiographic vasospasm and the development of ischemia. Historically, vasospasm was regarded as the principal cause of DCI, and the two were often treated as closely equivalent disease processes [,]. However, this assumption was fundamentally disrupted when clinical observations showed that substantial angiographic vasospasm can occur without ischemia, whereas DCI can develop despite little or no large-vessel narrowing [,]. This raised questions about the relationship between vasospasm and DCI. The proposed framework addresses this uncertainty by positioning vasospasm as one contributor to progressive NVU failure rather than as the defining disease process [,]. Within this framework, the apparent paradox is no longer unexpected, because different combinations of vascular, microcirculatory, inflammatory, barrier, and metabolic disturbances may drive the system toward the same endpoint of neuronal metabolic failure. Vasospasm may therefore contribute to DCI as part of cumulative network dysfunction, but its presence alone does not determine whether clinical ischemia will develop.

On that same note, the clinical dissociation between vasospasm and DCI also helps explain another long-standing challenge in aSAH research: the limited success of therapies directed solely at large-vessel vasospasm. For decades, the assumption that vasospasm was the principal driver of DCI led to the development of therapies aimed primarily at restoring large-artery caliber. Although several interventions successfully reduced angiographic vasospasm, their effects on delayed cerebral ischemia and long-term functional outcomes were often modest or absent [,]. Similarly, the STASH trial found that statins did not improve functional outcomes or reduce complications after aSAH []. This therapeutic discordance further challenged the concept that vasospasm alone defines the disease process. However, within an NVU-centered model, correcting arterial narrowing addresses only one component of progressive NVU failure, while dysfunction across the wider neurovascular system may persist. This rationale is further supported by nimodipine, the current standard of care, which improves neurological outcomes despite having only modest effects on large-vessel vasospasm []. Its clinical benefit is thought to reflect broader actions on neurovascular function, which could be viewed as being consistent with the proposed model and the multifactorial pathophysiology of DCI [].

A further clinical feature addressed by the NVU framework is the variable timing and presentation of DCI. Its delayed onset is more consistent with progressive system failure than with an immediate, isolated event []. Within the proposed framework, this delay reflects both the time required for disturbances to develop across the NVU and the system’s temporary capacity to compensate for their effects. For example, neuroinflammation evolves progressively as circulating leukocytes are recruited and the microglial response becomes established, allowing inflammatory injury and its effects on endothelial, microvascular, and metabolic function to accumulate over time [,]. Meanwhile, autoregulatory adjustments, collateral perfusion, metabolic reserve, and restoration of ionic gradients may initially preserve substrate delivery and neuronal function, thereby delaying the clinical expression of the underlying dysfunction []. DCI emerges when the growing neurovascular burden exceeds this compensatory capacity and the NVU can no longer maintain an adequate balance between cerebral substrate delivery and neuronal metabolic demand []. Clinical microdialysis findings showing that disturbances in cerebral energy metabolism may precede radiographic hypoperfusion and infarction by up to two to three days are consistent with this sequence, as they indicate a period of progressive metabolic decompensation before irreversible tissue injury becomes established [,]. By placing these temporal disturbances within a compensatory system, the NVU framework may account for the delayed onset of DCI.

The same progressive and threshold-dependent process may also explain the clinical heterogeneity of DCI. Patients may differ in both the burden of NVU dysfunction and their capacity to compensate for it []. Differences in collateral circulation, autoregulatory capacity, metabolic reserve, and susceptibility to secondary injury may allow a similar pathological burden to remain clinically silent in one patient while producing earlier or more severe deterioration in another. Heterogeneity may also reflect variation in the dominant pattern of NVU dysfunction, as different contributing processes have been associated with distinct pathological and radiographic expressions of injury []. Taken together, these differences can be interpreted as variable expressions of progressive NVU failure, although existing multifactorial models can also accommodate them.

The pathophysiological understanding of DCI following aSAH has evolved predominantly from large vessel vasospasm-centered towards a multifactorial framework which comprises microcirculatory impairment, neuroinflammation, blood–brain barrier disruption, cortical spreading depolarization, and metabolic disturbances [,]. Clinical trials investigating clazosentan, a selective endothelin-A receptor antagonist, which represents the complexity between angiographic vasospasm and neurological outcomes, were not able to demonstrate significant benefits that translate into improved functional outcomes [,,].

In contrast, two randomized Japanese phase III trials demonstrated significant clinical benefits of clazosentan when administered at 10 mg/h following either surgical clipping or endovascular coiling. The incidence of vasospasm-related morbidity and overall mortality decreased from 39.6% to 16.2% in the clipping study and from 28.8% to 13.6% in the coiling study. A predetermined pooled analysis also showed decreases in overall morbidity and adverse functional outcomes on the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) []. However, the REACT trial, which evaluated clazosentan at 15 mg/h in patients with thick, diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage receiving standard care including nimodipine, did not demonstrate a significant reduction in its primary endpoint of clinical deterioration due to DCI (15.8% versus 17.2%; p = 0.734) [].

These apparently conflicting findings should be interpreted considering the methodological and clinical differences present in the studies. The CONSCIOUS trials and the Japanese phase III trials assessed a comparable primary endpoint framework related to vasospasm-associated morbidity and overall mortality within 6 weeks. In the Japanese trials, all-cause morbidity and mortality were assessed as a second primary endpoint. In contrast, REACT concentrated on clinical decline due to DCI, assessing cerebral infarction and long-term functional results independently. The trials varied in regional demographics, procedures for securing aneurysms, clazosentan dosages (5, 10, or 15 mg/h), timing for starting treatment, standard care, and eligibility requirements concerning hemorrhage severity. Specifically, nimodipine is not commonly employed as standard treatment in Japan, while it was utilized in REACT. These variations may have influenced the inconsistency in treatment results, although the specific impacts cannot be definitively established [,,,].

Overall, these results indicate that addressing endothelin-induced vasospasm can reduce significant ischemic complications in specific groups, although its impact on overall neurological recovery varies across studies. Thus, the lack of functional advantage in specific trials should not be seen as evidence that macrovascular constriction is irrelevant in DCI development. Instead, the varied therapeutic responses align with a complex disease process where macrovascular dysfunction interacts with microvascular, inflammatory, electrophysiological, and metabolic issues. In the suggested neurovascular unit (NVU) model, vasospasm is viewed as a significant, potentially modifiable factor in secondary injury rather than the sole cause of DCI.

The NVU framework does not discard historical models; rather, it proposes the NVU as a biological architecture in which these mechanisms may intersect. Rather than functioning as a distinct competing hypothesis, NVU dysfunction may represent the common pathway through which vascular, cellular, and metabolic insults interact to cause tissue injury. The integrated historical paradigms are presented in .

Relation to previous reviews Earlier comprehensive reviews, notably Budohoski et al. [], and later Geraghty and Testai [], Dodd et al. [], and Stragier et al. [], established that DCI is multifactorial and described its contributing mechanisms, and Solár et al. [] examined the BBB and NVU in SAH at the molecular level. The present framework does not add new mechanisms. It may differ in emphasis in four respects: (i) it proposes an operational distinction between compensated NVU dysfunction and NVU failure, with candidate markers in patients (); (ii) it specifies where non-additive interactions between NVU compartments would be expected and how they could be tested, while recognizing that existing multifactorial models can also accommodate synergy (); (iii) it organizes biomarkers by the NVU compartment they reflect rather than by assay type (, ); and (iv) it states prespecified predictions under which it would be revised or rejected (). Whether these features improve prediction or treatment remains to be tested. Accordingly, the present work should be read as a hypothesis-generating perspective rather than as an established disease model.

If the hypothesis that DCI reflects progressive neurovascular unit failure, rather than a delayed arterial event alone, is supported, then activities that depend on how the disease is conceptualized, including biomarker design, therapeutic strategy, and hypothesis generation, may benefit from being reorganized around the NVU as the unit of analysis, not around individual cell types or individual mechanisms.

Under the conventional model, biomarkers are typically grouped by assay type: imaging markers, serum protein markers, electrophysiological markers, and cerebrospinal fluid markers are studied and reported as separate literatures [,]. This organization is a direct consequence of treating vasospasm, inflammation, and neuronal injury as independent processes, each deserving its own biomarker program. If NVU failure is a unifying process, as proposed here, biomarkers should be organized according to the neurovascular compartment they interrogate, like endothelial and microcirculatory function, blood–brain barrier integrity, glial–neuroimmune signaling, and neuronal metabolic status, rather than by the laboratory technique used to measure them. A single compartment can then be interrogated by multiple modalities simultaneously: microcirculatory dysfunction captured by both perfusion imaging and circulating endothelial markers, or BBB breakdown captured by both permeability imaging and serum barrier proteins [,]. This reframing has an immediate practical consequence: no single biomarker, however sensitive, should be expected to reliably predict DCI, because of the possibility that no single compartment failure may be sufficient to produce the syndrome. Multimodal phenotyping, combining markers from at least two compartments, ideally with serial sampling that captures the transition from initiation to amplification, is therefore a natural implication of the framework rather than a purely methodological refinement: biomarker studies would be more informative if they specified which NVU compartment a given molecule reflects []. Whether panels built on this compartment-based logic actually outperform single-compartment markers in practice is a distinct empirical claim, and it is stated explicitly once as one of the framework’s testable predictions in the following section.

The clinical trial record in DCI is dominated by single-target interventions, calcium channel blockers, endothelin receptor antagonists, magnesium, statins, each designed to interrupt one node of the cascade, typically vasospasm [,,,]. Their modest and inconsistent efficacy may reflect, at least in part, intervention on a single output of a multi-component process, although trial design, patient selection, timing, and dosing may also contribute. If EBI initiates a process of reciprocal endothelial–glial–neuronal decompensation that amplifies through feed-forward loops, then blocking arterial narrowing alone may not restore coordinated NVU function, because vasospasm may be a downstream manifestation rather than the origin of the failure. This reframing suggests that future therapies may need to adopt combination strategies aimed at restoring communication across NVU compartments—for example, pairing early endothelial and barrier stabilization with downstream neuroimmune modulation and hemodynamic support—rather than escalating the dose or specificity of a single-pathway drug [,]. It also reorients the timing question: because the framework proposes that the decisive injury occurs at initiation, not at the moment vasospasm becomes angiographically visible, interventions delivered in the early brain injury window should, in principle, carry more preventive value than those delivered once microcirculatory and barrier failure have already propagated. This does not diminish the clinical importance of vasospasm treatment or hemodynamic augmentation; it repositions them as management of a late network consequence rather than as management of the disease process itself [].

A framework earns scientific standing only if it generates predictions that could, in principle, prove it wrong. This framework generates five such predictions, each traceable to a specific stage of the proposed hierarchy:Abnormal endothelial and BBB markers measured within 24–72 h of rupture should precede clinical or radiographic DCI by at least 24 h in most patients who develop DCI. A vasospasm-centered model would instead predict that these markers track angiographic vasospasm severity [,,].A panel combining markers from at least two NVU compartments should show significant incremental discrimination over the best single-compartment marker (for example, an increase in AUC or a net reclassification improvement) in a prespecified validation cohort [,].Serial multimodal data should identify reproducible NVU phenotypes (for example, endothelial-, barrier-, or neuroimmune-predominant) that predict outcome independently of hemorrhage burden [].Phenotype-guided combination therapy targeting at least two compartments should outperform single-target treatment on a prespecified DCI or functional endpoint in adequately powered trials [,].Within the same vascular territory, concurrent abnormalities in two NVU compartments (for example, an endothelial or barrier marker together with clustered spreading depolarizations or a microdialysis metabolic event) should increase DCI risk more than the sum of their separate effects, detectable as a significant interaction term in prospective multimodal monitoring studies; purely additive effects would argue against the framework ().Not all of these predictions are unique to the NVU framework. Predictions 1–3 are also compatible with existing explanations of DCI, including early brain injury and multifactorial models; confirming them would be consistent with, but would not specifically support, progressive NVU failure. Prediction 4 is likewise expected under multifactorial models. Prediction 5 is the most discriminating, because it specifies compartment- and territory-specific interactions; even so, it would test a specific expectation of the framework rather than establish NVU failure as a distinct disease model.

Abnormal endothelial and BBB markers measured within 24–72 h of rupture should precede clinical or radiographic DCI by at least 24 h in most patients who develop DCI. A vasospasm-centered model would instead predict that these markers track angiographic vasospasm severity [,,].

A panel combining markers from at least two NVU compartments should show significant incremental discrimination over the best single-compartment marker (for example, an increase in AUC or a net reclassification improvement) in a prespecified validation cohort [,].

Serial multimodal data should identify reproducible NVU phenotypes (for example, endothelial-, barrier-, or neuroimmune-predominant) that predict outcome independently of hemorrhage burden [].

Phenotype-guided combination therapy targeting at least two compartments should outperform single-target treatment on a prespecified DCI or functional endpoint in adequately powered trials [,].

Within the same vascular territory, concurrent abnormalities in two NVU compartments (for example, an endothelial or barrier marker together with clustered spreading depolarizations or a microdialysis metabolic event) should increase DCI risk more than the sum of their separate effects, detectable as a significant interaction term in prospective multimodal monitoring studies; purely additive effects would argue against the framework ().

Not all of these predictions are unique to the NVU framework. Predictions 1–3 are also compatible with existing explanations of DCI, including early brain injury and multifactorial models; confirming them would be consistent with, but would not specifically support, progressive NVU failure. Prediction 4 is likewise expected under multifactorial models. Prediction 5 is the most discriminating, because it specifies compartment- and territory-specific interactions; even so, it would test a specific expectation of the framework rather than establish NVU failure as a distinct disease model.

Each of these predictions is falsifiable: if early microcirculatory and barrier dysfunction do not reliably precede DCI, if combined panels add no predictive value over single markers, if no reproducible NVU phenotypes emerge, if abnormalities in different compartments combine only additively, or if combination therapy fails to outperform single-target treatment in adequately powered trials, the framework would need to be revised or abandoned. In short, the value of this framework lies in the questions it generates rather than in its explanatory scope; it is offered as a hypothesis to be tested and should be revised or abandoned if these predictions fail. Neurovascular Unit-Based Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the proposed NVU framework. A major limitation is that, although the available evidence demonstrates that endothelial dysfunction, microvascular dysregulation, BBB disruption, neuroimmune activation, and metabolic abnormalities occur after aSAH, the proposed temporal hierarchy linking these processes remains incompletely validated in humans. Much of the mechanistic evidence is derived from experimental models or observational studies examining individual components at different time points. Consequently, temporal association does not necessarily establish causality, and it remains uncertain whether the proposed sequence of early NVU disturbance, progressive amplification, and metabolic decompensation represents a consistent trajectory across patients or a pattern restricted to specific biological phenotypes.

Importantly, the failure of vasospasm-directed therapies to reliably improve functional outcome supports the insufficiency of vasospasm as a standalone model of DCI, but does not, by itself, establish NVU failure as the primary causal substrate. Vasospasm may remain an important contributor in selected patients, and its pathological significance may vary according to hemorrhage burden, vascular territory, collateral circulation, and the underlying pattern of NVU dysfunction. More broadly, integrating established mechanisms into a common NVU architecture risks becoming overly inclusive if the framework can accommodate virtually any biological abnormality observed after aSAH. The strength of this framework will ultimately depend on whether it can generate specific, testable predictions that distinguish NVU-mediated mechanisms from alternative explanations of DCI.

A further challenge is the proposed heterogeneity of NVU failure. Although the framework suggests that patients may exhibit distinct endothelial-, microvascular-, barrier-, neuroimmune-, or metabolism-predominant patterns, these phenotypes have not yet been defined or validated. The relative contribution and temporal relationship of these compartments may differ substantially between individuals, potentially explaining why single-target interventions have produced inconsistent clinical benefits. This heterogeneity also complicates the clinical identification of DCI, particularly in poor-grade or sedated patients in whom neurological deterioration may be difficult to detect reliably and may not correspond to a single biological mechanism.

Future validation should therefore focus on prospective, longitudinal studies that simultaneously characterize multiple NVU compartments within individual patients from the early brain injury period through the development or resolution of DCI. Multimodal approaches integrating vascular and perfusion imaging with biomarkers of endothelial function, BBB integrity, neuroinflammation, electrophysiological dysfunction, and cerebral metabolism may establish whether early NVU abnormalities consistently precede DCI, identify reproducible biological phenotypes, and determine which components are most predictive of irreversible tissue injury. Critically, these studies should test the framework’s predefined, falsifiable predictions rather than merely demonstrating the coexistence of multiple NVU abnormalities. Therapeutic studies should subsequently determine whether interventions guided by specific NVU phenotypes can improve outcomes beyond conventional pathway-specific treatment, while accounting for the potential toxicity and complexity of combination strategies. Ultimately, the NVU framework should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than an established disease model or a replacement for established mechanisms; its validity will depend on whether it can prospectively predict clinical trajectories, identify biologically meaningful patient subgroups, and demonstrate therapeutic implications that cannot be explained by existing paradigms alone.

DCI after aSAH cannot be fully explained by large-vessel vasospasm alone. The dissociation between angiographic vasospasm, tissue ischemia, infarction, and clinical outcome, together with evidence of early endothelial, microvascular, BBB, neuroimmune, electrophysiological, and metabolic disturbances, supports a broader pathophysiological model.

This perspective proposes, as a hypothesis, progressive NVU failure as a framework that may link these processes. EBI may destabilize neurovascular homeostasis, after which dysfunction across vascular, glial, immune, and neuronal compartments can interact and amplify tissue vulnerability. Within this framework, vasospasm remains an important contributor to DCI in some patients but represents one component of a broader process rather than a sufficient explanation for delayed ischemic injury. Progressive loss of neurovascular and metabolic reserve may ultimately culminate in metabolic failure, tissue injury, and clinical DCI.

This framework remains a hypothesis rather than an established causal sequence. Current evidence does not demonstrate that NVU disturbance occurs in a uniform temporal order or contributes equally across patients, and much of the mechanistic evidence is derived from experimental and observational studies. Longitudinal multimodal studies should determine whether early NVU abnormalities predict subsequent DCI, whether distinct biological trajectories can be identified, and whether targeting multiple NVU compartments can improve outcomes beyond pathway-specific treatment.

An NVU-centered model therefore does not replace vasospasm or other established mechanisms of secondary brain injury. Rather, it offers a hypothesis-generating framework for exploring how these processes may interact to produce DCI and offers a basis for more precise biomarker development, patient stratification, and mechanism-informed therapeutic strategies.

neuroscience.title: Neuroprognostication in unconscious patients after cardiac arrest: considering the time course of prognostic markers
neuroscience.text:
The neurological consequences of cardiac arrest (CA) are well established: the circulatory interruption can cause widespread and extensive brain damage, which can be exacerbated by ischemia-reperfusion mechanisms following the restoration of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). The first and most common consequence of this brain injury is loss of consciousness, explaining why most patients remain comatose and require intensive care. During the following hours and days, the subsequent course is variable, ranging from complete recovery within a few hours to a complete lack of neurological improvement indicating irreversible damage. Approximately two-thirds of deaths observed in unconscious patients are directly related to these hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI), most often due to withdrawal of life sustaining therapies (WLST) decisions made because of a neurological prognosis deemed too unfavourable [,]. For intensive care teams, the ability to reliably predict a favourable or unfavourable outcome is a major challenge, as it is both essential to pursue maximum therapeutic commitment when the hope of improvement persists, but also because reflection on the care plan is necessary when there is no longer any hope of improvement. The definition of a favourable outcome remains highly debatable, as the perception of an acceptable level of disability in daily life vary considerably according to individual values and beliefs []. Most recent studies define favourable neurological outcomes as a Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) score of 1–2 or a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0–3, corresponding to no or mild-to-moderate neurological disability. Conversely, a poor neurological outcome is generally defined by a CPC 3–5 or an mRS 4–6, encompassing severe neurological disability in conscious patients, persistent coma or vegetative state, or death [, , , ]. Importantly, neurological outcomes should ideally be assessed at least 3 months after CA, rather than upon ICU discharge, as some patients may continue to experience neurological recovery after ICU discharge [,].

Considerable efforts have been made in recent years to clarify the respective performance of the markers that can be used in this situation, leading to the recommendation of a multimodal strategy combining different clinical and paraclinical indicators []. The prognostic value of this strategy depends not only on the proper mastery of the indicators used but also on adherence to the timeframes for their collection, as their prognostic value varies according to the time elapsed since CA and the onset of acute brain injury. The present review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the temporal evolution of neuroprognostication markers after CA—including clinical examination, biomarkers, electroencephalography, somatosensory evoked potentials, and neuroimaging—and to highlight the importance of adhering to recommended assessment timelines to ensure optimal prognostic accuracy.

HIBI develops through a dynamic process that unfolds over time following CA. The initial phase begins with the abrupt cessation of cerebral blood flow, resulting in global cerebral ischemia and oxygen deprivation. This primary insult rapidly leads to energy failure, loss of ionic homeostasis, cellular membrane dysfunction, and neuronal injury. Following ROSC, a secondary phase of ischemia–reperfusion injury occurs during the first hours after resuscitation [,]. This stage is characterized by excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, endothelial dysfunction, microvascular abnormalities, blood–brain barrier disruption, and cerebral oedema, all of which contribute to the progression of brain injury. In the subsequent hours and days, secondary brain injury may be further aggravated by systemic insults such as arterial hypotension, hypoxemia, dysregulated carbon dioxide levels, fever, electrolyte disturbances, or dysglycemia [,]. Over the following weeks and months, the injured brain undergoes a phase of remodelling during which competing restorative and degenerative mechanisms coexist. On the one hand, neuroplasticity, synaptogenesis, and, to a lesser extent, neurogenesis may promote functional recovery and neurological improvement. On the other hand, persistent neuroinflammation and delayed neuronal and glial apoptosis may contribute to progressive tissue loss and cerebral atrophy, which can sometimes be detected on follow-up neuroimaging. Because different brain regions exhibit varying susceptibility to ischemic and reperfusion injury, the extent and distribution of damage are heterogeneous, resulting in a broad spectrum of neurological outcomes ranging from complete recovery to severe disability, prolonged disorders of consciousness, or brain death [,].

When assessing the prognostic value of a marker, particular attention is paid to its specificity, sensitivity, and false-positive rates (FPR). When predicting poor outcomes, specificity is prioritized to minimize the risk of false-positive predictions. A marker is considered highly specific for poor neurological outcome when its specificity exceeds 95%, corresponding to a false-positive rate <5% []. However, such high specificity inherently comes at the expense of sensitivity, which is often low to moderate []. This explains why some patients may experience poor neurological outcomes despite the absence of poor-outcome predictors according to the 2025 ERC–ESICM guidelines [,,]. Conversely, when predicting favorable outcomes, both sensitivity and specificity should be considered and an optimal balance between the two should ideally be sought for quantitative markers, such as NSE cut-off values []. Importantly, the interpretation of prognostic accuracy must also account for potential methodological biases. Most deaths following CA occur after WLST for neurological reasons, raising concerns about self-fulfilling prophecy bias: indeed, prognostic test results may directly influence WLST decisions and patient outcomes. Nevertheless, studies conducted in countries where WLST is not routinely practiced for cultural or religious reasons have reported comparable prognostic performance to that observed in countries where WLST is commonly considered, suggesting that this bias may not fully explain the predictive accuracy of these markers [].

About 80% of patients with ROSC following CA are comatose at ICU admission and nearly 50% of survivors are still unconscious at 72 h []. Most patients with a favourable outcome begin to recover consciousness a few hours after cessation of sedation []. According to the ERC–ESICM guidelines, awakening is defined as the ability to reproducibly follow verbal commands, corresponding to a motor score of 6 on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) []. Nevertheless, delayed awakening is not uncommon after sedation weaning. In some cases, awakening may be observed up to 12–25 days after ROSC []. Recognized risk factors for delayed awakening include post-resuscitation shock, acute renal insufficiency, older age, and use of long-acting (e.g., midazolam) vs. short-acting (e.g., propofol) sedative agents [,,].

The neurological state of consciousness after CA is highly heterogeneous and subject to time-related variations. A complete physical examination using adapted scales and rigorous definitions is recommended to accurately assess the neurological state and predict recovery of consciousness [,]. Thus, clinical examination remains a cornerstone of neuroprognostication, although it is subject to important limitations. To avoid underestimating the level of consciousness, assessments should only be performed after adequate clearance of sedative agents. Any potential confounders that could lead to superimposed encephalopathy must be systematically identified and corrected. These include fever, renal or hepatic dysfunction, electrolyte imbalances, antiepileptic drug toxicity, and exposure to neurotoxic agents such as neuroleptics or antibiotics []. Additionally, fluctuations in the neurological status of brain-injured patients, as well as inter-observatory variability, should be carefully considered. Several clinical parameters should be systematically collected, including: 1/ brainstem reflexes (particularly the pupillary light reflexes - PLR and corneal reflexes), 2/ early myoclonus or status myoclonus occurring in the first days after CA, 3/ motor response to stimuli, as assessed by the Glasgow Coma Scale (mGCS), and 4/ patient’s level of consciousness using appropriate validated scales, such as Coma Recovery Scale Revised (CRS-r) []. Because these different clinical data can fluctuate over time, repeated assessments are required, ideally multiple times per day.

During the early phase (i.e., usually within the first 7 days), the literature provides relatively abundant data on clinical prognostic markers. During this period, brainstem reflex monitoring is essential. While the bilateral absence of PLR or corneal reflexes demonstrates low specificity and high false-positive rate (FPR) for prediction of poor outcome within the first 24 h post-CA, the FPR decline after 24−72 h. A combined bilateral absence of both the PLR and corneal reflexes after 72 h has 100% specificity in predicting an unfavourable outcome, despite having a sensitivity of only 20% [,]. Using pupillometry to quantitatively assess the PLR may improve accuracy, particularly when pupils are pinpoint. Automated pupillometry enables an objective assessment of the PLR by providing a Neurological Pupil index (NPi) ranging from 0 (non-reactive) to 5 (normal). Although the optimal NPI threshold is still being debated, an NPI of less than 2/5 after 72 h seems to indicate a poor outcome with high specificity, despite limited sensitivity of around 20−35% [,]. Regarding abnormal movements, early isolated myoclonus (i.e. brief, sudden muscular contractions affecting muscle segments, individual muscles, or muscle groups) observed in the first 72 h is associated with unfavourable outcome in most cases. Nevertheless, according to studies, the FPR ranges from 0 to 22%, suggesting that this criterion is not a robust marker for predicting a poor outcome, due to the risk of making pessimistic predictions that are not accurate []. Conversely, early-onset status myoclonus (defined as generalized, continuous myoclonic movements persisting beyond 30 min) demonstrates nearly 100% specificity when observed within the first 72 h, although it may be masked by sedation []. The prognostic value of the motor component of the GCS score for predicting poor outcomes is limited. Thus, the 2025 ERC-ESICM guidelines recommend combining it with at least two other markers of poor outcome []. Nevertheless, a motor score of less than 4 (i.e., absent motor response, decerebration, or decortication) correlates with an unfavourable outcome. Conversely, scores of 4 (i.e., flexion withdrawal) or 5 (i.e., localization to pain) when observed within the first 96 h after CA may indicate a favourable outcome [,,].

Beyond the early phase (i.e., usually after day 7), there is still limited prognostic data for CA patients. However, the bilateral absence of both PLR and corneal reflexes at this time appears to be highly specific for prediction of unfavourable outcomes []. Late-onset myoclonus, which appears after a symptom-free interval of more than 72 h after CA and is typically triggered by spontaneous movements (action myoclonus) in patients recovering consciousness, is consistent with Lance-Adams syndrome [,]. Lance–Adams syndrome is usually treated through gradual escalation of anti-myoclonic therapy (e.g., levetiracetam, perampanel, and/or sodium valproate), and requires an evaluation by a specialized expert team. Although Lance–Adams syndrome is not generally considered a poor outcome, its most severe forms, characterized by persistent involuntary movements despite appropriate treatment, may substantially impair functional independence []. Regarding the level of awareness, patients may recover arousal (i.e., eyes opening) after the initial period of coma, without showing evidence of consciousness. These entities are usually referred to as disorders of consciousness (DoC). They include the unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS). Both conditions are characterized by preserved brainstem-mediated arousal and persistent dysfunction of the supratentorial networks that support consciousness. It is critical to distinguish between these DoC subtypes, as patients in MCS are significantly more likely to regain consciousness and have a better functional outcome after 1 year than those in UWS []. For these reasons, daily clinical assessments for emerging signs of consciousness are recommended [,]. The CRS-r is the most widely used and sensitive tool for classifying patients as UWS (i.e., eye opening without environmental interaction), MCS (i.e., minimal interaction without functional communication), or conscious (i.e., reliable communication code established) (ESM - Table S1) []. To maximize the detection of consciousness signs, the clinical examination should be conducted in a distraction-free environment. Prior stimulation of the patient should be used to achieve optimal arousal and attention. The observations of caregivers and family members should also be considered []. Indeed, stimulus familiarity may be particularly relevant in patients with DoC []. Likewise, assessing command-following using instructions delivered in the patient’s native language is strongly recommended in order to minimize the risk of misclassification of the patient’s level of consciousness. Late awakening (i.e., after 14 days) with favourable outcome is rare but documented [,, , ]. Nevertheless, a prolonged time to recovery of consciousness seems to be correlated with an increased risk of neurological cognitive sequelae [,,,]. Finally, a persistent coma or UWS without confounding factors at 25 days or more than one month after CA substantially diminishes the possibility of neurological recovery [,].

It is recommended to wait at least 72 h before beginning to analyse the indicators used to assess the prognosis of a comatose patient. However, it is crucial to include prognostic markers obtained during the first few hours following CA—such as electroencephalograms (EEGs)—in this analysis. EEG findings are typically categorized according to background, superimposed abnormalities (epileptiform discharges also called rhythmic or periodic patterns, or RPPs), and reactivity (ESM - Fig. S1). Regarding background activity, the severity of HIBI is correlated with the predominant frequency, amplitude and continuity. It ranges from slow background activity (theta or delta frequency), to low voltage (10μV < amplitude<20μV the majority of time), sub-continuous (amplitude <10μV, during 0–10% of the recording), discontinuous (amplitude <10μV, during 10–49%), burst suppression (amplitude <10μV, during 50–99 %) or suppression background (amplitude <10μV all the time). RPPs, electroencephalographic seizures or unreactive EEG could also reflect HIBI, with varying degrees of severity. Regarding classification, the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society (ACNS) critical care EEG terminology [] was adapted by Westhall et al. [], resulting in three main categories: highly malignant, malignant and benign EEG. This classification is now the most commonly used for prognostication after CA [,, , , , , , , , ]. This enables standardized interpretation by classifying each tracing into one of the following three EEG categories ():•“Unfavorable” EEG patterns (historically called “Highly malignant patterns”), including 3 main patterns: suppression, suppression with superimposed periodic discharges, and burst suppression. These patterns are recognized as robust markers of poor outcome (i.e., specificity 95–100 %, FPR 0−5%, sensitivity highly heterogeneous according to timing of EEG recording) when observed at least 24 h after CA [,,]. Therefore, these profiles are considered one of the six prognostic markers of poor prognosis in the 2025 ERC-ESICM guidelines []. The morphology of bursts in burst-suppression patterns can also be very informative. Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is characterized by highly stereotyped bursts with nearly identical morphology, whereas burst-suppression without identical bursts exhibits greater variability in burst morphology. BSIB appears to be more specifically associated with severe HIBI, while non-identical burst-suppression may also result from high doses of sedative agents. After CA, BSIB is strongly associated with poor outcomes, and its prognostic accuracy appears less dependent on EEG timing than that of non-identical burst-suppression [].•“Indeterminate” EEG patterns (historically called “malignant patterns”) include abundant and generalized rhythmic or periodic patterns (RPPs), electroencephalographic seizures, discontinuous background, low voltage, unreactive EEG and antero-posterior gradient reversion. Most studies assessed the prognostic value of these patterns as a whole, rather than evaluating their individual performance [,]. The prognostic value of “indeterminate” EEG remains very heterogeneous among the different EEG patterns that can be observed. According to studies, the FPR for predicting a poor outcome ranges from 0 to 33%. Thus, these EEG are not recognized as robust markers of poor outcome, due to the risk of false pessimist prediction.•“Favourable” EEG patterns (historically called “benign patterns”) are defined as absence of malignant or highly malignant features, corresponding to a continuous or nearly continuous background, normal voltage, no superimposed abnormalities and preserved reactivity to stimuli. A “favourable/benign” EEG is highly predictive of good outcome when recorded during the first 12, 24–72 h after CA (specificity 56.5–100 %, predictive positive value - PPV 70–94 %, sensitivity 30–80 %) [,,,, , , , ]. A major point is that, in neuroprognostication after CA, the background is the most important component of the EEG. “Unfavorable” EEG patterns (historically called “Highly malignant patterns”), including 3 main patterns: suppression, suppression with superimposed periodic discharges, and burst suppression. These patterns are recognized as robust markers of poor outcome (i.e., specificity 95–100 %, FPR 0−5%, sensitivity highly heterogeneous according to timing of EEG recording) when observed at least 24 h after CA [,,]. Therefore, these profiles are considered one of the six prognostic markers of poor prognosis in the 2025 ERC-ESICM guidelines []. The morphology of bursts in burst-suppression patterns can also be very informative. Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is characterized by highly stereotyped bursts with nearly identical morphology, whereas burst-suppression without identical bursts exhibits greater variability in burst morphology. BSIB appears to be more specifically associated with severe HIBI, while non-identical burst-suppression may also result from high doses of sedative agents. After CA, BSIB is strongly associated with poor outcomes, and its prognostic accuracy appears less dependent on EEG timing than that of non-identical burst-suppression [].

“Indeterminate” EEG patterns (historically called “malignant patterns”) include abundant and generalized rhythmic or periodic patterns (RPPs), electroencephalographic seizures, discontinuous background, low voltage, unreactive EEG and antero-posterior gradient reversion. Most studies assessed the prognostic value of these patterns as a whole, rather than evaluating their individual performance [,]. The prognostic value of “indeterminate” EEG remains very heterogeneous among the different EEG patterns that can be observed. According to studies, the FPR for predicting a poor outcome ranges from 0 to 33%. Thus, these EEG are not recognized as robust markers of poor outcome, due to the risk of false pessimist prediction.

“Favourable” EEG patterns (historically called “benign patterns”) are defined as absence of malignant or highly malignant features, corresponding to a continuous or nearly continuous background, normal voltage, no superimposed abnormalities and preserved reactivity to stimuli. A “favourable/benign” EEG is highly predictive of good outcome when recorded during the first 12, 24–72 h after CA (specificity 56.5–100 %, predictive positive value - PPV 70–94 %, sensitivity 30–80 %) [,,,, , , , ]. A major point is that, in neuroprognostication after CA, the background is the most important component of the EEG. Thus, early continuous or nearly continuous, with normal voltage and no superimposed abnormalities (especially within 12−24 h or even in the first 72 h) is now one of the four prognostic markers used to predict a good outcome in the 2025 ERC-ESICM recommendations [].

Thus, many patients with an “Indeterminate/malignant” EEG patterns remain in prognostic uncertainty. Nevertheless, the prognostic implications of a single malignant EEG feature are likely to differ from those associated with multiple concomitant malignant EEG features in terms of the severity of HIBI. A bicentric study including 1076 patients assessed the prognostic value of combined malignant EEG criteria observed on a single early EEG towards poor outcome and evaluated the effect on prognostic uncertainty. A single malignant EEG feature had limited specificity (81.4%) for predicting poor outcome. Conversely, the presence of 2, 3, or 4 malignant EEG criteria was highly indicative of poor outcome (specificity of 98.1%–100%). Finally, multiple malignant EEG features reclassified approximately 31% of patients from the “indeterminate” category to the "likely poor outcome" category, substantially reducing prognostic uncertainty []. The same results were found in a previous study []. Nevertheless, these criteria should always be considered as a part of a multimodal approach, to minimize the risk of falsely pessimistic predictions. Finally, the presence of an isolated malignant criterion should prompt clinicians to observe and re-evaluate the patient, as neurological recovery remains possible, according to guidelines [].

This new EEG-based approach may significantly reduce prognostic uncertainty in this population. Indeed, the current algorithm for predicting poor outcome - which includes “unfavorable/highly malignant” EEG patterns > 24 h - appears to be very effective, classifying 50–60% of patients as “poor outcome very likely” [,]. Conversely, criteria predictive of a favourable outcome - including “favourable/benign” EEG patterns < 72 h - allow for the reclassification of approximately 20% of patients who were initially considered with “indeterminate prognosis” []. These favourable prognostic criteria have been extensively validated [,,,,,] and have now been incorporated into the 2025 ERC–ESICM guidelines []. Consequently, the proportion of patients with prognostic uncertainty could be reduced to only 20–30%. Within this subgroup, using multiple “indeterminate/malignant” EEG criteria could reclassify about a third of patients from “indeterminate prognosis” to “poor outcome likely” [] (). However, these “multiple indeterminate/malignant” EEG criteria are not currently included in ERC-ESICM recommendations [], as their prognostic performance requires further external validation before they can be recommended for routine clinical practice. Finally, future research aimed at identifying and validating new prognostic markers will likely focus primarily on this subgroup of patients with an indeterminate outcome.

The timing of the EEG recording varies considerably between studies. It ranges from 6−12 h (under sedation) to 7 days or more [,] (). As EEG reflects “real time” cortical activity, patterns of evolution over time could provide interesting prognostic information(). However, both the timing of EEG recording and the effects of sedation, commonly administered during the first 24 h after CA, must be carefully considered. When the EEG is performed immediately after ROSC, the EEG background is sometimes suppressed, even in some patients who will subsequently experience early awakening after sedation is stopped. For this reason, the EEG pattern should not be used for predicting poor outcome within the first 12 or even 24 h after CA, due to the risk falsely pessimistic prediction. After 12−24 h, it typically evolves rapidly towards different “unfavourable”, “indeterminate” or “favourable” patterns, highly correlated with the severity of the HIBI and the neurological outcome.

Regarding poor outcome prediction, the timing of EEG recording is a major issue. Indeed, “unfavorable” EEG patterns tend to disappear in the first days after CA, which reduces their sensitivity for predicting a poor outcome [,,,,]. Thus, “unfavorable” EEGs, recorded as early as 6−12 h after CA, have the greatest sensitivity (71–91% according to studies), despite moderate specificity. This sensitivity becomes more variable (10–84%) between 12 and 24 h, then decreases sharply between 48 and 72 h and beyond (6–48%). Moreover, in a large prospective cohort study, the sensitivity of a “unfavorable” EEG was 47%, 30% and 22% at 12, 24 and 36 h after CA respectively, with a very high specificity in all cases []. Thus, some patients with an unfavourable outcome may initially present an “unfavorable” EEG at 12−24 h (suggesting a “poor outcome likely”) which then evolves toward an “indeterminate” EEG (in favour of an “undetermined outcome”) (). These findings should encourage intensivists to perform EEG recording as early as 24 h after CA - ideally in the absence of sedation or with the minimal effective dose - in order to assess long term neurological prognosis, and to repeat the EEG at 48−72 h in the absence of favourable clinical evolution []. Finally, data regarding “unfavorable” EEG performed beyond 72 h are more limited and less robust. Nevertheless, it may be highly specific of poor outcome, despite a very low sensitivity [].

Conversely, in the vast majority of patients with an early awakening and a good outcome at 3 months, EEG background activity becomes continuous or sub-continuous, of normo-voltage and reactive within the first 12, 24 or 72 h after ROSC, even with low to moderate dose of sedation. Thus, the early recording of this pattern is considered as highly specific of a good outcome. Interestingly, the prognostic value of a “favourable” EEG recorded at 12−24 h after CA was higher (specificity 86–95 %) compared to a “favourable” EEG observed at 72 h (specificity 65–78 %) [,,]. Data regarding “favourable” EEG observed beyond 72 h are more limited []. At this stage, EEG background activity tends to be more continuous in all patients (including those with poor outcome at 3 months), which probably reduces the specificity of this EEG criterion for predicting a good outcome. Thus, the prognostic value of this “late favourable” EEG appears to be limited and, in all case, inferior to that of “early favourable EEG” (i.e., first 24−72 h after CA).

Sedation is often used in the first 24 h after CA, to facilitate post-resuscitation care (mechanical ventilation, management of post-resuscitation shock, temperature management) but it can alter the prognostic assessment in different ways. Sedation may delay awakening [,], confound pupillary and corneal reflexes and alter EEG patterns [,]. These different points encourage the use of light to moderate dose of sedation with short-acting drugs, such as propofol [,]. The question of whether EEG remains a reliable prognostic tool in sedated patients has been debated for a long time. Most sedative drugs have similar effects on EEG spectrum, namely decreasing frequency, continuity and amplitude, in a dose dependent manner. More specifically, high doses of midazolam and propofol could generate burst suppression patterns, which is an important predictor of unfavourable outcome []. Nevertheless, the induction of a burst suppression pattern is usually observed with higher doses than those used for the management of post-CA patients [,,]. Thus, an increasing amount of data suggests that light to moderate sedation (i.e., median doses < 3.0–3.5 mg/kg/h of propofol or midazolam < 63–68 μg/kg/h) does not affect the prognostic value of EEG. Moreover, patients who displayed a continuous background seems to be sedated with higher doses (2.67 mg/kg/h of propofol) compared to patients with burst suppression or suppression EEG patterns (2.07 mg/kg/h and 1.94 mg/kg/h respectively) []. These results, with some others [,,,,, , , , , , ], suggest that light to moderate sedation used of the post-CA management does not significantly impair the prognostic accuracy of the early EEG (i.e., at 12−24 h after CA) compared to recordings carried out after 48−72 h. Thus, EEG should ideally be performed in the absence of sedation or under the lowest effective sedative dose, as early as 24 h after CA to avoid missing the early time window during which EEG provides the highest prognostic accuracy. Caution is needed when patients required deep sedation with two different drugs, as the association of midazolam and propofol decreased the probability to detect “favourable” EEG patterns [].

SSEPs are valuable neurophysiological tools to assess subcortical and cortical integrity in comatose patients after CA [,,]. Bilateral absence of the N20 cortical wave in SSEPs of the median nerves, recorded from 24 h after CA, is one of six prognostic markers already recommended for poor outcome prediction []. Indeed, a bilaterally absent N20 SSEP (defined as no responses or a response with an amplitude <0.20 μV according to recommendations []) is considered to be the most robust predictor of poor outcome. This criterion is highly specific (specificity 100%, FPR 0%) despite a moderate sensitivity (30–65 %, according to studies). Interestingly, the SSEPs N20 responses are not affected by usual doses of sedative drugs in the post-CA context []. However, N20 results could be affected by hypothermia (<35 °C), and low blood-pressure (mean arterial pressure – MAP <60 mmHg) [].

Regarding the prognostic value of the bilateral N20 absence in the first 12−24 h post-CA [,,,, , ], the specificity appears to approach 100%, comparable to that observed with recording performed after 24 h. Nevertheless, some rare cases have been reported of patients with bilateral absence of N20 at this early stage who subsequently showed a favourable outcome at 3 months []. In some cases, the cause of a false-positive result was an incorrect reading of the SSEP records []. Studies assessing interobserver agreement of SSEP reading have shown that the risk of misclassification is higher in the presence of artefacts or low amplitude of the N20 wave [,]. Thus, interrater agreement among SSEP readers increases significantly after neuromuscular blockade. Moreover, a recent study suggested that N20 SSEPs may provide high prognostic accuracy as early as 6 h after CA, possibly because they allow the assessment of a larger proportion of patients before their progression towards awakening or death []. Regarding late SSEP recording (i.e., after 4–6 days), data remain limited, but some studies suggested that the bilateral absence of N20 remains an excellent predictor of poor outcome [].

Regarding the amplitude of the N20 wave, some studies have shown that a very low bilateral amplitude of the N20 (<0.40, 0.60 or 1 μV according to studies) is as specific as its bilateral absence in predicting a poor outcome, including when recorded at the very early phase (6−12 h post CA) [,, , ,, , , , ]. Conversely, the preservation of a bilateral N20 responses with high amplitudes (>3, 4 or 5 μV across studies) may be associated with favourable outcomes [,,, , , , ]. The prognostic value of the N20 amplitude may evolved over time after CA. First, the prognostic value of high N20 amplitudes for favorable outcomes could decreases between 12 and 72 h after CA, due to a progressive increase in N20 amplitudes among patients with poor outcomes []. Second, initially present but low-amplitude N20 responses may progressively disappear in patients with poor outcomes []. As N20 amplitude is strongly correlated with the severity of HIBI [], these findings highlight the dynamic nature of HIBI and the potential evolution of N20 responses over time.

The prognostic value of a unilateral absence of N20 for predicting poor outcome remain also discussed. Two studies suggested that unilateral absence with a preserved but low voltage contralateral N20 response is highly specific of poor outcome, when recorded at 12, 24 or 72 h after CA [,]. Another study assessed the prognostic value of an unilateral N20 absence at the acute (i.e., 72 h after CA) and sub-acute phase (day 20 after CA): unilateral absence of N20 was highly specific of poor outcome (specificity 96.7%) despite very low sensitivity [].

Finally, data concerning the N20 amplitude and unilateral absence of N20 are currently scarce, explaining why the ERC-ESICM 2025 recommendations do not recommend their use for assessing neurological prognosis after CA. Thus, further evidence is needed before these criteria can be incorporated into prognostic algorithms [].

Brain imaging remains a major tool for neuroprognostication of unconscious patients after CA. Current 2025 ERC-ESICM guidelines recommend the use of either CT (at any time) or MRI (after 48 h but ideally before day 7) in the multimodal strategy []. Although significantly less sensitive than MRI, CT is frequently performed in the early phase after CA, to investigate the underlying cause of CA []. CT scan may be informative when early signs of poor outcome are observed, such as loss of differentiation between grey and white matter (using low values of G/W matter ratio, for example) or cerebral oedema [,]. However, because the optimal timing for detecting these abnormalities is beyond 48 h, CT performed at admission as part of the etiological assessment may be insufficiently sensitive to highlight these signs. Thus, the 2025 ERC-ESICM guidelines recommend repeating brain CT at 72−96 h from CA if the patient is still unconscious and the early brain CT does not show signs of HIBI. Otherwise, a normal CT scan is not systematically associated with a good outcome. In patients with an unremarkable CT, brain MRI should be considered, ideally beyond 48 h and within the first 7 days, when diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) abnormalities are most reliably detected []. Indeed, MRI may help to predict poor and good outcomes, and remain more sensitive compared to CT. The 2025 ERC-ESICM recommendations suggested to consider “diffuse and extensive anoxo-ischemic injury” (i.e., diffuse and bilateral cortical and basal ganglia injuries) observed on the DWI sequence as highly specific of poor outcome [,]. Conversely, a normal DWI sequence in the first 7 days seems to be highly predictive of good outcome [,,,].

However, MRI findings evolve over time and across brain regions, which may result in potential misinterpretation and misclassification (). Although the data are not very robust, it appears that the timing of MRI acquisition is crucial to ensure the detection of abnormalities predictive of poor outcome:-Within the first 24 h, brain MRI may appear normal, including in patients with a poor outcome at 3 months [].-Between 48 h and day 7, MRI may begin to reveal cytotoxic oedema. This leads to restricted extracellular water diffusion, typically manifesting as DWI hyperintensity with corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) reduction (ADC values < 0.6 × 10−³ mm²/s). The affected regions often include the cortical area and particularly the posterior cortical ribbon, the striatum, the splenium of the corpus callosum, and the hippocampi []. In this acute phase, FLAIR sequences may also demonstrate hyperintensity and thickening of cortical ribbon and basal ganglia. At this stage, the presence of extensive lesions (DWI hyperintensity) in all the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia is highly specific of poor outcome. Nevertheless, the assessments remaining potentially subjective and lacking a clearly established quantitative framework.-After day 7, the subacute phase is characterized by vasogenic oedema, which appears hyperintense on both FLAIR and DWI, accompanied by a normalization of the ADC map (loss of diffusion restriction) []. Reduced DWI within the corona radiata may also appear, especially in patients with poor outcome, indicating the onset of white matter degeneration secondary to diffuse cortical injury. Finally, micro-haemorrhagic changes due to blood-brain barrier disruption typically emerge later in this phase on the susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI). At this time, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) could provide additional insight into white matter microstructure. Although of limited accessibility, some data suggested that reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) and increased diffusivity, markers of microstructural damage derived from DTI, are strongly correlated with functional outcome [,].-After day 14, FLAIR imaging may be normal or demonstrate residual hyperintensities in some regions (cortical area, basal ganglia, and/or bilateral white matter), sometimes accompanied by cortical atrophy or heterogeneous signals due to necrosis. At this stage, DWI typically appears normal due to resolution of cytotoxic oedema, thus offering limited prognostic value [,]. SWI may show necrotic-haemorrhagic lesions, which are more frequent in this phase. Cortical or basal ganglia contrast enhancement on T1-weighted imaging after gadolinium administration could also be observed, related to blood–brain barrier disruption, and suggesting laminar necrosis. This criterion seems to be associated with poor outcome, although the data remain limited [].

Within the first 24 h, brain MRI may appear normal, including in patients with a poor outcome at 3 months [].

Between 48 h and day 7, MRI may begin to reveal cytotoxic oedema. This leads to restricted extracellular water diffusion, typically manifesting as DWI hyperintensity with corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) reduction (ADC values < 0.6 × 10−³ mm²/s). The affected regions often include the cortical area and particularly the posterior cortical ribbon, the striatum, the splenium of the corpus callosum, and the hippocampi []. In this acute phase, FLAIR sequences may also demonstrate hyperintensity and thickening of cortical ribbon and basal ganglia. At this stage, the presence of extensive lesions (DWI hyperintensity) in all the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia is highly specific of poor outcome. Nevertheless, the assessments remaining potentially subjective and lacking a clearly established quantitative framework.

After day 7, the subacute phase is characterized by vasogenic oedema, which appears hyperintense on both FLAIR and DWI, accompanied by a normalization of the ADC map (loss of diffusion restriction) []. Reduced DWI within the corona radiata may also appear, especially in patients with poor outcome, indicating the onset of white matter degeneration secondary to diffuse cortical injury. Finally, micro-haemorrhagic changes due to blood-brain barrier disruption typically emerge later in this phase on the susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI). At this time, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) could provide additional insight into white matter microstructure. Although of limited accessibility, some data suggested that reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) and increased diffusivity, markers of microstructural damage derived from DTI, are strongly correlated with functional outcome [,].

After day 14, FLAIR imaging may be normal or demonstrate residual hyperintensities in some regions (cortical area, basal ganglia, and/or bilateral white matter), sometimes accompanied by cortical atrophy or heterogeneous signals due to necrosis. At this stage, DWI typically appears normal due to resolution of cytotoxic oedema, thus offering limited prognostic value [,]. SWI may show necrotic-haemorrhagic lesions, which are more frequent in this phase. Cortical or basal ganglia contrast enhancement on T1-weighted imaging after gadolinium administration could also be observed, related to blood–brain barrier disruption, and suggesting laminar necrosis. This criterion seems to be associated with poor outcome, although the data remain limited [].

Blood biomarkers of neuronal and glial injury are very useful for assessing neurological prognosis in comatose patients after CA (). Currently, only serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE) is recommended by the 2025 ERC-ESICM guidelines to assess both favourable and unfavourable neurological outcomes. Indeed, a blood NSE level >60 μg/L at 48 and/or 72 h appears to be highly specific for predicting poor outcome []. An increasing NSE trend between 24, 48, and/or 72 h is also associated with an unfavourable outcome [,, , ]. Conversely, low plasma NSE levels at 24, 48 and/or 72 h are highly predictive of a favourable outcome [], as is a decrease in NSE levels over the first 72 h after CA [,,,, , ]. Regarding the best threshold of NSE, current guidelines suggest considering NSE levels <17 μg/L within the first 72 h after CA as a highly specific, although poorly sensitive, predictor of favourable outcome []. Other studies have identified thresholds of NSE <30 or <45 μg/L within the first 72 h as providing the optimized balance between (higher) sensitivity and (slightly lower) specificity [,,]. Thus, the currently recommended threshold may need to be reassessed and potentially raised, although further studies are warranted. In any case, low NSE levels combined with a decreasing trend over time should encourage intensivists to continue observation and reassess the patient's neurological status rather than making premature prognostic decisions. Regarding NSE trends, the NSE peak occurs around 72 h after CA in patients with poor outcome, and as early as 24 h in those with favourable outcome. Data regarding the potential benefit of measuring NSE beyond the very first days remain limited, and no clear threshold has been identified for values ​​obtained from 96 h onwards [,]. Therefore, late NSE measurements appear to be of limited utility. However, if measurements could not be performed within the first three days and a late value exceeds 60 μg/L, it may still be considered suggestive of poor outcome, given the known temporal kinetics of this biomarker [,]. Regarding NSE, several confounding factors must be considered: for example, haemolysis (for example, related to ECMO or other extracorporeal circuits) may increase serum NSE levels, or neuroendocrine tumours.

Regarding other biomarkers of neuronal (TAU protein, Ubiquitin C-terminal Hydrolase L1- UCH-L1, and neurofilament light chain - NFL) or glial injury (S100B protein – S100Bp, Glial Fibrillary Astrocyte Protein - GFAP), the available data are more limited and less robust. They are not currently recommended for clinical practice, as cut-off values associated with good or poor outcomes are not well established [,]. Regarding their kinetics, TAU protein and NFL appear to reach a peak around 72 h after CA, similar to NSE, but their temporal evolution does not seem to have major prognostic value []. However, available data remain very limited, and further studies are needed to characterize the temporal kinetics of NFL levels (CINEFIL study, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07760636). S100Bp is the earliest biomarker, peaking around 8 h after CA and within the first 24 h. Finally, GFAP and UCH-L1 appear to peak between 12 and 48 h after CA, although data remain scarce [] (). Some recent data suggest that the prognostic performance of NFL (Area Under Curve - AUC 0.90–0.95) [,, , , , , ] may be superior to that of NSE (AUC 0.80–0.90) at 24, 48, and 72 h [,,,,,,]. However, the cut-off values of NFL for predicting good or poor outcomes are not yet well defined, and variability in assay techniques may explain the wide discrepancies in reported thresholds across studies) [,, , , , , ]. Additional data are therefore needed to establish reliable cut-offs before considering NFL in clinical practices.

Available data confirms that clinicians now have clinical and paraclinical tools with well-established prognostic value for predicting neurological outcomes in comatose patients following CA. Combined within a multimodal algorithm, their performance has been confirmed in various clinical studies. These data also confirm the critical importance of strictly adhering to the recommended timing for collecting these parameters, as their interpretation and prognostic value can vary considerably over time. Future clinical research efforts should continue to strengthen this strategy, particularly by examining the added value of new indicators (biomarkers, late auditory evoked potentials, brain imaging techniques such as functional MRI, etc.) and testing them in clinical trials that minimize the risk of bias.

neuroscience.title: Relic of the Past or Clinical Compass? Re-Evaluating the Diagnostic Utility of Proton Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (1H-MRS) in Encephalitis and Infectious CNS Diseases
neuroscience.abstract: Neuroimaging of inflammatory and infectious CNS diseases using conventional MRI has limitations, such as the challenging differential diagnosis of visible lesions, as well as the absence of neuroimaging abnormalities despite severe symptoms. The aim of this review is to evaluate the diagnostic utility of proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) as a complementary method in inflammatory conditions and CNS infections of viral, bacterial, autoimmune, parasitic, or fungal etiology. We searched the PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases, including studies and case reports evaluating 1H-MRS across age groups in the acute, subacute, and chronic phases of CNS disorders. The review demonstrates that MRS can serve as a valuable, non-invasive method capable of revealing metabolic abnormalities within normal-appearing brain tissue on conventional MRI. Furthermore, 1H-MRS detects specific metabolites-including cytosolic amino acids, acetate, and succinate in bacterial abscesses, trehalose in fungal lesions, and guanidinoacetate in tuberculomas-assisting in their differentiation from neoplastic lesions. Neurometabolite levels may correlate with clinical status, symptom severity, and cognitive deficits, while longitudinal observations enable monitoring of disease progression and treatment response. Although 1H-MRS is limited by spectral overlap, it represents a valuable complement to conventional MRI; however, further longitudinal studies on larger patient cohorts are required.
neuroscience.text:
Inflammatory and infectious diseases of the central nervous system (CNS), including viral, bacterial, autoimmune, parasitic, and fungal disorders, represent significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. These challenges result from the wide spectrum of possible pathogens and the often nonspecific clinical manifestations []. Although standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is valuable for evaluating structural CNS abnormalities, it has considerable limitations in diagnosing certain encephalitides, such as anti-NMDAR (anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor) encephalitis and tick-borne encephalitis. In many patients with these conditions, MRI findings may be unremarkable despite clear clinical symptoms [,,].

Conventional MRI also has limitations for focal infectious CNS lesions, where differentiating infectious entities from neoplastic lesions can be difficult because of their nonspecific imaging appearance and resemblance to other intracranial pathologies, including tumors. In these cases, additional MRI techniques may provide complementary information to support differential diagnosis [].

Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) is a non-invasive modality that evaluates the metabolic profile of brain tissue. Key metabolites detectable by 1H-MRS include N-acetylaspartate (NAA), an indicator of neuronal integrity; choline (Cho), which reflects membrane turnover; creatine (Cr), associated with cellular energy metabolism; myo-inositol (mI), a marker of glial activity; glutamate (Glu) and glutamine (Gln), involved in glutamatergic metabolism; lactate (Lac), indicative of anaerobic metabolism; and lipids (Lip), which may signal membrane breakdown and necrosis []. By assessing these metabolites, 1H-MRS provides metabolic data that can indirectly evaluate neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative mechanisms. Additionally, 1H-MRS can detect specific metabolic products of microorganisms, including amino acids, acetate, succinate, and trehalose. Identifying these compounds may help diagnose specific CNS infections and distinguish them from other focal intracranial lesions [].

This review summarizes current evidence on the application and diagnostic utility of 1H-MRS in inflammatory and infectious CNS diseases, with particular focus on characteristic metabolic profiles and the potential role of this technique in differential diagnosis.

The PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases were searched using the combination of (1) AND (2) of the following keywords: (1) ‘magnetic resonance spectroscopy’, ‘MR spectroscopy’, ‘proton MR spectroscopy’, ‘1H MRS’, ‘MRS’, MRSI, MR spectroscopic imaging, CSI; and (2) ‘encephalitis’, ‘neuroinfection’, ‘autoimmune encephalitis’, ‘limbic encephalitis’, ‘viral encephalitis’, ‘parasitic CNS infection’, ‘brain abscess’, ‘fungal CNS infection’, ‘postinfectious encephalopathies’, ‘HIV-associated encephalopathy’, or ‘PML’.

Our review includes studies published between 1996 and 2026 (until 1 September 2026). We have included relevant articles in order to assess the utility of proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy among patients with inflammatory and infectious central nervous system disorders as accurately as possible. The included papers were original research studies or clinical case reports that used 1H -MRS with patients of all ages (both pediatric and adult) in acute, post-acute, or chronic stages of infectious, autoimmune, or inflammatory central nervous system disorders. A total of 63 unique publications, comprising original research studies and clinical case reports, were selected for the review. The included articles were analyzed with regard to: (1) disease-specific metabolic profiles identified by MRS; (2) the potential advantages of MRS over other neuroimaging modalities in the investigated conditions; (3) the potential role of MRS as an adjunctive tool in the differential diagnosis of these conditions; (4) the relationship between MRS abnormalities and the severity of clinical symptoms; (5) the potential use of MRS for monitoring disease progression and treatment response; and (6) the prognostic value of MRS findings and (7) methodological considerations, including echo times (short vs. long TE), voxel placement, and acquisition technique (single-voxel vs. multi-voxel).

We included data on the following: (1) deviations from normal values in spectral profiles of brain tissue and pathogen-derived metabolites, including NAA, Cho, Cr, mI, Lac, Lip, Glu, Gln, total creatine (tCr), Glu/Gln complex (Glx), cytosolic amino acids (alanine, leucine, valine), succinate, acetate, guanidinoacetate, trehalose, and pyruvate; (2) stage-dependent variations in metabolic profiles across acute, subacute, and chronic stages of the disease, as well as the reversibility of observed metabolic abnormalities following therapy; (3) the capability of MRS to identify diffuse, global, or occult metabolic alterations in normal-appearing brain tissue beyond focal lesions visible on conventional MRI; (4) the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of MRS relative to other neuroimaging modalities; (5) correlations of individual metabolic peaks and metabolite ratios with clinical severity scores, functional tests, and overall patient prognosis; and (6) the spatial concordance between the localization of MRS metabolic alterations and conventional MRI findings.

Previous studies using MRS in the acute phase of HSE have shown reduced NAA levels and a decreased NAA/Cr ratio, indicating a loss of neuronal integrity associated with the acute inflammatory process in affected areas [,]. However, these values partially or fully returned to normal within one year after disease onset [,]. In addition, the acute phase of the disease was defined by increased Cho levels and an elevated Cho/Cr ratio, associated with macrophage infiltration, as well as increased mI levels and an elevated mI/Cr ratio, reflecting pronounced gliosis. During the acute phase of necrotizing encephalitis, elevated lactate and lipid levels have also been reported [].

It is worth noting that the studies and clinical case reports included in the present review (as summarized in ) differ in terms of technical acquisition parameters, which are often not reported at all. These discrepancies may have affected the comparability and interpretation of the findings across individual studies. In the context of HSE, the previously cited study by Sämann et al. [] reported elevated lactate levels during the acute phase of HSE and increased mI levels during follow-up examinations, whereas Takanashi et al. did not describe such changes in their patient []. However, this does not necessarily indicate that these metabolic alterations were absent in the patient reported by Takanashi et al. The long echo time (TE) used in their study (136 ms) limited the reliable assessment of mI and lipids and introduced the risk of Lac peak inversion [].

Moreover, MRS has shown that HSE is a generalized process not confined to the temporal lobe affected by the disease on conventional MRI. Hitosugi et al. also demonstrated metabolic abnormalities in the contralateral temporal lobe, including a mild decrease in the NAA/Cr ratio and an increase in the Cho/Cr ratio [].

The pattern of metabolic abnormalities observed in HSE provides insight into the disease’s pathophysiology. It may help assess the severity and reversibility of neurodegeneration, the degree of gliosis, and the extent of necrosis. However, MRS has limited diagnostic value in differentiating HSE from other conditions, as the metabolic profile can resemble that of other encephalitides and gliomas, including decreased NAA and increased Cho, Lac, and lipid levels [].

The study by Zawadzki et al. on TBE showed that although conventional MRI findings are often normal, MRS may disclose significant metabolic abnormalities in the central nervous system [].
