Patients in the acute phase of TBE exhibited a decreased NAA/Cr ratio in both thalami and in the right basal ganglia, as well as an increased Cho/Cr ratio in the left thalamus and the left cerebellar hemisphere compared with healthy controls.

The study was performed using a long echo time (TE = 135 ms), which facilitated the assessment of signals from major metabolites, including NAA, Cho, and Cr, but limited the detailed characterization of the overall metabolic profile, particularly with regard to myo-inositol (mI) and glutamate–glutamine (Glx). This represents an area that warrants further investigation. In addition, studies using multi-voxel proton MR spectroscopy, or magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI), could provide valuable complementary information, as Zawadzki et al. used single-voxel spectroscopy (SVS), with voxels positioned only in selected brain structures. This is particularly relevant given that conventional MRI revealed no structural abnormalities in the patients studied.

Considering that nearly half of patients with TBE develop post-encephalitic syndrome (PES), characterized by persistent symptoms such as cognitive impairment and neurological deficits that may last for many years after the acute phase of TBE, longitudinal studies comparing metabolic profiles between patients who develop PES and those who do not appear particularly warranted. Another important research direction would be to investigate the associations between metabolic profiles and clinical symptom severity.

Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is often associated with a serious clinical course, although conventional MRI does not show any abnormalities in about half of the cases; this is referred to as the clinical-radiological paradox [].

Splendiani et al. reported the case of a 17-year-old patient who had been diagnosed with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and in whom the cerebellar lesions displayed a moderate decrease in the NAA peak (together with a moderate reduction in the NAA/Cr ratio), which suggests metabolic dysfunction or neuronal loss, and a moderate rise in the choline peak (along with a moderate increase in the Cho/Cr ratio), indicating an inflammatory process and increased cellularity []. The spectrum did not show any rise in lactate or lipid concentrations-findings that would point to necrosis or severe hypoxia. The authors stated that MRS can be of help in distinguishing an inflammatory process from high-grade neoplastic lesions (these being characterized by a considerably higher Cho/NAA ratio) and from HSE, in which a markedly reduced NAA concentration, greatly elevated choline peaks, and frequently detectable lactate and lipid peaks due to tissue necrosis are more commonly seen. Following treatment with methylprednisolone, the symptoms disappeared, and a follow-up spectroscopy carried out six months later revealed a complete normalization of the spectrum, showing that the initial changes were due to reversible neuronal damage and not to permanent necrosis. Kataoka et al. also described similar findings concerning a lowering of NAA levels during the acute phase of the disease in the basal ganglia and thalami, followed by a normalization of the metabolic profile in the later phase [].

The observations described above concerned individual clinical cases; however, Hudasch et al. recently published a study describing the use of whole-brain MRS in 20 patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and 20 healthy controls []. The study showed that metabolic changes in anti-NMDAR encephalitis can be diffuse. A decreased NAA peak was observed in the right temporal lobe, an elevated Cho peak in the left frontal and parietal lobes as well as both occipital lobes, an elevated tCr peak in the left frontal and occipital lobes, and an increase in mI was noted in the left parietal lobe and both occipital lobes. Furthermore, MRS may help assess the patient’s clinical status, as Cho concentration in the right occipital lobe correlated with the results of the HPT for the left hand (fine motor skills test) and the walking speed test. Meanwhile, mI concentration in the right occipital lobe correlated with the disease severity evaluated by the NEOS score (anti-NMDAR encephalitis one-year functional status score). However, it is worth emphasizing that these results should be considered hypothesis-generating. For multi-voxel analysis, the 2019 ISMRM expert consensus (Wilson et al.), which defines current standards in 1H -MRS, requires rigorous Type I error control (e.g., FDR or Bonferroni correction) due to the large number of voxels compared []. In contrast, the study by Hudasch et al. utilized uncorrected Student’s t-tests, meaning these findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger, independently validated cohorts.

Fortea et al. examined 32 patients during the post-acute stage of anti-NMDAR encephalitis []. Their study found decreased levels of glutamate and glutamate + glutamine, along with elevated mI in the left dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) compared with healthy controls. No statistically significant differences in NAA concentrations were noted between the study group and the control group. Interestingly, the observed metabolic disturbances persisted throughout the entire follow-up period (24 months). The authors suggest that the persistent impairment of glutamatergic neurotransmission may result from an earlier increase in glutamate concentration during the acute phase of NMDARE caused by excessive activation of AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptors by anti-NMDAR antibodies, which subsequently leads to their desensitization and lower glutamate concentration in the post-acute phase. Conversely, the increase in myo-inositol concentration is linked to astrocytic activation and persistent inflammation. Interestingly, this study did not show significant differences in the metabolic profile of the medial temporal lobe, a region commonly implicated in NMDARE []. However, it cannot be overlooked that the loss of a portion of the data due to low spectroscopic spectrum quality may have contributed to the lack of statistical significance []. The quality of the data could have been substantially affected by the use of the PRESS sequence, which is highly sensitive to magnetic field inhomogeneities (in this case related to the proximity of the paranasal sinuses), and the aforementioned expert consensus recommends using the semi-LASER/LASER sequence, explicitly noting that the application of PRESS at 3T can cause a significant chemical shift displacement error (CSDE).

To sum up, the present scientific evidence shows that MRS is able to detect metabolic changes which are not visible on standard MRI, thereby facilitating the resolution of the clinical-radiological paradox. Moreover, MRS can assist in distinguishing anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis from neoplastic processes, as well as in assessing the reversibility of neuronal damage, the patient’s clinical condition, and prognosis.

Limbic encephalitis (LE) is a clinical syndrome caused by an autoimmune or paraneoplastic process, characterized by a subacute course of symptoms involving the limbic system, along with structural and functional signs of damage to the medial temporal lobes []. Depending on the etiology, LE may be associated with antibodies against LGI1 (Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1), GABA-BR (Gamma-aminobutyric acid type B receptor), AMPAR, and CASPR2 (Contactin-associated protein-like 2), as well as intracellular antigens such as Hu and Ma2 [].

The most common subtype of LE investigated in studies using MRS to date is anti-LGI1 encephalitis. Hang et al. reported that, in a patient with anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis, they observed a moderate reduction in NAA and the NAA/Cr ratio, accompanied by a slight increase in Cho and the Cho/Cr ratio within the left hippocampus [].

Larger study has focused on patients in the post-acute phase following LE. Szots et al. used MRS to examine nine patients who had experienced LGI1 antibody-associated encephalitis an average of 33 months earlier []. This form of encephalitis typically involves the limbic system, which was also demonstrated in the study population, with 8 of 9 patients developing hippocampal atrophy and sclerosis. However, when searching for metabolic abnormalities suggestive of more widespread brain involvement, the authors placed voxels in the right centrum semiovale and mid-occipital gray matter. The study found reduced glutamine/glutamate concentrations in the centrum semiovale white matter compared with healthy controls, indicating persistent alterations in the brain’s metabolic profile beyond the hippocampi. The study also noted lower NAA levels in the study group compared to the control group, although the difference was not statistically significant. The authors note that the mean age in both groups was approximately 60 years, suggesting that the lack of an observed difference could potentially be influenced by confounding aging effects.

In patients who were in the post-acute phase of autoimmune encephalitis, Taraschenko and colleagues found that the concentration of myo-inositol was increased []. They observed alterations in the metabolic profile of the hippocampus (in AE patients with various antibodies (anti-NMDAR, anti-GAD65, anti-LGI1, and the seronegative form of AE)), but no such changes were seen in the prefrontal cortex. Methodologically, the study adheres to high-standard expert consensus guidelines for MRS by employing a short-echo semiLASER sequence (TE = 30 ms) and FASTMAP shimming, which ensured optimal spectral quality and minimized chemical shift displacement errors in the hippocampus.

Interestingly, a correlation was noted between a higher level of myo-inositol and poorer performance on memory recognition tests, as well as better attention in the patients. Furthermore, a correlation was found between a higher concentration of tCr in the hippocampus and a faster rate of information processing. This indicates that MRS might be able to reflect the functional consequences of previous encephalitis, and in the future myo-inositol could act as a potential biomarker for monitoring the recovery process and as a target for cognitive-protective therapies [].

To the best of our knowledge, MRS has been used in only one case of paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis. Isik et al. described a patient with anti-Hu antibodies in whom, during the early stage of the disease (3 weeks from symptom onset), they noted a slight decrease in NAA and an increase in mI in the right superior temporal neocortex. In the later stage, however, the authors demonstrated progressive neuronal loss (decreased NAA), increased gliosis (increased mI/Cr), accelerated membrane turnover (increased Cho/Cr), and anaerobic glycolysis (lactate peak) in the medial temporal lobe regions []. It is worth pointing out that this case report complied with the technical standards of the time (the paper was published in 2004). However, from the perspective of the current 2019 consensus, it exhibits several methodological limitations, namely: the use of the PRESS sequence instead of semi-LASER, the absence of an unsuppressed water reference scan, and the use of peak-based measurements rather than automated spectral fitting with a simulated metabolite basis set. Given these methodological limitations and the paucity of published evidence, further studies are needed to characterize MRS findings in paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis.

Villanueva-Castro et al., although they studied only patients with Low-Grade Glioma, emphasize the utility of MRS in differentiating LE from Low-Grade Glioma, as all patients who were ultimately diagnosed with a tumor presented to the hospital with suspected LE []. However, high Cho/NAA ratios, which averaged 2.3, suggested a neoplastic diagnosis. Importantly, this study did not specify the acquisition parameters due to a lack of standardization in the study protocols.

Rasmussen’s encephalitis is a chronic, progressive, and most often unilateral encephalitis, the pathomechanism of which has not been fully elucidated. Current data indicate that a T-cell-dependent immune response and microglial activation play an important role in the disease’s pathomechanism []. The disease leads to progressive atrophy of one cerebral hemisphere, permanent neurological deficits, and often drug-resistant epilepsy [].

To date, research does not show evidence of abnormalities specific exclusively to this disease entity. As in the case of other types of encephalitis, MRS examination reveals a reduced NAA level and an elevated or normal Cho level, which leads to a decrease in the NAA/Cr and NAA/Cho ratios, suggesting neuronal loss or dysfunction [,]. Increase mI levels have also been reported [,].

In patients who have recently experienced uncontrolled epileptic seizures, a transient lactate peak has also been described [,,]. It is also worth noting here that the metabolic profile in Rasmussen’s encephalitis fluctuates, and after status epilepticus, a transient decrease in the concentration of NAA, Cr, and Cho may also occur, as well as changes in Glx concentration [].

Sundgren et al., utilizing multivoxel MRS, demonstrated that this technique may be more sensitive than conventional MRI for detecting brain tissue abnormalities in Rasmussen’s encephalitis []. In addition to abnormal metabolic profiles in the affected hemisphere, they observed decreased NAA/Cho and NAA/Cr ratios in the morphologically normal frontal periventricular white matter of the contralateral hemisphere. These abnormalities preceded the onset of neurological symptoms involving that hemisphere by 4 months.

Faria et al. also observed that metabolic changes in MRS may correlate with disease severity, as among patients with a milder disease course whose seizures were pharmacologically controlled, MRS showed no significant metabolic differences between the affected and contralateral cerebral hemispheres, whereas in cases with a more severe course, metabolic disturbances were observed, i.e., a decrease in NAA and an increase in Cho and Lac [].

For the interpretation of the findings discussed above, it is important to acknowledge that the literature on the application of MRS in Rasmussen’s encephalitis is based predominantly on small, heterogeneous case series and individual case reports, which frequently lack standardized acquisition protocols and established quality control measures for spectral data.

In summary, the available data indicate that MRS can show both focal and diffuse metabolic disturbances in autoimmune and paraneoplastic encephalitis. Depending on the disease entity and stage, the observed changes primarily include decreased NAA peaks, increased mI, and altered choline and Glu/Gln metabolism. Changes in brain tissue metabolic profiles during the post-acute phase of the disease, as well as their associations with the severity of cognitive deficits and clinical symptoms, appear particularly interesting. Moreover, reports suggest that MRS can detect metabolic abnormalities before the onset of overt clinical symptoms or the appearance of abnormalities on conventional MRI. In some cases, spectroscopic abnormalities normalized alongside clinical improvement, implying the possibility of reversibility of some observed disturbances. The lack of a specific MRS profile for individual entities, combined with a small number of studies and small sample sizes, limits the utility of MRS as a standalone diagnostic tool; however, this method can serve as an important adjunct to conventional MRI, supporting differential diagnosis.

A brain abscess is an encapsulated collection of pus resulting as a complication of a focal intracerebral infection, most commonly caused by bacteria of the Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species [].

In the case of bacterial brain abscesses, MRS can provide valuable clues in differentiating them from other cystic lesions, as it detects bacterial metabolic products and tissue degeneration products within the abscess [,]. Normally occurring tissue metabolites such as NAA, Cho, and Cr are significantly reduced or completely absent. Importantly, the presence of NAA, Cho, and Cr does not reflect the intrinsic metabolic profile of the abscess cavity itself, but rather stems from the partial volume effect.

In a spectrum obtained from a bacterial abscess prior to or in the initial phase of antibacterial therapy, characteristic amino acid peaks (alanine at 1.47 ppm, leucine at 0.95–1.05 ppm, and valine at 0.97–1.03 ppm) can be observed, which are products of protein proteolysis in the necrotic center of the abscess, alongside succinate peaks (2.4 ppm) and acetate peaks (1.9 ppm)-products of bacterial metabolism-and lactate (1.3 ppm), a product of anaerobic glycolysis [,]. Studies indicate that peaks corresponding to bacteria-associated metabolites (acetate, succinate, and pyruvate) disappear most rapidly during effective antimicrobial treatment [,]. Dev et al. additionally observed the disappearance of amino acid peaks following prolonged antibiotic therapy (4 weeks), with only the lactate peak remaining []. The peak at approximately 2.4 ppm is commonly attributed to succinate in the context of bacterial brain abscesses. However, it is worth noting that pyruvate signals may also occur in this spectral region. Therefore, metabolite identification based solely on chemical shift should be interpreted cautiously, particularly when spectral resolution and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are limited []. A study of 194 patients showed that the amino acid peak was present in 80% of patients with an abscess, while the sensitivity and specificity of amino acids as an abscess marker in this study were reported as 0.72 and 0.30, respectively [].

The presence of an amino acid peak can therefore be a sensitive marker for a bacterial abscess; however, the absence of amino acids cannot rule out a bacterial etiology. Studies indicate that the presence of an acetate peak, with or without an accompanying succinate peak, suggests that the infection is associated with an anaerobic bacterium [], although these peaks can also be observed in certain facultative anaerobes [,]. Therefore, while MRS may facilitate the selection of more targeted antibiotic therapy, caution should be exercised when assigning etiologic agents to specific groups solely based on the spectroscopic spectrum. It is also worth noting that a brain abscess caused by S. aureus does not display the characteristic acetate, succinate, and amino acid peaks, and the spectral profile is dominated by lactate and lipid peaks, which, in the absence of an NAA peak, may mistakenly suggest a diagnosis of glioblastoma [].

Additionally, it is useful to know that at 1.3 ppm, both lactate and lipid signals can overlap, making these metabolites difficult to distinguish; however, using two different echo times (TE 135 and 270 ms) solves this issue. In a spectrum acquired at TE 270 ms, amino acids appear as a positive peak at 1.3 ppm, whereas at TE 135 ms, this peak becomes inverted (negative), allowing it to be differentiated from the lipid peak, which remains positive at TE 135 ms [].

To summarize the above findings and aid in the differential diagnosis of focal brain lesions,  has been provided. This table also highlights the difficulty in differentiating bacterial abscesses from neurocysticercosis, as these lesions may exhibit very similar metabolic profiles on MRS. However, a study by Agarwal et al. suggested that the presence and relative predominance of succinate and acetate peaks may be useful in differentiating these lesions []. Lesions associated with neurocysticercosis are characterized by the presence of succinate alone or by a higher succinate concentration than acetate. In contrast, anaerobic abscesses demonstrate either acetate alone or a higher acetate concentration than succinate.

MRS could be of use in distinguishing between a tuberculoma or a tuberculous abscess and other focal brain lesions since the spectrum shows a particular lipid resonance peak at 1.3 ppm. This occurs because of the high lipid content in the cell wall of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as well as the abundance of fatty acids in the caseating necrotic material of the lesions [,,,].

Moreover, studies show that a guanidinoacetate peak at 3.8 ppm serves as a specific marker for tuberculomas and can therefore act as a potential biomarker for distinguishing tuberculomas from high-grade malignancies []. Tuberculomas that are highly cellular may show Cho peaks at 3.2 ppm []; however, as indicated by Parry et al., who utilized a multivoxel 3D CSI technique, the Cho/Cr and Cho/NAA ratios remain lower in tuberculomas than in high-grade gliomas and metastases []. Due to the simplified spectral analysis used in this study, which involved calculating metabolite ratios from the areas under the peaks rather than fitting the entire spectrum using parametric methods, and the lack of CSD correction, the measured Cho/Cr ratios may have been subject to measurement error. However, given the substantial differences in Cho/Cr ratios between tuberculomas (1.36), metastases (2.63), and gliomas (3.34), the overall diagnostic conclusion remains consistent with established neuroradiological knowledge. Nevertheless, further studies adhering to the latest ISMRM consensus recommendations are required to establish specific numerical cutoff values []. Furthermore, it is worth emphasizing that comparing metabolite ratios across different scientific reports remains challenging due to significant methodological discrepancies and the varying evolutionary stages of tuberculomas. Voxel placement (depending on whether it is positioned within the highly cellular, enhancing rim or the caseating core) and the choice of TE directly influence the relative levels of Cho, Cr, and NAA. Additionally, differences in analytical techniques account for further numerical discrepancies between studies, underscoring the need for standardized MRS acquisition protocols.

Tuberculous abscesses may exhibit a lactate peak [,]; nevertheless, in contrast to pyogenic bacterial abscesses, tuberculous abscesses do not have cytosolic amino acid resonances, nor do they show peaks of acetate and succinate []. Moreover, the lack of a trehalose peak (3.6–3.8 ppm) enables tuberculous abscesses to be distinguished from fungal abscesses [].

It is difficult to tell the difference between a tuberculoma and a tuberculous abscess simply on the basis of MRS findings; yet it is stated that this distinction does not affect clinical management since in both cases antitubercular therapy is given and surgical treatment is carried out when needed [].

Moreover, MRS has potential use in monitoring the response to antitubercular treatment since a progressive decrease in the lipid peak is observed after treatment has started. It acts as a valuable adjunct to conventional MRI when carrying out the diagnostic evaluation of tuberculomas and tuberculous abscesses, particularly in children, since the diagnosis is still difficult in this group [].

Elicer points out that MRS can be useful in differentiating focal lesions visible on conventional brain MRI in patients with HIV(Human Immunodeficiency Virus)/AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) []. They observed that lesions in toxoplasma encephalitis are characterized by markedly elevated Lip/Lac peaks around 1.3 ppm, accompanied by reduced peaks of other neurometabolites (NAA, creatine, choline). However, it is worth noting here that Lip/Lac peaks are not a specific marker for toxoplasmosis, as they result from necrosis and hypoxia, which can also occur in other disease entities (e.g., glioblastoma multiforme) [].

Barcelo et al. also reported similar observations regarding the metabolic profile of cerebral toxoplasmosis when analyzing a single case of atypical cerebral toxoplasmosis with a single ring-enhancing lesion in the pons, where MRS helped differentiate a toxoplasma abscess from lesions associated with primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) []. The authors suggest that despite a similar profile of changes observed on MRS in these disease entities (most commonly associated with HIV/AIDS), a decrease or normal level of choline in cerebral toxoplasmosis may be a feature that distinguishes it from PCNSL, in which choline levels increase. However, Simone et al. point to the low specificity of MRS in differentiating toxoplasmosis from lymphoma, while emphasizing its high sensitivity in detecting metabolic brain tissue damage itself and the value of MRS in monitoring response to treatment []. A modern systematic review also confirmed that MRS has a limited ability to differentiate toxoplasmosis from PCNSL [].

It is also worth emphasizing that choline levels in cerebral toxoplasmosis can be slightly elevated as well, which further complicates the differentiation from neoplastic lesions. Ferraz-Filho et al., after analyzing 42 cases of toxoplasmosis and 39 gliomas, suggested that concurrently considering Cho/Cr ratios > 1.97 and NAA/Cr < 1.12 allows for the detection of neoplasms with a specificity of 97.6% (using a TE of 144 ms) [].

Batta et al. conducted a study to evaluate the utility of new MRI imaging techniques in diagnosing neurocysticercosis-a parasitic CNS infection caused by Taenia solium larvae []. The study included 85 patients, in whom the most common finding on conventional MRI was cystic, ring-enhancing lesions accompanied by mild edema. The authors state that MRI spectroscopy alone cannot serve as a standalone diagnostic method for neurocysticercosis because the lesions’ spectral profile is insufficiently characteristic. However, they point out the value of MRS in differentiating parasitic/inflammatory lesions from malignant neoplasms. They base these conclusions on observations in 24 patients, showing low Cho/Cr and Cho/NAA ratios (<2) inside 96% of the lesions, which argues against malignant neoplastic tumors []. However, it should be noted that the authors did not provide detailed technical parameters of the MRS acquisition, which limits the ability to assess the comparability of their results with those of other studies. Consequently, a value of 2 should not be considered a universal cutoff point for differentiating neurocysticercosis lesions from malignant neoplasms.

Additionally, unlike some neurocysticercosis studies [,,], Batta et al. did not observe parasite-specific metabolites inside the lesions (such as alanine, succinate, or pyruvate) []; however, this may have been related to the small lesion size, which made precise voxel localization in MRS difficult. The described pyruvate peaks pertained to the racemose form of cysticercosis (racemose neurocysticercosis) and further help differentiate this form of the disease from cystic gliomas. Elevated lactate peaks within the lesions were also reported in some patients.

Hernández et al. also indicate that MRS can help distinguish neurocysticercosis lesions from tuberculomas []. The authors suggest that tuberculomas are characterized by significantly higher lipid peaks, choline peaks, and higher Cho/Cr ratios, as well as lower NAA peaks compared to neurocysticercosis [,,]. Pretell et al. reported a Cho/Cr ratio greater than 1 in all tuberculomas (4/4), whereas none of the six neurocysticercosis lesions exceeded this threshold []. However, this value should be regarded as a preliminary discriminatory threshold rather than a validated diagnostic cutoff, given the small sample size and the lack of spectral fitting using simulated metabolite basis sets, as well as the absence of reported fitting quality metrics and measurement uncertainty. However, it is worth noting that elevated choline peaks apply to only a subset of tuberculomas (due to the inflammatory response in the lesion wall) []. In contrast, in most cases, the choline peak is low or absent [].

Jayasundar et al. also compared neurocysticercosis lesions with tuberculomas []. The authors found very low levels of all metabolites and a low signal-to-noise ratio in NCC lesions. Additionally, they observed a statistically significant difference in the NAA/Cr ratio between the groups. This ratio appears to be exceptionally low compared to the study by Pretell et al. [] (), but this fact may be explained by the different evolutionary stages of the studied lesions. Jayasundar et al. included patients with NCC whose lesions consisted of active cysts (vesicular stage) or calcifications. In contrast, Pretell et al. studied exclusively patients with single enhancing lesions containing degenerating parasites surrounded by an active inflammatory response.

CNS cryptococcosis is a fungal central nervous system infection caused by yeast of the Cryptococcus genus, primarily C. neoformans and C. gattii, occurring most commonly in immunocompromised individuals (HIV infection, post-transplantation, immunosuppressive therapy) [,]. A cryptococcoma, on the other hand, is a form of CNS cryptococcosis-more frequently observed in immunocompetent patients-in which the host’s granulomatous response forms a mass-like lesion within the brain parenchyma. In neuroimaging, this can mimic a primary brain tumor or metastasis [].

Previously reported proton MRS findings in patients with cryptococcoma were non-specific, denoting an inflammatory process with neuronal loss and gliosis []. A decrease in NAA and Cr, as well as elevated lipid-lactate and Cho peaks, have been observed [,]. In some cases, very high Cho/NAA ratios were described, which can raise suspicion of a high-grade malignancy and complicate differential diagnosis [,]. However, crucially for differential diagnosis, numerous peaks between 3.6 and 3.8 ppm have been reported in cryptococcomas. These suggest the presence of trehalose-a compound that constitutes the fungal cell wall-which can point toward the fungal nature of an ambiguous focal brain lesion [,]. This characteristic spectral profile may facilitate differentiating a cryptococcoma from gliomas and bacterial brain abscesses. It is worth noting, however, that while the detection of a trehalose peak is a specific marker, its sensitivity is limited by the resolution of the method and depends on the fungal burden within the voxel-the signal may not reach the detection threshold in the early stages of the disease, in small lesions, or during effective antifungal therapy []. MRS can play an assistive role in the diagnosis and differentiation of cryptococcoma, potentially helping to avoid a brain biopsy and facilitating earlier initiation of targeted antifungal therapy.

A fungal abscess is a focal infection of the brain parenchyma that leads to the formation of a necrotic center surrounded by an inflammatory capsule. Fungal abscesses mainly affect immunocompromised individuals, but they can also occur in immunocompetent patients []. A study by Luthra et al. comparing neuroimaging findings of abscesses of various etiologies describes, among others, 8 patients with a fungal abscess who underwent MRS []. The most characteristic finding turned out to be trehalose peaks between 3.6 and 3.8 ppm, which were reported in 5 out of 8 patients and did not occur in abscesses of any non-fungal etiology. Furthermore, the authors suggest that the absence of these peaks in 3 patients might have resulted from a concentration of trehalose too low to be detected by a 1.5 T MRI scanner. High lipid peaks in the range of 0.9–1.3 ppm and high lactate peaks (1.3 ppm) were frequent but non-specific findings. Amino acid peaks, which occur almost always in bacterial abscesses, were also present in 50% of cases (4/8) of fungal abscesses, which may indicate intra-abscess proteolysis. In the above study, acetate and succinate peaks—frequently observed in bacterial abscesses—were not found in any of the fungal abscesses; however, clinical cases of mucormycosis featuring acetate and succinate peaks have been reported []. NAA, Cho, and Cr peaks are usually absent or barely visible in fungal abscesses, and their presence may result from partial volume effects [].

In summary, MRS may represent a valuable adjunct to conventional MRI in the diagnosis of focal CNS infections, providing information on their metabolic profiles and facilitating their differentiation. In particular, the identification of characteristic metabolites such as trehalose, guanidinoacetate, amino acids, pyruvate, acetate, and succinate may be useful. In , we have summarized the metabolic profiles of the above-described lesions reported in the literature to facilitate their differentiation. At the same time, the use of MRS is associated with several limitations, including the often low specificity of the observed metabolic alterations, overlap between the metabolic profiles of different disease entities, and the dependence of MRS findings on lesion size and location, acquisition parameters, and the ability to accurately position the voxel. Therefore, MRS should be regarded as an adjunctive technique, and its findings should always be interpreted in conjunction with the clinical presentation and conventional MRI findings.

Interestingly, MRS may also prove clinically useful in encephalopathies caused by acute infection (most commonly HHV-6 (Human Herpesvirus 6) and HHV-7, as well as the influenza virus). A study by Takanashi et al., conducted on 16 children with excitotoxic encephalopathy (8 with AESD and 8 with MEEX–Mild Encephalopathy associated with Excitotoxicity), aimed at evaluating the prognostic value of brain metabolites, showed that a decrease in NAA in the frontal/frontoparietal white matter within the first week of AESD onset was associated with a poor neurological prognosis measured by the PCPC (Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category) scale []. A decrease in Cr and an increase in Lac proved to be less prognostically valuable. Furthermore, the use of MRS supports the hypothesis that AESD may result from excitotoxic damage combined with delayed or apoptotic neuronal death [,].

Single-voxel spectroscopy demonstrated that in the frontoparietal white matter, Glu levels rise on days 1–4 from the onset of AESD, followed by an observed increase in Gln on days 3–12 []. These observations may suggest a process in which an excess of Glu is released from neurons, exceeding the capacity of astrocytes to convert Glu into Gln. The increase in Glu concentration detected via MRS can occur even before the changes described in AESD become visible on standard MRI; therefore, using MRS in the early phase of AESD may facilitate the differential diagnosis of prolonged febrile seizures, and may contribute to early therapeutic intervention.

ANEC is a rare clinicoradiological syndrome most commonly triggered by common viral infections, characterized by rapid neurological deterioration and high mortality [].

Ibrahim et al. performed MRS in 15 patients with ANEC using the single-voxel technique, placing the voxel within lesions visible on conventional MRI while avoiding areas of hemorrhage and necrosis []. Results in all patients in the acute phase demonstrated lipid-lactate peaks, which significantly decreased or normalized over time. Decreased NAA peaks were found in 8 out of 15 patients, and glutamate/glutamine complex peaks were observed in 4 out of 15 patients, suggesting potential excitotoxicity. The use of MRS in ANEC thus provides insight into the pathomechanism of the disease and enables monitoring of its progression, while other clinical case reports also suggest that this method may help assess the severity and prognosis of ANEC. Specifically, it was observed that the presence of the Glx peak (2.0–2.5 ppm) and a markedly elevated, broad Lip/Lac complex peak (0.8–1.5 ppm) correlate with a more severe clinical condition and high mortality [,]. Ibrahim et al. also proposed using MRS parameters as one of the components of a multi-parametric MRI scoring system correlating with the patient’s clinical state [].

SSPE is a rare CNS disorder caused by a persistent measles virus infection. Research using MRS in this condition focuses primarily on small patient cohorts or individual case reports; however, it indicates that the application of MRS can offer several benefits in certain scenarios. The metabolic profile of CNS lesions is relatively non-specific, yet it appears to vary depending on the disease stage [].

In the early stages of the disease, only a slight decrease in NAA peaks has been described, whereas an increase in the Cho/Cr ratio pointing to inflammation and membrane turnover was particularly notable []. An elevation in mI/Cr suggesting glial activation in stages II and III, followed by a subsequent drop in mI/Cr in stage IV (which may be associated with necrosis), has also been reported [].

As the disease progresses, a decline in NAA/Cr occurs, which correlates with worsening clinical symptoms. The appearance of lipid and lactate peaks has also been documented in later stages of the disease. Consequently, MRS may allow more precise monitoring of disease progression than conventional MRI.

Furthermore, a series of 3 clinical cases reported by Cakmakci et al. indicates that MRS can detect metabolic alterations in normal-appearing white matter (an increase in mI/Cr) even prior to the onset of structural changes on MRI []. Seo et al. reached similar conclusions; however, they demonstrated a decrease in NAA/Cr and an increase in Cho/Cr in structurally unaffected areas of the CNS []. Moreover, as suggested by a case reported by Takashima et al., MRS may aid in evaluating treatment response, as they observed an increase in the previously reduced NAA/Cr ratio 6 months after initiating therapy, which correlated with clinical improvement [].

In summary, MRS in SSPE enables the early detection of metabolic alterations before structural changes appear on conventional MRI, allows precise monitoring of disease progression, and may support the evaluation of treatment response.

HAND comprise a spectrum of cognitive impairments ranging from mild deficits to severe dementia occurring in people living with HIV and persisting despite effective antiretroviral therapy []. The pathogenesis of HAND is associated with the early entry of the virus into the central nervous system (CNS). Yet HIV does not directly infect neurons; neuronal damage takes place indirectly as a result of viral proteins, chronic neuroinflammation, and dysfunction of the blood–brain barrier [].

A meta-analysis of 27 studies involving a total of 1255 patients with HIV showed that the MRS metabolic profile in HAND is marked by elevated levels of Cho and mI, especially in the basal ganglia and in the frontal white matter. Furthermore, disease progression was linked to reduced NAA, with lower NAA levels being connected with the occurrence of cognitive impairment [].

A study of 14 patients who had HIV-associated encephalopathy indicated that a higher mI/Cr ratio might be one of the earliest and most reliable spectroscopic indicators of HAND. However, this result was obtained from a relatively small number of patients and its diagnostic importance needs to be confirmed in larger groups [].

MRS may be a potentially useful tool for assessing the severity of brain involvement and for monitoring the response to combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), since improvements in the metabolic parameters have been noted several months after the start of treatment. Even though cART is effective, a chronic inflammatory process may still persist in some patients, possibly causing subclinical and progressive damage to the nervous system [].

In HAND there may also be an increase in Glx, which could be indicative of excitotoxicity and thus offer some insight into one of the mechanisms causing neuronal injury in this condition. Yet this finding is considerably less well established than the more consistently reported increases in mI and Cho and the decrease in NAA [].

To summarize, the use of MRS in HAND may provide several possible benefits. First, the metabolic profile may reveal abnormalities before structural changes become apparent on conventional MRI. In addition, MRS may help assess the severity of CNS involvement and may be useful for monitoring the response to cART, as reductions in Cho and mI peaks have been reported following treatment initiation, potentially denoting a reduction in neuroinflammation. MRS may also provide complementary information for clinical assessment, as decreased NAA and increased mI have been associated with cognitive impairment.

PML is a demyelinating disease of the central nervous system caused by the reactivation of the John Cunningham virus (JCV). The primary predisposing factor for the development of PML is HIV infection. Typically, MRS within MRI-visible lesions in PML demonstrates a decrease in NAA peaks along with an increase in choline, lactate, and lipid concentrations [].

PML lesions may show varying metabolic profiles depending on their stage. Newer lesions, characterized by active demyelination, feature a higher choline peak and a less pronounced drop in NAA compared to older lesions where permanent neuronal loss has occurred [,].

Dominant lactate peaks can be characteristic of PML-Kozić et al. reported that they were 2 to 3 times higher than choline peaks, 4 to 6 times higher than Cr peaks, and up to 4 to 11 times higher than NAA []. However, these observations were based on only 3 cases, so a very marked increase in lactate cannot be considered a pathognomonic metabolic abnormality for PML.

Myo-inositol (mI) concentration, similarly to Cho, also fluctuates depending on the lesion stage. In the initial phases of PML lesion development, mI concentration rises sharply, which is associated with high glial repair activity. Interestingly, a high mI level can serve as a positive prognostic indicator associated with longer survival and disease remission. In contrast, later-stage CNS lesions are characterized by a gradual decline in the mI peak.

MRS in PML has also been applied to compare the metabolic profile of brain tissue in patients with PML-immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) versus those without IRIS []. The chemical composition of lesions in IRIS reflected a more severe inflammatory process and tissue destruction (lower NAA/Cr ratio, higher Cho/Cr, mI/Cr, lipid/Cr, and lactate/lipid ratios).

A study by Simone et al. evaluating MRS in the differential diagnosis of CNS lesions in HIV indicates that this technique has low specificity []. However, they observed that PML lesions (as well as lymphomas) are characterized by a statistically significantly lower NAA/Cr ratio than lesions in toxoplasmosis and HIV encephalopathy.

Nevertheless, the described metabolic profile can overlap with other CNS diseases, and MRS should be used as a complementary tool in the differential diagnosis rather than a standalone technique.

Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) is a valuable, non-invasive method supporting the diagnosis of inflammatory and infectious CNS disorders. It enables the detection of metabolic alterations that remain invisible on conventional magnetic resonance imaging. Metabolic disturbances demonstrated by MRS provide insight into the pathogenesis of clinical symptoms and may help resolve the clinical-radiological paradox observed in various types of encephalitis.

Our review demonstrated that the detection of specific metabolites in the spectrum can be particularly useful in the differential diagnosis of focal infectious lesions. The presence of cytosolic amino acids, acetate, and succinate supports a bacterial etiology of a brain abscess. Trehalose, on the other hand, serves as a specific marker for fungal infections (cryptococcoma, fungal abscess). The presence of guanidinoacetate and prominent lipid peaks points toward the diagnosis of tuberculoma, while varying choline concentrations help differentiate infectious/inflammatory processes from neoplastic lesions.

Studies indicate that key neurometabolite levels (e.g., decreased NAA, elevated mI, and alterations in the glutamate–glutamine complex) may correlate with the patient’s clinical state, the severity of neurological symptoms, and cognitive deficits. Serial MRS examinations may also enable monitoring of disease progression, evaluation of the reversibility of neuronal damage, and assessment of treatment response.

However, despite its significant advantages, MRS also has limitations. Existing studies indicate that metabolic profiles among different disease entities frequently overlap, thereby complicating differential diagnosis. For this reason, MRS should not be considered a standalone diagnostic tool, but rather a complementary modality to conventional MRI, other advanced neuroimaging techniques, laboratory testing, and, above all, the clinical presentation.

To fully evaluate the potential of MRS as a diagnostic adjunct, a tool for monitoring disease course and treatment response, and an indicator of patient prognosis, further large-scale, multicenter longitudinal studies in patients with neuroinfections are necessary. Furthermore, a significant challenge emerging from the literature review on MRS studies is the substantial heterogeneity of acquisition protocols and data processing methods used, as well as the widespread lack of reporting of key technical parameters (such as chemical shift displacement, shimming quality, and precise basis set modeling). Adherence to the ISMRM expert consensus methodological guidelines and technical parameter reporting standards will be crucial for future research [,]. Standardization of acquisition sequences (e.g., implementation of semi-LASER sequences to minimize chemical shift displacement at 3T magnetic field strength) and comprehensive reporting of methodological details will be essential for inter-center comparability and reproducibility of MRS findings in inflammatory CNS disorders.

neuroscience.title: JWA as a context-dependent redox regulatory hub linking stress responses with aging hallmarks and age-related diseases
neuroscience.abstract: JWA (also known as ARL6IP5) is an evolutionarily conserved multifunctional protein increasingly implicated in redox homeostasis and cellular stress adaptation. Its functions intersect with redox homeostasis through signaling pathways including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), and adenosine 5′-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), as well as interactions with key proteins such as X-ray repair cross-complementing 1 (XRCC1), nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4), and excitatory amino acid carrier 1 (EAAC1) involved in oxidative-stress adaptation. As a redox-responsive regulatory protein and mediator, JWA exhibits context-dependent roles in disease pathogenesis: in oncology, it acts as a tumor suppressor by mitigating oxidative stress-induced DNA damage and reversing chemoresistance, with reduced expression correlating with poor prognosis in gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and other malignancies; in neurobiology, it exerts neuroprotective effects through suppression of ferroptosis, regulation of glutamate homeostasis, and proteostasis-related mechanisms, with the strength and direction of redox involvement varying across experimental contexts; beyond these fields, JWA regulates intestinal barrier integrity, radiation response, and adaptation to environmental oxidants (Cd, B [a]P, H2O2), while specific polymorphisms influence redox-related disease susceptibility. As a potential aging-associated regulator, accumulating evidence suggests that JWA expression or activity may change during aging, although age-, tissue-, and disease-specific patterns remain incompletely defined. Current evidence links JWA dysregulation to oxidative stress and tissue dysfunction in several age-associated diseases, whereas its direct roles in the aging process remain insufficiently established. This review, centered on redox regulation as the unifying framework, comprehensively synthesizes current knowledge on JWA’s multifunctional roles across disciplines, highlights its potential as a candidate redox-related biomarker and experimental therapeutic target, and proposes an evidence-based research framework for future investigation and translation. By emphasizing JWA’s role in maintaining redox balance and its regulatory function in aging process and age-related diseases, we provide novel insights into its significance in future clinical-development considerations and offer directions for targeting redox dysregulation in refractory diseases.
neuroscience.text:
JWA is an all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)-responsive gene initially cloned from human tracheobronchial epithelial cells and maps to chromosome 3p14, a locus associated with cancer and epilepsy susceptibility (). Evolutionarily highly conserved from Caenorhabditis elegans to humans, JWA encodes a cytoskeleton-associated protein that functions as a key mediator of redox homeostasis, linking oxidative stress signals to fundamental cellular processes (; ; ). Unlike conventional redox regulators that act through single pathways, JWA can be viewed as a redox-responsive regulatory hub that integrates multiple stress-adaptation mechanisms, including modulation of redox-sensitive signaling cascades, regulation of DNA damage repair under oxidative stress, and participation in autophagic and proteostatic processes. Direct molecular sensing of ROS by JWA has not yet been established (; ; ).

The biological significance of JWA’s redox regulatory function spans diverse fields including oncology, neurobiology, environmental toxicology, and gerontology. In cancer, oxidative stress-induced DNA damage and redox imbalance drive tumorigenesis and chemoresistance, while JWA counteracts these processes by enhancing DNA repair and normalizing ROS levels (; ). In neurodegenerative diseases, excessive oxidative stress and ferroptosis contribute to neuronal loss, and JWA exerts neuroprotection through ROS scavenging and inhibition of iron-dependent lipid peroxidation (; ). As an environmental stress-responsive gene, JWA is rapidly induced by oxidants such as H2O2, Cd, and B [a]P, indicating its responsiveness to cellular redox perturbation (; ). As a potential aging-associated regulator, JWA expression has been reported to change with age, but the extent, tissue specificity, and functional significance of these age-related changes remain incompletely defined. Current evidence mainly links JWA dysregulation to oxidative stress and dysfunction in selected age-associated diseases rather than establishing a universal role in the aging process ().

Research on JWA has traditionally focused on its multifunctional roles in specific diseases, but the centrality of redox regulation as the unifying mechanism underlying its diverse functions has not been systematically elaborated. This review reorients the narrative around JWA’s role as a stress-responsive regulatory protein associated with redox homeostasis, integrating findings from tumor biology, neurobiology, and environmental toxicology to highlight its diverse roles in aging-related processes and age-associated diseases. We emphasize its dual potential as a candidate redox-related biomarker and experimental therapeutic target, propose a standardized research framework to address current methodological limitations, and outline an evidence-calibrated roadmap for future preclinical and clinical evaluation (). By synthesizing current knowledge through the lens of redox regulation, this review provides a novel perspective on JWA’s biological significance and offers directions for future clinical-development considerations strategies targeting redox dysregulation in complex diseases.

This narrative review was developed through targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus, covering literature available through August 2026. Core search terms included combinations of “JWA,” “ARL6IP5,” “redox,” “oxidative stress,” “reactive oxygen species,” “aging,” “senescence,” “age-related disease,” “DNA repair,” “ferroptosis,” “autophagy,” “reticulophagy,” “biomarker,” and “therapeutic.” Additional studies were identified by screening the reference lists of relevant JWA-focused articles and recent reviews.

Priority was given to studies in which JWA was experimentally manipulated or directly measured and linked to a defined molecular mechanism and functional outcome. Generic studies addressing redox biology, aging, or disease pathways were used primarily for contextual interpretation and were not treated as direct evidence for JWA. Evidence was classified as (i) direct mechanistic evidence, when JWA perturbation was experimentally linked to a defined molecular event and functional outcome; (ii) context-dependent or disease-associated evidence, when JWA-related effects were demonstrated in a specific stress or disease model without establishing a universal causal relationship; (iii) candidate biomarker evidence, when JWA expression or genetic variation was associated with clinical or pathological features without prospective validation; and (iv) mechanistic extrapolation, when a biologically plausible relationship between JWA-associated pathways and aging hallmarks was proposed but not directly demonstrated.

The JWA gene maps to human chromosome 3p14, consisting of 3 exons, 2 introns, and a 567 bp intronless coding region that generates two transcripts (1447 bp and 2112 bp) (; ). A key feature of its promoter is the enrichment of stress response element (SRE), heat shock response element (HRE), and retinoic acid response element (RARE), which enable rapid transcriptional activation in response to oxidative stress, ATRA, and 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA) (). Functional polymorphisms in the JWA promoter (-76G>C) and exons (380G>A, 454C>A, 723T>G) have been linked to altered redox stress sensitivity, increasing susceptibility to bladder cancer and leukemia by impairing JWA’s oxidative stress-induced transcriptional activation (; ).

JWA exhibits high interspecies homology, with the rat JWA coding region differing from humans by only 4 nucleotides (resulting in 4 amino acid changes that do not affect key functional domains) and mouse JWA (localized to chromosome 6D3) sharing a conserved gene structure (; ). The JWA protein (≈21–22.5 kDa, 188 amino acids) is a hydrophobic, cytoskeleton-associated protein containing a conserved prenylated Rab acceptor 1 (PRA1) domain, transmembrane domains (TMDs), and kinase phosphorylation sites critical for redox signaling; The PRA1 domain, consisting of 4 TMDs, forms short hairpin structures via TMD1-TMD2 and TMD3-TMD4 pairing, which are essential for endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane shaping, oligomer formation, and ER-phagy regulation, key processes in mitigating ER stress-induced oxidative damage (; ).

As a novel microtubule-associated protein (MAP), JWA stably binds α/β-tubulin regardless of microtubule polymerization status, localizing to the cytoplasm, microtubules, mitotic spindle, and partially to the ER/Golgi (). This localization enables JWA to integrate cytoskeletal dynamics with redox signaling, as microtubules serve as scaffolds for redox-sensitive kinases and ROS-producing enzymes (; ). JWA’s redox regulatory functions are further supported by its direct interactions with key proteins: binding to NCOA4 to inhibit ferritinophagy and iron-dependent oxidative stress (), forming a complex with XRCC1 to enhance base excision repair (BER) of oxidative DNA damage (), and associating with EAAC1 to regulate cysteine uptake and glutathione (GSH) synthesis, an essential antioxidant pathway (; ). Additionally, JWA contains two Protein Kinase C (PKC) phosphorylation sites (Serine-Aspartic acid-Arginine (SDR): 18–20 aa; Serine-Leucine-Arginine (SLR): 138–140 aa), which contribute to MAPK signaling activation under oxidative stress conditions and cellular adaptation to oxidative stress (; ; ). The lysine 158 (K158) site is critical for ring finger protein 185 (RNF185)-mediated ubiquitination and degradation, and its mutation enhances JWA protein stability, potentiating redox protection ().

JWA expression is tightly regulated at transcriptional, post-translational, and extrinsic levels, with redox signals playing a central role in this regulatory network. This precise control ensures JWA can rapidly respond to redox perturbations and adapt cellular processes to maintain homeostasis.

The JWA promoter contains multiple redox-responsive elements that mediate transcriptional activation or repression in response to oxidative stress. Nuclear Factor I (NFI), a multifunctional transcription factor involved in development and stress responses, specifically binds the CCAAT element (-58/-28 bp) of the JWA promoter to activate transcription under oxidative stress; NFI silencing abrogates this redox-induced upregulation (; ). CCAAT/enhancer binding protein (C/EBP) family members, which regulate cell cycle and stress responses, bind the JWA promoter CCAAT box to modulate HeLa cell proliferation and apoptosis under oxidative stress conditions (; ). The 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate-response element (TRE) in the JWA promoter mediates TPA-induced transcription in a cell-specific manner (inhibiting in NIH3T3 cells, upregulating in K562 cells), linking JWA expression to redox-sensitive pathways involved in tumorigenesis and therapeutic sensitivity (; ).

Transcriptional repressors also modulate JWA expression in response to redox signals. C-terminal binding protein 1 (CTBP1) directly represses JWA transcription, while Yin Yang 1 (YY1) binds the JWA promoter motif (5′-GAGAATGGCATA-3′) to inhibit expression, blunting JWA’s tumor-suppressive and pro-apoptotic effects under oxidative stress (; ; ; ). In contrast, inhibitor of growth family member 4 (ING4), a tumor suppressor that regulates chromatin structure, binds the JWA promoter (-107/-27 bp) to activate transcription, forming an ‘ING4-JWA’ axis that has been associated with reduced melanoma angiogenic signaling in experimental models, whereas whether redox normalization is a causal mediator of this effect remains unresolved (; ). The JWA -76C polymorphism reduces promoter transcriptional activity and abolishes oxidative stress-induced activation, highlighting the importance of promoter redox responsiveness in disease susceptibility and age-related redox imbalance (; ).

Ubiquitination and phosphorylation are key post-translational modifications that regulate JWA protein stability and stress-response functions. RNF185, an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in protein homeostasis and stress responses, directly interacts with JWA, mediates its K158 site ubiquitination, and promotes proteasomal degradation, providing a mechanism for stress-associated regulation of JWA protein stability (; ). JWA also regulates the ubiquitination of downstream redox-sensitive targets: it facilitates ubiquitin-mediated degradation of transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (Sp1) (), which promotes cancer cell proliferation by upregulating tumor-associated genes under redox imbalance (; ). In normal cells, JWA maintains XRCC1 function to promote repair of oxidative stress-induced DNA single-strand breaks (). In cisplatin-resistant gastric cancer cells, JWA inhibits casein kinase 2 (CK2) activity, blocking XRCC1 phosphorylation, promoting its ubiquitination/degradation, impairing DNA repair, and reversing cisplatin resistance; this links post-translational modification of JWA to oxidative-stress-associated chemoresistance (; ; ). JWA’s PKC/Protein Kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation sites are critical for mediating stress-responsive MAPK signaling, as phosphorylation status directly affects JWA’s ability to regulate cell migration and oxidative stress responses, and its abnormal modification is associated with age-related cellular dysfunction (). These apparently opposite effects of JWA on XRCC1 should not be interpreted as a single intrinsic direction of regulation. Instead, the available evidence suggests that the outcome is context-dependent and may be influenced by cellular state, basal redox environment, stress intensity, CK2 activity, XRCC1 phosphorylation status, DNA-repair demand, and proteasomal regulation. In normal cells exposed to oxidative stress, JWA is associated with preservation of XRCC1 function and BER capacity, whereas in cisplatin-resistant gastric cancer cells, JWA-mediated inhibition of CK2 and subsequent changes in XRCC1 phosphorylation and stability contribute to reduced repair capacity and drug resensitization. The molecular switch that determines these opposite outcomes remains unresolved and should be considered an important mechanistic boundary condition for future studies.

Extrinsic factors, including differentiation inducers, environmental oxidants, and small molecules, regulate JWA expression in response to cellular stress and redox perturbation. ATRA, which induces cell differentiation and inhibits proliferation, enhances JWA transcription via the −194 to +107 bp promoter region; low-dose arsenic trioxide (As2O3) synergizes with ATRA to upregulate JWA, while TPA antagonizes this effect, thereby linking JWA to redox-sensitive differentiation pathways (; ). Environmental oxidants and toxins (H2O2, B [a]P, Cd) upregulate JWA via oxidative stress signals or direct promoter binding, activating JWA’s redox protection functions, and this induction capacity declines with age, contributing to age-related oxidative damage accumulation (; ). Small molecules and drugs modulate JWA expression to target redox imbalance: JAC1 upregulates JWA by promoting YY1 ubiquitination/degradation, inhibiting HSF1, blocking the cell cycle, and suppressing triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) proliferation through the YY1-JWA-p38 MAPK pathway (). JAC4, a JWA-activating compound, exerts therapeutic effects on epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-driven lung cancer growth and metastasis via the AMPK/Neural precursor cell expressed developmentally downregulated 4-like (NEDD4L)/EGFR pathway, the contribution of redox changes to this pathway remains unresolved (). Targeted agents (Cis-wog, Pt (IV) prodrugs) inhibit JWA-mediated redox signaling by binding JWA or interfering with its interaction with XRCC1 (; ). Nicotine, whose metabolism generates ROS, negatively regulates JWA transcription via cholinergic receptor nicotinic alpha five subunit (CHRNA5)/protein kinase B (AKT), exacerbating redox stress and increasing disease risk (; ; ; ). Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), an antioxidant that scavenges ROS and promotes endogenous antioxidant enzymes, upregulates JWA via antioxidant effects, enhancing redox protection (; ; ; ). JWA regulation exhibits cell specificity and pathological dependence: TPA’s effect varies by cell type; JWA is downregulated in Parkinson’s disease and aging (contributing to redox dysregulation), but compensatorily upregulated in prion-induced chronic ER stress to mitigate oxidative damage (; ).

In this review, “redox-dependent” is reserved for mechanisms in which experimental manipulation of redox status or ROS alters the JWA-associated pathway. Where such causal evidence is not established, we use “redox-sensitive,” “redox-responsive,” or “associated with oxidative stress” to describe the relevant biological context. JWA intersects with cellular stress and redox homeostasis through diverse signaling and protein-regulatory mechanisms, contributing to cellular adaptation and tissue homeostasis. Its functions are characterized by cell-type specificity and environmental dependence, with redox status representing either a mechanistic component or an experimental context depending on the pathway.

JWA exerts tumor-suppressive effects through multiple pathways, including MAPK signaling, DNA damage repair, and target-protein degradation. Several of these mechanisms operate in oxidative-stress-associated tumor contexts, whereas direct causal dependence on redox status has been established only for selected processes (; ). It forms a repair complex with XRCC1 to participate in the BER pathway, which repairs oxidative stress-induced DNA damage: low JWA expression enhances tumor cell sensitivity to platinum-based drugs by impairing BER, while JWA-targeted Pt(IV) prodrugs reverse chemoresistance by inhibiting the JWA-XRCC1 pathway, modulating oxidative-damage-associated DNA repair (; ). JWA promotes proteasomal degradation of Sp1, thereby suppressing Sp1-associated phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) tumor-promoting programs. These effects have been described in oxidative-stress-associated tumor settings, but direct causal dependence of JWA-mediated Sp1 regulation on redox status has not been established (; ). Notably, the tumor-suppressive effect of JWA is weakened in elderly tumor patients, which is related to age-related JWA downregulation and redox imbalance (; ; ).

JWA exhibits context-dependent functions in some cancers: in hepatitis C virus-associated hepatocellular carcinoma, it inhibits the MAPK/MMP-2 pathway in association with reduced oxidative-stress status, while accelerating tumor progression by promoting hepatitis C virus replication, highlighting the context dependence of JWA-associated signaling and the unresolved contribution of redox status (). Co-expression patterns of JWA with p53 and XRCC1 accurately assess prognostic risk and chemotherapy benefits in gastric and esophageal cancer patients by reflecting the redox status of tumor cells, and this assessment value is more significant in elderly patients (; ; ; ).

JWA regulates neuronal homeostasis through context-dependent stress-response pathways, with protective effects demonstrated in several oxidative-stress and Parkinson’s disease-relevant models (). In Parkinson’s disease, JWA binds NCOA4 to suppress ferritinophagy, reducing iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation and thereby protecting dopaminergic neurons from ferroptotic injury (). It activates the Nrf2 pathway or upregulates glutamate transporter 1 (GLT-1) expression via the ERK/Akt/cAMP-response-element-binding protein (CREB) axis, enhancing glutamate uptake and alleviating excitotoxicity; both processes are redox-sensitive and critical for neuronal survival and preventing age-related neuronal loss (; ). JWA interacts with EAAC1 and regulates cysteine uptake and GSH synthesis, thereby contributing to cellular redox homeostasis and oxidative-stress defense (; ). In cognitive function regulation, JWA deficiency enhances hippocampal neurogenesis and long-term potentiation through the FAK/PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and improves spatial cognitive performance. Changes in redox balance have been associated with this phenotype, but a direct causal requirement for redox modulation in the FAK-dependent mechanism remains unresolved ().

JWA is involved in maintaining intestinal epithelial homeostasis, regulating oxidative stress responses, and providing radiation protection, with oxidative stress serving as an important biological context, and its dysfunction is an important cause of age-related intestinal barrier damage and radiation sensitivity increase () via the ERK/F-box and WD repeat domain-containing (FBXW7)/notch homolog 1 (NOTCH1)/peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (STAT5) axis, JWA regulates intestinal stem cell function and cell lineage distribution, maintains intestinal barrier integrity, and promotes post-radiation injury repair by reducing redox stress (; ). As an environmental stress-responsive gene, JWA is induced by H2O2, Cd, and B[a]P, alleviating DNA damage and inhibiting apoptosis by activating the BER pathway or regulating the ROS-MAPK signaling pathway, and this inducible protective capacity declines with age (; ). As an ER membrane-shaping protein, JWA mediates ER tubule formation via the PRA1 domain and cooperates with family with sequence similarity 134, member B (FAM134B) to regulate ER-phagy, maintaining ER homeostasis and reducing ER stress-induced oxidative damage, which is critical for alleviating age-related proteostasis collapse (; ; ). In prion infection, JWA induces reticulophagy/ER-phagy via the Ca2+-AMPK pathway, clearing abnormally folded prion protein (PRNP/PrPc) and alleviating ER stress, an important stress-associated mechanism, although the causal contribution of redox changes remains incompletely defined, and this mechanism also plays a role in clearing age-related abnormal protein aggregates ().

JWA’s downstream redox signaling pathways exhibit significant cell type specificity and environmental dependence, and also show age-dependent differences. In esophageal cancer cells (Eca109), it mainly regulates the ERK1/2 and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathways to maintain redox balance, whereas in normal esophageal cells (HET-1A), it relies solely on the p38 MAPK pathway (). In normal gastric epithelial cells (GES-1), JWA positively regulates XRCC1 stability to enhance BER under oxidative stress; in cisplatin-resistant gastric cancer cells (BGC823/DDP, SGC7901/DDP), it promotes XRCC1 degradation to reverse chemoresistance by modulating oxidative-stress-associated DNA repair (). In aging cells, JWA’s regulation of MAPK pathway subtypes is altered, leading to weakened redox balance maintenance capacity (; ; ). These differences highlight JWA’s ability to adapt its redox regulatory mechanisms to specific cellular contexts and aging status. The major JWA-centered mechanisms described above are integrated into a unified context-dependent regulatory framework ().

JWA has been implicated in multiple disease and tissue contexts, including malignant tumors, neurodegeneration, intestinal injury, and environmental stress responses. Across these settings, JWA-associated effects involve DNA damage repair, stress-responsive signaling, ferroptosis, autophagy, and tissue protection. However, the strength and direction of these relationships vary substantially according to cell type, disease state, stress intensity, and experimental model. In the context of aging, it is therefore important to distinguish direct evidence obtained from aging-specific models from findings derived from age-associated diseases and from mechanistic extrapolation. To avoid conflating disease-associated observations with direct evidence for biological aging, the evidence discussed below is considered at three levels: (i) direct aging evidence, including studies using aged tissues, aged animals, senescence models, or age-stratified human cohorts; (ii) evidence from diseases commonly associated with aging, including cancer, Parkinson’s disease, and intestinal dysfunction; and (iii) mechanistic extrapolation, referring to biologically plausible links between JWA-regulated stress responses and aging hallmarks that have not yet been directly demonstrated. This distinction is particularly important because aging-specific models, longitudinal datasets, and systematic tissue-level analyses of JWA remain limited.

JWA exhibits broad-spectrum tumor-suppressive properties in most malignancies, primarily by maintaining redox homeostasis, while exerting oncogenic effects in certain contexts. Its mechanisms involve regulating tumor cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, drug resistance, and immune responses via redox-sensitive pathways, with clinical significance in prognostic assessment, therapeutic efficacy prediction, and targeted therapy development (; ). Notably, JWA expression is significantly downregulated in elderly tumor patients, and its functional deficiency is closely associated with the occurrence, development and poor prognosis of age-related tumors (; ).

JWA regulates tumor progression through several context-dependent stress-response mechanisms involving MAPK signaling, cytoskeletal regulation, protein degradation, and DNA repair. JWA counteracts these processes via multiple redox-sensitive mechanisms. In metastasis inhibition, JWA regulates cancer cell migration through the MAPK-F-actin pathway and promotes CXCR4 degradation through the proteasome, thereby suppressing PI3K/AKT-associated invasion in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma models. These mechanisms have been demonstrated in specific tumor contexts, whereas their direct dependence on redox status has not been established (; ). In angiogenesis inhibition, JWA downregulates the NF-κB/STAT3/VEGF axis through the ING4-JWA-ILK pathway, thereby reducing angiogenic signaling and melanoma progression. These findings were obtained in tumor models associated with oxidative-stress signaling, but they do not establish with associated changes in redox-related signaling as the causal mediator of the ING4-JWA-ILK pathway (; ). In proliferation and apoptosis regulation, JWA promotes tubulin polymerization through p38 MAPK signaling and enhances chemotherapy-induced apoptosis, whereas JWA deficiency is associated with altered redox homeostasis and increased tumorigenic phenotypes in specific cellular contexts (; ). JWA also regulates tumor differentiation: in acute promyelocytic leukemia, its expression synchronizes with ATRA-induced differentiation, enhancing induction therapy efficacy by modulating redox-sensitive differentiation pathways (; ). Notably, JWA exhibits a dual “tumor suppressor-oncogene” pattern in leukemia and bladder cancer, related to tumor type, microenvironment, and redox context, and aging status is an important factor affecting this functional pattern (; ).

JWA is a key regulator of this process: high JWA expression stabilizes XRCC1 to enhance BER pathway activity and DNA repair, inducing platinum resistance by enhancing XRCC1-associated DNA-repair capacity in tumor cells (; ). JWA-directed Pt (IV) prodrugs (e.g., Cis-wog, Cx-platin-Cl) reverse chemoresistance by inhibiting the JWA-XRCC1 pathway and reducing tumor-cell DNA-repair capacity. And regulating the tumor immune microenvironment (promoting effector T cell infiltration, inhibiting regulatory T cell recruitment) to achieve chemo-immunotherapy synergy (; ). Additionally, JWA-related modulation of the CTBP1-JWA-AMPK/NEDD4L/EGFR axis has been reported to enhance the response of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma models to osimertinib. The contribution of redox changes to this sensitization remains unresolved, and the therapeutic relevance of this combination in older patients remains to be evaluated in age-specific preclinical and clinical studies (; ).

Low JWA expression has been associated with metastasis, recurrence, and shorter overall survival in gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, esophageal cancer, and melanoma (; ). Co-expression of JWA with p53, murine double minute 2 (MDM2), XRCC1, or FAK has been associated with prognostic stratification in retrospective clinical analyses; in gastric cancer, the “low JWA + high FAK” combination has been associated with poorer prognosis and differential treatment outcomes in patients receiving fluorouracil-leucovorin-oxaliplatin chemotherapy (). These findings support the potential value of JWA-related expression patterns for retrospective prognostic and treatment-response analyses, but their incremental clinical utility requires prospective validation.

JWA expression has also been investigated in relation to sensitivity or response to platinum-based chemotherapy, ATRA differentiation therapy, and radiation therapy in selected experimental or clinical contexts. These observations may reflect differences in tumor-cell stress-response and DNA-repair states, but they do not establish JWA expression as a validated predictor of treatment sensitivity or a treatment-selection tool. Similarly, JWA polymorphisms, including −76G>C and 723T>G, have been investigated as candidate susceptibility markers for bladder cancer and leukemia; their potential value for risk assessment requires prospective validation JWA-activating compounds such as JAC1 and JAC4, as well as JWA-targeted agents including Cis-wog and recombinant JWA, have been investigated in preclinical tumor models. These approaches provide experimental evidence for JWA modulation as a candidate intervention strategy, but their therapeutic efficacy, safety, and disease- or age-specific applicability remain to be established (; ).

JWA has been investigated in several neurodegenerative disease models, particularly Parkinson’s disease and prion disease, where oxidative stress, ferroptosis, protein aggregation, and proteostasis are prominent pathological features JWA plays a critical regulatory role in these diseases via maintaining glutamate homeostasis, inhibiting abnormal protein aggregation, regulating autophagy, and resisting oxidative stress, mechanisms associated with oxidative-stress responses, thus providing an important molecular target for intervention in age-related neurodegenerative diseases (; ).

JWA expression is synchronously downregulated with dopaminergic neuron marker tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) in Parkinson’s disease patient brain tissues and model mice, indicating impaired redox regulation; JWA deficiency exacerbates ferritinophagy and ferroptosis, accelerating dopaminergic neuron degeneration, while JWA overexpression or JWA-activating compound JAC4 activation inhibits ferritinophagy via NCOA4 binding, reducing Fe2+ accumulation and lipid peroxidation, improving motor symptoms and brain dopamine levels in Parkinson’s disease model mice (; ; ). JWA eliminates α-synuclein aggregates by inducing autophagy: it directly binds autophagy-related gene 12 (ATG12), inhibits its ubiquitination and degradation, promotes formation of the autophagy-related gene 5 (ATG5)-ATG12 complex, and enhances autophagic flux to alleviate α-synuclein-mediated protein toxicity, an important redox-sensitive process critical for clearing age-related α-synuclein aggregates (; ; ). In astrocytes, JWA upregulates GLT-1 expression via the ERK/AKT/CREB pathway, enhancing glutamate uptake and mitigating excitotoxicity; its deficiency exacerbates 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)/paraquat-induced neurodegeneration by disrupting redox balance (). Additionally, JWA antagonizes paraquat-induced oxidative stress via activating the MEK/ERK/PI3K/AKT/Nrf2 pathway, delaying neuron loss and motor dysfunction (). JWA expression has been reported to be reduced in dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson’s disease-relevant human tissues and experimental models, and experimental manipulation of JWA influences ferritinophagy, ferroptosis, and neuronal injury in Parkinson’s disease models. These findings provide disease-associated evidence for a role of JWA in Parkinson’s disease pathology. However, the available evidence does not establish that JWA dysregulation is specifically caused by biological aging or that the observed effects constitute a general mechanism of neuronal aging. Therefore, the relevance of the JWA-NCOA4-ferritinophagy axis to age-dependent neurodegeneration should be considered a disease-associated mechanism with potential aging relevance rather than direct evidence of an aging mechanism (; ; ).

JWA participates in neuroprotection via regulating glutamate transporters: it specifically binds EAAC1, modulating EAAC1-mediated glutamate transport and cysteine uptake to maintain GSH levels and redox balance, and its downregulation leads to glutamate homeostasis disruption and disrupted GSH homeostasis. (; ; ).
