Abnormal JWA expression disrupts glutamate homeostasis and GSH synthesis, enhancing neuronal sensitivity to oxidative stress and contributing to epilepsy and Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis (). Targeted JWA regulation or blocking its excitatory amino acid transporter 3 (EAAT3) binding restores glutamate transport balance and alleviates excitotoxicity-associated damage while restoring glutathione and redox homeostasis (). Additionally, JWA selectively regulates glutamate and taurine homeostasis in PC12 cells, avoiding glutamate-induced excitotoxicity while preserving taurine’s neuroprotective effect; both processes are redox-sensitive ().

Prion protein (PrP) misfolding (PrPˢc) triggers fatal neurodegenerative diseases, which are also associated with aging, characterized by abnormal protein aggregation and redox dysregulation (; ). Misfolded PrP induces normal PrP conformational changes, forming toxic aggregates; the disease is highly infectious with 100% mortality and no effective therapies (; ; ). In prion disease, JWA induces reticulophagy/ER-phagy via the Ca2+-AMPK pathway, specifically clearing ER-aggregated misfolded PrPˢc, alleviating ER stress and neuronal damage by reducing redox stress. JWA overexpression reverses PrPˢc-mediated cytotoxicity, and this autophagy-regulated abnormal protein clearance mechanism also applies to α-synuclein, suggesting that related JWA-associated proteostasis mechanisms may warrant investigation in other protein-aggregation disorders sharing related stress-response mechanisms (; ; ; ). Cognitive function relies on hippocampal neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity, which are redox-sensitive; abnormalities induce cognitive decline (typical in Alzheimer’s disease, the most common age-related neurodegenerative disease) (; ). JWA deficiency enhances hippocampal neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity via the FAK/PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, improving spatial cognitive function by normalizing redox balance. It is speculated that JWA overexpression may inhibit neurogenesis and exacerbate cognitive impairment, this finding raises a hypothesis that JWA-dependent regulation of hippocampal neurogenesis may differ from its protective effects observed in Parkinson’s disease-relevant models; however, whether JWA directly contributes to Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis or represents a therapeutic target remains unknown (). These findings indicate that JWA does not exert a uniformly beneficial or detrimental effect on neuronal function. Instead, its functional direction may depend on cell type, brain region, disease context, developmental or aging state, basal stress level, and pathway dependence. In Parkinson’s disease-relevant models, increased JWA activity is associated with protection against oxidative stress, ferritinophagy, and ferroptosis, whereas reduced JWA activity in the hippocampus can enhance neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity through FAK/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. The biological switch underlying these context-specific effects remains unresolved. The distinct neuronal contexts and JWA-associated effector programs described above are summarized in .

JWA regulates intestinal stem-cell and epithelial homeostasis through the ERK/FBXW7/NOTCH1/PPARγ/STAT5 axis. Available evidence supports a role in oxidative-stress-associated intestinal injury, whereas its direct contribution to biological intestinal aging remains incompletely defined (). Radiation-induced intestinal injury impairs mucosal epithelium integrity, triggers inflammation and hemorrhage, and inhibits intestinal stem cell regeneration, all associated with excessive oxidative stress (; ). The JWA-activating compound JAC4 protects against radiation-induced intestinal injury via JWA-associated antioxidant and anti-inflammatory signaling, providing preclinical evidence for further investigation of JWA activation in normal-tissue protection during radiotherapy (; ).

In response to Cd and B [a]P exposure, JWA participates in ROS-MAPK-associated stress responses and cellular damage control (; ). As an environmental stress-responsive regulator, JWA responds to Cd and B [a]P exposure and participates in the regulation of cellular damage and apoptosis through the ROS-MAPK pathway (; ). Its expression level reflects the degree of pollutant-induced cellular redox damage, providing a molecular basis for environment-related disease risk assessment. Importantly, persistent exposure to redox-active environmental stressors can promote cellular dysfunction, raising the possibility that JWA-mediated stress responses may intersect with aging-related processes. However, a direct role for JWA in environmentally accelerated aging has not been established.

JWA has also been investigated in cardiovascular injury, bone metabolism, and other redox-related conditions. Because several of these disorders become more prevalent with advancing age, their JWA-associated mechanisms may be relevant to aging-related disease biology; however, age-specific JWA mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized (; ; ; ; ). For example, JWA-associated regulation of vascular endothelial repair has been linked to oxidative-stress responses in OSAHS-related cardiovascular complications, but the causal contribution of redox changes and the therapeutic relevance of JWA modulation remain to be established (; ). Taken together, the disease-specific evidence supports a context-dependent model of JWA rather than a uniform disease-modifying function. Across cancer, neurodegenerative disease, and intestinal injury, the most consistently supported JWA-associated mechanisms involve DNA repair, stress-responsive MAPK signaling, iron/ferroptosis regulation, glutathione homeostasis, and autophagic or ER-phagic processes. However, the strength of evidence differs substantially across disease contexts, and the extension of these mechanisms to biological aging remains partly inferential. This distinction provides the basis for the evidence-weighted aging framework presented () and the evidence summary and development potential of major JWA-associated mechanistic modules ().

Evidence summary and development potential of major JWA-associated mechanistic modules.

JWA expression, gene polymorphisms, and combinations with downstream proteins have been investigated as candidate biomarkers for disease classification, prognosis, and treatment-response assessment. However, most available studies remain exploratory or retrospective, and prospective multicenter validation, particularly in aging populations, is limited (; ).

Key detection approaches used in JWA-related biomarker studies include PCR-RFLP, RT-qPCR, western blotting, and immunohistochemistry (IHC). PCR-RFLP has been used to characterize JWA polymorphisms (−76G>C, 454C>A, and 723T>G) and their associations with disease susceptibility; whether these variants can serve as susceptibility markers for age-related tumors requires prospective validation (; ). RT-qPCR has been used to quantify JWA expression in experimental and disease-associated studies, whereas the value of JWA expression for early detection or risk assessment of age-related tumors remains to be prospectively validated (). Western blotting has similarly been used to assess JWA protein abundance and associated pathway changes in research settings, but its clinical utility for treatment selection or response monitoring has not been established. IHC has been used to evaluate tissue JWA expression and its associations with clinicopathological and prognostic features; however, standardized assays and prospective validation are still required before clinical implementation (; ).

Regarding clinical associations, JWA-related biomarker findings can be considered at several levels. For risk assessment, JWA expression measured by RT-qPCR or western blotting has been investigated in relation to malignant transformation and disease-associated redox imbalance, but its value for predicting cancer risk, particularly in aging tissues, remains to be established prospectively (). For prognosis, IHC-based JWA expression has been associated with clinicopathological features and survival outcomes in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and melanoma, with lower JWA expression reported in association with tumor progression and poorer outcomes (; ); Combined detection of JWA with p53, MDM2, XRCC1, or FAK has also been associated with prognostic stratification in gastric cancer; however, whether such combinations provide incremental clinical utility, particularly in older patients, requires prospective validation ().

JWA-related measurements have also been investigated in the context of treatment response. RT-qPCR and western blot analyses of JWA and XRCC1 expression have been associated with platinum-based chemotherapy response or resistance in selected experimental and clinical contexts, potentially reflecting differences in oxidative-stress-associated DNA-repair capacity (; ). Combined assessment of JWA and breast cancer susceptibility gene 1 (BRCA1) mRNA has likewise been investigated in relation to cisplatin or docetaxel response in advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (). These findings support the potential value of JWA-related measurements as candidate biomarkers of disease characteristics or treatment response, but they do not yet establish their clinical utility for screening, treatment selection, or response-guided management, including in older patients.

The reported JWA/TH expression pattern in Parkinson’s disease provides disease-associated evidence, but age-stratified validation is required to determine whether this association is specifically modified by patient age (). JWA and GLT-1 expression analyses have been investigated in relation to dopaminergic neuronal injury, glutamate homeostasis, and oxidative-stress responses in experimental models (). These findings support the use of JWA-related measurements as research readouts of neuronal stress and injury, but their value as diagnostic biomarkers of age-related dopaminergic neurodegeneration has not been established. For prion disease, RT-qPCR and western blot analyses of JWA and downstream molecules, including CALCOCO1, PrPˢc, and ATG12, have been used to characterize abnormal protein aggregation, ER-phagy/reticulophagy, and associated stress responses (). These measurements currently support mechanistic investigation rather than clinical diagnosis, and their diagnostic value in other protein-aggregation diseases requires independent clinical validation.

RT-qPCR or western blot detection of JWA in intestinal tissue or peripheral blood has been investigated in relation to radiotherapy-associated intestinal injury and responses to protective interventions, potentially reflecting changes in cellular stress responses (). These measurements may provide research readouts of intestinal injury and stress responses, but their value for predicting susceptibility, evaluating disease severity, or monitoring treatment efficacy has not been clinically established. Analysis of JWA and ROS/MAPK pathway molecules has been used to characterize cellular responses to Cd-induced cytotoxicity and environmental pollutant exposure (). Similarly, detection of JWA and MEK/ERK/Elk pathway components has been investigated in relation to cellular responses to chemical carcinogens and chemically induced skin cancer risk (). These observations provide experimental or disease-associated evidence, whereas their value for individual risk prediction or clinical decision-making remains to be determined. JWA has also been associated with pathological processes in osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease through effects on bone metabolism and vascular endothelial homeostasis, but age-specific biomarker utility remains insufficiently characterized (; ).

Several experimental strategies have been investigated to modulate JWA-associated stress and signaling pathways, including JWA-inducing compounds, pathway-directed interventions, combination approaches, and targeted delivery systems (; ; ). However, the available evidence remains predominantly preclinical and varies substantially across disease models. To maintain an evidence-calibrated interpretation, the following discussion distinguishes three levels of translational evidence: experimentally demonstrated interventions, preclinical candidate strategies, and mechanistic therapeutic hypotheses. Experimentally demonstrated interventions refer to effects directly supported by intervention and outcome measurements in disease-relevant models; preclinical candidate strategies are approaches supported by disease-model evidence but requiring further validation of efficacy, safety, mechanism, or generalizability; and mechanistic therapeutic hypotheses are proposed applications inferred from JWA-associated mechanisms that have not yet been directly tested in the relevant disease context.

For chemotherapy sensitization in low-JWA-expressing tumors, JAC1, JAC4, or modulation of MEK/ERK/p38-associated signaling has shown enhanced apoptotic responses when combined with chemotherapeutic agents in experimental models (; ; ). These findings support candidate preclinical strategies for further evaluation in age-relevant tumor models rather than established treatment approaches. In platinum-resistant tumors with high JWA expression, JWA-targeted Pt(IV) prodrugs, including Cis-wog and Cx-platin-Cl, have been investigated for reversing chemoresistance through modulation of the JWA-XRCC1 pathway and associated tumor-cell responses (; ). Their efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetics, and disease-specific applicability require further preclinical validation. In metastasis-related models, JWA-associated interventions targeting MAPK/F-actin, CXCR4, or FAK-related signaling have shown inhibitory effects on invasion or migration in experimental systems (; ; ). These observations provide a mechanistic basis for future preclinical investigation but do not currently support JWA-guided treatment selection or clinical risk stratification ().

For Parkinson’s disease-relevant models, JWA activation, including JAC4 treatment, has been associated with protection of dopaminergic neurons through suppression of ferritinophagy, modulation of Nrf2-associated responses, or enhancement of GLT-1-mediated glutamate uptake (; ; ). Combination approaches involving ferroptosis inhibitors or autophagy modulators have also shown protective effects in experimental models. These findings support candidate preclinical strategies for further investigation rather than an established therapeutic strategy for age-related Parkinson’s disease (; ). For prion disease, JWA activation or modulation of the Ca2+-AMPK-CALCOCO1 pathway has been associated with enhanced reticulophagy and PrPˢc clearance in disease models (). This mechanism may warrant investigation in other protein-aggregation disorders sharing related stress-response mechanisms, but its broader therapeutic applicability remains hypothetical. In hippocampal neurogenesis models, JWA downregulation or inhibition has been reported to activate the FAK/PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and promote neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity. This represents a context-dependent neuronal phenotype; Alzheimer’s disease-specific studies involving direct JWA manipulation remain lacking, and no Alzheimer’s disease-specific therapeutic implication can currently be established ().

In radiation injury models, JAC4 treatment has been associated with protection against radiation-induced intestinal injury through JWA-associated antioxidant and anti-inflammatory responses (). These findings support further preclinical evaluation of JWA activation for normal-tissue protection during radiotherapy, including assessment in age-relevant models. In environmental-stress models, JWA-associated interventions have been reported to enhance cellular responses to heavy metals such as Cd and chemical carcinogens such as B[a]P, whereas the therapeutic efficacy of these approaches in age-related or systemic disease models remains to be established (; ). In intestinal disease models, JWA activation or modulation of the ERK/FBXW7-NOTCH1 axis has been associated with improved epithelial repair and homeostasis (). Whether these effects translate into a strategy for preventing or delaying age-related intestinal dysfunction remains a mechanistic therapeutic hypothesis requiring validation in aging-specific models.

At the drug-development level, structure-guided optimization of JWA-modulating compounds such as JAC1 and JAC4 should be considered only after their direct compound-target relationships and binding determinants have been experimentally resolved. Current evidence supports modulation of YY1/CTBP1-JWA-associated pathways, but the structural basis required for definitive structure-guided optimization remains incompletely defined (; ).; PRA1-domain-targeted compounds may represent a future drug-development strategy because of the potential role of the PRA1 domain in ER membrane organization and ER-phagy; however, their direct target engagement, pharmacological activity, and therapeutic efficacy remain to be established (; ). Tumor-targeted nanocarriers, brain-targeted systems, and intestinal-targeted delivery approaches may likewise be explored as preclinical strategies for JWA modulation, but their biodistribution, target engagement, efficacy, and safety require experimental validation before translational development can be considered (; ). Importantly, the therapeutic direction of JWA modulation should not be assumed to be universally activating or inhibitory. The evidence reviewed here indicates that JWA may preserve XRCC1-dependent DNA repair in one cellular context but facilitate drug resensitization through XRCC1 destabilization in another, while JWA activation is associated with neuroprotection in some disease-relevant models, whereas JWA loss enhances hippocampal neurogenesis in a different experimental context. Thus, the therapeutic question is not simply whether JWA should be increased or decreased. Rather, future intervention should be guided by cell state, disease context, basal stress/redox state, DNA-repair demand, proteostatic burden, and the specific downstream effector program being targeted. This context-dependent principle should be established before JWA modulation is considered for disease-specific therapeutic development.

Key JWA-associated redox mechanisms remain unresolved: direct binding sites, atomic structures, and regulatory patterns between JWA and redox-sensitive targets (MAPK molecules, NCOA4, XRCC1) are undefined, these structural uncertainties also limit the extent to which current JWA-modulating compounds can be subjected to definitive structure-guided optimization (; ); the tubulin-binding domain and microtubule polymerization regulatory mechanisms in redox signaling are uncharacterized (). Functionally, key regulatory factors governing JWA’s bidirectional stress-response roles (tumor-suppressive vs. oncogenic) are unknown (); the molecular mechanisms underlying cell-type-specific MAPK subtype regulation in redox signaling remain unclear (; ). Additionally, how JWA polymorphisms influence redox stress sensitivity (e.g., effects on protein structure and promoter redox responsiveness) and the balanced regulatory network of JWA ubiquitination in redox signaling (e.g., deubiquitinating enzyme identity at the K158 site) have not been fully addressed (; ). More importantly, the molecular mechanisms by which JWA regulates aging hallmarks and how aging affects JWA’s redox regulatory function are still unclear, which is a key gap in current research (). The age-dependent post-translational modification of JWA and its impact on protein stability and downstream pathway regulation have not been systematically explored, and the crosstalk between JWA and other classic aging-related signaling pathways (e.g., mTOR, SIRT1) remains to be elucidated, which restricts the understanding of JWA’s core role in the aging regulatory network (; ; ).

JWA-related clinical translation remains limited due to insufficient clinical validation and incomplete characterization of its context-dependent molecular functions, and the aging-related clinical research is even more scarce, which severely limits its application in age-related disease intervention. In biomarker research: Most studies are single-center, small-sample, and retrospective, lacking multi-center, multi-ethnic prospective validation of JWA and combined redox-sensitive biomarkers (p53, MDM2, XRCC1) (; ; ; ); clinical data on JWA expression correlation with redox dysregulation in disease progression/chemotherapeutic efficacy (e.g., Parkinson’s disease) remain scarce, and there is almost no large-sample clinical data on JWA as a biomarker for age-related disease risk stratification and prognostic evaluation, although age-stratified clinical validation remains limited (; ; ; ). In therapeutic translation: Human pharmacokinetics, long-term safety, and optimal dosages of JWA-targeted redox modulators (JAC1, JAC4, Cis-wog) are undetermined, with no candidates entering clinical development (; ; ); the therapeutic effect and safety of JWA-activating compound in the elderly population have not been verified by preclinical or clinical studies, and the age-related pharmacokinetic changes of JWA-targeted drugs are still unclear; JWA-related gene therapy and targeted delivery technologies are in preclinical stages, lacking in vivo efficacy and safety verification (; ); JWA’s causal role in redox dysregulation-related diseases remains unclear, hindering its direct translation as a clinical intervention target (). In addition, the combination strategy of JWA-targeted therapy with traditional anti-aging interventions (e.g., caloric restriction, antioxidant supplementation) has not been explored, and there is a lack of research on personalized JWA-targeted intervention based on age and genetic background.

The current research on JWA and aging is further limited by the lack of aging-specific standardized models and detection methods. In research models: Most mechanism studies rely on single cell lines (e.g., HeLa, PC12, K562), lacking validation in primary cells, humanized animal models, and disease subtypes under different redox contexts (; ; ; ); key JWA redox functions (e.g., radiation protection, neuroprotection) are only validated in mouse models, with no systematic verification in aged animal models and human aging tissue samples (; ); there is a lack of conditional knockout animal models of JWA in specific tissues of aged mice, which cannot accurately simulate the tissue-specific regulatory role of JWA in the aging process. In detection technologies: JWA expression detection methods (IHC, qPCR) lack unified standards for antibody selection, staining scoring, and primer design, leading to poor inter-study result comparability in redox-related studies; there is no standardized detection framework for JWA expression across age-stratified human blood, tissue, and aging-cell samples, which restricts the clinical application of JWA as an aging-related biomarker; gene polymorphism studies are severely limited to the southern Chinese Han population, lacking large-sample validation across ethnicities/regions and different age groups (; ). Additionally, insufficient focus on JWA interactions with key redox pathways (e.g., mTOR, gut microbiota-related redox pathways) in the aging microenvironment limits understanding of its regulatory network in complex physiological/pathological microenvironments (; ).

In terms of breadth: Regulatory networks of JWA in emerging redox-related fields (ER autophagy, iron metabolism, amino acid homeostasis) are incompletely elucidated; for example, molecular kinetic mechanisms of JWA-mediated ER membrane remodeling and specific stress-responsive transport pathways regulating taurine/glutamate homeostasis remain unclear (; ; ); functional studies in non-neural/non-tumor redox-related fields (e.g., bone metabolism, drug addiction) are fragmented (; ), and the research on JWA’s role in age-related cardiovascular diseases, and immune senescence is still in the preliminary stage, with no systematic exploration of its core regulatory mechanisms. In terms of depth: Downstream redox-sensitive target genes and key signaling nodes of JWA have not been fully identified; core mechanisms, including the E3 ubiquitin ligase mediating Sp1 degradation and detailed Nrf2 pathway activation processes in redox signaling, remain undefined (; ); research on JWA’s long-term regulatory effects and molecular mechanisms in aging-related redox dysregulation and environmental pollutant responses is scarce (; ), and the dynamic changes of JWA expression and function during the entire aging process (from young to old) and its correlation with aging-related physiological and pathological changes have not been clarified. In addition, the sex-specific and tissue-specific differences in JWA’s redox regulatory function during aging have not been explored, and the impact of environmental factors (e.g., diet, exercise, environmental pollutants) on JWA expression in the aging process and its underlying mechanisms are still unclear.

For JWA research, the future focus should be on integrating aging research into the core of molecular mechanism elucidation, and systematically exploring the crosstalk between JWA and aging-related signaling pathways. For protein interactions and structural bases, crystal structure analysis and cryo-electron microscopy should be employed to clarify JWA’s core binding sites, atomic structures, and regulatory patterns with redox-sensitive target proteins (NCOA4, XRCC1, MAPK pathway molecules) (; ; ); resolve the amino acid residues mediating JWA-NCOA4 binding and the molecular network regulating ferritinophagy inhibition, and explore the age-dependent changes of this binding interaction (; ); define the key JWA-tubulin binding domain and detailed regulatory mechanisms of microtubule polymerization in redox signaling (); elucidate the balanced regulatory mechanisms of JWA post-translational modifications (ubiquitination, phosphorylation) in redox responses, and clarify the age-dependent changes of JWA post-translational modification and its impact on protein stability (). For functional regulatory networks and specificity mechanisms, systematically decode the switching mechanism of JWA’s bidirectional stress-responsive functions, identifying key regulatory factors (e.g., tumor microenvironment, redox context, aging status) and downstream signaling nodes (); explore the molecular mechanisms underlying JWA’s cell-type-specific and age-dependent regulation of MAPK subtypes in redox signaling (; ); decipher the functional mechanisms by which JWA gene polymorphisms (−76G>C, 723T>G) influence redox stress sensitivity and disease risk in different age groups (; ); focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms of JWA regulating aging hallmarks such as genomic instability, cellular senescence, and stem-cell dysfunction, and explore the crosstalk between JWA and classic aging-related signaling pathways (mTOR, SIRT1, AMPK, etc.) in the redox regulatory network. In addition, explore the age-dependent epigenetic regulation mechanism of JWA (DNA methylation, histone modification) and its impact on gene expression and redox regulatory function.

For JWA research, the future clinical translation should focus on the elderly population and age-related diseases, and prioritize validation of JWA as a candidate biomarker and experimental therapeutic target through appropriately designed preclinical and clinical studies.

For biomarker clinical validation and standardization: Conduct multi-center, multi-ethnic, large-sample prospective clinical studies to evaluate the reproducibility and incremental value of JWA-associated biomarkers and its combined redox-sensitive biomarkers (p53, MDM2, XRCC1) in prognostic prediction, efficacy evaluation and age-stratified risk assessment for age-associated diseases (; ; ); across age-stratified human peripheral blood, tissue samples, and relevant aging-cell models, unifying antibody selection, staining scoring criteria, and primer design to improve the comparability and reliability of results (; ); expand clinical validation of JWA gene polymorphisms, in different age groups and ethnicities, exploring their synergistic effects with environmental redox factors (e.g., smoking, chemical toxin exposure, diet, exercise) (; ). Future studies may evaluate whether JWA expression and genotype add predictive value to established clinical risk models based on JWA expression level and gene polymorphism, and verify its clinical application value in the early screening and prognostic evaluation of age-related diseases (tumor, neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular diseases).

For targeted drug development and translation: Further characterize existing JWA-modulating compounds (JAC1, JAC4, and Cis-wog) with respect to direct target relationships, pharmacological selectivity, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, toxicity, dose-response relationships, and disease-specific efficacy. These studies should proceed through appropriate cell, primary-cell or organoid, animal, and, where relevant, aged-animal models before consideration of clinical development. Brain-targeted or intestinal-targeted delivery systems may be explored as preclinical strategies, but their efficacy, biodistribution, and safety require experimental validation.

For JWA and aging research, it is necessary to construct aging-specific research models and optimize detection technologies to simulate the in vivo aging microenvironment and accurately detect JWA’s expression and function in aging cells and tissues. For model construction and application: Construct JWA conditional knockout, tissue-specific overexpression and knock-in animal models in aged mice, and age-stratified PDX models representing relevant patient age groups and humanized aging mouse models to simulate the in vivo aging redox microenvironment, verifying JWA’s functions in tumor metastasis, neurodegeneration, intestinal homeostasis and other aging-related physiological and pathological processes (; ); establish a cell model library covering multiple aging stages, disease subtypes and redox contexts (e.g., primary human aging fibroblasts, neural stem cells, intestinal stem cells) to investigate JWA functional specificity in different aging states (; ). Construct human gut microbiota-aged mouse chimeric models to explore the crosstalk between JWA, gut microbiota and redox balance in the aging process.

For detection technology and research method innovation: Develop high-sensitivity and high-specificity JWA expression detection technologies (e.g., digital PCR, single-molecule immunoassays) to achieve precise quantification of JWA and related redox molecules in body-fluid and tissue samples collected across relevant age groups (; ); combine single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to analyze JWA’s cell-specific expression patterns and redox-context-dependent functional heterogeneity in the aging tissue microenvironment (e.g., aging brain, intestinal tissue, tumor microenvironment) (; ); utilize bioinformatics to construct a panoramic JWA redox signaling pathway network in the aging process, and explore potential interacting molecules and target nodes (); develop non-invasive detection methods for JWA expression (e.g., circulating exosome JWA detection) for the future biomarker evaluation and longitudinal monitoring of age-associated diseases.

For JWA research, it is necessary to expand the research scope to various age-related diseases, explore the common regulatory mechanisms of JWA in oxidative stress and aging, and develop personalized combination intervention strategies. For cross-disease functional research: Expand JWA functional studies to redox-sensitive age-related diseases, metabolic diseases, and environment-related diseases (; ; ); further verify JWA’s broad-spectrum neuroprotective potential in clearing abnormal protein aggregates via stress-associated reticulophagy in other neurodegenerative diseases, and explore its regulatory role in cognitive decline and memory impairment in aging or neurodegenerative disease models (; ); investigate JWA’s role in regulating gut microbiota-intestinal epithelial redox homeostasis in the aging process, and clarify its impact on age-related intestinal barrier damage and systemic inflammation (; ); explore the regulatory role of JWA in immune senescence and age-related inflammatory responses (inflammaging), and clarify its mechanism of action in regulating the redox regulation of immune cells during aging.

For combination therapy strategy exploration: Explore synergies between JWA-targeted redox therapy and existing treatments in the elderly populationexisting treatments in age-associated disease context includes evaluating the combined efficacy of JWA-modulating strategies in gastric cancer models representing relevant age-associated contexts; verifying synergies of JWA modulators with chemotherapeutic drugs and immune checkpoint inhibitors in relevant tumor models, with age-dependent effects requiring future evaluation, and identifying optimal combination regimens to reduce toxicity and adverse effects (; ; ; ; ). Explore combined application of JWA with other DNA repair pathway inhibitors (e.g., poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors) and neuroprotective agents (e.g., neurotrophic factors) to provide more efficient treatment combinations for age-redox dysregulation-related diseases (; ). In addition, strengthen the research on the long-term safety, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and age-dependent toxicity of JWA-targeted strategies, and provide a scientific basis for its clinical application.

JWA is best understood not as a universal regulator of redox homeostasis or a direct ROS sensor, but as a context-dependent stress-responsive regulatory protein that intersects with redox-associated cellular processes. Its functional consequences depend on cellular identity, basal redox state, stress intensity, DNA-repair demand, proteostatic burden, and disease context.

This context dependence provides a framework for interpreting apparently divergent observations across the JWA literature. For example, JWA can support XRCC1 stability and oxidative DNA repair in normal cells, whereas distinct regulatory states in therapy-resistant cancer cells can produce an opposite effect on XRCC1 and chemotherapy response. Similarly, neuronal studies indicate that JWA can protect dopaminergic neurons from ferroptotic injury while JWA deficiency enhances hippocampal neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity in another experimental context. These findings should therefore not be reduced to a single universal direction of JWA activity.

Within the aging framework, current evidence supports an association between JWA-related stress regulation and selected age-associated disease processes, but direct evidence establishing JWA as a universal regulator of biological aging remains limited. The major unresolved question is whether age-dependent changes in JWA expression or activity are causal determinants of tissue dysfunction or instead reflect downstream responses to altered cellular stress, DNA-repair demand, and proteostatic burden. Addressing this question will require aging-specific models, longitudinal studies, tissue-resolved analyses, and age-stratified human datasets.

From a translational perspective, JWA-related expression patterns, genetic variants, and pharmacological modulators remain candidate or experimental opportunities rather than clinically validated tools. Future studies should prioritize mechanism-specific validation, biomarker standardization, pharmacological characterization, and disease-specific preclinical evaluation before clinical development can be considered. Thus, the principal value of JWA research at present lies in defining when and how this context-dependent stress-response network influences redox-associated tissue adaptation, rather than assuming a universal therapeutic direction. The central challenge is therefore not simply to determine whether JWA is protective or detrimental, but to define the biological conditions under which JWA-associated stress regulation produces distinct functional outcomes.

neuroscience.title: ID-SCAN: a functional MRI protocol for neurophenomenological phenotyping of dissociative identity disorder without trauma provocation
neuroscience.abstract: Background: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a trauma-related dissociative disorder in which two or more identity-agents recur within one person, each experiencing and evaluating itself and its surroundings. Most existing neuroimaging paradigms rely on symptom provocation using trauma-related autobiographical material. Identity-agent effects that are independent of symptom provocation need to be disentangled from emotional responses to trauma-related material and from the co-consciousness of other identity-agents.Objective: To introduce ID-SCAN (Identity-agent State Characterisation and Analysis), a functional MRI protocol without trauma provocation for within-person neurophenomenological characterisation of identity-agent expression and switching, and to test its feasibility in a co-conscious case.Method: A woman with DID living with persistent co-consciousness between two identity-agents (Adu and Ado) completed two fMRI tasks: identity-cued evaluation of identical insect photographs the agents made sense of in opposite ways, and trait judgments about self, the other agent and a shared intimate other. Within-person analyses combined Bayesian general linear modelling, generalised psychophysiological interaction, representational similarity analysis and a pooled identity-cue switching analysis, with cross-task overlap providing a task-general baseline.Results: Adu and Ado made sense of the same insect photographs differently. Ado showed greater activation in striato-thalamic regions, whereas Adu showed greater activation in the amygdala and in the orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex; the two also differed in task-evoked connectivity. Adu-as-self and Ado-as-self occupied separable positions within self-referential regions. Cue-locked activity differed by switch direction, with greater reconfiguration when switching to the less-foregrounded Adu. Cross-task overlap localised to posterior visual and dorsal parietal cortex.Conclusions: Two co-conscious identity-agents showed distinct, convergent neurophenomeno-logical signatures of expression and switching in this single case without trauma provocation. ID-SCAN suits single-case and groupwise, simulator-controlled designs and provides a candidate framework for future longitudinal and treatment-related research whose test–retest reliability and clinical sensitivity remain to be established.
neuroscience.text:
Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a severe trauma-related dissociative disorder associated with chronic functional impairment, elevated self-harm risk and high treatment utilisation (Brand et al., ; Myrick et al., ). Historically its status was contested, but converging neurobiological evidence now supports the clinical observation that DID is a trauma-related disorder on the same spectrum as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), moving it, as Reinders and Veltman () put it, ‘out of the shadows’ of psychiatry (Reinders et al., ; Reinders & Veltman, ; Roydeva & Reinders, ). What still sets DID apart methodologically is that its defining phenomena are lived privately: within a single nervous system, shifts in who one takes oneself to be, and in what one feels, wants or fears, can be abrupt and pervasive, yet an observer has access only to testimony and behaviour. This epistemic asymmetry motivates neurophenomenological approaches (Nijenhuis, ; Varela, ) that measure phenomenological and neural features in relation to one another, and it calls for clinically tolerable paradigms that can characterise identity-agent expression and switching without relying on trauma-related autobiographical recall or symptom provocation.

Functional neuroimaging has begun to meet this need. Studies report identity-dependent activation and connectivity profiles in limbic, paralimbic and default-mode systems (Reinders et al., , ; Schlumpf et al., ), and, critically, these profiles are not reproduced by healthy participants instructed and motivated to simulate DID (Reinders et al., , ; Vissia et al., ). Independent samples have replicated these simulation-independent differences, together discrediting the view that DID is a product of suggestion or fantasy (Dimitrova et al., ; Reinders & Veltman, ; Strouza et al., ). The theory of structural dissociation frames DID as an organisation of the personality into agents that differ in affective and defensive tendencies and coexist with partially overlapping access to memory and agency (Nijenhuis & van der Hart, ; van der Hart et al., ), predicting that identity-agents are implemented as distinct, recurrent network configurations rather than transient fluctuations of a unitary self. Much of this literature, however, relies on symptom provocation or trauma-related autobiographical material. That reliance raises ethical and interpretive difficulties: it can burden or destabilise patients, and it entangles identity-agent effects with the neurobiology of trauma-related remembering, which may proceed differently from ordinary recollection (Kearney et al., ; Kearney & Lanius, ; Rubin et al., ; Shaw et al., ). There is therefore a practical need for tasks that avoid trauma provocation, are standardisable and are closely tied to brain systems that can be interrogated within a single person.

Co-consciousness, simultaneous awareness by more than one identity-agent, is recognised in clinical description and treatment guidelines (Beahrs, ; International Society for the Study of Trauma and Dissociation, ) but has been comparatively neglected in imaging, which has mostly studied patients whose switches are accompanied by marked inter-identity amnesia (Reinders et al., , ; Savoy et al., ; Schlumpf et al., ; Tsai et al., ). How identity-agents are instantiated when co-consciousness is the typical mode of experience thus remains open. Because sustained co-awareness and blending between agents could, if anything, reduce the measurable neural contrast between them (rather than making the agents subjectively more alike), a co-conscious presentation offers a conservative first test of whether tasks that avoid trauma provocation can still recover identity-agent signatures.

Here we introduce ID-SCAN (Identity-agent State Characterisation and Analysis), an identity-cued functional MRI protocol, without trauma provocation, for neurophenomenological phenotyping of identity-agent expression and switching in DID, and we report its first application to a woman with persistent co-consciousness between two identity-agents. The protocol comprises two identity-cued judgment tasks, a pooled cross-task switching analysis and a cross-task overlap analysis, and its architecture separates fixed structural components (trial design, Bayesian single-case statistics, cross-task overlap) from participant-identified components (the images and the intimate other, established with the participant in a semi-structured pre-scan interview). Our aims were to test, within one person: (i) whether identical benign images engage distinct valuation-related brain patterns depending on which agent is foregrounded; (ii) whether each agent occupies a distinct, self-like position within canonical self-referential regions rather than producing a generic identity-cued response style; (iii) how switching between agents is expressed as a task-general signature; and (iv) which processing is shared across agents, providing a conservative within-person baseline. Following structural-dissociation theory, we expected identity-agents to be realised as distinct, recurrent configurations, with self-referential organisation preserved for each agent, with switching costs graded by which agent is less foregrounded, and with the shared baseline confined to domain-general perceptual and attentional systems. Experiment 1 uses naturally occurring, agent-dependent differences in how benign images are appraised to probe valuation and salience with identical input (Craig, ; Critchley & Harrison, ); Experiment 2 adapts a trait-judgment paradigm and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to examine how each agent represents self, the other agent and an intimate other within self-referential regions (Courtney & Meyer, ; Denny et al., ; Heatherton et al., ; Kriegeskorte et al., ).

The participant was a right-handed woman diagnosed with DID according to DSM-5 criteria (American Psychiatric Association, ). The diagnosis was made by a senior psychiatrist with more than 30 years of clinical and research experience in dissociative disorders, on the basis of a clinical interview; the Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) was administered at intake and was markedly elevated. No structured diagnostic interview for dissociative disorders (such as the SCID-D) was administered; we state this explicitly so that readers can weigh the diagnostic evidence directly. The participant reported a history of childhood trauma, consistent with the trauma-related aetiology of the disorder.

Two identity-agents were studied, referred to throughout by the short names Adu (the adult-presenting agent) and Ado (the adolescent-presenting agent). No other identity-agent was currently active. The two lived in persistent co-consciousness with little or no inter-identity amnesia in daily life; the Ado was usually foregrounded and energetic and managed everyday activities, whereas the Adu remained in the background in a watchful, supportive role and was experienced as more fatigued and less active. Their relationship was cooperative and non-antagonistic, resembling a supportive parent–child dynamic, with the Ado relating to the Adu as a maternal figure; overt antagonism was rare. The two differed markedly and stably in everyday preferences (for example in foods and colours, and in the attitudes towards certain small animals used here) and in temperament, while sharing autobiographical continuity. On the advice of the treating psychiatrist, these two clinically stable agents were selected for study; their stable, opposite appraisals of specific everyday images are what the protocol exploits. This cooperative, strongly co-conscious organisation, together with the absence of other active agents, is what made it feasible for the participant to alternate dominance between the two agents rapidly, repeatedly and on request in the scanner, a boundary condition we return to in the Limitations.

At scanning she had comorbid major depressive disorder and was taking duloxetine (20 mg). The protocol was approved by the Kyoto Institute of Technology ethics committee (approval No. 2024-06). Written informed consent was obtained, and the participant consented to the inclusion of anonymized material relating to herself. A safety plan was implemented; during the first session, the participant's attending physician was on site to confirm clinical stability and support predefined stopping criteria.

ID-SCAN uses a rapid event-related design. Event-related timing suited this participant; a block design is equally compatible with the protocol and may be preferable in other cases. Each experiment comprised three runs acquired in a single scanning session, with the two experiments conducted on separate days; the identity cue that opened every trial served as the unit for the pooled switching analysis. A single, clinically tolerable session per experiment was chosen deliberately: because trauma provocation was avoided and the two agents could alternate dominance on request, a within-person design with many trials per condition was feasible without the burden and destabilisation risk of repeated trauma-related scanning. Rather than null-hypothesis power analysis, which is not well defined for an N-of-1 design, inference rested on (i) single-case Bayesian estimation with explicit posterior-probability thresholds, (ii) permutation testing for the switching and RSA analyses, and (iii) internal replication: the same underlying hypothesis was tested with analytically independent methods (activation, task-evoked connectivity, representational geometry and a pooled cue analysis), so that convergent results provide multiple within-person constraints rather than a single test that could be a false positive.

Task fMRI data were acquired on a 3.0-T Siemens Prisma with a 32-channel head coil using the Brain/MINDS Beyond Harmonised MRI Protocol (Koike et al., ), with a multiband gradient-echo echo-planar imaging sequence (TR = 0.8 s, TE = 34.4 ms, multiband factor = 6, 60 axial slices, 2.4-mm isotropic), a T1-weighted MPRAGE structural scan (0.8-mm isotropic) and a dual-echo gradient-echo field map for distortion correction. Full sequence parameters are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Preprocessing was conducted in SPM12 (Friston et al., ) and included slice-timing correction, realignment, field-map-based unwarping, coregistration, normalisation to MNI space and resampling to 2-mm isotropic voxels. No spatial smoothing was applied because the Bayesian estimation framework used for activation analyses estimates spatial noise structure via an internal spatial prior (uninformative global Laplacian, UGL), making conventional Gaussian smoothing potentially detrimental to the resulting posterior probability maps. A 128-s high-pass filter was applied, and six motion parameters per run were included as nuisance regressors. Detailed motion summaries are reported in the Supplementary Methods.

Experiment 1 targets the valuation component of ID-SCAN: whether identical benign images engage distinct valuation-related brain patterns depending on which agent is foregrounded. In a semi-structured pre-scan interview, the two agents identified categories of images that they made sense of in stable, opposite ways. Three insect categories (spiders, Cephonodes hylas, dragonflies) were used because the Adu consistently found them aversive while the Ado found them appealing, allowing rapid appraisals of benign content while holding the visual input identical across agents.

Images and post-scan rating. For each category, seven photographs were obtained from iNaturalist () and paired with phase-preserving grid-scrambled versions, yielding 21 insect and 21 scrambled images. After scanning, each image was rated on a 0–100 visual-analogue scale separately by each agent.

Trial structure. Each trial comprised (i) a 3.0-s identity cue (‘Adu’ or ‘Ado’) with jittered fixation, (ii) 2.0-s image presentation, (iii) a forced-choice perceptual judgment (‘insect or scrambled?’; 5.0-s window), and (iv) an identity-check screen (‘Did you perform this trial in the instructed identity-agent?’; yes/no; 5.0-s window), separated by jittered intervals.

Activation and connectivity analyses. First-level analyses used SPM12's Bayesian general linear model (GLM) with four regressors per run for the 2 × 2 design (Adu/Ado × insect/scrambled), modelled at image onset with the canonical haemodynamic response function, AR(3) noise modelling and UGL priors. Identity-selective ‘spotlight’ contrasts isolated insect-selective responses within each agent (weights: Adu-insect [3, −1, −1, −1]; Ado-insect [−1, −1, 3, −1]) and were evaluated within an a priori valuation mask spanning orbitofrontal, insular, striatal, thalamic and midbrain regions from the Automated Anatomical Labelling atlas version 3 (AAL3; Rolls et al., ). Generalised psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analyses (McLaren et al., ) examined task-evoked coupling for spotlight nodes. Detailed parameter estimates, thresholding rules and rationale (including small-volume thresholding for the masked spotlight contrasts) are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Experiment 2 targets person-knowledge within self-referential regions. Sixty personality adjectives were drawn from a Japanese Big Five adjective set (Wada, ) to test whether each agent instantiates a self-like representation rather than a generic identity-cued response style.

Trial structure. Each trial comprised (i) a 3.0-s identity cue with jittered fixation and (ii) three successive 3.0-s ratings (one per target: Self, the Other identity-agent, and an Intimate other, a person emotionally significant to and well known by both agents, identified with the participant in the pre-scan interview), each on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 4 = strongly agree), separated by 0.5-s blanks and a jittered inter-trial interval. Target order was randomised within trial, yielding 360 rating events across six conditions (Adu-rates-Adu, Adu-rates-Ado, Adu-rates-Other, Ado-rates-Adu, Ado-rates-Ado, Ado-rates-Other) in three runs.

Searchlight multi-regression RSA. Single-rating beta images were estimated with a Bayesian GLM (one regressor per rating). Within 3-voxel-radius spherical searchlights, neural representational similarity matrices (Pearson correlation) were regressed simultaneously onto four binary model matrices: rater identity-agent, target identity, self-versus-non-self, and the full rater-by-target model (Kriegeskorte et al., ). Statistical inference used 1,000 voxel-wise permutations of the rows and corresponding columns of the neural similarity matrix. Maps were thresholded at p < 0.001 with cluster extent > 20 voxels.

Visualisation of person-knowledge geometry. The rater-by-target significance map was intersected with an independent meta-analytic mask from Neurosynth (Yarkoni et al., ) (search term ‘self-referential’; uniformity-test z-map thresholded at false discovery rate q < 0.01). A condition-level representational dissimilarity matrix was computed for the six rater-by-target conditions and metric multidimensional scaling (MDS) was applied; dimensionality was set to three based on an elbow analysis of STRESS values ((D)).

To isolate task-general signatures of intentional switching, identity-cue events from both tasks were pooled and coded by switch direction (switch to Adu versus switch to Ado), independent of task content. In total, 204 cue events were modelled across six runs (84 from Experiment 1 and 120 from Experiment 2; 102 switches to Adu, 102 switches to Ado). Compliance was confirmed on 96.4% of Experiment 1 trials via the on-screen identity-check (81/84; non-confirmed trials coded as a separate error regressor); Experiment 2 had no forced-choice identity-check. A Bayesian event-related GLM modelled the 3-s cue epochs using two switch-direction regressors and an Experiment-1 error regressor, with motion parameters as nuisance regressors. Cluster-level asymmetry was tested by permutation: cluster boundaries were defined from the thresholded contrast maps using 26-connectivity labelling, and cluster-level mean betas were randomly reassigned across contrast directions over 10,000 permutations.

To delineate an identity-invariant, judgment-related substrate shared across tasks, identity-invariant maps were derived independently from each experiment and intersected. In Experiment 1, the perceptual judgment period was modelled separately from image viewing and a judgment > viewing contrast was computed for each agent; voxels reliably expressed in both agents were summarised using a conjunction (Adu AND Ado) map. In Experiment 2, a rater-invariant target map was defined by inclusively masking voxels with significant Target and/or Self-versus-Non-Self effects while exclusively removing voxels with significant Rater and/or Rater × Target effects. The two identity-invariant maps were intersected to identify convergent cross-task regions.

The participant confirmed performing 96.4% of trials in the instructed identity-agent via the on-screen identity-check (81/84 trials; three non-confirmations, all during Adu-cued trials, were modelled as error trials and excluded from activation contrasts). Post-scan ratings confirmed the intended appraisals: across insect images, the Ado rated images as more likable than the Adu (paired t-test across images, p < 0.001). The insects versus scrambled contrast engaged visual cortex ((E); Table S1). Collapsing across image type, picture-viewing activity differed between agents: Ado-cued viewing showed higher responses in dorsal and medial frontal cortex together with sensorimotor territories (Table S2), whereas Adu-cued viewing showed higher responses in orbitofrontal/medial prefrontal and striato-thalamo-cingulate and temporal systems (Table S3).

Within the a priori valuation mask ((E), white outline), identity-selective spotlight contrasts revealed dissociable valuation-related ensembles for the two agents evaluating the same insect images. Ado-selective insect responses were most prominent in striatal and thalamic loci (caudate/putamen and mediodorsal thalamus; Table S4). Adu-selective insect responses were broader, spanning right amygdala, orbitofrontal and medial orbital prefrontal cortex, insula, putamen and thalamic nuclei (Table S5).

Generalised psychophysiological interaction analyses showed that identity-selective spotlight nodes were embedded in dissociable task-evoked networks during evaluation of the same insect images ((F); Tables S4–S5). During Ado insect trials, striato-thalamic seeds (caudate/putamen/mediodorsal thalamus) exhibited increased coupling with insula and medial temporal regions (e.g. parahippocampal cortex), together with action/attention-related territories including precentral and supramarginal cortex and dorsal frontal regions (Table S4). During Adu insect trials, seeds in amygdala and orbitofrontal/medial orbital prefrontal cortex, together with insula, putamen and thalamic nuclei, showed broad coupling with medial and lateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal parietal regions and temporo-occipital visual cortex, as well as medial temporal structures (Table S5).

Multi-regression RSA demonstrated robust representational structure related to both the rater identity-agent and the judged target ((C)). The rater model produced the broadest footprint. Target-related structure was most prominent in posterior medial regions, including precuneus, with additional clusters extending into temporal and cerebellar regions. A Self-versus-Non-Self component was also detectable.

Within the canonical self-referential processing network ((C), white line), the full rater-by-target model accounted best for representational similarity and defined the mask for geometric visualisation. Metric MDS of the six rater-by-target conditions yielded a stable three-dimensional configuration ((D–G)). One dimension separated Adu-as-rater from Ado-as-rater across targets, consistent with a ‘rating identity’ axis. A second dimension separated self-judgments (Adu-as-self; Ado-as-self) from cross-identity judgments, consistent with ‘rater–target compatibility’, with judgments about the shared intimate other occupying an intermediate position. A third dimension captured perspective effects for the intimate other. Ado-as-self occupied a distinct but self-like position rather than collapsing onto Adu-as-self or shifting towards other-judgments.

Cue-locked activity differed by direction of switching ((B); Tables S6–S7). Switch-to-Ado > switch-to-Adu emphasised orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal cortex, anterior insula and striatum, whereas switch-to-Adu > switch-to-Ado showed broader modulation including visual and temporal cortex, medial frontal/cingulate, insula, brainstem, cerebellum and sensorimotor regions. Cluster-wise parameter estimates separated Adu-cue beta values between Adu-ward versus Ado-ward clusters (mean difference = 4.30; permutation p < .0001) more than Ado-cue beta values (mean difference = 0.85; permutation p < .0001). Cluster boundaries were defined from the thresholded Bayesian contrast maps using 26-connectivity labelling (60 Adu-ward, 50 Ado-ward clusters) and fixed before permutation; the null distribution was constructed by pooling cluster-level mean betas from both directions and randomly reassigning them over 10,000 permutations.

In Experiment 1, separating the perceptual judgment period from image viewing yielded judgment greater than viewing effects for both agents, and a conjunction identified voxels reliably expressed in both (). In Experiment 2, a rater-invariant target map was derived by retaining target-related structure while excluding rater-dominated structure. Intersecting these two identity-invariant maps isolated a constrained overlap localised primarily to posterior visual and dorsal parietal cortex (), including calcarine/cuneus regions and a superior parietal locus (Table S8).

We asked whether a protocol without trauma provocation could recover coherent, within-person brain signatures of identity-agent organisation and switching in a co-conscious presentation of DID. As a result, three findings stand out. First, the two identity-agents made sense of identical images in different ways, engaging dissociable valuation-related ensembles and task-evoked networks. Second, within self-referential regions each agent occupied a distinct, self-like position in person-knowledge space, and the same intimate other was evaluated differently depending on which agent was judging. Third, switching between agents was accompanied by a direction-dependent asymmetry, with larger reconfiguration when switching to the typically less-foregrounded Adu. Against these identity-selective effects, only a limited substrate (posterior visual and dorsal parietal cortex) was shared across agents. The overall pattern is one of selective reconfiguration within a shared brain, not a global change in task engagement.

These signatures are neurophenomenological in the sense of Varela (): each was defined by relating a first-person feature (how an agent appraised an image, judged a person, or was cued into dominance) to a neural feature measured in the same person. We read the findings this way rather than as a search for a mechanism behind the person because it fits the phenomena: following Nijenhuis (), the two agents are not merely different response settings but embodied, environmentally embedded centres of experience and action.

The valuation profiles (Experiment 1) were not mirror images of one another but engaged qualitatively different experiences supported by distinct brain patterns. The Ado-associated response centred on caudate/putamen and mediodorsal thalamus, circuitry linked to habitual or cue-driven valuation (Alexander et al., ; Bartra et al., ), with coupling to insula and parahippocampal cortex, consistent with viscero-affective, memory-inflected appraisal. The Adu-associated profile spanned amygdala, orbitofrontal/medial prefrontal cortex and insula, with broad coupling to lateral prefrontal and temporo-occipital regions, consistent with aversion-tagged, top-down evaluation (Bartra et al., ; Phelps & LeDoux, ). This topography converges with the emotion-regulation patterns reported for the apparently normal (neutral) part of DID patients in the PET work of Reinders et al. () and, more habitual and reactive, for emotional parts (Reinders et al., ; Schlumpf et al., ). Because these differences appeared across coordinated regional and connectivity measures, and because analogous personality-state differences are not reproduced by instructed simulators (Reinders et al., , ; Vissia et al., ), they are difficult to read as a uniform response bias; the convergence across paradigms (trauma-related recall versus benign appraisal) and modalities (PET versus fMRI) indicates that identity-agent-dependent brain organisation is not an artefact of trauma-provocation procedures.

Experiment 2 extended this to person knowledge. The key result was not that ratings differed but that each agent occupied a distinct self-like position within self-referential cortical midline structures (Northoff et al., ; Qin & Northoff, ), with target-related structure most prominent in precuneus, a region tied to autobiographical self-knowledge (Qin & Northoff, ). That both Adu-as-self and Ado-as-self were self-like, closer to each other than to non-self judgments, is consistent with two self-configurations realised within overlapping cortical populations, so that identity cues select among existing configurations rather than rebuilding the self anew (Seth & Bayne, ). That the same intimate other was evaluated differently by each agent, aligning with distinct neural patterns, suggests reorganisation rather than mere relabelling; that is, each agent enacts its own second-person perspective as well as its own first-person one (Nijenhuis, ).

The pooled cue analysis moved from state to transition. Larger cue-locked reconfiguration when switching to the Adu indicates a direction-dependent switching cost, consistent with the task-switching literature, in which costs are larger for the less-practised or less-dominant set (Rogers & Monsell, ; Wylie & Allport, ), and with clinical descriptions of dominance asymmetry (International Society for the Study of Trauma and Dissociation, ; van der Hart et al., ). Because the Ado usually managed daily life, the Adu is the less-automatised agent to enter; regions more modulated for Adu-ward switches (medial frontal/cingulate, insula, brainstem) overlap networks implicated in reconfiguring task set (Wylie & Allport, ). Earlier switching studies (Savoy et al., ; Tsai et al., ) reported frontal and temporal involvement but lacked the task-general pooling and quantitative asymmetry used here.

Localisation of the shared substrate to posterior visual and dorsal parietal cortex is consistent with the domain-general perceptual and attentional demands common to both tasks (Corbetta & Shulman, ; Duncan, ; Todd & Marois, ); its identity-invariance indicates that these systems are engaged similarly whichever agent is foregrounded. Posterior-association and parietal regions also figure prominently in our identity-selective effects (in the Adu-associated connectivity and in the switching maps), and this is what the neurobiology of dissociation predicts. These regions are among the most consistently reported neurofunctional correlates of pathological dissociation across disorders (precuneus, supramarginal gyrus, intraparietal sulcus and angular gyrus; Roydeva & Reinders, ), have been linked specifically to the neutral, trauma-avoidant identity state (Reinders et al., ; Roydeva & Reinders, ), and index active but not consciously deliberate cognitive control that implements inter-identity avoidance rather than amnesia, a frontal–parietal signature that simulators do not reproduce (Dimitrova et al., ; Strouza et al., ). That prefrontal and self-referential regions are largely absent from the shared map yet strongly present in the identity-selective effects indicates that higher-order, self-related processing is more agent-dependent than low-level perceptual encoding.

Compared with script-driven imagery in previous studies, which has been central to establishing the neurobiology of DID (Reinders et al., , , ), ID-SCAN trades direct engagement of trauma-related material for three practical strengths. It holds the external input identical across agents, so that differences cannot be attributed to different images; it avoids trauma provocation, widening access to patients for whom symptom provocation is contraindicated or destabilising; and it yields several analytically independent, within-person tests whose convergence constrains interpretation. These properties make ID-SCAN a complement to, not a replacement for, trauma-based paradigms.

Clinically, ID-SCAN's value is that it turns lived identity-agent differences into reproducible, within-person read-outs obtainable under tolerable conditions, which is a prerequisite for tracking change. Because the trial design and analysis are fixed while only the images and the intimate other are established with each participant, the protocol can be applied to new cases without redesigning its core. If replicated, three within-person metrics are candidates for longitudinal use: the switching-asymmetry ratio, the distance between self-positions in the RSA geometry, and the extent of the cross-task identity-invariant overlap; treatment-related integration would be predicted to reduce the first two and potentially expand the third. Establishing these as clinical read-outs will, however, require the trauma-related extensions discussed below.

The main strengths are the identical-input design, the avoidance of trauma provocation and the internal replication across analytically independent methods in a single, well-characterised person. Single-case methodology has a long and productive history in cognitive neuroscience (Caramazza, ; Rosenbaum et al., ), and the present design provides internal replication across two tasks and a pooled cue analysis that together constitute multiple within-person tests of the same hypothesis. The limitations are equally clear. This is one co-conscious case; without trauma-exposed controls, clinical comparison groups and instructed simulators, claims about diagnostic specificity are premature, and a formal simulator comparison in the manner of Reinders et al. (, ) and Vissia et al. () remains necessary. The protocol also requires that the studied agents can alternate dominance rapidly and on request; here this was feasible because the two agents were strongly co-conscious and cooperative and were the only active agents, but it may not generalise to presentations in which agents are mutually phobic or antagonistic, which clinical experience suggests is common. For such presentations, the protocol could be adapted with minor modification, for example to a block design that does not require rapid on-request alternation, though any such adaptation would require separate validation. Because the tasks involved only mild appraisal rather than trauma-related material, they may under-sample precisely the agent differences that emerge around trauma-related cues; extending ID-SCAN to trauma-related cues (the material most relevant to treatment) is an essential next step, to be undertaken with appropriate safeguards. The person-specific images and intimate other are, moreover, intrinsic to the design rather than a confound: idiosyncrasy is what makes the appraisals meaningful, and it is the fixed analytic framework, not the particular images, that is intended to generalise. Because each experiment was acquired in a single scanning session and no task was repeated, the test–retest reliability and across-session reproducibility of the reported effects remain unknown; an independent repeat session in the same participant would provide a stronger within-person replication. Finally, the functional meaning of maintaining the two agents partly separate, the origins of their differing preferences, and their detailed evaluations of one another were not systematically assessed and are not inferred here.

A protocol without trauma provocation recovered coherent, convergent neurophenomenological signatures of identity-agent expression and switching in a single co-conscious DID case, alongside a limited shared baseline. ID-SCAN offers a clinically tolerable and extensible foundation for the cohort, simulator-controlled and longitudinal studies (including trauma-related and treatment-tracking work) needed to establish the specificity and clinical utility of these signatures.

neuroscience.title: An MRI template of the female C57Bl/6N mouse brain
neuroscience.abstract: Brain templates are pivotal tools for standardized image analysis and interpretation in neuroimaging studies. However, matching data and reference remains essential. With growing awareness of sex as a relevant biological variable and male-centric biases in past medical investigations, the continuous limited use and availability of female-specific brain templates, particularly in preclinical research are alarming.To address this gap in preclinical neuroimaging, we created a high-resolution, in vivo structural MRI brain template for female C57Bl/6N mice, a population-average derived from 153 axial and coronal scans of 80 female mice. We further analyzed the template’s characteristics regarding the achieved effective resolution and compared it to currently available standard brains. Validation was performed by spatially normalizing external data to established templates and the novel reference, contrasting the degree of deformation.We present a readily applicable and accessible set of files (structural images, tissue probability maps, anatomical annotations, and transformation matrices) as reference for female-centric neuroimaging research questions. The novel template brain exhibits high nominal and effective resolution, differs significantly in spatial and cohort characteristics from previous references and shows improved performance with external data of female mice.We propose that integrating sex-specific tools into preclinical neuroimaging studies is essential for reducing sex bias, enhancing data reproducibility and strengthening the translational validity of neuroscientific findings. Research further disentangling (sub-)strain- and sex-differences is warranted.
neuroscience.text:
Brain templates and atlases are essential tools in neuroscience research []. They serve as references for standardized image processing, translation, interpretation, and reporting of experimental data. Specific resources for different species and developmental stages are currently available, that represent various dimensions of structural, functional, or genetic modalities of the brain. Despite their vital role in advancing our understanding of the nervous system, the applicability and limitations of these resources should be carefully considered when working with or referring to a specific brain atlas or template []. The underlying (imaging) modality and methodology, but more importantly, the oftentimes very specific and restricted input data set needs to be taken into account [,].

Tailored tools for certain age groups [], nationalities and/or ethnicities [] and pathologies [,] are available for the human brain and deemed essential [], to avoid biases from the application of ill-matched references []. However, specific templates appear to be used to a lesser extent to cover sex-specific aspects, particularly in preclinical research. The limited number of previous works were either not widely disseminated or are not openly accessible [,,]. However, differences between sexes in total brain volume, structure, function and temporal development have been widely reported [,]. Models have even been applied to classify human brains by sex based on anatomical characteristics (e.g. [,], but discussed critically in [,]). Recently, dimorphism in the Drosophila central nervous system’s connectome has also been reported [].

A by no means exhaustive selection of templates, aiming to provide a gross overview of human and mouse (one of the most common preclinical models in neuroscience research []) neuroimaging templates and their underlying data characteristics can be found in . A more in-depth review of available mouse atlases, also highlighting the aforementioned paucity of and need for female data-sets in in vivo mouse studies, has been provided elsewhere [,]. To the best of our knowledge, there are currently only two annotated female templates openly available [,], one of which is derived from the most studied C57Bl/6 strain, but it exhibits low, highly anisotropic resolution across slices. Physiological, morphological and potentially related behavioral differences between various inbred [,] and outbred mouse strains, including J and N C57Bl/6-substrains [] (see also ), may further limit their broad applicability.[]

Female-only templates are marked in grey. Squares (□) denote MR templates accessible to the authors online at the time of writing without personal request. N is used to indicate the population size, n the number of female individuals included.
