To bridge the existing gap in the availability of sex-specific resources, we report the availability of a high-resolution, cohort-derived, template of the female mouse brain. It includes tissue probability maps, spatial transformations from other common standards and spatially matched annotations. The underlying data was collected within a multi-armed, longitudinal structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study in female C57Bl/6N mice.

Despite their smooth surface and lack of gyrification, mouse brains may differ significantly between strains, both in structural and functional aspects. Genetical manipulations, different physiology, vulnerability to certain diseases and various behavioral phenotypes extend the spectrum.

Scholz et al. have previously shown that three common mouse strains (C57Bl/6J, CD-1, 129S6) significantly differ in brain surface anatomy, specifically in motor, anterior somatosensory, retrosplenial and entorhinal cortex. Already two principal components could be used to differentiate strains with 91% accuracy []. Skeletal, specifically skull measures were also found to be divergent between mouse strains [] and sexes in rats []. Importantly, phenotypical differences are not only prevalent between strains, but even between sub-strains []. For the C57Bl/6 sub-strains C57Bl/6J and C57Bl/6N, substantial divergence in behavioral and neurological function has been reported [,].  summarizes the most prominent differences in these two C57Bl/6 sub-strains. Even between 6J sub-lines, neuroanatomical and behavioral divergence has long been observed [,]. Against this background, there is a justified need to create currently lacking brain templates and atlases for the N-sub-strain.

Sexual dimorphism in murine brain structure and function has repeatedly been reported. Interestingly, studies in humans reporting males to have larger and more variable total brain volume, have not been reproduced in rodents []. However, neural differences at the cellular and synaptic levels (e.g [,].) have been observed, complementing macroscopic differences [] and sex-dependent results in structural and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging [,,,,]. These data strongly indicate specific brain areas including the (medial) amygdala, bed nuclei of the stria terminalis and hypothalamic subregions. In awake rats, resting-state functional MRI identified sex-specific network organization and connectivity strength []. Male and female mice on the other hand showed differences in BOLD activation to mechanical stimuli [].

Hence, although in comparison to the human brain, the mouse brain might show less striking anatomical variability, known sexual dimorphisms may still bias nonlinear registration and atlas-based quantification of (f)MRI data. A brain template derived of scans of female and male brains constitutes an average that might not be optimally suited to represent either sex. Consequently, registering female datasets onto a mixed-sex template may result in local deformations and/or diminish sensitivity to the detection of female-specific neuroanatomical effects. It remains to be determined if and how sex-related registration bias may have impacted the results obtained in previous studies relying on the use of mixed-sex templates, but this is inherently depending on the availability of a sex-specific resource.

All experimental procedures were approved by the National Ethics Committee on Animal Care and Use (Bundesministerium für Wissenschaft und Forschung, GZ: 2021-0.150.413) and were conducted by trained personnel. ARRIVE guidelines were adhered to as applicable (see Supplemental Material).

Eighty female C57Bl/6N(Crl) mice were obtained from Charles River (Sulzfeld, Germany) in two cohorts of forty mice each. They were housed in pairs, in individually ventilated cages (Tecniplast, Italy), on a 12-hour dark-light cycle, with ad libitum access to water and standard chow (Breeding/Maintenance Diet - Rats/Mice, Altromin Spezialfutter GmbH & Co. KG, Germany). Cages were equipped with nesting material and a wooden gnawing stick. Upon arrival in the facility, the mice were allowed to habituate for a minimum of 13 days prior to the MR scan. A larger age span of 69–108 days at time of scanning was consciously chosen to robustly represent the ‘adult’ female brain. Covering a range of several weeks ensures wider applicability [,] and aligns with age ranges used in templates for healthy human adults [].

Magnetic resonance images (MRI) were recorded at the facilities of the Preclinical Imaging Laboratories, Department of Biomedical Imaging and Image-guided Therapy, Medical University of Vienna. A 9.4 T μMRI scanner (BioSpec 94/30 USR, Bruker Germany) running ParaVision 360 v3.3 software, in combination with a mouse-brain-specific, transmit/receive, helium-cooled surface coil (CryoProbe Z125365) was used.

Anesthesia was induced by placing an animal in a chamber filled with 3.5% isoflurane in medical air. The mouse was positioned in a headfirst, prone position on a water-heated MRI bed. The head was fixed using a bite bar and net dressing, fastened at the rear end of the bite bar and 3D-printed anchors. Ear bars were not used. Eyes and ear canals were covered respectively with ointment (Bepanthen® Augen- und Nasensalbe, Bayer Austria, containing 50 mg/g (+)-Panthenol) and cotton balls to reduce scanner noise.

The maintenance phase of anesthesia was initiated by an intramuscular injection of 0.1 mg/kg medetomidine hydrochloride (Domitor®, 1 mg/ml, Orion Pharma) in the hind legs. Subsequently, the isoflurane concentration was gradually reduced during the anatomical scans to 0.5% for later functional MRI acquisitions, for which combined anesthetic regimens such as isoflurane and medetomidine are currently regarded as state-of-the-art []. However, the analysis of and reports on the functional data are beyond the scope of this paper. While deep anesthesia may be favorable to limit movement during structural recordings, this sequence order (structural, followed by functional scans) allowed for gradual isoflurane reduction, without having to pause functional image acquisition for isoflurane effects to subside, hence reducing the total exposure to anesthesia. Due to aforementioned head fixation, motion artefacts were nonetheless negligible.

As overall acquisition time was less than one hour, medetomidine was only injected prior to and not infused continuously during scanning. Venous cannulation could therefore be omitted. Of note, due to physiological effects such as vasoconstriction, at a small scale and high resolution, both functional and also structural images might be affected differently by various anesthetic substances [].

Upon positioning in the scanner and verification of placement and signal quality (matching and tuning), shimming, B0 field mapping, and two consequent anatomical scans per mouse were performed. To retrospectively confirm the absence of significant image distortions in the center of the scanner bore, a 3D-printed phantom featuring both a regular, orthogonal grid and the shape of a mouse skull was constructed and measured with both CT (i.e. inherently free of distortions) and MR (see Supp. Figure 1).

The respiratory activity of the animals was constantly monitored during scans (SA Instruments, Inc., Stony Brook, NY, USA). The structural sequence parameters were T2 TurboRARE: 1) TE/TR = 40/3200 ms, 3 averages, matrix 256 × 256, resolution 75 × 75 µm (axial), slice thickness 250 µm, scan duration 05:07 (excluding gating), and 2) TE/TR = 40/3163 ms, no averaging, resolution 78 × 38 µm (coronal), slice thickness 500 µm, scan duration 01:41 (excluding gating). As respiratory gating was observed to introduce subtle, but nevertheless notable intensity inhomogeneities between planes of axial scans, and movement was generally low, gating was abandoned in the course of the study. This resulted in even shorter acquisition duration and total time under anesthesia (<45 min). Twelve minutes of resting-state BOLD fMRI (480 frames) data were also recorded.

A post-mortem scan of a single perfused brain was recorded for additional quality control steps: To rule out that combining anisotropic, axial and coronal scans during template creation introduces a volumetric bias, the image protocol was extended with a T1-weighted, 50 µm-isotropic sequence. Due to its much longer acquisition time (around 30-fold), this high-resolution scan was not implemented in the in vivo measurements.

Structural scans were exported from ParaVision as Dicom and converted to NIfTI via dcm2niix [] as implemented in MRIcroGL []. These files were spatially upscaled (10x), realigned, bias-corrected (N4BiasFieldCorrection with default values) and masked, using custom MATLAB scripts (R2023b, MathWorks), SPM12 (v7771) and tissue probability maps (TPM) of the TMBTA template for initial segmentation of brain tissue, by thresholding the sum image of individual TPMs. Manual mask refinement (i.e. additional inclusion or exclusion of voxels), as depicted in , was performed in 3D Slicer (Slicer 5.6.2, www.slicer.org) []. Scans were visually inspected for image quality and homogeneity, leading to a final selection of 153/160 scans (76 axial, 77 coronal).

Advanced Normalization Tools [] (ANTs, http://stnava.github.io/ANTs/, antsMultivariateTemplateConstruction2.sh, running on Debian GNU/Linux 11 (Bullseye)) was then used for template creation and spatial transformations (antsApplyTransforms, antsRegistrationSyN.sh). The resulting Female Black Six template brain (FeBls, ‘Fabulous’) was then masked once more for any remaining non-brain tissue.

To achieve a 60 µm isotropic, high-SNR structural template, we combined axial and coronal scans using ANT’s multivariate template construction (antsMultivariateTemplateConstruction2). A schematic with representative images and code of the described procedure are shown in .

To exclude the possibility of introducing a volumetric bias by this procedure, a perfused brain was not only scanned at the same anisotropic resolutions previously described, but also at 50 µm isotropic. Each of these three scans, as well as a second isotropic image, derived from the anisotropic recordings by applying the approach described above, was then normalized to the template space and parcellated. Consequently, the segmented volumes in the individual space were compared to the high-resolution image, which was considered as the ground truth.

Tissue probability maps of the template brain derived with SPM and TMBTA priors are provided as both original outputs and smoothed by a Gaussian kernel (FWHM = 0.2 mm).

MRI brain templates, even within the same (sub-)species and imaging modality, often differ in scale, particularly across planes, owing to a range of technical and biological factors introduced during image acquisition. However, their resulting nominal resolution (voxel size) is not sufficient as a quality measure on its own. Other metrics for scan quality are typically only well-defined in artificial settings and phantoms, but do not translate well to in vivo imaging and derived templates.

Thus, we employed a parameter-free estimate of microscopy resolution [] to our data, which has previously been applied to assess the quality of isotropic, super-resolution MRI []. In brief, the cross-correlation coefficients d(r) are calculated from a normalized, Fourier transformed planar image and its original, with variable filtering (mask radius r in Fourier space). The cut-off frequency kc with the best noise rejection-signal preservation ratio is then used, along with the nominal pixel size, to derive an effective resolution using .

(1)Resolution=2⋅pixel sizekc

This decorrelation analysis was performed for both our template and several preciously published templates. Due to the algorithm assuming square pixels, only planes with isotropic resolution were considered. As contrast and resolvability between adjacent (sub-)structures vary throughout the brain, the overall, minimal calculated effective voxel size was used as criterion for the maximally achieved resolution.

To put the FeBls template into perspective, we quantitatively describe the underlying cohort’s and average brain characteristics. Common similarity metrics such as mutual information, cross-correlation, or Dice coefficients provide qualitative measures only, or lack a reference value. They are furthermore sensitive to the images’ different contrast mechanisms and intensities, or only apply to binarized segmentations. Additionally, the optimal (dis-)similarity between templates of different strains, sex, and age is unknown. Thus, all of these similarity measures defeat the purpose and are not reported here. Log Jacobian matrices derived from non-linear registrations between templates, however, may visually indicate spatial similarity and local deformations. Using histograms, one can judge the directionality, magnitude and distribution of spatial transformations.

Transforming one template to another can help locate their differences, but only indicates magnitude and direction, not significance thereof. Thus, we also subjected the axial, anatomical and respective functional baseline scans of 55 mice who fully completed the longitudinal study to the RABIES preprocessing pipeline [], spatially normalizing their brains. Resulting warp fields were then transformed to log Jacobians and smoothed. In this deformation-based morphology (DBM) analysis, SPM12 was ultimately used to test for regions in our cohort’s brains consistently and significantly being adjusted to match the DSURQE template. Confirming such differences between FeBls and DSURQE template substantiates the independence and necessity of the FeBls brain. As a further check of reproducibility, data of 17 C57Bl/6N males and 33 females recorded a year later with a similar imaging protocol underwent the same procedure.

Lastly, we normalized independent MR data of 42 female C57Bl/6 mice, kindly provided by Martínez-Tazo et al. [] and Rahman et al. [], to TMBTA, FeBls, and DSURQE (down-sampled to 60 µm) templates. We then calculated the log Jacobians as a measure of distortion from individual scans to the average space, assuming that the more representative a template of a cohort is, the narrower and more closely centered around zero the log Jacobians are distributed.

Brief characteristics of the imaged cohort and the resulting template can be found in . The brain template we derived is shown in exemplary coronal, sagittal, and axial slices, as well as a surface rendering in . Differences in MR contrast, especially for cerebrospinal fluid, and brain volume compared with the TMBTA brain are well-distinguishable. The former is being attributed to different sequence parameters, such as the higher RARE factor used. The 3D-template itself in NIfTI format and accompanying files have been uploaded to a public repository and are free to download at the Neuroimaging Resources Registry of the NeuroImaging Tools & Resources Collaboratory (NITRC) (see ). To enhance the applicability of our template, we provided data both in native resolution, and scaled by a factor of 10, for implementation in human-centric analysis software.

Biological and volumetric characteristics of the FeBls template.

additionally shows a selection of other templates, spatially warped to FeBls-space (antsRegistrationSyn.sh -d 3 -m -f -o), along with their atlas annotations (antsApplyTransforms -n GenericLabel), and FeBls tissue probability maps for gray matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid. Due to its importance as a reference for invasive procedures (virus injections, electrode or waveguide placement) and in histological studies, the AMBA was further included as a non-MRI template. With its entirely different resolution and contrast mechanism and limited coverage of the olfactory bulb, the resulting spatial transforms are expected to be less reliable, though.

We found that the minimal effective voxel size (defined as half the effective resolution, as in []) for the isotropic template (constructed from both axial and coronal scans) approached the nominal one (60 µm, < 0.5% difference) for major slice orientations (axial, coronal, sagittal), see also . Some rodent templates such as TMBTA [] and DSURQE [] share this characteristic. A T2w template derived from 10 male C57Bl/6 males by Hikishima et al. [] has been found to have effective voxel sizes exceeding the nominal resolution in sagittal planes by more than 15%. The Mortimer Space [] average template’s effective resolution was estimated to be approximately 139 µm, contrasting its nominal resolution of 70 µm. Despite the small variation in effective resolution, a 60 µm isotropic template derived from only axial, non-isotropic scans appeared visually grainier and blurrier on coronal slices. The sagittal and axial slices were perceived to have similar quality, except for the transition of posterior part of the olfactory bulb/the anterior part of the secondary motor area, where the axially derived template exhibited more pronounced borders.

For the single ex-vivo brain scan acquired at high isotropic resolution, we observed that it agreed well, both visually and also regarding anatomical segmentations, with the computationally derived isotropic scan. Furthermore, the parcellated volumes of the computed isotropic scan were on average closer to the ground truth than volumes derived from either axial or coronal scans.

In direct comparison, the FeBls template brain (≈ 483 mm3) is considerably larger than TMBTA (of significantly younger, RjOrl:SWISS mice, ≈ 346 mm3, see also  and supplement) but differs much less from MouseX_female-only [] (≈ 495 mm3) and DSURQE [] (≈ 487 mm3) brain volumes (both C57Bl/6J). Wang et al. further stated that C57Bl/6J total brain volume across sexes averages around 460 mm3 at approximately 90 days of age [], whereas Badea et al. reported more than 508 mm3 and standard deviation of ≈ 23.42 mm3 for a cohort of 9 weeks old C57Bl/6J mice []. This closely matches our cohort’s average of 505 ± 18 mm3 (averages within subjects across parcellations of either slice orientation or resolution).

Looking at the TMBTA atlas segmentations specifically, which encompasses the same regions at the same nominal resolution, as well as the warp fields from one template to the other and the resulting log Jacobians (), it becomes apparent that the volume difference is not merely caused by overall scaling of the whole brain, but that different brain regions scale to a different extent. Despite the lower total volume (resulting in negative log Jacobians, as the FeBls template needs to shrink to match the TMBTA, ), some small brain regions may be larger in the TMBTA than in the FeBls template. However, as these are generally located closer to the trunk, this effect could be influenced by the different contrast in our acquisitions and lower signal intensity. In such low-contrast regions, reduced segmentation performance is to be expected. The DSURQE template is not only more similar in overall volume and dimensions, but also the log Jacobian values are, on average closer to zero.

Visually, the overall shape of the FeBls brain appears less round along the anterior-posterior axis, when drawing a straight line between the base of the olfactory bulb and proximal-superior part of the midbrain, but extends slightly more downwards at the height of hypothalamus and medial septum (, top left). Among other regions, pronounced differences between DSURQE and FeBls were observed for parts of the olfactory bulb, nucleus accumbens, hippocampus, thalamus and bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (). As shown with DBM (), regions significantly different between DSURQE and FeBls’ underlying data are the thalamus, hippocampus, insula and piriform cortex, many of which are known to be either dimorphic or involved in differently expressed behavioral phenotypes between C57Bl/6N and 6J. Findings in hippocampus (dentate Gyrus, CA3) and corpus callosum were particularly robust and consistent in C57Bl/6N females and males. Sex differences found in an exploratory analysis (e.g. cerebellum, mesencephalon, primary somatosensory cortex, hippocampus and lateral septum) should be verified in a more balanced sample.

Consistent with aforementioned observations in the template cohort, externally scanned, adult female C57Bl/6 brains were on average larger than TMBTA, as seen by the shift towards the right in the distribution of log Jacobian values (). As hypothesized, for the three templates at the same resolution, the distribution corresponding to normalization to FeBls is both narrow and most symmetric around zero (), indicating a good agreement between the independent data and the template.

Herein, we present a novel brain template, aiming to address the paucity of female mouse template brains and C57Bl/6N strain, specifically. We show that the FeBls template significantly differs from mixed-sex and female-only (C57Bl/6J) references. The evaluation of external data not used for generation of the FeBls template showed a narrower and more symmetric log Jacobian distribution than with DSURQE, indicating a closer match between female individuals and our reference.

Although we lack a direct comparison, given partially consistent structural findings in three data sets (55 and 33 females, 17 males), we have reason to assume that some, but not all differences in templates are caused by mixed-sex versus female-only data. We hypothesize that in a sufficiently large sample also C57Bl/6N and C57Bl/6J are anatomically distinct, and template differences between FeBls and DSURQE shown are partially strain-specific. Whether the rate of congenital anomalies and variability (portosystemic shunt) drive these differences, and their respective prevalence in C57Bl/6N are still to be determined in future studies.

Naturally, our work is not without limitations: Despite best efforts, transformations between templates and resulting annotations may exhibit local deviations. Thus, atlas files should be used cautiously and placement of volumes of interest should be individually verified. A general issue with anatomical atlases is their varying degree of parcellations and usage of inconsistent nomenclature. Unifying and implementing levels of anatomical hierarchy (e.g. in 4D annotation files) is important and should be covered in future work.

While in many mouse studies narrow age ranges are used, we explicitly opted for a wider range to truly reflect adult brain morphology and broaden applicability. However, this may not fully align with study designs where the earlier sexual, instead of the brain morphological maturity is considered as criterion for adulthood.

Finally, covering a broader range of (structural) imaging contrasts (T1-weighted, proton density, diffusion) was unfortunately not possible within the experimental timeline and scope of this study.

neuroscience.title: Harmonization of Longitudinal Multi‐Scanner Neuroimaging Data With Nonlinear Biological Associations
neuroscience.abstract: The aggregation of neuroimaging data across multiple sources, typically scanners or imaging sites, has the potential to improve statistical power when conducting inference. The added benefits of increased sample size to inference, however, can be obstructed by unwanted source‐specific technical variability that increases difficulty in estimating biological signals of interest. To address this issue, recent methods based on ComBat, a batch‐correction procedure originally developed for genomics, have been developed for both cross‐sectional and longitudinal neuroimaging data. While these approaches have successfully removed technical batch‐specific variability, they restrict their consideration to linear biological associations. In this article we introduce a ComBat‐based method to harmonize longitudinal multisource imaging data that can account for nonlinear biological associations of interest. We demonstrate via simulation that, in the presence of nonlinear biological signal, our method outperforms existing ComBat‐based approaches designed for longitudinal imaging data, particularly in settings where observed values of relevant biological covariates lack substantial overlap across sources. Using volumetric measurements for 504 subjects combined from both the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we identify the presence of both additive and multiplicative study‐specific effects for a substantial number of brain regions and demonstrate the effective removal of their presence on data harmonized by our method. The flexibility of the proposed method towards capturing many types of biological associations makes it a versatile procedure that can be used to harmonize longitudinal biomedical data.
neuroscience.text:
In neuroimaging, harmonization methods seek to enable the effective aggregation of datasets across multiple sources; this strategy potentially increases statistical power for performing inference. These approaches attempt to preserve biological signals of interest while removing unwanted technical variability that occurs due to differences across scanner hardware, software, and site‐specific data acquisition strategies (Han et al. ; Jovicich et al. ; Takao et al. ). In recent years, a variety of harmonization approaches for neuroimaging data have been developed based on ComBat, an empirical Bayesian method originally designed for applications in genomics (Johnson et al. ). These approaches have been developed for diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and radiomic features derived from positron emission tomography (PET) scans (Fortin et al. , ; Yu et al. ; Orlhac et al. ). For cross‐sectional studies, a ComBat‐based harmonization method has been developed to assess structural brain changes across lifespan using generalized additive models that allow flexible biological associations (Pomponio et al. ). In a longitudinal context, a recent approach introduced a ComBat‐based framework for neuroimaging data that accounted for within subject‐correlation inherent to longitudinal datasets (Beer et al. ). This approach addressed limitations encountered in prior work seeking to harmonize longitudinal neuroimaging data (Venkatraman et al. ; Müller et al. ).

ComBat‐based harmonization enjoys several distinct advantages over other attempts at batch (i.e., site, scanner, or study) correction for aggregated neuroimaging data. First, the method is flexible to study design and only requires the same features to be measured for each participant observed. This property is distinct from other approaches effectively employed for harmonization that rely on overlap of participants between sites or scanners considered (Erus et al. ; Dewey et al. ). Second, ComBat‐based approaches have shown robustness to outliers. This property is due to the empirical Bayes framework employed by ComBat in contrast to approaches that treat batch as a fixed covariate (Johnson et al. ). Within each batch (i.e., site, scanner, or study), ComBat assumes that all feature‐specific batch effects derive from a common distribution, which allows information to be borrowed across features within a batch and shrunk towards a common mean. Furthermore, ComBat also removes heteroscedasticity of model errors across batch; this location‐scale adjustment has previously been shown to have benefits over approaches that solely adjust for mean effects (Fortin et al. ).

Inherent challenges exist when attempting to harmonize longitudinal neuroimaging data while preserving biological signal that has complex, potentially nonlinear biological associations. For longitudinal data, using cross‐sectional harmonization approaches ignores dependencies of within‐subject observations across time and can lead to the introduction of spurious biological signal due to inconsistencies in batch correction across time points. In addition, leveraging subject‐specific dependencies via a longitudinal method can lead to gains in statistical power (Beer et al. ). However, the presence of nonlinear signal can negate any potential benefits due to the introduction of spurious artifacts (Pomponio et al. ). The high risk of mischaracterizing biological associations highlights the importance of a method that is flexible enough to both capture complex biological associations and leverage additional structure inherent to longitudinal data.

In light of the challenges above, in this article we propose a method to harmonize multi‐scanner longitudinal neuroimaging data that flexibly preserves nonlinear biological associations. Our method accounts for within‐subject dependence inherent to longitudinal studies. In simulations designed with a variety of nonlinear biological signals, we demonstrate our approach's superior performance at removing batch‐specific technical effects over existing longitudinal ComBat‐based approaches; this improvement is most prominent in settings where biological covariates lack substantial overlap in observed values across batches. We demonstrate our approach using longitudinal volumetric data combined from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (Weiner et al. ) and the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) (Ferrucci ).

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section  outlines our method in detail. Section  is a simulation study. Section  describes the combined ADNI–BLSA dataset, demonstrates the presence of study‐specific technical effects, and applies our approach to the ADNI–BLSA data. We conclude the article with a discussion in Section . Software is available for our approach at https://github.com/nmd1994/NonlinearLongitudinalComBat/.

Nonlinear longitudinal ComBat model: We begin this section by outlining our overall proposed model. Given batch (i.e., scanner, site, study) index i∈1…m, participant index j∈1…N, participant‐specific time t∈1…Kj (where t is not necessarily identical across subjects), covariate index p∈1…P, and feature v:
(1)
yijvt=αv+γiv+∑p=1PfvpXjpt+ηjv+δivϵijvt,
where yijvt is the observed data for feature v, participant j, batch i, and time t, αv is the overall mean for feature v at baseline, γiv is batch i's additive effect for feature v, Xjpt is participant j's possibly time‐varying covariate p that varies with yijvt by smooth, possibly nonlinear function fvp, ηjv is a subject‐specific random intercept for participant j and feature v, δiv is batch i's multiplicative scaling factor for feature v, and ϵijvt is an error term. Xjpt includes both baseline covariates that do not change with time (e.g., sex, baseline diagnosis) and time‐varying covariates such as age at visit time t. We assume the random intercepts ηjv's and error terms ϵijvt's are mutually independent and are distributed as ηjv∼N0ρv2,ϵijvt∼N0σv2.

Representing nonlinear fits as random effects: To represent each function fvp we utilize smoothing splines; smoothing splines use a spline basis with penalized coefficients to encourage smoothness to balance between interpolating observed trends and fitting each fvp with a linear function. In particular, we use a parameterization of these penalized splines that separates linear and nonlinear components of each fvp and enables each function's degree of nonlinearity to be estimated as variance components of random effects in a linear mixed model. Mathematical details on this parameterization can be seen in Wood (). Given this representation of penalized splines we observe:
(2)

where XjtT is a p×1 vector of potentially time‐varying covariates for participant j at time t, βv is a p×1 vector of coefficients for p covariates, Zjvp is a 1×k vector of k nonlinear basis components of fvp (i.e., the nonlinear portion of the basis representation for covariate p) for subject j, and βvpNL∼N0Ikλp are the k×1 vector of coefficients for nonlinear basis functions Zjvp. Before providing explicit details on how we conduct harmonization, we represent our overall harmonized data in terms of our proposed model below:
yijvComBatt=yijvt−α^v−γ^iv−XjtTβ^v−∑p=1PZjvpβ^vpNL−η^jvδ^iv+α^v+XjtTβ^v+∑p=1PZjvpβ^vpNL+η^jv

Standardization step: Before applying the empirical Bayes estimation of location‐scale parameters inherent to ComBat‐based harmonization, we first standardize features to have overall mean and variance on approximately the same scale to prevent biased estimates of batch effects (Johnson et al. ). In the context of our approach, we estimate fixed effect parameters (αv, βv, γiv) with the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) and produce unbiased estimates of variance components (ρv2, σv2, Ikλ) with the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimator. Likewise, subject‐specific intercepts ηjv are estimated with the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP). Standard constraints are imposed to ensure identifiability of nonlinear smooth components and random intercepts (Wood ). Standardized data is computed as follows:
zijvt=yijvt−α^v−XjTtβ^v−∑p=1PZjvpβ^vpNL−η^jvσ^v

We estimate, but do not remove, scanner additive effect γiv during the standardization step. Post‐standardization, we assume that zijv∼Nγivδiv2. Batch‐specific effects are assumed to follow the following prior distributions: γiv∼Nγiτi2 and δiv2∼IGωiθi.

Empirical Bayes estimation of batch effects: Following standardization, additive and multiplicative batch effects are estimated by an empirical Bayes procedure typical of ComBat‐based approaches. From standardized data, method‐of‐moments (MoM) estimators are used to estimate hyperparameters (γi,τi2,ωi,θi) and (γiv, δiv2) are estimated by their conditional posterior means. Derivations for these empirical Bayes estimates can be seen in Johnson et al. ().

Producing nonlinear longitudinal ComBat‐harmonized data: Given additive and multiplicative batch effects estimated by empirical Bayes, γ^iv and δ^iv, we now provide an equation for data harmonized by our procedure:
(3)
yijvComBatt=σ^vδ^ivzijvt−γ^iv+α^v+XjTβ^v+∑p=1PZjvpβ^vpNL+η^jv

To remove batch effects, a location‐scale adjustment is first performed to standardize data. Following this step, which puts features back on its original scale, the estimated biological variability of interest is then added back to the data.

We conduct all analysis using the R programming language. We fit all additive mixed models using the mgcv package (Wood and Wood ). To test for additive batch effects, we compared models fit with and without batch as a fixed effect using the package pbkrtest to carry out hypothesis tests with the Kenward–Roger approach. We tested for the presence of multiplicative batch effects using the non‐parametric Fligner–Killeen test on the residuals of our data.

Given a description of our approach, we now design a simulation to demonstrate our method's benefits in the presence of longitudinal data with nonlinear biological signal. Specifically, we test our approach's performance against LongCombat and ComBat‐GAM. LongCombat is a harmonization method designed to correct batch effects for longitudinal data in the presence of linear biological signal and ComBat‐GAM is a cross‐sectional harmonization method designed to correct batch effects in the presence of nonlinear biological signal (Beer et al. ; Pomponio et al. ). We simulate 100 datasets per setting and vary the following between settings: functional form of biological signal, level of covariate overlap (i.e., range observed) between batches. We fix the number of batches to 2 per simulated dataset (of equal sample size), the number of features to 20 per dataset, the covariate considered (Age), and the number of subjects to 200 (each with observations at 5 time points). We simulate features from the normal distribution, generate batch‐specific additive and multiplicative noise from the normal and inverse‐gamma distribution, respectively, and can represent our simulated data from the following form: yiv=fAgei+ϵi, where vϵ1…20 and iϵ1…1000. Simulated ages were randomly sampled and ranged from 10 to 90. Age overlap intervals are defined as follows: Low: Batch1ϵ10,35–Batch2ϵ30,90, Moderate: Batch1ϵ10,40–Batch2ϵ30,90, High: Batch1ϵ10,60–Batch2ϵ30,90, Full: Batch1ϵ10,90–Batch2ϵ10,90. Functional forms considered include the following: linear (fx=Xβ), decreasing (fx=−x3), floor (concave) (fx=−lnx), ceiling (fx=lnx), and bump (fx=logNormalx). We flag batch remaining batch effects if tests for their significance fall below a p value of 0.05 (with a Bonferroni correction applied). For results taken from our approach, we set the number of knots for each spline basis to k=45. Specific details about our simulations can be seen in our software, which can be found at https://github.com/nmd1994/NonlinearLongitudinalComBat/.

Simulation results, visualized in Figure , indicate that our method outperforms both LongCombat and ComBat‐GAM in removing additive effects when nonlinear biological signal is present. Importantly, our method also performs extremely similarly to LongCombat when biological signal is linear, providing evidence that our method is not meaningfully penalized for being overly flexible when our model is mispecified to the data. Linear longitudinal harmonization approaches, while effectively removing additive batch effects when signals are linear, do not remove these effects well when biological signal follows a nonlinear function. For removing multiplicative effects, our method outperformed ComBat‐GAM and performed comparably to LongCombat, which appeared to remove slightly more multiplicative batch effects when true biological signal was nonlinear. It is important to note that LongCombat can only preserve linear biological signals, meaning some signal beyond linear complexity will be lost during the removal of batch effects. The ability to remove multiplicative batch effects appears to slightly worsen when the overlap between the range of observed ages between batches is not substantial. For additive batch effects, the relationship between covariate overlap across batches and the ability to remove technical effects seems to be function‐specific. We note that our approach appeared to remove all additive batch effects and the majority of multiplicative effects regardless of the signal function considered or the level of overlap between observed covariates in each batch. An additional simulation setting in Table  of Appendix  shows similar performance for our method when an alternative smoother is used post‐harmonization, demonstrating robustness to smoother choice.

Null case: Method performance when no batch effects present: We now examine the performance of our approach, ComBat‐GAM, and LongCombat under a variety of biological signals when no batch effects are present. To do this, we use the same functional forms for biological signal as our main simulation and restrict consideration to the Full overlap case (Full: Batch1ϵ10,90–Batch2ϵ10,90). We still simulate 100 datasets per setting with the number of subjects fixed to 200 per setting, with observations at 5 time points for each subject. Twenty features were simulated for each dataset and two batches were generated for each dataset. Our results, highlighted in Figure  below, show that our approach effectively avoids introducing spurious additive or multiplicative batch effects. Most notably, LongCombat appears to introduce substantial spurious additive batch effects when underlying biological signal is nonlinear, highlighting the importance of having a harmonization approach flexible enough to properly specify the shape of biological signal.

We analyzed longitudinal volumetric measurements for 504 subjects combined from both the BLSA (254 subjects) and the ADNI (250 subjects) (Weiner et al. ; Ferrucci ). ADNI acquired data from modalities including structural, functional, and molecular neuroimaging for participants across multiple sites using standardized protocols to maintain consistency during acquisition. Protocols provide guidelines for factors including imaging sequence parameters, scan timings and frequencies, data sharing, and other quality control procedures. For more detailed information on standardized protocols, including guidelines on scanner calibration and patient positioning, please refer to (https://adni.loni.usc.edu/). In contrast, the BLSA study follows cognitively healthy adults and follows them longitudinally for decades. The study acquires data via dedicated scanners to control for continuity from different patients across decades (Ferrucci ). For more information about BLSA, please refer to (https://www.blsa.nih.gov/). Ages for subjects from the BLSA study range from 27 to 96 while ages from ADNI ranged from 55 to 96 years old. We selected the following 20 anatomical areas based on visualizations indicating nonlinear associations with age: left accumbens area, right amygdala, left cerebellum white matter, right hippocampus, left pallidum, right putamen, cerebellar vermal lobules, left basal forebrain, left fornix, right anterior limb of internal capsule, left anterior orbital gyrus, right angular gyrus, left calcarine cortex, right central operculum, left posterior cingulate gyrus, right precuneus, left precentral gyrus, right planum temporale, left superior temporal gyrus, and right temporal pole. Along with the nonlinear function representing age, the following covariates were treated as additional linear fixed effects when performing this analysis: intracranial volume (DLICV) at baseline, sex, and diagnosis.

Identifying and correcting batch effects: Figure  shows a distribution of age in each study and Figure  shows, for a representative subset of ROIs, estimated age‐volume curves (adjusted for sex, intracranial volume (DLICV) at baseline, and diagnosis) for unharmonized data from both BLSA and ADNI. The results provide evidence for the presence of technical variability across batches, as estimations in overlapping age intervals between studies show clear differences. Tests for additive batch effects using pbkrtest (with Kenward–Roger method) and a Bonferroni correction showed 13 out of 20 features to have batch effects. Likewise, tests for multiplicative effects on residuals using the Fligner–Killeen test and a Bonferroni correction revealed 13 out of 20 features showed statistically significant heteroscedasticity. Results from data harmonized by our method showed no statistically significant additive effects using the Kenward–Roger method and a Bonferroni correction. Similarly, only 1 multiplicative effect remained on data harmonized by our method using the Fligner–Killeen test and a Bonferroni correction. Residuals of our analysis model fit to data harmonized by our method in Figure  similarly demonstrate no obvious multiplicative differences between batches for any features.

As an additional validation step for our method, we also split our data into a training set and a test set to see how additive and multiplicative batch effects (estimated on the training set) performed at removing batch effects on the test set. We found that no additive batch effects and 2 multiplicative batch effects remained on the test set post harmonization, indicating very similar performance to our main analysis.

In recent years, ComBat‐based approaches have been introduced as an effective solution for removing technical effects in neuroimaging data from multiple sources. These methods are flexible to study design and have been developed for both cross‐sectional neuroimaging data with flexible biological signal and for longitudinal neuroimaging data. In this article, we introduce a ComBat‐based method to harmonize longitudinal multisource imaging data with flexible, potentially nonlinear biological signals of interest. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate the benefits of our method via its superior performance in the presence of nonlinear biological signal against both harmonization approaches for longitudinal data that restrict consideration to linear biological signal and against harmonization approaches that allow flexible nonlinear biological signal but are not designed to handle longitudinal data. We also show that our method performs very similarly to these approaches in the presence of linear biological signal, mitigating concerns about potential risks of added modeling flexibility. We also highlight the importance of properly specifying biological signal by showing that LongCombat introduces spurious additive batch effects in the null case (no batch effects present) when underlying biological signal is nonlinear. We apply our dataset to volumetric neuroimaging data from the ADNI and BLSA studies and show our method's effectiveness at removing additive and multiplicative batch effects, even in the presence of limited overlap in age ranges between studies (Ferrucci ; Weiner et al. ).

Our method has several limitations which present opportunities for future work. First, we assume biological signal that can be identified by a smooth, continuous function; some settings may not have signal that can be characterized by these types of shapes. Second, our method controls for longitudinal effects via a subject‐specific intercept; more complicated temporal structure may need to be addressed by a more intricate modeling framework. Finally, our method relies on technical variability to be identified by clear categorical differences such as scanner type, site, or study; future work could more comprehensively capture and correct technical variability in a way that is not directly addressed in this work. Examples of what a future approach could capture include differences in scanner vendor, differences in field strength, studies where participants switched scanners over time, and differences between studies in population selection (e.g., ADNI selected for cognitive impairment while BLSA selected for healthy volunteers). Future work could also evaluate the performance of our method on a broader set of metrics outside of strictly anatomically‐based ones.

Overall, we see our approach as a tool that expands the scope of ComBat‐based harmonization to include longitudinal data with complex biological patterns. The value of the proposed methodology may be especially important in real‐world data observed as part of clinical care longitudinally. We hope the added flexibility of our method, which should encompass a more general class of problems than existing approaches, allows researchers to effectively aggregate data and quantitatively address scientific questions that they were previously unable to answer.
