Prediction performance was comparable when applying the BF-Lifemulti model to TESTCROSS for cross-sectional prediction of figural memory using ENR (explained variance of 12%). It showed slightly higher explained variance than both single lifestyle factor and data-driven models (Table  and Fig. B, C). For episodic memory, the performance of BF-Lifemulti (explained variance of 7%) was higher than that of the SMO single-factor model and comparable to the ALC, PA, and SI single-factor models (Fig. ), BFdata-Var and BFdata-Match (Fig. ), but remained slightly lower than BFdata-Var(Train) and BFdata-Match(Train) (explained variance up to 10%; Fig. ). For long-term memory, the performance of BF-Lifemulti (explained variance of 5%) was higher than that of the PA and SI single-factor models, while comparable to the SMO and ALC single-factor models (Fig. ) as well as the data-driven models (Fig. ).

Predictive performance was markedly reduced in TESTLONG across cognitive domains (Table  and Fig. ). For figural and episodic memory, BF-Lifemulti failed to achieve meaningful prediction in both cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses. Similar reductions were observed for the BF-Lifesingle and data-driven models (Suppl. Fig. ). For long-term memory, BF-Lifemulti showed limited cross-sectional performance (explained variance of 4%) but no meaningful longitudinal prediction. In this domain, BF-Lifemulti showed higher explained variance than the PA single-factor model, but lower explained variance than the SMO, ALC, and SI single-factor models (Fig. ). Performance of the BF-Lifemulti model was comparable to BFdata-Var and BFdata-Match (Fig. ), but remained lower than BFdata-Var(Train) and BFdata-Match(Train) (explained variance up to 8%; Fig. ).

For figural memory, adding demographic variables improved prediction performance in DISCOVERY and TESTCROSS, but not in TESTLONG (Table  and Fig. ). However, adding lifestyle variables on top of this model provided little additional benefit across cognitive domains (Fig. ).

Our next main analysis step was feature importance analysis via SHAP focusing on figural memory, specifically for the predictions in TESTCROSS using the ENR algorithm, which showed the most reliable R² scores (see Section “Predictive performance and model comparisons”).

From a summary perspective, analysis of TESTCROSS showed distinct feature importance patterns across BF-Lifemulti and BF-Lifesingle models. The BF-Lifemulti model showed the largest contributions from structural features (CT, GMV) in SAN, SMN, and DMN, while also incorporating functional and diffusion-derived information (see Suppl. Fig. ). In contrast, BF-Lifesingle models showed more heterogeneous and less integrative patterns: SMO and ALC single-factor models were dominated by structural features with minimal diffusion or functional contributions. Compared with BF-Lifemulti, the PA single-factor model showed a similar multimodal profile with less consistent structural dominance and greater diffusion contribution, particularly FA in commissural tracts. The SI single-factor model relied primarily on structural and node-level functional features and diffusion metrics other than FA, with minimal contribution from FA-related metrics.

To further characterize these patterns at the feature level, we examined the top 30% of features in the BF-Lifemulti model (Fig. ; SHAP values 0.042–0.243), which together accounted for 81.27% of the total SHAP contribution. Features that also appeared in the top 30% of any of the other four machine learning algorithms are highlighted (see also Suppl. Table ).

The highest-ranking features were primarily located in the SAN, VIN, DMN, and SMN. The top three SHAP contributors were: (i) GMV in a cluster spanning the right insula and frontal operculum (SAN_FrOperIns_2; area Id6); (ii) CT in the right temporo-parietal junction (SAN_TempOccPar_6; area PF); (iii) SA in the right visual network (VIN_10; area hOc4v). Other highly ranked features encompassed multiple parameters. GMV and CT contributions were observed across several cortical regions, including the left superior temporal sulcus (DMN_Temp_5; area STS2), left medial prefrontal cortex (DMN_PFC_13; area p32), right superior temporal gyrus (SMN_1; area Te3), and left frontal operculum (SMN_9; area Op4). Contributions of node-wise FC segregation were mainly derived from the left visual network (VIN_20), the right superior temporal gyrus (SMN_8), and the right orbitofrontal cortex of the limbic network (LIN_OFC_3; area Fo1). Diffusion-derived white-matter metrics were also among the top features, spanning major projection, association, and commissural fiber tracts such as the posterior and superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum bundle, anterior corona radiata, genu of the corpus callosum, and external capsule (Fig. ).

Overlap between BF-Lifemulti and BF-Lifesingle models was limited and varied across models, with the greatest overlap observed for the SMO single-factor model, followed by the PA and SI single-factor models, and no shared features for the ALC single-factor model (Suppl. Fig. ). For diffusion-derived metrics, no identical features were shared, although similar white-matter tracts (e.g., the left anterior corona radiata and left external capsule) were identified using different indices across models (Fig. ).

Across alternative cluster solutions (k = 2–4), predictive performance was generally comparable to the main k = 5 solution, with k = 5 showing slightly higher performance in some cognitive domains. Predictive performance in TESTLONG remained limited across all clustering solutions (Suppl. Table  and Suppl. Fig. ).

Lifestyle-only reference models based on the original eight lifestyle variables showed weak predictive performance for figural memory in DISCOVERY and did not generalize to TESTLONG (Suppl. Table  and Suppl. Fig. ).

For a global cognitive component, performance of the BF-Lifemulti models was similar to that of the BF-Lifesingle models, whereas data-driven models showed slightly better performance in DISCOVERY and TESTCROSS. Again, predictive performance in TESTLONG remained limited across models. Inclusion of demographic and lifestyle variables further improved the predictive performance of the BF-Lifemulti model (k = 5) across datasets (Suppl. Table  and Suppl. Fig. ).

We examined whether brain features derived from differences between groups of participants defined by overall lifestyle profiles provide predictive information for domain-specific cognitive functions. Overall, the model using brain features derived from overall lifestyle profiles showed modest domain-specific predictive performance, with the highest effects observed for figural memory. However, it did not clearly outperform fully data-driven models based on principal component representations of all brain features. Incorporating demographic variables into the BF-Lifemulti model improved prediction performance, whereas further adding lifestyle information itself on top provided little additional benefit. Together, these findings suggest that lifestyle-profile-informed brain features capture a specific portion of cognition-relevant brain variance, although this did not translate into broadly superior predictive performance.

Building on these results, we consider the domain-specific predictive pattern of the BF-Lifemulti model in relation to prior work. Prior studies in comparable aging cohorts using unimodal and multimodal neuroimaging approaches have reported explained variance of up to 12–14% for global cognitive performance,. In this context, the BF-Lifemulti model showed its strongest predictive performance for figural memory and a global cognitive component, while demonstrating limited predictive sensitivity for other cognitive domains, including working memory, language-related functions, and executive control.

The BF-Lifemulti model did not achieve the higher levels of explained variance (e.g., >20%) reported in studies of young adults using task-based or resting-state FC to predict fluid and crystallized cognitive performance (i.e., intelligence-related measures)–. However, prediction of cognition in population-based samples across the adult lifespan has generally remained modest. For example, multimodal neuroimaging predicted visual working memory across the adult lifespan in Cam-CAN (~16.2% explained variance; N = 547, aged 18–88 years), while processing speed showed limited predictability using resting-state FC (~8–11%; N = 99, aged 62–71 years; Cam-CAN, N = 295, aged 25–80 years). Consistently, a large-scale UK Biobank study explained only a small proportion of variance, with up to ~6% for fluid intelligence and ~2% for neuroticism (N = 18,550, aged 44–80 years).

Although higher predictive performance has been reported in smaller or clinical samples, such as individuals with MCI or Alzheimer’s disease–, these findings are only partly comparable to population-based studies, given the more specific and pronounced neural changes in clinical cohorts and the increased risk of overfitting in smaller samples,. In this context, the modest predictive performance observed here is broadly consistent with large-scale population studies such as the UK Biobank and likely reflects realistic effect sizes in normal aging. Taken together, while the predictive performance of the BF-Lifemulti model in older adults may appear modest compared to studies in young adults or clinical cohorts, its performance, particularly for figural memory and the global cognitive component, remains informative and broadly within the expected range in the context of age-related variability.

Within the present framework, the BF-Lifemulti model showed an advantage over BF-Lifesingle models mainly in predicting figural memory. Specifically, in DISCOVERY, the BF-Lifemulti model outperformed the ALC single-factor model. In TESTCROSS, the BF-Lifemulti model showed a modest advantage over BF-Lifesingle models in predicting figural memory (Fig. ). Although the absolute effect sizes were small, integrating multiple lifestyle-related brain features captured lifestyle-informed brain variance more comprehensively than modeling brain features based on individual lifestyle effects, supporting multivariate approaches in cognitive aging research.

Furthermore, the BF-Lifemulti model showed an advantage over the fully data-driven models (without prior biological hypotheses) when both used the same feature-extraction procedure. In this procedure, features were selected or reduced from DISCOVERY before any model training. However, this advantage was conditional: the BF-Lifemulti model did not outperform data-driven models when a more rigorous machine learning workflow was applied, in which PCA was performed separately within each training fold.

Importantly, the advantage of BF-Lifemulti over both BF-Lifesingle and comparable data-driven models was sensitive to the granularity of the brain–lifestyle representation. When the cluster number was altered (k = 2–4), this advantage was not consistently observed (Suppl. Table  and Suppl. Fig. ), suggesting that predictive performance may depend on how lifestyle-related variance is represented. In the present framework, the five-cluster solution appeared to capture a balance between aggregating shared lifestyle-related variance and avoiding excessive fragmentation.

Given the stronger prediction of figural memory, we next examined which brain features contributed most strongly to the BF-Lifemulti predictions. SHAP feature importance analyses revealed that contributions to the predictions of the BF-Lifemulti model primarily came from the salience/ventral attention, default mode, and somatomotor networks, as well as node-wise functional segregation within the visual network. These networks are broadly associated with attentional control, internally directed cognition, and visual processing–, functions relevant to figural memory performance.

At the feature level, important contributors included gray-matter morphology in salience/ventral attention and visual regions (e.g., right insula and right lingual gyrus), node-wise functional segregation within the visual network (e.g., left calcarine fissure), and microstructural integrity of projection fibers such as the posterior and superior corona radiata. Several of these regions have been reported to show structural associations with lifestyle factors, including smoking, and are also implicated in visual processing. This overlap is consistent with their contribution to figural memory prediction in the present model. The high contribution of node-wise functional network segregation within the visual network may be viewed in the context of prior research on network dedifferentiation during aging and network reorganization in visual impairment,, where alterations in network segregation have been linked to differences in perceptual performance. Although the direction of this contribution remains unresolved, these findings suggest that visual-network segregation was one of the important contributors to the figural-memory model. In addition, the inclusion of projection-fiber integrity features suggests that white-matter microstructure may also be relevant to this domain, although the specific relationship remains to be clarified.

In contrast, BF-Lifesingle models reflected more specific aspects of lifestyle-related brain variability by emphasizing particular modalities or network subsets. BF-Lifemulti integrates structural, functional, and microstructural features across multiple lifestyle domains, providing a more comprehensive representation than single-factor models. This multidomain perspective is consistent with previous work showing that combined lifestyle patterns are informative for cognitive aging. Previous studies have also linked individual lifestyle factors to differences in brain structure and function–,. Against this background, the present study examined whether brain features associated with multidomain lifestyle profiles also provide predictive information for cognitive performance. However, the modest prediction observed here indicates that lifestyle-related brain differences do not necessarily represent the brain differences most strongly related to cognitive performance.

The predictive advantage of the BF-Lifemulti model was mainly observed for figural memory, whereas prediction was weaker or negative for other cognitive domains. This pattern may reflect the specific brain networks engaged in figural memory, which involve higher-order visual regions, whereas episodic memory relies more on medial temporal lobe structures and verbal abilities depend on widely distributed language-specific networks (e.g., prefrontal, temporal, and subcortical regions). The limited prediction of verbal tasks may also reflect the relative stability of these abilities across aging, and they are strongly correlated with sociodemographic variables such as education and language exposure, which already encapsulate much of the neural information relevant to verbal performance. By contrast, approaches such as connectome-based predictive modeling, which use target-dependent feature selection to target specific networks, have successfully predicted verbal abilities, underscoring that prediction of different cognitive domains may benefit from tailoring feature selection and modeling approaches to the specific networks involved. However, the present study addressed a different question by selecting brain features based on lifestyle-profile differences, independent of cognitive outcomes. This design allowed us to test whether lifestyle-related brain variation carries predictive information for cognition without using the cognitive target itself to guide feature selection. The weaker prediction of verbal tasks therefore indicates that this lifestyle-profile-based feature set was not equally informative across cognitive domains.

Interestingly, the BF-Lifemulti model also showed positive predictive performance for the global cognitive component. This may partly reflect that global cognitive functions rely on widespread and distributed neural networks, which tend to show relatively consistent large-scale organization compared with highly localized, domain-specific processes and are therefore more amenable to multimodal characterization. Although the explained variance was modest, these results may reflect associations between lifestyle-related brain features and cognitive aging, especially for functions supported by distributed neural networks.

While the current study did not explicitly test aging frameworks, it exploratorily identified brain patterns—particularly in salience/ventral attention and visual networks—that may contribute to the prediction of specific cognitive domains. These brain patterns have not been directly examined in the context of established aging models in the current study, such as brain maintenance. This refers to the relative preservation of brain structure and function over the adult lifespan that is associated with better cognitive outcomes in aging, and STAC–r, which suggests that older adults recruit additional neural circuits to compensate for age-related declines. The present findings may nevertheless provide a basis for future studies examining how multidomain lifestyle-informed brain differences relate to domain-specific cognitive performance. Future studies could further investigate these links, for example, by incorporating task-based functional measures or additional lifestyle variables to enhance prediction.

Despite these brain-based findings, neuroimaging features alone accounted for only a small proportion of variance in cognitive performance. When demographic variables (age, sex, and education) were incorporated as additional predictors, predictive performance for figural memory improved substantially, consistent with prior findings that demographics capture a large share of explainable cognitive variance,,. By contrast, the incremental contribution of brain features remained modest, and adding individual-level lifestyle variables did not yield further gains. This pattern suggests that variance associated with lifestyle may already be partially reflected in demographic and brain measures, leaving little additional predictive value for lifestyle variables themselves. This interpretation was also supported by the lifestyle-only sensitivity analysis, in which the original lifestyle variables by themselves showed weak prediction (Suppl. Table  and Suppl. Fig. ). Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of variance in cognitive performance remained unexplained, indicating that future work may benefit from incorporating additional non-brain factors, such as socioeconomic status, physical health, cardiovascular risk, genetic predisposition, or social network characteristics.

In TESTLONG, predictive performance was markedly reduced. Neither BF-Lifemulti nor the comparison models (BF-Lifesingle and data-driven models) showed meaningful predictive performance for figural memory at baseline or follow-up, even after incorporating demographic and lifestyle variables (Table ). This consistent lack of performance across modeling approaches underscores the difficulty of predicting figural memory from brain features in this subgroup. Several factors may have contributed to this difference in prediction performance. Despite random assignment, TESTLONG differed from DISCOVERY and TESTCROSS in key characteristics, including education level and baseline figural memory performance (Table ). In addition, the available training sample size may have been insufficient to learn patterns that generalize to a more distinct subgroup. Together, the TESTLONG findings provide an important boundary condition for interpreting the present prediction results: predictive patterns observed cross-sectionally in DISCOVERY and TESTCROSS did not translate into reliable prediction in TESTLONG. This may partly reflect heterogeneity within the sample and differences between the training and test samples, as well as the general challenge of predicting individual differences in cognitive performance from brain features, particularly across longitudinal assessments.

Furthermore, several methodological limitations warrant consideration. First, model performance was sensitive to clustering granularity, and separation between lifestyle subgroups was relatively weak (low silhouette scores; Suppl. Table ), reflecting the difficulty of discretizing complex, multidimensional behaviors. Treating ordinal lifestyle variables as categorical inputs may also have reduced magnitude information. Some lifestyle indicators were also correlated and should therefore be interpreted as complementary indicators of broader behavioral domains rather than fully independent lifestyle dimensions (Suppl. Table ). While clustering enabled the examination of broad lifestyle heterogeneity, future work could explore alternative methods and stability criteria to improve interpretability and robustness. Future work could also explore alternative feature-selection strategies that use the original lifestyle-variable structure without deriving discrete lifestyle subgroups.

Second, BF-Lifemulti features were identified using exploratory between-group analyses without correction for multiple comparisons across all brain variables, with correction applied only across lifestyle subgroups. In addition, baseline health status or pre-existing disease may confound findings. Thus, results should be considered exploratory. In addition, since clustering and feature selection were performed once in DISCOVERY rather than repeated within each cross-validation fold, partial information leakage from validation folds into feature selection cannot be fully excluded. Cognitive outcomes were not used in these steps, so the potential leakage did not involve direct information about the prediction targets. The fixed feature set allowed the same lifestyle-informed brain representation to be evaluated across analyses.

Third, generalizability is constrained by lifestyle-variable selection, sample characteristics, and measurement design. The lifestyle profiles derived here reflect a selected set of behavioral and psychosocial domains and do not comprehensively capture all potentially relevant lifestyle or dementia-risk exposures, including domains such as diet and sleep. Furthermore, because the complete lifestyle-variable set required for clustering was not available for TESTCROSS, we could not directly evaluate whether this unseen dataset was comparable to DISCOVERY with respect to lifestyle profiles, and potential differences in lifestyle characteristics between the two subsets cannot be excluded. In addition, lifestyle behaviors were self-reported and subject to recall and social desirability biases, although this method is widely used in population neuroscience,.

Moreover, although longitudinal cognitive outcomes were examined, lifestyle and neuroimaging data were cross-sectional, limiting the ability to capture changes in these predictors and their relationship with cognitive change over time. Future research could further benefit from repeated behavioral and neural assessments over longer time spans to better characterize intraindividual differences in cognitive performance. Finally, given the sociodemographic characteristics of the training sample, external validation in cohorts with broader educational, ethnic, and cultural representation is warranted before generalizing these findings.

Despite these limitations, the current study suggests that brain features derived from overall lifestyle profiles provide modest domain-specific predictive information for cognitive performance in older adults, with positive predictive performance primarily observed for figural memory when using ENR. These lifestyle-related brain differences did not consistently surpass fully data-driven models and did not reliably predict longitudinal cognitive outcomes, but they provide a structured, lifestyle-informed representation of brain differences for combining lifestyle and neuroimaging data. Future work integrating larger and more diverse samples, repeated lifestyle and neuroimaging measures, and improved modeling of lifestyle heterogeneity may further clarify their relevance for cognitive aging.

The current study used data from the 1000BRAINS study, nested within the population-based Heinz Nixdorf Recall Study. We used lifestyle and psychosocial variables (hereafter referred to as lifestyle factors) from self-report questionnaires, along with baseline MRI and neuropsychological assessments at baseline and follow-up. We focused on participants aged ≥55 years (n = 969). Participants with DemTect scores in the impairment-indicative range (<8) or missing values were excluded (n = 23),. Of this eligible sample, 859 participants had available structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion MRI, and resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI). An additional 79 participants were excluded from further analyses, including 62 due to insufficient MRI data quality identified during initial quality control (see Section “Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)”) and 17 due to additional quality issues (incomplete brain coverage, n = 1) or processing failures, including failures in diffusion model fitting (n = 2), spatial normalization (n = 9), and functional connectivity construction (n = 5). Additionally, participants missing more than three of the 13 cognitive assessments were excluded (n = 6), leaving 774 participants (mean age 67.0 ± 6.7 years, 46.1% females), of which 255 participants had both available lifestyle behavior data and follow-up cognitive measures (follow-up interval: 4.0 years).

Participants were divided into three non-overlapping subsets to allow model development and evaluation of cognitive prediction cross-sectionally and longitudinally: (1) a main dataset (DISCOVERY), used for lifestyle-profile derivation, feature selection and model training; (2) an unseen dataset (TESTCROSS), used to test the trained model in unseen participants cross-sectionally; and (3) a second unseen dataset (TESTLONG), used to test model performance in second-visit data.

In detail, (1) in DISCOVERY lifestyle-profiles were derived with cross-validation used for internal model evaluation (n = 453; mean age 67.7 ± 6.6 years; 47.0% females); (2) TESTCROSS consisted of participants with baseline MRI and cognitive assessments who were held out from lifestyle-profile derivation because the complete lifestyle-variable set required for clustering was not available for this test subset, as several of these variables had not been collected under the participants’ original study protocol (n = 211; mean age 66.3 ± 7.1 years; 47.4% females); and (3) TESTLONG participants (n = 110; mean age 65.3 ± 6.2 years; 40.0% females; follow-up interval: 4.0 years) were randomly selected a priori from the 255 participants with available lifestyle behavior data and follow-up cognitive measures, providing an independent evaluation set while retaining sufficient sample size for model training. The remaining eligible participants (n = 145) were retained in the DISCOVERY dataset.

All participants provided written informed consent. The 1000BRAINS protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Duisburg-Essen, Germany, and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Lifestyle and psychosocial data used here were retrieved from the database of the third examination of the Heinz Nixdorf Recall study (10-year follow-up),. For the present analysis, we focused on eight lifestyle and psychosocial indicators spanning smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity/mobility, and the broader social engagement domain. These domains were selected to capture distinct but partly related aspects of everyday lifestyle and psychosocial behavior that could be operationalized consistently within the present analytical framework, with prior evidence supporting their relevance to brain and cognitive aging as outlined in the Introduction–. Specifically, we considered: (1) smoking [packyears of smoking = years of smoking × self-reported number of cigarettes smoked per day (CPD)], (2) alcohol consumption [total monthly consumption of pure alcohol (g/month)], (3) physical activity [sum of metabolic equivalents of task (MET) values assigned to each of the activities (sports/daily physical activities) participants engaged in multiplied by duration in hours (per month)], (4) flights of stairs [number of flights of stairs participants climbed daily], (5) count of sporty activities [number of different types of sports-related activities (e.g., running) that participants reported engaging in during the previous month], (6) count of physical activities [number of different types of physical activities (e.g., gardening) that participants reported engaging in during the previous month], (7) social integration, and (8) count of visits [sum of visits from children, relatives, and friends within one month]. Social integration was assessed following the adapted Social Integration Index used by ref. , based on the established epidemiological index described by ref. , and comprised three domains: marital status, close ties, and membership in organizations. Visit count was not included in this index and was entered separately as an indicator of visit frequency. We replaced missing values with the mean values from the first two examinations. Thus, MET reflected intensity- and duration-weighted activity, whereas stairs and activity counts captured specific mobility behaviors and activity diversity; similarly, visit count was entered separately from social integration to capture visit frequency.

Variables were transformed into ordinal categories for subsequent clustering analysis. Smoking (SMO) was coded as never, former, or current, while alcohol consumption (ALC) was coded as never, former, current non-spirits, or current spirits drinkers according to longitudinal self-reports. The remaining six variables—physical activity (PA), social integration (SI), flights of stairs climbed, count of visits, count of sporty activities, and count of physical activities—were divided into quartiles (Q1–Q4). All variables were coded such that higher values reflected higher risk for brain health (e.g., heavier smoking, higher alcohol intake, lower physical activity).

All participants underwent a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment during the 1000BRAINS data collection, which covered a broad range of cognitive functions. Thirteen cognitive tests were included in the present study, covering cognitive status (DemTect, indicating overall cognitive performance), language, memory, working memory, verbal fluency, and executive control. The prediction targets were labeled by cognitive domain for readability; the corresponding test names, references, cognitive domains, and scoring definitions are provided in Suppl. Table ,. Participants missing more than three cognitive tests were excluded (n = 6). For tests with fewer than 3% missing data, missing scores were replaced with the median value of the four participants nearest in age (the two closest younger and the two closest older than the individual).

In addition to domain-specific analyses, we included a global cognitive component score based on previous 1000BRAINS work,, which was constructed using a partly overlapping but not identical subset of neuropsychological tests compared to the 13 cognitive assessments used in the present study, to ensure comparability with prior findings and to assess whether prediction performance generalizes beyond individual domains.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was carried out on a 3T Siemens Tim-TRIO MR scanner with a 32-channel head coil (Erlangen, Germany) during the 1000BRAINS data collection, on the same day as the neuropsychological examination. Out of the full study protocol, T1-weighted, diffusion and resting-state functional MRI were included in the present analysis with the following sequence details. High-resolution T1-weighted imaging data were acquired with 176 slices, slice thickness = 1 mm, repetition time (TR) = 2250 ms, echo time (TE) = 3.03 ms, field of view (FoV) = 256 × 256 mm2, flip angle = 9°, voxel resolution 1 × 1 × 1 mm3. Diffusion-weighted imaging (dMRI) data were acquired using a twice refocused spin-echo diffusion-weighted EPI sequence with the following two parameter sets (each with FoV = 216 × 216 × 132 mm3, voxel resolution = 2.4 × 2.4 × 2.4 mm3, and 55 interleaved transversal slices without inter-slice gap): (i) 120-direction subset: 120 diffusion-weighted images (b = 2700 s/mm2), 13 b0-images, TR = 8 s, TE = 112 ms; (ii) 60-direction subset: 60 diffusion-weighted images (b = 1000 s/mm2), 7 b0-images, TR = 6.3 s, TE = 81 ms. Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) data were acquired using a blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) gradient-EPI sequence with 36 transversal slices (slice thickness = 3.1 mm, TR = 2200 ms, TE = 30 ms, FoV = 200 × 200 mm2, voxel resolution 3.1 × 3.1 × 3.1 mm3), lasting ~11 min and producing 300 volumes. During scanning, participants were instructed to keep their eyes closed, remain relaxed, and avoid falling asleep.

T1-weighted data preprocessing is detailed in the previous 1000BRAINS work. We adapted FreeSurfer’s ‘recon-all’ pipeline (version 7.1.0; https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/) to include the 400-node Schaefer parcellation, which was transformed into individual subject space using mris_ca_label. Morphological values for each node were then extracted with mris_anatomical_stats.

The dMRI data were preprocessed, including correction for eddy currents, head motion artifacts, and slice-wise signal dropouts, using FSL (version 6.0; https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/). Multi-shell data (b1000 and b2700) were then aligned to the b0 image of the b1000 shell using linear registration (FLIRT) and merged into a single dataset. Diffusion tensors were fitted to the b1000 shell using dtifit to generate fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) [(λ1 + λ2 + λ3)/3], radial diffusivity (RD) [(λ2 + λ3)/2], and axial diffusivity (AD) (λ1) maps. For NODDI modeling, we used the Microstructure Diffusion Toolbox (MDT, https://mdt-toolbox.readthedocs.io) based on combined multi-shell data, generating voxel-wise maps of intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) and orientation dispersion index (ODI). Diffusion MRI quality control metrics were obtained from the EDDY QC framework (Study-Wise Quality Assessment, SQUAD). Among these, the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) was used for quality assessment, and participants with CNR values exceeding ±2 standard deviations from the group mean were excluded to reduce the impact of low-quality data (n = 15).

For rsfMRI preprocessing, we followed the established pipeline from previous 1000BRAINS work, including volume removal, motion correction, ICA-based Automatic Removal Of Motion Artifacts (ICA-AROMA), filtering, and normalization to MNI152 space. Participants were excluded based on the following quality control criteria: (1) missing AROMA outputs (n = 19); (2) failures in CAT12 preprocessing (i.e., missing scans in the homogeneity check output; n = 5); (3) outliers identified by CAT12 sample homogeneity checks (>2 standard deviations from the group mean; n = 8); (4) inconsistent numbers of functional volumes (n = 9); and (5) excessive motion-related artifacts identified using DVARS, defined as >10% frame dropout across 300 volumes (n = 6),.

For brain structure, gray-matter volume (GMV), cortical thickness (CT), and surface area (SA) were extracted for 400 nodes (3 × 400 features) of the Schaefer 400 parcellation using mris_anatomical_stats, and summarized using the aparcstats2table program in FreeSurfer.

Individual DTI and NODDI metrics of all subjects were nonlinearly transformed into MNI space using ANTs. Within white-matter regions of interest as derived from the ICBM-DTI-81 white matter label atlas, which comprises 48 labels, we extracted the average values of FA, MD, RD, AD, ICVF, and ODI for each participant using fslstats tool. These white matter region-wise DTI and NODDI metrics (resulting in 6 × 48 features) were then used as input features for subsequent analyses.

To capture large-scale functional brain organization across the cerebrum, cerebellum, and subcortical regions, we constructed FC matrices using a combined parcellation consisting of 400 cortical parcels, 14 subcortical regions, and 7 cerebellar regions, resulting in 421 nodes in total. RsfMRI time series were averaged within each node, and pairwise Pearson correlations were computed between nodes to obtain FC values per each node pair. This resulted in a symmetric connectivity matrix of 421 nodes × 421 nodes. Non-significant connections were excluded by permutation testing, and Fisher’s r-to-z transformation was applied,,. Absolute values were used to prevent positive and negative weights from offsetting each other when estimating connection strength. To avoid distortions caused by differences in network density and overall FC, no additional thresholding was performed to sparsify the network,,. From the absolute FC matrices, three graph-theoretical parameters were derived node- and network-wise using custom R scripts, following previously established definitions: (i) within-network FC strength, (ii) between-network FC strength, and (iii) a segregation score that quantifies the relative balance of connectivity within networks versus connectivity between networks. The 421 nodes each yielded a segregation value, producing 421 node-wise features. In addition, network-wise metrics were extracted. With the regions of the Schaefer 400 parcellation being assigned to 9 large functional brain networks (i.e., visual, somatomotor, dorsal and salience/ventral attention, limbic, frontoparietal control, default mode, subcortical, and cerebellar networks), a total of 27 network-wise metrics (9 networks × 3 FC graph-theoretical parameters) could be derived.

Together with structural MRI and dMRI features, this resulted in a total of 1936 whole-brain features used for subsequent analyses.

This study aimed to evaluate if prediction of cognitive outcome from brain parameters would benefit from a model setup which is based on dedicated brain features associated with a person’s overall lifestyle profile. Thus, in our main analyses, we developed a model using brain features resulting from analyses investigating differences between groups of participants with different lifestyle profiles (BF-Lifemulti). We compared the BF-Lifemulti model against (i) a model using features related to a single lifestyle factor (BF-Lifesingle), (ii) a fully data-driven model, trained on principal components from the total amount of 1936 brain features (BFdata), and (iii) a model that incorporated demographic and lifestyle data in addition to the brain features into the BF-Lifemulti model. A schematic overview of the machine learning workflow is shown in Fig. . Details are described below.

The BF-Lifemulti model was developed in four main steps: lifestyle clustering, identification of lifestyle-related brain features, model training using multiple algorithms within a nested cross-validation framework, model evaluation, and model interpretation using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations).

The lifestyle clustering analysis aimed to identify groups of participants with similar lifestyle behavior within groups and differing behavior between groups. Therefore, K-modes clustering was used to group participants in the DISCOVERY dataset based on their individual profiles. Each DISCOVERY participant was represented by the eight lifestyle factors described in section “Participants”, forming a participant-by-lifestyle-variable matrix. These ordinal lifestyle variables were treated as categorical inputs in K-modes clustering (version 0.12.2) to reduce sensitivity to extreme values. This categorization was used to emphasize relative lifestyle levels in this relatively healthy sample, and K-modes was chosen because it is designed for categorical variables and supports a person-centered derivation of interpretable lifestyle profiles. Brain, cognitive, and demographic variables were not included in the clustering procedure. In detail, the algorithm was run with (i) 1000 random initializations for robust centroid selection; (ii) participants assigned to the nearest cluster using Hamming distance; (iii) cluster modes updated; and (iv) steps 2–3 repeated until assignments stabilized or 300 iterations were reached. The optimal number of clusters (k) was chosen by balancing statistical criteria and interpretability, using SW/SB ratio (within-cluster to between-cluster standard deviation ratio), R-squared, Silhouette score, and Davies–Bouldin index (DBI), where lower SW/SB and DBI, and higher R-squared and Silhouette values indicate better clustering. We tested k = 2–10 and evaluated the clustering solutions using these indices. Because such indices often favor simpler solutions (e.g., lower k values), the final k = 5 solution was selected by balancing statistical performance with biological interpretability.

To identify brain phenotypes related to different lifestyle behavior, feature selection was performed by identifying brain features that differed between our 5 lifestyle subgroups. In detail, feature selection was performed by comparing all 1936 brain features between the identified k = 5 lifestyle subgroups. Cognitive outcomes were not used during this feature-selection step. Due to the very large number of brain features relative to our sample size, univariate ANCOVAs were used for feature selection, adjusting for age, sex, education, and intracranial volume (for morphometric measures), to reduce demographic and head-size confounding during feature selection. This adjustment was used only to identify lifestyle-subgroup-related brain features; the selected brain-feature values were not residualized for these covariates before entering the prediction models. Brain metrics showing significant differences between any subgroup pair were retained. Significant group differences were identified at p < 0.05 with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests between subgroups (q < 0.05). Non-parametric Quade ANCOVA was applied when variance assumptions were violated. The resulting BF-Lifemulti feature set was held fixed during cross-validation and subsequent testing to maintain a consistent lifestyle-subgroup definition and corresponding brain-feature representation across analyses. No correction for multiple comparisons across neuroimaging metrics was applied, allowing richer input for the exploratory identification of potentially lifestyle-relevant features; accordingly, the selected features should be interpreted as an exploratory input set for prediction.

The primary goal of the current study was to test whether the BF-Lifemulti feature set provides helpful information for cognitive prediction. However, we assessed the robustness of prediction patterns across different modeling assumptions by applying five regression-based algorithms commonly used in neuroimaging analyses: elastic net regression (ENR), ridge regression, support vector regression with the radial basis function kernel (SVRrbf), relevance vector regression with linear kernel (RVRlin), and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Model fitting used a nested cross-validation (CV) framework within DISCOVERY, with an outer 5-repetitions × 10-fold CV for training/test splits and an inner 10-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning. For ENR, the regularization strength (α) was tuned over logarithmically spaced values ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10³, and the L1 ratio varied between 0.1 and 0.9. For ridge regression, the regularization parameter α was tuned over the same logarithmic range. For SVRrbf, the regularization parameter C varied between 10⁻³ and 10³, and the kernel width parameter γ was set to either scale or auto. For LASSO, the regularization parameter α was tuned over logarithmically spaced values from 10⁻¹ to 10⁵. For RVRlin, the hyperparameters α and β were tuned over values spanning multiple orders of magnitude (10⁻⁶, 1, and 10³). In all cases, hyperparameter selection was performed exclusively within the inner cross-validation loop. To evaluate generalization beyond model development, models trained in DISCOVERY were applied to the unseen TESTCROSS and TESTLONG subsets. Features were standardized (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1) within each cross-validation split, using parameters estimated from the training fold and then applied to the corresponding test fold and unseen datasets. All predictions were based on baseline MRI data.

Performance of all prediction models was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R²), indicating the explained variance, and the mean absolute error (MAE). For example, an MAE of 1 point means that predictions deviate from observed scores by an average of ±1 (e.g., seconds or correct words). Feature importance was assessed using SHAP analysis for the BF-Lifemulti model in the unseen datasets. To avoid interpreting feature contributions from models without meaningful predictive performance, SHAP interpretation was restricted to the algorithm and unseen dataset showing positive and comparatively stable prediction. Linear explainers were used for ENR, ridge, and LASSO, and kernel explainers for RVRlin and SVRrbf. For each feature, contributions were calculated as the average absolute SHAP value across the 50 cross-validation iterations (5 repeats × 10 folds).

For region-wise features, each feature label includes the functional network (e.g., SAN), the Schaefer parcellation region (e.g., FrOperIns_2), and the corresponding cytoarchitectonic area from the Juelich brain atlas (e.g., Id6), allowing precise anatomical interpretation.

Given the high dimensionality of the voxel- and region-wise features, we improved interpretability by aggregating SHAP values into broader, biologically meaningful categories (e.g., GMV in the visual network, FA in the association fiber tract), defined according to established brain atlases or tractographies. Category-level importance was then obtained by summing SHAP values within each category and ranking the results. All analyses were conducted in Python (v3.10.9) with scikit-learn (v1.1.2).

For comparison, three comparison models were constructed alongside the BF-Lifemulti model (see below). Among the five algorithms evaluated within the BF-Lifemulti model, one algorithm was selected for focused model comparisons based on its overall predictive performance across cognitive targets in DISCOVERY, as quantified by R². To ensure comparability, all comparison models were implemented using this selected algorithm and the same hyperparameter-tuning procedure.

To assess whether brain features derived from overall lifestyle profiles provide predictive information beyond those related to individual lifestyle factors, we constructed four models based on brain features reflecting the effects of a single lifestyle-related factor (BF-Lifesingle): smoking (SMO), alcohol consumption (ALC), physical activity (PA), and social integration (SI). For each BF-Lifesingle model, participants were grouped separately according to one corresponding lifestyle factor. Lifestyle-specific brain features were then identified using the same ANCOVA-based procedure as in BF-Lifemulti. In these analyses, age, sex, education, intracranial volume (for morphometric measures), and the remaining three lifestyle-related factors were included as covariates to isolate the effect of the factor of interest. The resulting brain features were used to construct separate machine learning models. SHAP analysis was applied to all BF-Lifesingle models using the same settings as for the BF-Lifemulti model.

To compare the BF-Lifemulti model against fully data-driven models, we applied principal component analysis (PCA)-based dimensionality reduction to all 1,936 brain features (Suppl. Table ). PCA was applied either to DISCOVERY or to the training set within each cross-validation fold only. For each case, the number of components was defined in two ways: either to explain 80% of the total variance or to match the number of features used in the BF-Lifemulti model. This resulted in four feature sets: BFdata-Var and BFdata-Match (PCA applied to DISCOVERY), and BFdata-Var[Train] and BFdata-Match[Train] (PCA applied to the training set). All hyperparameters were kept identical to those in the BF-Lifemulti model to ensure comparability, and analyses focused on the algorithms and cognitive targets that showed the highest predictive performance in that model.

We extended the BF-Lifemulti model by incorporating demographic variables (i.e., age, sex, and education; BF-Lifemulti +dem), as well as the original eight continuous lifestyle variables (BF-Lifemulti +dem+life), to assess the added predictive value of these non-brain variables beyond the selected, non-residualized brain features. Although the same eight lifestyle variables, recoded as categorical variables, were initially used to derive the lifestyle subgroups and thereby indirectly informed brain-feature selection, their original continuous values were not included as predictors in the BF-Lifemulti model.

As sensitivity analyses, we assessed three alternative model setups using the algorithm that showed the most stable predictive performance in the main analysis, with the same hyperparameter search settings (see section “Machine learning framework for cognitive function prediction”). First, for cognitive targets with positive predictive performance in the main analysis (R² > 0), we evaluated the impact of alternative clustering solutions for deriving overall lifestyle profiles (K-modes with k = 2–4). For the cognitive outcome with the highest predictive performance in the main analysis, we further conducted SHAP analyses to characterize feature contributions. Second, we implemented lifestyle-only models using the original eight continuous lifestyle variables as predictors to provide a reference for the predictive performance of lifestyle variables themselves. These analyses were restricted to datasets with complete lifestyle data and were treated as sensitivity analyses because the main focus was lifestyle-informed brain-feature selection. Third, sensitivity toward specific cognitive domains was examined by extending the predictions to a global cognitive component score as a supplementary target.

Basic characteristics of the total sample, DISCOVERY, and unseen datasets are summarized in Table . Differences between the DISCOVERY and unseen datasets were assessed using ANOVA for normally distributed variables, Chi-square tests for sex, and Mann–Whitney U-tests for non-normally distributed variables. Pearson correlations among the eight lifestyle variables were calculated to characterize overlap between lifestyle indicators and are reported in the Suppl. Table . For post hoc characterization, lifestyle subgroups were compared in terms of demographic, lifestyle, and cognitive variables using Chi-square tests, ANOVA, and Quade's ANOVA, where appropriate. To describe broader brain patterns after subgroup assignment, BF-Lifemulti features were averaged within each feature category (e.g., GMV and CT) and analyzed using ANOVA. All analyses were performed in IBM SPSS Statistics 29.0.

neuroscience.title: Effect of Trataka on Visual, Cognitive, and Psychophysiological Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
neuroscience.abstract: Trataka studies show a preliminary, statistically insignificant trend suggesting longer practice durations may be associated with higher cognitive scores, requiring confirmation through larger studies.As a healthcare technique, Trataka shows preliminary evidence of cross-modal neurocognitive modulation across visual, cognitive, and psychophysiological domains.High heterogeneity-centric studies underscore the need for an integrated, evidence-based public health approach to Trataka that ensures reliability, replicability, and reproducibility across ages, and evaluates duration–response correlations.Objective: A complementary and alternative healthcare practice such as Trataka, a Yogic visual concentration technique (YVC) rooted in Ayurvedic tradition, links cognition, visual, and psychophysiological well-being. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the moderating factors, including variations in study design and intervention protocol, to understand the efficacy of YVC across multiple domains. Methods: Systematic searches of eight scientific databases obtained 34 studies from 280 records until December 2025. Based on task scores, meta-regression and statistical heterogeneity were assessed using a random-effects model to obtain standardized mean difference (SMD) and risk of bias (RoB). Results: A pooled meta-analysis showed a significant YVC effect over control conditions across visual, cognitive, and psychophysiological domains (SMD of 0.92, 95% CI [0.44, 1.41]), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 74%) and a wide prediction interval (−0.22 to 2.07), which indicated that the true effect size could range from negligible to large, while extending to future studies. Meta-regression across the nine cognitive studies (K = 4 for each study design; k = 1 outlier) revealed no statistically significant duration–response relationship between session length and cognitive outcomes. RoB assessments indicated unclear to high risk among included studies. Discussion: Our results indicate that regular YVC practice could be associated with potential benefits for ocular and cognitive wellbeing, and for stress reduction, aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 3. However, given substantial heterogeneity, methodological limitations, and RoB concerns among included studies, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Standardized protocols, larger controlled trials, and neuroimaging approaches are needed to more precisely characterize YVC-related effects.
neuroscience.text:
Trataka, a structured yoga-derived attentional practice involving sustained time-limited focus aimed at strengthening visual attention over time [,,], is referred to as the Yogic visual concentration technique (YVC) in this study [,]. A type of complementary therapy rooted in Ayurveda [] that uses visual concentration, based on yogic principles and neurophysiological studies []. Many complementary therapy practices in yoga, including Asana (exercises) [], Pranayama (breathing exercises) [], and Dhyana (meditation) [], have been recognized for their role in changing people’s lifestyles and improving their mental health [,,].

More than 2.2 billion people globally are reported to suffer from various forms of vision impairment, according to the World Health Organization []. Following the COVID-19 pandemic [], the increased use of digital screen time has led to eye strain [] and vision problems such as myopia, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration [,]. Increased online learning and remote working have raised global health concerns [], underscoring the importance of preventive methods to reduce the impact of ocular diseases that aid in achieving Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG3) []. With the growth of digitally reliant sedentary lifestyles, complementary therapies are being evaluated to meet the new challenges [,]. Studies [,,] have shown that traditional methods in mental resilience address the growing burden through non-pharmacological, cost-effective, and sustainable approaches [,]. While measuring traditional techniques, such as YVC limited information is available in terms of its neurophysiological correlates [,]. However, there has been limited focus on visual attention and cognitive effects related to YVC. To tackle these challenges, there is a need to understand the neuroscientific basis of visual attention in terms of cognitive health []. Neuroscience research has been interested in exploring the neural mechanisms underlying attentional control [,] and perceptual processing [] to develop sustainable treatment strategies [].

Visual attention is one of the essential cognitive-functional domains [,,,,,,] that enables individuals to focus on significant details while selectively ignoring distractions [,] through both top-down (cognitive) and bottom-up (stimulus-driven) processes [,,]. Different forms of visual attention have been reported in studies, involving selective attention [], divided attention [], and sustained attention [], which includes YVC, providing valuable insights into how attentional control influences perception and higher-order cognitive processes [,,,] that are mediated by distributed cortical and subcortical networks []. Studies [,,] have proposed that YVC practice effects have a role in the neural basis for sustained attention and cognitive modulation, activating higher-order visual regions from V1 to V5 [,,] involving ipRGCs, which transmit signals beyond the primary visual system [,].

In meditation research, studies have hypothesized modulation of the default mode network (DMN) [], where reduced DMN activity during focused attention [] was generally associated with decreased mind-wandering [] and improved task engagement [,]. Studies have indicated that sustained visual fixation [,] was linked to oculomotor and attentional regulation [], recruiting neural circuits related to the frontal eye fields [] and superior colliculus [,]. Theta and alpha oscillatory activity in the prefrontal and occipital regions [,] during sustained-attention tasks is associated with default-mode [] and salience-network connectivity []. Related work [,,] has linked sustained visual cues to attention regulation and cortical plasticity, with cortical mapping studies having reported changes in visual, executive, and emotion-regulation regions in the cortex following sustained practice [,]. In general, yoga and meditative studies [,,] have used neuroimaging methods including fMRI [,,], EEG [,,], and MEG [] for brain-mapping [], while microstate-based network analyses provide an additional framework for understanding multi-scale brain organization [,,]. Despite the lack of data supporting pathways for visual and cognitive processes, YVC has been characterized as a low-cost, non-invasive, and accessible practice [,] with potential to improve eye health, attention, and stress reduction, aligning with public health objectives [,].

Evidence from the YVC studies on direct neurophysiological assessment of YVC practice remains limited. Short-term practice has been associated with reduced EEG entropy across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions, indicative of altered cortical activity patterns [], and with an increase in Critical Flicker Fusion frequency, suggesting enhanced cortical arousal []. Improvements in shooting accuracy following structured YVC technique have similarly been interpreted as evidence of enhanced oculomotor coordination and visual-motor integration []. However, a previous study on visual evoked potential (P100) latency had reported no significant change among short-term practitioners []. YVC’s effects across health-related domains remain to be addressed in the context of brain function and processing of oculo-sensorimotor functions. Classical texts describing YVC, including the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā and Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā [], do not specify a standardized, step-by-step protocol for duration, frequency, gaze-target characteristics, or progression, and contemporary studies consequently vary in these parameters as well as in visual cues and outcome measures [,,], contributing to substantial heterogeneity that limits reproducibility. No prior meta-analysis has quantitatively synthesized YVC’s effects across visual, cognitive, and psychophysiological domains while accounting for this methodological diversity.

The use of RoB in evaluating the literature suggested a lack of unified assessment of how YVC may influence distinct cognitive domains such as attention, working memory, processing speed, and inhibitory control. Owing to its simplicity, minimal resource requirements, and ease of practice, YVC is being explored as a feasible attentional training approach across diverse populations and settings. This study assesses the methodological efficacy of YVC techniques across diverse study designs to explore how YVC can contribute to sustainable health practices. Integrative approaches to lifestyle management such as YVC that align with SDG3 can ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all ages [].

This preliminary meta-analysis aims to achieve the following:

1. Evaluate the pooled effects of YVC on cognitive, visual, and psychophysiological outcomes compared with control or baseline conditions, and characterize the methodological quality, study-level heterogeneity, and risk of bias underlying this evidence across between-subject and within-subject study designs.

2. Examine, on a preliminary basis, whether session duration can act as a potential moderator of cognitive effect size through meta-regression analysis.

This meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines (see ) []. Eligibility criteria and the analytic approach were defined by the authors before study selection and data extraction. Prospective registration for the review protocol was not undertaken with PROSPERO or any other registry. As the study did not involve animal or human participants, no ethical approval was required. Only studies published in English or accompanied by a comprehensive English abstract were considered. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were independently screened by all authors. Given the limited number of available studies on YVC, no formal reviewer agreement was required. All discrepancies were resolved through discussion until a general agreement was achieved.

A systematic search was performed across eight electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, DOAJ, ProQuest, and JSTOR, to identify articles related to Trataka or YVC. The search strategy combined practice-related terms (Trataka; Yogic visual concentration; Yogic gazing) with domain/outcome terms (cognition; visual attention; EEG; fMRI; physiology; neural mechanisms; visual pathways). These term sets were used with Boolean operators as detailed in . No records were identified prior to November 2010. No field restrictions or limits were applied when retrieving records, and no predefined stopping criterion was used for the Google Scholar search. From 280 studies, 34 met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis. Eligible studies included publications in English up to December 2025 and included research articles, conference papers, dissertations, and relevant academic web sources.

The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram illustrated the identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of studies in the meta-review on YVC and its effects on cognition and visual attention-related outcomes. Out of 280 records, 195 duplicates were removed before screening, yielding 85 records. From 85, 34 studies were included in this review (see ).

This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using the PICOS framework (Population, Intervention, Comparators, Outcomes, and Study designs) [] to ensure methodological clarity and transparency (). The study design includes randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental designs, pre–post intervention studies, and within-subject repeated measures that precisely evaluated the effects of YVC.

Population: The review focused on human participants of all age groups, including children, adults, and older adults, regardless of their prior experience with yoga or meditation practices.

Intervention: YVC is practiced as a standalone technique. Studies in which YVC was combined with other yoga or meditation methods were included only if YVC-specific effects were reported as a separate outcome.

Comparison: YVC was composed of no-intervention or waitlist groups, routine daily activities, or standard care, using within-subject designs and participants’ own baseline measures.

Outcome: Cognitive functions such as attention, memory, processing speed, and executive function. Emotional or psychological parameters, including stress, anxiety, mood, or sleep quality. Visual health, including digital eye strain, refractive symptoms, visual comfort, or ocular fatigue. Physiological markers, such as heart rate, blood pressure, and insomnia symptoms. Neurophysiological responses, such as EEG, fMRI, or other indices related to brain activity. Published in English or with a comprehensive English abstract that provided sufficient methodological and results information for analysis.

Lack of empirical data: review articles, conceptual papers, editorials, commentaries, or anecdotal accounts without primary data or statistical analysis.

Intervention ambiguity: Combined YVC with other interventions (e.g., Pranayama, general Yoga) without isolating YVC-specific effects or reporting them as a distinct intervention.

Unrelated outcomes: Outcomes that are not relevant to cognition, emotion, vision, or physiology, or are focused on unrelated physical health markers (e.g., cholesterol, diabetes, musculoskeletal pain).

Duplicate or redundant data: Repeated or overlapping data from the same research group already included in the review, unless new outcome domains or participant groups were analyzed.

Methodological limitations: Lack of baseline or comparison condition or sample size too small (n = 3) to permit statistical analyses.

Data extraction was performed by two authors (SK and SB) and verified by three independent authors (SNS, SK1 and SD) as in previous studies [,] for accuracy, and discrepancies were resolved during the extraction process. No disagreements occurred during the verification of extracted data. When a study did not report sufficient data to compute an effect size (missing means, standard deviations, or convertible statistics), the study was excluded from the quantitative synthesis. Data extracted from these studies included study design, participant characteristics such as age, gender, methods used, key findings, and observations (). Eligible studies were systematically reviewed to examine patterns in YVC technique duration and variations in study design and the primary outcome measures. Key methodological characteristics, including participant demographics (a), intervention protocol, and assessment tools (), were extracted to identify trends and variations across the literature, which were represented in .

A comprehensive meta-analysis was conducted to explore the rationale for YVC-based interventions. A total of 34 studies were included, each selected based on methodological quality and relevance to the research objective. Among the included studies, 12 were randomized controlled trials, 7 were quasi-experimental designs, and 10 were pre–post intervention studies that examined the practice of YVC over time (b,c). Three studies using a self-as-control approach were examined. Two repeated measures contributed to the dataset. The distribution of YVC-related parameters was documented for the session duration and had moderate variability, with a median of 25 min and an interquartile range of 15–40 min (d). Training duration showed a distribution with a median of 4 weeks and an interquartile range of 2.25–8 weeks, indicating that most experiments were conducted for short to medium duration (d). All study types were considered and weighted in the synthesis process, ensuring that methodological variations were addressed in the final analysis. A list of keywords was used to represent an overview of participant characteristics, health conditions, outcome domains, and reported effects related to the included YVC studies [,].

Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB1), as described in the Cochrane Handbook (Version 5.1.0) and operationalized per [,], was applied uniformly across all included study designs to enable direct comparison within a single reporting framework. The Cochrane ROB 1 domain-by-domain assessment was applied only after eligibility screening to characterize the risk of bias profile of the retained studies. Domains specific to randomization were marked as not applicable for non-randomized or quasi-experimental studies rather than scored. The six standard ROB1 domains assessed were selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, reporting bias, and other sources of bias, each rated as low, high, or unclear risk. The risk of bias assessment was performed independently by two authors (SK and SB), and there were no disagreements in this study due to the limited literature on YVC.

All 34 eligible studies were included, and risk of bias was assessed. Five studies were excluded [,,,,] from the meta-analysis because of insufficient statistical information for reliable effect size estimation. No effect sizes were imputed. For the quantitative analysis, 29 studies were included.

The included studies were classified and listed based on their outcomes and study designs in .

Statistical analyses were conducted to evaluate the effects of YVC-based outcomes on cognitive, visual, and psychophysiological domains, including within-subject (pre–post) and between-subject (YVC–control) study designs. Raw outcome data were extracted from the included studies and classified into the prespecified functional domains. Individual study-level Hedges’ g, standard errors, and 95% confidence intervals were calculated separately for within-subject and between-subject studies using design-specific formulas. When a study reported multiple outcomes, their corresponding outcome-level effect sizes were averaged into a single composite study-level Hedges’ g to preserve the study as the unit of analysis []. All the notations and parameters used are described in . All the parameters were calculated using jamovi (Version 26) [] and PythonMeta (Version 1.26) [].

Effect magnitudes across diverse outcomes were computed using the standardized mean difference (SMD). Effect sizes were calculated separately according to study design. For between-subject studies, Cohen’s d was calculated from the difference between group means and the pooled standard deviation:(1)d=M2−M1SDpooled

Within-subject and between-subject random-effects meta-analyses were performed across each functional domain using Cochrane Review Manager (RevMan 5.4) [], with inverse-variance weighting and REML estimation of between-study variance (τ2), with HKSJ-adjusted confidence intervals. To provide an overall descriptive summary of magnitude and direction of effects across functional domains, domain-level composite Hedges’g and standard error estimates were calculated using the arithmetic mean.

Heterogeneity was assessed using Chi-square (χ2), I2, and τ2, and pooled confidence intervals were calculated using the HKSJ method. Heterogeneity across the included studies was classified using the following thresholds: 0–24% (low), 25–49% (moderate), 50–74% (substantial), and 100% (considerable) [].

For the meta-regression analysis, 9 studies that involved the cognitive domain were included to assess whether variations in intervention duration, measured in minutes, were associated with different outcomes across studies. This analysis reveals how extended practice durations may enhance intervention efficacy. A linear regression model was used to test their association, with the fitted line illustrating the trend linking session duration in minutes to domain outcome.Effect size = β1 (Duration) + β0(15)Change in SMD across the individual study was calculated as β. The p-value tested the null hypothesis that β = 0 (no linear relationship between duration and effect size).(16)β=∑ [(xi−x¯)(yi−y¯)]∑[(xi−x¯)2]t=βSE(β)

Positive SMD values were interpreted as indicating improvement in YVC outcomes compared to baseline conditions.

Effect sizes were interpreted using Cohen’s conventional thresholds: SMD = 0.2–0.4 (small), 0.5–0.7 (moderate), indicating improvement in the intervention compared to the control or baseline condition, but not uniform across all studies, and SMD ≥ 0.8 (large). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

Studies have shown varying levels of distribution, prominence, and co-occurrence across the literature for the obtained keywords related to various domains of neuroscience. These keywords have been clustered horizontally by relevance to YVC studies, and the word size indicates how often they appear in the literature, while their spatial proximity indicates how closely they are related (a). The central words “Trataka”, “Visual”, “Stress”, “Yoga”, and “Cognitive” are the most often listed. The overlap between cognitive and visual clusters has led many YVC-based studies to conceptualize both visual training and cognitive performance as interrelated rather than independent domains. Methodological terms (including measures, tools, designs, functional, and intervention) remained more isolated, which indicated heterogeneity rather than a standardized approach.

Across the 34 studies, the thickness and flow of the ribbon model represented the distribution of studies with diverse populations across different age groups and genders, participants with distinct health conditions, and mixed outcomes after practicing the YVC (b). These 34 studies have included participants from different age groups, from 8 to 11 years [,,], 18 to 25 years [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,], 25–40 years, and 40–80 years [,,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. This suggests the diversity and predominance of young populations, while one study did not report the age group []. A gender-based heterogeneity was observed across the 34 studies, among which 10 studies labeled them as heterogeneous (mixed population) [,,,,,,,,,], and 7 studies specified males only or females only. Furthermore, six studies did not report any information about the involvement of participants [,,,,,]. Various vision-related conditions, especially myopia, digital eye strain, visual strain, asthenopia, and glaucoma, were reported in 15 studies [,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Four studies included stress- and anxiety-related conditions, insomnia, and hypertension [,,,]. Cognitive improvements have been observed in visual-related studies after YVC practice [,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Only six studies did not report any improvement or had heterogeneous results, which may indicate inconsistent intervention effects or differences in the methods of measuring the outcomes [,,]. The existence of heterogeneous and non-reported data depicts differences in reporting practices and outcomes among the studies. These visualizations provide a descriptive and exploratory characterization of the included studies and participant characteristics and are not part of the quantitative statistical analysis and were not used to estimate intervention effects.

The RoB evaluation indicated differences in methodological quality across studies, including eligibility criteria, search strategy, study selection, reporting transparency, and interpretation. RoB was assessed in the following domains: selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, reporting bias, attrition bias, and other sources of bias. The domain-specific assessment was applied to randomized studies, while the same domain structure was used to consider descriptively for non-randomized and quasi-experimental studies to facilitate consistent reporting across the evidence. Randomization-specific domains, including sequence generation and allocation of concealment, were marked as not applicable for studies without random allocation rather than being assigned to a risk category.

RoB assessments indicated that the random sequence generation was rated as low risk in 11 studies (33%) (green). Allocation concealment was computed as low risk in seven studies (21%) and unclear in four studies (12%) (yellow). The remaining studies were not considered applicable as they involved no randomization or used quasi-experimental designs ().

For blinding of participants and personnel, 21 studies (65%) were classified as unclear risk and 11 studies (32.4%) as high risk (red), reflecting the practical difficulty of blinding participants in YVC-based studies. For self-reported outcomes, approximately 9 studies (30%) were at low risk, 15 studies (41%) at unclear risk, and 5 studies (15%) at high risk. However, objective outcome assessment demonstrated a comparatively favorable profile: 22 studies (65%) were low risk, 11 studies (29%) were unclear, and 1 study (3%) was high risk. Incomplete outcome data were classified as approximately 15 studies (43%) low risk and 18 studies (57%) unclear, whereas selective reporting showed 22 studies (68%) low risk and 10 studies (29%) unclear. Other biases were not applied as a substantive risk domain in the assessment. Overall, the evidence base demonstrated a relatively lower risk for objective selective reporting and outcome assessment. The individual study for each domain, from selection to other sources of bias, was assessed separately to summarize this risk of bias graph ().

Among the 29 studies, 10 primarily focused on the cognitive domain, including a minor psychophysiological task, and analyzed the total task-based score. The studies included a pre (before YVC practice) and post (after YVC practice) within-subject study design and a between-subject study design (YVC–control). The change in score for each cognitive task showed a consistent pattern of improvement after practicing YVC across the different cognitive domains. After following the YVC practice, the positive and negative differences in task scores across various cognitive measures, ranging from Stroop reaction time (−20.00) to the word score (10.47), indicate positive effects in the control and YVC groups (a). Similarly, the pre- and post-YVC groups showed positive and negative scores across the various cognitive tasks from the Trail-Making Test-B (TMT-B) (−59.31) to the SLCT net score (16.87), indicating positive effects following YVC practice (b). Psychophysiological measures such as electrodermal activity, anxiety (assessed by the Hamilton scale), Mood and Anxiety symptoms (MASQ), Stroop reaction time, perceived stress scale (PSS), and TMT-B showed negative scores, which indicate improvement because lower scores signify reduced anxiety and faster reaction time performance after YVC practice [,,,,,,,,,].

A meta-regression analysis was performed to identify whether improved cognitive task scores were associated with the duration of YVC practice sessions (10–60 min) as the indicator [,,,,,,,,]. Across the nine studies, the results showed that as the duration of YVC practice increased, the effect size increased. Cognitive outcomes were converted to Hedge’s g, and multiple outcomes within the same study were summarized into a single study-level effect size. Five between-subjects studies were included in the regression analysis, where one study remained an outlier due to its observed effect size of 3.21, which fell beyond the 95% prediction interval of the regression model fit to the other four studies (SMD = 2.65), and exceeded the model’s predicted value at its corresponding session duration (a). A sensitivity analysis was conducted (K = 5; see ).
