Both including (β = 0.009, p = 0.7891, K = 5) and excluding the study (β = 0.018, p = 0.2201, K = 4) showed no significant association between session duration and effect size, indicating that duration alone may not be a strong moderator. The mean effect size across four studies was 0.94, and individual effect sizes ranged from 0.44 to 1.57.

Similarly, session duration did not show a statistically significant association with effect size in the within-subject cognitive studies (β = 0.029, p = 0.083, K = 4). The mean effect size across the four included studies was 0.946, while individual study effect sizes ranged from 0.530 to 1.741. All four study-level estimates were positive, with the lowest effect observed at 20 min (0.530) and the highest at 60 min (1.741) (b). Although the trend shows larger effects with increasing duration, it was not statistically significant. No outliers were identified. Therefore, the current evidence from both between-subject and within-subject designs was insufficient to establish a duration–response relationship for cognitive outcomes. The wide confidence and prediction intervals indicate substantial uncertainty in the estimated relationship and may reflect factors beyond duration.

Within-subject designs showed a statistically significant pooled effect favoring YVC (SMD = 1.20, 95% CI: 0.33–2.07, p = 0.03), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 41%; χ2 = 3.39, p = 0.18). Between-subject designs also favored YVC, but the pooled effect was not statistically significant (SMD = 0.61, 95% CI: −0.36–1.58; p = 0.11), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 62%, χ2 = 5.44, p = 0.07). The subgroup difference between within-subject and between-subject pooled estimates was borderline statistically significant (χ2 = 3.70, p = 0.05, I2 = 72.9%), with a larger pooled effect observed in the within-subject designs (). Overall, the pooled estimates favored YVC in both study designs, although the magnitude and statistical significance differed between designs. The pooled analysis, stratified by study design, showed a significantly positive effect in the within-subject studies across all domains and a smaller pooled positive effect for between-subject studies, with moderate heterogeneity reported in .

In the RCT-only analysis, the psychophysiological domain favored YVC with statistical significance (SMD = 0.68, 95% CI 0.04–1.32, I2 = 87%), whereas the cognitive effect was positive when Hedge’s g favored YVC over the baseline condition, but not statistically significant (SMD = 1.02, 95% CI 0.25–2.29, I2 = 90%). The vision domain showed no significant effect and substantial heterogeneity (SMD = 0.86, 95%, I2 = 99%). Overall, the pooled RCT estimate was positive with statistical insignificance (SMD = 0.62, 95% CI 0.03–1.26, I2 = 95%), with a wide predicted interval (−1.78 to 3.02) (). Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis showed that the pooled effects remained positive across both study designs. In within-subject analyses, the largest changes were observed after removal of three studies (Δ = −0.37, Δ = −0.36, Δ = 0.30), while in between-subject analyses, removal of one study produced the largest increase and decrease (Δ = 0.56 and Δ = −0.40) ().

This review and meta-analysis synthesizes the evidence on Trataka (YVC) across visual, cognitive, and psychophysiological outcomes. The frequent key phrases across the 34 studies indicated the relevance of YVC in the critical domains, and the study characteristics have reported diversity across participants’ age, gender, assessments, and YVC outcomes (visual strain, hypertension, anxiety).

The RoB assessment of the reported studies highlights several methodological inconsistencies, including participant selection for study designs, detection of diverse outcomes in the same domain, reported participants’ performance, and self-reported, selective, or inadequate outcomes. These reported factors led to a highly biased evaluation of YVC-based interventions, underscoring the need for stronger research designs in future studies. Participant selection in the studies indicated that only the younger population limited the interpretation of YVC effects among the children and the elderly populations. Diverse outcomes were observed due to several assessments (word score, HRV, sleep quality, MASQ, TMT-B, SLCT, Stroop reaction time, HARS, and PSS) and variation in protocols (gazing duration, intervention length, and session frequency from single sessions to weeks or months). This diversity limits the comparability of individual participants’ performance to employ generalized standard tools for further research. These selective protocol-based variations on YVC have led to diverse research objectives (visual strain, cognitive and psychophysiological stress) and study designs (including pre–post, quasi-experimental, repeated measures, and limited RCTs), indicating heterogeneity across the studies and implying the need for specific RCTs and domain-focused reproducible protocols to minimize bias.

In the meta-regression analysis, no statistically significant duration–response relationship between session length and cognitive outcomes was reported. Even within brief sessions (10–30 min), effect sizes on cognitive-related measures were slightly favored, suggesting that the short- and long-term duration protocol may impact YVC’s efficiency across all domains. Sensitivity analysis in the between-subject meta-regression yielded no significant association between session duration and cognitive effect sizes to interpret duration–response relationships.

Although several studies showed effects in a favorable direction, the number of studies showing such effects was not taken as the primary basis. Some studies reported no significant change between baseline and YVC practitioners. The overall findings in relation to the magnitude of the pooled effect estimates, confidence and prediction intervals, and between-study variability suggested substantial heterogeneity observed across the studies. This variability was also evident across the study characteristics, including differences in participants, intervention duration, comparators, outcome measures, and study designs. These factors may contribute to variation in the observed effect sizes. The preliminary findings support a favorable overall direction of effect associated with YVC across the evaluated domains, although this favorability remained inconsistent. The findings from the RCT-only sensitivity analysis indicated that the pooled evidence showed a favorable effect of YVC, with a larger estimate among within-subject designs than between-subject designs. The potential benefit may rely on evidence from within-subject designs rather than the moderate effect provided by the RCTs. The difference in effect estimates between RCT-only and combined analyses highlights the influence of study design on the observed effect magnitude. Leave-one-out analysis showed that exclusion of individual studies did not reverse the direction of effects in either within- or between-subject designs.

Several methodological limitations affect the interpretability and generalizability of findings. Most research focused on young adults (18–25 years), with limited attention to older adults (25–40 years), the elderly (40–80 years), or children (8–11 years). A secondary concern is the imbalance of gender representation. Many studies limited their data to only male or female populations, which may influence the observed outcomes. Heterogeneity in the duration protocol further limits comparability. YVC session durations ranged from 2 min to 2 h, with frequencies from weekly to daily and total durations from 2 weeks to 3 months. This variability complicates the identification of optimal practice parameters. Many studies considered YVC alongside other practices, thereby limiting YVC efficiency among participants. Studies assessed a wide array of variables (e.g., flicker fusion thresholds, Stroop tasks, working memory, heart rate variability, and visual strain) using diverse instruments. Small sample sizes increased the risk of statistical errors, and many studies relied on subjective or self-reported outcomes rather than validated objective tools. Together, this contributes to the substantial heterogeneity observed in the quantitative synthesis and suggests that current evidence may not completely indicate the true efficacy of YVC. Standardized protocols defining session length, frequency, and duration are needed to improve consistency and clinical applicability. Substantial heterogeneity across the studies limited direct comparability and may have influenced the consistency of the observed results. A methodological limitation of this review was the reliance on the common RoB1 tool across studies with heterogeneous designs. This review was restricted to studies published in English or accompanied by a comprehensive English abstract, which may introduce language bias by excluding relevant evidence published in Hindi, Sanskrit, and other languages. Publication bias and selective reporting could not be formally assessed because the domain- and design-specific subgroups contained fewer than 10 studies, limiting the reliability of small-study effect tests.

To better understand the effects of YVC, yoga-related neuroscience research using physiological and neuroimaging methods is needed. Longitudinal EEG with functional connectivity analysis and cortical mapping studies may help characterize how repeated YVC practice modifies large-scale brain network organization over time. While further mechanistic and longitudinal studies are needed, the existing evidence supports YVC’s potential role in cognitive enhancement, attentional training, and emotional regulation. Though the heterogeneity remains unclear, the cumulative evidence supports YVC’s potential as a holistic practice for improving cognition, visual function, and psychophysiological balance. YVC demonstrated observable effects across visual, cognitive, and psychophysiological domains that remain to be fully explored. However, the current evidence lacks definitive conclusions regarding its effectiveness. Overall, analysis suggests potential benefits across selected outcomes but does not establish YVC as an effective technique across all domains, underscoring the need for standardized protocols, larger controlled trials, and neuroimaging-based investigations to establish clinical relevance. Future studies should include broader age ranges and conduct age-specific analyses. Standardizing YVC protocols, including duration, visual cue type, preparatory practices, and session design, may reduce heterogeneity and enhance comparability across studies.

The findings from this preliminary evidence suggest potentially beneficial effects across the domains of cognition, vision, and psychophysiology. However, substantial heterogeneity among the included studies, concerns regarding risk of bias, small samples, and variability in intervention protocols limit the reproducibility and generalizability of these findings. To better understand the benefits and limitations of YVC practice, future studies need to adopt rigorous trials with adequate sample sizes, standardized assessments, and follow-up evaluations to assess both short- and long-term effects. Development of a core outcome set for YVC would further improve consistency and comparability across studies. By addressing these methodological limitations, future investigations would be better positioned to generate reliable, reproducible evidence on the cognitive and neurophysiological benefits of YVC practice, thereby potentially aligning with the United Nations (UN) SDG 3.

neuroscience.title: Precision Laboratory Diagnostics for Autoimmune Encephalitis and Paraneoplastic Neurological Syndromes: Autoantibody Testing, Fluid Biomarkers, and AI-Assisted Integration
neuroscience.abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) and paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (PNS) are leading causes of potentially reversible but frequently misdiagnosed neurological disability, and delayed recognition worsens outcomes and impedes timely tumor detection. This narrative review is written from a laboratory medicine perspective and focuses on the analytical determinants of early and accurate diagnosis: appropriate test selection, dual-method confirmation combining tissue-based and cell-based assays, phenotype-guided interpretation, and assay harmonization. We summarize the expanding spectrum of neuronal and glial autoantibodies, quantitative biomarkers of neuroaxonal injury—most notably neurofilament light chain—and investigational cerebrospinal fluid markers, including cytokine profiles, kappa free light chains, and markers of astrocytic injury, whose ability to discriminate AE from infectious mimics has not been established. We highlight novel autoantibody discovery through phage immunoprecipitation sequencing, research-stage multi-omics approaches, and early, retrospectively evaluated artificial intelligence-assisted classifiers, and we address the growing challenge of neurological adverse events triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitors. Priorities for translation into routine care include external quality assurance, certified reference materials, age-adjusted reference intervals, and prospective validation of integrated biomarker panels within reference-center networks. The review provides a structured framework to support precision laboratory diagnostics in neuroimmunology.
neuroscience.text:
Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) and paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (PNS) have emerged as leading causes of subacute encephalopathy, seizures, and rapidly progressive cognitive and psychiatric syndromes, often affecting previously healthy individuals [,,,]. Importantly, many of these conditions are potentially reversible when diagnosed early [,], whereas delayed recognition is consistently associated with worse neurological outcomes [,] and, in paraneoplastic disease, missed opportunities for timely tumor detection.

From a diagnostic perspective, AE and PNS represent a paradigm of complex neuroimmunological disorders in which conventional clinical, imaging, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings are often insufficient, particularly in early disease stages. A substantial proportion of patients may present with normal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or only subtle CSF abnormalities, and a subset remains seronegative despite strong clinical suspicion. These challenges have shifted the diagnostic focus toward advanced laboratory-based approaches and biomarker-driven strategies.

This review is written deliberately from the perspective of laboratory medicine, a vantage point that remains underrepresented in the predominantly clinical and neuroimmunological literature on AE and PNS yet is decisive for diagnostic accuracy. Laboratory investigations are widely regarded as central to a substantial proportion of clinical decisions across medicine, although the frequently cited “70% claim” should be interpreted cautiously; their value derives not from test volume but from appropriate test selection, methodologically sound measurement, and context-aware interpretation []. In autoimmune neurology this principle is especially consequential: the diagnostic performance of neural antibody testing depends critically on the specimen tested (serum versus CSF), the combination of assay methods (tissue-based and cell-based screening with confirmatory steps), and the pretest probability defined by the clinical phenotype []. When testing is uncoupled from this laboratory-medicine framework—for example, single-method serum testing in low-probability patients—false-positive results are common and drive misdiagnosis, unnecessary immunosuppression, and missed alternative diagnoses; recent yield audits report low true-positive yield and frequent false-positive results, particularly when testing is performed in poorly selected populations or serum-only contexts []. A staged, phenotype-driven, dual-method testing strategy interpreted within its analytical and clinical context is therefore not a technical detail but the central determinant of whether these reversible disorders are recognized correctly and early. This laboratory-medicine lens is the unifying thread of the present review.

Over the past decade, the field has undergone a profound transformation driven by the expanding spectrum of neuronal and glial autoantibodies [,], improvements in assay methodologies including tissue-based assays (TBAs) and cell-based assays (CBAs) [], and the introduction of quantitative biomarkers of neuroaxonal injury, most notably neurofilament light chain (NfL) [,]. The updated 2021 PNS-Care diagnostic criteria introduced an objective scoring system that, for combined definite and probable diagnoses, showed a sensitivity of 93% and a specificity of 100% in a retrospective single-center cohort of 484 patients with suspected PNS, compared with 67% and 99% for the 2004 criteria [,,]; these are cohort-specific estimates that may not apply to unselected populations or to all AE/PNS presentations. In parallel, CSF cytokine and chemokine profiles are being investigated as adjunctive markers of intrathecal inflammation, particularly in antibody-negative cases, although their patterns overlap between autoimmune and infectious disorders and validated cutoffs are lacking [,,].

Beyond individual biomarkers, there is growing emphasis on integrative diagnostic models that combine serological, CSF, and imaging data with emerging multi-omics technologies and artificial intelligence (AI)-based analytical tools. A new and critically important clinical challenge is the recognition and management of neurological adverse events triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), which closely resemble classic PNS but require severity-adapted management within multidisciplinary oncological care [,,].

The aim of this review is to provide a focused, biomarker-oriented overview of innovative diagnostic strategies for the early detection of autoimmune and paraneoplastic disorders of the nervous system. Particular emphasis is placed on the clinical integration of autoantibody testing, fluid biomarkers, and emerging multi-omics and computational approaches, with the goal of improving diagnostic accuracy and enabling earlier therapeutic intervention.

This narrative review was based on a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE for English-language articles published between 1 January 2014 and 31 August 2026. Disease terms (“autoimmune encephalitis”, “paraneoplastic neurological/neurologic syndrome(s)”) were combined with methodological and biomarker terms (“neuronal antibody”, “neural antibody”, “cell-based assay”, “tissue-based assay”, “neurofilament light”, “cerebrospinal fluid”, “biomarker”, “PhIP-Seq”/“phage immunoprecipitation”, “immune checkpoint inhibitor”, “machine learning”, and “artificial intelligence”) in titles and abstracts; the full PubMed search string is given in . Inclusion criteria were (i) original clinical or laboratory studies, diagnostic-accuracy and validation studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, consensus criteria, and guidelines; and (ii) relevance to laboratory diagnosis, assay methodology, fluid biomarkers, or diagnostic decision-making in AE or PNS. Exclusion criteria were single case reports (unless describing a newly identified antibody), conference abstracts, non-peer-reviewed material, and articles without laboratory or diagnostic content. The documented PubMed search (re-executed on 26 October 2026 for reproducibility) identified 1752 records. Titles and abstracts were screened, and approximately 250 articles were assessed in detail for eligibility, by four authors (D.S., D.Z., Z.Š. and P.K.). As in other narrative reviews, no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed, and selection bias cannot be fully excluded. In total, 58 publications are cited, including foundational studies published before 2014 and clinical guidance identified through manual screening of reference lists, which were retained where they define established concepts, methods, or criteria. Recent laboratory-medicine-oriented syntheses and harmonization surveys were incorporated to reflect the current analytical landscape [,].

AE and PNS encompass both antibody-mediated and predominantly T-cell-mediated immune processes, with distinct implications for reversibility, cancer association, and therapeutic responsiveness.

Antibodies targeting neuronal cell-surface or synaptic antigens—including N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR), leucine-rich glioma-inactivated protein 1 (LGI1), contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2), α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR), and γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptor (GABABR)—cause potentially reversible neuronal dysfunction through receptor internalization or altered synaptic signaling [,]. These disorders typically respond well to immunotherapy when diagnosed early [,,].

In contrast, classic paraneoplastic antibodies directed against intracellular antigens (e.g., Hu/ANNA-1, Yo/PCA-1, Ri, Ma2, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin) primarily act as biomarkers of cytotoxic T-cell-mediated neuronal injury, often predicting irreversible neuronal loss and limited response to immunosuppression [,]. Anti-IgLON5 disease represents a unique paradigm bridging autoimmunity and neurodegeneration, with antibodies targeting the cell-surface IgLON5 protein leading to cytoskeletal disruption and secondary tauopathy [,,].

In PNS, ectopic expression of neuronal antigens by tumor cells breaks immune tolerance, triggering immune responses that cross-react with the nervous system []. Antigen localization informs both cancer risk and therapeutic expectations: high-risk intracellular antibodies mandate intensive and repeated tumor screening, whereas many cell-surface antibodies are associated with lower malignancy risk but excellent immunotherapy responsiveness when recognized early. Immunopathological classification is therefore central to diagnostic risk stratification and clinical decision-making.

Autoantibody testing represents the cornerstone of laboratory diagnosis in AE and PNS. However, its clinical utility depends not only on analytical performance but also on appropriate test selection, timing, and interpretation within a phenotype-driven diagnostic framework.

Autoantibodies can be broadly categorized into those targeting cell-surface/synaptic antigens and those directed against intracellular antigens, with distinct implications for pathogenesis, malignancy risk, and treatment responsiveness. Cell-surface antibodies—including NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, AMPAR, GABABR, DPPX, and IgLON5—are typically pathogenic and mediate potentially reversible neuronal dysfunction through receptor internalization or synaptic disruption. These disorders are strongly associated with favorable responses to early immunotherapy and exhibit relatively characteristic clinical phenotypes, such as faciobrachial dystonic seizures in LGI1 encephalitis [] or prominent psychiatric manifestations in NMDAR encephalitis [,]. For LGI1/CASPR2-associated disease, the first randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial demonstrated superiority of intravenous immunoglobulin over placebo in reducing seizure frequency, although the trial was terminated early because of slow enrollment and did not reach its planned sample size [].

Intracellular onconeural antibodies (Hu, Yo, Ri, Ma2, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin, and SOX1) are most often associated with PNS and underlying malignancy and primarily reflect cytotoxic T-cell-mediated injury. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65), although intracellular, are associated with a comparatively low frequency of malignancy, in contrast to classic onconeural antibodies, and are best regarded as lower-risk markers requiring high titers and cautious interpretation []. From a diagnostic perspective, this distinction provides a biologically grounded framework for risk stratification and guides both oncologic screening and therapeutic urgency.

Antibodies to glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) define autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy, an increasingly recognized entity that typically presents as meningoencephalomyelitis, often with characteristic linear perivascular radial gadolinium enhancement on MRI and a variable association with neoplasia (e.g., ovarian teratoma). GFAP-IgG is most reliably detected in CSF by cell-based and tissue-based assays, and its inclusion in modern neural antibody panels improves recognition of this distinct astrocytopathy [,].

Recent years have witnessed rapid identification of novel autoantibodies through advanced discovery techniques. Phage immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-Seq) incubates patient serum or CSF with a bacteriophage library displaying overlapping 36-amino-acid peptides that span the human proteome; antibody-bound phages are immunoprecipitated and identified by high-throughput sequencing []. Because the library displays short peptides, the method is best suited to linear epitopes and may miss conformational cell-surface targets; it is a research-based discovery tool whose candidate antibodies require orthogonal confirmation (e.g., TBA and CBA with the full-length antigen) and clinical validation before diagnostic use [,,]. PhIP-Seq enabled the identification of anti-KLHL11, an intracellular antibody targeting Kelch-like protein 11, initially described in men with testicular seminomas presenting with a brainstem-cerebellar syndrome (rhombencephalitis), though the clinical spectrum has since broadened to include other germ cell tumors, female patients, and diverse malignancies; a recent cohort of 17 patients identified by a Dutch national reference laboratory further detailed the clinical manifestations, tumor associations, and long-term outcomes of anti-KLHL11 encephalitis [,,]. Similarly, SKOR2-IgG was identified via PhIP-Seq in an initial report of two patients with lung and gallbladder adenocarcinoma, respectively, and requires confirmation in larger cohorts []. These discoveries can resolve the etiology in a subset of patients previously labeled as seronegative and underscore the evolving nature of the autoantibody repertoire ().

A key advance in recent years has been the shift from isolated antibody testing toward structured, phenotype-driven diagnostic algorithms. The 2021 PNS-Care criteria introduced a scoring system (PNS-Care Score) that integrates clinical phenotype, antibody type, presence or absence of cancer, and follow-up duration to classify patients into definite, probable, and possible PNS []. A retrospective validation study of 484 patients with suspected PNS evaluated at a single tertiary center reported, for the combined definite and probable categorization (PNS-Care Score ≥ 6), a sensitivity of 93% and a specificity of 100%, compared with 67% and 99% for the “definite” category of the 2004 criteria [,]. These are cohort-specific estimates from a selected referral population that excluded ICI-related presentations and syndromes not covered by the 2021 criteria, and they should not be generalized to unselected populations or to all AE/PNS presentations; notably, 15 patients with a PNS-Care Score ≤ 5 were judged likely to have PNS, most often KLHL11-IgG brainstem encephalitis []. These pooled figures should not be misread as the performance of the “definite” category alone, which is more specific but less sensitive.

For suspected AE, current expert consensus recommends a phenotype-driven, multi-step approach: (1) define the clinical phenotype; (2) perform first-line investigations (MRI, CSF analysis, electroencephalography) to establish an inflammatory context; (3) select targeted antibody panels based on phenotype and cancer risk profile; (4) apply a combined TBA–CBA testing strategy; and (5) integrate results with pretest probability [,,,]. TBAs using indirect immunofluorescence on rodent brain sections provide high sensitivity and enable recognition of characteristic staining patterns, including previously unrecognized antibodies, whereas CBAs offer high specificity by confirming antigen-specific binding, particularly for conformational cell-surface epitopes [,].

A complementary two-tiered TBA–CBA strategy is recommended to maximize diagnostic accuracy, with TBA screening followed by antigen-specific CBA confirmation []. A recent prospective comparison of commercial and in-house TBA and CBA platforms further demonstrated substantial inter-platform variability in performance for several antibodies, underscoring the need for assay standardization []. The diagnostic performance of antibody testing also differs by specimen compartment. For several antibodies—most notably NMDAR—CSF testing demonstrates superior sensitivity and specificity compared with serum; therefore, combined serum and CSF analysis is recommended whenever feasible [,].

Despite advances in assay technology, misinterpretation of autoantibody results remains a major clinical problem. It has recently been highlighted that increased awareness of AE has led to two unintended consequences []: a high frequency of misdiagnoses and the inappropriate use of diagnostic criteria for antibody-negative disease. Misdiagnoses typically arise from: (1) testing in low pretest probability settings, leading to incidental antibody detection without clinical relevance; (2) overinterpretation of low-titer antibodies, especially GAD65 or CASPR2 in serum; (3) use of incomplete assay panels (e.g., line blot-only strategies); (4) failure to confirm unexpected results with TBAs or repeat testing; (5) exclusive reliance on serum testing in conditions where CSF is more informative; and (6) ignoring alternative diagnoses such as neurodegenerative or psychiatric disorders.

Seronegative AE represents an additional diagnostic challenge. The criteria for probable antibody-negative AE require rigorous exclusion of alternative etiologies and well-substantiated absence of neural antibodies in both CSF and serum, ideally using both TBAs and CBAs covering a broad antigen range [,,]. Accurate classification of these cases is essential for identifying homogeneous populations for treatment trials and outcome studies.

Fluid biomarkers have emerged as essential complementary tools in the diagnostic workup of AE and PNS, particularly in cases where autoantibody findings are negative, inconclusive, or difficult to interpret. In contrast to autoantibodies, which primarily provide etiological specificity, fluid biomarkers reflect key pathophysiological processes, including neuroinflammation and neuroaxonal injury, and therefore contribute to disease stratification and monitoring.

NfL is an analytically well-characterized biomarker of neuroaxonal damage across neurological disorders [,]. The introduction of ultrasensitive immunoassays, such as single-molecule array (Simoa) technology, has enabled reliable quantification of NfL in both CSF and serum, facilitating its implementation in clinical practice [,]. In multiple sclerosis and several neurodegenerative disorders, serum/plasma and CSF NfL concentrations correlate with disease activity, severity, and long-term outcome [,,]; in AE, however, the evidence is more limited and less consistent, as summarized below.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating NfL in neuronal surface antibody-associated AE (NSAE) demonstrated that both serum NfL (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.909; 95% CI, 0.536–1.282) and CSF NfL (SMD 0.897; 95% CI, 0.508–1.286) were significantly elevated in patients with NSAE compared with controls []. However, the meta-analysis also noted that NfL levels were not consistently associated with disease severity, prognosis, or MRI/electroencephalographic abnormalities in NSAE, highlighting important differences from multiple sclerosis and suggesting that neuroaxonal injury, while present, may not be the predominant pathological feature. In anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, serum NfL levels are elevated and correlate with neuroaxonal damage; however, their independent prognostic value at diagnosis remains limited, as any association with long-term outcome appears largely confounded by age []. In a 2026 multicenter prospective cohort of 92 patients with anti-NMDAR, anti-LGI1, or anti-CASPR2 encephalitis, CSF NfL z-scores were associated with baseline disease severity, and longitudinal NfL changes with severity and disability at follow-up []; these findings await independent replication. Taken together, NfL elevation in AE is well supported as a marker of neuroaxonal injury, whereas its prognostic and treatment-monitoring applications remain insufficiently validated.

From a laboratory standpoint, NfL interpretation requires age-adjusted reference ranges, strict standardization of sample handling, and awareness of inter-assay variability [,]. NfL lacks disease specificity, as levels rise across a broad range of neurological disorders, and should therefore be interpreted in the context of clinical phenotype, neuroimaging findings, and complementary laboratory biomarkers.

Traditional CSF parameters—pleocytosis, elevated protein, and oligoclonal bands—remain important indicators of central nervous system (CNS) inflammation but lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity for early diagnosis. A subset of patients with AE may present with entirely normal CSF findings in the early disease phase.

Cytokine and chemokine profiling has been explored as a means of characterizing intrathecal inflammation. A systematic review of 83 studies found overlapping cytokine/chemokine patterns across neuroinflammatory syndromes, with some trends—B-cell-related markers such as CXCL13 and B-cell activating factor (BAFF) predominantly elevated in autoantibody-associated disorders, and interferon-γ mainly in viral encephalitis—but no disease-specific signature or validated cutoff []. A 2026 cross-sectional study of 43 patients with AE (29 seronegative) reported higher CSF CXCL10, CXCL13, IL-6, IL-13, and other cytokines than in 34 controls, with comparable profiles in seronegative and antibody-positive disease []. However, the control group comprised 33 patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and only one patient with viral encephalitis; the study therefore cannot establish discrimination of AE from infectious encephalitis, and its authors presented the findings as exploratory []. In a 2026 prospective multicenter cohort that included varicella-zoster virus encephalitis controls, cytokines showed limited diagnostic or prognostic utility []. CSF cytokine and chemokine profiles should therefore be regarded as investigational markers of intrathecal immune activation that lack standardized platforms, validated cutoffs, and adequate infectious-disease comparator data, rather than as diagnostic discriminators.

Intrathecal kappa free light chain (KFLC) synthesis, assessed in paired CSF–serum samples, has emerged as a sensitive adjunctive marker of intrathecal humoral activity. In the 2026 prospective cohort described above, intrathecal KFLC synthesis was detected in 94% of patients with anti-NMDAR, 50% with anti-LGI1, and 53% with anti-CASPR2 encephalitis, exceeding the sensitivity of CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands or pleocytosis; specificity was moderate (44%) against pooled control groups that included multiple sclerosis and viral encephalitis, but reached 90% against non-inflammatory neurological controls []. KFLC therefore supports, but does not establish, an inflammatory context and cannot by itself discriminate AE from other inflammatory or infectious CNS disorders.

Complement activation has been investigated as a potential marker of humoral immune activity in antibody-mediated neurological disease; however, its pathogenic role appears disease-specific. In anti-NMDAR encephalitis, brain analyses did not support a major complement-mediated mechanism, arguing against broad clinical utility of complement markers in this specific disorder []. Soluble GFAP, a marker of astrocytic injury measurable by Simoa, has also been studied in AE. In a cohort of 42 patients (31 with active and 11 with stable disease), CSF GFAP correlated with the albumin quotient (r = 0.59) and IgG quotient (r = 0.55) and weakly with CSF cell count (r = 0.29); serum NfL (r = 0.41) and serum GFAP (r = 0.30) correlated with the Clinical Assessment Scale in Autoimmune Encephalitis, and the serum NfL/GFAP ratio was higher in active than in stable AE, whereas CSF GFAP and NfL did not differ according to epileptic activity or inflammatory MRI lesions []. GFAP showed limited diagnostic or prognostic utility in the larger 2026 prospective cohort [], so soluble GFAP should be regarded as an emerging, not yet validated marker. It must be distinguished from GFAP-IgG, which remains the defining biomarker of autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy [,]. Emerging markers such as YKL-40 (chitinase-3-like protein 1) reflect microglial and astrocytic activation and have been associated with disease remission in AE, but require further prospective validation [].

The greatest diagnostic value of fluid biomarkers lies in their integration with autoantibody testing, neuroimaging, and clinical phenotype. Combined biomarker approaches may: (1) support an inflammatory or neuroaxonal-injury context in antibody-negative cases with high clinical suspicion; and (2) provide adjunctive information on disease activity. The use of NfL, GFAP, or other fluid biomarkers to guide treatment intensity, monitor treatment response, or detect early relapse in AE has not yet been validated and should currently be confined to research settings. Future diagnostic strategies will increasingly rely on multimarker panels rather than single biomarkers, necessitating assay standardization, age-adjusted reference ranges, and prospective validation in larger cohorts.  summarizes, for each biomarker, the sample type, intended use, and analytical availability separately from clinical validation status; apart from conventional CSF parameters, GFAP-IgG, and NfL as a marker of neuroaxonal injury, the listed markers should be regarded as investigational in AE.

Recent advances in high-throughput technologies have enabled the application of multi-omics approaches—including proteomics, transcriptomics, and immune repertoire sequencing—to the study of AE and PNS. These methods provide an unbiased framework for identifying molecular signatures associated with neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and tumor-driven immune responses.

PhIP-Seq, described in , is the most advanced example of such discovery-oriented profiling in AE/PNS [,]. Like other multi-omics methods, it remains a research tool: findings are typically derived from small, highly selected referral cohorts, require orthogonal confirmation, and have not been evaluated prospectively for diagnostic yield in unselected patients.

From a laboratory perspective, proteomic, transcriptomic, and immune-repertoire analyses are hypothesis-generating tools for studying antigen-driven B- and T-cell responses [] and may eventually help characterize seronegative cases. Their clinical relevance to AE/PNS diagnostics, however, is not established: analytical validity (reproducibility, batch effects, and sensitivity to pre-analytical conditions) is rarely reported, cohorts are small and selected, the number of measured features greatly exceeds the number of patients—creating a high risk of overfitting—and no multi-omics signature has been validated prospectively.

AI-based analytical models have recently been proposed to integrate heterogeneous data sources, including clinical features, neuroimaging, CSF parameters, and serological findings. A single retrospective two-center study developed an AI multiclass model that classified the etiology of meningitis and encephalitis (autoimmune, bacterial, viral, and tuberculous) from clinical and laboratory variables available within 24 h of admission; in an external validation cohort of 220 patients, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.916 and outperformed three clinicians in that study []. This estimate derives from one retrospective dataset, in which the etiological reference standard was itself based on CSF laboratory results, and has not been confirmed prospectively or in other populations. Separately, MRI-based machine learning approaches have been explored for predicting antibody serostatus in suspected AE []. However, most studies remain retrospective, involve small and highly selected cohorts, are at risk of overfitting, and none has yet demonstrated an effect on diagnostic or patient outcomes. Prospective, multicenter validation and attention to model interpretability are essential before AI tools can be safely integrated into clinical workflows.

MRI abnormalities, including fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities, may occur in both AE and infectious encephalitis. These findings show considerable overlap and cannot, in isolation, reliably distinguish between the two conditions [,]. Electroencephalographic findings often support an autoimmune etiology when combined with appropriate clinical features [,]. Specific patterns—such as mesial temporal involvement, brainstem–diencephalic lesions, or longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions—may suggest particular antibody profiles and guide targeted testing. Radiologists can be among the first to suspect AE and trigger a comprehensive neuroimmunological workup.

18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (18F-FDG PET) demonstrates high sensitivity (pooled sensitivity ~87% in a systematic review and meta-analysis), frequently revealing characteristic metabolic patterns when MRI is normal or inconclusive [], and exhibits antibody-specific hypometabolic or hypermetabolic signatures [,]. PET can help differentiate AE from neurodegenerative dementias and support early immunotherapy initiation in patients with rapidly progressive cognitive decline and atypical MRI findings.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)—including anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, and anti-CTLA-4 agents—have revolutionized cancer treatment but can trigger a broad spectrum of neurological adverse events (NAEs) that closely resemble classic PNS. The incidence of neurological immune-related adverse events (irAEs) has been reported between approximately 1% and 12%, depending on the agent, combination regimen, ascertainment method, and definition used; severe (grade ≥ 3) events are uncommon and generally occur in fewer than 1% of treated patients [,,].

The clinical spectrum of ICI-related neurotoxicity encompasses myasthenia gravis, myositis, encephalitis, peripheral neuropathies, meningitis, and myelitis. A particularly important overlap syndrome is the triad of myocarditis, myasthenia gravis, and myositis (the “3M syndrome”), which carries high mortality and requires urgent recognition []. Encephalitis occurring after ICI therapy may present with or without detectable neural antibodies. Some patients harbor classical paraneoplastic antibodies (e.g., Hu, Ma2), which may have been unmasked by immune checkpoint blockade, while others have novel or unidentified antibody specificities.

From a laboratory diagnostic perspective, ICI-related NAEs pose unique challenges. The 2021 PNS-Care criteria include specific recommendations for ICI-triggered syndromes, acknowledging that a substantial proportion of cases remain seronegative despite comprehensive antibody screening [,]. NfL has emerged as a promising, but still insufficiently validated, biomarker in this context. Elevated NfL may reflect neuroaxonal injury in cancer patients with acute neurological complications, including PNS and ICI-related neurotoxicity, while longitudinal NfL monitoring could potentially assist in assessing recovery and treatment response [,].

Management of the neurological immune-related adverse event should be distinguished from management of the underlying malignancy. For the adverse event itself, management is graded by severity: ICI therapy is usually withheld temporarily for moderate events, with possible resumption after resolution, whereas permanent discontinuation is generally advised for severe (grade 3–4) events and for specific syndromes such as myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, or transverse myelitis; corticosteroids are first-line treatment, with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange in severe or refractory cases [,]. Decisions on rechallenge and on further cancer treatment are made within multidisciplinary neuro-oncological care, in which oncological treatment remains an integral component [,,]. The distinction between ICI-triggered PNS (where tumor immunotherapy unmasks pre-existing antitumor immunity) and direct ICI neurotoxicity has important prognostic and therapeutic implications. Early clinical recognition supported by appropriate laboratory testing is critical, whereas the value of systematic biomarker-based surveillance in patients receiving ICIs has not yet been established.

Substantial inter-laboratory variability exists in assay platforms, antigen constructs, cutoffs, and reporting standards for neural autoantibody testing. A recent European survey of laboratories performing PNS autoantibody detection confirmed considerable heterogeneity in assay execution, reporting, and quality control, and highlighted the need for laboratory-specific recommendations to harmonize practices and improve diagnostic quality []. External quality assurance programs and harmonization initiatives are essential to ensure reproducibility, particularly for cell-based assays where fixation, cell substrates, and cut-off definitions vary widely. Recent laboratory-medicine syntheses have reinforced the importance of appropriate patient selection, pre-analytical control, and integrated serum plus CSF testing pathways in reducing false-positive and false-negative results [].

In current practice, paired serum and CSF should be submitted for neural antibody testing in suspected AE, because some antibodies (e.g., LGI1 and CASPR2) are more sensitively detected in serum with commercially available assays, whereas others (e.g., NMDAR and GFAP) are more sensitively and specifically detected in CSF; serum-only NMDAR-IgG positivity with negative CSF is a recognized warning sign of a false-positive result [,]. Samples should ideally be collected in the acute phase and before immunotherapy, because plasma exchange or neonatal Fc receptor inhibitors may cause false-negative results and intravenous immunoglobulin may cause low-level false-positive results (e.g., GAD65), which can be clarified by repeat testing after 3–6 months []. Specimens should be refrigerated at approximately 4 °C for short-term storage or frozen at ≤−20 °C when testing is delayed, avoiding repeated freeze–thaw cycles []. Assay-specific pre-treatment should be documented by the laboratory; for example, some in-house live-cell CBAs heat-inactivate serum before testing (35 min at 56 °C in a clinically validated flow-cytometric AQP4-IgG assay), a step that inactivates complement [].

Cutoffs and titers are method-specific. CBAs and TBAs are usually reported qualitatively at a laboratory-defined screening dilution, which differs among laboratories—in a recent European Autoimmunity Standardisation Initiative (EASI) survey of 139 laboratories, only 61% were aligned on sample dilution []—and endpoint titration helps to interpret weak or isolated serum positivity (e.g., CASPR2 or MOG) []. For GAD65, only high concentrations support neurological autoimmunity, and thresholds differ by method (e.g., >20 nmol/L by radioimmunoassay versus >10,000 IU/mL in serum and >100 IU/mL in CSF by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay), whereas low concentrations occur in type 1 diabetes and in healthy individuals []. Isolated line-blot positivity for intracellular antibodies without corresponding TBA staining has a positive predictive value below 50% and should not be reported as diagnostic without confirmation []. Antibody titers correlate imperfectly with disease activity, so repeat testing for disease monitoring is not established, although CSF NMDAR titers relate more closely to outcome than serum titers [,].

Testing should be performed in accredited laboratories participating in external quality assessment (EQA); in the EASI survey, 46% (indirect immunofluorescence) and 42% (line/dot blot) of laboratories held ISO 15189 [] accreditation, and 43% participated in more than one EQA program []. In our view, a standardized report should state the specimen type, the methods used (TBA; fixed or live CBA; line blot; enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay or radioimmunoassay), the screening dilution or titer, the result of confirmatory testing, and an interpretive comment relating the result to the pretest probability, with recommendations for CSF or reference-laboratory confirmation where appropriate. Direct communication between laboratory specialists and clinicians—through interpretive comments, discussion of discordant results, and agreed reflex and send-out algorithms—remains the principal mechanism for correlating laboratory results with the clinical evaluation [,].

For emerging fluid biomarkers, harmonization is similarly critical. NfL quantification requires standardized pre-analytical protocols, certified reference materials, and age-adjusted reference intervals to enable meaningful cross-study and cross-center comparisons [,]. Cytokine profiling faces analogous challenges, with no consensus on optimal platforms, sample handling requirements, or clinically validated cutoff values.

Reference centers play an indispensable role in confirmatory testing, interpretation of rare antibodies, and access to experimental biomarkers and emerging techniques such as live neuron studies. Clinically, over-testing in low pretest probability settings risks incidental positives and inappropriate immunosuppression, whereas under-testing perpetuates diagnostic delay. Evidence-based diagnostic pathways that integrate pretest probability, staged testing, and clear triggers for immunotherapy are essential, alongside health-economic evaluations of advanced biomarker and imaging strategies.

Integrated panels combining autoantibodies, NfL, intrathecal KFLC synthesis, and other CSF markers with MRI/18F-FDG PET features may outperform single tests for early AE/PNS diagnosis and cancer-risk stratification, but this hypothesis requires prospective testing. Personalized diagnostic algorithms tailored to age, syndrome, and comorbidities can optimize test selection and timing and could be implemented as clinical decision-support tools in electronic health records.

Continued application of PhIP-Seq and other unbiased serological discovery methods will likely identify additional autoantibody targets, which, once confirmed by orthogonal assays and clinically validated, may further reduce the proportion of seronegative cases and refine risk stratification [,]. Point-of-care and rapid assay platforms for key biomarkers such as NfL may enable faster triage in acute settings.

The expanding use of ICIs in oncology demands dedicated biomarker surveillance programs and prospective registries to characterize the spectrum and predictors of neurological irAEs [,]. Development of predictive biomarkers for ICI-related neurotoxicity represents an unmet clinical need.

Prospective multicenter studies should validate biomarker thresholds, AI-based prediction models, and imaging-guided diagnostic pathways, with outcomes including time to diagnosis, treatment initiation, and long-term disability. Standardization of biomarker assays and harmonization of diagnostic algorithms across centers will be critical for translating these advances into routine clinical practice. These efforts will underpin the transition toward precision neuroimmunology.

Early, accurate diagnosis of autoimmune and paraneoplastic neurological disorders is critical to prevent irreversible neurological disability and enable timely tumor detection. The 2021 PNS-Care criteria provide an objective framework for diagnostic certainty; their high sensitivity and specificity for combined definite and probable diagnoses were demonstrated in a retrospective, selected single-center cohort and require confirmation in unselected populations [,]. Phenotype-driven autoantibody testing using combined TBA–CBA strategies, complemented by NfL as a marker of neuroaxonal injury, conventional CSF inflammatory parameters, intrathecal KFLC synthesis, and MRI/18F-FDG PET, provides the current diagnostic platform for earlier recognition, whereas cytokine profiles, soluble GFAP, and prognostic use of NfL remain investigational.

Novel autoantibody discovery through PhIP-Seq has expanded the recognized antigen repertoire, resolving a subset of previously seronegative cases [,,], while early AI-assisted models, so far evaluated only retrospectively, may in future help integrate complex multimodal data [,]. The growing recognition of ICI-related neurological syndromes as a distinct clinical entity demands heightened clinical vigilance and appropriate laboratory testing in oncology settings.

Crucially, the impact of every one of these advances is realized only through the discipline of laboratory medicine: the diagnostic value of neural antibodies, NfL, CSF inflammatory markers, and emerging multi-omics or AI-derived signatures depends on appropriate test selection guided by pretest probability, dual-method analytical confirmation, and interpretation within the clinical context rather than on test availability alone [,]. Failure to apply this framework—particularly reliance on single-method serum testing in low-probability patients—generates false-positive results that drive misdiagnosis and inappropriate immunosuppression, underscoring that a staged, phenotype-driven laboratory strategy is the principal safeguard of diagnostic accuracy []. Positioning AE and PNS diagnostics squarely within laboratory medicine—rather than treating biomarkers as isolated clinical add-ons—is, in our view, the most actionable lever for earlier and more reliable recognition.

Ultimately, the integration of multimodal biomarkers into clinically applicable, harmonized algorithms—supported by reference center networks and prospective validation studies—will be essential to achieve precision diagnostics in neuroimmunology and translate these advances into equitable, routine clinical care.

neuroscience.title: In Vitro Generation of Neural Cells with Regenerative Potential from Seabream Radial Glial Stem Cells: A Preliminary Study
neuroscience.abstract: This study establishes an in vitro primary neuroglial culture system from Sparus aurata to model radial glia-mediated neurogenesis, demonstrating the capacity of radial glia to function as multipotent neural stem cells that drive neuronal differentiation and migration. Characterized through immunophenotypic profiling and time-lapse imaging, this cell culture model reveals active, continuous neurogenesis within proliferative UCHL1-positive central zones of radial glial colonies, effectively recapitulating the cellular plasticity observed in the in vivo teleost brain. Immunocytochemical analysis confirmed the establishment of a stable, highly viable primary in vitro neuroglial system. This central nervous system (CNS) model outlines the morphological and immunophenotypic profile of neuronal differentiation observed over gilthead seabream long-term culture. Overall, this standardized in vitro central nervous system (CNS) model provides a reliable experimental framework for future hypothesis-driven studies on teleost neurogenesis, functional CNS repair, neuropathological modeling, pharmacotoxicological screening, and neural tissue engineering.
neuroscience.text:
It was long believed that neurons and glial cells in the central nervous system arose from separate precursor populations that diverged early in development. This view stemmed in part from observations that neurogenesis and gliogenesis occur at different developmental stages, with neuronal production thought to end around the perinatal period. Previous studies indicate that, unlike mammals, teleost fish retain the vast majority of their radial glia (RG) throughout life, as observed in most freshwater species such as the Oncorhynchus mykiss []. Teleost RG display a characteristic morphology with somata predominantly localized in the periventricular zone. In species like the rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), this spatial architecture supports the persistent neurogenesis and indeterminate brain growth typical of teleosts []. Whereas mammalian RG differentiate into astrocytes during development, rendering astrocytes the predominant mature glial population [], the teleost brain maintains an extensive adult RG network []. For instance, in the hindbrain and spinal cord of the rainbow trout, the predominant cell population consists of GFAP-immunoreactive RG whose somata form a pseudostratified periventricular epithelium, giving rise to long radial processes that extend to the subpial surface and terminate in intensely immunostained endfeet []. This radial glial morphology is consistent with earlier descriptions in Cyprinus carpio [,]. Functionally, adult RG guide young migrating neurons from proliferative niches to their destinations, as demonstrated in Apteronotus leptorhynchus [], and undergo asymmetric cell division to self-renew while generating neuronal progeny []. Consequently, the persistence of adult RG is strongly linked to continuous neurogenesis and robust regenerative capacity []. Although adult CNS neurogenesis occurs within dedicated niches across vertebrates, its efficiency varies widely [,,]. Contrary to mammals, which possess limited regenerative scope, teleosts and amphibians reconstruct extensive CNS regions by enhancing neurogenesis and progenitor transdifferentiation [,,]. However, the specific mechanisms governing RG-driven neurogenesis in marine species remain to be fully elucidated.

As vertebrates, zebrafish (Danio rerio) share extensive genetic and functional homology with humans, underscoring teleost models valuable for elucidating human neurobiological mechanisms []. In adult zebrafish, the premier in vivo fish model, brain lesions or complete spinal cord transection trigger robust neuroregeneration that functional motor recovery ensues. This repair is driven by resident neural stem cells (NSCs), multipotent radial glial progenitors capable of long-term self-renewal and differentiation into both neurons and glia []. Upon injury, these constitutive stem cells reactivate essential developmental signaling pathways to sustain ongoing neurogenesis. Conversely, mammalian CNS injuries exhibit restricted neurogenesis and insufficient axonal regrowth, failing to achieve complete functional repair [].

In teleost models, adult neural stem progenitor cells (aNSPCs) persist lifelong, residing in various stem cell niches within the brain and spinal cord. Advanced studies have examined how various stimuli, such as neurotrauma, act on distinct populations of stem and progenitor cells, altering their cell cycle activity through the activation of normally quiescent aNSPCs or the modulation of niche-specific constitutive cell cycle rhythms []. The study of teleost neural stem progenitor cells (NSPCs) provides fundamental insights into the organization, differentiation, and proliferative dynamics of adult neurogenic niches []. Across various fish species, neural cell generation occurs throughout the lifespan []. Widespread proliferation zones across all subdivisions of the adult teleost rostrocaudal axis indicate ongoing adult neurogenesis in these brain regions [,]. For instance, adult zebrafish exhibit an extraordinary capacity for widespread neurogenesis throughout the central nervous system (CNS), with active proliferation zones located in the telencephalon, diencephalon, midbrain, cerebellum, and spinal cord [,]. In an in-depth study on zebrafish, Grandel et al. [] identified approximately 16 distinct neurogenic niches along the ventricular surface, which harbor both self-renewing stem cell populations and mobile pools of neuronal precursors. Notably, Kaslin et al. [] demonstrated that the adult zebrafish cerebellum contains bipotent radial glia-like stem cells capable of generating both neurons and glia for tissue homeostasis and repair. Following traumatic injury, radial glial cells act as neural stem cells by proliferating and giving rise to differentiated neurons that seamlessly integrate into pre-existing circuits. This extensive neurogenic capacity establishes the zebrafish as a premier model for studying neural repair, structural plasticity, and regenerative medicine []. Expanding our understanding of the niche-specific proliferative dynamics of adult neural stem and progenitor cells (aNSPCs) requires detailed investigation into the surrounding microenvironment and extracellular matrix components [,], which promises valuable insights for neural tissue repair []. A recent review by Caron et al. [] underscores that adult zebrafish preserve lifelong developmental stem cell populations, including continuously dividing neuroepithelial cells (NECs) and quiescent or cycling radial glial cells (RGCs) []. Within stem cell niches, RGCs exist predominantly in quiescent or actively cycling states, whereas NECs undergo continuous proliferation []. Characterization of aNSPC kinetics in zebrafish typically relies on exogenous S-phase markers, such as the thymidine analogues BrdU and EdU [], or the endogenous cell-cycle marker PCNA [,]. However, these approaches have rarely been applied to in vitro culture systems designed to mimic the native neurogenesis.

The scarcity of validated in vitro neural systems for Mediterranean teleosts has long constrained mechanistic research in marine neurotoxicity and neuropathology, necessitating reliance on whole-animal in vivo exposures or short-lived ex vivo brain slices. Consequently, despite the well-documented neurogenic potential and structural plasticity of the adult teleost brain, the cellular behaviors, morphological organization, and stem cell properties of radial glia-derived lineages in the gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata) remain poorly characterized under cell culture conditions.

Therefore, this study aimed to investigate radial glia-derived neurogenesis in a primary neuroglial cell culture model established from the brain of the teleost gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata). Although the freshwater zebrafish (Danio rerio) remains the benchmark teleost model for in vivo neuro-repair, its minimal brain mass severely constrains primary cell yields, presenting substantial technical limitations for complex downstream in vitro mechanistic assays. Conversely, the larger tissue biomass harvested per S. aurata brain facilitates the recovery of highly viable primary neuroglial suspensions that maintain structural and functional stability in long-term culture [,]. Despite these practical advantages, the specific neurogenic dynamics of S. aurata radial glia remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we systematically evaluated neural stem and progenitor cell (NSPC) dynamics, radial glial subpopulations, proliferative niche organization, and nuclear kinetics during neuroblast locomotion along elongated glial scaffolding. This reproducible primary culture system provides a robust experimental framework for comparative neurobiology, CNS repair modeling, and neurotoxicological research.

Juvenile gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata) with a mean body weight of 35 ± 5 g (n = 50) were obtained from a commercial hatchery (Panittica Pugliese, Brindisi, Italy). Fish were transported to the cell culture laboratory at the Department of Veterinary Medicine, University of Bari (Italy), in two 60-L oxygenated transport tanks filled with natural seawater (O2 at 10 mg/L, 37.5‰ salinity, 18 °C) at a density of 10 kg/m3. Upon arrival, fish were deeply anesthetized by immersion in seawater containing 0.02% (200 mg/L) 3-aminobenzoic acid ethyl ester (MS-222; Sigma-Aldrich, Milan, Italy). Anesthetized individuals were processed sequentially, wiped with 70% ethanol, and euthanized via spinal transection followed by decapitation. Only healthy individuals, as confirmed by anatomopathological examination, were selected for tissue sampling. Whole-brain tissues (~0.1–0.2 g/brain) were aseptically excised, pooled, and collected in sterile, pre-cooled Ca2+ and Mg2+ free Hank’s Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS; Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 10 mM HEPES, 0.5 mM EDTA, 25 mM NaHCO3, 200 IU/mL penicillin, 200 µg/mL streptomycin, 200 µg/mL amphotericin B, and 100 µg/mL gentamicin (Washing Solution, WS). Unless otherwise specified, all reagents and chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Milan, Italy).

Phosphate buffered Saline 100 mM (PBS 10×, pH 7.4, autoclaved, 14.2 g/L Na2HPO4, 80.5 g/L NaCl, 2 g/L KCl), 1× PBS for cold washes and for the preparation of enzyme and antibiotic mixtures.

Hepes solution (pH 7–7.6, sterile filtered with Stericup 0.2 μm filter unit 500; Millipore, cat. no. SCGVU02RE,1 M-H0887, Sigma-Aldrich).

Washing buffer (pH 7–7.4, sterile cup filtered, HBSS; Sigma-Aldrich 250 mL/10 mM HEPES/0.5 mM EDTA/25 mM NaHCO3/2X antibiotic–antimycotic solution).

Digestion Medium (DM) (pH 7.2–7.4, sterilized by 0.22-µm filter unit, Leibovitz’s L-15 supplemented with 7 mM CaCl2/10 mM HEPES/25 mM NaHCO3/1× antibiotic–antimycotic solution).

Basal Medium (BM) (pH 7.2, sterilized by 0.22-µm filter unit, Leibovitz’s L-15 supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine/10% FBS/1× antibiotic–antimycotic solution/1 mM sodium pyruvate/5 mM D-glucose/10 mM HEPES/12 mM NaHCO3/0.05% ITS+ (insulin/transferrin/sodium selenite/oleic acid/linoleic acid/BSA)/0.01 mM MEM non-essential amino acids/0.01 mM MEM vitamin mix/0.1 mM ascorbic acid/20 mM NaCl.

Enriched Differentiation Medium (pH 7.2, sterilized by 0.22-µm filter unit, L-15 BM supplemented with 10 ng/mL epidermal growth factor (EGF)/0.2 µg/mL hydrocortisone/10 mM glucose/10 µg/mL insulin/4 mM L-glutamine.

Primary neuroglial cultures were isolated from freshly excised brains under a vertical laminar flow microbiology safety hood, according to a recently developed method []. Briefly, cerebral hemispheres were excised using sterile surgical blades and scissors, and carefully cleared of meninges and blood vessels. After three washes with equal volumes of WS, brains were mechanically disrupted by pressing with a glass pestle through a 380-µm stainless-steel mesh filter. The resulting cell suspension was filtered and collected in enzyme-free Digestion Medium (DM), consisting of Leibovitz’s L-15 medium supplemented with 7 mM CaCl2, 200 IU/mL penicillin, 200 µg/mL streptomycin, 200 µg/mL amphotericin B, 100 µg/mL gentamicin, 10 mM HEPES, and 25 mM NaHCO3.

Enzymatic dissociation was performed by adding an enzyme cocktail containing 0.05% collagenase Type IV, 0.03% hyaluronidase Type IV-S, 0.3% dispase Type II, and 0.03% DNase Type I to the homogenate in DM for 20 min at 20 °C. Digestion was terminated by adding Leibovitz’s L-15 medium supplemented with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS; BioWhittaker, Lonza Walkersville Inc., Walkersville, MD, USA) to inhibit enzymatic activity. The mixture was sequentially filtered through 104-µm and 60-µm stainless-steel filters, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was resuspended in cold 1× phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) containing 5% fetal calf serum (FCS), followed by two centrifugations at 150× g for 10 min at 4 °C. The white cell pellet was recovered and incubated with 0.45 µg/mL DNase I in cold PBS; cell clumps were dissociated by gentle pipetting with a Pasteur pipette, followed by centrifugation at 70× g for 5 min at 4 °C. The final pellet was resuspended in L-15 medium containing 10% FBS and subjected to isopycnic separation via density gradient centrifugation to purify viable neuroglial cells from myelin debris, cellular fragments, and lighter, lipid-rich oligodendrocytes. The cell suspension, diluted 1:1 (v/v) with Leibovitz’s L-15 medium, was layered dropwise and gently onto a double density gradient (1:2 v/v cell suspension:Percoll) consisting of 15% and 60% Percoll (2:1 v/v) in 10× PBS. The 50 mL Falcon tubes containing the double gradient were prepared prior to isolation and maintained at 4 °C until use. Centrifugation was performed at 150× g (1400 rpm) for 10 min at 4 °C. Following centrifugation, a clear stratification of cell bands was visible: viable cells concentrated at the lower interface (forming a distinct white ring), whereas myelin debris and lighter, lipid-rich oligodendrocytes floated in the upper layers and were removed by aspiration. Using a fine-tipped Pasteur pipette, the white ring of viable cells was carefully collected, taking care to avoid the underlying erythrocyte pellet. The recovered cell suspension was washed in cold 1× PBS via two sequential centrifugation steps at 70× g (788 rpm) for 5 min at 4 °C. Finally, the cell pellet was resuspended in 3 mL of Leibovitz’s L-15 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, and the resulting suspension was subjected to cell counting. Cell viability was assessed via trypan blue exclusion. Brain tissue processing yielded 5.2 × 107 viable cells/g tissue weight, with a mean viability of 92.8 ± 0.06%.

The purified neuroglial cell suspension was adjusted to a density of 1 × 106 cells/mL in Basal Medium (BM), consisting of Leibovitz’s L-15 supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 10% FBS, 100 IU/mL penicillin, 100 µg/mL streptomycin, 100 µg/mL amphotericin B, 50 µg/mL gentamicin, 1 mM sodium pyruvate, 5 mM D-glucose, 10 mM HEPES, 12 mM NaHCO3, 0.05% ITS+ (insulin/transferrin/sodium selenite/oleic acid/linoleic acid/BSA), 0.01 mM MEM non-essential amino acids (MEM-NEAA; BioWhittaker), 0.01 mM MEM vitamin mix (BioWhittaker), and 0.1 mM ascorbic acid. BM osmolality was adjusted to seabream serum osmolarity (369 mOsm/L) by adding 20 mM NaCl as reported by other authors [,,].

Cells were seeded at a density of 3 × 104 cells/cm2 onto 0.01% collagen type I-coated substrates. For morphological characterization via phase-contrast microscopy, cells were seeded into 25-cm2 Falcon Primaria™ culture flasks (T25 flasks); for immunophenotyping via immunofluorescence, cells were seeded onto 12-well plates (Falcon, BD Biosciences; Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). Cells were allowed to adhere for 12 h prior to replacing the culture medium with fresh BM, which was subsequently refreshed every 48 h. Cultures were maintained in a refrigerated incubator in a humidified atmosphere (97% air/3% CO2) at 18 °C (CO2-170 Innova; New Brunswick Scientific, PBI, Milan, Italy). During the second week of culture, to purify the neuroglial culture, microglia and oligodendrocytes were detached by shaking the T25 flasks on an orbital shaker. The initial agitation step was performed at 100 rpm for 1 h to detach microglia, which were subsequently discarded along with the supernatant. Following a brief wash with cold 1× PBS and the addition of fresh basal medium (BM), the T25 flasks underwent a second agitation step at 240 rpm for 6 h to release and remove oligodendrocytes. After a final wash with cold 1× PBS and the addition of Leibovitz’s L-15 Enriched Differentiation Medium (EDM), a purified layer of astrocytes and neurons remained adhered to the vessel surface. The absence of MBP (myelin basic protein) immunoreactivity confirmed that the resulting cell culture was devoid of oligodendrocytes.

Confluent monolayers were obtained after approximately 3–4 weeks. To establish neuroglial cell enriched cultures, cells were shifted after the 1 week to L-15 EDM, consisting of L-15 BM supplemented with 0.01 µg/mL epidermal growth factor (EGF), 0.2 µg/mL hydrocortisone, 10 mM glucose, 10 µg/mL insulin, and 4 mM L-glutamine. Adherent cells were monitored daily, and phase-contrast images were captured using a CCD camera mounted on a Motic AE31 inverted epi-fluorescence microscope (Motic, Milan, Italy). Given the low cellular yield per animal (0.1–0.2 g of brain tissue) and the laborious isolation procedure, brain tissue from all 50 animals was pooled into a single large-scale preparation to ensure a homogeneous cell population across all experimental groups. To ensure reproducibility, five independent seeding sessions were performed using T-25 flasks and ten sessions using 12-well plates (with six wells analyzed per antibody test). For each well, five microscopic fields were randomly selected and quantified. T-25 cultures were used to evaluate growth over time (up to 2 months) and for time-lapse imaging. Overall, a minimum of three independent tissue isolation procedures were conducted.

For indirect immunofluorescence, primary antibodies were diluted in PBS containing 3% BSA as follows: mouse anti-glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) monoclonal antibody (mAb) (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# G3893, clone G-A-5; 1:500); rabbit anti-ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1) polyclonal antibody (pAb) (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# HPA005993; 1:1000); mouse anti-vimentin mAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# V5255, clone VIM-13.2; 1:200); rabbit anti-neurofilament 200 (NF200) pAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# N4142; 1:200); rabbit anti-microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2) mAb (Abcam, Cat# ab183830; 1:1000); mouse anti-neuronal nuclei (NeuN) mAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# MAB377, clone A60; 1:100); rabbit anti-CD44 pAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# HPA005785; 1:1000); rabbit anti-myelin basic protein (MBP) pAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# M3821; 1:200); and mouse anti-nestin mAb (Abcam, Cat# ab22035, clone 10C2; 1:250). Secondary antibodies were diluted in PBS containing 3% BSA and applied for 45 min at room temperature (RT) as follows: TRITC-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# T7028; 1:50); FITC-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# F6005; 1:50); FITC-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# F0257; 1:50); and FITC-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# F9887; 1:50). For direct immunofluorescence, the following fluorochrome-conjugated primary antibodies were diluted in PBS/3% BSA and applied: FITC-conjugated mouse anti ß-III-tubulin mAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# F2043, clone Tub 2.1; 1:100) and FITC-conjugated mouse anti-proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) mAb (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# F0167, clone PC10; 1:100).

Brightfield and fluorescence imaging were performed using a Motic AE31 epi-fluorescent inverted microscope equipped with a DAPI/TRITC/FITC filter set (DAPI/Hoechst set: excitation D350/50×, emission D460/50m; FITC/RSGFP/Fluo-3/DiO/Acridine Orange set: excitation D480/30×, emission D535/40m; TRITC/DiI/Cy3 set: excitation D540/25×, emission D605/55m). Digital images were captured using a Moticam 3000C cooled CCD digital color camera (3.3 Megapixel, 1/2” CCD) controlled by Live Cam 1.0 and Motic Images Advanced (v3.2) acquisition software (Motic, Seneco, Milan, Italy). Image analysis, processing, and multi-channel overlay/merging were performed using Motic Images Advanced (v3.2) and Adobe Photoshop 8.0 (Adobe Systems Inc., San Jose, CA, USA). The images shown are representative of the consistent phenotypes observed across all 446 analyzed wells and microscopic fields.

For indirect immunofluorescence, cells were rinsed three times with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS for 15 min at room temperature (RT), washed twice with PBS, and permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min at RT. Following three 5-min washes with PBS, non-specific binding sites were blocked by incubating cells in PBS containing 3% BSA (blocking buffer) for 30 min at RT. Cells were then incubated with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer for 60 min at RT. After three washes with PBS, cells were incubated with the corresponding fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies for 60 min at RT in the dark. Following three additional PBS washes, cell nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; 1.5 µg/mL) for 10 min at RT. To mitigate photobleaching, stained cells were mounted in an antifade mounting medium composed of 90% glycerol and 100 mg/mL 1,4-diazabicyclo [2.2.2]octane (DABCO) in PBS, which was applied directly to the wells prior to microscopic examination. Negative controls were processed following the exact same protocol, omitting the primary antibody incubation step.

Live-cell imaging was used to evaluate the cellular dynamics of Sparus aurata neuroglial cultures in 2D. Cells were seeded at a density of 3 × 104 cells/cm2 onto 0.01% collagen type I-coated 25-cm2 Falcon Primaria™ culture flasks with plug-seal caps (T-25 Falcon Primaria™, BD Biosciences; Sismed s.r.l., Bari, Italy) containing Leibovitz’s L-15 BM. To permit gas exchange, flasks were incubated with slightly loosened caps at 18 °C in a refrigerated incubator with a humidified atmosphere of 97% air/3% CO2 (CO2-170 Innova, New Brunswick Scientific, PBI, Milan, Italy). On day 10 of culture, flasks were tightly closed, sealed with Parafilm, and incu-bated overnight at 18 °C under CO2 free conditions in a temperature-controlled chamber. Leibovitz’s L-15 medium is specifically formulated for CO2 free or low CO2 systems via phosphate and amino acid-based buffering system rather than a sodium bicarbonate system, rendering it suitable for cultures where CO2 usage is temporarily restricted. Live imaging of cell dynamics was then monitored over a 12-h period. The imaging system comprised a Motic AE31 epi-fluorescent inverted microscope equipped with a Moticam 3000C Cooled CCD digital color camera (3.3 Megapixel, 1/2″ CCD), controlled by Motic Images Advanced (v. 3.2) acquisition software with Live Cam 1.0 (32-bit) (Motic, Seneco, Milan, Italy). The T-25 flask was secured under a 20× objective within the temperature-controlled chamber maintained at 18 °C. Time-lapse images were automatically captured every 15 min for 12 h. Image processing and video sequence assembly were performed using Motic Images Advanced (v3.2).

The migration trajectory of individual cells was automatically tracked over time at 15-min intervals. Cells were classified as undergoing radial migration if the angle be-tween their primary vector of displacement and the radial glial scaffold was between 0° and 30°. Conversely, cells were classified as undergoing tangential migration if their trajectory was orthogonal to the glial scaffold, maintaining an angle between 60° and 90° relative to the radial axis, while exhibiting a characteristic multipolar or branched morphology.

Mitotic somal translocation (MST), a specialized dynamic behavior of cycling radial glial progenitor cells, was distinguished from standard interphase somal translocation based on the criteria established by Wang et al. [] and Ostrem et al. []. MST was defined as a rapid, directed soma translocation along the primary basal process covering a distance >20 µm (approximately one cell diameter) at a velocity of >20 µm/h within a short time window (<60 min) immediately preceding cytokinesis. This translocation event culminated in cell rounding, apical-to-basal nuclear displacement, and horizontal cleavage division.

Firstly, we evaluated the development and differentiation of neuronal lineages from radial glial stem cells (RGSCs) in gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata) primary cultures using direct and inverted phase-contrast microscopy. Morphological analysis revealed that 24 h after plating, freshly isolated neural stem cells (NSCs) displayed a distinctive ovoid shape (A).
