By day 2, early elongated, adherent RG stem progenitors (RGSPs) exhibited initial proliferative activity along their cellular extensions (B,C,E,F,J). As shown in  and , phase-contrast microscopy of Sparus aurata RGSPs identified the emergence sites of initial polar protrusions within the first few days in vitro. Over the first 2 weeks of culture, microscopic examination confirmed three distinct cell populations: radial glia stem progenitors (RGSPs), which formed clusters with high proliferative capacity and an irregular, polygonal morphology (B,C,E); neural stem cells (NSCs), characterized by an ovoid shape at day 1 that progressed to a bipolar or tripolar elongated morphology from day 2 (D,I) to day 6 (A,B); and neural progenitor cells (NPCs), which committed to neuronal lineages without generating glia (F–H).

Representative images of newly formed and actively dividing RGSP colonies are presented in A,B,D and . Within 1 week of plating, radial progenitor cells extended their processes radially around the colony periphery, acquiring the characteristic morphology of mature RG cells (D and A). High-magnification microscopic analysis of these multipotent RGSP colonies revealed prominent growth cones at the emergence sites of radial processes, representing the early stages of glial fiber development (C,C’). As RG progenitors initiated process extension, they formed basal cones that generated long, directional processes while simultaneously emitting small lateral extensions for substrate attachment and intercellular interaction (B). Within the colony, these early basal cells (bRGCs) divided rapidly to form clusters of newly generated post-mitotic cells, establishing distinct microenvironments that function as actively proliferating stem cell niches (D and A–C).

During the proliferation of basal radial glial (bRG) cells via symmetric division, which expands the parental progenitor pool, the nucleus of the newly generated daughter cell distal to the basal origin is displaced longitudinally into the growing apical extension (D, yellow dashed outline). The basal portion of the glial cone subsequently extends via an elongated process toward the distal tip, giving rise to new RG progenitors (D–F). Conversely, during asymmetric division, the daughter cell distal to the proliferating base is smaller and becomes basally displaced relative to the mother cell, subsequently giving rise to a neuroblast during neurogenesis (F).

During the early stages of in vitro neurogenesis, radial glial progenitor cells (RGPs) undergo asymmetric divisions to generate a new apical progenitor alongside a basal progenitor, with the latter driving expansion of the radial colony (D). Most basal progenitor divisions are vertically oriented relative to the colony axis, thereby promoting self-renewal. Cleavage plane alignment demonstrates that vertical cleavage planes typically result in symmetric division, whereas horizontal or oblique cleavage planes frequently trigger asymmetric division, likely due to the unequal inheritance of polarized apical and basal cellular components. The transition from a proliferative to a neurogenic state gives rise to the primary parental progenitors that initiate neurogenesis: radial glial stem cells (RGSCs). Notably, the division patterns of RGP cells shift predictably across distinct culture stages.

Specifically, symmetric proliferative division predominates during early development, wherein RGP cells divide symmetrically to yield two identical daughter cells, thereby expanding the initial progenitor pool ( and ). Asymmetric neurogenic division becomes prevalent during intermediate differentiation stages; during this phase, one daughter cell retains RGP identity to maintain the progenitor pool, while the other differentiates into a committed neuron or an intermediate progenitor cell (IPC) (D). Finally, late stage development is characterized by symmetric gliogenic division, a terminal symmetric division in which both daughter cells commit to glial lineages, such as astrocytes, ultimately depleting the progenitor pool.

Neural stem cell (NSC) division utilizes tightly regulated mitotic mechanisms to maintain the long-term progenitor pool through three distinct pathways. Symmetric self-renewal involves an NSC dividing into two identical multipotent NSCs to expand or replenish the stem cell reservoir (D,I and D). Asymmetric self-renewal occurs when an NSC yields one self-renewing NSC and one committed progenitor cell, a process that operates continuously within mature neurogenic niches. Alternatively, this division mode can directly generate small neural progenitor cells along the soma or within bipolar and tripolar processes (). When basal radial glial cells (bRGCs) proliferate via symmetric division, the nucleus of the daughter cell distal to the basal origin translocates immediately following mitosis. This longitudinal displacement propels the nucleus into the growing distal extension (D).

This longitudinal displacement occurs during the expansion of the parental progenitor pool; these frequent symmetric divisions within the bRGC colony are demarcated by yellow dashed outlines in . Conversely, during asymmetric bRGC division, the newly generated daughter cell distal to the proliferating base is smaller and basally displaced relative to the mother cell, subsequently giving rise to a migrating neuroblast (). Early-stage neurogenesis initiates with the proliferation of these neural progenitor cells, where highly abundant basal radial glial progenitors (bRGPs) drive final neuronal output (A), followed by functional maturation of neurons and glia in subsequent stages.

Morphological analyses of S. aurata primary radial glia in vitro reveal a reversal of the classic in vivo apicobasal polarity axis. In classical cortical neuroanatomy, the developmental axis is defined as apicobasal, extending from the ventricular zone (apical) to the pial surface (basal). Conversely, in S. aurata neuroglial cultures, the developmental axis originating from the colony core follows a basal-to-apical (distal) orientation ( and C), extending outward from the adherent bRGC parental colony base toward the upper radial fiber scaffold.

The primary distinction between radial and tangential migration lies in the structural scaffold utilized and the degree of nuclear deformation required during nucleokinesis (A–C and ). During radial migration, neurons utilize radial glial fibers as a physical scaffold, which consists of long glial processes spanning the entire thickness of the monolayer (A,B). The neuron adheres to and enwraps the glial fiber via fibrous extensions (). Throughout this process, nucleokinesis is strictly guided; the neuronal nucleus remains aligned with the fiber and undergoes continuous longitudinal elongation to advance along this narrow track (A,B). Concurrently, cell adhesion sites maintain extensive contact with the glial scaffold (F). Conversely, tangential migration does not rely on a perpendicular scaffold; instead, neurons move transversely parallel to the substrate ( and C). In this configuration, the migratory scaffold is more dynamic, and neurons frequently utilize pre-existing axons as tracks, interlace with one another, or migrate transversely by transitioning between adjacent fibers along the periphery of the radial glial cell (RGC) colony (A,B,C,F). This structural arrangement grants the cells greater directional freedom to traverse extensive distances (B,F and C). Here, nucleokinesis is characterized by saltatory movements, and the nucleus undergoes irregular morphological changes because it is not mechanically constrained by a single glial fiber (C). Consequently, locomotion relies heavily on the dynamic exploration of the microenvironment by the leading process (C).

Radial migration predominates during the first 3 weeks of culture. Specifically, neuroblasts migrate along radial glial cell processes, which serve as directional tracks. The migrating cell adheres to the glial fiber via specialized adhesion mechanisms and translocates along its outer surface toward the distal tip (A,B and ). At this site, mitotic division initiates, generating neuronal progeny anchored to the fiber tip (A,B). Upon completion of cytokinesis, the neuroblast resumes migration in the opposite direction, translocating proximally along the fiber, while the newly generated, small neuronal cell concurrently extends adhesive processes around the fiber shaft (A,B). This rapid, terminal shift to the division site is driven by mitotic somal translocation (MST), as revealed by real-time imaging of a bRGPC undergoing MST in a 2 week-old culture (A,B). In migrating neurons, the centrosome is consistently positioned ahead of the nucleus, oriented toward the leading process. This anterior localization of the centrosome confirms that the enrichment zone of contractile proteins (the cytoplasmic bulge) is situated strictly on the opposite, posterior side of the cell during forward somal translocation (B). Furthermore, newly generated neuroblasts utilize these fibers as tracks to undergo gliophilic migration. Through nucleokinesis, a highly coordinated two-step mechanism, the neuron adheres to the glial fiber and translocates from its site of origin toward the expanding fiber scaffold or the injury site (B). The coordination of nucleokinesis during cellular scaffolding is a dynamic process that enables the nucleus to advance along a structural track by modulating its morphology. In this context, nuclear elongation is not a passive phenomenon but a critical mechanical adaptation required to navigate dense or confined environments (C). Nucleokinesis generally occurs in two alternating phases coordinated by cytoskeletal remodeling (B). The initial phase involves protrusion, during which the centrosome and the Golgi apparatus migrate forward into a cytoplasmic dilation within the leading process (B). This phase is characterized by neurite elongation and the orientation of the centrosome toward this cytoplasmic bulge (B). The second phase consists of nuclear translocation, where the nucleus advances toward the previously displaced organelles. This movement is driven by contractile proteins accumulated at the cell rear, which generate the mechanical forces required to propel the nucleus forward (B). During migration back to their site of origin, neurons extend a leading process and form a cytoplasmic dilation within its proximal region, into which the elongating nucleus translocates. Conversely, within the long processes of radial glial progenitor stem cells, a cytoplasmic swelling forms in a relatively distal region, followed by nuclear entry. Concurrently, the newborn daughter cell begins to establish adhesions and extend processes around the parental glial fiber, thereby facilitating the expansion of the cellular scaffold. Time-lapse images reveal that the cell soma exhibits a dynamic, comet-like behavior characteristic of migrating cells (A,B).

During neural development, neural progenitors proliferate to generate immature neuroblasts, which undergo sequential morphological transitions as they migrate radially along radial glial processes (E,F and C). Upon initiating migration along the internal culture scaffold, newly formed neurons enter a multipolar phase. Crucial maturation events occur during this stage, including the establishment of neuronal polarity and axonal outgrowth ( and ). Many primary neurons begin emitting neurites within 4–6 days post plating, with extensive branching completed after 2 weeks in culture ( and ).

Subsequently, these cells assume a bipolar morphology characterized by an anterior process that develops into a putative apical dendrite (). During neuritogenesis, neurons emit neurites that grow increasingly larger over time, completely covering the culture with filamentous processes (). When maintained in enriched medium, primary neuroglial cultures initially differentiate into a mature monolayer of stellate astrocytes (). Following 2 weeks of culture, long, branched neurites become visible (A,B), and this astrocytic monolayer begins to actively generate neurons ( and ). Within this microenvironment, astrocytes provide critical migratory cues and structural scaffolding support (A). Concurrently, sequential neurogenesis proceeds; RGPs generate early-born, deep-layer-like neurons that remain intimately intertwined with the glial fiber scaffold, before transitioning to produce later-born, upper-layer-like neurons that overlie the astrocytic monolayer (). This sequential production establishes a cooperative scaffold composed of radial glia and astrocytes that promotes collective neuronal migration.

During terminal maturation, late differentiation of RGCs into astrocytes occurs via gliogenesis ( and ). By the fourth week of culture, the astrocytic monolayer is densely covered by neuritic-like and dendritic-like branching, alongside well-defined neuronal-like morphology (B). Neurite-like arborization and length progressively increase over time, peaking at 2 months in vitro (B–C’).

We characterized the temporal dynamics and expression profiles of neuroglial markers via immunofluorescence microscopy. Following three weeks in vitro, radial glial cells (RGCs) displayed marked immunopositivity for both glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and vimentin (A). Proliferating colonies exhibited prominent nestin expression, particularly within the processes of intermediate progenitor cells (IPCs) in 1-month-old colonies, confirming a radial glia-like progenitor phenotype (B).

Differentiated astrocytes expressed both CD44+ and GFAP+ (H). Those located at the outer periphery of RGC colonies possessed elongated processes aligned with corresponding βIII-tubulin+ neuronal fibers, eventually acquiring a classic stellate morphology upon maturation (E–G). In contrast, the inner zone retained specialized niches of mitotically active glial stem-like cells that sustained robust neuronal production throughout long-term culture. Regarding the neuronal lineage, β-III-tubulin effectively labeled microtubules, somata, and neurites across both immature and mature neurons, providing a reliable marker to track early neurogenesis within RGC colonies (E,G).  and  demonstrate that during neurogenesis, cells undergo a definitive shift in their molecular marker profile as they transition from dividing progenitors to post-mitotic, mature neurons, progressively acquiring a mature phenotype.

Whereas NeuN expression was absent in actively mitotic cells (L,L’) after one month in vitro, differentiating neurons exhibited a high density of neurofilament-positive (NF+; ) and MAP2-positive (MAP2+; ) processes, with β-III-tubulin+ neuronal fibers running alongside and intermingling with the elongated processes of GFAP+ astrocytes. However, after 2 months in culture, actively replicating neuronal progenitors (UCHL1+/PCNA+) were clearly visible within the center of a GFAP+ radial glial colony, suggesting the maintenance of a stem/progenitor phenotype (A–D). After 2 months in culture, strong UCHL1 immunoreactivity indicated ongoing neurogenesis, characterized by newly generated neurons migrating along established radial fibers (C,D), thereby confirming the production of neuronal progeny. Neural progenitor cells were NeuN−/PCNA+, indicating their proliferative capacity. As neuroblasts differentiate, they exit the cell cycle, downregulating PCNA expression (PCNA−), and enter a permanent post-mitotic state while simultaneously upregulating NeuN, confirming their commitment to a mature neuronal lineage. This gradual process is clearly illustrated in L,L’, where differentiating neurons (NeuN+) progressively cease dividing (PCNA−), slowly reversing the PCNA marking, and acquire the marker profile of post-mitotic neurons (NeuN+), surrounded by actively proliferating progenitor cells (NeuN−/PCNA+).

The images in  illustrate the expression of specific markers via double immunofluorescence showing tangential and radial neuronal migration, as well as structural interactions along radial glial cell fibers. After 2 months in vitro, β-III-tubulin+ neurons (A,A’; green) appear aligned with a radial glial fiber (GFAP+; red). While the neuronal soma displays a prominent cytoplasmic protrusion (green), the β-III-tubulin signal highlights the perinuclear ring and the centrosome/microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), indicating phases preparatory to nuclear translocation and cell migration as reported by Powers et al. []. Punctate β-III-tubulin+ foci, corresponding to the centrosome and MTOC, migrated in tandem toward the leading process as positive signals invaded the growth cone filopodia (). Such dynamic behavior aligns with previous observations from time-lapse microscopy, where saltatory or comet-like soma movement was characteristic of actively migrating neurons. Concurrently, real-time imaging demonstrated dynamic, transient extension and retraction of membrane protrusions (or neuritic varicosities) along motile segments of the neural fibers (A,B). During tangential and radial migration, a characteristic nuclear orientation is observed; specifically, elongated nuclei are aligned along the axis of the extending neurites (B–D; green). Along migration and nuclear translocation, nuclear elongation is accompanied by asymmetric cell division of precursor cells (B,C’). Visualization of GFAP+ regions (C,C’), combined with UCHL1+ neuronal clusters (D) and PCNA+/DAPI+ nuclei (B,C’,D), reveals the proliferative capacity of cells assembled within the radial glial scaffold. High-contrast, inverted grayscale images highlight the complex structural organization and branched processes of the scaffold guiding migration. D shows specific physical contacts that facilitate the adhesion of neuroblasts to radial glial processes along structural radial fibers during nuclear elongation.

Neural stem cell colonies established a specialized niche for radial glial cells (RGCs), where cell polarity and anchoring relied on cell–cell adhesion (E,F). In D, white arrowheads highlight initial adhesion filaments extending from neural cells at the onset of migration, as the nucleus undergoes elongation (B,C’). This localized expression suggests that N-cadherin-mediated interactions facilitate the adhesion of RGCs and migrating neurons to structural radial fibers, thereby maintaining the architectural integrity of the neurogenic niche.

Radial glial cell (RGC) colonies exhibited a precise spatial segregation of distinct cell types. Staining for PCNA, a marker of DNA synthesis during the G1/S phase, revealed ongoing replication localized to the central core, in contrast to the mature peripheral zones (). Within the first week of culture, early-replicating cells in the central core began differentiating into committed neurons along the colony margin, reaching full maturation within a timeframe ranging from 2 weeks to 2 months in vitro ( and ). Double immunofluorescence demonstrated that the outer rim consisted primarily of differentiated GFAP+ astrocytes, closely intermingled with neuronal processes. Conversely, the inner zone harbored clones of mitotically active RGCs (DAPI+/PCNA+). These central aggregates constituted highly active neurogenic sites, where UCHL1 immunoreactivity revealed newly generated neurons migrating along pre-existing radial fibers (C–H). Counterstaining confirmed that these emerging neuronal cells, positive for MAP2, derived directly from the proliferating progenitor population (). To distinguish between the two distinct radial glia populations and the coexisting, clonally related glial and neuronal cells, GFAP labeling was combined with UCHL1 labeling. GFAP+ regions were UCHL1-negative, whereas the newly formed neuronal aggregates were UCHL1+ and PCNA+/DAPI+, strongly suggesting that these actively proliferating precursor cells originated from radial glia (). At various stages following lineage commitment, neuroblasts cease dividing (rather than continuing to expand the precursor pool), aligning their elongated (DAPI+) nuclei along short β-III-tubulin+ neurites. This highlights the evolution of arborization with intersecting branches during the phases of tangential and radial migration along the neuritic tree ().

β-III-tubulin serves as a benchmark pan-neuronal marker, as this cytoskeletal protein is expressed almost exclusively in both developing and mature neurons, making it ideal for visualizing neuronal cell bodies, axons, and dendrites. In A,A’, neurons labeled with β-III-tubulin–FITC display a cytoplasmic swelling (green bulge) adjacent to the nucleus along with punctate, bead-like markings along the fiber. Single dots containing both the centrosome and the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), positive for beta-III tubulin, migrate in concert, while the positive dots invade the filopodia of the growth cone (A). Morphologically, this profile represents neurons undergoing development, preparing for migration, or undergoing regeneration; specifically, the staining highlights the perinuclear ring, the centrosome/microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), or an early growth cone []. By 1 month in culture, the cells formed a confluent monolayer of polygonal–stellate astrocytes that were Vimentin− but strongly immunoreactive for CD44 and GFAP (CD44+/GFAP+).

The modes of neuronal migration along the primary radial glial scaffold in marine teleost radial glial cells (RGCs), as well as their regenerative potential, remain poorly understood due to a paucity of stable in vitro systems. Findings regarding the neurogenic zones of the Sparus aurata brain remain scarce. To date, only Zikopoulos et al. [] have investigated its in vivo plasticity, utilizing 5-bromo-2′-deoxyuridine (BrdU) immunocytochemistry to map proliferation zones across different life stages and sexual phases. Their analysis of adult male and female brains revealed ongoing adult neurogenesis within ventricular and subventricular regions, primarily corresponding to embryonic proliferative niches. The highest mitotic activity was identified in the molecular layer of the corpus and valvula cerebelli, with significant proliferation also observed in hypothalamic, thalamic, and telencephalic ventricular zones, as well as along the margins of the optic tectum. This proliferative pattern, characterized by a higher density of newly generated cells in females, supports the hypothesis of continuous neurogenesis in the adult teleost brain []. Our study demonstrates that radial glial cells (RGCs) serve as the primary adult neural stem cells (NSCs) responsible for continuous neurogenesis in the Sparus aurata brain cultures.

We observed that NeuN+ cells constituted 15% of the population in 3–4-day cultures (compared to Nestin+ cells, which accounted for 85%), rising to 45% at 2 weeks and stabilizing at 30% between the third and fourth weeks. Given that the NeuN+ population in early-stage cultures is markedly lower than in later stages (2 and 3–4 weeks), it can be inferred that the culture undergoes a significant temporal enrichment of the neuronal lineage; this is consistent with the active progression of the progenitor lineage rather than the static maintenance of neurons in vitro. Early-stage cultures (days 3–4) showed active synthesis of both neurofilaments (NF, 23%) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, 18%). This early NF expression begins in neuroblasts that have just committed to differentiation, prior to complete nuclear maturation of NeuN. Meanwhile, GFAP is expressed not only by differentiated astrocytes but also by RGPCs and the RGCs themselves. The delayed appearance of NeuN+ cells relative to Nestin+ cells indicates an initial predominance of neural stem/progenitor cells over mature neurons. Over the 3–4 week culture period, the progressive increase in NeuN+, GFAP+ (up to 49%), and NF+ (up to 78%) cells demonstrates the active differentiation of progenitors into mature neural lineages, giving rise to new mature neurons in vitro. NeuN expression naturally increases as post-mitotic neuroblasts undergo nuclear maturation; conversely, had mature neurons simply survived the initial tissue dissociation, their proportion would have steadily declined. Concurrently, astrocytes differentiate alongside neurons from bipotent or multipotent neural progenitor cells (NPCs). In the absence of microglia or oligodendrocytes, the glial population consists almost entirely of GFAP-positive astrocytes and RGCs.

Previously, we demonstrated that S. aurata brain cultures harbor radial glia displaying a distinct morphology, a characteristic molecular signature, and notable proliferative capacity [,]. These findings prompted us to further investigate nuclear translocation and migratory behavior during neurogenesis, as well as glial lineage progression and neuroblast differentiation. Using this in vitro model, we identified basal radial glial cells (bRGCs) as multipotent, self-renewing progenitors capable of generating both neurons and astrocytes ().

Furthermore, as previously demonstrated in mammals [,], these cells exhibit mitotic somatic translocation (MST) and interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM), underscoring their utility as a comparative model for central nervous system (CNS) neuronal migration during tissue regeneration. Unlike the mammalian CNS, where radial glial cells are transient embryonic structures, radial glia represent the predominant neuroglial population in the adult teleost CNS []. Morphologically, however, teleost RGCs closely resemble their mammalian counterparts, displaying long radial processes that are immunopositive for Vimentin and GFAP, as our findings demonstrate. In the mammalian neocortex, these embryonic progenitors generate both neurons and glia, with Noctor et al. [] definitively establishing that proliferating radial glia directly give rise to neurons. These progenitors maintain mitotic activity throughout neurogenesis before differentiating into astrocytes post-migration []. Parallel to these mammalian mechanisms, our findings confirm that teleost neurons migrate along progenitor radial extensions toward their functional destinations, confirming that the fundamental role of radial glia in choreographing neuronal migration is evolutionarily conserved [].

During neurogenesis, radial glial fibers regulate the direction of nucleokinesis within extending processes, highlighting that the centrosome, or microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), serves as a key indicator of cell polarity. Recent studies have demonstrated that centrosomal positioning is precisely regulated during neurogenesis, migration, and differentiation, enabling efficient nucleokinesis and directional neurite outgrowth []. Several investigations converge in stating that this process requires cytoplasmic dynein, cell polarity proteins, and microtubule-associated proteins that coordinate microtubule remodeling []. These proteins first coordinate the positioning of the MTOC in the anterior process ahead of the nucleus, subsequently driving the movement of the nucleus toward the centrosome. A similar finding was previously reported in mouse RG-like cells undergoing mitotic somal translocation, a process in which centrosome movement within the basal process during interphase precedes nuclear translocation []. Consistent with our findings, centrosomal positioning, alongside the dynamic regulation that couples and uncouples the nucleus, underlies the directional migration of neurons []. Centrosome behavior governs the neuron’s mode of migratory advance. During classic two-phase saltatory movement, the centrosome first advances into a swelling in the leading process; subsequently, the nucleus translocates toward the centrosome via a forward leap, completing the step [].

Moreover, our findings demonstrate that radial glia not only generate nascent neurons but also maintain or reconstruct the scaffold required for their migration. This scaffold self-renewal occurs because RG undergo symmetric divisions to produce new glial cells that extend long cytoplasmic processes. These fibers span the entire thickness of the culture, establishing a structural network that provides critical physical guidance. In 3- to 4-week-old cultures, an intricate network of dense glial processes integrated within neural networks becomes evident. Based on immunocytochemistry results evaluating cell culture composition over time, cells from purified neuroglial cultures were demonstrated to synthesize proteins recognized by neurofilament (NF) and GFAP antibodies after 3–4 weeks in culture. This confirms the presence of a mixed population of functionally active neurons and astrocytes capable of long-term survival and growth. By week 4, this structural maturation was evidenced by extensive neurite elongation and dense axonal arborization overlying the underlying astrocytic layer (). Pre-coating culture plates and flasks with 0.01% type I collagen was crucial for maintaining long-term viability and structural complexity by enhancing cell adhesion stability and facilitating cell–cell interactions during network assembly. Additionally, enriched differentiation medium (EDM) proved essential for preserving precursors in a stem-like proliferative state while providing the metabolic support required for neural differentiation.

Further analysis revealed that within 2-month-old long-term cultures, prominent fibrils are interspersed between neuronal and glial cell bodies, establishing complex structural connections between glial filopodia and axonal branches. Neuronal migration involves extensive morphological remodeling characterized by sequential nuclear dilation and elongation. Long-term neuroregeneration depends on coordinated neural stem/progenitor cell (NSPC) proliferation, migration, differentiation, survival, and network integration. Here, the dynamic network of radial glial fibers forms a flexible structural scaffold that drives neuronal growth and migration, as confirmed by the presence of dividing nuclei along these processes. Elucidating these cellular and molecular mechanisms may reveal signaling pathways to modulate neural remodeling through neurogenesis and gliogenesis, or to accelerate the differentiation of newborn neurons.

Over the past decade, studies on the adult zebrafish have highlighted the contribution of quiescent radial glial cells (RGCs) to proliferation following brain injury. Following optic tectum injury, RGCs possess the capacity to generate newly generated neurons [,]. Such in vivo studies conducted in zebrafish demonstrate that the neuronal regeneration process is driven by a combination of reactivated RGCs and constitutively proliferating neuroepithelial cells (NECs) []. In young fish, RGCs play a major role in the regenerative process alongside NECs, giving rise to neuronal phenotypes similar to those produced during constitutive neurogenesis []. To enhance repair, regenerative strategies could target neural stem/progenitor cell (NSPC) migration, differentiation, and lesion-site survival by modulating the neurogenic niche via growth factor stimulation. Because gilthead seabream basal radial glia (bRGs/bRGCs) exhibit highly efficient neurogenic capacity, they offer a powerful model to accelerate damage repair mechanisms. Consequently, this model of regenerative neurogenesis is particularly well-suited for the in vitro screening of cell therapies, neurotrophic factors, and pharmacological agents aimed at enhancing the regenerative capacity of neural stem cells.

Immunocytochemical analysis using DAPI and PCNA identified distinct proliferative subpopulations among NSPCs in newly seeded and long-term neural cultures. In this teleost model, molecular markers of adult-like glial precursors, such as Vimentin and GFAP, exhibit high specificity in adult NSPCs. Crucially, basal radial glia (bRGCs) exhibited long-term maintenance of their neurogenic capacity. Within these long-term cultures, specialized neurogenic niches maintain cells in an undifferentiated state, ensuring the spatiotemporal generation of mature phenotypes within a continuously evolving developmental context. Furthermore, the specific expression patterns and subcellular localization of vimentin and GFAP observed in these marine cultures facilitate the phenotypic characterization and cell-type identification of radial glial cells. Previous studies on the characterization of an adult tilapia (Oreochromis sp.) neural progenitor cell line demonstrated that these cells co-express GFAP and vimentin while exhibiting classical radial glial morphology []. However, in those cultures, the con-fluent monolayer predominantly comprised thin, fibroblast-like cells aligned in parallel, interspersed with occasional islands of epithelioid cells. Within the core of radial glia colonies in our primary cultures, immunocytochemical staining for UCHL1 (also known as PGP9.5), a highly specific marker of neuronal lineage and structural integrity, confirmed the presence of substantial neuronal production. This neuronal marker belongs to the ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase (UCH) family of deubiquitinating enzymes, specifically used in neurobiology to demonstrate consistent neurogenesis []. The morphology of seabream neuroglial cell bodies in this model aligns with previous in vivo brain section observations evaluating domoic acid neurotoxicity, thereby validating our novel marine neuroglial system as a reliable platform for neurotoxicological research [].

Although research remains limited, existing evidence demonstrates that Sparus aurata shares the high neurogenic and regenerative capacities observed in other major teleost models, such as the Danio rerio [,]. The presence of adult neural stem and progenitor cells (aNSPCs) and lifelong neurogenesis in the gilthead seabream has been documented in a limited number of in vivo studies, which are highly consistent with our current findings. Unlike zebrafish, S. aurata exhibits distinct slow- and fast-cycling NSPC populations, providing a robust platform to resolve neural stem cell kinetics. By overcoming the tissue mass limitations and technical scaling bottlenecks inherent to smaller model organisms, this marine teleost system offers a distinct advantage for advanced neurobiological applications and cell-based therapeutic screenings.

The high viability and long-term stability of these primary cultures validate Sparus aurata as a scalable, high-value cell source for biomedical applications and future tissue engineering. Elucidating the mechanisms of regenerative neurogenesis across different biological contexts is essential for repairing CNS lesions, reversing neurodegenerative processes, and developing effective therapeutic strategies for neural disorders in both teleosts and mammals. Our findings confirm that radial glia serve as the primary neural stem cell reservoir in the gilthead seabream brain, conferring exceptional structural and cellular plasticity to regenerating nervous tissue and establishing this marine species as a premier comparative model for adult neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and tissue repair.

In addition, data from gilthead seabream neurotoxicity assays underscore a historic reliance on in vivo and ex vivo exposure regimes, highlighting a distinct lack of validated in vitro screening systems for marine xenobiotics. This limitation is compounded by the dearth of Mediterranean fish cell lines suitable for examining viral neurosusceptibility and subsequent neurological damage []. Because various viral taxa cause extensive CNS inflammation and neuronal injury in fish, engineering novel in vitro models to investigate host pathogen dynamics is highly advantageous []. Ultimately, these systems allow investigators to precisely track viral evolution concurrently with host pathogenic responses, providing an indispensable framework for deciphering viral neuropathogenesis [].

Undoubtedly, pioneering in vitro studies of this nature require suitable, readily available, and purified antibodies directed against specific fish protein markers. However, species-specific antibodies, particularly for seabream, targeting CNS cell differentiation markers remain scarce due to the limited number of suppliers catering to fish research. We therefore utilized commercial antibodies whose cross-reactivity with fish proteins has been documented in the literature. Because commercial antibodies are almost exclusively raised against mammalian antigens, success depends on selecting polyclonal antibodies or specific clones known to cross-react with teleosts []. In our previous research on Sparus aurata, we evaluated the potential cross-reactivity of commercial clones with target fish proteins through sequence homology analysis [,,]. For instance, Alunni et al. [] demonstrated that GFAP is highly conserved across evolution, confirming cross-reactivity with mammalian anti-GFAP. The antibodies used in this study (e.g., GFAP, NeuN, UCHL1, NF200, Vimentin, β-III-tubulin, CD44, MAP2, Nestin, PCNA) have been previously validated for teleost tissues or Sparus aurata primary cultures in published literature (e.g., neurofilament and GFAP in zebrafish embryo cultures by Ghosh et al. []; vimentin and GFAP immunoreactivities in the brain of gray mullet by Arochena et al. []; characterization of GFAP and astroglial architecture in the rainbow trout brain by Alunni et al. []; all aforementioned antibodies in seabream liver and brain primary cultures via immunocytochemistry or immunoblotting in our previous studies [,,]). Ultimately, further advancements in marine biotechnology are required to expand the suite of molecular tools and markers available for primary marine cell cultures.

This study provides fundamental evidence demonstrating how a marine teleost model can facilitate advanced neurobiological applications, confirming the high viability of primary Sparus aurata neuroglial cells for long-term experimentation and clarifying the regenerative potential of radial glial stem cells. Evolving methodologies now enable the controlled and reproducible fabrication of bioengineered neural constructs designed to repair damaged nervous tissue. Recent ex vivo studies have leveraged neuroanatomical and functional data to guide neuroregenerative strategies using pre-engineered 3D neural constructs developed via neurosphere cultures or biohybridized microsystems []. By leveraging the developmental mechanisms underlying cell migration and axonal guidance, it is possible to create transplantable, microengineered neural constructs; these act as pro-regenerative living scaffolds, providing synergistic signals aimed at accelerating the functional reconnection of neural pathways compromised by disease or injury [,]. Furthermore, insights from scaffold-based designs have enabled the development of engineered neural networks that utilize physical microchannels to guide long-distance axonal growth []. Nevertheless, several significant limitations regarding future translational applications must be acknowledged. First, current bioengineering approaches rely on evolving methodologies for the controlled fabrication of engineered neural constructs; while these constructs are promising for repairing damaged nervous tissue or establishing predictive in vitro models, they currently serve more as tools for formulating research hypotheses than as definitive proof of therapeutic efficacy. Second, the absence of validated interspecies co-culture models limits our ability to replicate the host’s native microenvironment, representing a critical obstacle given the structural and functional complexity of nervous tissue. Finally, there remains a scarcity of mechanistic studies evaluating regenerative therapies based on the implantation of such neural networks.

Therefore, future research must utilize living neural scaffolds to develop transplantable, bioengineered neural networks while systematically mapping interspecies compatibility and functional recovery. Standardized longitudinal studies are required before transitioning from preclinical animal models to translational applications. Additionally, validating these cellular platforms will enable the development of high-potential cell products to evaluate therapeutic efficacy in neurodegenerative disease models. Ultimately, this specialized teleost model bridges the gap between basic neurobiology and applied bioengineering, providing a versatile platform for seeding next-generation 3D bioengineered scaffolds and interspecific biohybrid constructs []. Future investigations leveraging this system will be pivotal in unraveling the precise evolutionary and molecular mechanisms that govern constitutive CNS regeneration in teleosts.

In conclusion, this study establishes a well-characterized in vitro model of the gilthead seabream (Sparus aurata) CNS, demonstrating that its RG cells function as multipotent, self-renewing neural stem cells with high neuroregenerative potential. Our morphological and immunocytochemical profiling delineates the structural organization of teleost neurogenic niches and maps the pathways through which RG progenitors sustain the long-term production of neuronal and glial lineages. Furthermore, by tracking live nuclear dynamics and cellular translocation, we provide direct evidence of distinct, highly efficient modes of neuronal migration along primary radial scaffolds, a mechanism previously uncharacterized in seabream. The morphological shifts observed in these migrating neurons, including sequential nuclear dilation and elongation, represent a defining hallmark of teleost locomotion. The dynamic architecture of RG fibers serves as a structural scaffold that actively supports sustained neuronal growth, as evidenced by mitotic and translocating nuclei along the glial processes.

By serving as the primary reservoir of neural progenitors, these niche cells confer exceptional structural and cellular plasticity and regenerative capacity to the nervous tissue. From a comparative biology perspective, the consistent neurogenic activity and prolonged proliferative dynamics observed in Sparus aurata primary cultures reflect the extraordinary neural plasticity inherent to the adult teleost brain. Consequently, this model represents a pivotal comparative framework for CNS repair. Deciphering these conserved cellular pathways offers actionable evolutionary insights that may guide the development of innovative, translationally viable neural repair strategies for the brains of higher vertebrates. Furthermore, by faithfully replicating the teleost CNS in vivo environment, this alternative in vitro platform offers an immediate and accessible resource for screening applications in pharmacotoxicology, physiology, virology, neuropathology, and marine neuroimmunology, fields that remain under-investigated.

neuroscience.title: Neural Remodeling Across Cancer Evolution: Temporal, Spatial, Cellular, and Functional Principles of Tumor–Nerve Ecosystems
neuroscience.abstract: Many cancers contain nerves, but the presence of nerves alone does not reveal whether they help or restrain the disease. Research shows that tumor cells, immune cells, support cells, and nerves can change one another over time. This review explains how these interactions differ between early lesions, established tumors, metastases, and treated cancers. It proposes a practical way to map small tumor regions where neural fibers meet defined tumor and neighboring cell states, while distinguishing nerve amount, molecular state, and activity. It also separates observations in patient samples from mechanisms tested in laboratory models and clinical trials. This approach may help researchers compare studies consistently and identify neural targets that are measurable in patients and safe enough to investigate without disrupting essential nerve functions.
neuroscience.text:
The tumor microenvironment (TME) is an evolving ecosystem in which malignant cells interact with fibroblasts, endothelial and lymphatic compartments, the extracellular matrix (ECM), metabolites, immune populations, and neural structures. The nervous system is unusual within this ecosystem because neural signaling combines spatial precision, rapid temporal dynamics, electrical excitability, local neurotransmitter release, and systemic control of organ physiology. Cancer neuroscience has therefore shifted from the descriptive question of whether nerves are present in tumors toward a more demanding question: how do tumors recruit, redistribute, reprogram, or co-opt neural circuits as malignancy emerges, progresses, disseminates, and is treated [,,,,,,,]?

Two complementary perspectives frame the field: cancer may exploit or become dependent on neural circuitry, and neural components intersect with multiple cancer hallmarks and immune programs [,]. Recent reviews have surveyed therapeutic opportunities, neural–tumor microenvironment reprogramming, and repurposing of neuroactive drugs [,,,]. These syntheses provide essential conceptual maps, while primary studies demonstrate context-specific effects across prostate, gastric, breast, pancreatic, colorectal, lung, liver, skin, and central nervous system malignancies [,,,,,,,,,,,]. Together, this literature establishes that tumor–neural communication is neither confined to one organ nor reducible to a single neurotransmitter pathway; the relevant target may be a nerve projection, a reprogrammed neuronal state, glia, an immune intermediary, or a local circuit.

The major challenge is interpretive. A higher density of nerve fibers does not establish that nerves drive tumor progression; a receptor–ligand pair detected in a transcriptomic dataset does not establish signal delivery; and denervation does not necessarily isolate a neural mechanism because nerve interruption can change injury responses, vascular tone, inflammation, and tissue repair. Conversely, apparently negative or paradoxical findings may reflect differences in disease stage, neural branch, receptor repertoire, host tissue, or experimental mode [,,,,,].

The present review makes five linked dimensions explicit: temporal emergence, neuronal and glial identity, spatial architecture, functional consequence, and causal perturbation. Its contribution is not the general claim that tumors interact with nerves, nor a new label for neural niches. It is an operational and evidence-calibrated workflow: define what neural feature changed, locate it in a specific disease stage and spatial neighborhood, determine whether abundance, state, or activity was measured, and state what level of causality the design can support. The neural microdomain is specified through reportable spatial and cellular criteria, and observations from human tumors are kept distinct from mechanisms established by perturbation in experimental models ().

The overlap with recent reviews is substantial, and the present review does not claim novelty from discussing neural addiction, neural hijacking, neuroimmune crosstalk, or therapeutic neuromodulation alone [,,,,,,,,,]. The “neural addiction” and cancer-hallmarks perspectives describe broad conceptual relationships; the therapeutic reviews emphasize repurposing and intervention; and recent neural–tumor microenvironment syntheses discuss reprogramming, systemic circuits, and perineural invasion. These approaches complement the present review rather than replace it. Our distinctive contribution is to turn the broader concepts into a practical comparison framework that links (i) time and disease stage, (ii) projection and glial identity, (iii) spatially measured neural microdomains, (iv) separate readouts of abundance, state, and activity, and (v) an explicit evidence label for each claim. The framework is designed to expose rather than erase contradictory findings and to clarify what would be needed to move a candidate mechanism toward a reproducible patient biomarker or an intervention trial.

This critical narrative review used targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher-indexed records, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Search terms covered cancer neuroscience, tumor–nerve interactions, neural remodeling and innervation, axonogenesis, perineural invasion, neuroimmune crosstalk, neural microdomains, denervation, Trace-n-Seq, spatial transcriptomics, treatment-associated remodeling, and neural biomarkers, combined with terms for pancreatic, colorectal, breast, melanoma, lung, liver, prostate, gastric, and brain cancers. We prioritized mechanistic primary studies, human tissue and cohort studies, methodological reports, and recent reviews relevant to chronology, neural identity, spatial organization, causal evidence, or clinical readiness, considering the literature through 31 August 2026. This was not a systematic review; no protocol was registered, independent duplicate screening and formal risk-of-bias assessment were not performed, and no meta-analysis was undertaken.

For consistency, five evidence domains are distinguished. Anatomical evidence establishes where neural structures are located. Molecular evidence identifies altered ligands, receptors, neuronal states, or associated programs. Preclinical functional evidence demonstrates that perturbing a neural component changes a phenotype in a controlled model. Human observational evidence establishes relevance in patient material or clinical datasets but does not by itself establish causality. Prospective or interventional clinical evidence is the highest translational level and is currently sparse. These categories should be interpreted as cumulative rather than mutually exclusive.

The same principle applies to technologies. Histology can establish morphology but usually cannot establish function. Single-cell RNA sequencing can resolve cellular states but can miss distal neuronal somata and cannot directly measure neurotransmitter release. Spatial transcriptomics provides molecular geography, but its spatial resolution and sensitivity vary by platform. Retrograde tracing establishes projection identity, not functional dependence. Electrophysiology, calcium imaging, optogenetics, chemogenetics, genetic perturbation, receptor blockade, and rescue experiments can provide stronger causal evidence, but each has model-specific limitations [,,,,,,,,,,].

Terminological precision is essential because the field contains several partially overlapping phenomena. In this review, neural remodeling refers to disease-associated changes in neural architecture, neuronal identity, neural connectivity, neural activity, or glial state. Axonogenesis refers specifically to growth, sprouting, branching, or extension of axons. Tumor innervation refers to neural projections entering or surrounding a tumor, without implying their origin or function. Neurogenesis should be reserved for evidence of neuronal generation or expansion and should not be used simply to describe axonal sprouting. Perineural invasion (PNI) refers to malignant cell invasion involving the nerve sheath or nerve microenvironment according to pathological criteria; it is a route of tumor spread rather than a synonym for neural remodeling [,,].

A second important boundary concerns the CNS. Gliomas and some brain metastases arise within tissue in which neuronal activity is itself a major physiological variable. Direct synaptic signaling, membrane depolarization, and electrical coupling are therefore mechanistically distinct from peripheral axonogenesis. Glioma cells can receive glutamatergic synaptic input and integrate into functional neural circuits; human-induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived co-cultures have also demonstrated cholinergic neuron-to-glioblastoma synaptic interactions [,,].

A third boundary concerns neural guidance versus PNI. Tumor cells may use axonal structures as directional substrates or respond to axon-guidance receptors without satisfying histopathological criteria for PNI. Conversely, PNI can involve Schwann-cell-mediated cancer-cell migration and tissue injury programs that are not equivalent to physiologic synaptic signaling. Schwann cells are particularly important because they can provide a permissive interface between nerves and invasive cancer cells, and their behavior may change before overt malignant invasion is established [,].

These distinctions are not semantic refinements alone. They determine the appropriate endpoint. A study of axonogenesis should quantify branching and projection geometry; a study of PNI should define pathological invasion; a study of neuronal reprogramming requires projection-aware neuronal profiling; and a study of synaptic integration requires functional measurement. Combining these endpoints without operational definitions can produce apparent contradictions that are methodological rather than biological.

Some of the clearest experimental evidence that neural remodeling can precede overt malignancy comes from pancreatic carcinogenesis. Neuroplastic changes were detected during precursor stages, demonstrating that the neural compartment can respond to tissue transformation before invasive PDAC is established. Early pancreatic lesions may therefore act as active organizers of their neural environment rather than simply as passive recipients of nerves [,].

Recent multimodal work has made this concept mechanistically more precise. A 2026 study implicated ganglioside-mediated neural-acinar crosstalk as a molecular interface between epithelial lipid remodeling and neuritogenesis during ADM and PanIN development []. Independently, Netrin-1 expressed by metaplastic and precursor pancreatic lesions promoted sympathetic axon growth and branching through neuronal DCC; inhibition of Netrin-1 reduced local remodeling but accelerated PanIN formation in the experimental model, supporting a stage-specific protective role for lesion-associated sympathetic plasticity during this early phase [].

The same ligand can therefore participate in biologically different circuits at different times. In established PDAC, Netrin-1 and its receptor NEO1 can promote tumor-cell growth, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), stem-like programs, and sympathetic innervation, with Ntn1 deletion reducing these features in experimental models. These apparently contrasting findings can be reconciled provisionally by considering ligand source, receptor, disease stage, cellular target, and neural output as components of a context-dependent circuit rather than as isolated pathway properties [].

This stage dependence cautions against assuming that “more innervation” is intrinsically oncogenic. The recent pancreatic literature illustrates at least three possibilities: neural remodeling can restrain precursor progression; the same broader neural compartment can become tumor-supportive after malignant transition; or the neural phenotype can be a parallel adaptation with limited causal influence. Disease interception strategies must therefore avoid treating precancerous and established tumors as biologically interchangeable.

Once malignancy is established, neural remodeling can involve increased or redistributed fibers, altered branch composition, transcriptional reprogramming of tumor-innervating neurons, changes in neurotransmitter output, and reciprocal remodeling of tumor and stromal states. The Trace-n-Seq approach demonstrated that neurons innervating PDAC can be molecularly distinct from neurons innervating healthy pancreas, illustrating why bulk tumor sequencing provides an incomplete representation of the neural compartment [].

The temporal interpretation of established disease should also account for neural degeneration and apparently divergent colorectal findings. One 2025 study reported that greater nerve density was associated with poorer outcome and that denervation suppressed tumor growth, whereas another reported local sympathetic neurodegeneration and found that sympathetic ablation exacerbated progression in an experimental model, with evidence that sympathetic signaling supported chemokine-mediated CD8+ T-cell recruitment. The direction of effect therefore cannot be generalized across colorectal cohorts and models; differences in disease stage, neural compartment, host immunity, and experimental perturbation may contribute [,].

Metastatic disease introduces a second temporal problem: the neuronal environment of the target organ differs from that of the primary tumor. Neural biology may therefore influence metastatic organotropism before arrival, provide a niche after dissemination, or modulate the fitness of metastatic cells once they establish. Direct evidence remains heterogeneous, but the distinction is experimentally important because preconditioning and post-arrival support make different predictions and require different interventions.

Treatment should be treated as a biologically active stage, but treatment-associated neural changes need to be separated into three mechanisms. First, direct treatment-related nerve or Schwann-cell injury may follow surgery, radiotherapy, neurotoxic chemotherapy, or a drug with direct neural effects. Second, neural architecture may change secondarily as tumor burden falls, inflammation resolves or flares, vessels remodel, and tissue repair proceeds. Third, residual tumor and its neural ecosystem may actively adapt or be selected under therapy. These processes can occur together but are not mechanistically interchangeable. Direct human-tissue evidence in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma shows that neoadjuvant chemotherapy is associated with increased nerve density and tertiary lymphoid structure abundance, more mature nerve-proximal tertiary lymphoid structures, and chemotherapy-associated Schwann-cell transcriptional changes []. These group comparisons support treatment-associated remodeling, but they do not establish that neural changes cause treatment response or justify denervation as a therapeutic strategy. Serial pre/post-treatment specimens, matched untreated controls, neural-function assays, and immune/stromal measurements are needed to distinguish injury from regression-associated remodeling and active adaptation.

Recurrence therefore deserves explicit inclusion in the neural timeline. Key unresolved questions are whether neural states normalize after complete tumor removal, whether residual nerves retain a “memory” of the tumor, whether therapy selects for neural-adapted residual cells, and whether recurrent tumors rebuild neural networks differently from untreated primaries. These questions are particularly amenable to serial spatial pathology and longitudinal imaging because they cannot be answered reliably from a single static specimen. The temporal stages, representative neural phenotypes, and associated evidentiary requirements are summarized in  and illustrated conceptually in .

Tumors recruit and reprogram neural structures through overlapping classes of trophic and guidance cues rather than through a single canonical pathway. NGF, BDNF, GDNF and related neurotrophins can promote neurite growth or neuronal survival, whereas netrins, semaphorins, ephrins, slits and plexin-family pathways regulate directional growth, adhesion and tissue positioning. Developmental guidance programs are particularly attractive cancer mechanisms because malignant tissues can reactivate signaling systems that are normally restricted to development or tissue repair [,,,].

The breast cancer literature illustrates a distinct principle: neural signals can change tumor-cell behavior through axon-guidance receptors without necessarily requiring a large increase in total nerve density. Sensory nerves are enriched in human triple-negative breast cancer, and direct neuron-cancer contact can increase tumor-cell attachment and migration through PlexinB3-dependent mechanisms. The important variable is therefore not simply whether nerves are present, but whether tumor cells are competent to recognize and exploit specific axonal cues [].

Semaphorin signaling further illustrates pathway multiplexing. In pancreatic cancer, SEMA3D promotes disease progression through macrophage reprogramming, showing that an axon-guidance molecule can have a major tumor effect through an intermediary stromal compartment rather than solely through neuronal recruitment. This expands the concept of neural guidance from “neurons attract tumors” to a broader developmental signaling network that can simultaneously organize neural, immune and malignant states [].

Neural remodeling is also embedded in tumor metabolism. The recent pancreatic ganglioside study suggests that epithelial lipid remodeling can actively induce neuritogenesis during ADM and PanIN development, identifying glycosphingolipid metabolism as a molecular interface between epithelial state and neural plasticity. This is important because it links neural remodeling to a metabolic phenotype that may be measurable independently of nerve architecture [].

Neurons can reciprocally influence tumor metabolism. Pancreatic cancer models have shown that neurons can release serine to support protein synthesis in malignant cells, providing an example of a neural metabolic contribution that is not captured by classical neurotransmitter-centered models. Such findings imply that the neural niche can function as a local metabolic resource as well as a signaling compartment [].

Catecholamines provide another metabolic bridge. In experimental prostate cancer, adrenergic nerves activate vascular and metabolic programs. In hepatocellular carcinoma, human tissue analyses identified abundant sympathetic fibers near the invasion front, while catecholamine exposure induced inflammatory, proliferative, and ECM-remodeling programs in differentiated tumor hepatocytes and primary human hepatocytes. These findings support a mechanistic link between catecholaminergic signaling and the tumor-cell state, but they do not by themselves establish that sympathetic innervation is a clinical driver of human HCC progression [,].

Primary experimental evidence supports a tumor-to-nerve role for extracellular vesicles in axonogenesis. In head and neck cancer, tumor-derived exosomes induced neurite outgrowth in neuronal models, exosome-deficient tumors were less innervated in mice, and exosome-packaged EphrinB1 potentiated axonogenesis. These data establish a mechanism for structural neural recruitment in an experimental setting but do not by themselves prove that extracellular vesicles broadly reprogram neurotransmitter release or neuronal transcription across cancers [].

Stromal cells increasingly appear to be intermediates rather than bystanders. Fibroblasts can provide the ECM and trophic support to axons, while neural signals can modify fibroblast phenotype and matrix deposition. In TNBC, sensory-neuron-derived CGRP was linked to a dense ECM and immune-excluded state, indicating that neural activity can reshape stromal architecture and thereby alter immune and mechanical properties indirectly () [].

Peripheral organs contain sympathetic, parasympathetic, sensory, enteric and organ-specific neuronal populations. Their projections, receptor repertoires, neurotransmitters and target tissues differ; consequently, “nerve density” is biologically under-specified unless the neuronal population is known. The prostate literature demonstrated that sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs can have different effects on cancer initiation and dissemination, while gastric models established cholinergic dependence of epithelial growth [,].

Projection-aware neuronal profiling is therefore critical. Trace-n-Seq directly addresses the anatomical problem that neuronal somata are often located in distant ganglia rather than within tumor tissue. By retrogradely labeling projections and sequencing the corresponding neuronal cell bodies, this approach can identify the neurons that actually innervate a target organ and can reveal disease-associated transcriptional states that conventional tumor scRNA-seq cannot capture [].

The next conceptual step is to distinguish lineage from state. A sensory neuron remains a sensory neuron while its transcriptional program, excitability, neuropeptide production, or response to tumor-derived cues changes. In pancreatic cancer, single-neuron analysis demonstrates this possibility at scale. In head and neck cancer, loss of p53 in tumor cells has been linked to acquisition of neuronal features, illustrating that tumor-cell plasticity can complicate the distinction between neural recruitment and tumor-cell reprogramming [,].

Glial cells warrant parallel attention. Schwann cells participate in nerve repair and can be co-opted by tumor cells. They can promote dispersion, migration, and invasion through direct contact and NCAM1-dependent mechanisms, while Schwann-cell recruitment has been observed near neoplastic sites before classical invasion. These observations support a broader definition of the neural ecosystem in which Schwann cells are active regulators of tumor movement and tissue remodeling rather than inert components of the nerve sheath [,].

This glial perspective also clarifies the relationship between neural remodeling and PNI. PNI is a pathological manifestation of tumor–nerve interaction, but the cellular machinery that permits neural migration may begin before malignant cells have entered the nerve sheath. Future studies should therefore map Schwann-cell states together with axonal architecture and tumor-cell phenotypes to determine whether PNI represents a late endpoint of an already established neural niche or a distinct biological transition.

Global nerve density is an incomplete phenotype because neural fibers are elongated, branched structures. Two tumors with similar neural density may differ in axonal orientation, branching, terminal density, distance to vessels, proximity to fibroblast-rich regions, and adjacency to distinct tumor-cell states. Fine unmyelinated fibers and terminal structures may also be underestimated by conventional two-dimensional histology [,,,,,,,].

We propose the neural microdomain as an operational spatial unit, but do not imply that a universal radius or validated clinical assay already exists. A candidate microdomain should be defined within a prespecified tissue compartment and imaging/sampling window; dimensions must be reported in physical units and selected according to specimen architecture and platform resolution rather than an arbitrary universal distance. At minimum, its record should include four elements: (1) neural identity, established by a validated pan-neural marker and subtype or projection evidence where available; (2) topology, quantified at a stated 2D/3D resolution using measures such as fiber length, branch density, orientation, terminal distribution, or distance to neighboring cells; (3) a molecular neighborhood containing at least one defined tumor-cell state and one adjacent immune, stromal, or vascular compartment; and (4) at least one spatially localized molecular interface, such as a ligand/receptor pair or protein/RNA signal. These criteria define an anatomically and molecularly characterized candidate microdomain, not proof of communication. A claim of functional validation additionally requires direct neural activity/output measurement or a controlled perturbation linked to a phenotype, preferably with an orthogonal test or rescue. Archived human tissue alone will ordinarily support anatomical/molecular characterization, not functional causality.

Reproducibility must be tested rather than assumed. Studies should prespecify sampling boundaries, marker panels, spatial resolution, segmentation rules, distance metrics, and the denominator used for density or topology. At least a subset of fields should be annotated independently and blinded, with interobserver agreement reported using a suitable statistic (for example, an intraclass correlation coefficient for continuous metrics or kappa for categories). Segmentation agreement, within-specimen variability, between-specimen variability, and cross-platform concordance should be quantified, followed by validation in an independent patient cohort. Spatial transcriptomics provides broad molecular context but varies in spot size, sensitivity, and transcriptome coverage. Image-based methods such as MERFISH permit finer localization but require targeted panels and imaging infrastructure; near-cellular platforms improve granularity while retaining trade-offs in coverage and scalability [,,,,,].

For neural biology, multimodal integration is particularly important because axons can extend far from the transcriptional soma. A spatial dataset can identify a tumor or stromal state adjacent to an axonal structure without proving which neuronal population generated it. Conversely, a traced neuronal population can be molecularly defined without revealing the exact cells it contacts in the tumor. The most informative experiments therefore connect neuronal projection identity to local spatial context through coordinated tracing, morphology and spatial molecular profiling [,,,,,,,].

Three-dimensional imaging adds network topology that is difficult to infer from serial sections. Tissue clearing and light-sheet or confocal reconstruction can quantify branching, trajectories and proximity to ducts, vessels, and tumor nests. These approaches reduce the risk of mistaking a section through a neighboring nerve bundle for genuine intratumoral innervation, but they introduce processing-dependent changes in tissue dimensions, antibody penetration, segmentation, and signal detection. Such measurements should therefore be normalized against appropriate anatomical references and, whenever possible, validated by orthogonal histology ().

The strongest causal evidence for neural regulation arises when a defined neural component is perturbed and the intervention changes a measurable tumor phenotype while alternative systemic explanations are addressed. Neural inputs can influence proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, cell-state plasticity, metabolism, ECM organization and, in selected settings, direct electrical activity [,,,,,,,].

Autonomic signaling can act directly on epithelial or stromal compartments. Prostate studies demonstrated branch-specific effects on tumor development and dissemination, whereas gastric denervation reduced tumor growth through effects involving muscarinic signaling and Wnt-dependent stem-cell programs. The gastric model is especially informative because denervation was accompanied by reduced tumor incidence and progression and because organoid experiments linked neuronal input to epithelial growth [,,].

Pancreatic models show why pathway effects must be interpreted by stage and cellular target. Netrin-1/DCC-associated sympathetic remodeling can restrain progression in precursor lesions, whereas Netrin-1/NEO1 signaling supports growth, the epithelial–mesenchymal transition and stem-like programs in established PDAC [,]. The mechanistic evidence is summarized in ; here, the key functional lesson is that one ligand cannot be assigned a universal pro- or antitumor role without specifying disease stage, receptor-bearing cell, and measured endpoint.

Neural cues can also alter tumor-cell migration without increasing bulk growth. In TNBC, sensory nerves enhance adhesion and migration through PlexinB3, suggesting that neural interfaces can selectively increase dissemination competence. This is conceptually important because a neural phenotype may change the probability of invasion or metastasis without producing a proportional change in primary tumor volume [].

Neural regulation extends beyond direct tumor-cell signaling. Adrenergic nerves can activate vascular and metabolic programs, illustrating how neural input can organize the physical conditions needed for tumor expansion. In TNBC, sensory-neuron-derived CGRP can alter fibroblast phenotype and collagen deposition, producing a dense ECM associated with immune exclusion [,].

The ECM should therefore be viewed as a major interface between neural and malignant compartments. Matrix stiffness, collagen organization and interstitial architecture can affect cell migration, immune-cell access and drug penetration. A neural intervention that changes the ECM may consequently have effects that are not visible in tumor-cell signaling assays alone and may interact with therapies whose efficacy depends on tissue penetration or immune access.

Neural influences on antitumor immunity are not uniformly suppressive or stimulatory. Their direction depends on neuronal branch, receptor expression, immune-cell target, tissue context and disease stage. In TNBC models, sensory-neuron-derived CGRP is linked to fibroblast activation, a dense extracellular matrix and immune exclusion; the mechanistic perturbation evidence is preclinical, whereas the presence of corresponding neural features in human tumors is observational []. In colorectal cancer, human tissue analyses have reported local sympathetic degeneration, while experimental work indicates that norepinephrine acting through α2-adrenergic signaling can increase chemokine-associated CD8+ T-cell recruitment and restrain progression in an immune-competent model []. This result contrasts with studies of broader chemical denervation and tumor-volume endpoints, discussed in . Other work has identified a sensory–sympathetic tumor–brain axis associated with immune suppression in lung adenocarcinoma models; this is an emerging preclinical circuit, not evidence that the same causal pathway controls human lung cancer immunity []. Accordingly, a neural immune phenotype should be reported with the responsible neural population, immune compartment, assay, disease stage and evidence level. Human spatial association, transcriptional co-occurrence and preclinical perturbation should be described separately; no universal “neural immunosuppression” mechanism can be inferred across cancers.

CNS tumors provide the clearest demonstration that neural signaling can be electrical rather than primarily chemical. Glioma cells can receive glutamatergic synaptic input, depolarize, and participate in electrically coupled networks. Human iPSC-derived co-culture models have demonstrated cholinergic neuron-to-glioblastoma synaptic interactions, providing an experimentally tractable human platform [,,].

The biological boundary is now becoming less absolute. The 2025 SCLC study found that pulmonary innervation contributes to primary tumor initiation and development in experimental models, while analyses of human brain metastases and functional neuronal co-culture models showed that neuronal activity can promote intracranial SCLC growth. This illustrates a single cancer type engaging distinct neural mechanisms by anatomical site and reinforces the need to distinguish peripheral neural signaling from direct CNS circuit integration [].

Neural regulation of dissemination can be conceptualized at four levels: local tumor-cell migration, access to vascular or lymphatic routes, preconditioning of distant tissues, and post-arrival adaptation within the metastatic site. These levels should not be conflated because the same neural signal may influence one stage without controlling another.

At the primary site, nerve fibers can provide directional or adhesive interfaces that promote tumor-cell movement. This mechanism differs from PNI because the relevant phenomenon may occur before malignant cells invade the nerve sheath. At metastatic sites, the pre-existing neural architecture of the target organ provides a different environment, and disseminated cells may encounter organ-specific neuronal, glial and stromal states.

An important emerging example is colorectal cancer, in which a polysynaptic brain–gut circuit linking the lateral septum and enteric cholinergic neurons sustained tumor growth in mice, and chronic stress potentiated the circuit. This study demonstrates a testable systemic mechanism in a preclinical model; its clinical relevance and generalizability to human colorectal cancer remain uncertain []. The recently described lung tumor–brain–sympathetic axis likewise expands the possible circuit scale but is supported by experimental mechanistic evidence rather than clinical causal data []. These results should motivate—not substitute for—human validation and do not establish that systemic neural circuits determine metastatic organotropism.

Metastatic organotropism remains unresolved. A rigorous test would require matched primary and metastatic lesions, projection-specific tracing, lineage barcoding, spatial profiling, and longitudinal perturbation. Studies should distinguish neural preconditioning of a target organ before tumor-cell arrival from local neural support after colonization; endpoint data from established metastases cannot discriminate these possibilities. Current claims of neural control of organotropism should therefore be labeled emerging or preclinical unless pre-arrival timing and causal dependence have been directly demonstrated ( and ).

Histopathology and multiplex immunofluorescence remain the anatomical foundation. Broad neuronal markers can identify nerve fibers, while subtype markers such as tyrosine hydroxylase, choline acetyltransferase, vesicular acetylcholine transporter and sensory-neuropeptide markers provide lineage information. However, marker positivity alone does not establish functional activity and can be influenced by tissue injury, inflammation, treatment, or altered differentiation [,].

Three-dimensional imaging adds network geometry and can distinguish true intratumoral fibers from adjacent bundles. Retrograde tracing answers a different question: which neuronal cell bodies project into the target tissue? Trace-n-Seq links these approaches to single-cell transcriptomics and is particularly valuable because distal neuronal somata are systematically missed by conventional tumor sequencing. Newer transsynaptic tracing approaches can interrogate circuit connectivity in glioblastoma, although these methods remain primarily preclinical and require careful control of tracer specificity and experimental perturbation [,].

Single-cell and single-nucleus sequencing resolve cellular states but should be interpreted in anatomical context. In extracranial tumors, neuronal somata often lie in distant ganglia; a tumor scRNA-seq dataset can therefore underestimate the neural compartment even when neural processes are abundant. Conversely, neuronal transcriptomes may not represent the local axonal output reaching the tumor. Paired ganglion-tumor sampling or projection-specific labeling is therefore preferable when neuronal molecular identity is a principal endpoint [,,,,,,].

Functional assays provide the bridge from anatomy to mechanism. Dorsal root ganglion cultures, whole-mount co-cultures, organoids and microfluidic systems can control distance and contact between neurons and cancer cells. Electrophysiology, calcium imaging, optogenetics and chemogenetics can manipulate activity with greater subtype or temporal specificity than global denervation. Genetic deletion and receptor-selective pharmacology can then test whether an identified pathway is required for the phenotype [,,,].

No single perturbation is definitive. Surgical and chemical denervation can induce injury responses, while receptor antagonists may affect non-neural cells, genetic deletion may produce developmental compensation, and optogenetic or chemogenetic tools may impose nonphysiological activity patterns.
