To our knowledge, no local study conducted among the Moroccan population has yet examined the impact of poor sleep quality in patients with T2D and its association with psychiatric factors using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scale. Our study is the first to assess the association of poor sleep quality with glycemic control and anxiety in the Moroccan diabetic population.

According to this study [], which revealed that the prevalence of sleep disorders in Morocco shows marked regional disparities, with Fez-Meknes having the highest rate (23.76%), followed by Beni Mellal-Khenifra (11.88%) and Marrakech-Safi (11.28%). In contrast, Rabat-Sale-Kenitra had the lowest rate (0.29%), which may reflect better access to care.

We therefore conducted a regional cross-sectional study in the Rabat region to assess the prevalence of poor sleep quality and associated factors, such as mental health disorders, among Moroccan patients with T2D at the Mohammed V Military Instruction Hospital (HMIMV) in Rabat, Morocco. We also assessed the impact of sleep quality on glycemic control and psychological factors in a Moroccan adult population with T2D. We sought to determine whether there were correlations between subjective sleep quality and glycemic control, on the one hand, and psychological factors, on the other.

The present cross-sectional study was designed to identify the factors that affect sleep quality in 120 patients with T2D admitted to the internal medicine department of the HMIMV, in Rabat, Morocco, between 30/09/2024 and 30/12/2024.

Consisted of any type 2 diabetic patient (age ≥ 18 years), diagnosed >1 year ago, under regular treatment for diabetes disease, scheduled for consultation or hospitalization in the internal medicine department at HMIMV, Rabat, during the study period, and who had previously undergone biological analysis and agreed to participate in this study ().

Any patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus, gestational diabetes, a patient who had not previously undergone biological testing and who came for consultation during the study period, who lacked interest in participating in the study. Diabetic patients with any psychiatric or neurological disorders or other serious diseases were also excluded because these conditions significantly affect sleep quality [], and to minimize potential confounding effects associated with established clinical conditions ().

We assessed body mass index (BMI) derived from: weight (mass in kilograms)/height2 (in meters) and laboratory tests, including; (1) Glycemic control: glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level, fasting plasma glucose levels, and (2) lipid profile levels: low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL), triglycerides (TG), and total cholesterol (TC).

Data collection was conducted over a three-month period, from 30/09/2024–30/12/2024, during the internship. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire comprising sociodemographic and clinical variables, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scale. The questionnaire was administered through structured interviews to ensure standardized data collection. It was initially prepared in French and translated into Moroccan Arabic to facilitate participants’ understanding.

Clinical and laboratory data, including biochemical parameters, were obtained from the most recent laboratory assessment performed before the interview. For hospitalized patients, these data were retrieved from their medical records. Missing information was obtained from medical records when available. Data completeness was checked throughout data collection, data entry, and analysis.

In addition to the PSQI and GAD-7, the questionnaire included an additional question regarding perceived sleep need. Participants were asked, “How many hours of sleep do you think you need?” This question was administered independently of the PSQI and assessed participants’ perceived sleep requirement rather than the sleep-duration component of the PSQI. No specific recall period was specified because participants were asked to report their perceived need for sleep. For descriptive purposes, responses were classified into three categories: short perceived sleep need (<7 h/night), moderate perceived sleep need (7–9 h/night), and long perceived sleep need (>9 h/night). This additional measure was not used in the calculation of the PSQI score.

The basic demographic information of participants included: Age, gender, educational level, marital status, residence, lifestyle (smoking, coffee consumption, and physical exercise activity), employment status, and smartphone/interactive media use. Height and weight were measured during the consultation on the first day of admission to the service to calculate BMI.

In addition, data on family history of diabetes, duration of diabetes mellitus in years, number of hospitalizations due to diabetes, the mode of diabetes diagnosis was assessed based on the circumstances leading to the identification of diabetes. Participants were categorized into three groups: diagnosis following diabetes-related complications, diagnosis prompted by diabetes-related symptoms, and incidental diagnosis during routine screening or medical evaluation unrelated to diabetes symptoms. This information was collected through structured interviews and verified using available medical records. Therapeutic regimen, medical history, and diabetes-related comorbidities were also recorded, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, hyperuricemia, autoimmune diseases (including autoimmune thyroiditis “Hashimoto’s thyroiditis”, Graves ‘disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis), and cardiovascular diseases. Biochemical parameters such as fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c (%), TC, HDL, LDL, and TG levels were recorded during the interview based on the most recent laboratory assessment performed before the interview. For hospitalized patients, these laboratory results were obtained from their clinical medical records. The questionnaire served as a data collection tool to recording the available clinical and biochemical information.

The first measure used in the present study was the PSQI, an internationally validated questionnaire that evaluates subjective sleep quality and disturbances during the month preceding the survey []. The PSQI score is calculated from 19 items divided into seven subcategories of sleep quality, each rated on a 0–3 point scale (no difficulty to severe difficulty). The total score for each subcategory constitutes the PSQI total score, which varies on a scale from 0 to 21 points (from no difficulty to major difficulty). An overall PSQI score above 5 has been validated as having a high sensitivity of 89.6% and specificity of 86.5% for distinguishing good from poor sleepers in some populations [], including people with T2D [].

The second scale in the present study was the GAD-7, a 7-item self-report tool used to screen participants for anxiety and the severity of GAD-7 over the last two weeks []. Every item was scored between 0 and 3 points. The overall scores can vary between 0 and 21. According to a recent meta-analysis, the threshold recommended by experts for estimating generalized anxiety is 8 to optimize sensitivity without compromising specificity.

The present study was carried out with respect to the dignity and ethics of the participants. Data collection was carried out in accordance with patient confidentiality. All procedures in this work involving patients complied with the ethics standards specified by the national and institutional research committee. All participants received information on the project's nature, context, and objectives and signed an informed consent form. We obtained all the official authorizations required, including the approval of the ethics committee, which referenced CERB 132−24, the hospital director, and the heads of the clinical neurophysiology and internal medicine departments. Confidentiality and privacy were guaranteed to all participants. We have respected the Moroccan Arabic dialect [,].

Descriptive statistical analysis methods (median, mean, frequency, ratio, standard deviation, minimum, maximum) were used to evaluate the study data and were analyzed using Jamovi version 2.6.2. The data are expressed as the mean ± SD for continuous variables and as percentages for categorical variables. Mean ± SD and frequency (%) were used in descriptive analysis to describe patients’ sociodemographic and medical characteristics, sleep quality, and anxiety scores.

Sociodemographic, biochemical, and clinical variables were analyzed with a chi-square (χ2) test for comparisons of categories and a student’s t-test for continuous measures. The seven PSQI components were analyzed to identify the prevalence of good/bad sleepers. The Mann-Whitney U test was used for variables that were not normally distributed. All associations with a significance level were P ≤ 0.05.

We performed binary logistic regression to determine the significant predictors of poor sleep quality (coded 1). We included significant variables (i.e., age, HbA1C values, GAD-7 score) in the preliminary analysis of the model. The odds ratio (OR) and Pearson's correlation coefficient were used to identify sleep-related factors in the analysis. As the GAD-7 and HbA1c variables do not follow a normal distribution, we used Spearman's correlation coefficient (rho) to assess their relationships.

Multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that age and anxiety symptoms are significant predictors of poor sleep quality (). For each additional year of age, the estimated odds of poor sleep quality were 6% higher (adjusted OR=1.06; CI:1.00 to 1.14; P = 0.04), holding the other variables in the model constant. Similarly, each one-point increase in the GAD-7 score was associated with a 21% increase in the estimated odds of poor sleep quality (adjusted OR=1.21; 95% CI:1.06 to 1.39; P = 0.005). In contrast, HbA1c was not a significant predictor of poor sleep quality (adjusted OR= 1.13; 95% CI: 0.79 to 1.64; P = 0.48). Gender and night-time social media use were also not statistically significant predictors of poor sleep quality (adjusted OR= 0.61; 95% CI: 0.18 to 2.03; P = 0.42 and adjusted OR=1.06; 95% CI: 0.30 to 3.71; P = 0.92, respectively). In the multivariable logistic regression model, age and anxiety symptoms were independently associated with higher odds of poor sleep quality, after adjustment for glycemic control (P = 0.04 and P = 0.005, respectively).

Sleep quality is an integral part of health quality. Poor night sleep is associated with depression, anxiety, impaired social performance, chronic illness, and mortality []. In addition, poor sleep quality is associated with an increased risk of insulin resistance and complications in T2D patients. A bidirectional relationship exists between sleep and diabetes management. Improved sleep management can increase the chances of improved diabetes management, and vice versa []. Difficulty in initiating or maintaining sleep increases the risk of developing T2D twofold or more [].

Sleep disorders are common in diabetic patients, increasing their morbidity and mortality []. Disturbed sleep alters insulin sensitivity, leading to hyperglycemia []. In response to poor sleep, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal system increases glucocorticoid production, leading to increased glucose production and reduced glucose consumption, worsening glycemic control []. In addition, polyuria and nocturia, which are characteristic of diabetes, are major causes of sleep disorders, affecting sleep onset, and sleep maintenance, and aggravating these disorders []. As a result, diabetic patients often suffer from poor sleep quality due to physiological imbalances and associated sleep pathologies [].

We hypothesize that sleep quality, in addition to being influenced by sociodemographic factors such as gender, age, and occupation, is also modulated by lifestyle habits (smoking, coffee consumption, and physical activity), disease-related characteristics (years of diabetes, complications, and treatment methods), emotional factors (depressive symptoms, anxiety, stress, fatigue, and concentration) and clinical parameters (BMI, HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and blood lipid profile). The nocturnal complications of diabetes have a direct impact on sleep quality, and sleep management is crucial for improving patients’ health and well-being. The present study aims to evaluate the effect of sleep quality on glycemic control and psychological factors in Moroccan adult type 2 diabetic patients and to explore correlations between subjective sleep quality, glycemic control, and psychological factors.

The present research revealed that 84.2% of the people surveyed had poor sleep quality, with a PSQI score > 5. Poor sleep quality was statistically greater in women than in men: 57.5% versus 26.7%, respectively. Earlier studies reported that women had poorer sleep quality than men did [,]. Older age and menopause may be linked to this phenomenon [], babies’ crying, partners’ snoring, and daytime causes such as sleepiness or lack of concentration []. Notably, the women included in the study were younger than the men: 64.3 ± 9.60 years versus 67.7 ± 8.38 years, respectively.

The high incidence of poor sleep quality according to the PSQI score is consistent with the results of a study of diabetic patients in Jordan, where the PSQI score (PSQI>8) of patients was 81.0% []. Furthermore, the findings of several other studies are consistent with the results of the present study on poor sleep quality. In, Kenya (PSQI>5) (53.4%) [], Singapore (47.1%) [], Ethiopia (PSQI>5) (47.2%) [], Iran (PSQI>5) (50.7%) [], Qatar (PSQI>5) (35,8%) [], Saudi Arabia (PSQI>5) (41,1%) [], Brazil (PSQI > 5) (65,5%) [] and Korea (PSQI>5) (49%) []. In addition, Cappuccio et al. reported that 47.1% of T2D patients were poor sleepers [].

T2D patients have more sleep disturbances compared with controls (Lecube et al. 2016). Comparing studies using the PSQI index is complex due to differences in patient characteristics, such as age, diet, lifestyle, and sleep measurement thresholds. The complications of diabetes, such as neuropathy and nocturia, aggravate poor sleep quality []. In addition, sleep quality influences glycemic control, with established links between inadequate sleep duration and elevated glucose and glycated hemoglobin levels [].

A person's sleep time could be crucial in determining the risk of developing metabolic syndrome, including T2D [–]. In the present study, the average sleep duration per day was 7 hours, 4 hours at 9.2%, 3 hours at 0.8%, 6 hours at 16.7%, and 5 hours at 6.7% suggesting that a majority of type 2 diabetics suffer from sleep disorders. In addition, our results show that 40.5% of patients declare having sleep disorder triggers of psychological origin (e.g., posttraumatic stress, emotional shock, mood disorders), physiological origin (e.g., illness, sleep apnea), while 16.5% of our patients define their sleep disorder triggers of environmental origin (e.g., stress, noise, bad bed), and the remaining 2.5% define them of hygienic origin (e.g., work schedule, medication, diet...). In this sense, 10.8% of diabetic patients reported using sleeping pills 3–4 times a week, and all of them were poor sleepers. However, only 0.8% reported taking sleeping pills at least once a week, which can alter the sleep-wake cycle and lead to stress [].

In the current study, glycemic control, which was based on an HbA1c level of <7%, was reported in only 33.3% of the T2D patients. Similarly, other studies have reported that 24.3%, 39.1%, and 12.2% [,,] of the patients with T2D expressed glycemic control. This is an indication of a major failure in the effective management of diabetes, even in a specialist hospital, which needs further investigation into the underlying causes [,].

Our findings revealed no significant correlation between HbA1c and sleep quality (OR = 1.13, P = 0.486), which is in line with several studies [,–]. However, Cappuccio et al, reported a significant difference between good and poor glycemic control in relation to sleep quality [] using PSQI. Other research has shown positive associations between HbA1c and sleep quality [,,].

Tsai et al. revealed an inverse correlation between HbA1c and sleep quality, suggesting that improved glycemic control is linked to better sleep quality []. This relationship is probably due to the complications of diabetes [], such as neuropathy and osmotic symptoms, which disrupt sleep by frequent visits to the toilet during the night []. Controlling blood sugar levels can be an effective therapeutic strategy for diabetic patients. To this end, it can be beneficial to set an appropriate sleep time to optimize patients’ sleep duration and help them improve the quality of their sleep.

Regarding the treatment type of diabetic patients, this study showed that 11.8% of diabetic patients on insulin complained of poor sleep quality, compared with 57.1% of oral hypoglycemic Agents (OHA) patients. This result contradicts the study by Cappuccio et al, who reported that insulin users more often complained of poor sleep quality than those on OHA alone did []. This finding is similar to the findings of Rajendran et al, who also reported no significant relationship between sleep quality and the type of diabetes treatment []. This may be explained by social and environmental factors, such as the average duration of diabetes, in addition to neuropathy and nocturia, which are more common in long-term diabetic patients. We suggest that the choice of antidiabetic medication in type 2 diabetic patients does not have a significant impact on sleep quality, regardless of other variables.

The role of sleep is to modulate glucose metabolism and energy absorption, which has a direct or indirect action on the maintenance of satisfactory glycemic control in patients with T2D. In addition, the increased prevalence of low levels of glycemic control in cases of sleep deprivation and/or poor-quality sleep could be due to upregulation of appetite, increased time spent eating, and reduced energy expenditure. In addition, nocturnal arousal and excitement could be associated with altered leptin levels and leptin resistance, leading to dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and resulting in altered glucose metabolism [].

The two best-known pathways by which sympathetic nervous system activation is likely to predispose individuals to obesity, altered blood glucose levels, metabolic syndrome, and T2D are the inhibition of leptin secretion and stimulation of the HPA axis, leading to excessive cortisol secretion, which in turn alters glucose homeostasis [].

The pathophysiological pathways linking sleep to diabetes mellitus are not simple linear cascades but complex cascades that involve neuroendocrine and metabolic networks []. The sympathetic nervous system and the HPA axis are activated during sleep disorders, resulting in increased cortisol secretion. In addition, this glucocorticoid has adverse effects on metabolism, such as insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome, by increasing glucose production and decreasing its utilization. Thus, sleep disorders can alter carbohydrate metabolism, favoring the risk of T2D, and can be caused by hyperactivity of the HPA axis, leading to various sleep disorders [].

In our patients, comorbidities such as arterial hypertension (67.5%), dyslipidemia (40%), obesity (45.8%), hyperuricemia (45%), autoimmune diseases (11.7%), and cardiovascular diseases (33.3%) can lead to poorer sleep quality than the absence of comorbidities. However, comorbidities can lead to poor glycemic control, chronic complications, and increased emotional distress, which can result in disturbed homeostasis and poor sleep quality. While we did not find a significant association between BMI and sleep quality, this type of association was not materialized by significant rates after the application of logistic regression. This differs, however, from some previous studies that reported significant associations [].

The results also showed numerical differences in the mean levels of fasting blood glucose (FBS), TC, and TG between patients with poor and good sleep quality; however, these differences were not statistically significant. Similarly, a study conducted by Khorasani et al. found that serum TG levels were higher in patients with poor sleep quality than in those with adequate sleep []. Based on experimental and clinical data, certain mechanisms have been suggested to link the relationship between sleep disorders and lipid metabolism. A decrease in leptin, a decrease in insulin sensitivity, an increase in sympathetic nervous system activation, and an increase in cortisol production have all been proposed as explanations [,].

Our data indicate that greater lipid disturbance is associated with higher levels of TC in poor sleepers, as observed by []. In addition, a significant correlation between sleep quality, as measured by the PSQI index, and HDL levels was found, which is consistent with the findings of [], but differs from the study by Jennings et al., who did not observe this association [].

HDL plays a key role in reverse cholesterol transport and possesses antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Fanni et al. 2020). The lack of such relationships could be due to variations in sleep quality measurements across different studies. However, hyperglycemia and insulin resistance alter HDL particles, rendering them dysfunctional, as is frequently observed in T2D [].

Furthermore, no association was found in our study between poor sleep quality in diabetic patients with no occupational status and poor sleep quality in employees. However, joblessness can lead to psychological disorders such as anxiety, low self-esteem, and depression. These consequences can translate into poor sleep quality and quantity [,]. This explains the high rate of poor-quality sleep in the unemployed group in this study (42.5%) compared with the non-employed group with good sleep quality (12.5%).

Our findings regarding the high prevalence of poor sleep quality and its relationship with anxiety are consistent with growing evidence suggesting that sleep and mental health may be influenced by broader metabolic and lifestyle factors. In this context, Shirased et al. reported that greater adherence to Mediterranean and DASH dietary patterns was associated with better sleep quality among women with overweight or obesity, while adherence to the Mediterranean diet was also associated with lower level of anxiety [].

The present study showed that anxiety was a significant predictor of sleep quality, suggesting that for each one-unit increase in the GAD-7 anxiety score, the risk of poor sleep quality was multiplied by 1.21. This study, one of the first in the Moroccan context, also showed that anxiety and poor sleep quality negatively influence glycemic control, reinforcing the idea that clinicians should monitor these two variables in patients with T2D.

The results of the study indicated that there was a significant difference (P = 0.007) in GAD-7-rated generalized anxiety state when comparing groups of patients with good and poor sleep quality, and this variable was a significant major predictor (P = 0.005) of poor sleep quality in our T2D patients. The associations between poor sleep quality and anxiety were stronger than the associations between poor sleep quality and T2D and sleep quality and high blood pressure, respectively. Dong et al., also found a significant interaction between poor sleep quality and anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 ≥ 10) [,].

Inadequate sleep quality and anxiety both activate the HPA axis, stimulating the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal responses, increasing cortisol levels and inflammation, decreasing insulin sensitivity, and worsening glycemic control [,]. Both factors are also directly linked to impaired glycemic control [], sleep quality and poor diabetes self-management, increased food intake, changes in time and quantity of food intake, a preference for energy-rich foods, impaired glucose tolerance, and insulin sensitivity []. In contrast, a chronic high-fat, high-protein diet and delicious foods can raise fasting blood glucose levels, which can intensify anxiety []. Anxiety disorders are also associated with poor diet adherence, inadequate glycemic control, and increased adrenergic activity []. These findings suggest that the combination of poor sleep quality and anxiety may affect quality of life in people with T2D [].

It's also worth noting that recent work has highlighted the bidirectionality between sleep disorders and anxiety, with anxiety being predictive of sleep disorders and vice versa []. In this regard, findings suggest that clinicians investigating anxiety complaints in T2D patients should investigate poor sleep quality, and vice versa. Behavioral and pharmacological treatments are effective for anxiety disorders and poor sleep quality in people with T2D [,].

Furthermore, a recently published meta-analysis established the association between diabetes and an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia []. The reason for this is that inadequate control of diabetes, along with increased plasma glucose concentrations, can lead to cognitive impairment. Not only is hyperglycemia dangerous because of the long-term complications it can cause, including cardiovascular diseases, but it also has a direct negative impact on the central nervous system (CNS), contributing, among other things, to the slowing down of cognitive functions, and can also be associated with sleep disorders []. In this regard further investigation needed to explore the association of cognitive dysfunction and anxiety in diabetic patients with poor sleep quality.

This study demonstrates that the total prevalence of poor sleep quality in diabetic patients was 84.2%, with the mean ±SD of the global PSQI score (9.18 ± 3.73), highlighting the importance of assessing sleep quality in patients with T2D. Regarding GAD-7 score, 43.3% of participants were classified as anxious with the mean ±SD of the global GAD-7 score (8.0 ± 6.11). In addition, our findings demonstrate that’s 66.66% of the participants have an uncontrolled HbA1c (≥7), with Mean±SD (8.02 ± 1.63). Our results revealed a highly significant association between poor sleep quality and high levels of anxiety, as measured by the GAD-7 scale in the diabetic patients, independent of their glycemic control according to the Multivariate model used. These findings underline the crucial role of psychological factors in diabetes management. In conclusion, it is essential to integrate sleep and anxiety assessments into the care of diabetic patients to improve their overall well-being and optimize their treatment.

Firstly, the present study was based on a group of patients with T2D and without a control group, whereas studies like a case-control study and an equal percentage gender participants can boost statistical power. Secondly, in this study, it is difficult to examine the causal relationship because both variables are examined simultaneously and it is difficult to know which appeared before the other. For this reason, we will be studying this bidirectional relationship in an experimental animal model in future research. No objective tool was used to measure sleep quality, and sleep duration was estimated using a self-reported questionnaire. we found no significant correlation between HbA1c or BMI and sleep quality, which may be attributed to the small sample size of our study. Finally, recruiting participants from a single military hospital, even so, it may be representative, given that it is home to most of Morocco's specialists, may limit the representativeness of the sample and, consequently, the generalizability of the results to the entire Moroccan population with T2D.

Based on the findings of the current study, the following specific recommendations are made: healthcare professionals should pay greater attention to early detection of poor sleep quality in patients with type 2 diabetes and consider appropriate measures to improve sleep quality when necessary. A more in-depth assessment of sleep quality in type 2 diabetic patients using objective methods such as polysomnography in addition to the subjective tool to obtain more reliable results. Providing additional intervention for type 2 diabetic patients with poor sleep quality. More stringent interventions should be offered to for patients with poor glycemic control. To gain a clearer idea of the situation, a full survey including type 2 diabetic patients from other healthcare organizations in Morocco is required.

neuroscience.title: Case Report: Hyperactive delirium with psychotic symptoms associated with severe hypothyroidism during pembrolizumab therapy. Complete remission after levothyroxine and no recurrence after pembrolizumab rechallenge
neuroscience.abstract: Thyroid dysfunction is a common adverse event during pembrolizumab therapy, but severe hypothyroidism accompanied by acute neuropsychiatric symptoms is rare. We present the case of a 78-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal cancer who developed agitation, hallucinations, and confusion three months after initiation of Pembrolizumab. Evaluation revealed profound hypothyroidism (TSH 37.9 mU/L, free T3 <0.60 pmol/L and free T4 <0.5 pmol/L) and moderate hyponatremia without acute findings on neuroimaging. Levothyroxine therapy led to complete remission of neuropsychiatric symptoms, and pembrolizumab was safely restarted with close monitoring and no recurrence. This case underscores the importance of assessing thyroid function in acute psychiatric presentations during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and supports cautious rechallenge after stabilization. Severe hypothyroidism was considered a major contributor, although a multifactorial delirium, including the contribution of hyponatremia and the absence of CSF/EEG evaluation, cannot be excluded.
neuroscience.text:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of several advanced malignancies but may cause immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affecting multiple organ systems. Endocrine toxicities are among the most frequent immune-related adverse events, with thyroid dysfunction being particularly common during programmed cell death protein 1 inhibitor therapy, including pembrolizumab (, ).

Most cases of immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated hypothyroidism are detected through routine laboratory monitoring or present with nonspecific systemic symptoms such as fatigue, cold intolerance, or weight gain (). In contrast, severe hypothyroidism presenting predominantly with acute neuropsychiatric symptoms, including hyperactive delirium, hallucinations, and persecutory delusions, is rare and may be difficult to distinguish from other neurological, metabolic, or psychiatric causes ().

We describe the case of a 78-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal cancer who developed hyperactive delirium with psychotic symptoms in the context of severe hypothyroidism during pembrolizumab therapy. The symptoms remitted completely after levothyroxine replacement, and pembrolizumab was subsequently restarted without recurrence under close laboratory monitoring.

A 78-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal cancer began palliative pembrolizumab on July 4, 2025. Baseline thyroid-stimulating hormone was normal at 1.99 mU/L. Relevant comorbidities included chronic kidney disease, KDIGO stage G2, and mild aortic stenosis. She had no known previous psychiatric history and had lived independently prior to the index presentation. Approximately three months after pembrolizumab initiation (after four administrations), the patient developed progressive confusion and functional cognitive decline over about three weeks, followed by marked agitation and psychotic symptoms with persecutory/poisoning delusions. On October 3, 2025, she was brought to the emergency department for severe disorganization and agitation; she was disoriented in all spheres with incoherent responses and a nonfocal neurologic examination.

During the subsequent medical hospitalization, the clinical picture fluctuated. She was intermittently more accessible but remained at times disoriented, motorically restless, and increasingly agitated, with prominent visual hallucinations, persecutory and poisoning delusions, ideas of external control, evening and nocturnal agitation, barricading behavior, and verbal and physical aggression toward staff.

The diagnosis of hyperactive delirium was made clinically, consistent with an acute/subacute disturbance of consciousness and cognition, disorientation, incoherent thought and speech, psychomotor agitation, hallucinations and delusions, sleep-wake disturbance, and a fluctuating course in the context of acute medical abnormalities.

On physical examination during the initial hospitalization, the patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, without focal neurological deficits. During psychiatric hospitalization, the thyroid was not enlarged or tender, no nodules were palpable, and no peripheral edema was present. Cardiovascular examination showed a regular normofrequent pulse and blood pressure within the normal range. Neurological examination showed normal strength and tone, lively symmetric reflexes, no pathological reflexes, and no ataxia.

Medical evaluation was notable for severe hypothyroidism. On September 8, 2025, during interval monitoring, TSH had already increased to 41.20 mU/L. On October 3, 2025, TSH was 37.90 mU/L, free T3 was below the assay lower limit (<0.60 pmol/L; reference 3.74-6.11), and free T4 was below the assay lower limit (<0.5 pmol/L; reference 11.5-19.6). The relatively modest TSH elevation despite very low free thyroid hormone levels was interpreted cautiously; a rapidly evolving ICI-related thyroiditis with incomplete TSH equilibration was considered possible, whereas a partial central component could not be fully excluded from the available data. Concomitant laboratory abnormalities included moderate hypoosmolar hyponatremia and mild hypokalemia. Sodium was 135 mmol/L on July 4, 2025, 130 mmol/L on September 8, 2025, 124–125 mmol/L on October 3, 2025, with serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 21 mmol/L, and urine osmolality 202 mOsm/kg. Sodium improved to 128 mmol/L on October 4, fluctuated between 126 and 131 mmol/L during the acute medical hospitalization, and was 130 mmol/L on October 10. After transfer to psychiatry, sodium increased from 129 mmol/L on October 15 to 132–133 mmol/L during October and normalized to 139 mmol/L on November 3. Potassium was 3.3 mmol/L on October 3 and normalized after supplementation. Corrected calcium was within the reference range. CRP was mildly elevated during the acute admission. Vitamin B12 was borderline low, folate was normal, and treponemal serology was negative during the psychiatric admission. Neuroimaging did not reveal an explanatory acute lesion: cranial CT showed a small punctate hyperdensity in the left parietal deep white matter interpreted as possible hemorrhage versus calcification, and subsequent MRI described an occipital cavernoma without acute hemorrhage. Available cortisol values did not support clinically overt adrenal insufficiency: cortisol was 269 nmol/L on July 4, 619 nmol/L on September 30, 492 nmol/L on October 4, and 516 nmol/L in January 2026. However, adrenocorticotropic hormone values, sampling details, and a comprehensive assessment of other pituitary axes were not available in the records reviewed. Thyroid antibody testing was not documented during the acute episode. Delayed follow-up testing in August 2026 showed negative TSH receptor antibodies (<0.8 U/L; reference <1.8), mildly elevated thyroperoxidase antibodies (44 IU/mL; reference <20), and negative thyroglobulin antibodies (20 IU/mL; reference <115). Because these measurements were obtained several months after onset, they could not reliably define antibody status during the acute thyroid dysfunction. Lumbar puncture and EEG were considered but were not performed, initially because of severe agitation and later because of rapid clinical improvement and unremarkable MRI findings.

The main differential diagnoses included immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated encephalitis, acute structural brain pathology, adrenal insufficiency or hypophysitis, metabolic encephalopathy related to hyponatremia, and a primary psychiatric disorder. However, the temporal association with pembrolizumab exposure, the profound biochemical hypothyroidism, the absence of previous psychiatric illness, and subsequent remission after thyroid hormone replacement supported severe hypothyroidism as the principal contributor to the hyperactive delirium with psychotic symptoms. However, causal attribution remains limited by the probable multifactorial nature of delirium and by the absence of CSF and EEG evaluation.

Pembrolizumab was paused, and Levothyroxine was initiated on October 3. During medical hospitalization, symptomatic treatment with sedating/antipsychotic agents was limited by medication refusal and insufficient clinical response; severe agitation required intravenous midazolam, and she was transferred to inpatient psychiatry (October 12). At psychiatric admission, she had an agitated delirium with psychotic features, including vivid visual hallucinations, delusions of poisoning and persecution, altered consciousness and few clear moments. She arrived on levothyroxine 50 micrograms/day; the dose was increased to 100 micrograms/day on October 23 and to 150 micrograms/day on November 6 because of persistent biochemical hypothyroidism. Clinically, psychotic symptoms and agitation regressed during the psychiatric admission, allowing discontinuation of benzodiazepines and tapering of risperidone. On October 21, she still reported persecutory ideas. By October 27, staff documented fewer psychotic statements and increasing independence. By October 31, she reported no longer feeling persecuted, describing the previous experience as similar to a nightmare. On November 6 and November 11, she was awake and clear in consciousness, calm, coherent, euthymic, and without hallucinations or delusional thought content. At discharge on November 12, 2025, she was fully oriented, coherent, without positive psychotic symptoms, independent in basic and complex activities of daily living. At follow-up in April 2026, she remains on levothyroxine 150 micrograms/day, and pembrolizumab has been restarted at 3-week intervals. The thyroid laboratory is monitored every 6 weeks. She lives independently, and tumor staging showed stable disease. The clinical course, key laboratory findings, and treatment timeline are summarized in .

Timeline of symptoms and laboratory values.

This case describes hyperactive delirium with prominent psychotic symptoms associated with severe hypothyroidism and hypoosmolar hyponatremia during pembrolizumab therapy. The patient developed hyperactive delirium with prominent psychotic symptoms, including agitation, vivid visual hallucinations, and persecutory delusions, approximately three months after initiation of pembrolizumab. The complete remission of neuropsychiatric symptoms after levothyroxine replacement, together with the absence of previous psychiatric illness and the lack of an acute explanatory lesion on neuroimaging, supports severe hypothyroidism as the principal contributor to the clinical presentation. However, given the concomitant hyponatremia and incomplete neurological evaluation, causality cannot be established definitively.

Thyroid dysfunction is among the most frequent endocrine immune-related adverse events during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, particularly with programmed cell death protein 1 inhibitors such as pembrolizumab (). Antibody negativity does not exclude ICI-associated thyroid dysfunction (). Most cases are detected through routine laboratory monitoring or present with nonspecific systemic symptoms (, , ). In contrast, severe hypothyroidism may rarely present with acute neuropsychiatric manifestations, including delirium, hallucinations, and psychosis (, ). In the present case, the temporal sequence was clinically suggestive: thyroid function was normal before pembrolizumab initiation, severe hypothyroidism was documented at the time of acute neuropsychiatric deterioration, and symptoms resolved after thyroid hormone replacement and correction of metabolic abnormalities.

The diagnostic assessment also illustrates the complexity of acute mental status changes in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Relevant differential diagnoses included immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated encephalitis (), structural brain pathology, adrenal insufficiency or hypophysitis, metabolic encephalopathy, infection, and primary psychiatric disorder. Neuroimaging did not demonstrate an acute explanatory lesion, and normal cortisol and adrenocorticotropic hormone levels argued against adrenal insufficiency or hypophysitis. However, lumbar puncture and electroencephalography could not be performed because of severe agitation, which limits diagnostic certainty. Moderate hypoosmolar hyponatremia was also present and may have contributed to the delirium. Nevertheless, the profound hypothyroidism and subsequent complete clinical recovery after levothyroxine make pembrolizumab-associated severe hypothyroidism the most plausible primary driver. The diagnosis of hyperactive delirium was supported by altered consciousness, disorientation, incoherent thought and speech, psychomotor agitation, sleep-wake disturbance, hallucinations and delusions, and a fluctuating course. This presentation overlaps phenomenologically with myxedema psychosis; however, the prominent disturbance of consciousness and orientation, fluctuating cognitive status, motor agitation, and medical precipitants favored delirium with psychotic symptoms rather than a primary psychotic syndrome.

This case has practical implications for both oncology and psychiatry. New-onset agitation, hallucinations, psychotic symptoms, or delirium in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors should prompt rapid assessment for potentially reversible immune-related endocrine toxicities, including thyroid dysfunction and adrenal insufficiency before the symptoms are attributed to a primary psychiatric disorder. This is particularly important because such presentations may initially resemble primary psychiatric illness, especially when psychotic symptoms are prominent. Early recognition and treatment may avoid prolonged morbidity, unnecessary psychiatric treatment escalation, and premature discontinuation of effective oncological therapy.

Another relevant aspect of this case is the successful rechallenge with pembrolizumab. After clinical stabilization and adequate thyroid hormone replacement, pembrolizumab was restarted at three-week intervals with close laboratory monitoring and without recurrence of delirium or psychotic symptoms. Although conclusions from a single case must remain cautious, this observation suggests that rechallenge may be feasible after stabilization of endocrine immune-related adverse events, provided that careful interdisciplinary follow-up and regular thyroid monitoring are ensured.

The main limitation of this report is that causality cannot be proven definitively. The clinical presentation was probably multifactorial, with hyponatremia, sleep disruption, psychosocial stress, and possible medication-related factors potentially contributing to the delirium. No structured delirium scale was applied, although the clinical documentation supported the diagnosis. In addition, the absence of lumbar puncture, electroencephalography and serum antineuronal or onconeural antibody testing means that immune-mediated encephalitis or subclinical epileptic activity could not be fully excluded. A further limitation is that thyroid antibodies were not measured during the acute episode. Delayed testing in August 2026 showed mildly elevated thyroperoxidase antibodies with negative TSH receptor and thyroglobulin antibodies. These results suggest thyroid autoimmunity but cannot determine whether antibodies were already present at the onset of thyroid dysfunction or emerged later during the course of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. In addition, the thyroid assay platform, ACTH values, and a comprehensive assessment of other pituitary axes were not available in the records reviewed. Finally, as a single case report, the findings are not generalizable. Despite these limitations, the case highlights an important and reversible cause of acute neuropsychiatric deterioration during pembrolizumab therapy and supports systematic endocrine evaluation in similar clinical scenarios.

The patient reports good tolerance of the ongoing pembrolizumab therapy, which is currently administered every three weeks. Following the temporary interruption during hospitalization, restaging demonstrated stable disease. With regular follow-up, including laboratory monitoring every six weeks (including TSH and cortisol), she feels clinically stable and expresses satisfaction with her present condition and the ongoing treatment.

neuroscience.title: Reward Prediction-Error Fidelity: a testable hypothesis linking reinforcement learning mechanisms to applied behavior analysis for autism and neurodevelopmental conditions
neuroscience.abstract: Applied behavior analysis (ABA) has developed an effective technology of reinforcement delivery, including Discrete Trial Training, Natural Environment Teaching, and token economies, largely on functional-behavioral grounds. Computational neuroscience has independently produced formal accounts of reinforcement learning centered on prediction errors and credit assignment. I propose a testable hypothesis connecting the two: the effectiveness of a reinforcement procedure depends on the quality of the learning signal that its delivery produces on each occasion, a property I term Reward Prediction-Error Fidelity (RPE Fidelity). The property is decomposed into four dimensions, temporal credit, contingency, prediction, and outcome value, each corresponding to a construct long studied in behavior analysis. Formalized within an actor-critic model with eligibility traces, the four dimensions enter the learning update multiplicatively, which implies that they cannot compensate for one another and that the effect of each depends on the others and on the learner’s history. The combination rule distinguishes the hypothesis from the separate behavioral constructs it draws on, and its dependence on learning history distinguishes it from steady-state quantitative models of reinforcement. I situate the hypothesis within an integrative framework, discuss its application to autistic learners, including differences in reward processing and volatility estimation and the role of learner assent, and compare it with procedural fidelity, quantitative behavioral theory, and alternative learning models, including attentional, timescale-invariant, successor-representation, and Bayesian accounts. I derive nine predictions, specifying for each the result that would favor the hypothesis and the result that would favor its strongest competitor, and outline a staged research programme compatible with single-case experimental designs.
neuroscience.text:
Reinforcement is one of the few constructs studied with comparable rigor at both the neurobiological and the behavioral level of analysis, yet the dialogue between these two literatures remains surprisingly limited in practice. Neuroscience has, over the past three decades, produced a detailed mechanistic account of how the brain represents and updates value, from the discovery of the dopaminergic reward prediction error to the cellular dynamics of eligibility traces and synaptic plasticity. Independently, applied behavior analysis (ABA) has developed, refined, and empirically validated a technology of reinforcement delivery (encompassing procedures such as Discrete Trial Training (DTT), Natural Environment Teaching (NET), and token economy systems) almost entirely on functional-behavioral grounds, with comparatively little explicit reference to the underlying neurobiology.

This separation is not merely an academic curiosity: it means that many long-standing ABA practice principles (the immediacy of reinforcement, the differential durability of intermittent versus continuous schedules, the value of pairing tangible and social reinforcers) are empirically well supported but rarely explained in terms of the mechanisms that produce them. Conversely, neurobiological findings on reward learning rarely engage with the applied, real-world contingency management systems in which reinforcement is most systematically and repeatedly deployed. This article addresses that gap by proposing a specific, testable hypothesis; it does not attempt an exhaustive review.

I propose the following hypothesis. The effectiveness of a reinforcement procedure depends on the quality of the learning signal produced by each delivery, beyond the identity of the reinforcer and adherence to the written protocol. I term this property Reward Prediction-Error Fidelity (RPE Fidelity) and decompose it into four dimensions: temporal credit, contingency, prediction, and outcome value. Each of these variables corresponds to a construct that behavior analysis has long studied, namely immediacy of reinforcement, response-reinforcer contingency, schedule arrangement, and motivating operations. The claim specific to this article concerns how they combine. When the four dimensions are formalized as terms of a single learning update (Section 2.3), they enter multiplicatively rather than additively. This implies that they cannot compensate for one another: a severe deficit in any one of them limits learning regardless of the others, and the effect of improving one depends on the level of the rest. The combination rule distinguishes RPE Fidelity from the separate behavioral constructs it draws on, its dependence on the learner’s history distinguishes it from steady-state quantitative models of reinforcement, and together they make the hypothesis testable in a discriminating way (Section 7.2). RPE Fidelity is also distinct from procedural fidelity: a procedure can be delivered exactly as written while producing a degraded learning signal.

The argument proceeds from neural and computational foundations to applied reinforcement procedures, competing models, and discriminating empirical predictions.

The neurobiological basis of reinforcement is largely attributed to phasic activity in midbrain dopamine neurons, particularly within the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which project to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and prefrontal cortex. The seminal work of  established that these neurons do not simply signal the occurrence of reward, but rather encode a reward prediction error (RPE): a bidirectional signal reflecting the discrepancy between expected and received outcomes. Dopamine neurons are activated above baseline when reward exceeds expectation, remain unchanged when reward is fully predicted, and are suppressed below baseline when an expected reward is omitted.

This RPE signal has since been characterized as a biologically plausible teaching signal, capable of adjusting synaptic strength until an organism’s internal estimate of value converges with actual outcomes (). More recent work has complicated this picture without overturning it: dopamine neurons show functional heterogeneity, and a purely scalar, unidimensional account of the RPE signal appears insufficient to capture the full range of dopaminergic responses observed across tasks and brain regions (; ; ). Recent single-neuron recordings add a further complication: at least part of what was traditionally interpreted as a pure learning signal may instead reflect ongoing regulation of behavioral performance and motor vigor, indicating that distinct dopaminergic subpopulations may encode parallel value functions (). Alternative accounts go further, proposing that mesolimbic dopamine conveys causal associations between events rather than prediction errors (; see Section 6.10). The present hypothesis therefore requires only that the RPE constitute one important computational mechanism through which dopaminergic signaling contributes to reinforcement learning. It does not require a unitary account of dopamine function.

The RPE hypothesis derives much of its explanatory power from its correspondence with formal computational models of learning developed independently in psychology and machine learning. The  model first formalized the notion that learning is driven by the discrepancy between predicted and actual reinforcement, a principle later generalized by temporal-difference (TD) reinforcement learning algorithms (), which extend this logic across sequences of states and predictions rather than single associative events. The convergence between the firing patterns of dopamine neurons and the error term of TD models is widely regarded as one of the more notable points of contact between computational neuroscience and behavioral theory, while the field continues to debate how completely this convergence generalizes given documented dopaminergic heterogeneity (Section 2.1); it nonetheless provides a principled, if partial, bridge between operant learning as conceptualized in ABA and its underlying neural implementation.

Operant learning requires the learner to estimate not only the value of situations but also which response to emit in them. I therefore formalize the hypothesis within an actor-critic architecture (; ), which has been proposed as a model of the functional division between ventral and dorsal striatum (; ). The critic learns state values V(s) from the temporal-difference prediction error:

The actor maintains response preferences H(s,a), which determine the probability of each response through a softmax policy, and updates them using the same error:

where et(s,a) is an eligibility trace marking recently emitted responses as candidates for credit:

with λ ∈ [0,1] governing how quickly eligibility decays [TD(λ); ]. A formulation based on action values Q(s,a), such as SARSA(λ), leads to the same qualitative conclusions. Eligibility traces in this algorithmic sense are distinct from, but have been proposed to correspond to, the synaptic tagging processes described in Section 3.1 ().

Consider a single teaching trial in which the target response a* is emitted in state s and followed, after k time steps, by the first stimulus that reliably signals reward, and then by the outcome o. For simplicity, the outcome is treated as terminating the trial, so that V(st + 1) = 0. The four dimensions of RPE Fidelity then correspond to specific terms of the model.

When the error is computed, the eligibility of a* is (γλ)k. Temporal Credit Fidelity is therefore defined by k, the delay between the target response and the first reliable reward signal, rather than by the delay to the primary reinforcer. This distinction is central in applied settings. Once a stimulus such as praise, a token, or a marker has acquired value through pairing, its onset itself generates a prediction error [δ = γ·V(smarker) − V(sprev)], so that conditioned reinforcers can bridge delays far longer than the cellular window described in Section 3.1 (). The window of approximately 0.3–2 s therefore constrains, at the synaptic level, the interval between the response and the first reliable value signal, not the interval between the response and a backup reinforcer.

The reward term is r = u(o)·m, where u(o) is the unconditioned value of the outcome and m ∈ [0,1] is the learner’s current motivational state with respect to it. Motivating operations () act on m: satiation and habituation lower it, deprivation raises it. Outcome Value Fidelity is thus defined by the product u(o)·m at the moment of delivery, not by nominal reinforcer preference.

Outcomes that occur in the absence of the target response are learned by the critic as value of the context c, which forms part of V(st) at the time of the outcome. Because the error following the target response is computed against this baseline, δ = r − V(c), noncontingent outcomes that raise V(c) reduce the error that follows a*, and therefore reduce the actor’s update. Contingency accordingly acts through the value of the context, not only through the representation of the response. In the Rescorla-Wagner model with the context treated as a competing cue, asymptotic associative strength corresponds to ΔP = P(O|R) − P(O|¬R) under the conditions analyzed by , which provides a formal link between Contingency Fidelity and the classic contingency literature on operant behavior (; ).

Prediction Fidelity comprises two quantities that must be kept distinct. The first is the signed prediction error δ itself: an outcome that is fully predicted produces no error and supports no further learning, whatever its value. The second is associability, the rate at which the learner updates in response to a given error, which attentional models tie to recent unsigned error ():

The uncertainty-related dopaminergic signal described by  is more closely aligned with this associability term than with δ (Section 4.1). Prediction Fidelity therefore has two components: whether the delivery leaves the outcome informative given current expectation, and whether the schedule sustains associability appropriate to the current stage of learning. Replacing the fixed learning rate in  with αA·αt yields a hybrid formulation of the kind proposed by .

Substituting these terms, the update to the preference for the target response at the time of the outcome is:

describes the update on a single reinforced trial. Averaging over emissions of the target response that are and are not followed by the outcome, and assuming that the value of the context reflects noncontingent outcomes of the same kind and value, V(c) = P(O|¬R)·u(o)·m, the expected update per emission of the target response is:

In this form, all four dimensions appear as factors of a single product: temporal credit through (γλ)k, outcome value through u(o)·m, contingency through ΔP, and prediction through αt and through the dependence of the realized error on the learner’s current expectation. The derivation makes its assumptions explicit. The product form holds when noncontingent outcomes are of the same kind and value as contingent ones and are not signaled by a distinct stimulus; when they are signaled, V(c) does not rise and the contingency factor tends toward P(O|R), which is the basis of Prediction 2. Three consequences follow from , .

First, non-compensation. The dimensions enter  as factors of a product, not as terms of a sum. If any factor approaches zero [a delay long enough that (γλ)k ≈ 0, a context that already predicts the outcome as well as the response does, a fully satiated learner, or exhausted associability], the update approaches zero regardless of the other factors. At the level of the learning update, the combination rule is therefore multiplicative; whether the observable ratings of the profile (Section 6.8) show the same structure remains an empirical question, because the mapping from dimensions to ratings is itself imperfect.

Second, interaction. Because the dimensions multiply, the effect of improving one depends on the level of the others; the cross-partial derivatives of  are nonzero. For example, increasing outcome value should produce a smaller gain when temporal credit is poor than when it is good. This property of the model is tested directly by Prediction 1.

Third, history dependence. V(c) and αt change with the learner’s history, so identical delivery conditions produce different updates at different stages of learning. As expected value approaches u(o)·m, δ shrinks; this is why Prediction Fidelity is defined relative to the stage of learning, and why the same reduction in predictability can impair acquisition yet support maintenance (Prediction 3).

The multiplicative structure of ,  is not specific to the actor-critic formulation. A product of an error term, an eligibility or salience term, and a learning rate is shared by error-driven learning rules generally, from the  model, in which the prediction error is scaled by salience parameters of the stimulus and the outcome, to three-factor synaptic learning rules (). The combination rule is therefore a robust property of the family of models on which the prediction-error account rests, not a consequence of a particular modelling choice. The hypothesis does not claim to introduce a new learning algorithm. Its claim is that the variables applied behavior analysis manipulates on each delivery are the arguments of this product, so that a structural property of error-driven learning becomes an empirical constraint on applied procedures, where it has not been tested and where practice recommendations typically address timing, contingency, schedule, and reinforcer value as separate considerations. Where the present formulation does depend on specific modelling choices, namely the absolute scaling of the eligibility trace, the role of context value in contingency, and the history dependence carried by V(c) and αt, these choices generate the predictions that distinguish it from alternative accounts (Predictions 2, 3, and 6–9).

Each dimension corresponds to a construct already studied in behavior analysis: delay of reinforcement (), response-reinforcer contingency (; ), schedule arrangement (), and motivating operations (). These constructs specify the effect of each variable, but not how the variables combine, nor how their effects change with learning history;  specifies both. The account also differs from  Mathematical Principles of Reinforcement, which likewise has a multiplicative structure and whose coupling coefficient plays a role analogous to the eligibility trace. The difference lies in the third consequence: the Mathematical Principles of Reinforcement primarily describe steady-state response rates, whereas  describes trial-by-trial acquisition and contains terms, V(c) and αt, through which learning history modulates the effect of identical delivery conditions. The discriminating tests between the two accounts therefore concern learning trajectories rather than asymptotic performance (Section 7.2).

– describe model-free learning. Sensitivity to contingency degradation and to outcome devaluation are, however, classic signatures of goal-directed control (), and instrumental behavior is thought to reflect an arbitration between the two systems that shifts with training (). The hypothesis does not require that ABA procedures be learned exclusively through model-free computation; it requires only that the delivery conditions captured by the four dimensions determine the quality of the experience from which both systems learn. The two systems nonetheless make different predictions about Outcome Value Fidelity, which provides an additional test. Under goal-directed control, a change in m (for example, satiation before a session) should alter responding immediately, before the devalued outcome is experienced; under model-free control, it should alter responding only after the outcome has been experienced and the error updated. Because goal-directed control tends to predominate early in training and habitual control after extended practice, this difference should itself depend on the stage of learning.

The formal account specifies what would have to be true of the underlying computation for the hypothesis to hold; it does not show that ABA procedures are implemented by this computation. Alternative learning models, including attentional, Bayesian, successor-representation, and retrospective causal accounts, treat some of the same dimensions differently and are compared with the present formulation in Section 6.10.

A central question in translating dopaminergic mechanisms into applied practice concerns the temporal window within which reinforcement remains behaviorally effective. At the cellular level, this question has been addressed through the concept of a synaptic eligibility trace. Using optogenetic stimulation of dopaminergic and glutamatergic inputs separately in striatal medium spiny neurons,  showed that dopamine promotes spine enlargement only within a narrow window, approximately 0.3–2 s after the preceding glutamatergic input, with the precise boundaries of this window set by the kinetics of cyclic AMP regulation in thin distal dendrites. This work, together with the behavioral correlate described by , provides a candidate cellular mechanism consistent with the well-established behavioral principle that reinforcement is most effective when delivered promptly after the target response, while also showing that this window is a range with a specific molecular basis rather than a single fixed threshold. As formalized in Section 2.3, this window constrains the interval between a response and the first stimulus that reliably signals reward, which in applied settings is frequently a conditioned reinforcer rather than the primary outcome.

This finding offers a candidate mechanism for what applied behavior analysts have long formalized as the immediacy principle: reinforcement delivered without delay following a target response is, in many paradigms, associated with stronger and more reliable learning than delayed reinforcement, a pattern consistent with the eligibility-trace window described above. As Section 3.2 details, this should not be read as a fixed biological threshold that transfers directly to instruction; the size of the delay effect depends on whether the learner has other information supporting correct attribution of the outcome to the response.

Complementing this cellular evidence, behavioral studies in humans confirm that the timing of reinforcement shapes not only the rate of acquisition but also the durability of what is learned. In a motor-skill learning task, delaying reward delivery by a few seconds altered the trajectory of learning: training with a short delay (1 s) produced continuous improvement in performance, whereas a long delay (6 s) produced high initial learning rates followed by an early plateau, lower performance at the end of training, and reduced overnight consolidation (). The authors motivated this comparison with earlier neuroimaging evidence that short and long reward delays preferentially engage fronto-striatal and hippocampal systems, respectively; the study itself did not measure neural activity, so this dissociation remains a plausible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

These findings should not, however, be read as establishing a fixed, universal delay threshold that transfers directly from single-synapse recordings to classroom instruction. A substantial literature on human causal learning shows that the detrimental effect of a response-outcome delay depends heavily on whether the learner has structural knowledge of the relevant timeframe:  found that providing cues to the trial structure significantly improved causal judgments in the presence of delay, and a follow-up study showed that the negative effect of delay on causal learning could be abolished entirely by a change in instructions alone (). These studies measured explicit causal judgments in adults, and whether the same effect holds for implicit operant learning, particularly in children who cannot report their expectations about timing, remains an open question. Analogous findings from the behavior-analytic literature on delay-of-reinforcement gradients () and temporal discounting (), which do concern operant behavior directly, show that delay effects are well documented independently of any neurobiological account. Together, this evidence indicates that temporal contiguity and correct credit assignment are related but dissociable: a response and its consequence can be separated by several seconds and still be attributed correctly if the learner has adequate information about the response-outcome relationship. I therefore treat reinforcement timing not as a fixed biological threshold to be imported directly into instructional design, but as one input, among others, to the temporal credit assignment problem formalized in Section 2.3.

Discrete Trial Training (DTT) typically pairs a discriminative stimulus, response, and reinforcer within a tightly controlled and immediate sequence, while Natural Environment Teaching (NET) often involves greater variability in the interval between response and reinforcement due to its embeddedness in naturalistic activity (). Rather than treating this as evidence that DTT is intrinsically better aligned with the eligibility-trace window than NET, which is not a necessary property of either technology, the more precise question is how well timing and contingency are controlled within each method on a given occasion. Framed this way, RPE Fidelity becomes a property of how a procedure is implemented on a specific trial, independent of which ABA technology is used.

Once a target behavior has been established, the schedule by which reinforcement is delivered becomes a critical determinant of both its strength and its resistance to extinction, as established in the classic behavior-analytic literature on schedules of reinforcement (). Continuous reinforcement (in which every instance of the target behavior is reinforced) produces rapid initial acquisition but yields responding that extinguishes quickly once reinforcement is withdrawn. Intermittent schedules, by contrast, particularly variable-ratio (VR) arrangements in which reinforcement follows an unpredictable number of responses, generate higher and more sustained rates of responding that are considerably more resistant to extinction.

This behavioral asymmetry, known as the partial reinforcement extinction effect, has well-established behavioral explanations, including frustration theory () and sequential theory (), which attribute it, respectively, to the conditioning of responding in the presence of anticipatory frustration and to learned associations between sequences of nonreinforced responses and subsequent reinforcement. Neurobiological findings are compatible with these accounts but do not replace them. Phasic dopamine responses to reward-predicting stimuli vary monotonically with reward probability, whereas a slower, sustained component of activity has been reported to covary with outcome uncertainty, which is maximal at a probability of 0.5 (). The interpretation of this sustained component remains debated: it has been argued that it may arise from averaging, across trials, prediction errors whose positive and negative values are coded asymmetrically, rather than from a distinct uncertainty signal (). Under either interpretation, the finding bears on the associability component of Prediction Fidelity (Section 2.3) rather than on the prediction error itself, and it concerns the informativeness of reinforcement rather than unpredictability as such; it should not be read as implying that unpredictability should be maximized (Section 6.4).

A pilot study in an elementary school classroom embedded variable-ratio contingencies within a token-based game, with the explicit aim of eliciting reward prediction errors, and reported increased student engagement (). The study did not measure prediction-error signals, so its results are compatible with, but do not demonstrate, the involvement of the mechanism proposed here.

More broadly, the token economy, in which tokens earned for target behaviors are later exchanged for backup reinforcers, is among the most extensively evaluated reinforcement-based classroom strategies. Meta-analyses report large effects in general and special education classrooms, moderated by components such as backup reinforcer type and exchange schedule (; ), although an evaluation against What Works Clearinghouse standards concluded that methodological weaknesses in the single-case literature prevented classifying token economies as a best practice ().

The practical relevance of this evidence is sharpened by a systematic review of 96 published token-economy studies, which found that only 19% (18 of 96 articles) provided replicable, complete descriptions of all primary procedural components (). Token economies are known to be effective on average, but the specific configuration of their parameters, the token production schedule, the exchange schedule, and backup reinforcer characteristics, is often left underspecified in the published literature. This is precisely the gap that a dimensional account such as RPE Fidelity is positioned to address: rather than asking only whether a token economy was used, it asks which specific configuration of timing, contingency, predictability, and value parameters was in place.

Beyond token economies, differential reinforcement procedures, in which reinforcement is delivered contingent on a specific, targeted response class while other responses are placed on extinction, represent a second major family of reinforcement-based classroom interventions. A recent systematic literature review of differential reinforcement in applied settings for individuals with autism found large to very large effects across seventeen studies, with differential reinforcement of alternative behavior and of low rates of behavior producing particularly strong outcomes (). A complementary systematic review focused specifically on skill acquisition, rather than behavior reduction, found that differential reinforcement conditions favoring independent responding over prompted responding produced faster skill acquisition across the studies reviewed (). Together, these findings extend the evidence base for reinforcement scheduling beyond token economies to the broader family of differential reinforcement procedures used routinely in DTT and NET.

Meta-analytic evidence supports the effectiveness of Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention for young autistic children, although the scarcity of randomized designs introduces uncertainty into these estimates (, ; ; ). Because the present hypothesis concerns the parameters of reinforcement delivery rather than the effectiveness of comprehensive programmes, studies that manipulate individual reinforcement parameters, such as those reviewed above, are more directly relevant to testing it.

The evidence in this section bears on the Outcome Value and Prediction dimensions: it concerns the conditions under which the value of a reinforcer, and of the activity it follows, changes as a result of reinforcement itself.

The same reward circuitry that supports reinforcement-based learning can, under certain conditions, undermine motivation once extrinsic reinforcement is withdrawn, a phenomenon described as the overjustification effect. When performance-based monetary reward was introduced for an intrinsically engaging task and subsequently removed, activity in the anterior striatum and prefrontal regions declined in parallel with voluntary task engagement (). A meta-analysis of 128 studies found that tangible rewards contingent on engagement, completion, or performance undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation, more strongly in children than in college students (; see also ), although later syntheses show that incentives and intrinsic motivation jointly predict performance and that the effect depends on how directly the incentive is tied to the behavior measured ().

Two findings qualify the relevance of this literature for applied behavior analysis. First, a quantitative review of 65 data sets from individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities found a mean effect that did not differ from zero, with outcomes consistent with overjustification only somewhat more likely for behaviors already occurring at high levels without extrinsic reinforcement (); the risk therefore concerns mainly behaviors that already occur spontaneously, which bears on target selection rather than on the use of reinforcement as such. Second, the type of reinforcer appears to matter: in a recent functional imaging study, both monetary and social rewards preserved neural intrinsic value after withdrawal, but only monetary reward reduced behavioral motivational drive (). This dissociation offers a partial rationale for the common practice of pairing tangible reinforcers with social praise, and bears directly on the treatment of social reward in Section 6.5.

The same unpredictability that makes variable-ratio schedules effective for establishing durable, extinction-resistant behavior (Section 4.1) is mechanistically related to reinforcement dynamics documented in the behavioral addiction literature, where both the variability and frequency of reward delivery contribute to the addictive potential of a reinforcer (). This is not a reason to avoid variable-ratio schedules in ABA practice, which remain well supported, but a reason to apply them deliberately and with planned fading once a skill is consolidated, rather than sustaining high variability indefinitely.

The evidence reviewed in Sections 2–5 spans cellular, computational, behavioral, and instructional levels of explanation. I organize it around a single principle: a reinforcement event supports learning to the extent that its delivery allows the learner to answer four questions. Two concern credit assignment in the strict sense: what produced the outcome (contingency), and when the relevant response occurred (temporal credit). Two concern the computations that operate on that attribution: how much the outcome differs from what was expected (prediction), and how much it is worth at that moment (outcome value). I refer to the degree to which delivery conditions support all four as learning-signal quality, and to its measurable counterpart as RPE Fidelity. Because prediction errors shrink as an association is learned, the aim of a well-designed procedure is not to sustain large prediction errors indefinitely, but to keep each reinforcement event informative at the current stage of learning.

RPE Fidelity is conceptually distinct from the well-established construct of procedural fidelity, also termed treatment integrity, which quantifies the extent to which an intervention is delivered as designed and written (). A reinforcement procedure can be delivered with high procedural fidelity while still providing a poor learning signal, for instance when its schedule has become fully predictable. This distinction corresponds to the difference between M0 and M3 in Section 6.10.

The Neurobehavioral Reinforcement Translation Framework (NRTF) organizes this evidence across six levels of analysis. It is intended as an integrative heuristic rather than as an independently validated model.
