PubMed and Web of Science were searched for English-language publications from January 2010 to July 2026. The start date follows the formal proposal of HD as a DSM-5 diagnosis. The PubMed search string was (“hoarding disorder”[tiab] OR “hoarding symptoms”[tiab] OR “compulsive hoarding”[tiab]) AND (“obsessive-compulsive disorder”[tiab] OR OCD[tiab]) AND (genetics[tiab] OR heritability[tiab] OR polymorphism[tiab] OR epigenetic*[tiab] OR neuroimaging[tiab] OR MRI[tiab] OR fMRI[tiab] OR PET[tiab] OR SPECT[tiab] OR “functional connectivity”[tiab] OR “resting-state”[tiab] OR EEG[tiab] OR neuropsychology[tiab] OR cognition[tiab]), limited to English-language publications from January 1, 2010 to July 31, 2026. The equivalent Web of Science Core Collection search used the Topic field (TS) with the same three concept blocks and the same date and language limits. Results from the two databases were combined and duplicates removed. It was supplemented by backward citation tracing from every systematic review retrieved. Studies before 2013 were mostly within-OCD comparisons of symptom subgroups, whereas studies after DSM-5 began to recruit participants diagnosed with HD and to compare them directly with OCD ().

A study was eligible if it met any one of three criteria: (i) it reported original genetic, neuroimaging, or neuropsychological data from a case-control or cohort design with an explicit diagnostic or phenotypic definition for its hoarding or OCD sample; (ii) it was a published systematic review of one of these evidence types; or (iii) it was a foundational study published before 2010, identified by citation tracing from the systematic reviews retrieved under (ii) and included regardless of publication date, because it established the question under review (for example the first PET, fMRI, and clinical-comparison studies of hoarding). Conference abstracts, sources without obtainable full text, and commentaries without original data were excluded. Where two included studies drew on overlapping cohorts, both were kept because they report non-overlapping outcomes, and this is noted at first mention. Background and overview sources were used mainly to set context; for OCD neuroimaging, where primary studies are very numerous, narrative reviews and large mega-analyses were used to summarize the field.

Literature selection, the classification in , and the checking of findings against original sources were done by a single reviewer; no formal risk-of-bias instrument was applied. The 66 sources cited comprise 31 primary empirical studies, 12 systematic reviews, meta-analyses, or mega-analyses, and 23 background, clinical-overview, or narrative-review sources. The synthesis rests on the primary studies and systematic reviews; every primary study of hoarding, and every direct HD-OCD comparison, is characterized individually in ; OCD-only primary studies are described in the text.

In the mid-2000s, Pertusa et al compared five groups (severe hoarders without OCD, n = 27; OCD with hoarding, n = 25; OCD without hoarding, n = 71; an anxiety-disorder group, n = 19; and community controls, n = 21; total n = 163) on hoarding phenomenology, comorbidity, and functioning. They concluded that, in most cases, hoarding appeared to be a syndrome separate from OCD, linked to substantial disability and social isolation, although in about a quarter of the OCD patients with hoarding it was tied to typical OCD obsessions and compulsions. They called for replication, larger samples, and operational diagnostic criteria before any classification decision.

Saxena’s commentary of 2007 went further and argued that compulsive hoarding was a genetically and neurobiologically discrete syndrome. His reasoning drew on several lines of evidence: clinical features that set hoarding apart from other OCD symptoms (such as earlier onset, poorer insight, greater impairment, and a different comorbidity profile), strong familiality with suggestive linkage to chromosome 14, imaging findings of lower cingulate activity without the orbitofrontal and caudate hypermetabolism seen in other OCD (including his own PET study), and the consistently poor response of hoarding to cognitive-behavioral therapy. This argument is important because it supplies the neurobiological hypothesis that the present review tests: if hoarding rests on distinct biology, genetic, imaging, and cognitive studies should show it. The position was contested. A published rebuttal argued that hoarding overlapped substantially with OCD, was too heterogeneous to stand alone, and that the linkage evidence, which counted any hoarding symptom and not clinically significant hoarding, did not yet support a discrete syndrome. Saxena replied that studies recruiting patients specifically for compulsive hoarding found that many had no other OCD symptoms.

Mataix-Cols et al then reviewed the evidence for DSM-5, concluded that it was sufficient to recommend a new disorder, provisionally termed hoarding disorder, and noted a more conservative alternative, placement in an appendix pending further study, that was not adopted.

Under the earlier classification, hoarding was treated as one symptom of OCD. Yet the household clutter, fire risk, and interpersonal conflict caused by hoarding often occur independently of other OCD symptoms, and hoarding alone may cause substantial impairment in people who do not meet criteria for OCD. Hoarding also responds less well to standard treatment for OCD, and dimensional models of OCD overlap and cannot be divided along absolutely discrete boundaries.

Typical obsessions are experienced as intrusive and distressing thoughts that patients try to resist. The core of hoarding is excessive retention of possessions and difficulty discarding them; patients often lack the resistance and shame characteristic of OCD, and some view their hoarding favorably. Patients with HD are also more prone to poor insight, with many not regarding the accumulation as a problem, unlike most patients with OCD.

Onset and course differ: hoarding typically begins insidiously and follows a chronic course that worsens with age, rather than the waxing-and-waning pattern of classic OCD. Rates of comorbid attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and major depressive disorder in HD also differ from the typical OCD profile.

Treatment response is a further line of evidence. Hoarding symptoms typically respond less well to standard exposure and response prevention than other OCD symptoms, which has driven the incorporation of specialized elements, such as organizational skills training, into HD treatment protocols. For differential diagnosis, HD must also be distinguished from ordinary collecting, depression-related household clutter, and hoarding secondary to neurocognitive disorders such as dementia.

Neurobiological evidence was a supporting rather than a leading argument for the reclassification, and it is reviewed in detail in the sections that follow.  shows the timeline of the main contributions. Clinical and nosological milestones (red in the figure: Saxena 2007, Pertusa 2008, Mataix-Cols 2010, and the DSM-5 decision in 2013) are distinguished from neurobiological evidence (neuroimaging in orange, genetics in green, neuropsychology in purple). The figure shows that the clinical and nosological argument was built first, that early imaging and genetic studies appeared in parallel, and that structural imaging under DSM-5 criteria, the large genome-wide association study, and the most recent neuropsychological review appeared only after the reclassification. It shows chronology only and does not indicate the weight of each study.

Taken together, the clinical observations in the three sections above were the principal basis on which DSM-5 designated HD an independent diagnosis.

McKay et al evaluated the dimensional systems proposed by earlier factor-analytic studies of OCD, organized around symptom presentation and neuropsychological features such as contamination/washing, harm-related obsessions/checking, pure obsessions, and hoarding. By consolidating this dimensional evidence rather than treating OCD as a single entity, the review offered an analytic approach for stratified genetic and neuroimaging research, although the subtypes overlap.

Whether hoarding emerges as a separate dimension depends on the sample and method. In a multinational study of 1366 children, adolescents, and adults, Cervin et al assessed 87 specific symptoms with combined factor and network analysis and identified eight broad symptom dimensions; hoarding was clearly an independent dimension. In a study of 153 families comprising 330 diagnosed patients, Balachander et al found that symptom dimensions showed high concordance within families, suggesting that genetic factors may act at the level of symptom dimensions rather than uniformly across the OCD diagnosis.

Hoarding is not unique in this respect. A review by Proshina et al describes comparable dimension-level biological evidence for contamination/washing and symmetry/ordering, and the clinical correlates of the symmetry dimension have been examined in a Brazilian multi-site study of 1001 patients. The dimensional studies included in this review treated hoarding as a separate dimension; studies in which hoarding was merged into a broader factor were not captured by the search, and this is acknowledged as a limitation.

The heritability of OCD is moderate to high. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Blanco-Vieira et al, pooling twin and family studies from five databases, estimated phenotypic heritability at about 50%, with additive genetic effects accounting for 46% of variance and non-shared environmental effects for 54%, and monozygotic co-twin concordance for obsessive-compulsive symptoms of about 47%. Twin-based estimates reflect genetic contribution at the population level and cannot reveal specific risk variants. An early genome-wide association meta-analysis of clinically diagnosed OCD (2,688 cases) estimated SNP-based heritability at about 28%, but no locus reached genome-wide significance; the gap between twin and SNP-based estimates is sometimes termed missing heritability. Larger samples have since changed this picture: a Psychiatric Genomics Consortium analysis of 14,140 cases identified the first genome-wide significant locus, and the largest meta-analysis to date, of 53,660 cases and 2,044,417 controls from 28 European-ancestry cohorts, identified 30 independent loci, with a SNP-based heritability of 6.7% (higher, 16.4%, in clinically ascertained samples) and enrichment of signal in excitatory neurons of the hippocampus and cortex and in medium spiny neurons.

Candidate-gene work has focused mainly on serotonergic genes (for example SLC6A4) and glutamatergic genes (for example SLC1A1), in line with cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit models of OCD, but the more than 100 candidate-gene studies have produced inconsistent results. A meta-analysis of 113 association studies covering 230 polymorphisms found significant associations for 5-HTTLPR and HTR2A, and for COMT and MAOA in males only, each with modest effects, consistent with a polygenic model. Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation and other regulatory modifications, are also thought to contribute, although the studies summarized by Mohammadi et al remain exploratory and have not yielded a replicated epigenetic marker. A narrative review by Peedicayil found that most epigenetic studies of OCD examined DNA methylation (13 studies), mainly of the oxytocin receptor (OXTR), serotonin transporter (SERT), and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) genes; histone-modification and non-coding RNA studies were fewer, and the review concluded that findings were inconsistent across studies. A study that combined genetic and epigenetic data illustrates both the promise and the limits of this work: Grünblatt et al found, in a meta-analysis of family-based and case-control samples, that the LA allele of the SLC6A4 5-HTTLPR variant was associated with OCD (OR 1.21, p = 0.00018), and in a preliminary subset found higher methylation of a region at the start of the first intron in pediatric patients than in controls and adult patients; the authors state that the methylation result needs confirmation in an independent, larger sample. No epigenetic study specific to hoarding was identified among the sources retained for this review.

Most of the genetic studies below assessed hoarding symptoms in community or twin-based samples, mostly by self-report measures, and not in clinically diagnosed HD. In 5022 twins (about 89% female) from a UK registry, Iervolino et al estimated that genetic factors accounted for about 50% of the variance in hoarding in women, the only sex in which models could be fitted, with negligible shared environment; hoarding was measured by self-report and other OCD symptoms were not modeled. Nordsletten et al, in 2529 pairs of female twins from the same registry (the two samples overlap), decomposed two hoarding sub-components and reported heritability of 0.45 for difficulty discarding and 0.49 for excessive acquisition, with a genetic correlation of 0.77 between them, indicating substantial but imperfect overlap. In 7906 adult twins, Mathews et al estimated heritability at 36% for hoarding and 40% for OCD symptoms, with a genetic correlation of only 0.10 between them. This indicates a largely distinct genetic contribution to hoarding, although a correlation of 0.10 is not zero and does not rule out some shared genetic basis.

In a genome-wide association meta-analysis of seven international cohorts comprising 27,537 individuals, Strom et al reported a twin-based heritability of 26%–48% and an SNP-based heritability of 11% in an independent subset, with no loci reaching genome-wide significance. The architecture is therefore likely to be highly polygenic, and larger samples are needed for gene discovery. Twin-based and SNP-based heritability are estimated under different models and cannot be equated or used to cross-validate one another; together they indicate only that hoarding symptoms have a heritable component. The low SNP heritability is not an anomaly: for OCD, population-based symptom measures generally yield SNP heritability of 6%–14%, compared with 25%–43% for clinically diagnosed OCD.

Three further studies extend this picture. In 5293 adult twins from the Netherlands Twin Register, Zilhão et al estimated, from self-report questionnaires, a genetic correlation of 0.41 between hoarding and obsessive-compulsive symptoms and 0.35 between hoarding and tics, with genetic factors accounting for about half of the covariance between hoarding and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. This estimate is higher than the 0.10 reported by Mathews et al, so the degree of genetic overlap depends on the sample and measures. In a community sample of 5213 children and adolescents, Sinopoli et al found that a 5-HTTLPR variant in SLC6A4 was associated with hoarding without other obsessive-compulsive traits in males (OR 1.43, p = 0.009 after correction) but not in females, whereas SNP associations in SLC6A4, HTR2A, and HTR1B did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Finally, Cheung applied a transcriptome-wide association approach to published summary statistics from the hoarding-symptom GWAS (27,537 individuals) and an OCD GWAS (53,660 cases). Genetically predicted expression of gene sets for cellular senescence differed between the two phenotypes (p = 0.009), and gene sets for complement activation and synaptic pruning showed opposite directions in OCD. These results are hypothesis-generating only: the analysis is a single-author computational study of predicted, not measured, expression; the hoarding GWAS had lower power; there was no global multiple-testing correction, colocalization, or fine-mapping; and only European-ancestry data were used.

Twin heritability of hoarding (26%–48%) is of a similar order to that of OCD (about 50%), and in the same twin sample the heritabilities of hoarding and OCD symptoms were similar (36% and 40%) while their genetic correlation was low (0.10). This supports separability at the level of trait structure. Genome-wide significant loci for OCD emerged only with much larger samples, whereas the hoarding genome-wide study (27,537 individuals, symptom-based) found none; the two cannot yet be compared on equal terms. Candidate-gene and linkage studies of hoarding have been inconsistent, and larger samples are likely to be needed., No study has compared risk variants between clinically diagnosed HD and OCD; the only direct genetic comparison of the two phenotypes is an exploratory in silico analysis of summary statistics. The genetic evidence therefore supports a partly distinct heritable trait but not a disorder-specific genetic architecture.

Early neuroimaging from the 1980s focused on the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit. A narrative review by Hazari et al argues that this model is no longer sufficient alone and that findings of the past two decades implicate a wider associative network that includes the parietal cortex, limbic structures such as the amygdala, the cerebellum, the default mode network, and the salience network. Skarstam et al described the general view that genetic susceptibility and functional abnormalities in this circuit act together with maladaptive learning in forming obsessive-compulsive symptoms; this model synthesizes decades of heterogeneous findings and does not readily distinguish the circuit abnormalities underlying different symptoms.

By modality, the picture is as follows. Structural MRI findings are summarized below. PET and SPECT studies have mostly reported increased metabolism or blood flow in orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and caudate in symptomatic patients, which tends to attenuate with effective treatment. Task-based fMRI shows exaggerated orbitofronto-striatal responses during symptom provocation and error or conflict processing. Resting-state and connectivity studies report altered connectivity within and between CSTC loops and in the default mode and salience networks. EEG studies have linked neurophysiological features to symptom severity and treatment response, but the studies are few and results inconsistent.

To overcome the small samples of single studies, the ENIGMA-OCD working group combined 1830 patients with OCD and 1759 controls for subcortical volumes, and 1905 patients and 1760 controls from 27 sites for cortical thickness and surface area. Thalamic volume was larger than in controls in pediatric patients but smaller in adult patients, a reversal rather than a difference in effect size. Widespread cortical thinning was found mainly in medicated adult patients, and reduced surface area mainly in medicated pediatric patients, suggesting that adult and pediatric OCD may be affected by partially separable processes.

Task-based fMRI meta-analyses show how heterogeneous the OCD literature is. In a seed-based d mapping meta-analysis of statistical maps, patients with OCD (239 for error processing, 245 for inhibitory control) showed hyperactivation of the dorsal anterior cingulate, supplementary motor area, and right anterior insula during error processing, but hypoactivation of rostral and ventral anterior cingulate, thalamus and caudate, right anterior insula, and medial orbitofrontal cortex during inhibitory control. A separate activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis of 35 experiments (394 patients, 410 controls) found no convergent abnormality across all inhibitory-control experiments and a dorsal anterior cingulate effect only in cognitive-inhibition tasks. A narrative review of PET, SPECT, and fMRI studies similarly describes orbitofronto-striatal hyperactivity, especially during symptom provocation, with broader dorsolateral and posterior involvement and heterogeneity linked to symptom dimensions. In a resting-state mega-analysis of 1024 patients and 1028 controls from 28 ENIGMA-OCD samples, connectivity was widely reduced, mainly within and between sensorimotor, default-mode, and frontoparietal networks, with few increases involving the thalamus and no fronto-striatal difference.

Links between specific symptom dimensions and brain structure are far less developed. The ENIGMA analyses compared patients with OCD as a whole with controls and were stratified mainly by age group, medication, and clinical characteristics rather than by symptom dimension., Dimension-level work in OCD has so far concentrated on clinical correlates, for example for the symmetry dimension, and on symptom-provocation fMRI, so the relationship between structural alterations and symptom dimensions such as washing, checking, symmetry, or hoarding is still largely unexplored.

With the exceptions of Yamada et al, the Tolin et al studies, and the HD-only resting-state studies described at the end of this subsection, the studies in this and the next subsection are within-OCD symptom-grouping designs, not direct comparisons with an independently diagnosed HD sample.

Neuroimaging of hoarding goes back to PET. Saxena et al compared resting-state cerebral glucose metabolism in 45 patients with OCD (12 predominantly hoarding) and 17 healthy controls, at the time the largest sample studied with any functional imaging modality in OCD. They found significantly lower metabolism in the posterior cingulate and cuneus in the hoarding group than in controls, and significantly lower dorsal anterior cingulate metabolism than in non-hoarding OCD patients, and proposed that compulsive hoarding might be a neurobiologically distinguishable subgroup. All participants were free of psychotropic medication for at least four weeks, so medication was controlled in this study, although not in several of the others. The study used DSM-IV criteria and a hoarding subgroup of OCD patients; it can support heterogeneity at the symptom-dimension level but cannot be taken as evidence for an independent disease entity.

Yamada et al applied DSM-5 criteria and used voxel-based morphometry to compare gray matter in 17 patients with HD, 17 with OCD, and 17 healthy controls. Gray matter volume (p < 0.05) was significantly greater in Brodmann areas 10 and 11, the frontal pole and orbitofrontal cortex, in the HD group than in the other two groups, with no significant difference between the OCD and control groups. This runs counter to the earlier lesion-based hypothesis that frontal damage causes pathological hoarding. The difference does not by itself establish an independent etiological mechanism and may relate to illness stage or symptom severity.

Resting-state studies add network-level evidence but do not include OCD comparison groups. Levy et al compared 17 patients with HD only, 8 with major depression only, 10 with both, and 18 controls, and found lower connectivity in a task-positive cognitive-control network and greater connectivity in default-mode regions in HD only. In 24 patients with HD and 31 controls, Tomiyama et al found no difference in low-frequency fluctuation amplitude at a strict threshold, but reduced amplitude in the right inferior frontal gyrus at a more lenient voxel threshold (p < 0.005, cluster-level FDR p < 0.05) and, in patients with comorbid attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, reduced connectivity between this region and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. SPECT evidence in HD is limited to a single case report of a patient with OCD and severe hoarding, who showed fronto-temporal hyperperfusion and striatal, middle cingulate, and medial temporal hypoperfusion during severe symptoms; after improvement the hyperperfusion shrank and the hypoperfusion widened, but medication and treatment also differed between the two scans and no orbitofrontal abnormality was seen.

Mataix-Cols et al were the first to use a symptom-specific provocation paradigm: 16 patients with mixed-symptom OCD (DSM-IV) and 17 healthy controls each underwent washing, checking, and hoarding-related conditions and a symptom-unrelated aversive control within one design. Hoarding-related stimuli activated the left precentral gyrus and right orbitofrontal cortex, a pattern distinct from washing and checking. Because every patient contributed to every condition, this shows differing activation across symptom dimensions within one mixed-symptom OCD sample and cannot be extrapolated to HD as a separate entity.

In an fMRI study of 29 patients with OCD (13 with hoarding symptoms) and 21 healthy controls, An et al compared hoarding-related with general anxiety provocation. Patients with prominent hoarding showed stronger bilateral ventromedial prefrontal cortex activation, which correlated positively with anxiety ratings, whereas general anxiety provocation produced no such difference. This study also enrolled a hoarding subgroup within a DSM-IV OCD sample.

Two studies used formally diagnosed HD samples and direct HD–OCD comparisons. Tolin et al compared 24 patients with HD, 24 with OCD, and 24 controls on a response-inhibition task and found no difference in task performance but greater right precentral gyrus activation in HD during successful inhibition, distinct from OCD. In 43 patients with HD, 31 with OCD, and 33 controls, Tolin et al found reduced anterior cingulate and insula activity in HD when deciding about items belonging to others, but excessive activity when deciding about their own possessions, a pattern absent in OCD and controls. The pattern correlated with hoarding severity and self-reported indecisiveness, and the authors reported that it was not attributable to OCD or depressive symptom severity.

Four later studies compared HD with OCD directly using executive-function paradigms or electrophysiology. Suñol et al scanned 17 patients with HD, 18 with OCD, and 19 controls during stop-signal and switch-signal tasks: patients with HD responded faster and made more commission errors than both other groups, and showed right lateral orbitofrontal hyperactivation during successful switching and frontal deactivation during error processing, whereas patients with OCD showed hyperactivation of the right rostral anterior cingulate during error processing. Hough et al used Go/No-Go and Stroop tasks in 15 patients with HD, 17 with non-hoarding OCD, and 25 controls and reported greater activation in HD than in OCD in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula, and orbitofrontal cortex during response inhibition, and greater medial prefrontal activation in OCD than in HD during Stroop conflict. Hough et al relied mostly on uncorrected voxel thresholds and their groups differed in age and medication, whereas Suñol et al applied family-wise error correction within a frontal region of interest. Two EEG studies from the same group add a related electrophysiological signature. Error-related negativity during a flanker task was attenuated in 14 patients with HD relative to 27 with OCD, and the attenuation was larger in younger patients with HD. In a larger flanker-task sample (33 HD, 26 OCD, 35 controls), phase locking of the EEG signal was lower in HD than in both OCD and controls in the alpha and theta bands, and the effect was partly attenuated after adjusting for age. Despite its title, the latter study tested group differences with permutation-controlled mass-univariate statistics and did not report classification accuracy. An earlier meta-analysis of 13 studies (18 samples) had suggested only a marginal difference in error-related negativity between OCD with and without hoarding, limited to probabilistic-learning tasks and based on a subset of four studies.

While imaging findings in OCD as a whole center on orbitofronto-striatal-cingulate hyperactivity and increasingly distributed network changes, the hoarding studies report findings in orbitofrontal and frontal pole gray matter, the precentral gyrus, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate and insula., In the one structural comparison, OCD did not differ from controls where HD did, and in the decision-making study, hypoactivity and hyperactivity of anterior cingulate and insula depended on whose possessions were involved, a pattern absent in OCD. Whether these regions reflect hoarding-specific processes or the general features of OCD that are summarized above cannot yet be determined, because only seven studies compared HD and OCD directly and their regions and tasks differ. Orbitofrontal involvement is the most recurrent finding: it appears in studies using structural MRI, symptom provocation, and two different executive-function fMRI tasks,,,, although the direction and task context are not the same. The OCD-side meta-analyses report hypoactivation of medial orbitofrontal cortex during inhibitory control, whereas the HD studies report greater orbitofrontal activation in HD than in comparison groups, but the tasks, orbitofrontal subregions, and comparison groups are not equivalent, so this contrast should be read as hypothesis-generating. Electrophysiological studies add a different signature, reduced error-monitoring and phase-locking signals in HD relative to OCD.,

Reporting is uneven across the first six studies. Saxena et al required at least four weeks free of psychotropic medication (five for fluoxetine) before scanning, and Tolin et al reported that their key finding was not attributable to OCD or depressive symptom severity, indicating some statistical control for comorbidity but not necessarily medication-free status. For the other four studies, medication status and comorbidity control were not clearly reported in the sources consulted; this should not be read as evidence that they were not controlled. None of the six reports a standardized effect size, and none pre-specified a primary outcome, as expected of exploratory studies of this era (2004–2018); where several contrasts were examined, the contrast emphasized by the original authors is reported here as the main finding. The four later studies are similarly small (14 to 33 patients with HD per study), and one of them (Hough et al) explicitly relied on uncorrected thresholds; in the EEG studies the HD group was older or differed in sex or medication from the comparison groups.,

A meta-analysis of 115 case-control studies (3,452 patients) of adult OCD found medium effects for all executive-function subdomains, processing speed, and sustained attention, a large effect for nonverbal memory, and small effects for visuospatial ability, working memory, and verbal memory. A second meta-analysis of 88 studies found worse performance in patients with OCD on visuospatial memory (the largest effect), executive function, verbal memory, and verbal fluency, with small-to-medium effects overall and preserved auditory attention. These meta-analyses pooled patients with OCD as a whole; they do not tell us whether patients with predominant hoarding differ from other patients with OCD.

Genetic and neuroimaging research both point, directionally, toward partially distinguishable neurobiological features in hoarding-related phenotypes, although they are not fully consistent about genes, regions, or direction of effect. Neuropsychological research is more complicated.

A narrative review by Grisham and Baldwin summarized neuropsychological and neurophysiological findings in HD and attributed many inconsistencies to differences between samples with OCD and hoarding and samples with hoarding alone, and to the frequent use of OCD-only comparison groups. The earliest systematic review, by Woody et al, covered research on cognitive function in hoarding published before 2014, focusing on decision-making, categorization, and attention. It concluded that deficits in categorization and inhibitory control needed further investigation, and noted that comorbid depression and age had not been consistently controlled and that diagnostic criteria were not uniform across samples. Gledhill et al reviewed 12 studies, generally requiring a clinician-delivered interview to establish the hoarding diagnosis, and found relatively consistent evidence of deficits in sustained attention, motor inhibition, and organization, with inconsistent evidence in other executive domains. The authors flagged three limitations: many included studies drew samples primarily diagnosed with OCD, their search window (2011–2013) predated DSM-5 criteria, and some studies did not use a clinical interview. The most recent review, by Stumpf et al, searched MEDLINE, SCOPUS, and LILACS, retrieved 197 studies, and included 22 case-control studies totaling 1757 patients, far more than the previous two. Apart from categorization, patients with HD showed no significant impairment across most cognitive domains, including attention, memory, and decision-making.

The three reviews therefore agree only that some studies report impaired sustained attention and inhibitory function, whereas evidence in working memory, decision-making, and cognitive flexibility is inconsistent. This does not necessarily contradict the genetic and neuroimaging evidence. Three methodological points are relevant: sample heterogeneity (illness duration, severity, and instruments vary), the limited ecological validity of laboratory tasks, and inconsistent operational definitions of cognitive domains combined with generally low statistical power.

Cognitive impairment is reasonably well documented in OCD as a whole, whereas in HD it is limited to a few domains and inconsistent. Direct cognitive comparisons between HD and OCD are rare: the three HD reviews do not report an OCD comparison (), and the few primary comparisons disagree. Morein-Zamir et al found that patients with OCD and severe hoarding and patients with HD without OCD showed similar deficits relative to controls in response inhibition, set shifting, spatial planning, and probabilistic reversal learning, with no significant differences between the two hoarding groups. In 20 patients with HD, 19 with OCD and minimal hoarding, and 14 with OCD and high hoarding, objective performance on inhibition, attention, and immediate and delayed nonverbal memory was comparable across groups, although the OCD-high-hoarding group was more often impaired on delayed verbal memory. In a decision-making task under risk, 29 patients with OCD, 29 with HD, and 28 controls showed shared differences in risk attitude, but hoarding severity and compulsion severity related to probability weighting in opposite directions. Performance on the imaging tasks did not differ between HD, OCD, and controls in one study, whereas patients with HD performed worse than both other groups in another. The preceding sections organized evidence by discipline. Here it is organized by how far each finding travels toward answering whether HD is a genuine diagnostic entity, using the four questions introduced above. Evidence that settles one question does not automatically settle the next. This section synthesizes and does not introduce new studies.

At the symptom and phenomenological level, hoarding and OCD differ in the following ways. OCD is driven by intrusive, distressing obsessions, with doubt, perceived threat, and a need for control or certainty leading to compulsions that relieve distress. In HD the core is difficulty discarding and a perceived need to save, usually with emotional attachment to possessions, little resistance or shame, poorer insight, and prominent indecisiveness, attention, and organizational difficulties.,, In a similar uncertain situation, OCD is therefore more likely to be marked by threat and doubt, and HD by problems of control, attention, and decision-making. This is an interpretation from clinical accounts, not a tested finding.

The biological evidence on separability is suggestive but not yet consistent. Mathews et al found a genetic correlation of only 0.10 between hoarding and OCD symptoms. Twin studies also show that hoarding itself is heritable, at about 50% in women in one study and with partly distinct genetic influences on difficulty discarding and excessive acquisition, but these studies did not model other OCD symptoms and so do not bear on separability directly. Two non-genetic lines point the same way: hoarding emerged as a distinct symptom dimension in a large factor and network analysis, and dimensions, including hoarding, clustered within families. The genetic correlation between hoarding and obsessive-compulsive symptoms ranged from 0.10 to 0.41 across twin samples, so the overlap is not yet well estimated. These studies rarely used a formal DSM-5 HD diagnosis. Comparable dimension-level evidence also exists for contamination/washing and symmetry/ordering, so separability of a dimension is not by itself evidence for a separate disorder.

Neuroimaging: twelve studies, one using PET, one structural MRI, eight fMRI, and two EEG, each reported at least one significant between-group difference, although for one of them (Tomiyama et al) only at a lenient threshold.,,, Seven compared HD with OCD directly. The regions implicated, namely posterior cingulate, orbitofrontal and frontal pole cortex, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, precentral gyrus, anterior cingulate, and insula, overlap only partially, and the most recurrent are orbitofrontal cortex,,,, anterior cingulate,, and the precentral gyrus, but in opposite hemispheres., The two executive-function fMRI studies from independent groups both found greater orbitofrontal activation in HD,, the closest the field comes to a convergent result, but they used different tasks and small samples. Several of the earlier studies do not clearly report whether findings survived whole-brain correction for multiple comparisons, one of the later studies explicitly used uncorrected thresholds, and another applied correction only within a frontal region of interest. A group-level difference has been shown repeatedly; a specific, reproducible neural signature has not.

Genetics and cognition: genetic differences are limited to heritability and genetic-correlation estimates from community samples, with no genome-wide significant locus yet reported for hoarding symptoms. The only direct comparison of risk-related signals between the two phenotypes is an exploratory in silico analysis whose opposite-direction pathway signals still need validation. Neurocognitive differences are inconsistent, as discussed above. Other biological systems, such as immune and endocrine processes, were not part of this review’s search, and we are not aware of direct HD–OCD comparisons of them among the sources reviewed here; they are a plausible target for future integrative work. Group-level evidence is therefore clearest for neuroimaging and electrophysiology, exploratory for genetics, and inconsistent for cognition.

Here the evidence becomes markedly thinner. A group difference could reflect a mechanism unique to hoarding, but equally illness severity, chronicity, comorbid depression, medication exposure, or a general marker of psychiatric distress. None of the neuroimaging studies was designed to adjudicate between these possibilities: among the first six, only one controlled for medication, only one controlled statistically for comorbidity, and none controlled for both, and the later studies report group differences in age, sex, or medication that limit interpretation. The neuropsychological evidence adds a complication: if the brain differences reflected a specific, behaviorally consequential mechanism, a corresponding behavioral impairment would be expected, yet the three systematic reviews found impairment limited to a few domains (such as categorization, sustained attention, and inhibition) and none across most others. This does not disprove etiological specificity, but it removes one form of supporting evidence, and no other has taken its place.

This is the question a clinician actually needs answered, and the literature is silent rather than merely cautious. None of the primary studies or systematic reviews examined reports a diagnostic accuracy statistic for any genetic, imaging, or cognitive measure of HD, none has validated a classifier in a held-out sample (including studies whose titles refer to “discriminating” HD from OCD, which tested group differences only), and none has shown that group-level differences separate individual patients from OCD patients or controls. Even for OCD vs healthy controls, a machine-learning classifier trained on resting-state connectivity from 1024 patients and 1028 controls reached an area under the curve of only 0.57 to 0.67, which shows how far imaging markers are from individual-level diagnosis. The gap between “groups differ on average” and “this measurement can diagnose a person” is the gap this literature has not yet crossed. Individual-level diagnostic utility should be a major focus of future research.

Read across the four levels, the evidence forms a gradient, not a single verdict. Trait separability is partly supported. Group-level differences have been reported repeatedly but do not converge across studies or replicate. Etiological specificity is asserted more often than tested. Individual-level diagnostic utility does not yet exist. Multimodal approaches that integrate genetics, neuroimaging, cognitive measures, and longitudinal clinical data may eventually provide stronger evidence than any single modality, but no study has yet applied them to HD vs OCD, and this does not alter the present conclusions.

Differences in treatment response were among the clinical reasons for the independent diagnosis. Treatment for HD has not been standardized, and standard cognitive-behavioral techniques for OCD, including exposure and response prevention, show only limited effect. Components specific to hoarding, such as organizational skills training, are described in the clinical literature, but whether they outperform standard protocols has not been established in high-quality randomized trials.

There are only speculative links between treatment and the biological findings. The anterior cingulate and insula pattern during decisions about possessions and its association with indecisiveness, and the ventromedial prefrontal activation associated with anxiety during hoarding provocation, would fit treatment elements that target decision-making and organization. However, no study has tested whether these neural measures predict or change with treatment response. At present, treatment response is clinical, not biological, support for the distinction. Marker-based treatment selection remains a research aim, not a clinical practice.

Has the DSM-5 reclassification of hoarding disorder been supported by subsequent neurobiological studies? The answer is a cautious partial yes at the group level and no at the individual level. Hoarding behaves as a heritable, partly separable trait, and a few small studies report group-level brain differences, but these have not converged on a replicated circuit, neuropsychological differences are inconsistent, and no study has tested individual-level diagnostic utility. Neurobiological evidence therefore provides supplementary, not definitive, support; the reclassification rests mainly on clinical evidence.

The conclusions are limited by small, heterogeneous, and mostly unreplicated primary studies, by the mixed use of DSM-IV and DSM-5 definitions, by the narrower coverage of OCD than of HD evidence, and by the review design itself: a single-reviewer narrative review without dual screening, risk-of-bias assessment, or formal evidence grading, drawing mainly on samples from high-income countries and not covering immune or endocrine evidence.

Future work should use larger, pre-registered, multi-site studies with standardized DSM-5 criteria and direct HD–OCD comparisons, control medication and comorbidity, and use multimodal and longitudinal designs. Testing individual-level diagnostic utility should be a priority.

neuroscience.title: Applications of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of children with cerebral palsy: a narrative review
neuroscience.abstract: Noninvasive brain stimulation has emerged as a promising adjunctive strategy for pediatric neurorehabilitation, particularly for children with cerebral palsy. This narrative review, informed by a structured literature search, summarizes current evidence on transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in children with cerebral palsy, with emphasis on neurophysiological mechanisms, brain network targets, clinical outcomes, safety, and future translational directions. Cerebral palsy is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent motor impairment and frequent sensory, cognitive, communicative, behavioral, and musculoskeletal comorbidities. Although multidisciplinary rehabilitation remains the foundation of clinical management, improvements in higher level motor control, cognition, communication, and real world participation are often constrained by training intensity, adherence, developmental heterogeneity, and resource availability. Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies indicate that children with cerebral palsy may present with corticospinal tract impairment, altered cerebellar thalamic cortical circuitry, interhemispheric inhibitory imbalance, and atypical development of frontoparietal executive control and language related networks. These findings provide a rationale for targeting the primary motor cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and selected language related cortices with neuromodulatory interventions. At the mechanistic level, transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation may influence cortical excitability, NMDA receptor mediated long term potentiation and long term depression like plasticity, interhemispheric inhibition, and functional connectivity within distributed neural networks. Current evidence from small to moderate sized randomized trials and recent systematic reviews suggests that these techniques, when combined with task specific rehabilitation, may provide additional benefits for gross motor function, gait, balance, upper limb dexterity, spasticity, and selected cognitive, dual task, and communication outcomes. Available data also suggest acceptable short term safety and tolerability when appropriate pediatric screening and recommended stimulation parameters are applied. This review summarizes the current research progress on noninvasive brain stimulation in children with cerebral palsy and highlights its potential value for optimizing individualized neurorehabilitation strategies and improving motor, cognitive, and communication related outcomes.
neuroscience.text:
Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of neurodevelopmental disorders originating in the fetal or infant period that result from non-progressive disturbances or lesions in the developing brain. Its hallmark features are persistent disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation (). International consensus further emphasizes that CP is not merely a motor disorder; multisystem involvement, including sensory, cognitive, and communication impairments, epilepsy, and secondary musculoskeletal complications, is common in clinical practice, making CP a highly heterogeneous syndrome that spans the entire life course (, ). Epidemiological data indicate that the prevalence of CP among live births is approximately 1.5 to 3.0 per 1000 in most countries. A substantial proportion of affected children, in addition to limb motor limitations, also present with visual and auditory impairments, epilepsy, and cognitive and language difficulties. These comorbidities are closely associated with functional independence, academic performance, and social participation, yet may still be underestimated in routine follow up and rehabilitation decision making (–).

Current management of CP is centered on multidisciplinary comprehensive rehabilitation, including physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, orthotic management, and pharmacological interventions. These approaches have moderate level evidence for improving gross motor function, muscle tone, and certain activities of daily living (, ). However, several systematic reviews have shown that most rehabilitation therapies require long term, high frequency training to achieve clinically meaningful improvements. Treatment effectiveness is highly dependent on family resources and adherence, and traditional rehabilitation often reaches a plateau for complex functional domains such as higher order motor control, cognition, and communication, with limited additional gains thereafter (, ). Therefore, integrating adjunctive interventions that can directly modulate central nervous system plasticity into existing rehabilitation frameworks, so as to enhance training efficiency and raise functional ceilings, has become an important research and clinical priority.

Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) comprises a rapidly advancing class of neuromodulation techniques, primarily including transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). tDCS delivers low intensity direct current through scalp electrodes to modulate cortical excitability and plasticity in a polarity dependent manner. rTMS, based on electromagnetic induction, applies repetitive stimulation at specific frequencies and patterns to induce synaptic plasticity changes resembling long term potentiation or long term depression (, ). In adults, NIBS has demonstrated moderate to good efficacy as an adjunct to medication and rehabilitation training for post stroke motor and language impairments, Parkinson's disease, and depressive disorders, and it is generally safe and well tolerated when applied within recommended parameter ranges (, ).

The pediatric brain is characterized by heightened plasticity, which theoretically provides an advantage for NIBS in promoting neural network reorganization. At the same time, it raises greater concerns regarding dose response relationships, developmental stage specific mechanisms, and long term safety (, ). Existing systematic reviews suggest that tDCS and rTMS are overall safe and feasible in CP and other pediatric motor disorders following brain injury, with promising signals for outcomes such as upper limb function, gait, and balance. Nevertheless, most studies have focused primarily on gross motor outcomes, and evidence remains limited for more complex domains, including cognition, language, and cognitive motor dual task performance. In addition, stimulation parameters and target selection lack standardized guidelines (, ). Against this background, this narrative review aims to summarize the applications of NIBS, with an emphasis on tDCS and rTMS, in the treatment of children with CP. We outline the main techniques and their characteristics in neurological disorders, review brain network alterations in CP and the neurophysiological mechanisms of tDCS and rTMS, synthesize evidence on motor, cognitive, and language outcomes as well as safety, and discuss future research directions and translational strategies to provide clearer theoretical and evidence based support for target selection and individualized intervention protocols.

This review addresses the neurophysiological mechanisms of non invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) and their network level interpretations, together with clinical outcomes across motor, cognitive, language and communication, and dual task domains in children with cerebral palsy.

English language literature was searched in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and reference lists of included articles were screened to identify additional relevant studies. The search covered database inception to 25 December 2025. Search terms were grouped into condition and population, intervention, and outcomes or mechanisms, and combined using Boolean operators. An example PubMed search string was: (“cerebral palsy” OR “perinatal stroke” OR “hemiplegia”) AND (“child” OR “pediatric” OR “adolescent”) AND (“transcranial direct current stimulation” OR “tDCS” OR “repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation” OR “rTMS” OR “TMS” OR “non invasive brain stimulation”).

Eligible studies included interventional research evaluating tDCS or rTMS in children and adolescents aged 0 to 18 years with cerebral palsy or closely related motor disorders attributed to non progressive pediatric brain injury. Eligible study designs included randomized controlled trials, controlled clinical studies, crossover studies, and prospective or retrospective studies reporting clinical outcomes after stimulation. Relevant systematic reviews and meta analyses were also included to support synthesis across outcomes and protocols. Studies were required to report at least one outcome in motor function, gait, balance, upper limb performance, spasticity or muscle tone, cognition, executive function, attention, language or communication, dual task performance, and or safety and tolerability outcomes. Exclusion criteria included non English publications, conference abstracts without sufficient methodological detail, case reports with fewer than five participants, and studies not involving tDCS or rTMS or not including an eligible pediatric population.

Records were screened at the title and abstract level, followed by full text assessment for eligibility. Two reviewers independently screened records and assessed full texts, disagreements were resolved by discussion, and a third reviewer adjudicated when consensus could not be reached. For studies meeting inclusion criteria, information extracted for narrative synthesis included participant characteristics and functional severity when reported, stimulation modality, target and stimulation parameters, number of sessions and total dose, concurrent training content, outcome measures and assessment time points, follow up duration, and adverse events. Adult studies and studies in other pediatric neurodevelopmental disorders were cited only when pediatric cerebral palsy evidence was limited, and were used as supplementary support for mechanistic interpretation and safety considerations.

The pathological substrates of cerebral palsy include cortical and subcortical gray matter injury, perinatal white matter injury including periventricular leukomalacia, periventricular white matter lesions, and developmental brain malformations. These abnormalities may involve multiple systems, including the corticospinal tract, cerebellum, brainstem, cortico cortical circuits, and frontoparietotemporal connectivity (, ). Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies indicate that children with spastic CP commonly exhibit reduced fractional anisotropy in the bilateral or unilateral corticospinal tract, reflecting compromised tract integrity. The severity of these alterations is closely associated with abnormal muscle tone, co contraction, and deficits in gross motor function (). In this context, effective descending drive from the primary M1 to anterior horn motor neurons is weakened, while activity in compensatory pathways, such as the reticulospinal tract, may be upregulated. This pattern is considered an important neurobiological basis for motor phenotypes characterized by the coexistence of spasticity and weakness (, ).

Beyond descending motor pathways, the cerebellum and basal ganglia may also be affected, particularly in children with ataxic CP and in a subset of those with spastic CP. In these cases, reduced cerebellar volume and abnormal diffusion metrics in the cerebellar peduncles and cerebello thalamo cortical pathways are more prominent, and clinically they are often manifested as impaired postural control, increased gait variability, and reduced balance capacity (). Functional MRI studies further suggest that, during lower limb motor tasks, children with CP show decreased functional connectivity within cerebello motor cortical networks. During relatively simple voluntary movement tasks, more widespread and non specific activation may be observed, suggesting that basic motor performance may require recruitment of additional neural resources but with lower network efficiency (, ). Collectively, M1 and cerebello cortical circuits can be considered key network nodes underlying motor impairment in CP and represent major potential targets for NIBS to modulate motor function.

In hemiplegic cerebral palsy, imbalance in transcallosal interactions is thought to contribute to maladaptive reorganization of motor networks. Transcranial magnetic stimulation studies have shown increased transcallosal inhibition from the contralesional M1 to the ipsilesional M1, whereas cortical excitability and corticospinal output from the ipsilesional M1 are relatively reduced. This asymmetric inhibition is associated with poorer motor function of the affected limb (). A similar pattern has been observed in children with hemiplegia secondary to perinatal ischemic stroke, in whom some individuals exhibit atypical motor representations, with increased bilateral limb output from the contralesional hemisphere, which may further diminish the contribution of the injured hemisphere ().

Based on this model, NIBS in cerebral palsy commonly adopts two complementary strategies. One strategy is to enhance excitability and descending output of the ipsilesional M1 using anodal tDCS or high frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. The other strategy is to suppress excessive activity of the contralesional M1 using cathodal tDCS or low frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, thereby reducing pathological inhibition of the ipsilesional hemisphere and promoting restoration of interhemispheric functional balance (, ). Notably, the interhemispheric inhibition model may vary across etiologies and developmental stages, indicating substantial heterogeneity. Therefore, clinical application requires more refined stratification and individualized selection informed by neuroimaging and electrophysiological phenotypes.

Beyond the motor system, children with cerebral palsy commonly exhibit cognitive and language impairments of varying severity. The neurobiological basis of these deficits primarily involves atypical development of prefrontal and parietal networks, as well as language related networks (). Structural imaging studies suggest that a subset of children with cerebral palsy show reduced volume and compromised integrity of frontal white matter and the anterior portion of the corpus callosum, which are closely associated with poorer executive function, reduced attentional control, and slower processing speed (, ). Task based functional MRI and functional near infrared spectroscopy studies have shown abnormal activation patterns of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and frontoparietal networks during working memory, inhibitory control, and dual task walking. These patterns are characterized by more widespread or higher magnitude activation compared with typically developing peers, together with reduced efficiency metrics associated with task performance, such as decreased task related desynchronization amplitude. This suggests that children with cerebral palsy may recruit greater neural resources to sustain relatively lower behavioral performance (). Resting state studies have also reported altered functional connectivity between the default mode network and the frontoparietal control network, which may be related to attentional fluctuations and cognitive fatigue ().

With respect to language, a substantial proportion of children with spastic or mixed cerebral palsy present with expressive language delay, dysarthria, and childhood apraxia of speech. Neuroimaging studies indicate structural and functional connectivity alterations involving the left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area), the supramarginal gyrus, and their connections with the auditory cortex (, ). In some children, language lateralization is incomplete or atypical, with greater involvement of the right hemisphere in language processing. This pattern may reflect post injury redistribution of language function in early development, but it has also been associated with constraints in language efficiency and fine grained expressive abilities (). Collectively, these findings provide a neurobiological rationale for considering the DLPFC, Broca area, and adjacent cortical regions as key targets for NIBS to modulate cognition and language.

Children with cerebral palsy have substantially higher rates of anxiety, depression, chronic pain, and sleep disturbances than typically developing children (, ). Although the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain incompletely understood, accumulating evidence suggests that imbalance within prefrontal and limbic systems plays an important role (, ). In adults with depressive and anxiety disorders, abnormal functional connectivity between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala is regarded as a core mechanism of impaired emotion regulation. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and tDCS targeting the DLPFC have been shown to improve mood and certain cognitive biases in these populations (). Although direct evidence in children with cerebral palsy is limited, findings from chronic pain, neuropathic pain, and sleep disorder research in other populations suggest that persistent pain and sleep related symptoms may involve maladaptive cortical plasticity, altered thalamocortical dynamics, and disrupted sleep wake regulatory circuits (). Moreover, evidence from other populations indicates that tDCS can alleviate chronic pain and insomnia by modulating activity in M1, S1, and the DLPFC, providing a theoretical basis for future investigation of NIBS as an adjunctive approach for comorbidity management in cerebral palsy (, ). The multisystem brain network alterations and candidate NIBS targets discussed above are summarized in .

A shared feature of tDCS and rTMS is the ability to modulate excitability of targeted cortical regions under non invasive conditions and to induce durable changes in synaptic and network plasticity. tDCS applies a weak continuous current that can slightly depolarize or hyperpolarize neuronal membrane potentials, thereby altering the probability of neuronal firing during stimulation. Post stimulation effects can persist for tens of minutes to several hours and are commonly linked to NMDA receptor dependent mechanisms resembling long term potentiation and long term depression (, ).

Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation induces activity dependent changes in synaptic strength by delivering repetitive magnetic pulses that influence cortical excitability and inhibition. Stimulation frequency and pattern are key parameters that shape the direction of rTMS related plasticity. In general, low frequency protocols tend to reduce excitability, whereas higher frequency protocols tend to increase excitability, although responses vary across individuals and clinical phenotypes (–).

Moreover, the effects of rTMS are not restricted to the cortical area directly beneath the coil. They can propagate along structural and functional connections and reshape activity patterns at the network level (). Studies combining TMS with functional MRI or EEG show that stimulation targeting M1 or prefrontal regions can alter connectivity and synchronization within motor and cognitive networks, and these network changes may relate to behavioral outcomes (, ). In practical terms, this supports choosing stimulation targets based on the functional network that needs support, rather than assuming a purely local effect. It also supports pairing stimulation with task specific training, because NIBS is more likely to facilitate learning during practice than to replace practice.

In hemiplegic cerebral palsy and in children with hemiparesis following perinatal stroke, imbalance in transcallosal interactions is relatively common. This imbalance is characterized by increased inhibition from the contralesional M1 to the ipsilesional M1, together with relatively reduced inhibition from the ipsilesional to the contralesional hemisphere. Such asymmetric inhibition is considered to constrain reorganization and motor output of the injured hemisphere (, ).

In cerebral palsy, emerging evidence supports the feasibility of approaches that facilitate the ipsilesional hemisphere or suppress excessive contralesional activity in combination with intensive upper limb training. Trials have reported improvements in fine motor outcomes when inhibitory low frequency rTMS over contralesional M1 is combined with constraint induced movement therapy, including gains in standardized upper limb measures and related functional tasks (, ). Systematic reviews and network meta analyses suggest an overall favorable signal for M1 targeted rTMS, although heterogeneity in stimulation parameters and study quality limits the certainty of conclusions (, ). Clinically, this model provides a rationale for selecting M1 based protocols in unilateral presentations, but it also highlights the need for stratification using neuroimaging or neurophysiology, because reorganization patterns differ across children and may influence responsiveness.

The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and its connections with parietal regions form a core network for executive function, attentional allocation, and cognitive motor dual task control (). Connectivity within this network is associated with working memory, attentional control, and dual task performance (). Adult trials and meta analyses suggest that DLPFC targeted stimulation can improve executive outcomes and may benefit dual task gait, potentially through more efficient network activation and connectivity changes (). These mechanistic links are largely derived from adult evidence and should be interpreted cautiously when applied to pediatric cerebral palsy, given developmental differences in network maturation and lesion related reorganization.

In children with cerebral palsy, a trial applying 10 Hz rTMS over the left DLPFC reported improved manual and cognitive performance under dual task conditions, with no serious adverse events (). Evidence for tDCS remains limited. A pilot trial combining anodal DLPFC tDCS with cognitive training suggested feasibility and possible gains in cognition and language related measures, but the small sample limited between group conclusions (). From a clinical perspective, DLPFC targeting is most relevant when the rehabilitation goal involves attention, executive control, and performance under real world cognitive load, rather than isolated strength or range of motion. Future studies should evaluate whether gains translate to daily participation outcomes such as classroom tasks, complex self care, and communication demands. The proposed neurophysiological mechanisms of tDCS and rTMS, including their effects on cortical excitability, interhemispheric inhibition, and network-level function, are summarized in .

Key systematic reviews and meta-analyses of non-invasive brain stimulation in children with cerebral palsy are summarized in .

Structured summary of key reviews and meta-analyses on non invasive brain stimulation in children with cerebral palsy.

tDCS, transcranial direct current stimulation; rTMS, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation; M1, primary motor cortex; DLPFC, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex; GMFM, Gross Motor Function Measure; GMFCS, Gross Motor Function Classification System; MACS, Manual Ability Classification System; CIMT, constraint induced movement therapy; PT, physical therapy; OT, occupational therapy; VR, virtual reality; ROM, range of motion.

Most lower limb studies applied anodal tDCS over primary M1 combined with gait or balance training. In a double blind randomized controlled trial, Duarte and colleagues randomized 24 children with spastic cerebral palsy aged 5 to 12 years to anodal tDCS over lesioned side M1 plus treadmill training or sham plus treadmill training for 10 sessions over 2 weeks. Functional severity may influence responsiveness, and GMFCS levels should be considered when interpreting outcomes. The trial stratified randomization by GMFCS levels I to II versus level III (). The active group showed greater improvements in Pediatric Balance Scale and postural sway measures, with partial maintenance at 1 month follow up. Related trials using 1 to 2 mA for 20 min per session combined with treadmill or gait training reported improvements in gait speed, step length, and 6 min walking distance, with favorable safety profiles (). A single session study combining anodal M1 tDCS with virtual reality based gait and balance training reported immediate improvements in selected postural sway parameters ().

Across trials, systematic reviews and meta analyses suggest that anodal M1 tDCS combined with lower limb training yields small to moderate improvements in gait and gross motor function, while effects on balance are less consistent (, ). Lower limb rTMS studies typically use low frequency stimulation to suppress contralesional M1 or high frequency stimulation to facilitate ipsilesional M1, combined with conventional therapy. Small trials and pooled analyses indicate potential benefits for gross motor function and muscle tone, but evidence is limited by small samples and variable parameters, so rTMS remains a promising adjunct requiring further optimization ().

Upper limb studies commonly combine CIMT or structured upper limb training with tDCS or rTMS targeting M1. In a sham controlled trial, Gillick and colleagues applied cathodal tDCS over nonlesioned M1 plus CIMT versus sham plus CIMT. Both groups improved, while the tDCS group showed larger effect sizes in selected fine motor and bimanual coordination tasks, with neurophysiological signals consistent with increased corticospinal excitability in the lesioned hemisphere ().

For rTMS, Wu and colleagues applied inhibitory low frequency rTMS over contralesional M1 combined with modified CIMT in preschool children with unilateral cerebral palsy. Improvements were reported in Assisting Hand Assessment and related measures, with no serious adverse events (). A systematic review concluded that combining tDCS or rTMS with upper limb training is generally safe and feasible and may produce moderate effects, but overall evidence quality is low to moderate due to small samples and protocol heterogeneity, supporting the need for larger multicenter trials ().

Spasticity outcomes are often secondary endpoints in NIBS studies. Systematic reviews suggest that tDCS, commonly anodal M1 or cerebellar stimulation combined with physical therapy, may reduce Modified Ashworth Scale scores in the short term and may improve muscle stiffness and joint range of motion, but heterogeneity limits conclusions about dose response (, ). Network meta analysis findings suggest that low frequency rTMS over contralesional M1 may be more favorable for reducing muscle tone and improving hand function, whereas high frequency rTMS over ipsilesional M1 may be more favorable for gross motor recovery ().

Recent studies increasingly target DLPFC and frontoparietal executive control networks to address attention, executive function, and cognitive motor dual task performance. Adult evidence suggests that anodal DLPFC tDCS or excitatory rTMS can improve working memory, attentional control, and dual task gait performance, with changes linked to frontoparietal connectivity and activation efficiency, providing a rationale for pediatric investigation (, ).

In children with cerebral palsy, Ko et al. conducted a pilot sham controlled trial in 13 children with comorbid cognitive impairment. Anodal DLPFC tDCS plus cognitive training was feasible and well tolerated and was associated with within group improvements in cognition, activities of daily living, and language related measures, although between group differences were not significant (). Evidence for pediatric dual task outcomes remains limited. One randomized trial combined anodal motor cortex tDCS with cognitive motor dual task training in 30 children and reported greater improvements than sham in functional activity capacity, selected cognitive measures, and cortical excitability, with persistence at 1 month follow up and no serious adverse events (). Overall, DLPFC and executive network targeted NIBS combined with structured cognitive or dual task training shows acceptable feasibility and signals of benefit, but evidence remains exploratory due to small samples and heterogeneous protocols. Larger studies with mechanistic endpoints and participation relevant outcomes are needed before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

Language and communication impairments contribute substantially to participation restrictions in children with cerebral palsy, but evidence for NIBS in this domain is limited. Available studies suggest feasibility and acceptable safety when stimulation is combined with language or communication oriented training, with preliminary efficacy signals. In children with cerebral palsy and cognitive impairment, anodal DLPFC tDCS plus cognitive training was associated with improvements in language related measures, suggesting indirect facilitation of language processing (). A small prospective study reported that left DLPFC tDCS combined with augmentative and alternative communication training improved Communication Matrix levels and spontaneous expressive behaviors, with generally mild transient adverse effects (). Evidence from broader pediatric developmental language delay also suggests added benefits of tDCS combined with language and cognitive training, supporting cautious extrapolation to cerebral palsy (). For rTMS, meta analytic evidence suggests potential improvement in language response rates compared with speech therapy alone, but prescriptions vary and overall evidence quality remains limited ().

The current evidence base for NIBS in children with cerebral palsy is unevenly distributed across clinical phenotypes. Most available therapeutic studies have enrolled children with spastic CP, particularly those with unilateral involvement, and ambulatory participants, commonly within GMFCS levels I to III. Studies targeting lower limb function, gait, and balance have also included children with spastic diplegic or bilateral spastic CP. Therefore, the existing evidence is not restricted to unilateral CP alone, but the strongest and most consistently reported findings are derived from spastic and relatively ambulatory populations. In contrast, evidence for dyskinetic, ataxic, mixed, and more severe non-ambulatory CP remains limited (, ).

Motor dysfunction in unilateral CP is often discussed in relation to corticospinal tract injury and interhemispheric inhibitory imbalance, providing a rationale for M1-based stimulation strategies (, ). However, this model may not adequately explain other CP phenotypes. Dyskinetic CP is characterized by fluctuating muscle tone, involuntary movements, and impaired motor control, and is commonly associated with abnormalities involving the basal ganglia, thalamocortical pathways, and broader sensorimotor networks (, ). TMS has been used to investigate corticospinal excitability, inhibitory circuitry, and motor network physiology in CP and other pediatric movement disorders. In addition, rTMS and tDCS have been explored as non-invasive neuromodulation approaches for dystonia in broader clinical populations, although the reported effects are modest and protocol dependent (). These pathophysiological differences suggest that evidence derived from M1-centred protocols in unilateral or spastic CP should not be directly generalized to dyskinetic CP or other movement disorder presentations. For dyskinetic, dystonic, ataxic, mixed, and more severe non ambulatory presentations, the available evidence remains preliminary, and clinical applicability should be considered uncertain.

Although this review focuses primarily on tDCS and rTMS, several non invasive and technology assisted rehabilitation approaches are increasingly being used to enhance motor learning, sensory feedback, engagement, and task specific practice in children with cerebral palsy. Mechanical and vibration based interventions, including whole body vibration and local vibrotactile stimulation, may influence proprioceptive input, muscle activation, postural control, and sensorimotor integration (, ). Game based and virtual reality assisted rehabilitation provide enriched, repetitive, and feedback driven environments that may increase motivation and support motor learning. Systematic reviews and meta analyses indicate that VR assisted or exergame based interventions may improve selected outcomes related to balance, upper and lower limb function, daily activity performance, and cognition, although effects differ according to immersion level, task design, training dose, and comparator intervention (, ). Other technology assisted approaches, including robotic gait or upper limb training, functional electrical stimulation or neuromuscular electrical stimulation, wearable haptic feedback systems, and brain computer interface based rehabilitation, may also contribute to intensive and individualized training by providing assistive movement, sensory feedback, task repetition, or closed loop control (, ).

This review has several limitations. Although it was informed by a structured literature search, it was designed as a narrative review rather than a systematic review. Therefore, no formal risk of bias assessment, certainty of evidence grading, or quantitative meta analysis was conducted. In addition, the available studies varied substantially in participant characteristics, CP subtype, lesion profile, stimulation modality, target selection, stimulation parameters, adjunct rehabilitation protocols, outcome measures, and follow up duration, which limits objective comparison across studies. Some mechanistic interpretations were also supported by evidence from adult or non CP populations when pediatric CP specific evidence was limited. Accordingly, the findings should be interpreted as a structured narrative synthesis of current evidence rather than definitive evidence for clinical implementation.

Future research should move beyond feasibility studies toward mechanism informed and phenotype stratified trials that improve reproducibility and clinical translation. Given the heterogeneity of lesion type, developmental stage, motor severity, and network reorganization, neuroimaging and neurophysiological markers may help guide target selection and protocol matching. Candidate markers include DTI measures of corticospinal and cerebello thalamo cortical integrity, functional connectivity within motor and frontoparietal networks assessed by functional MRI or functional near infrared spectroscopy, and TMS measures of interhemispheric inhibition and cortical excitability. Large multicenter randomized controlled trials are needed to standardize stimulation parameters, model dose response, and clarify the optimal timing of stimulation relative to task based training. Outcome assessment should extend beyond impairment scales to include participation, real world dual task performance, quality of life, caregiver burden, longer term maintenance, and pediatric safety monitoring during repeated NIBS applications.
